I didnt hate Nathan, but i didnt love him either. The way he handed Tessa over, and just didnt care about here really ticked me off. The Magister isnt all that great either. I cant wait to see them gone. Hopefully some but-kick from our adorded shadowhunters. 
 I honeslty can say i really enjoyed this book! Hats of the Cassie for another great Shadowhunter story! I cant wait to start book 2! And hey, arent all the stories true? ;)
I just don't like her books, I keep wanting to look away from the page, it's like they repel me or something.

2013 Review: 
 this book was AMAZING!!! i loved it SOOOOOO much!! It got me into the Shadowhunter world :3 I can keep reading this book and it'll never get old. Will, Jem, Gabe all the guys are so perfect. As well as the girls! 
 2016: 
 Cringing a bit at what I wrote ^^ 
 But what I said was true. The way Cassie wrote the characters and the way Will Herondale is so mysterious, its so beautiful. I could read this book over, and over again and I wouldn't get tired of it. I remember walking into Walmart towards the books and I found Will, on the cover, attractive. So I read the back then bought the book. I love books that take place in the 1800's. I don't know why, but the way they spoke and dressed made me happy. I was happy to see that Tessa was an american girl who traveled to London to see her brother. 
 The way Cassandra writes, it's beautiful. I say this in all the reviews I've done about her books 
 I recommend reading TID before TMI, that is what I did. I didn't know about City of Bones until I heard it was coming out into a movie, and when I was reading one of the TID. Or you can read them in the order they came out.

I'd read almost all of the books in The Mortal Instruments (TMI), except for the last book, City of Heavenly Fire, which is now long overdue since I cannot remember some scenes in the series. Anyway, I read this book because soon enough it will be a TV series, that a true Shadowhunter should not be missed. 
 Moving forward, for the review; I could neither say that this first book of The Infernal Devices (TID) was bad nor good. But it clearly did not blow me away like those I read in the comments and reviews; it was very average in every way. Though I must admit, this book was way better than the City of Bones. And I couldn't help but see similarities between them - a spy inside the institute, arrogant and annoying male leads, mysterious and unknown past, father issues and whatnot. And I was a bit confused about the terminologies and what they do (iratze, seraph blades, etc.) in this book, yet Clare described everything more clearly than her debut novel. 
 Additionally, the way Cassandra Clare wrote this story was very elegant. Not sure if it had something do with the Victorian settings, but regardless she still richly created a very vivid era. London in 1900s was dark and gloomy and, well, rainy. Still, I found the period setting along with Tess' abilities more interesting. (Surprisingly, London in 1900s was very gloomy and dark and rainy which was far from what I imagined! But anyway I don't really know London since I've never been there. LOL.) 
 I rated it two stars because the story was a bit dragging. Too much history, too much talking and recon. For me, it went too long. There were parts that I skipped because I could not fathom a thing Clare said. 
 Then again, there were still good things in the story. The kickass action scenes and the twist, in the end, were oh so awesome. I liked Tessa and her power to Change and how she can touch their minds, that's impressive. Yes, Clare's strategy on how to keep us going by concealing the truth about their past and backgrounds still made me want to read the second up to the last book. Also, I want to know who she ends up with. Don't we all want to? 
 So, all in all, the plot was not so bad at all. If Clare could make the narrations and storytelling short, and stop having so much drama about their past then it'll be better. 
 "One must always be careful with books and what is inside them, for words have the power to change us."

I absolutely loved this book! We get a new bit of the Shadowhunter world, and a bit of a peek into Magnus Bane's past. I actually love that he was in this book, because it takes that tie and familiarity from TMI into this new series. 
 I didn't catch the plot twists ahead of time, which was really nice. I did have one tiny bit of an issue. Will sounded a lot like Jace. It was a little distracting in the beginning, but after his character started building a bit it got a lot better. 
 I can't wait to pick up book 2! Picking up Clockwork Prince now!

** spoiler alert ** 
 2/19/2011 - So, I was a little worried about starting this book. I am deeply, deeply in lust with Cassandra Clare's Mortal Instruments series and I was afraid this book wouldn't measure up to the high standards I have set for this particular author. I am quite happy to find out that my fears were for nothing because this book is fantastic. 
 This is set in the universe of the Mortal Instruments series but is set in Victorian England and the Institute in London. The book centers around Tessa an American fresh off the boat from New York. She is searching for her brother and is taken in by some rather deplorable characters but thankfully is saved by members of the London Institute, specifically Will Herondale. 
 Throughout the book Tessa is busy trying to figure out why the bad guys want her and what they have done to her brother. She is also trying to figure out her romantic feelings towards Will and Will's best friend Jem Carstairs. On top of which is her budding new power and the knowledge that she isn't quite as human as she has been led to believe. 
 The best thing about this whole book is how the author always leaves you guessing. Never quite sure what is going to happen or what the characters' exact meanings are. I love how well developed all of the characters are and how smoothly they interact with one another. I find that as much as Jace pissed me of in City of Bones it is nothing compared to the irritating abilities of Will. I can't imagine coming across someone who was so rude to everyone all the time, no matter what his past was like. 
 I was thrilled to see Magnus Bane again. I'd kind of forgotton that he was rather old and would be appearing in this book. I also liked hearing references to families that are very important in the Mortal Insturments books. 
 I'm curious to see what happens with Tessa's brother Nathaniel. I didn't like him from the get go and I couldn't believe that Tessa kept protecting him. I have a sister and if she did even part of those things I would have completely cut her out of my life. I hope in the next book Tessa doesn't forget how many times her terrible brother has betrayed her. 
 I find that Jessamine is annoying and I'm wondering if she has any redeemable qualities. I can't figure out what part she has to play in this story? She doesn't really lend anything to the story and I don't think anyone would miss her when she's gone. I guess we'll just have to wait and see. 
 I'm very glad that the Clave decided not to kick Tessa out because who knows what would have happened to her if they had. Plus I want to see what happens with her and Will, although I'm secretly rooting for Jem. 
 Great story, great characters, great book. I'm really looking forward to the next book and am anxiously awaiting it's release.

This was just... meh. I'm not really sure why I read this, because I wasn't too crazy about the Mortal Instruments trilogy. But, whatever, I borrowed from the library, so at least all that I've wasted is time. 
 Clockwork Angel starts with Tessa on her way to London to stay with her brother, because her aunt just died, and her parents passed away when she was young. However, dun dun dunnnnnn, she is met by two strange women who say they were sent by her brother. These women are evil :O And it turns out that Tessa has strange powers and a questionable lineage :O (Clary anyone?) So, she is held captive by them for a while and is told that she is going to be given to the ominous Magister, when suddenly, she is rescued by two Shadowhunters! Yay! One of them is the completely dreamy super mega gorgeous totally ripped Jace, I mean.... wait, what was his name again? ***this is a side thought. I finished the book two days ago and I can't remember the characters' names. Ok. Nate is her brother, Jem is the sweet one, Charlotte is the head of the institute..... Ok. For all intents and purposes, this male character is the 1800s version of Jace, so we shall continue to call him Jace, because, evidently, it is too much pressure for Cassandra Clare to come up with a whole new set of characters.*** 
 Anyways, Tessa is rescued by the Shadowhunters and taken to the institute, where they are trying to figure out what evil scheme the Magister is up to. There are evil robots involved. Seriously. Evil robots. And of course, this would not be Cassandra Clare if the main character, Tessa, did not have two guys developing feelings for her. The first is the typical Jace. He is gorgeous and wonderful and oftentimes, he acts like an ass, but every now and then, there is a glimpse of a good person under that callous exterior. The second is the sweet and caring Jem, who is patient and good and, like almost every fictional character in the world, he has a special place that he likes to go when he wants to think or relax, and he takes Tessa there to be super cute. 
 And you know, just for once, I would like the main girl to pick the healthy relationship. I mean, seriously, is it that hard? Is it really so impossible for a fictional girl to choose the guy that isn't a jerk? To pick the one that is honest and doesn't jump back and forth between personalities like a mental patient.... Or even if Tessa decided that she is really overwhelmed right now, and she is vulnerable, and it isn't right for her to be jumping into a relationship with someone that she doesn't know. That would be ok too, but an author like Cassandra Clare would never have the guts to do that, because she knows that the majority of her fanbase comes from girls that just cannot wait to whip out their cell phones and tweet of fb status that they are "TEAM _________" 
 I never really intended for this to become a rant, so I think that I'm going to stop now, but I'm just getting kind of frustrated. One more thing though; the twist at the end could be seen from about a quarter into the book. Just saying.

This book was unbelievably good. I can't wait to read everything else she's written. 
 Pros: Great writing. Obviously talented writer. Good characters, and great character development. Great world building, I plan to read the entire series after this. 
 Cons: The library has the second book checked out and reserved for the next two months...so I'm going to have to wait a little while to get my next fix. I also suffered from major 'book hangover', which made it almost impossible to start any other book because I was so focused on getting my next Cassandra Clare fix. 
 I'm not ashamed to admit this: The writing on this was so good I had to take a break and go edit my own W.I.P. while reading. Because I learned a lot about the writing craft just from reading this book.

I admit I read this because my daughter loved it. I mean- really loved it-and very passionately begged me to read it. I enjoy reading books she loves because it gives us so much to discuss. That being said, it was very easy to understand WHY my almost 14 year old daughter loved this story. The character of Hazel is so well written, she is SUCH a teenager, that kids can't help but get her. And add to that the gallant, smart, slightly disrespectful but still nice Augustus Waters. Who wouldn't love this guy?? Even Hazel's parents like him. I know that almost everyone out there has already read and reviewed this, so I won't go into the story, except to say it was wonderful, romantic, funny, and extremely sad. Originally posted on my blog: www.book-scents.com 
 The Fault in Our Stars is something I've put off reading for forever. The subject matter scared me! Kids and cancer. That is a recipe for heart aching disaster for me and for my heart's sake, I put it off. However, with the movie coming out and all, I wanted to read it before watching it. I mentally braced myself. I started reading, preparing to have my heart ripped out. 
 Now, I don't know if it was the hype or the fact that everyone touts it as a masterpiece, amazing, life changing and all that but... I feel like I didn't have that same connection with it that everyone else did. Which is kind of disappointing to me. I feel like I need to inform: I cry easily. Very easily. I get emotionally invested in all books or movies and I cry during them all the time. I expected to cry. I teared up but I didn't have the gut wrenching sobs I thought I'd go through. I'm not heartless I swear!! The story was sad and touching but I felt disconnected from it. 
 I think one of the main things that made me feel the disconnect was the dialogue. I realize that Augustus Waters is supposed to be witty and funny and clever and everything but I just can't imagine a 17 year old boy talking the way he does. 17 year olds just don't spout eloquent monologues on the spot! Or even craft them ahead of time as beautifully as he did! It just didn't seem plausible and sometimes Augustus and Hazel's dialogue just came off as pretentious to me. Don't get me wrong, Hazel's snark made me smile but most of the time I found myself tilting my head to one side and thinking, "really? did this speech just happen?" 
 I can practically see the mob coming for me now. *hides* Granted, there are amazing quotes from this book. They're poignant and insightful and I love it -- but it really didn't seem natural coming out of a 16 and 17 year old. 
 Maybe the dialogue was what took me out of the story enough that I didn't cry. I'm not sure. I don't know what it is. The story was sad to be sure but this book didn't leave the lasting impression on me that I expected it too.

Once again, I've tried to read it. First time, I made it to about page seven. I didn't even get to the bit on America's Next Top Model. This time, I made it to page nineteen. See, I made progress? To me, from what I read of the book so far and what friends have gushed about to me, Green writes perfect prose -- and he does, the quotes I've read from this book are amazing -- and his characters are teenagers. Teenagers that don't exist. I know that these guys speak and think differently than I do because they had cancer, but I still grew up with teens. Not even the ones who read Green speak like his characters do.

After all the hype, I expected more. I was not impressed by this book. A bit too "teen" for me. I've read books like this before that are better. Yes, it was sad in the end, but it's like everything was okay in it's separate parts and didn't quite come together.
I didn't cry, what's wrong with me? I wasn't as connected as most of you, I guess. I liked it...but maybe being a nurse made me relate and understand on a different level. First JG book.

sample_reviews.review_text:
The mark of the inmmature man is that he wants to die nobly for a cause, while the mark of the mature man is that he wants to live humbly for one 
 -- Wilhelm Stekel 
 That's phony!

"Read and Pass. Salinger gives a look under the hood of the teenage social outcast. The novel depicts both the common experiences adolescence as well as the unique thought processes of some kind of personality disorder all while recovering from some significant traumatic life events. It is compelling and unsettling. Holden has constant judgmental thoughts of superiority while often blind to his own display of the very things he hates. At other times he has some recognition of his own hypocrisy. Various people attempt to help him along the way. The most interesting is a former teacher who is a friend of the family. He tries to get Holden to let go of his hatred of the world and his arrogance of believing he is the only one who sees these things in society, and accept the kind of learning he will need to be able to articulate helpful observations like great men before him. Ultimately it is his little sister, who he has the greatest respect for, who motivates him to continue in society. 
 The novel captures both the restless outside of society feelings we all have in adolescence as well as the horror and sympathy we feel towards those who never do seem to process life in a socially accepted way."
I would rather light myself on fire than read another sentence of that again.

This book reminded me a lot of Flowers for Algernon (which I preferred). Whereas this book was highly "disturbing" and "out there" according to my parents who read it in high school, I thought of it as an excellent lens to society (what was acceptable/unacceptable at the time). The only reason I rated it 2 stars is the author writes as if he was the teenager in the story; which I understand why he did that, but I thought the "thinking about girls" and "sex" were a little lengthy/teenage-like, which was what the author was striving for, but I didn't much care for the style.
I'm sorry, but I hated this book. The kid is crazy. And seeing as this was one of my sister's favorites...yeah we are opposites lol

The website "thegreatestnovels.com" ranks "The Catcher in the Rye" as the best (#1) novel that was ever written. Time Magazine's All-Time 100 Novels rates the book as the 4th greatest novel. Other lists that I have seen on the Internet have this novel ranked high, too. After seeing these lists, I wanted to read the book to see why it is considered one of the best novels ever. 
 The story is about a few days in the life of a cynical teenage boy that has been kicked out of prep school, again, because of poor performance. He leaves the prep school before the Christmas break to spend time in New York City before his parents find out he has been dismissed from school. The story is about his adventures (misadventures) with friends and acquaintances, pimps, hookers, older women, and his younger sister. 
 There are two words that describe why I disliked this novel, "Holden Caulfield", the teen-age protagonist of the novel. The book is written from Holden's point of view so the reader gets to know this pessimistic, selfish, lazy, knucklehead well through his thoughts, relationships and actions. By the end of the book you want it to end so you don't have to experience anymore stupidity and negativity. About the only redeeming attribute that he had was his love for his younger sister. 
 I liked the writing of author. You can tell that he is a great writer. I could picture the different characters, situations and scenes through his deft descriptions. I just could not enjoy the book because of the central character being the type of teenager that needs his butt kicked daily. 
 There must be many folks who think this is a great novel, (see the high rankings in many lists of the all time greatest novels) but I found the story difficult to enjoy due to the irritating and depressing lead character. I also wonder why this is one of the books that high school teachers select for their students to read. What can they learn from this story? I guess a negative example; not to be a jerk, to study hard in school and to care others rather than be obsessed with their own issues. 
 Quotes 
 "The mark of the immature man is that he wants to die nobly for a cause, while the mark of the mature man is that he wants to live humbly for one." Quoted in the story but written by psychoanalyst Wilhelm Stekel.

I didn't like the main character, I didn't like the history, I didn't like the way it was written, and I don't understand the hype about this book, it isn't that good, just an apathetic boy about everything without any good reason, this isn't about depression, is about how a teenager boy can be a pain in the ass for everybody, even himself, and the worst is that the hole history doesn't have a real reason to be.
This classic is not for me.
This book is a phony.
A must-read classic (though I admit it was probably most enjoyable to read while you are still an angsty teenager).

Obiknovena po edin mnogo priiaten nachin. Zabavliavakh se dobre i chakam s net'rpenie da si kupia sledvashchata chast. 
 Epichnoto fent'zi naposled'k strada ot efekta na "Saga za og'n i led" - nasilie i falshivi geroi, koito figurirat samo za da b'dat izm'chvani i ubiti. Koronovanata kula e po-skoro kato dobrite po-stari fent'zita - Tolkin, Reim'nd Fiist. Ima khanove i se iazdiat kone i geroite se pridvizhvat ot tochka A do tochka B po opasni p'tishcha. Magiiata e navsiak'de i nik'de, s'shcho kakto goblinite, elfite i dzhudzhetata.

First of all, this is a review for both the Riyria Chronicles and the Riyria Revelations. I had already bought The Crown Tower before I realized the Chronicles were the prequels to the Revelations, so I read the series in "chronological order" and that worked just fine. I'm sure publication order would have been good too. Up to you. Now, for the actual review, in which I will try to put my many feelings into words. 
 "The battle between Good and Evil is a theme of much of fantasy. But I think the battle between Good and Evil is fought largely within the individual human heart, by the decisions that we make."- George R. R. Martin 
 Now I shall do what I should not do in a review and start comparing this to other books. I'll say that this series fulfills Mr. Martin's quote better than his own series does. I will say that I have not loved a series this much since the Harry Potter series ended. And I will say that these books felt just a bit Tolkieny. 
 I'll address that last one first because you're probably saying "Well of course it did! Doesn't all fantasy these days?" That's not what I meant. Yes, much fantasy these days is just cheap imitations of Tolkien's fine art. Some authors break the mould. Some try too hard to break the mould and forget to just tell a good story. Mr. Sullivan has told a wonderful story. 
 "Even in literature and art, no man who bothers about originality will ever be original: whereas if you simply try to tell the truth (without caring twopence how often it has been told before) you will, nine times out of ten, become original without ever having noticed it."- C.S. Lewis 
 Yes, this story has magic and elves and dwarves and goblins. Yes, it takes place in a quasi-medieval world (though I would argue that it corresponds more with our late Middle Ages/early Renaissance era) with kings and kingdoms and sword fights. Perhaps this is why the publishers of the book, trying desperately to convince readers that the book is cool, gritty and original, proclaim "There's no ancient evil to defeat or orphan destined for greatness, just unlikely heroes and classic adventure"! Which is ironic because Yes, there is and yes, there is. And while this book is, in fact, original in many ways, I think it has an equally important quality of feeling familiar. 
 Example: For some King Arthur fans (like me) people will ask what books and movies about King Arthur they like. The answer is none of them because they all mess up the story. "So what story are you looking for?" people ask. I don't know. But I'll know it when I see it. 
 Similarly, I don't really like fantasy. I mean, I read it more than any other genre and I love everything about it (dragons, castles, swords, dragons, elves, heroes, monsters, dragons, quests, dragons) but there are very few fantasy books I truly love. (Pretty much just Tolkien, Lewis and Rowling). In one of the interviews in the back of the book, Mr. Sullivan said he tried to write the kind of book he'd like to read. I'm glad he did, because it's exactly the book I didn't know I was looking for. 
 Don't get me wrong. I didn't expect to love this series, and I didn't at first. Much like Hadrian and Royce when they first met, I had my own preconceived notions and didn't expect much. "Oh, look, the main characters are thieves, I bet the author thought that was such a novel idea, not like its already its own sub-genre or anything." Oh and Royce. I was probably visibly cringing when he introduced Royce. Of course everyone could immediately tell he was dangerous 
 I could have practically told you Royce's life story right then and there. Cliche anti-hero. Of course he was an orphan, of course he was dark and broody and sarcastic and of course he didn't believe in right and wrong, but obviously its not his fault... 
 So what changed you ask? A lot. Dynamic characters are a beautiful thing. 
 And on the subject of characters, they are amazing. I love me a good character. The first one I fell in love with was, naturally, Hadrian. A good old-fashioned hero archetype with a strong moral sense who was neither an obnoxious holier-than-thou nor a withering pansy? Oh my, were you a breath of fresh air! And then there was the friendship (*ahem* bromance! *cough cough*) between Royce and Hadrian, and this was the aspect that drew me in. 
 In fact, let me be honest, I was expecting the bromance version of smut and I would have been totally okay with it if this book had been no more than that. 
 But it was so much more! Because pretty soon I didn't just love Hadrian, or even just Hadrian and Royce, I loved a whole slough of characters that I never never expected to care about. This is one of the (many) things that Sullivan did much better than Martin. In GoT, I could only muster up enough feeling to care about two or three characters, and the book is told in about 85,000 different perspectives. I really couldn't care about those perspectives and was tempted to just skip them and get back to the people I liked (and I almost did, until I realized I'd be skipping enough of the books that it didn't really warrant continuing the series at all). In the Riyria books, I found myself caring about barely significant side characters almost as much as the two heroes which is fine because most of the barely significant side characters actually turn out to be pretty significant 
 But none of the above ranting really explains what I meant by Tolkieny. One of the only good things Peter Jackson did in the new Hobbit movies was give Gandalf this brilliant quote: 
 "I found it is the small everyday deeds of ordinary folk that keep the darkness at bay. Small acts of kindness and love." 
 And doesn't that pretty much sum up Tolkien? Where the small and un-extraordinary defeat evil through means of hope and mercy? That is what I mean by Tolkieny, and this book has a bit of it. And frankly, that's the best compliment I know how to give it. You see, as far as I can tell, if the battle between good and evil is in the human heart, GRRM's characters have pretty much lost that war. These books though; yes, they are classic adventure and a rollicking good story, yes, they are quite dark at times, and yes they are original, complex and epic, but strip away all that and you have, at its core, a story about friendship, and love, and hope, and Mercy. 
 But most of all it is a story about redemption. That is why it is, in fact, a tale of Good and Evil. For that is exactly what redemption is; the victory of Good.

I'd probably rate it 2.5 stars. 
 What makes me like the book: 
 - I read and enjoyed Riyria Revelations. 
 - I like Michael Sullivan as an author (and an active member in the fantasy community) and want to support/like his books. 
 - Royce's musings and thought/process about Arcadius. That was interesting... 
 What I didn't like: 
 - Having read the Riyria Revelations, everything felt extremely too predictable. There wasn't any mystery. 
 - The "fore"shadowing felt overly obvious. 
 - I understand this is the beginning of their character arc... but Royce and Hadrian felt very 2-dimensional. 
 - Half the book was about Gwen trying to establish her own whorehouse. 
 1. Running a classy whorehouse still seems poor goal. 
 2. I dislike almost all use of predestination. 
 3. It didn't seem like there were really any particularly interesting/challenging obstacles.

Brilliant prequel to the Riyria saga featuring two of my favourite characters in fantasy. This book, although could be read as a standalone, slips in gems for those who have read the Revelations series. This perspective gives the reader a more intimate understanding of the characters and really brings them to life. To witness how these two crafty crims and the cast around them have ended up together is an exciting and fun journey.

A fun book. 
 I did like Gwen and her story, but at the same time I felt like it never had any stakes. It felt smooth sailing for her. 
 The main story line did have high stakes however, because I have read the other series I felt like I knew things were going to work out. 
 That said, I liked Pickles!

What's not to love. Enjoyed the story of how Royce and Hadrian first met. After reading Revelations I really enjoyed the backstory on these intriguing rogues. Michael's writing is great and I keep coming back for more. I "read" via audiobook and Michael couldn't have a better narrator for his Riyria book. Tim Gerard Reynolds brings each character to life. The characters are very easy to distinguish from each other. On to The Rose and The Thorn.

Royce and Hadrian are at complete odds but not for one thing they both agreed upon- their mutual resentment for each other. Circumstances caused them to become partners for a mission, though grudgingly and reluctantly. While they can barely tolerate each other in the beginning, the slow spark of what might be a possible partnership is kindled as they find themselves complementing each other in times of danger. 
 Can't get enough of Royce's disdainful and sarcastic remarks at Hadrian and their constant bickering is entertaining and hilarious as hell!XD 
 I also like Gwen who is smart and brave and how her story coincides nicely into the plot. Pleasantly surprised at Pickles' contribution and I must say Professor Arcadius is indeed a wise, crafty man. Definitely looking forward to more Royce and Hadrian in epic action together!!

I am a complete newbie to this author. I'd seen the books from The Riyria Revelations series and thought about buying them. This book is the first in a pair of prequels to that series, and I am glad I read this first. I prefer to read a series in chronological order rather than it's published one. If you're like me and this is your first taste in this world it is extremely important to remember that this is a prequel and that there are four more books to read after this. 
 The story has a very slow start and at times it was hard for me to focus. While it was well written there really wasn't very much going on action wise, but main characters were being established. The action does eventually pick up, but it occurs in little bursts. And although there was danger it wasn't until the very end of the book that I felt a sense of urgency. If I had read this book thinking it was a stand alone novel with the potential for more books I would have thought the ending was lame. This book is 400 pages of set up, but from the style of writing and the lovable characters I can see how people fell in love with this series, and I will be sticking around to read the punch line.

I really enjoyed the books in the Riyria Revelations and even picked the first for my library's science fiction/fantasy discussion group. 
 The Crown Tower is volume 1 of the Riyria Chronicles, a series of prequels to the events in the Riyria Revelations. It is not quite as good as the other titles by Michael J. Sullivan. This is partly because we already know that Hadrian and Royce survive the dangerous situations they are in, but that's not the only reason. The pair move very quickly, too quickly, from hating each other to being partners. Also, I found the back story on Gwen very slow moving. I am a reader who values character development over plot, but even for me I wanted the pace to pick up. Royce's willingness to kill anyone anytime is also easier to take in the later books, when we know he is beyond that behavior. 
 The book ends very abruptly. I know a sequel is due out soon, but I would have liked a somewhat tidier ending. 
 There is a definite Butch & Sundance vibe to this book. If you are a fan of Royce and Hadrian already I do recommend The Crown Tower. If you are not yet a fan, start with Theft of Swords instead.

book_a.title: Becoming Nicole: The Transformation of an American Family
book_a.user_review: A very interesting book about a transgender girl and her identical twin brother

sample_reviews.review_text:
A solid book exploring the obstacles that a young girl faced as a transgendered person. The further reading section at the back is well stocked, and the resources section is extensive. 
 The thing that keeps it from being a 5-star book is the writing. It is written very much like a piece of journalism, and we, the reader, are told more than shown things about emotional states, etc. I can't help but compare it to Raising my Rainbow which was more personal, and less "tell-y." This book is much more interested in establishing a timeline than getting too deep into conversations. 
 Still an excellent book, though. Recommended.

A very well written account of the true story of twins - both born as boys, but one of whom knows at a very early age that he/she is different. Even before the age of three, Wyatt (now Nicole) insisted that he wasn't supposed to be a boy - and this is the story of the challenges that lay ahead for the whole family.

I just finished reading Becoming Nicole: The Transformation of an American Family by Amy Ellis Nutt. I've been looking forward to this one for a long time! For those of you who don't know, this is the true story of an inspiring and brave transgender girl, her family, and her identical twin brother and the journey that had to underwent in order to ensure that their daughter was treated fairly. 
 This is a beautiful story about being true to yourself and how important it is to stand up for what you believe in. I greatly appreciated how informative and inspirational this book is. It does a wonderful job of explaining the struggles that the family endured and that many transgender children have to experience on a daily basis. I do wish, however, that the narration was told more through the perspective of Nicole and her brother rather than the perspective of the parents. I would have been more interested to hear about the experiences that the family went through, through the voices of the teens. Nevertheless, this story was very powerful and moving.

Despite having been born biologically male, Nicole Maines knew without a doubt from an early age that inside she was a girl, not a boy. Initially flummoxed, and then cautiously and, later, wholeheartedly supportive, her parents and twin brother journey with her as she grapples for acceptance in school and in her community, their fight for equality eventually leading to the Maine Supreme Court. 
 I had a difficult time putting this book down. Nicole's bravery in the face of discrimination at such a tender age, and her family's unwavering support in the face of incredible financial and social pressures, are awe-inspiring.

Very interesting story, and really educational for me. I appreciate the perspective of the family and of course Nicole herself. The scientific thinking about how one identical twin may be transgender when the other one is not was a useful component as well. I wish the author had been able to share the facts in a less saccharine manner.
Nicole's story is interesting, but about halfway through the book drags.

I suppose that this is an entry-level book, for people who have never encountered anyone trans ever before. There are a lot of things that I found off-putting, but were written in what I imagine we were meant to read as a "honest, just telling it like it is"-way. Not meanly, but especially the descriptions of Nicole's girlhood seemed really essentialist (BUT I grew up as a queer girl in the Germany of the eighties and not in the apparently more gendered US). All descriptions of how Nicole always preferred girl-coded-things like pink and dolls seemed to come from a very loving and supportive place. I don't know how much use this is to the non-femmes out there, but I realise how low the bar is and how desperately positive stories about success, triumph and acceptance are needed, and this one does that. 
 A lot of the thoughts shared by the parents on all the many memories our main character is now supposedly missing out on also made me roll my eyes, like a memory shared late in the book which has a male homosocial group of friends on a road trip peeing in the snow as the ultimate male bonding experience which Nicole is now excluded from. I'm not if this memory just fails to cross the cultural gap and I'm just unable to understand it, but none of my outdoor peeing experiences in homosocial groups ever seemed to bring me closer to my fellow urinators, but maybe I'm peeing wrong as a woman.

Extremely accessible introduction to gender identity issues. This heartwarming story of an ordinary family fighting to make a safer world for their transgender daughter is both engaging and informative. While the Maines family is central to the book, there is also a ton of information on the science behind gender development. This is one of the few non-fiction books that I have stayed up way too late reading! 
 Lesson number one: "Sexual orientation is who you go to bed with," he told Spack. "Gender identity is who you go to bed as." 
 Kelly and Wayne Maines are thrilled to start their family when they adopt, by all appearances, twin boys. Wayne can't wait to share his knowledge with his two little guys. But almost as soon as the twins are verbal, one of the them makes it clear that she identifies as a girl. As the years go on, it is obvious this is not just a phase. Becoming Nicole tells us about Nicole's journey, but it is just as much about Wayne's "transition" to acceptance, Kelly's fierce determination to support and protect her daughter, and her twin brother Jonas's struggle to find his own role in the world and in his family. 
 Nicole's story had started before she was even born. So had Jonas's--in atoms and molecules, in liquid beginnings. One DNA, two souls, and a billion possibilities. 
 I was especially curious about this book because of current issues in my area: an uproar over a transgender substitute teacher in my hometown and Houston's recently failed equal rights ordinance. The twin aspect was also intriguing: (1) Identical twins from the same egg, the same DNA, and eventually the same environment. (2) The twin's interaction with each other, both Nicole's frustrations that her twin is allowed to express himself in a way she can't and Jonas feeling like he is a supporting character in his own life. I was also very interested in the parents, who had two very different reactions. Wayne has a difficult time handling it all and deals by pulling away from the family. Kelly doesn't really know much about gender identity, but she throws herself into research and does the best she can for Nicole. (Jonas was never in any question. Nicole was always his sister.) The author begins the book with the family backgrounds of Wayne and Kelly and it really helps illuminate why they each react to their unexpected circumstances the way they do. Wayne comes a long way and eventually becomes Nicole's biggest champion. 
 Sometimes it all made Kelly and Wayne's heads spin. But just because they didn't understand it all didn't make it any less true. 
 The book is written in a detached journalistic writing style, with the occasional literary flourish. It reads like a long magazine article. It is a fantastic mix of human interest, science, history and psychology. I learned the most with the chapters on the brain and fetal development. The complex processes that make us who we are are fascinating. 
 Recognizing that the sexual differentiation of a fetus's brain happens later in pregnancy than genital differentiation and that both are complex biological processes, the fact that variations in gender identity exist should ultimately come as no surprise. 
 The hardest part to read was the bullying of Nicole, which began when an adult actively encouraged his grandson to intimidate her at elementary school. This eventually becomes the impetus for the discrimination lawsuit the Maines file against the school district, which is a central focus of the book. The landmark case "marked the first time a state's highest court ruled that a transgender person has the right to use the restroom of the gender with which they identify." (TIME). 
 Ultimately gender identity is the result of biological processes and is a function of the interplay between sex hormones and the developing brain, and because it is a process that takes place over time, in utero, it can be influenced by any number of environmental effects...Beyond chromosomes, any kind of mutation, or change, in the balance of hormones will tip the sexual development of the fetus toward one side or the other independently of what the chromosomes "say." 
 Since I have seen complaints about this on other forums, I will say that for historical clarity there is a very clear shift in the names and pronouns used, which occurs at the time of the official name change. It appears that the Maines family was extremely involved with this book and Nicole has been supporting the book heavily on Twitter, so I assume that this was okay with her. 
 The book ends after Nicole's gender confirmation surgery, right before she heads off to college. Nicole is extremely confident and happy, which is probably in no small part due to a loving and supportive family. Becoming Nicole is both inspiring and informative. I would recommend this book to anyone who is interested in knowing more about gender identity issues or is looking for a book about an ordinary family dealing with extraordinary circumstances. 
 For so long Wayne had tried to analyze kids, including his own child, looking for the right descriptions, the right terms, to explain it all, but here in Machias, in this dormitory suite, he finally gave up. It didn't matter to these kids whether someone was called gay, transgender, genderqueer or whatever, so why should it matter to him?

This is a hard book to write a review for. It reads much like a college thesis paper, only using the story of Nicole Maines as a vehicle for many chapters of historical info on transgender issues. I suppose for someone who is seeking more information, that's helpful, but it was frustrating for me because I only really wanted to read about the Maines family. This book includes a glossary of terms and resources, which would be helpful for parents/kids. I want to say that I wish there had been more about the family, but I feel like maybe the author was trying to protect them in some way? It just all seems very surface, even though it includes journal entries and poems and personal narratives from all four family members. 
 The rage I felt at the school system hit very close to home. I had a student the last two years who was required to use a staff bathroom because a JANITOR had a problem with it. Not a single student complaint, but an old janitor held the power in this school. The book addresses this truth as well-- the kids are all ambivalent-- it's the adults who can't deal with any challenge to their ingrained ways of thinking. 
 I remember the story from the news and I only wish the same level of common sense regulation would make its way south. Off to find their interview on StoryCorps...

The true story of the Maines family and their lives after they adopted identical twin boys. It wasn't long before they noticed a marked difference between Jonas and his brother, Wyatt. Jonas preferred sports and trucks and many of the things little boys were "supposed" to like; but Wyatt liked princess dolls and dress-up and playing Little Mermaid. By the time the twins were toddlers, confusion over Wyatt's insistence that he was female began to tear the family apart and the years that followed were not much easier either although the family managed to stay together and make great strides in civil rights for others who came after Nicole. 
 I found it captivating that Wyatt saw him self (and drew himself) as a girl as early as age 3-4 years old and never once identified as a boy. Kudos to the mom in this book who has never once wavered and was there from the very beginning and an perhaps even more acknowledgment for Nicole's Air Force republican veteran father who overcame his deepest fears to become a vocal advocate for trans rights; of a loving brother who bravely stuck up for his twin sister when all he wanted to do was have a normal teenage life.

book_b.user_review: WTF?? I didn't get past page 28; I'm glad I got this book from the library and didn't buy it (the author suggests you on't buy this book and for good reason. Time to get back to the story of Kvothe.

sample_reviews.review_text: Tal como dice el autor, no es un libro que le pueda gustar a todo el mundo. Despues de leer con tanta ansia El temor de un hombre sabio, quede bastante decepcionada ya que me esperaba a otra cosa. Sin embargo, me encontre con un libro muy aburrido y sin accion. Segui leyendo esperando a Kvote, tal como lo hace ella pero sin exito. El corto relato del final del libro me parece una escusa para tratar de justificar la explotacion de sus fans. Al final, todo esto es una industria y tenemos que pagar por estas pequenas escapadas que nos hacen sentir mejor. En mi caso, no es un libro en el que me pude refugiar y no me hizo sentir mejor, me hizo sentir enganada.

This book was reviewed on Dark Matter Zine; for more reviews, interviews and articles, go to Dark Matter Zine. Alternatively, this link is just to Dark Matter Zine's reviews. 
 A review by Nalini Haynes 
 I have a confession to make. Up until The Slow Regard of Silent Things, I hadn't read any of Rothfuss's books. Shortly after Name of the Wind came out, I edited a one-off issue of a zine for a club. A teenage girl gave me some notes for a review scrawled on both sides of a scrap of paper. I spent over an hour deciphering the notes using the internet as my Rosetta Stone and putting the notes in some kind of logical order. After this experience I was not keen to actually read the book. 
 Fast forward a year or two. My son read Name of the Wind and loved it. I acquired a hardcover copy with the intention of reading it but postponed the actual reading until the trilogy was complete. Wise Man's Fear came out; my son again nagged me to read Rothfuss's work but the feminist critiques of book 2 were off-putting. My son looked awkward as I cited, in detail, criticisms I'd read. 
 "Yes, but the PROSE!" he replied. "You must read his work FOR THE PROSE. You will kick yourself when you finally read it." 
 The Slow Regard of Silent Things allowed me to enter Rothfuss's world from an unconventional and -- according to the author's note -- not recommended point, by reading a novella that is much less of a commitment than a doorstopper. 
 Plus my son took David Mitchell's Bone Clocks and hadn't given me a review by the time The Slow Regard of Silent Things reached publication date, so someone had to review it. [shifty eyes] 
 So. Here we are and here is my review: 
 Auri is a solitary creature, a girl obsessed with Kvothe (the central character of the doorstopper trilogy) although he's never mentioned by name. When she's not obsessing, Auri tends her underground world, setting things to rights. It is her slow regard because she is a silent thing; it is also the slow regard of inanimate objects in Auri's world. 
 Rothfuss's voice in The Slow Regard of Silent Things is part Neil Gaiman in detailed simplicity and part Isobelle Carmody in her Red Wind children's SFF series for eloquent lyricism coupled with simplicity. Rothfuss's larger series (pun intended) is not suitable for younger readers, but The Slow Regard of Silent Things is suitable for a wide range of ages as it's quite chaste. It has one animate character who is, herself, quite modest and proper although there are implications for the future of her relationship with Kvothe within the story. 
 The black and white artwork provides points of interest to the story, enhancing the misconception that this may be a story-book for primary school children (who could read it if they can cope with some stretching language but who aren't the target audience). Pipes trail across the page as Auri follows pipes to ensure she does not become lost. Footprints trail a path cross-wise through the text as Auri fearfully recalls an incident -- an invasion -- that occurred some time ago, motivating her to action. Auri's halo of dandelion hair catches the eye as she sits on a chimney stack reflecting on the night scene. Artwork enhances this quaint novella. 
 The Slow Regard of Silent Things 
 is a descriptive novel of an odd creature's life, her solitary existence, her feelings of isolation and possible mental illness. Told in the very close third person, this novella delves into Auri's world and world-view, including her struggles to remember to eat, needing to give herself permission to eat and difficulties finding food. Without traditional plot arcs or character development, the entire novella is Auri's 'moment'. Tension focuses on Auri's belief that she must tend the world while denying herself, simultaneously seeking to provide sumptuous gifts for Kvothe whose visit is imminent. A simple rhythm blends with lyrical phrasing to create prose worthy of reading for its own sake. 
 This novella is too far outside the mainstream to fairly rate it, even from my personal perspective. I have NFI how to rate it or even what measure to use. Read it and judge for yourself. Writers should read The Slow Regard of Silent Things for the prose. 
 Happy now, Son? [image error]
Weird little story. But I like Auri.

The author warns both before and after this story that you might not like it. I did like it. This one contains only one character, Auri. I have read too many books since I finished his last novel to remember Auri or the world in which she resides. His most recent story about the boy who provides answers for a fee also concerned one character, but at least he interacted with others. 
 Auri seems to have a bit of OCD, and subscribes to something like feng shui. She attributes emotions and characteristics to objects. She also senses things such as "this will be a making day," and "HE is coming in seven days." Auri fancies herself a caretaker, fixing leaky pipes and ensuring that the mirror is happy by putting it facing the window. She also conducts herself correctly at all times even though no one is observing. 
 The author wields words as a painter would, and creates something here poetic and lyrical. He uses archaic and obscure words I often had to look up. My only tiny complaint was that he used a couple words too many times: sweet and maybe grin. 
 In the end notes, the author states that there is no plot and very little action. I disagree. Auri is constantly busy, and the overall theme is preparing for a special visitor.

If you like the first two books and a big fan of Auri, then this book is for you. If you like reading about a whimsical girls with OCD then this book is for you. If you like reading stories with no plots and extensive soap making then this book is for you. 
 I absolutely adored the first two books. I even got a signed copy on the day it came out, but it was such a labor to get through. horribly boring. 
 In the Author's Endnote, Patrick writes "It doesn't do the thing a story is supposed to do," I said to her. "A story should have dialogue, action, conflict. A story should have more than one character." 
 Yeah Pat I agree with you it should, so why hell did you write like this?

I found this to be a poetic glimpse into the world of a fascinating character, and I noticed myself reflecting on my own state often while reading. Five stars for the writing, but only four for the work as a whole - because I just cant help but feel there was a fair amount of opportunity left unexploited with this project.

I loved the 2 REAL books in this series. Patrick Rothfuss was correct in his Forward when he said (paraphrasing here) 'Do not read this book.' 
 The novella is terrible because it killed all interest I had in the main character of this book. I really enjoyed Auri's quirky, mysterious actions in the other books. 
 Further, it's boring for me and probably for any reader that cannot relate to, or suffer from, Obsessive Compulsive Disorder. 
 Also, the author should have left the audiobook portion to actual performers that normally read audiobooks. His voice is not right for an audiobook format. Patrick, Leave it to the pro's! You stick to the prose! Please. 
 Lastly, I have to wonder if this book is a money grab by the publisher or editor. Mr Rothfuss should have never shared this with the Publisher. This story feels like a character study back story that authors may use for themselves to help develop a character. This doesn't even feel like a real story (maybe it's the lack of a plot though). However, this is giving the author the benefit of my doubt. I really hope he realizes this novella is so far below par for the expectation level he set with his epic first 2 books of the series.

Touching, sweet and sad, The Slow Regard of Silent Things is really a gift for fans of Rothfuss' KingKiller Chronicles. Auri was without a doubt one of my favorite characters in the series and to spend this time with her in the Underthing was a complete treat. Sparse, intimate and without a speck of dialogue we follow Auri through her world while she waits the seven days for "him" to arrive. Like Auri, Rothfuss is careful with his word choice, stepping between moments much like Auri walks in the footsteps of other people. Quiet in its telling and simple in its execution it is a work of magic. It's only a matter of time before Rothfuss finishes his series and if the other goodreads reviewers are any sign, he better get on it (man are they impatient) but I believe in the end, this book 2.5 will become a small good thing within the larger world that he has built.

First not a story. Not sure what to call it... (and yes the bullet points are utterly necessary. ) 
 # a fluff character insight 
 # an acid dream 
 # a zombie like deleted scene that could not be killed 
 # just a cash exchange between writer and a asshole with a print press 
 Had I read the series this is attached to I might have understood it better. This doesn't encourage me to cuddle up with anything wtitten by this author. 
 It was mindless fluff. If the author wanted it out there publish it as a free story or in the back of one of your books. I don't know you and I just lost all respect for you!
A lovely, quiet vignette about one of the trilogy's more mysterious characters.

reference_books.title: Smokin' Seventeen (Stephanie Plum, #17)
reference_books.review_text:
Posted at Badass Book reviews 
 You don't know me. I'm a fan of your work, have been for years. I have gotten many friends and family hooked on Stephanie, Joe, Ranger and Lula. I had every one of your books. I love your work with Charlotte Hughes and the Full Series. I have laughed and teared up, I have giggled and gasped for years, but it's time I stand up and shout. 
 Your last three Stephanie Plum Novels have left me feeling cheated. With each new installment I hope for more. But I get the same old antics. I read a recent interview with you, in which you say that when an author finds a winning formula, to stick with it and milk it for all it's worth {Paraphrased}. I take issue with this. How can an author expect their fans to keep buying a novel with the same plots, same games, same lines, same everything? The books seem to be getting shorter, the font larger, and the quality poorer, all with a hardcover price. I used to recommend your books to all who would listen, but now? I shy away and that sucks! 
 In your latest installment of the Stephanie Plum Series, Stephanie turns into a Hoochie. I'm sorry to say it. I don't like the word, I don't like the meaning, but it's what you turned her into. I didn't mind so much previously when she would steal a few kisses here and there between Ranger and Joe (and hell Diesel) but having her sleep with both men, in the same book, on back to back nights is just shameful. Gramma Bella SHOULD put the eye on her! Joe SHOULD dump her, so should Ranger. So what, now that Joe and Stephanie have an 'open' relationship they can sleep with whomever they want, whenever they want, and each other? Yuck. I was a Joe fan in the beginning of the series, but then he turned rather chauvinistic, spouting how she should be barefoot and pregnant and not working, and that got my feminist hackles all up and pissy. I've always been a Ranger girl, but I can't understand how he can still be around playing for scraps. Is her vagina magic? Are you gearing up to make her like Anita Blake? Because if So, please for the love of books don't!!! 
 Characters need growth in a series. Stephanie has not grown, in fact I could argue that she has regressed. After seventeen books, she STILL can't shoot her gun, she can't use handcuffs, she blows up cars, and has no desire to learn self defense. I'm sorry, but she's an idiot. And not a funny one anymore. 
 To me, and I know that I am not alone, Stephanie used to be a source of comic relief. She made me laugh and took me out of the seriousness of my life or other more suspenseful books I was reading at the time. But she's no longer funny, she's a joke. 
 If you are tired of writing her, then please stop. 
 If you think your fans will stop reading if she chooses to stay with ONE of the men, they won't. 
 If you are doing this for the money, I'm sorry. 
 I won't be buying anymore of your novels. 
 If this alienates me in the book blogging world, so be it. I can't stand it anymore. I've held my council for the last three books and I can't do it anymore. It's my opinion, but I am not alone. I implore you to see reason. Please go back to writing meaningfully. Make Stephanie grow up a bit. Make her see that she has to learn. 
 I hate to see her the way she is. I hope you have a plan. I pray to the editors that you have a plan. Please don't string us along. Don't make us hate her. We fans, and Stephanie as well, deserve better than what you are giving us.

 So, here I am again. I swore I wouldn't read another Evanovich Plum Novel--after my last review of 17, I swore tooth and nail to my husband, my mom, and my blog readers that I wouldn't read it! So...I went to the library. I really just had to know if it was as bad as the previous one. After being teased that she might make a decision in 18, I let my small curiosity overshadow my intellect. 
 Remember back in the day of the early awesome plum books, where Stephanie felt BAD for kissing Ranger when she was dating Morelli? Remember back in the day where she swore she would never be like Joyce the whore? Remember? Well, it seems Stephanie has inhaled too many donuts, smoke fumes--from her cars always catching fire, and hair spray, because after she slept with Ranger and Morelli on back to back nights in 17, cementing her in my hoochie hall of fame; She is now sleeping with both men regularly in 18. How many times was it? 3 or so with Ranger? 2 or 3 with Morelli and then I'm sure her and Ranger had more sex in Hawaii than we were told. I mean, dudes--it's Ranger...and Hawaii. I would! Well, I would if I wasn't conflicted or dating another man, but hey, that's me. I have morals and scruples and a code of non-whorism.

But it doesn't make up for the complete 180 degree turns every character in the Plum series has taken. Her mom is a lush, Steph is a whore, Ranger has no sack, Joe lost his possessive balls too, Lula still thinks too much about food, but she at least strives to be better...sometimes. When it's easier ;) 
 It seems that after 18 books, Ranger and Morelli have lost their balls. Huh. Who would have seen that one coming. Heh, I said coming. Did Stephanie here that? She probably is one of them right now, and while in the throes with whomever it is, is secretly wondering how long she has to wait to sleep with the other one so she doesn't seem tacky. Should she take a shower first? Nah. Why bother? She is just going to get sweaty again. 
 I jest. Sort of. I know, If I get so angry about the direction, why do I keep reading? I keep hoping things will change and they have! Finally, they have! Only for the worse. I remember thinking, why does she keep getting back with Joe? She should give Ranger a turn. Only, not this way. Why can't she have a relationship again? For a whole book, let her be with Ranger! Then at the end, have Joe tell Ranger to meet him at midnight, in the dark park, alone. with no guns. Only fists. YAY! 
 Pulease. 
 Janet Evanovich? What on earth are you doing to your characters? They have completely morphed into pod-people. They have been replaced with robots!

sample_reviews.review_text:
Ironically, the first Kim Harrision book I ever picked up was this one. I returned it to the CLC library after the first chapter because I realized that starting with Book 5 of a complex series was a really bad idea. 
 This time (with the first four books under my belt), the opening chapters made much more sense. Rachel Morgan, witch, adrenaline junkie, and magnet for trouble, is not having a good week. She wakes up possessed momentariy by a demon, the church she and her vampire roommate live in is de-sanctified in the process (repairs of which are mind boggling expensive), and now someone seems to be killing weres (just one of the Interlander species that populate Cincinnati in this alternative universe.) As if these issues weren't enough, Rachel is also caught up in a confusing vampire love triangle between her roommate, Ivy, (who Rachel loves just as a friend or does she really want more), and her boyfriend, Kisten. Add in a powerful supernatural object that Rachel has and everyone else seems to want and you've got a fast paced adventure where Rachel has to use all her skills just to stay alive.

This is the first of the Hollows stories to really grab me by the heart. I've held the contention that the cases that the witch Rachel Morgan takes on are merely vehicles for us to see other facets of the characters. I never felt that these stories were about her work as a "bounty hunter" but more about the relationships she has with those around her. This story was the first, in my opinion, to truly mesh those two ideas together. We have love, and all the attendant difficulties that come with matters of the heart, we have loss, a really deeply felt loss, we have the defining of family, and what it means to find ones place. Rachel Morgan became a more solid character in these books, and I finally had a handle on who the character Ivy was, and her motivations for the things she does. I am definitely enjoying learning more about the people who make the Hollows, and am glad I made it through the first four books to this one.

reference_books.review_text: I've loved Terry Pratchett's work for years, but he seems to be falling into the same trap American sitcoms do: as the series goes on he spends more and more time on the "big serious themes" of his books and less on the off-the-wall humor. This one's no exception. As the Unseen University finds itself forced to field a "Foot-the-ball" (what we Americans call soccer) team, the dark past of their star payer comes to light and there's a lot about prejudice, redemption, and not blaming people for the sins of their ancestors. Still, there are some pretty good laughs, especially when Lord Vetinari the Patrician is onstage. reference_books.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo (Millennium, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Boy, does this book need an editor. There's actually a pretty good mystery here, but it's buried under layers of tedious exposition, unnecessary description, and especially Stieg Larsson's transparent Mary Sue-ism. 
 For those who aren't familiar with the term, a "Mary Sue" is a derogatory term in fan fiction for a character that is just a little too good to be true, and who is clearly an avatar of the writer. A Mary Sue character's painfully obvious purpose is fantasy fulfillment for said writer. 
 In this case, the late Stieg Larsson, a middle aged Swedish magazine writer, has penned a novel about...a middle-aged Swedish magazine writer. Every woman in the book, including the title character, wants to sleep with him, because he's such a nice, mellow, undemanding guy. He solves a mystery that no one else could. After he solves the mystery, he spends a completely unnecessary 100+ more pages getting his revenge against people who were mean to him at the beginning of the book. And so on. 
 All that said, once the story actually gets going, it's interesting enough to keep you reading. I did finish it, but I doubt that I'll be reading the next two. I'll take a friend's advice and just watch the movies on Netflix.

It kept me up way past my bedtime, and really, what more can you ask for in a mystery? Definitely recommended.

book_a.title: Dreadnought (The Clockwork Century, #2)
book_a.user_review:
Summoned to the bedside of her dying father, Confederate nurse Mercy Lynch embarks on an odyssey across an alternate-history, steampunk 19th century America where the Civil War has been dragging on for twenty years. The cool stuff from Priest's other "Clockwork Century" books is here, including airships and zombies, with the addition of steam- (and new fangled petroleum-) driven mechas and railroad engines armed and armored like rolling battleships. The action, once it finally gets going, is non-stop, and Priest does have some truly evocative descriptions. 
 I liked the last Cherie Priest book I read (Boneshaker) a lot, and I really wanted to like this one as much. It has its moments, but what costs this book a star is the dialogue. It gets really stilted and clumsy at times, even making allowances for the 19th century. So it ends up being only fair. I have Fiddlehead, a later book in the series, and I hope it gets better.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Well, this was fun! Priest found better pacing in her second in the series, pacing that pulls you along like the train the characters ride, keeping plot moving and interest up even though it theoretically took a while for the "real" action to start. Civil war, steampunk and zombies. 
 So why not a better review? First and foremost, the book ends just as it gets to its point. Yes, there are further books in the series, but it is a series that only shares setting and the cast as a whole while switching focus and point of view. Second but most bothersome, the female interactions are horrible. They are combative and fraught with suspicion, and throughout the novel it is impossible for more than one strong female character to exist, to be allowed in the scene or the action. For example, Mercy suspects multiple characters of being the spy in their midst, yet only one of them, the female, gets physically locked out at every opportunity while Mercy continues to communicate and bond with the men despite her concerns. 
 At least the brown font was slightly less grating on this second go-by, thanks to an exclusive insider explanation ;)

This was the perfect book to read and finish for International Women's Day (completely unintentional)as it featured a wonderfully strong female lead. 
 So, I would classify this as borderline steampunk. It has some steampunk elements but I thought it was more of a dressed up Western. It takes place on a train...that is travelling across country...with secret cargo...and people are trying to steal it. I'm pretty sure that is the standard set up for every train-robbery-gun-firing-cowboyish movie out there. 
 Either way, it was an entertaining read. It started off fairly slowly but it became infinitely better around the 150 page mark. Things finally started moving and shenanigans were beginning to appear. By the last third of the book, it was an all out shootout (literally and figuratively). Slow start but an explosive finish: 3.5 stars

The American Civil War has raged for over ten years, with both sides inventing newer ways of killing. In better times, these grim technologies might have been the harbinger of a nation's golden age, but for Mercy Lynch, they are just more efficient mechanisms for sending Confederate soldiers to the Richmond Hospital where she's been working as a Red Cross nurse. Amidst the din of injured soldiers, Mercy receives some news she can't ignore, which sets her on an impossible path to the other side of the continent. 
 Loosely connected to Boneshaker, the first installment of Priest's Clockwork Century series, Dreadnought fills in the mystery of the American East only obliquely mentioned previously, but no knowledge of Boneshaker is required to enjoy this steampunk adventure that rumbles along just as quickly as the infernal engine it describes. To get to Tacoma, in the Washington territory, Mercy travels aboard airships, riverboats, horseback, and finally a train that holds more secrets than, it seems, all the spymasters of the Union army. 
 Priest uses well-known character types to perfection in realizing the alternate-yet-all-too-familiar world of her 19th century America. Mercy as the plucky heroine who knows better than to cuss but is ready with a cutting remark anyway, who doesn't let modesty keep her from poking her nose into any mystery, is the perfect point of view for this story. Plucky, in this case, isn't an insult because her actions and responses to situations and people are nuanced and consistent. When she begins her journey, Mercy seems dubious about her identity as a nurse, but she fully steps into that identity and takes on a position of authority and strength that doesn't change her as a character, but instead more fully illustrates her personality. 
 Anyone looking for a steampunk novel with worldbuilding to fall straight into should check out Dreadnought and its companion novels. Priest has written a novel with strong themes of both loyalty and rule-breaking that will appeal to many people, especially set against the backdrop of an American Civil War alternate history. Readers looking for characters who are more than meets the eye need look no further than Dreadnought. 
 I write book reviews and essays at I Am Booking.

This was a story that got more interesting as it went along. The suspense, the impossible situations, and then an ending that surprised me. I could see it coming at the end, but in the beginning I had no idea who this person was or where they were.
Another book in the Clockwork Century, this story pulled me along in a fantastic way. I really enjoyed Boneshaker but it this novel Priest's prose seems tighter and the viewpoint was enthralling.

In my opinion, Cherie Priest is the reigning queen author of Steampunk novels, and Dreadnought is a solid example of why. It's hard to explain Steampunk to someone who doesn't already know what it is - I mean, you can bring Verne into the picture and then try to bring the word "mash-up" into the mix (citing Glee for those who tend to not read much) and then finish off with a flourish of "something like that" and hope that they get it... or you can just hand over a copy of Boneshaker and tell them to read it. 
 Sure, the historical aspects have been twisted and pulled a bit - but these aren't historical fiction novels (unless your world actually does contain zombies). The thing about Cherie Priest's books are - even though you know they aren't historically accurate, the manner in which she writes them makes you doubt that more than once as you are reading the story. In Dreadnought, there are many scenes in which Mercy is treating soldiers, in which relationships are being developed between the North and the South on the Dreadnought itself (which alone is.. man, so awesome to read about), and it seems plausible that these things did, in fact, happen. Another thing that helps is the way that Priest implements things such as dirigibles and zombies without batting an eye at how unusual they really are. Everything is incorporated into the story in such a matter-of-fact way that if you, the reader, seems to bat an eyelash at it, you would be the one out of the ordinary. 
 Mercy Lynch's journey from Virginia to Seattle, Washington is a fun, romping good time. There's adventure, there's flying vehicles, there's massive trains and there's zombies... and it all makes perfect sense. Boneshaker and Dreadnought are two shining examples of just how great Steampunk books can be, and I cannot wait to see what Cherie Priest comes up with next.
