I feel whatever I write about this book won't really do it justice and at the same time won't adequately reveal its flaws. It was very powerful and also imperfect. For me, it was a five star piece of writing. No doubt. But honestly, I can see others giving it 2 stars and hating it. It's not a book I would recommend to many. Or possibly any. It's nearly impossible to enumerate upon all the themes Yanagihara touches upon here, but ultimately, this book is about the power and limitations of love in all its forms (parental, friendship, romantic). 
 Yanagihara writes a tale of childhood trauma and the endless repercussions that stem from it throughout one person's life (Jude) and the ripple effect upon the lives of others. For me, her writing itself was wonderful and insightful. She really can paint a picture of people's innermost emotions in ways that are very fresh. 
 For me, her characters came alive in all their glory and their flaws. I cared about all of them and agonized when they agonized, was happy when they were happy (which unfortunately wasn't often). 
 The book has some serious flaws, but I felt the writing overcame most of them. The amount of trauma seemed over the top to me. I didn't feel the author was being gratuitous, but it felt almost unrealistic after awhile. So many bad things happened to one person. Personally, I felt like the initial incidents described were enough to justify the adult protagonist's behavior - - but there were multiple instances of trauma at the hands of various unrelated characters. It was over the top. 
 Second, where was the editor? I'm serious here. I'm imagining that the editor thought to him or herself, "the writing here is so good, I can't even bear to cut anything." Yeah, it is all very, very well done, but it could have had more emotional impact if the editing was better. It could have been The Road in terms of power and impact. It wasn't. 
 Another issue, which I didn't think was a mistake, but believe to be intentional, was that much of the book was told from the perspective of the protagonist, Jude. Jude is filled with self loathing and some pity which renders him not the most likeable person. The reader feels a lot of empathy for Jude without really being able to like him. The author gives the reader a sense of what is inside a person like Jude and the thinking process. It's fascinating and very original. But it is also risky because the reader can't completely relate, can't really love this character who can't love himself. His friends love Jude dearly, and you see glimpses of why . . .however, in the end, the reader is left wondering to some degree why they cared as much as they did. The reader has to trust the ancillary characters to some degree to fill in the missing pieces of the puzzle that is Jude and the parts of him that are loyal, hardworking, caring. 
 In the end though, the insights in this book and the way they were written really won me over and left me thinking, yes, this is a great book. Few authors really try to plumb the depths of the human psyche like this one does, and if you are interested in the psychology of humans and what drives human behavior, you can't help but find it engaging. I loved writing like this: 
 "Why wasn't friendship as good as a relationship? Why wasn't it even better? It was two people who remained together, day after day, bound not by sex or physical attraction or money or children or property, but only by the shared agreement to keep going, the mutual dedication to a union that could never be codified. Friendship was witnessing another's slow drip of miseries, and long bouts of boredom, and occasional triumphs. It was feeling honored by the privilege of getting to be present for another person's most dismal moments, and knowing that you could be dismal around him in return." 
 Now, a paragraph like that could be boring if the context wasn't so perfect. Or if it stopped the forward trajectory of the plot. But Yanagihara seamlessly weaves her insights into the story so that you never want to put the book down and yet want to pause to take in what you've read, to ponder it. I just loved that tension.

3.5 Stars 
 I was really back and forth on this book. At times I thought it was extraordinary and others times I found it tedious. 
 This is the story of a group of best friends from college and follows them through 4 decades of their lives focusing on one of the friends, Jude, who has always been a bit of a mystery to his friends. 
 What I liked: 
 Very introspective look at the life of a survivor. Questions whether or not a person can ever truly recover from a series of traumatic events and become whole again. Questions what qualities make a person loved, valued and worthy of love. Questions forgiveness, particularly forgiving ones own past. Questions what makes living a life worthwhile. 
 It was interesting living vicariously through four cool, talented ivy league grads forging their way through NYC after college, finding their niche in the world, developing their talents, managing their careers, developing as people. Another interesting aspect was that the main characters ran in art and theater circles which added to the reading experience. 
 What I found annoying: 
 If felt like the author was trying to cram every bad, sad and tragic experience she could ever dream up and stick it into one character's story line. If would be sad but believable for ONE, two or even three of those bad things to happen to a person, but it's way too much for all of it to have happened to one person. It's hard to believe. I know the point was that Jude had suffered very significantly, but it was way way too much. 
 The characters annoyed me. How is it that pretty much every single person Jude encountered in his childhood was not just bad but awful, like "should be in prison" awful?? Then about the time he turned 15, every person (with one or two expectations) was just so darn good? Only one character, JB, was both good and bad enough to be interesting and believable. I thought that was pretty far fetched ust seems very manufactured. 
 There were parts of the book that seemed long and unnecessary. For example, several pages were used to describe the eulogy of a minor character. There were several similar incidents. 
 This book is definitely worth reading, I just didn't love it as wildly as most of the other reviewers. I think the themes; friendship, love, abuse, survival, self abuse, loss, self reflection and self-esteem would make great book club discussion topics.

I save my 5 star reviews for this exact reason. If you give every book a 5 star review because it was good, what do you give a book that is simply put, so exceptional that you wish it could go on forever and even its 720 pages doesn't seem long enough. 
 I don't have words to express how moving and sad, yet how incredibly rich this book is. I don't think I've ever read anything that has moved me to tears like A Little Life. 
 I could feel Jude's pain, I could feel what he felt, even though I knew that the book could only end one way, I still hoped for more for him. 
 I could go on forever of the things that made this book what it is, but for now, I'm going to say this is THE BEST book I've EVER read. 
 Now I'm just going to carry it with me in my bag for a little while, to keep Jude and Willem, Malcolm and Harold and even JB around with me a little longer.

reference_books.title: The Secret (The Secret, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Meeeeh. 
 The ideas are ones I've been exposed to before, in much more thoughtful ways, in Buddhist writing. I can go with the concepts, but the writing's not very good, and I also don't like the way this book "blames" people for the bad things that happen to them. Buddhism itself actually would say that there are things that happened in past lives that are causing that suffering now. The study of the Chakrahs that I've done would say that although you can use your mind to aid in your own self-healing, just because you stay sick doesn't mean you've messed up. But this book, no. If you're sick, if you're poor, if bad stuff is happening to you, then it must mean that you aren't attracting enough positive energy with your thoughts. 
 I mean, I'm totally on board with the idea that good thoughts attract good things to your life. I've seen negative people continue to attract the bad stuff. But I think this book oversimplifies the idea so that it could be a successful pop-culture book. It talks about the importance of meditation and then never teaches you HOW, and talks just about focusing on positive things in your life. It says that when dealing with negative things you should just focus on the positive instead because otherwise you will attract more negative stuff. (The Dali Lama has much more useful things to say about this topic in THE ART OF HAPPINESS) 
 Nonetheless I didn't give it one star, because there were actually some good ideas in it--like to create a board that has pictures of all the stuff you want for your life on it, to start every day with gratitude for the things you do have, to remind us that the world is largely created through our mind. If you think you will be late, you probably will be. People will see you as you see yourself. Because I actually found some of those nuggets to be useful, I kept reading it.

If You're Like Me... 
 you have trouble getting organzied 
 you have trouble staying organized 
 you write list, after list, after list 
 you have piles of paperwork, books and files piled on every flat surface 
 Can you solve this with some organization? 
 Thankfully, the answer is a very simple, YES. Yes you can take care of all those piles of paperwork, etc, with some simple organizational techniques. There are a number of very good books out there that claim to show you easy steps to reduce that clutter, better organize your workload, and help you be more productive. 
 So What is "Get Things Done" aka GTD? 
 "Get Things Done" by David Allen, is one of those books, and has a lot of useful advice. The biggest trick it taught me is that if I can do a quick task NOW, then I should do it NOW, and not put it off until later. This is really fundamental to the organizational approach used by the author, and has helped me be more productive in my daily work, which involves a lot of paperwork, and filing. 
 Process every input as if it was a task, and decide what you need to do with it. 
 Do it 
 Defer it 
 Delegate it 
 Drop it 
 Do it, means DO IT NOW! Defer it, means it needs doing, but is not something you can do with the time, tools, or information available. Deferred items should always become tasks, or projects, depending how complicated they are. If you are going to delegate a task, then you need to decide who to delegate it to, notify them, and set a time or date to follow-up. If you are going to drop a task, then simply remove it from your list of things that need doing. 
 The next trick I learned is to organize my tasks by project, context, time required, and create task lists for each project. For each project, identify the very next task that is required to move the task forward. If that means you are waiting on someone else to complete something, or provide input then add it to a list of required followups. 
 Setting deadlines, or followup dates for every task will help keep your mind off things you don't need to worry about, and free you up to concentrate on things you do need to get done. This is where the review processes come into play, and at several levels. The system allows for reviews on a number of different schedules. 
 The daily review makes sure you have a grasp of what needs doing in the course of a given day, and allows you to decide what is feasible, and what might have to be deferred. The weekly review allows you an oversight of the entire week, and gives you a chance to setup the following week, as well as make sure you have nothing undone from your current week... And so on. Every review should take into account the various goals you have set yourself, and give you the chance to reassess the tasks, projects and goals you have set. 
 What worked for me! 
 I'll be completely honest. Some of the systems the book suggests work just fine for me. I have used it to help me at work, and in my professional writing. I have a much better grasp of what is required at each stage of my various projects, and where I am with them. 
 At work, I am far more productive, and a lot less stressed, even though I keep a lot of my task lists in my head, rather than in any formalized format. Since I am dealing with customers, and a hectic retail environment, this has proved easier than trying to write things down all the time. 
 This was a very successful adaptation of the system, to deal with the immediacy of my work environment. 
 What didn't work for me! 
 I've tried to use the system to organize my apartment. I am the first to admit my single-room apartment is a wreck, with piles of paperwork, books, and clothes everywhere. I have been using the system to try and bring some organization to the chaos, and failed. 
 I have been fighting several factors, time, space, and available surfaces on which to work. My wife and I both work, and are often on incompatible schedules. What little time we have together is considered valuable. What available flat surfaces we have are covered in piles of stuff, and that includes large areas of the floor. 
 So, we set ourselves the goal of getting a bigger living space, which means spending more money on rent, or purchasing a place. That means paying off our existing debts, which I delegated to my lovely wife, who is doing a great job of getting things paid on time, and with extra payments when we can afford them. 
 So, while I don't have the dedication to turn around almost nine years of clutter, I have high hopes of being able to adapt the system for the move, and remaining organized afterward. 
 Final thoughts... 
 Overall, I would recommend this book to anyone who has problems getting organized, and staying that way. There is a lot of good advice throughout the book, which is based on the author's personal experience, and successful application by his clients. 
 I've spoken to people who have instituted some, or all of the material from the book, and adapted, or dropped what didn't work for them. I have a feeling I fall into the lower end of the spectrum of GTD adopters, but I have intentions to extend my usage of it, as time and space allow.

Why You're Reading It: 
 - You are a Christian looking for comfort. 
 - You are interested in Christianity. 
 - You want to be open to reading about afterlife stories from all types of faiths. 
 What I Thought: 
 I was really hoping that this book would be inspiring and hopeful. I was really hoping that because it was number one on the New York Times bestseller list, it was a book that could speak to a variety of people. It was not. And it was a reminder that bestseller lists are just that -- lists that tell you which books are selling, not which books are good. It was also a reminder that there are a lot of Christians in this country and, if you don't already know this, Christians really like to support each other. 
 For anyone who has been to church and heard the message -- that is what you will be getting in this book, although with a personal twist. Yes, it's interesting to hear about what this family claims happened to them. No, I am not convinced it is all false (that would be pretty demented of a proclaimed Christian family to use their young son's near-death experience as weird spiritual scheme, so I'm giving them the benefit of the doubt... mostly). However, the only parts of this book that were unique were also parts that could be explained away. Other than the very clear message that if you don't have a personal realtionship with Christ, you are most certainly going to hell (displayed many times and in particular through a scene where Colton -- the child whom this story is based on-- has a screaming fit at a man's funeral because he's not sure the man is going to heaven), the long passages of Scripture, and an incredibly touching account of almost losing their toddler, there is not much to this book that you haven't heard. 
 No doubt, if this story actually happened, it was jarring to the family. However, having any experience at all in Christian based land (and here I reveal that I grew up in America, where one would actually have to try to not know anything about the religion), the things that this three/four year old with a pastor father and a sunday school teaching mother was saying about heaven and God was not at all out of the ordinary (though Burpo would have you believe they were, stating that he knew for a fact this his son had never heard about the spiritual things he described to his parents). 
 There was only one thing (ONE thing) that I couldn't explain away (the picture of the grandpa, for those of you who have read it), and though that was a "hmmmm" moment for me, it was not overall convincing. If you are a Christian and you already believe in the Bible (and this Nebraska family takes their Bible very literally), you'll most likely eat this up with a knife and fork and ask for seconds. If you are not -- you may want to spend your money on something else.

sample_reviews.review_text: Didn't like the book much, but did like the message.

I'm probably going to be unpopular in some circles when I say this, but I really just didn't like this book. The plot seemed to me to just be a retelling of "The DaVinci Code", only set in Washington DC using different symbology. I find the style that Brown writes in to be overly dramatic; in some places it reads like a romance novel: a little too flowery. It was interesting to read the parts of the plotline regarding Noetic sciences, but I am left unconvinced that they added a whole lot to the overall story arc. I'm pretty disappointed in this story; "DaVinci" and "Angels and Demons" were well crafted books overall, the plot was tight and kept my interest, even though portions of writing which I found atrocious. A bit more editing, better characterization, and a tighter plotline would have improved this book.

Ok. To start I want to make it clear that I like and enjoy Dan Brown's books. Sure they're generally crap - think of them as heaving bosom novels for the intellectual set. (I also like a good heaving bosom novel...). The theories are complete fiction but the puzzles and National Treasure style adventure are entertaining. 
 Not the Lost Symbol. 
 The Lost Symbol is long and boring and terrible. Every once in a while you hit a chapter or two that are vaguely interesting, and they make you think "maybe it will get good now." Sadly it never does. I had to force myself to finish it, and it wasn't worth it. 
 Tl;dr - the Langdon books are fine assuming you skip this one.

I was extremely anticipated to read this book. I had many great expectations for it. I am sorry to say; But I was very disappointed. It was all very interesting in the beginning, good plot, great story. But as i went through it didn't get any better unfortunately. I can't give it more than a 2.5 out of 5. 
 The plot 
 Okay so the plot was good. It had that thing that kept you curious and interested to read through the book, and wonder about things. There were things I didn't expect to happen which we're shocking. And there were things I just didn't care what happened to. But you could've guessed the main story from the first 100 pages or so if you read any other by Dan Brown. 
 Ideas and Themes 
 Now here comes my problem with the book. I will try not to reveal too much so there wont be any spoilers. I think I understand what Dan Brown hoped to achieve by proposing such ideas, he kind of went to the edge. I can picture a lot of people no so happy with what he wrote down. Not because of people with different opinions and not because they don't suit the way I think. It was just too delusional, too far away from anything. He kind of picked an angle to view the situation, and there was this factor of persuasion to get the reader to believe. I just think It was all nonsense, and it a big reason why I didn't like this book that much. 
 The text and characters 
 The writing was very good. It was all very smart and kept you interested. But really it was far too much writing for such a story. I just kept reading and reading and .... Really he could've gave the same idea in two pages only. There was far too much unnecessary details he could've skipped. It would've been much better that way. 
 The characters were good. I like that all of them were smart. There wasn't much of an error concerning them. I liked katherine (Peter's sister) the most. Just because she was strong and intelligent. And I could understand her and relate to her. 
 At last, I wasn't very impressed with this book. It's not in my favorites but I respect people and their ideas and it was kind of informative . but if you are religious, you're probably going to be disappointed so you wouldn't want to read this.

I pretty much just waited for this book to end. Though the DC runaround was fun to read as someone who lives there, the actual premise was uninteresting to me. Maybe I just don't care about symbols enough to be intrigued by a lost one. Just go to Symbols R Us next time, Mr. Langdon?

Okay, so I actually want to give this a 3.5 stars or a 3.75 stars but...Goodreads rating system is very limited. And I don't know if I want to actually give this book 4 stars, but I will say it was a vast improvement over the first book. 
 Less melodrama, more plot. Less stupid romance, more action. The story started to feel like it was coming together, and I was pretty interested the whole way through. Of course, some parts of the plot were a little anticlimactic and underdeveloped (I want so much more from the Earthborn/Sasha plot, but that could be the T.V show blurring the two lines) and it could have put in a few more punches, but it was overall good. Not perfect. Not the best thing ever. But enough to keep me reading, and help me flow over to the third book. 
 However, forever eye-rolling at Kass Morgan making Bellamy and Clarke say "I love you" to each other when they've been dating for like 2 seconds. As much as I like having canonical Bellamy/Clarke (*shakes fist at TV producer*) I actually prefer the agonizing development of their relationship (romantic or not...who really knows right now) on the T.V show. 
 Anyways, I'm already reading the third book, so you can tell I'm going to keep going no matter what. I still haven't seen any stills from Season 3 of the T.V show or any vines from Eliza or Devin. I'm holding on to nothing. All I've got are these books for now. And the Comic-Con interviews. 
 (Disclaimer: If any T.V show fan goes into these books seeking more story, these are completely different beasts. The T.V show and the first book were written around the same time. They're so different it's insane, so just expect two different things and you'll be happy. Same goes for people moving from the books to the T.V show.) 
 3.5/5 stars.

reference_books.title: End of Days (Penryn & the End of Days, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! 
 I knew there was a reason I waited so long to pick up the third book. I knew I needed to savor them for as long as I could, because now there are no more books. 
 Guess I'll just have to go back to the first book. 
 Wow. This was such a good finale. So much action. So much intrigue. And Penryn, oh Penryn, you have grown up so much. That's my little girl, going out and saving the world. You go, Penryn Young. You go, girl. 
 I just...words...not...happening. I'm still not over what Raffe did near the end of the book. I literally clapped my hand over my mouth and went, "no." I just...feels...those feels. So many feels. 
 Everything just worked out so well. There was never a dull moment, and that final showdown was just so stellar that I don't even care how much sleep I lost to finish the book. Okay, maybe I care a little, but it was worth it. 
 My only complaint was there was not enough Raffe/Penryn sass. Like, come on Raffe, did you forget how to be funny? There was such a lack of banter that it made me sad. But I will forever be lololing about how Raffe's friends are all "hey is that your girlfriend?" and he's all "no guys, we can't date humans, duh," and they're like "well, technically you're already screwed so you can do what you want and it doesn't matter" and then Raffe goes "hmmmmm" and five minutes later he and Penryn are making out while flying in the sky. Smooth, Raphael. Smooth. 
 My Raffe/Penryn feels were not as strong as they were in say, Book 1 or Book 2, but hey, there was a lot going on. This book was incredible nonetheless, and such a good finale. Sure, it ended a little abruptly, but I feel like it ended in a satisfying way. 
 But. I am a little peeved that I got robbed of the scene I've been waiting for for three books. The moment that everyone realizes that Penryn has been dating an angel this whole time and everything is like "wait what?" I was ROBBED. I wanted it so badly. 
 Gosh. This series. Such a perfect mix of humor, action, darkness, and romance, all wrapped up into an incredibly vivid post-apocalyptic San Francisco Bay Area. I mean, what more could you want? I WILL be re-reading it. Probably in the near future. I'm just going to miss it so much. 
 Goodbye, Penryn and Raffe. Until next time. Thanks for the wild ride. 
 5/5 stars. 
 Sidenote: Penryn Young IS Asian. I will accept no other head canons or fan casts. I don't care that it was never specified in the books. She is Asian. The end.

reference_books.title: Mansfield Park
reference_books.review_text:
<3333333333333333333333 
 Goodness, why did it take me nearly two years to finish this book? It is so good! And so cute! I was absolutely riveted page after page, and I am still healing from how disappointed I am in a certain character who had so much potential and now basically sucks. Boo on him. Boo. But whatever, it's over, it's done with, and the two main lovers have found each other at last and I love them so much but then whenever I start to gush I have to mentally remind myself that they are COUSINS. COUSINS. Jane Austen, why do you have to give me such complicated feelings about my ships? Whyyy? It is incest...but it is so cute...but it's gross...but it was the 1800's. So many complicated feelings. 
 ANYWAYS. The plot was really slow, but for some reason I was okay with it. Every little scene had me captivated. Jane Austen is so good at making us see something big in something little, such as the significance of a glance or the double meaning of an off-hand comment. And I loved all of the characters. With 400 pages you really get to know the people and the story, and now I feel so disconnected and I wish there were a sequel. But at least there's movie adaptations! 
 I'm so glad I decided to pick this back up again. I love, love, love it! 
 5/5 stars.

reference_books.title: The Girl on the Train
reference_books.review_text:
Very good. I was entertained the whole way through and I thought it was pretty well-done. Sometimes the narrations of the different characters blended together, so I would have liked if the different POV chapters had more distinct voices, and I also had a hard time keeping track of time because the dates at the beginning of the chapters got confusing. sample_reviews.review_text:
This was a very interesting and quirky book, and I have to admit, I don't think I've ever read such a weird story. Peculiar children is putting it mildly, these kids were downright scary. The story involves time travel, WWII, and some scary otherworldly beasts, that come together on a remote fishing island off of Scotland's coast. What was pretty unique about this book, is that there are "real" photographs to go along with the story, and you find yourself studying them. I was fascinated with the story, which becomes a page-turner, and slightly surprised at the ending. 
 This is a first novel for the author, Ransom Riggs, and I can't wait to see what comes next.

2 stars for the writing 3 for the story and 4 for the amazing photos. I will give it 3.5 stars 
 I think this book tries a little bit too hard to work around the photos. Sometimes they are pointlessly added. I think if they were just shown as the story moves on and not described by the main character- which takes away the effect of them- like they are in most times. Don't get me wrong. The story was interesting, the kind that sucks you in, the writing was nothing spectacular, the characters unusually immature, especially given how long they have been alive, although Jacob was the biggest problem when it comes to this. Some of the scenes are a little too forced around the pictures, but the story is interesting no less. 
 I loved this pictures, especially the second creepy Santa in the interview in the exclusive copy, they all have a certain mysterious aspect around them, which could have been better used if not so throughly described, they could have just been inserted with subtle hints so people could wonder what is going on in the scene. 
 Point is, if you can get past the basic writing and underdeveloped characters, it is an alright book, I still read it in a day so it wasn't putting me off too much. I would recommend it for the pictures alone.

The hype for this book truly did not deliver for me on this book. I found Jacob to be an unreliable narrator, and the character development to be very weak. I did not attach myself to any of the characters and felt the relationships were not well-developed. The beginning was very long and drawn out. I wasn't expecting the first 100 pages to be set in Florida, and it felt like it took a really long time for anything exciting to happen. Jacob seems like a whiny and spoiled teen that became disconnected from the author. I am having a hard time explaining why I didn't particularly enjoy this book, but there was something about it that completely irked me - maybe I was just hyper-aware that I was reading a book and couldn't become fully engrossed in the book. 
 Read For: Teen Book Club, August 2016 
 Recommend For: YA/Fantasy/Time Travel/Books to Movies

As with most books that manage to gain such mass appeal, choosing to give it a try should come with a bit of a caveat: expectations might be unfairly elevated. 
 Did it reach my expectations? To be honest I still haven't decided. Admittedly I entered into Rigg's world knowing very little (likely less than most) about the actual narrative. 
 What I liked: 
 1. The use of pictures: The buzz around the book has a lot to do with its unique use of pictures. What is interesting is that this was probably the most noted element that I remained unaware of until the end of the book. I recognized that the author was using pictures to enhance the narrative of course, but it wasn't until I reached the end of the book (that contained the author's interview) that I recognized why he chose to use the pictures (namely, that they were real and not staged, and that they were lost pictures in history that he had dug up, discovered, chased after, and gotten ahold of in the name of a personal passion project). Understanding that the narrative flowed from the visuals and helped create the storyline through his imaginative take on the people behind the photographs actually changed my experience with the narrative itself. What at first had felt somewhat lacklustre writing actually ended up gaining a few interesting layers in the aftermath, helping it to linger longer than it might have otherwise. 
 2. The concept: I will address more of this in the stuff that I didn't like, but, at a grass roots level I found the theory of his concept (of peculiar children, timelines, and loops) interesting enough to hold my attention. Given that not very much happens for the first three quarters of the book, this is actually to it's credit. 
 3. Jacob: I wouldn't be surprised to hear that the story lived or died for some on how they felt about Jacob. He is the main narrator of the story after all. I actually liked the character. He plays that always difficult role of privileged child with a complex. I think the reason why this role is always particularly hard to pull off (at least well) is because it is hard to get readers to truly care about his well being. In the case of Jacob he comes from a good home with two well-meaning parents, and to top it off he also manages to have a job that he fails to care about and a best friend that he treats like crap. 
 Honestly, with that premise it would be less than surprising if people in general had a hard time connecting. But I think Riggs deserves some credit here. He could have taken the easier path and given us a poor, likable (but turmoiled) outcast. But he doesn't, and he commits wholly to trying his best to give Jacob a recognizable soul. I liked how he spends time connecting us to his relationship with the Grandfather, and I even enjoyed how he uses the relationship with the father throughout the book to examine Jacob's motivation. By the time I arrived at the end I felt like I was beginning to learn how to care about this character, and that is a difficult thing to manage for any writer. If anything I think he suffers from a weak supporting cast more than the presentation and development of the character himself. 
 4. The Cinematic presence in the story: It made complete sense to me to read the author talking about how the book was written with a film in mind. It's the feeling I had carried all through the story. I can't remember the last time I felt myself saying "this scene would work great on screen" at so many different moments. It turns out this was intentional, so I guess it's a credit to say it worked. Of course the downfall is that it sacrifices on the literary level (although that is of course subjective). But I appreciated the ability and desire to try and fuse these two worlds together. 
 What I didn't like: 
 1. The literary sacrifice that the cinematic form demands: To follow up on my last point to the positive, the negative side of this is a story that struggles immensely with flow. How a book can feel so bogged down and yet move so quickly is puzzling to me, but this was my experience. For all of the time it takes to develop nearly nothing gets developed by the time we hit the real action (a full three quarters in unfortunately). 
 I think a part of the issue here (which might be worth mentioning) is that the author can't seem to figure out which characters and which moments to sit on and let develop, and which ones are simply tools to bring the cinematic form of the story to life. It is a shame that we get to know next to nothing of the fantastical characters living in Miss Peregrine's home, as the mere mention that they all arrived at this home with tension filled past (revolving around the fact they were all peculiar children trying to find a place in a normal world) left me as a reader intrigued to know more. 
 2. Emma: If I managed to find a way to enjoy the character of Jacob, Emma found my on the other side of this coin. A character that should have been immediately likeable (and in her mysterious introduction she kind of is) derails in to all of the characteristics that I expected to hate about Jacob. I can't remember the last time I have encountered a character that was so back and forth and emotionally confused, and for no apparent (or good) reason. And again, this is a bit of a shame because there was so much good stuff there that the author could have explored (with her different personal connections to Jacob himself). Instead, she ends up so erratic and so annoying (I love you Jacob/I hate you Jacob, Please stay Jacob/You are responsible for everything Jacob) that nothing of her complicated past ends up having any real bearing on the story (at least emotionally). 
 3. The fact that it feels like a dumbed down version of the popular YA format: I need to be careful with this point, as the last thing I mean to suggest is that good, smart readers can't enjoy this story. I actually think the story has a ton of potential. My issue is in the way it meanders through its story without a really good sense of it's audience. In the beginning, I thought it was aiming for something akin to The Magicians, something a bit more mature but still in the spectrum of recognizable YA material. The entire portions given to explaining the stories dramatic and complicated theories made me think it belonged with something more along the lines of Divergent, which would be perfectly fine if I hadn't been expecting something different. And then we arrive at the book's persistent meandering in to the cliche (most notably in the eye-rolling romance of Jacob and Emma), and the ridiculous dialogue that forms the book's climatic showdown. It all seems to hamper the ability to figure out the book's core audience. 
 The book is not terrible. In-fact, there were a few moments where I didn't want to put it down. There were also a few where I was perfectly okay with putting it down. The end result left me intrigued enough to tackle the sequel, but probably more intrigued to see with Burton can do with the film. That is, after all, where I think the book truly belongs.

sample_reviews.review_text: I almost stopped reading this book several times, but made myself finish. The storyline was very hard to believe and felt overtly didactic. I liked Jack and Ally's characters, but they just couldn't carry the others. There were times I enjoyed the story, but they were few and far between my eye rolls. Clearly, I would not recommend this book.

Thousands of people gather at an isolated campground, hoping to watch a solar eclipse. Among them are three teenagers--Ally, Bree, and Jack--whose lives will never be the same. 
 The story is told in first person and smoothly shifts between the three main characters. This was excellent! The author created three likeable, dynamic main characters as well as fleshed out several sub characters. 
 I learned a lot of things about astronomy that I didn't know before, and this book makes me want to watch a solar eclipse. The next one in the U.S. will be in August 2017. 
 Rated G, young adult fiction.

Set in campground constructed for the sole purpose of being at "front row, center" for a total solar eclipse this story is told from three different teenagers' points of view. 
 Each narrator has different reasons for being at Moon Shadow Campground. They all learn and grow through the book. 
 This book totally makes me want to see a full solar eclipse

reference_books.title: Agnes and the Hitman
reference_books.review_text: The dialogue is trite. The sex is bland. The characters are cardboard cutouts. The plot is inane and unbelievable. It seems that the author(s) can't figure out what kind of book this is. Is it a comic crime caper? A mystery? A romance? A mafia thriller? A cooking cozy? Bodies pile up left and right, plot lines disintegrate or appear from thin air. Even the editing is bad ... the electricity goes out, thanks to a bad guy who "did something" to the power, but early the next morning Agnes is in the kitchen using her coffee grinder and CD player. The authors would have us believe that her cooking is so great that people set their guns down to feast on pancakes and ham (and where does all this food come from when she never goes to the store ... and remember that the electricity was out ... we're talking South Carolina summer HEAT). Oh, and what's with the psychiatrist (who just disappears in the middle of the book). Crusie (or Mayer) does manage to write a few humorous scenes that tickle me, but if it weren't for a Shelfari book group Challenge I would not have finished it at all.

reference_books.title: To Kill a Mockingbird
reference_books.review_text:
Audio book narrated by Sissy Spacek 
 5***** and a 
 Is this the quintessential American Novel? Will it stand the test of time as Mark Twain's The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn has done? Time will tell. 
 I do know this, however. This is a singularly powerful novel that had a great impact on me when I first read it at age 13 (shortly after it was first published), and has never failed to move and inspire me as I've re-read it over the years (at least 20 times by now). It has touched generations of readers in the 50-something years since it was first released, and remains high on many "must be read" lists. 
 There are many reasons for this. It's a well-paced novel, a fast read with elements of suspense, family drama, humor and moral lessons. Scout is a wonderful narrator, both as a child and as an adult looking back on her childhood; and the fact that Lee was able to seamlessly move between these two viewpoints is a testament to her skill as a writer. 
 Many people feel this is a book about racism. I don't think that is the core theme of the book, though it is the central plot device Lee uses. I think the major theme of the novel is personal integrity and courage - doing what you know is right when all about you seemingly disagree and even when it may be dangerous to do so, being true to your own moral compass, and instilling those values in your children by example not just words. 
 In this respect Atticus Finch shines as the protagonist of this work. He is a man of strong moral fiber, a man who is "the same in his house as he is on the public street," a man "who was born to do our unpleasant jobs for us." He embodies the lessons he tries to impart to his children: that courage is not a man with a gun in his hands but rather, "It's when you know you're licked before you begin but you begin anyway and you see it through no matter what." 
 The novel aims a spotlight on a particular time and place in America's history. Lee writes with clarity and colors this world for the reader with descriptions that put us squarely in Maycomb, Alabama circa 1935: Somehow it was hotter then: a black dog suffered on a summer's day; bony mules hitched to Hoover carts flicked flies in the sweltering shade of the live oaks on the square. Men's stiff collars wilted by nine in the morning. Ladies bathed before noon, after their three-o'clock naps, and by nightfall were like soft teacakes with frostings of sweat and sweet talcum." 
 The minor characters, especially the women, are as richly drawn as the major players. I was struck by what a wide range of personalities, strengths, weaknesses and ethics Lee was able to express using characters such as Calpurnia, Aunt Alexandra, Helen Robinson, Mrs Merriweather, Lula, Miss Maudie, Mrs Dubose, Miss Caroline and Mayella Ewell. Some of them appear for only a page or two, but they come alive on the page and remain in the reader's memories. 
 The audio book is performed by Academy-Award-winning actress Sissy Spacek. She does an admirable job, though her accent is wrong. She is a Texan, and the Southern Alabama accent is softer than her twang. Still, by the second disc I had stopped noticing this, and allowed myself to be carried into the story by her expert reading. 
 ******* 
 NOTE: The above is a fresh re-write in July 2015; compiled from notes I've taken over several re-reads: May 1998, July 2004, 14Aug2010, 22Oct2011, 07July 2013, 13July 2015

reference_books.review_text: I expected an Italian "Year in Provence," but Mayes is not Peter Mayle. Here is the rare instance where the movie is much better than the book.

reference_books.title: The Night Bookmobile
reference_books.review_text:
A lonely young woman stumbles upon a Winnebago on a street one night when out walking. It's the Night Bookmobile, and what she discovers within is magical and inspiring ... and disturbing. 
 Niffenegger is perhaps best known for The Time Traveler's Wife. Here she turns to the graphic novel format. The illustrations are wonderfully drawn, and I found there was a good ratio of text to art. But I did not like this story at all. I can't say much without spoiling it, but I am left wondering what Niffenegger was trying to say by having Alexandra kill herself in order to work in the Night Bookmobile, when she already had an apparently "dream" job in a real library. Is the point of this supposed to be Mr Openshaw's statement that "only living people can be Readers."? Is she saying that librarians are lonely and depressed people who can only relate to books? Or that loving books will lead to a life spent alone? Clearly, I just don't get it. 
 Although I am not a great fan of graphic novels (In the four I've tried previously, I found the text difficult to read, and the art mostly dark.), I do admire the illustrations here. They are wonderfully detailed and the characters lifelike. Too bad the story is so bad. 1* for the art.

reference_books.title: The Husband's Secret
reference_books.review_text:
Audiobook performed by Caroline Lee 
 From the book jacket Cecelia Fitzpatrick has achieved it all - she's an incredibly successful businesswoman, a pillar of her small community, and a devoted wife and mother. Her life is as orderly and spotless as her home. But a letter is about to change everything, and not just for her: Rachel and Tess barely know Cecilia - or each other - but they too are about to feel the earth-shattering repercussions of her husband's secret. 
 My reactions 
 Well, this sure went in directions I didn't expect. I can't say much more without giving away key plot elements, which I definitely do not want to do. 
 I will admit that the multiple points of view did confuse me at first, as the narrative switched from Cecelia to Tess to Rachel. This confusion was compounded, I think, by my listening to the audio rather than reading. It always takes me a little longer to sort out the characters when I'm listening to an audio performance, especially when the voice artist does not use unique voices for each character. But once the various threads became clear to me I was fascinated by how Moriarty was going to weave them together, by the connections - both obvious and subtle - that she made. 
 I thought the weakest link (to the letter) was Tess's story line, and there were a few times when I felt that story was more chick-lit beach read than serious contemporary fiction. Still I couldn't help but consider "what would I do" if I were in the position of any one of these women. And some of their actions and reactions took me by surprise. 
 I was not a fan of the epilogue which gave additional information not found in the main book. Was Moriarty afraid her readers would not tolerate an ambiguous ending? To me this weakened the novel, and I nearly deleted that fourth star because of it. 
 Caroline Lee does a fine job performing the audio version of the book. I did not recognize much difference in the voices she used for the central women in the novel, but after a few chapters I had no trouble keeping them straight.

book_a.user_review: WOW ... murder, greed, plotting. The movie (which was terrific) has a somewhat different ending. I'm torn as to whether the movie or the book is better. But the book is fantastic.

sample_reviews.review_text: I can't say that I liked this book very much at all. After enjoying Smith's more recent novel, The Ruins, I harbored some high hopes for this, his debut novel. But, It hardly seems like it was written by the same man writer. There isn't much connecting the stories at all. Although I suppose they are both books that basically consist of one bad thing after another happening to the characters... But otherwise a jungle adventure involving a mysterious plant and younger main characters does not share much in common with this family and friend drama in the snowy Midwest. The main character, Hank, is convincingly portrayed by Smith. The author really does a wonderful job of getting into Hank's head and revealing the horrible justifications (and motivations) for his bad decisions. But Hank, for me at least, went too far in his spiraling descent into mad violence. After a scene involving Jacob, I simply stopped caring about learning where any of these bad decisions would ultimately lead. I just couldn't get re-absorbed into the fast-paced novel. I did not ultimately hate the novel - it had too interesting of a set-up - but I did not really enjoy reading it. The end did not satisfy me at all. I had been looking forward to checking out the film version initially, but now I think I will just wait and see if it is ever on television...
I think the movie is better.

What started with an interesting premise turned into a bloody, pointless killing spree. That was kind of the point of this moral story, with a lot of whining by the first person narrator. Towards the end I started skipping the introspective BS. I'm kind of curious about the movie. I have hopes that Raimi can do something good out of this mess...

A found some Scott Smith books at a discount bookshop, and I picked them up knowing that there are times when you want to shy away from the masterpieces and have something more simple. Well, it was simple enough. The plot was ok, some of it did not make too much sense, by the very end the plot was off the rail. But the book was entertaining enough.

It began wonderfully, but by the first third of the book, I was becoming annoyed at the over-the-top noirishness, and the author's constant badgering of how else could the protagonist be expected to act? (Novel is in first person, and very quickly, I became annoyed by the protagonist's stupidity and greed). I have serious problems with noir when I can't emotionally identify/empathize with any of the characters. By halfway through, I was tired of the characters. I'm surprised I gave it as high a grade as I did.
Nice story about how plans to make off with some found loot go awry.

Notice that I don't have any Bookshelf/Tags like "suspense," "thriller," or "painful"? That's because I Don't. Like. This. Kind. Of. Book. Well, every now and then I get out of my comfort zone and don't regret it--Beat the Reaper is a perfect example. But I think what redeemed BTR, despite its unpleasant heart-poundingness, was that it had a sly sense of humor. A Simple Plan has NO humor that I could find. My husband suggested I should read this because it was a prime specimen of a great first novel. I read it because my husband is really smart and I needed to rise to the challenge. But I must say, I dreaded reading this every night before bed. Such violence from such ordinary people, and then mountains of regret, all because they were greedy. Gross. Plus I just knew as soon as Mary Beth the dog was introduced that he (yes, it's a male dog) was going to suffer too, and god knows I can't take that. Anyway, for all you fans of this book, I'm sorry for the 1-star review. I realize it is a riveting story if you go for this sort of thing, but that star indicates "didn't like it," and that's the truth. Now I must go read Babe to cleanse my palate.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Hank and Jacob Mitchell and Jacob's friend Lloyd find a crashed plane in the woods. The pilot is dead but he has a duffel bag with 4.4 million dollars in it. The three men agree to sit on the money until they're sure no one is looking for it. But can they keep their mouthes shut? And what will happen when someone talks? 
 A Simple Plan is the story of three men in a difficult situation that quickly escalates into violence. The underlying theme seems to be how one lie inevitably leads to one more. 
 The main characters are fairly complex. Hank wants to protect his brother but also wants the money. Jacob wants to buy back his parents' farm with the money but he also wants to please his brother. Lloyd needs the money to pay back some gambling debts and can't wait six months. See where this is going? 
 Once things start going off the rails, they continue going off the rails for the rest of the book. The first murder is just the tip of the bloody iceberg. How much killing does it take to cover up one murder? Quite a few, it turns out. 
 Scott Smith's writing packs quite a punch. It's a cut above most thrillers and really makes me wish he wrote more than just this and The Ruins. Much like the Ruins, I wasn't sure how any of the characters would live much longer at the 50% mark. 
 The series of revelations near the end spell out the book's message: Crime doesn't pay. If I ever find a bag of money in the woods and I have people with me, we're turning it in to the cops. Alone, I could probably handle it... 
 Four out of five stars. Where's the next book, Smith?

Midwestern morality porn, where bad things happen to people who behave badly. When bad things happen to them, they change from archttypes of American homey goodness to more unpleasant folk; character steps match plot naughtiness. Dull, preachy, pointless.

book_b.title: The Christmas Train
book_b.user_review:
Book on CD read by Tim Matheson 
 2.5** 
 Former war correspondent turned magazine features writer Tom Langdon is taking the train from Washington DC to Los Angeles to spend Christmas with his girlfriend. He's also researching an article on modern-day train travel. Having in mind the spacious compartments of classic movies, he's in for a rude awakening, but he certainly finds plenty of interesting characters to profile, including a young couple planning to wed on the train, a big-name movie producer, a Bohemian fortune teller, a retired priest, and a woman who is such a frequent passenger everyone knows her. There is also a thief aboard. 
 I'd never read anything by Baldacci before and somehow thought of him as a writer of "legal thrillers" so I was surprised to find this holiday romance with a little bit of mystery involved. I was quickly drawn into the story. I loved Regina and Roxanne, the two women Amtrak employees who showed such an interest in their passengers, though I thought several of the other characters were little more than caricatures. I had figured out who the thief was fairly early and this part of the story seemed really incidental to the central romance, so I'm not sure why Baldacci even included it. For the genre, it was fairly entertaining, but the resolution of the central conflict was just too over the top for me. The novel lost a half star with that. 
 Tim Mathewson does a fine job performing the audio book. He is a gifted voice artist and had many different voices for the big cast of characters. The audio also includes sound effects of train whistles and the clackity clack of rail cars over the rails, as well as some seasonal music. Usually this kind of embellishment irritates me, but it really added to the atmosphere of this story.

sample_reviews.review_text: nice love story with a few twists and railway turns. I'll reread this one around christmas just to make me feel warm and fuzzy again.

So if that's what you're looking for, this is probably a good novel for you. If not, you'll find the characters one-dimensional & the ending not that surprising. The one good thing I did take from this book is a desire to ride a train for a long period of time.

2.5 stars 
 The premise is super schlocky but it's the sort of thing I might have loved under other circumstances. 
 Firstly, Lara Jean is very young for her age. Sixteen, but you'd think she was fourteen at best. This is understandable, because she's a homebody and close to her family, so she's been sheltered from both dysfunction and typical teenage mischief. However, it becomes grating when she's constantly crying over everything or when she's shocked that, yes, people in long term relationships have sex. Before marriage even! 
 Secondly, none of the potential love interests struck me as both appropriate and likeable. There's a certain ick factor with Josh, as he's her sister's very recent ex, and he and Lara Jean spent years acting like siblings. Peter I just didn't like. He seems like a jerk and it just isn't a ship I'll sail on. 
 Thirdly, there are quite a few distinctly punchable tertiary characters. Lara Jean's best friend Kris (sp?) Seemed both bratty and disrespectful, and not a very good friend at all. Peter's ex was such a bitter cliche I just couldn't deal with her. The little sister, Kitty, is plainly at least a touch spoiled, though she may be salvageable with maturity. 
 Also, not plot relevant but bothersome, we learn that the dad (a gynecologist) let his eldest daughter go to college in a foreign country without having discussed sex or birth control. That is a massive freaking oversight dude.
"Boys care more about their reputation than yours. You've just gotta hold your head up and act like you don't give a shit."

I loved Jenny Han's SUMMER series and so when I heard that Han was coming out with a new book, I got really excited. This book was one of my most anticipated contemporary picks for 2014 and I was psyched to find out what happened to Lara Jean and her letters. 
 Here's the thing. 
 This book isn't about the letters. Well, it is, but in a lot of ways it isn't at all. It's more about Lara Jean's rekindled romance and relationships with the boys who receive her letters. I would say about 98% of the book isn't really about the letters at all. 
 Nevertheless, I was determined to like this book. I continued on long after the letters were all sent out. Another thing here is that it's not really any big mystery who could've possibly sent out the letters. There's two possible people, and Lara Jean is genuinely shocked when she finds out it's one of the two people who could've sent the letters out. 
 There are five letters in total. Two of them end up not making any significance at all, and out of the remaining three, they all matter. Except two of them end up as love interests and the one left over ends up as a friend type because he's gay, which is clear but Lara Jean refuses to accept for a long time until she receives the confession face-to-face. So let's talk about the two love interests, shall we? 
 The real plot to this story is made up of a half-formed 
 love triangle 
 between Lara Jean, Peter and Lara Jean's older sister's boyfriend, Josh. Oh yes, and this crushing-on-older-sister's-boyfriend thing has been going on for quite a while. 
 [caption id="" align="alignnone" width="500"][image error] Uh yeah, excuse me for a second. This repeated storyline is making me sick.[/caption] 
 Lara Jean starts fake-dating Peter to try and get rid of Josh, because she doesn't want Josh to love her because he's her older sister's boyfriend and Peter is into this deal because he wants to make his recently-turned ex girlfriend jealous. That's as far as I'm going to go with this storyline so I don't give away spoilers, but you get the gist of the plot. This is really all there is to it, folks. 
 Oh yes, but I forgot to tell you about the ending. Don't worry, there's no spoilers here because THERE IS NOTHING TO TELL. 
 The ending is completely unresolved. There's no cliffhanger, no sense of closure, nothing. And this is a series. 
 [image error] 
 This ending gives me nothing. I don't feel excited at all to read the next book, or the book after that, or whatever comes out of this series. Part of this has to do with Lara Jean herself and the relationships she has with other people. 
 Lara Jean herself is at times childish, at times irritating, at times silly, at times too grown up and a lot of the time immature. Sometimes she sounds like a five year old, at other times it's like she's twenty. She never speaks as her age. Maybe this is due to her sisters, but I'm not convinced. There's nothing that I loved about her. She consistently disappointed me and created a train wreck wherever she went, always needing people to save her. 
 Then there's how she is with her family. We don't really see much of Lara Jean's dad in this book and her mom is dead. Margot (her older sister) spends most of her character portrayal through emails, phone calls and Skype chats since she's going to college abroad. Margot basically takes care of the family, especially their father. However, Margot's personality is incredibly frustrating. Her sisters and family depend on her, and yet she's selfish and doesn't see past what's right in front of her. She stabs Lara Jean in the back because of something that was Margot's fault to begin with. 
 Then there's the little one, Kitty. She's the only Song sister I actually liked, even though her choices toward the end frustrated me a little bit. Kitty's the relief of this story. She's funny and snarky, everything that I had hoped that Lara Jean would be. She also has a good dynamic with Peter as he gives her and Lara Jean rides to school since Margot's car (which Lara Jean borrowed) is in the shop (due to Lara Jean's stupidity). 
 Now on the boys. 
 Josh is invisible for half the book. The other half he's either professing his love to Margot or Lara Jean. 
 On the outside, I would've loved him staying a friend figure, but when you really get to know him, he and Lara Jean are made for each other. Or him and Margot. Whatever way he ends up going (WE DON'T KNOW BECAUSE THERE'S NO CLOSURE) he'll find a person just as insufferable as him. 
 Then Peter. The jerk of it all. There's no love between him and Lara Jean, they just think there is. No matter what, he's got to make up his mind, because while he's supposedly falling in love with Lara Jean, he also still loves his ex girlfriend. 
 Ugh. 
 I thought that this book would blow me away, but apparently not. If you're looking for something with this style, I would recommend Jenny Han's other books, her Summer Series or The Art of Lainey by Paula Stokes, which is an awesome summer read as well and much better written than this book. 2 stars.

reference_books.title: The Couple Next Door
reference_books.review_text: I'm sure Shari Lapena will become a great mystery author. She knows how to properly set up a suspenseful narrative, and that did keep me going to the end of the book, but it's repetitive, the characters are wooden, and some of the paragraphs (even the ones that are two sentences long) are in desperate need of editing. I like the idea of entering each character's head to find out their personal motivations, but sometimes it was an excuse to remind the reader the very questions you were asking a page ago. I find this sloppy. The sloppiest example is that a character is holding a knife in one scene and four times in one page, the other character thinks "why does she have a knife??? I should get that knife away from her." OK. Show don't tell.

reference_books.title: The Martian
reference_books.review_text: About as interesting as reading the Armageddon screenplay. Don't get me wrong, it moves fast, and has its moments. The jokes and little asides are well-timed but become tedious (they always appear at the end of a chapter, are about 70s TV, and just aren't worth the wait). It also felt like there was a lack of research and Weir dangled that lack of research in front of your face: "let me explain to the layman how this fictional device from NASA works..." (you made it up. Don't act like I wouldn't understand it.) "according to my boring math...." (it's boring because it's arithmetic. What would make it less boring is if you actually explained it. Then I'd find this part realistic). I felt like I was being talked down to while watching an action movie. An action movie with the same dialogue repeated every scene. Skip it.

 Pertama-tama, harus saya akui Dan Brown memang pengarang yang cerdas dalam membelokkan arah dan tujuan kisah ini. Saya tidak menduga akan begitu plotnya. Having read a couple of Robin Benway novels before and quite enjoying them, I was enthusiastic about the prospect of reading Emmy & Oliver. Unfortunately, the reading experience did not end up being quite what I expected. This is my attempt to explain why. 
 Emmy and Oliver have known each other since the day they were born. Growing up, Emmy had always realied on the fact that Oliver was there for her, and vice versa. When Oliver suddenly disappeared, everything changed. Emmy lost her best friend and her confidante, as well as any remeblance of freedom, which became a problem the older she got. Her parents, shaken by Oliver's destiny, have since his disappearance kept her tightly close to home, just to make sure that nothing similar happens to her. 
 Ten years since seeing Oliver the last time, Emmy is given a new chance when Oliver comes back home. Confused by what has happened to him and the way he is supposed to feel about his father and what he did, Oliver is not the same little boy anymore. He has grown up, whereas to Emmy it feels like not much has changed in the past ten years; her parents are still in control, still treating her like Oliver had just disappeared. 
 Connecting with Oliver does not come easily, but when it happens, Emmy feels like she has gotten her best friend back. What remains for her to do is to show to her parents that she has grown up, that Oliver is safe now and that it is time for them to loosen their grip and let Emmy make her own decisions. 
 The main thing that bugged me about this book is the way that it discusses parents, almost like they are just this caricature of overbearing paranoids. Emmy clearly loves her parents, but at the same time she talks about them like she has nothing in common with them, which in my opinion, is not true at all (I definitely was able to notice features of both her father and mother in her). For most of the book, her parents just seem like this "evil" entitity that do not let her to do what she wants, where in fact they just care about her. I feel like Benway intents the reader to identify with Emmy and her struggles, but I continually felt like I wanted to side with the parents and hoped for better representation of them - a representation that does not rely so heavily on the stereotypical "my mother is a ballbuster" trope and would have shown them more as individuals, not just caricatures of causes for teenage angst. I get the whole "my parents don't get me" argument - I think everyone who has been a teenager gets that - but in my opinion, it was taken way too far with this one. Or maybe I just miss my mother so much now that I am not a teenager anymore and she does not daily tell me what to do, that I just did not understand why Emmy complains all the time. 
 The premise of getting someone important back to your life after a long time of confusion sounded interesting to me, but unfortunately much of the discovery that could have been done on this topic was overshadowed by the whole teenagers-parents conflict. While reading, I love the feeling I get when I feel like I know the characters and can in some level identify with them, or at least understand their actions. Unfortunately, with Emmy & Oliver, I felt like I did not really connect with any of the characters and as I kept reading, I started to feel like I did not even want to connect with them. Oliver definitely is the most sympathetic of the characters in this novel, but I hope that Benway would have taken more time to his thoughts and his feelings. But since the novel is from the point of view of Emmy, we only get to experience Oliver's struggles through her eyes and unfortunately Emmy's point of view is most of the time clouded by her own problems and struggles. 
 To be completely honest, at around 60 % into this book, I almost gave up. I just did not see myself finishing this one and started to think about the next book I would read. But since I had accepted this book for review, I felt like it was my possibility to finish with the book before making any sort of judgements about it. Yes, now that I am writing this, there is a part of me that wishes that I would just have given up and spent the time reading something else, but on the other hand, now I can at least justifiably express why I did not like this book in a form of this review.

Emmy & Oliver is a book that is really hard for me to review. I think I might have suffered from skyscraper syndrome when it comes to this one. I had seen far too many glowing reviews, every one praising this book and it's adorable romance, and this made my expectations skyrocket. It's not that I ended up crushingly disappointed by the story, I just didn't end up loving it anywhere near as much as I thought that I would. 
 This story centres around Emmy and Oliver - hence the title - and their growing relationship, after Oliver returns ten years after being kidnapped by his father. Now the story is adorable and cute, and everything that most people would be looking for. But it didn't completely work for me, and I was disappointed that I couldn't just love this as much as everyone else seems to. 
 My main issue with the book came down to the whole kidnap storyline with Oliver and his father. My issue wasn't that the storyline was unrealistic, it's something that happens a lot and you would frequently see similar storylines on the news. No, my issue was more with how long it took for Oliver to be found. He's living in a world with the internet, where people google absolutely everything. But he doesn't think to try and google his mother, the woman he believes abandoned him. And I also have to forgive eight-year-old Oliver for being so dumb and not questioning why, if his mother was the one who left, why he and his father were the ones moving and taking new names. I mean, maybe I am surrounded by ridiculously intelligent children, but any eight-year-old I know would question that. The obvious answer for why Oliver didn't google his mother is the fact that then we would lose a big part of the plot to this story. But still... I am bothered. 
 The adorable, cutesy romance aspect to the story seems to be what so many people loved about it. And, yes, it's adorable and super cute, but it felt like it was just too cute for me. It felt almost too easy for these two characters to fall back into one another after all they had been through, and the fact they were just children when Oliver left. 
 Maybe I'm just turning into a horribly negative human being. 
 Or that I was not in the right frame of mind for a cute, teen romance when I read this. That's probably ridiculously close to the truth, I remember being rather stressed out about other things when I was reading this particular book. I feel like maybe, if I read this when in a much better and happier frame of mind, this could be a book I love. 
 Emmy's family were also utterly ridiculous and frustrated the hell out of me as I as reading this. A small part of me understands them and why they are so overprotective and overbearing. But then there's a bigger, much louder part of me that's screaming at my book in utter frustration and confusion. It's not like Oliver was snatched away in the middle of the night, by some evil, murderer/paedophile. He was taken by his own father, who was afraid of losing custody and went the stupid route when coming up with a way to deal with it. I know it was hard for them to watch their friend struggle with losing their child. But I still don't understand the way it made them act toward their own daughter. They were afraid of everything and anything and were smothering their own child because of it. I felt they were utterly ridiculous and Emmy needed to grow up and take control of her own life. I honestly wouldn't have been able to handle those two as my parents, Emmy clearly has way more self control than I do. They were making Emmy live her whole life for them, which is a shitty thing to do as parents. 
 3/5 Butterflies 
 I didn't have any strong negative feelings towards this book, and it's not that I didn't like the book either. It is a very cute contemporary read, with an adorable romance that I am sure many will love. But I had read a lot of better contemporaries around the same time, and this one just didn't manage to impress me in quite the same way. I think the gushing reviews I read and my high expectations didn't help either, it made it almost impossible for this book to live up them. But I honestly would recomend it if you want a cute contemporary, you won't be disappointed.

Kidnapping, missing best friend and potential romance between these two best friends but halted because of the said kidnapping? One is to expect that it'll be a heavy, dramatic sort of story. Well, wrong. I was wrong. It isn't like that at all. Oh, but I was very glad that it wasn't. I liked that premise wasn't as predictable as I thought it'll be (or dramatic for that matter). Emmy and Oliver by Robin Benway presented a story that it might sound intense at first but it came to me as a very light read. 
 Emmy and Oliver were besties. In fact they live in the same neighborhood, born at the same day, in the same hospital. Everything was going well until Oliver was hauled inside truck and drove him miles away from her. But the confusing part of it was that the one that took Oliver was his own father. Years had passed and Oliver returned, along with him was his experience with his father and the lie he grew up with. But it wasn't just about him; because him leaving the town scarred many people, including Emmy and her relationship with her parents. 
 He was kidnapped by his own father might elicit some reactions already. You know what, he might look like the antagonist of the story, but Oliver's father wasn't all what people had judged him. Sure, his reasons and judgment weren't appropriate. But I can firmly say that I can understand his reasons as why he did what he did. In fact, Oliver's memories with his father weren't bad at all. He told some fond memories he had with him. In a way, the word kidnapping was overly dramatic term for me (although what he did is actually that) when in fact he was just scared man longing for his son. 
 Now, let's go to the romance/friends' angle. Does absence makes the heart go fonder? Personally, no; especially if they were separated at such a young age. I just don't believe a romance in such a short span of time was possible; when ten years had passed and lot of things can/will change a person. The transition wasn't too favorable for my taste so I hardly connected with the romance. That said, when Emmy decided on things, she was brave enough to stand her ground. In some stories I've read they all go for love first, the rest next. But if you think about it, love should also mean understanding & cooperation. Well, at least on me. 
 I understand Emmy especially on how her parents treated her like fragile item. But I do know why they acted that way. Oliver's situation added that anxiety/fear for them. But know what, just because you made the decision doesn't mean it's automatically right or it will go well. Or when parents' decide for you it's not always mean removing your freedom to choose. But there's still that sense of individuality to be able to decide on your own. Emmy didn't want to be inside that bubble wrap anymore. This is the aspect I liked about the story. 
 It's weird for me that title of the story is Emmy and Oliver when it felt like it wasn't significantly just about them. But to me it's more Emmy, Oliver and their parents (but that's mouthful though, haha). Because I think they played such crucial part in their stories. 
 Originally published at The Aeropapers.

After ten years Oliver is home. Everyone must adjust to his return and learn what it really means. Oliver is this great kid that a really crappy thing happened to and you can't help but love him. Emmy's whole life has been affected by Oliver's kidnapping and now that he's back she find a new way to live her life. Every charterer in this book is great, and you can't help but feel each and everyone of them.
