Another excellent Kasie West contemporary romance that I devoured in one setting (after a very long and trying day no less). Oh the banter is sooooo perfect.

***3.5/5 Stars*** 
 The Distance Between Us was such a cute story, yet I struggled with quite a few things. So here are some of my thoughts........ 
 An adorable storyline - 
 He laughs a little. "You live above a porcelain-doll store; your best friend lives in a cemetery. You've pretty much grown up surrounded by creepy things. Is there anything you're afraid of?" 
 You. 
 Carmen and Xander both wanted to figure out what they were going to be when they're older, since they're both slated to take over their family's businesses. They created these career days that I loved. And those moments always led to scenes where my emotions were the strongest. But even before that I loved watching their tentative friendship form. It was such a cute story, and it was so easy to devour. 
 A girl I wasn't the hugest fan of - 
 Before him, I thought I knew if a guy was flirting with me. But he says things so subtly, so smoothly, that it's hard to tell if it's purposeful or if he's just playing along with my jokes. 
 So confession time, I'm awful at getting sarcastic humor at times. My whole family laughed at me, during our weekly Sunday dinner last weekend, because I didn't catch my Aunt being sarcastic. Multiple times in her texts. So my sporadic ineptitude towards sarcasm may have played a huge role in why I never clicked or connected with Caymen. You see, Caymen's like the queen of sarcasm and dry humor all rolled into one person. I tried again and again to connect and get her humor, yet I continually failed at it. It was so frustrating. 
 A boy that I was obsessed about- 
 He lowers the visor in front of me and flips open the mirror. "You still have paint on your face." He runs a finger down my cheek, tracing the paint line. My breath catches for a moment when his finger seems to linger a second longer than necessary. 
 Xander MADE this book for me. He was thoughtful, caring, and compassionate towards Caymen. He was also persistent, charming and I loved how he initiated the friendship between the two of them. And that he kept coming around and helped the friendship grow. He was such a good guy, and it was impossible to not fall hard for him. 
 Lack of communication - 
 I didn't want my mom to have bad feelings toward him. Somehow the guy had managed to climb out of the box full of people I had already labeled off-limits with a permanent marker and he'd become different. And now, much to my irritation, I feel some form of loyalty to Xander Spence. 
 I had to change this immediately. 
 So the two main conflicts in this book stemmed from lack of communication. And it wasn't like the people involved in the lack of communication weren't around one another countless times. They didn't have missed opportunities to ask questions. It was just never done, and the questions were never asked. Unfortunately that can be a book pet peeve of mine depending upon how it's handled, and I struggled with how both of the situations were handled. 
 A HFN that didn't sit well with me - 
 This is the second book I've read by this author where that last page didn't leave me feeling all smiley and happy. Sometimes I struggle with HFN (Happily For Nows) because there's still so much up in the air. And in this case there were still sooooo many things that needed to be worked out, figured out or I just wanted to know what happened. I wish there were a few more chapters explaining what happened so that way some of the outstanding issues would be resolved. 
 So now I'm left wondering if maybe this author and I aren't that great of a fit after all? Oh my gosh, I just don't know. I loved Over the Fence, but The Fill-In Boyfriend had one of those HFN endings where I needed more. I still have PS I Like You sitting on my shelf and Pivot Point sitting in my Kindle, so I guess I'll find out if this author truly isn't a good fit for me after reading those two books. Here's hoping if you pick this up you'll enjoy it much more than I did!

Truth-loving persians love to dwell upon that oh-so-trivial skirmish fought near Marathon. Not really, but we really are dealing with Persians, particularly one: Ms. Marjane Satrapi, the author of the graphic novel Persepolis. 
 I first heard about Persepolis as an independent film some years back, and then it slipped completely from my mind. Fast forward to a week or so ago as I wandered aimlessly through a Barnes and Noble. I was looking for a book, the kind that you don't know that you're looking for until you see it, when I saw it. I suddenly remembered that spark of interest from years ago, bought the graphic novel and finished it in a day. 
 It was good you see. 
 Persepolis is a memoir of Satrapi's childhood in Iran before and during the Islamic Revolution. Historically, the title refers to the ancient capital of the Persian nation, which is modern day Iran. In skipping about the Internet, I was surprised to see that Iran had openly decried the film based on the graphic novel, although I can't say why I should have been. 
 I liked this story because it really makes the people and culture of Iran tangible to readers. Marjane is a vivacious, headstrong and intelligent girl who is just trying to make sense of life. She is passionate about her religion (as a child she wants to be a prophet), tender toward her country (like a good patriot) and rational in her quest to figure out why her secular lifestyle suddenly takes a turn toward a more zealous one. 
 What struck me also was how I had to be careful with my prejudices as a reader. For instance, in the beginning, Satrapi writes that the West, i.e. Great Britain and the U.S.A., were greedy meddlers in her country's history. She also writes that Iranians have suffered under a long list of dictators. My knee-jerk reaction as a Westerner was to say, "Nooo! You're wrong!" But my rational self quickly surpressed that thought. As Americans, I don't think its often that we learn non-Western perspectives of history, and who is to say they aren't "true"? Satrapi writes her memories of Tehran as a diverse center of thought. Her parents are liberal intellectuals. Her father is a loving husband and family man who respects the independent natures of his wife and child. Her mother is a strongminded individual who is not afraid to stand up and speak. Satrapi does hint that her family did have a very close connection to influential politicians, which could explain this nonstereotypical Middle-Eastern family lifestyle, similar to Malika Oufkir in Le Prisonniere. However, the simple illustrations and clear story really sweep you up in the emotion and chaos that takes over the family and country.

As an Iranian growing up in a family with political background, a communist sister (Parvaneh Emam) executed at the age of 22 and, having read many books on the history of Iran's struggle for freedom and justice, I see that the book talks about the true Tudeh Party members, real communists as they were, who fought hard and sacrificed their lives for equity, freedom and justice. 
 What I like about Persepolis is that it leaves out the back-stabbing counter-revolutionaries of today's Tudeh Party who are very active in Iran and abroad and have been able to infiltrate literary organizations and political movements to destroy them from within. 
 This group of Tudeh members are also very busy writing the history of Iran and among them I can refer to "Rosewater", which is full of lies and simply a propaganda tool for today's Tudeh Party. Of course by giving the example of Rosewater, I do not wish to promote that book, although those books are also useful to show the real identity of that Party. 
 I highly recommend Persepolis to my Goodreads friends and I will be happy to participate in any discussions.

I found this book in my classroom and was instantly taken with it. Satrapi tells an internationally relevant story with all the wonderful hallmarks of memoir and graphic novels. I read it while my students read and then I ran to the library for the sequel.

3.5 stars. I can see why this graphic novel has gained so much popularity -- for example, I would not have read a prose memoir with this same storyline. The cartoons bring levity to the dense content (there are a lot of cultural facts to pick up along the way), while the seriousness of the text brings meaning to the cartoons. It's a good balance, though be aware that there's a lot of heartbreaking content in the narrative. 
 I would recommend this book to anyone interested in Iran or the Middle East. If that's not your interest then don't be afraid to skip this one.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Imagine you're a 8-year-old girl and a lecherous older man reaches toward you, intending -- well, nothing good. You lash out at him and he falls dead at your feet. From that moment, you're feared and shunned for your special talent: killing. 
 Thus is the life of Katsa, niece to the king of Sundoria. She is a Graceling, a child born strongly talented in at least one way. Gracelings are easily identified by their eyes, which are two different colors. Easily identified, in Katsa's case, means easily ostracized. It doesn't help that her uncle uses her to abuse and frighten those who cross him. 
 With few friends to call her own, the appearance of Po, a Lienid prince and a fellow Graceling, shakes her world. He's gifted at fighting, which means he can hold his own against her. Somewhat. But Po's gift goes beyond mere fighting, and Katsa's discovery of its true nature -- and her decision to accompany him on his investigation of his grandfather's kidnapping -- changes both their lives. 
 "Graceling" stuck with me. Katsa starts as a wounded, half-formed character who is so frustrated by her life that she can't even put it into words. She hates what her uncle asks her to do and the lack of control she has over her own life, but she sees no way out: 
 "Who are these fools who continue to resist Randa's will? Haven't they heard the stories? Don't they know he'll send me?" 
 "Isn't it in your power to refuse?" Po asked. "How can anyone force you to do anything?" 
 The fire burst into her throat and choked her. "He is the king. And you're a fool, too, if you think I have choice in the matter." 
 "But you do have choice. He's not the one who makes you savage. You make yourself savage, when you bend yourself to his will." 
 With the slightest nudge from her friends, she breaks away from her uncle's control and blossoms into a pretty kick-ass heroine. It takes the better part of the book, as it should. All the while, Cashore avoids the temptation of letting Katsa slip into more traditional female roles -- she doesn't come to relish pretty clothes or getting dolled up, nor does she relent on her determination to remain unmarried. It's refreshingly true to her bone-deep and oft-repeated desire to never let another person dictate her fate. 
 Some stories look like they'll be a light, entertaining read and leave you considering, seriously, what it would be like to walk in their characters' shoes. "Graceling," to my surprise, was one of those books. 
 "Graceling" is listed as a young adult/children's novel, but the writing and the handling of some pretty mature themes make it an enjoyable read for adults. Teenagers/children reading this book will encounter at least one obvious, but not graphic, sex scene.

HOWEVER...I found the ending to not only be very lame, but extremely irritating in pushing the ridiculous notion of mutual attraction/sex + friendship - commitment = true love. The whole concept of "being tied down to one man is like slavery" was so overdone in this book, and it was hard for me to enjoy the ending when I just felt like it was part of the author's personal agenda.

reference_books.title: The Beach House
reference_books.review_text:
I read this book to punish myself. 
 Next time, I'll just wear a hair shirt.

reference_books.title: Batman: The Killing Joke
reference_books.review_text:
This book is so good that even though I hate Batman I fell in love with this little piece. 
 Let's be honest, no one reads Batman because they want visionary Blake-esque poetry or the historical grim-satire of Gore Vidal. You read Batman because you want some pulp-style action, some crazy villains, a plot twist, and some weird stuff to happen. 
 Alan Moore provides all of this in "The Killing Joke". In fact, he provides so much of it for you that you almost need an enema to remove it from the deepest crevices of your colon. He flips the dichotomy on its head. 
 Without revealing spoilers, I will say this: If this book had been about just some random Raymond Chandler-detective and his long-running criminal nemesis instead of Batman and Joker, I would not have enjoyed it an ounce less. This is a work of art with macabre beauty in every inch of the plot.

reference_books.title: Interview with the Vampire (The Vampire Chronicles, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
God, did I ever want this to be good. I'm not big on vampire media but I love the sleek, sexy decadence of Rice-style vampires and I wanted that desperately. In fact, I think that I was biased in the first place against this book because I already had an idea of what I wanted: a vampire novel written by Oscar Wilde. 
 The first third of the book is, in my opinion, phenomenal. It is romantic (which overtakes technique too often in my reading) and beautiful and languishes tantalizingly over pale, thin, doomed things that beckon teen-goth-bedroom-walls and androgynous Goodreads book reviewers's loins. Setting the conversion of a vampire in antebellum New Orleans was a master stroke of a setting that I would never have considered. 
 Unfortunately Rice runs out of steam very quickly after the sensual eroticism of the platonic relationship between Louis and Lestat cools. In truth the novel turns trite so quickly after the peaks of their subtext 'relationship' that I often wondered if Rice was originally just writing fanfiction and knocked out the rest of the plot lazily after the juicy bits ended and her interest waned. Things happen that don't inspire you to care, characters appear who are forgettable at best, and the ending barely manages to save what little there is to save by being about as ambigious as a Predator movie.

reference_books.title: The Shining Girls
reference_books.review_text:
I really wanted to like this novel because it carried themes that I enjoyed and the plot was interesting. 
 But it wasn't good at all. 
 It was boring, most of all, which I found to be a little annoying since the plot was interesting. I was a third of the way through the book before I realised that the story wasn't what was lacking, it was the storytelling. This was made worse by the style. 
 The style is hard to describe. Imagine, for example, you have a bunch of large wooden blocks, all of which are in a variety of pointy or edged shapes, as well as a bucket that is round. Now imagine that you pour all of those blocks willy-nilly into the bucket. Of course they won't fit right, they'll pile on top of each other at weird angles, they'll clatter and hold each other up with strange angles, they'll leave large gaps that could be better used, and they'll probably stick out of the bin to take up unnecessary space that could've been reduced by simply arranging them carefully. 
 That's the style of writing you encounter in this book. 
 I will note, though, that Beukes became 100% better with her next novel, Broken Monsters. So much so, in fact, that I wondered if I was reading the same author.

book_a.title: Inferno (Robert Langdon, #4)
book_a.user_review: This is the book that made me decide that Dan Brown should be tried at the Hague for crimes against humanity.

sample_reviews.review_text: I have mixed feelings about this one. It's not as intriguing as Brown's previous works but I still managed to find myself mesmerized by the beauty of the Italian skyline as described by Brown's extensive historical vocabulary. Another plus is the philosophical standpoint (a sentiment which I deeply share) with regards to overpopulation and management of ecological resources. Humans have become so egoistic that nature suffers in our wake of population explosion. The ending is a little divergent from the usual resolution in other thrillers, but illustrates something thought-provoking that needs to be addressed in the real world.

A fun read! I now know more about Dante's Inferno than I thought I ever would...and there were great descriptions of classical Italian art and cities, etc. This book was a typical exciting Dan Brown, with many adventures, fun pursuits and escapes, and a some surprising twists along the way. A very entertaining read!

It isn't that the story isn't interesting; it is. It isn't that the plot doesn't move along well; it does. It's just that Robert Langdon is the Ken doll of literary characters, good-looking on the surface but bland and without genitalia. It did seem that Dan Brown gave a little more detail to his main character but if an author is going to have a continuing character at all shouldn't that character be well-detailed? All I find really distinguishing about Rober Langdon is his attachment to his Harris Tweed jacket and his Mickey Mouse watch.He may have claustrophobia but it doesn't play a part in the plot so it just seems thrown in there.
So not impressed with this book. I thought he was a better writer than what I found here.

At chapter 5: 
 Not off to a great start... I can usually get past Dan Brown's writing because he's so good at high-intensity, page-turner storytelling and peppering in history and facts. But starting with a dream sequence? Packing THIS many cliches into each paragraph? An incredibly unrealistic exchange with a hot nurse? Where was his editor on these? Maybe my standards have changed, but I don't know if I can make it through this one. Hubby and I have read other Dan Brown novels together, but I think he's dropping out and leaving me to fend for myself. I'll give it a few more chapters, but I might be switching over to the original "Inferno." 
 *Update* 
 At Chapter 49: 
 Not gonna finish this one. I tried, I really did. I encouraged hubby to keep reading, and he's enjoying it now, but I've gotten bored and can't stay focused on it. Unfortunately, I think the Dan Brown formula is just too stale for me at this point. I've been able to predict every scene so far, and that's no fun. And DB's social commentary started to get old (really, most 20-somethings are not obsessed with Googling themselves). 
 Also, DB, why not add some depth to Langdon? By book 4, I was hoping he'd be more than just a claustrophobic know-it-all with a Mickey Mouse watch. Haven't all these life-threatening adventures affected him at all? At this point, it seems more likely that he'd be a paranoid PTSD patient, unable to hold a job and dragging his therapist through a bunch of imaginary adventures, than a stable professor off to save the world from anther conspiracy. Poor guy. 
 That being said, if you like Dan Brown and just can't get enough of high-intensity chase scenes through art museums, this book is for you.

Boring. 
 Dan Brown - you need a new formula.

Good quick read but it is pretty formulaic, especially for Brown. He continues to put the existence of humanity at stake in every novel and in every novel there is a nicely wrapped ending with a bow. It was a good read, but NOT my favorite.

Never having before read a Dan Brown novel, I really felt that it was time I got round to filling this little void in my reading landscape, especially as he has such a huge fan base; then along came a copy of Inferno. 
 Sadly, it turned out to not really be my thing. I found the writing too mechanical; I do like a nice, rythmic flow to whatever I am reading and Inferno does not have that. I found that I developed little empathy for the lead character, Robert Langdon, who never made any kind of meaningful connection with me. On the other hand, I did find one of the other characters, Sienna Brooks, a far more engaging individual and certainly more intriguing. 
 I assume the author spent a good deal of time researching the fabulous cities that provide the backdrop for this story and he makes considerable use of what he learnt. The trouble is, there is too much of this, with repeatedly long, detailed, and sometimes uninspiring passages describing individual buildings or specific aspects of a room. 
 For me, the best parts of the book are those where Brown simply gets on with the action, at which point things move along quite nicely.

Oh dear why was I surprised? 
 The action picks up in Florence where Robert Langdon has just woken up with amnesia, what happens next can only be ripped from scenes of a Hollywood action blockbuster as he and the latest femme rush across the city in a murder mystery plot, all revolving around the text of Dante's Inferno. 
 Things take a drastic turn for the ridiculous as the novel continues and finishes in a way so unbelievable that I was actually speechless for a moment. Just think of a magician waving their hand over your eyes and murmer, 'Science!'.

I give 2stars for its pertinent subject-population explosion and a diabolically scary solution. Book is more a travel brochure for Venice etc than a thriller. Pace is sluggish/action mediocre. There are no hair pin bends that wake you from reverie or keep your nerves crackling. I finished the book, well, coz I always do (barring 'The Satanic Verses' that I couldn't go beyond 8-9pgs). I could pre guess the turns that the storyline was going to take-hence found the book to be 'mediocre'. Boring.

book_b.title: Altered Carbon (Takeshi Kovacs, #1)
book_b.user_review:
Hardboiled cyberpunk detective novel. Military past. Old enemies. Scandal. Intrigue. Romance. Betrayal. Murder. Technological advancements with judicial, practical, moral, and philosophical ramifications. The works. 
 Done pretty well and written in an approachable style. There are original terms but no overflow of off-the-cuff, try-hard fiction jargon. Characters are fleshed out and varied though, at times, it becomes difficult to remember the characters that reappear after 60 pages. Particularly interesting plot with a somewhat predictable but satisfying ending. 
 Overall a book that I enjoyed reading, which is high praise.

sample_reviews.review_text:
The basic idea of Altered Carbon is a world where you can live "forever" by being put into different sleeves, magnifying the disparity between rich and poor now that humanity is spread throughout the universe. Some people are even hired and their sleeves are modified or purchased by their employers or governments. Takeshi is hired by a wealthy meth (short for Methuselah) who hires him by force/obligation to solve what he thinks is his murder. It is Takeshi's first trip to earth and there are a few cultural adjustments that he had to make. 
 I read the first half of the book and skimmed the rest. The ideas were good but I got tired of reading about unimportant details. The author spends an inordinate amount of time talking about gun selection, sleeping arrangements, and bodily functions and it makes what could be an interesting story into something tedious. I would forgive it by saying this style is not my thing, but I've found many post-human novels that I have really enjoyed.

Dobra je ovo knjiga! Nije bravura od koje zastaje dah, ali je brza, hiper zabavna i vrlo jednostavno pisana. Ideja ,,digitalnog ugljika" je odlicna, inovativna i u smecu kvazi inovativnosti zaista osvjezavajuca. Ako shvatimo da je pisanje umjetnost prenosenja emocije na papir, onda Morgan ima mali problem jer prebacio je emociju samo na jednog lika, koji je bez emocija. Takeshi Kovacs je nabrijan, lud, bezkompromisan lik; bezobrazan i nikome se ne mice s puta (malo me i podsjeca na mog Callana Brennu, ali je Callan ipak malo senzibilniji i nervozniji :) ). 
 Ipak generalna zamjerka je velicina romana. Ovakvu knjigu punu tempa trebalo bi napisati sa 200+ strana ali nikako ne vise od 300, a ovo je romancina od 500, pa se ta brzina malo izgubi i ne trenutke postaje zamorna kao i zaplet kojega je dugo odlagao. 
 Ipak, vrlo plitko i zabavno da s radoscu ocekujem nastavke koje cu citati. I da, nije to SF u pravom smislu rijeci, vec detektivski maco tres, ali ovih dana mi to godi.

Great book! Similar to a Cyberpunk mystery style but with so much more. I have had several people tell me the book was good and now I understand why. 
 Morgan has a style of writing that takes you through time and you aren't even aware. The protagonist Takeshi Kovacs is a hard man to figure out but he seems to want to do the correct thing in the end. 
 I think anyone with interest in Science Fiction should definitely pick up this book.

I gave it two stars for the Raymond Chandler tribute, because that was fun, but really the Coen Brothers did that more entertainingly with the Big Lebowski. Also, Charles Sheffeld had a more interesting take on the on the various cultural and social permutations of a world in which people's consciousness could be digitalized, stored on computer and uploaded to new bodies in his book Tomorrow and Tomorrow. The extended life in this world of Richard Morgan's doesn't seem to offer any advantages and just results in a much more degraded mass of humanity. 
 Altered Carbon lacks the character development that is needed to maintain interest in a novel that's more than 500 pages long. The main character Takeshi, the Japanese ninja type character who is trapped in a white man's body in future San Francisco, now called "Bay City" doesn't seem remotely Japanese. He seems more like someone who used to like to slurp noodles in Japan Town. The sex scenes weren't convincing because the female characters were such stereotypes, and to be honest I skimmed them as well as the torture scenes. That's how I got through the whole 500 pages.
A gritty scifi detective story with one of the best antiheros I've ever encountered.

Storyline: 2/5 
 Characters: 2/5 
 Writing Style: 3/5 
 World: 4/5 
 --Below information added approximately one year after original reading-- 
 The technology was awesome. The book was surprisingly coherent as well. For me, the problem was that everything - the technology, the world, the characters - was pointed at and understood in context of the mystery. I'm really not a murder mystery fan. Nothing here changed my opinion about the subgenre. Mostly, I felt that the mystery was a wasted use of neat gadgets, a detailed culture, and an anti-hero. Few series have so decidedly turned me off at the first installment.

couldn't finish the bloody thing. The premises of the story are interesting, classical, rather than cliche, and the prose, while well south of excellent, is still very well done, well enough to be praised as, the best prose can be praised as, which is to say, involving. 
 Its shortcomings however, quickly become evident. 
 The main character, is meant perhaps to come off as "hardboiled" and dangerous, but I only ever empathized with him as an exhausted man instead, whose only true danger is the one he implies towards himself. 
 A bigger sin, on another hand, are the archetypes it eventually resorts to, masked as something new. Here a skeptical police lady, there a mysteriously murdered billionaire, and then comes the promenade of missing brothel girl and her caring prostitute sister, the random hot sex with a disgruntled housewife (which was so pornographic and squeaky, I swear I thought my mum would come into the room and give me a stern finger wagging), and all basic noir arch-littany that makes the sci fi frankly just feel like baggage. 
 And frankly, I called the big mystery reveal moments after the victim first presented himself. 
 Which is not to say there weren't the odd curveballs once in a while, but at the end, one questions the author's commitment to the story. 
 I couldn't finish the bloody thing. Maybe once I do, I'll edit this review, but frankly, I stopped halfway through, picked up a little Terry Pratchet instead and read that book, and then three more seemed more enticing and exciting than the idea of finishing one I was already more than halfway through. 
 It's always bad when you get upstaged like that, so alas, my rating must reflect that

The plot of the book was a good thriller, nothing special but interesting enough. 
 But what makes this book important is not the plot itself, but the characters. They present to you a future where Real Death and Death are different things and by doing so you find yourself questioning what it is to be human. Is it our bodies? Our conscious? can they be separated? If we lived something and don't remember it does that means it never happened?

The modern reader often encounters a problem with noir, sci-fi and other genre fiction written in the 40s and 50s. Mores on race and gender can come across as anywhere from awkward to offensive. This is part and parcel of reading a book from that era. One would hope for better from a contemporary author. Unfortunately, the depiction of women in this novel ranges from bald objectification to (one suspects) outright misogyny, as the author enthusiastically embraced this aspect of the genre. No more Morgan for me.

Altered Carbon has already been reviewed by everyone and their grandmother, so I won't bother to rehash the concept or storyline of this hard-boiled detective noir/cyberpunk hybrid tale set in the 25th century. It was tough to give an overall star rating (I settled on 4 stars, but I'm not sure if I can include this in my "favorites", since I liked some aspects of the book much more than others (a lot of people had that experience, it seems). I'll break it down as follows: 
 World-building (5 stars): This was excellent, as Morgan really explores the implications of what cheating death by transferring digitized identities to different "sleeves" (bodies) would be for a future society, especially in relation to homicide (called "Organic Damage"), and how those with power (the "Meths", short for Methuselahs) can abuse this advantage. When death is more of a setback, criminals and soldiers are more willing to take reckless risks, which makes for a steady stream of violent mayhem in the book. And the rights of identities held in virtuality are also fascinating, especially when someone is interrogated or tortured. I like the details that Morgan has taken the trouble to add, including a comprehensive set of future terms and expressions to describe things. That's what makes the world feel real, and he did great (why other authors don't bother is "another disk to spin"). 
 Characters (protagonist: 4 stars, supporting cast: 3 stars): Takeshi Kovacs is a sufficiently hard-boiled, cynical, world-weary Envoy (super spy/soldier/covert ops type) who is dragged unwillingly into the story. He is prone to extreme violence, but that's the world he has grown up in and that is what his line of work demands. But he tries on occasion to help others when possible. Still, his main motivations are revenge against the Meths who have put him in this mess. Other than Kovacs, however, the supporting cast members like the Bancrofts, Ortega, Trepp, Kadmin, Elliot, Kawahara, while serving to further the storyline, didn't resonate so much. And that despite a book length of 526 pages that takes place over just a few weeks. 
 Storyline (3 stars, way too complicated and meandering): Frankly, this book could have been great at around 350 pages, since there are long stretches when the plot wanders down various dark alleyways (both literally and figuratively) for reasons that are unclear. The world is already vividly described, but with so many side-stories I started to lose track of the main storyline, and the Bancrofts who initiated the story disappear for very long stretches. The motivations of Kawahara are also unclear to me. All the dots don't need explicit connections, but it seemed like a Jackson Pollock by the end of the story, with a prefunctory 20-page epilogue to explain "whodunit". 
 Overall, it's definitely a worthy read for anyone who likes cyberpunk and crime noir (as I do), but it could have been better. I do plan to read at some point the next two books, Broken Angels and Woken Furies, but I'll take a little break while the bodies are cleaned up and identities are put back on the "stack".

reference_books.title: The Story of the Lost Child (The Neapolitan Novels, #4)

reference_books.title: The Best of Adam Sharp

I kept reading way past the point where I wanted to stop, hoping for it all to come together. The author does a good job of letting you into the mind of Adam Sharp. reference_books.title: Tell the Wolves I'm Home
reference_books.review_text: The characters treat each other badly and yet supposedly love each other. Yes, that does happen in real life, but it is not what we aspire to. In this novel, a fourteen-year-old takes the brunt of everyone's emotional baggage and that is accepted even by her.

book_a.title: The Bookshop on the Corner
book_a.user_review:
I love Jenny Colgan! This newest book has all the usual lovely bits (I always feel rather British after emerging from her stories): flawed but loveable and plucky heroine who does her own rescuing, wonderful, but not perfect, romantic leads, and an immersion into a locale with a community of supporting characters. The Bookshop also has books, books, books! It's full of homage and references to books, both familiar and tantalizing new, plus a nod to The Little Paris Bookshop and Summer at the Little Beach Street Bakery. This was published in the UK as The Little Shop of Happily Ever After, a much better title. Thanks to Edelweiss for the digital ARC. 
 Now I have to find a copy of Up on the Rooftops!

sample_reviews.review_text:
Most disappointing. First of all, US publisher, shame on you for changing the title. This is not about a shop, but a van, and it never stays in a corner. 
 The characters are cardboard, everything is predictable. Reading is only a stop gap until real life happens, or so Colgan implies. Lots of books and authors are name dropped, and not all of them even real books. Good grief!!! 
 I read through courtship, pregnancy, new motherhood, divorce, re-marriage, widowhood- I'd say that's real life. Nina can't find solace in a book through melodramatic man problems? 
 The thing that made me angriest... the most raved about book in the novel is a "beloved children's classic" that touches everyone's lives is a FAKE. Up on the Rooftops does NOT exist!! The three children she names in it are her own kids!! (Yes I researched it). 
 Nice tribute to your kids but a real book would have been more effective, something many of us could have turned to share the novel's experience. Plus it's a disservice to all of the wonderful pre-Harry Potter British fantasy that many might not have read - Diana Wynne Jones, Eva Ibbotson, Joan Aiken... 
 This is not a keeper. It's just lucky it's not embedded in my wall right now.
This just made me happy to read it. I started it while my daughter was ice skating and before I knew it, I had read 150 pages and wanted to have my own van with books to sell. A sweet story.

This was a light enjoyable book for a book lover like me. Nina a librarian loses her job because of the library is closing and the books are being discarded. Surinder her roomate refuses to let her bring anymore books home. Nina takes a chance and purchases a van, loads up the books and moves to Scotland and begins a new chapter in her life.

I really liked this book a lot. It had excellent plotting and a perfect love story. Very good read. 
 I will say, however, that there was no bookshop on the corner. There was a bookshop in a VAN, but it didn't always park on the corner, or at all, really. So perhaps a better title would have been The Mobile Bookshop. Or The Scottish Bookshop. A little bit strange, that.

3.5 stars! This is a delightful little romance which has a lot about books and Scotland thrown in. Enjoyed it for the quick read that it is. 
 Recommended
Cute book! Makes me want to read even more & visit Scotland :)
A fun little romance with a big helping of book love thrown in.
Real rating 4.5 stars. Only the predictability of the romance kept me from giving it a 5.
This is chick lit at its finest. A light read.

I feel badly because other reviewers loved this book WAYYYY more than I did. It wasn't terrible, but I was ready to be done with it. The writing style was very hard to read...I think it's because it wasn't written in first person, and this story felt too informal to have this omniscient third person narrator. Weird in that way. Based on the reviews and the synopsis I had really hoped for a 5 star out of the park homerun, but had to settle for a foul ball instead.

book_b.title: Winter's Tale
book_b.user_review: DNF Well-written, but not my cup of tea.

sample_reviews.review_text: After attempting to read this book (I got as far as Beverly dying before deciding it wasn't for me) I felt as if I was drowning in sticky, sweet marshmallows. The writing style takes 500 words to say what 5 would do well. As a reader, I prefer straight-forward prose written in a clean style.

Peter Lake is high on my list of favorite literary characters for sure. Not only does Helprin write poetically and create an adventurous story of magic and transformation, he adds a surreal quality to it all and a real love of New York City. For some reason I'm totally attracted to Arctic tales, as well. This is like a grown up Golden Compass.

People seem to either love or hate this book. I don't hate it, but it is unnecessarily long, redundant, and over-described. It's hard to forgive the first chapter being written from the horse's point of view. If I was at all interested in New York City's history, I might have found something to pull me through it. As it is, I look forward to the movie, which if nothing else will take less time out of my life.

Full disclosure: "Winter's Tale" is the literary equivalent of a date with a crazy person. You've arrived and immediately realized that this was a bad idea, because though you've only just sat down, they're already going on about how cute their new little cousin is, or son, or dog - and oh, don't you want to see a photo? Meanwhile all you can do is just sit there, sipping your lukewarm water, shredding a napkin in your hands, begging the hours to tick by faster. Then they start telling you how they love to masturbate between the pages of their favorite novel. "What's the novel?" You ask, suddenly interested. Why, "Winter's Tale!" They say. But oh, if only the pages really were stuck together to the point that it was impossible to read another horribly written page. 
 Yes, this is THAT book. The one that people rave about endlessly like it saved them from suicide in the middle of a dreary night, and all you can think about is how you would have been spared the current agonizing conversation if they had just done it. 
 I can't even type the title without flying into fits of rage. First off, where is that damned indefinite article? Because if this is really going to try and stake a claim to being the definitive tale of old man winter, than I say bring on global warming! 
 So what is this story actually about? Well, this is what I gathered from the first 50-pages or so, before I decided to warm myself up by tossing the book into the fireplace. 
 1. There's a guy named Peter. Peter Lake (ugh). His parents were immigrants who were rejected entry into the U.S. (and they weren't even Muslim!) but because they really wanted their son to spend his life all on his own in America, they set him adrift in a little basket (or something) from where their ship is moored in New York harbor. He ends up in some fantastical marsh lands around New Jersey or something, a Moses to the marsh people. 
 2. There's a white horse. The story is initially being told from the horse's point of view, but it shifts after about 10 or so pages, never to return (at least, not in the next 40 pages or so). That's a pity because this horse is magical or something. On my book cover it's shown flying over the title ... perhaps it made off with the missing "A". 
 3. There's a villain named Pearly who heads the menacing "short tails" gang. If that doesn't have you shaking in your boots, the fact that Pearly is apparently attracted to shiny objects might. He's got a particular obsession for gold, not because it's valuable, but because it's shiny. He wants to make a room out of the stuff, and to do so hatches a plot to steal lots of it from an armored ship. He tells his gang this while in their usual meeting place - in an underground, non-golden (for now) room in the tunnels of New York's sewer system. And no, I didn't make any of that up. 
 This is how Pearly's obsession with gold is explained to the reader, and I quote: 
 "Pearly Soames wanted gold and silver, but not, in the way of common thieves, for wealth. He wanted them because they shone and were pure. Strange, afflicted, and deformed, he sought a cure in the abstract relation of colors. But though he was drawn to fine and intense color, he was no connoisseur. Connoisseurs of paintings were curiously indifferent about color itself, and were seldom possessed by it ... Not Pearly. Pearly's attraction to color was like an infection, or religion, and he came to it each time a starving man. Sometimes, on the street or sailing along in a fast skiff, he would witness the sun's illumination of color that was given (like almost everything else in New York) a short and promiscuous embrace. Pearly always stopped, and if he froze in the middle of the street, traffic was forced to weave around him. Or, if he were on a boat, he turned it to the wind and stayed with the color for as long as it lasted." Oh yeah, there's more where that came from. 
 Now, if that's the kind of writing you enjoy reading, you'll be thrilled to know that "Winter's Tale" is chock full of the stuff - over 600 pages worth to be exact! 
 For me though, "Winter's Tale" belongs to "The English Patient" school of writing. Which is to say, a school for people who like to read words because they like the way words look on a page, not because they like what words mean. They just want to inject words into their pretentious little veins and become numbed by them. And there are many, many, MANY words here to get high on. They mean nothing, and the way they are used and overused is so "high-brow American lit" as to be practically infantile. 
 Ultimately, "Winter's Tale" is clearly the result of a New York wet dream Mark Halprin had. I've read my fair share of erotica, but I have never read anything as disgustingly pathetic, as perverse, or as rapey, as Mark Halprin's treatment of New York here. This is the kind of thing that, had it been written about a woman, you'd probably think that the author was writing out of frustration for the restraining order that she'd had placed on him. 
 Every character - even the magical white horse - has a line about how much they love, not just New York, but Manhattan. Oh, I couldn't stay away, the horse thinks, that's why I am so willing to break out of my owner's barn - simply strutting the streets of Manhattan in my horsey way makes it worth the beating that I'm sure to get when I return! Peter Lake too, is willing to risk life and limb and leave the protection the marsh people and the, ahem, "cloud gate" offer him in order to go to Manhattan. And Pearly loves the place so much he holds his meetings, as mentioned above, in the city sewer! 
 There was a film adaptation released some years ago with Colin Firth in the lead. The movie got terrible reviews. Why? Perhaps it's because in movies you can't just go blah blah blah for hours and expect people to care. "Artless grace" says Joyce Carol Oats. "Artless" as in "without effort or pretentiousness; natural and simple"? Seriously, Joyce? Did you read the same book I did? 
 Oh, but the book has brought a smile to my lips at last, because it does crackle so nicely in the flames. Winter is over.

I'm going to be generous and give this book two stars, because I was engaged in the first 30-40%. After that, it became a huge struggle to finish this book because I just could not get interested the next parts. I'm sure I missed a lot of things in this book because honestly I was just skimming to completion. Too many things introduced/started and then not explained properly for my taste.

Premiere impression: totalement deconcerte. Un premier chapitre cinematique extremement impressionant tant la texture de la realite y est palpable. Puis des chapitres tres etonnants. Un element totalement inexplique, un "mur de nuages" qui flotte a l'exterieur de la ville... Serait-ce du realisme magique? Car j'aime pas beaucoup ca, moi, le realisme magique... Read & see... 
 Finalement: j'ai arrete de lire. Les personnages principaux sont trop parfaits, la narration insiste trop sur a quel point ils sont merveilleux. Le realisme disparait peu a peu et du coup la credibilite d'ensemble s'evapore et je cesse d'etre interesse parce qui arrive a ces personnages qui ne sont pas reels. Bref, a force de vouloir faire du merveilleux, la suspension d'incredulite ne fonctionne plus et je n'ai plus envie de lire. Dommage.

Everything I thought I knew about this book going was was completely untrue. When I read the description of a book on the book, I expect it to be right, but this was completely misleading. The love story it talks about isn't really a love story. Sure, there are several couples in love in it, but it's not so much a love story as a story about love - and justice, and God. 
 I was quite disappointed with the plot in this book. Mark Helprin writes a wonderfully detailed book, but the details mean nothing if the plot isn't there.

I don't think I've ever before come across a style quite like Helprin's. He makes the use of the English language seem easy the same way Cirque du Soleil acrobats make the rebellion from physics as we know it seem easy. His imagery and original metaphor is so thorough and imaginitive it's almost exhausting to read it. Winter's Tale is basically a fairy tale set in NYC (at various times), and it requires a lot of suspension-of-disbelief, but Helprin's writing is so smooth and unapologetic that you find yourself buying it, almost without questioning it, because if you question it you interrupt the narrative, which almost seems like a sacrilege. It's a story which arrives at its height when you surrender yourself to it, and it's among the easiest surrenders I've ever experienced.
I can see how some people might have trouble with this book or get bored with it -- it is chock full of similes and drawn-out descriptions. But I loved it!
I had to put this book down after reading about 1/3 of it. Arduous, groanable prose, I just couldn't finish.

Our Kind of Traitor by John le Carre is a novel about a Russian money-launderer (Dima) who seeks the help of a friendly British couple (Perry and Gail) when they meet on the island of Antigua. Dima's need: to reach British intelligence and defect, not from the USSR, but from the Russian mafia he is fatally associated with. 
 Perry is a dissatisfied academic; Gail is a rising barrister. Neither of them is connected to British intelligence, but Perry hazards a guess that an Oxford associate might be able to put everyone together. 
 Enter Hector, who leaps at this opportunity to catch a big fish and engineer payback within the "Service." He's been trampled, not enjoyed it, and now, in a semi-rogue fashion, he confirms not only that Dima knows incredible amounts about incredible sums being laundered worldwide but also that there is a pathway to extracting Dima (and his family) from the clutches of the Russian mafia dons (led by someone known as the Prince) who want to kill him. 
 le Carre is a professional espionage writer who in this book, at least, shifts the focus of the "Service" from intelligence to crime fighting. The ironies, bits of tradecraft, hardened characters, long-lived rivalries of his earlier novels remain more or less the same, though. 
 At the heart of such writing there's always a competition and it's not necessarily plot-related. It's a competition between proceduralism and character. Intelligence as le Carre portrays it is an elaborate sequence of getting things right; this is what moves the story more than the typical mix of iconoclastic spies, smarmy bad guys, and unwitting accomplices. 
 As a consequence, Hector, Perry, Gail, Dima and others are somewhat forced. There's "backstory" to each of them, but it doesn't add up to three-dimensional characterization. Why? Perhaps because some features of character development are contingent upon characters in idle moments, adrift, floating this way and that. And in a spy or crime book you need to keep them pointed in a given direction which, again, le Carre works out according to the idiosyncracies of secrecy. 
 Having said that, I did find the final passages, when finally released from bureaucratic purgatory, almost touching. A part of Dima that has been presented earlier in the book emerges with genuine pathos: he realizes that he is in the process of becoming what you might call a free prisoner. 
 le Carre writes to entertain. He's not a moralist like Graham Greene. But he does do a lot with this theme of the free prisoner (my phrase, not his) because in the end, he seems to be saying, we're all such creatures. No matter how ingenious and persistent a rogue like Hector might be, or idealistic Perry might be, or perceptive as Gail might be, they all (we all) live in a world governed by the abstract collective behavior of vast, intertwined sectors that are called, for instance, bureaucracy, the economy, science, the Internet...impersonal, irritating, not always rational processes that in the 21st century are determinative. 
 At one point in the novel, Hector's nemesis in the "Service" asks, "So what?" He means so what if there is a black world in which money gets laundered white, just as long as Great Britain and the City of London get their share of it when it's clean. 
 Again, a Graham Greene would take this question, focus hard on the nemesis, make a psychological study of him in crisis, and give us a true lesson in darkness. Likewise Conrad or Dostoevsky. In le Carre's fictional world, the nemesis is asking a great question that's never answered; le Carre reduces motivation to bureaucratic revenge and criminal expediency. This is what separates someone as talented as he from greater literary talents. He entertains us, he may know enough about espionage and crime to engage us, but his descriptions of existential imprisonment in the modern era are more for fun than enlightenment. 
 For more of my comments on contemporary writing, see Tuppence Reviews (Kindle).

I went into this having read a review stating that Le Carre has got his mojo back with this novel. I found a lot of his more recent novels to be way to preachy about the evils of modern international commerce and corporations. Not a bad premise, so long as you don't bore me with a lame story along the way. Anyway, this book has a pretty good premise, but drags oh so slowly with very little occurring. I mean, I love tennis and Roger Federer is the bomb, but I don't need to hear about how awesome he is quite this much or get a brief summary review of the 2009 French Open Men's Final. As the pages turn and the end comes ever closer, I wonder what if anything is going to happen? The finish was better than expected but not by much. Overall, this was a disappointment.

The latest novel by John le Carre is getting positive reviews all over the place with sentiments exclaiming that the old le Carre is back and that he has dropped the preaching tone of his last few efforts. Personally, I like it when he preaches to us about the ills of our modern world. 
 In Our Kind of Traitor, I felt the master of spy literature was holding back just a tad and I purely hated the way this novel ended. I just felt lost through much of the story, but that could be because I do not understand global finance. Not one bit. 
 My take is that this is a gangster-trying-to-go-straight story. Percolating beneath that is the picture of British government being so in the grip of vested interests and greedy politicians that the true traitor lies there. Is that the meaning of the title? 
 A Russian gangster, an idealistic young teacher from Oxford, his much more realistic girlfriend, the usual failed spy and the usual rogue spy; all the elements are there but it didn't come together well for me. John le Carre has stumped me before. I remember feeling like I was really missing something in The Little Drummer Girl. My husband liked Our Kind of Traitor just fine and explained some of it to me. 
 If you have read it, liked it and are now laughing up your sleeve about me, please...comment!

reference_books.title: Steve Jobs
reference_books.review_text:
A fascinating read about a very interesting and creative man. 
 Jobs told President Obama that schools should stay open until 6 pm, 11 months a year. 
 All books, learning aids, and tests should be digital, with feedback in real time. 
 Then Jobs told the President directly that Obama would be a one-term president if he did not become more business-friendly. 
 Bill Gates and Jobs agreed that computers have made surprisingly little impact on schools, 
 which need to be serving up personalized lessons and motivational feedback. 
 Jobs next item on his to-do list--he wanted to make TVs simple, elegant, with an easy user interface. 
 Jobs' quest for perfection led to a compulsion for control of every Apple product. 
 A desire to delight the user led to resistance to empowering the user. 
 A measure of Jobs' business success is seen in the relative values of Apple and Microsoft. 
 In 2000, Apple was worth 1/20 of Microsoft, but by 2011, it was worth 70% more. 
 Jobs approach was to figure out what people are going to want before they do. 
 Isaacson calls Jobs the "greatest business executive of our era," the one most certain to be remembered a century from now, next to Edison and Ford in the business pantheon. 
 Isaacson paints an impressive picture of Jobs' legacy--Apple II, Mac, Toy Story, Apple Store, Ipod, Itunes Store, Iphone, Ipad, ICloud, and Apple Corp. itself. 
 Though Bill Gates had considerable respect for Jobs, it was not reciprocal. Of Microsoft, Jobs said that it "had become mostly irrelevant." 
 Of his own efforts, Jobs wrote that he "tried to use my talents ... to show appreciation of all the contributions that came before us, and to add something to that flow." 
 Would that we all could not only think that way, but act that way.

book_a.title: The Unwinding: An Inner History of the New America
book_a.user_review:
The Unwinding portrays the dissolution of American values over the past 30 years. Biographies of celebrities are interwoven with profiles of ordinary citizens embroiled in extraordinary times. 
 Some very disheartening news for the future of our people and culture!

sample_reviews.review_text:
Here's another book I hoped would explain America to me. I'm beginning to worry that I just don't like the answer. 
 The Unwinding is not a book with a thesis to prove. It is instead an account of the 15 years leading up to 2013 presented through the eyes of a series of subjects--some famous, most just average citizens. They are third person accounts, but Packer presents them as if he has gotten deeply into the heads of his subjects. Sometimes this feels condescending but mostly it is powerful. Many of these characters begin Republican and drift left (or at least populist) for the first Obama campaign. Others (e.g., Peter Thiel) remain resolutely libertarian. Their struggles are about America and their feelings are, nearly unanimously, that the system is rigged and the institutions have failed. But nearly everyone maintains hope that a singularly focused individual might still get ahead. Years before "fake news" became a ubiquitous phrase, Packer is looking closely at journalists and how they are believed. He examines the housing bubble in painful detail and does not spare any of the participants--from top to bottom. Politicians--with the exception of Tom Periello--are excoriated as sellouts. There are few heroes, even amongst Packer's most sympathetic subjects (except for the Indian immigrant who loses her hotel but fights the big banks tooth and nail to a somewhat pyrrhic victory). 
 This is not a hopeful book, although the last vignette ends hopefully. In the Unwinding, much of what once bound America after the Second World War has come completely unglued.

This book hinges on the compelling nature of the individual stories, many of which I wanted to experience even more deeply, perhaps as their own books. And while connected through time and shared descent into crisis (the unwinding), I never really felt that George Packer intertwined the stories as much as he could. The ending also left me feeling empty, as if the author had introduced the unwinding and was saying to the reader "here's a glimmer or two of hope, but really, I don't have any suggestions for how we get out of this hole." Overall, tremendous writing and journalism that keeps you interested and invested in the characters. You may pass them on the street everyday, but it takes a storyteller like George Packer to get you to stop and contemplate their history, challenges, fears, and dreams.

sloppy sloppy journalism. i had high hopes for this book and enjoyed the stories about his 'average americans', but have to question his research skills after his horatio alger, slobbering lap dog, wikipedia puffery on celebs and and notable americans (like oprah and jay-z). at the end of the day his 'unwinding' narrative is all pretty standard stuff about flawed americans who make mistakes and pick themselves back up even when 'the man' keeps knocking them back down. hardly any grand linked narrative about how modern society has failed us. if you are intersted in that i suggest watching david simon's 'the wire' as a much more coherent and more grounded in reality starting point.

I enjoyed Packer's "The Assassins Gate," so I wanted to read this one by him too. He does a good job of telling the stories of everyday, regular Americans and the effect that the past forty years have had on their lives and America as a whole. Since the 1970's, America's middle class has suffered at the hands of corporate America, Wall Street, and the politicians. This book tells that story, and how those everyday, regular citizens are trying to make a difference. I enjoyed reading this book, it was eye opening and very informative.
The chapters detailing the demise of Youngstown would be great texts for our area high school students to read and discuss.

Parts of The Unwinding I enjoyed (the account of the Occupy Wall St movement through the perspective of one organizer and one participant, and the Elizabeth Warren portrait, for example); other parts bored me nearly to tears (please not Jeff Connaugton again); and one section actually did bring me to tears of frustration and despair (the story of the impoverished Hartsell family of Tampa). And the chapter epigraphs were pretty entertaining in the audio book context - disjointed and unidentified snippets from the media of each year. These reminded me of my obsession with reading the year-in-pictures and quotes issues of Rolling Stone and Life Magazine when I was a teenager in the 1980s. But the short portraits of public figures appear to have been written without doing interviews - kind of a Wikipedia-level of information there (Oprah, Alice Waters, Raymond Carver, Jay-Z [not a flattering portrayal, FWIW], Newt Gingrich etc.). 
 Also, the entire book is presented without analysis, interpretation, authorial commentary (and there is only a cursory introduction and no epilogue, postscript, or afterword). Yet any savvy reader knows that Packer's opinions are embedded in every sentence he chose to write and every portrait he chose to include/ exclude. But Packer never offers an overarching narrative to tie this all together, instead, he's left it to readers to write their own meaning on all of it. In fiction and other sorts of nonfiction narratives that can be generative, but here I thought more was needed. 
 I do retract my complaint about gender representation - there were plenty of women in the second half of the book, but then I could ask: why weren't there more African Americans, more Hispanics, more immigrants of any national origin; what about children and young adults, the elderly and aging; what about a discussion of education, or climate change, or celebrity, or religious culture; or arts and entertainment culture, or any of a thousand issues that have changed America over the last generation? I can't name them all and Packer wouldn't have been able to write them all, of course. But a book like this raises these objections because its tone and authority make its subjects normative - and as many reviewers have mentioned, it could be on reading lists twenty years from now. Even now I predict it'll be on the big newspapers' best-of-2013 lists, because it's just the sort of book that appeals to editors of the NY Times and the like.

 One question so far about this "must-read" book of summer 2013: Where are the WOMEN? I've listened to 40% and all Packer has offered to represent American women's lives of the last 35 years is the story of an underprivileged crack addict named Tammy Thomas, who will likely remain impoverished her entire life, and a snide and uncharitable portrait of Oprah Winfrey that focuses on her superficiality and her hypocrisy vis-a-vis the "average" American woman. Since it's audio I don't know where this is going, but I am getting a little pissed.

It was OK. A series of personal stories about people affected by the recession, and about some of the bozos who caused or exacerbated it. Maybe I was expecting something else. I got maybe halfway through it before losing interest.
A gripping account of the inequality reshaping America.
There were parts that were interesting, but overall I just thought it was ok.

book_b.title: The Man in the High Castle
book_b.user_review:
Dick was one of the most visionary writers of the 20th century. This book is one of the best of his imaginary tales. 
 The United States has lost WWII, and is occupied by Japan and Germany. 
 A haunting vision of history as nightmare!

sample_reviews.review_text: I'll start by saying that the only commonality between this book and the Amazon Prime show purported to be based on this book is its an alternative universe where the Nazis and Japan won WWII and the name of the female protagonist. This book won a Hugo Award, but I thought it was a mediocre and rather disjointed approach to what is an interesting premise.

I started this book awhile ago- and read it 1 or 2 kindle pages per night before falling asleep mid-sentence. 
 So what comes first? The chicken or the egg. Did I just completely not get it BECAUSE I kept falling asleep? Or did I fall asleep BECAUSE the book just wasn't that awesome? 
 Either way, I didn't care about any of the characters throughout the story- was trying to figure out how they intertwined somehow- and then the book just ENDED. My first thought was "Wow. I COMPLETELY missed that one." Read every page, every line, (often times twice because I couldn't remember where I drifted off the night before) and really just didn't GET it. 
 Perhaps I should have read the Cliff-notes version beforehand to help me catch the nuances I missed. 
 Or I just need to go back to school and learn how to think again.
Abandoned after half way. Stopped and started because I had visitors, but I suspect that wasnt the only reason this was so hard to get into...

Great concept but I didn't like this book as much as I thought I would. Some of the story lines were interesting, but all the political intrigue was lost on me. Maybe if I knew more of the real history of WWII I might have liked it (or understood it) better.
I was not the right reader for this book.
Tripe.

Dust Jacket Summary 
 It's America in 1962. Slavery is legal once again. The few Jews who still survive hide under assumed names. In San Francisco, the I Ching is as common as the Yellow Pages. All because some twenty years earlier the United States lost a war--and is now occupied by Nazi Germany and Japan. 
 Good Points 
 - a unique story set in an alternative history in which the Axis powers won World War II and divided United States into two territories. 
 Bad Points 
 - the story is very disjointed and fails to deliver on its premise. 
 - characters are uninteresting, bland and for the most part unlikable. 
 - plot elements introduced in the book but never resolved 
 - page after page of mostly boring descriptions of making jewelry, trading of antiques, etc. 
 - the book doesn't so much as end as it just stops. 
 Final Word 
 For me, this the first PKD novel that was an absolute disappointment. It was a chore to read, my mind wandered through out the story and I really dreaded picking the book up. It finally reached a point that I just didn't care anymore.
feels unfinished

PKD has never failed to amaze me, to entertain me, to enlighten me--until now. 
 This was a train wreck from beginning to end. And not in a good way. What the (blank) was he thinking when he wrote it? Was he even thinking when he wrote it? Was he even conscious? 
 Never mind that the characters were so thin and poorly drawn they barely existed. Never mind that the stories of these characters were equally as thin. Never mind the over abundance of I Ching involved. The great sin was that it was BORING! Yes, that's right. I wouldn't believe it myself if I hadn't read the whole thing. This is a PDK book that is BORING. 
 I'm still in shock.

After seeing and enjoying the 2015 Amazon mini-series, I reread this 1962 novel, which underwhelmed me the first time. This time I enjoyed the world-building more (Germany and Japan won WW2), but I still found the characters underdeveloped and the plot talky and wandering. At times the psychobabble dialogue reminded me of a bad, serious Woody Allen movie. Philip K. Dick is not known for his great characters, but for his ideas, humor, and audacity. There is less humor in this book. The ideas are there, but the execution feels unfinished. Mr. Tagomi, a Japanese official, muses on a piece of jewelry made by Frank Frink, a struggling Jewish man. At first, the piece has little effect on him, but eventually it does, and he realizes what's important is what he (Tagomi) brings to the jewelry. I feel similarly about this book. With its loose construction and undefined ending, it is very much open to interpretation. Many have interpreted it as Dick's finest work. I, apparently, am unable to bring enough to the book to feel that way.

reference_books.title: Before I Fall
reference_books.review_text:

Part of this might also be that I typically am not a fan of books written in the form of diaries, because they tend to be kind of staggered and don't go into enough detail on any one topic. Also, I expected it to be much funnier. It definitely had its funny moments, but I only had a couple times where I actually laughed out loud. 
 What I did find interesting was the vaguely parallel plot to Pride and Prejudice. Coincidentally, I just read Pride and Prejudice a couple of weeks ago and the story was fresh in my mind. P&P had been sitting in the back of my mind for much of the book, especially w/ the main male figure being named Mark Darcy. Mark being at first quite a rude fellow then eventually ending up quite a nice catch after all. Then w/ the situation with Bridget's mother. Not only did Mr. Darcy save the day and fix the entire situation, but there was also the connection of the behavior of Bridget's mother. I wanted something lighthearted, but found myself simply frustrated.

A wizard criminal named Sirius Black has escaped from the top-security prison, Azkaban, and all signs point to him targeting Harry Potter. The soul-sucking guardians of the prison, the Dementors, are installed at Hogwarts to protect the students, but they're much more of a disruption than a comfort. But when Ron's rat does turn out to be somewhere--and someONE--that he'd never suspected, other old friends come out of the woodwork, including Sirius Black himself. But exactly whose side is Sirius on--and who are his allies? It could very well be that Harry may finally learn a few things about his family. 
 The Dementors are a horrifying idea. They were expertly handled as an eerie presence in the book, though I had trouble imagining any grand wizarding society would accept their widespread use for the cause of order when they can suck people's souls out. I liked the switcharoo of loyalties and the way the characters' pets figured in, but I again got frustrated at how nobody tells Harry anything for the sake of a nifty reveal at the end. The red herrings are kind of out of control sometimes.

This review (and others) can be found in all its proper formatting glory on my blog Beauty and the Bookshelf. 
 *Note: This review would be waaay more flaily and gushy if I would've been a good person and written this review when I finished Crown of Midnight...like three months ago. 
 This (Smeagol's so-not-dramatic despair) is how I felt when I finished Crown of Midnight: 
 (Caption may or may not be how I feel dying waiting for Heir of Fire.) 
 I didn't looove Throne of Glass, but it reaaally made me want to read Crown of Midnight (which I'd heard was EPIC), and ohmygosh, Crown of Midnight made me like Throne of Glass more. Seriously, THIS BOOK. It's a feels-fest, swoonalicious, fantasmical adventure that usurps its predecessor and leaves you with an alcohol-free hangover. 
 One of my biggest issues with Throne of Glass was the use of exclamation points. They were, like, everywhere and drove me crazy. So I am very happy that the use of them was cut down here, because YAY. And really, I can't think of any complaints with this book (minus me wondering WHAT IS BEING DONE TO MY FEELS), so double yay! 
 Crown of Midnight follows Throne of Glass, where Celaena became (spoiler alert) the king's royal assassin and, in order to gain her freedom, must do his bidding. But Celaena isn't the most compliant of people, so she decides to twist the orders given to her by the king and be more in control herself. However, it's never that easy when evil is afoot and magic is brewing. Oh, and when there's sexual tension like whoa. 
 Celaena is an extremely badass protagonist whose bad side you DO NOT want to get on. Plus, she's an infamous assassin, so she'd kill you faster than you can blink. She's under a lot of pressure in this book, with trying to keep what she's been doing (or hasn't) a secret, attempting to figure out what on earth is going on in the castle made of glass and some heebie-jeebie things, and she's doesn't quite know where she stands in a kinda-sorta-not-really love triangle with Prince Dorian (ew) and Captain Chaol Westfall (yes yes yesss). New character Archer was simultaneously sketch and likeable (also, sucky job, dude), and I've always been kind of whatever about Celaena's BFF Nehemia. The king, as usual, can go die. Some oddball things happen with Dorian in this book, and I do like him...but he needs to back up/off of Celaena. Because I have a MAJOR SHIP, and it's between her and *siiigh* *googly eyes* *fluttery heart* CHAOOOL. I love him. I love him. I love him. I loved him in Throne of Glass (oh my gosh, that whole "get up" scene at the end?!), and that love just grows even more here. Chaol and Celaena (or, Chaol and ME) go together better than peanut butter and chocolate. Their sexual tension in this book KILLS ME, and it frustrates me, but my gosh is it AWESOME. (Major spoiler alert: My ship set sail! And it was beautiful. Then it anchored and I will go DOWN with this ship, but why, Sarah J. Maas, WHY? End spoiler.) 
 Can we talk about the last half of this book? Because WHAT HAPPENED? It was all so beautiful, and then my heart broke, and then my feels were being pulled apart and I just COULD NOT and CANNOT and yes, I HAVE EMOTIONS. You know, I think a book is successful when it gives me a whirlwind of emotion-barfing, so well done, Crown of Midnight. No matter how you felt about Throne of Glass--seriously, even if you hated it--please read Crown of Midnight. TRUST ME. (And if you don't like it then I think you need to see a doctor.) 
 In short: READ THIS BOOK. (But read Throne of Glass first, obvi.) In the meantime, I'm going to wait for The Assassin's Blade to magically appear in my hands, and I'm going to impatiently wait for ALL THINGS Heir of Fire. (Yes, I would kill for that book, sorry not sorry.) Seriously, fantasy--something I haven't read much of--might be becoming my new favorite genre. Crown of Midnight has everything: suspense, tension, adventure, murder, mystery, romance, humor, magic, shockers and surprises, a ship that'd eat the Titanic for lunch, a swoony boy (who's mine, I'll fight you for him), a KILLER ending, and so much more, oh my! Really, NEED I say more?

HOLY CRAP. 
 I'm speechless. This book was everything I could have possibly wanted in a sequel and more, I don't think I could love a series more. WOW.
WHAAAAATTT?!?!! I NEED HEIR OF FIRE LIKE NOWWWW.

I received an advanced copy of this book through Netgalley. 
 Indie witnesses a man falling from the sky and dying. He has a crumpled note in his pocket with the name of her mother's shop on it. And that is when everything gets really messed up. 
 This was pretty weak as far as world building goes. There are two warring factions, but you don't learn much about either one of them. There is some romance but it's a little wonky and has bad timing. The main character wasn't my favorite. She comes across pretty shallow through most of the book. 
 This book wasn't bad, it just didn't make much of an impression.

HEXED owes a strong debt to Buffy the Vampire Slayer, but fortunately stands on its own. Indigo Blackwood sees a man die, then two very creepy men come to interrogate her about what she witnessed. It all leads to an important family heirloom being stolen and Indigo discovering that she's a witch. 
 Indie shows great courage in tough situations, which really endeared her to me. She's determined to help people, but unable to do anything effective until she's trained in how to use her abilities. The other characters ranged in interest for me. 
 I liked Paige, the hanger on who turns out to be there for Indie in a way her other friends aren't, but she disappeared for long stretches of the book. (Until the cliffhanger ending, I totally forgot about Paige.) Bishop is the bad boy in leather who Indie of course falls for. I am still boggling at a romantic hero with a naked Betty Boop tattooed on his neck. Just what. (I hope I am not spoiling anything for anyone by mentioning that Indie insists that he cover it up, thank goodness.) Indie and Bishop do have a nice amount of snarky, belligerent chemistry. 
 The bad guys, sorcerers who want to kill witches, are quite threatening. These are not villains who just stand around posturing. Indie is very lucky that they want her alive to break a spell on the heirloom. Those around her are not always so lucky. 
 HEXED is an entertaining debut for fans of witches and stories with lots of action. It's nothing too original or exciting, but it's not totally paint by numbers either. There is a complete story here, but be warned that there is a sudden cliffhanger ending that sets up a sequel. I must admit, I wasn't a big fan of that hook. I might read the second book, I might not.

 Hexed by Michelle Krys was on my radar as soon as I found out it is about witches. If you know me, you know I devour any witch book I can get my hands on, thanks Cate Tiernan for that! Also, the cover is beautiful, even better when seen in person. The book follows Indigo, a girl who had no idea that witches and magic are real until she is plunged into a deadly war between the witches and sorcerers. I enjoyed Hexed, albeit it didn't capture my attention all the time, I thought it was a pretty interesting book and had a ton of twists, left and right. 
 Indigo was a good character, even though initially she had the typical horrible best friend and popularity getting in the way of her logic thinking. The introduction of Bishop finally gets her thinking and while I didn't care for the romance at all, I did like the way he made her look at who she is and what she's become and let her re-think everything she believed in.. including the existence of witches. I have to admit though.. I didn't get much magic or powers in here.. it felt a bit more like they have supernatural powers rather than them being witches.. maybe because I've read so many witch books and now always compare them to the ones I read. 
 Still, I wished I got more on the background of the witches and just the witch-y stuff.. you know what I mean! Still, the author held nothing back. There were many gasp inducing moments that I had to reread to make sure I understood what just happened right. unbelievable is the right word. I even took it to twitter and discussed with people the shock. haha. It's a good thing when an author takes us by surprise so early on in the novel. I definitely recommend it to paranormal fans and even contemporary fans since I feel this reads as a mash up for both. I'm excited to read the sequel, now that Indigo has a better hold on her reality and the hopefulness that we'll get more involved in the magic aspect of the story.
