sample_reviews.review_text:
Ok so here's the story... I have been a huge fan of Danielle Steel since I can remember. She was my favorite author as a pre-teen and a teenager. I have soooo many favorites by her 
 such as "Daddy" One of the most heart warming books and yes it made me cry. I believe Alan Thicke played in it when it was made into a movie..."No greater Love" "Jewels" all great books... However; Big Girl didn't impress me much at ALL! I was actually disappointed, because I predicted the book from the start. She made Victoria into such a victim throughout the whole book, that whenever I read about her in another scene, I already knew. So Victoria was born to two college sweethearts. Her father is such an A**... Because his daughter was born with blond hair and blue eyes and didn't look like them, he always made fun of his daughter and basically told her in such little words that she was ugly, also flat out told her that she was fat and no one would want her because of it. Then her mom was a spineless skinny woman that believed her husband was never wrong and had the same feelings towards her daughter that her husband had as well. 
 Now she was given a sister Grace at around age 7 or 8. Her sister was born looking just like her parents and Victoria didn't look like either of her parents. Grace got all the good looks, perfect parents and even better sister. She was the apple of their eyes. 
 Victoria graduated from college with her bachelor's degree, immediately started working at the best private school in NYC. But nothing she ever did was good enough for her parents. It didn't matter to Victoria that she had friends that loved her and supported her. Even as she found a hot guy who was interested in her for whom she was. He didn't see the "poor big girl." He was someone positive in her life. But the way Danielle finished the book, she didn't give you much but to imagine what happens to them in the long run. Basically this book made me feel like "oh poor fat rich girl" no one loves her. I just didn't feel drawn to the story, the characters, nothing. Only thing I felt was that the father was an A** and the mother was a spineless woman... lol 
 I honestly feel disappointed in this book. Her older books are soo good. I feel like my time was wasted on this one. Sorry Danielle, but this is only an opinion of a "poor big girl."
If you want to read the same sentence over and over and over again, then read this book.
gw banget.. somehow! :D
Bad as helll

My mother has been a fan of Danielle Steel's books for the better part of three decades. I'd never read a single one until I stumbled across this one at the library. I was intrigued by the name, enough to read the book jacket, and decided I wanted to read it. 
 It occurred to me about 80% of the way through that it was less like reading a novel, and more like reading a case study. It zoomed through decades, skipping four years or more at a time. It contained very little dialogue, considering the length of it. It wasn't anything like what I expected from a Danielle Steel novel, considering how popular they are. 
 I'd have preferred to like the character for some unique or quirky trait that made me laugh or even made me wince in vicarious embarrassment, instead of constantly being clunked over the head with descriptions of her "sweet and generous nature". The characterizations of her parents were paper-thin. Honestly so was Gracie's. 
 I have a question for those who've read DS books before: are they always like this? Is this typical of her writing style - racing through years while the situations her characters face have her repeating the same paragraphs over and over? Perhaps you could reply in the comments. :)

This book is about a "big girl" from L.A. who moves to New York to pursue her dream of becoming a teacher and to escape her belittling family. As a "big girl" myself, same size as Victoria, the main character in the book, it was painfully obvious to me that Danielle Steel isn't and has never been a big girl before. In the first 3/4 of the book, it seems the only thing Victoria thinks and talks about is loosing weight. Even though she has a great career and good friends, the story still can't stop revolving around her weight. I would have liked to get a better feel for Victoria's personality. I wanted to scream to the author "Bigger people think about more important things then dieting!! We have lives!" Not until she finds a man does she feel validated. I really enjoyed the book once he stopped feeling bad for herself!! And that didn't happen until a man told her she was beautiful. Won't be reading another D.S. book for a while.

Ellen Gleeson is the happy adopted mother of a 3-year old son - until the day she receives a missing child flyer in her mail. The boy on the flyer looks exactly like her son. She is obsessed with finding out if indeed her son is the missing boy and she sets her journalistic skills on the path. She ignores the responsibilities of her position and begins doing everything she can to locate Will's birth parents. 
 Although I like LIsa Scottoline's books in general, I had major issues with this one. First of all, her ability to locate the birth mother was just a tad too convenient. Her boss is drop dead handsome with a sexy Brazilian accent. This makes it all the more annoying when Ellen hears Spanish being spoken later in the book and is reminded of Marcelo. 
 Secondly, her babysitter is like an on-call nurse. Oh, you need me to sit with the child because you will be late? No problem. Oh, you stopped off to have sex with your boss and you did not get home until midnight? No worries, after all you said you would be late! Oh, six inches of snow and more is falling? Never fear, I will be careful when driving home. 
 A backstabbing co-worker is trying to undermine Ellen every chance she gets. Lay-offs are imminent and the co-worker is trying to cement her position. This become irrelevant when she reports Will's presence to his actual parents and they pay her a $1,000,000 reward. 
 Thirdly, that action causes the real mother to show up at Ellen's house demanding she turn over Will (Timothy). Simultaneously a man is at the house trying to murder Ellen and Will! One thing leads to another and Ellen ends up with two dead people at her home - Timothy's (Will's) mother and the murderer, who it will come as no surprise to you later - is revealed to be the baby's natural father. 
 So, to make a long review short - the story is interesting - though very similar to the Face on the Milk Carton. Ms. Scottoline is a good writer but this outing is too predictable, which causes it to be less of a suspense thriller than her novels usually are.

My book club met on Tuesday night after some small confusion about which house we were going to be meeting in. The woman that was going to host had sick kids, so it had to be moved to another nearby household. I think perhaps this book resonated with most of the other women in the book club more than it did with me, since on average most of them have at least 4 children, and I don't have any. 
 A good part of our discussion revolved around the question "What would you do in that situation?" As the author portrayed, it's a hard, no-win question in this scenario. If your adopted child turned out to have been kidnapped from another family, would you willingly return him? What effect would this have on them later in life? And there is no good answer. (Nor did the book provide one, though it ended happily enough) 
 Personally I was most relieved to know that it was entirely a work of fiction, and I questioned some of the methods used for proofs in the story..but that's one reason it's fiction. 
 I can't say that I particularly -enjoyed- the book. It dragged in the beginning quite a bit, and I found it hard to empathize with the main character, but it did provide good fodder for a book club discussion, and for that I am grateful. Too often we end up reading books that are so bland there's nothing to discuss. 
 I get to pick next month's book, so we're reading Good Omens: The Nice and Accurate Prophecies of Agnes Nutter, Witch by Neil Gaimon. I wonder what the ladies in the club will think of it.....

 What I particularly like about this book is how the straightforwardness of a child brings others into looking at the situation from a fresh point of view, or perhaps I mean into looking at the situation and themselves from a broader point of view than their usual.

This was an engaging read but really not a great book. According to the 'meet the author' section, it is supposed to be a book about American politics, race, class, and family. These topics do come up, but only superficially. So, I'd say it's a good read if you're at the beach or stranded at an airport, and want something that will keep you occupied but not make you think critically. But, if you're expecting another Bel Canto as I was this is likely to be a disappointment.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Just stay as far away from this book as possible. It's terrible, from start to finish. I cannot even begin to imagine why there are so many people who want to read this thing. 
 Imagine if you will the the following. A man adopts two black children in what has to be roughly the late 70s or early 80s and goes on to be Mayor of Boston. He wants to be governor but his son--the biological one--screws things up for him ala Kennedy, in a terribly written passage told for "the first time" without any reluctance to a perfect stranger. Now he lives for one of his sons to carry on the political legacy but they have no desire to do so. Suddenly a woman saves a life in our upper class family, and everyone's perspective changes as her ties to the family become known. What happens when a poor girl with a strong resemblance to the adopted boys is thrust into their lives? 
 This gets worse. 
 The two kids grow up with no desire at all to know who their biological mother was and all three children are drifting about--one steals drugs in Africa, one studies fish, and the other thinks he might want to be a priest. As the story progresses, switching from viewpoint to viewpoint so the author can tell us things we have to know about everyone, we add more characters than a Shakespeare history play--each of which gets to play narrator, jarring the reader all over the place. 
 As the story goes on it gets less and less believable--how could a man with the power of the mayor's office not know where the biological mother was? Just how bad are Boston hospitals that people can zip in and out of intensive care? How does a poor person afford going to concerts, political speeches, and other things that are barely affordable by a middle class person? 
 The book just gets progressively worse in terms of writing style. When a shocking--well, not to me because by this point I'm just reading to finish the book--secret about the girl's mother is revealed through a dream sequence, I lost any hope I had for this book to even claim to be mediocre. 
 The king of all "you've got to be kidding me" moments is saved for the end, when as a result of all this, and told several years into the future, when all of a sudden the father who wanted everything to work perfectly for his family--GETS EVERYTHING WE WERE TOLD HE WANTED. 
 Yes, 287 or so pages later, this book forces us into a happy ending for the one character in the book who up to that point had no compelling reason to be the one we give a shit about. 
 There's so much wrong with this book that I could go on for pages about it. Even without using spoilers, there's so much I can describe as being wrong. Let's start with the fact that people jump in and out of this book without comment--there are lots of white relatives at the start of the book who dislike the idea of the family having black relatives. Guess who we never see again after the opening pages? Of the characters we do have, they drop in and out seemingly at random. Sullivan the screw up son has no purpose at all, and his namesake uncle is about as needed as a third shoe. 
 Then there's the practical part of all this. Our patriarch is a former mayor, right? Has security guards, at least while being mayor, right? Yet he's had a stalker--there's no polite way to describe what happens in this book but stalking--for ALMOST 20 YEARS. Umm, either the security team hated him or they're more incompetent than the keystone cops. That's if you can believe that a powerful political figure wouldn't use his influence to find--and keep at bay--the mother of the boys if he were so worried about her, as well as the other problems I mentioned above. I could add more but that would require looking over the text again and I'd really prefer not to. 
 This book reads like a Hallmark movie, and if that's your thing, go for it. However, the only way to enjoy this one is to take the concept of suspension of disbelief and toss it off the side of the Empire State Building. I can do that in a comic book, but not in a real book. I'm willing to overlook some things in fiction, but this is like trying to ignore DNA, fingerprints, and a confession all in front of your face. Combined with the poor writing style that tells instead of shows for much of the novel, it leaves me as cold as the fish Tip should still be studying. 
 If you want a book that has believable characters, a plot that makes sense, and characters that logically progress from the book's beginning to the book's end, well, this one isn't it. (Library, 03/08)

sample_reviews.review_text:
Craig Johnson's well-honed and crafted Walt Longmire mysteries are engaging page-turners that are as fresh and raw as they are multi-layered and nuanced. Furthermore, Johnson doesn't back down from the socio-economical issues taking place in today's West and bringing them to a roaring boil. 
 Johnson's mysteries keep us turning the pages, but as we do, he gives us glimpses into the contemporary west, the people who live with the imposing presence of the looming Rocky Mountains, and the undercurrents of modern technology, and social ills. Dichotomies abound with cowboys on horseback with I-phones, raging snowstorms and the futility of technology in their midst, western machismo and the women with balls enough to stand up to it. 
 As you read Johnson's works, he will divulge his characters' souls to you. We learn, bit by bit, about their weaknesses, their wounds, and their paths that led them to inhabit this remote corner of America. We also share in their triumphs and victories -- even if it is small as an ice cold Ranier beer after a day of driving dusty roads. 
 The "Walt Longmire Mysteries" series explore our world and our psyches with their imagery, symbolism, mythological archetypes and spiritualism. He does this without stereo-typing or rehashing old cliches, but with spot-on dialogue, engaging characters, and complex suspenseful plot-building. And that is what makes the reading of the Walt Longmire mystery series so very addictive. 
 We root for Walt Longmire because he fights the good fights that must be fought--no matter what the costs are to him. In "A Serpent's Tooth," Walt must deal with a splinter group of a renegade polygamy group of Latter Day Saints who have built quite the arsenal of weapons and an old vendetta that crosses time-lines and cartels. How Craig Johnson interlaces water rights in the West, Shakespeare, physics, Lost boys, flying saucers, Lamanites, corsages, L.D.S., slow car chases, "My Friend, Flicka," and the C.I.A. into a fast-paced, suspenseful novel is truly a testimonial to his storytelling ability. 
 "A Serpent's Tooth" by Craig Johnson earns five stars from Chanticleer Book Reviews. Find yourself mesmerized by a great storyteller! Be forewarned: You will not be able to stop at just one Walt Longmire mystery. [Reviewer's note: Not since reading Jim Harrison's works have I encountered writings that are so satisfying to read.]
intriguing and suspenseful just as I would expect from a Longmire mystery/adventure.

When a mysterious youth starts making repairs on a widow's house, Sheriff Walt Longmire and his staff come in contact with a breakaway Mormon sect that has acquired a large ranch in his county. Then an old man claiming to be Orrin Rockwell, a 1800s Mormon Avenging Angel, appears on the scene thing start to heat up. Johnson has written a darker story than normal in this hard to put down modern day Western but it does the series justice.

Wow. This one made me stay up until 2 am to finish it. Walt, Vic and Henry feel like old friends, friends I care about enough to stay up half the night worrying about. I so enjoyed the 200 yr old Mormon tough guy, the CIA connection, and the fact that we get to see more of Walt's territory. I am glad to see Vic growing up and coming to love Walt entirely-though I still deplore her language. I really feel a professional woman would use vulgarity more sparingly-for effect, not as everyday vocabulary. Henry Standing Bear's use of language, his sophistication and erudition continue to draw me in as much as the landscape, the situations and the events. Full disclosure: I have listened to this entire series on audiobook. George Guidall does a stellar job.
A decent read.

Another volume in the Sheriff Walt Longmire saga. An interesting plot about a runaway boy, a CIA operation and a religious cult. 
 Johnson has to tread carefully with all the plot baggage he has created over the past novels. It often seems that it doesn't mesh quite as well as it should with the particulars of Walt's criminal case. Also, Johnson is prone, at least in this book, to use repetitively certain descriptive adjectives which a good editor should have spotted. 
 Otherwise, the level of tension and humor a pretty good.

I discovered Craig Johnson by watching Longmire on A&E. While the show is wonderful, the books are so much more. This one doesn't disappoint. As always, past and present, personal and professional mix for Sheriff Longmire and at times it seems that I understand his world better than he does. I read this one out of sequence because I received a signed copy as a birthday present but it didn't matter. The plot is timely and complex, clues and red-hearings plentiful, and joys and sorrows intermingled to a satisfying whole. I recommend this book to anyone who loves a good mystery where the characters are as developed as the plots.

The Walt Longmire series continues with A Serpent's Tooth, which has a little more romance and a little less humor than its predecessors. Still, for fans of the series, it's satisfying, and will leave you wanting to read the next book as soon as it's published.

reference_books.review_text:
I have never, EVER read a book with more infuriating characters than this one. I found a reason to loathe nearly every adult character in this book. The only reason I'm giving this book 2.5 stars is because the author did a good job of making me feel real disdain towards fictional characters. By the time this book was over my face hurt because I spent the last 50% of the book donning the "stank face." 
 Let me begin with Tessa. I know some people won't understand why I would have an issue with Tessa, since she is the "victim" in all this. However, she is also an idiot. Over half of what she thinks when she speaks to her husband is not what she says. All because she is afraid to "to rock the boat" or make problems where there aren't any. God gave women intuition for a reason, so it stands to reason that if you have been with someone for 7 years and have never suspected him of cheating before, never been paranoid, never been jealous and now you are suspicious, there might be a problem. "Rocking the boat" should be the least of her worries because if I were in her shoes somebody better call the Coast Guard because I would be willing to blow up the ship to find out the truth. Nick would be like 
 I also have an issue with the way the author portrays Tessa. By the end of the book I knew Tessa-the-mom, Tessa-the-wife, but nothing about her as a person. And then thanking the skank at the end...WTH?!!! 
 The skank being Valerie. OMG I hate her, she is a negative, selfish horrible person. The only thing going for her is her son and she is doing a bang job of screwing him up too. I loathe her very imaginary existence because she knew precisely what she was doing and precisely where things were going and she allowed it to happen. And I could say she did it without thinking about Nick's wife and kids and how what they were doing would affect them, but that would be a lie. She thought about them, she thought about them a lot, she spent whole paragraphs thinking about his wife and kids...she just didn't care. All she cared about was what she wanted and what she felt she and her son deserved. I don't mind books showcasing controversial issues, but if you're going to put me in the head of the "other woman" you damn sure better make sure she's likeable or even relatable on some small level. What we needed to find out about her is why she uses her son as a shield against the world, why is her outlook on life so negative, why is it that the first woman she genuinely liked the thing she initially noticed was that her clothes were ill-fitting which made her less of a threat, and most importantly why does she keep attaching herself to emotionally unavailable men. In her personal life, she expects failure so therefore she fails. I just feel sorry that her son has to be taken along for the ride. 
 It's quite convenient that she didn't have any friends who could tell her that what she was doing was wrong. I was disappointed that she and her brother have the kind of relationship where they tell each other everything but not the kind where they actually give each other sound advice. 
 And my least favorite character of all...NICK! I wish the reader could have experienced some of this from his point of view because I have no idea why he did what he did. I saw no justification for his actions. The culmination of Tessa and his problems was so unextraordinary and lackluster until it can't be justified. I need his point of view to at least try and rationalize his infidelity. He claimed he wanted to help Charlie and liked being needed but that's a cop-out because he is a surgeon and he helps people every day. Help me understand the lying cheating bastard who tells his mistress that what they did was beautiful and he doesn't regret it and tells his wife it was a mistake and he wishes he never did it with the same tongue. Why was his love for his family enough to make him want to stay but not enough to keep him faithful? 
 I was also very underwhelmed by the faceoff between the women. Tessa said she wanted to know everything and I feel like she let Valerie off too easy and didn't dig deep enough. There were no true revelations. This should have been the climax of the story and it just felt like the buildup was wasted.

book_a.user_review:

sample_reviews.review_text:
Fallen had been sitting on my shelf for a year now. After watching an interview with author Lauren Kate at a book fair early November, I finally cracked its spine. My expectations weren't that high, nor were they exceptionally low. The considerable hype surrounding this series definitely had something to do with both the high and the low part. All the same, I ended up disappointed. 
 I just couldn't get into it. Part of that is the fact that it's written from a third person perspective, which nearly always makes me feel distanced from the characters and the events. I strongly prefer books with a first person narrator, books that make you - when you look in a mirror after you've read them - surprised not to see the main character's face looking back at you. 
 A second reason is the setting. It was bland and gray and boring and the fact that it was a disciplinary boarding school added little or nothing to the story - when it could've had. In my opinion, it would have been so much more interesting (and realistic. And creepy!) if Luce were sent to an asylum of some sort. 
 I also found myself being slung back and forth between my impression of the surroundings (being: rainy, dark, coldn gloomy - as Luce's mood) and the actual surroundings (being: sunny, warm, beautiful trees etc). Somehow it didn't seem to fit, leaving me confused whenever Luce commented on it being hot outside. "Wait a second, wasn't the sky weeping in despair just a second ago? No? Sunny skies all around? Well alrighty then ..." 
 Third reason: it took forever until something supernatural started occurring. 3/4th of this book is basically about a girl getting sent to boarding school, doing research, falling in love with 2 guys at once and being chased by rather harmless shadowy thingies. Yawn. Only at the very end things started getting interesting, but then there was too much happening all at once. I honestly couldn't be bothered anymore at that point. I wanted to get it over with. 
 Fourth reason: although the idea of Luce's incarnations always finding Daniel is, of course, extremely romantic, I didn't feel anything at their developing love. No nostalgic sighing, no latent butterflies. Nope. Nothing. Sorry. 
 Fifth and maybe most important reason: I - once again! - made the mistake of reading a translation from English to Dutch. As a general rule, they suck. And I suck for trying to keep reading them. From now on: only English books and Dutch books that were actually written in Dutch.

Reading this on a suggestion of a student...not impressed so far. 
 Eh-that's my overall comment. I know, I know, teens across the nation dig this series but I found it dark, murky and a little confusing (again, my beef about the author's obligation to give the reader a clear explanation of the fantasy land they create). I'm discouraged that I have a lot of girl students who are glued to this. It's another Twilight-esque romance with a human and non-human type: your run-of-the-mill inner-species romance. Ugh. 
 P.S. The main character is a big whiner, which is annoying and it's the same formula as all the books in what I call the "Inner-Species Dramovel" (new word meaning "drama-novel"). If you are unfamiliar with the formula, here it is: Girl meets hostile non-human boy appearing to be human. Girl figures out what non-human boy is as said non -human boy starts to warm-up to her. Girl is inept at almost everything, non-human boy must protect her from herself and forces of evil that will destroy her. Girl discover she and non-human boy have history and/or are destined to be together. Said destiny will take 3-5 books to fulfill. AND, odds are that non-human boy will talk girl out of taking on some non-human qualities, but she'll do it anyway. AND, count on a love triangle. YAWN! 
 Twilight CHECK 
 Fallen CHECK 
 Wolves of Mercy Falls CHECK (although this one had redeemable qualities) 
 City of Ashes CHECK 
 Vampire Academy CHECK (haven't read it...just assuming)

sample_reviews.review_text: The plot of this book was a MESS. I wanted to like it, but I was so confused about what was happening. It was like the author made a book with a combination of Harry Potter and the Walking Dead and had no idea where he was going with it.

I could not finish this book. Absolutely no suspense, very flat characters, forced dialect. And heavy handed--my goodness, so heavy handed about its messages about women's power, importance of community, etc. Not a very well structured book. I don't consider this urban fantasy as much as horror, since the world building is kinda weak. 
 I have heard so many good things about this author. Maybe I will pick up another of his books and give him another chance.

This is a deceptively deep little urban fantasy that treads a familiar path, plot-wise, but has some very interesting things to say about gentrification, culture appropriation, and the inherent power of a strong community. I think it suffers a bit from first-book syndrome; the dialogue is a definite weak point, and I really wanted all of the really compelling things that Older weaves into the story to connect into something deeper. Instead, the reader gets an abrupt ending that's just a bit too neat. Still, it's a tight, fast-paced story that is perfectly pitched to younger readers, and depicts some cultures and settings that don't get near enough page time in contemporary YA.
I'm a fantasy fan, so appreciated the general plot but didn't care for writing style.

Buy this for all of the young adults in your life and also all of the adults.

Such a good book! Great characters, an interesting magical story, Brooklyn. Art and magic and folklore and riddles and commentary about anthropology and monsters and.... 
 I am rethinking several other books I gave a 5-star rating to, just because this book is so above-the-others good. 
 And I'm doing what I almost never do- going back and rereading it immediately. 
 2017 update: listening to and loving the audiobook.
I wish I could give this 3.5 stars.
Darned entertaining. The description promised a cross between The Mortal Instruments and Caribbean folklore, and that's pretty much exactly what the book delivered. What I was expecting, I got.

I really, really wanted to love this book. The absolutely beautiful cover! Urban fantasy! Half Puerto Rican, half black heroine! PoC characters! Art! Ghosts! This book had so many things going for it, and then it just fell flat. There were some wonderful moments in this book, and some of the writing is beautiful, and funny (also, love Nydia - she speaks to my inner archivist nerd), but the world building was meh - there's almost no explanation about the shadowshaper's magical abilities - is it inherited? Is it learned? How do you pass on the magic to someone else? Why did Lazaro, a fiercely proud Puerto Rican man with strong family and community sensibilities, trust an outsider with the shadowshaping knowledge? Everything happens much too quickly, and leaves too many gaping holes. 
 I also have to take issue with the blatant stereotyping of white people. The casual "white people" jokes (which, lets face it, if the joking was reversed, would not fly in a white populated story), the idea that white people are all rich and have no cultural pride or identity, and the fact that the only white character was the natural "bad guy" - there was literally no other speculation about who could be behind all of the evil things going on; Sierra decided in the middle of the book that it was the white dude, and that was that. 
 Hopefully, there will be a sequel, and all of the questions (who and where is Sierra's father? Does her other brother know about shadowshaper magic? Who the hell is Timothy, and what was the point of him? How long can a spirit inhabit a painting, sculpture, etc.? How do regular people not notice a giant mural literally leaping to life off of a wall? Who are the Sorrows, what are their powers, and what is their connection to the Shadowshapers?) will be answered.

reference_books.title: Damned (Damned, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
You know that sensation when you're unable to shower for a day or two? For example, you're camping, or on a marathon car trip or long international flight... your skin develops an ultra-thin film; an ever-present additional layer of grime that hugs you and leaves you feeling uncomfortable until the next time you can clean yourself up. 
 That's exactly what the experience of reading a Chuck P book is like. Each one explores a different rabbit hole in the burrow of human depravity. They're certainly not for everyone. 
 Just as reading a Brett Easton Ellis novel will leave you feeling that there's no point to life and people are just nihilistic, narcissistic douchebags, Chuck P (gave up trying to freehand-write his last name years ago) novels leave you feeling that, deep down, we're all disgusting creatures, unworthy of the regal notions we ascribe to ourselves. 
 Like I said, not for everybody. 
 In Damned, Chuckers take us on a trip through hell via the experiences of 13-year old Maddy Spencer, and her journey to find meaning in the afterlife. 
 The good: the setting. I mean, c'mon, how many books are set in hell? (right, right, Dante. Shut up.) From the start, I was excited to see how the twisted mind of Chucky P would build the world of the damned. And he's smart about it... the details are given out achingly slow at the beginning. He does, over the course of the first half, build a demented and funny world for Maddy to explore. One little example (no spoilers after this, I promise): everyone in hell has to work. You have a choice of two jobs: you can either perform depraved and vile sex acts on webcam for earthlings, or you can work in telemarketing. 
 The bad: like most Chuck P books, there's a plot twist near the end. While it's well-done and surprised me, it doesn't really go anywhere. Maybe that's because there's a sequel coming out next year and Chuckkity P planned it that way, but I thought this story deserved more of its own resolution. Fulfill me, Chuck, I've earned it.

This really is a good read. Recently there have been many truly excellent young adult titles, but popularity is no guarantee of excellence, so I wasn't expecting much, and I have been more than pleasantly surprised. After feeling resistant to the first page or two, the book won me over. Who doesn't love a good survival story? I began to find the narrator's voice is very appealing, the way she can figure things out. Always great to have a strong, capable female protagonist. I like that she comes from Appalachia and has all those nature skills. Also, I guess it doesn't hurt that I like reality TV - I think the author is spot on in creating a future that present-day readers can really relate to, by giving us a survival reality TV show set in a post-apocalyptic world.
I've never watched an entire episode of Survivor, but this book is an interesting juxtaposition of Lord of the Flies and reality TV. Much edgier that her Gregor series. I can't wait for the sequel.

The Hunger Games is a controversial young adult dystopian novel that is a highly competitive death-dealing game, and a fight for survival. I couldn't watch the film - there wasn't enough to grab my attention - but the book was bought as a gift and was the only dystopian one on my shelf. As a result, I didn't begin reading with much expectation that I would take to the novel: I'm not a fan of the young adult genre in general, with some exceptions. 
 The novel had quite a potent political message, especially early on. It illustrates simply and yet strongly how inequality can lead to resentment between the starving and the better-off, even if both groups know better on a full stomach. It's a clever ploy of the Capitol's system to divide the people so that their hold on power is relatively undisrupted. The Capitol uses official excuses for those who have starved to death, burying their guilt and complicity at ridding many of the districts of their inhabitants. The population are not fooled, but what can they do to act against the Capitol when the Treaty of Treason is an intimidating warning to those who would oppose them, in the form of a reminder that past uprisings have bitterly failed. It's at this point the reader must wonder how accurate this history is, and if it is, why do the Capitol need to remind the districts not to rebel if there weren't weaknesses? 
 Let's start with the positive. There were more than a few lengthy passages that sustained my interest, mostly between Katniss and Peeta's struggle to understand and trust each other before they entered the Hunger Games as the two Tributes representing District 12. The battle for survival in the arena started off very well, capturing my interest and impressing upon me the severity of Katniss' predicament. The conclusion as well, was well written, emotionally tense, and with enough peril to make it impressive. First-person point-of-view worked well at intervals, bringing Katniss' personality, likes, and dislikes to the fore and engaging the reader. 
 Katniss' voice did bother me, rendering her emotionally numb to any related or past events. This is where first-person point-of-view didn't work well, and the switches were occasionally noticeable. Katniss and Peeta's mostly passive and tolerant attitude to following rules irritated me. I know why they did it - to protect their families - but it almost seemed to justify the need for a sycophantic totalitarian regime, bloated by wealth and superficiality. It made the characters sick, and it made me feel sick, but the characters still went along with it more often that I would have liked. I'm obviously only commenting as a reader/observer here and not a participant in the Hunger Games; maybe that would make a difference to my opinions. 
 Katniss's boundaries were pushed once or twice, causing her to act in rebellion, but her actions only really made a difference where it concerned the Capitol's perception of her and to me reinforced the idea that if you have enough talent you can become popular enough that it doesn't matter that most districts are starved and oppressed. The bottom line is that Katniss and Peeta were absolutely helpless, and had to do as they were told. I didn't think this philosophy did much to encourage young adults in life, even if the suspense and gory deaths were appealing to some.

When I saw the movie with my daughter I knew I needed to read the books. I think it would be difficult to review this book without having read the series, and I recommend reading all three books. I will not detail the plot or charaters, as these are welll known at this point. As a series they are well written and the first person narrative is perfect for the nature of the story. As Borges once noted, the amount of suffering that can be known and understood at one time by a person is that of one other person. We cannot feel the suffering of millions save through the suffering of one. The Hunger Games trilogy makes this clear. 
 The Hunger Games is part a young adult read, part adult cautionary tale. Read alone, which it can be, it is a reflection on how children can be used to punish the sins of their parents while keeping the parents under political and economic control. It can be read as ancritique of current times. My 12yo daughter saw this clearly, which was startling. 
 A final note-- There has been some critique that the second book, Catching Fire, was not as good as the other two, but that is not the case.

Firstly I want to say I didn't particularly want to read The Hunger Games. I have found that books with such hype around them are rarely that good. However my husband who is incredibly critical read the book and liked it and recommended I did the same. So I gave it a go. 
 I have to say that I was presently surprised; despite the slow start (I found Part 1 slightly unbearable) the story really got going once the contestants hit the arena and the Hunger Games began. Set in a dystopian North America the Hunger Games are used to control the population of twelve districts which surround the Capitol. Two children/teenagers are picked every year from each district to fight to the death while the population watches. 
 This was all round a good story, Katniss (the heroine) is actually quite badass (Bella from Twilight could learn a lot) which is refreshing. The action sequences are exciting and the conclusion of the book seems to lead nicely to the second book, although obviously I know this is a trilogy so that point is irrelevant. All in all I enjoyed.

book_b.title: Inferno (Robert Langdon, #4)
book_b.user_review:
Damn you, Dan Brown, you got me again. 
 You know in prison movies, when the con slips the guard $20 so he and his boys can brutalize some fresh fish in the shower? That's a bit what reading a Dan Brown book is like. Not the prison rape, I mean, more like looking the other way. A Dan Brown book reads like a mixture of thriller and art history textbook. You have to ignore a lot of bad prose and overly long pretentious lecture sections to get to the good stuff... fun chase scenes and plot twists. This book, however, had none of that fun. 
 My troubled history with Dan Brown: 
 The DaVince Code - the first Robert Langdon mystery I read. I know that it's pretty much literary-snob standard to shun this book, but I liked it. Despite some cringe-worthy prose, pointless sections about art history, and wooden characters, the thriller parts were enticing and the plot twists were unexpected. 
 Angels and Demons - next, this. And it sucked. Too long, too talky, and never gripped me. I let it go, because it was the first Robert Langdon book. Maybe he was just getting warmed up. 
 The Lost Symbol - somewhere in between those two. The story wasn't all that great, but it did have a nice plot twist near the end. It was what a plot twist should be: when you read it, you smack your head and go "omg that's so obvious, why didn't I see that before?" 
 And now, Inferno. This may be the worst book I've ever read. 
 The Robert Langdon books are becoming formulaic at this point. Take Robert, add in a sexy female costar who- despite some mild sexual tension with Robert- only serves to act as an ear while Langdon explains the universe. Add in a death and a mystery that ties into symbols (Langdon is a symbologist, which I find hard to believe that these guys get so much work) and art history, then send them both on a scavenger hunt to piece together the puzzle. 
 Sample chapters go like this: 
 Robert Langdon and [insert name of sexy platonic soundboard female] rushed into plaza of the [name of European landmark] to escape the police. "Did you know," Robert Langdon said, "that [name of European Landmark] was originally..." [3 paragraphs copied straight from Wikipedia about said European Landmark]. 
 Things that drove me crazy in this book: 
 Plot twists. Hallmarks of the series, maybe the law of diminishing returns has made these less effective. Near the end of the book, there are a series of them, in rapid fire (where some characters LITERALLY sit Robert Langdon down and explain everything to him). Whereas in The Lost Symbol, the plot twist was surprising and clarified certain elements of the story, in this book, the plot twists muddle everything. One massive one twist flips the whole story on its head, and I was immediately ripped from the action. It contradicted so much of the previous story that the damn just broke loose. All I could think was "If X is really Y, then how come Z happened?" The kind of story reveal that you're sure just can't be possible because it seemingly nullifies multiple events that have come before (think Shutter Island). At one point in the midst of this craziness, Robert Langdon says "none of this makes any sense." I'm right there with you, Bob. 
 The pretentious use of language. Most of this book is in Italy, and so characters will have a conversation in Italian, and then Dan Brown will translate after each sentence. Maybe he was going for authentic, but it just comes off as snooty. "I'm Dan Brown, and I spent a bunch of time on Google Translate, so I want to make sure that gets in the book." Just tell us they're talking in Italian, and then write it in English. Could have saved a lot of word count. 
 Completely useless and unbelievably baffling over-explanatory adverbs and descriptions. Early on, Brown says that the woman moved her fingers "purposefully" when she was pressing buttons on a phone to call someone. Seriously? Do we really need that adverb to heighten the mood? Also, he uses pointless extraneous descriptors, which drives the Harsh super-crazy... saying things like "unbelievably beautiful" and "surprisingly smooth". 
 Out of touch with the modern age. Much of this book is about Dante's Inferno, and paintings inspired by it. On more than one occasion, he describes people (even young people) looking at pictures of paintings of hell, with its lake of fire, and tormented souls, and the people looking at these pictures become very disturbed by their graphic nature. Really? Do you actually think, in the era of 2 Girls 1 Cup, that looking at a picture of a centuries-old painting will disturb anyone, particularly college students? 
 The breadcrumbs left by the bad guy. AAAARGH! OMG THIS MAKES THE HARSH SOOO MAD!!! For no discernible reason, the villain leaves Robert Langdon a seemingly-deliberate series of clues for him to explore and thus foil his plans. Why the %^*#* does he do that? I understand there'd be no story without it, but you have to to give me some kind of explanation as to why he'd do this. Come on, I'm begging here. When you leave your characters' motivations a mystery, the reader is left to imagine, and it's a terrible distraction from the story. 
 DaVinci Code was so popular not for being a great book, but largely for being a book that had a modicum of controversial statements about religious types... the other three Robert Langdon books have little of that. If Dan Brown really wanted to drum up book sales, he should have set the book in Iran, and it would have been about a murder, about which Robert Langdon uncovers a conspiracy that the Prophet Muhammad was actually Jesus' half brother. BOOM. Billions of books sold. Inferno is no conspiracy, or controversy. The plot never gets exciting or edgy at all. Langdon just runs around Italy, looking for stuff, then some people tell him that everything isn't what he thought it was. Then they chase somebody at the end. At that point, I had completely stopped caring. I was barely able to finish the pile of crap. I feel like I should be compensated for my time (looking at you, HuffPo, if you're hiring). 
 In all fairness, there was one (of the dozen or so) plot twist at the end that was fairly clever. 
 And so, despite hating this book, I'm such a sucker that when Dan Brown releases the next book about how Robert Langdon uncovers the conspiracy behind the disappearance of the settlement at Roanoke three years from now, I'll probably read that one too. Damnit.

sample_reviews.review_text: I have mixed feelings about this one. It's not as intriguing as Brown's previous works but I still managed to find myself mesmerized by the beauty of the Italian skyline as described by Brown's extensive historical vocabulary. Another plus is the philosophical standpoint (a sentiment which I deeply share) with regards to overpopulation and management of ecological resources. Humans have become so egoistic that nature suffers in our wake of population explosion. The ending is a little divergent from the usual resolution in other thrillers, but illustrates something thought-provoking that needs to be addressed in the real world.

A fun read! I now know more about Dante's Inferno than I thought I ever would...and there were great descriptions of classical Italian art and cities, etc. This book was a typical exciting Dan Brown, with many adventures, fun pursuits and escapes, and a some surprising twists along the way. A very entertaining read!

It isn't that the story isn't interesting; it is. It isn't that the plot doesn't move along well; it does. It's just that Robert Langdon is the Ken doll of literary characters, good-looking on the surface but bland and without genitalia. It did seem that Dan Brown gave a little more detail to his main character but if an author is going to have a continuing character at all shouldn't that character be well-detailed? All I find really distinguishing about Rober Langdon is his attachment to his Harris Tweed jacket and his Mickey Mouse watch.He may have claustrophobia but it doesn't play a part in the plot so it just seems thrown in there.
So not impressed with this book. I thought he was a better writer than what I found here.

At chapter 5: 
 Not off to a great start... I can usually get past Dan Brown's writing because he's so good at high-intensity, page-turner storytelling and peppering in history and facts. But starting with a dream sequence? Packing THIS many cliches into each paragraph? An incredibly unrealistic exchange with a hot nurse? Where was his editor on these? Maybe my standards have changed, but I don't know if I can make it through this one. Hubby and I have read other Dan Brown novels together, but I think he's dropping out and leaving me to fend for myself. I'll give it a few more chapters, but I might be switching over to the original "Inferno." 
 *Update* 
 At Chapter 49: 
 Not gonna finish this one. I tried, I really did. I encouraged hubby to keep reading, and he's enjoying it now, but I've gotten bored and can't stay focused on it. Unfortunately, I think the Dan Brown formula is just too stale for me at this point. I've been able to predict every scene so far, and that's no fun. And DB's social commentary started to get old (really, most 20-somethings are not obsessed with Googling themselves). 
 Also, DB, why not add some depth to Langdon? By book 4, I was hoping he'd be more than just a claustrophobic know-it-all with a Mickey Mouse watch. Haven't all these life-threatening adventures affected him at all? At this point, it seems more likely that he'd be a paranoid PTSD patient, unable to hold a job and dragging his therapist through a bunch of imaginary adventures, than a stable professor off to save the world from anther conspiracy. Poor guy. 
 That being said, if you like Dan Brown and just can't get enough of high-intensity chase scenes through art museums, this book is for you.

Boring. 
 Dan Brown - you need a new formula.

Good quick read but it is pretty formulaic, especially for Brown. He continues to put the existence of humanity at stake in every novel and in every novel there is a nicely wrapped ending with a bow. It was a good read, but NOT my favorite.

Never having before read a Dan Brown novel, I really felt that it was time I got round to filling this little void in my reading landscape, especially as he has such a huge fan base; then along came a copy of Inferno. 
 Sadly, it turned out to not really be my thing. I found the writing too mechanical; I do like a nice, rythmic flow to whatever I am reading and Inferno does not have that. I found that I developed little empathy for the lead character, Robert Langdon, who never made any kind of meaningful connection with me. On the other hand, I did find one of the other characters, Sienna Brooks, a far more engaging individual and certainly more intriguing. 
 I assume the author spent a good deal of time researching the fabulous cities that provide the backdrop for this story and he makes considerable use of what he learnt. The trouble is, there is too much of this, with repeatedly long, detailed, and sometimes uninspiring passages describing individual buildings or specific aspects of a room. 
 For me, the best parts of the book are those where Brown simply gets on with the action, at which point things move along quite nicely.

Oh dear why was I surprised? 
 The action picks up in Florence where Robert Langdon has just woken up with amnesia, what happens next can only be ripped from scenes of a Hollywood action blockbuster as he and the latest femme rush across the city in a murder mystery plot, all revolving around the text of Dante's Inferno. 
 Things take a drastic turn for the ridiculous as the novel continues and finishes in a way so unbelievable that I was actually speechless for a moment. Just think of a magician waving their hand over your eyes and murmer, 'Science!'.

I give 2stars for its pertinent subject-population explosion and a diabolically scary solution. Book is more a travel brochure for Venice etc than a thriller. Pace is sluggish/action mediocre. There are no hair pin bends that wake you from reverie or keep your nerves crackling. I finished the book, well, coz I always do (barring 'The Satanic Verses' that I couldn't go beyond 8-9pgs). I could pre guess the turns that the storyline was going to take-hence found the book to be 'mediocre'. Boring.

This was exactly what I wanted it to be. The writing style was engaging and highly readable from the get-go, and the creepiness started almost immediately. 
 I love the way Koontz combines psychological horror with action. Both types of excitement are balanced perfectly, so there are no long, boring segments of one or the other. The protagonist spends a satisfying amount of time contemplating a terrifying moral dilemma, but before the dilemma is overly fleshed out and analyzed, something super violent will happen. It isn't pointless violence, though- everything ties back into the psychological horror later on. 
 The characters are realistic, especially the protagonist, Billy. He is not always likable, but he never does anything unjustified enough to make me stop rooting for him. This is extremely important in this type of genre, because the moment I view the protagonist as evil, all bets are off when it comes to psychological distress. Who cares if an unforgivable person has to make a moral choice? I couldn't see myself in that character, nor would I really care that he felt guilty- he should! However, I always liked Billy, despite his flaws. 
 He also reacted well to everything. There were enough personal details involved in his decisions that I felt like his character was realistic, but not so many that I wasn't also forced to think about what I would do in his situation. I also wasn't bored by pages and pages of nothing but character development. Billy also doesn't have endless abilities or strengths. Although the plot isn't very realistic, I could easily suspend reality because of the characterization. 
 If the plot sounds at all interesting to you, I highly recommend this book. It does not disappoint.

It has a promising start: A guy gets a note on his car that one person will be killed if he goes to the police or another person will be killed if he doesn't. After that, it is not about humans anymore, but instead cardboard cutouts with traits tacked on. In Velocity, Koontz is pretty much writing at this level.

book_b.user_review: An awe inspiring book. one of those true books out there that can really change your outlook on life. the book reads as if there are many short stories woven together, and what comes out is true brilliance. I feel as each story or perspective highlights the main theme of destroying the anchors that come in the way of our true happiness.

sample_reviews.review_text: Although this book was well written, and at times pulled me in. It just didn't grab me the way Khaled Hosseini's other books have. It's more like a collection of short stories, that while are linked, really don't come together in the end.

It's been a few days since I finished this book and I can't figure out why it was on some of the best of 2013 lists. I enjoyed the story, Hosseini is a really beautiful writer, but the plot fell short. The entire book revolves around reuniting brother and sister torn apart as children. Their story is told through lives of a slew of other characters you meet during the novels duration. Unfortunately, while it was a great idea, this is where the book falls short. Hosseini introduces new characters for a chapter or two at a time, spends a lot of time getting the reader invested in them, and then never mentions them again. These characters were important for the overall story but about a third of the detail was needed describing these people so when they are pulled away, the reader wasn't left confused. I honestly couldn't tell you why many of these details were even shared, since they had no overall investment in the plot. It weighed the book down immensely. I would've like some more character development in the correct direction. In the end, the novels two protagonists still felt like strangers while you were very well acquainted with minor players in this whole story. I finished the book feeling it wasn't complete and not because Hosseini meant for it to be this way, but simply because he didn't finish writing the book the way it needed to be written. 
 I would still recommend this novel because Hosseini's writing style is always a joy to read, but do not expect it to be of the same caliber as his past books.

Khaled Hosseini writes a good story, the style of this book though did not suit my style of reading. 
 As always Hosseini has a way with words and what I did read was enjoyable and would recommend this book to his followers.

The writing in this book was beautiful but the plot was confusing muddled with characters whose stories went nowhere and had little bearing to what I felt was the main story, that of Abdullah and Pari. The side stories of Markos and Thalia, the Bashiri cousins and Iqbal and the commander and his son were never developed and had little to no bearing when it came to the central story of Abdullah and Pari. There were minor connections but sometimes the connections were allusive. I kept thinking that Hosseini would tie them all together at one point but he never did. There were also sudden jumps from past to present with no warning which at times made the book hard to follow. I found the book wandered from idea to idea without any real clarity of plot. I am not sorry I read it but it was not as well done as Hosseini's other works. It almost would have better served as a collection of stories rather than a novel but maybe I missed something. Overall rating: disappointed.

sample_reviews.review_text: After having consumed the entire Fallen series, I was so excited to hear bad boy Cam was getting his own story and possible HEA. In some ways, it lived up to the earlier books about Lucinda and Daniel. However, despite Cam's charm and desire to help Lilith, the story didn't ring as true for me. It was a pleasant, easy read but just didn't pack the same emotional punch as the other books. For the most part, I felt it was because I didn't quite buy Cam's adoration of Lilith. I don't recall ever hearing about the girl he loved and lost and she seemed to have come out of the blue for me. I am a huge fan of Lauren Kate and continue to be so. I guess I'm just Team Daniel.

I remember really enjoying the first few books in this series but since it's been years since I've picked up the first book, it was difficult for me to reenter the series again. I basically had to re-fall in love with Dan and Luce and the whole premise once again. Surprisingly, I ended up enjoying the spin-off (the last book in the series is actually a spin-off and not at all related to Luce or Dan) more than the conclusion of Dan and Luce's cursed love. 
 I also enjoyed the novella, Fallen in Love, mainly because it allowed me to understand the other angels a little more even though when I first picked up the book, I had no recollection on any of the characters so the first couple in the novella, Miles and Shelby, were completely lost on me. Actually, now that I think of it, I'm still not 100% sure who they are...LOL. However, Roland and Arianne's own stories made a lot of sense because they were still prominent characters in the fourth and final ("final") book. I particularly liked Arianne's story because I did not know she geared that way. It was a little shocking but I liked it because even angels do not have boundaries on love and I think that's great. 
 I'm not going to talk too much about Dan or Luce mainly because I think most of the character building occurred in the beginning of the series and I was essentially only reading the conclusion in book 4, Rapture. Therefore, I will discuss more about the plot and the conclusion. First of all, I was shocked with the ending. I thought the whole purpose of the series was a cursed love between an angel and a human. However, Lauren completely skewed from that and revealed the ultimate reason as to why Dan and Luce have a cursed love to start with. Second, I think that ultimate reason is bogus. I found it ludicrous and ridiculous because, I mean, these are angels. Why do they need to pick a side and failure to do so would end up in a lifetimes of lifetimes of a love that will ultimately lead to death? Needless to say, I was not satisfied with that reasoning but it did give a good introduction into the "final" book of the series. 
 The whole premise with Unforgiven was fascinating. The idea of Lilith being sent to a purgatory of different aspects of hell that circle on the main thing - revenge - was interesting. You don't really understand what the story behind was until later on in the book and then you're like "OH, so that's what happened" and then you feel bad for the two of them. To be honest though, this whole drama stemmed from Cam's inability to trust in Lilith enough. If he only had the guts to tell her or show her, then they would have lived a happily ever after and maybe Cam wouldn't even have sided with Lucifer to start with. But no, he had to be stubborn and scared. I'm just glad it all worked out for them because I simply cannot imagine living different kinds of hell over and over again because of a deal gone bad. 
 Overall, I still think this series was good mainly because I do remember enjoying the first and the third book a lot with the second one being a bit of a lull. And Cam's story in Unforgiven was enlightening. I also like you not only got a closer glance at Cam's background but also more on Lucifer's personality. There were a lot of LOL moments between the two.

Let me start off by saying that I am among the seemingly few that actually enjoyed the Fallen series. I have always put that down to people having different tastes in books, etc... now, however, I am beginning to think that I was too young and stupid to NOT like them. 
 Because, let me tell you, I do not really remember the specifics of them all that well, but if they are written at all like Unforgiven is, then I don't know what I was thinking all those years ago. This book was terrible. It was more than terrible - it was so, SO bad that I cannot put into family-friendly terms how much I hated it. 
 I always, ALWAYS finish books, okay, but this was SO close to being a DNF for me. Every time I picked it up, I wanted to put it down, but in the end I settled for so many exaggerated eye rolls that I had a headache after thirty pages. 
 It was just so incredibly annoying - and the worst thing? I can't even pinpoint exactly what was so bad about it. The writing was terrible, the book an easy read and not in a good way, the characters were inconsistent and shallow, and the story... OH THE stORY. It was one giant freaking cliche (please note that 'freaking' was not the first word that came to mind here), and the fact that it was written terribly did this horrible, over-used plot line no favours. 
 So, to sum up, do NOT read this book. It doesn't matter if you enjoyed the Fallen series or whatever, this book will make you reevaluate everything - and possibly, God forbid, re-read them. Don't. I have made this mistake so that others don't have to. Please, don't let my sacrifice be in vain.

My review - Anyone who knows me knows that I ADORED the Fallen series! It was one of the first series that got me really into reading and when I found out that Lauren was writing a book from Cam's POV I may have done a little squeal and an even bigger squeal when it came through my door, it was such a great surprise that I jumped right into reading it! 
 In this story Cam made a bet with Lucifer, has 15 days for Lilith to fall in love with him and they can be together but if he fails he will be sent to hell. It doesn't help that Lilith hates his guts. 
 This story had me in so many different emotions that I really enjoyed every second of it! 
 I am a big Daniel fan but there was always something about Cam that I loved. I just didn't love him with Luce so I was really excited to read about him hopefully getting his happy ending! Even though he is a bad boy he can be so lovely some times. 
 I also loved that you got to see some familiar faces. 
 It had the same amount of humour, romance, drama that the other books in the Fallen series had and I am so happy to be back in this world. 
 Lauren has done a brilliant job with this book that I didn't put it down once until I finished it and even after that I didn't want the book to be over. 
 It was just really brilliant! 
 I really hope there will be more because I need MORE! If you haven't started this series then you need to get too it so you can read this wonderful series and read this fantastic book that is Unforgiven.

No plot Spoilers! Let me start by saying I was not a huge fan of the Fallen series. I liked the idea but it is not a series I ever plan on rereading, like some others I have enjoyed. I felt the series went on way too long and went down hill with each new book. When I found out whole reasoning for the curse and Satan's fury I was like....what????? That's it???....how silly!!! Anyway, one character I did really like from the series was the dark, enigmatic, charming, witty and over all sexy Cam. I was interested when I found out the author decided to delve into his history more so I checked it out. 
 The main thing I can say about this book is ...where is Cam?????? 
 OK so Cam is a main character but he is not the Cam we know from the Fallen series. Subtract most of the dark, charming, witty and sexy...add in some major teen angst, insecurity, fading looks, weakness, and at times down right stupidity and you have the Cam in this book. No spoilers as you can read most of this in the blurb above. The book is about Cam trying to save his lost love Lilith from Satan and her personal hell. Her life sucks and it is his fault ( not sure exactly why) so he goes into her life and high school to right the wrong. We very briefly met her in one of the Fallen books (the 3rd?) and saw a moment of their history and how it helped turned Cam to the dark side. Most of this book is told from Lilith's point of view and her head is not fun to be in. It is not badly written and the story had promise, but Lilith is rather two note ( angry or infatuated) and most of the other characters besides Satan are throwaway. ( the brother being the most interesting). The romance is bland because there is no real chemistry between them. Some of the Fallen characters do appear ( not Daniel or Luce) but their roles are really minor and not sure what they are doing there except to make the Fallen fans happy to read their names again. 
 My main problem (other than the personality change in Cam) is that it is repetitive and DRAGS, seriously you could read just the first and last 3 chapters and be fine. The action ( or lack thereof) in the middle seems like filler. I had to force myself to finish and once it got exciting BAM it was over. 
 I am not sure why the author decided to write this book other than to return to her successful series since her new one is not doing well. She can write well but this book was a waste of time. Also from a few lines at the end I have a feeling this may be the beginning of a new series. The premise has been set up to continue on. Time will tell. Overall I can recommend this book only to die hard loyal Fallen fans if you go in with LOW expectation on Cam and this story. 
 For others I say this is one to skip. If you do read it get it from the library like I did. It is not worth buying.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I really though I would enjoy this book. The overall story looked really interesting to me. I was expecting a romance thriller. I defiantly got a little bit of both. 
 I really liked the whole concept of the book, but I lacked connection with it. When I'm reading books i can really tell if i love the book when i feel what the character feels. I didn't during this book. When the main character Stella/Estella gets attacked the first time by trigger i felt a little scared but didn't really care. Then during the end of the book when the member of Danny's cartel came to kill stella i wasn't scared and honestly didn't care if she died. When Chet came down to save her I got upset when he "got shot" but i wasn't overflowing with emotion. 
 Ok the romance part. I really liked Chet, but the overall romance part of the book lacked for me. I was drawn to this book partially because i love teen romance stories, BUT THERE WAS NONE OF THAT. I mean they kissed like twice and the fell in love there was nothing there. It was like 5% of the whole story. This really bothered me. 
 I thought the ending was very predictable. I guessed that dusty was the father of inny's baby. I guessed that Chet didn't die, and that the gun shot was Carmina. Overall I think the whole book was very predictable. Besides that the big shock that came at the end wasn't very shocking. First of all the main character stella didn't mention that she lied and that lie was"tearing her apart" inside until the last 100 pages of the book. Doesn't seem like it was that terrible at all. When I found out that her mom killed the drug dealer instead of Danny i was like okay whatever.

3.5 stars - this was no literary masterpiece, but it definitely kept me turning the pages!!
This book pissed me off. Full of stereotypes, nothing original, and a non-conclusive, strung-together ending. The plot was thin, jumped around a bit, and was not compelling or convincing.
I loved this book!!!!

I put this on my mysteries and thrillers shelf, but there was little mystery, and even fewer thrills for me. 
 The style of this book was just so wooden and stiff. I just don't think it's realistic for characters to have twenty minute long conversations where they give you all the exposition in a neat, easy package. Conversely, I felt like all the movements in the plot were kind of abrupt. People's emotions and opinions changed, seemingly over the course of a single page, and it didn't feel like any character had a realistic story arc. In fact, none of the characters really had any development at all, really. 
 The audiobook narration wasn't my favorite. It wasn't terrible, but the narrator liked to differentiate male voices by just putting large pauses between all the words (this is also how she indicates tension). That's...pretty weird. 
 I guess this would be good for fans of Fitzpatrick, since other reviews seem to indicate that it's fairly consistent with her style. This was definitely not the book for me, though.

This is not a thriller, I can surely say. The storyline is slow paced and not really one you can get so intrigued about. 
 I just felt it as a general teen story with a just little, very little hint of suspense, which is not so exciting either. 
 Well, it's not completely boring or bad, but just not as expected (of a thriller). Good for a casual read.
I generally enjoy these types of stories with a bit of suspense and romance. There were a few unresolved questions after the climax that bothered me.

Mentiras peligrosas de la escritora Becca Fitzpatrick (Tambien escritora de la saga Hush Hush) fue todo lo que siempre espere de esta autora... !Una completa monotonia aburrida, de historias ya antes dichas, que se repetiran hasta el cansancio 1001 veces mas! Sus personajes carecen de fuerza, la protagonista es muy insulsa y mononeuronal, por otra parte Chet (Muy parecido a Patch no...) fue un personaje tierno y sincero pero demasiado falso y poco realista a la hora de compararlo con un plano real. Aqui ocurre lo que siempre sucede en este tipo de libros, un amor instantaneo y ferviente donde darian la vida por el otro sin dudarlo y no hay suficiente espacio ni en el cielo o en la tierra para todo el amor y comprension que se tienen. 
 Personalmente yo ya me rendi con este tipo de libros, ya no son lo que yo espero, no aprendi nada nuevo, malo o bueno, y la verdad no es de mi agrado este tipo de lecturas, no estoy teniendo una mala epoca con las historias romanticas, estoy teniendo una mala racha de historias romanticas sin sentido (Aunque se supone este libro es genero "Policiaco") que culminan casi siempre de la misma falsa y triste manera, es muy deprimente observar como estos son los tipos de libros que se venden de manera fugaz e instantanea, me parece que son hechos por autores en decadencia deprimidos y con poca imaginacion. 
 Estos libros ocasionan una enfermedad, encapsulan las mentes y no dejan volar, no aportan nada que ya no exista, es como cuando juegas scrabble y alguien pone "vaso" pero tu viste la oportunidad de colocar una "s" al final de la palabra y colocas "vasos" ?Esos puntos obtenidos son realmente tuyos? La verdad es que la palabra ya estaba echada, existia esa base, tu solo conseguiste una manera de alargarla un poco mas y lograr una cantidad mayor de puntos. 
 Admito, que me gusta que la protagonista alcanzara un nivel de conciencia e inteligencia mas alto, de hecho, al nivel al que deberia haber estado tras pasar todo lo que le habia tocado vivir, y ya tan al borde de los 18. Desde un inicio deseaba que Estella pudiera madurar, pero me parecio un poco tarde y ridicula la espera, y ademas fue como por acto de un golpe que crecio, y puedo decir que eso gritaba hacia todas direcciones: !FALSO! 
 P.d.: Otro punto positivo del libro es que emplearon la palabra, etereo, y me encanta esa palabra. 
 P.d.: De todos modos senti que perdi mi tiempo.

"We spend our lives running from our past, never realizing it's hitched to us - we can't ever outrun it." 
 As a fan of Becca's works since the Hush, Hush Saga, it's been my habit to read all of her books. I don't know, it's just that her writing and her stories really got a hold of me so when I saw this book I got a feeling of excitement and thrill. 
 Dangerous Lies is definitely not a perfect book but I believe that this is a good read. There are some parts of the book especially in the middle that lack some happenings. Also I'm not satisfied with the ending, it left me wondering what happened to some of the characters like Reed and what will come next to the people in Thunder Basin. 
 Overall I still like the book with its plot twist even if the story lack some things that may have made the book better and also kudos to Becca for not entirely focusing on the romance between Chet and Stella. I'm looking forward for her next book.

After reading (and loving) the Hush, Hush series and Black Ice, I was excited to get my hands on this book once I saw it at the bookstore. I SO BADLY wanted to love this book too but it was a major disappointment for me. The synopsis made the entire book sound exciting but, sorry to tell you, the only exciting part happened near the end of the book. The rest are just plain MEH for me. *sighs*

reference_books.title: The River at Night
reference_books.review_text:
Winifred who is basically the main narrator of the story. Her character is so complex that it is hard to describe her in one sentence. She seems to be at that point where she is just overwhelmed by everything happening all at once. Her long marriage has just ended, her beloved brother has died, and she is wondering where her career is going and why she chose it to begin with. 
 Enter her three best friends who have decided to go extreme hiking and river rafting in the remote wilderness. Winfred is the cautious one but is talked into going on the trip despite her concerns.

 friends stranded in the wilderness trying to survive against all odds. The story is unique because of the complex relationships between the friends and Wini herself.
