 it dragged some parts

reference_books.title: Behind Her Eyes
reference_books.review_text:
BEHIND HER EYES by Sarah Pinborough is such a fiercely chilling thriller that will leave you wondering about the characters the entire time you're reading. Three people become entangled in each other's lives. A woman meets a man in a bar. Sparks fly. They share a kiss. Low and behold the woman walks into her office the next morning and the guy in the bar is her new boss. Next thing she knows, she is walking back from dropping her son off at school, and who does she bump into and become fast friends with? Yep. The man in the bar/new boss' wife. 
 This is one tangled web. The poor gal in the middle, decides she can't let her interest in the man in the bar/new boss' wife/now good friend's husband lead to a full-fledged affair but that doesn't last long. Soon there is an affair, the two women have become close friends, and there are feelings, newly discovered 'other' moods, and things start to get complicated. Oh, how they get complicated. 
 There is a sordid past that is about to unfold and our girl is right smack in the middle. This is a soap opera waiting to implode and just wait. The end is nothing; I mean absolutely nothing that you could possibly imagine. Even in your wildest dreams.

reference_books.title: Every Secret Thing
reference_books.review_text:
It has been seven years since Olivia Barnes, a baby from a prominent Baltimore African-American family, disappeared. Her killers, two 11-year-old white girls, have only recently been released from prison when children again start to disappear. 
 Cynthia Barnes, the slain child's mother, is certain that the pair is at it again, and the police aren't far behind. But which of the teens is responsible? Is it good girl Alice or bad girl Ronnie? Or is it another killer altogether? 
 Every Secret Thing deals with difficult subject matter, portraying children as both victims and perpetrators of the worst kind of violence 
 Every Secret Thing will stay with you for a long time.

reference_books.title: Mrs. Fletcher
reference_books.review_text:
. It's a literary, coming-of-age story journeying thru personal growth, respect and acceptance. The topics explored cut to the emotional quick as most readers will be familiar in some way. But they are presented in a light manner which keeps the story upbeat. Tom Perrotta's well-defined characters, engaging narrative and thought provoking subject matter really took this story to another level. Written from both Eve and Brendan's perspectives, I felt like Perrotta nailed it perfectly coming from both angles. 
 Eve Fletcher is a single mom and brand new empty nester. After getting her son Brendan off to college she channels her loneliness in a gender studies course at the local community college. One night she receives a wildly anonymous text, U R my Milf! This text sets the wheels in motion for Eve's indulgence in MILFateria.com, an erotic website that gets mileage out of middle aged women. 
 Eve is enjoying her new found freedom, a student pondering feminist theory, she's drinking and dancing, exploring her sexuality and making stupid mistakes. One evening things really heat up after a small gathering of friends and this event is the defining moment where Eve realizes she's just plain lonely. And it doesn't help that her married friends plaster their Facebook walls with sappy Valentine's Day messages. 
 Meanwhile, Brendan's jerk-like behavior isn't winning anyone over at college. After finally getting a date with pretty Amber he screws up any possibility of a relationship due to his chauvinistic sexual behaviour. His roommate Zack has pretty much ditched him because he doesn't like the person he becomes when he's around Brendan. He quickly realizes he is a big disappointment on campus and drops out of school and moves back home. 
 Eve's freedom is stifled with Brendan at home again. She gives up taking another class at the community college to spare Brendan the embarrassment of running into his mom at school. Her freedom and carefree lifestyle is quickly swapped out for domesticity as she falls back into daily life as 'mom'. 
 That hot and heavy night plays over in Eve's head as she comes dangerously close to making a regrettable mistake. Fighting back her inner desires not a moment too soon, she offers up one lasting memory that is sure to never fade away. 
 I think the biggest takeaway from this book is our views and acceptance of others. This really came thru in Brendan's transition as the story progressed. I think anyone who enjoys an entertaining story will appreciate this one. It's light, funny and interesting from start to finish

reference_books.title: My Husband's Wife
reference_books.review_text:
This is a good psychological thriller. It is the story of Lily and Ed, a married couple struggling within their marriage. Lily has a secret from her past that she has not told to anyone, including her husband. She works as a criminal lawyer and meets Joe who she is drawn to. Ed is a struggling artist and begins to paint Carla, their neighbours daughter, who is only nine at the time. Carla has already learned that secrets are a powerful weapon. 
 When Carla ends up on the doorstep of Lilly and Ed, many years later, a chain of events is set into motion. 
 These people are all flawed individuals. Can these damaged people move on? A good story with a lot of ups and downs. fantastic start, didnt like second half. too much mention of daniel at the start 
 Lily and her husband Ed - newly married, following a whirlwind courtship. They've moved into a little apartment - Ed is pursuing his hopes of a new career in art and Lily has just begun her career as a lawyer. Her first case is an appeal for a murderer that she finds herself strangely drawn to. Down the hall live nine year old Carla and her single mother Francesca. We meet and get to know all four. How are the lives of these four going to intersect? 
 Well, they do - in a most unexpected and clever way. The book covers a period of fifteen years - then and now - lives change and little girls grow up. Every one of the four is guarding a secret - from both the past and the present. But secrets have a way of coming out. As do lies. The opening prologue of the book has an unnamed character thinking...."So it's true what they say about dying. The past comes back to go with you." A great hook to draw the reader in. Those italicized entries continue throughout the book, narrowing down who it could be. 
 Lily and Carla are the driving narrators. Each one is a master of rationalizing the decisions they make. All four are flawed characters, and I found it impossible to muster to find sympathy or empathy for any one of them. (Okay, little Carla did get some) They're all distinctly unlikable. But it's impossible not to keep reading - I was fascinated with Corry's plotting - and the secret machinations of each player.

book_a.title: The Couple Next Door
book_a.user_review:
Anne and Marco, new parents to a 6 month old baby girl Cora, are invited over to their next door neighbours, Cynthia and Graham, to celebrate Graham's birthday. Only at the last minute, the baby sitter cancels. Marco persuades Anne to go any way, that they'll bring the baby monitor to their neighbours, which is literally next door as they live in 19th century row houses, and check on their sleeping baby every 1/2 hour. Anne is suffering from postpartum depression. Graham thinks it will be good for Anne to get out and have a little fun. Anne who feels she's been disappointing him as a wife and mother, doesn't want to disappoint him further, so she goes. 
 However, an innocent night of fun, becomes a nightmare when Anne and Marco return home to find their front door ajar and their baby gone. Marco was the last to check on Cora and insists she was fine. Anne is a little hazy on her memories, slightly drunk, exhausted from lack of sleep as a new mother, begins to have doubts about herself and what she did or did not do. The police naturally suspect Anne and Marco as their are no obvious signs of an intruder. But there is no concrete evidence either to link them to the disappearance of their baby. If Anne and Marco are not responsible, then who is and why? 
 Its a great premise but I was ultimately disappointed in the book. The problem for me was both the writing style and the plot structure. The story is told from the characters point of view, primarily Anne and Marco, but even so I never really felt I got to know them, they were very one dimensional for me (as were the other characters). The other problem for me was major plot developments were revealed by the inner musings of the characters, which for me were a bit jarring because I didn't feel these revelations and been properly foreshadowed. It also sapped a lot of the suspense and seemed a lazy way of moving the plot forward.

sample_reviews.review_text: Found on holiday and looked interesting, an easy read, full of twists and amazing plot...a little bit of exaggeration goes a long way but passed the time in the sun.
It was entertaining, lots of twists and turns, but I have so many unanswered questions!

Meh.... 
 This book moves fast. I'll give it that. Not a single character that the reader can like or root for. Not even an intriguing villain to both deplore and love at the same time. I thought this was a pretty disappointing story overall.

This book is intense and follows a lot of really fucked up characters. This thriller is a story about a couple: Anne and Marco who leave their six month old baby Cora in the house to attend a dinner party with their neighbors. They decide to check on the baby every 30 minutes, but shortly after midnight, the baby is kidnapped and mayhem ensues. I was suspicious of every single character and this story is written in a way that forces you to question everyone and trust no one (as every good thriller should do.) 
 Anne is suffering from post par tum depression and has a history of strange behavior. Marco's business isn't doing well and he's desperate for money. Anne's parents are beyond rich and they dislike Marco with a passion. But every single character in this story has something weird and fucked up going on and it was very intense to watch this play out. 
 The beginning of this book was difficult for me to get used to. The writing felt very odd and choppy in the beginning and it took some adjusting for me to get used to it. The writing is also very wordy and there are several paragraphs every chapter that aren't really necessary and this book could have been cut down by a lot. Also, all the characters are unlikable and dull, even though I do think this is intended. I enjoyed the character Detective Rasbach, even though I would've liked more backstory with his character because we never find out anything about his personal life. 
 Overall, I was completely shocked by the amount of plot twists at the end. I liked that the mystery behind who took the baby was shown somewhat early on and then the rest of the story had so many more plot twists and had so much more depth than I was expecting. This turned into something I wasn't really expecting and I enjoyed that a lot. The last page had me shook and I love when a thriller ends like this. I smiled and screamed at the same time after reading the final page and it was just so amazing alsdklajslkajlsda. This is definitely one of my new favorite thrillers. I highly recommend giving this one a shot.

I liked this one. It held my attention enough that I got through it fast. I didn't see that ending coming though!
I really loved this book with all its crazy twists & turns. Up until the end & then she blew it. It just didn't fit.

This one was sooo good! I didn't expect it to be as good as it was! Such a fast paced plot. I was never once bored. I could not put it down. I had to keep reading "one more chapter" so I could figure out what happened next. The only complaint I had was the present tense writing style. At the beginning I kept noticing it read differently than most books. It would said "she walks into the other room" instead of "she walked". I don't know why I kept noticing that. I guess I'm just used to past tense. After awhile though I didn't even notice that. Such a great thriller!
I feel like this was written as a hi-lo book for adults. Predictable plot, unimpressive writing, just not that great.
entertaining, but predictable. and the ending was weak.

book_b.title: Smoke
book_b.user_review:
Beth used to fight forest fires. She left that vocation in order to concentrate on her marriage and to focus on trying for the baby she and her husband so desperately want. The baby that she hopes may save their marriage. Things don't go quite as planned and on the eve of discussing the possibility of divorce a forest fire erupts on the outskirts of town. Instantly, she is drawn back into the excitement she, admittedly, has missed. This fire might not only destroy her home but her marriage as well. When all is said and done, will anything good be able to rise out of the ashes? 
 I am a bit ambivalent about this book. While the story is good - I did enjoy reading about the forest fire and the tools used to fight it as well as the stress both the fire and the investigation surrounding it had on the inhabitants of the town. However, it seemed to be lacking the page-turning excitement I thought it might have. With an out-of-control forest fire raging all around them I found it a little difficult to believe that a town would go ahead with an annual fund-raising dance? Add to that the fact that for the most part I didn't really care for the character of Beth I wasn't drawn into this book as much as I had hoped I would be. 
 The action did pick up in the last third of the book, but it was not until that point that I began to care about what happened to this town and its inhabitants. Two-thirds is a lot of book to read through before things become captivating. 
 All that being said I think I went into this book with the wrong idea about the story. I was anticipating a little more fire-fighting. Someone else reading this without that mistaken preconception will probably enjoy the whole book rather than just, as I did, the last third. The book was certainly well written and I would not hesitate to pick up another book by Ms. McKenzie.

sample_reviews.review_text: Oh good lord.

The story about a raging fire inside people and out- who caused it, itself is engaging. I have heard so much about this book that I came to it with high expectations, which is a terrible thing to do with any book. So, reading on- sometimes slowly, I let go of any reviews I read and kept my mind open. 
 In the beginning we know a marriage is ending but not so much why. There is something there, dying marriage, cleansing fire (could be symbolic) except for the devastation of both. I don't believe in Ben, he came across as a non-person. Elizabeth got on my nerves to the point I didn't care what she wanted or if she would get it. The fire was the most interesting character in the story, because it kept me caring. Maybe it blazed so bright, was the most destructive thing that the characters turned to ash. 
 To be fair, there is a lot of insight into failing relationships. If any character is one a reader can relate to, it's Mindy. Mindy is flawed and lost, drifting from her children (any parents with teens can have empathy there) drifting from her place in her life. She is the bones a reading group can chew on. The problem is Elizabeth didn't feel alive enough for me to enjoy her. It's a good read, but I was expecting something that would burn into my memory.
I thought this book was a very entertaining read.

I was given a copy of Smoke from NetGalley for an honest review and this is my review. 
 I found this book very interesting. I also enjoyed the style that was used to tell the story. Being told by two different narrator's perspectives who were at one time friends and had totally different things at stake with the outcome how what happens with the fire and the investigation into the fire was very interesting. 
 The character of Mindy who was telling the story as a mother who was worried that her son had something to do with starting the fire to me evolved the most throughout the book. I like how she started out a bit broken because she lost her best friend but by the end she was a strong progress fighting for her son and trying to prove that he was not the one who started the fire that did so much damage to the area surrounding the town their family lived in. 
 As for Elizabeth, the other character whose perspective the book was told from I felt that she was on okay character but she did not impress me all that much. She seemed to have had it all but she was not satisfied with it so she wanted to escape her marriage was looking for excuses to explain away why things were not going her way. To me she was a bit annoying and could not accept things as they were and had to look for the next thing that may explain it a bit better or may make it a bit more exciting. Elizabeth was an adrenaline junkie who needed her next fix it felt like and I did not like that about her. 
 I really did like the storyline for the most part. It did drag on a bit in some parts but for the most part it was pretty good and it kept you wondering how the fire really started until the end. 
 I am giving Smoke four out of five stars.

"Smoke" is the story of two estranged friends whose town and homes are threatened by a forest fire. Elizabeth, a former firefighter, is investigating the cause of the fire. Mindy is the mother of a teenage son who knows something about the fire. I didn't immediately connect with the characters, but 1/3 of the way through I was hooked. I liked the unique firefighting theme and liked the fire reports to the town that were interspersed through the book. I enjoyed learning the complex nature of Elizabeth's and Mindy's relationships with their families and personal struggles. Definitely an enjoyable read!

I love books that give me a view in to a world that I do not know. "Smoke" did this in spades. The author gave me an insight in to firefighting, which was the backbone to a book about a troubled marriage, a broken friendship, and a town where everyone is blaming one another for starting the flames. 
 The relationships were especially well written. The marriage was flawed, real. Neither perfect nor disastrous. The friendship fell apart over something that was said, but again - the author handled it in an authentic way. It can be so tempting, I'm sure, to squeeze maximum drama out of those types of moments. 
 I look forward to reading other books by Catherine McKenzie.

I am a big fan of Catherine McKenzie and this is my forth book by her. I wouldn't sat that this was my favorite one but still definitely a good read. 
 This book started out a little slower for me. And it was really more about the characters and their relationships than the fire and I was kind of hoping for more fire action (My hubby is a long time fireman!) It took me a while to get into the characters and their personalities. But once I did I started liking them and the book much better. The character development didn't jump out at me like her others books though. 
 The more I read the better this book got! The beginning was just ehh for me but the end was great! Once all the drama started to unfold and it appeared that there was going to be some suspense and controversy I started loving it. There are a few twists and turns and a couple edge-of-your-seat moments that make it more interesting ;-) 
 And, I loved this quote - 
 "Chaos theory." 
 "What's that?" John says. 
 "Oh, just this thing my dad used to say. About how if a butterfly flaps its wings in South America, it might cause a hurricane in the Atlantic..." 
 All-in-all a good suspenseful read. 
 I received this book in exchange for my honest review.

I really enjoyed this one. I liked the alternating viewpoints and the characters were distinct enough that you didn't get confused by the transitions. I thought the writing was quite vivid and the storyline was just complex enough. I enjoyed the pieces on firefighting and the mystery of the fire starter, mixed in with family and relationship storylines.

The story carried me along and I liked the two personalities that were struggling with their own problems. The story centers around a town threaten with a forest fire, which had echos of Chasing Fire in it. 
 A great read.

Review by Carol M. Boyer 
 Outstanding and Breathtaking Novel!! 
 A stunning novel that captured me immediately with the frightening realization of smoke waking Elizabeth, the adrenaline speeding through her body telling her to join in the rescue to help save her town. The reality of the divorce she and Ben had just agreed upon,was clouding her thoughts but not her actions, to fight this fire. Elizabeth had given this previous career up and was now an arson investigator, however the old Elizabeth followed her gut instinct to join in the active fire fighting, ignoring a reason for the failure of her marriage. Suspicions arise about how the fire started and by whom. Elizabeth is torn between her ex-friend Mindy's goal of helping a victim who may not be who everyone thought. A beautiful story of commitment, losses, hope and forgiveness. Catherine's novel is breathtaking. your heart will race and not slow down till the end. A must read!! I was lucky to have received a copy from Lake Union in exchange for an honest review

reference_books.review_text:
06/06/16 - 5/5 
 How I wish I could erase my memory of reading this........ and get terrified, shocked, and entertained as much as I did the first time. I remember reading this one night and freaking out- seeing a dark corner, imagining evil lurking spirits, etc etc haha idek. In this first book, we don't know what the hell is happening. We are clueless and scared (or in my case, terrified) as Mara Dyer, and it felt amazing no doubt haha. It's not that she is an unreliable character (like most characters tend to be in a lot of books nowadays) but everything is just so mysterious and wicked. I don't understand how some people don't like this and some gave up after waiting for the sequels' release. It's really good and worth it, I recommend this to everyone- please keep an open mind. Definitely not great in a literary sense, but I really enjoyed it as it is nonetheless.

This review pains me a fair amount. The words I have to write about this book are not the ones I wish they were. 
 Let me begin by stating that I'm a huge fan of David Wong and I wanted to love this book. 
 The new setting and characters he's created for FUTURISTIC VIOLENCE & FANCY SUITS (FV&FS) seem like they could be a lot of fun, so I was ready to follow him on his first novel-length fictional outing sans John and Dave. 
 That being said, there are signs throughout the book that point to this endeavor as being a rushed production. Both JOHN DIES AT THE END and THIS BOOK IS FULL OF SPIDERS were uneven in spots - the former particularly so - but the moments of sheer brilliance and hilarity scattered throughout more than made up for the rough prose and bumpy plotholes. 
 FV&FS has a strong opening, briefly leading me to believe that David Wong had unleashed his inner Douglas Adams; however, the book quickly devolves into a messy collage of lengthy expository dialogues that are nowhere as sharp or witty as they strive so hard to be. 
 The book's villains started out as somewhat interesting tech-heavy Mad Max warlord-types, but midway through the characterization became so one dimensional that the baddies morphed into comic book characters straight out of 80's Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle cartoons. Rocksteady and Bebop would have fit right in with these guys, and seemed to be the inspiration for the cadence of some of the dialogue. 
 The prose throughout would have benefited from several more rounds of editing. I picked up at least three or four major typos - a small amount to be sure, but more than you'd expect from a wide release from a large publisher. The errors didn't end with typos and spelling, but extended into point of view problems and sudden tense shifts. Even the name of the main city - spelled "Tabula Ro$a" throughout the majority of the book - was spelled randomly as either "Tabula Rosa" or "Tabula Ro$a" towards the end. 
 All of these quibbles can be excused to a certain extent if the story moves quickly and amuses, but FV&FS strangely spends most of its time watching characters sitting around having discussions: what happened in the past, what they might do in the future, etc. The book is at its best when actual action is being presented, which is regretfully not often - and that really leaves the reader plenty of time to focus on the poor workmanship presented throughout. 
 There is some fun to be had with the book, but not nearly enough to justify its length. Shaving off 100 pages or so and rewriting the prose until it ceased to sound like direct transcriptions from audio notes may have turned a so-so book into something special, but as-is this book is a flawed experience. Seldom have I read a book that feels like such a last-minute, "weld whatever we've got together by the deadline"rush job, but I'd bet money that's exactly what happened here. 
 I'm still a David Wong fan, and I'll buy the next book he publishes, but here's hoping the next one is polished more thoroughly before it's released to the public.

Oh, authors these days... Always looking for different ways to be THE book chosen in the bookstore by the buyer. In order to do that, they push into new ideas, new boundaries, crazy plots... Sometimes it works out well, but not always.... 
 The marketing material about the book is very vague about the plot, so I will try to be the least spoilery possible - but there might be light spoilers ahead. 
 Zoey Ashe is a normal mid-twenties woman living in a trailer with her mother and her cat ("Stench Machine"). All goes well in a poor but honorable life, until a day a serial killer shows up and decides to make Zoey into his next victim. She escapes, only to learn that there is a bounty on her head - something related to her very rich but totally absent father - and she has to go to Tabula Rasa, in order to untangle the mess and hopefully survive in the process. 
 The plot is set in the near future, with some well-done insights future tech: self-driving cars, customized advertising, and an expansion of real-life streaming videos (called "the blink"), that makes almost impossible to do something in secret. Even mass murderers have blink channels, and compete for views by promising gruesome deaths in the name of "entertainment". On that aspect, Tabula Rasa adds on it by being like a "new Vegas", a place with little in terms of Law and Order, other than those provided by private security to rich people. 
 All good and well, the scenario looks promising. My whole problem with this book was about its tone and narrative style. You see, this book is supposed to be at the same time very funny and very violent, but the end result was... neither. Someone posted on our discussion group one line that serves as an introduction to its style: "This city is a butt that farts horror." You can get the general idea from there. 
 The book is full of jokes and cartoonish characters (and this was intentional). However, at the same time, it depicts very serious aspects of violence, like serial killers, sexual violence threats, exploitation of poverty and so on. The violence itself is not so explicit, but its impacts are. One example is when Zoey picks up and examine a portrait showing a family (mother, father and two kids) having fun in a shopping mall. It was the embodiment of happiness itself - only problem was that the mother had just been casually killed by the bad guy on his way out of a building - red shirt style. 
 So the reader is constantly being reminded of the horrors of the violence depicted on the book, but then is expected to laugh on the joke that follows. And to be honest, although there are a few lines that cracked me up, most of them simply did not. Most of them sounded like a desperate comedian in a poor day in a stand up, trying to save the show. 
 Consequently, that brings another problem: keeping the sense of disbelief. One can be perfectly ok with dragons breathing fire, magic, super-powered villains all the way through, as long as everything is coherent within the story. However, when you are asked to believe in a world where a cartoonish super-villain is threatening the world despite being obviously dumb, but at the same time, you are reminded of an all-too-real violence scene just as the one depicted on yesterday's newspaper, you start to notice the strings behind the curtain. Then, once they call your attention, you start to actively search for them - more clues to internal inconsistency. Until eventually, you stop caring about the plot. 
 That was what happened to me. I did start liking the book somewhat, although the jokes were not that good from the start. As it went on, I started to care less and less, and by the end I was trying to rush it just to get rid of it. 
 There are some good points within book, some interesting criticisms on technology and our use of the Internet. However I do not think it was worth the time spent. Also, considering the comments on my group, seems to be the majority's opinion. 
 So, unless you get a really strong recommendation from someone you like, just avoid it.

Predictable (it wears its twists heavily) and populist. Fairly objectifying of women. The reader is also meant (I think) to be pulled in by a heavily materialist aspirational fantasy lifestyle represented by a series of different characters and perspectives who have an uncannily similar voice. 
 I know that this kind of thing doesn't go for realism, and it clearly isn't realistic. An essentially pointless book in poor taste. Nevertheless, I think that the author knows his readership and I am sure that this will appeal to readers who like J Archer/D Brown and people who don't like literature or their characters with any degree of complexity.

reference_books.title: Sweet Tooth
reference_books.review_text: Ian McEwan is normally pretty reliable when it comes to producing engaging, thought provoking novels. His last few books aren't quite as profound as earlier work promised, and this book continues that trend. It is readable, but the central characters are not convincing, and I am afraid that by the time it got to the big "reveal" at the end, I didn't much care any more. There is an idea in there about ownership of narratives and versions of truth, but it is a bit underdeveloped and doesn't take a novel to make the points McEwan is trying to make.

 The two steal a car and a bunch of money from a dead meth dealer. They are followed onto an airplane by two members of a four-person team (two of the members had previously warned Jack to get out of Dodge). Jack incapacitates these men, Susan ends up killing one of them (whoops) and the fourth gets arrested.

sample_reviews.review_text: I was a decent book. It seemed too short though. Just as it gets started it was over.

Short Review 
 An interesting premise wrapped tightly in a layer of jingoism and then splattered with poor writing and a noticeable lack of editing. There are one or two solid, well-constructed, emotional parts but they are isolated islands in a sea of long winded speeches and telling-over-showing. Not a painful read necessarily, but it's probably better for you to look up EMP on Wikipedia and skip this to save time. 
 Long Review 
 First off, I'm a progressive liberal. If you read that and immediately think that my review cannot hold merit because of that - fantastic, move along. There are probably some five stars down the page. 
 Liberal as I am, I did my very best to approach this book from a place of neutrality. The fact that the foreword was written by Newt Gingrich tipped me off early that this was likely to be a book that stood in some way contrary to my political philosophies, so I wanted to come at it with an open mind. 
 Goddamn though if one of this book's defining problems isn't the fact that it might have been written with one hand while the author masturbated furiously to the Statue of Liberty as America the Beautiful blared on repeat. Let's look at some of the issues I had with this book. 
 1. The editing and dialogue. The editing has to come first because it, or the complete lack thereof, is something that really grates on me. Repeatedly throughout this book the author has characters use 'of' instead of 'have'. As in, "It must of cost a fortune", or "You should of told me." This is a book written by a 'Professor of History and Factory Fellow at Montreat College in North Carolina' who it says has authored over 40 books and won several awards. Additionally it was ostensibly edited by a professional editor. 
 Confusing 'of' for 'have' or even for the contraction on the end of words like could've, should've, etc. is an error I would expect to occur no later than third grade, and that's probably being generous. There is no excuse for this. 
 Also no human being talks the way these people talk. First names are used repeatedly in the same conversation even where there are only two or maybe three people present. People also respond in strange ways to things, include an inordinate amount of 'damn's and so many 'what's that I think everyone in this town has hearing issues. 
 2. The monologue and 'telling' obsession. There are so many impromptu speeches it's painful. The vast majority of this book already happens in meetings. Town council meetings, college/militia leadership meetings, public gatherings, you name it. People don't go around giving exposition-filled or uplifting patriotic speeches every third conversation. 
 This reliance on speeches makes it reasonably clear the author just has a narrative in there as an excuse to bludgeon you with talking points and rhetoric. 
 As if that weren't bad enough, a huge amount of action happens off frame and then gets explained to you afterward. The giant, defining battle of the book is treated this way. Our main character talks about prepping for the fight, then basically says, "Then I got knocked out during the fight, here's what happened." Ben (a major-ish character you should care about) turns up dead in such an off-hand way the main character literally walks right past his dead fucking body and doesn't notice and then gets told about it. Washington's death in that same battle is treated the same way. 
 Do we get to see him heroically rallying the troops to hold the line and make sure the town survives the battle? 
 No. We get told that he died. We're told that he did heroic things immediately prior to aforementioned death. Then we get to see kids cry over his corpse. It takes all of the emotional weight out of it. 
 The author, via the main character, also has this weirdly pervasive habit of referencing movies to set the tone, or to describe what he wants the reader to connect it with. So he'll have John think something like, "They were looting. It was like I could of been watching a scene from a movie where people run around all crazy, like Independence Day." You might as well have him come out and just write "I don't have the imagination or technical skill to appropriately and vividly describe a scene to you via the written word so... picture a scene from this movie you ought to know and lets move on." 
 He also has never met an adverb he didn't like. People say things angrily, sadly, calmly, sadly, excitedly, worriedly. All presumably because you, dear reader, are far too dense to tell from context the emotional state of the characters. 
 3. The author insertion and jingoism. Our protagonist is a colonel, and a professor, who's smart and good at just about everything. He's specifically a history professor at Montreat college. Just like the actual author. This might explain all the special treatment John gets in the book. Do they amputate his hand when it gets severely infected? No, he gets the special reserve extra-strength antibiotics. Because it's fine if some other person dies, John needs both hands. For all that flag waving probably. 
 And man is there flag waving. Remember those long inexplicably frequent speeches I mentioned? They are stuffed full of it. Characters constantly reminding other characters that 'this is still America, damnit' and how all the liberal hippy computer programmers are soft and going to die, and how we spent so much time worrying about global warming and gun control and abortion that we didn't prep for an EMP and so on and so forth. 
 You can bet if a character is important, in charge in some way, or positively impactful on the group that they have some kind of military background. 
 There isn't even any point/counterpoint situation going on. Like you could have had a liberal hippie organic gun free vegan commune pop up and be at odds with the main town, create some kind of thematic comparison between these two methods of approaching and solving a problem, and then having had the hippies get raided and slaughtered because 'Merica needs its guns. 
 That would have still furthered the agenda, and it would've been a potentially interesting narrative element. But nope. None of that. We just get lots of instances of characters saying things like, "Boy can you imagine places where most people are ivory tower intellectuals and computer programmers and stuff? They're all dead because they're not red-blooded American folk like us country prepper types. Let's high five in front of this American flag." 
 Alright, deep breath, and now I'll explain why this book got two stars instead of one. There were at least two scenes - the death of the first dog after it protects the family, and the death of Jennifer and subsequently the second dog to feed the other daughter and her unborn child. 
 You can't kill the dog without hitting me with the feels. So maybe it was just that doing it to me, but I feel like that section was better written. You were in the action, characters were having genuine emotional reactions to things. The same thing was done with Jennifer's death, you were actually there for a change. It didn't just cut to her grave with John going, "Oh yeah, by the way, my daughter finally kicked the bucket. Sucks, right?" like so much else in the book. So those couple elements redeemed it a touch for me. 
 Don't get me wrong. Still don't read it. Just giving a little credit here. 
 Lastly, for those who give this five star reviews because it's supposed to be 'educational', much of his 'science' about EMPs he includes is flawed. If that really were the sole intent, and he wasn't attempting to also write an enjoyable narrative, he still failed utterly. What am I to glean from this book? That bad shit happens in what is effectively an apocalypse? No shit. That under extreme circumstances sometimes the worst of human nature is revealed and sometimes the best as people either come together in supportive communities or devolve into their more base animal tendencies? Yeah, I've watched Walking Dead. I know. Is that educational too? 
 It was suggested I read the other two in the series. I might. I don't know if I hate myself that much though.

I had to DNF this book because it was just so badly written! You know, I hardly ever one-star a book if you notice my reviews. It takes a lot to annoy me.

 The whole plot promises a lot of action but fails to deliver. It's not that nothing happens in the book, it's more like the characters spend most of their time TALKING about the action AFTER it happens. That's right, we have a book where the 'action' takes place in meetings. I remember thinking during one such meeting where, damn, why couldn't the author plonk our main character in the thick of the action so that we can see and experience it through his eyes?

This book is fiction but wrapped in a very scary and serious National Defense problem America has ignored. What would happen if an EMP attack would to occur and send the nation back to before the Dark Ages. 
 It is very realistic and detailed look into the potential downward spiral of civilized people turning into survivalist animals. No medicine, water, food supply, or basic organization and laws. 
 Stand alone it is a pretty good, not great, sci-fi doomsday book. However, there are very realistic and current political inserts about the situation that makes it a little more scary and makes you think truly what would happen and are we prepared. 
 Without a spoiler, a comment at the end of the book a character comments that a direct nuclear detonation in the middle of the city would have been more humane than the EMP. 
 I would recommend this to anyone. It is a little slow in the middle but wraps up quickly and fast paced.

When the power blinked, Colonel John Matherson wasn't alarmed. These things happen. But they don't happen at the same exact time as failing phones, stalling cars, and falling planes. As night fell and nothing changed, he began to suspect the worst: that America had been attacked. One Second After turns a Norman Rockwell life into a horror story, taking readers through a town trying desperately to hold on to survival after its entire world collapses. 
 Like any horror story, this is grisly and exciting; as Matherson quickly realizes, his city has been the victim of an electromagnetic pulse, probably generated by a nuclear detonation in the atmosphere. Virtually every electrical device is now kaput. Cars, computers, even telephones and clocks are dead. One character notes in alarm that they've been thrown into the Civil War era, but their fate is far worse than that; as the historian Matherson notes, the world of 1865 had its own infrastructure. That was a world of widespread farming and home industry, of self-reliance. With electricity went every tool and system the modern world depends on; the trucks, trains, and ships that moved food from across the continents; the computers that managed the money. The integrated world economy, David Ricardo's dream coming true, meant the utter dependence of every community on thousands of others. With thousands of people needing medicine and food every day, and without the means to produce it or import it again as needed, One Second After is a tale of slow death. 
 The technological order having collapsed, and the old traditional skills having been forgotten, the people of town are in a bad way. An early scene in a nursing home overwhelms Matherson and readers with a hint of the tragedy that is to come; its staff unable to come to work, and medications running low, four medical personnel are alone in a building filled with dozens of elderly who need constant care. Matherson is there to evacuate his father in law, but when he arrives he finds death, disease, and despair; the staff are overwhelmed, unable to cope. It's a gut-wrenching scene, but devastation won't be limited to the nursing home. Those dependent on medications in the civilian population are first to decline; food poisoning, disease, and strife ravage the population in turns. Without comforts, ferality rears its head; as some give in to their inner beasts, Matherson and others do their utmost to preserve some dignity. They study the situation, make plans for the future, organize defense against what mobs and nature are throwing at them, and strain not to break themselves. 
 While rock bottom is never reached, and there is some marginal reason for hope at the end, this is a truly harrowing story. There are minor issues with the style -- the characters often remind themselves that "we're still Americans", invoking memories of higher ideals, but in too unvarying a way -- but this is a small fly in the soup. As devastating as the barrage of crises is, the main character continues to hold on, making it inspirational. There's no question that this novel was written as a warning; the story is bookended with notes from a congressman and a military intelligence officer who remark on the dire need to prepare for the aftermath of this kind of an attack. That warning applies not just for Congress, however, but for people, too; Matherson's city profits from the skills of a few survivalists and hardcore Civil War reenactors, but the townsfolk on the whole are not prepared. Accustomed to buying everything as needed from the store, no one has any extra provisions or supplies set aside. Little wonder 'prepping' booklists often include this one. 
 While I don't know how likely an EMP attack is, One Second After is a chillingly effective warning of how fragile everyday life has become. 
 Related: 
 Lucifer's Hammer. An apocalyptic novel following an asteroid impact, this also has a cannabalistic horde. It's also more firmly a science fiction novel.

I read this book as something different to read. I wanted a break from my normal genre and this book was highly suggested to me. After reading the description I was pretty excited. it sounded like an action packed book with a life lesson in it as well. Forstchen started off really strong with his writings the plot. After the halfway mark it really went down hill from there though. I was really disappointed with this book. I felt as though the second half of the book was nothing but rambling to try to fill in space. It just felt as though it went on and on and on and was never going to end. I also felt as though the story actually sucked in the second half of the book as well. Great idea but poorly executed. If you like military type book with a lot of political talk that rambles on and on then go ahead and read this book. I guess I'm just not into all the politics. And for how highly this book was suggested, I'm seriously disappointed.

So apparently this is one of the best apocalyptic novels ever, at least according to large swathes of the Interwebs. 
 Personally, I don't see it. The plot is interesting and the research is excellent, but the writing itself is execrable. I have expectations of professional novelists. These include being able to remember what the beginning of a sentence was by the time you get to the end - if you start a sentence with 'after' I expect that sentence to have something happening after something else. 
 The characters are flat and uninteresting and I found myself not caring about their plight in the slightest. 
 Also, he nicked a number of plot points - not vital ones, but several of the surrounding atmospheric details, like who became president after Air Force 1 went down and so on, from Alas, Babylon.

What a poorly written mess. Even once you get past the fact that the author doesn't know the difference between "must've" and "must of," it doesn't get better. Every character other than our hero serves simply to praise the hero for every action he takes, no matter how ridiculous. And the repetition. The ceaseless repetition of information we already know. Three times in four pages the character "smiled" because a situation reminded him of ancient kings negotiating. Twice to himself, and then he announced it to the group. This book sorely needed a capable editor. If you want a book about America after technology stops working, do yourself a favor and read "Dies the Fire" instead.

I like to read books that are well written, or at very least, well edited. This book, unfortunately, is neither. I couldn't finish it, knowing all too well how many other unread books I have on my shelf ready to read. 
 There's a part about halfway into the book where the plot completely falls apart. You'll know it when you read it.

reference_books.title: Company Town
reference_books.review_text:
~3.5 
 "A man without a past and a woman without a future."In the future Ashby envisions, bioaugmentation has become so universal that Go Jung-Hwa, unedited and suffering from Sturge-Weber Syndrome, is effectively unique, a black swan whose interaction with the world is not fully saturated by augmented reality. Hwa is just trying to live her life, working as a bodyguard for the local sex workers' union and teaching them self-defense on the side when her duties bring her into contact with Daniel Siofra, a mysterious fixer who works directly under the man who now owns the whole town. Suddenly, Hwa finds herself tasked with protecting a vulnerable child while around her, her old start dying under horrific circumstances. 
 The strongest aspect of Company Town is the worldbuilding. Ashby's new future is gritty and immersive, familiar and yet imbued with an alien strangeness. The story takes place in a near-future mining town in Canada that is undergoing the same sort of rusting as so many current industrial towns. The single-product economy is on the brink of failure, and while the town's new owner/investor may bring it back to life, everyone in the town is on edge about the potential cost. However familiar the social and economic situation might be, the people themselves walk around in augmented reality, their vision tagged with identifying information of the people they see, their forms obscured and defined by virtual reality instead of physicality. Botflies--no, not those botflies; these are flying robots-- buzz around everywhere, acting as tiny and ubiquitous paparazzi. A post-human civilization seems to be just on the horizon. 
 The concept is fascinating and the book itself is packed with nonstop action. However, I found the plot itself rather more problematic, from the core concept to the solution of the underlying mystery. I felt that not even the basic setup could withstand cursory examination; for example, I was completely puzzled about why Hwa, hired as a bodyguard for a kid, ends up attending school with him as a fellow student rather than actually guarding him. Everyone knows what she's doing, so it's not a disguise, and having your bodyguard take classes and do homework seems a great way to keep them distracted. Outside of school, Hwa spends basically all the time on her own rather than actually guarding the kid, again without any explanation. Not only that, but Hwa herself ends up as a target, and even though her very presence puts her charge in danger, they keep her as his bodyguard, with no explanation for why anyone would keep a bodyguard who is clearly getting the body into danger rather than guarding it. And then the point where they both stay home because the bodyguard is getting rape/murder threats? And they both skip school because she's in danger? Really? Very little else about the plot could bear scrutiny, from the action scenes to the final reveal. For example, when they duck into the bathroom to avoid the killer, why doesn't he just come in after them instead of politely waiting outside or wandering away so they can regroup and have a nice chat before heading to the elevators? Why did Hwa so quickly forgive the freaking destruction of the city? And the whole singularity thing just didn't work for me. The problem is that as soon as you set up a killer who can come back over and over again, you've set up an inherently losing situation. Forget the whole time paradox issue; you now have a protagonist who simply cannot win, unless the author cheerfully ignores the rules she put into place. The book is also a good example of a common device used in mysteries that I call "plot-driven obscurity," where characters withhold facts or wrap them in cryptic statements solely because doing otherwise would reveal the mystery. This was most visible with everyone talking about the unknown teacher's proclivities. Why wouldn't anyone just say the name? However, such issues aren't out of the ordinary for thrillers, and if you're in the right mood, I think they can easily be overlooked. 
 Plot issues aside, Company Town is an interesting story tackling some compelling issues ranging from post-human life to the politics of prostitution. Throughout, Hwa struggles to be seen--and to see herself-- as a person instead of a disorder. She also fights to come to terms with her frustratingly appearance-obsessed mother, and a culture in which people prefer to edit her out rather than see her disfigurement. Despite a few plot weaknesses, Company Town is an interesting scifi read with an interesting protagonist and a vivid vision of a near future.

 Kate and I had a rocky start. I read the first book and my detestation for Curran was so strong that it outweighed my appreciation for Kate. When I was finally galvanized to try again, I decided to test things out a little later in the series: this book, in fact. reference_books.title: Already Dead (Joe Pitt, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
**edited 11/28/13 
 There's a certain stereotype about the streets of New York City. To non-City-dwellers, the phrase can conjure a claustrophobic skyline blocked with lowering buildings and blinding lights, anonymous figures studiously avoiding eye contact as they rush past each other on the sidewalks, seething masses of pedestrians pouring onto the streets at random to the furious honks of stultified drivers, and snobby natives glaring at gaping tourists. Basically, the stereotyped New York is a place where people on the streets don't see each other as human. In Joe Pitt's NYC, "inhuman" is a pretty good description.

reference_books.title: Dead Until Dark (Sookie Stackhouse, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
**edited 12/04/13 
 Sookie Stackhouse is a pretty, demure, and (extremely) naive blonde with a "disability": the ability to read other peoples' minds. (Apparently, despite the direct contradiction in the term, an additional ability is the new disability in Sookie's world.) When Sookie uses her skill to prevent the murder of a vampire, she finds herself with a doorway into this only recently exposed world. Determined to discover who has been murdering the various "loose women" around town, Sookie teams up with the enthralling vampire Bill (ugh) to find the answer. 
 I felt compelled to read this because, as far as I understand it, Sookie Stackhouse, along with Patricia Brigg's Mercy Thompson, are to "female-protagonist urban fantasy"/paranormal romance (I'll call it FUF) what Harry Dresden is to "male-protagonist/hardboiled urban fantasy"(which I'll call MUF): the template, archetype, the most prominent example, and the series to set oneself up against. In other words, Sookie is who we get to blame for all of the tropes that are common to all subsequent FUF. So I must admit that I enjoyed trying to unearth which of these tropes are due to Sookie. 
 ...And that's all I'm going to post here. 
 The rest of my (rather verbose and quote-filled) review is posted over here at Booklikes. 
 Why? Because I disapprove of GoodReads' new policy of censorship. 
 ~2.5

sample_reviews.review_text:
This was a great book. A mystery with enough suspense to keep you wondering if you'd figured it out but not so many twists and suspects to be contrived and exhausting. 
 A young pair of friends bump into each other one afternoon and agree to have some tea and catch up. While chatting they bemoan their prospects (the war is over and both find themselves unemployed and broke). They decide on the spot to form a company of sorts called the Young Adventurers and plan to put an ad in the newspaper offering their services to do anything as long as it's well paid. This conversation is overheard, the woman is later approached to take on a mysterious - but well paid - assignment. She insists on involving her male friend. 
 One thing leads to another, and another, and another, and... People are kidnapped, memories are lost, trusts are betrayed, new friends are found, money is made, criminals are located.... 
 A fun read, never over the top, perfectly unbelievable when you take a step back, but nothing in the book causes you to step back so you get sucked in and just enjoy the ride.

"To all those who lead monotonous lives in the hope that they may experience at second hand the delights and dangers of adventure." 
 "His face was pleasantly ugly..."
I haven't read a lot her books yet, but this my favorite so far. Enjoyed it!

The Secret Adversary was a fairly interesting read, and quite amusing at times. But overall, I'd have to say I was disappointed mainly because part of the fun of reading a mystery is being kept in suspense and I was able to figure out who "the secret adversary" was very early in this story.

I've read this (and all the other Agatha Christies) many times before, but I never noticed before how much it sucks. On the one hand: Tommy and Tuppence, what's not to love, but on the other hand, NOW I KNOW WHERE J.K. ROWLING LEARNED TO WRITE IN ALL CAPS.

Agatha Christie's books are very hit-or-miss for me. I hadn't read any of her books for a few years because they began to frustrate me, but then I read 
 Five Little Pigs 
 and couldn't put it down. Because I enjoyed that so much, I decided to immediately read another Christie book, which was this one. In sharp contrast to my previous read (which I finished in a single sitting), it took me 10 days to finish this short book. The writing style seemed amateur, the characters weren't interesting, and the plot didn't engage me. 
 More than once the characters stated that their experiences (i.e., their adventure, the mystery) reminded them of dime novels. Aside from how irritating it is when a character in a book says, "Wow, what's happening to me is like what you read about in books!", the dime novel comparison was actually pretty apt. This was a cheap, quick, "you'll enjoy it more if you don't think too much" story. Unfortunately, the plausibility of events and characters' actions is essential to my enjoyment, and there were too many ridiculous and convenient turn of events in this story for me. I finished this book just to finish it, not because I wanted to know how it ended.

I adore Tommy & Tuppence! 
 They stumble on a mystery when Tuppence is offered an odd job, that suddenly disappears. Thinking something is wrong (which of course it is) she starts trying to figure out the mystery around one girl. 
 Intrigue, scandal, close calls and amnesia. 
 Love, love & love it!
Fun and a really fast read.

Tommy and Tuppence are really charming characters, but when Christie writes thrillers all of her classism comes to the fore, and it's all about the good solid middle class English people defeating the forces of evil which are causing Labour Unrest. Christie doesn't seem to be able to imagine that the striking workers of early 20s Britain may have had actual grievances, so she imagines that they're the dupes of evil masterminds and if the evil masterminds are just taken care of (by the middle class) then the workers will go back to being good workers and the world can get back to normal. I'm sure this sort of thing was very comforting for most of her contemporary readers, but it makes me gnash my teeth with annoyance.
It was okay for a mystery--figured out the "Secret Adversary" out about a quarter the way through. I did not like the writing style especially the use of all capitals words - throughout the dialogue.

book_b.title: The Call of Cthulhu and Other Weird Stories
book_b.user_review:
**edited 02/02/14 
 Lovecraft has had a tremendous influence on the modern fantasy, especially urban and comic fantasy. Terry Pratchett, Charles Stross, Jim Butcher, and several other major authors utilize Lovecraftian critters from the dungeon dimensions and the deepest depths as primary antagonists in their mythologies. I don't know if it's because I read the stories when I was too young, or if perhaps I encountered spoofs of his creatures before I read the real thing, but somehow, half-and-half fish/octopus men just aren't a terror trigger for me. Even in his more psychological works, I tend to find Lovecraft's writing a bit overblown, so much so that it tends to invoke laughter rather than horror. Granted, only a few of the antagonists of his stories are amphibious, but they almost always invoke an external influence. My classic horror stories of choice are the more internal/psychological ones-- The Yellow Wallpaper, The Turn of the Screw, etc. 
 For all that, I have a great appreciation for Lovecraft's ideas and influence.

sample_reviews.review_text: I had no idea what I just read. Were they stories or just ramblings? I felt like I had to do all the work imagining anything.

Astonishingly poor, particularly when considering that Lovecraft is regarded as a cornerstone of the horror genre. His stories are repetitive and predictable, and his authorial style is marked by florid, baroque word choice that borders on the laughable. (Of all the words in the English language to get sick of, I never thought "eldritch" would be on my list.) I will grant that Lovecraft has some flair for stirring up gruesome and macabre imagery, but I found his talents in that respect to be frequently obscured by the terrible quality of his writing. 
 This book is a collection of 18 short stories, although the latter two-thirds of the book is composed of the five longest stories. These five are generally more readable than the others, the best of them being "The Whisperer in Darkness." Of the shorter short stories, "The Rats in the Walls" is the only one I can recommend. The bad ones of this lot are reaaaaally bad, reading like literary regurgitation from a story-generating machine. 
 The stories are footnoted in extensive detail by editor S.T. Joshi - it is too bad that his industry was not devoted to a better author.
I feel like I didn't get it or missed something. Never really felt very spooky, just weird and distant.

So every hipster and geek worth their salt knows who Cthulhu is, and I, as all good posers do, had pieced together enough about him to get most of the jokes about him. (Most of these jokes, by the way, are basically name-dropping, so I feel that many people are posers about having actually read Lovecraft, but I digress.) 
 My other exposure to Lovecraft was the movie "Die, Monster, Die," a movie starring Boris Karloff based on one of HPL's stories that I watched one night on the classic movie network. I remember getting really drawn into the suspense of the story, and then finding the ending really silly and predictable. I also remember Robert Osbourne coming on afterwards basically saying that the movie tanked for being so lame, as though saying, "Ha ha, you just watched a terrible movie that we got the rights for next to nothing." 
 What does this have to do with this book? 
 Well, I listened to a version of this compilation on audiobook. The bad part (I guess) is that it didn't have all of the stories. The good thing is that I think that Lovecraft is tailor-made to be listened to. 
 The books in the collection were Call of Cthulhu, The Hound, the Dunwich Horror, and Dagon. 
 The good: There's a real poetry to the way Lovecraft puts together a sentence. When he does describe the horrors the narrator sees, they are the sort of thing that brings fire to the imagination. His stories are part horror, part sci-fi, and part fantasy, really. There is a scope to them that I think we don't often see anymore. Horror on a cosmic scale. Monsters with the powers of Gods that are tireless and unstoppable. I think this is the essence of Lovecraft, horror on the grandest scale. Horror that questions our place in the universe. 
 The bad: Two of the books out of four were suicide notes. A third was a note from someone who writing this because he was sure he would be killed soon. All of the stories have at least one instance (and often many instances) of someone encountering a horror and going instantly mad. Part of the way the suspense is built up is that our narrators often say, "It was a horror so terrible I will not describe it." There are definite patterns to his writing, patterns that dull the effects when you read them one after the other. And they weren't, by the way, meant to be read one after the other. They were often published in compilations like "Weird Tales" so it would have been harder to spot all of the similarities for story to story. 
 The ugly: So all the narrators are the most privileged of white males, that happens all the time, right? 
 Except you keep hearing about "mongrel people" and evil "negros" and dark-skinned savages. Attention college students, if you need a source for a paper where there are evil "other" characters, this is the writer for you. 
 I've heard it said that the racism of H.P. Lovecraft just shows him as a "man of his time." Yet there are so many other authors from even farther back in history whom we can read without being exposed to such blatant racism. Historians agree that his ideas about race are even more backwards considering the time and place he was raised. So, I'm not in to making too many excuses for the man. His racism is something that you will definitely notice as you read, and it will tarnish it for you. 
 What do we owe Lovecraft? His horror is interesting, but not all of it is brilliant. Lovecraft himself disavowed some of his work, including the so beloved Call of Cthulhu. He did keep writing in the Cthulhu mythos though, so as you read you will hear more whisperings of the Necronomicon and the elder gods, which leads to the idea that there is a horrific side to the universe that we are simply ants in comparison. That idea ignited the imagination of scores of writers to this day. Thank him for the Necronomicon in Evil Dead, for all those Stephen King Plots that ended with "it's aliens," and for Guillermo del Toro's...everything. 
 But, I think there's a reason that someone so influential is still basically a niche for those nerdy, completionist literary and scifi types out there. He's not the best at what he did, and he was definitely not the best of men. His influence on writing is really more interesting than the writing itself, and I think that the things that turn off modern readers to him (pacing, repetition, uneven storytelling, and racism) will continue to reduce him to a footnote in history. 
 Some may be sad about this, but I'm okay with it. Poe and Jules Verne will persist, the Lovecraft's of this world will be replaced.
Nah.

I was unable to finish all the short stories in this book; after a while, no matter how interesting, my reading was going very slowly and I had too many books on my TBR mountain to keep on trying to read this one and keep it for longer than necessary. I did like the stories read very much. I'd never read anything by this author so it was very interesting to be witness to his vivid -- if weird -- imagination. A true master of the horror.

Lovecraft ar varje gang en slags trygg hamn, oavsett hur lange man varit och last annat ar det alltid som att kliva in i ens eget hus igen nar jag laser hans verk. Denna gang med mer mer aktning an innan, dessutom, da flera av novellerna var battre denna gang an gangen innan. Som med den forra Penguinsamlingen kommer jag inte att ta upp mannen sjalv da det, i min mening, inte har med diskussionen att gora. Mannen var rasist, ja, speciellt i sina yngre ar. Sa. Klart. Hans asikter, vidriga eller inte, har ingen inverkan pa den genialitet som finns att hamta i det livsverk han lamnade efter sig. Det ar ingen storre ide att prata om hans stil da jag gjort det sa mycket tidigare. Bade i den prunkande stilen som aterfinns i hans tidigare verk och den mer aterhallsamma som den senare utvecklades till ar fantastiskt bra. Naval. Till saken. 
 Urvalet i denna samling ar snappet battre an den jag last innan. Den andra halvan ar inte i narheten lika seg som den forra (The Thing on the Doorstep and Other Stories av samma forlag) av den enkla anledingen att jag gillade de novellerna mer. "At the Mountains of Madness" brukar ses som hans magnum opus men jag forstar inte riktigt varfor da de langre stycken som ar med har ar vida overlagsna. I grova drag kunde jag dela upp samlingens innehall foljande - de riktigt bra - 
 "The Colour Out of Space" far till paranoia-kanslan perfekt och sedermera aven isoleringen. Beskrivningarna av naturen och de andra omgivningarna ar ocksa bra beskrivna. Dock ar Lovecrafts ovana att skriva ut dialekten fonetiskt dryg som fan. "The Call of Cthulu" ar nog den novell som han ar mest kand for, med all ratta, trots ett antiklimax i slutet. Men Lovecraft lyckas anda med exakt vad han tankte gora; beskriva hur tunt manniskans begrepp om sin egen verklighet faktiskt ar. "Celepahis" ar annu en Dunsany-pastich men som alltid sa lyckas han fantastiskt anda. Stamning och sprak ar fantastiska. Likasa "The Festival", speciellt da beskrivningen av staden i borjan och da berattaren traffar det gamla paret. "The Outsider" ar en gammal favorit som trots en ganska ologisk handling fortfarande ar guld vard. "Nyarlatothep" ar en ny favorit som stoltserar med fantastiskt sprak och harlig undergangskansla. "The Whisperer in Darkness" ar nog det basta exemplet pa Lovecraft bar han skriver som sig sjalv, utan de uppenbara influenserna fran Poe och Dunsany. Mer SF an skrack och med an hel del fysiksnack inblandat. Ocksa med harligt malande beskrivningar av landskapet i Vermont och isoleringen som Akeley kanner. 
 Sa finns det de som ar godkanda men inte mer, trots flera riktigt bra passager. "Dagon", "Shadows over Innsmouth" och "The Hound", till exempel. De ar inte sadana man skulle skippa men inte heller toppskiktet. De samsta ar egentligen inte rent ut daliga, heller, men knappast bra.

Behold! The eldritch other in all its cosmic horror, brought to you thru Lovecraftian prose and a cascade of increasingly dismal and slightly unbalanced vignettes. 
 This comprehensive collection of Lovecraft stories focuses on the Cthulhu mythos. There are early and later tales and the book contains an introduction about the author, and explanatory notes which are footnoted throughout the text. The supplementary material included does a great deal to flesh out the person behind these strange tales and provide some context and perspective. The footnotes help illuminate the author's life and provide interesting insights into the genesis of inspiration that permeated into the evolving creative process that formed these tales. Lovecraft's personal worldview is problematic, to say the least, but it's useful to have some background on him before delving into his works. 
 In some cases, the reader gets very early tales such as "Dagon" which is a short almost incomplete vignette. Yet, there is something there; a weighty thing, hiding in a tumultuous fog. A hint of evilness lurking in the darkness, just beyond human senses or comprehension. Even in his less expansive works, Lovecraft is able to hit the heavy notes. Strike an echo in the soul. 
 Lovecraftian prose can be overwrought and wordy, even troublesome. The language may be off putting to some modern readers due to the arcane text and alternative spellings, but nothing is insurmountable. 
 When it works, however, the author's use of sparse words hit just the right notes to paint a vivid picture. By laying off the throttle of verbiage, Lovecraft makes things real and plumbs the depths of the reader's personal demons. He is particularly good at this. 
 There is a certain distancing in Lovecraft's tone of phrase. He is sparse in dialog and when he does use speech, the characters often carry on in monologues. Other times the narrator recounts letters or diary entries--or simply tells the reader about everything going on. A sort of "removed" air pervades the writing. However, you do manage to slip in among the cracks between the words, and somehow the author slowly slides you (almost imperceivably) closer to the action-often at the very bitter and horrifying end. 
 Something about the author's word choice, even when buried in the arcane vocabulary of his time, creates certain undulations that rise above the waves and crest over into the subconscious archetypes of the mind. When he makes up words or monsters ot other devices of horror they feel real and not contrived. The Necronomicon, Cthulhu, Shoggoth, the Old Ones-what are these things? Lovecraft barely hints at them in his sparse descriptions, and yet we know them each and all. 
 The unknowable other, just beyond the reach of our senses is where most of Lovecraft's tales lead. As many others have noted, Lovecraft is a master of taking familiar things and skewing them just slightly enough so as to create a sense of being uncomfortable. Something is just not quite right, but it's difficult to pin down exactly what it is until you realize you are too far into the endless abyss to turn back. Sometimes we get fleeting glimpses of the monsters lurking in the fringes of our universe, ready to usurp mankind and begin a new age for the Old Ones. Yet, mostly we don't even get this, we hear second or third hand accounts about stuff going on in more isolated parts of the world. Something is out there, just beyond the corner of your eye. 
 Lovecraft's plots occasionally hinge on predicable device that could be tiresome for experienced readers who have seen such tropes raked over the coals in media and popular culture. I think keeping a historical perspective while reading these tales helps to alleviate this. The other thing is Lovecraft's style. His ability to bring characters to a predicable fate, of which often they are powerless to resist, is somehow captivating. Sometimes the characters can do absolutely nothing, but submit to that which is beyond their power and comprehension (while the reader just cringes with one eye over the protagonist's shoulder). 
 Yet, Lovecraft manages to make this relentless ride worth it. We know how the roller coaster works, where it starts, what will happen along the way, and where it will end--yet we scream just the same when we feel that first rushing drop.

I thought the stories in this collection were kind of uneven but it was quite fun seeing how they influenced authors like J.K. Rowling, Stephen King and Joe Hill. Plus I didn't realize that Arkham Asylum came from him.

A collection of short stories from H. P. Lovecraft, one of the horror genre's most celebrated authors. And why is he so celebrated? Because he was the first to discard gothic constructs--ghosts and witches and whatnot--and instead envision mankind as a tiny outpost of sanity in an otherwise chaotic and malevolent universe. More specifically, he envisioned his protagonists losing said sanity upon encountering a race of ancient and alien fish-people. That's right--fish people. Dum dum dum! 
 Honestly? I'm not a big fan of regular ol' horror, much less the fish-based variety. Doesn't seem scary to me. Just weird. Really weird. Really omg-why-don't-you-seek-counseling-for-how-much-you-clearly-fear-seafood weird. But that's just my opinion.

reference_books.review_text:

 Rating: 3,5 stars 
 So, the book was pretty good. The story was entertaining, the rythm was perfect and the writing was simple but good. I just found myself drowning in cliches between a Winchester-like family, an evil father that had disappeared and a compounding love story between a heartless hunter and a inocent half-breed girl. Despite that, I really enjoyed the book, even though I'm not a real romance lover; cliches don't make a bad story, they just make a normal story. 
 Apart form that, the plot was really good, and I found myself enjoying the moments between Dean Winchester Alex and Willow, the slow evolution of their relationship and, above all, all the cool moments like the battles, escaping through motel bathroom windows, being chased by cars, being chased by angels, being eaten by angels, and more battles. The only "episode" I didn't like were the few chapters when they were hiding in the cabin, where the rythm slowed down too much and the only thing they talked about was their love and yadda yadda yadda. Nonetheless, the descriptions were pretty awesome, and I could picture every character, scene and situation in my mind. 
 Oh, and Dean Alex is a hot hunter. No need to say anything else.

 Praise be to angels

 Meh. The book wasn't awful - I really enjoyed some parts of it, truly - but I had to force myself to read and finish it; I didn't pick it up looking forward to read it. 
 I had a major problem with the main character, Zoe. She is a conceited little brat and a bit racist towards non-GAP people. She claims to love her brother but after his death, she cries for about one hour then goes to LA to see Noah. Yes, it's true that she's trying to find the motive behind Liam's death, but the story revolves mainly around the romance between Noah and Zoe. 
 Also, every time they have a problem or they find themselves in a difficult situation everything is sorted out super quickly and easily. For example, in the end Zoe has amnesia and doesn't remember anything about Noah, but he manages to get undercovered into Sol City and kidnaps her during a party full of people. Even if she's scared and trying to escape from him, Zoe has these super convenient dreams that are in reality suppressed memories about her and Noah and that make her trust him. 
 There are plenty of examples for this throughout the book. Another major problem that I found was the lack of descriptions; everything just seemed so rushed, Noah and Zoe fall in love for each other so quickly (they go from hating each other to loving each other in a few pages), and their feelings and thoughts (mainly Zoe's, because she narrates 70% of the story) seem so superficial and irrelevant that it is hard to be attracted to their love story. 
 In short, it wasn't a good read, but it wasn't bad either. It was just meh.
