Someone Like You, by Sarah Dessen, should not be confused by Adele's "hit" song. Though every time I read the title and sang it as Adele would, it was actually a little similar to the story the song's lyrics tell. A mix of mother-daughter relationships, friendship, love, and teen pregnancy (yes, pregnancy in the teen genre), Someone Like You addresses each of these issues with Grace. 
 The book came out to be a wonderful surprise. If I had just simply gone with the words on the back, I would have put it down and missed out on a great book. The summary did not do the book justice, and I am glad that I try not to judge a book too quickly. 
 Haley and Scarlet, the main characters and best friends, has stayed together, side by side, since they met. They help each other through their toughest times. For Haley, her mom gets too overbearing for her and she runs into trouble with a guy she starts dating. As for Scarlet, she falls in love with a boy who is killed in a motorcycle accident to later find out she is pregnant by him. Haley and Scarlet stand by one another through each of their millstones, despite what is in store for each. 
 Sarah Dessen knows how to keep a person reading her books hooked throughout. I would recommend this 
 book to anyone, not just Sarah Dessen fans. Someone Like You would help you realize some things about your own life, like what love really is and the importance of close relationships in your life (family and friends). The book may also prevent you from making mistakes by learning from these two great friends' obstacles.

Generally Dessen's work feels very real and as though I cracked open a diary of someone who is going through this storyline. However, this one fell flat for me and I didn't really like any of the characters. Just not as good in comparison to many of her other work.

sample_reviews.review_text:
"Siege and Storm" takes off immediately where the first installment "Shadow and Bone" concluded allowing for readers to easily transition from one book to the next. 
 I enjoyed this installment. However, this novel contains mostly filler. Even though certain events and elements that are integral to the overall plot of this series happen in this installment they felt like they could have been shortened. Instead these essential parts could have been placed at either the end of the first novel or at the beginning of the conclusion. 
 Although, I personally enjoyed the filler in this novel because it allowed us to dwell more on Mal and Alina's relationship and gave us a chance to get to know Nikolai, Tamar and Toyla. Nikolai is a new favorite of mine and made me even more invested in this book. He's lively personality gave me a break from the large array of dark brooding characters that haunt these novels pages. That isn't to say I don't love dark brooding characters because in all actuality I enjoy them immensely, but you always need that vivacious cast member (for ex: Jace/Simon in the Mortal Instruments, Rose Hathaway in Vampire Academy, etc.) Sometimes you need a little break from the dark. 
 It was great to see Alina struggle with the power she has obtained. In most young adult novels, you don't see the main characters struggle between good and dark. Usually they aren't swayed from the morally right side. However, as Alina obtains more power she actually has to struggle with the concept that she might be losing herself to the dark force of power and how it feels to control people through fear. I give Bardugo props for giving Alina this issue. It makes her feel even more tangible because people struggle everyday with right and wrong and in the end your choice makes you. 
 The reason this sequel fills like filler is that a lot of it contains preparation for a battle to come, but the battle itself only lasts a few pages. The planning and political aspects of this novel made it feel real, but some may find themselves bored. I didn't but I could see how this would happen. However, hopefully people will be intrigued enough by the plot and characters of this story to continue onto the third installment "Ruin and Rising." 
 I love this world. It is dark and filled with vivid details that make it come alive inside my mind and I can't wait to see what awaits Alina next. Will she defeat the Darkling? Will her and Mal reconnect? Will Alina take the throne for herself and rise to power? What waits in the conclusion? I guess, I will have to read it to find out.

 A more detailed review. Originally posted at Disquietus Reads 
 I do not promise that this post will have anything resembling coherence. I am just so incredibly blow away by this book. Stayed up until 3:30 a.m. finishing it, crying for an hour afterwards, then not being able to fall asleep for another couple of hours because I couldn't stop thinking about it, blown away. I don't even know where to start with this review because I have so many feelings to process. I was so excited to get my hands on this book. Excited enough that on the drive home after purchasing it I may or may not have been stroking it and repeatedly cooing "my precious" to it. And I was not at all disappointed. If this book does not convince you that Leigh Bardugo and the Grisha series are the best thing out there in the YA world, I don't even know how to talk to you. 
 The writing remains spectacular. Gorgeous, and evocative, I just want to drown myself in it, and read it again and again. In fact I will probably take it with me on vacation next week and re-read it just to make sure I didn't miss anything. And find all my favorite quotes. The world Leigh has built is so incredible and complex, the relationships, characters, countries. I can't even wrap my head around her talent, but I can tell you that it is everything a Fantasy book should be. 
 Alina is my favorite protagonist in the history of all the protagonists. I loved her in the first book, but pages 103 and 232 of this one sealed the deal for me. She is glorious, magnificent and yes, terrifying. She truly comes into herself in this book, embracing her power, her connection with the Darkling, the reality of her relationship with Mal and the fact that she is no longer the scared little orphan girl she was when she first came to the Little Palace, and never will be again. While she is definitely frustrating at times, and still has her moments where she is scared and doubtful, she is all about kicking ass and taking names in this book and her journey was the best part of this book. Her last words in the novel literally gave me chills and I cannot wait to see what she has up her sleeve next. 
 Siege and Storm also introduced three new characters who I am madly in love with. Sturmhond is everything he was hyped up to be. When I first heard about his character, I had some suspicions about his true identity and I may have let out a little AH HA I KNEW IT when I discovered I was right. Leigh constantly surprises me, so being right about this made me extremely happy. I can't properly express his charm and wit and how much his presence adds to this series. While I don't ship him with Alina at all, I can definitely see why the pairing appeals to my fellow readers. The golden-eyed twins, Tamar and Tolya are also new favorites of mine. I enjoyed them immensely. 
 I should probably talk about Mal too. I'm so conflicted by him. While I don't love him as much as my other book blogging friends do, I don't dislike him at all. I'm not sure why he seems to be getting so much hate in other reviews I've read of this book. Yes, some of his actions are definitely frustrating, but I just couldn't be mad at him over them because I empathize with him. He's loved Alina his entire life, even when he didn't realize it, and he isn't quite ready to accept that she is no longer that same girl. It's hard not to swoon at that kind of love. At the same time I do find the whole concept of your first love being your only possible true love to be incredibly boring, which is why I couldn't sell myself on the idea of Mal/Alina, even though I tried. I appreciate their relationship and the love they share but I don't think it's sustainable because they are not the same people they were before Alina discovered her power, and people outgrow each other. It's a fact of life. 
 Honestly I don't even know how I feel about the so-called "love triangle" of this series. Part of this is because while the romantic relationships are important aspects of the series, they are by no means its driving force. I wouldn't at all be surprised if Alina ended up alone at the end of everything, so I don't want to get myself invested in any pairing, but despite my best efforts my heart still aches and yearns for the Darkling/Alina. If my feelings hadn't already been sealed on this in the first book, and survived despite his truly horrific actions toward her, pages 418-419 and two particular lines: "I've seen what you truly are and I've never turned away. I never will." and the "And he was my monster, too" line would have done it. The Darkling and Alina are connected, through their powers and because, at least in my probably slighltly deluded mind, their souls are made of the same stuff. They need each other in the elemental way the darkness and light have always needed each other throughout time. One cannot survive without the other. Of course I could be reading way too much into it all. Just let me have my delusions. 
 Naturally, I saved my discussion of the Darkling for last because he is the dearest to my heart (I'm still sad that I don't live in the anywhere near Hollywood and couldn't go to the Siege and Storm release party and get one of the Darkness Never Dies totes) this may take a while. I was anxious going into this book, because I'd heard that he was absence for most of it, but I did not feel that absence at all. While he wasn't physically present as much as he was in Shadow and Bone, he was seeped into every page of this book, constantly in Alina's head, which caused me to have a lot of emotions, most of them the exact opposite of everyone else. Every scene with him caused my heart to ache and tears and pulled so much emotion out of me, but it was the scenes on page 238 and again pages 418-419 in particularly destroyed me and left me sobbing like a baby. He causes my heart more conflict than any character, ever. I hated so many of his actions. The way he treated Alina, his new creations, what he did to Baghra, the way he seems to have been completely corrupted to the point of being wholly irredeemable at this point. Most of his actions in this book were horrific. I can't deny that. One in particular had me wanting to rip his head off out of sheer disappointment, especially after having read the recently released Genya POV piece, The Tailor. But I just do not share the same feelings of terror and creepiness that my fellow readers seemed to have. Maybe it's because I have never been scared of the dark, maybe it's because I have a thing for characters who aren't afraid of themselves or doing what needs to be done, even if the rest of the world thinks it's obscene, but I finished this book more in love with this character than ever. I may not agree that everything he does is necessary, some of his actions were probably definitely done because he has been utterly corrupted by his desire for power, but I can understand why he does them. Part of that I'm sure has to do with being in Alina's head while she faces an inner conflict over her power that I suspect, and hope, the Darkling faced before he became what he is now. I could be reading way more into this than is actually there, but I have faith in Leigh and I just can't believe that the Darkling is only about being creepy and scary and all about being desperate for more power. While I fully expect my love for him to cause my heart to be shattered to pieces in the final book, I can't deny the fact that if loving him is wrong, I never ever want to be right. 
 I honestly can't even think of anything to criticize about this book, other than my constant need for more of the Darkling, but the entire series could be written from his POV and I'd probably be saying the same thing. I know that I will be reading these books again and again while I wait for the final installment.

Rating: 4 1/2 Stars 
 Warning, warning! Danger, danger! SPOILERS for SHADOW AND BONE ahead! Avast, there be spoilers! If ye have not read Shadow and Bone and wish to do so, TURN BACK, me hearties! 
 . . . 
 . . . 
 . . . 
 [This Book in One Sentence: Alina Starkov returns in Shadow and Bone's thrilling and heart-wrenching sequel; war is brewing, and no one is safe.] 
 Upon completing Siege and Storm, I immediately bought it on Amazon after a near-lethal injection of fangirl into my veins. Thanks, Darkling. Thanks for being such a magnificently crafted character. You're gonna kill me one day. 
 "I've seen what you truly are," said the Darkling, "and I've never turned away. I never will. Can he say the same?" 
 Siege and Storm picks up where the previous installment left off. Alina and Mal are attempting to build a new life together-away from Ravka and the Darkling's influence. As Shadow and Bone sadly revealed, the Darkling has much bigger plans for Alina than anyone could have guessed. With Mal's help, she manages to escape, but not before being traumatized by events that were gory, sorrowful, and could have been stopped. 
 Alina and Mal are hiding out in a dirty foreign hostel, but fate cannot be so easily ignored. The Darkling is growing more powerful by the day. Ravka is in more danger than ever before. Alina is aching to use her powers. Will she return? Is the Darkling after her? How can she be useful to Mal without her abilities? These are the questions that plague her nightmares.. 
 I absolutely adore this book. It might be a trilogy favorite-perhaps. There are swashbucklers, adventures, kickass character developments, sob-worthy scenes, politics with a side serving of violence, horrific happenings... 
 woah 
 . I'm getting dizzy, and I wasn't even halfway done. 
 Complex, interwoven themes are present in Siege and Storm: the hero's journey; the pain of sacrifice; the cost of hubris; the balance of death and life; an unending struggle for human power. 
 I really admire Alina's character development; it reflects the harsh reality of trauma combined with magically induced ambition. This new amplifier has changed her-and what's more, it's given her an unbreakable connection to the Darkling. She's not the same girl that she was in Shadow and Bone; she's better. I positively love Alina in every way... but I think that Mal holds her back more than anything or anyone else. 
 Sometimes I wanted to stab him with a giant fork. 
 Mal is an expert tracker and a handsome human being, but his positive qualities stop there. He's certainly 
 not right 
 for Alina. It felt like he was clinging onto her for dear life, complaining about anything that he could while, um, they were in the middle of fighting a war! People were dying left and right while Mal glared at Alina for talking to another man about military strategies. 
 Mal disrupted the story for me because I have never wanted Alina to end up with him. He's an excessively jealous love interest who has slept with ten times as many people as Alina ever has or will. Hypocritical, much? 
 The Darkling is not present as much as he was in the first book, but as one of the main characters, he is still much-discussed. Scenes with him were lacking; this was a disappointment- 
 I consider the Darkling to be one of the greatest characters that literature has ever seen. 
 However, the scenes that did feature the Darkling were not wasted. He made me angry, tugged at my heartstrings, and caused me to cry out in frustration numerous times throughout the novel. His relationship with Alina has been twisted and gradually becomes 
 deliciously disturbing 
 . So, he's there; Shadow and Bone readers will just have to get used to his occasional place on the sidelines. 
 Additionally, a plethora of new characters are introduced. They are 
 total 
 game-changers. These people will make you question everything you know about Shadow and Bone's setting. There are pirates, princes, warriors who worship Alina as a saint, and so many more. If you thought that this world was fleshed out before, then you're going to be positively overwhelmed by the new information in Siege and Storm. 
 From love squares to Darkling lairs, this book's plot is seductive and shadowed. 
 Siege and Storm is highly recommended for anyone who appreciated Shadow and Bone; if you're a lover of magic, adventures on the high seas, high-stakes politics, dark characterizations, or having your heart ripped out while sobbing uncontrollably, you will enjoy every minute of this masterful work.

sample_reviews.review_text: This was my least favourite Jennifer Weiner... I had to force myself to finish it.

Welcome to Upchurch Connecticut where the moms are snobs and your husband is barely there. One day you receive a phone call from one of the other moms (Kitty Cavanaugh). What could she possibly want? 
 Synopsis: 
 Kate Klein is a young mother of three who brought her children to this lovely house and makes a discovery. Kate does the responsible thing and let the police know, but she can't let it go of what she has discovered. She starts to pursue leads as to who did it? While her best friend Janie is game to help solve the case her husband is not. What about a blast from the past? What changes does this bring for Kate and her family? 
 My Thoughts: 
 I was very entertained by this classic Jennifer Weiner novel. I listened to the audio version where Emily Skinner narrated. I very much enjoyed her narration. This novel was one of the more humorous mysteries I have ever read. 
 Who doesn't identify with moving to a new town and not fitting in? I had really hoped that the husband would come around. I felt sorry for her with his ignorance. I had thought the novel would last longer than what it did! I sort of hoped for a different ending.
This book will make every mom in suburbia crave for a neighborhood murder to spice up their lives. Or maybe that was just me.
http://www.segredosemlivros.com/2015/...

** spoiler alert ** 
 For mystery club theme "Murder Meets Chick Lit." I have really enjoyed Ms. Weiner's chick lit novels and was very excited to see a crossover into mysteries. Alas, this novel didn't quite work for me. I loved the flashback chapters to the beginning of Kate & Janie's friendship and the introduction to Evan McKenna. Those read like classic Weiner. The mystery itself was okay. I didn't see the resolution of the mystery until it happened and I like when I'm surprised. The mystery could have used a little more support through the plot. 
 My main complaint with this book was that the final chapter or two came out of left field. There was nothing in the previous 360 pages to support the conclusion. Kate complains, whines, moans and groans, and otherwise expresses her unhappiness with being a mother and housewife. Then, in the last 2 pages of the book decides that it is the greatest thing ever, her true higher calling. If there had been ambivalence throughout the book, I could have accepted the ending better, but such was not the case.

In Goodnight Nobody, Jennifer Weiner tells the story of Kate Klein, a city girl who suddenly finds herself stuck in the suburbs of Upchurch with her two kids while her absentee husband devotes himself to furthering his career. Everything changes for Kate when she stumbles upon the dead body of one of the seemingly perfect mothers of Upchurch. Although the writing is terrific, I'm afraid the ending was just too far out to be believable.

Originally posted on NOT ENOUGH BOOKS, NOT ENOUGH TIME 
 So, there are a few things you all need to know about this review and myself. But I don't know if I want to tell because it shows how idiotic I can be. 
 - I did not know this was a series. 
 - This book has been on my bookshelf since 1997. 
 - This book was a filler. I was not expecting to like this book as much as I did. Over the years, I think I have tried twice to read this book and didn't get through the first three chapters. But I needed a short, quick read while waiting for books from the library. I was greatly surprised at how good this book was. 
 - But my biggest reaction to this book was how on earth is this a children's novel. 
 I know there were a few times while I was reading that I had to put the book down and regroup because what L'Engle discusses is so deep that I couldn't comprehend what she was getting at. I would have to go back and reread sections. This wasn't a bad thing per say but for a child, I think the meat of the story would be missed. I think this is one of those books, like To Kill a Mockingbird, where the reader can go back at any given time in their life and learn something new and gain another lesson from the story. That is what makes a really good novel. 
 Another thing I did not know, again I must have been living under a rock when it came to this book, but I did not know Madeleine L'Engle was a Christian author. Sure, when I was reading A Wrinkle in Time, I couldn't miss it, but doing more research, L'Engle was compared to other Christian authors, but knowing this it allowed me to see parallels to Biblical parables throughout the story, much like with Lewis and Tolkien. Some of it did seem a little forced to me, like it didn't quite flow with the plot, but overall, it was another story of good versus evil. 
 Finally, because you all know me, I have to talk about the heroine. 
 I have never been a spectacle, red-headed ten year old, but I related to Meg so much, but it was on a emotional level. It was strange being an almost 24 year old relating to a 10 year old girl but at that age, I didn't feel I was adequate. I had an older brother who was brilliant and athletic and frankly, I thought, my parents favorite. I tried my hardest at school and athletics, I was great at sports but education took effort. I just never felt good enough. Meg went through these same emotions. Reading this book brought back some of these feelings. They were so raw and there, L'Engle didn't drill it into your head but I think Meg was so relatable that a reader doesn't have to put themselves into Meg's shoes so much as they slip comfortably in. She isn't the typical, strong, smart heroine that we expect in a young adult novel, but she comes into her own skin. Like we all must do in our own time. 
 In closing, I think this was a well written book, though you can tell it's dated. But that doesn't take away from the novel. Like I said, some of the Biblical references were forced but overall, enjoyable. The characters were fantastic, they felt like your next door neighbors. I'm not sure if I will go back and read the next installment in the Time Quintet but I don't think it should be taken as a bad thing. I think I missed the window where this book was mysterious and enthralling, who knows I might go back in a couple years and find that window. I never say never, because you never know.

3.5 out of 5 
 A Wrinkle in Time is a wonderful children's book. It has creative characters and situations. It has a moral compass guiding the story. It follows an adventure through the pov of children. It teaches them positive lessons about life. As a book for adults, however, it is somewhat more shallow of an experience. 
 First off, many elements were too simplistic to be completely satisfying (as an adult). For one, the universe/place this took place in was more magical than 'possible.' There's nothing wrong with that, but I would consider this more fantasy than science fiction. Usually science fiction deals with possible things (which this does in the science aspects), and focuses on that science as a way of explaining the world (which this does not). Instead of setting up the rules of the world and then having conflicts that come out of those rules, in AWIT, obstacles arise and are explained when needed to serve the story (say for a plot point, or to add drama. Things like the magical glasses only being able to be used once). This gives the story a more magical, fantasy vibe. 
 The story too was overly simplistic to be totally satisfying for me. There really was no overt danger visible here. There were threats of being threatened, but no one was really threatened. And in actuality, there were only really a handful of scenes. While this might be appropriate for children (keeping things short and not showing anything too dangerous or frightening), I wanted more to happen. 
 Lastly, the logic here feels designed for kids as well. To quote the book: "IT could only give pain, never relieve it. The beasts must be good. They had to be good." This clear cut blank-and-white division of right and wrong is good to teach children concepts, but as adults, we know that it isn't the way the real world really works. We've learned sometimes the worst things feel good (that is why they are so destructive). We've also learned that this kind of conflict and ambiguity is more appealing (to adults), because it reflects the real world. 
 But those things aren't saying this is a bad book. They are just pointing out how this book would be more appealing to children than adults. There is a lot to like here. I enjoyed the style of writing here. It was very simple, not particularly 'amazingly' written, but the dialog struck me as interesting. It reminded me a lot of The Lion Witch and the Wardrobe in its style and elements. The characters too were interesting, and I particularly like Meg. Her inner struggle with confidence was both interesting and realistic. 
 The only real negative thing I found with AWIT was there was definitely a religious analogy going on. I felt, however, that it got in the way of the story instead of really serving it. If the "God" element would have been edited out, the story really wouldn't have changed. The message would be the same, and so would the story. But with the occasional reference to serving God and the like, I got the feeling that I was being subliminally preached at. This turned me off at parts of the story. 
 A Wrinkle in Time is a nice little book. It's quick, interesting, has a nice fantasy flavor, and a good message (I especially liked the non-conformist sentiments). If I had kids, I wouldn't think twice about reading it to them.

 I enjoyed how lighthearted the story was. Lewis has a really unique voice that I don't think I've ever seen even close to replicated in anything else I've read. I also didn't miss the religious parallels, but I didn't think they were obtrusive as they could have been. 
 Pretty interesting start to a fantasy series I'm really looking forward to allowing my inner child to work his way though.

Although The Magician's Nephew was published originally as the sixth book in the series, the publisher of the edition I'm reading arranged it as first to be read to fit the chronological order of the story, and so began my journey into Narnia. The story explains the origin of Narnia, and the origin of things related to it in later stories, such as the magic wardrobe, and the lamppost etc. 
 The first half of the story reminded me of that wonder and mystery that all of us feel as children in the big world we find ourselves in. It really spoke of that feeling you got as a child when you were away from the grownups for a few hours with another kid in the neighborhood, experiencing your first feelings of real independence off on some adventure. This feeling associated with the book was my favorite part about it. 
 But I didn't appreciate other parts of the book as much. For example, the Christian religious parallels were so prevalent that there were certain parts that were almost exact copies of stories that occurred in the Book of Genesis. For example, the queen tempting Digory to eat of the forbidden fruit, or the creation of Narnia being like Eden, or a powerful tree being placed in Narnia (as in Eden), the children being called "sons of Adam," Aslan being representative of God (or Jesus Christ) etc. I'm not against the author using the stories as a way to present religious values in a different light, but they were so obviously taken from the Bible that it felt like this wasn't a story all on its own at all. 
 Other than that complaint though, the book reads easily and I found myself flying through it. I've heard that this is usually most people's least favorite book of the Narnia series, so that makes me look forward to the other stories as this was still enjoyable.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Fallen had been sitting on my shelf for a year now. After watching an interview with author Lauren Kate at a book fair early November, I finally cracked its spine. My expectations weren't that high, nor were they exceptionally low. The considerable hype surrounding this series definitely had something to do with both the high and the low part. All the same, I ended up disappointed. 
 I just couldn't get into it. Part of that is the fact that it's written from a third person perspective, which nearly always makes me feel distanced from the characters and the events. I strongly prefer books with a first person narrator, books that make you - when you look in a mirror after you've read them - surprised not to see the main character's face looking back at you. 
 A second reason is the setting. It was bland and gray and boring and the fact that it was a disciplinary boarding school added little or nothing to the story - when it could've had. In my opinion, it would have been so much more interesting (and realistic. And creepy!) if Luce were sent to an asylum of some sort. 
 I also found myself being slung back and forth between my impression of the surroundings (being: rainy, dark, coldn gloomy - as Luce's mood) and the actual surroundings (being: sunny, warm, beautiful trees etc). Somehow it didn't seem to fit, leaving me confused whenever Luce commented on it being hot outside. "Wait a second, wasn't the sky weeping in despair just a second ago? No? Sunny skies all around? Well alrighty then ..." 
 Third reason: it took forever until something supernatural started occurring. 3/4th of this book is basically about a girl getting sent to boarding school, doing research, falling in love with 2 guys at once and being chased by rather harmless shadowy thingies. Yawn. Only at the very end things started getting interesting, but then there was too much happening all at once. I honestly couldn't be bothered anymore at that point. I wanted to get it over with. 
 Fourth reason: although the idea of Luce's incarnations always finding Daniel is, of course, extremely romantic, I didn't feel anything at their developing love. No nostalgic sighing, no latent butterflies. Nope. Nothing. Sorry. 
 Fifth and maybe most important reason: I - once again! - made the mistake of reading a translation from English to Dutch. As a general rule, they suck. And I suck for trying to keep reading them. From now on: only English books and Dutch books that were actually written in Dutch.

Reading this on a suggestion of a student...not impressed so far. 
 Eh-that's my overall comment. I know, I know, teens across the nation dig this series but I found it dark, murky and a little confusing (again, my beef about the author's obligation to give the reader a clear explanation of the fantasy land they create). I'm discouraged that I have a lot of girl students who are glued to this. It's another Twilight-esque romance with a human and non-human type: your run-of-the-mill inner-species romance. Ugh. 
 P.S. The main character is a big whiner, which is annoying and it's the same formula as all the books in what I call the "Inner-Species Dramovel" (new word meaning "drama-novel"). If you are unfamiliar with the formula, here it is: Girl meets hostile non-human boy appearing to be human. Girl figures out what non-human boy is as said non -human boy starts to warm-up to her. Girl is inept at almost everything, non-human boy must protect her from herself and forces of evil that will destroy her. Girl discover she and non-human boy have history and/or are destined to be together. Said destiny will take 3-5 books to fulfill. AND, odds are that non-human boy will talk girl out of taking on some non-human qualities, but she'll do it anyway. AND, count on a love triangle. YAWN! 
 Twilight CHECK

 Wolves of Mercy Falls CHECK (although this one had redeemable qualities) 
 City of Ashes CHECK 
 Vampire Academy CHECK (haven't read it...just assuming)

 The characters are pretty well developed though I did think Lex could have used a bit more work. I mean the girl not only has a hero complex but also doesn't seem to learn from her mistakes really. 
 I adored Pip and Bang and of course Uncle Mort is one of my favorites. 
 Coming back to the Harry Potter comparisons, I think Norwood and Heloise did an Umbridge once they got control over Croak. I certainly hate Norwood as much as I hated Umbridge. Zara is more of a Malfoy in my mind even after that crazy last chapter. 
 A great read for me and I just couldn't stop reading it. Though be warned, if you're looking for a happy ending, this book doesn't exactly have one.

reference_books.title: The Assassin and the Underworld (Throne of Glass, #0.4)
reference_books.review_text:
So I finished The Assassin and the Underworld before I had to take a break from Celeana. Because, how do I put this nicely.... Celeana is a fucking moron! Let me tell you why, so, she fucks over Arobynn by screwing up his trade agreement with Rolfe the pirate king by freeing two ships filled with slaves, destroying his(the pirate kings that is) island defenses and buggering most of his boats. She then makes said pirate king promise never to get into the slave trade with Arobynn and not allow anyone he notices to get into the slave trade. If you aren't with me so far let me shorten that out for you, she fucks Arobynn over a lot of money and what is to him a perfectly good business opportunity and she thinks he'll get over it. 
 Ok, then, then once she's back after a hiatus to the Red Desert that was meant to be a punishment, Arobynn is showering her with gifts again and wants to make amends to her by giving her an opportunity to stop another slave trader in the making. Of course, Celeana isn't the brightest bulb on the tree because she thinks the psycho who beat her and Sam senseless is being honest and actually doing something good. Makes total sense given Arobynn's character and the fact that while he might be nice to Celeana, he is still a dick to Sam. 
 Don't take my word for it though, Sam tells Celeana what Arobynn's punishment for him was. And Arobynn tells Celeana Sam still has to pay for his suit while Celeana's is a gift, but hey, I'm sure Arobynn is totally being upfront with you Celeana. 
 So when (predictably) Arobynn manipulates Celeana into the exact opposite of what she thought she was doing she actually thinks to herself that sure, she can stop the person who needs stopping and ruin the whole slave trade agreement thing......but she can't be bothered. You know why? Because, She. Doesn't. Want. To. Get. Involved! 
 OMFG! You KILL the person who was fighting against the whole slave trade agreement, because you're anti that but then when you know who is actually going to be running it to decide to not stop them because you don't want to get involved!? 
 Moron! 
 The other novella's in this series aren't bad at all. In fact they are fun, however because of Celena being a selfish, stupid git and pissing me off this isn't going to get as high a rating as it would have otherwise. 
 Also, can someone explain how Sam was supposed to know Celeana would choose him over Arobynn when, in her own words Celeana never loved Sam before suddenly discovering her feelings for him and until recently would be more likely to kill him than anything else? Did she really love Sam at all? She brings him up often enough in the series and says she loved him but seriously? 
 All I'm saying is, he deserves better.

reference_books.title: House of Leaves
reference_books.review_text: What the ever living fuck!? What am I missing about this book. I want to kill it. No really, I would like to murder this book in the most painful way possible. Reading it was like having sleep paralysis. Anyone whose ever suffered through that will understand the reference. It was just so painful.

reference_books.title: The Awakening (The Vampire Diaries, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
So since vampire diaries, the series is nearly done(or is it done already?), and I'm super behind on watching it I decided I could just read the books to get my fix of delicious Damon. I was mistaken. 
 Now generally, the series usually follows the books, at least in GOTr it does but that isn't the case so much here. Bonnie is a red head, Meredith is the third best friend, Elena is blonde, minor things i know. But the most major change I think is how much less annoying Elena is in the series. And that's saying something because I hated the Elena Gilbert is the series, she was whiny and all woe is me, but of course everyone thought she farted fairy sprinkles. The Elena Gilbert of the book puts her to shame however. This Elena is on a whole seductress power trip, she's manipulative of everyone and dismissive of anyone she believes is beneath her. She takes the whole queen bee thing too seriously and is so cookie cutter in some of her thoughts and words that she reminds me of Marsha from The Brady Bunch. Add the insta-love/lust with Stefan whose whole conflicted mysterious characterization does nothing for me and this book just became a steaming pile of disappointment. I'm trying to power on through the second book hoping Elena grows as a character or you know just dies but it's slow going.

book_a.title: Storm Glass (Glass, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Opal Cowan is more annoying as a character than Yelena, which isn't saying much because I sorta love Yelena. The only thing Opal has got over Yelena is how much more shit her life is/has been/will be. Poor thing. Yes, Opal develops as a character in the book but too slowly imo. She's still manages to become a likable character towards the end though. 
 The most annoying thing in this book is the bloody love square. Yep, Opal has 3 potential love interests which is a bit ridiculous and I normally love a good love triangle. 
 3.5 star read for me.

sample_reviews.review_text: Maria Snyder has a great way of making a simple story line enjoyable. This is the beginning of a series so the character connections are still developing but it was a good story.
Not as good as her others.
This was a really quick, engaging read. Read it if you like the Study series.
Good book, but kept feeling like I was missing some back story. Maybe there was just a prequel I didn't know about. But Opal was a character with interesting magic.

Opal Cowan is a glass magicians, so when the Stormdancer's glass orbs begin to shatter, she is called upon to attempt a fix. When she determines the glass-maker's ingredients have been sabotaged, the question becomes who would do such a thing, and why? Her quest for answers takes her from the Magician's Keep to the far reaches of the kingdom, and brings back old demons she thought had been put behind her forever. 
 Opal's not as strong a character as Yelena from the Poison Study trilogy. While I was interested in the story, Opal's constant self-doubt was a little hard to take. Plus, the love story left me completely confused--just when I thought she had settled on one guy, she would turn around and go for the other one, without any apparent logical reasoning. My favorite part of the book was when 2 characters from the other series showed up. Not sure I'll go on to the second book...other reviews I've read indicate that the issues with Opal's character just get worse.

Where do I begin... I'll start by saying that this may, kind of, but not really include a Spoiler... 
 For the most part, I really enjoyed this book. The plot was pretty well placed and I never felt bored with the action or dialogue, and I was easily absorbed into the world of glass magic. My biggest problem was with the protagonist of Opal Cowan. I really like her for about 80% of the story but then I realized just how indecisive she was and how much that bothered me. Yeah, she was pretty awesome with her magic and inner fight, but Synder really lost me at the very end of the novel. I should probably say first: I am not a fan of love triangles. At all. They infuriate me to no end. But I dealt with this one, until the end when Opal, who appears to have made a decision, decides that maybe it would be fair to explore another avenue. I just didn't get her and to me this decision made no sense. But maybe that's just me. 
 So, while I enjoyed reading this book, it was a very quick and entertaining read, I don't think I'd continue the series.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I'm honestly not sure why I'm interested in reading the next book, but I am. The plot of this book seems to be Opal complains about being a one trick wonder and not having any friends, then she's kidnapped, she gets free, whines some more about being a one trick wonder with no friends, is nearly kidnapped, whines some more, is kidnapped, whines, followed by someone who turns out to be a friend, whines and kidnapped yet again. 
 I like her style of magic. It would be interesting to see what else she can do with glass. 
 I also like the stormdancer, Kade, but I'm a lot less thrilled about the other love interest who never trusted her to be on her own. It wasn't abusive (yet) but certainly stifling. 
 I really hope the next book has more of a plot than a series of kidnapping and escapes.

Sorry to say it was disappointing. Loved the Inside/out series. Really really liked the Study series but the Glass books just aren't up to par. Probably because Opal is not as likable as Yelana and to me the story was choppy and many parts just did not make sense (and I am pretty good at going along with the paranormal) Mostly I think it was just Opal's personality or lack thereof that made this just ok. I bought the 2nd book, because the library did not have a copy so I will give it a look and then donate it.

I wish Opal's story would not have been dragged out over 3 volumes, as apparently there is not enough plot to fill so many pages. The Study Series had the same problem, actually. I like Opal, her glass magic and the stormdancers, but apart from that there is not enough substance to keep me reading this spin-off. 
 The good: 
 - Opal is not an over-powered Mary-Sue as Yelena has become. It was refreshing to have a heroine that has to think and strategize Reaching the end of the book, I might have to take that back. Opal also discovers new abilities to get her out of danger and might become just as over-powered. 
 - Opal is not as stupid as Yelena who never listens and runs into trouble without thinking. 
 - Storm magic, glass magic, horses 
 The bad: 
 - Possibly to make Opal different from Yelena, the author took her character too far into the opposite direction. Yelena is too hot-headed, while Opal hesitates all the time, has zero self-confidence and constantly doubts herself. Granted, she does get some character development towards the end, but her self-loathing is a bit too extreme, given that she really has no reason to be that disregarding of her quite impressive achievements. 
 - Love triangle/rectangle - I am so over them. In this case particularly, it is very disturbing that by the end of the book a guy who tortured Opal repeatedly is set up as a possible love interest. 
 - Teachers sending their students into dangerous missions without proper protection or even thoroughly teaching them self-defense and other skills (lock-picking) that don't involve magic 
 - Too much talking about the incredible amazing marvel that is Yelena. Seriously, people will pick up your other books if they like this one. No need for so much publicity.

This book was a fun read and I really enjoyed the idea of glass magic-- I really haven't read anything like this before. Still, it did not catch me as some of the other Maria V. Snyder works I've read recently (Poison Study, Night Vision) which was a little disappointment. 
 Still, I'm interested enough to keep reading and see where it goes. I'm not too fond of Opal yet, but hey! She might grow on me. I just found it annoying that everyone was telling her she was too hard on herself or too timid, yet I did not feel that attitude from her.

book_b.title: Pride & Popularity (The Jane Austen Diaries, #1)
book_b.user_review:
Having previously read two books from Jenni James' Faerie Tale Collection I don't know why I thought the Jane Austen Diaries would be a huge improvement. It's not. There is a slight improvement, but not huge. I wanted huge. 
 The problem with Pride and Popularity is that while it's a modern retelling of Pride and Prejudice(which I love obsessively btw) it does absolutely no justice to the original or the current century(or the ending of the previous century for that matter, because I'm fairly sure I was here for the end of that). 
 Chloe is trite. Taylor is trite. Chloe's mom makes no sense and is trite. Chloe's dad is a bit of a star, but only because he seems sane and marginally less trite. I had a point I promise, I just don't remember what it was. 
 Let's start with Chloe, she's allegedly 17, but sounds like Marta from the Brady Bunch(what decade were they from exactly?). She's sarcastic, dense, shallow and unlikeable. The original Elizabeth was sarcastic, humble, smarter than was expected of her and got you on her side simply by acting like a mature adult with spine of course. The only reason Chloe is in love with Taylor is that he's hot. She doesn't know he's a good person, she doesn't bother to find out even when evidence is present to the contrary. She doesn't even try to get to know him. 
 Taylor is allegedly a good person like the original misunderstood Mr. Darcy, however that is not an excuse for his immense ego in the starting of the book (that whole basketball scene annoyed me, I mean who does that?) as well as throughout it in bits and pieces when he's not doing an impersonation of Dr.Jekyll and being super nice. I also thought Georgiana speak was unnecessary, it did not make me think she was any cuter really and was faintly annoying. 
 Chloe's mom who is the life of her Halloween party and also appears to have multiple personalities, is suddenly forcing her daughter to date some guy?! She reminded me of a pimp to be honest, it may have been acceptable in the 18th century and in say I don't know, an Indian family but I thought this was a modern retelling. 
 Im tired of complaining now so I'm going to stop, however I don't think I'll be continuing on with reading any more of this authors books.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Loved it. This is a great modernisation of the Austen books. It is far enough removed from the original that it doesn't feel like a word for word retelling but James lets all the important parts shine though. Reading these and having met the author, you can just tell that Jenni is truly passionate about her books and in general about Austen. 
 It's also great to see a YA book that is actually suitable for a YA audience - no sex, drugs and teen pregnancies but the book is better for it. Definitely should not be missed out on !!!

This one is also one of my holiday books. 
 Since lately I've been kinda obsessed with anything related to Pride and Prejudice, when I browsed Goodreads, I found this book. With good ratings and reviews, I decided to go for it. 
 This book is well written retelling of Pride and Prejudice in modern day. I love Chloe and Taylor as a couple, and Chloe's parents is one of a kind. Their dating ritual is so funny. 
 For a light reading on a holiday, it could brighten your day :)

Ma ne sentivamo veramente la mancanza di questo libro? 
 A parte insipienza della trama, i rimandi piu che ovvi a P&P, e una realta completamente avulsa dalla nostra. Insomma, mi dispiace, ma non mi sembra niente di che; non c'e neanche nulla da criticare ...

I LOVED THIS REMAKE!!!! Its sooo different because most Mr. Darcy's don't talk a lot, but boy oh boy does this one:). the only thing that bothered me was that is was a little to "perfect american society" for me (Not trying to be racist at all)
This is a light hearted retelling of the Jane Austen p&p classic. It is for 14-18 year olds. It is a very sweet story.

I 'sugarin' love it! <3 It's one of the feel-good books. I'm looking forward to read more of Jenni James master pieces. It's a clean work and I'm satisfied with that because I'm not looking for stereotypes definitely because I'm not a fan *wink* :D
Claramente, no la mejor version actual. Lo odie.
Oh, this was painful.

Loved it! I did not think I was going to like this book. I am a huge Jane Austen fan, and specifically Pride and Prejudice. I thought I would give it a try. This modern day take was an enjoyable read from start to finish!
Solid 3 1/2 stars. I love P & P so it was a fun, easy, and sweet read.

reference_books.title: Princess in the Spotlight (The Princess Diaries, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Hmm... 
 Lily is a horrible friend. I can't stand her. 
 Mia's obsession with controlling her mother was creepy. If my teenager gave away the groceries I ordered because she didn't approve of them, she'd be grounded - AFTER her allowance repaid the cost. 
 I'm going to keep reading these for a bit, as I hope Mia gets smarter or something, and maybe Lily gets some therapy.

reference_books.title: Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell
reference_books.review_text:
DNF 
 Made it 13 hours into the audiobook before giving up. I loathed this book. It is boring, twee, pretentious, and winks at the reader so much I'm surprised the book doesn't get eye cramps.

reference_books.title: Rogues

 But it was simply too gross for me. I dry heaved for 5 chapters straight. Nope. Not for someone with a weak stomach at all.

reference_books.title: Best Served Cold
reference_books.review_text: I wanted to like this book. For a while, I did. But by about the third mark, I just didn't care about Monza nor anyone else. I just did not care. The torture/death scenes became monotonous. I started skimming by the halfway mark and by 3/4, gave up.

book_a.title: The Dispatcher
book_a.user_review:
This was ok. It's urban fantasy more than science fiction, honestly, which is fine. For reasons no one knows, people who are murdered re-appear back in their homes alive. So dispatchers are licensed to murder dying people so that they can be saved and not actually die. 
 So the idea behind it was interesting. I just didn't really care about the actual story or the main characters. It was a police procedural, which I wasn't expecting. The characters were pretty bland, honestly, as the focus (common with procedurals) was focused on the mystery. Just not what I was in the mood for.

sample_reviews.review_text:
There were two factors that drew me into buying this audio book. One, was that it's written by John Scalzi and two, it's read by Zachary Quinto. Combine these two things together and it was an easy purchase for me and one I didn't regret at all. I'd say it's more of a novella than short story and Scalzi drops us right into the world he's created, where for some unknown reason, people who die unnaturally immediately finds themselves back home and whole again. However, people who die a natural death do not come back, which is where the main character Tony Valdez comes in. He's called a Dispatcher and it's his job to "murder" anyone who is facing a natural death so that they'll come back. His position is a formal one with the government and his work is sanctioned, but as is bound to happen with anything, there exists an underground in which criminals or people who even just people who want to engage in ultra dangerous activities such as dueling hire off duty dispatchers to be around in case their activities go awry. Tony gets caught up in an investigation into the kidnapping of one of his fellow dispatchers who was one of the off-duty dispatchers who worked these type of jobs on the side. 
 This is the third book by John Scalzi that I've read and he continues to impress me. He's able to create his worlds without bogging the books down in unnecessary description, and yet I was able to picture exactly how this new society was. Zachary Quinto's voice was perfect and I'm hoping he either has other books he's narrated for or will in the future.

This was a nice short read, and my first time reading anything by Scalzi. The concept of the Dispatchers and their work was intriguing and something different. However it felt unfinished and not completely worked through. I would have enjoyed more about the loopholes of people coming back to life once they've been murdered or more theory or what qualifications these situations have to meet for someone to come back to life. On a positive note I found the main character to be witty, sarcastic, and blunt. These qualities weren't anything new but a breath of fresh air from what I've been reading. Overall this book was a nice change of pace.
Loved the premise and the world building and the story left me wanting more. I wonder if there will be more
Good intro to this author, very brief novella. Will try other works from him.

The concept was fascinating and the events intriguing enough in the first chapters. But by the end, the story became somehow predictable and kind of dull. 
 Nevertheless, I found the writing style direct and simple, which I liked a lot, so I will definitely give a shot for another book from the same author.

If J.J. Abrams wrote an episode of Law and Order this would be the script. If it were a film, Tom Cruise would no doubt play the lead role. It's that kind of commercial product that reeks of packaging. Plastic and formulaic. Not terrible, but I'm glad it was short and didn't overstay its welcome. 
 This was free on Audible yesterday and is, as of 10/06/2016, still free. It's worth a listen for that price.
A good detective story exploring an interesting (if somewhat off the wall) premise. And it was free!

This was a short quick novella that took a lot for me to process. In the end, I realized I did really like the story. At first, I was unsure about my feelings regarding not having questions that I had answered like, "How does the universe know someone died or got murdered?" But then I just 
 Decided that, like those in the book, I don't know and I didn't have to know--because either way, the phenomenon was happening and it had to be accepted. 
 Basically, the book takes place in the nearby future and when you die from natural death, you die forever. If you are murdered, you come back to like as you were hours before your murder. The Dispatcher is about a man, Tony Valdez, who is a dispatcher--someone hired and to murder people before they die of natural causes--giving them a second chance at life. 
 The story unfolds when they find out another dispatcher goes missing. The thrill is finding out who took him, why, and how he survives. 
 It's a very interesting concept and well thought out. Loop holes were discussed in the book, but I still had the overwhelming thought, "Why?? How?!?" Throughout the novel. 
 I had to listen to this audiobook twice in order to get the full story. I think the first time I wasn't paying close attention, because I thought it was going to be an easier listen to. Plus, I fell asleep. But the second time gave me a clearer picture of the story and setting. 
 Overall, I'm sticking with my 3 stars, primarily because the story didn't grab my attention right away and I'm 
 Most likely not going to remember parts of this book in a year or so.

Narration 3/5 
 Zachary Quinto has a nice voice to listen to and was good at making slight adjustments to his voice for each character without going overboard. I wouldn't pick up a book just because he reads it but if he reads one I'm interested in than yes, for sure. 
 Story 3/5 
 I was impressed by how complete the story felt even though it was just under three hours. The beginning was very interesting and the world Scalzi created where no one can truly be murdered was unique & intriguing. However, once it turned into a missing persons investigation it began to feel like an episode of Law & Order and lost a bit of that unique draw. There's so much more I'd like to know about this world Scalzi created and would be interested to see more short stories within it that maybe follow other dispatchers.

Disappointing, it was an okay story, but it lacked a good bit of the humor and the cop that was supposed to be the stand in for the reader was WAY to obvious and didn't know enough. It was a really good concept I just feel it got messed up somewhere in execution.

book_b.title: The Aeronaut's Windlass (The Cinder Spires, #1)
book_b.user_review:
DNF. 
 Started well, but it fell off the mark hard.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This book was obnoxious. The characters were for the most part one note and the most memorable one were the ones I wanted to strangle. Like Gwen. Gwen was completely repressible. Really, the characters seemed so interchangeable in some instances that I started not paying any attention at all to the names. The steampunk was there of course, mostly winding its way in places in the social structure of the book, and of course the ships. Then there are the cats, if Jim is trying to make some sort of statement of against or criticizing humans, except that the cats came across as even more shallow and self centered and backstabbing than humans. Basically they did nothing to convince me of their superiority. It was awful. I don't want to see another cat for a while because he got the way they act so great, and the cat that took up most the time in the story getting the spotlight was the most self-centered, racist or speciest, piece of crap that ever got any time and was treated as if he was in the right and a really cool guy. 
 I mean really, there is a way to write this character that makes him not something I want to kick him as hard as I could across the street. Or at least not feel as if the author is insisting he is a great guy in this universe. I hated the cats, they, in the end, seemed to be entirely too human, their politics even more convoluted and mixed in with useless posing then ours. Basically, while I can see why you have to be political, I also understand that society reaches a point where their own rules about that sort of thing basically means that horrible things are allowed to happen and they basically shoot themselves in the foot. The cats passed this boundary line apparently when they were created. 
 That said, unfortunately, because of how many characters there were, or because of the steampunk genra (I haven't read enough novels to feel savy enough to know their characters and how they are supposed to act beyond talking about what is proper every five seconds) the characters appeared rather flat in this story. Gwen was completely unlikable as a hair trigger idiot who thinks she has the moral high ground. Her cousin is easily confused with who I think was the prince. The girl with the cat, Bridget I believe, was a put upon but missing any real substance "good person" character. And poor Grimm's character. You look at the book cover and you think you're getting a genuine rogue of a character who yes has morals, but their pirate morals, and he drinks, and he fights, and he protects his crew but no one else. You get that a little, but mostly he's just built up as this tragic guy who got the shaft by politicians. He is the most uninteresting character in his blandness. He is perfect in basically everything he does, and his mistakes and weaknesses come from his moral high ground and how perfect he is. Let me explain that second point. You know how some people try to play up a desirable trait as their weakness, like their too kind, or too orderly. That's what this character feels like he would put down as his big weakness, perhaps with the standard "pride". 
 That said, I might be the only one to think this, but I liked Folly. The best part was when she talked to the puppet master or said something particularly clever, which wasn't often, but it happened. I thought she be this whinging, weak character the first time we were introduced to her, but no, she really took off and captured my heart. She was surrounded by bland and infuriating characters, but her insanity was something that I (though I might be alone in this) actually greatly enjoyed her parts. 
 That said, I'm sorry Jim. I know that the Dresden Files was apparently the type of book you had to write because that's what the stupid masses would read, but... I'm just one of the stupid masses. I loathed the Code of whatever and now while this book was readable after the first hundred pages or so, I just didn't like it. You're one of my favorite author's but unfortunately I appear to be a favorite of one I'm afraid you might not like. Still, I think I'm in the minority here, so hopefully one of the masses rejecting this isn't any loss at all. I know it's not. I just wrote this part because I genuinely feel bad. I wanted to like this, I really did. The problem was that, in the end, I really couldn't.

I freely admit to being a Jim Butcher fan boy. Dresden Files is a very close second to my favorite series of all time. I've also had the pleasure of meeting Jim a few times now, and he's a great conversationalist, tells wonderful stories, and is amazingly generous with his fans. All of this is to say I may possibly be a bit biased. 
 That to one side, I've never been a huge steampunk fan. It just hasn't really done much for me. But, with Butcher writing, I thought I'd give it a whirl. I'm glad I did. 
 In this world, humans don't live on the dangerous surface of the Earth. The live in Spires, floating cities far above the Earth. Travel is by various kinds of airships, held aloft by the power of special crystals. Each Spire is like a country, and relations are strained. 
 As this book starts, war is brewing between Albion and Aurora (thinly disguised England and Spain). Along the way, we meet Captain Grim of the airship Predator, disgraced from the Fleet and now a privateer; Gwen Lancaster, scion of a noble house; Benedict, one the "warriorborn" who seem to be humans engineered with animal traits; Ferus, an ethericist (closest they get to wizards) and his apprentice Folly, and Bridget, a young woman from a minor noble house who has joined the Spire's military out of obligation. 
 The world is nicely fleshed out, with different cultures and peoples. Cats are intelligent in this world (yes, yes, cat owners) and are another power to be bargained with. When Albion Spire comes under sneak attack, our heroes must work together to overcome their foes and stop their wholesale destruction and murder. On the bad side is Captain Ransom, the powerful Madame Cavendish, and a host of Auroran Marines. 
 There are monsters, sword fights, duels, and ship to ship combat, all with a steampunk flavor. I enjoyed it a lot. It was a good start, and I look forward to rest of the series.

This was my first introduction to the steam punk genre and I have to say it was an awesome way to start. Jim Butcher did a wonderful job depicting his rather colorful cast of characters and I couldn't help but become entangled in their stories. Some of the technical jargon seemed to slow the reading down a bit, but since this is a new genre for me I figure its a learning curve type of thing. One thing is for sure, I can't wait until the next one is released.

I'm starting to hate that thing Butcher does, where there's always a character who knows the future or the whole plan and speaks only in riddles and warnings. We get it - you're the author, you know the whole picture.

Urgh so damn boring for 50% and then it was amazing. Honestly, I feel like if I started this book in the middle I would have liked it more (and missed nothing.). The beginning is unnecessary and so slow and dragging...I didn't even really understand why this novel was considered a steampunk genre book until 75% through - which is a huge problem. After that point though it was brilliant (until the craptastic ending trying to lure me into enduring more of this series!) with machinations of the power crystals and air ships and goggles! I know the book tried to start that way but it didn't work until 75% through. 
 Also cats are assholes....but amusing enough to read about. Clever concept.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Another fantastic series by Butcher. I absolutely loved this and it was a perfect first novel in the series. It rounded the characters gave us a mysterious evil shadowy figure an exciting and unique new world and it gave us Rowl. I approve

So. Good. 
 But ridiculously marketed/summarized. This is not a book about Grimm. The jacket copy doesn't even mention the cats! Not to mention that there are two female characters who are just as prominent! Argh!

I was disappointed. I am a big fan of Butcher's Dresden series so I was terribly disappointed when this one fell flat in comparison. Perhaps I should not compare, but I do. It's true: this book has no pictures. What it does have are interesting fonts, and silly words, and text that makes the reader say things they would never actually say in real life -- things that will have listeners laughing out loud throughout. 
 This book is hilarious, and it captures children's sense of humor well. It's perfect for a read-aloud -- and, in fact, seems to be written specifically for it. One caveat: readers should practice it first in order to master the individual voices and made-up words; it's worth the extra time. Highly recommended, especially for readers who can make fun of themselves in order to let children enjoy a good joke.
HILARIOUS.

This book is the reverse of a wordless book, in that it's in the format of a picture book, but with no pictures, which is the story itself. 
 It's also designed to drive parents crazy, because the other part of the story is that the reader has to read it out loud, no matter how goofy the words are. After all, a young child can't be expected to read it him or herself, right? 
 It's cute and clever.
I read this in the store to my sister and we were both cracking up! What a perfect book for a read aloud.

So I have really mixed emotions about this book because it was definitely cute and originalish and fun, but I don't think it's wise to tell kids they have to read every word of a book or that they cannot stop reading a book until they reach the end. 
 I know that that was a joke, and that the book is not geared towards readers, per se, but rather toward those being read to, but I don't agree with the aforementioned idea. I don't think many children will be negatively impacted by this book; in fact, I think most children will enjoy The Book with No Pictures. 
 But, yeah, that's what I think about that.

"Small kindnesses and simple pleasures shared were so important, whether given or received, regardless of what quarter they came from, that they brought home to me powerfully that I was not alone in this world, in this life. I shared the most basic operating system with people who ostensibly had little in common with me. I could connect--perhaps with anyone." 
 Piper Kerman (omg I adore her name) was studyibg at Brooklyn when her friend Nora, who eventually became her girlfriend, gave her the chance of the lifetime; it took her to places she's never been too. Because she was a fan of adventure, it was too good to be true. Unfortunately, what took her to this journey also took her the worst ride of her life. 
 We never look at the bad guys as living things who actually have their own stories too, right? This book got me interested to what jailers were in for and whether they were incarcerated for a mistake they recklessly made. 
 I like this book because it showed me that the other little things I don't thank God for were actually part of the pillars of my temple; that I should be happy of what I have now; that I should stop judging people by how they look like; and be zen and stoic. 
 I would give a 5-star review, but some parts were just too predictable and some parts got me bored because they couldn't cut to the chase.

Honestly the main reason I was able to get through this book was because after four seasons of the Orange is the New Black show I've gotten pretty accustomed to TV Piper's WASPy, self-congratulatory bullshit. Let's just say the writers of the show have done a damn good job picking up the voice of the real-life Piper. 
 You can easily cut half the book out by removing every mention of her pretty blonde hair and blue eyes, how well educated she is, all her comments about what a good person she is, and the comments from everyone surrounding her about how she is the most keen, kind, intelligent, amazing person on the planet. And maybe the several dozen times it's mentioned how surprised people were that such a person like herself could EVER wind up among the lower masses. 
 As a memoir... alright, she discusses her own experiences in prison for about a year, which mostly involved lots of running and making friends, some electrical work and whatnot. A bit bland. But as an account of prison life for women, a task to which she gives quite a lot of lip service, this is just not accurate of most peoples' experiences. She had a job lined up outside before she was ever released, a house, a fiance... hell, she had a WEBSITE dedicated to her while she was in prison. We're presented with constant reminders about how much mail she got and gifts she received, how her phone list and visitor list were always overfull of eager friends and family ready to give her attention, how supportive everyone around her was, and so on. That's a drastically different picture from the majority of the prison population, and frankly I wish she'd have spent more time (like the show) on bringing to attention the real issues, rather than more stilted and embarrassing dialogue where yet another person comments on her great ass.

This was a great read! It was a great insight into life in a women's jail. The humanity of it all was very surprising to me (the very aspect that the author was trying to convey). I would recommend this to anyone.
Very different from the show, go figure

I slogged through Orange is New Black. I felt so sure after every page it was going to get better. Piper Kerman will make a cohesive narrative at some point, right? 
 Wrong. Orange is the New Black is full of two paragraph vignettes about what feels like million characters Kerman interacts with prison. It's supposed to document her year in prison, but it feels like a mess. I could almost picture her with this big bowl in her hand, small pieces of paper scrawled with two word memories shoved inside, wine she picked them up at random. 
 The tone of the book did not help. It felt like prisoner procedural and almost like an information book. Through the whole book, it does put on a privileged air. "Look how cultured I am. I went to all these cool places (with a criminal , transporting drugs. Then I went to prison. Everyone loved me there." *HEAVY EYE ROLL* 
 I mean, I've never been to prison, but I know it's no girl's summer camp. 
 Near the end of the book she had a real great paragraph on finding sisterhood in prison. It showed humble growth and did not match any of the book. Maybe that's why it was so great... 
 I find it at the thrift store and it's going right back.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I tend to not like the surprise pregnancy trope in romance novels because they all generally follow the same plot. Girl finds out she's pregnant, panics and automatically assumes she's going to be a single parent, questions the father's intentions when he tries to be there because he couldn't possibly be into her for any reason other than the baby, then something tragic usually happens, leaving one or both parents to try and "set each other free" because, again, the only reason they were together in the first place was because of the baby. Only then do they realize that they really do love each other. It's tiring.

I enjoyed the first in this series of stand alone interconnceted stories. 
 this time we concentrate on the brother of the H from the first book, Wyatt and the best friend of the h from the first book, Angie. 
 After a casual hook up with Wyatt while visiting her friend Presley, Angie returns home to her life only to discover a couple of months later that she is pregnant. This isn't happy news for her. 
 Feeling conflicted and unsure of what she plans to do she returns to stay with Presley in Tennessee, and to break the news to baby daddy Wyatt. 
 Wyatt, self-confessed womanizer, with a history of being commitment phobic, and preferring casual hook ups only, takes the news of impending fatherhood surprisingly well. He is secretly all in but needs to do some ground work to convince Angie to stay with him. She agrees to live with him for a few months to work it out. Wyatt woos! 
 This book was chugging along quite predictably when it hits a HUGE speed bump and took me completely by surprise when it totally veers off plot into new territory entirely. It takes a bit to surprise me so this was welcome and certainly elevated this book for me. 
 As a reader the only complaint I have is the unlikely and irritating change in the H from manwhore/ commitment-phobe to insta love, this-woman-has-a-golden-vagina so I'm all in, boyfriend of the year. Its too much fantasy for fiction! 
 Still a great book.

reference_books.review_text:
Stolen Songbird is a fun fantasy read. It is the first in a series, but the pace wasn't bogged down by setting up the series. I really enjoyed the characters and the world of the trolls. I liked the fast pace of the events and the magic systems. I also enjoyed the angst-ridden romance, although it got a little tiresome towards the end. 
 There was an elusive issue that kept me from rating this book higher. The political situation of the trolls is complex, to say the least. Often, a character would establish an intricate argument against an action. Later, they would ignore the well-established consequences and perform the action with the equivalent of a mental shrug. It felt somewhat haphazard and disjointed. 
 However, I did enjoy the story overall and will read the second book in the trilogy.

reference_books.title: End of Days (Penryn & the End of Days, #3)
reference_books.review_text: End of Days is a brilliant conclusion to the trilogy. The beginning of the book focused mainly on the romance aspect of the book, with quite a bit of angst. Luckily, I love that. But then, it settled back into Susan Ee's usual balance of romance, politics, action, and comic relief. There were some big surprises and some new characters that provided action, insight, and a few laughs. At first, I was left with a few questions, but I later realized that the author wasn't spoon-feeding me. Once I used my brain, it all made sense. I thought this was a perfectly fitting conclusion to the trilogy. So glad I read this. I mean, who knew angels were so attractive? I can't wait to see what she writes next.
