I'm not entirely sure whether this book was just not that great or if it just wasn't for me. When I was a kid, I loved the story of Jane Eyre, probably because of her harsh childhood and because I found the whole Rochester part to be very romantic. After rereading the novel as an adult, though, it lost a lot of its charm, to the point where I'm not really sure how I feel about it. 
 Unfortunately this fey-fantasy version did not convince me that it's time for me to reread Jane Eyre again. I found myself skimming through the last one fourth just to get through the book, even though it ended predictably enough. Initially, I thought the fey war and Jane's curse of rage, plus the mask aspect, would make an interesting combination of Beauty and the Beast and Jane Eyre. Something about it just never really came together for me though. Jane in her role as governess seems alternately spiteful and ineffective, far more concerned with controlling Dorie than understanding the child, even though supposedly she is sympathetic and at least doesn't give up like the other governnesses. Considering this is a storyline that takes up a large part of the book - despite the low page count, it feels like a much longer book - it's just too dull to retain my interest. 
 As for whatever I remember liking about the Jane/Rochester romance, it is definitely not here in this book. From the beginning, the author seems determined to characterize Jane as desperate for affection or attention. Right off the bat, she's obsessing over whether or not she can or will be touched because no one has touched her voluntarily since she was 14 or something like that, aka since the war. I mean, what romance? Apparently what Jane sees in him is that he's the only one who has shown her interest... As for what he sees in her, I never got any sense of that from the book. This romance was as dull as it was unbelievable. 
 There is a lot of obsessing about beauty or lack thereof, but whatever themes could have been developed from this never got past the most shallow exploration. The fey magic aspect of the masks might actually be more interesting if it was about actual plastic surgery. I expected some sort of point about inner strength over shallow beauty but at the end, it seems like the author was too tempted to have the cake and eat it too, which negated whatever theme about beauty or appearances there might have been. 
 I am honestly not sure where the praise for this book is coming from. I would say that maybe it's just not suited for me but given the ratings both here and on Amazon, there's definitely a discrepancy between the glowing official reviews it got - "astonishing" and "evocative"? - and what readers experienced.

1st in a series. The Great War between humans and fey is over. But everyday Jane has a reminder, her face is scarred with the curse of rage. She must keep it covered with an iron mask or it affects others surrounding her. Even though she sustained her scar in the war people turn away from her, she's looked down upon. Jane applies for the job of governess to a little girl who needs help with an affliction like Jane's.

3.5 stars rounding up: This was a goooooood retelling, I think, even for those who do not like Jane Eyre. The fun, non-ridiculously angsty/tragically tragic backstory elements were all there or toned down and the inclusion of the fae and the twist on the 'woman in the attic' trope was pretty twisty. 
 That being said--to quote Grace, as lovely as the story was, it was a story I wish a stronger/more prose-adept writer had written? A lot of the world building read shallow to me--it was hard to get a good read on exactly how the the magical races and humans interacted, let alone how the Great War truly came to be. Furthermore, this is the type of story that really shines in the hands of gorgeous prose, and that just...wasn't really here. Not that the writing was bad, but that it simply didn't weave the type of gothic, entrancing tale that was being told. 
 There's a good story here. It's simply a bit more buried than I would have liked.

err im not sure what was going on. this was such an odd book. i know it was based off the original Jane Eyre and there was a lot of parallels with that novel but this retelling just fell short of good. First of all, this NOT a retelling of "Jane Eyre", unless one considers every gothic novel to be such. 
 This is a classic gothic romance, albeit with fey elements. Here, Jane has a sister, and traumatic experience as a warrior; there is no mad wife in the attic; and the child Jane is hired to look after is central to the plot and not peripheral. The main thing that differentiates this from most gothics- including "Jane Eyre"- is that here the heroine has a Past with secrets just like the hero does. 
 The fey element was essential to the plot(s), and very well thought out. Most of the novel kept a considered pace and revealed things to Jane- and us- at a well-measured rate. If that had continued to the end, I would have given this 5 stars; as it is, the ending seemed chaotic and rushed. While it didn't end on a cliffhanger, it's pretty obvious by the end that there are more books in the series. 
 I did enjoy most of the book, including the development of the various primary characters. However, the hasty ending detracted from my enjoyment, and I likely will not read more in the series. 
 That being said, this was a pretty good modern novel in the gothic tradition.

"Ironskin" is an unfortunate example of chemistry gone wrong. Sometimes you combine the correct ingredients but your technique is off, and Bob's-your-uncle, you've got no eyebrows. Like many of the other reviewers, I wanted to like Ironskin. I really did. I was sincerely looking forward to this galley. I stuck with it to the bitter end, hoping against hope that things would improve, that the plot would develop, that the clumsy writing would even out. I was not rewarded for my patience. Perhaps in the hands of a more experienced author with a better editor this could have been a good novel, but as it was, it was indulgent, tedious nonsense. Save your money and time. If you need a good Gothic romance send-up with a fantasy twist, read Sarah Rees Brennan's upcoming title "Unspoken" instead.

Ironskin is a book that had great potential to be a rewritten fairytale or a magical adventure; a srory about accepting who you are, helping others, facing enemies stronger than yourself and learning to work with what you've got. 
 Unfortunately it didn't end up being any of these things. The story was nice for only about 2/3 of the book, the romance seemed a bit forced, something about the writing just didn't work and in the end all this ended in a cliffhanger. It's not a horrible book, I'm just disappointed. I was hoping for more and didn't get that.

What a beautifully layered story! For what seemed like a Jane Eyre retelling with supernatural elements, I was expecting something more straightforward and recognizably similar to the plot structure of Jane Eyre, but this novel was full of the unexpected! It does not directly follow the arc of Jane Eyre, but infuses the spirit and romance of the original novel into a new story. I found the relationship between Jane and her pupil, Dorie, unexpectedly complex, as Jane struggles to get through to her and in the end through Dorie, Jane comes to realize something very important about herself. The author also sets up a strong history in the narrative, with the Great War, and the influence of the ultimately treacherous fey adding to an intricate fictional/ alternate reality where humans are still struggling to recover from the effects of war and the loss of the fey-technology. The details of this history and Jane Eliot's involvement is slowly meted out however, so there is a feeling of tension as you try to catch up on what everything means. 
 What I liked best about this story is how the author weaved in many elements - fantasy romance with touches of steampunk, and nods to Beauty and the Beast as well as elements of Jane Eyre - to create a heavily atmospheric, dark tale of love and beauty and secrets. The nature of the secrets are very unpredictable, just like Edward Rochart, the mysterious widower artist, who sees Jane Eliot not as fey cursed, but as a brave, strong woman. And yet Jane struggles to cope with her past, and her curse, and to find the self-respect she needs to accept love, making this novel a gloriously touching romance between two damaged people. Although I could have used a little more development between Jane and Edward's relationship, and there are still some unanswered questions as to the nature of the fey (but this is the first book in a series), I loved this intricate, intelligent, Gothic tale and I highly recommend it to fantasy and Jane Eyre fans!

Five years have passed and the Great War between human and fey has long gone. But the tragedy brought upon the world still lurks within the victims of the war. They are called, the ironskin, and Jane is one of them. 
 Seeming to want nothing more than to live as normal as possible, Jane takes on the job of a governess for the mysterious Mr. Rochart's fey-cursed daughter, Dorie. 
 As Jane struggles to teach Dorie to learn how to suppress her curse, she begins to develop feelings for Mr. Rochart... but does he have the same feelings for her in return? 
 Later then, curious Jane suddenly uncovers mysteries surrounding Mr. Rochart's residence... and although the fey seem to have disappeared and let the humans live their lives after the war; it doesn't mean they have yet left them alone and live in peace... 
 Let's get to the good stuff first: 
 That cover. Can you say awesome? And the fact that Jane actually did wear a gown exactly like the girl posing on the book cover. It's not often that I see book covers [with girls in gowns] lately that actually show significance with the actual content of the book. 
 I was really intrigued about the Ironskin world. How the fey had this technology that helps humans in their everyday lives, and how humans seemed to go back to square one after relying so much on that technology. That was one unique setting. 
 I finally found a YA novel with a protagonist who is twenty-one! Yay! Seriously, when you say young adult, it's not just in the teen years. Just saying. 
 So what could've possibly made me find this not to my liking? 
 Here's the bad stuff: 
 There was a lot of brooding around going on with Jane's mind. I don't get her fascination with Mr. Rochart. There's only a few times that he ever made his appearance. His most consistent one was way near the ending. So why fall for someone who isn't even around that often to develop even a slight tinge of friendship? Yes, he's charming (or so Jane says, I didn't seem to recognize such personality though), but what did he do to prove it? 
 I would have liked it if the author gave more details on how exactly the fey technology worked. It was just more focused on describing it as something blue...and then what? And what else did the fey give to make people rely on them so much, aside from that blue something? 
 Now with regards to Mr. Rochart's studio and his occupation, it was good, fascinating even. But I don't get why he had so many guests come all at the same time. And why do they have to stay so long? Healing process? I don't know. 
 And then there's the inconsistency of the storyline. Everything happened too slowly for me. Most of the time I see Jane with Dorie, and I'm glad to see that it goes through an actual process - baby steps as Jane says. But the rest just came out imbalanced. One moment I'd see Jane having a few second "moment" with Mr. Rochart, the next she's out helping Dorie, then the fey come along threatening them, and then she goes off to her sister's party??? I thought no one was supposed to leave the house for safety reasons? 
 This would have been an amazing book with all the steampunk, fey fantasy theme, but the way it was executed was not really something I appreciated.

 The Blair Book Project @ www.theblairbookproject.blogspot.com

Becky is unbelievable shallow and annoying, but I still wanted to continue the series.

Those who know some things about personal finance will immediately hate this book. I know I do. Becky Bloomwood's spending habits make me cringe in terror. Just from reading the first chapter, I'm already planning out her budget. Of course, that means no Prada or any other high-end fashion apparels. I get the temptation, but no... 
 So there. That is already a mark against the book. Little to none emotional attachment to Becky Bloomwood. I'm highly unsympathetic towards her spending and "stuff unpaid bills in her draw" approach. Plus, her habit of lying and just avoiding the truth? Yeah... She and I won't do very well if we are in the same room. 
 Also, let's talk about originality. After reading two books from Sophie Kinsella (Can You Keep a Secret? and I've Got Your Number), I'm starting to see a real trend here. Lying heroines. Sort-of mysterious love interests. (Or in Jack Harper's case, totally secretive and mysterious.) Rich love interests, too. And a lot of embarrassing moments? Oh, yeah. Check, check, check them all. One is okay. Two is just a coincidence. And three... Well, that just marks the spot. It gets so tedious. 
 (Of course, I'm saying that one of these three books is copying the format and subplots of the other two. It might not be Confessions of a Shopaholic that is unoriginal.) 
 Let's talk about the movie and the book. Yes, I watched the movie first. Honestly, it is Luke Brandon's actor that draw me in. (Hello, Hugh Dancy.) Nope. The movie and the book are not very similar. Other than than the same names of characters, I could mistaken the two as unique works. Not a book and its movie adaptation. 
 If we talk about Luke Brandon, all I'm going to talk about is Hugh Dancy's face. So no. No, I'm not going into this. 
 Despite the highly embarrassing moments, the painful similarities to other Kinsella books, and the annoying main character, there are some moments that are worthy. Good, noteworthy. But would I suffer through the book to read that part again? Nope. 
 In conclusion, Confessions of a Shopaholic is not a favorite of mine. I will never touch it again. Even with a ten-foot pole. 
 Rating: One out of Five

book_b.user_review: Retelling of Sleeping Beauty.

sample_reviews.review_text: I loved this new spin on Sleeping Beauty. I want some of it to be true!

This book is best described as "interesting." It was definitely a page turner, but not so much for the characters and storytelling as for Card's unique take on history, fairy tales and the melding of modern and ancient worlds. I also enjoyed learning a little about Slavic history and legend that I never knew before. 
 Part history, part legend, part fantasy, minus truly compelling characters and plot. Worth reading, especially if you like Card. Warning: it takes a little while for the book to become interesting.

This book I pondered for many days after reading it. There were some things I didn't like about it that I thought the author could have left out (if you've read it you understand what I mean) but overall I liked it. It was original and interesting.

I enjoyed this book well enough, it had good characters and decent world building. The more I read of Orson Scott Card the more I see his tendency to narrate the story and simply deliver in plain text what the reader needs to know about the history. I am beginning to realize that I prefer writers who leave some things to the readers imagination, and allow the history and story to unfold throughout the book.

It was ok. I found it entertaining merely because it was so different from what I normally would choose to read. I grabbed it out of desperation and it being the only thing I had on hand at the time. 
 The romantic relationship was tiring in it. Frustrating and to me not so believable. I didn't know enough Russian history to make that part interesting. The main character was without clothes a lot. Couldn't figure out why the author wanted him that way so much. Mostly pointless I thought. I don't get Mr. Card's humor the way he probably intends, so it wasn't as funny to me.

I had read several negative comments before reading this book, and I was all set to disagree with all of them, but wound up, instead, agreeing with nearly every single one. 
 The story starts off sweet and fun enough. But by the time the Princess is woken up, things take a turn for the weird and disjointed. At a few points I felt like I had picked up one of those super cheezy romance novels- completely unrealistic sex scene included (gross). 
 The religious aspect of the book was really random as well. She's Christian, he's a Jew, but neither one is REALLY practicing their faith- it's pretty much a cultural thing. And, between all the witchcraft and unanswered questions on God's existence, I didn't see the reason why the author should of bothered to include any Christian or Jewish aspect into the plot at all. 
 It's one thing to have an unbelievable plot, but when you can't believe in the characters either- well, then you've got a recipe for a bad book on your hands.
It had a bit of a slow start and there were parts where I felt it dragged on unnecessarily but I did enjoy the expansion of and twist on the Sleeping Beauty story.

Ancient tales twisted with romance creates a great story in Enchantment. Card writes romance like no one else can - making true love appear before every reader's eyes. And the best part is that his plot doesn't suffer for the love theme.

This was a very mediocre book. There were times when I thought it was going to be really good, but that never actually materialized. Perhaps Card was looking for a very simply story style since it's a retelling of a fairy tale. But either way, he ended up with a fairly weak plot that involved some leaps of faith to maintain any sort of believability (which is saying something in a fantasy novel!). It was certainly an interesting take on Sleeping Beauty - but that didn't really add enough to make it a winner.

I picked up this book because I enjoy modern retellings of fairy tales. The story managed to hold my interest about halfway through. However, it seemed to shift into a completely different book later on, when the characters became talking heads and seemed to be lecturing the reader instead of telling a story. I'm not even sure what the point of the lecture was--that Jewish people had the only true magic? I couldn't make it out. Regardless, I was very disappointed.

reference_books.title: Charged (Saints of Denver, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Jay Crownover has this magical ability to evoke so much emotion with a single book that aren't quite sure you'll survive. But survive I did. Heart-wrenching, exciting, inspiring. That's what Jay does and Charged is no different. 
 Quaid and Avett are a great couple. Their internal struggles to accept themselves exacerbated by the horrible circumstances that mashed them together was difficult. At one point, reading Avett's POV, I was so sad I had to stop reading and simply stare at the wall in front of me. I internalized her battle to the point where I felt every single emotion like a pin prick to the heart. It's a small sting, but if there are enough, you're gonna cry. 
 I love reading characters that remind me of my own personal hell. I survived mine, and "seeing" someone else do the same inspires me; it reminds me to keep pushing forward and strive to be better than I was yesterday. Avett is that inspiration, and I hope she does the same for you. 
 Quaid was a bit more confusing (like most guys). There were certain things I didn't quite get (like his behavior outside the courthouse...). But at the same time, he was confused. He's been trying to prove something since he was 18 - to himself, to his parents, to the world as a whole - and meeting Avett puts a crack in his well-formed shell of an image. While it took him some time to come to right choice for his heart, he was absolutely dedicated to helping Avett the entire time. Quaid just needed to let go of who he thought he should be and allow himself to be who he was. We change as we age, and sometimes we need to veer from the path we choose at a young age to account for those changes. 
 Avett and Quaid's journey to self-love was absolutely wonderful and is proof positive of Crownover's talent and willingness to lay her heart on the line for her readers.

Ultimamente no he leido ningun libro que me tenga enganchada como las series de Kristen Ashley (me ha arruinado para otros escritores), pero decidi darle una oportunidad a este libro, por favor no le den esa oportunidad, companeros lectores habla hispana no pierdan su tiempo. 
 Este libro nada mas NO esta editado, tiene miles de errores de ortografia (el ingles no es mi lengua materna, pero simplemente es imposible no darse cuenta), hay momentos en donde percibes que la escritora traia una idea y en el siguiente capitulo la aterrizaba de una manera completamente distinta, este libro grita con desesperacion una falta de edicion.

book_a.title: Rose Harbor in Bloom (Rose Harbor, #2)
book_a.user_review:
Review originally posted: Traveling With T 
 Jo Marie, young and widowed, opened the bed and breakfast as part of a dream she had. Her husband was killed in Afghanistan and she is working through her grief the best way she can. The never ending duties of the B&B seem to be a place to help keep her mind occupied, while she grieves and moves on with her life. 
 Jo Marie has a cranky man doing odd and ends jobs for her around Rose Harbor. Jo Marie wanted a garden of roses planted for an event- and Mark, the cranky handy man, did not finish it. He seems to be dragging his feet for a reason- but being a secretive man- it's not obvious as to why. The friendship between Jo Marie and Mark is odd- and filled with misunderstandings! 
 Annie has planned a perfect weekend at Rose Harbor Inn to honor her grandparent's 5oth wedding anniversary. Because of past complications with her love life, she needs a weekend of basking in her grandparent's obvious adoration of each other. However, someone needs to tell her grandparents to act like the loving couple Annie remembers- as they are spending their anniversary weekend fighting. Annie is beside herself, and mad that Oliver, a boy she used to have a crush on, is spending the weekend at Rose Harbor Inn. Oliver used to tease Annie, but now, he's interested in her. Annie can't see beyond the years ago Oliver, though. Can Oliver show Annie he's changed and that a good love is right before her eyes? 
 Mary comes to Rose Harbor Inn to escape her life for a bit. Diagnosed with cancer, Mary is looking back at her life- and some of the mistakes she made. There is a huge mistake in Seattle- and Mary is looking for the strength to connect with George, a past love. Mary knows she broke his heart years ago- and wants forgiveness- even though she is not sure she deserves it. Can George forgive Mary for the past heartbreak? Is their story over? 
 Love. Forgiveness. Dreams. Happiness. Second chances. Rose Harbor in Bloom has it all. 
 Traveling With T's Thoughts 
 Being a fan of Blossom Street series, I wanted to really like Rose Harbor in Bloom. Being written by Debbie Macomber, I did not see a problem with this wish. Something fell flat with me about this book. Maybe it was the cantankerous handy man? That storyline seemed to take up a good bit of the book. Perhaps it was because this is the 2nd book in the series and I need to read the first to get more of a feel for the characters. 
 It's not a bad read. It's just not as good as I expected. However, the heartwarming aspects of a Debbie Macomber book are there.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I had originally won this from a goodreads giveaway a few years go and since then it has sat on a shelf in a my room, waiting to be read. I can honestly say that it was not one of my favorite and I don't know that I care to read any more from this author. 
 The story is told in three plot lines; that of Jo Marie, Mary, and Annie. The first woman is who I assume binds this series together, as I have not read the others, and as such plays a smaller part in the narrative than the other two. Annie's part was enjoyable, revolving around the love story of both her and her grandparents. However, Mary's story frustrated me. The woman was horrible, constantly being rude to those who tried to help her as well as remembering how she had walked out on her ex-boyfriend (who had proposed to her) without really letting him know, and then also never letting him even know that their daughter had been born despite her saying he would have made the best of fathers I couldn't help but George to give back to her as she had dished out to him, especially since he was such an awesome guy that he didn't do just that. 
 As to the writing itself, there were many moments that involved huge info dumps along with repetition of the same thoughts throughout. And with the way the three plot lines were written, it constantly felt like I was being jerked back and forth through the space of a day because everything was happening at the same time. 
 The story is not such that I believe no one will enjoy it. For those who love stories about people who have completely messed up their lives and are now desperately striving to fix them, this should be enjoyable. However, that was not the case for me.

Read ARC from Netgalley.

Twisted and full of surprises, The Marriage Pact reminded me a little of The Firm. Alice and Jake receive an unforgettable gift on the day of their wedding: membership to The Pact, a club that promotes healthy marriages. No one has ever left it and none of their members has ever divorced. Some have died under mysterious circumstances, but let's not talk about that. Alice and Jake find some good things about it, but little by little it takes over their lives and, as much as it helps their marriage, it starts stressing them out. The way the plot turns subtly menacing is masterful. Is it really happening or could it all be a misunderstanding? Nobody is there against their will, or is being coerced into anything so why does it fell like Jake and Alice are being bullied? The tension builds up slowly until it is almost unbearable and then the author ties everything up in a great, great ending. 
 I chose to read this book and all opinions in this review are my own and completely unbiased. Thank you, NetGalley/Random House Publishing Group - Ballantine!

Alice and Jake are newlyweds with great careers, a lawyer and psychologist, who enter into The Pact, a mysterious and elite group of married couples. As soon as they sign the contract, they are required to be on their best behavior and give their all to their marriage, at all cost. 
 The Marriage Pact is a creepy way to keep couples married. Everything about the contract and the rules makes me cringe. If everyone had to sign this contract when they got married, I would never get married. A good read that is very different - just stay away from The Pact!

The beginning of the book took forever to get going and when it finally does it's "twist" and "turn" every where that it really becomes to much. After all of that I found the ending to be lukewarm at best? Really at the end of the book I was quite annoyed I had invested a week in this book for it to end that way.

This book was seriously, seriously weird, as was my reading experience with it. On the one hand, I never really liked the main character as I found him obnoxious, pedantic, and emitting a faint whiff of undeserved superiority. Yet something about the book's chatty narrative style drew me in. 
 I guess you could say this book is a meditation on marriage and its challenges, ups, and downs. I felt like the cult-like Pact that the characters belong to was a framing device for these meditations on marriage. It's a really weird device, though. It was hard to suspend my disbelief at times, since the cult-like Pact is just so weird, but then I didn't think the book was all that far-fetched given the weirdness of cults that have actually existed. 
 In the end, I don't even know what to make of this book. It was suspenseful, trying to figure out what was going to happen with the Pact, but it was also oddly detached. I didn't dislike the book, but I don't think I really like it either.

I was able to get a copy of this early from Netgalley and WOW! 
 I have always known that marriage takes work between both parties, but The Pact is a bit extreme in its measures! Most of us might call The Pact a cult because of its rules the punishments if you break the rules. 
 Alice & Jake might seem like an unlikely couple but they complement each other quite well and this induction into The Pact (TP) tests even their love for each other. Are the rules really there to help or are they there for some other nefarious reason? 
 This book had me on the edge at various times wondering if belonging to TP was a good or bad thing. Sometimes it seemed like a good thing but as they delve further into the organization it is not all it is cracked up to be but there is no way out.  Before I even begin with my review, there is one thing I must admit (in-spite of my mixed feelings towards the book) - The Marriage Pact is a total page-turner. Once I started reading this book, I simply could not stop. Also, with the short, evenly paced chapters, it was a relatively quick and easy read. Before I knew it, I had a hundred different theories, I was procrastinating chores, and cutting on sleep to race through this book. 
 Which is also possibly why the grand finale left me disappointed. No, actually, that's not entirely true. Yes, I had big expectations, but the climax would have been a let down either way. After all that amazing build up, I was expecting something which would blow my mind, but instead my dominant thought was - wasted potential. 
 This story could have wrapped in so many different ways, so many amazing ways, and yet the author eventually led it in a very mediocre, very predictable direction, bringing the story to a point where the concluding sequence could have gone one of two ways, but by then all was lost anyway, 'cause the choice was really between Option #1 = WTH! and Option#2 =Whatever! Sigh. 
 Wrapping Up: All the stars are for the first 75-80% of the book, 'cause it was an experience I truly enjoyed. However, I would only recommend this book to folks who are obsessed with the genre of psychological suspense, and would enjoy the ride no matter how it all wrapped up. Others, I believe, can skip this one. 
 -Shantala (Book Blogger @ Shanaya Tales)

I really enjoyed RAIN REIGN. This is a touching story told by a girl named Rose who happens to be high functioning autistic. She is bright and verbal but she is also obsessed with homonyms, rules, and prime numbers. Rose has trouble at school connecting with other kids but she has no trouble connecting with her dog Rain. 
 Her father brought Rain home one rainy night and they have been fast friends ever since. But then a superstorm hits and Rose's father lets Rain out without her collar on. Rain doesn't come back. Once the storm passes, Rose develops a plan to find her dog. She makes a make and locates all the animal shelters within 50 miles. She makes phone calls and often repeated phone calls checking for her missing dog. 
 One day, the Happy Tails shelter says that they have found her dog. But there is a problem. When Rose arrives with her Uncle Weldon, she learns that Rain has a microchip that says her name is Olivia and that she belongs to the Hendersons. Because Rose is also an obsessive rule follower, she next goes on a quest to find the Hendersons who have been displaced by the storm and return their missing dog. Rose decides that it is only fair to give up her friend. 
 Since this story is told from Rose's viewpoint and in her voice, the sentences are short, precise and direct. We can easily see when she is getting sidetracked by her obsessions. There isn't much about Rose's feelings. She doesn't like to touch people and can't articulate how she feels. She has a great relationship with her uncle who seems to understand her and love her despite her peculiarities. Her relationship with her father is more problematical. Readers can see his frustrations with her and can see that Rose is a little bit afraid of him. He has anger issues but has never hit her though it appears he has come close. 
 Readers who are interested in how autistic people see the world will enjoy this story. So will fans of stories of kids and dogs.

As someone who always looked forward to teaching my lesson on homophones, I knew I would be endeared by the main character's fascination with them. What I didn't foresee was how much I would identify with Rose's love for her dog, Rain, and appreciate her struggle to function in a world where most people don't follow the rules since I admit to being a bit of a rule follower myself. This book will appeal to upper elementary and middle school students who gravitate toward realistic fiction, especially books that have quirky characters and/or dogs. Rain Reign most certainly lives up to the hype.

Category/Genre: Realistic fiction/Disabilities/Family Life 
 Estimate age level of interest: 3-7 
 Estimated reading level: 3rd-4th grade 
 Brief description: Rose is a young girl who has Asperger's syndrome and LOVES homonyms. Rose loses her mother at a young age and her Dad struggles to raise Rose on his own while suffering with his own alcoholism and losing his job. He has a hard time understanding Rose's condition and frequently gets angry with her or leaves her home alone. One night her Dad brings home a dog that she falls in love with. However, one morning after a big storm finds him missing. While this dog was a gift to Rose it tears about the relationship between her and her father even more. 
 Identify two characteristics and explain how they are used in this book: 
 Characteristic 1 (realistic fiction): Helps children enlarge their frames of reference while seeing the world from another perspective 
 -This book allows for students to explore autism and asperger's by connecting with the main character Rose. Rose knows that she is different and she wishes she could change that so she could make friends more easily or not make her father so angry but she can't. I think this book would serve as a strong teaching tool for students to be able to understand what it is like for people they might know with the same condition. By connecting with Rose, students will gain deeper understanding for those with autism. 
 Characteristic 2 (realistic fiction): Features aspects of coping with the problems of the human condition. 
 This book did a great job of exposing the hardships and consequences that alcoholism has on a family. That being said, I do think this book is not appropriate for the suggested interest level of 3rd or 4th grade. Even though it is at that reading level in terms of complexity this book is more suitable for 6th and 7th grade audiences. 
 In what ways and how well does the book as a whole serve its intended audience? This book does a wonderful job of allowing students to understand autism and the hardships of families. However, the suggested interest and reading level begins at 3rd grade. I don't think that this book is completely appropriate for 3rd graders because of the layer of alcoholism that is included in the plot. Additionally, in the end of the book Rose's father leaves her instead of persevering with the challenges he faces. This book is much more suitable for 6-8th graders despite its lower reading level.

Best western I've ever "watch". Simply leave and watch it from out of my mind. Must read.

I have often faced the question (and am sure so have you) - "What attracts you to a book?" One of the most poignant reasons for me is the 'Cover.' To me, the image or the visual representation of what the book might hold, has great significance- though to this, many will state that the writer and the artist are different individuals, most likely with varying perspectives. So what we see might have very little to do with what the book holds- and hence the proverb "Don't judge a book by its' cover.' To all those who have this opinion - well since I am going to do the reading bit, so I don't mind taking my chances. I always have and in future, will, often choose a book by its cover. 
 The Sisters Brothers is one such book that I have chosen solely by its cover and am so glad that I did. I am usually liberal with my ratings and don't mind grading a writer well, if he/she has been able to arrest my attention- and DeWitt is one such writer. It is amusing, thought provoking, full of irony, comical and so so much more. 
 The Plot ??? It's really blatant - The two notorious 'killer' brothers- Eli and Charlie Sisters, have an assignment- to kill a 'thief' named Warm who is presently located in San Francisco, California. It's the Sisters brothers journey from the Oregon City to California as the Commodore's henchmen- a quest none the less, full of several anecdotes and short dialogues which are nerve racking! Once in California, after a few other incidents, they eventually find Hermann Warm, but instead of killing him (as commanded) they have a change of mind and join Warm in his quest for gold. Warm dies eventually (with nothing to do with the brothers) and after some adventure the brothers return to their Mother, an act of final retribution. There - not even a paragraph, where story line goes. 
 Now for the more interesting part- what I liked about the book. 
 *	The simplicity for sure and the dialogue. Those were honest, curt, emotionless and kind of brutish dialogue 
 *	The relationship between the brothers. I would call Charlie a professional, but even he has a soft corner for his Eli. Eli is more humane- dumb when compared to Charlie, but with a heart that does not belong to the 'killers community'. Throughout the book, it is Charlie who outsmarts Eli, even looks after Eli. But in the end, with certain turn of events, it is Eli who cares for his brother and even kills the Commodore 
 *	Charlie's loss of an arm - is that poetic justice ? That hand which killed so many men, was it hence divine intervention that lead to his losing an arm ? Rubbish - it was over confidence and lack of preparation. But this loss has its own significance. Not just for taming the two brothers but also revealing the transcendence of everything 
 *	The final retribution - meeting the mother after many years and the final coming together 
 It is a classic book with the backdrop of a perfect western. Read it for it smoothness. Read it for its' style and read it for its genuineness. 
 My Rating - 3.5/5
Not really sure what I think of this one. The first half I blazed through, couldn't put it down. the second half was just sad.

book_b.title: Fresh Off the Boat: A Memoir
book_b.user_review:
Love this guy. I'm not sure if the book deserves 5 stars on merit or writing, but I am really glad it exists, so, 5 stars. 
 I've been following Eddie Huang online for awhile. This book wasn't that different from his blog or his show on Vice (both of the same name). Sure, he's a little full of himself and the "I don't care what people think" trope gets old. But he's smart, he's funny, and I'm not sure modest people would be able to so aptly call out racism with the detail that Huang does. At base, he's dealt with a lot of undue criticism or judgment, and he wants a better country moving forward. He's extremely sharp in writing about it, and listening to the audiobook was definitely the superior way to ingest this piece.

sample_reviews.review_text: The beginning is a joy to read. The middle and ending are insightful in terms of race, but is otherwise really narcissistic.

I enjoyed the stories from Huang's childhood and hearing some of his observations about food and culture. Alas, Huang seemed determined to challenge "model minority" stereotypes by reveling in stories about his petty crime, drug dealing through law school, and his felony conviction. He's clearly successful now, but most of Huang's stories paint him as an overprivileged underachiever. If he engaged in any self-reflection or acknowledged his privilege (e.g., instead of jail, he went to Taiwan for a year), I wouldn't have found his stories and personality so obnoxious.

I loved this book. His audio version of it was good. I wouldn't tell other people to spend more money to get it (than to purchase the book or rent it) but if you can get it for the same price I'd say do it. It was a good story that I wasn't familiar with in a lot of ways. I had lots of Asian friends growing up and was a regular fixture in their homes so I was familiar with a lot of parts of the culture Huang talks about. What I was unfamiliar with was Florida in the 90s, especially through the eyes of a Taiwanese family. That was new and very interesting to listen to. Huang does a great job chronicling his life; he keeps it interesting and detailed and really hooks the listener/reader in via his passionate explanations and interpretations on parts of his life. He's a good storyteller and I found myself interested in each story. Though I will admit, when he talks about food it's really wonderful and you can hear the love and appreciation in his voice. Great book for those that love bios, food, pop culture, and just decently written books in general. Loved this so much I bought a copy to send to my old roommate, a chef who is a serious sneaker freak. Good stuff.
Good, but not knowing what to expect is probably the best way to get into this book. He jumps around often but ends up going on about how he got the restaurant off the ground.

Kudos to ABC for spotting the potential for a pretty funny comedy in this dark,angry memoir. Yes, the characters and basic situation (of at least the first few chapters) are the same - but this is no sitcom family. In the real world, this is the story of a dysfunctional "shotgun" marriage between an ex-Taiwan gangbanger and the angry college girl he got pregnant; who go on to become both physically and emotionally abusive parents. Eddie starts off getting in fights and selling porn page-by-page in middle school (with his mom's tacit approval), then moves up to doing and selling all sorts of drugs pretty much throughout his late teens and 20's. Eddie frequently (and correctly) refers to his father as "a real dick" and himself as a punk. What he doesn't add is that he is also a total asshole. Doesn't like America, doesn't like white people (or most Asians, for that matter), doesn't really like much of anything except African Americans and hip-top culture. Oh, and he's smarter than everyone else, too. At the end of the book he tries to do standup comedy, (sample joke: "White people aren't scared of kung fu, but you know what they are scared of? Black people!;" also, Asian girls have flat butts because they drink soy milk instead of whole milk - hilarious!!), and then ultimately opens a successful restaurant and gets good reviews - yay! But (SPOILER), by the last page he is still just as much an asshole. 
 Much of his story is told in rap, basketball and drug slang that I couldn't understand. And granted, I'm a 60-year-old white guy who cannot relate to a lot of what he went through. But I did spend over 18 years living in Taiwan (including in his dad's old neighborhood of Yong Kang Jie); and I have a lot of experience with young Taiwanese (including family members) and what they go through moving to and living in the U.S. And yeah, it can be tough, and some kids gets picked on - hell, I got picked on; my sons got picked on. Welcome to childhood, idiot. Luckily, I don't believe Huang's experience is representative of what most ABC's go through. Instead, his own negative experience is largely the result of his own anger. Would have given this 2 stars, but knocked off another one as the book has now ruined the TV show for me. Jerk.

Interesting. I received this as an advanced reader's edition from Goodreads, and, as a older midwestern Caucasian woman, I had real difficulty relating to this book. It was often like trying to read a foreign language, since so much of the book was based on hip-hop or references to hip-hop. Unlike many of the other reviewers, I did not find Eddie Huang a lovable character. He was raised in what I would consider an abusive home and grew up with a gangster mentality. However, the story did have glimmers of redeeming value and I'm not at all sorry I read it.
Wow, this dude is whiney. This book goes down as the most annoying memoir I've read to date. Save yourself the trouble and go listen to a two year old for a couple hours.

This wasn't my cup of tea, though I found Huang a very interesting narrator. His own antics entertained him and he broke out in laughter throughout the book. He is a smart man that thinks about race and identity much more than probably most people. His almost rap lyric narrative interrupted the flow of his own story for me, so I had a hard time with this book.
Clearly not for everyone, but hilarious for those who get it. Eddie is awesome!

I didn't know what to expect when I was handed Fresh Off The Boat. I wondered who was Eddie Huang? And what made his story worth reading? The title suggests it would be a new beginning for him and his family. His parents come to the United States from Taiwan looking for opportunities; his father grabs it by the throat and eventually finds success in owning restaurants. 
 But the picture of Eddie eating what looks like a piece of chocolate during a family photo reveals two things: Eddie loves food and he doesn't succumb to cultural norms. The readers see Eddie best when he's writes about food. He explains how dishes were cooked and also how particular dishes fit into a cultural context. His memoir is not a cookbook but it will make you curious enough to try some of the dishes mentioned or stop by Baohaus, his restaurant in the East Village in New York City. 
 At times I swore Eddie was African American for his cadence of the language. His love of Hip-hop and sneakers destroyed my limited view on what it means to be Taiwanese in America. But I would of liked to see more scenes created through his words. Instead, he tells how he navigates growing up. He tells the results of his poor choices. I wanted the same finesse in revealing how he became the guy with a law degree and owner of Baohaus, he showed when describing the intricacies of food.

Sleeping Beauty is my favourite Disney princess movie so I'm instantly on board with retellings or reimaginings. Forget a happily ever after. I want to know what the hell is going on! 
 Aurora is reasonably shaken up after her reawakening, as the life and people she had always known are gone and they aren't coming back. I wanted her to fight back right away because the people "handling" her were treating her like crap and it was driving me nuts. But honestly, she handled situations in a way that was very believable for someone in her position. 
 I definitely wouldn't say there's a love shape of some sort. There are three guys present in Aurora's life but they all play vastly different roles. One is her "true love" who is just a kind stranger. The second is a rebel hoping she'll aid their fight. The last is a foreign diplomat whose intentions are difficult to pinpoint. I'm excited to see the roles they'll play in the sequel as I'm quite unsure what they'll be up to. 
 This is a slower story but one that never felt lagging. I loved seeing Aurora slowly transform from a timid, scared, lost girl to a stronger young woman ready to take her life and future back into her own hands. The story closes on quite the cliffhanger and I'm eagerly anticipating what happens next!

I felt this story was a little slow in parts, particularly in the beginning and yet still has a lot to offer. The plot is interesting and the characters are definitely my cup of tea. reference_books.title: Eyrie
reference_books.review_text:
I wanted to love this book and I'm so disappointed that I didn't, but for me it was very mediocre. The characters and the plot felt undeveloped and it just seemed to meander on and on without ever going anywhere. 
 The main character Tom Keely is a broken man who is so jaded and bruised by his attempts to save the world that when we meet him it's hard to believe he could ever feel passionate about anything. He's on a downward spiral when he runs into a childhood acquaintance and is drawn into her world. Gemma is a woman who has never known security or love, apart from the brief time she spent with Tom's family as a child. She is looking after her grandson while her daughter is in jail and her life has been marred by disadvantage and violence. She is permanently damaged and Tom senses that Kai is in danger. The whole book basically follows his developing relationship with Gemma and Jai as he becomes a permanent fixture in their lives. 
 Tom is searching for redemption by saving Kai and trying to forget about his own problems, but it takes so bloody long for anything to actually happen that by the time the plot finally reached its climax I'd had it. 
 There is a lot of anger over corruption and greed by the powerful expressed in the novel, but unlike many other readers, I sensed a deep fear of the underclass who are portrayed as universally hideous (Gemma's one and only redeeming feature is her love of Kai). Then again, pretty much everyone in this book is portrayed in a negative light. The 'ocker' language just makes the book seem dated and the complete lack of hope that anything can be done to change things was depressing. I'm not sure what this book was striving to achieve, but sadly it fell short for me, which is such a shame because I do love Tim Winton.

reference_books.title: Let the Great World Spin
reference_books.review_text:
This book suffers from the same flaws as so many of the books I've read lately. Maybe I'm just becoming ultra-critical the more I read, but there was very little in this book that worked for me. 
 It's so frustrating to hear over and over again that writer's need to show and not tell, only to come across award-winning books that break this cardinal rule. Let the Great World Spin provides a very good example of why it doesn't work: It's extremely tedious to read. Being a fan of 19th century fiction I have a high tolerance for detailed scene setting, subtle nuance and limited action. I don't mind lashings of backstory when it's done properly, but large portions of this book read like a first draft. 
 I love that the author was trying to portray an iconic event in New York city history from many different perspectives, showing the diversity and also the connections between characters from vastly different backgrounds. He also touches on contemporary issues in the wake of September 11. Unfortunately the characters were flat and stereotypical for me. Flicking from one perspective to the next did not allow me to connect with any of them in a significant way. Despite the detailed descriptions, the portrayal of New York city didn't feel authentic and I found myself becoming increasingly frustrated as I went along. The connections between characters seemed contrived and I got a strong sense that the writer had no real plan for the ending as it just got thinner and thinner and petered out. 
 There was also a problem with overwriting. This is my favourite example: "The sunset was the color of muscle, pink and striated gray." Another disappointing read for me.

reference_books.title: Unaccustomed Earth
reference_books.review_text:
This book is about experiences of Bengali immigrants in the United States who are part of a wealthy, educated milieu. It is an area that is very ripe for exploration and I don't have any problem with the fact that all of the stories focus on this particular group. Unfortunately I don't feel that Lahiri has done justice to her characters. 
 The first problem I have with this book is the writing. So many reviewers have commented on how "beautiful" it is but for me it was frustrating. Despite the abundance of detail the author uses very few descriptive words or literary techniques. I longed for it to take off and capture my imagination but it never did. It is spare to the point of being bland and mind-numbing. The other issue I had was the very liberal use of exposition which slowed the stories down immensely. The stories don't have much of an arc to them and I found myself wondering what the point was on many occasions. 
 Nearly all of the characters appear to be suffering from low-level depression and there is a repressed tone to the stories which seems to be deliberate. The major theme running through the book is the generation gap between parents and their children who were raised in America. Again, a very worthy subject for exploration, but the lack of genuine affection between these characters did not help me to care about them and their dilemmas. Most of the characters are extremely self-absorbed and display no generosity of spirit, humour or insight and, more gallingly, no recognition of their extremely privileged positions in both Indian and American societies. They remain wrapped up in their own problems, oblivious to anything beyond their insular little worlds. 
 Lahiri does try to introduce a wider perspective in the last story through Kaushik's career as a photographer but this sudden concern with bigger issues didn't ring true for me. In fact, I found it a bit offensive when Kaushik compared his own family's situation with the people he saw in refugee camps who had been forced to flee with just a few possessions. I realised how much I'd come to dislike this book by the end when I was supposed to be swept away (no pun intended) by the doomed love affair between Kaushik and Hema, but all I felt was relief that I'd finally reached the end of the book.

reference_books.title: May We Be Forgiven
reference_books.review_text:
This is a book which tries to be everything and ends up being nothing 
 There were some great moments and a point when I actually considered giving it 5 stars, but it casts its net far too wide and isn't nearly as satirical as it seems to think it is. After a while the flatness of the writing becomes painful and many of the jokes are in extreme bad taste. The ending was beyond ridiculous. It felt like the author gave up even trying to make a satirical comment about society and just rambled about the holiday to Africa. It reads like "then we did this....then we did that...then I was given some tea by a traditional African medicine man which gave me explosive diarrhoea...then we went shopping......and met the woman who got Claire's heart....and look what a great big happy extended family we are! The American dream isn't dead after all." 
 I know the African bit was supposed to be about the way rich Westerners exploit third world countries and shallow materialism etc.(at least I'm assuming this is the case. If not the book is even worse than I've given it credit for) The `servants' in Africa are all black and we are supposed to pick up on the racial inequality, but the problem is that Homes wants to have her cake and eat it too. She wants us to enjoy this family holiday and appreciate Harry's awakening, while at the same time mocking Western behaviour. It doesn't work. Instead what starts out as a sharp satire ends up being the worst kind of feel-good, cliched, all-American redemption story that reaffirms that everything is really okay with society. The message is we just have to find new ways of connecting with each other and thinking about family and the pieces will fall into place. Yeah, that's all it will take. 
 I'd like to say I'm surprised that this book won the women's prize for fiction, but this award was also given to We Need to Talk About Kevin, so nothing much can shock me. WNTTAK was another book that raises serious issues about school shootings but then sheets the blame back home to psychopathic individuals, creating the impression that nothing can really be done to prevent such atrocities. It also ends in a sickeningly cloying way with a reunion of sorts between Kevin and his mother. 
 I understand that female authors aren't obligated to write about gender or create empowered women characters, but I did find it interesting that May We Be Forgiven opens with the violent death of a Puerto Rican woman whose legs fall off when paramedics try to get her out of the car wreck. She survives long enough to experience extreme terror and agony while her husband is killed instantly. Shortly after this Claire is bashed with a lamp so badly that her brain matter is visible. She also lingers for a while before dying. Then there's the missing girl whose remains are found in a garbage bin and the elderly woman who is raped by her husband while Harry and Amanda watch on a baby monitor and the sexual abuse of 11 year-old Ashley by a female teacher at her school. She also goes through the humiliation of inserting a tampon into the wrong `hole' and then defecating all over the floor when removing it while sharing it all with her uncle on the phone (very sophisticated humour). 13 year-old Nate on the other hand saves a village in Africa (and lectures the ignorant natives on the evils of consumerism when they raise money to send to them. This was one of the most appalling scenes in the book). I can't think of any male characters that experience the same degree of violence and humiliation in this book as the female characters. 
 I also found it interesting that a book purporting to be a satire of contemporary society doesn't even refer obliquely to the GFC. Then there are the racial stereotypes. These stereotypes can be very funny when used satirically but this book just ends up being shallow and offensive. It actually reminded me a lot of Where Did You Go Bernadette, another vastly overrated book, which follows the same trajectory. It too started out as a sharp satire but then because almost unreadable as one ridiculous event was piled onto another finishing with an implausibly happy ending where the family unit is preserved. It's like the authors are trying to emulate Arrested Development but with none of the finesse or critical perspective that made this show so good. 
 It says a lot about the literary world that anything that pushes boundaries or seems `edgy' (like jokes about sexual abuse of children) is considered great, when in fact it is deeply regressive. To me this book is another symptom of the disorientation felt by many who realise that something is profoundly broken in American society but have no idea how to fix it. I'd love to believe the whole "happy family at Thanksgiving reminiscing about the journey they've all taken over the last 12 months" was a joke, but sadly I fear it was completely sincere. 
 May the judges of the Women's Prize for Fiction be forgiven for choosing this stinker.

reference_books.title: The Sense of an Ending
reference_books.review_text:
*This review contains spoilers 
 "You still don't get it. You never did, and you never will. So stop even trying." 
 These are the last words that the narrator Tony's former girlfriend from 40 years earlier writes to him after Tony has arranged several meetings with her in an attempt to get to the bottom of the mystery as to why her mother (whom he met exactly once) left him 500 pounds and his old school friend, Adrian's diary in her will. Adrian and Veronica started dating after Tony broke up with her and he lost contact with both of them. How Veronica's mother ended up with the diary is one of the things he hopes to find out when he gets his hands on it. 
 Through Tony's reminisces we learn that during their liaison at university he spent much of his time feeling peeved with Veronica for not having sex with him (she did once after they broke up in an attempt to win him back which only made him despise her). When she started going out with Adrian he strongly suspected she was a little freer with her favours. He resented the fact that she didn't like some of his music and when he stayed at her more upper-class parent's house for a weekend she went for a walk with her father and brother, telling them Tony liked to sleep in, which was a blatant lie because he liked to get up early (to Tony this shows that Veronica has been "damaged" in some way, possibly through sexual abuse). While the others are out Veronica's mother cooks him some eggs and tells him not to let her daughter get away with too much. She also gives him a funny "horizontal" wave when he's leaving which for some unexplained reason made him wish he'd talked to her a bit more. 
 His anger towards Veronica and jealousy of Adrian caused Tony to pen a scathing letter after which they didn't speak to him again. A short time later Adrian decides to" reject the gift of life" which he hadn't asked for and he kills himself in a grand, apparently noble, gesture in keeping with his philosophical beliefs. 
 Tony goes on to live a disappointing and uneventful life that makes him wonder if maybe Adrian had the right idea, until he learns of the diary bequeathed to him. At this point he undergoes some kind of emotional regression and he can't stop obsessing about Veronica and the SINGLE weekend he spent at her parent's house which is remembered in great detail. After 40 years, marriage, parenthood and divorce he still has the same adolescent feelings towards her and the same resentment towards her father and brother for making him feel inadequate on his lone visit to their house. There's no growth or insight whatsoever and he's still burnt by the fact that she wouldn't sleep with him. 
 Tony tries to discuss his feelings for Veronica with his former wife Margaret, who is a straightforward, no-nonsense woman as opposed to a mysterious one like Veronica, because all women, it seems can be divided into these two simple categories (the fact that this comes from a female character's mouth doesn't make it any less offensive). After trying to fob him off about the diary which she has in her possession, a "whiskery" Veronica agrees to meet Tony at a cafe, but then just gets up and leaves midway through his monologue about his life (who can blame her really?). Undeterred, Tony arranges another meeting with her, in which she drives him around town in an erratic manner that makes him fear for his safety only to stop on a street in order to show him a group of "special needs" people, one of whom calls her Mary when she gets out to talk to them. She greets every attempt at conversation during this trip with single word answers eg. "driving," before dumping him back at the station with no explanation. She then replies to his email by berating him for not "getting it." (Is this also Veronica's subconsciously cruel way of reminding him that he didn't "get it" while he was with her?) 
 When the secret is finally revealed the reader can completely understand Veronica's scorn towards Tony for his totally obtuse, self-centred ways which prevent him from recognising the truth (heavy sarcasm alert). How could Tony not have realised that the nasty letter he wrote to Adrian all those years ago, briefly mentioning that he should talk to Veronica's mother about her selfish, opinionated daughter, would lead Adrian to sleep with the mother and beget a child who would then turn out to be developmentally delayed due to her advanced maternal age? Of course he is to blame for everything that happened and of course Veronica has the right to act like a crazy b in light of all of this. Adrian, it turns out was not a noble, brave person for topping himself for no particular reason and with no thought for anyone else as Tony had believed for the last 40+ years. He was rather a coward running away from "the pram in the hall." The fact that it took Tony 40+ years to stop admiring Adrian for his existential act of suicide says it all. 
 The Sense of an Ending is one of the lamest books I have ever read. Its "deep" philosophical insights are worthy of a pretentious undergraduate. Its insights about the nature of memories, history and perception are banal and very poorly executed. The Booker Prize has lost all credibility with me.

Having an admittedly not especially bright little girl as the first-person narrator did not seem to work out well. Too much "What Dreams May Come"-ish (I mean the movie, did not read that book) blurry nonsensical wish-fulfillment crap. And how often is a rapist and murderer a boring character? :/

Audiobook , read by author

 this was some sort of torture , the story started well ( up to 30% ) ,and then it deteriorate swiftly , the only reason i kept on with it because i wanted to find something good in the end, something worth all the hype , on the CONTRARY the ending was utter crap . it was a wast of time.

I hated this book.

It took me a little while to get into this book, but once I did it was fascinating. Narrated from such a unique viewpoint. I can see why it was made into a movie, it reads very much like a movie. Absolutely amazing!

I would actually give this 3 1/2 stars and maybe 4, because I honestly couldn't put this book down. I think I gave it 3 because I like happy endings and this book started out with an unhappy ending so it was hard for me to read. The author did a really good job with the characters and their emotions, although there was a scene in the book that I thought "Really? She chose that to be her wish?" and when you read it, you'll probably understand what I mean!

So here's the summary: Beginning of the book, amazing; middle of the book, slowly gets annoying but didn't lose interest; end of book, stupidest ending ever! Not satisfying and honestly... 
 SPOILER 
 The dead girl inhabiting another girl's body and using it to have sex with her ex boyfriend??? WTF???? I know the point of the book is to appreciate life while you have it and it has a charming way of making you feel warm and sad at the same time. I loved that about it, but they didn't even catch the bastard that killed her and they never found her body???? How unsatisfying an ending is that??? And I hate the tendency for contemporary authors to HAVE to put sex into their books even when it's creepy and unnecessary. Sharing a kiss with her ex would have been sweet on many levels. The author didn't need to take it that far, but she had to go there. Ugh.

When I picked up this book a few years ago, I'd heard only good things about it and, as such, didn't even fathom that I would dislike it. Oh, how ill-prepared I was. 
 Now, it has been years since I read this and I am nowhere near willing to pick it up again, so I apologize for not going into specifics. The writing did nothing for me. I could tell the author was going for something pretty and poetic with her descriptions, but often, it just came across nonsensical. Even though I was privy to Susie's most intimate thoughts, I found myself uncaring towards her. She didn't hook me, she didn't interest me, and that is the kiss of death for a book. I didn't care about Susie, I didn't care about what she was doing. The supporting characters fell flat to me as well, and, without any interest in any of the characters, I just could not appreciate the plot. I remember forcing myself to finish this, thinking that it must get better, there must be a reason for such high praise. Sadly, it seems that this book just wasn't for me.

Could not finish. The story idea was a good one but it was not well executed. The characters were hard to like and the plot was dragging and never got interesting. The writing, well, I have seen much better. I tired and I tried to finish but there was nothing holding me in the book: the language, the characters, nor the plot.
I just really liked the writing style - and the suspense in place where, even though you know what happened to her, you're kept turning pages to see if and when other people might learn that.

book_b.title: The Uncommon Reader
book_b.user_review:
This was an amusing read but not as sharp or witty as I was hoping it would be. Ultimately however it is much more subversive than expected and this is what elevated it from 3 to 4 stars for me. 
 On discovering a latent love of literature, the queen also discovers that despite being considered one of the most powerful women in the world she has no voice of her own. She is merely a figurehead who is trotted out to open hospitals, chat with the common folk and give occasional speeches, but it soon dawns on her that no one really listens to what she says. She becomes increasingly interested in discussing authors and ideas, but the only person she has to share her thoughts with is Norman, a young man who she meets on her visit to a mobile library parked in the palace grounds. Most people around her are hostile to her new-found passion for the written word and they do not want to see the queen expressing an opinion or stepping beyond the boundaries set for her by history and tradition. She begins to rebel against these restrictions, first in very subtle ways and then more openly. 
 One of the great strengths of the book is its potrayal of the cultural backwardness of the political leaders of today which I feel is very realistic. The ignorant prime minster whose eyes glaze over whenever the queen tries to discuss literature with him is a thinly veiled portrayal of Tony Blair. I loved the ending when she announces to her Privy Council that she is going to write a book of her own and quickly disabuses them of the hope that it will be something uncontroversial. "I was thinking of something more radical. More.....challenging." 
 She later tells the gathered minsters: "One has met and indeed entertained many visiting heads of state, some of them unspeakable crooks and blackguards....One has given one's white-gloved hand to hands that were steeped in blood and conversed politely with men who have personally slaughtered children. One has waded through excrement and gore....Sometimes one has felt like a scented candle, sent in to perfume a regime, or aerate a policy, monarchy these days just a government-issue deoderant." 
 Yes indeed! One can only hope the real queen has an opportunity to peruse this quirky little book with a deep message at its heart.

sample_reviews.review_text: This is a charming little tea cake of a book - sweet, delicious and ultimately a treat, not a meal. The character of the queen is delightful; a sensible no-nonsense woman who becomes familiar with the ways of the world only when she begins reading books (I found myself hoping that the real Queen has exactly this temperament), and the details about the oddness of her world are lovely, and of course, any reader would be delighted by how much reverence is given to reading itself. I found myself starting to wish there was more given of the world outside of the queens books, but that being said this is a lovely little book.
Meh! :/

not a fan of British lit i found this book endearing . just the mention of a traveling library brought back memories of days long ago. not only did i use a bookmobile, i also drove one.i have come to a conclusion- either you love reading or you do not. there is no in between. but to have a life with no reading i can not imagine.

A cute little story that essentially celebrates the lure of reading. The Queen (of England) notices a mobile library parked in front of the palace when her dogs make a fuss about it; she checks out a book out of politeness and things develop from there...
Cute novella about what might happen if the queen of England fell in love with reading.

A book about the pleasure of reading, so it's why I was attracted to it at first, and as it is the Queen of England who is the protagonist, I thought is could be really funny. 
 A pleasant, short and easy read, this book is indeed funny and witty too. It is simple but interesting. 
 The Queen discovers reading and becomes passionate about it. This doesn't please everyone at Buckingham as she grows more and more bored by her duties - which she used to enjoy. 
 Good and very humorous at the beginning but I lost a little of the excitement towards the end. Anyway, I liked it - it reads like a little treat to enjoy with a cup of tea.

1.5 stars. 
 I feel oddly guilty writing this review as a book lover. However, I found this book about loving books unbearably pretentious and wholly tedious to read. The constant name dropping of authors and the (blatant) implication that readers see the world not only differently, but also exponentially more accurately than nonreaders, was akin to reading self affirmation phrases over and over again. The entire book suggests that the reader, as a reader, is making himself or herself better than everyone else by engaging in the activity of reading. It felt to me like being constantly and heavy handedly bludgeoned by "intellectual" propaganda. And while I may agree with some of the ideas behind this propaganda, I find a book, not literary or enlightening in the least, about those ideas to be almost offensive. 
 For those who thought this was just a "fun" little read, I felt it missed the mark there too.

Several people had recommended The Uncommon Reader to me over the last year, but somehow I only got around to it this morning. Don't be as slow as I was! The idea is very simple - the Queen gets hooked on reading - but Bennett handles it perfectly. It's a delight, and takes about an hour to read. 
 Maybe a short extract will do the job:'Exploded?' said the Queen. 'But it was Anita Brookner.' 
 The young man, who seemed remarkably undeferential, said security may have thought it was a device. 
 The Queen said: 'Yes. That is exactly what it is. A book is a device to ignite the imagination.' 
 The footman said: 'Yes, ma'am.' 
 It was as if he was talking to his grandmother, and not for the first time the Queen was made unpleasantly aware of the hostility her reading seemed to arouse. 
 'Very well,' she said. 'Then you should inform security that I shall expect to find another copy of the same book, vetted and explosive-free, waiting on my desk tomorrow morning. And another thing. The carriage cushions are filthy. Look at my gloves.' Her Majesty departed. 
 'Fuck,' said the footman, fishing out the book from where he had been told to hide it down the front of his breeches.
Boring and overly quaint. I had to make myself read this. It seemed much longer than 58 pages. And the ending, blech, give me a break...
Call me stupid if you like but this book had way too many dictionary on hand words. It really took me out of the story to have to look so many up.
