reference_books.review_text: This was a good one in the series. Dresden is dealing with a lot this go-round but all my favorite characters are there to keep him from getting his @$$ handed to him. The snarky wonderfulness of this offering did not disappoint.

reference_books.title: A Countess Below Stairs
reference_books.review_text: This was a fun, quick story about a Russian countess during the revolution who ends up as a house maid in England, post-WWI. The characters were enjoyable and the story well-told. The plot was a little predictable, but as a fun read, I didn't mind that very much and was amused by the way things were tied up in the end.

reference_books.title: Inheritance (The Inheritance Cycle, #4)
reference_books.review_text: A good end to the series. Some of the wrap-up was predictable, but it was a good fantasy romp.

book_a.title: Ghost Story (The Dresden Files,  #13)
book_a.user_review: This one was not my favorite. Hoping the next is better.

sample_reviews.review_text: I think that someone got a thesaurus for Christmas.

I liked this book. Really, I did. It's the Dresden files; I think it'd be impossible for me not to like this book. But that's all I did- like it. I didn't love it and I wasn't blown away, which for the Dresden series is pretty problematic. 
 My main issue with this book stemmed from the state Dresden was in, i.e. dead. I've seen and read that whole plot line where the main character somehow ends up as a spirit one too many times for me to find it fresh or innovative. Jim Butcher took a risk. Fans clearly expected Dresden to miraculously pull a save out of his ass. They expected him not to be dead and back in the action right away. So Jim Butcher decided to change things up. He took a risk, and I can appreciate that. Authors that don't try something new every once in a while get boring fast. I just didn't like the risk very much. 
 Ghost Story has a slightly dystopian, post-apocalyptic feel to it (something I've never liked). Chicago clearly went to hell after the events at the end of Changes. Harry didn't really think or care about the consequences of his actions during his quest to save Maggie, and now we get to see those consequences in Ghost Story. A lot of the people close to him suffered as a result, and we get to see that too. 
 Unfortunately, Murphy, the Alphas, Butters, etc...none of them played a huge role in the plot. This probably also contributed to my disappointment. They were off dealing with their own problems, and therefore only showed up in a big way toward the end. I really wish we got to see more of them. In the end, their condition is a mystery. 
 I will say this, I honestly wasn't expecting a lot of the events or characters that turned up. The plot was interesting, but I wasn't all that drawn it. It's hard to read a book where Harry isn't right in the middle of all the ass kicking, all the time. It was humbling, because it forced Harry to see that he wasn't a superhero. 
 An interesting confluence of events brought the book to a close. I wasn't expecting the characters that saved Harry- I thought they'd be someone else completely. So JB continues to surprise me. 
 All in all it was a satisfactory book, and definitely necessary to continue the series. I'm in no way ready to give up on Dresden because of one mediocre book!

Not what I expected, and that's a good thing. Based on how the previous in the series ended, I thought I could see what was coming. And while I wasn't completely wrong, Butcher threw in quite a few twists. 
 He still occasionally talks too much. He had Dresden spending a few paragraphs pondering what style of dwelling he might want while at the same time the guy was rushing into battle. Not too likely, but I don't really expect five-star quality. 
 The mere fact that this series got so much better after the first few volumes and has remained a guilty addiction into Volume 13 is pretty darn impressive enough. 
 Makes me wonder how long he's gonna spin the series out... I'll definitely read Volume 14 if there is one.
Well, that was emotional. Cried twice while reading this

This book is horrible!!! It has all the trademarks of bad Sci-fi from the 60's and 70's. First it is a conclusion to a cliffhanger ending from a previous book were he was killed by an unknown sniper's bullet in the last two pages. Now in this book, surprise surprise Harry comes back to Chicago as ghost to solve his own murder. Wow!!! How original. One of the endearing traits of Harry is he is willing to pay the price of his choices come hell or high water. In this book wimpy Harry whines about the how the outcome of his choices affected those around him. The ending which is suppose to shock the reader, but it is just another major disappointment we find out Mister Bad Ass Harry Dresden is actually Mr.Chicken Dresden. And Oh yeah in the end we find out the death of Harry Dresden is not the end of the series another Shocker.

Must admit that I was torn in my feelings on this one. Liked some parts of it, was immensely frustrated by other parts. Overall I found it middling satisfying. At least they had the good sense to go back and get James Marsters to record the audiobook after the disappointment that was the original with the "fill in" narrator. I can't listen to an audiobook series for a dozen books with the same narrator and make the switch to a new voice easily and the response to that original audiobook release shows I'm far from alone in that!
2.5 stars. Probably my least favorite of this guilty pleasure of a series.

Terrific book. A nice change of pace with a fair amount of action but lots of Harry's view of what it all means. Some good background mixed with an expansion of the "rules" of the "Dresden Universe". A very reflective story that finds Harry coming to terms with his previous dubious, yet necessary decisions. One of the best in the series. It will open up a lot of good future story lines.

Butcher's writing is vivid, but the plot is weak in Ghost Story. He transitions forward in time to (almost arbitrarily) alter many members of the extensive cast. Harry's priorities aren't as strong as they are in other books of the series, like Changes. The climax is great, except Butcher averts it to have another, weaker climax, focusing on lesser characters. 
 The last thirty pages are the worst writing I've ever read from Butcher. 
 I'll not be reading the next book.
I think it was the ghost thing that didn't work for me. I just don't do ghosts. This was not my favorite in the series but it was still good.

book_b.title: Skin Trade (Anita Blake, Vampire Hunter #17)
book_b.user_review: I really thought this was going to be one of my favorites, a la Obsidian Butterfly, but unfortunately, even though it has all my favorite characters (Edward, Olaf, etc.), the ending was a weak culmination of the great plot. If the end had been better, this would be one of the best Anita Blake books.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 Skin Trade is enough of a step in the right direction that I'm sorely tempted to give it a higher rating than it actually deserves. There's a plot! With murders! And investigating! And I turned out to be right about Marmee Noir's plans for Anita. And the two explicit sex scenes are better-written and less icky than what I've come to expect from Hamilton. And she's being copy-edited again, so there are only a few typos. I get the sense, reading Skin Trade, that Hamilton is trying to blend the mystery/horror style of the early Anita Blake books with the erotic style of the later installments. The results are mixed, but I have to admit that Skin Trade is her best in years. 
 That said, I can't say I truly enjoyed it, hence the 2-star rating. Skin Trade has its moments, and I'm quite happy that the plot never gets lost and is never far from Anita's mind, no matter what else is going on. However, there are a lot of problems. 
 First, there's the macho posturing. Especially in the first half of Skin Trade, Anita seems hell-bent on bickering with every male character she meets and trying to prove she's tougher than they are. The female characters don't even seem to rate that kind of treatment. Anita pretty much never gets along with any woman, ever. In one scene, she decides that a female cop is "one of those women who seem to hate other women." The woman hasn't even opened her mouth yet; how would Anita know this? Projection much? Anyway, all this bickering and posturing wouldn't be so bad if it didn't take up such a vast amount of page space. I wanted to shout at the characters to just go solve the crime already. 
 Second, I think Hamilton is trying to push the envelope further in terms of sex, and the results are sometimes pretty disgusting. Anita is far too friendly to creepy serial-killer Olaf (thank goodness she doesn't sleep with him) and does end up sleeping with a 16-year-old (thank goodness it's not "onscreen," and thank goodness she's disturbed when she realizes what she's done). 
 Third, we know that Anita is the most super-special person to ever walk the face of the planet. We get it. She doesn't need more powers, or more men, or to turn out to be one of the very last carriers of blue tiger lycanthropy (Blue tigers? What the...), but all of these occur. 
 Finally, several promising plotlines end anticlimactically. I hope that, in the most egregious case of anticlimax syndrome, the "end" is not as final as it seems. 
 There was one bit that really struck me as clever, though: 
 "Why?" I asked. "Everyone knows what a pain in Jean-Claude's a** I am. Why do you want to deal with that?" I couldn't call for help in any way, or someone else died. I couldn't go all lycanthrope, because it wouldn't help me. What could I do? What the f**k could I do without a gun? 
 He laughed again, but this time it was lower, more attractive, more seductive. "The power, Anita. You are the first necromancer in centuries, and with so many other powers." 
 Vittorio is answering Anita's spoken question, but in a way he's also answering her unspoken question. Indeed, Anita does end up being forced to enter Skin Trade's final confrontation without firearms, so that her powers are the only weapon she has. (That said, she has so many powers at this point, and it's been ages since she actually shot anyone, so she's probably more formidable metaphysically than physically.) 
 All of my grumbles aside, I really do think Skin Trade is a good start, if Hamilton intends to move the series back toward a focus on plot. 
 Read this and other LKH reviews at FantasyLiterature.net

On a whole i love the Anita Blake novels. But in all honesty they were starting to head way too far into romance and out of the sci-fi horror. The sex alone was becoming gratuitous. I wasn't really keeping my hopes too high on this one. But i was pleasantly surprised. First off you get almost half was through the book before sex. Big change from the last one where it was hitting almost from page ten. It's closer to the older books where its more about Anita and her attitude and Anita and her vagina. I loved it. Though still not the best of the series it was a very enjoyable read. Though it seemed to climax a little late and yet abruptly as with some parts that just kinda end with now build up.

I guess Laurell finally got the message from her fans. Sex is finally not the main topic in this tale. While it has to be there for the character to exist, it was minimal. I for one, appreciate the effort. While there were similarities to Obsidian Butterfly, another book I liked, it as different enough to keep me reading. I actually enjoyed this read.

Rereading this book still is as enjoyable as when I first read it. This is one of my fave books in the series. The new characters introduced were intriguing especially Victor. Funny "in -the-head-only-conversations" of Anita with herself is very amusing. Like the scene where Olaf was "checking out" the corpses... Anita mused about Dr. Memphis... "..was he just one of those people who didn't cuss much and needed practice? I'd be happy to help him practice.". Made me smile... Really it did... And rereading it, it did not fail to make me smile again.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I don't usually write reviews with spoilers - and this doesn't have major ones, but I've clicked the box just to be safe ;) 
 Let me say, I enjoy reading Ms. Hamilton's books. She can create some wonderful characters. The problem is that there are just too many. The lady desperately needs a good editor. I miss Damien and Jason. I really miss Jean-Claude. I also like Requiem, but he at least made an appearance here. It's as though the early characters just can't hold her interest any more, so Anita has to have more men... 
 For this installment, Anita travels to Las Vegas. Alone. Now, given all that's happened in the series, Anita travels *alone* out of state?!? I was looking forward to some good bad-guy-hunting, so maybe there's some redemption in the story. Maybe moving the overall arc forward. 
 Well, Anita seems to have gained a new power. She can freakin' stop time. Her "day" in Vegas is over 370 pages long. And it's the usual rambling interspersed with marshall-stuff (Edward, Bernardo and Olaf have joined Anita in Vegas. Yeah for Edward and Bernardo. Olaf...no thanks) and a host of new law enforcement characters (thankfully they all stay clothed). I've been to Vegas. I know the city layout. They traverse the city and cram a *whole* bunch into those daylight hours. 
 I will say this isn't the non-stop orgy that the last few books have been. Anita stays clothed (well, other than injuries) until the last quarter of the book. Then she's her usual screaming self. 
 Overall, it was ok. It did end up moving the overall story arc forward a click or two (again, in the last pages) and they did get the bad guy. But, I really would be thrilled if Ms. Hamilton returned to her original characters and allowed Anita to "limit the menu" as she keeps whining about.

I have conflicting thoughts when it comes to this book. For those of you who liked early Anita before the major turn to erotica, you will like this book better than her recent ones. There is very little sex compared to her recent books. Only two scenes (well three, but one is glossed over something fierce). So don't read this for the sex - read it for the crime-solving action that is reminiscent of her early early books. 
 The time pacing in this book is odd - it takes place in about one or two days. And there isn't enough time to fit in everything they were doing in that time, so it's impossible to get a sense of the time of day. With everything that goes on it should be closer to a week's timeline, not a day or two. 
 Not a huge deal, but that restricted time frame doesn't allow for much character development or revelations of relationships or anything along those lines. It only really allows for action and dialogue to further the plot. Which I think is sad because Anita as a character and how she interacts with her relationships and how those develop are what make me like her story. When she was getting to know Richard and Jean Claude in the beginning stories, I was so hooked by the relationships. The only relationship that was really developed in any way this time was with freaky Olaf. Which wasn't bad...it was interesting but there it was limited with no resolution or ending or actual change because let's face it - it was about 48 hours. 
 There were also none of the 'home' characters. The major players were missing and it felt like they were missing. Sure, there were others, but I think those who love the series will find it rather sad. 
 Lastly, I worry that I am growing tired of the series. I gave this three stars because although I did read this in a couple days because I was anxious to see what happened, I am not excited about the next book. Not for anything specific in this book, but more because I think the series is getting too convoluted. Not because of her harem - that I can keep straight! It's the power-issues that are throwing things out of whack. Weird things happen because of ties to various people, sexual and otherwise, and they aren't explained. The 'explanation' is Anita saying "I don't know what happened." Or it is explained by the Mother of all Darkness or Belle. There has to be some underlying truths to the series that allow these power things to happen. Or at least some consistencies. I'm tired of Anita having a dream/experience with Marmee or Belle, and then all of a sudden have a new skill in her repertoire that no one can explain and no one even tries. It chips away at the credibility of the Anita Blake world. 
 Maybe the series has just gotten too big with too many main players in Anita's life. I don't envy the author trying to keep them all in the forefront and meld all the powers, animals, and cop feelings of Anita's into one character. I don't think it's possible to do that and create a stable fictional world.

These books just get stranger and stranger. This wasn't a bad book, but it wasn't a great one either. For once, there was a plot, but for having spanned several books, it had a pretty weak conclusion to the arch.
Much better then the last. I love that Anita was away from her many "sweeties" and that there was hardly any sex. Progress!

I would like to start by saying.. I read this book after Lover mine by JR WARD who is one of my fav authors and one of my Fav series. So anything after Lover mine is going to be a very tough act to follow. 
 I missed Nathaiel JC Asher, Micah, jason and etc. I felt that alot of this book was Anita and the police standing around talking about who's got the biggest balls, her or them, not enough doing. 
 however, it redeemed itself in the end when action finally happened. I liked the ending it baught me back into it but the majority of the stuff at the beginning was just skimming to try and get to something good. 
 I really like Olaf's character. okay not the sick gross side, but the confuing doofas side that is willing to try and be "normal" don't know how long that will last though and I am actually looking foward to a showdown between him and ANita, if there ever is one. 
 All up this wasn't bad, but wasn't the best one either.

I was NOT PLEASED! The only saving grace for the second star was Edward! I hope that LKH pulls her head out of her butt, and at least pays attention to her grammar and repetition for her future books!

book_a.title: Columbine
book_a.user_review:
Like Iris Chang's Nanking, this is clinical, detached and compelling telling of a tragedy. 
 Cullen's book does not sensationalize any aspect of the Columbine High School shooting of 1999 -- if you're looking for hagiography for the victims, or a blood-and-guts retelling, this isn't it. But if you want something insightful that may help you better understand, for the first time, the motives and goals of instigator Eric Harris and the follow-along of Dylan Klebold, this is the one to read. 
 The author spent ten years researching, interviewing and writing, and his patience and skills show on every page. This is illuminating. 
 Apparently a revised edition includes some corrections but that's not the one I read, so I can't comment.

sample_reviews.review_text: This extremely well-researched and well-written book was considered one of the best non-fiction books of 2009, and I can certainly see why. Always gripping, it tells the horrifying details of the Columbine massacre and what lead two high school students to commit murder in an interesting, non-linear manner. Many of the things we were lead to believe about Columbine were not accurate, and Dave Cullen respectfully debunks the myths. Highly recommended.

This book was excellent! So many times I pick up a book about some unimaginable event trying to find out what made a person act in such an unbelievable way. Usually I am disappointed because it is so hard for anyone to get in the head of another person whose mindset is so foreign. Fortunately Eric Harris and Dylan Klebold left journals and videos that opened up their minds.

I found this book both creepy and fascinating. I liked that it didn't so much as focus just on the killers and their actions, but everything that followed in the aftermath, the stuff that got lost in the horrible tragedy. for example, I had no idea about the cover up that Jeffco officials perpetrated or how long it took for the families to get the information. 
 Also, I remember very clearly some of those rumors that circulated, especially how it was two kids who were bullied and that's why they went crazy. And I remember thinking at the time, "most of us have been teased/bullied and we don't go on a murdering spree and kill people who had nothing to do with our abuse." 
 It's quite thorough, pulling from many different sources, but there are some areas where the write admits that he made his own guesses as to what people were thinking/saying/doing/feeling. It's also a pretty hard book to digest at times. 
 I do recommend it, if only so more people are aware of what actually happened in the dealing with the situation.
Good factual discussion about what actually happened and what happened in the months before.
I say this not having finished the book. It's a really well researched account, but I just couldn't keep reading about these sad, sad people. I want to finish it though, I do.

On April 20, 1999 Eric Harris and Dylan Klebold went to school not with the goal of passing that days Math test but to blow up Columbine High School and leave a lasting impression on the world. 
 Columbine has since become synonymous with school shootings, the expression needs no definition, and unfortunately leaves a lasting impression, Eric and Dylan's goal. 
 Like most historic events or tragedies you can remember where you were and what you were doing. (i.e.9/11) Anyway, I was only fourteen at the time so don't remember exactly that but have a very vivid memory just a few weeks afterward. I was in 8th grade and a boy a class behind mine brought two walkie talkies to school, which were promptly confiscated. Somehow, it snowballed that said student was bringing a gun to school on Tuesday and would shoot anyone wearing the color green. Tuesday came with a large number of the student body surprisingly in attendance. I recall a large pile of book bags at the front entrance and lots of police and bomb sniffing dogs. Tuesday came and went. Nothing happened. It was all a rumor. If Rockwood Valley had panic it could not even have been a tenth to what Columbine experienced. 
 The novel Columbine, has been hailed as the "In Cold Blood" of this generation, like Capote, Cullen had the reader connect or feel empathic towards Dylan and Eric, I know that might sound strange considering their actions but somehow, despite their wrong-doings made the killers into real people and not the psychopaths that they were. I also liked that the author flashed back and forth between the day of the massacre and then to its aftermath. He also addresses some rumors or bogus "urban legends" if you will, such as the trench coat mafia or one of the victims professing her devotion to God before her death. Columbine is not for everyone, it is disturbing, unbelievable and even though Dave Cullen maps out the 5Ws (&H) it still leaves you stun.

This was not even on my radar, mostly because of the heavy subject matter. Children killing children is not something I want to devote a lot of time thinking about. I decided to give it a chance, however, after seeing the high reviews on here. This is a masterpiece of reportage. The author does not shy away from the details, so brace yourself, and thought the subject matter is heavy, the narrative is engaging. There is so much information he is giving us, but it never feels like we're being fed just the facts. It is astounding at how the author pieced the narrative together from all the different resources to create a narrative not only of the day of the event, but events leading up to and after the event as well. I appreciated the fact that he alternated the happenings from the actual day of the event with stories of the survivors and people otherwise affected by the event. You get flashes of the shooting in pieces. It didn't feel too overwhelming that way, and I thought it was a clever way to handle it. My favorite part, by far, was the section on psychopathy. It was so fascinating, and such a small part, but it has stayed with me. Highly recommend this one.

This was refreshing to read, in the sense that it provides much needed context and hind-sight to the events that occurred around the time of the shooting. At the time, people (media, politicians, residents of Columbine) jumped the gun and started pointing fingers without any tangible proof or information. 
 This book gives a detailed account of the follow up, the shooting, and the aftermath in an accurate and journalistic way. I enjoyed that Cullen attempted to stay as informational and unbiased as possible with the trick subject matter. To how he debunks some of the myths surrounding a variety of martyrdom stories, and how he handles analyzing the killers Dylan and Eric. It is frightening to think what Eric may have become had he not killed himself in 1999, after reading what Cullen had written about him. He very easily could have gone onto to become a serial rapist/ serial killer. It really was an example of "the perfect storm". 
 I admired Cullen for finally giving faces and names and stories to the victims. With the recent shootings in the U.S. it is again demonstrating how society has the tendency to focus on the killers and not their victims. On a personal level, the one aspect of reading this book that will never leave me was reading about Kyle Velasquez. His background and his story probably touched me the most. He is one of the least well known victims, his family never really came forward and there were no false martyr stories published about him. He was just a nice boy, who was quiet, and trying to make his way through high school. Kyle is the person I think of when I think of Columbine. Those who were murdered that day are the kids and adults who deserve to be remembered. 
 Kyle Velasquez was 16 born on May 5th 1982, died April 20 1999.

I was super excited when my English teacher told my class we would be reading this book. So excited that I started researching more about the topic to better understand the event before reading about it. That being said, I found Dave to be biased (something he admits to in the epilogue) and it frustrated me throughout the whole book making it extremely difficult for me to enjoy. If I hadn't had such high hopes for this book, I probably would've liked it more, but given that I was told this is the account that's mostly regarded as true and then seeing so many flaws, I was very upset. 
 In my opinion, Dave discusses the deaths of those who were "interesting" or had drama surrounding them. I came into this book expecting to hear about all of the people killed and was really only told (with detail) about 5 of them, which left me extremely unsatisfied. 
 That being said, I did enjoy reading the book. I enjoyed learning more about the tragedy (even though I wanted to know so much more) and despite feeling like Wikipedia could've given me the same story in much less words and time, I don't regret reading this.

My rating isn't a reflection on the author's ability, but of my own issues with this topic. Columbine affected me deeply as a young adult (I was a freshman in high school when it happened). It was the first time (not the last) that I truly realized the dangers in the world, in places you thought (or assumed) were safe. I was obsessed with Columbine at the time... reading everything I could get my hands on, attending Rachel's dad's speech in town, etc. It was a bit obsessive. Anyway, I couldn't wait to read this when it came out but every time I picked it up I wouldn't be able to get far and I would get sick to my stomach reliving what occurred. In the end I decided that I wasn't going to force myself to finish the book since I was having such a reaction to it.

book_b.title: Belgravia
book_b.user_review:
Ugh. It was painful. Not really, but not at all my cuppa, although I like Fellowes' others works, like Gosford Park and of course Downton Abbey . Plus I'm a big "fan" of the Napoleonic wars ... and maybe that was my problem, it just didn't ring as true as the works of Patrick O'Brian or Jane Austen. 
 Fellowes had an "historical consultant" help him with this - not a good sign. I mean sure, if you write historical fiction, you should have an expert review it to see if you made any major mistakes, but to credit them on the outside cover would imply you're kind of out of your depth. 
 I look forward to the miniseries this seems to have been a treatment for. The dialogue is much better suited to be acted than read, or even said by real people, if that makes sense. It's theatrical and not at all natural. 
 I'm certainly glad he made an effort to get the history right but ... ugh. Just ugh.

sample_reviews.review_text: Very predictable and somewhat uninteresting. I was a little disappointed. The characters had a lot of potential but never reached it. I actually skim read a lot of the pages at the end. It was a good storyline but nothing new. Just okay.

This was a good story but written poorly. Like the last seasons of Downton! This could have been good but far too much internalizing and not enough direct dialogue. it reads more as a brainstorming session for a book than the finished thing. What a shame

** spoiler alert ** 
 Julian Fellowes is becoming the Jane Austen of the 21st century, except that she wrote books set in her own time, and he writes about the past. 
 It's the typical class warfare struggle, rich vs. poor, with a couple of plot twists. Premature death, illegitimate baby, titles to inherit, debts to creditors. Yet it all works out in the end, wrapped in a big red bow. 
 It reads like a watered down rehash of his Netflix series, Doctor Thorne. Next time I want to read a historical fiction, I'll look to the romance aisle, where the descriptions are more vivid, and the characters are 3-dimensional.

From Waterloo to the 1840's, this is a story of two families - one an up and coming trademan family and the other high society - whose lives become involved do to a love story with the young man being killed at Waterloo and the young woman dying in child birth.
Absolutely delightful.
The audio was so much fun, like reader radio. Not sure if the book would be as enjoyable honestly because it's easy to figure out how it's going to play out. But listening to it- an adventure.
Well researched but shockingly poor writing. Dull, dull, dull.....I'll stick to the Downton Abbey reruns.

book_a.title: Spying in High Heels (High Heels, #1)
book_a.user_review:
I would expect better writing and command of the English language from someone who has been the "recipient of numerous awards" (according to her website). There were times I had to stop and re-read a sentence to make sense of it, due to lack of punctuation. I had to stop counting the dangling participles and incomplete sentences, which were very distracting. 
 Aside from the language and writing errors, this book is a light beach read at best. By the time I hit the halfway mark in the book, I really didn't care much about the characters, the end of the story was predictable and it was the literary equivalent of eating a couple bowls of cotton candy. Not that I expected it to be much else, but don't get this book thinking there will be red herrings or twists and turns that keep you on the edge of your seat. Many words are spent detailing driving the Los Angeles freeways, which seems to have little, if anything, to do with moving the story forward. I live in Los Angeles and not only are the freeways not that interesting, on a normal day you'd find it impossible to get from point A to point B as fast as this character does. 
 In general, this book is a messy fluff piece and I've deleted any subsequent books by this author from my Nook sample reading list.

sample_reviews.review_text: This was really good frothy mystery. Lots of humor. Reminded me of Janet Evanovich's Stephanie Plum. But with LA, not Jersey.

Spying in High Heels is delightful! Maddie Springer's boyfriend has disappeared and Maddie is determined to locate him. After all, she may be pregnant with his child and as soon as she gets her nerve up she is definitely going to do "the test"! As Maddie investigates, she gets a little too close to the truth about the missing 20 million dollars, a couple of murders and becomes a target herself. She needs a weapon but what does she have on hand? Maddie searches her studio and finds the perfect weapon, a dusty Thigh Master! You see why I gave this book 5 stars? It's hilarious, fast paced and has a little romance and a little mystery.
Didn't finish

It was cute. At first. 
 See, in the beginning Maddie was a cute combination of Becky from Shopaholic meets Nancy Drew. She was charmingly adorable with a great sense of humor and an awesome boyfriend. But that quickly changed. Soon, Maddie was ameteur sleuth judging everybody by their body type and career, being a prissy princess and making all the wrong decisions that had my teeth on edge. Her character became increasingly superficial and transparent (the way she thought about jasmine just because she had a lot of surgeries, the way she thought about Althea). She was an awful person. Her character was shallow and one dimensional. She had no depth at all. There were no facets to her personality. It was a horrible experience, reading the main body of the book. 
 The plot was flimsy and predictable. I knew from the start who the killer really was. And frankly I was just racing to finish it up because I have this nasty habbit of not being able to skim. It's a curse really. 
 So yeah. This was a very blah read.

3.5 stars 
 What I didn't like: First, all the endless details about what everyone is wearing every second of the day. Bor-ring. Second, the heroine spends the first half of the book unwilling to take an EPT test to know if she's pregnant or not (it starts to be funny in the second half of the book when she finally has the balls but keeps screwing up the test). 
 What I did like: The author's voice. That's what kept me reading. She's funny as a crutch. (I mean that in the best possible way.) And Ramirez. He's one hot cop. Loved his family, too.
Cute. Light. Funny. Good summer read!

A friend gave me the book because she knew how much I like the Stephanie Plum series. 
 So this is more or less the same cliche - female character starts to investigate two murder because the suspect could be the father of her "perhaps" child; add a hunk of a cop, a great friend and voila ... 
 But, even though a nice story, it just hasn't got the same touch not to mention the same class as the Plum books. AND I more or less had an idea of who the killer could be half way through the book. 
 It seemed to me that the main character Maddie was constantly either on some numbered high- or freeway or was eating some take away place, oh, that's right: or drinking diet coke because she's "late" late - which in an annoying way everyone seems to emphasise, because she seems to be one of those who are constantly late - as in not on time. 
 The plot itself is good, though, as I mentioned before, with just too many cliches. 
 If you haven't yet read the Plum books, you might enjoy this one for a nice rainy weekend or a light read at the beach.
Super funny! Can't wait to read more from Gemma Halliday!

A humorous story. Maddie designs children's shoes in LA. Richrd, her boy friend lawyer, disappears and a business client of his turns up dead. Richard is suspected, and Maddie learns more than she wants to as she investigates to prove his innocence. Despite warnings from a chunky detective and then anonymous threats, she plunges on. Strong voice, nice tension. Think Janet Evanovich's Steffan Plum on the West Coast. Not a literary novel, but written and fun. Enjoy.
Cute and fun read.

book_b.title: So Cold the River

I couldn't put this thriller down. It reminded me of a classic Dean Koontz - taking something really and tilting it just a bit to the strange and supernatural so that the reader starts thinking yeah, that could happen! 
 I thoroughly enjoyed reading it and look forward to reading more from this author.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I'm not sure about this book. Everybody is so unpleasant, it's hard to care about the characters. I'll give it a little more time... 
 Okay, I'm over half way through the book and I still don't care diddly for the protagonist. As bad as he is, the villians are worse. There's just no one to like or care about in this book. I'm giving up.

I really liked the setting of this book, but that was about it. I listened to this as an audiobook and I never really got into the narrator (while I often dislike a narrator when I start listening to a new book, I mostly ease into their way of speaking after a while, and start to appreciate it, but that never happened this time). So I might have enjoyed it more if I'd read it or if someone else had narrated it, but I don't really think so. My thoughts kept wandering; I'm not too sure how everything fit together in the end, and I'm not interested enough to go back and look it up. I think Michael Koryta probably just isn't for me, even though those two books of his I have read weren't bad by any means. Just not enough to make me want more.

I read Michael Koryta's So Cold the River as a library checkout, since I'd never encountered the author before yet was in the mood to try a suspense-oriented horror thriller. And while I found it competently done in some ways, in others, it was ultimately kind of disappointing. This was an uncommon instance of a book I read and wound up not actually wanting to buy. 
 Eric Shaw was once an up-and-coming filmmaker, and now he's slogging through his days by filming memorials for funerals while he avoids dealing with how he's walked out on his wife Claire. A wealthy socialite, Alyssa Bradford, hires him to do a documentary about her father-in-law--and when Eric agrees to take the job, he comes to a town full of the obligatory layers upon layers of disturbing secrets. At the heart of them all lurks something evil, something Eric begins to see in visions once he starts taking drinks from an old bottle of Pluto Water. 
 At its core the plot wasn't bad, I'll happily give it that, yet some aspects of its execution rubbed me the wrong way. One big one was that while you initially are led to believe that drinking this old mineral water is what's causing Eric to have visions, it comes up at one point that he has this ability anyway--and his wife actually has to remind him of an incident where he'd exhibited precognition. That yanked me RIGHT out of the story, because I found it impossible to believe that a person could forget something like that. 
 The other thing that bugged me was that a good deal of time is spent in the POV of the primary mortal antagonist. I acknowledge that this was necessary for the development of his character, and you do ultimately see where his character is going. But that said, more than once I found that character repugnant enough that I was almost driven away from the book. 
 On the good side, there were several genuinely creepy passages, and I had no issues with anything about Koryta's prose; more, my quibbles were with aspects of his characterization and plot. In the end, though, this book didn't seize me well enough to make it permanently into my collection. I'd recommend it as a library read, or if you need something to read on a trip, but nothing more than that. Two stars.

I hate to give a one-star rating, but this book deserves one. It just didn't make any sense, really, and was tiresomely cliched, full of questionable or downright silly motives, cornpone dialogue, and waaaay too long. The main question I had to ask after reading it was "Why?" And at the top of my long list of "Why" questions is, why did I waste the time and money? If you must read this, please check it out of the library, and don't say you haven't been warned.

Eric was formerly involved in shooting movies, but now uses his talents to make videos for weddings and funerals. He is offered a lucrative job to go to a small Indiana town, find out details of a wealthy dying man's early life there and make a short film. He finds a dangerous supernatural mystery to unravel. Very enjoyable, look forward to reading more from this author.
Ho Hum

So Cold the River by Michael Koryta 
 A down and out want-to-be Steven Spielburg find himself immersed in water, deceit and confusion. A trip to a famous resort for a simple project lands him in the most danger fraught period of his life. 
 Eric Shaw is a man with an enormous ego that has been shattered by failure. His self loathing promotes his driving of those who love him to despair. Koryta truly paints a man who conspires to destroy himself. The characterization is poignant and colorful. Small towns with secrets are a frequent topic of scary novels. This isn't scary like a slasher film but more thought provoking scary. 
 The books is primarily an exploration of Eric's personal redemption but ancillary characters such as his wife, Claire and Kellen Cage are also well done. I particularly enjoyed the quirky Anne McKinney looking to the sky for personal redemption. 
 Josiah Campbell was almost a stereotypical red neck haunted by a desire to be someone and no ambition to get there. This book was overflowing with memorable characters that added both their own nobility and despicable behavior. 
 I highly recommend the book.

Comparisons to Steven King and Dean Koontz were apt. Kortya has a good voice, and it's not too crazy. He doesn't go off the deep end as King did in IT, and his characters are pretty strong. Very nice setting in rural Indiana, makes me want to visit there and see it for myself. Wondering if these characters will recur in a future Koryta book.
utterly disappointing. I'm forced to boycott the authors who wrote positive blurbs for this guy. not fun, not scary, not sharp. boooo.

reference_books.title: Opposition (Lux, #5)
reference_books.review_text:
Con esta entrega finalizamos la saga Lux, una saga que nos dio alegrias y nos hizo pensar sera que si tiro el libro contra la pared la cosas cambiaran (si de acuerdo no lo hizo pero se puede hacer el intento). 
 Mi rating de 4 estrellas es debido a que a pesar de no ser un mal final y de tener ese y vivieron felices para siempre, le falto algo no se si fue que al ser "los villanos" los luxen malos esperaba mas de esa batalla porque como se ve al principio del libro esos tipos no estan dando vueltas van por lo que quieren conquistar La Tierra. Pero con semejantes villanos Jennifer no supo usarlos bien es decir todo lo resolvio volando al mejor estilo de Austen y los Arum se encargaron del trabajo sucio sin que nuestros protagonistas siquieran llegaran a sudar y luego tenemos a Nancy una mala como villana que casi logra el cometido de acabar con el Happy Ending por dios ya habian sufrido como mucho. 
 Resumiendo el libro fue increible en su primera parte no lo podia soltar, me comia las unas por saber si nuestro lindo Daemon se habia pasado o no al lado oscuro de la fuerza (si me gusta Star Wars), luego sus interacciones con Kat, sus ocurrencias, la fuerza de la misma Kat ella es increible, el viaje por carretera y conocer mas a los Arum fue genial perode ahi en adelante el libro decae mucho y Jennifer no hizo nada por darle mas vida. 
 Uno de los mejores momentos fue de Kat y Dee, vamos esa pelea fue sublime, magnifica y quedara registrada para mi como una de las mejores que he leido, yo estaba como dale mas duro Kat a ver si reacciona y deja la zorra y cosas por el estilo; los demas momentos pertenecieron a Daemon fueron maravillosos esa mezcla de ternura, romance y egocentrismo lo hace ser quien es. 
 Esperaba algo mas de otros personajes como Dawson y Archer pero es una muestra mas de que no se debe esperar tener todo en la vida, Dawson fue un completo 0 a la izquierda su parte brillante fue la del Candy Crush y Archer a pesar de la ayuda con el viaje no tuvo mas fuerza algo que no me termino de cuadrar, me gustaria un libro sobre el y Dee pero bueh Jennifer ya lo sabes. Luc hizo su parte no fue como justo que no tuviera alguien con quien compartir la victoria pero fue bueno ver que sigue en contacto con los chico despues de un tiempo. 
 En fin para finalizar un buen final que se pudo haber desarrollado mejor pero no defraudo y si le doy un chance a los demas libros de Armentrout asi escriba bajo su psudonimo.

reference_books.title: Heir of Fire (Throne of Glass #3)
reference_books.review_text:
Puedes leer esta y otras resenas en --> Mi Biblioteca 
 Con Heredera de Fuego Sarah leva la historia de Celaena a un nuevo nivel. Luego de enterarnos del pasado de Celaena (estoy haciendo mi mayor esfuerzo por no darles spoliers grandes) y de la idea de Chaol de enviarla lejos para salvarle la vida con la excusa de infiltarse en el reino de Wedlyn, ella se encuentra en una fase deprimente donde piensa que nada vale la pena, recuerden que en Corona de Medianoche Celaena se enfrento a una situacion horrible y eso la cambia. En Wedlyn debera enfrentarse a su pasado y su otra mitad, es decir debe abrazar la herencia magica que sus padres le han legado, Celaena es mitad Fae y su poder es capaz de consumir todo en llamas de ahi el titulo del libro. 
 Pero en Wedlyn no solo se enfrentara al pasado sino que tambien conocera a su tia Maeve la Reina Fae quien considerara a Celaena una amenaza por lo que se enfrentaran en voluntades. Y junto con ella concocera todo un mundo nuevo donde aprendera a controlar sus poderes y conocera gente maravillosa. Aunque no todo el mundo es tan amable con ella, Rowan Whitethorne es ese vivo ejemplo, el le ensenara todo lo que necesite saber y con eso aprenderan las fortalezas y debilidades del otro, lo que los llevara a tener un vinculo profundo. 
 ELa trama dee ste libro es increible, al expander el mundo de la saga Sarah nos lleva aotros parajes y con eso as secretos y mas magia seran revelados. Tambien anexa a esta mezcla personajes nuevos cuyas voces se escuchan al lado del trio protagonico. Tambien nos muestra nuevas facetas de nuestros queridos protagonistas lo que solo le agrega mas a la historia. 
 Un personaje nuevo pero que me sorprendio mucho o mejor dicho me intrigo fue Manon Blackbeak heredera de su clan dentro de la Brujas Diente de Hierro Manon esta segura en el papel que debe ejercer, sin embargo conforme avanza el libro nos damos cuenta de que ella no es completamente sadica y violenta como su abuela u otras brujas. Su relacion con su dragon es increible y me impresiono que alguien qu fue criado como ella demostrara esa amabilidad hacia un dragon con discapacidades. 
 Aedion Ashryver es el otro personaje que Sarah mete en la ecuacion, este chico es conocido como el Lobo del Norte y a pesar de que jura su lealtad al Rey, pronto nos damos cuenta de que es solo una farsa. Aedion esta infiltrado y trabaja con los rebeldes en busca de la Princesa perdida de Terrasen y su legitima Reina, sin embaro esta unido a Celaena Sardothien la asesina del Rey de una manera que ni se imagina. Aedion le aporta a esta historia calor, sarcasmo y otro hombre sexy (en serio que Sarah nos quiere matar). 
 Rowan es nuestro nuevo crush literario y aunque terminamos conociendo mucho de este chico, a la final no terminamos de ver todo lo que su personalidad nos puede ofrecer. Rowan seguira siendo un personaje que iremos descubriendo mas en los siguientes libros. Una cosa que quedo pendiente es si habra romance o no con Celaena, aunque muchas quisieron que solo quedara como amigo, yo personalmente no se que opinar. 
 Chaol empieza a mostrar un lado terrible de el, jamas pense tan mal de el pero las cosas que ocurren en este libro lo van cambiando y no precisamente para bien, no sabe que hacer su trabajo lo obliga ser leal a la corona pero el sabe que su lealtad es para Dorian y adonde el vaya Chaol lo seguira. Dorian por su parte muestra su faceta de hombre enamorado y romantico, aqui Sarah le da la oportunidad de ser feliz, pero tristemente no lo disfrutaremos mucho. 
 El libro es impresionante el ritmo no decae porque Sarah juega con los puntos de vista de cada uno de los personajes, y solo nos deja con ganas de mas debido a que Celaena llega a perdonarse a si misma y a rescatar a la chica que dejo abandonada cuando en Terrasen todo se va al diablo. Ella buscara venganza y tratara de recuperar todo lo que por derecho es de ella. Solo podemos esperar mas y mas de esta saga.

reference_books.review_text:
Le doy 5 estrellas no por la profundidad sino que nos da un vistazo al comienzo de la vida de Cinder en la tierra luego de todas sus cirugias cuando Linh Garan se la lleva a vivir con su familia y de una se ve como su madrastra Adri la detesta desde el comienzo pero como su relacion con Peony empieza desde el primer momento en que se ven, ella fue la que ayuda a Cinder a adaptarse al mundo nuevo un mundo del cual ella no sabe mucho sino es porque su cabeza va descargando la informacion a un ritmo vertiginoso. 
 Tambien uno de los puntos importantes es que nos muestran como Cinder rearma de nuevo a Iko y como Garan desaparece de su vida casi al momento de llegar a ser parte de la misma. Es una linda historia algo para conocer mejor a Cinder y seguir con la historia principal.

book_a.title: La élite (La selección, #2)
book_a.user_review:
2.5 esta segunda parte fue un fiasco total ahora me pregunto como diablos logro este libro salir a la luz, escribo esto escuchando Make Me Wanna Die de The Pretty Reckless y si ese es el sentimiento que le doy al libro. 
 America me habia gustado durante el primer libro, su personalidad fuerte de no dejarse llevar por lo que La Seleccion es, tratar de resistirse al Principe Maxon y terminar enmaorandolo mas solo por ser como es ella, me habia gustado mucho. Pero en este libro es ella la que se pierde dentro del triangulo amoroso, sobresale Maxon al ver una parte de el fuerte y decidido que no cree en el sistema de gobierno actual y que mediante pequenos pero fuertes cambios planea cosas buenas y distintas para su pueblo, eso habla de lo bien que lo quiere hacer como Rey, pero como hombre al fin no va a perder la oportunidad de conocer a las chicas y mas si la indecision de America no ayuda, una indecision que me traia al borde, ya nina es a Maxon a quien mas a escoger punto deja el drama. Por su parte Aspen es la decoracion de pared no aporta nada bueno excepto darle dolores de cabeza a America y darnos dolores a nosotros los lectores por saber si los descubririan. 
 La trama en general no es muy pulcra salta mucho, hay escenas claves si pero muchas no dirigen a ningun lado y la chicas con sus conflictos de melodrama no deja que uno se meta mas en la historia. La parte de los rebeldes es interesante pero Kiera no sabe como explotarla esperaba mas secreto y misterio por esa parte solo sirvio para darle momentos intimos al triangulo una lastima. 
 Espero mas del final de la trilogia porque sino fue una perdida de tiempo. Por cierto hasta la portada es la que menos me gusta quien diablos escogio ese rojo que yo veo como anaranjado y jamas le quedara bien a la modelo con el tono de su cabello, ven una mala segunda parte.

I had a lovely review for you all. Then THIS happened when I hit preview. 
 Okay, so there's no way to prove that my review was actually lovely, but I'm going to say that it was because you can't prove otherwise.

 3.5 stars. 
 ~ This is erotica, not contemporary romance. Expect just as much sex as there is plot. However, this is a good intro to Olivia Cunning. If you haven't read Backstage Pass, try this one first. You'll get a handle on this author's writing style in much less time and it's slightly less intimidating (read : less anal play/voyeurism) than BP is for hesitant erotica readers.

The characters meet, find they're attracted to each other, then engage in kinky sex. Again, this is a short. I don't mind when the focus is more on sex if I'm reading something that is meant to be read in about an hour.

reference_books.title: Stories of Your Life and Others
reference_books.review_text:
I for one had never heard of Ted Chiang. I've always enjoyed science-fiction and all of its sub-genres, from the space opera to alternate history, but I wasn't one to seek it out. In fact, as I'd gotten older, science-fiction began to seem less essential to me. Unless I stumbled across a novel that had received rave reviews, I wouldn't consider it -- because as I grew older, I began to see the genre as so many snobs do -- as a secondary or even tertiary consideration when presented with the option to read a good book -- because science-fiction is for kids. 
 Of course, deep down I knew this wasn't always the case. A Canticle for Leibowitz is a perfect example of great science-fiction, and I mention Leibowitz only because it's a personal favorite. But it seemed harder and harder to discover good science-fiction by anything more than trial & error. And frankly, as the 80s wore into the 90s, I simply became tired of trying. It became a waste of time. There's so much more that is bad than good, and blurbs on a book can be so misleading. Oh, and mediocrity often sells best. The stuff I consider good simply doesn't populate shelves like mediocre efforts by mediocre writers. 
 Now who's sounding like a snob? Point taken. 
 But the internet has changed everything for someone like me. I can sift through blogs and forums and those more learned than I as to what constitutes the good stuff -- the stuff that received limited print runs -- or saw the light of day only in an obscure anthology -- or found its way on a library bookshelf, only to sit there in obscurity, unless the borrower already knew it was there in the first place -- can point me in the right directions. 
 Not that I always agree, but I think of blogs and review forums and the like as aggregates of good taste -- kind of like Metatcritic or Rotten Tomatoes -- so I find there to be less error in the trial and error process. 
 So to my point, which should be painfully obvious by now: Ted Chiang's obscure short story collection, Story of Your Life: And Others, which unfortunately seems out of print, is very much worth the effort to track down and read. 
 I so tire of those who consider "literary science-fiction" an oxymoron. They merely demonstrate ignorance. 
 That's not to say every story is a genius collection of words. Some I felt decidedly superior to others. But the collection of ideas here, some certainly not knew, but all presented in unique, original, timely ways, is simply one of the best collections of "ideas" that I've ever read. 
 Highly recommended. All here are above average, and several are decidedly brilliant. Ironically, let's hope a literary version of Chiang's invention -- calliagnosia, the idea at the center of the final story in this collection -- never appears.
