reference_books.title: Drood
reference_books.review_text:
Oh, Dear Reader, 
 The best thing about this book IS its cover. 
 I'm no stranger to Dan Simmons, having read seven of his novels, all of which are significantly better than this horrendous misfire. For those with a keen eye for science fiction, I strongly recommend the Hyperion books. For those who enjoy historical imaginings, by all means, pick up a copy of Simmons' previous publication, The Terror. For those who like a good old-fashioned horror novel, one filled with lots of vampires, you simply can't go wrong with Carrion Comfort. 
 This mess of a novel should be avoided at all costs -- though I did choose to finish it. Like those who simply can't quit dinner with food on their plate, I have a tough time abandoning a novel once I've started. But goodness gracious what a slog -- what a predictable slog. 
 There is no horror here, no tension, no suspense, and no real mystery. No surprise. And a novel like this hinges on surprise. There are hundreds, thousands of words devoted to banal detail that, by novel's end, come close to amounting to practically nothing. 
 I struggle to criticize this novel without giving dreary plot points away. 
 Told strictly from one individual's viewpoint, we find ourselves reading the same trains of thought over and over again, and they become so tedious and predictable. I can't even begin to tell you what happened over spans of a hundred or more pages because there was nothing compelling enough there for me to remember what occurred. I endured endless discussions of the same things over and over and over again. 
 The writing is very mediocre and the novel is way, way too long. It's bloated with contrivance after contrivance from beginning to end. The antagonist simply isn't strong enough, compelling enough, or likable enough to sustain a story of this length. The narrator isn't even remotely, deliciously UNlikable. Oh, and had I ever cared to indulge in opium or morphine addiction prior to my reading of Drood, I've experienced what amounts to the strongest dose of aversion therapy in reading this novel. The descriptions of Opium addiction go on, and on, and on, and on. 
 I don't think I've ever read such heavy-handed pretension in a novel as long as this, that is also so undeniably filled with hot air. I've never read such an empty novel of this length. 
 When we come to the climax, it's simply ridiculous. Success of the denouement hinges upon the reader's acceptance that a certain character actually has IN his or her character the capability of committing a specific act. Yet there is nothing in all 771 pages, not one ounce of characterization, that prepares for or allows any reader with a remotely critical eye to actually believe what the character claims. Particularly given the amount of time involved. The ending is one of the weakest I've ever read -- although I did like the very last couple sentences. 
 Simmons simply fails to create a suspension of disbelief. Simmons fails to characterize believably. So the ending fails in rather spectacular fashion. 
 I kept thinking -- surely, something more was going to happen -- Drood can't stay this dreadful. But it did. 
 It's almost as if Simmons didn't actually write this -- perhaps he hired some ghost-writing hack to take a stab at an idea he was having trouble with. 
 Stay away from this one, Dear Reader. Simmons phoned this one in from a very, very distant place.

reference_books.title: Wolf Hall (Thomas Cromwell, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Caveat: I'm not a devoted fan of historical fiction, so take my opinion with a grain of salt, but I simply didn't find the story engaging. In fact, I felt Mantel's prose kept me at arm's length from any visceral enjoyment of events, and instead felt more like reading a "textbook reenactment" of events--a text version of what one sees on the History channel's episodic treatments of historical events, for example. It just didn't work for me. 
 Which was a little surprising, if only because I was initially drawn in. I enjoyed the opening scenes, particularly the introductory dialogue between Cromwell and Holsby. It was lively, informative, engrossing. But it felt, somehow, as though Mantel's paintings of events and multitudinous character introductions, not to mention her fondness for pronouns, began to feel more like oratory than entertainment. 
 Consequently, finding the novel unfinishable (which is a rare event for me), I reluctantly give it just one star. It simply wasn't satisfying.

book_a.title: Taipei
book_a.user_review:
There is no beautiful writing in Tao Lin's Tai Pei, there is only deliberate, stilted effect. 
 There is no compelling narrative, merely severely affected happenstance. 
 There is no emotion to be found, no sense of empathy, or even sympathy for the characters in the story. They could have been named ants going about their days in the ant hill. 
 Tao Lin is too busy scoring style points to be bothered with something so inessential as his reader. 
 There is nothing to be learned here by the well read. He merely taps the notion of the disaffected twenty-something and contorts his writing to seem as though he is enlightening us to a new way of saying something about what hasn't already been said, when actually it has been said, and much more effectively, much more articulately, and far more beautifully. 
 Nothing to see here, move along.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Agh. Why. I wanted to enjoy it. But it was just so bad. I didn't even finished it. Just got to page 80 with SO much trouble. Then decided to toss it. My precious time... gone. 
 Everyone seems to enjoy this. I hated it.

A few thoughts just because a book is well written or brings something new to the table doesn't mean that it's good or worth your time. To sum it up some of the most self-centered , self-involved writing I have come across, if anything positive can be said about this book is it hits the nail in the head in it's portrait of NYC Hipsters/Yuppies a whole generation or subculture that is totally disconnected to anything that's not an electronic device, the type of people who seem to like things only in a self-loathing ironic way who are always quick to make a punch line and who seem to lack a genuine bone and believe in nothing but their cut-off closed-off niche circle of jag-off friends! Perhaps Tao Lin is making a statement about a part of a generation. A cause for alarm. It seems a number of people loved this book but if I had to bet it was in an ironic way. Don't waste your time there are far too many books ,that matter and have a soul, to read and so little to read a fraction of them. This was a horrible book!!!

Emepece la lectura de Taipei mas entusiasmado de lo que esperaba encontrar y termine nuevamente convencido de que la narrativa y el proyecto estetico de Tao Lin no me interesa para nada. 
 Hay un uso virtuoso de la prosa, un muy delicado ensamblaje formal que se agota en su propia experiencia: la trama es nula, los personajes son planos, intercambiables y el imaginario hipster melancolico que maneja resulta completamente unidimensional. ?El resultado? Una novela de casi trescientas paginas acerca del sentir y vivir de chicos pretenciosos de Brooklyn con sus necesidades basicas satisfechas. 
 El "realismo sucio" de Raymond Carver o la narrativa descarnada acerca de la Generacion X que impulso Bret Easton Ellis (quien no casualmente aparece en la contratapa diciendo que Lin es una de las mejores voces de su generacion) ofrecieron al menos la novedad de sus tramas semi-vacias y exprimieron hasta el fondo el procedimiento del iceberg hemingwayiano. Tao Lin no lo hace. Mientras que en "Less than Zero" de Easton Ellis, por dar un ejemplo, teniamos un punto de tension que punzaba sobre el retrato social de su epoca o en Carver podiamos vislumbrar una oscuridad en los comportamientos y los modos de sus personajes, en Lin se resume en jovenes experimentando con drogas, filmandose y viviendo apaticamente, rechazando reglas basicas de sociabilidad, etc.

I was underwhelmed, even bored by Taipei. Tao Lin's great trick is to describe in uncannily precise detail his protagonist's shifting state of mind. It's clever, and I was briefly interested from a writerly point of view, but ultimately, I found the characters uninteresting and their dilemmas minor - though it should be said that this book did suffer from my reading it straight after the extremely affecting and (also beautifully, keenly observed) Half of a Yellow Sun. Still, it struck me as navel gazing of the sort that never even gets down that hole.

This book was not what I expected or anticipated at all. It was on Buzzfeed's Junkiest Books About Drugs List AND it received a starred review from Publisher's Weekly so I decided to give it a whirl... Ugh, I shoulda gave it up 20 pages in when I couldn't get into it. I powered through all 248 pages hoping that it would at least pick up... nope! 
 The story follows Paul, a twenty something author living in Manhattan, who plows through life using a combination of drugs and medications. We're not meant to pity him, just observe, as he goes from literary event to restaurant to Taiwan, etc. Paul is a loner and aimlessly drifts around until he finds a girl to attach himself to. When he meets Erin their drug use intensifies and their quest for the meaning of life becomes hopelessly muddled. 
 It's well written, but not exciting. I couldn't find myself relating to any of the characters. Read at your own risk.

This book will solve my insomnia problems. No, really. I usually can't sleep on trains, but this little gem made me fall asleep not only once, but twice during a long train journey and that's something. 
 Also, my internal "reading voice" for this book isn't the usual one, but a very specific one from the past. I recall the time when I listened to the old audiobook version of Neal Stephenson's "Snow Crash", narrated by the excruciatingly boring voice of Robert McIntyre. It's like hypnosis. A monotone voice reading me a flat-lined story with a repetitive usage of certain words is enough to sedate me flat out. 
 Oh, and speaking of repetitive usage of certain words...during my reading, I invented a little game. I started to write down what I supposed were Tao Lin's favourite words, since they had a tendency to show up on every other page. Here's the list so far: 
 1. Words that end with -y. Even if they shouldn't. 
 2. Vague, vaguely. 
 3. Grinning, grinned. 
 4. Seem, seemed, seeming, seemingly. 
 5. Any word that implies that someone didn't really do it, or that something wasn't really genuine but almost or mimicking the Real Thing. You know, what we today like to end with -ish, but Tao Lin likes to end with -y, or describe (oh, the shitload of descriptions) as -looking. 
 The only unfortunate outcome this little game of mine might have, is that it might transform my reading experience from a pleasantly sedative to an enraging one. In that case, I will have to abort my mission and cure myself with some other book. 
 ............ 
 Now that I've finished it, I have another list of stuff I'd like to happen in this book. But first, a little plot background: 
 It is a thinly veiled biography of the author (called Paul here) and his 20-something hipster junkie friends who are just as privileged and bored as he is. They pass their time walking aimlessly around town, ingesting a shitload of drugs or eating fine dine or healthy meals which the reader has to wade through excruciatingly boring accountances of. Nothing much else happens. An accidental Las Vegas wedding and a trip to Taipei, sure, but it is wasted on these whiny dopeheads. 
 Now, what I wanted to happen, but never happened (possible spoiler alert) was: 
 1. Paul or anyone of his equally pretentious good-for-nothing friends get into a drug shootout. Or get paid a visit from some angry dealer who's been packing heat. The car scene with 'Peanut', WTF? 
 2. Anyone gets found with his or her face buried into the toilet with their pants down? No, no, nothing of the really ugly drugginess is featured (except Paul vomiting a lot.) 
 3. Someone tries to get sober. Naaah. Life is too boring for that for a 20-y (as Tao Lin would have put it) physically and materially content junkie. Oh, let's do some shitty movies instead, tralala... 
 4. Someone (preferably EVERYONE) loses their money, MacBooks, iPhones or fucking anything they are as addicted to as the MDMA they're constantly ingesting. That would have caused a refreshing buzz. But no. No...they are like bored, sugar high kids with way too many possibilities at hand. I wanted to see some starvation. Sure, the depression Paul and Erin are trying to Xanax themselves out of is present, but that does not explain some of the horribly stupid things they do. 
 5. Tao Lin finds another descriptive word for 'vague', 'grinning' or 'seeming.' FFS, MR LIN, YOU'RE AN AUTHOR! It is your fucking JOB to INCREASE your readers' vocabulary, not place it in a roundabout!

I'm about 50 pages from the end, and I really don't care for this book. It's like trickle-down Brett Easton Ellis, and I already am not a fan of that style (the attempted-depth-of-shallowness), so ... yeah. That, on top of the author's continued use of things like 'six to eight strangers' at a bar or 'between five and forty minutes,' his overuse of the term 'vague' (twice on a single page! ugh), and other irritating minutiae of diction/syntax, I just want to finish the book and be done with it (I had nothing else with me to read on the plane, otherwise I doubt I would've gotten this far in to begin with). Oh god it gets worse - I must've seen 7 'earnestly' in the span of a couple pages. Seriously? Just. Use. A. Thesaurus. 
 So, this is definitely one of the worst books I have ever read. I struggle to find something positive ... I guess the author can spell correctly, and most of his sentences are grammatical. That's about it. The dialogue is realistic, but it's dialogue that does a) nothing to advance the 'plot,' b) doesn't lend any insight into characters (beyond repeatedly ramming home their shallow self-centeredness and inability to cope with the bare fact of existence). 
 Riveting stuff. You can write about shitty characters and *still make it interesting for the reader.* Reading this book is like reading a book about 3-year-old babbling - it may be well-executed, but as a novel it adds nothing to my understanding of the world/other people unless the author makes more of an effort than his listless characters to write it well and meaningfully. 
 In summary, 'I read the book in 7-10 days, more or less not enjoying it, but earnestly wanting to feel like I was wanting to enjoy the vapidity of its exposition. I must've toked four to eight times, various things, while vaguely gazing neutrally at the blank, mildly-expectant face of someone near me with whom I may or may not be romantically interested in a vague way. I worried that I might be depressed but can't really decide if I am, even after explicitly discussing it with others in a roundabout fashion.'

Sorry, I can't finish it. I had it on my device for a month and would dip in and out, hoping it would start capturing me, and did make it halfway through before abandoning it. I really wanted to like it the way the Publishers Weekly reviewer did, but I found it self-indulgent and far too specific/repetitive about drug dosages to be halfway interesting. After one chapter, the routine of new city + drugs + new girl to sleep with + new book reading with warning e-mails from publisher and/or parent just wasn't interesting anymore. Someone really interested in casual drug use and ennui would probably devour it. I'll keep clinging tightly to the belief that there is more to life.

"On the plane... Paul thought of Taipei as a fifth season, or 'otherworld' outside, or in equal contrast with, his increasingly familiar and self-consciously repetitive life in America, where it seemed like the seasons... formed a square, sarcastically framing nothing...." 
 And there you have it: we knew this restive, underachieving art scene was lurking in the hip coffee shops of Manhattan, and now we have a tortured first hand account. And like this book, it is repetitive, and boring, and empty. Paul goes to parties. Paul takes pills. Paul writes books and promotes them. On drugs. Paul rationalizes his drug activity in terse emails to his mother, chiding her to ask questions about the drug experience rather than to judge him. Paul marries a girl who can't say no. (At least she's from Baltimore. But GIRLS FROM BALTIMORE PLEASE KNOW I EXPECT MORE FROM YOU!) They never once say "I love you." Paul can't say no, either, which is why I was hoping to turn that last page to an overdose. Nope. Instead, Paul's final words in this book are of gratitude, which might be a welcome death in itself -- a death of one sad selfish era of his life. Who knows. 
 All my churlishness aside, there are some things this author did very well. His characters record the tiny movements of emotion from minute to minute -- the gestures, mumbles, eye contact that shape the course of relationships. His characters use technology the way we know other people use technology (Me? No, no, not me!) -- as a new reality where people go to resolve their conflict and record their existence. His characters use anti-anxiety drugs and MDMA to simultaneously enable erratic performances that will blow up on social media and dull the throb of disapproval from parents, industry, readers, anyone else. Obviously, you can add me to that list. 
 Finally, quite ingeniously, this author has created a story in which I am as unattached to his characters as they are to... well... anything. Their Macbooks notwithstanding.

Navel gazing tosh of the highest order. Tao Lin is celebrated as the crowned prune of Alt-Lit. I think I'll stick to Good-Lit in future. However, if the following quotes don't cause you to cringe in horror, then this kind of claptrap might be right up your street: 
 "Paul followed a slow-moving Laura through a long, dark, almost boomerang shaped hallway, which felt briefly room-like, as they lingered in it, or like it wanted to be a room, with furniture and guests, but was maybe too shy and too afraid of causing disappointment, so impaired itself with two conspicuous openings to conventionally shaped rooms, a sort of recommendation against itself." 
 When a hallway is invested with more character than the actual characters, you know you're in a whole, steaming heap of trouble. Furthermore, the non-existent plot and page-by-page tedium make for a dry salad of a novel, albeit devoid any nutritional value. B-O-R-I-N-G.

book_b.title: The Pillars of the Earth (Kingsbridge, #1)
book_b.user_review: My first and last Ken Follet book. I came away marveling at the utter mundanity of it all: boring, repetitive, connect the dots plot development, grade school characterization and unimaginative writing, all adding up to a complete slog. Looking back, I'm surprised at this disappointing Oprah Book Club selection. While I've only read a small handful of her choices, I'm aware of many of her more recent recommendations. On the heels of books like Love in the Time of Cholera, The Road, Anna Karenina, I simply wasn't prepared for something so weakly imagined and executed. I'm giving it 2 stars, if only because I finished it, even though I can't really say what compelled me to the end other than the fact that I hastened toward it and began skimming pages as I approached the predictable conclusion. Stay away from this one unless you've heavy interest in historical fiction, medieval architecture, and display profound tolerance for bad, boring writing. You'd think a writer with this level of success would stay away from so many adverbs. Seriously!

sample_reviews.review_text:
What an epic book. While I loved the characters and the way all of their stories intermingled, I was underwhelmed by the story itself. I felt like it continued on a level field with tiny hills of excitement. I found myself 3/4 of the way through the book and wondering if there would ever be a climax. 
 Strangely, if I stopped the book for a few days, I missed the characters; but the second I picked it back up, I would think about how bored I was. I think Pillars is one of those books that is better in memory than it was during the actual story. 
 I gave this book 3 stars, but would prefer to do 2.5. I'm not quite sure why this is deemed the best book of time.

The unrelenting mindless smashing of women and their spirits just wore me out. Yes yes medieval times, I get it I get it. But this book does not leave me with a heroic soaring sense of the masterful creation of gothic cathedrals, it leaves me spitting mud out of my mouth. Wore. Me. Out.

Well despite the fact the book is super long and it took me 2 months to complete, it was well worth it! I really liked it! It kept my attention almost the entire time. There characters were so well developed and the book so well written I felt like I knew the people and was right there with them. My heart raced at times and I found myself smiling also. Towards the end I did start to get a little confused with the story but the small details didn't take away from the main story line that ended just about how I would have liked! Worth the time!

Posle bredovogo poiska rebionka po lesu i posledovavshei stseny "zharkogo" seksa v lesu, a takzhe iz-za muchitel'no topornogo iazyka i sloga avtora ia poniala, chto moio otnoshenie k knige okonchatel'no stalo negativnym, a, znachit, ot chteniia ia ne poluchu udovol'stviia. Muchit' sebia eshchio 1000 stranits -- durakov malo.

Anachronistically strong female characters. The male charcters are are all evil, useless/bumbling, pathetically impotent due their faith, or accomplished only insofar as they have been supported by a woman. That's probably why this appeals so widely, reaching even the "Oprah's Picks" types.

I kinda hated this book. Ludicrous plot lines dependent on both ridiculously melodramatic behaviour and startling coincidences. I read historical fiction in part because it offers a entertaining way to learn more about the past, but the detail was actually pretty scant. And the main female character was rarely mentioned without an explanation as the current state of her boobs (firm or dropping, swaying, bouncing or restricted. Yes really). Which was at least pretty funny, albeit unintentionally so.

This is one of the most amazing books that I have ever read. A friend loaned me his book, back in the early 90's, because he said I just had to read it. It was the hardback and I said okay. I was a bit nervous to take it on because it was over 1,000 pages. When I was done.....I simply could not give the book back. I loved it so much it was like giving up a child...giggle. My friend told me I could keep the book because I obviously loved it more than he did. It became a treasure to me. I read it again a few years later and I was still wrapped up in it's magic. What an incredible story of love....travel....architecture....witchery....prince and princesses....evil....and the building of cathedrals. Everyone needs a story like this at least once in their lifetime!!! I have this book on my TOP TEN LIST of books that I have read. I am very selective about the books that go on there and this one simply had to be on it!!!

Okay. First off, I am a picky reader. Secondly, I'd seen the miniseries first, and liked it, but I knew in advance many of the major events, so I wasn't dying of suspense. I think that's why it took me like 4 months to read it- I kept switching to other books. 
 Gets a star: Follett can describe and not make me yawn! 
 Minus a star: He writes stuff like "Aliena was anxious" even though it's apparent that she's anxious because we have seen her in similar circumstances many times over hundreds of pages and she was anxious then. Follett does something like this at least as often as every other page and I couldn't bear it at times. 
 Gets a star: Thumbs up to the medieval history provided about the common people- it was interesting learning about the processes to build cathedrals and turning wool into cloth. That sort of thing is taken for granted in most historical fiction. 
 Minus a star: The ending seemed rushed to me- despite that this book is nearly 1000 pages long and it took me ages to finish. 
 Gets a star: It's a good story from multiple points of view of people who are at odds with one another. That's not easy to do. Every time he switched to another character's point of view, I was sorry, but half a page later I was engrossed. 
 This is the first Ken Follett book I've read, but I'm not sure it is the last. I hear his thrillers are very good and I'd like to give one of them a try.

Epic in length & scope, bits of diaglogue & characterization were somewhat unconvincing, and I wouldn't say that Follett is a literary master. However, this was an entertaining, fairly well-researched read that I was able to escape into this fall while touring some European cathedrals built around the time the story takes place and through this long winter. I enjoyed it enough that I am about to embark on the next part of the story in "World Without End." Recommend this novel for those interested in the Middle Ages, Architecture, or who enjoy historical fiction.
GREAT book. I actually bought a copy just to lend to friends. It's THAT good.

reference_books.title: Reading Lolita in Tehran
reference_books.review_text: To be fair, my rating is not based on reading the entire book. Its' based on my attempting to read the book twice on two separate occasions and utterly failing to get engaged enough to get more than a few chapters in. Not that the memoir doesn't have potential: but the author is windy, spending forever setting the scene and being nostalgic before the reader has developed enough interest to understand the nostalgia.

reference_books.title: Shantaram
reference_books.review_text:
About 1/3 through this book I want to shake up the author/narrator so badly that I think I have to stop reading. Perfect characters in fantasy autobiographies are tedious in fiction, but pathetic in faux-non-fiction. 
 The narrator has made mistakes before, but most occurred before page one. He committed crimes. He landed in jail. But then he executed a perfect, daring escape to India where he fell in love with the perfect woman, fell in with friends who enjoy conversations of pseudo-philosophical crap, and knows just how to react to every situation so it turns out to his advantage. The few times he screws up it's something small and forgivable, like getting drunk with a friend, and serves to advance the plot, by getting him robbed so he has to move to the slums, become a "doctor" somehow, armed only with a first aid kit, and fall in the good graces of a mafia boss. Yep, he's got a charmed life. 
 For all that, he wallows in being haunted by the past he left behind and can never return to, which he mentions once. Or twice. Every few pages. You're supposed to feel sorry because he broke out of prison, poor soul, which he got into via armed robbery, oh the victim he is. 
 He is respectful. Always sees the good in everyone and everything. Always knows what to say or do in every situation. Which is good because the entire freakin' India revolves around him. Heck, you can't run a Mafia in Bombay without thinking that Lin is the son you never had. 
 Basically, if you met this guy you'd want to punch him in the face, except of course you wouldn't cuz you'd see the deep pain in his heart, be charmed by his deep regard for you, and become deep friends while having deep conversations because that is just how every chapter in this book seems to go. 
 At first I enjoyed, at least, the descriptions of India. Because what American doesn't love to read about third-world people who are te victims of circumstances or participants in colorful, "exotic" cultures? But I'm done with this. Otherwise I might throttle my iPod.

reference_books.title: Amazonia
reference_books.review_text: I did not realize this was going to be a cheap thriller.

reference_books.title: Saving Francesca
reference_books.review_text: It was a somewhat predictable teen angst tale, and I thought the jump from "Jimmy is the grossest person in the world" to "Jimmy is coming home for dinner" was a bit abrupt (it took about 1 page). But, for all that, it was an entertaining read.

reference_books.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo (Millennium, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
YAWN! 
 I tried listening to this book during my morning commute, but my mind kept wandering. 
 Part of it is the sheer quantity of extraneous detail provided. Do we really need a list of items Blomkvist unpacks, followed by his decision to go for a walk, then his hunt for a key, then the coffee shop he found, that he was the only person there, that he sat sipping coffee and reading a novel described as an important feminist voice, and his eventually putting it down because he didn't get the point of it? 
 Not only does this not advance the plot, but it doesn't advance his character much. WHY IS IT THERE?! And it goes on and on in this vein. 
 Part of the trouble may also be that I knew what happened to Harriet. Given that, it all looked rather obvious. Actually, it looked kind of obvious anyway. The flowers give it away. 
 Anyway, shortly after Blomkvist crawled into bed with one of the myriad Vangers, and shortly after Lisbeth's first incident with her guardian, I switched to a lecture series on medieval Jewish history. It kept my attention far better.

book_a.title: American Rust
book_a.user_review:
An attempt at a Steinbeck-esque capture of rust-belt despair. The author creates a world in which there are no options, and how that drives people to drive their lives into the ground. 
 I had trouble caring about many of the characters. Maybe it was their incredible passivity. The only times they take action is in order to do something incredibly stupid. Although I did at least care about them then. That's what made Isaac and Billy's narratives somewhat compelling. Everyone else was "meh." 
 To contrast, the Okies in "Grapes of Wrath" are forever *trying* to improve their lives and getting smacked down. In "American Rust" nobody tries. They give up before page 1, and then spend the entire novel justifying themselves. Then they all make grand gestures that are too little too late, and the last page leaves off with you knowing they're all going to sink right back into their same old malaise. 
 Toward the end I was skimming chapters. That's why I'm giving it two stars instead of three.

sample_reviews.review_text: you'd think i would be more into a book all about how much pennsylvania sucks. maybe i have just been hardened against sympathizing against people who make stupid mistakes.

The author seems to have no understanding of the use of a comma making for rather jumbled writing. His editor, if there was one seems to have allowed him to get away with it. 
 Any community that lost 150,000 jobs would undergo great trauma and rapid decline. The lads in this novel are a product of that social upheaval. 
 The point of view shifts between Isaac English, William Poe, Poe's mother Grace, Isaac's sister Lee, and police chief Bud Harris. 
 An ominous sense of doom hangs over the story as each player falls victim to a fate they seem powerless to escape. The reader learns not to expect happy endings. 
 The entrepreneurs who own industries make sure they are looked after when they walk away from failing enterprises but their hourly paid employees pay the price for their cushy lifestyles. The entire community pays the price.
Rather pointless.

This is a high 3, btw. And I still consider it one of the better books of 2000+. Meyer's prose is smooth, and the manner in which he deals with SoC is perfect, and melds right into the prose. I read this entire thing in one night. The tension drips off the pages. It is a thrilling read (actually cared more for the prison scenario than Poe's). But I was looking for more (having read the reviews) and expecting something on the matter of the rust belt. It's there, of course, in the background and occasional snippets. But IMHO it was skipped over... That's a very idiosyncratic thing, and you should take that into account. I'm of the thought that most anyone who likes dramas will like this book. 
 That being said, there is great talent at work here, and I look forward to his next book and will buy it as soon as possible. I suggest the same for others.

I do not understand why "good literature" is, nowadays, synonymous with "poor grammar." The run-on sentences in this book gave me a headache. It was not written in close enough third person to warrant the bad grammar, especially since the Yale graduate in the novel was also written with poor grammar. 
 The summary of this book is: 
 Chapter 1: Characters expose their inner angst. 
 Chapter 2: Someone murders someone else. 
 Chapters 3-End: Characters expose their inner angst. 
 Seriously. NOTHING ELSE HAPPENS. If you cut out three-quarters of the rambling inner angst in this book, you'd have a short story. And it would have been better that way.

The story, picking up as I got into it, was truly "Steinbeckian" in nature. Meyer painted the scenes well thruout the book...dark, depressing, empty, fearful, lonely. 
 Two quotes really hit me: 
 p. 297 "He wasn't sure of the direction but he followed the flowing water. That was easy, he thought. You knew you needed that coat, didn't have to think about it. Allow things to happen and they work out fine. Overthink, get self-conscious, that's when your mistakes happen.. . ." (How true--when we have choices, it can be a challenge to select "what's right." Sometimes, it's liberating to simply be given the direction to go.) 
 p. 333 (refer back to 332) "There's no mystery for your generation. . . ." (How many times I have thought this for our grown children and my students. No surprises left to discover...nothing to "grow into." It all feels so rushed. Makeup, dating, formals, cars...so much comes so easy for too many, today.) 
 AK, thank for the loan! I'll keep it safe for you.
good story, but the stream of consciousness, run on style writing was really distracting for me. I never really invested in any of the characters beyond a detached curiosity.

Read this book with my book group and folks were on opposite sides of the fence on this one -- some having a strong dislike. It took me time to get into the narrative and begin to relate to the characters. Interestingly, many of the discussion questions below center on character development and viewpoint. In the end, I liked the book and the characters have stayed with me. 
 Discussion questions: 
 In what ways does seeing the novel through the eyes of six different characters change the experience of the book? How would the book be different if seen from only one point of view? Which characters would be more or less likeable if the reader could see them omnisciently? Do you think Meyer was trying to make a broader point by writing this way? 
 I think Meyer's point in writing the novel this way was to show how often random acts between two people can have a lasting and sometimes devastating ripple effect. In that sense, I thought he did a very good job of threading these acts (and their consequences)through the story. The book certainly would have changed dramatically if only seen through the eyes of one character and it would be an interesting question for the author, which character he would choose. While I struggled in the beginning with this, I'm glad he offered the different perspectives in the end. 
 Does your opinion of various characters change throughout the book? How and why? Isaac, Poe, Lee, Grace, and Harris are all faced with important decisions that will affect not only their own lives, but also the lives of their loved ones. Whose choice was hardest to make? 
 Yes, my opinion of some of the characters changed throughout the course of the book -- some negatively -- particularly Harris and Grace. Poe and Harris were faced with the greatest challenges and those that were the hardest to make. In choosing to compromise his morals for Grace, Harris in the end is ruined. The consequences of Poe's decision to not to be truthful about Isaac's role in the murder put him in great physical danger. 
 Which characters behaved in the most unexpected ways? 
 I was the most surprised bu Harris's actions as the novel ran its course and maybe the most disappointed. In the end, I have to say I was more annoyed at the way the Isaac and Lee characters were developed. 
 When the book begins, Poe, despite his athleticism, considers himself a coward. Do you agree with his as- sessment? Has it changed by the time the book ends? 
 I liked Poe's character and thought Meyer did a great job at showing how a persons insecurities influence behavior. Poe's athleticism gets him into more trouble than he can handle and distracted him throughout his life into actions and choices that were damaging. His perceived strength was actually his greatest weakness. 
 Harris, by most conventional measures, is a "good" man at the book's beginning. Has he changed by the book's end? Is he still good? Would society agree with you? 
 He most certainly has changed by the end of the book. I think Harris is a good man who makes some bad choices and yes, society generally disfavors a man who commits murder -- particularly when you are in a position of upholding the law. Harris is a perfect example of how a toxic relationship can lead to peril. 
 Lee says in her own words at the beginning of the novel, that she abandoned her family to save herself. Do you agree with this self-assessment? Does your opinion of her change as the story unfolds? What would you do in her shoes? How much responsibility does Grace have for Harris's actions near the end of the book? Does she have moral responsibility? Are her actions more or less pure than Harris's? What would you have done in her or Harris's position? Is Grace still a good person? 
 I saw Lee as a pretty selfish individual from beginning to end. In many ways, I think her character was the least developed and I never really related to her or understood her presence in the novel. I think Meyer's point with Lee was to show that because a person is well educated or well-off doesn't give you adequate survival skills or make you a better person. Grace is also a fairly weak and selfishly motivated character who used her influence to cause Harris's falling. 
 I'm glad I read the book and look forward to Meyer's next work.

I just wrote a review about 10 seconds ago were I was disappointed and I felt like the story moved really slowly....then I read this book and everything just took off running and never stopped! I thought it was great. First of all, I am a huge nerd and loved every aspect of the networked world it was set in, plus the way these guys interacted with each other was just hilarious. It didn't take itself too seriously but at the same time I thought it was a really running editorial on issues that are currently in the news all the time. 
 It made it's point in a funny and engaging way and that's why I enjoyed it. I think I did want a little more from the characters in terms of back ground and morals and other things but overall I think it really shines as a book I've never heard before telling a great story so I'd recommend giving it a look and maybe you'll be surprised at what you find.

Hmm. I admire this author as a person, and I agree with his message, yet I grew bored reading this book. The main character starts out as cocksure and remains that way, despite torture by a disappointingly typical sadistic female-in-power character. A good book makes me believe what's happening in the story. I just didn't believe it. 
 Why would the entire Homeland Security Department want to torture innocent teenagers? Surely there is some inherent flaw in the government's approach that leads to massive corruption. But no. These were apparently bad guys just for the sake of being bad guys. They let an evil sadist go wild because, apparently, that's just how they roll. I got halfway through the book, waiting for some hint of insight, but there was none; just a lot of ranting from the main characters about "F the police." That's not good enough for me. 
 The main character won't tell his sympathetic and loving parents that he was a victim of criminal torture, but he'll tell 500+ strangers. Why? Because "Don't trust anyone over 25!" 
 Uh huh. That's not a character I can care about. After a while, he just seemed stupid. The premise of this book has a ton of potential, but I didn't like how it was handled.

Marcus Yallow and three of his chums are innocently playing Harajuku Fun Madness in the streets of San Francisco when terrorists blow up the Bay Bridge. Homeland Security, which can't tell the difference between kids on a heroic scavenger hunt and terrorists, picks them up. Some days later, they release Marcus and two of his friends, telling them if they ever tell anyone, what happened, they will disappear. Meanwhile, a police state is imposed by the feds on San Francisco. Marcus strikes back against the empire. The empire strikes back. Awesomeness ensues. 
 The characters sometimes faded into mouthpieces for various political perspectives. That was intrusive sometimes, but hey, that might have been an homage to 1984 right there. But unlike 1984, near the end, I couldn't put it down. Plus, I'm always up for Karl Rove being the real villain of the piece.

Listened to the audiobook for this one. I liked the guy's voice--actually liked it more than what he was saying cause often I would zone out and just listen to the pitch of his voice. So I technically didn't finish this book, meaning my review is pretty unreliable... I hope one day I'll give this book another try and pay attention. But I didn't like all the stuff I actually listened to; it seemed like things were mentioned when it was a little too convenient. I mean, I know that whole "don't mention the red jacket unless it adds to plot" thing, but it felt too deus ex machina. The author gets away with it because the story takes place in a technological world, so of course why not have super-computers and amazing hacker friends to solve your problems? Anyway, like I said, I think I need to give this book another try.

I read this after seeing the theatrical adaptation in Chicago this past summer. Doctorow's vision of techno-rebellion in the face of increased surveillance/"security" certainly resonates (just last week we had yet another attempted bomber on a plane) but... there's part of me that vividly remembers what happened on Sept. 11 and is not convinced that we have gone too far in our methods. Sure, some are stupid and some are just ill-planned (really? a color-coded alert system??) but we do have an enemy with whom there is no middle ground for bargaining. 
 His love of technology led to several passages I just had to tune out (how one sends a tunnel in or through DNS, for example) but the rest of the story sounds relatively plausible, particularly the bits about the rest of the country not caring about SF and the gradually creeping increased measures. One would like to think that we couldn't get to that point here, but it's a definite possibility. When he went off on a tirade, as with the conversion of a "real" neighborhood to create City Center, again: tune out time.

I can't believe I waited so long to read this book! It was amazing! I've been giving it to select students for years, but clearly didn't know how great it is. Watch out students; I'm going to tell all of you about this book. I'll give it to gamers, programmers, hackers, rebels, slackers, and thinkers. It's a really scary near future scenario where everyone is surveilled by the uncontrolled Department of Homeland Security and everyone's rights are denied in order to catch "terrorists." Readers of all ages will go through a roller coaster of emotions. Fear, amusement, disgust, empowerment, excitement, despair, and hope. Technology enables new methods of terrorism, but also new ways to be activists and teens really can change the world.
YA novel that engages readers in timely controversy of freedom and safety in a world in which surveillance is an issue.

sample_reviews.review_text: As a huge fan of 18th century British Literature, this book never fails to give me a few chuckles. Swift satirizes the British and their habits so well; he was a master.

Swift is such a snarky cynic. Honestly, it's no wonder from what I read about his life that he was so miserable and everyone hated him. He really was one of the least likable authors of his time. I only had to read half of this as a school assignment and thankfully I was not expected to finish it because the entire thing is absolutely ludicrous. I love fantasy and imaginative books, but this entire story was just so bizarre it makes me wonder about Swift's sanity. Surely all that isolation was not good for him?! I also read his famous essay "A Modest Proposal" as well and found this much better despite the disturbing questions it raises about the cheapness of human life. Here his cynicism actually works for him instead of against him, but honestly Swift will always leave a bad taste in my mouth. What can I say? I am a romantic at heart and Swift's stark view of the world doesn't jive with me.

To be discussed by the Powells Beaverton SF group on Tues Sept 10th at 7pm. I had not read this before and I do not expect to read it again. I did find it interesting and there was certainly more to it than I was aware - in that I knew about out Lilliputia and Brobdingnagia and little-endian versus big-endian but nothing about the speaking horse people (the Houyhnhnm). I thought of Laputa as coming from Myazaki's Castle in the Sky and yahoos from yahoo.com. It was well written but tedious in the extreme to read. Yes I know it is supposed to be satire, but without the footnotes I'd never have realized to what level the author reached - and even with them it was hard to care.

This book, along with Robinson Crusoe and The Scarlet Letter, forms an unholy trinity of the driest, dullest classics I've ever read. I'm not intimately familiar with the British political system in the 18th Century - hell, I'm not even vaguely familiar with it - nor do I particularly care to be, so obviously the satire went flying right over my head. But even with that in mind, the book could still have been entertaining. It just wasn't. There was way too much measuring, way too much minutiae, and for someone who constantly used the phrase "I will not trouble the reader with" ... you troubled me with a lot of shit. 
 I'm thrilled to have finally finished this, after starting it three weeks shy of a year ago. I almost cried tears of pure joy when, thinking I had another twenty pages to go, I turned the e-page to find a biography of Swift. My pain had ended. Halle-fucking-lujah!

This could have been good, but it was just boring. Swift got very technical in things that didn't add to the satire, story, or environment and did not aid in the pretense that this was a travel book. Swift made his points about larger themes by attacking people and smaller groups without really distinguishing between those who perpetuated and those who suffered from negative attributes of society. I would much rather read a story about things that happen instead of the narrator starting long conversations with almost everyone and everything. Even in the more active parts the writing is passive and dull.
I loved Gulliver's Travels and the different chapters. This was a very good read.
I thought I'd never finish! Tedious, boring and not funny at all.

This book was dry. Like a saltine left in the sahara desert in july. It was detailed, I'll give it that, but the utter lack of plot and how blatantly manufactured it was just aaaaaaagggh. "and then I got shipwrecked again and it was a different place! Oh my gosh! But it's okay I learned the language" 
 I spent so much of my life reading this book, I can't spend one more second reviewing it. It's dry. And boring as heck. And only a little bit stimulating to the imagination. That's all. Someone breathe some life into this concept and it'll be worth something. But this is only valuable because of it's existence as an early novel. 
 P.S. Read as an assignment for British Literature 1, Freshman Year. 
 The most entertaining thing that came from this is linking the houmnhyims to My Little Pony. the primest of humor.

Wendy Everly n'a pas eu une enfance de tout repos. Lors de sa fete de six ans, sa mere a essaye l'a poignarde en tentant de la tuer. Sa mere l'a toujours detestee car elle etait convaincue que Wendy n'etait pas sa fille. La mere de Wendy a ete internee et suite a ca, Wendy a ete elevee par son grand frere protecteur et sa tante. Ils ont du se promener d'ecoles en ecoles car Wendy avait du mal a s'adapter. En fait, elle n'a jamais senti qu'elle etait a sa place nulle part. 
 Suite a une rencontre avec un garcon seduisant et intrigant de l'ecole (Finn), une serie d'evenements l'amene a decouvrir la verite sur elle-meme. Finn lui apprend qu'elle est une enfant substituee, qu'elle a ete echangee a la naissance. Voila qui expliquait le comportement de sa mere (fausse mere). Il lui mentionne qu'elle est en danger et qu'il est temps pour elle de retourner vers sa vraie famille. Wendy finit par accepter. Elle croyait se rendre vers un lieu plus merveilleux ou elle sera aime a sa juste valeur. 
 Elle dechante assez rapidement lorsqu'elle arrive dans cette ville mysterieuse. Elle apprend qu'elle a de grosses responsabilites qui l'attendent. Elle a beaucoup de difficultes a obtenir des reponses claires a toutes ses questions. Elle devra tenter de faire sa place dans ce nouveau monde. Elle peut compter sur Finn qui veille sur elle et sur Rhys, un garcon de son age qui devient un bon ami. Arrivera-t-elle a se faire a ce nouveau monde? Que vont penser son grand frere Mark et sa tante qui l'aiment du fait qu'elle les a abandonne? 
 Mon avis : 
 J'etais assez emballee par cette lecture au debut du livre. L'aventure s'annoncait palpitante du moins, elle en avait le potentiel. J'ai cependant ete un peu decu au cours de ma lecture. J'ai trouve qu'il y avait des longueurs a certains endroits et j'aurais prefere plus d'actions. L'histoire est tout de meme bonne et je lirai surement le tome 2 a un moment donne. Je suis curieuse de savoir ce qui va se passer ensuite. 
 Petit point negatif, le livre est ete drolement traduit. On retrouve des verbes conjugues au Subjonctif Imparfait. Voici ce que ca donne : "Il m'avait explique qu'il fallait que je me preparasse en un eclair et que je me tinsse bien toute la journee." Ouchh, jamais un auteur ecrit a ce temps de verbe et c'est tres derangeant comme lecture. Heureusement, ce n'est pas continuellement comme ca mais bon, j'eviterais a tout prix a l'avenir.

It is not often that I give half stars but in this case I will, I enjoyed Switched very much and read it very quickly, however I was not in love with it. The premise of the story is that a girl realizes that she was switched at birth and learns where she belongs is not where she thought. This is an older book, but I still don't want to give too much away - I thought going into this book it was going to be about Fairies.... it was note, I was pleasantly surprised though by how the author played the switch and the cast of characters. 
 The plot climax seemed a little rushed at the end of the book, but my real concerns were about Wendy, the main character. I feel like as she was learning who she was and how to live in this new 'world' she didn't ask enough questions, nor did she ask the questions that I think that she should have. I found it a little frustrating to read when I wanted answersto questions she was late to ask or didn't ask. 
 I think that this first book did have some good world building and I think if given the opportunity I would read the next installment but not right now...I liked the book but I was also more frustrated than pleased as I read most of it. The ending saved it from getting a lower rating, there is some romance and obviously, like I mentioned the real action happens then as well.
Not very well written but for some reason I liked it anyway. A quick read.

meh. I don't want to finish this. It started off with a bang and quickly withered into nothing special. Once I found out exactly what being "switched" was, I was bummed out. Holly Black did this exact concept way better. 
 I can predict everything that's going to happen. I'm annoyed that she would be falling for Finn when he keeps secrets, and has been a total jerk to her. I see where it's going and I don't want to take the journey.
I luuuuurve this book. I've read it within a day eheehe. The beginning was a lot like Hush, hush though. But it gets better and Better. I can't wait to read the next book.

Ahh, yes! Switched was, is highly delectable, delicious and devouring. Addictive, yes indeed! Amanda Hocking has ever so graciously introduced us to the story of Wendy who everyone will fall in love with. 
 How devastating for Wendy that as a child, her mother tried to kill her, seeing her as a wicked and evil creature. The woman was locked up, and Wendy and her brother Matt, who has always been there to protect her ever since the incident, went to live with their aunt and uncle. 
 Now, time has passed and Wendy still can't help but think about that day from time to time. She does feel different from other people. Just like her mother always told her. She wouldn't dare mention this to anyone else though. But then she starts to notice guy at school. His name? Finn. She catches him staring at her every once and a while. Once they finally talk and he finally opens up to her, and explains the different feeling she is having, he has reasons for it. He explains that she doesn't belong here. That she was raised for a purpose. His story that he tells her is exactly what she thinks it is-a story. But it isn't. Could her mother really be out there and have sent her off to live with strangers, a mother who tried to kill her? Was she really switched? Who is she really? As she learns who she is, and finds her true background, she also finds love, loss, and the hard laws that stop her from happiness.

This book is not as good as The Year of Living Biblically, but it's still a terrific read once it gets going. The story has a fascinating arrangement - each chapter covers one letter of the alphabet (except XYZ, which are lumped together), and the story is guided by alphabetical subheadings. A section with the title of an artist may lead to a snarky one-liner about the man's fetishes, while a section with the title of a mountain range yields a revealing meditation on a time that Jacobs was lost in that range (and the effect that the incident had on his relationship with his father). These longer musings, which are much more frequent near the end of the alphabet, make the book truly worthwhile, and Jacobs really seems to be baring his soul (as opposed to the difficult first sections, where he is only willing to bare his pop culture fluency and his most unusual trying-too-hard-for-attention personality quirks). 
 The basic story is interesting, as Jacobs embarks on a quest to read the entire Encyclopaedia Brittannica, but the quest is a self-centered one, and it is difficult to read the inconveniences suffered by Jacobs' wife and other family members when the reader knows that even Jacobs doesn't seem convinced that his pursuit has a worthwhile goal. As the book progresses, though, Jacobs matures as a storyteller and presents beautiful studies of intelligence and wisdom, along with honest struggles with infertility and with his larger-than-life father. By the end, this is a truly wonderful book, and I highly recommend it.

I expected more. I was one of those weird kids who actually read two different encyclopedias . Read one the summer after 5th grade and another in 7th grade. The 1st was the world book and I continued to read the update volumes until I went away to college. 
 I expected less personal anecdotes and more interesting knowledge.

This just never really clicked for me, but it improved about 3/4 of the way through. Maybe it's because I got use to the style, but I think it was because it became less facts from the encyclopedia and more of a story.

I've been looking forward to reading this book since I heard that A.J. Jacob's was going to do another one of his projects. (When it came out, I read his book The Know-it-All and enjoyed it a lot.) The Year of Living Biblically is just what it sounds like: Jacobs decided to follow the rules of the Bible as literally as he could. He read the Bible, and made a list of everything that was considered a rule. He also assembled a spiritual guidance team-rabbis, preachers, scholars-who could help answer any questions he might have... 
 Read the rest of my review at A Bookish Type.

An annoying book about reading the entire Encyclopedia Britannica that I was compelled to finish. Humour is subjective and I found Jacobs' nebbish, hypochondriac, regular Jewish guy persona to be pretty fake and forced (as well as pretty old, Woody Allen did it much better). (He's an Esquire editor, roomed with a Kennedy in college, goes on fab vacations, all while trying to portray himself as a bumbling oaf. If he had just fessed up to being an elitist with some intellectual pretensions I would have found the book way more enjoyable.) For human interest he shoe-horned in a rather pat telling of he and his wife trying to get pregnant. It is okay that Jacobs didn't really want to share his and his wife's private life, but it is painfully obvious he was being jokey to cover the real thing. 
 Yet I was compelled to finish the book. I loved how it was organized, going from Chapter A to Chapter XYZ. Jacobs comes up with interesting factoids. I wish he'd just relaxed and let himself appear a little more intellectually engaged. 
 If I'll take away anything from Jacobs' quest to read the Encyclopedia Britannica, it is this: Ebbinghaus. 
 ------------- 
 My counter-recommendation: 
 Vanishing Point by David Markson. Fiction that stretches the definition of fiction - composed of index card length bits, much of which are quotes or facts about writers and visual artists, the other part the slow deterioration of a mind. What a strange and delightful book. I think I first heard about it from the Time Best Books list, but didn't know much more about it than that. I'm so glad I walked into it blind, because each little twist and turn was exponentially more charming from the surprise. The French Lieutenant's Woman has tentatively vaulted on to my favorites list- it was tempting to flip right back to the beginning and start again after I finished. I'm going to spoiler the plot discussion because it is too difficult to discuss otherwise. 
 TFLW starts out as a typical Victorian novel, kind of in the vein of a Jane Austen or a Rebecca. I love this stuff so cool, but not totally anything new. All of a sudden, though, the narrator starts dropping these intriguing little hints that he's not writing from the point of view of a Victorian at all, with all these subtle mentions of computers or feminism. It's really well done, and introduces a sort of dizzying third wall to the story. (At this point I googled and found out the book was actually written in the 1960s). 
 Still, there's nothing entirely nonconventional about the narrative to this point. A Victorian gentleman is confronting the issues of being part of a decaying milieu in the time of the beginning of industry. He becomes engaged to the daughter of a scion of industry. At first all is love and (polite) roses, but he slowly realizes that she is a bit shallow and perhaps not all he could wish for in a life partner, although endowed with an attractive dowery. After a reversal in his own fortunes, he realizes marriage with her would involve a compromise in what he thinks the life of a gentleman should be. Cue the entrance of an intriguing "fallen" woman. 
 What happens now is really cool. Fowles zooms out from this very particular story told at a very particular moment in time and makes you realize that this choice point is meant to be much more universal than that, that at some point we all face a similar choice between ideals and realism, between being left behind and being part of the future. He sets up three alternate endings, one of which he just tells without telling you until afterward that it is only a possibility, and the other two semi-simultaneously. The narrator (=Fowles) enters and exits as a not entirely sympathetic character a few times. 
 What it made me think of most was the way that I sometimes play out certain scenarios for my own life to the end, how my own daydreams become the choices I make or don't make. I was so entirely intrigued by the way the endings were written. We see the characters from all angles, and at one moment I would hate Sarah and the next love her, at one point despise Charles and the next feel sorry for him. I can't describe exactly why, but the way he wrote the characters was just so fascinating. I couldn't look away. 
 TFLW definitely deserves its place on the list.

Steve Martin can string a sentence together, sure, but his characters are poorly developed and he relies on cliche catch phrases to get across his sentiments instead of writing complete thoughts. His characters are stereotypes, except he has a hard time sticking to one stereotype. The main character of this novel, for example, is a mishmash of conflicting attributes, including antisocial and outgoing, confident and insecure, and sexy and modest. She is everything a man would want in a woman and everything about her is unbelievable. His gender stereotypes make me want to gag. In one conversation, the characters discuss the terms of their relationship, except the narrator didn't bother telling us exactly what was said. So in this conversation, the female protagonist felt the boyfriend confessed his love to her and told her he wanted to spend the rest of his life with her and in this same conversation the male protagonist believed she understood it was just sex with no strings attached. How could such a misunderstanding happen between two non-mentally ill (i.e., non-erotomanic people)? We'll never know because we weren't privy to the conversation. Convenient. Lazy writing if you ask me. 
 If I weren't so supportive of the freedom of speech and the rights of individuals to choose what she or he reads, I would have burned this book to save someone else from reading it.

You know, I really don't mind foul language when it's used by a character in the story. But when the 3rd person narrator sinks to that level... I just don't think that it's necessary, and I think that it's the sign of a lazy writer who wants to go for the shock value. I may keep reading from that point (as I did in this case) but it really takes a lot of really good story telling to remove the lazy cloud from over the book. 
 Didn't happen in this case.

It took me a long time to plow through, mostly because it felt so fantastical I couldn't connect with any of the characters. The action started immediately with no build at all. 
 I also felt like there was way too much sex. The author certainly makes sex, inappropriate sex, sex for in, sex for love etc part of the story but I think I just felt it was relied on too much and at time gratuitous. Humans are sexual beings, sure, but it seemed to drive nearly everything in the storyline. I also didn't realize how much of the story was about sex, so maybe if I had known it wouldn't have been so jarring. 
 Basically, I think that it was just not a book for me, it was too long and I did not connect with the characters at all. If sad, tragic love/sex stories set in the Great Depression are more your thing it might me more for you.

It really wasn't the dark themes that got to men (even though I feel they could've been handled a little more subtle) but the writing style. It sort of felt really repetitive when it came to the similes in every single sentence. Really, there were a lot. And the dialogue felt rushed and just didn't have character. Sadly, only one star:(

This is the story of Rose and Pierrot who were left as babies at a Montreal orphanage during the depression. As they grew, they developed a close bond to each other and also began displaying great talents; Pierrot is a piano prodigy and Rose is a dancer and comedian. After years of traveling the city and performing in homes to earn donations to the orphanage, Rose and Pierrot are separated. Each leads very different lives through several years until they find each other again. Even though their lives are filled with poverty, being together renews childhood dreams and they take steps to make them come true. The Lonely Hearts Hotel follows Rose and Pierrot through the years of love, dreams, hardship, addiction and fame. The narrative is melancholy but lyrically magical filled with delightful descriptions of hotels, performers, good and bad characters and, most of all, the lives of Rose and Pierrot. The Lonely Hearts Hotel is comical, heartbreaking, haunting and overall wonderful. 
 I received an advance reading copy through Penguin's First To Read program in exchange for an honest review.

I'm not at all sure how I feel about this book. The main characters, Rose and Pierrot, meet as orphans in the same orphanage and immediately form a life lasting bond. They are different than the other children as Rose fancies herself a clown and Pierrot can play the piano like no other. Unfortunately, they are destined to grow up during the great depression in Montreal and face unbelievable hardships. I enjoyed most of this story. It did get a bit weird for me, a bit drawn out, I felt the story seemed to drag and lose its center. Some of the hardships the 2 face are tough to stomach. If I wasn't reading this for First 2 Read I might have stopped after 100 pages.

The synopsis for this book compares it to The Night Circus. Now The Night Circus is my all-time favorite book and I've been burned a few dozen times by other books making the same claim and falling way short. ONE DAY I WILL LEARN. The Lonely Hearts Hotel resembles The Night Circus (if you squint...in the dark) in that the protagonists are two orphans (one boy, one girl) who grow up to perform in a show and fall in love and the boy treats another girl badly in his love for Girl #1. That's it. Sum total of their similarities. While The Night Circus is beautiful and magical and lyrical, The Lonely Hearts Hotel is dismal and depressing and downright ugly. 
 I should've figured that out when a child is raped by her cousin on THE VERY FIRST PAGE OF THE BOOK. It only gets more depressing from there. This book needs every trigger warning ever: there's rape, child molestation, incest, child abuse/neglect, domestic abuse, verbal abuse, emotional abuse, physical abuse, victim blaming, slut shaming, drug abuse, animal cruelty, dog fighting, graphic descriptions of 3 miscarriages...I'm sure I'm forgetting some. 
 Now the prose is beautiful in places until the author's relentless need to beat you over the head with metaphors gets annoying. (It happens roughly 25% of the way through, by the way.) She can't go a paragraph without jamming a nonsensical metaphor into the prose. And for all the author's love for flowery, beautiful language, the constant use of terms like "cunt", "tits", "bush" and "fuck" is extra jarring. 
 And then there's our protagonist Rose. She's sweet but misused. All she wants to do is marry her childhood sweetheart and start a traveling show starring clowns. She finally does both, only to decide at the peak of her happiness that she also wants to be a Mafia boss and run heroin between Montreal and New York City. Not even joking. And she's willing to throw everything else in her life away for that. I get that it's largely revenge on her former kingpin lover but it comes out of nowhere and it's infuriating and absurd.

DNF at page 146. This book just did not work for me at all. Basically, it's just an ongoing string of sexual descriptions, sexual references, sexual fantasies, sexual violence, sexual obsession, etc., but not in a beautiful or even interesting way, all in a dark, dirty, guilt-ridden way. Nobody is even enjoying the sex without serious baggage. Everyone (and I mean EVERYONE) in this book is essentially unpleasant and a mess. The characters, to me, were like weird 2-dimensional illustrations - distant, removed, colorful - but only worth looking at briefly because they really just make you feel worse.

reference_books.review_text: HAHAHHAHAA I AM NOT OKAY! THIS WHOLE BOOK HAS TAKEN MY EMOTIONS AND TWISTED THEM UP AND I AM BROKEN! This book. What can I say other than that this book solidified why Victoria Schwab is one of my all time favorite authors? She manages to put so much into one book. There is action, adventure, discovery, character development, diversity, so much in her books. This is the second book in her Monsters of Verity duology, thus the end and I was so sad to reach the end. I was actually sobbing when I finished this book because the ending was that heartbreaking but that good. In every book she has a message and this one came through loud and clear so much that it gave me a lot of emotion. I loved it so much. I loved being back with August and Kate and seeing them grow and learn and develop as characters. I loved getting new characters including one who I believe is gender neutral meaning they don't identify as male or female. And it was fantastic. I can't say much without ruining the story or the ending but know that this duology is worth reading. It's worth all the pain, the emotions, the heartbreak because Victoria Schwab is a beautiful writer who crafts stories that are amazing.

reference_books.review_text: Wow is about all that I can say about this book. This book was simply fantastic and so refreshing to read. I have heard it compared to The Night Circus by Erin Morgenstern which I loved but this one is totally different from that book. This book blew me away. First off it's a debut novel and Stephanie Garber hit it right out of the park on this one! This book managed to capture the whimsy of Caraval and the danger of it all in one go. I loved all the characters in this and I was ALWAYS at the edge of my seat. I consistently wanted to know what would happen next and would gasp and scream at every twist and turn that happened in this book. Overall, if you want something fantastical and whimsical that will capture you and never let go I highly recommend this book. I also recommend when you buy this book to take the cover of it and look at the hardback as there are different pictures under the cover. reference_books.review_text: Rick Riordan is one of my favorite authors for a reason and this book added to that reason. First off, the diversity in this book is astounding. It's not just characters of different colors but different faiths, there is a gender fluid character and it's just amazing. Secondly, I laughed way, WAY too hard at the jokes about the show Cheers in this. I watched Fraiser first but I am currently watching Cheers on Netflix and I had to stop reading for a few minutes to laugh when they mentioned that the bar looked like Cheers because I could see it in my mind right away and I was losing it. And when they said the giant looked like Norm, I lost it. All joking aside, this book was fantastic. While the plot wasn't as crazy as the first book was, I still loved it because it held such an emotional impact in it. The ending of this book actually had me screaming because we are getting a character from Percy Jackson in the next book and I'm so freaking happy. Overall, I loved this book. It was such an interesting take on Norse mythology, I'm learning so much about Norse mythology because of it. Rick Riordan did a fantastic job with this book and I can't wait for the next one.

 I just...have so many questions, honestly. Like why are we supposed to find any of the characters sympathetic in this? I mean, the Academy students are split between Simon the author darling who can think no wrong, George who thinks it's not rape if you're sexy enough, and everyone else who thinks faeries are worthy of extinction because of a political move by one of the faerie queens (and remember, we know there are other courts who stayed out of this entirely). And considering the kind of teacher they have, this isn't likely to change. How am I supposed to root for the Shadowhunters, exactly? 
 And then halfway through the story just grows bored with itself and decides it's much more interesting to advance Simon and Isabelle's relationship. The entire date is a pain to get through, and it gets more and more obvious that Clare has no idea who Isabelle is as a person and has her act however she needs to create cheap tension. There's nothing Clare can do like she can create meaningless romantic pseudo-tension. I'm not even convinced that this is the last bump their relationship will experience. 
 Also, Helen Blackthorn is getting married. Yay? I don't know enough about her to care, and she and Aline are too young for this, in my humble opinion. But hey, whatever.

 Jesus fucking rollerblading Christ.

 We meet our female lead, Tatiana, the day the Nazi's invade Russia. Her family freaks the fuck out, like everyone else in the country does, and they immediately spring into action, sending their only son to "safety", other family members to get money out of the banks and their idiot youngest daughter, Tatiana, to go get food to stockpile.  IMAGINE FUCKING THAT. 
 Of course she starts to frantically run around the city in fucking high heels and a pretty dress because it was Sunday and she wanted to look nice. How dafuq you gonna carry that much food in ill-fitting heels, Tania? You think about that? No, no you fucking didn't. You were too preoccupied with looking pretty, you vapid little nitwit. 
 So, running around, running around. "I have to catch this bus to get to the next grocery store in time but OH, IS THAT ICE CREAM?" No. No you are NOT going to stop and eat fucking ice cream right now (<-this is my disbelief talking). But oh yes, yes she fucking is. Because she is a self-centered asshole. 
 It's while sitting on a bench and eating her ice cream, her beautiful long blonde hair flowing around her in the summer breeze, that she meets the second most self-centered asshole in the history of literature, Alexander Belov. Guess what? He's hot. He also saves her day by letting her into the officer's section of the grocery store so she can buy supplies to her heart's content. Then he and a buddy carry them all home for her because she can't because she's in fucking heels and has blisters. 
 IMAGINE FUCKING THAT. 
 And so begins the basis of their entire relationship. It can be summed up in one quote: 
 "She needs me so much to take care of her... And I desperately need to take care of her." 
 That's it. That's the entirety of this "love" story. It's nothing but Tatiana being a fucking TSTL little Mary Sue and Alex playing the fucking white knight to her damsel in distress. 
 I know what you're thinking. 
 Welp, sorry to break the news but 
 So Alex and Dimi, his rat of a friend, help Tania bring the supplies home and lo and behold what do we discover? That the handsome soldier our female lead has been lusting after is actually DATING HER SISTER. 
 Meet Dasha, the only decent person in the first two hundred pages of this book (that's as far as I got). Because Dasha is a good person she gets completely fucked over. Wanna know how??? Her boyfriend and sister proceed to fall in love behind her back. 
 Does Alex realize what's happening and do the right thing by breaking up with her? Hell no, he's a self-centered asshole, remember? He's also a fucking sadist because he parades his relationship with Dasha in front of Tatiana, who he secretly sees every fucking day. 
 Does Tatiana tell her sister what's going on? Hell no, she's a self-centered asshole, remember? She's also a fucking masochist because she continues to see Alex even with him dating her sister and acting like a monumental douche. 
 So that's it. Self-centered asshole sadist with a hero complex meets self-centered asshole masochist with princess syndrome. They fall in love and their theme song is FUCK EVERYONE ELSE. They'll probably dance to it at the wedding, wide smiles on their asshole faces as they fucking tango across the graves of those they sacrificed on the altar of their love. 
 This review can also be found at The Alliterates.

"Call it sentimentality. Call it curiosity. Just don't call it madness." 
 Her Dark Curiosity is the first book that failed to meet my expectations this 2014. Never, in my years of reading books that I encountered characters making stupid decisions, have I ever face-palmed myself so much (physically and mentally) than I ever did while reading Her Dark Curiosity. 
 When The Madman's Daughter debuted in 2013, I wasn't keen on reading it. But when I was urged to pick it up, it was perplexingly good. The grotesque and sinister plot combined with Megan Shepherd's enthralling writing style made for an incredibly interesting story, even though those visuals would've made me feel queasy under normal circumstances. So imagine my disappointment over reading Her Dark Curiosity and finding Juliet wallowing, making senseless and inconsistent decisions, and just going about freakishly aggravating! 
 WARNING: Spoilers are coming up! 
 The ending of The Madman's Daughter was upsetting that even I still haven't gotten over Montgomery's decision until now. Finding Juliet in a state of grief over his absence, I said, "Go on, and grieve, girl." But I really didn't need to see that ALL THE TIME! It was like every page I turn I'd get a whine here and a whine there. It just didn't end! Even after he got back... This just boarded over ridiculous! 
 I've mentioned over my review of The Madman's Daughter that I didn't really appreciate the love triangle between Juliet, Edward and Montgomery, and this book just happens to solidify that statement. Juliet was infuriating! I would have accepted it if she truly had fallen for Edward and that maybe this was her way of moving on after what Montgomery did, but no. This was her way of covering up her loneliness, throwing herself at Edward, leading him on a chase that he has no chance of winning her heart over, and blatantly making the BIGGEST mistake of her life. What makes it a lot more terrible is that it happened right after a fresh kill! Idiot, I tell you! 
 Oh, and don't get me started on her opinions about science. She has been voicing out how evil her father was for creating Edward, blah, blah, blah (I can't remember the words she said that infuriated me but it was excruciating to read) and more whining going on. I don't know if she is simply naive or just utterly stupid that even Lucy, her socialite best friend who knows nothing about the kind of morbid science these practitioners are conducting has to point out something she couldn't realize herself; something that seemed completely obvious in my opinion. 
 To make it even worse, with how Her Dark Curiosity ended, it is a given she's bound to do another idiotic thing in book 3.
