 The biggest negative was the narrator Nancy Travis. I have enjoyed her acting performances but she was not a good narrator. She rushed and didn't give the characters different intonations. She read everything the same except for one character towards the end. 
 Overall, I did enjoy the story and like how it all intertwined.

It was pure stubborness that got me through the first 100 pages of this book. I found it difficult to follow the jumps in character perspective, and I didn't care about the people who I would have tagged as the main characters. But the last 2/3 were really good. But, at the end, I found myself caring more aobut the "main" characters, who disappeared entirely. Not my favorite Alice Hoffman book, but a nice read.

book_b.title: Gilead (Gilead, #1)
book_b.user_review: I read this right after I finished Housekeeping, which I enjoyed more. Gilead's main character, John Ames, was less compelling for me, but I did enjoy the flow of his thoughts, the process of his gradual revelations.

sample_reviews.review_text: Boring!!! Didn't finish it.....just rambled on and on and on. How did it receive a Pulitzer????

Read it for a book club. Could *not* get into it. Some interesting historical tidbits but was otherwise so boring that I had a hard time getting motivated to read it. I hear there are some amazing parts, but they were lost on me. 
 That being said, I am intrigued by the other two stories in this series. I am curious to see what the others characters' backstories are. Hopefully not as dribbling as Rev. John Ames...

Complex and kind of meandering, I found this a strangely beautiful tour through faith and human interaction as the dying priest writes a letter to his young son, prompted by the return of the prodigal son of his oldest friend.

Beautiful story, written in a sort of stream of conscious narrative (taking the form of letters written by an elderly father to his young son)... Gilead is a very well-written and insightful book. BUT a little too sweet and sentimental for my tastes.

The best description of this book might be 'a meditation'. Slow, gentle and soft, yet heavy on character development and themes. 
 An old dying father is writing a letter of reflections and life truths to his now 7 year old son who now is seeing a man of withering force and failing health. The father is a reverend in 1950s America who spent decades writing sermons and who still admits that some questions are still unanswered. 
 It is full of religious debate but not too heavy with it, contrary to some of the critique. The old questions of belief, predestination and forgiveness seem to be timeless. The same discussions were held centuries before, then and there, and even now. 
 Take time with it because it will demand quite a bit of it. But it's all worth it - this book just stays with you for a while after you've read it. For a simple reason of it being simply made so well.
Can't believe it won the awards.

I gave the book one star, that was probably one too many! it took me a week to finish it, reading myself to sleep. I might have missed some of the ramblings of the awful old man, so glad it is finally over! In the beginning I tried to keep an open mind, even though I don't like religious books of ang kind. But the narrator is so irritating, full of self righteousness only the old can master, the ever angry old guy, still full of hate and bile after so many years. There is a perversity in this old guy marrying the woman young enough to be hus granddaughter.

Picked it up as a late summer read and found it tedious and unnecessary. The narrator of a book is a dying preacher. He's telling his young son about his life growing up in Kansas or Iowa or someplace like that. Long dusty recollections of dusty impressions. The preacher does have an "enlightened" element to his personality. He's a pacifist, non-racist, stoic salt-of-the-earth midwesterner who tries to do the right thing while instinctively and with grace absolving those around him of sin. This book is a Garrison Keillor Woebegone musing absent of any levity.

I just finished this book. It was beautifully crafted, though quite preachy and heavy handed at times. I found that I couldn't read it in long stretches because it felt so heavy and morose. I did enjoy looking at history from a new perspective though.

Heavy Christian theology. 
 Originally read December 2014, re-reading in Jan/Feb 2016 for book club.

reference_books.title: The Good Earth (House of Earth, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I very much enjoyed this classic by Pearl S. Buck. I had wanted to read it for a very long time and finally had a chance to pick it up in a school library where I was subbing. I am very glad I did. 
 Wang Lung goes from rags to riches in this coming of age story. His father arranges a marriage for him to O'lan who is a slave in the big house. She is not good looking but is wise and a hard worker. She helps Wang Lung in the fields, delivers her children herself and goes back to the fields. After nearly starving in the drought and going south, Wang Lung and O'lan acquire wealth and return home. Wang Lung invests in land and becomes wealthy. 
 Very worthwhile read.

reference_books.title: The Woman in White
reference_books.review_text:
This book was first published in 1868. It is quite wordy, and I did put it down after 50 pages as it moved so slowly. I read another book then picked this one back up. It moved smoother after that but I still think it could have been many pages shorter. I did like the intrigue of the mystery and it kept me turning the pages. 
 Walter Hartright is commissioned by a man to teach art to his nieces. On the way there, Walter encounters a woman dressed all in white. They have an interesting conversation along the way and he puts her in a cab for the rest of journey when they part ways. At this fork in the road, another cab pulls up with two men in it who ask Hartright if he has seen the woman, that she has escaped from an asylum. He does not give her away and continues on his journey. Hartright and the two nieces' lives intersect with the "woman in white" throughout the rest of the book.

reference_books.title: Fifty Shades of Grey (Fifty Shades, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I've read better and I've read worse. I probably would give it a 2 1/2 if that were possible. I liked some parts better than others. James tended to use some expressions to excess and although attractive, Christian has some real issues. Ana seemed like such an innocent and I did feel sorry for her. I may read the next one just to see if James gives us more insight into the characters.

reference_books.title: The Tea Girl of Hummingbird Lane
reference_books.review_text:
Lisa See does it again, another beautifully written story, this time about a mountain village steeped in tradition and superstitions. Li-Yen is a very intelligent young girl who lives in the village and goes to school. They usually finish that schooling then move on to picking tea leaves and helping their families make a living. Li-Yen's teacher talks her parents into letting her continue her schooling but she will still learn her A-ma's trade of being a healer. 
 This is a coming of age story and follows Li-Yen to adulthood. See writes her characters with such depth that I am sorry I've finished the book, I want it to continue. There are a lot of details about the tea industry also that I found interesting. This book will stay with me for a while.

reference_books.title: Murder on Astor Place (Gaslight Mystery, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
A good Victorian mystery about a widow, Sarah who is now a midwife. She comes from an upper crust family but has been estranged from them since the murder of her husband. 
 While attending the delivery of a baby in a boarding house, she sees a young girl who looks a lot like someone Sarah knew while in school. She realizes that it is the sister of someone she went to school with. She believes Alicia is pregnant but not quite sure because she only had a fleeting glance while delivering. 
 A couple of days later Alicia is found dead in the boarding house and Sarah calls on her old school chum. Things just don't seem right by the girl's family when they learn of the death. Sarah and a detective Malloy look for clues to solve the case.

book_a.title: Kiss the Girls (Alex Cross, #2)
book_a.user_review:
Another fast paced page turner from Patterson. 
 This one has Alex up against not one but two serial rapists and killers. One is more brutal and on the West coast while the "collector" is on the East coast. It becomes personal when Casanova (the East coast monster) kidnaps Cross's niece. He tries to solve the case before she is killed.

sample_reviews.review_text: DNF - I've decided that Patterson's books are very hit or miss for me. I just couldn't read this one so I'm done with the Alex Cross books.

This is the first Patterson novel I've ever read, and it will be my last. I enjoy police procedurals, but not when the writing is so awkward, and the plot so full of holes. 
 The main character is Doctor-detective Alex Cross who is such a hot-shot super detective that he continuously misidentifies the killer, and makes really poor decisions. 
 There are certain chapters which go into excruciating detail (worryingly, the sex assault/murder chapters are included in this), while there are sudden unexplained gaps in time in other places in the book, which make no sense. 
 Avoid.

Still loving Alex Cross character, and still excited to read the next book in the series, however I thought this book was much weaker than the first, the story was slow and sometimes unnecessary, it felt more like character building and setting up the story for the next book to establish his biggest fears and driving forces. Still a good detective story but I have higher hopes for the next one.

This is genuinely the worst book I have ever finished. 
 To be fair, it is tolerable when there is action, which is often. But every time James Patterson tries to put words coming out of a characters mouth, it makes you want to punch yourself in the face. When he writes descriptive, emotional paragraphs, it makes you want to punch him in the face. 
 I actually dog-eared a couple pages because the writing was so bad, I wanted to be able to quick reference it to people to show them how bad it was. 
 Want another example of how bad a writer he is? One of his other books is called, "Night of the Machete." I am not a God-fearing man, but if you believe in God, maybe throw in an extra prayer for James Patterson's English language murdering soul.

3.5 stars 
 I am becoming quite the fan of Alex Cross, he intrigues me. although so far both books have left me expecting a little more from him. 
 This book was fast paced and was well equipped with memorable bad guys. I will have to keep reading.

I can't get enough of the Alex Cross novels by James Patterson!! I own them all, but haven't finished the series yet. 
 I read it because I really liked the movie, and a friend told me that the book was so much more graphic - it was!

I never saw the movie so didn't really know what I was getting into with this. Finished it in one night it was that much of a page turner. Definitely not for the faint of heart, or one to read alone though. It is 451 pages of complete creepy, diabolical sadism that will make you want to sleep with the lights on. 
 Would've given it more stars but for a few things...there is a relationship that develops that feels wholly unbelievable given what one of them has gone through. It doesn't seem to give justice to the trauma this person would have gone through. Secondly, how the crime is solved. The initial tip-off to the guilty party seemed to be an afterthought and we're given very little background on how this person ever even came up as a suspect. 
 Solid read, but with some holes. Don't read it alone, or late at night.
Read this book years ago and absolutely loved it. One of my favorites by Patterson.

Wow, I can't believe I used to like this book. All of the things I came to hate about the later books of the series are actually WORSE in this book. Spoilers are about details, not the plot so it shouldn't ruin much/anything. Also, fair warning, a lot of this review is a C&P of the first Cross book since a lot of my issues are the same. 
 1. The fact that Patterson spends half the book writing about how evil white people are drives me nuts. Keep in mind that Patterson was a 46 y.o., married, wealthy, while male from Palm Beach, FL writing about what it's like to be a 38 y.o. single father living in a crime-ridden poor neighborhood in DC. Really!? If it were only Patterson's apparent self-hatred, I would just feel pity for him. However, he managed to repeatedly glorify reverse-racism while fitting in more racist cliches than I ever would have thought possible. Check out how many times fried chicken and ribs shows up in the first three-four books. Also, Alex's obsession with white women. To say nothing of the language and the discussions of "the man," slavery and why the blues is the only good music ever created. Oh, and every white cop is an A$$ 
 2. *SPOILER ALERT* The plot is completely improbable. 
 - Cross is allowed in a crime scene involving a close relative that isn't even in his jurisdiction. When that gets far-fetched, the FBI allows him onto THEIR team because of Kyle Craig, an agent that Cross met ONCE and didn't appear to care much for. He is now described as a "close friend" and breaks a ton of regulations to get Cross on the case with no oversight. 
 - Cross breaks at LEAST 3 major laws. The incident of aggravated assault on a law enforcement officer is a federal crime and would have been a jail sentence of many decades if committed by anyone else. Also, many areas consider martial arts a deadly weapon, so he might have been looking at a near-life sentence. But they were white and MIGHT have been profiling, so it's okay... 
 - Cross' new g/f is allowed along on VERY dangerous stakeouts, including being on the scene when they hope to arrest the bad guy. At one point she is even described as wearing a short skirt, heels and a "peasant blouse." The first scene where they are hoping she will ID the guy - okay. But after that, WHY!? 
 3. Cross is revoltingly perfect. He balances family, women and job perfectly. He never gets angry with his kids/nana or they with him. He is gorgeous and impervious to beatings, shootings, etc. (sorry, I already forget which violence took place in which book). And he has NO issues what-so-ever except for the occasional "oh ya, and I miss my wife." Another reader said this, but I must take the time to agree - why does every characters have to have crappy relationships? Cross comes from a broken home himself and is a single dad due to a murdered wife. His love interest has a broken home and everyone around her died of cancer. 
 4. Cross' women: This is more of a pattern than anything. Date Alex Cross = end up dead or attacked horrible. Congrats to this one for being attacked, not once, but THREE TIMES in the book. She might be the only one in the series not attacked because of Cross though. Apparently women exist in Cross' life only to be killed so he can have more angst. 
 Also, In this case, he takes a crime victim on as a patient (unofficial or not, he still does therapy with her in an official capacity) and then becomes sexually involved with her. So now he should lose his job, his freedom AND his license as a psychologist because that breaks the NUMBER ONE RULE in psych. 
 5. I hate the writing style. The tendency to go from first person to third person (and MANY third persons at that) drive me tweaky. Pick one. I also don't like the short, abrupt chapters that appear to do no more than lengthen the book. Also, why does Patterson feels the need to RANDOMLY EMPHASIZE PASSAGES FOR NO GOOD REASON? I mean, is there really a need to confuse the reader by adding italics not only for thoughts, BUT FOR SUDDEN BURSTS OF WRITING THAT APPEAR TO MEAN NOTHING? This gets worse in the second and forth book (I skipped #3 this time around), but IT'S PRETTY ANNOYING HERE TOO. See what I means? Oh, and learn how to write a 4 year old's thoughts so that she doesn't sound older and wiser than Nana. Actually, she and Nana might as well be the same character except that the girl is there to be cute and Nana is there to be racist. 'Cause apparently being racist when your old is okay. 
 All in all, a book to be avoided - especially if you actually read and THINK about what you are reading. If you are the kind of person who listens to the beat of the song and has no idea what the words are, you might like it just fine. And if you are white and feel guilty about it, you will probably even find it "deep."

book_b.title: Traveling With Pomegranates: A Mother-Daughter Story
book_b.user_review:
This was a biography written by Sue Monk Kidd and her daughter Ann Kidd Taylor. Sue is turning 50 and going through the change and has decided that her life is over and she is now an old woman. 
 Ann has been declined at a school she wanted to attend and feels dejected. They take a trip to Greece more or less to find themselves. 
 There was a lot of symbolism and introspection in this book and I just could not relate. I appreciated Mother and Daughter trying to connect better, but it seemed as if they were very close already.

sample_reviews.review_text: Well I gave up. After 2 hours of listening to this book, out of a 9 hour CD set, I had had enough. It was so boring it was hard to focus. Shame - I really wanted to like it. Maybe I just need to be in a different frame of mind for this book.
I liked this one a lot better than Dance of the Dissident Daughter--similar themes, more memoir, and the voice of Kidd's daughter Ann adds some variety.

This is a very well written book about nothing. About 300 pages of self discovery and reflection. It is a long journey to self discovery, but as a secondary observer things seem much more clear. I wanted to yell at the narrators to snap out of it the entire time I was reading. Even though I realize that a process such as self discover is not so simple or short, I didn't want to read about it. I have my own hamster wheel in my head going round and round, I didn't need to hop aboard one belonging to someone else, no matter how well written. For those readers interested in memoirs filled with philosophy and self discovery this could be a very interesting book, but I prefer things actually happening in my books.

I abandoned this one when I was 90% finished. It was less about traveling than about new-agey pop psychology. I grew irritated with the "big" revelations about their lives that came through their dreams. 
 If you haven't read her fiction, a good deal of this will be incomprehensible.
I related a lot to the women in this book. I especially related to both of their inate desire to write that won't go away. And now I want to visit Greece so badly.
I liked the first 2 chapters and then it got to be too much. Too much feminism and interpreting dreams. If I hadn't already read The Secret Life Of Bees I don't think I would after reading this book.

I appreciated the author of Secret Life of Bees more for reading this work. She is a different and very careful thinker. If you want to write a book people find meaningful, first fill your head with meaningful things.

I enjoyed reading this book that addressed the complex mother-daughter role. Ann in the book has reached young adulthood (23 if I remember properly) and Sue (author of "The Secret Life of Bees") is going through menopause. This mother/daughter pair travel to Greece and Paris, face health issues, and plan a wedding. It was so nice to hear that even though both faced some conflicts how much they cared for each other. I wish I could have this type of a relationship with my mother, but sadly I do not. However, I do hope to be close to my own daughter as she matures into adulthood. I would also love to be able to travel the world with her some day! 
 I found Ann's conflict with marriage and changing her last name interesting. I could hardly wait to marry and change my name - perhaps due to conflicts growing up and a desire to shed what I didn't like? I had never thought about how a man being addressed as Mr. is according to his gender where a woman is address Miss, Ms., or Mrs. according to her marital status. True but I never gave it much thought before! 
 Good book, but not my favorite, thus the 3 star rating.
yawn
I didn't completely finish this book. It's not interesting enough to make we want to finish off those last few chapter.

reference_books.title: The Help
reference_books.review_text: I think my experience with this book suffered because it came so highly recommended. It was an interesting idea and basically well-written, but I didn't enjoy it that much.

reference_books.title: The Chaperone
reference_books.review_text: Great summertime read, well-written. Too long; too many endings. Great central idea, but it felt like the author shifted gears in the middle of the book.

My first Stephen King book. And probably my last. Came highly recommended by many people I respect. Great premise, but the book was toooooo long. If he had tightened up the book, it would have been great; otherwise, for me it was a slog.

reference_books.title: Eat, Pray, Love
reference_books.review_text: Again, this book came so highly recommended that it made for ultimately disappointing reading for me. I didn't love Gilbert and I didn't particularly love her journey. The book came off as self-indulgent, though I'm happy for her.

reference_books.title: The Good Earth (House of Earth, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I don't think I have ever HATED a book more than I hated this one. In fact, I don't think I have ever hated a book, period. If I could give it negative 10,000 stars I would. But after slogging through this entire book, I found the ending so cynical and deflating that it made me want to dig up Pearl S Buck and throw this damn book in her face.

book_a.title: Gone Girl
book_a.user_review: Well-written and interesting. Didn't love the cynical ending.

sample_reviews.review_text: One of the best books I've read. I was completely hooked and couldn't stop thinking about the plot when I had to put it down.

I was so keen to read this..but found it an enormous let down. Kind of clever, but in a self-conscious and showy off kind of way. Kind of unpredictable but in a kind of predictable way because of the alternating narrative viewpoints. Characterisation is unconvincing. Awful Amy is odious and nasty Nick is a good pupil. Desi and the supporting cast are transparent and insubstantial. Little literary merit and even less narrative tension. But... Couldn't give up on it!
What was with the last quarter of that book?

This was an interesting psychological thriller, more psychological than thriller. Nick and Amy are a typical American couple; in their late 30s, married, celebrating their 5th wedding anniversary, recently lost their jobs to the recession, and moving away from their adult home and closer to Nick's childhood home to care for his aging parents. It would seem they are average in every way. But when Amy disappears, the cops begin digging below the surface, and each piece that is revealed paints a different picture of their marriage. 
 Gillian Flynn has created a unique story, with characters that are incredibly different and... psychotic. I recommend this book for anyone who likes a good character study.
Liked it. Had some memorable quotes throughout. Interested in the film version and how they are going to change the ending
It's a sneaky page-turner, and now I wonder why did I let it steal any of my time.

This book was brilliantly written. It probably deserves a 5 star review. But it won't get one. Why? Because fuck Amy. And Gillian... well you're on my list with George R.R. Martin, Nicholas Sparks, and Karin Slaughter for robbing me of my happy endings. Hell I'll just take a satisfying ending. So one star is all you get from me.

Great twist in the middle - and the twists keep coming! Once you get through the first half, it's a thrill ride! 
 My one criticism is that the author seemed to only have one voice for her characters, she sounded like a woman trying to see things from a man's point of view. Overall great read though!

Sometimes there are times where I wish I could quit a book half way through, and not finish the rest. However, when you're already half way through the book you want to finish reading it and see what the ending is like. With Gone Girl, I wish I quit the book for good. I am going to try and write up this review because I haven't read a book in a long time where it just makes me so mad. 
 Gone Girl is a story of Nick Dunne whose wife goes missing on their 5th wedding anniversary. It was a who did it type of novel, and what made it different is that you saw the events from his point of view and you were able to read journal entries from Amy's point of view leading up to her disappearance. 
 The first half of this book was great. It kept me on my toes, and I want to read more. I wanted to find out what was going to happen to Nick. Will Amy ever be found? Nick became their first suspect. I can see where people were finding this sexist, but in a way it was like all other major crime stories. It goes to the person you think is the most accountable. Nick had holes in his story from the start, and he was hiding things from the police. It's no wonder they suspected him. I first started rolling my eyes when the affair was announced. How predictable. Then, once we found out that Amy's personality was just crazy is when I really started getting mad. I don't know why it just infuriated me. This also goes with Nick. He was starting to get on my wrong side. 
 The book continues on. You find out about Amy's past, and how she has framed people before. Nick tries to use it against her. The only sum what redeemable thing was Tanner and his wife. The rest just I can't even. 
 I stopped reading the book fully at about 88% left in the book where the rest of it I just scanned. I couldn't handle it any more. The sad thing was I have read more enjoyable young adult fiction books then this book. The ending made me even madder. You sit there and want to frame your wife, your wife uses you for a pregnancy so you are trapped, and yet you stay with her?! Worst ending in a novel since Jacob and Bella's baby became soul mates in Twilight. I apologize now for those that I recommended this book originally too in the beginning. The first half was great, but ugh.
I'm torn on what to rate this, I really loved it as I was reading, total page turner, but the ending fell so flat, all that building and then nothing. So liked the book, hated the ending.

book_b.title: The Last of the Mohicans (The Leatherstocking Tales #2)
book_b.user_review: SOOOOOO BORING.

sample_reviews.review_text: Did not enjoy it. The story itself was okay-ish. Not my thing, not realistic in some respects. Extremely violent in other. The telling style was very detailed, but it were often not the details i cared about. There was not enough depth in character description to get attached to any of them. The character of David was plain annoying ugh!
I read this for Hawkeye on M*A*S*H and oh, it was just hilariously terrible.
I remember reading this book in high school. My sister skipped my bookmark ahead one chapter while I was getting lunch and I didn't even notice for 10 pages.

It's said that James Fennimore Cooper wrote this on a dare because he didn't like a certain book and said he could do better; so someone told him "Okay, then do it." Well, I didn't like this book that he wrote, so I will say that I could be dead sleeping for a solid month, wake up with five minutes left before a deadline, and STILL come up with a more interesting story than this. Save trouble and boredom...watch the much much MUCH better 1995 movie, starring Daniel Day-Lewis. They changed almost the whole story, but in this case, that's a good thing.

This came with the BN eReader software. I just finished Arthur Conan Doyle's "The Refugees" and adventure story which ends among the Iriquois tribes in the late 1600s. I thought I might see if James Fenimore Cooper's classic tale could hold my interest in a similar genre and setting. 
 The first couple of chapters were slow going as Mr. Cooper was suffering from a pompous display of erudition. The story then settled down and read quite well as an adventure story. I identified with some of the lead characters, though not as well as expected with a more modern novel. The descriptions of Native American life in the Northeast captured my interest, though I have suspicions about their accuracy. His depiction of the Native demeanor, though possibly flattering for his time, was about as cardboard and one dimensional as his portrayal of the women. 
 The book was OK. Given the mix of its appeal to the juvenile elements of a male mind, and it's portrayal of white males as the only interesting heros, and indian males as the only interesting villains, I can't recommend this book.

I don't say this often, but man, the movie is SO much better. 
 Probably thrilling and groundbreaking in its time, the writing has not aged well. Apparently the rule of "show, don't tell" wasn't around yet. Sample page: '50 word sentence, 50 word sentence, 75 word sentence. "In short... 100 word sentence".

The Last Of The Mohicans is a great great read. Though not for everyone I found it to be informative, adventurous, and fantastic all at once. 
 Set in 1757 it follows the adventures of a group of "fish out of water" Brits and three extremely skilled woodsmen. The main character, Hawkeye, is probably one of the most exciting heroes I've come across in fiction. His constantly drawn contrasts between "book smarts" and "woods smarts" really turned the notion of what a 'savage' is on its head. 
 While I don't want to give anything away, the book does have some surprises at the end that will surely shock you and make you re-read the passage to make sure you actually saw what you think you saw.

Dear god no. This book was so boring. It does not deserve the movie it got. It's waaaaaay too long, jam-packed with overused adjectives and sentences so long that I've forgotten the beginning of them by the time I get to the end, and it's just so casually racist. I know that the author didn't intend for it to be that way; I feel like he really cared about the cause of preserving Native American lore. But it's just so patronizing and pitying and ... misunderstanding. On top of that, it simply isn't good. The story is boring, repeats its own action over and over, has very little tension throughout, and reads like it's trying to be nonfiction, with factual-sounding sentences that veer away from anything resembling a story. It's very dull. Just stick to the movie, which even had to fabricate a bunch of subplots that aren't in the book to make the movie script even remotely interesting from what was written in the book. Skip this one.

Written in an English long forgotten, Cooper's tale of Hawkeye and his friends remains a classic. Those willing to work through the barriers of style and language will be rewarded with a thrilling book filled with adventure and tenderness. While a "true to the book" movie might be rated R because of the violence, which some might regard as over the top, Cooper brings to life the perils of war and the savagery of combat where the fighting was done hand to hand. A very good read, surprisingly quick.

One of the few times I will ever admit to a movie being better than a book. While it is highly descriptive the language is polarizing to modern times and the book lacks the epicness which was captured in the cinematography of the movie.

reference_books.title: Vampire Academy (Vampire Academy, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I don't understand why these books are so popular. The main character is supposed to be this kick-ass girl, but really is just mean and cold, not relatable at all. 
 I could barely finish the book because I really didn't care about any of the characters or the story.

reference_books.title: The Alienist (Dr. Laszlo Kreizler, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
If this book were half as long, I would have given it 3 stars. I love mystery/crime/forensics stories. Unfortunately, the story only adds up to about 40% of the book. The rest is just fluff. It was so bad that I was actually becoming ANGRY that it took so long to move the story forward. I began skipping 2-3 pages at a time and did not miss a thing! 
 I like authors like James Patterson who get right to the point--I don't need to know what color the curtains were and how they felt to the touch as the character walked past them. If you like authors who give pages and pages of filler, (Sorry, but Steven King's one of the worst,) then you won't mind devoting so much of your time to a story that is just ok.

reference_books.title: The Passage (The Passage, #1)
reference_books.review_text: This book is not nearly as great as everyone is saying. I liked the characters, but I found the tone of this book extremely depressing. There is no sense of hope. Nothing good happens to anyone. I love paranormal, especially vampires, but this book is too dismal.

reference_books.title: A Game of Thrones (A Song of Ice and Fire, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This book had too many characters to keep track of. There was so many supporting characters with similar names that it was a very confusing read at times.

book_a.title: Wicked Appetite (Lizzy & Diesel, #1)
book_a.user_review: I hate that I wasted my money on this book. I'm a long-time fan of Evanovich and have read about 75% of her work. This is the worst book of hers that I've read. It's basically a dumbed-down, fluffed-up, re-hashing of the Stephanie Plum novels. And the Plum novels have started getting stale and repetitive, so a bad imitation of them can't be good. Even Diesel seems less appealing than he was in the "Between the Numbers" books. Evanovich used to be one of my favorite authors because of her smart-assed, whacky style. I hate to say this but I'm afraid she's slipping.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Although I thought this was a funny book, I really do think the characters and plot devices were too similar to the Stephanie Plum series. I liked the infusion of magic but I would have liked Lizzy to have a different personality. The only visible differences between Plum and Lizzy are that Lizzy loves waking up at 5am, is a baker (and can therefore cook really well) and that she doesn't live anywhere near her family. There are surface differences but their base personalities are irritatingly similar. 
 This was an enjoyable book but I wanted something new and different rather than a set of standard commonly used ideas.

I'm not sure what shelf this new Evanovich series belongs on... A super silly, sweet and not very wicked blend of mystery, romance (teasing of the kind to be expected from this author) and paranormal. I wanted it to be better than it was...the kookiness just outweighed the lightweight story. Save it for the beach!
Read my review at http://hippiebookreviews.blogspot.com...

 And in my imagination, Diesel is NOT blond. (Frankly, neither is Lizzy.)

Life is just to short to be finishing bad books. What. Great start to 2015.

So this is the first book in a new series by Evanovich that follows Wulf and Diesel. As people may remember these characters were seen in the "in between numbers" Stephanie Plum books. But there are no other people that are seen in Wicked Appetite. 
 The premise of the book, Diesel is trying to stop his evil cousin Wulf from doing naughty things. Wulf's new scheme is to find what are called "The Stones" (no joke lol), and they represent the Seven Deadly Sins. Diesel is trying to stop Wulf from acquiring the stone of Gluttony. The other main character is named Lizzie. And she is also an unmentionable (like Diesel and Wulf). She's not sure what her ability is and when she first encounters both cousins she is suspicious of both. There's also a cast of animal characters and rather amusing side characters with strange behaviors and "collections". You just have to read it to understand. 
 I gave this one three stars, but in reality it does not compare to the Plum series. The characters, while funny, felt very similar to many characters that are seen in Stephanie's world. Lizzie seemed like a lesser replica of Steph and Diesel was Morelli and Wulf was a badder version of Ranger. It was a nice read that can hold me over while waiting for the next Plum book but it wasn't fantastic. 
 I'll still read the next book, but this is a series I won't be investing in financially.
I didn't care for this one at all; I will skip this series.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I hope you won't ever read a simplified version of this book. Simplified books are parodies and caricatures, good for nothing. Even people trying to learn a new language had much better plunge in the deep end. 
 If you haven't read this book yet, and are skimming the reviews to see what it's like, and if you happen on mine then this is my advice, don't read any more reviews and read the book at least twice. And then come back and read about how other people have experienced it. 
 If you have read the book, then you may be among a large group of brilliant people who hate it, or join the other group of equally brilliant people who love it. Though using the word love may not be the correct term! There won't be any ambiguity. And right there, is one of the charms of this work of art. 
 For second time readers, for what it's worth this is my suggestion if I may, don't think much while you're reading and don't try to analyse, just let your emotions come to the surface and observe your Self. Not the book. You will see you are drawn in and are experiencing the emotions and life lessons of souls who only ever existed in Emily Bronte's chest, and then in the book she wrote. Who knows how she did this? My mind can't fathom how she and other prodigies and creators of any great work of art in any field did it. But no matter if you love or hate it, this book shall leave you a bit changed. The hours you spend reading it will somehow amount to years of experiencing life. I hope you will have, indeed, read it even before you read my review. Because that way, I wouldn't have set your expectations in anyway, or clouded your eyes. Or your feelings.

Their relationships verging on pathology... I think this book to be highly overrated. Whether I was just in the mood or it was so well written, I don't know, but I didn't mind that fancy, descriptive language I usually have only loathsome feelings for. Additionally, it rekindled my longing for solitary heights and munros of the north, thus I could not grade it any lower.

I can see how English teachers could have a field day with essay questions from this book but I'm not sure if I see it as something that I would recommend for recreational reading. Heathcliff is so evil, and Catherine is such a flighty witch, yet they're both also somewhat justified in their initial reactions that ultimately formed their adult selves. I'm glad that everything ended reasonably well in the last ten pages, which was totally unexpected, but I don't really think I'll be reading this again any time in the forseeable future. Frankly, I hated the book! I've never been one for tragic love stories, and the characters in this book were so extremely unlovable. Selfish, self-obsessed and extremely weak in different ways, it left me rather disgusted. I can appreciate Bronte's (perhaps rather realistic) depiction of how humans really work, and the ending with the graves were rather touching all the same, but I just couldn't bring myself to like this book.

This is not a love story. Stories like this contribute too much to why people have such a skewed version of what love is supposed to be, and why so many girls think abuse in a relationship is acceptable and normal (Do you hear me Stephenie Meyer!?!). 
 Synopsis: A guy with reactive attachment disorder meets one of the most narcissistic chicks in all of literature. When he's the only game in town she'll "love" him because hey, narcissism has to be fed, but he'll never get the fulfilling love out of the relationship that he needs. And he'll never know how to "love" anyone else because he thinks that obsession is love and is incapable of forming any other attachments-- Lord help you if you do anything that smells like abandonment (she does). So they blithely go about wrecking havoc on the lives of everyone around them, even their children and the one or two truly decent people they know... all in the name of "Love" (selfishness). 
 It's a train wreck. I can see someone enjoying it for it's literary merit. I can see enjoying it as a horror story or psychological thriller. But as the ultimate end-all and be-all of love stories, or even a love story at all? No thank you. 
 Blech.

reference_books.title: The Night Circus
reference_books.review_text:
Buddy read with dearest Mia, but because she has a long week assignment so I've finished this one first. Ton of good luck for you, dear! 
 "The circus arrives without warning. No announcements precede it. It is simply there, when yesterday it was not. Within the black-and-white striped canvas tents is an utterly unique experience full of breathtaking amazements. It is called "Le Cirque des Reves," and it is only open at night." 
 The Night Circus was a book that has magical feeling for me! It just swept me off from reality to that magical land. I was so enchanted by the setting, it took place between 1873 until 1903. The concept of this books seems so original for me, it's unique, wonderful and dream-like! Really, really beautiful. The beginning of the story was really promising and engaging. The writing was very lyrical, descriptive and (this is what I like the most) imaginative! It's utterly easy to imagine the world that written by Morgenstern. UGH, I couldn't even tell how much I love that world! The costumes and the settings were just awesome! It's just gorgeous and captivating! 
 BUT... 
 Yeah, there's reasons why I give this book 3 stars. For me, the characters here were so lack of depth, not vivid enough for me to being attached to them. I kinda felt nothing when one character died, even I couldn't feel anything for Marco and Celia's relationship. I couldn't feel the love and their desperation and endeavor for being together. The pace was really slow-as-snail, I found some part kinda dragged on. I waited for the good part when it claimed as duel, but for me it's end up annoyingly flat. It took so much time to build all of these things up, but it took so little time to tear and explain it down. Oh c'mon, you don't want it to be wasted in vain, right? 
 But don't get me wrong, I liked this book, I loved the world and that magical feeling but I had expected more. Book wasn't only made of setting, but also the characters and story itself. The Night Circus is the kind of book that every person should read at least once in their life if you don't mind the slow-paced story ;)

Like most previous reviewers stated, the first 1/4 or so of this book is completely pointless. You could skip it and not miss much. The main character starts the book with a strange amnesia and so must learn everything about his world starting anew. The only problem is that no-one wants to talk about anything. Everyone is so secretive and resistant to talk that you gain absolutely no knowledge of the world he is thrust into until about 90 pages in or so. Its very frustrating. It's as if Dashner is trying to replace suspense with long drawn out world building. To be perfectly blunt, Dashner needs to go back rewrite the beginning and re-release an updated version. 
 Once you get past all the secrets the book starts to get much better. The transition between no one talking and everyone sharing is sudden and poorly handled, but you're so excited that things are finally being explained that you can easily look past the poor writing skills. The story progression and suspense and such after the first hurdle is actually quite good. The monsters in the book are so creepy that I actually started having incredibly stressful dreams about the grievers chasing me after reading those parts. The character building is average, but the world they are caught in is quite interesting and really drives the book forward 
 I have to give the book 2 stars, because of the horrible beginning. It could have had 3 or 4 stars if not for the incredibly slow and frustrating start.

Kind of an interesting concept - Thomas wakes up with no memories and finds himself trapped in a deadly, ever-changing labyrinth in a sort of Lord-of-the-Flies meets Theseus situation. None of the other inhabitants ("Gladers", people who live in the Glade, which is a little oasis in the middle of the maze where they can farm and stuff) have memories either, or understand why they've all been put into this place. But they've cobbled together a complex community to keep order, keep their minds occupied, and try to find an exit. 
 I have always liked stories where the protagonist is thrown into a chaotic, dangerous world with no memory or information and we as the readers have to uncover the information at the same pace as the protagonist(s). I also liked the Grievers (labyrinth monsters), once we finally got a description of them; very grotesque and Lovecraftian. 
 There were some definite flaws in this book, though. The book obviously banks on us being curious and seeking answers to the many, many questions posed (where/when is this taking place; who is behind it; who designed the maze; why does nobody have memories; etc.). But so often when Thomas asks a question, the Gladers shut him down fast - "Stop asking questions! Do what you're told!" Also, some people who have been affected by the Grievers' poison and survived have regained some of their memories -- but they are never willing to talk about it to the others! At that point, it starts to feel like the mystery is being artificially drawn out, like a magician milking his stage act with a lot of unnecessary swooping hand gestures. 
 Also, dear god, the kids' jargon and slang gets old REALLY fast, though. I guess it's in line with the trope of sci-fi stories using made-up words as curse substitutes, but the dialogue is absolutely saturated with it. "Hey, you shucking slinthead, what kind of klunk are you trying to pull? Tell that greenie to slim it before the Grievers find us!" (Not a direct quote, but very much in line with some of the dialogue). Oh, and don't forget the Random Capitalization of Many Things, another sci-fi writing trope. Grievers, Grief Serum, the Maze, the Glade, the Changing, the Flare, etc. It grates after awhile. 
 Despite the flaws and stylistic things that aren't my cup of tea, I'm likely to check out the next book because I want to know where the story is going. We're introduced to a few new characters and concepts at the very end that have caught my imagination.

The writing style is terrible. The dialogue sounds forced, you can't connect to the main character, the plot drags, the word choice is lacking, etc. I just finished the book because I wanted to know the ending. Now, onto something more enjoyable.

I liked the ideas and story in this book, but I was not a fan of the writing style. It's about a bunch of teenage boys, but the tone of voice the book is written in is very adult. They have way too many insightful thoughts and self reflections for a bunch of teenage boys. But if you can get around that, the story is fairly creative and original, and I do want to read the next one in the series so I can find out how it all turns out. I do have a soft spot for a nice dystopic futuristic book!

After reading a certain amount of dystopian books, you'd think the same patterns would form, that they'd start to become predictable. Not in this case. 
 Thomas wakes up one day in "the Glade"--an enclosed village of sorts, surrounded by a giant ever-changing maze. Every day for the past two years, "runners" have gone out into the maze trying to find an exit. The doors close at nightfall and the "grievers" come out, snarfing up anyone left behind. Thomas remembers things about the maze that the other boys don't and does everything he can to help them escape. 
 I flew through this book in about a day and a half. The plot moves at a perfect pace, so you can't stop anywhere. The end is completely different from the rest of the book and left me kind of sketched out, but wanting to read more. 
 The characters however lacked development, in my opinion. Not that they didn't have personality or weren't likable. All I know is, I didn't really care when one of the main characters was murdered--not a good sign. (unlike the Hunger Games where I completely broke down). 
 Will I buy the book and read it again? No. Will I borrow the sequels? Absolutely.

This was a hard book to read at the beginning. It was hard to read the slang and I still don't have a clear picture of the setting. After reading the slang for a bit it started to make sense and fit in with the story (it had a purpose). The one thing that was hard for me what that I was lost as to where the story was going, which is a great in a way. If the author intended for the reader to be in a haze just like the main character, he did his job. I think he meant for the reader to experience the confusion Thomas felt. I have mixed feelings about this book. I'm not sure I liked it but there's part of me that wants to read the next books in the series because I want to know how it all ends. We shall see if the pull is strong enough....

sample_reviews.review_text:

 It probably would have been fine if the 4th book had a story or a plot, but I'm not sure that it really did. Instead, it left me feeling disappointed. It didn't really answer of the questions that it needed to and it glossed over things it should have given more attention to. 
 Sure, some of the sex scenes were fun, hot and creative. That's why I bumped the rating up to 2 stars, honestly. 
 Ultimately, though, this book felt an awful lot like filler. 
 I'm not excited about book five at all. 
 I'm not even sure if I'm going to read it.

3.75 stars- 
 RELEASE DATE: November 18, 2014 
 Gideon calls me his angel, but he's the miracle in my life. My gorgeous, wounded warrior, so determined to slay my demons while refusing to face his own. 
 The vows we'd exchanged should have bound us tighter than blood and flesh. Instead they opened old wounds, exposed pain and insecurities, and lured bitter enemies out of the shadows. I felt him slipping from my grasp, my greatest fears becoming my reality, my love tested in ways I wasn't sure I was strong enough to bear. 
 At the brightest time in our lives, the darkness of his past encroached and threatened everything we'd worked so hard for. We faced a terrible choice: the familiar safety of the lives we'd had before each other or the fight for a future that suddenly seemed an impossible and hopeless dream. 
 ~~ 
 3.75 stars--CAPTIVATED BY YOU is the fourth installment in Sylvia Day's contemporary, adult Crossfire erotic romance series focusing on Gideon Cross and Eva Trammell. Told from alternating first person points of view (Gideon and Eva) CAPTIVATED BY YOU follows immediately on the events of book 3-Entwined With You. If you have not read the series, be aware there may be some spoilers in my review. The series must be read in order for cohesion and understanding. The entire series, to date, covers but a few months in real time. 
 The storyline focuses on the continuing relationship between Eva and Gideon-two broken and wounded souls whose earlier years were destroyed by betrayal and abuse. Secretly married in an island ceremony, our couple returns to civilization where revealing their 'engagement' is anything but a happily ever after. Events will set into motion a destructive path that may be too difficult to overcome. 
 CAPTIVATED BY YOU will see secrets revealed, heartbreak and betrayal for one family when the past comes crashing down. Eva and Gideon's relationship is as destructive and unhealthy as it is strong. Gideon's need to protect and control forces an ultimatum from Eva that will shatter all semblance of Gideon's self discipline. He is a man possessed; haunted by his past; and broken by the demons who continue to destroy his soul. The chaos that ensues finds Eva and Gideon on the verge of sabotaging their own relationship-one ex at a time. Eva is Gideon's weakness, his strength and his heart. Eva continues to push Gideon's buttons; and they equally manipulate one another's emotional fragility and strengths. 
 We will revisit with Cary's love triangle of Trey and Tatiana although there is very little closure for Cary or the reader. Gideon's dysfunctional family dynamics is a major stumbling block in Gideon's recovery and some issues of the past will be confronted. Brett Kline remains a point of contention between Eva and Gideon-one that is slowly tearing away at Gideon's control. And some questions will be answered as to the who, what and how. 
 CAPTIVATED BY YOU is an intensely personal and in depth storyline. The sex scenes are numerous, aggressive, continuous and erotic. As Gideon begins to lose control in his personal life he sets into motion a diverging set of controls in the bedroom. A different and previously unaddressed side of Gideon will emerge. 
 Sylvia Day's CROSSFIRE series and CAPTIVATED BY YOU is a compelling read. There are moments of intimacy, seduction, arousal and love juxtaposed with heartbreaking betrayal, painful confessions and destructive realizations. Eva and Gideon's relationship is intensely seductive and alarmingly toxic to everyone and themselves. 
 Copy supplied by the publisher.

This first volume was okay, but I was a bit disappointed with some of the gender stereotypes/roles. I mean, it's great that Tohru is an independent young girl, but the fact that the Sohma men allow them to live with them so she can clean up after them and make their meals is a bit chauvinistic.

Honestly, I didn't think I'd like this so much. I've always said "Anime is weird. I have no interest in it." But my friends were reading it and loving it and recommending it... so I borrowed it. And devoured it. A fun, witty, fast little read. ^.^ And I love the different style! I'm a classic british lit kind of girl, and so this totally different format is a great change of pace.

I loved this as a kid. It was one of my favorite romance-comedy manga series. I stopped at Volume 11 because the story was repetitive and it was becoming increasingly and unnecessarily darker. I was right to do so because the series is even worse than I'd thought. 
 The "darkness" I was talking about is how child abuse, domestic abuse, womanizing, self-harm, and all kinds of disorders and triggering situations are romanticized. STOP ROMANTICIZING AND GLORIFYING TRAUMA AND ABUSE!!!!! It's not cute to throw yourself in front of a gang of people who want to kill you and then proceed to try to "fix" them by lecturing them about how friendship is magic and love is rainbows and flowers and everything will be okay~*~la dee da dee da~*~*~ 
 I remember as a little girl thinking, "You poor boys, I want to take care of you like Tohru (the main character) does!" and wishing I was in the position where so many boys needed me, wanted my help, and gave me pseudo-love while I gave them pseudo-psychological/emotional rebound. Exactly how Tohru does. I really hope people understand the sheer fuckton of bullshit that is and just how much pressure that puts on women. This series perpetuates the notion that women must control men and look out for them all the fucking time. That is all Tohru is--a gigantic babysitter for immature boys who don't know how to take care of themselves and refuse to learn how. We have to teach our boys to be more responsible. Not to be abusive, not to be destructive, not to be so selfishly carefree. Every single male in this series is self-interested and self-serving. Because of it, they get into these fights about whose dick is bigger and wreak havoc wherever they go. Then they go "oh my god I just hurt this person wtf have I done?! I have got to calm down!" only to go back and do it again. Come the fuck on, stop with these ego-laden sausagefests and stop trying to make it "cute" because it isn't. Stop using trauma as an excuse to be an asshole because trauma is not something that needs to be trivialized for your shitty romances. 
 The only thing that helped this series keep its 1 star is that this may contain one of the best portrayals of female friendships and mother-daughter relationships I've read. There's probably only a handful of media where the women are active in one another's lives and they don't resent each other or have some kind of rivalry with one another. They truly and deeply care for each other. However, outside of the three best friends and one deceased mother, all the other female characters are nonchalant, hateful, resentful of Tohru, or they rarely ever show up again. In addition to that, I love that physical femininity on a male is not a problem. However, they are still masculine-coded due to their abusive nature which is still problematic. Stop writing like this. It's not cute. It's not progressive. It's stupid and it's disgusting.
