book_b.title: Dodger
book_b.user_review: I definitely need to read more Dickens, and then maybe read this again. Sir Terry's humor, perfect turn of phrase and his deft handling of language remain, even when Discworld is left behind. What often stands out to me in Pratchett novels is they way the plot seems to take something of a back seat to the language and the details of each scene. To be clear, this does not detract from the experience. However, in this book, I thought we might benefit from a bit of a stronger story line. I enjoy hearing all the words in my head, and sometimes forgot to care what was happening to poor Simplicity.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This was delightful, and well fleshed-out, and rung through with the author's fascination with Victorian london. Not just "oooh, Vicotoriana" but "ooh, sewer architecture" and "nitty-gritty little details of poverty at the time" and "little-known historical figures". The original characters were excellent, my personal favourite being Dodger's patron Solomon, a mysterious pork-eating Jew who has personal deals with God and is equally happy in the company of the Queen as that of guttersnipes and theives. 
 It did not quite feel like *Pratchett*, though. Nevertheless I await the TV serial with bated breath.

Ah, Sir Terry. What a treat. Set in Victorian London, where "Charlie" Dickens plays a key role, young tosher Dodger goes on his hero's journey through the sewers of London, assisted by a golden-haired girl he saved, a wiser-than-Solomon Solomon, an extremely stinky dog, and even Queen Victoria. Wonderfully told, would read aloud wonderfully too, I suspect.
Discworld or nothing! Sorry, Sir Terry...
Well written with twists and turns everywhere. Thought provoking and enjoyable.

I tried to like this book... and did not. I could not seem to follow the writing... too much rambling and nonsense. I made myself read the first 100 pages before making the choice to abandon... Not for me.

This is the first stand alone Terry Pratchett book I've read that wasn't a Discworld novel, so I wasn't totally sure what to expect. Fun and delightful, it's everything you want a Terry Pratchett book to be, sprinkled here and there with some truly profound gems of insight. A short and rollicking read, Pratchett weaves his characters and his narrative together seamlessly- just like always.

I have enjoyed Terry Pratchett's Discworld books in the past but this standalone historical fantasy for teens was flat and boring. The title character, Dodger, is a teenage boy in early Victorian London. He supports himself by his wits and toshing (basically picking through garbage) in the London sewers. After foiling an attempted beating of a pretty young woman, Dodger meets some of the soon to be eminent figures of the day (Charles Dickens, Henry Mayhew) while trying to save Simplicity (the woman's assumed moniker) from an evil husband. 
 I listened to this on audio and perhaps it would have been better in print. The action dragged at times and I cared little for Dodger or the cardboard Simplicity. The historical information was interesting but I found myself wondering if this book will appeal to teens. The humor didn't reach Pratchett's usual heights. 
 I am puzzled by the rave reviews and think teens are better off reading Dickens if they are curious about the time period.

First, a disclaimer: I have a love/hate relationship with Terry Pratchett, and this book is no different. I loved his Discworld series, hated Nation. This books falls more on the hated side. You may love everything Terry Pratchett does. If you do, good for you. You'll probably like this book. I just...didn't. 
 Now the summary: "A storm. Rain-lashed city streets. A flash of lightning. A scruffy lad sees a girl leap desperately from a horse-drawn carriage in a vain attempt to escape her captors. Can the lad stand by and let her be caught again? Of course not, because he's . . . Dodger. 
 Seventeen-year-old Dodger may be a street urchin, but he gleans a living from London's sewers, and he knows a jewel when he sees one. He's not about to let anything happen to the unknown girl--not even if her fate impacts some of the most powerful people in England. 
 From Dodger's encounter with the mad barber Sweeney Todd to his meetings with the great writer Charles Dickens and the calculating politician Benjamin Disraeli, history and fantasy intertwine in a breathtaking account of adventure and mystery." 
 Okay, keep in mind that the audience for this book is teens. TEENS. Teens who don't necessarily care about Charles Dickens or Oliver Twist or Benjamin Disraeli. From that view point, this book is a snooze fest. Sure the plot sounds exciting, "Who is this unknown girl? Dodger will be a detective and find out!" but Terry Pratchett has managed to turn this more into a "fun time with historical figures". And unless you care about the historical figures, this book is lackluster. So if you are a die hard Terry Pratchett fan, or a Dickens fan, or you just like historical London, go ahead and check it out. If you are not one of these....maybe give it a pass.

I enjoyed all of the historical figures etc, but I much prefer Terry Pratchett's more modern Discworld novels, or when he's playing with different literary styles, his non-Discworldesque forays into the Discworld with the Tiffany Aching series.

Excellent! I read it twice through just to get all the details and characters and Anglicisms down but it was a joy both times and I'm sure I will pick it up again soon. Unlike Pratchett's fantasy novels, this one takes place in the underbelly of Queen Victoria's England, where "toshers" comb the sewers for coins and things to sel, try to keep healthy and stay out of trouble with the law. Dodger transcends his station by rescuing a woman who has been beaten and then gets himself invited into society. A great, galloping read and very interesting as well.

reference_books.title: The Curse of Chalion (World of the Five Gods, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
What a wonderful book! It is fantasy, with very little magic and violence. It is a book about political intrigue, and the quest to lift a dreadful curse from a royal family. No word is wasted, and there's not a single moment where you feel bored or uninterested. Not only that, but it also adds some interesting theological discussions about the relationship between Man and God, and the importance of free will on one's faith and beliefs. 
 This is the best book I've read this year, and one of the best ever. 
 Note: the audiobook version is particularly good, with Lloyd James doing one of the best performances I've listened to.

reference_books.title: The Sword of Shannara (The Original Shannara Trilogy, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Terry Pratchett once wrote: "J.R.R. Tolkien has become a sort of mountain, appearing in all subsequent fantasy in the way that Mt. Fuji appears so often in Japanese prints. Sometimes it's big and up close. Sometimes it's a shape on the horizon. Sometimes it's not there at all, which means that the artist either has made a deliberate decision against the mountain, which is interesting in itself, or is in fact standing on Mt. Fuji." (from A Slip of the Keyboard: Collected Non-Fiction). 
 That sounds absolutely, true, but if that's the case, let's say mr. Terry Brooks was really, REALLY, close to Mt. Fuji when he wrote The Sword of Shannara. 
 This book was published in 1977, and it has a huge importance to the literary genre. After The Lord of The Rings, in the 50's, no other large work of fantasy reached anything close to success, until The Sword of Shannara. If Tolkien created Fantasy, it could be said that Brooks made it into a genre, where editors started to believe there was money to gain by publishing it. 
 The basic plot is about Shea Ohmsford, a young man from a small village that sudden receives a visit from a mysterious Druid, Allanon, who tells him that due to his bloodline he's the only one who can wield the mythic Sword of Shannara to defeat the Dark Lord. And by the way, hurry, because the bad guys are already upon you. So he and his foster brother Flick flee their hometown to retrieve the sword. 
 The book has been hugely criticized for the ideas ripped-off from The Lord of the Rings. And although Pratchett was right, and every fantasy story has something of Tolkien, there was no need to be so blunt about it. The Nazgul, Gandalf, the council of Elrond, the crossing of Moria (including the battle with the Balrog), Grima Wormtongue, you name it. If it was cool in the Lord of the Rings, you'll find something similar in The Sword of Shannara. 
 But this was not enough to make me grant just one star to the book. I've read plenty of books full of Tolkien influence, and they ended up pretty fine. I had serious problems with the author's narrative style. The characters are so... heroic! It feels like they'll win no matter what, just out of their own bravery and honor, no matter the size, number, or ugliness of the bad guys. The battles are non-descriptive, but at the same time, the author applies such an abusive use of adjectives that it remains a wonder that so little can be said with so many words. It sounded a lot like someone telling me a D&D adventure he played with his friends - entertaining for him, not at all to me. 
 By the end of the book it has some good moments, mostly during the siege of Minas Tir... i mean, the siege of Tyrsis, but by then over 500 torturing pages have already gone by. 
 So, one mystery is left to discuss. Why the hell was the book so successful? For that, I'll borrow the words from Wastrel, another book club member, which was very incisive in his observations: 
 "(...) Brooks replicated the superficial material of Tolkien - the plot, the world, the characters, and in doing so he somehow managed to capture a small part of the magic of Tolkien. But he stripped out all the 'difficult' or 'complicated' elements. He stripped out much of the sense of wonder, and he stripped out the ethical and religious significance, and he streamlined the Revivalist prose style into something more familiar to modern american readers, and he simplified and sweetened and rose-tinted the worldview and cut out the diversions and distractions and superfluous worldbuilding elements, and he emphasised the coolness and badassery... and then, in a genius move, he aged down the main characters and targeted it specifically at YA readers. [I suppose a modern analogy might be to say that Brooks is a copy of Tolkien in the same way The Hunger Games is a copy of Battle Royale...] 
 Essentially, what Brooks did was observe the popularity of complicated, long-aged, artisanal French red wines (made the traditional way, the way it's been made for centuries), recognized the key chemical ingredients, and decided to start selling 180 proof rectified spirits (flavored with essence of grape) outside school playgrounds (...) To put it in less evocative terms: The Lord of the Rings is a neo-medieval Romance; The Sword of Shannara is a boy's adventure novel that looks like The Lord of the Rings" 
 So, if you are interested in the History of Fantasy as a literary genre, The Sword of Shannara is a must. Otherwise, stay clear.

reference_books.title: Golden Son (Red Rising, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Golden Son, by Pierce Brown, is the second book in the Red Rising trilogy. As such, I'll do my best to avoid spoilers, giving just a general sense of the series plot and setting, moving then to point out general virtues and flaws within the book. 
 That said, WOW! Ever since Ready Player One I haven't read a book that made me actually sad halfway in, regretting it was coming to a close. It is so intense, action-packed, filled with critical moments, that it is a wonder it doesn't start spontaneous combustion still in the reader's hands. Golden Son received the Goodreads Choice Award for Science Fiction in 2015. 
 In a distant dystopian future, a revolution within the human race toppled regular government, and the winners replaced the old regime by a system of colors. Humans were genetically modified to specific tasks, and each color would then be tasked with that work only. Each color also determines one's place in society. Reds are labor workers, and are at the bottom. Golds, on the other hand, are the rulers, and the apex of genetic-modified human race. Darrow, a Red worker living in Mars sets out to topple the Gold's regime. 
 The first book deals with Darrow's time in the "Institute", a training camp for the best among the Golds. This second book handles what happened in the first few years afterwards. 
 Red Rising, the first book, has strong elements of both Hunger Games and Ender's Game, but way better than both. In this one, I guess that Game of Thrones would be a better comparison, although not as fitting as the first ones were. The scope is vast, and multiple political plots among the main houses set the tune for the book - yet do not expect the depth of political intrigue within GoT. 
 On the other hand, this series has a couple of unique characteristics that set it apart from all others. Pierce Brown is a master when dealing with dramatic moments, and whilst one may wait the entire book to get to that peak moment in the story - the one that makes you want to punch the air in celebration - here you'll find one every fifty pages or so. You may be thinking: "That can't work" - but somehow, it does. It is hard to put the book down - hell, sometimes it is even hard to breathe! 
 The second unique aspect of the series is that the author likes to toy with science fiction and adventure tropes. The plot changes direction many times, but almost always it sets in a direction where the reader thinks "oh, I've seen this before, I believe this will happen next"... and then, BAM! - The author shoots the story in another direction, pulling the metaphorical rug from our feet. It can't be an accident; the author must be doing this on purpose! He toys with the readers as much as he toys with his characters. 
 To avoid being too biased, I'll try to point out some flaws I was able to find in the story, If you think they can be a bother, maybe you won't like this book as much as me. Darrow is the over-the-top hero; even though he is arrogant, rash, and sometimes unnecessary violent, one can be pretty sure he'll succeed in the end. After all, the story is totally focused on him. His friends and sidekicks, however, may not survive his crazy ideas. Also, do not expect Hard Science Fiction - some gadgets made me frown when described. The tone of the narration might also sound a bit melodramatic - especially when we are confronted with Darrow's thoughts. However, the audiobook, narrated by Tim Gerard Reynolds, nails the tone and delivers one of the best audio experiences ever, changing what could sound like a drama queen whining into a Shakespearean ethical dilemma. Finally, this is a revolution plot. Too many books on dystopian revolutions have been written, and you may be simply tired of that. I assure you, though; this one stands apart from the rest. 
 I am itching to grab the last book and see how the story ends. If you don't believe my review, and think I am exaggerating, please go on and check other reviews. Check the ratings on Goodreads and Audible. Then, hopefully, you'll be convinced that this is a series worth reading. And get the audiobook! 
 On a final note, a film adaptation of the book is in the works. I am concerned about it, though. The melodrama I've mentioned earlier walks a thin line, and I think that a movie won't be able to keep such fine balance.

reference_books.title: The Hallowed Hunt (World of the Five Gods, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
Lois McMaster Bujold has definitely been included on my (very short) list of amazing authors. I can't say she thrills on character building, when compared to other authors, but she has mastered the ability to create and deliver a plot like no one else. It does follow a certain pattern. When she starts the book, she introduces the main character, and then throws him in a plot. And you think "ok, I understand, this book is about this." And then she adds a little twist, and you go "oh, I see what you did there, the plot is about that". Not before long, she moves the story a bit sideways - always presenting the other important characters, adding new ideas, not deviating from the original open scene, but thickening the script. Only when you are about 50% done you can really say what is the book about. 
 This is the third book in the series, and it is totally independent from the other two. Different characters, different scenario. The only thing that links the three books together is the world building, and most important, the theology. Gods DO exist (five of them), but they can only really affect the world of the living if they can find a person WILLING to be his tool. The importance of free will is always paramount on her story, giving opening to some interesting debates about religion and their relationship with oneself. 
 In this third book the plot is more complex that in the other two, and there's a different style of main character, more akin to fantasy - a strong warrior, which has to coexist with a wolf spirit within him (in the first one it is a young man that once was a proud warrior, but after year of slavery becomes a humble person, without aspirations. In the second, it is a middle-aged noble woman, that brings age and maturity to the way she handles her troubles). This is the least interesting character of the three, but with some merits nonetheless. This book also expand the theology of the series by introducing Shamans, and the mixing of animal spirits with humans. 
 All in all, another priceless work. I feel I enjoyed the first two more than this one, but it still deservers 5 stars for the quality of the writing, and intelligence of the plot.

reference_books.title: The Kingdom of Gods (Inheritance, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
... And I'm done with the series. 
 I'm finishing it more with a sense of relief than accomplishment. The first book (A Hundred Thousand Kingdoms) is very good, but the other books miss something. 
 This one focus on Sieh, the Child-God, the Trickster, one of the most interesting characters in the series. Something happens, and he starts to age. Then, more things start to happen. A lot of things, which wouldn't just be spoilerish, but also confuse to explain. The Arameri are losing power, and the world is changing. 
 If at first the idea of exploring Sieh sounded good, the result wasn't as predicted. I actually ended liking the character less than before. There are a lot of good concepts built over these gods mythos. I particularly like the idea that the godling needs to find his nature, and act accordingly to it, to get stronger. Sieh, for example, can never break a promise he makes to a child. Why, if he's a God? Well, he can (like everyone), but to go against his nature would damage him. 
 Don't get me wrong. I respect N. K. Jemisin a lot - she writes very well. But I feel that this should not have evolved into a series. Maybe a couple of short stories, to delve into the Universe... It is not easy to write about Gods.

book_a.title: Throne of Jade (Temeraire, #2)
book_a.user_review:
Sometimes the book goes a different direction you expected. This was my case here, at least. The Temeraire series is a fantasy/alternate history story about the Napoleonic period with Dragons. Other series have explored this period a lot, due to amount of conflict going on around the globe. However, Naomi Novik chooses not to go down this venue, and instead focus on what would the world be if there were be Dragons on it. 
 Early on the first book we learn that Temeraire is a rare Chinese Dragon, given as a gift to the French but captured by the British before hatching. Well, the Chinese did not like at all that the gift was misdirected, and on this book they come back looking to recover the gift. The British crown is highly interested on increasing its diplomatic relations to the Chinese, and since a Dragon will not accept to be separated from its handler, Captain Laurance and Temeraire depart to China, by means of a not so pleasant invitation from one of the Chinese princes. 
 The plot is plausible, but the book feels like it is mostly world building. The trip to China itself takes almost half the book, and the other half serves mostly to display China on this time period, and how is the relations between Men and Dragons over there. 
 The world building part is done well, but the overall plot lacks some punch. The story comes to a conclusion quite suddenly, and although there are some action scenes, I ended up a bit disappointed. I'm still unsure about the series: the man/dragon relation is interesting, but the series itself needs to pick up the pace, otherwise it will soon become rather dull. 
 Recommended only if you like dragons.

sample_reviews.review_text: Not quite as good as the first but still very enjoyable especially when they finally got to China

Oops, forgot to review on time again! My belated impressions: very neat to see characters' perceptions slowly broken down and reformed, and Temeraire developing even more as an independent. Ending felt a little abrupt and, perhaps anticlimactic? But glad that she didn't go for any kind of cheap big finale, so you win some, you lose some.

Much of the charm of His Majesty's Dragon was lost in this second installment. In that book, it was a gradual build up to the awesome end action scene against Napoleon's armies. In this novel, we get to ride a boat and talk about food and clothing for about 300 pages before anything interesting even happens. 
 Some of my favorite parts of the first book were the completely endearing and sweet conversations between Temeraire and Laurence. For example, "I should rather have you than a heap of gold, even if it were very comfortable to sleep on." BEST DRAGON EVER! I wanted more of the exact same interactions, but unfortunately, most of the book it seems Temeraire and Laurence aren't even speaking. Whenever they do speak, it feels like they are always on the verge of cross words. Most of their conversations revolve around 19th century politics, bringing up slavery and bigotry, and Temeraire is even forced to ask if he owns himself - or is he the king's property. Some of it was interesting, but by the end of the ship voyage I was tired even of these minuscule conversations Temeraire and Laurence had, as it was invariably going to be brow beating us with politics. 
 They spend 8 months on a boat, traveling to China. And boy, do we really get to FEEL those 8 months. The entire ship story line took an insanely long time, and it was just straight up boring. I wanted some action in China damn it. We eventually arrive in China, sure, but only about the last 100 pages of this 400 page novel is devoted to that. Talk about feeling rushed. We are bombarded with new characters who we never really get to know, and then a deus ex machina ending is thrown at us out of the blue. And then...it was just over. 
 I was completely disappointed by this novel. I will be continuing the series but I hope it returns to its roots.
A continuation of the story of a dragon and his captain. They travel to China and see how different dragons are treated there. Long in some parts, but always relating new ideas.

This book combines two of my least favorite aspects of the fantasy genre--unnecessary sequels and endless travelogues--into a vortex of boredom. I almost never give up 320 pages into a 400-page book, but I am already kicking myself for having read as far as I did and see no point to wasting any more of my life on it. 
 The first book is great fun, but this one did not need to exist. The characters who were great came back dull, the okay ones came back interchangeable, and there is absolutely nothing going on except a very slow voyage to China,* because the Chinese want Temeraire back, which of course we know isn't going to last because there are half a dozen more books featuring him and Laurence in places that aren't China. 
 Now it's no secret that I have little patience for series and even less for the episodic type, but good grief, if you're going to write that kind of series, at least bring in some complex new characters or interesting plots or something. 
 I propose a new rule for fantasy book writing: if more than a quarter of any sequel is spent traveling, it's because the author doesn't really have anything more to say in this world or with these characters, and is simply drawing it out for the sake of writing a sequel. The manuscript should be scrapped immediately. 
 *I assume that by the end of the book the characters did in fact reach their destination? Because 80% of the way through, I was still waiting for it.

More adventures with Laurence and Temeraire, the dragon, during the Napoleonic war. This time they take a trip, that lasts 7 months by sea, to China, who is determined to get Temeraire back because he is one of their very rare Celestial dragons.

I didn't love the first book in this series but it was pretty short so I thought, hmm maybe this is just getting started. So to give the series the benefit of the doubt I read Throne of Jade. Also I listened to the audio version and the narration by Simon Vance was amazing. Really, that man could read me anything, any time. 
 But grown... it was even slower than the first book. 
 A good bit of the book is spent on a ship to China. I'm a sucker for a sea voyage but this was just too long and uneventful. Once they get to China, there are some interesting and quirky culture clashes between the Brits and the Chinese but overall little happens. Oh Temeraire checked out some female dragons. Wow, I can't handle all this drama. 
 Like the first book, this one is largely about the growing relationship between Lawrence and Temeraire. I think this is what a lot of people really like about the series but it just didn't cut it for me. Maybe I read this too close off the back of Hobb's Farseer Trilogy which was also a lot about the bond between man and beast. And while, Hobb did this so richly and deeply, it fell a little flat in Temeraire. Or maybe I just hit man-and-beast-bonding fatigue. Who knows? But whatever the reason, this failed to give me all the warm and fuzzies. 
 I couldn't help but roll my eyes every time Temeraire asked Lawrence to read him another bedtime story. 
 I mean, I was already half asleep... zzZzzzzzZzzz

Such an entertaining story! Beautiful writing, very interesting characters. I love the friendship between Laurence and Temeraire, they are precious. Yes, the pace is slow and there is less action than in the first book. Still, I enjoyed reading it. I will read the third book soon, hoping to finish the entire series by the end of the year!

Loving this series. This second book was not quite as good as the first, with more military/political bits than I prefer but still truly enjoyed it, I found myself losing focus during some of it. Looking forward to the next one.
Not nearly as good as the first book, just a decent follow up.

book_b.title: Uprooted
book_b.user_review:
I'm a father of two little girls, and as such, I've been heavily bombarded by fairy tales on the past few years. Even though I like the stories, I'm already nauseated by the same themes used on them over and over. And that is the cool thing about Uprooted. Let's call it "fairy tale for grown-ups". 
 Once upon a time, in a land far far away, there was a valley where people lived, worked and were happy. On the dark wood, however, evil things lurked, and no one came near it willingly. High on the valley there was a tower, and on top of it lived a Dragon. Once every ten years, the Dragon came to the valley, chose one young girl, and took her to his tower. Sounds familiar? 
 Warning, minor spoilers ahead. I won't tell anything that isn't told very early on the book but if you don't want to keep on reading, just know that it is a great book, and you should read. Ok? Right... 
 Moving on... The Dragon isn't really a winged creature. It is a mage, sort of the lord of the valley. Our heroine, lovely and clumsy Agnieszka, has the right age to be chosen, but everyone knows that the Dragon will choose Kasia, the beautiful and talented girl that everyone loves, but no one dares to get too attached, for obvious reasons. When the dragon comes, however, Agnieszka is the one chosen, after a strange magical test. She is taken to the tower, and after some initial struggle, she finally understands that she's to be trained to control her own magical powers. 
 That is enough of spoiler for now. Sufficient to say that like a tree, the story grows and grows, until it becomes really large. And it kept surprising me over and over, one climax on top of the other. At some point I said to myself - "hey, this book is heading toward a great conclusion!" But then I realized that I was just halfway through the book - and each apex was actually the opening scene for yet another complication to the plot. 
 Before I go, I'd like to point out some other good things about the book: the strength of the friendship between Agnieszka and Kasia (which drives a good portion of the story); the Dragon's personality, one of the grumpiest and surliest mages I've ever seen; and the magic system, which shows lovely contrasts between the Dragons by-the-book magic vs Agnieszka's intuitive one. 
 I wouldn't recommend the audio version, though. Didn't like the narrator very much - she has (or does) some sort of Russian accent that takes away some of the fun of the story.

sample_reviews.review_text: Great book, although there were points I was frustrated with how much they seemed to repeat the same thing through out the chapter. Otherwise the book had a great plot line and great character development. I loved how it started and finished within the same book and didn't drag on to other books. I would recommend this book to anyone

Actual stars 3.5-3.75 
 I'm not much for fairytales but Uprooted was pretty enjoyable for the most part. 
 Sarkan is a wizard who lives a solitary life except for the company of one girl. He would choose a girl at the age of 17 from one of the villages surrounding the evil and corrupted Woods every 10 years and keep them in his tower. After the 10 years are up the girls could leave and return to their village. But the girls now women would never remain in their villages for very long or decide to marry, their lives now seem destined for a different course. 
 It is that time again when Dragon (aka Sarkan) is about to choose a new girl for his tower. Everyone one in the village thinks that Sarkan is going to choose Kasia because she is the more beautiful of all the eligible girls and therefore taught by her mother to cook and other domestic duties that she will need. But to everyone's surprise Sarkan picks Agnieszka, definitely not the most put together girl with rips and stains regularly on her clothes and her hair in a tangled mess most of the time. And no domestic abilities to speak of. 
 Sarkan and Agnieszka have a tumultuous relationship from the start. He barely speaks to her and when he does he insults her and is very impatient with her clumsiness in cooking and household chores and especially her appearance. Agnieszka is not sure what reason Sarkan would have for choosing her until he shows her what she has to offer and it will alter her life as well as the future of the villages surrounding The Wood. 
 Sarkan and Agnieszka have a complex relationship. First of all, Sarkan pretty much abducted her, or I guess she was technically "given" to him by her village so poor Agnieszka is scared to death of this cranky reclusive old but not old man. And everything she does is not right. She can't cook, can't clean without making a mess. If the kitchen were a person and she fought the kitchen, the kitchen looked like it won with food and dirt on her clothes and her hair unkempt all the time only earned Agnieszka sharp looks and biting comments from Sarkan. She could do no right and his impatience was constant. 
 Somewhere along the way things started to change. You felt a companionship of sorts grow between the two. Not exactly comfortable but civil. Through their both trying to stop The Wood from corrupting of all of the land Sarkan and Agnieszka became even closer. But their was still the awkwardness of her being held against her will. 
 This was a fairytale type of story I could get into for the most part. It had a bit of a romantic feel at times as Sarkan and Agnieszka got to know each other a bit. But there was still an irritation he had with her and she had to deal with being kept in the tower. Plus once they got into a routine than they had to deal with The Wood. So sentiments went to the wayside. 
 Even though Sarkan was a bit crotchety most of the time but it was endearing because he was never cruel and nice not to see an insta love develop. That gets old sometimes. Sometimes you need some good old tension. 
 The only thing I think really annoyed me was how much time went into the battles with The Wood. It felt too long and I got bored some of the time. 
 I guess I just wanted more development between Sarkan and Agnieszka and less Woods fighting. 
 This book gives me hope that they are other enjoyable type of fairytale reads out there. I'm looking forward to trying a couple more.

3 1/2 really, and sometimes 3, there were many things that i didn't really like but the overall feeling is one of enjoyment. loved the writing and the world, really didn't like the fighting scenes (but then that's me) but they were portrayed superbly and left you breathless. the characters, well can't say they were all that well defined, maybe and didn't like that it all came so easy for Agnieszka. and oooh i didn't like the maybe unnecessary sex scene, it felt shoved it and couldn't see any reason for it. so piece by piece alot of things that i didn't like but overall liked it alot and enjoyed it alot and would love to see what friend think

I think what Uprooted suffered from most in my reading of it was the over-hype it received before I even started it - Honestly, it didn't have a chance to live up to all of the accolades it had to stand against. First, it had five "Employee Recommendation" stickers on it at my local bookstore - That's an absurd amount, so I knew it must be good. Then, some people that I know were talking about it with an excitement and reverence that made me think that Uprooted is going to be the Next Big Thing, so my expectations were great indeed, but the clincher was when my wife devoured it over a rainy weekend and expounded her love for the story and its characters. No book could live up to such heady praise, and Uprooted, to put it bluntly, didn't. It couldn't. 
 That all said, this was a very well told story with some very interesting takes on magic and fantasy, and Novik is clearly an imaginative juggernaut with her well considered planning and unveiling of twists. Very enjoyable, but I do feel that the book possibly suffered from a lack of copy-editing - There were some parts that meandered unnecessarily (but never for too long, luckily), some obvious tropes come in to play where I was hoping to be surprised by a different angle, a couple of awkwardly worded sentences that took me out of my groove, and at some parts the pacing just didn't feel right or slowed down when I was ready to speed up, but even that was forgivable thanks to Novik's attention to the details of the scene. 
 Was it the best book I've ever read? Of course not. Was it well-written and enjoyable? Absolutely.
Outstanding fantasy with a unique voice and compellingly original plot. Very impressed with the writing.

For someone who doesn't read high fantasy, being me, I read and loved this book so that says a ton. I'm always pro girl power 110% but this book had me falling for the heroine's counterpart...who was a guy. Great magic concept and I loved watching the heroine develop and grow and react as the story went on. I hope so badly for a sequel because I did not want to leave this world! The imaginary was spot on and was not over detailed or dragged out like how I felt in a Tolken book. The ending totally blindsided me which I love because usually I foreshadow correctly in books and it left me guessing. beautiful cover and story and it makes me even more want to become a tree more than I ever had before. This is one of those books you read by a new to you author then you crave ALL their books which I will begin to collect as soon as I find them! loved it!

Update: Re-read this in conjunction with the notes I'm taking from Structuring Your Novel by KM Weildand and this book is actually perfect in terms of the plot structure and pacing. Reading it as a writer rather than a reader has given me a greater appreciation of how Novik is able to keep cranking up the conflict. This book kept me on the edge of my seat, even as a re-read! I purchased the audiobook for this exercise...these factors have led me to change my rating from 4 to 5 stars. 
 What a perfect book, and I cannot say THANK YOU enough to Naomi Novik for writing a standalone fantasy in the era of series that authors do not finish in a timely manner! There's so much to love here. The magic system/spells were reminiscent of those found in Harry Potter, Agnieszka was a plucky heroine, the Dragon was a curmudgeon that you couldn't help but admire, the evil Wood was scary as hell. The only reason I didn't give it 5 stars is that I wish it had a little more in the way of romance. Nonetheless I really enjoyed this book and the patrons of my library are about to be bombarded with recommendations to read this if they haven't already.

Holy crap. I don't have words that can do this book justice. 
 Without a doubt, easily the best book I have read this year (and it's the 96th book I've read in the last six months if that puts it into perspective for anyone). It might honestly be the best if not one of the best books I have read ever. I don't even really life fantasy that much. I often avoid fantasy books like the plague. But I'm converted. If other fantasy authors put this kind of effort and love into the writing, I'll give them a try. 
 I have so much love for this book. It was a truly enchanting and magical experience. The world building was so beautiful and rich that it was timeless and seamless. The mythology was logical and it stayed within its confines in such a satisfying and comforting way that I felt like I actually understood how it all worked, like it could actually be real. 
 The emotional element was incredible, all the characters were well rounded and even the minor characters were easy to understand. Just everything and everyone was incredible. 
 I'm struggling not to just ramble amorous verses about the wonders of this book. 
 The treatment of death was almost comforting.. when I die I want to be encased in a tree, please. 
 Even the ending was well executed and the whole this was just a beautiful experience and this book is just 
 it's so good okay 
 please believe me 
 buy it 
 read it 
 please 
 your life will be better for it. 
 Excuse my while I just drown in my feelings for this book.

This book was very promising at the start. I loved the premise and I liked the narrating voice and the magic was very interesting but the story developed quite slowly and somehow, I lost interest along the way. What seemed quite magical at the start became dull, as if it was too convoluted and I was anxious for a resolution. It felt like a missed opportunity, I don't know why since the book was well written and imaginative, but it fell a bit short for me. *shrugs*

What an excellent book. The writing style was very clear, I greatly enjoyed reading from Agnieszka's perspective. The characters, the world and the flow of the book was excellent. I highly recommend this book, it's definitely one of my favourites this year.

reference_books.title: S.
reference_books.review_text:
Prieks par gramatu sakas jau tas sanemsanas bridi. Beidzot ari gramatu lasitaji var aprakstit gramatas izpakosanas procesu. Gramatai par noformejumu uzreiz dodu miljons punktus no desmit. Sakuma viss ir iepakots smuka melna vacina ar uzrakstu S. Tad tu atples uzlimiti un no kastites iznem jau pavisam citu gramatu ar nosaukumu "Ship of Theseus". Gramata izskatas ka no bibliotekas nakusi. Vina ir maksligi novecinata, lapas ir nodzeltejusas, vaks nedaudz apbruzats uz mugurinas bibliotekas uzlime. Ieksa vakos saspiesti zimodzini, kad gramata panemta lasisanai un atgriezta. Un, protams, blakus tekstam sarakstitas citu lasitaju anotacijas. Bet viss jau nebeidzas tikai ar anotacijam, gramata ir saliktas ieksa piezimju lapinas, avizu kserokopijas, vestules, atklatnites un pat kads mistisks sifresanas disks. Tas viss kopa rada iespaidu, ka tu tiesam esi atradis svesa cilveka milako gramatu. 
 image 
 Ari pati gramata pec satura neliek vilties. S. stasts ir aizraujoss, un, iespejams, tiesi seit ir iesifreta Starka patiesa identitate. Varonis sak no nulles, un vina personibas attistibu varam noverot tiesi. Ka no cilveka bez atminas un pagatnes S. klust par revolucionaru, slepkavu un teroristu. Par biznesa aklumu pret cilveku ciesanam un naudas varu par cilvekiem. Jau si stasta del vien ir verts gramatu izlasit. Lasitaju komentari ir paralela gramata, vini te risina ne tikai savas attiecibas, bet megina atminet to, kas ir Starka. Atskiriba no manis, vini ir lasijusi ari parejos Starkas darbus, vinu pasaule sim autoram ir veltiti daudzi raksti un konspiraciju teorijas. Lasitajam no malas ir jaiztiek ar sim pamestajam zinasanu drumstalam, lai kaut nedaudz censtos lidzdarboties saja petniecibas procesa. Un tad vel ir gramatas tulkotajas Filomenas vestijums Starkam, autoram, kuru vina ir milejusi lielu sava muza dalu. Vinas velme pavestit autora, kurs tad ir nodevis vina identitati, un kas ir noticis patiesiba. Tas viss ir nosifrets zemsvitras piezimes. Lai lasitajam butu vieglak savienot visus gramatas pasaules gabalinus kopa, te paliga nak gramata ieliktas pastkartes, vestules un uz salvetes uzzimeta karte. 
 Pats lasisanas process ir diezgan nogurdinoss, esmu paradis uzreiz izlasit visu, kas rakstits lapaspuse un tad doties talak. Ja ar pamattekstu problemas nav, tad ar komentariem gan ir grutak. Jo viena lapaspuse var atrasties dazados laikos ierakstiti komentari un var gadities, ka tu vel nemaz isti nesaproti kontekstu. Tad tu nedaudz paskir uz prieksu vai atpakal un tiec skaidriba (vai ari netiec), ka tads kugis, kur vejs pus, tur ari kugo. Sakuma bija gruti ielasities, bet ar laiku lieta aizgaja. 
 Vispar iesaku izlasit visiem, kuriem ir interese ari par gramatu, kas nav sarakstita tiri pec tradicionalas modes un ir gatavi veltit laiku tam, lai atrastu teksta sleptas nozimes. Gramatai lieku 9 no 10 ballem. No tam, kuras man tik driz neaizmirsisies, un loti iespejams, ka pec kada laika parlasisu, lai atrastu to, ko esmu palaidis garam. Lasisana sagadaja patiesu prieku.

reference_books.title: The Player of Games (Culture, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Banks ir viens liels negantnieks, izlasiju vina pirmo Kulturas serijas gramatu un sagribejas man izlasit vinas visas. Otro saku lasit bezmaz vai tulit pec pirmas pabeigsanas. Ta sakot, kamer vel nav katla tvaika spiediens nokrities. 
 Kads kulturas iedzivotajs Gurgeh ir vislabakais speletajs kads vien jebkad visuma bijis. Protams, no tiem, kuriem saprata koeficients ir 1. Vinam vissarezgitakas speles noteikumu iemacisanas aiznem vien paris dienas. Un pec neliela trenina vins ir praktiski neuzvarams. Tomer ar laiku tada dzive vinam klust garlaiciga un sak pietrukt istu spelu. Tacu salidzinosi nesen Kultura ir sastapusies ar kadu imperiju, kura pats galvenais ir spele Azad. Tikai no tavam prasmem Azad spele ir atkarigs katra imperijas iedzivotaju stavoklis sabiedriba. Gurgeh tiek piedavats uzspelet. 
 Ta ka Kultura valda pilniga laimiba un saticiba, maksligo intelektu stingra uzraudziba. Katrs var nodarboties ar visu, ko vins vien velas, galvenais nekaitet citiem, resursi ir neierobezoti, un visi dzivo ka miljardieri. Kad lasiju, tad man prata ienaca doma, tad tada bus Riga, kad pie varas tiks Elerte un ieviesis robottehnologijas. Bet vispar vilka pec sen berniba lasitiem attistita komunisma ieskicejumiem. Autors gan nav gajis tik talu, ka apgalvo, ka te katrs strada tapat vien, jo vinam to nosaka iekseja parlieciba. Te cilveki lielakoties citigi slaistas. Tomer tie, kuriem ikdiena ir apnikusi vienmer var iestaties kontaktu nodala un censties parliecinat citas civilizacijas pievienoties Kulturai. Gurgeh gan nav tads laimes mekletajs, tomer ari vinu var piespiest darboties Kulturas intereses. 
 Pats Azad speles apraksts autoram ir sanacis labu labais. Nav pateikts nekas konkrets, nav iztirzati likumi vai figurinas, lasitajam tiek lauts izteloties speli pasam, un tas ir vislabakais. Vinam, lasitajam, pietiek zinat, ka ta ir loti gruta un pat tris gadu laika vins neiemacisies pat mazu dalu no tas likumiem. Ari pasi spelu apraksti ir aizraujosi, gandriz it ka lasitu realus notikumus. Autoram ir izdevies radit ari trisdzimumu hominidu rasi, kur ir skaidri saprotams, ko kurs isti dara pecnaceju radisanai. Tradicionali zinatniskaja fantastika autori sada gadijuma iztiek ar "sepulas" analogu. 
 Kopuma labs lasamais, interesanta socialpolitiska sistema, kas balstita uz individa prasmi spelet kadu noteikti speli. Dzimumu lidztiesiba vai precizak nelidztiesiba trisdzimumu rase. Pardomas vai sada veida izraudzitie labakie lideri nerada sabiedribu, kas ir orienteta uz katra individa totalu dominanci par parejiem zemak stavosajiem. Gramatai lieku 9 no 10 ballem. Patlaban labakais no cikla darbiem ko lasijis. Iesaku izlasit jebkuram zinatniskas fantastikas cienitajam, var drosi lasit nelasot parejo ciklu.
