What did I just read? I'm so excited when it came out, and I went to the bookstore right away, and I went home to read this. It's very clear I had finished reading this during our FINALS, and I'm so mad and disappointed. DID I JUST READ A FANFICTION? I know it's just a script, but my anticipation of this book went downhill right away, after I close the book after reading it. But there're things I loved about this book, but the majority was a disappointment. Sorry Potterhead, I myself also a Potterhead, but this script to the magical play is nothing.

My expectations were pretty low going into this, and I was still underwhelmed. The story was juvenile and the dialogue so cheesy. Perhaps the actors delivered the lines in such a way that they came off as profound and meaningful. But, I felt like I was reading a children's book about the value of friendship. 
 By using time travel and dream sequences, the writers brought back so many characters from the books that it was too much. Do I really need to see Umbridge, Cedric Diggory, Moaning Myrtle, and Aunt Pentunia again? Not really. This kind of story manipulation in order to mention as many Harry Potter things as possible reminded me of Ready Player One and its overuse of 80's references. I hated that book. 
 There were several moments that had me thinking, "WTF?" but I will focus on just two here. First off, I'm still not over the fact that VOLDEMORT PROCREATED. Let that sink in for a second...okay, so Voldemort allegedly had sex with Bellatrix Lestrange, knocked her up, and has a daughter that the entire Wizarding World knew nothing about. Not only does the concept of Voldemort having sex carry a major ick factor, it makes zero sense. Voldemort was a villain and a monster. An elaborate spell/potion was required for him to even return to a somewhat human form. And he emerged from that cauldron with his fertility? Really? Plus, Voldemort didn't respect anyone but himself. You could argue that Lestrange had romantic feelings for Voldemort, but I'm pretty sure that Voldemort would have viewed relations with Lestrange, or anyone really, beneath him. Plus, he believed he could make himself immortal and rule over the entire wizarding world, so why would he have any desire to have a baby? Voldemort doesn't need a sidekick. And if he's immortal, he doesn't need someone to take over for him when he's dead. So...how does this make any sense at all? Secondly, Ron was so drunk when he married Hermione, that he doesn't remember their wedding? Really? Ok, wait, maybe I can't stop at just two things...I was also really bothered by the fact that Albus, Scorpius and Delphi were able to get into Hermione's office using Alohomora. Hermione would have used more protective spells. Also, the trolly witch randomly sprouting talons from her hands was creepy and weird. I am sighing, shaking my head, and choosing to believe that nothing in this play is canon. 
 Overall, I think the most disappointing part for me was finding out what happened to Harry, Ron and Hermione after the seventh book ended. A large part of me would rather have remained ignorant. We Harry Potter fans got seven wonderful books with a happy ending. I have closure. I don't need to read a story about a 40-year old Harry and his tumultuous relationship with his son. And if I ever get an inkling to revisit the Wizarding World, I have so many options. I can re-read the books, re-watch the movies, visit the theme park in Orlando, try to make butterbeer at home, listen to the movie soundtracks, visit Pottermore, etc. This play is fan-fiction. And fan-fiction is probably the only part of the Harry Potter fandom that I have not explored, and don't have a desire to. 
 Rowling should have just left Harry alone with All was well. 
 Further Reading: 
 1. Initial Reactions to "Harry Potter and the Cursed Child": A Rage Filled Catharsis 
 2. Top Five "Cursed Child" Plot Holes 
 3. Why It's Important Albus and Scorpius Aren't In Love 
 4. Top Five Random "Cursed Child" Moments 
 5. Why I Was Able to Enjoy "Cursed Child"

I really wanted to give 2.5 stars to this, but I can't, so I am constrained by the laws of mathematical rounding to give it three. I wanted it to be a home run, but it was a double, because of a bad throw from the outfield. 
 The first half of the play was not very well written, it seemed hackneyed and contrived. None of the characters, as I know them from the books, were acting or speaking in ways consistent with their development over 7 novels. It was frustrating. 
 The second half was better, but was not good enough to pull the 1 star I was prepared to give the book--based on the reading of the first half--a higher rating. 
 If you are a fan of the novels, you will find this screenplay passable, but I don't think you will enjoy it any more than I did and you will reach the end of the book wishing there were more to give praise about.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I'm not going to go super into this, but this read like bad fanfiction. 
 I felt like it undermined the characters and the message of the original books. The fact that Harry, Ron, and hermione supposedly taught their kids to hate Malfoy doesn't make sense and I don't see that actually happening after all they went through. 
 The second act is a slight against Hermione and her wonderful character. She did not need to marry Ron in order to be a successful and kind person. She was all that and more before Ron even had a slight clue that he liked her. Absolute garbage. 
 In general though, the story doesn't make much sense and I don't feel like it should have even been written. I'm sure seeing the play is a bit of a different experience, but the story and the characters are the same so I don't think it would change my opinion much.
Oh. Oh dear God. Oh, that just wasn't fair, making me feel all the feels again!!

After seeing the heavily mixed reviews for Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, I went in with low expectations but a forgiving attitude (J.K. Rowling can do no wrong, after all). However, I don't accept this story as canon. It's good fanfiction, but it's not gospel. 
 Although there are touches of the magical whimsy that never failed to fill my heart with giddiness, the play format ultimately robs the reader of any true emotional connection. There's simply not enough time to provide the characterization and depth that the Harry Potter universe deserves. Some of the dialogue was hilarious and poignant; at other times, it felt cheesy and forced. Even so, it's clear that the story has good intentions, and I appreciated the complex father-son relationship between Harry and Albus. The conflict between the two of them was what felt most authentic and interesting to me. In addition, the plot provides a lot of fan service in terms of referencing past characters and events, which made this a fitting tribute to the series. 
 Some readers hate Albus for being whiny and imperfect, but I think that's the point--he's a misfit. Still, I doubt anyone would disagree when I say Scorpius is the real MVP. Many fans tend to view Draco Malfoy through an idealized lens, one that Rowling didn't intend for a villain, and Scorpius is a reflection of Draco's soft caramel center. I'm cutting the writers some slack for giving certain characters more stage time than others; it's impossible to involve everyone in the action when you have time constraints. 
 The plot surprised me in a good way, at least for the first third. I would've never thought of that concept, and the narrative arc itself was very tightly constructed. Buuuut...the deus ex machina moments and one-dimensional villain ruined it for me. They felt like cheap solutions to complex problems. Plus, all the logistical issues involving time travel and government security made it difficult to suspend disbelief. The ending was kind of interesting, though, with the parallels between Albus and Harry when it came to both of them feeling responsible for the death of an innocent. 
 Despite the story's flaws, I can't wait until this play makes it to the States.

This book was an amazing instalment to the Harry Potter collection. You follow Harry, Ginny and his three children through their own experiences of Hogwarts, in particular, Albus. Albus feels as though he has some big boots to fill following his dad's heroic legacy. However, we find that through the ups and downs of Albus' experiences, friendship still wins over anything else. 
 The way in which this is written is so magical, even as a scripted piece, however, it would have been nicer to have experienced this in the form of a novel instead. I truly would love to see how the theatre transforms the magic in the book onto the stage, something which would probably still baffle me! The main love that I had for this book was the relationship between Scorpius Malfoy and Albus Dumbledore, it was something that I felt as though was weaved into this plot very well, and it should be emphasised more in literature. Overall, it pacified my need for magic and the world of Harry and his friends as they complete another task, but this time to protect their own children. I would highly recommend this to anyone who has a profound love for the magic of Harry Potter.

A faithful continuation of the story right from where the epilogue to the previous book left off. Although others disagree, I find the characters, both new and familiar, to be just as fully fleshed out and engaging as in the previous adventures. It also fleshes out a vital little part of the prior story that gives a little more dimension to some of the characters that we only encountered briefly in the past.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Drivel. Pure drivel. The only reason this gets two stars is for Harry Potter-based nostalgia. I think the characters of Albus and Scorpius were interesting, and I'd have liked to read more about them, but the horrid, fanfiction-y plot made this an unbearable read. What an utter disappointment.

reference_books.title: The Penelopiad
reference_books.review_text: I have to admit that I've only read The Handmaid's Tale by Margaret Atwood before now. To remedy that, I read The Penelopiad which is the story of Odysseus and Penelope of Homeric myths, but from the point of view of Penelope. I enjoyed the insertion of the twelve maids that were hung by Odysseus when he returned from his Odyssey as a chorus, much like how most Greek epic poems included a chorus of maidens that told a bit of the story from a third person point of view. Overall, since I have always enjoyed books based on Greek myths, like Rick Riordan's Percy Jackson series, I really liked this book. At only 198 pages, it's not overly long at all. My only beef is that a portion of the book, towards the end, got a bit hyper-feminist for my taste, but this is Margaret Atwood we are talking about!

reference_books.title: Ready Player One
reference_books.review_text: I would give this book five stars if only there a bit less gaming jargon, and if it hadn't taken a few chapters to really start to capture my interest. However, total props to the author for coming up with such an original concept and capturing my heart with all its wonderful 80s nostalgia and pop cultural references. If a sequel is in the works, count this girl excited!

reference_books.title: Winter (The Lunar Chronicles, #4)
reference_books.review_text: I would say that I was upset that the series has ended, what has become my favorite YA series, and indeed one of my favorite series period, but then I would be forgetting that I still have Stars Above and I'm so excited about that! Winter was a bit long, but I still gave the book 5 stars because the ending completely satisfied me.

reference_books.title: The Hunt for Red October (Jack Ryan Universe, #4)
reference_books.review_text:
This was my first Tom Clancy book! I chose this book because it was the first Jack Ryan book he wrote, and also because it was the one Jack Ryan movie I haven't seen yet. I love Patriot Games, Clear and Present Danger, and The Sum of All Fears, so I hoped I'd like the book. The book centers around a Soviet nuclear submarine captain, Marko Ramius, and his crew aboard the Red October, as Captain Ramius hatches a plan to defect to the United States with his more senior officers who want to defect too. Jack Ryan is a CIA analyst living in London. When he sees pictures of the Red October and their "caterpillar" propulsion system which allows the submarine to sail virtually undetected, he hops a flight to Langley, and from there the adventure begins. 
 I'm of two minds about this book. Certainly the tension is very well written. There's lots of twists and turns that keep your attention. On the other hand, I bored with all of the technical details found throughout the book. It made the book feel very long, longer than it actually is. However, because the story itself was so good, I hope to get my hands on Patriot Games soon. I genuinely think that the only reason why I don't give this book a higher rating is because the technical jargon, and that should be not as prevalent in Patriot Games. I can see why men like Tom Clancy more. That said, I definitely recommend the Jack Ryan series to anyone who likes Brad Thor or WEB Griffin.

reference_books.title: Middlesex
reference_books.review_text:
I just finished "Middlesex" for the transgender category for BookRiot's #ReadHarder challenge and I really enjoyed it. The book is long, and I listened to the audiobook, so that was 21 hours for the book. Nevertheless, I didn't feel too daunted and the story of Cal's grandparents and parents, was really interesting. Jeffrey Eugenides builds a story that feels like it had to be an actual true story, by using real events in the Greco-Turkish War, the beginnings of the Nation of Islam, and the rise and fall of Detroit. 
 However, that is only the first half of the book. The second half focuses solely on Callie/Cal and the journey Callie takes to learn of her origins and her sex. Since the book was published in 2001, some words like "hermaphrodite" have fallen out of fashion in favor of "intersex." Bear that in mind while reading the book. Otherwise, I highly recommend it!

book_a.title: Men Explain Things to Me
book_a.user_review:
I only read this because I needed to read a book on feminism for my #ReadHarder challenge. I had hoped it was going to be a funny book about men "mansplaining" stuff to an intelligent woman. That was only the first chapter. The ensuing chapters pretty much were the author talking about how violent men are, how violence is only a male thing, how they rape, murder, and abuse and get away with it. If there had been one chapter on the subject, that'd be fine, but it was the whole rest of the book. 
 So, not much by way of humor in the book. Just a lot of anger towards men. I'm not saying I'm disagreeing with most of her premise. There are a lot of men who are abusive or feel entitled where women are concerned and that's a problem. I just started this book with different expectations.

sample_reviews.review_text: I really really wanted to like this book more- I think it started off strong, got really ramble-ey and muddled in the middle, and then ended on a good note. I liked the strong parts, but through the middle it felt like I was just reading to finish. Despite this, her writing and feminist stances are great, and I'd like to check out some of her other books.
Mandatory reading, not only for women.

Rebecca Solnit is often credited with originating the now-popular term, "mansplaining". I love using that word. It's a funny word. It captures an important social injustice/stupidity. 
 Anyway, I reeeeally disliked the only other book by Rebecca Solnit that I've read and, alas, beyond the first essay (on the dark hilarity of mansplainery), I really disliked this. Her writing just ain't for me. I find it so humorless (excepting the first essay), so self-important, so indulgent; pop intellectualism of the worst kind. I was also a little leery of her occasional notes about the awful fem injustices in those Other Lands. White privileged lady speaking for poor oppressed Arab ladies... gah. Or even worse: just ALLUDING to it, leaving us to fill the blank with our own stereotyped ideas. Gaaah.

rather than detailing the subtle sexism in the unconscious actions and conversations women have with men, this author dives deep into the weeds of sexist war where every woman fears for her life. ironically her idea was spoiled and not properly explained in this book which provides a history of sexism rather than details on mansplaining.

"There are other things I'd rather write about, but this affects everything else... Think of how much more time and energy we would have to focus on other things that matter if we weren't so busy surviving." 
 Rebecca Solnit writes passionately and well (I've never seen so many apt uses of quotidian!) about a pervasive culture that encourages masculine dominance and control to the detriment of women and those in the LGBTQ community, who are subjected to physical and emotional violence and eradication. The Virginia Woolf essay has a tonal dissonance, but is still worth reading.

Overall, the essays were well-written and poignant (though the Virginia Woolf-centric one barely held my interest), but it wasn't exactly the light material to read before bed. Only the first essay was humorous, so be prepared for some academic reading and analysis.

The first two essays in this should be required for all men to read. I think the second essay, about violence against women, is even more powerful than the first, but the first is probably more actionable for readers.

These essays are like hearing feminism argued by a well-read, news junkie friend. Topics like rape culture, gender pay gap, mansplaining, marriage equality and Virginia Woolf -- all of which have been done to death -- feel fresh. For instance, there's the idea that feminism allowed same-sex marriage to become an issue by arguing for equality within relationships: "Those who are threatened by marriage equality are, many things suggest, as threatened by the idea of equality between heterosexual couples as same-sex couples."

I'll be honest, I tend not to read feminist books because they tend to make me even more angry than I already am. I am the kind of person that waits in the dark for a man to try to mansplain to me, so i ban bite his jugular. 
 But I gave this a shot and it was hightly recommended and I thought, why not? 
 I was afraid that it would say the same things that we already know, but instead this book gives several interesting inputs, like how the battle for LGBT rights has helped the women's cause because it has changed the idea of what a man has to be and how gay marriages are truly between equal, and their recognition will eventually help with the distruction of the hierarchical models in eterosexual marriage. 
 There are some slow parts, but despite that it deserves to be read.

3.5. 
 Thought provoking, and as a woman really made me reconsider what's going on in the world.

book_b.title: World War Z: An Oral History of the Zombie War
book_b.user_review:
Wow! I had no idea that I would ever like a zombie book! This was recommended to me by one of my Readers' Advisory classmates and it was a GOOD recommendation. I think I only got a bit bored once, but it was only for a couple of pages. That's what is magical about this book. The premise is that the narrator of the book compiled the transcripts of dozens of interviews with people who were touched by a decade long world war against zombies that occurred a few years before. Each interview is only a few pages long. Interviews were conducted around the world with people in the military, former world leaders, an astronaut, some everyday ordinary people, and one interesting greedy pharmaceutical businessman. I only got bored once when a submersible expert was interviewed. 
 The interviews lend insight into how the zombie apocalypse started, the years during the war, and how the living finally began to gain victories against the undead. Although the imagery was a bit gross, especially during the beginning of the book, it was not too much for me, and I don't like gross stuff at all. It was well written. The author did a great job of changing "voices" between all the different characters introduced in the novel. It was a very unique concept and it was executed quite well. 
 ***UPDATE*** 
 It seems I wrote the above review four years ago when I was a library science student. I've just finished listening to the audiobook version and the book is still just as good as I remember it. This audio book is definitely one of the best productions, mainly because they got such a great cast to play all of the different characters. Max Brooks was the interviewer, and he did a great job reading his own book. My favorites were Jeri Ryan, Mark Hamill, and Masi Oka. Totally recommend!

sample_reviews.review_text: I did NOT like this as much as I had hoped. In fact I did stop reading it. I had to put "read" in order to get it off my "currently reading" list. It is basically testimonies given by various people around the world and is absolutely NOTHING like the movie. Which is usually a good thing, but in this case the movie was fairly good and entertaining. This book just bored me. Sorry, and I did not finish reading.

This book is a series of interviews from various survivors of the Zombie War that takes place in the future (and not too far, it seems). It goes from Patient Zero in China through how people fight to survive, then to fight back and finally, the clean up. 
 I hate zombie movies. I don't even like parodies of them, which makes me really surprised I enjoyed this book so much. I think it's the notable lack of zombies (they were shoved into the background). I don't know a lot about politics or economics, and I'm sure someone more learned in those areas might have a problem with what Brooks did with global politics and economics, but it worked for me. I have a feeling Brooks had a fun time with the breaking down of various countries and organizations. People who follow politics will probably get more out of the clever things slipped in. Or at least, be more annoyed by them. 
 I hooked a friend on to the audio book version and he pointed out to me something I missed about the description of Yonkers, where men faced down countless zombies and were defeated. I went back and reread and I laughed for five minutes. Because, no, it is horrific, but the people Brooks mentions that die--I don't know how I missed it, but I don't watch much Fox News, either. I do think it's easy to make this book political commentary, but I also think it depends on what the reader brings to the table. I missed a lot of the digs at the left and right because I don't pay attention to some of these people. Caricatures are what they are. People will exploit them, but I don't think it has to ruin the book, unless someone lets it. It was the stories of the people that drew me, in the end. I think the most horrific interviews were the ones where there are holes or silence. The interview about Korea was an example of this. 
 The relation between the zombie virus and the avian flu is pretty pronounced, and I think my experience of the book was a result of listening to a friend talk about his History of Medicine lectures with me over the subject. I am fearful of outbreaks. 
 This isn't a novel in the standard sense. Actually, it reminded me a lot of The Laramie Project, how through interviews you piece together a horrific event and the aftermath of it. I liked the book, but I also liked the audio book version since it gives you more of the individual "character" in each piece. It was my first time listening to an audio book all the way through, so it was interesting.

I don't really know what to say. I went into this book with high expectations. I always try my best to finish a book I have started, so this is a rarity. I liked the guys writing style. He was very informative and you could tell he enjoyed what he was doing. There was no plot to this one and I couldn't stay interested. He jumped around so much that I didn't even care where he was anymore. I ended up reading over 50 pages of it and couldn't tell you what happened. I regret to say, I could not finish.
Great book! Even if you aren't a "sci fi" fan, I think it's worth the read.

Everyone told me I would love this book, but no. With no main characters to give a crap about, and pretty much just technical story after story of how zombies came and how they fought them off I just couldn't get into it. I found my mind drifting after only 3-5 pages every time I picked the book up. I can see why it appeals to people, but when I get zombies, I want zombies attacking, not explanations of how people stopped zombies from attacking. The only story I enjoyed in the whole book was that of the rich people making a TV show out of their fortress from the zombies, only to be overtaken by the living. This just wasn't my thing... in any way shape or form!

Terrible, boring, awful, stupid, dumb.... 
 Hope the movie is better. I always like the book better than the movie, but this was no good.
I don't get the hype, made zombies boring.

Recommended to me by a friend who usually has spot-on taste in books. But I'm not really a zombie fan (I like vampires instead) and I just wasn't feeling the "testimonial" style of the book. It was a little dry.

This is a great book. A very pleasant surprise and not what I expected. It is about so much more than zombies. A real indictment of the times we live in and our reactions to events. I really loved this one!
Zombie fans should really enjoy this .

reference_books.title: Red Rising (Red Rising, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Red rising was a new experience for me in reading as it was quite different to the things I've read before. It forced the reader to use their brain with the constant tactical and strategical thinking of the characters. The plot was super intriguing and I'm very interested to see what will happen in the next book! 
 The characters is what really made this book. Darrow really reminds me of Jon Snow. They're both 'outcasts' if you will and gain trust from their people, break the system, and are more insightful than the current leadership. Sevro is my favourite and I'm super excited to see him in the next installments. He was probably made me laugh the most. Mustang is a really smart and kickass girl and i loved her so much. *SPOILER* When we found out she was the Jackal's sister i was shook! I thought she would betray Darrow* 
 One thing that i kind of had a problem with is that Darrow was basically invincible. Not in the fight with Cassius but in every other situation, he couldnt be defeated. Maybe because Eo's dream drives him but it was unrealistic. for example, why was every other house to easy to take?? 
 Overall, an entertaining read!

reference_books.title: Red Queen (Red Queen, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Red Queen was an alright book. I couldnt connect with Mare or any of the characters and the book did not have me invested in the story. The relationship between Cal and Mare was forced as heck and i did not feel a spark of anything while reading it. It took me a while to get in to it and when i did, it was spoiled for me. So lets start from the beginning. I liked the world building in this book as we got to learn about the different parts of the land that were effected by silvers. The main character was alright. She is supposed to be strong and independent and yes that is what she was but she wasnt anything special. The plot is so much like Hunger games and Throne of glass mixed together. Overall this book is alright. Mediocre at best as my friend Nat would say.

reference_books.title: A Court of Mist and Fury (A Court of Thorns and Roses, #2)
reference_books.review_text: I read it. I loved it. I'm excited to see what happens in the next book! I really didn't enjoy the first books as i found it bland/boring and I did not get attached to the characters. The only character that was interesting was Rhys ;). One of my favourite scenes of the book was the star fall scene, it was beautiful. If I were to write a whole review it would take too long so I'm just going to say that it was absolutely awesome!!

reference_books.title: Falling Kingdoms (Falling Kingdoms, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I enjoyed this book A LOT. It was a fast and easy read and the plot and characters were so good. I gave it 3 stars because compared to the other fantasy I have read it wasn't that well written but I feel that in that in the future books the writing is going to improve. I'm excited to continue with the series!!! :-)

reference_books.title: Carry On
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I loved story line of this book and the characters but I felt that the romance between Simon and baz was rushed and a bit too open for people who hated each other for seven years. It was a bit unrealistic. However I still loved them together OMG. I still had a lot of fun reading this book and would recommend to everyone. It's a fantasy book but it's written just like a contemporary so even non fantasy lovers can enjoy

book_a.title: A Game of Thrones (A Song of Ice and Fire, #1)
book_a.user_review: It was an okay book. The first book was to get the ball rolling but I still think it was an average book. If i do choose to read A Clash Of Kings then I do hope it is more action packed and that the story is more fast paced. If i could rate if i would have given this book 3 1/2.

sample_reviews.review_text: After reading through a few chapters, I skipped anything that didn't have "Daenerys" written on the top. She was the only remotely interesting character in the series because I actually cared what happened to her. I pretty much fell asleep when anyone else was narrating (particularly if it was one of the interminable chapters at the Wall...). How could a book that starts with the walking dead on page 1 be so bloody boring?
...Wow

UGH ok I had to stop myself from commenting in the thread because it would serve no purpose, but I have to vent here a little. 
 Just got done reading a series of posts on here where readers expressed their shock that people who didn't fall all over themselves for Game of Thrones existed (great quote here "god forbid they should hate the series" - and then they speculated as to why that is. 
 To date the thread has two main speculations: 
 - they can't stomach the rape (it's realistic in a medieval setting!) 
 bullshit - GRRM *MADE UP* the world that GoT takes place in. He intentionally chose to include rape. As for realism? So dragons and magic and whatnot is believable but omfg a medieval-ish fantasy without rape.. NO WAI! 
 My "favorite" of these was 
 "GRRM is still the best out there, so it's a huge shame that some people can't get past whatever pre-conceived notions [referring to the sex and paedophilia] they have to enjoy these books. " 
 Not liking rape is a perfectly valid reason for not reading a book, the part that bugged me is that this was frowned upon. Which implies that I should "get over" being offended by something (one commenter actually says this) in order to enjoy the books. No - I am sorry.. I don't think I'm going to _get over_ rape being portrayed as ok. Also childbrides and their subsequent rape - no thanks not in my fantasy! 
 - they can't read long books 
 That _must_ be it. I am just not intelligent enough of a reader to make it through a long book. Also the tie-in that because I don't read long books I also won't read books twice. (for the record I've read LoTR about 23 times AND I've made it through the Simarillion SO BITE ME) 
 I wish these people could take a step back from their fanboy/girl ism and take a minute to actually read what it is that they're typing and consider what it is that they are saying. 
 I didn't comment in the thread because doing so would make me have to join the group - something I didn't want to do. But thanks for reading the rant!

I don't know what else can I say that has not already been said about this book. But for those who are still thinking about reading it, I highly reccomend. It's damn good fantasy, well written, never boring.

Lo que no me gusto: 
 - El estilo de escritura. El autor hizo un info-dump masivo en este libro. Pienso que existen mejores maneras de dar informacion sobre el mundo, los personajes, etc. 
 - Lo aburrido que fue el libro. Me costo mucho mantenerme interesada, creo que me tomo mas de un mes terminarlo. La idea es buena, pero a mi parecer estuvo mal ejecutada. 
 - Que no me importo ninguno de los personajes. Sinceramente, pudieron haber muerto todos y me hubiese dado igual. 
 - Tener que lidiar con Sansa y Danaerys. No se que tanto le ven a esas ninas... 
 - Haber gastado dinero en el boxset. 
 Lo que me gusto: 
 - Que logre revender el boxset lololol.

Finished the ebook with less than an hour before it expired... whew! 
 What a great story! I expected the kings and knights of old; I didn't expect the undead, mages and dragons! Can't wait to get my hands on book 2: A Clash of Kings.
I did think the ending was a pretty good surprise. It just took a long time to get there. A long, long time...

I was pretty daunted by the prospect of starting this book, mainly because I had trouble making it through Lord of the Rings, and I had heard there were lots of names and families to keep track of in this book, too. However my fears were pretty much unfounded. I did look in the appendix once to check who somebody was, but most of the names aren't too weird or anything. Even though the book is pretty long, I had trouble putting it down because there was just so much intrigue. This isn't the kind of book I normally pick up, but I had heard so much about it that I just had to find out. It turned out I really liked it! I'm sure I'll be continuing with the series, but might have to read a few shorter books first.

Excellent book. Great character development and intricate plots lines. Throughly entertaining. 
 I'll do a full review when I finish the series.
Even if you have watched the show it is still well worth reading this book. There is much that is not covered in the tv show as is always the way.

book_b.title: Black Ice
book_b.user_review: Black Ice was given to me by my friend to read. She loved it and said I would to. The plot was interesting and it had you hooked from the first chapter. However, the book was very unrealistic. It isn't realistic that a man that has abducted turns out to be a smoking hot guy who happens to be good all along and falls in love with you. The story with Calvin was tragic and so sad. I know he was bad but his dad mentally abused him by telling him he was never good enough. The ending was very stupid. It was a happy ending for everyone but extremely unrealistic. The main character lives the rest of he life with this man that has perfect hair and body and lives on the beach. I don't know guys, this book wasn't bad but it didn't wow me at all.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Spoilers btw. 
 So I found this story overwhelmingly frustrating. I was actually sucked in right away. The first description the author used when explaining what a young girl who had been drugged was seeing ended up being an incredibly imaginative and beautiful piece of writing. Then we moved on to the actual story, and dear lord was it 80 leaps and bounds backwards for feminism everywhere. 
 I decided I hated the main character the moment she was complaining about not wanting her hands to smell like gas if she had to fill up her car by herself. However, I shrugged that off and expected that as this story continued, she would learn to be more self-reliant and less shallow. The sad thing is, I think the author really thinks that she accomplished this. I don't know in what universe girls make out with their kidnappers in the middle of the woods, good intentioned ones or no, but I just couldn't believe that was even included. I also couldn't believe she was supposedly in love with him in the end. I really wanted Britt to just become a bad ass, but that never happened. As a matter of fact, she bases her perception of herself on what men think of her. She's supposed to have gotten over this by the end, but it's still based on what her love interests see her as, and has nothing to do with being strong herself. And there was the whole grizzly bear story line that just kind of... went away. I really wanted the bear to eat the bad guy in the end. Instead it just stopped existing and everyone went about their business. Over all it's got some nice descriptions, but the story isn't really worth it.

I am utterly disappointed in this novel... 
 I'm not sure why but something about this story was off for me and it may be the unrealistic characters or love triangle. The characters annoyed me to no end in this novel and while the love story shored between Britt and Jude is fantastic the context in which it is set throws me for two. In a hellish scenario I couldn't imagine someone becoming romantically involved with one of their kidnappers, no matter their motives. 
 Overall this novel is sadly not going to become a favorite of mine.
Didn't care for the story line or the characters, just not a great read for me.

Lo lei por que me lo recomendaron y decian que era lo maximo. No soy de este tipo de genero pero decidi darle un chance a este. Esta por demas que es de lo mas estupida y llena de cliche. Unas estudiantes tontas y las estupideces que hacen... Definitivamente es lo peor que he leido (hasta hoy). 
 Definitivamente le puse [?] por que es la figura que mas me gusta, no se merece ni un piquito de estrella. Oh...! Y si esperas como yo, que al final se mejore, de un vuelco o te paguen por leerlo: eso no sucedera.

I really enjoyed this book!! I had it sitting on my bedside table for awhile and hadn't picked it up due to not so great reviews... I shouldn't have waited so long! I loved the setting and the mystery and the action! I also liked watching Britt find herself and her strength. What a great read!

Seriously? This book has such a weird plot. Talk about creepy. Honestly I didn't finish this book and I probably never will because of this deranged idea for a story. No offense to anyone who likes this book but I just can't get my head around it.

This book.... Was annoying as hell. 
 1) The main character and her best friend were extremely dim witted and irritating throughout the entire book. So stupid. Wow. 
 2) Why is Britt thinking of romance and how sexy her captor is? HE KIDNAPPED YOU. STOP IT. 
 3) Most of the book was "we hiked through the snow. Found shelter. So cold. Repeat." I wish there had been more action. 
 4) Shaun and Calvin are both EW. 
 5) The ending was too cheesy considering this book was supposed to be a thriller type story. 
 6) AND PROBABLY WHAT ANNOYED ME THE MOST, considering I am an astronomy lover, you wouldn't be able to see the Orion constellation in May. So that was an epic fail, Fitzpatrick.

i really liked the mystery in this book and how it somehow kept me on edge. Mason was a character that was dark and mysterious & that kept me intrigued. However as the story progresses i found it a little stupid as the characters were falling in love...??? Maybe this book was trying to portray Stockholm syndrome and was trying to allow readers to explore these areas?? It was an interesting read since ive never read about these situations before.

3,5 stars. 
 A great book with a very interesting story. I loved the mysteries and the fact that you couldn't trust a single person. A negative thing for me was the fact that it was a bit predictable at times. I didn't like how some characters were portrayed and the fact that the main character was kidnapped and her only concern was about her feelings for a boy she broke up with 8 months before. Other than that it was alright.

Well, I finished it. I blame the Fear Street books I read as a tween for enabling me to predict the endings so early in books. Eh, if this is all you have on hand read it and if there is anything else nearby, try that instead.

reference_books.title: Diary of a Wimpy Kid (Diary of a Wimpy Kid, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Worst book I have ever read. You may be thinking that I am taking this too far, but I'm not. If you read the book (which you really shouldn't) then you'll see what I'm trying to say. This book is way too short and every page is filled with pictures. This should be for second graders, not middle-schoolers. And even if it is for second graders, it is about middle school, which is a thing only middle-schoolers can relate to. The font size it too large, and the font is hard to read, because it's supposed to look like handwriting. There are no "worthy words" in this book, and it is a bad choice all around. DON'T READ THIS BOOK!

reference_books.title: Rodrick Rules (Diary of a Wimpy Kid, #2)
reference_books.review_text: I only read this because I was bored. I didn't want to read it, but I was just so bored and I had to. I feel that you need to finish a book series, even though it is bad. Let me tell you that this is NOTHING like middle school. Middle School is way more "normal" than that. The author probably just took all the middle school stereotypes and put them into a book series. Jeff Kinney is way past the middle school age, and that stuff may have happened in the 1980's, but not now. This should be written by middle schoolers who actually experience middle school life and remember it. Realistic Fiction? Yeah, right. This should be Fantasy because none of this stuff ever happens.

reference_books.title: The Last Straw (Diary of a Wimpy Kid, #3)
reference_books.review_text: Horrible. I really hate these series. These books take me about 20 minutes to read and less then a second to hate. Almost the whole book is full of these stupid pictures. I don't think this had anything similar to middle school at all. Never read this book ever.

reference_books.title: Dog Days (Diary of a Wimpy Kid, #4)
reference_books.review_text: I hate these books. Summer is nothing like this. I have a brother who is in middle school, and he is supposed to relate to this? No way. This is such a bad series. I literally cannot see why this series of books are so popular. None of these are funny or cool. And, after four years, you wouldn't even be in middle school anymore. These books are repetitive, horrible, picture-filled, and boring.

reference_books.title: The Maze of Bones  (The 39 Clues, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Not the best book, not the worst. I would rate this book 3/5 stars. The first books in the series are usually the worst because they introduce all the characters. I like some of the quotes, but there is not enough hard words in this, so it is at the reading level of about 5th grade, which is way too easy for me. I like the action and the genre, so I read this book. It's Ok, but not the best. You should read this if you like Realistic Fiction/Fantasy books and if you are in the 5th grade. I am not in 5th grade, but I still thought the book was Ok. I think this book deserves the rating of "Average."

book_a.title: Cabin Fever (Diary of a Wimpy Kid, #6)
book_a.user_review: Another horrible novel. I really should stop reading these. All these books have are pictures. They take me about half an hour to "read." You know why I put quotes around read, you really don't read these books, you look at the pictures and throw up. They are really badly drawn and I just hate these novels. They are really boring. Do not read these books.

sample_reviews.review_text: Another solid entry in the Wimpy Kid series. I feel that Kinney has already used up some of his best material, but he still came up with some solid stories and events that had me really laughing. Even if this book is not as good as his first three, it is still better than most books on the market. And any reader would be hard-pressed to find a series with more laughs/page than the Wimpy Kid series!

A lovely heartwarming humorous book which is dedicated for kids and also ADULTS!! (yeah why not?) it would be perfect to read it especially during winter season since it's all cold, christmasy and snowy. I loved the cartoon drawings covering the pages which made it easier to imagine some situations, and most of the times, the illustrations were hilarious.

Diary of a Wimpy Kid is like a legend.While writing, authors always think too deep about the plot of the story.This is where Jeff Kinney overruled the other authors. Why write a book so complicated when you can write a simple one which everyone will enjoy?I think it's the simplicity of the book that attracted so many readers.And the doodlings make it even more interesting.It also makes us realize how there are funny stuff going on around us all the time which we don't even notice.Maybe we do, but we just don't take the humor in it.Makes us realize how dull we have become.
A cute quick read, with a touch of confusion at the end plot wise. Wimpy Kid fans will love it.

Gue bener-bener keganggu banget pas baca buku ini. Bukan karena ceritanya nggak aneh tapi kocak lagi. Tapi karena gue kehilangan 16 halaman kosong tidak tercetak. Dan Penerbit Atria yang sudah gue keluhkan via twitter tidak ditanggapi sama sekali. Hihhh..mengesalkan. Yang dulunya Penerbit Atria salah satu favorit penerbit gue. Sekarang tidak lagi. Gue tidak akan beli buku-buku terbitan mereka lagi. Anda berurusan dengan orang yang salah. CIH!!!
I hope I have time to read other volume of this series. I would like to know more abou Greg thought and his life. Greg's idea make me smile.
Greg Heffley's misfortunes pile up during the Christmas Season. Funny as usual.

I generally find these books pretty entertaining, and this is no exception. I don't know if this one is the funniest in the series or has the most surprising storyline, but for a quick read, I can't complain.
I haven't read or listened to any of the other Wimpy Kid books, and while this book wasn't bad, it didn't make me want to go out and grab the rest of the series, either.

This edition of the Diary of a Wimpy Kid series revolves around the month between Thanksgiving and Christmas. 
 Mom produces a Christmas Scout (akin to Elf on the Shelf) to keep an eye on things. Of course, Greg has some issues. He eats chicken nuggets only. The school has a special area where they sell them. Later he finds the same nuggets at the store. He buys them all with the idea he and Rowley will open their own restaurant and undercut the school and make money. 
 They print their own newspaper when the school refuses to advertise their event. They get the local pizza joint to foot the cost, but they run their advertisement adjacent to a scathing review of the pizza joint. They find they can't sell the newspaper so they begin giving it out for free. The school confiscates the balance of the newspapers. 
 The boys make posters and hang them on the wall outside the school. Rain causes the ink to stain the wall. Rowley confesses (kind of) in a way that gets Greg in trouble but not himself. After scrubbing the walls, Greg comes home to a note from the police. He's now worried they want to arrest him. 
 Dad gets snowed in on business. The Hefleys are snowed in. Eventually, the snow melts and floods the basement. Rodrick moves in with Greg. Things are a big mess. 
 On Christmas Eve all works out. Greg delivers a toy for a toy drive at the police station. He wears a ski mask to protect his identity. He checks on his Giving Tree present (that wasn't there). He ends up shoveling the church's in search for the present. The newspaper snaps a photograph. In Greg's newspaper, he reveals that it is he who was the masked shoveler.

book_b.title: Seedfolks
book_b.user_review: I didn't like this book. We had to read it for school, and I read ahead (sorry!) There was detail, but only in certain areas. The chapters were too short, and they introduced a new character in every chapter, with not much detail about the character. I didn't like the format of the story, and there are hardly any good words in this. The reading level of this is about 5th-6th grade, but I read at a much higher level than this, so it was easy for me to read. I really didn't like this book.

sample_reviews.review_text: This was an ok book. I didn't like the constant changing of the characters in every chapter. But I thought the general idea was good. I think it would be cool to have a small, community controlled garden in the city. Then, you wouldn't need space at your house, you could just visit your patch of whatever in the community garden.
Like an urban stone soup. A book both my boys have read in Fifth grade and truly enjoyed. I agree!

I can understand why people like this book. It's short but unfortunately I thought it dragged on and on. There weren't any memorable moments for me either. Seedfolks is a story about coming together as a community, and has a good message, but this isn't one of those books that everyone should read at least once. There are many other stories that I prefered about people putting their differences aside for the sake of the community.

I loved this book, especially because I am involved in a community garden and have found the community there to be a very important part of this season of my life. The thing about gardening is that everyone can do it, whoever you are and wherever you are from. Gardening brings people from different backgrounds together for a common cause and gives us a sense of working together for the same goals: growth, life, and finding your place in the natural world. This book of short snippets sharing the lives of community gardeners was so enjoyable and a quick read, and I definitely recommend it to everyone.

This very short novel is a beautiful story about what it means to be a community and how a community comes from having something in common - even if it's as small as a garden. Each chapter has a different character and a different point of view about this community garden which made it feel more like a short story collection instead of a novel. I enjoyed reading it in that format since it gave me a chance to see the garden in so many unique and interesting ways. The cast of diverse and interesting characters was delightful. One of my favorite characters was the old lady who kept drinking a tea made from flowers and her doctors told her not to. She outlived all those doctors and would say their names like a "chapter in Genesis." I just love that! 
 When we discussed this book in book club, we wondered who the main character was since it was told from so many points of view. I liked my friends idea that the garden was the main character since it changed and grew the most. I also liked where the term "seedfolks" came from. One of the characters talks about her ancestors who were the first black family in Colorado and she thought of them as her "seedfolk" since they planted their roots there for her. This was a cute story about community and how we have more in common than we think.
Summer reading for sophomore year in high school. It was pretty good. Short and sweet.
What a lovely, lovely little book.

I really despised this book. I was required to read it for school, and would refrain from reading as much as possible. I thought the problem and solution in this story was weak, and i felt like nothing really exciting happened. The chapters were really short, and i found my self flipping back in the book to refresh my memories of each character.

The cover puts me off, but picked it up to pass by time. This was a great find to read. The book is about a community who begins a garden because of one little girl. Each chapter is about a person in the community trying to remember a past that no longer is there. The stories all come back to the garden that brought a community together no matter color or race. 
 It is a wonderful book for struggling readers. I would definitely recommend this book to others.

I like the idea of a book about a community garden that brings people together. However, Fleischman's book which lets his audience "see people making something of themselves instead of waiting for a welfare check" (spoken by Florence on pg. 85) is hugely problematic given that Fleischman is a white guy from California that doesn't seem to be on welfare. I found his depictions of people of color to be essentializing and derogatory, while the character that he admitted to crafting after himself, the caucasian Sam, is just about the nicest, most balanced, and respectable member of the "Seedfolks." This is the YA version of The Help. A for effort. 
 If Fleischman's designs were to show the healing effects of collaboration and unplugging from technology, wouldn't it have been so much better to turn Seedfolks into a collaborative effort? He could have gathered friends and asked them to write a short monologue about their family's immigration experience and the way that a community garden might have benefitted them. That would be a more honest and respectful representation of diverse voices in America.

reference_books.title: Me Before You (Me Before You, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Read my full review here: http://mimi-cyberlibrarian.blogspot.c... 
 Me Before You by JoJo Moyes is a romance novel that subtly turns the corner from a love story to a book that poses profound moral questions. And the questions stay with the reader long after the last page is read and the last tear is wiped away. 
 Will Traynor, is a 35-year-old wealthy and successful businessman--a man who has it all. In one brief moment, an accident takes everything away from him, rendering him quadriplegic, angry, and suicidal. Enter Louisa Clark, a 26-year-old village girl. She is hired by Will's mother to be his caregiver for six months--not to do the medical work, but to make Will's life easier. Louisa (Lou) has never traveled, has had the same boyfriend for 7 years, still lives in her family home, and has no education beyond high school. She is a bit spineless, but in order to do the necessary job for Will, she is forced to develop skills that she didn't know she had and to grow beyond her expectations for herself. 
 The moral question posed is a universal one; what is quality of life? In her attempt to find ways to encourage Will to enjoy life, Lou communicates with other quadriplegics and their caregivers, many of whom have found ways to improve their quality of life. Her greatest fear is that Will will go through with his plan to travel to Switzerland for an assisted suicide. He has promised his parents that he will stay alive for six months before he completes his plan. Lou's self-assigned task is to get him to decide to live. 
 This is no ordinary romance novel, because in an ordinary romance novel, Lou would have prevailed; Will would have repurposed his life; and all would have ended in sweetness and light. The conclusion would have left the reader with tears of joy; and I would not have been left with significant questions. 
 Here are the moral dilemmas I struggled with as I read Me Before You. Is Will selfish in the decisions he is making? Does a person have an obligation to live? Is choosing to die a person's moral right? I just finished reading Zero K by Don DeLillo, which is about cryogenics. I was already filled with questions about death and dying, although DeLillo's perspective is quite different from Moyes. 
 The last 100 pages move very rapidly, and as soon as we begin to grasp the novel's conclusion, we become as confused as Lou. We continually ask ourselves about Will's quality of life. What is the best solution for him? Can he really change? Should he change? The reviewer in the New York Times suggests that the circumstances "lead noncontemplative people to contemplation." As I began the book, I really expected to finish the book, sigh, wipe my tears, and move on. I didn't expect to be haunted with the unanswerable questions that assail me now. 
 Moyes' writing style is subtle. The New York Times reviewer says that Moyes "disarms the reader with the normalcy of her voice. Her language is never lofty; she exposes her characters' flaws with the literary equivalent of a fluorescent bulb's naked light." The characters are all finely drawn; we have a clear vision of each one, which makes the impact of their decisions all the more profound. 
 As I discussed the novel with my husband, he brought up the life of Stephen Hawking as an example of a person who made different life choices from Will Traynor. And I remembered the biopic, The Diving Bell and the Butterfly about the Elle editor, Jean-Dominique Bauby, who was totally incapacitated by a stroke. The movie asks many of the same questions about quality of life that Me Before You is asking. A movie based on Moyes book comes out in the next couple of weeks. I am not sure that I have the spiritual energy to live through this twice. 
 This is my book club choice for the month. We meet next week. I am always curious about what my friends will think about the book.

reference_books.title: The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up: The Japanese Art of Decluttering and Organizing
reference_books.review_text:
Read my full review here: http://mimi-cyberlibrarian.blogspot.c... 
 My daughter's best friend is a house organizer and cleaner. My daughter is not. Besides that, she has two pre-schoolers. One evening her house organizer friend was trying to help her tidy up, and my daughter told her: "Really I never learned how to clean. We were all taught how to clean up for the cleaning lady." Ouch! 
 Everyone has been talking about The Life Changing Magic of Tidying Up. You've heard about it, haven't you. I decided to give it a try. 
 I listened to The Life Changing Magic of Tidying Up in the car on a long car ride Tuesday. Like many people of my age bracket, there is a huge accumulation of stuff that comes from having lived as long as I have. I have been trying to start the process of "tidying up" by working to get rid of 3 things every day. Well, listening to Marie Kondo, I realized that my method was not the appropriate way to do the job. Kondo has a very specific method and works to advise people about their tidying up habits. She teaches a method that she assures the reader is foolproof. 
 As I drove, I thought about where I would begin putting this book into practice. I thought about my messy office, my messy sewing room, my messy closet. I mused that Kondo's method might work for me. It was when she started to tell me the precise fashion in which to fold t-shirts in order to make them happy that I turned off the book in disgust. As one Goodreads reviewer said, "She is 'batshit' crazy." 
 I do need to start liberating the things in my house, but these are things--inanimate objects--they do not have feelings!!! At the same time, I realize that this is a system that works well for a lot of people. And Kondo guarantees that if you use her system, you will get control of your house and your stuff. 
 Oh--and one more thing. Kondo began tidying up when she was 5-years-old. Wait a minute! This is the only child I have ever known that tidies up at age 5. If she had been my kid, I would have taken her to the psychologist for treatment for OCD! As it is, she has made a whole career of tidying up.

reference_books.title: The Power of Habit: Why We Do What We Do in Life and Business
reference_books.review_text:
Read my full post here: http://mimi-cyberlibrarian.blogspot.c... 
 The Power of Habit by Charles Duhigg is an entertaining and instructive look at how habit influences the behaviors of individuals, organizations, and cultures. If you are seeking a self-help book that will instruct you in how to get and maintain a good habit or get rid of a bad habit, this is not the book to read. But it is a clear-eyed look at how habit influences every aspect of life. 
 A Pulitzer Prize winner, Duhigg writes in a clear, narrative style in keeping with his career as a reporter at the New York Times. He has done his research, and his stories are entertaining. The section on the power of habit in personal life was extremely engaging and made my husband and I look at our daily activities with new eyes--the pleasure my husband gets from going upstairs at night to a bed that he carefully made in the morning and the habit I have of checking my email the very first thing in the morning, which is pleasing to me because I like to get them out of the way first thing. We also discussed the habits that we are not so proud of--the ones that drive each other crazy. (Those I won't go into here!). 
 Duhigg traces back personal habits to their origins and then looks at the ways in which those personal habits can change. He tells the story of Tony Dungy, a pro football coach who became convinced that the key to producing a winning team was to change players' personal habits so that behaviors on the field would happen automatically. He taught the team moves that would operate on a three step plan, find the cue, change the routine, and feel the reward. Duhigg believes that to change the habit, you must find the cue and the reward. Then you can change the routine and change the habit. He adds one more ingredient--belief. Dungy took these three steps, cue, routine, and reward, added in belief, and changed the makeup of the way his team played. His team became winners because whenever they felt the cue, they moved into the routine, and received the reward. However, it was only when belief entered the picture that the team really became winners. 
 I particularly liked the chapters on corporate habits because so many of them were very skillfully illustrated by Duhigg. He tells of how Paul O'Neill changed one keystone habit at Alcoa Aluminum and turned the faltering company around. Most significantly, he tells about how the climate at Starbucks helps individual employees become responsible members of the corporate and cultural community. There are a couple of horrifying stories about how counterproductive keystone habits can be. For instance, the habits taught to the employees in the London Underground were very disconnected from one another. On the one hand, the employees knew their own jobs very well, but they didn't know what the other employees' jobs were or how those jobs were interrelated. So, when a small fire began in one of the underground stations, everyone continued to do his/her own jobs, without taking any personal responsibility, and a huge fire erupted which killed several people. 
 One of the major strengths of the book are the stories. One amazing story line is about how Target figures out its' customers buying habits. For instance, their technology can tell when a woman is pregnant--before she tells anyone--and target (no pun intended) ads to fit her condition. They determine probable purchases because of subtle changes in shopping habits. 
 The reviewer in the New York Times had a criticism of The Power of Habit. He says, "The point is that habitual behaviors come in many different forms, and squeezing them into one framework misses some of the nuances of how to change behavior effectively. In recent years social psychologists have developed many effective interventions to help people improve their lives, only some of which involve breaking bad habits in the way Duhigg describes." Duhigg's framework of cue, routine, reward may be too small a framework. 
 I asked my husband what he learned most from The Power of Habit. He said that he hadn't realized how much of life was dictated by habit. He thought that he could identify the good and bad habits in his life, but now he realizes that habit is everywhere in his life and the lives of the people, the companies, and the culture around him. 
 I tried to hone in on a few personal habits that I am not proud of and consider my options regarding those habits. I have had to chuckle at myself. I am trying to keep a food diary in the weeks before I visit the doctor in January. I am using an app called My Fitness Pal. I have had to "do over" using this app several times over the last several months because I stop using it when I have a day when I want to eat something that I don't want to keep track of and have it show up on my food log. I don't want to look at the daily calorie count on the days when it is going to go over what I have allotted for myself. Denial is one of the weak sisters of habit. 
 My husband and I read this book together and it engendered a great deal of conversation. Sometimes we had to pull ourselves away from the breakfast table and begin our day. Reading together has become one of the enjoyable habits that we have created as a couple. 
 Duhigg closes The Power of Habit 
 by writing "If you believe you can change--if you make it habit--the change becomes real. This is the power of habit: the insight that your habits are what you choose them to be. Once that choice occurs--and becomes automatic, habitual--it's not only real, it starts to seem inevitable, the thing, as (William) James wrote, that bears "us irresistibly toward our destiny, whatever the latter may be." 
 The Power of Habit comes out in paperback on January 4. It is a thought-provoking, highly enjoyable book. We both can recommend it. 
 New York Times review: http://www.nytimes.com/2012/03/11/boo... 
 Charles Duhigg's website: http://charlesduhigg.com/

reference_books.title: Ginny Moon
reference_books.review_text:
Read my full review here: http://mimi-cyberlibrarian.blogspot.c... 
 Ginny Moon, a 14-year-old on the autism spectrum, has had a rough life. Her drug-addicted mother, Gloria, lost custody of her when Ginny was nine, and Ginny was placed in several foster homes until she found her "forever" home with a high school counselor and his doctor wife. At each stop, Ginny tried to escape, always wanting to get back to her mother and her "baby doll" Now, however, life is somewhat normal--she likes her family, her school and her classmates; she plays in the band and on a Special Olympics basketball team. 
 The story is told by Ginny, "deep in my brain," where she lives most of the time. What we know about autism is that each person afflicted with the disorder manifests it in different ways. Ginny has some obsessive characteristics, such as marking the time for every event in her life, keeping a rigid schedule, and eating exactly nine grapes for breakfast every day. For Ginny, time stopped when she was taken away from her mother and her baby doll. When her "forever parents" have a new baby and Brian, her "forever father" suffers a heart attack, everything in Ginny's world becomes even less secure, and she does what she needs to do to protect herself; she sets out to find her mother. 
 The amazing thing about Ginny, as we hear her voice loud and clear, is that she knows what she wants. She mostly understands that her brain is unique, that she views the world differently than others, and that sometimes she sees herself as (-Ginny), a girl with no place in the world. This is the Ginny that the reader hurts for. This is the Ginny that the reader wishes that they could just reach out and hug--she is hurting so badly--except that Ginny doesn't want to be touched. But most importantly, this is the Ginny Moon that is resilient. She can concoct a plan and follow it through. 
 One of the crucial people in Ginny's life is Patrice, the psychologist. She has been Ginny's counselor since she was first taken away from her mother, and Patrice understands and loves Ginny. Her compassion is boundless. But even Patrice doesn't understand Ginny's obsession with her baby doll until half way through the book, and this is a pivotal moment in the plot. At that point I couldn't stop reading until the end. One reviewer said that the ending is a bit Disney-esque, but it ended exactly where I was hoping it would end, in a satisfying and loving way. 
 Ginny Moon is the debut novel of Ben Ludwig, a teacher and adoptive father of an autistic teenager. He said he got much of his inspiration from his own experience but also from the parents he met at Special Olympics games and practices. I really loved this book because Ludwig has an uncanny way of getting "deep in my brain" with Ginny and helping the reader understand and love her. The Kirkus reviewer says, "By turns heartwarming and heartbreaking, Ginny's quest for a safe home leads her to discover her own strong voice."

reference_books.title: Far From True (Promise Falls Trilogy,  #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Read my full review here: http://mimi-cyberlibrarian.blogspot.c... 
 Remind me, please, never to move to Promise Falls, New York! 
 Far from True by Linwood Barclay picks up where Broken Promise, the first book in the Promise Falls trilogy, left off--and I do mean left off, or more appropriately, left hanging. Nothing gets solved in Broken Promise. 
 In the startling first chapter of Far from True, a bunch of young adult guys decide to go to the last night at the local drive-in movie theater before it is torn down to make way for progress. Derek, who we met in Broken Promise, decides to hide in the car trunk as a prank. Just as they arrive at the theater, there is a huge explosion and the movie screen falls on two cars killing four patrons. At that point, nobody cares about Derek, the stowaway. Is it terrorism? Or from what we already know about Promise Falls, it may be something far more sinister, although I do have to reassure you that the sinister force (or forces) are neither vampires nor aliens. Oh--but I don't know that for sure. 
 Several more of the characters from Broken Promise show up in Far from True, although some of them just wander in and out. This time out, Cal Weaver, a local PI is investigating a break-in at the home of one of the victims, while Detective Barry Duckworth has got a caseload full of murder, mayhem, and violence. The number twenty-three appears and reappears throughout this episode as well. 
 As I am writing this, I am wondering how in the world there could be so much bad stuff going on in such a small town. Yet, Barclay is so good at juggling all these subplots, that the reader just keeps reading and reading, totally immersed in page turning. Another of Barclay's skills is character development, which keeps the huge number of characters unconfused in the reader's mind. Several of the characters are memorable, including a treacherous ex-mayor, a highly conflicted college professor, and a little girl who seems to have psychic powers of some sort. There is even some colorful sex to spice things up a bit. One reviewer called it "a Richard Russo novel gone off the rails." 
 And frankly, we get no satisfactory ending. Some crimes are solved, some sort of disappear, and we are reminded of some from the last book. We are left hanging, once again. However, the third book in the trilogy is called The Twenty Three. Maybe we will get some justice yet. 
 Barclay is a great storyteller. There are almost 1500 pages in the Promise Falls trilogy. It is incredible that one little town could have so many stories. Read on! Read on!

book_a.title: The Invention of Wings
book_a.user_review:
Read my full review here: http://mimi-cyberlibrarian.blogspot.c... 
 "We are all yearning for a wedge of sky, aren't we?" 
 Sarah Grimke is a girl of eleven in 1803 Charleston SC when her parents give her a slave girl, Hetty (or Handful as she is known), the daughter of the family dressmaker. Sarah is indignant. She does not want her own slave; she hates the idea of slavery, but her voice is a minority in one of the leading families of Charleston. Having slaves is just "as natural as breathing." Sarah is drawn to Handful and Handful decides that she can gain some advantage by being kind and helpful to Sarah. Sarah vows that someday she will set Handful free, but it takes many years for that to happen. 
 Sarah and her sister Nina, spend their lives defying the custom of the South, and end up in as leading abolitionists in the country by the mid-1800s. Sue Monk Kidd has fashioned her novel, The Invention of Wings on the lives of Sarah and Angelina Grimke, who were very famous in their day, but whose fame as abolitionists and suffragists was supplanted by others whose names are better remembered. The character of Hetty is based on a real slave girl in the Grimke family, but one who did not survive until adulthood. The fact and fiction of the lives of these two women, Sarah and Hetty, are woven together in alternating chapters. Both stories are powerfully told, although quite often Hetty's words resonate with the horror of the downtrodden. Sarah comes across as noble as she leaves the South, becomes a Quaker, and speaks the truth of slavery throughout the North. 
 Kidd has very carefully researched the times and the circumstances--the treatment of the slaves is so graphically told that the reader recoils in horror at what was expected punishment for minor infractions, such as stealing food or fabric. As is typical of Kidd's work, the characters are extremely finely drawn, although she may have had some constraints with the character of Sarah, because she had an actual life history. 
 One of the best characters in the book is Handful's mother, Charlotte, who is very rebellious and clever. She is the family seamstress and teaches Handful everything she knows, both spiritually and creatively. She crafts a story quilt that tells the story of her life. Charlotte tells Handful that "spirits live in the trees with the birds, learning to fly." She tells her that her shoulder blades are the nubs of wings. Charlotte puts small black triangles into her quilt, the wings that she tries again and again to use as she attempts to escape from her captivity. 
 Two summers ago, we visited the National Underground Railroad Freedom Center in Cincinnati and experienced an exhibit of African American story quilts, similar to the one that Charlotte creates and plays such a significant role in the novel. I could truly imagine what Charlotte's quilt looked like as I was reading because of the example of the incredible quilts in the Museum. 
 Although my experience with black vernacular and the black experience are really limited, I believe that Kidd's own experience as a white Southern woman with domestics in her parents' and grandparents' homes resonates in her characterizations. For example, my friend Jean frequently says of her mother, "She is getting on my last nerve." The character, Hetty, says that in one of the early chapters of the book. I told Jean that her saying, "She's getting on my last nerve" goes back to the early 1800s in the African American slave community. She was pleased and amazed to know that. 
 I very much appreciated The Invention of Wings. I appreciated knowing about the life experience of Sarah and Nina Grimke, about Handful (Hetty) and I appreciated learning about an era of American history that I knew very little about. 
 Kidd has created a powerful novel full of truths to ponder for a long time after the book is closed the last time. Our book club had a terrific discussion. I would highly recommend it for your book club.

sample_reviews.review_text:
4.5 I started this with a little reservation. I found the narratives of Sarah and Handful under-developed. As they were introduced as aged 11-12 and then grew and aged I initially thought that their 'voice' should have developed more. However, this became less important as the story grabbed hold of me and took me back to plantation and slavery and the patriarchal society of the first half of the 19th century in the Southern states of the US. Read to the very end! The author's note was fascinating. Highly recommended. 
 (Just realised I review the review of this book!)

1/3 of the way through this book and I'm bored. I fell asleep reading it several times. This is unusual for me so I'm giving up on it. I had such high expectations since the author wrote The Secret Life of Bees. I loved that book.
And then I found out that the audio production uses the same cast as "The Help" and things made so much more sense. Grrr.
Loved it!!

This was a wonderful book! Kudos to Sue Monk Kidd for her rendition of the story of the Grimke sisters. I hadn't even heard of them, but they were pivitol in the process of the coming of age of women's rights and the abolition of slavery. Beautifully written, I couldn't put it down!

I loved this story about Sarah, an 11 year old girl in Charleston in the early 1800s who refuses the"handmaid", Hetty (also known to her mother as Handful) she is given, whose story we also follow through the decades. Handful's story, entwined with her mamma and grand-mauma's, as portrayed through their sewing and quilts was beautifully told. As I was nearing the end of their tale, I realized that Sarah is based on the true story of Sarah Grimke, who grew up into a woman who spoke out against slavery, which made me love the book even more. This is my favorite book of Sue Monk Kidd's since the wonderful Secret Life of Bees.
Well written, but predictable and stilted text. Took me awhile to finish.

"You got to figure out which end of the needle you're gon be, the one that's fastened to the thread or the end that pierces the cloth." 
 Reading The Secret Life of Bees just meant I had a favorite book. Reading The Invention of Wings means I have a favorite author. Sun Monk Kidd is tremendous, folks. 
 This book pulls at your heartstrings in a way that isn't cheesy. It's authentic without being boring, it's about slavery without chastising, and it's about abolition without pride (well, at least the bad kind of pride). It gives the bad guys of the story hearts while it keeps the good guys with their feet on the earth. Sun Monk Kidd weaves in so much symbolism you can see it without the help of your English teacher. Instead of feeling overdone, though, the nuances of water and wings and sewing makes the story so full-bodied you feel like you'll burst. 
 There's a lot I love about this story but probably my favorite part is how this novel, at first glance, is about slavery and it's impact on two women - Hetty and Sarah. When you actually read it though, I think each reader will pick out something else that's important to him/her. For me, I adored how much this book was about women. Men play very minor roles. The men in this story do little more than hinder the women along the way. Each step for these women are taken on their own - and it's beautiful. 
 To sum it all up? 
 GUSH! 
 (Also - the audio version of this is excellent!)
Beautiful and haunting book sadly based on our own American history. Moving characters and story.
3.5 Informative retelling of the Grimke sisters' story entwined with fictional slave character--incredible bravery and determination.

book_b.title: The Truth According to Us
book_b.user_review:
Read my full review here: http://mimi-cyberlibrarian.blogspot.c... 
 Here is how Annie Barrows sets the stage for The Truth According to Us on her website: 
 "It all began at the Decoration Day Parade, when the Rotary Club band honked out the last notes of the "Battle Hymn of the Republic," and Willa Romeyn, age 12, made a solemn vow to discover all the secrets that adults hide from children. 
 It all began when Miss Layla Beck refused to marry Nelson the Citronella Scion, was tossed out of the lap of luxury, and landed--in white high-heels--at the train station of Macedonia, West Virginia. 
 It all began when the Town Council of Macedonia decided to commemorate the town's Sesquicentennial with a dignified yet lively recounting of its history, to be entitled The History of Macedonia.
