***UNPOPULAR OPINION AHEAD*** 
 DNF 22% 
 I don't know where I started to have a lot of criticism about books. I guess it began when I started writing novels by myself, got all kind of critiques, and did my best to become better. 
 I love Sarah J. Maas's books, and I think she has a great potential as a writer. I don't think any of her books quite hit the mark of what I expect in a fantasy novel, but she's getting closer with each book she publishes. Also, being in Facebook groups for TOG and ACOTAR fans, I learned a lot of new things about her as a young, up and rising author. 
 If I look at her books in total, I loved the Court series better than TOG. But if we talk particularly about TOG, I liked HoF the best. I believe that after HoF, she lost some of her touch, but I still enjoyed QoS and EoS. 
 Tower of Dawn, however, missed everything that I wanted to read about in a book, as a fantasy, and as a part of a series. 
 Let's start with the basics. The writing. Oh my God, the writing was so slow and flat I felt nothing and wanted this book to end from the moment it began, because I already felt it was going to be excruciating. And it was. For the entire 22% I read, I had to force myself to continue. The conversations were dull, the descriptions boring, and it felt so slow I wanted to throw my kindle to the other side of the room. 
 As for the characters, it's basically the same. I am not a big Chaol fan, but I did try to keep an open mind going into this book, yet I couldn't stand it. Chaol, as always, is dull and plain and stupid. Nesryn was there for only one purpose; being the colored other main character. Yrene was the typical Mary Sue, and everyone else blended in the background. 
 It seems to me SJM tried so hard to make this book something that it shouldn't be, and it was frustrating and annoying to read. The male characters start to become similar to each other; all so possessive and sarcastic and honorably and lacking any sort of personality. I hate them all with passion (I'm looking at you, Rhysand). I just can't with these characters, and honestly, I want to give the entire TOG series up. 
 Another problem for me, and not just about this book but this series as a whole, is that if I don't reread it when a new book comes out, I forget everything else and I can't get into a book. I just can't. Sarah can make fantastic endings to books. But she can't frigging start them! I don't want to drag myself through half a book I don't enjoy just to get to the enjoyable, faster parts. I want it all to be well-paced and enjoyable! And I'm sorry to say this, but Sarah doesn't do that anymore. 
 So I can't continue reading this book. I just can't. I don't know even if I care enough to read the last book that will come next year. I'm that done with this series. I'll try to keep up with ACTOAR but that's about it. 
 I truly hope Sarah will grow to be a better author, because I don't want to waste my barely-there free time on books that are so slow I want to punch a wall. 
 That's just my opinion, though, and obviously not a popular one. Please no hate comments. Everyone is entitled to their own opinion and I know how this fandom tends to get brutal to those who disagree with the majority. If you want to state your opinion, please do. But in a respectful way. 
 Also, I am not changing my mind about this book, so don't bother trying.

Lesson #1 - Don't read A Drop of Night alone. 
 Lesson #2 - Don't read alone at night, especially right before bed. 
 Lesson #3 - Just.. don't read it alone, okay? 
 A Drop of Night was so much more than I was expecting. It's a genre-mashing thrill ride that took my imagination to new heights. I swear, my body was covered in goosebumps while reading this book. There were times when I would shudder and set the book down because I was wholly freaked out. But yet, I loved it. 
 We actually get two stories told parallel together that are equally important. We see the events between 1789-1790 that started it all, and then we get the present; 5 teenagers thrust together in an underground palace fighting to live. It flowed nicely, never giving us a dull moment or time to breathe. 
 Anouk was strong-willed, tough and borderline unlikable. She has that unrealistic narration I like in thrillers, too. Her sass and dark humor made light on some of the scary parts darker situations and how she handled everything with bravery was to be admired. 
 It was hard to connect to Anouk, well all the characters really, on the level that I like to. But after finishing and thinking about it, this wasn't necessary for me. It doesn't take a strong connection to root for a group of teenagers to live. To bite your nails in anxious anticipation because every room has a trap and you aren't sure who will survive. While yes, at times their actions and lack of thought process frustrated me to no end - I mean who wouldn't assume something shady is probably going on when going to France alone? - I was rooting for them from the start and their development with each other was nice to read. They still bicker and frustrate each other but a bond was formed in the process. 
 The ending took a turn I didn't see coming - which isn't saying much with the twists A Drop of Night had within its pages. I was hoping for more, but this is all me and wanting to know about THE AFTER. That's not the story, though, and considering all the different ways it could have went, leaves much to my imagination. And.... to keep me up at night. 
 All in all - I loved it! A Drop of Night is unique with its blend of genres and creeptastic shenanigans. It's ability to hook from page one and keep me up at night, speaks volumes in my book. I highly recommend it!

 There were a few times while reading A Drop of Night, I wondered "What is going on?" A Drop of Night is one of those stories that will keep you on your toes and make you wonder what is going to happen next. There were only a couple small things that I was able to guess while reading, but everything else completely surprised me. 
 A Drop of Night is a very interesting, sometimes crazy and weird, thrilling story. There is a lot of action and mystery to keep the reader engaged. Overall, I enjoyed reading A Drop of Night. It definitely surprised me and made my heart race. 
 There are a lot of mysteries and secrets in A Drop of Night, so I have decided to write a vague Things I Liked vs. Things I Didn't List Review. 
 Things I Liked: 
 The Mystery: I honestly didn't figure out most of the mystery for this story. I only guessed a couple small details correctly. So the ending really surprised me! 
 Unique Story: I can honestly say I haven't read anything quite like this story! There were several times I wondered what was going on. I also think the story was a bit crazy and weird at times (in a good way)! 
 The Historical Parts. I really liked that there were some historical parts to this story. I found them very interesting. 
 Entertaining: There is a lot of stuff that happens in this story. I think there was almost something constantly happening once the characters reach the palace. A lot of action and creepy situations. I think that this is more of a plot-driven story. 
 Things I Didn't Really Like: 
 I guess the only thing that I didn't like that much was the main character, Anouk. I'm not really sure why, but I just didn't really click with her. I did want to like her and I didn't hate her. Overall, she just wasn't a character that I really liked or loved. 
 My Recommendation: 
 Overall, I enjoyed reading A Drop of Night. The story had an interesting plot and mystery. There were twists and surprises. There were parts that made my heart race and some that really made me wonder what was going on. If you enjoy horror and mystery type stories, I recommend giving A Drop of Night a read!

 I was excited going into this, having seen the comparison to The Cabin In the Woods and expecting something just as trippy and unpredictable. In hindsight, I'm disappointed. File this one under "could have been." Or maybe "almost there." The elements were present, but the presentation was lacking. 
 Where should I start? The synopsis was a little misleading, for one thing. Bachmann's style was rough and choppy, which kept me from sinking into the story. The threads of the plot only ever remained threads, tying themselves together at the last minute and never weaving into anything substantial. Anouk herself was a major hurdle, abrasive and unpalatable at the start and taking way too long in developing into a sympathetic character. 
 Those are the nitpicks. And the fact remains that this could have been a really awesome book. Lots of action and suspense, a few really tense moments, and I had to guess my way through the whole thing. The ending was a letdown, and I was left feeling frustrated that the concept never lived up to its potential. It could have been the intense fantasy thriller it promised to be, but by the last page I still hadn't budged from my "meh" reaction. 
 Skip this if you want. You're not missing much. Rad cover, though...

book_a.title: The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao
book_a.user_review: This was one of the best books I read this year. It was one of those books I just couldn't put down. I would recommend it to almost anyone. I enjoyed the Dominican history lesson within the book, especially because most people probably don't learn about Trujillo's dictatorship in school, and it's a really interesting (albeit crazy and depressing) topic. If you don't speak Spanish, you may have to use a dictionary to understand Diaz's liberal use of Spanish curse words and phrases, which are hilarious.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Any novel that can toss around casual references to comic books like Watchmen and the Fantastic Four is going to attract my attention. The book is enjoyable; I liked the title character, although Diaz's style seems to keep Oscar at a frustrating distance. I thought the language and narrative structure was inventive, posing the kind of time-bending challenges that postmodern readers love. 
 But I can't help but think about Everett's Erasure when I read Diaz's book. There were moments when I was troubled that my lack of understanding regarding cultural norms and attitudes in the Dominican Republic would lead me to be less critical about the story's constant images of misogyny, hypermasculinity, and violence, or overlook the author's larger message about how we should view Oscar's family and experience in American vs the DR. Is the Brief Wonderous life, praised by some for its "magic realism" and others for its "verisimilitude," really just another version of Everett's racial parody and media spectacle, "My Pafology"?

A sweep of voices, a multi-faceted approach to one small life that left me a little dazzled and envious. Women, men, old, young - he nailed every section. Interesting and inventive. And a hell of a lot more that I ever knew about the Dominican Republic before reading it. One beef: lose the footnotes.

The history of the DR was new to me (amazing to learn after having gone there several times) and horrifying that it seems to be largely accurate. The writer is clearly brilliant. Can't even say whether you should read it or not because it's so different.

sample_reviews.review_text: I read this while camping over the Thanksgiving weekend and really enjoyed it.

Mindy Kaling is very funny and wonderful and I love the Mindy Project. I probably would have loved the Office if I'd watched it, but I didn't. Anyway, I think I'd end up liking the Mindy Project better, because I am shallow and love Mindy Lahiri's fashion and am insanely envious of her collection of handbags. She seems to own about 20 Chanel bags in colours she can match to her outfit. I also love that she's smart, gets all the sexy boyfriends, and can be funny and frivolous. 
 This is a very gentle, enjoyable book by a funny woman who can tell a great story. I've mostly covered how much I love Mindy Lahiri, and Kaling has a list of how she isn't like her character. I love and admire what she's created. This book isn't full of her childhood and what made her what she is today. She talks about what she's really like, what it's like to be famous but most about the amount of fame she has. She has funny anecdotes but she isn't very biographical. While she notes that she has her moments, I loved how clear-sighted she was about how annoying it is to be a woman in comedy. She just seems to want to take it in her stride. 
 My absolute favourite part was where she 'Sliding Doors' fictionalises herself as a high school Latin teacher at a posh New York school who falls in love with a 40~ish US history teacher. Mindy Kaling could write romance and I would read it. I know she already writes romance which I watch, but if she ever decided to give away the glamour of being a famous television person to write five + Harlequin romances a year, I would totally and slavishly buy all her novels and give them 5 star reviews on Good Reads.
I love Minday Kaling. This book was great, fun, and light.

Funny and fresh, but we were already expecting that after the success of her first book, as well as just her professional success in general. While this book didn't quite grab me as much as her first, I still definitely appreciate Kaling's signature sarcastic candor, tongue-in-cheek anecdotes, and, yes, relatable demeanor.

 I really liked Mindy Kaling's first book, Is Everyone Hanging Out Without Me? and I hoped this book would live up to her first book. In my opinion, this did not. Kaling had such a wildly successful and good first book, that like any sequel, there is a lot of hype for this book and so I was really expecting a lot more. Furthermore, because I have read her first one, this book didn't feel like a different book. It felt it was the less funnier continuation of the first book. 
 This felt very disjointed and all over the place. The book was difficult for me to read because it fell flat from the expectation I had that her jokes would be funny. However they did not translate from the page as well as they did in her first book. 
 Overall the writing is good, even if it is conversational writing. Her voice really shines through in the book and I think I would enjoy listening to the audiobook of it. In the end, I think because it did not seem as original and witty as her first book, I had difficulty enjoying it as much as other may have. 
 2.5/5 stars.

Read on audiobook, and mostly really liked it. I adored Is Everyone Hanging Out Without Me? and really related to the insecurities Kaling talked about there. This book is from a more confident Kaling, who has created and starred in her own show, and while I relate to that too, it's a less compelling thing to read. That said, I love what she has to say, and I ate this up.
3.5 stars. Laugh-out-loud funny at times, typical Mindy in tone, but not quite as enjoyable or insightful as her first book.

3.5 STARS 
 I liked this book slightly better than Kaling's book "Is Everyone Hanging Out Without Me?" Maybe it was the fact that this was the second book by Kaling that I read, so I had some knowledge of her writing style and was not expecting it to be a humorous book. Similar to IEHOWM, Kaling narrates different events from her life and tries to give some insight and advice. It was a quick read and I enjoyed it for the most part. These were my favorite quotes: 
 "But my secret is: even though I wish I could be thin, and that I could have the ease of lifestyle that I associate with being thin, I don't wish for it with all of my heart. Because my heart is reserved for way more important things." 
 "The best kind of laughter is laughter born of a shared memory." 
 "I can't for the life of me not eat something that I want to eat. You know how if you turned on a faucet in your sink to wash your hands, the idea of leaving the bathroom without turning it off is insane? That's how I am about ignoring delicious food."

Let me just say, this book was not bad. I know that I only gave it two stars, but that's mostly because I didn't think this book was as funny for me as Mindy meant it to be. I, too, have a wet sense of humor that just doesn't appreciate her book and tv show like the rest of America. Sigh. That being said, you should still read this book.
Read it on the beach as some candy lit so I'd enjoy reading ON the beach. It's a nice snack-type thing---something you can munch on in a couple of hours killing time.

Who cares if he can't read or write. He's someone to spend the rest of her life with. They don't have much in common but he's the first one to look at her and not see her for her birthmark. Oh well everythng comes to an end and this was a quick ending for this group.

reference_books.review_text: There was a lot of description in this book but I liked the story line. I skipped the details a lot of the time because it was too much to read. Terrible what people have to go through. People should be aware that there is suffering all over the world.

book_a.title: The Girl Who Chased the Moon
book_a.user_review: I really like these books by Sarah Allen. They're fun, romantic and full of surprises. They are a bit odd so don't be expecting a serious work of fiction but their quirkiness makes them light and airy.

sample_reviews.review_text:
The Girl Who Chased the Moon one of those books where you can pretty much tell where it's going and know everything is going to turn out okay, but it doesn't really matter. In fact that is just what I need sometimes, like a fairy take for adults. 
 It's a fun read, very light, fluffy and sweet. I read it in one night. The style reminds me somewhat of Alice Hoffman. It is more magical realism that full-out fantasy. I could see Sarah Addison Allen becoming an author I go to whenever I need a little bit of cheering up.

Enjoyable and magical, yet left me wanting more (not necessarily in a good way) 
 I guess it's been a while since I've read such a short novel, and while I did find it whimsical and a lovely read, 'The Girl who Chased the Moon' needed just a bit more 'oomph' for me to fully engage with its charm. 
 However, it was a nice read with intriguing, inter-woven plots.
Perfect pick for my mood, quiet & beautiful.
This book was a fun easy quick read. I liked the whimsical nature of it. I liked the two parallel stories of Emily and Julia, who are both trying to find happiness. Highly recommend.

Two words: MAGICAL REALISM. My opinion: NOT FOR ME 
 I know, great reviews, etc. BFD

It was a nice fantacy. A little town with an unsual story to tell. The family with the moon glow was a little too much but the rest of the story was a nice escape to a little friendly suspicious town.
This was an interesting book. I was not as impressed as I have been after reading the author's previous books.
Adorable
A little schmaltzy but perfectly readable

(3.5 stars) This is definitely for someone who likes happy endings and cute romance. It took me awhile to get used to the writing, but after that I was pretty immersed in the story. Her use of simile to create an air of magic is successful, and I soon found myself fond of the paralleling stories of Emily and Julia. There were a few moments where I didn't quite understand something, but overall this was a lovely read. It was nice to get away with this story and I look forward to reading The Peach Keeper which sits unread on my bookshelf.

book_b.title: Where'd You Go, Bernadette
book_b.user_review: Couldn't finish this cause it just wasn't my thing. Got a little too strange for me. Too choppy and it was a bit crazy.

sample_reviews.review_text: I tried, I really did but sadly couldn't finish. I just couldn't get into the story.
Loved it. Read it within 24 hours. Infinitely original, very funny, and with some real gravitas. Great read.

I don't understand what all of the fuss has been over this book. But I have also never watched Arrested Development and don't have a lot of patience for satyrical fiction. I found all of the characters to be highly aggravating and the plot to be thin. It did get better once Bernadette actually disappeared, but it still was one of those books that I just finished to finish. 2 1/2 stars
couldn't put it down. funny, snarky and sweet. some of my favorite things, but 4-1/2 stars...didn't make it to 5. not quite sure why not; will ponder.

I was 90 percent extremely excited to read this book; It was on my wishlist on Amazon for most of this year, and it was touted as being one of the best books of last year. If I hadn't saw that it was in at the library, I would have probably purchased it later this year. The 10 percent that wasn't excited was because I had attempted to read her previous book but found it to be pure chick lit. So I started this book, and realized that an author isn't going to do a complete 180 most of the time in their writing style. Is this a bad book? No. I consider it to be evolved chick lit, but at the core, the characters are shallow, the situations are silly and trite, and I didn't really root for any of the characters.
I liked it and it kept you reading. The parts about the weirdness of Seattle were my favorite.

Bernadette Fox has lost all interest in life. Her career as an architect failed. Her marriage is on the rocks. Her house is in shambles. She's hired Manjula Kapoor, an India woman she met on the Internet, to shop online for her, pay her bills, make her dinner reservations, and arrange for her family vacation to Antarctica. Bernadette is an artist who has stopped creating, a menace to society. She's become a recluse whose sole focus is her 15-year-old daughter, Bee. 
 Nothing about Where'd You Go Bernadette is conventional, including Semple's writing style. The novel is a compilation of documents--emails, handwritten notes, FBI documents, reports from a psychiatrist. Not to mention correspondence between helicoptering parents at Bee's school, the shallow women Bernadette calls gnats. Bernadette finds herself in the middle of one riotous crisis after another involving the gnats, yet she maintains her dignity while remaining true to herself. And to Bee. 
 Semple adds depth to her characters with funny antidotes of their past lives. Their voices are spot on. 
 Bee--On the verge of going off to boarding school, even though she is naive in her own charming way, Bee is intelligent beyond her years. Her loyalty to her mother is paramount. She even goes as far as to cheer her mother on in her battle against the gnats. The mother/daughter relationship is rock solid, which is why Bee refuses to believe the worst when her mother disappears off the planet. 
 LG--Bernadette's nerdy husband who is tolerant of his wife's eccentricity but too preoccupied with his career at Microsoft to notice she's falling apart. 
 Sue Lynn--gnat and administrative assistant for LG, who sets her sights on him when she senses trouble in his marriage. 
 Audry--gnat and neighbor, the focus of Bernadette's temper tantrums. 
 Where'd You Go Bernadette is imaginative, spunky, and oh so much fun.

I can't remember what year it was but I remember being really sad when Steve Irwin died. I can still picture that smug Australian smile painted on the face of a guy wrestling with a crocodile. What is it with him and crocodiles? At least, I know what's with him and stingrays. But really, killed by a stingray? I couldn't believe it. But then again, there were lots of things I couldn't believe back then. I'm pretty sure I didn't believe in goodreads back then, or Obama, or glee. If you would've told me that Morgan Freeman would be a god, or teenagers would fall in love with a sparkling zombie, or bdsm novels would be a thing, I might just have laughed in your face and called you ape-shit. Cause ape-shit was a thing back then. I might or might not also have been obsessed with John Grisham back then. Objection! heh heh! Anyway, now I've got Bear Grylls. He drinks his own pee and eats lots of gross stuff. I vividly remember him drinking liquid from squeezed elephant shit. So there, he makes the passing of Irwin just a bit bearable. Sometimes I think that it would be cool if he gets poisoned by his own piss and dies. That'll top Irwin big time. Then I remember that I wouldn't have anything interesting to watch so I'd just wish a tsunami at the set of Jersey Shore. Then suddenly, Jersey Shore gets canceled. I honestly dunno if I'm gonna be happy that the crap got axed or to be bummed-out cause they won't get hit by a tsunami. So then I realize that's why I prefer reading over watching TV. Wait, I think Family Guy's on, nope, just a commercial. Sorry. Where was I? Well, what's with commercials these days? They're all creative now. They got robots, animation, even animals but all these got nothing to do with the product. Selling milk? Robots for you! Credit Card? Monkey and champion sprinter! Burgers? Sexy women...well, I guess this one's okay. But to be fair, I'll include: detergent? macho bald guy! Alright, enough, enough. But really? What am I saying? What has this got to do with the book? I dunno. Nothing I guess. This book's one crazy blob of crazy-satirical-explorer-bitHeartwarming goo. I can't really say that it's beautiful or great prose-wise or story-wise. It's funny as hell, also offensive as hell. There was this part where the uncanny comparison between Canadians and Cows are made. I couldn't control myself. Sorry, Canadian friends. It's something you should experience yourself to understand. Or not, since you might be offended. Also where a great many words are exhausted to lambast the beautiful city of Seattle. Remember Sleepless in Seattle? Yep, I really dunno why that movie never had any scene where it rained. Weird. Semple lives there, so I guess her claim that one of the richest cities in the world is dominated by bums and hobos are pretty credible. I also wouldn't want to live anywhere where I'd be thankful if the shit I stepped on is a dog's. I hate shit. At least they have great coffee. Well, let's give them that, they've lost the Sonics already. So I guess the big question is: Why should you read this? Well, for starters a lot of super cool Beatles references. Also, Al Gore is a superstar! That counts for something, right? Right, guys? Guys? Guys? Guys? Oh! You're still here? Well, if you're still interested... Honestly, it's one crazy novel. Everything's random and some things seem superfluous, but you gotta be crazy if you don't enjoy this one.

This was a fun and creative book. The story is told via emails and correspondence between various parties reflecting their different perspectives on the mental illness of the main character. She hires a personal assistant in India who does her shopping, travel arrangements, banking, etc. The main character seems to be agoraphobic and has problems coping on many levels. She has a very sweet daughter who attends private school. The husband is a high level executive at Microsoft. It is a fun read and particularly endearing since references so many familiar places in Seattle.

Fun, Fast read. 
 There were a couple times where the author put information in that didn't need to be there. I just started skipping left and right, but it was a fun little story.

reference_books.title: The Stranger
reference_books.review_text:
"Here we have a perfect reflection of this trial: everything is true and nothing is true" 
 Honestly, wasn't a huge fan of this book. It was kind of boring and kind of weird and I'm not really sure I got a whole lot out of it. Had to read it for a grad school class and it's definitely not something I would have picked up on my own.

reference_books.title: American War
reference_books.review_text:
"Sarat thought about how easy it would be to fix the mistake, to simply redraw the stars properly. But she knew that even broken history is history. The stars, cast wrong, must remain that way. It would be wrong to change them" 
 Set in a future where global warming has reduced America's land mass and a second civil war has broken out over the South's refusal to give up fossil fuels, American War follows the story of Sarat, a young girl who is growing up in the South. After surviving a massacre at the camp she lived in for six years, Sarat desires revenge on the people who killed her mother and injured her brother. But revenge will not come easy, and it will not come without a price. 
 --- 
 This was definitely a dense, slow read for me. I wish there had been a little more background about the causes of the war and the divisions that separated the country at the beginning of the novel, since these divides seemed crucial to understanding a lot of what was happening. Sarat as a character was an interesting person to read about, but felt pretty one dimensional motivation wise. I felt incredibly disappointed by the end of the book, because instead of closure it felt like the novel just ended back where it started and I wanted more for the characters. 3.5 stars.

reference_books.title: City of Saints & Thieves
reference_books.review_text:
"If you're going to be a thief, the first thing you need to know is that you don't exist" 
 Tina is out for revenge, and her revenge is so close she can almost taste it. After 5 years of training, she is ready to seek out the man she believes murdered her mother - the man who is also her sister's father. But when things don't go as planned and Tina is caught by her childhood friend Michael, the son of the man she is trying to kill, Tina is forced to question her certainty about her mother's murderer. When all signs point back to her childhood home in the Congo, will Tina find the answers that she is expecting? 
 --- 
 I want to start by saying that I really enjoyed this book: I was only planning on reading this for a little while before switching over to the book I have to read for my class, and I ended up reading this book in a single day. I couldn't put it down. The characters are compelling, the mystery draws you in, and the writing is fantastic. I did feel that some of the supporting characters were a little lackluster and could have been more developed - I hardly know anything about most of them and wish I knew more. The Goondas, the gang in this book, felt a little lackluster compared to the Dregs we all know and love in Six of Crows/Crooked Kingdom, so I wish that there was just more to them as a whole. It felt hard to connect to some aspects of the ending because these secondary characters weren't as developed. Otherwise, I loved the story and would recommend this book to anyone looking for a mystery novel with POC characters that really throws curveballs at you. 
 Would give this a 4.5 out of 5

reference_books.title: The Language of Thorns: Midnight Tales and Dangerous Magic
reference_books.review_text: I really love how Bardugo took some classic fairy tales and twisted them into something different and unexpected. Each one of these stories took a surprising turn and explored different aspects of humanity. I think my favorite one was The Witch of Duva.

reference_books.title: The Lover
reference_books.review_text: This is another book I had to read for my class, and I just found the story hard to keep straight. The narrator jumps around in time a lot and I struggled to figure out when we were in the "past" vs the "present" vs the "future", as the narrator writes about how she started writing, her mother, her brother's death, and the Chinese lover she took when she was 15 for money. IT wasn't a BAD story overall, but it was just incredibly hard for me to keep straight. 2.5 / 5

book_a.title: When Dimple Met Rishi
book_a.user_review:
"She did the only thing she could think to do in the moment - she flung her iced coffee at him and ran the other way" 
 Dimple is an Indian-American girl who has just graduated high school and is set to attend Stanford in the fall to study coding, much to the disappointment of her mother, who is extremely traditional. This sets up a lot of tension between Dimple and her mother, as Dimple is much more progressive compared to her mother. When Dimple's parents agree to let her attend a summer coding program that allows the winning team to market their new app, Dimple is shocked and ecstatic. Until she meets Rishi, an Indian boy who is the son of one of her parent's family friends. The two families have arranged for them to meet in the hopes that eventually they will get married. And Dimple does not take the news well. But will Dimple's disgust with Rishi fade over the coming six weeks? 
 --- 
 This book was SO cute and SO fun. It literally had me laughing out loud at times. I absolutely loved that both of the main characters were Indian, as I can only think of a handful of books with an Indian main character. I also loved that one was more traditional than the other, as this created some realistic tension between the two characters. I also absolutely loved that Dimple was so into coding, something that many females are not interested in - particularly in YA. This book had so many things going for it and none of it felt overdone or kitschy. It was such a fun read, perfect for summer trips to the beach! I highly recommend that you pick this one up.

sample_reviews.review_text:
gY"sSynopsis: The Shah family & Patel family both set up their children Dimple & Rishi for an arranged marriage & sends them off to a summer program, so they can get to know each other & get married ASAP. Dimple doesnaEUR(tm)t want a husband right now but is totally unaware of her parentsaEUR(tm) sinister plan. Whereas Rishi is a hopeless romantic & is ready to woo her, upon his parents request. 
 gY"sAnd tada it's Bollywood movie-in-the-making! IaEUR(tm)m serious! There is song & dance & Hindi dialogs running rampant in this book. Even a typical Hindi-movie Airport scene! I was warned this book would be too YA for me. I simply didnaEUR(tm)t know it would be to THIS extent! The writing isn't bad. ItaEUR(tm)s got all the feels too! But itaEUR(tm)s beyond my mental capacity to relate to 18-yr olds thinking of marriage! I had this strong urge to shake the parents & tell them are u guys for REAL???gY~+-Like let the kids 1st graduate please! And I'm baffled - which 18-year old, that too a MALE readily accepts the idea of marriage before graduation?!

What a disappointment. At first I thought this book was cute but the more I read the more annoyed and bored I got. 
 The biggest problem with the book is that there's no romantic or sexual chemistry between Dimple and Rishi. They're supposed to go from (one-sided) dislike to friends to lovers but it just wasn't convincing to me. If the book was about their friendship, it would be much more believable. It didn't help that the POVs kept switching way too fast. And that subplot with Ashish and Celia was unnecessary and just as unconvincing. 
 Both Dimple and Rishi are competing in Insomnia Con (really bad name). It's supposed to be a web development program, and we never get to find out much about it, but if I understood correctly they're making a mobile app. Web development and app development are very different things, so this doesn't make sense. The book takes place during the six weeks of Insomnia Con but it doesn't seem like they're there at all, that's how little they talk about it. They spend much more time talking and preparing for some ridiculous talent contest. This talent show has nothing to do with tech industry but apparently everyone has to participate. And there's a statistic that says 78% of talent show winners also won Insomnia Con - but those are completely different competitions that have nothing to do with each other! Why would your ability to dance or sing have anything to do with how good your app is? 
 I really wanted to like this book, it had so much potential. But it was too predictable. And I think the author avoided writing about the details of app development because she doesn't know anything about it - but that's why writers need to do research. I feel like I would have enjoyed this much more if I read it ten years ago.

I think I am just gonna DNF this one. It is too damn cliched for my liking. Found the story quite.. not mature too. Romantic or sentimental readers might love this but too bad I'm neither romantic nor sentimental. 
 Plus I am quite unhappy with the Hindi terms in the book. If the author wanted to make the story original and unique, at least insert some side notes or footnotes of the meaning of the terms and not expect all the readers to understand Hindi. I mean, what the heck man. I like to know every details in the story. Stuff like this is just not cool.

What a disappointing read! I read great reviews of this pre-release and expected so much more from this book. I loved the idea of protagonists from an Indian background and that the book was set in a coding environment, particularly for the female character. Sadly, the unconventional background and associated gender issues were almost entirely ignored - the author appeared to have no knowledge of coding and therefore the setting was referred to very little which meant that Dimple's passion for coding felt flat and not very credible. Rich's enjoyment of comic book art was much better understood and discussed more thoroughly. 
 The romance itself developed far too quickly in my opinion, particularly in relation to two characters from conservative backgrounds (one of whom is supposed to treasure their traditional values). Rishi seemed to be put forward as entirely flawless which began to irritate whilst Dimple was either full throttle 'Independent Woman' or completely loved up and incapable of holding any other thought in her head. The plot was thin and seemed only to be there as an excuse for the characters to be kissing. 
 Honestly, I wouldn't recommend this to anybody. I'm sure there is far better fiction out there - Rani and Sukh by Bali Rai being a much better example!

This might be my favorite book of the summer. Dimple and Rishi are engaging characters who shuck many YA conventions while the story plays out in a relatable way. The cover and back cover photos make this one to snap up in hardcover while you can. A high point for me was seeing how different their Indian families were, and how their connections to each other did not feel contrived. I'm happy this book made the NYT bestseller list!

2.5/5 stars. This was a very sweet YA story, but some of the dialogue seemed very contrived and unrealistic. Some of the side characters seemed really stereotypical. Lots of juvenile behavior and shenanigans. My favorite thing was a male protagonist who was really earnest and expressive.

4 dYOEY's (BLOG LINK IN BIO) 
 One of the nicest books I've read in awhile. dY~S It's gotta be teen "chick-lit" over "general" chick-lit, the last one of those I read was trash...dY~' 
 Who knew a YA rom-com revolving around arranged marriage would be so good! 
 The characters are immensely likeable & goofy, whilst it's full of nerdy references - perfect for fans of the book Geekerella. 
 It's also a gentle look inside another culture; so I think it's great that this book's been so popular.

I almost DNF this book. The only thing that kept me going 1/2 - 3/4 of the way through was the audiobook narrators. It was pretty slow moving for me, and a little long. I really enjoyed the emotion and realistic feel they brought to the book. Overall, glad I stuck it out.

Book: When Dimple Met Rishi 
 Author: Sandhya Menon 
 Rating: 1 Out of 5 Stars 
 Okay, I really do feel like I'm the only one of my friends who didn't like this book. I don't know what it was, but I just could not get into this book at all. There was just something that really off for me. 
 I really did try to like this book, but it just felt forced to me. I was expecting an Indian girl who went off to coding camp and am almost Sarah Dessen or Morgan Matson style book. What I got instead was a childish character mixed with even childish writing. I don't know what it was, but the writing and the characters made me feel as if I were reading a middle school level book-a poorly written one for that matter. I really can't remember the last time I disliked a book this much. 
 My biggest problem was Dimple. I have never seen a more immature character in a long time. She is rude, annoying, and disrespectful. She needs grow up. I really did feel like she was in junior high, not just graduated high school. She is supposed to be this coder girl who wants nothing more than to go to coding camp and get away from her family's goal of finding her a husband. Sounds pretty cool right? Yeah, right...That is not what we got. Instead, we got a very self-centered and annoying character. I think I would have liked the book more, if the main character was actually well written. 
 The writing....Don't even get me started on that. I don't remember the last time I winced that much on so few places. There was no flow and it was way, way too choppy. I have read a number of close writers who write so much better than this. Plus, there was no plot. If there was an actual plot to go with the summary, it was missing. 
 I don't know what went wrong with this book and I don't see how it is so popular. Maybe I'm just missing something, but I did not like this one at all. I don't even know if I'll read more from this author. 
 Don't judge the book based on my review. I usually tend not to like books everyone does and I love books that everyone doesn't.

book_b.title: I Wrote This For You
book_b.user_review:
"And we clutch that picture to our hearts because we expect each other to always be the people in the picture. But people change. People aren't pictures. And you can either take a new picture or throw the old one away." 
 --- 
 While I thought that this poetry collection was well put together and the images in it were stunning, I wasn't blown away with the overall feel of the writing. There were a few entries that I absolutely loved, but some of the others felt less impactful, particularly the large number of one liner pages. I do think this book is worth paging through if you're a fan of poetry collections (Think Milk and Honey, Wildly into the Dark, etc.) but I wasn't as impressed as I was hoping to be.

sample_reviews.review_text: HOLY SHIT this book is amazing. They all seem to have the same thing in common and that's heartache but whatever atleast it sounds good?
There are parts I love, there are parts I did not like so much. Overall, it was still great. Better than Lang Leav's Love and Misadventure. Posted my favorites below.

$4 on Kindle. For some reason I assumed it was a story, a love story, so I wss taken aback a little when I saw the pictures and short poems of love and life. 
 I ended up really enjoying the quotes, poems, stories and bookmarked freely relating to them and and likely in the future. Nice item to have stored on my reader for future references.
Lovely words.

I have mixed feelings about anthologies, so it shouldn't come as a surprise that I would have mixed feelings about poem books too. This time I tried reading this book when I'm in a more contemplative mood, and maybe it did help a little, I suppose? 
 I have to say, I don't like the pictures. I don't feel like it adds value to the poems at all, and in comparison to the words, they pale in art. The poems are okay - some I actually enjoy. My favourite is "The Twins" and it goes like this: 
 "I like to think that somewhere out there, on a planet exactly like ours, two people exactly like you and me made totally different choices and that, somewhere, we're still together." 
 I thought that the idea of doppelgangers in an alternative universe making the choices that you wish you have made, is quite a sweet but sad way of describing a breakup. 
 Other than that, I'm pretty much 'meh' about this book, although I'm appreciative of the way the tone picks up towards the end. It had a nice message at the end too, so that wasn't too bad.

Some passages were beautifully written but most, I didn't find appealing. There were cliche passages and some didn't go well together that they kind of didn't make sense. It also didn't give me the "feels" that I was expecting before reading it--maybe because I focused too much on how it is written.

I wrote this for you is a magnificent, highly emotional, and unforgettable experience that is uniquely different for each person who reads it. The photographic images combined with the sheer simplistic beauty of the prose is stunning. It grabs at your heart as it seeks to reveal its emotional depths. More than once I found myself in a fog of memory as experiences and people crashed inside me. This book is a good reminder that there is more to life than the whirlwind of activity and that much of true living is found in quiet moments and the relationships you have with others.

This book had such great potential with a captivating title and an alluring abstract. However, it fell far from my expectations, to the point where I am happy this book was gifted to me rather than going out and spending the money myself. This is a book of what I would loosely call poetry. It may be poetry in an extreme Tumblr-esque type way (not that there are not good poets on Tumblr), however I personally viewed it more as pieces of flash fiction mixed with quotes about life and love. 
 The "Poems" 
 Let me start by saying there were some good pieces in this book. There were gems hidden throughout that I personally really enjoyed ("The Circus Is Cheaper When It Rains," "The Seconds Before Launch," The Fragments Belong Together," "The World Is Better Backwards," and "The Dwindling Conversation" were what I personally found to be the best). However, a majority of the book felt like I was scrolling through a word porn page on Facebook, reading recycled quotes, or reading another one of those open letters to *insert literally anyone* that you could kind of connect with but left you with this yearning for more. Some of the quotes are speaking to you as a reader and could apply to most anyone (see the last 30 pages), and the rest feel like I'm reading someone's diary entries cut up and reorganized into a letter to a significant other. One redeeming quality to maybe a third of the poems is the use of the titles in relation to the overall meaning. There were times when the title made the quote actually noteable, such as "The Leftovers." Other times, however, the title seemed a little too askew and abstract, such as "The Seraphim And The Pirate." 
 The Pictures 
 The worst aspect of the book is the pictures. They do not fit. Most of them look like stock photos someone found during a google search and don't offer much insight into the poems. Each piece had its own picture, but only a few seemed to correlate with the poems. Maybe if I took the time to reread the book a handful of times I would be able to see some deep artistic connection that I am just currently unable to appreciate. However, this book doesn't give me any inclination to want to read it. 
 Formatting 
 I did appreciate how some of the poems turned sideways. While it probably wasn't necessary, it did make it more interesting and caught my attention in the midst of the stream of poor quotes. However, the arrangement of the poems felt sloppy. I could not really tell a difference between the various sections until the last one--the attention of the poems seemed to be pointed back at us as readers and not the lost lover. Otherwise it seemed like a back and forth fight within every section to decide if the atuhor loves or hates their last partner with "insights" to life randomly stuck in. Maybe the author was trying to convey the back and forth emotions following a break up, however it could have been better executed if that is the case. 
 Personally, I won't be rereading this book again any time soon. I wanted more from it the entire time and I think if I had put it down (it is an entirely easy read and only took me an hour), I wouldn't have picked it back up. This book is for people coming right out a break up, or deeply in love, or dealing with a break up horribly because they are still deeply in love. It isn't worth your time if you are looking for poetry with real depth.

reference_books.title: Soumission
reference_books.review_text:
"Soumission" is weer een echte Houellebecq - enorm controversieel, lastig te interpreteren en al voor de verschijning spraakmakend. 
 Het is 1922 en in Frankrijk wint de "Moslimbroederschap" de verkiezingen van het Front National. Dat betekent een ommekeer in Frankrijk (en in Europa). De Sharia wordt ingevoerd en het economisch systeem wordt gebaseerd op een theorie van o.a. G.K. Chesterton als "derde weg" tussen Kapitalisme en Communisme: familiebedrijven zijn de ruggengraat van de economie met forse financiele steun van de "oliestaten". 
 Houellebecq's hoofdpersoon, Francois, is een 44 jarige liberale professor aan de Sorbonne die alles met nogal afstandelijke belangstelling gadeslaat. Eigen idealen heeft hij niet en de ontwikkelingen vervullen hem met een vage angst maar als blijkt dat hij weliswaar ontslagen wordt maar wel zijn volledige salaris krijgt doorbetaald vindt het het allemaal wel best. Behalve dan dat hij niet meer in staat is het bed te delen met veel van zijn studentes en dat zijn huidige Joodse studente-vriendinnetje met haar ouders vlucht naar Israel. Hij voelt zich ontheemd, uitgeblust en oud. Maar er gloort hoop. Als hij zich zou bekeren tot de Islam kan hij zijn oude baan terugkrijgen met veel meer salaris en krijgt het onder de nieuwe polygamie bepalingen van de Sharia het recht meerdere vrouwen te hebben. De beslissing die hij neemt is, laten we maar zeggen, niet het gevolg van existentiele gewetenswroeging. 
 Je kunt het boek op talloze manieren interpreteren. Ik lees er vooral een satire in op het liberale atheistische vrijdenken in het gelaiciseerde (goed woord ?) Frankrijk. Maar je kunt het ook lezen als een satire op de onredelijke angst voor de Islam. Het is natuurlijk heel bijzonder dat het boek uitkwam op de dag dat de aanslagen in Parijs werden gepleegd - terwijl Houellebecq betoogt dat de reguliere Islam die niets moet hebben van terrorisme, de overwinning behaalt via de verkiezingen. Je kunt het ook lezen als een satire tegen de Islam, als een religie waarvan de werkelijke waarden en normen zo door en door westers-conservatief zijn niemand (behalve buiten links) er echte bezwaren tegen heeft. 
 Als je wilt weten wat hij zelf zegt te bedoelen moet je het [interview in The Paris Review](http://www.theparisreview.org/blog/20...) maar lezen (het is van 2 januari, dus voor de aanslagen).

reference_books.title: Invisible Cities
reference_books.review_text:
The city has always been a fascinating model for human society. From the Great Babylon, the source of all evil, until the New Jerusalem with golden streets and pearl gates it appeals to humans as the realisation of dreams, bad or good. 
 Italo Calvino provides a wonderful mixture of these dreams in this beautiful book as Marco Polo describes the cities he visited to his host Kublai Khan. Gradually the great Khan realises that the cities are dreams, images of Marco's Venice but aren't they also the images of the Khan's own dreams about his vast empire ? 
 And while reading I come to realise that these cities also represent my own dreams about society, my hidden fears and my personal hopes. 
 This is the best any book can achieve. Magic-realism at its best. One time reading is not enough for this book, you have to read it again and again.

reference_books.title: Days Without End
reference_books.review_text:
A well written novel about two soldiers in the US Army during the civil war and the wars against the Indians. What I like about the book is the extensive descriptions of the scenery and weather during the long marches and the realisation that the lives of the extremely poor Irish lads in the army were not that much different from those of their adversaries (both the Indians and the confederates). Also the description of the tender love between the two men is a pleasure to read. 
 What I do not like about the book is the graphical description of horrible atrocities agains the Indians. This is already the third book in this years MBP after The Underground Railroad and the Ministry of Utmost Happiness that contains too much violence to my taste. 
 I also like open endings so I would have given four stars if the last chapter would have been left out.

reference_books.title: Back to Blood
reference_books.review_text:
Het nieuwste boek van Tom Wolfe is een Comic in zwart-wit, een tekenstrip in een orkaan van woorden. Uitvergrootte emoties en inktzwart aangezette tegenstellingen leveren een theatraal plot. "Terug naar het bloed" is een "roman noir", een echte rechtschapen held, een beeldschone maar o-zo-verdorven vrouw als verrader en een samenloop van omstandigheden die je zelf nooit zo zou kunnen bedenken. 
 Het verhaal speelt zich af in Miami, explosief vat vol tegenstellingen. Met volkomen gescheiden bevolkingsgroepen van onder andere Cubanen en Haitianen en met extreme tegenstellingen tussen puissant rijk en straatarm, een stad "waar iedereen elkaar haat". Het boek staat vol Spaanse en Creoolse begrippen en woorden, exponenten waarmee verschillende generaties zich tegen elkaar afzetten: de oudere provinciale Cubanen die alleen Spaans spreken, de jonge Haitiaanse gangs die Creool gebruiken als geheimtaal en de schmierende Russen die elkaar bedreigen in het Russisch. Taal is een wapen bij Tom Wolfe. 
 Spannend en onderhoudend geschreven werpt het boek een genadeloos fel licht op een moderne samenleving waarvan Reality-tv, uitzinnige kunstvormen en porno de hoekstenen zijn.

reference_books.title: The Remains of the Day
reference_books.review_text: Geweldig verhaal in fraai Engels. Kazuo Ishiguro suggereert veel en je moet echt tussen de regels door lezen. Maar dan zie je ook een mooie lovestory en een prachtig tijdsbeeld van de tijd tussen de beide wereldoorlogen.

I really wanted to like this as it is a classic however I failed. 
 As a piece of literature I am sure it is quite remarkable however I detested the characters and their attitudes - there was not one likeable character amongst them. I am guessing I was supposed to find their "shenanigans" amusing, unfortunately I didn't - I felt they were a bunch of self-centred people completely lacking in any insight.

Before reading any book, it helps to understand the time and place that inspired it. I feel this is vital for taking in On the Road, the story of a group of friend that didn't want to get a job and settle down. These were the free spirited Beat generation, which came right after WWII and rejected the morality of the time. The book describes Jack Kerouac's multiple journeys across America and into Mexico with his friends, taking drugs, sleeping around with numerous women, and doing whatever it took to keep them on their grand journey - be it beg, borrow, or steal. The story shows a lot of amoral behavior but is sincere, perhaps showing the need of people who feel spiritually lost to continually seek out that part of them that's missing.

I did not finish it. For some reason, I kept thinking of the book Of Human Bondage. One character kept bring down the main character. Perhaps I read them too close together. I felt like I was not getting anywhere anytime Dean came into the picture.
A disappointing book about irresponsible men who treat women terribly. There was very little endearing about the self-absorbed characters. Dean Moriarty seems like a classic case of bipolar disorder.
I may never go on another road trip again, just on prinicple.

Contrary to my expectations, this book was actually a pretty entertaining read-aloud. Jack/Sal is full of bs and so are all his buddies, and they run basically run around aimlessly between NYC and SF for about 300 pages, which is alternately amusing and awfully dull . . . which I think is part of the point. And for those interested, pieces of Sal's narration expose some of the inner workings of old-fashioned American sexism and racism. You could call it a kind of cultural study.

I'm really wanted to adore this book. I really did. I'd heard so much about it, seen quotes of it on pinterest. The guy behind the counter at Boarders when I purchased it even told me "It's the kind of book that you remember where you were when you read it". There's beautiful mysticism interwoven in passages of On The Road, which Kerouac would later take up in The Dharma Bums. But the momentum of the story doesn't allow you to mull over these passages. They hit your consciousness fast, and leave just as quick. This is largely in part to the run-on sentences that Kerouac uses. This is a stream of consciousness flow, that is quite loosely structured. The guys in the novel booze, chase women and flee from their responsibilities. And the women, well they wait on their men and plead for them to stay. All but Mary-Lou, who is referred to as a whore for hitting the road just like Sal and Dean do. 
 A good woman in the novel is one who will put up with the men boozing, having affairs, taking to the road and 'never say a harsh word, never a complaint...her old man can come in any hour of the night with anybody and have talks in the kitchen and drink the beer and leave any old time'. I had to remind myself that this was written in the fifties, before the civil rights movement, before the women's movement and before gay and lesbian rights. 
 The novel begins with Sal's fascination with Dean and ends with it. He writes of him as crazy, a goof and an angel. Ultimately, On the Road is a bromance. Sal and Dean pining for each other and the escapism that the road offers.

book_b.title: The Ocean at the End of the Lane
book_b.user_review:
Soms is de grens tussen literatuur en "gewone boeken" wat grijs. Neil Gaiman schrijft knap en creatief maar soms legt hij alles ook wel heel goed uit en valt er voor de lezer weinig meer te raden. The Ocean at the end of the Lane heeft het niet gehaald voor de longlist van de Man Booker Prize 2013 maar hij staat wel (nummer een zelfs) op de alternatieve "Not the Booker" lijst in The Guardian. 
 Een man gaat naar een begrafenis in de buurt waar hij zijn jeugd doorbracht. Impulsief besluit hij even op bezoek te gaan bij het huis waar een vriendinnetje woonde, dichtbij zijn oude huis. Wanneer hij er komt treft hij de inderdaad de situatie aan zoals hij zich herinnerde. Of toch niet helemaal? Wanneer hij op een bankje gaat zitten komen plotseling herinneringen boven aan een angstaanjagend avontuur dat hij hier beleefde toen hij 7 jaar oud was. Gaat het om verdrongen herinneringen die plotseling bovenkomen ? Is het echt gebeurd of heeft hij dit gedroomd ? 
 Neil Gaiman schreef een prachtig modern Fantasy verhaal dat zich afspeel in een tijd en ruimte die raakt aan onze werkelijkheid maar die er niet helemaal mee samenvalt. Hij schrijft in de stijl van Roger Zelazny (De prinsen van Amber) en Daphne du Maurier (The House on the Strand). Het is een tijdloos verhaal waarin kinderlijke angstdromen zijn vermengd met een verhaal over grootse zelfverloochening.

sample_reviews.review_text:
My first experience with a Gaiman novel and I'm still trying to sort through it in my head. I did really enjoy the story, and the story telling style he has. I'll definitely be reading more of his works, when I want something a bit more challenging and emotional than my usual escapist fare. 
 All the feels are present in this book and at the end I found myself with more questions than answers. But I suppose that was the point of the story all along, and in that it succeeded mightily. I was uncomfortable with the narrative for a short bit (child endangerment trigger) but thankfully that part was short lived, even if the resolution (erasing the incident as though it never happened) left me uncomfortable as well.

2.5 stars. Do you ever read a book that's good, on a technical level, but which you kind of hate anyway? I feel like that's what just happened to me. 
 You know what the problem is? I knew all the themes and the places this book would go. Do you know how I knew everything? Because it's the exact same themes as The Graveyard Book. And Coraline. And probably some of his other books too. It's about letting go of your childhood. Which is cool. It's a good theme. But I can't read an entire book with no other appeal. 
 I can acknowledge Gaiman is a great author. His imagery is pitch-perfect. Unfortunately, I don't know if that's really a good thing. If you've read this book, you know I'm talking body horror. The whole worm thing genuinely brought me one inch from DNFing this. Or dying, whichever came first. Don't read this if you're not a fan of body horror. Genuinely, do not. 
 The whole thing honestly just felt like a repeat of The Graveyard Book, but with less compelling characters. Yes, there were some nifty twists, but I somehow didn't care about any of it. This just felt so mediocre and angering to me, as a book. I felt like I should have loved it and I just didn't.

Sometimes books come at just the right time. Another time, I might have been put off by the fanciful story in "The Ocean and the End of the Lane", but this week in November, days darkening and nostalgic, it was a tale in which I didn't mind getting lost.

The essential fairy tale has returned. 
 Great short book - set up is quick and efficient, no worries with all the background information on every character - it just dives right in. We are again brought back to the essential - the imaginative - the simple in order to tell and retell a story. Complete with heroes, heroines, evil doers, and a twist here and there. 
 I dare not go into details - what fun would that be? Go, and discover for yourself (and I bet you only need a day or two to in fact discover). Instead, I'll just leave with a few favorite quotes from the book - it gives a great snapshot of the tone of this little treasure. 
 "Adults follow paths. Children explore. Adults are content to walk the same way, hundreds of times, or thousands; perhaps it never occurs to adults to step off the paths, to creep beneath rhododendrons, to find the spaces between fences." 
 "Nobody actually looks like what they really are on the inside. You don't. People are much more complicated than that. It's true of everybody." 
 "When I left, I went with Lettie Hempstock and her mother out of the front door, and the moon was a thin white smile, high in a cloudy sky, and the night was gusty with sudden, undecided spring breezes coming first from one direction, then from another; every now and again a gust of wind would contain a sprinkling of rain that never amounted to anything more than that."

 Note (added later 8/17/16): I feel the need to add that I've thought about this book for a little while now and I've come to a conclusion as for why I don't really care to dissect this book.... I found it somewhat depressing. The writing was terrific, as is the case with all of the writing I've read by Neil Gaiman, but ultimately this was not a book that made me feel all that good about myself and the world in the end. While I'm usually a fan of Jodi Picoult's novels, have read several of them, I'm growing weary of the format.  As other reviewers have noted, this one was much too similar to My Sister's Keeper and I simply couldn't get through it.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I'm seriously considering putting Jodi Picoult in with the "No Anitas" section. It's funny how some writers are derided for playing the same song over and over again, viz., John Grisham, when Ms. P does the same thing. 
 The book is about a serious dilemma a woman has when considering future care and expenses for her six year old daughter who has Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI or Brittle Bone disease). 
 When she approaches a lawyer about a wrongful birth suit against her obstetrician, she creates a rift in her family, her friendships, and her town. 
 It was kind of icky to find recipes in this book. I know the main character found it very stress relieving to bake pastry (I find great relief in eating pastry), but seriously, to include recipes was jolting. 
 I have no doubt Ms. Picoult will enjoy continued success, even if she is dangerously near Dan Brown country in the realms of quality.

** spoiler alert ** 
 They really need a 'stopped reading before finished' option on goodreads. I generally love Jodi Picoult. Her stories deal with tough subject matter, have great characters and are very well researched. This one was the exception for me. I kept trying to like it. I made it more than halfway through. 'The Pact' follows the story of two families, and two highschool sweethearts, Chris Harte and Emily Gold. The story begins with the tragic event, what looks like a murder/suicide, that ends with Emily Gold dead and Chris Harte in the hospital. The story then goes on to show the history leading up to the event. The Gold and Harte families were extremely close and Emily and Chris grew up as best friends. Until their friendship turns into something stronger. Both seem devoted to each other, from the outside. I guess for me, one of the problems was Emily Gold's character. She seemed to have some serious issues leading up to the 'event' that stemmed from something traumatic in her childhood. What seemed unbelievable to me is not that this event should from that point on lead her into what seems to be a serious depression, but that she was able to hide it for years from everyone in her life until she succeeded in ending her own life. Her inner feelings seem completely at war with her outer actions throughout most of her young adulthood. Even more unbelievable is the extent to which her mother blames Chris for her death, even after finding out about her daughter's possible depression through a diary found in her daughter's own room. As a mother, maybe I just don't want to believe that you can so completely misjudge your own child. That you can live with them and not know how much pain they are in....that you can not really know them at all. That Chris, Emily's seemingly uber-dedicated boyfriend, would not notice some serious warning signs and not ask questions of actions that seemed to really be important. Denial is one thing, but these characters seemed to not be cognizant of her troubles at all. For all their flaws, this complete avoidance of Emily's problems seems completely out of character for both her very loving mother and her very devoted boyfriend and lifelong best friend. Maybe these problems are solved, or at least acknowledged in the end of the book but I was so frustrated that I was unable to finish it. The PactJodi Picoult

Didn't enjoy this. Picoult seemed to want to explore the polemic, contemporary phenomena of teen suicide, but the result is unsatisfying, long winded, pretentious and boring. 
 Why? Three reasons. 
 1) The book feels constructed, unnatural. Take eight people. Four relationships. Two families joined at the hip by their lovebird teen kids. And a lawyer and his assistant. Make the girl a beautiful, promising teen artist, kill her (suicide or murder, only Chris, the loyal, love-blind, sports-star boyfriend, knows for sure) and "explore" how this suicide/murder affects them all. 
 Sounds interesting, and it might have been if it wasn't for stereotypes playing themselves for all they were worth. The Romeo and Juliet teen romance. The (unbeknown to all) troubled girl and the simple, WYSIWYG boy. The secret childhood molesting in a McDonalds toilet, and an undesired pregnancy. The cold, perfectionist, vindictive mum and the warmer, supportive mum. The tormented, reasonable dad and the distant, head-in-the-sand image-conscious surgeon. And, to round things off, there's the obligatory yuppie defence lawyer (an arrogant, hooker-using, win-at-all-costs divorcee with a rebellious teen kid), his hot is-she-isn't-she-a-reforming-influence assistant, a bumbling female cop and an ice-maiden take-no-prisoners prosecutor. 
 The plot plods along as you'd expect, everyone dealing with it in their own way. Relationships crumble and reform. Lifelong friendships disintegrate overnight. Enemies meet for coffee and solace. The truth-has-no-place-in-the-courtroom lawyer doesn't want to hear what his client has to say and weaves a web of fabrications into a house of cards that comes tumbling down with the first words from his client. 
 Thing is, none of this goes anywhere. There are no real conclusions. Things start and fizzle out. Or don't start. Nothing gets resolved. The toilet molesting is never developed, so we don't really know its role in Em's state of mind, which isn't explored either, and which is central to the believability of the story. Yes, we find out what happens eventually, but what we discover is that not even Chris really knows why she felt the way she did, and we're left with the impression he didn't really try to find out. Which, given his apparent communicating skills and the lengths Picoult goes to to convince us that Em and Chris are joined at the heart and know what the other is thinking, just doesn't wash. 
 One could argue that this is real life, and I wouldn't disagree at all. Thing is, if I want real life I can read a newspaper. And if I want a treatise on teen suicide I'll read one done by someone "qualified" to write one, no disrespect meant to Picoult. The reason I'm reading this is because I want entertainment, and this didn't entertain me. It annoyed me. 
 2) As I said, the above may sound interesting, but it comes across as contrived as we skip between the past and present in an attempt to create context. Here, this literary ploy is used and abused with the intention of raising the tension and keeping us guessing. Instead, in my opinion, it falls flat on its face and serves only to prolong the agony of "finding out" - and to add a dozen superfluous chapters that can be skipped on the way to the Big Reveal, which is, after all, the only thing we care about. Did he or didn't he? The thing is, we already know. The answer is in the title. 
 3) There's no real climax to the story. Even the expectedly unexpected verdict comes as an anticlimax, and the tension Picoult tries to introduce to build up to it comes over as false. Why? Because she uses Chris' point-of-view to tell Em's story, and the only way she can maintain said tension is by "not telling" us what only he knows, and must spend every waking hour in jail thinking about. Which is bad storytelling. 
 Picoult wants to keep us guessing, and instead of staying away from Chris' POV and revealing the story through the other protagonists' recollections and discoveries, she takes the easy way out using the past/present, backwards/forwards ploy and the staunch refusal to shine the light of her erratic, sometimes third-person, sometimes omniscient narrator on all of Chris' thoughts, and thereby answer the question bugging us from the beginning right up until until the last chapter. 
 I just wanted to cry out: "He knows! Just tell us!" 
 Annoying.

reference_books.review_text:
I watched the movie a long time ago and loved it incredibly much, so when I finally read the book, I was happy to say that I loved it just as much! 
 It actually surprised me how similar the book and the movie are. 
 Every single character was great, but I especially loved Kissin' Kate Barlow. She's the definition of badass. 
 The back story (told through flashbacks) is fantastic, too. It's surprising to me that a children's book has such an unusual (and important) love story, but of course I'm very happy about it. 
 There really isn't a single bad thing I could say about this story. It's one of my favorites and I would recommend it to everyone.

reference_books.title: The Wave
reference_books.review_text:
Unfortunately, this was a huge disappointment for me. 
 Although the topic and the fact that this book is based on a real story are very interesting, it was rather poorly executed. 
 The major problem for me were the characters. 
 They had absolutely no depth to them and I was left with many questions. 
 Why does the teacher decide to keep the experiment going in the first place? Why do the students just go with it, without any questions? What makes them decide to tell other students about the movement? How come everyone suddenly cares about Robert? Where do Laurie's doubts come from? What made David change his mind so suddenly? How did Mr. Ross finally realise that his experiment went too far? What made him accept that he needed to stop it? What were the reactions of the students when they realised what they had become? 
 Maybe not knowing the answers to these questions is the point of the book, but it just left me frustrated, confused and annoyed. 
 In addition to that, everything happened very fast and at times I felt like I was reading a newspaper article and not a book. 
 Right after I finished reading, I decided to watch the german movie based on the same true story, and although it ended in a quite dramatic way (bit of an overkill, in my opinion), it still seemed more realistic than this book.

Review posted on A Keyboard and an Open Mind May 16 2016: 
 I remember getting this book from the library not long after it was published in 2011, but the fact that I couldn't remember many details at all made me think that I had DNFed it. However, going by my GoodReads status updates, I did get all the way to the end, but I only gave it two stars. I thought that maybe I should give it another chance to impress me, but sadly, I ended up feeling the same way again. 
 When Constable Peter Grant meets a ghost while supervising a crime scene, it ends up leading him into a world he never imagined. The string of murders his team are investigating are revealed to have a supernatural bent, and before long, Peter is taken on as an apprentice to a wizard, trying to get his head around Latin while also meeting the Gods of the London rivers, among other events. 
 One of my main issues with this book was Peter, and the way he was written. Some will argue with me that he's just a typical hot-blooded male, but it gets not only tiresome but a bit gross when nearly every time he lays eyes on a woman (whether it's one he knows or not), we got descriptions of her perky breasts, or the hardness of her nipples, or how he'd really like to do certain things to her. The book is in first person, which I am picky about anyway, but when I've got a character spouting things like this, it bugs me. If it hadn't been for that, I might have liked him okay, but I think I would have found his character a bit flat anyway. I thought the narration was a bit similar to Mark Watney's in The Martian, i.e. fun and snarky at first, but then forever fun and snarky, to the point where it's just annoying and boring (I know, I know, I'm a crazy weirdo for not liking the Martian). 
 The plot as a whole was not terribly exciting until maybe the last fifty pages or so. I had trouble keeping track with all the players in the murder investigation, not to mention the subplot that didn't really have a lot to do with anything, other than to introduce some side characters. Some of the world-building to do with magic was interesting, particularly to do with the history of magic and also Peter's lessons, but I felt the procedural aspect of the book outweighed the magical aspects by far, which was disappointing, given that it was supposed to be a supernatural crime! 
 As you have probably concluded by now, I'm not going to continue with the series. While its premise promises all my favourite things, the execution just didn't do it for me.

Mi sono annoiata tantissimo :-( 
 E lo dico con grande dispiacere, viste le premesse: romanzo ambientato a Londra (yeah!), poliziesco sovrannaturale (m'ispira!), con i fantasmi (evviva!) e gli stregoni (ri-evviva!) e toni di stampo gaimaniano (potrei commuovermi)... ed e una serie, libri e libri per godermi ambientazioni e personaggi (parte la hola). 
 E invece. (due parole tristissime, "e invece".) 
 Non so perche, gli elementi per una deliziosa lettura d'evasione c'erano tutti, e l'idea era piuttosto originale, ma qualcosa non ha funzionato; e stata una lettura lenta e fiacca, che piu di una volta ho pensato di mollare. 
 Forse perche ho trovato il 'mondo magico' di questo romanzo poco affascinante, poco definito, anche se ho apprezzato l'aver dato un approccio scientifico alla magia, con suoi limiti, rischi e difetti. 
 O magari e stata colpa del protagonista, Peter, e voce narrante, che ho trovato quasi sempre tra l'irritante e il barboso, e il vagamente patetico quando gli parte l'ormone. L'ho rivalutato nella parte finale del romanzo, pero, dal 'viaggio temporale fantasmatico' in poi... magari nei prossimi romanzi migliorera, ma non ho ancora deciso se dargli un'altra possibilita. 
 Il suo maestro stregone e stata la delusione piu grande: mi aspettavo carisma a palate, invece per ora e abbastanza insipido, almeno per essere un potente mago, ufficialmente l'ultimo rimasto in Inghilterra; certe volte persino Peter sembra piu intelligente di lui, e Peter, per sua stessa ammissione, non e proprio una cima. 
 L'umorismo non mi ha fatto ridere, la chimica fra i protagonisti non funzionava, uno dei due personaggi che mi stavano simpatici ha fatto una brutta fine... disastro, insomma. Meno male che ho preso l'ebook in inglese e l'ho pagato pochissimo. 
 Considerazione non attinente con la qualita del romanzo: non ho capito perche la maggior parte delle personificazioni dei fiumi londinesi siano donne di colore. Capirei, giustamente, quelle dei fiumi del continente africano, ma Fleet, Tyburn, Thames... io tenderei piu a immaginarmeli con caratteristiche fisiche tipiche degli antichi nativi luogo. O devo allora supporre che gli spiriti del Nilo e dello Zambesi abbiano tratti nordeuropei? Ma puo anche darsi che mi sia persa qualche spiegazione lungo la strada: quando la noia e alta, la soglia d'attenzione s'abbassa.

This is the story of the orphan girl Sophie who accidentally happens to see a Giant one night. Not wanting to be known by "human beans", the Giant decides to take Sophie with him to the Giant country. He is a very nice Giant, a Big Friendly Giant, but the other Giants are not... they gobble up humans every single night of their lives. 
 As the BFG is able to mix dreams and make people dream them, Sophie forms a plan to get the most powerful woman on the planet on the case: the Queen. With the help of a dream, she convinces her to act and act fast, and very soon, the army is helping the BFG to arrest all the murderous Giants. 
 The BFG and Sophie receive luxurious living quarters close to the Queen, and with the help of his new human daughter, the BFG even manages to become a writer, starting his career with a novel about himself and Sophie... 
 A nice little story. A bit brutal for younger readers, but entertaining and especially funny for everyone who likes word-plays.
