reference_books.title: Freakonomics: A Rogue Economist Explores the Hidden Side of Everything (Freakonomics, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
The thing that bugged me most about this book was the randomness of the things compared in it. The authors tried (very hard in some parts) to show causal relatonships that, upon reflection, seem slightly forced or misapplied. 
 That said, it is a novel concept - and I don't mind chaos, or randomness to a certain point, but then my inner statistician comes to life and starts working the numbers. 
 ***SPOILER ALERT*** 
 Like when the authors try to show a relationshp between the legalization of abortion and a drop in criminal activity over the last 25 years, basically postulating that those aborted fetuses would be criminals had they been born. A bit inflammatory, no? 
 I think some of that appears a bit more reckless on second glance - and there are no known studies that show that this is true either way. So, it's supposition. Entertaining, in its own way, but also purely 'fun with numbers'. It shouldn't be taken as some sort of statistical gospel, that's for sure. 
 However, Freakonomics is interesting in that it does try to go beyond the traditional barometers and barriers built into the world of economics and works very hard to get people to think about things from differing angels. 
 In that, it succeeds.

reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 This one started out with an interesting hook. The prologue was promising, and necessary to the plot. 
 However, it took a long time to get it to reconcile with his plot and I grew restless waiting for that to happen. Eventually, enough action started to happen and the lulls disappeared. It flowed pretty smoothly after that, and I'm glad I stuck it out. 
 It's a huge book, around 1000 pages. Wow. I haven't read a book this long in a while. So, it was good that it engaged me, right up until the end. 
 A couple of commments: The bad guys seemed almost cartoonishly bad, and predictable. They rape, torture, murder - all for pleasure, even sexual arousal. It's an over-used plot device. It's supposed to make you hate the bad guy so much you want him to have a grisly demise. However, in this case, with the baddest baddy of them all, the conclusion isn't particularly gruesome or satisfying. It's rather a let-down, especially since he was built up to be so bad. 
 There were a lot of storylines competing for your attention: I can see how they were interwoven, but I could equally see how one or more of them removed would have made for a tighter story, an easier flowing writing style. The book was ambitious, I'll give it that, and it largely worked. 
 I felt it didn't do enough to inspire you as to why the cathedral was being built; too much was hung on the dreams of the men (and few women) involved in the building. However, those aspirations didn't necessary seem lofty enough, or perhaps they weren't adequately described? 
 The most compelling are the undercurrents that show through; the love stories, the families, the lives affected by the building of the cathedral and the town of Knightsbridge. 
 I thought, for the most part, that the characters were a bit better than two dimensional, and in some particular cases particularly well drawn. Ellen, in my opinion, seemed to come to life more than others. Prior Phillip, too. But many of them were rather flat and seemed to only serve to move the plot along - cardboard cut-outs could have done the same. 
 All in all, it was worth the read. It was quite the epic novel, and while I don't feel I learned anything particularly new, I also felt mostly entertained. 
 ****SPOILER ALERT**** 
 NOTE TO AUTHOR: It's likely one raid would have succeeded on the town, but I find it unfathomable that they would wait to fortify the town only under the shadow of another raid. Wouldn't they more likely have fortified the town immediately after the first raid, therefore nullifying the second? Perhaps it's a small point, but I noticed.

book_a.title: Infinite Jest
book_a.user_review:
Right now, I'm finding this book virtually unreadable and it seems the author is trying way too hard to be relevant and hip. It's really too bad, because I want to like this book. 
 I'm going to give it a bit more time. 
 Okay, I gave it 100 pages, which is like 95 more than I should have. It was awful. Self-conscious, laborious, tragically hip and riddled with obscure references that neither seem relevant or worthy of the time it takes to look them up, I simply gave up on this book. 
 Where was the plot? Who were the characters? I still have no idea. And I tried. 
 It very rarely happens. I wanted to give it a shot because the author died earlier this year. I wanted to see what all the fuss was about. It certainly wasn't about the readability of the writing. 
 Anyway, not a fan. Probably won't attempt it again.

sample_reviews.review_text:
The last of the great 'doorstop' books that I hadn't read (well there are still plenty of doorstop sized books out there, but not many are considered great). 
 Wallace can be brilliant, and there are passages, and pages, and page-sized passages, that are thrilling to read; but, in the end, this is a fantastic 400 page masterpiece mired in the bulk of the extra 600 pages of masturbatory non sequiturs and rambling musings that disguise any sort of discernible plot. 
 In light of DFW's demise, much of this book now seems prophetic, a thousand page cry for help, but the tortured genius could still have been aided, in this, by a strong editor.

Ok, before you read this and before I have to say what I have to say, I DID NOT finish the book. I made a conscious choice to cut my losses and bail out of this one and I am sincerely glad that I did. After bailing out of this book I preceded to quickly read three or four novels in the time that I would have read it, and those novels rewarded me much more than anything I read in Infinite Jest. 
 I am not opposed to reading challenging texts, I wrote a fifty-page paper on James Joyce's Ulysses and although it was a challenging read, I was glad that I did it. Infinite Jest does use some similar techniques as Ulysses with the disjointed narrative and using different kinds of writing styles, but the difference is, is that Ulysses had a purpose: The book was meant to simulate the thoughts of one person throughout an entire day and Infinite Jest just rambles on to seemingly no end. After reading ten very dense pages about the color of the protagonists bong, I decided that this book was entirely too long and much of the detail was just beating you over the head. 
 I was told that this book was funny and I must say I rarely laughed, outside of a tepid chuckle. It had none of the sardonic language or satire that I had expected and is prevalent in other texts like Candide, Don Quixote, the work of Jonathan Swift, and some of the better work of Kurt Vonnegut. 
 I was sincerely let down by this work.

David Foster Wallace seems to be--have been, rather. He hanged himself in 2008--one of those writers with, as a friend of mine put it, an empty wastebasket. Like William Vollman and Joyce Carol Oates, he's in love with everything he writes and never discards a word. I picked up Infinite Jest because it's gotten plaudits as a revolutionary work and Wallace as a wunderkind recipient of a MacArthur, etc. Sui generis David Eggers calls it in his foreword (For Writer Working's previous commentaries on Eggers and his work, see September 1, 2008 and July 3, 2007.) Alas. 
 I am now at page 184 of this 981-page (1079 counting footnotes), and I'm giving up. Wallace has an amazing mind, and he welcomes us into every nook and cranny of it, whether we want to go or not, whether it moves the tale or not. 
 The central action of the book revolves around (though is not limited to) a tennis academy boarding school near Boston devoted to turning out net phenoms, taking them in as youngsters and sending them into the pro world. Such an environment of high intelligence and competition offers rich environment for extensive conflict and intrigue, and there is plenty of that. What's more, the book is filled with some amazing characters and wonderful language. This street character, for example. No one would ever write or sound exactly like this, but the essence is pure: 
 It was yrstruly and C and Poor Tony that crewed that day and everything like that. The AM were wicked bright and us a bit sick however we scored our wake ups and boosting some items at a sidewalk sale in the Harvard Square where it were warm upping and the snow coming off onnings and then later Poor Tony ran across an old Patty citizen type of his old aquaintance from like the Cape and Poor Tony got over and pretended like he would give a blow job On The House and we got the citizen to get in his ride with us and we crewed on him good and we got enough $ off the Patty type to get straightened out for true all day 
 So, if all this is so good, why am I quitting. In short, I could have used a lot more of the above, but got instead too many heavy doses of stuff like this: 
 Some ... never do get comfortable with them and use the less garish auditory side-doors; and the abundant sulcus-fissures and gyrus-bulges of the slick latex roof make rain-drainage complex and footing chancy at best ... a kind of safety-balcony of skull-colored polybutylene resin, which curves around the midbrain from the inferior frontal sulcus to the parietooccipital sulcus .. 
 I have a fairly healthy vocabulary, but not an all-inclusive one, and I don't mind heading to the dictionary from time to time. However, Infinite Jest is full of passages like that one, which are not just challenging. They're annoying as hell, and unnecessary. Then, there are the footnotes, which often seem to take a chemistry and/or math degree to even comprehend, and once you do understand them, you're left with that empty feeling you get when someone has to explain a joke to you. Usually when I find myself critical of a work that has received as much positive press as this one, I think the problem is with me rather than the book. This time, I wonder if the people are just jumping on the wunderkind bandwagon. Right or wrong, wading through all that for the occasional literary thrill is just not worth it for this senior citizen.

I feel SO ashamed of myself. I have been wanting to read this book FOREVER! I have kept this on my shelf for a very long time. I know I will have some time off this summer, what a better time than now to savor it....to take on the challenge. 
 I am about 125 pages in...and I JUST CAN'T. 
 I am unsure what to "rate" this book. I supposed it is somewhere between a 2 and a 3. But since I CAN'T finish it, is it REALLY a 3? 
 Is this a GREAT piece of work? I'm not sure. It is a HUGE piece of work that's for sure. But it is confusing, illogical, and tangential...to say the least. 
 I mean NO disrespect to Mr Foster Wallace, but I wonder if this was written during a manic episode. It does sort of read like something like that 
 Having said this....I have NOT finished the book. But I can't....as sad as that is....

I very rarely ever do not finish but the opportunity costs of continuing this pretentious piece of #$%* with its little boy humor...The year of the adult depend undergarments...wink, wink, snicker, snicker... are just too great. No point, rapidly becoming dated, self indulgent...I'll stop here..The fact the book makes a list entitled Hipster Life Recommendations says it all.
It was too much for me. I had to return it to the library mostly unread so my star is just because I couldn't even get partially into the book. I wish they had an "I gave up" option. :)

Not sure about this book. Had heard about it from a couple different people and finally say down to read it. Warning, this book takes TIME to read. Took me almost a month and I typically read 2-3 books a week. DFW has an amazing grasp of the English language and can string together some very poignant and thought provoking phrases, yet in the sheer verbosity of this book much of his points (I feel) are lost. I never got the point of this book. And the footnotes are maddening. Should probably be 2 1/2 stars but I always round up. Like I said, it's great writing, just no point to any of it. I came away with nothing from this novel. Maybe I'm just not smart enough to grasp what he's saying.
I thought it would be more jesty.
Not sure exactly why but I just did not enjoy this at all. I usually power through even stuff I don't care for but I abandoned this one. Maybe someday I'll try again.

Just picked this one up from the library yesterday. I've never read anything by David Foster Wallace, so I guess it is about time... I'm always running into references about this book in other things I am reading. But all I have to say is it better be good if I am going to commit to reading 1,104 pages of it! We'll see... 
 LATER: ok, I feel as though someone completely cheated me out of a week's worth of my life. How in the WORLD has this book gotten so many good reviews? My only guess is that people who give it five stars are in fact giving themselves the high rating as a result of being able to read the whole thing! So many times I wanted to stop, but as always, once I start a book I have to see it through to the bitter end. Only this one didn't even have a real ending. It's like it just stopped at a completely random point, as though the author was tired of writing and just said, "Ok, it's done." 
 There are so many things wrong with this book. I don't mind reading a book that requires me to have a dictionary in one hand... honestly I enjoy improving my vocablulary. But this one was ridiculous. But that isn't my main complaint. The big problem, as I see it, is that the many, many parts of the story never fit cohesively together at all. There are at least 34 main characters, not including Les Assassins des Fauteuils Rollents. I kept thinking that at some point they would all be drawn together into the plot, but alas, it was not meant to be. At around page 400 it looked hopeful, by page 800 it was less so but I was still thinking "This has to get better", but it never did. And, really, over a hundred pages worth of footnotes? I stopped reading them halfway through the book because they were so pointless. 
 Trust me, don't waste your time with this one. And don't believe all the hype. Yes, David Foster Wallace was obviously a genius, and yes, it's sad that he killed himself, but that doesn't excuse this poor excuse for a novel. Oh one other thing that drove me crazy: he started so many sentences with "And but so.." or "So but and..." What is that???

book_b.title: The Society of S (Ethical Vampire, #1)
book_b.user_review:
This was okay as half-breed vampire stories go. 
 There was really only one creepy part, and so it will be obvious what it is; I won't spoil it here. :) 
 But, it was an easy, quick read and entertaining.

sample_reviews.review_text: One of the few books I actively hate. In lieu of ASKING her father ANYTHING about her heritage or her mother, this 13-year-old girl just walks out of the house and hitchhikes to Georgia, where she smokes marijuana for six months. Then, against all odds, she actually does find her mother -- and everyone acts like all this behavior is perfectly normal. No one is the slightest bit upset about ANYTHING. They stand there and talk to each other about it like robots, without actually answering anyone's questions. It's SO frustrating. DNFed.

What a strange book. I picked it up because it had a Horror label on it at my library, and we are doing an all-staff genre study for the horror genre. I don't think I could possibly have found a less scary book with a Horror label. I only found out later that the series name is Ethical Vampire, so that should give you a clue. The tone of the story was philosophical and somewhat mournful (almost Gothic!), and it contained very little that was actually frightening. There are a couple of murders, so I guess that could be scary, but it's not anything more intense than your average P.D. James mystery. Actually... yes, P.D. James fans who want to read a vampire novel for whatever reason should definitely pick this up.

Ari lives with her father. Her dad homeschools her and almost never discusses her mom, who disappeared pretty much right after she was born. Because she's an only child and homeschooled, she has no friends (not counting her dad, the housekeeper and two other people who are over to the house most of the time), so her dad finally lets her go over to the housekeeper's to spend time with her kids. 
 Once she gets a glimpse of normal life, she realizes just how strange her own life is. And then she starts to think that maybe there's something going on with her dad. 
 (There is, but I think it's cooler if you find out for yourself.) 
 I really enjoyed this and I'm psyched to hear that there's a sequel. :) I'll try and pick it up this week sometime.

This was by far, the most boring vampire book I have ever read. I nearly gave up several times, but decided to plug along, in case it got better. Well, it really didn't. The idea of vegetarian vampires, is just about as ridiculous as sparkling vampires. And really, oysters? I suppose I just prefer bloodthirsty or broody vampires to those that try to blend in with humans and take supplements rather than actually do what a vampire is supposed to do, you know, drink blood.
I finished this book only because I can't stop reading a book. Terribly boring and in my opinion poorly written.
I didn't care for this book. It was pretty lame in my opinion. You know I'm not enjoying a book when it takes me a week to read 300 pages. I won't be continuing this series.

The idea for this book was very promising but I just never connected with the characters. The main character got less and less relatable as the story went on and the plot was not strong enough to overcome this.

Review courtesy of Dark Faerie Tales. 
 Quick & Dirty: The book is about a young girl who tries to discover who she really is (cough, vampire.) 
 Opening Sentence: I stood alone outside our house in deep blue twilight. 
 The Review: 
 The story of this girl is based on her trying to find her own identity because her father has sheltered her from so much throughout her life. She works on trying to ease as much information from her father that she possibly can. With the help of her friend Kathleen, Ari is pushed out of her shell and is given enough strength to get the truth from her father in little tidbits. 
 But overall the plot of the book itself is very confusing from the beginning and as I started to read more I realized it was non-existent. When reading there was not much lead about what was going on. The book was simply about the life of a confused little girl who is slowly being exposed to the outside world. 
 When first reading the book the syntax used by the author is also utterly confusing and definitely unnecessary. It seems as if she tries to write as a sophisticated young lady who has been raised reading Shakespeare and Edgar Allan Poe. In this case, it would make sense with the personality Ari was given but in reality she falls extremely short and instead simply makes the book dull. However, it is quite interesting how the writing style changes. When speaking to her father, Ari speaks in a that sophisticated manner using a wide variety of advanced words. But when speaking with her friend Kathleen, Ari becomes more relaxed and she speaks like any other young teenager. 
 Ari is the main character of the book but her intentions are not entirely well known. She is eager to discover who she is and enjoy life but the extent that she will go to achieve these goals are unknown. 
 Kathleen McGarritt is Ari's first true friend. She pushes Ari to do things she would not have otherwise done. She is daring and bold; just the kind of friend Ari needs to escape her ignorant life. Kathleen is indeed an enjoyable character. 
 Raphael Montero is Ari's father. He is the typical over protective father but with a cold breeze. He is unemotional with Ari and from a young age started to home school her himself. Being an extremely successful independent researcher, he teaches his very young daughter subjects only taught in college level courses. His treatment of her is what makes Ari such a mature and adultlike figure. 
 Malcolm Lynch is a so called friend of Raphael Montero. Ari doesn't know this man but soon he makes an appearance in her life to make things more complicated than they already are. He is a poised gentleman at first look but his dark interior motives are mostly unknown by many non vampires. 
 The book itself is slow and without direction. The only interesting thing in the book is the change of writing style which shadows Ari's changing personality. There really isn't any lead that there would be not only a sequel but two books to follow this one. The ending is quite bland. I wouldn't recommend to read this vampire book. 
 Notable Scene: 
 They moved through the alleyways of an imaginary city, picking up cards representing coins and special tools and weapons,feigning at fighting and biting while barely touching. In fact, all five of the boys struck me as shy by nature, overacting in their attempts to socialize. Besides me, Kathleen was the only other woman present,and she moved around the room aggressively, as if she owned it. At times the others tried to gang up on her, and she fended them off effortlessly. She knew the most spells, and apparently she had the most detailed notebook. 
 Occasionally the players robbed one another and deposited their stolen coins in imaginary banks-ever the good capitalist, I thought. The game centered less on fantasy than on greed and domination. 
 FTC Advisory: Simon & Schuster provided me with a copy of Society of S. No goody bags, sponsorships, "material connections," or bribes were exchanged for my review.

A very interesting take on vampires. I loved the story, but I wasn't thrilled w/ the 1st person POV, writing style, & typos. The 1st person POV felt very limiting and not intimate. It was as if SH was trying to tell more outside of Ari's designated perspective and missed the internal aspects of the main character.

A very creepy read. I really enjoyed the twists in this book. But I was confused about Ari's age. The blurb wasn't really the same as the story. Overall, I learned a lot of about vampires. Recommended for people ages 13 and up. WARNING: YOU MIGHT HAVE NIGHTMARES.

reference_books.title: Fifty Shades of Grey (Fifty Shades, #1)

It's not well written which didn't allow me to get invested in the characters. If they, and the writing, were developed and executed better, the erotica parts would've been better. But I found it boring. Shelved for now but maybe a revisit.

reference_books.review_text: I think I would've liked this book several years ago but my taste has changed and I no longer care for chick lit. So three stars it gets. Not a bad book but not a great one either. I was bored and ready to be done.

reference_books.review_text: Huh? Say what, say who? All the characters sound the same and I don't care about any of them!

reference_books.title: Beautiful Disaster (Beautiful, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I think it was free on my nook? Maybe? The characters are a hot wreck. I felt like bashing both their faces in and calling it a day. I hate them, I love them, I hate them some more. t wasn't a great book but I couldn't stop reading it. It's like a train wreck where you can't look away. I don't know how that happens and I'm not sure how I feel about my confusion. So, yeah. Don't judge me! 3 stars for keeping me hooked.

reference_books.title: Hush, Hush (Hush, Hush, #1)
reference_books.review_text: So this book has some major storyline flaws and is borderline neurotic with it's jumping around and over abundance of villians. I like the premise. I like that the bad-boy really was bad. It had confusing moments and its share of eye-rolling-cheesefest. But here's the thing, it kept me entertained and I read it in one sitting. I read to be entertained and so for that, I give it 3 stars. I'll overlook some of the pathetic (eek, I'm sorry...kinda) aspects, such as bomb threat, the police force "investigations", and Vee (the character as a whole! Ugh!), and I'll give the sequel a shot.

book_a.title: Etiquette & Espionage (Finishing School, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Finally a book that has caught my attention! Love me some Gail Carriger so I have high expectations. 
 DNF... Tried twice but I just couldn't get into it.

sample_reviews.review_text: My review is here http://www.darkmatterfanzine.com/dmf/...

This newest offering from Gail Carriger does not disappoint in the slightest. Sophronia Angelina Temminick is a young lady of England, packed off to finishing school after one too many unfortunate incidents--the latest involving a dumbwaiter and an unfortunate trifle. Mademoiselle Geraldine's Finishing School is not quite the kind of finishing school her mother envisioned; in addition to the proper way to curtsey, Sophronia is educated in the shadowy arts of espionage. 
 Fans of Carriger's Parasol Protectorate series will immediately recognize the properly irreverent writing style and fall in love with Sophronia's madcap adventures. This is a wonderful introduction to the world of steampunk and Carriger's revision of Victorian England for any reader.

This was a fun read. I just love the wit that is so characteristic of Gail Carriger. This series is supposedly set 25 years prior to the Parasol Protectorate series. And lots of steampunky goodness - mechanimals, airships and mechanical servants!
This inventive steampunk is funny and clever with some great characters.

What's funny is before this class, I had tried reading this book. I saw it in a bookstore and the cover caught my eye. However, I didn't care for the first chapter and put it down. 
 But I'm so glad I gave it a second chance. It was amazing! Hilarious! I really need some comedic relief in my life rn. It felt a lot like Harry Potter - boarding school, friendship, hidden talents, supernatural (not magical) elements, and an overall arching mystery. Most of the characters are girls and they each have a different quality that makes them suited for the school - super important for young girls to read about! I adored it and I am definitely going to pick up the rest later! =D

Gail Carriger is delightful. I discovered her Parasol Protectorate series and eagerly devoured each book as they came out. I was quite pleased to hear that Carriger was writing a YA series set in that same daffy steampunk world. 
 Many things from the Parasol Protectorate carry over here: the over-the-top character names, the supernatural mythos and the devotion to proper curtsying and fashion. But the books - if not dumbed down - have been crafted to fit a younger audience. The sex is right out. The messages, of friendship and self-acceptance, are more on-the-nose. The characters are silly but relatable. All in all, this is the perfect book for that geeky, awkward teenage girl to find comfort and fun in.

On page 5: One of the main character's names is Mrs Barnaclegoose. You know what I'm thinking of? 
 On page 126: Sophronia seems like such an adventurous character, but I have a slight reservation. 
 She loved the lessons in espionage and deceit -- so many possibilities! -- and remained only a smidge disturbed by the analytical approach to murder. 
 Now, why on earth would you not question that?!??!?!? 
 On page 145, where I stopped: I generally enjoy historical fiction and books about spies, but I really didn't enjoy this book! I was expecting suspense and fight scenes, but instead got Sophronia sneaking around a school that I couldn't visualize. 
 I would give this book 1 star, but I really enjoyed how Gail Carriger added some mythical creatures into the storyline-- werewolves and vampires teach and train the girls.
This story...The fucking stupid names, the stupid story... I can't even...

YA steampunk. Delightful characters, including some younger versions of minor characters from the Parasol Protectorate series, fun action scenes, good world-building and Carriger's amusing turn of phrase. A lot of fun. 
 Quibble: Sophronia never really had much at stake, so I had trouble caring about the mystery prototype.
I'm thinking 3.5 stars. It was fun, but I think I find the cover and synopsis to be misleading. Will discuss and elaborate soon. It was cheeky enough to consider continuing. We'll see!

book_b.title: Bewitching Season (Leland Sisters, #1)
book_b.user_review:
I'd really give this 3.5 stars, which is still a solid rating for a debut author. Hopefully Marissa Doyle keeps growing and the books keep getting better. There are enough reviews giving the summary. I'll just simply say I enjoyed the bok. It was a fun read with magic, mystery, and romance. Several storylines intertwine and clean up nicely at the end. I don't always like clean endings but it works for this book since I think its perfect for younger YAs and reads almost like a fairytale. I think a lot of younger YA (age 12-13) want to read about romance but aren't quite ready for ALL YA that is available. This book is perfect for that maturity level. 
 This book focuses mainly on Persephone and not so much on her twin, Penelope. My biggest gripe of the book is Persy's constant self-loathing. UGH! She constantly compares herself with her sister who looks exactly like her! She never thinks she measure up and at times she gets irritating. Regardless, I am looking forward to Betrayed, the second book.

sample_reviews.review_text: This was such a great book. And it's in one of my favorite genres, gaslamp! (Magic and Victorian England. Fantastic!) I loved all of the characters, including the main one, Persephone Leland, but sometimes you just wanted to punch her. She was basically the epitome of shy, nervous girl around a handsome man. And she seemed to love making the man she truly loved insanely jealous! But overall, a great book.

Maybe I was just in the mood for a fun, lighthearted read - but I really liked this book! It was kind of like Harry Potter meets historical fiction meets regency romance for young adults. 
 Sure the plot was predictable. Sure the main characters could get whiny. Sure sometimes I wondered if they could really be as clueless as they were in the choices that they make (but then again...I was 17 once upon a time). But still, it was an enjoyable read - one that I didn't want to put down! I loved that it was clean, and good-natured, and fun. 
 I didn't give it five stars for some of the above reasons, but mostly because of a sub-plot love story where the kidnapped falls in love with the kidnapper. It just seemed too easy, too obvious, and, well....disappointing. 
 I'm going to be reading the next one in the series without a doubt!

I read the first 100 or so pages and then read the last 10 pages. I don't feel like I missed anything. I guess I can't really say I READ the book, but since I probably didn't miss anything, I'm calling it a "read". I grew tired of Percy's constant, "I'm not good enough," diatribe. Blah blah blah. While one reviewer said that it's exactly like a teenager feels, I think it's more appropriate for a new teenager...like 13...not someone who is almost 18 and "coming out". It was tiresome.

It gives me back my faith in this genre. This charming mix of magic in nineteenth century England. One can't take it for serious. But as a light, enjoyable story it was worth my time. 
 It was funny. I laughed reading banter between siblings. And who wouldn't want to have Charles as a brother? ;-) 
 A love story was sweet, clean and with a little spark. 
 I didn't mind that was totally predictable, (I knew very soon that Lochinvar was a wizard. ) that the world here was black and white (each character was utterly good or bad) and that the whole novel was evidently for young adult (teenagers). It was written in a way that everyone who is open to such genre can enjoy it. 
 Nonetheless, I give only 3 stars because I think that Marissa Doyle should give us here also a love story for Pen or make the book a little shorter. I felt sometimes that she was pushing too hard. But perhaps it was just my adult voice that thought so ;-) 
 Still, I think I will try another Doyle's book in the future.

Bewitching Season by Marissa Doyle is a fun YA historical fiction of twins and magic set in pre-Victorian England. The twins, Persy and Pen are about to have their first season, which basically means they go to balls in pretty dresses and try to look for somebody to propose to them. The problem? Their governess who taught them how to use their magic gets kidnapped by this evil Irish dude. 
 Read the rest of my review here

I love historical fiction. I love the manners, the balls, the dresses, the courtesy... it all feels so romantic (No, don't touch me with reality)... fueled by the likes of Jane Austen's works. 
 I wanted to love Bewitching Season. I've been waiting to read this and when I finally bought it and read it... 
 I love the manners, the balls, the dresses and the courtesy well enough but they couldn't detract for the utter silliness of one Persephone Leland. She may be a bluestocking but that didn't help her at all from being over-anxious, over-thinking things and at times pretty stupid. I rather think that Penelope was the more level-headed of the two even if she was, uhm, more inclined towards the balls and meeting eligible men. But I was reading the book from Persy's point of view so I couldn't say much of Penelope. I still say she's more level-headed. Both were impulsive. I like Charles though. 
 Full review at Whatever You Can Still Betray.

Decent effort for a first time author. I have great hopes that her next book will be much better. I enjoyed her setting and her characters, and the mystery kernel of the plot could have been really spectacular, if she had done more with it. Instead, the characters seemed to have the same conversations and interactions over and over, while the plot languished in the background.
a beautifully done and addictive book!

I got through a fourth to a third of this book before I had to start skipping ahead and skimming through. I think maybe ten to fifteen years ago I would've really enjoyed this book. It had simple writing, immature characters/relationships, and a stereotypical plot line. Back when I was ignorant of how things were in the early 1800's and back when I was immature myself, I would've liked the cliche situations and relatable characters. However, now that I know better and am (hopefully) no longer as immature, I just found this book incredibly ridiculous. As I said before, the writing style was incredibly simple though not stinted and jumping around all over the place, which was good, and I recognize that this book is aimed at girls about ten years my junior, but still. Girls ten years my junior can handle more complex writing styles than this. It was a little TOO simple. 
 As for the characters, I didn't believe a single one of them. Except MAYBE Pen. The author seemed to think that people in the early 1800's would think and act exactly how we do in the modern age. They didn't. They had a different set of rules to live by and were raised in a different kind of society. That changes how you view things and how you act. No one in this story acted as if they were from the 1800's and that killed me. These are high born ladies, sitting on tables, and calling their governess Ally. I'm sorry but that would NEVER happen. EVER. Also it was hard to tell them apart as their nicknames for each other were Pen and Persy. It took a few chapters to successfully know which was which and even then there would be occurrences of me mixing them up. Plus I really hated Persy. I liked the idea of her, but she really annoyed me in the end. Here she is constantly talking about how her sister is so much prettier, and so much more interesting, and has such greater hair than she does.... when THEY ARE IDENTICAL. And when the love interest is interested in the same things she is and tries talking about them with her, she just sits silently and thinks to herself how happy he looks sitting next to her gorgeous sister who is carrying on a great conversation with him (but only because Persy refuses to talk or answer his questions. So in order to not appear rude and to cover up Persy's awkard silence, she talks to the guy instead. Which is really quite considerate of her really). It's just obnoxious. 
 They never take the magic thing seriously. None of them. Except perhaps Ally. It made me annoyed and nervous the entire time that they were going to get themselves exposed (and maybe that happens later.. I didn't actually finish reading this so I don't know for sure). 
 Then there's the plot. It was so cliche and predictable. Half of the events weren't necessary, they were just there for over the top drama. Which I find annoying and unrealistic. 
 The only slightly redeeming quality was the love interest but after two chapters of that I was fed up already. So it wasn't redeeming enough. The reason I got fed up with that situation was because of Persy's handling of the situation (which was always in terribly immature ways - and she's supposed to be the intelligent one) and the love interest himself. I didn't believe him. I didn't believe that he would go from being what sounded like the worst little boy that walked the earth, to the most charming, handsome, gentlemanly 18 year old in just one summer and to just continue getting better from there when they finally see him again at 21. I just didn't believe it. You don't tease someone for your entire life and then just suddenly turn into a different person who's in love with them instead. I can see being an immature little boy and teasing because it's funny and they're girls and whatever, but to do it until you're 17 and then suddenly decide that you're going to stop and have a normal conversation with them which leads to love when the girl is 13.... I don't know... Seemed forced and fake. Again, unnecessary drama that was added to complicate things. 
 I know I'm railing on this book pretty hard, especially when I didn't even read the whole thing. And my main problem is just that I waited too long to read it because now I'm too old for it. But this is my honest opinion on it at this moment. 
 I recommend this for a really young audience....like 10-13 maybe. But nothing higher than that. Unless you're SUPER into the immature fluff of historical inaccuracy. Your call :)

I bought this because it seemed kind of like Harry Potter and was set during the 1800s in London. It's a little juvenile, but I think I'll stick with it, because so was the first Harry Potter. (First couple, really.) 
 It's about twin sisters Persephone and Penelope (okay, seriously, is it now be a rule that every historical fiction YA book have a character named Penelope--The Luxe series, this and The Season?), who have the ability to do magic. (Their governess gives them magic lessons on the downlow, but she cautions them to never do magic where anyone can see (because the time when witches were killed isn't so far in the past). So when she (governess) disappears suddenly, they decide to find her. 
 And, of course, they do magic all over the place, with no regard for who can see them. 
 Fun book.

reference_books.title: Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil
reference_books.review_text: This book dragged for me...I had a hard time getting into it. Sure, it had all colorful characters that were actually based on real people and real events, but most of the time it just read like a history lesson.

reference_books.title: The Interestings
reference_books.review_text: "Interesting" in multiple ways; this book touches familiar territories, both in life itself and especially in the fine arts side. Relatable, understandable, and all too real.

reference_books.title: Something Wicked This Way Comes (Green Town, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Love the concept and idea, really. It was not what I thought it would be at all. 
 The language and writing style turned me off. It was choppy and over-descriptive to the point where I didn't even know what the author was talking about at times. The dialogue was so 1950s cheesy I couldn't get into it!

reference_books.title: Needful Things
reference_books.review_text: There are a lot of characters in this one to keep up with, and they are actually all either directly or indirectly important. Everyone starts a new chain of chaotic reactions that leads to something else--about someone else--and then the process starts over with new people! Seeing how they all become intertwined in this very tangled webbing is exciting! You find yourself wanting to root for at least some of them to see if any of them are strong enough to outsmart the mysterious shopkeeper who seems to be in control of them all.

reference_books.title: Leaving Time
reference_books.review_text:
Well. 
 If it's one thing Ms. Piccoult did right that she always does, it's mess with my head. 
 This book was good for what it was, not my favorite, but it did the job of making me second guess everything I read...and want to turn back and re-read to look for the clues I missed. 
 She steers away from the moral dilemma and courtroom action in this one and focuses on the behaviors of elephants in grief to compare to the behaviors of humans in grief. The symbolism is there and constantly flashed before your face. You can't escape it and you can't ignore it. An elephant never forgets and it protects.

book_a.title: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child - Parts One and Two (Harry Potter, #8)
book_a.user_review:
** spoiler alert ** 
 A better title for this would be "Harry Potter's son and the Questionably Stupid Plot involving a Time-Turner and Cedric Diggory." 
 I just want to know... HOW and WHY? 
 This was hard to get through to read, how in the world are people watching this as a play? 
 It is too long and it jumps all over the place as far as storyline and time period. One minute they're 11, then they're 16. What gives? Who has the patience for all of this cluster? 
 The storyline and main plot could have gone in one direction, instead it unraveled into something completely unimportant. WHY? 
 If it really were about Albus struggling with the fame associated with his father, we should have seen that. We should have seen his life at Hogwarts and how much of a different person Albus is. What is his life like as a Slytherin? 
 The time turner should have been used to go back to PREVENT Harry from becoming the chosen one, as it was a personal vendetta of Albus. Instead we are thrown all over the place into something that goes nowhwre. There is a little plot twist in there that could have been better...but it seems like it was thrown in at a last minute attempt to make something bad into something good. 
 The only thing I enjoyed? The little references to the actual books that were able to bring us back to Hogwarts. That was it. Completely.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I feel now how I felt such a long time ago...when I finished the Deathly Hallows. It was so nice to be back in the world and those characters--old and new. 
 However, the writing was clearly not J.K. Rowling's and it didn't genuinely feel like a Harry Potter book...at least not like how I had expected it to feel. It just feels more like someone paying homage to her and her work instead of staying true to the real writing? I don't know if that necessarily makes sense... 
 All-in-all, I think my enjoyment was still genuine because I missed (SO MUCH) reading Harry Potter and of the wizarding world. 
 Final rating: 2.75/5 stars
For me, this is not canon.

Oh dear. I should have listened to my gut, and simply borrowed this from the library versus buying it. This was ok. Barely ok. And only because I simply loved Harry Potter, and with the play/screenplay format, could envision my beloved characters once again. 
 So disappointing.
I expected nothing and I am still disappointed.
I loved it - I did not expect the story line it followed but it was perfect and I wanted to shed a tear when it finished

I have dreaded reviewing this book. Dragged my feet, avoided sharing my disappointment....sigh. All of it. I LOVE Harry Potter. I love the book, I love how it is written....the characters, the magical world, how it is a gateway to get kids to fall in love with reading....LOVE IT. I have taught the first two books in class numerous times and melted every time I see my students bitten by the HP bug....but I was not as excited to read this book....it isn't written by Rowling, it isn't her characters....it isn't a novel....it isn't Harry Potter. It isn't. I don't care how you try to explain it....it didn't feel the same and it kills me that this book is now part of the Harry legacy. Gah. I tried my best to go into this book without any pretenses, but it is hard...I was excited to see the play write's interpretation...but the deeper I got into the play the more annoyed I became. 
 1) I don't feel like the play write truly understood JK's characters....I hated his interpretation of Hermione and Ron. Hermione is not that annoying....and Ron isn't the dumb guy that all the jokes are made on....I mean maybe in the movie? But not the characters I fell in love with! 
 2) The play write does NOT know teenagers....no teenager I have hung out with would hug his friend ESPECIALLY when no one is around...that's not how teens act. Nor how they talk....it really bothered me. 
 3) The end was obvious....the villain was obvious....JK is never obvious. 
 4) Just don't touch what is good. Please. I feel very protective of this world....write your own play about your own characters. 
 So....in the end....should you read it? Sure. Should you gush and love every second? No. It is not the same as the original books. This is a whole different world--- I shall pretend this is fan fiction that got published because he knew the right people....but it isn't the same and I am not inspired to go see the play....I prefer to let the characters live on in my imagination without being clouded by someone else's point of view.

Muddled thoughts on this one, what can I truly say except for what is in my heart? Tbh, it reads like a piece of simple fanfic, and that's the bottom line. I could add that I think Rowling might have sold out but that is speculation on my part. I have my reasons to think it however. 
 So, I give it two stars - It was ok.
Good if you want Doctor Who-ish meets Harry Potter fan fiction but don't want to search for it.

Gaah I never thought I'd ever give anything related to Harry Potter 1 star and yet here I am. 
 SPOILERS BELOW 
 Now if you go in expecting another Harry Potter book, you will be sorely disappointed. If you go in expecting a play which borrows your favourite characters for a story, you'll probably still be disappointed considering JK Rowling's name is attached to this and you expect a certain level of clever writing from her. Alright so she didn't write the whole thing, she did give her stamp of approval. 
 Firstly, no one is in character. Yeah, sure 19 years have passed but there is so much incongruence it's just making my head hurt. I love Ron. I have always loved Ron. But it seems like they forgot how to write Ron. It reads like movie Ron and not book Ron. Do you not remember Ron Weasley who shared his family and home with Harry after only a year of knowing him? Do you not remember Ron who told Sirius that he would have to go through him before killing Harry, when he thought Sirius was a mass murderer? Do you not remember Ron who Hermione fell in love with because he remembered the house elves and went to warn them during the Battle of Hogwarts? But you know, whatever. Let's have Ron only for comic relief, who only thought about food and wore a gravy-stained napkin when his best friend's son went missing. Fuck you. 
 I get Albus. I get it, it can't have been easy being Harry Potter's son and living up to his name. I can understand his frustration and his anger. What I can't get is Harry's reaction to his son. Really, you really think Harry is going to tell him he wished Albus wasn't his son?? Are we basing Harry on his 5th year when he got mad at everything? It's so out of character for him. And don't give me the bullshit that JK Rowling obviously knows her own characters better, because if she did, no way would she treat Cedric like that. 
 Which brings me to Cedric. Cedric Diggory, the boy who was kind above all, became a Death Eater because he was humiliated during the Triwizard Tournament? Is this the same Cedric Diggory we are talking about who wanted a rematch because Hufflepuff won only because Harry fell off his broom? The one who wanted to be fair so told Harry about the Second Task? The one who wanted Harry to take the cup because he felt Harry deserved it more?? Okay, as long as we're clear. This is especially shitty, considering Hufflepuff has almost no other heroes. 
 What about how the only reason Ron and Hermione are together is because Ron got jealous about Krum?? What are you even on about?? 
 Yes, completely murder Draco's character, why don't you?? 
 The worst of all was the plot. The really weird bizzaro plot. Time- Turner? Is this even a plot? It sounds like those memes where people keep suggesting why didn't they just go kill Voldemort when he was a kid? The wacky plot had so many loopholes it'll make you laugh. 
 The only good thing was Harry confronting Dumbledore about leaving him in an abusive household for ten years. 
 Scorpius as a character was really good. He was funny and smart. 
 But the plot. Ugh. 
 My head hurts from all the bullshit. 
 tl;dr I've read fanfics by 15 years old with tighter plots and better characterisation.

Having grown up in the south, there was much I could relate to in this book. It was recommended to me by my friend Kelly. I'm glad I read it. The relationships in it are both heartwarming and heartbreaking.
It felt like reading a play in some ways--depicting what the characters aught to do and say rather than how people truly think and behave.
So boring, what is this about?

I picked this book up because of Tennessee William's review: the greatest prose writer that the South has produced. Let me tell you, he hit the nail on the head. This was lovely. Carson McCullers is a wonderful writer. She plays with words so skillfully that even the mundane and every-day appear special and grand. 
 This novel is set in the 1930s in a Southern town where its inhabitants deal with race inequality, poverty, lack of education, barely scraping buy, hard and difficult physical labor, diseases, and the first traces of Communism and Fascism. There really is no major plot. Instead, McCullers highlights the lives of several townspeople but two stuck out to me - probably because in a way they are quite opposite of each other: a deaf-mute gentleman and a music-loving, penniless teenage girl. McCullers beautifully brought across their thoughts and beliefs, their desires, and their sorrows. This novel is truly a character-study, something that is amongst my favorite topics to read about. 
 I can only highly recommend this book if you are like me and you love to read novels built on language over content. 
 See my blog (spoilers possible!) here: https://ichleseblog.wordpress.com/201....

As usual with these books I feel I am missing something personally that only I am not getting. Tried to get into it, but I felt dragging and reading became a chore, could not finish did not want to tread on.

It could be slow at times, a little too descriptive for me. Maybe too deep for me too? Kept wondering what the meaning of the title was. 
 I could tell it is a classic; I really felt for all the characters.

Hmm...so many people raved about this book in the reviews I read, but I had to make myself finish it. I kept thinking it would get better, but it never did, not for me anyway. There isn't really much of a plot to speak of. It jumps from character to character without a lot of rhyme or reason, and although their depressing lives in this small town are all intertwined in one way or another, they feel oddly disconnected. Each one of the characters is strangely drawn and feels ridiculously close to a deaf/mute man that none of them actually know. The story is an embodiment of hopelessness and despair, and it just left me wanting in the end.
Read for my novel workshop. One of the most horrible things I have ever read. Yuck. The characters are unrelatable and the language is simplistic and relies on empty adverbs like "very" and "really."

I'm going to lead with: not really my type of book. I read this because it was the May pick for The Perks of Being a Bookworm group; what I like about book clubs is that they are introducing me to books I would never think of reading. Sometimes this is a success, this time it wasn't. 
 I did not enjoy actually reading this book, in fact I was somewhat reading it; I didn't have to force myself to read it, but I didn't care if I read it, I had no 'need' to know what happened. If it had not been a group read and reasonably short, I would have stopped reading before I got halfway. Maybe it was the fact that I didn't really care about any of the characters apart from Singer and Biff, partly because of their selfishness regarding Singer, projecting their need onto him without caring about him for his own sake. I don't think it was simply that because even unlikeable characters can be compelling to read about, but not these. 
 I did like the writing; I got a sense of each of the characters fairly quickly, some more than others, Dr Copeland in particular. 
 This style of story does not grab me; I suppose I need a 'quest' or similar to drive the story for me, even if that is used for social commentary. I recently read Post Office by Charles Bukowski and I was reminded of it whilst reading that; I didn't particularly enjoy it either (2 stars again).

reference_books.title: The 5th Wave (The 5th Wave, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
The idea behind the 5th wave has potential to be very good. It's not the same old alien invasion that has been portrayed a thousand times. However, the book is written almost as if it's a girls journal/thoughts and in many places, is all over the place. I think the author intended it to be read fast and make you feel out of breath at times, which he succeeded at. But the trade off is that there feels to be almost no plot for at least half the book. It's almost a hopeless, survival story. The book is well written but fails to deliver that thick plot that causes you to sit on the edge of your seat throughout the book. However the last 75 pages or so are very good. 
 The reason for this book getting 2 stars is mainly because of the lack of a plot halfway through the book and because the story repeats itself. Some places it goes between other people's point of view and retells the same event from their stand point. In other places it's as if the author is trying too hard to convey an image, like; "There are the stars. the pinpricks of light stabbing down. There is the empty road beneath the light stabbing down and the girl on the road with the smudged face and twigs and dead leaves entangled in her short, curly hair, clutching a battered old teddy bear, on the empty road, beneath the stars stabbing down." 
 This book could have easily been shrunk down to less than 300 pages. It is unnecessarily long. I also did not like the main character too much. She seems almost unbelievable in certain situations. The world as you know it is gone, aliens have invaded, at one point you think your the last human on earth, and she can't stop thinking about some boy she had a crush on. A boy she has never held a full conversation with. so I give 5th wave 1 wave out of 5, I was left unconquered. 
 Out of 5: 
 -Character development: 3 
 -Plot: 1 
 -World building: 1 
 -Writing style: 1

sample_reviews.review_text:
"Jonas's world is perfect. Everything is under control. There is no war or fear or pain. There are no choices. Every person is assigned a role in the Community. When Jonas turns twelve, he is singled out to receive special training from The Giver. The Giver alone holds the memories of the true pain and pleasure of life. Now, it is time for Jonas to receive the truth. There is no turning back." 
 The Giver is such an amazing book. I literally couldn't put it down. I got in from the library and I've had it just sitting on my shelf for weeks and weeks and I kept renewing it. I can't believe how long it took me to finally pick it up and actually read the thing. Every time that I had the chance to read, I would read. This book is filled with so many twists and turns and I absolutely loved it! I loved it so much, that I actually just bought The Giver Quartet from booktopia.com. 
 How beautiful is that book? I mean come on, it's gorgeous! 
 When Jonas and his friends become a Twelve, everyone except for him gets chosen for a job based on the volunteer work they had done over the past few years. Jonas is chosen to become the next Receiver of Memories, which at first sounded like a 'great honor' as everyone told him it was, up until he really did experience pain. I hated reading about how he got turned away when The Giver was in too much pain to give him some memories and I almost shed a tear on the train at one or fifteen moments. 
 This is one of the books that I had down to read for the Treesof Reverie readathon, and the only psychical book I read for it, unfortunately. 
 A few weeks ago, a youtuber that goes by the alias abookutopia, posted a review on the movie, at first I didn't understand why it went from black and white to suddenly going into colour, as I hadn't read the book yet, but now I understand, and I think it's so smart how she did that. 
 I'm actually planning to watch the movie after I finish writing a few blog posts, and I honestly have a high expectation. 
 I love the relationship between The Giver and Jonas, and I understand how frustrated the two of them must be, with no one else understanding colour, and all the memories. I'm so excited for my gorgeous copy to come in the post so I can enjoy the rest of the story. 
 I strongly recommend this book to pretty much everyone. Although the book has some mature topics such as 'releasing' where people get killed for not being adequate enough, and even suicide, I really do think it's a great book for anyone to read. 
 Kaylee 
 -readerxpro

I remember reading this in school and I remember liking it. I'm very interested in seeing the movie. I don't remember reading the other books because back than it wasn't easy to keep track which books were in a series. 
 I can't wait to see where the author decided to take her book.

** spoiler alert ** 
 An amazing book. I would've given it five stars but I was a little disappointed how the story got increasingly abstract in the last two pages. 
 Yes, I understand the whole book was filled with symbolism, and some artsy fartsy people might think it doesn't really matter what exactly happened to Jonas and Gabriel, but I just spent the last hundred pages growing to love these characters and caring where they ended up. 
 Were they really safe or were they lost in some abstract future where we all learn to love? 
 Did the Giver leave the sled there for them? Where the heck did it come from? 
 I need concrete answers! I'm not what you'd call cultured or imaginative!

I liked it, but I wish a few things... I wish the ending had been a bit more, a bit more descriptive? A bit longer? A bit more uplifting? Just more. The book did affect me though. The character of Asher especially. His joy for life was wonderful. One moment during the book I was brought to tears and it was by the scene involving Asher as a cheerful child being corrected in his speech. I can say that I am moving on from dystopian books for now, I have had my fill.

I hated this book. The writing was excellent, I will say that much, but this book left me unsettled and feeling just downright icky. It takes a heck of alot to put me off, but this one made me super uneasy, and I don't really know why. Could it be the vivid scenes of infants being put to death, or the creepy old guy who puts his hands all over a young boy to transfer memories? I dunno, but I really, really, really found it seriously creepy.

I've read other books with almost the same contained and controlled setting (e.g. Divergent and Delirium). But The Giver is probably the most frightening of all. Imagining life stripped off things that are most essential, is depressing but intriguing. Let's see how Lowry resolves conflict that arised from what seems to be a resolution to chaos in itself.
I feel like I reread this book every year just for fun.

Basically... In the future, a fundamentalist community adheres to a strict society standard of sameness in exchange for safety from pain and strife. This pain is adverted due to one person being the recipient of the community memories. This "receiver" is often burdened by such memories, they need a successor. This is where the story opens, as a 12 year old boy is assigned this most unique of positions to be hold. While others were beginning more traditional training of labor they'll be providing, Jonas must undergo a rigorous process where he'll experience more than anyone has ever seen or felt since before the sameness. He'll learn about the good, the evil or something in between the two, and weather it's possible to have one without the other. As well as learning more about their fragile community, enough that will drive him to the point of eloping. 
 A great story! I can easily see why the hype was behind this well told dystopian/utopian novel. It made me eager to continue on with the "series" the author has going even if they are relatively shorter story than I prefer. I shall certainly be looking for another book from this author in the future.

I remembered George Orwell's 1984 because of 'sameness'. The story is introduced in a futuristic, utopian setting and slowly turning into a dystopian. It made me ponder about God's beautiful gift of freedom of choice. History remind us of wars and tragedy brought by our errors in practicing freedom. The Giver has portrayed an alternative world without suffering. But would I choose the latter? My answer is no. The novel depicted how colorless, dull and lacking life could get without freedom. It's life aching to live. The most terrifying scene for me is Jonas' father 'releasing' a baby. I dared not imagine it. 
 The novel conveys sensitive social issues such as euthanasia, suicide, & infanticide. The graphic & detailed depiction of its horror is amazing.

I won't officially review this as I don't really remember enough about this to properly review it. I rated this 2 stars because I remember being unimpressed, a little bored, and very unsatisfied with the ending.

book_b.title: The Way of Shadows (Night Angel, #1)
book_b.user_review:
A novel about an assassin you expect to have some dark characters who kill for money or other personal gain, but this story has a bit of a reluctant assassin. Azoth - later is Kyler- a orphan boy who grows up in the slums as a part of a guild mostly made of children. Kyler longs for a life free from the abuse he endures from the older boys. He longs to become a wetboy - a super assassin with magical powers. After a run in with Durzo Blint, the living legend, the greastest wetboy, Azoth seeks Blint out to become his apprentice. But Blint gives him an assignment in order to become his apprentice, and of course it involves a murder. 
 As the story progresses, the lines between hero and villain get blurred. It's almost a anti-hero hero. Weeks does a good job of making you feel pity for young Kyler. How he is almost forced to do what he despises and then seeks redemption for it. 
 There are some unexpected events and secrets revealed that make the story better, taking you on a roller coaster of emotion. The book is pretty dark and at times depressing but this adds to the story. Weeks does a good job dictating your emotion and even baiting you into thinking certain things about characters. At times the story is hard to follow and some of the characters get confusing to keep up with. The plot doesn't really show up in its entirety until about halfway through the book. Of course the first half is a coming of age story with sub plots to carry you through. 
 I debated over 3 or 4 stars but decided on 3 stars because the foul language was a bit over the top and some of the sexual innuendo was pointless and just thrown in to be there which took away from the story. If you like overly powerful characters, alot of magic and a lot of action you should enjoy this book. It is part of a trilogy but ends in a way that it could be a stand alone book if your ok leaving a few things in the air. 
 Out of 5: 
 -Character development: 5

From all the hype I'd read, The Way of the Shadows was a fantasy novel chock full o' the standard fantasy tropes, full of slam-bang action, and more fun that it deserved to be considering it doesn't really explore new ground in fantasy fiction. 
 Well, the hype was correct. I did indeed enjoy the novel. The adventures of Kylar Stern reminded me why I got into fantasy as a 12 year old kid. Done right, it can be loads of fun. 
 Was some of the novel obvious to a seasoned fantasy reader? Sure, lots of it was. A main character who starts from nothing, is trained by a gruff and sometimes ruthless mentor, suffers greatly along the way, only to persevere and become a bad ass . . . yeah, I've read loads of novels that traveled that well-worn path. 
 Do I care? Nope. 'Twas good stuff. Give it a read of you are looking for a fun romp.

I liked the book, there were some pretty brutal parts to the story but was a ok read. This book is sort of the book series you read when your in between series and you can't decide what to read next. Definetly not for children to read, there are some pretty graphic things in this novel. I really like the world he created and have bought the remaining two books in the series, not something I will probably read again but don't think I have wasted my time in doing so. One interesting this in this novel was how children are treated. I have NEVER read a novel that contained that sort of content, except from possibly George R. Martin. Which is what made me this novel stand out for me. Anyways, not something I recommend other people read, but if you do you won't regret it but your life won't be changed for reading it.

A street urchin vows to escape his hardscrabble life by becoming an apprentice to the best magically-enhanced assassin in the city. He grows. Drama unfolds. Inot the most original story but I really enjoyed this fast paced bit of bad assed escapism (although I gagged at an awkward profession of love). The writing reminds me a lot of Joe Abercrombie...good times!

My biggest complaint with this book was I was not invested at all in the world. Big things seemed to be happening, but I didn't really care beyond the main character. A bit of humor might have been nice too. Overall I was intrigued by the magic system, I'm a fan of the assassin set-up, and I'm interested to see what will happen in the next books.

I got quite a few chapters into this book--far more than I was really comfortable with--when I found myself sitting there and watching this character doing horrible, immoral stuff with absolute callousness (and I'm not even talking about the assassination gig!). And I pulled away and sat there watching myself watching him, and I thought, "What am doing? Is there any way in which I can justify what I am exposing myself to right now?" And I realized I couldn't. So I left it unfinished. 
 Rating: Extra R. Also, I didn't even get to the worst stuff. Violence, deviant sexual attitudes, yada yada yada. Did I mention I couldn't finish it?

I don't even know why and how I got this book, but I found it lurking around my bookshelf one day and decided to get it over with. It has a high star rating and glorious reviews after all. 
 I can divide my experience into two parts. The first 2/3 of the book is good. It's not extremely well written, but there is a lot going on, and the story is delicously complicated. There are a lot of characters, which some people don't like, but I do. I finished almost 1/3 of it in 2 days. But then we come to the second part. The last 1/3 of the books is almost unreadable. It's full of action scenes. I'm not that big a fan of action packed books, but I never had such difficulty with another book. It's so confusing, long and simply boring. The story in general continues to be alright, but the fact that all of it is sword fights and people jumping around ruined it all for me. I don't even know how I got through it. It never finishes. Just goes on and on and on. 
 I gave this book 2 stars because I liked the first part and the story is good and kind of reminds me, in a very vague way, The Song of Ice and Fire, but of course half of this one is painful to read. I had already gotten the rest of the series while I was actually enjoying it, so I guess more pain is in store for me. But there's a bright side: the day I finished this book was one of the happiest days of the year for me.

Whats not to love about this novel? 
 A orphan raised in the gutter as a thief and scavenger, who triumphs over adversity to become an assassins apprentice. And add a touch of magic near the end of the book (that's the essence to the next two) Okay that the simplistic view, and a lot more's happening here than solely that. 
 Azoth who is an orphan who lives in the Warrens of Cenaria City. He has two friends, Jarl and Doll Girl. Then there's Rat who rises to be the leader of the guild and hates Azoth and his friends to the point of murder and buggery. We see his life in the warrens and his struggles to over come that life. He wants become Durzo Blint's apprentice but has to prove himself. - okay any more here adds spoilers. 
 Meanwhile the cities ruler is Duke Gyre and his heir Logan Gyre. Duke Gyre leaves the city to fight invaders leaving his son behind. Add to this a travelling mage Solon Tofusin who seems to be following a prophesy involving Lord Gyre but isn't sure if its the Duke or his son. 
 Once Azoth, now known as Kylar Stern has become Blints apprentice we get to witness some training and grooming that's addictive in the telling. He becomes a blade master and we learn he has a wealth of magical mojo, but the connection to it is broken. However a "kakari" would bridge the connection but is a very powerful weapon and only 7 are in existence. 
 Kylar eventually gets the black kakari which has some unusual qualities including defying death at a dire cost to Kylar. 
 The book then goes into overdrive with a fight between Kylar and Blint and Khalidorans invasion arrives by sea with vurdmeisters (powerful mages) and amongst the chaos Logan Gyre becomes King and hides in a most unusual place. This end part of the book had me on tender hooks the entire time, and I refused to put the book down until I had finished it. 
 Its an old story of waif to assassin but it has a whole new feel here. The Black kakiri and the vurdmeisters magic are a new twist on magic as we normally perceive it in these books. Told in a new and ruthless manner this book is simply addictive. The characters are endearing. And the ending climatic.

sample_reviews.review_text:
How about a perverse, semi-literary, demi-autobiographical, dark, meandering novel about an self-absorbed author who writes a perverse, semi-literary, demi-autobiographical, dark, meandering novel. Sound like fun? Just about as fun as other meta-disasters such as films about making films, poems about writing poems, and musicals about putting on musicals. Just about the world's most aggravating gimmick. 
 The plot meanders like the Maine coastline-- lots of twists and turns, no Northwest Passages. In fact so much happens in the plot-- two whole generations of a family come and go with lots of bizarre and tragic events-- that every sentence has to say, "and then." No setting, no expansion of moments, just, "this happened next." And the plot is completely ridiculous. If it wasn't so ugly, dark, and self-consciously authorly, it would be kind of funny. Kind of. If rape, infidelity, and self mutilation are your kind of comedy. 
 I resent books where the author smugly stands in front of the Wizard's curtain-- Harlan Ellison is one of those. [auhtor: A.S. Byatt] and Dorothy Dunnett are more my cup of tea-- their storytelling is so masterful that the author completely disappears.

I really enjoyed the fact that I could not tell what was going to happen in this book from one moment to the next. I was just content with enjoying the ride. Towards the end I felt like it got a little sloppy, which is why I only gave it 3 stars, but I would recommend it.

Decided not the finish this book. I don't like to start a book and not finish it, but I was less than 1/3 of the way through and was just bored to tears. I was not relating to any of the characters and when it started talking about Garp and Helen both having affairs with a couple that were there friends I decided I had had enough.
I can't finish this book. I'm really bothered by a character ummm trait? Habit? Depravity?
books within a book within what I suspect is John Irving's life.

A work of writing that will take your emotions by surprise because of how unpredictable it is. You will find yourself having to re-read some parts just to make sure that that's what really happened. It's dirty, humorous, heartbreaking and incredibly honest, so much that you feel John Irving is your friend telling you a life experience in a casual sitting at a coffee shop. 
 It also highlights that being a writer can sometimes be the most difficult thing in the world.
My favorite Irving book.

This was the first Irving book that I read. I remember choosing it for a class where we searched for great American writers who would become classics. My thoughts are Irving is a great writer, but I cannot imagine him becoming the required reading for class. But who knows?
Freaky but good.

T.S. Garp is a somewhat known writer with a peculiar mother who is a more famous writer than he is. Jenny Fields, his mother, was a nurse who was strong-willed and she enjoyed caring for folks but didn't have a desire to be in a relationship with anyone. She saw herself as asexual. When the desire to be a mother overcame her, rather than foster a relationship she didn't want, she copulated with a mentally injured soldier who died soon after inseminating her. Jenny raises Garp on her own, in her own peculiar way, instilling an interest in wrestling and literature into her boy. The first quarter of the book about Jenny raising Garp and his awkward adolescence is the best part of the entire book; the quirky premise of an asexual, feminist nurse raising her son at an all-boys school was a promising start for this novel. 
 When Garp graduates, the book segues to Jenny and Garp traveling to Europe together where Garp befriends a hooker and Jenny doesn't get out much to sight-see. Jenny declares a desire to write a book about herself even though she's never written before and Garp is inspired to write because of his time walking the streets. One of the themes Jenny harps on in her book is lust and her lack of having it. She both emasculates and sympathizes with her son for lusting after women, foreshadowing later events with Jenny's "fans" and their perception of Garp and his place in Jenny's life. 
 Garp and his mother return to the U.S. having both completed a manuscript: Jenny's autobiography A Sexual Suspect and Garp's short story with the awkward title of The Pension Grillparzer. Jenny's book gets published through the first publishing contact she makes (really?) and her book becomes a huge bestseller. She becomes nationally known as the asexual feminist who wears a nurse's uniform wherever she goes. Garp's short story is published with little fanfare. The bulk of the rest of The World According to Garp follows young Garp into adulthood as he marries his wrestling coach's daughter, Helen, and the two have children. Garp stays at home with their kids and is a doting father who worries tremendously about his kids. Garp writes a couple of novels that are mediocre and not very successful; his readership is considered small yet astute. He and Helen have consensual affairs with another couple. And the novel goes on and on, not giving much insight into any of these plot points. Even though Garp is described as a doting father, he gives very little insight into being a parent. Although Garp is a writer, he gives very little insight about the process of writing or pursuing writing as a career (Irving as narrator does offer a zinger or two about the process of writing, though. I'll get to that later). And the consensual affair seems to neither strengthen nor diminish their marriage; it ends simply because Helen tires of it and their marriage carries on. 
 Mostly, that's the way the entire novel goes, by just carrying on. Irving introduces quirky characters and premises but does not really dive into the quirkiness of the characters and premises very deeply. It's like he is creating a laundry list of interesting ideas then leaving us simply with the list. Asexual nurse and single mother who miraculously becomes a bestselling author? Check. A football player that becomes a transsexual and Garp's best friend? Check. A college student, Michael Milton, who has an affair with Helen then whose penis is bitten off by Helen in a car accident? Check. It all sounds more interesting than it plays out with very little insight into these weird characters' motivations or feelings or desires other than to say "Look at these loonies! Next." For being such quirky characters, the interactions and conversations between them are a real drag. Their lasting love or friendship for each other through one bizarre event to another mundane event seems to be the only thread through the entire book; their lives are entwined simply because they held on together and that's it. As Garp states, "Life ... is sadly not structured like a good old-fashioned novel. Instead, an ending occurs when those who are meant to peter out petered out. All that's left is memory. But even a nihilist has memory." 
 Sadly, that's what this novel does: peters out. All the characters summarily die off, their lives ending in mundane fashion, except for Garp and his mother, who are both murdered for being famous writers. The rest of them just live on, then die, as is life. The youngest of Garp's children--Jenny-- outlasts them all. She finds a career in medicine, just like her grandmother. The novel ends with young Jenny's observation, "But in the world according to Garp, we are all terminal cases." 
 Duh. 
 Not very insightful, if you ask me. I can tell Irving has a knack for dropping an occasional zinger or two but I really wanted more of that from him. Lines like "A writer's job is to imagine everything so personally that the fiction is as vivid as our personal memories" were so few and far between that I was left wanting. Irving's novel was just teasing, just flirting, not really following through, then it petered out.
