In 1909, a wealthy businessman, form the deep woods of Wisconsin, places an ad for a "reliable wife". A woman with a dark, mysterious past, accepts the offer. The first half of the book kept my interest but the relentlessly bleak tone and unpleasant characters, finally wore me down. I guess the author's message was that repression of feelings is "bad" but I felt hammered to death over it. Lighten up, buddy! Yes, there is plenty of torrid (not the fun kind!) sex here but I did not find it very engaging.
There were some parts that were poetic but I did not enjoy this book.

I don't know what to make of this book. It was so dark and yet not *really* miserable. The characters suffer terribly yet somehow they are essentially...I don't know, not really at peace with the misery, but stoic. Accepting. It makes their fates seem not so awful somehow. Reading A Reliable Wife was definitely an intense experience but it didn't completely depress me the way books with self-destructive characters usually do.

I just finished a marathon reading of A Reliable Wife. It was one of those books that I literally couldn't put down. 
 A Reliable Wife is a beautifully written novel set in the harsh winter of Northern Wisconsin in 1907(location: Fictional town of Truitt somewhere on the shores of Lake Superior). Ralph Truitt has lived a lonely past twenty years after a very tragic and mysterious married life. He advertises for a mail ordered "reliable wife." Catherine Land answers his advertisement and upon arrival is not the plain Jane in the picture that she sent to Ralph. She is beautiful, and has many secrets of her own to hide. There is a roller-coaster of events that I will leave off as to not spoil the book. 
 The lyrical prose of this book was wonderful, starting with the first line, "It was a bitter cold, the air electric with all that had not happened yet." The setting of the novel in the cold, bitter winter in a land of depressed people was stark and perfect for the novel. Ralph and Catherine are both troubled souls seeking redemption. As the book progresses, it is interesting to see how two people who start off seeming so un alike are actually quite similar. I enjoyed their characters and learning more about them. 
 The story was unpredictable and twisted and turned to an ending I certainly did not predict. It kept me riveted. I really wanted to read this book after seeing it compared to my favorite authors, Daphne Du Maurier and the Bronte sisters. While it did have a gothic sinister darkness to the plot that was also driven with despair, it is really its own novel. I did love it, but I wouldn't rank it above Jane Eyre or Rebecca. 
 With the setting of the novel in 1907, one would expect it to be staid and sexless, it is anything but. At first I was put off by Ralph's constant thoughts about sex as it just wasn't something I was interested in reading. But sex and the way different characters handle it or have issues with it is definitely a main part of this book and I grew accepting of that. 
 One small complaint I had is that sometimes the setting did not seem accurate. I lived for six years in Houghton, Michigan in the Upper Peninsula, which is isolated and routinely receives 300 plus inches of snow in a year. I now currently live in Northeast Wisconsin. It seemed strange to me that the world would be so winter locked in the fall. I could see that happening around Thanksgiving and especially in January or February, but not before. I also wondered about the trips to Chicago without mention of Milwaukee or Minneapolis, both of which would be closer to Wisconsin on the Lake Superior shore. Like I said though, these were small items that seemed only out of place to me as I've lived in the area. It just showed to me that the author had not, but he still wove a fantastic story. 
 Overall, it was a great riveting tale that will keep you guessing until the end.

sample_reviews.review_text: I don't want to be disrespectful, but I feel as if C.S. Lewis was a bit high - like, Lewis Carroll high - when he wrote the last book...or maybe he had desperately run out of ideas...

This is my favorite book in the series. I like it so much because it brings everything together. Eustace and Jill go to Narnia. I loved how they told the king about the magic rings. It just comes back to the first book. They also brought old characters. I also like how the trouble is started by a monkey. I loved the ending it's like a big reunion. The downside is probably in the middle of the book where I lost interest. Other than that it's great.

Racist, boring, and a very unsatisfying conclusion to the series. When I read this in 6th grade, I was like, "WTF?!" Now I'm like, "WTF?!" 
 At least this series proved that in some ways, I have not changed from Young Me.

Sinopsis: 
 Durante los ultimos dias de Narnia, el lugar se enfrenta a su desafio mas cruel; no se trata de un invasor de fuera sino de un enemigo interno. Mentiras y traicion han echado raices, y unicamente el rey y un grupo reducido de seguidores leales puede impedir la destruccion de todo lo que mas quieren en este magnifico colofon de Las Cronicas de Narnia. 
 Mi opinion: 
 No me gusto este final de la saga que prometia mucho. 
 En esta entrega no senti nada de lo que venia mostrandonos Lewis (a excepcion claro esta, de su cristianismo). 
 En pocas palabras: aburrido... 
 Lo unico que me gusto fue la reunion de todos los amigos de Narnia, aunque no tuvimos a Susan presente.
I like the Narnia series as a whole, but this was such a disappointing ending. It's Lewis at his most heavy-handed. And don't even get me started on Susan and her ending.
Loved this book!!! The last chapter was amazing! What a picture of heaven!! Still not sure I agree with Emet part of the second to last chapter but it made me think!! Love Narnia!!

I make no apologies for the following review. 
 This book is badly written, racist, sexist and boring. 
 I have not enjoyed the Narnia series. C. S. Lewis was a deeply bigoted writer and excusing this on the fact that he was a "man of his times" just does not wash for me. He may have been an Oxford scholar, but at times his writing is poor, (e.g. "I'll give you up my cabin of course, Lucy" & "Wouldn't it be lovely if Narnia just went on and on - like what you said it has been?") (HEAVEN FORBID!) unless I have downloaded an eBook with a great many typographical errors. The dialogue between the children is dated to the point of being ridiculous at times. Lewis obviously did not like grown women, as he cast the Witch (Devil) in female form and he motivated Aslan's rejection of Susan in the final book due to the fact she harboured doubts about Narnia, and also liked wearing lipstick and nylons. Horrors! 
 As for reading this to my own children (now grown) I am very glad I did not, as I imagine after the horror of this last book, they would have been traumatised for life. I am still wondering how this series could have become a children's Classic. Did parents wish to terrify their children and give them recurring nightmares? 
 I take back what I wrote about "The Silver Chair" and "The Voyage of the Dawn Trader"- this book is far worse. 
 In conclusion, I have cast Narnia into Outer Darkness; together with Gaiman's "American Gods" and Ishiguro's "The Unconsoled".

Where can I start with this review? I find it hard to collect my thoughts after reading The Last Battle. I really wanted (and expected) to have a worthy ending to the series where the magic lives on. But I was quite surprised and dissapointed with the way it concluded. Honestly its an odd story, it lacks the fantastic imaginative stories that I fell in love with in the Narnia chronicles, and had a much darker storyline, which doesn't really get resolved. Its also harder to ignore the christian theme in this book, something I didn't appreciate. It was sort of nice to see the characters from the other books, but it wasn't really the way I expected to revisit them, and I was quite dissapointed with the situation with Susan. 
 Thoughout writing this review I've been reflecting back on the book, and I feel more and more dissapointed by this ending, it gives such a bleak last look at Narnia! I won't go as far as to say I regret reading the book, but I also wouldn't really recommend it. Hard-core Narnia fans or those that appreciate the christian analogy might enjoy the book, but for others I think you can be just as happy leaving your last impression of Narnia with the Silver Chair.

C(hronic) S(odomite) Lewis brings his "Carnia" series to an explosive close with this dreadful dreck. The Satanic uber-Beast Asslan destroys "Carnia" via some sort of disgusting evacuatory expulsion of his heinous, hellish halitosis. The usual unholy shenanigans occur with the entire cast of unbibled sodomite drug users from the other books making desperate cameos. Shocked...shocked I am that this filth peoples the curricula of our "schools". Further proof that the end times are nigh. Part of the text is given over to an ode celebrating an obscure early 70s satanist named William Lung, noteworthy for his proto-disco hit "Shaved by the Bell". Avoid at all costs.

These are my favorite books, but I will admit that I struggled with the prejudice against the Calormene, people of Middle Eastern ilk, in this title. Still, I found the metaphor lovely, and I wept with the beauty of Aslan's land in the final chapters.

sample_reviews.review_text: This book kinda dissapointed me because it had sooo much potential and it just sort of fell flat. The story seemed so rushed to the point that I really didn't see the characters fall in love. Plus a lot of things happened that didn't really seem realistic.

Disappointing. I was attracted by the premise of His Eyes where a girl, Amy, is hired to babysit a blind guy named Tristan who is having a hard time accepting his current condition. I expected that it will be more about Amy reaching out to Tristan but it seems like the book loses its focus entirely the moment Tristan's ex-girlfriend makes her entry. 
 The sad thing is I cannot really see the authentic reason to put the ex-girlfriend's character in the story at all. She doesn't add on anything important and the reason that she suddenly comes back to Tristan is beyond ridiculous. It feels that the only reason of her abrupt, superficial entrance is to heat up the book a little bit, though to me, the effect is completely the opposite. 
 All in all, His Eyes does have a potential to be a good book but it suffers, severely, from choppy writing and poor editing.The storyline does not seem to progress anywhere while the character development is nearly non-existent. Despite being a very quick read, this isn't something I would recommend.

Found the book on a list and kind of intrigued by the synopsis. And I learned that it's a story from fiction press, though I never heard of the story I decided it's worth to check. 
 A young girl, get a job to babysit a rich newly-blinded boy. I thought it'd be interesting. Amy is an average teenage girl whose big brother skipped town after graduating high school and her mother lived in some kind of bubble, or she thinks so. Tristan was very rich, ex-jumping horse athlete and yes, newly blind. He was in denial stage, refusing both training and helping hand, kind of stubborn. 
 For a teenlit, it's good, I guess. It's just ain't for me. But, I think there could've been more depth or something. Or I guess these kind of books aren't for me. 
 My favourite part is the bits of letting go the people you love, allow them some space to grow and discover who they really are. And this wise view came from Amy's mother, looks can be deceiving.
Check out my review and a teaser here: http://frommetoyouvideophoto.blogspot.com/2011/06/feasted-on-his-eyes-by-renee-carter.html

I wanted MORE, especially near the end. I felt like emotions were covered very clearly in the beginning, but faded a bit toward the end. That's my only complaint. I loved the voice of this novel. The circumstances were unique and i was definitely caught by surprise several times. That was refreshing. A great love story, and a great story about overcoming.

It was short and light to read but it can definitely warm your heart and tug some strings.

 So I read it. I wish I didn't know the twist going in. The very beginning was actually GREAT, but then I didn't understand what her dilemma was regarding which guy to "choose." I mean, duh. One has a girlfriend and she's your cousin/roommate! I didn't even feel that the taken twin was on the table as a possibility - even though they were "attracted to each other." And the other twin, Cash, was definitely INTO her. And what made him a "bad boy" exactly? A tattoo? That he didn't go to college? That he drove a motorcycle? He owns a successful business and he's up front with her (or so we believe at the time). So again, I didn't get her confusion. I'm not sure if I liked HER really. She slept with a guy and she didn't know which twin it was and she didn't even CARE which one it was. Just ewwwww. 
 There were some sweet moments ( with the single twin) and this book definitely had some steam. 
 Then it just ended. Unfinished. WHY?? A book like this does not need a sequel! Just finish the story and give us a good epilogue please! I might read the next one because I don't like to leave a series hanging and it looks like it gets better going by the reviews. But I'm not dying to read it.

Down To You was a good book, first of all can we talk about the cover, that made me want to read the book right away, and then to go into and start to read the book and to see it from three characters different points of view was refreshing and something that I love to read in books keeps me guessing what is going to happen next, I wasn't expecting the twist that came into the book but I am glad of the outcome. Once I got to the end, I thought that was it, but then I see there is a continuation in the story,I am looking forward to seeing what happens next in Olivia and Cash's story.

Olivia Townsend is nothing special. She's just a girl in college trying to get through it so she can return home and help her father out on the farm and run his business for him. Living an hour away, she's determined not to be the second woman in his life to abandon him so she's going to get through college and move back home; even if it means putting her own life on hold to be with him. 
 But then she meets Cash and Nash Davenport. Sexy twins but completely different to each other. Cash is the bad boy and everything she wants in a guy, whereas Nash is successful and everything she needs in a guy. Only problem is he's taken. But staying away from both of them is proving hard and thus starts a love triangle...that's not really a triangle. But you'll have to read to find out what that means. 
 Olivia is a shy, insecure girl but with the boys, they bring out her feisty and confident side. After Nash and Cash meet her, they are instantly attracted to her. They think she is gorgeous, funny, witty and smart but she doesn't understand why they think that. She's instantly attracted to both of them, but she has to decide which one she wants...both of them made her insides crumple every time they spent time together, so I know picking would have been so hard to do. 
 Cash. Swooon. What can I say about him? Well he's a club owner, he's successful, goes after what he wants, a bad boy (which I loveeee), and has tattoos. The first time he sees Olivia, he knows he wants her for himself, it's just trying to make her see he isn't like all the other bad boys she's dated, he's different - hence the secret he's been keeping most of his life. 
 Oh Nash! I'm sorry but Cash stole my heart. Albeit, you were career driven, ambitious, taken by Olivia's cousin and everything Olivia wanted in a man, but it just wasn't enough. But where does Nash come in to the secret? 
 I completely loved Down To You. Everyone had been raving about it for weeks and although I had it on my Kindle, I had yet to read it. But I am so glad I did. I was captivated by the book and it took me about 3ish hours to read; that's how involved I became. There are three POV's in the book, from Olivia and the boys, and it worked amazingly well. It gave in insight into their feelings about the situations and about Olivia and how they felt about her. The POVs worked also; because of the twist at the end...well I didn't see that coming at all. 
 There was so much chemistry between the boys and Olivia, but I must admit, Cash stole my heart. I felt he and Olivia were much more suited. They were just drawn together no matter how much Olivia didn't want to be a badboy's girlfriend again, she just couldn't stop the attraction to him and Cash was the same. He wanted and needed Olivia for himself and to prove he wasn't like all the other men she's dated. He wouldn't want to crush her heart or cause her pain. 
 When the secret came out, I wasn't all that surprised by Olivia's reaction. There are two parts to this secret, and the first part surprised me. It showed a more sad time of Cash's past and to be honest, I felt for him having to go through it and do it for his family. It proved that Cash was like Nash. He was educated, he was sensitive and he was head over heels for Olivia. But those long days that Olivia ignored him, you could see he was in so much pain that he needed to get her back. And that's exactly what he did. 
 I just can't wait to Up To You to be released now. The ending was a pure shocker and I definitely need to know what is going to happen to Cash and Olivia! The teasers on M. Leighton's website are totally not enough, I need more! And that club scene in the teaser. HOLY HELL GIVE ME THE BOOK NOW. I can't wait until January!

sample_reviews.review_text:
This is the novel I would name as an ideal romantic novel. Sparks has beautifully portrayed the depth of emotions. 
 Some of my favorite parts from the letters to the ocean: 
 "I miss you, my darling, as I always do, but today is especially hard because the ocean has been singing to me, and the song is that of our life together." 
 "At night when I am alone, I call for you, and whenever my ache seems to be the greatest, you still seem to find a way to return to me. Last night, in my dreams, I saw you on the pier near Wrightsville Beach. The wind was blowing through your hair, and your eyes held the fading sunlight. I am struck as I see you leaning against the rail. You are beautiful, I think as I see you, a vision that I can never find in anyone else. I slowly begin to walk toward you, and when you finally turn to me, I notice that others have been watching you as well. 
 "Do you know her?" they ask me in jealous whispers, and as you smile at me, I simply answer with the truth. 
 "Better than my own heart." " 
 "But now, alone in my house, I have come to realize that destiny can hurt a person as much as it can bless him, and I find myself wondering why--out of all the people in all the world I could ever have loved--I had to fall in love with someone who was taken away from me" 
 "Life passes by now like the scenery outside a car window. I breathe and eat and sleep as I always did, but there seems to be no great purpose in my life that requires active participation on my part. I simply drift along like the messages I write you. I do not know where I am going or when I will get there. Even work does not take the pain away." 
 The story has its own uniqueness although the characters are entirely common people. The male protagonist Garrett is deeply aggrieved at his wife's accidental death. He writes letters addressed to his late wife for his own catharsis and throws them, enclosed in bottles , into the ocean. Now Theresa, a column writer living in another city, discovers one of these bottles and is deeply moved by the depth of Garrett's love. She has some serious trust issues with men after having to endure her husband's infidelity. So she is automatically attracted to Garrett who is faithful to his wife even after her death. And she decides to find him. In this way, they enter into a relationship. 
 As Theresa gets to know him more closely, she feels emotionally conflicted about his love for his late wife. And eventually it leads to their breakup. Later, Garrett realizes that he has to move on but here destiny comes into play. 
 The best part is the beautiful message conveyed by the story as Theresa writes in a final letter. 
 "Because of you, I am hopeful that there will come a day when my sadness is replaced by something beautiful. Because of you, I have the strength to go on." 
 She is not left depressed forever but finds strength from her love for Garrett. 
 True love is that which gives you hope and strength instead of leaving you dejected that happens in all the famous classic love stories. And that is why it has that uniqueness and likability.

This book was easy to read but didn't manage to hold my attention for long. I felt that the progression of the story was unnecessarily slow and rather predictable. The only shocker came in the last 50 pages. I was really disappointed, as I expected so much more from a Nicholas Sparks novel, given all the hype surrounding his works. 
 My mum had read it before I did and, being a major fan of any book that even remotely falls within the romance genre, even she didn't find this book romantic, heartwarming or touching in any way. It all just seemed unreal and unbelievable. I felt that everything fit too neatly into place for Garret and Theresa and then steadily began to fall apart once distance became an issue. I may seem hard-hearted and horrible for saying this, but I didn't think there was anything romantic about Garrett's letters to Catherine. Yes, sure, they were sad. But not because of their content or the feelings behind the words, but because it was sad to see that a man hadn't made the effort to move on and stop doing wussy stuff like writing letters to his dead wife and throwing them into the ocean, not expecting them to wash ashore and be found. If he was so touchy about strangers reading his letters and publishing them, then he shouldn't have risked sending the letters out into the open ocean. He could've just kept a journal or seen a therapist. 
 This book just left me feeling depressed and seemed to suck all the hope from the world for a good day or two after I was done with it. I'd planned on reading The Notebook, another Nicholas Sparks novel, before I watched the movie (which I recently acquired a copy of) but I'm not so sure if I want to.

sample_reviews.review_text:
THIS. BOOK. WAS. SOOOOOO. GOOOOD!! 
 I have been a HUGE fan of the lovely Lisa Mantchev since the Theatre Illuminata Trilogy came out and with her newest book, TICKER, I just grow in my admiration and stalking of her! 
 Miss Penny Farthing lives in a world filed with a variety mechanical contraptions, where a brilliant yet deranged with grief surgeon--Calvin Warwick--is determined to save her Ticker heart even if it comes at the expense of people's lives. He kidnaps her parents and depends that Penny turn herself over to him in order to save them. Penny sets out with her twin brother Nic, her best friend Violet, and the gallant Marcus Kingsley to rescue them. Along the way they encounter betrayal, traps, near death experiences, and spiders. Tons and tons of black, silver, and gold mechanical spiders that are hella scarier than real ones because, you know, mind control! 
 Penny was just so wonderful! She's sarcastic, stubborn as all hell, a jump-head-long-into-battle-make-no-apologies type of girl and I would SO be friends with her if she existed in real life! She's so protective of the people she loves and loyal. No matter the cost to herself, she will fight. She also has like two stomachs and a particular obsession with sweets which I am in TOTAL agreement *hehe*. Even with her life literally on the line and life falling apart around her, Penny is a woman of action. She sets her mind to something and does it. She's got a lot of spunk and can raise hell with the best of them. She's also a wicked shot with a pistol *wink*. 
 Marcus Kingsley. The name alone should cue massive amounts of swooning *dreamy sigh* Marcus is a gentleman and fine specimen of a gentleman at that! He has the physique to prove so *wink wink* Those broad shoulders and muscularly built body in a soldiers uniform was just enough to make a girl giggle uncontrollably while reading (Guilty!). Marcus is a man of his word and a brilliant leader. Having the Ferrum Viriae--elite rescue soldiers-- newly placed under his command as acting Legatus (General), Marcus is doing his best to be a leader in a position that belonged to his brother before he died. He is headstrong, orderly, has a mind that work countless different battle strategies under a minute. But when it comes to Penny, Marcus is softer and open. He's a man of action with a good heart and good principles sent in place. 
 Nic--Penny's twin, Violet--Penny's best friend, and Sebastian--Penny's childhood friend were all thoroughly entertaining and well-developed secondary characters. You'll love them as much as Penny and Marcus. Nic is an inventor with a sharp mind and fiercely protective of his sister. Violet is a true friend through and through. She's got guts too! She leads a troop of soldiers in the book when she has to go hunting for the one who betrays them and is determined to protect the man she loves (Nic) no matter the danger. Her and Nic are just so cute together! Sebastian is the rich playboy of the group and many a lady will find themselves swooning over him too. He's charming, handsome, and up for creating mischief at any time. But he's humble enough to admit when he's wrong and to find a way to make amends. 
 Calvin Warwick is the surgeon who gave Penny a ticker heart to help save her life when she fell of a horse. He broken up by grief and has gone quite insane because of it. Unable to let go of the love he lost, he thinks rescuing Penny at whatever cost, before her Ticker runs out of time, will be a way to honor his beloved. He's all kind of cuckoo BUT his madness makes sense for those who have lost people they love. I for one could understand his unbearable grief and could sympathize with him. Not with his actions but with his brokenness. Part of me wanted Calvin to have freedom even after all he had done because in a warped way, his intentions were good, he just did very ugly things no good human being would agree with. 
 The many contraptions throughout the story were really fun to read. My favorite was the parasol that could electrocute people! How I would just LOVE swinging one of those around *mischievous grin* The mind controlling spiders were just creepy enough to make you shiver and yet awesome enough to make you want some of your own. The action throughout the book builds up and keeps you turning the pages, especially the moments when Penny has near-death experiences and when Marcus rushes in like a knight in shining armor . . . except Penny can take of herself, what with her amazing shooting abilities. 
 TICKER was a splendidly, fantastic read full of delicious treats, hilarious dialogue, and imaginative action! You will find yourself laughing out loud, giggling nonstop, and your heart swooning every time Marcus Kingsley comes on the scene. It reads with a poetic ease where the words just fall into place like a dance, one part fast, one part sweet, one part heart-broken, one part steady. 
 One of my FAVORITE books this year! 
 GO. BUY A COPY. NOW! 
 FAVORITE QUOTES 
 Penny 
 "I doubt anything untoward will happen, but should the romance of the situation overwhelm him and he attempt to ravish me before your very eyes, you may knock him out with a tray." 
 "I'm allergic to fuss." 
 "I might be able to look after myself, but I'm safer when I'm with you." 
 Marcus 
 "Everyone who is going will do so with hopes for the best and prepared for the worst. In other words, armed to the teeth and carrying a few extra surprises." 
 "He reached up, trailing his fingers along my jawline before cupping my face in his hands. 'But some treasures are more important than others.'" 
 "I think she's safe from my advances, at least until morning." 
 "A tigress doesn't change her stripes." 
 "My dearest Miss Farthing, will you do me the unutterable honor of wearing this cheap bit of metal that will most likely turn your finger green, pretending to love and honor me as your husband for the purposes of subterfuge and stratagem?" 
 "Dimitria was very sick. None of us knew the extent of it.' 
 'That doesn't make a damn bit of difference to your heart. Grief doesn't take such things into consideration.'" 
 "We've all had terrible things happen to us. Only the weak use it as an excuse to prey upon others." 
 Warwick 
 "Don't you understand! We've both had our hearts broken. Death took from me the thing I loved most in this world. Now I am going to cheat it at every turn." 
 Sebastian 
 "Penny, my darling, I hoped that someday I would wake to find you by my side. I just didn't think it would be because you tried to kill me." 
 SNEAK PEEK 
 At that precise moment, Deadnaught returned carrying yet another tray, this one laden with missives and parcels, with Marcus Kingsley right behind her. 
 He didn't appear at all taken aback by my ridiculous frills or my foul language; instead, he made a lovely bow, hat tucked under his arm. "Tesseraria." 
 "Legatus." 
 "I'm glad to see that you are well." 
 "If by 'well' you mean I look a right monkey," I said, "then verily, I am well." 
 "You have to admit she looks fetching, Marcus," Violet said. 
 "Far be it from me to pass judgment on a lady's attire," the clever man replied. A few stiff steps brought him within feet of the bed. "I'm glad you're going to recover. It was terrifying to watch you fly through the crossfire on the Vitesse. If I find a dozen gray hairs of my head, I'll know who to blame." 
 I studied the military-short haircut, ignoring the temptation to run a hand over the closely cropped black curls. "Not a one." 
 "Yet," he added. "Give it time and a bit more of your reckless behavior." 
 "Without a doubt, driving through a gunfight was the most reckless thing I've ever done," I admitted. "And I've done quite a few reckless things in my life." 
 He reached for my hand. "I shouted to you when you shot out of the driveway and took off down the street." 
 "I heard you." I stared hard at the place where our fingers met, thinking it better to look there than into his eyes. 
 He didn't seem to care that we had an audience of two. "But you didn't stop." 
 Startled by the note of concern, I looked up. "I had to get to my brother." 
 Marcus's grip tightened to the point of impropriety. "You should have waited. I would have gone with you." 
 "You were a bit preoccupied at the time, what with all the bullets whizzing past you." I tried to extract my hand from his, but his gloves might as well have been coated in glue. "You were protecting Violet and Sebastian, too." 
 "I've never been more tempted to abandon a post."

This bordered on a 1.5 for me. There was a lot of crises managed by a lot of bravado. No character development, which left the whole thing flat. I enjoyed the clever steam-punkery.

The base of the story is good, had so much potential. It's just all thrown together in a cook pot and boiled. Then written by an excited toddler. Was the author even trying? 
 Really terrible. Aside from the story making little sense it jumps about with random explosions, kidnappings, chases and insta-love. We get the barest bones of the society the characters exist in. We learn everything's clockwork, they have a military & it's similar to victorian era. 
 The plot makes little sense at points. If this society is so dependent on mechanics why would they condemn a certifiable genius to death? Even if he is a killer, someone would make him quietly disappear & encourage him to continue his work. this becomes a point the author even makes when Sebastian is revealed to be a turncoat.<\spoiler>

"...Her prototype clockwork heart might be delicate, but Penelope Farthing is not. She is every bit the fashionable yet sassy young woman I would expect a female steampunk protagonist to be, even if constantly referring to her heart as her "Ticker" - capitalized and all - got kind of annoying to me... 
 ...Ticker starts out with what feels like an over-abundance of description. Everything in Penny's immediate surroundings is described with such detail that it ended up feeling more forced to me than anything else, particularly with regard to the gadgets and gizmos aplenty. My guess is that Mantchev was trying to get across the steampunk world-building, but it doesn't feel genuine to me for a character who comes across these types of things in everyday life to go on about them in such detail... 
 ...there is some insta-love action between Penny and Marcus, the young head of the military police force. I don't care for this trope in any type of novel, but it seemed particularly unnecessary here. Now, I'm not saying there shouldn't have been any romance between them at all - just that it really did not need to happen in this way...This part of the story would have played out much better had Penny been able to develop feelings naturally through the course of the adventure, having been thrown into each other's company... 
 ...Each of the main characters has some wit, intelligence, and depth to them; and although world-building descriptions could have been taken down a notch, I will say that Mantchev surprised me a little by adding elements that I would not have thought to connect with the steampunk genre, such as tasers, flying vehicles which are not airships, and fortresses powered by material mined from distant lands. 
 I don't really have too much else to say about Ticker, apart from the fact that once the story actually got going and I'd gotten past the mire of description, I rather enjoyed it. It became a fun read, and it's a book that I think would translate very well to a film adaptation if done properly. I look forward to reading more from this genre in the future."

book_b.title: The Selection (The Selection, #1)
book_b.user_review: Part Cinderella, part bachelor, part hunger games...

sample_reviews.review_text:
Summary: 
 America Singer is chosen to be one of the Selected, a handful of teenage girls who will compete to win the affections of the crown prince and become his future Queen. America, whose "true love" is from a lower cast, has no interest in gaining the affections of the prince, but eventually the two start to become friends as the competition is narrowed down. 
 Review: 
 Not every book is for every reader, and that is probably why I put off reading this one. This was a book group pick so I felt obligated to read it. I know how popular this book is, but it never held much appeal for me--just not my thing. 
 Essentially this book is "The Bachelor" for teens. I think my biggest problem with the book is the predictability--it is all so cliche. Of course America doesn't want to be chosen to be the future queen, she has no interest in that. Of course the prince would be intrigued by American who just wants to be his friend. Of course they will begin to fall in love. Sorry, but there is nothing original here--it is very stereotypical. 
 Despite that teens love these books, and apparently quite a few adults do too (judging from the reactions of most of the members of my book group). I think the appeal is that the everyday girl gets the unattainable and then there is the happily ever after. Entertaining fluff, but that is sometimes what people want. I may pick up book two someday when I am looking for something light and entertaining, but that's for another day. 
 Overall: 
 Light and entertaining, but lacking depth. Perhaps the sequels will have more meat to them, but this didn't really hook me. It was okay, but it wasn't a favorite. Still, I might pick up book two someday should I feel the need for something light. 
 Cautions for Sensitive Readers: 
 Language: Mild--I don't remember anything graphic. 
 Violence: Some, though mostly off in another part of the palace from the narrator. 
 Sex: Some kissing and groping, but nothing explicit. She is informed that she must be a virgin to compete in the Selection and that the prince may ask anything of her. 
 Drugs/Alcohol: Some alcohol consumption.

Hi, I'm baack! And here's my first book finished in 2015. The first book in The Selection series which I finally start due to curiosity and I'm a sucker for long pretty dresses I could never wear nor own, not a good reason to start a book, but it's something. 
 Anyway, The Selection is about a selection, thirty-five girls competing to win the heart of seventeen year old Prince Maxon of Illea. The heroine, America Singer, is, yes, a singer. And here are a few things I thought of the book: 
 The start of the book is slow, I'm so close to give it up, but I held on and finished it. Entertaining read, yes, but it left me with a lot of unaswered questions. 
 Like, I still fail to see the need of a monarchy heir to marry a true daughter of the country, as it was put in the book, unless there was a written agreement to do as such or else the people will overthrow the crown. It seems like Illea is a weak, developing kingdom, unsettled in their international relation (past princesses sent off to marry foreigners) and also its own internal matters, I mean, weekly televised report? 
 And the rebel attacks. While, Maxon's theory on North and South rebels is interesting and I expect it to be explored more, I still wonder, how the rebels even get past the gate? I mean, this is the royal palace, the king and the royal family live there, the current king is not its first monarch, so I assume the palace has been around for a long time, and rebels get past the gate and into the property. HOW in the world? What are the guards doing? The rebels got in to their bedrooms, for god's sake. While the purpose might be to emphasis the danger and threats these rebels posses, that's plain ridiculous. I expect a much, much better security measure for a royal palace. Like, invest in a impenetrable wall as high as you can build, a strong, defendable gate, a new security head. It doesn't matter how many of them are, they should be well prepared. People like these rebels just can't be allowed to go waltz into a royal palace like it's a freaking open-for-all shopping mall. 
 And on the second attack, the king himself was also in the safe room along with the Selection ladies. Oh my God. And Maxon was also there. As the palace was attacked. Perhapts Kiera Cass was trying to be unconventional, the monarch's life is important, I know, but having him in that safety room looks even more ridiculous. (I thought the king, and the prince, would be out there leading the fight back? His kingdom needs a more than an administrative, doing-office-works king in its current state, it needs a king and heir who could also defend it in actual fights.) 
 And our dear girl America saw this situation as the king defending the palace like a ship captain. Then she just kind of remind me of Bella Swan. Average, but kind of okay, wanted by two men, uncertain whom she wanted to be with. (The start of The Elite has even got me disliking her character.) 
 Oh and the whole China invading USA and got labor instead... wait, China actually needs more labor force? Their population is much bigger than USA's, unless it declined drastically for some unknown reason, they don't need any more people to do anything for them. And the American State of China, what kind of a state was that? Is it like the Dutch East Indies? 
 What I'm trying to say is while the story idea is good, its base is not. For a universe to be believable, it needs a strong base for the whole thing to grow on. This lack of strong base might be due to America Singer's own lack of knowledge regarding her own country's history and current affair. But, still, when you dig deeper as reading the book, there is nothing much. 
 As I previously said, it's an enough entertaining read, but nothing more. I don't expect much as I begin reading, but even it still fell short of what I expect to find. 
 I'm not sure if I'll finish the second book, I'll give it a few more chapters.
Predictable but it's been a nice experience reading it. And really liked Maxon. :)

reference_books.title: What-the-Dickens: The Story of a Rogue Tooth Fairy
reference_books.review_text:
In WHAT THE DICKENS a terrible storm wipes out the power and everyone is told to evacuate their homes. One family decides not to evacuate. Just when the mother's insulin runs out, Gage (her cousin) shows up at the house and ends up taking care of the three children while the parents go out into the storm for medical supplies. During the storm, Gage tells the children a story of a rogue tooth fairy. 
 I'm not quite sure what I think of WHAT THE DICKENS just yet. The writing was good. The story was interesting. But.. It didn't go anywhere. From the back cover it seemed like the story of What The Dickens was going to tie into the storm. It implied there was a fairy war going on and the storm was happening because of that.. Now.. I didn't get that from reading the book. The book ended when the story ended. Nothing changed in real time. Not much changed in the story. The two didn't seem to tie in. I guess it could be that Maguire wanted us to make up our own ending, but why have this crazy storm that makes a whole town evacuate their houses and move into a shelter and not do anything with that? I don't get it. This story had a lot of potential, but I feel a bit let down.

reference_books.title: Rampant (Killer Unicorns, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Killer unicorns, badass teen huntresses, hot boys in Italy? Yes. 
 RAMPANT tells the story of Astrid, a teenager who's been listening to her mother's crazy stories of being from a line of unicorn hunters for years. When Astrid actually sees a unicorn attack her skeezy boyfriend, she starts to believe. 
 This story was full of man-eating unicorn action! I think the general response to unicorns is a raise of the eyebrows, but these aren't your average sparkly, shiny unicorns. Peterfreund did massive research into unicorn myths for this book. So if you want to read about evil creatures and teen girls who kick ass, this is your book. My only concern was that the story ended too abruptly for me. Other than that, I quite enjoyed it.

reference_books.review_text: Damn. That's all I have to say other than this book made me really sad and at the same time it was so smart and amusing.

reference_books.title: Forever . . .
reference_books.review_text:
This book is about Kath who thinks of nothing but her new boyfriend, Michael. I didn't particularly like Michael. He was a bit two-dimensional. I never got a good sense of what he was like other than he liked to ski and he really wanted to have sex with Kath all the time. I got a better sense of Theo (and liked him more) even though he was introduced near the end of the book. But maybe that was the point. 
 The writing seemed a little bit too simple to me for a YA like this. I wanted more substance but didn't get that. The story was good and the subject relevant for teens. I enjoyed reading it but it would have been better with some more character development. It would have been especially nice to see the before-Michael Kath and during-Michael Kath and the differences involved.

reference_books.title: Eyes Like Stars (Théâtre Illuminata, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
It took me about 250 pages to really get into this story. That's a lot of pages before you start to like a story. My main issue was the vague setting. This book took place in a theatre and the theater seemed to exist in its own world. The rules for this theatre were not the same for the rules of the world around it. What frustrated me was not knowing this until halfway through the book. Also, it didn't make sense to me that if the people in the theatre had no exposure to the outside world, how was it possible that they then had jeans to wear and knew of things like "laser-triggered alarm systems"? These disconnects didn't work for me. 
 If we knew the setting early on, I probably wouldn't have had such issues with the book. But Mantchev didn't provide a clear picture of where her story was taking place. That being said, I love the idea of a theatre that lives to its own rules and exists in our world. I thought Ariel was a great character and by the end of the book I was interested to know where the next book would take us. It just took me 250 pages to get to that point.

book_a.title: The Magicians (The Magicians #1)
book_a.user_review:
I finally finished it! Not the best response when I finish a book. I've sat down and tried to determine how I feel about THE MAGICIANS, but I've still come to no conclusions. I don't know if I liked it or hated it. I don't know if I thought it was good or bad. This doesn't happen to me very often. 
 I will say this: it's not as steeped in the magical realm as I expected. THE MAGICIANS is a story of highly intelligent misfit teenagers who are selected to go to a wizard school. The world is our own world and except for finding the will and the discipline to learn how to alter the elements or reality or whatever you want to call it (magic), this book offers barely any escape from our world (like most fantasy novels might). 
 I think what bothered me the most was the importance of Fillory to the characters in the book. (Fillory was reminiscent of Narnia. Even with the two kings and queens from Earth.) I love books, don't get me wrong, but I couldn't understand how a series of books could impact these teens so strongly that they couldn't let go of the fact that Fillory might be real. 
 There were certain characters whom I really enjoyed (Alice, Mayakovsky...), but most of the characters fell flat for me. Everyone in the book is so unhappy. I also found it hard to see what was going on (and usually when I read a book it plays out like a movie in my head) and I think it was because the characters were two-dimensional. 
 Though I don't want to discourage people from reading this book. There were certain parts that I really enjoyed and then certain parts I had to wade through. Don't expect your average fantasy novel, you won't get it. This isn't really fantasy. It's more a coming of maturity/age story that has elements of magic in it.

sample_reviews.review_text: I really wanted to like this or love this, but the whole thing was just so slow. Really, I don't like Quentin at all, I get him, but at the same times its not an excuse for him to get away with half of the stupid things he does. The first 300 pages consisted of Brakebills, learning magic, them turning into geese, and really the arctic fox intercourse? And all of the unnecessary drunk, sex, and party scene that happens in this book. The first 300 pages can have been written in maybe 150 pages or less and then finally in the last 100 pages of this book we get something! We get Fillory and finally some actions. But boy, did this book really put me to sleep! I fell asleep reading this book because it was just so long and slow. What I did took away from this book is that you can never be happy, you will find something new to be excited about, but sooner or later the excitement will die down, and you will be just back to square one, back to feeling lonely in your life, and wondering why are you not content with your life. This book is depressing, whining, dark, slow, and really of just Quentin whining 75% of the time. I am however curious what will happened in the next two sequels, but I'm not willing to put myself through that misery again. I will probably just read some summaries online and maybe put the next two books on the bottom of my to-read list. Really disappointed with this book. I really think Grossman could have make this such a better book than it is. And again I speak for myself, entitled to my own opinions. You may enjoy this book, a lot of other people did! But this was just not my cup of tea.(

I hated this book the first time I read it, but when it was chosen for book club I decided to try to give it a second chance and try to be more objective. It didn't work. I still hate it. 
 When I first read it I thought I only hated it because of the way it completely twisted some of my favorite novels from childhood (The Narnia Chronicles) but I realize now it's much more than that. This novel has been described as being "Harry Potter for adults" but that statement couldn't be more wrong. This is Harry Potter for adults who have become completely disillusioned by books about magic. There's nothing even magical about this book - Grossman turns magic into science and takes away everything that's magical about magic. The book feels completely sterile and antiseptic, with no heart or imagination at all; instead of the creativity and color Harry Potter inspires in my imagination, I pictured this whole world dreary and grey. The style and tone of the book made the narration feel toneless, and uninterested, which made it hard for me to care about what was happening or get into the story. I didn't like any of the characters in this novel - not because they were unlikable, but because I simply didn't care about them at all. 
 And I haven't even gotten into the minor things that bugged me, like the fact that the school's calendar is randomly 2 months off from the rest of the world for no apparent reason. I've discussed this book with some other people who defended it based on the fact that the tone is intentional and the author is trying to make a statement on these types of novels, but even if this is the case it just put me off the book entirely. If you're looking for Harry Potter for adults, do not read this book. Check out Jim Butcher's Dresden Files instead.

I'm still not entirely sure how I feel about this book. The structure is unusual in a way that might be flawed, or it might just be different from what I'm used to. There isn't a conventional story arc, but it's not arranged as a series of interludes connected by a device, either. Normally, a story with school at its center will be structured around the school time frame, but this isn't. Sometimes a lot of time passes with the narrative just skimming and skipping over things, then other times we stop and zoom in on things that don't necessarily move the plot or develop the characters, although they aren't really objectionable to read. And then the whole school thing turns out to be not so important, in a way. 
 I think the protagonist is problematic for me. I don't really like Quentin, but then he is an anti-hero and I'm not really supposed to like him. It's more that, while Quentin may be more realistic than a conventional hero, he doesn't feel real to me as a fully developed character. After everything he experiences, I still don't feel like I know him or understand what makes him tick. In some cases, I might say that was the desired effect, or I was just not connecting to that particular character, but in this case I'm afraid it's because the character isn't whole. 
 Overall, I still enjoyed the book to a reasonable extent, and I'm looking forward to seeing how the second book picks up the story and pushes the characters in hopefully new directions. I guess I'm supposed to talk about how the book is and is not like Harry Potter, or how Fillory is or is not like Narnia, but really, that's tiresome. It's refreshing to see the Hogwarts-like situation given such a different treatment, and the Narnia stuff seems like perfectly acceptable and somewhat traditional literary signifying.
Fantastic read. Can not wait to start the next book in the trilogy.
Got halfway through before the Young Adult and "don't think about things that are happening in the book" aspects got too large.

I'm giving up. Not only does this book really have no point behind it but it has stolen so much from other books that I just can't understand how Grossman could do it. First he actually uses some of the same made-up words and ideas from Harry Potter and then the last straw was when I realized that he used the same exact in-between type world as was used in the Magicians Nephew by C.S. Lewis. I mean come on.

Quentin is sort of the lovechild of Harry Potter and Holden Caulfield; this is his magical "coming of age." Q is self-centered, petty, insecure, and awkward...in short, your average teenager. This is a novel of his dreams and fuck ups, both spectacular. I really liked it, tho the pacing was a little off for me, and most of the time you want to strangle the protagonist. I'm not running out to devour book 2, but I'll get to it eventually.

I might change my two stars later when I have calmed down a bit, but good lord this book made me livid! If it was written well, all of the blatantly obvious references to The Secret History and fantasy literature (Harry Potter and Narnia in particular) would have been forgiven as they could be passed as homage or intertextuality. But the writing is so terrible (has anyone heard of an editor?), it came across as blatant freebooting (in print form). 
 A magical land visited by four English children (where only human children can sit on the four thrones)? 
 A wizard's school? 
 A hunt for a white stag? 
 A group of precocious and bored university students drinking themselves to death? 
 Drunken orgies in the woods? 
 A time-turner disguised as a pocket watch? 
 A form of wizard chess? 
 A world-between-the-worlds with ponds to jump into? 
 Seriously - are Donna Tartt and J.K. Rowling getting any royalties from this? 
 And lets not forget the worst line in the book: "Of course it matters, Vix," Quentin said. "It's not like they're all the same." "Vix" was a term of endearment with them, short for vixen, an allusion to their Antarctic interlude, vixen being the word for a female fox.
I really wanted to like this more than I did. I like the idea and might pick up book two to see if I like it any better.

I have no earthy idea why this book is or ever was popular. The idea that SyFy bought the rights to the property and has made a television series from it blows my mind. To me this book read like J. K. Rowling's older, 'cooler' brother mansplaining all the ways in which Harry Potter was juvenile drivel. And true to form, by doing so the quibbler missed one of the very coolest things about Harry Potter: good or bad, rich or poor, gifted or average, cool or uncool, all of the students at Hogwarts are just that: students. The great social rift of girls below and boys above is practically ignored. 
 I tried to give The Magicians the benefit of the doubt. I mean, it is written from the POV of a teenage boy. The fact that Quentin's self-absorbed isn't a huge surprise, nor are his more neanderthal views on women. 
 Where I fell off the joy train was during the Antarctic portion of the program. First up, the Russian who runs the concentration camp they call a school is creepy to the point of vulgarity. The whole 'theft of voices' thing boded ill, but it wasn't until the 'hammer and nail' game that Grossman really hacked me off. 
 The scene is set thusly: a dank stone cell, a table and chair, a block of wood, a hammer and nails, and a fiddly spell so oft repeated to suit various conditions as fill the provided book. Our hero is set the task of completing every iteration of this pointless spell that's purpose is simply to allow the caster to drive a nail into a piece of wood with one whack of the hammer without bending said nail or crushing their thumb. The narrative expounds on the conditions covered ad nauseum: different locations, altitudes, weather -- some examples specific, some not. Finally, only three variables remain to be tested: the caster's gender: male, female or 'hermaphrodite.' Naturally, the protagonist balks over the last option like any genderist prig. 
 Obvious irks aside, why exactly are those the final three options? Wouldn't every iteration of the spell have three versions based on the caster's gender? Is it just a given that only a man would find himself having so much trouble driving a nail into a board 'on a tropical island during a snowstorm' that he would have to resort to magic? How does that even make sense? 
 I actually lasted a bit past that. It was when the entire fourth year class was turned into foxes as an excuse for wholesale rape that I gave up. The protagonist describes how the object of his desire's 'eyes roll in terror' as he penetrates her only to 'fog with pleasure' seconds later. (That was written by a true man...with no real sense of spacial relationships.) Our hero describes how uncomfortable things are the next day, wonders if his lady love is still a virgin...and all the other ridiculous garbage anyone with a lick of sense would avoid voicing at all cost. 
 I plan to return my copy to Audible because I just can't justify giving Lev Grossman a single dime.

book_b.title: Fifty Shades of Grey (Fifty Shades, #1)
book_b.user_review:

sample_reviews.review_text: Okay, so I knew the book was going to be about sex. "Fifty Shades of Grey" I hoped that meant an older woman with grey hair was going to have great sex. But no, I was disappointed. Anyway, there was lots of sex but I would have told Mr. Grey to go F*** himself from the beginning and then there would be no story.
Utter drivel.

The success of Fifty Shades of Grey is the very definition of viral marketing. A book that was originally self-published as an eBook and a print-on-demand paperback, it somehow caught the imagination of women everywhere and it's said that a copy now sells every sixty seconds. Amazing. There are three books in the series and they are numbers 1, 2 and 3 on the New York Times best seller list, and have been for months. 
 I have three words for this phenomenon: WTF?? I mean really...have you read this thing? 
 I bought a Kindle version ($9.99), just to see what all the hoopla was about, and got through about 1/3 of it (31% according to my Kindle), rolling my eyes and saying, "Oh, please," on every other page. With one exception (from Jessica Reaves of the Chicago Tribune) it seems to be immune to criticism of any kind (because it's made a boatload of money?), and as an author it's probably bad form to say this (you know that won't stop me), but it's crap. I don't mind the concept of it or the genre of eroticism itself, but something that's selling like the latest iPad release should at least be...well, good. 
 Fifty Shades of Grey is not good. That's not hurting sales in the least. It doesn't seem to matter that the writing stinks, the characters are unappealing and not engaging, the storyline is non-existent and, worst of all, the sex isn't even good, just lots of murmuring and moaning and gasping, and heartbeats quickening and racing. Kinda trite. At least be original. 
 The protagonist, Anastasia Steele, is a 21 year old virgin, and the narrative (told from her point of view) is sprinkled with lots of italics: holy crap! holy fuck! holy shit! jeez! and so on. And her inner goddess talks to her, and does "merengue with some salsa moves." Need I say more? Now, you can't argue with that kind of success - it's phenomenal - and good for E.L. James. She seems as amazed by this as everyone else. But seriously...what are you people thinking? Whatever it is, could you please transfer it to my book? And when mine becomes a runaway best seller it won't bother me a bit when E.L. James trashes it on her blog.

The author will be the first to tell you she isn't a great writer, and it's evident in Fifty Shades. The gratuitous sex scenes got ridiculous and tired very quickly, the language used was very asinine, especially in the everyday conversations of the characters, and the main character's thought process was like a balloon with the helium slowly leaking out. 
 At first the sex scenes were fun and thrilling, and then they never stopped happening and I began skimming through them in order to get to more of the story-- which was, sadly, lacking. There isn't much to this book other than a whole lot of sex. 
 If you've never read a sexually explicit romance novel before, then this might float your boat. I've read my share of romance novels (ones that actually had characters you could care about and plots with mysterious twists that make you want to keep reading), and this one was so ridiculously bad, in my opinion, that it was hard to finish reading.

The story, I've gathered, seems to about a girl called Anna and her absolutely perfectly damaged hunk, Christian. 
 Anna seems to act like a bratty 16 year old. Well that was my first impression anyway. 
 But no, Anna is actually in her mid 20's who happens to be the most childish virgin in history! 
 I've known puritans less repressed than this lady! 
 Anyway, when her friend commits the horrific crime of asking Anna to do her interview for her, Anna stomps her feet a bit but ultimately accepts the proposition. She travels to a very big hard........office and meets Christian. The manliest man that ever maned. 
 A manly man so completely manly, in fact, that he can make you drop your panties with a single smile. What a virile bastard! 
 With some schoolyard flirtation and some encouragement from the crazy voices er I mean her inner Goddess, Anna decides that he is absolutely dreamy. A conclusion many people who've read this book, seem to be agreed upon. 
 What follows is some heavy petting, with some kind of awkward sex scenes and some strange metaphors. Oh and lets not forget consultation from the crazy voices/the Inner Goddess and lip biting. Lot's of lip biting. 
 The writing style is not terrible, but I personally didn't find it appealing. Then again, I hated Anna from the first page and this is in first person, so perhaps it's all her fault. As a 21 year old, I found the portrayal of Anna weird and unrealistic. I felt she was nothing but walking hormones ie a teenager. I also found broken but otherwise "perfect" Christian a little bit creepy and a control freak. I haven't even gotten to the infamous "tampon scene" either. 
 It just seems like Twilight attempted to grow up, but kept it's teen angst. 
 Sorry, this is one bandwagon I just cannot climb aboard.

Everyone probably knows what this fan-fiction novel is about already, but I'll just summarize it briefly. One day when Ana's friend falls ill and calls in a favour, requesting Ana to interview one of the richest, successful men in Seattle in her place. Although it should it was indeed a formal interview, Christian and Ana both realize that this encounter was anything but ordinary. They start to form a curiosity and fatal attraction for one another. But as all businessmen know, sometimes the only way to keep something is by signing a contract... 
 I read this book because there were so many people raving about it, and of course it was also because it made it onto the top 20 list of best sellers on Indigo etc. If you ever watch or read the Vampire Diaries, Twilight or any other similar television shows or books, it is a definite possibility that you will enjoy this novel. I think the most captivating part about this novel is Mr. Grey himself. What kind of girl does not have an attraction to a bad boy? A handsome bruting one? A mysterious, rich, powerful and charming one? When you combine all of these aspects into one character, it becomes irresistible to desire more information, and the only way to gain more information is by blazing through the pages! 
 So why do I give this three stars? As explicit as the sexual content in the novel is, there is quite a bit of repetition. Not only in vocabulary, but also events in the story. The higher the predictability, the less enjoyable it is (excluding fairy tales, the ones where we watch because we expect the feel-good happy endings).

Ok, I'm just going to start this with an apology to my friends who really enjoyed this book. You are entitled to your own opinion and I respect that. However, I wholeheartedly disagree with you. I went into it with zero expectations, and somehow it fell beneath zero into a negative WTF wasteland. 
 I know this whole thing got started as Twilight fan fiction, but after it got popular shouldn't she have changed some more details? This is just barely skimming the edges of plagiarism and if I were Stephenie Meyer I would be very pissed off. It was set in the same city, with similar characters--down to the zany scatter-brained mother, all-adopted siblings, and clumsy inexperienced main character. Take Twilight, change the names and remove the vampire aspect and you have 50 Shades of Utter Crapola. 
 I'm not even going to get into the bad writing. It speaks for itself. 
 The storyline was DEEPLY disturbing and I'm sure it had domestic violence counselors cringing across the world. Anastasia literally called him a control freak, said she felt smothered, and actively worried that he was going to hit her again if she made him mad. Her eating was controlled by him, who she could hang out with, her behaviors--everything. He would randomly show up where she was and somehow even after she told him he was a "stalker" she was in the same breath talking about her feelings for him and how much she loved him. She just knew he was damaged and complicated and SHE would be the one to change him! Ignoring the fact that he'd had over a dozen other women in the same situation and none of them had ever changed him. 
 Sound familiar? That's because it was an ABUSIVE relationship with a ton of mixed messages. He'd tell her he was incapable of love and didn't want her to touch him, and then later that night he'd be excited about introducing her to his mother. Um... no. It doesn't work that way. To quote He's Just Not That Into You--"you are not the exception, you are the rule." 
 (I'm going to ignore the obviously incredible things--like that the main character was in her 20's and had never had sex or been drunk at all in her life.) 
 I'm just extremely confused as to why all of this is considered hot to some people. I was revolted all the way through the book and for a lack of a better term, I can't get it up for someone who is a fucking psycho. I agree with the memes out that there that say if he wasn't hot and rich the book would go nowhere because women would see it for the garbage it is. 
 Honestly I'm terrified that women are going to take this to heart and stay in an abusive relationship because they are trying to save their abuser from his own mental issues. Please please please realize this is a STORY that was written by a woman and in no way mirrors your situation because it is a completely ridiculous piece of FICTION. 
 If you are looking for erotica that is not full psycho-stalkers, try Anne Rice's Sleeping Beauty series. It is WAY better and doesn't contribute to the dumbing-down of women everywhere. 
 One star. 
 I've had better.
An insight into intelligent, artistic, and original writing.

I'm about as confused as much as Miss Steel about this book. I really hated this book....I loathed it, and 1/2 way through it I set it down and didn't pick it back up for months, but I wanted it cleared off my night stand so I finished, and ...........I hate, hate, hate to admit......I liked the ending. It went from a 1 star to a 3....Just for the ending.
This has to be a joke.

reference_books.title: The Magicians (The Magicians #1)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 Just about every character in this book is an absolute shit. 
 There's also no question that Quentin makes my list of worst protagonists. He is such a goddamn douchebag 90% of the time. 
 BUT the fact that there's not really any redemption for him and he continues to be one of the world's biggest fuckups until he gets Alice, who I liked about 60% of the time (which is much more than I liked any other character here), killed. 
 This book also needed a better editor. There is so much stuff in here that's not relevant to anything (all scenes from Quentin's and Alice's final year only serve to show us that they both got excessively douchey? Alice wasn't much like that before or after that chapter so that was weird) and yet the question of Quentin's Discipline was brought up for the test and then they said they'd test him again the next year. His Discipline wasn't mentioned again until like the last page of the book. In his first test the teacher administering it says how unusual that is. It doesn't make sense to never have it brought up again while he was at school. 
 I managed to get to the end of this book because I really wanted to see if somehow Quentin was right that Fillory held his redemption. Then when it became clear that that wasn't going to happen, I was basically waiting for Alice to die. Then when she was dueling Martin I was hoping that he would experience a sudden irrepressible burst of magic that would help indicate his Discipline and defeat Martin. But of course that didn't happen because Quentin is ridiculously useless. This book earned a third star because he FINALLY accepted that he's been a fucking dickhead his whole life. The old Quentin would have taken solace in Emily telling him that it wasn't his fault, that it was the school and magic in general but he wouldn't accept that and he was right not to. He finally grew up a little bit and I think Alice would have liked that for once he wasn't being such a pussy.

reference_books.title: House of Leaves
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I think I expected to love this book as much as I did the first time I read it some six years ago. It wasn't nearly as scary the second time around. But the first time I read it my main focus was on the tapes and the house. Those parts of the book haunted me for quite awhile. I would stay up thinking about how quickly Halloway devolved. Wondering if once the house gets you alone, no companion or radio, if time works differently. Wondering why, for the rest of them, time didn't change despite the fact that space and physics meant nothing beyond that door. 
 This time I was much more swept up with Johnny's madness. There are so many reasons he's not a reliable narrator so we don't have the best grasp on what's true. I think he believes he's telling what's happening but the longer he spends with Zampano's the less sure he seems to be about what's true. Johnny acknowledges when experiences are hallucinations but he loses a lot of time. Thinking about the check mark you notice on the corner of a single page while reading only to later read Johnny's mother's letters. Wondering if Johnny's increased mental instability is caused by the story, begging the question of the house somehow being real despite the fact that the beginning all but tells us that these tapes, these people, and most of the texts referenced seem to not exist. Are the hallucinations he experiences actually the beginnings of schizophrenia, inherited from his mother, only taking the form of whatever seems to be haunting the house because he has become obsessed with the story? The inclusion of the index card in an appendix that considers a rewrite that leaves Navy and Karen losing both their children to the house suggests that the whole of The Navidson Tapes is fiction. But who does that index card belong to? Whose fiction is it? And if we don't know that how can we know it's really fiction at all?

reference_books.review_text: Absolutely the cutest thing that has ever existed. I've been a huge fan of My Cardboard Life for years and I associate Philippa Rice with awesomeness (not only because MCL is awesome but also because I started reading it when I first discovered Doctor Who) and this 100% did not disappoint. It's so simple and a completely accurate reflection of those day-to-day moments spent with someone you love. Perfect.
