book_a.title: Mrs. Dalloway
book_a.user_review:
I kept wanting to put this book down and couldn't quite make myself do it. Not knowing anything about this book when I picked it up, I wasn't prepared for the lack of structure. I got about fifty pages in before I realized that this was all the book was, a day in the life of some people who are unhappy in very ordinary ways. 
 As simple as a book like this seems on the surface, Virginia Woolf is completely amazing for being able to pull it off. While the characters are pretty unlikable it's easy to stay interested in their day. Almost everything that happens is almost depressingly mundane but the writing turns it all into something much richer.

sample_reviews.review_text: Literally everyone should read this book when they're on the cusp of 60.

It is mid June just after the conclusion of the Great War - not yet know as WW1 since this was the war to end all wars. Armistice was November 11, 1918 so the spring following that was 1919. 
 I pick this bookswap book up on June 12th so I can look out the window at the right season, if the incorrect continent. Clarissa Dalloway is in London. I am in Virginia. 
 It's quite a day for 52 year old Mrs Dalloway by Virginia Woolf. As she is making preparations for a big party in the evening, an old flame comes back from India and drops in on her. She is not in a happy marriage as she and her husband lead lives on different tracks including separate bedrooms. With an outlook from the upper class, she remembers why she didn't marry Peter and wonders what to do about it now. 
 I struggle through this, finding that it is not an easy reading summer book too late. Why did I think Virginia Woolf would be in that category anyway? Brain spasm. Theoretically, I like stream of consciousness writing. But page-long sentences and semicolons and parentheses required more concentration than I had to give. 
 My two stars on Mrs. Dalloway is more about me than about the book. My head just wasn't ready for the high voltage this book required. I have Orlando on my book shelf but I think I will let it sit there for some time.

I think this book is a completely brilliant work of art, and successfully pulls off what was surely a highly experimental form at the time, but I don't feel like I was in the right headspace to fully enjoy it on a narrative level. It's the kind of book you need to read in one go (or as close to that as time allows) and I wasn't able to give it that. Beautiful sentences that cut to the core throughout, but it was a slog for me. I'd love to reread in a couple of years.

I chose to buy this book because I'd yet to read any Virginia Woolf. 
 Meh. 
 Yes, it is "the outline on paper of human consciousness" and yay for "transforming the art of the novel," but I was bored. 
 Also, the back cover is misleading; it made me believe the whole book was stream-of-consciousness from Mrs. Dalloway's point of view, so when it started jumping from character to character, I was like whaaaat. 
 Bravo for the definition of consciousness between characters. I'm sure that takes great skill. 
 It's a good book, and influential, no doubt, but I didn't enjoy it.
couldn't get into it - clearly it was beyond me. just not a fan of Ms. Woolf.

Oh, man, I really tried on this one, but I don't think it's worth my effort to finish the book. I totally get the historical significance of Mrs. Dalloway, but to me, that's just not enough to redeem the rambling story filled with silly people and thoughts of insignificant characters. Yes, the sentences can be very beautiful, emotive and paint a picture. But that doesn't turn the book into a compelling story with characters one would care about.

This is the first (and so far only) Virginia Woolf novel that I have read. It was assigned in one of my courses, and I had a really tough time with it at first; once I got about 40 pages in, I really started to get the hang of Woolf's writing and I started to enjoy it much more. There is something poetic and haunting about her descriptions of people, places, times, etc. It's not the easiest read, and understandably, there are a lot of people who don't like Mrs. Dalloway, but even if you don't enjoy the novel, you have to appreciate and applaud her innovative writing techniques.

This is beautifully written, if not hard to follow at times, and has some very quotable lines. 
 It is written in a stream of consciousness style and I view it as a raw look at social life, feminism, and mental illness during post World War I England. While the story is not heavy, but rather whimsical at times, the thoughts of this book will have you contemplating them for some time. 
 I quite enjoyed my first taste of Virginia Woolf.

It's not that Septimus was exactly my favorite character, it's just that I hated all the other characters in comparison. This is a weird feeling I get when I finish reading an acclaimed classic novel, I feel the need to cherry pick the things I like in order to gain some recognition of knowing what I'm talking about. Mrs. Dalloway is not objectively a bad novel by any means, it's just that I found so few things over the length of the story that I actually enjoyed. Septimus was the character I liked the most and look where he ended up. The most interesting part of the book for me were the beautiful descriptions of time being chipped away from the characters' lives and how they weren't finding what they wanted and were running out of time to feel fulfillment in their lives. I liked this in almost a sadistic way, because the characters themselves (Clarissa in particular) are so conniving and unlikable that by the end I was praying for the party to quickly turn into a train wreck of the most epic proportions. Sadly I got no such catharsis. But as mentioned before this is just coming from a person who sees these kinds of train wrecks of the dystopian variety more often than not, so perhaps Mrs. Dalloway just needs an acquired taste to enjoy.
could not finish.

book_b.title: One More Thing: Stories and Other Stories
book_b.user_review: These stories range from the merely pointless to the completely insufferable.

sample_reviews.review_text: The stories in this collection range from amusing to good to very good. A couple are even beyond very good. "Julie and the Warlord" was side-splittingly funny and "Sophia" was surprisingly tender and sad. My only criticism of this book is that, because the stories are so short and there are so many of them, it begs to be read all in a chunk. But when you do that, they start to lose their effectiveness after a while. I found that I wasn't paying as much attention to the later stories as to the ones in the first half of the book.

My opinion might be in the minority, but I did not enjoy this book. I am not the type of person who doesn't finish books; I always press on even in the bleakest of books. But this one...I finally put it down. Maybe that was easier because it is short stories, but in a way that is worse because I did not like even one of the stories I read. I kept hoping they would get better, that I would find that one or that I would feel a little bit of hope, but no. In fact, I can say I hated it. Then I felt bad for hating it but it was true, so I'll admit it. I hated it.

I had high expectations for this book, and unfortunately it fell short. The short stories were too short to derive any real purpose and the laughs were few and far between. A majority of the stories gave off a vibe of trying too hard and ultimately it fell flat.

Fun, nothing life changing here but some entertaining stories. A lot of them are not really "short stories" per say but more like vignettes. Some are just one page long, or just a few sentences. Some made me chuckle, others I thought were clever ideas even if they didn't really blow me away. The stories have the dialogue of someone that writes for TV (at least it seemed that way to me, but I already knew he was a writer for The Office in addition to being an actor on the show). I liked the one about John Grisham accidentally having his new book published with the title of "The Something" because his editor didn't realize that was just a placeholder and he hadn't decided on a title yet. Or the one about the diary of "the man who invented the calendar". I did grow a little bored of them by the end for some reason.

I was extremely disappointed-I loved B.J Novak on "The Office" & was looking forward to his writing. I did not get very far at all mainly because of the language. I do not enjoy reading the F word in any context nor do I enjoy other "gratuitous"profanity & this is filled with them. I could not get past it.
A collection of silly stories that fails to be anything else, just silly. Yawn.
I reeeeally enjoyed some of these stories while others were just duds.

B.J. Novak's stories are definitely different. They are a mixture of snippets, vignettes, and very short flashes of ideas. Most span only three to five pages with some ranging only a paragraph or two. Their impact varies greatly, anywhere from ecstatic to very flat and trivial. Even though a clear intent on humor pushes through in nearly every piece, many feel as if they could be more developed. The few instances that bring about smiles and laughs aren't enough to make the book enjoyable. One of the unique and intelligent "stories" that reflects Novak's creativity and him promise as a writer of fiction is the satire titled "The Comedy Central Roast of Nelson Mandela." Novak demonstrates an eye for addressing social issues and a cleverness with poking fun at serious topics. Where many writers wouldn't dare attempt such risks, Novak's penchant to pursue laughs is commendable. However, the elusiveness of the stories often prevents them from packing any type of emotional depth. These odd stories feel clever, but sometimes too much so for their own good.

An author friend of mine asked me to take a look at this anthology and tell what I thought. My main comment would be "disappointing." 
 The author does have a talent for being able to tell a full story within a page or two. A lot of writers can't do that, myself included. His short short works are better than his longer stories. Still, many of the works in this book are less than a page--some only a few lines. They aren't stories, but mere ideas. Some have a decent point to them, but they come across as Facebook posts or, the shortest ones, tweets. I can read stuff like that online. Spending money to read them in an anthology makes me feel cheated. 
 As for the real stories in this collection, content-wise, they reminded me of high-school creative writing assignments. Maybe that's when they were written. Most of the viewpoints sounded naive. It's listed under humor, but I only found a few glimmers of cleverness. Nothing laugh out loud. 
 I don't know. Maybe I'm too old to read a book like this. (Me who reads kids' books regularly.) I couldn't help feeling that the book was published only because the author was a TV actor.
Couldn't finish. Too dirty. Sad.

reference_books.title: The Perilous Sea (The Elemental Trilogy, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
The Perilous Sea book 2 of The Elemental Trilogy by Sherry Thomas. 
 Prince Titus and Iolanthe are still on their journey to overthrow the evil Bane. Along the way, an unexpected truth is revealed that shocks them both and shakes the foundation they have built their quest upon. 
 I loved how this time the book would switch between narration of the present to the past. A lot of minor characters become much more important. Secrets are revealed and beleifs are shattered. I also loved how I couldn't guess what was going to happen. I would think and think and I knew that something was fishy but I was not expecting the thing that happened to be it and that is AMAZING. I love when books keep me guessing. 
 The perilous sea wasn't as amazing as the first book,but it was still awesome. It was packed with adventure and not as slow as the first novel yet it was missing something I can't put my finger on it. Sometimes I felt like the interesting parts were rushed. 
 Dragons, flying carpets, magic wands, elixirs and charms. 
 Highly recommended for lovers of high fantasy. And yes you have to read book one before you read book two.

reference_books.title: The Girl on the Train
reference_books.review_text:
Reading this book felt like a chore (prepare yourself for a rant). It was so infuriating. This was very very very very slow and I couldn't even skip pages for fear of missing some important detail. Five chapters would be excruciatingly boring about Rachel's everyday life and then one of the entries would finally be related to the actual Mystery. which is the only reason I kept on reading. 
 In general, this is how the book went: Rachel sulking over ex husband, she feels sorry for herself, she drinks, she gets hangover, hates herself and swears she will never dink again, repeat. Occasionally some interesting parts that bring you back to the mystery and then to my dismay back to her hating herself drunk and thinking about her stupid ex. Now I understand that this is supposed to be some realistic description about a messed up women but COME ON we get the idea enough already. I was so over this stupid cycle of her's and almost pulled my hair out at 80% into the novel when it was still going. 
 Ok I'm done ranting. 
 The mystery parts were good. Great even. but you had to read about 30-40 pages before you actually happened upon them. The book could have been so much better. The character I loved the most was Megan. She was strong and didn't tolerate any bullshit but she was also flawed. 
 The narration fluctuates between three female characters: Rachel, Anna, and Megan. It is written in first person present tense. And there are dates to keep all the events in order. 
 Would I ever re-read this? NO 
 So who would I recommend this book too? 
 If you like mystery and are willing to push your self through long boring parts to finally solve the mystery then go on and read this. I understand why people compare this to Gone Girl (all the messed characters and the mystery) but honestly GG was so much better.

book_a.user_review: This was great I loved every bit. I loved how Feyre developed and all the new characters. I know a lot of people don't like how it played out but I really did. You really get sucked into the world and get attached to all the personalities. There was a lot of LOL moments that always add a nice touch. Highly recommended for all the fantasy lovers.

sample_reviews.review_text: soooo, I'm finally finished, thank god.

OH MY GOD. THIS BOOK. This book really broke me. I am still sobbing uncontrollably while I am writing this review. But let's get the usual stuff out of the way. I (as always) loved the writing style and writing itself. Every decision in this novel made sense, which I really appreciated. The characters went through drastic changes throughout this tome. Characters I loved, I now hate. And characters I hated I now love. I love almost every character that was introduced, the story line was sexy and badass and heartbreaking and everything I could ever want in this sequel. That being said, I did not see that ending coming. I didn't. And now my eyes are so swollen from crying, its pretty hard to keep them open. I actually really understand the ending in all seriousness, though. It totally makes sense and I like it even if it did cause me emotional and mental trauma. This is probably one of my favorite books of all time now and if you haven't read this yet, WHAT ARE YOU DOING WITH YOUR LIFE. READ IT.

This book is one of the few out there that's better than its predecessor. There was alot of growth in the characters, the world, and the plot of the story. Feyre comes into her own and learns to find a sense of healing caused from the events in the last book. 
 Compared to the first book, there are several references to sex and three major sex scenes that I had to skip over because of the explicit detail. 
 I was disappointed a few times but some of the decisions of the characters and the amount of sexual detail in this book but overall I enjoyed it.
I decided not to finish this book. I was not enjoying it, and it took too much energy to try to read it. Maas is a great writing, but the ACOTAR series isn't for me.

 A Court of Mist and Fury (ACOMAF) broke me. I am broken. I am liquified feels. I can't breathe. I can't think. My heart has been ripped out of my chest, shattered into a million pieces and stomped on. This book hangover I have will likely last until May 2, 2017 when A Court of Wings and Ruin comes out and I can gobble the story down within days. I thought A Court of Thorns and Roses (ACOTAR) was amazing, but I was wrong - I mean, it was really good. But ACOMAF was BEYOND amazing. It was a higher level of amazing that ACOTAR could never ever come close to reaching. I don't think ANY book can come close to the level of amazing that was ACOMAF. I've never been able to answer the question, "what's your favorite book?" But after reading ACOMAF, I can. I can 100% say this book is my absolute favorite book ever. 
 Feyre was BRILLIANT in ACOMAF. And that's saying a lot, because she was AMAZING in ACOTAR. But it wasn't possible for her to reach her full potential as a human in the Spring Court. No, Feyre as an immortal Faerie in the Night Court was.. Destined. Fated. Meant to be. I was debating going back and reading ACOTAR again because I feel like I'd see it SO differently, but then I thought.. How could I get through it? I loved it and it'll always be a favorite, but... Re-reading ACOTAR would mean having to see Feyre in the Spring Court again. It would mean seeing her human again, vulnerable and with Tamlin... *Vomits* 
 Okay, yeah, I loved Tamlin in ACOTAR. But that's because he was basically all we knew, except for the few times Rhys showed up. But now that I've seen Feyre with Rhys, I know she was never meant to be with Tamlin. He was too possessive, too dominating. He held her back, refused to let her spread her wings and fly (see what I did there?). And his behavior in ACOMAF is unforgivable, especially his betrayal at the end. I wanted to KILL him. I wanted to smack him so hard, his head would spin. He was so possessive of Feyre, so sure she belonged to him, that he refused to believe she was better off without him. God forbid someone be happy away from him. It was a completely foreign concept to him. He never treated Feyre like an equal. He never even treated her like a person; rather, he treated her like a possession. 
 Feyre was so broken in the beginning, so lost and withering away.. At first, when Rhys brought her to the Night Court, I wasn't sure how to feel. I loved his wickedness, but I was weary of him, of whether or not I should trust him. But as time passed, I shipped him and Feyre so hard, it can't even be described in words. HE HELD HER HAIR BACK WHILE SHE VOMITED! TAMLIN DIDN'T EVEN WAKE UP - OR PRETENDED HE WASN'T AWAKE, AT LEAST. LIKE... THE FEARSOME HIGH LORD OF THE NIGHT COURT HELD FEYRE'S HAIR BACK WHILE SHE VOMITED FROM HER NIGHTMARES. He had my heart from that moment on. 
 Feyre and Rhys together were dynamite. The sexual tension, the heat, the lust and the intensity between them was unbelievable. How could I EVER have shipped her with Tamlin the baby jerk? They were partners, equals, mates (!!!!!), bonded so deeply, even the King of Hybern couldn't break their bond. They were snarky and sarcastic with each other, but the love and attraction always thawed the bite of that snarkiness. Their banter was banter for the ages! Rhys treated Feyre like an equal, like her opinions and feelings matter. He trained her so she could protect herself. He gave her space when she needed it and stepped in when she didn't realize she needed that contact and support. He helped heal her heart in subtle ways, and she didn't even realize. Even letting her go with him on important court business... it's more than Tamlin let her do. Tamlin coddled her, told her it was too dangerous. But Rhys let her decide on her own what she could and couldn't handle. That alone made him the better man. 
 Also, can I just say how hard I laughed every time Feyre called Rhys an insufferable bastard. It was so fitting! 
 Feyre's character development in this was so wonderful and perfect and it felt so right. She was so strong and so brave. I loved her training and exploring her powers and her full potential. I loved that Rhys let her do that, let her grow and do what she needed to do to heal. I can say with absolute certainty that Rhys and Feyre are my absolute favorite Book Ship ever. They are my Bookish OTP. They are relationship goals. And Rhys making Feyre High Lady of the Night Court? icing on the cake. 
 Mor, Cassian, Azriel and Amren were squad goals. They were amazing. I loved the friendship between Mor and Feyre. I loved that, despite Rhy being her High Lord, Mor was still her own person, who didn't bow down to his intimidation (unlike that lap dog Lucien, but we'll get to that soon). When Feyre needed space and needed to get away, Mor helped her, without hesitation. YA needs more epic female friendships, with women supporting women. Cassian was another favorite of mine. He was so fierece and loyal to Rhys. And he protected Feyre when it was necessary, and without hesitation. He was also hilarious and snarky. I loved the direction he and Nesta were going in... Interested to see what her forced transformation will mean for them. 
 Azriel scared me a bit, but his steadfast loyalty was incredible. I was so terrified for him near the end.. for Cassian, as well. I didn't trust Azriel at all in the beginning and I'm not totally sure why. Maybe because I wasn't yet sure if anyone from the Night Court could be trusted. And if Azriel scared me a bit, Amren completely terrified me. But I was fascinated by her and her story. I can't wait to learn more about her and her past. 
 Finally, Lucien... Dude, what a pathetic welp. I used to like Lucien. But he was just a condescending prick in ACOMAF. He was Tamlin's lap dog and he barely fought for Feyre, even when he saw what Tamlin's iron fist was doing to her. He makes me sick, honestly. But it's terrifying that, at the end, he could see right through Feyre's tricks and lies. I wonder what that will mean for book three... But also, his love for Elain... The fact that they ended up being mates... ??!?!?!??! I don't even know what to think! 
 Sarah J. Maas did some incredible things with this book. I think this sums it up pretty well: 
 All of these are 100% true and 100% important. But think about it - "The first guy a girl meets is not her soulmate." This was not a love triangle. In ACOTAR, it seemed as though there would be a love triangle between Feyre, Tamlin and Lucien... Then maybe a love triangle with Feyre, Tamlin and Rhys. But Sarah J. Maas debunked all of that when she turned Feyre so permanently away from Tamlin - and for epic, sound reasons. How many authors have ever done that? I can't think of any off the top of my head. And the realistic depiction of anxiety, depression and PTSD? Not to mention the fact that she depicted a male recovering from sexual assault...? Like, HOW AMAZING IS SARAH J. MAAS FOR DOING THINGS RARELY DONE? Seriously, though! 
 AND THAT ENDING OMFG I CAN'T WITH THAT ENDING, I AM BROKEN AND I DON'T KNOW HOW TO PROCESS WHAT HAPPENED AND WTF?!?!?!?!? No, seriously, I can't even begin to TRY to process what happened. That ending has left me so conflicted and broken and damn excited for the third book, to see Feyre take Tamlin down from within his own court. It's going to suck, though, because it means Rhys and Feyre will be separated and who knows for how long? But I'm guessing, in true Sarah J. Maas fashion, their reunion will be filled with passion, lust and fireworks. 
 Wow... This turned into an epic essay, instead of a review. But I can't even begin to tell you guys how much I loved this book. It was just such utter perfection, I can't even begin to wrap my head around the level of perfection. I wasn't kidding when I said this book hangover will likely last until the third book comes out! It was so amazing, so perfect, so RIGHT. I enjoyed this book 1000x more than book one. I'm anxious to see what the consequences of the ending will be. I need book three now, but I'm also terrified of it and what it will bring. 
 Overall, if you couldn't tell from my super fangirly essay review, I loved A Court of Mist and Fury beyond words!! ALL THE STARS! ALL THE HEARTS!! ALL THE FEELS!!! SO BROKEN!!!! Seriously, if this isn't on your TBR, it NEEDS TO BE! If I could give this book ten million billion x infinity stars, I would! I know I've said it, but I CANNOT wait for book three - which actually has a title now: A Court of Wings and Ruin, ACOWAR for short! That alone - the fact that it has the word WAR in its abbreviation - should be proof in itself that all hell is about to break lose! 
 You can also find more from me on my blog: Pandora's Books

5 Stars 
 - I loved all of it but the first 200 pages were something else. The way issues like domestic abuse and PTSD are handled is incredible - probably better than in a lot of contemporary novels - and this is fantasy... 
 - I liked Feyre in the first book even though I got why people found her naivety annoying, but I unashamedly loved her in this one. She's learnt her own self worth and refuses to be kept in the dark, manipulated, etc. She loves Rhys but she calls him out on his shit when he's being over-protective, or makes a mistake. She also admits when she makes a mistake. The best thing about Feyre though is that she always thinks of other women as friends. At one point she gets jealous of another woman because Rhys is flirting with her, but she immediately acknowledges that this is not the other woman's fault. And I love how much she values her friendships with other women like Mor and Amren. The way she wants to bond with Ianthe at the beginning because she has been deprived of female friendship all her life is incredibly sweet and telling. 
 - The banter between Rhys and Feyre is hilarious. Also the fact they value each other so much as friends as well as lovers is wonderful. Their relationship is very different to Feyre's relationship with Tamlin. 
 - The sex scenes were OTT but kind of hilariously so. Also, to be expected. This series is NA, not YA. 
 - I love Rhys' squad. Especially Amren. 
 - The world-building in this was amazing. 
 - Even though this is a super-long book I can't believe it took me a month to read.
Wow, wow, wow! Just wow. So good.

Excited to see how Sarah finishes this trilogy. The only drawback (why not 5 stars) is that, while we had a teasing peek at Rhysand's true nature in "Thorns and Roses", we never got the opportunity to process some of the inconsistencies of Tamlin's. One moment Feyre adored him, the next she was a'runnin'! However, I can see why most readers feel that the author redeemed herself with this one. I thoroughly enjoyed the first book, but this one just blew it away!

reference_books.review_text:
This review is way better when you read it on my blog. It has pretty pictures and GIFs and lists of things I liked! 
 There's something so special about being part of a fandom... and Fangirl described it perfectly, without making it sound super lame. *shoves book in everyone's hands while making seal noises* 
 Rainbow Rowell has quickly become one of my favourite contemporary fiction authors. Like, she may have thrown Stephanie Perkins off the Adorable Romance Queen throne, which is pretty much impossible. 
 When I first got it in the mail, I was a little intimidated by the size of the book. 438 pages is pretty huge for a contemporary, so I had no idea what to expect of this. All I heard was that it was AMAZEBALLS. And it was. It so was. 
 Cath is easily one of my favourite main characters ever. She's funny, she's flawed, and she's a fangirl. She's one of the few characters I've encountered that deal with actual social anxiety that's realistically written, so I could really relate to her in every way. 
 I absolutely loved reading parts of Simon Snow and Cath's fanfiction. It made me wish Simon Snow was real, and with that, Simon Snow fanfiction. If it was, I would be Magicath's biggest fan. 
 I think we all know that Simon Snow is totally based on Harry Potter and it made me feel so nostalgic for the time when there were still books and movies coming out, the fandom was active, and Wizard Rock was a thing. 
 Anyway, Fangirl is definitely more fun if you have read the Harry Potter series and are part of the fandom, but even if you haven't, it's GREAT. (noV")

reference_books.title: What I Didn't Say
reference_books.review_text:
When I first picked up What I Didn't Say, I expected a heavy read, which it really wasn't. It's about heavy subjects but it isn't exactly depressing. I liked the book, if you just forget about the medical inaccuracy of the accident and the predictability of the story. Other than that, it's a great contemporary. 
 The story is told from Jake's point of view, a teenage boy who, after a terrible car accident, loses his ability to speak. From then on, he has to rely on notebooks and sign language to communicate with others. It feels like the worst thing that has ever happened to him, but when he starts talking more to Samantha Shay, the girl he has been crushing on for years, he realises that being mute is not the end of the world, he just needs to adapt, and find a way to live with it. It was truly inspiring to see how the both of them still had hope, even after all that's happened to them. 
 Jake's story is heart-wrenching. I can't even imagine how terrible it must feel to go through the things the characters in this book do. Even though they were going through really hard times and were experiencing the worst of things, they stayed strong, they stayed alive. This book has a really great message to it, that helping people will not only make them (feel) better, but yourself too. 
 It was beautiful to be able to go on this journey to recovery with both Jake and Sam, and see how much they loved and helped and needed each other. The romance was absolutely amazing. Jake and Sam seem perfect for each other. They can see each other's flaws, but still love the other. 
 Full review with videos, quotes, and other stuff can be found on my blog!

reference_books.title: The Reason I Jump: The Inner Voice of a Thirteen-Year-Old Boy with Autism
reference_books.review_text:
(Review by an actually autistic person.) 
 Oh, dear. I knew that when I started reading about autism, I was going to eventually find something horrific. I just wasn't expecting it to be this one. 
 This book is very negative about autism. And no, I'm not one of those autistic people who overly romanticizes autism. It's not that black & white for me. Autism makes my life very difficult and I'm often anxious & depressed because of it, but it also makes me who I am and I wouldn't want to be cured of all that autism is. (Just the negative parts, but I feel like that would be even more impossible.) 
 My autism comes with some awesome qualities like attention to detail and an unique perspective and special interests and hyperfocus and a great connection with animals. Also, like Naoki Higashida says in his book, "For us, you see, having autism is normal -- so we can't know for sure what your 'normal' is even like." 
 There are so many good questions in this book and I felt like none of them were answered in a way that would help neurotypicals understand us better. There's a lot of "people with autism do this but I don't know why". 
 This book is filled to the brim with generalizations. It would make for repetitive writing to always have to write 'some/most autistic people' all the time, but I feel like this is the other end of it. It should have been a mix, just like with the use of 'person first language'. Many autistic people prefer to be talked about as 'an autistic person', rather than 'a person with autism', because the latter makes it sound like a disease that needs curing, among many other valid reasons. Of course, there are some autistic people who prefer 'person with autism', but it's not the majority, as far as I know. Still, it's always best to always ask the person in question what they prefer. 
 There is a lot of 'we' and 'us autistic kids/people' rather than 'I', and that annoys me. I think some neurotypicals reading this might forget that Naoki cannot possibly speak for all autistic people. 
 On page 148, he explains that neurotypicals often think autistics 'won't be able to understand the plan for the day just by listening', and he says that us autistics will eventually get better at it. Then he says that 'being shown photos of places we're going to visit on an upcoming school trip, for example, can spoil our fun', in such a generalized way... And like, if my mom had read this and stopped helping me prepare for new situations, I would've had so many more meltdowns. 
 I hate to be the one to have to say, '#NotAllAutistics' but hey, someone's gotta do it. 
 The translation felt awkward, but maybe that's just the way Japanese to English translations end up. It felt very similar to the English translations of Marie Kondo's books. 
 And maybe they translated it word-for-word to stay true to Naoki's thoughts, but I felt like it could've been edited better. On page 149, he writes: "One of the biggest misunderstandings you have about us is your belief that our feelings aren't as subtle and complex as yours." Again, such a generalization. It would have been better to explain that autistic people not feeling as deeply is an autism stereotype. Just that changes the entire feeling of the sentence. 
 Most of the writing is very simple and straight-forward, as you can expect when the author is writing a book using an Alphabet Grid (the letters of the alphabet + numbers on a piece of paper that Naoki points to). And those simple parts sound very realistic coming from the mind of a 13-year-old, autistic or not. But then there are these weirdly poetic parts that don't feel like they were written by the same person. Almost like David Mitchell wrote them... But that's a theory for a different day. 
 This is what David Mitchell said about the translation process: "KA Yoshida did the heavy lifting from the Japanese into English, and in a sense I provided the stylistic icing on the cake. But I also needed to respect the fact that it was a 13-year-old boy writing, not a 44-year-old novelist, so it couldn't sound as if it was written for the New Yorker." 
 The absolute worst part was page 151, where Naoki Higashida (or is it David Mitchell?...) answers the question, "What are your thoughts on autism itself?" 
 "I think that people with autism are born outside the regime of civilization. Sure, this is just my own made-up theory, but I think that, as a result of all the killings in the world and selfish planet-wrecking that humanity has committed, a deep sense of crisis exists. 
 Autism has somehow arisen out of this. Although people with autism look like other people physically, we are in fact very different in many ways. We are more like travellers from the distant, distant past. And if, by our being here, we could help the people of the world remember what truly matters for the Earth, that would give us a quiet pleasure." 
 Sorry, but I call bullshit. Autistic people aren't here to teach neurotypicals anything. This is romanticization and I don't like it. Also, can confirm that autistic people are not in fact time travellers. 
 If you want to learn about autism, you're not going to learn much from this book. Instead, Find An Autistic Person Near You! That's always the best way to learn. And if you don't know any, there are plenty of autistic people from all over the spectrum who would love to help you understand. Me included. 
 All my other recommendations are about autism in women specifically, so if you're interested in that, pick up Rudy Simone's Aspergirls: Empowering Females with Asperger Syndrome or Dominique Dumortier's From Another Planet: Autism from Within. 
 And if you want even more reasons why this book is problematic, here's a good article: No, autistic children are not the spiritual saviours of mankind.

 I really liked Fracture! I liked how the whole accident didn't just drag on all the way through the book: when she got out of the hospital, other things were going on right away. I was reading this while travelling through the airport and I hated when I had to put it down because there were security checks or we had to walk to the gate and everything. 
 The characters were pretty good. I loved Delaney and Decker, and I wasn't really sure about Troy--he was just always kind of mysterious to me, and not in a good way. Delaney was very easy to relate to. Even though she went through a lot of things I haven't been through, I sympathised with her. 
 The pacing was excellent. Things weren't revealed too soon but not too late either. 
 I absolutely love the cover art. It's the thing that made me buy it in the store. (I know, I shouldn't judge books by their covers or whatever, but come on. It's gorgeous.) 
 Fracture is a emotional, suspenseful, and fast-paced debut novel that I highly recommend for people who like contemporary with a paranormal twist.

book_a.title: 172 Hours on the Moon
book_a.user_review:
Read my full review on Lauren Reads YA (with GIFs and pretty book photography!) 
 Imagine if a horror book and a science fiction book made a book baby... 172 Hours on the Moon is that baby. 
 All I knew about this book before going in was that it was creepy, and I'm so glad I didn't know any more. That made the twists even more exciting! The first half of the book I was thinking of all kinds of crazy (conspiracy) theories, and once you find out what the twist is, you're like, "WHAT?!" 
 The only thing that made me give this 4.5 instead of 5 is the blandness of the characters. The three main characters were all very stereotypical, and I felt myself caring more for the secondary characters. And God, Mia was annoying in the beginning! Girl, your band is never going to get anywhere... Also, stop acting like you're too cool for space. *hand emoji* 
 This book gets ALL THE EXTRA POINTS because it made me SO EXCITED ABOUT SPACE. Even if there's something terrifying in space (on the moon, to be specific). Just... SPACE!!! 
 After finishing it late in the evening, I spent the rest of the night reading about the Apollo 11 conspiracies and learning about how to do your business in space and basically watched everything available on SciShow Space. I think the fact that this book made me excited about space is so important, and everyone with even a slight interest in science should check this out. 
 I was so creeped out by the whole thing and the ending was absolutely MIND-BLOWING. I've read a few books since then and still find myself thinking about this one pretty regularly. I highly recommend 172 Hours on the Moon. What a page-turner!

sample_reviews.review_text:
This did not frighten or surprise me half as much as I had expected. Maybe that was my mistake. 
 172 Hours on the Moon follows the story of three incredibly annoying teenagers who win the lottery and get to go to the moon along with five austronauts. Once on the moon, mayhem ensues. 
 The thing is, there was so much mystery from the start, and it all amounted to nothing, or at least nothing worth reading. It wasn't as if the secrets they were keeping from the oblivious teenagers made much impact on what was happening. The secrets had no value once they were revealed because everything was already happening. I didn't like that. I also didn't care much for the characters since they didn't have much of a personality. And all of that added to my lack of sympathy for any of them. So what if these characters were scared to death on the moon? Do I care? Not really. 
 However, I was entertained at first. It was a quick read that at times even creeped me out a little bit. I do think this book would make a better movie. I would love to see that.

Well. I'm terrified now. Holy crap. I enjoyed this book, but I feel like the ending kind of went nowhere and the translation was a little odd; hence why I only gave it 2 out of 5 stars. HOWEVER, I definitely still recommend that you check it out. It was unlike anything I've ever read.
I don't understand the hype. It was too far fetched. Characters were annoying. The premise was so unbelievably unrealistic it bothered me the entire time. Didn't like this book at all.
What the everloving fuck just happened :v

Let me start off by saying that the premise of this book was really awesome. However, I don't think it lived up to its full potential. I didn't enjoy how slow paced the first two-thirds of the book was. I just kept sitting around waiting for something interesting to happen. The story also kept skipping around which caused a lot of confusion for me. I didn't like the lack of detail when it came to certain things like the training the characters had to do before going to the moon. They showed one "class" they had to attend (with hardly any detail) and then before you know it, they're boarding the rocket. Overall, the pacing was just really, really strange. Also, the writing wasn't that great. I'm not sure if that is because it was translated from Norwegian or what. 
 The last 1/3 or so is what saved the book for me. This is when the genre of horror truly comes in. I understand now why other people described this book as being scary. My heart was pounding so loud, especially for the last 50 pages or so, that I thought it was going to come right out of my chest. Just the things they were describing and the possibility that they could exist in real life is so terrifying to me. I'm shocked I didn't have nightmares. 
 Overall, this book wasn't amazing but it wasn't awful either. It had a great idea that was unfortunately poorly executed. I don't necessarily regret reading it, but it's not a book that I'm going to go around recommending to other people.

All a book has to promise me is space and aliens and I'll be picking it up. Unfortunately that's all this book offered me. I don't even understand, were those some sort of aliens? 
 Anyhow, the writing and story was just all over the place. I wasn't confused by the story (well for the most part). I felt like I was being messed with. Conversations between characters were so random(I know the book was first published in Norwegian, so maybe it got lost in translation? But I find it hard to believe it got that messed up by translation), a ton of stuff with the plot was random and then I didn't even get to be scared by some awesome aliens. 
 The book was definitely dark and had the creepy factor. But what made it dark is that Harstad went in thinking I'm just going to kill everyone off in space(on the moon!) and then give a massively nonsensical ending. WTF ending? WTF? 
 I picked this book up because a few reviewers I follow and love had just finished reading it and gave it 5*, saying "it's intense, dark, creepy and mind blowing." Yea, I don't know what book they read, but it must have had a different story under the cover. Oh, there's a positive; the cover makes sense with the story. And I like it (which is about only 1 of 2 things I liked).

With a claustrophobic environment and an unidentifiable dark presence, 172 Hours had all the pieces. They just never fell into place. 
 Our main characters Mia, Antoine, and Midori are the most stereotypical, unlikable, fictional teens you will ever have the displeasure of reading about. They constantly complain about how much they hate their parents and how hard their lives are (and Antoine's a stalker...?) The reader never develops any attachment whatsoever to the main characters so it's hard to care when they start getting killed off in space. 
 Midori, who is Japanese, doesn't have the best representation in the book. (Though I'm not Japanese, the way her character was portrayed felt off to me). 
 She has some brilliant lines like: 
 "'Well, then I hope you guys have some Asian food up here, too, and not just a pile of hamburgers.'" 
 Which is responded to with: "'I doubt you'll find any sushi in there, if that's what you mean, but we may be able to dig up some noodles.'" 
 ... am I the only one who feels like that's weird? ... no... just me... okay.... 
 Her sole purpose in the book is to provide the reader with Japanese urban legends (which did not add anything to the story if you were wondering). 
 There's A TON of not so discreet foreshadowing throughout the book. The characters are sometimes just like "Wow we could die up on the moon I don't know why I'm thinking of that now but I am you should be scared for me." Nothing creepy actually starts happening until after page 200. The first 200 pages (out of the 350 pages) are filled with nothing but pure teenage angst. 
 We also have, what may possibly be, the worst fictional romance ever. There's this weird insta-love thing between Antoine and Mia that pops up twice and adds nothing to the actual plot. 
 The ending of the novel was supposed to be creepy and plot-twisty but it was more strange and confusing than anything. 
 Ultimately, I gave this book two stars. I would have given it one star but I think the concept of the book is unique. Everything was there and the book could have been fantastic; It just fell flat for me. (Really, really flat).

Disappointed, to say the very least. Not only disappointed, but I'm also really angry with this book because almost nothing happens in the whole book, nothing! Although it is a very fast read this was one of the least exciting books I've read in my life, I may be speaking for the work of a translator but I wasn't such a big fan of the writing and for the exception of a few chapters, I didn't think this was a creepy novel at all. 
 I just couldn't get into the author's idea of a horror novel, the only 'scarier' parts were towards the end but still... everything felt so juvenile and the characters were so annoying. The romance (why there even was a romantic relationship in a horror novel about space travel?) was unnecessary and ridiculous. 
 So much wasted potential because the premise is great. I thought about not finishing this book a couple of times but decided to stick with it and actually, I quite liked the ending but it really was one of the rare parts I liked. Sadly, I'm just so glad to be done with it.

What an interesting horror story - and one with very little chance of a sequel (I hope!). 
 NASA, for various reasons, has decided to go back to the moon but they need an excuse and a way to gin up public interest. The excuse is a search for a mineral that would give America the edge in nanotechnology, the public interest angle is that three teens (between the ages of 14-18, of a certain height, in good physical and psychological health) will be chosen as passengers. In reality they're gong back to activate DARLAH 2, a Top Secret lunar base set up in the 1970s. 
 Mia only wants to play in her punk band, possibly cut an album and go on tour before moving to an artists loft with her band mates; her parents, rather that recognizing that she's nearly an adult treat her the same as they treat her 6-year-old brother and cannot believe she isn't eager to be one of the teens, so they enter her into the contest. Midori is a disaffected Japanese teen who only fits in when she's at Harajuku, spending all her money on items for her outlandish costumes; entering the contest is a way for her to escape and gain fame to spur her move to New York. Antoine has just been dumped by his girlfriend, stalking her by using the telescopes on the Eiffel Tower to peer into her bedroom; the contest is the perfect way for him to change his life (and possibly get her back). 
 The three join the NASA trained astronauts on the trip, which goes very, very wrong indeed. There's a reason why the moon trips stopped, but the people who were involved were sworn to silence or - like Oleg Himmelfarb - suffering from Alzheimers. Or dead. Mr. Himmelfarb, sitting in his nursing home, has flashes of memories but can't do anything about them. 
 There are some logic issues with this book (for example, wouldn't NASA have tested the three, or had a cadre of teens from which to ultimately choose, like some reality show?) but the subtle horror will render them unimportant. This is horror like that in Let Me In, with a higher psychological component than most American writers allow for. 
 ARC provided by publisher.

"A chilling, shivers-down-the-spine thriller...a high-quality piece of meticulously researched and realistic sci-fi/horror." 
 If only. 
 The storyline plodded along laboriously, at first detailing each of their lives, then moving onto the moon where every inch of it were covered in predictability. The characters were stock (rebels with good intentions, over-concerned parents with whom they clash repeatedly with) and I disliked each of them from the start. 
 Boring. 
 I wasn't scary, well thought out or meticulously researched (more like googled). I can't fathom why this got lots of positive reviews. 
 Oh and don't get me started on the ending. It's so bad I want to tell you what happens so you won't have to read it for yourselves. I won't though.

I adore Oliver's writing style and extra points because Hana was awesome but seriously I felt like Oliver must have said "I'm tired of this series so I'm just going to write a bunch of pretty fluff with no conclusion because I can't be bothered to figure out an ending."

I knew this crap was coming when I finished book two but that was in a league of its own Second nothing actually happens on Lena's side of the story. reference_books.title: The Casual Vacancy
reference_books.review_text:
JK needs a little work on her Second/Third POV presentation. I found it distracting being in the middle of a POV then having another POV butt in unexpectedly. I dunno if that's a normal writing style, but I didn't much care for it. 
 As a HUGE Harry Potter fan, I found it odd to be reading about Sex, Incest, Rape, Drugs and all those dark scenarios I associate with PNR. I did find it intriguing and frustrating which for me is a good thing. 
 I'm still a bit lost about what the whole point of the story was. It seemed as though JK wanted to cram in as much "Scandalous" storyline as she possibly could. The council and the election kind of passed without so much as a whimper. The election was MEH. In other words BORING and POINTLESS. 
 The sex scenes were tame and highlighted JK's debut into that kind of genre. It came of as a YA author TRYING very hard to be sexy. I know it's not a HUGE part of the story, just thought 'd mention it.

reference_books.title: Life After Life
reference_books.review_text:
So far I am struggling to read this one. The format is a new one for me and I think it would be better to separate each POV as they seem to intersect and confuse me. It would be nice to identify the narrator as well as sometimes the person just babbles on with no introduction. 
 I like the concept though and will forge on to see where this goes. It almost seems as though Ursula is a doll, yet she is human. I don't like the blase attitude the mother has, nor the lack of interest or discipline. She almost seems cruel locking her kids up and such to toughen em up. My ass. 
 Be interesting to see how Maurice turns out at boarding school. As he seems like a total handful. Likewise Ursula, why on earth did she murder that bloke! Or was she the one murdered? So I am interested in how her lives shape her over the years to lead her to that point in her life. 
 I still don't understand Maurice and his "I don't give a fuck" attitude. To his family, to his wife and kids. Is he copying his mother's "Toughen up" stick? I absolutely HATED Howie and what he did, so I'm glad Ursula learned, and came back stronger. I loath that her mother scorned even hated her for what happened with Howie. Did she know the truth though? Ooh, I bet it's Howie that raped and killed them little girls! 
 The illegal abortion clinic, what a fucking pack of animals! And yeah, I am mad at Isobel for taking her there. Not because it was an abortion, but because it should have been done at a proper clinic. It's a hard thing for a woman to go through, little own a child, a child that was raped at that. 
 The "Teacher" and his damn blind folds!!! Honestly, how fucking ignorant can one be. It doesn't feel right, it doesn't sound right, so tell him NO. Then tell anyone and everyone who'll listen about the fucking creep. What is with all these damn filthy old men pawing at her through the novel anyway. I understand she is just a child or VERY young, but it does grind my gears about how Ignorant/Innocent she is. Did the mother teach her nothing about Rape/Sex/Child birth? Sister? Aunt? School? Brother? Friend? even a damn book! Grr 
 One thing I hate more than a rapist is a violent person, and a person who lies. Be you man or woman. Derek I will never understand. Like Ursula said, "Why marry her?" why the fuck go to all that trouble and make yourself and another person miserable. Why potentially drag children into such a poisonous situation? It boggles the mind, it truly does. Glad she remedied the situation and left. Still don't know how Derek found her. Glad Teddy smashed the prick, hopefully he killed the bugger. 
 I like Pamela, such a awesome sibling. It is nice seeing her lead a happy life filled with laughter and children. Oh, and a good man. Isobel I like, but she's so darn reckless. Maybe broken? 
 YES! So she smashed Howie each time he got fresh with her, and eventually told Millie about him. Oh, and it was a broken veteran that was interfering with the little girls. Glad Ursula managed to save Nancy from him each time. 
 What happened to Ursala's mom and dad? They seemed like such a beautiful, loving couple but ended up so distant. Can I say how pissed I am the mom offed herself over Teddy. Nothing wrong with favorites, but damn, way to make the others feel insignificant! Jimmy to, what happened to his friendly, lovely manner? 
 So Ursula had contact with Hitler and his family is that right? Kill the bastard and stop the damn war going on so long! She had a "Reincarnation" feeling, so kill him, get killed, and ta dah. Would it work? 
 Speaking of war . . NEVER read a war time novel so it's damn tragic reading. I was never good at time travel novels, so I'm still struggling with that, but I'm following a lot better as I go. I can't stand all the random "Foreign Language" dropped through the novel like a German bomb. It's unnecessary, and annoying. 
 I don't understand all the bickering that went on near the end. What was that about? So Ursula killed Hitler (God how many wish we actually could?) yet it seemed Teddy was still in a war? flying anyway and still went down BUT survived. So, did her killing Hitler change anything? 
 Was it reincarnation then and not just time travel? She seemed to be in different bodies during the same events. I still found it confusing to be laying in a bombed out puddle with Ursula, then her rambling on about past shit. It did my head in. 
 Over all, I thoroughly enjoyed it. Mentioned my issues so I wont again. Some high's and lows, and a lot of confusing time travel and back stories that quite frankly didn't need to be mentioned for about the fifth time. Yet some horrible, beautiful, and intriguing stuff as well. World War 1-2 told in a way that is unique and interesting, yet can feel long. Read as a E-Book, but I may hunt down the paper back :) Well read Ms Atkinson.

Spoilers ahead, read at your own risk. 
 I picked up the first book in the trilogy because everyone was talking about it and I wanted to know what the fuzz was all about. I didn't put it down because once I start a book, I feel the need to finish it, regardless of how repetitive, plotless, cliched, annoying and poorly written it is. I picked up the second book because I hate cliffhangers: I got more of the same. I picked up the third book because I said to myself: "hey, you've made it through the first two, might as well finish the story and see if SOMEHOW the author manages to redeem herself". She didn't. 
 I'll give it one star and a review though, because it is the one and only book that actually managed to not only annoy me, but also make violently angry. Every bad cliche in cheesy Latin-american telenovelas is there. The sappy ending with the kids and whatnot: why?? Why would you do that? You couldn't think of anything else?? Give me tragedy, God knows both characters are better off dead, anyway. I hated it and I hate myself for wasting my time reading this rubbish. It's not even entertaining, or fun, it's just a waste of time. 
 This is a brief summary of the whole trilogy: 
 * girl meets boy 
 * boy has serious pychological issues and can't have a relationship but somehow (!) just can't get enough of this girl 
 * girl wants boy, but doesn't, but does 
 * girl wants to have sex, but doesn't, but does 
 * they are together, then not, then get together again 
 * they have babies, buy a house and are happy ever after. 
 Everything else is filler and pointless and only offers different locations to have sex. There's no drama, no unexpected plot twists, no nothing. Like... really???? That's it??? Three books to tell a story that shouldn't take more than 10 lines?? 
 And the sex... Oh, man... Being an erotica book of sorts, you would at least expect a decently written sex scene. Well, guess again. All of the scenes are not only badly written, they're all the same (with MINOR changes here and there). The S&M is poorly portrayed (obviously the author doesn't know enough of this practice), looks like something only a depraved and insane person would do (which is not), does not sound healthy, fun or sexy (which SHOULD be) and it's just boring. Sex. Boring. I can't believe I'm putting those two words together. And yet, it got an overall rating of 3.92??? I weep for mankind... 
 If there's anyone out there, reading this rant: Please, don't waste your time on this crap, don't do what I did. There are millions of books out there, and I'd bet the shittiest one of them is still better and more entertaining than this shit.

Stupidest fucking thing I've ever read. There's literature, bad literature, 50 feet of shit, and then this book. Everything about it is horrendous: the writing, the "plot", the pacing, the characters. I mean, the first two books were terrible in their own right, but the "relationship" between Ana and Christian in this book goes to a whole new level of unhealthy and pathetic. 
 And James has absolutely no concept how to build a plot. Things happen without any precedent and then an out-of-nowhere infodump explains it away between the crappily written gratuitous sex scenes. And the epilogue is even more nauseating than the Harry Potter one, and that's saying something. 
 I know they say people have a right to enjoy what they want but I have the right to judge anyone who actually likes this garbage.

Well... it's time for the final battle... and it takes a whole book to get there... and yeah, we know how it ends, but it's fun getting there. 
 With the death of Octavius Sextus, the princepts fury, Alera, trains and counsels Tavi - mostly when they are on the ship returning to Alera. She has existed since the beginning, and has a verylong term view on things - she came to consciousness/atavar status with the first First Lord of Alera - and some stones used in a mural at the castle... and with the destruction of the castle/city by Sextus, Alera's avatar is aging, to be absorbed into the underlying spiritual plain... she teaches and advises, but cannot do harm to any... 
 Isana and Auraris are captured by the Vord Queen - and while Auraris is encased in her 'gel', he is fed and not harmed - to control Isana. And Isana, Invidia, and the queen are making a kind of dysfunctional family unit (the queen calls Isana 'grandmother') - and we see that the queen, having a drop of Tavi & Kitai's blood, is abnormal - she seeks bonds - and seems to get closest to a human bond with Invidia... hmmmm... and at the end, when the remaining High Lords make their attack on the queen and fail - Isana & Auraris step up to rescue, heal, save them when the queen leaves to confront Tavi. 
 Lord Aquitaine, as Sextus' adopted son, steps into temporary First Lord status - fully planning to knock out Tavi through fair or foul means if he returns. But he does an admirable job of utilizing alera's resources - soldiers, people, lands, etc. in preparation against the Vord... an excellent tactitian, but not innovative. hmmmm... and he does so selflessly... as they are falling back, towards the end.. Ehren (whom Sextus recommended to Aquitaine as head spy, but whom he deputized to remove Aquitaine in favor of Tavi) by suggestion sets up Aquitaine to confront Invidia, leading to further injury to Invidia and ultimately to Aquitaine's death (she slashed him in the gut, and they could only extend his life, but not cure him). 
 and as ____ is falling, Amara & Bernard tell Aquitaine that Bernard has spent the last years preparing the Calderon Valley to defend against the Vord, since no one would take their reports seriously, so they retreat again. And Bernard has some innovative defenses - many based on Tavi's suggestions - including a non-fury craft catapult (based on Tavi's & _____ archeological dig of Roman sites) but where they flung fury crafted fire balls. But they are being pushed back are at their last wall... 
 And once landed, Tavi et all (including the Canim) need to get to Calderon quickly - Tavi is getting intel from Alera - and Kitai negotiates with the Icemen to work with them to ice over the causeway, and Tavi converts the ice ships to large sleds, to carry them to Calderon in a fraction of the time. Along the way, Nasag's Sha (canim cursor) and Fidelius conspire to get rid of one of the magicians who is making trouble for Nasag and Varg via earthcrafting - where they 'tunnel' underneath, get into his room, take him out of a inside locked room, and leave him in an underneath tunnel to die... and it worked, at least in the short term. 
 and Kitai tells Tavi that he's been doing her wrong - not courting her properly, not treating her like a lady... so she separates from him (at least the sharing of his room/bed)... so Tavi woos her (when he can make the time) and before they face the vord queen, they have a night together, and when they awake in the morning, he is aware of 2 cuddled next to him - Kitai and the fetus she is carrying. and then we have a nice conversation where Tavi to be true to self must protect Kitai, and Kitai to be true to herself must fight alongside him... and they both accept this - and Tavi allows her to be with him in the 1st confrontation, but leaves her when she is injured - but she joins him as soon as possible - and he needs her (she shares in his fury crafting abilities) - and he draws the queen to a crazy, fury mountain - and when she is trying to control the mountain, Tavi via Alera's advice, cuts their connection - and they end up in his father's tomb, and the queen is injured, and she tells him she is defective, not a typical vord queen, and he gently reassures her - and kills her quickly... and the vord are 'headless', killing each other... hmmm... victory! 
 and the story ends with Ehern's daily report of kingdom business, plans that include lands portioned to the Marat & Canim, treaties with them as well as the IceMen, a university that invites all to attend, not just the patroned/fury crafting citizens, a new series of causeways that run as a wagon wheel, some steadholts who were keeping their vord, whom the queen had instructed to protect and assist them, the knowledge that the Vord in Cananea would someday attack and they needed to be prepared - using the enemy of my enemy is my friend to forge those treaties, a 2week old baby who is included in their wedding ceremony, Fidelias as Tavi's valet & advisor, Amara's pregnacy, as her reproductive system was healed when given the ____ of life in the queen's den - and Tavi & Kitai's wedding.. ahhhh

 This is the final book in the Codex Alera series and for me this book, as well as the series as a whole, delivered. The Characters are fun, brave, and smart with a crazy magic world to run around in. 
 A minor point of dissapointment for me (but it still earns 5 stars):

Let us talk about Sweet Peril or as it should have been titled "I Can't Keep A Secret aka Horrible Relationships Decisions aka How to Get a Bad Boyfriend" 
 The two main themes in this book are a) No one except Belial understands the concept of a secret and b) Anna doesn't understand the concept of a non-abusive relationship. 
 On relationships 
 As a dude I don't sign up to care about abusive relationships. It's my man privilege and I acknowledge that. For us, as long as we're not abusive, most of the time we're good with that. That's why it takes a concerted effort for dudes to care. Most of us make the effort but it's not something I normally look out for when I'm reading YA fiction. But I have sisters and ex-girlfriends and girls who are friends and nieces and little cousins. I'm surrounded by girls. And like with Television our girl, in this book, reminds me not a lick of any of them, to a point where it's off putting. 
 Anna is unhealthily obsessed with Kaidan. That in and of itself isn't much of an problem. I've been unhealthily obsessed with a girl before. She was likewise with me and hilarity ensues. The problem is that Kaidan is a bad dude and she has other options. Options that do everything Kaiaen doesn't, like express their affection for her, or make themselves available to her, or not lie to her. And still her response is 
 Watching [Kaidan] look me over, I flushed. Nobody else could make me hot like that from a single look. Nobody 
 Except yes they can. Kopano clearly makes her hot and she obsesses over it all the time they're together. He turns her on just as hot, AND he likes her, AND he tells her he likes her. This seems like a no brainer especially when the other option is doing everything in his power to make her hate him. The idea that of all the characters we would vote to kill Kopano makes me sad. 
 They've know each other for such a little amount of time and for most of that time he's been antagonistic towards her. It makes no sense that he should be so well regarded by her. He doesn't let down his guard for her. He doesn't let her in. Yet because he didn't curse around her she obsesses that it might have all been fake. 
 We'd had such precious little time together, and I didn't want to think that any of it had been fake. 
 On top of all that when an incident happens, and she kisses another boy, in fact the same African boy who gets her motor running Kopano . Kaidan gets insanely jealous. 
 He was beyond pissed, which made me angry in my own defense 
 You might be wondering why her defense matters until you find out that at this point in the story Kaidan has not only broken ties from her, but moved away to LA, to get away from her, and she kissed this boy Kopano one time in a heat of passion moment. (Not that he could possibly make her feel the way Kaidan does whatever that means) 
 [H]is face flushed from angry hardness to sad softness, and I realized that's exactly how he felt. Betrayed, Forgotten. Even though he'd been the one who'd left 
 In the face of such emotional manipulative accusation Anna's response is odd to say the best: 
 What could I say to make this right? 
 She hasn't done anything wrong? She kissed a boy when she was ACTUALLY single. Not like when Jay kissed a girl last book and he was "not official". Anna's been told many times that Kaidan is done with her. He doesn't talk to her, he changed his number. This apologetic line of thinking starts a huge unrespectable spiral where Anna is compelled/forced to apologize for her actions of kissing a single boy when she has been told repeatedly to her face and behind her back that Kaidan has no interest in her. That Kaidan has moved on with a new girl. I understand Kaidan being jealous. We all get jealous when our ex moves on, but being jealous and acting jealous are two different things. He has no right to act jealous and yet his response 
 Nothing I said could've pushed you into his arms if you didn't want to be there 
 How romantic. After the blow up, she dejectedly decides that since she's told the prophecy, and she had no other business (because [emotions]), that she will just go home. Whereupon Kaidan calls her stubborn. This to me is one of the most mystifying pieces of writing I've ever read. I have no idea what part of her wanting to go home is supposed to be stubborn and I understand (even if I vehemently disagree) with every other aspect of the fight. Kaidan and his BFF Nephilim Blake beg her to stay and she still says no, whereupon she now internally agrees, that she's being stubborn. It's not until he grabs her and mandhandles her to stillness that she relents. Acknowledging that he came at her with a fierceness that frightens and excites her because he's not in his right mind. This is the very opposite of what we're supposed to be telling girls. A guy that out of control isn't the guy you want to stay around, but hey who needs to make smart decisions it's only the risk of your life and eternal soul at stake. 
 Her defense when they do talk about it, starts with the suggestion: Emotions that I'd buried for so long rose inside of me, impassioning my words.. No. These are emotions that have been rolling on the surface of her mind for like a year now. Only Kopano has been able to get them quiet but hey he doesn't turn her own like Kaidan does with a look inspite of every look he gives her making her skin flushed. But even after finding out that her father orchestrated the separation with Kaidan, she's still apologizing. She still caves first when she's attacked by Kaidan who demands: "Show me your emotional color aura". Just no backbone whatsoever which would be fine if this was book 1 paragraph 1 but as I'll say later time is passing. Anna is acting the party girl, drinking partying, turning good people bad. She should be growing up. Instead she's still upset when she thinks people are being fake around her by not swearing 
 He's been such a punk, all heartbroken and shi-iiz." I rolled my eyes. "Not this again, Black" 
 "I'm tryin' to be good 
 This is a weird things to get so vehemently upset by. It's the closest thing to backbone she shows and it's at a point when people are respecting her. Even Silent black man Kope has more backbone when defending the kiss her shared with Anna. 
 Do not play victim [Kaidan] when you are partly to blame 
 This man is the new Jay. This book is seriously lacking some Jay but this guy acknowledges that Kaidan can't be mad when people follow his words. He's brilliant. No one else does this. No one. But just like in Twilight she will pick the abusive "I'm so emotional about you I can't control myself or those I harm in the process. Please stay away from me when I yell at you but don't even show a hint of attraction to anyone else" guy. 
 The main point of this book unfortunately is that Kaidan and Anna get together. I would spoiler that but it's such a minor spoiler and it'd would be obvious from the context of the rest of this section. Because that's one sloppy one sided relationship. Conversely to Kopano who is open with his feeling any time he has a chance, Kaidan refuses to acknowledge his feeling towards her. She says she loves him and his response after "emotionally shivering" is to ask her to spend the night. In real life this would be a hilariously bright red flag. She harps on the fact that he doesn't even need to say it and then the closest he comes is 
 "The thing is, I can't share you. I need you to be mine. Only mine. When I think of someone else touching you--" 
 Wherein he breaks off and refuses to even say the word boyfriend. Even with context that's a pretty scary thing to say. It comes off less romantic and more possessive. Why you would find this attractive is beyond me. Especially coming from someone for whom sex is such a big part of his life. This guy is a lust demon who specialized in having sex with women to get them to give in to lust. One might think his perspective towards sex and "touching" might be somewhat appropriately relaxed. Considering how much she has and will push him to have sex with other girls to keep his demonic father unknowing. The closest he ever gets in the book is when a group of Nephilim are forced to hide clinging in the water under a dock for hours sans Scuba gear (something I'm not sure would be physically possible but they're magically healing so we let that slide) when Kaiden: 
 At first I thought he was reaching for me, but then he slowly signed, I love you 
 Now as a minor point. I'm no sign language expert but I remember a few signs from elementary school. One of which being "I love you" because it's such a simple sign. You don't really sign anything. It's a hand shape. it looks like this 
 View post on imgur.com 
 . 
 It's really that simple you don't really do it "slowly". Now you might think that the whole "no touching" thing was a bit of romantic hyperbole but after staying in the water for hours and facing death from pneumonia Anna needs to get into dry clothes. And when someone else is helping to save her life by helping her out of her wet clothes in a manner so respectful you'd be forgiven for forgetting that they're about to die and maybe they should hurry up: 
 "I can't, [push my shorts all the way down" [...] under the circumstances the entire scenario of undressing was a necessity. Nothing more. 
 Kopano grabbed a blanket from the bed. "Here," he said, laying it across my midsection. "I will not look. Try again." He stared down at the floor next to me. 
 [...] 
 When they were at my knees [he] grabbed the bottoms and tugged down my calves, keeping his eyes averted. A growl of fury sounded from the doorway and my heart stopped. 
 "Get. Your. Bloody hands. Off her." 
 Sure why not get spitfire mad at a dude for saving your girlfriend's life while not looking at her. But of course Anna's take on this is apologetic for HER behaviour. 
 Had I been in my right mind, I would have told him to focus on Zania while I waited for Kaidan [...] to come down 
 Heaven forbid this girl needs open heart surgery. Woe to the doctor who dares to touch her chest. 
 View post on imgur.com 
 On Secrets: 
 The other main theme is that Anna is part of a prophecy that will bring down demonic rule on earth. This is fairly serious business so of course Anna uses every opportunity to tell everyone she can think of about the prophecy. You might think such a naive move might be punished by her being found out. Nope. just nope. 
 Upon hearing the prophecy: 
 "Oh, my gosh," I said. "I need to call Dad." 
 and then a few hours later 
 I was burning with the urge to call [Kaidan]...Because he needed to know about this. Like, now 
 But did he? did he really? at three in the morning really need to know about a prophecy that is going to be so complicated to pull off it's going to take months? Couldn't wait till say the afternoon? 
 When meeting a secret ally Zania for the first time 
 "It's harder for me [to deny myself] with drugs." 
 hmm like really? The Demonic overlords think her weakness is alcohol. She dedicated a significant amount of effort to convince them of that, and yet so easily the truth spills from her. What is recruiting Zania fails? What if she's overheard? What if Zania is captured or coerced? These are thoughts that don't occur to people who don't understand the concept of a secret. 
 Anna never being punished for making stupid decisions is such a repeating trope in this book alone that even when it's called out she fails to fall. \ 
 "Tell me one mistake you've ever made in your perfect little life," [Ginger] challenged..."Okay. For one, I fell in love with Kaidan and showed him my colors [...] When we went on that road trip last year [...] I wanted to ... be with him. You know. But he said no." 
 This was such an excellent choice of Truth or Date question because she's never made a mistake. In her ENTIRE life the only mistake she's ever made was saying yes to a guy and she didn't lose her virginity in a manner she finds inappropriate. He wasn't rough with her. Instead of living with the consequences (and I apologize if that comes across as victim blamey but I'm speaking to a very very specific circumstance here) the guy actually says no so she doesn't have to suffer any consequence. Her life is literally filled with secret sharing with no regard and she's never caught by it. 
 The two people who appear like they CAN keep a secret are Kopano and of course her father Belial. This man has a the most powerful demon as his errand boy passing messages in a way that's basically deus ex machina all over the place. Oh no you're in danger about to be found out. Azael to the rescue. What do we do about the Duke of lies who can is a human lie detector. No worries Belial already got her mother on the side. The man even arranged to hook his daughter up with a nice guy that she finds attractive by just putting them together and seeing if it happens. He's the real MVP. 
 I wondered how many other unknown allies we had, but he would never tell me. Need to know basis. 
 Oh would that such control and understanding was genetic. Maybe everyone wouldn't know that Anna is faking, Anna is weak to drugs, Anna is in love with Kaidan. Anna is a virgin. Anna is running the revolution. Heck it's so obvious even the demonic overlords suspect it. 
 You know..." Pharzuph began, almost hesitant, lowering his voice even further. "Rahab thinks the daughter of Belial is the one." 
 On things the book did right: 
 Time. I don't normally see this in a YA book but time passes. I suspect it's just so they can age Anna up to make her 18 and therefore legal for sexual purposes, but I was actually sort of impressed by how much time passed with nothing happening. The story would focus on an event and then it would be a season until the next digetic event happened. It was a disoriently unique and surprisingly pleasant experience.

The author could've killed one of the dukes off but no .... It had to be the way it was written!!! Not what I expected but there's always casualties in any battle - still not acceptable in my opinion!!! And finally some HEA with conditions. Looking forward to the last book in this trilogy. Hoping more action in the last book!!!
