PJV Quickie: Conversion is probably one of the strangest books I've read in a while: there was quite a bit of WTF happening, yet I couldn't stop reading. 
 Review: 
 I was a fan of Ms. Stephens' Thoughtless series, so when I saw she had written a vampire series I was very interested. I knew going into it that it would be different, but what I got was totally unexpected: 
 The two main characters, Emma and Teren, have a meet-cute and the attraction is instant. They quickly get into a relationship but Teren seems to be taking it slowly... until he accidentally pricks her lip while they're kissing. She takes the news that he's "sort of" a vampire pretty well. I enjoyed the twist on traditional vampire lore. Then it gets weird. They visit his family and secrets are revealed; things are not as happy-go-lucky as Teren has led her to believe. Emma must make some pretty momentous decisions, and she doesn't have a big window of time to make them in. Then it gets weirder. I'm not going into spoilers, but it felt like I was reading a category romance with a paranormal twist. Just as I'm thinking I know what's going to happen, a villain pops up out of nowhere with a weak premise. 
 There were some funny bits, but even so the story itself kind of dragged in spots; it definitely could have been shortened and the plot would not have suffered. Throw in a self-centered best friend, a horribly scarred sister, and a really sweet ending, and you end up with a book that left me wondering what the heck I just read... and looking up the next book. I have issues, I know. 
 Recommendations: 
 If you're looking for a vampire tale that's a little different and not too dark, you might enjoy Conversion. It's lighter than traditional vampire lore, not dark and broody, and the hero is pretty likable.

I love S.C. Stephens, but I am sorry this story just did not grab me. I have been reading it just to get to the end and I have decided it is not going to happen. 
 Why didn't I like it? 
 Well, Teren is... blah... I get it, he is sexy and too good to be true. A vampire who is fighting his changing nature to prevent hurting humans and the woman he loves after dating for mere days. I have read this exact character so many times by now and he doesn't even have any layers of emotion to set him apart from the others. 
 Emma, she is altogether too accepting and the whole, 'Yeah we have only been dating a month but I think we should have a baby' thing is too much. Then she is trying to force a lifestyle she doesn't understand on her sister just because she is disfigured? So selfish. Her sister is fine being the way she is. The character doesn't have enough positives to outweigh her constant complaining and selfish behavior. 
 Perhaps if I hadn't ever read something in this genre I would be more forgiving, but I just could not finish this story.

Did not finish. Such a slow and boring start. For me, Conversion is just words on paper. I have no connection with the characters AT ALL. I love SC Stephens, but this didn't work for me. I gave up at 25%...

I loved the Thoughtless series and was thinking about starting this and just kept pushing it aside.My sis-law told me how good it was so I gave it a go...now i'm like "why didn't I read it sooner"!!! 
 Teren is so swoon worthy :-) 
 I love His and Emma's relationship with tons of funny banter between them and just the right amount of sexy! 
 Definitely recommend!!!!!

Oh. That was unexpectedly disappointing. A rushed and unbelievable romance with a boring male lead that appears to have no personality whatsoever. He didn't even ask her to marry him for crying out loud. Are these two actually in love? Because I just don't see it. Although I have to say I ended up skimming a lot of it just hoping that there would be a plot. Got pretty good at 80%. So do hang in there. I think the next one will be better so am treating this first one as kind of a prequel and more of a setting the scene-type of book. I love this author. And I love PNR. So I'm not sure what's gone wrong here.

reference_books.title: Openly Straight (Openly Straight, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Muy muy bueno. Me identifique mucho con la historia y me encantaron los personajes, aunque siento que el final fue un poco precipitado y mas bien un anticlimax.

reference_books.title: Silence (Hush, Hush, #3)
reference_books.review_text: (Leido en el 2013) Para mi, el peor de la saga. Si en un comienzo Norah se me hacia intolerable, en este libro con su amnesia llego al punto en que no la soportaba. Y eso fue lo que pense durante todo el libro. Nada mas que anadir.

reference_books.title: The Eye of Minds (The Mortality Doctrine, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Resena completa: El Juego Infinito de James Dashner 
 Este es el quinto libro que leo de James Dashner, y aunque no me sorprendio mucho, tampoco me decepciono. Sabia que no podia esperar algo tan bueno como Correr o Morir, asi que no tuve expectativas muy altas, y el libro me gusto. 
 Como era de esperarse, el libro esta lleno de accion y suspenso, todo el tiempo te mantiene en vilo por lo que va a suceder. Ademas, cada capitulo tiene giros en la trama que no se esperan, lo que hace la lectura muy dinamica y activa. 
 Los personajes fueron uno de los pocos problemas que tuve con el libro. No es que sean malos, pero nunca llegue a tener una conexion con ellos. Son muy planos y James nunca llega a profundizar en sus personalidades, ni siquiera en su fisico. 
 La trama es muy novedosa y atrapa facilmente, especialmente por la forma de escribir de James, quien siempre busca tenerte en suspenso y le da mucho misterio a la historias. 
 Calificacion: 4/5.

reference_books.title: If I Stay (If I Stay, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Resena completa: Si Decido Quedarme 
 Si decido quedarme es un libro que te hara reflexionar y te ayudara a valorar las cosas que tienes en tu vida. Nos mostrara que nadie esta exento de que una situacion de estas le suceda. Nos muestra lo importante que es valorar a nuestras familias y amigos. Muy bien narrado, con personajes entranables y una historia tomada desde un punto de vista muy particular. Con amor, comedia, ternura, reflexion y muchos otros aspectos, este libro entra a ser una de mis mejores lecturas de este ano y me deja con ganas de mas. Lo recomiendo completamente.

reference_books.title: Paper Towns
reference_books.review_text:
Lo primero que debo decir sobre este libro es que me lleve una leve decepcion con el, ya puede ser porque tenia las expectativas muy altas, o porque en realidad no es tan excelente como lo pintaban. Pero a pesar de esto, el libro me gusto. Cuenta con ese estilo de escritura tan peculiar de John Green que tanto cautiva en sus libros, ademas tiene ese toque personal que los hace mucho mas bonitos. 
 Pero, ?por que no lleno mis expectativas? 
 Pues, principalmente, no lleno mis expectativas por las grandes similitudes del libro y Buscando a Alaska, otra novela de John Green. 
 Su trama es muy similar, los protagonistas en ambos libros buscan resolver un misterio sobre una chica completamente enigmatica. Ademas, en los dos libros, los protagonistas son unos jovenes comunes en la secundaria, para nada interesantes. 
 Y hablando sobre personajes, debo decir que gran parte de los personajes de este libro no me convencieron. Quentin, en gran parte me agrado, pero en ocasiones se hacia muy egocentrico y aburrido, cansaba con sus eternas explicaciones, dudas y cuestionamientos. Los mejores amigos de Q, Ben y Radar, son demasiado extranos, me sacaron muchas risas pero en momentos se me hicieron super extranos. Y ahora, Margo Roth Spiegelman, uno de los personajes mas complicados que he leido. Enigmatica, egocentrica, me estreso mucho a lo largo de la historia, y solo logro convencerme en las ultimas paginas. 
 En terminos generales es un libro MUY aburrido, que practicamente solo se salva por la narracion tan particular que tiene y por las ganas de resolver el susodicho misterio.

book_a.title: This Is Water: Some Thoughts, Delivered on a Significant Occasion, about Living a Compassionate Life
book_a.user_review:
"The really important kind of freedom involves attention, and awareness, and discipline, and effort, and being able truly to care about other people and to sacrifice for them, over and over, in myriad petty little unsexy ways, every day." 
 This is Water es el discurso dado por David Foster Wallace en la ceremonia de graduacion del Kenyon College en 2005. En el, hablo de aspectos muy importantes en el dia a dia y que solemos olvidar, y tambien creo una gran reflexion en torno a la forma en que estamos siendo educados. Todos deberian leerlo, simplemente espectacular.

sample_reviews.review_text:
An interesting speech on how you can change your viewpoint from the automatic, default way of thinking to one with more meaning and possibility. 
 I highly recommend not buying it though. It's about $10 for ten pages. Find the free copy on purdue.edu. 
 The author is clearly intelligent and insightful, but I can't help but also be critical of a person who advises us on how to think about life and make it a better experience, and yet committed suicide himself. 
 :-|

"The really important kind of freedom involves attention, and awareness, and discipline, and effort, and being able truly to care about other people and to sacrifice for them, over and over, in myriad petty little unsexy ways, every day." 
 I generally refrain from holding authors in such high regard until I've actually finished one of their works. I'm still working through Infinite Jest, although I guess this speech would technically count as one of his works... regardless, David Foster Wallace was undeniably brilliant. 
 For future reference: 
 The speech, published in The Guardian on September 20, 2008. 
 The speech, read aloud by David Foster Wallace. 
 A full review for this may appear once day... probably after a few dozen more reads, once his words fully sink in. I'm hoping to someday purchase the book as well, or at least see for myself what the format is like. 
 DFW has the remarkable talent of somehow making you laugh while feeling introspective and somewhat depressed at the same time. I am in awe of him.

I picked this up at Borders because it was one of the few David Foster Wallace books they had and I wanted to become familiar with his style. I didn't know at the time that it was a commencement speech given three years prior to his suicide and published one year afterward. Despite some clever analogies and good advice in general (which equates to Wallace saying, "Don't be like me"), it very much reads like a suicide note. Needless to say, I was very disturbed and disappointed that Little/Brown chose to publish it at all, especially after the author's death. Shame on you, Little/Brown.
If you want something that will change your life in under an hour just by reading. This is it!

Oraia omilia!O Wallace den leei kati prototupo-alla oi gnostes autes aletheies xekhniountai eukola,kai mas tis thumizei me omorpho tropo.To keimeno kulaei gregora ki eukola! 
 "A huge percentage of the stuff that I tend to be automatically certain of is, 
 it turns out, totally wrong and deluded. Here's one example of the utter 
 wrongness of something I tend to be automatically sure of: Everything in 
 my own immediate experience supports my deep belief that I am the 
 absolute center of the universe, the realest, most vivid and important 
 person in existence."
A very nice, very thought provoking commencement speech, but did it really need to be stretched over a 136 pages? Methinks the publishers are just trying to make another buck.

This tiny book is one of my absolute favorites. Even though you can find the entire text of DFW's commencement speech at Kenyon online here, having a physical version of it (in really attractive, simple packaging) is worth it. One thing about this that has drawn complaints, but that other people have liked, is the way that the sentences are divided. Instead the normal formatting, each sentence has its own page. One person on amazon accused the publisher of trying to make it seem like every sentence was its own nugget of wisdom, which I don't think was the intent at all. This is a text that benefits from a slow, thoughtful reading, and the format encourages that. As far as whether or not the book was published as a cash-grabbing attempt by the publishers (another common criticism of some reviews), I'm not sure, but I am happy that I have the opportunity to buy a nice book I can keep nearby and let people borrow.

Disappointing from the mind behind "Brief Interviews with Hideous Men" and "The Broom of the System". 
 The basic premise here is that everybody worships something, there is no such thing as true non-belief, and given that, it is much better to worship something supernatural than anything else, because worshipping the supernatural is "the only thing that won't eat you alive." 
 So disappointed. Then again, he was deeply damaged and troubled for as long as he lived, so I'll do my best not to be offended by what I perceive to be a rather long index finger pointing accusingly at my forehead. The only reason I pushed through my indignation and finished it, is that it is all of 16 pages long. (That is, 16 pages as measured by ereader software. I realize it is over 130 pages in hardcopy, but there is only a single sentence per page. So let's say "16 page-equivalents".) 
 (BTW, the stuff about controlling the way you think about other people in the daily grind, and giving people the benefit of the doubt, I absolutely agree with all of that. I just don't agree that it has anything to do with worship.) 
 Edit: I have seen people describe this talk/text as a suicide note. I think that is too easy. Might as well call all his works some kind of suicide note, as he always suffered from deep depression and it shows. But I will not underestimate him so, or excuse the uncharacteristically inane arguments he sets forth.
A lovely and moving address made at a commencement. Very quick read, would make a perfect gift for a graduate.

A graduation speech delivered by David Foster Wallace at Kenyon College in 2005, now published as a short book. I read it online, back when it was still freely available, and it was worth visiting, though I am unconvinced that it demands publishing by itself rather than in a new DFW essay collection.

book_b.title: An Abundance of Katherines
book_b.user_review:
Resena completa: An Abundance of Katherines 
 Algo que me gusto muchisimo de este libro es que la historia es muy particular. Como es de esperarse por la trama, el libro contiene muchos terminos matematicos, ecuaciones y graficas, pero esto no es molesto y considero que es algo muy importante para la historia. Ademas, ninguna de esas graficas ni el teorema son inventados. Al final del libro podemos leer un apendice donde Daniel Biss (un profesor de matematicas) explica como funciona el teorema. 
 La portada francesa, mi 
 favorita. 
 El libro tiene muchas partes que son muy comicas, no tanto como los otros libros de John que tienen un contenido mas dramatico. Me rei mucho a lo largo de toda la historia y no sufri casi nada. Tiene de todo un poco: romance, personajes divertidos, accion, un poquitin de drama y hasta matematicas. 
 Los personajes son muy muy buenos, todos me gustaron en general porque le aportan mucho a la historia. El unico que no me convencio del todo fue Colin, porque en ocasiones se me hacia muy egocentrico y solo le interesaban las cosas que tuvieran que ver directamente con el. Los otros personajes, especialmente Hassan y Lindsey, me gustaron mucho, me divirtieron mucho con sus ocurrencias.

sample_reviews.review_text: Mot the most riveting John Green book I have read but it does have some action scenes that the other books don't have.. (a fist fight for example) The setting and plot were also fairly unique even though the ending was very predictable, and I thought the character of Hassan was a great portrayal of an American Muslim teenager, a group generally under represented in YA lit.

Reading any John Green book is a treat. I'm usually sucked in from the first paragraph. I don't think this is his strongest work, but it's still a good book. As always, entertaining and quirky supporting characters make the story more than a one-note plot. I loved the use of graphs and footnotes to illustrate Colin's obsession with a theorum to predict his future relationships. Yes, it's a little unbelievable that such a socially awkward kid would have had 19 girlfriends by the time he was 18, let alone 19 NAMED KATHERINE), but I suspend disbelief here for sake of a clever story.
I loved this book! I thought that Colin was a smart and interesting character. I loved the ending and will definitely be reading more John Green in the future.

Not my favorite. I was annoyed for the majority of the book by Colin's singlemindedness when so many wonderful things were happening in the plot. It kept coming back to the Katherine's which is extremely realistic when you're dealing with a person going through a breakup but nonetheless. Not my favorite.

Like all John Green books, this one does not disappoint! 
 Love the witty charm that is always good for a few chuckles :)
Not my favorite John Green book, though it got better towards the end. I wasn't a huge fan of the main character, Collin. I found him to be slightly annoying.
Too old for this sort of thing.

It was a good read but not my favorite John Green. Two things, though: 
 1) I LOLed at the Archduke Franz Ferdinand stuff because I learned more about the Archduke in this book than I did in the book I am currently reading about the start of WWI, which had only a page and a half on the Archduke and didn't really tell me anything other than that he was assassinated. 
 2) I miss calculus. (Loved the mathy bits & especially the appendix.)

Just no. Annoying characters, annoying repetition of words. An incredible smart kid meets other smart kids. Focus a lot on the "natural good looking, smart, forward girls". Main character has an obsession with girls looking better without make up, and want some sort of award for this. A lot of focus on the character Hassan and his body type (overweight). We are made to pity Colin, because he's oh so smart and oh so misunderstood - but really I pity the people next to him; especially Hassan. Unrealistic. Very niche. Couldn't find a part in the book that I could relate to, will it be a character or scenario. Privileged people doing maths while proving every stereotypes out there. Instead of being rich in content, the book focus on banal situations and then somewhere in a sentence or two bind all these together to make some sort of deeper "point". 
 I wasn't a fan of Looking for Alaska either, but if one were to compare Alaska was definitely better. Same archetypes, unfortunately. Not my thing to be honest.

Actually, more like 3.5. 
 I know this is people's least favourite of John Green's. And while I can see why this can be so, I don't think it deserves all the bad press that it's getting. It's by far the funniest of the bunch (sure, not HAHA funny, but happy chuckles, and that's good enough for me). And I LOVED Colin! Lots of people don't, but I do, I truly do. I like the contradiction that is him - a nerd to the core, but c'mon, he gets some pretty real good action from the ladies too - and the words that come out of his mouth are such a delight to read. I love it when he starts speaking random foreign languages too (I mean, that's pretty neat right?), especially the conversations between him and Hassan. This book was also ladened with many mind-blowing facts that I have never known, and I think it made me somewhat smarter. 
 So yeah, I don't think this is the worst of John Green's book.

book_a.title: The Hating Game
book_a.user_review: This is a very good option ... if you want this kind of book!

sample_reviews.review_text:
Going in, I thought it'd be a classic romantic book, using the enemies to bickering allies to lovers trope, which is my favourite trope of all time btw, but it was a bit different. First of all, it was obvious from the get-go that both characters were really into each other, so I was super excited to read it. 
 The two main characters are Josh and Lucy who work together but "hate" each other. Josh, is a tall, muscular, smart, athletic, rich, shy, stylish guy who knows how to cook and likes to clean up but is a "loser" because he didn't complete med school. This guy is so obviously supposed to be the perfect guy that the everyone who reads the book has to fall for it's kind of cringy. As for Lucy the main girl, she is the usual blank "insert-personality-here" girl whose most consistent character trait is the shade of lipstick she wears and that the readers can shamelessly project themselves on. 
 It was a very predictable book and the writing was not that great. The one thing that saves it is the chemistry the two characters have. From the beginning, their "hate" games, were so much more than foreplay then acts of hostility, and it was obvious they were really into each other. Their sex scene was also really great. 
 But, and it's a pretty big but, I didn't get how Josh was so in love with her. There is a difference between really liking someone and then writing down what they wear every day to perform a statistical analysis on their outfits (?), paint your room the colour of their eyes three days after you me them(???), break up with your long-term girlfriend for them even if you only know them for like a week and barely talked to them at all (????) and leave your job so you don't compete against them in an interview (?????). Like, woah Josh buddy, you're hot and all and I appreciate your muscles and your interest but it's getting creepy. 
 All in all, it wasn't really that bad. It had some cliches that kind of made me want to vomit, like Lucy solving years of family resentment in a single 5-minute-long rant to Josh's father, the waiters listening to her and being all "hey girl that was awesome, you don't have to pay woo" and clapping when she and Josh kissed. That whole scene was a disaster from start to finish. Other than that, it was quite ok. Kind of sweet, kind of sexy, kind of funny, it made me wish I was lying on a beach while reading it.
What a breath of fresh, rom com, air! Lovely story, wonderful characters, intricate and delicate writing. Such a fun, fresh take on the office and romance trope. Really well done!

** spoiler alert ** 
 "I haven't wanted you this long, and gone through so much, and given up so much, to have you for one night. It's not enough." 
 "When you get so little of someone, you take what you can get." 
 These quotes, and so many others, are why this book is one of my all time favorites.

I finished this in one day (if you don't count my 8 h of sleep in between haha...) and I COULD NOT PUT IT DOWN (except for when I really, really had to sleep...) 
 The banter was hilarious and I absolutely loved the games going on between Lucy and Joshua. It was with excitement and a racing heart that you followed their conversations about strangling each other while you could practically feel the tension building up between them. I'm a sucker for hate-love stories, and this one was not an exception. 
 These two practically live for making each other's lives miserable, and they are used to having the other person in their field of vision whenever lifting their heads up from their computers. 
 Lucy knew Josh's entire wardrobe and what he would wear everyday - which isn't normal, but nevertheless quite funny since he wore the same color every Monday etc. 
 You laugh out loud at the things they do to step on each other's toes at work, and EVERYONE knows how much they hate each other which just makes the situation even more entertaining. They are of course thrown into situations where they have to cooperate and face one another, but the tension and feelings simmering beneath the surface are palpable and you squeak at times because you just want them to realize what's so obvious! 
 Some scenes were cliche, but somehow the author managed to make them less cringeworthy by remaking small details and adding credible dialogue to smooth it all over. For instance the following happened: 
 1. An elevator kiss (YES, and it was GOOD) 
 2. A wedding they had to attend together (yes, she walked down the stairs and he was dumbstruck) 
 3. Lucy being sick so Josh had to take care of her (what are the odds even?) 
 4. Other love interests being present (that weren't really up running for winning their hearts but still) 
 All these situations are very cliche, but they make you fangirl nevertheless... and rightfully so ;) 
 I need to point out how time and time again Josh's muscles and body were described. His taunt stomach, and his big, big biceps and his amazing back muscles. I love muscles, like I LOVE muscles - but it was becoming redundant and as if nothing else but Josh's muscles were of importance. Lucy kept saying that she liked him for more than his muscles, yet she kept pointing out his muscles every chance she got. 
 On the other hand, and this is what I appreciated for once. Josh was insecure about himself, despite being this oh-so-swoonworthy muscular male, and I couldn't help but feel grateful for him not being overly confident about himself like every other male character we get to read about in stories like this one. He was battling with his personality instead and thought that women only liked him for his body, (he probably knew he looked like a model), but he wanted them to see him and not his body which justified him looking so handsome and being big and bulky. I liked that he wasn't this perfectly sculptured guy (even though he sort of was...) So deifinitely bonus points for that since it wasn't expected. 
 The ending felt somehow very rushed; so an epilouge would've been preferable but other than that I really liked Sally Thorne's debut novel! 
 This is an entertaining read and I recommend it to everyone that feel like they need an intoxicating chick-lit.
I really liked this angsty, fluffy, novel, but was disappointed with how much sex the author included in the last 15% of the book.

I read this in exactly 5 hours and 3 minutes. 
 Sally Thorne is now an insta-buy. 
 I need a sequel. 
 ... 
 Okay, now what do I do with my life?
Oh my god I am completely in love.

Heartwarming (adj.): 
 Causing pleasant feelings of happiness (and silly, stupid tears you can't stop). 
 By all means, it was not a sad book. On the contrary, The Hating Game was a funny, sweet, adorable, intoxicating office romance about two sworn enemies that fell in love. And I'm crying because it filled me with so much joy, and hope and love my body can barely contain! 
 "Both love and hate are mirror versions of the same game-and you have to win. Why? Your heart and your ego." 
 Josh is Lucy's nemesis. They work together while they plot each other's murder. They play juvenile games, they keep filing complaints to Human Resources, and they make each other miserable. Their competition is tough, and with a promotion on the horizon things escalate quickly. But after one mind-blowing elevator kiss, and some unexpected kindness from Josh, Lucy starts to wonder whether beneath his cold and cruel behavior exists a Nice Guy after all, with the potential to break her heart. 
 The line between love and hate was never so blurry. 
 "No one can kiss me like you do." 
 Dear Sally Thorne, I'm yours. 
 I can't get rid of this ridiculously wide grin on my face, I'm one step from looking like Joker. And then I remember all those moving and sweet moments and I start crying, and people wonder who murdered my cat. I don't have a cat. 
 Josh and Lucy's story tugged at my heartstrings in an unexpected way. They were two characters beautifully crafted, with their flaws and insecurities. Lucy was always sociable and charming, she wanted people to like her but in the end, she was lonely. Josh was a clinical asshole that made everyone tremble, and tiny Lucy was the only one that stood up to him. Little did she know how shy and caring he was. 
 "Shortcake." 
 "Stop calling me Shortcake." 
 "Watching you pretend to hate that nickname is the best part of my day." 
 Hilarious banters, crackling tension, tenderness and passion, The Hating Game has everything you could ask for from a romance novel. Every single touch spoke straight to my heart, and made my blood warm and my head dizzy! There were times I forgot how to breathe, and times I couldn't help but sigh. Josh is such a dreamy guy, yummilicious and sexy and so, so swoonworthy! 
 While I would have liked a few chapters from Josh's POV, I enjoyed Lucy's narrative so much! She was such a sweet and funny and adorable person, and you could understand her reservations and her fears! 
 I'm so in love. 
 "What are you imagining? Your expression is filthy." 
 "Strangling you. Bare hands." 
 "So that's your kink." 
 "Only where you're concerned." 
 If this sappy review didn't convince you to read this little gem, please do check Arianna's review! [?]

I read this book because many of my fellow Avon Addicts were raving about it. Oh, my goodness. I love this book. I don't know that there is anything else I can say. It is one of the best books I've read it a long time. I inhaled it! Read this book!

I have quite a few thoughts about this book! I inhaled the whole thing yesterday. 
 1. Before I start nit-picking, let me just say that this is a superb and impressive debut novel. Sally Thorne has a unique voice, which is one of my favorite things in romantic fiction. 
 2. The beginning of this book is stellar. As in...brilliant. Quirky, sucks you right in. I usually hate first person POV, but once I got settled in for the ride, the POV didn't irritate me as much as it usually does. In fact, it was used perfectly at the beginning--which is to say, the heroine's perspective reflects her state of mind...moody, bumpy, insecure. All the things that help to establish who she is--and, more importantly, make us wonder about the events unfolding around her--are accomplished with this POV. 
 3. The best part of the beginning is the hero. Why? He is full of surprises. The story is full of surprises. He hardly talks. We have to figure out who he is, and what his intentions are, from his actions alone. This is absolutely brilliant. But, unfortunately, this is also the downfall for the rest of the story. Once he starts talking, a big chunk of the fizz is released from the book. The beginning was the best part. The end turned into a regular old romance novel--not that it's necessarily a bad thing. It just lost the magic of the beginning...the mystery, the unknown, the building tension. After the elevator scene--which was FABULOUS--the tension in the story goes downhill. 
 This is my main observation about this book. It's clearly divided for me into 2 books...the beginning, which is freakin' amazing...and the end, which turns into a somewhat contrived and predictable romance novel. If I had read the end first, I would have thought...Hey, this is good! But that first part of the book set me up for something spectacular. It was so good, it was hard to follow up. 
 4. This book is too damned long. A good chunk, maybe 25%? or more, needs to be edited out. By the end, their fun and silly banter was starting to drag and feel repetitive. So were some of the cute gimmicks like the titles for their "battles." 
 5. I was confused about the paintball scene. It was unclear if the heroine was "unwell" because she was bruised and battered by the shots she received, or something else. It was a weird plot turn to have her seriously ill at this point. The overlap of her getting her butt kicked with an unknown illness (virus? food poisoning?) caused some confusion in the story. I just found that odd. 
 6. The humor is insanely funny. I laughed out loud multiple times. Thorne's sense of humor is quirky and hilarious and spot-on. Extremely well-done. 
 7. The charming details here--about their clothes, her family, the strawberry farm--are precious. His family was not as well defined...the characters were flatter, not as well fleshed-out. 
 8. The sexual tension is delicious, but eventually the love scenes dragged on too long. I got bored and started to skim. I think these could have been edited down also. 
 9. My biggest disappointment was the final scene at the wedding. This book, which started out with so much charm and quirkiness, devolved into an unbelievable confrontation with his family. The heroine unleashes a profanity-laced tirade at his father to defend him. This felt forced and not authentic to this character or the story itself. Would I expect this scene in a regular old romantic comedy? Maybe. But this book--and these characters--deserved something more authentic and quirky. Yes, it neatly wrapped up the storyline at the end, but it didn't work for me. It didn't feel believable. The hero's grand gesture was lovely and surprising and worked perfectly. Loved it! 
 10. Overall grade: 4.5 stars. The beginning of the book gets 10+ stars. It is simply brilliant. The end was fine. I am eagerly looking forward to reading more by this author. 
 Exciting discovery!

3.5 stars 
 Death, friendship, and Heartbreak turns into a wonderful new love story. Belly grows up in book 2 and the story has intensified. Coping with death and resulting grief of having someone so significant pass away was a major theme. 
 I really missed Belly's brother Steven in this book. They had such a strong and developed relationship in book 1 and having him be absent for the entire second book was a mistake. I wanted to see Steven come to Belly's rescue at the funeral even after she made a scene. 
 The weekend spent helping out Conrad was confusing. These boys and Belly have loved each other their entire lives as summer faux-siblings/ teenage love interests. The writing didn't get me to feel either boy loved her the same way she is twisting herself inside out to love them. I know they are all broken from the death of Susanna, however, Belly seems to shoulder all the effort in making either relationship(friendship/loyalty/love) work. I wanted to see them work for her love a little more. I wanted to get a glimpse of how much she meant to them and not just how much she ached for the boys. 
 As this story revealed itself, I admit I began liking these boys less and less and hoping she would get a break from both of them. Secret girlfriends, unspoken feelings(is that because he loves her as a sister or loves her enough to let her go?)and brothers that love the same girl enough to want to be with her but not enough to fight for her? The scene felt like a high school hallway conversation and not a brothers diving into their feelings for the same girl. That one true lifetime love even boys dream about actually finding. The author could have saved several pages of angst with this simple dialogue and still gotten to the same place. 
 "Do you want her?" 
 "No, I tried it and it didn't work for me. You go ahead." 
 "Ok, I think I'll give her a shot and see how it goes. Stay cool bro." 
 Eager to get through Book 3 to see what happens and who she ends up with so I added an extra half star for book 2.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This book is BOMB. I love how Conrad was seen as 'running away' at first. And the moment when the real estate agent came, everything just made sense. I love their attachment to the summer house. I love how Laura sternly convinced Mr Fisher. I love how Bel and Jere helped Con in his studies. & the last Belly Flop :) 
 But my goodness the love triangle hits sooo hard in the sequel. I feel really sad for Jere. I can feel the jealousy, the love-hate feeling with Con. I just get him. In fact, if I were Belly, I would pick Jere over Conrad everytime. Jere is such a sweetheart, really upfront about his feelings and tries so hard to protect Belly. Conrad on the other hand, has mixed feelings towards Belly. One moment he's there, next moment he's not. He loves Belly but in a distant way, more subtle way. 
 Well, first love will always be the most treasured one in heart, won't it? Especially with Conrad's on-off gestures. 
 I was quite hopeful about the 'last night' in the summer house to be honest. Especially when the Red Sox girl's there. I was hoping for Cameron to appear, at least to tie the loose ends from the first book. Sigh didn't happen though.

I hate Belly so much. I think hate is not enough to describe how much I dislike her, I loathe her. 
 She's the most annoying fictional character I've ever encountered. She's so self-absorbed. How can she be like that? How can she only care what she feels? Can she be atleast selfless? Yes, I do understand that she needs to be there for Conrad and Jeremiah because they've been childhood friends. But, the thing that really pissed me off when she said all those awful things to Taylor, Conrad and specially.. specially her own mother. 
 How can she be so naive? She had a bestfriend that can put up with her when she was dejected and wretched. And, she snapped her just because she called her selfish, which is true, because she want all the attention to herself. 
 And to her mom, Oh god. She was so cruel, every mother would be worried when you saw your daughter drunk with all the mess everywhere. And, what did she get for worrying over her daughter? She said: 
 "I wish Susannah was my mother and not you." 
 I can't help it, but to despise her. Seriously, SHE'S NOT THE ONLY ONE WHO'S MISERABLE WITH THE LOSS. She doesn't need to be a bitch. Is she blind or what? I just hate her so much, I want to shave her head. What pissed me more is her mom was the one who apologized, it's not right. Her mom had the right to be mad, not Belly! 
 I also felt sorry for Jeremiah for loving a girl like her, he deserves better than that. How can Belly kiss Jeremiah back if she still loves Conrad? And feel glad about it when Conrad was hurt? It's like she's using a guy over again. Ugh. 
 But, the ending.. who's the guy?

It was super cute, which is what I was hoping for when I picked it up. After reading the intense stuff that Ellen Hopkins wrote, I needed the break and wanted something sweet. This one did make me tear up more than the first one, both in a good way and a bad way. But it was good.

From Its Not Summer Without You 
 This wasn't the way I pictured it. Me, in a white dress in the pouring rain, running for the car. Him, running ahead of me and opening the passenger door. 
 "Are you sure?" he asks me. 
 "No," I say, getting in. 
 The future is unclear. But it's still mine. 
 I wonder what that means but I guess ill figure it out soon enough
I really liked this one a lot. Way better than the first book. I'm enjoying how much character growth there was between book one and two and I can't wait to see how they grow even more in book three.

* 3.5 stars * 
 A solid second installment to the series, but I'm not sure if Jenny Han will break my heart again. Although, I like the way she breaks it.

It is a known fact that I did not care for the first book. I wasn't able to connect with Belly. The way she would string along all the guys in her life irritated me beyond belief. Not only that but she came across as self centered and childish. I don't think she changed much from the first book. 
 This book finds Belly and Jeremiah in search for Conrad. Their search leads them to Cousins Beach. When they find Conrad everyone has decisions to make that will forever change them. 
 While writing that short summary I realized that not much has happened in this book. 
 Belly's relationship with Conrad is not perfect. He is flawed in many ways, but I felt like Belly doesn't want to accept that. She refuses to see how Conrad is not the "perfect" guy and that he is struggling with the death of his mother, the potential loss of their beach house, and anger at his father. Most girlfriends or even friends would want to help or at least stand by their friend through these tough times, not Belly. She wants Conrad's entire focus. 
 I felt like as I read this Belly would be jumping in a corner yelling, "look at me, look at me!" 
 I have a major problem with Belly jumping from one brother to the next. Yeah, both boys have feelings for Belly, but who asks their brother if they are done with a girl so they can have them??? I struggle with that. Maybe it's the fact that I grew up with 2 brothers as good friends and I can't see dating both, or even one for that matter. 
 It just feels wrong... like you are forever driving a wedge between family members, forever destroying that bond. 
 The thing that irritates me beyond belief is Belly. She is 17, but I felt as though I was listening to a 13 year old tell her story. Where was the growth from the last book??? 
 Why hasn't she matured?? 
 The storyline was lacking. Looking back nothing happened. There was a party, a fight, a few flash backs, a smaller fight and that was it. I was looking for more.. more meat.. something... anything. 
 I will find myself reading the final installment because some sick part of me needs to know who Belly ends up with and in what manner. Is she going to destroy Conrad or Jeremiah on her journey for the perfect boyfriend?? I wish I were continuing to read because it was good story, but I can't say that.
meh

reference_books.title: Sharp Objects
reference_books.review_text:
1.5 stars 
 Gillian Flynn, reporter-cum-bestselling-author, is most famous for her publishing juggernaut, Gone Girl, which went on to inspire the Oscar-nominated film of the same name. But, long before Nick and Amy Dunne were making you rethink your desire to ever tie the knot, Flynn was busy penning her debut novel, Sharp Objects. 
 So, what's it about? 
 Reporter Camille Preaker is, to put it mildly, deeply unhappy with her latest assignment: return to her tiny hometown of Wind Gap, just south of Chicago, to cover the violent murders of two preteen girls. But it's not the murders that trouble Camille. It's returning to her hometown. She hasn't been back in eight years, a streak she has no interest in ending. Her boss, however, is adamant, and so, all-too-soon, Camille finds herself back in Wind Gap, back in her moneyed family's Victorian mansion, and back in the presence of her ice-cold mother, indifferent stepfather, and mercurial stepsister, Amma. 
 Needless to say, it's not exactly a nurturing environment--especially for Camille, who is a self-cutter fresh off a stay in the psych ward. She's also using--okay, outright abusing--alcohol in a desperate attempt not to return to old habits, i.e. cutting, something that, not coincidentally, gets harder and harder the more time she spends with Mommy Dearest. 
 But why did Camille become a cutter in the first place? And why does she identify so strongly with the preteen murder victims? And why did her mother never even mention the murders, easily the biggest piece of town gossip in decades, to reporter Camille? 
 Family secrets abound, and--spoiler alert!--it should come as no surprise that the killer is much, much closer to Camille than she initially suspects . . . 
 And that's a bit of problem. Whereas Gone Girl held its secrets close, Sharp Objects is weirdly predictable, telegraphing the killer's identity almost from the dust jacket. This is so obvious, you think. It must be a red herring. But no. It's exactly what it seems. And whereas Nick and Amy Dunne were so awful that you wondered--curious but detached, like an eyewitness watching a train wreck--just how twisted things would become, Camille Preaker is oddly endearing. You want her to find happiness, despite all of her flaws. Heck, maybe because of them. Surely, she deserves better than she gets in this unrelentingly dark story. 
 And that, in the end, is my real problem with this novel. A story can still be entertaining if it's predictable or unrelentingly dark. But not if it's both! What's the point of slogging through the darkness if you already know exactly where you'll wind up? 
 Still, it's a well-done debut novel with all the hallmarks of Flynn's later, better writing: secrets, murder, missing persons, and enough family dysfunction to make you reconsider attending a family reunion any time in the next century. 
 But it's no Gone Girl.

reference_books.title: The Taming of the Shrew
reference_books.review_text:
Everyone in the town of Verona, Italy, wants to marry the beautiful Bianca. But--alas!--her father refuses to let her wed until her older, tart-tongued sister Kate takes a husband of her own. Enter Petruchio, a canny young man looking to make some big bucks--which is exactly what Bianca's suitors promise him if he marries Kate. So how will he woo seduce tame his bride-to-be? Why, with a charming mixture of starvation, sleep deprivation, and such honeyed words as: 
 "She is my goods, my chattels, she is my house, 
 My household stuff, my field, my barn, 
 My horse, my ox, my ass, my anything." 
 Romantic, no? No. In fact, it's hard to believe that Shakespeare, penner of such sensational heroines as Juliet and Viola, could ever produce this sexist drivel. Because he certainly didn't do women (or men) any favors with the character of Kate (or Petruchio). Blah!

reference_books.title: Squirrel Seeks Chipmunk: A Modest Bestiary
reference_books.review_text:
Sixteen fables featuring mice, cats, dogs, and, yes, squirrels seeking chipmunks. Sounds pretty adorable, right? 
 Wrong. 
 This is, after all, a work by David Sedaris, a writer who managed to show the seedy underbelly of even the Macy's store Christmas elves in his popular piece, "SantaLand Diaries." 
 Accordingly, these fluffy little animals are plagues by a whole host of human ills--racism, homophobia, infidelity, etc.--and so act in a decidedly unadorable manner. And while the stories are clever in an oh-look-he-made-the-storks-bad-parents sort of way, they also lack the wit and charm of Mr. Sedaris's more personal essays. 
 It's not that all the stories are bad. Some, in fact, are quite good. The title story, for example, is a haunting meditation on interracial dating--or, perhaps, any opportunity missed out on due to simple miscommunication. And "The Vigilant Rabbit" is a wryly observed look at xenophobia that stars a bunny determined to protect his forest by killing everything in sight--even, it turns out, the one animal that could have saved it. 
 But most of the stories are crude, bordering on tasteless, the absolute worst of the bunch being the last one--the piece de resistance, as it were--entitled "The Grieving Owl." It stars a hippo plagued by anal parasites, an owl determined to remove them, and, not to put too fine a point on things, a greased up gerbil covered in lube. 
 See? Tasteless. 
 It's a tone purposely reinforced by the drawings of Ian Falconer, best known for illustrating the popular Olivia children's books. Here he depicts Sedaris's odd menagerie in the same storybook style, just in black and white--with, of course, the occasional splash of red thrown in to highlight the blood on a lab rat, say, or the anus of a parasite-ridden hippo. 
 Ick. 
 Ultimately, Mr. Falconer's illustrations are like Mr. Sedaris's fables: deliberate, jarring, maybe even brilliantly so, but off-putting all the same. So while I applaud their willingness to step outside of the box creatively, I can't help but hope that they return to their proper places. Soon.

book_a.title: The Sleeper and the Spindle
book_a.user_review:
5 stars. 
 Neil Gaiman's previously published short story, "The Sleeper and the Spindle", gets the gift book treatment in this lavishly illustrated edition, complete with gorgeous artwork by Chris Riddell. (Side note: Click here to view more of Riddle's lovely illustrations.) 
 But wait, you say. The Sleeper and the Spindle? Isn't that the lesbian retelling of Snow White and Sleeping Beauty? Yes and no. Gaiman's story does, indeed, feature an all-important, spell-shattering kiss between the two central characters . . . 
 But they're not in love, and this retelling is not a swoony romance. 
 Rather, it is the story of a young queen on her wedding day, a queen who decides to don chainmail instead of a wedding dress and ride to the aide of a nearby kingdom, where a sleeping curse has gotten entirely out-of-hand. There she does kiss a princess and break a spell, but so what? That's not where her story ends, nor even where it climaxes. The so-called lesbian twist is just the first of many surprises Gaiman has in store for the reader in what is, at its heart, a story that's much more concerned with women forging their own destinies than finding the love of a good man (or woman). 
 And that, my friends, is a message well worth repeating.

sample_reviews.review_text: Creepy twist on Sleeping Beauty and several other fairy tales (Rumpelstiltskin? Snow White with the wicked stepmother) has a queen rescuing a princess.

I have sort of the opposite feeling about this book compared to other popular reviews - I loved the story but detested nearly all of the illustrations. 
 I think the story is just about perfect - as always, Neil Gaiman gives us just enough to let the reader know what's going on instead of wasting pages on useless details. Along that same note, I would disagree with other reviews that complain about lack of character development. Well, for starters it's a short story. But he's very good at describing a character with a minimum of words. Just the brief description of how the Queen placates her fiance with a quick kiss prior to leaving on her adventure, or how she tells the rescued castle dwellers to take good care of the old woman tells the reader that this isn't your ordinary heroine. 
 However, the illustrations were very creepy. I thought the Queen was evil for a while because of the skulls on her bed. The townspeople covered in cobwebs are terrifying and I didn't have to look hard at the drawings to see some hidden (and even creepier) Easter eggs.
Heroes come and go, but the story goes on.
The twist on Sleeping Beauty was interesting, but it was a bit too short for me to really get into. The illustrations made up for it though.

I loved this book. I picked it up on a whim and went in with no expectations. The Sleeper and the Spindle is a wonderfully remained fairytale. The only thing I wish is that there was more of the story.
Love the writing. Love the illustrations. A book for everyone.

This was interesting--a picture book designed for adults. The Sleeper and the Spindle is a twist on the Sleeping Beauty/Snow White fairy tales with a plot line featuring empowered women going on adventures and leaving the menfolk behind. (The Queen is due to be married but postpones the wedding so she can go on a journey with 3 dwarfs.) 
 The pictures are lovely, complex and not designed to appeal to children. They're clearly for adults. The story is well written (Neil Gaiman wrote it after all) but a bit odd. I liked the new take on an old fairy tale but the author's failure to name any of his characters keeps the reader from fully engaging with them. 
 Still, this was an interesting project although the form may not lend itself to being a best seller. 
 Recommended.
More like a *3.25*

I thought this book, while original in its twist on the Sleeping Beauty fairy tale, was not great to simply ok. I read it because I needed a book less than 100 pages for my Book Riot challenge. Otherwise, I doubt I'd ever have chosen it as it's outside what I'd typically read. I really liked that the protagonist was a strong female.

** spoiler alert ** 
 There's a great twist to the story which is why the one star. But the rest is a bit if whimsical nonsense really. 
 So many things about this story don't make sense. If she's the queen, why is she feeling trapped by marriage she's in charge of, why is she marrying someone she doesn't like, why have so many people lost their lives trying to find a way over the mountains when they could have just waltzed through the tunnels like the dwarves do? None of the characters have any motivation for what they do, they just seem to be going through the motions. 
 In the end the queen just wanders off into the sunset with her dwarves, abdicating all responsibility for her kingdom.

book_b.title: Crown of Midnight (Throne of Glass, #2)
book_b.user_review:
4 stars. 
 HO. LEE. SHIT. 
 How can an author improve so much from one book to the next?! Because while Throne of Glass could best be summarized by the words "perfectly fine", "adequate", and "acceptable", Crown of Midnight had me literally whooping with joy. 
 But I'm getting ahead of myself. 
 First, Crown of Midnight's plot. In a nutshell: 
 Celaena Sardothien, assassin extraordinaire, is now officially the King of Adarlan's Champion--a.k.a. crown-sanctioned killer--and she is not enjoying her new career at all. She neither likes nor trusts the King (understandable, given that his army brutally butchered her parents a mere 10 years ago), and she doesn't approve of killing the so-called traitors rebelling against him. Which is why she's not. Instead, she's only pretending to kill his enemies, while actually helping them go into hiding. Of course, if the King ever discovers her betrayal, he will have her--and all her friends--executed. 
 But Celaena is not the only one keeping secrets. 
 All of her newfound friends--Prince Dorian, Chaol, and Princess Nehemia--are keeping secrets of their own, and when those secrets finally spill out into the open, heartbreak--and death--abound . . . 
 Seriously, this plot gets intense! The last one hundred or so pages of the book is a pure adrenalin rush to read, with double cross after double cross, explosive secrets, and near-constant action. Chase scenes! Fight scenes! Murder and mayhem! And the Fae! Oh my god, the Fae! 
 This story works so much better than its predecessor that it's mind-blowing. Freed from the constraints of Throne of Glass--the Tournament of Champions, the murder mystery subplot, the meh love triangle--Maas constructs a plot that can legitimately be called a page-turner. I stayed up until 3 a.m. to finish this book (no regrets!), and by the time I reached the last page, I was emotionally exhausted--although I did still have enough energy to be delighted by Maas's final revelation . . . 
 (Spoilers ahead!) 
 . . . Celaena is--as any regular fantasy reader could have guessed from early on in Glass--the long-lost heir of Terrasen, the half-Fae kingdom conquered by Adarlan's king 10 years ago. For Celaena's parents were not just any Fae lord and lady, but the King and Queen of Terrasen, meaning that Celaena, in addition to being an assassin and ex-convict, is royalty and half-Fae, too. 
 It's nice to see the mystery of Celaena's heritage finally confirmed, and, while not surprising, it's an excellent way for Maas to end Midnight. It sets up a ton of drama for the next installment in the series--especially between her and Chaol, her (now former?) lover and the King of Adarlan's current Captain of the Guard. 
 Bring on Heir of Fire!

sample_reviews.review_text: I didn't really enjoy this book.

Not bad at all. The beginning was too cheesy for me and slow and a bit boring. However, later it picked up the tempo and it was quite good. The big plot twist was a bit predictable but yeah, okay it was good. The ending made me actually quite hungry for continuation.

2.5 stars. 
 I'm not entirely sure why these books are so popular. Until the very end of the book when all the twists were revealed, the only scenes I found remotely interesting were those with Celaena and Chaol and I'm not even a romance reader. The plot twists are the only thing that bumped this from 1 to 2.5 stars. I'm not sure if I will read the other books or just Google what happens to save myself the trouble.

Actual Rating 4.5 stars 
 Review: 
 Protagonist: Celaena is back and this time it's as the King's Champion. Trying to keep herself alive and hold on to her own morals is hard though, when one slip up, one mistake could cost her everything. I've always loved Celaena's character. She's strong, independent, and at times down right ruthless. While she may be an assassin, and now one employed by the corrupt king, she also has a strong moral compass and will do whatever she deems necessary to ensure the welfare of her country and her people. 
 Romance: I just, I can't you guys. One of the things I loved about the first book was that while it did have an edge of romance to it, and a really great love triangle too, it never really filled in parts of the story. Meaning, it was never really filler, it was just an extension of the story rather than something to fill time between the better parts of the plot. In this installment though the romance moved way too fast and took up much too much of the story which left me feeling a bit uncomfortable. In fact, while I didn't really have a preference of who Celaena ended up with in the last installment, in this one I really didnt like a love interest purely because their relationship was going too fast. I felt that there was no real build up and maybe it's because I haven't read the first book in so long, but I just didn't really feel the chemistry. Also, another thing is I'm so confused, is there a love triangle anymore? Did Celaena choose? Or is there still a chance for (spoiler) to end up with her? Honestly I was so very confused and a bit irritated by the romance of this installment, especially since it's going to be such a long series. 
 World-Building: I loved the world-building in this book. In the previous installment there was very little that went on outside of the competition to become the King's champion, in this installment however, we get to see so much more including more political intrigue, rebellion, and knowledge about magic and what exactly happened to it. Celaena discovers some dark secrets and learns more about not only herself, but the corrupt ruler she is serving. This book goes beyond the set up of the first installment and begins to show readers the world beyond the castle of glass and show them the impact one tyrant can bring upon an entire continent. 
 Predictability: So I have to say that while I was spoiled on a few minor plot points, thanks BEA Heir of Fire line, for the most part i was extremely surprised at what occurred in this installment. While I'll get to the bombshell that was dropped in the ending during the next part, I'd also like to touch on a "Game of Thrones" moment that happened in this book. I mean holy crap there was no way I thought something like that would happen, in fact I vehemently denied that it was true until all the evidence pointed to the contrary. I mean there are some great twists in this book, but there are only really two that steal the whole show and this was one of them. 
 Ending: And the other one was the bombshell dropped at the very end of this installment. Now, before I get into that let's talk about the ending in general. Honestly it was a pretty strong ending, though it is the thing that confused and irritated me most about the romance, but let's not rehash that again. It really helped set up where the next book was going and Ill be interested to see what happens next. Now for the bombshell, I mean holy crap it was just... I mean I was surprised it took the person who discovered it so long to figure out what it was because he had his suspicions, he had the info he needed, but even with all the clues laid out before him he was so dense as not to figure it out when I had figured it out a couple pages before. The guy was dense, to say the least. 
 Rating: 
 So one of the many things I was told about this installment was how much better it was than the first (and the first was amazing.) However, I'm not sure if it's the expectations I had or my own opinions on how the romance progressed but this, while great, couldn't really measure up to the first installment.
Loved it, loved it, LOVED IT!! The feels are just insane, and I can't wait to continue! And can we all just take a minute to appreciate Chaol Westfall for a minute please, because he's bae!!
When she's running around trying to figure out the riddle, the first location is so obvious. And she gets hurt SO much in this book, isn't she supposed to be the greatest assassin in the world??

This review (and others) can be found in all its proper formatting glory on my blog Beauty and the Bookshelf. 
 *Note: This review would be waaay more flaily and gushy if I would've been a good person and written this review when I finished Crown of Midnight...like three months ago. 
 This (Smeagol's so-not-dramatic despair) is how I felt when I finished Crown of Midnight: 
 (Caption may or may not be how I feel dying waiting for Heir of Fire.) 
 I didn't looove Throne of Glass, but it reaaally made me want to read Crown of Midnight (which I'd heard was EPIC), and ohmygosh, Crown of Midnight made me like Throne of Glass more. Seriously, THIS BOOK. It's a feels-fest, swoonalicious, fantasmical adventure that usurps its predecessor and leaves you with an alcohol-free hangover. 
 One of my biggest issues with Throne of Glass was the use of exclamation points. They were, like, everywhere and drove me crazy. So I am very happy that the use of them was cut down here, because YAY. And really, I can't think of any complaints with this book (minus me wondering WHAT IS BEING DONE TO MY FEELS), so double yay! 
 Crown of Midnight follows Throne of Glass, where Celaena became (spoiler alert) the king's royal assassin and, in order to gain her freedom, must do his bidding. But Celaena isn't the most compliant of people, so she decides to twist the orders given to her by the king and be more in control herself. However, it's never that easy when evil is afoot and magic is brewing. Oh, and when there's sexual tension like whoa. 
 Celaena is an extremely badass protagonist whose bad side you DO NOT want to get on. Plus, she's an infamous assassin, so she'd kill you faster than you can blink. She's under a lot of pressure in this book, with trying to keep what she's been doing (or hasn't) a secret, attempting to figure out what on earth is going on in the castle made of glass and some heebie-jeebie things, and she's doesn't quite know where she stands in a kinda-sorta-not-really love triangle with Prince Dorian (ew) and Captain Chaol Westfall (yes yes yesss). New character Archer was simultaneously sketch and likeable (also, sucky job, dude), and I've always been kind of whatever about Celaena's BFF Nehemia. The king, as usual, can go die. Some oddball things happen with Dorian in this book, and I do like him...but he needs to back up/off of Celaena. Because I have a MAJOR SHIP, and it's between her and *siiigh* *googly eyes* *fluttery heart* CHAOOOL. I love him. I love him. I love him. I loved him in Throne of Glass (oh my gosh, that whole "get up" scene at the end?!), and that love just grows even more here. Chaol and Celaena (or, Chaol and ME) go together better than peanut butter and chocolate. Their sexual tension in this book KILLS ME, and it frustrates me, but my gosh is it AWESOME. (Major spoiler alert: My ship set sail! And it was beautiful. Then it anchored and I will go DOWN with this ship, but why, Sarah J. Maas, WHY? End spoiler.) 
 Can we talk about the last half of this book? Because WHAT HAPPENED? It was all so beautiful, and then my heart broke, and then my feels were being pulled apart and I just COULD NOT and CANNOT and yes, I HAVE EMOTIONS. You know, I think a book is successful when it gives me a whirlwind of emotion-barfing, so well done, Crown of Midnight. No matter how you felt about Throne of Glass--seriously, even if you hated it--please read Crown of Midnight. TRUST ME. (And if you don't like it then I think you need to see a doctor.) 
 In short: READ THIS BOOK. (But read Throne of Glass first, obvi.) In the meantime, I'm going to wait for The Assassin's Blade to magically appear in my hands, and I'm going to impatiently wait for ALL THINGS Heir of Fire. (Yes, I would kill for that book, sorry not sorry.) Seriously, fantasy--something I haven't read much of--might be becoming my new favorite genre. Crown of Midnight has everything: suspense, tension, adventure, murder, mystery, romance, humor, magic, shockers and surprises, a ship that'd eat the Titanic for lunch, a swoony boy (who's mine, I'll fight you for him), a KILLER ending, and so much more, oh my! Really, NEED I say more?
Amazing! Better than the first.

sample_reviews.review_text:
'The Bees' by Laline Paull is an adventure novel set within a beehive, starring Flora 7-17, a sanitation bee born with special skills that set her apart from her kin. It's filled with fascinating detail and plenty of action. 
 I listened to The Bees as an audiobook over the course of a couple of months on my runs. I'm not sure how well this book would have held my interest had I read it on paper; as it was it provided a very welcome distraction from running.

3.5 stars, really. Strange book, and though I was interested enough to read to the end (after the first third, which was a bit of a slog), I'm still a bit divided about it. I thought the setup, which is kind of The Handmaid's Tale meets Watership Down meets 1984-slash-Animal Farm, was interesting. And I like what she took on with world-building--in this case a beehive. But the storyline got repetitive in places, which ended up making the social commentary feel heavy-handed, and that kind of thing is always better in less-is-more mode, as far as I'm concerned. 
 Also it was somewhat hard to latch on to the main character, especially once the drones--the males--came into the picture and were given all personality in the story. Which I realize was the point: the hive is full of female bees that are basically interchangeable within their given roles, and this is what happens when one bee breaks out of hers. I get it. But there was something slightly off-putting about the males being the only really interesting personalities, at least until the main character's hubris kicks in. 
 But in spite of those complaints, it kept me reading. The world-building was a lot of fun, and the fact that the world was a beehive was fascinating in itself. I think, in the end, what flattened it for me was how little humor or any sense of irony there was. Even a serious book has room for a bit of edge, and I wish there had been more. Still, it was such a different book--which ultimately kept me reading straight through, so kudos to Paull for pulling it off.

Although this book is very different from most books I read I really enjoyed it. The story is told from the point of view of Flora 717, a worker bee. How the author has humanized bees is hard to describe; you start to forget that the characters aren't human.

I had really high hopes for this book, despite some of the reviews I read. The premise, a narration by a bee about class, caste, loyalty, ability, race, etc. has so much potential...but I just couldn't get into this book. I stuck it out hoping I was either missing something or that it would get better. Unfortunately neither happened for me. 
 I don't recommend this book.

Laline Paull is a British playwright. Her debut novel, The Bees describes life in a cultivated beehive. In this text, we follow Flora 717, a bee born with something unique-- something unique which makes her stick out in a society where being the same is critical to success and survival. 
 What drew me to The Bees initially was an interview with the author I discovered on io9. See, science fiction is often exploring where science can take us in the future. We push the boundaries of what is known in texts like Orson Wells The Time Machine, or in Issac Asimov's I Robot. New planets, races, and technologies are discovered, which in turn inspire humanity to keep reaching further and further. Science fiction rarely explores the science we have in front of us for what it is. And what's exactly what Laline Paull does here. 
 Paull felt this book was just waiting to be written when she learned about bees. About the drones who are massacred once a year, or how multiple princesses will fight each other for dominance and the crown, or the scientifically defined "fertility police" who will hunt down worker bees that end up laying eggs instead of the queen-- killing the bee and eating the eggs. It's terrifying stuff! No wonder she was inspired to write a book! I picked up The Bees expecting a dystopian science-fiction novel with anthropomorphic bees. Bring it on. 
 Yet, once I started reading, nothing about the book really grabbed me (Honestly, I was so bored with it, I put off writing this review for three months to get away from it). I realized around halfway through I had been waiting for the next thing to happen so the book will really get started since the beginning. And yet, nothing seemed like "the next thing". I was always waiting without knowing why. Waiting for Godot anyone? 
 Laline's prose was beautiful at times. I found some gorgeous lines that I read over and over purely out of the enjoyment of the phrase. And yet, it seemed like the author herself wasn't certain where she was going with the story. It seemed she lacked follow through to her own metaphors of humanity. One second I'd feel like I was being beaten over the head with a metaphor, and the next minute it would vanish as though it had never been there. 
 By the end of this book, I just didn't understand why Laline's primer book was such an "It" book of Summer 2014. It's intriguing and different. I love some of the truly poetic phrases, as well as how it challenges science fiction to explore what is in front of us a bit deeper. But I just couldn't find myself caring.

book_b.user_review:

 ******Spoilers****** 
 Notes to self - not a review. 
 I cannot believe this is my first Ray Bradbury book. It would have scared the bejesus out of me when I was 12 or 13. Must Rent Movie! 
 Cooger and Dark's Pandemonium Shadow Show arrives in town the week before Halloween. There's just something about a carnival! This particular show has a house of mirrors that drives visitors insane and a carousel ride that adds or subtracts years to the rider. And the freaks are freaky.

 A couple faves: 
 *pg 222 re the fortune teller: "her great proboscis with the nostrils caked like tobacco-blackened pipe bowls" 
 *pg 190: ...and the boy with the eyes that had seen all the glistery tripes of the world shaped like hung-and-dripping sins and all the sins tenterhooked and running red and verminous, this boy with the eyes of a man who has lived forever, seen too much, might like to die but doesn't know how...

sample_reviews.review_text:
The carnial arrives in Green thumb Illinois between midnight and dawn. Cooger and Dark's Pandemonium Shadow Show has lured two young boys who share a deep and binding friendship into its malevolent mysterious world. Their dreams and hopes soon become nightmares. 
 I don't quite understand why this novel has long been considered a 'classic'. The writing was inconsistent. Bradbury apparently had some very specific thoughts he wanted to convey but these remained in his head and were never sorted out in the narrative. The philosophical ruminations of a middle aged man while eloquent and lyrical were somewhat disjointed and did not serve to tie the plot together. 
 I am generally empathetic to stories written in their time but I found some of the 'chauvinistic' tendencies difficult to tolerate. 
 Totally a 'boy book' and would thereby be attractive to young reluctant readers and to the child that remains in the man.

Something Wicked This Way Comes is the story of two boys (about 11 or so), presumably sometime in the 50s. A dark carnival comes to town promising to fulfill your dreams. But nothing is for free - not even dreams. The two boys are exposed to the dark underside of want and desire and fight to save themselves and their town. 
 I wanted to like this book much more than I did. In mulling over my reaction to the book, I thought about expectations. How evil are expectations? With no expectations (or low expectations) I will be pleasantly surprised and think about how great a book is. With high expectations, it is almost impossible for a book to live up to what I want it to be. Something Wicked This Way Comes is a good book. It is just not a great book. And I was expecting (for whatever reason) a great book. Something dark, and creepy, and sinister. Something wicked. It wasn't. 
 At times the book was downright awesome. When the boys are hiding beneath the grating and the carnival is parading through town... wow. Very intense. I can smell the carnies even now. 
 The writing, I think, is part of what bugged me about the book. Bradbury uses an almost lyrical tone to the book. Something, for example, isn't just "slick" or "slippery." Instead it is "slick as silk off a cat's back." This is OK, but it is not to my taste. I prefer more direct language. 
 Three out of four stars. A good, October read.

I finished this on a jog while the slaughter in Nice, France was fresh on my mind, so maybe that helped me appreciate the idealistic, feel-good mechanism used to end the book more than I would have otherwise. Bad guys use fear as a weapon. They thrive on instilling it in others. But how do you fight an enemy you don't understand? Can love defeat hatred? 
 Before you read this, go look up a bunch of quotes from this book. It's almost like poetry in novel form. That can be good or bad. Me, I'm not so good at poetry, and often in this book the charming prose unfortunately made it hard to follow. Other times it was very compelling.

I'm sorry. I really wanted to like this book but it just did not work for me. I could give you a plethora of reasons as to why this might be so, but the bottom line still stands in that I just did not like this. I think I somewhat understood what Bradbury was trying to get across, but I had such a hard time sifting through his words that even that may not be true. In a nutshell, I feel the underlying theme was 'Don't worry, be happy,' for lack of a better term. Laughter is the best medicine. Appreciate who you are. These are some other themes I took away from it. I also saw in the book what could be compared to an addict in early recovery. In that I mean, the main characters were being tempted by their innermost desires and it was essentially a book long struggle only to come to its inevitable climax in which I will not ruin. It was a book for me where I really had to struggle in getting through a page and was actually getting angry at many times because I just could not get it. It just was not sinking in for me and was a chore and that is just not fun when trying to read. I kept hoping it would get more 'readable' but it didn't. A lot of the book just did not make any sense to me, like he was speaking in a completely different language. It was like trying to read an incredibly boring and monotonous history book in school and you knew you had to get through it to understand it for the upcoming test, but found yourself spending an hour on one page and mentally chastising yourself because your mind would keep wandering to what you were having for dinner and the like, rather than being able to absorb and love what you had in front of you. All this being said, I can still see where some folks may eat this right up and as a Goodreads buddy said, it is a very divided book in terms of like and dislike and I most certainly fall on the latter side. I should also say that I am not a big fan of poetry. I respect the hell out of it and would never bash anyone on their love for it, but it just has never been for me for whatever reason. I bring up poetry because I do believe that if you are into poetry and deep prose then this might be right up your alley and would be willing to bet that the major dividing line in terms of those who like and dislike this book would be comparable to those who like and dislike poetry. Of course there are going to be those who dislike poetry and love this book and vice versa however I do think that there might be some truth behind this. So that about sums up my thoughts on this and would love to hear what others think about it!
