book_a.title: The Handmaid's Tale
book_a.user_review: Really enjoyed this book. It was quite different. Loved the futuristic concept. It was way ahead of it's time for 1985.

sample_reviews.review_text: A theocratic military dictatorship has taken over the United States and declining births due to widespread sterility threatens society. Handmaids are concubines assigned to members of the ruling class in order to bear their children. Women have no rights, existing solely to reproduce. Atwood's vision is quite horrific, but I think the real story of gender inequality at present and throughout history is much worse. As history has shown, there doesn't need to be the threat of sterility for men to attempt to control every aspect of women's bodies and lives. A commendable novel, but a bit clumsy and underdeveloped.

Let me tell you something about Margaret Atwood. She is truly poetic. The Handmaid's Tale was a really good novel, but what I loved most about it was the writing style. 
 But I'm getting ahead of myself. 
 Lets discuss plot. Offred is a handmaid. What's a handmaid you ask? They're hired mistresses - although hired is a loose word as they didn't APPLY for this job. In Offred's society, women were stripped of all their rights, and select few women who were fertile were taken and forced to be handmaids. They were placed with rich Commanders - and their wives - and forced to have sex in order to produce a baby for the family. Offred remembers a time when she was in love, married and had a child of her own. Everything was taken from her. Everything was taken from everyone. Then the Commander Offred is placed with tries to be her friend - in secret of course. She realizes just how much better the upper class has it. Along the way, Offred meets Ofglen - her partner to walk to town with who teaches her about the resistance. Offred also meets Nick - who inspires in her a very illegal desire. 
 Like I said, the plot - while good - was not the shining glory for this novel. 
 Here are some examples of amazing writing in this novel: 
 "Waste not want not. I am not wasted. Why do I want?" 
 "My self is a thing I must now compose, as one composes a speech." 
 "In hope.Why did they put that above a dead person? Was it the corpse hoping or those still alive?" 
 Chills, right? 
 The novel was amazing, and it gets better with analysis. If you still want dystopian - but want REALLY good dystopian - this is the book for you. 
 Also, if you LOVE poetic writing - also the book for you. 
 Seriously, read it.

i've been struggling to write a review on this one because this is one of those extremely rare and special books--in fact, i'm trying to think of another that i can put in this category--that hit me in a VERY personal way. i don't mean that in a "this book was beautiful and made me cry and really stuck with me!" kind of way. i mean that in a "this book struck me in the core of what i believe and identify with" kind of way. i mean that in a "i'm getting a 'nolite te bastardes carborundorum' tattoo on my body" kind of way. my reaction to reading it was physical. i haven't stopped thinking about it since i finished it. no, i haven't stopped thinking about it since i read its first page. i am friggin flabbergasted that i didn't read it until i was 30 years old (the same age as this book!). because it is everything. how to put that into words? i'll try. 
 i love being a woman. it sounds like a duh, but my femaleness is such a massive part of my identity. i think about being a woman every day. i suspect most women do. i think about all of the wonderful things that come with being a woman every day. i celebrate other women every day. i celebrate myself every day! i also think about all of the terrible things that women have to endure every day. 
 i'm not overly familiar with dystopia as a genre. i suppose an essential element is that the society depicted has to have some basis of reality in history. they're scary because they're possible, because they've happened before, whether in bits and pieces or scattered throughout time and cultures. they're commentaries about what can happen when a structure of damaging practices or ideals becomes the norm. i've read a lot of reviews of the handmaid's tale on here over the past couple of days, and it's clear to me that a lot of readers experienced the story in this way--as a warning. as a terrifying visualization of what COULD be possible. as a literal interpretation of the dangers of extreme right religion (even though i feel that the text is pretty straightforward that religion is simply a guise here), or as something that felt implausible in our reality today but might have stronger correlations to what women endure in other countries where their liberties are far more endangered than they are here (valid, of course). 
 but here's the thing. i read this book as a woman, living in america, in 2016, and the real scary part is this: regardless of what margaret atwood's intentions were, regardless of when it was written or the circumstances that created it, it is disturbingly relevant today. this is happening NOW. there is so much that resonated with what i have experienced, what women i know have experienced, what women i DON'T know but read about every day have experienced. this is a commentary about female bodies and ownership, about women's autonomy, about how our society views rape and violence against women and victimhood and how it forgives and humanizes perpetrators, about patriarchy, about female sexuality, about silencing, about complacency. and it is chilling. 
 i'm going to just do a series of excerpts here to wrap up, because i'm failing at expressing how much this book impacted me and how important it is, and there were so many passages that were so powerful and so relevant to the kind of thinking i read on facebook, in news stories, from court rooms and police stations and the media. like this one: 
 "But whose fault was it? Aunt Helena says, holding up one plump finger. 
 Her fault, her fault, her fault, we chant in unison. 
 Who led them on? Aunt Helena beams, pleased with us. 
 She did. She did. She did. 
 Why did God allow such a terrible thing to happen? 
 Teach her a lesson. Teach her a lesson. Teach her a lesson. 
 Last week, Janine burst into tears. Aunt Helena made her kneel at the front of the classroom, hands behind her back, where we could all see her, her red face and dripping nose. Her hair dull blond, her eyelashes so light they seemed not there, the lost eyelashes of someone who's been in a fire. Burned eyes. She looked disgusting: weak, squirmy, blotchy, pink, like a newborn mouse. None of us wanted to look like that, ever. For a moment, even though we knew what was being done to her, we despised her. 
 Crybaby. Crybaby. Crybaby. 
 We meant it, which is the bad part. 
 I used to think well of myself. I didn't then. 
 That was last week. This week Janine doesn't wait for us to jeer at her. It was my fault, she says. It was my own fault. I led them on. I deserved the pain. 
 Very good, Janine, says Aunt Lydia. You are an example." 
 or this one: 
 "She did not believe he was a monster. He was not a monster, to her. Probably he had some endearing trait: he whistled, offkey, in the shower, he had a yen for truffles, he called his dog Liebchen and made it sit up for little pieces of raw steak. How easy it is to invent a humanity, for anyone at all. What an available temptation. A big child, she would have said to herself. Her heart would have melted, she'd have smoothed the hair back from his forehead, kissed him on the ear, and not just to get something out of him either. The instinct to sooth, to make it better. There there, she'd say, as he woke from a nightmare. Things are so hard for you. All this she would have believed, because otherwise how could she have kept on living?" 
 or this one: 
 "He stops at the foot, his fingers encircling the ankle, briefly, like a bracelet, where the tattoo is, a Braille he can read, a cattle brand. It means ownership. 
 I remind myself that he is not an unkind man; that, under other circumstances, I even like him. ... 
 He is not a monster, I think. I can't afford pride or aversion, there are all kinds of things that have to be discarded, under the circumstances. ... Fake it, I scream at myself inside my head. You must remember how. Let's get this over with or you'll be here all night. Bestir yourself. Move your flesh around, breathe audibly. It's the least you can do." 
 or this one: 
 "Maybe none of this is about control. Maybe it isn't really about who can own whom, who can do what to whom and get away with it, even as far as death. Maybe it isn't about who can sit and who has to kneel or stand or lie down, legs spread open. Maybe it's about who can do what to whom and be forgiven for it. Never tell me it amounts to the same thing." 
 a favorite: 
 "The newspaper stories were like dreams to us, bad dreams dreamt by others. How awful, we would say, and they were, but they were awful without being believable. They were too melodramatic, they had a dimension that was not the dimension of our lives. We were the people who were not in the papers. We lived in the blank white spaces at the edges of print. It gave us more freedom. We lived in the gaps between the stories." 
 there are endless examples. the handmaid's tale is brilliant, beautifully written, soul crushing and disturbing, and i love it and i hope i keep thinking about it all the time forever.

This book was so boring, I kept waiting for it to pick up and it never did.

Margaret Atwood is a filthy hypocrite. Apparently she considers herself an environmentalist, but she has to be the biggest tree-murderer in history. This is a short story. Not a novel. But for some reason it's spaced out over 150 pages, with another 150 being used as a lengthy prologue to the actual plot, and a 20 page epilogue that would be very satisfying if it were attached to the end of a well-written novel. 
 It is one of the most painfully tedious books I've ever read. 
 Feeble character building through overly abstract description (it's like reading drunk: you get a vague idea of one thing in a scene, an egg or a fence or some nonsense, and nothing else) and wishy-washy reflections from the narrator that don't actually serve to develop her. As a consequence, the few things Offred does (and she really doesn't do a lot at all) don't really make any sense. "Oh, she believes this now. No, wait, she doesn't. She wants to kill herself? Yes? No? She wants to be defiant? Maybe. She's having sex with someone and probably has feelings about it. Let's randomly flashback to some other vague scene and change tense and maybe take speech marks out or maybe not. Yay! This is Good Literature!" 
 Despite the fact that the plot could very nearly be boiled down to a piece of flash fiction, the remaining space isn't used to build a detailed picture of the setting (and no wonder, because as soon as you examine the few details Atwood feeds you, you find the whole thing falls apart and your Suspension of Disbelief hangs itself from a chandelier). 
 And on that note...yeah, this isn't a good dystopia. It's not 1984 or Brave New World. Somehow, it's not even Hunger Games. The best dystopias reflect a real and terrifying possibility. Brave New World does that even today. 1984 certainly did at the time of writing, even if it doesn't any more. But this... 
 Listen, America. I know y'all (am I doing your slang right?) couldn't run a country to save your lives. 
 I know you've gone so far to the right that you consider anyone who walks past a homeless man and doesn't gun him down with one of the six uzis that you're all permitted to carry (for some reason) while screaming something about welfare to be a "filthy socialist". 
 I know your fundamentalist Christian communities are zealous enough to make Oliver Cromwell say "Now, hold on, I think you're taking this God thing a bit too seriously" and that even your average person can't get through a sentence without loudly decrying the principle of separation of church and state and trying to bully a gay teen into committing suicide in the name of Jesus. 
 I know you just elected Donald Trump (no snarky hyperbole needed here; this one's mental enough as is). 
 I know all that. But I still don't think this is a plausible dystopia. 
 Because if there's one thing your government is good at, it's grinding to a halt without everyone dying (except the poor, but I understand that poor people dying is business as usual for you). It's pretty much designed to grind to a halt (which is a good thing, apparently). And you have levels of devolution that would make a Scottish Nationalist laugh in derision. 
 So the idea that the USA could be turned into a straw-man Christian theocracy that oppresses half the population simply because terrorists gunned down two-thirds of a central government that doesn't function anyway is absurd. 
 And it's absurd that women like Offred, who were born and raised into a society that wasn't Saudi-Arabia-on-steroids (modern America, of course, is Saudi-Arabia-taking-a-coffee-break), would suddenly become all passive (and weirdly philosophical but in a way that doesn't produce any meaningful conclusions) just because a bunch of right-wing nutters killed another bunch of right-wing nutters. 
 So what is this novel for? It's not entertaining, it's not clever or innovative. We've established (by reductio ad sarcasmus) that it isn't prescient or socially valuable. 
 Thus, I can only assume that its primary purpose was to kill trees.
It was fine but ultimately not much happened.

I read this for my book club. I wasn't expecting too much, because 1) it wasn't fitting with my "reading what you feel called to read" plan, and 2) I've read two other books by Atwood, and although they were decent, I felt they were lacking something. This book is probably my favorite of hers that I've read. I still felt like it was missing something to a certain extent, but I felt less that way after finishing it. I did like the way it ended. 
 For those who somehow don't already know about this book, it's dystopia that's actually set in the past (it was published in 1985, but by that point in the book's own timeline, things were already starting to go down). The main features of the new regime are totalitarianism (of course), heavy surveillance (I guess this goes along with totalitarianism), and super rigid gender roles. And lots of sexism. It's pretty bleak. 
 For me, it wasn't scary in the way of "oh I'm so worried something like this could actually happen" (although, knock on wood, why not). It was the parts that reminded me of things that already happen in my life that were the most disturbing. I think the most unsettling scene of the book was where the main character simultaneously has her bank account frozen and is fired from work at gunpoint because women were no longer allowed property or work, and her husband was like, "o cmon is just a job u kno ill always take care of u babe." Ughhhhh. Yeah. Unfortunately, I feel like that was super realistic. I think this book is so impactful for many readers not because they're scared of the future it presents but because elements of it remind them of how things stand currently. 
 Atwood is not a great world builder here, although I guess she thought it was somewhat unnecessary as her purposes here are more about the concept than the plot, and she pays special attention to mood and tone. And that she does well. It's an ominous feeling book. 
 Overall, it's a worthwhile book. I am definitely looking forward the book club discussion for this one!

book_b.title: Back to Blood
book_b.user_review: Just hated the writing. The conversations between the characters are terrible. He's trying too hard to sound young and hip which just makes the book irritating to read.

sample_reviews.review_text: Five word review: Bonfire of Miami police vanities
couldn't get into this story.

I don't even know what I just read (technically listened to as it was an audiobook). 
 I hated how Magdalena didn't know what certain phrases meant. She is a nurse which implies medical training. Pretty sure she would know what a metaphor is. 
 And what happened to some of the characters? They just disappeared! No explanation. 
 I almost lost my mind during the early boat scene when the narrator shouted SMACK a million times.

I listened to the hachette audio version, and almost gave up after two hours of Lou Diamond Phillips. In retrospect the enjoyment of the story overcame the quality of narration that put me off, and I end up giving it three stars as a compromise. Wolfe comes through as a great storyteller, and although I've spent almost no time in Miami I feel as though he's given me a good overview of life there. What is it about Phillips? He almost does a reasonable job with making me believe he's is voicing a Cuban, or Black English, or Russian speaker - but that seems the limit. It was difficult at times to sense the switch from dialog to narration.

What an ordeal!!!! BAM!!! POW!!! WHAMMO!!!! Annoyed yet? This is just a tiny taste of what Back to Blood was like to read. Tom Wolfe's first novel in 8 years looks at Miami the same way that Bonfire of the Vanities addressed Manhattan, and A Man in Full explored Atlanta. Wolfe repeats his usual formula of a vast array of characters, satiric tone, and paragraphs full of irritating onomatopoeic devices, over-punctuated with caps on steroids and exclamation points. At 704 pages, Wolfe could easily have accomplished the same effect with a mere 500 pages just by eliminating the verbal histrionics. I finished the book just so I could say that Wolfe didn't defeat me, but it was a tough go. If my own writing students had handed in similar pieces, I would've returned them with one word: EDIT!!!!!
I will have to try this one again, maybe in the summer.

As much as I wanted to believe this book would be better than the reviews, it was a huge disappointment. Could not get into the story or like any of the characters, and the funky punctuation and sentence structure was really grating.

Unless you are considering relocating to Miami, or live in Miami I cannot recommend this book. It makes me want to crawl back into the loving embrace of the 19th c.--Jane Austen, Henry James, Dickens, Edith Wharton "time machine take me away." I have had it with the genre of Jonathan Franzian existential ethnology of modern 21st alientation and ADD. If I want to feel bad, I don't need to shell out $23.00 in hardcover and slog through 700 unentertaining pages, all I gotta do is get on the Miami Dade Metrorail and schlep my post millenial Anglo ass to work in this city "where everyone hates everyone" (which is the most quoted and patently hyperbolic excerpt from this well-written "feel bad" read).

An interesting look into the country that is Miami, focusing on Art Basel, the Miami PD, the struggle that some Cubans face as they try to fit in, and the struggle that other races have in relation to the high Cuban population. 
 Fast paced, thrilling, and insightful. I dug it.

Ghastly boring...boring...boring. Gratuitous, inane sex scenes. Incoherently obnoxious plot twists. Characters you just don't care about. Any positives...book design is phenomenal...unfortunately the book is not.

reference_books.title: Clockwork Angel (The Infernal Devices, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I am leaning towards to this series more than The Mortal Instruments, probably due to a bias I have regarding Victorian England, English guys with accents IMO better than American accents, the COVER OMG STEAMPUNK COVER, and the amount of feels this book [edit: ENTIRE TRILOGY] is able to instil in me - a cold, unfeeling person. 
 Other than that, this book has things I relate to, such as: 
 drinking tea, playing the violin, and hating ducks (I see them at uni and regard them with mild suspicion whilst everyone coos over them). Will also makes references to hedgehogs <3. 
 And there are TWO HOT GUYS one who is a 'halfie'. 
 Just...ALKASLDKLLKGHDL! I have no words.

reference_books.title: The Knife of Never Letting Go (Chaos Walking, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This book, amongst other things, have made me realise my brain is different and weird. 
 I don't understand the appeal of Peter Alexander pyjamas or Body Shop products or Tiff & Co. sometimes...like why is it OK to buy someone necessities such as soap as a gift but only if it is from The Body Shop? "you smell but this is from The Body Shop so it's socially appropriate,"? 
 Anyway, much like the above, I encountered the same problem with this book. 
 I found the plot was interesting and fast-paced, but I feel like there's supposed to be some deeper meaning, something poignant, hidden in this novel...and I'm missing it somehow? I thought I'd find it more thought-provoking than I did? 
 I mean, my thought process was: 
 "Are Ben and Cillian gay?" "Are they 'together'?" 
 "Aaron is a religious nutter. Oh this is beautifully ironic." 
 "Ben is a beautiful soul." 
 "hahaha the dog said 'poo'!" 
 "Why would they say 'whirler'? I don't get it." 
 "When Todd says, 
 'Each of us knowing the other.' 
 about him and Viola -- is that 'knowing' in the biblical sense?" 
 "I wanna know what's in the diary...hey it sounds like a Moleksine...ooh Hobbit Moleskine...I don't get why Moleksines are so expensive; they're not even leather and are merely designed in Italy but manufactured in China. oh look, yet another well-marketed product where it's OK to get someone necessities but only if it's a particular brand!" 
 "I wonder what their profit margin is...?" 
 As you can see, I was thoroughly emotionally detached from this book. I didn't even come close to almost crying or tearing up at all. Not even when Ben sacrificed himself or when Manchee died . 
 I enjoyed it I feel like I should've enjoyed it more than I did -- I mean, DYSTOPIAN!, the ideas and concepts were interesting; Ness portrayed the effects of mob-mentality on humans and how something insane becomes OK if enough people believe it, and wow humans are such sheep. 
 Also, this is pretty sexual - the sexual tension between Todd and his knife: 
 "Take me, it says-- 
 Take me and use me, it says-- 
 Never let me go, says the knife-- " 
 If you don't think that's sexually inappropriate then you're wrong.

reference_books.title: Fallen (Fallen, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
The cover is the only redeeming factor of this book. 
 The 'protagonist' is a total Mary-Sue. This is pretty much Twilight but with Nephilim and a nicer cover. 
 It has a good plot *idea*. Key-word: IDEA. But it is really tragically-written. Because, you know, if you were immortal, you'd want to spend your days in reform school instead of say, finding a cure for cancer. 
 Why do higher-beings always hang out and chill incognito in school? 
 I can't believe I finished reading this book. 
 I don't know why I didn't register that this book was badly written until I finished it...I think I kept telling myself it would get better.

reference_books.title: The Girl in the Steel Corset (Steampunk Chronicles, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This (supposedly) had everything I'd've thought I'd like: kick-ass heroines, hot Irish ranga chick, guys with English accents, Steampunk etc., but unfortunately, I found this novel very average. 
 The Steampunk genre felt almost exploited here; there were a few interesting (but unoriginal) concepts added (Organites, the aether, maybe?), but other than that it just felt like the author threw every Steampunk cliche into a mixing pot and splattered the mixture on paper and called it The Steampunk Chronicles. 
 There was nothing spectacular about the plot, in fact it was thoroughly predictable. There was something "off" about the writing style too - it was pretty poor, if I'm perfectly honest, and I think the word to describe it is "trashy". 
 There was a ridiculous love triangle and the guys were so tacky or cardboard - one or the other. 
 I do want to know what happens but I don't think I can bring myself to read the sequels.

reference_books.title: Torment (Fallen, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
I don't know why I bothered to continue...I blame the covers again, and also, the clever *idea* for the plot which I wanted to see through to the end... 
 It's great because unlike Twilight people DIE. 
 At least the protagonist was a bit more assertive and less Mary-Sue in this book, but still, what I don't understand is, WHY THE HELL (hah hah no pun intended - OMG it's a double entendre - geddit??) IS SHE HIDING OUT IN A SCHOOL? WHY ARE THERE NEPHIL IN SCHOOL? WHAT'S WITH THE NEED TO PUT IMMORTALS AND HIGHER BEINGS IN SOMETHING AS MUNDANE AND UNNECESSARY AS SCHOOL?!?! It just RUINS it. Even more. Nothing screams 'LAZY' more than other-world beings pretending to be mere mortals and hiding out in school. 
 The worst bit is, I feel like I need to find out what happens in the end. I just wish it was written...well.

book_a.title: Bones of Faerie (Bones of Faerie, #1)
book_a.user_review:
2.5 stars 
 Read this while listening to: "Ghost River" by Nightwish. 
 This story was like a cross between The Knife of Never Letting Go (the post-apocalyptic setting, the dangerous adults, the story of a journey) and Coraline (the dark fairy tale, creepy world, untrustworthy adults)... 
 I found the plot dark and oddly beautiful, but the novel suffered from a lack of characteriasation. All the main characters were basically nothing more than a name on a page to me. 
 However, my little (9-year-old) sister, being the child of darkness that she is / I have been raising her to be, has been stealing this book to read whenever I put it down, so I foresee her enjoying this a lot more than I did, since she LOVED Coraline.

sample_reviews.review_text:
A war between Earth and Faerie has left the world changed and ruined forever, where even the plants and trees are no longer to be trusted and will even kill you if they have the chance. Sound awesome? I think so! But unfortunately for me, the execution made on this story about a post-apocalyptic future touched by the effects of magic just didn't live up to my expectations. 
 As I said, I really liked the idea the author was working with here and is the reason I read this book. A war between the people of Earth and Faerie sounded too good to pass up, and the general story itself was interesting enough to hold my attention the whole way through. However, the characters were so flat and uninteresting half the time that I felt zero connection with any of them save for perhaps Allie. I felt like I was thrown head first into the story without getting to know the characters so that I could feel for them or care about their struggles. Matthew is a great example of this. Even the elements of surprise, those I felt that the author was trying to achieve, were lackluster and had no meaning because it was like they were dumped on me too soon without any sort of build up. I did like some of the characters, but I wish they could have been fleshed out more so I didn't have to feel so disconnected. 
 My biggest criticism about the story is the main character. I just plain didn't like her. And the fact that the narrative was spoken by her, it made it all the worse. She was two-dimensional, depressing, and straight out annoying. However, considering her situation, like her father abusing her and other sad things that's revealed about her life, it's somewhat understandable. But again, the writing here couldn't bring it all together in a way that I could relate to her. If you don't mind an "emo" (couldn't think of a better word for it) character and narrative then you will probably like this book a lot more than I did. I'm just not into that sort of thing. 
 A lot of the description in this book was really nice, and the way the author painted this post-apocalyptic world was, as I mentioned earlier, interesting enough to hold my attention, although some of the ideas to describe somethings were just plain bad in my opinion. For example, magic touched people have clear hair. Hair as clear as glass. I can't help, I think that's really stupid. On the other hand, the way the forest operated was awesome. I wouldn't want to live in such a place but reading about it was great. 
 So, you may be thinking "why give this book three stars if you sound like you didn't like it that much?" Perhaps it sounds that way but I honestly did like the story itself well enough. Even though I found the execution not to my liking, the main character annoying, the characters two-dimensional, I thought it was a good little story about a post-apocalyptic future and magic. It's not the best story I've read but it was still good.

Maybe it should be retitled to The Absent Faeries because this book has no interaction with the fey at all. Besides a world that's gone slightly wonky, the fey were absent. I understand the title of the story (BONES of Faerie) might mean that the plot takes place in a time when the fey have come and gone. 
 But how boring is that? 
 Some of the characters have magic, the world is a little dangerous, but what makes that plot any bit unique? I got myself too hyped for this book.
Fae

This book really has so much promise that I'm more disappointed for it than anything. It started off really well. The writing is beautiful in it's simplicity, the characters are immediately likable and sweet. I was confused why people on my friend's list had rated it so low. As I kept going, I finally started going "Ah, now I see." 
 Unfortunately throughout 75% of this story, I felt like I had been dropped into a book halfway through. As though this was book three in a series and I hadn't read the first two. Nothing is ever really explained. The war, Faerie as a land, the extent of magic and who has it, what the world is really like now. It's all very shallow and self contained. Had the author opened it up to a grander scale, this would have been an incredible story. 
 As it is, I probably won't pick up the next book. But this was a quick and mildly fun read on its own.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Major Spoilers!!! 
 I stopped reading this book because I found out the cat gets killed near the end. That might seem like a silly reason to stop reading a book, but I'm not the kind of person who enjoys the death of a characters beloved animal (as im sure most people do not) and i just dont want to read about it in this particular case, so I'll be giving this book to a friend or to the library...
Wonderful first book in the Faerie series! Janni's books reflect her incredible creative personality!!

Fun Fairytale Remix 
 Bones of Faerie is an interesting mix of the post-apocalyptic and fairy-tale. Set in a not-too-distant future, after a cataclysmic war between humans and the fey that left their world a radioactive wasteland, and ours in deadly, never-ending enchantment (where trees have a taste for blood, and even the smallest creature cannot be trusted ), it tells the story of Liza, a 15-year-old girl who has grown up in a town where possessing magic is an automatic death-sentence. Even her baby sister, born with clear hair like spun glass, an obvious sign of fey contamination, falls victim to the cruel law. And now Liza, with something growing inside of her that could bring that death-law down on her own head, must make a choice, for herself, and for children like her sister who may be the future of their world. 
 Interesting enough to keep me reading, a little juvenile although that's not surprising as it is a children's book (more children or tween than teen or young adult). A little sparse on the magic (literally and figuratively) but solid overall. Three ***

This is a fantastic read for the Young Adult genre. Filled with faeries, magic, shape-shifters and, of course, mere humans, this book has everything that a younger reader could hope for. The story pulled me in from the first page, as the story unfolded, the writing simply flowed so that I was half-way through, then promising myself "one more chapter" I finished the entire book. The relationships in this story are unlikely, yet remarkably sweet, and somehow, just right. The fantasies are subtley woven throughout real-life matters, making a more believable and intriguing story. The twists and turns leave the reader unsure of what he/she hopes the characters will do next, yet the ending is satisfying. 
 I am giving this book 5 stars specifically as a Young Adult book. As a non-young Adult, the book could seem somewhat cursory---the story-line is great and the characters are rich; however, as a Young Adult book, the depth for an avid non-young adult may not be there.

Really interesting concept. I kinda wish the author had expanded it a little more; I was intrigued, but still had questions about the history of the whole situation. 
 In looking further, I noticed that this book was actually a result of NaNoWriMo, so AWESOME!
I simply hated this book!

book_b.user_review:
3.5 
 I was expecting to receive something poignant and life-changing from this but no...just nothing... 
 I guess my thoughts can be summarised as follows:

sample_reviews.review_text:
There isn't anything unique about this book. 
 However, there are pretty words and amazing meanings. 
 It's a book that you read quickly, with much emotion, and you'll probably remember forever. 
 And even though it wasn't unique, or magical, it was special and worth the read.
I enjoyed this young adult book with very smart characters who are doomed and suffering from cancer. Still not my favorite in the upcoming Tournament of Books.

Finished re-reading The Fault in Our Stars again today. It was just as tear jerking as I remember it being the first time I read it. It brought back memories of my own trials, triumphs and losses in life. And as I came to the end I had the same reaction as I did the previous time I read it- It's over?! I want more!

Rip my heart, why don't you?! 
 You'll need a tissue box. But read it.

This is a reread and was originally finished August 9th 2012 
 My review got deleted for this but basically the 4 stars stay because it's beautiful, but not giving it 5 stars 
 because the writing is very very flawed.

I admit I read this because my daughter loved it. I mean- really loved it-and very passionately begged me to read it. I enjoy reading books she loves because it gives us so much to discuss. That being said, it was very easy to understand WHY my almost 14 year old daughter loved this story. The character of Hazel is so well written, she is SUCH a teenager, that kids can't help but get her. And add to that the gallant, smart, slightly disrespectful but still nice Augustus Waters. Who wouldn't love this guy?? Even Hazel's parents like him. I know that almost everyone out there has already read and reviewed this, so I won't go into the story, except to say it was wonderful, romantic, funny, and extremely sad. If you haven't already, please read this book as soon as you can. And let me know how you liked it! 
 (and if you have a 14 year old daughter, get her this book)
Full of truths, the way only John Green can write. But writing about cancer is tricky, and by the end I found it a little too sentimental. Still a good book.

Once again, I've tried to read it. First time, I made it to about page seven. I didn't even get to the bit on America's Next Top Model. This time, I made it to page nineteen. See, I made progress? To me, from what I read of the book so far and what friends have gushed about to me, Green writes perfect prose -- and he does, the quotes I've read from this book are amazing -- and his characters are teenagers. Teenagers that don't exist. I know that these guys speak and think differently than I do because they had cancer, but I still grew up with teens. Not even the ones who read Green speak like his characters do.

After all the hype, I expected more. I was not impressed by this book. A bit too "teen" for me. I've read books like this before that are better. Yes, it was sad in the end, but it's like everything was okay in it's separate parts and didn't quite come together.

This is the first book by John green I've ever read. I was hesitant to read it because I try to stay away from hyped books and best sellers, and also because I knew it was YA and its not really my genre. However I enjoyed this book. It is fast paced, easy to read, funny and sad, and very complete. I liked the characters, they were very real and relatable. But the thing I enjoyed most in this book was the approach of cancer and death and life. It does not turn the characters into victims, it does not make you feel sorry or pity any of the characters. It celebrates life and the message of living the life you are dealt comes across very strongly. 
 It's pretty deep for a YA book. And although I did find the whole romance thing a bit cheesy, It made me be very grateful for being healthy and alive, and also I think that people who have struggled or are currently fighting cancer would appreciate it, I people treated them like regular people, and see far beyond their illness, because cancer does not define you. 
 I recommend it widely and I'm also curious to read more of this author.

reference_books.title: The History of Love
reference_books.review_text: This was a gorgeous book, with finely drawn characters. I put off reading it for a long time because the cover (an upside down picture of the ocean horizon) makes me dizzy. I'm glad I read it--however I wasn't entranced by it as I thought I should be, given how much many of my friends loved it. I thought it was a little too predictable (and I'm not actually that great at predicting plots). It was very evocative, but not actually enjoyable.

reference_books.title: My Real Children
reference_books.review_text:
I don't know how I feel about the whole "trigger warning" phenomenon, but I do think some books might benefit from notes to the potential reader. (Of course, that's also a good use of Goodreads.) So let me say up front that this deals with the aging of an old, beloved woman, and her gradual loss of memory. It's a wonderful book. And one that I would probably burn before giving to my mother, whose own mother occasionally has memory problems. This would be a very hard book for someone on the front lines of that kind of struggle. 
 However, it's also a well-written and fascinating book. Two stories interwoven that ask questions about the significance of single people in shaping world events and the nature of happy endings. 
 This book made me miss college literature classes. It would be very fun to read, discuss, and analyze this book alongside Life After Life.

reference_books.title: Zoo
reference_books.review_text:
I picked this book up, not because I had even the smallest expectation of enjoying it, but because I kept seeing copies of it at the airport when I was on my way to the annual Association of Zoos and Aquariums conference, and I was curious. I was shy a book to read on the plane, and the first 24 or so chapters were free on my Kindle. (This isn't quite as impressive as it sounds, given that the chapters run about 1,000 words each.) 
 Plus, I reasoned, even if it was awful, it'd be interesting to see how Patterson deals with anthrozoological issues. I figured it'd be interesting on at least a anthropological or sociological level. I looked forward to analyzing its fears and arguing with it. (Notice all the excuses I'm offering. That's because I deeply regret the poor decisions I made that resulted in me reading this book.) 
 Instead of an academic interest, though, as soon as I began reading a sickening sense of horror crept over. This book is worse than The Da Vinci Code. This book is worse than Twilight. This is, in fact, the worst book I've ever read. 
 I'm not sure which is the worst facet of this festering heap of detestableness, but I could break it down into a few headings of horrible: 
 1. The writing style. It's just awful. The chapters average about three or four pages. The sentences are all short and choppy and written in such an action-adventure cliche style that it comes off as a parody of itself. In fact, Dave Barry writing a parody of a Dan Brown novel has better prose than this. He actually used the phrase "rosy-fingered dawn," which I thought was illegal. He also threw in all sorts of things meant to be cute such as, when a grizzly is attacking his SUV in DC, "I assumed he wasn't from AAA." Ha ha. Very clever. At this point, I was rooting for the bear. 
 2. The stupidity of all the characters, without exception. The gist of the story is that the protagonist Jackson Oz is a "scientist" (more on this later) who believes that animals are going nuts and attacking humans. And yet he thinks nothing of keeping a chimpanzee in his apartment. Chimps are dangerous even if you're not confidently expecting the animal world to run amok. 
 3. The sexism. The first (and actually only) sex scene in the whole book is so flagrantly written to play up Oz's rampant masculinity and dominance that it was unintentionally hilarious. Later, when Oz meets his obligatory Sexy Science Babe, every single time she's mentioned he reminds us how gorgeous she is, how very pretty and delicate and small, how totally unlike every other scientist woman he's ever met. Blargh. Not only that, but her whole role is to admire, cheer-lead, support, fall in love, and need comforting and defending. 
 4. The "science." Patterson read, at maximum, two Wikipedia pages as research, and that was it. I would be surprised if he even got all the way through both of them. He may be able to spell hydrocarbon and grasp some extremely basic (third-grade-level) concepts of pollution, but clearly not chemical dissipation, bio-accumulation, or any other chemical, biological, or ecological process. He's just throwing around the words to sound important. And don't get me started on the acronyms. Also, no, Oz is not a "scientist." He got an undergrad in science. That's not the same thing. He's a hack. 
 5. The fact that, at a critical point in the plot, Patterson skips five years for no apparent reason except that he apparently got bored. 
 6. The totally unnecessary violence and sickening detail on animal deaths. I'm not even going to go into this. Seldom has a book given me the actual physical urge to regurgitate. 
 7. The ending. Or lack thereof. In a better, braver, deeper book, Patterson's choice for an ending might be brave or bittersweet or thought-provoking. Here it's an admission of defeat. If you're going to come up with some big thorny problem, you owe it to Science Fiction to at least try to come up with a solution or at least a message. "I dunno, we're screwed" doesn't cut it. Plus, do you expect me to believe they're not burning fossil fuels to stay warm up there in their ivory tower beyond the Arctic Circle? 
 This is a book that had to be downed quickly, much like a very unpleasant shot of hard liquor you're drinking for some unimaginable reason. I saw someone had it shelved as "burn so as not to inflict upon other library patrons." I thought she was exaggerating, but now I whole-heartedly back that decision up. This book has absolutely no redeeming qualities. 
 Deep down (Very deep down. Thousands of miles.) this book has two good points: 
 1. Humans are more distanced from animals than at any other time in history or pre-history and this is not a good thing. 
 2. We're affecting the environment in unknowable and dangerous ways. 
 But that's it. This is an execrable excuse for a book. It shouldn't even get a star. No one at all should read it, even as an example of everything you shouldn't do as a writer. Or an editor. Or a publisher. Or a human.

reference_books.title: To Say Nothing of the Dog (Oxford Time Travel, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
This is a time-travel story that is exceptionally well-done. The writing is witty, wry, and wonderful. I never quite did grasp all the nuances of the MacGuffin, but that's OK. 
 The plot twists, as they relate to characters, are a little bit predictable, but not any less enjoyable for that. 
 A sterling book.

reference_books.title: The Eye of the World (Wheel of Time, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This series lures you in. The author is a passable world builder. book_a.title: All the Birds in the Sky
book_a.user_review: What a beautiful, wonderful book. Neither strictly fantasy nor purely science fiction, this book marries both genres and, in the end, transcends both worldviews. There characters were remarkable and enjoyable. This was a perfectly balanced, incredibly joyful, optimistic, lovely book. It was exactly what I needed right now.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Not for the first time, Laurence thought this was one of the annoyingly incommunicative features in the English language. Much like the inability to distinguish between "x-or" and "and/ or," the lack of delineation between "x-we" and "in-we" was a conspiracy of obfuscation, designed to create awkwardness and exacerbate peer pressure--because people tried to include you in their "we" without your consent, or you thought you were included and then the rug got pulled out from under you. Laurence dwelled on this linguistic injustice as he watched his parents walk back to their car, across the crunchy parking lot, without him. 
 This was...I'm not sure what adjectives to use - the story was in parts charming, heartwarming, disturbing, sad and terrifying; optimistic and pessimistic in turn. 
 The writing was certainly delightful, but given how troubling parts of the story are, 'delightful' feels like the wrong word to use. The writing absolutely hooked me in from page 1 until around 2/3 of the way through. I love the juxtaposition of children's book style prose with adult themes, and I think the combination worked really well and kept me both engaged and off balance. (Actually that would work very well as an one phrase review - kept me engaged and off balance, and I loved it!) 
 In general, I enjoy following characters from childhood into adulthood (or at least getting flashbacks of protagonists as children), it sets context for their actions and shows us not just who they are, but why they are the way they are. I loved watching Laurence and Patricia (particularly Patricia) grow up. My favourite part of the book is her entrance back on to the scene as an adult - I could see it happen in my head and I could believe how Patricia's childhood led to her becoming Adult Patricia. I loved how all the elements of the story and major characters come together at the end, in weird, unexpected ways. 
 I really liked the romance developing in the background, subtle and absolutely integral to the plot. I love romance in sci-fi/fantasy, especially in books where one wouldn't otherwise expect it. Liked it enough to shelve the book under 'romance' since it is handled so well. 
 This book started off at a 5, and went down to about 4 in the middle. This is one of those books where the writing is also a character (unlike say, Sanderson, where the writing itself is unobtrusive), and I much preferred the writing in the first third of the book to the middle bits, where it sort of slowed down the story. 
 Such a strange, wonderful book though. I'm really looking forward to my reread.

This book is split into two sections. Part I is the childhood and teenage years, Part II is young adult/early adulthood years. There are two main protagonists, a male and a female. Personally I enjoyed Part I but could not get through Part II and didn't end up reading the book. It just got very tedious and I felt the author was trying too hard to be hip. It just didn't feel genuine. Got very bored.

Completely gripping, super-fun novel mostly set in speculative near-future San Francisco, set up as a sort of magic vs. tech conflict with an actually satisfying understanding of both magic AND tech--by which I mean, there's none of this Rowling bullshit about boy wizards and their mighty power wands. In Anders' universe, magic means balance, interconnectedness, the earth. I mean, finally! How hard is it? If, like me, you hated the way Rowling (& Lev Grossman etc) portray magic (as yet another way for humans to use the earth as a resource), and you also don't hate tech, you'll want to bring this book to the beach.

It's been a while since I've so failed to connect with a book, and I find myself honestly confused at the amount of acclaim and awards this book has received. 
 Based on premise and author I was looking forward to picking this one up, but as things got going I found the writing, dialogue and even characters to be jarring and shallow throughout. I also feel this book has serious pacing problems. It unfolds in awkward spurts and feels more like a series of vignettes than a cohesive work. 
 I went into this book with middling expectations and I'm sorry to say that I was still disappointed.

cross douglas coupland with rainbow rowell & throw in a little cixin liu for good measure, and you might come up with something like this genre-hopping ya novel. 
 the first and second halves of the book don't quite match up, but not a bad read otherwise.

The book didn't let me into its' world. 
 I hardly felt any connection, or sympathy, to any character of the book (well, that's something to say, being the characters are magicians and environmental villains..). 
 The lead characters, being abused mentally and physically by their families in their childhood, anti-social and bullied, suddenly grow up into this 'hip' magician and super-rich nerd, with lot of fine shag histories to tell. Whoop whoop. 
 (I say hip, because somehow the author apparently has this need to accentuate and insert the 'hipness' into any place the characters hangout) 
 Patricia is quite okay, actually. In fact, I really like the dark tone in the beginning of the novel, when she found out that she can talk to birds. But Laurence? Meh. Teenage Laurence is a whiny, self-absorbed, coward. And Adult Laurence is just the same apparently, seemed like that he never finish his puberty phase. 
 Main story is just ridiculous. A big storm coming in America and the leads somehow became the only saviors/heroes/saints of the world! While having overpriced coffee! 
 Why? because the world is collapsing when U.S military not there! 
 there's Arab Winter! (whatever that supposed to mean, it didn't explained) 
 the North Korea is coming! 
 Russians troops are moving west! 
 China's claimed border on South China Sea, OH NOOOOOO~~~!! 
 (not actually a news. it's already happening since the 19th century, dear.) 
 The solution? immigrate human population to a new planet. through a wormhole-sort-of-thing machine. 
 The time setting was questionable (twenty something years has gone and apparently nothing is quite different, in social-media tech and all). The trying-to be-hip-in-everything were gag-inducing. The sarcasm and the ironic jokes failed. The serious parts felt like joke. Hard to say anything about the quirky characters (Ernesto, Mr.Rose), because there's not enough to tell, even though they probably worth an attention. 
 Not that the imagination is not imaginative enough. 
 It's just so..unconvincing. 
 I don't feel any magic.

There were things I liked about this book and things I disliked, but overall I have to say that I was not wowed by All the Birds in the Sky. 
 In short, I liked the beginning of the book and the end but not so much the middle. The beginning is set during Patricia's and Laurence's childhoods, and it reads almost like a YA book. Like a really dark and sad YA book, I guess, as there is abuse, bullying, and a general feeling of darkness that runs alongside the story. There were certainly moments of fun and humor, but neither of the two really had great childhoods, and Anders doesn't shy away from showing the reader just now not great things were for them. I liked the two of them as kids - they were both awkward, shy, basically two nerds who really connected with each other. Something that bothered me about the beginning, even though I generally liked it, was that the abusive and destructive behavior of several characters was never discussed in-depth or dealt with in any way. There were some scary things that happened to these characters, stuff that was pretty much ignored and never talked about again. It did not ring true for me at all. 
 The transition in the book from their childhoods to adulthood felt shaky and really took me out of the story. And once we got into adulthood, I almost put the book down several times. It felt to me like it wasn't going anywhere, like it was rambly and not much was happening and I was just, frankly, bored by it. But there was one point where THINGS start happening, and I drew back into it, and I did really like the last third of the book. 
 The end of the book really shows the world falling apart, and it was scary but I loved how Anders described the slow unraveling of everything we know to be necessary in modern life. That part reminded me a little bit of Emily St John Mandel's Station Eleven. I liked the clashing of science and magic, and I liked how Patricia's magic wasn't this huge fantastical thing, but rather a minor element of her personality that came in handy sometimes and in some major ways. There's also a particular element of the book, it's a minor plot point but quite a spoiler, that I absolutely loved. One of those connection things that you go "ah!" as you read it. 
 So overall - not my favorite book, but I did enjoy parts of it. I'm glad I read All the Birds in the Sky and would still consider reading something else written by this author.
I liked the beginning, but the rest of the book was a mess.

I still don't know what to make of this book, but I enjoyed the first third or so. The tone was reminiscent of Lemony Snicket and Roald Dahl with its acerbic and good-hearted children navigating a cruel and absurd world. There was humor and wonder and an interesting friendship. 
 Then it gets a bit muddled once the protagonists became jaded and disaffected adults. Perhaps a stylistic choice, but it wasn't particularly enjoyable. Laurence's supporting cast wasn't as interesting as Patricia's and their parallel stories meandered until their rekindled friendship became an inexplicable romance. Not only did the romance feel forced, it was thematically redundant. The key to averting the destruction of Earth/hive collapse of humanity was their childhood melding of magic and science. There wasn't a need to reiterate the importance of this combination. 
 The result of this fantasy/science fiction conflict was akin to mixing chocolate and peanut butter and tasting lemon.

book_b.title: Lord Foul's Bane (The Chronicles of Thomas Covenant the Unbeliever, #1)
book_b.user_review:
I've been told for years now that this book is one of the pillars of fantasy. If that's true, then the whole genre is due to collapse any day now. The man is addicted to adverbs, and his writing is loose and weak. The storyline is almost slavishly Tolkienite. There are some creative touches (the hero is a leper) but I don't feel like it's original enough to merit being a "pillar." Also, it's poorly written, poorly plotted, and horribly insulting to women. 
 I hope people don't judge fantasy novels based on this one. It's really awful.

sample_reviews.review_text:
'The Bees' by Laline Paull is an adventure novel set within a beehive, starring Flora 7-17, a sanitation bee born with special skills that set her apart from her kin. It's filled with fascinating detail and plenty of action. 
 I listened to The Bees as an audiobook over the course of a couple of months on my runs. I'm not sure how well this book would have held my interest had I read it on paper; as it was it provided a very welcome distraction from running. 
 http://www.50ayear.com/2016/08/05/35-...
I think I just took on board a lot of misinformation about bees. If it was true, then it was very personal. Rude.

3.5 stars, really. Strange book, and though I was interested enough to read to the end (after the first third, which was a bit of a slog), I'm still a bit divided about it. I thought the setup, which is kind of The Handmaid's Tale meets Watership Down meets 1984-slash-Animal Farm, was interesting. And I like what she took on with world-building--in this case a beehive. But the storyline got repetitive in places, which ended up making the social commentary feel heavy-handed, and that kind of thing is always better in less-is-more mode, as far as I'm concerned. 
 Also it was somewhat hard to latch on to the main character, especially once the drones--the males--came into the picture and were given all personality in the story. Which I realize was the point: the hive is full of female bees that are basically interchangeable within their given roles, and this is what happens when one bee breaks out of hers. I get it. But there was something slightly off-putting about the males being the only really interesting personalities, at least until the main character's hubris kicks in. 
 But in spite of those complaints, it kept me reading. The world-building was a lot of fun, and the fact that the world was a beehive was fascinating in itself. I think, in the end, what flattened it for me was how little humor or any sense of irony there was. Even a serious book has room for a bit of edge, and I wish there had been more. Still, it was such a different book--which ultimately kept me reading straight through, so kudos to Paull for pulling it off.

Although this book is very different from most books I read I really enjoyed it. The story is told from the point of view of Flora 717, a worker bee. How the author has humanized bees is hard to describe; you start to forget that the characters aren't human.

I had really high hopes for this book, despite some of the reviews I read. The premise, a narration by a bee about class, caste, loyalty, ability, race, etc. has so much potential...but I just couldn't get into this book. I stuck it out hoping I was either missing something or that it would get better. Unfortunately neither happened for me. 
 I don't recommend this book.

Laline Paull is a British playwright. Her debut novel, The Bees describes life in a cultivated beehive. In this text, we follow Flora 717, a bee born with something unique-- something unique which makes her stick out in a society where being the same is critical to success and survival. 
 What drew me to The Bees initially was an interview with the author I discovered on io9. See, science fiction is often exploring where science can take us in the future. We push the boundaries of what is known in texts like Orson Wells The Time Machine, or in Issac Asimov's I Robot. New planets, races, and technologies are discovered, which in turn inspire humanity to keep reaching further and further. Science fiction rarely explores the science we have in front of us for what it is. And what's exactly what Laline Paull does here. 
 Paull felt this book was just waiting to be written when she learned about bees. About the drones who are massacred once a year, or how multiple princesses will fight each other for dominance and the crown, or the scientifically defined "fertility police" who will hunt down worker bees that end up laying eggs instead of the queen-- killing the bee and eating the eggs. It's terrifying stuff! No wonder she was inspired to write a book! I picked up The Bees expecting a dystopian science-fiction novel with anthropomorphic bees. Bring it on. 
 Yet, once I started reading, nothing about the book really grabbed me (Honestly, I was so bored with it, I put off writing this review for three months to get away from it). I realized around halfway through I had been waiting for the next thing to happen so the book will really get started since the beginning. And yet, nothing seemed like "the next thing". I was always waiting without knowing why. Waiting for Godot anyone? 
 Laline's prose was beautiful at times. I found some gorgeous lines that I read over and over purely out of the enjoyment of the phrase. And yet, it seemed like the author herself wasn't certain where she was going with the story. It seemed she lacked follow through to her own metaphors of humanity. One second I'd feel like I was being beaten over the head with a metaphor, and the next minute it would vanish as though it had never been there. 
 By the end of this book, I just didn't understand why Laline's primer book was such an "It" book of Summer 2014. It's intriguing and different. I love some of the truly poetic phrases, as well as how it challenges science fiction to explore what is in front of us a bit deeper. But I just couldn't find myself caring.

reference_books.title: Before I Go to Sleep
reference_books.review_text:
I started this book in December. Since then I have read 6 other books and 
 watched 3 seasons of House of Cards. IF this does not hint at dissatisfaction 
 with the read I don't know what does! 
 Continuing to read this book has been like a forced march through a slog of 
 redundancy! 
 I kept reading on as 3 out of 4 in my reading circle raved about it. If I did not 
 know better I would say that busy,little elves were re-typing this story each night 
 after I put it down and lacking imagination kept on writing the same stuff over and 
 over and over again! 
 I am no stranger to the damsel in distress,psychological thrillers having read many 
 over the course of the years. I was so disinterested in what was really going on 
 with this boring character and her equally appearing to be,long suffering husband 
 that I wasted no mental energy in trying to figure out what the heck was going on. 
 Then my first thought was to throw the book across the room as I said to myself 
 "all this for that plot twist"? What a waste of my time. 
 So I am going back to another amnesia story,Stella Bain. Some did not like this book 
 but Anita Shreve is a far,far better writer with her excellent but sparse prose......nary 
 a word wasted!

reference_books.title: The Flight of Gemma Hardy
reference_books.review_text:
The novel,The Flight Of Gemma Hardy takes the basic template of the Jane Eyre story and gives it 
 a modern twist. Gemma is a mid-centruy Scottish girl who is,like Jane an orphan. The journey Gemma takes is updated for these times and this makes it quite an engaging story. Gemma is a resourceful, 
 plucky heroine in every sense of that description even at ten when our story begins. 
 I have a slight issue on how the book ends but that does not take away from the excellent writing 
 and story. This book will definetly be on my top ten reads for 2012.

reference_books.title: Commonwealth
reference_books.review_text:
Like so many reviews before my brief one I can most totally agree that the writing was top notch. However the plot, chronological flow and large amount of characters made this a ho-hum read for me. When I do not look forward to picking up the book again that is a bad sign or this reader. 
 I am not one to shy away from books that move back and forth in time or between multiple characters. However THIS novel would change eras 
 I swear in the middle of the page! There was not real plot to the story,just a rambling on about two families joined by a re-marriage down through the years. 
 Having read other novels by this author I was not expecting this book to be what I call kookie books. That is strangely written tales with a cast of many who were generally all " life's burnt toast" and done in an odd style. 
 I guess I have reached a stage where I really only want to read books with a usual plot and if it does go back and forth in time at least not to three or four different eras! Lately when a book is slightly unusual sounding but has tons of raves I usually find it has no appeal to me!

book_a.title: Secrets of a Charmed Life
book_a.user_review:
This was a novel with the Bliz in the background. In 1940 with the threat of invasion children from England's major cities were sent out into the provinces to live with foster families. Emmy age 15 and Julia age 7 were two such kids. They had lived with a single mother and had two different fathers. 
 Emmy has a real talent for drawing and makes herself be discovered by a bridal shop owner. 
 Her employment there is cut short when their mother is forced to send them to the country. 
 There they are taken in by age 66 Charlotte Havelock who lives in a Cotswold cottage with her 
 mentally disabled sister. This could have been an easy going war for the sisters but Emmy's 
 ambition and fate intervene. The Blitz begins just as Emmy and her sister arrive in London again. 
 the book chronicles the tragedy that happens and has different consequences for the sisters. 
 I found the writing style to be very good and it flowed well. 
 My daughter,ever the English major,found serious fault with historical things. To sum up the 
 girl's life before the Blitz,their language and attitudes were very 21st century not 1940's England. 
 This did not bother me as I just got used to it and it was over shadowed by a good story that propelled you forward. My only objection is that the ending dragged on a bit too much. 
 There is a very good interview with the author at the end of the book which shows she is an educated,deep thinking person who does not churn out "drug store literature"!

sample_reviews.review_text: Workd war II and a tragic story-my kind of book. Heartbreaking. A good quick read

London during the blitz - an old woman recounts the truth of what happened to her during the war years, a secret she has held for decades, of lives lost, and regret for what might have been. What a great read, but have the tissues ready - this was another book that had me crying on the elliptical machine.

Isabel McFarland believes it is time to tell her story. Through her telling comes thee recounting of the lives of Emmy and Julia Downtree. They are sisters living with a single mother in London during the bombings from the Luftwaffe in WWII. Their mother sends them to the countryside to be sheltered by a foster family. They are fortunate to be taken in by a caring couple of sisters. But Emmy's dreams cause her to make some poor choices that change the course of their lives. The sisters are left to pay for those choices, changing their futures. 
 A couple of wonderful quotes: 
 "Fear is worse than pain, I think. Pain is centralized, identifiable and wanes as you wait. Fear is a heaviness you can't wiggle out from under. You must simply find the will to stand with it and start walking. Fear does not start to fade until you take the step that you think you can't." 
 "...truth is a strange companion. It devastates one moment and enthralls the next. But it never deceives. And because of that, in the end, it comforts." 
 I would highly recommend this book to fans of historical fiction. 
 Really 4.5 stars

Loved. This. Book. 
 One of my top 3 summer 2016 reads! 
 I was a little hesitant to start as I knew that it is another book about WW2... But this story is different. More about the Blitz and how they evacuated children out of London...emotional, but not as heart wrenching.... 
 I may even like this more than The Nightingale! Not sure.

I could not have forced myself to read another word. Every sentence was painful. An excruciating reading experience. It's a novel full of sentences like: "Her left ankle ached ferociously." "She just stood there." "She stood there stunned." "She looked eighteen." "He looked like he hadn't slept in weeks." 
 Here are some comments I wrote while interacting with the text which help explain my critique of the novel: 
 Give me a break. 
 Immature style; 
 Is this the unedited version? 
 Melodramatic not real 
 Telling, telling, telling! Author doesn't seem interested enough in theme, plot, characters to develop. Telling is good enough. 
 Cheap trick! Julie's journals tell what happen to her. Just detail after detail. Little showing. Less work for the author that way. 
 Would Julie's story have made a better novel? Was most interesting story actually given? 
 Oh my gosh! A simile! Isn't that original! (The simile: "white surf hitting the shore bubbled like bridal lace." I'm not sure if bridal lace "bubbles" but she tried.) 
 "Assertain" not a word a kid would think 
 Childish 
 Too convenient. 
 How can this (novel) be any longer? 
 I think she entitled the novel "Secrets of a Charmed Life" so anything at all could happen in the novel. After all, the characters lived a charmed life.

"Ah, but what is history? Is it a record of what happened or rather our interpretation of what happened?" 
 "I think it's both," I answer. "It has to be both.What good is remembering an event if you don't remember how it made you feel. How it impacted others. How it made them feel. You would learn nothing and neither would anyone else." 
 A truly touching story about two sisters during the Blitz. Although some might call this a dual narrative, the contemporary character serves only as a bridge between the present and the past. I couldn't stop turning the pages as Isabel revealed more and more of herself to history student Kendra. 
 This differs from any other dual narrative I've read because a) the whole present part of the book takes place over the course of one afternoon and b) Kendra's story isn't ever fully brought to our attention. I found myself not really minding this because Isabel's story and her life during WWII was quite fascinating. 
 Great storytelling!

I loved it!! This book is full of WWII history, familial love and loss, romance and mystery. Susan Meissner is a master storyteller (read The Fall of Marigolds) who delivers more than necessary to keep me enthralled. I would give it 4 and a half stars if I had that option. The only reason I'm not giving five is that I can't give five to every book. And apparently I am an excellent book picker outerer.
I loved this book! A great read about family bonds that get stretched but not broken!
I enjoyed this book but I didn't love it. The story is interesting but parts of it are a bit drawn out. However, I would read other books by Meissner.

sample_reviews.review_text:
3.75 stars 
 This is definitely a character driven story and, as can be the case with character driven stories, that means that it is a bit of a slower story to get through. 
 I thought the author did an amazing job of developing the characters. Characters that I liked at the start, I despised by the end and vice versa. All of the characters had a lot of depth. 
 My main gripe with the story is just that it seemed as though it was not supposed to be obvious to the reader about the switch in babies, but I personally had guessed what was going to happen before it had even occurred. However, I appreciated that it was not explicitly stated to the reader in the same way that the characters never specifically said what had occurred until later in the story. 
 Definitely one to check out if you enjoy character driven literary fiction novels.

Mort and Abe are brothers who live in a two family house. Their wives, Helen and Rose get along very well. Mort is the father of girls and Abe is the father of only boys. Both of their wives get pregnant and they are very excited to be introducing new life into the world. They both go into labor during a blizzard in which a midwife has to come in and assist them. Helen gives birth to a girl, Natalie and Rose to a boy named Teddy and the two babies soon become friends and even closer when they get older. But every family has its secrets and this one is no exception! The book had very very short chapters that reminded me a bit of a James Patterson novel. The story itself wasn't bad but I had wished that there were just so many different children who seemed underdeveloped. I really liked the character of Mort and the path he ended up taking by the end of the novel. Overall, an average read.

In spite of good reviews, in spite of wanting to love the story line just had to give up. Found the characters flat and one dimensional and did not want to give up any more of my time to be with these folk.

Very fast and easy read. It contains nothing complicated beyond the practicalities and occurrences of the close but problematic relationships between two brothers' families, especially their wives- over a period of decades plus. 
 They begin living in a two flat house. One family upstairs and one down within mid-century 1947 plus Brooklyn. Both brothers hold a box making business and have children. Both are single sex children families: one with 4 boys, the other with 3 girls. 
 And consequences effect large change. 
 I adored the first part and well into the 2nd. But by Part 3, the character of Rose! Well, several features just didn't jive. All at once, it became almost the opposite of heart-warming. Sad in the opportunities lost and neglected. 
 It was a window. I especially enjoyed the perceptions of Judith and Natalie over time. But also found the book as a whole within the play out of its premise a little hard to swallow. Possible, of course. 
 I did find the old-fashioned style of telling/ prose for all the minutia and nuance of interplay between the families and effects of those attentions, refreshing. Everyday people. And apt to make me reminisce in a positive sense for that period of closeness when we lived with extended family, just like this.

What a great book! I'm thrilled this is my first book of the year - definitely started my reading year off right. Terrific prose, tight story, and well-rounded characters - what more can a girl ask for? 
 Though the big secret of the whole plot was always suspected and therefore didn't come as a complete surprise, it didn't bother me in the least because the characters reacted to it in what's I wasn't anticipating. So even though the big reveal wasn't that big of a reveal, there was still plenty that I didn't anticipate. 
 I also really enjoyed how the characters developed - how I first went from siding entirely with Rose and hating Mort and finding Helen annoying to doing a 180. Each person developed and changed gradually, or rather at a realistic pace that I almost didn't notice my sentiments changing in the same way people often don't notice gradual shifts in real friend/family dynamics. 
 My only complaints are the presence of two or three swear words (but nothing compared to other books) and one scene hinting at premarital sex but without any explicit details for which I was grateful. 
 Marvelous book. I hope Loigman writes more!

The characters were flat and unbelievable. The dialogue was contrived and phony. About a quarter into it I cursed myself for spending good money on it and then just speed read it to get it done with. I confess I finished it because the end of the year is coming, and I want to make my goodreads goal. But literally, I finished it and said aloud, "That was by far the worst book I've ever read."
