This book was a letdown for me. It had the potential to be a great novel, but the way the author treated her characters and topics brought my enjoyment of the story waaaaaaay down. On the one hand, I enjoyed the language with which the book is written. It's a story told in a very quaint, very plain way that's easy to follow and easy to relate to. The setting is in a "simpler time" when families could make do with a single working parent and 5 hungry mouths to feed; when a college education cost nearly nothing; when a family of 7 somehow could ride in a single automobile; when "ladies were ladies and men were men." I mean, charming, right? I thought so. What I didn't like was that everything was oversimplified in this way. The story deals with a tremendous amount of very serious circumstances. Verbal and emotional abuse in a household, for example. I found it extremely bothersome that this was used as a method to tug at heart strings and then allowed to fall away in a shallow show of "redemption." I'm all for characters learning and growing, but that's not what the characters in this book did. They were generalizations of what someone might behave like in a certain set of circumstances and then they'd suddenly perform this relentless about-face without any sort of real catalyst and the reader is just expected to accept this change without question. Themes of forgiveness are at the forefront, and I'm all for forgiveness, but it seems almost irresponsible to treat such serious topics so flippantly. I felt like I needed to see each of the characters in a more raw and exposed way. I needed to see the stripping away before we came to the sudden change of heart. I needed to see WHY they were growing and see the STEPS that occurred. What I got instead was a poorly developed group of characters who were set in their ways until it became necessary for the lesson in the story to have them change. As charming and as emotional as I found the general story line, I can't forgive the author's treatment of her characters. She clearly possesses the writing skill. I would like to know why she chose to oversimplify when there was so much opportunity to delve deeper and create something so much richer than this books was.

Fairly well written but predictable plot. Overall, I found this book depressing; very draining to read. All of the main characters were full of sadness, negativity, or anxiety-page after page. I may try this author again, but not because of this story

reference_books.title: The Iron Traitor (The Iron Fey: Call of the Forgotten, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
I am a huge fan of The Iron Traitor, and I'm so glad I got an ARC of it! I liked The Iron Traitor a lot more than the Iron Prince, and while I wasn't completely sure about this series with The Iron Traitor, I've decided that it's just as interesting as Kagawa's Iron Fey series. 
 I really like the relationship Kierran and Ethan have, and it really reminds me of Puck and Ash. Their relationship is definitely complicated, and I'm really curious as to how their relationship will be different in the next one, given the huge cliff-hanger of an ending. Which is all I'm going to say about that. Actually, in general, I'm wondering how things are going to be in the next one, given everything that's happened in The Iron Traitor. 
 I really liked Ethan in this one, and while he still has some anger issues, I feel like he's calmed down since The Iron Prince. Not much, but a little, and I don't know if it's because he's grown on me, or he's changed or if it's because it's been a while since I've read The Iron Prince. At any rate, Ethan was a lot less irritating in The Iron Traitor, as was Kenzie (although there were times when she did get annoying). I did feel like the things Ethan learned in this book changed him a little. But for the most part, he's still him, even though he does have a better understanding of things that happened in the past. 
 I did feel like I got to know the characters so much better. They REALLY came to life in The Iron Traitor, and while bringing characters to life is something Kagawa is just good at in general, I felt like the characters really changed and came to life in this one. 
 And I'm glad we saw Puck and the rest of the gang, because things seem so much more lively when Puck and Grimalkin are around. I'm glad Puck and Ash and Grim were around to help out Ethan and Kierran, even though Kierran was acting like a moron the entire book. There were times when I was glad I was reading The Iron Traitor at work, because it ensured that I *wouldn't* be yelling at Kierran. Because I definitely wanted to a few times. I like Kierran's dedication and loyalty to Annwyl, but he also did some stupid things because of it. 
 Final Thoughts: The Iron Traitor really is a good addition to the Iron Fey series, and Kierran and Ethan are definitely the most interesting characters. I can't wait to read the next book, because I really need to know what happens! The Iron Traitor gets 5 stars. 
 *The Iron Traitor is from netgalley.com, which hasn't influenced my review in any way!

reference_books.title: Wildwood Dancing (Wildwood, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Honestly, I didn't like Cezar at all, and it turned out, I had good reason not to like him. His older brother "drowned" when Cezar, Jena, and Costi (Cezar's brother) and Cezar did nothing to save him. It turns out the witch of the forest saved Costi, and turned him into a frog...who happened to be named Gogu. 
 I also found Jena to be somewhat unlikeable too, especially with all her fights with Cezar about how she was in charge of the castle while her father was gone and could manage just fine without Cezar's help. She whined and complained about how she was responsible and in charge, and yet she didn't seem to be very good at running the household in her father's absence. 
 I loved the setting, and the descriptions of the forest and area were amazing! It started off slow, and then everything picked up. 
 I liked Gogu/Costi, as well as Jena's younger sisters, and I wished that the 3 younger sisters had more of an appearance. She drew on the mythology and folklore of Transylvania, and she wove in elements of the frog prince as well. The cover art is really pretty, and it definitely went well with the title of the book, and the whole Other Kingdom element of the book. 
 Rating: It gets a 3 out of 5, because Cezar and Jena were annoying, and I hated the fact that the family troubles were attributed to a witch, but there were a lot of other things that I really liked.

reference_books.title: Soundless
reference_books.review_text:
I was really intrigued by Soundless, because not only is it a fantsasy inspired by Chinese mythology, but it's a village comprised of people who cannot hear. Unfortunately, Soundless was really lackluster, and I didn't like it as much as I thought I would. Actually, I didn't like it at all. 
 First of all, this book is a stand-alone, and I don't know that fantasy works very well as a stand-alone. It's just, how do you give enough world-building to make the world feel real, while also keeping the story contained to one book? It seems like something that's very hard to balance and do well, and things were really vague and pretty much happened because they needed to happen with no real explanation. 
 As for Fei's village...I was intrigued by the fact that they couldn't hear, but it didn't work for me. It came across as them being telepathic, rather than signing to each other, and I actually forgot that they couldn't hear until signing was mentioned. I don't know if it's something that doesn't come across well in print, or if maybe it can be done well in print, but not with how Mead did it in this book, but it really came across as mental telepathy. I did like how some of their signs were different than signs in a couple of near-by villages, and I wish we got more of that. And back to the vagueness of world-building, I thought why they had issues with hearing and, for some, seeing, was interesting, but could have been a lot more interesting with more background. 
 And...I didn't really get the sense that the book was steeped in Chinese mythology. Granted, I know nothing about about Chinese mythology and folklore, so maybe that's why I didn't get the connection to Chinese mythology. But at the same time, I felt like, if you changed the character names, Fei's village could have been on any mountain on any continent. It seemed like the names were the only part of the book that were Chinese. 
 Overall, I really wanted to like the story, but I couldn't. Which is a little disappointing, because her Vampire Academy series was a lot of fun too read, and the concept is such a cool idea. Maybe Soundless would have worked better as a series, instead of trying to fit everything into one book. 
 My Rating: 1 star. Soundless fell really flat for me, and it could have been really interesting, but unfortunately, it had a lot of things working against it.

reference_books.title: Liar
reference_books.review_text:
I thought Liar started off really strong and I initially liked it, but I slowly became indifferent towards the book by the end of it. 
 What really lost me was the revelation of the family illness- that her family were werewolves. That was when the book started to lose me- and while it was first at first, by the end of it, it just felt like a lame excuse for why she lied all the time. I get that things run in the family, which I could have handled. And if the werewolf thing is a stand-in for something else (mental illness and period-related issues seem like the best possibilities, but the second one doesn't explain the fact that her one uncle seems to be affected by the family illness), I thought it didn't really do a good job of it, just because it turned into something I wasn't expecting, and it felt out of place. 
 I'm fine with unreliable narrators, and one who's a compulsive liar makes for a really interesting unreliable narrator because you're never sure what's true and what's a lie. What became really clear to me was that Justine really needed help. She really did- her brother being a good example of this. At different points in the book, she has a brother who hates her, he never existed, or he died and she was involved somehow. Not only that, but it's never resolved, and it's randomly mentioned, but you don't really hear about it after a certain point. Which makes me wonder why it was even included...I guess to show how much of a liar she is, but you definitely get that throughout the book. Maybe to show family issues? Anyway, one of the very few things that you could actually trust is that she's in desperate need of help, and it's a shame that she doesn't get it. 
 She gets sent up to the Greats (how they're related to her, I could never figure out) in the country, and she runs away because her life will end if she's not in the city. I really wish we could trust her stories about her family, because I am oddly curious about what they're really like, and if they noticed that Micah needed help. And if they did, why they didn't try to get her more help. Maybe they did, but Micah never talked about it? 
 While you couldn't trust a lot of what Micah said, something I could trust (and actually liked) was how she felt out of place- race being a big one, since she's bi-racial. Part of me wishes that had come up more, because it really doesn't in the book. Which is fine, because there are so many other things going on, and just because a character is bi-racial doesn't mean the story has to focus on that. But there is a part of me that wishes we saw the impact it had on Micah's life. 
 My Rating: 2 stars. Micah definitely has a strong voice, and I liked that she's such an unreliable narrator, but the big reveal about the family illness made me feel indifferent about the book.

book_a.title: The Forgotten Ones (The Danaan Trilogy, #1)
book_a.user_review:
If there's something I love, it's a story that centers on fairies. And I was pleasantly surprised that The Forgotten Ones is not your typical fairy story. 
 I really liked how Allison's dad became immortal because he spent too much time in fairie. As far as I can tell, Allison is not a fairie, which is definitely different, but a different that I'm intrigued by. And Allison's mom? I totally didn't see a certain plot point coming. At all. Actually, I have random thought about her mom: for some reason, the portrayal of Allison's mother as a schizophrenic who's heavily sedated and can't go anywhere without being sedated bothered me, and I have no idea why. 
 The Forgotten Ones is pretty short, but it moved at a pretty good pace, and I felt like things were wrapped up really well, while also leaving things open for the next book. It's because things get fairly resolved that I wasn't annoyed by the length of the book. It doesn't end in a cliffhanger, which is also nice, but given that last line, and everything that happened in The Forgotten Ones...let's just say that I really want to know what that means for the characters after finishing the book! 
 I'm feeling pretty neutral about the characters. The fairies seem pretty interesting, and I wanted to know more about them! At the same time, I liked what we did learn about them, and I'm sure there's more to learn! Other than that...no one really has made a lasting impression. I will say that I think the length played a part in this, because I felt like I didn't really get to know the characters, and maybe a book that was slightly longer would have helped in their development. Hopefully, we'll learn more of them in the next book. 
 Let's Rate It: I liked The Forgotten Ones, and how it's a different take on fairies. It's pretty rooted in Celtic mythology, which seems pretty rare in fairie novels. Still, I wish I knew the characters a little bit better, but I really am hoping to learn more about them. The Forgotten Ones gets 3 stars. 
 *I got The Forgotten Ones from netgalley.com, in exchange for an honest and fair review.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Review to come on August 26th as part of The Forgotten Ones blog tour hosted by Xpresso Reads 
 Favourite line: "I'm perfectly happy with a good book and a bowl of Double Fudge ice cream." 
 Yes, Allison, so am I! 
 Firstly, I have to say that the cover of The Forgotten Ones is pure awesomeness. I love it! So, so pretty. The font, the image, the colours, everything is beautiful. 
 Okay, so I went into this book with a preconceived expectation that was fulfilled, but not in the way I assumed it would be. The cover and title lent towards something magical and mystical, so when I was almost half way and hadn't encountered anything in the way of magic (as in waving wands and stuff, not romantic magic, although there wasn't much of that either), I was convinced I was reading a contemporary romance. 
 Then bam! We have magic faeries flitting around causing all sorts of trouble. Cool. 
 I'm going to back-track and start with Allison and Ethan's relationship. I loved the tension between them, but sometimes I wanted to smack her over the head. Seriously, she'd been in love with this guy for forever, and he was obviously into her, but Allison kept making excuses. Her main reason was because Ethan was a player, but I didn't really see that. If a girl was hanging off him, he made the effort to untangle himself and run to her. There was never any big event that Allison witnessed Ethan doing to suggest he was with heaps of girls. I wanted Allison and Ethan to get it on more. 
 Now, back to the bam! moment. 
 The first half of this book read like a contemporary romance, then all of a sudden I was thrown into a magical world with conniving faeries, some of them imprisoned, others creepy, and way too many complicated names to make sense of, or try and remember. At one point there were two guys fighting each other and their names both started with A. I got confused and it took me a while to work out if the guy who won was the guy I thought he was. I ended up skimming over the names because I didn't know how to pronounce them. There was a pronunciation guide at the back of the book, but I didn't know it was there until I'd finished. I think I wouldn't have struggled so much if I'd read this first. 
 The reason for all the faerie fighting: Allison's mum is schizophrenic. Allison has grown up with no father and spends all her time worrying about her mother. She also believes she is the reason for her mum's illness. Cue creepy faerie man, Liam. He turns up looking for Allison's mum, and is actually Allison's long lost dad, and everything goes to hell. She disappears, Ethan disappears, and Allison goes to faerie land to save them. 
 Despite the things I didn't like, I did enjoy The Forgotten Ones. It was a fast and easy read, but not one that grabbed my complete attention. There were too many characters for me to get invested in anyone in particular, and Allison was a little boring really. My favourite moment by far was the one kiss Allison and Ethan shared, but it was over so quickly. I really like Ethan, and I wish Allison had given him more of a chance. 
 The ending: We're left with a cliff-hanger, but I didn't feel as if there was a huge lead up to it. The story just sort of stopped. I love a good cliff-hanger, but I'm not a fan of this sudden-stop type of ending, and for me there was no satisfactory resolution. I know it's part of a trilogy, but the second book isn't out yet! This is the kind of book where you need the next one to keep going with the story, and I do want to find out what happens. 
 Overall I liked The Forgotten Ones, but I didn't love it. That's okay though, because there are plenty of people that will love it, and I encourage you to give it a go for yourself. You never know, it may be your favourite read of 2013.

This book had a lot of potential but left me a little bit confused. Even at the end I'm not sure who the characters were and why they are so important - what their roles are in this other world. I think I give this a 2.

The Forgotten Ones is about Allison's quest to help her mother Elizabeth. Elizabeth became schizophrenic the day Allison was born but not because of the baby: Allison's father is part fairy and was stolen away from Elizabeth, breaking her heart and shattering her mind. When Elizabeth and later Allison's (almost) boyfriend Ethan are kidnapped, Allison teams up with her long-lost father and his fey comrades to rescue them. 
 The book was okay. The story was even-keeled: little to dislike but little to get excited about. Scenes that could have been action-packed were brief, and Allison played a weak role in the climax. I was satisfied with the ending; although there's a cliffhanger, the tension did not really build throughout the story, so the cliffhanger is more of a bunny slope. 
 The characters were forgettable. Allison liked to read, was surprisingly willing to accept the existence of fairies, and didn't allow herself to love the heart-wrenching Ethan because of... some reason, I wasn't quite sure. Some of the secondary characters were interesting, like her cousin Nicole, but they weren't fully fleshed out. The author also introduced a ton of characters in the second half of the book that will likely become a fairy army in the sequel but were unnecessarily complicated in a short span. 
 The Forgotten Ones was a quick read, so it might be good to read this and the sequel during a long beach weekend. The tension might build better over the course of two books. 
 One last note... Although this is New Adult based on ages, it definitely feels like Young Adult. If it wasn't written out that the characters are in their 20's, I would have assumed they were in high school. Concern for a parent, living at home, first love: these are all YA themes.

View the full review here: 
 http://www.iswimforoceans.com/2013/10... 
 As most of you know, I've avoided the new adult genre like the plague, simply for the innate fear that it will become host to a bevy of novels that are trite, cliche and altogether meaningless. I am, however, a sucker for a gorgeous cover and a unique premise, so I was instantly sold on the premise of The Forgotten Ones by Laura Howard. The author presents readers with a rich and imaginative world, all the while grounding us in reality with characters readers will relate to and situations that feel all too real at times. 
 It must be said though, that I was expecting a much more new adult content from The Forgotten Ones. With Alison being 21 and Ethan being 23, it's completely acceptable to class the novel as such based on that alone. However, I found that the budding romance had a much more YA feel to it, as it was sweet and, if I'm entirely honest, innocent. The beauty of NA is that readers can expect more sexual tension without blurring the lines of age-appropriate material. It felt as though The Forgotten Ones teetered somewhere along the middle of these genres though, blurring the lines. 
 Ms. Howard gives readers a completely exciting paranormal premise in which we follow Allison to Tir Na Nog, uncovering the truth behind the myths of the fairies, and the truth behind Allison's own nature, as well. The story is rich and intriguing, and we're offered careful subtle glimpses into an amazing magical realm complete with spells, paranormal creatures and a backstory that is, for all intents and purposes, to die for. 
 The main problem that I had with The Forgotten Ones was simply that it was so short. Had we been offered another hundred pages or so, we might be able to fully envelop ourselves in the world. As it is though, The Forgotten Ones teases us with tempting details, but it never fully absorbs us into its magical escapism. I also felt that, at times, the novel warred between a contemporary romance and a paranormal tale. Both elements were prominent and strong, but I think the emphasis on romance might have taken away from the actual paranormal offering in the end. 
 Overall though, I'm intrigued by the premise of The Forgotten Ones. The pronunciation of a multitude of names was tricky to grapple with at times, but it didn't really detract from my enjoyment. It's a solid series opener, and I'll definitely be looking to see if the series improves as it progresses. I give it a 3.5 out of 5, and I recommend it to all fans of both NA and YA, especially those who enjoy romance and paranormal. 
 I received this book free of charge from the author in exchange for an honest review. This, in no way, affected my opinion or review of this book.

I received a free copy in exchange for an honest review. 
 The Forgotten Ones by Laura Howard is about Allison, a 21 yr old girl who is getting ready to go to grad school. Ever present in her mind, and her main purpose in life, is taking care of her mother who has schizophrenia. She has been mentally ill since Allison was young, since she came home from a study abroad in Ireland knocked up and heart broken. Allison, along with her grandparents, make taking care of her mother their main priority. For Allison, that means forsaking a social life. She has a reputation for being "no mans land" but the super-hot Ethan doesn't let that deter him. Towards the middle of the story we meet Liam, who is buying land near Alison's family but is also her dad who she has never met. He also looks 25 yr old, despite the fact that Allison herself is 21. Obviously, this causes lots of questions. Liam explains that he is human but has lived with the Tuatha De Danaan, or faeries, for so long that he does not age and has developed some of their special skills. He has returned to protect Beth, Allisons mother, from a jealous and vindication faerie princess who original lured Liam there back in the 17th century. They must journey far to save her mom, a journey Allison is determined to go on. 
 This is the first of three books, so there is a fair amount of plot development. The author did a great job with that, not getting bogged down with it but letting us know what is going on. The only detail she didn't get into was the circumstances around Allison and Ethan's infamous kiss. Would have liked to hear about the circumstances around that, but obviously not essential to the story. She also does ALOT of scene description, which is great in a foreign land of faeries but did get tedious after awhile. 
 I felt like the character of Allison could have been flushed out more. We know she likes to run, where she works, about her mom. But that's about it. Towards the end we see some glimpses of her growth with her opening her heart to Ethan, whom she has kept at arms length because of the situation with her mom and not wanting to saddle him with it, too. She also steps out of her comfort zone while trying to help her dad and his fiery friends defeat the evil Princess. 
 Overall, a decent read. Not my favorite but I have high hopes for the next books in the series.

You can find this review and more at Such A Novel Idea. 
 The Forgotten Ones is a book I've had on my TBR list for a looooong time, so I was excited to have the chance to be a part of the blog tour. 
 This book was such a fast read! I couldn't believe how I zipped through it, partly because of length, but also because it was easy to keep reading and fast paced. 
 The story revolves around Allison: Allison is a young girl who lives with her mother and grandparents. Her mother, who was diagnosed with schizophrenia when she was pregnant with Allison. Allison's grandparents have been taking care of the two since she was born, and Allison is ready to take over her mother's care. 
 So of course, the pleas of her cousin Nicole and the attention of Ethan (quienticinal bad boy who turns good around Allison) are pushed off for the idea of becoming a responsible adult. 
 Despite the short length, the story was well thought out and the world building was flushed out. This is definitely a talent of the author considering it is a fantasy book at such a short length. The concept of this book was AWESOME! I definitely found myself wanting more. MORE, MORE, MORE. 
 The romance was similar to Finding Meara, in that it was there, but it was by NO MEANS the main focus of the book. I really enjoyed that a lot, although of course I wanted MORE (I feel like a more monster today). 
 Even though Allison is a bit older than the normal 'young adult' protagonist, she read just like a YA character. I think this book could be easily read by the younger YA audience, especially for content and language. 
 I'm not normally a fairy reader, but this book was just so engrossing and entertaining that it changed my mind. And I love that the faieries were not Tinkerbell-esque. The ending was great and I cannot wait to see what happens next! 
 Rating 4/5

book_b.title: Fast Food Nation: The Dark Side of the All-American Meal
book_b.user_review:
Fast Food Nation is an interesting book. I first read it for a sociology class years ago, and I decided to read it again. 
 It's about the fast food industry, and how it's changed over since World War 2. He also talk about marketing to kids and what it's like working in the slaughterhouses. 
 The part about the meat-packing industry was interesting and yet disturbing. He describes what it's like working there and what happens to the animals. The workers work in terrible conditions, with injuries not being reported. If they are, then a lot of them are falsified so the slaughterhouses don't get into trouble. And the workers that keep working no matter how sick they felt and no matter how bad any injuries were sustained. 
 I've had my copy for several years now, so I'm sure some of the statistics are out-dated. And while I loved the book the first time I read it, this time, it was just okay. We all know fast food is bad for us, but the book felt like a one-sided argument on why fast food is evil. It's definitely implied that fast food is the reason for all of society's problems. 
 It is fairly well-researched, though, and it did make me think about where my food comes from and how it's processed. 
 I would give it a 2 out of 5. It felt one-sided, and not terribly focused, but it does get points for making you think.

reference_books.title: The Iron King (The Iron Fey, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I have nothing much to say about this- I think almost everything's been emphasized already, from the characters, the romance, and the plot, so I'm just gonna focus on its clever and original concept instead. Yes, the faery concept isn't entirely unique, but it also isn't well-recognized. And I love how Julie Kagawa made it as if it is her own; the familiar tales weaved into an original plot. 
 Meghan Chase is a mortal, or so she thinks she is. She's actually a half-faery, and the faery world actually exists. There are 'trods' or portals in the mortal realm that leads into the faery realm, so faeries can come and go to the mortal world as they please. Mere mortals can't see them for what they truly are, because the faeries use 'glamour' which covers their true self to blend in with the humans. However, people who have extreme imagination and belief could see through the disguise. 
 How the faery world and the faeries exist is what really amazed me, they weren't just suddenly born into the world at the beginning of time. The existence of the faery world, called the Nevernever, and its inhabitants, the fey, is caused by the dreams and imagination of humans. They existed because once upon a time, humans believed they existed. As long as humans don't stop believing or imagining, as long as humans don't stop writing stories and ballads about them, then the faeries are basically immortal. Otherwise, they will cease to live. That is where the conflict of the fey begins. 
 According to what we know about faery mythology, faeries are terrified of iron. It is the same for the faeries in this book. Iron repels them, it burns their skin and it sucks the glamour out of them. Iron and technology are their primary weakness because it contradicts their existence. The Nevernever and the fey came from the people's fantasy and dreams, whereas iron and technology is of science and logic. So what would happen once humans start relying solely on science? The mortal world would not stop progressing, thus having an ample amount of technology as time goes by. What if humans start dreaming and imagining about different things then? What if they start dreaming about futuristic devices and technology instead, how would that affect the faery world? 
 So that is basically where the story will revolve, aside from Meghan's rescuing of her brother and her romance with the Unseelie prince. I noticed that people were more focused on Meghan's side of the story, primarily because she's the main character after all. But the concept of the faery world and how it works are what really pulled me in. I am looking forward to more of it. I don't mind the excessive romance and Meghan's serious case of damsel in distress, as long as there'd be progress and more compelling eventualities in the Iron-Fey aspect.

book_b.title: The Bad Beginning (A Series of Unfortunate Events, #1)
book_b.user_review:
The beginning was indeed bad. 
 We start with the Baudelaire siblings being informed of their parent's deaths due to the fire at the family mansion, leaving them with no home and no guardians. They were also left with no choice but to be sent to live with Count Olaf, a distant relative who turns out to be quite unlikeable. 
 Count Olaf is not merely a mean and snobby adult, but evil. He hit Klaus Baudelaire, the second child, once across the cheek. He locked Sunny, the youngest and only an infant, inside a bird cage and hanged it at the top of a tower, swinging dangerously high above the ground. He tried to trick Violet, the oldest though only fourteen, into marrying him just so he could steal their fortune. He also said that once he gets his hands on their fortune, he will then 'take care' of the children. Go figure out what he means by that. 
 I'll admit, I didn't really like The Bad Beginning. I mean, who would like a children's book about twisted adults and child abuse? But I get it. I get that this is about the Baudelaire children's unfortunate lives. I get that there will always be bad things happening and there will be no happy endings. As if Lemony Snicket did not point that out hard enough. But this book is different in a way. There are a lot of books about tragedies upon children which are still for children (by "for children" I mean less violent and disgusting), take A Little Princess for example. Why should this book be violent, abusive, and disgusting in a way that an adult relative forces a fourteen year old girl to marry him? In a way that he locks an infant inside a bird cage and leaves it dangling on top of a tower? 
 I also find the author's writing too redundant. The blatant throwing in of definitions is becoming repetitive, I bet he does that in the following books as well. He also kept on reminding the readers that this is not a happy book, and that there will be no happy endings despite the bits of happy moments that might currently be happening. We fucking get it. Instead of enjoying some parts of the book even though it's mostly about misfortunes, I get to feel mad and annoyed all throughout just because of his never ending reminders of how the readers should feel/become aware of. 
 Nevertheless, I still enjoyed the earlier part of the book, before all the twisted stuff happened. I also liked Justice Strauss' interactions with the Baudelaires, I like that she's the only person who's sweet and cares for the orphans even though she's kinda stupid and utterly gullible, and also the part in the play when Violet outsmarted Olaf, of course. Even though I didn't like this a lot, I'm still going to give the second book a chance. My continuing or dropping of the series might depend on The Reptile Room.

What did I learn from this book? That when he says this book is unhappy, he really, REALLY means it. It's a miserable piece of writing, and it utterly fails to involve me. I'm only glad it was a gift, so I didn't have to pay for it.

I couldn't pass that up, and since I had enjoyed the movie I figured it was pretty much a given that I would enjoy the books as well. I was not wrong. I highly enjoyed reading this. 3.5 stars. 
 I like the way this was written, and the three clever characters Violet, Klaus, and Sunny. I really only give it 3.5 stars because I am not a fan of books that do not have happy endings. It was an entertaining and quick read. The evil foster parent situation reminded me of James & the Giant Peach, which I read many times as a child and was semi-obsessed with.. Whoaaa. I wish I read this as a kid! I loved this! Gothic and postmodern. I like how the narrator is also a character in the book. I also like how as much as the author talks down to the audience...it deals with dark themes like death and pain. I think that it's a great book for kids, it will enhance their vocabulary but its not so dark that they will be traumatized. It's even really funny!
I remember reading this series back when i was a little girl. It was like the first 'big' series that i read.

I wish I had of read this book when I was younger because I think it would have fascinated me alot more. However, I liked how Snicket explained the words he was using. I think this book and the rest of the Series of Unfortunate Events would be good books for children to read because of the way he describes bigger words to make it easier for children to understand. All in all it is a good childrens' book.
I am reading this on my Nook. It is ..... interesting. I saw the movie and read enough reviews either loving or hating the book that I was intrigued.

I've been hearing about this series since like forever. Thank God for Scribd, all 10 or 13 books in the series are there, and I intend to finish them... 
 I told my younger cousin, Ore, that I was reading this first book. He started laughing hard and said Snicket was a sadist...he had read it when he was 13 or 14.. 
 All in all, I enjoyed the book and his weird style. I don't know who he is yet, but I suspect he had a hard childhood, and this is his way of telling other children that life is not always rosy. 
 Fun stuff. 5 solid stars.

sample_reviews.review_text: I spent so much time trying to connect dots that weren't meant to be connected. Entertaining, not a favorite.

The Shining Girls is one great idea that is unfortunately poorly executed. My main issue with the book is that at no point do any of the three main characters - Kirby, Dan, and Harper Curtis - ever become more than descriptions on the page. All three exist only insomuch as the author is telling you they do so: they don't become real or three dimensional in the mind of the reader, and neither does their world. The Harper character in particular was annoying because he never achieves any sort of depth: he's a serial killer like pretty much any other serial killer you've ever read about or seen on television. He does bad stuff just because. We know nothing about his background or anything about his life before or after his experience in the House that somehow just pushes him over the line from really bad guy to serial killer. The author offers up one scene that describes some minor animal torture and watching his brother get crushed under a tractor but again, it's par for the course for any serial killer and it offers nothing insightful about *this* particular serial killer. 
 At the start of the book, Harper is running away from a group of people out to do him some sort of harm but it's basically irrelevant in terms of learning anything about him. It's a very drawn out sequence of events, the purpose of which is just to get him to the House where he has this sensory experience while high on morphine that somehow just puts him on this path to hunting and killing the 'shining girls'. And that's about it for Harper in the character development front: he spends the rest of the book stalking and killing girls, and a few other people along the way because that's what serial killers do. At no point does he question what that transformative experience might have been about, or the very idea that this house is somehow a time traveling device/portal. He just immediately goes along with the entire situation. Alrighty, then. 
 Kirby isn't much better. She's a typical alternative/punky kind of girl who doesn't really fit in with mainstream society. Her history with the serial killer doesn't help matters but really, we're not offered much in the way of character development to know her better or sympathize with her much more than that. We get some scenes from her life as she grows up with her flakey, artistic mother Rachel. As an adult she's on the hunt for the man who tried to kill her but the sleuthing/mystery aspect of her story is woefully underdeveloped. Much like the characters in this story, the meat of the plot doesn't get much deeper than the page it's written on. Kirby doesn't really get far at all in terms of finding clues or making connections to Harper until near the end when the whole thing suddenly comes together for apparently no other reason than the author figured it was time to wrap things up. There's a really jarring chapter near the end where Kirby is in the House (which up to this point she didn't even know existed), hiding upstairs as she hears Harper (she doesn't know who he is then but knows he's the man who tried to kill her) coming in and up the stairs. This scene just pops up out of nowhere, and I actually flipped back a few pages to see if I missed something, or if this was supposed to be something she was dreaming about. No, it's just a weird prelude to later on near the end of the book when Kirby actually does find the House and goes inside. It was just a very strange choice structurally as the reader gets thrown right out of things. 
 Another small bit that frustrated me was an exchange near the end between Kirby and the police - she's pointed them to where Harper is living and having been in the House herself, she's seen how it's so different inside than out. Of course, the police go there and it's just a dilapidated abandoned house, inside and out. But when Kirby goes back, this time with Dan, and they both go in, Dan sees the House in the same way as Kirby and Harper: so why does it 'work' for him and not the police? Well, that's another cliche, isn't it? The protagonist tries to convince those in authority about her theory but they are unable to verify what she's said or what she's seen etc. So they think she's crazy and she has to go off to the scary house/location whatever and deal with it herself, thus triggering the final battle between plucky heroine and bad, evil man etc. etc. 
 I lost interest about half way through and just skimmed to the end. I figure if you haven't made the characters come alive and be more than descriptive words on the page by the halfway mark, then there's a problem. This book is big on its ideas but is woefully short on its ability to deliver.

A serial killer that moves through time and his only surviving victim who refuses to give up on finding him. Avoids the confusion that accompanies most tales that flip through time. Engrossing and believable characters lend weight to a fantastic tale. Some moments of true horror, not for the squeamish, well worth the time and accolades.

Well, at least I can say I've dipped my toe into the world of serial killer fiction though I don't when I'll have the stamina to revisit it. Still, this was interesting despite the usual hang-ups that accompany writing time travel. I'm looking forward to reading more of Beukes' work I have waiting in the ranks.
I was really looking forward to this book but it was a big disappointment. Great story idea but it didn't fulfil it potential. Disappointing ending.

This was not a good book. It was an interesting concept, but I found that I was not actually interested in any of the characters, and didn't really care about the plot, and none of the plot twists were surprising or even vaguely amusing. 
 It was billed, in the library, as a thriller, with a time travel twist (the part that makes it spec fic) - it was not thrilling. There is a time traveling serial killer, but even though we get many interminable scenes from his perspective, it's a little hard to say exactly why he was motivated to be a serial killer. (Not good. The guy is basically a Murder Hobo.) The house that allows him to time travel is cool, but is a concept clearly ripped off from Dr Who. Why are these particular women targeted? Why only women? They "shine". No more explanation. 
 The pacing also needed work - it was very choppy, the POV character switched constantly, and there were not very many cliffhanger moments, as there should be in a thriller. Scenes were overlong, without adding much to either characters or plot - inanimate objects and scenery were described in excessive detail. 
 I was disappointed that I picked this as a book for a long car ride.
Flojo, una forma mas de desaprovechar un argumento prometedor.
So good, but I need someone to put this in chronological order for me. Get to work, Internet!

This falls outside of my typical genre but I was intrigued. I ended up not really liking it. It felt so disconnected and I never really understood anything about his motives or The House. Maybe Im not into time travel enough and sometimes you just have to go with it but the book left me with basic plot questions that I feel like should have been addressed.

interesting and involving, but ultimately not satisfying. it felt a bit like a jigsaw puzzle that you feel compelled to finish but don't care what the final image turns out to be. 
 the characters were lively and the relationships were well crafted. the writing shows promise and I'd be curious to read another book by the writer.

reference_books.title: The Royal Ranger (Ranger's Apprentice, #12)
reference_books.review_text: A long time fan of the Ranger's Apprentice series, I always recommend John Flanagan to teens looking to get into the fantasy genre, without too much of the suspension of disbelief required. It's a nice cross between fantasy and historical style writing. In the final book in the series, Will Treaty is about the age Halt was when he was taken on as an apprentice, and he takes on the royal princess as his own ranger-in-the-making. In this book, there's a lot going on that is outside the series norms. First, we introduce a girl ranger. Next, we find that Will, and rangers in general, are not infallible, and finally, we have a closer-to-home adventure. If anything, I enjoyed this book as an ending to the series, but felt kind of jipped that Alyss had to die for really no reason. It's how life is, but it's also something I had trouble coping with throughout the book.

reference_books.title: Wither (The Chemical Garden, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This book was awful. I won't say the writing was terrible, it was good enough, but it wasn't enough to redeem the absolutely illogical and boring progression of this book. Other people have stated in their reviews how this book had terrible world building, and I absolutely agree. Take Ship Breaker by Paolo Bacigalupi for example. Fantastic world building with absolutely realistic possibilities you can get lost in. The beautiful thing about dystopia is that you are able to see it get from World A (Our world today) to World Z (The world in the book) and you can see the progression of the worlds between t hose points. Wither was nothing like that. The book gave you a ridiculous premise that I kept hoping would be better explained, but wasn't. There's absolutely no way AT ALL that the entire population of the world, or the USA, would go for genetic alteration. Unless it was government mandated it would never happen, and even then the country is HUGE so you would inevitably get some back-water individuals who escaped the alteration. It's absolutely irrational to expect that an entire nation would, all at once, have genetic engineering done on their children within a 20 year period. 
 Combine that with the shallow characters and you get a very boring, irrational book. Because yes, dystopia does need some rationale. Take Rhine - despite being the main character you know almost nothing about her! You don't know her favorite color or food or place in Manhattan or memory with Rowan. Jenna you know was a prostitute with sisters who were taken and killed in the van (how many sisters?) and Cecily who must be heartless to not care about the girls who died in the van after she was chosen and who you know came from an orphanage and that's about it. What!? Worse yet, you learn even less about their personalities despite seeing them interact for almost a year! Rhine is not dynamic. She has no emotional changes or worldview revelations. She comes in one way and exits exactly the same. 
 I had high hopes for this book and I kept waiting for something good and interesting and with some kind of explanation to happen, but it never did. Awful.

reference_books.title: The Adventures of Captain Underpants (Captain Underpants, #1)
reference_books.review_text: For all the hype Captain Underpants gets, I didn't think it was anything that special. Let's be fair, though.... I'm 24 and not 12. I do like to think that even at an older age I can enjoy things written for children, and I found myself laughing in my head at many of the jokes and illustrations, but I just didn't see why this series is so stand-out among the kids. Perhaps because it involves trouble makers, fake doggy-doo, and turning your principal into a crime-fighting underwear-wearing hypnotized superhero. That's probably it.

reference_books.title: Girl Online (Girl Online, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I picked this up when everyone was going crazy about it and decided it would be a cute beach read. The story was adorable, and very teen without being so angsty I couldn't handle it. However, I have issues with characters who SAY they like and trust someone, and then rely on hearsay to make judgments about that person without asking. The entire conflict in the book could have been easily resolved with a simple conversation, and that irritates me. Otherwise it was a fun, super light read.

reference_books.title: Life As We Knew It (Last Survivors, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
It's modern day America. Teens go to school, strive for college, do extracurricular activities, listen to the radio and watch TV, download music and record shows on DVR. That is, until an asteroid hits the moon and knocks it out of its path around the earth. The asteroid was more dense than expected, and the moon is now closer to earth and its gravitational pull is wreaking havoc on the earth's oceanic tides, volcanoes, and tectonic plates. 
 Miranda and her family live on an isolated street, and struggle through life in a world where everything they once knew and loved is gone. It's family first, and this harrowing tale of post-disaster Earth and human sacrifice is not just depressing but is also encouraging. The trials that Miranda and her family endure bring to light the jealousies and dark sides of human emotion, but also the beauty of family bonds and self sacrifice. 
 Most post disaster, post apocalyptic or dystopian teen novels suffer from bad world building, but this was one of the exceptions. The characters were human and emotional and yet dynamic, and they felt real, so their experience was nerve wracking. It didn't hurt that I started reading this during an early October snow storm that took out power to 2/3rds of the entire state where I live. Being without power for 3 days with an early winter outside, and destruction all around from fallen trees that couldn't bear the combined weight of their leaves and the snow, and a warm but not warm enough fire to sit by really made this book come alive for me. I would put down the book and have to tell myself "Hey, it's not you. Power's coming back, this is just temporary." But the atmosphere was perfect for making this book meaningful. It could happen. Let's just hope it doesn't.

book_a.title: Odd and the Frost Giants
book_a.user_review:
I enjoyed this book in that it was an interesting enough story and it was extremely easy to read, and the illustrations are wonderful. 
 Unfortunately I know little to nothing of Norse mythology and couldn't tell up from down with the Norse gods, except for what was explained to me and perhaps a little more garnered from American Gods so long ago. I think as an introduction to Norse myth, it could be stronger, but as a story for children with a little Norse myth thrown in, it was just right. 
 I have to admit that my very favorite thing about this book was actually one of the illustrations. I loved the illustration of the Frost Giant holding Odd up to speak with him. My husband listened to the audio version of this, which he said was fantastic and read by Mr Gaiman himself - but he asked to go back and look at the pictures in my copy and I pointed out my favorite parts. 
 Overall I would definitely recommend this book for any young reader (or adult!) who likes adventure, and overcoming the adversities in the world.

sample_reviews.review_text: I love it that Neil Gaiman narrates his own books.

It was a very nice retelling of a Norse legend of the Asgard gods, Odin, Thor, and Loki and seemed to imply at the end that the boy Odd may have been our boy Bod (From the Graveyard story) in a "different" form. 
 In brief: Odd is a young man, whose leg has been severly smashed and broken when a tree fell on him in the forrest. He does not fit in the community and runs away to live alone in the forrest. He is not alone long, when he meets an eagle, bear, and fox. The animals are the gods from Asgard who had been thrown out by a Frost Giant. He welcomes them to his fire, feeds them and manages to help them get back to Asgard. He confronts the Frost Giant who has stolen Thor's hammer and manages to convince him that he really wants to go home. :) 
 It is a story after all, and told simply and wonderfully by Mr. Gaiman. The only thing better than reading it, would have been to listen to Mr. Gaiman read it to me.

A fun short read. A cute fairy tale type story, with some nice writing elements, but one major plot point seems a bit too deus ex machina , namely that Odd somehow gets the ability to carve this amazingly beautiful thing like his father could have, and it's good enough to satisfy the frost giant . I still enjoyed it a lot as a quick read and a good one to share with kids.

I love juvenile literature and I adore Neil Gaiman and I collect fairy tales. That means that this book was a big hit with me. I love this tale involving the Norse gods. It was a quick, well written read that I totally recommend.

So I really love Neil Gaiman this little story is no exception. Its a very quick little read with a story about a little boy who loves the father who passed away. He always had a smile on his face, even when his leg is crushed by a fallen tree. He lives in a little Norse town and soon comes in contact with Odin, Loki and Thor, trapped in animal bodies. He goes on a journey to Asgard to save the land. It almost comes off as a hero myth. Good.
The more kids we have reading JF Norse mythology, the better. :D

The first introduction for the boys (aged seven and five-and-a-half) to any Norse mythology, and to Vikings. They appeared to enjoy it. Master Seven did ask if Loki and Thor were in a movie. 
 It is a pleasant story, easy to read aloud.
Probably good for kids, but not one of his kids books that an adult will really enjoy too.

Another nice little Gaiman story, making clever use of Norse Mythology - especially the snide remarks about Loki and a certain stallion ;-) - but in a style typically his own. Quite an enjoyable little read.
Read with the boy, we both enjoyed it.

book_b.title: Seraphina (Seraphina, #1)
book_b.user_review: The cover reminded me of the Jonathan Stroud books, which I loved. The story was decent...interesting concept. Just going on gut feelings here not anything definitive.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I just got a galley! This is my lucky day! I've read a total of two pages and so far, it's major, awesome, rufus, terrific and out and out perfect. 
 More later . . .

A clever fantasy that centers on complex and believable characters. Yes - believable, even though some of them are actually dragons walking around in human form, and others are half-dragons. The narrator, 16-year-old Seraphina, is one of these. Dragons, regardless of what sort of body they happen to be wearing, are supremely logical and inclined to be cold and selfish. On the plus side, they are natural scholars, and relentlessly honest. Because of their gifts for mathematics, many dragons are good musicians. But they lack the ability to convey emotion with their music. Seraphina, in contrast, can play with great heart - but, as a half-dragon, she's not even supposed to exist. That's only one of her problems. The crown prince has been murdered - probably by a dragon - and the peace that has endured for forty years is in danger of collapsing. If it does, the kingdom of Gorred will most likely be overwhelmed. What can one young girl do about such a danger? And what can Seraphina do about falling in love? Unlike her uncle Orma, Seraphina is fully human in her emotions. She has other responsibilities at court, too, both as a teacher and as a musician. I haven't even begun to talk about her garden of grotesques -what do they have to do with the whole situation? It's no wonder she often feels overwhelmed and exhausted. 
 I can't even begin to give a summary of the plot. Suffice to say that, if you like fantasy centered on political intrigue, such as the "Queen's Thief" series by Megan Whalen Turner or the books by Kristin Cashore, you'll find Seraphina well worth a look. And, as I said, Seraphina, her uncle Orma, the crown prince, and the princess, are all very interesting characters.

I really liked the world building in this novel and I have to say that for the most part I really liked the characters. This is a book I would have loved when I was a young teen. 
 It wasn't perfect but there is enough here to keep you going through the plot and enough world and culture building that you get a sense of why various things are happening. 
 I had a bit of difficulty with the falling in love bit, but I guess hormones rage at that age and in a weird way it could happen. Do teenagers make sense? 
 I will probably read the next book in this series to see if the odd bits get tied up in the next book. 
 Pretty good.

So so good! This fantasy novel has a complete compelling world, with the most interesting and unique dragons ever! The main character, Seraphina, is torn between her loyalties to the humans and dragons at a time when dragon-hatred is reaching a fever pitch and a human prince has been murdered. I loved the way Rachel Hartman wove this world, with questionable morals on both sides, and how she made music such an integral component. Wonderful! 
 First read: July 6, 2014 (hardback) 
 Second read: January 7, 2015 (Audiobook with fabulous narrator)
A big disappointment...I couldnt wait to read this one. Sorry to say, I could not find the voice of the main character. The plot was hard to follow. It was just all over the place.

The description on the flap sounded so amazing, I was pretty much dying to read this book. When summer rolled around and I was finally able to sit down and delve into this majestic tale, I was let down a little bit. There were a fair amount of confusing terms that weren't properly explained and things seemed to jump around a lot. To be honest, I'm not exactly sure what even went on in the whole 453 pages I just read. I got the gist of things, but I was expecting a much more masterfully crafted book. I understand that writing takes a certain amount of skill (believe me, I've tried writing a book myself and things didn't end well) and that this was her debut novel, but still. The story had so much potential, it could've been pretty spectacular, but it fell flat for me. Maybe I've read too many medieval/fantasy books and things are starting to become cliche, but this one had sounded different. I did enjoy the half-dragon concept, and Seraphina's struggle to keep her identity hidden, but things were incredibly predictable. I could pretty much guess how things were going to pan out from a mile away. The instant Kiggs and Seraphina started making love eyes at each other I was just screaming with impatience for him to find out her secret and then have a feud or something and then make up at the end. I admit I skimmed some paragraphs just to get to the sexually tense parts with Kiggs and Seraphina. The ending was satisfactory enough, but it didn't really match the rest of the book, the way it was written. I do believe that Hartman will be an amazing writer, and that Seraphina was a pretty good first book. Props to her and I hope that her writing will get even better the more she practices her trade. Anyway, it was good, but nothing too spectacular. Younger readers first introduced into the realm of dragons will probably be blown away, but for a reader like me, it just didn't jump out.

The timeline near the beginning confused me a bit--either due to shoddy editing, intentionally disorienting writing, or just to my skimming and/or falling asleep on the bus while trying to read. And I was a tiny bit disappointed with the inclusion of a romantic aspect (though it was admittedly well-handled) in a story otherwise full of strong, independent female adventuring. But it was otherwise an absorbing fantasy, with a carefully-constructed world (whose world-construction didn't encumber the actual telling of a story, unlike some storytellers *cough, Tolkien, cough*) that was fun to get lost in. The glossaries and whatnot in the back were even good. (I half-chortled to myself at the way they retained Seraphina's voice...)

The prince has been found with his head missing, which points toward a dragonly demise. It threatens to unhinge the tenuous treaty between humans and dragons in the kingdom of Goredd. There are humans and dragons who want this treaty to fail, but who is responsible? Hatred and fear run deep on both sides, and Seraphina, whose father is human and whose mother was a dragon finds herself caught in the middle. To tell more would be to spoil such a wonderful debut novel filled with courtly intrigue, romance and mystery. 
 In spite of the murder and courtly intrigue, the heart of this novel beats with joy and wonder and soars like few I have read. There have been other dragon books, but the view here is refreshing. Dragons can become human-shaped (it's not explained, nor is it really needed. Just trust me on that). Dragons rely more on their superior intellect and are clueless about feeling, but this has severe drawbacks. 
 The character Seraphina is a strong heroine who shows bravery when it is needed, but is vulnerable about her greatest secret and not fitting in to either world she is a part of. The worldbuilding is solidly populated with music, cultures and a plethora of interesting saints and unique characters. Although most of the action takes place in one city of the Kingdom of Goredd, there is plenty to suggest fully formed lands, people and creatures exist outside of the city walls. 
 This is the best book I've read so far this year. I did not want to finish this book and leave these characters behind, and that hasn't happened with me for a while. Rachel Hartman has created a masterful debut that deserves a wider readership than the Young Adult shelves of a bookstore. It also needs to be remembered next year when fantasy books are nominated for awards.

I had higher expectations for this book, given the promise of the subject matter and all the rave reviews. It was a little disjointed and slow-moving for me, especially in the beginning. It picks up later. The writing is beautiful, the story is unique, and the series has potential. It just didn't have the quality I was looking for...the one where you bust out your iPhone kindle app every few minutes you get to sneak in a couple paragraphs.

I really enjoyed this audiobook - great reader, UK accent, and she sings the songs well. The imagery and language in this book are fantastic: Hartman deftly created a world where humans and dragons are laboring to keep the peace despite prejudice and distrust among their people. Seraphina, a secret half-dragon working for the court composer, uses her dragon power and maternal memories to track down a rogue dragon wreaking havoc in the countryside, meeting more of her kind along the way. 
 Morris winner 2013.

reference_books.title: The Ice Twins
reference_books.review_text:
There's a fairly common sitcom plot where the characters don't communicate an important fact or feeling and hilarity ensues from the misunderstanding. The viewer realizes afterward that the entire episode would not have happened if the characters had just spoken to each other. This whole book is like that. 
 Gus and Sarah have the perfect life. Perfect family. Perfect house. Perfect perfect perfect monozygotic twins with perfect blonde hair and perfect icy blue eyes. You hear? They're perfect! Until one of the twins dies and a year later as they're picking up their not so perfect anymore lives to move to a private island (seriously?), the surviving twin says she's the twin that died (or is she or what is going on here?) 
 For some reason Gus and Sarah don't have this little girl in therapy before this happens. Her identical twin sister has been dead for 14 months and she wasn't in therapy!?!? What's wrong with these people? They uproot a lonely girl who has just lost her identical twin and move to a private island?!? Everybody needed therapy! 
 The rest of the plot only happens because nobody talks to each other. Gus and Sarah each have their own secrets and theories and problems with the surviving twin and they don't talk to each other about anything important. Just the dog and groceries basically. So if they had, maybe discussed things this book would have been a lot shorter. :) 
 It was fast and it kept me interested on a frigid day (it was 7 degrees here in Chicago today brrrrrr).

reference_books.title: Pretty Girls
reference_books.review_text:
This was an okay mystery. The plot points are covered in the blurb and other reviews but here's the gist: Young woman missing in the past, young woman missing in the present and they're both connected (maybe?) to the main character. MC's husband is murdered and a whole lot of heck breaks loose. Jennifer McMahon does the woman-missing-in-the-past/woman-missing-in-the-present thing a little tighter than this. 
 I've been reading a lot of these mysteries the last few years and the theme of the perfect husband with a violent past is a common one. This story however, goes on a little too long. Like another reviewer, I was ready for the climax but there seemed to be too much book left for what I felt the story had left to tell. Around the halfway point, it starts to drag. 
 Overall: kept me mostly interested but the characters are kind of stupid and it's too long for what it is.

reference_books.title: All Things Cease to Appear
reference_books.review_text:
Life is too short for bad books. I slogged through 100 pages of this empty monster and nothing much has happened except we switched POVs with nothing much to indicate a connection. I understand from other reviews that even more POVs are coming and it's pretty slow throughout. 
 It's too frustrating to read with no quotation marks to indicate when characters are speaking. If I have to re-read many paragraphs just figure out if someone's talking, I don't want to keep reading. There's way too much flowery description and not enough actual story. I don't need action all the time but all this introspection and overly flowery-trying too hard-MFA language just turns me off if there's no story behind it. 
 There's nothing to see here-move along.

reference_books.title: The Widow
reference_books.review_text:
I was really looking forward to this. The Widow is this year's Gone Girl. But it's really not. It has nothing on Gone Girl. See my rant before my review of Try Not to Breathe. Jean's husband has just died after he was accused of a horrific crime a few years ago, she hopes the press will finally leave her alone. Until she invites a journalist inside her house in her new widow haze. There follows a lot of time jumps and POVs: from the detective, the husband, the journalist, the widow herself. 
 This was a pretty simple story, and should have been simply told. The husband is accused of kidnapping a two year old girl - who has not been found - he's arrested but the evidence falls apart. Jean stands by him throughout the ordeal and the blurb indicates that now that he's gone, she can tell the real story. However, this seemingly simple story is told in a muddled way. I don't mind jumping around in time or multiple POVs if they add to the story. But here, it feels like they padded the story just to get it out of novella territory.

reference_books.title: The Trouble with Goats and Sheep
reference_books.review_text:
I hate giving up on books. I HATE it! But this... This was booooorring. About 100 pages in and not a whole lot has happened, except we've been told it hot about 75 times and that Mrs. Creasy is missing. That's all. I could not make myself care about Grace or Tilly and all their adult neighbors and parents are pretty much the same character over and over. 
 I have much more interesting things to read.

book_a.title: No One Knows
book_a.user_review:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I'm not sure how to rate this one. I read it in 2 days and for the first half I was up in 4.5-5 star territory. I could not put it down. Aubrey's husband, Josh has been missing for 5 years and has just been declared legally dead. And there's a $5 million life insurance policy that his mother (Daisy) wants to fight Aubrey for. I love horrible mothers-in-law in novels. Especially when the main character daughter-in-law is the worst. Aubrey was arrested and tried for Josh's murder, even without a body and has just now come out of the bell jar she's been living in. 
 Told in third person limited with varying time periods and POVs, there are hints that almost everyone has secrets and no one is who they seem. Aubrey had a rough childhood that Josh "saved" her from; growing up in foster care with a prostitute foster mother. Daisy gives little peaks at her secrets in her chapters. "Does he know? Does he know?!?" We go back and forth to when Josh and Aubrey are kids, when they're in high school and fall in love, and to the night Josh disappeared five years ago. 
 It was great until about the halfway mark. Then I just felt disconnected. The story dragged somehow. Not that the action changed at all. Maybe it just became a little repetitive. The ending is bananas and doesn't jive with the rest of the book. If Aubrey knew Josh was alive the whole time, why the breakdown? Why does the third person limited narrator tells us that she's thinking Josh must be dead? It seems like a big twist just for the purpose of a big twist. 
 I have a couple problems: In Chapter 31, we flash back to the summer before Josh's Junior year in high school. Aubrey is just going to be starting high school and Josh is happy about that and planning a romantic weekend. A few pages later, it's mentioned that Aubrey is on the pill and that the school nurse hands them out like candy. I'm sorry but isn't she still in GRADE SCHOOL at this point?!?! I don't think her Montessori school nurse is handing out birth control pills. Neither is the high school nurse. You need a prescription for those (except now in Oregon). 
 And of course, Aubrey is perfect. She seems to have a magical effect on every single man she comes across, even a psychotic lifelong criminal. It's like the magical penis trope only in reverse. With all that "perfection" I was hoping her mother-in-law would play a bigger part in making her suffer. But that subplot dies away about the halfway mark. 
 I read it super fast and was enthralled for about 200 pages. Four stars for the buildup, 2 stars for the second half and the ending. So...3!

sample_reviews.review_text: A worthy addition to the unreliable narrator canon. This would be a 5 star book but for the last chapter (not the epilogue), which felt like the author was forcing readers to come to a specific conclusion, one with which I happened to disagree. Even still, I was fascinated by the main character and the depiction of grief. The twists kept the story pulsing forward and even once key pieces were revealed, I knew there was more to come around the corner. What a ride!

Super confused by the ending ...

Have you ever read a book where there are twists and turns and then BOOM you get punched out? That's what I felt when reading No One Knows. I was really into the novel, loving the twists and then WHACK! I felt like I had been punched. I was so taken back by the final twist and I hated it! I felt that the whole novel was ruined. 
 Aubrey's husband has been missing for over 5 years that he has been recently pronounced as dead. Aubrey believes that her husband is dead because he would of never done this to her. However, when his life insurance payout is looming, Aubrey is realizing that she never really knew her husband. 
 I find it hard to rate this novel, because for the majority of the novel I believed that it was a 4 star novel. However it was a 1 or 2 star ending. I can see the why reason for the majority of the negative reviews for the novel. I felt that the reader got blindsided and it wasn't in a good way.

Need a book that will keep you on the edge of your set and having you staying up too late? No One a Knows, is the book for you. There are so many twists and turns you will not know which way is up. I promise you the ending will have you feeling blindsided. Enjoy! This book comes out today and will make a great Spring Break read. E-ARC by NetGalley.

This was one of SheReads spring book choices and is also on ModernMrsDarcy's Summer Reading list. I almost put it down a couple of time because it didn't grab my interest right away, but in the end, I was glad I kept reading. After about 100 pages, I actually had time to sit and read more than a few pages at a time and found that that made a difference, either that or the story just got better as it went along and sucked me into it. The last 150-200 pages really drew me in and I became engrossed in how this story would play out. Aubrey and Josh were childhood sweethearts, they grew up, married, he went to medical school and by all appearances they had a good life. Then one night, they went to bachelor and bachelorette parties at the Opryland Hotel and Josh just disappears. This story jumps around a lot which I usually don't like, but this was well used to tell the story, both past and present. The present is 5 years after Josh disappears and he is finally being declared dead officially and it goes back 5 years to the night of his disappearance and back to their childhoods when they met, so it hopped around a lot but the chapters were well marked with the years, so it was fairly easy to follow. In the end, I wanted to keep reading because I wanted to know exactly what happened before and after Josh disappears. I was hooked. It was an enjoyable read.

No. No. No. Don't bother. 
 I am not even going to review this one. I could barely get through it. I am done reading books that are compared to GONE GIRL and GIRL ON THE TRAIN. I am done reading books with unreliable narrators and those that have twists that really don't make any sense other than to be a "gotcha" -- know what I mean? When you know there is one and are looking for one, you're prepared and it is a gimmick. I want to believe my characters and like them -- and even if I can't, I still expect plausibility in context.

book_b.title: The Walls Around Us
book_b.user_review:
It seems like I'm giving a lot of books 2 star ratings this year. Maybe I need to find other books to read. This started out well, albeit confusing. But that's to be expected when starting a new book perhaps. The writing was a little too MFA for me and the story didn't make up for it and draw me in. 
 We follow girls in a juvenile detention facility and the world of ballet, if you can see those two worlds colliding. They don't really collide but a former ballerina is accused of killing two other ballerinas and is sent there. 
 It seems like The Walls Around Us is told through a mist of dreams and supernatural visitation. I wasn't always sure what was going on due to the flowery-ness of the writing and the effect Ms. Suma was going for here. I can see what she wanted to do, but I would have enjoyed following the mean girl cat fight world of the small town ballet more than the prison.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This book touched on a lot of important issues (class, competition, jealousy and the legal justice system are just the first to come to mind) while at the same time creating a fantastic atmosphere and mystery surrounding what really happened between Orianna Speerling and Violet Dumont. Ori is imprisoned for the brutal murder of two ballerinas in her ballet class (company?), but no one really knows the truth of what happened out behind the theater except for Ori and Vee. The novel shifts perspective between Amber, Ori's cellmate in the female juvenile detention center, and Vee, who had been Ori's friend throughout childhood. 
 Amber's perspective from within the detention center is so well-drawn, and I loved finding out about her back story. She was actually much more interesting to read about than were the chapters narrated by Vee, who turns out to be quite a piece of work. This book probably would've been 4 stars, except that I really didn't care much for the last 50 pages. It was difficult to understand what was happening and I found the ghost story angle a little silly. The how and why of Vee and Ori's switch is too blurry and bizarre, although I do like that Vee gets justice done to her in the end. 
 Digital ARC from NetGalley.
Oh my god.

A friend of mine said she'd heard this book was described as, "Orange is the New Black Swan." And I wrinkled my nose a little when I saw it was described as a ghostly story, because I don't care for paranormal and I definitely don't care for ghosts. I got this as an advanced reader copy from my darling friend Marisa, and I was going to give it a shot no matter what I thought it might be about -- she knows books way better than me, so I trust her to bring me a great read. 
 But this story. This book. These girls, and the way their stories were woven together. 
 All of what she describes it as is there -- Violet and Orianna are ballerinas, Amber is in prison and there is this ghostly feeling surrounding everything while you're reading, because you know something is not quite real about everything. And you're right. 
 The story revolves around Violet, Amber and Orianna -- three girls who were so entirely different yet were so hauntingly beautiful and damaged and incredibly deep that I didn't blink when their stories intertwined. It's told in the point of views of both Violet and Amber, who are so very different from each other yet very much the same at the same time, and whose lives are connected without either one of them knowing it because of Orianna and her fate. I'm being vague because even the slightest bit of information would ruin the beautiful story for you, and I don't want to do that. 
 There are a lot of characters to keep track of in this tale, but I find that each one is full and real and easy to picture, from the girls in prison with Amber to the people who danced with Violet and Orianna. 
 I have one bit of advice for anyone who reads this one: Don't spend too much time trying to understand. Don't let yourself get confused. Immerse yourself in the book, in the beautiful words, and just go with it. Look back later, when you take a break from reading. I let myself get confused sometimes and I would try to reread what I had already read, and I lost the magic. You don't want to lose the magic in this one. 
 A new favorite, for sure.

What was this book even about? I seriously am so confused right now. This book has a beautiful cover and a poetic title, but there story inside does not match. This was nothing like I thought it would be and I was confused for most of the book, and the ending didn't clear anything up. 
 For about half of the book I suspected what was going on, but I still don't know how it happened. I don't understand why it keeps happening. Basically, there is no explanation at all through the whole book and you only get a piece of really important information at the very end of the book. 
 I do not recommend this book. Much to hard to follow, and it took me awhile to get through it because it is just hard to read. The pacing is odd, there are too many characters to keep track of, and it's hard to tell who's POV you are reading from at first. I'd suggest saving your time and skipping this book.
