3.5 stars. 
 Okay, this was a really weird book. 
 I'm not even sure how to write this review because I have such mixed feelings about this book, that it's hard to pinpoint what I really liked and what I didn't. 
 I guess this is a disclaimer, but this is nowhere near the usual books that I read. Like at all, and I'm not a huge fan of the genre, either. But, this is still a spectacularly written book. 
 It follows the story of Amber, who is in juvie, the story of Violet, who is on her way to Julliard, and the story of Ori, who links the other two together. 
 It's also, very, very confusing. 
 As in, I as confused all the way through, until the end, where I was just slightly less confused. I hope in the finished novel, the chapter separations are a bit better, because I often lost track of who was narrating at the moment. 
 This is an intricate tale of guilt and innocence. Full of surprises, and interesting angles. Definitely a good book to read if you enjoyed Rooms by Lauren Oliver. 
 **Thank you Algonquin Books and NetGalley for an egalley of this book. This is my honest review*

My Thoughts On The Book: 
 "Some of us had been running all our lives. We ran because we could and because we could not. We ran for our lives. We still thought they were worth running for." 
 The Plot Of The Story: 
 Well, if I'm entirely honest I must say that I didn't entirely get this book. It was a little confusing for the most part until the threads were tied together somewhat at the very end but for most of the book I was left feeling like I had no clue what was actually the point of it. 
 The book is told via dual POV's, the first is Amber from the detention centre and the second is up and coming ballerina Violet. They seem to have little if nothing in common until you realize that their common thread is Orianna. Orianna is Violet's friend and another ballerina, a more talented ballerina it would seem. Events lead to Orianna being incarcerated with Amber for murder. That's the book in it's most basic terms but it isn't as simple as all that and to say too much more will give the plot ad the excitement of the book away but put it this way it's not at all as it seems especially when you have to factor in that some of the story is told in the present and some of it is told from the past....... confused yet? Yep, you get the gist of how this book made me feel. Don't get me wrong though as I did enjoy reading it and I was left with a sense of satisfaction when the book was finished, I did kind of get where it was all going but getting there was a little mind boggling for me. 
 What Is There To Love? 
 The characters are well-constructed and complicated beings, with great depth to them, especially the girls in the detention centre. We get a good sense of who they all are, how they think and what their motives are for the way they act and the moves they make within the bounds of the story. 
 The idea behind the story was a fantastic one, it was a unique idea and sounded as if it should make for a wonderful read, I know a lot of other bloggers have loved this book and I wish I could say that I was one of those that was blown away by it but it just didn't..... makes me more than I little sad as I had really great hopes for it. 
 The Walls Around Us is a book about emotions and about perception, how people view each other and how it leads to the worst kind of preconceptions about who and what people really are. It shows how the simplest cases of jealousy can lead to bloodshed and blame being pointed in the wrong directions, and it also shows how if you believe a person to be a certain way that no matter how hard that person tries to fight that preconception it oftens sticks and never goes away. 
 What Is There To Dislike? 
 Umm, overall it was okay and I did quite enjoy reading it as I said but it was all a little confusing. Some of the problem for me was down to the simple issue of the books format, being a very early ARC from the end of last year the formatting wasn't all in pace yet and it made it a little challenging to read. I am sure if I read it again in the finished form that it might make an awful lot more sense and maybe it is something that I should do for me own piece of mind as the idea for the book was a ingenious one. 
 How's The Writing? 
 There is nothing majorly wrong with the way the book was written and as I said I think it may have been more of a formatting issue in this case but in saying that the way the book was structured did leave me bewildered at times as it didn't make the most sense, I couldn't see the threads that joined the story together to begin with it took a while for the two POV's to join together and start making sense to me. 
 After finishing the book I did feel that it was cleverly put together and the story did build up nicely until the final reveal, the final twist and then everything fell nicely into place, it was relief to finally get what the author had been building up to. 
 Final Thoughts: 
 This was my first book by Nova Ren Suma and while this particular book hasn't quite hit the spot for me it doesn't mean I won't be reading more of the authors work in the future and she has quite an intriguing touch to her writing that I am curious to discover more about. 
 I am sad that this book didn't live up to my expectations but a I said this may have been down to the formatting of the early ARC and I do intend to read a finished copy of the book in the future to see if this was truly the case for my confusion or whether it was the befuddling structure of the book that led to the book not grabbing me that way I wanted it too, so read this review with that in mind and I would always recommend that you read this book for yourself and make up your own minds about it.
Loved it!!! Unexpected twist!

What. Just. Happened. ??!!? I feel like that was less of a book and more of a huge jumble of book parts all mashed up that I had to plow through just to get to the end in search of some sort of closure (sense would be entirely too much to hope for). The bits about stabby ballerinas were definitely sensational, though.

4.5 
 This was a very intricate weaving of a story, jumping back and forth between points of view, and I enjoyed it so much. 
 One point of view is Amber's, a girl who's been in juvenile detention for over three years. One night, the locks on the doors open of their own accord, and the girls are able to run free. What follows in her narrative is the story of how 42 girls managed to die on the same night three years ago. 
 The other point of view is Violet's, a talented ballet dancer about to leave for Julliard. One night, she makes the decision to visit Aurora Hills Juvenile Detention Centre, where her best friend was sent three years ago, dying not a month into her sentence. 
 What was interesting about this story was that it was not about neither Amber nor Violet, but about Orianna, Violet's best friend and Amber's cellmate. It's a spectacularly told ghost story about truth and justice and toxic relationships (friendships, relatives) and what the consequences can be. 
 What I also liked was that the two different POVs are in two different tenses. We know straight off the bat that Amber's story is taking place in the past, while Violet's is taking place in the present. I actually enjoyed Amber's narration a lot more, though I don't think this was why. Amber was just, to an extent, a better person, and the author has managed to convey this, even though Amber is behind bars and Violet is not. 
 This was essentially a cover borrow, and I'm glad that I'm occasionally so vain as to pick something so gorgeous up without knowing too much about it. Very interesting read.

This book had all the things that make a great book at least for me. It had a great plot, kickass heroines, romance that was not over the top plus some feminist undertones. 
 The Alice Network is a story told through the interchanging views of two women, Eve and Charlie. Eve's storyline is set in France during the first world war where she is a spy while Charlie's is set in different places where they travel to but in the present which is post the second world war. 
 Spies, the Nazi, a queen of spies, revenge, love and betrayal what is not to love about this book. From the first time I began this book I could not put it down I was totally hooked. I could not stop reading Eve's story! I have to confess that I actually read this book in a weird way. I first read all parts about Eve then I went back to Charlie. I mean compared to Eve, Charlie was boring plus she had this hero complex where she tried to save everyone which annoyed me. 
 The best part about this book was the characters. They were strong, dysfunctional, brave 
 "Are you ever afraid?" 
 "Yes, just like everybody else. But only after the danger is done--before that, fear is an indulgence." She slid her hand through Eve's elbow. "Welcome to the Alice Network." 
 They are also very rude but they were real. 
 I could totally picture Lili when she ordered a brandy. 
 "It's been an absolute pisser of a day," 
 My favourite characters were Lili, Eve and Charlie in that order. The plot did not disappoint even when there was a lull in Charlie's part you could look forward to some action when it came to Eve. 
 This is definitely worth 5 stars. I totally recommend it:)

** spoiler alert ** 
 Quinn combines facts and fiction in this novel about a spy ring, The Alice Network, that actually existed during World War I. The novel moves from 1914 to 1947 with two different stories. One is Charlotte's, an unmarried pregnant college girl in search of her cousin. The other is Eve's who served as a spy for the Alice Network. Moving back and forth in time interrupts the narratives and breaks the flow, making it harder to read and hard to stay interested in the novel.

Wow. This blew me out of the water. What a historical gem - based on real life figures from WWI and tying into WWII fiction with plenty of character development and a chase to find someone that turns into a hunt for revenge. I will definitely be re-reading this, as I'm sure I missed quite a bit the first time! I've never heard of Louise De Bettignies, the "Queen of Spies", and what a shame. This easily ranks up there with The Nightingale and All the Light We Cannot See.
Very good.

This came highly recommended and I forged half way through and tried to keep up with the dual story line and enter into this story. I finally did what I rarely (if ever) do - decided to be done. Just could not keep investing my time in such a dark and slowly evolving tale. I do leave wondering what happened to cousin Rose and Charlie and Eve - just not enough to spend several more hours with a so/so book when I have so many more on my stack to read!

3.5 stars 
 I'm a sucker for a good spy novel, and 20th century female spies/Resistance fighters are my preferred escape stories. This one checked all the boxes: strong women fighting stereotypes, outsmarting the enemies (both the Germans and the sexist society), parallel narratives, and unfolding mysteries. It was a good escape read, and it gets its stars for that, but it doesn't stand up to scrutiny. I was disappointed by the obvious editing mistakes (like describing someone as "tall and gaunt" twice in the same paragraph) and the pat, dragged-out ending. Characters who could have been complex and interesting (some of these were real people, with real issues) all became good-or-bad stereotypes, and went through the series of predictable steps, obviously overlooked clues, and a completely predictable final confrontation and happily-ever-after ending. 
 In the end, the whole thing felt shallow and staged, and I left disappointed.

 The whole plot line of this story was just brilliant. I also loved the fact that Olivia wasn't 100% confident in her own skin, which just made her that much more relatable. I personally saw myself in Olivia in so many things. SO. MANY. THINGS. 
 I don't know what else I can say about this other than I loved it. I loved every part of it. It wasn't full of suspense like the other two novels were, but it was addicting all the same. I have become so emotionally invested in this gang, I don't know what I'll do once it is over. I'm also not one to focus on the setting of a story, but this setting is just perfect. 
 Nothing else to say except, if you haven't read it yet please do so! 
 Also what would have taken 11.5 hours to listen to on Audible took me 3 hours. I FREAKING DEVOURED THIS BOOK. I want more Nate though :(

I don't even know where to begin on this one. WOW!!! Before Jamaica Lane is the third, full novel installment of the On Dublin Street series and it is simply amazing. Nate and Olivia are best friends. Nate is extremely HOT, SEXY, and CHARMING. He is also a commitment-phobe and a total player, yet you can't help falling in love with him. Olivia is a sweet, quiet, and insecure girl. She is beautiful but doesn't see herself that way and lacks not only self-esteem but confidence as well. This is the story of best friends who cross the lines to friends with benefits, and eventually to lovers. The story unfolds beautifully. There is humor and sass, angst and sadness, paid and fear, and finally joy and beautiful love. If one book has it all, it is this one. 
 "If you were just some woman in a bar, I'd pick you out from all the others, take you home, and fuck you so hard you wouldn't be able to walk straight in the morning." Nate 
 I gulped. 
 In fact, I think I might have had a little mini-orgasm." Olivia 
 Olivia finally gets tired of being the shy, insecure girl who can't talk to men; who can't flirt or even consider herself in the same league as her beautiful friends Joss and Jo. She decides she needs someone to teach her how to be confident and make her feel like she can be someone's perfect girl. Who better than her best friend and chick-magnet, Nate, to help her out? She has her eye on a post-grad student named Ben but her lack of experience is holding her back so she asks Nate to teach her how to be that sexy, sensual, and confident woman that can attract a man like Ben. 
 "Okay, we'll take it step by step. Strip to your underwear." 
 A shiver went through me at his demand, but I found myself replying, "You could ask nicely, you know." 
 His lips twitched. "Olivia, sweetheart, would you please strip down to your underwear for me?" 
 Let's just say that from the very first lesson, things get downright steamy! Their chemistry is undeniable and right then and there I knew that this "friends with benefits" or "teacher/student" arrangement was not going to work. They are obviously attracted to each other, they get along great, and they laugh and play together so adding hot sex to the mix? Yeah, things are going to get messy. As the "lessons" move forward, the lines start to blur. Soon they are spending all of their time together, Nate is sleeping over, and Liv is falling deeper and deeper into this world that revolves only around her sexy best friend. 
 "Liv's perfect. She deserves perfect. She won't be settling for anything else." Nate 
 As Liv starts to see the change, Nate is in complete denial. He suffered a terrible loss and vowed never to give his heart away again. So what does he do when Liv finally confronts him about what is really going? He runs. I swear I felt my heart breaking for Liv and even for Nate because this wonderful man just didn't know how to deal with what was really going. 
 "You taught me to be brave again, Nate.' 
 I swiped at the tears, my heart catching painfully as his eyes seared into mine. 
 'How can such a coward teach someone to be brave?" 
 Before Jamaica Lane will capture your heart and it will take you on a rollercoaster of emotions. It is flawlessly written and it will make you fall in love with these two courageous characters. On Dublin Street will probably always be my favorite of the series and Braden will always be my number one alpha male, but let me tell you, Samantha Young brings it with Nate and Liv's story. Plus, an added bonus to an already terrific story, we get to catch up with all of our favorite characters from previous books. It is intertwined seamlessly with Castle Hill and that just made this even more perfect. Read it, devour it, and good luck putting it down! Now the wait begins for Hannah and Marco's story in Fall From India Place. 
 "I didn't just want Nate to love me. I wanted him to love me the way I loved him. The kind of love that's so big it would last beyond a lifetime."

4.5 Stars

 Nate is in turns a nice guy, a great friend, a superb lovaaahhh, a complete douchey-ass hole, and a good groveler. I love a good grovel.

 My only complaint: The tattoo...saw that coming from a mile off. Awkward. I wish they'd have left that out completely. For me, it took away from the story rather than add to it. Not sure how everyone else feels but it was kind of a cheesy downer for me toward the end.

The chemistry between these two was sizzling. Like, seriously. Great build-up was given to these friends and my ovaries were in danger of combusting on several occasions. I liked both the characters. The heroine had confidence in all areas of her life, bar one. It would be absurd to hold anything against her for being a little unsure in one area in her life, especially since there were valid reasons for her insecurity.

Again Auntee's review says it all. I really liked this book. Olivia is such a great heroine. She is sweet, smart, strong, and doesn't take BS. Nate is a complete rake. But, as we know, sometimes rakes turn into the best men. :-P This can be a tad of a tear jerker too.

True, it took a lot of reading as per the references to get this one written by Philippa Gregory, but it was just painful to read for me... with all the deceit, killings, plotting and narrow-mindedness, and bad ones at that. Awful. There wasn't any climax to the book, sure there were a few high and low points here and there, but they were so sparsely situated that I'm not even sure if those can be counted as points. Reading a Philippa Gregory book is like hopping into a freshly laundered bed after a hot bath with newley shaved legs! It's simply divine! She masters historical fiction with ease and is on point with her "guesses" that fill in the blanks where history has kept it's secrets from us. The Red Queen is no exception when it comes to her masterful story telling. A pure joy to read as the story jumps of the page into my mind creating a beautiful movie that plays in my head with no effort on my part. I forget I'm even reading!

Margaret Beaufort's only desire in life is for her son, Henry Tudor, to become the King of England. This book is the story of how she sacrificed everything to ensure that that happened. 
 She believed she was special and that the Lancaster House was blessed by God, she spends hours on her kness in prayer and her heroine was Joan of Arc, in fact she often asked herself 'What would Joan do now?' when she was faced with a tough decision. 
 I am a highly intelligent, highly educated woman, from a royal family, called by God to great office, guided personally by the Maid, and constantly hearing the voice of God in my prayers. 
 It is narrated by Margaret who comes across as not very likeable, incredibly pious, very jealous of her rival, Elizabeth Woodville (The White Queen), single-minded and devious. Philippa Gregory has really brought her to life and I was gripped by the seemingly endless battles between the armies of the Lancaster and the Yorks, but Margaret never stopped hoping and plotting and scheming, even when her son had to be raised by her enemy she continued telling him that he was still a Lancaster and that one day he will be the King, and not to give up believing. 
 I enjoyed the first book in 'the cousins war' The White Queen but I enjoyed this even more, I thought the writing was more descriptive and flowed easier. Although I really didn't like the emotionally cold Margaret Beaufort I did admire her determination and self-belief.
Well written, but Margaret was not someone I could sympathize with.

Philippa Gregory tackles the figure of Margaret Beaufort, the mother of Henry VII of England, in this novel chronicling the Wars of the Roses. While it is interesting to learn about Margaret, who married at an extremely young age and endured a difficult childbirth, she was far from a likable character. Margaret displays a self-righteous belief in the Lancaster cause and particularly that her son Henry is destined to be King of England. The ends justify the means to Margaret and she even orders the children of the rival York family murdered at one point to further her son's claim to the throne. I simply could not find much that was sympathetic about Margaret and I found myself hoping her enemies would put this woman in her place, simply because she was so unlikeable.

I finished this book...out of sheer will and force. I really wanted to like it as much as The White Queen, but the main character is so unlikable you are actually rooting for her demise. She has no saving grace. You NEVER feel bad or sorry for her, even when she is a young child. She plays too much the victim and does nothing but complain. This book made me not want to continue forward with the rest of the series.
I didn't care about Margaret or her son... This book bored me and I couldn't finish it. That hasn't happened with Philippa Gregory before; either I am in a bad mood, or my tastes have matured.

I finished this book ten minutes ago. It took me nearly two months to read, and here's why: 
 1. The protagonist was a whiny, self-absorbed, annoying twit who was afraid of growing old. 
 2. This book combined my two least favorite genres: romance and historical fiction. 
 3. The ending, if you can call it that, was horrible! 
 4. Some authors can pull off writing very long books (J.K. Rowling, anybody?). Some can't (Kathleen Winsor, I am talking to you). This was an eight hundred and twenty page story that should have been three hundred pages, tops. I might have even rounded my rating up to 2 (my official rating of this book is 1.5 stars) if this book wasn't so long. 
 I started Gone with the Wind when I was about halfway through this book, and so far, it's a thousand times better. Amber St. Clare cannot stand up to Scarlett O'Hara!

I'm a historical fiction junkie who loves a bit of romance, whether or not it's the primary feature of the book. Let me tell you, this is the one that started it all. Forever Amber is a classic of its genre and it deserves to be. I LOVE anti-heroes and Amber is lovable bawdy lass that makes you root, makes you groan, and gives you the best ride you will ever have wandering through Restoration England. You really feel like you're there and you don't stay in one class system. You see it all: the thieves, the whores, the royals, and the nobles, and everyone and everything in between. I devoured its nearly 1000 pages at many different locations in New York City. When I revisit those places sometimes, I think about how much I enjoyed reading the book at that spot. Though it gets a little confusing if I was at the cafe at Discovery Times Square or if I was at a ball in the 1660s. This is a favorite of mine and it always will be.

 Description: 
 Olivia Cunning knocked the ball out of the ball park with this stunning series of a group of twenty something rockers on tour. The readers are given an indepth look into the world of metal rock bands and the interactions between members of the band, the band and their fans and the band. These books are also in a lot of ways a coming of age story as these "boys" turn into men book by book in the series. The 5 stories weave a back story through out each novel to end up with a nice bow tie at the end of book 5. OC weaves descriptive hot sex (erotic) in with her character development and she also uses it as a vehicle to move the story in the direction she wants us to go. 
 In Double Time a menage/mfm/mm book we finally get Trey's story. Now Trey has been a book boyfriend of mine since book 1 and I am excited OC did him justice. Through Trey's bisexuality we see how he tries to change for the woman he loves and how he grows and learns so much about himself as he develops his relationship with Reagan. Ethan was a wonderful mix of protector, little boy, dom and boyfriend...as part of this relationship we do learn more about him. I did find Brian's angst a wee bit over the top and would like to have seen him a bit more stoic and perhaps behave slightly out of character in his pining for his family.

This book reveals things about Eric's story that you just don't get cause of not having the background of reading Eric's book. . 
 I give this book and the series a 5+stars they are firmly on my personal favorite's shelves as I know I will want to reread this rockin adventure. I recommend the series to lovers of erotic romance with a strong contemporary setting and characters. The series is edgy and fresh and I truly hope OC writes Dare and his band's stories next. ROCK ON OLIVIA!!!

I didn't have high expectations coming into this book. Book one, Backstage Pass was fun and really dirty, but the story line was just okay. And then I really didn't like book two (the hero and I did NOT get along.) But I wanted to give this series one more chance and I'm glad I did. I also want to note that although this is the third book published in this series, it is actually the fifth book. By that I mean, band members Eric and Jace already have their HEAs in this book, although their books are not out yet. I don't like that this book is out of order and I don't know why the publisher decided to do this (we get Jace's book in January and I assume Eric's book after that) but there you go. 
 Trey has been in love with his best friend and fellow band member Brian, for a very long time. As teenagers, they share some intimate moments, but Brian is now very happily married to a woman, and he has just become a new father. While Trey never wants to lose his friendship with him, he has to deal with the fact that that is all they will ever have together. Trey is bisexual, and enjoys the very nuemerous hook-ups he has in every city The Sinners tour in. Trey's brother is also in a band, and Trey helps them audition a new guitar player. The one that blows them out of the water is Reagan. She works at a coffee shop but has some mad skills at playing the guitar. She can't believe she won the audition and that she is going to be an actual rock star. She also can't believe how sexy Trey is. They have an immediate connection (total insta-lust but it worked okay for me). Trey decides it is time for him to have a steady girlfriend (After 24 hours of knowing her.....a little fast) and Reagan feels the same about him. 
 Trey keeps his bisexual side a secret, as Reagan once found her BFF (and boyfriend at the time) Ethan, having sex with another man while dating her. She was betrayed and hurt, although her and Ethan have patched things up and are friends again. But Trey can't hold off his urge to have sex with another man, and eventually Ethan comes into the relationship, as he loves Reagan and is very attracted to Trey. 
 This book gets high marks for its enjoyment factor. It's so sexy, and dirty and the story moves along at a nice pace. I really adored Trey and his emotional struggle with his bisexuality and falling in love with Reagan. He is a good-hearted guy, and you can't help but root for him in this story. I also like Reagan. More of a tomboy, she could care less about glamming herself up for the press. Her reaction to becoming a big-time rock star played out well for me too. I also love the vibe of the band in general, while they are on tour or just hanging out at each other's houses. They are family and I really enjoyed their interactions. 
 There are a few things that didn't work for me. First of all, in each book in this series, there is a small suspense part and I don't understand why its there. It never really fits in or in this case it is so predictable, I'm just not a fan. It takes away from the other stuff in the book. 
 I also had problems with Ethan. I never warmed up to him, as he is so forceful and on the colder side. I found his scenes with Trey hot (we get some really good m/m scenes as well as m/m/f in this book) but at one point he tries to steal Trey away from Reagan for his own, and that bothered me. If he was suppose to be Reagan's BFF, and he already cheated on her once, why would he want to hurt her again? When Reagan comes up with the idea that Ethan should join their relationship, it seemed rushed on Reagan's part. I felt like she really didn't give it consideration. The sex is hot between the three of them, but I wanted more depth. 
 But like I said earlier, while I have some reservations about this book, I also found it just plain fun to read. If you are in the mood for rock stars and dirty sex, you will like this one.

Review originally posted at http://fictionvixen.com/joint-review-... 
 My joint review with Sophia at Fiction Vixen Book Reviews 
 Angela and I are both fans of this series and we are both fans of m/m/f romances so we decided to do a joint review of Double Time by Olivia Cunning. 
 Sophia: This was such a fun book to read. It's one of those kind of books where I set aside my need for some semblance of realism and just sit back and enjoy. I think it's because the rock star lifestyle is so far beyond my reality and when I read about it, I want it to be as outrageous and crazy it can be so I can just kick back and immerse myself for 400 or so pages. There were several things that did not work for me in this book, and that's mostly what I'll talk about here, but overall this was a really sexy, super-fun read. 
 The Timeline 
 Sophia: This review assumes you're familiar with this series and you know the characters we're discussing. That being said, this book was clearly published out of order and we jump way ahead in the timeline. I'm not sure why the decision was made to do this, but as a reader I am a little disappointed. As much as I love Trey and was eager to get to his story, it will be weird going back in time to read the other Sinners' stories since I've already gotten a glimpse into their (now) current relationships. 
 Angela: I have no idea why the publisher thought it would be a good idea to jump ahead in the timeline and release Trey's book before Eric and Jace's. Not only do we already know what their kinks are, but also have an idea of their HEA. I was not a big fan of this. As much as I adore Trey, and I do have much love for him, I would have rather waited and had the chance to see him go through his issues and have everyone's story told in order. That would have made more sense to me. I always like a big wrap up at the end of a final book in a series to give us an idea of where everyone has ended up and how they are all doing... and I'm not sure how they will do it here seeing as everything is out of order. Plus we will see Trey in the next two books and already know what's in store for him. Confusing. 
 Trey 
 Sophia: Trey is my favorite Sinner. He is bisexual and has been in love with Brian, his best friend and band mate for 13 years. The time has come for Trey to let go of the hope of Brian loving him back and Trey is going to try to move on not only from that but he is going to give up men entirely. When he meets Reagan, he believes he can be happy being only with her. Trey is selfish, and impulsive but we see a sweet, generous side of him too. He's loyal to his band mates, loves his brother and is damn sexy. 
 Angela: I have a whole lot of love for Trey. He's always been my favorite, but that may be because he's a bi-hero and I'm a big fan of bi-heros. Or it could be because Trey is awesome and I'm a big fan of awesome. I really felt for him in the first book of this series, Backstage Pass, where Brian meets the woman of his dreams and Trey realizes that there isn't ever going to be a chance of them being a couple. I really wanted him to get his HEA, and find out that Brian isn't the only man in the world. I felt like he got what he needed with Reagan and Ethan. Something to satisfy all of his needs. 
 Reagan 
 Sophia: I thought Reagan was awesome. I liked that she was a guitarist because that's such a male dominated profession. I'm glad she wasn't hired to be Exodus End's new guitarist simply because she was female, instead based solely on her skill. 
 I also liked that she was brash and a little bit crude, just like her band mates. She made me laugh constantly. 
 Angela: I thought Reagan was the perfect heroine for Trey. She's wild and crude and crazy, but then you'd have to be to fit in with this rock-n-roll set and have a relationship with someone like Trey. I liked that she was comfortable with her sexuality and had no problem with jumping into sex with Trey. The hot tub scene where she is flirting with Trey, while checking out his brother at the same time was funny. I liked her, I even understood her needing to be reassured that she was just as good a guitarist as the men she had always idolized. She was strong and vulnerable. 
 Ethan 
 Sophia: Ethan is Reagan's former lover and now roommate. They broke up when Reagan caught Ethan cheating on her with another man. They managed to stay friends after the breakup, and Ethan has remained close with Reagan because he loves her, but knows he can't be faithful to her. Reagan believes Ethan is gay. 
 I had a hard time with Ethan. I was so annoyed he tried to interfere with Reagan and Trey's relationship. He supposedly loves Reagan and wants her to be happy but then he comes on to Trey simply because he wants him and knows Trey wants him too. Not cool. 
 Angela: I still don't know if I really like Ethan or not. I just don't get the whole reason why he let Reagan continue to think he was totally gay and not bi and in love with her. He cheats on her with a man, she catches him, they break up, he pines after her from the role of a friend, but when Trey comes on the scene he does the same thing? That just did not make sense to me. Who does that? You're right, not cool. 
 The Three Way 
 Sophia: The way the three way relationship came about seemed a little far-fetched. There wasn't enough emotional build up for Trey and Ethan and the relationship was under developed. It was just sex, "let me service you" so you can keep your girlfriend. I get that this is a way for Ethan to be close to Reagan and bang Trey and I can overlook some things for the sake of a fun read, but this was one of those things in this book that was hard to accept. It was convenient and really HOT, but not very believable. 
 Angela: As much as I love menage stories, they are very rarely in any way believable to me, but this just seemed weirder than normal. The "here you can have him to take care of your bi needs" thing was odd. Especially since it involved Ethan, who Reagan had had a serious relationship with at one time and still considered her best friend. I mean I went with it for the sake of getting to the hot man on man sex, but... weird. Then when they are starting out and they are snapping pics of each other doing dirty things to each other to send to Reagan.... When they don't even know how she is going to react to it? 
 I do tend to find m/m/f menages more authentic than m/f/m menages. Wouldn't you think a man would almost have to have some bi-curiousity to be in a bed naked with another man? You know, just in case of accidental touching. 
 Insta-Love and Sex 
 Sophia: Trey and Reagan fall in love right away. I wasn't surprised by the insta-hookup, but Trey's decision to commit to Reagan was so impulsive, even for him. But strangely, I totally believed in his commitment to Reagan, or at least his commitment to being committed. He seemed to really want to make it work. 
 The insta-love between Ethan and Trey...well, the sex was hot. Not convinced on the love. But let's get back to the sex. Trey and Ethan were smokin' hot together. If I remember correctly, didn't they get an entire sex chapter? 
 Angela: I hate insta-love story lines I mean I really hate them. One night stands, okay, insta-dating and liking, okay, but I just don't care for storylines where someone is saying I love you and committing in a week. I don't know if I believed Trey's love for Reagan at first, I think he committed to her because he found someone who was just as intriguing to him as Brian and wanted to hang onto that feeling. 
 As far as Trey and Ethan, I didn't believe their insta-love at all, but the sex was hot. Like singe my eyeballs hot. I could have done with a few more chapter long sexy scenes. Ethan might be an ass outside of the bedroom, but inside the man is dirty. The "bondage"scene with the three of them..:) Even if I didn't believe the love between them, I did feel the chemistry was there. 
 The Suspense 
 Sophia: In past books I kind of wished the suspense was left out. It just didn't work for me. Pretty much the same in this book even though it was minimal. It didn't add much to the story nor did it take away for me. 
 Angela: The suspense plot was just background noise for me... I could have done without it. I think this was just the author's way of giving Ethan an "in" with the tour since he was the security expert, or maybe so there will be that moment where everyone realizes that they love each other so much. It didn't really add or take away any enjoyment of the storyline for me. 
 Conclusion 
 Sophia: I love an emotionally intense story, but sometimes I just want a fun, "rock your face off" read and that's what this book was for me. The wild, free lifestyle is just fun to escape to for a while and the no holds barred sex is hot, plain and simple. I had a few issues, but this series draws me in with the wild rock star lifestyle and the strong brotherhood style relationships between the band mates. I love Trey and I enjoyed his unconventional love story. Final grade: B- 
 Angela: I like that:..."rock your face off". I had a lot of fun reading Trey's story. Initially I was a little disappointed that this would be a menage instead of a straight m/m, but this story ended up working for me. This series caught my attention with the first book by being about a bunch of guys who are wild, sexy and kinky and I continue to be entertained with their rock-n-roll living. The next book is going to be a little strange reading since we're going back in time, but I was glad to get Trey's love story, even if it was out of order. Final grade B

I mean, if you take out all of the sexual references, comments, descriptions, innuendos, mentions, and, well, the sex, all that's left is a bunch of thes, ands and exclamation points. Then I had an epiphany (Google it - it's not the Big O): I was completely going about this book in the wrong way. I was looking at it from a reviewer's standpoint, a good book/bad book angle, and that is absolutely not how this tome is meant to be devoured. 
 There are plenty of books about scarred college guys who are hunky and tattooed and pumped up and have slept with hundreds of faceless lasses because he can't give his heart to just one girl yet because of that thing that happened in his past and he's just waiting for that perfect girl to break through his defenses. This un-novel novel is about going a step further, though, because it has lots and lots of descriptive sex. And almost sex. And inner dialogue about glances that make man parts twitch. And vajayjays yell "holla!" And less of a story. (Sheesh; that again...I must move past that.) 
 But can I? I know people enjoy different kinds of stories, like heavy Russian novels in your Ice Palace and light, frothy beach reads on vacation, but I can't really see any point to this story other than making your ladybits tingle and getting the vapors. So what do we talk about here, then? The main characters, virginal Baya (echhh that name) and studly Bryson have a "meet cute" that can only be here, nestled amongst these pages of gutteral sounds, flashing, flapping, tingling, yearning, and aching body parts, endless sex by a roommate who Baya doesn't even meet (face-to-face, anyway) until the end of the book and a tally of conquests that Baya's overprotective (of course) yet hypocritical brother has on his door-frame.

Their voices alternate in chapters, so you know from the get-go that sweet, lovely, innocent baby Baya is tired of her brother's protection and is ready to do the deed immediately, if not sooner. We also are happy to know that while Bryson has as many notches on his door-frame as her brother Cole, he was only reacting to something bad that happened to him that he can't talk about. So it's OK. He didn't mean any of that sex with those people; at least his heart wasn't in it. Which makes his attraction to Baya, even with all of his penis saluting talk, pure and true. So noble. Gag. 
 So blah blah blah, have to hide their relationship from Cole; blah blah blah, Bryson is even awesomer because his little sister is deaf; blah blah blah, Baya has to wear some tiny short shorts (that she stole from her sexually adventurous roommate) to work in Bryson's bar because that's all she had though she would never normally wear that sort of thing (several times); blah blah blah there's the bitch who wants Bryson at any cost; blah blah blah dang it, I am tired of being the innocent virgin; blah blah blah I can't live with that roommate so I have to stay in my brother's apartment with him and Bryson don't worry nothing will happen...blah blah blah BLECH. 
 Look, sex in novels is all well and good, but for me, bottom line, it can't take the place of story. Seriously, if you removed everything not having to do with sex from this novel, there would be no changes. And like I've complained about before: New Adult is now code for PORN LITE. But I work at a library and the amount of cat books that the younger kids come looking for, this seemed to fit right into that world. 
 The writing style also bothered me quite a bit. One second she's being cowardly and scared the next she's full of courage and will fight the world if she has too. It made my head hurt trying to keep up with her. Not to mention I found the writing to be extremely botchy.  The thing that bothered me most was that I felt that the idea of the book was actually quite amazing. I could totally see it. Fantastic "bones" and strong concept/world building - few issues of the pace dragging and over description when not needed; and sometimes the immaturity of the narrator's voice was too annoyingly grating on my nerves...but overall not a horrible read. 
 Nisha and her relationships with the cats that communicate and sometimes protect her is great! Thought at first it would get too Disney-ish but it didn't.

In short: City of a Thousand Dolls by Miriam Forster is an entertaining and addicting read with lush and fascinating world building. 
 At six-years-old, Nisha was abandoned by her parents at the City of a Thousand Dolls - a community that takes in unwanted girls, trains them in a specialized area like fighting, beauty, healing, or pleasure, and then sells them off to the highest bidder at sixteen-years-old. When one of the girls is found dead in the City, Nisha decides she is going to track down the killer in order to protect the girls, as well as herself. Along the way, she also uncovers secrets about her past. 
 The world building is where City of a Thousand Dolls truly shines. Debut author Miriam Forster integrates South Asian culture into a lush and fascinating world to pleasing effect. I loved spending time in the City of a Thousand Dolls, learning about the different houses and castes, and the training and schooling for the girls. And, OH YEAH, Nisha can speak telepathically to the cats that roam the city and these cats are basically her makeshift family. I thought that was cute! There are so many ways that the concept of telepathic cats could have gone awry, but for some reason, I found it worked and was never super silly or cliched. 
 I feel a bit conflicted about the plot and characters in City of a Thousand Dolls. On the one hand, the mystery was a good one and the reveal was shocking. But the execution of the mystery was a little clumsy at times and the plot twists were predictable. And the ending was tied up WAY too neatly and quickly for my tastes. Similarly, I did like Nisha most of the time - she was ultimately brave and good - but she often made questionable choices and could be a little slow on the uptake. The romance was very limited and nothing particularly special - but sweet just the same. 
 Okay, okay - so that may sound like a lot of faults that I've just listed, but the fact of the matter is that I enjoyed myself while reading City of a Thousand Dolls. It was addicting and easy to read. And I must reiterate that the world building was super interesting! There may not have been as much depth as I was hoping for, but I had FUN reading it and isn't that the most important thing? 
 City of a Thousand Dolls works well as a standalone, but there is room for a sequel. Recommended for readers who like fun and easy books and cat people.

City of a Thousand Dolls is not...bad. It was my most anticipated book of the year and unfortunately it did not live up to my expectations but it certainly wasn't terrible. When a novel is touted as high fantasy and comes with a synopsis like the one this one does, some expectations will latch themselves on to the book. If expectations were sentient beings that is. And sometimes it feels like they are but that's just me being crazy. Caitlin, the awesome, picked up a copy for me at ALA and honestly, when I saw the length (or rather the lack of thickness) of the book, I was somewhat concerned. And with good reason. 
 The book lacked the detailed world building that is so essential in novels of this genre. It lacked the complexity that is so important when creating a world from scratch. The characters had the potential to be emotionally rich with complicated relationships but the potential remained untapped. The names of the characters used were Indian and to some extent, the author does dip into Indian customs and traditions but then she also brings in Asian customs (or so it felt like to me) but it all needed more work for that construction of culture to work. It just felt cobbled. 
 I needed more time with the creepy woman who wanted to possess the main character whose name is Nisha which is interesting as all heck if I were to start analyzing but I'll restrain myself. I wanted to know why she wanted her and for what purposes? Why was Nisha so afraid of the woman, was it because of her cruelty or because she would demand from Nisha things she didn't want to give. It would have been a fascinating look into sexuality and desire but ah well. 
 There are talking cats but alas. The book feels really superficial. Not that it doesn't address some more substantial themes but that it does so very superficially. There is a lack of depth, a lack of substance that interfered with my enjoyment. And okay, so I admit, I was looking for something Eona-esque in the sense that peoples' motivations and backstories are considered and I am fully aware of how difficult it is to do such a thing but that is part of the challenge of writing. 
 Also, the romance. When we come into the book, it is already in progress and that is a gamble I do not advice any author to take because you can get a LOT of tension from relationships that are in its nascent stages and when you plonk the reader in the middle of a relationship that seems like it's all about the physical (which is not necessarily bad) and then do not develop it any further (heck, the love interest isn't even present in the novel for more than ten pages) until Nisha goes "I know I love him!" it makes the reader (well...me) unhappy. 
 So yeah, this book is okay. I probably won't be coming back to read the second one but I might. The talking cats didn't do it for me but I may give it another chance. We'll see. You guys may like it better than I did. Just...lower your expectations.
Predictable from start to finish. Stupid.
Not the greatest book ever written, but a decent story of murder, fantasy, some magic and talking cats.

So how does the City of a Thousand Dolls come about? Well, we give society a two-child limit and let everyone know that only men carry the family name and can own property. Does this sound familiar? Yes, the feminism in mean screams to tear some people apart for making up stupid rules like that. Anyways, we got a safe haven for girls where they will learn things and grow up into something society wants: a wife, a mistress, a medic, a musician, etc. And we add the mysticism around the city and how nothing really gets in or out past the barrier. And we hear a dozen or so variations on how the barrier came about, but it doesn't seem like any of the city's background really gets explained. 
 Truly, I never became vested in this story. It was too slow for me to get into, and I felt like it was slightly childish for me. It might have been the talking cats that did it for me. Although there is an explanation for that. But it just seems like every aspect of this story was forced into fitting perfectly that it really just fel flat. Don't get me wrong, the murder mystery had me guessing all the way through. But I just didn't care for this one. 
 I recommend people interested in this one read other reviews before making a decision. I was bored, but I'm sure there are those out there that really enjoyed this read (that's how I added this one to my reading list).

** spoiler alert ** 
 *sigh* 
 You know I feel bad.. The story was interesting and the world was intriguing.. But the author missed a lot of intricate and story-building details. The main character had a very bland personality and it just looked like she was trying sooooooo hard to be something she's not. In addition, she would remember her secret boyfriend/courtier in very critical moments, and that ruined the whole story. The only character I liked was Tanaya, even if she ended up being one of the villains. 
 See I love cats. Cats are adorable and fluffy and I just want to sit on them. But having your main character talk to cats is kinda cheesy, to be honest. And no... having one of the cats become this super sexy bodyguard is very silly. I didn't like this book and won't be continuing the companion book to it.

sample_reviews.review_text: It takes a while to get going, but there is lots of intrigue going on.

I'd really give this a 3 1/2. The main character, Cat, was just a little too passive, and when he did act, it was to do things that even he suspected were foolish. The castle and characters, though, were wonderfully drawn, and the story was engaging.

Gwendolyn is one of the most blindly, unabashedly atrocious characters I've ever read, and is obnoxious to read, to boot. Cat was equally as annoying, but in the other, more pussy direction. 
 A resounding, bored sigh is kind of what I felt about this book. 
 2/5, for the ability to craft a decent story around entirely unlikeable characters.
I read this book as a child and loved it. I was surprised to discover that it's by the same author who wrote Howl's Moving Castle. This reminds me of childhood...

It's been a long time since I read Charmed Life but I do remember being utterly charmed by it. I was really invested in the characters, and the worldbuilding was somewhat unsettling (in a Dahl kind of way) but amazing to me.
I can only give this 3 stars. The only thing I recall about it is that it was very forgettable!

This was a cute story about kids living in a magical world. It interested me enough to order the rest of the series from the library, but it's mostly because I know that it won't take me long to read them. It seemed to be aimed at a pretty young reader.

This was my favourite book as a kid. I read and re-read it. Like the best kids books, it's laugh-aloud funny and break-your-heart sad at the same time. I love Diana Wynne Jone's writing, but to me, this was always the best. Highly recommended for middle-school readers, especially those who don't like an ending to be too obvious.

Really fun, quick read. Gwendolyn was a piece of work! But of course it all works out in the end. 
 I love how DWJ doesn't talk down to her readers so that even though this is a kids' book, it's still easily enjoyable by adults. I'm looking forward to reading more in this series.

reference_books.title: Solar
reference_books.review_text:
I'll say up front that I'm a big McEwan fan. This novel is not so dark as many of his are and is actually the first time he has ever made me laugh. It is excellent! 
 .....SPOILER alert (but only a small one, and not plot related...)....listening to the scene where he describes his main character trying to get dressed in Artic gear had me in stitches - how many times did he put the gloves on only to have to take the gloves off again to stow his lipsalve, to put on his boots etc etc....then a rework of the classic "don't go to the toilet when its 20 below story" and I could see slap stick and cinema houses erupting. Very unusual for this writer, I am trying desperately to think of another truly rip-roaringly funny episode in a McEwan and failing. 
 The typical McEwan "twist"/ "incident" tipping point comes quite early on and from them on it has you hooked as to exactly where he will take the storyline. By the end part of me felt just a tiny little unsatisfied with the ending plotwise, but another part of me just smiled as ......SPOILER ...as all his lives work is falling down before him, he found what had been alluding him all the time because he hadn't been looking for it. 
 That said, I absolutely loved reading this book. It has one of McEwan's best characters ever in Professor Michael Beard. He was just so real to me. With his inability to look after his balding, overweight, drunk body, his inability to hold together any of his 5 marriages whilst having no problem at attracting the opposite sex, with him being a Nobel Prize winning physicist who finds himself working on artificial photosynthesis as an answer to the world's energy needs and potentially a way to combat climate change - saviour of body Earth versus destroyer of his own! 
 Throughout I had this vision of Bill Nighy doing a Robert De Niro / Raging Bull and putting on several stone to play Micheal Beard. It seems to me that this part is made for Nighy's mix of straight and comic acting ability, his droll voice, his on screen chemistry. Can't wait to see what they do with it as a film.

reference_books.title: The Goldfinch
reference_books.review_text:
I listened to the audio read by David Pittu who I have to say did a marvellous job of all the characters' voices. I didn't know his name but immediately recognised his face from TV dramas like Law and Order. He's now on my "good narrators" list although a quick search reveals he's done lots of children books but not much else, shame. 
 I struggled to get started with the book as I found the museum bombing scenes confusing and actually listen to them three times before deciding just to go with it and carry on. I'm glad I did. My first Donna Tart and all I can say is there is something about this book. I did feel it was long, overly so? not really sure. There is something I can't quite put my finger on which gives me a love/hate relationship with it. Yes it is a ponderous marathon, yet I cannot see where Tartt could have shrunk it without losing the sense of time and age passing in the boy's life. 
 As for the ending, I loved it. In many ways made it for me and I do feel I want to reread them and give them more attention that one listen. If not an ending like this, where else would you end it? With Theo's return from Amsterdam to Hobie's ( not sure if that's how it is spelt as I listened to the book), with an embrace of reconciliation and return? - too Hollywood. For me Theo HAS to make things right, he has to track down the pieces of furniture he deceivingly sold, to make recuperations. It's part of his rehab and of him finally growing up, taking responsibility etc. The treatise at the end on art, the line of beauty, the illusion of artworks and of the faces people put on in life is all about this. Certainly it works on the audio as him reflecting and philosophising about life and art. I particularly recall that both he and Boris (chalk and cheese?) both loved the painting and how the goldfinch was real for them, it was an individual gold finch and if he saw it today in its cage he would go and let it go free. No longer the illusion of a bird, no longer the illusion of life but of real life, lived. 
 I just found the Audie awards site which has a snapshot of his narration for which he won the Literary fiction category in 2014.

book_a.title: Nocturnes: Five Stories of Music and Nightfall
book_a.user_review:
All the reviews in the newspapers that I have read about this book have dismissed it. I think they have miss the point completely. I've heard it called light, not funny. without plot, with some of the stories ending abruptly, characters not named etc etc. But for me the delight of Ishiguro's writing is that it is to quote my friend Vicky, he is "like a water colourist" - his writing has a light but deft stroke, well chosen and well positioned with just the correct amount of colour and form to create a compelling picture. I find his stories remain with me and pop back into my head with the weirdest provocation. I read his A Family Supper a bit back and only recently has it popped into my head again, vividly seeing son, daughter and father at the dinner in the story as I prepared some fish. 
 Nocturnes should to be read in my opinion not as a collection of short stories but as a suite of stories, with a more intimate linkage between them. It was I understand written as one work and should be read as one. It has a cyclical nature to it with both the first and last stories taking place in Venice, with musicians playing in the squares for tourists, with a character from the first returning in the fourth of the five parts. 
 Its themes are music, played and or listened to, talent not "unwrapped" through circumstance, underfulfillment, or choice, conscious or unconscious, people's relationship to music and the place of music in their lives. Whether it is the old singer serenading his wife in "Crooner" Neapolitan style from a gondola, the Swiss couple searching for themselves amongst Elgar's "Malvern Hills", or the young Eastern European Tibor, almost selling his soul for perfection to the 'false' virtuoso American woman as she tries to recapture what might have been then settles for what is in the unmusical husband to be in "Cellos". The stories are sad in that in each of them there is a real sense of chronicling the unattained success, the unaccomplished talent, but his deft touch provides humour to counterbalance and reinforce. The whole scene of the friend trying to help save his friends' marriage, trying to cover up the crumpled read dairy page by claiming a rampaging dog by creating a "soup" of doggies smells in "Come Rain or Come Shine" and the slap stick escapades of the bandaged couple running amuck through the hotel by night in "Noctures" are incredibly visual and had me in stitches. Yes I enjoyed this Ishiguro very much

Five separate stories all relating in some way to music. This is a new author to me and he is very pleasant to read. The stories all deal with some level of general unease and moderate discontent. There is really no resolution ever and the stories are not "exciting" or "gripping" in any way, but are well written. Probably likely to appeal to those in mid-30s and older since much of the subject matter deals with life's disappointments.

Here's a nice diversion I was glad to have picked up, in part because the stories are short, pleasant worlds that I could dip my toes into on a sunny day, but also because I have an interest in the craft of writing, and the quality throughout the book varied so drastically that I found my curiosity piqued. 
 The collection boasts two standout stories about love, life and music. The simple prose in these offerings hint at a deep pool of emotion. However, the three other stories made me think the hints were just outright bluffs. As with every Ishiguro book that I've read, I had to wonder if the feelings he traced were actually substantive and true, or if they were just random lines he doodled in the air, then crossed his fingers in the hopes that our imaginations would fill in the rest. 
 Beyond that, the characters and scenarios sometimes verged on unbearably twee. I can certainly see why Nocturnes would feel like a tender hug to some readers. But for the most part, it felt like a half-hearted pat on the back to me. Then again, maybe I'm just dead inside.

sample_reviews.review_text:
If Stephen King and Anne Rice had a love child, it would be The Passage. I was surprised to find King's blurb on the dust jacket, and wonder what he was really thinking: "Holy crap! It's The Stand with vampires!" Suffice it to say, if you like Stephen King and vampires, then you'll salivate like Pavlov's puppy over this fat slab of a book. But if you don't normally enjoy books like this, but are tempted to pick it up because you've heard that this is the cross-over book for people who don't normally enjoy books like this, don't do it. It's another vampire fantasy, not the next religion disguised as a door stop. 
 Still, there's lots to admire. I especially liked the beginning, where the ominous seeds are sewn. I liked the human foreground and the fantasy background. I like some of Cronin's narrative flights and earnest over-the-top action sequences. But on page 160, I finally lost my tolerance for stuff like this: "He was everywhere and nowhere all at once, moving not over the landscape, but through it, into and out of it, breathing the dark city that was also breathing him." Really? You can do all that? Whaddaya say we just get to the blood-on-blood action because this is the kind of prose that invites parody and gives fantasy a bad name. Not to mention it makes me want to stab myself in the throat with a fork. I read further at a considerably accelerated pace, because I didn't want to get pulled into more verbal quicksand, but you know what? In spite of Stephen King's blurb, "Read this book and the ordinary world disappears," I'm going to put this guilty pleasure aside. After 250 pages, the ordinary world is looking pretty good. I'd give it 2.5 stars.

This novel was terrific. It had government conspiracy, viral 'vampires', real life struggle after the apocalypse, and a story with a wide range of characters. 2012 is too long to have to wait for the next installment!

I wanted to love this book. Several people I love and whose opinion I respect loved this book. And I really liked it, but I thought it needed an editor. And I couldn't help but notice the similarities between it and "Firefly/Serenity." Amy and the virals reminded me SO much of Summer and the Reavers. Because of this it didn't seem as original to me. I also don't like the plot device of getting to the point of major action, and them starting a new chapter that starts 8 days later and recaps what the action was. They seems lazy to me, and a better use of ones word count eould be on handling the action. But I did enjoy the book and I imagine I will get the sequel from the library.

This author really needed a good editor. It could easily have been cut in half. Whenever the plot started to gain a little momentum, it crashed against the author's literary pretensions, encrusting the story with long baroque descriptions. Overall, it had the pace of a dead snail.

The Passage by Justin Cronin is one huge cliche (and I mean this literally, at around 1000 pages it's a HUGE cliche) that offers nothing new to the genre and was more of an exercise in endurance than entertainment to read. 
 A grieving scientist, having been unable to find a cure for his late wife, heads off into the jungle in search of the secret ingredient for immortality. The US government get involved, and hijack the project in an attempt to use his findings to create indestructable super-soldiers in their secret evil mountain base. Shady FBI officers scour the country for 12 death-row inmates for the human experimental tests which turn them into vampire type creatures that, surprise surpise, break out of the secret base and wreak havoc on the world. Since these terrible god-complex scientists and immoral military types apparently know no bounds they also do the experiment on a little six year old girl who now has some sort of telepathic link to the vampires and predictably represents humanities only hope of a cure. The story then jumps ahead by almost 100 years, and we find that the US population has been all but wiped out except for small pockets of people living a basic lifestyle and relying on the remains of 100-year old technology to keep the lights running at night and the vampires out. After almost 1000 pages of pulling out every cliche and well-worn plot device Cronin can think of we finally arrive at the conclusion that if the original 12 vampires are killed then all their progeny will conveniently drop dead. I am dismayed to see that Cronin intends to make a trilogy out of this, but I certainly won't be reading it. 
 It is competently written, but so unoriginal that it is obvious from very early on exactly where the plot will go, so that all that remains is the arduous task of slogging through the book to get to its inevitable conclusion. What makes me all the more maddened by Cronin is the self-congratulatory epilogue materials in which he has the audacity to give his readers a suggested reading list (of books all far better than his own I was amused to note) and a justification for his reasons for writing a horror book when he is in fact a serious author of proper books...what an ass.
It really was an amazing ride. Find my full review on my blog here if you are interested in more details, but hopefully not too much! :)

I usually never write out a review, but in this case, after having (only in my opinion, of course) wasted precious time reading through 800 pgs of this book (I might actually skip the last 60 or so pages), I just felt I might actually keep some people from making the same mistake. 
 REALLY don't understand how this book got to be so highly acclaimed. Up to the apocalypse, I guess this book tells a decent story. The book also basically skips over the events of the apocalypse almost completely, this could have served as the most interesting part of the book (however, I did like the part with Amy and Wolgast up in the cabin). Also, the origin story of the virus is rudimentary and vague at best. 
 I understand that the author was not going for this, he wanted to focus on the the human aspects of this story, their interactions, background stories, how they would deal with being the last survivors, etc. that would be fine, if it weren't for that fact that all these characters are incredibly bland and I just couldn't find myself to care for any of them. I could go on about this, but I want to keep this short. 
 More importantly, this "blockbuster" vampire/apocalypse novel is not ever at all scary...in fact, the most entertaining part about this book might be one of the quotes on the back, by Ron Charles, of the Washington Post: "Engrossing..By the third chapter, trash was piling up in our house because I was too scared to take out the garbage at night." Trust me, this is laughable and make me wonder how much he got paid for that quote and if he ever actually read the novel. I should admit at this point that I am notoriously faint of heart when it comes to horror books/movies/games. This book, even though people are being ripped apart, is remarkably PG, and in the end, just a dull, yet long read (pagewise, there is nothing to think about, the language is extremely straight forward, so at least it is still a quick read). 
 This is a book for the masses. But as a fan of Fantasy/ScyFy/Apocalyptic/Horror novels, stay away, there are countless better options. 
 Like I said, I usually don't write reviews on here, but this book let me down again and again. I did want to know what would happen, but mainly to see if finally something interesting would happen that would warrant the critical acclaim. In my opinion, that was never the case.

The opening sucked me right in with a fast-paced, well-written, tragic look at a woman's life unraveling until she hits rock bottom. Unfortunately, the rest of the book was nothing like that first section. For every chapter that was thrilling and full of nail-biting suspense, there were four chapters that were slow, aimless studies of characters I couldn't give two shits about. (Peter is the most boring first-person character I've ever met. Which cardboard cutout will he end up falling in love with??? Who. Cares.) The overarching plot: meh. And yet, mingled with the dross, are occasional lines that are exquisitely lovely. 
 So yeah. Not particularly thrilled with this one. Didn't love it. Didn't exactly hate it. Just . . . meh.
The story is interesting but I lost track halfway through the book and had a hard time wanting to keep reading. Might pick it up again later.

reference_books.review_text: I liked this book, it had a very different point of view and I think the author did an excellent job telling the story. The perspective of a 5 year old boy is carried through very well through the whole story, and I can see why this is a popular choice for book clubs. There is a lot of content to digest from a social and psychological aspect, it's a fascinating thought process to watch unfold.

reference_books.title: Enchantment
reference_books.review_text: I enjoyed this book well enough, it had good characters and decent world building. The more I read of Orson Scott Card the more I see his tendency to narrate the story and simply deliver in plain text what the reader needs to know about the history. I am beginning to realize that I prefer writers who leave some things to the readers imagination, and allow the history and story to unfold throughout the book.

reference_books.title: Under the Dome
reference_books.review_text: This book held me captive for about 6 days - a very long time for me! It was a monster, and WELL worth the investment of time. The antagonist is served up in true Stephen King style, but with a strictly human makeup ( reminding me more of The Stand than Pet Cemetery). Despite the other-worldly element of the Dome, the fact that the events under it are entirely plausible makes this story even more frightening. It's not the bogeyman under the bed, but the one you know, the one you go to church with or serve breakfast to or buy your coffee from. This story is a scathing statement on the evils of politics, and a rather defeated memoir of how easily people follow the wrong leader(s) when afraid and faced with uncertainty.

reference_books.title: The Stolen Child
reference_books.review_text: Good book! Very interesting concept, not sci-fi at all, but an exploration of alternative reality. It reads very much as reality, just one that you've never heard of. Fascinating. I might just believe in faeries...

Koontz sacrifices a cathartic end in favor of a quicky "buy the next book to find out what happens" end that can't help but feel a little like a cheap ploy.

 Blossom the Happy Monster - the book indicates that Blossom will join Odd on his adventures in the future. Two books later, I'm still waiting.
