Easily this reader's least-favorite of all four books in the series, New Moon does show a degree of style growth as we're introduced to a storytelling shift from the first book: Dual-POV. Not only are we given Bella's first-person perspective, but also Jacob's. Edward features little throughout most of the story (aside from Bella's semi-hallucinating moments brought on by self-inflicted danger--in which some semblance of her own conscience/common-sense seems to manifest as Edward, with the request that she STOP risking her safety.) Sound a little insane? Well, to be fair to realism, I've known few teenagers in love who weren't leaning pretty far over the cliff-o-craziness... 
 I digress. 
 At a base level, New Moon is a highly emotional YA urban fantasy continuation revolving around an inadvertent love-triangle--and a girl who deals with her relational co-dependency in less than healthy ways. Readers are also allowed inside the head of a somewhat whiny male protagonist, who happens to be going through some physiological changes that make puberty look like a hormonal walk in the park. The world-building expands to encompass both vampires and shapeshifters, rounding out a far broader sense of conflict than was conveyed in the 'star-crossed lovers' plot of the first book. 
 While some have contended that Bella's period of depression was overly dramatic, there are many who may find her response entirely believable. For this reader, the primary detraction to enjoyment was spending too much time in Jacob's head. Purely subjective, to be sure, but the guy annoyed me. If this reader wanted to end up in any male's head, it would have been Edward's. (16-year-old male mind vs. 100-year-old male mind? Not really a contest, there. Just sayin'.) 
 I did appreciate the vampire socio-political aspects that came into play toward the end. The book managed to stand well on its own, while hinting more at future issues that would likely need to be faced.

New Moon happened to be my least favorite book in the Twilight Saga. At the time when I was reading it, I couldn't put it down. But when I finished the Twilight Saga and really thought about it, the whole book was very boring. In fact I probably read it so fast only because I was very eager to read the rest of the series. The ending was confusing to me as well.

reference_books.title: Sunshine
reference_books.review_text:
I'm torn on this one because the two central characters are really good, but the story can be very wordy and spreads its focus on things of little interest. 
 The Good 
 I don't generally care much about vampire tales but this one hit the notes I like. Imagine you were once human and are now made into this undead being that must prey on your own kind, live away from society, and are generally shunned and reviled. Many of us would probably be sad creepy loners. Not charming Oxford scholars. Or sexy/creepy high school students. Or even campy hyper-sexed creatures. Which brings me to the vampire of this book, Constantine. He is very alien and inhuman in the way he is described and the way he speaks as opposed to be written as some 'hot-guy-that-never-dies-and-has-powers' but in all other ways feels comfortably human. He's not glamorous and you don't remotely envy him or any of the others. I especially love this description of him late in the book when (for reasons I'll not spoil you on) he is trying to pass as human: 
 "There was a kind of threateningness to his ugliness but you couldn't have said why. There was a study once about whether ugly or good-looking people are more imposing. Generally the uglier you are the less imposing, till you reach a sort of nadir of ugliness and then you get really imposing. I thought Con just missed the nadir. Just." 
 LOL. Kudos to McKinley for not annoying me with talk of his immortal hotness. I loved Constantine who was at once creepy, alien, and sorrowful but possessing of a sort of hesitant old school chivalry. 
 Alas it didn't feel like he was in the book all that much. And while I also loved Sunshine who was in focus from start to finish I didn't love all the things Sunshine loves. 
 And here comes my big issue. For every cool development or event with Constantine and the vampires you get endless pages of Sunshine's life and times as a baker at her family coffeehouse and all the hangers-on pertaining to. 
 I cannot even convey how much of this there was, how little any of it seemed to matter to the story, and what a book-killer it was in a novel that otherwise had so much going for it! I don't think I am exaggerating in saying this sort of minutiae took up 3/4 of the pages. 
 I loved the main characters (and even a side character or two). Loved the world building and general idea of the plot. But eek. This was my first McKinley book so I don't know if this is typical or not but it was sort of a shame. However, others may not be bothered by this at all in which case I'd say give it a shot as the characters and story were otherwise interesting.

reference_books.title: Entreat Me
reference_books.review_text:
4.5 Stars! 
 Well, I just loved this. Entreat Me is a really fun and mature Beauty & the Beast retelling. 
 The protagonist, Louvaen, has instantly become one of my favorite fantasy heroines. At first all you really see of her is how over-protective she is with her sister and I was on the fence. But as her other qualities came out she became the highlight of the book. She's funny, confident, and full of sass. She frequently is all three of those things at once (like that time she threatened to make a necklace of someone's teeth). Occasionally she would not listen to someone more knowledgeable when she should have, which can be a pet peeve of mine. But it only happened once in a big way. She is also loyal and tenderhearted. I ended up loving her to death. 
 Just earlier this week I posed a question on twitter asking for fantasy heroines that are 30+. I had come to notice that even in adult fantasy the protagonists are usually very young. In YA they are 16/ 17 but most of the time in adult they are 22/23. I'm sorry that is not enough of a difference. Then I started to get really annoyed about ageism in publishing not being talked about like it is in film. Many people said they picture the person they are reading about as being their own age, but I want to call some bullshit on that because honest on-the-page representation MATTERS. 
 Grrrrr ....anyhow the point of this rant is that here is a real adult character! I don't know how old Louvaen is, it never seems to say. She is probably in her late twenties vs. thirties. But she is a widow with plenty of life experience, not some angsty girl coming-of-age. *sigh of relief* I picked this up at a time when I really needed it. 
 Ballard (the beast of this story) is ... a really good guy. I didn't really blame his previous wife for hating him and neither did he. But there was also nothing malicious about him past or present. I loved that he is shown having such devotion to a son that is biologically not his and that he was fine with that. His son Gavin: also a great guy. No angsty assholes here using their pain to be jerks to everyone around them. And these two really could if they wanted to. But they don't. So refreshing! 
 The curse-breaking in this was interesting as it had several components that all had to happen, making it something that came apart piecemeal and kept me on edge wondering how it would all eventually come out right. 
 If you are looking for a well done fantasy romance with great characters and a surprisingly hot main couple I highly recommend this one.

reference_books.title: The Fifth Season (The Broken Earth, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
4.5 Stars! 
 Riveting and awful! I love how completely nonlinear the three POV's were and how perfectly they worked together. I'm a bit shy about dystopia because the real world is depressing enough and I read for escape -but this was just so damn interesting and different. 
 Just keep the immortal words of Eomer son of Eomund close to your heart and you'll be fine... 
 Do not trust to hope. It has forsaken these lands.

book_a.title: Gilded Cage (Dark Gifts, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Due to a thing called the "slave days compact" drafted hundreds of years ago, anyone without magical gifts has to perform ten years of servitude between ages 10-50. They get to choose when. Luke's father has been accepted to three medical schools but now he and his wife have decided to get their mandatory "slave days" over with and bring their children along so they can too! All as one big family! 
 Only there is a snafu, as it turns out the aristocratic magical family they were all supposed to go slave for together didn't have any need for Luke and he will be sent elsewhere. Well, his parents draw the line there and get pissed and are all like "he comes with us" and "stuff your paperwork" and after they got roughed up for dissenting "You can't just assault people." 
 To which they are reminded "You all began your slave days and entered a state of legal non-personhood. You are now chattels of the state. To explain for the little one here, " he said, looking at Daisy, "that means that you are no longer 'people' and have no right at all. At All." Abi gasped and Mum made a low moan, pressing her hand to her mouth. 
 Why is this news to them, the people who have apparently been going along with this for centuries? Why have they not revolted before now? 
 Contempt all around. 
 This book has a high amount of four and five stars reviews, so take mine with a grain of salt as I am dropping this sucker in the electronic DNF pile at only 7% in. I just can't.

sample_reviews.review_text: This book is going to appeal to a lot of people (more than it already did to make it a "wattpad sensation"). It's a gritty alternate history urban fantasy with hints of Never Let Me Go by Kazuo Ishiguro and a society reminiscent of the Light and Dark cities in Tell the Wind and Fire by Sarah Rees Brennan. Unfortunately for all the detail and world building, this book lacks nuance in most other areas. The unequal power dynamics of setting up a character acting as a slave in a romance with one of her masters (even the "kindhearted" if ineffectual one) is immensely problematic and not something that needs more page time. Maybe you'll like this one. Maybe you won't. For me it was definitely a hard pass.
Honesty this book was way to messy. Political as well. It was for me extremely hard to follow. I didn't fall in love with any character. Nothing excited me. Over all it was a disappointment.

Gilded Cage by Vic James is a page turning fantasy novel set in a a dystopian British society where the world is divided into people with and without skills. The story focuses on two families ; 1 family who is set to begin their mandatory 10 year slavery service and 1 family who rules the country. 
 I could not put it down. The story was so vivid, the characters so engaging and grow along with the story, and there is no shortage of political intrigue and magic. 
 I really enjoyed it and cannot wait to read Book 2.

Our setting is stereotypical dystopia. In an alternative-universe the Equals have risen to power. They possess Skills, magical abilities, and in one swoop took over the governance of the entire world. In each part of the world, Equals rule differently. In Britain, those without powers are required to commit 10 years of servitude to the Equals. In most cases, these are in harsh work camps where you can practically smell the want for rebellion... 
 Right off the bat, I struggled with a lot of the world building. James did a great job showing us how the other side lives by alternating perspectives between characters living in the Millmoor work camp and those living on Kyneston Estates, where one of the most powerful Equal families lives. But, how we got to this point is fuzzy. I was left with more questions than answers. And I was frustrated. 
 I also struggled with the multiple points of view. There were seven different perspectives in this first book, all of whom are introduced in the first half of the book. It was challenging to keep everyone straight, and honestly, it made the story less interesting. It was distracting for the first 45%-ish, but eventually I got used to it and appreciated it. 
 I can see where James is going in the future. She packed a ton into this first book, and I was on the edge of my seat for the entire second half of the book. These are complicated characters with complicated motivations. James did a wonderful job dropping clues to the reader throughout, but I was still shocked by many of the twists and turns taken in this novel. 
 By the end, I was hooked. James's voice is unique. The story is a bit of a regurgitation at first, but it quickly evolves into something exciting and refreshing. Mostly, I am intrigued by the moral compass and ethics of the different characters. I am also interested to see if the other countries of the world get involved as more political intrigue and potential rebellion unfurls. We shall see. 
 Recommended to all lovers of dystopian YA. For sure.

DNF at 41% 
 Fuck it. I'm done. I can't do this anymore. I gave it a damned good try and I couldn't do it. 
 The book starts out not explaining anything. Who are the Equals? Why did they do this? What the hell does Skill have anything to do with this? Give me something! Anything! Not random info-dumping at all the wrong places, either, because this had that too. I would get interested with Luke's story (Was it Luke? The characters were so uninteresting that I've forgotten.) and then the chapters afterwards would ruin it. Such as Abi. For such a smart girl, she really doesn't show it. 
 I get the world was an AU on British nobility, but that's about it. There was no point to it. I hate books that don't explain anything and expect me to just go along with it. Give me some reasoning behind why things happen and I'll go with it. But, this? I can't. Even then, it's unrealistic. How would that one brother whose name starts with an S have this much political maneuvering at 17 years old? Yeah, he's special and all that, but so? He's 17! Then, you have Luke (I think) and that was realistic given the situation. If the book had just stuck with him, I would have read it. Forget the magic shit that's unexplained. Give me rebellion against a corrupt governmental system and I'll read the hell out of it. 
 This book? Not so much. It's going to appeal to lots of people, I know, but I'm not one of them. Thank you for giving me a chance, Netgally, but not for me.

** spoiler alert ** 
 OMG I love this book so much!!! 4.5 Stars!!! I have to wait soooooo long for the next book :(. 
 This book takes place in an alternate reality in England. There the ruling power are people called The Equals who have a magic power called The Skill. Everyone else are commoners. Every commoner has to serve 10 years as a slave. Luckliy Abi, an 18 year old girl, arranged it so that her family would spend their servitude at Kyneston instead of the slavery camp of Millmoor. The family packs up their belongings and as they are about to get into the van to take them to Kyneston, they find out Luke, Abi's 16 year old brother, will be sent to Millmoor instead for hard labor. In Millmoor, Luke meets a young 13 year old girl named Renie and a Doctor named Jackson who introduces him into the rebellion. Meanwhile Abi and the rest of the family are working for the Jardine. This is the most powerful family in all of England. There Abi works in the family office alongside the second son Jenner. As she's working there, she starts to fall for him even though it is forbidden. Gavar is the first son, and heir to the Jardine name. He has sired a young girl with a slave named Leah named Liberty. He is engaged to Bouda Matravers, a young heiress with the goal of becoming the first female chancellor. The third son is probably the most mysterious and powerful. Silyen seems indifferent to most of his family, seeming to do whatever he wants. 
 The ending completely had me hooked. Like what's going to happen to Luke, Jackson, Renie, and Abi. It ending on such a cliffhanger that I really need the next book, but i'm sure Vic James isn't even done with it! I will definitely be recommending this book to my fellow booklovers!

In the alternate reality of "Gilded Cage," slavery is still alive and well, though it has nothing to do with race. Instead, commoners -- ordinary people -- are forced to give up a decade of their lives in unpaid, often miserable service to the ruling class. Those in power are known as Equals, and they have innate hereditary abilities to do things like heal themselves from injury, read minds, wipe memories, cause pain, and so much more. You can surely see where this is going: time for a revolution. 
 Luke and his family -- his mom, dad, older sister Abi and 10-year-old sister Daisy -- end up smack in the middle of the excitement when they decide to do their slavedays together as a group, and Abi has arranged for them to be house slaves at the estate of one of the most powerful Skilled families in Britain. They expect it to be a comparatively cushy 10 years, but things go awry when Luke is whisked away from them to a horrendous slave town filled with treacherous factories, malnourished "property," violent guards -- and faint stirrings of subversion. 
 I thought the author made the right choice in using multiple points of view to tell the story, giving us a commoner's look at life in a brutal slave town and at the estate, as well as Equal perspectives. As with any uprising story with a political bent, there are plenty of secrets, intrigue and people who are not what they seem, and while I was disappointed that there wasn't as much fantasy as I expected, there was enough excitement to hold my interest and I enjoyed getting to know the characters (especially a dark, inscrutable and terrifyingly powerful Equal named Silyen). I'll most likely read the next installment of this series, which feels to me like a somewhat less-impressive Hunger Games with a tinge of fantasy. 
 *I received a free advance copy of "Gilded Cage" from the publisher via NetGalley in exchange for an honest review.

Part of me wanted to give this 3 stars just because of the ending. I'm not a fan of the cliffhanger ending trend at all. If a story is well told and interesting enough to continue into a series then I will already want to know 'what next?' I don't want the story to end in the middle of a scene, it's just annoying. In general I liked the book though and went with 4 stars. 
 Vic James created a fairly believable dystopian story set in Great Britain. Here, the class division of haves vs have-nots is not separated economically but magically-those that have magical 'Skills' are the rulers and everybody else is simply a commoner regardless of wealth and must spend ten years at some point in their life as a slave, mostly working in industrial slave towns. The story is centered on a family who has just entered their mandatory 'slave days' and mainly focuses on the teenaged brother and sister, Luke and Abi, as they deal with their situations. 
 While parts of the story were a little predictable, there were still several things that surprised me, which is always a plus. Overall I liked the book and look forward to the next in the series, hopefully there won't be another mid-scene cliffhanger though. 
 *received review ARC from netgalley

Well, I feel like I read a different book than everyone else. This book was described as "exciting," but it's really not. The characters were all flat and I couldn't bring myself to care about any of them. As others mentioned, the names are also very distracting. 
 But the worst part was, I couldn't wrap my head around the world-building. So we have a modern world, complete with cell phones, tablets, modern medicine, etc. Everyone who is not born with "skills" is required to serve 10 years as a slave starting between the ages of 10-50 (they get to pick). Oh, and children don't get an education while they're a slave, so we can figure there's a large portion of the population who will enter into their 20s completely uneducated and another large portion of the population who will never get an education beyond high school (because let's face it, not many will go to college in their 30s after being beaten and given mindless work for the entire length of their 20s). One of the main characters has just finished high school with great marks and is accepted to med school, but she has to defer her enrollment for 10 YEARS because she starts her servitude. Is she going to finish school? Doubt it. Assuming she survives, she probably won't even remember half of what she needs to make it in college. Most of the slaves seem to end their servitude with extreme physical and/or mental issues. Yet somehow this society is still able to get enough skilled and educated labor to survive in the modern world? With all these people doing manual labor, who then fills in as doctors and scientists and developers, etc. etc. etc.? Also, what would be the incentive for anyone to better themselves into a position knowing it's all going to be stripped away during their servitude, especially since there doesn't seem to be a way to buy your way out of being a slave. And let's say you have someone who is a developer and starts their servitude when they turn 30. Guess what, when they get out at the age of 40 they won't know anything about their field anymore. Same with doctors, lawyers, etc. Anyone with a trade that changes over time is shit out of luck. I might have bought this premise a little more if it was during the industrial revolution or earlier, but literally none of it makes sense in the modern era. 
 I can't even comment on the plot because that's how little I cared about it.

The story itself was interesting, after getting more then half way through. It was a close DNF at the beginning though. There were a lot of character POV changes and new character introductions too soon for my liking in the story, and I never felt the "I like her/him!" with any of them. Though while not a cliffhanger, don't expect any type of happy ending at the end either. In fact, this book was so dark, and the world was so miserable, I have a hard time seeing a HEA at any point in the series. It had a bit of a Hunger Games feel to it in that sense. However, I am interested to see where the rest of the series goes from here. Full review to come...

sample_reviews.review_text: The entire series is a keeper. Mary Balogh writes beautifully.

This is the last the in Bedwyn series and, I think, the best of them all. The Duke of Bewcastle is cold and very certain of what is proper. Then he meets the woman who can make him laugh again. One of the things I liked best about this novel was how Balough manages to make Christine klutzy without making her seem stupid or goofy.

SNOOZEFEST.

 Wulfric was dull. Christine had a severe case of Regency Manic Pixie Dream Girl. 
 There was ONE SCENE I enjoyed (the quarrel in the woods when she threw his quizzing glass, because: lol). The rest of the book I blacked out from boredom. And it WASN'T A SHORT BOOK, PEOPLE. 
 Sidenote: This book is an example of why people hate jumping into a series. Let's spend more time running through the entire roster of Bedwyns, their spouses and various offspring. That was SUPER FUN.
Ahhhhh I'm so sad that it's over! This book was absolutely amazing!
Upon re-reading upped my rating. 12/2013

Absolutely brilliant. A very Pride and Prejudice story, where you can't help but wait until the main heroine dashes through the shell of the main hero. And when it happens, it's such a thrill to read. Definitely WAY better than the first of the series and highly recommended.

i was expecting so much more from wulf and i just didnt get it, this book left me wanting for more and not in a good way. hpnestly christine most of the time acted like a child and just couldnt make up her own mind, jesus christ, wulf proposed like a million times (more like 3 maybe 4 times) and she kept saying no even thou she "loved him" the more i remember about the the story the more i want to give this book a lower rating. ah, WTH, it started with 2 stars but i cant possibly think of favorite part of the story so it goes down to 1 star. you let me down MB with wulf's story.

This is my second reading of this story and it's been awhile. It is as good as I remember. Wulfric is the 35 year old duke of a very wealthy, powerful family. Christine is the daughter of a gentleman schoolmaster. It helped that I reread the previous books in the series as Wulfric's personality is drawn little by little in each one. Not reading them is not a loss however, just that the picture of his personality will be stronger. 
 And strong is a good word. He has eyes of ice with a demeanor to accompany it. He does not waste words. He speaks softly but his words are powerful. He is not fanciful, never smiles let alone laugh. Christine is his opposite. She is cheerful and an optimist. Easily laughs at herself and any other situation that catches her fancy. She does not know how to control her honesty in order to follow the rules of polite society. Refreshing. And that is exactly what attracts Wulf to her. 
 If you have read the previous books you'll also get an epilogue of sorts as the Bedwyn's make appearances with their children. 
 This is my favorite kind of romance. Why? Since I am not a writer I find it difficult to put into words but I like that Wulf is honest with himself about his feelings even if they are terrifying to him. No true alpha runs away from anything even feelings. He gets to know himself and come to terms with the reality of who he is and isn't. He has two roles, one is the duke and one is Wulfric. Christine helps him find the latter. I LOVE Christine. I want to be her or have her as my role model. No matter what, she finds it within herself to be positive even when she wants a hole to open up and swallow her. She is a light in a room without meaning to be or meaning to draw attention. 
 August 2017: I needed to re-read this book. I may have to get the ebook so I'll always have it. The binding is coming loose.

I really liked this book. It had interesting characters and an interesting love story. It has a bit of a twist that was not that obvious at first, but it made a lot of sense. My only complain is that at times it felt too worldly. There was too much description or lingering of things that were not relevant to the plot, which distracted me. 
 3.5

reference_books.title: Bared to You (Crossfire, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This book started out really hot with all the sexual tension. 
 I'm really curious as to what happened to Gideon to make him have those nightmares. 
 This book didn't really interest me that much. I mean I love the times that Gideon and Eva were together because they were so sweet. 
 I just couldn't connect with any of the characters. Eva's mom and Gideon were both "stalking" Eva by getting every single detail of their life. Cary is a good friend but he doesn't deal with relationships well. Neither does Eva and Gideon so it's like one big mess of relationships. 
 Eva gets jealous numerous times and is mad at Gideon but Gideon always seem to just kiss it away. Sure they talked things out but not fully. 
 There was no development of the characters other than they learn to deal and basically sweep their problems under the rug for now and that they can't live without each other. 
 Need to read the rest of this series but I have to wait because both the library book and library ebook is checked out.

reference_books.title: Dark Wild Night (Wild Seasons, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
This book was more sweet. I love how oblivious and slow both Oliver and Lola is. They have this love that formed from friendship. It was the sweetest thing to read about them. 
 It was sweet reading about how they got together but there just wasn't enough content for me. I felt like some parts were too slow. As much as I love the comic aspect, I found it a bore when Lola had to deal with all the stuff she is working on. 
 I loved reading about Mia and Ansel and Harlow and Finn. 
 I did like the little sneak peak at Luke making an appearance. Definitely excited to read about Luke and London.

reference_books.title: Thief (Love Me with Lies, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
It was interesting to read Caleb's point of view. To see how much he loves Olivia despite the lies and things was sweet. It is interesting to read how many times he almost goes back to Olivia and the things he's done that Olivia doesn't know. 
 I rejoiced when he officially left Leah. I was glad to find out what he gave Olivia for her birthday. 
 It took two marriages and lots of trying for them to finally get together.

reference_books.title: Reflected in You (Crossfire, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
The reason this didn't get 5 stars is because of the first and middle part. I hate how their relationship goes from being perfect to not all because of some misunderstanding. It was just and endless cycle. It didn't get good until the end. The end almost made it a 5 but then I remembered how hot and cold their relationship was and how annoyed I was about Eva thinking if she should let Gideon go and how they felt bad about what they were doing to each other. 
 I disliked how throughout the whole book Gideon didn't open up to Eva. Only when she threatened to leave did he open up a little. It always felt like he used sex to avoid discussing things and even though she wanted to talk and let him open up or was mad at him, she always relented. Didn't care much for that. 
 I'm not sure how to fell about her going out with Brent to make Gideon jealous just like she is of Corinne. I'm proud she's standing up and she did get through to him but I don't like the idea in general. 
 I mean it's a solid 4.5 out of 5 stars. 
 I loved that Eva started snooping around to find answers that Gideon wouldn't tell her. What the detective told Eva at the end was mind blowing. I was not expecting all the details to line up with the actions Gideon did. It was a good way to end this book. I almost want to go back and read all the things Gideon did and see them in a different light. 
 I loved seeing them evolve as a couple though. At the end, they were not jealous of the other and trusted each other. That was sweet. 
 This book was better than the first because it had more plot with the whole Nathan business. Then again I always end up liking the second book more than the first. It was the same for Fifty Shades series and Gabriel's Inferno series.

reference_books.title: On Dublin Street (On Dublin Street, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This was such a sweet story! I loved every moment between joss and Braden from he moment they met to the end. 
 They had some hot moments together and I felt their pain. Braden is so sweet and I like that they understand each other. 
 I loved how you could see how joss was changing throughout the story and how she dealt with her past. 
 I loved her friendship with Ellie and the problems that came up. 
 It was a great read. Although when the scenes changed to her therapist visit, it confused me because then it went back to the situation. 
 I loved that the story was in Scotland. I love reading about places I've been like when she went to Edinburgh castle.

sample_reviews.review_text:

Great book but left me broken hearted!

"He was my crack. I could never get enough, and when I had him I was already thinking about when I could have him next." 
 The ending brought tears in my eyes. That is something that I didn't expect at all and it's hard to put words on this review when your heart is too crushed from it. I want to scream my frustrations on top of my lungs and shit... IT HURTS. THE ENDING HURTS. I need a moment. I. AM. MESSED. UP. 
 All the characters here are undeniably flawed, twisted but bold. The story is really twisted and definitely a mind fuck love story. I love Olivia Kaspen no matter how broken she is or the mistakes she did to hurt a person she loved. She got the angst, sarcasm and sass. Her emotions felt so real to me. When she found out her ex-lover Caleb Drake have an amnesia, she took the advantage of making him falling in love with her again. She'll do everything to get what is hers. However she is scared that he will know the truth that made their relationship fell apart. 
 When I'm reading this, my anticipation starts to build up every time I finish a chapter. I keep waiting for something to happen until the last 5 chapters of this book (including the Epilogue). I was on the edge of my seat and just couldn't stop reading! All left me with surprises and took me in an emotional roller coaster ride. I've got to be honest, this book is depressing. 
 What makes it beautiful? 
 First love never dies, yes, but it doesn't mean that he/she is the one till the very end. 
 We may found our soulmates but because of wrong choices, we lost them and could never get back. 
 That will scar us for life but if you really love a person, you'll know how to let them go and wish them happiness they deserved. 
 See? it's perfectly imperfect.

sample_reviews.review_text: Nostalgic at best. A very easy read, but I felt it wasn't true to many of the characters. It felt unnecessarily heavy and even predictable. It didn't manage to tap in to the everyday wonder of the magical world, which is what was so lovable about Harry Potter.

What did I just read? I'm so excited when it came out, and I went to the bookstore right away, and I went home to read this. It's very clear I had finished reading this during our FINALS, and I'm so mad and disappointed. DID I JUST READ A FANFICTION? I know it's just a script, but my anticipation of this book went downhill right away, after I close the book after reading it. But there're things I loved about this book, but the majority was a disappointment. Sorry Potterhead, I myself also a Potterhead, but this script to the magical play is nothing.

My expectations were pretty low going into this, and I was still underwhelmed. The story was juvenile and the dialogue so cheesy. Perhaps the actors delivered the lines in such a way that they came off as profound and meaningful. But, I felt like I was reading a children's book about the value of friendship. 
 By using time travel and dream sequences, the writers brought back so many characters from the books that it was too much. Do I really need to see Umbridge, Cedric Diggory, Moaning Myrtle, and Aunt Pentunia again? Not really. This kind of story manipulation in order to mention as many Harry Potter things as possible reminded me of Ready Player One and its overuse of 80's references. I hated that book. 
 There were several moments that had me thinking, "WTF?" but I will focus on just two here. First off, I'm still not over the fact that VOLDEMORT PROCREATED. Let that sink in for a second...okay, so Voldemort allegedly had sex with Bellatrix Lestrange, knocked her up, and has a daughter that the entire Wizarding World knew nothing about. Not only does the concept of Voldemort having sex carry a major ick factor, it makes zero sense. Voldemort was a villain and a monster. An elaborate spell/potion was required for him to even return to a somewhat human form. And he emerged from that cauldron with his fertility? Really? Plus, Voldemort didn't respect anyone but himself. You could argue that Lestrange had romantic feelings for Voldemort, but I'm pretty sure that Voldemort would have viewed relations with Lestrange, or anyone really, beneath him. Plus, he believed he could make himself immortal and rule over the entire wizarding world, so why would he have any desire to have a baby? Voldemort doesn't need a sidekick. And if he's immortal, he doesn't need someone to take over for him when he's dead. So...how does this make any sense at all? Secondly, Ron was so drunk when he married Hermione, that he doesn't remember their wedding? Really? Ok, wait, maybe I can't stop at just two things...I was also really bothered by the fact that Albus, Scorpius and Delphi were able to get into Hermione's office using Alohomora. Hermione would have used more protective spells. Also, the trolly witch randomly sprouting talons from her hands was creepy and weird. I am sighing, shaking my head, and choosing to believe that nothing in this play is canon. 
 Overall, I think the most disappointing part for me was finding out what happened to Harry, Ron and Hermione after the seventh book ended. A large part of me would rather have remained ignorant. We Harry Potter fans got seven wonderful books with a happy ending. I have closure. I don't need to read a story about a 40-year old Harry and his tumultuous relationship with his son. And if I ever get an inkling to revisit the Wizarding World, I have so many options. I can re-read the books, re-watch the movies, visit the theme park in Orlando, try to make butterbeer at home, listen to the movie soundtracks, visit Pottermore, etc. This play is fan-fiction. And fan-fiction is probably the only part of the Harry Potter fandom that I have not explored, and don't have a desire to. 
 Rowling should have just left Harry alone with All was well.

 1. Initial Reactions to "Harry Potter and the Cursed Child": A Rage Filled Catharsis 
 2. Top Five "Cursed Child" Plot Holes 
 3. Why It's Important Albus and Scorpius Aren't In Love 
 4. Top Five Random "Cursed Child" Moments 
 5. Why I Was Able to Enjoy "Cursed Child"

I like that we weren't stuck in Hogwart's the whole time, that we got to see the 'adults' at work, making the mistakes that adults make just as readily as children, and I love that the dynamics between characters (old enemies or old friends) has shifted and changed. Because that is what happens in real life. And being a script, it explores the characterisation and interaction more fully which I loved. 
 People's main beef seems to be the fact it's a script, not a regular prose story (probably because a script, if you're not used to them, can seem quite distancing, but the reason it's like that is it's leaving room for actors to fill the spaces - or the voices in your head if you like performance!) This book has made me feel about 1000 different ways, each of them conflicting with the others. It has both confused and thrilled me on some level, and now I'm sitting here having no clear idea how I feel about it. It's not great, it's not terrible. It's neither necessary or unnecessary. It neither furthers the story of Harry Potter nor harms it. It just kind of... is. 
 It's hard to really be disappointed in this book. We weren't supposed to get any new Potter material, so it's not like our expectations were set very high. Rowling basically promised at one point that there would never be another Harry Potter book written by her. And in a way, there still hasn't been. Her touch is definitely on the plot and characters, but this is much more of a Jack Thorne play than it is a J.K. Rowling novel. As such, the writing style and restrictions of a play have sucked a lot of the life out of the story. 
 Also, reading this as a play confounded me a little bit as a fan of theater. It has SO MANY SCENE CHANGES. I can't imagine what this thing must look like on stage, but it must be chaos. It has as many scene changes as a movie, with very few of them lasting more than a minute or two. It almost feels like they wrote it as a movie first, then decided to make it a play after the fact, without adapting much of it to the stage. I don't know, maybe it's a great play, but it seems unwieldy as hell. 
 Anyway, the story itself. It's fine. There's a decent development of the relationship of Harry and his youngest son, Albus, and it's nice to see where all of the Potter crew ended up decades after the Battle of Hogwarts. But, this play is almost exclusively about the big, crazy, magical plot, and as such leaves a lot to be desired in terms of character connections. People spend most of the play stating their emotions and desires out loud rather than actually feeling or acting upon them, mostly because there's not time to really live in any of these incredibly short scenes. 
 I found it very hard to care about anyone in this story. The best plays are all about relationships, about how people affect each other, usually very deeply. This play is about a series of magical errors and the attempts to fix them. The relationships it does contain are mostly surface-level, well-trod types: father-son, best friends, husband-wife, and never really explored beyond those simple starting points. It doesn't feel like any character truly grows or changes or realizes anything about themselves because of the story, it just kind of feels like these changes were written in because they're expected to happen. It's ultimately kind of lazy. 
 All that said, the plot I'm complaining about is kind of fun. It's got a lot of big, Pottery energy and twists and magic creatures and all that. There are some pretty huge logical leaps you have to go along with, though, and they kind of hurt the story. I won't spoil anything, but I'll just say the way the story progresses kind of contradicts itself and makes it very difficult to suspend disbelief, and the plot in the latter quarter of the book or so suffers for it. 
 So, I'm not making this sound very good, and I honestly don't think it IS very good. But, it has enough going for it with Rowling's involvement and its lighthearted tone, plus it's a quick, decently-fun read, that I still think it's worth the very small amount of time commitment. I also think someday it will make a great blockbuster movie, assuming they smooth over a few of the weirder plot problems that seem fixable. Here's hoping they don't make it a trilogy.

I really enjoyed this book because it was unlike so many books I've read. It was scientific, which I loved, but also extremely readable. The main character is so endearing that you are automatically rooting for him. At first I thought there was no possible way that this book would have a conceivable plot, but everything was explained so well, and from what I hear, it was very scientifically accurate with a couple of exceptions. I did eventually get tired of him explaining every tiny detail of what he was going to do, but overall, I found myself highly entertained.

reference_books.title: Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell
reference_books.review_text:
This is the kind of book that I want so badly to like, but I just didn't. There are some readers who appreciate this style of writing, and I'm just not one of them. I want to say that I think Susanna Clarke is most likely a brilliant author and applaud her creation of an alternate history. The things I dislike about this book are the same things that make me like the movies better for Lord of the rings. I think it's great that Clark and Tolkien know this world they've created so well, but truthfully, I'm looking for a story. It reminds me of what Mark Twain said in a telegram when someone asked him to write a two page piece in two days. "NO CAN DO 2 PAGES TWO DAYS. CAN DO 30 PAGES 2 DAYS. NEED 30 DAYS TO DO 2 PAGES." I think it's easier to include every detail ever imagined than to really refine your story to include only the pertinent ones. 
 My major dislike for this book was the length and amount of detail. I don't mind a long book, as long as the story line is still progressing well. I honestly had no idea where the story was going for about 2/3 of the book. There were so many tiny details that the story got weighted down and put into the background. I listened to this book rather than reading it, so the footnotes were ridiculous because I often didn't know when they ended and the story picked back up again. Besides, the footnotes are not my thing. There's enough gratuitous detail in the story alone. 
 Another thing I did not like is how distant the story and characters were. Although the characters were well defined, I never did really find myself caring about any of them. I occasionally felt sorry for Lady Pole, but really not as much as she deserved. They were all just kind of flat to me. 
 I hesitated to give this book a rating because I know that many people will love all the things that I dislike, but the people who don't like long detailed stories, maybe this will help them not waste time with this one.

reference_books.title: Lonesome Dove
reference_books.review_text:
If you had told me a month ago that one of my favorite books I would read this year was about Cowboys moving cattle from Texas to Montana, I would have laughed at you. However, on the finished side of this book, I can definitely see why it is. I became so obsessed with this book and its characters for the time I was listening to it, that I ended up buying the movie because I didn't want it to end. 
 I think what really makes this book is the characters. Each one is so rich and real that I just ended up feeling like I knew all of them. Deets is absolutely one of my favorites. Even the "bad" characters in the book seemed simply human and flawed. I think that it takes a talented writer to evoke sympathy for the worst characters in a book. 
 The plot is definitely slow, but it didn't feel like it was while I was in it. I listened to the audiobook from audible and I think that was a good decision. The narrator did a great job of really helping the characters come alive for me. 
 Overall, I really loved this book. And it is likely one I would recommend to others.

reference_books.title: Murder as a Fine Art (Thomas De Quincey, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This book started out so good in the beginning for me. I enjoyed the first chapter (dark as I am), but it seemed to fall apart for me as time went on. My biggest issue with this writing is the overt history lessons that were not so much peppered in, but jarred in. When I was in choir, we were practicing a song that was quiet but powerful. My teacher used a metaphor for how we should feel while singing. It's like we're in a ferrari, and we know we can go really fast, but we're doing 25 just because we can. I feel like the author could use this advice as well. He is clearly very intelligent and has learned a lot about Victorian London and so he wants to show how much he's learned, but he needs to learn to drive his ferrari at the speed limit. This analogy seems to have gotten away from me a bit. 
 The other major issue that I had with the book was the inconsistency of the murderer. He started out as a cool, calm and collected serial killer. But at the end he was this impassioned maniac who was fighting to stop the opium epidemic? What happened? 
 Overall, this was definitely not my book, but most people in my book club enjoyed it and I would therefore not hesitate to recommend it to someone else.

 Philip K Dick has some of the more brilliant "what-ifs" in literature. 
 They're so compelling that they've inspired several movie adaptations, some of them Legendary. 
 However, 50 years passed, I could not finish this book, has it is so ... boring. 
 I guess several writers have left their legacy in thw beauty of words, some in the talent to craft stories, while others construct genres.

I had high hopes when I read the premise of Philip K. Dick's alternate historical account of post WWII with Germany and Japan being the victors. What I was left with at the end was some unanswered questions and the feeling that this could have been so much better. I did enjoy the story and found myself becoming engaged with the characters - especially the pawn store owner Robert Childan and the jewelry maker Frank Frink - but no conclusion was made at the end of the book as to how these characters ended up. Not that I would no recommend the read, I would just recommend tapering the expectations of bit. Not a masterpiece....
Tripe.
Great book in idea and premise total failure of an ending and total package.......

The Man in the High Castle tells the story of an alternate history where Germany and Japan won WWII, taking place in 1962. Really, this is shows that the best part of Dick's writing can also be the worst. Namely, as was suggested in the introduction for Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? that Dick can briefly mention one concept that another science-fiction writer could spend an entire novel on. 
 Therein lies the ultimate problem with this novel. There is so much going on, but too many characters. Any one of them could've been a great story, but the story cuts off too fast. By the end, half of the plots aren't really even resolved. I would've gladly taken a tighter focus on say...Childan and Frink (since they're connected) or Tagomi and Baynes, or Juliana's visit to the titular man in the high castle. But instead, it's so spread out and ends abruptly. 
 That being said, I did like all the various innovations of the book. The use of the I, Ching to predict the future was very interesting, even if I never fully understood it. I also really enjoyed the alternate history within the alternate history with The Grasshopper Lies Heavy (an author's idea of what the world might've been like if England and the USA won the war instead, presenting a third view). It's all really creative (and harrowing when you consider what a Nazi Germany in charge of the world would've been like), but again, it's a world that ends too fast.

PKD has never failed to amaze me, to entertain me, to enlighten me--until now. 
 This was a train wreck from beginning to end. And not in a good way. What the (blank) was he thinking when he wrote it? Was he even thinking when he wrote it? Was he even conscious? 
 Never mind that the characters were so thin and poorly drawn they barely existed. Never mind that the stories of these characters were equally as thin. Never mind the over abundance of I Ching involved. The great sin was that it was BORING! Yes, that's right. I wouldn't believe it myself if I hadn't read the whole thing. This is a PDK book that is BORING. 
 I'm still in shock.

book_b.title: The Book of Mormon: Another Testament of Jesus Christ
book_b.user_review:
I really hesitate to write a review for this book because I think it can hardly be compared to other books. It's intention is not to entertain (although some parts are thoroughly entertaining). It's purpose is to provide a belief system for its followers. Now, as an adult, I would like to reread this without the pressure of feeling like I have to be inspired on every page. Objectively read it. That would be quite nice. Just as I have objectively read quite a lot of the bible. 
 I read this book several times (at least parts of it several times) growing up in the LDS church. I have always felt oddly detached from this book that everyone else around me seemed to constantly praise and find so much inspiration and comfort from. If you are taking this for what it is supposed to be, than you can't really find any fault with the writing style as it is apparently an inspired journal of the history of the Americas. However, if you do not believe that, than you are just left astonished as to how this book could be filled with so many empty words. I have had people tell me that there is purpose behind every verse in the Book of Mormon, but I would definitely argue that. Even as a young believer in the religion. 
 I find it odd now that so many have talked about how inspiring the messages are. I have found that the things that are inspiring in the Book of Mormon are few and not entirely original. I think that, absolutely, you can find inspiring messages in this book (especially if you are looking for them in every verse), but you can find inspiring messages in many works of literature and especially in religious works. 
 Let me quickly say, I have no hard feelings about the LDS church, and I have nothing against the Book of Mormon. I just don't believe it. So take this review with that in mind.

Target audience: the entire world; this book was meant to be the true word of God, the last testament of Jesus Christ and a sort of second Bible. It was supposed to revolutionize Christianity. 
 About the author: If you are a Mormon believer, the author of the book is the angel Mormon (he is explained in the overview). If you are a non-Mormon, the author is Joseph Smith, Jr., an American religious leader and founder of Mormonism and the Latter Day Saint movement, Mormon prophet and founder of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Smith came from an unremarkable New England family. Although privately religious, the Smiths rarely attended church, and after they moved to Palmyra they became involved in magic and treasure-seeking. Religious differences within the family and over religious revivals in the Palmyra area left Smith perplexed about where to find a church. When he was 14, he prayed for help, and, according to his own account, God and Jesus Christ appeared to him (there are various versions regarding the persons in the vision). In answer to his question about which was the right church, they told him that all the churches were wrong. In 1823 he received another revelation: while praying for forgiveness, he later reported, an angel calling himself Moroni appeared in his bedroom and told him about a set of golden plates containing a record of the ancient inhabitants of America. Smith found the plates buried in a stone box not far from his father's farm. Four years later, the angel permitted him to remove the plates and instructed him to translate the characters engraved on their surfaces with the aid of special stones called "interpreters." Smith insisted that he did not compose the book but merely "translated" it under divine guidance. Completing the work in less than 90 days, he published it in March 1830 as a 588-page volume called the Book of Mormon. 
 Structure of the book: The Book of Mormon is organized as a compilation of smaller books, each named after its main named narrator or a prominent leader, beginning with the First Book of Nephi (1 Nephi) and ending with the Book of Moroni. The book's sequence is primarily chronological based on the narrative content of the book. Exceptions include the Words of Mormon and the Book of Ether. The Words of Mormon contains editorial commentary by Mormon. The Book of Ether is presented as the narrative of an earlier group of people who had come to America before the immigration described in 1 Nephi. First Nephi through Omni are written in first-person narrative, as are Mormon and Moroni. The remainder of the Book of Mormon is written in third-person historical narrative, said to be compiled and abridged by Mormon (with Moroni abridging the Book of Ether). 
 Overview: I know I'll upset many Mormons around here, but, as a non-Mormon (half-atheist actually), I think that the Book of Mormon can be truly understood only if we understand the context that surrounds its appearance. So, I'll divide my overview in two sections. 
 Content of the book: According to the information from the plates, when the languages were confounded by God at the Tower of Babel, a group of people known as "Jaredites" migrated on the American continent. Although they managed to build a flourishing empire, centuries later the Jaredites self-destructed in a massive civil war. Almost two million people died in a single battle on the hill Cumorah. While the Jaredites exterminated themselves, in the year 600 BC, just before the Babylonian captivity, a family of Jews from Jerusalem migrated to America. The father of this family was called "Lehi." Lehi had a wife and several sons and daughters. Nephi, an obedient son of Lehi, was the father of a race of white people known as "Nephites," while Laman, a rebel son of Lehi, was the father of the "Lamanites," cursed with dark sin due to their rebellious nature. The two nations (races) were in constant conflict with each other. But in the year 34 AD Jesus Christ descended from heaven (right after his ascension in Jerusalem) in America, visiting the Nephites and the Lamanites. This event brought a total Christianization of the two nations and centuries of peace. Nevertheless, the conflict was reignited, and the hill Cumorah was once again the witness of a huge massacre. The Lamanites destroyed the Nephites, until there was only one left, Moroni. So, the native people of America are in fact the descendants of the Lamanite people, and the stone ruins that are spread across the continent are former cities of the civilizations described in the golden plates. Fourteen centuries after the destruction of the Nephites by the Lamanites, the Nephite prophet Moroni appeared in the form of an angel to the young Smith and guided him to find the golden plates. Moroni was a Nephite prophet in his mortal life, the son of the prophet Mormon, the compiler of the buried text. From the author of the golden plates, Mormon, Smith named the translation of the texts as the Book of Mormon, and those who adhered to this doctrine have been called "Mormons." 
 Context of the book: To be fair, most Christian leaders have expected their religious works to revolutionize Christianity. First and foremost we have to understand that the Book of Mormon appeared in America at a time of the Second Great Awakening, after the American War of Independence and before the American Civil War. At that time the American nation was virtually a nation without history. And a nation without history is like a man without a soul or without an identity. So, Smith forged a history for the American continent, a history which conveniently conferred divine legitimacy to the new nation and his new cult. He linked and conditioned the eschatological destiny of the world to the eschatological destiny of America, promoting nationalism and American exceptionalism. He stated things that many Americans wanted to hear, even if they were contrary to the truth. 
 Smith's strategy was to present a version of the past in order to support a certain scenario of the future. Thus, starting from the sacred history of America contained in the Book of Mormon, together with the subsequent visions and signs, Smith built an apocalyptic scenario that has at its core the glorious destiny of the United States and the Mormon group. According to the Mormon doctrine, between the ascension of Christ and the revelation of Moroni there was the great apostasy - a long period populated by false prophets and false doctrines. The pure Christian teaching was corrupted immediately after the death of the apostles. But God began to restore the truth before Parousia; first through the discovery and the colonization of America, and then through the restoration of the true Church. Jesus's sermon in America gives hope to the Mormons that the Zion of the latter days would be established in the New World. Smith is (self-proclaimed) the one and true prophet of God after the apostles, while the Book of Mormon is the everlasting gospel revealed to the people in the last days and preached in the entire world according to Revelation 14:6-7. So, the expression "latter day saint" signifies three things: the restoration of the prophecy and priesthood that died in the Hebrew tradition, the imminence of Parousia and the divine authority of the church established by Smith. 
 Joseph Smith Jr. and all those who have succeeded him to the leadership of the Mormon group, presidents and prophets alike, have claimed that the Book of Mormon is a true description of the history of America. While the Bible is considered to be a historical description of the Old World and of the former Christian Covenant, the Book of Mormon is a historical description of the New World and of the new Millennial Covenant. 
 Strong points: Creativity: I personally know how hard it is to write a book, and I'll say that creativity is a strong point. Even if I do not agree with what he wrote, I have to admit that the author - in my opinion Joseph Smith Jr. only - put a lot of work to imagine it and write it, more than 90 days for sure. 
 Weak points: Arogance: In the 19th century the Book of Mormon could not be confuted because the history and the geography of the American continent were little known and the mass media was relying only on paper products: books and newspapers. But today, in the light of 21st-century knowledge, the Book of Mormon is nothing but a religious fiction. The introductory line of the Book of Mormon says that it "is a volume of holy scripture comparable to the Bible. It is a record of God's dealings with ancient inhabitants of the Americas and contains the fulness of the everlasting gospel." Mormons say it is infallible, the most accurate book that ever existed: "the Book of Mormon was the most correct of any book on earth, and the keystone of our religion, and a man would get nearer to God by abiding by its precepts, than by any other book" (Joseph Smith, History of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, vol. 4, ed. Brigham Henry Roberts (Salt Lake City: Deseret News Press, 1905), 461). The evidence, however, do not support this statement. 
 Lack of historical support: Historical support is the backbone of any religion because the scenarios of the future become legit only if they rely on scenarios of the past. But, while all the empires of the world left behind proofs of their existence through coins, inscriptions, jewelry, weapons or buildings, there is absolutely no material evidence to support the existence of the three great civilizations described in the Book of Mormon. On the contrary, all the archaeological evidence show the opposite. Likewise, there is not a single evidence that Jesus descended in America or that Christianity existed before the coming of Europeans (Mormon 9:32); there is no evidence about the extensive use of metals; in reality Native Americans mainly used stone and wood. 
 Factual errors: It wrongly describes the presence in America of horses, goats, donkeys, elephants, cows, sheep, wheat or barley - elements that had been totally absent from the flora and fauna of the continent (1 Nephi 18:28; 2 Nephi 12:7; Mosiah 9:9). In contradiction to the Bible, the Book of Mormon says that Jesus was born in Jerusalem (Alma 7:10), and not Bethlehem. Also, Lehi built a temple in America as Solomon did in Jerusalem. But Judaism rejects this scenario because it is forbidden to build a temple in a different location than Mount Moriah. 
 Lack of originality: The main themes of the book - American exceptionalism, the Lost Tribes of Israel and Parousia - were major concepts of the Second Great Awakening. The Bible seems to have been a source of inspiration as well: Lehi is a copy of Adam and Eve, while Laman and Nephi are a repetition of Cain and Abel. Laman is the rebellious son as Cain, while Nephi is the obedient son similar to Abel. And, as Cain killed Abel, the Lamanites destroyed the Nephites. The Book of Mormon copied even the biblical language, using certain linguistic constructions, expressions, phrases or words meant to create the impression that it was divinely inspired. But in 19th-century England John Turner, the adept of Joanna Southcott, also copied biblical language in his prophetic works about Shiloh (the future Messiah).

reference_books.title: Sunset Park (Five Boroughs, #2)
reference_books.review_text: Solid, interesting study of Raymond, a twenty-something guy coping with a serious case of internalized inferiority and unexplored bi-curious impulses and his preppy, very out friend David. Raymond gets high and blows off work, but then has complex about his brother's, friends', and girlfriends' low expectations. David has been madly crushing on Raymond and when they become roommates they embark on relationship that they both struggle to define. Their obstacles are not particularly defined, and are more an outgrowth of both of their immaturity and difficulties communicating. In that, the book lays out a realistic and compelling story of two guys who have to grow up in order to be with each other.

reference_books.title: When Breath Becomes Air
reference_books.review_text:
We live and die, but by the grace of God we can find and create meaning in both the living and the dying. Paul Kalanithi was a brilliant man, a neurosurgeon neuroscientist who, if he had lived, would have healed many people and contributed enormously to our understanding of the brain. But at the age of 36 he learned he had terminal lung cancer and had to forge new ways of living, relating to the people around him, and identifying himself. 
 First, this is not a why me? story- Paul quickly thinks why not me? But finding ways of living and sources of meaning in the face of suffering and mortality is his challenge, with which he grapples until his final breath, drawn very young but surrounded by family and love. 
 Paul and his wife Lucy decide to have a child, and his last paragraph in the book, addressed to their daughter Cady, demonstrates how he has found that deeper meaning, that hope for the future, in her: 
 "When you come to one of the many moments in life where you must give an account of yourself, provide a ledger of what you have been, and done, and meant to the world, do not, I pray, discount that you filled a dying man's days with a sated joy, a joy unknown to me in all my prior years, a joy that does not hunger for more and more but rests, satisfied. In this time, right now, that is an enormous thing." 
 When discussing whether to have a child, Lucy asks, "Don't you think saying goodbye to your child will make your death more painful?" and he responds, "Wouldn't it be great if it did?" 
 Paul meditates on what he sees as medicine's primary calling- a pastoral role beyond the clinical in which a doctor helps the patient articulate what matters most in his life, and then helps that patient regain the functions needed for those valued things, or cope with the fact that those functions cannot be regained. Medicine for Paul is not and should not be a job- it is a calling. 
 I read this cover to cover, crying all the while, on a rainy weekend day I had planned on whiling away to no real purpose. If this book is one of Paul's legacies, and indeed, its publication was his deathbed wish, then I have been a grateful recipient of his wisdom and his insight. Words do have a longevity that he, that none of us, do not. Worlds, minds, enclosed in amber and kept as long as we keep these records alive- it is a beautiful gift, a grace in the face of great pain and suffering.

reference_books.title: Rainshadow Road (Friday Harbor, #2)
reference_books.review_text: Ever since I read Jacob Have I Loved in middle school, I have loved books of sisterly competition and betrayal (probably because I only have brothers). That was the hook that excited me about Rainshadow Road; however, Kleypas's ever-growing tendancy to narrate in therapy-speak sucked all the drama and angst out of that plotline. The hero was bland to the point of invisibility. A final note- the supernatural elements were awkward and nonsensical. It rather reminds me of Nora Roberts's 'Born In' trilogy where the first two books were delightful (Born in Fire is a great and non-hokey description of artistic inspiration that Kleypas should have taken note of) and the third completely bombed thanks to the bizarre faux-mystical elements. Alas.

book_a.title: The Proposal (The Survivors' Club #1)
book_a.user_review:
Oh, Mary Balogh. If I lived in the same country as a public library, I would never shell out cash for a new release ever again... First, let's start with the whole premise of a "Survivor's Club." Also, by this point all of her previous characters, populating every other scene, merge together in an unwholesome muddle of dukes and viscounts. Finally, I've seen all of this before. If Lady Muir's first marriage had an interesting spin, nearly everything else in The Proposal was classic Balogh, in a been-there-done-that sort of way. 
 Will I read the next one? Of course (public library please!). Why? Despite everything, Balogh knows how to put together the bare bones of an excellent, angsty love story. She may then procede to kill all of the angst with her heavy-handed pen, but pretend for a moment that rather than heavily editorializing the opening meeting of wounded vets, she let the group speak for themselves? Tone down the titles a few notches, leave the corny group moniker for the marketing department, and carry the story forward with snappy dialogue vice plodding internal exposition and what do you have? A classic Balogh regency- sweet, poignant, a little angsty, and wonderful. If I have to wade through crap to get at the ghost of those really excellent books, I guess I'll do it.

sample_reviews.review_text: Love Mary Balogh books. This is a nice book, but my least favorite so far.

Thank you to Goodread and Mary Balogh for the win. The Proposal is the first of what is to "The Survivor's Club" series...seven wounded friends that recuperated together after the Nepoleonic wars. 
 This is the first book of Ms. Balogh that I have read and I enjoyed it. The Proposal is a cute, romantic love story about Gwen and Hugo, although the secondary characters were quite entertaining and added depth to the story. While I was not bored reading, I do acknowledge it was fairly tame and slow-paced with no dramatic events or plot twists. 
 I liked the other members of The Survivor's Club and will continue the series with the next publication.

2 stars 
 I wanted to love it. It checks a lot of boxes for me--found family, stoic hero, emotional baggage, etc. But in execution it was terribly boring. This is due, at least in part, to the author's writing style. She seems fond of repetition. For example, she would describe a character from one person's perspective, and then again ten pages later from another perspective. That sort of thing really irritates me.

We first meet Gwen, Lady Muir in One Night for Love. She is the slightly lame sister of the hero, Neville, of that book. Although One Night For Love has spawned a metric ton of spin-off books (The entire Bedwyn series being one of them), at no time did I ever suspect we'd be getting Gwen's story. 
 It took me awhile to realize the connection, but it was a fun aha! moment when it did. Gwen is long widowed with a lot of buried guilt regarding her marriage. She is visiting a friend who is newly widowed, when she sprains her ankle on the beach and meets the hero, Hugo Emes, Lord Trentham. 
 I have to say I simply fell in love with Hugo. What a great character. He is a war hero who came back from the war suffering from PTSD and his own incredible guilt. He formed a friendship a small group of survivors of the war who also carried their own scars, both physical and mental. 
 At heart Hugo is a decent gentle sort who comes from an upper middle class background. He has never had any great ambition, he only has ever wanted to live a quiet comfortable life. But his foray into war changed all that. He is feted and given great honors because of what he did on the battlefield, all the time he doesn't feel at all worthy of it. 
 When he rescues Gwen they are immediately attracted to one another. Although Balogh is very subtle in how she lets their attraction manifest. It isn't bolt of lightning and immediate lust, but it is an acknowledged attraction and Hugo speaks very frankly about how much he likes and wants Gwen. 
 The meat of the story is their courtship. They fall almost reluctantly in love with each other. Each one of them has internal issues that doesn't allow them to completely let go. And Hugo, although he has been elevated to a Lord, is conscious of a class divide between him and Gwen. But they talk to each other and get to know each other. The build of their romance is well done and completely sweeps the reader along. 
 There are nice bits of humor strung throughout. You smile as Hugo and Gwen get comfortable enough with each other to have inside jokes. 
 Fans of Balogh who have read all the books that have spun from One Night for Love will be treated to a who's who of walk-ons by various characters from those books. There is even a memorable scene that includes Wulfric Bedwyn (who remains my favorite Balogh hero ever). 
 When I finished the book I closed it with a happy sigh. A good book should always elicit that reaction. 
 review is from an ARC through the Amazon Vine program
Typically like Mary Balogh's books but this read like a very poor rehash of Pride and Prejudice, and I mean poor. I managed to finish it but won't be reading anymore in the series.

I think I need to read more romance novels to be able to compare and contrast a bit better. Nonetheless, this was a pleasant-enough read. Now I'm discovering that this is the 13th with the same family but I didn't felt lost and now I want to know more about Lauren and Nicholas, each one with his own book.
