 The only thing that I didn't care for was the lots and lots of paragraphs showing the heroes doubts about their feelings and the wisdom to accept love, it was tiresome... If not for some repetition it would be a 5 star.

I must say I enjoyed this book a great amount. It was like picking up a series that had already been going on and seeing the characters and knowing you were going to be going on a journey with all of them soon. It is the first in a new series by this author. This story was following one of the wounded and introducing us to all of them. I can feel the other interesting characters champing at the bit to tell their stories. I can't wait to read those stories. This author is good at drawing out your interest in the character's back story. She holds back lots of details and reveals them a little at a time. I enjoyed getting to know the characters slowly and really getting a feel for them. So about the story... it is your usual historical romance set in England and it has a sometimes dark feel to it. I enjoyed the nuances of each character and had fun reading it.

Lord Trentham or Hugo, has been home from the Napoleonic War for a few years now. But he didn't come home unscathed, much like many other soldiers. The Duke of Stanbrook who lost his son in the war, and eventually lost his wife due to her grief, has opened up his home to Hugo and six other wounded former soldiers (one is not a soldier, but a widow whose husband was tortured and then shot, which she witnessed). Some are wounded on the outside, and all are wounded on the inside. Every year for a few weeks, these seven people meet at the Duke's house and just hang out. They talk, they share how they are faring, and they find peace in the companionship. 
 Hugo was brought up middle class, but due to a heroic move on the battlefield, he was handed a title. That along with inheriting his father's vast business empire upon his recent death, Hugo finds himself a titled and very wealthy man and it makes him uncomfortable. He bought himself a decent sized house, but still feels more comfortable out in his gardens or tending baby animals. But he knows he has a duty, which means he must marry and beget an heir. Joking with his fellow companions (and by joking, I mean maybe a slight smile, Hugo isn't one to joke) he decides to take a walk on the beach and find a wife. What he doesn't realize is how accurate he is. 
 Lady Muir or Gwen is visiting a friend who recently lost her husband. Gwen knows the sadness of losing a husband, as hers fell off a balcony a few years ago. Before that, she also lost her pregnancy when she fell off a horse (she also permanently injured her leg and walks with a limp). Gwen has had much trauma in her life, but her friends and family who she lives with have kept her spirits up. Gwen goes out for a walk and due to her limp; she falls on some rocks and sprains her ankle badly. Luckily, Hugo just happens to be in the area and swoops her up and takes her back to the Duke's house for a doctor. Gwen is embarrassed and feels like she is imposing on their house party. Hugo doesn't really know what to do around a Lady. As Gwen is forced to stay at the Duke's house for a week until her family can send a carriage, she ends up spending a lot of time with Hugo. 
 As I mentioned earlier, this series is all about "The Survivors Club", six men and one woman who have been deeply affected by the Napoleonic War. While Hugo has no physical injuries, he is deeply tormented on the inside. He led a "Forlorn Hope" where 300 men died, yet it was a successful attack. He has been given a hero status for this, but has a hard time letting go of all the men that died and now being rewarded for that. The others in the group include a blind man, one with crushed legs, one with a scar, one with a bad stammer and a woman who watched as her husband was shot after an extended torture. So, if you like tortured characters, this very well might be a good series for you. There is much drama. This set-up really intrigues me and I very much look forward to getting into all of these characters heads and learning their story. 
 With all the hurt in this book, I found it to be very slow. Hugo is very blunt, and not a man with a lot of words. Pairing him up with Gwen, who is a little cold at first, it was hard to get into this couple. Things eventually start to move along, and that warmer, well done banter that I love from Mary Balogh peeks in every once in awhile. But I did find myself wandering off through a lot of this book. There just wasn't a ton to keep my interest. 
 What I did appreciate is that there isn't really a suspense plot, or a revenge plot or even really a villain. The villain manifests internally in these characters. Hugo must accept what he did in the war, and who he is now. And Gwen must accept the circumstances of her husband's death and that she is allowed to have a happy future. I appreciated the fact that this is a very character driven story. But like I said, it felt sluggish at times. 
 I have to read the next one though, because I'm so intrigued by this Survivor group. 
 Rating: C+

I think Mary Balogh has outdone herself with this book. 
 It's perfect. This book tells a story much deeper than romance. It's about the essence of long lasting love. It's about compassion, patience, understanding, hard work, and rational mind. 
 The pace of this book is quite slow. Plot wise, there is no big climax or twist throughout the book. In this book, Mary Balogh put much effort in the characterization. 
 Gwen is the kind of character who is beautiful,charming and kind. But it doesn't just stop there. She has a strong inner spirit that make even Hugo fell in love with her. 
 Hugo is the kind of hardworking, blunt, and solemn kind of man. But behind his gruffness, he has a soft and kind heart. 
 Mary Balogh also did a great job in the characterization of every secondary characters in this book ( and there are a lot of them). 
 The main issue happening in this book is the fact that Hugo come from middle class background and Gwen from aristocrat background. Each of them thought that the other was not what he/she looked for. 
 We can blithely say that love conquers all. But in reality, it's not that simple. It takes hard work to make that saying true. 
 There is a saying in this book that I like. "Marriage is not just between two people, but also between two families and two societies" 
 Gwen and Hugo didn't rush into marriage. Their courting include their families and they found out that they are not so different after all and they can make it work.

book_b.title: A Kiss For Midwinter (Brothers Sinister, #1.5)
book_b.user_review:
A really excellent novella. Milan shines here, given the format, as the characters are as rich as those found in any full-length book. 
 I believed the big mis was really well done- it was only natural for Lydia to be defensive and I thought her insistance on holding out only made sense given the deep, shaming experience she had lived through. As for Jonas- well. There's something about the medical hero, and he just displaced my previous favorite, Jesse from The Wedding Journey. The final scenes were delicious, truly.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I know I hold an unpopular opinion about this story, but I just couldn't bring myself to like it. Everything was just wrong for me. The dialogue, for one, was uninspiring. I had to grit my teeth at the writer's pathetic effort to be witty or funny. 
 "But you see, Miss Charingford, I must be a doctor before I allow myself to be a gentleman. I do not recall such a thing in order to hold you up for moral condemnation. I state it as a simple medical fact, one that would be relevant to further treatment. Certain female complaints, for instance--" 
 "Put it out of your mind. You will never treat me as a patient. Ever." 
 "Ever?" he asked. "So if you're trampled by a runaway stallion, you'd expect me to express my wholehearted regrets to your parents. 'No, no,' I will say. 'I couldn't possibly stop your daughter from bleeding to death on the cobblestones--my professional ethics forbid me to treat anyone who has unequivocally refused me consent.'" 
 Lydia gave him a firm nod instead. "That's exactly right. I would rather bleed to death than have your hands on me." She tucked her gloves under her arm and reached for her shawl. 
 He was still smiling at her. "I'll pay my respects at your funeral." 
 "I don't want you there. If you dare come, I'll haunt you in your sleep." 
 But that only sparked a wicked gleam in his eye. He took a step closer, forcing her to tilt her head up at an unnatural angle. He leaned over her, bending his neck. And then he whispered. 
 "Why, Miss Charingford." That smile of his tilted, stretching. "There's no need to wait until you're dead to visit my bed. In fact, I'm available right now, so long as we finish before--" 
 Uh... Was that supposed to be seduction? Wow. Way to go, Lothario. 
 Aside from the horrible writing, another thing I didn't like was the fact that Lydia and Jonas lacked chemistry. Their romance was not convincing and totally not natural. In Chapter 1, for example, Jonas just decided that he wanted Lydia after an argument. And then he put off all his plans for marriage and decided that he would wait for Lydia to fall for him. Um, what? Was that really a natural reaction of a man who had just been dissed by a woman, who, by the way, was soiled (pardon the term)? Bloody ridiculous, especially given the historical context. 
 This is my first Courtney Milan book, and I'm not particularly tempted to read more of her works.

For such a short book, it packed a punch!!! 
 I enjoyed it immensely. Well done, Ms. Milan, well done!
Not as good as Duchess War but needed to read it to fill in the blanks about the family.

This has my most hated "hero" in 2013. I found him completely, utterly despicable. 
 I haven't been able to write a review yet because every time I attempt it my blood pressure goes up. 
 Standing by while a sham doctor prescribes poison for a young, pregnant girl, knowing it will likely kill her and her unborn baby, because he wants to inherit the doctor's practice? Are you kidding me? And then choosing a list of wifey-candidates (which he wants so he can have lots of sex and not worry about contracting a STD--fabulous) based on their beauty....um, okay. And then, getting irked w/ one of the candidates because she has freckles, and her "smile is too wide"--WTF! And then when he realizes who she is, he wants her because "he always wants what he can't have"....and then, even after he realizes how vulnerable she feels because he knows her big secret, during one of their first conversations, he comes onto her and says he wants her sexually--because that's something a real stand-up guy would do. 
 Oh wait a minute. No, it's not. 
 Oh crap. My blood pressure is going up. Must. Stop. 
 I really enjoyed some other stories by this author, but this was certainly not one of them.

This was a sweet, clever little novella. So much packed into this heart wrenching, sensitively executed short story. 
 Lydia Charingford at the tender age of 15 has been diagnosed as being pregnant by a narrow minded, unsympathetic Doctor who advises her parents to have her put away as she is ruined. In the company of this physician is a young man named Jonas Grantham about to embark on his medical training and accompanying the elderly Doctor to gain experience, warned to keep his opinions to himself, Jonas feels unable to intervene in the treatment proposed, although he does not agree with the medication prescribed....a decision he forever regrets. 
 Six years later Jonas returns, he is by now a fully qualified Doctor with some ground breaking ideas. Young, enthusiastic, tactless, sarcastic and incapable of being anything other than direct and truthful, he is on the lookout for a wife. He draws up a list of eligible young women of which Lydia...whom he does not recognise...is no.11 on said 'wife list'. Lydia is immediately aware that this tall, good looking young man was present at the moment of her disgrace and this knowledge puts her on the defensive. She decides she does not like him and even after Jonas is made aware...by Lydia herself...that it was she 6 years previously, she is convinced he thinks her easy and could not possibly be attracted to her. This is the catalyst for Jonas to decide that no other will do and he embarks on a 16 month pursuit of Lydia, during which, due to the directness of his speech and his inability to lie, she misunderstands every remark he makes to her. To his credit Jonas will not be turned from his goal and doggedly carries on trying to win Lydia's heart. As a physician he recognises that she has not recovered and that she is really very badly affected by her ordeal six years previously, he patiently tries to help her, his methods and manner of speech, however, do not endear him to her. 
 Courtney Milan has tackled a taboo subject in a brave and sensitive manner, in an era, where disgrace of this kind would have, under normal circumstances, completely ruined a young woman. Lydia may have escaped wider censorship with the aid of her friend Minnie and her own caring and loving parents, but she is deeply troubled and hides it with a cheerful and happy disposition, her own worst critic, she is resigned to never allowing herself to find love and is afraid of the natural urges of her own body. 
 There are also warm and evocative scenes with Jonas and his own Father, a self made man who is desperately ill....real tear jerkers....hankies at the ready! 5 well deserved stars for this wonderful little gem Courtney Milan.

I kept putting this one aside to read other things on my TBR for some reason. It was cute. I appreciated how sex-positive it is - Grantham's clinical nature was weirdly a good vehicle for that. I wanted to slap Lydia for her cluelessness with regard to Grantham's affections - seriously. Thank god that was a short-lived situation, I literally rolled my eyes. The resolution felt rushed, and the banter was just ok. The relationship between Grantham and his father did build well and I was a little choked up over it a couple of times. I am certainly looking forward to the next in the series!
I just loved the characters! I think that anyone who reads this falls a little bit for Dr Grantham and even for Lydia. And am I the only one who just loved his dad?!

Re-rated in November, 2016 - 3.5 stars rounded-up for the historical feminist setting 
 I mostly read male/male romance, but I do enjoy the occasional, "traditional" male/female romance. The more I read across these genres, the more I appreciate this author, especially the juxtaposition of the historical setting with strong/feminist heroines facing discrimination and challenges to the most basic aspects of life. 
 I really appreciated the theme of this book, how it wove serious issues into an easy-to-read romance.

I enjoyed this book so much up until the last 15% or so. That I did not enjoy. It brought it down 1 star for me but I still really enjoyed this story and I recommend it if you want a light holiday read!

I think Courtney Milan's career may eventually reach an integrity ceiling. Her books are absolutely beautiful for the raw honesty of emotion and history, of suffering and ignorance and strength that they portray. If you're sensitive, as I'm sometimes sensitive, it makes it hard to use them as escapism. I like historical novels because history is just as much another world as any second world fantasy can present. But I like escapism, too. I like exceptional people. I like to believe, when I'm seeking escape, that somebody will save all the sick and starving children _this_ time. But Courtney Milan is all too aware that mostly, those children didn't get saved. They lived short, brutal, unpleasant lives. She doesn't focus on it, oh no. But she knows. And that knowing shines through the seams of her stories. It makes them something other than romance. They're beautiful things, but they rarely make me comfortable.

reference_books.title: If on a Winter's Night a Traveler
reference_books.review_text:
About halfway through the book, I thought I was reading a 260-page middle finger from Italo Calvino to his readers. Toward the end, I realized that wasn't fair - it wasn't a giant middle finger, because Calvino probably really believed what he did was edgy and clever. 
 In 1955, maybe this would have been edgy. In 1979, which is when he wrote it, it's hard to believe people were fooled into thinking this was anything but a bunch of smug sputum. In 2008, it's just a waste of time. 
 I learned one thing from this book. I was supposed to read this in college and never did, and finished out of a sense of obligation to Kevin McManus, my English teacher way back when. So what I learned is: if I could force myself to finish this, I can read anything.

book_b.title: The Lottery and Other Stories
book_b.user_review:
Not what I thought at all. I intended this to be a Halloween read, because, you know, Shirley Jackson. Except for The Lottery, it was much more like J.D. Salinger, where you read the story, go "bwuh?" and then go back and say, "oh, that part when she dunked her cruller in the coffee must have meant she lost her virginity that same night, because otherwise the story makes no freaking sense." And then look it up at Grade Savers to see if you got the story right. 
 So kind of like Encyclopedia Brown, too. 
 Really. Turns out anybody with a name James or Jim Harris is evil. Maybe just a smalltime jerk, maybe the devil in human form. Also, if you ever throw anything out that's monogrammed, you lose your identity. Or if you leave your house, for that matter. 
 The obvious exception is the story The Lottery itself, so I think it's kind of false advertising to call out that story in naming this collection. It should be called Afternoon in Linen (that's one where passive aggressive tendencies are observed in a conversation) and Like Mother Used To Make (some guy gets used by a neighbor to make dinner for some other guy, but you suspect the used guy is gay anyway, so what's the problem) and Other Stories.

sample_reviews.review_text: Shirley Jackson has a great way with the uncanny. That creeping sense that something is not quite right. She tunnels the same sense of melancholy and horror as Robert Aickman would later, but she does with even less warmth. She can be funny, Charles is a great example, but there is always something unsettling about her writing. The Lottery, the short story itself, lives up to its infamous billing; what an ending, the perfect disturbing end to a perfect collection. The perfect Autumnal reading.
Creepy, intense and in short story form...
I have only read The Lottery, and found it didsturbing.

Just like with any short story collections, there was a grab bag of good, bad, and what? The lottery is the strongest of all of them by far, and I can kind of see how they connect thematically. Each story leading up to the lottery presented a character that was easy to judge, and I found myself easily doing so. Then the selection in The Lottery, to me, represented the idea that we all are dealt certain cards, sometimes there is nothing we can do, and it is wrong to judge people based on those cards.

When I read "The Lottery and Other Stories" by Shirley Jackson, the first thing I did, was read "The Lottery" aloud to my mother who'd never read it before. Shocked and disgusted by how the ending contrasted so drastically with the pastoral setting of the beginning and the middle of the tale, it showed Jackson's true gift as a writer of suspense and drama. Throughout this collection I grew to appreciate how diverse, yet consistent, her short story skills were. There's an undertone of malice and humor in whatever she writes in this book, whether it's as simple as a woman believing she has a suitor in "The Daemon Lover" to a more psychologically complicated account of a bookseller and his customers in "Seven Types of Ambiguity". I also noticed a macabre twist to this selection that made all of her characters unforgettable and richly drawn.

Shirley Jackson had this amazing, albeit negative, perspective of people. Throughout all of The Lottery and Other Stories, she shows an underlying lack of trust and disregard for others. In The Lottery, she's basically saying, look what can happen when people stop questioning what's happening, and just start to go with the flow. People end up killing each other, senselessly. And oh...........how this happens all over the world. It's the "group think", I think, that she abhorred. 
 So many of these stories have underlying themes of paranoia, and mental instability. Which carries over into her novels as well...Hill House...We Have Always Lived in the Castle. I read that alot of her stories stem from her experiences of trying to "fit in" in small-town Vermont. Which begs the question...are people really the way she saw them, or was the paranoid, mentally unstable one actually SJ herself? 
 I think my favorite here was "Dorothy and My Grandmother and the Sailors" because, while being a short little tale, it says so much. It's amazing where paranoia and panic can set in, once a little seed is planted. Shirley Jackson could say so much about people in such a few, short pages. 
 As far as leaving you with a sense of completion, I think it was Jackson's style to end before the climax. She left the reader with very open endings, and we were meant to deduct our own meaning. I have to admit after reading a few of them, I was like...what the heck???? Actually, I guess in particular the second one, about the Demon Lover. 
 Throughout all of these stories, Jackson uses a man's name or a variation on his name...James Harris...also called Jamie, and other nicknames, too, that I can't recall right now. I thought it was genius the way she weaved him throughout the stories..like he was this evil force, or the devil himself.
Painful. I enjoyed "The Witch" and "The Lottery". The rest were just difficult.

The only bad thing I can say about this collection is that it makes me want to suffer head trauma so that I can forget the stories and read them again in their NEWNESS. Singing Shirley Jackson's praises is like pointing out the blueness of the sky. Just read this. It'll ruin you for all other writers, but in the most divine sense.

My personal favourites of this collection: 
 The Intoxicated 
 Like Mother Used to Make 
 The Witch 
 Charles 
 Flower Garden 
 Seven Types of Ambiguity 
 Come Dance with Me in Ireland 
 Of Course 
 Men with Their Big Shoes 
 and of course 
 The Lottery (it still stuns) 
 Every one of the stories in this collection is well worth your time, but of course we all have our favourites. Wonder what yours will be.

Some of the stories were great. I particularly liked The Daemon Lover, the Witch, and the Lottery. I probably would've enjoyed some of the other stories more if I had studied them in a class, but when I'm reading for pleasure I really don't want to have to overanalyze things.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I was disappointed in this book, because I had heard so many rave reviews. I give it 3 stars because, even though it wasn't very good, I couldn't put it down. I'm not sure why I couldn't put it down, but I stayed up late all week reading it. 
 It's the story of 30 years of friendship between 2 women and the ups and downs they travel through. Neither character is likeable. Kate is a spineless pushover and Tully is narcissistic and bitchy. They are each jealous of the other's life, starting from when they meet at age 14 and through the end of the book. It didn't seem to be a solid basis for a lasting friendship. I still don't understand why they stayed friends - they had nothing in common and I would not have been friend with either of them! I was also bothered that the characters never matured, even though the book spanned over 30 years. Tully had mommy issues and was never satisfied, and Kate never really stood up for herself and what she wanted in life. 
 At the end, Kate dies from cancer. It's really sad. I could barely hold it together. The last 10% of the book dealt with her diagnosis, treatments and death. It was a little too much for me, since I have lived through a relative's sickness and death from cancer. It's not something I want to re-live in my spare time. Additionally, I felt that the author tied everything up too neatly with Kate's death. Everyone made their amends and they all loved each other and were there for each other and her life was cleanly wrapped up. That's not how real life works, especially with something as vicious as cancer. It made me mad. 
 Overall review: Kate was depressing, Tully was annoying, there was to much cancer and it was too sad.
A little sappy for me but the characters drew me in and I cried at the end. Gotta love books that make you cry.

book_b.title: The Book of Ruth
book_b.user_review: Another dreary choice from Oprah's Book Club.

sample_reviews.review_text: I read it for a book group. It was so depressing.

Another book I had a hard time getting through -- this one just seemed to drag on and on. The story itself could have been so interesting, but I feel like the writing should have been much tighter to hold my attention.

We were assigned this book as part of a writing course, with the intention that the instructor would have us read a few chapters per week, for us to discuss the author's use of craft. Our first discussion opened with the group unanimously loathing the book so much that it was never brought up again. I read it to the end to see if things got better - they did not, a tedious downer to the final sentence.

c. 1988 
 Funny and tragic.
I love her writing. These are characters I can relate to. I prefer her early writings... this book, Map of the World and The Short History of a Prince.

Ruth is a very complex character -- beaten down, made to feel that she is unintelligent, stuck in her smallest of small town lives. She begins corresponding with her estranged Aunt Sid, the only person to encourage her and lift her. Ruth says that Sid saved her life a million times over. 
 Even after becoming a mother and wife, Ruth exists in a childlike, innocent state, until a violent act throws her life into complete upheaval. There is a sense of hopefulness throughout that things will turn out okay for Ruth in the end. Despite her awkwardness, she has dignity and resilience.

My mother-in-law read this on Oprah's suggestion, then she asked me to read it so we could discuss it. We both hated it. There is no way the reader can accept the self-consciously literary narrator as Ruth, who tells us repeatedly how stupid and illiterate she is. Likewise I found Hamilton's attempts to empathize with her characters both shallow and condescending. The only reason I finished this book was to discover what horrible thing had happened, as was referred to on the first page...the answer wasn't worth it. Hamilton has used every literary device at her disposal, and she is clearly a skilled writer. Unfortunately, her dislike or disrespect for her characters distances the reader, and the literary skill is wasted.
Spawned or maybe spawned from the White Trash chic genre. Bleak as bleak can be.

3.5- Such a sweet story!

This is a short, heavily illustrated chapter book about a dog and a cat who live very different lives in Paris but when they meet, they each help each other become more brave. The illustrations are charming as is the text.

This was a cute story of an unlikely friendship. It was a little simplistic for my third graders, so I think it might be better suited for 1st or 2nd graders. I did like the characters, though, and the overarching theme of friendship.

I am a serious Mo Willem's fan, but I was hesitant to read anything other than the picture book sensation that the Pigeon, and Elephant and Piggie series, is. I had definitely been missing out! The story of Diva and Flea captures the reader from the title page which portrays an inviting rooftop view of the city of Paris complete with a friendly gargoyle statue. The idiosyncrasies of both Diva, a small dog, and Flea a street cat, are presented to the reader, not as flaws or strengths, just as part of who they are. Both come from different backgrounds, Diva is the pet of a building administrator, Flea is a flaneur or an individual who is a wanderer, curious about the world around him. They meet and are curious, rather than wary, of these differences. As they get to know each other and conquer fears and have adventures that strengthen the bond between these two friends, they also evolve and mature. One of the many virtues of this story is that its characters deal with many situations young readers are dealing with themselves, allowing for an introspection without the possibility of feeling self-conscious. The way the characters face each issue is an excellent model of how all of us can tackle difficult situations and celebrate the small successes. This is an excellent introduction to chapter books for younger readers, with short chapters and illustrations that function as a portal to the streets of Paris, and the Parisian way of life. Every element of this book, from the raised lettering of the title on the dust jacket, to the ornate frames that enclose each chapters' title, to the rich, thick paper used, and the detailed illustrations, communicate to the reader that this book is special, and was made carefully for him or her. Teachers that are searching for a read aloud that will engage students and set the stage for many literary conversations will love this book.
Sweet!

Wonderfully illustrated chapter book of two opposites teaching each other bravery in Paris 
 A lovely collaboration between the talents of Mo Willems (usually the creator of picture books himself) and Tony DiTerizzi. 
 I whipped through this as I checked it through before reading it to my son at bedtime. It's a little like Lady and the Tramp - a protected and sheltered pooch (Diva) meets a street-smart 'flaneur' (wanderer), here a cat called Flea - and opposites soon find a connection. 
 In a city of adventure and beauty, the two show each other the excitements of their relative worlds and may even have some reciprocal lessons to offer. 
 Fully illustrated in colour, the pictures of a nostalgic Paris are beautiful, with artfully drawn dogs and scenes suited to the tale. Each chapter is no more than a handful of pages long, making it an easy read for fairly young children (my son wanted several chapters in one go) and you could read the whole thing in just 2 or 3 bedtime sessions. 
 I loved the clash of personalities, and how it wasn't all a one-way relationship (Diva being taught to look outside her own courtyard) - the street-smart cat also got to learn a few things about life and contentment. 
 My son really enjoyed the story, the conclusion, and even the French words. 
 Great setting, simple characters that still manage to grow, a lovely story about friendship. Could be read to ages 3-7 by parents, or by 7-10 year olds who like animal stories and accessible chapter books. 
 With thanks to Walker Books for the advance reading copy.

reference_books.title: The Last Time We Say Goodbye
reference_books.review_text:
First of all, I want to say that this book does a great job of not romanticizing suicide. It's told from the perspective of a girl whose brother committed suicide and manages to both get across the heartbreaking effect it had on her, and give a glimpse of what her brother was going through. Even though she didn't understand it or completely even notice her brother's struggles, she doesn't try to delegitimize them or suggest that her brother should have just fought his demons, which is so, so important. 
 But. 
 There are other books in YA that deal with suicide, and do it in more interesting ways, with characters that are easier to grow attached to. To name a few from this year alone, My Heart and Other Black Holes, All the Bright Places (I am 100% in disagreement with anyone who says this book glorifies mental illness. It does not.), and I Was Here. Another sibling-suicide book I'd recommend over this one is Saving June. 
 My main problem with The Last Time We Say Goodbye was that, while I praise it for not romanticizing terrible things, it doesn't do much else either. It's very dull. Not a whole lot happens in this book at all, in terms of both plot and character development. By the end of the book, Lexie still feels like the same person she was in the beginning. Of course, her brother's death shouldn't have just been a device for her to learn something about him or herself, but I didn't feel her growing as a person throughout the novel either. In truth, she was kind of unbearable until the last few chapters, when she finally seemed like an actual human being. It's not that there is an appropriate response to something like what she went through, but it was just difficult reading from the point of view of someone who had essentially turned herself into a robot: she pushed her friends away and shut herself in her own little Grief Box, where she was only allowed to care about math. Literally. But that's another issue altogether. 
 You see, my other problem with this book is the way it depicts high school, which is to say: it gets its high school characters from '80s teen movies. Lexie is a self-proclaimed nerd who loves math, relates everything to math, and hates English and cheerleaders (who are all blond, because of course they are). No, really. She complains about how much she hates the books she has to read for English class, because she likes them until the teacher starts explaining things like symbolism and metaphor. Because obviously those things are so terrible, right? They just make so many books worse! Surely The Great Gatsby would be more enjoyable if the green light could just be a green light! Why not just remove Hester Prynne's scarlet letter altogether?!? 
 And yeah, sure, some nerds are probably like that. But the problem is that this book treats them as if they're all like that. Every nerd in the book is obsessed with science or math, or maybe history, because apparently if literature or art or music is your thing, you're not a nerd. Which feels a lot like saying: you're not worthy. At least not to our main character, who gets her kicks from making fun of cheerleaders because she's a Special Nerd and they're just Regular Athletes. Never mind that, you know, a lot of times cheerleaders are the overachievers who also happen to be at the top of the class academically, or that the smart kids can also be the ones with no extracurriculars, who like to just go home after school and watch TV. Or read The Great Gatsby. 
 Perhaps even more insulting is the suggestion that nerds are, by nature, mean-spirited people who feel superior to everyone around them. Lexie says in the book that "Nothing gives nerds more innate satisfaction than poking fun at cheerleaders." Aside from the blatant falseness of this statement, it is completely useless for any reason other than to make us hate her. I was in the nerd crowd in high school*, and she is not someone we would have been friends with. 
 *For the record, I graduated from high school almost 6 years ago, and even when I was there it was not at all like it is in this book. I was a blond nerd--AP classes, a 97% GPA, and I didn't hate going to classes--with one extracurricular activity, which happened to be the school newspaper. Not a math club, not whatever that robotics club was, not debate, or chess club, or whatever qualifies someone as a nerd in Lexie's book. My best friend was the stereotypical science/math nerd, but she was also captain of the varsity cheerleading squad. Most of my friends had straight As and they also liked their teenage debauchery--you name it, at least one of them had done it. 
 This is how it is in most high schools. We don't live in the world of The Breakfast Club, where people are one thing until proven to be more. Cliques exist, sure, but they are labeled by popularity, not shared interests. Everybody hates the kid who thinks she's smarter than the teacher [Tangent: there is a scene in this book where Lexie argues with her English teacher, saying that love is "just chemicals." Not only was this irrelevant to the actual topic of the class--any real teacher would have cut her off instead of humoring her lunacy--but the idea itself is a rip-off of the show Bones (see gif below), which Lexie was marathoning in the beginning of the book. Not to mention, this was an honors class, and people in honors classes do not tolerate one of their peers arguing so viciously with the teacher. It's annoying and everybody hates it. An argument like Lexie's feels more like someone trying to prove their intelligence than someone who actually knows anything, and I guarantee that in real life, at least one of her classmates would have defended the teacher's point of view.] 
 Moving on from all that, I did like the last few chapters. They finally got me. I just wish the whole book had been like that. All in all the book was okay, but it was too dull and relied too heavily on stereotypes for me to give it anything above 2.5 stars.

reference_books.title: A Thousand Pieces of You (Firebird, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I've decided to be more liberal with my 1-star reviews, because I realized recently that I haven't given a book one star in a few years. Why does the 1-star option exist, if not for books I couldn't even finish? 
 Which brings me to my confession: I did not finish this book. You can choose whether to take heed of my review or not. I mean, personally, I think the whole "You can't review a book if you didn't finish it" rule is totally invalid -- people have reasons for not finishing books, and knowing what they are might stop you from wasting your time. Sometimes it's just a "This book wasn't for me" situation, but sometimes it's not. 
 This one was not. 
 "My hand shakes as I brace myself against the brick wall." 
 That, my friends, is the first sentence of A Thousand Pieces of You. Wow, what a rousing start. How am I ever going to put this book down after that?! Forget The Knife of Never Letting Go and "The first thing you find out when yer dog learns to talk is that dogs don't got nothing much to say." Forget The Night Circus and "The circus arrives without warning." This one clearly has them beat with that epic line about a brick wall. 
 Snark aside: this first sentence tells you absolutely nothing, right? It's not specific to this book at all, which raises a red flag because it's a clear promise of bad writing. 
 And bad writing ye shall receive! Where do I even start? Okay, I know this book is YA, but here's the thing: I love YA. At least ninety percent of my favorite books are YA. But as a YA reader, I felt like Claudia Gray was talking down to me in this story. Every. single. thing. is right there on the page. There is nothing to infer, nothing to think about. Reading is supposed to be an experience where I can feel with the characters; I don't need their every emotion and question and thought spelled out for me. The writing in this one leaves nothing for me to do other than, well, read. And that's the most unsatisfying kind of writing there is. ("But, Paige," you might say, "you're not a teenager! This book isn't intended for you!" -- to which I say, "BALONEY." All books are written for the people who like them. I like YA books, so this book is supposed to be written for me.) 
 All this transparency left nothing for me to attach myself to. Everything feels flat, like I'm being told This Is The Story You Are Reading instead of getting to feel like I was a part of it. I don't know if Claudia Gray (or whatever her real name is) has a degree in writing, but I'd venture a big no on that one -- which is fine, because I don't think you need a degree in writing to be a good writer. But it would definitely help in her case, because reading this book felt exactly like workshopping a grad student's manuscript. It would have been easy to improve the writing quality and make it feel less like the author didn't trust the reader to understand, but nobody put forth that effort. 
 Unfortunately, the writing style wasn't the only bad thing about the book. The main character, Marguerite, is every bit as unbearable as her name. In the half of the book that I read, she did nothing but complain, contradict herself, fawn over her two love interests, and judge people. I think the fact that she's an "artist" (throw in a couple generic art references and bam! Your heroine is supposedly an artist!) is supposed to make her interesting, but we never actually see her doing any art. She doesn't look at the world with an artist's eye. Being an "artist" changes nothing about her perspective, other than making her the self-declared black sheep of the family, the special snowflake who likes art instead of science. Oh, the poor little runt. 
 The love interests were not much better. You've got the probable drug addict and the accused murderer, great! I could totally get behind that, if I believed that either of these guys were actually either of those things. But they're not. They're both Bad Boys Lite(tm), and Marguerite cares more about them than she cares about accomplishing anything. She starts off the book promising to kill Paul Markov, and then not even halfway through it he's all "But I'm innocent!" and she's all "Oh, okay." [implied: "What a relief because I never really intended to kill you anyway, on account of I am way too bland and also have no experience killing people. Also I think, maybe, not sure because apparently I haven't thought about it enough even though it's all I've been talking about, I might be in love with you."] They're both in love with her for some reason (I believe Paul more than I believe Theo, who's pretty much just a pathological flirt, but neither of them totally convinced me) and she's basically willing to go for Theo because he makes it more clear, until Paul tells her his feelings and that's the end of that. The bromance between the two of them totally could have hooked me -- I am a bromance fiend, after all -- but it was barely even there! Why do you promise me a beautiful platonic relationship and then not deliver?! 
 At this point I don't think I need to get started on the plot, so I'll just say that it was half-assed at best. So many things go unexplained in this book: questions that characters can't answer because the author couldn't answer them. Other reviewers have mentioned this, so just read the other 1-star reviews if you need examples. I'm off to read something that's actually worth my time. 
 Shame about that cover, though. It deserved better.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I received this e-ARC for free on netgalley.com (Thank you!) and in exchange I will do an honest review. 
 So the start was pretty good: one day Sia wakes up on a bench in the middle of the day and she has no clue where or who she is. Only her iPod says her name Sia and that's it. A really promising start, but somehow it went downhill from there. I really liked the first chapters, but after Sia meets her parents again, the story becomes so unrealistic and ridiculous. Everything felt like "happily ever after" and I couldn't buy the whole amnesia plot twist, sorry. Solving your mum's drinking problem (which she had for a year) in two weeks? Check. Getting the boy, although he hated you nuts before? Check. Sorting out your father's money by attending the Oscar's afterparty? Check. 
 The Story and writing was nice though, but definitely a light, unrealistic read.

Kyle is precious just wanted to say that off the bat. He is right to be wary of letting go and letting Sia in but he still precious. 
 Okay so Sia has fugue amnesia. She remembers nothing about her time before she lives on the streets. When Kyle sees her in a food kitchen, anger bubbles over and he scares her, she runs and gets hit. This has her wake up in a hospital and her parents are there. Only she doesn't remember anything. She goes home to live her life again but she is changed. Change by the experience. Only for all around her, they are wary because let me tell you she wasn't exactly susie sunshine to people. 
 Her best friends are horrid to others as well. So Sia begins to see this and she doesn't like what she sees. She's changing for good and this doesn't sit well with some. Kyle sees this and starts to let her in especially after her standoff with her friends and boyfriend. 
 Sia has lots of issues to deal with. Who she used to be, her life now, who she is becoming, family problems all of it but no one knows. Well not true she does trust one person. Kyle. Kyle who she is beginning to like and who secretly likes her. 
 As all this is going on Sia is trying to do good and offers to help Kyle with a fundraiser. Man she excels in this area. So anyways, she gets this great opportunity to raise money and convinces Kyle this is a good thing. He goes and they do some serious damage to people's pocketbooks but they also realize how they feel for each other. Except Kyle is afraid. Can you blame him? She was horrible to him before her personality change. His fears are valid: what if once she remembers, she doesn't like him anymore or goes back to her old ways. She understands and they stay friends but don't go further although both want to. 
 So will she remember? Will her family life get better? Will her and Kyle become the super totes cute couple they should be? You will just have to read this sweet and wonderful book on how only you have the power to change you into a better person and empower yourself against peer pressure and choose the love you deserve book.
DNF... I got decently through though. And I did skim to the end... overall this book was NOT my cup of tea

A very sweet, lovely story with a great deal of predictability. 
 Sia awakens on a park bench to realize she has lost her memory. The only reason she knows her name is from a playlist on her ipod, which says "Sia's playlist". Instead of going to the police or a hospital to find out either what is wrong with her or if someone is looking for her, she becomes homeless for about a week. She meets Carol, a wise and lovely homeless woman, who helps her maneuver through soup kitchens, getting clothing, and sleeping under a bridge. 
 When Sia is in an accident, she wakes up in a hospital, still without her memory, but at least with an identity. Sia finds she has fugue amnesia, which is caused by some form of stress. As she tries to return to her normal routine, Sia discovers several family issues which could be the cause for her amnesia. She also finds the person she has been was a cruel fashionista who "ran the school" with her best friend Amber. 
 The best part of this YA novel is Sia getting a second chance at life. Due to her amnesia, she starts over as a much more loving and giving individual. Her father helps her to see this is more consistent with the young child she was than with the teenager she has become. Even when her memory returns, Sia stays the sweet girl she has become. 
 What makes the story difficult, is Sia's life now does a 180 due to her amnesia and everything works out amazingly well. All of her family issues, and her personality concerns disappear in the blink of an eye. The new Sia is loved by all and has a totally giving, loving personality. In addition, she is beautiful, confident and able to turn around the lives of her family, her friends and her community. 
 This is a sweet story with a very interesting premise. It is not difficult to like Sia, the person, but it is difficult to believe Sia, the book. I would recommend this for a very young and innocent preteen as a sweet coming of age story and an opportunity to think about those who are less fortunate. A more savvy, high school teen may just find this a bit too saccharin.

Dnf at 40% because honestly, I'm tired and I deserve better.

 Sia is embarrassed by her old self, which is fair, I get that, but oh my god does "new Sia" have to be so incredibly stupid? And do her friends have to be so vapid just because they're popular? And being homeless for a week doesn't make you an expert on being homeless. Fucks sake. I'm done.

The cover is very pretty and I loved the name Sia it's a beautiful name. 
 Sia wakes up on a bench at the park with memory loss. After a week on the streets with her new friend Carol ,she ends up at the hospital and finds out she is beyond rich and a bitch.

 What I was missing where the deep emotions off not realizing who you are? And the sadness off the realization that her relationship with her parents and other people are not that good. Her friends and boyfriend were walking cliches.

 I received an ARC of this book from Net Galley. The synopsis of this book greatly intrigued me, as I haven't read anything like this storyline before. Right from the beginning, I was hooked. 
 Sia starts out waking up in a park with no recollection of why she's there or who she is. I liked where the story was going when it started. After a while of being homeless, which I found very interesting to read about, Sia ends up reuniting with her family. In the life she had forgotten about, Sia had been very wealthy, popular, and also mean. I really enjoyed how she decided to change her life to become a better person, and how she stood up to her former friends and tried to get them to turn nice and caring as well. Sia is a likable character. The other characters I really liked were Carol, Kyle, and Beatriz. Sia had great interactions with them and it was nice to her true friendships evolve.

It also seemed like Sia barely struggled with her memory loss at all, except for a short amount of time in the beginning. A lot of things in this book felt too fast.

book_b.title: First & Then
book_b.user_review:
I don't know what book everyone else read, but this is not a 5-star book by any scale that I would use. The writing is mediocre, the characters are frustrating (Devon, Ezra) or flat (Cas, Devon's parents) or can't seem to decide how old they are (Foster, Marabelle), and the plotting was strange. Every scene felt like it was cut short, like they ended in places that didn't make sense for them to end. The whole book felt this way, actually. I didn't get enough of anything from this book, and I can't decide if that's because it tried to do too much or it didn't try to do enough. 
 Like, we've got the whole Foster-moving-in-with-Devon thing. Okay, fine. Go with that. Show her struggle to adapt to having a new family member around all the time; show the growth in her relationship with Foster. Instead, what I saw was Devon complaining for no apparent reason that this kid came to live with them, not explaining what was really going on with his mom (really. the whole book goes by and you can't say the word "depression," or whatever it was that sent her into rehab (or wherever she was, since I'm pretty sure the word "rehab" is never said either)?), and then becoming an overprotective "big sister" the moment something mildly bad happens to him. Basically what I wanted in the Devon/Foster relationship was for the author to dig deeper. 
 The focus on everything that happens to Foster takes away from Devon's involvement in the action--nothing ever really happens to her, and for that reason she doesn't have a ton of character development, either. The book opens with her being told that her personal essay for a college application wasn't good enough, but never comes back to it. She never really starts to care about college; we don't see her apply at all, and the extracurricular that she halfheartedly signs up for comes way too easily--literally all she has to do is hold a camera bag, and she even complains about that. She gets a byline in the school newspaper just for emailing with the guy who eventually becomes her love interest. Woe is Devon, it's a hard knock life. 
 The romance takes a backseat and relies on the all-too-convenient "all of our conflict comes from lack of communication" trope, so I don't have a lot to say about it. I took a break from reading to text my friend and tell her how tired I am of contemporary romance authors defaulting to miscommunication as a source of tension. [Don't get me wrong, some books do it well--like Anna and the French Kiss--and some contemporary authors continually succeed at avoiding it, like Morgan Matson and Sarah Ockler. But alas, those few authors can't come out with dozens of books a year and sometimes I have to settle for stuff like this.] 
 The Jane Austen stuff is the book's main draw and frankly, I felt like it didn't need to be there. Devon says the one criticism she has of "Jane's" books are that the couple-finally-gets-together scenes are too short and there's not enough kissing, AND THEN SHE GIVES US EVEN LESS OF THAT EXACT THING. Everyone at least remembers the scene in Pride & Prejudice when Darcy confesses his love and all that jazz, but I finished First & Then two days ago and I could not even tell you if Devon and Ezra kissed at the end. I assume they did, but I legitimately don't remember. 
 Here are the three bullet points that I did like about this book: 
 -it was funny, and I liked Devon's voice 
 -I appreciate that the author at least tried to emphasize female friendship, even if it was only once in the whole book 
 -I loved Jordan. Loved him. Why wasn't he the love interest? Ezra was okay, but Jordan was like sunshine on the page. 
 This is not a book I'd recommend if you're looking for a cute, swoony contemporary romance, because there barely is a romance. It's not a book I'd recommend if you want a moving family story, because the family situation is neither explained well nor very nuanced, and I was not moved. If you want a fast read with a funny but irritating narrator, well then go ahead and grab a copy of First & Then.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Ugh, I want more Ezra and Devon. 
 From the first few pages I knew I was going to love this book. Devon was sarcastic and funny and Ezra was the mysterious quiet football player. 
 I'm so glad the author took her time with their story. It was messy and true and just what I've been looking for. Everything I've been reading lately has characters jumping into relationships and I never get that sense of connection. This is how it's done. 
 There was some parts like all the talking about college and having to get involved in extracurricular activities that were a little annoying to me. They felt so long. I also feel like I still don't really know who Devon is besides her love for Jane Austen. 
 I'm not sure I liked Cas. I feel like they didn't really have a lot of dialogue and I felt bad for Devon. I'm glad she found Ezra. 
 I also loved the growing relationship with her and Foster. It was a little weird with him being in 9th grade and everyone else being seniors though. 
 I enjoyed this story, minus all the college stuff. 
 I've also never read a Jane Austen novel but I love Friday Night Lights. The author doesn't make you feel like you have no idea what Devon is talking about when she references her work though, which is awesome.
#ThatMomentWhen you get to the final character revelations and they leave you with a stream of tears.
This book was adorable and I really enjoyed the (not so subtle) parallels with important Pride and Prejudice scenes. My only gripe is that I NEEDED IT TO BE SO MUCH LONGER.

This book grew on me slowly, and affected me a lot more than I thought. It became not just a book about high school problems, it became a lovely piece about family and pain, and how those things change you. I saw a lot of myself in Devon, the author captured a lot of my inner turmoil and sarcastic comments and I felt one with Devon. Good read.

4.5* I read this book from 11pm one night to 5am the next morning. It's not that I couldn't put it down, it's just that I didn't want to. It was an extremely cute, yet simple story. I enjoyed the relationship between Devon and Foster and how it developed over time. Ezra is an interesting character to read about and his and Devon's relationship warmed my heart. However, I wish the author showed Devon's personality more because there weren't a lot of unique traits for her. If you're looking for a quick and simple, yet very cute read, this is it.

Holy guacamole this book was adorable!! I'm just gonna go ahead and say what was a bit disappointing. Like others have said, this book did address a lot of things that weren't given more in depth explanations or solutions. With that said, I don't think that is a total downfall. We'd all like to see every problem come with an answer within a novel. Truthfully, that doesn't always happen. 
 This book takes place in a girl's senor year of high school for goodness sake. I don't know about you but high school was a mess haha. So in my views, unanswered things are a bit of a reality check for me. 
 On to the good, Devon was absolutely relatable as a character! I remember not knowing what to do with my life(then & now) either when adults were badgering me about college and what not! Devon embarks on a self journey on what really matters to her--from the people in her life to discovering herself. This was such an easy and fun read embedded with some serious issues that we tend to ignore. I'm a sucker for a some romance, yet I quite enjoyed the fact that romance wasn't the first priority here. Devon's growing relationship with Foster moved me so much! Emma Mills did a great job on this novel!

Not quite the "Friday Night Lights" meets "Pride and Prejudice" type of novel I was expecting, but still pretty good. A typical high school drama with some interesting features. Devon's struggle to get through her senior year was relatable but not very unique. What was unique was Foster and how his quirkiness and football skills pulled Devon out of her self-isolation. I liked the guys on the football team, especially Jordan and his advice, and I liked that the relationship between Devon and Ezra wasn't perfect but still felt real. Loved that he read Austen for her. 3.5 stars.

mientras toda mi TL de Twitter estaba viendo y comentando El Ministerio del Tiempo, yo he empezado y terminado este libro. todo un merito para mi. 
 le he puesto 4 estrellas porque me ha parecido muy entretenido, pero la calidad literaria igual no llega pa tanto. 
 su principal problema es que intenta luchar contra los estereotipos para acabar cayendo en ellos de nuevo. tienes toda una paleta de personajes secundarios que rompen con ellos, para que luego vaya la protagonista y caiga en el peor de todos, el de pensar que las chicas monas y maquilladas que se interesan por la moda no tienen dos dedos de frente, y encima cuando se da cuenta de que las ha juzgado mal, se para medio segundo a reflexionar sobre su error. 
 por otro lado, me han ENCANTADO los personajes principales, sobre todo Foster y Ezra, especialmente Ezra porque es la cosa mas cuqui del mundo (y me recuerda a otro personaje pero no se a cual). 
 Devon me ha gustado como protagonista y narradora. al principio entendi su indecision y su "no se que hacer con mi vida pero de momento estoy bien asi", y me ha gustado ver como va pasando de "no se lo que quiero" y "me da igual todo" a "eso es lo que quiero y voy a luchar por ello". tambien me han parecido geniales sus reflexiones y paralelismos con las historias de Jane Austen, eso mereceria una relecturas para pillarlas mejor. pero a veces me costaba ver su personalidad. por momentos parecia mas un titere transmitiendo ideas que no eran suyas (de la autora, imagino), que la persona que ella decia ser. 
 me ha ENCANTADO sin embargo como evoluciona su relacion con Foster y como aprende a apreciarlo y a quererlo. y su relacion con Ezra me ha gustado mucho mucho. aunque el tema del enfado entre ellos dos me parecio un poco mal llevado y mal explicado, pero se sobrevive bien. 
 en fin, le falta quiza un poco de profundidad para hacerlo mas memorable, pero es un gran libro para leer en una tarde, me ha dejado con buen sabor de boca, a pesar de que se me ha hecho corto, y yo esas cosas las valoro mucho. 
 muchas gracias a Alhana por regalarmelo para mi cumpleanos.

"When you love something, you can't be happy all the time, can you? Like, that's why you love it. It makes you feel all kinds of things, not just happy. It can hurt, it can make you fucking mad, but... it makes you feel something, you know?" 
 Esto ha sido una monada de libro. Dulce como un banquete de bollos rellenos de crema y pepitas de chocolate. Emma Mills nos presenta una pareja de personajes adorables, con unos miedos e inseguridades con las que puedo sentirme muy identificada. 
 Pero mi mayor problema es que el libro en si peca de superficial. Es imposible que se alcance la profundidad requerida -tanto en personajes y tramas, como en sus resoluciones- en menos de 300 paginas. La autora tenia un elenco de personajes fantastico y original, pero no llega mas que darles dos pinceladas a cada uno.... lo que es una pena porque donde muchos autores al final solo tienen un nombre en el papel con su correspondiente lista de caracteristicas, Emma Mills crea personas en carne y hueso. Pero les faltaba mas espacio, mas desarrollo para que se puedan oir sus voces. 
 Y honestamente, adoro a Austen como la que mas, pero la forma en la que estaba incluida en la novela (aparentemente es un retelling de Orgullo y Prejuicio y Austen es la autora favorita de la protagonista) parecia metido en calzador: no solo no tenia sentido alguno, si no que llegaba a resultar pesado y absurdo.... quizas tambien porque el estilo de la autora, en general, necesitaba pulirse bastante mas (cambios de escena torpes, acciones mal llevadas... me entendeis). 
 Finalmente, es simplemente una lectura comoda y dulce, perfecta para leerla en una tarde -si sois como yo, con una sonrisa bobalicona en los labios y los ojos en forma de corazon- y olvidarla al dia despues. 
 "Close your eyes, real tight, and then count to three hundred. That's all you have to do. You just count to three hundred, and when you open your eyes, five minutes will have passed. And even if it hurts or things are shitty or you don't know what to do, you just made it through five whole minutes. And when it feels like you can't go on, you just close your eyes and do it again. That's all you need. Just five minutes at a time."

Definitely a 4.5 star. 
 This book was just adorable. It's really hard to find a solid Pride and Prejudice retelling, but Mills really takes the cake here--strong, relatable characters torn apart by miscommunication and judgments. I can't pick a favorite character, and I was sad but happy when the book came to a close--sad to have finished so quickly, but happy to see the characters where they ended up. And I don't think there's a better way to leave a book.

reference_books.title: Enchantment (Channie, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I am not sure if Abel wrote this book intentionally funny or not but I thought it was pretty funny. All the awkward moments of first times and love and just being a teenager and everything that comes with the territory fused with magic made 'Enchantment' and incredible read! 
 Channie and Josh go through this whirlwind friendship/relationship even with all the curses he keeps getting knocked on his bum with. Josh, I had to very much admire because even though he kept getting hurt time and time again he kept enduring it to be with Channie. Channie, I understood, had almost no control over these curses that kept escaping her and hitting Josh. 
 I read it less then a day because I was fascinated to see where the story would take me. There was so much adventure that I couldn't put it down (for which I now have the oh so amazing bags under my eyes). Every time I thought I knew where this story was headed, I was wrong and instead I was taken in a complete different path then what I had thought. 
 I did feel as though their relationship was a bit rushed but then again isn't that how pretty much every hormonal ridden teenage relationship goes. Now throw in some magic and a crazy family out to kill Channie and her family and you have 'Enchantment'. 
 Trust me, you want to read this book!! It is an awesome read and you won't be sorry!! 
 -martha :D

book_a.title: Half-Blood (Covenant, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Very annoyed with this book! Yes! I know a whole lot of people love it but nope not me! 
 First off Vampire Academy came out in 2007 whereas Half Blood came out in 2011. There are too many similarities in these two books to not think plagiarism! 
 Here are the similarities: 
 Rose leaves the school with someone 
 Alex leaves the school with someone 
 Rose has Dimitri (who is a legend in the Dhamphir world) stand up for her 
 Alex has Aiden (who is a legend in the Pure blood world) stand up for her 
 Rose has Dimitri training her 
 Alex has Aiden training her 
 Rose has someone she cares about very much turn evil 
 Alex has someone she cares about very much turn evil 
 Rose is a half blood 
 Alex is a half blood 
 Rose has Dimitri find her and bring her back to the school 
 Alex has Aiden find her and bring her back to the school 
 Ok seriously shall I go on and on? Nah I think you get my point. I am Vampire Academy all the way on this one because it came first and Russians trump the Greek gods any day in my book. 
 Alex was a very whiny, annoying, teenager. I mean I know many of us were annoying too as teenagers but Alex was wayyyyyy over the top. The characters are a complete failure because they weren't even as spunky as the VA characters. No originality Ugh I am just disappointed. 
 If you were going to read Half Blood don't bother. Read Vampire Academy instead it's better then the knockoff.

sample_reviews.review_text: I enjoy all of JLA's books, and this would did not disappoint! This wasn't the most original book I've ever read (it started off resembling The Vampire Academy), but it branched off into its own thing and I loved it! I really like the little bit of Greek mythology we get, and the pure and half-blood concept is very intriguing. Aiden is super swoon worthy so that helps ;) I'm super excited to see where this series goes!

I really wanted to like this book, and I did like it, but the reason for the three stars is because I couldn't help but draw comparisons between this and Vampire Academy. It felt as though JLA had just taken the idea/plot of VA and made different characters/villains and implemented them in her own story. 
 Also she added Greek Gods. 
 But those changes aren't enough for me to truly recognise this as a piece of it's own. It's almost a carbon copy of VA. 
 The reason I gave it three stars instead of 1 or 2 is because I did really enjoy the story line, I enjoyed the characters and I enjoyed the story. Like I usually do with anything written by JLA. This one however fell flat due to the similarities between this and VA. 
 I will continue reading this series just to see whether the similarities continue or whether the book lands on its own feet.

2.5 the second book might be better but I'm not sure I'll read it. 
 I liked the prequel a lot but the more and more I read this book the more dissapointed I got. You just can't ignore how damn similar it is to Vampire Academy. 
 Secondly, at times the dialogue was rather painful. Alex was supposed to be so clever and insightful at times (psychoanalyzing Aiden) and was so blind in her judgement of others (Lea, Marcus). She felt inconsistent - one moment aware of the seriousness of the situation - training, dealing with grief, the next -partying, mouthing off and doing her best to fail at her goals, apparently. So I found it hard to emphasize with her. 
 The first half of the book -there is barely any plot. Parties and high school dealings and pseudo deep talk between Alex and her love interest. Then things speed up a little and it becomes more original. But too little too late. 
 You could substitute the Greeks for any other pantheon and it would not be much different. It's just that thinly presented. A shame, as I love mythology and Greek myths in particular are so easy to research too, but here it's just a couple of words here and there, exclamations like 'gods' and that's about it. Very americanized. 
 There were times were I felt some more description was needed. It felt very bare. Alex makes a big deal of wanting to wear a uniform when she meets her step father but it's not at all described other than color. 
 The way Alex obsesses over Lea and vice versa I was half expecting them to have a fling or something. At least that would have been a nice change from the 'vampire academy' feeling of this book.

I really enjoyed this book I thought it was fun, exciting, fast paced and easy to read. 
 The storyline was intriguing and easy to follow. I really liked the characters and world that this book created. This book is also very funny I laughed many times while reading it. 
 This book has the kind of ending I like, an obvious ending/conclusion but it leaves hope and prospect for a sequel (or many.) 
 I can't wait for the next book

As I said on my EYE ON INDIES post, one of the things I love most about this book is the fact that our heroine is utterly unafraid to fight for anything and everything precious to her. This is so rare in YA lit these days, and I'm so sick of damsels in distress that do nothing but wait for their princes to save them. Alex becomes the prince and takes control of her destiny and I had to stop myself from standing up and cheering loudly while reading it. 
 Thanks to the kind folks at Spencer Hill, I've been granted permission to bring you my thoughts on "Half-Blood" a few months early, bless their hearts. Read on if you want to find out more about the world of the Hematoi, and why it's so important to YA lit today. 
 It needs to be said: the blurb is a bit misleading. Yeah, Alex is crushing on Aiden, but that's not all to the story. If anything, that's just a fraction of the story. 
 Alex is one of the few non-dystopian (though whether or not the Hematoi society is dystopian is genuinely arguable) heroines that is active in taking control of her life. Whether this be about protecting her mother and choosing to live her life on the lam because of it, or after, choosing to fight her way back into the Covenant school to become a Sentinel, or having to fight her own desires in order not to fall for Aiden, her pure-blood instructor/friend/love interest so that they both don't get destroyed by the Hematoi higher-ups for their relationship. She actively takes control every second of this story (even in the prequel "Daimon", she's an active heroine) instead of passively waiting to be rescued by Aiden/other Sentinels/her friends from the Covenant academy. 
 So much of YA lit, I've found, especially contemporary-set normal-life YA lit doesn't really encourage girls to take control of their lives, but instead to passively wait until they get rescued. This is one of my hugest pet peeves with YA lit today, and something that I actively seek out not to read when possible. Girls need to take control, period. I used to self-harm because I let society command what I should have been, and I wasn't, not naturally by design. I still am not today, and I still have to fight self-harm urges because of it. But because of heroines like Alex, I have to remind myself that there are worse things than being labeled "too aggressive" - waiting for the prince that never comes, the cavalry that never arrives is far worse, being left in despair is on top of all of those. The only answer, of course, is to take the reins. And the fact that this seems to be (unconsciously) encouraged in so much YA lit is absolutely infuriating. 
 So, if you want a heroine that's a positive role-model in that respect (regardless of her misadventures in naughtiness at the Academy - she is a teenager, after all) and something new in terms of a new look at both the vampire and Greek Myth/Gods-related mythos, I highly suggest you take a look at "Half-Blood". It's definitely a debut not to be missed. 
 (posted to librarything, goodreads, shelfari, and witchoftheatregoing.wordpress.com)

She has no idea why other than that her parents were killed by a Hunter who is also after her. Once she is cleared to return to the pack by her alpha, she slowly starts to realize she is different. She is part magick and Lycan. Not only is she different from everyone else but she is also a part of a prophecy said to change the world. This book is not your typical werewolf story....so much better! Loved it!!

My opinion :

 Lets see, what we have.. 
 1. Lucien the wolf pack's 24 year old alpha
