loved it, kinda annoyed how it ended with caia and luciern. hopefully in the next ones they will be back together!

I'm actually really confused by this. I expected...not this? I guess I felt that the structure of the plot was just...messy. I wanted to read this because I enjoyed Samantha Young's Slumber, and I read the beginning of On Dublin Street and I enjoyed it, so I thought I'd try her Lunarmorte. I've been craving a little werewolf/vampire action lately. And after a terrible run-in with...another series, I'd hoped this would be an interesting diversion. 
 Caia's finally going home, after ten years of living in isolation with her guardian Irini. She's finally able to go back to the Pack Errante, after being in hiding from The Hunter who killed her parents. A moody senior in high school, this obviously is going to be a shocking transition. Is he ready to reassimilate into a Pack she's practically strangers with and meet the new Alpha? 
 There. That's as much summary I'm willing to give. It starts in media res (for those who haven't learned that term in English class, it means "in the middle"). Like I mentioned, Caia's finally going home to her pack. And when she does, she's/the reader's practically bombarded with names and relationships to remember (but honestly I don't remember who's related to who), and these relationships keep getting referred to throughout the story in the most unhelpful way. Literally there cannot be a more vague way to introduce a family tree into a story. 
 That's the biggest tiff I have with the story. And this doesn't include the lack of anything constructive that I'd like. Random things keep springing up, with also some predictable details and some vague details. For example; obviously, because the new alpha is unMated, Caia's practically his wife anyway. But then comes the details about her heritage (because we all knew this was coming, too); she's not only a lykan, but also some sort of hybrid (totally expected). But a hybrid of what? This detail, I feel, is very unclear. Why? Because the alliances of the races to the Midnight and Daylight Covens aren't highlighted as well as they should be. 
 Forgettable, hard-to-recall, and just plain vague details litter this book. Maybe I'm harsh since I recently re-read Sarah J. Maas' kick-ass books. Or maybe it's really that messy. Overall, yes, I definitely regret reading this book.

This was one of those awfully written books, in terms of atrocious grammar, lack of punctuation,the stupid, appalling plot, the pathetic world building, odious, idiotic character development, nauseatingly cheesy one liners and just overall dreadfulness, after finishing which one hates oneself for wasting one's time and life energy, and degenerating one's intelligence over reading it. Needless to say I do NOT recommend this book.

reference_books.title: Scarlet (The Lunar Chronicles, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
This book was entertaining but I was pretty disenfranchised with most of it. By the end of the book I found myself telling the book "Oh my god wrap it up already!" 
 There was just so much fluff! I realize that it's written for grade levels lower than I usually read but I think that is one of the reasons that I was so critical of the parts I didn't like because I hate it when books send those certain messages to young people. 
 NAMELY The "Oh my god it's only been one day and i'm in complete love with you for reasons unexplained." I HATE THAT. I hate it so much because all it does is reinforce these terrribbbllee ideas of what romance and relationships should be like, especially because the character was so abusive in the first place. Yes it's his wolfish nature but oh my god why are we still reinforcing that this behavior is tolerable and something that can be overcome!? 
 Thankfully it didn't also feature a love triangle because i'm pretty sure I would have just been 500% done at that point. 
 The new characters Scarlet, Wolf, and Thorne had as much depth as Iko and she's a robot! I expect it from Iko but so far the only characters i'm actually interested in are Kai, Cinder, and Queen Levana who thank god we saw more about in this book. Really all this book did was serve to interest me in Fairest. 
 Overall the action was fun and the plot was okay but there was just so much going on that was utterly unnecessary, too much fat that should have been cut or written better. 
 I'll finish out the series but I really hope that these characters evolve more because if they don't it's going to be a long ride.

reference_books.title: The Sword of Summer (Magnus Chase and the Gods of Asgard, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Solid meh. 
 It is however a step up from the Red Pyramid which I stopped reading because Riordan couldn't stop pandering to the audience and treating them like they weren't intelligent enough to get the book which was a serious downgrade from his other books. 
 This book still did weird fourth wall breaks where Magnus would make weird self depricating comments that definitely sounded like what an adult thought a kid would say to excuse the "totally lame" aspects of their personality. No Rick. Just stop, 
 Other than that I definitely thought the characters were fun and I found the basic idea to be good. However the book adhered to the quest archetype WAY TOO MUCH. Like okay, we get it. You need to go somewhere to get a thing and then that person who has the thing will need another thing. This book was a series of vaguely connected mini journeys that did nothing more than just introduce the reader to the world. Which I get for middle grade readers is fun, but once again the pandering. You can't just say "oh it's simplistic and choppy and really obvious because it's for younger kids" nope. Not while Garth Nix exists. Not while Harry Potter is a thing. You can write good plots and have meaningful adventures without really choppy mini quests. 
 I do think it's super useful for teaching text book examples of a heroes journey and a quest. I just think it's missing heart and meaning. It's missing the depth and it's missing what usually makes the adventures exciting which are actual stakes. The ultimate goal was so abstract and seemingly out of left field and it never felt urgent. 
 Like I said, it's a step up from Red Pyramid, but it's still not on par with Lightning Thief.

reference_books.title: When the Moon Was Ours
reference_books.review_text:
Magical realism, exploration of identity, LGBTQIA issues, brujaria! This book has got it ALL! 
 First and foremost this book is about self discovery, self acceptance, and the love that we accept from ourselves and I LOVED IT. Sams journey of acceptance and discovery as he realizes who is and the lies he has been telling himself is simply breathtaking. 
 Miel's journey as she slowly faces her greatest fears about who she is, where she's from, and what she's worth to herself and to others hurts to read because it resonates so deeply. 
 I think that this book is a worthwhile read for anyone who has ever felt like they've needed to grow into who they are. Beautiful book!

reference_books.title: Aristotle and Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universe (Aristotle and Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universe, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I appreciated this book for a number of reasons, the primary being the depiction of mexican american teens in El Paso that was authentic, not forced, and allowed them to explore their identities. My fiance often told me about the "pocho" identity crisis you go through as a young boy when you don't feel "Mexican enough" so it was really interesting for me to see this fictionalized. I recommended it to him immediately and I can easily see my students loving this book for the same reason. 
 I also loved it because of the way it explored those really hard parts of growing up. Saenz made it very apparent that at some point they were children and then they weren't anymore without ever spelling it out. I think the shoe game was probably the thing that made that most successful. 
 He beautiful explored boy hood, complicated relationships with friends, partners, and parents. I loved it. 
 I think many kids will see themselves reflected in the pages of this book and i'd recommend it to anyone.

book_a.title: The Forest of Hands and Teeth (The Forest of Hands and Teeth, #1)
book_a.user_review: Meh. I've read another book by Ryan and I knew that I didn't like the main character in that book but I just thought it was that one character. after reading this book I'm starting to think that she doesn't know her main characters are insufferable. That being said I feel like this is a good novel for reluctant readers around 9th grade. I'm an avid 25 year old so my view is skewed. it's fun, the action is consistent, and there is romance! My difficulty came with that there were so many interesting parts that I felt weren't developed as much as they should have been while she spent so. much. time on some seriously boring details, all the while never giving us much from those moments. Example:main character and love interest alone in a house for a good 20 pages. tons of unresolved stuff and plenty to go off of during that time but does any of that happen? nope. Some of it happens during an action sequence and the other stuff just never happens because I think she forgot. it's just not satisfying and the characters are weird. the story line has weird pacing and I wasn't thrilled with it. But I'd definitely still recommend this to a student.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Mary is a teenaged girl living in a small village surrounded by high fences to protect the inhabitants from the Unconsecrated, i.e., zombies. The villagers call the world outside the fence "The Forest of Hands and Teeth." Growing up, Mary's mother told Mary stories about a wider world, with tall buildings and even an ocean, but no one believes these tales except Mary. And when Mary's mother is lost to the Unconsecrated, as had happened to her father, Mary's world becomes even more restricted: 
 "In my village an unmarried woman has three choices. She may live with her family; a man may speak for her, court her through the winter and marry her in the spring ceremonies; or she may join the Sisterhood." 
 Mary's brother Jed blames Mary for their mother's fate, so he refuses to take her in, and thus she is forced to join the Sisterhood. Unexpectedly though, she falls in love. The object of her feelings is already spoken for, however, and then, unexpectedly, a second boy speaks for her. (Females have no say in the matter.) Mary thinks her chances of finding happiness (not to mention the ocean) are gone forever. But things get even worse: the boundaries of the village are breached by the Unconsecrated, and those who can must find a way to escape. 
 Discussion: The author lines up the usual YA Post-Apocalyptic/Dystopia suspects: a rebellious teen girl who narrates in the first person and who exhibits both bravery and idiocy; the inevitable triangle with two boys vying for her affections; an evil female adult who stymies the heroine's attempts at freedom; and a host of bloody, slack-jawed, drooling and moaning Undead to act as the Greek Chorus. 
 Does this one stand out from the rest of them? Not really, in my opinion. Mary, the main character, is a bit too self-centered and idiotic for my taste. The two boys of her triangle are both milquetoasts. World-building information is barebones, with background explanations non-existent. 
 Was there anything to like? Well, I have to say my favorite part is that Mary and her group, running from the zombies, keep encountering Roman numerals, and can't figure out what they mean or how they are ordered. I could so relate! LOLOL 
 Rating: 2/5 Wait: Make that II/V

Man I wanted to like this book. But I honestly don't know much I liked about this story which just makes me sad to say. I couldn't connect to the characters and honestly couldn't stand any of them. Mary goes through alot but most of the time I felt she deserved it or I just didn't feel sorry for her at all. I was interested in the world and still am curious about alot of things but I unfortunately just did not enjoy this story. But who knows maybe you will.

I really wanted to love this book for many reasons. First of all it was my first zombie read,second the cover was amazing and 3rd the synopsis sounded great. I will say the first quarter of the book had me riveted but as I got to know Mary more ans see the love triangle(if you can even all it that) develop it just all fell flat for me. I really started to loathe Mary and her thought process as well. I always try to put myself in every characters shoes and try to understand their thoughts and choices, Mary's lost me and kept me frustrated. It has been a year since I have read this book and since the other 2 are not from Mary's point of view, I might read them at a later date.

Ryan's first novel in the Forest of Hands and Teeth series is gripping. Mary lives in the future when the world has been overrun by zombies, called the Unconsecrated. Her town is the only safe bastion left. Surrounded by a chain-link fence that no one ever goes beyond, her world is small and simple. You marry for commitment and to have children, not love. You listen to the governing body, the religious Sisterhood and never question them. Life within the fence is safe, there hasn't been a breach in years. But Mary's father is missing, assumed to be one of the Unconsecrated now. Mary's story is about love, following dreams, and trying to make it in a world that is dangerous and oftentimes depressing. I can't wait to pick up the second novel.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I like books about zombies. I like that zombies are an enemy you can't negotiate with, win over or sexualize (unless you're into really, really weird stuff) but are still disturbingly human. Zombies are not the problem in this book. In fact, the zombie world Carrie Ryan has created is very interesting to me: the intricately linked yet isolated villages; the Sisterhood and the extent /limits of their influence; and the seemingly human-made fast zombies. The problem is the protagonist, Mary. I don't know if I've ever hated a main character like I hate Mary. I dislike her for two reasons: 1- Everything she does has the same emotional intensity. Everything from her mother dying to Harry grabbing her hand in the river to her choosing to be the one that decapitates Travis has a shrill, one-note panic that just becomes maddening over 300 pages. Every book needs to have an arch in plot and emotion to make the story truly satisfying. "The Forest of Hands and Teeth" has neither, it's just Mary freaking out the whole time. 2- Mary has no gumption. She stumbling into situations blindly, led only by emotion and when things go wrong she curls up and wishes she can rewind time or just gives up and waits for death. Then, she's miraculously saved. . .
Absolute drivel. This book is exactly why YA(fantasy) has such a bad name.
This woman owes a lot to the remake of Dawn of the Dead!

Another post-apocalyptic teen novel, this time with zombies! I just finished this in time for book-group discussion with some high school students. One pointed out that it's like the movie 'The Village' -- with the paths and gates added. The story is an odd mix of zombie horror and choked romance; a curious combination! Not anywhere near as compelling on any level as The Hunger Games or (my favorite of this genre) The Knife of Never Letting Go.

FOREST OF HANDS AND TEETH by Carrie Ryan 
 The story had way too many loose ends that were never resolved. I don't even like thinking about this book because it makes my head ache. Regardless of that, while reading it (ahem, listening) I was completely immersed in the intense story. Carrie Ryan kept me riveted. 
 The most important question I must ask myself: Why was Mary's father on the other side of the barrier? Why were any of them? The way I understood it was that people find their loved ones all zombie-fied on the other side of the barrier on a semi-regular basis. But since this has been a problem for centuries, why would their loved ones be found there, of all places? 
 *confused* 
 If Mary's mother was never bitten, the whole story would have turned out differently. So I guess that's where I'm stuck. Why. . . . 
 (Don't get me started on the other 89403290432 questions I have that are unanswered.) 
 And really--doesn't anyone know what a flame-thrower is? Jeez. Problem solved. The end.

I struggled to understand why she makes the (dumb) choices she does, and there were many many inconsistencies that affected my enjoyment (or not) of this book.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Prequel! Now even more excited for the upcoming sequel. 
 Also, kind of inspired to do a series of Current Books/Current Events blogs... If I do, I'll link Clariel's below.

I'm a huge fan of Garth Nix's Old Kingdom series and have waited - with barely contained anticipation - for a new installment, while I wouldn't say I was disappointed, I also wasn't entirely enamored by this novel. 
 On the plus side - returning to the world of the Old Kingdom was still utterly enthralling and the magic of the writing is undeniable. As always, Garth Nix creates a complex and captivating world - it is dark and dangerous and he sets high stakes for his characters. It is also interesting that this novel is a prequel rather than a sequel, and entering this world in this time made for a fascinating experience given that the other books in the series means that the reader knows how the world will change with time. 
 However, it is the characters that were the reason why I didn't fall in love with this novel as I had expected to. The protagonist is Clariel, and Garth Nix has previously created complicated, vulnerable and likable female protagonists - both Sabriel and Lirael are excellent examples. Clariel was an exception, at least for me. She is not relatable or likable - I found her to be whiny, spoilt and entirely lacking in depth. While some of the supporting characters are much more charming, they are completely blind to Clariel's shortcomings and almost fall over themselves to help her and this somehow made them less relatable by extension. 
 I still think that this novel is a worthwhile read, especially for serious fans of the Old Kingdom series, but for me, it didn't quite live up to the previous books in the series.
That Mogget, such a rascal. Kind of a slow start and I never much came to like Clariel. I'd be interested in seeing more of Bel and Mistress Ader though.

I loved it! 
 I read the original trilogy a few years ago and din't even know this had come out. 
 The pacing was very fast, especially in the second half so that there was something major happening every few minutes. I really liked how Clariel made many mistakes and they had actual consequences. For most stories like this in the end the main character is shown as the amazing supreme hero despite their mistakes, but at the end of this book Clariel is definitely no hero and almost more of a villain. 
 I also like how determined she is. When she was locked in a hole she actually climbed up the wall instead of waiting around to be rescued. I also don't mind how much she talks about the forest because she isn't just crying and angsting about it, but actively making plans to try to get there and when outside obligation calls her away from the forest she may regret it, but she follows her obligations. 
 I do wish the book had been a little longer, but it was good the way it was.
The best thing about this book was Mogget. He pretty much stole the show when he appeared. Lol.

I loved being back in the Old Kingdom. However, I was sad about the ending. I can not wait for the next book to come out in October. I am probably going to marathon the rest of the series before I get the next one.

I read Sabriel as a teen and it quickly became - and remains - one of my favorite fantasy novels of all time. I love the setting; the magic system; the characters of Sabriel, Mogget and Touchstone; the exciting story - everything just worked so well. Then I read the sequels...and I was disappointed, over and over again. And honestly - Clariel is the most disappointing of the lot. Why? 
 Awkward writing. It's like Nix suddenly thought "tell don't show" was the new rule of writing. There are so many exposition dumps, especially at the beginning. Nix doesn't build his world and characters through action, dialogue or actual scenes - but just by telling you what to think. It's terribly clunky and graceless. 
 An unlikeable main character. Clariel is like Katsa if she had absolutely all her unique, interesting personality features surgically removed. She is a caricature of the emotionally distant, pointlessly violent "strong female character". Sabriel was intellectual, martially trained and a bit socially awkward - and it totally made sense, based on her upbringing. And she was a very likeable POV. If I met Clariel in real life I would throw her off a bridge. 
 I'm just going to pretend that Sabriel is a standalone novel, and I recommend you do as well, dear reader. More is not always better.

Much like the Legend of Korra, this long-awaited sequel follows the ostensibly dramatic and exciting adventure of an uncharismatic and constantly whining main character in a setting that is nostalgic until you realize its rather whiny as well. Wonder how a setting can be whiny? Supporting characters fade into the background, until you look around and wonder "is this inn haunted by a complaining ghost or what?". 
 The story somehow fails to convey the sense of urgency and humor that characterized the previous installments of the series, and is only kept alive (alive being a rather generous description, think more semi-vegetative and on life-support) by cameos by characters from the other stories (I'm looking at you Mogget). Nix makes an effort to do so, but doesn't manage to reconcile the Old Kingdom in its prime (well, not prime but much better than the crumbling wreck it was in the original trilogy) with the story itself. 
 Oh yeah, and the book was far too short. I mean, it's like 300 pages, but nothing ACTUALLY HAPPENED. 
 I know I'm older now, but I reread the goddamn series a couple lonths ago and it felt a lot better than this so its not childhood nostalgia.

It took me over a month to read this book. That almost never happens, especially for YA books. This book just didn't hold my interest until I hit chapter 18. And then I was interested, for about four more chapters and the. I was just interested in finishing. 
 Okay, so I loved the Abhorsen trilogy. But, I also read it a long, long time ago. In fairness to this story, perhaps I should have re-read them prior to reading Clariel because, well, I couldn't remember who the heck she was supposed to become. Obviously a bad guy. Obviously a necromancer. But...hm....just can't remember and that took out some of the pleasure away from reading an origin story. I fully recognized that this is my experience, and not the fault of the author. (However, what if someone was just picking up this book and not starting with the trilogy? I think showing the descent into evil would have been much stronger.)

I liked the first three books in the series well enough but in comparison Clariel is just mediocre. 
 Hopefully the next book will be better.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I was disappointed that this book did not end with the two deciding that they were "better off friends" - JUST friends. I knew they would probably get together because of they way they didn't act like brother and sister, the way a boy and girl who were best friends probably would. I want a book that has a guy and a girl as FRIENDS and they STAY that way and be AWESOME.

It was a good book, but I thought the characters were so annoying sometimes. If they just talked to each other and said what they wanted to say the book could have been 100% less annoying. Plus, I felt that the ending was way to abrupt. I felt like we could have used one more chapter so everything would've ended perfectly.

(3.5 stars) 
 Can girls and boys ever be just friends?... is a question I've struggled with for years myself. It's a fact of life that we're wired differently. Things change when we grow up. That's what best friends Levi and Macallan (yes, like the whiskey) have to contend with, when Levi moves to Macallan's Wisconsin hometown in the seventh grade. 
 I've read all of Eulberg's books by now, and I have to confess I love her style of narration. The things her characters go through feel realistic. They make me think about being a tween/teenager again. 
 Take a Bow 
 remains one of my favourite YA contemps, while 
 Revenge of the Girl with the Great Personality 
 (which I got a signed copy of, mwahaha) was a great insight into the beauty pageant scene. Better off Friends looks at how a girl and a boy who are best friends slowly realise how they're, well, made for each other. 
 I can certainly relate to that. I have a fair number of close guy friends. I hung out with them a lot in primary school, being taller than most girls and having to sit/stand with boys instead. Just a few years ago, one of them confessed to thinking I was "hot" and asked if I wanted to make out with him. Cue Lou's horrified expression. XD 
 I guess the point is, Levi and Macallan are both really different people brought together as almost-teenagers by a British TV show, who eventually realise, after a lot of trial and error, that they may not be better off friends. It's not a new twist. But it spoke volumes to me. Screw insta-love or love at first sight or falling in lust with the smell of her hair. This was exactly the kind of relationship development I wanted in a YA - something that reflects real life. 
 Aaand also now I want some fried cheese curds, damn it!!! 
 (Two problems I have with the book: 
 1. The constant back-and-forth between Levi and Macallan gets old after some time. In their defence, misunderstanding and miscommunication play big parts, which I'm all too familiar with, especially at the 14-16 year-old stage. 
 2. The span of the timeline throughout. For a relatively short book it jumps quickly from one time period to the next. It didn't bother me much, but it might for other readers.) 
 If you've been looking for a light read, perhaps this is the one for you! And I won't pass up the chance to recommend Eulberg's other novels. :)

OUNNNN 
 This book was so Sweet!!! 
 I just wanna hug this couple! 
 I'm a emotional diabetic so I don't really like to much sweetness... I get a terrible case of boriness when I start tasting sugar in my heart... So I give only two stars.. 
 But I would totally recommend this book for a 13 year old...
The protagonists start off as seventh graders, and the story goes into their high school years. The book was written from both perspectives. It made some good points about friendship and family.

"This entire time I've been thinking about where my home was. At first it was California, then Wisconsin. But in truth, home isn't necessarily where you sleep at night. It's where you feel like yourself. Where you're most comfortable. Where you don't have to pretend, where you can just be you.I had finally reached that place because Macallan is home to me." 
 Vaya libro mas adorablee!, que te deja con una sonrisa en la boca todo el tiempo que te engancha desde la primera pagina y eso que yo ultimamente no conseguia engancharme a ninguno asi es tan ligero sencillo fresco amor todo lo que diga es poco para lo que me ha gustado, vemos la historia de Macallan y Levi que se hacen mejores amigos desde los 11 anos y vamos viendo como son sus vidas hasta la adolescencia toda esa etapa con sus momentos buenos y sus momentos malos el no decirse las cosas y bueno algo que me ha gustado mucho que en cada capitulo vemos na pequena conversacion de los protas comentando lo que nos cuentan en cada capitulo y te hace enamorarte mas de ellos 
 Por favor Elizabeth espero que hagas una novelilla o algo y nos cuentes de sus vidas y tiene tantas quotes que me han gustado aunque la de principio de la review la que mas 
 "On a scale from one to ten, how much of a pain was I after my injury?And please be honest. 
 Do you think I would hold back on you? 
 Unfortunately, no. 
 On a scale from one to ten? Thirteen. 
 Fair enough. 
 Now I have a question for you. On a scale from one to ten, how annoyed were you that I was going to the dance with someone else? 
 Infinity." 
 "So, as I was saying, guys and girls can be friends.' 
 'Best friends.' 
 'And what is better than falling in love with your best friend?' 
 'Nothing.' 
 'You always have to get the last word in, don't you?' 
 'You know it.' 
 'Yes, I do.' 
 'Yep.' 
 'Oh, Macallan...' 
 'Yes, Levi?' 
 'I love you.' 
 'I love you, too.' 
 'And there you are again, having to get the last word in.' 
 'But I don't think you mind.' 
 'Not at all.' 
 'Good."

Conoci a la autora en la FIL 2015 de Guadalajara, cuando asisti a su presentacion, lo hice porque queria conocer a la presentadora ( a la booktuber clau reads books), no tenia el mas minimo interes en la autora o su trabajo, pero a medida que los asistentes le preguntaban sobre este libro, decidi que queria leerlo. El libro me parecio muy bueno, los primeros capitulos que es cuando los personajes son muy jovenes (11 anos) se me hicieron muy infantiles pero es comprensible, sin embargo a medida que la situacion se tornaba "mas oscura" el libro me tuvo enganchado. 
 me gusto mucho la forma en que se retrata el punto de vista tanto de Maccallan, como de Levi y el realismo con el que la relacion esta construida y la quimica que se siente entres todos los personajes. 
 No le doy 5 porque senti momentos que la historia se quedaba corta, pero la lectura ha sido bastante buena.

I honestly don't know how to begin this review. Everything I wrote and then deleted sounded super awkward, so I'll just get straight to the point: YOU NEED THIS BOOK IN YOUR LIFE. Seriously guys, you have to own, or at least read Better Off Friends. I guarantee you - Better Off Friends will constantly tug on your heartstrings, maybe make you tear up a little (it certainly made me tear up a bit), and have you happily smiling at the very end, wanting more, and then proceed to reread your favorite parts all over again. I regret not reading this one sooner. (And could you believe that I was planning on not even giving this book a chance since I've never heard of it before? Very foolish decision.) 
 Read the full review of Better Off Friends on Effortlessly Reading.

This book was fantastic! 
 Better off friends is an AMAZING book!!! This is a really hot topic lately. Can girls and guys be just friends? I think yes however this book is the one where the answer is no. This book tells the beautiful tale of two best friends, Macallan and Levi, and how they try and ignore their feelings for each other. They share everything together, do everything together but they are just friends. Right? ... 
 For more review go to: http://crackthespine.weebly.com/revie... 
 Recommended Age: 
 13

I was looking for a cute contemporary book. I almost got it. I'm a sucker stories of best friends falling in love, but this book was okay. It was good and kept me entertain, a little predictable, but I wanted more cuteness haha. I wanted a book like the ones of Perkins (lola and the boy next door). Maybe someday i will find more books like that.

Suzy lives a quiet, well structured life and when her car breaks down she finds her life turning into a tailspin she is not sure she wants to control. Joey goes by the name City he isn't looking for a relationship but when he meets Suzy he knows he has to have a taste, or two, or three. Neither were looking for each other but they seem to have found it, now if they can only accept it. 
 Fantastic read, I liked that Suzy and City are opposites of one another. Suzy struggles with the fact that City is not her ideal "perfect persona" of a man she should be with, he is erratic and it frightens her. I thought his idea of a date was delightful and that he has a way of letting his special memories with Suzy distract him during the day. Can't wait to read more.

Motorcycle riding, tattooing hot alpha men that can make the woman melt into a pile of goo quick while making her feel safe and loved? Yup, that is this book. It was an enjoyable read that followed a predictable formula for me. I enjoyed the characters for the most part. Suzy at times annoyed me, as did the name. I don't know why. I just couldn't wrap my head around it as her name. 
 I liked City, I liked the way they met and several aspects of the story. This game me a taste of what I needed, a light read with great steam and low on emotion. I will consider moving on and reading more in the series as it looks to focus on the brothers of the tattoo shop. 
 For 0.99 not a bad read, not a great read, but still hit the spot.This review was originally posted on Back Off My Books

Mainly enjoyable. Daft but fun. I am, however, plagued by the knowledge that I've really at least four thousand books with identical storylines. 
 Also, 1) Derek. Just no. Why does this trope keep showing up? 2) Kaylee. Again, no. Didn't add anything. Just stupid. 3) the word Whore. My best friend would smack me if I called her that. It's not okay, it's not funny, it's not a term of endearment.

A great start to this series. I love the Gallo family and how close they are and I can't ever get enough of a tattooed man on a Harley that treats cherishes his mother. *swoon* 
 I'm not sure why I've waited so long to meet the Gallos, but I'm kicking myself for it. I just adore Ma Gallo. She's a loving mother with a firm hand. All her grown children revert back to kids when she's around and it's absolutely adorable. 
 Joseph Gallo aka City has enjoyed bachelor life. Riding his bike and inking his customers and Inked he's content with life. Having loved and lost, he's not looking to go down that road again but when he meets prim and proper school teacher, Suzy McCarthy, everything changes. 
 These two share an instant and undeniable attraction from the moment they meet. Since Suzy is nothing like the women he's dated in the past, he's quite taken with her no cussing and ladylike manner. She's a lady it only makes her more desirable in his eyes. He can tell that deep down there is a dirty girl aching to be set free but he has to work hard to get the chance to chisel his way in and work his magic. 
 Suzy is somewhat a control freak. She has a path and a literal checklist for the man she plans to spend her life with...City doesn't meet any of those requirements so she's not too keen to continue things with him. Thank good for his tenacity because he proves that not everything is black and white and a man in a suit can be just as much of a jerk as a man on a bike can be just as much a gentlemen. 
 I loved that City never gave up on her and eventually got to see that Suzy wasn't as prim and proper and she was on the outside. Things got quite hot and heavy with them. He pushed her passed her comfort zone and they both got to reap those rewards. 
 FAVORITE QUOTES: 
 She was the girl next door, the untouched bookworm that every guy wanted to conquer. I wanted to make her dirty. I wanted to make her scream filthy words while I fucked her. I wanted to corrupt this girl in the worse possible way. She would be a challenge and maybe I'd found someone worthy of my time. 
 "You think too much. Stop making a list of why you shouldn't be here. Feel the reasons you should," he said. 
 "Sometimes life doesn't give us what we're looking for, but it gives us what is supposed to be. We just have to be willing to take the plunge. Live a little. Take a risk for once." 
 "No more talking, my mouth has other things to do that are more important." 
 Oh, hell. I knew trouble when I saw it and it was standing right in front of me. City would be the death of me, but hell, at least I could say it was fun while it lasted. 
 Love would come someday if he didn't f*ck me to death first. Death by d*ck. Didn't sound half bad. 
 I didn't want to be Suzy Q, the goody two shoes anymore. I wanted to be a woman that could let her hair down and be who I wanted instead of what everyone expected.

I just couldn't get into this book. I found Suzy incredibly annoying and City was just all over the place. The drama was too manufactured, and the relationship was not believable to me at all. I doubt I'll go any further into this series. Very disappointing.

I love Chelle Bliss, every book I have read I could not put them down. I was so stoked to read this book. I fell for the hot and sexy City. Then there is Suzy from Untangle me, I loved her then and love her now. you wouldn't think that they would work but they do. I love them together and when they are together getting down, damn it was sexy. They do work together and I love how they are together and you wouldn't think City had some sweet side but he does. absolutely amazing book I can't wait for book 2.

Sweet, passionate, sexy love story of finding love in someone unexpected. Chelle Bliss teaches the reader that making a list and what makes sense on paper does not fool what the heart desires. It often chooses the opposite. 
 Fall in love with Suzy and City and get caught up in their passion for each other.
What can I say, I love hot tatted alpha men with a soft heart, & City is definitely that!!! Loved him!! Can't wait to read more in the series. Would love a tatt by him!
oh my freakin gosh this was one hot story i loved every second it took to read it it never lost my interest i cant wait to read book 2 Chelle Bliss you are an awesome author cant wait to read more

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 Skin Trade is enough of a step in the right direction that I'm sorely tempted to give it a higher rating than it actually deserves. There's a plot! With murders! And investigating! And I turned out to be right about Marmee Noir's plans for Anita. And the two explicit sex scenes are better-written and less icky than what I've come to expect from Hamilton. And she's being copy-edited again, so there are only a few typos. I get the sense, reading Skin Trade, that Hamilton is trying to blend the mystery/horror style of the early Anita Blake books with the erotic style of the later installments. The results are mixed, but I have to admit that Skin Trade is her best in years. 
 That said, I can't say I truly enjoyed it, hence the 2-star rating. Skin Trade has its moments, and I'm quite happy that the plot never gets lost and is never far from Anita's mind, no matter what else is going on. However, there are a lot of problems. 
 First, there's the macho posturing. Especially in the first half of Skin Trade, Anita seems hell-bent on bickering with every male character she meets and trying to prove she's tougher than they are. The female characters don't even seem to rate that kind of treatment. Anita pretty much never gets along with any woman, ever. In one scene, she decides that a female cop is "one of those women who seem to hate other women." The woman hasn't even opened her mouth yet; how would Anita know this? Projection much? Anyway, all this bickering and posturing wouldn't be so bad if it didn't take up such a vast amount of page space. I wanted to shout at the characters to just go solve the crime already. 
 Second, I think Hamilton is trying to push the envelope further in terms of sex, and the results are sometimes pretty disgusting. Anita is far too friendly to creepy serial-killer Olaf (thank goodness she doesn't sleep with him) and does end up sleeping with a 16-year-old (thank goodness it's not "onscreen," and thank goodness she's disturbed when she realizes what she's done). 
 Third, we know that Anita is the most super-special person to ever walk the face of the planet. We get it. She doesn't need more powers, or more men, or to turn out to be one of the very last carriers of blue tiger lycanthropy (Blue tigers? What the...), but all of these occur. 
 Finally, several promising plotlines end anticlimactically. I hope that, in the most egregious case of anticlimax syndrome, the "end" is not as final as it seems. 
 There was one bit that really struck me as clever, though: 
 "Why?" I asked. "Everyone knows what a pain in Jean-Claude's a** I am. Why do you want to deal with that?" I couldn't call for help in any way, or someone else died. I couldn't go all lycanthrope, because it wouldn't help me. What could I do? What the f**k could I do without a gun? 
 He laughed again, but this time it was lower, more attractive, more seductive. "The power, Anita. You are the first necromancer in centuries, and with so many other powers." 
 Vittorio is answering Anita's spoken question, but in a way he's also answering her unspoken question. Indeed, Anita does end up being forced to enter Skin Trade's final confrontation without firearms, so that her powers are the only weapon she has. (That said, she has so many powers at this point, and it's been ages since she actually shot anyone, so she's probably more formidable metaphysically than physically.) 
 All of my grumbles aside, I really do think Skin Trade is a good start, if Hamilton intends to move the series back toward a focus on plot.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I don't usually write reviews with spoilers - and this doesn't have major ones, but I've clicked the box just to be safe ;) 
 Let me say, I enjoy reading Ms. Hamilton's books. She can create some wonderful characters. The problem is that there are just too many. The lady desperately needs a good editor. I miss Damien and Jason. I really miss Jean-Claude. I also like Requiem, but he at least made an appearance here. It's as though the early characters just can't hold her interest any more, so Anita has to have more men... 
 For this installment, Anita travels to Las Vegas. Alone. Now, given all that's happened in the series, Anita travels *alone* out of state?!? I was looking forward to some good bad-guy-hunting, so maybe there's some redemption in the story. Maybe moving the overall arc forward. 
 Well, Anita seems to have gained a new power. She can freakin' stop time. Her "day" in Vegas is over 370 pages long. And it's the usual rambling interspersed with marshall-stuff (Edward, Bernardo and Olaf have joined Anita in Vegas. Yeah for Edward and Bernardo. Olaf...no thanks) and a host of new law enforcement characters (thankfully they all stay clothed). I've been to Vegas. I know the city layout. They traverse the city and cram a *whole* bunch into those daylight hours. 
 I will say this isn't the non-stop orgy that the last few books have been. Anita stays clothed (well, other than injuries) until the last quarter of the book. Then she's her usual screaming self. 
 Overall, it was ok. It did end up moving the overall story arc forward a click or two (again, in the last pages) and they did get the bad guy. But, I really would be thrilled if Ms. Hamilton returned to her original characters and allowed Anita to "limit the menu" as she keeps whining about.

3.5 Stars 
 I'm pretty much going to restate what I said about the first three Kitty Norville books -- they're light, entertaining fluff. I wouldn't have read this far into the series if I didn't enjoy the story or feel some suspense and attachment to the characters. However, it's simply a quick, fun read for a rainy day, nothing spectacular. Although a few aspects are rather cliche, the premise and plot contain twists of originality that set it apart from other series of its kind, which seem like a dime a dozen nowadays. All in all, I recommend it for pure, escapist pleasure, but don't expect to be blown away.

3.5 stars 
 When I choose a book to read, I have several series that are my "go-to" books. They aren't fantastic literature but when I am in the mood for entertainment, I really don't care. The Kitty books are perfect for this. It's a series that I can just sit back and enjoy. 
 In Kitty and the Silver Bullet, Kitty and Ben return to Denver for a few reasons, but mostly because Kitty's mom has been diagnosed with cancer and must undergo treatment. Kitty is still "officially" banned from Denver by Carl and the Denver pack, so she and Ben must "sneak" in. 
 Kitty endures several events in this book that further develop her character. She continues to realize the implications of being a werewolf. She can't have children, not that she even thought of being a mother, but because the decision had been taken away from her because of her lycanthropy. Kitty worries about the security of her family and the health of her mother. She even offers to "infect" her mother to "cure" her from the cancer. 
 Kitty's freedom of movement is affected by Carl and Meg. I did find it odd that while Kitty did sneak into Denver, she went about her business in the open, going as far as to air her radio program in Denver and Carl did not react. Carl and Meg's abusive hold on the Denver pack is a sore point for Kitty and Kitty decides to make a stand. Kitty even agrees to work with the local police detective. 
 The vampire politics and deceptions in this book were incredible. The posturing for position and authority created some interesting, if not bloody, situations. 
 Kitty's radio show was still the highlight for me. I loved her interview with Mercedes Cook, who chose to "come out" as a vampire on the air. 
 Throughout the book Kitty questions her relationship with Ben. Their relationship is strained at times and Kitty wonders if they would be together. This book marks a turning point in this relationship. 
 All in all, another solid book in the series. I'll keep reading these books. They are a fun read.

This whiny protagonist needs to grow a backbone. I am over her wimpy approach and attitude. She has to get saved repeatedly and spends the entire book whimpering. And the relationship between her and Ben is completely unbelievable. The author has not managed to convince me of any chemistry between the two of them at all.
Second time I'm reading this and still as good as the first time.
While this book is enjoyable, it raises concerns for where the future of the series will go.

This review has also been posted on my Happy Indulgence blog. Check it out for more reviews! 
 After vacationing and working on The Midnight Hour out of town, Kitty finally returns home in this installment, finally able to face what she has left behind. Carl and Meg are alerted to her presence and partner with age-old vampire Arturo to expel her out of town, but Kitty's backed by a police and opposing vampire Rick. 
 Caught between some territorial wars between vampires and werewolves, and facing a very personal battle against Carl and Meg, how does Kitty fare in Kitty and the Silver Bullet? 
 As always, the world of Kitty Norville is a refreshing and light read. Kitty's always enjoyable to read about because she's just so real, even though she's a werewolf. She's got a life and family to care about, and with the new addition of her co-alpha Ben, she's got a lot to live for. 
 That's why she stands up to Carl and Meg, her previous pack leaders where she was the most submissive in the pack. For those who cringed seeing Kitty being used and abused in the first book, you'll get your vengeance here. 
 This book was much more action packed than the previous ones, and there are a LOT of characters that you'll come across here. I found it a little more difficult to follow than previous installments, but still enjoyed it a lot. Kitty really grows and stands tall in this book and it's refreshing to see such a turn around since the last time she was here.

The summary of this novel made me immensely interested and I looked very much forward to read it. It took me a while to find time but I am glad to have now finally read it. 
 I've seen a lot of negative criticism, particularly regarding the characters but I would actually like to give praise to Kim Edwards for creating such complex characters. The novel has a very complicated plot and with even more difficult characters. Because of this, I can imagine that for many it would be hard to empathize and sympathize all of their actions and feelings. For example, how easy is it exactly to empathize Dr Henry's life-changing decision of giving his sick daughter away in the beginning? Truth to be told, I was myself shocked at how someone, particularly such a loving doctor, could do so but as the story continued, we got a deeper insight into Dr Henry's personality and more importantly, his past. 
 All the other characters were somehow the same yet different - they had their huge flaws and strengths, their emotions and thoughts and they were after all humans who had to undergo certain trauma of loss and neglect. One character that particularly touched me was Dr Henry's son, Paul, and the conflict he had with his father. Although I could not empathize, I could indeed sympathize and I think that this could be common for many of the readers to one or more characters. 
 Other than the characters, I also really enjoyed Edwards' style. It wasn't the most exquisite and creative form that I had encountered but it was simple, easy to follow and nice. Sometimes it was confusing to keep track of the ages of the characters, despite the year given. 
 However, one of the reasons why I gave this a four star and not five was because of the angst and dark mood of this novel. Indeed, there were light scenes. The love scenes were beautiful and the imagery was although not incredible descriptive, it was still good. However, there was always a brooding and sad tone. Sometimes it was not even sad but blank and neutral in a negative sense. I also wasn't too fond of the ending but that's because I like to leave a book, happy and satisfied. The ending was well but very bitter-sweet and I wish that one of the things that happened in the end did not happen. I'm not going to be explicit though because I don't want this review to contain spoilers. 
 So overall, I enjoyed this book a great deal. I wouldn't recommend it for everyone as it is a rather dark and complex but if you like complicated characters with a controversial plot, then sure, why not. Give it a go.

 It's hard for me to describe how I felt about this book. Astonishing. Astounding. Amazing. Awesome. (Does anybody notice a pattern here?) 
 This is a book about secrets. It's about loss, and the grief you deal with when it happens to you. But what I came away with after reading it was this: it is also a book about love, of lovers, of family, of friends, of strangers. The impression it left on me was one of love, hope and forgiveness, which, when you consider the plot, probably makes a whole lot more sense. 
 It's also a study of contrasts - we see how one man falls because of a choice he made, while one woman rises because of the choice she made. Everything changes for David Henry and for Caroline Gill on the night that Norah Henry gives birth to twins. The book traces the effects of the David's decision to give up his daughter Phoebe, who was born with Down's Syndrome, and Caroline's decision to keep her. We see how there's growth and pain, how there's a space that could never be filled, or a love unexpectedly found. 
 This, however, I would say, is probably one of the more difficult books I've read. There's a lot of lengthy passages, and I had to stop a lot to absorb what was happening and make sense of it in the context of what had already happened. I honestly felt like I was slogging through it, but, at the same time, I felt like the struggle was worth it. 
 Kim Edwards paints a lovely, descriptive story for the reader - and it's one that deserves to be read.

This book was definitely not one of those "fairytale" books. In fact, the events that occurred were extremely believable. One man, in the heat of a moment, and in a desperate attempt to save his wife from pain and misery, tells a lie. It isn't a small lie. In fact, it's the largest lie he would ever tell. And then, for years, this lie eats at him and destroys his life and tears away the happiness he had wished for his wife and his son. The lie, ultimately, destroys their family. It should have been the happiest day of his life, the day he delivered twins...his own twins. But, something is wrong with his baby girl so he makes a brash decision to send the baby girl away. It's the right thing to do, he decides. If he were to keep her, it would only be difficult for his wife and he and to fall in love with her and watch her die a slow death. So, he sends her away with his long-trusted nurse to a home. But, when Caroline gets to the home, she cannot go through with it. The home is too horrible. So, she leaves town with the baby girl, Phoebe. Phoebe grows up, raised by Caroline, while her brother is raised with her natural father and mother. It's only expected that one day, somewhere, somehow, the two would meet again.

 I loved Harriet and I loved both of her parents too. I'm proud to be a bit of a geek myself (although I am definitely not at Harriet's level - I'm good at random facts and interested in strange things but not like she is!) and I could see a lot of myself when I was younger in her. To start with her crazy Dad was where it was at for me and Annabel her stepmum was the clueless one who was boring. But then her true colours came to light as the book progressed and I came to love her too, probably more than Harriet's dad. 
 I could relate a lot with Harriet's desire to change herself and become something she's not. Even now at 31 I have times when I feel like I'm not good enough and need to be more. Thankfully I've gotten to the point where that doesn't happen often any more and I've learnt that if others don't like me that's their problem not mine.. For a while in the book I was beginning to think I'd come away disappointed with the message in the book but it proved me wrong and although Harriet's true to life journey is painful at times alls well that ends well as they said. 
 This is one of those books I feel like I can't recommend highly enough. If I was to describe my thoughts as I finished the book in just three words it would be these three: "I Want More." And luckily for me rumour has it Holly Smale is already at work on the sequel.

 An Open Letter To Geek Girl, 
 You made me laugh. Roll on the floor, wipe tears from my eyes laughter. I haven't read a book as sweet and funny and snarky as you in ages and I am happy that I've found you. There is nothing better than your average girl being thrust into something she doesn't understand and you delivered so well on that front! Thanks for all the laughs.

 I for one am so glad that this UK book finally got published in the US! I'm also really glad that it's part of a trilogy and I almost never say that about contemporary novels. Smale has delivered a debut that will make you laugh your face off. 
 The plot is pretty simple. Geeky girl accidentally gets scouted at a fashion field trip for school and becomes an overnight success as a model. Thing is, she never wanted it. In fact it's her best friend who loves fashion. It's quite enjoyable to watch Harriet as she navigates the world of fashion. She's out of her depth and it's so much fun to watch her try to make sense of her life as it's changes right in front of her. She goes from a gangly red-head to a trending model and it's a grand adventure. Harriet's quirks make her character for me and I'm so glad that Smale has given her almost too much character. Sometimes that's not a bad thing and Harriet proves that. 
 On top of this being a novel about Harriet coming into her own, it really focuses on family and friendships. Harriet's family is an interesting mess, but they all love each other and it was nice to see that they were featured so prominently in a novel where they could have just been in the background. 
 It also looks at friendships when you're a bit of an outcast. I love books that have protagonists like this and Harriet really does her thing, as do all of her friends. I must mention that there is also a bit of budding romance that I just adored. Lion Boy is darling and I can't wait to see what happens between them in the next installment. Add in the fact that the fashion industry that Smale gives us is full of satire and you really can't go wrong.

Ok, so maybe the plot wasn't the most realistic but I loved the humour! I can't wait to tackle the other books in the series.
Did enjoy as much I as I wished, but nonetheless I loved author humour and book was okay. I think if I would be 15 years old or younger, then probably I would enjoy it even more.

This is probably a very subjective review - my little sister ADORED this book - but I personally had to give up on it halfway through. The voice ruined it for me - the main character, Harriet, was so annoying I just couldn't put up with her for more than 50 or so pages. 
 Plus, I love comedy books and a bit of slapstick, but this one just went so over the top that I couldn't even suspend my disbelief and get through it. Particularly the scene at the Clothes Show Live, with the stalls falling over. I mean, *really*? 
 I do think that the author will do well though, in future books where the main character ISN'T Harriet Manners, because she is a good writer. 
 And the love interest, Lion Boy/Nick, was pretty dreamy, so kudos for that.
Overall, a funny, interesting book, but I there were certain things that just bugged me and made this book slightly less enjoyable.

This review first appeared at http://www.adventureswithwords.com 
 There's been so much buzz about Geek Girl that I was really looking forward to grabbing a copy - Harper Collins sent me a fab badge and pair of 'geek' glasses but not an ARC, so I eagerly headed into the kids' section of my local Waterstones on the day of release, and there it was, in all its papery glory. This is a variation of the coming-of-age, My Fair Lady type story, but updated for the 21st Century, and aimed at readers of 11+. I can testify that it's hitting its target audience as I've already seen more than one 11-year-old girl getting stuck into a copy. 
 Reading this after Oblivion by Anthony Horowitz was quite a jump, and after reading the first few (nice short) chapters, I had a bit of a break before coming back to it with my reading head in the right place. Once I picked it up again, I couldn't put it down. This is such a funny, sweet but also very perceptive journey through the horrors of teenage-hood, some bits seeming horrifyingly familiar from my own time at school. 
 To say that Harriet has a hard time fitting in at school is putting it mildly. At one point, she describes herself as like a polar bear in the rain forest, which also explains what draws Toby, another ultra-geek, towards her like a magnet. Polar bears have to stick together. But the thing is, Harriet doesn't want to be a polar bear, as cool as they are. She wants to be a monkey, or a parrot, or maybe even a bird of paradise, because that way she'd fit in with the other wildlife in the jungle that is secondary school. 
 I'm sure that all teenagers find it hard feeling like they really do fit in, for all sorts of ridiculous reasons. Too short; too tall; too fat; too thin... But being a 'geek', or in other words, being really curious about the world and possessing an excellent memory, but not overly concerned with your outer appearance, can be particularly hard, I think, because other teens don't realise that the geek isn't showing off, or trying to look clever. The looks you get after correcting the headmaster's pronunciation of 'diplodocus' in assembly... Well, it doesn't bear thinking about. 
 I don't think I was quite as badly off in these stakes as Harriet, though; by 15, I'd discovered make-up and fashion and even leg-shaving. But I knew exactly where Geek Girl was coming from. I'm not sure I wouldn't still sign that contract to be whisked away to some faux-glamourous photo shoot if I could! I loved going on the journey with such a funny narrator, too - Harriet is brilliant company; I really enjoyed all her funny sayings, and the descriptions of the other characters from her point of view. Wilbur, from the modelling agency, is particularly hilarious, incredibly over-the-top but very affectionate. 
 I was glad to see that there will be a follow-up to Geek Girl starring Harriet again in her reluctant adventures in the fashion industry. I'm looking forward to seeing how it all turns out.

 Blech. Boring story; only the thinnest sliver of plot; puerile writing; a heroine who is a weak and stupid damsel-in-distress cookie-cutter character; completely unmotivated characters. Vampires do not sparkle. Hate it
I just can't believe that this series is anywhere close to a list of best books of all time. It's insulting really.

Vampires that sparkle? What about exploding into flame in sunlight? And if you can live forever, why the hell would you choose to be in high school, which most of us hated? I rate this book a huge yawn.

God, this book. It was /horrible/ to read. I literally spent three fucking months reading this. And it wasn't even worth it.

I was so keen to read this..but found it an enormous let down. Kind of clever, but in a self-conscious and showy off kind of way. I don't know what to say about this book. I know a lot of people really were blown away by it, but I really could have done without the diary parts written by Amy. In fact, after the first three or four, I skipped them completely and didn't think it detracted from the book at all. 
 If I ever go batshit crazy someday, though, I only hope I could do it as well as Amy Dunne.

This was an interesting psychological thriller, more psychological than thriller. Nick and Amy are a typical American couple; in their late 30s, married, celebrating their 5th wedding anniversary, recently lost their jobs to the recession, and moving away from their adult home and closer to Nick's childhood home to care for his aging parents. It would seem they are average in every way. But when Amy disappears, the cops begin digging below the surface, and each piece that is revealed paints a different picture of their marriage. 
 Gillian Flynn has created a unique story, with characters that are incredibly different and... psychotic. I recommend this book for anyone who likes a good character study.
Liked it. Had some memorable quotes throughout. Interested in the film version and how they are going to change the ending

I was a little disappointed. The plot was cleverly written. I was certainly gripped at the beginning, but then my opinion just changed. I didn't think that Go's character was authentic, she seemed slightly forced and I sometimes found the same to be true of other characters. 
 The book was great at building up towards the later chapters, but it was predictable. Towards the end however, as I was waiting for the predictable twist - it didn't happen. What I was left with was unsatisfying and seemed unnatural. I understood why the characters made their decision toward to end but that didn't mean that I believed it. For all that I'd learnt from the characters - it didn't seem a likely ending. 
 Yes this book was gripping and the plot was clever, I kept reading right until the end - but it was more out of frustration.

This book was brilliantly written. It probably deserves a 5 star review. But it won't get one. Why? Because fuck Amy. And Gillian... well you're on my list with George R.R. Martin, Nicholas Sparks, and Karin Slaughter for robbing me of my happy endings. Hell I'll just take a satisfying ending. So one star is all you get from me.

Great twist in the middle - and the twists keep coming! Once you get through the first half, it's a thrill ride! 
 My one criticism is that the author seemed to only have one voice for her characters, she sounded like a woman trying to see things from a man's point of view. Overall great read though!

Sometimes there are times where I wish I could quit a book half way through, and not finish the rest. However, when you're already half way through the book you want to finish reading it and see what the ending is like. With Gone Girl, I wish I quit the book for good. I am going to try and write up this review because I haven't read a book in a long time where it just makes me so mad. 
 Gone Girl is a story of Nick Dunne whose wife goes missing on their 5th wedding anniversary. It was a who did it type of novel, and what made it different is that you saw the events from his point of view and you were able to read journal entries from Amy's point of view leading up to her disappearance. 
 The first half of this book was great. It kept me on my toes, and I want to read more. I wanted to find out what was going to happen to Nick. Will Amy ever be found? Nick became their first suspect. I can see where people were finding this sexist, but in a way it was like all other major crime stories. It goes to the person you think is the most accountable. Nick had holes in his story from the start, and he was hiding things from the police. It's no wonder they suspected him. I first started rolling my eyes when the affair was announced. How predictable. Then, once we found out that Amy's personality was just crazy is when I really started getting mad. I don't know why it just infuriated me. This also goes with Nick. He was starting to get on my wrong side. 
 The book continues on. You find out about Amy's past, and how she has framed people before. Nick tries to use it against her. The only sum what redeemable thing was Tanner and his wife. The rest just I can't even. 
 I stopped reading the book fully at about 88% left in the book where the rest of it I just scanned. I couldn't handle it any more. The sad thing was I have read more enjoyable young adult fiction books then this book. The ending made me even madder. You sit there and want to frame your wife, your wife uses you for a pregnancy so you are trapped, and yet you stay with her?! Worst ending in a novel since Jacob and Bella's baby became soul mates in Twilight. I apologize now for those that I recommended this book originally too in the beginning. The first half was great, but ugh.

For the last two years or so, whenever I'm in a group of people discussing books, someone asks me if I have read Gone Girl. Now I have read it. The End. 
 Seriously though, I am trying to write book reviews so I will think more critically about what I read, and write something other than legal analysis for the myriad cases that cross my desk. So here it is. 
 Gone Girl reads like watching a thriller whodunnit movie, or a particularly messed up episode of 48 hours. The thing is, if I wanted to see a film or watch a true crime show, I would do that. I read novels because I love the poetry of the written word. The character development that films usually only approximate. The description or turn of phrase that makes me say "yes, exactly." I did not learn anything from this book and the writing, while fine, was nothing that gave me pause. As a side note, I probably would not watch this movie. Except maybe, MAYBE, if it starred Matt Damon. 
 I suppose this book is trying to make the reader consider how, in this age of Nancy Grace and 24-hour CNN coverage, media and public opinion hijacks and blurs the legal process in high profile criminal cases. If any readers did not already know this, then I applaud the effort. That said, the storyline in this novel is so improbable, I doubt even the sharpest law enforcement officers would crack the case. This, of course is the point: the goal is to keep the reader guessing, and guessing wrong. 
 Some aspects of this book I found disturbingly misogynistic. To suggest (and this may be a spoiler) that a female character elaborately staged a sexual assault to frame the alleged perp is distasteful to me. I'm not saying it does not happen, but given the reality of date and partner rape and the hurdles in proving it, why toss a bone to the many, many perpetrators who argue consent? This is not to say Ms. Flynn presents such conduct as representative of women, far from it. In my view, including this was unnecessary, and disappointing. 
 Finally, I found the two main characters of this book to be completely unlikable and unsympathetic. I guess we're taking the old adage that beauty is only skin deep to the nth degree, but I need a little more than that to get excited about a book. The moral of the story is that when people ask me if I have read X hot best seller, I should confess that I'm kind of a snob about my novels, and change the subject to the latest reports on Kimye. 
 PS: if you like this kind of thriller, check out Ron Rash's Serena. Similar black widowy theme, better writing, and a NC writer to boot.
