reference_books.title: The Dark Divine (The Dark Divine, #1)
reference_books.review_text: There wasn't anything spectacular about this one but I tend to like most books from this genre.

reference_books.title: All of You (Between Breaths, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Meh. It was okay. Same ol' theme with the new adult genre. Abused characters that find one another. It was good for the long flight to Italy. Not for conservative readers.

book_a.title: The Big Over Easy (Nursery Crime, #1)
book_a.user_review: I got a lot of good laughs out of this one. So bizarre and quirky but funny. Fforde is such a creative author.

sample_reviews.review_text: A very unique and talented approach to fiction! My rating would be higher, I'm sure, if I were more used to reading works of fantasy. It's just so hard for me to get into something that's not real. However, I loved the nursery rhyme approach and the subtle (and sometimes not-so-subtle) references to various rhymes. I'll definitely never be able to recite Humpty Dumpty the same way again.

In the tradition of Thursday Next, fiction and reality meet in the middle of this book where Nursery Rhyme characters clash with the 'real' world characters. Detective Spratt is charged with solving the murder of womanizing, alcoholic, ex-con Humpty van Dumpty. Many people had a reason to want him dead, but which one actually killed him? Follow Jack Spratt and Mary Mary as they go into the world of Detective Guild politics, anthropomorphic animals, and Nursery Crime. 
 A fun and witty romp full of colorful and quirky characters. I loved playing find the nursery rhyme. There were so many you could start a drinking game. It was hilarious and full of crazy twists and turns, especially toward the end. A book nerd will really appreciate the different kinds of literary references. Even a mom might appreciate some of the references since she might have seen them more recently than I have (Solomon Grundy, Rapunzel, and three bags of wool anyone). Now I don't want to give too much away but Jack is not immune to the world of the nursery rhyme.
This series wasn't as much fun as Thursday Next.

The Big Over Easy is the first in Jasper Fforde's Nursery Crime series. DI Jack Spratt and his Official Sidekick Mary Mary investigate the suspicious "fall" of Humpty Dumpty. Fun for mystery fans and anyone familiar with nursery rhymes.

This was really cute! I always enjoy Jasper Fforde's creative storytelling, and The Big Over Easy is no exception, as Detective Jack Spratt of the Nursery Crime Division investigates the tragic demise of one Mr. Humpty Dumpty. Fans of classic detective stories - Sherlock Holmes, Miss Marple, etc. - will find plenty to chuckle about in this mystery romp.
Very entertaining. Hilarious and serious. Had me on edge for all through the book.

This book was OK. It was cute at first, since all the characters have nursery rhyme names, but then it got really boring. Then, the author seemed to cram all the excitment into the last 10 pages or so. If only the middle of the book was half that interesting. It took me a while to read because I kept getting so bored, I'd fall asleep on BART. Definetely not one to buy, maybe rent from the library if you have no other idea what to get.

I like the Nursery Crime concept, but the plot stalled at times. The story could have been shorter, not enough plot twists. I read The Fourth Bear, for some reason, and enjoyed it more. Nonetheless, he does with this series what he did with the Thursday Next series: create a unique twist on fairy tales.
Maybe it's the British writing which can be a bit dry but this wasn't as fun as I thought it would be.
Pointless, silly fun. Not brilliant, but makes me smile. That is worth 3 stars at least!

book_b.title: The Will (Magdalene, #1)
book_b.user_review: My husband moved before us so I was in the mood for a good love story. Looking through books on my to-read list, this one stood out with its pretty cover, high ratings and approval from a few goodreads friends. I forgot that I had attempted one of this author's books before. Man oh man, I wish I had not forgotten that experience. I could have saved myself the money I wasted on this one. I can see why some would like it, but the characters and writing style were not my cup of tea AT ALL. They were annoying and trashy and I found myself cringing over and over until I finally gave up. I did give it two stars because I cared enough to skip to the end to see how it all wrapped up.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Yikes, I looked at my friend reviews, and all that read gave very high ratings, and I'm like crap what's wrong with me? 
 I didn't like it, like at all. 
 It seemed every male talked the same. If there were that many alpha males in the world, I would probably be single because well.... 
 It wasn't just that, the heroine, while quirky, it was OTT, and that rich coming from me, because about as socially awkward as they come. 
 I swear she was from the 1800's. I was bored. 
 So since this is very popular among all of my friends, this seems to be one of those times, that it's not you its me.
KA at her best. Can't wait for the next in this series.
Such a loooooonnngggg dramatic book. Like how many problems can one person have? how many people can fall in love? and for more than 20 years? I love KA book's, but this one was not for me.

A radio station in my country has successfully matched up several couples in their 'two strangers and a wedding' on air marriages. This is a lengthy process behind the scenes involving both family and friends of the two people involved to make sure the right match is made before they meet at the altar. 
 This story is kind of like that. Josie's late Grandmother Liddy pretty much betrothed her to Jake and his children in her will. She knew that Jake would be the perfect man for her, with the added bonus of his lovely children. She also knew that Josie would be a wonderful partner to Jake. A loyal and loving woman, something that has been missing from his life for a long time. 
 Sometimes the people that love you the most know you better than you know yourself. 
 Josie's life changes when she moves into Lavender House and begins spending time with Jake and his family. She has been working in a completely opposite world, living a fabulous lifestyle that is nothing like living in Magdelene. The longer she is there, the more entrenched she becomes and her desire to return to her old life is weakening. 
 There is definitely something growing between Josie & Jake and it is really sweet. I just loved the way Josie interacted with the children and how her influence completely enriches their lives. I love who she becomes when she is with them all, they are also changing her. 
 This is a life changing journey for Josie and Jake. I have to say that he is now my favourite KA male lead character :-)

Well, one of the quickest DNFs I've ever had. I absolutely loved the premise of this book, and the fact that the H and h are older, but I couldn't make it past chapter three. The author is prone to meandering, run-on sentences. In addition to the poor sentence structure, the book was riddled with errors. Here's a sample sentence: "I also didn't think much of the fact that the man, nor his kids, approached me to tell me they were sorry for my loss." This sentence should say "...NEITHER the man, nor his kids..." The sentence has a completely different meaning sans that one word. The errors were so numerous, and of such breadth and depth, that it seemed as if NO copy editing or proofreading had been done. I can't speak to the book's structural editing, since I only read a few chapters, but I have my doubts about that, too. Hard to believe a big five publisher didn't do better by one of their bestselling authors...

When I noticed THE WILL recommended on twitter I was intrigued by the premise and bought the book. I was surprised, EUR3,49 for a 600+ page novel was cheap in my opinion. 
 When I started reading I was instantly drawn into the world of Josephine and Jake. I loved the small town setting and the 'everyone knows everybody attitude'. What I also noticed was the elaborate descriptions, especially about clothes, make-up and looks. It dragged the story for me and while it was an aspect of Kristen Ashley's writing it created a push-pull effect. She pulled me in with personable characters but she pushed me away with descriptive writing which slowed down the story considerably. 
 Jake is my kind of male; honest, gruff and rough around the edges, sexy and a family man. Josephine is uptight with the vocabulary to match but also with a generous and warm heart. Her past delivered some internal conflict while there was also some external conflict, enough to keep the story going. 
 Jake and Josephine together, that was where THE WILL delivered for me. I loved their chemistry, their banter and the day-to-day conversations. Their romance was a slow-burn but when their romance reached inferno temperatures it singed the pages! 
 Conner, Amber and Ethan give the adult romance a different kind of flavor I enjoyed. Humor, day-to-day stuff, teenage drama, I liked it all. Problems arised and were solved a little too easy for me. 
 Even though THE WILL didn't knock me off my feet, I was still warmed by the story. Like I was slowly sipping on a warm cup of chocolate; each character made me feel home in Magdelene and the romance was felt in all the right places of my heart. 
 I definitely want to return to Magdelene and its inhabitants. 
 3.5 stars

I'm a long time reader of Kristen Ashley's books. For me she has a wide ranging appeal because she writes characters who are funny, flawed, and sexy. Since her heroine Josie speaks in first person you definitely see all those traits up front and center. Ms. Ashley is also a girl's girl who knows every girl needs friends and a fabulous outfit. Her male protagonists usually put the A in alpha. In this story Jake does that but you also feel for this guy on a different level because of his vulnerability to Josie. I was a little worried about the pace starting out on this book because it is LONG. Not that I mind long books, that's what e readers are for in my opinion. It moved along at a nice clip though and even surged in a way I didn't expect near the end which was exciting. The story itself was a solid one and intriguing from the beginning, which also made it a good read. I liked a lot of scenes in this book but my questionable favorite was actually between Josie and her boss Henry near the redbox in the garden. For many reasons that blew me away. I suspect anyone reading would feel the same. My only complaint and it's a minor one, was that I felt Josie's affected speech patterns were occasionally overdone. I'm still giving this one 5 stars though cause it's a great beginning to a new series.
Loved this book x

I enjoyed this. You had a clueless heroine, but her naivety was believable and an alpha hero who didn't go alpha-hole. I liked both characters individually and together and enjoyed the cast of secondary characters.

Kristen Ashley makes kickass stories that make you swoon and give you toothache from. And sometimes I complain about her books. But most of the time, I love them. And I truly enjoy reading them. Like this book for example. 
 KA just knows how to give readers a hero who's so alpha it's almost ridiculous but also one with a big heart, a soft spot for certain things, and an unbelievable way with words. So what it these heroes already sound like each other? If lots of men talked like them in real life, oh well, there'd be more women swooning. 
 I enjoyed this book because the usual KA formula works perfectly with the characters and their development. I love all the quirky things and details that complimented the story. I enjoyed the secondary characters as well. It's no wonder why KA is such a successful author. She knows what women like.

reference_books.title: The Lost Continent: Travels in Small Town America
reference_books.review_text: I just couldn't get into Spartina & this book jumped off the shelf ... So far - it's great fun. This book became slightly less amusing as I continued reading. There were few towns along the way that Mr. Bryson didn't bash & he made it seem as though he really needed to get back to Europe. This book was a good break from the heavier things that I'd been reading, but I didn't love it.

reference_books.title: Water for Elephants
reference_books.review_text: Loved it!!!! This is a book that had a bunch of characters that were easy to dislike. I think that I really did love learning about the circus train. It isn't part of my own history & I enjoyed peeking in.

reference_books.title: Suite Française
reference_books.review_text: I finally finished this book on vacation while curled up on the couch on the Outer Banks. I had purchased a copy for my daughter's father-in-law & he said it was "ok". I know that he has very high standards & the book had come highly recommended, so I bought a copy of my own to read. At home the book moved slowly as I would only read at night after long, tiring days. On vacation the story line moved right along. I found this book to be well-written. I had some trouble keeping the characters straight, but I think it was due to my own mental state when I had too much on my mind when I decided to read. This book is not light-hearted, but it's worth taking the time to follow the twists & turns.

reference_books.title: Ape House
reference_books.review_text: It may come from having a son that was fascinated by primates from the time he was very small (& still visits zoos as an adult) but I enjoyed this book & even its quirkier characters (strippers in a dingy hotel??) I picked it up as I have a hold on Sara Gruen's newest book & thought I'd read this one while I was waiting. It didn't disappoint & if Koko the Gorilla means something to you I think that this book may be worth reading.

reference_books.title: The Memory Keeper's Daughter
reference_books.review_text: This is one of those books that stays with you. I read it over a weekend, but thought about it for the next month. This author does a great job with setting... You really feel as though you're standing nearby while the story is being told.

book_a.title: The Friday Night Knitting Club (Friday Night Knitting Club, #1)
book_a.user_review: I expected a bit more from this book as it's been on the Booksense bestseller list for quite awhile. The book did give wonderful insight into NYC life & neighborhoods & mentioned one of my favorite places to eat (Ellen's Stardust Diner). A good choice for a summer read, but have the kleenex handy near the end.

sample_reviews.review_text: This was a good book. Had a little bit of strong language. I was completely taken off guard by the ending...I'm not sure if I can read the second, still mourning and not ready to move on with the lives of the characters.

What a horrendously boring book. This was unexpectedly the only other book that I'd rank alongside Twilight. Like Twilight, I actually just skimmed through the entire second half of the book and couldn't wait to finish it just because it dragged on and on, I just wanted to go straight to the end. 
 It had so much promise in the beginning. I'm a sucker for stories of different women from varied walks of life, backgrounds and ages coming together and traversing the journey of life. I like exploring the depth of each character and looking at them from the lenses of a reader vicariously experiencing someone else's life for a few hours. 
 But the characters in this book were at best, mediocre and lackluster. 
 WARNING: SPOILERS AHEAD 
 The main character Georgia, I found to be quite annoying. While I appreciate her struggles from the point-of-view of a woman, I disliked the ambiguity of her character. I couldn't understand if she was strong or weak, a whiner or a warrior. She spent the better part of the book whining about being abandoned by a man who cheated on her, who walked out on their daughter too. He attempted contact, tried to make amends, to no avail. And after that build-up about her refusal to take him back, all it took to get her to relent was a night in Scotland. I know fiction often mirrors real life, but this is just preposterous. 
 The frustration I felt at her character led me not even feeling a smidgen of emotion at her death. And don't even get me started about the manner of her death, and how abruptly it was introduced in the story. Nothing about the whole book even led to this plot possibility. While I appreciate unexpected endings, this one just came from left field. Her death did not add any value to the story's end. I got even more frustrated that she died without really having any form of resolution or at least a version of a happy ever after. 
 The secondary characters Anita, Cat, Lucie, KC and Darwin were merely women who were lost struggling to find their place in the world. However, I felt that the tension that brought them to where they are today were feeble attempts at even creating some sort of tension. In my mind, they just seemed weak and tentative. 
 The only characters I actually responded well to were James and Dakota -- and yet, when THEY could finally have their "ever after", their Georgia died. 
 It was quite a disappointing book - character-wise and plot-wise. I wish I could say that there's a redeeming quality in the book, but even the writing style and story build-up was disappointing. It was slow, went too much into the nitty-gritty details of the mundane everyday. Maybe my unfamiliarity with knitting was a contributory factor, but I've somehow managed to enjoy books before that also had parallelisms to things foreign to me -- even something as technical as coal mining. 
 All in all, I guess this is the last of Kate Jacobs that I'll ever read.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I wish there were half stars...this seems it should be more than 3, but for various reasons, not quite a 4. The description on the cover was "Steel Magnolias set in NYC." This intrigued me, but I was having a hard time understanding that until about 3/4 of the way through the book. The storyline, overall, was a fantastic one, but this book should have been longer (I NEVER say that). There were a couple of peripheral characters that could have been flushed out more and the whole (SPOILER ALERT) cancer/dying thing happened in what? 3 chapters? I guess what it comes down to...I read this at the pool, could hardly put it down, but finished it thinking "Great idea, could have had better execution." Afterward, I read that this was her first novel, in which case, I still think an editor should have said "Do more with these ladies...spend more time on the dying thing," but I commend the author for a first time out. I will be curious to see if a second novel learns from the first.
Although this was entertaining, I found it to be very predictable. I tended to like the ancillary characters better than the leads.
I just couldn't get into it...
Light travel reading. I was definitely drawn into the story.
Formulaic, couldn't relate to the characters.

I wanted to like it, I really did but I just couldn't finish this book. I thought it would be something I would like since I enjoy knitting and books about women who have a "sisterhood" type relationship but I just didn't like any of the characters enough to keep reading.

post-read: so, now i'm finished. this book was basically chick-lit. i felt the story wasn't too shabby, but writing style/tone made me feel like i was reading a high schooler's creative writing assignment. SO prosaic and cliche. in another author's hands, it could have been much better. the ending, as jeni said, was surprising, and i think the author used it to separate it from its chick-lit sistren, but it didn't work. it did make me tear up a LITTLE, and i was entertained, and the characters were likeable, but all this wasn't enough to pull it into a 3 star rating. i put it a little higher than the shopaholic books sophie kinsella and a little lower than jennifer weiner books jennifer weiner. 
 i got this for a dollar at borders. it's not like i was super pumped to read it, friends giving it only a medium rating. i'm really just too tired at home to read anything too taxing. i think it's related to how much brain power i use at work. i'm still pretty busy and doing big, new projects, so my ability to read novels that do more than skim the surface is lacking. but the pendulum will swing the other way soon, i'm sure.

I gave this book two stars because I have actually read cheesy chick-lit that was even worse than this, but not for a long time, so I had forgotten what a tortuous experience it could be. At about page 200, I had just had it and can only describe the rest of the read as an exercise in self discipline as I pushed through it a few pages at each sitting. Imagine the cheesiest Lifetime movie ever made then drag it out from two hours to four hours, and you would have something akin to this novel. The story was so very soap opera. I know, there are a lot of people who like histrionic melodrama, but I'm not one of them. Of course, in keeping with soap opera cheesy, the author tried to end with a tearjerker by killing off a character; too bad she didn't nuke the entire cardboard crew about midway through the book and spared us the remaining hours of hokey. Then there was the weird stuff like the dress with a mandarin collar that showed the buyer's collar bones, then there was the "petite" grandmother who grew to 5'5" to be as tall as her granddaughter within the next two paragraphs...and don't get me started on the eye-rolling implausibilities. All things considered, I wished I'd have spent the time knitting.

book_b.title: Olive Kitteridge
book_b.user_review: I kept telling myself this was supposed to be a great book & I didn't like it. It felt very scattered & if it were any longer I would have quit after the first 50 pages. Maybe it was just bad timing ...

sample_reviews.review_text:
first and foremost, i would like to congratulate myself for finishing this. for what i thought would take no more than two days to get through; it took about a week. A WEEK! i read the same paragraphs over and over, thinking that perhaps i was missing something. something elegant, ruminating, and unforgettable that the pulitzer board saw, which clearly i couldn't. but no, i wasn't missing anything (except for maybe hours of my life). ooh, i feel like old ladies will see this and hate me ... but i don't care! this book was borrring and lackluster; a snoozefest. 
 there was such an initial appeal to these stories; set in coastal maine (how i looove it there) and an irrational, old miser of a lady to connect them all. i was sorely mistaken. this time, my soft spot for an old crank didn't beat, nor did it beat for anyone else around her. oh, and not only were these stories boring, but painfully depressing as well. how can anyone under the age of 50 read this w/o feeling dejected of their future?? if this book is representative of what truly happens with the ravages of age, maybe we're better off dying quickly and young. then again, i'd like to think that by a ripe, old, stinky age, i'd have lived a meaningful and sensational life, unlike olive kitteridge. so far, i feel i've already had. so there, take that elizabeth strout, just you try and break me...

I put this on my "read" shelf without finishing it, really. I read all but the last two stories, which I just skimmed. Oh my goodness, this was so boring I could barely focus. I don't particularly enjoy this kind of writing style, where everything is hazy and gray and is told as if you're looking at the story through a dirty window. I can see how a lot of people would enjoy this book because it's so raw and gritty and gives a deep view of each character and slowly exposes pieces of Olive, the main character, until you know every part of her. But I? I just don't care! Nothing happens in this whole entire novel. Or rather, lots of things happen, but they are not the focus. The focus are the thoughts and feelings of the characters which are so abstract and always so melancholy that it made a story that would otherwise be interesting, something matter-of-fact and boring that I didn't care to even know. I guess I would compare this book to looking at a still lake while sitting on a peaceful dock all alone. Some people could find that peaceful and contemplative and beautiful and ruminative, while I'd find that boring and uneventful and tedious to the point of tears. I gave this book every chance, I really did try, but ultimately I did not enjoy it at all.

I'm going to have to reread this lovely book. I started a few weeks ago and then had to return it to the library. Then I had to go to the bookstore and actually buy. I enjoyed it but I felt like I didn't really READ it as carefully as I should. Will return to edit this review. But I do have to say, Olive Kitteridge is my mother if she was white old biddy from Maine (which she is not).

Through the angry and unpleasant personality of Olive Kittridge and the juxtaposition of the beauty of the natural world and the follies and sorrows of human beings we are meant to understand the amazing gift of life. The book is written in 13 stories, some from Olive Kittridge's viewpoint and some from other people in the town where Olive lives. In the reader's guide the author says, "I chose this form primarily because I envisioned the power of Olive's character as best told in an episodic manner. I thought the reader might need a little break from her at times, as well." As a reader I think this is very true. I needed a break from Olive, if this book had been straight Olive I would have liked it a lot less. 
 Winners of the Pulitzer Prize are often depressing, with signficance that is supposed to be uplifting, and this one is no exception.

I feel like I have to have kids or not be in my twenties to get the full effect of this. I got about as much out of this as I get out of watching Louis CK. Being old sucks, no one's marriage is happy, everyone cheats, your kids will be failures and/or colossal disappointments, time moves too fast, my heart will go on. 
 However, the story "Tulips" was outstanding, mainly because the character of Louise, an insane shut-in with a murderous son, was awesomely creepy. You can pretty much predict most of the small town blues after the first few stories, but "Tulips" was like the origin story of a Batman villain. Awesome. 
 All in all, the prose was above average, but painfully predictable, and I just couldn't relate to anyone enough to ever get into it. Olive's character was not very likable either. And this wasn't a novel at all, despite the half hearted effort to make it one. 
 What I'm saying is, you should read Winesburg, Ohio instead.

This books reads like mini short stories with a common thread running through each of them. The thread? Olive Kitteridge. The author deftly unveils Olive as though one is unpeeling an onion; slowly, methodically, and subtly. 
 Thoroughly enjoyed reading this book.

I love the concept of taking an aged matriarch and funneling the rifts and eddies of time through her relatively-static perception. The story Security along with the ending were particularly heartwarming and well-written. However, I do think that it fails to come together with a stronger thematic link than simply the character of Olive herself.

My invite to the Elizabeth Strout party got lost in the mail. I have heard about her books for years, but wasn't sure they would be my cup of tea. And the first story here, Pharmacy, didn't do much to change my mind about that. It wasn't until the third or fourth one that I got hooked. 
 It seems to me that these stories were belatedly linked instead of it being planned out from the beginning. That doesn't affect the quality of them or the way they link together, it just means that certain characters are more interesting than others, and I wanted to spend more time with some of them versus others. 
 Strout's characters and her portrayals of them remind me a lot of Kent Haruf, who chronicled small town life on the eastern plains of Colorado. He might be a good recommendation if you want more writing in the same vein.
didn't like the language in this book and found the life stories to be sad. Not a fun or light read.

Written in the style of Alice Munro, this book is a collection of short stories with one character who is common in all of them. In some stories, she is central and in other only peripheral. Well written and expressive. Heart-warming and heart-breaking. A good read that is easy to put down and pick back up again. Recommend.

reference_books.title: Mockingjay (The Hunger Games, #3)
reference_books.review_text: A great end to the series. I really wondered where it would go next...but I'm very satisified with this book and it's ended. It echoed a movie I once saw with Donald Sutherland and Ralph Fiennes called "The Land of the Blind." I'm glad that Katniss's character remained true and she was able to work out some feelings, mature, grow and survive.

reference_books.title: Wink Poppy Midnight
reference_books.review_text: It's been a loooooong time since I've read a book within 24 hours, but this one delivered. It's pretty much like reading a modern fairy tale starring three high school aged teenagers.

reference_books.title: Nevermore (Nevermore, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Great book! I am so impressed with Kelly's first book. You rock girl! 
 This nearly 600 page book is a breeze to read, you literally fly though the pages. I was up in the middle of the night two evenings reading this...a very appropriate read in the wee hours. 
 I love that Isobel is a strong character, that her brother's a twerp and her mom likes Varen. And Pinfeathers and the other goblins? Very spooky (reminiscent of the Shinigani in Death Note or straight outta Harry Potter - - but totally unique and original).

reference_books.title: The Ruins of Gorlan (Ranger's Apprentice, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This story took me 3 months to read aloud to Eli at bedtime. Geesh! I know this is a series and all, with most likely dozens of books yet to be penned...but it seemed to lack a good editor. Short phrases were repeated within paragraphs, which really annoyed me. And I'm not really sure the novel could decide who was the main character, as it fluctuated between Will and Horace (but of course the series title makes you think Will...as does the last quarter of the book.) The two female characters Alyss and Jenny were thrown in for color, but they had a lot more potential to make the story richer. Yet, they were completely absent from the middle half of the book. 
 Boys will like this series; and the idea of Rangers is absolutely wonderful. I just thought the author needed a bit longer to work out the details and make the story flow more strongly. 
 And why is it that all male protagonists in teens and kids books seemed to be named Will these days?

book_a.title: The People of Sparks (Book of Ember, #2)
book_a.user_review:
Well, this has taken me two months to read to my sons at bedtime, as we found some other more exciting things to read this summer. 
 The People of Sparks is the story of what happens to the people from Ember in the author's first book of the series. It was mostly about relationships and getting along with another group of people. It touched on the ease that people decide to go to war and some options for peaceful prevention of war. A bit teach-y for an adult to read, but useful for a child to read/hear. 
 There is a third book to this series, which is evidently a prequel examining how the disaster happened, but I don't think we'll read it.

sample_reviews.review_text:
The first half of this book was just plain annoying. Our heroes have made their way out of the cave and are learning about all the wonders of the outside world, but it feels like a learning-to-read book aimed at kindergarteners. "What is that marvelous thing that flies through the air?" they'll ask the people they meet, and learn it's a bird. "What is that huge tall plant?" and learn it's a tree. There has to be a better way to tell that part of the story which captures the awe and learning without being so pedantic. 
 After a while, the book picked up steam, though. I liked the roamers, and (even though it was heavy-handed) the main conflict had a good moral. I'll keep reading at least the next book.

The People of Sparks is a follow up to City of Ember, which I really enjoyed. The City of Ember is now above ground and new adventures begin. I had a difficult time getting into the book and the events were not all that exciting. My enthusiasm for the character definitly died down. I felt the adult characters in the book were shallow. The ending was decent, but it took too long to build up to that point. Based on this book, I will not be reading the Prophet of Yonwood (book 3).

I get that this series is a YA series, but I feel like it was written for first graders. I like the story line, but not the way the author writes. But I have to finish the series now. Also, it bothers me a bit the the morals are so painfully obvious.

I'm just going to mark this one abandoned because I took it back to the library and have no real desire to pick it up again. It just doesn't have that same draw as The City of Ember and I don't feel compelled to finish it.

I haven't typically written book reviews on this site before (although I plan to change that in the future) but I have to say that I was disappointed with this book. The premise and first half of the story was intriguing...but the way the second half was carried out was way too PC for my taste (borderline preachy). A more in-depth review to come....
Great book! Read it in one day.
Great sequel in that it was the right amount of same and different from the last book. I am recommending it like crazy to the kids at my library!
I liked reading this book, and it's a great sequel to the city of ember.
good kid book, nice anti-war message

book_b.title: Death Comes to Pemberley
book_b.user_review:
Well, for a mystery...it's not bad; but for an Austen tribute novel, eh?? How can the author set the book at Pemberly, use characters from "Pride and Prejudice" and NOT have a strong female main character? I don't understand it; there wasn't even a central character in the whole novel. 
 The author writes well, no doubt about it; but what did Elizabeth and Jane really feel during this novel? Who knows they were in the background somewhere taking care of their children. 
 While I love that the male characters of Darcy, Wickham and Colonel Fitzwilliam all get more of an depth look into their characters...I'm still not sure who the story was about. 
 9/14/14 update; just heard this is a PBS BBC miniseries that is actually better than the book. I'll give it a chance and report back.

sample_reviews.review_text: Very disappointing !
I found it to be too slow. I guess it wasn't for me.

I will be honest. I watched the miniseries before reading this. So, going into this, I knew what was going to happen and who did it and yadda yadda yadda. 
 However, this is my second attempt at reading it. First time, I got it from the library with good intentions to read it. I opened it, took a glance at the language, and set it aside. I really wanted to do the same thing this time, but now that I saw the show, I really needed to read the book. 
 The show was excellent! It had character depth for all of them, showing the issues with the marriages and then just in general. God, the character depth. It was gorgeous. Then, there was the mystery. It was completely brilliant and well woven. It ticked all my boxes for things I want in a period murder mystery. 
 This book was nothing like it. 
 Characters felt terribly off. There was barely any depth, and when it was attempted, it was incredibly awkward. The plot was plodding, even though I knew what was going to happen. Too many side stories. I know, she was trying to keep period accurate. But that, for me, killed it. She could have had tangents and side stories, but I just do not care about a letter that Lady Catherine wrote or Elizabeth's relationship with her old friend Charlotte or Mr. Collins or whatever. I don't care. It's not relevant to the plot or mystery in any way. 
 I'd say, skip the book. Watch the miniseries.
This was okay. What I really recommend is watching the BBC miniseries of this book. That was excellent. This just felt a bit flat.

I saw the series/movie of this and enjoyed it. And thought that the book had hope. I have been struggling to read through the 75 pages I got to and finally decided I could do it anymore. The story drags and drags and makes it frustrating to want to concentrate on it.
Not great... Not awful... Just silly
Tedious and ridiculous.

Holy cow! Someone actually managed to suck all the charm and wit out of Pride and Prejudice and leave behind a dry, plodding chore that I had to force myself to read. 
 To begin with, James assumes that the reader isn't even remotely familiar with P & P and spends several pages recapping the entire book. THE ENTIRE BOOK. Even parts that aren't relevant to the current story. Because if there's one thing James loves, apparently, it's back story. There's back story for everything, including peripheral characters that only appear in a couple of scenes. The result of this is that the present story is constantly being put on hold to reveal more irrelevant back story, and ends up moving along in fits and starts and never really advancing at all. 
 The details surrounding the murder itself are repeated again and again and again. At the inquest. At the trial. By Darcy. By the colonel. Over and over. The same boring details as if we didn't get them the first time around. 
 But my biggest complaint - the biggest crime in this flop of a mystery - is what James has done to Darcy. My dear Mr. Darcy has been turned into a flat, dull, uninteresting shadow of his swoon-worthy self. There's no spark between him and Elizabeth. There's not much spark anywhere in this book until the epilogue, when the characters finally (FINALLY) show a little pep. But then it's too little too late. And, of course, it's ruined by more back story.

I was disappointed by this book. As a sequel to Pride and Prejudice I was hoping for something with the same vitality as the original, paired with P.D.James's flair for ingenious plotting, but I found neither. Perhaps James was seeking to adopt a style more in keeping with the early nineteenth century, when the original book was written, but I found her prose plodding and verbose. Because so much of the story depends on a previous knowledge of events in the original book, there is a great deal of summarising of the 'back story', with characters reminding each other of past events in order to ensure that the reader is up to speed. Even when the plot moves on, much of the action takes place 'off stage' which again requires it to be related at second hand. 
 The murder mystery itself seemed to me to lack James's usual flair for unexpected plot twists. There is only ever one suspect and as the evidence stacks up against him we know that at some point there must be a revelation that proves his innocence, but when it comes it struck me as unconvincing. The idea that a young man at the point of death, from some undisclosed sickness, could find the strength to deal the blow which leads to the victim's death takes some believing, but even less credible is the fact that he waits months, until the suspect is brought to trial and found guilty, before confessing. He does not, after all, face any danger that he will be accused of murder in his turn, since the actual death was an accident; and he knows anyway that he has not long to live. There are other revelations to follow, but again they are all delivered at second hand. 
 Meanwhile, we have to sit though the inquest and the trial itself, where the same evidence is repeated over and over again by various witnesses. And when the final denouement is reached, this has to be explained to us repeatedly by each participant. This is interspersed with long internal soliloquys from Elizabeth and Darcy about the effects of their marriage on those around them, their responsibilities to Pemberley and its occupants, and their previous relationships. 
 There is a well known adage constantly quoted to aspiring writers; 'Show, don't tell.' In this respect I am afraid 'Death comes to Pemberley' falls short.
The real mystery is not the murder, but how this book got past editors onto bookshelves.

reference_books.title: Catching Fire (The Hunger Games, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
From http://rhiannon-hart.blogspot.com/200... 
 In the aftermath of Katniss and Peeta winning the Hunger Games, Katniss must come to terms with the consequences of thwarting the Capitol. Leading up to the Quarter Quell, the seventy-fifth anniversary of the games, she must prove to everyone, including President Snow, that she's head-over-heels in love with Peeta and that her "cousin" Gale means nothing to her. There will be dire consequences for Katniss and the people she loves if she fails. 
 Reading Catching Fire made me angry, and there's nothing I like better than a dystopian novel making me angry. Down with the President! Chunks of this reminded me of the sweet parts of Nineteen Eighty-four, the middle third in which Winston and Julia have their dalliances in the forest and the room above the shop, talking carelessly and indulging in love-making, a big no-no in Oceania. (I've always rather fancied going to a party dressed in overalls with a red sash tied around my waist like a member of the Anti-Sex League, but I think the reference might be a tad obscure.) I half expected Katniss to spy a microphone hidden in the woods or for a painting to fall down in her house revealing a telescreen inhabited by President Snow sporting a Stalin mo. "TWO MINUTES HATE!!" Unlike in The Hunger Games, I found the romance in Catching Fire to be touching and thoroughly heart-wrenching. The love triangle isn't just about who Katniss thinks is spunky and can play up to the audience with; it becomes a matter of life and death for many people. 
 The pacing starts off a tad slowly, but it's hardly a disadvantage. It's like the calm before the storm, the ominous quiet before everything "catches fire". Fantastic title, by the way! It works literally and metaphorically on several levels. Where does Collins get her ideas? Such imaginitive ways to kill people. So sadistic and flamboyant! Rather like the thoughtless indulgences of the people of the Capitol. While Collins borrows from your typical grey, stony totalitarian dystopian novels, she also throws in a bit the destructive extravagance of Brave New World and Westerfeld's Uglies as a wonderful contrast between the bleakness of several districts and the frivilousness of the Capitol. 
 Gale remains a mystery. Peeta I have gained rather more respect for. He's the one to watch in book three I think. Gale needs to really pick up his game or he's going to fall off the radar for good! So have I picked a team? You bet I have! 
 Yep. The boys just pale into comparison to Katniss's awesomeness. This girl rocks. I don't think I've ever adored a female protagonist so much. I love hearing what's going on in her head, the way she pieces things together. Her voice (and Collins' writing) is thoroughly readable. And boy is she feisty when she's angry. I think I feel a girl crush coming on. 
 It's the people that really make Catching Fire, and not only the main cast of characters. There's a real sense of the masses, how people are reacting to this or that bit of footage; the unrest; the partying. Every bit character has a personality sketched in just a few short sentences, and they all have a purpose in Collins' grand scheme. (I had to look up who Seneca Crane was, but the bit with the dummy was genius!) Those who called The Hunger Games "simple" can't do the same for book two. 
 Catching Fire goes off with a bang. I adore it.

reference_books.title: Wintergirls
reference_books.review_text:
From http://rhiannon-hart.blogspot.com/200... 
 Lia's ex-best friend Cassie is found dead in a motel room, alone. On the night of her death Cassie called Lia thirty-three times. Lia never picked up, and now she's being haunted by Cassie as she slides back into dangerland: her all-consuming struggle to be thin. 
 First of all, how popular is the name Lia in books right now? She's the main character in this book, Crashed by Robin Wasserman and my current read, Prophecy of the Sisters. 
 I read several books in my teens about anorexia, all very powerful books whose titles have been lost in the mists of time. But none came close to the lyrical power contained within the pages of Wintergirls. The theme is ripe for revisiting. The internet has brought a new facet to body-image disorders since I was a teenager: pro-ana forums, short for pro-anorexia. Proponents argue that anorexia and bulimia (pro-mia) are lifestyle choices, not psychological disorders. The forums are a place where those with eating disorders can go for "thinspiration", tricks for not getting caught, and support. (There are also several forums of the same name that are actually there to help anorexics recover and heal. Why they call themselves pro-ana is a sweet mystery to me.) 
 There has always been the concern that YA books about eating disorders "teach" teenagers how to be anorexic or bulimic. The portrayal of these disorders in books is so bleak, so heart-wrenchingly awful, so downright shocking that the idea that anyone would claim that a teenager would get to the end of a book like Wintergirls and decide to jump on the eating disorder band-wagon is ridiculous. 
 Lia views the world through a prism that makes everything about food; not only what she puts in her mouth, or what other people put in their mouths, but their actions as well. 
 He regurgitates his chewed story for me, another paying customer feasting on the dead blonde. 
 She's been institutionalised twice, both times against her will, and fed until she reaches a "safe" weight. She's disgusted by the idea of food in her body, but at the same time she craves it, knows she needs it desperately. As her weight drops she feels stronger, but her hallucinations grow worse. Her character is drawn with such sensitivity that instead of wanting to grab Lia by her bony arms, shake her, and scream "Eat, Lia, EAT!" as her parents do, the reader knows it's not as simple as that--Lia won't get better unless she wants to, and she's so lost that she has no idea even where to begin. So she tries to make herself disappear instead, one pound at a time. 
 The novel is told in first-person present tense, and if it weren't for Lia's dry and evocative observations, being right there with her as she runs on empty would be too heavy to handle. The telling is brisk and honest. Lia's compulsions to eat, to stuff her face with box after box of cereal, slice after slice of pizza, are stricken from the record--literally--and replaced with affirmations that she hates eating, that she loves not-eating. Her parents are dealt with similarly. She replaces mentions of "mum" and "dad" with Professor Overbrook and Dr Marrigan. 
 Memories of Cassie are revisited almost reluctantly, with more about their unhealthy friendship revealed as the haunting grows worse. They make a pact as pre-teens to be the thinnest girls in school. Their progression from lively little girls who play with dolls into teens with full-blown eating disorders is somewhat obscure, especially for Cassie, as we aren't inside her head. At one point Lia muses that she's not particularly smart or beautiful or talented, so her way to be special is to be thin. I was gob-smacked when I read this. I could read you a page from my diary when I was sixteen that is almost identical. The only difference is that I've never had an eating disorder. Anderson's portrayal of Lia's struggle is one that any who is or has once been a teenage girl will in some way identify with. 
 I thought Elijah was vaguely redundant. At first I thought he symbolised what Lia was missing out on: a real life, part of which could include a boyfriend. There's a fantastic scene on page 131 on the way to Cassie's funeral that illustrates a fundamental difference between men and women: our stubborn attitude to clothes and footwear that hurt us. In Wintergirls it goes like this: 
 "They look good." 
 "No, they don't," he says. "If they hurt you, they're hideous." 
 Which is, of course, a metaphor for anorexia: you're killing yourself, you're dying--you think you look good but you don't. Elijah's role petered out so unsatisfactorily that it made me question why he was included at all. 
 Apart from secondary character issues--that are somewhat due to the close-first narrative--Wintergirls is a complex, thought-provoking read. I'm extremely pleased with my first foray into Laurie Halse Andersons work. It's little wonder she is the "issues" queen.

3 1/4 stars
I absolutely love Brian Vaughan's work with Saga, but Paper Girls might've been a bit too obscure for me. 3.5

The story was awful and made no sense whatsoever. The characters were basically caricatures of teens...except they were all supposed to be 12. Twelve!!!!! No 12 year old known to man has ever used language like that, and certainly not with that level of talent. Usually at 12, kids are starting to learn their way around profanity. These girls sound like sailors. And don't get me started on the fact that one of them smokes. At. Twelve. In a graphic novel touted as being feminist and something every girl should read. 
 I disliked it intensely. I think Vaughn must be just going for shock value. Either that or he's never met an actual child before. If this was supposed to be full of 17 year olds, it would have at least been more realistic, though not any better. The story was bad, the characters were bad, and writing was awful. I can't recommend this to anyone.

I received PAPER GIRLS, VOL. I as an ARC through NetGalley.com. 
 3.5 STARS 
 Comics that focus on female characters get an automatic thumbs up from me, just for bucking the totally false assumption that women don't read comics and male characters are more universally relatable. I dare anyone of any gender to read this book and not find yourself identifying a little with at least one of the four main characters. 
 While I don't think this is a book universally appropriate for the YA crowd, I DO think there are a lot of young women out there who could use a tough group of 12-year-olds dealing with Twilight Zone shit to put some spice in their reading material. (If that sentence piques your interest, I gotta drop a LUMBERJANES recommendation here; that one leans more toward fun than scary, while PAPER GIRLS leans more toward scary than fun.) And another note: if you do give this to folks in YA's target age group, I suggest reading it yourself and discussing some things with them afterward. There were several spots where I felt jarred by a character's words or actions, and I had to keep reminding myself that it's meant to be taking place in 1988, and things have changed a lot in the past thirty years. 
 The art in PAPER GIRLS isn't my favorite--I've read several comics lately with art that is exactly what I like best--but it feels like the right art for this story. It adds to the atmosphere and the sense of danger, and while I don't foresee wanting any prints on my walls, I also can't imagine feeling as wrapped up in the story while reading if it had different art. It definitely feels like a major part of the character of the story. 
 And the last few panels have me REALLY looking forward to Volume 2.

I'm super excited to read the next bind-up when it comes out! I really like the concept of this comic series, and you really can't go wrong with some Brian K. Vaughan. 
 Read this if you like: BA chicks, the 80s, space, allegory, and suspense.

I absolutely loved Paper Girls Vol. 1. It tells the story of a group of Paper Girls in a small town near Cleveland in 1988 who are faced with what appears to be the end of the world. This volume ended on a cliff hanger that left me on the edge of my seat wanting more. I received a free digital copy for review purposes, but I can't wait to get a physical copy and to pick up subsequent volumes. Overall, I would highly recommend this book and it is one of the best graphic novels I have read all year.

Between 3 and 4 stars on this one. I like the idea of it, but this volume read as though it was a single issue. There was so much going on and yet nothing was ever explained, I expect a bit more in a volume. Like I said, I think this can really grow into an amazing story, but right now I'm just left a bit confused. 
 However, this is one of those graphic novels I would still suggest simply so that you can look at the stunning artwork. I'm obsessed with it.
A little too similar to Stranger Things and other nostalgia type stuff coming out this summer, but also fun and good.

book_b.title: For Such a Time
book_b.user_review:
This book was terrible, but for reasons other than I expected. It was also a DNF, for reasons that will become apparent. 
 This book has been controversial because: 
 -- It's a romance between a Nazi camp commandant and a Jewish woman passing for a gentile. 
 --Romantic leads have to be worthy of love by the end of the novel. (See above dynamic.) 
 --It's also a Christian Inspirational romance and the Jewish woman converts to Christianity at the end. 
 It was nominated for a RITA (the Academy Awards of romance) and people got angry about the above -- though they conceded that it was a technically good book. 
 I love historical novels and I'm not afraid of a bit of controversy. The opening chapter was rather enjoyable -- the heroine hiding in a room, weak and afraid, where she's been stashed by a Nazi and doesn't know why. The commandant turns up, severe and inscrutable, but dashing all the same in that just-look-at-my-tailored-uniform-and-chiselled-features thing that German officers often have in books/films. 
 But it all quickly fell apart -- the heroine was oddly over-reactive to things when she should probably have been deadened/embittered/resigned after months in Dachau. The hero was worse. The big pull for reading this book for me was HOW will Breslin redeem the hero? How do you go from Scary-Nazi-Runner-of-Deathcamp to happy-ever-after? Breslin solved the problem by making him bland and sensitive from the get-go. I didn't get to how he felt about Jewish people but he probably thought they were "all right really, all humans are worthy of life but I've got these orders you know, what's a commandant to do ..." There was pretty much nothing internally that he needed to develop and struggle with. It was all external conflict for him (i.e. the setting, his orders, the war.) 
 At one point his actions were semi-questioned by his men and he actually explained himself to them. PLEASE. Show me any officer in any army who would do that. 
 The very last nail in the coffin was when we switched to his POV in chapter 5 (for the first time, a big no-no) and he didn't know why he'd saved the heroine, he just had this compulsion that he needed her. Oh fuck off. Your romance is bad and you should feel bad. 
 So yeah, this is not only a controversial book, it's a bad book, which is a far worse crime.

sample_reviews.review_text: Wow. This is a tough book to put down, especially the last quarter or so. It is definitely hard to see how it can ever be possible for the heroine to get her hero in the end. A fantastic rewrite of the story of Esther set amongst the Jewish ghettos and camps during WWII.

Toto bola asi jedna z NAJHORSICH KNIH, ktore sa mi pocas mojho zivota dostali do ruk... Pardon, aby som bola presna.. O 2 tyzdne nie je problem sa zalubit do velitela koncentracneho tabora, velitel, ktory ma akoze pod palcom tabor Terezin kde len tak mimochodom vaznia jej stryka.. no problem, laska je laska... WTF WTF WTF !!!!), nutena propagacia krestanstva (objavovanie krestanskej viery hlavnej postavy pretoze jej viera ju "zradila"), neuveritelne za vlasy pritiahnute konanie a myslienkove pochody vsetkych postav a neskutocne, do neba volajuce vyslovene "historicke" SPROSTOSTI, pardon okolnosti, ktore sa za ZIADNYCH OKOLNOSTI nemohli odohrat... I love the idea of the story, which was a modern retelling of the story of Esther in the Bible. Overall, a good read, just written in a way that didn't really keep me hooked. I put the book down for a couple of days at a time.

I don't give a lot of one star reviews, but I feel that the subject matter of this book was so inappropriate that I have no other choice. I did read this book (via my library), so I would agree that it is well-written. Just because something is well-written, doesn't mean it should have been written. A romance between a Jew in a concentration camp and a Nazi commandant is such an imbalance of power as to violate all the standards of both the romance and inspirational genres. I feel that the use of the concentration camp background here, as well as the difference between the statuses of the characters feels like an emotional shortcut to establish credibility. The magical realism with the frequently reappearing Bible is insulting at best. Miracles happen, but anyone who believes said miracles are focused on the conversion of Jews amidst the Shoah needs to reread Romans 9-11. 
 I have written a longer reaction here: http://revgalblogpals.org/2015/08/17/...

I try to make it a point to never, and I mean NEVER, read romance novels. 
 To me, a whole book that's plot is just about two people falling in love is about the most boring, stupid, and pointless thing in the whole world; heck the universe for that matter:) 
 That being said I picked up For Such a Time because I thought, sadly mistaken though I was, that it was a historical account of WW 2, which I love. Not some dumb, 'Christian' romance novel that relied upon silly story lines, unbelievable plots, and unfeeling descriptions of one of the most horrific, and terrifying events in history. 
 The holocaust and WW 2 are subjects that I do love to read about but they MUST be well written, and moving accounts that show what it was like. 
 "For Such a Time" is just another stupid, sappy romance novel. (Oh yes, did I mention its a "Christian romance?" Basically the only difference between "Christian Romance" and "regular romance" is that there are a few bible verses thrown in, a faith driven old uncle or something, and in the end everyone turns to God after screwing each other across half the world-well then, I guess it's ok) 
 The book was a mockery of WW2 and those who suffered and died and a horrible account that didn't do justice to what the Jews and other minorities that were targeted went through. 
 I found it highly offensive that the author down played the horrors of war and WW2 in general. 
 Now don't get me wrong, I do believe that Jewish people/other minorities and Nazi's probably fell in love; love appears in the strangest of places. But just the way this was done was so stupid, and unbelievable and just....wrong. Wrong because, as I said, it didn't do justice to WW2 and what people went through, and wrong because it tried to make some sappy love story out of it instead of a haunting, beautiful tale that could be done. 
 One last thing; I know I've been quoting "Christian romance" a lot. Please don't get me wrong, I am a Christian myself and I am not trying to mock Christianity. Just "Christian romance" because the people that write said romances basically, as I said earlier, slap a 'Christian' label on their works of porn; clean them up a bit (No blatant sex scenes but still enough innuendo and comments to be just as bad) for the Christian audiences, and stick a few bible verses in them thinking that that will make everything ok.
Even the summary is offensive. This is disgusting and horrifically antisemitic. I am offended as a writer and as a non Jew.

In the classic re-telling of the plot from the Book of Esther, Kate Breslin brings us to Nazi Germany in 1944 in her novel, For Such a Time. It begs the question: What could you have done to save the Jews? 
 Aric first sees Hadassah (or her assumed name, Stella) in Dachau. He appears to rescue her from certain death and takes her to his transit camp of Theresienstadt in Czechoslovakia where Stella becomes his secretary. From here, the plot follows as closely as possible to the story from the Book of Esther. Stella's Uncle is one of the prisoners in the camp appointed by the Nazi's to choose who will go to Auschwitz. When telephone lines go down, Stella gets a bag of cards to type up from the captain of the camp. Aric, in spite of his compassion, doesn't stop the Jews from getting on the train, and Stella does the unthinkable and courageous by taking 160 names off of the list. 160 Jews were saved. 
 Stella lives in fear of being discovered and struggles with her choices. She wants to save all the Jews. Aric detests his job, too, but does his job anyway knowing he could lose his life if he takes any chances. The question that is asked throughout this book is: What would you have done in their place? You can't save everyone without losing your life. If you lose your life, more die. If you save some, but not all, you live to save more people. Many stories in history show us the courage of people in Nazi-occupied territory and in Nazi Germany who struggled with this question every day of the war. 
 The book of Esther show us a similar recounting where Esther braved the wrath of a king to reveal her true identity, and in doing so, saved his life and the life of her people. We can choose to go along to get along, and someone else will be chosen to save people; or you can choose to do the right thing no matter the risk. While this is a work of fiction, Kate Breslin gives us a history lesson on the back of the book. I encourage you to read that when you are finished reading this novel. For Such a Time is a romance novel set near the end of World War II-an unlikely set up of a Jewess and a Nazi Wehrmacht Officer who runs a transit camp. It was riveting. I gave it five stars. 
 *book given by publisher to review.

I first saw this book on Goodreads months back, and after reading some of the reviews and seeing that it was being received as controversial, I decided to forgo reading it at the time. 
 So you would imagine my surprise when my dear friend at church handed me this book and Saving Amelie and told me how much she enjoyed both of them. If you read my review for Saving Amelie (which I very much loved) you'll see that the holocaust is not one of my favorite subjects to read about. My head is not buried in the sand, and I strive to keep myself well informed, but it is undoubtedly a very depressing subject. 
 Aside from all of that, I found myself completely ensconced in this story. 
 *What I don't understand is why nowhere on the cover of the book did it say that this story is inspired by Queen Esther's life in the bible? That was what I enjoyed the most about the story! 
 I had to constantly keep that in mind because at many points in the story my brain kept shouting Stockholm Syndrome! Stockholm Syndrome! I'm assuming that's where a lot of the controversy stems from because I don't remember in detail the reviews I previously read. It's also a given that any book with a character that converts from one faith to another is inevitably going to be controversial. 
 Having said that, aside from the inspiration from Queen Esther's life, and the scripture taken from the book of Esther at the beginning of each chapter, this book didn't strike me as being overly "Christian" because there was a huge disconnect between the characters who were changing their lives and (God) who was bringing about the change. For the most part, I feel, it was left up to the reader to decide why these characters were miraculously changing their entire world view, and to whom to give the credit. It was kind of a nebulous non-issue but ultimately, I feel, should've been the crux of the story. 
 The star rating might change in the future but I like it where it's at for now.

Struggling to understand how a novel that features a Jewish woman in a concentration camp falling in love with a Nazi commander is getting so many accolades. Maybe it's well-written--I'll never find out--but this very concept is so offensive it's unbelievable. The fact that so many people--the author, the publisher, readers, RWA judges--found this acceptable baffles me.

The subject is offensive. It's conversion porn. You lost me at Nazi.

book_a.title: Nineteen Minutes
book_a.user_review:
This book was difficult to read, not because it was written badly but because it was written so well. I found myself torn between sympathy, disgust, pity, anger, and so many other emotions for all the characters involved. It's frightening because it depicts so well the helplessness that kids who are bullied feel. It also depicts the inability of school systems to effectively deal with bullying, sometimes resulting in terrible consequences. 
 My only criticism of this book(and most of Picoult's books) is that the ending seemed rushed and wrapped up a little too neatly. While reading it, I kept wondering HOW this could end, and I was disappointed by the way it did. But I'd still recommend it and I still rate it amazing, as it covers exactly the kinds of things kids deal with on a regular basis.

sample_reviews.review_text: This. Is. The. Single. Best. Book. I. Have. Ever. Read.

audio. I've been affraid of this book. tough topics, I just couldn't imagine..... 
 Once I got through the beginning of the book, I was through the tough part and we were hitting the "character building." I did enjoy the author's attention to detail ~ how tough it would be for the police to be detached and yet, they have to be good and break down the crime scene, get evidence, etc. I enjoyed seeing the human side of everyone as well. 
 ** (possible spoilers??!!) ** 
 But, true to the author's history, the end let me down. It always does. I thought it really could have been gutsy and inventive. Instead, it made me wonder why I'd worked so hard to finish 18 audio cd's (trust me, this took WORK!) 
 Oh well, off to another.

I heard about Jodi Picot's Nineteen Minutes back in May when a NH parent complained his 14 year old daughter had to read it for school and he hadn't been notified despite some sexual content he found objectionable. I pretty much never agree with parents wanting to protect their teenagers from information contained in books - especially when that reading is taking place under adult supervision. 
 I still don't agree with this parent but, to be fair, the scene he objected to is a quite graphic description on teens having sex. I was never given anything remotely like this when I was in school. Nobody had sex in the classics I was assigned. 
 I mostly read this book to see why it's being assigned to high school students. The premise is that there has been a school shooting committed by a student who'd been bullied. I do think this book could open up conversation about bullying, gun control, and sexual consent - all issues kids should be thinking about. 
 The structure of the book is very clever. With multiple narrators, it shifts back in time before these particular children were even born, showing the events that shaped them. Of particular interest is the midwife and mother of the future shooter who delivers at least one future victim, befriending her mother. This structure allows Picolt to give several different perspectives without telling the reader what to think. 
 I don't know if Picolt typically writes from the perspective of teenagers, but it didn't work for me here. It seemed like a caricature of how adults think teens talk. Also, her use of metaphors and similes were universally awful. Her editor should have cut them all. 
 The book drags toward the end but I kept reading to find out what the hinted at plot twist would be. Actually, I had an idea what it could be, but thought "oh no, that's way too stupid." But, that's what it was. I won't give it away other than to tell you to imagine the worst plot twist possible. That's it. 
 I probably wouldn't recommend this book to a literature class. For the benefit of conversations it could inspire, it might work for health class or even politics. And that's coming from someone who wants high school students reading more books by women that have greater relevance to contemporary life. 
 But not this one.

Ms Picoult really knows how to keep your attention. I feel manipulated, but I keep on reading. Unfortunately, I don't know any answers to the problems that Picoult is concerned with, but she has me thinking about them. Picoult has a good video on her website that you might want to watch.

I have read this book twice. The first time, I was really hit by the tragedy, and the second time I really paid attention to the backstory. It was so interesting to be inside the boy's mind and see what he was thinking. I really loved the story, I did not love the language. The swearing made the book less endearing to me. Also, something about the actual writing wasn't as great as you would hope.

Another great novel from the amazing Jodi Picoult. As someone who has suffered bad bullying at school and later into teenage life, and also someone who can actually sympathize with Peter's character, I felt this subject was handled exceptionally well!

I had a hard time with the violence in this novel. I was disturbed for a long time after reading this. 
 This was my 3rd Jodi Picoult book to read and I feel the formula is the same with her books.

Terrible. The modern sections at first seem promising, but the outcome becomes a foregone conclusion fairly early on, and I cannot bring myself to care about a courtroom drama where I know the outcome. The flashback sections are horribly written, entirely pointless, and destroy the pacing of the novel. The characters are at best bland and uninteresting and at worst entirely unsympathetic. This book could have been interesting had it been half the length and dispensed with the unnecessary flashback portions, but as it is I cannot recommend it to anyone.

This is a great air travel book, with short scenes and shifting perspectives that make it easy to read while being frequently interrupted ("gate now boarding"...). Overall I found the premise engaging and the pacing quite good. Picoult's observations about the power of popularity were certainly thought-provoking. 
 What kept this from being a five star was the lack of character development for a few key characters--especially the shooter's parents. In real life, I suspect that after the event they would have also been bullied and threatened (and possibly forced to move away) and might thus begin to better understand their son. Their passivity and lack of push-back from the community didn't quite ring true to me, and felt like a lost opportunity for drama and more satisfying closure.

Leave it up to Jodi Picoult to take a completely unsympathetic character and situation and force you to see the humane side of it. 
 The setting of the book happens in the first couple of chapters. A seemingly ordinary student - a bullied kid named Peter - walks into his school and starts shooting at everyone. It starts out pretty simple. No room for debate over what's right or wrong here. It's very clear at first who you hate and who you sympathize with. I'd never read a book about a shooting, so I didn't expect to find any sympathy for the shooter. But that's Jodi Picoult's gift I guess. She humanizes every character and forces you to understand them. Not necessarily like them; she doesn't try to erase their flaws or sugarcoat their feelings. She just explores every other side of their lives to make you realize that there's more to them that meets the eye. There's more to that criminal's life than what he did, there's more to him that why he did it; there's his whole life. 
 I loved the honesty in narration because it really captures how complicated and emotional people are. How sometimes their actions or feelings don't make sense. How we need our families need to lean on for support. What we can end up being if we keep so much hatred bottled up. 
 Nineteen Minutes wasn't just thought-provoking and well written, it was empathetic. I'm really glad I picked it up when I did because the last few months of 2016 made me feel like there was no empathy left in the world, so it was good to read about some humanity again instead of the daily evils that are the everyday news. 
 Of course, the ending wasn't cheerful or happy. That would've been sugarcoating it. But it was just I think, so it didn't upset me as much as other Jodi Picoult endings did (Yes, Handle with Care, I'm talking to you...). So I can say that this is the best Jodi Picoult book I've read (so far). 
 It's not an easy read, none of Jodi Picoult's books are - being as raw and emotional as they are. But I really do recommend it, because it opens up your mind and helps you find compassion in the most unlikely of places.
