sample_reviews.review_text: Sometimes funny, sometimes excruciating. Rusty, one of the children was my favorite character.

Someone described this book as "Richard Russo meets Big Love" and that's exactly right. Like Russo, Udall has perfected the comi-tragic tone of disaster snowballing around a hapless protagonist. Like Big Love, the novel chronicles the day-to-day lives of a very large polygamist family (28 children!). Although the writing is top-notch and the characterization terrific, I found myself very frustrated with the main character, Golden-- and I can't quite put my finger on whether that's because of Udall's plotting, or whether he specifically tried to make Golden this sad-sack with no agency. Throughout the book, Golden makes mistake after mistake with a "ho-hum, things are falling apart around me, everything is terrible" attitude. But his mistakes have very real, and very grievous consequences on the people he supposedly supports, namely his four wives and 28 children. I feel that there is a (male) attitude of entitlement where he can constantly fuck up, let people down, and make people miserable, but because he never cognizant makes a choice, he's just a passive bystander rather than an actor. But the decision not to do something is a decision. And his wives do not have that option, and his children are living in what to my mind are pretty unforgivable conditions. 
 Perhaps this is to show the flaws of polygamy as a patriarchal institution, but I think that's giving Udall too much credit. Of the three main characters, two are male, and throughout the book, prostitution is a constant running force. Both polygamy and prostitution (as it's traditionally practiced) are patriarchal traditions that cement the power of men and treat women as property. And I think making Golden a character who literally cannot handle the patriarchal reigns he's been handed is a very weak way to critique those institutions. It makes both seem like something people just fall into, men as well as women, and takes away the responsibility of the men practicing them. 
 Despite all this I really enjoyed the book and would recommend it; I think it's going to be a huge hit in paperback.

In the beginning I was worried the main character would be the butt of the jokes unrelentingly. Thankfully a third of the way through the main character, Golden, is given more depth and the book is saved. Up until that point my favorite character was the sheriff who was in it for about two pages. 
 Towards the end, it was hard to stop reading. I wanted to know what was going to happen to the family and to Golden.

This book will make you LOVE a POLYGAMIST who CHEATS ON HIS WIVES and CAN'T SUPPORT HIS FAMILY. Trust me on this one. 
 I'll admit it: I judged this book by its cover. With a title like "the Lonely Polygamist," how can you NOT read it? In addition to having one of the best titles of all time (right beside "the Amazing Adventures of Kavalier and Clay" and "the Curious Incident of the Dog in the Nighttime"), it was a tremendously good story full of lovable, deeply developed, and flawed characters. Never would I have thought I could sympathize with a polygamist who cheats on his wives and can't support his family. But Brady Udall will make you love him! While Golden Richards has four wives and over 20 kids, the book only follows three characters: 
 Golden Richards, the father, age 47, 6ft 5in and hopelessly slow, 
 Rusty Richards, an extremely lovable 12 years old, and a typical "plyg kid" who will do anything for attention, 
 and Trish, 27 years old and the neglected fourth wife. 
 All three characters go through amazing transformations by the end of the book, and you will not predict the ending. I also loved the use of symbolism and imagery. The turning point in every character's life is accompanied by an explosion (literally). 
 Probably the best book I've read all year. I will be reading more from Udall.

This book was good, but far too long! I couldn't listen in long stretches so I lost track of the characters and all those wives! But despite that it was a solid story. I was really sad about poor Rusty. He didn't deserve any of what he got, especially being blown up. Golden pretty much caused his own problems by being such a push over! I would give this another listen to get some parts I missed.

Not a bad book--it picks up quite a bit at the end. I didn't have a great deal of sympathy for the protagonist, who with 4 wives and 28 children and one mistress seemed to invite his own troubles. However, I thought the ending was well done in its attempt to show how lonely and disconnected from each other we so often are.

The title of the book grabbed me, the book, however, did not. 
 About half way through, bored to tears, I just gave up. I didn't find the characters well developed, sympathetic or remotely interesting. I had such high hopes and wanted to read a narrative about something I know nothing about. I went in open minded and excited and gave up bored. 
 I don't even care what happens to the characters!

What a sad and heart wrenching story; though very well written. Warning: there was a lot of swearing and "sex talk" in this book. This story gave a very disturbing picture of polygamy. I am not sure I have read any book on polygamy that was very uplifting. I just felt so sad for most of the characters.
Couldn't finish it. I wanted to slap the dude across the room. Life is too short. Too many books to read. Too little time to waste another day on this book.

3.5 stars 
 I liked this book more than I expected to. I thought I'd really hate the main character, and in most of the parts, I sort of hated him, but not enough to make me hate the book. The parts about the other characters were interesting and entertaining enough to make up for all the boring, despicable parts about the main character. Unfortunately, it seemed like the parts from other characters' points of view were few and far between. I would have liked to see more of Trish's story, and the stories of the other wives. We really never get to see anything but a few glimpses of the other wives. I enjoyed Golden's flashbacks, but otherwise, his parts were very boring to me and I thought the author could have cut out about a hundred pages and the book would have been better. He was so weak as to be pathetic and dispicable for neglecting his children and wives. We're supposed to feel sorry for him, I think, but he chose to live that life so I didn't feel sorry for him at all. I just thought he whined and made a lot of excuses for what a poor excuse for a human being he was. 
 The author's writing style was pleasant to listen to (I had the audiobook), and I liked his descriptions. I also liked the parts about nuclear testing and the after-effects. The only thing about the writing that bothered me was how the author jumped around in time so much. I liked the flashbacks, but usually a chapter went something like this: present day--yesterday--five years ago--yesterday--back to present day. It was sometimes hard to remember what was going on with all the circular time frames. Other than that, I enjoyed Udall's writing quite a bit.

reference_books.title: Cress (The Lunar Chronicles, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
My Review: 
 I'm not even sure where to start but this review might contain spoilers, not major ones but maybe a few if you haven't read the other books. The reviews for this book are outstanding so I was super excited to start reading it. I was fine with reading about Cinder, Scarlet, Thorne, Wolf and Iko but when it came to Cress I wanted to RIP my hair out. Since this book is sort of mainly about her I was so sad that I just didn't like her at all. She is whiny, her obsession with Thorne, was annoying to the point I felt the relationship that they had is forced and didn't feel at all that natural. When it came to reading in her POV I usually had to stop myself from throwing my kindle. I would have preferred a lot more of Kai and Cinder since we never got that LOVE story that we all have been waiting for. They spend more time apart than together and that drives me crazy. 
 The story, sort of, didn't progress as much as I would have liked until about 60% and once it got to that point I felt like I wasn't sure what the beginning of the book was really for. I, however, LOVED the last 40% and I am excited to see what happens, since I have a lot of questions that were not answered and the end left me feeling like WHAT....I need to know what happens! 
 Scarlet and Wolf are still my favorite but let me say lets not talk about Scarlet right now since I just can't. I am sure Wolf feels the same way. I adore Cinder, always have, I just want her to get a happily ever after but I know it will take her a little time seeing as she is a fugitive and a wanted criminal (which is basically the same thing) Iko and Thorne just crack me up but Cress, poor Cress, I just couldn't get past the damsel in distress. She had such potential to be a bad ass hacker genius but it sort of just didn't happen. I wanted more from her and I understand being trapped on a satellite could make you a little whiny and child like but this was way more than I would have wanted. 
 The last 40% really had me on the edge of my seat, I had a bit of anxiety about what was going to happen next and the end was just awesome. I am really looking forward to Winter, you get to meet her in this book, she sort of reminds me of Alice in Wonderland, just a little mad. 
 If you read the others you will totally enjoy this, just keep in mind the beginning is a little bit of a stand still and the story progression is a tad bit slow but over all I rather enjoyed it. 
 An InLinkz Link-up 
 Thank you so much for stopping by to check out my review 
 Hope you have a great day and Happy Reading! 
 This review was originally posted on Because reading is better than real life

reference_books.title: Wanting My Stepsister
reference_books.review_text:
This started off pretty good then half way through it took a major left turn and I was totally confused. Libby has loved her stepbrother since they meet and Jasper has felt the same way. For years they have denied their feelings for each other but now they can't seem to keep their hands off each other and they don't care. 
 I was good when this started. I lot of tension and protectiveness that makes you feel like Jasper was a great protective guy. I liked how much he loved her and how much she loved him. I honestly didn't realize until the half way point how awkward the relationship was. It was creepy possessive, like in the middle of him realizing they both liked each other he started calling her baby girl and while fooling around he asked who's your daddy now? I'm sorry...what? Plus they were both virgins but he seemed to have a lot more experience than a virgin would. It was an unhealthy possession of her and she didn't seem to mind at all. When they finally had sex all he wanted was to get her pregnant....Did I miss something? All he talked about was planting his seed and getting her pregnant. I was so confused. The last half totally spiraled out of control and I just sort of didn't understand what I was reading and rolled my eyes more often than I had wanted. 
 I didn't like the possessiveness he had over her and it wasn't romantic. Every time he told people, she's mine like she was a dog, I wanted to punch him. The sex wasn't bad and when the parents found out I was even more confused. Overall, it was ok, not my favorite stepbrother/sister book. 
 Thanks for stopping by to check out my review. 
 Have a great day and Happy Reading!

book_a.title: Truth or Beard (Winston Brothers, #1)
book_a.user_review: Just wasn't feeling the characters, felt the love story was all over the place. Was hoping I would like it but I didn't.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Over the course of one sleep-deprived, but laugh-filled, week, I devoured Penny Reid's Knitting in the City series, thus starting a (perfectly healthy) obsession with her writing. Reading a book by Penny Reid is like being inducted into a world of adorably quirky characters and writing that is both intelligent and humorous. She injects an unparalleled zaniness into each of her books and I'm thrilled to say that her newest release, Truth or Beard, follows suit. Charming, refreshing, lively, and entertaining - any and all of these words can be used to describe Truth or Beard. It's undoubtedly the kind of book you read from the comfort of your own home, unless, of course, you're perfectly fine with people giving you strange looks as a result of your frequent and loud bouts of laughter. 
 What's not to love about the pairing of a math teacher whose Halloween costume of choice is a sexed up Gandalf the Grey and a mechanic whose unrequited crush prompts him to pretend to be his own twin? In case you're wondering, the answer is nothing. Every minute of the love/hate relationship between protagonists, Jessica James and Duane Winston, is just plain fun, from their whip smart conversations to their heated intimate encounters, and everything in between. When I read a book, I tend to gravitate more towards either the hero or the heroine, yet with Truth or Beard, I was equally enamored with both Duane and Jessica. Their unabashed honesty and genuineness made me feel as though I got to know all aspects of their characters; there was no mystery with them because they each laid everything out for the other to see. 
 ...Having said that, I will admit that I'm a tad bit enamored with Duane Winston. A guy who reads book, acts like a gentleman and has a dirty mind is pretty much my idea of perfection. The fact that he could say something inconspicuously sensual like "you're a siren who doesn't need to sing" in reference to Jessica's effect on him and not induce an eye roll speaks volumes to his level of charisma. Duane is so amazingly sweet and sexy, I couldn't help but swoon over his words and actions during his and Jessica's every interaction. I'm well aware this guy is a fictional character but that didn't stop me from giggling like a schoolgirl and fanning my face every time he opened his mouth. Did I mention he's a redhead? There just aren't enough redheaded heroes and I, for one, am glad Penny Reid is taking it upon herself to fill the void. 
 With its large cast of eclectic characters, the budding romance between Duane and Jessica, and a subplot to add a bit of action and suspense, there is never a dull moment in Truth or Beard. Like the Knitting in the City series, the Winston Brothers series is made up of interconnected standalones - a fact that fills me with immeasurable amounts of joy because, after reading Truth or Beard, I am more than anxious to become better acquainted with the remaining Winston brothers. There are six Winston brothers in total, which means there are five books in the series I have to look forward to. Five! If I could, I would set up camp in Penny Reid's mind so I could witness every story as it springs into existence. Until then, I think multiple re-readings of Truth or Beard are in order... 
 *complimentary copy provided by author in exchange for an honest review
SO freaking good! Penny's books only get better and better! Review to come at Red Cheeks Reads.

When I read all the reviews I feel like I'm the only one who didn't like this book, which surprises me. First of fall, the plot was SO obvious, from page one I already knew what was going on, which ruined the book for me, as expected it wasn't very interesting... This book just wasn't it for me, I really didn't enjoy it.

Just one single question - How many areas of life are you an expert in, Penny? Your books never cease to surprise me, especially when it comes to those geeky little tidbits!

I knew I shouldn't have picked this back up on Easter Sunday but I started to really enjoy it a few days ago and I wanted to get back into it. I loved the idea of a "twin switch" situation and the two MC's had a fun and electric chemistry right off the bat. 
 Unfortunately within the first two chapters I found them both clawing at each other with no time to get reacquainted after years of infatuation on the heroine's part and growing up together as kids. They just jumped right into full on groping within earshot of a Halloween event at the town community center full of children. I could've powered through the utter tackiness of the moment because it had been somewhat funny and I wanted to watch the circus of what was surely to come; had the Hero not ripped himself away from the heroine taking God's name in vain. 
 I'm sorry but is it really necessary to use THAT swear to sell a story? There's curses out there that are stronger and less degrading to God than that particular epithet. I'm not trying to be a religious prude or anything, but the combined tackiness of the moment between these instances just left a bad taste in my mouth. I'm disappointed because I was looking forward to this one but I couldn't even get past the first two chapters before deleting from my library. I don't recommend this for anyone who is sensitive to reading about characters who take God's name in vain. Just saying.

 Not only did I finished this with a smile on my face, but also now, a couple of days since I finished, I haven't deleted this off my kindle yet because every time I see the cover it makes me smile again. I loved so much about about Truth or Beard, Reed does such an awesome job with her characters and relationships - and not just the romantic ones, there are great friendships and fabulous family ties too. I really liked that Reid gave us POVs for both Duane and Jessica, and knowing what they were thinking and feeling heightened the emotional level and the steam level too. 
 I would never have imagined from our first introduction to the Winston brothers in Beauty and the Mustache that any of them would make a great leading man, but I truly loved Duane - and I am prepared to fall for his brothers as well.

sample_reviews.review_text:
A great start to a series. 
 I loved how it went back and forth seamlessly between modern day Ireland Crane and the past with Ichabod Crane of history and legend. Going back and forth ties past and present together so you get the entire story, not just snippets. 
 Ireland is an interesting character; I hope to see her develop more in future books. Rip was a fun sidekick character that added humor to the story. Noah...I hope there is more romance to come. 
 This was a great new take on the headless horseman tale with a few twists I didn't see coming. 
 I can't wait to start on book two, Raven.

If you're looking for an awesome Halloween read, check out Crane right meow. Revolving around a Sleepy Hollow retelling, this exciting, gory, and hilarious novel flips back and forth through time and the present to introduce new characters in a priceless spooky tale you thought you knew. I loved, loved, loved Rourke's writing style and how she seamlessly threaded in humor with horror. (I especially loved Rip.) The book is well-written, extremely entertaining, and the perfect fall read. I definitely need to get the sequel, Raven, soon. That ending gave me chills! If you love feisty heroines (and villains), a bit of mystery, and a historical, paranormal twist, you will love this book as much as I did. 
 ~SAT 
 Recommended to: Sleepy Hollow lovers and all things paranormal and spooky. Must enjoy horror and humor. 
 Favorite Quote: We all change for love. It's just a matter of what you let it change you into.

Thank you to Patchwork Press for providing me with an egalley of the book to review. 
 I expected something really unique when I read the summary for this book. The high ratings also seemed to reassure me that this would be a book that'll be memorable, witty, and full of adventure and characters that put an unusual new spin on a much loved story. It reminded me of The Hollow Trilogy by Jessica Verday as well as the Sleepy Hollow TV show, both popular new adaptations of the story. 
 This one, however, turned out nothing like that, and at 40% I ended up dropping it. 
 There was honestly nothing keeping my attention or interest in this story. The main character, Ireland Crane, attempts to be a strong female protagonist that has experienced difficulties in her past, including a pretty brutal break up after her boyfriend cheated on her. But there's no substance to her, no backbone that she attempts to have. She wasn't a female lead that I was fond of or could connect to, instead choosing to take the route of many other female protagonists who have emotional fits, jump to conclusions, make hardly any sense with their actions or words, and use cliched jokes and sarcasm to try appealing to the reader. None of these worked for me. 
 Not much happened in terms of the plot either. There's a lot of going back and forth between the past and present town of Sleepy Hollow, between Ichabod and Ireland Crane. Ichabod turned out to be just as flat and undeveloped as Ireland was (in which case the apple doesn't fall far from the tree I guess). There wasn't much going on and the details that were added into the story, such as describing how the villagers treated Ichabod, Rip Van Winkle, and Washington Irving, only added fluff to the story in what felt like an attempt to make up for the lack of a skeleton underneath. I didn't learn anything about Van Winkle and Irving, and I had already read 40% of the book. It's not a good sign when so much goes on but it feels like nothing significant has happened. 
 The development in the plot wasn't a shocker either, and although I presumed the plot would be something I could more or less foresee it was disappointing nonetheless to see that it was even more predictable and, well, BORING than I anticipated. 
 Definitely not the book for me. I didn't find anything interesting or new here. The cast of characters is simple and standard enough to appeal to most people, the plot is pretty predictable and, again, standard. Perhaps I should stop approaching books with such high hopes, or not rely so strongly on other reviews - the disappointment level will be lower.

I was given an ARC in exchange for an honest review free of persuasion from the author or anyone else affiliated with this book. 
 Stacey Rourke has hit it out of the ball park with this one for me. I went into the book expecting a normal paranormal book from her. What I did not expect was a telling of Ichabod Crane from the past and joining it with the present with the Headless Horseman living on. The adventures of Ichabod and Ireland Crane live on in CRANE through the delightful Rip Van Winkle. Not who you would expect to be the one telling Ireland, who is living in this century, the story of how Icabod met his untimely death with his first hand knowledge. I was so memorized by all of the activity and the going on of the Headless Horseman in this century that I didn't even notice the little clues on who it was until it was revealed. 
 I highly recommend this book to anyone of the ages 15+ because of some of the gore factor and a few sexual innuendo's. Other than that I highly recommend this book! I know for a fact that this will be a book I will go back to and reread just so I can see if I get all of the little hints the second time around.

Ireland Crane has a new haircut, a new tattoo, and a new home in Sleepy Hollow, where she can get away from a cheating ex. When people start losing their heads...literally...she refuses to believe in the legend of the Headless Horseman. Until she comes across an old man in her basement who's been sleeping for years and knows that the legend is, indeed, real. 
 I'm a sucker for retellings, and I think this is the first Sleepy Hollow retelling I've ever come across. This first in a trilogy is really fun! The story flips between the present and past. In the present, Ireland is haunted by bad dreams, annoyed by her house guest, and reluctant to start a relationship with the good looking and very gentlemanly Noah Van Tassel. The past narrative tells of Ichabod Crane, his two friends, Rip and Irv, and his love for Katrina Van Tassel. Both narratives give an interesting take on the classic tale, then blend together to form a parallel story. The pacing and blending of the two different timelines is well done, and the plot moves along, mixing familiar aspects with new twists. 
 For me, Rourke's characters are the key element in this story, mostly due to the dialogue and the way the characters interact realistically while still retaining some quirk. Ireland is sharp witted and snarky, which I love, but her contrast to the other characters is perfect. Her snarkiness plays well off the old-fashioned sweetness of Noah and the wackiness of Rip Van Winkle, who goes narcoleptic during moments of high stress. The back and forth between Ireland and Rip was entertaining, second only to later dialog between her and another key character. I don't want to spoil it, but let's just say I really hope there's more of that banter in the second book. 
 While this book isn't actually a romance, I'm still giving it a Romance Factor of 3/5, because at the core of what's going on is a ghostly love story. No Sex Factor in this one, but there was a Spook Factor, and I'm giving that a 3/5 as well, because there were a few scenes that gave me that "edge of the seat" feeling. The Horseman is sufficiently menacing at times, and though I didn't expect to be scared, I got a few chills. 
 There wasn't really anything I didn't like, though there are a few questions I had at the end, mostly regarding the connection between Ireland and Ichabod and the purpose of Rip falling asleep under stress. Those questions might actually be answered in there, but I seriously flew through this book and when I do that, I tend to miss little things in favor of the big scenery. I think another read through will be in order. 
 The second book in the series is available, and since I'm currently using books to reward myself for reaching certain goals, I've bumped this one to the top of my reward list so I can read it soon. This is a great modern twist on Sleepy Hollow, and I can't wait to read the next one, which incorporates the tales of Edgar Allan Poe into the continuing story of Ireland Crane.

Being a fan of everything that I've ever seen about Ichabod Crane and Sleepy Hollow I suspected that I would enjoy this greatly! I was fabulously not disappointed! 
 This is a variation and a completely new take on an old story. I wouldn't let that scare you away. The old characters are still there but this is now set to today and how the story affects Ireland Crane. 
 I have to say, I love the characters. I have so many highlights in my Kindle and I wanted to highlight even more! They are all quite different but at the same time they are all snarky or funny in their own ways. In the middle of battle I always found myself laughing! This also, of course, attributes to Stacey's fantastic writing and world building. Everything was believable so I didn't have to push to understand what the characters were going through and I completely understood when a character broke out in a one liner. 
 This also helped the ebb and flow of the book. It can't be all blood and horseman, there has to be something to the characters and to the storyline. Again, she built this beautifully! 
 If I were to pick a favorite character I would have to say I loved them all. I was quite curious what was going to happen to everyone. Even the horseman! He is a great villain and I love great villains! 
 The only slight downside for me was twofold. Firstly, it is a bit of a mystery and I found myself getting tired even though I really wanted to continue reading! The second was about 75% through and there is a redundant portion of the story. I understand why it was happening but I was on the edge of my seat by that point and that part kind of slowed me down. What happened with Ichabod and Katrina at that part though was fabulous and I actually liked how THAT ended. Whew... this is hard without spoilers! 
 So... all in all the storyline was fantastic. The characters were built brilliantly and left me wanting more! I'm glad I already have Raven or I might be having a book hangover! 
 In short: Not too gruesome. There's some blood but not too much. The storyline is definitely worth reading! Great for the upcoming fall season! 
 This review was originally posted on Creating Serenity

Told in both present and past, Ireland and Ichabod are both Cranes. Both arrive in "The Hollow" right around the same time as a few murders where-in the victims' heads are taken. 
 It was alright, I liked seeing Ichabod's part in the book although I wish we got to know him as a character more. Ireland was alright but I have to admit, I liked her character better after she embraced who she really was.

I must say that I'm very disappointed on what I had read so far, I stopped at 41%, it felt like it was going nowhere and I was almost half way done with the book. I went into this book with high expectations with all the five and four star reviews and found it quite lacking and boring. The characters for me were dull, none of them made me love them or at least like them. Ireland was kind of annoying, her actions doesn't match her inter monologue, she does the exact opposite, knowing it was a dumb thing to do. Also, what really upset me about her as a character, was the way she acted towards a student was beyond uncalled for. I don't understand how she got a job as a school counselor with that attitude.  Okay, so what really threw me off was the whole someone from the past, waking up in the present time. It reminded me too much of Sleepy Hollow and I thought this was going to be different from the show.

This is a fantastic book. It is The Legend of Sleepy Hollow retold. The characters Irving, Rip, and Ichabod were so great to follow. I read this book in one sitting as I just couldn't put it down. The book had my interest right from the first page all the way till the end. I love how the author took an old story and redid it with a nice twist. 
 I highly recommend this book and it gets 5***** from me

A generous upgrade from a 2.5 star rating. 
 The good: as far as retellings go, this one had an interesting twist to the original; had moments of creepiness and I didn't dislike Ireland Crane. 
 The bad: the writing often felt like fan-fiction, and yes, I realize that as a retelling there is a certain amount of that to be expected, but felt like there were pop culture references dropped in all the time that just weren't relevant; most of the characters felt very flat and I just couldn't care if they would/had died. 
 I will probably end up reading Raven at some point, because I felt like this picked up towards the end, and I would like to see if it continues in the next book in the series

reference_books.title: Handling the Undead
reference_books.review_text:
This is not your typical zombie story. 
 Yes - dead people come back to life. 
 No - they aren't really there to harm anyone...yet. 
 A strange electrical "reverse" power surge has an odd result: the dead come back to life. The term "reliving" was born. 
 What does one do with those who are "reliving?" No one is certain. Could this be the end of the world? Or, is it just that the dead want to return home? 
 The story examines the lives of 3 families, and how their living lives were impacted by the "reliving." It is creepy in a sad way, instead of in a horrifying way. Its actually quite sad, and it does raise the question of what one would should a dead loved one suddenly make its way back to you. Do you try and give them life? Is it selfish? Or do you set them free back to the afterlife? 
 This is not at all like Let The Right One In, and those who expect it to be might be disappointed. I loved Let The Right One In, but I enjoyed Handling The Undead as well. It was almost poetic, and written with lots of emotion from the characters.

Chelsea Handler is a freakin riot.

OK, I am giving this one star because chapter one is hysterical and about half of the chapter about the midget is hilarious. Beyond that the book was a bore. It was self-indulgent accounting of some of the men she had sex with or didn't have sex with. She clearly enjoys being drunk/high and sleeping with someone new regularly, and every once in a while there is a funny line about it. Mostly it's dry rambling about nothing funny. I was disappointed because chapter one suckered me into buying the book.

I love raunchy, and outrageous situations, like the TV series Californication. Speaking of Handler, Evan Handler is very good in it. I like TV's Girls enough to keep watching it. I've never seen or heard Chelsea. This book was boring. I can't believe I read it all, hoping it would get better.
This was a pretty quick read. Not as funny as I was hoping for, but it had its moments. Recommend for a short flight.

Everyone loves Chelsea or so I hear. Admittedly in the acting roles I have seen her in she has been quite funny, but I have not watched her show at all. But I have had this book and Its Me Vodka in my To Be Read Pile for some time. With my 2014 Reading Challenge to not buy a new book until I read 10 from the TBR pile, I decided it was high time that I actually see why everyone loves Chelsea. Conclusion...I am not sure I get it. 
 The Good and The Bad: Someone suggested that the book itself is very much like the one night stands she describes: brief, meaningless, but kid of fun. I would completely agree. It is the result of one too many cocktails, bad judgment and a self-deprecating attitude. It is a cotton candy book for sure, fluffy and fun. And yet I am not sure it is ultimately my thing. I couldn't relate to the stories as much as I thought I might. Though I have had a couple of one night stands myself on the whole one night stands are not my thing nor are drunken stupors and complete lack of judgments. 
 This is not to say that I didn't laugh. I did. Though I may not be a walk of shame sort of girl, I certainly could relate to a few of her escapades (I just dated them for 2 months rather than a few hours). Told in a series of short little stories, Chelsea chronicles her search for...well, a good time. She is snarky, self-deprecating, and candid. She gets shiny gold stars for being all three. Each chapter involves one of her sexual misadventures and for the most part each is funny for a very different reason. The stories range from fetishes, a string of men she hopes her father won't approve of, and her personality shines through whether it is her true personality or the Chelsea persona she sells as a living. Often she is quite good at delivering punchlines, though other times they are a bit forced and by the end many of the stories are similar. 
 I think my biggest problem though as it felt less like an empowered woman who is comfortable with her sexuality and her adventures and more of a this is why you should do drugs or drink heavily. I seriously cannot fathom half of the situations happening and when I have that disconnect, it gets hard for me to continue reading since I don't really like the person telling the stories. She gets points for being witty and awesome in a few can't believe that happened moments, but overall it's not a book that will remain on the shelves, but I had fun for the few hours while it lasted. Sorry Chelsea, I guess you were my one night stand as well. 
 Buy or Borrow: Borrow 
 Part of: Stand Alone 
 Also Recommended: For more anthologies I recommend any of Laurie Notaro's books or I was Told There'd Be Cake by Sloane Crosley. Mary Roach's Bonk is also hilarious 
 2 out of 4 happy bibliosnark bookmarks

book_b.title: The Devil in the White City: Murder, Magic, and Madness at the Fair That Changed America
book_b.user_review: Not one of my favorites. It took me a while to get into it. I think I expected more than what I got, and that is why I was disappointed. Its not a bad book, its just not my style.

sample_reviews.review_text: Parts were good, but it was sooooo slow!

RATING: 3 out of 5 stars 
 SUMMARY: This nonfiction work tells the tale of two different men who grow in power during the Chicago World's Fair. One is Daniel Burnham, the architect of the Fair. We follow his struggles to build the fair and his continual work at making it successful throughout. The second man is HH Holmes, who perfected his murder technique using visitors of the Fair. We follow Holmes manipulation of multiple women as he selfishly fulfills all of his desires. 
 REVIEW: I'm going to review this in two parts, since it basically is two novels in one. Daniel Burnham's story easily takes up more of the space of this novel. Larson gives you many very specific details and facts, rattling off people's names so fast it can make your head spin. His section would get me confused at times with the sheer amount of information Larson gave you. However, there are a lot of fascinating aspects to his story. There are so many things in our world that exist because of the World's Fair. I just wish Larson streamlined the story a bit more. HH Holmes' story kept me more interested. We saw the same story play out with different victims. Larson tells you about the multiple women Holmes wed (this was a shock to me) and what he did to them once he was bored with them or they served his purpose. It rarely went into super graphic detail, however I felt Larson should have explained Holmes hotel more. This is what connected him to Burnham/ the World's Fair and I felt I didn't know enough about it. I think this book is marketed as telling a lot of Holmes story, when in reality it did not. Overall though, I did enjoy it, it just moved a bit slower than I would have liked.

Fascinating! Can't believe that this is a nonfiction book. Love the simultaneous story of the world's fair and the life of H.H. Holmes - so great that Larson chose to highlight something that many people have heard of, but few people really know about - particularly how influential and lasting the impact of the Fair really was, and how enormous. 
 Can't wait to delve into Larson's other works next.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Terrible. The descriptions were overly gory and disturbing. I was so turned off that I was nauseated. I should have thrown it in the garbage. Why are serial killers glamorized?

After reading Larson's "Dead Wake," I knew that I would find his other works to be equally enlightening. I found the pages of "The Devil in the White City" to be packed with historical information. I had no idea how much of our American culture, inventions, and traditions were founded during the Chicago World Fair. Nor, how many famous individuals and businesses were involved in this massive undertaking. I won't deny that there were parts where the details of what went into the constructing of the fair were a little too in depth for my taste and at moments found myself losing interest. However, it seemed that whenever my loss of interest began to occur, Larson would transition into the unveiling of the life led by sociopath, Holmes. His story was eerily captivating and gruesome simultaneously. Overall a very fascinating read.

nonfiction about building of Chicago World Fair and a serial killer in Chicago at the same time. Alternating chapters of the architects making the fair and the killer killing. killer killing was entertaining but those chapters were always very short compared to the endless stuff on building boring fairs. got kinda interesting in the end once the fair actually opened. mark this one down as a disappointing recommendation from Ashley. Her stock is falling

While I appreciate the writing (which was excellent) and the story of the Fair was fascinating, the whole book felt like prologue to me. I kept expecting more (though, to be fair, I read very little historical non-fiction). To his credit, I felt like Larson was somewhat trapped by the facts.

This is a very well researched and well written book. It is an enjoyable read for anyone who enjoys historical non-fiction. It was a little dry for me in places but obviously a really good piece of literature.

Oh, man. This book was so frustrating for me. I first learned about H.H. Holmes through an episode of Haunted History, and his story is strangely fascinating. So I picked this up thinking I'd learn a lot more than I could in a one-hour TV show. I didn't, though. I still liked the parts about the architecture of the World's Fair, especially at the beginning when there was more of a balance between the two subjects. However, the book is called "The Devil in the White City," not "The White City That the Devil Passed Through Once and Was Barely Connected With His Murder Spree." Just very weighted to the fair with no revelations about Holmes himself, which I would have been okay with had the book been presented differently. If you wanna write about the World's Fair, just write about the World's Fair. 
 Mostly, what bothered me was Larson's writing style. It's very fictionalized--to the point of sensationalism. It's already a story about a guy who built a murder castle. It doesn't need any further sensationalizing. There were a lot of moments that made me think, "How could Larson possibly know that?," which pulled me out of the story. Perhaps I went in with my hopes too high.

The book is really about 70% history of the great Chicago Worlds' Fair and Exposition and 30% crime novel so if you're looking for the straight crime thrill, you'll probably be disappointed. But, if you love history, this book is for you. You'll like both parts. 
 This book marries the amazing Chicago Fair and Exposition of 1893 (dubbed the White City) and the tale of one of the most prolific serial killers in US history (Herman Webster Mudgett/H.H. Holmes). 
 While I was completely amazed by the history of this book, I wished there had been more information about Holmes/Mudgett. I am not a literary rubber-necker but his brief history did not satiate my curiosity about this little-known man. In all, though, this was a fascinating book and completely captured the magic and hope of the time, a period of time when Chicago came into its own as a city. It's hard to imagine it was ever second-class. Some other things hard to imagine? 
 So many momentous things came from the fair--it was the first time moving pictures were shown; Nikolas Tesla displayed his lightning coils; the first zipper was showcased; the first electric kitchen was debuted, with an automatic dishwasher; Aunt Jemima's Pancake mix was introduced as well as Shredded Wheat, Pabst 'Blue Ribbon' beer and the Dewey Decimal System. What's more, Walt Disney's father helped to build the darn thing; L. Frank Baum visited; Columbus Day was instituted and AC current was used for the first time. Can you imagine a world without any of those things? 
 The author is a true master of his work, weaving between the two story lines and showing how this serial killer could not have become the monster he was without the Chicago Exposition, a fair that showcased all of what was brilliant and evil about man.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Imagine you're a 8-year-old girl and a lecherous older man reaches toward you, intending -- well, nothing good. You lash out at him and he falls dead at your feet. From that moment, you're feared and shunned for your special talent: killing. 
 Thus is the life of Katsa, niece to the king of Sundoria. She is a Graceling, a child born strongly talented in at least one way. Gracelings are easily identified by their eyes, which are two different colors. Easily identified, in Katsa's case, means easily ostracized. It doesn't help that her uncle uses her to abuse and frighten those who cross him. 
 With few friends to call her own, the appearance of Po, a Lienid prince and a fellow Graceling, shakes her world. He's gifted at fighting, which means he can hold his own against her. Somewhat. But Po's gift goes beyond mere fighting, and Katsa's discovery of its true nature -- and her decision to accompany him on his investigation of his grandfather's kidnapping -- changes both their lives. 
 "Graceling" stuck with me. Katsa starts as a wounded, half-formed character who is so frustrated by her life that she can't even put it into words. She hates what her uncle asks her to do and the lack of control she has over her own life, but she sees no way out: 
 "Who are these fools who continue to resist Randa's will? Haven't they heard the stories? Don't they know he'll send me?" 
 "Isn't it in your power to refuse?" Po asked. "How can anyone force you to do anything?" 
 The fire burst into her throat and choked her. "He is the king. And you're a fool, too, if you think I have choice in the matter." 
 "But you do have choice. He's not the one who makes you savage. You make yourself savage, when you bend yourself to his will." 
 With the slightest nudge from her friends, she breaks away from her uncle's control and blossoms into a pretty kick-ass heroine. It takes the better part of the book, as it should. All the while, Cashore avoids the temptation of letting Katsa slip into more traditional female roles -- she doesn't come to relish pretty clothes or getting dolled up, nor does she relent on her determination to remain unmarried. It's refreshingly true to her bone-deep and oft-repeated desire to never let another person dictate her fate. 
 Some stories look like they'll be a light, entertaining read and leave you considering, seriously, what it would be like to walk in their characters' shoes. "Graceling," to my surprise, was one of those books. 
 "Graceling" is listed as a young adult/children's novel, but the writing and the handling of some pretty mature themes make it an enjoyable read for adults. Teenagers/children reading this book will encounter at least one obvious, but not graphic, sex scene.

The first thing I thought while reading this book was that the style wasn't that good. I blamed it on the French translation, though, and kept on reading. The story in itself isn't really original, and it seems like Kristin Cashore just chose to follow the "rules" on how to write a fantasy novel - which seems to be quite trendy nowadays, using the same basic figures, revamping them and embellishing them. In some cases, it is a success, in others, the book just "vaguely seems" like something that you've already read- In this case, I would tend to choose the latter. 
 However, I wouldn't say that this book was disagreeable, or that I really disliked it. The characters, even though I wouldn't call them complex, still have a certain depth -Katsa's rashness and stubbornness, for example- 
 All in all, if this book doesn't stand amongst my favourites, it is nice to read something that doesn't demand concentration and intellectual effort. It makes a good read for a sunday afternoon. But if you want to read good fantasy, it isn't the first book that I would recommend.

Graceling is about a world wherein some people are born with special talents. They are marked with eyes that are two different colors, and are known as Graced. Katsa has the Killing Grace. What she chooses to do with that grace is the source of this story. Strong female characters (although Katsa can be a little dense at times-- she doesn't like "feeling" things and doesn't know her own mind), some romance (the love interest is actually interesting!), and lots of action scenes. Dialogue is not great, but I don't expect that from fantasy novels. 
 notes: there is sex in the novel, so I would say 14 and up.

sample_reviews.review_text: Got halfway through and couldn't go on. It was somewhat nice as an audiobook to listen to as I drove around Ireland, but it was hard to follow and not quite what I was looking for in a good travel book.

Rutherfurd has done it again; perhaps not as well as before but his batting average remains impressive. 
 The Princes Of Ireland is not a novel you'll devour in a single night--some might; most of us are slower readers. It undertakes to give us the panorama of Irish history from the time of the Druids down to the reign of Henry VIII, replete with love, lust, battle and political intrigue.
I really like the history of Ireland and these time periods in particular, but this book was just too slow and disjointed for me. I'll just have to find other books on the subject.
long, dull.

 I was a bit disappointed that until the point where I stopped, there were no explicitly homosexual characters. Not a one in eleven centuries, y'all. Like, the single mention of it was when a monk character was being cruised by some of the other "sinful monks" who were "going down a dark path." Please! Using homo monks as a means of emphasizing how noble and chaste a character is is SO 1960s and just sick. 
 Otherwise, if you want to read a textbook on Ireland with a bunch of flat characters who ultimately just disappear when the author skips centuries, read this book. It has like a million 5 star reviews so don't take my word for it.

reference_books.title: Blood Song (Blood Singer, #1)
reference_books.review_text: When I started this book I immediately felt as though I had skipped a book in the series, like there were big chunks of information that I should have known, but didn't. There were so many characters being thrown at me that I started to forget who people were. Then there were all the "by the way" moments. Like, "by the way, I can see ghosts." and "by the way, you're a siren." and "by the way, your best friend who we never even met and don't really care about is dead" . It was like the author(s) couldn't decide which direction to take the story, so they went in every single direction all at once. It made for one big, hot mess. I'll admit that it was interesting enough to keep me reading, mostly because I had a bunch of questions that I wanted answers to. Unfortunately, those answers never came which was unsatisfying and disappointing. Even though I'm kind of OCD about finishing series, I don't think I'll be continuing this one.

reference_books.title: Once Dead, Twice Shy (Madison Avery, #1)

reference_books.title: Murder on the Orient Express (Hercule Poirot, #10)
reference_books.review_text: This was one of the first Agatha Christie novels I ever read and it's one of my favorites. book_a.title: Black Coffee (Hercule Poirot, #7)
book_a.user_review: I was going to skip this one because I had read some of the reviews beforehand, but my OCD kicked in and I read it anyway. Poirot, the curious little Belgian detective, becomes a rather mundane Englishman and Hastings is little more than a cardboard cutout, smiling idiotically in the background. I was not impressed by this novelization.

sample_reviews.review_text: intrigued by idea of making an old play of Christie's into a novel. Read it with a weird fascination about how bad it could be. has a sort of interesting twist at end.

Black Coffee by Agatha Christie (play script) adapted into novel form by Charles Osbourne is story number seven on the reading order list I'm following. This story to me felt like what can be best described as a game of Clue. Yes, the famous board game. As the novel opens, no crime has been committed yet and it takes eight chapters for a lead character to appear in the book. To me, this was a wee bit to slow and could've been trimmed down. In some respects, I felt the case was to simple for a great mind like Poirot. However, this could've been because I've read a great many Christie novels at this point and know how well she can twist and turn the climax of her narratives. This might be because Osbourne didn't quite translate the play well enough or the play had to be simple for it's audience to follow. I figured the ending out far before it came which made the last third a slog to get through for me. The characters had the typical Christie vibrance and were a true bright spot for the story for me. Black Coffee was still great it just at times felt like a Poirot paint by numbers. Black Coffee like the drink is strong, but sometimes bitter going down. I am still glad I read it though, and it gets a solid 4 Goodreads stars (3.5 really). Peril at End House is next up in the Poirot series and I can't wait to get there!
A play featuring Hercule Poirot turned into a novel by Charles Osborne. Well, all I can say is, he shouldn't have.

Well......Its a good read. 
 You can finish this in one sitting. 
 Now as far as the plot is concerned it fails to grip the reader... 
 It seems as if you have seen a similar storyline in some other works of Agatha Christie....... 
 Please note that this book was earlier a Drama by AC. It has been novelised by Charles Osborne......

Although Black Coffee had all the standard Christie tropes, it fell flat. Somehow neither the characters nor the crime were as interesting as usual. Once I remembered this is, in fact, an adaptation by another author, it began to make sense.

Sir Claud Amory has telephoned Poirot. A famous physicist, he seems to think that a member of his household is trying to steal an important secret formula from him. This formula, if placed in the wrong hands, could cause great harm. Will Monsieur Poirot come down to Abbot's Cleve? 
 Poirot, he will come down. But before he arrives, Sir Claud is found dead. Dead in a locked room with half a dozen other people in it... 
 Also, the plans have been stolen. Who could have taken them? The secretary? The mysterious Italian friend of Mrs. Richard Amory? Mrs. Amory herself....? Poirot takes on a case in which almost each suspect had the opportunity to steal and kill. But which of them did it? 
 Discussion. 
 I purchased Black Coffee thinking that it was an Agatha Christie novel. Wrong. It is an Agatha Christie play which has been adapted into a novel by Charles Osborne. 
 It's amazing how easily genius can be taken for granted - until it is suddenly removed. Black Coffee has made me appreciate Christie's real novels, because this one, sadly, is not up to standard. Here's why. 
 The story was originally a play. I love plays. I think they're wonderfully fun to read. But there is nothing worse than a novel which feels like a play. And this novel did. The way the movements of the characters were described felt exactly like instructions from a play. [exit, left stage] Also, the actual setting of the story hardly shifted - in one scene (yes, scene as in play scene) we are at Poirot's flat. The next scene we are in Sir Claud's library. We stay in the library. Characters move in and out. Just like a play. It feels awkward. 
 Then there's the description and conversation. Christie has the wonderful talent of explaining things subtextually. She does not need to hit you over the head with information to have you know it. She glides it in. Osborne engages in major head-hitting. And then there's the dialogue - it, too, feels playsy - information is stated which would have felt more natural had they been conveyed in the form of description - but this was too busy describing the all-important movements of the characters. 
 All in all, Black Coffee, at least in its novelized form, is not a favorite for me. 
 Conclusion. Read Murder on the Orient Express and The Murder on the Links. Read Black Coffee only if you're desperate.

I'm not much of a mystery reader, but I've never read Agatha Christie and I wanted to, so thus, this book. I read the first fifty pages in a flash. This is not what I'd expected from Agatha, I thought. This is light reading. Lots of dialogue, minimal action. 
 As I looked more carefully at the book, I found out why. Despite the enormous AGATHA CHRISTIE written on the front cover, Black Coffee, the book, was not actually written by Christie. It is derived from a play Christie wrote, but it was actually written as a book by someone else. 
 So, have I read Christie or haven't I? I think not. I must still seek out a Christie for the whole experience. Black Coffee was watered down Christie.
Not the best of poirot cases, i admit. the plot is predictable. This book is only for those who love Poirot and do not want to miss out on any of his novels.

So here's my problem; why on earth there this line "...took some tablets from ** pocket and dropped them into the cup ** was holding" in the very beginning of the story? 
 I feel like reading the rest of the story after that scene is useless.

Perhaps because this one was adapted into a novel from a play by someone other than Christie, this one doesn't seem to have the same feel; it comes across as quite flat. The material is still there, though; a decent read for Christie fans.

book_b.title: Hercule Poirot's Christmas (Hercule Poirot, #20)
book_b.user_review: It's no secret that I love Agatha Christie. Not only does she know how to weave an excellent mystery, but her ability to create characters that you can't help but love to hate is superb. This is one of the novels where that talent shines especially bright. The ending was definitely one of Christie's most creative and is sure to shock the reader.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Read under the alternate title "Murder for Christmas." 
 It's far from Christie's best book, or her best puzzle, but it's a solid read, albeit on the weaker end of the spectrum.

Es sollte eigentlich ein langersehntes Familientreffen auf Gorston Hall werden. Der alte und gebrechliche Vater und Herr des Hauses mochte all seine Sohne noch einmal an Weihnachten um sich haben. Denn wer weiss schon, ob er das nachste Weihnachtsfest noch erleben wurde? Allerdings herrscht unter den einzelnen Familienmitgliedern kein eitel Sonnenschein. Niemand ist mit den anderen wirklich grun und jeder hat sein Steckenpferd zu tragen. Als dann an Weihnachten ein Mord geschieht, beschuldigt jeder jeden. Doch wer war am Ende der Tater? 
 Da meine Ausgabe keinen Klappentext besitzt, konnte ich mich vollig unvoreingenommen in die Geschichte fallen lassen. Allerdings muss ich sagen, dass das Kriminalistische, sprich der Mord, recht lange auf sich warten lasst und man schon von vornherein zu wissen glaubt, was passieren wird. Zumindest erging es mir so. Leider konnte mich das Buch auch sonst kaum von sich uberzeugen. Es las sich zwar recht flussig, aber war leider nur wenig spannend. Erst ganz zum Schluss gibt es doch noch einen kleinen und einen grossen Aha-Effekt, was ich wiederum sehr gut fand. Aber dennoch konnen diese das komplette Buch nicht mehr aufwerten. Ich habe durchaus schon bessere Bucher rund um Hercule Poirot gelesen.

An enjoyable time in a classic Christie setting: a big house with a limited list of suspects, each of whom had a reason to wish the very disagreeable victim dead. 
 This would have gotten 4 stars from me were it not for the wince-inducing dialogue given to the victim's Spanish granddaughter, Pilar. Not all things in Christie age well!
A closed room murder, a family gathering at Christmas, and Poirot's little gray cells at work, what more is needed for a good Christmas mystery!

This was excellent. It was a real treat. It's felt like at times I was playing the game clue. The ending was quite a surprise and as usual to Christie form very pleasant. She really does an excellent job.

A classic murder mystery with (as the author herself says) 'lots of blood'. A locked room mystery with a very limited circle of suspects. The crime seems preposterous and almost impossible, occurring in a very tight time window. The investigation is satisfactory, but what stands out is the identity of the killer and the final explanation. They are surprising and yet satisfactory. Summing up, a good and quick read.

This is my first Agatha Christie book ever. It was silly and felt like watching an old movie. Some of the editing was imperfect and the punctuation choices were odd. Still, I really enjoyed reading it because it's a classic and now I can say that I've done it. I may even read another.

Skip this one completely.
