reference_books.title: Paperweight
reference_books.review_text:
DNF at 50% 
 It's a shame that a book with this beautiful of a cover didn't really do much for me story wise. I'm not going to write a long and lengthy review as I usually do, because I didn't finish this book. I wasn't interested enough to continue reading. I picked this book up because that cover was too gorgeous to pass up, and because I'm intrigued by stories that deal with different types of mental illness. This book deals with a lot of graphic content, which is expected. It's about a girl named Stevie who gets put into a rehab facilitation type of place for her eating disorder, and she decides on the 27th day she's there she is going to kill herself on the anniversary that she killed her brother. It wasn't the darkness of this book that bothered me, because I read plenty of dark books that deal with dark subject matter, but it was the way Stevie narrated it. She's one of those characters who try way too hard to not care about anything. She's aggressively rude and annoying to everyone in this book. I know this is the behavior that put her in this rehab place in the first place and I should've expected this, but I don't know. I just can't stand Stevie's narration in this book. Even in the flashback scenes her narrations are just boring and dull. I don't really know how to explain it. Maybe it's just me. I gave this book 2 stars as opposed to 1 because this book has potential and somebody else would probably like it but it just wasn't for me.

reference_books.title: A Million Dirty Secrets (Million Dollar Duet, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This book could have been so much better if Delaine hadn't been such an annoying character. I literally couldn't stand her throughout most of this book. She has a bitchy attitude and the nicknames she gives everything is annoying. Who the hell names their vagina "Double Agent Coochie"??? That was really stupid and it made me cringe every time that nickname came up, which is every 2 sentences. 
 This book has had a lot of comparisons to Fifty Shades Of Grey, and for the record, Noah Crawford is way way way better than Christian Grey in my opinion. I didn't like Fifty Shades of Grey at all, but this book is different and I feel like Noah is actually a sweet and decent, while Christian Grey was just a controlling, disgusting freak. I couldn't stand him. So I did enjoy this book much more than Fifty Shades Of Grey. 
 I gave this book 3 stars because I enjoyed Noah's character, he intrigued me and I was curious to know more about him and why he is the way he is. He is the main reason why I enjoyed the book, since Delaine was so annoying to me. I don't think I'll be continuing this series.

reference_books.title: Landline
reference_books.review_text:
This is my 2nd time reading this book, and it makes me sad to say this but I didn't enjoy it as much the second time around. I still love Rainbow Rowell's writing, and I think she has really realistic and relatable characters, but this time around Georgie kind of drove me nuts. I know sometimes people say reading a book at the right time in your life can have an affect on how much you enjoy it, and I enjoyed it a lot more the first time I read it three years ago. This time around it was okay, definitely more of a 3 star than a 4 star. I kind of felt bad for Seth and at times I was hoping Seth and Georgie would end up together (even though I read the book before and I know how it ends.) But I think Seth deserves better. Neil can also be an asshole at times and I guess I don't really see what Georgie sees in him. She spends most of her time with him forcing him to talk and he never smiles and he's always grumpy and he seems perfectly fine without her and it just rubs me the wrong way. I adored some things about Georgie and Neil's relationship, but most of it was so toxic and they just don't seem like a good match. She's too dramatic and obsessed and he's too emotionless an robotic and as they say in the book: it's a tragedy that the funniest girl in the world is married to the guy who never laughs. I could appreciate some of the cute moments in this book, and I love that there's an LGBT character in this book, but honestly the best thing about this book is when Georgia meets Cath and Levi at the airport, and notices that they're engaged. A glimpse at Cath & Levi from Fangirl was easily the best part of this book. I don't know, I guess this time around I just didn't enjoy Georgie and Neil as much this time around. I still love a lot about this book, just not as much as the first time I read it. I also thought it was really offensive when Georgie says kids don't need a Dad as much as they need a Mom. It's so inconsiderate and rude to say that to Neil, and so untrue. I just thought it was really immature on her part. 
 _____________________ 
 My first review: 
 4-4.5 STARS 
 I had the honor of winning this book in a giveaway on Good Reads, (THANK YOU SO MUCH). I adore Rainbow Rowell's writing style and her characters and everything about her books. Although I didn't like this book as much as Fangirl, I still really really loved it. I feel like I would appreciate this book a lot more when I am older and married, but even now I understand that marriage is difficult and has it's ups and downs. This book had so many beautiful quotes and beautiful moments that made me teary-eyed. I will admit, this book started off pretty slow for me, and I kept putting it down, then picking it up a few days later. After about 100 pages in, the story finally started to pick up and I couldn't put it down. After I passed the 100 page mark I finished the rest of it in one day. Even though Neal could be a dick at times I still really loved and admired his character. I love how he calls her sunshine and how he says "I love you more than I hate everything else," and how she wakes up in the middle of the night to jot down a script idea, and Neil tells her he will remember it the next day, and he writes it for her on the bathroom mirror in the steam from the shower. Their relationship was just so adorable and I like the alternating story lines from the past and the present. 
 Through the entire book I was rooting for Neil and Georgie to be together. I loved all the cute moments in their past that Georgie would reflect on so often. It was so beautiful to watch their relationship develop and grow, and I was actually surprised at the twists towards the end because I wasn't expecting it. I also loved all the scenes about the proposal and when she's having the babies just because I'm mushy like that and I love reading about things like that. Seth's character was so funny and I really enjoyed every scene he was in. 
 Since this book takes place around Christmas time, it would probably be better to read this in December instead of summertime haha. But I really did enjoy this book and I loved all of the characters. Rainbow Rowell has a beautiful way with words, and I always love her books.She writes the most relatable characters I've ever read and I really appreciate that. This book will be added to my all time favorites shelf, and I definitely plan to re-read this someday down the road. 
 I also wanted to add that for some reason I kept picturing Seth as Zac Efron (because she constantly mentions how sexy and attractive he is, and that he's a blue eyed brunette so..) and I pictured Georgie as Rose Byrn for some reason. I'm not sure why. And I pictured Neil as Jake Gyllenhaal because of the comic strips and his character in Zodiac, I don't know.

reference_books.title: Always and Forever, Lara Jean (To All the Boys I've Loved Before, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
Closer to a 4.5 stars 
 Gosh, these books get better and better with each one. I loved To All The Boys I've Loved Before, and then I loved P.S. I Still Love You even more, and now I think this one is my favorite of the three of them. I just love these characters, I love Lara Jean and I relate to her so much. I know some people say she's "childish" but honestly, when I was in high school I was exactly like she is in this book. I love her older sister Margot and the way this book shows their relationship and how it's difficult to stay close when she's away at college. I love Lara Jean's Dad and seeing him finally settling down again and being happy with someone. I love Kitty, Lara Jean's little sister and her sassiness and watching her grow up in this trilogy. I have a really special place in my heart for this family and I adore them all to pieces. 
 "She always picked love; she always picked adventure. To her they were one and the same." 
 I love following Lara Jean through her senior year of high school, with all the highs and lows and stress of getting into college and making plans for the future. It was all so exciting and it made me feel so nostalgic for when I was in high school doing fun things like prom and planning for college and all that. Lara Jean is an extremely relatable character for me, in this book especially. Like when she is on the bus and all their friends start playing "Never Have I Ever" and she starts freaking out because she can't leave and she hates playing that game because she's never had sex or done drugs and that's all anybody cares about. SAME AF. I love the way she handled peer pressure from her friends and I love that even though her and Peter have been together for over a year they still haven't had sex. I think that's so realistic for a lot of real life teenage romances, and it goes to show you can still have a great YA romance with no sex. I loved all the scenes with Lara Jean's Dad and his wedding to Trina! All the proposal scenes and the bachelorette party and wedding planning and the wedding itself was so much fun! I loved seeing Margot visit the family and the tension with her not feeling included anymore. I loved the struggle of Lara Jean debating whether or not she wanted to go into college with a boyfriend. I feel like if I had a serious boyfriend in high school, I would be debating the same things she did, since her Mom said it's never a good idea to go to college with a boyfriend (which I do think is true.) 
 "One day all of this will be proof, proof that we were here, proof that we loved each other. It's the guarantee that no matter what happens to us in the future, this time was ours." 
 I am probably one of the only people who loves this series but still doesn't like Peter... It's like he grows on me sometimes and then he'll do something that pisses me off and I go back to not really liking him very much. He's just so.... ehh. After three books of Lara Jean + Peter I'm still convinced that Lara Jean deserves better. He just constantly disappoints me. Like when she was ready to give him her virginity and he totally blows her off.... and starts arguing with her like what??? And he gets all offended when she puts her education before their relationship like I'm sorry... what's more important? Don't you want her to have the future she wants and go to the college she wants? Idk he just got so selfish at times. When she made him the french toast after they had a fight that was mostly his fault and he barely even noticed and said he can't because he's on a diet, I nearly lost my shit. So uncool. 
 "I guess that's part of growing up, too--saying goodbye to the things you used to love." 
 I just love this series and I'm going to miss these characters so much. Is it so much to ask for a new series that follows Lara Jean through her years of college? I would love that. I just want to read more about Lara Jean and her family. Even one more book that takes place in ten years when Lara Jean is an adult and Kitty is graduating, that would be SO COOL. I miss these characters already.

reference_books.title: 99 Days
reference_books.review_text: This book is one big no. It was so bad. I only made it to Day 34, which was about 100 pages in before I decided I had enough of this bull shit and I would prefer to not waste any more of my time reading this. Molly is an inconsiderate asshole and she's one of the most idiotic characters I've ever seen. Often times I found myself wanting to slap some sense into her because she apparently has none. This is the second book in a row that I've read that involves a love triangle between one girl and two brothers. Like what are the chances? The only thing worse than a love triangle is a love triangle with two brothers that destroys their relationship for life. I don't like Gabe. I don't like Patrick. And most of all, I don't like Molly. Even though Patrick and Molly were in this crazy "first love" relationship, they literally had no chemistry at all. It kind of defeats the purpose of everything. And the chemistry between Gabe and Molly was pretty much non-existent as well unless you consider lust as chemistry (I don't). The characters are supposed to be 17 or 18 years old but they speak and act as if they are 13 or 14. It sucks too because I really had high hopes for this book and I wanted to love it. I even had it on my Most Anticipated Books of 2015 list. I hate when books disappoint me like this. Overall, this book is a waste of time and Molly will repeatedly make you roll your eyes and feel disappointed.

book_a.title: The Sun Is Also a Star
book_a.user_review:
4.5 stars 
 "Everything happens for a reason. People say these things to make sense of the world. Secretly, in their hearts, almost everyone believes that there's some meaning, some willfulness to life. Fairness. Basic decency. Good things happen to good people. Bad things only happen to bad people. No one wants to believe that life is random. I am a realist. It's better to see life as it is, not as you wish it to be. Things don't happen for a reason. They just happen." 
 I wasn't expecting to love this book as much as I did. This book was like a breath of fresh air. This book inspires me so much and I absolutely love Nicola Yoon's writing style. I read Everything, Everything last year and I wasn't a huge fan of it, I thought it was just okay. But this book is easily a new all time favorite of mine. This book follows a Jamacian girl named Natasha whose family is getting deported in twelve hours. She wants to be a scientist and she doesn't believe in love or God or anything really except or sceince. I really like Natasha's character because she's so strong and she's such a realist and she is desperate to have a future in America. On the day her and her family are being deported she meets Daniel, a Korean-American boy who is a hopeless romantic and a poet and he's rebelling against his family's wishes for him to become a doctor. I love Daniel's character because he's so optomistic and he believe sin love at first sight and he doesn't really know what he wants to do with his life at the age of seventeen years old. 
 I really appreciate the diversity in this book. I've never read a book like this before, a person of color and a korean. I just love seeing diverse books like this in YA because there isn't nearly enough of it. This book reminds me a lot of Eleanor & Park, not only because Daniel is asian just like Park, but because of the way the chapters are written from both characters perspectives and the chapters are short and sweet. It also reminds me of November 9 with the way it follows a couple who meets and falls in love on the same day. The one down side of this book is that it has some serious insta-love. I usually roll my eyes at insta-love but this one was just written so well I honestly believed it myself, which is crazy for me because I hate insta love 99% of the time. 
 I love how Daniel believes in love at first sight and how he tries to use sceince to prove that love at first sight exists. I love one of their first converstaions in the cafe when Natasha says love doesn't exist. It reminds me of that scene in 500 Days of Summer when he tells her love isn't like Santa Clause, love exists whether we want to believe in it or not. I love the way the romance is written, it's so passionate and beautiful and it never feels forced. With beautiful quotes like this: "Touching him is order and chaos, like being assembled and disassembled at the same time." 
 I also love how well-devloped their families are, and each member of their families have fleshed-out, interesting back stories. I especially enjoyed the back story with Natasha's Dad and his dream of becoming an actor and how their whole family suffered because of his unwillingness to let go of that dream. I also loved seeing the relationship with Daniel and his older brother Charlie who is a complete douche bag, and Daniel's Father who desperately wants him to become a doctor and be successful in life. His father is protective of him and doesn't want Daniel to grow up poor like he did. I love getting to read from the perspective of two families who moved to America to start a new life, and the struggle of never truly feeling accepeted in a new country. Daniel talks about how his parents want him to act more Korean but everyone else expects him to act "more American". It's such an interetsing perspective. 
 This book brings up a lot of things I think about a lot. Daniel doesn't know what he wants to do with his life and he questions why should we know what we want to do with the rest of our lives at seventeen years old? I completely agree and relate to this, as I felt the same way at seventeen. It also talks about fate and coincidence and whether or not things happen for a reason or if things just happen. I like this quote: "Life is just a series of dumb decisions and indecisions and coincidences that we choose to ascribe meaning to." In a way I think that is true. Maybe things don't happen for a reason maybe things just happen and that's life. 
 I also liked getting chapters form random characters that would appear throughout the book. Like Irene, a security guard at the building Natasha is going to. It's so increidbly random and at first I didn't like it, getting random chapters from the perspectves of ranodm characters - but some of the short stories were so interesting and heart breaking. I like the idea that every single person around us is living a life as complex and vivid as ours. I'm a curious person and I always wonder about other strangers lives, so to actually get little glimpses of the strangers in Natasha and Daniel's lives is really interetsing. I love that Irene's character is who brought them together in the end. Natasha saved Irene's life years ago in New York, and now in a way it's like Irene is saving Natasha's life, by bringing her and Daniel back together. It's such a beautful full circle. I also loved the side story with the lawyer leaving his wife for his paralegal. I loved how Hannah, his paralegal talked about how she wanted to be like a fairytale and then her final chapter was: they all lived happily ever after. I also love that scene where Daniel and Natasha both see a flash mob on the subway and as a reader you are hoping they see ecah other, but they pass right by each other. I also love their first kiss scene when they are singing kareoke. That is one of the most passionate first kiss scenes I've ever read in a book and I enjoyed it a lot. I felt so bad for Natasha's family at the end when they did end up getting deported. I thought the pacing of the last two chapters was weird, considering almost the entire book took place in one day and then those last chapters skipped ahead by five years or so? And then THAT ENDING. I almost threw the book across the room. How could it just end there? I was so shook. It was beautiful but tragic at the same time. 
 Overall, I'm very impressed with this story. I'm still shook by that ending, and I can't even believe it ended like that. I really love this story and I will read anything Nicola Yoon writes. Knowing this story is personal to her because she is a woman of color who is married to a korean makes it even better. We need more diverse books like this in YA (and in general). I just really like books that make me think about life and force me to consider things I never thought about before. I will be thinking about this book long after I finish reading it. This book is just insanely beautiful and I recommend it to everyone.

sample_reviews.review_text: Bought this on holiday after finishing all the books I had brought with me, I was really desperate and I would probably never consider a book like this otherwise... god I am sorry it wasn't my thing

BLAH, I hate it when I'm against the current and judging from all the 5 star reviews for this book, I know I'm part of the minority that didn't like this book. 
 First off, I want to say that I didn't have super high hopes for this book b/c I didn't like Everything, Everything; yet, so many people loved this book that I thought I would give the author another chance. Besides, it was just one book, so I tried to go into this one with a clean slate. I have to say that aside from the cover being gorgeous (really is eye catching), I like the formatting of Nicola Yoon's books. Her chapters are shorts and we are able to get multiple perspectives, which makes the story more grand and interesting. I wasn't super invested in Daniel or Natasha's chapters, but I really did like Kingley's chapters on his past. It's weird to think about parents having their own lives before us, and in Kingley's chapters that is exactly what he confesses to the readers. He did have a life before getting married and having kids, and he had big dreams as well. It was really touching to read about his struggle, and to understand that a decision can both be the best and worst choice you've ever made, at the same time. 
 I also liked the chapters on Daniel's parents, and their struggle with being immigrants in America. I definitely related to Daniel when he was talking about how his parents were so focused on giving their children a better future, that they didn't bother to get to know them in the present. I used to get really annoyed with that as well, but I know my parents do it because they want what's best for me and I think that is what Daniel realizes as well. They want a better life for their kids, a life their parents couldn't provide for them, and to do that they sometimes have to turn into people they didn't want to be. 
 Okay what I mainly didn't like about this book is the exact same reason why I didn't like her first book-the insta-love. This is probably one of the most used/annoying tropes ever-it gets me every time, and not in a good way (obviously). I'm all for a good romance, but I don't like how some authors glamorize attraction/lust and call it love. Most of the people reading this story are young adults and they are going to think the next person they make eye contact with is their one true love. Love takes time, you have to know someone fully before you can say that you love them. For Natasha and Daniel to spend a few hours together and then claim they are meant to be is unrealistic, and is a cheap way to write a romance story. Don't even get me started on that epilogue though -___- I'm not saying that there is an age limit for falling in love and finding the right person, but this is a story I couldn't take seriously because it is so unrealistic and extremely, extremely cheesy. 
 Mild Spoiler Below 
 I also didn't like how this book in a way romanticized adultery. I understand that people fall out of love all the time, but the way this book was written made it seem like cheating is an okay thing to do when it's not. It's fine to leave when you're not happy, but to try to break up a happy home all because of selfish needs is horrible and shouldn't be glorified in any way. This part of the story really irritated me as well because it's basically saying "what I want is the most important and I don't care who I hurt in order to get it." I hope people won't take away the wrong message from this situation. 
 All in all, I think I have to throw in the towel for this author. I had the chance to meet Nicola Yoon at a signing and she's so sweet and funny, so I really wanted to like her books because of that. Yet I've always been an advocate on separating the author and his/her works, which unfortunately in this situation I had to do. 
 Maybe I would have liked these unrealistic, angst-y romance novels back when I was in middle school/high school but for where I am now, it just makes me cringe a little...

When I reviewed Everything, Everything, Nicola Yoon's other book, I commented on the sparseness of the cast but how it all balanced out anyway. I really liked how in The Sun Is Also a Star that the peripheral characters in Natasha and Daniel's day also have their own little chapters summarizing their stories, pulling their motivations and reasoning into the narrative. 
 I didn't know what this book was about when I got it -- I just knew that I liked Everything, Everything and had been recommended Yoon's second novel -- but it seemed especially important now, as Natasha's story as an undocumented immigrant facing deportation unfolded. Yoon is wonderful with voices and characters. My only issue that kept tickling the back of my mind was that this ~*~love~*~ was so sped-up. It was a whirlwind 12 hours. And I kind of get it in a way, having experienced a date that went on for continuous days, but it also felt really constructed in this novel. That's my only criticism, really.
Sweetly adorable but also so, so real as this book deals with tough topics. The writing style is fantastic. Absolutely loved this book.

Reading this book is like skipping all your meals for the day, and then once you start reading...you gulp and gulp, intoxicated by the loveliness of the feeling. 
 Yoon nailed it. 
 I was really, effing scared and fascinated by the prospect of this book and she slayed it. In my humble opinion, it's way better than Everything, Everything. 
 Will my students like it as much or better? Probably not. 
 But as an adult, I appreciate the romanticism and longing and disappointment of this complicated love story on a much higher level. This made each twist and a turn so delicious. I simply cannot fathom that Natasha and Daniel are not real. 
 Daniel is one of the most amazing, male characters that I've ever read. He's lyrical and loyal and earnest and touching and tender and endearing and naive and brave. 
 Natasha is fantastically crafted and so stoic and complicated and forceful, too. 
 I loved al the unique points of view. I loved the humor and the softness. I.Loved.It.All.
This was really good. Let me just honestly say that this is something I would totally be reread. This book made me laugh it made me cry and it made me realize the meaning of love.

"God is the connection of the very best parts of us" 
 Daniel, a Korean American, is gearing up for his big interview for admission to Yale, pressured by his parents after his older brother is suspended from Harvard. Natasha is struggling to get her family's deportation revoked after her dad tell's an officer their whole story during a DUI. When their stories cross, Daniel sees it as fate and thinks it is a sign that they are meant to be. Natasha, a skeptic, doesn't believe in fate and tries to push Daniel away - why would fate bring two people together only to have them forcibly apart in less than 24 hours? 
 --- 
 Honestly, I didn't have a whole lot of thoughts or expectations about this book going in, which was probably a good thing. This felt like a very typical contemporary YA novel - boy meets girl, fall in love, problems ensue, someone they overcome the odds and end up together again. The writing itself was beautiful and I thought that the characters that were chosen were what set the book apart from other YA books but didn't get to the point of being gimmicky. I personally think that the book would have felt more real or satisfying without the last chapter, because the ending, to me, felt kind of forced to give the reader a happily ever after, but just read kind of awkward to me. While I liked it, it's not something I would want to re-read, but I would recommend to people who like contemporary YA novels or novels with non-white lead characters.

This book was a major disappointment and the most pointless story I've ever read. 
 The characters were impersonal and mostly dislikeable even all the side characters were completely screwed up. The insta love was the most ridiculous and unconvincing one I've ever encountered and the whole story was completely unrealistic (way too many coincidences) and entirely pointless since in the end nothing had been achieved. 
 The way the Korean family and Korean culture and language were depicted displeased me greatly and the random use of Korean words was ridiculous (also please learn to transcribe correctly!) Furthermore, wtf was wrong with Charlie?! I didn't get him AT ALL. His whole point was being an asshole and having a fucked up life and a fucked up future. Congrats. 
 I've never read a story with such unrelatable and weird acting characters. And if you've ever wondered how many stereotypes about Koreans can fit into a single book, this one gives you the answer: ALL of them! -.- Can't believe nobody here is criticizing that. 
 Also the topic of immigration isn't discussed properly and just plays a background role. 
 I guess I will never read a book again by this author. I actually would love to shred this one into pieces but I'll refrain... at least the cover art is decent.
I loved this beautiful little book. Despite some quirks that stuck in my craw, I thought it was hopeful, structurally inventive, and lovely.

book_b.title: Wish You Were Here
book_b.user_review:
I love Renee Carlino, Before We Were Strangers is one of my favorite books of all time, so it kills me to say I really didn't like this book. A one star review might seem extremely harsh, but I honestly couldn't think of one thing I actually liked about this story. This book follows this girl named Charlotte who is a waitress in Los Angeles, randomly one night she meets this guy named Adam who recently quit his job as a lawyer to paint full time. They share one night together, and then he acts weird the next day and they lose touch. Seven months later, she is still hung up on him (even when she casually starts seeing someone else), and then she finds out why Adam was acting so strange with her. 
 Charlotte is one of the most obnoxious, judgmental, selfish protagonists I've read about in a long time. She was constantly bitching about something, and her attitude and judginess really got on my nerves. She judges people over the stupidest shit all the time: for example, she's always judging "dog people" and she does it more than once. Like excuse me, what the fuck is wrong with liking dogs? She also judges someone for still being in college at the age of twenty-five. She judges her best friend for wanting to do something spontaneous and romantic even though she LITERALLY DID THE SAME SHIT WITH ADAM. She only thinks about herself, and is constantly bitching about how hung up she is on Adam and treats Seth like shit. She bitches about how much it sucks to be rejected by Adam and then literally does the same shit to Seth all the time. I just couldn't fucking stand her. 
 Not to mention, Adam and Charlotte's first night together was totally cringe-worthy and ridiculous and he was giving off so many red flags and he was way too forward for a first date. I didn't think he was "charming" he was actually giving me really creepy vibes but of course our protagonist thought he was just so cute. Charlotte keeps commenting on it too, in her inner dialogue, she's wondering why he's so strange but she just chooses to ignore it and have sex with him anyways because that is totally the right thing to do if someone is acting strangely. 
 This book tries to be like Me Before You and I couldn't stand that book either, so I guess that's another reason I didn't like it. So Adam is dying of a brain tumor, and now she wants to take care of him and act like he's the love of her life even though she's technically still only known him for a day. It was just so cringe-worthy and insane. I didn't feel their chemistry at all. Also, Seth was nothing but sweet to her and her constant attitude towards him really got on my nerves. Like he's a baseball player, he's sweet as fuck and he's patient with her and all her Adam drama bull shit. He's way too good for her. I skimmed from the halfway point to the end because I honestly couldn't give two shits about Charlotte and her dramatic life, so I skimmed to the end and I was not shocked to see the story line just get even worse towards the end. She marries Adam and he dies, and then she goes back and marries Seth, like wtf? Seth deserves better than that bull shit. 
 It fucking sucks because this was one of my most highly anticipated books this year and Renee Carlino is one of my favorites, but this book was a fucking mess. I could not stand any of these characters, especially Charlotte. I am so disappointed, I never thought I would hate a book from this author, but I do.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I'm completely confused as to whether I loved this one or not. 
 I'm pretty sure I loved it but the whole middle was the kind of story I usually stay away from because I'm just not a fan of sobbing over sad things in books. I like happy. But even though this had that thing (I'm trying not to spoil) I liked it. I cried and it bummed me out for a while but by the end I felt...i don't even know, hopeful? 
 so. yeah. little confused after this. I can say I loved the writing as always and I really did like the characters too. They were real and I always enjoy that. 
 wow. this is a terrible review and I'm sorry!

This book completely and utterly blew me away. It demolished my heart in the most raw and honest way, but it also slowly and surely pieced it back together. Wish You Were Here was so emotional and moving that I'm still struggling with my thoughts and feelings, long after finishing the book. 
 There are very few books that I have read where I have loved each and every character and am rooting for them to thrive and flourish. Yes, the story centered on Charlotte and Adam, but there were also many incredible secondary characters as well. Renee Carlino has created quite the cast in this book, each with their own individual journey to embark on. The genius, however, is that this motley crew will feel so familiar and relatable to your own life. I thought of my own brothers, parents, sisters, friends, and lovers as I read this book. I'm still in awe at how accurately and honestly the author captured these emotions and experiences. 
 Wish You Were Here isn't simply a girl meets boy love story. It's also a story of connection, understanding, friendship, growth, death, timing, and of truly living. You will cry as your heart breaks, but even through the sadness, there is beauty and hope. We watch our characters rise up and grow and are left feeling a little lighter and optimistic. This is definitely one of the best books I have read in a very long time. While reading, I was often reminded of a line from The Summer Day by Mary Oliver, 
 "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" 
 You don't want to miss this poignant and thoughtful book! Another truly stunning masterpiece from Renee Carlino. 
 *I voluntarily read an advance reader copy of this book*

Ugh. I had a lot of problems with this book. I read it very quickly in two sittings in less than 24 hours. It does read well. It's not boring. The beginning was very intriguing which I think is why I kept reading it. But by the end I was skimming just to be done. I had been meaning to read Renee Carlino's books for a little while. Didn't know which one to start with I chose this one because the synopsis did sound really good. This review has a ton of spoilers in it so fair warning now. If you really want to read this book and don't want to be spoiled and know important plot elements please don't read below. 
 **************** 
 We have Charlotte a protagonist I really liked mostly because she was a damn mess and it's really refreshing to see a main character in her twenties who doesn't have her life together. Charlotte meets Adam and they have a really weird and sweet night together. When we are first introduced to Adam he seems kind of spacey. He doesn't remember much. I figured this might be like a 50 first dates situation where he has a short term memory problem. After spending the night together Adam is weirdly pissed at Charlotte and she leaves. Charlotte then joins match.com meets a nice guy there and he stands her up. Flash forward six months. She meets match.com guy again who is a hot baseball player. He's super boring and I don't really care about their relationship but I'm sticking around to see what happened with Adam. Charlotte goes on a wild goose chase and eventually meets his neighbor who in turn tells her Adam has a brain tumor and is currently dying in a hospital. 
 This is where I start to not like this book. And here is my very long list of reasons: 
 1. Cancer as a plot device. 
 That is so overdone at this point like can we not? Didn't Nicholas Sparks already beat this dead horse enough? I also really hated that that was like a twist. If I had known going in that this was a cancer book I wouldn't have read it. Both my mother and my grandmother died of cancer so I have a really hard time romanticizing it. 
 2. Manic pixie dream boy. Oh, my god! Adam was the epitome of the MPDB. He was spontaneous and weird but he's also hot and rich and in his final days he takes Charlotte to France and teaches her to sail and they fly on private jets and have an on-call doctor. Um...seriously? Like I said romanticizing cancer. Also I felt like the only purpose Adam served was to develop Charlotte so she can 'find her way. Like wtf? 
 3. The other dude. So like at first I was indifferent to him. He seemed fine but I knew he wasn't the star of the show here so I didn't get attached. But then after the dude dies she meets this guy again and oh they get married...awww. Are you kidding me? 
 I honestly do not know the point of this book. I really regret reading it. I wish I hadn't wasted my time.

5 freaking [?]'s !!!! What can I say Renee does it again . This story gave me all kinds of emotions that I never think I will never forget . I think I will never be as strong as Charlotte and with all the things she goes thru and still stays strong and never gives up . Everyone should experience this wonderful love story .

2.5 stars. 
 This felt like a "Me Before You" rip off except the guy has cancer (yeah, shocker). 
 I'm sort of a fan of Carlino's novels but this felt cliched and really disappointed me idk why. 
 I didn't like how Charlotte led Seth on while she knew she was in love with Adam and technically cheated on Seth as well. Yeah, not my cup of tea.
This was a very moving and wonderful story. All about living life to the fullest, loving, dreams, and heartache. I loved the characters and found the plot to be original with some romantic cliches.

"Love is a wordless secret; it's an inside joke. Only the two of you have to understand it." 
 There was not anything obviously wrong with this book. There are stories that you connect with and stories you don't. This one was a story I just didn't connect with. 
 Charlotte, main character, is hard to like. She's not nice and completely irresponsible and her frustration at having a paying job with descent hours that she didn't like was equally frustrating and eye rolling. 
 Neither Adam nor Seth were interesting. The conversations felt fake and forced. Her best friend is awful. I wish I'd liked it more.

Normalmente antes de leer un libro leo algunos reviews para guiarme un poco y saber con que me voy a encontrar posiblemente. sample_reviews.review_text: Very bizarre idea, but oh, so cool. I had it on my Caldecott hopeful list. I'm not usually a big fan of clowns... but this warmed my heart.
Sweet.
Wordless book. A little clown falls from the circus train. A farmer finds him and takes him in. It changes them both as they figure out how to fit together.

The illustrations are all black, white and brown - except for the red of the little clown, the farmer's long underwear, and a checked tablecloth (and of course the circus train). Don't miss this one! 
 Fall 2015 - tried it on a whim with Ben and was thrilled when he "got" it - "he's sad" on the face-washing page. 
 June 2017 - Ben chose it again and totally followed the story. He especially liked the hat swap at the end (but kept calling the clown a mermaid!)
I love this! A great word-less story about an unlikely friendship.

Even though, I am only giving this 3 stars; it is definitely a Caldecott contender. A young clown is thrown off the circus train into the Amish looking farmer's field. What will happen next? This could be a great story for making and checking predictions.

A feel good picture book.

book_a.title: This Star Won't Go Out: The Life and Words of Esther Grace Earl
book_a.user_review: I cried during the introduction... Need I say more

sample_reviews.review_text:
As a parent, I found it extremely difficult to read this book. Esther...beautiful, smart, creative...gone WAY too soon. I had to stop reading this book after every couple of pages, just to let the words sink in..the art, the prose...the truth. Esther was the truth. She was strong but she was a kid. We have to remember she was a kid who dealt with the blow of sickness, cancer. It's devastating to read Esther's words, to know she was so talented and was fighting for a life. You can feel the torments of adolescence in her words, even while she is smart enough to access her medical situation as adult-like as possible. 
 Everyone should read this book. I find myself questioning humanity almost every day. Why can't we be good to one another? Why do so many feel the need to be hateful? Esther shows us the good in people, the strength, the power of hope we can instill in others. Truly a heartbreaking story but also a must-read.
Rest In Awesome Esther

This novel was inspirational, and I liked the introduction by John Green, as well as the fact that Esther tried to stay positive even through her struggles, but through the novel, you were able to tell that she is definitely sad, definitely worried about when her life may end, but her relationship with her family and friends, as well as God gets her through it. The fact that she wrote the words, and nothing was manipulated made it more inspirational. The only thing is that sometimes her writing felt so repetitive that I had to put the book down, read something else or do something else, and come back to it.

This book was honestly one of the most incredible and personal things I've ever read. I wish I got to know Esther in her short time on this earth, as she was such an incredible girl. She impacted the Nerdfighteria community in such a huge way, and this star certainly will NEVER go out. <3

Como les digo en todos lados yo no me creo ser "fan" de John Green ni tampoco de sus libros porque no me terminan de sorprender y de cerrar. No digo que sea el mejor autor del mundo como la mayoria de sus fanaticas porque creo que hay autores mejores. 
 En fin, les contare como descubri el libro de Esther. Lo conoci cuando salio en espanol y Me gusta leer Espana lo anuncio en sus redes sociales y comento en grande que ERA LA VIDA DE LA CHICA QUE INSPIRO A JOHN GREEN A ESCRIBIR BAJO LA MISMA ESTRELLA. Yo estaba como si nada y jamas me entere que el autor se haya inspirado o algo por el estilo, la editorial lo tenia y lo fui a buscar. Punto. 
 Por otro lado los bloggers hispanos agasajaban el libro y yo no sabia si era por el mismisimo Green (porque en esos momentos no me terminaba de cerrar) o porque escondia una gran historia llena de emocion. 
 Muchos de nosotros estamos acostumbrados a leer tipos de novelas que vienen de la mente de un escritor que en la mayoria de los casos son pura ficcion. Pero cuando nos encontramos algo escrito desde lo vivido y desde el momento suele chocarnos y ponernos a pesar "esto de verdad paso..." o "esto es real, totalmente real". 
 Una estrella que no se apaga no habla solo de esa inspiracion que tuvo el autor de Bajo la misma estrella, sino de la corta vida de Esther Grace Earl una chica que a los 12 anos le diagnosticaron Cancer. Esta no es una pelicula o un libro que tiene ficcion, sino es algo real que existio y permanece vivo en miles de personas que a penas conocemos. 
 Esta chica llamada Esther lucho contra el cancer por mucho tiempo y luego fallecio en el ano 2010. A lo largo de esta especie de biografia tenemos partes del diario suyos, entradas que escribian sus padres en un blog dedicado a ella durante su corto tiempo de vida, cartas de amigos y familiares, textos hechos por amigos y un monton de cosas mas que nos cuentan que hizo Esther. 
 Esther fue una chica normal: rio, lloro, se deprimio, tuvo amigos, amo y todo lo que hacemos normalmente los humanos. Fue una chica con gran corazon y un gran luz que al parecer aun no ha dejado de brillar (segun lo dice el libro). 
 Es un libro que te choca porque no cualquiera puede sentirse un hombre de piedra leyendolo. Yo cuando lo empece a hojear decidi dejarlo porque me deprimi de lo que leia, pero lo retome mas adelante para ver como estaba compuesto. La vida de Esther no es una historia de ficcion, repito, es real y paso hace casi 5 anos atras. Es dura y es una batalla que tuvo que enfrentar ella y toda la familia. 
 A mi parecer es un gran libro porque tiene eso de ponerte a pensar sobre lo que ocurre en el mundo: No solo el Cancer esta en miles de personas, sino que hay otras enfermedades que profunden la misma tristeza. Es una novela fuerte y que quiza deberia leerla mucha gente para entender lo que esta pasando en el mundo y para tener una vista mas abierta. 
 Yo tengo casi 17 anos y se que hay chicos que se estan muriendo con Cancer, pero leer este libro me ha abierto la mirada porque creo que no todos sabemos exactamente como sucede o como actua. No todos tenemos familiares con esta enfermedad o con otra, pero les digo que si todo el mundo leyera este libro u otro que sea parecido tendriamos una mirada mas abierta. 
 Por otro lado el libro nos demuestra que la esparanza y el amor siempre estan presentes en el aire. Nos ensena a querer y a mirar mas lo que tenemos al lado y a disfrutarlo. Tenemos que vivir la vida como si fuera nuestra ultima semana de vida porque es una bomba de tiempo. Quiza lo mas poco que tengamos sea lo justo y necesario para vivir y ser feliz. 
 Esther y su historia me dejaron demasiado perpleja que a la hora de terminar el libro me quede mirando a la nada pensando. No puedo transmitirles todo lo que siento pero les aconsejo que dejen el miedo de lado y leanselo. No importa la edad que tengas. 
 Por cierto: Me molesta la gente que lo lee porque cree que todo esto tiene que ver con Bajo la misma estrella. Okey, puede que un poquitin, pero Esther es Esther y Bajo la misma estrella es Bajo la misma estrella. Los que buscana el enigma de Bajo la misma estrella (No se cuantas veces escribi ya Bajo la misma estrella en este parrafo) no se van a encontrar con lo que desean. 
 Se van a encontrar con la historia de Esther que segun todo lo que lei fue una gran chica y creo que si la conociera seriamos grandes amigas. Me han encantado sus escritos y su forma de ver el mundo que tenia. Me habria gustado saber de ella cuando estaba viva y me alegra que su historia haya ayudado a cientos de personas... porque sinceramente ella es una estrellla que no se apaga... y nunca lo hara. 
 Si sus padres llegan a leer esta resena dejenme darles las gracias por hacer llegar esta historia a mi manos :) 
 Una estrella que no se apaga es la viva historia de Esther Earl compuesta por partes de su diario, historias y cartas que nos llevan a conocer lo que fue su vida. Fue una nina bella y muy animada que creo que a muchos nos hubiera gustado conocer. Es una historia real fuerte y que te golpea, pero te dejara pensando y encantado.

I originally had no intent of purchasing or even reading this book when I entered the book aisle of Target. Not to say I was against it, but I simply had not considered it. The photo on the front drew me in and I found myself flipping through the pages and before I knew it, reading the book, right there in the middle of the aisle. I felt compelled to buy it so I could finish it. I'm most certainly glad I did. The story of Esther is both touching and inspiring. Reading her writing made me feel like I knew her; I wish I had. I have a feeling we would've gotten along. I love reading the work of other young writers, so this book was great for me. It even encouraged me to get back into my own writing, something which I've neglected as of the last few weeks. The story is a sad one, and I couldn't shake a feeling of inevitable, impending doom while reading it. But input from Esther's family not only added to the personal feel of the novel, but put a hopeful spin on it. They all seem like extraordinary people. The only downside to the book was sometimes I missed some of Esther's references-but hey, what would you expect when reading someone else's diary? With this book on shelves, this star truly won't go out.

I normally don't write reviews about the books I read but I really needed to put my thoughts down in words for this one. I consider myself a nerd fighter, I hold the opinions of the Green brothers to very high esteem, and I do find Esther Earl to be a interesting person that I would have definitely gotten along with as a young tween/teen. I also wanted to check out the book about the girl who was an incredible influence on John Green's best seller "The Fault in Our Stars" 
 Now onto this book. This book, as most of you know is the compilation of Esther Grace Earl's life during her fight with aggressive thyroid cancer. That being said, its a compilation. Its literally just a pile of semi-organized writings/photographs from both Esther, family, friends, and doctors. Its kind of just a mish mosh of everything her parents could dig up and hand to the editors. Also, the overall style of the book looks like this project was headed by a tween. Yes, the book is about a teen/tween but it just makes the whole thing seem immature or just overall off. It was just too cheery. Every page is a different color and the stars theme is incredibly heavy handed throughout. It's almost like if you slapped Lisa Frank stickers all over an edition of Anne Franks' Diary. I'm not saying those girls are the same or that Esther Earl comes even close to the impact of Anne Frank, I'm just using the age and gender of the two people as a comparison. 
 Yes, you have to take at face value that she wrote these things at a very young age and that like most individuals at that age, the writing is all over the place and left me constantly groaning. I wouldn't want to read my diary from those times It is cool to read the progression of someone evolving as a person but even still...we all sucked at that age and our writing reflected this. Tween/Teen years are a purgatory of suck that we can one day climb out of and Esther is not immune to this. I feel that its hard to even critique it because its about a girl with cancer. That being said, sweet christ, did this book feel so forcefully inspirational and pandering. I get it, she had cancer and she fought bravely til the end while Its almost as if the publishers and Esther's family are shaking their love of that girl in your face while shouting "DON'T YOU SEE HOW IMPORTANT SHE WAS TO US?". 
 As a reader, I don't have the emotional attachment that her family,friends, and doctors have/had to her. I didn't watch Esther struggle so there is a point where it becomes so hard to relate to. I didn't know Esther and I'm also past the point in my life where I can identify with the tween/teen issues Esther was dealing with sans cancer. It's obvious that this was edited to be a symbol of hope for those who read it. Shes credited as the main author...but she didn't edit it. Her parents did. Even if she was actually like this when she was alive, Esther Earl is just too damn perfect on page. Even her worst days are filled with saccharine sweet inspirational quips and personal examinations of faith/her relationship with God that always end positively. I just don't see how her story is more stand out than the millions of other young adults/tweens/teens that are suffering with cancer. 
 Overall, I understand why people have been raving about this book but it is not my cup of tea.
There's really no way for me to review this book without sounding like a heartless asshole - so I won't. Didn't care for it, that's it.

I feel very unempathetic writing this, but c'est la vie. This book started off wonderful. I loved the forward from John Green, enjoyed hearing about Esther, the time line, treatments, enjoyed her mom's Caring Bridge entries, but after a while it was just overkill. It became very mundane and I was no longer as interested. It could have been much shorter and still made the same point. This is one of very few books I would suggest skipping around as a strategy.

My low rating of this book should in no way be interpreted as a statement that the book is not worth reading. It has merit; it just failed to connect with me, personally, on all counts. I would recommend it to anyone whose experiences with serious illness are limited, in that it helps the reader to understand that people who are terminally ill are not defined by their struggles. I would recommend it to young people in general, as they may be more accustomed to the writing style than I am (this book is, after all, largely comprised of journal entries and letters; While I respect the intent to preserve Esther's work as close to its original form as possible, I am old and curmudgeonly, and I found the inclusion of the natural "ums" and smiley faces distracting). I would recommend it to people who have a religious faith that they identify with, because those readers will be more inclined to connect with the religious aspects of the book. I think that my limited pre-existing knowledge of Esther Earl hindered my reading experience, as well. If you know her well, or if you know nothing about her at all, your reading experience will probably be much richer than mine. Going in with a little bit of knowledge was, in my case, very damning.

book_b.user_review: It was just so long. There was no emotional connection between the reader and the character. I shouldn't have finished the book. The plot twist was indeed massive. However, at that point I couldn't care less about the characters, the plot twist, or anything else Card threw at me. sample_reviews.review_text: Cracking coming-of-age story, set against the background of a fierce battle for survival for mankind.

I couldn't finish this book. The writing was mediocre at best, the characters uninteresting and unrealistic, the plot completely devoid of any actual conflict. There was nothing happening that Ender, the bland, gary stue main character, couldn't solve within a page or two. 
 Other than that, I decided to read the book because I thought the movie was sort of decent and since usually movies are worse than the boom, well. You can see my reasoning. Turns out the movie was only decent because it took out all the misogynistic, xenophobic, racist, and religious content from the book. I'm not sure why anyone was surprised that Orson Scott Card is a nasty homophobe. 
 Since this is considered a sci-fi must read, it seems to me the sci-fi community should up its standards.
Excellent book. I loved that nothing was as it seemed. I really want to read the other Ender's books now.
thought-provoking!

I enjoyed this book. After a long stint of reading only non-fiction, and studying for the degree, it was night to spend an evening an relax with this book. I might have to say that, like eating the first meal after a 24 hour fast, my pleasure in reading might have been affected by the desire to just cuddle up with some good fiction. 
 There were several components from this book that reminded me of "The Power of One," though it was definitely more mellow in terms of the tortures Ender went through vs. Peekay. The perpetuation of the "genius" stereotypes/tropes also doesn't sit too well with me, but nevertheless, I also derived some merit from the actions of the main characters.
Simply one of the greatest books in contemporary literature.

I had to finish this book because I'd like to see the movie. I saw the same flaws that those who hated the book did, but I don't hate it. It was okay. I am pretty disappointed in Card, though. He writes a lot of books on writing, and based on the advice he gives, I thought he'd be a better writer. 
 Why I didn't LOVE it is this: 
 1. The book is extremely repetitive. From the Battle School games to the simulator on Eros, the entire book was a repeat of this or that. It got dull, but I trudged on anyway. 
 2. Except for Mazer, who only wished to prove a point instead of hurt him, Ender always won. He was too smart. He was more-or-less a prophecy child. I'd hate to say this. The people who know the word might object, but I believe Ender is a Sue. He has no flaws. In fact, he's pretty flat as a character. The only thing that gives Ender any dimension at all is 1. His fear and hatred of Peter. 2. His love of Valentine. 3. That he doesn't want to hurt people or be manipulated (but does anyway). 
 3. The ending was very anticlimactic. I kinda liked the last chapter, but the battle with the Buggers? Ugh...I swear I blinked at the page and wanted to shout, "Really!?" 
 As for the Demosthenes and Locke chapters...kinda pointless. 
 I'm kinda curious about the rest of the series. Where could it go? But I probably won't read it. I think the movie will be good, and hopefully will give more dimension to the characters, but I don't think I'll read anymore Ender.
I loved it. One of my favorite sci-fi books ever. Ender Wiggin is so funny, innocent and charming.

I seldom read sci-fi. I'm more of a fantasy girl myself, as for some reason I can imagine magical worlds better than futuristic ones. I find sci-fi worlds a bit cold and lackluster, and the idea of aliens is just too farfetched for me. But elves and wizards and fairies aren't. Weird, I know. 
 But this book just blew me away. I can't help but empathize with its main characters, as alien as their world might be to me. And by the time I reached the ultimate twist, all I could think of was "What the WHAT?!?" I almost threw away my kindle in surprise. 
 So Ender's Game certainly changed my outlook, and I can't wait to get my hands on the next book! And the next sci-fi series!! I've got a lot to catch up on.

book_a.user_review:

 Shusterman is a consistently inspiring author, and I can't wait for the third installment!

sample_reviews.review_text: I actually thought this book was a great follow up to UnWind... i really enjoyed the intertwining story lines, and the climax was fast and emotional. The unfortunate thing, now, is waiting for the next book.

Unwind enthralled and infuriated me. I was totally satisfied with the conclusion and did not need or expect a sequel. Nonetheless, when I heard a sequel was forthcoming I preordered it. Other reading obligations left me no time to read it when it arrived, but this weekend I finally took it in hand. Wow! Shyster an weaves together many threads from the original, adds a new villain, and provides plenty of twists to keep fans reading. My only quibble is that tree is no real conclusion. Readers cannot walk away from Unwholly and be wholly content to let the story end there. I can only say, please write quickly, Mr. Shyster an. I need to know!

This was an enormous disappointment for me. I had really waited for about a year for this one to come out, and read it within a few weeks of it's release. Maybe my expectations were too high? Or maybe the author was just phoning it in on this one. 
 Something which struck me immediately was that the first chapter summarizes this hero-esque unwind and his brush-with cum escape-from the cops, life on the run, and then winding up at the graveyard. In the first book, that took two thirds of the book, and was very detailed and interesting and involved developing characters and relationships. In this book, it's simply a chess move: setting up the board for later action. 
 And that's what makes this book disappointing - the conflicts appear contrived right from the start with these magically placed - or literally manufactured, even - people, and there is no actual character development. 
 And it continues to get worse until the final scene in which it becomes obvious that this book is a holding action for some grander battle or comeuppance that clearly is about to happen - just after the final page.

A visceral and intellectual sequel of the first order; I loved the first book and although I was skeptical it truly surpassed my expectations. Shusterman expands enormously upon his original plot, weaving the most insignificant of details into fully-fledged sub plots. Alhough it works as an action-packed dystopia series, it loses some of the allegorical resonance of the original, foregoing existentialism for sci-fi intensity. Some of the details, like the Frankenstein-esque character of Cam, showed real promise, but never fulfilled their true potential. Again, I have to mention my disappointment in its dismissal of the abortion-issues it so deftly paralleled the last time; this time around "unwinding" just felt far less likely, if still equally terrifying.

Danger! Danger - this is a review of the Audible version of "Uglies" by Scott Westerfeld. If you want to read a review of the printed or Kindle Edition, there are plenty to choose from - folks that see the story as commentary on all that is wrong with 21st Century American to those who simply cannot endure another dystopian love triangle. Take your pick. 
 My lament is with the narrator's voice in the Audible Edition - Carine Montbertrand. Somehow Miss Montbertrand has decided that all teenagers need to blow their noses, and so she has depicted every character with renditions of a shrilly head-cold. I highly recommend the Kindle Edition instead so you can create your own voices for each character. Because once you spend 12 hours listening to these teenage whines - shrilly and slightly congested for Shay, morose and nasal for Tally, sulky and overly-tired for David, Cruella DeVille meets Gilbert Gotfried for Dr. Cable - you will never again be able to enjoy these characters.

I've wanted to read the Uglies quartet for years, ever since they showed up on my little sister's shelves. The series takes place in a post-apocalyptic society where all of humanity is gathered into a few independent cities. In every city, when citizens reach their 16th birthday they undergo a surgery to change them from "uglies" into super-model gorgeous "pretties". There is, of course, a catch. Both the catch and most of the other plot points were quite predictable, although the motivations of those in charge surprised me; I just don't feel like they got enough out of it. But the idea was novel and I appreciated that. The world was also very well developed and the details of the procedure by which people became pretty were fleshed out enough to make it very believable. 
 Read more here...

 The other characters are just as bad with the only interesting one reverting to type over the same, completely under-developed boy. 
 And the writing is just awful. Not Stephanie Meyers disturbing, but still annoying. I want to send the author a thesaurus with a note thanking him for making it clear that the setting is in the future by putting "hover" in front of everything (hoverboard, hovercraft, hoverstruts).  Finally, the book doesn't even live up to its main goal of commenting on societal norms and the perception and definition of what is beautiful. It really offers no argument against conforming toward the mean,and, therefore, ends up subtly supporting it. 
 Waste of time. Waste of neurons. Waste of paper.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Although the ending of this wasn't quite what I wanted it to be, I thoroughly enjoyed this book and look forward to reading more of Cat Clarke's books. Although it's quite a simple story once you've read it all, it seems quite confusing and complicated when you start reading it - just like how Grace feels. With her pen in hand, she slowly unravels her story and more and more secrets and lies are unfolded. I loved the Grace spoke, the witty sarcasm a constant. Ethan is a character I would love to learn more about but he serves his purpose and does it marvellously. 
 For a debut novel, this is one of the best I have read. Cat Clarke presents a world with is mixed up, confusing, full of sex and bad language but beautifully written, very vivid and moving too.

If only I could rate a book on the cover alone. I think the cover is gorgeous. The story? eh not so much. I really liked the beginning and I thought I was really going to like the entire thing, but it fell flat for me in the second half. I knew what was going on right away and it was just dragged on and on and on...the ending came and went and I was like "thats really it?" oh well. I hate endings like that though!

ENTANGLED is author Cat Clarke's debut novel. It is the story of Grace, a suicidal teen, who suddenly finds herself being held captive in a white room by a mysterious man named Ethan. She is supplied with a table, paper and pens. She has no remembrance of how she arrived in this room. She decides to make the best of the situation and writes down her complicated life story. 
 I picked up this book because the cover intrigued me, and I felt like reading something contemporary. The book is gripping and intense. As it starts out, Grace has been abducted and I was worried about what might happen to her. As she sits down to write her story I became increasingly interested in her messy past and what led her to contemplate taking her own life. 
 Grace as a character is complicated and rough around the edges, yet vulnerable at times. She is a party girl and drinks, sleeps around and cuts herself. She does not have much in the way of family support. Grace has never had many friends before she meets Sal, who she begins an intense friendship with. Grace is a mess and heading on a downward spiral when she meets and falls hard for Nat. She feels that her life is turning around and that she has it all with her loyal best friend Sal and gorgeous boyfriend Nat. 
 The story is told in first person and is difficult to read sometimes, as Grace's head is a dark place to be. The plot is full of pain and teenage angst, and Grace is brash and tough. I did ultimately feel sympathetic towards her, though her manner makes it hard at times. The character of Sal seemed well intentioned but I did not feel that I got to know her that well. Their intense friendship and falling out is one of the major themes of the book. Nat and Grace have a torrid love affair that makes Grace feel wanted and loved, and hopeful that her life is turning around. Nat's brother Devon is a breakout character who I wish would have appeared more in the book. 
 The white room scenes helped to move the story along and provided a break between the flashbacks. These scenes and the character of Ethan kept me guessing what was going to happen next. 
 It is hard to put this book down once you are getting close to the end. The story has many twists and turns and surprises. Although I did have an idea how it was going to end, I still enjoyed the book to its conclusion. I liked this debut novel and felt that the author nailed Grace's troubled voice, and also succeeded in sharing the intensities of friendships and relationships, and depression. The writing is well done, with a thoughtful and consuming plot. Recommended for older teens or adults due to the explicit themes. 
 ENTANGLED is a British novel that has not been released in the US. You can find it through Alibris or Amazon Marketplace.

*THIS ISNT MARKED AS CONTAINING SPOILERS BECAUSE I DONT THINK THAT IT DOES. BUT THIS IS A WARNING JUST IN CASE...*

Despite that it was still quite good. It was alarming identifying with the character so much even though she's so different. 
 I felt it ended a little too suddenly, that there should have been more. I even checked to see if it was going to be part of a series (it doesnt seem to be.) because even though you can figure what'll happen next really quite easily and sometimes it's good to let the imagination roam, some time's it's also nice to READ it. 
 The end made me cry, BUT I got rather stuck in the middle somewhere so, 2 stars ^^

Powerfully written and deeply heart-wrenching, but it was far too depressing for me. There is too much hurt in the world to read something so sad...Despite the fact that I had figured everything out half-way through the book, all I wanted to do when I finished it was cry and that's not my idea of a good read.

"in the end it always comes back to me. That's what I'm left with: just me. And that's what scares me more than anything. Me." 
 I hate that I didn't enjoy this one more. I love the cover. I bought this book just for the cover. But I just could not like the main character. It wasn't even her horrible habit of lying about everything - even small things - I just did not think she was a good person. She was horrible to her best friend, horrible half the time to her boyfriend. I didn't understand the relationship or their want to be together. 
 And I felt like the twist was obvious from the very beginning so the rest of the book was just a struggle to get through.

Hated it in the middle, trying to figure things out. Then, as I came near the end, thought(felt) it was exactly how it should be. Good ending. Yet, wanna know more. Cannot talk about it without revealing things about...well, myself. Also, a good mystery. Even though it was a bit predictable. 
 Feel glad to have finally finished it. (Although, it took less than one day; was still exhausted and frustrated while reading and trying to understand what was gonna happen[or rather, what had happened].) 
 I was thrown off by these lines at one point in the book...they made me see inside and understand myself better...and also made me terribly angry for some reason. 
 ... "It's when I'm alone that the doubt sets in. It's been that way for years. As long as there are people around, I can pretend that everything's OK. But I need that audience to pretend for, otherwise it doesn't work. 
 Alone, I'm not that easy to fool. It's not that I mind being alone, not really. I can distract myself with silly fantasies and daydreams for hours, but in the end it always comes back to me. That's what I'm left with: just me. And that's what scares me more than anything. Me." 
 .......... 
 "The memories that seem to get louder and brighter the harder I try to forget." ... 
 I couldn't not finish the book. I still think I hate it, for making me sooooo depressed. But the end made up for it. I liked the bitter taste of the end. It was not a happy ending, or a sad ending. It just was. -_-

From the first few pages I was confused, but so was the main character. The story starts out with Grace believing she's been kidnapped and locked in an all white room by Ethan. The only thing she can do is write about what's happening and what happened in the past. Slowly day after day we start to learn about Grace's life before she was kidnapped including her relationship with her best friend Sal, her home life, and her own self-esteem. 
 Gracie's voice is very real in the way she thought and how she talked. Grace was in, I wouldn't say normal, but realistic life situations that too many teens and even adults have to face. She had many things in her life she needed to figure out and we learned and sorted through those things right along with her. 
 Even after reading the last page, I was still slightly confused. I ended up discussing the book with someone else who had already finished reading it to try and clear some things up. We both came to the same conclusions so maybe Cat Clarke wrote it to be puzzling and didn't write everything out in black and white. While reading Entangled, I kept trying to figure out the significance of the title or if there really was one...I'm still not 100% sure as to why it has that title, but I can think of a couple of reasons why.

Very predictable, was it supposed to be? I knew the "twists" about 30 pages in. Also, I know being preachy isn't really cool in books, but the feminist in me was so disappointed. Girl meets boy, girl can't live without boy, loses all her interests and friends, and *spoiler* Attempts suicide when it all goes wrong? 
 Grace was so brick wall dumb about everything. I get that she had to be thick so that the repression/reveal of the twists works out... But if this was on tv I'd be throwing things at the screen

I hate this book. And I don't say that often. Hell, it's even killing me now typing that about the book. But it's true, because the book was going so well, it was really interesting and heart-wrenching. And then the author suddenly ended it. The book was not resolved in ANY way. SO many important plot questions were left unanswered. Some, I can understand. MOST of them? And the really important ones at that? Please excuse me while I scream with rage and sob helplessly. Because I really did love the book until the end. It seemed as though the author had gotten tired with writing and decided to just stop. Literally, just stopped writing and handed it to the editors. Because what this book really needs is a good two chapters. Or at the very least, a very jammed-pack-with-information epilogue. I have never been more disappointed and angry at a book than I am now. I really, really wish I had never read it. 
 If anyone is offended by my review, I apologise. But please remember this is my view alone, and I am not saying that everybody should despise this book. It's just that I do, very much.
