sample_reviews.review_text: For a paranormal romance, it wasn't truly awful. I liked the idea of a djinn instead of a vampire or what have you. Kind of weird energy sex.

SPOILER, SPOILEEEEEER 
 Guao, la autora mejoro muchisimo en este libro, se siente un crecimiento. 
 Grace es el oraculo pero tiene problemas economicos y tambien con su rodilla por el accidente que vivio con su familia, luego de los sucesos en serpent kiss, se queda con ella un Djin que la vuelve loca, y la saca de su zona de confort ayudandola con los ninos, sus sobrinos y con ella misma. 
 Khalil el Djin que vimos en storm heart y serpent kiss, pero que aca conocemos realmente, es un principe entre su gente, un inmortal. Un genio sin un cuerpo carnal, pero que con Grace cambia su perspectiva del mundo, de si mismo. El comienza a amar a los ninos y a Grace dandoles a los tres su corazon poco a poco. 
 Juntos se enfrentan a las visiones de Grace y la toma de su poder del oraculo, ese reclamo que hace que ella, sea ahora la verdadera duena del poder, es decir es un ser valioso para muchos sobre todo para los djin ya que sana a Phaedra la hija de Khalil, rota producto del secuestro que vivio por parte de su madre. Lo que hace a Grace la salvacion de muchos Djin. Ambos luchan con una comunidad de brujos que no quieren el oraculo y los mismos son culpables de la muerte de si hermana y cunada. 
 Este libro es algo distinto el amor se da poco a poco, las escenas eroticas son mucho mejores, los misterios se resuelven, sin embargo eso de Grace quitandole el poder a Phyton no tuvo mucha explicacion, tampoco lo de el sueno con la diosa del oraculo, la autora deja muchas cosas sin resolver. 
 Sin embargo fue un libro con una trama fuerte, rico en descripciones del paisaje y las emociones. Atrapante, y lleno de amor con los dos ninos de la historia. 
 Grace es una mujer guerrera, no es una damicela y Khalil es un alfa sin ser un grosero y juntos tienen sentido, tienen quimica, tienen mucho para dar a los demas. 
 Recomendado!

I've been enjoying this paranormal series, but I think this book is the best yet. Harrison worked a lot of emotion into this tale of Khalil the Djinn and the human woman who's inherited the mantle of Oracle. Really well done emotional growth, and some great dialogue. I'm looking forward to the next book in the series.
Not for me. I preferred the Wyr to the Djinn, and the other women to Grace.

I had some misgivings about this book I will confess. 
 I really enjoyed the first three books in this series and I was intrigued by Khalil from the first time he made an appearance, no problems there. It was the two children I worried about. 
 I usually don't like romances where there's kids involved. Often they take away from the romantic tension. 
 I shouldn't have feared though. Harrison knows exactly what she's doing and managed to balance the family stuff and the romance in a way that had me totally engrossed in both the romance and the relationship Khalil forges with the children. 
 I really loved Khalil: he's sexy, dangerous, all powerful and still caring and human when it counts. Grace was a bit too hard on him at times in my opinion, but all in all the romance between them was very satisfying to read. 
 Although this story is mostly a story about family and love Harrison also managed to put in a suspenseful action storyline that had me invested as well. 
 So in the end I enjoyed this book much more than I expected and while 'Storm's Heart' is still my favorite book in this series, 'Oracle's Moon' is an unexpected second.
Excellent series fans of pnr should read these

I would like to start by saying that I was so looking forward to this book! A Djinn hottie with an Arabic name and a southern belle? Now that is a book to look forward to! 
 As always and one of the elements that what makes this series so fantastic are the characters. 
 I had fallen in love with Khalil from the time he made his appearance in Storm's Heart and even more when we saw him again in Serpent's Kiss; especially when we find out more about his connection to Carling and that he needed to save his daughter from something. That was my hook and I was so looking forward to knowing more about his backstory and what had conspired. 
 Grace is an absolute gem, true she did have her ditsy moment where she didn't think stuff through but that's part of her character. i love that she generously stepped up and took responsibility when it was given to her, her sister's children. She shows that she does put them first above all else. Though she had not fully embraced her responsibility as the Oracle at the beginning, I was glad to see her growth in that aspect in her life. 
 Sadly there was a missing element in what makes this series so fantastic; world building. We got so much inside into the world of the Wyr and Elves in terms of politics and how their societies function but I felt that we didn't get anything out of the Djinn Society or their politics; there were some but it felt lacking to me, I needed more! 
 Second problem in this book, the plot 
 While the first books had plots that gripped me till the very last word, with impending danger at every corner of our heroes lives; this book felt slow ... there wasn't much at stake; I mean there wasn't much the characters could lose if things don't go their way. Compared to assassination attempts, gang members and a life threatening disease; bills and babysitting don't sound that exciting. True there was a moment towards the second half of the book where things get a little more threatening but it seemed rushed to me, I feel that it could have been done much better. Instead of just babysitting and going on dates, why didn't the book focus on the prophecy that Grace saw? It heavily involves Grace and would have added a lot to the plot 
 What I wanted more than anything in this book was to see interactions between Khalil and his daughter. We not only find out early on that his daughter is physically damaged and his on the verge of being a 'rouge' but we also realize that Khalil's relationship with his daughter is also damaged; you can sense the pain in Khalil's voice and actions about that and you feel that this character wants to fix things with his daughter. We get none of that! None! His daughter makes two appearances and they are both to interact with Grace. I found it to be so disappointing that the only interaction she had with Khalil was just spoken of. I wanted to see emotions and struggles. I wanted to see development in both the relationship between Khalil and his daughter but also wanted to see more development in his daughter as well. She is such an interesting character and it is a shame that we didn't get a lot of her in this book. We just see her being cured at the end, I wanted to see her struggle and get in her head. I seriously hope she gets a book of her own that includes her own struggles and demons as well as REAL interactions with her father. 
 One thing I will say that I am so relieved that Khalil did not fall into flesh! I was yelling out loud to him not to fall into flesh the whole second half of the book. Becoming human will make him loose some of that sexy appeal XD 
 3.5/5 stars

Once again Thea Harrison exceeds my expectations. 
 At first I was a little disappointed that the next story in the Elder Races series wasn't about another of the Sentinals. But, gods, how she weaves this world all together continues to blow my mind. 
 I was so worried about how this story would turn out for Grace (who's the Delphinian Oracle) and Khalil (a Djinn) that I spent way more time reading than I meant to. Oops. I'm not sad about that. The way the author worked everything out had me totally satisfied. 
 Now I have to get my library to order more in this series!
LOVED IT!!
I am biased as all hell, but this is definitely my favorite Harrison book since Dragon Bound.

sample_reviews.review_text: It was ok. I felt like if id read this straight after I read the others I would have enjoyed it more but the big gap between volume 5 and 6 took me too far out of the story. It took me over halfway through to get back into it.
Det forste jeg gjorde etter a ha lest ut denne var a forhandsbestille nesten volum.

I don't read many comic books, but I fricken love Saga. 
 To be quite honest, the only reason I love this series as much as I do is because Prince Robot IV is one of my all time favorite characters. He is flawless because he is so not flawless. And I love love his dialogue. I adore his storyline. He is seriously the best thing ever. So anyway, I have yet to be disappointed in this comic series. My Robot is just as charming as ever. 
 (Okay, I do enjoy all the other characters, and they are all so fantastic. But MY ROBOT).
Oh no. More stuff is getting real. Hazel is so cute!
4.5 stars
Really happy with this volume!! Starting to get even better than before! The end was my favourite part definitely and can't wait to see how this continues.

I will now attempt something more like an actual review. 
 My brother passed me volume 6 of Saga while I was waiting for him to finish work. And we're talking a couple of weeks ago, it was the first time I'd seen or heard anything about Saga. The art and character designs caught my attention first, along with similarities characters shared with people I know, which made me curious. We went straight up to buy the 1st volume and thus it began. After handing it over to my father, I later got an excited text from him once he'd read it. Then I found library copies on Overdrive and since then have been instagraming its beauty and falling apart here on goodreads. 
 So, the initial attraction was art and design. A girl working with my brother had described it as an alien Romeo and Juliet and, on a core level, that's fair. Although this is larger scale differences and none of that suicidal teen malarkey. Two planets (or one planet and its moon) are sworn enemies. United by the power of fiction, two opposing soldiers fall in love and make a baby that stands against everything the war has raged on for, a war that has sucked neighbouring planets into. This is the story of a family built through love trying to protect itself from hatred. 
 There's swearing, robots, gore, heartache, cute things, gross things, twisted things, unfair things. And there's humour and love and, most of all, literature nerds. 
 Oh! And a language that is probably made up but looks vaguely Romanian. It's cleverly done so that it pulls scraps of other languages (maybe it's Esperanto?), and can usually be understood by my weak brain. 
 I love it, it's awesome, I'm forcing it on people.

Still a fantastic series that's entertaining and drives home it's message of diversity and the importance of family (both biological and logical). 
 Can't wait to see where Vaughn takes this story next.

I will love Saga forever. I squealed with delight when this arrived and I devoured it as quickly as possible. I wanted to give it 5/5 just because it is Saga and I love it. But then I ended it just feeling like I wanted more. This felt like filler a little. Even though it wasn't. I just think it is my utter impatience and need for more from this world, these characters and this story. I WILL NEVER BE SATISIFIED!

A roller-coaster of emotions! 
 This series continues to deliver with plenty of gasps, humor, and heartfelt moments. 
 Hazel and her grandmother are separated from Alana and Marcus, as they are prisoners on Alana's home planet. We catch up with Prince Robot is is living on a secluded planet with his son. The Will is drugged out and seeking revenge for the death of his sister. So glad the family is reunited, Marcus and Alana are feeling the romance and expecting another child. We end on a happy note...for once!

book_a.user_review: Hated it. I thought if give Faulkner another go and have decided that my first impressions were right. He's not for me. Ugly storyline. Mostly disturbing and dis likable characters. There were a few intriguing phrases - "emotional barbecue" one example.

sample_reviews.review_text: All the way through, I felt I should be enjoying it more than I was.

While I believe that the Sound and the Fury is still Faulkner's paramount novel, Light in August is a close second and it is definitely an easier read. The tale of Joe Christmas, a half black and white man, who is outside of any society, accepted by no one, and treated as an pariah, is compared and contrasted with the tale of Lena Grove, a pregnant woman who is acknowledged and assisted by everyone and lastly the first two are compiled with the story of Reverend Hightower whose tale presents a kind of powerless southern morals, unable in the face of racism and lack of knowledge to change anything. The ebb and flow of the intertwining stories is classic Faulkner. 
 4 Stars
The best Faulkner ever wrote. That says it all!

There are two kinds of people--those who like Faulkner and those who don't. I'm one of the latter. There's a 1959 movie of the Sound and the Fury though starring Yul Brynner with hair if anyone knows who Yul Brynner was anymore. And there's a screamingly bad movie called Anastasia where Yul accompanies himself on the balalaika--just FYI.

I'd give it five, but wanted to indicate that--for me--it's second-tier Faulkner, which makes it utterly amazing--just not as good as Absalom, Absalom. A problem with stars. The way the mode of storytelling shifts, the intertwining of pronouns with the third-person point of view... these are disorienting, their subtlety packed with what WF learned from his most radical work. Race and sexuality shown as overstuffed with history, so that in this South the past (personal or collective) is almost literally crushing everything. Incredible prose, incredibly disturbing.

I desperately tried to grasp what this author was attempting to accomplish. I endured these ramblings right to the end. I do not recommend this book. Chased too many rabbits in too many directions. Whew! Glad this novel is OVER!!

Okay. Maybe I just don't have the frame of reference to appreciate Faulkner. Maybe I went at this one with the wrong mindset. Maybe it's just generational and 1932 doesn't carry well to 2010. 
 I hated Light in August. It's overblown, tedious, and none of the characters rang true. Every minor tension or imagined slight becomes a lifelong grudge. Everyone is either angry or stupid or both. There's not a single redeemable personality or act of courage to speak of. 
 Pages fly by with nothing happening. Irrelevant streams of consciousness and ponderous flashbacks occupy much of the substance of the book. Overwrought passages distract rather than add ambiance. Example: "It just lay there, black, impenetrable, in its garland of Augusttremulous lights. It might have been the original quarry, abyss itself." Translation: it's dark. 
 I've heard it lamented that many of the classics of the 20th century would have never made it to publication today or would have been edited beyond recognition. After Light in August, I can't help but think that's a good thing.
Absolutely the greatest American novel ever written. Nothing comes close.

It was a school book, I will openly state that first and foremost. But honestly, it was fine, even entertaining, up until the scene where he is caught and has....THAT done to him. Sorry, but I don't recommend this one. It's too graphic.

Club Read: On the Southern Literary Trail 
 Comments: 
 It was only last year that many club readers like myself were looking at 'Go Down Moses', a set of thematically related but chronologically separate stories that Faulkner believed, contrary to all external appearances and the view of his publisher, constituted a fully integrated novel. 'Light in August', which was written before GDM, covers the same geography and many of the same GDM themes but is conventionally plotted, a straight-ahead narrative that relies on defined excursions into the past as a context to the single developing narrative. Why then does the first book have greater continuity, seem more grounded, and feel less fragmented than the second? 
 Chained Links 
 At times, reading LIA feels like following a relay race in which different participants carry the baton separately across different intervals before handing it off to next one down the line. Writing LIA, Faulkner may have been thinking more along the lines of chained links, with each new link in the narrative set off by a change in tone or viewpoint or by the introduction of a new character. It's nowhere more apparent than at the end of the novel. Faulkner first queues up Percy Grimm as the militia commander that kills the mixed-race anti-hero Joe Christmas , then follows with Yoknapatawpha stalwart Attorney Gavin Stevens, making arrangements for Christmas' burial (while strangely voicing God's possible thoughts on the respective curses and blessings on the white and black races), and finally concludes with the nameless furniture salesman amusing his wife with a road story about a peculiar, uneasy family (Lena, Byron and baby), trying to map out, literally and figuratively, the road ahead. Purely on the basis of mechanics, Faulkner generates interest by anticipating the reader's need to see how the new material hooks up with the other plot links. 
 Faulkner's fiction and the fictionalized setting of Yoknapatawpha, on the map 
 Yet, some of these changes in focus feel capricious and arbitrary: why do we need the furniture salesman to conclude the Grove-Bunch liaison when it started out, simply enough, as a plain-faced depiction of Lena walking into the sawmill in search of her straying boyfriend? One moment, we're inside the head of the lead principal, Joe Christmas, witnessing the unraveling of his psyche via an intensely personal interior monologue on his involvement with the Yankee, Negro-loving Joanna Burden, then later we're put by the author at some considerable distance from Christmas -- say about 500 miles -- hearing the story of how he was apprehended in connection with her murder from a nameless Jeffersonian. It's the modernist in Faulkner, I think, playing with my head. 
 Misfits and Miscreants 
 The technique of the chained links helps obscure the fact that, unlike GDM, all the principal characters in the stories, taken together, are a bunch of outsiders, transplants or community misfits of one type or another. We know LIA takes place in the fabled Yoknapatawpha county -- along with Steven's cameo appearance, there's Will Varner's store (from the 'Hamlet') as a noted landmark. Still, this setting or any other setting constructed along the lines of a small Southern town is not fundamental to the writing. Each link in the chain is focused on the stranger that comes to town or the native estranged by the town or in the town, nary a hero in sight. Think of all those fiction reviews in which the critic comes to the idea that a book's ambiance, its physical presence and sense of place and a shared culture, is so powerfully rendered that it becomes as yet another major character in the story. GDM gives us this with 'The Bear' or 'The Fire and the Hearth', no structural chaining required because all the linkages are built into the thematic material. With LIA, not so much. 
 It's not just that Faulkner's agents here have washed up as outcasts. Members in this group seem uniquely qualified by their history and temperament to remain forever separate, broken off not just from community, but from each other and from some part of themselves. With the possible exception of the millworker Byron Bunch, there is no sense in this novel that one character can be changed significantly and permanently by the interaction of another character. Of course, there are reasons for this that go to the heart of the major psychological themes Faulkner is developing -- the alienated self, the psyche crippled and deformed by fundamentalist denunciation of human sexuality, the subtle power of racism to twist identity and distort both who you are on the inside and the need of belonging. But these characters come off the shelf with no attachment DNA and that's limiting for the storyteller interested in character psychology. Beyond the basic premise and the fleshing out of the dynamic, there's no place for the author to go that will lift the characters up from the vortex of emotional suffering to the higher ground. As a result, LIA often functions more like a series of psychological monographs than an organic narrative. 
 Power in the Back Story 
 Perhaps, another way of saying this is that Faulkner's 'back stories' in LIA resonate more than the 'front story'. The back story to the Hightower narrative, originally a short piece called 'The Dark House' before it was incorporated in LIA, especially excels with its portrait of the over-eager minister on his first commission who is undone by powerful emotionally charged memories from his childhood. The author here provide just enough requisite detail to generate sympathy; first we get congregation's reaction to Hightower's strange homilies, likened to Confederate calvarymen on galloping horses, followed by material on the wife 'gone bad' and the scandal of her death in Memphis that will lead to Hightower's forced resignation from the church. When rogue elements in the town endeavor to run him out of town, suddenly there's a change in the weather and the abject minister becomes, almost over night, an object of pity and even Christian charity, not scorn. Hightower will stay in Jefferson, despite his disgrace. It's, as Faulkner characterizes it, the 'storm that blows over' and it's just the kind of storytelling detail I would expect to find in Yoknapatawpha county. 
 But what about his 'front story? 
 It occured to me that Faulkner might choose to deliver Hightower out of his isolation and self-loathing by shaping his timely delivery of Lena's baby as an element of his possible recovery. The author shows Hightower taking pride in his midwiving skills and you can sense him, at his home after the birth of the child, moving towards the redeeming light. But instead, accompanied by a description of another kind of light, the filtered coppery August Light coming into the Hightower study, Chapter 20 starts us down a different path. It's filled with disturbing memories of 'three phantoms and a ghost' (Hightower's mother, father, and his grandfather's slave cook, along with ghost grandfather himself) and a string of unpleasant Civil War related associations that rise to the level of incapcitating neurosis, a kind of brain fever. At the end of the chapter -- one filled with enough ambiguous antecedents to drive careful readers to read rage -- the old minister remains haunted by the galloping horses and the circumstances of his grandfather's death in battle, nearing his own death, perhaps, and utterly bereft of hope. 
 Back Door Man 
 Likewise, Joanna Burden 'back story' strikes me as great material. Here's a tale of a spinsterish woman of a certain age whose forbears were northern Calvinists and abolitionists, but who now finds herself friendless, without family, and isolated in the heart of defeated Confederacy. As her sexual relationship with Christmas gets underway, we learn further details of her background and kin -- two family family members were killed by former Jefferson mayor Colonel Sartoris over Reconstruction issues -- and of her desire to unburden herself of these shadows in her past. As the front story takes over, we read updates from Christmas, which suggest Joanna, for the first time in her life, in pursuit of the sheer exhiliration of being alive. The sex gets a little kinky and though the religious taboos must still be in play, Joanna clearly revels in the idea of inter-racial hanky-panky with her back door man. At one point, Faulkner has her echoing the thoughts of St. Augustine before his conversion to the path of righteousness: Lord save me from the sins of the flesh, but please not right away! 
 But then the front story goes off the rails. Faulkner finishes the Burden tale by again shifting the viewpoint, so we learn only selective details -- and those only at some distance -- of how she suddenly re-embraces her pieties, puts together a crazy scheme for Christmas to become a lawyer, then fatally asks him to kneel down and pray with her, threatening him at the point of an old civil war revolver. Such I guess is the power of menopause onset to produce calamity and snatch defeat from the jaws of victory. As carefully as Faulkner delineates Christmas as a violent misogynist and Burden as the mercurial but desperate woman, I credit neither the gun nor the instrument of Burden's death, Christmas's razor. The facts in the monographs may support them, but surely the drama that should logically build to these developments and to make them inexorable falls way short of critical mass. Put it down to the modernist reaching for a coy enigmatic subtlety at the wrong place at the wrong time. 
 Paging Temple Drake 
 In his biography 'One Matchless Time: A Life of William Faulkner', scholar Jay Parini quotes the author as saying "I began Light in August knowing no more about it than a young woman, pregnant, walking along a strange country road". Though I can't offer much else in the way of scholarship to buttress my argument, LIA to me manifests as the product of a probable Faulkner decision to find a way to make the Lena Grove opening work with other story ideas kicking around in his head, maybe for some time. Perhaps, the fact that these ideas had no natural affinity for each other was all the more reason for Faulkner to invoke his modernist muse once again and put them all in the same novel. Certain LIA details -- the sex jelly at the orphanage, the near decapitation of Burden, the castration of Christmas -- also suggest Faulkner was reaching at times for the same shock value found in the edgy, financially successful 'Sanctuary', published just at the time the author was hard at work on LIA (the link below conveys how readers and critics reacted to Faulkner's stylistic choices circas 1931). 
 But I believe these artistic choices were counter-productive and inimical to Faulkner's great strength as a southern storyteller, on full display in such works as GDM and the Snopes Trilogy. In a parallel universe, one in which this author was less in thrall of technique and modernism, the LIA material might well have made its way forth as a set of stories -- all with unique endings -- tacking to a different wind. His famous quote from the Nobel Award acceptance speech is always worth citing but perhaps has special meaning here: 
 I believe that man will not merely endure. He will prevail. He is immortal, not because he alone among creatures has an inexhaustible voice, but because he has a soul, a spirit capable of compassion and sacrifice and endurance

book_b.title: Mrs. Lincoln's Dressmaker
book_b.user_review: Chiaverini's writing style seems to me to be flawless. The pacing of the plot gives a deep look into day-to-day living for the primary characters. The rich, expressive descriptions of characters' feelings and actions keep readers from being bored or exhausted. Her writing feels like a beautiful handcrafted quilt...with all of the coordinating and contrasting colors of characters and textures of action finely and evenly drawn together, one stitch and one word at a time. At first, it bothered me that this book wasn't footnoted. Yet the details - either imagined or real - are so believable, if I have to look up and research some of the "facts" myself, so be it.

sample_reviews.review_text: Very slow at times but an interesting story of Lincoln family from another perspective.
History heavy. Wished there was more plot.
One of the worst books I've read ever. Simplistic, plagiarized, boring, flat --

When I began reading this book, I was under the impression that it was a novel, from the perspective of Mrs. Lincoln's modiste. This was not that at all. The book started off SO SLOWLY, telling little to nothing about Elizabeth at all. Sure, she was there, but nothing was told from a 1st person POV, and for many of the tiresome scenes, she wasn't even present. All the accounts of the war read like a history book, and were extremely hard to follow. 
 If I were a less stubborn person, I would've given up on it before I reached 20%. Luckily, the book did pick up, and seemed to be more about Elizabeth by about halfway through, but since I imagine most people abandon it long before that point, I just couldn't rate it any higher.

I thought the story of the dressmaker got lost in all the narration of the generals, battles, etc. of the Civil War. I don't think a dressmaker (or most the the civilians) would be that informed of the specifics of the war and it wasn't necessary to have that much detail about the war to tell her story. I decided not to finish the book and probably won't read any other books of this type by this author.

I really wanted to like this book, because I am so fascinated with Mary Todd Lincoln. Unfortunately this fiction book read like nonfiction and seemed to be more of a list of historical events than a narrative.

Mrs. Lincoln's Dressmaker is an account of a friendship bond between two women that blossomed out of one of America's most tragic times, the Civil War. Elizabeth Keckle, was a very talented dressmaker, sewed for many of the Washington, D.C. socialites including Mary Todd Lincoln. The connection forged by these women went beyond their professional association toward a kinship developed through the personal struggles ad tragedies these two women faced. Jennifer Chiaverini provides the reader with a personal view of what life was like at that time. We get a different view of Mrs. Lincoln. Additionally, the reader gets a better understanding of what it was like to be a black free woman trying to make a living at this time.

What an awfully dry and boring book. The characters were not developed at all. It felt as if I was being told facts and not a story. I felt no connected at all to Elizabeth. I forced myself to read this for a Book Club or else I definitely would have given up reading it by the end of the first chapter. 
 Read For: Historical Fiction Book Club - April 7, 2016 
 Recommend For: Historical Fiction/Lincoln Fans/Civil War Reads

I usually read a couple of books a week -- but don't let the fact that I read on this one for more than a month (March 30 to May 4) lead you to believe it was because I didn't enjoy it or because it was a "slow reader". It was my life, and the various deadlines that kept me from reading. This whole month I could only read one or two pages before I was asleep. 
 This is a very interesting and different view of Mrs. Lincoln, her foibles, problems, joys and friends...and her relationship with the president. And it is reported from the viewpoint of her seamstress who became her friend and confident -- a former slave who bought herself and her son out of slavery and into freedom. Now I want to do some research and see if this is based on fact. It certainly felt as if most of these people were real and not just in the imagination of Ms Chiaverini -- although I've read other of her books and she does make characters live. 
 It's well worth your time -- and I KNOW it won't take this long for you to finish. 
 Added: 
 The internet search brought up a photo of the quilt this figures in the book and the verification that Elizabeth Keckey was very much a real person and her life has evidently been well represented in this book. Soiler alert: See: http://www.quiltersworld.com/webbonus...

I am so disappointed. I was really looking forward to reading this book after seeing the movie Lincoln and finding Mrs. Keckley, a minor character in the movie, to be intriguing. Unfortunately, I was expecting a novel and got a textbook instead. I am surprised this is classified as a novel, since it read much more like a straight forward non-fiction book. Granted I only got about 100 pages in. The text (note I didn't say plot) was dry and slow moving and it began to get painful to read. When I start dreading having to pick up a book then I know it is time to throw in the towel.

reference_books.title: The Book of Ruth
reference_books.review_text:
It's definitely better than the movie adaptation, as most books are, but I found myself missing the chemistry between Nicholle Tom as Ruth and Christine Lahti as May. Still, the novel moved deftly through the concept of complex characters, if the plot itself was a little clunky in places. The movie was much more direct with the theme of how all people have a little meanness inside of them, though also tempered with goodness and sympathy; we got to see that through Ruth and May, and ultimately Ruby and Justy living in the farm house stewing in bitterness and regret; from the opposite end we saw it a little in Ruth's brother, Matt, and her Aunt Sid, who were so different from the main characters in personality and experience, and yet hurt them by holding themselves aloof. 
 The writing was a bit uneven as well, as told through Ruth's voice; usually the diction was simple, but sometimes Hamilton would throw in complicated statements that would throw me from the story. She made up for it with some physical descriptions of Ruth's life, and the visceral foreshadowing elements, like with the dead crows. And Ruth herself was so frustrating in a wonderfully human way--her life was so limited, and oftentimes angry, that I wanted her to do better for herself, but how could she without proper encouragement? She built up Aunt Sid like an idol, but she was too shamed to be truthful in her letters, and Sid herself never initiated anything until the end. Ruby was tragic from the start--quite obviously only of interest because he was the sole person to actually pay her a bit of attention. The three of them, plus Justy once he was born, ultimately made do day by day, and although you could feel the tension simmering in the narration, I wish there had been slightly more of an arc for Ruby, to signify his growing issues. 
 That being said, I dislike when things are quick and convenient, and I found myself appreciating the ending, which was rather en media res. Definitely less final than the movie, though Ruth still had a sense of where she wanted to go. I still would say, in book and adaptation both, that the relationship and its effects between mother and daughter were smothering, simmering and alive. 
 In personality I'm probably more like Matt, feeling somewhat appalled by their bitter resentment, their stewing ignorance. So I really appreciate Hamilton for putting me in Ruth's head, for showing me that she was more than a simpering victim or bullying idiot--she had her own, idiosynchronatic, and often empathetic way of seeing the world. She wasn't even named until after the big climax. The other characters didn't really know Ruth, but she'll stick with me.

reference_books.title: The Namesake
reference_books.review_text:
I came into this book figuring that I would like it, and I was not disappointed in the least. I took the book to work this week and spent my entire lunch hour on just one chapter, pouring over the exquisite descriptions of each scene exposited upon and the flow of the narration. I especially admire how Jhumpa, who covered decades in less than 300 pages, knew exactly which scenes to center on, and which to let roll by. 
 Not that this is overly important, but I found that the movie was more or less en tandem with the book, despite having a slightly narrower focus on Gogol's name issues as the main conflict. I suppose my one complaint with the book was giving Moushumi a chapter to narrate- not that I didn't like the deeper look into her character and motivations, but it broke the more natural flow of telling things from Ashima (or more likely) Gogol's persepctives. Ashoke's brief forays into the hot seat, though, didn't bother me, perhaps because his story in particular was so central to his family's collective narrative. 
 All in all, an excellent read for anyone interested in immigrant experiences and/or great literature. After I finished the book, I listened to an NPR interview with Jhumpa online where she admitted near the end that writing is an incredibly taxing and difficult task- and I can believe it, really, because how else could it be so good? :P Yet on the page, it is effortless, and it makes me feel- even though I have no direct experience with Indian life- that this culture is second nature to me. Brava.

reference_books.title: The Casual Vacancy
reference_books.review_text:
I wasn't sure what to expect with this one since several friends and etc seemed to have mediocre reactions, but I really loved JK Rowling's first post-Potter novel. It took a little while to get into, I mean by way of introducing all of the characters and understanding/remembering their connections to one another, but the chapters were interesting and filled with such fully realized people that it held my attention from the off. 
 Must've been a relief for Rowling to get into the heads of so many folks, what after seven books of Harry and a couple of outlying prologues. At the beginning I did a lot of comparing to the Potter books--particularly, and perversely, with with Andrew's biological response to Gaia (I mean sheesh, Jo, it took you five books for Harry to just get one chaste kiss with Cho. :P) But as time went on and I grew more engrossed into this story, I basically just came away with seeing Shirley Mollison as Pagford's version of Aunt Petunia. 
 I'm a sucker for well rounded characters, and I found in all of their POV portions I could relate to at least a little bit of all of them, even if my opinion overall was less than flattering. In particular I was drawn to the kids--Sukhvinder and Krystal were my favorites--and also the middle aged women, who looked, acted, and felt middle aged. Mothers and wives, particularly those who aren't lithe and unopinionated, tend to be ignored or dressed up as one-dimensional ninnies without any motivations for their actions. Rowling's also a stickler for physical details--very important for a story with such a large cast of characters. 
 The issues raised in the book ranged wildly, from mental illness, teenage bullying and depression, pining for lost youth, and then the violence and drug culture that encapsulated the poorest family. These characters and situations were perhaps Rowling's finest. Against the backdrop of the middle class Pagford council arguing about services to the poor (and particularly the sins the Wheedon family,) I got to look first-hand into their lives and feel disgust, pity and even admiration for their choices, which peeled away the truth about how difficult it is to pull yourself up after a life of abuse and neglect. "The casual vacancy" that Barry Fairbrother's death brought to the Pagford council was a far more serious one when it came to his family and others to whom he reached out; it made me think that really, our lives are less dictated by socioeconomic factors but by the people who occupy space in them. 
 The book was perhaps a little long, and the ending featured a rush of tying up many character's storylines, but overall I found the novel to be an empathetic look into the human condition. It's very different than Potter, which, as a fantasy, embodies characters dealing with larger than life issues. There's no Voldemort in Pagford to inspire groups of followers vs opposers, or threaten a mass war or public exposure beyond a few forum posts on a website. :P It is a book that, if set in the Wizarding World, would deal more thoroughly with the conditions House Elves, centaurs, giants and the underlying prejudices surrounding magical bloodlines. It's a more subtle story, but perhaps more moving in how it addresses everyday people in their everyday lives.

reference_books.title: Ender's Game (Ender's Saga, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I skimmed the battle school parts, and focused more heavily on the Peter/Valentine subplot. I have mixed feelings. I appreciate that Card understood, and in the eighties, the power that the Internet would have to bring certain political (and other) voices to the masses. And I can probably excuse the fact that he didn't have enough future vision to understand how unlikely it would be for the two to remain anonymous, at least in our world, where the internet has catered more focus on celebrity. If "Locke" and "Demosthenes" were truly that popular to the masses, there would be more demands for proof of identity. They'd certainly be called for speaking engagements, plastered all over YouTube, whatever. But what I don't buy at all is that pre-teens, even genius pre-teens, could pull this off (and I note that Card didn't once actually write a full-fledged article so as to show the readers their skills.) 
 The entire novel is more or less based on the predilection that the term "genius" means these young kids can basically get away with/had the propensity to accomplish pretty much anything. It's a lazy, shallow premise, especially in a book that, as I understood it, was supposed to probe the complexities of war and politics. The idea of a "video game genocide" was certainly troubling, but I found more meaning in John Kessel's criticism of how Card handled the issues at stake and the character of Ender, in his 2004 essay "Creating the Innocent Killer: Ender's Game, Intention, and Morality" (which apparently has a GoodReads page! https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/8...) It's also archived here: https://web.archive.org/web/201409061...

book_a.title: The Red Tent
book_a.user_review:
I debated how I wanted to rank this book. I know I have bias, and I thought it unfair that Jacob's tribe seemed so set apart for strong critique (then again, seeing as Jacob's family was the only one Dinah knew growing up, that makes sense.) Certainly changing Dinah's story from being raped to just falling for a guy that her family didn't like changes the outcome quite a bit, but objectively speaking, all aspects of the story made sense, so kudos. 
 My main prop to this book has to go to how completley it dropped me into this absolutely foreign, alien (and terrifying) world. I certainly would be terrified to be a woman during that time, so I admired Dinah's strength all the more to embrace life (and love and childbirth) to the fullest. I appreciated, and was fascinated by, the way Anita wove the pagan cultures and the Hebrew "tribal" culture together- note, this was before Moses, before the giving of the Ten Commandments, and before the Israelites became "Jewish" in a way that we can relate to today. I also, of course, loved the fullness of character afforded to the matriarchs, Leah and Rachel (and Rebecca and even Sarah a little), and their handmaidens, Zilpah and Bilhah, which is missing from the male-dominated bible. (One thing from the bible was crystal clear, though- the way that a "family" was a "tribe" in ancient times, which was self-sufficient and nomadic, in my tradition. It was intriguing to get a glimpse into how these "tribe-families" may have interacted.) 
 My one big critique is that I wish Anita didn't link Jacob getting the name of "Isra'El" to his shame over what happened with his daughter, but kept to the original story about wrestling with the angel of Gd- which is, after all, such a powerful message to Jews, even of the modern day. Then again, I felt grim satisfaction that the story of Dinah finally seemed to have repurcussions and get it's due. No matter which way she was cast off from her family, she at least deserves that.

sample_reviews.review_text: Something in the way this was written made it feel like torture to read. I muddled through, but it felt like really hard work! Fiction should not be such hard work!

This was incredibly different from what I normally read. For this New Year I want to explore different genres out there instead of reading my usually Science Fiction/Fantasy. Don't get me wrong now, I will still be reading my favorite genre, just slipping in some contemporary and historical fiction here and there. 
 I'm not a super religious person and I know only minor parts of the Bible. I never really paid attention in church. So when I read this, I became very intrigued by these women of the Bible and their stories. I could not imagine living during this time. The women back then seem to hold so much power yet none at all because men ruled the land. So they gathered together in The Red Tent to talk about their struggles and their dreams, they build friendships and share secrets. They bleed together and helped each other when sick or in labor. 
 This book was compelling and truly beautiful. It made me feel so powerful to be a woman.
Laborious and boring. I almost finished it, but went into labor with my daughter and never had the time or desire too finish it afterwards.

I admit I'm a sucker for any worth-while stories written between the lines of known history. Add a woman-centric element and I'm sold. I really enjoyed the story of Dinah's life and had to remind myself that it is only fiction.

I loved this book. I am a christian, so I was not sure how this would read for me. I really learned a lot from the book and fell in love with the story. I love reading new things, new ideas, viewpoints and prescriptive; this book gave me all of that. The characters were vivid, the story was clear. I have recommend this book to many of my fellow readers. Enjoy.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I'm re-reading it as well in anticipation of the movie being released next weekend. I had forgotten how this style beget so many other female oriented Biblical stories. I believe I heard her at an AJL convention oh so many years ago.
Hmmm, I couldn't get past the first chapter. Too much menstruation.
I hated this book. It's supposedly based on one of Jacob's wives from the Bible. It was gruesome. I guess life was like that back then, but it didn't appeal to me.

I found myself constantly putting this book down because it was dull and slow. The story itself was interesting, and embellished, from the Bible. I understand it was a fictionalized account of the lives of women in biblical times, but it was horribly drawn out and rambling. I finally started to enjoy the book about 70 pages from the end (for about 40 pages) but it dropped off again. If it wasn't a book group selection I would have dumped it at about page 50.

I read this book for book club, and wouldn't have bothered to finish it if it weren't for that. I guess you can't really call skimming over all but the first few chapters of the book just prior to book club "finishing" it, but that's what I'll call it. Anyway, I am no biblical scholar, and the author admits that the book is intended to stand on it's own as fiction, but I have enough knowledge of the Bible to know that this author took the basic story and pulled the rug out from under it, so to speak. The author suggests that sex with sheep occurs while tending the flock, that a father has no problem touching his daughter in inappropriate ways, and that premarital sex as teenagers is all part of the daily norm in the lives of these nomads. I just couldn't enjoy the story on any level. 
 I guess that knowing the actual characters role as written in the Old Testament could have worked against me in this case because honestly everyone else in my group seemed to love the story. There was just far too much of the authors imagination in it to make it an enjoyable read for me. 
 So my advice is, if you're familiar with the story as it stands and don't really see the need to invent more drama into an already dramatic story then don't bother reading this book. But that's just my opinion.

book_b.title: The Lowland
book_b.user_review:
It was one of those books where I found myself growing depressed by the end, just because characters' lives (and page count) were growing thin. Lahiri reprises her formidable ability to make 40 years' worth of academia, politics and family life sound completely relatable. I was also struck by some broad similarities between the frustrations surrounding the war in Vietnam, abuse of power and civil rights issues here vs the tumult of a fledgling nation, terrorism and raised awareness of the poor in India. But the clicker for me is always Lahiri's insistence on the focus of individual desires as manifested through family relationships. Word events provides a poignant backdrop, but personal relationships are more universal. Maybe all of this boils down to why I related the least to Udayan of all of the narrators. 
 This was really Shubash and Guari's story, and although other characters occasionally made an appearance as narrator I'm glad it wasn't for long because that would take away from the narrative flow. I remember I had similar issues in "The Namesake" when Lahiri would jump into a side character's head. Part of me wanted to see things from their perspective, but the rest was wrapped up in the protagonists. But overall, the characters in this novel felt very different from Lahiri's first. For those who have finished this one (or who don't mind spoilers,) I would suggest reading Savita Iyer-Ahrestani's essay in Paste Magazine about how characters here break out of traditional Indian-American molds, particularly the unlikable, self-centered Guari. She might be Lahiri's most complicated creation--a real feat. 
 In terms of weaknesses, I'll pick on the beginning and the ending. It took me a little while to get into this story for a few reasons. Lahiri writes in a very narrative, prosey style, and Udayan and Shubash, frankly, weren't as interesting as young boys as they became as young men. The first few chapters read more as rambling background material. 
 As for the ending, well I had my biases about it ending at all. :P (Spoilers to come!) Turning Shubash into "the universal man" in his final chapter rather than addressing him by name felt a little pretentious. And I'm not sure I buy that Meghna was so completely taken by Guari's one, brief visit (which was fraught with tension) that she'd want to see her again, though maybe this was Bela hiding her own desires behind her daughter. And ending with Udayan's shooting, jumping back years before the previous chapters, well I guess there was little way that would not feel too esoteric and ungrounded. But the closing lines, where he's slipping from life and thinking of Guari's hair or whatever, just left me disappointed. In general, I suppose that Udayan worked better as a ghost, someone to haunt the other characters, rather than a person in his own right. In life, he was just young, sad and misguided.

sample_reviews.review_text: More like 3.5 stars. I love Jhumpa Lahiri, but I am not a huge fan of jumping back and forth between points of view. I did enjoy the story and I was surprised by the revelations at the end. I think I just expect more from this author.
No rising action or breathtaking climax but a good story.

The Lowland started out as a book that showed promise. I didn't care much for Lahiri's writing style, it didn't have a natural flow or grace to it somehow, but the story had enough potential to hold my interest for a while. Two brothers, two sides of the same coin; each representing the paths laid out before the youth in 1970's Bengal. Themes are introduced into the book some are particularly intriguing like the Naxalite Movement's effect on the Bengali Youth. But Lahiri never runs with any of them. She leaves them relatively unexplored. She chooses to focus on her characters instead. Unfortunately, it doesn't do the novel any good. They come across as weak or selfish or both. You don't resonate with any of them. It could have been more. Much more. 
 Maybe instead of stretching the book across 50 years and over the lifetimes of Subhash and Gauri it could have focused on the lives of the two brothers instead. Contrasting Subhash's life in the US with Udhayan's in Calcutta. The final chapter could have been the same along with the mistake committed.

Well, I liked the book but its not as good as The Namesake. One thing that would like to say is that I lived almost 60 years reading this book. The ups n downs of the characters and the silent pain each one of them was facing sometimes left me thinking with a teary eye.

This was recommended at the bakery, and really delivered. Shades of strained family relations bleed into weird blasts of lost time behind the ranch. Heart breaking, gold and overcast, and most fantastic!
People love this book! But I just think it doesn't flow like the others.
I liked some parts, but over all: what a drag
Kind of slow book, but very well written, interesting character development. Will read more by her for sure.

This book was a disappointment for me. I've loved Lahiri's other books, especially Unaccumstomed Earth which was a 5-star read for me. The story is about 2 brothers who grow up together in India. Subhash leaves for the United States to study and work and Udayan stays in India, becomes involved with a revolutionary group and is murdered. Subhash returns to India and tries to rescue his brother's young wife by bringing her to the United States. What I disliked about this book is that the tragedy of Udayan's casts a permanent shadow over everyone's life - Subhash, his wife Gauri, and even their daughter. And not just a shadow for a few years, but decades. People are resilient, but not these characters. They wallow in their sadness, and spread their unhappiness around. I hated seeing how this cast of characters didn't develop or grow, but stayed stuck in their sadness.
This book is very lonely. Might have liked it more if I hadn't read most of her other books, but this is similar in tone.

book_a.title: Wintersmith (Discworld, #35; Tiffany Aching, #3)
book_a.user_review: Available on Kindle.

sample_reviews.review_text: Very sweet.

3.5 
 Not my favorite in the Aching series, but still a good entry. It had touches of Hogfather and Small Gods, what with all the god making and whatnot. And it was cool to spend some time with Nanny Ogg, who's often overshadowed by Granny Weatherwax who was, of course, an important part of this story. 
 I like how Tiffany is sort of coming into her own, that mix of confidence and doubt. If anything, though, my biggest complaint about the book is that there's quite a lot of her going around in circles in this book, and it felt a bit repetitive after awhile. 
 That aside, I also liked seeing Roland develop a bit more in this story, and the Feegles were fun, though not quite as 'on' as in the other stories. 
 A good book that suffers only in comparison to the other two in the series, which sparkled a bit more.

Pratchett is a wordsmith. He creates a divine world into which he spins his stories... stories of magic, where seasons have personalities and can become ... almost human. This is the case of the Wintersmith, when young witch Tiffany Aching leaps into the midst of the winter dance and takes the place of Summer. Wintersmith is captivated by her and wants to become human so as to be with her. He starts courting her with wintery magic, including millions of little Tiffany snowflakes. But as Granny Weatherwax knows, a season becoming a human can be dangerous... 
 I like these books. They are simple but sweet, profound yet funny, and full of unforgettable characters -- in this case, a witch who digs her own grave (literally). Tiffany is a delightful heroine -- sweet, sincere, intelligent, and kind, with an unusual amount of insight into The World. 
 As for the rest? Well, what can I say except CRIVENS!!

best pratchett opening scene ever; a whole lot of witch practice meta, and tying all the knots, and awesome nanny ogg cameo; some really pretty bits; but overall weaker than first and second books, with plot getting sloppier near the end and ending sort of rushed. but still, but still.

book_b.user_review: I just got too tired of the characters, and the trip back into Ember seemed too predictable.

sample_reviews.review_text: I was pretty much done with this series before the end of this book.

Vote: 3,50 
 Class: L-A1 (FP) 
 (Fourth Book of the Ember Cycle; it must be read after "The City of Ember" and "The People of Sparks"; the third book, "The Prophet of Yonwood" can be skipped) 
 I found The City of Ember and its sequel (except for "The Prophet of Yonwood") an enjoyable reading. It's a good series, with fantastic characters and a well written story. It's clearly a very young young-adult dystopian novel. 
 - the setting (3,50) of this book is the village of Sparks some month after the coming of the people of Ember, while the people of Sparks, all of them, are struggling to survive against many problems. 
 - the characters (4,00), Lina and Doon mostly, but Torren and the others too, are great, moving, real human being with all the good and evil inside them. 
 - the story (3,25) is very simple: Lina and Doon are going to explore their home city of Ember to find a way to help their people; a simple story but likable. 
 - the writing style (3,50) is easy and enjoyable and simple to read; only thing is: as in the others books of the series, the titles of the chapters reveal too much about what is going to happen and so nothing is really unexpected (and this is another characteristic of a very young young-adult book). 
 I found this book an enjoyable reading even if not a great book. I'm going to recommend it to many of my friends.

Sometimes I hate reading series books, because usually my expectations are way too high after a good first book. This happened to me with His Dark Materials. The first books in Ember and HDM knocked me out, but they ended on such disappointing notes. 
 One thing that kind of annoyed me about the Ember series is how Duprau continually introduces some kind of helpful device that immediately gets destroyed. I wanted to know what was in that book, but no! Guess what! Not this time! Arrrgh! 
 This book just ran out of steam for me around the middle. The ending was 'surprise' was cool, though. I wasn't expecting that (which makes me question how well I paid attention while reading; did anyone else see it coming?). 
 Not horrible, just ok.

The City of Ember was best and this 4th book might be the next best in the series. It answers some questions and sort of gives you closure on the characters while still presenting a possibility for further stories. Don't you love an author who closes the book, but doesn't quite seal it shut? I listened to the audio version of all the books. This is one series that does well on audio.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I seriously love this one the most. The adventure in this one and after so much I finally FINSIHED. AND I WAS SOOO HAPPY. LINA FINALLY GOT HER HAPPILY EVER AFTER. I couldn't really celebrate because I finished in class, but I caught myself smiling. 
 I heard bad reviews about the 3rd book, so I skipped that one until I finished this one. You don't really need it expect theres a reference to it at the very last 2nd page which ur like "ok whatever." So the 3rd book didn't really matter. 
 Things I love: 
 -CHARACTERS: LINA AND DOON ARE LIKE THE MOST INTERESTING CHARACTERS EVER, 
 -PLOT: god, I just love this. It's has so much adventure in it. I was super happy with that because it stopped having adventures in the 2nd book and I just love having the rush and mystery again! 
 -ENDING: ah... They finally put a bit of romance, even though it was 0.00000000000001% of the story. It was cute. AND NO MORE BAD GUYS, YAY!!. 
 -best saying: "It's called e-lex-tricity. have you heard of it?"
I enjoyed this installment, and liked getting to see Lina and Doon again, and appreciated the way the very end gave some fast-forward perspective on how things ended up working out.
The story may have been a little better than the 3rd book, but the writing was disappointing.

Far better than book #3 in the series, The Diamond of Darkhold returns to the story of Lina, Doon, and their neighbors who joined the people of Sparks when they fled the dying underground city of Ember. Winter hardships with a doubled population threaten everyone's survival, so the pair of friends plan an adventure to retrieve critical supplies their people left behind. Unexpected dangers await, and the mysterious, partial clues left by the builders do not prepare them for the challenges they will face. 
 I enjoyed this one as much as books #1 and 2 in the series. If you have not read any of them, start sequentially, but do not bother with the 3rd, as it has very little relation to the other three.
if your kids have read "The City of Ember" I would encourage them to read the rest of the series. It is very good!

The Diamond of Darkhold returns the story back to Lina, Doon, and the people of Sparks as they try to survive in a desolate world. In many ways, Darkhold resembles Ember with the kids needing to decipher mostly destroyed instructions left by the Builders for the Emberites. This leads me to my chief complaint of the entire series: for the Builders to be so prescient in creating a society that would be protected from world destruction, why were they so awful about informing said society about how to survive back in the world upon their reemergence? One set of instructions? In paper, of all things? If time doesn't destroy, ignorance will, and that is what has happened. 
 I continue to enjoy Lina and Doon with their ingenuity and bravery to help their people. They are young and hopeful, resembling youth at its best before cynicism and pessimism have a chance to overcome those attributes into adulthood. Also, for the most part, no one is inherently evil in these novels. Instead, DePrau shows us that ignorance can be just as detrimental as any enemy. In contrast, DePrau also shows us that even when things become most difficult, there is always a solution if one looks hard enough. 
 I really enjoyed The Book of Ember series. It's a great series for kids. I read this series alongside my 9 year old son (who quickly outpaced me: if only I could have the free time to read that he has!). We had some good discussions about the choices characters made, what we might have felt or done in their place, the consequences that follow. Recommended.
