book_b.title: The Day of the Duchess (Scandal & Scoundrel, #3)
book_b.user_review:
I want to like this author's books...but sometimes it's hard. I have a hard time with her writing style - I understand not everyone will think it a big deal, obviously or she wouldn't be so successful. For this book, I think the story itself is good but the way we get there is a challenge. 
 Her style is very contemporary for a historical romance so if you are a stickler for the proper use of a word for the time period, you will be frustrated. I don't consider myself a complete purist, but I do notice, the more historicals I read, when "ass" is used instead of "arse" but it doesn't deter me from reading. In this book there is more than that. Maclean's use of the term "full stop" had me rolling my eyes each time I read it as it's pervasively used throughout all her books, and really, overused. I believe I counted it used six times in this book. Granted, it wouldn't be a bad thing if it were used once to emphasize with great feeling how strongly someone felt, but to be used so much, just got annoying. 
 Also, while this might be fine to another reader, I found the sisters to be distracting and obstructive to the story. I did not find them likeable. I loved the Rogue Not Taken, Sophie and King's story, so she was fine, but the other sisters are just crass and rude. I love sarcasm, but they were rude, full stop. (see what I did there) 
 I loved how Haven redeemed himself and finally came to realize the error of his ways. Sera was all over the map and when she doubted Haven again and again, even though he provided her with more than enough opportunities for her to believe in him, I was again frustrated. 
 The last frustration I had with the book was the back and forth through time periods. It was confusing as I couldn't read the book all in one sitting. It took me several days to read where I needed to stop and start and I'd have to recall where it was we were in the story because there was no clear pattern. 
 There was something I liked - I loved the debutantes who were a part of Haven's plot to win Sera back. They were awesome and I loved when they went against their momma's censure. It'd be great to see stories developed from these characters. 
 Bottom line, this one was a miss for me. I feel like that's the thing with Maclean's books these days - they are either hit or miss. I say this in all my reviews of Maclean's books that I've read and reviewed, I loved Nine Rules to Break When Seducing a Rake. This was her debut and her best. I wish all of her books mimicked the style she used in that book and didn't slide into contemporary-isms like her other books. I would probably enjoy them if that were the case.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 Oh, dear. I saw this at the library and I thought I should break my historical romance drought with something juicy and angsty and controversial. 
 Let's put it this way - it did not rain in my historical romance desert. 
 This was the strangest book in tone and in world-building. The characters talked and thought like 2017. They acted like a horny insta-lust couple who had been steeped in a modern sex positive philosophy. That glibness contrasted greatly with the very real danger of ruin and a dangerous pregnancy. The hero's reaction to being forced to marry was ridiculous. As was his revenge. As were her expectations for marriage in that day and age. The hero was supposed to be an all powerful Duke, but he wasted all of his time on mind games. 
 I didn't believe the heroine walked into the House of Lords and demanded a divorce so she could run a pub. I didn't believe the Bachelor-type reality show the hero conjured up in the last half. Good lord - this isn't a historical - this is an alternate universe. Things didn't work that way then. They don't work that way *now.* 
 The flashbacks and time shifts were annoying. We go from the angst fest of the heroine almost dying to a flashback of their flirty banter when they first met. The characters said in their thoughts how much they loved each other, blah, blah, blah - but they sure didn't show it. The Merope story seemed a stretch for these characters. I can see what the author was trying to do and points for including a similar story to highlight this couple's situation- but that sweeping story had a poor imitation in these unlikable characters. 
 The big gesture of the hero at the end was the prefect bookend to the beginning where the heroine made a spectacle of herself. What ever happened to the stiff upper lip? What about emotions conveyed with the slightest lift of an eyebrow or the slight quiver in a voice? These are historical romance delights - the nuance - the staying within the lines while creating something new and unique. Exploration of public vs private, desire vs. duty, role vs. identity is a longstanding tradition in romantic literature. This story didn't explore any of those tensions because those tensions barely existed in this universe. 
 By the end, I was exhausted by both of them and I didn't care if they got together or not. They seemed to enjoy their drama so much, I don't know if they'll be happy without more reindeer games to play.

I had to read the book a second time to make sure that the review I was giving was accurate, and after the second reading I still do not understand how so many can give this five stars or even like Serafina at all. 
 2 years and 7 months prior Serafina lied, colluded, tricked and captured the man she "loved". Her love was very short lived though, for when he reacted as any lied to person would, she blamed HIM for her "ruined life" (no sweetie you ruined your life) and ran away. For all her sorriest she admits she would do it again if she knew she wouldn't get caught. That is not sorry at all, only sorry she got caught. 
 Yes after she did all the above he told her to go away and had an affair, (every woman who reads this book condemns him for his "affair" but gloss over her actions with "but she loved him", please let no one love me like that, I have no use for liars and tricksters). 
 He got over his anger and wanted her back but she was no where to be found. 
 Fast forward she comes back for a divorce and we get this silly 1800's version of the bachelor and you have a mess of a book. Mess mainly because while throughout Malcolm realizes his mistakes at no point does Sera EVER admit to her wrong doing. Never does she admit or even see that had she not been wrong from the first all the horrible things would never have happened. 
 I cannot stand book where men are humiliated and women celebrated for actions that had a man done them the same readers would call for his head. That is not women empowerment that is sexism. 
 Had Sera ever once stated yes, I lied when I first met you, yes I tricked you and didn't trust you enough, yes I started things badly I might have rooted for her, in the end I wanted her alone and lonely looking at the life she tricked herself out of and wanted Malcolm happy and whole with someone who was honest, because at no point did the author bother to redeem the woman as she felt only the man needed redeeming. 
 I hope better for Sesily's book and will only read it to finish the series but I doubt I will purchase SM again. Seems she gave her best with the number series.

When I read The Rogue Not Taken, I never could have imagined MacLean would try to redeem the Duke of Haven or that I would end up loving him as much as I did. His past actions were pretty unforgivable but somehow I was rooting for him from the start. Sera was such an incredible heroine and I loved watching her keep her head held high in spite of unfortunate circumstances. I also loved how feminist this whole novel was, even while being limited by the constraints of the time. (The madness of women not being allowed to own a business!) Sera and Haven's tension built at quite a clip throughout the story and neither was willing to budge but the interesting thing is how Haven thought he was going to win her back when he hadn't done anything to show her he loved her. Which given their history, is crucial. An apology would have gone a long way too. I kind of wanted to shake him. But there were so many moments when I could see his heart and see why vulnerability was so hard for him. The scene when they were underground was so moving and really set the tone for the rest of the novel. Watching Haven and Sera finally get together was worth the wait, particularly when Haven finally puts his money where his mouth is. I thoroughly enjoyed this one and I cannot wait read Sesily's story next!

Ugh. The couple had every quality I hate in people. They were Immature, selfish, impulsive adults who act like whiny children and didn't feel anywhere near enough remorse for the hurt they inflicted on themselves or others. The romantic gesture at the end was way too overdramatic, I couldn't help rolling my eyes. 
 I also swear the author copies and pastes her sex scenes from one book to another and just makes a few changes.
Depressing.

I love Sarah MacLean books and I am just obsessed with her Scandal & Scoundrel series , when I found out who The Day of The Duchess was about my first thought was how is this going to work out because after reading about this couple in the first book in this series, I thought there was no hope for this couple at all , however after reading this story I was just blown away . The Day of the Duchess was fantastic. 
 In this book we follow Seraphina and Malcolm and as I said , when I first read about these two I had no hope what so ever that they would reconcile, Malcolm did some very horrid things and honestly just based of what I knew about him prior to the start of this book , If Sarah decided to get rid of him of him early off in the series I would not have been sad about it, I could not stand him . However, I have complete faith in Sarah MacLean, she always deliver fantastic romance so I dived into this book intrigued to see what would happen and I was just amazed. I loved that we got to see so many flashbacks in this book as well as read from both of their perspectives, it was perfect because you got to see both sides of the story and really understand how they got to this stage. Reading this romance was like watching a beautiful flower grow in the most unusual conditions. Watching Seraphina and Malcolm find there way back to each other, forgive each other and in many ways start over was just amazing and again shows you just how powerful love can be and of course lets not forget the steamy sexy time lol. I loved this story !!! I had the biggest smile on my face reading the epilogue, I had so much joy in my heart for these two. The Day of The Duchess is one of the best historical romances I have read this year. If you are looking for sexy, swoon-worthy historical romance filled with redemption and second chances with an epilogue that fills you with all those happily ever after feels. Then you should definitely pick up a copy of The Day of The Duchess as soon as you can.
So much angst, so little reward.

This is the second book I've read by Sarah MacLean, and it is the one that ensures I will be a lifelong reader. This is an absolutely gorgeous romance about two damaged souls finding the strength to move forward with their lives and allowing themselves love and happiness. This book affected me in a surprising way, and I began limiting myself to a chapter at a time to draw it out. It's definitely my favorite romance of 2017, and one of my overall favorite reads of the year. 
 Malcolm and Sera are first introduced in MacLean's The Rogue Not Taken. Full disclosure: I didn't read that book. Those who have may come into this with intense feelings of dislike for Malcolm, and when it came out that he had cheated on his wife, I was skeptical of his ability to transform into a true hero. I don't enjoy romance novels that involve adultery, and I normally would never recommend one. But MacLean handled the incident incredibly well in this, revealing that there is much more to both sides of the story than had originally been shown. The first chapters, alternating between the present and past events, kept me hooked with each new revelation. It's heartbreaking to watch the pair fall in love and then fall apart through these flashbacks, and it made me root for them to find a way to make it work. 
 This is a couple who has been hurt by life and have spent time trying to hurt each other. But now, they simply want closure. For Sera, closure is a divorce and a fresh start. For Malcolm, there is no future without Sera and he's determined to win her back. I connected to them both strongly, and felt each of their emotions intensely. 
 The only critique I have is the epilogue: Sera is heartbroken over her infertility throughout the book, and Malcolm's acceptance that they will never have children together is huge. It's a beautiful moment that proves their love is all they need and that they can be a family of two in a time when women are expected to be breeding machines. And then... surprise, the doctor was wrong and Sera is pregnant multiple times over. I think this was a huge missed opportunity to create a very different ending to typical historical novels, and I felt MacLean sort of pulled back here and defaulted to a traditional storyline in a book that is otherwise pretty unique. 
 I'd highly recommend this to MacLean's fans, lovers of historical romances, and readers who enjoy romances that gut you emotionally and then make you believe in love.

Finally! I loved this book more than the story of the others. The angst and regret, love and forgiveness, i loved Sera and Malcolms story. Their journey to love was punctuated by the Talbots sisters mayhem.

THIS BOOK IS EVERYTHING. I cried twice in the opening thirty pages. The HEA is so incredibly hard-fought and powerful. I don't think there's ever been a reunion romance better written than this. I started the book hating Haven so much, and by the end I adored him. I immediately started re-reading it, I loved TDOTD that much.

reference_books.title: Men at Arms (Discworld, #15; City Watch #2)
reference_books.review_text: My second Discworld book. Since I gave the last one 4 stars, I'd like to give this one 4.5. Continue to particularly enjoy the characterization. Storyline is formula but in a good, cozy way. More complex plot than Guards Guards. Fewer goofy pop culture refs for humor. Still don't care for the Librarian. And Carrot's intelligence feels very inconsistent. But will definitely continue with the series.

reference_books.title: Mistress of the Art of Death (Mistress of the Art of Death, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This is one of those mysteries that's pure formula and regularly predictable yet still totally enjoyable. Not everything has to break new ground. And although I knew early on who the murderer was -- along with which supporting characters wouldn't survive, the name of the candy, etc. -- the climax still resulted in an overcooked dinner and a pouting spouse. Mental junk food but very tasty. 
 I've never watched any of those forensic shows, so I can't speak to those analogies, but I was pleasantly surprised by how little gore was actually involved. It was discreet. 
 I guess there was one very original bit. I've never seen a deus ex machina at the *beginning* of a story before. (Although there was still one at the end as well.) That stroke of luck was distracting and a bit irritating throughout the rest of the book. Produced some good characters, but still too easy. 
 Will probably read the rest of the series if I can continue to find them on a remainder table like this one. I did really enjoy the historical context.

reference_books.title: Soon I Will Be Invincible
reference_books.review_text: Well I enjoyed it. As a longtime comics reader who is saving all kinds of money by not buying DC's pathetic attempt at 'mature' comics (same kind of mature-audiences-only as slasher films; ie, not at all), it was nice to read something more balanced and fun. And I never hold genre books to particularly high literary standards anyway. Yes, it's all about the cliches, but I enjoyed seeing which specific ones Grossman went with. And again, it was a relief they weren't turned on their heads in gritty brutal your-hero-has-a-dark-side fashion. Interesting how some readers see the characters as obvious DC analogues and others seem them as equally obvious Marvel. The mystery elements were reasonably portioned out. I didn't entirely figure things out ahead of time but the reveals didn't come out of left field. I pictured Doctor Impossible throughout as Doctor Venture; I think that helped set a good tone.

reference_books.title: The Umbrella Academy, Vol. 1: The Apocalypse Suite
reference_books.review_text: Fun, expressive art and your standard hipster-quirky characters and plot, but there seemed to be a lot of details that the writing just sort of skipped over. Like he planned to go back and fill bits in later and then forgot. Still, I'll certainly get the sequel. To support the whole indie diversity thing if nothing else.

reference_books.title: Outliers: The Story of Success
reference_books.review_text: Disclaimer: Gladwell is my favorite writer, especially his New Yorker pieces. So I was predisposed to like this. But I was still pleasantly surprised by the subject matter being more interesting than I expected. I'm not very ambitious, so learning about how people succeed isn't nearly as catchy as learning about, say, how people make decisions. But there were plenty of fascinating random tidbits to chew on. Again. His stuff is great for making conversation at parties. But, as with Blink, you don't really come away with any sort of action plan. There were a few references to ways of giving more people the opportunities for success, but they weren't very practical (more hockey leagues, for example).

book_a.title: Gentlemen of the Road
book_a.user_review: Very Fafhrd and the Grey Mouser. The twists were predictable, but it's the kind of story where you want them to be. An action movie of a book. Fun and fast. Wish I had the British cover.

sample_reviews.review_text: Hard to resist the exuberance and enjoyment Chabon must have had in writing this adventure story set in both a remote and obscure time and place.

I should have trusted the good reads community and not bothered. But the book was so beautiful and enticing.. Who doesn't love elephants and middle eastern adventures? I have thoroughly enjoyed some of his other books but this one... Just downright goofy.
Makes up for the dreadful, FARSHTUNKENEH Yiddish Policemen's Union. FEH!!
not a book that i would usually be drawn to so i'm a little hesitant to recommend it, but i couldn't put it down.

An entertaining and fast read. I didn't walk away with any grand thoughts or new insight, but I enjoyed the adventure tale for what it was. The story was cleverly constructed, well-written, and had plenty of action to keep the story moving. The illustrations were also lovely. A perfect choice for a short plane ride or other travels and was great for reading on the subway during my commute.

Chabon's working title of this short novel was "Jews with Swords." The opening kind of reminds me of _The Three Musketeers_, too, although this is set in the 950s in the Caucasus. Two adventurer/swindlers fall in with a kidnapped heir to the kingdom of the Khazars, and find themselves at the middle of a mercenary army...a revolt...and more. There are some lovely surprises in this book and every main character is indeed Jewish.
...but I never was much of a Kipling fan, come to think of it.
Kind of meandering, not really gripping. Maybe that's a consequence of switching point of view so many times. Didn't have time to get attached to any of the characters. Disappointing.
Blech.

i knew many here would like this book but i have to disagree. the vocab is impossible with words that can t be looked up in a normal dictionary so i had to skip most of those words. the review here is better than the book and helped me understand it. i enjoyed the illustrations and short chapters which allowed me to finish it. i like michael chabon and have read many of his books. i think he is trying too hard to prove he is one of the most brilliant writers writing in america today. i hope he settles on a style soon so i can read more of his books.

book_b.title: Scott Pilgrim, Volume 4: Scott Pilgrim Gets It Together
book_b.user_review:
The series is staying consistently good. I'm fine with the books coming out late if that's what is keeping the quality up. 
 There were a few laugh-out-loud moments ('sexy phase'). Unfortunately, I was reading on an airplane, returning home from Thanksgiving. 
 Felt dumb I hadn't figured out the 'evil exes' thing sooner. Very sad we will probably be seeing less of Wallace now.

sample_reviews.review_text: Some mildly interesting developments but really feeling like a soap opera. I just feel he could be doing so much more with the format!
A fun contination of the series.
It's about at this point that I decide I'm not a huge fan. It's not terrible, just really random and feels like it's trying too hard.

The evil ex girlfriend is one of my favorite characters! And I love that Mae Whitman played her in the movie! She was perfect for that role! 
 I am so excited that Scott and Ramona exchanged I love you'S and are living together! They are such a cute couple! 
 Scott reminds me of me. So much. You have no idea. 
 That ending scene was too freaking cute! 
 Probably my favorite installment in the series so far.

God....this volume added nothing to the story for me. Nothing at all. I stopped reading it half way through and was able to read and understand vol 5 and 6 without that nagging feeling that I'd missed out on some critical part of the plot.

Scott finally starts to grow up! Well, a little and we see Scott and his friends all begin to mature and act more like real people. The story line of having to fight Ramona's evil exes falls into the background which is fine with me, because I find Scott and his friends maturing and changing much more interesting.

The story keeps building, and improving. I would recommend reading the books closely because they keep you wanting more. I like this book the best so far because it really shows a new angle on Scott. His character is developing and it's fun to watch him grow with all the craziness that surrounds him.
Better than number three, I liked the surprise twist on boyfriend number 4. I am looking forward to seeing what happens to Scott in number 5.

Scott Pilgrim does get it somewhat together in this volume. He makes strides in his relationship with Ramona, gets/loses/gets back a job, and fights one evil ex (the female one.) This is more of a transitional book in the series. It was cute, O'Malley's visual punchlines are clever as always, but it wasn't my favorite.
It was nice read.

reference_books.title: Dark Matter
reference_books.review_text: Meh. Not for me.

reference_books.title: The Word Exchange
reference_books.review_text: Meh. This is more like 2.5 stars. I think there's a writer in her but i don't think we've seen it yet.

reference_books.title: Behind Closed Doors
reference_books.review_text: Ugh, this is awful. It's one note, no real change in tone throughout, so it's one long desperate monologue without any character development or reason to care about or believe in the protagonist. Notwithstanding its 300-page length, the type is large and the margins are wide so it's really more of a novella which is appropriate for the plot. Don't waste your money and certainly do not buy this in hardcover. The quality of the paper is so poor that it seems like a deliberate comment by the publisher.

reference_books.title: Reasons to Stay Alive
reference_books.review_text: I wanted to like this more than I did. There's a good chance that Haig will capture other readers for the precise reasons he didn't capture me so take my rating with that grain of salt. It just wasn't for me.

reference_books.title: Smoke Gets in Your Eyes: And Other Lessons from the Crematory
reference_books.review_text: She's no Mary Roach, but her light hearted perspective is welcome. I think that Thomas Lynch will alwsys be my favorite mortician, but I'm glad we have Doughty, too.

book_a.title: The North Water
book_a.user_review: This one requires a strong stomach throughout. Having just finished it, I'm inclined to take a long hot bath to recover from the grime and cold in the story, which I think is a good indicator of how vividly McGuire brings his book to life.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Moby Dick meets Blood Meridian, and then some. Gripping. Fast-paced. Stomach-churning, but poetically (hold those two adjectives simultaneously in mind) so. (I mean, consider a man's head, stove in with a brick: "there is a fine spray of blood and a noise like a wet stick snapping.") Deeply researched, brilliantly hatched (perhaps in the end a bit too tidily). Memorable, superbly drawn characters, and the two principals in particular: conflicted ships-surgeon Patrick Sumner and arch-fiend harpooner Henry Drax, a villain for the ages. 
 All said, The North Water is emphatically not for every taste, and particularly not for squeamish readers, given its overall mood and tone, which are carried along via many scenes of graphic violence and depictions of various excresences, pustules, animal viscera, and medical procedures. (I seldom wince from the page: here, more than a few times.) 
 Nevertheless a taut, nervy, offhandedly philosophical (think Hobbesian) adventure novel.

Lu certes d'une traite comme un thriller mais que m'en restera-t-il dans quelques mois ? pas grand chose ... quelques personnages sinistres, un vocabulaire cru, et une avalanche de "fuck" de sang et de morts, 
 Je retiendrai peut-etre le destin de ce chirurgien, amateur d'Homere, confronte a la corruption et aux aleas de la vie, sans grand courage lui meme, mais avec quelques principes auxquels il semble parfois s'accrocher et pour qui ce voyage s'avere une veritable epopee vers un nouveau destin 
 J'ai regrette que le marin visionnaire Otto n'est pas ete plus "developpe" j'aurais aime plus de conversations avec Sumner pour etoffer les differentes visions de la psychologie et des croyances (le scientifique vs le visionnaire) 
 Je recommande la lecture de On the Proper Use of Stars de Dominique Fortier qui lui, m'a laisse une vision moins horrifique et certainement plus realiste de ces marins du grand Nord (des aventures du commandant Charcot, de Paul Emile Victor en Terre Adelie) dont l'univers me fascine depuis l'enfance ... 
 nota : il me reste dans ma PAL The Terror de Dan Simmons mais bou diou, quel pave ! 
 Many thanks to Jane Rawoof 's review ...

A gritty, crude, coarse and raw narrative that seemed appropriate to the setting. Descriptive passages seemed set to shock and lay bare each difficult situation. The story was engaging and tied itself up well...I felt that it wandered a little towards the final quarter of the book, but all in all it tightened up. Of the books longlisted for the Booker prize 2016, I think it would deserve a place in the shortlist and, given the similarities in style to recent winners The Luminaries and The Narrow Road to the Deep North, it could even stand a chance at winning.

If you like your historical fiction bleak, bloody and barbarous, then Ian McGuire's Booker long-listed The North Water is the one for you. Think Moby Dick by way of Quentin Tarantino and you're not far off. 
 It tells the story of a doomed whaling voyage in the 1850s. The Volunteer sets sail from Hull with the motliest of crews, made up of brutes and savages and skippered by the dubious Captain Brownlee. In the first few pages we meet Henry Drax, a vicious harpooner with a thirst for murder. He casually slaughters a drinking partner and rapes a young boy in the harbour before even setting foot on the ship. "The law is just a name they give to what a certain kind of men prefer," Drax declares. Clearly not an upstanding member of society. We follow the action mostly through the eyes of Patrick Sumner, an Irish surgeon who is both mentally and physically burdened from serving in the siege of Delhi. He seems to be one of the few morally sound people on board, even if he has a few skeletons in his own closet. But will he survive the unforgiving Arctic conditions and this dangerous, unscrupulous crew? 
 The graphic violence in this absorbing, fast-paced novel has drawn comparisons to the more gruesome aspects of Cormac McCarthy's work. I wouldn't consider myself squeamish in the least but I must admit to wincing at some of the more grisly passages: 
 Cavendish, without raising the rifle from his hip, tilts the barrel upwards and shoots him through the throat. The top portion of the Shetlander's skull detaches and flies backwards against the steeply pitched canvas roof, leaving a broad red bulls-eye and, around it, a fainter aureole of purplish brain matter. 
 I quite enjoyed The North Water for the most part. It is a gripping tale of survival and a convincing vision of legendary nautical adventures, populated with a cast of memorable characters. McGuire's sharp dialogue and stylish prose help to create an unnerving atmosphere of peril and suspense on the high seas. However the violence eventually loses its power to shock because of its frequency. And while it is an entertaining story, there is nothing particularly *new* here - I don't really understand why it is deemed Booker worthy. I would describe The North Water as a very well-written thriller rather than literary fiction. It's an enthralling, vivid and unsettling novel.

Good book....a very "manly" read, about "manly" men in the past. I enjoyed the language, the images......some of the content was a bit upsetting but it was genuine and real.
Great book.
Incredible. A must-read for Cormac McCarthy fans, as McGuire invokes his style and sense of tone.

I started this one a few days ago but gave it up pretty quickly. Now I've read some of the one-star reviews I'm giving it another go. No female voices? After The Miniaturist that sounds just the tonic I need... 
 Finished. 
 Hmm. Odd sort of book really. The descriptions of life on a whaling ship and then the subsequent stranding on the ice are very good. It's gritty, visceral and utterly realistic. Perhaps too much to be honest. There is nothing to redeem the unremitting unpleasantness of this story. The main character is too flawed and self-centered to be a heroic figure. He occasionally does good things, but not for the right reasons. He has no sense of humour at all, so even that can't lighten the bleakness. The other characters to a man are despicable. This could have been a very good read, if there had just been someone to root for. I was rooting for the whales and the polar bears and seals, but that (as you can probably predict) didn't help me much (they all died horribly). 
 Would I recommend this? I would if you really, really like violent and realistic stories about extremely unpleasant things, but I feel a bit flat after reading it. 
 It had no point to it at all except to make me realise that however challenging and unpleasant life occasionally gets, be glad I'm not on a whaling ship.
No. One chapter, and done. The reviews were stellar, the beginning sickened me. Not my cup of tea.

book_b.title: March: Book Two (March, #2)
book_b.user_review: This volume includes the March on Washington and, accordingly, my hero Bayard Rustin. What a great service this series is.

sample_reviews.review_text: The second book of the March trilogy is as good as the first. John Lewis is the last living speaker from the March on Washington, and the book continues his story while lining up with the inauguration of President Obama. Everyone should be read these.
Even Better than the First Book
Wow! John Lewis's story is so compelling.

The second in this trilogy documenting Rep. John Lewis' experiences in the civil rights movement is just as wonderful as the first installment. The division between the different factions in the civil rights movement - and the different methods they use and message they send - speaks to me as I work through the struggle today to protect the freedom that Lewis and his friends and colleagues worked so hard for - and gave their lives to.

The second in a planned trilogy based on John Robert Lewis' experiences during the Civil Rights Movement. With the power that was created in the second, the illustrations and research of the others, Andrew Aydin and Nate Powell, make the second an absolutely perfect second one. The events are vivid and detailed as well as energetic and painful. The visualization of the struggles, the in-fighting, the power of children and groups to fight against oppression collide to detail a piece of history that's a bit different than reading a nonfiction text-- it's one thing to real about Bull Connor, it's another to see the venom he spit as people were fighting for desegregation.
Just as wonderful as book one.

This series is truly wonderful and inspirational. Again, everyone should read it. I really liked this second book. The illustrations were again spot-on. If I could give this one 4.9 stars I would, only because I felt that the first book was more emotionally raw and a bit more personal. I cannot wait for the third book though. I'd say this graphic novel series is worth owning as I think it's perfectly suited for re-reads. 
 See my blog (spoilers possible!) here: https://ichleseblog.wordpress.com/201...
This is an outstanding series. I'm not much of a graphic novel fan, but I love how this series is done. Can't wait to read the 3rd.

4.5/5 
 Scary how relevant this is to current political climate. Never forget the past. Otherwise we are doomed to repeat it.

I read this volume shortly after the Denver Freedom Riders started organizing around the continued racism perpetuated by the police, prisons, and our culture. I was not actually aware of the term "freedom riders" before and when I was asked to join the group, I assumed it was a motorcycle club. 
 Volume Two of March focuses a lot on the original Freedom Riders of the civil rights movement, but anyone who thinks the depicted era of racism is "bygone" has been blinded by a lot of privilege. We still have blatantly racist politicians and police. Black people are still being murdered by the state at fucking ridiculous rates. We still need Freedom Riders. We still need civil rights movements. 
 The game has changed, the rhetoric used has changed, and the system of oppression has learned from its movements such as the one John Lewis participated in. So we must also learn from these significant examples of painful resistance. The ways they organized, the tactics they used, the punishments they faced, and the infighting that always occurs must be reflected on as we continue to organize for racial justice.

reference_books.title: P.S. I Love You
reference_books.review_text:
I find it very difficult to believe Ms. Ahern wrote this book at the age of 21. Her understanding of people and how they cope with a tragedy such as young widowhood is astounding. All of the characters in this book are incredibly believable and genuine. Holly is easy to relate to even if you haven't been in her situation and has such an unique voice. The only detail that might reveal the tender age of the author is in the simplicity of her prose, but in a book like this, it reads as well. The message is more important than the words used to convey it. 
 This book goes beyond "chick lit" to entrance most any reader.

reference_books.title: Blackwood Farm (The Vampire Chronicles, #9)
reference_books.review_text: Refreshingly, a new story set almost entirely in the recent past, a new (well, slightly related) family with paranormal secrets to explore, and a new lovable vampire hero. Tarquin Blackwood seeks out Lestat to tell his story and ask for help in banishing his lifelong companion, the spirit Goblin. Tarquin's narrative meanders with Rice's usual rapt attention to the details of architecture, clothing, and decor, which stretches the book to more than six hundred pages. Truthfully, my hand hurt from holding the book, but that's because I really couldn't put it down. I was fascinated, and really pleased, particularly since I just read Blood and Gold and Pandora which were basically the same story for the third and fourth time, from a slightly different perspective with slightly more detail. I am excited to finish out this series by reading Blood Canticle next.

reference_books.title: The Catcher in the Rye
reference_books.review_text: I really didn't see what all the fuss was about...

reference_books.title: The Book of Illusions
reference_books.review_text:
Professor David Zimmer's wife and two sons have died in a plane crash and he is at loose ends, slowly drinking himself to death, when he sees a clip from one of Hector Mann's silent films on a TV retrospective show. It makes him laugh. He embarks on a project to see all of Mann's films and write a book about them. Mann disappeared in the 1920's and no one has heard from him since. When David's book is published, he receives a mysterious letter that may shed some light on Hector's disappearance. 
 David is an elegantly realized character with a dynamic arc throughout. I found his story, and that of Mann, rather fascinating. However, there were a few things that didn't work for me. First of all, there are no quotation marks around any of the dialogue. This becomes very confusing, particularly when a character's thought or a small sentence about the action is inserted between lines of dialogue and it is not readily apparent who is speaking. Second, David describes several of Hector's films all the way through. While this is generally pretty well done, with a lot of detail, it is difficult to picture all of these scenes and becomes kind of a slog. Third, I felt as though I had invested quite a lot into both David and Hector, and was very disappointed by the ending. I won't spoil it for you, but if you're a fan of "they all lived happily ever after" you will definitely not be pleased.

reference_books.title: A Streetcar Named Desire
reference_books.review_text: I'm not generally impressed with plays and movies of this era, as they portray a time when it was considered acceptable for men to treat women as property. Women endured physical as well as emotional and psychological violence, without a inkling that something may be wrong about that. When Blanche encourages Stella to leave Stanley after he hits her after the poker game, I agreed very firmly with her. I was amazed that Stella returns, and that she still stays with him after what he does to Blanche near the end of the play. Blanche is written as flighty and slutty and her final fate is galling because I believe she's the only character in the play with a lick of sense. I found myself reading this quite quickly because I just wanted it over with. The whole thing repulsed me.

book_a.title: Ender's Shadow (Ender's Shadow, #1)
book_a.user_review:
This companion book to Ender's Game follows Bean's story as he grows up a street urchin in Rotterdam and is finally selected for battle school. Every effort has been made not to contradict the earlier work, but things are very different from Bean's perspective. Depth is added to battle school and people are not necessarily who they seemed to Ender. 
 Excellent work. Bean is a fantastic character and it will be interesting to see how his trajectory differs from Ender's after the Bugger War.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This is another book that I started and didn't finish. And before anyone discredits my opinion because I didn't finish the book, let me tell you why I stopped. 
 1. Bean is not a relatable main character. He has no emotion, and thus makes it really hard for me to empathize with him. He's basically a genetically mutated 2-dimensional genius. 
 2. Thanks to Jared's 2 star review (you'll see it if you scroll down), I was completely done with Ender's Shadow. And I don't say that with anger, I actually say it with relief. Because what happens in Ender's Shadow is complete and utter crap. Orson Scott Card tried to make Bean the mastermind behind Ender's victory over the Buggers, thus making Bean the real hero, and dulling the point of Ender being the main protagonist and hero of Ender's Game. 
 So all in all, it started out good and interesting, but when it became all about Bean, the book turned into a slow crawl down hill.

One of the most disappointing books I have ever read. What on earth would possess an author to destroy his greatest work? Cause that is what he's doing here. Oh wait. I know why he did it. Money. Bad move.
As always, Card had me captivated with the characters and intensity. The mystery surrounding Bean had me flying through the pages.
Better than Ender's Game.
I liked this one because it was sort of about Ender, but not.... and so it gave a different point of view
Excellent side by side story of Bean from Ender's Game!!! Would love to see a movie of this one too!!!

Wow! I wasn't expecting to really enjoy this book. I loved Ender's Game, and thought that a "retelling" of the same story would be boring. It wasn't at all! I was just as enthralled and loved learning more about Bean.

I have been putting off reading this book as I had already read "Ender's 
 Game" and this book was suppose to be the same event but from another 
 kid's (Bean's) point of view, so I was worried that there would be a 
 lot of overlap. 
 As it turns out, Card did an excellent job of creating essentially a 
 new story with little overlap, and a very interesting story at that. 
 We learn Bean's background and what he did to prepare for the main 
 event of both stories, and what happened to him on that journey. 
 Because Bean's focus and interests were different from Ender, there 
 was a lot of good stuff for Card to work with. 
 I would recommend reading "Ender's Game" before this book. I didn't 
 feel that spoiled this book at all, but reading in the reverse order 
 would spoil "Ender's Game" I think.

Poignant and entrancing, this book put a new spin on life for me. I'm surprised I haven't been immersed in this series, before. It questioned the meaning of humanity, and what makes us human, a surprisingly deep thought in an enjoyable sci-fi novel. Perhaps, it is what made it so enjoyable. I've decided it is the selfless sacrifice we silently sacrifice, whether emotionally, or in life or death situations in the street or full-fledged war. 
 As always, Card is effective in portraying many dimensions in a character, bringing them to life for the reader. After reading To the Lighthouse I've realized the dilemma of what people actually feel and think is a much bigger reality than I realized, even (or especially) in fiction. 
 One thing is certain, I will be delving further into the Bean/Ender series, and as we speak am putting the remaining books on hold at the library.

I absolutely adored Ender's Game, so naturally Ender's Shadow had been on my 'to-read' list for quite some time. After hearing fantastic things about this 'parallel novel', I was ready for an action-filled and highly intriguing story of at least the same caliber as the original. Perhaps I was disappointed because my expectations were too high, but this book contained far, far too much thinking for my taste. Bean feels the need to thoroughly analyze nearly every action and decision made by both himself and the people around him. I think Card tried a little too hard to make him interesting and analytical, to the point where it actually detracted from the story. Hard-core Ender's Game fans may enjoy this novel for its new insights into the story and characters, but it only works as an accompaniment, not a stand-alone.

sample_reviews.review_text: Historical fiction. The first part of the book centers on the story of Rachel Pizzarro, mother of impressionist Camille Pizzarro. She leads an independent and rebellious life, and brings scandal to her home when she marries a relative of her deceased husband, which was forbidden in her culture. One of their children is Camille Pizzarro (often credited as the father in Impressionism), and the second part of this book is the story of his struggle to become a painter. The measure of a good book for me is if I learn something -- and seek more information on the subject. This one had me headed to the library to look at Pizzarro's work and see if I could spot the St. Thomas influence.

Historical fiction based on the life of famous artist Camille Pissarro's mother, Rachel Petit Pissarro. 
 Hits: Vivid descriptions of St. Thomas and Paris. Hoffman's portrayal of the love between Rachel and Frederic, *sigh*. 
 Misses: Slow. Often unlikable main character.

This book was a gripping story in the beginning, but really petered out toward the middle and end. I usually am a fan of Alice Hoffman, but this tale was really repetitive (if I heard references to hait blue or turtle women one more time...). Also, I never figured out where the marriage of opposites was. Was it the younger girl marrying an older man? Was it the non practicing Jew marrying a supposed Christian? Also, in the story There were several conversations that appeared to be leading to some juicy tidbit and then got cut off because the maid came in or the person didn't want to speak ill of anyone and that was that...just hanging there wishing something interesting had been revealed. There were several characters with an African father and a white mother who everyone took for being white. I know this can happen on occasion, but this book made it seem like a very common thing. Overall, it was just an ok book. If you are looking for a better one by Alice Hoffman, I would recommend "the museum of extraordinary things."

Decent read - I echo other reviews requesting the capability to award 1/2 points - I would have given it 3.5 if possible. 
 Quote: 
 "Mattei's old adage came to Zee's mind now: Everybody lies. Maureen and Lily had both lied to Zee. That was no big surprise. Bit it was more than that now. The lies or stories that Maureen and Lily told were not lies they were telling Zee, the were the mythology they were creating for themselves. When they were no longer able to believe their own fairy tales they lost all hope. 
 It was a huge revelation, and it explained a lot." 
 Do we create a mythology as we live our lives and does it sustain us through the difficult times...is reality to difficult to deal with unless we cushion it with "mythology".

I positively adored this book--its many layers, its use of symbology, its strong and compelling voice, the complex, true-to-life characters who shadowed other characters throughout, the beautiful way Barry has of revealing character through setting. (One of my favorite scenes described a child's wild scribblings buried under wainscoting--a brilliant hint to the main character's layers, buried via her relationship with her mother.) I loved the plot of this book, along with its strong literary core. Lastly, though I don't want to give anything away, I'll say that Barry has a gift for developing characters who surprise. A truly fantastic read--definitely my favorite book of 2013 to date.

Why didn't I read this sooner? Essential reading for understanding intersectionality (in the context of being poor, black and female) and, I suppose, polyamory - the love polygon between Mr._______, Celie, Shug and Grant. 
 Celie must be one of my all-time favourite fictional narrators - my test of a good fictional narrator is if I can hear their voice inside my head. Celie really jumps off the page as a fully-formed woman. 
 The novel does deal with some difficult and challenging subject matter (sexual and domestic violence, racial discrimination) and may be triggering for some readers, but avoids melodrama or exaggeration - everything seems eminently believable. The darker subject matter is balanced out by lighter, humorous moments, normally revolving around Shug Avery's appearances. 
 I cannot recommend this novel enough and I don't really know how I've managed not to read it sooner.

I understand that it's a classic, and it does provide an interesting perspective on an important period of time, but I just didn't like the way it was written. I really lacked desire to finish the book, although I'm glad I did because the end was good. However, I wouldn't read it again.

This book has found me at different points in my life and reminded me identity is always evolving as we grow into the person we were always meant to be. Walker's novel is also one that explores the nature of spirituality, though that side of the novel tends to get overlooked as its more feminist aspects are focused on. At the core of it all, this is a very human and very moving book. Celie literally writes herself into existence over the years. That's powerful stuff, indeed.

A bad book, even with noble aspirations, is still a bad book. This is Forrest Gump meets Steel Magnolias. If you like simple-minded homilies spun by a good-hearted dolt, this is the book for you. It won the Pulitzer in 1983, giving further credence to my belief that voters of literary awards get it wrong more often than they get it right. 
 According to Wikipedia, "the novel has been the frequent target of censors and appears on the American Library Association list of the 100 Most Frequently Challenged Books of 2000-2009 at number seventeen because of the sometimes explicit content, particularly in terms of violence." I'm skeptical of it being banned because of violence as opposed to its depiction of homosexuality and marijuana. More generally, it's probably banned because of its unapologetic dogma that most would categorize as liberal. I sometimes wish I were a librarian so I could ban books, but for different reasons. "This book is banned because of insufficient character development." 
 This novel is very dogmatic. Bad black men are horrifically cruel to women and keep them down. Spunky black women fight back, but when they come against white people in power they get beaten down. Lesbian love is A-OK. Black skin is beautiful. Africa was a paradise until white men came in and ruined it. Frankly none of these dogmas is particularly controversial to all but dyed-in-the-wool reactionaries. Maybe these dogmas were controversial in 1982, but I doubt it. How edgy could it be if it became a Steven Spielberg movie just a few years later? 
 (Note: I recently saw the first half of the movie. Let me just say that Steven Spielberg directed the shit out of that movie. The screenplay corrects many of the novel's shortcomings. But beyond that, Spielberg does heroic work squeezing every bit of narrative juice out of a tale that doesn't have that much drama in it. He was at the top of his game when he directed it. And young Whoopie Goldberg is adorkabe in the role of Celie. It's a role that is a far cry from the in-your-face persona she nurtured afterwards.) 
 I would be remiss if I didn't mention one area where Walker veers into a ditch. Namely she defends the practice of female genital mutilation as it was practiced in Africa. I can't remember her exact words, as I listened to the audio book, narrated by herself. Of that, I will say she did an ok job. Still, it would have been better if she had relinquished the job to a voice actress. But back to female genital mutilation. Nettie, a missionary in Africa, describes it as merely a small cut or nick. It's part of the tribe's Culture with a capital C, and therefore ok. Surely Walker has changed her opinion on the practice which is so misogynistic. I think when writing the book she was so hell-bent on showing the super-awesomeness of the tribe was that she lost perspective. 
 An ongoing debate is the question of what is literary fiction and what is genre fiction. A typical answer is that literary fiction is more focused on language and character development as opposed to plot. This is true, but I think the answer obscures a key point about character development. In genre fiction characters run into figurative brick walls when it comes to characteristics that violate the genre's tropes. Nuance is not allowed if it means that a character will act in a way that's not acceptable to the genre. They're put in an emotional straightjacket. My belief is that readers of the genre want realistic characters, but not so realistic that their motivations become murky and confused. Genre readers don't want characters that challenge pre-conceived notions. 
 There was a study published in Science recently that shows that readers of literary fiction are more empathetic than readers of genre fiction. As quoted in Scientific American, one of the study's authors said "Although literary fiction tends to be more realistic than popular fiction, the characters disrupt reader expectations, undermining prejudices and stereotypes. They support and teach us values about social behavior, such as the importance of understanding those who are different from ourselves." 
 I'm sure the Pulitzer voters in 1983 thought that The Color Purple undermined prejudices and stereotypes by showing they humanity of African Americans. And not just any African Americans, but ones who are lesbian and even smoke a joint once in a while. Wow! How revolutionary! Let's give it an award and in so doing, , give a giant fuck you to racists and white supremacists everywhere. 
 But The Color Purple never disrupts readers expectations. Celie is good and always good. Nettie is good. Shug Avery is good. The African Tribe is good. Celie's step-dad is bad. Mister is bad, except in the end when he becomes good. Mister's transformation is made easy for readers as he is shown to have Found Religion. If you're over the age of 12 and these characters truly disrupt your expectations, then you're kind of a dumbshit and quite probably a racist. If reading this book makes you less racist, then yay! But you probably voted for Trump last year, and you'll vote for the son of a bitch in 2020 if he hasn't been impeached by then. 
 So if this is genre fiction, what genre is it? I would classify it as "women's fiction." I know that the name of this genre drives some women insane as they see it as ghettoization and demeans novels they know and love. "Upscale" or even "Commercial Fiction" is less offensive. Whatever. The bottom line is that this weak-ass novel is not canon-worthy, and it's a travesty that it's taught in high school and college. Its only academic worth is that it serves as a snapshot of the issues that academe thought were important in the later part of the 20th century.

This book was amazing. As angry as it made me feel how Celie was treated all her life, I was so caught up in her story. I had to read this for college and it is one of those books that you enjoy reading and forget you have an exam on it, but I am so glad I read it and gave it a chance.

"There is a way that the men speak to women that reminds me too much of Pa. They listen just long enough to issue instructions. They don't even look at women when women are speaking. They look at the ground and bend their heads toward the ground. The women also do not "look in a man's face" as they say. To "look in a man's face" is a brazen thing to do. They look instead at his feet or his knees. And what can I say to this?" 
 What a sad and splendid book. The Color Purple tells the tale of 20 years of Celie's life through her letters. A poor black woman whose father abuses and rapes her at the age of 14, Celie soon loses her sister as well as her independence after marrying "Mister." Only by meeting Shug - the most fierce, unapologetic woman Celie's ever encountered - and learning the truth about her sister does Celie start to move toward her reawakening, her self-acceptance, and her love for even those who have hurt her. 
 Alice Walker delves into so many important issues in The Color Purple. Even though the book focuses on a black woman oppressed in the first half of the twentieth century, a myriad of the behaviors and themes found within the book still apply to all women today. Not only does Walker weave in timeless feminist ideas, she also relates Celie's struggle to domestic abuse, lgbtq culture, the strength of sisterhood, and so much more. 
 My favorite concept in The Color Purple was the use of storytelling as healing. Celie gives herself a voice by befriending Shug and eventually writing letters to Nettie, and even the epistolary format of the book exemplifies the power of writing, talking, and sharing one's struggles. Whether it's a veteran with PTSD sharing their story with a therapist or an angry teenager writing on their blog, human connection and communication poses so many benefits, and Walker's book highlights that in the most wonderful of ways. 
 Highly, highly recommended to anyone interested in feminism, historical fiction, overcoming abuse, or any intersection of those topics. Definitely a classic I wish more people read.

reference_books.review_text:
Walk away Richard! 
 Silly me. I mistakenly thought this was a work of non-fiction. I kept shaking my head and thinking." Come on!" Then about half way through I checked and realized it was fiction. 
 Silly writing. Publishers hoax.

reference_books.title: Skeletons at the Feast
reference_books.review_text: Don't think I'd recommend this one. Story line was fractured, ending was BAD and atrocities depicted were graphic beyond need. I don't know how many timers the author used the wor "violated" but it was OVERKILL. Highly recommend THE BOOK THIEF in its staed.

reference_books.title: The Darkest Part of the Forest
reference_books.review_text:
This is not my typical genre so I feel unqualified to review this. I borrowed it from the library because I like the title and because I am always on the hunt for good books for my precocious eight-year-old granddaughter. 
 First: This is NOT a book I recommend to ANY eight-year-old, no matter how precocious. More teen-agers and young adults as there are a few steamy (well done) sex scenes. 
 I esp. liked that women were depicted as very strong and capable, even as sword-weilding warriors! Also issue of gender-orientation sensitively portrayed. 
 Found the story, as one amazon reviews so aptly said, "strangely satisfying", though it could have used some editing. There was a lot crammed in here and the ending lasted a long time. Lots of action and adrenalin-flowing scenes. It seemed as though the author was so absorbed in her characters and their story that she just couldn't let them go.

reference_books.title: Gone Girl
reference_books.review_text:
Excellent narration by Julia Whelan. Her portrayal of these loathsome characters (except Go and Boney) gets to the heart of their pathetic thoughts and yearnings. It will take me a L-O-N-G time to hear the names "Nick" or "Amy" without feeling ill. 
 Storyline had way too many implausible events to make it believable. Horrible ending.

reference_books.title: Boy, Snow, Bird
reference_books.review_text:
DANG! This is one helluva story! 
 Not sure why I took away one star. Took me a bit of a while to get into it, but whoa baby (!), once I did...............

book_a.title: A Million Little Pieces
book_a.user_review: I quit on this one. Just didn't buy it. Felt like someone asked the author to do this and he wrote a slurpy, pseudo-dramatic version of rehab. Too much didn't jive so I dumped it. Perhaps I am being rash (I got to p.207) but I'd had all I could stomach.

sample_reviews.review_text: I didn't read the entire book, so the label "read" is not quite correct, but it's definitely neither a "to-read" or a "currently-reading." There ought to be a label for "not-worth-finishing," although this is the only book I've ever started that would deserve it. I'm not sure if it counts to have ATTEMPTED to read this book. I am not sure I was able to finish a single chapter, no matter which one I attempted. The writing was an atrocity, and the story was false but published as non-fiction. I could have possibly accepted one or the other, but not both. Can I give negative stars? This is the only book in which, if someone asked me, "Well, could you do better?," my answer would be, "Unequivocally YES."
I read this book a while ago but I enjoyed it. He writing style is a bit different than what I am used to, but overall it's a very interesting book.

What a (million little) piece(s) of crap! By the time I finished this book I was craving a few stiff drinks, desperately tearing up the house looking for a syringe and spoon. If I had only thrown this one in the Goodwill bin sooner! I have no clue why anyone would think this was worthwhile reading material. I found it to be vapid, self-aggrandizing bullshit from start to finish. 
 I read this book before the whole Oprah controversy/confrontation, so that really had no impact upon my lowly opinion. This book was so badly written and sophomoric, I never had an inkling of empathy for any of the characters, particularly the author himself. So why am I wasting my time writing this review? Just in hopes that you will decide not to read this shite! Thank you for just saying no to "A Million Little Pieces" - you would have a much better time reading the operating manual for your toaster oven while smoking a rock.

I won't write a review because I don't think I can jot down in meaningless alphabetical letters how this book made me feel. It's not an easy story to love or relate to but it's all about human vulnerability, temptations, loss, anger, love, and it's so full of literary goodness. This book took a part of me with it.

I read this book before all the SHIT hit the fan that this author is a fraud. While reading it, I felt it was pretty damn obvious it was a lot of fabrication, it just didn't ring true and was honestly surprised that Oprah like or recommended it.

I am not sure why I like reading about people with completely screwed up lives but I do. This is James Frey's true story about addiction and recovery. Although, I have heard that this story may not completely be true but embellished to be a crazier story. Either way- entertaining read.

I liked this book for the same reasons I didn't like this book. The protagonist (the author) is very stubborn throughout the book and doesn't like to listen to other people. I liked that he holds onto his beliefs because for a second I thought he was going to give in and it was going to turn into a religious book, which I totally would have been disappointed with. However, at the same time he doesn't open himself up to any of the ideas of the rehab center. Basically, he is saying "I am supreme over any 12 steps of rehab and you should just have enough will power to overcome addiction." I wouldn't recommend this book to someone who is an addict for that reason. Also I felt like the author kind of brags about how he was tougher than everyone else in this rehab place, and although it's a memoir some of it I have a hard time believing. I have never had any real experience with addicts, so I really have no idea how that life is, but I still felt like it was overflufffed a bit. The other thing I did not like was the way it was written. Here is an example of how I felt a sentence would be "I read the book. I liked it and didn't like it. I wrote a review and hit enter. The review went off into the universe for everyone to read." There were just took many words and it was very simple. It took a long time to read because there were just too many unnecessary sentences. It was like he literally just wrote down everything he thought and it was too much for me. That being said, the way it was written also made me feel like he was just a normal person going through a very hard thing which made me feel more connected to it. Overall, I guess what I am saying is that I am on the fence about this book which is why it gets 3 starts from me. Happy reading!
yuck.

Crushing, devastating, underscores the absolute futility of everything. I want to like the guy and I do, but I hate him as well. It is a sickening book and I never even want to look at the cover again. The pain in this one is a sledgehammer. It has a happy ending in that he has not relapsed, but I don't trust that it will stay that way, and I've asked the G-d he doesn't believe in to help him.

I picked up this book from a Goodwill for a quarter, I think. Given all of the controversy surrounding it, I bet that's all that most people would pay. Certainly, if I had read it along with Oprah's book club, I would be furious to learn that James Frey made up or exaggerated much of it. 
 I already knew about all of the controversy, though, and I practically devoured it. I thoroughly enjoyed the stream-of-consciousness writing style and plot. I suppose you can tell by now that I read it as a novel. It's a good novel. My question now is, why did he or the publisher try to market it as a memoir? Is it really that hard to break into fiction these days? Or is he just a jerk who wanted money, and was unwilling to place an "Inspired by actual events" line at the beginning of his book? I'm not sure what happened, but I still enjoyed the book. It's exciting, touching, and inspiring, even if it didn't really happen. I just wish James Frey had let the James in the book be a character, instead of claiming that it was really him.

book_b.title: The Stranger in the Woods: The Extraordinary Story of the Last True Hermit
book_b.user_review:
The Last True Hermit? This is a sensational and unnecessary by-line as even the author includes information on many present-day hermits. That put aside, a very good listen (read), well-written and very engaging. I wish there had been more detail about Christopher's Knight's day-to-day existence and less psychology. I found it heartbreaking that this man was forced to return to a society/life that he felt so alienated from. Also put off by the author's continued insistence on making contact with Knight when he so clearly did not want it. I understand and empathize with Finkel's commitment and concerns about Knight, but the poor guy had to beg and plead to be left alone. 
 Excellent bibliography for other works on solitude included. 
 As always, superbly read by Mark Bramhall. (I would listen to anything that this man narrates.)

sample_reviews.review_text: Probably closer to a 3.5. I enjoyed this book as I found the character of Chris Knight, a "hermit" who essentally walked into the woods with his backpack and didn't emerge for 27 years. He is a controversial figure, as he sustained himself by stealing thousands of times from local homes and cottages. However, I was so curious to understand how this individual seemed to have no drive for connection, relationships, and contact, which are the very things that I feel give life its meaning. I also enjoyed some of Finkel's reflections on solitude, other famous recluses and hermits, and what it means to be alone. Definitely an interesting read.
Very well done

Not my favorite book. Unfortunately I had to forward through several of the pages due to the writing style employed. Finkel writes this like a term paper, as if he is proving a thesis through research. What I wanted was the story of Christopher Knight. It was difficult to sustain close reading through the drudgery of philosophic and psychologic references. 
 Just OK.
This book was very interesting. I learned more about the history of Hermits than I ever knew existed!
Truly fascinating.

I have mixed feelings about this book about a man who lived in the woods for 25 years in Maine. On one hand, it is excellently written and a good investigation on what it means to live a solitary and isolated existence. On the other hand, Chris Knight, the hermit, is so disillusioned when he re-enters society that it's really disheartening. He also, despite one tearful moment, seems genuinely annoyed by the author's persistent interviews and repeatedly tells him to stop bothering him and wait until he's dead to publish anything. Well, the author didn't wait, which made my annoyed! Very interesting, though, and I can't believe Chris didn't light one fire that whole time, for fear of being caught.

Very straightforward and readable without making more a myth out of the man than needed. I particularly liked the well researched medical interpretations as well as the appropriately placed quotes about silence. If you are even marginally introverted I highly recommend this book.

This felt very exploitative, particularly when you learn how much this family and Chris did not want to talk to this reporter. 
 The only parts I really enjoyed were the sections on the history of hermits. I'm interested in further reading in the future on isolation and hermits throughout history.

I didn't expect to like this book, but I loved it. It is very interesting, honest, and well researched. It is the story of Christopher Knight, the "hermit" discovered and arrested in Maine after 27 years living in the woods without any human contact.

This book was well researched and fairly well written, but the pacing was on the slower side for my tastes. The actual story of Chris Knight was padded with so many factoids from literature, psychologists, scientists, and history that I at times forgot what I was even reading. The extra information was necessary to make this a full book length piece (and some of it was genuinely interesting), but the fascinating and bizarre story of the actual hermit got lost in all the extraneous info.

reference_books.title: Come to Me Quietly (Closer to You, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
It's no secret that I am a HUGE fan of A.L. Jackson's books. The first book I read Pulled stayed with me and to this day I still remember how hauntingly beautiful the story and her writing was. Her books have never let me down and Come to Me Quietly just reminded me of how amazing of a storyteller she is. 
 This book is deep... the storyline and the characters have so much depth at times you feel like you are drowning with them in their sorrows. As with all her books I was sucked into an emotional battle. 
 Jared is BROKEN! I'm a sucker for the broken boys, but I have to admit I didn't love him at first. It took me some time to get used to his character. As the story developed and I heard his full story I couldn't help but fall in love with this broken man. He just needs someone to help him out of the black hole of self destruction and that person happens Aleena Moore. She's a light in the darkness for Jared but he's too messed up over his past and the mistakes he's made to let her become anything more then another mistake. Your heart will BLEED for him and what he's been through. I cried and cried when I learned his full story. 
 Aleena or Aly, is one strong character. She has been hiding ever since the day Jared was stripped from their lives. Hiding behind the pain and hiding behind her secrets. It took a while to get to why Aly let this affect her so much. I mean friends come and go it's part of life, but this was so much more to her. She never really let anyone in, as much as people tried she was truly closed off. I know that she was in love with Jared when they were children so there had to be more to the story and oh boy was there EVER! I didn't see that twist coming which is rare for me. Sometimes I have the plot figured out long before we get to the heart of the story, so this was quite refreshing! I was so torn up when she revealed her story and Jared and she discussed it I seriously used a box of tissues sopping up the tears... It was an UGLY cry but I've come to always expect that from this authors books so I was prepared!!!! 
 I don't think that I could recommend this book highly enough!!!!! I totally am in love with Jared and Aly's story and July can't get here soon enough to see what happens next... The only one thing that I was left questioning and I'm hoping that is coming in the next book is Jared and Christopher's relationship. They were best friends in the past and I really wanted to see a heart to heart with these two, but after reading the ending of the book I have a feeling there will be a lot more discussions in the future... I wouldn't say it was a cliffhanger but more of a lead in of what's to come in book #2! 
 I happily give this book 5 stars. It deserves that and so much more....

reference_books.title: The Dark Prince (Dark Light, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
God I don't even know where to begin with this one... WOW WOW WOW WOW!!!!! Fans of this series I am going to tell you right now that you are going to LOVE this book it is so crazy good. After I finished my reading I immediately messaged her and told her that I was just not worthy. 
 If you haven't read the first book in the series yet then this won't make much sense to you so I highly recommend you go and read this book IMMEDIATELY and tap your toes and wait for this book to publish... You won't be sorry.... 
 So The Dark Prince really rocked my world. It continues with more of the smoldering HOT Dorian Skotos the GREEK GOD! You will need to fan yourself several times through this book I'll warn you now! Gabriella is hopelessly in love with Dorian that was pretty clear in the first book in the series. That love grows, intensifies and becomes downright dangerous to both Gabriella and Dorian. And not just dangerous because of who they both are but dangerous to their survival. 
 There are many, and I mean MANY deep dark secrets in this book that will make you EEEEPPPPP and GASP and SIGH.... I couldn't hold my emotions in check at times and I had some ugly cries. Gabriella just tugs at my heart strings and even though I got really angry with Dorian at times throughout the book I remained enamored by him. The question is can we trust anything that he says. As the information unfolded I questioned everything and constantly found myself saying NO WAY he didn't just do or say that... 
 This book introduced one very LOVEABLE character and I found myself completely in lust for this one immediately... I'm not going to give anything away because it would just be unfair but when you read his parts I think that you will want MORE MORE MORE of him as well... sigh.... 
 The most brilliant and astounding part is contained in the last paragraph to the last word on the last page and your HEART will STOP and you will immediately do a double and then a triple take at the ending... If you are anything like me and reading this ending at 2 am with dreary eyes but just cannot put the book down you will re-read the same part repeatedly and say THAT JUST DID NOT HAPPEN!!!! Then you will run and post about the moment anywhere you can because you feel like you need to tell someone about this crazy unexplainable moment! Now I have you totally intrigued and wanting to read The Dark Prince right???? 
 SOOOOOOO AMAZINGLY GOOD!!!!!! I had no words for several days and I hate being as vague with you all as I am but giving away any part of this story would just be completely unfair at this point... Don't worry you don't have much longer to wait! 
 5 BIG BEAUTIFUL BRIGHT SHINING "LIGHT" STARS for this awesome sequel. I was worried because a lot of times they just don't live up to their hype but this one far exceeded my expectations and I think that you will all love it as much as I did! The 15th isn't far off now so you won't have to wait much longer...

reference_books.title: Undeclared (Woodlands, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I really enjoyed this story. The characters were well developed, there was just one plot line that I thought got lost somewhere in the mix but it didn't deter me from enjoying this book. 
 Grace is a girl that is confused as are most girls her age. After years of writing to a solider that started out as a school project, she fell hard and fast for Noah. They wrote beautiful letters back and forth for years before Noah decided to leave the military. Grace was certain that he was her prince charming, but when Noah decided to send Grace a Dear John type letter letting her down she completely retreated into herself... Grace had already led a difficult life now she was away at college and lonely, so lonely, no meaningful relationships because she vowed to never feel the hurt again she felt when Noah's letter arrived... 
 Noah Jackson was a Marine, having had a rough childhood and a father he hated, once Noah graduated high school he knew his way to break free was the military. He and his best friend Bo enlisted and were sent to Afghanistan. Life in the desert wasn't easy but it was made a lot better when he started getting letter and care packages from a high school student working on a school project. What he didn't know is that Grace would become his reason for wanting to be a better man and wanting something he never truly had. A family. After years of being overseas when he was discharged from the military he was in a bad place. Needing to get his life in order he spent his time making himself someone that Grace would be proud of, someone deserving of her. What he didn't know was that blow off letter may have ruined any chance he had at winning her over... 
 Grace was a stubborn girl, and when Noah came back into her life she was hell bent on making him suffer the way she had since receiving that letter... She was so funny, she made me laugh a lot, but she also made me sad. Noah was infuriating at times, boy did he make me crazy! The story was done very well overall and I really enjoyed getting to know these characters. Bo, Noah's best friend cracked me up and I loved how protective their roommates were of Grace. 
 Overall this was a good read and I do recommend that you give it a shot... There is another book coming out that will be Bo's story and I'm excited for that one. I really loved his character and think that there is a lot more to him then meets the eye... He is portrayed in a specific light but I have a feeling deep down it isn't who he truly is, he's hiding... We shall see if I'm right... 
 I give Jen a solid 4 stars on this read. The only thing that I would have changed was moving forward one part of the plot that sort of disappeared at the end. But other then that it's a great read and a beautiful love story about finding yourself and discovering that sometimes what we want in life is worth fighting for...
