Shallow. Boring. Badly written. Terrible dialogue. No plot. No ending. Too many characters. Too many tedious descriptions of the brands characters were using, wearing, living in. Too many pages (almost 500!). But I made myself finish this utter drek. 
 It's supposed to be satire, and the cover blurb says "Snarky . . . wicked . . . funny" (NYT). I could see the author attempting humour but it didn't even make me smile. 
 The most annoying thing was that every time I picked it up, I had to flip back a few pages because I could never remember what was going on and who these characters even were. There was a character list in the front of the book, but it only listed about half the characters in the novel. I had to keep checking it until the end. 
 A nice break with a fluffy novel can be therapeutic, but this one was just crap. 
 Recommended for: creative writing teachers to use as an example of what not to write. Others looking to read some lifestyles of the rich and famous should just dig out a Jackie Collins novel from the 80s.

Not as good as the first book in this series - this felt like too much very far fetched stuff was going on. I still enjoyed Nick and Rachel's adventures, but I missed some of the other Singaporean characters and got a bit fed up of Michael. Still fun, just not as much fun.

reference_books.title: The Library at Mount Char
reference_books.review_text:
Excellent premise, but I just cannot with this book. Got maybe 20% in and gave up. 
 The writing is so lazy, most of the times the characters don't even finish their thoughts, whether they're speaking or thinking. A lot of "tension" and "mystery" is being manufactured through their inability to express themselves, either because they're being pointlessly interrupted or because they just cannot English. 
 The gore is gratuitous and psychologically unsound. And there's so much of it, by the time I gave up on this book, all I could think of was Eddie Izzard's sketch about genocidal tyrants, 
 "Whoa, you must get up VERY early in the morning!"

reference_books.title: Little Women (Little Women, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Had I only read Part 1, I would have given this three stars, but as one whole narrative, the effect is odious. 
 I've read plenty of novels written in the same period, so I cannot in good faith dismiss the grating narrative voice and the many, many preachy lessons as just a thing "of the time." 
 This book is dull, sexists and psychologically unsound, to put it mildly. There's no story as such, just an awful lot of vignettes that maybe offer a window into the characters' adorably comfortable lives, but don't truly forward the story or justify the characters' actions.

reference_books.title: The Psychopath Test: A Journey Through the Madness Industry
reference_books.review_text: If you're looking for a thorough, clinical review of the field, this is not it. Instead, as the title states, it's one man's journey through some of the aspects of the industry, in his personal search for answers dictated by the unique questions he's interested in and the specific people he encounters on his journey. Still, it's a great, if harrowing, starting point, and an interesting glimpse into both the psychiatric industry and journalism.

reference_books.title: Throne of Glass (Throne of Glass, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Errr, no. Mostly because by about page 100, I was completely distracted from the story by random thoughts: 
 - A throne room at a remote salt mine? WTF? 
 - Why would a loss in an assassin competition mean just being sent back to where one came from? Wouldn't assassins fight to the death? 
 - How does the best assassin in the world get so easily distracted?! Stop daydreaming! 
 - Why would a murderous prisoner get washed by others?! Why not just give her a pail of water and order her to do the job herself? 
 - She's still a prisoner, so why dress her in silks right away? This shit's expensive and impractical, and she's about to embark on a long journey, riding horses and presumably sleeping al fresco in her clothes along the way? 
 - Disney princess alert! I think she's about to break out into a song, accompanied by forest animals. Focus, Miss Assassin! Focus! 
 - Why would she tell her servant who she is when she was supposed to come to the capital under an alias? WTF? 
 - And why is the servant such a sexists bitch? Surely not to ham-handedly remind us what a total cutie our assassin is: 
 "Don't make such a face," Philippa called over her shoulder. "It squishes that little nose of yours." 
 - The "let me tell you all about our realm and how totally hot that girl assassin is" conversation between the king and the prince is just... I have no words. 
 - Why is she being "practically dragged out" of places so often? Also, if she's such a terrifyingly skilled assassin, why would anyone dare to even try to "practically" do anything to her? 
 - WTF is she doing considering playing piano, penning pretty notes, and reading books the night before the competition starts?! Did I miss somewhere where she mentioned she grew up in a noble family and practiced her music skills and penmanship from an early age? (While, obviously, also practicing stealthy murder of the highest quality and remaining completely undiscovered in this pursuit until she was 17.) 
 - Is she an assassin (a person who gets paid to ply their trade and expected to deliver) or an impetuous homicidal floozy? Why is she randomly throwing flowerpots at people who have done nothing worse than call her names? And why does she miss?!! 
 - She's spent a year in rags at a salt mine and she's complaining that her shoes pinch?! 
 - I'm getting a whiplash from the way the guard goes from unceremoniously dragging her around to imparting caring tidbits or compliments and then back to growling. 
 - As an assassin, wouldn't you want your competition to underestimate you? Then why does she resent it so much when the others don't think much of her at first glance and suddenly regrets wearing a pretty dress? The girl has zero agency and no plan. Sheesh. 
 - She's spent her life killing for the highest bidder, and now suddenly she's got scruples? Because doing it for the king and a lot of money suddenly would be "murder?" WTF? 
 - A wise person once said that, if you want a woman to appear attractive and a true love interest in a story, you should portray her as graceful. If you want a tramp, focus on how pretty she is. I'm not even 15% into this story and I'm already so bored of how pretty the assassin is... 
 - Oh, and now she's calling another woman "unfairly stunning." WTF? Also, I've always thought the point of an assassin was to be inconspicuous. 
 - And now they're being catty about who's the prettiest! Whaaa!!! 
 - She's spent a year at a prison mine and now she's "starved" because she's missed lunch?! 
 - How does she sleep like a log when she's supposed to be an assassin?! She's acting like a spoiled princess, not somebody who's had to be on her guard all her life. I know this time it's because she's read till four in the morning (on the night before the competition? WTF?!), but by now it seems like she's got trouble getting out of bed in general... 
 - 20% in, and if I hear another arrogant, condescending internal monologue about how much superior she is to everyone else without a shred of evidence to prove it, I'm throwing the book in the trash. Little Miss Conceited. 
 - Also, how did she manage to conceal her identity for so long - as an inexperienced child! - when now she's so attention- and recognition-hungry? 
 - "You all have five minutes to put away your weapons and catch your breath." WTF?! The 24 of them just stood around introducing themselves for what I imagine must have been at least 15 minutes, so what do they need the extra 5 for? 
 - She got distracted and MISSED A BREATH?! OK, I'm done. I cannot read this anymore.

reference_books.title: The Reader
reference_books.review_text:
A star for the subject matter, but otherwise this is as poorly written a story as they come. 
 *SPOILERS* 
 I still don't understand why the author has to spend such a long time setting up the dysfunctional, abusive relationship in Part One. I didn't know the subject matter when I picked the book up (based on the stellar reviews), so I dived straight in and for almost half of the book was led to believe I was reading about the physical, psychological and sexual abuse of a child. And then, suddenly, wham! Part Two, the abuser turns out to also be a Nazi, and the narrative becomes just the author using the abused kid (who doesn't consider himself abused and never stops to consider that now his PTSD is affecting other, innocent people) as a suddenly all-knowing and understanding mouthpiece to fit his own agenda. It was interminable, painfully tedious and utterly forced. Part Three is just as dreadful narrative-wise, but now you will wish the dialogue remained as nonexistent as it was before, because here everyone spews the same flowery monologues that don't sound like real people talking, or like anyone trying to have an actual conversation. Finally, the main character closes with this: 
 "The tectonic layers of our lives rest so tightly one on top of the other that we always come up against earlier events in later ones, not as matter that has been fully formed and pushed aside, but absolutely present and alive." 
 That, kid, is the definition of a flashback. You've got PTSD. Get some help, because you've been dead inside since 15 and nobody who's known you is any better for it.

book_a.title: The Wind in the Willows
book_a.user_review:
What a horrid, horrid story, full of violence, insults and evasion of any consequences. I suppose it's a good parable for what life's like if you're filthy rich, but I really don't need a reminder of the fact that some of us are above the law by the "virtue" of money and enabling "friends." 
 And no, I do not believe the ending to be in any way redeeming. The best predictor of future behavior is past behavior, so one instance of submitting to the rules of "good" society (and for just a few hours) does not in any way convince me that the character's lifetime of being an utter self-indulgent jerk is over.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Trevor Phillips OBE ,head of the Equality and Human Rights Commission, has chosen to discuss Kenneth Grahame's The Wind in the Willows, on FiveBooks (http://five-books.com) as one of the top five on his subject - Equality, saying that: 
 "...Essentially there is a bad reading and a good reading of this book. The bad reading is that it is a parable about class, where the stoats and weasels are working-class oiks who invade Toad Hall. But the good reading is what underlies all this: Badger as a symbol of the values of decency and fair play. He is somebody who will take people for what they are and treat them decently.....". 
 The full interview is available here: http://thebrowser.com/books/interview...

At least now with it on my Kindle, I'll always have Mole, Rat, Toad and Mr. Badger at hand for my own reading pleasure.

I rather disliked this book, and as such, have no inclination towards writing a review. I will say that Kenneth Grahame was sexist and annoying, and the Toad was the most annoying character I've read in a long time. Peace out~

This was a lovely book with colorful characters and subtle morals. It isn't the fastest paced book you will ever read, but it doesn't have to be. This is a book to relax to and just enjoy the adventures these characters are going through.

V etoi knige plokho vsio - nachinaia s siuzheta (esli on tam voobshche est') i zakanchivaia personazhami i atmosferoi, tsariashchei v knige!!! Kak tol'ko eta kniga umudrilas' stat' klassikoi - ne poniatno. Geroi zdes', v osnovnom, ediat (s podrobnym opisaniem chto imenno) brodiat po lesu i vedut glupye i neestestvennye dialogi (khotia, mozhet byt', skuchaiushchie dzhentl'meny v Anglii deistvitel'no tak razgovarivaiut, tochno skazat' ne mogu). Ochen' khotel by poznakomit'sia s rebionkom, kotoromu eta kniga ponravilas' ili kotoryi khotia by dochital eio do kontsa (ia sdelal eto s bol'shim trudom). V etoi knige detskogo net nichego. I v pervuiu ochered' strannoe nazvanie, po kotoromu ni za chto ne dogadaesh'sia, chto pered toboi skazka! Personazhi zhivotnye, no oni ne deti, a skoree muzhchiny srednego vozrasta, kotorym absoliutno nechem zaniat'sia. Iazyk knigi ochen' slozhnyi: pestrit nazvaniiami rastenii, zhivotnykh i slozhnym postroeniem fraz. I samoe glavnoe - v knige prakticheski nichego ne proiskhodit, net samogo glavnogo, chto dolzhno byt' v detskoi knige - net prikliuchenii (esli ne schitat' za prikliucheniia ugon mashiny, pobeg iz tiur'my, krazhu loshadi m eio dal'neishuiu prodazhu, chto, konechno, delaet chest' klassicheskoi detskoi knige!). V ocherednoi raz ubedilsia, chto klassika klassike rozn'!
Such a delightful tale. I really enjoyed the adventure as such and Grahame has some really nice things to say about life and friendsdhip. I look forward to reading more books by him.

I seem to have an opposite view to most of the reviewers on here. I loved The Golden Age, but had trouble with this one. 
 I watched the movie when I was a child. I did not like Toad then and I don't like him now. 
 If the author's intention was to really make me hate this character, he succeeded. And as a consequence I developed a low opinion of Rat, Mole and Badger as well, because they allowed themselves to be repeatedly taken in by this disreputable character. 
 Pros: 
 1. Rat, Mole and Badger. All interesting characters, gentleman. 
 2. The fantasy elements when they searched for Otter's child. 
 3. The peaceful, idyllic river life was lovely to read about. 
 Cons: 
 1. The world doesn't make sense. How tall are the creatures? It sounds as though they are the same size as humans, but at one point one of them is easily lifted, bodily, into the air. And Toad has hair? How can an animal be mistaken for a human? Why is Toad happy that rabbits are being hunted? 
 There have to be some rules to a world. 
 2. Toad. 
 3. The narrator becomes unreliable, unintentionally, I believe, when he states and reiterates that Toad is a good-hearted, decent fellow. 
 If you care very much about right and wrong, and that people must go out of their way to accommodate those around them, then Toad may spoil this book for you as well. If not, go ahead and give it a go, there is much else to recommend it, despite the world-building flaws.

There are two types of people in this world: 
 1) Those who like the Toad from Wind in the Willows. 
 2) Those who do not like the Toad from Wind in the Willows. 
 I hated him. The rest of the book was okay. Not terrible, but nothing special.

This book had its ups and its downs. Toad's adventure was most definitely the meat of the book while the rest of the chapters read like tangents (or short stories). 
 The first 4 chapters could have been compacted into 2, one about Rat and Mole and the other about Badger. Chapters 5, 7, and 9 were entertaining to read, but mere tangents. It became frustrating after you realize those 3 chapters added nothing to the main plot line. With that said, I really enjoyed chapter 7 because it added a different layer to the world these animals lived in. 
 Overall, this book is a fun children's book, especially when it revolves around Toad. This story offered up humour, heart and suspense, which is more than I can ask for in a book written over 100 years ago.

This book is far more funny, imaginative, charming, and insightful to the ways of people--in spite of its claimed insight into animals--than I knew, or I would've read it ages ago. My only regret is that the version I had omitted one or two of Toad's songs (I'm sure they are bombastic) and had no illustrations. This will definitely be a repeat read and I am looking forward to introducing my children to all of the animals herein.

book_b.title: The Book Thief
book_b.user_review: Ah, what a gloriously written piece of nothing! Somebody's been paying attention in their writing class, that's for sure. Nothing like a paint-by-numbers tearjerker that predictably treats of the redeeming power of reading to please the sheltered reading masses. By the end, the trivialization of Holocaust was making me heave, the relentless synesthesia was setting my teeth on edge, but, hey, everything that happened was perfectly foreshadowed, and the humanity of humans was affirmed, so what's not to love? *sigh*

sample_reviews.review_text: What beautiful imagery and description in this book. It sort of jumps around a bit in parts and that made it difficult to really emotionally connect with the most poignant parts of the story. Really I was most impressed with the "showing, not telling" - I could write a whole book of just my favorite quotes from The Book Thief.
Great book. Well worth the read. Great story and well written.

Incredible. Every page had something that caught my heart and made me think. This book cultivates a unique perspective on WWII, friendship, humanity, and death. I very much recommend it, but it's heavy and dark so be prepared.

This book is interesting not just in subject matter, but in narrative devises. From the narrator to the overt foreshadowing (due to said narrator), it's all told in an interesting way. It's beautifully done.

Ah! Tear-jerker! I really need some fluff chick lit, I've ready too many sad books in a row. 
 Anyway, I loved the narrator of this book: Death. The characters were complex and lovable. I've read some reviews where people said they hated the mother character, but personally, I think they've just never been in a family who's Eastern European. She'd be considered loving in my family. 
 I liked the concept of the sort of flashes of bold highlights that Death made, but I think they were made a little too frequently. They got gimmicky in some places. I suppose, since this is a young adult novel, I will let it slide that it does come off a bit obvious. 
 So, five stars minus one because dang it authors! I HATE 'SUM UP' CHAPTERS! Maybe this is a personal thing, but they just seem tacked on and maybe even cliche?

This is one of those novels that I put down after a few chapters, came back to it later, and I'm SO THANKFUL that I did. I admit that the unusual narrative technique threw me off at first, and I nearly lost interest altogether if it hadn't kept popping up on my Goodreads update feed. 
 But after giving it another try, I have concluded this might be one of the most rewarding literary experiences I have ever had. The last few chapters -- and even the very last line -- of this book will stay with me for the rest of my life. 
 I have no idea how the film version turned out, but regardless, absolutely everyone should read this book. While that mandate might evoke some of the constructs and real events depicted within the novel, the world might be a better place if people acknowledged the truths learned by the narrator that are so obvious (and tragic) when you just sit down and think for a second.

Cover Blurb: Yes or No? I'm a little divided about the cover. The title is mostly what caught my attention, and while the dominoes now make more sense than they did before reading the book, I still don't quite get why it was chosen for the cover art. Hmmm. 
 Characters: Death as a character is a concept that doesn't always work, but I liked him quite a bit in The Book Thief. He made for a very interesting and surprisingly good narrator, and I enjoyed his odd sense of humor. While never truly a direct character in the story, he was perfect for seeing the events through his eyes. Hans Hubermann, Liesel's foster father, was my favorite character. I loved his easy, quiet manner and gentle teasing. If I could have an ideal uncle, I'd want Hans Hubermann. Rosa, on the other hand, took me a while to get used to. Verbally abusive, rude, and sour, I didn't much care for her form of affection, though in the end I did come to like her a bit. I loved Max and Rudy and of course Liesel. Rudy had a defiant streak and Liesel was spunky. She didn't always behave well, but she always felt horrible afterward; it was hard not to forgive her. 
 The Romance: Rudy and Liesel have a bit of a childhood crush on one another, though neither would ever admit it. With so much going on in this book, it never takes forefront. 
 Plot: This is a character-driven book. Many things do happen, but there isn't a main plot. When Max arrives at the Hubermann home, it is definitely a turning point in the story, but it is only one of many in Liesel's life. The Book Thief goes from 1939 to 1945, and follows Liesel's time in a little town outside of Munich. We meet the people who influence her life, witness the events that change it, all through the eyes of Death, who takes an uncanny interest in Liesel for many reasons. Liesel is forced to leave her home and her mother when her father is arrested for being a Kommunist, and when her little brother dies on their way to Himmel Street, where they are to live with the Hubermanns, Liesel turns to book thieving for comfort. She can't read, but there is something about books that she cannot resist. Life with the Hubermanns isn't easy. They are barely able to feed themselves, and Hans Hubermann isn't exactly in agreement with the Nazi Party. But Liesel likes her foster father and she makes friends with a neighboring boy, Rudy. But every once in a while, she still feels the need to steal books, and she soon finds herself taking them from the bonfires and the mayor's house. When a Jewish man shows up at Himmel Street one night, seeking refuge with the Hubermanns, Liesel discovers someone she can share her books with. But Max can't stay forever - not with the war looming ever closer to Himmel Street. Despite the lack of definite plot (because again, Max and even the book thieving is only a small part of the story), I couldn't help but be drawn into The Book Thief. The characters are interesting, I love the era, and the narration style is just so unique and emotional. This is a feels book, and I definitely had a lot of feelings going through me as I read - sometimes laughing, but mostly sad. 
 Believability: Nothing to complain about. 
 Writing Style: First person, past tense. Though every once in a while, Death would kind of start talking in present tense. The narration took me a little while to get used to. It comes across as choppy at first; Death doesn't have a linear way of thinking. He will jump around quite a bit from one event to another, and sometimes this event has happened before that other event. But in about 50 pages, I got used to it, and was able to follow Death's thought process. And I must admit that I really enjoyed it. His dry, dark sense of humor and sometimes bizarre metaphors and similes added an extra layer of bleakness and emotion to a topic that is already very bleak and emotional. 
 Content: 15 s-words, 8 g--damns 
 Conclusion: The Reader will see the end coming fairly well in advance, because Death keeps dropping hints. But it still hit me very hard when I finally read it. I was a little stunned, and for a moment I debated whether or not it completely ruined the book. What was the point, after all, if that was just going to happen? But I honestly liked it, though I cannot exactly say why. I just did. I first tried to read The Book Thief when it initially came out. A story about a young girl who steals books during Nazi Germany sounded like the sort of thing I would love. But I couldn't get into the narration and I thought it was a little too weird, so I didn't pick it up again until recently. The movie is being releases soon, after all, and I hate seeing movies without reading the book first. Now that I'm older, I was able to enjoy The Book Thief a whole lot more. It is a little odd because of Death's narration, and it can feel a tiny bit slow. But I honestly didn't want to put it down, it captivated me so thoroughly. And what exactly it was that captivated me, I'm still not entirely certain. The characters were good, the era was good, the narration was very interesting, and it was an extremely emotional read. But I can't say that the characters were my absolute favorites, or that this was even the best WWII novel I've ever read - or even the most emotional read I've encountered. And yet, there was something about it that just stuck with me. The opening lines and the ending lines will always stay with me. 
 Recommended Audience: Girl-and-guy read, better for teens seventeen and up, and adults. Anyone younger than seventeen probably won't stick with it for long just due to interest level. Fans of WWII, Holocaust, and emotional novels will like this.

The Book Thief is an extraordinary book. Narrated by Death, it chronicles Liesel Meminger's life from 1939 to 1943 - the time in which she lived with her foster family, the Hubermanns, in Molching, Germany, a suburb of Munich. Liesel is not Jewish, but an incredibly reluctant member of the Hitler Youth. Her daily life, at the start of the war, continues in much the same way as life before and after the war. She plays soccer on the streets with her friends, she attends school, she reads books, and she delivers laundry for her foster mother. But as the war progresses, her life changes in the ways one would expect a young German girl's life to change due to war - rationing, air raids, knowing people who have been drafted into the army, etc. 
 However, Liesel's story is not the typical WWII era narrative as it is, on the surface, the tale of the ordinary German, not very sensational or particularly moving. But Liesel is a literary powerhouse of a protagonist. Her brother dies and she copes by stealing a book - a book from which she learns to read. And learning to read, that changes the course of her entire life. 
 It was an interesting choice, on Markus Zusak's part, to have Death narrate the book - it adds a sense of foreboding but also a tone of almost "hyper-reality" - giving a voice to the one fact that we all know but don't like to confront - everyone dies. Death is exhausted by World War II, between the soldiers, the Jews and the civilians, he's exhausted. But Death is touched by Liesel, the girl who seems to see him and a girl he encounters more times than he believes he should (I use "he" because I listened to The Book Thief and the reader is male). 
 Personifying Death takes away the fear, Death narrates the book like Liesel's old friend, not as an inevitable outcome and I believe that makes Liesel's tale all the more profound and moving. My words are inadequate in describing the suffering Liesel endures but Markus Zusak does so with a great love for her, for all his characters. Throughout The Book Thief, Liesel is moved herself by the power of words and though she starts as an illiterate child, she quickly becomes a voracious reader. She recognizes the power words have, the words that stay with us long after they are spoken or read and she learns some valuable life lessons from her words and the words of others. Death reveals the outcome of the book long before the final pages but that doesn't make the end any easier to accept. While not a direct story about the Holocaust or a novel of expected and imminent danger, the outcome is heartbreaking and completely, harshly real to Liesel and the reader.

"Earnest, pretentious and over-rated. I can see the attraction, but it's not for me" 
 That was my initial review. But now, having re-read it, I'm of a slightly different opinion. Zusak does really well at showing the sense of panic and confusion faced by the German People during the Second World War, a perspective not often seen. His characterisation and plot is superb. But I just wish he didn't use that stupid 'death-as-narrator' device. It ruins anything. 
 If you want truly great Holocaust literature, read "Schindler's Ark". If you want truly great experimental fiction, read "If on a Winter's Night a Traveller". The problem with this book is that these two genres don't work as well together as Zusak obviously hoped.

I wanted to love this book. When I read the first few pages I thought I would. Sadly it did not meet anywhere close to my expectations. I just could not get over the fact that throughout the book it repeatedly told me what would happen later on. I hate spoilers, so when there are short one to two page chapters randomly placed around the book that tell me when and how someone is going to die I am extremely upset. Don't get me wrong, I love books full of emotion even if it kills of my favorite characters, but they don't tell you beforehand what's going to happen! I also would of preferred the book being from Liesel's point of view all the time, instead of having the grim reaper narrating it. 
 I also found some of the descriptions odd. Where I thought the book was supposed to be about a girl who saves books from being burned, she only does that once! The other books she stole was from a kind woman who was in debilitating depression from the loss of her son, and this is after Liesel chews her out for being in depression.

reference_books.title: Third Grave Dead Ahead (Charley Davidson, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
Love hanging with Charley and the gang! Another fun one that kept me coming back for more. Charley's humor makes me smile more times than I can count. While listening to the audio version, I can't help but laugh out loud when her antics get crazy and her thoughts even crazier. 
 I have a rottweiler for a dog and when she comes in contact with the one in the story it was very refreshing. They get such bad press for being a strong (and I'll admit scary if you don't know them) dog, but how Darynda showcased Artmeis, I am very pleased. 
 Can't wait to start the next one!!

reference_books.title: Wild: From Lost to Found on the Pacific Crest Trail
reference_books.review_text:
Well, this one took me much longer to finish than I anticipated. The beginning was very slow as we were brought up to speed with the backstory of how Cheryl decided to take this journey. Once she made it to the trail, I enjoyed it much more. I could handle the little flash backs at that point as it was what she was remembering while out on her own and trying to piece her life back together. I can say I did want to knock some sense into her for decisions that she made in her life. 
 There was some humor, which I always appreciate. The people she met on the trail seemed just as I would expect, welcoming and encouraging and proud of anyone who took on the same trek. I could imagine doing something similar myself as I like the outdoors and hike. I've never backpacked though and would imagine it to be an eye opening experience. I was impressed that she had bought her supplies and boxed them up prior to heading out, then gave them to her friend to have her mail to certain locations for when she was about to arrive. 
 I'm glad I stuck it out and finished. It was an interesting read, but it didn't have me wanting to read every chance I got. I give it 3.5 stars.

reference_books.title: Yes Please
reference_books.review_text:
I'm not totally sure how I feel about this one, but I do know that I am glad I am done reading it. It was on my tbr list, but was also this month's book club read. I wasn't sure what to expect, as I'm not much for reading biographies of a person's life. I guess I was hoping for more humor. Don't get me wrong, there was definitely humor in the book, but I think the melancholy sections of the tough times she went through overshadowed the humor for me. The insight into some of the SNL years was interesting, but overall I felt like the book was very jumpy. I would have enjoyed a more of a timeline approach, and instead it jumped through time (apparently Amy Poehler likes to time travel as she mentioned as few times, LOL) and I was lost and not sure if I missed a section, only to realize we were talking about something from the past again. 
 All in all it was interesting to get a back stage view at how some of the business works, but I'm not sure I would recommend it to anyone.

reference_books.title: Claim Me (Stark Trilogy, #2)
reference_books.review_text: I enjoyed the second book in this trilogy. While I do enjoy the steamy sex scenes, it seems like they fall back on that pretty quickly in lots of situations where a bit more dialogue would have been preferred by me. That didn't stop me from reading on to find out what was happening. You knew something big was going to be coming from all the "secrets" that Damien seemed to be keeping, but how it played out was a mystery. The ending had me wanting the next book in my hands to see how everything would unfold. Looking forward to the summer when I can get the past part of this story.

reference_books.title: Hard as It Gets (Hard Ink, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I love it when an author is recommended to me and I find the book addicting. That is exactly what happened with this book. I'm sure the fact that there were tattoos involved didn't hurt either! I found Becca very likable and was pleasantly surprised at how up front and direct she was. It took me a bit longer to accept Nick. After being discharged from the Army like he was, his attitude was understandable and I'm glad he finally started coming around after Becca fell into his life. I loved the fact that he wanted to draw on her and found her that inspiring. And of course when a book can make me laugh out loud, I'm usually hooked.

book_a.title: Wonder (Wonder #1)
book_a.user_review:
This was an easy read for my book club. So glad we chose it as it made me think about how I react when I see someone with different features. I grew up with a sister who had a hand that was smaller than her other one. It happened to be her right hand, the one you use to shake hands, so it was something that was noticed often. It never changed who she was, but peoples reactions can be harmful without realizing it. 
 As I read about Auggie's condition at the beginning, I liked how they didn't go into detail right away, but made you come up with your own image based on what they did give us. It helped to give Auggie his own voice without the immediate reaction of his looks to change what you thought of him. When the narration changed to his sister Via, I was bummed at first as I wanted to keep reading about AUggie. But then it changed again and was a friend of his and then another. I realized that it helped to hear what those close to Auggie saw in him and how they all had different reactions to what he went through and how they fit into his life. 
 Everyone has a right to there own opinions, but it makes you realize that you can't judge a book by it's cover. This is a very thought provoking book and I am looking forward to our discussion about it a club night!

sample_reviews.review_text: I had heard so many good things about this book from so many different people and I finally got it from the library so I couldn't wait to read it. It's a quick read, but seriously amazing. Loved it. I seriously don't have the words to convey how beautiful this book is and how much I loved it. Highly recommend.
This was a very interesting read. I wasn't a huge fan of the voice acting when it came to the main character but I understand why it was like that.

I expected to dislike this book but instead found it completely charming. 
 I would give it five stars but I felt like the graduation scene went a little to far and thus seemed forced. 
 Auggie is a great character and I appreciated the multiple POV. 
 Read it in one sitting.

A really interesting voice. A surprisingly light treatment of what can be a terribly depressing subject--a middle schooler with a severe facial deformity trying to integrate into public schools after being babied and homeschooled. I wish that the ending was less of a perfect, neat one. In fact, it almost ruined the book for me it was so over-the-top. Almost.

Courage. Kindness. Friendship. Character. So good! 
 I borrowed this via the digital library but I definitely will be purchasing a copy for my home library.

Augustus (Auggie) is ten years old and attending school for the very first time. He's been homeschooled for the first ten years of his life. You see, Auggie is an ordinary kid in most ways, but he looks different from most kids. He has been through hundreds of surgeries, attempting to correct the affects a wayward gene had on his face. Some look at him and run. Others look at him and feel sympathy. But what Auggie wants more than anything is for people to look at him and see him for who he is on the inside: a caring, bright, funny boy. Will his new classmates be able to look past his exterior and get to know the real Auggie? Or will they run in disgust and horror like so many other?

I loved this book and recommend it to all of my tutorial students, ages 10 and up, without reservation. I've even used it as a writing prompt because this story of an outcast-turned-hero, and the remarkable way he changes those who encounter and initially fear or avoid him, is so thought-provoking and stylistically beautiful. The characters are thoroughly realized--so real that I actually miss them, and want to revisit them even though I finished this book very recently! Thematically rich (prejudice, bullying, disabilities, bystanders, friendship, family, adaptation and personal growth...), this story is perfect for teachers to assign, knowing that kids will undoubtedly love and be enriched by this praiseworthy book. In fact, two of my own writing students recommended Wonder to me! This book gets five stars for me without any contemplation because it is MEMORABLE and REREADABLE, offering depth and an uplifting, honest look at how people learn to accept differences and look past appearances, despite initial fear, revulsion, disdain, or shyness. A book to touch readers of all ages, with no content for anyone to object to, in my opinion. I finished this book and wished I had written it.

This little book is like totally amazing. And I'm like super stingy with five-star reviews. 
 It's probably like maybe a YA, with chapters that are like only 2 pages long, but that really pulls you along and you can't help like cheering for this kid with his small size and his severe facial deformity. 
 Touching and compelling and had me in tears more than once. And a satisfying ending. 
 The book just arrived one day in the mail, but I have a vague recollection of signing up for it quite a while ago. Happy to have received it, because I'm not sure I would have picked it up otherwise.

This is now one of my favourite books of all time. I'm a bit late to the bandwagon, but after hearing so much about it I finally picked up Wonder and experienced the emotional roller-coaster. 
 August Pullman is a ten year old boy who was born with severe facial disfigurements. Thanks to the various medical procedures he has had to undergo, he has never been to a school before. Until now... 
 The novel is broken into chunks, from the point of view of different characters. Besides giving more context to the events of the story, the different perspectives remind us that every person has their own story and we may not know what is really going on in their world. 
 Moving, heartbreaking, and inspiring. It is clear why this brilliantly crafted novel has gained so much praise and is being used in many schools to teach PSHE. Read it!

I was disappointed. I thought the concept of he book was very interesting and thought provoking. That being said I didn't like the voice she gave her characters and the story felt very forced especially near the end.

book_b.title: To Tame a Highland Warrior (Highlander, #2)
book_b.user_review: Another enjoyable book by Karen Marie Moning. I have to read a series in order and this was the second book. It's nice when characters are in more than one book. Had some twists which kept it interesting. I'm looking forward to the rest of the series.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I enjoyed this book, part of the Highland Series by Karen Marie Moning, this is book 2. I have not yet read book 1 but this story stands alone quite well. 
 Gavrael McIllioch hides a secret that terrifies him - he is a Berserker. When he is extremely angry or the sight of blood tap supernatural strengths within him and risk him spinning out of control into violent mayhem, over the years he has learned to control the Berserker in him for most of the time. Something happened when he was 14 and he ran away from home thinking his father was a madman and he so his father was not able to explain what being a Berserker is. 
 He's known Jillian St Claire since her family took him in when he was 16, but even she doesn't know his real name or story. He has been known as Grimm Roderick for years. Through a peculiar ruse, the couple is thrown together and their childhood hair-pulling, insult-trading is shown to be a thin disguise for true love. Gavrael pushes Jillian away with his actions because he is afraid he'll turn on her. 
 Through it all though Jillian continue to love him and somewhere along the way she realized that Grimm loves her too.
My kind of love-story!

Love it! 
 On with the next one!

This book was ok like the first one. It's more of a 3.5 stars than a 4. It's a bit ho-hum in terms of highlander stories. The writing is not always "historical" which takes away from the historical feel and the stories aren't all that original. Several people say it's a fantastic series so I'm hoping they'll get better.
Loved it!

It pains me so to give a 1 Star rating to a Karen Marie Moning book as I just love her but 'To Tame a Highland Warrior' was absolute garbage! I had to slog my way through this story. The first book in the Highlander series was fun but this was nothing short of torture. 
 In a nutshell this book is about Grimm who has a sad past but is summoned to return to a place that haunts him to be a potential suitor for Jillian. However because of his said sad past Grimm is a giant douche to Jillian because he thinks he will go crazy and kill her if he marries her because his father did that to his mother. Makes sense right? 
 And even though Grimm was such an asshole, Jillian is still jonsing for him. He is cruel to her and even shunned her proclamations of love after a passionate kiss. I'm sorry but if I was spurned and my affections not returned I wouldn't waste my time on someone who didn't want it, let alone someone who's a dick. 
 But this is a romance novel so naturally the heroine yearns for the brooding highlander! Barf! Jillian is an idiot who shuns all other men because they are not Grimm. She just 'knows' there is a deepness to him so when he returns she is intent on figuring him out. Even though he is still really mean to her! Jillian could have a perfectly nice husband in Quinn but does she go for it? Nah, she wants to be treated like trash and hope for the best. 
 Grimm is just the typical 'Woe is me!' character that has no dimension at all. Instead of asking question about his what happened years ago he just assumes the worst and in doing so misses out on a lot life has to offer because he is dumb. We're talking dumb as a box of rocks here people! 
 Tortured 'hero' and stupid heroine is the name of the game in this book. There was no story progression at all! It was just constant whiny drivel for the first hundred pages that only got minutely better after that. The best part of the story happened in the last 62 pages! I hate when authors save all the good stuff for the end! 
 Everything else was a snorefest. I actually thought about not finishing this installment because I detested it so! Just a couple of immature people pining over each other with that whole 'I love him/her but it simply cannot be!' schtick. 
 There were no fae in this either which was a HUGE disappointment! I love when Karen adds in fae stuff but there was zilch in that department. Oh and another thing that wigged me out was the age difference. I get that this was a different place and time but Grimm met Jillian when she was 11 and he 17. He watched her 'grow into womanhood' and started to want her. 
 Dude, gross! That felt kinda incestuous to me. I know they are not blood related but it was icky! Granted nothing between them happened until she was almost 16 but he was still 22 so ew! You would think Grimm would feel for her as if she were a sister and vice versa but I guess not.

reference_books.title: The Sense of an Ending
reference_books.review_text:
No man ever steps in the same river twice. --Heraclitus 
 No woman ever reads the same book twice. --Karolyn Sherwood 
 I recently finished THE SENSE OF AN ENDING, by Julian Barnes, for the second time. The first time, I loved it. The second time ... I still loved it, but I took issue with a few things. TSOAE is the story of Tony Webster, a sixty-ish Englishman who is bequeathed five hundred pounds from his college girlfriend's mother whom he met only once. Tony has no idea why she thought of him at all--he hasn't even seen the ex-girlfriend for forty years--so he sets off to figure it out. This introspective journey turns into a mystery of sorts, which makes the already short novel (155 pages) read very quickly. 
 The primary theme of TSOAE is memory, and how it warps and wafts with time. There's also a secondary theme, and that is remorse, which Barnes describes as, "A feeling which is more complicated, curdled and primeval. Whose chief characteristic is that nothing can be done about it: too much time has passed, too much damage has been done, for amends to be made." (p108) This second idea makes the novel a sort of cautionary tale: Be careful with your words and deeds because they are more powerful than a young person might imagine and cannot be undone. 
 TSOAE won the Man Booker prize in 2011. It was Barnes' fourth nomination, and first win. There's no question he's an excellent writer, and this is a wonderful story. My teeny, tiny knock against it is that what I originally read as wise and eye-opening became pedantic on my second reading. Others in my book club described it as painfully slow, but I disagree with that. I consider it literary. (Maybe that's the same thing?) Anyway, TSOAE is chockfull of brilliant thoughts, lines, and perspectives on life. Although it's not quite as brilliant as I thought the first time I read it, I still give it 
 Five twinkling Stars 
 I wonder what I'll think if I read it a third time.

reference_books.title: We Are Water
reference_books.review_text:
I liked one line from the last page of WE ARE WATER, by Wally Lamb: "We are like water, aren't we? We can be fluid, flexible when we have to be. But strong and destructive, too ... Like water, we mostly follow the path of least resistance." 
 But that's it, that's the only thing in this entire book that I liked. 
 I suppose I might have liked the original premise. I can imagine Lamb saying, "I want to write a story about a mother who leaves her husband, the father of their three grown children, and marries a woman. I want to tell that story." That could have been a good story, especially considering the woman is an artist who marries her art dealer. (As a former art dealer, I was eager for a dip back into those waters (no pun intended).) 
 This is the first book of Lamb's that I've read so I don't know how it compares to his others. I "assume" they were different and much better because Oprah chose two of his previous books for her book club. However, I know this: This novel in five parts is told from the first person point of view of multiple characters in alternating narratives. There was quite a bit of "stream of consciousness" in the narrative which authors like Virginia Woolf did very well. These characters, though, came off as whiny idiots--especially the wife. Lamb made her sound like an eight-year-old with a mental disability. (That's as nice as I can state my true feelings.) He also failed the two daughters, especially the couple's youngest, Marissa. Is Lamb a misogynist?? The females were ridiculous, and he did marginally better with the male characters. Still, I EXTREMELY DISLIKED every character's dialogue, actions, reactions, motivations, and inner thoughts. This book was melodramatic to the point of being painful to read. The only reason I finished it is because I read it for my book club. 
 One last point ... (This might be a spoiler, but I won't go into any details.) We find out through the course of the book that Annie, the wife, was sexually abused as a child. Lamb gives her abuser 50+ pages of his own, as he details the shitty life he had growing up. I imagine this was Lamb's acknowledgement that most pedophiles and rapists were also victims in their youth. BUT, the way Lamb delivers the abuser's story it comes across as if he's defending the man!! Like, Hey, readers, it's not really his fault. Look how life failed him first! 
 Give me a bleeping break. 
 One drop of a Star

reference_books.title: The Whistling Season
reference_books.review_text:
THE WHISTLING SEASON, by Ivan Doig, is one of those enveloping, epic tales set in a distinct time and place--the winter of 1909 in rural Montana. This is the first book of Doig's that I've read. He died this year leaving a legacy of thirteen novels and several more non-fiction works. It's easy to see why so many people loved his work. I loved a lot ABOUT this book, even if I can't broadly say I loved the book. There are dozens of fantastic sentences and scenes. 
 The Whistling Season is the story of the Milliron family (a dad and his three sons) who live on a ranch in Montana. The boys' mother passed away, and their house is turning into a, well, somewhat of a mess. The father, a wonderful character, sees an ad in the newspaper and decides to hire a housekeeper from the Midwest. That, as they say, changes everything. Rose arrives in splendid dress with, as a surprise, her brother, Morrie Morgan. If the father is a wonderful character, Morrie Morgan is phenomenal. With a grand handlebar mustache and a personality to match, Morrie is a bit of an enigma. He is brilliant, or at least highly educated. Together Rose and Morrie teach the Millirons a lot about life. 
 My frustration with this book was its lack of focus. The first two chapters are backstory about the Milliron men. (Only a renowned author could get away with that.) The story is told mostly in flashback from the first person POV of the oldest son, so naturally we think of him as the protagonist. But ... the back cover of the novel leads an uninformed reader to think the story is about Rose, the housekeeper, who doesn't arrive until Chapter Three. Rose does play a vital role, but this book is billed (on Goodreads, et al) as "the first of three Morrie Morgan books." In fact, I learned at my book club discussion that the Milliron family isn't even in the two other Morrie Morgan books. Other than The Great Gatsby, this is the only book I can think of where the narrator is not the protagonist (and The Great Gatsby has a good reason for that). You see why I say the book lacks focus. 
 I imagine if a reader knows the book is really about Morrie, they might just fall in love with it. 
 For me, Three and a half twinkling Stars (but I rounded up because of the beautiful writing).

reference_books.title: 2 A.M. at The Cat's Pajamas
reference_books.review_text:
2 A.M. AT THE CAT'S PAJAMAS by Marie-Helene Bertino would have been a fantastic short story. No book has ever made me want to be an editor more than this one. I love the title and the premise of this book: Three disparate characters mashup fantastically in a unique setting. (That's essentially the premise of every Ann Patchett novel, and I love Ann Patchett.) The trouble with THE CAT'S PJs is that it lacks focus and Bertino tries way too hard to have a unique "voice." When I say "lacks focus," what I means is there are so many characters that it's nearly impossible to track what's happening to whom at any given moment. Soon enough, I just didn't care. 
 The three main characters, all residents of Philadelphia, are Madeline, a nine-year-old motherless, blues-singing protege; Sarina, Madeline's freshly divorced teacher; and Lorca, the owner of a nightclub called, yes, The Cat's Pajamas. The entire story happens in twenty-four hours, and the "chapters" are short, some as brief as a sentence or two. This makes for quick reading and an easy page-turner--a good thing because otherwise I probably wouldn't have finished it. 
 My biggest gripe with the book, though, was the improbability factor. First, poor Madeline's widowed father is essentially comatose with grief. She is being "looked after" by a neighboring deli-owner woman who was a friend of Madeline's mother. Madeline's house is so filled with roaches that she names them. (How is the father who never leaves his bedroom paying rent?)(If Madeline is "so much like her mother," why isn't the dad enamored with her?) Second, in the first five pages we learn that Madeline is nine, and in fifth grade. Unless she's a girl-genius (she's not), she would be in third grade. Third, supposedly Madeline sang along with a Billie Holiday record absolutely perfectly "before she'd ever spoken her first word." WTF? I could go on with more and more examples of this nonsense, specifically Lorca's completely unrealistic relationship with his drug-addicted son Alex, but you get the picture. 
 Bertino did scatter a handful of lovely truisms throughout the book, but for each one, I have a dozen passages underlined with negative comments--everything from my aforementioned "WTF?" to "This makes no sense to me." to "Ridiculous!," "Completely unrealistic!," "Who is this character again?" and "Why are we in the head of a dog?!" Because, yes, the novel is written in the omniscient POV to the point we even get into the head of a dog during one chapter. How did Bertino's editor let that happen? If they were going for funny/quirky, they should have referred to WHERE'D YOU GO, BERNADETTE, a funny/quirky novel that was at least well-written. 
 Enough said. This book found an agent and a major publisher, so there you go. 
 Two (and a half) stars

reference_books.title: The Big Sleep (Philip Marlowe, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This is a classic, undoubtedly, and an early influence on many of my favorite books and movies. I love Chandler's tight prose, twisting plots and hat-wearing, monochromatically dressed bad guys. 
 It's amazing to me (but then, I'm easily amazed) how much the English language has morphed in the past 70 years. There are so many words and phrases that I was completely unfamiliar with-but then, the LA underground of the 30s wasn't exactly my scene anymore than the LA underground of the 21st Century is. 
 Also interesting is how writing has changed. This classic and quintessential work of noir fiction now reads like a "what not to do" manual of cliched metaphors. 
 A classic, and yet, I'm happy noir fiction has evolved.

This is a family drama centred around three generations of women and their relationships with each other. 
 Maisie - 80 year old grandmother, living with a man 15 years younger than her. She loves her family but has something of a strange relationship with daughter Liz. 
 Liz - mother of Ashley and Ivy. Her relationships with her mother and daughter are complicated and her marriage to Clayton seems to be rather cooler than it used to be. Her mission in life is to do something to help victims of domestic violence and abuse. 
 Ashley is young, sassy, quirky and in love with the idea of being in love with Senator Porter Galloway. 
 The story is told alternately from each viewpoint but each sounds too similar to the other - quirky, sassy and sarcastic - with nothing to really mark out each narrative as being different from the others. Reading it is a bit like sitting down to a good gossip with your oldest friends and for parts of the book it really works. However, it does jar with the very serious issues raised of domestic violence and date rape, soft coating them a touch and diluting their effect. We are told by Ashley several times that the family is full of eccentrics, rather like "You don't have to be crazy to work here but it helps". To be honest, I didn't really "get" their eccentricities at all, they all seemed fairly sane and normal to me. Of the three women, Maisie is by far the most interesting and enjoyable to read about and possibly the closest you will get to eccentric, but even she has a good reason for wandering along the highway with a llama. It is a shame that she is not featured as much as the other characters as I would have liked to have read more about her.

Maisie is a feisty and independent 80-year-old who is in a relationship with her much younger driver, Skipper. Her daughter, Liz, a former swimsuit model, is now a conservative and rational wife and mother of two. Liz's husband, Clayton, is a wealthy investment banker who is having an affair in New York with a former fellow model of Liz. Their son, "Ivy" (Clayton the fourth) lives in San Francisco with his partner, James, and their daughter, Ashley, is a recent college graduate and struggling young artist trying to make ends meet while living in the family's beach house. 
 The story revolves around Ashley as she and her roommate plan summer parties to make some money (albeit illegally) and she falls in love with a young politician who ends up being both emotionally and physically abusive. Meanwhile, Liz is starting a shelter and outreach program for battered women. We later learn that Liz's sister, Juliette, was killed by an abusive lover. Maisie adored Juliette and believes that Ashley is her spitting image in every way. She supports her granddaughter endlessly while putting down her daughter Liz. Symbolically, an Atlantic coast hurricane is brewing while the drama of the story unfolds. 
 All the women in the story are doing their best to survive in a man-driven world and keep the peace in their family. They are resentful and jealous, and the mother-daughter relationships are interesting. However, I found the character development to be poor. Quirky Maisie is the only interesting character in the book, and she is pretty outrageous at times. 
 Not only was the character development lousy and the plot predictable, but I really had a hard time seeing where any of the characters were coming from. Liz didn't believe Ashley's roommate when she feared that Ashley was being abused, while Liz is the organizer of a safe house for women victims?! Clayton seriously cried to his wife when his mistress left him?! And Liz and Clayton are actually ashamed of having a gay son at this day in age?! It was a quick read, but pretty ridiculous at times. I had hoped for something more juicy and engaging for a summer beach read.

book_b.title: A Great Deliverance (Inspector Lynley, #1)
book_b.user_review:
I bought this book because it was on a list of the Greatest Mysteries of the 20th Century. Although Elizabeth George has written well over 20 books, I have never read any of them before this. Now I may have to search some of them out. Intelligent and well-written, A GREAT DELIVERANCE definitely earns its spot on the aforementioned list. It is layered and complex with several red herrings and complicated characters. I could barely put it down. 
 Set in England in the mid-eighties, A GREAT DELIVERANCE is the story of Sergeant Barbara Havers and Inspector Thomas Lynley of Scotland Yard who are sent to York to investigate a murder. Nineteen-year-old Roberta Teys was found sitting beside the decapitated corpse of her father with an axe on her lap. She says, "I did it. I'm not sorry." Yet the case isn't that simple, of course. Not only are the suspects and central players varied and complex, so are Havers and Lynley and their respective families. George has linked the multitude of layers in this novel together so deftly that they become intertwined and begin to feed off each other. One interesting thing I noticed in the story is that George continually strikes contrasts. For instance, Havers is an unkept and brooding woman; Lynley is handsome and suave. We meet a set of sisters, again one is beautiful and one is frumpy. This continues with locations, buildings, and other characters. In the end, I think George was trying to make the case that the world is full of good and evil. 
 My knock on this book is that it is so long and complex there were quite a few threads left untied. It makes me wonder if George's next book continued with some of the same characters. I guess I'll find out the next time I'm looking for a good mystery. 
 Word of warning: The ending is difficult to read. It speaks to the most horrendous of crimes. 
 Four mysterious Stars

sample_reviews.review_text: I like mysteries, they're my go-to easy reading. And I liked the BBC series based on these books. But George's character writing for women, particularly, makes me so angry that it ruins the story. I read these many years ago, but I still remember one or two scenes that were intolerable.

I'll probably read a few more in this series to see if it grows on me, but this wasn't really my type of mystery. The characters were engaging, and I think it was more them than the plot that kept me reading, since I was only mildly curious about the resolution. 
 Also, if you're at all into fat activism, this is definitely not a pleasant read.

I'm not a big mystery reader (sorry, Lin!), tending to read one every few years or so, so how A Great Deliverance ranks on the mystery-novel scale is pretty well beyond me. I'd read the novel before, and remembered almost nothing except Lynley and Havers themselves initially, but it didn't take long to sort out the motive behind the crime, and from there, who had committed it. 
 For the most part, this is easy reading. Its style is not elaborate or difficult. But then Ms. George throws in literary allusions and 50-cent words that bog it down. I don't object to higher-level vocabulary in a book, but in this case it made the style feel inconsistent. Some confusing head-jumping at times also made for a rough-edged read. 
 There's so much problematic about this book, and the style isn't all. Most or all of my major beefs with the book had to do with its depiction of women, so if you can't bear that being criticized, bail out now.... 
 For example, women in Deliverance mostly fall into three general types. (1) kindly, attractive woman who is somewhere on the desire/dalliance spectrum with Lynley (Deborah, Helen, Stepha); (2) pallid, defeated mother (Havers' mom, Olivia); (3) fat and/or unattractive woman (Havers, Roberta). Without exception, regardless of socioeconomic status, age, locale, or situation, adult women all wear dresses or skirts. Every single one. This novel was written in the late '80s, so that was really weird. 
 The whole novel is obsessively focused on poisonous relationships, whether sexual, familial, or professional, sexual being predominant. Non-main-character women have little to think about beyond attracting men or dealing with them in lousy, and always heterosexual, relationships. Hollow marriages, angry marriages, infidelity all over the place, sex to drive the demons away, agonized crushes, jealousy, sex where consent is at best questionable... not to mention the major-spoiler stuff, about which the less said the better, for a couple of reasons. Depressing. 
 As usual when I read a mystery, and particularly one of a long series, it was hard to care much about the people involved in the mystery itself. Gillian was exceptional in not falling into one of the feminine types above, and in how she had a story that didn't just run in place and which intersected in an effective way with Barbara Havers'. 
 As for Havers, her belief that obedience to Lynley was the saving grace for her job was uncomfortable. "She could stand to learn a lot from Lynley," her boss says, and she does. But why is it always her perceptions and prejudices that end up false? Why's she the one who has a big emotional explosion in the middle of a case, and that over a sex act? It would have been nice to have golden boy Lynley have similar ruptures in his preconceptions regarding Havers, for him to learn something about himself that didn't center around his own love life, for there to be some give and take there. 
 I'll follow up on the other novels in this series eventually. This one displays possible long-term potential rather than being all that good on its own, in my opinion.

Honest - I know that this book is like a wet dream for existentialism and what have you. Maybe because of my psychology background but it felt like reading a book where the main character has some variant of autism. So his behaviour wasn't that surprising from that angle. 
 Ironically, the entire book left me a bit indifferent.

The protagonist of this story is a 'stranger' indeed, in the way he reacts to events in his life. He seems impassionate with regard to everything and without deep moral feelings. In the view of his and each man's destiny, death, nothing matters for him anymore. This presentation of the character of this man tastes a bit artificial too me, too theoretically philosophical. Also, the trial seems rather absurd in the argumentations used (or is it only outdated?). The description of the thoughts of Meursault when he approaches the Arab he is about to shoot are very effectful as are the last pages of the novel.
This was a quick and powerful read, revelatory of social issues, existence and death. Albert Camus is a master writer to pack so much philosophy so casually in this short, simple book.

***Spoiler alert 
 Mersault was a sociopath. He was friends with shady characters. He had no problem with women being beaten. He was strangely okay when his mother died. And he shot and killed a man with the only explanation being "It was because of the sun." It struck me when, during his trial, the prosecutor placed much emphasis on premeditation and intention and Mersault thought to himself, "He was right though." The tone that Camus used throughout to tell the story left me, the reader, just as detached as the character himself. And the result of that was losing sight of terrible crime he committed. Mersault didn't show much feeling. And by much, I mean that he didn't show any at all. In fact, his negative reaction to his execution was almost too much emotion for him and a detraction from his apathetic character. 
 I know this book was supposed to make me "question my existence" or something of that nature. But reading it didn't make me feel any more or less human. I felt exactly how I should feel about the particular story - disgusted. I did not feel this disgust because society told me it is appropriate to feel it when a man is killed by another man. I felt disgusted because killing a man is a disgusting crime. The only thing Camus accomplished with this novel in my opinion was giving us readers insight into the mind of a puzzling character. A character who has no control over what he does and doesn't care how he feels about it. In other words, a sociopath.

The continuing story has Daenerys visiting strange and new places. places where she will be seen as a major poweress but the dragons will steal the attention. 
 Back in Kingslanding, war is closer than ever, and with Lord Tywin Lannister gone, the Red Keep's responsability must fall on Tyrion's shoulders while he encounters love an affection on a summer creature named Shae and will go to great lengths to keep her safe. 
 Meanwhile we will follow Arya Stark through her journey, as she makes herself pass as any other famished child on the streets of Kingslanding, to "hitching a ride" to the wall, safe from home and from her brother Jon; to being captured to being turned into a kitchen girl to finally, making it for a escape towards home, Winterfell. 
 Meanwhile, things at Winterfell go slow and safe, until Then Greyjoy under his father's blessing returns to claim Winterfell as his. The people thinking themselves safe see themselves threatened by Theon's need to prove himself a strong commander and cheif as well as prince. But his reign will be short as he will be overpowered by enemies using a white flag, the Boltons. 
 Further, by the Wall, Jon will start his climb upon the ranks to turn into the Lord Commander's "page", in order for him to be trained for the later role everyone plans he'll take. And a near brush with unkown dark creatures will have him wondering what's on the other side of the wall. 
 And we all know the words: Winter is coming.
Awesome book! I am loving this series.

7 reasons you should read A Clash of Kings before you watch GoT Season 2! 
 1. The detail. 
 The show is stunning, from costumes and makeup to setting, but the graphic detail that Martin weaves into his storytelling is astounding. 
 2. The emotions. 
 Oh, don't get me wrong - I've overheard enough of this season to know that HBO didn't disappoint when it came to the feels. The complex relationships and narratives shine in A Clash. I felt Tyrion's mixture of self-deprecation and need to please, Sansa's fear and hope, Catelyn's mixed emotions as she watches her family tear off into war. Reading their stories, feeling their emotions is extraordinary. 
 3. Joffrey. 
 And you thought he couldn't be more of an ass. 
 Read the rest of my review here! http://canireadeverything.blogspot.co...

Whoohoo! What a licentious saga!! The book finally veered off from the HBO series by the end, so it's all starting to surprise me. "A Storm of Swords" awaits, for which I'm as thrilled as a Arya would be slicing Joffrey's head off with Ice after skewering him with Needle for his incestual blood to shower Cersei and the Kingslayer unaware in a copious embrace. Not a spoiler, by the way.

This book is all about character development. 
 SPOILER 
 No one of any real note dies here. At least, I don't think Theon dies, that's unclear. Otherwise, Clash is just about a progression of all the things that were begun in Game.

Jumping from "A Game of Thrones" comes the story of what happens when the first book ends. 
 Two men are dead, and the Iron Throne is up for grabs. A red comet is seen by all across the sky, and its messages are mixed. A war breaks out in Westeros and many people are taking sides. And all in all, there is fighting and death to be spread across the pages of this book. 
 My review: Excellent sequel to a great book; I can't wait to read the third book. 
 Recommended for all fans of high fantasy

Great followup to the 1st book, albeit with a little more lulls in between the action. 
 Dany's story here was disappointing. I like how Theon's story was one you knew where it was heading but hoped there would be some sort of redemption. The main star of this book has got to be Tyrion! I loved how he concocts his schemes in somewhat an opposition to his sister yet all he does is for House Lannister wholeheartedly. His view of justice is an amusing one. 
 The little subplot involving Arya and her "three wishes" was excellent. 
 I won't say anymore than that except list some theories: 
 1- The face trees are inhabited by spirits of the dead. 
 2- The truth behind the Starks' crypt is to raise an army of Others in times of need. 
 3- The thing Ned wanted to tell Jon was that his mother is Lyanna (which explains why he's overprotective of him and the memories of her saying "Promise me, Ned..") which means he's Rheagar's bastard. 
 4- There will be a confrontation between Sansa and Joffery sometime in the future. 
 5- The Asshai people will interfere with the going ons in Westeros more. 
 6- Gendry and Arya will be a couple or he'll end up serving her. 
 7- More evil bastards will appear. 
 ON TO BOOK THREE!

** spoiler alert ** 
 I thought this book was stronger than the first one. 
 I wasn't particularly interested in the Lord Stannis/Davos storyline but at least the one God doesn't seem to be a thinly veiled Christian religion. 
 It's interesting which characters are giving POV chapters. For example, we never see Rob through his own eyes. I'm glad Varys and Balish don't get POV chapters. I think that would make them less interesting. 
 Daenerys' chapters continue to feel somewhat bland compared to what's happening in the Seven Kingdoms. 
 I feel really sorry for Tyrion. I think it's pretty clear his role in saving the city is going to be downplayed if not forgotten entirely. So is Cersei's part in nearly losing Kingslanding. 
 I'm glad Sansa seems to be growing up a little. 
 I'm really looking forward to the next book.
