book_a.title: The Calling (Endgame, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Endgame has begun....and is finally over! 
 Endgame follows 12 strangers as they fight to win a mysterious game and save their lines from extinction. First of all, I must say this book is extremely familiar to The Hunger Games, only not as good.12 players, each between the ages of 13-18....let's face it, it sounds oddly similar, sort of like a book series or blockbuster movies we all know and love. However, Frey made the fatal mistake of trying to balance between 12 different people with disastrous consequences. The characters were poorly developed and the one that had a little more depth was an American with a seemingly perfect life. Why not someone else? 
 The writing was also pretty sloppy, in my opinion. The fight scenes, as well as most of the plot, was redundant and tedious. I literally said out loud "I cannot wait to be done with this book". And that was not meant in a good way. 
 The book also falls under the juvenile fiction category, which I, SURPRISE SURPRISE, have a huge problem with. Ok, the writing reflects a juvenile fiction category, but the words do not. There are several f bombs thrown throughout with scenes of bloody, intense violence. If I were a mother and knew nothing of this book, I would be extremely upset if my kid was reading this kind of book without my knowledge. 
 On to the positives. I really like the interactive puzzles, but must they be so difficult? I mean really. I thought this was a young people novel? I just feel like there is too much information for people to actually sit there and pour hours and hours into. I know the prize is $500,000 but it seems like they do not want this money to be one. We all are not as intellectual as the poorly developed characters in this book. 
 Genre: Juvenile Fiction 
 Positives; Unique interactive twist 
 Negatives: Poorly developed characters; redundant and somewhat confusing plot. 
 Rating: 2 out of 5 stars

sample_reviews.review_text: I didn't finished it, it was just too bad

Thank god this is over. it is one of the worst things I have ever read, if I wasn't sent it to review I would have given up on it long ago and that's very unusual for me. The premise is weak and never fully explained. The writing is absolutely terrible. Everything. is. written. like. this. For some reason the author thinks that saying This is Endgame. Over and over will make it sound dramatic but it is just laughable. There are too many characters and they are so badly explained that I felt like I constantly forgot most of them existed. Most of it just didn't make sense, and the over explanation of action scenes managed to make it incredibly boring. How the author managed to make gun fights boring is quite impressive. I could go on and on but just avoid! It is clear me this has only been read by people in the hope of figuring out the 'clues' to win the prize at the end of the series. I think the author must have focused on this to the expense of the actual book. Interesting marketing ploy, terrible execution.
this book was so badly written it makes me sad :(

The plot was easy to understand and was quite intriguing. The let down was that the forever changing perspectives (once every three to five pages) for the large amount of characters. Sometimes the same scene would be told in four different perspectives and the characters lost their depth due to this constant change. Also, need more action! They have been trained to kill so why are there so few deaths. I skimmed the last half and won't be reading the sequel.
I am number four meets the hunger games - still rolling my eyes.

La verdad este libro no fue para nada lo mio muchos puntos de vista que solo me confundian y muy lento todo 
 Aunque bueno le hubiera puesto uno sino fuera por tres personajes que me gustaron desde el inicio y quizas podria agregarle un .5 por el final que mejoro bastante pero no se 
 Si siga con la serie

I am aware that the author, James Frey, has a really bad reputation at the moment, but I am not here to judge him as a person, I am here to judge this book. And I really did like Endgame. 
 At first, it took a bit of time to get used to the writing style, because it was more like someone narrating a story, less formal you could say. But once I got used to it, I found the book quite entertaining. 
 Of course, it's a fantasy story and some things are a bit "weird", but overall I really liked the story. Many people have said that it's similar to the "Hunger Games", but I disagree. I think the only real similarity is that 12 kids are fighting against each other for their lives. 
 But the rest IS different. There's no arena, but the players play across the world and that was something I really liked. And there's nothing like the capitol, other people that are controlling the games. It's gods. 
 I also liked that the story was told through the eyes of different characters, which made it easy to identify with them and even like some of them. 
 I think Christopher was super annoying, though. And I am seriously angry that the author killed my favorite character (I don't want to give any spoilers, so I won't say which of them it was). 
 But apart from that, I liked the book and I'll read the second book as well when it's published, because I really wanna know how it goes on.

DNF @278. 
 I couldn't.. 
 I tried.. I TRIED.. But I could absolutely not deal with this book for one more second!! 
 And what kills me is that the book HAD SO MUCH FREAKING POTENTIAL!! 
 As always I read the reviews of this book before pursuing it and I saw how many were comparing it to Hunger Games. I feel this book has it's own original idea. The ancient artifacts and civilizations. The players and their heritage and tribes. The numerous codes and riddles. All those were such exciting elements that made me want to keep going. 
 But the book itself is so DREARY AND DEPRESSING!! 
 The way it was written really made me loathe the whole idea of continuing it! The author made it extremely difficult to understand the characters because of their huge number and personalities. I don't have a favorite character because I couldn't relate to ANY! All of them acted in such an irrational way and I reached half of the book and still couldn't point out one character from the other. 
 And what's with creepy Christoper? Stalker MUCH?? 
 I feared for my own wellbeing because of the depressing atmosphere of this book and that's why I decided to mark it as DNF, although I was really looking forward to see who would win and how they would find the keys.. 
 Maybe I might pick up this book again in the future. But for now, I need something more upbeat and interesting and can allow me to read and comprehend its entities without feeling like I want to kick the wall.

Un libro muy bueno, con una historia que sorprende. 
 Resena completa aqui en mi blog: Librooks

Anybody who thinks this is a "Hunger Games" rip off needs to do some more research into the Hunger Games. The Hunger Games isn't originally by any means, either. The similarities between this book and The Hunger Games is 12 kids trying to kill each other. That's it. Period. This concept is also not new or original The Hunger Games (12 kids trying to kill each other). That aside, I couldn't make it past the first 100 pages for two main reasons: 
 1. The formatting SUCKS. Every heard of indenting a paragraph? If you refuse to indent, at the very least skip lines between paragraphs. It was too dang hard on the eyes to try to read. My eyes should not have to strain to read the page. 
 2. The present tense of the whole thing. It was annoying and took away from the overall flow of the story. 
 The premise is interesting and I did enjoy the Pittacus Lore series by the same author(s). However, this book just couldn't seem to deliver due it's format. Sorry. I have no intention of finishing this book or the series unless the author (for some strange reason) releases a new version of the story written in past tense and learns to indent his freaking paragraphs.

book_b.title: Cress (The Lunar Chronicles, #3)
book_b.user_review: Captain Thorne, how I adore you! 4.5 Stars!

sample_reviews.review_text:
If I could give this more than 5 stars I would. Very rarely do I not want a book to end, usually I cannot wait to get to the end, but with 'Cress', I never wanted it to end - and I cannot wait to read 'Winter' as soon as I get a copy. This was an amazing sequel to the first two books, and I can definitely say that it is my favourite in the series so far. 
 All of the characters are developed even further, and new links and relationships evolve, which made me even more invested. The separate stories all had enough detail and development, and when they joined or overlapped, it made perfect sense. The characters are deep and layered, and lovable, and the continuation of the story from the first 2 novels, didn't falter or cause me to lose interest. 
 I literally have nothing negative to say about this book, I adored it!!
Loved that Thorne was in it more. He is so humorous. :)

Again, I'm not sure if I'll keep going. The first book was too close to the Cinderella story. Each book the author takes more liberties with the fairy tale. 
 The story arch gets more involved and intricate with each story. We add more and more characters and more levels to each book. 
 I would love to see where this story goes. 
 It isn't dystopian. It isn't steampunk. 
 I don't know where it falls or how I feel about it.
Where's the next book?

This was probably one of my favorite books so far in this series. It's a filler book, but there is still a lot of character development and story progression. Cress is a very deep character, but I wanted to see more of her in a book that is titled after her. I also hope that we see some more character development from the villains because we all know power corrupts, but there has to be more motivation than just power. The action was good though and there were a few moments where I actually sat in the car after getting home just so I could see what happens next. (I'm listening to the audiobook in my car because it's the only cd player I have. Don't judge.) This is usually the point in a series where I start to get a little bored, so props to Marissa Meyer for keeping the story interesting!

Book 3 of the Lunar Chronicles brings us back to loving the series. 
 Cress has been alone on a satellite circling earth since she was a very young child, with only her netscreens and an occasional visit from her Lunar guardian for company. She has grown her hair very long and developed an excellent singing voice, a talent for computer hacking, and a taste for sentimental romances...and Cress longs for a handsome prince to rescue her from distress. 
 What comes along is not a prince exactly, but rather, a group of fugitives intent on de-throning the evil Lunar Queen Levana. And they want Cress to help them. 
 This story is much more than a science fiction re-casting of "Rapunzel." It is also a terrific, fast-paced, suspenseful and sweet coming-of-age tale. With plenty of cliffhanger chapters and chases through deserts, underground passageways and outer space, there is much to love...including the clever but naive character of Cress. 
 Cress is part 3 in a series that will include at least 5 books. Cinder starts the series, starring an unloved cyborg stepchild. Scarlet is second, featuring a girl in red cape and her rather dubious lupine companion. Winter (coming in September 2015) will focus on Queen Levana's beautiful stepdaughter. A "prequel" to the series, Fairest, is scheduled for release in January 2015. 
 The book and the audiobook narrated by Rebecca Soler are highly recommended. What is not recommended is waiting for Winter! Will we care what happened to Queen Levana in Fairest to make her the awful person she is?

** spoiler alert ** 
 I am just in awe. Wow. Powerful, unexpected and fun. I have such a good time reading this book! So let's just get into it. 
 I am so impressed with how much Cinder's character has evolved. She is so much stronger now, so much braver and more capable of love. And she is learning what it means to make friends. She is becoming the leader and "revolutionary" that is so demanded by the series and it is just flawless the transformation seen in action. 
 Scarlet was whipped out of view with an absolutely broken Wolf. But it is just so worth it to see them surviving. Because Scarlet is Wolf's Alpha star now. And I thought that was a beautiful comparison that fit just so perfectly. So I am hoping that in Winter I will see Scarlet rise from the ashes again like the independent girl she is and show her more vulnerable side to princess Winter. And I hope that wolf can learn that you don't have to be in control to survive and that he doesn't have to be the powerhouse all the time. 
 Thorne's character is completely evolved now. He was so selfish is Scarlet. So self absorbed. And that time in the desert with Cress, time when he was completely reliant on her- a complete stranger- well, it changed him. And Cress showed him that he can be a hero. Because she believes that he is a hero. And I think that Thorne learned how to be selfless and how it's not so much of a core as an opportunity. 
 Cress came out of nowhere! She is this light minded girl with this beautiful outlook on life that is so passionate. She was built into the independent side of character from the beginning of her life and she learned how to rely on someone else even though she thought that she was really taking care of Thorne. They built a bond in one book that many people have a hard time building in a lifetime. 
 But the thing about Cress is that she is so exposed. To everything. And she is so observant and curious and terrified and loving. I worry that in this next book, if Levana gets her hands on her, she could break her. And she doesn't deserve to be locked in a cage. She is too beautiful and strong hearted for that. 
 Kai never let go of Cinder. From the very beginning he decided that he was going to trust Cinder and he didn't stray. And now that they are together I am sure that the next book will be an epic beginning to the most charming ending that we have ever seen in the retelling of classic fairytales.

4.5-stars 
 Cinder is starting a revolution on Luna and I've to wait for Winter to be released. I am not a patient person. I might pretend that I am, but I'm not, especially when I have to wait for something awesome! 
 Because Cress was AWESOME! 
 And I'm not going to add more.

OMG. AWESOME. JUST AWESOME. 
 Okay, so Thorne and Cress are by FAR my favorite pairing (I called them being together since scarlet), but I LOVED all the Kai-Cinder moments too. 
 As far as Cress goes, I feel like she had the potential to become a very whiny character, but I think she may be my new favorite one. Don't ask me why. Just deal with it. 
 Okay, that JACIN GUY (UGH I hate him so much) is probably going to be with Winter (BTW I loved her introduction when she was with Scarlet, a great introduction and I can already see where Marissa is going with this). And so far even though Winter creeps the hell outta me, she seems like an awesome new character. 
 SOOOO what else? OH! Wolf was totally useless, which I'm fine with, because he's probably my least favorite and most underdeveloped character. Although I do have to say this: when Scarlet was captured and he got all depressed, I'm glad it wasn't the other way around, where the girl (AKA Scarlet) is all depressed because her love interest is gone, but the other way around. Switch things up! 
 Definetly my favorite book in the series, they just keep getting better and better. Also, I totally called the Cress/Dr. Erland plot twist thing. I remembered it from Cinder. So much forshadowing in this series, I love how all the hints are dropped, like the one in Cinder about Winter... don't know if you peoples remember that one, where Kai is in the meeting.... 
 Well whatever this book was awesome. Do yourself a favor and READ IT!
Another rollicking installment in this series. 'Rapunzel' is added, with her lovely long tresses (though the hair isn't a feature for particularly long). A few more surprises, and lots of action.

reference_books.title: Frigid (Frigid, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Actual rating 2.5 stars. 
 I love JLA's writing, it's always great smutty escapism, but with 'Frigid' I was so annoyed over the first few chapters I was close to DNFing it. The relationship and behaviour of our two main characters was really off-putting. With a narrative told from two differing points of view, that of Sydney and Kyler as they dance around each other in varying degrees of love, like, lust and hate... 
 Sydney was cute as a button - and I mean that sarcastically. Hopelessly in love with her best friend. Hey we've all been there, and I pretty much ignored it too, and fantasized in private. *sigh* But the manhandling and controlling behaviour from Kyler blargh! - and she enabled him. Big time. It was painful to read. But I did have some favourite parts about Sydney: her clumsiness. The head-to-chin-butt had me in stitches. 
 There also seemed to be some sort of sick fascination about people putting their hands on Sydney's hips - I think it was mentioned at least three times per chapter. 
 Kyler is so weak-willed, misogynistic, possessive, and controlling. Stereotypically the tall handsome hunk. It's okay for a man to sleep around, but somehow, not for Sydney. Everything about this guy rubbed me the wrong way. I really wanted to punch him in the face. Additionally, to top it all off, a pet hate of mine are guys calling you "baby," I winced every time Kyler said it. Sydney girl, you could do so much better. 
 I don't think the dual perspective of Sydney and Kyler did all that much for the narrative, jumping in and out, just to hear how hot they thought the other one was. Other than that, it didn't reveal anything new for the plot. 
 With what seems to be a lot of drinking and swearing, (again, unnecessary) it wasn't setting the mood or the scene, just made the main characters look like potty-mouthed lushes who wanted to hump everything that walked by. Made me feel like I had a dog latched onto my leg. That, and the F-bombs. Drained the romance right out. 
 There were some intense sex scenes: some of it titillating, some of it not. I also just about gagged when Sydney was described as being "tight and drenched down there"... I mean, ew. There's got to be some more passionate, creative ways to describe arousal that doesn't sound like leaky plumbing. Another aspect that had me cringing was the whole sex-while-Sydney-is-asleep-thing. Creeped me out - I know it was meant to be sexy, build the tension and angst between the pair, but it had shades of rape that didn't sit well with me. 
 And someone shooting a gun at some point felt like overkill. But, after all the bagging I've done, I got into 'Frigid' for the last third of the book. It felt like good old JLA again. 
 There's just something about this coupling, and the situation that hasn't sold me. The ending is very cutesy, but didn't wrap everything up. Very mixed feelings about this book, overall it was okay - I kinda enjoyed it. But don't think I'd recommend it. She has written so many other good books, this one pales in comparison.

reference_books.title: The Colorado Kid (Hard Case Crime #13)
reference_books.review_text:
As a lover of Stephen King's writing, and after discovering one of my favourite television shows, 'Haven' was based on his novel which I had not read yet - I raced out to purchase it immediately without looking into what kind of book it was... I wanted to be surprised. 
 Expecting the supernatural goings-on like its small screen counterpart, I was disappointed. 'The Colorado Kid' is far more poignant. For starters the main character is a intern newspaper reporter, Stephanie McCann looking into an unusual death for the local The Weekly Islander; and while researching the back story of the event uncovers facts which are left open to interpretation (due to narration which may, or may not be reliable). I actually enjoyed that I wasn't spoon-fed an opinion, but merely presented the situation to which I could draw my own conclusion. It's a crime mystery novel beyond anything else. 
 Given that I'm not a big fan of crime novels, I wasn't particularly taken with this book, but loved the subjective nature of the narration. I'm rating this book on it's style and development of plot above anything else because it is something well out of my usual reading comfort zone.

reference_books.title: Nick & Norah's Infinite Playlist
reference_books.review_text:
Actual rating 3.5 stars 
 I loved the novel, and am of the opinion that it is definitely the best of what Rachel Cohn and David Levithan have written together. It is gritty, artsy and embodies the soul of New York and garage bands. The characters are all painted with bright colours and flaws making them all loveable in individual ways. 
 Norah's dry sarcasm juxtaposes with being such an introvert, confidence is a big issue for her - and straight away creates conflict for nearly everything she does, making Norah a compelling character. Enter Nick, an all-around good guy seemingly out of his element. But that is just it - he's not. He embodies the millennium man. Age, race, gender and sexual orientation mean little to Nick, as he takes everyone on face value and how they treat him. Together, they both appear to not belong to the club and music scene in New York, but on closer inspection embody the pulse of the industry. And it takes meeting and accepting each other to start realising their place and the start of their journey. 
 Although the narrative is witty, and such edgy symbolism is planted throughout, 'Nick and Norah's Infinite Playlist' suffered from two of my biggest turn-offs in books: the flashback, and excessive embellishment of a scene (otherwise known as mental wanderings). I think if it hadn't exceeded my expectations in all other areas I would have abandoned it early on. 
 It is a very quick read, but heavy on content. Also, being true to the contemporary genre it concludes in a way you can interpret it as an ending or not... you must read between the lines to get the most out of this book.

reference_books.title: The Fill-In Boyfriend
reference_books.review_text:
This is a light and fluffy read, and I found, completely hilarious. 'The Fill-in Boyfriend' has to be one of the best Kasie West novels I've read so far (and has encouraged me to purchase her entire catalog). 
 Gia is a girl after my own heart - I relate to her. In fact I was a lot like her in High School. And who doesn't do silly things in their youth to save face in front of their friends? Gia possesses a hint of devil-may-care about her which is at constant war with insecurity. This drives her choices; some idiotic, some marvelous. I think it is also behind why she has never experienced true, gut-wrenching, all-encompassing love. She has always been guarded. I loved getting to see her grow and slowly test all of her preconceived notions - and even some she hadn't thought of. 
 Fake Bradley (Hayden) has cemented his place amongst my favorite fictional boyfriends. He crossed everything I have listed on my ideal boyfriend list (yes, I have a list). Tall and bookish with the right mix of compassion and bravado. His younger sister, Bec helps to balance out the cast. Her straight-talk and perception from the fringes of Gia's world, contrast the passive-aggressive niceness of the 'in' crowd. 
 All of that let 'The Fill-in Boyfriend' balance on the line between cheesy and realistic - perfect for a contemporary romance you want to escape with. With a saccharine writing style and a story line which continually drives you forward with its character development, this is a book you can read in one sitting if so desired (I did). As with most in this genre the overall plot is predictable - but the sub-plots were a delight. 
 Recommended to anyone who enjoys happy endings and meet-cute. Now... I need to find my own Fake Bradley/Hayden....

reference_books.title: Freak of Nature (IFICS, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
A nice little book - just nice. It could have been fantastic. I was lead to believe such great things from some fellow bloggers I follow, but it fell way short. Such a great premise for 'Freak of Nature' - waking up a cyborg, a clandestine company overlord and forced to perform nefarious stunts for someone else's regime. There is a lot to like. 
 For me, the biggest part that held my heart from falling in love with Julia Crane's love child, is that I could not relate to either of the main characters. Kaitlyn's mentality did not match her predicament. Her reactions varied from fantastic and engaging, to way off base. She was everywhere, and did not make sense to her character. Switching from mature to immature - it left her wishy-washy when I felt a great arc would have been about her rising out of confusion and uncertainty to assume her identity and ideals. 
 Lucas was the most frustrating. For someone intelligent enough to build a cyborg, he sure was dumb. I didn't feel any of the chemistry between him and Kaitlyn. His inner turmoil fell flat, and as it was dragged out for so long through the story line of the novel, soon became tiresome. He was in a great position to make this character amazing, with compassion and power, trying to buck the man and a yearning like Frankenstein for his monster, I wanted to experience some torment, angst, and covert operations... and it was there, but just like a whisper in the dark. 
 Gracie made the most sense, but still her behaviour and manipulations sometimes jumped out of character and left me grinding my teeth. She was allowed too much freedom for it to feel realistic, and the way she fell into fast friendship with Kaitlyn, superficial. She seemed to wave too much control over key players in the plot for me to swallow. I'd really have like to see her challenged and need to test her strength for the sake of her friendships and relationships. 
 Much of the science around Kaitlyn being a cyborg did not add up and annoyed me throughout reading the entire book. It turned in to a bit of a struggle, and I put it down on several occasions. As did some of the twists at the end... and left me rolling my eyes. 
 If you overlook the glaringly obvious shortcomings this is a fun escape. Free flowing narrative style, though a bit juvenile for my tastes. It did conclude nicely (also leaving enough open for a sequel), but even that felt a little too trite. I felt this book more suitable for middle graders with the way it was written - but some of the steamier scenes wrote it out of that category leaving it ill placed for its target market. 
 I really wanted to love this book - but in the end it just felt like a dog's breakfast.

book_a.title: Never Never: Part Three (Never Never, #3)

Actual rating 3.5 stars. 
 I couldn't wait to get my hands on this final installment of the Never Never series after loving the first two books so much. It had all the mystery, sass and heart of its predecessors, but there was something lacking... 
 For one, Silas remembers. And though it is a key point in the plot, at first it felt like a cheap storytelling tool. But this argument only stands if you look at 'Never Never part 3' as a book - not the third part of one book. Colleen Hoover was contractually restricted from co-authoring with another writer outside of her publishers catalog, so this method of three small novellas was a work around. 
 Another aspect was the solving of the amnesia mystery. Although I didn't hate it, it lacked some punch. We had all this angst and conspiracy theories being thrown about in the first to installments, so it would have been fantastic to still include some of these elements. Or alternatively, leave something unsolved or open ended, give one of the elements its own subplot. 
 Many characters and theories (like the voodoo angle) were completely ignored in part 3, which were the things that had grabbed my attention in the first place, so I felt a little ripped off that I was left hanging. (Me loves some paranormal stories :) ) 
 Ultimately, the conclusion felt "nice." 
 Though, I will say I lurved the character development. Especially that of Charlie. We see a different version of her in each book. Every time her memory is taken, that whole nature vs nurture aspect comes into play in forming her personality. There are certain traits that are intrinsic to her character, and the others grow from her experiences. It was captivating to read her reactions each time she woke with a clean slate and how those first events shaped her opinions for the next 48 hours. 
 If this series ever gets a bind up, it will be a completely different reading experience, and I am planning to re-read these end-to-end again at a later date to see if my opinion differs to the initial read. Great, quick paced novel with a paranormal element I'd recommend to all my friends.

book_b.title: The Heir (The Selection, #4)
book_b.user_review:
Actual rating 2.5 stars. 
 I was curious to see where Kiera Cass would take this series with the next generation... I have a love/hate relationship with these books, issues with the characters and their attitudes, but love the complexity of plot and tabloid allure. However, 'The Heir' failed to deliver on all of these counts. 
 I did not connect with Eadlyn as much as I did with America. I found Eadlyn entitled, and we never get to find out - due to the nature of the narrative - if she indeed has a worldly view as expected of her in the role of monarch. Her 'work' is always alluded to but never completely explained. It left me thinking Eadlyn as shallow, protected and scared. It builds great tension, but left me not all that invested in her future. I put it down to how she was written - educated, aloof and separate from everyone else. Eadlyn herself mused on this, how she had intentionally isolated herself in order to become a better ruler - it also made her hard to relate to, cold, and somewhat bitchy. 
 There was also a lot less going on in this novel in comparison to the Selection trilogy. We were aware of the caste systems, the politics and the plotting and planning of all the characters involved. In 'The Heir' we lost most of that and instead were dealt up a dish of Eadlyn's self discovery. I wanted more about the rebels, more conniving politics, more entwined storylines - like The Selection. 
 Even though this effectively re-booted the story line, it left me with much of the feeling of a middle book in a trilogy, setting things up, moving the story forward a small amount, but resolving little. 
 The ending was brilliant. A cliff hanger I did not see coming. Not in a million years. It is the one thing that has me wanting to read the next in the series. Plus, I feel as though I'm going to get more of what I want from this new generation of royals. 
 It was an easy read, but I ended spreading it out over a week, consuming the last half in a day; as I mentioned, there didn't feel like there was enough going on to hold my attention. It was fun, and enjoyable, but a little flat. Though not the best book of the series, it certainly has set things up for an explosive ending and I can't wait to find out what is going to happen. 
 We get glimpses of Maxon, America and Aspen, and many of the other characters from the first three books: it was entertaining to see how they had grown over the last few decades. There was less explained about the world and political landscape than I would have liked, and Kiera Cass seemed to spend a lot of time describing clothes more than anything... But the Selection series has been a guilty pleasure of mine, though I find many faults in the characters and tropes, the novels are undeniably compelling to read. I just can't stop. So Cass must doing something right.

I loved this book! I don't believe because it mentions Heaven that it is a holier than thou account of anything and it doesn't shove any religiousness down your throat. I thought the theory if this book was wonderful and it was written so that the ending is not discoverable by the middle of the book. 
 Following the life of Eddy who is, at 83, a maintenance worker at a pier amusement park, this story takes you to Heaven. Eddy dies this day, not knowing if he saved the little girl he intended to save before his life ends and he is swept into a totally new adventure. 
 When he gets to Heaven, he is told that he will meet 5 people and their explanations of why they are part of his lessons to learn about his life. Who will they be? What part did they play in the way that Eddy lived and died? How he lived? Why he suffered or rejoiced? 
 This book makes you wonder at who would be your own 5 people and shows that everyone is connected to some thread of existance even if we don't personally cross paths. What minute change did someone make in your life just by existing generations before you and what trace do you leave behind for someone yet to come?

You can read the full review and more on my blog.(: 
 I'm having difficulty putting my thoughts into words on this one. It just IS. It defys opinions. It's pure storytelling, with no problems or special features. It's just a story, Eddie's story. And eventually all of ours. 
 The plotline is original and fascinating- an idea of heaven that's very different from the various religions' views of it. It kind of gives you hope - that one day, you'll understand. It shows you the difference you made on others' lives, and them on yours. 
 I liked the writing more in this book than in Tuesdays with Morrie. I think it has to do with the quotation things he did in the above. What can I say, it really bothered me. Or maybe it's the fact that this is a work of fiction, as opposed to the former which is a memoir. Either way, The Five People You Meet in Heaven reads quickly, and touched more heartstrings for me. It really made for a beautiful read, good for all ages.

reference_books.review_text:
I devoured this book in one sitting. 
 I picked it up when I got home from work one afternoon, thinking that I would read a chapter or two before going about the rest of my day. Instead I read it straight through, walking around the house holding it in front of my face when I needed to go get a drink or a snack or dinner. 
 That being said, it wasn't an easy read. It had a lot of layers and depth. It was just so engrossing that I couldn't put it down. I have read quite a few Holly Black novels, and so was prepared for this to be a fairly dark and morbid book. (The title alone led me to expect bitter bleakness.) But somehow this work, while still having its share of shadows, was still hopeful and beautiful and heart breaking. 
 This is hands down my favorite Holly Black book I have ever read. And it is, thus far, my favorite book I've read this year.

book_a.title: Einstein's Beach House
book_a.user_review:
This is the first of Appel's fiction collections that I have read, and it was amazing. I can't wait to start The Man Who Wouldn't Stand Up. 
 Having previously read Phoning Home: Essays, I was used to Appel's style. He writes in an accessible but deeply contemplative manner. His word choice is precise. As a reader, I appreciate writers who use exact phrasing, who say "bright hues of amber and vermillion" rather than "yellows and reds." Appel also demonstrates an ability to fully flesh out characters that are quirky, sympathetic, and still relatable in the limited space of short fiction. 
 Each of the stories included in this collection stands entirely on its own, but Appel's appreciation for the ridiculous and slightly morbid condition of humanity tie them together. My favorite by far was "La Tristesse des Herissons," mostly because I have had friends who are that couple. 
 This book made me laugh out loud, to the point of disconcerting those around me. But it also made me think about life, mine and the lives around me. Who do we want to be as a society? How do we want to be seen by others? 
 I highly recommend this book for people who are willing to examine their own worldview, to be challenged, to walk a few pages in someone else's life. The style or the plots may not be for everyone, but there is true value here. And I think that those who are willing to give it a chance will find their spirits have grown after they are through.

 This is another example of great story telling. Several short stories that are contemporary and appeal to most everyone.

I too received a free copy of this book in exchange for a Goodreads review, but unlike most of the others I found these stories frustrating. I forced myself to read all of them in order to review the entire book, but I probably would have put it down before the halfway mark if I hadn't felt obligated to finish. 
 I've seen literary fiction described as truth told through lies, which is the goal of most of the short stories I like to read. The problem with these stories is I simply did not believe them; they didn't contain enough truth. The rhythm and the details were off (e.g. a 6-year-old describing "a colossal aquarium" where "angelfish and gouramis cross paths"; what 6-year-old do you know who can identify a gouramis? or "skyscrapers shimmer like bejeweled sea creatures"... Huh? I've never seen a sea creature that looked like a skyscraper.) 
 Almost all of the stories promised a premise that seemed enticingly odd and clever, but then let me down via a delivery that was somehow not clever enough. One other reviewer noticed a pattern of female characters who were always the crazy or limiting people, while the male were more stable and heroic. I noticed that too, but it bothered me even more that all the stories seemed to have a mean-spirited essence to them, as if the author didn't really like any of his characters. I want to enjoy the characters I'm reading about--the people I'm spending my time with--even those who are extremely flawed, and I had a really hard time giving a flip about the crazy, jaded, and bitter populace of Jacob Appel's worlds.
This is a collection of off-beat short stories written in a confessional style. Some of them are a little dark in nature and all are about some aspect of human nature. This was a free review copy.

I received this book free from the author in exchange for a review. This collection of short stories was a mixed bag for me. I really disliked half of the stories, but the other half was good to great. In the majority of the stories I disliked, the characters seem two-dimensional and unlikable to boot. The women are portrayed as overly-emotional (and in some cases, flat out crazy), and the men are viewed only through how they react to the women. In the stories I disliked the most, "Les Tristesse Des Herissons" and "Sharing the Hostage," the men in the two tales also show some serious issues with animals. They were very disturbing. 
 However, I thought two of the stories, "Strings" and "The Rod of Asclepius," really hit their mark. The characters' back-stories are rich and interesting, and Appel does a wonderful job of showing the depths of their relationships in very few words. Those two stories would get five stars from me. 
 The other four stories have good and bad points, but generally fall into a range between the four I've mentioned above. All in all, Einstein's Beach House is worth the read.

Funny, tragic and quirky. There's a custody fight for turtles; a girl's mother is killed by her stepfather; a family has a sex-offender move in next door. The stories are all thought-provoking and entertaining.

I don't usually like to read short stories, but this book has some real good stuff inside. Some of them are not unforgettable, but there are others, like the one about the depressed hedgehog, that are really great. So if you like not mainstreaming short stories, that's the book for you. 
 Non mi piace di solito leggere le raccolte di racconti, ma alcuni di quelli contenuti qui non sono niente male. Non che siano tutte indimenticabili, ma quella del porcospino depresso era veramente uno spettacolo. Quindi se vi piacciono le storie poco comuni, questo e il libro che fa per foi. 
 THANKS TO JACOB M. APPEL FOR THE ARC!

I am absolutely blown away by the quality of these stories. I found this author through a Goodreads giveaway for his new book and he was kind enough to share a few of his other works as well. The title of this volume caught my eye, and I absolutely could not put it down. The stories are reminiscent of David Sedaris and BJ Novak, full of humor and unique plots. Can't wait to continue reading his other works.

Just before Einstein's Beach House I read the Burning Chrome short story collection by William Gibson. The stories were all written in Gibson's trademark cyberpunk style, but the stories didn't benefit from being bound together as a collection. That's not the case with Einstein's Beach House. These stories are variations on various themes and settings: the stories of doctors and lawyers, of the suburbs, of mysterious women and runaway imaginations seem to describe the author's childhood and life to present. The stories do not overlap, but they have the effect of zooming in on the house down the street, opening the roof, and showing the reader how strange real life can be. The stories often crossed over the line of credulity, a funhouse mirror distortion of modern America. If you like funhouses you'll like this collection. 
 Strings (#3) is a beautiful, subtle story about a middle-aged rabbi, comfortable with her predictable life, reencountering a charismatic ex who needs her help to produce a 400 cello ensemble in New York. The story is a beautiful examination of the adventures we give up to ensure a happy, if somewhat predictable, life. Other stories such as Hue & Cry (#1) and Limerence (#4) contain a similar power to portray real life with the saturation nob cranked a bit higher than usual, and this neon reality is where Appel shimmers. 
 Other stories (La Tristesse Des Herissons, Sharing the Hostage) were fun, but too far from my own experience to leave a lasting impression on me. The concluding story Paracosmos was an excellent take on maybe-magical-realism-maybe-crazy that felt very fresh and rounded out the collection perfectly. 
 Einstein's Beach House is small press done right. I look forward to seeing more from Appel in the future, and I'll keep my eye on future Pressgang Prize winners.

sample_reviews.review_text: I could not get into this book

Gave up on the book halfway through. I was at the point where Violet finds out she's pregnant with what she believes is Edward's child and tells him. 
 At that point, I grew tired of 1) how shallow Violet was, 2) her incredibly childish attitude, and 3) her inability to learn, well, anything, really. It was like she was emotionally stuck at the age of 8. I didn't care about her and cared even less about what would happen to her because she was shallow, childish and dumb. 
 I nearly gave up on the book when Lulu Mimi acted incredibly ignorant for someone in a foreign country in turmoil who was also actively seeking to leave. It was an insult to my intelligence that this savvy business woman would become so stupidly in love that she would believe that there was no record of Violet's birth or that anyone could show up at an embassy and they would take their word that a child belonged them despite any proof of this. 
 It's like the author just made up stuff here and there to insert at random with no true plot behind it all. 
 My friend Ruth told me the rest of the book and I'm glad I stopped, because it just got dumber and dumber and ended without any true satisfactory resolution. 
 I guess what was really disappointing to me was how the author portrayed women as being basically foolish. Had a man written this book, he would have been eviscerated in review after review for this. But it's Amy Tan writing about Chinese women, so she can get away with it. 
 When I read a book, aside from the entertainment aspect of doing so, I also enjoy trying to figure out the author. You can't write 300 pages+ without revealing anything about yourself. The stories anyone creates describe who they are, what they believe, and what they value. This is why psychiatrists/psychologists don't care if a patient lies to them, they can figure out the patient by the underlying beliefs/values of what they are being told. 
 So, for me, I am not just being told a story, but I am spending time with the author, and I realized that Amy Tan isn't someone I would want to hang out with. 
 Ugh! I want my 12 hours back!!! I won't be reading Amy Tan again any time soon.

I very much liked the first half of this book but I feel like a lot of Tan and See's fiction is similar: woe, woe and more woe. This one had a somewhat hopeful ending though and I love her strong female characters and depiction of Chinese courtesan life.

While listening I was annoyed about what Amy Tan chose to discuss in detail. 
 It was distracting to later refer to an amazing period which brought so much happiness and a person that was so important to the character but it was skipped with a paragraph. Yet other details which seemed to matter little to the plot were described in agonizing detail. 
 However, she couldn't have done that bad of a job given my heart was in agony at the right points except for reference to the happy time with Edward. Though I might be able to blame that on my recent introduction to motherhood.

** spoiler alert ** 
 It's too bad about this book, because I really LIKE Amy Tan--Joy Luck Club is one of my all-time favorite novels, and I enjoyed The Kitchen God's Wife and The Bonesetter's Daughter, and also her book of essays on writing. But this is just dreadful. 
 Bad writing, basic grammatical mistakes, repetitive structure and language, annoying characters, strangely contemporary language, two hours of Amy Tan's vocal fry talking about courtesan training, boring sex scenes, descriptions of emotions that didn't feel remotely authentic.Aiya! 
 I've decided not to finish this book. I spent at least twelve hours on the road listening to it, and if I never hear the word "stem" again, it will be too soon. (Though the description of an "ivory stem on a girdle" was hilarious...so, you mean a strap-on, Ms. Tan?) Of course the annoying American guy the main character inexplicably falls in love with has TWO traumatic back-stories, not just one, and he doesn't even get to die of Spanish Influenza without a fake-out first. The only part of this book that I found gripping was the pivotal moment when Violet gets tricked into going to the House of Tranquility by Mr. Fairweather (gotta love when authors go all Dickensian in their name choices). Violet's struggle to identify herself as Chinese or American happened the same way over and over again, in the same words--it was like Ralph de Bricassart agonizing over whether he was a man or a priest first, except as soapy as it is, The Thorn Birds is the better book. 
 Speaking of name choices, HOW can you name a prostitute "Kumquat"? I laughed out loud. Tan uses those kinds of compound noun names in her other books, but it seems like she's maybe running out of ideas. All of the courtesans in Hidden Jade Path are named for clouds: Magic Cloud, Puffy Cloud, Billowy Cloud. I feel for the girl who gets stuck with the name Puffy Cloud. Oh, and what about Cracked Egg? All of the names felt contrived, even the English ones. 
 And worst of all, I felt patronized. Every time a new section started with "June 1919" or whatever, Tan felt the need to say "Three years later...", as if the reader needed to be reminded right away how much time had passed. And whenever a character referred to an event that happened in the past, we were treated to a complete retelling. When Violet met Loyalty Fang again, and he reminded her that he had been the boy that her cat had mauled at Hidden Jade Path, did we really need to be given that whole story again? As soon as he said the thing about the cat, I remembered the story. I swear, if a halfway decent editor had gotten ahold of this book, it would have turned out to be half as long. 
 Also, there should never be mispronounced words in an audiobook. Get it together, everybody--and if you're going to use the word "pudenda" 800 times, make sure both readers pronounce it the same way. Common sense.

I just don't get into the wizard books of the Discworld series like I do the other ones. They have their clever moments here and there, but all in all I find the wizards a tad annoying. I do like Rincewind, and especially the Luggage, but they were kind of eclipsed in this story by the bumblings of the rest of the wizard staff. 
 The story is meant to kind of poke fun at the quirks people have in Australia, but having never been there and not being greatly acquainted with how things are done differently down there, I think a lot probably went right over my head. 
 Another problem is I find I can't read more than about three Pratchett books right in a row or they start to lose their fun factor, and this was book three, so the humor was losing its luster pretty quickly in this one for me. Time to take a break and come back for more Pratchett later.

 I've never visited Australia, and I don't know too much about the culture there, so most of my appreciation of this book was based on pop culture; but that's okay. I'm sure I missed a few of the jokes, but overall it was quite enjoyable. The Wizards are goofy and typecast. All is well with the world.

reference_books.title: Fragments (Partials Sequence, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Much like the first book in this series, I was sucked in from page one. This was a very welcome change as the second books in trilogy's that I have been reading lately have felt watered down, and forced. Wells keeps an even, suspenseful and intriguing flow going all the way through to the last page. 
 In FRAGMENTS we see things from three different POV's: Kira, Marcus and Haru. Kira is definitely the dominant POV, taking up the majority of the book, and for good reason. She's on a mission - sure they cured one baby from RM, but now they need to cure them all, and to do this it's going to require a journey, both in the physical and mental sense. And they need to do it as fast as possible because every day children are dying and the Partial's expiration date is getting closer every day. 
 The details in the scenery are both outstanding, and yet a little too much from time to time. In a nearly 600 page book, where the vast majority of the main POV is travel, by foot or horse back across a desolate land, I found myself a time or two, being a little anxious for the real action to start. Don't get me wrong, I'm not saying there isn't any action - there's a lot of action, even more so that in PARTIALS. I just tend to have a bit of trouble focusing on great sections of description and inner monologue. And as they occur a handful of times, it felt like they took up more of the book than they actually do. Don't let my inability to be patient effect your choice to read this book. It's a must read for fans of PARTIALS. 
 The last 1/3 of the book was my absolute favorite part of the book. And since I really liked everything before it, this is really saying something. It literally explodes with an amazing twist that will have you flipping page after page, wanting more! 
 Have the found the cure? Who will survive? You are going to have to pick up a copy and find out for yourself! Oh, and I would be a total jerk if I didn't tell the fans of Samm, that you get a whole lot more of him in this book! (yay!!) 
 For more reviews and giveaways visit www.MeMyShelfAndI.com

It doesn't make the character's ingnorance any less realistic, but I can get really annoyed really quickly when I feel like screaming at Luce " figure it out already!"

It makes me want to punch her in the face so she'll have a bit of sense.

 No Cam, no deal.

Quite a fun book. Well-written, interesting protagonist, and kind of a strange take on the "vampire" concept. The conceit of this book is a "vampire finishing school," which basically means a private high school for vamps. The "vamps" are as non-vampy as you can possibly get, though, at least in this, the series' first book. In movie terms, think of it as MEAN GIRLS meets THE CRAFT. 
 I read the book because co-author Kristin Cast is a fan of my work. That, plus the fact that the HOUSE OF KNIGHT series has sold a bajillion books and generated a rabid following made me want to check it out. I'm glad I did. 
 If you dismiss this as "just another TWILIGHT," you'd be wrong. Yes, this is high-school vamps, but I felt the characters were far less starry-eyed and more typical of the clique nature of a real high school. These kids are kids, and only really succumb to the broader scope of the supernatural aspect near the book's end. 
 I won't read the rest of the series, but don't take that as a knock on the work -- as a middle-aged guy, high-school melodrama doesn't really resonate anymore (vamps or no vamps). If you're into this type of story, MARKED is a home run. The series just completed, by the way, so you can slam all of the books without worrying about a long wait for the story's end.

reference_books.title: Me Talk Pretty One Day
reference_books.review_text: At times laugh-out-loud funny, and most often crass, "Me Talk Pretty One Day" is generally a good and quick read. It's a bit cliche and tacky to write an intricate review of a book almost everyone has read, but Orwell's most famous book (or perhaps second most-famous, after "Animal Farm") left a distinct political impression with me, and the best way to make sense of it is to write about it: 
 What seems to me as a central theme of "1984" is the concept of liberty, with special reference to how it has been addressed in the various political ideologies in history. With respect to the book, the concept is largely literal - the loss of "liberty" with regard to where you work, where you live, what you eat, what you wear and with whom you associate. But beyond the literal "unfreedoms," as they would be called in Newspeak, hide the more terrifying, less tangible losses of liberty: the freedom to think and believe as an individual wishes, and without persecution. Looking back to the Inquisition, the uncertain era of the English King Henry VIII or even the American Revolution, civilization has always fought with the sentiment of wanting to liberate itself in some way, or of some thing. And although perhaps Orwell writes about it differently, I think one can argue that the Party in "1984" is no exception; it is fighting for liberation from usurpers to its "throne" of unrestricted power. In order to do this, as Winston learns, it is necessary to retard the entire nation's intelligence. 
 Stay with me here - let's apply this Orwellian concept to, say, the war in Iraq. We're fighting for liberation (supposedly from terrorism, but more likely in actuality from subservience to the Middle East in the oil industry - but that's a different essay), the Sunnis and Shiites are fighting for liberation (from us as much as from each other, I expect), and, as in "1984," the war is a continual waste of supplies and production, which in effect retards the American citizens' intelligence by squandering money that ought to be spent on our own country on a war that in reality has nothing to do with us, except that we started it for no good reason. Aside from keeping the nation dumb as to the state of affairs in Iraq, or what the war is doing to the economy at home (not to mention killing thousands of our troops), the U.S. government is, in its anti-terrorism movement, tending toward Big Brother-type surveillance with such pieces of legislation as the Patriot Act. I know this is kind of rambling, but my point here is this: Big Brother is watching, but his name is George W. Bush, and this is 2007, not "1984." 
 Just a little reflection on a book... didn't mean it to be political! ;)

reference_books.title: Middlesex
reference_books.review_text:
"Middlesex" is what you might call a true "Great American Novel." It is easy to see why Eugenides won the Pulitzer for this epic tale about family, coming-of-age, love, money, war, and, above all, identity. Why we are who we are and where our bodies and identities really come from. I minored in Sociology in undergrad and so was particularly interested in the author's exploration of the nature vs. nurture in the forming of one's gender identity. 
 The novel is split roughly in half, the first half being the narrator's family history, and the second half being his own life as a hermaphrodite and what happens as he reaches puberty after having lived as a girl for 14 years. My one complaint: I thought the ending lacked poignance. For such an engrossing, at times tragicomic story that evokes true empathy in the reader, Eugenides fails to deliver the final message with the ethereal, polished hand that sweeps throughout the rest of the novel. 
 However, despite its semi-weak final paragraph, I highly recommend "Middlesex" - it is captivating from start to (almost) finish. I read its 527 pages in two days, and literally could not put the thing down.

reference_books.title: Northanger Abbey
reference_books.review_text:
A delightful, quick little read. Although it was one of Austen's early books, it was not published until after her death, and it is a simple, though satirical, novel about her usual subjects: society and marriage. The character of Henry Tilney is wonderfully sarcastic and funny, Isabella such a wicked angel, and Catherine so placid and innocent, that one can immediately see that this book is primarily character-driven. In fact, there isn't much of a plot. I still liked it, but then, I love 19th-century literature, so I could be on my own here. (Yes, I realize it was written in the late 1700s, but I still categorize it as Victorian and 19th-century in style.) 
 If you fancy a quick foray into the Victorian love-and-marriage theme, grab this book -- and if you like it, read "Pride and Prejudice" and "The House of Mirth." Both are similar and very good. This theme is something I have yet to see played out in Dickens with his usual ingenuity and mastery, and the girly girl in me was enchanted with this glimpse of another author's take on late 18th/early 19th-century society.

I was grateful for the listening time because there were many parts of the book that I think I would have grown tired of reading and opted to put the book down instead of continuing to read. Bits of the story (before the inevitable lifeboat journey) are long and arguably side stories, possibly tangents. They're not boring information, but at times, they feel unnecessary for the story. 
 However, taking a step away from the book and thinking about it, I can see how every section connects to another, even if in small ways. Perhaps, Pi's actions and thoughts later are completely influenced by his religious studies and his time spent loving and learning about God. 
 The book is violent and graphic, which is realistic in a situation involving wild animals. Pi's journey is incredible, heartbreaking, and vivid. I rooted for him the entire time, and I never once wanted to see him fail.

reference_books.title: Making Faces
reference_books.review_text:
Difficile fare una recensione analitica e asettica su un libro del genere, perche dentro questo romanzo c'e talmente tanto che e quasi impossibile elencare tutto. 
 I personaggi, per lo meno all'inizio, potrebbero dare l'impressione di essere stereotipati, i classici personaggi cliche del romance e invece no, la Harmon riesce a rivoltare le carte in tavola alla perfezione. Inizialmente il protagonista principale - Ambrose Young - e bellissimo e il piu ambito. Campione di lotta nella squadra del liceo, ha quattro amici per la pelle con cui si allena e trascorre tutto il suo tempo libero. Ovviamente si accaparra la piu bella della scuola, Rita, con la quale si mette insieme. Rita e amica del cuore di Fern Taylor, cugina di Bailey, ragazzino malato di sclerosi multipla e destinato a una morte precoce, di cui ha una fredda consapevolezza. Va da se che Fern Taylor e bruttina, con denti imprigionati da un apparecchio poco sensuale e prorompenti capelli rossi che non si lasciano domare facilmente, magra e con indosso impietosi occhiali dalla montatura spessa e nera. Quanto di peggio puo esserci nell'aspetto di una persona? Fern ama segretamente Ambrose. E si presta a scrivere lettere d'amore per permettere a Rita di conquistarlo. 
 E poi l'11 settembre 2001 arriva e sconvolge la vita di tutti. La guerra in Afghanistan prima e in Iraq poi decimera la gioventu americana e neppure Ambrose Young e i suoi amici saranno immuni da questa scure di violenza e dolore. 
 Il romanzo cambia registro quasi immediatamente. Se pensate di leggere il solito Young Adult con la storia d'amore tra il Bello e Dannato del liceo e la goffa imbranata che diventera una Principessa siete ingannati. La storia e quella di tanti giovani di poco piu di vent'anni al giro di boa del dopo liceo, alle prese con le problematiche di vita futura. Con l'aggravante della devastazione della guerra, che, sebbene lontana e quasi irreale e concreta nel seminare morte e dolore. Meravigliose le figure degli adulti a contorno e il dolcissimo Bailey. Scritto meravigliosamente, tradotto anche meglio, Sei il mio sole anche di notte e un bel libro, di quelli che meritano di essere letti.

reference_books.title: One Night Stand (One Night Stand, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Divertente e simpatico si legge tutto d'un fiato e si fatica a sospendere la lettura. Ben caratterizzati i personaggi e la trama anche se ci sono un po' incongruenze si fa fatica a perdonare. Se puo essere plausibile che dopo una notte di fuoco e un incontro surreale ma simpaticissimo, ben descritto e intrigante al matrimonio della rivale della propria migliore amica, la protagonista si ritrovi il bellissimo uomo con cui ha avuto un'avventura di una notte seduto in casa propria poco piu di una settimana dopo e per giunta fidanzato di sua sorella - sorella peraltro antipaticissima, la classica odiosa che sembra quasi una macchietta tanto e dipinta in maniera "cliche" - poco plausibile sono le varie successive soluzioni per spiegare il perche l'Adone dei sogni della protagonista stia per sposare la sorella e soprattutto il come alla fine si risolve il tutto. Sinceramente un po' piu di sforzo dal lato fantasia non sarebbe guastato. Per cui solo tre stelline perche il romanzo e comunque carino e puo risultare comunque gradevole per lettori non troppo esigenti.

reference_books.title: The Bronze Horseman (The Bronze Horseman, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I liked the beginning, the sorrow that war brings to all Tatiana's family, the sacrifice she makes hiding her feeligs for Alexander and giving her man to her sister. I started having some discomfort when family behaviour starts being awkward towards her and everybody's profiting of her good character and spirit of self-sacrifice. The part along the Leningrad's blockade is creepy but depicted marvellously and full of angst and thrill. Then, the Lazaredo part starts to make all my interest in this novel to fall down, disastroulsy. I loved everything until the marriage. Then boredom starts to increase and my curiosity of what may happen next fades into a big yawn. I don't know why. I understand Tatiana is very young when everything starts, and her love for Shura is tremendously great, but her personality does not grow together with her experiences that should give her more awareness of living and maturity. She appears the same naif and gentle, and almost prone youth that was before, when her family was alive. And Shura is funny but too light in this part. I know that there will be more angst pages until the end, but I suddenly lost interest in knowing what comes next so... I dropped the book. Sorry. 
 p.s.: Too many repetition of the same act, concept, situation, poem! Paulina Simmons repeats and repeats and repeats... maybe it's also for this reason. A better editing intervention might have helped.

book_a.user_review:
I unfortunately have to agree with most of the other not-so-positive goodreads reviews because this book, among all eight read so far, has been the most difficult and boring and difficult to read up to the end. Too much deja vu, the island, the murders, the impossible and incoherent situations, apart from the beginning, when Ty and Zane rejoin from Ty's deployment, all their relationship dynamics went blank, as if the author wanted to wipe off everything written so far and start from ground 0. Ty in this book seems more close to a drama queen character while Zane follows his partner without a reaction, the real main characters of this book are Nick and kelly, and I don't know if I like this switch of events. What I have liked the most in this saga is the growing of the relationship and the conflicts, the secrets little by little unveiled, I loved the burst of conflict in book 7 when Ty reveals his secrets to Zane and Zane's violent reaction to that. Everything was so real and so passionate. Here I did not find passion whatsoever. Just lukewarm feelings from every part. 
 And I really have one question: why on earth such an important and powerful manager such as Stanton, Livi's father chooses an island to have his daughter's wedding and only a bunch of bodyguard at the security duty? A place - he knew about it - had secret passages between the walls, was so far from everything that might be easily isolated and if he knew about the tentative kidnapping of his grand-daughter why on earth not to choose a more suitable and american police protected place? that doesn't make any sense and even the end of the story with all culprits discovered did not convince me at all. I found everything some sort of deus ex machina in order to match with the surrounding and the environment. 
 I loved all this series but this book in particular made me yawn a lot of times. Hope for the final one then.

The writing wasn't that great either, it read like a cartoon with all the laughing, chuckling, raised eyebrows, and snickering that was going on. Doesn't exactly instill the seriousness that was mass murders they were suppose to be solving. 
 Plus all the really lame pot jokes? Seriously, how old do you think the readers are? In all honesty, had someone told me this was a fanfic and not an actual published novel I probably would have believed them. 
 Some of the "puns" in this one weren't even real puns! 
 I have to say that my faith was renewed in the series after the ending of the last book, but my faith has very thoroughly been crushed. Fortunately, there is only one book left, knowing that you could almost say that this one is a little bit of a filler. I'm ready to put these guys to rest, frankly at this point its gone on to long. 
 The author missed a HUGE opportunity here. Had she added anything about the 6 months gone or even actually addressed that at any point in time it would have added to the story. Ty and Zane don't even sit down and have some sort of heart to heart. Oh and the entire series is a run of contradiction, pretty sure Ty had said he'd tell Zane everything when he got out, he's out tell him all your secrets! Zane doesn't like lies of omission as stated earlier in the series, he can't trust people who aren't completely truthful with him. 
 Now though, Ty and Zane's engagement is going to have to be addressed. It'll probably happen in the Sidewinder book, there is just too much overlap that the series are both getting really repetitive. 
 I'm sorry to say as well that Zanes age throws me a lot when they talk about adopting kids. If they adopted now he'd be over 65 probably older by the time the kid left for college. I don't know, kinda just a side thing, but it's one of those things that if you don't mention his age maybe no one will notice that he's pretty much 50. 
 Anyway, I'd have to recommend this to anyone who is so heavily invested in this series/author that you have to read all the books. You know the people who read Cross's book, plus the Sidewinder series and Cut & Run. For everyone else just stay away, no I would not recommend this book/series.

didn't wow me at all

The official release date for this book is today which makes me disinclined to talk about the story. It would be too easy to spoil the story for those who haven't gotten around to reading the book yet and since I would never forgive a reviewer for doing that to me, I won't take the risk of doing so now. I'll limit myself to listing a few things I loved about this book and will hopefully manage to do so without revealing things that I shouldn't. Of course, the only way to make sure you don't encounter any spoilers is to do what I did, and stay away from reviews all together until you've read the book. 
 Let me start by saying that I loved this book. For me this book had everything I love about the 'Cut & Run' series. There was the mystery and all the high thrills action needed to solve it, not to mention some twists and turns that took my breath away. The fact that it was set in a Scottish mansion with secret passage-ways and located on a remote and private island only added to the sense of danger. I have always loved the interactions between the characters in these books and the addition of Kelly and Nick to Ty and Zane's double act meant a lot more quick fire dialogue. 
 The start of the book had me reading with a huge grin on my face, a grin that was semi permanent and only interrupted by moments of laughter. In fact, the grin was stuck on my face for a long time. But on those occasions when the grin did fall of my face it was because there was real pain in the story. 
 I'm not entirely sure what I expected when I started this book. I was ready for residue of Ty and Zane's last fight, especially since it was followed almost immediately by their separation. Conflict between Nick and Kelly wouldn't have surprised me either since their intimate relationship was so very new and almost nipped in the bud by their separation. What I was completely unprepared for were the issues between Ty and Nick I was confronted with; deep seated issue without any easy answers. Reading about those was as painful as it was fascinating and kept me glued to the page. 
 I loved Ty's struggles when he finds out about Nick and Kelly and his difficulty in determining what exactly is causing him to feel so off about it. 
 "Stop. The deal is I don't freak out, and you don't share sex stories." - Ty to Kelly. 
 And I have to admit that I'm falling deeper in love with Kelly and Nick as I read more about them. Kelly's support for Nick when he's facing one of the toughest decisions he'll ever have to make was beautiful. 
 ""The decision you make, you make it for you. Not him." Kelly whispered in his ear. "You make it for you. And I'll be here." - Kelly to Nick 
 But the Kelly's words towards the end of this book took my breath away. 
 "What words do I use for this feeling if 'I love you' has already been used." 
 Followed by: 
 ""I love you, Nick," Kelly whispered. "No matter what those words meant before, we know what they mean now. They're ours now. Just ours."" 
 Well, those two quotes all but melted me. 
 Now that I've finished the book I should say that I wouldn't have minded a bit more sexual action on these pages. It wasn't something I was missing or actively waiting for while reading the book though. The story with all its twists and turns, action and clever dialogue had me in such a tight hold that I didn't even realise how little sex there'd been until the story had ended. 
 It sort of breaks my heart that we appear to be nearing the end of Ty and Zane's story. Of course there still is the 'mole issue' to resolve but, as things stand now, it looks like that might be the end of their adventures. Having said that, the 'Sidewinder' stories have only started and this book set us up for what promises to be one hell of a storyline in that series. And since Ty is very much a member of the Sidewinder team, the future might not be quite as bleak as I fear. One thing is sure though; no matter where Abigail Roux decides to take her characters next, I will be following them closely, making very sure not to miss a single word in the process.

I picked this one up at 1:30 in the morning and had finished it by 9pm the same day. I really do enjoy New Adult novels but I find that a lot of them have an issue with toeing the line between abusive and romantic. With this novel I had her ahead of time that this one leaned more toward abusive. However, I was pleased to find that, in my opinion at least, this was not the case. The romance portrayed in this novel is not necessarily a romance I would ever want in real life (too much drama and head games!) but it made for a fantastic read. I really did like Travis, his family, Shep, Finch and America. Abby was a bit annoying at points with the mind games and not deciding what she wants, though. 
 Also, there were some cliches that the book could have avoided. Like how every 'whore' seems to looove Travis for no reason, as well as every guy being all over Abby - though I get that they're both supposed to be attractive it became a little too much. Also, I didn't particularly like the fact that Travis beat up like 50 people over the course of the book. Most for stupid as reasons, too. It seemed a little obsessive. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed the story and I felt like the romance was well paced. The writing wasn't fantastic but it was easy to read and I enjoyed most of the characters. It is one of the better New Adult reads I have read.

I have made a resolution not to search for books on goodreads anymore, because inevitably, the ones with higher ratings are ones that are liked by Bella-Edward fans, who write in their reviews "YAAAA!!!!!!!!!!!! HEART LOVE HEART LOVE ." 
 This book has a very cliched and boring premise: Good girl intrigues bad boy; bad boy tricks good girl into "hangin'" with him, bad boy falls in love with her. 
 However, I thought to myself that such a cliched storyline could not POSSIBLY have garnered such a high rating if it weren't special, right? Plus, that cover is pretty awesome -- I'm thinking to myself, Is the butterfly trapped in the jar representative of the characters in the book? Symbolic of societal issues? 
 Answer: I didn't get far enough into the book to find out. Basically, I didn't get even as far as the "good girl intrigues bad boy." What happens in the beginning of the book is that this good girl is somehow always pulled by her friend America to events, including an underground fight ring. The first fight she attends has the main guy "Travis Mad Dog Maddox" as a combatant. He does nickname her some really weird, random nickname, Pigeon, for no reason at all. I mean, does she look like a bird b/c she's skinny? Does she tilt her head to one side when she's thinking? Does she have beady black eyes and poop on statues? NOTHING is revealed as to this mystery. 
 Moving past that, let's discuss how such a "good girl" would be friends with America, who's hanging out with what I'm assuming to be kind of shady characters (um, such as a combatant in an underground fight ring?)? We're also led to believe at some point that Travis has aced his literature class. Also, the first time the main girl (I can't even remember her name) is tricked into eating with Travis is totally nonsensical -- granted, she made a promise to Travis to go to his dorm, but she went with America and her boyfriend. Granted, she did not have dinner, but how is she in any way obligated to go on what turns out to be a date with Travis??? Please, can we just call her the way I see it? A big giant hypocritical LOSER?? 
 The book is incredibly lame. Let's assume that Travis is the hottest stud in the world, sprays himself regularly with Axe cologne so that women are undressing around him and fall at his feet. I went to a high school with 2400 people, and there were TONS of hot guys everywhere. Seriously, we had some male models at my school (I realize not everyone has hot people at their school, but I really did. My yearbook looked like an Abercrombie advertisement), and no matter how hot or studly these guys were, I NEVER saw any girl (or two girls at the same time openly vying or) gaping after Travis Maddox in the fashion described in this book. I mean, we're assuming that alcohol isn't openly consumed on the school campus, right? 
 So, either every girl is drunk (and maybe doing drugs as well, hallucinogens, probably), or Travis Maddox is actually an alien sent to infiltrate and impregnate the human race, one college girl at a time. Which would make for a far more interesting book, if you ask me.

Wow!! There were so many feelings and emotions as I read this book that it was just amazing. While I put this as a romance book, it was not your typical sweet and mushy romance at all. It was rough at times, pulled at the heartstrings, made you mad, sad, and happy. There were times I wanted to close my eyes because I could not believe what was happening and then there were other times I couldn't turn the pages fast enough. I read this book in one day. 
 I don't really know what to say other than it was just amazing! I liked all of the characters from Abby and her supposed naivety, to Travis and his rough and toughness, their friends America and Shepley, and even Abby's roommate Kara. There was Travis' family of brothers and Abby's dad. This book portrays very well that families are not perfect, maybe a little dysfunctional or a lot dysfunctional, but that we are all seeking something better. 
 I also enjoyed the college setting. Having not actually attended college as a dorm student and living away from home, I really enjoyed the talk about the underground, the parties, the cafeteria, etc. I could picture the campus and excitement of college life.
