reference_books.title: Born to Run
reference_books.review_text:
If you have ever seen the Boss and/or the E Street band live this audiobook's strengths wouldn't be a surprise. It is long, unrelenting, poetic, politically minded, self effacing, and full of heart. Much of Bruce's musical catalog has long been comfort food to me, so I like, many other fans, are probably primed to enjoy just listening to him. But 18 hours is a long time, and it is noteworthy that his delivery held up throughout. ( I caught some volume changes at the beginning of chapters but most wouldn't.) 
 Bruce is gifted storyteller, and just like his music, the characters of his NJ upbringing and the music business come to life here. His religious past both informs his moral compass and confounds his self confidence in a ways that feel authentic to me as a Catholic school kid. 
 There is much to also appreciate about Bruce's candor around his relationships with his bandmates (especially Clarence and the role his race and physical size played into his stage mythology), his wife, family, and most especially his father. Much of this book examines Bruce's relationship with father and role mental illness shapes them both. As he writes: 
 " We honor our parents by carrying their best forward and laying the rest down. By fighting and taming the demons that laid them low and now reside in us." 
 I was excited to learn that the Bay Area played an important role his life: his early trips out West, trying it solo in SF, his parents place in San Mateo (his Dad drove a shuttle bus in SFO!), and even mentioned San Jose twice! 
 The one downside of buying the audiobook on Audible is that it does not come with the photographs found in the back. 
 Lived up to my expectations. Bruce always does for me.

book_a.user_review:
I reread this classic for kids book club later this month. As a adult reading this again a few things struck me. 
 1) Dahl is such a master of language. He manages to be descriptive and emotionally compelling. There was a ton of great vocabulary in those oompa loompa songs. He also does a great job playing with dual ideas of hunger. 
 2) Speaking of the oompa loompa - yeah, wow how colonisist/racist are little slaves from an island happily work in your factory? Apparently some of these describitions were changed in later editions. 
 3) What a morality tale. Again, those oompa loompa songs really spell out behavior guidelines. Dahl was very anti-TV. 
 4) All and all it is still entertaining and teachable. Impressive.

sample_reviews.review_text: The book was very good. Both of my daughters, who have seen the Johnny Depp/Tim Burton version of the movie more than once, listened intently as I read the book to see if "it actually followed the movie." :) As a 30-something adult, I have seen both versions of the movie. The "original" was okay but I wasn't as enamored with it as most people my age seem to be. I found the second movie to be very faithful to the story and would recommend the book to anyone with children or anyone who needs to remember what it was like to be a child!

Full disclosure: I don't like children. I don't have any, and never will. But that doesn't stop me from enjoying children's fiction. I don't see why it should, since there are so many beautiful examples out there that any age can easily enjoy. And in my reading, there are some books I read where I get the sense that the author loves children. Harper Lee, Betty Smith, both of them made me thing that they are the type that love children. I can see them smiling down at strange children who approach them and having an instant connection of kindred spirits. 
 Roald Dahl... not so much. In fact I question whether Dahl liked people at all. I know people love the man and I feel bad for saying bad things about him, but for heaven's sake, nobody in this book was likeable. The other children and parents were ridiculously over the top parodies, far too over the top to be funny. Charlie is this... empty shell of a child. He doesn't seem to have a personality, and the fact that he's quiet and withdrawn is made out by Dahl to be some sort of wonderful trait that Dahl wishes more children would have. Which is kind of creepy since those traits are likely from the extremely bad health Charlie suffers from, which Dahl describes in a somewhat disturbingly long introduction to the character, as living in extreme poverty and near-starvation. Charlie's grandfather is no more fleshed out, seems to be more childlike than Charlie but without anything to give him a personality. And Willy Wonka is a psychotic sadistic child-hating manchild with a penchant for third world labor. And this is a *children's book*??? Sorry, Dahl fans, but this book freaked me the hell out.

book_b.title: Ethan Frome
book_b.user_review: I picked up this classic again for two simple reasons: 1) It felt like a good winter time read. 2) I was forced to read it as a teenager in my American English class. Simply put, I hated it and I wanted to see if anything changed. I gave the audiobook version a try in attempt to adapt to language and writing style better. I still didn't find it that captivating of read, and wonder it would be a good match of highschool student. I understand that Wharton an interesting literary and more notably female figure. But I think there are other classics that can teach literary devices like flashback, and third person narration that better connect with young adults.

sample_reviews.review_text: Bleak story, with beautiful descriptive passages. Definitely recommended, but know what you are getting into: a classic tragedy.

I get what Edith Wharton was trying to do, and I have to give her credit for that. I think it is great that she was trying to get people to understand that divorce is needed sometimes. I just really hate how she went about it. She makes the wife a horrible person, and so it is hard not to hate her. Then she makes the guy loveable, but he is also a cheater. I just don't approve of making the wife a bitch, and making the cheating husband such a "wonderful" guy.

This is a short 'novella', and what's there not to like? Edith Wharton is undoubtedly compelling and evocative with her words, especially the descriptions of landscape, much as I usually resent having to waste time over descriptive passages rather than the plot. The plot is good, the suspense keeps you going. You'll love the 'ironic twist' at the end so much that you'll hate it. 
 That said, I found the sad, poignant story rather...unrealistic. Maybe I'm in a cynical phase about the power of love etc. I just couldn't digest all the sentimentality. There are probably layers and deeper meanings that I'm not able to immediately grasp. It seems to be a fairly popular, well read and respected book, given the number of classroom resources that show up in search results. Maybe I'll go read some of them and then update this review. Because right now, I cannot honestly say I loved this book or would recommend it to anybody else. 
 PS: This would have been a quick read but I'd found this book under the readings of one my favourite Librivoxdotorg readers Elizabeth Klett. So I spent a few hours listening to this, rather than reading it up in an hour or so. 
 PS2: After reading some sparknotes kind of pages on this novel, I can confirm several layers exist but they all reach to the same conclusion: this is ONE seriously depressing read. Some of the interesting insights I gleaned: the colour red against the "stark" white landscape as a symbol or motif, "inverted fairy tale", and that the cruel ending of the novel can be justified as containing the warning of moral paralysis. Phew. Deep.

Ethan Frome's dreams are dashed with his father's death. A promising education is halted so Ethan can run the family farm. It's not until his invalid wife's cousin appears that a spark is reignited within him. 
 Wharton does a terrific job in capturing this sense of lost hope and the story is only slightly marred by a trick/gimmicky ending.

I was a little underwhelmed by this one. I didn't buy the narrator, who had to have filled in a lot of gaps in his imagination to be able to tell this story of Ethan Frome. I wasn't compelled to pull the book from my bedside, where it sat as going-to-sleep reading. Ethan as a tragic character was just kind of lame in his wintry entrapment.

I picked this book up thinking it would be a short read of good literature. 
 I did not enjoy it and could not finish the book. Enough said.
Definitivamente creo que leer este libro fue perder el tiempo. Es una historia corta, simple y aburrida.
As always, Wharton has plenty of points to make about how society works, but this short novel was far too bleak for me.
Well that was depressing.

I absolutely hated this book. 
 OK, two things were good. The author draws New England landscapes, particularly in winter, beautifully. Secondly, the book was exceedingly short, so my misery wasn't prolonged. I need to joke after reading this sad, dismal, depressing book. Jeez, how can people look at life with such eyes?! Stop griping and do something with your life. It is your own fault if you just sob and moan. 
 You follow a couple that is ill-fit. The reader has to listen to their arguments. On top of this, the wife, Zeena, is a hypochondriac. You have to listen to her sob story, complaints and grumbles. Ugh. 
 Then there is attraction that arises between the husband and the wife's cousin who has been taken into the house as a maid. This is so corny, and so melodramatically described. Overly sentimental too. At the same time there is no fire in this love, and you scarcely see how it develops. You are instead supposed to moan about the impossibility of it all. 
 What others may think is if of prime importance. 
 I know this is maybe going to irritate those who love this book. Please excuse me, but this is how I react to the book. 
 It doesn't get better; the end is pure maudlin. 
 I listened to the audiobook narrated by Elizabeth Klett. The speed varies. It is not always read too quickly, but much is. Each new chapter starts out at a good speed. Then she seems to get carried away by the story, causing her to read faster and faster. The tone, the voices she uses for the different characters, is fine, so this is quite a shame. 
 It wasn't hard writing this review! I knew exactly what I had to say! If you are like me, avoid this book. It is depressing, sentimental and maudlin.

reference_books.title: Carter Beats the Devil
reference_books.review_text:
The book opens in 1932, when acclaimed magician Carter the Great puts on a grand show. President Warren Harding is a volunteer in the show and seems to enjoy himself. Hours later however, the President is dead, and Carter is on the run, suspected of being involved in the death. 
 The book then goes back to Carter's childhood, and tells the story of how he came to be a magician (turning to magic to overcome loneliness and defeat a bully). 
 The story progresses up to and beyond the night of the President's death, and as it does so, layer upon layer is added. This book is a sprawling novel, with Carter the Great right at the centre of it. 
 This is a highly fictionalised account of the life of Carter the Great, who was indeed a magician in the jazz age. It's enjoyable in many ways, and there is lots of wit and humour within the pages. However, there are just too many threads and sub-plots, which made it over-complicated. (I admit to feeling a sense of relief when I finished the book). If it had been edited and was about 200 pages shorter - my copy was over 600 pages long - it would have been an excellent novel. As it is though, it is an enjoyable one, and I bought Glen David Gold's second novel, on the basis of having read this one (and because Charlie Chaplin was on the cover). Recommended with some caution.

reference_books.title: The Jane Austen Book Club
reference_books.review_text:
I picked this book up a few years ago in a charity shop, because (a) it was ridiculously cheap, and (b) I like Jane Austen. I finally got around to reading it because I watched the film adaptation a few weeks ago, and really enjoyed it, and I wanted to see how the book and film compared. Of the many reviews I've read of this book since finishing it myself, the vast majority are unfavourable, but while I can see what might put people off, I actually enjoyed it a lot. 
 Six friends start a book club which meets once a month, to discuss the novels of Jane Austen. Each takes their turn at hosting, and while the novel does discuss their meetings, it takes much more time to describe each character's back story, and the issues which they are facing in their current life. The narration is quite unusual - it is as if the book club has a collective consciousness, and it is from the point of view of this consciousness that the story is told; I can see how that could irritate, but for me anyway, it worked. I did think that the characters were pretty well drawn, although two of them - Prudie and Bernadette - seemed slightly set apart from the other four, this possibly being because the other four had connections between them that excluded Prudie and Bernadette (this may also explain why these two characters were my least favourites). 
 It's a very charming book, if slightly predictable. Not entirely predictable however - the resolutions of Sylvia's and Allegra's stories were not what I had expected (or at least in Sylvia's case, it would have been unexpected, but I knew what happened, only because I had seen the film). However, as each chapter is devoted mainly to one character (that being whoever is hosting the book club that month), it almost feels like a series of separate short stories which relate to each other through shared characters. 
 I wouldn't say that you need to like, or even to have read any Austen novels to enjoy this book, as in truth, only small parts of the books are devoted to the actual book club meetings - in fact, you could probably have written this book about any author's works (Karen Joy Fowler is clearly a big Austen fan, as she notes in her acknowledgements) - but I do think it helps, as I found myself nodding along with the assessments of certain Austen characters. I enjoyed it a lot, but on balance, I'm not sure I would read it again, while I would certainly watch the film adaptation again.

reference_books.title: How To Be a Good Wife

reference_books.title: The Never List
reference_books.review_text:
After a traumatic childhood experience, best friends Jennifer and Sarah create the Never List - a list of things which they must never do, in order to stay safe. Despite all their good intentions however, they are abducted, and thrown into a three year long nightmare. The book opens thirteen years later, with Sarah still suffering from the effects of the ordeal. She never leaves her apartment, never has physical contact with people, works from home, and has no friends. However, the man who abducted her and Jennifer is being considered for parole, and Sarah needs to make sure that he doesn't get it, so she decides that the only way to secure her future is to revisit her past. 
 When I started this book, I thought I was going to really enjoy it. The first few chapters throw you headlong into the story at break-neck speed, and it seemed to pave the way for an intense psychological thriller. In fairness, it does keep up the quick pace all the way through, with plenty of twists and turns, and in many ways, was a quick and easy read. 
 Unfortunately though, I ended up feeling a bit frustrated by both the story, and the main character. At the beginning of the story, Sarah is suffering from severe paranoia and phobias, but she seems to overcome them so quickly, that it is just not believable. To assume that a woman who is too scared to even leave her apartment (even when she orders food in, the doorman to the apartments has to bring it to her, rather than the usual delivery person) is suddenly feel able to drive miles, and jump on planes, all in a matter of a few days, just felt inconsistent. In fact, most of the main characters seemed to act in an entirely inconsistent manner. 
 I had my suspicions about what was going to happen at the end, but there were a couple of twists I didn't anticipate - and it's always nice to be surprised when reading a thriller - but I did feel that the final denouement was a bit tangled up, involving a few characters that didn't really serve much purpose in the story. 
 The book did have some good points and there were some genuinely tense moments (and it's certainly had some rave reviews) but I think it was probably just not the book for me, with some of the themes, such as torture and rape, feeling particularly disturbing.

reference_books.title: The Measure of a Man: A Spiritual Autobiography
reference_books.review_text:
I don't listen to a lot of audiobooks and it's very rare for me to think that a book is better listened to than read, but in this case, I'll make an exception. The Measure of a Man is narrated by Sidney Poitier himself, and he has such a beautiful voice, that it really enhanced my experience of the book. It also worked really well as an audiobook because he is so conversational in tone - he peppers his narration with phrases like, "You follow?" or "You see?" 
 As for the content itself - wow! This is a wonderful autobiography and then some. While Poitier does tell the story of his life, it's not necessarily a straightforward chronological account of events. At times it comes across more as a philosophical discussion, where he uses his own life as a starting point. 
 His description of his childhood on Cat Island in the Bahamas was wonderful. Although his family lived in poverty, he points out that living in poverty on Cat Island was very different to living in poverty in some concrete jungle. As a child, he lived in a place with a beautiful climate, cocoa plum trees, sea grapes and wild bananas. 
 However, the most interesting - and in many ways upsetting - part of the book was when Poitier described his life in America which started when he moved to Florida aged 15, and then moved on to New York, and eventually started acting. This was a a time of racial segregation, and he realised exactly what it meant to be classed as a second class citizen. As an example - he recalled one event when he was already quite well known in films, and he went to a restaurant for a bite to eat. The black Maitre d' explained that he could have a table there, but they would have to put a screen around him, for the sensitivity of the white diners. When offered jobs on certain films, he was asked to sign papers disowning those of his black friends who were campaigning for equal rights (he always refused to do so). 
 Throughout it all, Poitier's dignity and strong sense of right and wrong shines through. He speaks strongly of his love for his parents, and how they inspire him in his life - whatever work he does, he does for them as well as for himself and his own family. He describes how he has always tried to be the best that he can be, his search for answers, his hopes for not only himself, but the world at large. He's honest about himself; those parts of himself that he is proud of, and the mistakes which he has made. 
 This is not a revealing, kiss-and-tell autobiography, and it is all the better for it. Poitier does not delve into the subject of murky or tawdry Hollywood tales, and is respectful of those people who he does mention by name. He does discuss some of his most famous films - which made me immediately want to go out and rewatch them - and reveals his motivation for playing certain roles, and refusing certain others. 
 Overall, I'd say that this is one of the best autobiographies I have ever read (or listened to). I would strongly recommend it, not only to anyone with an interest in Hollywood or film-making, but also to anyone with an interest in the civil rights movement.

book_a.title: Uncle Tom's Cabin
book_a.user_review: Historically and culturally significant novel. I admire Harriet Beecher Stowe, but did not enjoy this book as much as I had hoped. Certain parts made me cringe, such as broad generalisations and stereotypical views of black people. Also the overwhelming preachiness got tedious after a while. I felt like I was constantly being told that if you are not a Christian, you are inherently evil. I don't think this classic has aged particularly well. Still, it helped to change the widely held view that slavery was acceptable, and for that reason alone, I'm glad I read it.

Obviously it's me not you. This relationship just can't continue. I'm just not that into you. OK, that's just my internal banter with "Uncle Tom's Cabin." Long ago, back when mom first moved us up to Fairbanks, Alaska to live in a tent, I got this title in Classic Comics. I thought it was mind-blowing as a 10-year-old in 1971 (or whenever). But after my son read it, I decided to tackle the actual novel. It's good to read the classics, right? And this apparently displaced "12 Years a Slave" in the collective mindset of the the U.S. reader back in the day. So it's a good time. Maybe. But the tone and the style really disgusted me. I couldn't stand the reality of the picture painted by Harriet Beecher Stowe. Her characters seem shackled by more than simply being slaves. They're neutered by more than circumstance. And their masters should be pummeled by either fist or sledgehammer. I can see now why fellow whiteboy, director Quentin Tarantino, blessed his characters with the ability to actually rebel against the scumbag douches who felt it was their place to tell them what to do. That said, I'm still chipping away at this story. I just have to put it down frequently because it makes my blood boil. My biological father, who had nice white skin, was an immigrant who didn't care much for injustice. When he was treated like crap for his poor language skills early on during his time in this country, he got mad. Sometimes he'd pound the bastard who irritated him. Sometimes it was his foreman. Too bad for that guy. But Stowe's black characters can't do that. They should. But they can't. My step-dad, who's black and who raised me, dealt with this residual nastiness -- the legacy of slavery -- like a master. He deflected. He repurposed. He overcame. On a daily basis. I recall a job boss in San Francisco berating my own parent to me. The guy was an official of some standing. My dad and I were building a pretty significant addition to a train station. We had some minor issues, like any contractor. The official, thinking I was a hired hand, called my dad disparaging names and related that to his skin color. I don't recall if he used the N word, but it was that bad. I wanted to head butt him. Twist his neck. I'd been working 10 hours in the heat. Concrete work. And I was young, big and had arms like a gorilla. So I simply said, "He's my father." The guy paled, then turned red. He mumbled some apology and ran off. My dad returned about 30 minutes later. I told him. I was still angry. He shrugged it off. He said something like "If I got mad at stuff like that, I'd never get anything done." But it still makes me mad. So does this book.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This book is historically important, but as an atheist it was a torture to read. It's not even the lack of editing that concerned me, it's how things got so dramatic and revoltingly religious, especially after around page 400 where Eva dies. Oh my God my eyes were bleeding the whole time. It really got to the point where the Christianity propoganda became obnoxious. Everything was like an old, poorly animated Jesus cartoon. 
 Harriet Beecher Stowe was really writing about her wet dreams of how Uncle Tom was the black Jesus and damn she wanted to be in Heaven so bad, she wanted people to know that those black "creatures" were "actually like us". Like she knew her God would give her a free ticket to heaven for this. Not to mention the racism and sexism that she apparently wasn't aware of. I don't want to be unfair to her, I believe her heart was in the right place but I think she still had HUGE racial bias and deep down she still thought of them more like wild animals. Ugh it was so frustrating to read the parts where she was talking so highly about the white, blonde characters and how she was talking about Topsy like she was a circus freak. 
 Anyways, I love reading about black history so this book gave me a huge perspective on some things. But the writing and the Christianity bullshit, ugh please spare me that bullshit thank you.

I only managed 8 pages before I found myself unable to go on. Stowe's writing was very realistic and I suspect that if I could stomach the storyline I'd have appreciated what she had to say. Unfortunately I just wasn't in the mood to read a book depicting the realities of slavery. It annoyed the hell out of me and I'm not exactly sure why, as it's something that I'm used to reading about in fiction and in slave narratives. Maybe it was the non critical light that it shone on the practice that aggravated me, or maybe it's the right book, but the wrong time. I'm sure I'll give in another try in my lifetime, but not for a long while. 
 Rating? For what the book accomplished, 5 stars. For the quality of writing and story, probably 3 or 4. But for my personal enjoyment, which is how I rate my books, I can only give it 1 star.

Harriet Beecher Stowen klassikkoteos on selkea orjuudenvastainen aateromaani, joka otti jyrkasti kantaa orjuuteen Yhdysvalloissa. 
 Romaanin keskeinen hahmo on Tuomo eli Tom. Han on oikeamielinen ja jeesushahmoinen uhrautuja. Vaikka hanen ruumiinsa onkin toisten omaisuutta, Raamattu ja odottava paratiisi auttavat kestamaan. 
 Kertomus saa alkunsa, kun nahjusmaiseisen Shelbyn rappiotilan liepeilla alkavat korppikotka pyoria, yhtena pahimmista Simon Legree, joka on kuin pahuuden ruumiillistuma. Hanessa tiivistyvat kaikki julman ihmispedon paheet. Ne koituvatkin lopulta Tuomon kohtaloksi. 
 Lukija saa siis seurata oikeamielisen ja raamattuun turvaavan fiksun orjien johtajan tuhoutumista oman vakaumuksensa vuoksi. Pikku hiljaa Legreen kynsiin joutunut Tuomo kohtaa vaajaamattoman karun kohtalonsa. 
 Romaanissa on rinnakkaisjuoni, jossa Yrjo eli George Harris lahtee lipettiin ilkealta omistajaltaan, tavoitteena ihanteellinen Kanada, jossa pahaa orjuutta ei ole. Shelby-vetelys menettaa kiristyksen vuoksi kunnon orjansa Elisa ja taman pojan, joka on Yrjon esikoinen. 
 Niin kuin kunnon jannareissa on tapana, pahikset yrittavat saada karkulaisaidin ja pojan kiinni. Hekin lahtivat kohti Kanadaa ja Yrjon peraan. 
 Loppujen lopuksi Tuomo tapaa ennen kuolemaansa Simon Legreen luona Elisa aidin, jolta saa tietaa tyttaren olevan elossa, eli nyt aiti lahtee tyttarensa, tyttaren miehen ja lapsenlapsensa jaljille...

I read this during a college break in anticipation of a Civil War history course I was going to be taking the next semester. It is a real page turner and aside from some of the sentimentality, it has a real modern style.

book_b.title: Madame Bovary
book_b.user_review:
Oh, how I wanted to love this book. I enjoy the classics, and thought this one would be right up my street. How wrong I was. 
 The story concerns Emma Bovary - an incredibly selfish and unlikeable woman. She married the mild mannered Charles, but it's not long before she's cheating on him - he just doesn't give her any excitement, so she constantly seeks it elsewhere. In addition to her unfaithfulness, she also spends his money without thinking twice about it. 
 Also, while I like descriptive prose, this book is bogged down by it. It felt like on every single page there was a descriptive passage about the setting for that scene. 
 Sorry - I know this book has loads of fans, but I certainly won't be joining their ranks.

sample_reviews.review_text:
After giving it some thought, I decided that the book is a classic not because of the story and characters, but rather in spite of them. Although the characters are insipid, vain, pompous, silly, ignorant, grasping, dishonest, and self-important (yes, all of them) and the story chronicles their unintelligent flailing about into melodrama, vice, and bungling, Flaubert employed such a witty and realistically descriptive voice (and was the first writer to employ that level of realism in his descriptions, evidently) that the book is not a dime-store bodice ripper but rather a literary masterpiece. 
 {Read my full review here}

Wow what can I say I pushed through this hoping that it would get better but I should have just stopped at chapter 2. Sorry all you fans it just didnt move me. I think it was to winny for me. I like a female lead with a little more strength.

Henry James once said, "Madame Bovary has a perfection that not only stamps it, but that makes it stand almost alone; it holds itself with such a supreme unapproachable assurance as both excites and defies judgment." 
 That's right. Defies judgment. 
 I don't know... he looks kind of judgy to me... 
 Unfortunately, I had to read a translation as my French is nowhere near good enough to read the original. Though I am assured that the prose in the original French are amazing and inspiring. 
 I can certainly appreciate the characterization and story-telling ability but I personally struggled with the story as I reconciled what Flaubert seemed to be saying about society, women, women who had affairs, men and romance. 
 Now, I would like to take a moment to quote Manny's Review, since he is the one who convinced me to read this book in the first place. 
 "Flaubert makes no obvious attempt to judge Emma..." 
 No, Flaubert doesn't break up his beautiful prose at any point with, "So whilst that is a very nice tree, I would like to intrude and mention that Emma is, like, a total ho! So, now back to the tree..." 
 I feel he doesn't do this because that would be superfluous. In fact, it seems to me that he doesn't stop judging through this entire book. 
 [image error] 
 The judgement is like looking at vacation photos of a ninja family. You can't see it but you know it's there. 
 Why else would Flaubert so meticulously describe and relish in Emma's fall from grace? Every little detail is mentioned with the same eagerness as a kid dobbing in their little brother. He puts together a file of evidence for her complicity, a smoking gun as you'd say, and leaves it up to us to point the finger. 
 -She immediately decides after her wedding night that she doesn't love Charles. 
 -She then sets about creating her own misery by obsessing and romanticizing this unhappiness until it consumes her. 
 -She goes from a productive and proficient housewife to a morose, unrelenting mess. 
 -She quickly begins despising Charles and blaming him for everything while he dotes on her and grows increasingly content. 
 -Her home quickly falls into a state of shabbiness. 
 -Her daughter goes neglected. 
 -Her first romance uses her unforgivably but is eventually driven away by her incessant neediness and demands. 
 -Her second romance, whilst more earnest in his affections, is also driven away by her incessant neediness, deteriorating mental health and demands. 
 -She drives her husband into bankruptcy. 
 -Commits suicide to escape it all. 
 -Her husband falls into despair, neglects their child and quickly dies. 
 -The child ends up working in a cotton factory. 
 What would a child do working in a cotton factory, you ask? 
 Oh, just a little mill-scavenging. Their job was to crawl under the huge, spinning WHEELS OF DEATH to pick up the spare bits of cotton. They were not allowed to sit, rest, or take a break while the mill ran - which was always except for Sunday when they cleaned the huge, spinning WHEELS OF DEATH that caused these children to live in a constant state of grief and terror 
 Well, doesn't that just cheer you up! 
 The entire story arc and every unnecessary tidbit condemns Emma like one more nail in the coffin. Society is condemned, men are condemned, romantic idealism is condemned. Really, this novel thinks everyone is to blame. What is this novel's answer to it? It seems to be saying, "Well, that silly woman had so much and she threw it all away and look at her now, kids. She's dead! And poor, which is really much worse." 
 The novel seems to step back and tsk at Emma, saying that she had so much. A safe and comfortable home, a good husband who doted on her and she just couldn't be happy with that. 
 Then it looks at society and says, "Well, you created this and now you've helped destroy her too, you assholes!" 
 It shakes its head at Charles and says, "You weren't strong enough to keep her in line and then you pined over this worthless woman to the ruinment of your only child." 
 But I wonder what this book would have been if Emma hadn't been a victim to everyone and every circumstance except for Charles. I wonder what this book would have been like if it displayed a far more realistic approach to a woman having an affair and her reasons. Because, let's face it, this book's depiction of a woman and why she has extra-marital relations is very obtuse. Emma's life and situation is hardly the common for women who seek more out of life. This book makes her quest for more seem silly, unneccessary and ungrateful. 
 Most of all, I wonder what this novel would have been like if it had dealt with Emma as a real character. One who didn't need to be mostly insane to justify having an affair. One who wasn't both stupid and entitled and didn't lose all her money through a lack of self-control and ability to take five seconds to do the math. One who was capable of growing and learning from life. 
 Unfortunately all that is lost. Even in the end, Emma learnt nothing. All sound and fury. Signifying nothing. 
 Much like this novel. 
 My final criticism about this book... 
 This was a book about people gettin' it on... 
 AND THERE WAS NO SEX! 
 [image error] 
 Curse you, Flaubert! Curse you!
Another college read that kept my attention.

I read this book when I was a teenager and thought it was lofty and romantic. I read it as an adult, and thought it was completely ridiculous. I think Flaubert intended it to be ridiculous. A story about the excesses of materialism and the shallown nature of aquisitiveness. Paris and her ilk would really get a lot out of it.

Of course, two stars was my senior-year-of-high-school rating, for which I was one of two people - me and my best friend - who chose it over War and Peace or some such, so we just read (/talked) out in the hallway. It therefore needs a serious reread.

This story had a very dramatic main character. Many of the other characters were very static, but the drama that Madame Bovary for the most part brought on herself kept the story going. Glad I read it, but I also found that I disliked most of the people in the story.

2.5 stars. It's unfortunate that I find such an important and influential novel to be so slow. To be sure, Flaubert's attention to detail is precise, and his writing can be brilliant. But I found these details to be as excessive as the romantic flights of fancy that he mocks in Madame Bovary's life, just excessive in a different way. That is to say, Flaubert's verbal mise-en-scene can be overwhelming at times, much in the same way that a romantic work might be overwhelming in sentiment. The plot itself was no frills: a bored middle class housewife with romantic dreams of a better life has several affairs to spice up her life. Perhaps we have Flaubert to blame for making such a plot so common? In any case, straight-forward plot combined with the droning descriptions of the details of everyday life made this a slog for me. 
 Indeed, this was the third time I had attempted reading Madame Bovary. First, as a teenager, I didn't make it past the first thirty pages. In my twenties, I didn't make it much further. This is the first time I was able to make my way through the book. What kept me reading was that occasionally Flaubert would deliver these lines that would bowl me over. Example: "When she went to confession, she invented small sins in order to stay there longer, kneeling in the shadows with her hands together and her face against the grating, beneath the whisperings of the priest. The metaphors of betrothed, spouse, heavenly lover, marriage everlasting, that recur in sermons, awoke in the depths of her soul an unlooked-for delight." Those types of brief insights and beautifully conveyed ideas would keep me turning pages, even though this was not the most enjoyable novel for me to read. Much like Sentimental Education, which I found just slightly more tolerable, I felt equal parts frustration (in the novel) and awe (in Flaubert's writing), but never much joy in the reading experience.
Is there something wrong with for not really liking this book?

This is a hard one to review. I loved Flaubert's way of describing things, but I didn't love the fact that he looks at all his characters (maybe except little Berta) with discernible irony. Well - that's the hard thing - the irony IS, on one hand, enjoyable, but on the other - how to feel sympathy for wholly ridiculous people? But, it is the most colourful sociological ouevre I've ever read.

reference_books.title: Carter Finally Gets It (Carter Finally Gets It, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Will Carter, known to his friends as Carter, is a thirteen going on fourteen year old. That means he's going into HIGH SCHOOL! This is his chance - he will get jacked! He will be the best at every sport, and be the total ladies man. He is going to become the definition of Mr. Smooth with a few, okay a lot of bumps on the way. Hands down one of the funniest YA novels I have ever read. I listened to it on audiobook with Nick Podehl's genius impersonation of a young teenage boy. After Will Grayson, I can absolutely say I love this narrator, and I love this book!

reference_books.title: The Kitchen Counter Cooking School: How a Few Simple Lessons Transformed Nine Culinary Novices into Fearless Home Cooks
reference_books.review_text:
This book is perfect for anyone who has an innate fear of cooking. It provides enough basic tips and recipes that allows the reader to feel more comfortable when tackling everyday meals. The author also touches upon the problems with processed foods and grocery store layouts, giving a brief glimpse into the cruel and ruthless world of big food chains. Armed with a team of culinary experts, this author shows that cooking real food at home is not only a possibility but a necessity. 
 This is definitely one that I will recommend to everyone I know.

reference_books.title: The Adventures of Captain Underpants (Captain Underpants, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Words cannot express how thankful I am that Dav Pilky chose writing books as a career. The man is a comic genius and has kids in stitches from his Dumb Bunnies to his Silly Gooses to his Captain Underpants and Ricky Ricotta. He remains one of the funniest children's authors up there with Jon Sczieska and Mo Willems. 
 Kids and I'm sure some adults like myself cannot get enough of the two boys' antics and their mean principal turned super-awesome superhero, Captain Underpants. Though the toilet jokes and bad spelling may perturb some parents, it is obvious that this author knows how to get kids to read and want to keep reading all of the adventures.

reference_books.title: Paperboy
reference_books.review_text:
A boy growing up in 1959 Memphis takes over a paper route for his friend. At the end of each week, he must collect money from all the neighbors. It seems like an easy feat, except there's one problem. He stutters. Sometimes, he just can't get the words out. Most of the time, he can't even say his own name. 
 What an exquisite piece of literature. I am normally not a fan of historical fiction, but this story is so gripping. You fall in love with all the characters, and you really get to understand the time period. For instance, the boy questions why Mam, his family's maid, can't sit in the front of the bus or get her picture taken at the zoo with him. A few times, he talks about the concept of segregation. 
 Apart from these types of incidences, through the relationships he forms with the neighbors, he also encounters alcoholism and murder. He finds a birth certificate that changes his view of his father forever. There are many layers to this story which gives it depth and meaning. It's never just about one issue; just like real life, he deals with a multiple number of challenging situations. 
 I read this book directly after Wonder by R.J. Palacio. Both could be used as a class book for late elementary, early middle. Both could be considered classics one day. It will be interesting to see in the future which books stand the test of time, and which don't. I do believe, however, that this particular tale will. It's just that good.

reference_books.title: Cardboard
reference_books.review_text:
Unable to afford a gift for his son's birthday, Cam's dad buys a cardboard box for 78 cents. The seller tells him there are two rules that he must follow - any scraps must be returned to the seller, and he cannot ask for any more. Dad and son create a boxer out of cardboard that comes to life. When the kid next door sees the cardboard man, he wants one of his own and steals some of the pieces. Pretty soon, all chaos breaks loose as a cardboard world full of cardboard monsters is created. 
 Being a graphic novel, this is a pretty fast read. It's definitely a great book for reluctant readers - it's humorous at times and jam packed with action. It is sentimental, but not to the extreme. Many kids could relate to the relationships Cam has with his Dad and Marcus.

sample_reviews.review_text: I think is very similar to fifty shades of grey. Not a great book. Fifty shades is much better
Gave up at 73%. I just couldn't take any more of the whining!

I tried with this one, I really did, but when I got to the part where she describes anal sex as "anal play" I lost it. Anal play? Were there anal hooks or inflatable butt plugs? No. Fisting? No. Not anal play. The way she wrote about BDSM was so naive that I wondered if she'd ever actually encountered the scene. Why are these books so popular?! I hated it. HATED IT. Firstly, it was poorly written, had an underdeveloped plot, and was full of stereotypical characters. Secondly, the relationship between the two main characters was unhealthy in every way and the characters did not behave in a way consistent with the types of abuse they suffered. Thirdly, Day shows a lack of vocabulary, technique, ability, and imagination. Fourthly, Eva is exactly the type of woman I despise and therefore could not identify with in the slightest. Finally, the sex itself was inane and cliche. Day actually used "You're so tight", "You're so big", and "It's so good" in the space of two pages. I wrote better sex scenes than that in middle school.

I see many comparisons between this series and the clumsily written 50 Shades bores - actually I checked out the Crossfire series simply out of curiosity, wondering what another author could do with a similar-sounding concept. The Crossfire series is far better written. Granted, it contains an enormous measure of escapism and fantasy (no man like Gideon Cross actually exists outside of daydreams) but that is the point of these guilty pleasures. I was also impressed, and occasionally surprised, by the flashes of insight Ms. Day shows regarding obsessive relationships. Anyone who has ever been caught up in one knows they are destructive, irrational, stressful, and feel better than anything else ever has. The intensity of the relationship is addictive. Ms. Day gets it, or has convinced me that she gets it. Having struggled all my life to conquer my own tendency toward jealousy, I found something in common with Eva. So, a pleasant surprise with the Crossfire series. I was expecting little more than standard wish-fulfillment erotica and I got something rather smarter . . . but still with plenty of erotica. Nothing wrong with that!
Not bad, I didn't have to skip a lot like I did with fifty shades of grey, but the story is really similiar to FSOG.

Eva acaba de se mudar para Nova York, com seu amigo Cary, conseguindo um emprego em uma grande agencia de publicidade. Ela quer se sentir livre, comecar uma vida nova, sem estar a sobra do padrasto e da mae, alcancando suas proprias conquistas. E logo de cara conhece Gideon Cross, um famoso e bem sucedido empresario, e ambos sentem uma atracao irrefreavel logo de cara. O que Eva mais gostaria era se entregar a essa paixao tao forte, mas as coisas comecam a tomar proporcoes inacreditaveis muito rapido, e ela sabe que isso pode nao acabar bem. Gideon sabe que quer Eva, de uma maneira tao profunda e possessiva que ele mesmo nao se reconhece. O relacionamento deles comeca repleto de paixao e luxuria, mas fantasmas do passado atormentam ambos, e torna o relacionamento deles exponencialmente perigoso. 
 "He was the kind of guy that made a woman want to rip his shirt open and watch the buttons scatter along with her inhibitions." 
 A explosao de "Cinquenta tons de Cinza" trouxe uma onda de livros adultos, e Crossfire foi um deles. Um romance bastante erotico, que conquistou milhares de fas no mundo todo. Algo que tenho encontrado bastante em livros adultos atualmente e aquele comeco forcado, instalust. Adicione um CEO milionario e uma jovem inocente e... nao, espera. Nesse livro a historia e um pouco diferente. Eva nao e uma jovem puritana e inexperiente. E uma mulher que ja teve sua fase de rebeldia, seus momentos de luxuria. Sabemos que algo em sua vida a levou a uma fase de total descontrole. Nao sabemos muito sobre Gideon, publicamente ele e um notorio conquistador, visto com mulheres diferentes a cada semana, mas e um homem frio e reservado, pouco se sabe sobre sua vida pessoal. 
 "B.O.B. and I have a longtime understanding - when we're done with each other, we know exactly which one of us has been used, and it isn't me. Good night Gideon." 
 Comecei a ler o livro sem muitas expectativas. O plot misterioso-CEO-bilionario ja esta se tornando comum, mas nao e algo que me faca nao ler um livro. O maior diferencial desse, e um dos pontos positivos em relacao a grande maioria dos romances adultos da atualidade, e a protagonista: Eva Tramell. O livro e, em sua maioria, um romance erotico, e contem vocabulario bastante pesado, mas isso e uma caracteristica da serie. O passado dos protagonistas, que a principio desconhecemos, foi uma das razoes pelas quais gostei bastante do livro, e um misterio bastante intenso, que ajuda a compor uma historia mais interessante. Confesso que nao gostei tanto do livro, o comeco forcado, que ja citei, me desanima bastante, mas fico feliz por ter continuado a ler a serie, pois o segundo livro me agradou muito mais. Uma das coisas que tambem mais me agradaram no livro foi o romance, o sentimento tao forte, capaz de enfrentar inumeras dificuldades em prol do relacionamento. Os traumas e "demonios interiores" dos personagens foram muito bem trabalhados, e confesso que me surpreendi bastante com o caminho que a autora seguiu. Recomendo a quem gosta de romances adultos, bastante intensos, e nao se incomodem com vocabulario bastante pesado. 
 "I can let you in, Eva. I'm trying. But your first response when I screw up is to run away. You do it every time and I can't stand feeling like any moment I'm going to do or say something wrong and you're going to bolt." 
 Ja li os tres primeiros livros da serie, e em breve serao postadas as resenhas do segundo (Profundamente sua / Reflected in you) e terceiro (Para sempre sua / Entwined with you) aqui no The Serial Reader. 
 "What the hell are they in love with when they don't know how fucked up I am? If that's love, it's nothing compared to what I feel for you." 
 3.5/5 
 Love always, 
 Francielle 
 http://www.theserialreader.com/2013/0...

Not what I expected. I've seen many reviews comparing this book to 50 shades, (which I loved) I see some similar things, like some dom/sub action staring to come out, and sexual abuse. But this couple is very different. Eva has fought her way to being strong and Gideon has tried to move on with his life to be somewhat normal. The path for these two is so different I really hate to compare to the other book. Looking forward to seeing them work on the relationship. Can it work..will they make it and the supporting cast of characters , what will happen to them? Wish the price was lower..very expensive for a e-book.
Both Eva and Gideon have pasts that effect their present and while they are intimate, both struggle to keep the past from effecting their now.
Just another Fifty Shades of Grey :(

I'm ashamed to actually admit that I read all 4. Let me explain it though, I don't know about most of you but I'm the kind of person that will read it until the end even if I don't like it. Having said that, I really hated it! -.- I thought it was cringe worthy in parts (I laugh when I think about it), and soooo cheesy! I mean I was rolling my eyes at least 40% of the time (Specially during the 4th book). 
 Nevertheless I will probably read the last one (shame shame shame on me) but I will complain my whole way thru it.

book_b.title: Mary Poppins (Mary Poppins, #1)
book_b.user_review: OK, so Mary Poppins isn't exactly the rosy cheeked woman with the cheery disposition that we all know and love from the Disney version. In fact, she's kind of a B. The adventures are quasi-fun, but her attitude kind of puts a damper on things. She's just really mean.

sample_reviews.review_text: It's a series of short stories with adventures with Mary Poppins which is...pretty boring. I knew it wasn't going to be like the movie but Mary is hard to like and relate to, as well as most of the characters because they aren't developed. It jumps from one adventure to the next and it just wasn't very captivating. Just kinda meh.
I couldn't finish it. It really is a children's book...and not one you can read for the first time if you're already an adult. And Mary Poppins comes across as a snobby bitch to me.

Mary Poppins is one of my favourite films. Growing up I watched it a million times--or at least I feel like I watched it a million times. It was fun, and beyond imaginative, with a soundtrack I can still sing word for word. Mary Poppins was awesome and I remember being so enraptured by her. She had a bottomless purse! Her medicine tasted like candy and changed colours! She had friends who had tea while sitting on the ceiling! She could travel to other world's through artwork and she taught me one the longest words I've ever known: Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious! 
 So needless to say I was expecting something similar from the book, and I was left pretty disappointed. In the book--the inspiration for the film--Mary is self absorbed and rude. And not in any way that was remotely funny or endearing, well at least not to me. I mean I know she said " She was practically perfect in every way," but when Julie Andrews said it I smiled, in the book her vanity was irritating: 
 Marry sighed with pleasure, however, when she saw three of herself, each wearing a blue coat with silver buttons and a blue hat to match. She thought it was such a lovely sight that she wished there had been a dozen of her or even thirty. The more Mary Poppinses the better. 
 "I wish we were invisible," said Michael, when Mary Poppins had told him that the very sight of him was more than any self-respecting person could be expected to stand. 
 But the winter afternoons, she knew, were short, and they had to be home by tea time. So with a sigh she wrenched herself away from her glorious reflection. 
 Blah. If I could compare this to another children's book--but a book that got it right, it would be Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. That book was filled with wonder, great characters in both film (I prefer the 1971 version) and book format. I know not every children's book has to have loveable characters, but I'll put it this way, if I read the book first, I probably wouldn't have had any interest in seeing the film. I don't think I'll read the second book in the series either, since I could barely get into the first.
I'm sad I didn't like it that much. I just ended up preferring the movie to the book? I didn't like book-Mary as much as movie-Mary.
Mary Poppins seems much more selfish and hard-hearted than I expected, but she was written in a different time, and I am a product of my own.
I liked what I read and I really need to finish it I think...
I did not like this book.
Everyone's going to shoot me, but I love the movie more. *hides*
What a craggy character. Mary was completely UNLIKABLE. So disappointed.
Mary Poppins is mean. Lots of fantastical stuff; not much relation to movie.

reference_books.title: The Likeness (Dublin Murder Squad, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Another audio review--this had a great female reader, who did an incredible job of conveying many different (mostly male) characters' voices. 
 I keep going back and forth between three and four stars for this one. Ultimately, I liked it slightly better than her first mystery, "In the Woods." Like in that book, she starts with a compelling scenario--a detective discovers a body of a woman who looks exactly like her and is carrying ID with the detective's undercover identity. However, she seemed to throw out blessedly fewer red herrings in this one and wrap up the loose ends much more effectively. I also liked the focus on Cassie in this book. Ultimately, the ultimate revelation/confession scene really needed a tighter edit--it went on seemingly forever. But I thought this was a strong follow-up overall.

reference_books.title: Crime and Punishment
reference_books.review_text: I struggled a bit to get through this (admittedly it's not a summer read), and, I don't know that I had the best translation of the book. Still, there were certain parts I couldn't put down. This is a remarkable combination of a psychological thriller, a survey of ideologies, and character study.

reference_books.title: The Chaperone
reference_books.review_text: I listened to the audio version (narrated by Elizabeth McGovern, aka Cora from Downton Abbey) and she did a fantastic job (save for the German handyman, who sounded a little too much like Schwartzenegger at times). Made me want to watch a Louise Brooks film.

reference_books.title: Where'd You Go, Bernadette
reference_books.review_text:
I listened to the audio version. All in all, an engaging and surprisingly poignant satire that made a long road trip go quickly -- I'd say closer to 3-1/2 stars than 3. I thought a few of the plot twists (i.e., Sue Lynn's pregnancy) were unnecessary and distracting. But overall, it's a fun, quick read. 
 The audio reader was very good, but the performance could have used a sound editor or better sound engineering. Whispers came across as whispers, and yelling as yelling, which made me constantly have to adjust the volume up and down as we listened.

reference_books.title: Freedom
reference_books.review_text: Sometimes I think I'm a misanthrope. Then I read Franzen and think, Not even close. I love his writing and think no one captures details or fleshes out his characters as well as he does. But, dang. This one is tough to get through while retaining a sunny disposition.

book_a.title: Storm Front (The Dresden Files, #1)
book_a.user_review: "Hells bells." Super easy, fun read. The writing made me roll my eyes at times. But what's not to like about a noirish private eye who's also a wizard?

sample_reviews.review_text:
Is there any more fun, snarky Chicago wizard book than Dresden? 
 No way. 
 The whole Dresden files books are right up there with the Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy as being fun, fun, fun. 
 My teenaged daughter picked them up, and now she's racing through the series. 
 I can't wait until I forget them, so I can read them again. 
 By the way, the TV show stunk and was nothing like the books. It deserved to be killed after one season, but the same can't be said for the books. 
 Awesome!

I can't be sure if I my ambivalence towards this is due to the bleurgh audiobook narrator (he read the entire thing like it was some tired, lazy film noir), a hatred of the first person narration/narrator, or the plot and characterization which were completely submerged in the male gaze. 
 Do not recommend.

Hard-boiled detective that's a wizard! 
 Unfortunately, it didn't really gel for me. Must be successful, due to the number of sequels, but I didn't really buy either the premise or the characters.
What can I say; sometimes I just need some brain candy. Quick, light, fun, and problematic in places, but excellent for reading on the train.

Eug. The Dresden files annoy me so much. The main male character is a Gary Stu with unbelievable god-like powers, and he's a perv., because he ends up screwing his female assistant/student, who is a) waaay younger than him b) his own bloody student, which means there's a seriously nasty power imbalance. 
 I do like his dog, but I strongly dislike almost all of the characters and their interactions.
Nothing original in the world building or characters. A good, quick, popcorn book. I'll try the next one.

The world-building of Storm Front is top-notch--it doesn't even feel like the first in a series, the milieu is so fully realized--but Butcher's tendency toward "tell, don't show" characterizations and the tiresome cliche of Dresden himself make this a bit of a disappointment anyway.
Very entertaining mix of noir and fantasy. Fans of the TV series "Angel" might be especially interested.
The recent infatuation with the twilight series really spoiled vampires for me. It's nice to read something this exquisite and actually thrilling in this genre again.

Let me start by saying the Dresden Files series is probably my favorite series EVER (to date). That being said, I almost quit before I started based on Storm Front, the first published novel by Jim Butcher and the first Dresden novel. The rough edges of a fledgling novelist really show in this book making it a mediocre story at best IMO. Thankfully I kept reading and though book 2 (Fool Moon) was still pretty weak Butcher's writing was clearly showing signs of maturing. Book 3 was very good and by book four I was hooked. I have never looked back. 
 You have to read Storm Front to get the full Dresden background history and character introduction but I urge you not to base your opinion of Jim Butcher or The Dresden Files series on this book. I promise, if you make it to book three you will be happy you stuck it out. 
 WW

book_b.title: Prep
book_b.user_review:
** spoiler alert ** 
 This is one of those books where I got through it about halfway, was tempted to give up on it because it was too depressing, angst-ridden, and uninteresting. Still, I soldiered on, thinking I had already invested time in it, and maybe--who knows?--the self-loathing, judgmental, and utterly passionless protagonist would learn something, discover something about herself, grow, change, etc. 
 SPOILER: Nah, that didn't happen. Other than a few nice moments and observations, it's not worth finishing.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I recently read this for an encyclopedia entry I was writing on post-2000 coming-of-age novels, so my assessment, I fear, isn't really fair. On the one hand, I think Sittenfeld is a very talented writer, but on the other, I kept wanting to say GTFU (you know, grow the *#^$ up), which seems very, very ungenerous of me. In the end, I can appreciate what attracted people to this book, making it a surprise success. That doesn't mean the book sticks with me or changed my life in any drastic way---and isn't that what we crave from a novel? I guess the lesson I learned from writing the entry is that WAY too many of us authors (if I may call myself that) go the C-of-Age route early in life. If we're lucky, we mature to recognize that adolescence isn't the be-all, end-all of our lives---despite what the culture tells us about clinging to youth. I want adult books, and I want to say to Curtis, please, please, after THE MAN OF MY DREAMS (the follow up to PREP), take a risk, look beyond your own experience, imagine someone who's not a 16-28 year old girl/woman struggling with place/parental affection/identity, and write me a magnum opus about---oh, I don't know---exploited sugar cane workers in South Florida. 
 Then again, who am I to ask such a thing of an author?

The San Francisco Chronicle says about Prep, "[It] conveys the inner world of an entirely typical teenage girl with remarkable warmth. One of the most tender and accurate portraits of adolescence in recent memory." I would have to agree. I can't remember a book I've read recently or maybe ever for that matter that transported me back to my high schools days as much as Prep did. And I mean that in a good way. Although the main plot line (a 14-year old girl who decides to go to a private boarding school rather than public school) isn't all that typical, the life she lives within that boarding school is. Sittenfeld's writing is excellent. She puts you inside the head of a typical teenage girl, and you just can't get out. 
 From the memories of the great day with her secret crush to watching the queen-bee and wanna-be's, Sittenfeld includes everything to make you feel like you're living through high school all over again. I laughed out loud numerous times as I remember having so many of the same feelings that Lee (main character) has. You grow up as she does and feel for her as she just tries to make it through another day without screwing up. 
 Overall I really enjoyed this book. I was getting ready to tell my parents that my 15-year sister had to read it. And that all ended when I got to chapter 8: Kissing and Kissing. For me, the chapter was completely unnecessary and ruined any chance that I could recommend the book to anyone and feel okay about it because of the descriptive love scenes, especially not my 15-year old sister. 
 Even with chapter eight included, I still really enjoyed this book, and Sittenfeld ends it out well. I would recommend it to anyone that likes good writing and well really anyone could read this. Just realize this recommendation comes along with my forewarning about chapter eight. If not for that one chapter, I would have easily given it 5 stars.
The main character in this book is beyond annoying. She never changes during the whole course of the novel. I can't believe I made it through the whole book.

I hated the lead character (she doesn't really deserve the title "protagonist") so much that I was unable to enjoy any part of this book. This is not a character you love to hate; she's a character you hate. And hate. And hate. She doesn't grow as a person, doesn't learn from her mistakes, and generally sits there like a bump on a log throughout the whole book. She's a perfect example of the "new protagonist" so adored by Stephenie Meyer and her ilk - a girl with no personality and nothing to recommend her. Do yourself a favor and just skip it.

3-5-2005: Curtis graduated from Groton in the 90s. Supposedly this novel is not autobiographical, but the descriptions of the school are so clear that it's hard to separate fact from fiction. A disturbing book, even if it weren't about Groton: Lee Fiora, a scholarship girl from Iowa, is highly self-conscious and terrified of not fitting in. She moves through four years at the Ault School without ever seeming to understand herself or her environment. She doesn't seem to move forward or develop. Plus the school seems so heartless, all of the students so obsessed with coolness; what is Sittenfeld trying to show? Lee is so unsympathetic a character that it's hard to bond with her, and many other characters are two-dimensional. Frustrating book for a number of reasons. Though clearly I'm biased. It has certainly been highly praised, so I must be missing something. I will need to read this book again someday....
I only kept reading until the end because I hoped the main character would be hit by a bus. She wasn't.
Ok. I don't think I'll ever read it again. Highschool was not super for me, as it is not super for the main character in this book. The writing was good.
Loved, loved, loved this book!

The main character's awkwardness was eerily like my awkwardness in college, so I can't really give this an objective review. While I was reading it I was also sad that I would never have the experience of reading it for the first time agin.

After reading the American Wife, this book was a huge disappointment. I kept hoping it would get better, but when it ended I was so glad. 
 All I wanted was for the main character, Lee to grow or mature over the four years she was in high school. She does not. She is the same shy, anxious, self conscious girl from the day she enters the school to the day she graduates. Things change around her, but she doesn't. So I am sitting on an airplane thinking, 'Why do I care about this girl's story?' People are suppose to evolve, events are supposed to change a person..... but not this main character. Lee truly cares about no one, including herself. 
 One of the discussion questions asks how Lee's high school experience relates to my own. While I could relate to the lack of confidence, the rest was so unbelievable.

reference_books.title: If You Were Here
reference_books.review_text:
LOVED LOVED LOVED IT! 
 Just as I did with her memoirs, I found myself laughing like crazy throughout If You Were Here. For any Jen Lancaster fans, run (don't walk!) to get this book!

reference_books.title: Hungry Heart: Adventures in Life, Love, and Writing
reference_books.review_text:
Whenever I finish a book, I am usually good about jumping on the computer the same day and posting a review, or at least my rating. With this book, I had to take a while and noodle it over. On one hand the book felt like a good read...but the other hand had this nagging doubt that I couldn't put my finger on. 
 I am a fan of Good in Bed, and I have read a couple of other books of Weiner's and enjoyed them. I have quite a few sitting on my bookshelves at home that I need to read (one day...). I also enjoy reading the snarky tweets of The Bachelor series she does, even though I don't watch the show. It's also interesting to see what is going on in the world of publishing that she brings attention to that someone like me would only assume. Picking up this novel after seeing her promoting it, I thought it would be a great insight into her mind. 
 Enter a collection of essays on her life, that for some reason are not told in order. They mostly are, but a few times the timeline bounces around and I thought to myself, "oh we are going back to that again? Ok...." I went along for the ride though, because Weiner is a great storyteller (and isn't shy of saying so quite a few times throughout the book). Stories about her childhood. Stories about her mom. Grandma. Sister. We all have them and I am a sucker for them. As we progress we see how the relationships change all due to her father's spiral down and her feelings on them. We read about how Good In Bed came to be. How she found her agent and publisher. How In Her Shoes was a great novel but a not-so-well-received movie. We also read about her Twitter life and her relationships. (Be cautious with the miscarriage section as it can be quite graphic). 
 So why was I so hesitant to jump online and boast about this? I love reading these types of stories - just look at Marian Keyes and Lauren Graham - love them! 
 But Jennifer Weiner? Errrr...I just felt there were parts that were hypocritical and/or rubbed me the wrong way. 
 In the chapters about her tweets, she spoke of Joan Didion's dog and explained how she saw an author who capitalized on tragedy in order to sell books. Uhhhhh....ummmm...isn't that what this whole novel is? Didn't you just explain earlier in the book how Good In Bed was based on your feelings and experiences in your life? Didn't you just explain earlier in the book how Little Earthquakes came to be after your stressful delivery and caring for a newborn? Isn't the whole premise about this book capitalizing on your tragedies to sell a book? Sooooo then shouldn't your dogs be worried about you? Your family? 
 Then there was the section about her dad and how he made the news when a girlfriend of his ripped his *ahem* groin area open where he needed stitches. She made reference to the fact that because of their last name, a lot of news stations and people like Jay Leno picked up the story and used it for jokes. That's all well and good, until Weiner begins to complain about how it made her feel. Don't they realize that he has a family and his children are reading these things people are saying? What's good for the goose, isn't good for the gander for her, because she has no problems skewering the contestants on the reality tv shows she watches and live tweets about. Making fun of people who may not have the best grammar. Making fun of people for how they dress, what they say what they do...I love a good snarky read, as I do judge people, but I'm honest about it. Don't cry a river when people make fun of you, if you just turn around and do it to others. 
 Little things like that really stuck out in this book, and I found myself saying "but wait...didn't you say xyz earlier in the book?" And because of that, I just can't recommend this. But if you're a fan of Weiner's books and tweets, then by all means pick this up (hey look! I recommended it after all! Must be contagious...)

reference_books.title: Twisted Sisters
reference_books.review_text: I'm so disappointed in this book. I always want to love Lancaster's books regardless, but it was too difficult with this one. I never connected to any character, and felt like the premise of the book finally happened in the last 20 pages. Unlike the stuff I've read from her before there were too many "pop-culture" references that took me out of the story and 1 dimensional characters that I forgot about 30 seconds after I read about them. Wish I could feel differently. I still remember staying up nights to finish her stories. I hope those days aren't behind me.

reference_books.title: Look Again
reference_books.review_text: I loved this book! Although the ending was very predictable, the book held my attention throughout, from beginning to end. I found myself staying up late and bringing the book to work to read whenever I could. I hated certain characters, and felt for others - truely a mark of a great writer when you can connect to the story in such a way. I will be looking for other books from Lisa Scottoline now!

reference_books.title: If I Stay (If I Stay, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Yet again, here's another book that was very popular amongst my reading group friends that I was excited to read. And it left me feeling flat. I wanted to like it. I wanted to feel emotional throughout the journey and have my eyes opened. Instead I just kept waiting for...something...I never felt as though I connected to Mia. The flashbacks didn't add to the story for me as I kept wanting to go back to the present and see what was happening there. 
 Everything I felt while reading this has been said by other readers (and in a much more coherent fashion). I didn't feel like the flashbacks added to the plot line. The use of music was irritating to me - we get it author - you like music and can name a bunch of indie bands. Move on. I did not feel like shedding a tear (which speaks volumes given I'm pregnant and crying at anything). And I had to read the end a couple of times to figure out whether she stayed or went (ok THAT I'm chalking up to pregnancy brain!) 
 This just wasn't my cup of tea. I will skip the second book but will try this author again.

book_a.title: The Fault in Our Stars
book_a.user_review: Just not my cup of tea. I couldn't connect to either character and felt nothing at the end. Not for me I guess.

sample_reviews.review_text:
There isn't anything unique about this book. 
 However, there are pretty words and amazing meanings. 
 It's a book that you read quickly, with much emotion, and you'll probably remember forever. 
 And even though it wasn't unique, or magical, it was special and worth the read.
I enjoyed this young adult book with very smart characters who are doomed and suffering from cancer. Still not my favorite in the upcoming Tournament of Books.

Finished re-reading The Fault in Our Stars again today. It was just as tear jerking as I remember it being the first time I read it. It brought back memories of my own trials, triumphs and losses in life. And as I came to the end I had the same reaction as I did the previous time I read it- It's over?! I want more!

Rip my heart, why don't you?! 
 You'll need a tissue box. But read it.

This is a reread and was originally finished August 9th 2012 
 My review got deleted for this but basically the 4 stars stay because it's beautiful, but not giving it 5 stars 
 because the writing is very very flawed.

I admit I read this because my daughter loved it. I mean- really loved it-and very passionately begged me to read it. I enjoy reading books she loves because it gives us so much to discuss. That being said, it was very easy to understand WHY my almost 14 year old daughter loved this story. The character of Hazel is so well written, she is SUCH a teenager, that kids can't help but get her. And add to that the gallant, smart, slightly disrespectful but still nice Augustus Waters. Who wouldn't love this guy?? Even Hazel's parents like him. I know that almost everyone out there has already read and reviewed this, so I won't go into the story, except to say it was wonderful, romantic, funny, and extremely sad. If you haven't already, please read this book as soon as you can. And let me know how you liked it! 
 (and if you have a 14 year old daughter, get her this book)

Originally posted on my blog: www.book-scents.com 
 The Fault in Our Stars is something I've put off reading for forever. The subject matter scared me! Kids and cancer. That is a recipe for heart aching disaster for me and for my heart's sake, I put it off. However, with the movie coming out and all, I wanted to read it before watching it. I mentally braced myself. I started reading, preparing to have my heart ripped out. 
 Now, I don't know if it was the hype or the fact that everyone touts it as a masterpiece, amazing, life changing and all that but... I feel like I didn't have that same connection with it that everyone else did. Which is kind of disappointing to me. I feel like I need to inform: I cry easily. Very easily. I get emotionally invested in all books or movies and I cry during them all the time. I expected to cry. I teared up but I didn't have the gut wrenching sobs I thought I'd go through. I'm not heartless I swear!! The story was sad and touching but I felt disconnected from it. 
 I think one of the main things that made me feel the disconnect was the dialogue. I realize that Augustus Waters is supposed to be witty and funny and clever and everything but I just can't imagine a 17 year old boy talking the way he does. 17 year olds just don't spout eloquent monologues on the spot! Or even craft them ahead of time as beautifully as he did! It just didn't seem plausible and sometimes Augustus and Hazel's dialogue just came off as pretentious to me. Don't get me wrong, Hazel's snark made me smile but most of the time I found myself tilting my head to one side and thinking, "really? did this speech just happen?" 
 I can practically see the mob coming for me now. *hides* Granted, there are amazing quotes from this book. They're poignant and insightful and I love it -- but it really didn't seem natural coming out of a 16 and 17 year old. 
 Maybe the dialogue was what took me out of the story enough that I didn't cry. I'm not sure. I don't know what it is. The story was sad to be sure but this book didn't leave the lasting impression on me that I expected it too.

Once again, I've tried to read it. First time, I made it to about page seven. I didn't even get to the bit on America's Next Top Model. This time, I made it to page nineteen. See, I made progress? To me, from what I read of the book so far and what friends have gushed about to me, Green writes perfect prose -- and he does, the quotes I've read from this book are amazing -- and his characters are teenagers. Teenagers that don't exist. I know that these guys speak and think differently than I do because they had cancer, but I still grew up with teens. Not even the ones who read Green speak like his characters do.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I'd not read that many pages of the book before feeling of wandered into an episode of Dawson's creek, where all the children are supposedly good looking and super smart with their come backs.....now I think of it, didn't one of the gang there die of cancer...maybe that was inspiration? 
 I found the whole thing a little off to be honest...do you go home with a guy you just met, do your parents let you, based solely on the fact he must be ok if he's a cancer survivor too? 
 It seemed to me the oxygen got in way when story needed,but conveniently slipped into background when not. 
 It was fairly obvious from early on that Gus was going to die first, it's just how these things work, though I expected it to be sudden, not a return of his illness. 
 The whole author story wasn't great,and his attempts to become the nice guy laughable. 
 I didn't enjoy this book at all,but I read it to the end so it wasn't too awful...and I don't think I'm the target audience anyway.
I didn't cry, what's wrong with me? I wasn't as connected as most of you, I guess. I liked it...but maybe being a nurse made me relate and understand on a different level. First JG book.

book_b.title: Gossip Girl (Gossip Girl, #1)

 Illustrative quote: "And doesn't she look fucked? I think she's been thoroughly fucked." 
 Ah yes. This is one high-class book.

 Sometimes I read just to see what the kids are reading. I hope to recommend books or to make connections between books. This is not a series with which I can do either. The characters are shallow. They do not always act in character. We learn nothing from their situations. 
 Furthermore, book one ends horribly where an innocent girl is fondled. Her friends save her from the situation, but instead of recognizing the situation as the incredible life-altering experience it is, they decide that the answer is to take the girl home so that she can get some sleep. 
 Think Dynasty, The Kardashians and other characters of that ilk. The one saving grace (maybe?) to this series is that there will be teens interested in it. Gossip Girl says it all.
I expected more from this book. It goes too slowly and I didn't like it much. The TV show is way better...

Normally I don't judge people based on the choice of books they happen to enjoy. But this is an exception, anyone who managed to finish this book without feeling an intense need to put to it down and scream, or at least cringe at certain parts that resemble the Stuff White People Like blog, congratulation, you have a literary taste equivalent to overnight McDonald burgers.
