I like the TV series of the same name; I think it's well-written, and most of the actors do an excellent job with their roles. However, the book (and I assume the whole series of books) is dreadful. It's dreck--horribly written and tedious to read. This is undoubtedly the worst book I have ever read--and I've read a lot of books thus far in my life. I have no idea how this series was made into a TV show. Those producers and people-that-be must have been able to see the glimmer of something good that, when you take away von Ziegesar's horrible, vapid writing, is evident in the idea of what these novels should be.
this was awful. I want my time back.

Super quick, easy read. I expected to be more annoyed with the superficiality of the characters than I was. Very glad it did not take the route of other NYC socialite books that have annoyed me in the past, AHEM Candace Bushnell and Plum Sykes.

I borrowed this digital title from the library since I know there's a TV show out, and I was curious. Why is this a popular series and a popular TV show? I couldn't identify any redeeming qualities about it. A bunch of rich kids being mean to each other. Oh wow, that is fascinating!

Ugh. I read this in a few hours, and it's pretty horrendous. I found a few punctuation mistakes--without looking, which bothers me--like "...Cyrus Rose was a completely annoying, fat, loser." Honestly; that's one of the first things you learn about punctuation. 
 It's a book about a bunch of sixteen- and seventeen-year-old kids who are richer than rich, go to private school in New York, and are, of course, immensely popular. It's written like a cheap fantasy, complete with overt descriptions of the houses, clothes, and everyone's looks. The girls double-kiss everyone on the cheeks for greetings; even the "poor" kids can afford brands like Armani; the kids drink all of the time, everywhere, and never get carded or looked at strangely by adults; one popular girl gets asked to model when she goes to at an art gallery by, of course, two famous gay artists who happen to be brothers; and everyone is barely shocked, much less disgusted, when a senior strips an unwilling freshman naked to the waist to grope her boobs in a bathroom 
 I suppose they'd be an alright series for people who don't read much, but I was just left with a bad taste in my mouth. I've read fanfiction more realistic, complete with Mary Sues.

reference_books.title: The World Until Yesterday: What Can We Learn from Traditional Societies?
reference_books.review_text:
Much of this is material you know: agriculture, state societies, atypical, etc etc. Where Diamond differs is in his unromanticized analysis and recommendations: it's not useful to pretend that we'd be better off as noble savages, but there are important lessons we can (re-)learn about managing risk, pursuing justice, raising children, and living better in our circumstances. Diamond's illustrative anecdotes from his field work in New Guinea are profound and, IMO, helpful. 
 Sadly, this book will never reach policymakers or influencers. So it's up to us to recommend it, discuss its lessons, live by example and hope the next generations pick something up. 
 Oh, and it's slow going but worth toughing out to the end.

reference_books.title: The Omnivore's Dilemma: A Natural History of Four Meals
reference_books.review_text: It's 2010. By now you know about CAFOs, Big Agriculture, and destructive government subsidies. You'll chug DDT before touching HFCS. You think about your food... or you think you do. Is there anything you can learn from Omnivore's Dilemma? Any reason to read it? Well, yes. Do you know the carbon-sequestering adaptation that makes corn so efficient? Why the "NPK mentality" is so (seductively) dangerous? What about alternatives: what does "organic" mean? There may be much in here that you already know, but I'm confident that there's much you don't. More importantly, this is stuff we need to be reminded of, stuff we need to think about regularly.

reference_books.review_text: It felt forced. Obligatory Vonnegut absurdity, but somehow without any real meaning. No character development or growth. Too-frequent "...and then a miracle happens" to move the story.

That's fine for a fable, but in hindsight I was hoping for something more.

sample_reviews.review_text:
some teen books are also great reads for adults and this is not one of them...

Four and a half stars. 
 I'll admit to having high expectations for this book. Perhaps higher than I should have. I've read too many good reviews, had too many friends swear by it. 
 It's good. Very, very good. But through the entire novel I was stuck wondering when it would be more. 
 Don't get me wrong, I loved Speak. Melinda is witty and sarcastic, her narritive has an almost vicious bite to it at times. Her story is undeniably brilliant, masterfully told. The author's characters are genuine and her voice is honest. I read the majority of it in a day, reading through multiple classes. It flows and it's addictive. 
 It's good. Really, really good. But it's not that good. Read the book because it's good. Don't look for a message--the author didn't purposefully write one in {according to the interview in the back}. Don't get your hopes up; be pleasantly surprised rather than wondering what you missed.

8/10 Stars 
 The next time you work on your trees, don't think about trees. Think about love, or hate, or joy, or rage-whatever makes you feel something, makes your palms sweat and your toes curl. Focus on that feeling. When people don't express themselves, they die one piece at a time.

book_b.title: Independent People
book_b.user_review:
Pride. Pride has been the topic of beautiful and deep conversations with friends, some still ongoing. It's a multifaceted word, hard to talk about because of its many meanings. It's also an important and necessary part of the balance we humans must keep. 
 Cruelty. Not a word I'd ever associated with pride, but now I may never be able to look at pride the same way. Some may see Independent People as a book about sheep, or perhaps the Icelandic ethos, or about struggle. I found heartbreak. Some parts hurt to read. Physically hurt. Gut level. And it kept hurting more. 
 Bjartur of Summerhouses wants to be independent. Own his land, be indebted to nobody, be strong. This need, this pride drives him to an isolation that is especially pathetic because he isn't even aware of it. Unseeing, he drives away love and hope and promise. The dumbstruck reader is with him every cruel step of the way. And perhaps, at the end, seeing independence in a different light.

sample_reviews.review_text: This is the book I read when I can't get to sleep.

The back cover description makes this seem like the book that everyone should read if they only pick one for their life. I couldn't finish it. I just couldn't keep doing that to myself. I struggled to reach page 140, and doing another 340-ish pages of the same shit just wasn't on my agenda. I've only quit a book a few other times, and I've enjoyed a few that are full of Romanticism style writing, which can rightfully be called excessive by many... But there is just so much repetition that doesn't seem like anything will come along to change that. 
 And when something does, it's deprived of believable emotion. The main character is kind of an ass... I really dig his drive to attain true freedom, so I put up with it for a while. But anyone that questions him or his thoughts are met with unrelenting criticism and a sour attitude that reminds me of someone that says, "fuck off, I don't want to deal with you. And here's everything that's wrong with you, which I'll assume on first glance" upon introductions. I like some other Scandinavian authors, so I was hoping that this would have the same charm.. but nope. I wish I could finish it, because apparently it's supposed to be better at the end, but I'm not sure if that "better" is just because it's ending or if it's from a genuine change in writing. 
 If you like burrowing through a story that is about as thick as the blizzard that almost kills the main character about 100 pages in (which I call the hand of karma finally slapping him), then have at it. But I'm not going to keep running on a track that I see no purpose to staying on. It's a shame too, because there were a couple pages that had very valid, cultural insights. But I can only think of 2 pages out of the 140 I crawled through. I don't expect there to be many more further on.

Breathtaking shout for what Halldor Laxness understands for human freedom. If you have in mind all the medieval storytelling style, as well as the icelandic literature you can think of this book as the 'reinasance' of the sagas right in the middle of 50's.
I read half the book and it was ok but I just lost interest. Maybe, I will get back to it.

If I had a friend who had a dream of being a small farmer and how romantic a life in the country would be, I would give them this book if I wanted to crush all their dreams. I described it repeatedly as that "super depressing and dreary icelandic book I'm reading" and then I got over halfway to the section titled the Hard Years.

This superbly written novel pulls you into another time, another culture and a very unique family. Bjartur, a sheep farmer in early Twentieth Century rural Iceland, struggles his entire life to make a living and keep his "independence"--that is, not be beholden to any other man through loans or obligations. Ultimately, the system wears him down, but even at the end of this tale--when he is an old man, ruined financially, reunited with his long-lost daughter (now dying of consumption)--his stubborn, independent spirit carries on. Bjartur is crude, insensitive to his loved ones and more than a little idiotic throughout (not much of a hero to root for), yet is to the author's credit that you have affection for him. This both an exceedingly grim and strangely beautiful novel.
Endurance and love win out. Don't judge people by external appearances. Prepare to be moved (deeply). Love your sheep.

The ultimate libertarian's struggles against everything to maintain his freedom as a sheep farmer. It sounds long and boring but it's taut and compelling (and funny, who'd have guessed). The prose amazed me and the translation is a damn feat. So sick of daddy issues and rape being used as plot devices, but the power of this book is otherwise undeniable.

This book is... incredibly well-written, for a start. Fine-grained in its detail: SO MANY SHEEP DISEASES. Cynical and heroic at once. In the introduction, Brad Leithauser says he once rhapsodised to Laxness about his love of the hero Bjartur, and Laxness replied "but he's so stupid!", to which Leithauser answered "But he's so wonderfully stupid!". I think that hits the nail on the head: Bjartur's stark determination to independence is glorious, but his narrow-mindedness (eg, his opposition to the farmer's co-operative; his callous disregard for the health of his wives) is fatally stupid. 
 For all that, I would have preferred a book about Asta Stollija. She is very much Bjartur's foil throughout, and reasonably well characterised, but as soon as she's out of his orbit all her characterisation disappears. The other women are mostly cardboard cut-outs: the first wife's fears are explored in some detail, but not her hopes; the second wife's feelings are rarely considered; and the grandmother seems to have next to no character at all. Most annoyingly, even when the narrative focalises through one of the women, they never interact. 
 In short, surprise surprise: Nobel-winning book shows great command of literary skill, humour, historicity, social insight, etc, and is also sexist.
I tried this but couldn't get into it, and then had to return it to the library. This book has been languishing at the top of my to-read list for a while, and I'm letting it go.

reference_books.review_text:

reference_books.title: Changeling (Order of Darkness, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
What can I say about this book ... it's wasn't terrible. It wasn't terribly good, either. It was just ... ok. I have read many of Philippa Gregory's historical fiction novels, and I guess I was expecting the same level of writing. Just because a book is YA doesn't mean it needs to be dumbed down, in my opinion at least. This book, however, seemed to be written in the most simplistic way, as if the author didn't really care to put much effort into it. It almost reads like a really long children's chapter book - which given some of the content, I found strange. 
 The story strangely jumped from one story that seemingly resolved itself just fine and would have made an okay ending ... only to suddenly throw us into another storyline that was short, unnecessary, and fairly unrelated. Was this final tacked-on bit really needed? I found myself reading and wondering, what the heck is going to happen with this new storyline, there's not much left of the book! How weird if they throw this in last minute and then wrap it up right away. And then that's just what happened. It was just strange. 
 The characters were interesting enough, I guess. I didn't really feel like I really got to know any of them particularly well. Everybody seemed fairly one-dimensional. I did enjoy the character of Freize, with his odd dialogue. Otherwise, I feel like I was supposed to be far more invested in these characters than I really was. 
 The whole thing was completely predictable (and from me, often the most dense of readers, to say I know who was the villain from their very first introduction ... trust me, it's predictable.) It was entertaining enough, I suppose, and it read fairly quick so it didn't take up much of my time. I do plan on reading the rest of the series; hey, I'm a completist. We'll see if the level of writing picks up any in the next two books. Let's just say my expectations won't be set too high.

reference_books.title: Dragon's Keep (Wilde Island Chronicles #1)
reference_books.review_text: The writing style is quite disjointed and rambling, but you get used to it soon enough. It had the feel of an old story told by an elder by the fire. Interesting enough story and I'll be reading the sequel, so I guess I liked it well enough.

reference_books.title: The Princess and the Hound (The Hound Saga, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I picked up this book during one of my shifts at the library. We were weeding out some of the sad books that nobody seemed to want. This unfortunately (fortunately for me) was one of them. It has a decent cover and a mildly interesting jacket blurb, so I added it to my stack to take home. I inevitably end up with a big stack of books to take whenever we go through a weeding session. 
 I'm happy this one ended up with me. It was a good read, if a little on the lesser end of the "good" scale. The writing was a bit stilted and it took some getting used to at first. But once you get into the writer's style, the story starts to flow through. 
 The story is set in a medieval-like country where those who possess "the animal magic," i.e. the ability to talk to, command, and even transform into animals, is a serious offense. Those who are suspected of having it are often burned at the stake by crowds of angry villagers. This has been going on for as long as the kingdom can remember. Well, as it turns out, the queen of this country secretly has the animal magic, and is teaching it to her son, also "afflicted" with the magic. They are very careful about keeping it a secret, though of course those closest to them silently suspect. 
 Things come to a head when the prince is getting ready to marry a girl he's never met from a neighboring (formerly enemy) country in the hopes of bringing solid peace between the two. When he travels down to meet her for the first time, he is struck by her animal-like personality, not to mention the wild hound she keeps at her side at all times. He begins to fall in love, which is fairly predictable but not at all unwelcome for me as a reader. 
 There is of course a secret about the odd princess and her companion which comes out in due time, if a bit awkwardly. A lot of the writing and plot progression is awkward in this book, but as I said, you get used to it as you go. 
 As the book comes to what was probably several conclusions, which made the end drag on a bit, the prince comes into his own, the princess' problems are sorted out, the country is reprimanded for their violence towards animal magic (quite rightly), and some moral lessons about "being yourself" bounce around. The whole book was fairly mediocre and very teen-oriented, and as an adult of a relatively higher reading level, I wasn't necessarily blown away by this book. But I certainly found it entertaining and interesting enough to keep me reading through to the end. It was a decent light read, quick to get through and satisfying enough. Definitely worth keeping on my shelves for another read someday.

reference_books.title: Cinder (The Lunar Chronicles, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I'd been hearing great things about this book for a while before I finally managed to read it. I have to say, I agree with all of them. This was a great retelling of Cinderella. It had just enough of the original story to satisfy those looking for a retelling, but threw in so many other great elements that made it entirely original. The scifi story was just fascinating, though of course, as a scifi/fantasy fan, I am biased. It's been some time since I read this so I don't remember all the particulars, but I can tell you that I loved this book and am impatiently waiting for the sequel to come out. This imatience is compounded not only by the fact that the story was so good and I can't wait for it to continue, but by the fact that it ends on a bit of a cliffhanger that is most frustrating. I'm not even sure when the second book comes out, but I hope it's soon. I'd very much like to see where Cinder goes next.

book_a.title: Daughter of the Blood (The Black Jewels #1)
book_a.user_review: This series is a great set of books, but I don't really know what I'm reading until I finish the book. Everything is interesting, and I get the feeling I like the story, but it's hard to pinpoint exactly what's going on. It feels almost as if there's some prequel or companion novel that I should have read before starting the series ... except none such exists.

sample_reviews.review_text:
First, I like darker fantasy in general. This one was more than a bit "over the top" without the upside of being very well written... 
 The names are Daemon, Saetan, and Lucivar. Daemon is nicknamed 'the sadist'. The book includes things that seem a little out of place like cigarettes, and dildos... 
 The all-powerful "almost too good to be true" little girl Witch ("Jaenelle") is adored by Saetan and has him (and all the denizens of hell) wrapped around her little finger. Her "conflict" in the real world (i.e., not in hell) involves her being sent to a mental hospital where it is common to be drugged by the "Uncles" who are sadistic pedophiles and murderers. 
 On the other hand Daemon's "conflict" it to resist his sexual attraction to the Witch... Note - he's 1700 years old. She's 15. 
 In retrospect, I'm really not sure why I finished the book...
The subject matter of this book was appalling, the magic system confusing and the plot skippy at best. Having read Bishop's Others series I thought I would enjoy this one, I hated it.

If you can ignore all the trigger warnings that have ever existed in the history of trigger warnings (I literally mean all), you might like this book. Tends to get dramatically flowery at some points but the story still manages to captivate you and you really want to know what happens to the characters despite several contradictions and plot weaknesses. It's dark and twisted (and not always in a good way) and may not be everyone's cup of tea. 
 A fun read, anyhow.

Guh. 
 Terrible. So, so terrible. It's one of those books that you keep reading because you start to enjoy how terrible it is. 
 I mean, if you are going to decide to write one of your characters to be 50,000 years old (literally.... I'm not exaggerating.... Saetan is 50,000 years old), he probably shouldn't be surprised by preeeeetty much anything. Instead, every time this character appears in the pages, he is gasping with shock, or grabbing the edge of the chair so he doesn't fall over with disbelief. And he was continually portrayed as the baddest of the badasses, but every time he almost lost his temper and actual showed how much of a badass he was, he decided to be merciful instead. There was an actual Scrooge scene, where Saetan (ie: Satan) in HELL is wiping away his tears because he is so happy for the sad little undead children who were given a lovely little Christmas tree as a gift. 
 Yeah. Don't name a character Satan and make him 50,000 years old if he's just going to be a bumbling, friendly grandpa figure. 
 Also, don't include 25 characters if none of them are ever going to do anything except stand around and be shocked at how truly remarkable this young child prodigy is, omg, can you believe she did that amazing magic, no in hundreds of thousands of years has ever done that, it's just not possible, let's all grit our teeth and try to keep our eyes from rolling out of our heads for the 85TH TIME THIS CHAPTER. 
 Every character is totally one-dimensional, the descriptions of them are just horrendously repetitive (Sadi is just soooooo bored and sexy and cruel and chiseled and bored and sexy, and Jaenelle is just so whimsical and wise and innocent and wise and whimsical). The back stories for them all are really shallow and uncompelling (two lifelong friends became enemies because one of them called the other a bastard?), every single character who wasn't one of the "good guys" was just an extremely violent sexual pervert (NOTE: THAT DOES NOT MAKE THIS BOOK SEDUCTIVE OR EROTIC! WTF?!) (also, men are controlled by a "Ring of Obedience" placed around their "organ" because we have to be dainty and use euphemisms even though most of the characters are going around raping everyone they can find), and, oh, the real "main" character (since Jaenelle, the supposed main character, was actually just a pretty plot point all the men could be written around) was a super gross pedophile. Who, in the final pages, was HEROIC in his pedophilia. 
 Yeah. Tell me again how feminist this book is. 
 Plus, c'mon. The basic element of any good fantasy book is the world-building and the magic system. The most comprehensive explanation of the magic system in this book was in the table of contents at the beginning. I actually found it intriguing, but when you finish the whole book and there's still no actual explanation of it, you start to think maybe the author doesn't know what she's doing. There was continual reference to "landens" without ever actually explaining who they were (just regular humans like us? living regular 70-year long lives? who knows!), vague references to some kind of socioeconomic stratification (but were the landens the poor folk? or was it the less powerful Blood? who knows!), a billion different states and places named with no attempt to flesh them out (referring to someone solely as an "Eyrien half-breed" means very little if nobody knows what Eyre is). 
 Now, it is the author's first novel. So I think some of the bad, boring, repetitive writing might be attributed to that. I've seen authors make huge improvement between book 1 and book 2. But unless someone can tell me that the second book is just mind-blowingly incredible, I'm gonna go ahead and be done with this series.

I really enjoyed this book, and was very glad that I'd gone ahead and picked up books 2 and 3 while I was at it. 
 The idea of the jewels is very interesting, and different from a lot of other fantasy books I've read. I feel like the main characters are well rounded, and aren't too perfect. The only thing I didn't like about this book was the ending...but I guess if you know you're writing a sequel, it's ok to leave a book that way. It just felt very rushed and not fully thought out at the very end. No big thing, I'm already halfway through book 2.

book_b.title: Anna Dressed in Blood (Anna, #1)
book_b.user_review:
Such a great book - I don't usually enjoy books with a more horror/creepy plot as I rarely find I am as interested in them reading as I would be seeing. I'm a very visual person and for some reason, reading the words of something creepy happening just doesn't do it for me. I need to see it. I don't know what that says about my imagination ... 
 But every now and then I find a creepy book that truly creeps me out. I loved the story in this book; our main character and his life just fascinate me. He's someone who seems like he'd fit in well with Sam and Dean (points for getting the reference lol) which makes him my kind of guy. And our ghost! Anna is awesome, both her backstory which we slowly get to discover to her dual personalities that she can't control to her interesting relationship with our hero. 
 The book isn't really all that creepy or horrific, honestly, but for some reason the descriptions and flow of the story hit just the right nerve with me - some ghost is slowly creeping towards our hero ... I can just feel myself tense up. I actually found I couldn't really read this book right before going to bed because it actually made for some unsettling dreams. 
 I'm looking forward to reading the sequel, though it might take me some time as, like I said, don't really like to read before bed and that's my prime reading time. So it might have to wait for some weekend when I'm lounging around during the day and need something to curl up with.

sample_reviews.review_text: It just wasnt as scary as everybody made it out to be! I figured a little more blood and gore. I am slightly disappointed but on the up side I did like the story. Boy (hunter) meets girl (ghost). girl (ghost) kills people!! Awww young love!

Since his father was murdered, Theseus Cassio Lowood starts to be a ghost hunter. While waiting for the right time to get revenge on his father's killer, Cas killed the dead. His next target is Anna Korlov AKA Anna Dressed in Blood. Anna was murdered in 1958. When she died, She wears a long white dress, and now the dress is stained red and dripping blood. 
 Anna is different. She know that she is already dead and she is stronger than the other ghost. She kills everyone who step in her house. But when Cas's classmates trick him and send him to Anna's house, for some reason Anna doesn't kill him. Cas tries to figure out what make Anna so different and how to kill her. Can Cas kill her ??? 
 Anna Dressed in Blood is one of the horror book I can't put down. I read the book at night, and it give me chill but I still can't put it down. I really, really, really love the book. The book is told from Cas's POV. It's not too many book which is told from guy's POV, and it's refreshing. Cas is my favorite character.He is so charming, smart and witty. 
 Even if it's a horror book, we can find a little bit of romance in the book. Cas and Anna are such a sweet couple. The ending is so unexpected. I can't wait to read the next book. I highly recommend the book to everyone. Even if you don't really like horror book, I believe you would enjoy this book. 
 I give Anna dressed in Blood 5 out of 5 stars.
A teen-aged boy who kills ghosts gets in over his head when develops feelings for his latest target. Not very good.

Pues he estado pensando en mi opinion sobre este libro y llegue a la conclusion de que se me hizo entretenido, odie algunos personajes y ame a otros, el que mas me gusto fue Anna y el que mas odie fue a Carmel. El libro tiene una muy bonita y cuidada edicion esta escrito decentemente pero no asusta ni un poquito y la escritora siento que no profundizo en los personajes y pudo haberles sacado bastante provecho. Y ya por ultimo el protagonista Cas se me hizo medio estupido no es un personaje al que adore u odie pero creo que le falto mucho. 
 Para finalizar puedo decir que es un libro entretenido pero no llegas a amar y a desesperarte por saber que pasa. Es una mezcla de drama juvenil con tintes paranormales (algo asi como buffy y Angel, ?alguien recuerda estas series?) le daria 3.5 si se pudiera.

I liked it and I didn't! 
 I thought it was well written. It was disgusting and vivid and cringetastic but there was something about the whole Cas/Anna relationship that I just didn't buy into! 
 I'm a big Supernatural fan and this book did have me remembering certain scenes from the show! Not in a bad way though!

Thesius Cassio Lowood is anything but a regular 17-year old, he lives with his mom and goes out on escapades to..well..hunt ghosts. It is in his lineage to do so and thus believes it is his destiny to hunt the dead all over. One of the tips take him to Thunder Bay, Ontario to hunt the most ruthless ghost he has faced, the ghost of a 16 year old girl who was murdered brutally about half a century ago. Anna. Anna Korlov. Today she is just a night time story in slumber parties even though her brutal acts continue and the rational minds choose to find alternative explanations. 
 I went into the book not knowing anything but the title and the cover gave me some idea of what I was getting into..lots of creep and blood..and I was NOT disappointed! This book was such an amazing ride of creep and yet the author manages to keep it light with the narrator's wit.. boy oh boy.. I loved Cas! Cas may be a ghost hunter with a lineage, very certainly not an average boy, but I loved how vulnerable and soft he was when needed. Afterall he was just a 17 year old kid, a smartass witty one at that! And Anna.. Too bad I can't reveal much of her without revealing the story, but I sure can give a glimpse of her.. 
 "Anna is like nothing I've ever seen before. Her strength seems limitless, along with her bag of tricks. She's not some shuffling phantom, pissed off about being shot to death. She's death itself, gruesome and senseless, and even when she's dressed in blood and veins I can't help but stare." 
 The way Kendare Blake manages to strike a balance amongst all he elements in the story is truly commendable. This book creeped me out, made me laugh (thanks to Cas's comments), made me sad, happy and full of anticipation. It has been a while that I had been sucked into a book this way. I just couldn't stop reading.. A definite 4.5 stars! So if you haven't read it yet.. GO READ IT NOW!!!!

I just loved it so much! It's dark, thrilling but also romantic and beautifully written! It's a really short story, but it has everything we need to understand and love the book since the beginning. The characters are lovely and mature for their age, and I'm enchanted by Cas. Can't wait to read the next one!
I've held off on reading this series, and I was abit sceptical when I started, but wow did it surprise me! I really enjoyed this book and looking forward to the next one!

I was not even sure I should write a review for this book. But considering that the reviews that hyped me into buying it... well, maybe a few words will convince a poor soul into reading something else - something better, and that will be worth it. 
 I am easily scared. Truly. Once I rented The Ring (back in my time kids, we used to rent movies...). The scenes that played while you were selecting the subtitles and the language were enough to scare me, and I returned the DVD that same day. 
 When I was a kid I watched Hollow Men on a open TV channel. It's a movie about some scientists that discover how to make people invisible, and one scientist tests it on himself, becomes an invisible psychopath and start killing everybody. Well, how did I cope with an invisible threat? I convinced myself that if I used my glasses (i'm nearsighted), I would be able to see thru his invisibility. (Back then I HATED using glasses). Well, it worked. I use them till this day (for different reasons). But that got me started. 
 So if I am so easily scared, why I picked a supposedly horror book? 
 I love romance. Pride and Prejudice, Jane Eyre and even the more atual books such as Red Queen and The Bird and the Sword. And I was really attracted to the idea: a ghost hunter falling in love with a ghost. How would it happen? How would he gain her trust? Would he kill her? That feeling, that hope, made me face my fears and buy the book. 
 Of course none of that happens. Not even the dreaded scary part. They just fall in love like that. Puff. No development. No teenager doubts. 
 I mean, when i was young I was never SURE somebody loved me or even liked me properly (I'm not even sure nowadays). Yet, they simple knew... The ghost hunter and the ghost trapped for 100 years in a house alone killing people instantly in love. HOW PRETTY. 
 Well... besides that: 
 (i) none of the characters were likable. I would honestly like Cas (main character) more if he died some epic way. The 'supporting' characters were plain. (Seriously, read The Name of the Wind, even the doorman will have dept.) 
 (ii) He says "Anna Dressed in Blood" a hundred times. I feel like listening to "Bond. James Bond." but without the hottie actor saying it. 
 "I'm going there to kill her. Anna. Anna Korlov. Anna Dressed in Blood." 
 "I thing of her again. Anna. Anna Dressed in Blood. I wonder what tricks she'll try." 
 "Anna Korlov. Anna Dressed in Blood. Her name moves through the dark like a dancer." 
 (iii) IT WAS JUST TOO EASY. If Amy Harmon was not giving romance or something scary to read, AT LEAST she could've given us some action. Some fight. Damn. Within less than 24 hours of preparation they killed the strongest ghost/voodoo thing ever and it was DONE. Honestly. Want to know what happens? Read the chapter 33. With 20-something pages you can get all done and solved. 
 Nothing happens in the between. No skills developed. No drama. Nothing. 
 So if you find yourself needing some romance/action/horror - go find other book. Watch some Netflix. Eat. Just don't spend your hard earned money in this book.

I picked this up because of the cover and title. While the story wasn't terrible, it wasn't quite unique enough. Ok, so there's a kid who can kill ghosts. But his method of killing ghosts is.... lame. Really, a knife? No special description is given, no special powers, it's just... a knife. Wow. Not. The kid has no special fighting skills, took no classes on fighting or self-defense. He is described as trying to land clumsy and desperate knife lunges during fight scenes. Yet later he declares he has killed something like 200+ ghosts in three years. I find it very hard to believe he would have survived the first battle. Granted, his father was also a ghost slayer, but there is no mention of him training his son. As far as Anna goes, boring. Here you have a girl murdered and wearing a dress dripping blood, strong character right? Wrong. We are TOLD how terrible and beautiful she is but I never really feel it. The description of her is so minimal and even her dialogue is lacking. Again, one of those sad cases of good elements but a bad writer who didn't know how to harness them or flesh them out. Perhaps this was written for a much lower reading level than I was expecting but this really could have been pushed to be so much more.

reference_books.title: Fifty Shades of Grey (Fifty Shades, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I think I'm the only one who hasn't reviewed this damn book yet! But hey, better late than never. Actually, NEVER is probably better...this book was unsurprisingly bad. 
 The fact that FSOG was not well written didn't bother me very much. If it had had good characters and a decent plot, it could have earned itself more stars. My main issue was with the sex! 
 I first heard about this book when everyone was making a massive fuss about how "naughty" and "sexy" it was and for some reason, I assumed that it was going to be the next Marquis de Sade. 
 *laughs at younger self* 
 The book did not shock me in the slightest. But its biggest fault was the fact that it's so well known for being about BDSM and yet...It's just SO VANILLA. It makes me wonder where everyone is getting this idea that it's kinky from? The magical man in the moon? 
 Ok, so Christian has his little playroom and he's mega rich. So why doesn't he use all of the space and money available to him to buy awesome, kinky furniture? Or better toys? Granted, I've only read the first book. For all I know, in the second and third he might well whip out the violet wands, the needles, the snakewhips and the chastity devices...but really the kinkiest thing he and Ana do is to have period sex! 
 And towards the end, she literally pesters and pesters him to hurt her and when he eventually agrees, she gets mad?? Am I the only one who finds that strange? 
 And E.L. James seems to have some kind of problem with condoms. As far as I can remember, she never mentions them only "the rip of the foil packet." It's a pet peeve of mine, when writers of erotica are perfectly comfortable to use the word that rhymes with "block" but avoid using the word that rhymes with "hussy" like the plague and instead use odd terms like "flower" or "temple of Venus." (I'm looking at you Sade!!) James does the same with condoms here. By the end of the novel, I was tempted to hijack every copy of FSOG ever published and scribble the word "condom" in red ink over every mention of "foil packets!" UGH!

The Percy Jackson series was the first major series I had read; and I was obsessed from the very first word. Needless to say, I'm a big fan of the series. From the hilarious narration from Percy, to the wonderful combination of the modern world and Greek myths, this series was a recipe for goodness from the start. Even now, I am still reading Rick Riordan books. I just can't get enough. The characters he wrote were ( and still are ) memorable and full of heart, and that's hard to write off.
couldn't finish it

Percy Jackson, a troubled dyslexic 12-year-old withADHD, finds out that he is a demigod after some unusual events. He ends up at Camp Half-Blood after his mother takes him to Montauk for the weekend but they get attacked by a Minotaur and she disappears. At the camp, he learns more about life as a demigod, eventually learning that Poseidon is his father. He is sent on a quest to find Zeus's stolen lightning bolt with the help of Grover, a satyr, and Annabeth, a daughter of Athena. The story progresses as expected, adhering strongly to a Hero's Journey storyline with a cliffhanger ending beckoning for the next book in the series. 
 I understand that the series is intensely popular with children, perhaps due to their lack of exposure to better literature. It is incredibly derivative and predictable. The characters are flat, boring and irritating. Percy himself is annoyingly bratty and Riordan spends more time forcefully telling rather than showing Percy's personality. The novel is overall very choppy and disjointed, which really causes the novel to drag on forever. The fight scenes lack any suspense, it is obvious that the kids will succeed with hardly any trouble or loss. There is no question to their eventual triumph as they face each obstacle and that absence of tension bleeds the fun out of what could've have been a wonderful story. 
 Riordan goes for the punchline every time with his allusions and homages to the classical Greek literature, resulting in shallow and trite depictions of the various Gods, Goddesses and spirits. His treatment of the material makes it seem as though even he doesn't believe his story is real, as though the author himself was unable to suspend the disbelief necessary for the novel and it is infectious. Also, why in the world does Athena have children?!?

This series appealed to me when the movie was in the theater but I was busy and never got to it. When I saw that it was soon being released on DVD I decided I wanted to read the book before seeing the movie. I belong to the school of though that most of the time, the book is better than the movie and this is another story that I believe that holds true for. 
 I shared this book with my children, we read almost the entire thing aloud and then borrowed the audio book to listen to in the car on a long trip. One thing I liked about listening was hearing someone else pronounce the names for the Greek gods, I just wasn't entirely sure of the pronunciation of some of them which is no big deal when you are reading silently to yourself but becomes a bigger problem when you are reading aloud! 
 Parts of this book reminded me of Harry Potter (another series I am working through with my children this summer) and somewhat of the Spiderwick Chronicles which we have already finished. I like that this opened their minds to the idea of Greek myths because I think we are going to moving into those in a few weeks. This book was engrossing enough for adults or children and I highly recommend it. When we went to the beach last week my children were throwing shells back in telling me that they were offering for Poseidon the sea god!

 Percy Jackson and the Olympians and Harry Potter. Different books but the story is startlingly the same. 
 But what it failed to capture is the magic the boy wizard had cast to it's readers, or to me, for all I can remember from this book is it's just a great copy of a story I had grown to loved. i guess if i read this before HP i might have a different reaction/reception to this book, after all, it was a fun and quick read. sample_reviews.review_text: I couldn't finish this. It was slow, heavy going and bored me rigid.

Everybody knows the story of The Three Musketeers and their friend D'Artagnan, right? Well, if you're like me and you were basing your knowledge upon the various screen adaptations of the story, then you may be amazed by how much of the story - and the characters - that you don't know. D'Artagnan, a young man from the Gascony area of France, who goes to Paris with the aim of joining the King's Musketeers. After a few initial misunderstandings, he becomes firm friends with the melancholy Athos, the rambunctious Porthos, and the foppish Aramis. The book follows their adventures as they become embroiled in trying to stop the evil machinations of Cardinal Richelieu, who is determined to bring down Queen Anne, wife of King Louis XIII. 
 The book was a delightful and action packed adventure, full of humour, fighting and romance. I was surprised that there were chunks of the storyline that didn't actually feature D'Artagnan or the musketeers, and also by the fact that, unlike the screen adaptations, the four servants of the main characters featured almost as heavily as the main characters themselves, and were very instrumental in the musketeers' plans and actions. 
 The plot moves on very quickly, and there are LOTS of twists and surprises, but despite this, Dumas still found time to establish each main character's personality. It's fair to say that at times they act in a less than gentlemanly manner, but despite this, I still found myself regarding each character with affection. It is also, in parts, a very funny story (there is one particular scene where D'Artagnan visits Aramis, who is constantly planning to leave the musketeers to become a man of the cloth, and finds him in consultation with a curate and Jesuit superior, which had me laughing out loud all the way through). 
 The seductive but evil Lady de Winter, and Cardinal Richelieu are a substantial part of the story, playing the two main villains, with 'MiLady' always trying, and often succeeding to stay one step ahead of the musketeers who seek to bring her down. 
 Overall, this is a hugely entertaining romp through Paris, and I believe that everybody should read it at least once. For me, it's a keeper, and one I intend to re-read at some point.

Escrito em 1844, os "Tres Mosqueteiros" nasceram aquando da descoberta por Alexandre Dumas de um manuscrito intitulado As memorias do sr. D'Artagnan". Nessas memorias, d'Artagann refere que na primeira visita ao sr. de Treville, capitao dos mosqueteiros, encontrou tres mocos que se chamavam Athos, Porthos e Aramis, nomes que Dumas julga tratar-se de pseudonimos que disfarcam nomes ilustres. 
 Posteriormente e perseguindo a sua investigacao, Dumas acaba por descobrir um outro manuscrito intitulado "Memorias do conde de La Fere, respeitante a alguns acontecimentos que se passaram em Franca em fins do reinado de Luis XIII e principios do de Luis XIV". Manuscrito este que e pelo que Dumas diz, relata os acontecimentos descritos no livro "Os tres mosqueteiros" e um outro que me parece ser "20 anos depois", tambem da autoria de Alexandre Dumas. 
 Esta informacao, que desconhecia, vem no prefacio da edicao que possuo. 
 Verdade? Ficcao? Nao o sei dizer! 
 Certo e que li esta obra quando tinha 12, 13 anos e que, ate hoje, ficou guardado num lugar muito especial do meu imaginario. Uma obra de referencia no panorama da literatura que, e depois de a ter relido, ainda aconselho a uma certa faixa etaria e a pessoas que leem pouco e apenas pretendem distrair-se um pouco. 
 Quero com isto dizer que fiquei muito desiludido com esta minha 2a leitura. 
 Esta muito longe de ser um bom livro. A narracao, presumo que de Dumas, tem muitas falhas e os acontecimentos que se vao sucedendo, tem mais buracos que as ruas de Lisboa. A accao tem realmente factos historicos veridicos (lembro-me, por exemplo, do cerco de Arrochela), personagens que existiram (Luis XIII, Ana de Austria, Richelieu), mas a forma como os acontecimentos se vao sucedendo, sao extremamente rapidos, com pouco sentido e contem pouco rigor narrativo. 
 Se nao concorda, atente a alguns factos: 
 D'Artagnan, jovem fidalgo gascao, vem para Paris com aspiracoes a ser mosqueteiro. E possuidor de uma carta de seu pai para o sr. de Treville. Ate chegar a presenca do capitao, passa por alguns contratempos, perde a carta que Dumas nunca mais refere, e sobretudo assiste a uma impensavel e violenta repreensao do sr. de Treville a 3 mosqueteiros... e o sr. de Treville nem sabia quem era d'Artagnan. 2, 3 paginas depois ja d'Artagnan e grande compincha desses mosqueteiros e meia duzia de paginas adiante ja esses mosqueteiros seguem quase religiosamente d'Artagnan, e o jovem gascao apenas consegue ser colocado no corpo da guarda. Depois temos o papel de Richelieu que, a noite joga partidas amigaveis com o Rei e de dia conspira contra tudo e contra todos, nao olhando a meios para atingir os seus fins. Existe de facto um fundo de verdade, mas o relato de Dumas e bastante desconexo assim como a ligacao entre o cardeal e Milady e o papel desta e deveras incongruente, e confuso. Uma mulher que e tao bela que tem um poder hipnotizador sobre tudo e todos. Demonstra um odio tao grande por tudo o que se mexe. Esse odio nao e muito compreensivel porque tambem nao e muito compreensivel o percurso de Milady. Cheguei a parar para meditar no que lia, pois a ansia que demonstra em fazer mal e tao grande que e por diversas vezes, me pareceu que varias etapas do texto ou foram omitidas ou nem sequer foram escritas. Lembro-me de uma "cena" quase no fim do livro onde ela e presa. O homem que a prende coloca um tenente a vigia-la e, para que esse tenente nao caia nos terriveis jogos de Milady, adverte-o para que nao va em cantigas, que nao acredite numa palavra que ela disser, no entanto, esse tenente que tudo devia a esse homem, inclusive a sua vida, acaba por ser facilmente dominado por Milady em apenas 3, 4 dias, a ponto de a ajudar a fugir e de ele proprio cometer um terrivel homicidio. E o engracado e que ela nem usa grandes argumentos. 
 Mesmo a forma como o romance acaba e algo de impensavel, uma completa contradicao. Depois do que acabamos de ler, depois de os mosqueteiros terem passado o livro todo a lutar contra os homens do cardeal, com esse mesmo cardeal a demonstrar uma raiva mortal principalmente a d'Artagnan, e precisamente Richelieu que premeia o jovem gascao... certo que o cardeal sempre demonstrou uma certa admiracao por d'Artagnan, mas e estranho! 
 A historia em si e simples: 
 Situada em 1630 (+/-), 3 mosqueteiros e um jovem guarda, aliam-se a rainha contra o cardeal. D'Artagnan parte para Inglaterra para recuperar uma joia que a rainha havia oferecido ao duque de Buckingham como prova do seu amor. O cardeal, sabendo disso, manipula do rei no sentido de ele realizar um baile em que a rainha tera que apresentar essa joia. Mesmo com homens do cardeal atras dos mosqueteiros, d'Artagnan consegue chegar a Inglaterra e trazer de volta essa joia que a rainha, para grande raiva do cardeal, usa com visivel satisfacao. De notar que no caminho para Inglaterra, Athos, Porthos e Aramis vao ficando para tras sem nos sabermos se morreram ou nao. Dumas pouco se importa em explicar, so depois de d'Artagnan chegar e que o sr. de Treville se lembra dos mosqueteiros e la parte o jovem guarda em busca dos amigos. 
 Posto isto, os 3 mosqueteiros entretem-se com as suas conquistas e chulices amorosas (era uso e costume nessa epoca as amantes sustentarem os seus amados militares e eles ate tinham brio em o fazer). Sao entao convocados para o tal cerco de Arrochela e e dai que partem para a ultima aventura. 
 Eu assumo-me como um leitor muito exigente e um critico feroz. Como cada qual, tambem eu tenho as minhas preferencias e o que pode ser bom para mim, pode ser muito mau para outras pessoas e vice-versa. Esta obra desiludiu-me porque, sem ser pelas razoes ja apontadas, nota-se que Dumas se limitou a pegar nos textos ja existentes, nao lhe acrescentando mais valia nenhuma, nem sequer teve capacidade para criar um enredo mais elaborado, cuidado ou artistico. Repare-se que nao e por acaso que Dumas foi talvez o unico escritor que fez da arte de escrever um negocio de producao em serie, empregando varios funcionarios para escreverem historias. 
 Assim "Os tres mosqueteiros" e, na minha opiniao, um tipico romance de aventuras que aconselho a jovens que se iniciam neste magico mundo da literatura ou a pessoas que pouco leem e que apenas pretendem relaxar e divertir-se um pouco. 
 Para quem procura Qualidade, para quem deseje ler, absorver, pensar, analisar e estudar uma obra literaria, este nao e certamente um romance que aconselho. 
 Obviamente que continuara a fazer parte do meu imaginario, embora ja tenha mudado de lugar. E eu que estava a pensar em reler o "Conde de Monte Cristo", obra que tenho como uma das melhores que li ate hoje, depois de reler os "tres mosqueteiros", prefiro deixa-la onde esta e continuar a pensar no "Conde de Monte Cristo" como uma Grande Obra.

The Three Musketeers is awful. I think the last book I read with such a fury was Wuthering Heights, and now six years later, I'm willing to concede it may not be that bad. But The Three Musketeers is such a hypocritical and wanton display of immorality, hypocrisy and everything. Now hold up. I'm not saying the book should be banned from bookshelves because it might harm the children. I'm reading it. Going to finish and most likely try and beat D'artagnon with a spiked club when I'm done, and the sexism in this book is amazing. I can't figure out if Dumas is trying to show how unromantic, unchivalric, and not rose colored French society was or something else. I respect Dumas as a writer. I think the Count of Monte Cristo is an awesome book. Who doesn't like Edmond? As long as he's not mad at him. I just don't know how people can not see something wrong. Case in point. Opening chapter, D'artagnon's Daddy says, "Son here is money, an old horse I want you to love forever, a letter of conduct and advice to be nice to the Cardinal." On his arrival in Paris, he's lost his money because of duels, sells the horse, looses the letter and joins the Kings guards instead even though he could care less. In effect, everyone thinks he's the biggest king lover in all Christendom. Another example, a brave, beautiful young woman by the name of Madame Boniceaux is helping the queen with her little issues and is kidnapped. D'artagnon saves her, falls in love with her, worships her. The queen loves her, thanks her, is grateful to her. She gets kidnapped again. D'artagnon falls in love with another and says ho-hum, what can I do but hope all is well? The queen says I'll look into it. Ten chapters later she's forgotten. And don't get me started on Athos and his lady's story. Grrr!

3.5 stars, this was a riot and really enjoyable. time-appropriate sexism, not so fun, but it made me want to rewatch the 90s movie real bad. glad i read this, and looking forward to reading count of monte cristo too!

Just another good ol' classical adventure every youngster should read

This book is called "The Three Musketeers". It's about four swordsmen! 
 However, once you get over that, you're in for a thrilling ride here. Few writers can do adventure better than Dumas. A young, idealistic adventurer blunders into town to join the army, runs foul (separately) of the three best swordsmen in the regiment, and agrees to fight them all on the same day. From that moment, the action never lets up. 
 Sure, the prose can be a bit difficult for a fast read, some of the characterization is a bit exaggerated, and Dumas' jokes don't always come off for a 21st century reader. But you soon forget that, once you get into the story. If you like a good sword-and-no-sorcery adventure romp, you can't go past this one!

Why, oh why did I waste such valuable reading time finishing this? Because, apparently, I'm a glutton for punishment. 
 I will warn you ahead of time, this review may contain spoilers!!! I'm not sure yet because I don't really care enough to plan this out. This will mostly be whining, ranting, and general complaining. Remember, I warned you. 
 Before I dive into this review, I will tell you that I've heard the Cassandra Clare plagiarized arguments, and that this book is basically a reworked fan fiction like the famed Fifty Shades of Grey books. I will not go into those details. I'm just going to look at what has been presented to me in a digital style format for Kindle. So be prepared for jokes and snarky comments that most will probably think are not funny. 
 I decided to read this book because my fourteen year old cousin asked for the series for Christmas. I helped my family purchase it for her (because I'm their book guru) and I thought I would give at least the first one a shot. I've been trying to read more YA lately to familiarize myself with why it's so popular since I pretty much stopped reading YA when I was ten. I'd make the odd excursion into the wilds occasionally, but for the most part I didn't read much. 
 This was my reaction to the book: 
 WHAT DID I JUST READ! HOW IN HELL DID THIS GET PUBLISHED! DID SHE SELL HER SOUL TO THE DEVIL OR SOMETHING? 
 Yes, I bolded that. I currently want to rub my head along the floor as I walk in the futile hope that I'll rub this book from my memory. If Sherlock Holmes' Attic Theory is to be believed, that this book is taking up valuable space I can use for my writing and better books. 
 Let me start with the characters since they're probably the most appalling aspect. 
 Clary: This little lovely is a fifteen/sixteen year old red-head who loves her sketchbook and doesn't think she's pretty. Sounds like me in high school. I should relate right? Wrong. Clary is one of the angriest, self-absorbed, whiniest little brats I've ever had the displeasure of getting to know. 
 I've read my share of female protagonists who go down like cheap alcohol; they put up a fight and don't agree once you think you've stomached them. But I liked those gals anyway. Clary is not one of them. She bitches about everything. She gets angry at the stupidest stuff. She also can't keep a solid thought in her head. She wonders about the strangest things at the strangest times, like in the middle of a fight. And she slaps or scratches people with barely a reason. 
 Let's move on, shall we? Before I throw my computer. She really pisses me off that much. 
 Jace: I know he's supposed to basically be this popular ideal of fanfic Draco (Now with more leather!), but I honestly thought Draco was a waste of space to begin with. Not because Rowling was a terrible writer (because she's definitely not that), but because he was a terrible person! If I just look at this character without thinking about his developmental origin, I still don't like him. He's a conceited jackass. He's the kind of guy where you're friend looks at you and says, in the sassiest way possible, "Gurl, you can do better." Sure, he's got tattoos and blonde sex hair, but when are those boys good for you? 
 Now, I'll be straight with you, reader. Think of it this way. Cassandra Clare refers to Jace's blonde curls so often I was beginning to wonder if he was rockin' a perm. And he's wearing leather pants in hot, humid New York weather. His dangly bits have got to be chaffing. Seriously, ladies. That is not hot. All he's missing is an Ed Hardy shirt before he's the douche in the corner of the club you roll your eyes at. 
 Before any fans read this and freak out on me with: OH NO! JACE IS TOTES HAWT! YOU JUS HATIN BECAUSE YOU CAN'T HAVE HIM! YOU JEALOUS CAUSE YOU CAN'T WRITE LIKE CLARE CAN! (I can't even be a pre-teen girl right, and I was one once.) There are no pictures. You are living in your fantasy. All Clare describes most of the time are his eyes and hair. If you are a grown woman and your mad at what I've said, go drool over Supernatural. The Winchesters are hot, demon hunters, and have better personalities. Okay, marginally better personalities. Whatever. At least they aren't wearing leather pants. Or in puberty. 
 Simon: The child hood friend suffering from unrequited love syndrome. Yawn. He was awesome until he got all heart broken. Solid friend till the end even though he could have pushed Clary off a cliff and I would have felt it totally justified. The only character that the dry wit Clare tries to use fits. At one point he does tell Clary off and calls Jace an asshole, earning him my Favorite Character Award. 
 Isabelle: The bitchy hot chick Clary hates even though she isn't that bitchy. I actually kind of liked her despite being a totally undeveloped stereotype. The butt of cooking jokes. 
 Alec: Isabelle's boring older brother. He's gay for Jace. Hates on Clary because she's also making eyes at his dream man. He's just there for plot conflict. Too underdeveloped to be interesting. 
 Magnus Bane: I liked Magnus despite his unfortunate attire. He really seemed better than that. I would read the other two books for him, but I'm pretty sure I couldn't suffer through more Clary. Although, he could totally be that sassy gay friend Clary needs to tell her, "Gurl, you can do better." (I really wanted to say that again. I blame the lack of sleep.) Of course, nothing Clare writes is really that interesting, so I don't know why I expect it to happen. 
 Luke: Clary's mother's friend suffering from unrequited love syndrome. Also liked him, but he should have yelled at Clary more for being a little brat. 
 Jocelyn: a.k.a. Coma mom. That's how she spends the whole book. And ends the book. I felt cheated. 
 Valentine: The big bad. More like Bad-Guy-From-a-Can. He's not really menacing at all, or even memorable. Even his name sucks. I'm gonna call him Daddy V from now on because for some strange reason I can take that more seriously than Valentine. Who names their child that anyway? 
 That should handle all the characters, which I enjoyed writing about more than I thought. Now, onto the next biggest complain that I've read about and couldn't help noticing: the metaphors! Bum-bum-bum! I'll just list a few off: 
 "The night sky rippled overhead..." How does the sky ripple when you aren't looking at it through anything? 
 "The moon hung like a locket over the city..." So it just hanging there wasn't good enough? 
 "She wondered how often he let glimpses of his real self peek through the facade that was as hard and shiny as the coat of lacquer on one of her mother's Japanese boxes." This one broke my brain. 
 "... was black as velvet." Oh, honey. Didn't you know velvet comes in many different colors? 
 To describe a mausoleum: "... like an iceberg off the bow of the Titanic." 
 To refer to a restaurant building: "... like a collapsed souffle." 
 "... the lights of Manhattan burning like cold jewels." This would be a moment where Clare using glittering would make sense. 
 "The apple tasted green and cool." How do you taste green? 
 "She felt a bright surge of shame that burst behind her eyelids like a small sun." If shame looks like the sun to you, Clary, why do you still have eyes? 
 "... yowling like a foghorn." Does this woman think about what she says? This cat sounds possessed. 
 Okay, I'll stop there before I start crying. I swear, Clare doesn't think about what she's actually putting down. Everything in her world "sparks," "gleams," "glints," or "glitters." It sounds painful to look at. When I read the descriptions and think about what it would look like visually, it sounds like Tinkerbell covered Clare's world in pixie dust. Instead of making vampires sparkle, Clare made friggin' everything sparkle! Eyes, bracelets, bracers, weapons, random objects in the corner. It stopped making sense. I don't even want to know how many times she uses those words. I kept getting deja vu with those words as often as I saw "like" or "as." This chick needs an editor. 
 Plot wise it isn't much better. Three objects... blah, blah. Special snowflake girl... yadda, yadda. I actually got bored in the middle of the climax because Clare foreshadows with a brick. I guessed the ending at the beginning. Seriously, she lacks subtlety. 
 But I want to mention one main plot twist that should have made me gasp and drop my Kindle to clutch at my heart. Yup, you guessed it, dear reader. The Daddy V reveal. When I was reading the scenes with pacified Jace, I couldn't buy it. It became apparent to me that Clare had manipulated her character so it could suit the moment. There was no natural character progression to fragile, doubting Jace from jackass Jace. 
 This is how the scene should have went: 
 DADDY V: Jace, I am your father. 
 JACE: This isn't Star Wars. I want a DNA test. I know we use magic and all that, but science still exists. Hell, there's probably some magical DNA test. I mean, a couple of items and some convenient circumstances does not the truth make. Wow, I just sounded intelligent there. 
 Okay, I was pretty liberal with that, but I think I made my point. 
 That, of course, leads to the whole incest-love thing. I read Martin's Song of Fire and Ice before they were a cable show. Nothing will beat the creepiness that is that incest-romance. Well, nothing that I've come across. 
 Then there are the inconsistencies: 
 Mark scars are sometimes described as silver, sometimes as white. 
 Luke's dagger, then sword, then dagger. 
 The werewolves are strong enough to break through boarded up windows a couple stories up, but not a roof top door. 
 Light from the open front door doesn't affect Abaddon. Only the light coming through the skylight. Which, when I read it, I had to assume was dirty or frosted. She never clarified. 
 Yeah. Cassandra Clare, by royal decree, you need an editor. 
 There are a thousand other things I could go into like how all the characters have the same wit that isn't funny. Or I could go into detail all of the inexplicable rages Clary flies into. Or mention that Clare actually has Daddy V monologue and throw his head back to laugh. But I'll stop before I find myself bald because I've torn out my hair from looking at my notes. 
 Before I stop, let me put this in another perspective. As an unpublished writer who reads the work of other unpublished writers, I have come across much better. It's books like these that make me scratch my head. I understand if you want to blow an afternoon reading cotton candy fluff, you know, nothing really special, but there is stuff out there that has characters that are genuinely lovable. And the characters are what really matter because that is what the reader connects to. That is why Cassandra Clare's City of Bones got one star. In the end, I stopped caring. 
 If you liked this review, I've got more: 
 The Original Mortal Instruments Trilogy 
 City of Ashes 
 City of Glass 
 The Infernal Devices 
 Clockwork Angel 
 Clockwork Prince

'The Mortal Instruments series is a story world that I love to live in. Beautiful!' : 
 Says the front, by none other than Stephanie Meyer. 
 Live in, maybe, delve in, stay-up-late-until-finished , sink her fangs in (geddit?) 
 No. 
 I don't even know where to start with this book. One moment it was okay and the next it just... wasn't. 
 And truly, i was disappointed. 
 There was some potential in this book, but overall just no. 
 I liked Jace, he was witty, funny, hot , and just a cool guy. And that pretty much summed up what i liked about City of Bones. Not to mention that towards the end of the book, i really grew to hate him. It just DID NOT add up to why Jace would suddenly just believe all that jazz. Ultimately, that was a major problem of mine throughout the whole novel : not enough. Maybe my expectations are too high, or maybe i'm just Asian, but I felt that Clare could have included so much more to the story; more background, insight, flair,thought could have made the story so much more enjoyable. Instead, i felt like the author was just slotting in any hum dum of a reason to whatever motive the character had, like it was going to be okay? Well, it wasn't. 
 Speaking of characters, there was Clary. I did not like her from the instant (okay maybe not) i liked her in like Chapter one ; i really felt like she would make a great heroine, one that everyone roots for, gets the guy etc. etc. But i was disappointed, gravely. She was an annoying, spoilt brat, shallow-minded, weak (you get what i mean)for pretty much the whole book, and well, can i just say that was exactly the opposite of what i had in mind. Clary wasn't all bad, in fact, i preferred her in all her physical splendour : she was flat, short, and had short legs, which i have to say, was her best attribute. By far, that was the closest i could get to relate to Clary, to realism really. 
 And all that, was only characters ; the plot itself, was nothing i hadn't seen before, with your fair share of demons, angels, werewolves, vampires, seems like the whole package, for those of you who love such stuff, but the problem wasn't there. 
 It was the pacing, it was nice and quick, just the way i like my books ;) but a little too quick. I couldn't even remember what happened what... 30 pages ago? Everything was so rushed, which put me off, because there were moments that had soooo much potential to be developed further, but just like that,it was over. Where's the magic in that! 
 Next up, Clary's famous lines of 'why'. I cannot stress enough how shallow Clary is, flaws are only normal but even the most subtle of things she would ask : why. As if this was purely to annoy me. Not to mention Jace's :' I'll come with you' line, or somewhere along those lines. 
 What upset me most though, was just this one tiny TINY thing she revealed nearing the end of the novel. No spoilers but that just was it for me. /: I walked into this book with the hope of living up to it's hype, hell, even a decent read was fine enough, but not this... not this...

Giving this two stars is a gift. Had I realized the book was endorsed by Stephanie Meyer I would have skipped it. 
 Start with the bad relationship framework and angst of Twilight for your base. Add the least appealing elements of Harry Potter (the drama and angst of books 5 & 6). Throw in some of the demon fighting and hunting of Buffy The Vampire Slayer. And what the hell, have some more relationship drama and angst. And top it off with a weird smidgen of Star Wars. 
 Clare got her start writing fan fiction, which I can see because I don't feel like she committed to any character or story decisions. It felt like she was waiting for feedback from the audience so that she could change the story for approval. Fictional cowardice. None of the characters were defined enough for me to care about them at all. Clarey is not compelling. Not quite Bella Swan pathetic, but not far. Jace is a sarcastic jerk, and Clare is unable to generate any sympathy for his dark and mysterious past. Simon, Clarey's friend, fills out the obvious and weak part of the apparently necessary love triangle. But wait, there is more! Now you get an additional love angle for free! (I won't go in to particulars on that angle in case someone reads this and actually decides to read the book.) I would have rooted for the supposed evil mastermind, Valentine, but Clare was never able to generate any character traits or feeling of menace from him either. 
 The things that make Harry Potter and Hunger Games work is that they are not about the romantic relationships. The romance is secondary to the needs of the story. Harry needs to live, to survive, to defeat Voldemort. Katniss needs to put food on the table, to protect her family, to survive. Those characters had inner strength and hard choices to make. These characters are just pathetic to me.

SPOILER ALERT: DO NOT READ REVIEW BEFORE YOU HAVE READ THE BOOK. 
 When I picked up this book at the store, and bought it instead of a Neil Gaiman book, it was because I was in the mood for something simple and teenagery. I was not disappointed regarding that. City of Bones seems to me like a cross between Harry Potter and The Immortals. Harry Potter is a very good series, The Immortals is more the teenagery style that City of Bones is, but it's not a bad series at all. Sure CoB is flawed, but it is everything you should expect judging from the genre, cover, summary and reputation. If you expected more from this book, you are foolish. 
 You may be confused about the negative tone I have here, compared to the four stars I gave. The truth is, if I could have given it three and a half star, I might have done that. But there is also the thing that I genuinely liked this book. It has its strange descriptions and cliches (a lot of cliches), but I found it captivating and generally well-written nevertheless. 
 When it comes to Clary, I... I'm almost afraid to say this, because she is jealous and short-tempered and possibly violent, but I did take a liking to her, without really knowing why. And let it be said that I'm normally not a big fan of the main POV character. 
 BONUS POINTS for switching between POV characters, by the way! Some may say it just feels weird, but I'm a big fan of seeing different sides of things. I was even tricked at the beginning, thinking the demon was the one we'd be following. I liked him! I liked him even after his intetions of eating the girl (who we now know as Isabelle) became clear! I liked that Clary went against the Shadowhunters. 
 A little word on the Clary/Jace romance: I'm in a way glad the author took some time to let them get to know each other, and not actually have any hints of romance before it had been a while. However, I think that when it first began, it might have gone a little too fast. And if I can be allowed to skip to the end for a moment, I found it funny and realistic that everyone seemed to like Clary more after the big Valentine drama, not becase they had been through something together and had become a big, happy family, but because it was clear that it could never be Jace and Clary, so Simon, Isabelle and Alec didn't dislike her out of jealousy anymore (Isabelle is not jealous because she wants him, but because she doesn't want him to have another female in his life - I am a female, I know these things). Speaking of the big Valentine drama, I kind of wish they were all there, that might have been more fun. I liked that Clary didn't believe Valentine at first (I didn't either), but I think it should have been more focus on her slow way to believing. First a little doubt and then more doubt, and then she would be gradually more convinced. I'd like that. 
 I'm not even going to talk much about Simon. Although I'm not much a fan of him, I do accept that the story needs him, if nothing else, so for a counter-weight to all the freaky stuff going on. For God's sake, let him stay normal. 
 Luke, however, I want to talk about. I pictured him as Tim Foyle from Veronica Mars, and trusted him about in the same way. (Meaning I half-trusted him from the start, and stopped trusting him where the book asks you to do so, and then trusted him a lot in the end). 
 And while we're on it: Werewolves. I have a lot to say about the werewolves. I do feel like the author ripped the whole concept a little off Twilight, but considering Twilight is shit, I forgive her. I don't think it's unnatural that the wolves have packs, considering that they change so regularly. What I do think is strange is that everyone seems to be very wolfy ("you killed our leader? Hail! I shall follow you until I die!") except Luke ("they're just Downworlders"). Why has everyone else changed so much, and why does Luke think they're nothing when he too is one of them. Don't tell me EVERYONE else was born werewolf? My main problem with them, however, is how easily they change. The ONLY novels I have read that have realistic shape-shifting are those of the Animorphs series. The author of those books describe very well how how painful the process of CHANGING YOUR FREAKING SKELETON is. Come on, your skeleton does change from human to wolf, your face is stretched to a wolf snout and you grow fur and claws. How is this NOT painful? How can these people do all of this without the blink of an eye? Also, the clothes. I first reacted when they were rescuing Simon, and the wolves came and turned human, and the clothes of one of them were described. I mean, when you transform to something bigger, either your clothes are ripped apart, or change to fit your new form, depending on what kind of technology or nature that causes you to change. If you transform into something smaller, they fall off you (see Wormtail) or shrink. Animorphs do this well also. And then there is the ever-lasting problem about identity. In Animorphs they have to battle the identity of the animal, and it always takes some time before they get control over it. It's sort of the same here, how Luke the first time he transformed, had no control over his actions, but after a while learned to control the wolf. This human/animal thing is necessary in Animorphs, and I forgive it in this case too, but I personally prefer how it works in Harry Potter, where Lupin has no control over his werewolf self. He forgets who he is. He is no longer human, but wolf. I like this better because it is more realistic. Humans and wolves do not have the same brain, and you can not just mix them as you please. But as mentioned, I forgive the author for this. 
 And I think that's all I had to say. Now I'm off to finish Les Miserables, before I start on City of Ashes.

I first happened onto Cassandra Clare through her Infernal Devices trilogy because I am a fan of the Steampunk genre. I read City of Bones knowing it was set in the same world of Shadowhunters and Downworlders but I must say that it did not hold my attention quite as well as the previous books. Maybe it is because I was trying to piece together how everyone was related to the characters in the Infernal Devices, if at all, and maybe it is because it's not a Steampunk novel. Either way, City of Bones turned out to be a very good read and by the end, I couldn't put it down because I could not wait to see what happens to Jace and Clary. I am intrigued to find out if City of Ashes picks up right where Bones leaves off because the Epilogue in City of Bones seems to end rather abruptly to me.
