 Oh on a side note, I did not like the men factor (where they were either wanting to rape/sell/use women for their own purposes OR head over heals in love with one, I guess the plague got to all the homosexuals and nice guys) also another reason for the 4 stars and not 5.

sample_reviews.review_text: I wish I liked this more. Good premise for a novel- the world's population has been largely wiped out by a virus. Surviving girls are kept in "schools" to be educated and kept in excellent health. They are told that after graduation they will be released to the City of Sand where they will have a great life, except life really isn't that simple. When Eve figures out what will really happen to her after graduation, she runs away. This book is the first in a series, but I don't know if I'll actually read the rest. It was a very simplistic book. Lots of loose ends still need to be tied up in the sequels.
So many questions.. so very sweet and innocent Eve and so very mysterious Caleb.

I would have to put Eve by Anna Carey in my..I enjoyed it but not overly wowed...category. I really like the overall concept of the story. Having a plague ravage the world leaving few survivors that have to rebuild society. It's not something we haven't ever heard before but everyone puts their own twist on it. 
 It was an easy lighter read for me, which is not a bad thing. I could tell that this was the first book in a series because there were many questions left unanswered. I couldn't say the ending left me hanging from a cliff and salvating for the next installment but I did enjoy it. 
 I noticed some familar themes....Eve herself has a little Wendy from "Peter Pan" going for her, with the exception of having to fight of sexual advances. This of course is no Neverland though with the wild strays having a bit of "Lord of the Flies" going for them. 
 The romance was cute not epic but I did believe the chemistry of the characters. 
 I will probably read the second book because I feel an authors writing grows just as much as their characters do. So I'm curious as to how some of the issues will be worked out and how some questions will be answered. I wouldn't run up to you on the street and say you have got to read this book.
DNF...

That was a dumb ending. There are so many post-apocalyptic stories out there right now. This one is a tame kitten next to its sisters. Every edge seems blunt, dull, and a bit less terrifying than it could be. All the dangers seem more like Santa Claus, a bit imaginary. Just a bunch of made up stories to fill the gaps and keep us in line. The poor girls at that school are so conditioned to believe the oddest tales. It amazes me that no matter how much she has seen to the contrary she is still feeding herself one big lie. What gives her the idea that a happy ending is possible? No such luck sweetheart. 
 Eve is a bit annoying. A perfect girl, teacher's pet, who is high maintenance. She leaves messes everywhere she treads and lets others clean them up. Her countenance is a textbook definition of damsel in distress. There is no fight to her. She breaks so easily and is lucky that none of the threats never occurs. 
 Caleb is hard to swallow. Dirty hardly describes his true state. More like he is kin to the earth, he is that dirty. It doesn't sound the least bit attractive or snuggly. I wonder about him, what he is really thinking? Did his mind undergo a complete change toward Eve? He freely admits she isn't his type but doesn't hold to his declaration. How could he even know his type? There isn't a girl around and they certainly aren't raining from the sky for him to figure it out. Even when he is supposedly friendly toward her he isn't very emotional. He is hard to read. I guess he is a very restrained individual. 
 This story reminded me of The Host by Stephenie Meyer during the underground portion. An entire group of boys living secretly in an underground tunnel system. When they come to the old couple coming to their rescue and bringing them into their big house I was very strongly reminded of Article 5 by Kristen Simmons. I kept expecting betrayal around each corner. 
 Mostly I just wanted to slap the characters. Eve for all her talk of Romeo and Juliet and their downfalls. Going on and on about how she understands the importance of a moment and that she won't waste it. Umm, yeah. . . way to waste plenty of them. 
 The whole scenario didn't work well for me. An all powerful king turning all their girls into brainwashed broodmares and all boys into labor camp slaves. Really? Could people really be so scared they would just let that happen? How could they sanction that? To not ever fall in love or even see the opposite sex? Not to have families? That sort of thing is programmed into our very cells. How could a society exist like that? 
 In the end with all the hype and having met the extremely entertaining author this book was a let down. It felt like the bones of a young adult story but it was written with juveniles in mind. So it ended up as a shaky mix of the two. At least it was a relatively quick read.

 This book had me from the very first chapter. I personally haven't read a dystopian novel in quite sometime and so reading Eve was a like breath of fresh air filled with originality, reopening my mind to a fictional world of danger, destruction, and survival. It was exciting, incredibly fast-paced and all-out enjoyable. I finished it in two sittings. 
 I admire Anna Carey's "fast-paced-page-turning" skill of storytelling. It definitely kept me interested and on the edge of my seat throughout the entire novel. The characters are different because the time is very different. Understanding Eve as a character is refreshing and relatable in many ways and watching her character develop drastically throughout the story was really great. 
 One thing I did not like about the book in particular; it didn't feel like a dystopian tale until something was mentioned specifically in concerns to the time or situation. In other words, it didn't necessarily stick out as dystopia from sometime after 2035. Compared to other dystopian novels I've read in the past, I guess they stood out much stronger than Eve when describing a future catastrophic circumstance? Another thing that bothered me was the lack of character understanding. I felt like there was this briefness when coming across characters in the book. Like there was so much more to learn about characters like Arden, Caleb, Eve and even Leif. Hopefully when reading the next book, these factors will fade away and prove to be a build up to understanding everything and gaining a better glimpse at the secrets behind the dystopian premise of this book. 
 All in all; great read!

Eve / 9780062048509 
 I picked up "Eve" from Amazon Vine because it was sold to me as a cross between "The Handmaid's Tale" (which I love) and "The Hunger Games" (which I also love). That was, as we will see, a dirty lie designed by marketers with black holes where their souls should be. And now I'm stuck having to write a review for a book that I flung to the ground in disgust at about the halfway point. However! I am nothing if not interested in helping potential buyers decide whether or not to spend their hard-earned money on a book, so here is my Very Useful Summary of the first third or so -- if you like this, PRESS THAT BUY BUTTON NOW. 
 EVE: It's the evening before graduation, where I will present the valedictorian speech because I am the smartest girl in the entire world! Which is not terribly hard because 98% of the population was wiped out by a plague, but still. Also, I have no personality whatsoever besides being naive, obedient, and utterly unsuited for a dystopian environment, and am therefore intended to be a generic blank for the reader to sink into. 
 ARDEN: Hi! I'm the social outcast of the school and everyone rightfully mistrusts me because I lie and cheat and bully people! I have a personality, though, so you'll wish I was your protagonist instead of Meaningful-Name-Eve over there. I'm going to flee the walled school because graduates aren't sent to college; they're strapped to beds and forced to churn out babies in startlingly unsafe conditions considering how valuable they are as baby makers. 
 EVE: I don't believe you because that makes no sense: why would they teach us waltz and Russian literature if that were true? (NOTE: This really does make NO SENSE.) But despite the fact that you are an established liar, I'm going to break out of the dormitory, nearly break my foot, nearly drown, and get my hands torn to shreds on thorns JUST TO BE SURE. ... Oh, crap, she's right. Welp, nothing for it but to escape -- I'll go get my best friend. 
 TEACHER: Halt! Oh, Eve, I see you've decided to escape. I'll help you, but there's no time to get your best friend. 
 EVE: OK, if you say so. 
 TEACHER: I do. Oh, but go into the crowded dormitory and pack everything you own including the last letter your mother wrote for you before she died. Wouldn't want to leave that behind. 
 EVE: Of course not. I have priorities. And I'll try not to trip over my sleeping best friend while I pack. [later] Wow, it's really hard to find food and water when I've only ever been trained in waltz and Russian literature. Oh! Arden! Can I come along with you, despite the fact that my presence will hinder you and possibly get us both killed? 
 ARDEN: Sure, but I'll glower at you while the reader again wishes that I were the point-of-view character instead of you who are so impractical you refuse to use blankets if they've had a dead person touching them. 
 EVE: While you hunt food for me, I'll just wander off into this Walmart. Oh! A baby bear! Baby bears are dangerous; I know that much. But it looks like Winnie the Pooh. (NOTE: I am not making this up.) I'll just pet him for a bit. Oh! Look at the plot twist that is so obvious a dead man would have foreseen it: an angry bear mother. Whatever will I do? 
 CALEB: Hi. I'm a literal savior riding a literal horse. Sadly, though, I am not the Old Spice guy. 
 EVE: Er, how do you feed and shoe and nurture a horse in a dystopia? 
 CALEB: Look, just get on so we can escape the bear. 
 EVE: 'K. Don't rape me, though. 
 CALEB: I'm not interested. 
 EVE: WHAT DO YOU MEAN YOU'RE NOT INTERESTED. "The plague had killed far more females than males. As one of the few women in The New America, especially an educated, civilized woman, I'd always supposed I was every man's type. [...] I was intelligent, I worked hard. I was told I was beautiful. I was Eve, the valedictorian of School." (NOTE: That is a direct quote in the context of Eve being offended at being told by Caleb that she's "not [his] type" immediately after she's been indoctrinated her whole life -- and been worried for the entirety of the book -- that all men are degenerate rapists.) 
 ...and that was when I threw the book at the wall, because if Eve thinks that rape is a compliment, then she's officially too stupid to live. (Also, I'm pretty sure the book maintains this rape-is-a-compliment theme, since -- if I gather correctly -- the King of America will decide that Eve will be his own personal baby-maker, come heels or high water. BECAUSE SHE IS JUST THAT SPECIAL. Obviously.) 
 The one good thing I can say about "Eve" is that it demonstrates how not to write a YA dystopia. Eve has no discernible personality underneath her whiny naivete, and it occurs to me that one of the reasons why I love Katniss Everdeen so much is because she's a distinct person -- she's not a blank for me to sink into, but an actual character worth following in her own right. And in "The Handmaid's Tale" -- which "Eve" wants to be so much it hurts -- Offred's gaps in her personality was part of the point; society was doing its best to strip her self away and that was a tragedy, not something for an author to aspire to. 
 While I don't demand walls of text to explain world-building in my dystopias, I do require the setting to at least make sense. The hand-wave for why a tremendous amount of resources are sunk into the girls' education is quite ridiculous; the Latin and Russian lessons were supposed to keep them occupied so they wouldn't become suspicious (and would make them erudite protagonists, obviously). The fact that a HUGE number of years and resources are invested into these girls only to then keep them in unhygienic conditions that I *guarantee* would have them dead in a few years flat cannot be chalked up to the Bad Guys being evil and stupid; the system literally should have collapsed on itself before we even get to Eve. 
 And if it had, we all would have been spared a lot of bother. 
 NOTE: This review is based on a free Advance Review Copy of this book provided through Amazon Vine, and which I am required to review as a participant of the program. 
 ~ Ana Mardoll

reference_books.review_text:
The first novel I read by Mary Kubica was absolutely spectacular, so I was very excited with this one as well but it was not as well done as the first. 
 I do love that Mary Kubica writes the novel from various people's points of view and some are in the future talking about the past while others are in the present, much like her first novel. This novel focused on a homeless girl Willow and her baby being taken in by Heidi and her husband Chris. Heidi can no longer have children due to a cancer scare mere months after having her first child Zoe. Chris believes his wife has taken in this homeless girl and her child to help out the girl, but then he starts to think maybe it's more about the baby.... as we are going through present time with Chris and Heidi we are slowly getting Willow's back story, but from the future where she is telling her story to a detective. Quite intriguing and it was a good book, but it just did not have the amazing ending punch that the first one did. I enjoyed the book and I would recommend it and I will most certainly be sticking with this author as her novels roll out.

 It is a bit gruesome, dealing with so much death in a tiny village, and coming from the POV of a mad-scientist type of 11-year-old British girl... but it's perfect. Charmingly, gruesomely perfect. 
 In the book, the town is looking forward to the opening of Saint Tancred's tomb, 500 years after his death. For proper ceremonial purposes, not anything weird, of course. But the whole fun in digging up the patron saint is doomed when Mr. Collicut, church organist, is found DEAD. (How many more people can die in Bishop's Lacey, I wonder?) 
 But the ending... those last words uttered by Flavia's father... ARE TO DIE FOR. I must read the next novel. I MUST READ IT SOON!
Another fun Flavia.
Flavia de Luce has to be one of the best literary detectives ever, like a pint-sized, non-smoking Sherlock Holmes!

Having previously read Alan Bradley's "A Red Herring Without Mustard" and "I Am Half-Sick of Shadows", two Flavia de Luce murder mysteries, I was unprepared for this truly excellent novel. My biggest "beef" with the previous offerings had been that Flavia, who is supposed to be 11-years-old, sounded like a 30-ear-old man and that she seemingly was not permitted to get any older. 
 I had expected, when I read the blurb on the back of the book, that once again Alan Bradley, mimicking M C Beaton, whose hero and heroine Hamish McBeth and Agatha Raisin are not permitted to age, each story starting afresh as if the clock had been turned back, would show us the same boyish Flavia. But no, after several novels, and presumably comments from irritated readers, Alan Bradley is finally allowing Flavia de Luce to show signs of growing up and slip into puberty, not matter how much Flavia herself may be resisting the "awful" transformation this has on her mind and outlook. 
 Plot 
 Set in 1951, the story begins when Flavia, uninvited, sneaks into the local church to witness the exhumation of Saint Tancred's bones, which have rested for the past 500 years in the the church of St Tandred's in the fictional village of Bishop Lacey. When the workmen are unable to lift the massive gravestone that covers the saint's tomb, Flavia is quick to grab the torch from one of the workers and poke her head and his torch where she's not supposed to - only to discover the bizarrely staged corpse of the young organist Crispin Collicutt. 
 From this point onwards its a rip-roaring yarn of Flavia trying to beat the other local detectives at their game. There are newcomers Miss Tanty, an elephantine soprano with huge bottle-bottom glasses and strange habits, and there is the mysterious botanist-cum-private eye Adam, supposedly a friend of Flavia's father. And then there's the legitimate investigator, Inspector Hewitt and his lovely wife Antigone. 
 At home in Buckshaw mansion, things couldn't be worse. The bailiffs are staking their claim. Will Flavia manage to unmask the killer and will the mysterious Heart of Lucifer be the saviour of Buckshaw and the De Luce family's fortunes? 
 The ending comes as a real shocker - not the unmasking of the killer, mind, for that one we see coming a mile off. No, the final sentence leaves one racing to the nearest library or bookshop to get one's hands on the next instalment, for Flavia's life is about to turn up-side-down in a wholly unexpected way...and not just because she's going to turn twelve soon and become a "proper" girl!

sample_reviews.review_text: It is rare for me to not be able to finish a book but this was one that can honestly say I couldn't get in to so ended up giving up on.

I really, really wanted to enjoy this book. The author clearly put a lot of time and research into the historical context, but I was really interested in Antonia's story. When the author would suddenly come back to present day, explaining historical references, beetles, zoo animal facts, etc. it was hard to stay engaged and I really had to force myself to finish it. Hopefully the movie will be better.

Nazi occupation of Poland is recounted from the perspective of an ambitious Warsaw zoo, whose matron kept a memoir. The fate of various animals is juxtaposed against the fate of victimized humans, and the idyllic description of the lovely city and zoo is contrasted with the unspeakable brutality of the Nazi's inhumane and insane attempts at genocide. 
 It is painful to write a negative review of a book that treats such an important chapter of human history. But . . . . 
 Let's just say that it is a history book, it should not be shelved as historical fiction. And maybe I don't love animals all that much, but I just couldn't connect. 
 It depends on what type of book you like to read. I loved All the Light We Cannot See, it had such nuance and complex portrayals of characters and situations. This book seemed dry and superficial by comparison. All the nice people are really, really nice and nearly all of the evil people are unaccountably evil. Then there are the numerous rabbit-holes of cute-animal stories. 
 Sorry.
I expected to love this but the third party narrative style bored me to tears. I just couldn't keep going.

The Zookeeper's Wife: Or, Animal Carcasses of WWII 
 No one can take away from the merits and bravery of Antonina Zabinski and her husband, Jan. Their story is truly terrifying and uplifting at the same time. Their bravery and kindness and humanity shines through. It's truly beyond imagination what they went through in Warsaw during WWII, how much they did to help Jews, and how the city was destroyed. 
 However, this "book" reads more like a textbook glimpse into their lives. There is no straightforward narrative, no journalistic insight. It jumps from place to place, dropping massive amounts of info and relating it (sometimes) to Antonina and her journal. There's no cohesiveness or narrative flow. 
 It was all interesting and sometimes shocking information. It pained me to read about so much death, animals and humans. How could humanity be so evil? Yet, the Zabinksi's proved that goodness still existed. 
 I'm glad I read this story. I learned many things I never knew before. However, I just wish the story was better written and had a more concrete, purposeful flow.

This sat in my bookshelf for a while - I assumed it was a novel, but it was actually nonfiction, adapted from a diary of a Polish woman who, with her zookeeper husband, saved hundreds of people from the Nazis when Warsaw was under occupation. Lovely and heartbreaking all at once.

This was a good (true) story but I found it difficult to really be wrapped up in the book. I think this is because it was hard to keep track of the people written about. It seemed there were endless names, some of which were only mentioned once or twice in the entirety of the book.

I was so disappointing with this one. While the story was incredible, I just so hated the way it was written and couldn't get into it the way I had anticipated. I recently read The Nazi Officers Wife, and was captivated by it. This was my choice in a newly started book club; I'm interested to get others opinions.

This book suffered the "read-in-the-wrong-medium" syndrome. I did the audio book of this, and looking back I should have picked up the book. The narrator was fine, she did a slough of voices and different accents, had good tone, kept the right pace. But there are just too many tangents, veers from the plot, and references to keep the main plotline straight and concentrated. 
 Once you dig through the historical research and find the plot- it was very interesting. This follows a true story of zookeepers Jan and Antonina Zabinski, who end up smuggling Jews around their former zoo to save their lives, and essentially hide in plain sight. It also touches on other subjects of animal "bloodlines" in relation to when the Nazi's tried to "clean" European bloodlines by eradicating Jews, historical hunting, and zoo ethics and non-ethics during this time period. 
 Now this book is non-fiction, but you can tell it is intensively researched. The author is well versed on the subject- a little too well versed. There are often times complete semi-related tangents on subjects. If she wanted to write about this subject in this way- why not write a non-fiction book? I was left confused about what really was true (she actually puts "in an interview from...." and "cited by..." in the text of her book- which lead me to believe it's factual. But then the storyline is only semi true? The author just wants the luxury of writing historical fiction, and be able to take liberties with characters and scenes- but also want's to be informational and show off her research. I get the feel of historical fiction is much different than non-fiction. But this seemed to teeter the line, and get confused between the two. You can't have both! The characters, development, and actual plot of what was happening at the zoo fell by the wayside to the historical context.

It would be unfair for me to properly review this book as it took me AGES to read it and I'm not a huge fan of nonfiction to start with. So, I'm going to give it a solid 2 stars and leave it at that. It was interesting to read about the real heroes during this time period who risked everything to save others, but I just couldn't get into the story.

reference_books.title: Nexus (Nexus, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I'm a sucker for transhumanism and cool stuff you can do to your brain to make you better. That's only a short distance away from the slippery slope down into a shameful pool of YA-esque wish-granting plots and perfect characters, but we're still not quite there. Naam has managed to narrowly (hence the 4 stars and not 5) avoid all that and yet still serve up a exciting and gripping thriller. I love it! 
 We dive down the rabbit hole of human body and brain modifications and we come to understand, through the adventures of our unwilling protagonist Kade, how an imagined future human society will react to the possibility of being overtaken by modified humans, much faster, stronger, and smarter than any of them. It brings to mind familiar storylines - us vs. them, fear of progress, political fights, and laws in place that oppress the non-humans. 
 Naam's background as computer scientist and the fact that he is on the advisory board of the Institute of Accelerating Change and a member of Institute of Ethics, among others, means that he is able to realistically paint a picture of the imagined science behind Nexus, and that he nails the philosophical ramifications of having access to biology-altering technology. 
 It's a solid thriller, but it lacks all the things that thrillers usually lack, such as developed characters. Kade and the others do feel too polished, their motivations too dumbed down and quickly thrown in as not to throw off the fast pace of the story. I personally did not find it too jarring, though. The book sucked me in nonetheless. Can't wait for the next 2 installments!

reference_books.title: The Bone Clocks
reference_books.review_text:
David Mitchell once again manages to blow my mind with the sheer magnitude of his writing prowess. I read his books just to highlight, on my ebook, clever use of adjectives or beautiful little quotes, or even just only to remind myself what strong, distinct voices and beautiful descriptions (that don't get long-winded) looks like. 
 If David Mitchell's books were anything else they would be beautiful geodes: 
 I don't even use pictures in my reviews but his books really do remind me irresistibly of them - you crack one open, and out spills beautiful crystals of every color, sharp with jagged edges, as though you could cut yourself with them... but the light they reflect is soft, dancing, playful, mystical. 
 The protagonist Holly's story is rich, beautiful, and layered. I love following her throughout her life, getting that little pleasant surprise when I see she was doing well with her old friend turned husband, Ed, who helped her when she was down, feeling a pang of sadness when her family members passed, and feeling dread as she grew old and vulnerable and feeble. 
 I love that the fantasy part of it is merely a sprinkling at the side - much focus is on the characters and how their lives intertwine around Holly. I had to skim through the bit at the end where the fantasy part takes the center stage of the story, because I'm not a fantasy person, and it bores me, but I'm glad the story returns to Holly in the end. Even so, the fantasy scenes were well-written, fast-paced, and rich with details. 
 Beautiful, beautiful writing.

book_a.title: Station Eleven
book_a.user_review:
Mandel has brought to life a gem of a novel and this is now one of my favourite books. This is a story centered around the before, during, and after of the fall of civilisation, exploring the human lives that impacted each other during the process, some actions that happened years before the Collapse leading up a domino effect to impact events decades after it. We are taken through the lives and journeys of a select few people that are intertwined with each other, and as the flu spread too fast for denial to catch up with it, we also experience the character's disbelief and haphazard, reluctant preparation for the end of things that they have not yet accepted will come. 
 "The television newscasters weren't exactly saying that it was the end of the world, per se, but the word apocalypse was beginning to appear." 
 The dreaded and impossible 'a-word'. This sentence summed up the entire atmosphere of the book. I had my knuckles in my mouth. 
 We also catch a very well-written and well-imagined glimpse of the future after the Collapse - people start the calendar from Year One and we go up to Year Twenty - which seemed bleak and depressing, but Mandel has infused hope and the human determination in every part of the story and it was wonderful to watch. The Travelling Symphony was the representation of that. I enjoyed cheering along with them and delighting in their love for the symphony and for each other. 
 Another thing that occurred to me while reading - Mandel is rather like the opposite of some authors like Stephen King. While King has perfected bringing out the absolute worst in every person in his stories, Mandel is keen on bringing out the good. Even the antagonist in the events after the Collapse had a great backstory that will make it impossible to hate him. 
 I really enjoyed this book. It frightened me and yet lifted my spirits. Can't wait for the next Mandel!

 It has one feature that I really liked - instead of being a post-apocalyptic novel, it shows the apocalypse. People die on stage (pun intended), and you see what it was like to be there when it happens. And that was something I'd never seen done really well.

sample_reviews.review_text: If you like Agatha Christie, you'll enjoy this send-up of British murder mysteries. It's all there--country house, jealous lovers, shady vicars and antique dealers, and a mysterious dog death.

I REALLY enjoyed this book. The first "part" was tedious for me but I realize now it was supposed to be??...the best part of the experience comes later, so hang on! 
 I just posted my reflections here: http://lesliesbookcase.com/2017/07/09...

From the creator of Midsomer Murders and Foyle's War comes the most predictable mystery within a mystery that exhausts every cliche known to readers of whodunits. 
 Convoluted, unsympathetic characters, and what seems like 1000 pages of endless red herrings. You can't miss WhoDunIt though. 
 A monumental waste of time.

I adored this novel by an author that I have only just heard of. Where have I been? 
 The tale gives homage to the old fashioned murder-mystery, but the delivery is current, exceedingly well paced (not too fast, or too slow) and flows from chapter to chapter with ease, offering well crafted characters and lots of twists and turns. 
 The construction is exquisite, from my point of view. It is "literally" a story within a story. 
 Briefly: the tale is about an editor, Susan, who receives the latest manuscript from one of her authors, Alan Conway - Magpie Murders, the last book in the series featuring private detective Atticus Punt - which she begins to read in preparation for publishing. The story she reads is set in the 1950s, where Mr. Punt and his assistant, (much like Holmes and Watson), go to a small English village to investigate a recent death (or two). This is to be Punt's last case for reasons that you will find out. 
 The village, of course, has lots of secrets, quaint settings, and interesting characters. But the investigation never reaches its climax because the manuscript is unfinished. Pages are missing and the author, Alan Conway, is now dead. Suicide, or murder? 
 Susan now has to find if there are more pages and unravel the other mystery. Not just One, but Two. Conway's death and the missing pages. 
 This leads Susan - who is quite the sleuth herself - on a journey of investigation, mirroring Punt's own investigation in Conway's novel, this being the clever part. The author, Mr. Horowitz, manages to create some extremely educated parallels between the two stories that make him shine as a creative novelist. This was standout for me. 
 The insights into the publishing world were interesting, as were all the little word puzzles within the plotting. It certainly had me trying to decipher things well into the early hours. 
 By the end, I began to believe that there might actually be a series by Alan Conway, featuring Atticus Punt and I wanted to know the ending. Sadly, this is not so. Perhaps this might spur Mr. Horowitz to consider the challenge - the gauntlet has been thrown. I should mention that I recently finished reading the entire Arthur Conan Doyle, Sherlock Holmes series and loved it. I wouldn't mind putting the Atticus Punt collection right next to it. 
 I would gladly suggest that anyone who likes a well thought out mystery should read this novel. 
 Five stars. 
 Sergiu Pobereznic (author)

I got my copy of Anthony HorowitzaEUR(tm)s Magpie Murders from the library and almost immediately I was concerned that this might not be the right book for me. You see the previous reader had folded back the pages to mark their place. What kind of a sick, twisted individual would do this? Is this the audience that Horowitz writes for? Would Magpie Murders be full of this type of deviant behavior? In the South they angrily call bending the pages to mark your spot: poking the possum. My liberal leaning friends call it: dropping a Trump on America. In the U.K. it is scornfully referred to as: nobbing the jolly trousers. Nowhere is it accepted in modern society and those that perform this heinous act are considered ill-mannered troglodytes that do not realize the library is loaning you a book and it is not meant to be vandalized. 
 Luckily, the contents of Magpie MurdersaEUR|the story contained in this sorely mangled publication were fantastic. And it is apparent that not only is author Anthony Horowitz in opposition to the practice of folding over the pages of library books to mark places, but that he would not hesitate to administer an ass whooping to any chump he notices doing this. (Note: Horowitz would not be using any Marquess of Queensbury rules but delivering a straight up Seattle sockjob.) 
 Magpie Murders is a whodunit hidden inside of a mystery concealed in an enigma, comfortably snuggled in a conundrum, and then hidden in a quandary only to be surprisingly encased in the chocolate shell of a puzzle. Mystery writer Alan Conway has turned in the latest manuscript to his popular Atticus Pund detective series. But it is missing the last few chaptersaEUR"there are too many suspects and no killer! His editor, Susan Ryeland makes a note to see where these pages went off to, but before she can locate them ConwayaEUR(tm)s lifeless body is discovered sprawled at the bottom of a tower on his estate. He has committed suicide. But has he? As Susan struggles in her search for the missing chapters one thing becomes crystal clearaEUR"Conway was not very well liked and similar to his submitted mystery novel, there is a long list of suspects who just might have done him in! 
 Horowitz give us the Atticus Pund novel to read as well as following editor Ryeland as she discovers all may not be as it seems in the authoraEUR(tm)s demise. Both stories are riveting and share clues and hidden evidence to deciphering the mysteries. ItaEUR(tm)s all very cunning and artful. Yet Horowitz makes sure not to shirk on fleshing out his characters or the plot. There is real heart here and Magpie Murders is a standout novel.
an enjoyable fun, clever mystery
Twisty, meta, whodunnit fun. Also, 10/10 would watch Atticus Pund Investigates.

What can I, a mystery aficionado, say about Magpie Murders? Well to begin with, I liked the fact that this book had a rather novel literary device which isn't very common in the mystery and suspense genre, a book within a book setup. However it was rather derivative and toadying to the works of the greats. It was brimming over with literary nods like some books overuse pop-culture references. That especially felt forced as if it were marketing the books mentioned. 
 It began well enough even though it felt overly familiar following which it devolved into a boring tedious slog and a very predicable one at that. 
 In trying to be too clever, it became obvious and overlong. It needed better editing, which is ironic given that the book takes place in the publishing world and involves the sleuthing skills of a book editor. 
 Anthony Horowitz is an Agatha Christie fan, as am I. He even worked on the long running Poirot adaptation and his love for all things Christie clearly shows in his writing. With this book, he tries to mix vintage Christie with poorly written and even more predictable contemporary works such as The Girl on the Train with their obviousness, melange of detestable characters and ultimate hollowness giving it an uneven feeling. It's a case of been there and done that by a sleight of hand. 
 It wasn't bad per se, I just expected more. A mystery novel should have an engrossing mystery, suspense and thrills galore and depth, I didn't find much of that here but it was entertaining to a degree.

If not for the ending, I would give it a perfect 5-star rating, at the moment, the rating stands at 4.5. What I love most about this book is the ingenuity of creating a mystery within a mystery. Also, I think Horowitz has been really successful in recreating the atmosphere of the golden age period while not forgetting the fact that we're in the 21st century instead of the early 20th century. 
 While I have praises for the book and really enjoyed the story, it's not without its problems. First and foremost, the main narrator of the book (there are two and I'm referring to the heroine) is not particularly endearing and the end just made me want to wring her neck. All the other characters are not particularly lovable either and the conclusion! I think Horowitz should just end the novel at the point where the Punt's story ended and need not drag us out into the real world and get us to only hate the heroine more. 
 Another interesting aspect of this book is how Horowitz inserts excerpts from the plot of other books in the Punt series. I personally think this is a very clever idea as spices up an otherwise ordinary plot. Yet, I can also see readers hating these excerpts as they lead to nowhere and deviate from the main story. 
 To conclude, I love Magpie Murders and I would certainly recommend this book to other readers, but I'm a fan of Horowitz and so maybe more lenient when I deliver my rating of this book. Still, I appreciate his efforts at trying something new instead of repeating the same formula over and over again.

Two mystery stories in one book. In one, a copy editor must unravel mysteries surrounding the death of a famous author that occurs just as he has finished his successful mystery series ... and you have that book, itself.

 ... yet, I couldn't find myself rating this one higher. Maybe it's just me, but the book just didn't have that "wow factor". It's a good book, don't get me wrong. I guess I just didn't like it as much as I was thinking I was going to.

reference_books.title: A Wrinkle in Time (A Wrinkle in Time Quintet, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
3.5 out of 5 
 A Wrinkle in Time is a wonderful children's book. It has creative characters and situations. It has a moral compass guiding the story. It follows an adventure through the pov of children. It teaches them positive lessons about life. As a book for adults, however, it is somewhat more shallow of an experience. 
 First off, many elements were too simplistic to be completely satisfying (as an adult). For one, the universe/place this took place in was more magical than 'possible.' There's nothing wrong with that, but I would consider this more fantasy than science fiction. Usually science fiction deals with possible things (which this does in the science aspects), and focuses on that science as a way of explaining the world (which this does not). Instead of setting up the rules of the world and then having conflicts that come out of those rules, in AWIT, obstacles arise and are explained when needed to serve the story (say for a plot point, or to add drama. Things like the magical glasses only being able to be used once). This gives the story a more magical, fantasy vibe. 
 The story too was overly simplistic to be totally satisfying for me. There really was no overt danger visible here. There were threats of being threatened, but no one was really threatened. And in actuality, there were only really a handful of scenes. While this might be appropriate for children (keeping things short and not showing anything too dangerous or frightening), I wanted more to happen. 
 Lastly, the logic here feels designed for kids as well. To quote the book: "IT could only give pain, never relieve it. The beasts must be good. They had to be good." This clear cut blank-and-white division of right and wrong is good to teach children concepts, but as adults, we know that it isn't the way the real world really works. We've learned sometimes the worst things feel good (that is why they are so destructive). We've also learned that this kind of conflict and ambiguity is more appealing (to adults), because it reflects the real world. 
 But those things aren't saying this is a bad book. They are just pointing out how this book would be more appealing to children than adults. There is a lot to like here. I enjoyed the style of writing here. It was very simple, not particularly 'amazingly' written, but the dialog struck me as interesting. It reminded me a lot of The Lion Witch and the Wardrobe in its style and elements. The characters too were interesting, and I particularly like Meg. Her inner struggle with confidence was both interesting and realistic. 
 The only real negative thing I found with AWIT was there was definitely a religious analogy going on. I felt, however, that it got in the way of the story instead of really serving it. If the "God" element would have been edited out, the story really wouldn't have changed. The message would be the same, and so would the story. But with the occasional reference to serving God and the like, I got the feeling that I was being subliminally preached at. This turned me off at parts of the story. 
 A Wrinkle in Time is a nice little book. It's quick, interesting, has a nice fantasy flavor, and a good message (I especially liked the non-conformist sentiments). If I had kids, I wouldn't think twice about reading it to them.

reference_books.title: I, Robot (Robot #0.1)
reference_books.review_text:
Hard Sci-fi ages the least gracefully out of all the genres. I mean, Social Sci-fi usually reflects a problem in society, and those problems never go away, so the message will always be renewed and relevant. But Hard Sci-fi tries to make a realistic prediction of the future. While good writers and those with insight may get many aspects right, their 'time' will inevitably fail them. It is impossible to predict what technologies unrelated to ones story will come in to existence that will change everything and mess up one's predicted future. But more importantly, and more deadly to a story of the future, it is impossible to predict how things we take for granted 'today' (like phrases of language, modern activities, etc) will become extinct in the future. Those traits will date a piece, and sometimes, kill it. In I, Robot, the 'signs of the time' haven't directly done that. Yet. They have, however, made it fit more into the past with stories like Them, more than with cutting edge, brilliant glimpses into the future. 
 As an older book, I'm divided about many things here, because there are many things I liked and many I disliked. First, I, Robot is written very plainly. No frills. No dramatics. Almost all dialog. The robots are never really described, the places are neither. While this leaves things rather dull 'visually,' this does at least prevent some of the 'science' from being overly-dated (you can fill in the details with ones relevant to your current era). This focus on dialog also makes for an interesting read, leaving the inner monologue to a minimum. Unfortunately, a great deal of that dialog is dated. The use of phrases like "Sizzling Saturn" and "golly" litter the pages, making this feel like some 50's sci-fi B flick. 
 I, Robot is also intelligently written. Each story explores a paradox of behavior, usually exploring the 3 robotic laws Asimov establishes. These present some classic sci-fi dilemmas, which are fun. But since these short stories probably weren't originally intended to be a novel, booked together like this, those dilemmas become very repetitive. A majority of the problems are 'loopholes in logic,' and very similar when read back to back. 
 The idea of documenting the future history of robotics is cool too. It was interesting to see how things advanced in a realistic manner in self-contained short stories. But since these were short stories, not every one was great. I found Little Lost Robot and Evidence to be the most interesting (and the most 'modern'). At the same time, I didn't particularly care for The Evitable Conflict or Reason. And I found one thing to be particularly annoying in many stories -- a reliance on logical laws to create conflict or bounds, but then conflicts that weren't actually logical (often the robots making emotional decisions or showing emotion). I guess I was expecting more puzzle, mind-looping logic. 
 And that leads to what I, Robot is -- the grandfather of sci-fi books, not perfect, but the beginnings of the modern robot. As that, it is the foundation of what is being imagined today, but as is a grandfather, it is no longer functional today. I, Robot has established ideas that have now become standards, givens. It will never lose that crown. But in today's world, I, Robot is much like Robbie the Robot -- interesting, a bit goofy, and way dated.

reference_books.title: Slaughterhouse-Five
reference_books.review_text: Interesting book, although I'm not sure if I understood the significance of everything. I didn't know why there was 'framing' around the story (ie - a writer writing a book and then we read his book). I also would not say this is sci-fi (even though it's on the top 100 sci-fi books of all time). It reminded me of Donnie Darko (which I wouldn't say is sci-fi either). Both are physio-psychological journeys (involving things that are fanciful, and might not really be happening). Here especially. This sounded like how one soldier dealt with the tragedy of Dresden and the war and how his mind created this fantastic escape (the aliens and being unstuck in time/memories) to deal with it. Some of the concepts here were cool (especially the viewing of the 4th dimension concepts), and the style to the book was interesting. I can see how some modern writers (Palahniuk and even Richard Kelly) were possibly influenced by this. An interesting read.

Wow. What a book. Written over 60 years ago and still very relevant today. After reading (and being disappointed by) A Brave New World, I had my reservations about reading 1984, for out of all genres, Sci-fi ages the least graceful. But I found 1984 to not be a book written in 1948, but something that could have been written at any time (even today). The prose was surprisingly clear, non-complex and succinct. It evoked the senses and had action and pace, something very modern. The structure too was arranged to build in tension and complexity (something I find lacking in 'dated' fiction). And above all, the message being told is as relevant today as it was back when the book was first published. That is what I believe makes this book so great, and so truly frightening. 
 1984, however, can at times be uneven, devoting extensively large chapters to 'explaining' dogma and politics. That said, the things said in those chapters are just as interesting as the plot and in actuality, all that 'info dumping' is truly where the core of the book is. In these political sections, there is a truth to what is being said. Things that might sound familiar. Things that may have happened in some form in your own country. That is when this book becomes riveting. That is when this book becomes truly scary. 
 And that effectiveness, that thing that makes 1984 so influential, is its powerfully accurate message about society and government, a fact that has and always will be a true -- the power of a dangerous (or any) government is its control over its peoples thinking without them realizing they are being controlled. The totalitarian dictatorships of the past are obvious examples (look at the Nazis and making genocide 'acceptable'), but what is more frightening is, some of the statements describing the ridiculously oppressive Big Brother government, describe even some actions done by our 'free' democratic governments. It is truly disturbing to realize actions in your country's past may have had the same purpose this fictional government had -- trying to control your thinking. 
 That brings us to the purpose of all of this. 1984 isn't meant to be just doom and gloom, it is meant to be a wake up call. Like 1984 says: 'Who controls the past controls the future: who controls the present controls the past.' Knowledge is power. And the only way to prevent such terrible acts of control from developing is for the people to have real knowledge of what is happening. As such, I think this book should be read in schools. When a statement, even fictional, can be still relevant decades, even generations later, it is proof that it is in some way true. 1984 portrays accurate signs of an unjust governing system. Things everyone should be aware of. Things everyone should fight against so that 1984 never truly becomes reality.

 I did two things on my seventy-fifth birthday. I visited my wife's grave. Then I joined the army. 
 "Old Man's War" is the first book in the "Old Man's War" series, by John Scalzi. It tells the story of the protagonist, John Perry, a septuagenarian, who signs up to join the "Colonial Defense Force", which is tasked with aggressively defending Earth and its colonies, against aliens. 
 "Old Man's War" is, at its core, a love story set up as military science fiction. John Scalzi has made this unlikely combination work brilliantly by adhering to a straightforward, linear plot. The action, of which there is plenty, is fast and heavy. This action is judiciously interspersed with slower sections, which helps build the story and drive the plot. This balance keeps the reader interested throughout and the book never palls. There is never a stage where technical gobbledygook or military wanking (*cough* Tom Clancy *cough*) gets to you. 
 Read the full review at my site https://wp.me/p89tYT-dA

I didn't dislike this novel as much as two stars might suggest, but it does seem rather that Scalzi is more interested in developing a concept for a story rather than seeing through the actual writing. Worldbuilding is hard to do well, but once an author has achieved it, readers also want the action that occurs in that world to have a memorable and compelling central conflict that is consistently present. Perhaps if Scalzi would confining his scope of action to a shorter time period, he would never have to use any equivalent of "and then some time passed" to hurry himself along to the next thing he wanted to put into the book. When his ideas are this good, they deserve a decadent kind of attention. A plot that builds in a closely connected, cascading fashion could better carry the reader along as a thoroughly absorbed participant in the world.

Re-read this so I could finally get to the rest of the series. I got a big kick out of it the first time, and I enjoyed it just as much the second time. OWM is a quick read, and thoroughly enjoyable as a modern take on Heinlein-esque military SF. It's also very funny, particularly in the hilariously gruesome asides describing human-alien encounters. 
 Granted, the characters are a little flat, but that does tend to go with this sub-genre, and Scalzi keeps the story moving. In this case, that makes up for a lot. 
 File under, "If this is the sort of thing you like, you're really going to like this."

Really a 4.5 star book, and I'm looking forward to reading the rest of the series. I like Scalzi's writing style and the stories are great, even as they slip into battle descriptions. Not usually my thing, but a credit to Scalzi's strengths as a storyteller.

At the age of 75 John Perry joins the army. Not any army but the CDF which is responsible for fighting for us humans in space. Nobody knows how much advanced they are but it's clear that they have access to a technology that extends the normal lifespan. Having the choice between growing old and dying within the next years, spending a limited time with the CDF sounds like a reasonable idea. 
 Reasonable or not, soon John Perry finds out that the universe is a rough place for a soldier... 
 John Scalzi is often compared to Robert Heinlein and I have to agree. He writes in an amusing style and the protagonist could easily be from one of Heinlein's books. There is a big problem with the pacing though. It takes almost half the book to start the adventure. It was fun to read about the military drill and everything related to it but it's not new and I expect more from an SF novel. When it finally gets more interesting, John Scalzi can't deliver. The events are too short and didn't impress me much. Add to this the pseudo-ethical discussions and the ultra light science part and the result is a novel that I finished in 2 days but that I probably won't remember anymore in two weeks. 
 If you look for a light piece of military SF, this is your book. Enjoy the ride and move on. Serious SF fans should stay away. Fans of Heinlein can give it a try but my bet is that they will be disappointed.

This is the third chick lit book I have read this month and it is not bad. I am starting to have a better feel for what chick lit involves and what things I like about the genre. My opinion is that chick lit resembles women's books more than romance, although romance is very important to these stories. I think that women's books look at people's whole lives, work, friendship, etc. And chick-lit seems to do that too. 
 Rachel, the main character of Something Borrowed has always done what Darcy (her best friend) wants her to do. She has followed Darcy's lead for a long, long time - maybe too long. So when Rachel decides to not be the good girl anymore, not to always listen to Darcy all of her life is up for grabs. I think in the course of this book, Rachel grows up and how she does that is a great story. 
 I think Giffin does a good job with this book. The writing is excellent for a first novel and she held my interest for the whole story. I had a pretty good idea of where we were going, but I enjoyed the ride.

I won't lie; I read this book because I saw the movie and found it... problematically sweet. Perhaps because I relate to Rachel, I liked this book despite the fact that I sometimes found it hard to believe the story line. Each of these characters is flawed, pretty obviously, and I think that redeems the book for me.

I thought this book was a nice, quick read and found it enjoyable but I was a bit disappointed by the ending. I thought everything wrapped up a little bit too neatly for my liking, especially with the sudden revelation Darcy gives at the end. It was a little bit too convenient, a little too perfect really. Rachel does a good job of justifying her relationship with Dex in her mind, calling Darcy shallow and mean, but I think that the author manages to have some genuine moments shine through where personally I was left wondering if Rachel wasn't over exaggerating some of Darcy's personality traits to try to feel less guilty about sleeping with her best friend's fiance. 
 I'll probably get around to reading the sequel someday just to see what happens with Darcy but it's certainly nothing I'm feeling like I need to rush out and buy.

 Three words: InstafreakingLove

The Promise of Amazing pulled me in with the super cute cover. Normally I tend to stay in the Fantasy or Science-Fiction genre and only venture out when something gets enough hype to draw my attention, such as John Green's works. But sometimes you just need a cute romance story in your life. 
 The Promise of Amazing is your typical, Young-Adult romance novel, and I don't mean that in a negative way. You've got Grayson, the bad-boy trying to go good for cute girl. Then there's Gwen, the good-girl trying to come out of her shell, not only for the boy, but also for other reasons I won't revel because of minor spoilers. The most interesting thing I have to say about this novel is how the two main characters interactions affect their mindsets and personalities. It is very masterfully done, and the supporting characters are written very nicely as well. While I found them to be a bit of a generalization of teenage boys and girls, I do have to admit they are pretty accurate representations of some of that age group. 
 My main complaint is the insta-love fad that seems to have taken hold in romance literature. What really makes me love a novel is the growth to people share by interacting. Not the physical, "He's so hot and I love him." and that is where this novel fails. To a certain extent I can understand the insta-love when writing characters in this age range as love does tend to come quick. But it's more infatuation. The love part comes after the hardship, after someone has stuck by you and you've learned the dark things about them that they hide from the world, not before. There could have been a lot more to this novel, but all in all it's a decent story. It doesn't drift very far from the shy girl meets hot boy story line but there are enough small twists and turns to keep it interesting. It is told in alternating chapters between the two protagonists which allows us to see both their mindsets and the characters are significantly unique enough to make me feel like I'm learning about someone new and not just the typical run of the mill lovers. It's a fun, easy, read. Not too good, and not too bad, and just right for you if you're looking for a cute, heartwarming, "I've learned a lesson and found my true love." read.

 RESENA: Este libro fue tan... adorable. Eso si, una cosa es adorable y otra extraordinario. Y os puedo asegurar que esta novela no cumple la segunda. Hay libros extraordinarios, que releerias miles de veces y que se hacen un huequito en tu corazon y otros que simplemente terminas con una sonrisa en la cara y te dejan un buen sabor de boca. Quizas la autora tendria que haberse pensado un poco mejor el titulo, ya que no esta nada bien romper una promesa tan extraordinaria (Vale, pongamonos serios...) 
 La historia comienza cuando Wren una chica cualquiera, le salva la vida a Grayson justo cuando este esta a punto de ahogarse con un perrito caliente, en una boda organizada en el catering que llevan sus padres y en el que ella trabaja todos los fines de semanas. 
 Wren es el tipo de chica que podria ser tu companera de clase en el instituto, lo cual me ha encantado. No tiene un pasado oscuro, ni problemas familiares, ni esta deprimida... (?A que os suenan todos estos topicos?) Solo es una adolescente normal, con dudas sobre su futuro y algo timida. Me ha gustado que en algunos momentos me pudiera sentir identificada con algunos pensamientos que tiene, o con su forma de ser. La verdad, esta bien ver que a veces las protagonistas de los libros pueden ser gente cualquiera, sin cualidades especiales, ni una belleza sobrenatural, ni una vida salida de una mala telenovela. 
 Lo unico que quizas me ha disgustado un poco, es lo facilmente que perdonaba a Grayson por todas las estupideces que cometia y lo rapido que creaba excusas para redimirlo de su comportamiento (aunque, la verdad, no se que habria hecho yo si estuviera en su lugar...) 
 Por otro lado tenemos a Grayson. Dulce, mono, gracioso y con un expediente un poco negro, se gana el corazon de Wren y del lector. 
 Despues de ser expulsado por vender trabajos entre los alumnos y de envolverse en un negocio peligroso con los cerdos de sus amigos Grayson necesita empezar de nuevo. Al principio, me parecia un poco estupido, dado a su atraccion repentina por Wren (de la que hablare mas tarde) y su comportamiento de tonto enamorado, pero segun avanzaban las paginas, he ido comprendiendole mas y mas, hasta llegar a entender sus acciones y meterme en su piel. Me ha encantado que no tuviera un pasado demasiado problematico (Ya vale de tanto nino maltratado/abusado/abandonado/huerfano) y que no se comportara como un capullo machista y sobreprotector durante el 80% del libro, para luego salir con la excusa de "Es que te quiero" (Ja,Ja,Ja,Ja). Esta bien, cambiar un poco del prototipo cansino que usan para todos los protagonistas masculinos de los libros juveniles. 
 Aparte de ellos dos, hay un monton de personajes secundarios (y no tan secundarios), todos ellos perfilados a la perfeccion, desde la cinefila y romantica Jazz, hasta al cerdo controlador de Luke. 
 Y ahora viene el gran pero y a la vez punto fuerte de la novela.... La relacion romantica. Empezare con una pregunta simple: ?es el instalove, alguna vez, siquiera una buena idea? En mi opinion, la respuesta es un rotundo y absoluto no, por la simple razon de que las relaciones basadas en un enamoramiento, tan rapido como las palomitas al microondas, no son creibles y mucho menos, reales. Creo en los flechazos, pero no en que conozcas a una persona y sin siquiera haber hablado con ella, ya empieces a pensar en como ese encuentro te ha cambiado la vida, lo guapa que es o lo mucho que te gusta. No, simplemente no. 
 Y ahi ha estado el fallo de "The promise of amazing", Wren y Grayson se conocen y sin haber tenido siquiera una conversacion, el ya esta fantaseando sobre ella las 24 horas del dia, llegando a decir, que ella es la unica que le entiende y que a su lado se siente comprendido y libre (WTF?). En esos momentos, deseaba poder sacudirle hasta hacerle entrar en razon y conseguir que dejara de decir tonterias cursis sobre una chica a la que solo habia visto UNA vez en su vida. 
 Pero bueno, antes de que salgais corriendo, debo deciros, que a pesar de su catastrofico principio, la historia de amor que el libro cuenta, me ha parecido bonita y sobretodo muy dulce. Quizas es un poco precipitada, pero debido a lo bien que la ha desarrollado Robin, los pros ganan a los contras. Ademas a lo largo de sus paginas, nos podremos encontrar algunas escenas tan tiernas, que nos dejaran con una sonrisa boba en la cara. 
 "So if I had said I've got a key to the cottage, we can be alone, you would have said, Sure, let's go?" 
 "Are you nuts? I would have said, No way, I'm out of here" he answered, pretending to get up. 
 "Stop" 
 His eyes got serious again (...) 
 "I'd go anywhere for you, Wren" he whispered. 
 And then he kissed me" 
 El estilo de escritura de la autora es agil y fluido, con lo cual el libro se lee enseguida, sin hacerse pesado ni aburrido en ningun momento. Ademas me llamo la atencion, las multiples referencias que encontre a series de television, peliculas y libros: La princesa prometida, Veronica Mars, Supernatural, Una paz solo nuestra... 
 La narracion alterna capitulos contados por Wren y otros por Grayson, a mi particularmente, me han gustado mas los de la chica, aunque leer las cosas desde el punto de vista de nuestro protagonista masculino, no me ha disgustado para nada. 
 La verdad, no se que mas decir sobre esta novela. No es una lectura imprescindible, ni puedo decir que me haya encantado, pero para pasar una tarde de invierno, no esta nada mal. 
 En resumen: "The promise of amazing" es adorable y tierno, pero no hay nada que le haga especial. Si estas buscando un romance contemporaneo, que se salga de los topicos juveniles, te gustara. 
 LO MEJOR: Lo mono que es y lo reales que son los personajes. 
 LO PEOR: El instalove. Ugh 
 UN MOMENTO: 
 Any time I checked off the reasons to avoid him, I'd picture him in front of school, leaning against his faded car. Hands in pockets, swoon-worthy grin, deep brown eyes full of the promise of amazing. 
 CONCLUSION: 
 NOTA: 7/10

If this was my first time at the rodeo I would have highly praised this book for its quirky characters and all the hijinks they get into. I don't really know what to say about tropes. I mean there's a reason that parents are killed off mercilessly: can't have curfews if you're saving the world. But now that I'm no longer a noob, I'm beginning to question characters' motives. For instance, you're telling me Camilla (a rich, beautiful, popular girl) 
 would want to be with someone like Sam 
 (which objectively is not beyond the limits of imagination) 
 but I'm sure people were picturing this guy 
 which would defeat the justification of his suffering if he looked like that. But that's besides the point. I'm just saying that it's convienent for Sam that he has someone who accepts him for who is while he's still judgemental as fuck. Totally paranoid, unable to divert from expectations, and readily conforms as a defense mechanism. Since he's perfectly fine standing by as his friends get bullied as long as he's spared. He's not interested in anyone other than himself or things not benefiting him. That may be an overexaggeration. It's obnoxious to think that he doesn't have to change a single fucking thing about himself when it's painfully clear that the life he's living sucks. 
 So Camilla comes into town (and she's not an alien despite the title led me to believe) and decides to fix Sam since he's too pathetic to do anything about it. Why does she constantly and willingly give time and effort to this idiot, I don't know. Instead of the "you're beautiful without knowing" trope it's altered to "you're a genius without knowing". Family drama goes down and Sam pretends to care but never once does he asks his mother if she's okay. Maybe it's a "guy' thing but he's so terribly socially awkward that he expects everyone to meet his needs and won't do the same for others. Mind you these are people he's supposed to be close to, especially Mike. It became this weird subplot that I forgot was of any significance because Sam doesn't give two shits. So I'm supposed to? 
 And then there's Camilla who is perfect in that lovable and quirky way. She a fucking goddess bestowing her grace to the plebeians that crawl beneath her. She finds a seemingly lost cause and gets to work making a weekend project out of it. It's predictable. The only considerate things about her character is that she has dreams outside of Sam's world. She wants to sing and compose but fears failure. What the fuck are you talking about? You sing for the first time on stage and get a standing ovation and that doesn't give you any self-esteem. Bullshit. This is just unnecessay in order to give her a flaw that ends up being a quirk itself. Since girl should know her place and not think she has talent or that hard work would make her cocky (something within that line of reasoning). She's confident in everything else about her so why not the most important thing which is music? That doesn't make sense. 
 Anyways, those are really just nitpicks about this book. The real reason that I'm not impressed is the fact that I've read stories like this one countless of times. There's nothing to differeniate it. It even fills the quota of one diverse character which is Mike as the Gay Character. 15 year old me would give it 4 stars.

Life in Outer Space by Melissa Keil is a contemporary YA novel and the author's debut. It was an excellent read. 
 Life in Outer Space is not speculative fiction, but it's about geeks and nerds and contains a lot of pop culture references (particularly horror movies) so I expect it will appeal to spec fic readers who enjoy YA. I read the US edition (cover pictured top) and I was gratified to see that Australian spelling and slang was mostly preserved. I was particularly glad to see the words "arse" and "Mum", the former of which shows up many times in the first few pages. 
 At its heart, Life in Outer Space is a story about Sam, a year 11 boy, his friends and, to a lesser extent, his enemies. The book tackles a few common teen issues such as parents getting divorced and difficult parents. There's also Sam's best friend, Matt, who mysteriously quits karate after years of loving it and Sam doesn't know how to confront or deal with the issue. Although there were some moments of teenagers being silly, I thought it was all quite realistic, despite Sam navigating his life with constant reference to movies. 
 I quite liked that it was set in Melbourne and that Keil wrote various Melbournian landmarks into the story. Sam and friends see movies at the Astor and go to Brighton Beach for a party. Although in terms of realism, I felt that maybe slightly more complaining about how long it takes to get anywhere in Melbourne via public transport (there were a few trips that must have required two trains to reach) would have been more believable. But really, that was my biggest complaint. 
 Keil deserves an award for how she dealt with the period of the book in which Sam is moping. Often those sections of books are disheartening to read but Keil peppers hers with witty lines that had me laughing out loud, possibly even more than in the more upbeat parts of the book. We understand Sam's pain but, in reading about it, the we needn't feel it ourselves. 
 My favourite storyline involved Sam assuming his life was following a particular movie trope (one I personally am not a fan of) but then subverting that trope. I know that sounds very vague, but spoilers. Suffice to say it was a very satisfying resolution. 
 Life in Outer Space was a very fun and enjoyable read. I highly recommend it to fans of YA, particularly fans of nerdy contemporary YA. I am impressed with this debut novel and I will be interested to see what Keil writes in the future. 
 5 / 5 stars 
 You can read more of my reviews on my blog.

Quirky. Witty. Enjoyable. 'Boy Meets Boy' had me gripped from the first page. 
 It was pleasant to dive into a world full of colourful characters, no looming apocalypse, no life threatening enemies, just a rollercoaster ride for your heart. 
 David Levithan paints characters wonderfully unique, whether they are a part of the main cast or ensemble. It had me paying attention to every word on the page. The same goes for the dialogue - it is a laugh riot at times. 
 The biggest drawback about this novel for me was that it was a little too gay - in the sense that nearly every character has a touch of Dorothy about them. And I don't mean that in a derogatory sense, it's only that it pulled me from the story because of the lack of realism. It lost that contemporary feel. The landscape was very 'safe.' Though, this aspect certainly did not detract from my enjoyment and love of the story. Contradictory to that, the setting allowed exploration of sexuality in many forms which would have been impossible in a more realistic setting; and you would have lost that candy-crush-light-hearted-romantic feel of the novel, because you would be faced with some of the more ugly aspects of society and how it deals with difference. 
 Additionally, it mirrors how sub-cultures develop in the wider community, as like gravitates towards like to create their own safe haven. 
 David's characters are always so beautifully flawed that you just have to wrap your arms around them with a big hug. I love reading his books and get such a different view of the world from my own. 
 'Boy Meets Boy' is a light read, embracing diversity, positivity and dry humour in one boys journey to find love. A great summertime read, or for a break away from heavier content to lift your spirits.

This was the first book of this genre I have ever read and it was cute. I think it gave me a good start in this genre however, I believe it was for below my age group. Non the less it was okay if not completely predictable and forced.

"When it comes to true dance, it's not about how you look, it's all about the joy you feel. " 
 Boy meets boy es algodon de azucar, es el sol despertandote por la manana, es tu cancion favorita sonando en la radio, es una taza de te y una manta en un dia de lluvia, es el equivalente literario de un momento de felicidad. La magia reside no tanto en la historia, sino en el universo en la que esta se desarrolla. El pueblo de Paul y Noah, nuestros protagonistas, es un tanto especial, con su drag capitan del equipo de fultbol, la creacion de la Alianza Gay para ensenar a los heteros a bailar o la prohibicion de los boy scouts y su sustitucion por los joy scouts debido a su principios homofobicos. El pueblo de Paul y Noah es un pueblo normal pero sin los prejuicios, odios y estupideces con las que tenemos que lidiar todos los dias. No se trata de una representacion realista del mundo, sino de una version mejor. Leviathan nos ofrece una alternativa, nos dice que un mundo mejor es posible, lo cual no solo es inspirador sino poderoso. 
 Pero no solo el universo es interesante, la propia historia, con todos los topicos de partida que vienen asociados a una historia de amor de instituto, nos ofrece algo mas. El hilo conductor de la novela es la relacion o mas bien el proyecto de relacion de Paul y Noah, pero a su alrededor tenemos un grupo de adolescentes lidiando con sus propios problemas y dramas. He leido algunas resenas que decian que esto hacia que la historia perdiera el foco, pero para mi es justamente lo contrario. La vida de una persona no se centra exclusivamente en su relacion amorosa y el hecho de que Paul tenga que lidiar y ayudar a sus amigos con sus propios problemas hizo que la historia pareciera mas realista. Por no hablar de que esta historia coral tiene mucho mas interes que el romance entre Paul y Noah, que aunque son muy adorables no dejan de ser extremadamente tipicos. 
 Sin embargo, no toda la historia es de color de rosa. Aunque tenemos un tono desenfado en toda la novela, esta presenta problemas muy reales como la homofobia de tus propios padres. Paul tiene casi una vida perfecta, hasta el lo reconoce, pero sus amigos no. Sus amigos luchan contra los prejuicios de su familia, las dudas sobre su propia identidad o la incomprension de sus companeros. Estos problemas, que no llegan a ser dramas pero tampoco pasan desapercibidos, nos muestran que incluso en el mundo de Paul y Noah hay que continuar con la lucha. 
 Por ultimo, no queria dejar de recomendar el audiolibro de esta novela. Personalmente creo que el hecho de que haya disfrutado tanto de esta historia es en buena parte gracias a Nick Ridebau, que da vida a Paul. La voz de Nick Ribedau es simplemente perfecta y consigue que ese mundo utopico en el que viven Paul y todos sus amigos parezca real. El resto de voces igual de bien elegidas y el acompanamiento musical (especialmente la version de la cancion de Leviathan cantada) son simplemente la guinda del pastel. Si teneis la ocasion, escuchad en vez de leer esta obra, !no os arrepentireis!
