(review originally posted on my livejournal account: http://intoyourlungs.livejournal.com) 
 I borrowed this book from a friend because, for the most part, I like Levithan's work. I've read his collaborative novels Nick and Norah's Infinite Playlist (which was light and fluffy, but fun) and Will Grayson, Will Grayson, which I also liked a fair bit (that was also due to the fact that it was co-written with John Green, who I LOVE.) My favorite of his work that I've read though, is his novel The Realm of Possibility, which is very, VERY geared for teenagers, but I was just young enough for it to really touch my heart. So, I've always been keen on reading more of his work, and since I found this on my friend's shelf, I asked if I could borrow it. 
 Well, this novel was okay. It wasn't GREAT, but it was far from terrible. 
 I have to say, Levithan really does know how to write with teenagers in mind. He writes in a really fun and whimsy kind of prose, that while at times it seems to come off as a little pretentious (it feels like he's trying to appeal to 'hipsters', or people who very actively try to go against the grain) is a breath of fresh air from the mediocrity of a lot of YA fiction. He also creates really quirky characters, which will appeal to most teenagers who strive so hard to be different and to find themselves. Paul, our protagonist was the one of the least quirky of the bunch, but a lot of the supporting characters were so quirky they were almost caricatures. 
 The experiences these teenagers go through is also quite authentic: coming out of the closet to your family, having a falling-out with your friend because of boy/girlfriend, etc. etc. Nothing in this book comes off as OMG DRAMMAAA (unless Infinite Darlene has anything to say about it) but it IS dramatic at the same time, because these characters are still teenagers; it just doesn't come off as superficial, or soap-opera-ish. It helps that not absolutely everything in this book is resolved, save for Paul and Noah's relationship, which reinforces a realistic depiction of the teenage experience. It does end on a note of hope though, which is good of course. :) 
 However, there were little things in this book that struck me as kind of odd. For one, while Levithan is great at realizing quirky and distinct characters, it feels like the whole friggin' town/city this novel is set in is quirky; the record where nothing is organized in any particular order, the video rental store that only rents out VHS and refuses to put out DVDs, I mean, really? It's very cute and all, but it's completely unrealistic that those businesses would stay open. This little descriptions came off as pretentious, but I can see sects of teenagers (re: hipsters) gobbling this stuff up. I'm sure I would've if I had read this when I was 15-16, as opposed to 21. These are little things though, that when it comes down to it, don't detract from the story as a whole, so I can let it slide. It still managed to irk me just a bit though. 
 The other thing that nagged at me a bit was how fast Paul falls for Noah. Now, I can totally understand having a crush on someone after having only one conversation with them. When you first meet someone and you get those butterflies in your stomach after they talk to you? I dig that, and that's what Paul seems to experience with Noah at the beginning of the novel. But when they start to get to know each other and hang out and date and whatever, Paul starts musing that he might be in LOVE with Noah. That's when I'm like: "Whooaa boy, slow down. You've been dating this guy for what? A week? Two? MAYBE three?" It drives me crazy when *anybody*, not just teens, throw the word 'love' around like that. Sure, you can like the guy -- you can like him A LOT -- in that amount of time, but love is a big dealio. 
 And what the hell was with Paul's kindergarten teacher writing 'Paul is definitely gay' on his report card? I was in Concurrent Education for two years and let me tell, that is breaching ALL KINDS of teacher's ethics writing something like that. I also get annoyed when adults claim they can tell a child's sexuality at so young an age. I had a friend when I was little who loved to wear girl clothes -- dresses especially -- and would argue with me constantly over being the pink Power Ranger when we were playing pretend. Everyone in the neighborhood was *convinced* he would be gay, but as far as I know, he's straight. So, I don't know, that whole little tidbit annoyed the hell out of me. 
 The whole talk of these kids dating in grade school was also strange. Yes, lots of little kids say they have a 'boyfriend' or 'girlfriend', but Paul seemed very serious to me when he said that Joni and Ted have been dating on-and-off since the fifth grade. Uh, what? I'm sure they called each their 'girlfriend' and 'boyfriend', but that isn't "dating" when you're in the fifth grade. Paul also goes through the list of people he 'dated' while in grade school. Just, what? Maybe if it was more clear that he didn't actually consider them exes it would be funny, or something, but he seemed quite serious when listing these people to the reader. 
 I want to go back to stuff I liked though. I *loved* the friendship between Paul and Tony. It was very touching seeing how much these two cared for each other, and also refreshing that the love triangle wasn't between the two gay best friends and the third party. I was actually very impressed with all the friendships that Paul has, and how Levithan wrote each of them. The fall-out between him and Joni was kind of heart-breaking (who hasn't lost a friend because they started dating someone?). The side-story between him and Kyle was also nice, even if I was annoyed with Paul for kissing Kyle; way to lead someone on, even if he didn't know Kyle wanted to pursue something more. 
 Final Verdict: Levithan is really a great writer for teens: he writes quirky and distinct characters who really jump off the pages and is great at writing about stuff that most teens go through in a very authentic way. His writing as fun and quirky as his characters as well, which is a plus, even if it came off as kind of pretentious (for me) at times. There were a bunch of little things about this novel that just really irked me though. Yes, they were small things, but it was a bunch of small things, which kind of amassed into a bigger thing. This is too bad, because Levithan really is a good writer. Will I continue to check his stuff out? Probably. Is this a great piece of GLBT lit? Definitely, even if I found Paul and Noah's relationship moves a little fast; but that's more symptomatic of YA in general, really. However, their relationship is still much more authentically realized than a lot of other romantic relationships I've read in YA. 
 So, with all the said, a definite recommend if you're looking for some decent GLGT lit. However, as a *whole*, this novel had some kinks in it that bothered me a bit. Little things, yes, but they added up.
Maybe a little bit too idealized for my liking. If you like fantasy...enjoy.

reference_books.title: The Hunger Games (The Hunger Games, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Whenever I hear countless good things about a book I feel almost obligated to either prove them wrong or join their ranks. With the Hunger Games by Suzanne Collins, I have to agree with the majority that it is an amazing book. I've read others like it (The Running Man and The Long Walk by Stephen King, The Manhattan Hunt Club by John Saul, etc) but it is very different in it's own way. The story follows Katniss, a girl from District 12, who takes the place of her sister to fight for food for her family, and her life, in the Hunger Games. Two "tributes" are chosed from Districts 1 through 12 (a boy and girl between ages twelve and eighteen. The older you get, the chance of your name being chosen grows. There can only be one person left alive and that person will live in comfort for the rest of their lives including their family. To Katniss, this is greatly needed especially because in District 12 "you can starve to death in safety." The book is incredible, despite it's being written in present tense. I usually hate that but it really works with this novel. It is a bit predictable, but most novels are to some degree. It is worth the time.

reference_books.title: Rising Sun
reference_books.review_text:
Congo took us to Africa. Airframe took us inside and outside of airplanes. Pirate Latitudes took us back in time. Now Rising Sun takes us deep into Japanese culture. I know that it came out before a few of the books I just mentioned but I am amazed at how well Crichton can capture things that are not known to the majority of people whether it is scientific studies or other countries or both. 
 Rising Sun is a murder mystery and is one of the few mystery novels that impressed me both because of the skill of the author and because of the lengthy solution of the mystery. It was a very fun book full of details about Surveillance equiptment. Some may find that repetitive examination of a film boring but I enjoyed how that could turn something so small into a massive clue by skillfully inhanceing the film. Very fun book and very enjoyable with a ton of info as usual.

reference_books.title: James Potter and the Hall of Elders' Crossing (James Potter, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I am very impressed by this novel. Honestly, I can say that it is different from, but just as good as, the Harry Potter novels written by J. K. Rowling. It was well-written with new and likable characters and the format of the book was the same. It covers Harry's son James' first year at Hogwarts and his adventures with his friends Zane and Ralph. The adventure in this book is a little similar to the Deathly Hallows with the gathering of three relics, but it is totally unique as well. This book some how managed to compliment and expand upon the endlessly interesting world of Harry Potter. Also, the length of the book was what first made me take it seriously. It isn't huge, but it is longer in word count than the Half-Blood Prince and the following two are even longer. I haven't read the other two yet but I definitely will. In fact, writing this review is taking away from the time I should be spending on the reading. Lippert has rekindled that overwhelming feeling of curiosity that I had when waiting for the next Harry Potter novel. I am surprised that more people haven't read these yet. I recommend this book and the following two (even though I haven't gotten to them yet) to anyone who has read the seven Harry Potter novels. 
 Again, all I can say is that I am impressed.

reference_books.title: Handling the Undead
reference_books.review_text: Handling the Undead was my second Lindqvist read and, will wonders never cease?!?!?, because this zombie novel is "DIFFERENT"! "But, zombies kill people like the entire, like time, right?" Wrong, this has a little more depth than that. "But people get there brains eaten out of they're faces a lot, right?" Absolutely not. In fact, the zombies are about as normal in regular zombie terms as your grammar. Anyway, now that anyone reading this sits in slack-jawed wonder, I can say that this book is by no means fantastic, despite my sarcasm. Yes, it is a very fun read, but only because the Sweedish author takes the zombie genre and, if I may be so crude, reanimates it, not by ancient voodoo, lightning, or by translating something that really shouldn't have been translated, but rather by using the sometimes neglected powers of creativity. The zombies in this book are not hostile, at least not for quite a while. They are even creepier in my opinion because you as the reader do not know what to expect from them, just like the characters who are still alive. The zombies act like people with massive amounts of brain damage and are treated the same way that mentally challenged people are treated in society today. The book involves morals, something I can't get enough of. Should they just kill the zombies, again? Should they dig up the remains of those who may be reanimated? Are the undead the same people? What will religions have to say or do about this occurence? How will the families of the dead react to their newly risen relatives? What do we do with the dead? How do we...handle...the undead? Had to do it, but anyway, the book's characters didn't interest me all that much. The dead ones which lacked personality were more interesting and that isn't really all that great of a thing. I was intrigued with the plot from the beginning though and enjoyed the book as a whole. Not as good as Let The Right One In (unless it is the American film apparently hahaha...) but still a nice addition to the ranks of horror.

reference_books.title: The Restaurant at the End of the Universe (Hitchhiker's Guide, #2)
reference_books.review_text: The Restaurant At The End of the Universe is the "delicious" second installment in the HHGTG series. If you have forgiven that first statement, allow me to tell you that this book is no less brilliant than the first, but the feel of the story began to change for me. Things begin to happen with amazing rapidity and the laws of physics and common sense are broken, shattered, and recycled as firelighters. I urge all to read through the confusing bits though (if they are confusing to you) because this series is just that, a series, and it must be read in its entirety. The description of what the Restaurant at the End of the Universe actually is and the popularity of it will always stick with me as well as the band who's concerts are so loud, they change the climate of an entire planet forever. In short, no surprise here that this book is full of surprises. Good ones.

book_a.title: Bag of Bones
book_a.user_review:
Bag of Bones was a book that I only liked the first time I read it and loved the second. Perhaps this is because I listened to Stephen King read the audio the second 
 time or because I was a little older and more mature about fiction and not so easily driven to bordom by the story's sudden switch to dealings in legal custody and a 
 budding romance. When I first read it, I was immediately frustrated because, at the time, it seemed like typical King who just has to cram as much into a book as he 
 possibly can. Please remember that this is imature me thoughts. Now, in 2011, this change left me in awe at King's skill which shouldn't surprise me by this point but 
 still somehow does. His ability to create characters that I can relate to, even when I have nothing in common with them, is an art that I don't even try to understand. 
 The creepy factor is not lost in this novel either. In fact, Bag of Bones is in my top five list for King's scariest novels now. The only reason why I gave it four 
 stars instead of five was because it tended to drag on just a little bit and some of the romance between Mike and Mattie really annoyed me at certain times (her nearly 
 frantic attitude of trying to get him in bed for example). I guess the lesson I learned from this book, or rather from me giving it another try, is that, if you have a 
 favorite author, some of his books are worth a reread even if you weren't all that impressed with them the first time. Now, if it is something by someone like Chuck 
 Palahniuk, don't bother because your brain may be trying really hard to convince you that it is funny and good, but it will eventually self-destruct from the built up 
 pressure of its own delusions.

book_b.title: So Long, and Thanks for All the Fish (Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, #4)
book_b.user_review: This fourth book brings us back to the Earth, or should I say, brings Arthur back to the Earth after eight years of journeying the galaxy. sample_reviews.review_text:

Fun reading for those who enjoyed the previous books in the series.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Review originally posted on Nightjar's Jar of Books. 
 SUMMARY 
 After spending her whole childhood in seclusion, hidden away from the evil Queen Julia by her overprotective but emotionally distant father, Amelia is finally able to break away when she insists on leaving home for university. But, now exposed to the outside world, she finds herself pursued by mysterious people with extraordinary powers, and caught between her duty, and the life that she now knows is out there waiting for her - if only she has the courage to go after it.Bound by Duty was published in 2014, and was Stormy Smith's debut novel. It is the first book in the urban fantasy series, Bound, which continues in Bound by Spells and Bound by Prophecy (projected for release in November this year). 
 STORY [3/5] 
 The premise of this book is quite gripping: Years ago, the evil Queen Julia killed off all the Elders - a powerful group of mages - but not before their leader was able to make a prophecy of her downfall, at the hands of a girl born of all "the five families". Amelia is that girl, which I'm sure will come as no surprise to anyone who picks up this book. However, instead of trying to have her killed when she found her, Queen Julia arranged for Amelia to be betrothed to her son, the prince.A lot of the book was romance-centric, but I felt that Stormy Smith did a good job in making sure that the romance didn't overshadow the plot entirely - and Amelia probably spent about equal amounts of time agonising over her love life, and her duty and heritage, which was somewhat refreshing. 
 CHARACTERS [2/5] 
 Amelia is the main protagonist in this book, and she's a truly awful one. She's whiny and selfish, and she throws ridiculous tantrums whenever she doesn't get her way - and, worst of all, the other characters in the book almost always seem to act as if her behaviour is justifiable. She also has this incredibly hypocritical issue about people not telling her things (even when they have good reasons for it), but has no qualms whatsoever about hiding things herself - even when it's important information that could potentially save their lives, and which she has no reason to want to keep hidden!The character-rating for this book goes from "dire" to "okay" because of two of the side characters, however. The first is Micah, who was undoubtedly the most interesting character in the book: He's initially portrayed as a rather sketchy character (and his backstory is something of a mystery), but he does his best to help Amelia out, even though she doesn't fully trust him. The second character is Aiden, who spends the majority of the book seeming like your usual stereotypical dream-boy - wildly attractive, inexplicably devoted to Amelia, and distinctly lacking in the personality department - but towards the end, he began to show some promise.There are a few other important characters, too, who I should probably mention - but none of them are particularly interesting, I won't say too much: Bethany, Amelia's beauty-queen best friend; Cole, her overprotective brother; and Queen Julia, about whom we're told nothing, except that she's evil. 
 ROMANCE & RELATIONSHIPS [1/5] 
 First off, you should be warned that the main romance in this story (between Amelia and Aiden) is heavy on the insta-love, which I know a lot of people find off-putting. I personally don't mind it, as long as it's done well (e.g. Maggie Stiefvater's Shiver trilogy), but in this book it really isn't - mainly due to all Amelia's annoying character traits that I discussed above. They just make the whole relationship seem incredibly shallow and contrived. The other romance in this book is that between Bethany and Micah, which seemed initially like it might be quite interesting, but unfortunately we never see much of them when they're together.As for the platonic relationships, the most prominent ones are Amelia's relationship with her brother Cole - which is strained due to his long absence from her life - and her friendship with Bethany, which I found decidedly unconvincing: We're constantly told that they're the best of friends, despite the fact that, as first-years at university, they can't have known each other for more than a year. This might be believable on Amelia's part, since she's never had any friends her own age before (except her brother), but on Bethany's part it's definitely not. 
 WORLD/WORLD-BUILDING [1/5] 
 The prologue of this book reads like the introduction to an epic high fantasy novel, but this is misleading. The series is actually an urban fantasy, set in our own world, but featuring a hidden society of magic users who are divided into four races: Mages, Hunters, AniMages and Elders. Nothing about any of these groups is ever explained, however - we're told that AniMages can turn into animals, that Elders are very powerful, and that all the Hunters are on Queen Julia's side, and not much beyond that - and nor is the presumably-hidden world that they live in.World-building is certainly something that I think there'll be more of in the second book, but with fantasy series in particular, I really feel that a good amount of the first book should be dedicated to introducing the reader to this new world - something that Bound by Duty utterly failed to do. 
 WRITING [3/5] 
 The writing is probably the best thing about this book. There's nothing that really stands out about it, but it's incredibly engrossing, and it flows really well - factors which combined to make it quite difficult to stop reading. 
 OVERALL IMPRESSION [2/5] 
 An interesting, well-written story, which is, unfortunately, completely overshadowed by unconvincing relationship dynamics, and the most irritating lead character I've ever come across. 
 RECOMMENDED FOR... 
 Fans of Tahereh Mafi's Shatter Me series might like this, as the the books are quite similar in their attitude towards romance, and the writing was somewhat reminiscent of Jennifer L. Armentrout's work (but less witty). The relationship between Amelia and Bethany may also appeal to those who liked Rainbow Rowell's Fangirl, though Cath's friendship with Reagan was portrayed much more realistically.

This review was originally posted on my blog, Hiver et Cafe 
 I received this book as an e-ARC for a blog tour in exchange for an honest review. This fact does not affect my opinion in any shape or form nor was I compensated in any way for this review. 
 This book, I enjoyed immensely. I had been reading a bunch of "meh" books lately and this one really pulled me out of that trend! 
 I was a bit confused in the beginning because the setting seemed to be really "fantasy" in the beginning, but then it shifted into the modern world and I was like, "What??". And then it mentioned Brighton, which I only know of in England and so I was confused again. I eventually concluded that it was somewhere in the States, and everything was okay again and I could concentrate on the story. 
 I love the cast of characters in this book! Amelia has been belittled by her father her entire life. He constantly tells her to stay in control of her powers and because of his craziness, she's never had any friends before she moved away to college. She's also betrothed to a prince that she's never met before who also happens to be the son of the crazy Queen Julia, queen of all the people with powers. I totally sympathize with her and her frustration, especially as she learns to control her powers and learns of her destiny. Things just keep happening to her and for someone who's always being told to stay in control, she certainly doesn't have much of it over her own life. She's forced into positions where she must choose between what she wants and what is right. (Which is of course where the title comes into play. ;D) There were many times where I was mentally shouting at Amelia to just go for it and it was frustrating, but her reactions and hesitation were understandable, considering her background. 
 I love love love Bethany! She's Amelia's best (and only) friend and roommate. She's from Mississippi and she's got sass! She's a lovely character and a great friend to Amelia, especially when she doesn't tell Bethany all the crap she's dealing with. She's understanding and gives great advice. She doesn't get jealous and she pushes Amelia to leave her shell and go out into the world. I want Bethany to be my best friend too! 
 And can I just say. Aidan. YES! Aidan is so hot and also very very yummy. He's loyal to Amelia and I love that he's understanding of her limits and her boundaries. When she tells him that she wants to slow down, he slows down. He doesn't push her and he doesn't whine about it. He tells her of his intentions to kiss her and he literally says that she runs the show. (Can I have an Aidan please and thanks?) He's also tatted up and also has that "damaged" quota that fills my fictional boyfriend checklist. And I think it needs repeating that he's also hella hot. 
 That's enough about the characters. The plot! I understand that one of the things in the plot was supposed to be some big reveal, but I just about guessed it from the beginning. Another thing that happened was a tad predictable, I just thought that it wasn't going to happen in this one. Other than the vague things I'm saying about the spoilery bits, the concept of the powers is quite interesting. The different powers of the Mages are attributed to different colours. Amelia, being an Elder, has powers that are purple, while her brother has powers that are green. 
 While I wouldn't say that it's overly original, it's well written and well crafted. After I got over my confusion, I was sucked into the plot and I pretty much read it in one sitting. I also want an Aidan for myself. I think I'm going to add him to my fictional boyfriend harem. This is a fantastic debut novel from Stormy Smith and I seriously can't wait for the next installment in the story. I literally just finished this book! Look out for this one guys!

This was a BIG DNF! I hated all characters. Awfull! Amelia was so annoying. Some transitions were really bad. Out of the blue they got attacked and the next second they are safe (as if a door could safe you from really bad people). nOp! And I couldn't follow all decisions Amelia made because I think there were some thoughts missing..

So, as another commenter said, I can see how she got SOME inspiration from Rachel's Higginson's Star Crossed series, but that is where it ends. Also, because I am so in love with that series, this one was just what my little heart needed to get over the ending of that series. With that said, I love this book, I got the ARC and didn't put it down until it I was done, and I found myself cursing the author (jokingly, of course) at the end because I DIDN'T WANT it to END yet! Ahhhh, now I have to wait, such is the frustrating deliciousness that is a first book in a series. I'm going to have to go ahead and read it over and over until the next one comes out, just because I'm going to miss all my new friends. Alright, let's get down to the good stuff. 
 The heroine is Amelia, and she has been stifled her whole life, and at the mercy of the decisions of the men in her life. Can't blame her for wanting to make her own decisions and be in charge or her own life for once! So with spunky side-kick Bethany, she enters the world of dating, with a hunky guy who is just too human for those in her life. As her frustration builds, her magic build until she just has to release it. Noticing her struggles, Bethany's boyfriend comes to the rescue...I won't go any further than that. 
 Suffice it to say that things escalate, and Amelia slowly unravels the mystery of who she really is and her importance in the life of her people. She is bound by duty, but will she choose duty? Or will she choose love? Hmmm, guess we'll have to find out!

Book: 
 Stormy Smith has created a marvelous story. Bound by Duty is a tale full of magic, heart break, love, and mystery. When I started reading I was quickly drawn in and found it hard to put it down. I really like the characters, some more than others and found myself feeling right along with them. I could especially feel the pain of Amelia and Aidan. They have both been through so much and there is so much more to come. I did enjoy the little quips at times between the characters that would help lighten the mood and I just love Amelia's best friend. She is one of those characters that just brings a smile to my face. Amelia does seem to get herself into some pretty bad predicaments throughout the story. Then I got left on a cliffhanger that left everything so far up in the air that anything could happen next. Where will this journey lead us? It promises to be quite an adventure of love and sacrifice. 
 Audio Book: 
 Overall the narration by Kristin James is good and easy to listen to. She helped bring Stormy Smith's book to life. I love that she reads with emotion in her words. I do feel that she kept her voice too soft which made it harder to hear at times and she needs a little work on accents but other than that she did a great job. I did thoroughly enjoy listening to Bound by Duty.
The premise of the novel and the story itself are interesting, but the characters are very flat. It was a book I wanted to like, but one-dimensional characters kill me.

This author was brought to my attention by a follower of my blog and she had nothing but glowing things to say about this series. So when Stormy contacted me about reviewing her books I was ecstatic, especially because PNR is my absolute favorite genre. And when there's magic involved?? I'm so there!! 
 When I come across a PNR novel I'm always curious to see what kind of world the author creates and how it differs from others in the genre. The creativity alone never ceases to amaze me. Stormy has done a fantastic job of delivering a uniquely crafted, magical gem! Everything about this story had me all giddy. The different types of magical powers and their coordinating colors was an interesting touch, along with the variety of supernatural beings and their individual backgrounds. I was just like a kid in a candy store with this story, could not get enough. 
 Secrets, secrets, and more secrets! Everybody's got them, but what will it cost to uncover them?? Amelia has to overcome a lot of personal obstacles while trying to figure out what is fact and what is fiction. She's been giving quite a few different "truths" but she'll have to get to the bottom of it all to really understand who/what she is, what she's capable of, and why the safety of her peoples rests solely on her shoulders. Throw in a love interest, an arranged marriage to a prince, a human (mortal) best friend, a queen intent on controlling everything & everyone (resulting in the fight of a lifetime), and you've got one gripping story line! 
 Needless to say, I really enjoyed this book from start to finish, and would definitely recommend it!

DNF 25% in. I feel like everything is going on in different directions like the characters seem to have bi polar. They would just yell each other. To me the past wasn't really clear on the history nor from who we got it from this far. I was already feeling confused and I just didn't want to waste my time. It's sad bc the story seemed interesting. I also wished the author was more descriptive when it came to the magic instead of just describing as purple/green light.

Click here to see my review on my blog here! 
 I love that feeling when your reading a book and it's like your transported to that reality because you are so invested into the plot and characters, it's all you can think about. Bound by Duty by Stormy Smith did that for me. This was a epic new YA Fantasy Paranormal Romance that you won't want to miss! 
 Amelia our MC is a broken girl who is trying to find herself all while being told who she should be. At 18 she moves away from her Father and closer to her brother, for college, to get a little freedom before her life isn't really hers anymore, and to find out who she really is and why everyone says she so special when she doesn't feel an ounce of it. From there her life take a turn for the good and the bad. 
 The Good- she makes a great BFF, who would do anything for her. I loved Bethany. She is very happy go lucky all the time and looking at the bright side of things. Every girl should have a BFF like her. Amelia also meets Aidan, a mouth watering, swoon worthy guy who I can officially say is added to my Book Boyfriend list! Right from the start it is hard for Amelia to resist his charms and good looks,, but she tries because she knows it can never be. Over time though she finds it harder and hrder to resist and they have some earth shattering, hot moments that make you can't help but root for them. I loved the chemistry between them, and I really hope the best! Team Aidan all the way! 
 The Bad: Amelia's life was never as it seemed, and she's gonna find out things that change everything. People will deceit her and the life she was finally starting to feel like she could control may just be ripped right from her! My heart goes out to Amelia and I can't wait to continue her journey in the next installment! 
 This is Stormy Smith first published novel and I was blown away by how engrossed I was. I devoured the book quickly, reading every chance I could get between work and my little devils :). There's Magic, Mystery, Deception, Monarchy, & Swoon Worthy Men. What's not to love! The ending will leave you for sure wanting more too! Book 2 now please! :)

Amelia has grown up sheltered by her father. She has broken away from his hold to attend college and try to make friends and a life for herself. She has powers though that she has no idea what they are or how to control them. Amelia belongs to a group of Mage but she herself is an Elder. Since there are no other Elder females she is unsure of what it even means to be one. Amelia has also been promised to marry a prince, the son of an Evil queen that has wiped out the rest of the Elders. All Amelia really wants is to live her own life and make her own choices. 
 I picked up this book because it was classified as a New Adult Sci-fi/Fantasy. The biggest problem is it really doesn't even seem the characters are mature enough to be considered a Young Adult book. Amelia herself being the biggest offender of the characters very often comes across as an immature 12 or 13 year old. Her first interaction with Aidan she simply just runs off and from there it doesn't seem to ever get better. Even Amelia's older brother who is supposed to be 8 years older didn't seem to interact the way someone of his age should. Aidan's idea of getting a girl's attention is to steal her seat in class and call her doll.... just no no no. 
 The entire maturity level just seemed to be completely lacking throughout so no matter how good or interesting a plot could be it just couldn't save this one for me. The plot did have potential but the characters would need a lot of work to have gotten a better rating.

book_b.user_review: This reads just like a true crime show, exploring a scandal almost as unbelievable. Though the story runs a bit slow sometimes, it's worth the detail and preciseness in which David Grann lays out one of the most chilling conspiracies in American history.

sample_reviews.review_text: I can't believe this is a true story... and yet, I can. "White privilege" at its best, folks. Greed is a powerful, powerful sin.
Absolutely fascinating and eye-opening. A must-read.

Had no knowledge of these events at all (mass murders of the Osage Indians in the 1920's in Oklahoma). This book tells the story of the murders, the cover ups, the investigation, and how all tie in to the formative years of the FBI. Reads like a novel; hard to believe and devastating.

It was an excellent book and definitely an unknown topic for most Americans. However, I found the many characters somewhat confusing and hard to keep track of. I listened to it on CD so I'm sure that contributed to my not loving it since I couldn't flip back pages, etc.

There are three parts. The first is about the Osage and the riches they were given for their oil caches in the twenties. Over two dozen murders occurred in the Pawhuska, Oklahoma area. The second part is the investigation and the involvement by the beginning of what will become the FBI. It also documents the trials of prominent and not so prominent individuals. The former Texas Ranger, White is a hero on many levels. Part three is an account of David Grann's extensive research and new insight all these years later.

America, as a nation, will never not need constant reminders that its foundational crimes were not limited to particular moments in history, and to a few particularly bad actors. David Grann has written one such reminder.
I read this for a book club. I'm not really into this type of nonfiction, but the story was interesting.

Watch a mini-review in my August 2017 reading wrap up! 
 This book is an amazing blend of historical nonfiction and true crime. Because of that true crime element, is has more of a traditional narrative structure than a lot of historical fiction out there, and this made for some very engaging reading. That said, if you're not used to reading historical nonfiction, parts of this book can definitely come off as a bit dense. 
 Killers of the Flower Moon is heartbreaking, but not particularly surprising given the US's history when it comes to the treatment of American Indians. Grann's research is meticulous, and he's able to paint a vivid portrait of life in Oklahoma during this time, as well as just how atrocious the treatment of the Osage nation was. 
 Overall, a great nonfiction read, particularly for people who tend to stay away from the genre.

This book was really interesting primarily because of it's subject matter. I didn't know anything about the wealth of the Osage tribe and the Reign of Terror that violently took the lives of so many members of the tribe. Grann did a lot of research and he tells the story in a way that really helps characterize the main players in the events and keeps it interesting. Definitely worth picking up if you're into history or true crime.

reference_books.title: Love Letters to the Dead
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 This book is another epistolary novel about a girl going through the grieving process for the recent death of someone young. (Odd how I ended up reading two of these so close to each other for the staff book club. I wonder if the person who created the reading list realized how similar they were.) While this protagonist still seemed really young and naive and foolish for the age given, I found it more believable in a way. Perhaps because she was so openly grieving and repressing that grief, and because she clearly was so very susceptible to pressures from her friends and family. I also preferred the writing style to the last I read, though the brief biographies the author gave for each of the celebrities became more annoying the more of them I read. I suppose it's to provide a background for the younger audience for which this book was written, but I felt like it was a bit redundant and a bit too obvious, which stalled the actual story. 
 The story itself was an interesting growing-up and dealing-with-trauma type of thing. It dealt with quite a few heavy issues for a book with such a young-sounding protagonist (physical and sexual abuse, grief, depression, mental illness, alcohol, drugs, sexuality, etc.), but that's not necessarily a bad thing. I really liked and appreciated the emotions Laurel was going through, the grief and the guilt and the anger and the sadness. They resonated with me, especially as someone who suffered a personal loss at a young age, and I kind of wished the author had focused more on that feeling than on trying to remind the audience why the particular celebrities she'd chosen were supposed to connect to the story. The end came up quickly, but was fairly satisfying, if a little tidy. It left you in a comforting, hopeful place, which I think is what I need in a book with a theme of grief. I know this is Dellaira's only book thus far, but I think I'd like to read something in a different style from her. The way she handles heavy emotion has tons of potential.

reference_books.title: The Marriage Plot
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 This was another of those books that I wanted to like more than I did. I'm beginning to suspect that most contemporary fiction just may not be for me. The general coming-of-age concept is one with which anyone can identify and understand, especially when combined with "the marriage plot." I actually like Mitchell and Madeleine's stages of marriage age, because being around the "Stage Two" age, of course I notice the same patterns. It makes you wonder sometimes about marriage and how it comes about, which is a different story. 
 Or is it? After all, how does Madeleine and Leonard's marriage come about? Because they were in that stage, or because they were in love? In my opinion, it's because they were in anxious denial. Madeleine seems determined to believe that if she just keeps open-minded about mental illness and steady on the course, that will be enough to cure Leonard. He on the other hand, is a scientist who feels like science is failing him, understandably frustrated and anxious to get on with his life. What happens when obstinacy and panic fall in love? A rushed and ill-conceived marriage, which even poor Mitchell, soul-searching in India, can see coming. 
 Yet it's not the relationship woes, frustrating as they are, which make me feel unsatisfied about this story. Given the characters (whom I admit I didn't find easily relatable or likable), their conflicts are sadly true. I read one review which called the book "over-written," which it may be at times, but at others it can be nicely descriptive. 
 I think my main problem with this coming-of-age tale is that nobody comes of age. Nobody ends up anywhere. Nobody does anything. At the end of the novel, the three characters are in virtually exactly the same positions they were at the beginning. The sole exception is Madeleine, in that she finally knows (kind of) what she wants to do with herself. But considering that Madeleine has had virtually no personality for the majority of novel outside of being Leonard's caretaker*, I can't bring myself to feel more than just vaguely pleased for her. Most of that pleasure lies in the fact that I hope she can finally live some facet of her life now. 
 *This made me think multiple times of The Dive From Clausen's Pier, and that question, "What do we owe those whom we love?" Despite my weariness with Madeliene, she demonstrated the struggle with that question beautifully.

reference_books.title: This Shattered World (Starbound, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I normally try to keep my reviews as well-worded as I can, but I have to be honest that the first word that comes to mind for this book is "blah." It just seemed so needlessly long. Most of the first two-thirds of the book are spent with Jubilee and Flynn (great names) running back and forth between the caves and the base and reciting over and over "I shouldn't be thinking about him/her" or "I don't know why I'm trusting him/her" or "He/she isn't one of my people." It was redundant, annoying, and didn't even have the decency to face the tropes head-on as the authors did so bravely in the first book. Even the guest appearances of Tarver and Lilac didn't help, despite it being nice to see them again, because Tarver's trip to Avon seemed pretty useless. All the information he gave them could have been sent via computer - oh wait, it was. It's a shame, because I think the characters and the world would have been a really nice continuation of what the authors began in These Broken Stars, had it not dragged so painfully.

reference_books.title: The Flame Alphabet
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I finished this book over a week ago and quite honestly, I've been putting off writing a review because I simply disliked it. It was quite a disappointment because the premise was so intriguing. When I'd first read about this book online a couple of years ago, I immediately wanted to read the book. I wanted to know how language could become toxic, why only children were affected, how this epidemic would be addressed. None of these questions were answered. None. The characters were unrelatable and unlikable and underdeveloped. They inspired no interest and no sympathy. The writing is disjointed, which serves the premise, but not to the point that it makes the read worthwhile. I never leave books unfinished, but if I hadn't been reading this for Eclectic Readers (and facilitating the discussion), I would have dropped this one.

book_a.title: I Feel Bad about My Neck: And Other Thoughts on Being a Woman
book_a.user_review:
** spoiler alert ** 
 Now clearly, I am nowhere close to feeling bad about my neck yet, so perhaps I should have picked a different book of essays for my Book Bingo. I mean, I turned thirty several months ago, have been confused in the past eighteen months with a high-schooler, and I feel like a grade-schooler. That being said, there are several of Ephron's films that I absolutely adore, and I could not resist when this one showed up in the library listings. And in the end, no, I didn't really identify with a lot of Ephron's rants (albeit humorous rants) about aging as a woman. 
 However, I do identify with some of the simple frustrations of being a woman, being in need of an affordable home (though my definition of "affordable" is unsurprisingly very different from Ephron's), and hating how much I need my glasses sometimes. And her essay "On Rapture" is something every book lover will understand. Not to mention, I shamelessly snagged titles and authors to add to my reading list. 
 If I were to read this in ten, twenty, thirty years, I'd probably identify with more of it. I'd probably rate it higher. But as it stands, I ended this book feeling like I wanted to live more, write more, re-watch my favorite Ephron movies (When Harry Met Sally... is one of my favorite movies of all time still; I wish I still had the essay I wrote on it in college), and have Ephron by my side to guide me as I age (I may have to photocopy "What I Wish I'd Known" as what I really want is to have someone whisper the appropriate statement for my life on a regular basis). That's certainly not a bad takeaway for such a quick read.

sample_reviews.review_text: Nothing mind-blowing, but a fun and quick read!

I slogged through this book. I really wanted to like it, because, well, it's Nora Ephron. But it just wasn't humorous to me at all. I enjoyed her thoughts on reading/connection to books, but honestly, that's about it.

I read somewhere this book was hilarious. It wasn't. It was mainly a boring narration of author Nora Ephron's life. Although we catch glimpses of the same voice that wrote "When Harry Met Sally" and "Sleepless in Seattle" --which comically resonate in the universality of the banal details of our lives-- these stories are simply not funny enough to merit their becoming a book. She had a great life and a knack for pinpointing the little things we all go through, which should have made this book very appealing, but instead dragged on and felt pointless.
All the various subjects are kind of shambled together. It's part biography and part funny, girly, I mean womanly, advice.

From Silkwood to Heartburn to When Harry Met Sally, Nora Ephron is a genius storyteller with a lovely sardonic sense of humor. I picked up this book at a library sale for less than $1, and it proved to well worth the purchase. Ok, that didn't sound like a compliment, but I think it is a compliment that Ephron would understand. Besides, I have to get even with her for breaking the news to me that, being 41 years old, I have exactly one more year to enjoy my neck before it completely degenerates to the point that it must go into hiding under turtlenecks in various shades of black. I do not own turtlenecks. I feel my collar bone is one of my sexiest features and display it openly every chance I get. However, according to Ephron I probably will be having less and less sex as I continue to increase in years (goddess willing, it will be a good many, many years more), so none of my angst for the physical inevitabilities of age is probably worth the effort. 
 Ephron and I do not have much in common: I am not a foodie (beyond the fact that I will not eat anything that has been hormone induced, corn fed, contained in filthy and confining pens, and/or genetically modified...I don't eat much, in which case, I am not a foodie); my purse is organized and I own more than one (though see absolutely no point in spending more than $20 on anything that will, inevitably, end up worn and grimy despite being organized since I actually use my purses and not just admire the name on the tags); and I cannot dream of affording to have my hair done twice a week, botox, shrinks, or to fly to L.A. to purchase a pair of jeans from a boutique frequented by Nancy Reagan. 
 Still, yes, an empty nest is underrated, the joy of a good book takes priority over all other matters, and I remember every minute of being in labor 22 years after the fact (it hurt like fucking hell!). 
 Pour a glass of wine and enjoy the read. As for me, I must go find a sale on black turtlenecks.
Quick read, some funny moments and truths, but not all that great. Favorite line: Most everyone wears black-except for anchorwomen, United States senators, and residents of Texas...

Can't see what people like about this book written by a usually clever and witty woman. I didn't like it at all, it felt as if she wrote it during one weekend, flippently chatting with some girlfriends. Admittingly I would not have picked it up at all if it was not book of the months in one of my groups, but nevertheless as I like Nora Ephron's films, I had expected more.
Nora Ephron, please be my BFF.
So depressing and jumbled. It's a mix of stories she's done for magazines. I didn't laugh once.

Okay, this doesn't necessarily count as "read" because I stopped. I hated it. I was angry I wasn't reading my other book (this was a book club pick). I read it about 50% of the way and then realized I didn't have to take a test on it, I could just stop reading. So I did. The short snappy sentences that make Ephron's dialogue sparkle in movies are boring in a monologue. The content of the essays felt like all the worst cliches about women aging. No thank you.

book_b.title: A History of Glitter and Blood
book_b.user_review:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I was warned before reading this story that the book was "weird." It is, in fact, weird, but I get where the author was trying to go with it. It was an interesting world with an interesting premise, and I think I would have liked it if it had been told in a more traditional fashion. As it was, the jumps back and forth through time and the multiple interruptions in the narration really just made the book uninteresting at first (because the reader doesn't have enough information to actually care), frustrating later (because the information coming is now confusing or not communicating the stakes well enough), and a slog by the end (because you're just tired of trying to make sense of it all). The ending got a lot better, but there was still a lot missing. I think there could have been so much done with this world, these creatures, these themes, but it just didn't pull together in time for me.

sample_reviews.review_text: good book, strange but interesting.
I gave up around 40% because it was obvious the story was going no where. this was the epitome of dull fantasy. there was no worldbuilding, and the characters had nothing to them.
Such a strange book. It felt like I'd been tossed in the middle of the story and never got caught up.

I received this book for free in exchange for an honest review. This does not affect my opinion of the book or the content of my review. 
 First and foremost, thank you to Chronicle Books for this ARC. The synopsis had interested me previously, so when I saw it on display at BEA, I started chatting with some of the publishing staff. After a few minutes trying to hash out the book together (It's about fairies! And gnomes! And the gnomes eat the fairies and there's a war! But then they fall in love?!), they pulled out a galley for me and asked me to figure it out for myself and report back! 
 I'm still not sure how to describe A History of Glitter and Blood. It was... Weird. Odd. Bizarre. Dark. Interesting. Strange. Different. THERE'S the word I want, different. 
 The synopsis does a LOUSY job of summing up this book. A History of Glitter and Blood really is about fairies and gnomes (and tight-walkers), and there really is a war. But the war is more of a supporting subplot and not the main storyline, if that makes sense. The true story here is really about the characters and their interactions and relationships. This book is pretty dark, and involves some elements I wasn't expecting, like prostitution and polygamy. FYI, the storyline does revolve around sexual themes, but again, isn't the main plotline, if that makes any sense at all (probably not, because this book is crazy). The world building is pretty weak, but that's because, like I said, the point of the story is the characters and their relationships, not what's happening around them. 
 I won't lie, I struggled quite a bit with the way A History of Glitter and Blood is written. It's a total jarring mess at times, to put it frankly. There were a couple of times in the beginning when I seriously considered putting the book down because it was SO DISJOINTED, but then something would happen that would make me want to read just a bit more and figure out where it was headed. 'Cause uh, it's all real confusing at first, and the narrator is ENTIRELY UNRELIABLE. But if you stick with it, you learn why the writing feels so crazy, and then it actually all starts to make sense in a bizarre way. At one point I thought to myself, "Huh, the author was kind of brilliant with how she wrote this book!" 
 By the end, I was FEELING SO MUCH for the characters, and I think that was the point. I just wanted them to find their happy ending!!! I thought the court scene was genius, and by that time I was doing in-my-head cheering for the characters. 
 Overall, this definitely ranks up there for oddest/strangest/most different books I've read in a while. It's not going to be popular with a lot of people. You have to be looking for something totally different and be willing to push through the crazy writing and stick with the book. I think most people who DNF this book will do so because they didn't stick with it long enough to get what the author was trying to do. If you think you're wanting something different and don't mind hanging in there, then you might enjoy this one in the end. 
 This review was originally posted on Books Are My Thing

1.5 stars 
 "There is no narrative. 
 There is nothing about Scrap. 
 There is nothing about her. 
 There is dry, pointless, objective, timeless history." 
 Have you ever read postmodern fiction? If you haven't, count your lucky stars. It is the single most pretentious genre I have ever encountered; it leaves Augustus Waters and his unlit cigarette in the dust. 
 Postmodernist authors essentially go out of their way to make a story as weird as possible. Metafiction, pastiche, illogical magical realism--it all goes in one big pot of fragmented timelines and big flashy symbolism tags. A History of Glitter and Blood greatly resembles that genre. The narrative not only jumps between past and present in an inconsistent order, it has these out-of-place lines that remind you the person writing this is not the protagonist. 
 "Remember to take that out in the final draft, that's stupid, I've got to stop making things that aren't about Cricket about Criket." 
 Those aren't notes made by Moskowitz, like I originally thought. They're made by the character writing this book, who is an entirely different person than the protagonist Becks, whose thoughts and actions we see in third-person. No doubt it's creative, but almost too creative to the point it irritates rather than inspires. 
 Then there's the world-building. This reality is populated by fairies, gnomes, and another species called tightropers, which I still don't have a clue what they are. But practically every aspect of their life is the same as ours. They have hair spray and pasta and guns. They look the same as us. So are fairies humans then? Glitter-coated immortal humans that lose limbs and pieces of themselves, because apparently they're delicious to gnomes? 
 I told you this story is fucking weird. 
 No one ever questions the way things are. Machines exist, so science exists, but no one has ever thought to look into this losing-chunks-of-yourself thing. They just accept it and go about their gothic filter life, communicating themes and shit. 
 I read up to 58%, then just skimmed the rest. I feel no less because of it. 
 ARC received from Netgalley. quotes taken from an uncorrected proof and may be subject to change.

I received an eARC of this book from Edelweiss in exchange for an honest review. This does not affect my opinion of the book or the content of this review. 
 Initial Reaction: 
 A History of Glitter and Blood by Hannah Moskowitz was a pleasant surprise. I'll admit I had my doubts going in ESPECIALLY seeing so many DNF reviews on Goodreads. I can honestly say having read the entire book I don't know why people gave up! I loved it :D This book is nothing like I've ever read and this made it interesting and kept me on my toes. The book follows the story of three friends (Beckan, Scrap and Josha) as they navigate their way through a war. 
 As the title suggests the book is a history of the war, or at least it tries to be ;) At the beginning of the book I was slightly confused. The narration had a tendency to head hop, there were sentences that made no sense, and then there was an instance where the author told him/herself off! I didn't understand this! I thought surely it was a mistake and it was distracting to the narrative and quite frankly boring characters. 
 Then about 25% in I had an "ah-ha!" moment. This history was being written by one of the characters which explained the times in the story when things didn't make sense and as the author of the story wrote more he/she deviated from just the history and it became very similar to a love story! I LOVED this aspect. It was a story about friends who became family and the love they had for one another, what they did for each other, and what happened to each of them during the war. 
 The story begins with a hunt for Cricket one of the fallen members of their "family." Josha is mourning, refusing to leave his room, while Scrap and Beckan search for just a piece of their friend. You see they are fairies, immortal beings, and cannot die. Every piece of them, even the glitter they shed, is sentient. So begins the story. 
 I like the characters! Beckan is a strong leading lady. She's the glue of the family and the author's main interest. Scrap will do anything for his "family" even go down into the gnome mines. Josha is hurting and a bit on the selfish side in my own opinion. And Cricket, even though he is dead from the start of the story, his character shows up a lot and plays a prominent role. I fell in love with him and hurt for the friend he left behind. 
 Overall I enjoyed the story. I feel that if you gave up/DNF the book that maybe give it another go. If you can make it to the ah-ha moment of the book things really start to make sense and the writing gets better as the book progresses showing the progress of the character that is writing the story. I loved the paranormal/fantasy elements of the story as well. It was an interesting take on fairies and gnomes along with other creatures. And the war! Though it plays a large role in the background of the story it is over at the beginning. 
 Now there is a caveat to my review ;) While this book is billed as a young adult, I do not feel that it is appropriate for that age...maybe 16+. The characters have a very open relationships, along with two of the MCs being prostitutes to get by during the war. It can be graphic as far as the violence goes and there is quite a bit of strong language (the F-bomb being a favorite). Otherwise I enjoyed the book! It's not for the faint of heart and if you give it go, stick with it through at least 25-30% before you decide to DNF....pretty please :D I think anyone that enjoys fantasy, dystopians, and a little romance will enjoy this one. Plus the open ending has potential for more from these characters!

I received a free copy of this book via Netgalley. Thank you so much, Chronicle Books, for this opportunity! 
 So this book was very painful to read. 
 And I'm very disappointed because I expected a lot from this book. I'm a huge fan of fantasy (I love the genre to bits!) and I really love reading about fairies and gnomes and such. Plus, the beautiful cover was such a huge bonus to me! I thought, "HECK YES. This book would be perfect!" 
 But ha. I've heard that there were negative reviews on it, but I literally disregarded them. Now I feel like I've been slapped in the face and was told, "I told you so!" :( I am literally so disappointed! 
 Reasons Why "A History of Glitter and Blood" Didn't Work Out For Me: 
 1. Not that this was to blame, but the formatting of the e-ARC was INCREDIBLY MESSY. There were random photos popping out in different parts of the story, and it literally made no actual relevance to the story (well, maybe just a little bit, BUT STILL. What are they? :( Some paragraphs were broken from random notes, images, and "smudges," and the story will continue right after that huge line of images, and it was just too confusing!! And distracting. 
 2. The beginning was partially slow, and the writing was very easily to slip away from. I really couldn't connect well with the writing. Sure, I read the words in the story, but I really could NOT imagine any of the scenarios being described. Maybe it was the pictures or the weird formatting that was partly to blame...? 
 3. Characters were confusing. I couldn't really connect with them as well. I'm not even sure how the characters were related to one another because they were barely introduced well in the story. 
 4. Talks of sex and prostitution... I really don't know what to feel about that either. 
 Truthfully, I skimmed around 30% of the book because I was slowly losing interest. If only the formatting was done better, maybe I could've paid more attention, I guess. But nonetheless, A History of Glitter and Blood was a disappointing read, and I wish it could have been way better that what I've read today. 
 This is just my initial review. Full review will be posted at my blog much closer to the release date.

I will say that I TRIED to read this. I got a decent amount of the way through and still felt like I was confused. I felt like the writing was all of the place for me, and it was very hard to stay focused on what I was reading. There were too many names being thrown out there which didn't help me. I couldn't remember the parts that I read, so I decided to put this on my Did-Not-Finish (DNF) list. I honestly do not know if I will get back to reading this book., but for now its going to be checked off on my TBR list.

I'm confused. 
 There's not enough darkness to be Gothic, there isn't beautiful language to be lyrical, therw isn't an interesting main character, and there's too much going on in terms of magical beings for me to follow. 
 Sadly I had to give up on this one even with the killer title.

I just couldn't do it. I hate not finishing a book but this one was so messy and confusing. One minute they were in the present and the next there was a random flashback. Plus there were these random illustrations that popped up when nobody was even talking about them. I had high hopes for this one, but it was a huge bust, and I was only 23% in.

reference_books.title: Still Alice
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 This book was amazing. I finished it in about 3 hours because I just couldn't put it down. I didn't expect such an emotional read but I was crying by the time I finished it. 
 If you have a parent or a loved one with Alzheimer's, this book is extremely hard to read. On the other hand, I highly recommend reading it because it gives insight to what they might be going through. 
 The author makes the characters so real and makes you fall in love with Alice. You want everything to come out well but given the topic of the book, it is obvious that it is a sad read even though it had a "happy" end. 
 The one thing that I did not like was when Alice was unable to find her pills once she found her suicide message. It just seemed like the author wanted to have a happy end and therefore made her lose them. I felt that it would have been, in a way, happier if she could have found them and committed suicide because that is what she really wanted to do when she had the capacity to think it through. However, this is a book that I would like to read again to see all the little nuances that happens throughout. 
 Words cannot really explain how much this book touched me. I recommend it to anyone who is dealing with Alzheimer's or just wants a really good read.

reference_books.title: Slated (Slated, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Not as good as other dystopian novels I've read lately. Not much happens, other than a lot of talking. The ending is too rushed also, and just leaves everything open for the next book, which I probably won't read anyway. Sad because it seemed like a good concept for a book.

reference_books.title: Breathe into Me (Breathe into Me, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Couldn't even bring myself to finish this book. Typical teenage characters, which means not realistic in the least bit and typos everywhere. I usually always finish a book but there wasn't even a storyline halfway through that I wanted to know more about.

reference_books.title: Taken (Taken, #1)
reference_books.review_text: At first, I loved the premise. It reminded me a lot of The Maze Runner, which I really liked. I also liked that it was a male point of view because you don't get many of those in dystopian YA books. Unfortunately, it was downhill from there. It felt like the author tried to take every cliche of dystopian books and throw it into one, really quickly. Disappointed.

reference_books.title: Fade (Wake, #2)
reference_books.review_text: 3.5 stars - a great installment to the series.

book_a.title: Fifty Shades of Grey (Fifty Shades, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Horrible writing style, one dimensional characters, really flat sec scenes and an incredibly fucked up relationship. Can we please have a popular book with a strong female character and a healthy relationship? 
 2 stars only because I'm curious enough to read the next ones to find out what happens and it's a really quick read.

sample_reviews.review_text: Okay, so I knew the book was going to be about sex. "Fifty Shades of Grey" I hoped that meant an older woman with grey hair was going to have great sex. But no, I was disappointed. Anyway, there was lots of sex but I would have told Mr. Grey to go F*** himself from the beginning and then there would be no story.
Utter drivel.

The success of Fifty Shades of Grey is the very definition of viral marketing. A book that was originally self-published as an eBook and a print-on-demand paperback, it somehow caught the imagination of women everywhere and it's said that a copy now sells every sixty seconds. Amazing. There are three books in the series and they are numbers 1, 2 and 3 on the New York Times best seller list, and have been for months. 
 I have three words for this phenomenon: WTF?? I mean really...have you read this thing? 
 I bought a Kindle version ($9.99), just to see what all the hoopla was about, and got through about 1/3 of it (31% according to my Kindle), rolling my eyes and saying, "Oh, please," on every other page. With one exception (from Jessica Reaves of the Chicago Tribune) it seems to be immune to criticism of any kind (because it's made a boatload of money?), and as an author it's probably bad form to say this (you know that won't stop me), but it's crap. I don't mind the concept of it or the genre of eroticism itself, but something that's selling like the latest iPad release should at least be...well, good. 
 Fifty Shades of Grey is not good. That's not hurting sales in the least. It doesn't seem to matter that the writing stinks, the characters are unappealing and not engaging, the storyline is non-existent and, worst of all, the sex isn't even good, just lots of murmuring and moaning and gasping, and heartbeats quickening and racing. Kinda trite. At least be original. 
 The protagonist, Anastasia Steele, is a 21 year old virgin, and the narrative (told from her point of view) is sprinkled with lots of italics: holy crap! holy fuck! holy shit! jeez! and so on. And her inner goddess talks to her, and does "merengue with some salsa moves." Need I say more? Now, you can't argue with that kind of success - it's phenomenal - and good for E.L. James. She seems as amazed by this as everyone else. But seriously...what are you people thinking? Whatever it is, could you please transfer it to my book? And when mine becomes a runaway best seller it won't bother me a bit when E.L. James trashes it on her blog.

The author will be the first to tell you she isn't a great writer, and it's evident in Fifty Shades. The gratuitous sex scenes got ridiculous and tired very quickly, the language used was very asinine, especially in the everyday conversations of the characters, and the main character's thought process was like a balloon with the helium slowly leaking out. 
 At first the sex scenes were fun and thrilling, and then they never stopped happening and I began skimming through them in order to get to more of the story-- which was, sadly, lacking. There isn't much to this book other than a whole lot of sex. 
 If you've never read a sexually explicit romance novel before, then this might float your boat. I've read my share of romance novels (ones that actually had characters you could care about and plots with mysterious twists that make you want to keep reading), and this one was so ridiculously bad, in my opinion, that it was hard to finish reading.
Did not finish.

Everyone probably knows what this fan-fiction novel is about already, but I'll just summarize it briefly. One day when Ana's friend falls ill and calls in a favour, requesting Ana to interview one of the richest, successful men in Seattle in her place. Although it should it was indeed a formal interview, Christian and Ana both realize that this encounter was anything but ordinary. They start to form a curiosity and fatal attraction for one another. But as all businessmen know, sometimes the only way to keep something is by signing a contract... 
 I read this book because there were so many people raving about it, and of course it was also because it made it onto the top 20 list of best sellers on Indigo etc. If you ever watch or read the Vampire Diaries, Twilight or any other similar television shows or books, it is a definite possibility that you will enjoy this novel. I think the most captivating part about this novel is Mr. Grey himself. What kind of girl does not have an attraction to a bad boy? A handsome bruting one? A mysterious, rich, powerful and charming one? When you combine all of these aspects into one character, it becomes irresistible to desire more information, and the only way to gain more information is by blazing through the pages! 
 So why do I give this three stars? As explicit as the sexual content in the novel is, there is quite a bit of repetition. Not only in vocabulary, but also events in the story. The higher the predictability, the less enjoyable it is (excluding fairy tales, the ones where we watch because we expect the feel-good happy endings).

Muy mala, aburridisima, una historia tonta y predecible, y la escritura es tan repetitiva y superficial que me queria suicidar. 
 Es un crepusculo mil veces peor y ademas es tan cliche que me aburri un monton.
disturbing.

I'm about as confused as much as Miss Steel about this book. I really hated this book....I loathed it, and 1/2 way through it I set it down and didn't pick it back up for months, but I wanted it cleared off my night stand so I finished, and ...........I hate, hate, hate to admit......I liked the ending. It went from a 1 star to a 3....Just for the ending.

I don't get what the fuss is about! 
 Fifty Shades of Grey is poorly written, has no actual plot, the characters are extrimely uncredible and annoying, and all the sex scenes get pretty boring after 100 pages (the book has a total of 500!). This story could have been told in 100 pages MAX, without the boring repeated considerations of the narrator, without the millions of "Jeez", "Oh my", He's so sexy", "It's so erotic" and without alle the cliches. 
 The only thing that I liked in this book was the e-mail exchange between Ana and Christian, which was quite funny and to the point. 
 I read somewhere that the book was about to be made into a movie - maybe this interpretation will be more interesting, even though I don't see how you can make a movie out of this book without making it an adult movie - it's all about sex!

book_b.title: The Iron King (The Iron Fey, #1)
book_b.user_review: Although the story line did get better than I expected, I really didn't like Meghan. She was annoying, weak, dependent and selfish. I might continue the series because it is an interesting story line but she better grow up. And fast.

sample_reviews.review_text: Bit different but I enjoyed it. Book 2 at the ready.

Bagaimana bayanganmu mengenai dunia peri? Apakah seimut dunia Tinkerbell? Kamu salah! Dunia peri tidak seindah dan seimut itu. Malah terkesan mengerikan--setidaknya untuk dunia peri yang disebut Nevernever. Butuh ketangguhan ekstra buat bertahan disana! 
 Nggak percaya? Kalau begitu, inilah dia... 
 Meghan Case dari The Iron King! 
 Apa kabar, Meghan? 
 Meg: Baik. 
 Bisa kamu ceritakan, bagaimana awalnya kamu bisa masuk ke dunia peri Nevernever? 
 Meg: Kami bisa juga menyebut peri di Nevernever dengan fey. 
 Oke, fey. 
 Meg: Sejujurnya aku terpaksa pergi kesana sebab Ethan, adikku, diculik dan dibawa kesana. Pada awalnya aku nggak tahu, sebab ada Ethan lain di rumah. Tapi sikapnya yang aneh tidak bisa mengelabuhiku. Belum lagi Robbie Fellow, sahabat baikku, yang ternyata Robin Goodfellow, menunjukkan bahwa Ethan yang ada di rumah itu bukan Ethan yang selama ini kukenal. 
 Jadi, kamu langsung pergi ke Nevernever? 
 Meg: Robbie memberiku pilihan untuk menyelamatkan Ethan. Tapi pilihan yang lain sangat mengerikan dibanding mencari Ethan langsung. 
 Saat itu, apa kamu tahu siapa yang menculik Ethan? 
 Meg: Tidak. 
 Lalu kamu langsung pergi begitu saja? Kamu tidak berpikir Nevernever luas? 
 Meg: .... Tidak. 
 Wogh! Kamu datang kesana tanpa pikir panjang, lalu kamu juga tidak tahu darimana memulai mencarinya. Kamu nekat sekali, Meghan. 
 Meg: Aku bahkan rela menukar kebebasanku dengan Ethan. 
 Kamu benar-benar kakak... Bagaimana Nevernever? 
 Meg: Tempat yang indah sekaligus mengerikan. Disana kita mesti hati-hati dalam berbicara. Satu kata "terimakasih" saja bisa langsung membuatmu punya hutang pada orang pada siapa kamu mengatakannya. 
 Wooh! Tidak ada tempat di Nevernever berarti untuk orang yang suka berterima kasih. Lalu, apa kamu langsung menemukan petunjuk dimana Ethan? 
 Meg: Tidak dengan cara mudah. Aku terpisah dari Robbie, gara-gara... dan aku terpaksa membuat perjanjian dengan cat sith, Grimalkin-- 
 Grimalkin yang itu?! 
 Meg: Yap. Sama seperti Robin Goodfellow. Tak disangka ya ternyata makhluk dongeng kayak mereka benar-benar ada. 
 Lalu? 
 Meg: Kami mesti berjalan jauh dan bertemu dengan beragam fey dan makhluk fantastis lainnya yang ternyata semuanya mengerikan. Kami tidak hanya keliling Nevernever saja, tapi juga bolak-balik ke dunia nyata. Kenyataan bahwa ternyata banyak sekali fey di dunia nyata menohokku. Mereka ada dimana-mana. Bersembunyi dengan glamour--semacam selubung untuk menyembunyikan identitas fey dari mata manusia. 
 Apa hal paling mengejutkan yang terjadi selama petualanganmu? 
 Meg: Aku ternyata setengah fey. 
 Apa?! 
 Meg: Lebih tepatnya aku setengah summer-fey. 
 Summer fey? 
 Meg: Apa aku sudah bilang kalau Nevernever dibagi jadi beberapa bagian? Ada summer court, winter court, dst. Ada juga daerah liar yang tidak jadi daerah kekuasaan ayahku, yang merupakan summer-fey maupun ibu temanku, Ash, Ratu winter court. 
 Ash? 
 Meg: Sebenarnya dia ditugaskan untuk menangkapku. Tapi aku membuat perjanjian dengannya. 
 Aku jadi pusing nih. Balik ke Ethan ya. Kamu jelas ke summer court, sebab kamu anak Raja. Apakah kamu menemukan adikmu disana? 
 Meg: Tidak. 
 Berarti adikmur di winter court? 
 Meg: Tidak juga. 
 Lalu dimana? 
 Meg: Di wilayah yang kecil tapi berkembang pesat dengan hadirnya teknologi, Iron Court. Habitat asli Iron Fey. Wilayah kekuasaan Iron King. 
 Aku jadi penasaran, apakah Ethan juga punya darah setengah fey? 
 Meg: Kenapa Anda berpikir seperti itu? 
 Kenapa dia diculik oleh The Iron King? 
 Meg: Lebih baik akua tidak mengatakannya. Biarkan pembaca mencaritahunya sendiri. 
 Oops, nyaris sop iler. Tapi aku tetap penasaran dengan adik tirimu. Apalagi di adegan kalian di ending. Benarkah dia setengah fey? 
 Meg: Aku tidak bisa mengatakannya. Jawabannya ada di The Iron Prophechy. Novella setelah The Iron Prince.

 Meghan Case dari The Iron King.
