There's a special kind of magic that happens when a reader discovers on their own a book, or a series of books, that they love. I imagine that some of the first kids, teens, and adults, to discover Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone well before it began earning all the buzz and became a household name, feel a special bond to that series. I would assume that readers that discovered and loved the Twilight books without knowing that they were so popular, only to discover they were, would hold a special place in their heart for the series. 
 I remember the afternoon that I received my Nook clearly. It was just a couple days before I was scheduled to have my eighth orthopedic surgery. My Nook was part birthday present (I'd turned 25 just a few days before) and part something for me to enjoy as I recovered. I was also given a gift card to fill up my Nook with new books and I was looking to stretch that money as far as possible. I wasn't firmly entrenched into the YA genre yet. I was a card carrying Harry Potter, Percy Jackson, and Twilight fan. But beyond that, I really hadn't ventured into the genre on my own yet. And I only got to the aforementioned series because I'd heard about them through other people. The Mortal Instruments series sat on my shelf unread. But I really wasn't addicted to YA then like I am now. I just loved some things about the genre. 
 But because I wanted to stretch my money, I decided I'd look into some of the YA titles that were under $5. That night, Julie Kagawa's Iron King was on sale, as were the next three books in the series. They all had gorgeous and enchanting covers. I remembered seeing their print copy counterparts in Barnes and Noble and even at Walmart. I was able to get all four books for under $30, which was a good deal to me. I bought the first one somewhat hesitantly, but within the first fifty pages, I paused so I could go and buy the other three books before the sale ended, because I was absolutely in love. 
 When I first read the description, I wasn't sure how I would feel about reading a book about fairies. After all, I'd been reading books about wizards, vampires, werewolves, and demigods. How exciting could fairies be? 
 I was so thankful that Julie's writing showed me just how fascinating, enchanting, and dangerously charming the fey could be. I loved how she wove elements and characters from Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream into a modern day tale of fairies and juxtaposed with the ultra-modern threat of the iron fey, from whom the series takes its name. 
 The creation of the characters was just so clever. From the protagonist Meghan, to the hilarious Robin Goodfellow known as Puck (borrowed from Shakespeare), to the darkly dreamy Ash, and the most sarcastic and clever cat embodied by Grimalkin, every character is so dynamic. Beyond that, the world-building was just so wonderful. I fell in love with Faery here, with the mystery, with the magic, and of course, with Ash, who has to this day, remains my ultimate book boyfriend. I am not at all a romantic person, but the sort of chivalry that exists in these books makes me wish that Faery and all the characters in it -- even Queen Mab -- were real. 
 I went on to read the rest of the series (Iron Daughter, Iron Queen, and Iron Knight followed it) and now read the companion series, Iron Fey: Call of the Forgotten (The Lost Prince and Iron Traitor are out now with a conclusion to the trilogy coming this fall) and loved each book more than I loved the last. 
 The Iron Fey series wasn't referred to me by anyone. I hadn't seen it on Goodreads or heard about it on the news because it was generating such publicity. I found it on my own. And it's consistently the series that I recommend most to people who are new the YA genre. And while I've discovered I love EVERYTHING that Julie Kagawa writes (check out The Blood of Eden series if you haven't already -- dystopia + vampires = AWESOMESAUCE), Iron Fey has a very special spot in my heart as my first love.

4.5 STARS 
 I've admittedly had a bit of a bumpy road with Tarryn Fisher's last few books. I've loved some, I've left some, but none have given me the elusive feels I had through the Love Me With Lies series. Until now. In Atheists Who Kneel and Pray, a refreshing and intensely complex storyline, Fisher once again weaves love and infatuation with narcissism, bad choices, deception and the inability to just grow up and say what should be said. Instead, her characters, in all their brokenness and all their flaws, try and fail miserably at keeping the shards of their broken hearts in one piece by doing all the wrong things. And it hurts to watch. So so so much, it hurts. But I loved that pain, that heartache, that hopelessness laced with a glimmer of hope that maybe... just maybe... there'd still be a chance for them despite the fact that it felt so impossible. 
 Reading this book made me feel like I had a weight inside my chest, a heaviness that just wouldn't ease up at all until I reached the last page. I kind of hated that feeling. I also kind of loved it. 
 True to form, Tarryn Fisher had me reading much of this book completely infuriated, my heart often heavy with unwanted emotion. I was equal parts confused and frustrated at times, but through it all, despite the somber tone in this story, remained a sliver of hope. I stand by the notion that with Tarryn Fisher, you never know what you'll get. I stand by my opinion that I don't trust her, because I'm never convinced she truly believes in romantic happily ever afters in their traditional sense. And I suppose that's why I keep going back for more, for that uncertainty, for the emotionally turbulent stories full of flawed, messed up characters that riddle their own journeys with intense love and fiery heartache. 
 I have to be really honest here. The beginning of this book, the first quarter or so, I felt a bit disconnected, enough so that I almost considered DNFing. I didn't get where it was going and I was impatient. But then something happened. This little scene that had almost nothing and yet had everything to do with the storyline itself flickered the story to life, and I was transfixed. And once those fiery emotions were lit, I was consumed. I'm a reader that lives for pain, for anguish, for jealousy and rage. So for me the rest of the book was completely unputdownable. It only grew in intensity and angst with each turn of the page and it made everything that happened in the beginning just click into place. 
 Atheists Who Kneel and Pray is a messy, emotionally turbulent story of a screwed up woman who has no faith in the lasting power of love, doesn't believe she's worthy of it, but she tries to fake her way through a relationship anyway with a man who she inspires. She goes through the motions because it seems right, because she wants to believe in love and commitment and marriage even though her mind and her heart can't come to the same terms. I'm not going to lie and say I didn't spend much of this book trying to figure out exactly what was up with Yara. Yara is not an easy character to relate to. Her emotions, her distrust, her insecurity I understood. I even came to understand why she never felt worthy of love. But her actions, her reasons for always running, her narcissism, how unapologetic she was when she hurt people, I struggled with that for a while. But as this story evolved, that woman came to understand herself and she grew and changed and accepted, and because of that, so did I. 
 The Love Me With Lies series is still my favorite Tarryn Fisher storyline, but Atheists Who Kneel and Pray is a close second. It's angsty and heavy in all the ways I love a book to be, but with Fisher's signature storytelling, it settles in and twists in the way only her stories do. This book will hurt to read, it'll absolute infuriate most. But it's an honest look at what it truly means to love. It's messy and broken and it doesn't fit in the boxes we want it to, which is why I appreciated it so much.

I freaking love Tarryn Fisher. You start her books knowing that you have NO idea what the characters will be, but that they won't be cookie cutter, and that you don't know what to expect. 
 We meet Yara. She's mid twenties and from England. Currently working as a bartender at The Jane in Seattle, but having lived around the USA for a while. She's a "love 'em and leave 'em" type of girl. She finds men who "need" her, inspires them, and when it gets too close, she runs. 
 David removes a splinter from her finger then disappears. He eventually returns. We learn he is the lead singer of a band and has lost his inspiration. 
 Yara can be his inspiration. But things get more involved than she likes. 
 Things happen, and more things happen, and I can't tell you because it will spoil the book, but it's a roller coaster ride and, as always Tarryn did not disappoint.

You know, this one was hard. I would never doubted giving Tarryn Fisher less than a thousand stars on a review, but today I did. 
 'Cause, I didn't cry. 
 I've dried myself of tears everytime I've read her books, but now I'm thinking this could've been more than what it is. I'm not the observative kind, but I found a lot of things alike between F*ck Love and Atheists Who Kneel And Pray. She's developed a patron, and she's not creating that much of new stories. 
 However, I did like the book. And I can't give my fav author anything less, so there the five go.

Atheists Who Kneel and Pray is an all consuming self-discovery and romance. Yara is a frustrating character who discovers who she is, how she loves, and what she wants from life through falling in love hard and not knowing how to deal with what that means for her. 
 I loved everything about this novel, except the pacing. The beginning of the novel is slow and took a bit to interest me. It wasn't until Yara's flaws are fully on display that I really started to enjoy what Fisher was doing with the story and characters. 
 Yara is a frustrating character because of the specific flaws she has relating to the story. She's flawed in all the ways you don't want a character to be flawed in a romance. She holds herself back from truly feeling and experiencing by creating a narrative about the typical progression of her relationships that she believes to be true. Yara is a complicated character that the reader gets to know intimately to the point that she becomes predictable. This predictability isn't a flaw, but a testament to Fisher's writing. 
 As with my review of Mud Vein by Fisher, I've been purposely vague about Atheists Who Kneel and Pray. I went into this book knowing absolutely nothing about the plot or what to expect. I truly believe that that is the best way to enjoy Fisher's novels. Her characters remind me of Gillian Flynn's characters in that they are deeply complex and showcase undesirable traits. 
 Overall, Atheists Who Kneel and Pray was a fantastic novel despite the few pacing issues. It's a character driven story about a young woman who discovers who she is through falling in love despite the narrative she's created for herself.

Book review moment of honesty - I have read some really embarrassing things in my life. This is one of them. I bought all three of the Fifty Shades books, paying in cash and buying in a book store so there is no digital record of my trashy book reading habits. I own all of the Twlight books, in hard cover. I have no shame when it comes to actually reading something, but plenty of shame when it comes to admitting that I've read it. Picture me while I'm writing this review wearing a bag on my head with eye holes cut out like the Unknown Comic from the "Gong Show" tv series from the 1970s. This is fan fiction, which, yes, I've read before. And fan fiction about a boy band that I have no particular interest in (One Direction - I'm old enough to be any of their moms). But, it was in the bargain bin at Barnes & Nobles (it was $4.95 less the B&N store membership discount). And, I'd heard of it and was looking for a light romance as we approach Valentine's Day. So, why not. Warning - this is kind of gross, so if you don't actually know what this book is about (the methodical deflowering of an innocent), you might want to take a pass on this review. This means you, Mom. 
 Then I read the description on the back, and it is exactly the premise that my husband hates. The "good girl" is bored with decent guys and wants to be with the guy who treats her like garbage. And she loves him for it. Only she can fix him with her love. Yes, it is insanely frustrating. My husband is a genuinely nice guy. And he's also hot and smart and funny and reads lot of books (mostly sci-fi, but he did just finish A Man Named Ove to appease me). He is a catch, and when I met him over a decade ago, he was 36 years old and had never been in a relationship that lasted "a whole year." So yeah, he has now. He was single a long time before that though, and saw a lot of disastrous relationships. And he hates it when women ignore it when a guy flat out tells her that he is bad news. I think one of his mottos is: "When someone tells you that they are a train wreck and you shouldn't date them, you should believe them." Whenever we see this in a movie or book, he just shakes his head at the stupidity. And he is right. If you date someone who says that they will treat you poorly, and then who does in fact treat you poorly, you have given them permission to treat you poorly. Value yourself more, ladies (and guys who also put up with entirely too much crap in the name of "love"). He is not a fan of relationship power games, and this book was nothing but head games. He shook his head all day Sunday when I was reading it (during the Superbowl when Atlanta laid an egg and lost in OT after a commanding early lead). But, I didn't care, I was reading this book, despite how dumb it was. 
 This is smack your head with your hand level of stupid when it comes to Tessa's "attraction" to Hardin. And, I can't even type that name. Good lord, Anna Todd, you are naming your fake Harry Styles, Mr. Perma-boner whenever he is around Tessa character Hardin Scott? I'm surprised she didn't go with the surname Richard, or one of its nicknames, but then it wouldn't be H.S. like Harry Styles. I can't say Hardin, or even type it, so I'm going to call him Hayden as it close, and it reminds me of Hayden Fox on the old tv show "Coach" (and that character was named after iconic Iowa Football coach Hayden Fry). These are names, people, but Hardin is a condition; one that was explored thoroughly in this book. Ewww. Or maybe I'll just call him H. Which reminds me of Preparation H, as he was a complete pain in the a$$. I was mentally comparing H. to the protagonist Fred, in The Utterly Uninteresting and Unadventurous Tales of Fred, the Vampire Accountant and Fred is the clear winner, despite being undead. He's a nice guy. Seriously, that is a funny book (I got the audiobook) and the contrast between Fred, who treats people with respect and can't believe that his former classmate might actually be asking him out, vs. H. who thinks he is God's gift to women, is stark. 
 I don't think that Tessa should have stayed with Noah, though, as it was obvious that they weren't actually attracted to each other. I'm picturing Noah as a young Pat Boone. Tessa was actually quite cruel to Noah with how long she strung him along, ignoring his texts and calls, and inviting him up and then ditching him in her dorm room while taking his car for an entire night. Nice. But, Noah was a tool who was ratting her out to her mom about everything - wow. And why the mom thought Noah was some catch, this still in high school guy. No-one in college should be dating a high schooler. That isn't a thing that works out with someone who isn't living with their parents and commuting to school just for classes. I don't know why Tessa was surprised about this development, as she had allegedly done her homework about what college life would be like and wrote up a detailed schedule for every minute of her 4 years there in advance. This was dumb. And didn't give me warm feelings for Tessa. Why did I keep reading this? 
 I know why. I am strangely drawn to romances that feature the loss of innocence, thus the aforementioned Fifty Shades. My favorite of the "Black Dagger Brotherhood" books is the one featuring Butch and Marissa. OMG, did I just admit that I've read almost all of the BDB books? When will this series of embarrassing book confessions end? I stayed up until midnight last night finishing this book. On a work night. Midnight. Dang, that is late. And now I think I'm starting to sound like Tessa and all her whining about staying up late on school nights. Which is a thing, people. You should sleep at night. Unless you are a vampire. And then you can just hang out all night and watch the person you've got a huge crush on sleep. Because that isn't creepy and weird or anything. Oh, there is plenty of sneaking into your room and watching you sleep in this book, so if you are a fan of home security, this isn't your book. 
 Or boundaries. Fans of boundaries should also avoid this book. No seriously, this is not a feminist manifesto, shockingly. Trigger warnings abound in this book, where "no" means "maybe" and driving drunk is cool and stomping away angry after 1 million fights is sexy and all sorts of other immaturity that is passed off as "passion". This is also not a realistic portrayal of college life, as Tessa reminded us 1 million times that she is "getting a 4.0 GPA" despite the fact that she is still in her first semester of school, so she hasn't even received any grades yet, and she seems to be missing all of her classes after getting her internship. And let's spend one minute on her classes, as she is an English major (which I did too, albeit many years ago), and I never had a class called "Literature." Seriously, the class is named "Literature" like they are supposed to cover all of literature in one class that meets three times a week for one semester, a class with both first year students and upper class students? Intro to Lit? Nope. Literature. And we're talking about Pride and Prejudice and Wuthering Heights and Jane Eyre? Really? And the professor is letting H. add and drop his class on a weekly basis for months, and Tessa is somehow in it despite the fact that she is also working every day at the completely impossible internship. You know the one, where you get an office with a window (and a door that locks - seriously, locking doors in an office building), they let you out early every day, just because, that is how offices work?, and you get paid, while also getting school credit (for what class, mind you, doesn't matter, as you know the Dean - whee!) to read a manuscript and write notes. Um, cool? And she got it because she's getting a 4.0, and she knows this because during the first week of school she went to her classes. Ok, it is realistic that if the Dean put in a word for her, that she would get an internship, but everything beyond that is incomprehensible to anyone who has ever worked in an office, and seems to draw on Ana's "job" in Fifty Shades as the source of what work is actually like. 
 Ok, enough ranting. I kept reading, and at a ferocious pace, because I wanted to see the train wreck. I would say I wanted to know what would happen, but you and I both know what was going to happen. It was pre-ordained. This plot was not even slightly original. And, I don't need to actually read the second and third books to know what they are about. But, I might anyways. I'm still deciding. Anyone who is old and cynical like me but who enjoys the cheese (and this is quite cheesy) and who has read these other two books who wants to give me any indication of whether they are worth it, please, chime in.

When I first bought this book, I was very excited to read it. I'd heard very good things about this book, and had been wanting to read it for a while. I thought that when I read the first book, I was going to be totally engrossed in the story and never want to put it down until I finished the last book. 
 I was totally wrong. I hated it. I thought it was poorly written, had awful plot points, and I thought the main character, Tessa, was a pathetic and naive little girl. 
 For those of you that don't already know, After was originally written on Wattpad as a Harry Styles fanfiction. It become so popular that the story was slightly altered so every "Harry" became "Hardin" and the story was published as an actual four-book series. I knew this when I started reading it, but I didn't realize just how immature the author's writing was especially since the story was originally written as a fanfiction. 
 Anyways, the story of After is of a new freshmen named Tessa Young, at Washington State University. She is a petite, pretty, intelligent girl who always has everything planned out for herself, and always wants things to go well. She wants to focus on her studies, her boyfriend, and staying out of trouble. However, this doesn't go as planned when she meets her dorm roommate's group of friends, one of them being the (predictably) mysterious, tattooed and pierced Hardin Scott. 
 Obviously, despite Tessa trying her best to fight it, Tessa and Hardin fall in love. Of course, just like every other fucking novel I have read, Hardin is not one for relationships, besides (literally) screwing around and being a manwhore, but of course he falls in love with Tessa after they meet and she "changes" him. Lots of shit goes down, betrayal, and devastation. 
 Ok, that was just a run-down summary, and I could've probably done a better job, but to be completely honest I hated this book with a burning passion so I could care less about the summary. I thought Tessa Young was pathetic, too trusting, too naive, and honestly annoying. She thought she was so much better than she actually was. And don't even get me started on her and Hardin's toxic relationship. The only time they weren't fighting was when they were naked. 
 I probably would've enjoyed this book more if I read it like two years ago, but unfortunately I just read it now. I'm probably going to read the rest of the series, just to see what happen.

reference_books.title: The Given Day (Coughlin #1)
reference_books.review_text:
No one writes Boston like Dennis Lehane. Once again, he does not disappoint. 
 Set at the end of WWI in a city full of immigrants, major class divisions, racial tension and political unrest, the scope is huge. While the main focus is on the unionization battle between the Boston police force and the city (and the ensuing citywide riots), it seems every other significant event during those years is covered in detail as well... Babe Ruth's final season with the Red Sox. The 1918 Influenza pandemic. The Great Molasses Flood (Wikipedia it - you wont be disappointed). So much more. 
 The writing is pretty close to perfect. An impressive amount of research went into the creation of this book. But some of the relationships are unrealistic and some of the heroes a bit too indestructible. The inclusion of Babe Ruth as one of the main narrators confused me - I can only assume he was there to show how ignorant and blind the upper class of Boston was to all that was happening around them.

sample_reviews.review_text: This man knows how to write a book! He never fails to make me feel all the feels and I adore him for that. Such an awesome read!
Liked it, but didn't love it. Very raw, gritty, and ultimately, unresolved. Long, messy journey with characters you aren't sure you even like, but then you don't get to enjoy the destination.

One Last Thing Before I Go is a hilarious and bittersweet look into the life of a forty-something loser whose selfishness has torn his life and family apart. When Drew Silver (herein known as "Silver" because no one refers to him as "Drew") learns he has a potentially fatal heart ailment, his decision to forgo surgery and simply die sets off a chain reaction of events that threatens to monkey-wrench the lives his ex-wife and their daughter have created for themselves during his "lost" period. Oh, and to make matter worse, his daughter learns she's pregnant, and she comes to him (HIM!) for advice! 
 Silver is exactly the kind of man every man has the dangerous capability of becoming, a sad, depressed man looking back at all the mistakes he's made, knowing full well he could have turned left when he turned right, etc. Yet Silver is that lovable loser; you know deep down inside he really is a damaged soul needing to be loved, and wanting to love, but he can't help but fuck things up. So much so that he imagines his tombstone will be inscribed with the words "What the Fuck?" 
 Jonathan Tropper's latest is often times brutally funny and refreshingly honest. The characters, especially Silver and, most impressively, his 18-year-old daughter Casey, come to life with stunning clarity. I read this in a 3-day frenzy, not wanting this story to end. Alas, it did, and it left me both smiling and sad. Highly recommended.

Over the last few years, Jonathan Tropper has asserted himself something of a master of the genre I like to call Novels About Middle-Aged Suburban Men Whose Lives Aren't Awful, Just Unsatisfying. His latest, though, was surprisingly satisfying. I was a little underwhelmed by This is Where I Leave You, but I think that was mostly because of where I was in my life more than anything about the book itself. With that in mind, I did approach this with a small amount of skepticism but ultimately I came away with a nice, healthy dose of the feels. 
 The set-up here is just a little darker. Drew Silver is a washed-up one-hit-wonder playing the wedding-and-mitzvah circuit. His ex-wife Denise is getting remarried to a guy Silver can't bring himself to hate, and his teenage daughter Casey has just announced she's pregnant. He lives in an apartment building with a bunch of other middle-aged men whose wives have left them and together they make weekly trips to sell their semen to medical research. He cruises through life more or less on autopilot, not really noticing the hurt caused by his lack of engagement. 
 Then Silver has a ministroke and an aneurysm, diagnosed by his ex-wife's new fiancee Rich. Equal parts pride and surrender prevent him from allowing Rich to repair the tear in his aorta, meaning that Silver could literally die at any second. He's okay with that, because he's lost everything that's ever meant anything to him and he doesn't see how life is ever going to have meaning again. Then Casey reveals her pregnancy, admitting that she's telling Silver before her mother because she's less concerned about letting him down. So Silver decides that in the time he has left, he needs to make up for eighteen years of crummy fathering. 
 The first chunk of the book is a little too full of hyperbole and testosterone for my taste -- Silver and his fortysomething buddies ogling young women with perfectly taut everythings while exchanging excessively witty one-liners. After a while, though, Tropper finds his groove and the book finds the right balance between poignant and schmaltzy. You start to sympathize with Silver, genuinely root for this man who has never proven to be anything but an apathetic fuck-up. And yet he's anything but unlikable. There's maybe a little flash of George Bailey here, as Silver learns what he means to the people in his life, yet it never quite falls over into excessive sentiment.
Kind of an odd book.....it didn't grab me right away, but I did end up caring about the characters.

 I had never even heard of Jonathan Tropper before requesting One Last Thing because I mostly read Young Adult books. I was intrigued by the book's description, but I didn't actually expect that I would enjoy it. I'm definitely not the "targeted audience" for this one, but I surprisingly enjoyed. I am confident when I say that I'll definitely be reading more of Tropper's books. 
 Tropper succeeds on so many levels in One Last Thing Before I Go: this book is equally heartbreaking as it is humorous. Since the main character, Silver is terminally ill, most of the jokes are dark humor which is NOT for everyone. Keep that in mind if you plan on reading this book. Many of the jokes weren't laugh-out-loud, rolling-on-the-floor hilarious, the jokes are more subtle jokes that are meant to evoke a few chuckles. Don't expect to be laughing your head off! 
 One moment in One Last Thing you could be crying your eyes out and the next you could be laughing. This book is a strange book, but extremely engrossing one; I was hooked right from the beginning. This is a book that will best be enjoyed by "middle-aged" people who will be able to identify with Silver better than most readers. Even I as a teenager could oddly identify with Silver and his hardships; Tropper definitely has created a character that is easy to identify with and easy to root for. The other characters in this zany cast of characters are all extremely developed and are realistic with their insane, overwhelming personalities. These characters felt like they were breathing, like they lived beyond the page which is always a good sign. 
 In One Last Thing Before You Go, you have this premonition that you know what's going to happen; in the same way, you know what's going to happen in The Fault In Our Stars. You just know what's going to happen next, but you have this lingering doubt that it's not going to end that way. One Last Thing Before I Go does go down the route that I expected for the most part. It was a tad predictable until I arrived at the very end, the finale. The finale was so wonderfully crafted and yet so horrible at the same time; it was very open-ended and it kind of irked me. I felt that this was a good decision, yet I felt so annoyed by this decision and so pleased by it. I felt rather ambivalent towards the ending, but for the most part, it was excellent. 
 One Last Thing Before I Go is an extraordinary contemporary novel that I would highly recommend. I will definitely be reading more of Tropper's novels and I have a feeling that I will quickly become a fan of his. This was definitely a lovely surprising read and I'm so happy that I took the time to read this one. One Last Thing Before I Go isn't your typical contemporary novel and succeeds in both emotional depth and humor.

Tropper usually does well with stories of family dysfunction (please read This Is Where I Leave You!) but this novel does not rise to the level of humor, wit and insight I'm used to from him.

Five?! I never, ever spend that much time reading a book. The last time it took me that kind of time to get through a book was Frankenstein *shudder*. Admittedly, the last 1/4 of the book engaged me enough to read quickly and enjoy the climax and resolution, but everything that led up to the climax felt like work to me. Let us talk about Sweet Peril or as it should have been titled "I Can't Keep A Secret aka Horrible Relationships Decisions aka How to Get a Bad Boyfriend" 
 The two main themes in this book are a) No one except Belial understands the concept of a secret and b) Anna doesn't understand the concept of a non-abusive relationship. 
 On relationships 
 As a dude I don't sign up to care about abusive relationships. It's my man privilege and I acknowledge that. For us, as long as we're not abusive, most of the time we're good with that. That's why it takes a concerted effort for dudes to care. Most of us make the effort but it's not something I normally look out for when I'm reading YA fiction. But I have sisters and ex-girlfriends and girls who are friends and nieces and little cousins. I'm surrounded by girls. And like with Television our girl, in this book, reminds me not a lick of any of them, to a point where it's off putting. 
 Anna is unhealthily obsessed with Kaidan. That in and of itself isn't much of an problem. I've been unhealthily obsessed with a girl before. She was likewise with me and hilarity ensues. The problem is that Kaidan is a bad dude and she has other options. Options that do everything Kaiaen doesn't, like express their affection for her, or make themselves available to her, or not lie to her. And still her response is 
 Watching [Kaidan] look me over, I flushed. Nobody else could make me hot like that from a single look. Nobody 
 Except yes they can. Kopano clearly makes her hot and she obsesses over it all the time they're together. He turns her on just as hot, AND he likes her, AND he tells her he likes her. This seems like a no brainer especially when the other option is doing everything in his power to make her hate him. The idea that of all the characters we would vote to kill Kopano makes me sad. 
 They've know each other for such a little amount of time and for most of that time he's been antagonistic towards her. It makes no sense that he should be so well regarded by her. He doesn't let down his guard for her. He doesn't let her in. Yet because he didn't curse around her she obsesses that it might have all been fake. 
 We'd had such precious little time together, and I didn't want to think that any of it had been fake. 
 On top of all that when an incident happens, and she kisses another boy, in fact the same African boy who gets her motor running Kopano . Kaidan gets insanely jealous. 
 He was beyond pissed, which made me angry in my own defense 
 You might be wondering why her defense matters until you find out that at this point in the story Kaidan has not only broken ties from her, but moved away to LA, to get away from her, and she kissed this boy Kopano one time in a heat of passion moment. (Not that he could possibly make her feel the way Kaidan does whatever that means) 
 [H]is face flushed from angry hardness to sad softness, and I realized that's exactly how he felt. Betrayed, Forgotten. Even though he'd been the one who'd left 
 In the face of such emotional manipulative accusation Anna's response is odd to say the best: 
 What could I say to make this right? 
 She hasn't done anything wrong? She kissed a boy when she was ACTUALLY single. Not like when Jay kissed a girl last book and he was "not official". Anna's been told many times that Kaidan is done with her. He doesn't talk to her, he changed his number. This apologetic line of thinking starts a huge unrespectable spiral where Anna is compelled/forced to apologize for her actions of kissing a single boy when she has been told repeatedly to her face and behind her back that Kaidan has no interest in her. That Kaidan has moved on with a new girl. I understand Kaidan being jealous. We all get jealous when our ex moves on, but being jealous and acting jealous are two different things. He has no right to act jealous and yet his response 
 Nothing I said could've pushed you into his arms if you didn't want to be there 
 How romantic. After the blow up, she dejectedly decides that since she's told the prophecy, and she had no other business (because [emotions]), that she will just go home. Whereupon Kaidan calls her stubborn. This to me is one of the most mystifying pieces of writing I've ever read. I have no idea what part of her wanting to go home is supposed to be stubborn and I understand (even if I vehemently disagree) with every other aspect of the fight. Kaidan and his BFF Nephilim Blake beg her to stay and she still says no, whereupon she now internally agrees, that she's being stubborn. It's not until he grabs her and mandhandles her to stillness that she relents. Acknowledging that he came at her with a fierceness that frightens and excites her because he's not in his right mind. This is the very opposite of what we're supposed to be telling girls. A guy that out of control isn't the guy you want to stay around, but hey who needs to make smart decisions it's only the risk of your life and eternal soul at stake. 
 Her defense when they do talk about it, starts with the suggestion: Emotions that I'd buried for so long rose inside of me, impassioning my words.. No. These are emotions that have been rolling on the surface of her mind for like a year now. Only Kopano has been able to get them quiet but hey he doesn't turn her own like Kaidan does with a look inspite of every look he gives her making her skin flushed. But even after finding out that her father orchestrated the separation with Kaidan, she's still apologizing. She still caves first when she's attacked by Kaidan who demands: "Show me your emotional color aura". Just no backbone whatsoever which would be fine if this was book 1 paragraph 1 but as I'll say later time is passing. Anna is acting the party girl, drinking partying, turning good people bad. She should be growing up. Instead she's still upset when she thinks people are being fake around her by not swearing 
 He's been such a punk, all heartbroken and shi-iiz." I rolled my eyes. "Not this again, Black" 
 "I'm tryin' to be good 
 This is a weird things to get so vehemently upset by. It's the closest thing to backbone she shows and it's at a point when people are respecting her. Even Silent black man Kope has more backbone when defending the kiss her shared with Anna. 
 Do not play victim [Kaidan] when you are partly to blame 
 This man is the new Jay. This book is seriously lacking some Jay but this guy acknowledges that Kaidan can't be mad when people follow his words. He's brilliant. No one else does this. No one. But just like in Twilight she will pick the abusive "I'm so emotional about you I can't control myself or those I harm in the process. Please stay away from me when I yell at you but don't even show a hint of attraction to anyone else" guy. 
 The main point of this book unfortunately is that Kaidan and Anna get together. I would spoiler that but it's such a minor spoiler and it'd would be obvious from the context of the rest of this section. Because that's one sloppy one sided relationship. Conversely to Kopano who is open with his feeling any time he has a chance, Kaidan refuses to acknowledge his feeling towards her. She says she loves him and his response after "emotionally shivering" is to ask her to spend the night. In real life this would be a hilariously bright red flag. She harps on the fact that he doesn't even need to say it and then the closest he comes is 
 "The thing is, I can't share you. I need you to be mine. Only mine. When I think of someone else touching you--" 
 Wherein he breaks off and refuses to even say the word boyfriend. Even with context that's a pretty scary thing to say. It comes off less romantic and more possessive. Why you would find this attractive is beyond me. Especially coming from someone for whom sex is such a big part of his life. This guy is a lust demon who specialized in having sex with women to get them to give in to lust. One might think his perspective towards sex and "touching" might be somewhat appropriately relaxed. Considering how much she has and will push him to have sex with other girls to keep his demonic father unknowing. The closest he ever gets in the book is when a group of Nephilim are forced to hide clinging in the water under a dock for hours sans Scuba gear (something I'm not sure would be physically possible but they're magically healing so we let that slide) when Kaiden: 
 At first I thought he was reaching for me, but then he slowly signed, I love you 
 Now as a minor point. I'm no sign language expert but I remember a few signs from elementary school. One of which being "I love you" because it's such a simple sign. You don't really sign anything. It's a hand shape. it looks like this 
 View post on imgur.com 
 . 
 It's really that simple you don't really do it "slowly". Now you might think that the whole "no touching" thing was a bit of romantic hyperbole but after staying in the water for hours and facing death from pneumonia Anna needs to get into dry clothes. And when someone else is helping to save her life by helping her out of her wet clothes in a manner so respectful you'd be forgiven for forgetting that they're about to die and maybe they should hurry up: 
 "I can't, [push my shorts all the way down" [...] under the circumstances the entire scenario of undressing was a necessity. Nothing more. 
 Kopano grabbed a blanket from the bed. "Here," he said, laying it across my midsection. "I will not look. Try again." He stared down at the floor next to me. 
 [...] 
 When they were at my knees [he] grabbed the bottoms and tugged down my calves, keeping his eyes averted. A growl of fury sounded from the doorway and my heart stopped. 
 "Get. Your. Bloody hands. Off her." 
 Sure why not get spitfire mad at a dude for saving your girlfriend's life while not looking at her. But of course Anna's take on this is apologetic for HER behaviour. 
 Had I been in my right mind, I would have told him to focus on Zania while I waited for Kaidan [...] to come down 
 Heaven forbid this girl needs open heart surgery. Woe to the doctor who dares to touch her chest. 
 View post on imgur.com 
 On Secrets: 
 The other main theme is that Anna is part of a prophecy that will bring down demonic rule on earth. This is fairly serious business so of course Anna uses every opportunity to tell everyone she can think of about the prophecy. You might think such a naive move might be punished by her being found out. Nope. just nope. 
 Upon hearing the prophecy: 
 "Oh, my gosh," I said. "I need to call Dad." 
 and then a few hours later 
 I was burning with the urge to call [Kaidan]...Because he needed to know about this. Like, now 
 But did he? did he really? at three in the morning really need to know about a prophecy that is going to be so complicated to pull off it's going to take months? Couldn't wait till say the afternoon? 
 When meeting a secret ally Zania for the first time 
 "It's harder for me [to deny myself] with drugs." 
 hmm like really? The Demonic overlords think her weakness is alcohol. She dedicated a significant amount of effort to convince them of that, and yet so easily the truth spills from her. What is recruiting Zania fails? What if she's overheard? What if Zania is captured or coerced? These are thoughts that don't occur to people who don't understand the concept of a secret. 
 Anna never being punished for making stupid decisions is such a repeating trope in this book alone that even when it's called out she fails to fall. \ 
 "Tell me one mistake you've ever made in your perfect little life," [Ginger] challenged..."Okay. For one, I fell in love with Kaidan and showed him my colors [...] When we went on that road trip last year [...] I wanted to ... be with him. You know. But he said no." 
 This was such an excellent choice of Truth or Date question because she's never made a mistake. In her ENTIRE life the only mistake she's ever made was saying yes to a guy and she didn't lose her virginity in a manner she finds inappropriate. He wasn't rough with her. Instead of living with the consequences (and I apologize if that comes across as victim blamey but I'm speaking to a very very specific circumstance here) the guy actually says no so she doesn't have to suffer any consequence. Her life is literally filled with secret sharing with no regard and she's never caught by it. 
 The two people who appear like they CAN keep a secret are Kopano and of course her father Belial. This man has a the most powerful demon as his errand boy passing messages in a way that's basically deus ex machina all over the place. Oh no you're in danger about to be found out. Azael to the rescue. What do we do about the Duke of lies who can is a human lie detector. No worries Belial already got her mother on the side. The man even arranged to hook his daughter up with a nice guy that she finds attractive by just putting them together and seeing if it happens. He's the real MVP. 
 I wondered how many other unknown allies we had, but he would never tell me. Need to know basis. 
 Oh would that such control and understanding was genetic. Maybe everyone wouldn't know that Anna is faking, Anna is weak to drugs, Anna is in love with Kaidan. Anna is a virgin. Anna is running the revolution. Heck it's so obvious even the demonic overlords suspect it. 
 You know..." Pharzuph began, almost hesitant, lowering his voice even further. "Rahab thinks the daughter of Belial is the one." 
 On things the book did right: 
 Time. I don't normally see this in a YA book but time passes. I suspect it's just so they can age Anna up to make her 18 and therefore legal for sexual purposes, but I was actually sort of impressed by how much time passed with nothing happening. The story would focus on an event and then it would be a season until the next digetic event happened. It was a disoriently unique and surprisingly pleasant experience.

Original can be found @ Books & Swoons 
 Okay, So I had been procrastinating on reading Sweet Peril because I was afraid I would be disappointed with the story. Luckily that wasn't the case. Sweet Peril is the continuation of Anna's story in her quest to build an alliance in order to fight the dukes and gain freedom for herself and the rest of the Nephs. Basically what this means, is that she travels a lot and there is a lot of great descriptions of the different destinations she gets to travel to. The thing is that after a while I found myself speed-reading through said descriptions, just so I could get to the action part, and to Kaiden. 
 I already knew he wasn't a big part of Sweet Peril because Anna and him aren't supposed to be seeing each other, but I really missed his sense of humor throughout the majority of the story. I really enjoyed seeing how Ginger and Anna's relationship progressed as well as Anna's relationship with Belial. There was definitely more Kopano throughout the story and I was really upset at how Anna handled the situation with him. Anna was reacting to being hurt by Kaiden and used Kope in order to try and forget Kai. It was wrong on so many levels that even Anna was ashamed for acting the way she did. 
 All in all the plot kind of sagged in the middle but when the pace finally picked up towards the end there was a lot of suspense and heart ache going on. I was so happy when Anna and Kaiden where finally able to get together. Apart from the speed-reading through some of the excessive details I really enjoyed Sweet Peril.
Actually liked this one better than the first :)

book_b.user_review: Blaire and Rush are hot. All the sex? They were hot. But I was never a fan of instant romance so this book was just not for me.

Really Good... I already read NEVER TOO FAR also and I thought, I prefer Woods than Rush... Woods is a perfect man who cares about anyone (his Friends and his employee) I just love Woods... I wish Mrs Glines would be kind to me to write his own story :)

Gawd, I need to stop reading this crap. It's awful. Apparently editors are the only reason why commas exist in books, because none of these smutty indie books have them. Didn't anyone teach grammar in the 80s? 
 Seriously, these books are terrible - like crack, The Kardashians, or cheap potato chips. You know you're going to regret it but you go for it anyways. 
 The story sucked, the guy was horrendous, and not at all appealing, the main character shallow, there was no chemistry, and the sex scenes were boring. And the big scandal/secret? Just dumb. As I said in my review for Collide by Megan Hart, it's really sad when 50 Shades becomes good literature compared to this trash. 
 I honestly do not understand how books like these get a higher rating than Percy Jackson or Unwind. Apparent YA readers tastes are more discerning. And to think that I used to complain about the teenage fan girls that drove up the YA wannabe books! The writing for those are exponentially better than these "new adult" romances. At least this one cost me less than $1. 
 Sorry Abbi Glines - I'm sure you're a nice woman. Just invest in an editor - you can find them on craigslist.

This is well written book except for the repetitive Oh My's. It pulls you into the story and doesn't let you go until you finish it. I am kind of annoyed by the whole innocent, virginal, girl falling for the sexy, yet controlling stud, who bosses her around. Is this really how we still see woman in relationships? Can't Blaire be innocent and virginal, and yet be strong and self-assured at the same time? I'm also annoyed by authors who don't finish stories just so you run out to buy the next one. If the story is good, I will buy the second one but if the first leaves you hanging, I will be too inclined not to purchase another.

STORY: 4.5 stars 
 PERFORMANCE: 3.5-4 stars 
 OVERALL: 4 stars 
 STORY: 
 This was my 1st Abbi Glines book. It was a pleasant surprise with its' clever storyline and super hot sex scenes. I struggled with how fast some of the relationships became as deep as they did and how this occurred so quickly; for example, the relationship between the two main characters developed very, very quickly . While I was grateful that there was not an excessive amount of angst and tension-filled drama between them before they finally acknowledged their feelings, the magnitude of some of the feelings felt a bit rushed in my opinion. And though the ending was interesting, unexpected and made sense from a business perspective, I hated the cliffhanger ending! It did make me want to keep reading though... 
 PERFORMANCE: 
 Jennifer Lynn Bronstein is not a bad narrator yet because I have listened to so many other narrators, I kept wishing someone else had been chosen to read this particular series. I could be completely wrong but for me, Bronstein's Southern accent didn't not feel authentic. It was not absolutely atrocious though... What bothers me most about her performance was that she made little or no attempt to alter her voice between characters. I would have appreciated it if she'd at least attempted to speak with a more masculine voice while reading the male dialogue but she did not. Aside from the sex scenes, she did not put a lot of emotion into the dialogue, using the same tone of voice consistently which in my opinion was somewhat needy and whiny. And thought she did put emotion in her voice while recording the sex scenes, occasionally I felt that she put too much effort. Basically, if I hadn't listened to other, better narrators prior to hearing this audiobook, I don't think I would have had as many issues with Ms. Bronstein's performance but since that's not the case, it was hard for me not to compare.
I absolutely loved Blaire and Rush story. Couldn't get enough of those two. Can't wait to read more and see where there story will go.

Trate de escribir esto libre de spoilers pero se me puede haber escapado algo, lee bajo tu propio riesgo.

 Y luego hay una coleccion de personajes que me encantaria haber llegado a conocer mas:Woods, Bethy y Jace, Nan y sobretodo Grants. Claro, entiendo que esta no era su historia pero eso de lanzar personajes a diestra y siniestra y luego no contarnos sobre ellos, bueno, no me parece. 
 Y eso de que el papa aparezca en las ultimas paginas con una explicacion apresurada... !yo quiero saber mas! Quiero saberlo todo. Un par de paginas mas, con una conversacion un poco mas adecuada no hubiese dolido.

book_a.user_review: Gave up on this story. I have grown tired of the Lizard King and the Lot Lizards. When midway thru this book, I read a review of another C. J. Box book and discovered the heroine is still chasing the Lizard King in the next installment (Highway Quartet Novel #4). I didn't see any reason to finishing installment three - nor do I expect to read the next one.

sample_reviews.review_text: I hate reading a series out of order, but in the midst of reading this one I determined (accurately) that the back story being presented was an indication that the main character, Cassie Dewell, had appeared before. So, I'll go backwards and read the prequel, but that fact diminished none of the effect of this book. As murder mystery and police procedural it didn't break much new ground (outsider cop, corruption on the force, murderous gangs, innocents at risk), but in its short, sweet length, it was a very interesting portrayal of a modern boom town, and all the vice that comes with the riches fracked oil can bring.

Why do so many authors try to sell the idea that discovery of fact is more important than due process? And given the popularity of the books, I guess a lot of people buy the idea. And why do I worry about such things when I am reading fiction? Because sometimes fiction can give you a better idea of where people's thinking is than surveys.
So happy for a new standalone with new characters. I'm not a fan of joe Pickett, but I do enjoy box's other books

I enjoyed reading C.J. Box's THE BADLANDS. I loved that Cassie Dewell is your everyday woman: middle aged, concerned about the extra weight she carries, single mother, has issues, and too busy to worry about the right clothes or haircut. On top of that she's sharp, tough, good at her job, and yet has a soft maternal core. She's a character I could relate to and like. However the character that really drew me in was 12 year old Kyle. There were scenes in Kyle's POV that actually had me a little misty eye at times. 
 THE BADLANDS has an interesting world, an Old West feeling, and I enjoyed reading the tidbits Box showed us of gritty Grimstad, ND. The story is filled with interesting, well developed characters, dark suspense, and at its core a boy's quest to take care of his mother. 
 The was my first C.J. Box novel and I was impressed. Now I definitely have to read the first 2 books in this series and see what all fuss is about the Joe Pickett series, since all of Box's fans love that character.

This was a good stand-alone book, but not a great one by an author I have enjoyed before. To oversimplify, an autistic teen witnesses a crime, his mother can't overcome her addictions, and a new female detective is in town, a North Dakota town severely changed by the discovery of oil. The police are not portrayed very sympathetically, and the novel's fast pace just really doesn't allow the reader to engage all that well. It ends with a clear lead to a sequel which is fine, but there was just not enough suspense in this to hook me into another. One interesting inclusion was the observations about how the discovery of oil can profoundly affect a community in the form of drugs, instant money, loss of traditional ways, etc.

My interest in reading this title was the setting of the Bakken oil field in North Dakota. There were really no details depicted about life in this oil field that I was unaware of. The story did move along quickly and the "invisible" twelve year old young boy was an interesting character and he, Kyle, could always preserve onward. A gritty, gutsy kid is Kyle. 
 This was my first C. J. Box novel and while I was engrossed to see what was going to happen regarding the missing drugs, there is a bit too much violence in this author's writing for me. Probably will not choose to read another on of Box's books.
Another enjoyable suspense by C.J. Box. I look forward to reading the next in this series.

3.5 stars. Gritty, a bit grisly, and with a decidedly topical setting--a backwater town struggling to deal with both the good and the bad brought on by the economic boom of the Dakota oil fields. I do like the Cassie Dewell character and will be following her next adventure when Paradise Valley releases in July. Hopefully, that will include a resolution to the Lizard King, one psycho serial killer whose saga began in The Highway.

I really enjoyed this stand alone by C.J. Box. It involves investigator Cassie Dewell, hired by Grimstad, North Dakota sheriff Kirkbride to look into the reason for the high increase in drug trafficking and usage in addition to the increase in disappearances and murders involving bodies being cut up, etc. in the former small town. Because of fracking, the town has seen a huge growth in population due to all the workers involved in getting oil out of the ground, using a method involving fracking to do so. Cassie had been working in North Carolina prior to relocating to Grimstad, where the temperature often falls to 32 or more degrees below zero, so she has to deal with becoming acclimated to such a cold climate. She also had been working on a case involving long haul truck driver and serial killer, Ronald Pergram or Stradley, and had nearly been killed by him before she left for North Dakota. (This is a continuation of the book "The Highway" published in 2013 involving Cody Hoyt and Cassie Dewell, his partner). Sheriff Kirkbride fears that he has at least one dirty cop in his employ and Cassie is assigned to find out whatever she can about the situation. 
 The book starts off with newspaper delivery boy Kyle Westergaard seeing a fatal car accident, and finding a bag full of money, and pounds of both methamphetamine and black tar heroin already packaged for sale. Kyle doesn't know what he has found, but he takes the bag home, and of course the crooked cop(s) in addition to several other people are wondering what happened to the bag. It actually belongs to members of the MS13 gang from El Salvador, now located in the San Diego, CA area. Kyle, born with fetal alcohol syndrome, has a mother who is a recovering alcoholic and heroin addict who lives with a sleazy man who basically lives off her wages from McDonald's, T-Lock. When T-Lock finds the bag and sees what it contains, all hell breaks loose in one form or another because he is a meth addict and can't help spending the marked money to buy a new vehicle and also using the drugs. This brings the MS13 guys to the small town and the murders increase, so Casey and her new partner, Ian Davis, have their work cut out for them. 
 I thought the book was a great story and I was fascinated by how the MS13 gang got started. The US basically took people from this country in as refugees after many of them, including women and children were murdered by others in a civil war in their own country. (Author T.J. Parker also uses the MS13 gang as villains in several of his books). I am sure there will be at least one more book in this series, since the serial killer truck driver has not been prosecuted for his crimes yet.

(2 1/2) I am glad to say that I now have hope for this C.J. Box franchise. The first one was so formulaic and violent that it was not very good. This one is still formulaic and violent, but there is some good character development and much better plot development as well. Cassie Dewell isn't much of a protagonist yet and Box will have to work on making her a more compelling presence but if he keeps coming up with such a wide array of supporting characters and spinoff lines to the main story this could become a successful series. A quick read with a very realistic and up to date setting. I will hang in there for the next one.

book_b.title: Saturn Run
book_b.user_review: Interesting book, but not my normal reading material. I read this book because is was partially written by John Sanford.

sample_reviews.review_text: I read this not long after reading The Martian and at first felt like it was a retelling of the same story and almost didn't continue because I was disappointed. BUT, I gave it a chance and I am glad I followed it to the end because the ideas that developed were fresh and intellectual. It may have started slow, but I was pleased with how it came into its own. Give it a chance; I'm glad I did.

Flawed. But one hell of a detailed actual science science-fiction relatively near-future book. Bits were definitely clumsy and with too much detail. The pacing was uneven. And the characters were inconsistently done. And the ending wasn't especially believable. But the technology and the politics and how it rolled out made a lot of sense. Lots of ideas in this one but more realistic seeming then most. A mixed bag. But worth talking about. 3.5 of 5.

The plot was so interesting, I didn't quit. But I probably should have! John Sanford CANNOT write female characters! To him, women clearly should be dead, stupid, grasping, or traitors. This book offended all my feminist values. But I really wanted to find out what was going on on Saturn!
Really enjoyed this, some good near-future hard SF with aliens thrown in for good measure.

Alien activity is accidentally noticed near Saturn. The U.S. and China enter a race to see who can get there first. Both missions have problems and didn't have time for proper planning. This book follows the U. S. mission closely and tells about the lead up and trip to Saturn. They beat the Chinese by a couple of weeks and discover that the site is just a depot that provides information to whomever discovers it. The Chinese ship is badly damaged during the trip and needs a rescue. Should the Americans risk it? 
 This is my kind of science fiction. Set in the future where technology is more advanced yet people and situations are very familiar. Lots of fun.

John Sanford means nothing to me. I haven't read any of his other books, though I can tell you that when I was reading this and my mom walked in the room she marched right over and got all grabby to read the back cover. There was no back cover, for the record, since it's an ARC. 
 That was my first introduction that John Sanford has written books before, and enough that my mom knew right away who he was. She was surprised he wrote a book about space too, which gave me another indication--he doesn't generally write science fiction. 
 Okay, learned two things very quickly. What I learned from reading the novel is this: 
 A TON of research went into this. The entire story is pretty much focused on futuristic (I think?) rockets, strong enough and fast enough that we as human beings can get to Saturn and back in the span of a couple years. The story here is that we discover an alien space ship arriving near Saturn, then leaving again. Because we as a species care more about one-upping each other, it immediately becomes a nation vs. nation scenario where we try to beat the Chinese, so we can get the special alien technology first. 
 What follows is a lot of technical information, some of which was interesting but most of it I kind of glazed over for. Science and math were never my strong suits, and this focuses heavily on the science. When that happens I just sort of mentally check out until the plot comes back into play. 
 But the plot didn't play as large of a role as I thought it would. Nor did the aliens. You'd think that there'd be a pretty big portion about the aliens, right? Thing is, when they finally got to Saturn a really solid chunk of the book was already over, and that worried me. If so much time was spent on the minutiae of the travel, how were they going to give the aliens their due space too? Answer: we don't get to meet the aliens. 
 Action was few and far between, which made this drag after a while. I kept thinking we were building to this big bad climax with lots of drama thrown in the mix to keep things interesting. That is half true--we did get lots of drama, even a death. It just wasn't enough to wow me and I wasn't dying to find out what would happen next. 
 Ultimately, it was a character driven book on the wrong characters for me. I wanted ALIENS and you gave me people.

I love John Sanford but I delayed reading this book because I also feel like... ugh, crossovers by famous authors are usually bad - like the publisher is just thinking "Give the guy his crappy book he always wanted to write and then he will concentrate back on the moneymakers." 
 I was wrong with this one! 
 While Mr. Sanford seems to basically write the same main character in every book. albeit with a different name, the science and the fun and the character all added up to a great read!
Poorly written. Superficial characters, Lots of headhopping and viewpoint shifts. Lots of telling.
Great story. Really enjoyed this book.
Ruined by a terrible last few chapters.

reference_books.title: Burned (Burned, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I've read 4 of Ellen Hopkins' books in the last two weeks, going on a bit of an author binge after she was recommended by a friend. This book details the life of a Mormon teen in an abusive family. She is sent to a long lost aunt's house to "straighten her out", but instead she discovers love and a side of herself she never knew existed. Themes of religious doubt, teen sexuality and self discovery are explored, and the book is gripping. The conclusion of the book is abrupt, unsatisfying and rather inconsistent with the rest of the story, but otherwise the book is quite memorable.

reference_books.title: Breaking Dawn (Twilight, #4)
reference_books.review_text: I was awaiting this book very anxiously, having enjoyed the first three books in the series. However, this final book disappointed me as a reader- characters and plot lines were inconsistent and the tone of the book changed completely as compared to the first three. Maddening!

reference_books.title: The Last Straw (Diary of a Wimpy Kid, #3)
reference_books.review_text: This book has been fiercely anticipated by nearly every 3rd to 6th grader in the land for months. I found it to be the least enjoyable of the three "Wimpy Kid" books, it seems to be missing much of the quirky humor that made the first two hits with many tweens. This opinion was backed up by my own tween, who said the book was "just okay...nothing special, and not as good as the first one".

reference_books.title: Every You, Every Me
reference_books.review_text: I've read - and adored- several books by this author but his new book seemed quite different and I didn't enjoy it nearly as much. The literary device of using overstruck text (a line through the words, as if to cross them out) to show the characters true feelings is heavily used, over and over for large segments of the book. It is a nice way to express thoughts a few times, but it got very bothersome when used dozens and dozens of times in a fairly short book. The plot features an interesting mystery to be solved within a high school setting, but it just wasn't what I'd come to expect from this author's usually stellar output.

reference_books.title: Identical
reference_books.review_text: I would find it unlikely that any reviewer would say they "enjoyed" this book- it is both difficult and uncomfortable to read. However, this tale of incest, abuse, family secrets and intense psychological disorders is unforgetable. There is a twist near the end that throws the reader for a huge loop, forcing one to reassess the first 500 pages of the book. This book features very adult situations and language and is recommended for mature readers.

book_a.title: Everybody Sees the Ants
book_a.user_review: This dark, brave, touching book reveals the psychological effects of bullying on a 15 year old boy. Part realistic fiction, part hallucinogenic fantasy, it blends the two perfectly. Lucky Linderman struggles under constant, horrific bullying from a classmate and his very disfunctional family. Every time he dreams, he is transported to the jungles of Vietnam where he attempts to rescue his grandfather, missing in action since the early '70s. Each of these dreams leaves his with a solid artifact to prove that a great deal of reality lies within the dreams. Througout the book, a crew of ants offer constant commentary on his life, both the painfully real on and the one set in his dreams. This book is very highly recommended for older teens to adults, it is outstanding.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Sad, brutal, funny: well done, A.S. King. It's been awhile since I've read a realistic treatment of a bullied kid, one that captures the creative/banal cruelty of the perpetrator, the absolute ineffectiveness of adults in such situations, and the absolute despair of the victim who has done everything possible to disappear and is still singled out. All of that is here, but it isn't a weepy sort of book; it's wry and twisted, full of a lot of painful laughter and sarcasm. And it makes sense, because when you've been harassed your whole life by someone seemingly untouchable, and when the people who are supposed to protect you are too caught up in their own baggage to shield you from it, you have several choices: shut down, escape by any means, or get funny. Lucky Linderman does a little of each. 
 I liked the POW/MIA angle, both as a method for providing color and action in an otherwise very talky and emotional narrative, and as a metaphor for Lucky's situation. Usually dream sequences are a cop-out, but these served a definite function and were well-written - they make it possible for Lucky (and for the reader) to access emotions that would seem really sappy if they came out in waking life. 
 Loses one star because I don't quite buy some of the interaction b/t Lucky and Ginny + the gang of wise-cracking feminists. I want it to be believable but it feels like wishful thinking. Maybe I'm just cynical; it's possible that there are plenty of hetero teenage boys that are secretly that sensitive and open-minded and female-positive, but I've not met any yet (sorry guys - I hope you prove me wrong!).

I had mixed feelings about this book. It was definitely written well, and I found the story somewhat compelling, however I did not like the parts where he was dreaming and was in the jungle with his grandfather. I understand the relevance to the story, and why it was put in there, but I do not like books that combine some sort of realistic fiction with fantasy elements. For example, Revolution by Jennifer Donnelly. I really liked that book all the way to the end, when there were a few fantasy elements somewhat intertwined. Anyway, that means that I did not like this book as much as I had anticipated going into it. I give it 74%.

"The world is full of assholes. What are you doing to make sure you're not one of them?" 
 Like Lucky, I once did something that got me sent to the school counselor. Except I was in 5th grade. I was normally dropped off to school before the breakfast period. I typically spent 30 to 40 min. thinking alone in the school playground about things that occurred the night before. 
 After one particularly bad night, I decided I needed outside data. So I worked up the courage to ask a handful of kids at breakfast period: What's discipline? What's abuse? How can you tell the difference? 
 Answers were not forthcoming. I think I nearly caused one girl to cry with my bizarre arguments. (e.g. "If they don't beat you, doesn't that mean they don't love you?") I backed off. 
 The breakfast teacher asked what was wrong. I was terrified, but repeated my question: "What's the difference between discipline and abuse?" I didn't get an answer. She let me believe there wasn't a problem. But I got called out of class later. 
 I met the school counselor in a tiny room that felt like a closet. I didn't know her. She said I wasn't in trouble. I didn't believe her. 
 At some point, she asked if I had any injuries. I had a bruise on my left arm from when mom grabbed me too hard. I didn't want my mom in trouble. My mom had enough trouble. The other night, I watched dad plow mom with a chair, then throw it at her when she ran for the front door. 
 I was scared again. Here was an adult pretending to care. But they won't understand. They were gonna get it all wrong and make everything worse. 
 I had learned that there were good enough reasons to threaten your daughter with knives and throw chairs at your wife. But even by my standards, dad's logic that night made little sense. He was mad cause mom was late to cook dinner. She came home late cause she had to balance a full-time job in Flushing with evening Touro College classes. We lived in the Lower East Side. 
 I showed this woman my bruise. Said it was an accident. (My mom did not abuse me. If anything, I should've been the one to protect her.) And didn't say anything else. They called mom to pick me up. My teacher and the principal spoke with her. 
 Later, I showed mom the tiny knife wound dad left on my back. We went into hiding from dad. I missed 3 months of school. But in the end, we had to go back to dad anyway. 
 There's so much King gets right. And so much she gets wrong. Only the people who've been through it would know the difference. 
 For all the talk about standing up for oneself, in the end, the problem is solved by the intervention of other adults.
Loved it.

I really enjoyed this book. A.S King writes it so nicely. 
 The idea of the book, in balancing reality and dreams is powerful and realistic. And, each character is in-depth. The plot is brilliantly crafted. I love the writing as well. Love the book overall, and would definetely reccomend it.
Read it. Just freaking do it. So good.

It's ironic that a book about bullying can be so full of cruel, negative stereotypes that it verges on bullying itself. 
 Lucky Linderman, the teenage protagonist of A.S. King's young adult novel Everybody Sees the Ants, has been routinely bullied by an asshole named Nader McMillan since he was seven years old. Nader's antics grow ever more cruel until, one day at the pool, he uses Lucky's face to try to erase the cement. 
 With a giant wound in the shape of Ohio on his cheek, Lucky's mom packs them up and heads to Arizona to the safe confines of her brother and sister-in-law. They leave behind Lucky's father a chef who can only cope with his falling apart family by disappearing into work. 
 read more.
Deserving of its many honors. Amy King is a writers' writer.

What an absolutely beautiful book with such strong messages laced throughout. I had no idea what it was about before picking it up and I can say it was a great experience reading it that way. This is definitely one of those "everybody should read this" books.
