 ACTUALLY 3.5 STARS 
 I think I keep waiting too long after reading to write reviews, so please forgive me if this one doesn't make sense. And it probably won't. When I start Everybody Sees the Ants, I was expected a book very similar to Please Ignore Vera Dietz, which I adored. And although they had a lot of similarities, in my mind they were completely different. 
 Lucky, the main character per this one, is a huge nerd. I don't know exactly what makes him a nerd for me, but he'll be stuck forever as that in my mind. And the poor guy is bullied, he doesn't stand up for himself (his daddy made him that way) and one day it just goes too far. His mom gets sick and tired and leave town to stay with her brother. That's when the real story starts. Before that it was like we were just getting all the info for the build up of leaving, so we could see why. Good call there. (Completely off subject, but the bully: Nader. That sounds like a kid who would get bullied to me.) 
 But anyway. So they're gone. And Lucky starts explaining these weird dreams. Every time he has one, we get the down-low. And honestly, I have no idea whether Lucky is downright delusional, or if he's actually sane. Because the dreams...they're weird. And they're true to him, which makes it even harder to make a decision. Surreal is the best way to describe this entire book. 
 Lucky was really weird, too. On top of having all of these strange dreams, he's (as mentioned before) nerdy, and not only that, but he's a bit anti-social. I was so proud of him when he started to make friends! Because no matter how weird they were, I loved them. I mean, they're doing a public play named "The Vagina Monologues", and are doing it seriously. How are they not awesome? I mean, if it makes you uncomfortable it's probably not awesome, but I thought it was hilarious and actually kind of meaningful. 
 All in all, Everybody Sees the Ants was a very weird, surreal book. If you have problems reading about vaginas, or bullied boys, don't read it.

book_b.title: Wishful Drinking
book_b.user_review: I've read most of Carrie Fisher's fiction, when I saw her on a morning show promoting this book I knew that I had to read it. I did enjoy this autobiography, but I think that it would have been far more memorable if I had listened to an audiobook of it read by the author- her personality is so BIG (perhaps as a function of the manic phase of the bipolar disorder she discussed in this book)that the book would no doubt be greatly enhanced in audio. However, the book was very good and every aspect of her sometimes tragic and troubled life received Fisher's trademark highly intelligent, snarky treatment.

sample_reviews.review_text: Shame he dies in the end.
Disappointing. I wasn't sure if I was reading the script for her stage show or a book. In either case, maybe an outline would have helped during the writing process. This was all over the place.

I don't read a lot of celebrity memoirs, so maybe as things go this was pretty good but... Rick and I listened to an older NPR interview and the Fresh Air interview from November last week after she died. My interest was piqued in her life but between rehashing the exact anecdotes told in interviews and Star Wars which I've admittedly never seen, there was a lot of skimming going on. It was much funnier/wittier to listen to her than to read her.

I highly recommend the audio version! It really adds something to the narrative to have the author's own voice injecting her personality in. She does repeat herself a fair bit, but it doesn't really detract from the humor or meaningfulness of the stories. I wish I could give it 3.5 stars.

I no longer really like Carrie Fisher. I mean, I never really gave two whits about the Star Wars films. I like Debbie Reynolds... 
 In this book, Carrie Fisher was self-obsessed, repetitive and frankly, vulgar.
Tried too hard to be funny.
Just before I finished this Carrie passed away. I loved her sense of humor and her honesty.

What a lovely audiobook this made for, narrated by Carrie. What an absolutely unbelievable life she's had. It's true that real life is stranger than fiction. Carrie essentially narrates the course of her life, an endeavor spurred on by her decision to get electro-shock therapy, which at the time of the book's writing, resulted in the loss of a portion of her memories. She covers everything, from being born from two Hollywood icons to living a life surrounding by famous people, to getting entrenched in drugs and alcohol, to coming to grips both with her addiction and her mental health issues, to her various marriages, to being a mother, and all that comes in between. Carrie is completely honest with her life and herself in a way that is unbelievably refreshing. She fully embraces her life, her emotions, her anger, her addiction, her bipolar disorder, and every beautiful and ugly bit of herself. I found this so enjoyable.

Anyway, at a certain point in my early twenties, my mother started to become worried about my obviously ever-increasing drug ingestion. So she ended up doing what any concerned parent would do. 
 She called Cary Grant. 
 First of all, Carrie Fisher is hilarious. I had no idea that she was the Shiloh Jolie of her generation and that her mother had Ava Gardner on speed dial (or whatever they had back in the 1970s). Though the cover shows Fisher in her iconic Leia costume, very little focuses on her stint as a galactic princess. She has her hands full with manic depression, bipolar disorder, famous parents, an on-again off-again marriage with Paul Simon, and parties at which she regularly ran into Meryl Streep and George Harrison. No big. 
 It's obvious that this book came from a standup show. Most of the jokes would be great in a live setting. They revolve around pithy punch lines, and the whole book moves at a breakneak pace, from Fisher's daughter to her parents to her husband and back again. When I started reading "out loud" in my head, the book was much more enjoyable - with a good sense of comedic timing, Fisher's mediocre jokes become amusing. Unfortunately, that doesn't transfer well to paper, and I felt like I was being jerked around in the text. Fisher is a decent writer, but the constant subject changes and lack of direction mean that many of her shticks don't ... stick. (I'm doing it now, SAVE ME). As a side project, this book is a fun, fast read. As a true memoir, it falls short in several ways. 
 Read if you like: MTV True Life, Star Wars 
 Skip if you prefer: narrative continuity, prose that goes beyond standard standup jokes
Entertaining, engaging, and thoroughly approachable. Perhaps too approachable?

sample_reviews.review_text:
I'm really beginning to question my resolve to finish this series. I'm still plugging away at it--just started book 4 in fact--but I'm finding more and more that I have to force myself to pick these books up and read them. It's not a story that haunts me night and day until I finish it. I think there are a few reasons for this. 
 First of all--and I've heard other people say this--these books are so very long. And it's not that they're too rich with detail. I like detail in a book. No, the problem is that so many things happen that have nothing to do with the overall story and therefore do nothing to advance the plot. Like encountering the plague ship, for example. That had nothing to do with the characters' primary goal of finding Ian, so why was it there? And speaking of that primary goal, we were nearly halfway through the book before the situation with Ian even came up. Until then it was all about Claire getting back to the 18th century so she could be reunited with Jamie. So shouldn't that have been its own book, and the thing with Ian been saved for the next installment? I don't know. These books just seem to ramble on aimlessly about anything and everything. 
 I'm also not really digging the characters. I can't seem to identify with Claire very much, and I'm not attracted to Jamie, so there's an extent to which I don't much care what happens to them. That has nothing to do with the quality of the book and everything to do with my personal taste, but it's still problematic for me. 
 And what's the deal with Mr. Willoughby? Talk about your racial stereotypes. Okay, I know, the book takes place in the 18th century when people had very little contact with cultures outside of their own. I can understand that, and so if the story were told from Jamie's point of view I would have understood the portrayal of Mr. Willoughby's character. But the narrator is Claire, a modern, educated woman from the late 1960s. Surely she's been around Chinese people before. And yet she insists on referring to him as "the little Chinese". So maybe "little" is used only to refer to his stature, but it still comes off as condescending. Like there's something inherently cutesy about this character and the culture from which he hails. As I said, I would have been okay seeing this portrayal of him through Jamie's eyes, but I would have expected better from Claire. 
 I still plan on finishing the series, because I like to finish what I start, but it may take me a while to get through all the other books.
Libraries should have extended deadlines for books of this particular length...

I started this book SIX MONTHS ago. It got more and more ridiculous, and more and more difficult to pay attention. By the time I got to page 500, I should have just quit. But I was more than halfway through, so I pushed on. Slowly. So slowly. It was not a good decision. I think I'm done with the series. 
 The second star is for the beginning ... the Scotland stuff was ludicrous, but in keeping with the first two books. Then, however, the plot goes off the rails and into the ocean. So many ships. So many storms. So many islands. So many pages.

This was book 3 by Diana Gabaldon in the Outlander series, and I am a HUGE fan. I loved Books 1 & 2 and the tv series which wraps up right around that time, but my god, Book 3 was WAY way too much fast-moving PLOT that reeked of sea adventures, island rituals, bizarre characters, and some not-so-well-explained voodoo magic. YIKES! The dynamic between Claire and Jamie was neither explored further nor really had time to develop because Diana threw SO MANY fast-moving events in our direction. Way too much plot, way too little story. 
 I started losing interest after the boy gets captured. I won't give it away for those who haven't read it but those who have, you know what I'm talking about. The nature of the events seemed to be so made up, so incongruent to the overall story, and awfully put together that it made me think she was just stringing us along. I listened to the audio version and actually put it on 1.25x to make it move along faster. I also switched to reading on the Kindle here and there. The islands didn't do anything for me and honestly, the characters surrounding this event seemed as dull and uninteresting as it could get. 
 Gosh I'm just going to wrap it up by saying this was a most unsatisfying story, yet it included two of my favorite characters who manage to grow way less favorite to me. Is it possible to get seasick from reading a book and going through the motions of the storm with your characters? Well, I think I did. 
 Now I have to decide if I'm going to continue the story. Feeling let down and sad that I no longer can say I LOVE love love Outlander. I guess it's possible all this is because we're no longer in Scotland, folks!!!!
-- Yet again.....applause to Gabaldon....can't wait to read the next! --

So, OK... I admit that I liked Outlander and Dragonfly... but Voyager was just ludicrous. But after slogging my way through Voyager, I feel complete with the series. I realize that this book is supposed to be over-the-top action and people admire it because the lovers aren't in their 20's. But Gabaldon over-uses phrases and all judgements about people are based on what their eyebrows are doing. The setting of the various boats they are in are claustrophobic and Claire is taken hostage so many times in the three books I have read, you would think that she would be used to it. If you want non-stop action, then go for it. But this is definitely a book for plot junkies. 
 I like to call these people (affectionately) addicted to plot.

I was really torn about how to rate this book. On the one hand, I really enjoyed reading it. On the other hand, I had some serious issues with some of the events in the book. I didn't expect Jaime to be a monk after Claire left, but his marriage to Laoghaire just didn't make any sense to me (especially after what she did to Claire). I'm also disturbed by Claire's lack of anger and feelings of betrayal after Jaime lied (by omission) to her not once but twice. I would have expected them to take things slower once they found each other again too. I thought there would be at least one discussion about the twenty years they missed with each other! I was also surprised at the lack of concern over Young Ian. He disappears, they freak out and go after him, and then barely mention him again until after they're at Geillis' house.

Another great addition to the Outlander Series. It's disappointing that Claire & Jamie were separated for a whole 20 years! Although their devotion to each other never dies. They finally reunite to find out they don't know each other at all, they've become different people over those 20 years apart but their love still lasts. Lots and lots of drama and adventure in this book, I was reading this book when I decided gabaldon thinks of everything! Jamie an Claire get out through the craziest stuff. A wonderful book and a lovely introduction to some characters that we will soon fall Iove with in future books!
A little slower in places than the last two books but still amazing. Such a good ending!!
I honestly didn't mind the first half. The second half is so far fetched that I couldn't get into it. It was a struggle to get through. A shame since I enjoyed the first two so much.

I so loved this amazing book. I have loved the entire series to. So moving, beautiful and so ever romantic. Reese is a amazing strong heart girl. She has dealt with so many terrors in her life, with family, life and even love. But from the day that Mase met her he has always been for her.

Only Abbi Glines can put sweet and sexy together like nobody else. The story of Reese and Mase is every girl's fairytale. Having that strong sexy man there for you, and loving you through everything. 
 The struggles that Reese went through and overcame is so courageous. Having Mase there being her personal cheerleader is so inspiring. Captain! OMG!! Never, never saw that one coming!! Just wow!!! 
 Abby's stories always have some awareness brought to them. This story is no different. Dyslexia does not make any individual young or old stupid. Having a support system is the most important thing. Mase was that support for Reese. 
 Reese finally gets her HEA. Has the father she always wanted, friends who love her like family, and a man she will love for the rest of her life. Can't wait for more from Rosemary Beach. Will be sad to see the series end.

Thank goodness I did not have to wait long AFTER finally reading When You're Gone (Rosemary Beach #11) when we were introduced to Mase Colt Manning and Reese Ellis. I was feeling all warm and tingly by their connection and got hooked into their background and their story that I needed more especially the cliffhanger ending we were left with. 
 Reece is still fighting her demons but with the help of the love of her life, Mase it was getting easier. She had made some amazing progress and is ready to explore/experience more opportunities. She is a strong and determined woman out to prove she can overcome and accomplish things she has missed out on. She wants to prove her independence and with any new challenges there were obstacles that she had to face. 
 Whenever, wherever there was anything that entailed Reece, there was a guarantee that Mase was always there and/or knew something was up. He had fallen HARD for her and knew how to read her. This beautiful man constantly won my heart over and over again. Although there were times he was a bit too much but the reasoning behind any of his actions had made sense. I mean what is not to love a hot, overprotected cowboy who truly loves his dear family (& of course Reece) FIERCELY, and would do anything to see them happy? 
 "I can swear to you that you will always be it for me. No one fits me like you. No one makes me feel whole. No one else ever will." 
 As with any love that grows deeper, Mase and Reece began encountering obstacles in their relationship that will test them to the fullest with an ugly past that they will continue to face together, new people butting in and/or eyeing their attention..the getting the list goes on and on. 
 This book starts off where (obviously) book one leaves off, however, the first few pages felt rushed on something that needed just a little more insight that it had slightly thrown me off a bit. Although, as the story progressed it got more into what was going on and figuring out where the connections were at making the read intense, intriguing, and the need to know more not just about the main characters but the supporting characters as well. 
 The story of Mase and Reece continues to break and melt my heart <3 in ways that I had least expected. Their story is one that will give you goosebumps in good and bad ways. And the big plus...there were more swoony goodness from Mase! So much to say but at a lost for words about this fine specimen. :D 
 I have to quickly note that the ending of the book kinda of threw me off. A lot of questions were answered but It felt like a cliffhanger of sorts. I am hoping that we get more of them in the future. 
 If you have fallen for the characters' stories from the Rosemary Beach series this one definitely did not fall short and was filled with even more to the collection. ~Cristina, 4 stars 
 ************************ 
 GOOSEBUMPS. I had them all over once I read the very last word of this book. Abbi Glines just writes everything that can rock and shatter your world, then somehow put all the pieces back together again. I was blown out of my freaking wits. It was insane! The twists were just so unexpected. And that one chapter near the end? I did not see that coming. At all. You will definitely know which one I'm talking about when you read this--it was a solid and outstanding chapter from the book. But with everything that's been going on though, it was like waiting for the shoe to drop. Multiplied by ten. So much was happening in all angles that it would be hard for you to keep up if you weren't as engrossed in the book, which is close to impossible, by the way. 
 Mase & Reese were just hard not to love. I fell deep for both of them--take note on the both part--ever since When I'm Gone. I honestly like that better than this one though. I think I could've lived with that book alone for Mase & Reese, but then again, that's just my opinion. And I don't think I'd know anybody who's read When I'm Gone that didn't want more, more and more of Mase Colt Manning. I mean, Jesus Christ. Have you met the man? Have you heard him talk? Everything coming out of that man's mouth is magic. It is so darn impossible not to fall head over heels for him. Just plain impossible. It was like death by Mase's words. His words alone can give you butterflies in your stomach, make you hot and squirm, and melt you into freaking goo. 
 In When You're Back, everything in Mase & Reese's relationship is tested--down to the very core of it: trust. Love was never gone. As was told here, once you find that one person for you, you love hard. And that just never goes away, which was perfectly the case for this Rosemary Beach series couple. 
 And please, please let there be a book or two for Captain? I am craving to know more about him after his appearance here. He can't just not have a story after this one. Believe me, when you read When You're Back--probably 80%--you'll be agreeing with me. ~Renery, 4.5 stars

reference_books.title: Start with Why: How Great Leaders Inspire Everyone to Take Action
reference_books.review_text:
I first learned about Simon Sinek watching his famous TED talk many years ago. That talk helped me put into words WHY I write fantasy novels. It was not long after watching it that I wrote 'A Manifesto on Virtue' and posted it on my blog (http://www.jeff-wheeler.com/?page_id=447). And it was shortly after *that* when Amazon Publishing picked me up as an author. 
 So needless to say, I'm a huge believer in the power of WHY. I recently finished reading Simon's book and thoroughly enjoyed it. It went deeper and had more examples than his TED talk. You can't read it without re-thinking your own strategies. For example, before I started reading it, I was running some marketing ads for my new e-zine Deep Magic. The results weren't very good. Then I got to the part of Simon's book that talked about finding people who already believe in your vision. Who already have bought into the WHY. Those are the people who want to find. So I changed the marketing message to the WHY I founded and am publishing Deep Magic: because I love reading (and writing) clean fantasy and science fiction stories with strong moral values. I aim to bring a little goodness and light to this dark world instead of adding more darkness. I believe in my core that the pendulum has swung too far to the gritty and dark (think Game of Thrones). I believe books can be compelling and riveting and have *good* heroes. As soon as I changed the messaging, copies of Deep Magic started to sell. Go figure. Simon was right again. 
 Understanding your own WHY is so important. Read the book. It'll make you think about your life, your career, your reason to get up in the morning.

reference_books.title: The Queen of Blood  (The Queens of Renthia, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
The first thing I always look for when starting a new author or a new series is tension. It must be inherent in the plot and with the main characters or I won't read past a few pages. The Queen of Blood is full of rich tension from the opening scene to the nail-biting finale. The world of Aratay is teeming with elemental spirits with urges to create and destroy. Only the will and magic of the Queen keeps their bloodlust from destroying the civilizations of humanity that live within the creative tree cities in the woods. Barely. The story is about a queen-in-training, Daleina, who survives one such massacre and despite her inadequacies, strives to keep the balance that protects her people. She is joined by a disgraced champion named Ven who also seeks the welfare of the people above his own safety and comfort. While there are a few sexual references (offscreen) that don't quite make it a true cleanread, it's a step in the right direction and much tamer than most of the current crop of fantasy offerings I normally run across and avoid. The violence is related to the nature of the elemental spirits and adds well to the suspense by raising the stakes.

sample_reviews.review_text:
As easy as it would be to throw on one star and spend the entire review mocking Atlas Shrugged and Ayn Rand, I'm not going to. There's already plenty written about the glacial pace, the painful dialogue, the unbelievable characters, and the book's myriad other flaws, and to a great extent I agree with all of that. However, because that's all been said, I'm going to talk about why I think it deserves two stars instead of one. 
 It's much more of an allegory, like The Pilgrim's Progress or The Faerie Queene, than a novel as such. Like those two, most of the characters that appear in the book aren't fully-realized characters, but instead archetypes--either the Glorious Titan of Industry, the Vile Socialist Looter, or the Undecided Masses. Dagny Taggart and Hank Rearden are much more fully realized, and there are other characters that get some depth (Francisco d'Anconia, Cheryl Taggart, Eddie Willers, etc.), but mostly the names and behavior are interchangeable. If Midas Mulligan ran an oil company and Elias Wyatt ran a bank, the story and themes of Atlas Shrugged would only have to be changed in one place: the story of why Midas Mulligan is named "Midas." 
 That's another thing. You can usually tell which archetype a character is simply by their names. The Glorious Titans of Industry have names like Midas Mulligan and Judge Narragansett (well, that's a title, but you never learn his first name) and John Galt and Elias Wyatt and Ragnar Danneskjold, whereas the Vile Socialist Looters have names like Tinky Holloway and Balph Eubank and Kip Chalmers and Cuffy Meigs and Wesley Mouch (the most blatant example). 
 And speaking of interchangeability, the other countries in the world are all interchangeable. Literally every other country is repeatedly referred to as "The People's State of [x]," though in a couple cases the transformation into a Vile Socialist Looter country occurs during the course of the plot. Any People's State produces nothing of value and exists only to sponge supplies and money from America, the only country in the world which still counts Glorious Titans of Industry among its populace. 
 With this kind of cartoonish background, I think it's unfair to hold Atlas Shrugged to either the standards of a philosophical treatise or a novel, because it's not often trying to be those and where it does, it does it badly. As a philosophical treatise, the work is amateurish, relying on philosophical arguments that have already been effectively answered by people who wrote before Ayn Rand did (just one example--Objectivism smashes hard on the rocks of Hume's Is-Ought Problem). As a novel, it's long-winded, with stilted dialogue (example: I don't think there's a single instance where anyone says, "I know." They all say, "I know it." Every time), terrible pacing, and minimal character growth. As an allegory about the possible dangers of collectivism, which Rand was well aware of from her childhood in Russia, it actually isn't bad when it isn't being sabotaged by the aforementioned flaws. 
 And that's why I have to give it two stars. When judged under that standard, it doesn't do as badly as I had expected, and I finished the whole book and was pretty curious about what happened next at points, even if at other points my eyes were glazing over and I had to fight to keep going (*cough*TheSpeech*cough*). On the other hand, it still does pretty badly, because while the actions of the characters make perfect sense in the context of the world that Rand sets up, that world has so little resemblance to our own world that it's not actually useful as a guide to determine what to do or how to live your life. 
 Would I recommend this to anyone? Emphatically no. If you want to learn about Objectivism, just read Anthem, which is a fraction of the length and doesn't have to cram in a plot, and if you want a gripping business/economy-oriented novel, there are thousands of better choices. 
 And finally, I end with this Bob the Angry Flower Comic:
This book is simply the worst sort of dishonesty.

[Dear Reader: Have 20 minutes to kill? Excellent. Please enjoy my magical journey through the pages of Ayn Rand.] 
 *December 2012. 
 I am doing this. I slogged through The Fountainhead some years ago just to see what the fuss was about. But now, after so many patrons have come to the library in a wild-eyed search for the new Atlas Shrugged movie, and after hearing the expression 'going galt,' and then seeing some guy on the road with "John Galt" painted on his back windshield, it is clear to me that I tortured myself for nothing and read the wrong Ayn Rand. So here we go. 
 My copy is 1168 pages and seems to weigh about 60 pounds. It has been checked out a total of 162 times, but is in surprisingly good shape, which may indicate that no one has actually finished it. Still, I hope that there are penciled notes in the margins. From a library standpoint that would be bad, but it would increase my entertainment value. 
 *UPDATE, 1/6/13. I'm on page 100 or so, which is like being on page 5 of a normal book. I've decided that if I were going to be stranded on a deserted island, I would bring this title with me -- not for enjoyment or for spiritual consolation, but because editing it down would keep me amused for years on end. I suspect there's a weird but readable 400 page novel in here somewhere, but you'd have to pick it out line by line. And then, of course, you could start to argue with her philosophy and world view, which is good for another few years of entertainment. 
 *UPDATE, 1/11/13 
 Some characteristics of Ayn Rand heroes: 
 -- They are not good party guests. 
 "Darling, you take everything too seriously. One is not supposed to be intellectual at a ball. One is simply supposed to be gay." 
 "How? By being stupid?" 
 -- They like it rough. 
 "He took her wrist and threw her inside his room, making the gesture tell her that he needed no sign of consent or resistance." 
 "He seized her arm, threw her down on her knees, twisting her body against his legs, and bent down to kiss her mouth." 
 (So, the next morning, keep an eye out for injuries.) 
 "She saw a bruise above her elbow, with dark beads that had been blood." 
 -- They get real worked up about antitrust law. 
 "Excuse me for interrupting, Mr. Rearden...I thought I must tell you that the Legislature has just passed the Equalization of Opportunity Bill." 
 It was the stolid Mr. Ward who screamed, "Oh God, no! Oh, no!"--staring at Rearden. 
 Rearden had leaped to his feet. He stood unnaturally bent, one shoulder drooping forward. 
 Also, anytime these characters get remotely flirty, there's a noticeable amount of creepy silent laughter and "mocking." We get "mocking" gazes, "mocking laughter" (again, usually silent), "mockery" in people's eyes, & etc. Either Rand is a big proponent of angry sex (likely, see above) or, to misquote Inigo Montoya, that word doesn't mean what she thinks it means. 
 *Update 1/23/13 
 On page 488 and I am already exhausted. Rand spends fully half this book describing, at great length, what something is not, before finally naming what it is. At least another third of each page is devoted to rhetorical questions. So I am tired. But I will persevere, because I am increasingly convinced that when I finish I will join the ranks of a select few who have actually read this damn thing cover to cover. I can't believe that half of the people who say they live by this book have read more than a few key pages. (Which might be fine, actually. Rand is changing my mind about the merits of abridged literature.) 
 Anyway, as I read I am developing a multiple choice test to ferret out those Atlas Shrugged fakers, the Cliffs Notes skimmers, the people who listened on audiobook in the car but had the volume down while they were on the phone and then forgot to turn the sound back up. Here's my quiz so far. 
 When driving down a country road and gazing at the scenery, you say: 
 a) Isn't this gorgeous? 
 b) Look, a red-tailed hawk! 
 c) "What I'd like to see is a billboard." 
 If someone gives you a gift that they think you will enjoy, you: 
 a) Thank them -- how very thoughtful. 
 c) Give them a gift in return. 
 b) "Throw it in their face" for convoluted philosophical reasons. 
 Someone is wearing an orange shirt. How should you describe this shirt? 
 a) The shirt is orange. 
 b) The shirt is the color of a tangerine/marigold/something else that is usually orange. 
 c) The shirt was not white or black, nor brown nor any of the greys, dark or light, and was without any hint of blue, green, or other cool spectrum colors. Nor was the shirt yellow or red; it was something in between those two hues, an orange color, of a shade favored by people who do not like to pay taxes. 
 *Update 1/29/13 
 Last night I had a dream that one of the characters, Hank Rearden, had started to build some kind of steel structure. And in my dream I took this to be a good sign, and felt relieved, because it meant the tides had turned in a positive way. I cannot begin to describe how f***ed up it is that this book and its childlike, hero-worship philosophy have invaded my subconscious, and that my subconscious is apparently completely fine with that. 
 But I have turned some kind of corner. I'm on page 648 and totally into it. I cannot put this book down, even though it is heavy, and my arms are literally getting tired when I read for too long. I've also started skimming all the many political speeches so I can hurry along to the next plot twist, which defeats my original purpose for picking up the book. But forearm toning has been an unexpected benefit, so maybe I'm breaking even. 
 Btw, there is actually a scene in here where an honest-to-god pirate approaches that Rearden character on a deserted country road and tries to give him an honest-to-god bar of gold, because said pirate has long been an admirer of Rearden and thinks it is unjust that Rearden has had to pay so much income tax. This must be a vivid fantasy for about half of America. 
 *Update 2/4/13 
 On page 760. She has taken her perfectly good love triangle and distended it into a grotesque love quadrilateral. (I could call it a square, but I'm too irritated for that.) In other news, we have reunited with most of her characters and discovered that for the past several hundred pages they have been hiding out in the Shire -- except for instead of singing and ale, Rand's Shire is characterized by sanctimoniousness and lecture series. 
 Obviously, I have some frustrations. I've decided to seek my revenge by (heavily) abridging the last 100 pages I read and then translating them into lolcat. I believe this is an appropriate response to the text and you will just have to trust me on that. 
 [Scene - Our intrepid industrialist heroine, Dagny Taggart, crash lands in a strange valley.] 
 John Galt: Hai. 
 Dagny: Oh, hai. 
 Midas Mulligan, Ken Danagger, Ellis Wyatt, Richard Halley, Quentin Daniels, and ten other characters: Oh, hai. 
 Dagny: Wer iz I? 
 John Galt: U r in mah treehaus 
 Dagny: I can haz gold coins? 
 Tax Pirate: Yez. 
 Dagny: John Galt, I can haz sekz wif u? 
 John Galt: No, because even though I just told you that I have been creepily stalking you for 10 years, you must swear allegiance to the tenets of my cult before we consummate our love. Also, I am too busy being weird and inscrutable to take my clothes off. 
 Dagny: I haz a sad. 
 To be continued. 
 *Update 2/16/13 
 JR: What is this?...Get that tome off of here, I could hurt myself on that. 
 Me: Many people have... 
 On page 951. I certainly get the point by now, and since the book's central purpose is to make that point, it's hard not to feel like this show ended hours ago and I'm still in my seat. I suspect even Rand is beginning to fray. Having run out of vague-but-scary words to explain the outcome of anticapitalist philosophies, she recently had one character describe our dystopian future as "the end of the world, not fire and brimstone, but goo." I would have been less surprised by 'slime.' 'Goo' reads like Rand was writing at 4 am, perhaps drunk or high on pixie sticks. That same character later runs screaming at the sight of a social worker ("No! No! Not your kind of world!") and jumps off a bridge and dies. I'm wasting an opportunity for a joke here; choose your own adventure. 
 At the marked risk of summing up too early, my personal journey with this book has so far gone something like this. 
 1. Mockery (to use one of Rand's favorite words) 
 2. Fascination and mockery. 
 3. COMPLETE AND TOTAL FASCINATION. 
 4. Disappointment. 
 5. Fatigue and mockery. 
 Did you ever hear that Peggy Lee song, 'Is That All There Is?' That's kind of where I'm at, ever since we met Rand's imaginary friend, John Galt. The whole force of the narrative hinges on your approval of him, or at least your admiration -- without that, it's just a bizarre farce. But as a tent pole, he's not tall enough to lift the fabric of these 1200 pages. Or maybe I'm just bitter because I was on Team Rearden. 
 Anyway, I will finish, and when I do I may want to come back and surreptitiously delete these words, who knows. See you on the other side. 
 *Update 2/20/13 
 Surely, I must be done with the book by now, right? I was nearing the end. And then I arrived at John Galt's speech and I can't stop falling asleep. It is like trying to read Dianetics. 
 Here's the thing: I'm pretty sure Galt's speech is supposed to be the climax of the story. The Man of Mystery is revealed, and the appropriate people look suitably surprised about it, and when he finishes talking (if he ever finishes talking) I suspect we will begin our roll toward the finish line. But why did Rand spend all that time illustrating her philosophical argument with a cast of characters and a high stakes plot, only to punctuate that plot with a 69-page lecture? She was much better off with the novelization method. Her points are not more meaningful now that they are boring. 
 Galt mentions halfway through his speech that he's already been talking for two hours, and it's the biggest element of fantasy in this fantastical novel -- that anyone would be listening that long. I hear that people claim to have read, if not the novel, at least this speech, but I think they must also be fakers. No human could endure it. My quiz is in development. 
 This update is dedicated to Shek, who refuses to join my Objectivist Discussion Group. 
 *Update 3/3/13 
 I finally finished. I'm on the other side now. The weather is nice over here, I like it. 
 While I ruminate, on what, if anything, I have to say about this book now that it's no longer happening to me in an active way...let's do a literature review, shall we? The following are articles I would be pleased to read if someone would write them. Calling all academics: these titles have semi-colons colons [DUDE, SORRY], and one of them uses 'towards.' How can you resist? 
 Revenge of the Strawmen: How Rand's imaginary friends and make-believe enemies make her arguments irrelevant. 
 If Rand hates a 'Zero' so much, why does she write like one? Towards a better understanding of description through process of elimination. 
 Neutering Robin: the powerless sidekicks of Atlas Shrugged. 
 20 Questions: Or, why Rand's characters take two pages to order a sandwich. 
 Believe me that this urge is an exception to my rule, but the next time I see a teenager with this book in their hands, I'll beg them to put it down and go smoke some weed instead. Rand's writing style (perhaps I should say rhetorical style?) is particularly effective on youngish minds (those with long attention spans, anyway), and in addition to her infantile economic principles, she has some interesting ideas about what justifies murder, what level of consent is necessary for sex, & etc. The book is like a 1168-page a**hole pill. So please excuse me while I go visit all my neighborhood school libraries (damn, any of those left?) and mis-shelve it. The 800s should be a pretty safe spot. 
 *Final update OMG. 
 A couple of lovely people have congratulated me on finishing my Atlas Shrugged saga. Perhaps there was a little bit of relief in your tone. But I'm not quite done! Sorry. I have one more left in me. 
 I've had difficulty deciding where to stand regarding this book. My indecision, according to John Galt, is a sure indicator of moral turpitude. Quoth Galt: "There are two sides to every issue: one side is right and the other is wrong, but the middle is always evil." [Page 1054]. 
 I started reading because I assumed Atlas Shrugged's longevity and its apparent influence were due to something special about the book itself. I have to admit that I still think there's something particularly effective about the novel, whether in spite of or because of its flaws. I read that E.B. White once told James Thurber that if he actually knew how to draw, his cartoons wouldn't be any good, and Rand benefits from the same kind of raw, unembarrassed force in her fiction. What I'm saying, in essence, is that some parts did not suck. The scenes describing the first run of the John Galt line are rather fine. It's certainly a page turner at points, with a strong, if confusing, romance element. It is brave and bold in its scope, an early zombie novel, perhaps -- where the zombies are you and me, in case you were wondering. 
 But when I complained that few people have actually read this book, I meant it. So we have a contradiction, something Rand tells us, SIX MILLION TIMES, is not possible: 
 "Contradictions do not exist. Whenever you think that you are facing a contradiction, check your premises. You will find that one of them is wrong." [Page everypage.] 
 So let's try and play by her rules. 
 Premise A: This book is influential and widely read. 
 Premise B: Few people have actually read this damn book. 
 Which one is false? Premise A? Is Atlas Shrugged really influential, or do people just namecheck it, like they do Ronald Reagan? What if none of the Randites ever read it? What if Alan Greenspan never even read it, and just sweetly nodded and smiled along with the rest of her boy toys? Wasn't Paul Ryan embarrassed recently, after he claimed to live by Atlas Shrugged principles, but forgot that one of those tenets was unapologetic marital infidelity? Which is like, a third of the book? It's hard to forget all that rough extramarital luvin' if you've actually read this thing. 
 Or, maybe I'm wrong on Premise B, and people have do read this it. Could be. There are elements in here that would carry a modern reader along. Frankly, the whole thing is like some kind of economic episode of Super Friends, where the superhero hideout is Galt's Gulch, and everyone's superpower is making money. It also reminds me of that bit in Tom Sawyer where he crashes his own funeral. You'll be sorry when I'm gone is woven through every page of this book. In fact, it's the whole book. What Twain tossed off as a quick satire of self-absorbed adolescence, Rand made a career and a following out of. In that light, it does seem unfair that she's the one more frequently voted to the top of influential books lists. But at any rate, she has harnessed a kind of basic storytelling momentum here, and it might carry more than one reader across the finish line. 
 I must pick a premise to discard, or John Galt will call me evil. And, in the interests of my future business enterprise, the Atlas Shrugged merch store (Look for us in SkyMall!) I will trash Premise B, and conclude that people have actually read the book. Although how anyone gets through it without being able to vent on Goodreads, I can't imagine. Thank you for reading, or politely ignoring, as the case may be. I've obviously enjoyed myself. And I will now return this 10 pound instrument of torture to the library, where it is currently 90 cents worth of overdue.

Well, I've been thinking about writing a review for this book since I first got on goodreads. I've been saving it because I thought that maybe I can write it better a little later on, but I'm not getting any younger, and I hate this book only more. You know how sometimes when you're trying to get to sleep at night and you've previously had an altercation with someone, and you didn't get a chance to really speak your mind? Say it's with a teacher, or a parent, or a boss or something-someone in authority. That's what Ayn Rand is to me, but the really beautiful part is that Ayn Rand in a sense would approve of this review: namely the idea of better ideas putting lesser ideas to waste. 
 On the initially topic of waste Rand's magnum opus is a waste of paper-a lot of paper. In this book the world is not so evenly divided between those ubermenschen: Dagny Taggert (a clear stand-in for Rand herself), Hank Reardon, Francisco D'Ancona, and John Galt are all perfect-especially John Galt. John Galt is indeed so perfect he has a phrase named after him: "Who is John Galt?" that reappears throughout the text. These perfect individuals must now navigate and destroy a world not at all perfect and actually quite hideous and inept because of your everyday slack-jawed simpletons, and your high rise simpletons in positions of political power who have sacrificed every other country in the world to the lamentable fall of having "People's State" as their prefix, and now are poised to do the same to The Land of the Free itself, that is until Galt leads the whole lot of brilliant minds into his invisible Galt's Gulch where they will wait out the inevitable "Great Simpleton Die-off" to emerge at the end of the novel to finally recreate the world. There's a whole bunch of Dagny rape-but this is good rape mind you-and just terrible dialogue. Plus, as I alluded to earlier, there is a whole lot of nothing going on. The book sets itself up as a mystery: "Who is John Galt?" It then drifts off into railroad speak, bureaucratic ridiculousness, and continental meanderings that while seeking to show how the country is collapsing, only show some really terribly drawn foils for the main characters to gloat over how stupid they are. This is really more akin to a fictional treatment of a journey to an orphanage where the main characters just ridicule the orphans for not having parents, a private school education, or their own Ferrari. Ultimately though since none of the main characters have any development whatsoever the novel is more picturesque, although it's an impressively inaccurate view of the world and so doesn't even qualify for that label. But, again the point is that the only thing that actually happens in these pages is that the main characters are removed from this society which collapses only because of the stupidity of everyone else, but then the main characters are brought back in to no doubt make the world in their image. It's length implies complexity, but only succeeds in casting out the message that if one has a lot of money, one is inherently better, and better people ought to rule the world. Indeed, better people ought to rule the world. Unfortunately for Rand the people she says should rule the world already do. And they are really bad at it. 
 Back when the right wing urged everyone to read this book because "it was coming true." they were correct in that we are living after the events of the book; it just wasn't how Rand said things would work out. As it actually happens when you have the wealthy in charge, behaving selfishly, and then urging everyone else to follow their example you don't wind up with utopia, you wind up with 2014 and counting. You wind up with a sociopathic government that can justify cutting education to beef up the army to secure oil rights and property rights for a select few, you wind up with sociopathic business owners like Steve Jobs who can be applauded for the meaningless excess that iPods and Macs represent, a sociopathic media that proclaims "body image uber alles," and a socipathic economic system that champions growth over everything else. What's worse you produce a readership eager to behave without remorse for anything. The time has not come for Atlas Shrugged, the time has past for Atlas Shrugged, and it is a complete and total failure as work of fiction, and work of philosophy.

I wanted to like this book. It is filled with important ideas (ok, maybe just one important idea) and it did challenge some of my own values and assumptions. You would think that this qualifies it as a good book, no? Well, my problem with it lies not in the ideas it contains, but rather how they are expressed. 
 It is boring. I found it a chore to read. The characters are one-dimensional, and all the hero industrialists speak like the same person having a conversation with themselves. There is no depth in any of the characters introduced: either they're a brilliant beautiful hero who creates wonderful things and whose farts smell like cherry blossoms, or your a scumbag mooch who looks like a sloth and acts like one too. The only person that deviates from this two-part formula is Eddie Willers, and he's just an average joe who looks up to the industrialists in awe. Boring. 
 Railroads are an important symbol in Atlas Shrugged. I wouldn't say the book was a train wreck; rather, it reads like a train ride. Slow, long, boring, and you know exactly where it's headed the moment the train leaves the station. 
 Another problem I have is that the antagonist is a society who advocates, and indeed forces sacrifices of those with wealth/ability for those in need. All the advocates for this society are idiots who can't form a critical thought and just repeat unconvincing platitudes. There is not a single rational argument in the Anti-capitalist camp. Every time a hero explodes into a pro-capitalist monologue in the midst of a sea of moochers, they all just sit there attentively and look dumbfounded. I sat there, reading these speeches, and thinking, "ok, I don't even disagree with you, but nobody in the whole crowd can defend their position intelligently?" It's easy to look smart when everyone who disagrees with you would sooner accumulate a puddle of drool than interject with a thoughtful counter-point. The whole book was a straw man assault on the "progressive agenda" 
 All in all, interesting ideas, terrible storytelling. If you're looking to learn about Ayn Rand's philosophy, save yourself the punishment of Atlas Shrugged and try one of her shorter novels.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Theft of Swords is an exciting and fun fantasy novel. Basically two stories in one, Theft of Swords mainly follows the adventures of Hadrian and Royce, two jack-of-all-trades that work together to complete a variety of jobs for whoever can afford them. When a job comes up that seems too good to be true, the two set in motion a series of events that place them as well as a few other interesting characters in a plot that could effect everyone in the region. While this might sound like the plot for a multitude of fantasy novels, the way Sullivan presents the world, characters, and action differentiate it from many of the commonly used fantasy plot points. 
 Sullivan does a great job of presenting characters that you quickly grow interested and invested in, as I often continued to read on trying to find out what happens next. Some of the most frustrating things about stories of any genre that follow multiple view points is when there is that one character that kills the momentum of the story. In Theft of Swords, that problem never arises. I found all of the characters interesting to follow, including the brief view points of the "bad guys" on occasion, and never felt myself mentally groan when I started a chapter that switched view points. The conversations between the characters are also on point, mixing humor and depth especially between the two main characters. 
 The world that Sullivan created is equally as in-depth and full of history and quirks as the characters that live in it. Descriptions of locations and conversations about the history of the world between characters never feel like information dumps and help to paint a clear picture of the world that the characters are moving around and exploring. The author puts you in the cities, the country, and the other different locations by painting a clear picture of the locations through his description. 
 Overall, I highly enjoyed this story and look forward to the opportunity to see how these characters grow in the future novels.

Edit : 2nd read. I keep my rating (5 stars). Looking back at my first review, I smile at myself. My comment about the heir/heiress looks so naive seen from my new perspective and I wanted so much to know who/what Royce had seen inside the tower. I should have guessed. 
 That being said, I am still under Royce's and Hadrian's charm (if not more). 
 ****************************************************************************************************

I would probably have loved that book if I'd read it as a teenager but I do not now.

This book was really enjoyable, I've read some really good reviews and now I know why. I think I'll have to reread the last few chapters I finished it on a plane while exhausted and distracted by turbulence. So maybe it's not the authors fault I couldn't stay in the story towards the end. Because I was hooked from the beginning and especially enjoyed the first book... Perhaps though it started better than it ended. 
 This book is an omnibus of two shorter books cleverly titled a new "Theft of Swords." Two different swords, two different books, two tales of the same story, and captivatingly told. I'm looking forward to reading more from the author.

Really? Really? Really? I just don't get it. I honestly don't understand all the positive reviews. On the surface, this book looked really good. It had numerous positive reviews and what sounded like a good story. 
 I have read a lot of books in my time and this is only the second book I could not finish. It wasn't that it was bad, I just could have cared less what happened. I forced myself to read half way in hopes that it would redeem itself. It didn't. This book had no depth. I thought the character development was poor. I didn't like any of the characters. Overall, I was highly disappointed in this book. 
 If you want to read an absolutely beautiful fantasy book about two thieves, read, "The Lies of Locke Lomora" by Scott Lynch. One of my all time favorites.

These two thieves, they're fascinating. At first I didn't really understand them, but the more I learn about them, the more real they become. Their personalities are quite different, yet I feel their friendship, the trust of many years together. It's really great. I half the time paid little attention to the plot, being more interested in how they will react to whatever the other does. They trust and respect the other, make the important decisions together, yet at the same time they're their own people, choosing to walk their own paths even as they walk on the same road.

I wouldn't say the book is outright awful, but it barely kept my interest and seemed a bit childish. I do appreciate the author breaking some of the typical fantasy roles, especially how you're left trying to figure out if the wizard is actually good or evil, etc. Some of the world building was done through a character that remembers an entire library of knowledge, and it just irritated me to death that it was done that way. Also, most of the plot did not have me excited to see how it ends. That is where the book is really lacking.

I brought several thousand pages of Michael J. Sullivan with me on a vacation in a remote area. Four thick paperback tomes. I made it to page 192 of the first before I just couldn't read any more. The characters felt more like caricatures. Their interactions didn't seem plausible. The straw that broke the camel's back for me was when the uncle went into the princess' room obviously suspecting she was involved in some sort of plot and clearly searching for incriminating evidence. Somehow, he failed to notice that only one set of curtains was closed - which would be pretty suspicious whether it was day or night - and that seemed to be about to prove a fatal mistake (I don't know for sure, I put the book down immediately after he cried, "Wait! Why is only one set of curtains drawn?" after having been in the room for 20 minutes).
Fabulous, funny, and just classic. Two best friends, one grumpy and one funny, must clear their "good" name after being accused of killing a king. They are classic anti-heroes and super fun.

No doubt Michael J. Sullivan is quite a story teller and I was entertained as I ploughed through both books (Theft of Swords is actual two books in one). Fun with amusing dialogues, I definitely will be reading the next books. However, I finished this feeling a tad disappointed. It was all a bit too straightforward for me, not dark, not twisted, which after reading this has made me realise that's how i like my fantasy, Dark, full of grit, menace etc. In this book however, you have one of the main characters, Hadrian, a thief who is also remarkably an idealist. Alas, Hadrian's idealism throughout the book started to wear me down. But this is entirely due to my personal taste, the book itself is worth reading for people who like lighthearted fantasy filled with optimism and heroes whose only flaw is they can't say no to someone in need. (am I cynical or what?).

reference_books.title: When Breath Becomes Air
reference_books.review_text: Beautiful, this is a book I will read again. This is a book full of meaningful prose that I will take with me and use thoughtfully for years to come. In my personal life and my professional life as a nurse. So many lessons and epiphanies to be held dear in this poetic journey. I cried many times.

reference_books.title: The Handmaid's Tale

reference_books.title: The Bookshop on the Corner
reference_books.review_text: The main character in this book had zero substance and I found myself not caring at all what happened to her. The entire premise was unbelievable and underdeveloped.

reference_books.title: Everything I Never Told You
reference_books.review_text: This was a well developed family drama but with a lot of over-the-top "beautiful prose" that didn't seem to fit with the story. Several times it felt "over-written" with far too much descriptive narrative that didn't lend itself accurately to the story or the character it was coming from. The story itself was incredibly sad. It was hard to look from the outside in and see the train wreck of this family and not be able to help them. The author was successful in developing each character and allowing the reader to see the events unfold rather that just telling the reader what happened. It definitely makes the reader think about what it means to love, love your spouse, your children, yourself and how that love, no matter the best of intentions can be a catalyst to break someone apart. Particularly the expectations you have for those you love and what it means for the other person to try to meet those expectations. So very sad.

reference_books.title: Major Pettigrew's Last Stand
reference_books.review_text: This was a very slow moving book, definitely not a page turner but enjoyable! I liked the characters and dry British type humor. It was a good love story that remained classy through the end. Each relationship was easy to relate to. This was just a really nice and simple read to cleanse the palate after reading some heavier more intense novels. I really did enjoy it.

book_a.title: The Same Sky
book_a.user_review: This was an emotional and thought-provoking read without being overly emotional or disturbing. I am a huge fan of books that have alternating character views where one chapter is told by one characters point of view and the next chapter is told by another character. This was a beautiful story. I would definitely recommend it for a book club pick, a lot of discussion to be had here.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I can't remember the last time I was so disappointed in a book to which I was looking forward to so much. Possibly Anne Rivers Siddons' last book. 
 Jodi Picoult has been praising this book for months, and I liked the premise. I didn't know what to expect because I've never read anything by Ward before, but I found this amateurishly written, with largely unsympathetic characters and a plodding pace. I won't be reading any more of her books. 
 I see that Picoult is among those thanked in the acknowledgements. Amanda Eyre Ward ought to send her flowers every day for a year and also wash her car once a week in exchange for the rave review, because it was completely undeserved.

This book was achingly heartbreaking. It ripped me open in more ways than one. It just hit so close to home, so close. It's a story about the struggles and hardship of immigrants and the reasons why many come to the U.S. It's also a story of pain, loss, and the emptiness that consumes you when you lose a child. The author did an amazing job telling these stories, and I am grateful because books like this raise awareness. This isn't something that's covered by media or spoken of enough. But it IS a big deal, an ongoing tragedy, and too many lives are lost or destroyed on a daily basis. Read this book. Just do it.

The moral dilemma of illegal immigration. I think any normal person on earth would love to live where he/she was born! Be a part of your family,extended family and feel a part of big plan. But to do all this we need to have the basic needs of food,clothing and shelter.... Most of the illegal immigrants are desperate to survive in their own countries and there is no hope. They look to countries which look like promised land to them so that they reach a place where they can live with dignity with tools of survival ! 
 Author Amanda Ward has touched this subject well and spun the fictionalised tale of illegal immigration and how it clashes with the American life! 
 Alice and Jake own a famous barbecue restaurant in Austin Texas. Life is beautiful except that they mourn that they are unable to have a child. They almost adopt a child to have it grabbed from them at the last minute by the biological mother. 
 Carla a young girl in the Honduras whose mom has crossed over to the US to help the family is stuck in the life of poverty with her grandmother and brother. After her grandmas death she is desperate to reach her mother and starts the dangerous journey to crossover to America to reunite with her mom. So with the help of her mother from this side of the border she starts the horrible journey filled with dangerous train rides, and travelling through the desert, being a girl suffering indignities at the hands of ruffians, and keeping quiet since you do not want to be noticed. 
 She loses her brother on the journey and she does reach her mom, but there are consequences for all desperate situations! 
 The two stories of Alice and Jake and that of Carla collide in unexpected ways.....

This novel seemed to be written by two different authors. On one hand it was an interesting expose on illegal immigrants and the position they are making a better life in America for their kids. Then the other half was cloying sentmalism. I did like the character of Alice with her vintage dresses and colorful cowboy boots. The character of Evain was horribly drawn then it was as if okay she's a plot device let's just drop her from the novel. Also the writing was pedantic and reeked of being sickenly sweet.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I hate books with sad things and this book was full of them. The redeeming quality of a happy ending did not quite make up for it. The scenes were not super descriptive so I did not have to live in a depressed state too long either. There is some swearing too. Loved the Texas connection! There were definitely Texas only references, which I now get. Read this for book club and was not expecting the topics covered; I feel a little caught off guard.
Thought it was lame. Wrapped up way too tidily at the end. Sad I spent time reading it. In addition, curse words at the beginning of the book seem unnecessary.

Two heartbreaking stories set in strikingly different countries--America and Honduras. A little girl and a 40-year old woman with poignant, painful circumstances about which neither one knows how to resolve. 
 Amanda Eyre Ward has taken a young girl, Carla, feeling lost and lonely without her mother who has headed to America to make a living to provide for her daughter, four-year old twin boys, and her mother. 
 Ward paints an equally sad and arresting story of Alice Conroe, 40 years old with her biological clock wound down. Alice and her husband desperately want a child, and each attempt to adopt falls foul of success. 
 Alternating Carla and Alice's stories in each chapter, the reader gains insight into two critical areas of life not always familiar to every individual. 
 Carla's life in Honduras is one of seeking food in the garbage dump and living in fear of being attacked or murdered. It is no wonder these people take such chances to enter America, whether legally or illegally. And what they go through in their efforts to arrive here is unbelievable. 
 Alice's dream of a child of her own seem to be defeated at every turn creating problems between her and her husband. And yet their love is strong enough to survive. Just as Carla's determination for a better life provides for her survival. 
 I fell in love with both Carla and Alice, and I hoped they would become parent and child. But even better the comparison and contrast between the stories brought home with greater power the human will which carries us through times of despair, depression, want and immense need. 
 This is my first Amanda Eyre Ward read, and it will not be my last. Her writing is powerful and yet filled with bits of humor in Alice's story, which is needed from time to time. Ward draws evocative pictures of her characters, real people, people you want to know. 
 Recommendation: The Same Sky is not an overly long book, and the story line moves quickly. If you want a well written, heart tugging book filled with the human longing we all share, The Same Sky would be a good book for you to pick up. Perhaps you have read Ward's other books and if so, she has written a winner here. 
 Note: I received a copy of The Same Sky from Ballantine Books via NetGally in exchange for an honest review. The opinions expressed are solely my own.

I was given a copy of this book in exchange for an honest review. To read more reviews like this one, check out Obsessive Book Nerd! 
 The Same Sky was a pretty quick read for me, but unfortunately I just couldn't give it a stellar review. I'm actually pretty torn about what to say. The story follows two characters, Clara on her journey from Honduras to Texas and Alice dealing with the disappointment and numerous failed attempts of becoming a mother. I knew at some point the two characters would cross paths, but it just didn't happen quick enough for me. 
 I enjoyed Clara's story so much more than Alice's. Clara and her supporting characters seemed real. I felt that her journey was genuine. The struggles and hardships she endured were heartbreaking. There times however, when modern technology was mentioned (a.k.a. the internet) by Clara and this was confusing because Clara was living in a village where she slept on a pallet, robbed of cooking pots, had to walk miles to use the only phone in town, and ate flour paste for meals. So I'm assuming that she is referring to using the internet once she is older and living a better life in America. But, why even refer to it? I was just confused. 
 Alice's part of the book felt disconnected. Her character was more well rounded than the others but didn't feel fully developed. Just when I thought I had a good read on each of the supporting characters, they did/said something abrupt and out of character. It went completely against the already developed character. I found myself re-reading paragraphs because I didn't understand why a character just did/said the thing they did/said because it didn't make any sense. Every single character in Alice's story fell into this category of dissapoint me for me. 
 I'm a little concerned that this book is getting such great reviews on Goodreads. My review and rating does not follow suit. So I kind of feel like I'm not being fair, but I've thought long and hard about this book and I'm just not happy about it. The second I finished it, the first feeling I had was utter disappointment. I could tell at about 65% through the book that I might not like where the book ended, but I kept reading on. Overall, I probably would have given the novel a better rating had it just been Clara's story.

Alice is a middle-aged woman in Austin, Texas, married to Jake Conroe, of the famous Conroe's BBQ. Their marriage is happy and fulfilled but for one glaring lack: they have no children. Surrogates failed them; adoption has failed them; at the book's opening, they've just had an especially heartbreaking failure. Baby Kellan was in their home for a day and a night when the birth mother changed her mind. Alice and Jake's different ways of coping with this latest loss is putting some strain on their relationship. 
 Carla is a young Honduran girl whose mother has gone to the US to earn money and send it back to her family, leaving Carla and her younger brother with her own mother. When her grandmother dies, Carla, not yet twelve herself, struggles to protect herself and her brother in their increasingly dangerous, gang-controlled village. In the end, she decides she has no alternative but to take her brother on the dangerous journey to join her mother in Texas. 
 They tell their stories in alternating sections, relating what are for each of them the mundane details and incredible challenges of their daily lives, as well as the complex and sometimes confusing relationships they are a part of. Alice and Carla each become very real people, and I felt connected to each of them and to the people they care about. Austin is a place I and many other Americans have been, but Ward's writing makes the village of Tegucigalpa as real and present, and we feel Carla's love for and connectedness to her home as well as the fear and grief of what it is becoming. 
 We also experience Alice's complicated relationships with Jake's family, and her own, in both cases compounded by her childlessness. Jake's parents very much wanted grandchildren; Alice's sister Jane has three children and feels a little overwhelmed. 
 These two stories come together in an ending that is both satisfying and thoroughly earned. 
 Highly recommended. 
 I received a free electronic galley of this book from the publisher via NetGalley.

I originally gave this book three stars because there was a disconnect for me with Alice's story. After some reflection, I am bumping it up to four stars. Carla's story was so strong that three stars just seemed wrong. I'm still not completely sold on the necessity of Alice's story and found it dull and kind of manipulative - sort of a "the grass is not always greener" thing - except that for Alice, despite her sorrow at not being able to have a child, it really is. Carla's story is five stars and highly recommended for people to understand the tough choices immigrants must make and the harsh realities of the journey.
