book_a.title: Gossamer
book_a.user_review: very sweet story about dreams

sample_reviews.review_text: delightful. I loved it more than The Giver in so many ways.

This review was first posted on my blog at http://knowitnotsomuch.blogspot.com 
 A quiet story that intricately weaves the stories of a mother, an angry and abused boy, an old woman and two fairy like creatures, Gossamer is a perfect bedtime story. 
 Littlest One is a fairy like creature that delivers dreams to humans as they sleep. She is still being trained and she is a curious, playful little thing. Her teacher sees the potential in her and guides her through the processes that suddenly become much more difficult when the Sinisteeds appear. 
 Short and sweet. Truly.
Loved it. Great book. I wish there was a second.... Let us pray ( fingers crossed)
Lowry has such a fantastic writing style!

Not my favorite Lois Lowry book. I feel like it was not as well developed as her other ones, especially in terms of the conflict. I like the idea behind it....it really got me thinking about dreams and where they come from. It would be nice to think there is someone looking out for you and giving you dreams to help you out!

My main experience with Lois Lowry has been through The Giver, that I read years ago, but as an adult. The book recently came out as a movie, which I have not seen. I remember thinking the book gave some good fodder for thought for kids, and that it was well written. 
 Gossamer came to me via BookCrossing. Had I not been faced with an overwhelming task which required little brain power, and much patience, I probably wouldn't have popped the CDs into the player, but I was, and I did. This is a gentle story, mostly about where dreams come from, and the power of keeping hope over despair.

Lois continues to give her readers a world with rules that are meant to be broken; a mentorship of unusual proportions; and the love of small things that are really much, much bigger on the inside. Lois Lowry is the one author I know who writes with such a limited palette so she can punch up the color whenever she wants highlight something special. She truly writes about hope. I admire that in such a tiny text, she does more than most.

I listened to this one on CD, and the performed did a great job. It would be good for younger readers. 
 This book is a fictional story about dreams and nightmares. It follows a young gossamer and her teacher as they give pleasant dreams to an older woman and a young boy named John who is staying in her home as a foster child. Although the story is told mainly through the eyes of the young gossamer, the reader is able to follow the struggles and success of all of the characters. It is a great motivational book for younger readers. 
 The mood throughout the majority of this book was really calm and pleasant. Because of the mood and the message in this story, readers can be easily motivated to look for the good in life rather than focusing on the negative. It was also a rather short novel, and would therefore be easy for a student to get through.

This is a poignant and bitter-sweet book. The boy in this reminded my of some of the troubled kids I've worked with, so perhaps that was why this touched me. At times, it got a bit much. But I can see how this book appeals to older kids.
This book had great potential, but it just kind of ended without really explaining itself.

book_b.title: The Girl in the Red Coat
book_b.user_review: I loved this so much. None of the grisly criminal shades of a typical abduction story, something more spiritual and human, although very sad

sample_reviews.review_text:
Purchased in place of a book with a similar title but I read it anyway! 
 I began this book thinking it was something else and while I was disappointed it wasn't what I expected I kept reading as I was drawn into the story. 
 A page turner in places although I felt it glossed over 'years' and some elements seemed a little far fetched. Overall I enjoyed it.

A pre-release book from Faber given to my book group to review. Not my sort of thing at all. The only engaging character is Beth, desperate to find 8 year old Carmel who disappears at a book fair. Gramps is too spooky for words.
For me, this book was a chore to get through. Interesting at first, but I quickly lost interest. A lot of nothing in between the beginning and the end.

Reassurance if needed for potential readers is that this book is not about child sexual exploitation. 
 This book is a classic psychological thriller with a chilling undercurrent which is attention grabbing from the outset. It is really difficult to do anything else except read it. 
 The beginning of the book sets the scene explaining the relationship between parents and child leading up to the day of the event. Beth was always concerned that Carmel would go missing as she was considered to be highly intelligent but ' dream like'. 
 The reader is informed about Carmel's separation from her mother at a book fair. Carmel was a lover of the colour Red hence the red coat. Beth could see the red coat then it disappeared. The terror and desperation of her mother Beth is evident. She is searching for her young daughter with the clock ticking. Her anguish, panic and overall helplessness is evident. This is every parent's nightmare more especially as Carmel is an only child. 
 The book is told in two voices, Beth the mother and Carmel the child taking it in turns to tell the story from their individual perspective. The voice of Carmel was convincing especially the change from the child to adolescent voice. 
 The reasoning behind Carmel's kidnapping is quite original yet quite far-fetched depending on what the individual reader is prepared to believe. Some aspects stretch what is plausible. 
 Following this immediate panic the book develops into an interesting gripping read. Carmel was taken by a man reporting to be her Grandfather telling her that her mother Beth was in an accident. In essence she was tricked and isn't aware she is missing. The story moves to unexpected places. The abductors take Carmel as they think she has a gift which they want to use. Carmel is told that her mother has died and her father does not want her. 
 She is somehow smuggled to the USA. Exploration of Carmel's new surroundings ensues as well as her differing emotions. Despite encouragement and pressure from her kidnappers Carmel clings to her true identity and visions of her mother. Carmel is likeable, bright, strong willed, with spirit and does not come across as a victim. Narrating for a child in the first person can prove undoable for many but this follows well with Carmel's narrative maturing as she does. Beth is surrounded by guilt and of course self-blame. Although Beth does engage with the Police, this book does not focus on the Police investigation instead concentrating on the effects of the separation from the viewpoint of both Beth and Carmel. Beth has friends who wish to assist as well as Carmel's devastated father who is now her ex-husband. Carmel appears to cope despite low points it is Beth whose total existence is blown to shred. Beth never gives up hope that Carmel is still alive, she keeps searching, while at the same time trying to rebuild her life and taking something from her relationship with her ex-husband and his partner. 
 The writing is quiet poetic and magical ensuring that the story is not depressing. All the characters are well developed, with the descriptive passages aiding the overall story. Carmel is entertaining and it is lovely to see her innocent outlook on her new surroundings and individuals caring for her. Kate Hamer makes the story interesting from the perspective of a young child and I did miss Carmel when the story had ended. The story of the mother Beth was also believable. I didn't want the book to end yet driving the narrative from the start is whether Beth and Carmel will be reunited. I won't give any spoilers but suffice to say this book ended quicker than I would have liked. I found the closing paragraph particularly distressing and poignant. I would highly recommend this book but word of warning is that it is so difficult to put down and do anything else while reading. I would not recommend to parents of children who themselves generally have high anxiety levels.

Carmel is abducted by a roving preacher who pretends to be her grandpa. "Grandpa" is convinced that Carmel is a healing (which she may or may not be). This book follows several years of drifting while her mom continues to search. 
 Not the next "Gone Girl" nor is it a thriller.
A really good read. For once, you get to see two points of view. Add you're own angst (yes, that's the only way I can describe it, angst!) and you're spinning.
I liked this well enough, but its short chapters were a little jarring.

An exceptionally emotional read, Kate Hamer's prose is exquisite. The author brings us into an emotional and authentic world that somehow goes beyond the five senses; I am in awe of her writing. The story pulls you in, but more than that: the characters *feel* real. I lost one of my little girls for nearly an hour once and I remember the terror: Hamer evokes it so well, plus the horror of having to go on *just in case* you're reunited. Carmel's journey with "Gramps" and Dorothy, plus the colourful world of evangelists is really well drawn too. One of my favourites in recent times, was sorry to finish. Read this book!! You won't be disappointed.
Not what I was expecting, but very good. I couldn't stop reading!

Perhaps I read this at the wrong time, perhaps I wasn't letting it get to me, perhaps I simply did not understand it, but the book did not deliver the emotional punch I was expecting, and the feeling I'm left with can be best described as "lukewarm". I might need to read it again to see if I feel differently. 
 The book's take on the "missing child" story is not the usual mystery of "who did it" and the suspense of "where is she", as you have Carmel narrate her separation from her mother and the subsequent events, which takes away from the reader the anguish of not knowing. There are no intensely frustrating near-misses in the search for the child, there is, in fact, no intrigue, except for the strange mystical and religious undercurrent that is never fully resolved. Instead the focus is on the internal transformation of both, mother and child, and even though it's the first person perspective, it is told in a somewhat emotionally distant way (hence "lukewarm"). 
 *SPOILER AHEAD* 
 But what I found most unusual is how the abduction turned out to benefit the mother, who got a car, who started working, who finally settled the feud with her ex-husband and even became friends with his new partner to the point of taking their new-born for walk! This might be an author's way of saying that life goes on, but I just wasn't comfortable with it.

reference_books.title: The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
reference_books.review_text: The Adventures of Huckeberry Finn is touted as the sequel to The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. The story in a nutshell is about Huckeberry Finn. He escapes from Widow Douglas house and starts living with his drunken father. At first his enjoys his carefree life, but as his father's beating escalate he decides to 'sail' away. Here he befriends a runway slave, Jim. Their adventures are categorized in the next 200 pages. Huckeberry grapples with the idea of helping a run away slave and concludes it completely moral to be anti-slavery. It was a long and tedious read primary because of the use of colloquial language. I was lost numerous times and had to skip entire dialogs. The author gets two stars : one for his staunch anti-slavery stance and two for creating such fallible moral character.

reference_books.title: My Ántonia
reference_books.review_text:
Willa Cather's My Antonia is a story about a pioneer Bohemian girl who struggles to make headway into American. It was so beautifully narrated with descriptions that made me forget that I was stranded at airport for a day. Willa Cather's is American's George Elliot. Her genius lies in her use of language not necessarily the simplified plot. I actually cried when Antonia was abandoned by her husband and sent back to Black Hawk, Nebraska. There was a part of me that wanted Antonia to marry, Jim Bruden as he admired her so very much. I felt that My Antonia was a touch more tragic then Cather's masterpiece, O'Pioneers. The message of this book for women of today, if you feel is challenging, then our great-grandmother's was struggles a thousand times more than any of us do. Hats off to our ancestors's spirit. I was somewhat disappointed that Antonia life was so hard compared to the other girls. 
 Favorite Quotes 
 1.	She was a rich mine of life, like the founders of early races 
 2.	Whatever we had missed, we possessed together the precious, incommunicable past

Unenlightening whiny drivel.
The beginning was good, but once I got to the section of India it was a slow read..
A disaster.

This was a waste of time. I almost finished reading the first third and then thought, "What's the point?" The author is a very skilled writer and I did truly enjoy her POV and style of writing, however, it was not enough to save this book. We all need to take care of ourselves and to fulfill the needs to grieve for lost relationships, youth, whatever... We don't need to spend a year whining and letting our past decisions control everything we do. Deal with it and move on. So, since the lowest rating I could give this book was one star, that is what Eat, Pray, Love earned from me.

the author begins by explaining the reasons why her journey of self discovery from Italy, to India and then to Indonesia was a necessary diversion from her fast paced life in New York City. Each country shall have a theme (thus the name of the book). I was intrigued...the narrator's voice was perfect for audiobook, it was easy listening. Italy--oh the raptures of Italy! I feel I could soliloquize on the abundance of luxurious food, rich romantic scenery, and the melodious language of the locals solely from having read this book. The first third of the book made me want desperately to pack a bag and set out for Rome. The rest of the book was boring. Probably just not a good choice for audiobook.

ugh. I watched the movie and enjoyed it so i thought i'd read the book. They only part I really enjoyed was the eat part in italy. the pray part just dragged on and on. the love part was okay. i would recommend to others to skip the book, watch the movie.

book_b.title: Haroun and the Sea of Stories (Khalifa Brothers, #1)
book_b.user_review: A whimsical book that was difficult to understand in 9th grade English class.

sample_reviews.review_text:
about halway through the book, i realised it reminded me of something. but i couldn't put my finger on it. a very annoying feeling, it really is, to feel like you've read something that sorta kinda maybe looks like the thing you're eating throgh right now. 
 not to worry, i realised what it reminded me of. Douglas Adams' The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy. 
 yep. Salman Rushdie's writing reminded me of a radio show turned book. 
 is it bad? not really, no. it didn't remind me of easy, uncomplicated literature, which Adams writes, but it matched in absurdness. 
 now i know, people who read the series and liked it will say - no!, no no, it's not like that a bit. i'm tepmted to agree, on a larger scale. it's SF, it's extremelly funny and innuendo-ish and easy to engage in. 
 and this is a children's book i'm comparing it to, so this comparison shouldn't even exist. but, in my humble opinion, it exists. there's the "absurd" feeling of the characters, the story, the setting, the explanations and even the writing itself is shady, on some level. 
 this comparison only works one way, though. you can find Adams in Rushdie, but not that much Rushdie in Adams. Haroun is meant to teach you something about stories, about their importance, about how living without them is a curse and it should never befall upon us. the Guide is funny and lets you see how incredibly stupid humanity is and what a scam civilization is. 
 i read this because my History teacher asked me if it resembles a fantasy book or if it could somehow enter under the fantasy umbrella. it does have fantasy elements, but i don't see this going under that roof. it's not that it doesn't deserve it, it's just that it doesn't bring a certain style along with it. it's a children's book, and it's meant to be educational and entertaining on the simplest level, while still leaving space for a second read, where you can find other povs than you did before. fantasy is too big a name for something like this, and it's this opinion that i stand behind of.

Saya sudah lama punya buku ini dan setiap saya baca, saya terus merasa terhibur. Rashid dan Haroun, ayah dan anak yang saling mencintai, terlibat petualangan fantastis yang mengagumkan, memadukan semua unsur hiburan terbaik yang pernah kita dapatkan. Drama, aksi dan komedi bercampur saling memperkuat kisah. Bukan hanya happy ending yang kita dapatkan, tapi rasa ketagihan untuk terus membaca novel ini.

Not quite a children's book, not quite your typical Rushdie feast, I wasn't sure how I felt about this. I think if it had been by anyone else, I would have loved it. I'm spoiled by the Rushdie sprawl, though, so I was a little disappointed by Haroun. It's a pretty little story, funny and imaginative, but it wasn't wild enough. I need my Rushdie to be wild.
Prica za sve,da se setimo kako da budemo srecni. Citajte svojoj deci,trebace im.

I really wanted to like this book. But it was awful. It reminded me a lot of Alice in Wonderland, and I hated Alice in Wonderland. This book has a 4 star rating, HOW?! I would definitely rate this as one of the worse books I ever read.

Absolutely loved it. Has always considered Rushdie as a serious kind of writer, but this story was so magical, so believable and so fantastic. 
 Loved all the cute characters throughout the story, which ended way too quickly - Haroum, Hoppoe, Mali, Goopy-Bagha, Iff, Blabbermouth, and even Baat-cheat. And the others. 
 beneath the layer of simple story telling is another completely different universe, which lends light to how our lives are personally and professionally. And how the magic of stories hold us together, binds our dreams and hopes and wises into an intricate, positive pattern. 
 LOVED IT! What a lovely read! Would make for an excellent animation movie.

Reading this book is letting a colorful circus run in one's mind. It is a children's book, but being a Salman Rushdie book, still carries strong political messages. I wish Ghibli studio made a movie out of this!

Haroun is a wonderful blend of fantasy and reality. It tells the story of Haroun's adventures in the fantasy land of Gup with a telepathic tin bird, a floating gardener and a water genie, without avoiding 'adult' topics such as adultery, political corruption, and polution that he experiences in his real world, the 'sad city with factories in which sadness was actually manifactured.' 
 The beautiful message (the importance of wishing) that Rushdie gave to his son through this book is something I fantasize to ever give to my own son someday, through my own writing... Perhaps, it will happen one day, when I subscribe to the tap of warm story waters installed by a water genie..

This book is sort of the Arabian Nights with a little Alice in Wonderland thrown into the mix. ( And I don't know if it's just because I've finished the neverending story recently or these two books have really something in common) When Rashid, a storyteller known as the Shah of Blah, loses the ability to tell stories, his son Haroun sets out to find out what has happened. With the help of Iff the Water Genie and a cast of colorful characters he finds out that forces of Darkness are polluting the Sea of Stories. 
 It's all a thinly veiled allegory for Islam trying to silence the author after his Satanic Verses was published, but it's deftly handled & often quite amusing.

Clever -- parts of it made me think of Alice in Wonderland or The Wizard of Oz-- but the book never really grabbed me. I know the story was written for Rushdie's son, but I was still put off by the lack of female characters. There are only three: a princess who needs rescuing, a young girl who has to pretend to be a boy to hold her job, and a wife/mother who deserts her family to run off with another man. We don't need more stories that relegate women to such roles.

reference_books.title: The Indigo Spell (Bloodlines, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
The Indigo Spell is a solid addition to the Bloodlines series, picking up the pace and drive from the somewhat wallowing Golden Lily installment. I found the main storyline more engaging and the relationship between Sydney and Adrian a little more believable. I wasn't keen on the way that relationship stalled and became repetitive over a good book and a half, but at least things have moved along a little by the end of the book . At times the relationship teetered a dubious-consent knife-edge, but the consent was re-negotiated several times, which was a plus. 
 The tight couple focus of this book found me missing the ensemble/Scooby Gang feel of some of the other novels in the extended series, but that's a matter of taste - I know some readers want more Sydney and Adrian as a high priority. 
 What I didn't like was seeing many of the next moves and the big mistakes before the characters did. They're supposed to be so smart, so why was I feeling smarter than them? I also found myself at times seeing the bones of the book a bit too much, feeling the author moving the chess pieces into place, and this sometimes led to a failure to suspend analysis and get swept up in the story. This wasn't a major issue, but it did eat into my enjoyment a little. 
 Characterisation was a bit of an issue for me. As with The Golden Lily, I feel like I still know Adrian a lot better than I do Sydney. I still don't really have a feel for what makes her tick, for what drives her, for her individuality. I know she's diet-obsessed, I know she likes to wear dull khakis and buttoned-up matronly blouses, I know she has great aim, I know... not a lot more than that. The repeated efforts to tell us that Sydney likes a mundane, monotonous world end up at times just boring the reader. Things happen to her, she does what she's told, she doesn't really make a lot happen. Perhaps until she breaks the tattoo? Will she then come out of this repressed shell ? I'm hoping her insipidity is all just set-up for the progression of that series-long arc, but it does lend a bit of a dragging feel. 
 I love the addition of Warriors and magic users to the universe, and I'm really hoping that more supernaturals and covert groups will come to light as this six-book series continues on. I didn't quite get the purpose of the wee dragon, though. Was this just a set-up for future books? I was hoping he would play a substantial role in the denouement, but he didn't. Maybe it's just the Pern-lover in me, but more tiny dragons please! More!

reference_books.title: Where She Went (If I Stay, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I find myself at complete odds with my favourite YA bloggers on this book! 
 I picked up If I Stay because I heard it had a sequel, and I was really looking forward to a rehab book in the voice of a young woman with disabilities. I ended up really liking If I Stay, but had avoided spoilers assiduously for Where I Went. 
 Unfortunately, too assiduously. When I picked it up, I found that instead of being in Mia's clear, powerful, insightful, vulnerable, resonant voice, I found that the book was to be all about Adam's pain. I thought he was a bit of an arse in the first book, and he just became a giant arse in this one, meaning the ending made even less sense. And when he started comparing his pain at being dumped and becoming a bigtime rock star to Mia's pain at her entire family dying in front of her and having to recover from critical injuries, I just about threw it against the wall. This book was just a giant posturing waaahh for me. 
 I really hope that Forman (or a good fanficcer!) decides to write Mia's story.

reference_books.review_text:
This New Adult novel was just "meh" for me, I'm afraid. Set in college around naive middle-class virgin (yes, it's a plot point) Rory and bad-boy-from-the-wrong-side-of-the-tracks-but-with-a-heart-of-gold Tyler, it starts out as a consent issuefic, morphs into a class and drugs issuefic, and tries to be a romance all at the same time, without ever quite succeeding at any of the above. 
 Unfortunately, the writing was often awkward and stilted, the pacing was uneven, and there were some race and disability issues that threw me out of the story. 
 Mostly, however, I was bothered by an issue also highlighted by Ridley on a Death Author thread: "Sexual assault isn't a meet cute." The book opens with minor character Grant attempting to rape Rory, and this is all about showing us how manly and ethical Tyler is, when he saves Rory from the situation. The aftermath and consequences of the sexual violence are barely examined; it's just all about getting Rory to notice Tyler. Ugh.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Pride and Prejudice - 5 stars 
 Pride and Prejudice and Zombies - 3 stars 
 I enjoyed this book but it was not what I was expecting I thought the book would be a new story, not the old one with a few mentions of zombies. I was drawn to this book because of the movie and I still have high hopes the movie will be more original then this.

The best thing about this book is the cover. The second best thing is the concept. The execution doesn't live up to its potentional, mostly because too much of the original text is left intact, making it a redundant read for anyone familiar with Pride and Prejudice. There is not enough deviation from Austen's work, making the added zombie plot more of an insignificant side note than anything else. That being said, I can't imagine that it would make much difference if one were to read this and skip the original book altogether. If I had it do over and I could only read one, well, at least this one has a few awesome illustrations. I think it would have worked much better as a graphic novel; maybe there is still hope that it will be adapted into one.
Meh.

Quite possibly the worst book I've read in a long time. I know it's supposed to be a parody, but I honestly never laughed once. It seems as though the inclusion of zombies were just thrown in at random when they thought it deemed appropriate, but honestly it just felt like they added the word "zombie" on occasion because zombie was in the title of the book. Utterly ridiculous, and completely lacking proper flow. This one took me a long time to get through. At least it's done now, and I never have to read it again.
I read about a quarter of the book, and that was enough. Interesting concept, but not enough to make the whole book worthwhile. It mainly made me want to read Pride and Prejudice again.

I'm abandoning this. 
 My first problem: I actually liked Pride and Prejudice. 
 The title is true to the story. It's Pride and Prejudice ...and zombies. Literally passages are copied from the book with zombies tacked on. Example: We walked to Meryton, encountered zombies. It's as if a fourteen year old was assigned the book in English class and started doodling zombies in the margins. If I were fourteen maybe I would think this was a fun read, however, it's in the original language so somehow I doubt it. Plus, the zombie additions weren't original or suspenseful. It's just the same book, with added zombies. Nothing else. I think I chuckled once, but eventually I realized the only reason I was reading was in order to get to some of my favorite parts of the original, therefore it became pretty pointless to continue. 
 Maybe this is pompous, but honestly I know a dozen people who could have done a better job with this idea, myself included, if but for the simple reason that I would AT LEAST had some characters get it on. If you're going to have ninjas and beheadings, why not some smutty parts? That's all I'm saying. Go all the way. Pun intended. And for that reason, this was entirely disappointing. 
 Finally, perhaps this is a betrayal to my own sex but the author wrote Elizabeth Bennet as if she was in perpetual PMS. I could go on about why this book just did not do it for me but it would be rambling. Conclusion: underwhelmed and surprisingly unoriginal.
If you didn't like Pride and Prejudice, no amount of zombies will make it better.

Intriguing in concept, lackluster in execution. This book is ideally suited, I believe, for those who've never read Pride and Prejudice. For someone like me---who has not only read the book, but seen the miniseries, dabbled in fanfiction, read other interpretations of the same story, and inadvertently memorized whole passages---this was rather tedious than entertaining. Despite the inclusion of zombies, nothing changes. Certainly a handful of details are different, but the book remains in essentials unchanged. Which is a little hard to believe when you have zombies running around. 
 Add to this that the editor, or perhaps the writer, cared so little for continuity that they allowed "Bennet" to occasionally gain an extra T; "Kilkenny" to shift back and forth from "Kilkerry;" and characters to consistently reference statements they don't actually make in this version of the classic (e.g., Elizabeth refers to Darcy saying his temper is "resentful"---a statement he makes in the original but not in this book), and it's hardly any wonder that by the last third of the book I was desperate for the end. 
 If you've been meaning to read Pride and Prejudice, but can't quite bring yourself to struggle through early nineteenth century prose, this is the book for you. But if you already have a strong background in the book, you'd be far better off skimming this version for the zombie bits and paging through for the pictures.

The concept of adding zombie plots to books that didn't initially have any plot at all is certainly laudable, but Grahame-Smith's execution is utter shit. The writing is so poor and the humor so unoriginal I lost all patience with it even before the fucking ninjas showed up. 
 Perhaps it would have been better if the author had any experience with literature outside of compulsory high school reading (which I'm assuming is where he got Pride and Prejudice from in the first place; the reader's discussion guide at the end seems to confirm this), comic books, and Buffy fanfic. I guess we'll never know.

I am not a zombie fan and when Walking Dead is playing in my house, I avoid the room with the television. What I am is a Jane Austen fan and especially a Pride and Prejudice fan. I love the story more as time goes on. 
 So, when our library offered the opportunity to watch the movie one week and discuss the book the next, I decided it was time to check out this book. 
 It was a pleasant surprise to find out that the original text is preserved and the zombie parts added into the plot. In my opinion, Grahame-Smith did an excellent job of combining his zombie excerpts with Austen's original text. Hence, the four stars. 
 Now, a brief word about the movie. Worth watching, for sure. Don't expect the plot to follow P&P as closely as the BBC mini-series. They take a rather large detour and some rather creative plot points. With the exception of Darcy, the casting gets high marks. Colin Firth has spoiled me for eternity and no one else measure up. Also loved the costumes and the visuals of the Bennet girls preparing for battle.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I like Isabel Allende: I think she's fiesty, funny and a very eloquent when I heard that she hadn't written a book about sustainability issues, I was very excited. However, I admit that I read this book because it was recommended to me by a friend who described it as 'unputdownable'. 
 I disagree. 
 The language was far simpler than you would expect from an Allende novel but as the book is aimed at teenager readers this is not unexpected. You would expect the story, however, to be gripping and well developed. For me this was where the book was lacking. 
 We follow the somewhat nerdy Alexander (a naive 15 year old flute player with anger management issues... do all children nowadays have anger management issues?) as he accompanies his grandmother (a famous social anthropologist) on an exhibition to the Amazon. Once there he encounters all kinds of adventures with 'the people of the mist': an indigenous tribe. 
 I must admit I didn't follow a lot of what was going on (partly because I wasnt paying attention). I couldn't work out where all the mythical things fitted in with the plot. This might have been an excellent use of symbolism by Allende of modern societies inability to fully understand the lives of other cultures. Something tells me it probably wasn't. Too much time was spent on Alexander's personal journey and the last 50 pages (of a 400 page book) was where Allende packs in all of her critiques of modern society. It felt like a checklist. It was too much. 
 I am loathe to slate the book- I was not it's audience- and perhaps 12 year olds love it. I'm not sure they would understand the subtlety of Allende's critique but perhaps I am underestimating the average 12 year old. One thing is for certain, it's no Harry Potter.

Interesting book, makes you travel to a total different place, really liked it

Alexander Cold, a fifteen-year-old California boy, is sent to stay with his grandmother in New York while his mother is being treated for cancer. After arriving at the airport to find no one waiting for him, he wanders through an alternate-dimension New York where no one will give directions to a polite out-of-towner, has all his belongings except his passport stolen by a girl around whom, had the plot not demanded it, he'd never have dropped his guard for a second, and eventually winds up at the door of his grandmother's apartment. Grandma Kate is a reporter for International Geographic, so of course she promptly takes Alex off on an expedition to Brazil, to track a yeti-like creature reported to inhabit remote portions of the Amazonian jungle. (This expedition is, of course, the reason his passport couldn't be stolen.) The Amazonian version is known simply as the Beast, and the North American version, i.e., sasquatch, or "Bigfoot," has apparently never been heard of, or at least is never mentioned. The Beast is also rumored to have a city, hence the title of the book. 
 Besides Kate and Alex, the expedition consists of two International Geographic photographers, a pilot, Cesar Santos, who's an experienced guidefor jungle expeditions, the pilot's twelve-year-old daughter Nadia, the anthropologist Ludovic Leblanc, Doctor Omayra Torres, and assorted other hangers-on and spear-carriers. After enough initial obstacles have been overcome, the expedition sets out up the Amazon, encountering wild beasts and wild Indians along the way, until the two children become separat ed and have an amazing adventure, learning what the adults are not worthy to know. 
 As you may be gathering by this point, I found this book irritating rather than enjoyable. Some of the problems, the ones involving speaking styles and word choice, may well be problems of translation. For instance, in the sentence "Wheeling in the air were birds he had never seen before, some as translucid and filmy as jellyfish, others as solid as black condors" on pages 260-261, the use of translucid rather than translucent is probably not Ms. Allende's doing. (The idea of birds being either translucid or translucent is another matter, but leave that aside for the moment.) Likewise, when Ms. Allende wrote the Spanish original of "My parents do not tolerate guns. If they saw me with this they would faint" (page 130) or '"And to think that I have deprived myself of this delicious treat for more than fifteen years!" he exclaimed at the second mouthful' (page 240, where Alex finally breaks down and tries eating fish) she may well have had Alex sounding like a normal fifteen-year-old boy. 
 Other things are harder to blame on the translator. Ludovic Leblanc is a cartoon western racist, believing and actively promoting all sorts of claptrap about the bestial nature of the Indians a nd the essential brutality of human nature, even when he has to create the evidence himself. He's completely incompetent, impractical, and quite impervious to facts, reason, or experience until the end of the story, when a single experience changes all his opinions and transforms him, temporarily, into a clear-thinking plotter with nerves of steel. Much is made of the fact that Alex is an extraordinarily picky eater; in fact he allegedly doesn't eat for several weeks of the expedition, because nothing's on offer that's on his short list of acceptable foods. We are repeatedly reminded that Alex is not eating. Why doesn't he collapse from hunger? 
 Then there's the Magic Indian. Now, some of the Indians are magical because it's an integral part of the story. Matuwe, on the other hand, is just magical once, when the plot needs him to be: "His sense of orientation was so extraordinary that, although he had never flown, he was able to locate their position in that vast green expanse of jungle and to indicate with precision the place where the International Geographic party was waiting." (page 333, when Matuwe returns by helicopter with a rescue party.) 
 More generally, except for Kate, Alex, and Nadia, all the significant white expedition members are either villains or dupes--and even Kate is a bit of a dupe. All the Indians are good guys. Indian culture is pure, connected to nature, and good, while white culture is unnatural, fake, bad. It gets tiresome very fast. 
 Besides the failures of logic and characterization, Ms. Allende is also guilty of a simple failure to check easily checked facts. On page 139, we learn this important fact about anacondas: "They didn't dare probe around too much, because those reptiles were known to travel in pairs, and no one was inclined to chance another confrontation." This seemed odd to me, and I did a little checking. Amongst the several sources I found that told me the anaconda is ordinarily solitary are http://nashvillezoo.org/anaconda.htm and http://www.extremescience.com/biggest... And concerning the Beasts, on page 389: "...they're very ancient animals, maybe from the Stone Age, or earlier." Now, maybe Ms. Allende doesn't have web access, but I bet she has access to at least one good library. I bet a reference librarian could help her find out something about the habits of anacondas, or whether the Stone Age counts as "ancient" on the scale of biological evolution. 
 All in all, a disappointing and irritating book. Don't waste your own time, and don't give this to the younger readers it's intended for, who ought to be discovering what's fun about reading.
A little fantastical for my tastes. Probably meant more for kids, although it was in the adult section at the bookstore.

I have wanted to read an Isabel Allende book for a while so headed on into this one. When I picked it up i did not realize it was written for Young Adults, but ploughed on anyway. I think the operative word would actually be - plodded. Determined to finish, it has taken me three weeks - mainly because it just did not capture my imagination. I am not a great lover of fantasy fiction, and the plot just seemed to go all over the place, and I think there could have meant to have been some veiled messages in there somewhere too. 
 Oh well, at least I finished it and Jaguar and Eagle will no doubt meet again, but not in my company!

I've read better by Isabel. 
 This one was intended for an adolescent audience, clearly. That might account for it's simpleness/lack of subtlety, but even so parts of it seem hastily written and uncorrected. Other parts seem to be directly driven by where the author wanted the story to go rather than by what the characters would actually do if they were true to themselves and the situation. 
 Additionally, the novel showcased several instances where young teens take hallucinogenic drugs to arrive at truths otherwise unknown. I am really not on board with that. 
 Isabel did a good job of showing how two individuals from varying cultures can view the same situation quite differently...which is very good. 
 Then again, all the New Age air-supported beliefs were hard to take. I am thankful the author backed off claiming shaman healing herbs and water would actually save Alex's mother from cancer. I think she knew she'd be overstepping her bounds there.

reference_books.title: Manwhore (Manwhore, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Cards on the table? I barely skimmed the blurb as the title alone was enough to get me on board....I mean come on, an author ballsy enough to title their book Manwhore, I don't know about you but that was an auto-read in my book if for no other reason than to see if the audacity is a fluke or backed up by a kick ass novel. Spoiler alert- Katy Evans has the goods and she definitely delivered. 
 Rachel Livingston is a lovely young reporter on her last ditch big story at her hanging-on-by-a-thread-low-circulation magazine, Edge. Her assignment, get close to and write a hot expose' on billionaire bachelor Malcolm Saint. Rachel scores her interview and catches Malcolm's interest in the process. They tumble into a torrid affair that scorches the pages and singed my fingers. They break my heart when they fall apart when her initial motivation are revealed. Though you see the conflict and climax coming more than a dozen miles away, the ride is sooo worth the predictability of the destination. Malcolm Saint. Saint. More like Sin. More like the author absolutely blew me away with his characterization. I want him. I want to experience the storm that is Saint. He is the elusive, powerful wealthy stoic, scarred by his upbringing and parental issues hero that we all know well. But Saint is also an enigma with enough mystery and depth that makes a girl want to jump in- vag first- for the emotional layer peeling long haul. 
 "Oh no!" I laugh when he starts to lower his head. I clench my legs and stop him by grabbing a fistful of sooty black hair. "It's too intimate! I can't" 
 He trails a hand down my curves, his eyes glimmering, but not with a smile, with a challenge. "Let me taste you," he says husky and hot. 
 I go quiet and melt as his lips press to my stomach, my navel, lower. 
 "Malcolm." I protest first, holding my body tense on the bed. 
 His first lick- I tense up, my hands in his hair ready to stop him. "What if I don't taste good?" I breathe. 
 He runs the tip of his tongue over my clit and dips it inside to the complete massacre of my senses. 
 Mmm. You do." 
 The plot, though we've been here before reads exciting. It's 50 Shades meets you favorite rom com sans the lazy pace. Each chapter ratcheted up the angst and before long I was groaning (audibly!??!) imploring Rachel to just call the whole damn thing off, ditch that dying publication and put it all on the line for her man! Rachel is the perfect heroine for this plot. She is a smart balance of self-deprecation and confidence. She is proud enough not to want to be just one in the line of Saint's play-thing-toss away-booty brigade; and yet she is vulnerable and realistic enough to go with her gut and make the kinds of choices women make every day regarding being swept away in a play boy love affair. Rachel is utterly genuine and I root for her hardcore. I may even make a t-shirt. 
 Malcolm is alluring and he pursues Rachel with a full frontal seduction that leaves her breathless often. He is alpha to the core but does not beat her over the head with his control. He gives her room to graze - the little lamb to his wolf- allowing her space to retreat when she is overwhelmed by the magnitude of their mutual desire but he spares her no mercy when he decides that she is his. 
 "Rachel," he says as he takes my arm and pulls me out of the car. 
 "What...what are you doing?" 
 "Something I should've done before." 
 I refuse to take a step as he takes my hand and tugs me toward him. My eyes are huge. "You've lost your mind." 
 "I have," he agrees, then he lifts an eyebrow. "Are you coming up, or do you want me to carry you." 
 "Please don't carry me," I beg, aware of Otis's absolutely stunned stare. 
 "Then come with me." I take one step forward, his fingers lacing, strong, through mine and then we're back on the elevator. When the doors open, when nobody else can see us, he swings me up on his arms and folds me over his shoulder. "Saint! Malcolm SAINT! Put me down, what are you doing?" 
 "I'll put you down soon." I fall still and swoon inside, my heart done for. 
 "You're sleeping over. You're staying the night here." 
 The sensuality is tangible, and as the story unfolded it killed me that I could not insert myself into the novel and save them from themselves. Rachel makes an epic mistake allowing Malcolm to find out the truth splashed in the media instead of explaining herself. Why!! Why!! Argh! It is a talented writer who can make this archetypal trope so damn engaging. 
 Manwhore, the cool, little book with the big,salacious title deserves major kudos. Manwhore is a rich story with funny supporting characters; Malcolm's BFF Tahoe and Rachel's BFF Gina simply MUST spin-off somewhere, somehow, someway. I just know he would tame the little wildcat that is Gina! 
 The end is a cliffhanger and a bad one. I can take cliffhanger endings in small doses and under certain circumstances, however, the author ended Manwhore in a particularly cruel place, leaving way too much hanging. Seriously? *frowny face* The sequel, Manwhore +1 (Is this a "working" title? I'm not loving it) is due out this summer so I will have to wait (impatiently!!!) for some sort of resolution!

reference_books.title: Precarious (Jokers' Wrath MC, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Started last night, finished today and would not have it any other way. Beginning was a little awkward, I wasn't so sure it would be a MC or contemp romance, but a few chapters in and I was hooked. Krypt. He was an ass. I was SO annoyed when he behaved like a mental patient when Penny came around. I think Ash forgave him too quickly, but given the circumstances I guess it was for the best. Can't wait for Sept 15 for Maddox/Santana. Their story felt like the real story. More like this book was just an intro to the real show. This story had danger in spades, but I would have liked to have seen more about the MC. I feel like having a little more insight on the brothers would have really punctuated certain moments. Especially the big sacrifice at the end, I felt my heart strings pull but if I were to have gotten to know the brothers more, then I would have felt even more gutted. 
 Plenty of steam, legit action- some MC books have "danger" but this was written to be more dangerous, grittier than the usual MC gang drama. These heroines were not only shot at- their lives hung in the balance. Gave the book some authenticity that I appreciated.

book_a.title: Burned (Fever, #7)
book_a.user_review:
Very Meh. Plot holes. Makes me wonder what it was she scrapped to go in this direction...and if it was good... 
 SPOILERS BELOW: 
 Highlights Lor. His scenes were amazing. 
 -Dani aged. Good. Details. Bad 
 -Ryodan/Dani fans will not be jumping for joy. 
 Lor. Lor saved Burned from being in complete shambles. Where do I begin? The plot holes, the manufactured drama between Mac and Barrons? Seriously, Mac is hung up on some old douche bag shit that Barron's did after knowing her less than 24 hours? GTF over it Rainbow Girl, Black Mac, Mac 2.0 -whoever you are these days. I knew I was in trouble 1/2 way through, when I realized how damn bored I was and wondering for the upteenth time, where the hell is Dani? Then when we finally get Dani she is...Jada. Are.You.Kidding.Me. I get it. Dani had to age. I figured it would be in faery, via the silvers. What I did not expect is this fragmented personality business. No no no no no no no no. Just NO! I do not like Jada at all. Why absolutely ruin Dani as a character!!!!???? She could have come back just as kick ass- but still as HERSELF. Ugh.- 
 (Pardon me, damn near broke my ankle in another one of those pesky plot holes that plagued Burned. I'd do a better job of avoiding the gaps in shit-that-makes-no sense, if it were not for the tears of abstract boredom blurring my vision). 
 Kat, meh, I was disinterested for the most part, though I like her situation with Kasteo. He is one of the nine who I feel so sorry for. Talk about falling in love in the wrong century. He must want to kill Barrons and Ryodan daily. Need more of him. 
 Jo. Look who cares, really? I'm just glad she is not climbing the stairs for Ryodan any longer. 
 Lor is the man of the hour. KMM gets nothing but kudos from me when it comes to this male, he steals every scene. I completely agree, Moning is near unmatched when it comes to her alpha males. 
 Invisi-Mac was also a highlight. The best thing she ever did was watch Ryodan unguarded. For sure. 
 I haven't read Moning's Highlander series so I am far less OMG about Daegues being alive. I suppose that's great *shrug.* 
 Overall, it was very meh and a miss for me. I absolutely loved the Fever series, I have read them ALL several times over. The world building and writing was so damn amazing. Iced was fantastic. It felt trans-formative and fresh and I was super excited for Burned-the second Dani O'Malley book...and then I got this Burned which did an about face from Iced and freeze framed sprinted in the opposite direction. Burned just feels like something that was forced so badly it is puckering at the seams. 
 I hope Feverborn does not suffer the same pitfalls as Burned. I already know I can't take a full book of Jada and more faux Mac/Barrons strife. I also know that whether it be this fall or 5 years from now, I will be waiting like a freak at midnight for Feverborn to hit my e-reader on release day. 
 Gads!! I know right. But hey, fangirls unite...right!!!!????!!

*** 3.75 *** 
 A buddy read with my friends at the MacHalo Freaks group before the release of book #8 
 I am a bit reluctant to write this review, particularly since many of the people whose opinion I regard highly, are not very pleased with this book ... This usually doesn't influence my reviews, but in this case makes me think I am missing something ... I found the book perfectly fine for a transition book in a series, and I think of the last two books as a separate series, or Fever 2.0. I think that the author is setting the scene up for whatever OS going to develop in the next 3 books. So, we just have to be patient and let her tell us the story! 
 Even after reading this a second time, I have not changed my feelings about this book. Despite the way things are going with Dani, a path I despise for a myriad of reasons, this series, with the wonderful world building, with the numerous plot twists, and with the characters which we have grown to love or hate, this series with its triumphs and failures, is still one of the most imaginative, well-written and fascinating Urban Fantasies out there! 
 Tomorrow is the day book 8 is coming out and I am ready and nervous. I am also very hopeful that this series will gain back some of its magic and find its way back to the hearts of those, who lost their faith in it dew to the last two books direction... To all, I wish good health and good books:):):)

KMM is a terrific story teller. I liked her fever series and I LOVED "Iced" but I must admit "Burned" has definitely let me down. Maybe it was the over hype and long build up between books, maybe it's was the fact that, for me, Mac's story had ended satisfactorily in "Shadow Fever" , or maybe it was that she essentially "killed" the character I wanted to know the most about but I just couldn't engage in the story. The book is 90 percent depressed Mac, 9 percent "Other" and only about 1 percent Dani . Oh Dani we hardly knew you..... At first I was angry about it now I'm just bummed. I feel the author gave into pressure from a vocal minority instead of staying true to her original vision. This book should have been awesome but it's not.

I really love love love this series and so enjoyed getting to spend time in Dublin with Mac & Jericho. Their world is so much fun to hang out in and I miss all the characters when the book ends. Hopefully KMM is busy at work and won't keep us hanging for too long!

4.5 I think?? Maybe 5. Need to think on this!! 
 I missed Dani a lot but I am hopeful that the next book (which I will hopefully have in my grubby mitts within the year!!) will give us a ton of info that this book was missing and I am fairly confident that real Dani will come back to us. 
 Also, can I just say, on the record, that I don't understand the utter contempt so many readers hold Jo in? Like, am I missing something? I'm not saying I want to like spend a week with the girl or whatever but for the life of me I am just baffled when I read about the hatred so many feel for her. I feel like my book (and Iced as well) must have had pages missing from it or something. Except wait, I read these books on kindle. 
 Any input appreciated.
This gets a 5 instead of a 4 because of that ending that had me growling in frustration.

Finished the audio version this morning and, while I am still completely in love with the characters, plot, and setting of the series, it wasn't my favorite of Ms. Moning's books. I'm going to reserve judgment, though, because the last series that had a less than thrilling book in the middle ended up continuing with such force and passion that the less than thrilling one was quickly forgotten...or understood, once I saw where the author was going with the series. So, Burned is not my favorite, but I know something bigger, badder, and better is right around the corner...it has to be with Barrons and Riodan running things:-)

If you read the book with no expectations, it was really good. LOTS of characters in this one and kept me wanting more as usual. I really enjoy read Karen's books, she gets you with the first chapter and keeps you until the last. Thank you Karen for another good read.

Hmmm...it read like a filler novel. There were several points of view, including the Unseelie King for a chapter or two, though Mac was the dominate narrator. It was all very distracting. Why did Lor get his own POV? I hope to see more of Christian and Dani in the next book in this series.
WHAT.IS.THIS.CRAP?

** spoiler alert ** 
 I find myself thinking about this book at oddball moments, like this morning in the car on my way to work, and laughing. The author made choices here that are just... bad. Or sad. Or maybe both. One of the most likable characters in this universe was a smart-alec 14 yr old girl with superpowers and a dark past. Moning really ruined things by fast-forwarding Dani's life and morphing her into a 20-something femme fatale called Jade. Dumb. The "Jade" character is dull. She fights! She's cold as ice! She's fearless! Guys get ah-ooga cartoon eyes when they see her! As if that's not enough, the author has one of the other main characters (whats-her-name, Mac) rhapsodize over "Jade's" beauty, her now-straight hair and nice boobs. When you first meet Jade she's stalking through the streets in stiletto heels, oiled legs and a short dress (the oiled legs make me snort-laugh even now). There's absolutely nothing of Dani left, and she was the only voice in this universe who seemed to have something original to say... 
 And the whole reason for this smashup is because Dani/Jade is destined to be some ancient guy's love interest, and it's creepy for Ryoden to have romantic interest in a 14 yr old. Not that aging her 5 years matters -- tell me again why any man who's been alive for thousands of years (there's a whole group of them here, they're cursed with immortality) would be enthralled by a 20 yr old? It's icky no matter how you do it. The 20-something thing kind of worked in the first series with Mac because you learn along the way that Mac isn't all that she seems -- not even she's aware of her own abilities and what's lurking in her brain, so it sort of makes sense. And the romance stuff comes at the end of the series. But Moning had to mess with that, too, rewriting some stuff from the earlier books to add to or edit that storyline. Again, no. Leave it alone. 
 Back to this book: Mac goes invisible and creeps around the club, spying on people, which is completely awkward. There's a whole subplot with the unseelie king that makes no sense. Then another character gets locked in a dungeon (essentially - it's really a very nice apartment) to learn how to control her powers, but you don't see anything happening there, she just disappears from the storyline and you check in on her to find she's meditating. There's a rescue attempt where Mac and Jade a some of the cursed guys go tooling around Europe in a Humvee with Jade lying attractively across their gear in the way back. (I can't stop laughing, sorry) 
 I don't have any idea where the author intends to go here, but I really don't think I care to find out. Originally Mac et al were interesting to read about as their world imploded and they had to figure out who they were and what kinds of choices they were going to make (a lot of moral stuff), but the focus has switched entirely to hair, makeup, and sex. Too bad. Dani was cool and this could've been a good YA crossover character/series.

Every time I revisit Nalini Singh's psy -changeling world, I never want to leave. Three novellas, each finely crafted and wild. Dorian was a fav of mine and I adored seeing through his eyes once more. Felix is a submissive male wolf who completely stole my heart. I wasn't sure if I would be into him (subs don't really crank my wheel) fool that I am, why didn't I know that Nalini would make him irresistible and unfathomably endearing? Duh! Kenji and Gem were surprisingly the most underwhelming of the featured couples. Not to say that I didn't enjoy their story- it just gave me warm and fuzzies, but no real umph-omigosh. Tazia and Stefan had a sad sweetness that I really responded to. Their story taking place during a time when breaking silence is punishable by reconditioning! Their illicit romance felt very "early psy-changeling" and it is remarkable that Singh can switch back and write a story that feels just as desperate and yearning during a very dangerous time in series history. I wanted to shout that they were free! Free to love. 
 Yes. Nalini gives me majorly visceral reactions.

Nalini Singh is one of my favorite authors. I love the worlds in ALL of series. I absolutely loved the first story in this anthology. I liked the others too but I thought those were just okay.

I wish I'd waited to get this book from the library because it was disappointing. 
 I was most looking forward to Stefan and Tazia's story. While I liked it, it left me wanting more. More what? I don't know. I just wasn't satisfied by it. I guess I thought we'd see more of the deep-sea station rather than the desert setting where most of the story takes place, and more of them getting together rather than the quickie marriage/love scene. I like the stories with Psy heroes best--Judd and Brenna's being my favorite--so perhaps I just had too high expectations going in. 
 The next story was Dorian's and how he coped with not being able to shift while growing up. I really liked this one. It was very short but it gave a peak into how Dorian became the sentinel he is in the current books. I've always liked his character so it was interesting seeing how he grew into that role. 
 Next up was the story of a female dominant and male submissive. It was okay. I liked Felix. He was submissive but still his own person. I'm not sure I fully bought their HEA though due to the large disparity in their dominance levels, but it wasn't bad. 
 The last story was about Kenji and Garnett. I wasn't really looking forward to reading this story because the 7-year estrangement plotline just didn't interest me. The story was more of a murder mystery, though, with the romance as a backdrop. It was better than I was expecting, but I did get a bit bored with all the forensic investigating, which the story spends the most time on. Kenji and Garnett's relationship issues are wrapped up pretty quickly after the murder is solved. I thought Kenji's reason for pushing Garnett away was pretty stupid--he should've just talked to her 7 years ago. The story wasn't bad, but it wasn't great either. 
 Overall, kinda a meh read. I debated between 2 or 3 stars but will bump it up to 3 for Dorian's story.

First story: I liked this! It was a quieter kind of story, which I appreciated. 
 Second story: Fine, but didn't really do much for me. 
 Third story: I just don't love how Singh writes the submissive and dominant thing. There seems an element to sexism to it, that dominant woman mostly need to mate with dominant men. And that dominant always means solider. (I mean, I know there are maternal dominants, but they're not getting the stories. Even the one maternal dominant who got a story was a soldier.) 
 Made me want to read other authors's takes on submissive wolves. 
 Last story: REALLY, KENJI? You don't want to take Garnet's choices away from her? YOU LITERALLY DID THAT FOR SEVEN YEARS! And adoption exists, COME ON. Like, I don't mean demean his sorrow, but COME ON. Kind of did like the mystery plot, though. 
 I don't know. It's probably about time to for me and Singh to part ways. I'll come back for Nikita/Anthony. And maybe the rugby-playing brothers.

 by E. Lockhart 
 4.0/5 *s 
 The Boy Book is an honest YA fictional account of a group of high school girls navigating their ways through teenage challenges of boys, friendship, and life. Told from the POV of Ruby, and through the Boy Book (notes on dealing with the many aspects of relationships with the often confusing nature of their male peers), Lockhart has written a novel worthy of note. reference_books.title: The Fifth Witness (Mickey Haller, #4; Harry Bosch Universe, #20)
reference_books.review_text:
(4 1/2 /5. ***s) 
 This recent novel (#4) in Connelly's MICKEY HALLER (the Lincoln Lawyer) series is my favorite thus far (with stiff competition from The Lincoln Lawyer, the first book in the series). Not only did I enjoy the complex case taking place during the height of the home foreclosure disasters, which affected so many in the U.S., but I learned how and why the devastating problem developed. (Additional details regarding the plot have been well covered in other reviews and book synopses, so I won't reiterate that information here.) 
 Connelly did a fantastic job of bringing Mickey's character to life, providing details of his personal life as well as giving insight into the difficult and sometimes ethically challenging work of defense law. I usually prefer to stay away from books in a series, but this is one in which the author hasn't chosen to coast on prior successes. The subject is current, and the characters have changed and grown with each book, continuing to capture my interest and further increase my education in the practice of law. 
 Everyone accused of a crime is entitled to a defense, and Connelly effectively conveys how easily justice can be manipulated. The guilty will continue to be found innocent, and the innocent will always run the risk of being wrongly convicted. By explaining the legal system to clients through Mickey, and taking us into each aspect of building a solid case, Connelly helps us understand the delicate scales of justice. He shows how verdicts hinge on "facts" as presented to the jury, combined with lawyers' legal strategies, testimonies by witnesses and experts, and the judge assigned to the particular case. The truth doesn't necessarily dictate the verdict. 
 ***HIGHLY RECOMMENDED, for fictional as well as educational reading. 
 -Doc Aloha Reviews, 12/17/2014

reference_books.review_text:
THE CARTEL by Don Winslow 
 - narrated by Ray Porter 
 4.90/5.00 *****s 
 THE CARTEL is SIMPLY AMAZING; very possibly the BEST book I've yet heard on Audible. So interesting, educational, and a frighteningly "real life" read(/listen), serious readers will not fail to put this important work at the top of their lists! 
 This is one you will want to own... 
 one to recommend to any person concerned about humanity... 
 the lives of citizens of every nation, people of every culture, those who contemplate society and today's world. 
 Winslow brings to life the reality of the "War on Drugs", and why it's more of an issue of the human condition. Where demand/necessity exists, basic economic law tells us supply will be provided. Despite how the issue is spun, this is its core truth. 
 THE CARTEL is SUPERBLY written by Don Winslow, with Ray Porter providing perfect, award-winning narration. Both are at the top of their games; a formidable task for this incredibly detailed, character and action-rich work of fiction so believable, you'll continue to question how much is REALLY fictional! This is quite honestly one of the best works of historical fiction I've ever experienced, brought to literary excellence by a master coordinator of complex plot and very numerous, yet well-drawn characters. 
 Winslow's ability to handle both challenges, blending them into a rich, deep, culturally educational picture of this socially vital work (without leaving his audience lost in minutiae) is sheer genius. He conveys the stories of those associated with the surprisingly complex world of illegal drugs, illuminating their unique roles in the business. The reader (listener) gleans a comprehensive picture of the NARCO world, and how far-reaching the beast's tentacles are. Citizens of every nation, at every level of society, are affected by the business of drugs; willing participants in this world or not. This mutifaceted view of one of our modern world's greatest challenges should be considered required reading by scholars of life.
