I read this book a few years ago, and i did not get into it. However I was given this to read at my book group and I really enjoyed it. 
 I think it was because I was young at the time and didn't really appreciate the book, However now that I am older I have realised that I have appreciated this book more. 
 Ok so this story involves around a 9year old boy called Bruno- now this book doesn't aim for 9year olds its aimed at young adult and adults. 
 You follow the journey with Bruno you will then arrive at a fence. 
 I think this book has to be read in the same was a parable or fable. Its not an accurate historically text. To me this book it was simple to read very effective story telling.

I chose this book because the title looked interesting and on the back cover there were reviews and endorsements from the likes of Publishers Weekly, The Wall Street Journal, and USA Today. In fact, USA Today states, "Powerful and unsettling . . . As memorable an introduction to the subject as The Diary of Anne Frank." The Diary of Anne Frank? Wow, USA Today, now that is a very powerful comparison to make! And so, after reading the comparison of this book to The Diary of Anne Frank, I was sold and I made my purchase at the counter of Border's. Now three days later the only word USA Today got right was unsettling. This is written by John Boyne who apparently decided it would be easier NOT to do any sort of research before he wrote his book. Boyne, who gives an interview at the end of the book, states that he wrote this in a week. 
 Well, Boyne, we can see that. This manuscript would have been torn to pieces in a workshop. 
 What I liked: I loved the idea of two boys sitting on either side of a fence. I also noticed that this had been turned into a MAJOR MOTION PICTURE and to prove it there was a picture from the movie at the back of the book-- two boys sitting cross-legged on the ground, a chain link fence between them. It looked enticing to me and I let my mind run wild with the possibilities in which this author may have taken such a story. 
 What I didn't like: The book and the author John Boyne. 
 The year is 1942 and the setting begins in Berlin. However, Boyne has no sense of setting so Berlin very easily could look exactly like my backyard in southern Illinois for all I know. This is told through the eyes of nine-year-old Bruno whose father is a Commandant beneath Hitler. Hitler, by the way, actually eats dinner at Bruno's home with his girlfriend Ava, though Bruno doesn't really know who Hitler is or why he is so powerful. This makes me think that something is wrong with Bruno mentally because someone as powerful as Bruno's father would have a son who very much knew and worshipped Hitler. Bruno's family is sent to "Out-With" which is how Bruno pronounces Auschwitz because apparently Bruno mispronounces words as if he spoke English, not German. Oh yeah, and Bruno also mispronounces Fuhrer instead saying Fury. So the family, which consists of Bruno's father, mother, Bruno, sister Gretel, and servants, all go to live in a three story house one hour ( by foot) away from the concentration camp though Bruno can see thousands of people in striped pajamas behind a fence out of his bedroom window and before you ask, no he doesn't have binoculars. 
 Hmmm . . . that's very peculiar, John Boyne. 
 Bruno, a typical nine-year-old, asks his twelve-year-old sister, Gretel (who would've been away from home in the Girls Coalition, not at home playing with her dolls) who those people behind the fence are and she's says that they are Jews. Bruno then asks if they (meaning her and him) are Jews because apparently he doesn't know what a Jew is. 
 C'mon!!! John Boyne, you cannot possibly think that we readers are that stupid to think that Bruno is that stupid that he wouldn't know what a Jew was! Bruno would've been raised to hate Jews and to know very well what was going on behind that fence. 
 One day Bruno goes out exploring and comes to a part of the fence, a part of the fence that is not tightly secured and where the two boys can eventually touch hands beneath and/or crawl through. He sees a boy, Shmuel, sitting cross-legged on the ground with a shaved head wearing striped pajamas. They start talking, and can you believe it? They just so happen to be the exact same age to the day! 
 What a Ka-wink-a-dink, John Boyne, you're really using your imagination now! 
 The two boys meet every single day for over a year, sitting on the ground talking about their two lives and still, AND STILL, Bruno doesn't understand what those people are doing over there. In fact, he wants to go over because he thinks it's a village, a town with lots of fun things to do. And although the two boys are talking about how their lives are being lived, we as the readers have no idea what is being said because John Boyne just tells us that they meet and talk. We rarely get a glimpse into their conversations. 
 Now, let's stop and think about this for a moment. John Boyne are you really trying to make us believe that every single day these two boys can find the time to meet at the fence and talk for hours? First of all, a nine-year-old Jewish boy would've been killed after arriving at Auschwitz because they only wanted those strong enough to work. Also, Bruno would've been studying the war and probably at a camp for boys especially since he was the son of an SS. In addition to this, the fences were electrical at Auschwitz. This is not to even mention that the stench of death surrounding Auschwitz was so pertinent that it could be smelled for miles around. John Boyne, you should know these simple facts simply by graduating from high school. 
 John Boyne's characters are as flat as a paper doll and by page 200 (the book is only 216 pages) someone could've come into their home and gunned Bruno's family down and I wouldn't have felt the slightest moist of a tear forming in my eye. In truth, I would've felt nothing but sheer joy that the book was finally over. I felt absolutely nothing for Bruno who could see that his friend, Shmuel, was too skinny so Bruno brought him food although he ate most of it on the way to meet Shmuel. I felt nothing for his sister, whom I have no sense of what she may look like. His mother is faceless and his father is nothing but a no-speaking-uniform. 
 The Ending: what a joke! John Boyne would've been laughed at and sent into a fit of crying if he would've had the nerve to try and end a book in this manner in any workshop in any place in the world including amateurs in beginning creative writing. Bruno and Shmuel decide to meet one last time before Bruno moves back to Berlin. Bruno wants to slip beneath the fence and see what the "town" is like on the other side, so they hatch a plan and Shmuel "steals" a pair of pajamas from a hut that he can so easily walk into and do such a thing at a concentration camp in 1942. They meet, Bruno changes into the pajamas, crawls beneath the fence, and they begin to walk around. 
 Here's your big chance, John Boyne, use your five senses and let us see and smell and feel the concentration camp. Nah, that would make you work too hard, John Boyne, so instead just give us some old people sitting around staring off into the distance and crying and some soldiers playing with their guns and laughing. Good job, John Boyne, you've really got my interest now. What a way to paint the scene! 
 Eventually the soldiers blow a whistle meaning that the Jews are to begin marching and Bruno and Shmuel begin marching as well. They march everyone into a gas chamber though Bruno thinks it's a place to get out of the rain, because at this point it has started raining. And that's the end of the chapter. The next and final chapter starts with this line, "Nothing more was ever heard of Bruno after that." And then Boyne spends ONE PAGE saying how the sister and mother cried and a year later his father found the place in the fence, slipped beneath it, and then fell to his knees in agony because he figured out what must've happened to his son. Are we supposed to feel sorry for Bruno's father whom we don't even know? Hell, I don't even feel sorry for Bruno being gassed at this point! 
 In addition to this poorly written book, there are inconsistencies throughout from the spelling of pajamas/pyjamas to saying on one page that Bruno cannot remember his friends back home in Berlin to the following page where Bruno mentions all three names of his childhood friends from Berlin. I am going to throw this book away. I have never thrown a book away before, but I don't want to be responsible for someone young or inexperienced with the Holocaust getting a hold of this hideous book and reading it, thinking that this is well thought out or well researched. 
 Shame on you, John Boyne! You obliviously do not care about this subject or you would have given it the time and research that it deserves. You simply wanted to make a buck and somehow (though as a writer I am scared to think a publisher would find this good) you got lucky.

** spoiler alert ** 
 The ending was very sad. It was unexpected, but I'm glad it ended the way it did. I don't think the book would have been any good if it hadn't ended that way! It was very poetic, but sad. Probably would make Greek tragedy writers proud. 
 It was a little hard to read because of the fact that it was told from the view of a nine-year-old, though. But that was okay. 
 I liked the fact that Bruno never fully understood how to pronounce Out-With and the Fury. I liked the naievete and innocence in his character.

I cannot understand how a book so terribly flawed could be such a success, even without its really dumb premise (fury! furher! really) it is just standard terrible holocaust rubbish. Yawn, gas me, turn me into soap just don't get me so angry again.

I think there are plenty of other negative reviews on this book that perfectly sum up my feelings about it. But... 
 1) I absolutely cannot believe that the son of such a high ranking Nazi would know nothing at all about the war or any of the events leading up to it. 
 Bruno has no knowledge of the animosity for Jews at the time, no idea who Hitler is, why the lights have to be off every night in his house...the list goes on. The author attributes this to age of his character, but it is a very poor excuse for such an ignorant protagonist. Again, he is the son of a very high ranking officer. 
 2) The weird and out-of-place word play. 
 'Out-With' instead of Aushwitz, the 'Fury' instead of Fuhrer...the family is supposed to be German but the dialogue is written as if they were from England or America. As another review pointed out, that play on words only works in English, not German. 
 3) The relationship between Bruno and Schmuel is very forced. 
 Honestly, it's more of Bruno talking at Schmuel, complaining of the new three story house he is living in and eating the food he sometimes brings when he visits his friend. He rarely asks him any questions and the conversations seem stilted. This isn't helped any by how ignorant Bruno is about the events of the time he is currently living in. 
 Another reviewer really hit it on the head when they said this was written for adults who are already aware of the events of the Holocaust. I can see why so many others who read this book feel this is an insensitive portrayal of Holocaust. 
 In addition to all of those reasons, as if they weren't enough, it's also very poorly written. The plot was definitely culminating to it's shocking ending, but the author had to fill in the gaps before he got there. The result is a clumsily told story with no development (plot, character, relationships) that adds nothing to the stories that have been written on this part of history.

I read this for book club, the member who chose it, did so because she really enjoyed the movie. I am surprised this was made into a movie? it was a good read, easy flowing dialect. The story is told through the words and thoughts of a 9 year German boy, Bruno whose father becomes the commandant of Auschwicz Concentration Camp. xWhile out exploring one day Bruno meets Schmeul and they becomes friends through the fence that separates where Bruno lives with his parents and Schmeul lives with his papa, grandfather and other inmates. After 12 months of friendship and talks, Bruno finds out that he and his mother and sister are going back to live in Berline while his father stays on at Auschwitz. On his last visit he decides to come under the fence (where there is break) and join his friend for the day - and he never knew what hit him. 
 I was always reluctant to read this book or watch the movie as I thought it would be very sad but there is nothing sad about this book really. It just happened and his parents never knew where he disappeared to though his father may have an idea.
See the movie.

The Boy in the Striped Pajamas has been on my radar for a long time, and I'm very glad I finally picked it up. 
 This is an incredibly moving story about a nine year old boy who is the son of a Nazi. Seeing his life that exists in what is essentially a bubble of ignorance, he befriends a boy living on the other side of the fence. In a concentration camp. 
 It's a very fast read, but I came out of it feeling like I had just read something meaningful. I think this would be a perfect historical fiction book to teach in schools, and I highly recommend it.

Having only one previous experience with a James Patterson book, in which I didn't make it past the first chapter, The Women's Murder Club series was recommended to me. I have to admit that I did the storyline entertaining. Not great literature, but a good weekend read.
Love these girls!
Took me an awefully long time to finish this. It was good. Good cops always win in the end. Truth shall prevail.

After reading "1st to Die", I had to dive right into the second book in the Women's Murder Club series, "2nd Chance" by James Patterson. 
 I cannot say enough good things about this series thus far, each book has been a real page turner! Crime fiction at its best, and centering around kick-ass females. What more could I ask for? 
 In this book the ladies are shocked when a sniper shoots at choir kids coming out of a church. Miraculously only one child was hit, and killed, despite dozens of shots being fired. They soon find out that the child who died, may not have been a random unlucky one. 
 As more and more people are being targeted and killed, the ladies wonder if these are racially driven murders or if the sniper is targeting cops. 
 The women come together to put an end to the senseless killings. Can they make it out of this one unscathed? It seems unlikely once they find themselves the targets.
Another great book and keeps you guessing right up til the end. Loving this series!

I enjoyed this one, but I'm starting to wonder if they take down one person just to find out that it wasn't that person who was committing the crimes. If this continues I'm not sure I'll keep reading the series. I'll try the 3rd one.
This was a good second installment of the series. I liked the twist - didn't see it coming. Sometime soon I will read the next one!
Not as a thriller as the first one...but good to read if you want to keep up with the stories of the characters.

Don't get me wrong, I really love James Patterson and pretty much everything he writes. I like this series too but I honestly feel at times like he is trying too hard. 
 The whole girl power mix of every crime show and Sex and the City, had me rolling my eyes at times. I like that it is a group of professional women but there was just something off about it. Maybe because a man wrote it and did the stereotypical girly things, I don't know. 
 I will continue the series, and this whole book is literally #squadgoals but really unbelievable at times as well as over the top. 
 Decent Read!

reference_books.title: Supernaturally (Paranormalcy, #2)
reference_books.review_text: This books was not quite as amazing as the first, but a chance to get back in Evie's pink boots and zebra dresses cannot be passed up! This one has a less clear cut villain and more emotional drama. Evie is trying to figure out how to live a "normal" life and realizes she's bored. As she learns more about herself you discover hidden depths to Evie that are wonderful and let you in on a few of her secrets.

reference_books.title: Water for Elephants
reference_books.review_text:
I was really puzzled by this book. While it was an interesting story, I can't figure out what everyone is raving about! There were some interesting parts of this book. It was interesting to see this side of life during the Great Depression. It was interesting to view it from a 90-something year old man's mind and see that he was still there, he just looked different outside. But the story was not that compelling, and the characters were SO one sided. They were not multi-faceted at all. All of the main characters were either good or evil. It was so straightforward that it didn't seem realistic. 
 You know how when you go to National Parks and read the little signs about the plants, animals, and history, and think, "Oh, that's interesting?" That's how I felt about this book. The subject was intersting. The time period was interesting. The fact that almost everything in here was based on real events, was interesting. But not enough to read a whole book on it! I hate stopping in the middle of books but I couldn't bring myself to finish it! It just wasn't well written, and to top it all off, it also had tons of bad language and some sex scenes that were unnecessary. Those haven't even affected this review, it was purely based on the story and characters, which left something to be desired.

reference_books.title: Demonglass (Hex Hall, #2)
reference_books.review_text: Demonglass was so much better than Hex Hall! I loved the world and characters Rachel Hawkins created during Hex Hall, but I loved how much more we got into them during Demonglass. I'm not going to lie, I also love love loved that Demonglass lacked the petty high school squabbles since it takes place during summer break. And the cliff hanger? Aack! How am I supposed to wait a whole year? I loved that Rachel Hawkins didn't come straight out and say all the swear words and other things which were somewhat inappropriate. she'd say, "'You witch,' except he called me something else." Which I thought was much better than putting those words in there that I don't want to read. Can't wait for #3!

reference_books.title: Mockingjay (The Hunger Games, #3)
reference_books.review_text: I was really excited to read this. I loved the first two books and really thought that Peeta saved the book from being too dark/serious/depressing because of the pure sweetness he emanated. I was really frustrated to not find that in this book and sort of felt betrayed that this book was missing that so much. It's not a love story. None of them are really, but I think the love part has always been that no matter how bad things get, there are still bright spots in your life, like Peeta for Katniss. That was missing, and the whole thing was just depressing. Well written, good war type book, not a happy love story. The best part was that Katniss stayed true to herself through all 3 books. She never did something out of character.

reference_books.title: Fury (The Fury Trilogy, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Too much language and honestly, I was super annoyed by the Furies who seemed petty and meddlesome. It seemed very disjointed with all the jumping around too, and it seemed like the Furies were being overly harsh in their reactions. Not my favorite.

book_a.title: Hourglass (Hourglass, #1)
book_a.user_review: This story had an interesting premise and intriguin characters, but it seemed to drag for me. I found myself skipping ahead a few pages, and then chapters at a time waiting for it to get more... something. By the time I finished skimming I had gotten the jist of the entire book and had no desire to go back and get all the gritty details, so I didn't. I got the basics of the story and felt fine with it. Not my favorite, wouldn't read a sequel if there was one.

sample_reviews.review_text:
The synopsis and cover of this book over sells it completely. Seriously, this cover is freaking perfect, and the synopsis includes TIME TRAVEL !!!!! And of course, the cheesy romance. But I can totally look past a cheesy romance when the rest of the book holds its own. And TIME TRAVEL seemed quite capable of doing so. Seemed being the key word there. 
 Emerson has seen "ghosts but not ghosts" ever since her parents death. She was put in mental institutions and finally a boarding school far away from the southern ghosts of Tennessee. But now she's back in Tennessee with her brother and his wife oh, and the "ghosts but not ghosts." Enter Michael. He believes everything she says. And has more information. But can Emerson trust this alluring man who says she can time travel? 
 So, as one might guess, I expected this book to be mainly about Emerson learning how to time travel. Not about Emerson choosing which dress would make her appeal to Michael. Or about how unfair it is that her brother wouldn't let her go out with someone he's employing. Or how amazing she is at everything and god, "no one likes a crazy girl, especially one who is apperently so hot and athletic and sassy and just pure perfection." Which, I hate to break it to you Myra McEntire , 
 ABSOLUTELY NO ONE LIKES TO READ ABOUT. 
 I love characters with faults that make them perfect. Not perfection that makes them perfect. Plus, all these things Emerson is credited with being, she shows no example. Like she's apperently extremely sarcastic and hides behind it. SHE IS RARELY SARCASTIC! Like when she is you're shocked because it's just so not her. So there's Problem number one. 
 Problem number two is that it was so freaking obvious from the very beginning that Emerson and Michael would end up together. Like there was absolutely no doubt in my mind. Which made the two of them dancing around each other so very tedious. "But Emerson, you know what your brother said." "Oh, Michael. you pissed me off so back off." "Emerson Kaleb isn't for you! I am!" "It was just a kiss! Back off" These few sentences basically entirely encompass 5/6 of the book. 
 Which leads to Problem number three 5/6 of the book is nothing but Emerson and Michael's severe attraction to each other which they cannot act upon. And since it was so blatantly obvious they would be together, it wasn't even remotely interesting to read about. 
 Problem number four The entirety of their romance is basically based on physical attraction and the "we both do this, therefore we're meant to be together thing". When Michael "dies", Emerson never talks about how she misses the little things about him. Nope. There's only the physical need for Michael to be around. 
 And Problem number five The time traveling element of the book is practically non-existent. And can only happen if you are extremely precise. So basically, since Emerson broke the rules, she won't be able to do it again. Hurray for boredom. 
 I am honestly disappointed in this book. I was expecting so much more than plot-lost-in-the-romance book.

Really enjoyed this one! The writing was great, it kept me totally captivated. Emerson was a cool character, and I really liked her. Michael is pretty darn lovely as well, I have to say. Everything about this book was pretty close to perfect. I couldn't put it down. It was 3 am and I had to force myself to go to sleep because I still had more than 100 pages to go. I don't mind that the science of the science fiction/time travel aspect was a bit lacking, because I never understand all the complexities anyway (Wibbly wobbly, timey wimey... stuff. Oh yes, 'Hourglass' also has a very tiny Doctor Who reference. Yay!). One of the only things that I thought was a bit weak about this book was the semi-love triangle (actually, quadrangle) that emerged. It wasn't a huge part of the story, but I didn't really think it was necessary. There was enough drama between the two characters without that, I thought. I guess I didn't quite get the "villains", either. I would've liked more clear motivations from one of them in particular. However, when it comes down to it the strengths of this book far outweigh any possible negatives. I really (really!) enjoyed it, and I look forward to reading more about Em and Michael.

A solid 4 1/2. I don't know why I'm finding the hardest time dishing out 5 star ratings! My problem with the book was this...so she's in love, infatuated, obsessed (call it what you will) with a hottie. ok, I get it. so then the hottie has a hottie friend and you fall for him too? even after knowing him for a day? And there is so much miscommunication in YA novels! If you like someone, please tell them and save yourself all the drama. And if you have this deep dark secret, at least do a better job of hiding it. I can do without all of the painful facial expressions and sudden outbursts of anger! (but that's basically the definition of a YA book. all the tension and naivete.) But all in all the story itself was really cool. It kinda reminded me of the time that Harry and Hermoine went back in time to save buckbeak. haha. I really enjoyed the characters' personalities. They were fun and quirky. Definitely recommend it to my friends. Its another series to get hooked into.

The story is about a girl called Emerson, a seventeen year old, who sees and interacts with ghosts from the past or 'ripples'. After being hospitalised for the better part of her years, she returns to Ivy Springs to live with her brother and sister-in-law. Her brother, Thomas, suggests yet another consultant to try and help Emerson with her issues and after seeing Michael, the new consultant, she is instantly drawn and agrees to work with him. However, she learns not only does Michael share her gift too, but she also has other untapped abilities, such as time travelling. 
 My opinion about Emerson is that she is an okay character.....that's just it. There's nothing more I could say about her, other than that I did feel sorry for her when her parents had died on a ski trip that they were all on and soon afterwards she was hospitalised and pumped with numerous amounts of medicines that kept her like a vegetable. Aside from that, despite being a small, yet strong female, she was rather a dull female character. There wasn't anything new or fresh about her and because of that my opinions about her are just going to have to be that she is an okay character. Likeable, but boring nonetheless. 
 I liked Michael at the beginning. He came across as being charming, smouldering, hot and a mysterious new kid on the block. However, as the story progressed he became almost too good to be true. I know this sounds weird, considering we are talking about a fiction book, where nearly everything is unreal. However, it made Michael a really unrealistic character. I also got annoyed at him when he tried being the hero in EVERYTHING. He even got on my nerves when he always switched his emotions towards Emerson from desire to stubbornness to just plain angry very quickly. 
 The relationship between Emerson and Michael began at first very sizzling and hot but it soon died down very quickly. It became just like any other YA relationship. However, I am going to admit that there were some very funny bits between the two characters. 
 In terms of the plot, I got a tad bit confused in the beginning but I guess that the author wanted the readers to be slightly bewildered until she revealed the fragments that were missing in the first chapter. The whole aspects with time travelling that also including some sci-fi aspects lacked coherence and substance and at times the descriptions seemed fuzzy. It seemed like Myra wanted to use/create some fancy words to explain the whole time travelling aspect. However, all it really achieved was make the book sound silly, too unrealistic or too technical. I thought the powers that the other supernatural students had were really boring. I mean hardly any of the students' powers stood out.....how could they if the students themselves did not stand out! However, I did like the explanations about the 'ripples'....but that's about it. To be honest the whole plot was a bit of a mumbo-jumbo. 
 P.S after reading some discussions about 'Timepiece' (the second book) I am a bit gutted that nothing else happens between Emerson and Kaleb (for those who have read 'Hourglass', you know what I am talking about)!

Meh. Just meh. 
 - I don't know if I have anything to say, like it was just really long and boring and yeah. 
 - Emerson felt like the typical YA character. Even though she could see the past, and also travel through time with help. 
 - I mean, does everyone have to have powers by the end of this book? 
 - Also, the hiring of Michael ad a therapist was just weird because he was 20.....and then he becomes the love interest 
 - I ended up skimming the end, there was a lot of explaining done by the villains. Why explain everything? Why?

Hourglass by Myra Mcentire totally surprised me on how much I adored it and how amazing it was. The reason I believe I was so pleasantly surprised is because I went in believing this book was about a girl with the ability to see ghosts, nowadays a plot that isn't original, but I was nevertheless intrigued. So you can imagine my surprise that the concept of this book was something altogether different. 
 Hourglass is a story about Emerson Cole a teenage girl that has been plagued with ghostly apparitions shortly before her parents death in a tragic accident. Since then she has had a difficult time coping but after a stint in a mental institution and years away at boarding school she is back in town as her scholarship runs out. Luckily she has her older brother Thomas and his wife Dru that have become Em's anchor and support. It is Thomas who finds Micheal, a consultant from the Hourglass whom he hires to help Emerson with her "problem" and from that day on she is never the same again. Normal is so overrated anyway. 
 There are many aspects of this story that I enjoy and one of them is the strong adult presence in Emerson's life. Many times stories have absent parents and adult guidance but this story is not the case. It was refreshing to see Emerson confide in her brother Thomas and that they have such a special bond and that he doesn't treat her as if she is crazy and he truly looks out for her *sigh* so heartwarming. I also admire Dru for she is a great motherly influence that has an awesome sense of style and she gives Emerson that balance that she needs. 
 As for Emerson Cole she a kick ass protagonist and she has won a special place in my heart. Her wicked sarcasm is consistently hilarious. "Holy Hormones Batman" is one of my favorite Emisms and I totally admit to using it. Her interactions with Micheal are sizzling, fun and you just never know what is going to happen next between them but you know you want more of it. Micheal lends that mystery and intrigue to the story that keeps you on the edge and as you get to know and understand him you are already half in love with him. As with the another character Kabel, yowza talk about someone to get the blood pumping faster than a roller coaster ride. Whenever he made an appearance I would be left fanning myself, what a lady killer and I cannot wait to see happens with him in subsequent novels as with the other characters that also became endeared to me. 
 I admired the whole science fiction concept of this book and considering that I am totally not a sci-fi fan that is saying alot. The idea behind Hourglass is so very innovative that I was eager to know what it was all about from the very beginning. I was made a captive audience and I did not want to stop reading. Hourglass has so many amazing twists, and although I saw a few coming I was completely blind-sided by some of the others and I loved that about this book. 
 I cannot sing enough praises for Hourglass and I know that the YA genre of readers will devour it greedily and demand more because it is that engrossing and original of a novel and in this market of overused themes and characters, that says alot.
OMG so good! One minute my heart was pounding the next I was tearing up. Michael...THUD!

I actually enjoyed this book which is the start of a new series by a local author here in Nashville. It's a nice change from the typical sparkly supernatural beings and the main characters weren't filled with broody emo-ness which seems to be the YA flavor of the month. I'd like to see more of the supernatural aspects however and less romance. 
 Liked: Emerson's (the main character) ability to be tough as well as maintain her femininity, the lack of southern culture abuse, the secondary characters such as Kaleb and Lily, time travel! 
 Disliked: Being reminded how got Michael is every other paragraph, lack of depth on the main villain
Such a shame that this book turned out to be another YA novel with a non depth plot line and the same boy meets girl, girl falls in love with bad boy... twist. Really disappointed with this one.

I heard really good things about this book, but I didn't like it. 
 The characters were okay. 
 The love interest was annoying and the attraction was superficial in my opinion (similar to Twilight). 
 There was an attempt at a a love triangle but it failed. 
 Tried to have a huge finale and failed (I was a bit confused at the end) 
 I think there will be a sequel. I will not be reading the next one. 
 Horrible writing. I found many grammatical errors (I'm not even OCD about grammar) 
 I thought the concept was very interesting so I believe it had potential. 
 I do not recommend this book.

book_b.title: The Last Little Blue Envelope (Little Blue Envelope, #2)
book_b.user_review: I enjoyed this sequel, although I felt that the ending in the first book was much better than this one. Off on another adventure, Ginny finds that people are not always what they seem. Although the story is still wonderful, it seems like it was maybe not thought out quite as carefully as book 1. Still worth reading, even if just to find out what happens with Ginny and Keith!

sample_reviews.review_text:
I got this at the Texas Library Association conference and was absurdly excited to see it. I loved Ginny from the first book. She's so spunky, but she suffers from the occasional case of low self-esteem-- i.e., not thinking she is brave even though she backpacked across Europe by herself at 18! Ginny has the opportunity to evolve and mature further within this novel, and her relationships get accordingly complicated. 
 This book keeps the same characters from the first ones (thankfully), with the introduction of two new traveling companions. Neither are particularly wanted on the journey. If you recall, at the end of 13 Little Blue Envelopes, Ginny's backpack was stolen in Greece. She never did read the last letter. Well, as you can guess from the title, someone has found the last envelope-- and he's blackmailing Ginny to let him go with her (and split the art proceeds). Keith (from the last book) and his new girlfriend follow. While Keith is wanted, the new girlfriend is an unwelcome surprise. Anyway, adventure ensues. 
 Fast paced, great locations, nicely done romance. The ending was perfect. Highly recommended to anyone interested in contemporary teen fiction.

Very satisfying. A perfect ending to Ginny's story (not an ending for her, obviously, but for the reader). That 3 stars is really a 3.5; I liked it. I really liked it. But I didn't LOVE this one the way I loved the first one.

It has been a number of years since I last read Maureen Johnson's writing. I have to say that I loved it even better than I did years ago. The writing is still strong, maybe even better, and the stories are so captivating. This is a book that I'm not afraid to recommend to young teens. Reading this book felt like coming home again to my early teens years when there was so much to learn about life and myself. 
 I also like the fact that Ms. Johnson does not force her writing. She performs at her own pace and stays true to herself.
So fabulous. I think I might even like it better than the first one!

3,5 stars 
 The first one was better.

This is one of those funny times where I enjoyed the sequel more than the original. I feel like in this one, I flew right through it, eager to see what was going to pan out through the end. 
 In the last book, Ginny has her backpack stolen from her, along with the sacred thirteen letters from her aunt. This book is the story of how a young man named Oliver finds it by buying her stolen backpack and basically holding it hostage. 
 Let me just say that this book did a very good job with character development. I went back and forth from hating to loving to hating again to loving again multiple times with each character. Oliver especially. 
 I feel like if I say too much, I'll give most of the story away, so just read this book, it was very, very good!
Satisfying, and didn't tax my memory too much about the previous book, which I hadn't read in years.

I read the first book and thought there should be more resolution. Then I found out there was a sequel. I was like yeah! I enjoyed reading the rest of Ginny's journey. I would recommend these books just make sure they know about both.

Real rating: More like 3.5. 
 Originally posted this review of BOTH books on my blog, hello, chelly.
http://librarianosnark.blogspot.com/2...

reference_books.title: Just One Damned Thing After Another (The Chronicles of St Mary's, #1)
reference_books.review_text: This book is a History Geek's dream. I will certainly continue the series. Go St. Mary's!!!

reference_books.title: Candide
reference_books.review_text: BLAH, BLAH, BLAH.....BOO HOO HOO! Long winded and forever whining.

reference_books.title: The Opposite of Loneliness: Essays and Stories
reference_books.review_text:
I really hate to be the one to make a negative statement about this book. The hype was huge and said it was profound and everyone should read it and that there was a deep message in it that you would never have expected such a young person to have an understanding of. ALL of that is just a lie. 
 Sure , the internet loved the one item she wrote. I read that and thought it sounded like most anyone her age or younger. At that age most college kids believe they are ready to change the world and achieve their goals in life. Her writing simply did not astound me as I had been promised it would. Maybe, if she had lived and continued to develop her skills she would have written volumes we all would want to read over and over. 
 But, she did not live. Sad to see such a bright light no longer there. So very sad. 
 What did happen was that her parents had to have agreed to allow this to be published and are profiting from it(which is sick)or someone out there is profiting from it other than them (which is still sick). Furthermore, too many of the works in this book mention smoking pot or doing other drugs, which I found troubling, or had the female character speak about sex in some really disgusting way that most of us would not. Because we would not think in those words about anyone we were emotionally connected to. 
 I feel like I got sucked in and ripped off. How sad that I actually paid for a hardcover copy.

reference_books.title: Hammered (The Iron Druid Chronicles, #3)
reference_books.review_text: K. Hearne did an excellent job on this installment in the Iron Druid series. I continue to find all of the main characters interesting. There are many changes in this one and so be prepared to gasp a few times. The only negative was that this time there was a liberal spattering of Captain Kirk chatter ...and while I love that show....I can't stand William Shatner( and therefore Kirk). Spock rocks, though. The ending will only make you want to continue reading this series.

reference_books.title: My Sister's Grave (Tracy Crosswhite, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
My Sister's Grave had unexpected twists. It was very well written and the action was stellar. The characters became people you quickly related to and I will be interested to see where things go next. This plot was so well wrapped up that I was not left wondering about any of the different storylines within the plot, which is a pleasant thing to find in a novel. 
 This is one I would recommend to friends.

book_a.title: Hounded (The Iron Druid Chronicles, #1)
book_a.user_review: A bit of a new twist on ancient dieties , druids, and more. There's an Irish Wolfhound with a mental connection to the Druid...interesting. Above all else, this book caters to my sense of humor which ranges from amusing dry wit to the laughable goofy sort. It has some of the most hilarious dialogue I have read in a while. Definitely reading the next in this series.

sample_reviews.review_text: Oh, how I love these books! I'm not so into mythology, but Kevin Hearne's style is light, even in the midst of life and death action, and different. For most of the books in this series, I listened to the audio books. The narrator makes it more fun with good voices. In any case, I enjoy the action, the dialogue, the local setting, and especially the characters. How can you go wrong with an attorney who's a vampire?
Fun urban fantasy with the whole gamut of fantastical creatures and gods and wiches and so on. And the hero is a druid with pet wolfhound.

I picked up this series in part because it was recommended to me by several different people who are fans of Dresden Files and suggested I might like it for that reason. I did very much enjoy it! I appreciate original twists on urban fantasy, and the druid lore is a nice change of pace from vampires and werewolves (even though those feature as well...). Oberon is the best supporting character ever, and the book has a great sense of humor.

For some strange reason I was under the impression this series was targeted at YA readers. I was pleasantly surprised to be wrong. 
 Kevin Hearne has created an extremely interesting world in which supernaturals walk alongside man. But unlike most urban fantasy tales, he focuses much more on various deities in different pantheons and their modern day incarnations. There is, of course, the obligatory "usual suspects" - vamps, werewolves and Fey. But Hearne does an admirable job of putting a unique twist on them. More than enough to keep me coming back for more. 
 His protagonist, Atticus O'Sullivan, is, at first blush, a Harry Dresden clone with Druidic powers instead of more traditional command of magic. At least that is what I thought at first. Just a few chapters in and I realized how wrong I was. The character is very well-fleshed out, with virtues and flaws of a subtle nature. By adopting a first person POV, the author allows us some insights but more often provides tantalizing clues (show vs. tell) which draw the reader deeper in. 
 The plot was uncommonly varied and appealing, the pace of the work was very well done as well, with excellent balance between rising tension, release and building to greater peaks of tension afterwards. The dialogue was witty and funny but without sounding artificial. 
 My only negative opinion of the work is an old one. It is sometimes difficult to create a sense of genuine peril when it involves a character with functional immortality. Hearnes does make statements and creates an interesting pair up of two incarnations of Death at one fight, which I found quite interesting, but there was not quite enough genuine danger. 
 All that said, I'm delighted to have read this book and have already purchased the next 2 in the series.

I'd probably give this 2.5 stars (3.5 on Amazon). 
 I really liked the idea of all the Irish folklore and magic, and the different pantheons of gods. I struggled to reconcile a 2000 year old person with the voice of Atticus. He just didn't sound like someone who had been through that much stuff. I get that he was supposed to sound jaunty, like Harry Dresden, but I just think there would be more to someone who was that old. Even Dr Who had a deep scary dark side when he wasn't being child-like. I think Atticus walked the line with being a bit smug, he wasn't quite annoying but was very close. 
 I really wanted to like Oberon but I found his voice inconsistent, and preferred him when he was being doggy and not making popular culture references. The Morrigan was great, just weird enough to be non-human. 
 The bad guys weren't very well developed so I struggled to really root for Atticus against them. They were just one dimensional baddies. 
 I do think the bit about the elves dressed in cycling shorts, bashing Atticus with brooms was pretty funny, and there was a couple other funny bits too. 
 Overall, it was okay but not sure I'll read more.

Excellent read. I finished this in two days (because my library loan was about to end and because it was that good). It's written in first person, in a very entertaining style. The main character is a 21 century old Druid and the language is a pleasant mix of ancient and modern - as it should be when one lives for 21 centuries and needs to learn to blend but can't expunge every bit of the old formality or verbiage. 
 The story is suspenseful, the characters are quite varied (vampires, werewolves, witches, and humans) and there's a very entertaining dog thrown in the mix for good measure. 
 I am looking forward to reading the next book in the series.
Could be an interesting series. Entirely nerdy!

I stayed up late several nights in a row to finish this book. It was recommended by a friend, and I was hooked from page one. I enjoy urban fantasy that plays with mythological characters like gods and goddesses. This one focuses on Celtic Druids and their belief of fae creatures and acknowledges the many different religious figures that co-exist. I would recommend this to anyone who enjoyed The Lightning Thief; however, be aware that this is an adult book that at times is quite gory in detail and includes some sexual encounters.
This series is definitely a favorite! Kevin Hearne is one of the few writers who can actually make me laugh out loud while reading. And the Audible narrator is EXTREMELY talented!

book_b.title: The Book Thief
book_b.user_review:
The meat of this story was a worthy read. If only the author had done just that. Just TELL the STORY. 
 Using DEATH as a narrator is such a pointless novelty. Even as a kid, after the first time you read a story that uses this , it is annoying to see it again in future. Let's face it, Meet Joe Black was the closest drivel to succeed in using this ploy. 
 And, what a pain to have what lays ahead in the story bellowed out in bold letters and lists before you read it. It's bad enough that there are so many spoilers in book reviews. Now I find spoilers at the beginning of each chapter of The Book Thief. 
 Let's add to all of this that the main character is a cardboard girl. Her personality tastes like cardboard and glue. Only her actions and the actions of those around her saved the little hope I had of connecting with the collection of souls this story was about.

sample_reviews.review_text: What beautiful imagery and description in this book. It sort of jumps around a bit in parts and that made it difficult to really emotionally connect with the most poignant parts of the story. Ah! Tear-jerker! I really need some fluff chick lit, I've ready too many sad books in a row. 
 Anyway, I loved the narrator of this book: Death. The characters were complex and lovable. I've read some reviews where people said they hated the mother character, but personally, I think they've just never been in a family who's Eastern European. She'd be considered loving in my family. 
 I liked the concept of the sort of flashes of bold highlights that Death made, but I think they were made a little too frequently. They got gimmicky in some places. I suppose, since this is a young adult novel, I will let it slide that it does come off a bit obvious. 
 So, five stars minus one because dang it authors! I HATE 'SUM UP' CHAPTERS! Maybe this is a personal thing, but they just seem tacked on and maybe even cliche?

This is one of those novels that I put down after a few chapters, came back to it later, and I'm SO THANKFUL that I did. I admit that the unusual narrative technique threw me off at first, and I nearly lost interest altogether if it hadn't kept popping up on my Goodreads update feed. 
 But after giving it another try, I have concluded this might be one of the most rewarding literary experiences I have ever had. The last few chapters -- and even the very last line -- of this book will stay with me for the rest of my life. 
 I have no idea how the film version turned out, but regardless, absolutely everyone should read this book. While that mandate might evoke some of the constructs and real events depicted within the novel, the world might be a better place if people acknowledged the truths learned by the narrator that are so obvious (and tragic) when you just sit down and think for a second.

Cover Blurb: Yes or No? I'm a little divided about the cover. The title is mostly what caught my attention, and while the dominoes now make more sense than they did before reading the book, I still don't quite get why it was chosen for the cover art. Hmmm. 
 Characters: Death as a character is a concept that doesn't always work, but I liked him quite a bit in The Book Thief. He made for a very interesting and surprisingly good narrator, and I enjoyed his odd sense of humor. While never truly a direct character in the story, he was perfect for seeing the events through his eyes. Hans Hubermann, Liesel's foster father, was my favorite character. I loved his easy, quiet manner and gentle teasing. If I could have an ideal uncle, I'd want Hans Hubermann. Rosa, on the other hand, took me a while to get used to. Verbally abusive, rude, and sour, I didn't much care for her form of affection, though in the end I did come to like her a bit. I loved Max and Rudy and of course Liesel. Rudy had a defiant streak and Liesel was spunky. She didn't always behave well, but she always felt horrible afterward; it was hard not to forgive her. 
 The Romance: Rudy and Liesel have a bit of a childhood crush on one another, though neither would ever admit it. With so much going on in this book, it never takes forefront. 
 Plot: This is a character-driven book. Many things do happen, but there isn't a main plot. When Max arrives at the Hubermann home, it is definitely a turning point in the story, but it is only one of many in Liesel's life. The Book Thief goes from 1939 to 1945, and follows Liesel's time in a little town outside of Munich. We meet the people who influence her life, witness the events that change it, all through the eyes of Death, who takes an uncanny interest in Liesel for many reasons. Liesel is forced to leave her home and her mother when her father is arrested for being a Kommunist, and when her little brother dies on their way to Himmel Street, where they are to live with the Hubermanns, Liesel turns to book thieving for comfort. She can't read, but there is something about books that she cannot resist. Life with the Hubermanns isn't easy. They are barely able to feed themselves, and Hans Hubermann isn't exactly in agreement with the Nazi Party. But Liesel likes her foster father and she makes friends with a neighboring boy, Rudy. But every once in a while, she still feels the need to steal books, and she soon finds herself taking them from the bonfires and the mayor's house. When a Jewish man shows up at Himmel Street one night, seeking refuge with the Hubermanns, Liesel discovers someone she can share her books with. But Max can't stay forever - not with the war looming ever closer to Himmel Street. Despite the lack of definite plot (because again, Max and even the book thieving is only a small part of the story), I couldn't help but be drawn into The Book Thief. The characters are interesting, I love the era, and the narration style is just so unique and emotional. This is a feels book, and I definitely had a lot of feelings going through me as I read - sometimes laughing, but mostly sad. 
 Believability: Nothing to complain about. 
 Writing Style: First person, past tense. Though every once in a while, Death would kind of start talking in present tense. The narration took me a little while to get used to. It comes across as choppy at first; Death doesn't have a linear way of thinking. He will jump around quite a bit from one event to another, and sometimes this event has happened before that other event. But in about 50 pages, I got used to it, and was able to follow Death's thought process. And I must admit that I really enjoyed it. His dry, dark sense of humor and sometimes bizarre metaphors and similes added an extra layer of bleakness and emotion to a topic that is already very bleak and emotional. 
 Content: 15 s-words, 8 g--damns 
 Conclusion: The Reader will see the end coming fairly well in advance, because Death keeps dropping hints. But it still hit me very hard when I finally read it. I was a little stunned, and for a moment I debated whether or not it completely ruined the book. What was the point, after all, if that was just going to happen? But I honestly liked it, though I cannot exactly say why. I just did. I first tried to read The Book Thief when it initially came out. A story about a young girl who steals books during Nazi Germany sounded like the sort of thing I would love. But I couldn't get into the narration and I thought it was a little too weird, so I didn't pick it up again until recently. The movie is being releases soon, after all, and I hate seeing movies without reading the book first. Now that I'm older, I was able to enjoy The Book Thief a whole lot more. It is a little odd because of Death's narration, and it can feel a tiny bit slow. But I honestly didn't want to put it down, it captivated me so thoroughly. And what exactly it was that captivated me, I'm still not entirely certain. The characters were good, the era was good, the narration was very interesting, and it was an extremely emotional read. But I can't say that the characters were my absolute favorites, or that this was even the best WWII novel I've ever read - or even the most emotional read I've encountered. And yet, there was something about it that just stuck with me. The opening lines and the ending lines will always stay with me. 
 Recommended Audience: Girl-and-guy read, better for teens seventeen and up, and adults. Anyone younger than seventeen probably won't stick with it for long just due to interest level. Fans of WWII, Holocaust, and emotional novels will like this.

The Book Thief is an extraordinary book. Narrated by Death, it chronicles Liesel Meminger's life from 1939 to 1943 - the time in which she lived with her foster family, the Hubermanns, in Molching, Germany, a suburb of Munich. Liesel is not Jewish, but an incredibly reluctant member of the Hitler Youth. Her daily life, at the start of the war, continues in much the same way as life before and after the war. She plays soccer on the streets with her friends, she attends school, she reads books, and she delivers laundry for her foster mother. But as the war progresses, her life changes in the ways one would expect a young German girl's life to change due to war - rationing, air raids, knowing people who have been drafted into the army, etc. 
 However, Liesel's story is not the typical WWII era narrative as it is, on the surface, the tale of the ordinary German, not very sensational or particularly moving. But Liesel is a literary powerhouse of a protagonist. Her brother dies and she copes by stealing a book - a book from which she learns to read. And learning to read, that changes the course of her entire life. 
 It was an interesting choice, on Markus Zusak's part, to have Death narrate the book - it adds a sense of foreboding but also a tone of almost "hyper-reality" - giving a voice to the one fact that we all know but don't like to confront - everyone dies. Death is exhausted by World War II, between the soldiers, the Jews and the civilians, he's exhausted. But Death is touched by Liesel, the girl who seems to see him and a girl he encounters more times than he believes he should (I use "he" because I listened to The Book Thief and the reader is male). 
 Personifying Death takes away the fear, Death narrates the book like Liesel's old friend, not as an inevitable outcome and I believe that makes Liesel's tale all the more profound and moving. My words are inadequate in describing the suffering Liesel endures but Markus Zusak does so with a great love for her, for all his characters. Throughout The Book Thief, Liesel is moved herself by the power of words and though she starts as an illiterate child, she quickly becomes a voracious reader. She recognizes the power words have, the words that stay with us long after they are spoken or read and she learns some valuable life lessons from her words and the words of others. Death reveals the outcome of the book long before the final pages but that doesn't make the end any easier to accept. While not a direct story about the Holocaust or a novel of expected and imminent danger, the outcome is heartbreaking and completely, harshly real to Liesel and the reader.

I wanted to love this book. When I read the first few pages I thought I would. Sadly it did not meet anywhere close to my expectations. Don't get me wrong, I love books full of emotion even if it kills of my favorite characters, but they don't tell you beforehand what's going to happen! I also would of preferred the book being from Liesel's point of view all the time, instead of having the grim reaper narrating it. 
 I also found some of the descriptions odd. Where I thought the book was supposed to be about a girl who saves books from being burned, she only does that once! What Alex uncovers is that his niece was part of a call girl ring whose clients ranked as high as Congress and there were some connections with the White House. Some White House officials try what they can to thwart the efforts of Cross's investigation so that it does not go public, but Cross is determined to uncover and expose the evil that not only killed his niece but many other girls as well. A satisfying conclusion yet Kyle Craig strikes again with a last chapter phone call. To be continued with the next Cross installment...

James Patterson seems to write for an audience with limited intelligence. At least that is the way I often feel with these 2 page chapters, simplistic story lines, grade school vocabulary, and sexual serial killers often the main topic. 
 Washington D.C., exclusive sex club, someone killing young women for sexual gratification, cover-ups, and Detective Alex Cross to save the day (if not the women) and let the truth be known. 
 This book also contains a side story of Mama Nana, Alex's grandmother, having congestive heart failure and a heart attack, her time in the hospital and the family's reactions to this. This story seems more honest and emotionally connected to the author, and so to the reader, than the serial killer fiction. To connect the family theme with the serial killer fiction, the case comes to Alex's attention when his niece's remains are found.
This was not the greatest.
I like that Patterson continues to add depth and layers to this character and his family, both on the job and off.
If I could give this one a 10 I would! James Patterson does it again! mystery/intrigue, murder and scandal! a real page turner! awesome ending to a awesome book!

Contemporary, Thriller 
 Ani FaNelli endured a shocking, public humiliation when she was a teenager at the prestigious Bradley School. It also left her desperate to reinvent herself. Now she is living close to the perfect life she has worked so hard to achieve with a handsome blue blood fiance, an expensive wardrobe and a glamorous job. 
 Ani has a secret. 
 She is still haunted by something else that is buried in her past. It is something that is both painful and private and it is threatening to bubble to the surface and ruin everything for her. 
 Ani has a cutthroat ambition and some sharp edges that she uses to protect a scandalous truth and a heart that is actually bigger than it seems. 
 Now Ani has to decide if by breaking her silence she will destroy everything she has worked for or if she will finally be set free. 
 This is a book that takes so many twists and turns that you never know just where it is going or where it will end up. Ani seems cold and difficult but as the reader gets more into the story they find that there is a lot more to Ani than they first thought there was. The story is very engrossing as the reader will want to find out just what is going on and what Ani is hiding from her past. It has a very satisfying ending and the story will stay with the reader long after they have finished the book.

When I started this book, I thought I hated it. If I had DNF'd it, it would have been a one-star book for me. I hated TifAni, hated her name, hated how snotty she was. I kept reading though, and I will admit the twists got me. The ending was so clever, and it made me think for a while after finishing it. Maybe it's because I was not one of the popular kids. 
 In any event, I can't say that this is "like Gone Girl" because truly no one can compare to Amy Dunne. But of this summer's book offerings that have been compared to Gone Girl in the hopes of pumping up sales, this is one of the more entertaining offerings.
anti-climatic.

Which would be fine, and bearable, if she was in high school throughout the novel. She's not. Her primary timeline, the one she narrates from, is the character in her late 20's.

Overall, the book was just okay and kept me entertained enough to finish it. It dealt with some pretty intense and dark subjects, but I wouldn't go as so far to say it was just as good as Gone Girl like the reviews say.

 You meet Ani and find out she has quite the history. The story jumps back between 14-year old her and present day her. Definitely not akin to "Gone Girl." That twist was breathtaking. This was unexpected, but that only made it a twist. Writing was a bit awkward, had to backtrack several times in places to understand. Kept my interest, but only because on vacation.
