book_a.title: Uprooted
book_a.user_review:
** spoiler alert ** 
 So I've had great expectations as I started reading this book. I've heard great things about it, the synopsis was promising and I was eager to dive into the story. 
 The first two thirds of the book were phenomenal! I loved every bit of it. The story, the history (!), the characters, the romance, the fantasy ... I could go on with this list forever! 
 So there was me, devouring this story, and suddenly it changed settings. We were in the capital waiting for Kasia's trial and actually did ... nothing? I don't know it felt like this to me. Maybe it is because I fell in love with the Dragon's character the second he appeared in the book and he disappeared for what felt like 500000 pages but I wasn't just quite that invested as I've been before. 
 Don't get me wrong, it still was an amazing read and the story was well structured but it all felt a little bit ... rushed in my opinion. So many things happened at once, at the same time nothing seemed to happen at all and the absence of the Dragon stung like a thorn and then the whole thing kind of exploded and we were fleeing. 
 That's when the story got a bit back to its original pace I think. After the reunion with the Dragon, the whole story seemed to flow better and the end was just incredible. 
 The way Naomi Novik explained the roots of the Wood and showed Agnieshka a way out was just incredible! After our heroine defeated the "villain" of the story I first was a bit disappointed. When the Dragon took her to the tower and they had what seemed like a last goodbye I was like: What?! That's it? 
 And then Naomi Novik continued with her conclusion and never even mentioned the Dragon and I was really ... sad and mad at the same time. Maybe you can tell by now but I shipped the Dragon and Agnieshka SO hard. They were perfect for each other and it seemed as if they weren't getting their freaking happy end but then the last two pages came and I could relax! 
 So all in all I really enjoyed this book. I had some issues with it but the cons hardly outweigh the pros.

sample_reviews.review_text: Great book, although there were points I was frustrated with how much they seemed to repeat the same thing through out the chapter. Otherwise the book had a great plot line and great character development. I loved how it started and finished within the same book and didn't drag on to other books. I would recommend this book to anyone

Actual stars 3.5-3.75 
 I'm not much for fairytales but Uprooted was pretty enjoyable for the most part. 
 Sarkan is a wizard who lives a solitary life except for the company of one girl. He would choose a girl at the age of 17 from one of the villages surrounding the evil and corrupted Woods every 10 years and keep them in his tower. After the 10 years are up the girls could leave and return to their village. But the girls now women would never remain in their villages for very long or decide to marry, their lives now seem destined for a different course. 
 It is that time again when Dragon (aka Sarkan) is about to choose a new girl for his tower. Everyone one in the village thinks that Sarkan is going to choose Kasia because she is the more beautiful of all the eligible girls and therefore taught by her mother to cook and other domestic duties that she will need. But to everyone's surprise Sarkan picks Agnieszka, definitely not the most put together girl with rips and stains regularly on her clothes and her hair in a tangled mess most of the time. And no domestic abilities to speak of. 
 Sarkan and Agnieszka have a tumultuous relationship from the start. He barely speaks to her and when he does he insults her and is very impatient with her clumsiness in cooking and household chores and especially her appearance. Agnieszka is not sure what reason Sarkan would have for choosing her until he shows her what she has to offer and it will alter her life as well as the future of the villages surrounding The Wood. 
 Sarkan and Agnieszka have a complex relationship. First of all, Sarkan pretty much abducted her, or I guess she was technically "given" to him by her village so poor Agnieszka is scared to death of this cranky reclusive old but not old man. And everything she does is not right. She can't cook, can't clean without making a mess. If the kitchen were a person and she fought the kitchen, the kitchen looked like it won with food and dirt on her clothes and her hair unkempt all the time only earned Agnieszka sharp looks and biting comments from Sarkan. She could do no right and his impatience was constant. 
 Somewhere along the way things started to change. You felt a companionship of sorts grow between the two. Not exactly comfortable but civil. Through their both trying to stop The Wood from corrupting of all of the land Sarkan and Agnieszka became even closer. But their was still the awkwardness of her being held against her will. 
 This was a fairytale type of story I could get into for the most part. It had a bit of a romantic feel at times as Sarkan and Agnieszka got to know each other a bit. But there was still an irritation he had with her and she had to deal with being kept in the tower. Plus once they got into a routine than they had to deal with The Wood. So sentiments went to the wayside. 
 Even though Sarkan was a bit crotchety most of the time but it was endearing because he was never cruel and nice not to see an insta love develop. That gets old sometimes. Sometimes you need some good old tension. 
 The only thing I think really annoyed me was how much time went into the battles with The Wood. It felt too long and I got bored some of the time. 
 I guess I just wanted more development between Sarkan and Agnieszka and less Woods fighting. 
 This book gives me hope that they are other enjoyable type of fairytale reads out there. I'm looking forward to trying a couple more.

I loved it! And just because out there are writers like Brandon Sanderson, George martin or Patrick Rothfuss , i didn't give it stars, because those are reserved for them.

Update: Re-read this in conjunction with the notes I'm taking from Structuring Your Novel by KM Weildand and this book is actually perfect in terms of the plot structure and pacing. Reading it as a writer rather than a reader has given me a greater appreciation of how Novik is able to keep cranking up the conflict. This book kept me on the edge of my seat, even as a re-read! I purchased the audiobook for this exercise...these factors have led me to change my rating from 4 to 5 stars. 
 What a perfect book, and I cannot say THANK YOU enough to Naomi Novik for writing a standalone fantasy in the era of series that authors do not finish in a timely manner! There's so much to love here. The magic system/spells were reminiscent of those found in Harry Potter, Agnieszka was a plucky heroine, the Dragon was a curmudgeon that you couldn't help but admire, the evil Wood was scary as hell. The only reason I didn't give it 5 stars is that I wish it had a little more in the way of romance. I plan on posting a lengthier review to my blog, but for now, suffice it to say that I haven't devoured a book like that in a year. This book was very promising at the start. This book has been generating a lot of buzz, but I wanted to add my little shout into the void because I really loved this book! 
 Every ten years, the Dragon takes a village girl into his castle. After the decade is up, he lets them go, but they are never the same. Of course, the Dragon isn't an ordinary dragon but, in fact, a wizard. With that Novik takes this well known trope in a new direction. The whole village believes Kasia, beautiful and talented Kasia, will be taken; however, the Dragon takes Agnieszka. 
 The beauty of Uprooted is that it covers well-trod territory in fantasy, but it makes it feel lovely and new. Have you ever read a book and thought, "This author and I, we have loved the same books"? Many people have made these comparisons, but there were elements of my favorite fantasy stories, such as the Sevenwaters series or Tamora Pierce's books. Agnieszka's sheer determination to save the people and home she loves reminds me so much of the women of Sevenwaters. Her determination is interesting to me because, unlike the other wizards and witches in the story, she seems to wield magic through sheer will. Much of her strength comes not from her skill or learning but her belief in herself to make it happen. I loved how Agnieszka discovers other past witches from the valley who, like her, use intuitive and outdoorsy magic but aren't taken serious by learned wizards because they just help their villages survive and don't write down spells. The romance is slow and isn't really a main point to the story. It might turn a few people off if they don't like huge age differences (I think it's a bit complicated because of the whole live for hundreds of years thing, and I also cut my teeth on romances like Daine and Numair's in Wild Magic) and if the "bicker until they kiss, then bicker some more" things grates on the nerves (I personally love relationships with lots of bickering). 
 The most important relationship in the story, in my opinion, is that of Kasia and Agnieszka. I wish more stories showed how powerful female friendships can be, and this book places a high priority on this one. It is very clear how much the girls love each other; however, this relationship is complicated by being raised knowing one was going to be taken by the Dragon, and the fears and jealousies that came with that. It is a complex relationship, and the novel doesn't shy away from the complexities, making the friendship even more poignant.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Oh my god I can't believe I spent money on this book when I could have written it myself. 
 I did get a chuckle out of what she referred to as a period of "job promiscuity". The author claims she skipped around jobs because she was bored whereas I grew frustrated of people who couldn't keep up with me--including my supervisors. I eventually hung out my own shingle like Amoruso did...too bad nonprofits don't pay or I'd be as demonstrably successful as she.

I looked past this book's terrible title because I thought the founder & CEO of Nasty Gal might be an interesting voice on the topic of getting shit done. Alas, I was sorely disappointed. I couldn't help but think that Amoruso, a self-proclaimed "badass bitch," could only wax poetic about her youthful shenanigans - including stealing thousands of dollars worth of merchandise - because she's a pretty, white woman who's now also a millionaire. This book was a lot of empty platitudes about inspiration & working hard, built on repetitive reminders of how much money Nasty Gal brings in & how different & awesome Amoruso is. She writes, "It's not cool to get drunk on your own success," but I wish she'd taken her own advice.

Equal parts inspiring and masochistic -- reading this inspired me to go out and take on the world while also making me feel like the world is always out to get me. It's the type of book that has you cheering yourself on on one page and curled up, wrapped in a blanket, crying on the next, but maybe that's just me! I basically sped read the last two chapters because I felt like I'd extracted the message of the book (melted down it's be yourself because you're awesome!) and just wanted to move on to something that wasn't making me have an existential crisis.
This was great! It was an enjoyable read and really motivating.

Lo empece a leer porque la serie de Netflix me gusto pero el libro nada q ver,parecen los berrinches de una nina de 6 anos q paso de nini a empresaria porque se le ocurrio una buena idea 
 Algunas frases lo salvan y las historias de otras Girlbossesb

Rating: 1.5 stars (1/2 for pure entertainment, like a train wreck) 
 As a female entrepreneur, I initially liked the idea of a book about a #GirlBoss even if I wasn't sold on the title. Unfamiliar with the Nasty Gal brand, I had seen the hype around the book (Goodreads Best Business Books 2014) and am always on board for strong females discussing their success. 
 The first part of the book drew me in, and was relatively entertaining. I was surprised to learn the first thing Sophia Amoruso sold online was stolen (she used to steal a lot), and that she was once a dumpster diving freegan. She also believes in magic and planting wishes in her life via sigils and passwords. 
 It didn't take long to realize this was not going to be the kind of book with any strong takeaways. The writing style heralds Mad Libs for blockbuster books, and the "advice" is irritatingly basic and inane (geared for millennial girls): "Be a nice person at work . . . If you are a total terror to work with, no one will want to keep you around," "Life is short. Don't be lazy," "Being a girl is fun," etc. Any time the word "ain't" is used particularly makes my skin crawl, it seemed like she was talking to tween airheads, or was perpetuating one herself ("And the top of the chain ain't gonna like it."). The ditsy, magically successful fashion lady. 
 After she passed the "rags" portion of her story and got started on the "riches" ($250-million-plus), Amoruso started to come off, as a friend put it: "sounding like a condescending know-it-all." This portion was difficult to get through, but was peppered with other female success snippets that broke up the pomposity. 
 Yes, it is a Cinderella story with social media, fashion, and monetary success--but at the end of the day, it's just a marginally interesting, braggadocious tale. Post #GirlBoss (2014), Nasty Gal suffered layoffs, lawsuits, disgruntled employees, and Amoruso stepped down from CEO in 2015. She also was dropped from Forbes' Richest Self-Made Women when Nasty Gal filed for bankruptcy in 2016. It's not all bad news for Amoruso, she is producing an adaptation of #GirlBoss for Netflix in 2017. 
 Reading this, I felt at times I was being Punk'd. My favorite part was the end, and I would never recommend this book to anyone. 
 * Still, props to Amoruso for being a successful (no matter for how long) female entrepreneur. It was a bold move to write this book, and if you want to be rich, you've got to be a bitch. 
 "Bad bitches are taking over the world." -- #GirlBoss

Adquiri o meu exemplar assim que chegou as livrarias e estava super entusiasmada para ler, entao comecei logo. Nota-se pelo imenso gap entre a data de inicio para a data de conclusao que o entusiasmo nao perdurou. 
 Estanquei na pagina 41 no segundo capitulo e nao tive mais coragem de abrir o livro desde entao. E nao abri mesmo, ficou la, me assombrando esses meses todos. Ate hoje. Domingo mansinho e chuvoso, deu vontade de tirar a tarde pra leitura. E escolhi - novamente - o Girlboss. 
 Achei o inicio pouco cativante e bem enjoadinho, mas os capitulos seguintes conseguiram ser mais interessantes e instrutivos. Se voce ignorar algumas contradicoes, certamente conseguira tirar boas licoes em varios momentos. Sophia passa sua experiencia de forma sincera, e gosto disso. 
 No entanto, apesar de ter terminado o livro no mesmo dia, eu nao amei. Terminei por determinacao, nao por curiosidade ou vontade de saber mais detalhes.

In many ways, #GIRLBOSS is the Lean In of the millennial generation. I admire the success that Sophia managed to achieve despite barely finishing High School and failing to hold down the simplest of jobs in her youth. For the first half of her book I was consumed by her account of the beginning stages of Nasty Gal and the story of how she built an empire out of nothing. 
 Somewhere during the second half of her book, she lost me. It was as if she couldn't figure out what she wanted her book to be. A book can be many different things but her book was so directionless it failed to be anything. The cliche business/success quotes. Oh the quotes. It gave her book a certain irony that can only be achieved by someone claiming how important it is to be unique and then promptly quoting every success mantra known to man that each of us have already heard dozens of times. "Success works only if you do. Bet on yourself. You have to own it like you own your used car. Be willing to admit you don't know everything. First impressions are everything." - ok those weren't all direct quotes but that's how the last quarter of her book reads. She mentions how her customer wouldn't buy a $300 dress yet nearly every swimsuit on her website is about $300. She says you don't have to go to college to be a rock star at work yet most of the job postings on her site say you need a bachelors degree. She says you have to be a team player and be a nice person that others want to be around although glass door says that the Nasty Gal work environment is the exact opposite. 
 While I agree that she built Nasty Gal she continues to attribute every success her company has (even the success right at this moment) to her even though the success of Nasty Gal today is actually due to the collection of 300 or so employees. She overused analogies and at one point even described a barbeque where a guy started spraying her with a hose and she had to think quick and throw a hamburger patty at him as an example of why you always have to be on your feet and ready for anything to come your way. The book morphed from a badass bitch older sister I never had to a 12 year old who somehow got the keys to the car. 
 Not a waste but didn't live up to the expectations I had. She has also since stepped down as CEO but I actually admire her for admitting that it was perhaps time to let someone else into the drivers seat.
Finished the audiobook because it was downloaded and we have a new hands-free ordinance, making it easier not to stop.

I only made it about halfway through this book before I couldn't take it anymore. It's so incredibly slow-paced and wordy that it's easy to lose track of what's going on. For the record, I can't stand the movies for the same reason. 
 I have no idea what the appeal of these stories are for people because the actual storylines are so masked behind all the wordy narration that it's difficult to track with the actual story arc. By the time they move on in a scene, you've fallen asleep through the descriptions and meanderings that the author gives about everything. 
 For me, I will stick with C. S. Lewis and George MacDonald (who incidentally, were friends with Tolkien - maybe he should've learned from their more fast-paced writing styles).

Banyak pesan juga yang disampaikan dalam novel ini, terkait perebutan kekuasan, harta, kejujuran, pengorbanan, dan keberanian (keberanian untuk menghadapi ketakutan dan ancaman, serta keberanian untuk keluar dari zona nyaman kita, seperti yang telah dilakukan oleh Bilbo. Percayalah bahwa jika kita berani melakukannya, kita akan mendapatkan pengalaman yg luar biasa).

So much fun to read. I'd only been introduced to Tolkien through the LOTR movies (which I loved) and this is the first book that I have attempted and it was absolutely enchanting! The ease of the reading and the depth of the story encourages me to continue on with the trilogy... I had been reluctant with Tolkien and hesitant to get into this story; I think I felt intimidated by the scope of it all and I had never really known much about his writing until being shanghaied into seeing the first movie installment of LOTR in 2001 and really not caring a whit about it until I was swept headlong into this magical world. I only wish I had read this when I was younger and reading The Chronicles of Narnia. I guess we are never too old or too young.

 The road goes ever on...

I wonder, as I sit here, sipping my tea and sitting in my chair by a roaring fire in true Tolkien-ian fashion, why it's taken me so long to re-read 'The Hobbit'. It's one of the most enduring tales of my childhood, and I personally (upon reflection) account it in large part for my love of fantasy - well, of tales and stories and spoken word put to paper and ink, really. There is something so very magical about a tale told to an audience or readership, as it is by Tolkien here. A true adventure into the wild - a story told in the fashion of oral traditions that have long since faded into the depths of antiquity. But something about the tale of the hobbit - Mr Bilbo Baggins of the Shire - has endured in readers hearts and imaginations for almost a century, and will continue to do so for countless generations to come. 
 'The Hobbit' is truly a joy to read. I can't really describe it any other way. I found myself picking it up to continue reading and just...smiling. Not necessary in pure anticipation (I certainly savored and stretched out the experience, although I am always eager to re-join Bilbo and the dwarves exploits) but more with the happy contentment of a person eager to partake in a truly delightful past-time. I liken it very much to Bilbo's longing and gladness once he returns to his Hobbit Hole and the sound of his whistling kettle. For me, at least, reading 'The Hobbit' feels like coming home. 
 Rating a book (out of five stars) such as this one is (in all honesty) completely unjust. At best it's a waste of time, at worst a poor and stifling reflection of my honest and whole-hearted love for it as a piece of literature. It's certainly not perfect (what book is?), but there is something so wonderful about the themes it tackles - the fundamentals of good and evil, hardship and loyalty and honor and bravery and friendship, struggles and hopelessness and strength and endurance, and perhaps most importantly of all - the unspoken (and in my case, too often unacknowledged) desire for a real adventure! I relate so personally to all these themes within the construct of the story itself, and also the characters themselves, within it. Their struggles and desires and humor and perseverance to the verge of stubbornness in the face of adversity, their ultimate vanquishing of seemingly unconquerable odds will always remain a true inspiration in my life. Tolkien's soul truly lives on in the pages of this book. 
 That's really all I have to say. Everything else is feeling, and I'm truly not eloquent enough to articulate it all effectively. I hope this review gave you even a small taste into the impact that this book has had on shaping me as a person. My love for it only grows with every re-reading. 
 I ask you to please read it (if you haven't, or even if you already have), and to share the love. :)

sample_reviews.review_text: Quiet and wonderful. A perfect portrait of all of the things that go into being a family -- secrets, laugher, and pain.

http://charlotteswebofbooks.blogspot.... 
 Saints for All Occasions was one of those books that people are going to be talking about all summer. The characters are rich and the story is intricate

Courtney Sullivan is an excellent writer. But I never fully engaged with these characters. The book has received an average review of four stars. So perhaps it's just me. My lack of enthusiasm for this book, though, will not keep me from grabbing another Sullivan book. I already own "The Engagements." And I do love family sagas.

One of the things I loved best about J. Courtney Sullivan's Saints for All Occasions was how quietly and unassuming this story snuck up on me. I found myself about halfway through, reading along and realizing that I didn't want to put it down. I was thinking about Nora and Theresa in the car on the way to the grocery store and contemplating what it means to raise a family and have your children grow up and into themselves while I was stirring the spaghetti sauce on the stove. 
 "Taken together, the small choices anyone made added up to a life." 
 This quote, for me, is meaningful personally and alongside this beautifully written story. As Nora looked back over her life, as Theresa looked to the past wondering what she might have done differently....it was the realization that those small decisions along the way are what created the lives they led. And the lives of their children. 
 I enjoyed the sections that took place in Nora and Theresa's past immensely! One of my favorite things about a well written family saga is seeing the sequence of events, those "small choices", build upon themselves. Some parts of the story seemed familiar to me from other books. The Irish American experience, the dance halls, the girls making their way across the Atlantic. The stifled fifties housewife who is questioning her marriage and husband. But altogether, in this book, Sullivan writes a unique story all her own. 
 My favorite character was Nora, who wasn't able to see or understand the affect of her choices on herself until much later but still handled herself with grace. Her constant role as the family matriarch, her protective mothering and her avoidance of things she didn't understand was incredibly endearing. As a mother myself I often wondered what I'm going to do with my grown adult children, when they start making their own decisions and have their own opinions different from mine. Their own life experiences. I can't imagine being able to understand everything they choose, but hope for the grace to handle them well. 
 I would suggest this book to anyone who is loves a good family saga, one filled with secrets and regret and the love of family that perseveres throughout mistakes and misfortune. I enjoyed the historical aspects of the sections that took place in Nora and Theresa's past as well as the present day themes that were more relatable.

 Very nice read. I recommend it find it's place in your suitcase this summer as you head off to escape the daily grind!

I would give this book 3.5 stars. 
 The Likeness by Tana French is the second book in the Dublin Murder Squad Series. It has been a while since I read the first book, In the Woods, which I really liked. But I was pretty foggy on what happened in the first book (except I remember I didn't like the ending too much). The two books are loosely connected with some of the same characters, but each one works as a stand alone story. So it is not necessary to read In the Woods before reading The Likeness. 
 The Likeness features Detective Cassie Maddox, who is sent on an unusual undercover mission. A woman's body is found, and the woman happens to look identically like Detective Maddox. So Cassie pretends to live this woman's life, infiltrating her closest group of friends in an attempt to find the murderer. 
 If you are looking for a true to life crime story, this one doesn't quite fit the bill. The idea of Cassie looking exactly like Lexie, the victim, is hard to believe, not to mention the idea of Cassie being able to act exactly like Lexie and convince all of Lexie's friends that she is actually Lexie. You have to be willing to just accept this plot and go with it. If you can do that, it is kind of a fun story, even it is far fetched. 
 I listened to the audiobook version of this book, and it took me a really long time to finish the whole 22 hour book. I'm not sure if I would have felt this way if I was reading the book, but listening to it, I felt like it was just a little too long-winded at times. 
 I found this to be an entertaining crime story with interesting characters. I would definitely like to continue reading the books in Tana French's Dublin Murder Squad series, as I have read good reviews of her other books as well.
This was so awful I can't begin to understand why its got such good reviews. The storyline was totally implausible and the writing was frankly bizarre.
I would give the middle of this book a 4.5 - page turner. But for me the beginning and end dragged a bit.

 This book has kind of a crazy premise, but Tana French pulls it off beautifully. Lexie and her friends all turn out to be much more complicated and loving than they appear from the outside, and Cassie finds herself being seduced by their simple, tight-knit way of life. But, of course, things are never quite what they seemed to be. 
 This book is haunting at times. It's one of those books that feels like it's Saying Something, about the attempt to escape from the daily grind and the horrible things we do to the ones we love the most, but without ever being heavy handed.

It took a bit for the actual plot to get going. Though I just read the first book, I found that I didn't care that much about Cassie's feelings. But the ruined spiderweb of relationships was super satisfying to watch.

Good grief what a completely awful book! 
 This prickly detective goes undercover to replace her 'double' and instantly bonds with the roommates who are all suspects in her double's murder. And by instant I mean the very second she meets them, she BONDS with them, to the point where she hides vital information from her cop handlers who are trying to solve the crime. 
 Eighty percent of the book nothing happens. It's all just loads of nonsensical conversations about nothing, all in a bid to convince the reader that the detective is a multi layered complex personality not some half wit who can't seem to get anything right. She's great at profiling but dense at reading her boyfriend; she hates lying but loves working undercover; she has some sort of connection to her double instantly finding a hidden secret diary by working out how her double's mind works. She doesn't get pulled out when she loses objectivity because that would just be too logical!! 
 The whole thing is too moronic to even write a review on without shuddering in disgust at the extra wasted time. Bottom line is: If instead I'd read the first two chapters and the last two, I'd have saved time that can now sadly never be recovered.

reference_books.review_text:
So this was supposed to the next Gone Girl? And it is described as suspenseful? Sadly, I beg to differ. 
 Jean Taylor's husband was accused of a crime... and for a while she wasn't sure if he was guilty or not and has to pretend that she doesn't suspect him and doesn't notice his strange behavior. Then she finds out the truth. When he is gone for good, she no longer has to pretend and she can tell the truth to the press or make up her own version. 
 Unfortunately, I wasn't grabbed by the story, didn't find it suspenseful, immediately grasped what Jeans' husband's "nonsense" was and was not invested in the characters. I gave it 3 stars however, because the writing was good and the characters were well developed.

reference_books.title: Vinegar Girl
reference_books.review_text:
Anne Tyler's Vinegar Girl is a delightful re-telling of Shakespeare's Taming of the Shrew. 
 Kate Battista is a school teaching assistant and a 29 spinster who lives with her father. Dr. Battista, a scientist and her 15 year old sister, Bunny. Kate is not well liked at the school at which she teaches, except by her little students, who adore her. She is difficult, obstinate and rude. She takes care of her family's house hold and runs it efficiently to say the least. 
 Her father. Dr. Battista, runs a lab, with the help of Pyotr, whose visa is about to run out. Dr. Battista feels he is on the brink of a scientific breakthrough and that Pyotr is indispensable and comes up with a plan to keep Pyotr in the country. He wants Kate to marry Pyotr to give him a green card, even though she doesn't even know him! Kate immediately feels betrayed and imagines that she has been invisible to her father for her entire life. That he could completely ignore her feelings for the betterment of his own work enrages her. She then starts making his life more difficult by ignoring him, and being mean to Pyotr who is desperately trying to get to know her as he finds her interesting and intelligent. 
 After a while she decides to go along with the plan and agrees to marry Pyotr for a short while, only so that he can get his green card. Pyotr, who is a bit strange and quite eccentric, then tries to "woo" her. And somehow, he ends up doing just that. 
 This book is a sweet, easy read and was an extremely enjoyable. Anne Tyler has a way with words and this book is no exception. 
 Published: June 21, 2016 
 Published on: Goodreads and Amazon

reference_books.title: Blink
reference_books.review_text:
4 stars. 
 Blink is a quick, fast-paced, easy read that captures your attention immediately and won't let go till the very last sentence. 
 Toni Cotter had it all - a loving husband and a beautiful little girl named Evie. But that life didn't last. Her husband, Andrew got called back to Afghanistan and he died in an accident, causing her carefree life to go up in flames. Unable to care for her daughter on her own, she and Evie move closer to her mum as they are in need of a fresh start. There, five year-old Evie starts at new school and has a hard time adjusting - becoming extremely unhappy and very quiet. Meanwhile, Toni, who has had a hard time coping with the cards life has dealt her, ends up making some very poor choices ultimately putting Evie's life in danger. Unfortunately, in the end, these choices lead to catastrophic events: one day little Evie disappears. Years go by. And still there is no trace of her. 
 Yet Toni does not give up. She is a mother and even though she, and everyone else, blame herself for Evie's disappearance, she believes her daughter to be alive. And she will not rest until Evie is found. 
 Alternating between Toni's recollection of "Three Years Earlier" and the "Present Day," KL Slater does a phenomenal job in keeping the readers in suspense and in keeping us off guard. There were times when I was sure that I knew what was going on and was completely wrong. There were a few plot points that I felt were unnecessary (hence the 4 star v. 5 star rating) but all in all, this was a good psychological thriller. If you are looking for a thriller that will keep you guessing and surprise you till the end, this is it. 
 Thank you to NetGalley, Bookouture and KL Slater for an ARC of this novel in exchange for an honest review. 
 Published on NetGalley, Goodreads and Amazon on 2/23/17.

book_a.title: Commonwealth
book_a.user_review:
4 Stars. 
 One Blended Family's Life Portrayed in a Myriad of Different Ways. 
 In this family, dysfunction and neglect run rampant and have a rippling effect on everyone's life. The Cousin and Keating families are close as can be, spending time and partying together on weekends. Then, something happens that changes the course of these families lives forever: Bert Cousins falls for Beverly Keating - both of whom are already married to other people. Thereafter, two families become one, joining four children from one marriage and two from another. And more often than not, the kids, Cal, Caroline, Jeanette, Frannie, Holly and Albie are left to fend for themselves, with their parents never giving them a second thought, in essence letting their children run amok, for which in my opinion there was no excuse. Was this a sign of the times or was this a sign of neglect, plain and simple? I asked myself this question over and over, with my temperature rising and my heart beating faster and faster, my emotions running at an all-time high. That said - neglect is of course the answer, though I do think this happened more often than not in this generation. 
 This is a family who has gone through various trials and tribulations through the course of their lives - including marriage, divorce and of course death. They have experienced a deep sense of loss and even betrayal and though the dysfunction runs deep, somehow it doesn't break this family apart. For the Cousin and Keating children are resilient, as they have basically raised themselves. And though the family becomes distant over the years, they do not lose their bond to each other. 
 Commonwealth spans over the course of 50 years, and is told mostly from the perspective of Frannie Keating, though several of the other children and parent's perspectives are also featured. The time frame jumps around during the book and was at times hard to follow, as was the structure of the story, especially when the family's life was portrayed in different mediums (hence the reason for the 4 v. 5 star rating). The characters are vividly written by Ann Patchett - some are bold, some intense, some cold, some withdrawn and encompass a family masterfully. 
 Parenting styles and/or the lack there-of, and the neglect that went along with it, hit a nerve for me when listening to Ann Patchett's Commonwealth and yet I couldn't tear myself away (and I'm guessing I'm not the only one who felt this way). However, the strength of this family, their ability to endure and their love for each other, though misplaced it maybe have been, was brilliantly depicted and at times defied logic. 
 All in all, I found Commonwealth to be a complicated and intriguing characterization of a truly dysfunctional family, though it angered me and made my blood boil on multiple occasions. Further, the narrator of the audiobook did a stellar job and made the listening experience enjoyable. Strongly recommended. 
 Published on Goodreads and Amazon on 5.12.17.

sample_reviews.review_text: I liked this a lot more than I thought I would. It sounded like just another dysfunctional family book, but I found most of the characters to be finely drawn and interesting.

A very readable and well-crafted story about two families (2 kids in one, 4 in the other) that become blended through infidelity (the father of one family marries the mother of the other; the 2 nuclear families reconstitute themselves as several more fluid, overlapping families). 
 The book begins in the infancy of one child and ends about 5 decades later. There's plenty of dysfunction as the strengths and imperfections of the various parents manifest themselves in various ways, and the dynamics of the childhood relationships evolve. 
 This book shows the ways families change and the ways they remain the same in spite of the changes. Some of the parents married several times, and new parents moved in and out of the children's lives, yet the 6 kids somehow remained connected to one another, to one degree or another, for better or for worse, for the rest of their lives. 
 There's also a whole sub-plot about a book called Commonwealth within this book called Commonwealth. It's a thinly fictionalized version of the childhoods of these 6 children, written by an outsider.

I don't know if it's because I listened to the audio version rather than reading the print, but this just wasn't my cup of tea. It reminded me very much of the Interestings: it went on and on and on with know discernible purpose and I found the characters unlikable and hard to relate to. I also felt like it tried to cover too vast of a time period with too many characters, of which I had difficulty keeping track.

I found this novel fascinating. Patchett's writing is amazing, and the narrative structure was extremely unique. I noticed there were scenes I wanted more descriptions on that she quickly brushed over, and then there were some scenes she talked about for awhile that I wasn't interested in at all. However, overall, it was a truly wonderful read.
The characters and the set up were very good. It never came to the denouement it sets the readers up for. Read "Bel Canto" instead.

This is a moving novel about the blended modern family inspired by Ann Patchett's own personal family history. In the early 1960s, the married Bert Cousins is a deputy DA, out of sorts with his lot in life and family, and looking for something more. He rolls up uninvited to Franny Keating's christening party, and oiled by alcohol, falls in love with and kisses the beautiful Beverly Keating. This leads to the disintegration of the two respective families and a catalogue of repercussions down the years. In a narrative that shifts from person to person over 50 years in a non linear manner, with multiple threads, the greatest focus is on Franny. The story resonates strongly as so few of us today have experience of a family without divorce, separations, remarriages, and step relations. 
 Bert and Beverly move to Virginia where, during the summer months, the six children from their marriages run wild in a way that would be less common today. The six are subject to all the strife that afflict a group of children but form strong bonds over their disappointments with and hatred of their parents. Patchett lets us get to know her characters well through detailed descriptions and vignettes of events, incidents and secrets. There is much comic humour, sorrows and tragedy in the highs and lows of a blended family. Franny is a law school dropout and becomes a waitress. She becomes involved with a writer, Leon Posen, to whom she confides her family history. Like a parasite, Posen appropriates this history to pen a bestseller that spawns a movie. This triggers the revisiting of a hidden past as the truth emerges. Fix Keating, LAPD cop, has cancer and it is Franny that comes to care for her father. 
 Patchett gives us a a human and insightful look at the complexities of the dysfunctional modern family through the Cousins and the Keatings. Her character development is impressive, particularly with regard to Albie. There are perhaps an over abundance of characters but Patchett handles them adroitly. I was touched by her positivity with regard to the challenges of a blended family and of how time eventually is likely to iron out the wrinkles. A brilliant novel that I highly recommend. Thanks to Bloomsbury for an ARC.

book_b.title: The Girl Before
book_b.user_review:
One house (One Folgate Street, London) rented by two different women, at two different times. But this rental property is different: clean, minimalist and technologically advanced. And it comes with oddly severe restrictions: no furniture of your own, no clutter or personal affects. It also includes a list of questions that the applicants must answer and answer correctly in order to be considered and accepted. Oddly enough, the owner of the property is the architect, Edward Monkford, and he tends to only rent to women who look like his ex-wife. 
 The Girl Before, by J.P. Delaney is told in alternating chapters by the two women who rent the property at different times: Emma and Jane. Both have suffered hardship and both are looking for a lifestyle change. And One Folgate Street, with it's strange restrictions offers exactly that. And handsome Edward Monkford's presence is a welcome distraction for both women, who can't help but fall for him. Yet tragedy surrounds this property and for one or both girls, harm awaits. Only time will tell who is to blame and whether or not Emma and Jane are safe: with Edward and at One Folgate Street. 
 The Girl Before is a mystery novel that was fast-paced and kept my attention throughout. However, in truth, I found its premise to be quite odd and felt that book never really made complete sense and unraveled towards the end. 
 Thank you to NetGalley, Random House Publishing Group and J.P. Delaney for an ARC in exchange for an honest review. 
 Published on NetGalley, Goodreads and Amazon on 2/1/17.

Thinking I know what is going to happen but not having that happen. I also like how this story is told, one section from emma (the past) and one section from Jane (the present). Think "Sleeping with the Enemy" meets "50 Shades of Gray" meets Frank Lloyd Wright. 
 Fans of unreliable narrators and a plot that never leads you to solve the mystery will just love this one.

The Girl Before 
 by J. P. Delaney 
 Reviewed by Heath Henwood 
 www.books-reviewed.weebly.com 
 1 Star 
 Ever since 'Fifty Shades', or perhaps well before then, there has been a rash of books trying to imitate with a slight twist. 'The Girl Before', is just the latest one. 
 The idea behind the plot is actually good - the opportunity to live in the perfect house - but what are the catches. 
 This book fails to deliver though in delivering on the plot concept, and tends to get caught up in the sex (much more than is needed), rather than developing the characters and plot line. 
 The story follows two tenants of the house at different times. Emma the first tenant died mysteriously in the house, and Jane the current tenant is slowly unravelling the mystery. Enter into the story the handsome landlord Edward Monkton, who has more than a vested interest in the house and tenant. 
 Thus, the Skelton for an intriguing story is there. The delivery is not. 
 There are many other gaps in the plot, the thoughts behind the story, and why the female characters are painted as being so dumb. There are too many better books out there to read. 
 Thank you to Netgalley for providing a review copy in return for an honest review. All opinions expressed in this review are entirely my own.

I had to get a little more than a fifth of the way through this until the story really began, and once you hit the place where the story gets interesting, the rest of the book is creepy. If you liked to feel creeped out, you'll like this. 
 The story is about two women, both residents of a strange house, one who died, and the woman who came after her. Both experienced tragedies before moving into the home. They had to fill out questionnaires and send pictures and agree to a slew of rules to even be considered as renters (no simple credit check and steady job could get them into this sterile, odd place). The home won architectural awards, but residents who live there can't leave dishes out--even the cleaning supplies are well hidden in a secret wall panel. There aren't even book cases--no clutter is allowed whatsoever. I couldn't imagine living like that (I wouldn't make it a day), but both women are in dire financial situations, and the home is modestly priced because no one would live there with the millions of rules if they could afford a normal place. 
 I couldn't identify with Emma or Jane or the architect of the home, Edward, who is a perfectionist and possibly a sociopath (hence the creep factor). 
 There were some nice twists and turns I didn't see coming, which is great, but I didn't fall in love with the ending.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Any novel that can toss around casual references to comic books like Watchmen and the Fantastic Four is going to attract my attention. The book is enjoyable; I liked the title character, although Diaz's style seems to keep Oscar at a frustrating distance. I thought the language and narrative structure was inventive, posing the kind of time-bending challenges that postmodern readers love. 
 But I can't help but think about Everett's Erasure when I read Diaz's book. There were moments when I was troubled that my lack of understanding regarding cultural norms and attitudes in the Dominican Republic would lead me to be less critical about the story's constant images of misogyny, hypermasculinity, and violence, or overlook the author's larger message about how we should view Oscar's family and experience in American vs the DR. Is the Brief Wonderous life, praised by some for its "magic realism" and others for its "verisimilitude," really just another version of Everett's racial parody and media spectacle, "My Pafology"?
Enlightening!

I don't speak Spanish. I don't recommend this book if you don't speak Spanish. So I didn't like this book. I liked 2 chapters in the book. It was interesting to get background on the Dominican Republic, but not interesting enough to warrant reading the whole book.

This book is mostly written from the perspective of Yunior, our fictional narrator. It is unusual in that it is written as Yunior would speak, peppered with Spanish slang, geeky comic book references and plenty of footnotes about Dominican History. Incidentally, the footnotes are written by Yunior, not Diaz himself and therefore are to be read as part of the story. 
 Yunior starts off by telling us about Oscar's childhood. From here the book moves on to Lola's story, Oscar's mum's story, Oscar's Grandparents' story before moving onto Yunior himself and then back to Oscar. This is a peculiar structure for a novel, but not unheard of and it's one that works really well in this case 
 It was interesting to learn about the history of the Dominican Republic (I knew zilch beforehand) but the slang and cultural references made it a good fun way of reading. There's a touch of magical realism added by the fuku, but this is mostly a sub-plot.

I hate to do it, but I'm having to abandon this book. It came so highly recommended, but every chance I get I put it down and start another book. There are too many books in this life which I'll never have the chance to read, so I'm done wasting time on this one.

**SPOILERS FOR THE PLAY AND HARRY POTTER BOOKS** 
 So, I had to really think about this book before I rated it and gave it a thorough review. However, the more I consider it, the more I discover that I just...didn't like this story. First of all, I hate that it's considered the eighth Harry Potter book. In my mind, it's fan fiction. I know that J.K. Rowling helped come up with this story, but still. I can't consider this part of the Harry Potter cannon. For lots of reasons. 
 I suppose I'll talk about the characters first. And not just the main ones of Albus and Scorpius. No, the actual characters from Harry Potter. Before reading this, I would've said it was impossible to ruin my favorite characters. But ruin them, this play did. In the story, Albus and Scorpius use a Time-Turner to try to keep Cedric from being killed by Voldemort. In doing so, they completely mess up reality. The second time they try to change things, Hermione ends up being a horrible professor, just because she didn't end up marrying Ron and having children. Which is ridiculous. Hermione is an intelligent and strong woman. She never would have ended up as a sort of Umbridge-like teacher. I hated that. Then, we have Ron. Ron is pretty much relegated to a jokester character with no other traits. Which is obviously far from the truth. Ron is a flawed character, who had issues of being overlooked for the first years of his life. Ron is also a good friend, and I just didn't get that kind of vibe here. So in short, they messed with characters I love, and not for the better, either. 
 Then, we have the characters of Albus and Scorpius. Now, I did like the friendship between the two boys. But seriously, they were idiots. You're a fourteen-year-old wizard, and you know better than to mess with time. But they still do it anyway. I mean...I just couldn't buy into it. Plus, Albus's bad relationship with Harry is just unbelievable. As Harry's son, he should be well aware that it bothers Harry when he wasn't able to save or help someone. I just don't buy that Albus thought Harry was insensitive to Cedric's death. Or to Albus himself. 
 Now, let's talk plot. As I said, this play has a lot of Time-Turner use in it. While the fast pace was nice, I just don't think that it is necessary for this kind of thing. I mean...it's ridiculous that Albus and Scorpius go back in time in the first place. The fact that they do it three times? I just don't buy it. And then, when it comes out that the villain is Voldemort's daughter that he had with Bellatrix Lestrange? It's laughable!! Voldemort is a corrupt wizard bent on taking over the world and filling it with evil. When would he ever have had the time or inclination to have sex with Bellatrix? And Bellatrix's relationship with Voldemort was more that of someone following her master or god, and there was nothing romantic about it. 
 In short, I really don't like this play. I think it messed with a lot of the rules that the Harry Potter books set out. For example, Polyjuice Potion takes a month to make, and characters were talking about making it just like that. Not possible. Also, at one point, Albuss and Scorpius go back in time to the day when Lily and James were killed. They even watch it happen, and they saw Hagrid come and get Hairy out of the ruined house. Only problem, there was no Sirius Black. In book 3 we learn that Sirius showed up, tried to take Harry away because he was Harry's godfather, and was convinced by Hagrid to give him up to the Dursleys. Sirius also gave Hagrid his motorcycle. These details were completely left out here, and this stuff becomes a big deal when you get to Prisoner of Azkaban. In short, this play messes with the characters, rules, and plot of the seven Harry Potter stories. And as much as I want to say the friendship between Albus and Scorpius redeems it for me? It doesn't. It won't. I'm sure the play is a very nice thing to see, but....I just don't like the plot or the way it treats the characters and world of my favorite series.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This is the second book in the Six of Crows duology by Leigh Bardugo. After loving the first book, I was super excited to finally read this and complete the duology. A part of me is very sad that these characters' story has ended but I'm glad things have had a satisfying conclusion. 
 Reading this book reminded me of why I loved the first novel so much. The characters, once again, are the highlight of this story. They're still a gang of morally grey, misfits but I still can't help but love them. We learn so much more about everyone in this book; We delve into many of the character's pasts which made me love them even more than I did whilst reading Six of Crows. Each character develops during this story and this is an aspect of this series that I really loved. It's so strange how these characters continue to do terrible things but I still root for them to succeed in all their scheming. 
 I adored the relationships between all the characters. There is lots of romance in this book but it isn't overwhelming as it woven into the plot so well. There's such complexity in how each character interacts with every other characters which I also enjoyed. The characters that really stood out to me in this story were Inej and Jesper. Inej I loved in the first book a lot and we learned loads more about her in this story. She's such a brave and strong character, in an often quiet and unassuming way, which is something I really loved. Jesper is a character who I also liked in the first book, but he's become one of my favourites after reading this story. I loved learning about his past and how that has shaped what he's currently doing. 
 I loved how unpredictable this book was. I thought, when I first started reading, that I knew where this book was going. But nothing happened how I expected it to and I think this is what made the plot slightly stronger than the first book. I had no idea what was going on in this book, in the best possible way. And just when I thought the story was going one way, it turned out Kaz was plotting something crazy and things take a completely different turn. 
 The plot is fast paced and important character flashbacks were wonderfully mixed into the writing. I'm also very satisfied with how the story ended. There were lots of sad and happy moments that occurred, but overall I love how things were wrapped up. 
 The Grisha universe is so rich and developed and Leigh Bardugo does an amazing job of bringing this world to life. I loved all the references to the characters from The Grisha Trilogy as I enjoyed revisiting some of the people I loved from those books. 
 This book took me a while to get through but I loved every page of it. I'm sad that I've now finished this duology because I'd love to read more about these characters. But I'm so glad I read this series and it's definitely one of my new favourites.

Pacing and sequel setup aside, this was a lovely way to end this particular story, with every one of my heartstrings tugged and all the sweetness tempered by a fair amount of bitter. I love a good caper story, I love stories of families made rather than born, and I look very much forward to reading the next one in this universe.
Meh....

Just like the first book, this was super fast paced and exciting. I love having multiple perspectives not only because you get to know each character more but also because it keeps the pace going steady. I'm so sad this is only a two book series, I would so be down for more books about these characters! The world building is done very well in these two books and it never feels info dumpy. The plot in this one is interesting because it's constantly evolving as their plans and schemes have to change! Overall Loved it!

If it weren't for that ending, I would have given this four (0.5) stars. Without that thing, I would barely have anything to criticise about this book. Pretty much only the fact that there wasn't enough of Kaz because I adore him (in the other characters' POV's becoming more prominent, I felt like Kaz was sacrificed a little). Maybe the ending was a bit rushed and maybe I would have preferred more of a focus on the characters rather than the plot. 
 So, stop reading now if you haven't read Crooked Kingdom, because I simply can't talk about how angry I am without majorly spoiling it for you. 
 I honestly didn't see Matthias' death coming. At all. And in hindsight, perhaps I should have: isn't it bang on trend these days, in YA? Kill off a character for maximum shock value at the end of a series? That's Leigh Bardugo to add to the list of other YA authors guilty of the same thing....I'm sick of it. I'm sick to death of looking forward to a novel, getting it, reading it, and finishing it disappointed, because of their stupid decisions. And let me, for a moment, just highlight why, exactly, this is a tantamount to really poor writing: a character death is so heavy-handed, so unsubtle a way to leave the reader feeling bittersweet or to evince some kind of tragic loss. There are so many other, more interesting, ways in which to register that bittersweetness -- lets just imagine, for instance, that Matthias had been recalled back into the druskelle in Fjerda, separated from Nina, living a life he hated. That would have been sad, but there might have also been a smidgen of hope there, too, that one day they might be reunited. An ending with a melancholic tone does not have to to equal death. It can be done, very effectively, in different ways. Resorting to the same device again and again is boring, predictable, and most importantly, puts readers like me right off books. When Matthias died, I put the book down, at first disbelieving, checking to see that he definitely didn't come back to life, and then -- my interest in reading the rest of the book completely deflated. I skim read to the end. I withdraw my investment if I think that authors are just playing with my emotions simply for effect. 
 The other thing, the real kicker, in my opinion, about his death, was everyone else's reaction: limp. Vague. Nina. What the fuck. No despair. Just a sort of light sadness, ah yes, go and meet your god, Fjerdan, I will see you in the next life -- like, ah, did I just completely misread this relationship? Was I misinterpreting the signals when I thought you too were in love? Well. Nina didn't really act like it, to be honest. And the rest of the crew -- oh, no, Matthias appears to be dead? Oh. Sad. Anyway. Like. The fuck??? isn't the whole pointof this series about a band of people who initially really hate each other, then begin to form real bonds with each other and become friends?? Not really sure, now. Maybe Leigh wasn't bothered about the platonic side, just so long as the romantic couples got together. 
 And also, she killed Matthias off in the middle of a really interesting, and usually pretty much absent, process in modern narratives -- that of education to the privileged. Just as Matthias was beginning to question what he'd been taught to believe, just as he was beginning to reevaluate and reconstruct his outlook on the world and about Grisha -- he dies. He has to, doesn't he? The straight, white, neurotypical and able-bodied male. I just....It would have been so much more interesting to watch that mental conflict, the shift, the effort that it took for him to subvert and challenge his own prejudices: that is such an important thing to represent in literature BECAUSE IT NO DOUBT APPLIES TO SO MANY OF LEIGH'S READERS but Leigh cut it down just as it was flourishing into something really nuanced and refreshing to read about. 
 I don't have the energy to write anything else. This book was such a huge disappointment, I'm not sure that it should be even worth 3 stars. Maybe it isn't. I don't know. If it hadn't happened, I would be begging, here, for Leigh to continue writing in this world, about these characters, but instead, even if she did decide to do that, I'm not sure I would read it. I really loved Matthias. He was such a good, sweet, honourable and kind-hearted person that, yes, had a lot to learn, but he was learning. And I can't merit an author who decides that that isn't important.

Que puis-je dire qui n'a pas deja ete dit ? Un cast de personnages incroyables: ils sont tour a tour sublimes, terribles et touchants mais toujours d'une profondeur merveilleuse. Les tours, les rebondissements, les sentiments, les mots, les silences, les coups, tout est a couper le souffle. J'ai la larme relativement facile mais a deux reprises, j'etais presque a sangloter. De la tres bonne litterature YA.
Enjoyed the audiobook, however, I still feel the Grisha trilogy is better. This book was incredibly slow, and I understand the hype, but I just did not love it like everyone else did.
OMG good.

What a sequel. 
 Six of Crows had a plot and characters that were completely original to me. Maybe I haven't read enough books, but Kaz felt like a completely new beast to me in the realm of characters. His development sometimes seemed predictable, but Leigh would switch it up and send Kaz down a path i didn't see. 
 Crooked Kingdom continued the journey with these complex and beautiful characters. The plot was always a vicious, twisted creature. There were so many angles and corners to it that it was hard not to get lost or swept up in everything. I found myself saying 'oh, don't worry. They'll get out of it', several times through my time reading this novel. 
 Can't there be more books in this series?
I am now dead.

book_b.title: Crow's Row (Crow's Row, #1)
book_b.user_review: Could have been a good book but it feels like it was thrown together too quickly. I know reading is supposed to take you to a place where anything is possible but this just felt ridiculous. Though we are left with a major cliff hanger I feel no burning desire to see what happens next.

sample_reviews.review_text: 4.5 Really enjoyed this story. Cannot wait to see what happens in the sequel. Patiently waiting for it...
I really enjoyed this book... the beginning was a little slow but I was crying by the end!! If you haven't read it yet you really should!!
This is more like a 3.5 for me

Cuando vi la portada de este libro pense que iba a ser otro libro paranormal, pero !NO! me equivoque completamente, trata un tema de pandillas y droga lo que comunmente se da por todos lados, en fin, la historia te atrapa desde el primer momento y el romance ni se diga, aqui los personajes no se quedan junto desde el primer momento o se enamoran no su amor va creciendo conforme se van conociendo. 
 Lo mejor ese final cuando lo lei no podia creerlo, era simplemente imposible no podia dejar de leer hasta saber si era verdad, pero cuando lei el epilogo, uff mi corazon suspiro de alivio no puedo esperar al segundo. 
 Rocco estas vetado de mi vocabulario no quiero que sufra de nuevo mi corazon. 
 Lo mas seguro es que el libro 2 este lleno de VENGANZA, AMOR, Y PELEAS.

*3.5 STARS!* 
 I'm still actually very surprised. This book wasn't nothing how I was expecting. I'm a huge fan of the kidnapping books I just love the whole 'Captor to Lover' even though I know it's not realistic!! So I was kind of expecting this to be like that. Urm.. NO.. it wasn't, Crows Row was very different to any kidnapping book I have read before. 
 So why not 5 stars? 
 Even though this book was very well done and a lot of things grabbed at me and surprised me. I was more bored than entertained. I loved all the characters but with a kidnapping book I love the grittiness and the not knowing I like the whole figuring out hmm will he be a good egg in the end or not? With this you don't get that. It wasn't dark at all and for me we didn't really get the whole Captor to Lover experience. I'm not saying that's what the author was after its just that's what I was expecting and so I was left feeling a tad disappointed. Saying all that I loved the hero Cameron something fierce he was broody, mysterious and just loveable for me he was the reason I carried on, not saying I didn't like Emily/Emmy because I did but at times I wish she was a bit stronger, she was a little bit naive for my liking and when she found out certain things she didn't really think it was a big deal even though I was gasping for breath like she should of been doing!!! 
 I very much enjoyed the romance. I loved Emmy and Cameron together, they was sweet but then again I found the butterflies was missing and I just wanted MORE!! 
 "That's the problem Emmy. You're trying to understand me, but what I do isn't who I am." The full power of his gaze was on me now. "The thought of you seeing me this way, of knowing this other side of my life that is so... it makes me feel sick." Cameron took both my hands in his. 
 I did enjoy this book and I can see why others loved it but for me I was just left wanting more.

I love reading books that are completely different and have a unique storyline! This book was one of them, really enjoyed it although at some points I could guess what was going to happen next it did keep me wanting the read on and on

All I can say seriously about this book was that, it lacked that something something for me. you know..sure it was nicely written and the story had promise but then, i needed that extra spice and it just was not here..nevertheless, i read all of it so that' s saying that it is still a good book.

I'll just be honest.. I don't know if I liked this book or not. :) I only know that the ending pissed me off. I wanted more... more of getting to know the characters, more explanation, and more love. Overall it's not a bad book and I had no problem finishing it but it left me sitting like a deer in the headlights wondering what the hell just happened.

I think this is an instance of an author taking generally liked features of ya/na novels and putting them in 
 stalker boyfriend - check 
 instalove - check 
 annoying but 'unique' heroines - check 
 love conquers all - check 
 now this can work in some instances but when this happens in a contemporary setting its annoying, the main character whines about her life throughout even her hair is an issue... really?? thats not the end of the world. 
 Instalove is a main issue yes this may happen in novels but happening to a kidnapped woman who witness her love kill someone and ruins lives by dealing drugs how can you instantly fall for someone? Seriously at one point there is an offer, early on in the novel, where Emily (The my-life-is-so-crap-but-really-not-that-bad main character) is told that she will be rescued... she then tells them no? like WTF? she had one conversation with mister drug dealer/stalker and decides that he is good and wants to stay in a luxury prison situation. 
 Also speaking of cameron stupid drug dealer given that he is one of the best drug dealers in the US he needs to start acting like it he was not badass...at all just seemed like some sappy teenager, how he ran a business is beyond me. 
 From first page knew it was going to be tough to finish, in the end only did complete as I found it funny at this attempt of romance and thought it MAY get better. It didn't, and do not recommend to anyone.

Crow's Row started a bit slow for me but once it started going it was like an avalanche :) ... I was livid at the end of this book but once I saw a sequel life was good again! I am absurdly anxious for the sequel.
