Read more reviews like this at http://lovelybooksblog.blogspot.com! 
 Within the first 70 pages of The Goddess Test I was sure I would hate this book. It was cheesy, it was predictable, and it was completely unrealistic. To my compete shock I soon found myself loving this book; I read it in one day, unable to put it down. If you're looking for a book with a lot of depth and character development don't bother, but if you're looking for a fun read with an adorable romance search no further. 
 One of the major flaws with this novel, and the main reason I initially hated it, is the lack of logic. Ava lures Kate across a river by stepping on rocks and then proceeds to dive into the river in an attempt to leave Kate stranded and ends up killing herself. What I really don't understand is why Ava thought Kate would even be stranded, they just walked across rocks to get there... can't Kate just walk back across the rocks? This kind of logic made me want to throw this book against a wall. 
 Despite this major fault The Goddess Test had a lot of redeeming qualities. First of all the romance between Kate and Henry is adorable, it was different without being too strange and by the end I was rooting for them every step of the way. Second, I loved the mystery aspect of this novel. I've always been a sucker for mysteries and while this was not exactly a heart pounding mystery I did enjoy the climatic and unexpected turn of events when the perpetrator was unveiled. 
 I was pleasantly surprised by this novel, I initially hated it and loved it by the end. Part fantasy, part romance, and part mystery The Goddess Test is a fun read as long as the lack of common logic doesn't bother you. I would undoubtedly recommend this novel to someone looking for a light summer read.

**1 star** 
 I love Greek mythology. I try to absorb everything I find that mentions it, even in part. I've read countless books, watched all the movies involving it, and played Age of Mythology. So when I first heard about this book, I was pretty excited. A retelling of the myth of Persephone, but with a twist - she has to face a few tests in order to get the crown. 30 pages into this book, I wasn't excited anymore. 
 The problem is, Kate is your typical useless heroine. She cries a lot and whines a lot, but doesn't actually do a whole lot. What she is good at is delegating responsibility to other people. And crying. She's good at crying. At the end when the council decides whether or not she has passed all seven tests, I seriously just wanted to punch her in the face. I get her arguing with Zeus if she had been a strong, rebellious character this whole time, but nope. She's just annoying. Speaking of the results of the seven tests, what a cop out. All these tests happened unknowingly to the reader and to Kate. Kate just bopped around the whole book whining while passing all the super hard magical tests. 
 The romance? Wherein Kate is really resistant to accept the contract because she'll be Henry's "wife" six months a year, but it'll keep her mom alive longer so she agrees? Where there is actually little mention of Henry's sexiness/hotness until 200 pages in when Kate suddenly decides she loves that poor, sexy, tortured soul? A soul that's a powerful, ancient, virginal god of death. Don't worry, Kate takes care of that (with a little help from an aphrodisiac). But the whole book is just Henry brooding and trying to find a balance between giving her space and enjoying her company, and Kate is just like "I'm just doing this for my mom- WOW HE'S HOT!" 
 I think that yeah, while Hades as a sensitive virgin was a bad creative choice, I think he is a more realistic character than Kate. He struggles with his love for Persephone, and when he develops feelings for Kate he accepts she may never love him and keeps it under control until she reciprocates. Kate meantime is busy thinking about her mom <-- not really, she just revels in her dream world mom and forgets about the real one with cancer, dying a few miles away. 
 The sad part is that I only need to focus on Kate, Henry, and the romance in this review because that's central to the plot. Nobody else in the book really matters, not even the person that's been killing off all the other girls. Some characters were only good for slut-shaming (Ava), and some were only good for angry overreactions (James). But what did I like about this book? I liked the idea...and that's about it. I stared at that sentence for a long time and I have absolutely nothing to add to it. 
 Summary:

I'm sorry but this book was not what I'd expected and I don't mean it in a good way. The beginning was very promising, that few Henry's lines in prologue brought a mystery to the story and I couldn't wait for the action and romance to happen. And so I waited and waited and waited.... 
 This should have been a wonderful book. It should have been about Greek mythology being transformed into the modern world, it should have been about Greek gods it should have been everything the book description had promised and more. Yeah, the thing is, it wasn't and it makes me so angry, because it's not like there are so many YA books based on the old antique myths and I was really looking forward to read this one. 
 I found impossible to relate to Kate. It was like we experienced things through her eyes but at the same time we weren't allowed to see what was really happening inside her head. Everything felt so distnant. I couldn't break the invisible barrier which separated me from Kate and so after a while I just stop caring about her. And I think that's the worst possible thing, to stop caring about the heroine, because after that, there is just no more hope for the book. 
 What irritated me the most were the names. Henry? Diana? Really? The one and only thing, which could have saved the Goddess Test from the total fiasco of not having anything to do with Greek mythology was taken from us when Ms. Carter decided to change the names of gods to some ordinary English names. I know she did somehow explain it at the end but that doesn't change the fact that as far as I'm concerned, by calling Hades Henry, she put the last (or was it the first?) nail in the coffin. 
 I'm not going to start with the chemistry between Kate and Henry (which was nonexistent), because I already feel bad by publishing this negative review. I know Aimee is a very young debut author and I wish her lots of success in the future because it looks like people generally love The Goddess Test and I'm the one who just didn't get it. 
 Thank you, Harlequin Teen and Netgalley for giving me an opportunity to read and review this book. Despite my opinion, it's much appreciated.

(this'll be a short spoiler-free review) 
 I liked this book but I don't know, there's something about it that I didn't like either. 
 I started off reading this book thinking it was going to be horrible. I was greatly surprised to find it otherwise (for the most part). 
 It's really hard for authors to capture Greek gods, I think, ESPECIALLY in a YA book. I was waiting for Carter to turn Hades into the next Edward Cullen but to my surprise, I really enjoyed Hades's character. He wasn't portrayed as some teenage boy but as someone much much older, like it should be. 
 In fact, I liked Henry/Hades character the most. Kate was OK as well, but meh, she had her moments, both good and bad. 
 OKAY, the gist: 
 Hades needs to find himself a new 'wife', someone to help him rule the underworld as one sole ruler cannot handle the underworld. Persephone (not sure if you're well acquainted with Greek mythology, but that's his wife in Greek mythology) has left him for a mortal man, gave up her immortality and died with the mortal man thousands of years ago. Now the council, this includes Zues, Poseidon, Apollo, (all your big main gods), thinks that Hades can't handle the stress and role of ruling the underworld and will appoint a new god to rule it, this will lead to Hades downfall and 'death' of sorts. 
 This brings us to Kate, who has been chosen after many failed attempts to find a wife. All of his chosen 'girls' have ended up mysteriously dying. And now Kate has struck a deal with Hades, save her mothers life and she will become his wife, that is of course if she passes the test's the gods throw at her. 
 Can I just say I saw Caliope's facade. It's always those damn chipper characters you have to watch out for! I felt all high and mighty knowing who the mysterious killer was but I was absolutely thrown by surprise at the ending...... WHAT?! 
 WHAT!??! 
 ALL THOSE PEOPLE WERE GODS!?!?!?! AVA WAS APHRODITE?! ELLA WAS ARTEMIS, THEO APOLLO.... WAIT WHAT?!?!?!?! 
 I just, I couldn't really wrap my head around that. I just couldn't buy it. 
 HER MOM WAS DEMETER!?!??!..... HOLD UP. 
 The first thing I thought when I found out her mom was a god was, "shouldn't that make Kate a demigod?" .... and then I just stared at my kindle like it had just slapped me.... what? 
 I did not see that coming, I mean, her mom has cancer for like years and the fact that gods can have 'human' bodies and all just blew my mind in a good and bad way. Also, did Diana/Demeter/Kate's mom give birth to Kate for the sole purpose of making her Hades wife?!?!? I'm confused. 
 I liked the ending as much as I hated. 
 I liked that it shocked the hell out of me because I had NO idea that was going to happen. It's been a while since a book has been able to do that to me. 
 But I had a hard time BELIEVING the ending. It was bit far-fetched. I just... hmmmm, 
 . 
 . 
 . 
 My sister has all the books, so I'm just going to finish this series up but, oh man, I don't know. It was good, but.... what?

** spoiler alert ** 
 Yes, I could break this down into individual books. But, considering I read them all one right after the other, I think not. 
 I read this whole series in 3 days between LAN activities. (That is a gaming parting, for those of you who don't know.) 
 I read them all because the first book had an amazing plot that I enjoyed and I fell in love with some of the characters. I read the other two for the characters. 
 The first book follows Kate who must go through a series of tests (which thankfully we don't witness someone trying to kill her constantly) to determine if she has the character to become the new Queen of the Underworld, and the husband of Henry (Hades). This book was so lovely to read, and a great break from everything. I would have been happy with just this book, though I would have wanted to see more of Henry. 
 The other two books I kept reading to see Henry and Kate together. Honestly, the plot of both of those were just too far reaching without enough information. I wish they had been kept more simple and focus on the relationships more. That is what the Greek gods were all about, their relationships. 
 Still, I would definitely recommend the first two books, and if you want to read more about Henry and Kate keep going, otherwise the first book can hold up as a standalone. 
 In fact, I get the feeling that, like the Twilight series, this series suffers from unintended continuation. I would have rather JUST had a large collection of short stories about the two of them.

DNF - It just didn't hold my interest. It was a pretty brainless, easy read that seemed to use Greek mythology VERY lightly. Made it halfway through, and I already know who is supposed to be who (totally different names) and what is going to happen. Just to see if I was right, I skipped to the last 2 chapters and yup. Got it all right.

Reading this in the ebook version, I actually got to make specific notes as I went along and have a bunch to say about it. The cover of the book is beautiful, and the story started out intriguing and I was hopeful. Sigh. The story could have been good. It could have been juicy, wonderful and exciting but instead it was so meek, feeble and routine. 
 About Henry: 
 Everything about Henry, Kate, and Henry & Kate together was... dead (no pun intended, really. Really) Everything felt so calculated and cold. Their first kiss was a completely no chemistry kiss. If the story wasn't told from Kate's point of view, I would have thought she was actually some neutral character that no one cared about, lol. I didn't understand when and why (and how) she started to care for Henry enough to kiss him and make him a blanket like I swear they only talked like 3 times so far, and those conversations weren't even anything remotely meaningful. 
 About the Gods: 
 The whole idea of "Gods" was so underplayed! Henry, a millennium old god, was portrayed more as a tortured teenager. A teenager. A teen- okay, you get it. Every other god was the same. Greek gods, I'm pretty sure, were especially cruel and didn't care about puny humans. But these ones, these ones goddamn cared about every little stupid thing that even I wouldn't care about. They didn't have a presence at all. Gods? more like Blobs. Heh. Hehheh. 
 About the attacks: 
 If I was the target of some unknown assassin that had killed 11 girls before me, I would probably be really suspicious of everything and everyone. Now I realize she didn't really have to, because the attacks were so lame, I almost laughed one time. Kate was extremely bad at this suspicious thing, and it annoyed me to no end when she banished Ava and then started to think she was the culprit of the attacks. If you can doubt a person so quickly like that, you have to question if you ever really considered then a friend. Which brings me to the assumption that Kate just can't handle the idea that people die (Surprise!!) and that made her even stupider in my eyes. She was living in the underworld, for god's sake. She is stuck on staying alive no matter what, she is stuck on keeping her mother alive no matter what, she is stuck on saving Ava, who I doubt she even cared that much about. 
 Or, once again, I just failed to see the "chemistry" between Ava and Kate. 
 About the Tests: 
 They were such. A. Disappointment. This is pretty much where the book almost made me cry with boredom/frustration. A lot of spoilers coming up!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! 
 Okay first of all, eating my general three meals a day is not something I would consider gluttony at all. I, like other sometimes eat even when I'm not hungry, because- well, food. And I don't think this is wrong at all, unless you are costing someone else their meal. Damn, it's not like Kate is hogging all the underworld food and leaving all her maids and other underworld poor people staving and dying. Now that is gluttony. 
 Second, the humility test- wtf? Say I'm Kate. I tried my fricking hardest to win the test, and someone spiked me and I accidentally had sex- with someone I love, mind you, I'm not just gonna sit there and accept that I failed the test. I did nothing wrong and I sure as hell would yell until they admitted it. It's like saying rape happens because the girl has no humility. I do not get how accepting that I'm a failure when I'm clearly not will give me passing marks. 
 I wish there had been at least one fight, or anything otherwise... exciting related to the tests, and that they weren't all just about dresses and eating and mundane stuff like that- I mean, the story is set in the underworld, and there couldn't have been anything more interesting happening? Kate has only been given poison once in the whole book, and she didn't even eat it. /Eternal sigh/

I had a lot of problems with this book. This is the first book since I've started blogging where I not only didn't enjoy it, but was also kind of angry with as well. The author's writing itself isn't that bad, but it's not very good either. She has the tendency to use YA cliches, over-complicates her story to the extreme, and sets up her characters like Edward and Bella from Twilight. Except worse. 
 Right off the bat, the first chapter was pretty cheesy. Over-dramatic Henry acts like this the entire book. "It's all my fault," "My life sucks," "I didn't protect her" blah blah blah. Plus, just because a character is a god, doesn't mean they can't have personality. Every single character was shallow, under-developed, and lacked depth. 
 Believability 
 When we are introduced to Kate, I kind of liked her. She was a little whiny, but I thought she was alright. Then everything went off the deep end. First, the most popular girl in school (who is an immediate bitch, what a surprise!) Ava, pranks Kate in the worst possible way and ends up dying. Only it's okay, because Henry can bring Ava back to life, for a price. So yeah, this is the part where Kate should be kind of questioning this guy on how he raised her friend from the dead. Nope, instead she looks up the story of Hades and Persephone like Henry told her to, and doesn't even clue into the fact that he's Hades. Like, legit Hades, not symbolically, allegorically, metaphorically, whatever. That piece of information goes right over her head, even when Ava is walking around, alive, without her brain bashed in like it was before. 
 Now, all this stuff happens really fast, right at the beginning. When Kate moves in with Henry, all of a sudden everything is at a standstill. Things move at a snail pace. Most of it is Kate figuring out whether or not she likes Henry, and then she ends up loving him (shocker), which I didn't understand because the build up to their romance was non-existent. The author told her audience about Kate's feelings, rather than showing them. 
 Gender Stereotypes 
 Kate has servants, and when one of them asks her to wear a dress (when she doesn't want to), instead of putting up a fuss, she just gives in. She even has a to wear a corset. Umm, so much for feminism. Let's subjugate our character to physiologically altering lingerie for the purpose of being pretty and skinny. 
 This isn't the end to the gender stereotypes that permeate this book, either. Henry is so over-protective, and Kate constantly reacting to him. He's active, she's passive. He's in a bad mood, it makes her sad (but she barely knows him). She agrees to all these tests to prove herself capable of being his queen. Ugh. The whole thing is setting this girl up to the be the perfect ideal of a woman by passing these tests, which are the seven deadly sins. Um, I don't remember Henry/Hades having a perfect track records, or for that matter, any of the Greek gods. They mess up each other's lives throughout Greek mythology. But by subjugating Kate to these tests, it's only promoting this concept of an "ideal" woman, that nobody can actually be. 
 Another thing was her skinny-ness. At one point she says, 
 "I didn't gain weight, and that only gave me an excuse to eat as much as I wanted." (page 135). 
 You should always be able to eat as much as you want, and not have to constantly worry about weight loss or gain. If you're a healthy person, with an active lifestyle and good food choices, then that shouldn't matter! Whenever I eat, I want to have a full meal. That's how much I want to eat. I shouldn't need an excuse to do that! 
 Plot 
 So the whole idea is for Kate to stay alive, and all the girls that have gone before her have died terrible deaths, and no one knows who is behind them, and for some inexplicable reason, Kate is the last girl before Henry "fades." Why he's suddenly fading is beyond me. It doesn't sound like he has it that bad. Lots of friends, some nice family members, but he's severely depressed because Persephone left him thousands of years ago. Okay... 
 Anyways, so no girl has stayed alive past Christmas. Kate gets past it with barely a hitch. And then she's in the clear. She makes clear, moral decisions that anyone would have probably made in her place, but she's exalted for it in the end because apparently they were so hard to pass. Later on some serious stuff happens, but the whole time I'm screaming mentally at Kate, are you blind?? The whole story just did not make sense in my brain. 
 In the end... 
 This book really fell short of my expectations. The plot was so over-complicated with characters making decisions that really made no sense whatsoever. Henry and Kate are Edward and Bella cookie cutters, except Kate is really desperate for Henry's love for some reason, and Henry is a depressed robot. Kate is subjected to age old gender assumptions and just lets it all slide. Apparently feminism doesn't apply to Greek mythological retellings. I know some people really enjoyed these books, but I would personally not recommend them.

This book was an absolute disappointment. When I read the summary, I was excited because the idea had great potential to it, but after I finished it, I was extremely disappointed. This book had absolute great potential, but the characters were bland and not very memorable. They didn't leave an impression on me, not even the olympians. The olympians should have at least been memorable because come on, they're gods. The character that I even remotely liked was Henry. His development was somewhat constant, compared to Kate who was hot and cold about whether she should have stayed with Henry or not.The test was too easy. WAY TOO EASY. The only villain was Cassiope, or Hera, apparently. I expected it to be way more adventurous and since it was a first book and seven tests, each book would be some sort of test. But no, all SEVEN tests were passed in one book. And nothing remotely dangerous and exciting happens. It's just one big sigh wrapped into a book. All I can say is that it was an absolute disappointment. And to think that there are more to come. The idea in itself isn't bad, it's just the plot and the characters that are disappointing.

 I'm finding it difficult to sum up my feelings for this book. At first I was bored, then mid-way it was okay, but then it just got silly and I sat there contemplating what my rating would actually be. I settled on a good 2 stars. 
 I got this book with RavenPost with the theme 'Isolation', and it's a book I've definitely seen around but never really considered picking it up. Still, it was an interesting read. I've not read a story of someone who has to stay inside and never leave their house due to terrible allergies, so it was quite new to me. I just the story lacking in some areas. 
 Firstly, it was a bit slow. Maddy was inside and basically just reading and spending time with her mum or nurse, all the while pining for the normality of a regular teenage girl. Of course that's to be expected, she's isolated. But then her neighbours move in. And one of them a handsome young man called Olly who takes her fancy. From there, this book is mostly just Maddy wanting to be with Olly and cursing her illness for trapping her in her home. Which leads to my other issue with the book overall - romance. 
 Maddy and Olly speak a few times online, meet face to face twice and then THEY'RE IN LOVE. It's instalove, and it's too unrealistic for my liking. Not only that, but Maddy makes some terrible decisions and does pretty questionable things just to be with him, right up to risking her life. It's pretty careless of her. Literally risking everything just for a boy she's just met. Instalove isn't a seller, I don't know many people who like it, so I wish authors would stop writing that in. I, for sure, am not a fan of it 
 Also, there is a plot twist in this book. Sadly, I kind of suspected that there would be one. The book was a little too slow for there to not be. When it happened, I wasn't that surprised. I did have a reaction along the lines of 'WHAT' because I wasn't sure that would even be an option. If you know what it is, you'd think 'surely this can't be after everything that's happened.' Yet it did. It's not easy trying to explain without spoiling, so go read the book and let us know what you thought about the twist! 
 There was also a part of the story which I really didn't like (can't say due to it being a spoiler), but I felt that Maddy was really stupid and acted on impulse without thinking. It ended up being extremely bad for her and others around her. I was reading it thinking 'Why do this, and what made you think this was a good idea?' 
 She learnt the hard way. 
 With the characters, I wasn't a fan of Maddy. Her bad decisions, dramatic nature (mostly near the end of the book, crying over such a small issue), and her slight lack of consideration for others. As soon as she saw Olly outside from her window, she was obsessed. I got bored of that very quickly. 
 Near the end though, she was just so emotional and crying so much (for about an hour - maybe longer!) over something and I was like 'what is she even crying about?'. I know she's a teenager, but I was genuinely not sure what was wrong. If it's about Olly, it's honestly her own fault for making silly decisions, getting people in trouble and nearly dying for her reckless attitude. 
 Speaking of Olly... he was alright actually. He was quite patient with her, and he wasn't pressuring in any way. His penchant for climbing on everything and stuff was a little strange, but it's not really a bad trait. He was quite a nice guy. I do think he should have knocked some sense into Maddy, though. Sometimes it felt like he should say 'Alright, stop now. You need to be careful', if he really cares about her. He was just as reckless as Maddy in the end, and should have been a bit more decisive in some cases. 
 The other characters were interesting, but didn't really stick out much. I quite liked Carla - she was a warm and caring character, a bit more lenient and sometimes funny. There aren't many characters in this book, but considering the type of story it is, you don't need too many. The number itself was enough. I just wished that some were fleshed out a bit more. There was time, for sure. 
 Olly's family was quite interesting to read about. His overall story and what was going on in his life was sad and I wish we learnt more about that. Of course, the male lead as well as the female lead needs a sob story. We had quite a bit of pagetime with Olly, so again, more fleshing out of his life would have been good. Ultimately, it was all about Maddy. 
 I did like that the main character was half-Japanese and half-African American. It certainly makes a change. I'm all for diversity, especially in YA. I just wish I enjoyed the story more, considering it was a kind I'd never read before. I haven't read many books revolving around isolation and it's one of those rare ones that I read that's about sickness. As a hypochondriac, I tend to avoid them. 
 I'm not entirely sure how I feel about this book. I forced myself to read it, I did get into it but then I was left feeling like it was lacking something. Hence my 2 star rating.

And at least for JK, that probably would have worked since her plots were SO extensive.

Plus, my baby sister is seventeen and she does not speak this way, so what's the excuse for it. At the very least, this sort of choppy writting should be reserved for the dialogue parts of the book only. It's so choppy, and makes it so hard to read it in an easy flowy manner. 
 5. There are SO many grammatical, and character plotline errors. Who is your editor?! Fire the moron, stat! 
 6. These characters are not even worth getting to know. They're all the stereotype. How about making Kramisha a poet, who loves to shop and is well spoken and articulate?!?! I suppose that is beyond the writting capacity of Mrs and Miss cast. Which is saying alot, since they lack majorly in that department. 
 7. Lastly, and most obvious, there is NO plotline in this book. Sure there are some good points and i like a lot of the Wicca related rituals and so forth. But, that alone does not compensate for the rest of the mess that is this series. 
 The publishers need to stop feeding into this insanity and publish anything futher of this story. But of course, that won't be the case. It's like a drug. If there is demand, there will surely be supply. 
 Unfortunately, a new book is out and i am ashamed to say i am once again reading the sixth book. I am now up to chapter 6, and as you may have guessed NOTHING has happened, and yes... Zo remains a Ho. It's like a bad scab you cannot seem to stop picking at. You just can't help yourself. I suppose it's more curiosity than anything else. 
 At least, there's Aphrodite and her quirks to keep me going throughout the book. She's unexpectably become my only favorite character. And, i have a feeling that once Zo the Ho grows up, Stark is the one who will stop her from shoving her tongue down every male that crosses her way. Unfortunately, i suppose i'm only adding the fire, they'll just keep realeasing more of this crap, by buying another book, but as i said, "bad scab" 
 Finally, I have read some bad books in my past, but this is perhaps the worse. Please put us out of our misery and finish this.

 Rating: 
 Until The Sun Falls From The Sky:(3 Teacups / 3 Handcuffs) 
 With Everything I Am:(5 Teacups / 4 Handcuffs) 
 Untitled: He's said one word, "MINE", we don't know his name, but we are already in love. 
 Our Thoughts: 
 KA does an excellent job at crossing mythologies. The first novel focuses on vampires, the second on werewolves. There is an overarching narrative woven throughout the series. It will bring the three main couples together to fullfill the prophecy and restore harmony to the races. 
 KA knows how to write hawt alpha males. Callum is one of our favorite book boyfriends, in both his human and wolf states. 
 Even though these men are mythological, they are still surprisingly normal. They fail to understand women, human or otherwise. A lot of the novels' conflict is the men's inability to understand their women and express their emotions. 
 These women are are strong and independent. They are not afraid to go head to head with their men. It takes awhile for them to truly be claimed. 
 These men aren't afraid to go against the customs of their kind to claim their mates. They will fight and die if anyone tries to separate them. 
 Like most KA novels there is a strong sense of family woven throughout the narrative. The characters discover that family isn't necessarily about blood, but those you love. 
 Neither vampires nor werewolves are villainized; like humanity they just have a few bad apples which makes the cultures more relatable. All the main characters want to do is live, find love and happiness! Who doesn't? 
 We can not wait for the last installment. We do not know much, but from the short snippet at the end of With Everything I Am, it holds great promise

 "Her eyes narrowed. "You know, Lucien, you need to make up your mind. Either you're this guy or you're the jerky, controlling guy who I met at The Selection or you're the near-miss murder guy last night. Pick one. I'm getting confused."

sample_reviews.review_text: I have ruminated on this. I mean, SEP is kind of a phenomenon, right? Not so much this side of the pond (where romance is a somewhat sidelined genre of literature in general and thus no one is really a phenomenon) but in the States she's like a Big Deal? I certainly cannot remember the last time I read a book with Good Reads reviews of 20K+. So I suppose my expectations were high and this ended up on my TBR pile somehow, so some blog or reviewer I respect must have liked it. But I've got to say, it left me cold. The writing is good. Philips can do banter, I'll give her that and she sets a scene well. But I didn't feel a connection with the book at all and the romance just didn't do anything for me. Add into all that I had some serious suspension of belief issues. The multi-zillionaire (American) football player running into the broke zany artist and keeping her around seemingly just because she can pick on him in a witty way and then they fall into an angry sex kind of relationship. Then there's the Rocker Dad and the groupie Mother and the half-sister and the southern dragon lady in the cutesy town at the cutesy farm. And So Much Happening, my God. I was exhausted. The beav and her ex, the mum pretending to be the decorator and the sister running away, the dad showing up, the parental secondary romance, the kid sisters singing, the whole thing with Nita and owning the town and the paintings and prison at the end. Just: enough already. If I wanted this much going on I'd watch a glossy American soap or something. At least part of the reason the romance was lost on me is that the romance got lost amongst all of the other stuff going on. That said, I did read the whole thing. I didn't skim but it all felt like a bit of a slog. I can't say that I'll be hunting out any Philips in the near future off the back of this.

Aww, I feel really sad now. This is the final Chicago Stars book, I will ever read, unless Susan Elizabeth Phillips decides to ever write another one. I liked this one better than the last one 'Match Me if You Can', probably because Dean reminded me of the cocky heros that she wrote about in the earlier books (sorry Heath). To be honest, this book kinda felt like a mash-up of every other previous book in the series. I saw the money pushing of Bobby Tom, the drugged up mother like Heath, the mom hate of Kevin, etc. I can't remember many other clear examples, but I found little familiar tidbits that popped up. 
 The thing I liked most about this book was the characters. Each one was fully fleshed out, no cardboard cut-outs here. It was nice to delve into each characters past and learn why they are the way they are. I must say, pretty much everyone in the book was damaged goods. Never have there been so many people with such difficult lives. Aside from psychotic drunk Karen Ann, I legit ended up loving all these characters. I even ended up liking mean old Nita! This surprised me cause I hated her at first. Sure, I knew she probably had a sad past to account for her terrible attitude, but I was like 'pftt yea right! Nothing could redeem this hag'. She came off cruel, but it seemed like deep-down she was just lonely. Dean's mom April was another one I loved. From the stories, she was a terrible person and it was heartbreaking to see her try to redeem herself from her past wrongdoings. I legit cried when Dean finally introduced her as his mother . Total hallmark moment on my end... 
 As for Dean and Blue, I liked them from the start. They were both people with hurt and it was nice to see how they fit so nicely together. They started out as a kind of friends-with-benefits thing, but you got to see them slowly fall for each other. Towards the end when Dean confessed to Blue and she rejected him. I just wanted to be like 'NOO DON'T DO IT! He loves you!'. I didn't blame her for being upset with him though because even I cringed at the scene where she was around his football friends. It was alright though because they both did stupid things and say cruel words, so it wasn't just one person being annoying and ruining everything. 
 I must say, I loved their ending! It was SOO cute! There was the stereotypical last minute misunderstanding where the hero chases after the heroine. Dean flew over to the farm house because he thought Blue had run away. He'd been accidently photo snapped kissing another girl, but there was a whole story to explain it. What proceeds is Dean feeling like someone has shit all over his life and he's all sad. Then the next morning he wakes up and Blue hasn't left after all. I liked how she was super confused and he just started yelling at her . Things could have easily been really cliched, but I liked how things didn't end up like you expected. After that whole scene, I was totally happy with Blue and Dean getting their happily ever after. 
 Guess I will have to find something else to read. I'll probably read her other series next...

 They're soon heading for his summer home, where their already complicated lives and inconvenient attraction to each other will become entangled with a charismatic but aging rock star; a beautiful, fifty-two-year-old woman trying to make peace with her rock and roll past; an eleven-year-old who desperately needs a family; and a bitter old woman who hates them all.

reference_books.review_text:
Ok, my rating for this book is quite harsh, but now I get to explain it. The rating does not reflect my overall enjoyment of the series, nor does it take into account the annoying characteristics that have been consistent throughout. This rating is based on this particular story - where just about every decision Atticus made had me shaking my head, facepalming, or rolling my eyes. That makes a book pretty unenjoyable for me. I felt like Atticus was either way out of character, or he is an unreliable narrator. Either he is paranoid, wise after many years, and truly thoughtful about his master plans, as he says he is, or he is impulsive, easily embroiled in grade A dangerous situations that could probably have been avoided or mitigated by, finally, some sort of wise planning or course of action. So far, Atticus, you are the second and if I have to listen to your bragging about your craft beer and your healthy omelettes and running/biking habits, I want you to be up front with me from now on. Either you are a paranoid, clever survivor, or a hot-headed, overwhelmed Celtic warrior who is going to die very soon. I don't think I can handle you being both.

** spoiler alert ** 
 In lieu of an actual review (short version: it was good but a little challenging and took at least 2 reads to "get it"), a couple of observations: 
 (1) On the appeal of steampunk: I remain convinced (and in large part because of this book) that the big appeal of "steampunk" as a genre has to do with the archetypal Inventor/Tinkerer. Here we get this in Mieville's Isaac. In many ways he's an unlikely protagonist: a little hefty[+:], nerdy, self-aggrandizing, cowardly, and a bit of a pervert[++:]; but incredibly brilliant. He occupies a mental space with our real-world Thomas Edison and Nikola Tesla and (perhaps more so?) Benjamin Franklin. Our modern (20th/21st century) concepts of science are so laden with litigation and patent applications and funding cuts and notions of proprietary information... It makes sense to cast Isaac as a radical; it's as if he can see through the veil of the page into our own world, can see how science is encumbered by business and process, can see how disconnected the individual is from his work. There is no more Lone Tinkerer puttering about his basement workshop assembling the next great innovation. And something in our cultural consciousness years for that. 
 (2) On protagonists: Though I've (above) alluded to Isaac as the protagonist, Mieville's Yagharek serves as our narrator and by extension of convention this grants him a kind of protagonist emeritus status[+++:]. But in Yagharek we're given an interesting bridge between the novel and the reader. Yagharek is, in so many ways, the opposite experience of what I imagine a "typical" fantasy reader is after in his narrators: Yagharek is not heroic either; he is a rapist and a cripple and he is in many ways frustrated and impotent. Our vehicle into the story is hardly a vehicle for escape, hardly a means of escaping our own "real world" anxieties and limitations. What's more, Yagharek's ultimate fate (i.e., to desplumarate himself and "go as a man" into New Crobuzon) is a way of turning to the reader and saying: "Now get back to your life just as Yagharek has done." 
 --- 
 [+:] = The references to "his bulk" being a little bit mixed in that regard; but for the sake of argument, he could (in the parlance of our time) stand to lose a few pounds, for sure. 
 [++:] = Though let us not judge him here since his "perversion" is really just analogous to an interracial relationship (though that comparison is on par with calling the space shuttle an airplane). 
 [+++:] = To be honest though, Yagharek is enough of a protagonist to not need the "emeritus". 
 ---

This future fantasy world with typewriters and gaslamps and boilers and heliotypes is just too icky and corny to keep reading. I'd also like to point out the annoying things like "chymical" instead of chemical, hyperbolic overuse of the adjective "fat" and the constant use of the word "organic," which I expect has something to do with how everything else in this world is "mech." Also, could you think of a worse exclamation than "godspit?" Awful. I know this dude is crazy smart and that these are probably all deft and esoteric references to masterworks of this genre, but it's not for me.

book_b.title: Fables, Vol. 19: Snow White
book_b.user_review: The Bufkin story was amusing and creative. The Snow White story didn't flow or gel for me. The excessive foreshadowing and the uni-dimensionality of the antagonist was a let-down. I may have tossed the book across the room when I was done (gently, because it's a library book).

sample_reviews.review_text: Just couldn't get into this volume. I ended up skimming the book.
Not the best of the series. It seemed like it was a lot of filler for the next installment.
Very fun! Had a hard time putting this one down. I love Fables!

** spoiler alert ** 
 Fables has had its ups and downs over the years but this is the first volume to actively piss me off. 
 Major spoilers follow. 
 While Bigby and Brock Blueheart go hunting for the missing wolf cubs, Snow is surprised to be reunited with her long-lost first husband: Prince Brandish. Brandish is basically an asshat 50's husband who locks Snow up in a room, thinking that if he kills Bigby and their kids, Snow will love him instead. He never quite has the means to sway Snow's heart, though--he doesn't have mind control powers or anything. He just sort of expects her to love him after he kills her husband and children. Because ladies LOVE it when you kill their children. 
 Why does Brandish think this, you ask? Who knows? Maybe he's just nuts. Too bad there's never any justification for his madness. We never get a glimpse into his brain. We never see why he cares so much about Snow in particular. Why can't he move on? Why not give it up after allllll these years? No reason is given. As a result he isn't a very interesting or threatening villain. Is he repugnant? Sure. But there's no brain there. Even his presence as physical threat seems muted: he has a few magic tricks (he turns a dude into a bird, has a magic sword, and jumps around a lot), but it's not like he's a goddamn dragon or something. 
 And yet...we're supposed to believe that THIS is the guy who kills Bigby? Out of all the foes the Big Bad Wolf has slain, he ends up falling to THIS lame ass, undeveloped human? 
 What makes it all worse is this: just as Brandish never seems to be trying very hard to win Snow over, nobody else seems to be trying very hard to save Snow. Oh, sure, they express concern, and they try opening the door to the tower he's locked her in. But it always feels like some peculiar force is holding them back from trying very hard. It's almost as though they don't really give a shit about Snow at all. Hey, guys, our deputy mayor who's saved our bacon over and over again has been trapped in a room with a man who wants to rape her and kill Bigby! THINK WE SHOULD DO SOMETHING ABOUT IT? "Oh well but the laws say they're vowed to each other and the door is enchanted and" SHUT THE FUCK UP. FLY TO THE WINDOW, HELP SNOW, AND KILL THE FUCKER. 
 Even Snow herself seems unusually mild given the cicurcumstances. Here we have a strong female character who is trapped in a room with a man who slaps her, proclaims his plan to kill her husband and her CHILDREN, and presumably intends to rape her too. You'd think Snow would try a bit harder to get the fuck out of there, or would express a bit more emotion. Even ice queens can have fury in their eyes. But Snow just looks bored the whole time. The most she does is tie bedsheets into a rope, sling it through the window, and pout when they're too short to get her to the ground. That's it. That's her only plan. No point trying anymore after that. When Rose Red abruptly remembers that they have a fucking magic carpet at the end, it feels too little too late. 
 In a lesser series, I might think this to just be lazy writing. But maybe there's more to it. Maybe Brandish *does* have a power of mind control, and this manifests by making those he comes into conflict with not really try very hard to defeat him. Maybe that's his superpower, and the book just never makes note of it! 
 ...Orrrr maybe it's just lazy writing. 
 This was Snow's title book, so one might hope that it was her finest hour--her shining moment. But it's her weakest. This volume takes a strong female character and transforms her into a mild, dull woman who barely even tries to save the lives of the people she loves. This volume also kills off Bigby, the predominate hero of the series and everyone's favorite character. And it is a truly lame death, a death far weaker than a badass like Bigby deserves. Bigby deserves a hero's death: sacrificing his life to save lives, or to take down a genuinely threatening foe. Not getting pricked to death by a, well, prick in a duel that is ultimately meaningless. 
 The first third or so of this volume also collects the mini-comics showing Bufkin's adventures causing a revolution in Oz. It's cute but ultimately sort of meaningless. There isn't much conflict, and no real intrigue or depth. Bufkin tries, Bufkin succeeds. Too easy. The ending was amusing, but not enough to make up for everything else.

What the hell? Everything felt incredibly rushed in this volume. 
 The best part, was the first few issues bringing the Bufkin in Oz story to a close. My only problem was that it brought his story too a very final close, and he was becoming one of my favorite characters. I wasn't entirely satisfied with how his story ended, and I'm not sure why it needed to end. 
 There is a side story about Beast trying to get out of his servitude to the Blue Fairy...yawn. 
 The rest of the volume deals with Bigby driving off with Stinky to look for Dare, his missing cub. This is all narrated by a future Ambrose for some reason...? Once Bigby is gone Brandish holds Snow White hostage, and the rest of the Fables don't do a damn thing. It was ridiculous! Everyone pretty much abandons Snow and lets this Brandish guy do whatever he wants. Oh, and this Brandish guy is somehow more powerful than all the other Fables, including the witches of the 13th floor and Bigby. What? A few volumes ago they were planning on taking on Mister Dark and now they can't even face some random Prince?

After the excellent 'Cubs In Toyland" this is a disjointed and ultimately unfulfilling volume. 
 The Bufkin / Oz story was originally presented as a back up feature over a number of issues and doesn't really work that well when read in a single sitting. It comes across as disjointed and somewhat trite; there's also the problem that Bufkin just isn't as funny as Willingham thinks he is. 
 The Snow White storyline consists of 3 strands - the unengaging story of the Blue Fairy and Beast; the somewhat distasteful story of Brandis (Snow's ex-husband and apparent wannabe chauvinist rapist) and Brock & Bigby's search for the missing Therese and Dare in a flying Harry Potter car. All these don't really gel that well together and none are particularly interesting in themselves. 
 There's a few nice touches - Lake is a potentially interesting character, Reynard is as cool as ever and its going to be nice to see Bigby (literally) pick up the pieces - but overall it doesn't work as a consolidated volume. It feels very much as filler / interim volume. 
 However, the last page (no spoilers!)........I m still looking forward to the next volume!

A lot of craziness has happened in the last couple of volumes of Fables and this one is definitely no different. However, vol 19 is a lot more all over the place than Cubs in Toyland, which ultimately makes it less effective for me. Add to that a good helping of retconning (though to be fair, Brandish was based on an existing Snow White story, but to find that out I had to look it up on Wikipedia, so the series doesn't get any points) and this is definitely only a 3 star volume of a 5 star series.

2.5/5 
 Eh...look at that! It took me one year to read a graphic novel.

4 stars? Because Fables. Otherwise this is fairly ho-hum. The initial section about Bufkin etc is a bit silly but has it's moments - I liked the sentient rope. The main story with Snow etc is nothing too special but still enjoyable.

3.5, but I gave it the 4 over the 3 because it ended rather well. 
 Didn't love the Bufkin stories, but they had their moments.

reference_books.title: How to Live Safely in a Science Fictional Universe
reference_books.review_text:
There's nothing more frustrating than a book that starts good, has an interesting and unique setting and concept but instead of improving as the story goes on, it just goes completely off the rails. This is what happened with How To Live Safely in a Science Fictional Universe and I wish I stopped reading after the first half of the book because the second half is just a rehash of the ideas introduced in the first. This would have been perfect as a short story, instead the author preferred to drag it until I got sick of it. 
 It gets 2 stars only because of the beginning and the ideas that it introduced then, it was fascinating and really good, but the second part was the most frustrating reading experience of the year so far.

reference_books.title: The Hate U Give
reference_books.review_text:
"What's the point of having a voice if you're gonna be silent in those moments you shouldn't be?" 
 I had my reservations before reading this, I know better than to blindly follow the hype of a book, especially of a Young Adult one. But hey, the premise seemed good and timely, and even if the hype turned out to be an exaggeration there were still changes for this to be an okay book. Now I wish I knew nothing about this book because even with me expecting something good out of it, I was still surprised by how good The Hate U Give was. It was sad, infuriating but above all it was hopeful and surprisingly funny. 
 So the gist of the book is pretty simple, it follows Starr, a black high-school girl which lives in the ghetto but because of what happened when she was little when she witnessed the death of her best friend, her parents decided to move her to a private school in another neighborhood. Most of the students in that highschool are white, so Starr finds herself living a double live: the real her that can cuss and speak her mind, and the personality that she uses at school to not give the kids any reason to pick on her, judge her or simply be prejudiced towards her. 
 This is the status quo with which the book begins, moving on from that, things get insane. Yes, I know that the description of the book talks about what happens next but I never write spoilers in my review (or at least I try no to), even if those spoilers happen to be included in the book's description. It's just that when I started reading this, it had been like a month since I first got my eyes on it and when I finally got it, I refused to read the description again since I was planning to read the book anyway, and guess what? After finishing it, I read the blurb on Goodreads again, and there it was right there, the thing that happens quite early in the book but that was a complete shock for me. I understand why they do that, it's just like with movie trailers that give most of the plot away, but I really wish that just as with movies where there are teasers that don't (usually) spoil anything, something similar could be done for books too. I guess this is why for most book I just avoid the description and read some reviews from people that I know don't spoil things, if those reviews are available. If not, I'll probably cave in and just read the damn description. I'll end my rant and go back to talk about the book (I hope) by saying that there are books or publishing houses that know how to do a good, vague description, so kudos to those. 
 Back to the book, if anyone's still reading. The reason I avoid YA novels is because, and I'm going straight to the point here, they're shallow. They're mostly just entertainment, and I'm not going to be a hypocrite and say that this is a bad thing. It isn't, I read books for entertainment too but teenage angst and romance - not something I enjoy. The Hate U Give felt different. Yes, it still had the beats of a regular YA novel and most characters felt like they belonged there but the way in which the author tackled the subject of police brutality, racism and prejudice of all kinds and shapes felt, I'm not going to say mature, but something you don't usually see in popular YA novels, and The Hate U Give is shaping up to be the YA novel of the year. This can only make me happy. 
 The Hate U Give, for me, is an example of a Young Adult novel, done right. It has all the trademark characteristics: angst, some romance, conflict, drama, sadness and humor. The thing is that the author knew how to restrain herself from abusing the ingredients, because once you add too much of a thing, you can easily alienate your reader. 
 Before I end this review I have to give a big shout out to the humor in this book. From the way I fixate on it, you would think that this book has a lot of humor. Yes and no. There is some, not much, but it really stands out among all the suffering and drama. Probably also because the humor was right up my alley and I laughed out loud a lot while reading this. I could give some samples of the humor in this book, but the best parts I had highlighted were kind of spoilery. Here is one that I think is safe: 
 This is the first time she's spoken to me since our fight. I'm not complaining. She's been nonexistent to me too. I respond anyway. 
 Sorry for what? 
 I'm not being petty. Petty would be saying, "New number, who dis?" 
 The Hate U Give is an important book, with a political and social message that is worth discussing, especially by young people. What's even more amazing about this book is that it isn't just that, a book with an important message, no, this book has great characters, a story that is addicting, it's powerful, sad and humorous, all at the same time. This book was unique, I want to read more books like this.

reference_books.title: The Butcher of Anderson Station (The Expanse, #0.5)
reference_books.review_text: This I also read last year, so I don't have much to add, maybe just that I remember this making me hope to see more Dawes in Babylon's Ashes...which happened (I'll take credit for that).

reference_books.title: The Way of Kings (The Stormlight Archive, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Nothing can top George R. R. Martin's 'A Song of Ice and Fire' for me, but Brandon Sanderson's 'The Stormlight Archive' can easily take the second place. This book was that good, it starts confusing as hell throwing bits and pieces of history and filling your head with all sorts of terms and words without ever explaining them to you until later on. It looks as a really off putting book, but once you get the hang of things it doesn't let you go. I love all the characters, I love the world Sanderson created and the potential this series has.

reference_books.title: More Weird Things Customers Say in Bookshops
reference_books.review_text:
This was just as funny as the first book, guaranteed to offer some good laughs. Here are some of the bits I thought were especially funny. I had to settle for only 5. 
 CUSTOMER: Do you have Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Abracadabra? 
 CUSTOMER (pointing at the books on the shelves): Are these real books? 
 BOOKSELLER: ... Yes. 
 CUSTOMER: So, they're not e-books? They're real? I can look at them? 
 BOOKSELLER: ... Yes. 
 CUSTOMER: Do you have a book that interprets life? 
 BOOKSELLER: I'm not sure I know what you mean. 
 CUSTOMER: Well, I was out hiking the other day, and I saw a wolf. I want to know what that meant. 
 CUSTOMER: Do you have Harry Potter book seven, part two? 
 BOOKSELLER: Book seven, The Deathly Hallows, is just one volume. 
 CUSTOMER: But the movie has two parts, so there must be a second book! They don't just make movies from nothing! 
 (It's just after 6pm. There's a sign on the desk asking the customers to ring the bell if a bookseller isn't at the till. 
 A man rings the bell. The bookseller comes out from the back room.) 
 MAN (looking from the bookseller to the bell in his hand): Wow. Just like in a brothel!

book_a.title: The Ocean at the End of the Lane
book_a.user_review: I see that this is rated as Adult Fiction, aside from that disturbing sex scene, this reads more like a fairy tale. Anyway, this is not a complaint, just an observation, I liked it quite a lot.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Goodreads Description- Sussex, England. A middle-aged man returns to his childhood home to attend a funeral. Although the house he lived in is long gone, he is drawn to the farm at the end of the road, where, when he was seven, he encountered a most remarkable girl, Lettie Hempstock, and her mother and grandmother. He hasn't thought of Lettie in decades, and yet as he sits by the pond (a pond that she'd claimed was an ocean) behind the ramshackle old farmhouse, the unremembered past comes flooding back. And it is a past too strange, too frightening, too dangerous to have happened to anyone, let alone a small boy. 
 I'm not quite sure what to say about this book... it seemed so dark and sad. I felt bad for our unnamed narrator because of all he had to go through. I was a little grossed out about the part where he tries to pull the worm out of his foot, the bathtub scene with his father was upsetting, and Ursula Monkton would have been terrifying for a young boy. 
 This was a quick read and it kept my interest. I think I need to ponder the deeper meaning of this story to truly understand what Gaiman wants us to know. He definitely has a way with words though. He is able to articulate emotions we have all felt. 
 Some of my favorite quotes: 
 Grown-ups don't look like grown-ups on the inside either. Outside, they're big and thoughtless and they always know what they're doing. Inside, they look just like they always have. Like they did when they were your age. Truth is, there aren't any grown-ups. Not one, in the whole wide world." 
 "Monsters come in all shapes and sizes, Some of them are things people are scared of. Some of them are things that look like things people used to be scared of a long time ago. Sometimes monsters are things people should be scared of, but they aren't." 
 "I do not miss childhood, but I do miss the way I took pleasure in small things, even as greater things crumbled. I could not control the world I was in, could not walk away from the things or people or moments that hurt, but I took joy in the things that made me happy."

4,5* 
 I went into this book knowing nothing about the story. And it was probably the best thing that could happen to me. 
 Despite the simplicity of the storyline it was just amazing! Gaiman's writing style is so rich and beautiful... I finally understand what his fans are talking about when they rave about his work. 
 And I was SO lucky that I got to listen to the audiobook because listening to the author himself telling you his story (in that sexy voice of his) was just pure perfection! 
 The only thing that kind of threw me off was that 'fantastic' element of the story. But other than that it was great!

As I write this, I'm still feeling pretty emotional about this book (and that never happens, I read a lot so I've become rather hardened at the end of novels!). 
 The main character in this book is a 7-year-old bookish boy who lives his life vicariously through books. Soon, he finds himself in quite a fantasy of his own. Though I've read that an easy way for an author to make their characters endearing is to make their characters readers (something about us identifying with them), this didn't feel like a ploy at all. I fell in love with the main character, and friendship with the Alice in Wonderland-esque "rabbit," type character who leads him through his journey of magical realism. 
 I don't want to give away too much. But let's just say that this book brought to mind everything from IQ84 to Alice and Wonderland to Harry Potter. So read it and love it. It's my first Neil Gaiman book, but I know I've found an author I'll go back to again and again.

Classic Gaiman 
 In the manner of Neverwhere and The Graveyard Book, Gaiman explores the underworld of our childhood mind, and finds there a lesson for our adult self. Highly recommended.

INTERESTING. but not really my cup of tea. I'm like kind of wondering what the point of it all was???? the story itself made me want to keep reading, but the writing was not my favorite. that ending was great, tho. I liked it.
Neil Gaiman has such an amazing way of returning you to childhood. My heart was pounding reading a large section of this book. Gorgeous.

4.25* 
 I still don't know what I think about this book and will have to ruminate for a while.... 
 After thinking about this book for several days, I'm still not quite sure what I think about them. Neil Gaiman has such unique ideas. I would love to live in his head for a day! I'm not even quite sure how to classify this book - magical realism? Fantasy? 
 This book follows an unnamed character who goes back to the town he grew up in for a funeral. He leaves the funeral and wants to get away from people for a while so he drives around and ends up returning to the road he grew up on. He ends up "getting lost", so to speak, in something that happened to him in his childhood which leaves the reader wondering at the very ending of the book whether things were real or not. 
 I liked the magical qualities of this book and there were some parts that really got me thinking, but I was left confused (which isn't always a bad thing). I appreciated the symbolism throughout the book and think this would be a very interesting one for honors students to read and discuss. 
 The characters were very interesting (all of the main characters were females minus our narrator so I was feeling a bit of girl power going on) and I loved the setting of this book. Idyllic English country-side will always interest me! 
 Overall, I liked most aspects of this book, but was left a little too confused about things that I suspect were more symbolic in nature.

The only other thing I have read by Neil Gaiman is the first part of the graphic novel Sandman. There are similarities that makes me feel like I understand his basic MO. That is, he seems mainly focused on producing a visceral reaction in his readers. He enjoys making you squirm. There is a scene in this book of a boy pulling a worm out of his foot, and it is impossible not to feel a prick in your own foot and want to rub it. I have not read Coraline but saw the movie, and the most striking, frightening image from the movie (the one that made my daughters scream and run out of the room in tears) is that of a boy with button eyes. The canvas-clad monster in this book seems like an echo of that image. But he's not content to just give you a queasy feeling in the stomach, he's also interested in the flutterings of the heart, and so the monsters are balanced by charming folksy characters who demand to be liked. 
 This is all well and good, though I wasn't totally taken in by the story. I feel I've read it or seen it before in other forms, as it seems to follow a familiar Hollywood plot structure. Is it cynical of me to suspect that Gaiman had movie adaptation in mind when he wrote it?

Gaiman at his finest 
 I have been a Gaiman fan for years. His short story, "The Wedding present," was so powerful I had to put it down, wait a few days and then read it again. The Ocean at the End of the Lane is just another fine example of Gaiman's craftsmanship as a writer. If you like Gaiman's other works, you'll love this one too.

I am a little torn about what to rate this book. I loved the concept and I was interested throughout the whole book on what it was about and where it was going. The main problem I did have with it is that it did not flow. The story was choppy and I had a hard time knowing what was going on and when it was going on. Also, things were not explained very well and there didn't seem to be a very good explanation for what did happen. I will give this author another try, but I will not be rereading this book.

book_b.title: Free Will
book_b.user_review:
Free Will is a short but informative book (judging by its length calling it an essay would probably be more accurate) looking to prove that free will is an illusion, and I have to say, it managed to convince me. 
 Despite the daunting subject, Haris' ideas are clear and easy to grasp which is something I really appreciate in non-fiction. So many authors get so tangled in their ideas that they forget that what they're writing isn't meant just for them. 
 It was great, food for thought for a very long time. I highly recommend it.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Harris made the argument against free will from a neuroscience perspective. But really what he is saying is that free will is a logical impossibility. "I can do whatever I want" but who decides what I want? The unconscious self? Who decides what the unconscious self wants then? What is "I"? 
 This is a good argument but life goes on and people do what they do, whatever the reason.
Not my cup of tea!

A good read. 
 A bit obvious throughout, which is okay. Much more importantly though, it seemed intellectually honest.

This is a booklet, not a book. I have been pondering the problem of free will for twenty years, it is a central part of the book I am just about to publish, so I was very interested to see what Mr. Harris had to say. I was extremely disappointed. 
 I was shocked by the shallowness of his arguments. The scientific evidence he draws on are experiments that I read about 15 years ago; I can't understand why he doesn't include the copious evidence against free will that neuroscience has amassed in the last decade. His other arguments seem adolescent or circular. There are no definitions of what "free," or "free will" mean. He just blithely assumes that the meanings are obvious. 
 He begins his book with the statement that the cultural clash over the issue of free-will/determinism will be more explosive than that over evolution. But his discussion of the consequences of our culture letting go of the belief in free will is appallingly brief. He addresses the most obvious issue, crime, but that's about it. Nothing about the more personal issues of shame and pride. Nothing about how this would affect my attitude towards someone who has hurt me, or how it would affect our cultural belief in a meritocracy where people deserve better compensation because of their abilities. 
 He ends with a flippant "proof" of his lack of free will by saying "I can end this book any time I want, and since I can't think of anything else to say on the subject and I'm hungry I'm going to stop now." I could think of a dozen things he hadn't discussed right off the top of my head! 
 If you're interested in free will, don't read this book. First read Incognito, by David Eagleman, for the latest neuroscience research and what this means about free will. Then read The Atheist's Guide to Reality, by Alex Rosenberg, for a thoughtful discussion of what no free will means for our society. Then read my new book, We Are ALL Innocent by Reason of Insanity, for insight on what no free will means for the individual, in addition to the culture. You can read my blog posts on free will here: http://www.innocentbyreasonofinsanity... 
 I did get one memorable idea from Mr. Harris' book: "Don't confuse determinism with fatalism," but he got that idea from someone else (philosopher Daniel Dennett). 
 Frankly I can't understand why this book was published. It is so light on substance it should have been a blog post. The only reason I could come up with was Mr. Harris thinks that free will is going to be a major issue in the near future, and he wanted to position himself as an authority and original source.

Now I no longer feel guilty because I didn't use my college education. (Or because I ruined my children's lives(just kidding). Forces beyond my control conspired against me :) For the most part I agreed with the book, even though Sam Harris' premiss can be depressing. I can't say it was an enjoyable read but it's something that needs to be said.

His use of science and logic is sound but his prose style made the essay seem like a lecture. And not an enjoyable lecture, but rather the old-fashioned finger-wagging kind. Yet could he have written it another way? I reckon not, right?

There's some food for thought in here, but ultimately, I don't think Harris convinced me of his argument. 
 It seems willfully narrow, and though I agree that I can't know where my impulses and desires come from exactly, that doesn't necessarily mean I don't choose what to do with them.

Sam Harris is a crystal-clear and highly efficient author, and this book is not an exception. He captures the age-old debate and his own formulations in 66 pages, and I don't think there are any deep errors in what he says in these 66 pages, but his clear-cut attitude - which I usually admire - rings too naive to me here, precisely because the classic definition of free will that he attacks is so problematic that I don't think it's worth wanting in any case. Yes, we are not "free" in that sense, but why should we take that sense seriously? Why should we even care when we learn that we don't after all possess a weird, illogical, undefinable, magical kind of freedom? Why should we trash the whole concept of freedom if it's not supernatural? Shouldn't we already have more realistic and practical expectations from the concept of freedom? The fact that Harris accuses compatibilists - who are giving definitions of freedom in a deterministic world - of doing bait and switch just shows that he in fact wants that magical freedom himself, and wouldn't settle for less. It's his choice, and he is as eloquent as ever at that; the book deserves the 3 stars just for that.

After reading Lying by Sam Harris, I thought I would give Free Will another shot. I tried reading it awhile ago, but it didn't grab my attention. And I can see why. The concepts in Free Will are much harder to grasp than in Lying. I understand that free will is a much more complicated topic than lying, and the language tends to reflect that, but it simply doesn't make for as engaging of a read. This book is challenging on many levels, and even has the potential to completely dismantle your view on reality -- if only it were more accessible!

reference_books.review_text:
Can we go back in time and find healing love again? 
 The challenge of the book is to make us wonder about such a possibility. 
 And it is a wonderful book that moves and transforms the reader. 
 I loved it. 
 Maria Carmo 
 Lisboa 20th. January 2010

reference_books.title: The Orange Girl
reference_books.review_text:
This book is a journey of self discovery where the universe itself recognizes its existence through the eyes of a Father and Son. This book is a journey, a love story, a love letter, and a challenge from a dead Father to a future son: the question about life, death and the will to be part even of a brief period of wonder in this beautiful universe. Loved it, it is certainly a GOODREAD!!! 
 Maria Carmo, 
 Lisbon 19th July 2012.

reference_books.review_text:

reference_books.title: Proof of Heaven: A Neurosurgeon's Journey into the Afterlife
reference_books.review_text:
An interesting account of the direct experience of a neurologist during seven days of coma and his discovery of other levels of awareness. 
 For a spiritualist, the book does not portray anything radically "new", but it has the advantage (for skeptics) of rendering the experience of a scientist who was, himself, a skeptic. 
 It is certainly a touching account of a significant experience, and of a life full of discovery. 
 Maria Carmo, 
 Lisbon, 2nd. July 2013.

sample_reviews.review_text:

 3. This text develops the factual information in a description pattern. 4. Some descriptions are given with a problem and solution or cause and effect reasoning. I would use the description webbing of each person as they are defined. Many of the people represented overcame physical or racial challenges in developing their gift. A connection to each person as Americans leaving their mark could be developed in a critical thinking activity with the Venn diagram. How is that person celebrated for their contribution?

Based on who will receive the book, this book is fabulous because he uses the simple words to inspire their daughters. However, the profound meaning in this book is valuable. For example, he provides some panjandrums of american to rise their patriotic of their nation. 
 Honestly, I was disappoint because I thought that he would talk about his obstacles when he was youth and how he cope with them, and what the lessons are but unfortunately he did not. In fact, I enjoyed with it ^_^

A decent idea, and the illustrations are pleasant enough...but the text itself suffered from a severe lack of oomph. The attempt to market a message of I-love-America (and also everyone in it...especially you! with "you" being simultaneously my daughters and whatever child is being read to! this is a very personal yet very expansive message!)...was too transparently about the message itself, rather than making a nice reading experience for little kids. Maybe it was a complex, loving message for his daughters at one point...but it lost that personal touch in the process of mass-production.
Gorgeous. Such a beautiful book that filled me hope and light during these super sad last few days.

I was very leery of this book, because in my experience politicians and celebrities rank about equal for successful children's book writing. In other words, odds are good that it will be bad. But I am so glad that I did eventually pick this one up and give it a try. President Obama has written a letter to his daughters that asks a question like "Have I told you that you are creative?" He then offers an example of a famous American who exemplifies that character trait, summing them up in a few lines. This is a celebration of what makes America great, but also what makes for a great person. It is a celebration of all we hope our children will become. 
 President Obama's words read like verse here. The structure is a strong one with a question, a person as an example, and words that sum that person up simply and powerfully. One of the pleasures of the book is that when you read it, you hear the President's voice in your head, because the cadence matches the way that he speaks so closely. Thanks to this, the book reads aloud beautifully. 
 Long's illustrations feature the two Obama girls and their dog. Then, as each famous American is mentioned, a child appears who is like that great person. So a girl with paintbrushes and palette is there when Georgia O'Keeffe is featured. A boy with a baseball bat, glove and ball is there when Jackie Robinson is given as an example of bravery. And they join the group, so that by the end there is a crowd of diverse children listening to the book along with you. Long's style changes when he depicts the famous Americans. Where the children are lighthearted and full of whimsy, there is a more serious feel to the great Americans. 
 A beauty of a book no matter who the author is, this book is one to be appreciated by all Americans no matter their politics. This will make a great holiday gift this year. Appropriate for ages 5-8.

What a great inspirational book for children! 
 Yes, you can be anything you set your mind to! 
 Loved the illustrations!

The illustrations were nice, and I liked the sentiment of the book but I found it a little strange and I wasn't sure why the entries were written the way they were. They were a bit disjointed, so I kept expecting some sort of rhyming verse that never appeared. But, it gets three stars because I like the idea and the ideals.
Nice little children's book.

This is a wonderful book for children. A picture book that tells a short, but sweet story about human diversity, ingenuity, determination, heart, creativity, and compassion. It really reminds me of learning, as a child, that America is great because we are a melting pot, but it also reminds me of learning as a child that all humans are family to each other in some way. 
 It's definitely a great book to teach kids about being human and about being different and how both of those things are awesome. It's inspiring, but it also educates. I learned about a couple of people from our past mentioned in the book that I'd never heard about before. And at the back of the book there is a little blurb about each person mentioned. 
 The book is also wonderfully illustrated with vivid color. Definitely worth reading with your kids!

Subtitled "A letter to my daughters," this book gives kids encouragement by naming some inspiring historical figures. For some reason, the poetry of it really struck me. I choked up on almost every page. This would be a good readaloud, but I probably wouldn't make it through!

 Below is my review for the Immortals series as a whole. Don't worry it doesn't contain any spoilers! 
 The Immortals series is aptly named: at times I felt it'd last an eternity. 
 But, Alyson Noel finally completes the Immortals series with the sixth and final installment, Everlasting. Evermore, Blue Moon, Shadowland, Dark Flame, Night Star and Everlasting comprise the complete series. Throughout these six books, Noel introduces readers to immortals, rouges, witches, ghosts, magic, magical dimensions and some interesting special abilities. 
 Overall, I enjoyed the Immortals series. It is an enchanting tale packed with romance and suspense. With an original plot, well-developed characters and plenty of action this series has a lot to offer. 
 However, it should have been condensed to three or four books. Evermore and Blue Moon start the series off with excitement and promise. From the first page of Evermore, I was hooked and completely captivated by Ever and Damon. I couldn't wait to turn the page and discover more about their story. Then it felt as if someone hit SLOW MOTION! Shadowland, Dark Flame and Night Star really started to drag on, and all three books left me disappointed. Throughout these novels, conflicts were being resolved and things were happening but still I found myself growing bored. And then I read Everlasting, the final book in the Immortals series. It was as if someone hit PLAY again- everything picked back up. As I fell back in love with Ever and Damen, I remembered why I originally liked this series. Noel finishes things off with a bang and does a wonderful job of tying this series together in the end. 
 Evermore-4 STARS 
 Blue Moon-4 STARS 
 Shadowland-2 STARS 
 Dark Flame-2 STARS 
 Night Star-2 STARS 
 Everlasting-4 STARS 
 I gave the Immortals series by Alyson Noel 3 STARS because that is what I felt it earned as an entire series. I would recommend reading this series at some point in time! 
 -XOXO 
 Reading, Eating & Dreaming
