reference_books.review_text: I checked this out on audio and couldn't make it more than 15% through the book. So, be warned, I don't know if the tone turns around. I just couldn't like the narrator. What starts as fun snark in general becomes wearisome in its selfish, unrelenting incapacity for any sort of empathy for others. It's tiring more than funny, and makes me feel guilty for those times I may revel in sarcasm past the point of common courtesy.

reference_books.title: Carsick
reference_books.review_text: As another reviewer put it, this book is a bait-and-switch. The hitchhiking premise is interesting, but the first 2/3 of the book are entirely fictional (first best-case scenarios, then worst-case). I went through this title on audiobook -- though, perhaps, "through" is the wrong word for it. I made it through the first 1/3 being amused and occasionally left open-mouthed with shocked hilarity. During the second third (worst-case scenarios) of the book, I only made it through the first two "bad rides" until I couldn't stomach any more. When John Waters wants to get nasty, no one can top him. Skipped the rest of the "bad rides" for the sake of my own psyche. Then the actual non-fiction section -- the last 1/3 of the book -- I didn't even finish. It was a dead bore filled with bad weather, whining, and smarmy flattery of his rides. Pass this title as memoir. Worth a skim for the fictional bits.

sample_reviews.review_text: I had a really difficult time connecting with the main character, which made it difficult for me to become invested in the story. I hated this book the first time I read it, but when it was chosen for book club I decided to try to give it a second chance and try to be more objective. It didn't work. I still hate it. 
 When I first read it I thought I only hated it because of the way it completely twisted some of my favorite novels from childhood (The Narnia Chronicles) but I realize now it's much more than that. This novel has been described as being "Harry Potter for adults" but that statement couldn't be more wrong. This is Harry Potter for adults who have become completely disillusioned by books about magic. There's nothing even magical about this book - Grossman turns magic into science and takes away everything that's magical about magic. The book feels completely sterile and antiseptic, with no heart or imagination at all; instead of the creativity and color Harry Potter inspires in my imagination, I pictured this whole world dreary and grey. The style and tone of the book made the narration feel toneless, and uninterested, which made it hard for me to care about what was happening or get into the story. I didn't like any of the characters in this novel - not because they were unlikable, but because I simply didn't care about them at all. 
 And I haven't even gotten into the minor things that bugged me, like the fact that the school's calendar is randomly 2 months off from the rest of the world for no apparent reason. I've discussed this book with some other people who defended it based on the fact that the tone is intentional and the author is trying to make a statement on these types of novels, but even if this is the case it just put me off the book entirely. If you're looking for Harry Potter for adults, do not read this book. Check out Jim Butcher's Dresden Files instead.

I'm still not entirely sure how I feel about this book. The structure is unusual in a way that might be flawed, or it might just be different from what I'm used to. There isn't a conventional story arc, but it's not arranged as a series of interludes connected by a device, either. Normally, a story with school at its center will be structured around the school time frame, but this isn't. Sometimes a lot of time passes with the narrative just skimming and skipping over things, then other times we stop and zoom in on things that don't necessarily move the plot or develop the characters, although they aren't really objectionable to read. And then the whole school thing turns out to be not so important, in a way. 
 I think the protagonist is problematic for me. I don't really like Quentin, but then he is an anti-hero and I'm not really supposed to like him. It's more that, while Quentin may be more realistic than a conventional hero, he doesn't feel real to me as a fully developed character. After everything he experiences, I still don't feel like I know him or understand what makes him tick. In some cases, I might say that was the desired effect, or I was just not connecting to that particular character, but in this case I'm afraid it's because the character isn't whole. 
 Overall, I still enjoyed the book to a reasonable extent, and I'm looking forward to seeing how the second book picks up the story and pushes the characters in hopefully new directions. I guess I'm supposed to talk about how the book is and is not like Harry Potter, or how Fillory is or is not like Narnia, but really, that's tiresome. It's refreshing to see the Hogwarts-like situation given such a different treatment, and the Narnia stuff seems like perfectly acceptable and somewhat traditional literary signifying.
Fantastic read. Can not wait to start the next book in the trilogy.
Got halfway through before the Young Adult and "don't think about things that are happening in the book" aspects got too large.

I'm giving up. Not only does this book really have no point behind it but it has stolen so much from other books that I just can't understand how Grossman could do it. First he actually uses some of the same made-up words and ideas from Harry Potter and then the last straw was when I realized that he used the same exact in-between type world as was used in the Magicians Nephew by C.S. Lewis. I mean come on.

Quentin is sort of the lovechild of Harry Potter and Holden Caulfield; this is his magical "coming of age." Q is self-centered, petty, insecure, and awkward...in short, your average teenager. This is a novel of his dreams and fuck ups, both spectacular. I really liked it, tho the pacing was a little off for me, and most of the time you want to strangle the protagonist. I'm not running out to devour book 2, but I'll get to it eventually.

I might change my two stars later when I have calmed down a bit, but good lord this book made me livid! If it was written well, all of the blatantly obvious references to The Secret History and fantasy literature (Harry Potter and Narnia in particular) would have been forgiven as they could be passed as homage or intertextuality. But the writing is so terrible (has anyone heard of an editor?), it came across as blatant freebooting (in print form). 
 A magical land visited by four English children (where only human children can sit on the four thrones)? 
 A wizard's school? 
 A hunt for a white stag? 
 A group of precocious and bored university students drinking themselves to death? 
 Drunken orgies in the woods? 
 A time-turner disguised as a pocket watch? 
 A form of wizard chess? 
 A world-between-the-worlds with ponds to jump into? 
 Seriously - are Donna Tartt and J.K. Rowling getting any royalties from this? 
 And lets not forget the worst line in the book: "Of course it matters, Vix," Quentin said. "It's not like they're all the same." "Vix" was a term of endearment with them, short for vixen, an allusion to their Antarctic interlude, vixen being the word for a female fox.

As other reviewers have said, equal parts Harry Potter, Narnia and Catcher in the Rye -- without the depth of any of them. Intriguing concept and there were moments I wanted to love this, but it's too rushed to get truly invested and that's to say nothing of your childhood hopes and dreams getting crushed by the biggest Eeyore of all protagonists imaginable . I'm not sure what Grossman was gunning for with the oppressive negativity, but his characters' collective lack of wonder, motivation and compassion doomed this book.

I have no earthy idea why this book is or ever was popular. The idea that SyFy bought the rights to the property and has made a television series from it blows my mind. To me this book read like J. K. Rowling's older, 'cooler' brother mansplaining all the ways in which Harry Potter was juvenile drivel. And true to form, by doing so the quibbler missed one of the very coolest things about Harry Potter: good or bad, rich or poor, gifted or average, cool or uncool, all of the students at Hogwarts are just that: students. The great social rift of girls below and boys above is practically ignored. 
 I tried to give The Magicians the benefit of the doubt. I mean, it is written from the POV of a teenage boy. The fact that Quentin's self-absorbed isn't a huge surprise, nor are his more neanderthal views on women. 
 Where I fell off the joy train was during the Antarctic portion of the program. First up, the Russian who runs the concentration camp they call a school is creepy to the point of vulgarity. The whole 'theft of voices' thing boded ill, but it wasn't until the 'hammer and nail' game that Grossman really hacked me off. 
 The scene is set thusly: a dank stone cell, a table and chair, a block of wood, a hammer and nails, and a fiddly spell so oft repeated to suit various conditions as fill the provided book. Our hero is set the task of completing every iteration of this pointless spell that's purpose is simply to allow the caster to drive a nail into a piece of wood with one whack of the hammer without bending said nail or crushing their thumb. The narrative expounds on the conditions covered ad nauseum: different locations, altitudes, weather -- some examples specific, some not. Finally, only three variables remain to be tested: the caster's gender: male, female or 'hermaphrodite.' Naturally, the protagonist balks over the last option like any genderist prig. 
 Obvious irks aside, why exactly are those the final three options? Wouldn't every iteration of the spell have three versions based on the caster's gender? Is it just a given that only a man would find himself having so much trouble driving a nail into a board 'on a tropical island during a snowstorm' that he would have to resort to magic? How does that even make sense? 
 I actually lasted a bit past that. It was when the entire fourth year class was turned into foxes as an excuse for wholesale rape that I gave up. The protagonist describes how the object of his desire's 'eyes roll in terror' as he penetrates her only to 'fog with pleasure' seconds later. (That was written by a true man...with no real sense of spacial relationships.) Our hero describes how uncomfortable things are the next day, wonders if his lady love is still a virgin...and all the other ridiculous garbage anyone with a lick of sense would avoid voicing at all cost. 
 I plan to return my copy to Audible because I just can't justify giving Lev Grossman a single dime.

book_b.title: The Good, the Bad, and the Undead (The Hollows, #2)
book_b.user_review: This is one of the few series that I have read through more than three times.

sample_reviews.review_text: Book two of this series is far better than the first, taking less time to get up to full speed and creating more and more mystery surrounding the primary characters. If you've read the first book, no hesitation recommending this one.

Another funny and quirky installment in The Hollows series. 
 I love characters and like the development of Trent Kalamack as a bad guy. Also like the extra info on Ivy, Piscari and the history involved. 
 Removed a star from my original rating due to authors tendency to add racist phrases. This time we have Glenn pretending to be an 'angry black man'. How about we include characters from traditionally marginalized backgrounds and treat them like every other character. Thanks

I like this world that the author has built but I don't love the story. I plan to continue reading the series. I may not make it the whole way through, but for now, it has me engaged. I'm curious about what happens next.

Funny things - reviews. Perusing reviews of this one, it seems many were bored with the first compared to this, and reviews for the first commented on IT'S slow start. It seems I'm always in the minority - I think the original Dead Witch Walking is an amazing book, and I found it fast-paced from the start. I didn't find it slow and I thought the action was in your face from the beginning. With this one, though, the book is again excellent but the beginning is much slower than the firsts. 
 Even if the first book had an amazing, tense first half, this one took the slower path. In fact, if it weren't the second section being so impressive, I would have given it a four star rating. One thing's for sure - this one doubled with the first made such a killer impression on me that nothing could have kept me from immediately seeking out and reading the third. 
 The story starts cute with Jenks (love him) and Rachel working, earning money, and of course falling into pits of trouble. There's a bona fide crime whodunnit with this one. The murders are icky, dirty and horrid too. While Rachel isn't what I'd call a sleuth, she's awesome in her persistence and having bad luck stumble her way. The books focus is of course the protagonist Rachel. She discovers a big secret on why she survived her childhood illness, connections she had no idea existed, and that her abilities dab in darker areas than she could have imagined. 
 There's a nice climax with Piscary, the big bad master vamp of the city, and the demon who made a killer appearance in the first, Algaliarept (Nicknamed 'Al'.) Seriously, the villain spotlights? Best parts of the book. I LOVED the surprise when Al popped up and deals made, and Piscary in the pizza joint? Creepy. Kisten? OMG. Really. How hot can one of the scenes get? Nick as the boyfriend is still a bit dull but there was a juicy session. Ivy's okay and hasn't grown on me yet enough. I love that in this book you get to reach Rachel's mother, Alice, who is hilarious, tragic, and intriguing in one package. 
 Rachel's flaws make her easier enough to genuinely like. In this book she finds out something large about herself, and what she can do. Always she struggles with morals. 
 Harrison is great at adding credible detail to the magic, keeping it realistic, detailed and intriguing. I love her back history with all the supernatural communities and the comical history of the Turn. This one holds a bit more gruesome details than the other but it's still not considered a gory book. 
 The ending has an a big turn that made me nearly salivate to pick up the third and see where it leads off. Epic battle and great lead-up, even if the first half was a bit slow.

Much better than book #1 in the Rachel Morgan/The Hollows series. I don't even know why. Maybe because this one read more like a mystery? Because Rachel didn't behave like an idiot for once? Sure, she did have several spazzy moments - like when she tipped over the jar with Bob - but she didn't behave outright stupid this time. On the other hand, she blamed Nick for his recklessness in dealing with demons, but it was she who made the biggest, most awful blunder of all. 
 Though there were a couple of things that bothered me: 
 a) Her blind need to prove that Trent committed all those murders, the way she disregarded both Edden and Glenn's concerns, the way she kept blaming them and calling them cowards when they tried to reign her in. 
 b) Her relationship with Nick. I just didn't buy it. And the ending proved me right, when she was more excited about the car and her payment than worried about Nick and what she was doing to him using ley line magic. 
 Overall though, it was a nice read with fast action and an intriguing plot. And the fact that Trent Kalamack reminded me of Lex Luthor helped, of course. He was awesome!

Definitely liked the plot line more than the first book, but I am still having a hard time warming up to Rachel Morgan. She makes impulsive and at times stupid decisions, and basically survives from sheer luck and untapped skill she didn't know she had. 
 Be that as it may, I love Trent and Glenn, and this book and its characters really stepped up a notch with its small details such as Glenn's secret obsession with ketchup, and Trent's little rebellions against his handlers. These small things bring the characters out a little more. Too bad Rachel has none of that charm.

Review: 
 I had to put this book down several times for extended periods of time because I got irritated with the main protagonist. I knew from book 1 that she can be irritatingly stupid but after I put the book down for sometime I'd forget just how irritating and pick the book up again. It was like that, on and off, on and off, until I eventually finished reading it after more than two years. Maybe a more forgiving reader might find this book a quicker read than I did. 
 Rachel Morgan, the main protagonist, is just this side of stupid who blunders around from danger to danger and survived by sheer dumb luck. Not only does she endangers herself, but also people around her. WTF!! Character development? I think that rates really low. However, there is also Jenks. Who became my instant favourite pixie! Tends to fly around my head and sass every single character in the book! And then there's Big Al! Shrouded in mystery and not quite sure yet whether he would turn out to be the biggest bad guy in the entire Rachel Morgan world, but he's likeable to me! I hope he turns out to be not too bad... 
 Come to think of it, I think everybody else in the Rachel Morgan world is well developed, even the bad guys' characters. It's only the main protagonist who is too stupid to live. 
 I really like the world building. It's rich and vibrant. It's painted with skillfull and masterfull flair. It got all the good fantasy elements, fairies, weres, witches, and vampires, yet still feel authentic. The kind of urban fantasy world which really appeals to my fantasy buff self. However I couldn't stand the annoying stupidity of the main protagonist. It's just too irritating! I don't think I would be buying anymore books in this series. If ever, I would borrow it from the library than waste my money. 
 Empirical Evaluation: 
 Story Telling Quality = 3.5 
 World Building = 5 
 Character Development = 2.5 
 Pace = 1 
 Plot = 2 
 Ending = 1.5 
 Overall Rating: 2 out of 5

reference_books.title: Persepolis: The Story of a Childhood (Persepolis, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
A coming of age story, told via graphic novel, through the eyes of a young girl (of communist tendencies) during the Iranian Islamic Revolution. 
 Very good stuff!

reference_books.title: Laika
reference_books.review_text:
This is a lovely graphic novel that offers a fictionalized account of the life and death of the eponymous dog (and Hero of the Soviet Union), the first living creature launched in orbital space flight. 
 The story is at its heart a comment on the nature of human/ animal relationship, and one of the keys to its success (in my eyes), is Abadzis' refusal to anthropomorphise the central character. Throughout, she remains a dog, and her journey is shaped by those powerful forces around her. 
 Well worth checking out.

reference_books.title: Goldfinger (James Bond, #7)
reference_books.review_text:
Fleming's Bond is a vain, quite stupid, racist and misogynist pig. He's also reasonably rubbish at this spying lark. Seriously, he makes plenty of mistakes that should have ended up in his death. For the reader, alas he makes it out alive this time around. 
 Indeed, despite coming across as a vapid banality, somehow this Bond chap even manages to seduce a number of lesbians, who don't seem to be at all concerned with his casual racism. Oh, and he's the hero. The extended description of the round of golf must go down as one of the most tedious things ever put down on paper. 
 Even worse than the tedium, is the ludicrous plotline. Why on Earth the limp villain decides to spare Bond's life (despite having him as good as dead), is beyond this reader. I understand the need to further the narrative, but you'd think that Fleming could have come up with something a bit more believable than this. 
 This is a silly book with an odious main character. I see very little to recommend it.

reference_books.title: The Postman Always Rings Twice
reference_books.review_text:
The Postman Always Rings Twice, by James M. Cain was quite notorious upon its initial publication in 1934, and must be regarded as one of the more important crime novels of the twentieth century. It's a suspenseful race through a story filled with a raw mix of sexuality and violence that must have been shocking at the time. 
 The tale of a ne'r do well drifter, a young, beautiful broad and her much older husband "the Greek". Of course, a passionate affair develops, with more than a hint of sadomasochism underwriting their attachment. Thus, a scheme is hatched for them to be together. I expect that you don't have to have seen the film(s) to see where this is going... 
 Even better than Double Indemnity, this taut thriller is a rollercoaster ride from go to whoa. Double thumbs up.

reference_books.title: Into the Water
reference_books.review_text:
Sometimes a novel just has too much going on for the reader to keep on top of it. When you've got a lot of characters, and those characters are not particularly well constructed or differentiated, I'd recommend NOT switching between narrators each chapter. 
 Even a good author would struggle with this creative choice. Unfortunately, Hawkins is not that. I'm surprised it made it to print in this state, to be frank.

book_a.title: Housekeeping
book_a.user_review:
This one was quite a tricky read for me in some respects, and a really strong example of a 'feminine' novel. A melancholy, lyrical story, submerged in in water, light and cold about three generations of women stuck in the American Pacific North-West. 
 Ruth is our narrator, who guides us through a haunting story of loss, place and transience. Abandonment really is at the heart of the novel, both in a physical and spiritual sense. Robinson readily incorporates vivid descriptions of the natural environment to explore the fragility of human relationships and the transitory nature of the physical world. It's a hard book to talk about, and I'm still working some of it through my head, but I did appreciate the vibrant contrast of the violence, majesty and impermanence of the natural world with human attempts to control uncertainty. The tragedy of these particular women's lives and the failure of each of them to 'succeed' in maintaining conventional social relationships - especially that of 'family' !- is especially moving. 
 The (almost) complete absence of male characters is particularly telling, and I suspect that it is deliberate. Indeed, it does accentuate the marginality of these women in their society and subverts patriarchal notions of family, social order, and gender roles. That said, I'm not sure that the misfortune of their existence is much of liberationist statement. Maybe it isn't. This is a challenging and moving read. I think that I'd recommend it, but suspect I'll still be mulling it over for some time yet.

sample_reviews.review_text: I was just never able to get into this one; maybe it was the story that wasn't of much interest to me, but I can't pinpoint it.

Quotes from the book that I enjoyed: 
 "...one's destination was there from the very beginning, a measured distance away, standing in the ordinary light like some plain house where one went in and was greeted by respectable people and was shown to a room where everything one had ever lost or put aside was gathered together, waiting." 
 "It is, as she said, difficult to describe someone, since memories are by their nature fragmented, isolated, and arbitrary as glimpses one has at night through lighted windows." 
 "For when does a berry break upon the tongue as sweetly as when one longs to taste it, and when is the taste refracted into so many hues and savors of ripeness and earth, and when do our senses know anything so utterly as when we lack it?" 
 "For to wish for a hand on one's hair is all but to feel it." 
 "Though we dream and hardly know it, longing, like an angel, fosters us, smooths our hair, and brings us wild strawberries." 
 "For in fact I wore her coat like beatitude, and her arms around me were as heartening as mercy, and I would say nothing that might make her loosen her grasp or take one step away." 
 "The force behind the movement of time is a mourning that will not be comforted."

Typically, I am drawn to books with strong character development. I live vicariously through them - enduring trials and enjoying adventures. Housekeeping is not that kind of book. There is little plot, and the characters are neither developed nor memorable. However, the writing in this book is exquisite. The author's words evoke such imagery and mood. I often found myself pausing to let the words puddle and swirl in my mind, reflecting before moving on. 
 Examples: 
 Buttercups are the materialization of the humid yellow light one finds in such places... But the deep woods are as dark and stiff and as full of their own odors as the parlor of an old house. We would walk among those great legs, hearing the enthralled and incessant murmurings far above our heads, like children at a funeral. (98) 
 They were like the people in old photographs - we did not see them through a veil of knowledge and habit, but simply and plainly, as they were lined or scarred, as they were startled or blank. Like the dead, we could consider their histories complete... (179) 
 The fruit trees were all bare, and their leaves on the ground were as limp and noisome as wet leather. The sky was a strong, plain blue, but the light was cool and indirect and the shadows black and precise. There seemed to be no wind at all. We could watch the heat from the fire pull and tease the air out f shape, stretching the fabric of dimension and repose with its furious ascending. (199)

I have a real desire to love Marilynne Robinson. She takes literature seriously; she takes thinking seriously; she's a little defensive about how seriously she takes these things. She doesn't churn out novel after novel after novel, implying that she actually thinks about what she's writing. She's hyper-intellectual and the prose of her essays is very, very effective. 
 But this? This is not, Mr/s Blurb Writer, a modern classic and it does not, Paul Gray (Time Magazine) "brilliantly portray the impermanence of all things." It's intellectually ambitious, sure, but just as with Gilead, I feel like the characters, the ideas, the prose and myself are all keeping each other at arm's length. Here we have the typical 'smart' writer's dilemma of having an uneducated, quiet and unsocial character as narrator of a hyper-intellectual, language-loving and garrulous narrative. We have the common problem of intriguing literary symbolism (small town on lake/many drownings/ties to Noah's Ark, memory and human community) slowly but surely becoming child-like metaphysics, which might be nice sometimes, but, when treated with this much gravity ("It had never occurred to me that words, too, must be salvaged... it was absurd to think that things were held in place, are held in place, by a web of words"), is particularly tiresome. We have strunk'n'whitean simplicity masquerading as genius. 
 Now all that said, it's impressive and I love the ambition. This is a review of my re-reading, and I intend to re-read Gilead (which I remember being a little less adolescent-girl-with-camera metaphysically frou-frou than this one, thank the Lord) and finally get around to reading Home (which I am hoping continues Gilead's trend towards a more social-religious focus). But I have a hunch that when we finally move on from the deification of MFA programs, this will be the kind of thing that's re-discovered every few decades, rather than taken as definitive for its time. The alternative, I guess, is that we keep deifying MFA programs, this stays in endless print, but nobody outside of universities reads anything other than Maxim and Cosmo. 
 Addendum: it can't have helped that I read half of this before, and half after, Powers' Morte D'Urban, which similarly treats the theme of worldliness/unworldliness, and is similarly ambiguous about the relative merits of these traits, but does so with much humor and lightness of touch. It seems weird to say, but Robinson's book might well strike me as more successful if I was comparing it to Dostoevsky, for instance, than Powers.

I started reading this a LONG time ago, finally picked it back up this month and finished it. It's beautifully written, with sharp, gorgeous imagery. It's also deeply, deeply sad, profoundly lonely. I could only read it in short pieces, because it filled me with a sort of terrible, keen emptiness at times. Effective, in that sense, but not something I will be rereading.

Ever pick up a book that has so many good reviews, with a description reminiscent of other books you've liked, that it seems practically guaranteed that you'll love it? And then you get to the end and think, "That's it?" I guess this is one of those books that I just didn't "get." 
 Ms. Robinson uses some beautiful imagery; she probably spent years polishing and perfecting her descriptions of her characters and the setting. But it never clicked with me. I didn't feel particularly attached to any of the characters, aside from a vague sympathy for Ruth and Lucille. In fact, the characters that were most real to me were the two sisters-in-law who took care (by a loose definition) of the girls after their grandmother died and before Sylvia came; I thought the way they finished each others' thoughts was hilarious. But most of the book I just waited for something to happen. And waited. And waited some more. 
 Unfortunately, just didn't do it for me. 
 For more book reviews, come visit my blog, Build Enough Bookshelves.

One of the most touching, beautiful books I've ever read. Robinson takes us inside a sensitive but eccentric personality, shy, perhaps even neurotic, depressed--who knows? Some people were not meant to fit even, even when they try. I give this book to people all the time, sometimes they get it, sometimes they don't. Which of course tells me a lot about them. I love this book.
The plot wasn't particularly compelling but her writing had many moments of loveliness.
too boring to finish

one of the hardest books for me to get through (the only others being books by Virginia Woolf if that tells you anything about my tastes), because frankly nothing interesting happens. The heightened language the author uses to create mood in the very thin plot is self-conscious and unnecessary. book_b.title: god is Not Great: How Religion Poisons Everything
book_b.user_review: Hitchens calmly and succinctly dismantles the notion of 'God' across multiple religons a mixture of personal stories, documented historical anecdotes and critical analysis of religious texts. Fantastic. A-.

sample_reviews.review_text:
There are books where you can honestly say, "it changed my life," and god is not Great is one of those books for me. I grew up in the Episcopal church ("Catholic light" as Robin Williams so brilliantly put it once) and I attended a private Christian School. I'd like to say I always resisted, and that my being an atheist was there from the beginning, but I'm a terrible liar. I think I always was a skeptic, I just didn't have the language and emotional maturity to really just come out and say what I was. When I discovered Hitchens through the Daily Show I eventually bought a copy of god is not Great, and read it over the summer after I graduated high school. I don't remember it being a pleasant experience, in fact I often had to put the book down and cry or just breath because I had finally found the voice that made sense. 
 This was my fourth time reading this book, and having grown older (and I hope wiser), I'm mature enough now to realize what this book is: the first real effort for a public atheist to speak his ground. As Hitchens notes in the book, atheists and non-believers often suffered publicly for their non-belief and this book then is an attempt to publish the position of atheism without fear of severe public reprisal. That doesn't I don't have conflicts with this book. Reading it again there were plenty of times I felt that Hitchens was pushing his position to far, or else engaged in some generalization and "othering," but I still defend this book because of it's station. 
 god is not Great is a book that will give young, and old, atheists their first real argument against belief and faith in the divine. And from this reading they'll hopefully experience other books which will help them figure out what their own personal position is. Every atheist should read this book because it's a jumping point from which a deeper more mature atheism can develop. 
 At the moment I'm working on a chapter by chapter analysis of god is not Great for my site White Tower Musings, and as soon as I have the up I'll update this review. If the reader is interested though they can read the first post I ever wrote for WTM, which was about Hitchens and god is not Great and Letters to a Young Contrarian. 
 https://jsjammersmith.wordpress.com/2...

I gave it an honest try. I got to page 183 of 280. It took me 39 days. Why'd it take me that long to read 183 pages? 
 Because this book is ridiculous. I hate every word of it. It's biased, it's masturbatory, it's closed minded, it's self aggrandising, it's bigoted, and all the while it's congratulating itself on being so logical and rational and so much LESS biased and closed-minded than religion. 
 When my friend Alex recommended it to me I said I'd read it, and that is why I tried so hard. I can't remember though why he recommended it. I am already an atheist. All I can recall from the night he recommended it was how angry he got when we were talking about women in atheism, and how oblivious he was that his comments were so misogynistic. 
 Then Marie sent me this link today, on an unrelated matter: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I7izJg... 
 After watching it I gave myself permission to quit his book. He is a jerk. His book is rubbish.

I just finished reading Christopher Hitchens' exhaustive catalog of the violence and oppression perpetrated by the great religions from antiquity to the present day, God Is Not Great. 
 The book's subtitle, How Religion Poisons Everything, would have been a more fitting title. 
 Hitchens was a well-read atheist, a free-thinker and a good man, I think. In his book, he made the case that morality does not depend on religion -- just look at how religion itself has endorsed all manner of evil from genocide to slavery. 
 Too true. 
 If only Hitchens were still alive. I would have loved to see him give the same treatment to politics, which is becoming more and more like a religion and is proving to be just a divisive with so many all-or-nothing, no-compromise players in the game. (He was certainly aware of how cynical politicians have always known how to use religion -- and the religious -- to their advantage.) 
 Hitchens' book rightly promotes free inquiry and the scientific method. To him, the explanations offered by science were far more satisfying than those offered by religion. To me, science is great with the what and how of life but not so good with its ultimate meaning. 
 But there, I must admit, the explanations of the great religions aren't very satisfying either.

I hate not finishing books I start. I don't know why that is. But that first title, God Is Not That Great, was just soooo boring, that when I came across a free book pile that had books that I was actually interested in reading, I had to swap it. So I swapped it for The Kindness of Strangers, which greatly disappointed me because it wasn't that much better! I think it was a little too out of date for me to relate to, which is why I didn't like it. It was about this journalist from the Beeb and how she started out and worked her way up. I couldn't relate not because it was British but because of how things work. This women just stumbled through life and ended university like when the BBC was just starting its affiliates outside of London and they were like taking anyone who was interested and today it sooo doesn't work like that. The story ended before 9/11 and the end of the book was just like all complaining about how things are done today with like international journalism, which does suck that it's getting all condensed and stuff, but that is just the future. Companies can't afford to have like reporters in every city just waiting for something to happen. They have to use the local media from that city to get their details. And boohoo, online is making everything go quicker! Get with the times! This book was kind of a disappointment which I had such high hopes for the topic. 
 Grade: D+
Ugh... just awful

I don't know if I can write a review fitting for this book. It is not so much an argument against religion as it is a rant against it. As a collection of sins, it is a great collection. It is a starting point for an endless and perhaps pointless study of theism. 
 Do not read this as an argument against religion. It is one-sided, bombastic, and incisive, but it is not an examination of pros and cons, not in a traditional sense. Politics produces atrocities; do we do away with it altogether? Do we ban politicians? Males have a very long history of abusing women and children. Do we lock all males away for life? Yes, religion has been shameful, but does that mean it is all invalid? The author does not touch on its good points in any meaningful way. He does not acknowledge that schools and hospitals exist because of religion. He does not concede that charitable organizations exist largely because of religion. This is a rant, a justified and moving rant, but it is not a complete argument. 
 Hitchens' concept that religion is a fossilized philosophy is interesting. It is the point that hit me the hardest. Religion is philosophy with the questioning left out, and that bothers me the most. I question everything. 
 It is a difficult read. He makes obscure references with no backfill, makes multiple references per paragraph, sometimes seemingly unrelated, and he leaves lines of cause and effect open ended but states them as fact. As a university essay it probably fails miserably, but as a weekend read, it is powerful and staggering. Have Google open always.

Again, what is your argument? You don't like religion therefore there is no god? Like Dawkins, this author makes the argument from silence. Obviously (given current stats on religion in the developed world), there are few people that continue to be delighted with the impact of religion and religious authority throughout history but what has any of that to do with the god question? Clearly all the references to religion are much more damning of humanity. Using this logic we should also reject quantum physics because we cannot understand Descartes earliest impression of animals. I love the question but I simply cannot abide the simplistic and unintelligent arguments.

To find truth, I expect the use of logic, examination of the opposing view's strongest point, and as much objectivity as possible. We find none of this in the book. 
 Atheists and scientists are described as intelligent and anyone religious (Christian, Muslim or others) gets the most derogative adjective possible. This sheds no light on truth. 
 All religions and sects are considered much the same. This is not because Hitchens did not have a thorough knowledge of history, the Bible, church history and religions. He does. But by blurring the lines, he is able to paint a very negative picture of religion. Even the atrocities of atheistic regimes are traced back to religion. This is done by highlighting the interaction between religious leaders and the totalitarian systems; Hitler's Third Reich and others. 
 Why read this book? It is worth reading to get an understanding of the New Atheists propaganda and methods, but don't expect to reliable information on God's existence or goodness.

This book reads like a long, sometimes incoherent, rant. I mostly found myself hating Christopher Hitchens while reading it, especially during the times when he argues that it's biological destiny for men to want to masturbate all the time, kind of purports a pro-life stance, equates the physical & psychological trauma of female genital mutilation to male circumcision, and reduces the problems in Iraq to simply issues of religion. Frankly, if you are looking for a thoughtful book on atheism and/or religion, this is not it. If you are a 12 year old boy and really pissed off at religion, this is the book for you.

For a long time, I tried really hard to become a believer. In high school, I dated someone who wanted to be a youth minister. I would go to church with him, I would sing in the choir, go to youth group, try and pray and I never got anything out of it. I never felt what all these other people claimed to feel. He ended up breaking up with me because I didn't believe the way he wanted me to. And from then on, I just stopped trying and I never looked back. I have many problems with religion(especially organized religion) and this book outlines every single one of them. I understand it works for some people. I am not one of those people. People have been killing each other for thousands of years arguing over who has the better imaginary friend. Christopher Hitchens brings his own wit and personal insight into this book. It was very well researched and written so that each chapter is like its own essay. making it easy to put down and come back to when you have time to read it. I would recommend this book to nonbelievers and anyone interested in theology.

reference_books.title: The Vow
reference_books.review_text:
This books is an account of the true events that the movie is based upon, narrated by Kim Carpenter. That being said, I knew it was not going to be as compelling and dramatic as the movie was. Regardless I decided to read it anyway. 
 *SPOILERS SPOILERS SPOILERS* 
 In my opinion it started off well and was alright to read until after the accident which is around chapter 3. At this point it got unbearably repetitive. All Kim had to say was she didn't recognise him, he kept making trips back to see her but she was unresponsive, she didn't recognise that he was her husband and so on. These facts were repeated over and over on every single page!! It did my head it and I must have skipped at least 50 pages in between the chapters. 
 And then when its finally been made clear enough that she didnt recognise him/didnt respond to him blah blah blah, we get to the point where Kim is told that they need to start over and fall in love again. EXCEPT there is no description of how this happens!! All we are told is that they go out on some dates and Krickett decides she wants to remarry him! 
 I know this is not a novel but really the story could have been written better to make it more readable. As I mentioned before I got to then end of the book by reading the first line on each page and skipping ahead, it was that boring.

reference_books.title: A Game of Thrones (A Song of Ice and Fire, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Scarred for life, not listening to other peoples recommendations again.

reference_books.title: Unravel Me (Shatter Me, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
I couldn't stand this book. It made me want to rip my hair out. I wanted to throw it at the wall. I wanted to light it on fire. I wanted to rip out each individual page and then shred it and then light each of those on fire. It gave me a headache. It made my head throb and pound. Reading this book was awful. 
 So I think ive made my point. Unravel me is the epitome of redundant. And I couldn't handle it. Yes I know it's a literary device but seriously. I think I must have skipped 3 pages for each one I read throughout most of the book. Every other page we would come across juliette thinking something like "and im breaking, and my bones are shattering, falling into a thousand pieces. Each one of like glass, ripping my insides..."" BLAH BLAH BLAH on every-freaking-page!!! 
 In short this book was unbearable, and if you want to actually keep your mind sane, dont bother. I finished this today after a very painful 2 days, and I feel like my brain has melted. 
 If you can ignore the writing, the story is good. There was enough mystery to keep me interested, which is why i kept ploughing through the blizzard that was the prose. 
 All.in all I cannot give this more than one star because of how painful it was to read.

reference_books.title: The Fellowship of the Ring (The Lord of the Rings, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
To sum up my rant LOTR IS BORING AS HELL! Think of the most boring, dull, unentertaining experience of your life and LOTR is 10 times worse than that. In my opinion don't bother! But if your still thinking about it, here are a few reasons why I hated this soo much. 
 I really wanted to read this, I mean I really wanted to say "yes I read lord of the rings, it was pretty good" but JRR Tolkien did not want that. Honestly I have never read anything as dull as The Fellowship of the Ring. Even the Hobbit which was pretty boring was nothing compared to this. In the end I actually had to give up and here is why: 
 1) Hobbits are boring. All they do is eat, tell long boring stories, eat some more, sing a song, eat again, and then finally eat a little bit more because they still aren't satisfied. I swear in one of the scenes it said they spent a good 3/4 of an hour EATING NON STOP. Are you serious!? 
 2) The ring causes a lot of problems but we don't know why. for at least 70% of the book (which is all i could read) we don't know why the ring is bad, we just know it causes a bunch of problems. We also don't know anything about the dark lord who is supposedly trying to get hold of Frodo for the ring. And we don't know what frodo is going to do about it either. OHH and frodo has been told like 50 times to not use the ring but he does anyway. 
 3) 50% of the novel is about a group of hobbits on a journey and they don't know where they are going or what they are afraid of. The other 45% of the novel is about another journey, where they do know where they are going but that doesnt help them achieve anything or make it any more interesting than the first half. 
 4) The word "merrymaking" is honestly driving me up the wall. That's like all hobbits care about - eating and merrymaking by singing a bunch of really long and boring songs. I swear to god they do not do anything useful throughout the novel, all they care about is BLOODY MERRYMAKING! 
 5) WHAT THE HELL IS MORDOR? I guess I will never find out because the book was so boring i couldn't get through it. 
 Like I said I reallly wanted to finish this book because this is the second time I've tried to read it. I thought that last time I just couldnt get into it because I was really young, but honestly who actually enjoys this stuff? 
 Beleive me I tried to finish it, but after I got to the end of book one with a great deal of difficulty I could not go on. In book two I was at the point where I was reading one sentence in each paragraph. By the time i got to chapter 2 of book two, i read one paragraph and skipped three, until I eventually just skipped chapter 2 and went to chapter 3 which i skipped completely. The last thing I read was the first sentence of chapter 4 book two and that drew the line. That was when I shut it for good and I'm not going back!

reference_books.title: Insurgent (Divergent, #2)
reference_books.review_text: This book was slow. I didn't really get into it at all and found it to be uninteresting. The story might have been good but I found it boring. I forced myself along for a while but finally gave up.

book_a.title: Love, Rosie
book_a.user_review: Frustrating to no end. Completely unbelievable - as if a heart surgeon doesn't know the difference between "know" and "no". as if people write their life story in a great big long instant message. both Rosie and Alex are completely stupid. complete load of rubbish hated it.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Rei, llore y me enamore con esta historia, tan real y tan unica a la vez, Rosie y Alex son el uno para el otro pero no aun despues de tanto tiempo todavia no se han dado cuenta y eso a veces estresa, aunque dicen que lo mejor se hace esperar. 
 El que nazca todo de una amistad incondicional, lo hace perfecto porque ves todo paso a paso, como te dicen las madres que deberia de ser, asi que te da una buena idea del enamoramiento, aunque a veces doloroso, pero he ahi la delicia de la cruel realidad.
Good book but not amazing. 3.5

The only reason why I think I continued to read (or commit) to this book was because of the writing style. How it was written in letters or emails or chats, responding to one another. But honestly, it was so lengthy, and it had unnecessary drama. I am somewhat upset that I wasted time reading/finishing this book, but I guess that's the reality of the situation given. The beginning was, no doubt, adorable. 7 year old children writing notes to each other-incorrect grammar, naughty actions and funny nicknames. However, as things progressed, it became sad and lonely and somewhat annoying. Their problems became less problematic and more let me hit these characters in the head with a brick because this is too much. 
 Nevertheless, I committed myself to reading this because of the letters/writing style. Ahern doesn't do anything too special with the story or the characters, but she does create a beautiful friendship between a girl and a boy that every person desires. I think we all have friendships that either stick it out forever, which we would never know until the end I suppose, or friendships that fade away. It's important to understand or realize which ones you need to fight for and which ones are just bumps in your journey-either way, I guess it would be hard to know which ones are which at the time. 
 Love, Rosie is filled with heartbreak, betrayal, love and funny anecdotes. While I didn't seem to enjoy this, I am sure those interested in romance and realistic fiction would love to see the relationship between Rosie and her best friend Alex develop and shape who they become by the end.

I'm a huge fan of Cecelia Ahern, I've yet to read one of her stories that I don't love.

 If you're a fan already, then definitely give it a go.

I have some issues and some high praises to lend this book. Let me start by saying that I liked the movie better for so many reasons, and that the book's format actually came as the biggest shock to me. I think that's my greatest problem with the story, in fact. I spent the first 200 pages of the novel trying to recover from the discomfort a book made up entirely of unrealistic letters gave me. 
 That's the second problem I have with the book. The plot itself does have its loops and twists that make you scream "Oh, get real!" But it is a story and if you can remember that, you'll do yourself a fantastic favour. My problem with it lies with the unrealistic version of this story. 
 It is 500 pages of emails and letters spanning 45 years. Yes, the epilogue tells you that majority of them are kept by Rosie through her life, but still. NO ONE emails and mails letters as much as the people in this story do, and even if they do, they don't put painful details in their messages that creep as deep as the colour of the car being driven or the suit being worn. If this had been a story told in a normal context, those details would not have felt out of place, but because the letters are the only eyes we have to this plot, those details have to be there and therefore feel EXTREMELY forced. 
 A lot of the book feels forced in fact. Alex and Rosie both get divorced like a million times, divorcees in a chat room spend a literal decade complaining about their ex-husbands and half the letters/ emails are waaaaay too peppy. 
 The story itself has so much worth and potential. It's a beautiful and tragic tale about two best friends who just can't seem to get together no matter what. The characters are likeable, the book is actually hilarious at times - FREAKING HILARIOUS-- and the story line provides some unexpected turns. The boring parts aren't even boring. Overall it's well written and fresh and keeps you excited the entire way which deserves an applause. But the book attaches those great attributes with a feeling of forced detail and that goes in waves of being quite irritating as you read along. 
 Another point I must make is in regards to the truth of the story. There's so many lines in this book that are so true to life. I applaud Cecilia Ahern for being so perceptive and honest. I think the fact that these characters are literally finding their way through life really opens opportunities for there to be these moments of depth that the author can shine a light on and I loved it so so much. 
 Would I read this book again? No. Would I watch the movie again? Probably more than 100 times-- because this story really is beautiful and exciting, quirky and intoxicating.. I just think it needs to be told in a different way, and I'm happy that there's two running versions of it.

** spoiler alert ** 
 As you know, this is the 6th book in the Odd Thomas series and deals with Odd coming across a dangerous cowboy who has plans to kill a bunch of children. Odd starts a cross-state hunt to stop him and along the way he meets 86-year old Edie Fischer, who helps him on his way; she's as mysterious as AnnaMaria but far more action oriented. 
 I LOVED the first Odd Thomas, as most of us did, and didn't really feel I needed a sequel. But we got them, with varying success. I have found the odd-numbered books better than the even-numbered, and that is especially true for this book. I am not a slow reader and bought the UK edition of the book the day it came out - and one month later I'd barely gotten halfway through. Up until then I'd only liked chapter 14 and some few - VERY few - scenes that came before and after. That first half of the book is the most boring stuff I'd ever had to paddle through. I know, I could just stop, but I have promised myself to read all of the Odd series, even though I feel Koontz has lost his grip on what makes books, well, gripping. Back in the day I was the biggest Koontz-fan in Europe (maybe an exaggeration, but I was a BIG fan), but in recent years he's just been lacking in quality. I'm not only talking about him going overboard with his catholicism and right-wingery either, he seems to have lost the edge, to dare going to dark places, and in this book his descriptions of skies and seas and lakes and houses and rooms and the such REALLY went into overdrive, so much so, that I occasionally zoned out and just read the damn paragraphs without really absorbing them, but just to get them over with. We don't NEED half page descriptions of some room, ESPECIALLY not in the middle of a chase. Also, hammers on anvils isn't the best way to describe even the hardest rain, methinks. 
 Often his descriptions of the most mundane things are laughingly stupid. Like: "Blood has an odor faint but distinct, of conceit and modesty, of courage and cowardice, of charity and greed, of faith and doubt, in short the fragrance of what we might have been and the smell of what we are..." No, Koontz, the smell of blood is coppery and sweet, no more, no less. This isn't even clever or profound, it's just a ramble of the worst kind. 
 At one point he even had Odd mention that he'd read a book called Twilight Eyes. 
 Later, as he's driving with Edie, they start talking about laws and she says something about "idiot laws" and Odd asks "what law?" and she says, "Oh, all kinds of laws, sweetie. Idiot safety laws, bone-headed environmental laws that actually contribute to pollution..." I know that you're a Republican, Koontz, but you're still allowed to think for yourself and not believe every lie Fox News tells you about pollution and/or global warming; it's not a hoax, maybe if you actually READ the gazillion, independent studies on it and its effects, instead of equating science = evil, God = good, then you might actually avoid sounding "bone-headed" yourself. And idiot safety laws?? What, shouldn't there be limits on how fast you can drive? You DO know, that even a few miles extra an hour can cause severe damage that could be avoided by just driving a bit slower, right? 
 Then, as he and Edie are talking in a diner, he comes up with this gold nugget (he's talking about mottoes to live by when it all goes to hell and states some examples): "The secretary of defense announces from Sweden that he is having a sex-change operation, is in love with the prime minister of Russia, and has given his lover our nuclear launch codes." REALLY, Koontz? In that short sentence you display an ugly opinion of trans-, homo- and xenophobia. Transgendered and/or gay people are a threat to the US? This IS what you're saying with this, and it's a blatant lie, it is typical right wing-Michele Bachmann-paranoia crap; but it is no wonder, as it's well known that Koontz has supported Michele Bachmann, John McCain and Mitt Romney who all LIVE for installing fear for foreigners and gays in the American population. Shame on you for this, Koontz, you had a lot of gay readers back in the day and since none of them are hurting YOU, why do you have to be such a bigot? 
 Just a few pages later he, ironically, muses on this: "Usually I spare myself from the news, because if it's not propaganda, then it's one threat or another exaggerated to the point of absurdity [...], of bigotry and oppression misnamed justice, of hatred passed off as righteousness..." This IS all very true, but, again, Michele Bachmann and her ilk are the worst offenders in doing this, AND YOU SUPPORTED HER! That is bigotry! 
 Then he becomes delusional: "Among the nations of the Earth in all its hstory, ours is one of the few that has not brought forth its Hitler, its Stalin, its Pol Pot, its Mao Tse-tung, its Vlad the Impaler." A lof of nations haven't brought forth one of those, the US not being one of them: the massacring of Native Americans, Bush starting a war on grounds there were lies, bombings, shootings. Yup, it all adds up. You have just as much blood on your hands as a lot of other warring nations. 
 Near the end of the book, when all is ending with kids and dogs and happy sunrises, he writes: "I will not say that they were all beautiful by the standards of our culture, which is obsessed with models and airbrushed celebrities..." Well, dear Mr. Koontz, when was the last time you had a less attractive female lead in one of your books? They all have long black/blonde hair (never redheads) and deep almon-shaped brown eyes/deep truthful blue eyes, they all move with grace and have slender legs and full breasts and what have you. In a LOT of your books you have equaled beautiful = good, ugly = evil, so you're as much to blame in that culture you slam. That's bigotry too. I even remember in one of his earlier books, I think it was The Eyes of Darkness, where he had an elderly maid think about how this culture idolizes young people. Again, Koontz IS part of that culture, as it seems that the older he gets, the younger his protagonists are. 
 Which brings me to his slamming of Hollywood and everything it stands for; that is deeply ironic, since his books use every Hollywood cliche available. 
 His love for dogs is also too exaggerated; in one scen, Odd is attacked by three Dobermans, pacifies them, and freaking starts APOLOGIZING for having to do it! 
 And would it have killed you to kill off just ONE of the 26 children in this book? I don't wish death on anyone, but it's suspense fiction and the stakes are supposed to be high. ALL the bad guys die, ALL the good guys survive - where is the excitement in that? Booooring! 
 Of the five or so people Odd kills, one of them is a young woman, the only woman in the entire book who shows any sexuality and the only one of the killed ones whose death throes is disgustingly described. I'm not saying Koontz is a misogynist, but catholicism is and it's also afraid of sex and he's a self-proclaimed catholic, but I find it realy disturbing that he's in a way "slut-shaming", intentionally or not. 
 My last gripe with this book is his decriptions of Satanism. Maybe Koontz should take the time to read The Satanic Bible; Satanism is NOT about sacrificing children, or grown-ups, or goats or anyting else like that; it is NOT about summoning the devil. It IS, however, about not wanting to be shamed for all the stupid things the bible says and live your life as YOU see fit, without hurting anyone. That is ALL satanism is about. Of course, there's always some bad seed in every group, even catholic priests abuse kids, but get your facts straight, Koontz. Also, some of the symbols the satanists use are ankhs and Celtic crosses. These are NOT associated with satanism in any way, it isn't just catholicism that is good and loving, far from it, in fact! 
 Normally I hate spoilers, but for this book I actively sought them out to see if ANYHTING would happen that would make it worthwhile, but found nothing and thus had to FORCE myself to finish it. 
 Overall this is a very, very, very bad book; I WILL read the last Odd book, but then I think my 28 year long affair with Koontz is over. It seems like a loooong time since Whispers, Watchers, Midnight and Dragon Tears. MAYBE I will read Chris Snow #3 if he ever gets around to write it; I'm not sure, because even though they were alright books, they are not among my favourites. 
 Too bad, because you have given me many a good read.

Suddenly Royal starts with the arrival of a Duchess and the Prince to America and Sam's university. She just expects that they are donors and when they request a meeting with her - she is all prepared to plug the university's bird programme which she is heavily involved in. Turns out though that Sam is about to get the shock and surprise of her life as she discovers that on her mother's side she is in fact a Duchess and now being the last one in her family line - the queen of Lilaria is requesting that the original families return and the titles be re-instated. Sam definitely doesn't feel like a member of the royal family and is halfway through her Masters programme, not to mention her stepfather is currently recieving treatment for Cancer. Can Sam up and leave everything and show the world that this American young adult has what it takes to take a seat on the Queen's council as a Duchess and rule her own village as each royal member is in charge of a township ?

I could accept that the Prince and Samantha would come to love each other eventually however, their love at first sight/shared meal clipped the suspense of the plot and had me uninterested before I even got my footing into the story. Next, the introduction of Samantha to her royal standing was undercooked. If Chase wanted to make Samantha aware of her royal standing, she could have done it gradually instead of blurting it out within the first 20 pages. She even could have had Samantha venture to Lilria and been told there. Instead she sprung it on her in middle ofa hotel in a vastly cliched setting. After Samantha found out she was royal, there wasn't much more to hold my attention. Finally, the randomness of the "save the bird" campaign that Samantha was saddled with threw me. I could understand saving a lot of animals, but the whole bird thing seemed random and contrived to me.

sample_reviews.review_text: This was an interesting book, sometimes funny, sometimes sweet, sometimes annoying. It was like spending a week with Sheldon Cooper.

Unreadable. I couldn't get past the first six chapters. I found the writing banal and charmless and the depiction of the main character horribly patronising. If you want to read a book narrated by an emotionally challenged character try The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time. The big difference is that the latter is written by a proper writer who knows how to write. Whereas The Rosie Project, or what I managed to read of it, was void of any literary merit. I really enjoyed this book, urban fantasy with humor is exactly what I have been craving and this book delivered in spades. 
 There are a lot of reviews explaining exactly what is so great about this book, so I will just explain why I didn't give it five stars. The main reason is just that the author floundered a bit with her main character, I think that she wasn't 100% sure how much Sam should know and what Sam's true powers should be like until after this book. That really only becomes noticeable when you read further into the series, but here Sam's power/knowledge is a bit vaguely described (not knowing about werewolves, etc.) and later on she is much more powerful and better off. 
 Other than that, the book is great, it has a nice sense of humor, although it is not a laugh-out-loud book. It is pretty simple and I ran through it in just a few hours, but I couldn't wait to dive right into the next one :).
I honestly believe something is wrong with me. I can't get into ANY book. I must be in a rut.

First of all, the world building in this book is excellent. I could follow actions, descriptions, and imagine the areas Sam visits. This includes her slums - as she is a slumlord - and their tenants. It's so easy to picture this world in your head and enjoy the action. It's also easy to imagine the characters and what they look like. 
 Having said that, the characters are more or less a good base to start off a series with. Being the first book in the series, I don't think it's fair to expect the characters to be perfect because we must learn more about them as the series goes on. Wyatt did appear mysterious at first, and then after certain events we see how forgiving, clever and brave he is. 
 Michelle and Candy are also good characters, although we don't see much of Michelle. Her relationship with Sam also started long before this adventure and I'm not sure if she knows of Sam's nature. Candy was deceiving as a character, she did appear to be harmless at first but we realise soon that she is strong-willed and sly. Sam loves that. 
 Sam's character is a contradiction. She is evil in the sense that she has the urge to kill and Own people (take their souls into her and keep them with her for eternity) but at the same time she seems... harmless. Just an imp with a relish for trouble. There are little things she does like throwing gum on the floor of a bar/restaurant and hoping someone stands on it, and more extreme things like sending huge balloons floating down the highway to cause accidents. The strange thing is that her enjoyment of these things makes you giggle, or is that just me? Her thinking and comments also make me laugh; I thoroughly enjoy her strange and wicked thought-process. 
 If you have a sense of humour and can take things lightly, this book will make you laugh. It's quite different from anything I've read and I wish I found it a lot sooner. There is a good mix of humour, gore, investigation/tracking, action and romance. The world building is great, characters are good but could be better - a decent start to a series that a lot of potential. I would recommend it to those who love urban fantasy and have a good sense of humour. 
 Visit www.vigilantmind.com for other reviews.

I'm not sure it's possible for me to write an unbiased review of the Northern Lights (probably known as The Golden Compass to my American friends). I have loved this series since about 2000 and still own my original paperbacks that have been read countless times over the years so it's hard to be completely objective about a story that has been a part of your life for such a long time. Anyway, I'll do my best to try and explain why this story has always been one of my favourites but surely the fact that it's still on my shelf after 17 years is enough to hint at how good it is! 
 When her best friend, Roger, goes missing along with numerous other young children, Lyra and her daemon Pantalaimon, set out to find them and bring them home. What follows is an epic journey that takes her from her home in Jordan College, Oxford all the way to the frozen wastes of the North. She has help from numerous sources along the way - the gyptians who are also searching for their missing children, the witches of the North and even an armoured bear called Iorek Byrnison - but what she finds when she eventually catches up with the child snatching gobblers is something more horrific than she could ever have dreamed of. 
 Lyra is a brilliant character, she's fierce, stubborn and a little bit reckless, as an accomplished liar she can be cocky and thinks she knows everything but she's also very intelligent and will quickly learn from the mistakes she makes. I love how feisty she is and the way she jumps straight into the action because she is so determined to save Roger and the other children, she faces things that would terrify even adults and she does it with a great deal of bravery. The bond between her and Pantalaimon is brilliant, he's a bit more sensible than she is and is often the voice of reason when she's about to get herself in trouble, unfortunately for him she doesn't always take his advice but he is always there as her backup when she needs him. 
 While Lyra's world initially seems very similar to our own it quickly becomes clear that Philip Pullman has used his wonderful imagination to create something very different. Every human is born with their own daemon, a living, breathing entity that is basically the other half of their soul. Daemons can take any form throughout childhood, Pantalaimon often changes shape depending on the situation that Lyra finds herself in, but once puberty is reached it will choose one form to settle as. The bond between human and daemon is unbreakable and killing one will cause the death of the other so there are lots of strict taboos in place about not touching other people's daemons even though you can communicate with them. I love the sheer variety of different daemons found in these books and I've spent the last 17 years waiting for my own daemon to turn up! Unfortunately it's still nowhere to be found but I still live in hope. 
 Along with daemons this world also contains the panserborne, a race of warrior polar bears who have an affinity to metal and who are known to be brilliant protectors. Lyra is able to make friends with Iorek Byrnison, an exiled panserborne who has been living amongst humans for far too long, and he agrees to help her try to rescue the missing children after she frees him from captivity. Iorek is another brilliant character and a great ally for Lyra as she travels across the frozen wastes of a land similar to the arctic. Although this series has a lot of fun characters it also has some surprisingly dark elements, I'd actually forgotten how upsetting some parts of the story were so be warned it's not for the faint of heart but that darkness doesn't make it any less of a wonderful journey. There are lots of amazing elements to this story and from what I remember the series only gets more fantastical in the next two books. 
 I started this reread because I want to be ready for the new companion trilogy (the first book La Belle Sauvage will be released in October) and I can't wait to read new stories set in this world but I'm just as excited to continue with the original trilogy and remind myself of the rest of Lyra's adventures. There is a reason that this series holds up so well since it was originally published, it's something special and if you've not already read it you're really missing out.

My first Philip Pullman, and probably my last. 
 When I read a book I don't like, I usually figure it's just not for me, and I have different tastes, blah, blah, and move on. Not this time. The novel "deserves" a few notes. 
 Philip Pullman has awfully combined two of the greatest conundrums of modern science, dark matter and the nature of consciousness, into one very week element within his narrative, and has connected it with the transition from childhood to adolescence. After all this is a YA novel. 
 Pullman's suggestion is that children are not fully self-conscious until adolescence. This premise is nonsense, even for a book. Pullman's claim is that these elements of consciousness start streaming into the children and their daemons settle into a fixed form. Uhm...Come again?

This is one of my favourite books from my childhood/YA years, and it was fascinating to read it again and pick up on all the nuances I'd missed when I was younger. Looking forward to rereading the rest of the series!

Reread for the first time in about a decade. Still wonderful but I definitely understand the many layers of Northern Lights a lot more now, the metaphors feel more pertinent.

He crossed to the desk and took from the drawer a small package wrapped in black velvet. When he unfolded the cloth, Lyra saw something like a large watch or a small clock: a thick disc of brass and crystal. It might have been a compass or something of the sort. 
 The first book of the His Dark Materials trilogy was all set in Lyra's world and I think it was my favourite of the three. Academics in Oxford colleges and gyptians on narrow boats, witches from Lapland and panserborne from Svalbard, poisonings and kidnappings, alethiometers and spirit-powered flying clockwork spies, balloons and airships, Dust and the Aurora Borealis, and above all the concept of daemons. It is an utterly brilliant book and Lyra is a marvellous heroine. She is strong-willed, independent and resourceful, but she listens to other people and doesn't fall into the trap of insisting on doing things all her own way, no matter what. I love how subtly the differences from our world are painted - such as the references to the Skraelings and New Denmark, which make it clear that in Lyra's world the Vikings had continued to visit Vinland and colonised it, without the author feeling the need to spell it out. And what could be more exciting than my favourite bit of the whole book, the escape from Bolvanger?

I fell in love with this series about a year ago and I've reread these books a couple of times already. Once, they pulled me out of a book slump and the other time was when I was feeling down and reading them totally cheered me up. 
 Nothing beats the blues like a good second chance romance novel and The Trouble with Love has got to be best I've read so far. It is really good. The fact that I've read it in one sitting, this afternoon to be precise, just confirms it. 
 I liked the chemistry between Emma and Alex, but I really liked the fact that their relationship wasn't just physical, all about heated glances, lusting after each other and mistaking lust for love. Their issues were real, they both hurt each other and they were trying to live with it. It's what I appreciate most about these kinds of stories, when done right, they take you on an emotional ride and they melt your heart and break it, all at the same time. 
 The friendship between the Stilleto girls is another thing I really enjoyed reading about, because they had that kind of relationship where they tease and maybe even antagonize, but it's all good-naturedly and it's pretty obvious they care a lot for each other. 
 What I didn't quite care for was the reason Alex and Emma never went through with their wedding in the first place. Alex screwed up, Emma got mad and threw her ring at him the night before their wedding and he chose not to try to make it up to her for what he did, instead went straight out of town. Also, he threw his phone out of his car window, which meant he never got Emma's calls or messages when she was trying to work things out between them. 
 We don't get the reason they split up until almost the very end, but I was expecting something more substantial than a "Oops, I threw my phone away for no reason at all, so I'm sorry but I didn't get your message telling me you still wanted to get married.". 
 This was just too lame. 
 But at least he redeems himself in the end. And it was super sweet. 
 The Trouble with Love is definitely my favorite book from the Sex, Love and Stilleto series. I can't help but feel a bit sad because it's the last book, but then I'm also excited because the story continues with the Oxford men and I already have a feeling whose story we might be reading next. And I can't wait! 
 Special thanks to Random House Publishing for providing me with an arc via NetGalley.
