Where to begin. I didnt love this book, but I didnt hate it. I'm glad I read it because I love Jamie's writing style in the BD series.. I was so excited when I heard she was doing a Maddox brothers series. Maybe I had high expectations. But this book was underwhelming to say the least. There were too many plot points that didnt make sense and/or were unnecessary and left unfinished . I mean WTF is going on with her relationship with her brothers/parents for one . 
 The big secret was ridiculous. She chose not too say anything for absolutely no reason - Well technically 2 secrets but one she could have told especially when other people knew - it was like everyone knew except for Trent. People at her job knew, the boys in his fraternity knew but Trent - no one said anything to at all. Again - made no sense. 
 But all in all quick fast read but when I finished the book my reaction was like "ummm okay that's ridiculous. I mean I figured out the secret in the beginning especially since I finished the BD series before starting this one so to me it was pretty obvious especially since she dropped clues. But I just knew there had to be something more than what I was thinking. 
 Jamie tried to do too much with this story, she kept telling us something but never showed us that Trent "loved" her since they were kids but since she never showed us - it actually felt like she was contradicting herself. And she never explained why all of a sudden Trent made his move then . 
 And now I heard she's is going to give them a sequel? I dont know if I will read it depends on how the rest of the books in the series shape up.

I was so looking forward to reading about Trenton Maddox. I honestly was trying to figure out this big mystery the entire book until the last sentence. I felt confused most of the time. 
 Don't get me wrong, this was an awesome read once everything clicked into place. I had to listen (audibles) to the ending about 3 times and think back to Walking Disaster before I could really appreciate the writing skills... Geez I was like WTH!!! Loved it. 
 Now you can read this book without reading Beautiful Disaster and Walking Disaster but I think you would appreciate the story better if you read about Travis and Abby first since they are mentioned a few times. 
 I really love the friendship between Trenton and Cami. There is a love triangle going on but not one you expect. There are twists that keep you thinking throughout. 
 I was barely ready to give BO a 4 star rating because I wasn't connecting for most of the book. But once it all clicked and I took a day or 2 thinking about all the pieces, I had to give credit where credit is due. 
 4.5 stars for me and I can't wait for more of the Maddox brothers in the future!!!?

www.bookworm221.tumblr.com 
 The Maddox brothers are back! and now is time for us to know more about Trenton. 
 First of all I have no idea why but I was sort of expecting it to be from Trent's POV but it's actually from Cami's POV and it was perfect because we all get to experience what is like to be wooed by the allegedly bad boy Trent. 
 For those of us who have read the Beautiful Series Cami is a familiar character, she works at the bar Red and she knows the Maddox brothers but in Beautiful Oblivion we know how she knows them and since when and also we get a pretty good idea of how she feels about those bad boys. We also get a chance to know Cami, to know that she has to work to help her brothers, that her father as anger issues and when she was little they were all in danger of their father but despite those hurting memories of her childhood she still wants to see her family work for the sake of her mother. 
 Trent enters Cami's life with one purpose: to win her love. 
 "I was just thinking now was as good a time as any to acknowledge that you're perfect and it wouldn't suck if you fell madly in love with me anytime soon." 
 And this is why he goes above and beyond any expectation that she might had and he tries his hardest to win her heart even though he knows that she has a boyfriend who she barely even sees but for some reason she can't break up with him. 
 I wasn't expecting to like Trent that much right away but it is impossible to not fall for his antics, he was determined since chapter 1 to get Cami's attention then friendship and then love. I won't mention all the amazing things that Trent did for Cami because I want to give you a chance to be wooed by him. 
 Whenever I saw early reviews or comments about Trent they were always raving about him and how perfect he and the book were, and I have to say they truly are amazing, it has been quite a while since a book has left me in shock at the end when I didn't see certain plot twist coming, and after reading those last word and screaming WHAT! I was left with a huge grin on my face and I immediately wanted to start reading it again. 
 Great job Mrs. McGuire! 
 Keep Calm and Read On 
 Instagram and Twitter @bookquotes221

I absolutely love everything that Jamie McGuire writes and I have been anxiously awaiting Trent's story! I fell deeply in love with Travis in Beautiful Disaster and now she has me swooning over Trent in Beautiful Oblivion. 
 After dropping out of college at ESU because of a tragic accident that left him with a tremendous amount of guilt on his shoulders, Trent is now living at home with his father, and working at the local Tattoo shop, Skin Deep. Just like his younger brother Travis, Trent is quite the ladies man and is always taking a new girl home with him. 
 Camille "Cami" Camlin has been working since she was a teenager hoping to move out of her childhood home as soon as possible. Cami is now a Sophomore at ESU and is happily living the college life by attending classes and working as a bartender at the local hotspot, The Red Door. When Cami gets a phone call from her boyfriend saying he has to cancel their weekend plans she decides to go to the Red Door and hang out with her friends and unwind a little bit. 
 While at the Red Door Cami is a bit surprised when Trent Maddox walks up to her table and starts to flirt with her. She has known him most of her life and he has never shown any interest in her. We all know how hard it is to resist a Maddox brother, and Cami finds herself falling quickly for Trent. 
 "You can borrow me anytime. I'm perfect for sweater weather." 
 "Be careful. I might hold you to that." 
 "Don't threaten me with a good time." 
 Trent is relentless in his attempts to spend time with Cami but she is hesitant because she has a boyfriend. He gets under her skin and they become close friends very quickly. He tries to prove to her that she needs someone who wants to spend as much time with her as possible. Will Cami be able to resist the Maddox charm and stay faithful to T.J.? 
 I loved the chemistry between Cami and Trent. Cami is a little spitfire who doesn't take crap from anyone. Trent is a Maddox which means he will fight for what he wants and will never back down. Even though this story is told from Cami's POV I felt like we got a good glimpse into Trent's thoughts. I loved the supporting characters and their relationships with Trent and Cami. As much as I loved getting to revisit Travis and Abby I was a little disappointed that this story ran parallel to Beautiful Disaster. I would have liked to see Trent and Cami have their own story as I better connected with them during the scenes that didn't run parallel to Beautiful Disaster. I was also hoping that all of the family issues Cami was having would have been resolved by the end of the book as it seemed to be a large part of their story. The ending of the book definitely shocked me. I can't wait to read the next Maddox brother book!

sample_reviews.review_text:
So, I picked up The Girl Who Kicked The Hornet's Nest as that had been sitting on my 'To Read' pile for quite a while. 
 Seeing as I enjoyed The Girl Who Played With Fire so much, and the fact that it ends with everything so up in the air, I guess it's a bit odd that I hadn't got around to reading it before now as I had it sitting around. However, the Millennium books are all actually rather big and can be a bit daunting/cumbersome for my relatively short tube journey :D 
 I'm glad I finished the trilogy though - it was another fast-paced, action-packed., hugely enjoyable romp. However, although I was really drawn in with the whole tying the loose ends procedure, there were more things about this book that niggled me. 
 The first two books had a huge cast of characters, but this one includes all of the previous ones and introduces a whole load of new ones, and I found it rather overwhelming. There were just so many people that I found it hard to keep up with who was who - and sometimes their first names were used, and sometimes their surnames - and so many names were so similar (as I think is typical in Scandinavia) and I often got lost with who was talking/referring to who! 
 I also got a bit annoyed with a whole plotline concerning Erika Berger, who was always shown to be this strong, switched-on woman, and yet the whole plot relies on the fact that she's had the wool pulled over her eyes by a couple of people. It just doesn't ring true for this character that has been built up over the previous two books. 
 However, the small negatives didn't detract from the fact that it was an intensely enjoyable book, and a fitting end to the trilogy storyline. I highly recommend!
Another good read in this final one of the series, however, i do think that the first one The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo is by far the best in the trilogy
I'm sorry to those who liked it, I just couldn't get into this book.

The author Stieg Larsson provides a complete detailed understanding of the personalities as the plot expands. I know a lot of reader would not want such details but it is necessary to build the development of the multiple plots, which in turns build an excellent story line. 
 I viewed all three Swedish versions (Dubbed in English) and the books have provided more detail story line that cannot translate to big screen.

The first book I read on my IPhone. Endless details about the Swedish Government and Secret Service make parts of this book really boring. However, for anyone who wants to find out what happens to Lisbeth Salander, this is a must-read. The ending is a bit of a disappointment.

The first book was good, the 2nd book was very good (one of best thrillers I have read in the past several years), and this, the third and final in the Millennium trilogy, was pretty average. After reading The Girl Who Played with Fire, you are left wondering how things might end up. Looking for a few chapters to tie things up and put a bow on everything. Larsson wrote a 600 page book to answer all your lingering questions from book 2 and calls it The Girl Who Kicked the Hornet's Nest. 
 Very little suspense and no surprises. This is a novel that centers on an investigation by parties who do not know how things unfolded... yet the reader already has the knowledge. Granted, Stieg Larsson does it in style giving you his usual page turning account. While I think this book is somewhat mediocre, it is still must read material for anybody who has already read the first two (a requirement).

I am so sorry to have finished this book. I have thoroughly enjoyed all the books in this trilogy and I am disappointed that there won't be any more to read. 
 The Girl Who Kicked the Hornets' Nest is a thriller that is difficult to put down. So many books of this genre follow a similar, stale pattern, but with the books in this trilogy you could never guess what was going to happen next. I also like that the story took place in Europe and all the characters were European. I enjoyed the descriptions of the various towns, restaurants and cafes the characters frequented. This was a European perspective of Europe, not an Americans perspective of Europe; again, very unique. 
 That being said, there were a number of characters in the book with similar Swedish names. At times I had a little trouble keeping track of who was who. But it wouldn't have worked if they had names like Jones or Smith; I wouldn't change a thing. 
 The Girl who Kicked the Hornets' Nest is a fantastic book. I recommend it, and all the books in the trilogy.

I really enjoyed this blend of domestic fiction and mystery, in which the loves, hates and sorrows of three women intertwine around, well, someone's husband's secret. The plot (about which the less said the better for fear of major spoilers) is contrived, but gripping. The characters were well drawn, from the hyper-organized, impossibly cheerful Tupperware saleswoman to the shy wife devastated by her husband's infidelity, to an older woman understandably embittered by the loss of her daughter many years before. 
 BUT... 
 I hated the epilogue. Before reading the epilogue, I was really bothered by everyone's decision to let John Paul off the hook, because legally and ethically it's not their call. The community has a stake in prosecuting murder. That's my take anyway, and I'd welcome other views, because it's an interesting discussion. But the epilogue cuts off that dialog before it starts. It's as if Moriarty couldn't decide the moral issue herself, so she bailed on it.

This book was okay to me. I went into it expecting it to be sort of explosive, I guess, and I was disappointed. Oh, don't get me wrong, there were some great parts to this book, but for the most part, it was kind of plodding, and tended to drag on. The synopsis of this book is that a husband writes a letter about something he did many years prior to his wife finding it, and the repurcussions it has on their lives. The author (Liane Moriarty), takes us back and forth in time to explain what has happened, and how it all led up to the present. To me, the reactions of some of the characters in here were a little "off", or weird, maybe people in Australia express emotions differently, I don't know, but it took away from the overall punch of the book. Just not my cup of tea, sorry.

** spoiler alert ** 
 There were two reasons why I read this: first, because I like My Chemical Romance and the author is the lead singer of that band; second, because there's been a discussion on the YALSA listserv about whether this title should be in the Young Adult or the Adult section of the library. 
 On the first count: 
 I found the plot to be more confusing than it needed to be. I suppose there will be more explanation or backstory, since this is "volume 1," but I spent most of the story trying to keep the 7 superkids/adults' names and superpowers straight. The artwork is great, but not my taste. I mostly felt bad for the violin girl on the cover--her story goes: her family rejects her for having no superpower, so she joins the Orchestra of the Damned and is about to destroy the world by playing "The Apocolypse Suite." Then her brother tries to kill her, saying he never liked her anyway. She's still alive at the end of the story, but may never get to play the violin again, which may have been her only superpower. I just felt bad for her. The different characters, while interesting, just didn't come together for me. 
 On the second count: 
 What you see on the cover is about as graphic as this gets, nudity-wise. I see it more as a skintight bodysuit or abstract art rather than nudity. The story is quite violent, but nothing worse than other YA graphic novels I've seen. My decision is to keep it in the YA section. The story might appeal more to adult graphic novel/comic book fans, but they definitely browse the YA graphic novels too.
The White Violin is one of the more original villains I've seen in a while. And the book is worth a re-read for the story, but not the art, which at points seems underwhelming and lazy.

I thought this had the potential to be a really fantastic story, but it lacked organization, coherency, and required the reader to suspend their disbelief WAY too much. It also left far too many questions unanswered such as: 
 Why did the one sibling die? They just...disappeared. 
 Why were so many children born suddenly to women who had had no signs of being pregnant. This started everything, but was never even touched on or explained. What about the other children? 
 Why is the mom a talking mannequin with no limbs? 
 Why is spaceboy suddenly a gorilla? 
 What was Yanya's super power? Was she abused/neglected as a child? Why is she so emo? Why did she want to destroy the world? 
 How did an orchestra of school children manage to slow her down? 
 What was Rumor's power? "I heard a rumor....." Please explain this to me. 
 Why was there a talking monkey butler? 
 There were parts of this graphic novel where I was genuinely intrigued and driven to continue reading. Most of the time though I forgot I was even reading this, and had no desire to even pick this back up. 
 There
I thought Vanya would be really really special...but Mr. Gerard proved my mind wrong and poor Pogo. I hate Vanya for killing him! WHYYY!!!!!!!!!!!

Wow. This is the first comic that I've really disliked. So let's just dive in... 
 So right away, I didn't like that we just dove into the story without understanding who each of the characters are and what their specific powers were. We got a few flashbacks to their childhood here and there throughout the collection, which were okay. But again, because we didn't learn much about the characters to begin with, the flashbacks were just meh to me. 
 Further, these flashbacks still didn't give me enough information to understand, or even like, any of the characters. The characters themselves were so very bland to me. Partially because we didn't get any background information, but also because they were all so childish and rude. 
 I didn't love the way the narration flows either. It was pretty rough throughout, but specifically in the first few pages... It's very choppy and some of it just does not flow at all. For example, "the children were either abandoned or put up for adoption... ... The ones who survived." Then we're off on another topic. Granted it eventually leads back to where we were, but it was still rough. 
 I couldn't stand that things weren't explained at all. I need some level of world building here. I also would have appreciated more explanation about the siblings relations. We know that they were all born at the same time from various women that weren't even pregnant. But are they related? Whether they are or not, they were still raised as siblings...so the weird romantic relationships were super gross to me. 
 I didn't care for the artwork or the storyline. Some of the panels were better than others, but most seriously lacked a level of detail that I appreciate in comics. There's not much else I can really say here, overall it just wasn't for me. 
 The ending also seemed incredibly rushed. And ew, how old is that carton of milk with the missing child's photo on the very last page?! The kid had been missing for 20 years. Gross. 
 To end on a positive note, the one thing that I did like was how some of the chapter titles flow right from the storyline. Specifically, there is one chapter where a waitress is talking and someone asks her what was said, the next panel was the chapter break which was titled, "Thank you for the coffee." 
 I highly doubt that I will pick up Volume 2. Part of me wants to, just to see if it improves.... We'll see.

sample_reviews.review_text: I loved this book! I liked the art style, I really liked the time period/setting, I liked the characters. It was a quick and satisfying read. I also especially liked the Lovecraftian short story at the end but the whole thing was great and I can't wait to read the next one.

In simplest terms, this does for Victorian literature what Fables went on to do for fairy tales and Hellboy for mythology. 
 While the plot is simple enough: the league of extraordinary gentlemen, consisting of Mina Murray (recently divorced), Allan Quatermain, Captain Nemo, Hawley Griffin, and Dr. Jeckyll, are assembled and hired by M16 to protect England from threats which only their unique abilities can take on, the real highlight of this work comes from the sheer detail put into it. The background art is complete chaotic activity, affecting mood, and the stylization of the Victorian era is imitated brilliantly in the wordings, panel changes, and overall tone, which carefully treads the line between parody and cynicism, as many works of the period do. 
 While it's not required, the characters have almost no weight if you come in unfamiliar with such works as Dracula, The Strange Case of Dr. Jeckyll and Mr. Hyde, 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea, The Invisible Man, the Sherlock Holmes and Allan Quatermain stories, and myriad others due to the sheer ambition of this work. 
 It is elevated from a simple mashup of famous Victorian characters due to the sheer number of them, plenty of lesser known characters, such as Poe's Dupin and characters mostly outside of speculative fiction, such as Dicken's Artful Dodger and Pollyanna from the book of the same name, have cameo appearances. 
 Being the work of Alan Moore, of course this is more than a little bizarre, over the top, and bawdy in turns, but it's an enjoyable sticky love-letter to Victorian fiction, and a real treat, possibly one of the best entries there is, in the genre of intentional steampunk.

Previously read: 03/30/2009 
 Reading this with an eye for book discussion, and I can see why some people don't like it. There's a lot of misogyny and racism that I'm pretty sure is meant to be satirical but might come off as serious, and yeah, sometimes the art is a little wonky looking, and a lot of the characters are dicks. That said, I do still enjoy this book. Mina is kick ass, and I love the literary references.

Sorry...not my cup of English Breakfast Tea. I found it rather disappointing. I'd never read any of the League of Extraordinary Gentlemen before this, I'd only seen the movie (of course it was a bit disappointing to so...) 
 This, like a lot of books that I've been disappointed in is one I think is a good idea. It just doesn't, "come off". Willamina who is not Mina (am I the only one who actually read that novel????). Allan Quatermain is an opium addict, Captain Nemo is still trucking around under the sea...a bit. Edward Hyde is running amok... you get the idea. (At least I didn't see Tom Sawyer). 
 This just didn't draw me in nor even appeal to me. If you're a League fan, enjoy. Don't plan to follow it up.
I enjoyed the story and the inclusion of many fictional characters, ala Philip Jose Farmer. I'm not a big fan of the artist and I dislike the monochromatic coloring style.

It's good but it's not my favourite of Moore's work. Or my second favourite. 
 My beef was with the illustrations, particularly of Mina Harkness. The way she is drawn...Ugh. It seems poor. I know that women had corseted wasp-waists in Victorian times but to draw her waist pencil-thin with giant boobs...Ugh.
This certainly wasn't as amazing or gripping as it's been billed. I'm not really sure what the fuss was about - perhaps I missed something?

The graphic novel itself was fun and enjoyable (I especially enjoyed the little details hinting at past Extraordinary Gentlemen), although the illustrated Allan Quatermain short story at the end wasn't quite my taste. I was waiting in anticipation for the reveal of Mina's true nature but, alas, no luck. I'm dying to see how her companions will react, so I guess I'll have to read the sequel.
Can't get into this one. It wasn't all that exciting for me, sorry.

A clever read, not quite as layered as some of Moore's other works. But, overall it was still an enjoyable read, tying together some of England's more famous Victorian Era Literary heroes. I was on a sharp look out for any subtle messages that Moore usually hides in the background and I was surprised by how few there were. One that was funny was the statue of the Baron Munchhausen. reference_books.title: Faithful
reference_books.review_text:
'Faithful' by Alice Hoffman 
 3.5 stars/ 7 out of 10 
 I have several friends who are fans of Alice Hoffman's writing, so I thought it was time for me to read something by her. I decided to start with 'Faithful' (which will be published in November 2016). 
 The story centres on Shelby Richmond, who, as a teenager, was in a car crash with her best friend, and continues for many years to feel responsible for and guilty about what happened to her friend. 
 I was a bit concerned to start with, that the story was going to be over-simplistic. However, this turned out not to be the case. For me, the theme at the centre of this novel was the possibility of redemption, and I thought Hoffman explored this theme well through a variety of situations and characters. 
 I especially liked Maravelle and her family, and I'm glad that they became part of Shelby's life. I thought Shelby, herself, was a well-drawn character. Whilst the level of complexity in her life was more than that of most 'real life' people, it was relatively easy to empathise with her and the situations she found herself in. I found myself on several occasions thinking 'there but for the grace ......' 
 I found this an interesting and enjoyable book, and at no stage felt bored by it. I can imagine that Alice Hoffman will attract even more fans once this is published. 
 Thank you to Simon and Schuster, and to NetGalley for an ARC.

reference_books.title: Swing Time
reference_books.review_text:
'Swing Time' by Zadie Smith 
 3.5 stars/ 7 out of 10 
 I had read 'White Teeth' when it was published, so was interested in reading Zadie Smith's latest novel. 
 The novel is told in the 1st person; there are two interpolated narratives, one starting from the narrator's childhood, and the other relating to her adult life. The prominent 'other' in her childhood is Tracey (a relationship which has repercussions up to the present). In her adulthood the 'other' is is Aimee, an Australian pop star. Interestingly, we never learn the name of the narrator. 
 I was very amused, in the Prologue, by the narrator's descriptions of the differences between hers and Tracey's families and lifestyles. It sounded all too familiar to me from my own childhood. I had political parents, and was a political parent myself. Zadie Smith captures beautifully all the nuances and absurdities of this type of family life. 
 Throughout the book, I found the sections relating to Tracey, both as child and adult; and also those regarding the narrator's fraught relationship with her own mother, to be convincing and thought provoking. I found the sections relating to Aimee to be less successful, whilst still interesting . 
 This is a well written novel, with many strands to entertain, interest and raise issues for the reader. 
 Thank you to Penguin Books UK and to NetGalley for an ARC.

sample_reviews.review_text:
3.5 
 Interesting read about the history of gene, gene therapy and how technology is going to accelerate new ways of treatments, discovery and the ethics (the usual stuff). It is a pretty easy read but as I have no real interest, some scientific explanations are still hard to grasp.
Reaffirms the sense of awe in our Creator God and our smallness as we discover the complexities of his creation.

I hate to say it, but this is not my cup of tea. Too much 'then this scientist did this, and this scientist did that'. 
 Nothing artistic or creative about the writing, it is essentially a verbose history of genetics, complete with fantastical imaginings of what scientists thought/ said/ did (based on very flimsy evidence). The genetics is obviously explained for laymen, but I found it too reductive. 
 If you like scientific history, then go for it. After 250 pages, I skipped forward to the bits about his own family, losing track / interest in the historical detail at the 1970s stage. 
 Needless to say, this was a book club read, I would never have chosen it otherwise.

In this beautifully written, vivid history of genetics; Mukherjee takes us by the hand and walks us through the hall of fame of all the people who are the reason for modern biology as we study it today. His picturesque descriptions make the book a joy to read. 
 Starting with Mendel and ending with embryonic stem cell research and beyond; the fascinating story of genetic research is given in the book. There are life stories of many exceptional scientists. Unfortunately many examples of bad science and faux-scientists can also be found. I am particularly glad that Rosalind Franklin (who died at age 36 due to ovarian cancer; most likely because of Xray exposure from her experiments) and her work (without which DNA structure would not have been understood) is given the importance and acknowledgement in this book. 
 Students of medicine, biology and related fields as well as anyone with an interest in the history and future of science will enjoy and learn a lot from The Gene.

Summary: Although this lacked 
 The Emperor of All 
 Maladies 
 ' focus on moving human stories, it was one of the most ambitious yet accessible books I've ever read on the history of genome editing. 
 Throughout history, our understanding of heredity and the gene has become more precise and more nuanced. As a result, our ability to manipulate the genes of other organisms and eventually our own has increased as well. In The Gene, Siddhartha Mukherjee places our current genome editing abilities in the context of this history and insightfully presents both the promise of these abilities and the potential results of their abuse. 
 As someone who loved 
 The Emperor of All Maladies 
 and who works on proteins that are used for gene editing, I had high expectations for this book and it met or exceeded them in almost every way. My only real complaint is that the human side of the story was a much smaller part of this book than in The Emperor of All Maladies. The author's amazing empathy for his patients, which was part of what made me love that book so much, wasn't discussed here. However, the writing was equally, astonishingly good. The author also once again did an incredible job tackling ambitious scientific topics in detail, yet in an accessible way. I wasn't sold on every single one of this analogies and descriptions, but many blew me away with their combination of simplicity and attention to detail. 
 I also thought the perspective the author provided on this history was particularly informative. He told compelling stories about many of the researchers involved, weaving such delightful narratives that even the stories I've heard a million times (such as those of Mendel and Darwin) felt fresh. By bringing these scientists to life, Mukherjee was able to draw the reader into their world. More than any other author I've read, he made it clear why scientists wanted to answer particular questions and shared their sense of wonder with each new discovery. He also made the impact of every discovery very understandable. 
 Honestly, the only thing "wrong" with this book was that the author had the (mis)fortune to write a Pulitzer prize winning book first. Even though this didn't wow me quite as much as his first book, I enjoyed it immensely. I would particularly recommend it, not only because it is an amazing book, but because I think it provides a perspective that is essential (although not sufficient) for an informed opinion on the dangers and merits of genome editing and GMOs. 
 This review was originally posted on Doing Dewey

A complicated story and a long book. It details the history of medical science research into how we become what we are, through the interaction of our genes, inheritance and the other constituent parts of our DNA. The science was complex, and I freely admit to getting lost multiple times in the detailed descriptions of how the biology works. The author has a back story with an inherited history of mental illness in his own family and a desire to understand more about how such things are inherited and could be eradicated. The moral issues with tampering with genetics were well described in the end, although the author came to no real firm conclusions other than the highlight both opportunities and dangers. An interesting book, on a subject for which I had very limited knowledge.

sample_reviews.review_text: A beautiful book with a gripping story! This book was very hard to put down, I immediately got hooked on the story set in WWII era Malaysia! This book looks at so much, loyalty, family, grief, war... It is one of those long books that are quite easy to read but still beautifully written and informative. I loved this book. His writing was poetic. What a joy to read. The story was intriguing while learning about the history of this country. I love the way the author told the story through a reflection. This is a book I could read again and enjoy just as much as the first time.

Story set in Penang off Malaysia during the Second World War. The main character Philip Hutton is the half caste son of the current owner of the influential Hutton trading firm and his now dead second Chinese wife (who was in turn the daughter of the pre-eminent Chinese mining magnate who also appears to be a Triad leader). 
 One day when he is around 14 and his family are in UK Philip is visited by a Japanese man Endo-San to who his father has rented the island opposite their house. 
 Endo San practices a martial art involving hand to hand and sword fighting - Philip becomes his pupil, Endo his "sensei" - philosophical guide and inspiration (and at least it is hinted lover). At the same time and despite repeated warnings Philip shows Endo around the Island despite the fact he is blatantly preparing the way for a Japanese invasion. When the Japanese arrives his father refuses to join the rest of the Westerners in fleeing and supposedly to protect him (although not achieving this at all) Philip accepts the role that Endo has been grooming him for of liaison for the Japanese with the locals while (unlike his friend - son of a Triad leader and fellow follower of a Japanese sensei) he rejects an opportunity to join the British resistance working with the communist guerrillas. Over time he increasingly threads a fine line between collaboration and resistance - eventually openly assisting his old friend. The book is set in the present day when Philip is visited by the ex lover of Endo San who is dying from atomic bomb wounds and finally opens up on his life. 
 The plot is considerably more complex than above - rather than a first novel it seems to be his first four or five novels: a story of a half caste with divided loyalties dealing with the brutality and difficult choices (although one annoying thing is that he so clearly seems to have made the wrong choice in collaboration) of the Japanese occupation; a martial arts movie; a sub-Alchemist Buddhist meditative fable on the issues of connectedness and reincarnation, combined with elements of supernaturalism (the last two make it like a WWI version of "The Matrix"); a vignette on a variation on "The Last Emperor" (his Grandfather was tutor to a forgotten predecessor to the last emperor). 
 Within what is actually an annoying read there is actually a good novel buried.

Beautifully written. Has all necessary ingredients - historical significance, patriotism, filial piety, the unexplainable web that ensnares life. This book has managed to evoke a myriad of feelings, from awe to anger, from shock to inexplicable understanding. My kind of book! Should have won that darned ManBooker prize (2007) instead of just being longlisted for it!
An interesting look at Malaya/Penang during the time of WWII. Although I felt some remoteness to all the events . . . even horrific events.

Having been accused of never reading fiction, I selected this book partly to correct that impression, but also chose it carefully for its historical landscape and background (Malaysia just before and during the Second World War)--a period and geography I know something about but hoped to learn more. 
 On the content side, it fulfilled that wish. Set in Penang 1939, all its streets, peoples and history seemed authentic as I have walked many of these streets and seen many of the sites mentioned. The historical war facts, such as I know them, also rang sadly true: the naievety and eventual abandonment of Malaya by the British, the various campaigns lost and won, and the atrocities of its occupiers have all been recorded elsewhere. 
 I was not prepared, however, for the honesty of the story that wove all these factual elements together. There was more than a plot of a young Eurasian boy, half-British half-Chinese, born into two families resident in Malaya struggling to survive the war. There was the unfolding of some of the deepest issues that must have torn apart many families, and communities, during this war. The young protagonist who befriends a Japanese diplomat and finds meaning and purpose in his life while betraying much of what he has been taught to respect, surely reflects the painful decisions many who lived during those years had to make. To reveal more would be to destroy the tale. So let me conclude by saying that this is a book that should be read by anyone age 15 or older who wants to learn more about this special time and place in world history, or who has also experienced the struggles of living in more than one culture or within conflicting cultures. It is eloquent and thoughtful, and while it has not cured my bias towards non-fiction works, it has given me pause to consider well-written historical fiction.

This book has many of the things I love most in literature: a cohesive story, clearly drawn characters, a fascinating story, and true historical sweep. It is, however, clearly the work of a neophyte author, albeit a very skilled one. Eventually it becomes a bit plodding, the plot progressing predictably and with little variety. Still, I would recommend this book to anyone who has an interest in some little-known aspects of World War II history. I am not a big fan of "war books", but quite enjoyed this one.
Not as engrossing as his other book, still interesting as far as history.

When John wakes up, he watches the news, with a streaming of Five and Nine fighting. Sam and John go to get them before they kill each other. Six, Marina, and Adam exit The Sanctuary. Nothing relevant changes. 
 I'm in the minority with 90% of the people giving this 4 or 5 stars. I can't wait for this series to end, if you haven't realised by now. It's utterly boring and I can't believe there is the book 7.  All character are identical to the way the acted when they were introduced. I'll spare you the details, since I repeated it multiple times in the reviews of previous books.  Relationships aren't in the spotlight as they were in the previous books and that's the only upside. They were bearable only because of it. John Green is, really and truly, my favorite author. His characters, his plots, his prose, and his style just make me want to read his novels over and over again. "An Abundance of Katherines" is probably my favorite book of his. The characters are hilarious, creative, but simple and realistic enough to be able to relate to. The underlying theme in the novel opened my eyes (as his themes always do). I don't want to post any spoilers, so this review will inevitably be vague and unconvincing, but I recommend this book to any reader. I believe that even adults can enjoy teenage fiction, ESPECIALLY John Green. I also believe that is one of his goals -- to write a novel that will be loved by both teenagers and adults. He definitely meets that goal. His prose is mature enough to be a challenging read, but easy enough for a child to understand. His style is completely original, especially in this book. And it really just SHINES. That's the best way I can think to describe it. READ THIS BOOK. You will not regret it.

You've never met a family quite like The Family Fang by Kevin Wilson. Caleb and Camille Fang are performance artists who create scenes in public that will surprise, shock or amuse people and they video tape the reactions. They were inspired by their daughter Annie's first visit to Santa and from then on their children Annie and Buster were always forced into roles in their art. As adults, Annie and Buster find themselves due to different circumstances both returned to their parental home and suddenly they are in the middle of their parents' biggest performance to date. This story is incredibly quirky and intriguing. I loved the cross between present day and the look into past performances by the family that gained insight into the Fangs' childhood. It had many darkly funny moments, but ultimately the outcome of their parents final performance was sad and disappointing.
Absolutely love its dark humor and exploration of the intricacies of art and family.
i skimmed the last 200 hundred pages, and even then i was bored.

Oh, this is nothing but a quirky, quirky, quirky Wes Anderson movie waiting to happen. Owes a huge debt to The Royal Tenanbaums, from the cover to the family characters forced to deal with the disappointments of adulthood. It's about Buster and Annie, a brother and sister growing up in a family where their parents Caleb and Camille are famous performance artists whose art consists of making weird, uncomfortable spontaneous events in malls and on busy streets. The art is something Buster and Annie have to participate in as children, but then their adult lives take them in strange directions. Simultaneously spiraling downwards, both Annie and Caleb find themselves forced to move back home as adults. 
 There's something so movie-like about this novel - maybe it's that the descriptions of the bizarre performance art happenings seem perfectly suited to being adapted into flashback cutaways in the film version. But the writing is more of a series of vignettes, description rather than immersion, that ends up being a bit less than totally satisfying.

A novel about a couple of "artists" who stage live events (usually stupid stunts at the mall...) and incorporate their 2 children into the mix. The book is all about whether or not you think the parents were cruel to do this, or if it was all part of their love for the children, in trying to bring them into their world of "art". 
 For me, this novel did not work at all because a) I did not find it funny like I think it was supposed to be, and b) the "events" or "happenings" as they referred to the stunts were completely lame and stupid. From the book's description and reviews I've read, I was expecting them to be a lot more clever. But no. Instead I just kept thinking "why am I reading this again?". They just kept doing stuff like handing out fake coupons for the chicken place at the mall, thinking it was hilarious when people approached the counter trying to use their fake coupons. This is the best the author could dream up? 
 It wasn't completely bad--I did sort of enjoy the vignettes of the childrens' (now grown up) adult lives, and how their upbringing affected them, for better or for worse. It does make you think about what kinds of things are good for children or not, and how much you can really buck conventional wisdom on that without causing your offspring more harm than just embarrassment.
for me, a great blend of fun, effed-up, and mystery.

 Jhumpa Lahiri won the Pulitzer Prize for her short story collection The Interpreter of Maladies. I was first introduced to her work through an American Literature class where we read and discussed one of her short stories, "Hell-Heaven." Lahiri's writing style is simple, effortless, elegant. Her descriptions, while lengthy and take a while to get used to, are definitely a strength of The Namesake. 
 However, this being her first novel, I think her sense of plot is much more suited to the short story as this one doesn't seem to have an overarching conflict so much as it presents chronological snapshots of Indian immigrants in America. The first half of the novel deals with Gogol's hatred of his name because it's neither Indian nor American but Russian. To me, this seems an issue that can only take so long to get over. I'm a Filipino with an African-American name. You learn to deal with these things. 
 The second half of the novel chronicles Gogol's many relationships while Gogol himself hardly does anything. I was more invested in Moushumi, who was, in my opinion, the most three dimensional character in the novel. She appears in the last hundred pages and turns the last fifty into a sort of telenovela, but I appreciated the wrench she threw into Gogol's dreary life of inaction. 
 In fact, all the Gangulis seem quite privileged in the sense that there isn't any racial tension in their neighborhood, they can afford to go home every couple of years, and they even have a community of fellow Bengalis to support them emotionally. It must still be immensely difficult, of course, to make a new life from scratch in a different country, but the question that I found myself asking multiple times was, What makes the Gangulis so different from all the other immigrant families? Why are we reading about them when their lives seem so...neat? 
 I was expecting something like Ruth Ozeki's A Tale for the Time Being, which I reviewed some time ago and absolutely loved for its insight into both Japanese and Canadian cultures, mixed with a little bit of family lore a la One Hundred Years of Solitude or The House of the Spirits. I liked the peek into Indian culture, but it was just that--a peek. There weren't any critiques or commentaries on it. At best, there was Moushumi's rebellion from what was expected of her and we got a female point of view that's a little more expansive than Ashima's (Gogol's mother), but again, that only appears in the latter half of the book. Also, without magic realism, families are kind of boring. There are only four of them here so don't expect repeating names and superpowers either. 
 All in all, the book doesn't have much going for it in terms of plot, but if the writing style is enough to get you through the 150 pages it takes before the good part, give this a try. I'm still willing to read The Interpreter of Maladies though and I really want to see the film adaptation starring Kal Penn and Irrfan Khan, so we'll see how that goes.

Jhumpa Lahiri's ''The Namesake'' deals with the lives of Indian immigrants to America and their children- providing a portrait of the struggles of each generation to adjust with the culture of the other. I really enjoyed reading it. I won't say it was a great read. But it was an emotional, almost overwhelming book, that I'd recommend to people who like emotional stories dealing with the harsh realities of life. 
 The story deals with Ashoke and Ashima, an Indian couple, who had an arranged marriage, who have moved to America. Starting in the late 1960s, the novel starts with Ashima giving birth to a son. Near the very beginning of the novel, we are informed that several years ago, Ashoke had faced a railway accident, the train where he was in was crashed into pieces. Many passengers had died, and Ashoke was also near death, but in his hand he had page from a book by Nikolai Gogol, which caused the rescuers to understand that he was still alive and thus, his life was saved. 
 There is a confusion about the child's name. According to the family's customs, the baby will be named by Ashima's grandmother, who had named all of her great-grandchildren. But, however, the letter never arrives, and the great-grandmother becomes severely sick, not remembering anything. So, the child goes by the pet name ''Gogol'', kept in honor of Nikolai Gogol, whose book had saved Ashoke's life. 
 When Gogol is to start school, his parents decide to register the name ''Nikhil'' as the official name of Gogol, but Gogol never responds when he is called Nikhil; he cannot move away from the name Gogol. His parents are compelled to keep his name Gogol. As a little boy the name doesn't bother him. But as he grows up, the rather unusual name starts disturbing, and, at one stage, when he is in his late teens, he finally changes his name to Nikhil. 
 He starts living his life in his own way, but his names always haunt him. To some, he will always remain Gogol. At the same time, he comes across the realities of life, of harshness, loneliness, love, heartbreaks... 
 First of all, the book gives us quite a vivid picture about Indian American family life. The immigrant parents can never fully adjust themselves to the culture and traditions of the new country. To them, their home always remains India. The children, on the other hand, growing up with the culture of America, can never think of India as their home. To them, India is only a place from where their parents had come; to them, the place bears little importance, bringing conflict between the generation. None of the generations can be blamed. 
 The novel also gives a vivid picture of the realities of life. Gogol goes through a lot of troubles, a lot of agonies and heartbreaks in his life, teaching him the realities. Love, betrayal, heartbreak, sadness, deaths of close people- he faces everything in his life. 
 Filled with emotional content, this is a likeable novel, but not certainly a book to fall in love with. I enjoyed reading it; it was engrossing and well-written, vivid and quite powerful. 
 Review by: Shounak Reza 
 Review was originally published in my blog: Shounak's book reviews

Jhumpa Lahiri is one of my favorite authors, and one of the best voices writing today. It therefore pains me to mark her pivotal novel so lowly. Her prose is lilting and lovely, but so full of the everyday details of life that the story never gets to the heart of its characters. While I enjoyed the details of Ashoke and Ashima's immigration and history, the novel loses focus when it shifts to Gogol. What starts out as an interesting, anthropological novel becomes a parade of sad, shallow life stories. I'm still a fan of Lahiri ( 
 Interpreter of Maladies 
 is especially beautiful), and I'll gladly read anything else she publishes. Hopefully her next novel will employ the same strong characters and situations as her short stories.

Wow. I really hated this book with a passion. I was first moved to buy it because I had recognized the author's name and saw that she had earned several important accolades in the literary world. Further, the subject matter appeared to be about something close to my heart: the immigrant experience. Specifically the search for identity amid membership in two conflicting worlds, the old and the new. As someone who has immigrated from Ukraine at a young age, I am always interested to talk to and read accounts of others in the same boat (no pun intended). So I picked up this book expecting something profound, new, innovative- it had after all been written by the famous Jhumpa Lahiri- the very same that won the Pulitzer for Interpreter of Maladies. Besides that it had the added privilege of being called, a Heather pick. 
 Words cannot describe my disappointment. Very quickly after starting it, I resolved to finish it so that I could deliver a fair review. After all, if you don't finish a book, I don't think you have a right to criticize it. So here goes. 
 SPOILERS ahead 
 The omniscient perspective lent a very didactic taste to the book. The book focused mostly on Gogol Ganguli, his mother Ashima, his father Ashoke and at times his sister Sonia (though she was largely marginal) as well as his wife Moushemi. Even though the perspective was meant to give us exclusive insights into their secret inner worlds and motivations, the writing lacked depth and inventiveness. The characters were hallow similacra of real people, their flaws carefully fashioned to make them relatable but in the end just made them bland, forgettable and mundane. This is yet another example of the fact that in trying to appeal to everyone, you end up producing something so watered down and lacking in character it loses all fortitude as a work of art. Needless to say my BS detector was going off every few pages. There were times that I had to pause my reading just to digest the overwhelming stench of hackery. 
 The biggest disappointment was the way the author treated the main theme of 'names' as stand in for identity. In the book we learn that traditional Bengali culture requires each person to be given a private nickname to be used by close friends and family and a public "good name" to be used in all other situations. The main male character,the son in the story, grows up with the name Gogol because of a situation that arises as result of his immigrant parents not receiving his maternal great grandmothers name suggestion on time, forcing his parents to defy tradition by naming him themselves. His father settles on Gogol as that his favorite Russian author and also because that is that author he was reading when he was in a train accident that nearly left him dead years before his son was born. Therefore the name signifies survival, novelty and legacy at the same time. So much could have been done to develop this theme further or to delve into the significance of these themes. But no, the author simply walks us through a garden variety childhood and adolescence of an immigrant where his predictable struggles with identity cause him to resent his "pet name" as well as resolve to distance himself from his roots by changing his name, dating Western girls and fraternizing with Western ideals. While the idea of feeling guilty for embracing, even identifying strongly with a culture you do not share with your family is one that resonates with me, the way it was treated in this book fell short of profound to say the least. The triteness of the name motif and the circular , neatly tied up ending was highly disappointing.
I couldn't get into or therefore through it... I'm ashamed.
It was so fascinating to see life through the eyes of Gogol.
This is book is beautiful look at culture and a family in transition, as families constantly are. It's a necessary glimpse into the challenges of assimilation set in compelling theater of emotion.

American contemp....late 20th cent....first generation Indian, growing up between cultures, self definition. Telling of a life's trajectory in present tense - makes you feel like you're always ramping up to the point but never getting there.
Amazing, amazing! And if you get a chance, see the movie with Kal Penn - he does a superb job!
A little slow for me but overall a really good book about family. And how we fit in our family. Liked the story a lot.
Too depressing. My book club all hated it, particuarly the ending.

reference_books.title: The Witching Hour (Lives of the Mayfair Witches, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Ohmygod what a huge waste of my time. I feel like I might just have spent longer reading this book than Rice spent editing it. I swear a third of it was just descriptions of air. Another third was characters restating the main plot points over and over again until I wanted to beat them up. The final third was mostly a kind of written family tree describing a whole host of characters that were largely indistinguishable from one another and about whom I cared not at all. It was imposed right in the middle of the extremely sparse plot, of which there was maybe enough to support a book a quarter of the length of this one. But that book would also be extremely boring and ill-advised. 
 Also the characterisation was just terrible. I don't know how I'm supposed to relate to main characters who start the book as millionaires and end it as billionaires. Their love story was absolutely excruciating, as were the totally cringe sex scenes. Rice thinks we want to be told, again and again, that he is totally "pornographic" in the least thing he does, and there's also a sex scene in a shower in which he's wearing leather gloves and it describes in detail how the gloves feel on her skin and it's just like come ON, lady, are you eroticism-deaf? 
 Anyway.

reference_books.title: Reamde
reference_books.review_text:
This book really annoyed me. Which surprised me because I've quite liked other Stephenson books. I've found them sophisticated and interesting, whereas the more I read of Reamde the more I realized it was actually pedestrian and boring. 
 It started off relatively promisingly, with lots of talk about the worldbuilding, technology, and economy behind the virtual world of T'Rain, but descended much faster then I'd have liked into schlock action and completely out-of-place Amerocentrism. 
 This is something that's not even hinted at in the blurb, which makes me think that the publishers didn't really know what to do with this novel, and tried to mis-sell it to Stephenson's core audience. Instead, I felt like I was reading some less-inspired Tom Clancy novel. 
 Some of the things I didn't like about this book: 
 - Firstly, the action-movie villain, conveniently both Muslim AND British, and his slapstick band of one-dimensional 'Jihadists'. Also how many times Stephenson is able to refer to them as 'Jihadists'. 
 - How every character is either good or evil, and the good characters are wholly good, irrepressible, "kick-asssss" characters, and the evil characters are sadistic rapists bent on the destruction of civilization. 
 - The virtual world T'Rain, Stephenson's bread-and-butter subject, would just not work at all as an online game. It's derivative, impossible, and, frankly, sounds a real snoooooze. 
 - There's no sense of pacing or tension or anything. This is common to Stephenson's novels, but really bugged me here. It's 2 massive action sequences with a bunch of stuff in the middle, and it all proceeds at the same stately pace. 
 - The action sequences take FOREVER. And the guns are described in such DETAIL. Who needs such DETAIL? It's not INTERESTING. 
 - It's actually really quite racist and sexist. All the women end up being saved by men multiple times, but never the other way around. The main woman character gets to play damsel for nine-tenths of the book, and her asshole billionaire uncle gets to be the hero and kill the bad guy. How dumb. 
 Finally, a note on the audiobook version. The narrator can't do accents. Every British person sounds like the queen, even the Welsh Black Muslim terrorist leader. The Scottish character sounds vaguely Russian and the Russian characters sound vaguely Scottish. The French-Canadian RCMP officer sounds Spanish. The Chinese sound like squirrels. It's just terrible. 
 Gonna end my rant here.

reference_books.title: Undermajordomo Minor
reference_books.review_text:
A wonderful, bizarre little book. I'm being ungenerous in giving it 3 stars, but I can't say I really liked it. I don't think it set out to be really liked by anyone. It's curious, slight, digressive, and characterful, and a joy to listen to. I'd recommend it to anyone. But really liked it? No, I can't say that. 
 Lucy Minor's a great character; only one of many in the book. I could have listened to him chatter on for much longer.

reference_books.title: The Truth About the Harry Quebert Affair
reference_books.review_text:
Originally posted on Time Thy Pyramids. 
 IT'S SO BAD DON'T READ IT!! 
 Hopefully anyone who's just skimming this page will see the above and then refrain from spending actual time actually reading this terrible book. 
 Just like Graeme Macrae Burnet's His Bloody Project, the last book I reviewed on here, Joel Dicker's The Truth about the Harry Quebert Affair is an example of a novel that's been much better received by serious literary types than I can understand. Unlike His Bloody Project, though, which was an adept and enjoyable work, even though I don't get why it's on the Booker shortlist this year, Quebert is a silly, sloppy, flabby, idiot novel - a banquet of cliches pieced together with a nonsense plot and written by a teenager. And yet it won the 2012 Grand Prix du roman de l'Academie francaise and was nominated for the Goncourt, and it's an international bestseller. Hmm. 
 Briefly, the narrator, Marcus Goldman, a young celebrity novelist, decides to try to clear his mentor Harry Quebert, one of the greatest living American writers, who has been charged with murder following the discovery of a body in his garden. The body belongs to Nola Kellergan, a fifteen-year-old girl who went missing in 1975, and with whom the thirty-three-year-old Quebert had been having an affair. He basically ends up writing and publishing a tell-all book while leading the investigation (because, duh, that's how crime-fighting happens in America), and of course he finds all sorts of buried secrets beneath the friendly New-England-small-town veneer, revealed through interspersed flashbacks and documents. So far so compelling. 
 But the book lets itself down on every level. Let's start with the plot, which is multistranded and sprawling, but which very little effort has been made to make internally consistent. For example, on the same night Nola disappears in 1975, the old woman who sees her being chased through the woods is shot. However, because Dicker's decided that the novel's focus is going to be on Nola, everyone involved - from the police searching for Nola to the townspeople grieving for the missing girl to Marcus narrating in 2008 - completely forgets about the dead woman. Nobody really thinks to try to solve that mystery. She barely gets mentioned, to the point that I forget her name. 
 And this happens more than once over the course of the book. In the present day, people get killed, buildings get set on fire, suspects literally skip town overnight, and nobody really seems to care beyond the extent to which these acts affect the main question of who killed Nola? even though solving these peripheral mysteries is probably a much more direct route than going to the town diner and hoping to find someone to question about the events of thirty years ago which is how the investigation proceeds most of the time. 
 The police procedural aspects are just unbelievably bad. Towards the end of the book, Marcus and Gahalowood, his cop buddy, do a double facepalm because they FORGOT, legitimately FORGOT, to follow up a lead about events which happened in Alabama in the late '60s. As if neither of them, a WRITER, and a COP, thought to write it down. Later, an 'aha' moment comes when Gahalowood is casually looking at a key piece of evidence implicating a man they just arrested while IN THE DINER EATING HIS PANCAKES OR WHATEVER because maple syrup on incriminating photographs makes them even more persuasive to a jury. 
 And don't even get me started on the central love affair between Quebert and Nola, which is clearly intended to be the stuff of great literature - a love for the ages - but reads like a harlequin novel written by a teenager. Quebert falls in love with Nola at first sight when he sees her dancing in the rain on the beach, which is just sheer laziness on Dicker's part. In fact, we are told time and again about how Quebert found it impossible not to love Nola, as in this dialogue between Marcus and his secretary: 
 "Marcus, I think I'm crying." 
 "Why?" I asked. 
 "Because of that young girl, that Nola; I think I love her too." 
 I smiled and said, "I think everyone loved her, Denise. Everyone." Yet all we see is a naive child who is in turn manipulative, whiny, stalkery, and a little psycho. She's not smart or funny or anything to Quebert beyond a hero worshipper, which really underlines the creepiness inherent in the whole adult-child-relationship thing that Dicker tries so hard to make you think isn't actually problematic though it so is. 
 It's not just Nola who's a really bad character. Literally every single character in the book is an underbaked cliche.* There's the narcissistic celebrity novelist, the sage lovelorn mentor, the grumpy cop with a heart of gold, the shyster lawyer, the overbearing Jewish mother, the rich Harvard-educated businessman and his physically deformed chauffeur. There's the social-climber diner owner and her long-suffering husband. They talk like this: 
 "But my shirt is making me itch, honey-bunny." 
 "Shut up, Bobbo!" When Marcus and Gahalowood visit a mechanic, they meet him with his head under an old Buick, which makes sense because he's a cliche. There's even a police chief who turns up in the last chapter to say you've got 24 hours to close this case! as if that's not a totally arbitrary deadline dreamt up to keep the tension going. 
 This isn't helped by the fact that the writing is ridiculous, which makes every character sound like an idiot whenever they open their mouth. Here's a phone call between Marcus and Gahalowood: 
 "I'm on the Interstate. I'm going to see Elijah Stern." 
 "So you really think he's mixed up in all this?" 
 "That's exactly what I'm hoping to find out." 
 "You're totally crazy, Goldman. That's what I like about you." 
 Here's Marcus trying to comfort Quebert in prison: 
 I grabbed him by the shoulders. "We will always be friends. I won't abandon you. This book is the proof of my unfailing friendship." 
 Heck, at one point, Quebert, one of the world's greatest living writers, says "All I know is that Nola lived inside me, literally," which, this book won the Grand Prix, so, wow, is all I'm saying. The characters also do the remind-me-of-the-exposition...? thing way too often, as if they're lapsing into temporary amnesia, which might explain some of the plot holes. 
 Also the novel jumps between viewpoints pretty frequently, and will sometimes flirt with omniscience in a terrifically annoying, fourth-wall-breaking way. We'll get haphazard snatches of each character's thoughts in a manner totally unbefitting a murder mystery. Or one minute Nola will be thinking about how excited she is that she's going to see Quebert, and then we'll get a... she did not notice the figure hidden in the bushes. That's a real line from the book. I didn't make it up. 
 I finished the book though. I guess I thought it would get better, or have a satisfying conclusion, and there were one or two (actually one) halfway decent twists, but the solution was convoluted and had a bit of a comedy-of-errors feel to it, so even that didn't satisfy. 
 Oh man. I could go on. There's so many truly scathing reviews on here with some exceptional examples of why this is an awful book and you should never read it. But there's also a crazy amount of gushingly positive reviews, so go and try to reconcile all that because I just can't. I'm so confused. 
 Notes on the audiobook: 
 Robert Slade's narration is the best thing about this book. It's still pretty bad. He has two voices, moderately angry and moderately whiny, and the nasal New England accent doesn't help things. I think that I would have liked the book slightly more reading it the old-fashioned way (slightly, mind). But then again, I probably wouldn't have had the stamina to finish it if I had to actually hold something and move my eyes back and forth, so there are no winners here. 
 * I was talking to Daisy about how everyone in the book was a New England small town / police procedural cliche. She then proceeded to guess every single character in the book with no prompting. She's psychic and everything, but the point that I'm making is that the book is bad.
