book_a.title: The Last Policeman (The Last Policeman, #1)
book_a.user_review: I didn't really expect to enjoy this as much as I did. It's not a great piece of literature, but rather a well-done, well-written exploration about life going on with the knowledge that it might be meaningless. An exciting twist on the detective genre.

sample_reviews.review_text: I liked the parts that looked at how people react to the last days more than the murder mystery. Not being a big mystery reader, it seems to me that the detectives pull things out of thin air sometimes. I might read the next one in the series. I'm more interested in the last one in the series.

Enjoyable existentialism with everyday people told via a suicide investigated by a conscientious cop in pre-apocalyptic Concord, New Hampshire. 
 (There's more on my blog about The Last Policeman, here. Thank you to Quirk Books for the review copy.)

Odd take on the detective story. The conventions are here for your typical murder mystery, but Winters adds the twist of an asteroid hurtling to earth to allow characters to act in irrational ways that still conform to the internal logic of the genre.

What a rewarding little book this was!! But am I the only one left wondering why the current cover is so completely unappealing? Seriously, it's nothing like what's pictured here. Instead, it's a collage of photos, one of a man's feet left dangling in the air, another of the upper half of a man, and the 3rd and most prominent, of a house with a spacious front yard, with a meteor-like object in the sky above this scene. 
 More often than not, my best friend Rebecca reads the same books I do. When I sent her a picture of this cover, despite the glowing terms in which I described the book (I was about a third of the way through it then), she flatly stated that, "that [book] looks really dumb," and declared she had no interest in reading it. Undeterred, I bought her a paperback copy, and she finished the book a few days before I did. She loved it!!! 
 So yet again, we are reminded here to not judge a book by its cover. 
 The story was so likable, as was the main character. The fact that this was a mystery set against the backdrop of the world coming to a cataclysmic end in mere months, somehow "worked." I think this is a tribute to Winters' writing. The story flowed wonderfully, and the book was very difficult to put down. 
 Busy as I am, I simply HAD TO order book 2 immediately, and I bought books 2 AND 3 for Rebecca. She'll likely finish both before I'm half way into book two.... 
 I've always been envious of those who are able to use the simplest language to communicate something so much bigger than the words used to say it. Such is the case with this book. At least a couple of times, I highlighted a passage that I thought was neatly profound. I did not expect to find that in this particular book. 
 So I cannot wait to dive into the next one. I'm curious where the story will go, given the plot-imposed expiration date on the world as we know it. And I can't wait to find out. This is worth every moment spent reading it. For those of you who have not yet read the book, I urge you to give it a look-see. A great marriage of genres, and the mystery portion thereof? It did keep me guessing until the very end, which is always a huge plus to me! Happy reading, everyone!

3.5 
 Everyone in the world knows that in six months, a giant asteroid is going collide with the Earth, killing untold millions and forever changing life for the few who manage to survive. Faced with "all of this unbearable immanence," many people are walking off the job, turning to drugs or religion, or committing suicide. 
 When he first sees the body of Peter Zell in a McDonald's bathroom, Detective Hank Palace thinks it's just another in the string of suicides that have earned Concord, New Hampshire the nickname "Hangertown." But something doesn't seem right, and Palace becomes convinced that Zell was actually murdered. Although the other police officers mock him ("What's the point in solving murders if we're all going to die soon anyway?"), he begins to investigate, following twisting leads through a city braced for disaster. 
 This book has a really great hook, and the exploration of different ways people react to knowing the exact date of the end of the world is well-done. The mystery is suspenseful, and while the end of the book isn't exactly satisfying (It's the first in a trilogy, so the asteroid doesn't crash yet...), it's at least a natural stopping point. Some of the characters felt like hollow 'whodunit?' cariacatures, but Winters tries to get inside the head of others. 
 This book would be a good choice for those who want a unique mystery or apocalyptic fiction. Although it's written for adults, teens would probably like it too.

What an entertaining book! 
 Not only did I like the detective story, the detective himself, the upheaval of society context- all of that- but the WIT. The wit so filled with obvious human cognitive and psychological knowledge! 
 Scrumptious little gem. Sort of crossover mystery/dystopic/psychology of chaos. 
 It held some quotes that were priceless. Also a new phrase that just so describes current media driven belief/ cultural values of judgment and continual angst, as well: unbearable immanence. 
 I had to write that one down. Perfect to silkscreen on a t-shirt for a diva drama queen professor emeritus.

I was pretty excited for this book. a mash up of a thriller mystery and apocalypse. be still my beating Heart. 
 except I feel like it was poorly executed. like a strong creative writing project or a decent YA book but not well written or depth by any means. 
 characters were 2 dimensional. I don't think I was interested in any of them, especially the narrator. 
 dialogue was cringe worthy. no one talks like this. all their motivations and thoughts were childish and unrealistic. 
 holy mollely said the grown adult brutish male police officer/detective over and over again. 
 I felt lots of repetitive information. Lots of telling not showing. Lots of rehashing and summarizing in a book that's not that long, it didn't need so much reminder information. 
 I guess this is a series now, I want to know more about the meteor because it was very much background noise in this first one so maybe the series gets better? I'm undecided if I want to go forward.
The premise is great, but the question on if it will really payoff will have to wait until I read the remaining books in the trilogy. I enjoyed it, but wasn't enthralled.
I was really disappointed...I expected more of the murder case..maybe a link with the asteroid impact...
Not sure I'd class this as scifi...

book_b.title: The Orenda
book_b.user_review: It was recommended to me extremely highly, and so I was a little bit disappointed. Clearly masterful, thrilling, visceral, and enlightening, it's also occasionally hamfisted, confusing, reductive, and unenjoyable. The Tenderness of Wolves was better, just because I cared about what happened to the characters and making my way to the end of the story.

sample_reviews.review_text:
"The Orenda" is a book that tells the tale of Jesuits coming to Canada amid the fighting of two Native tribes in Canada: The Huran and the Iroquois. But is the threat now the third party the Jesuits? 
 How can all these souls fit into one country? 
 It tells a tale we might not have really thought about: The 17th century First Nations and European first contacts with each other and how hard it would be to understand who is the other. 
 I just finished reading "The Orenda" last night. 
 I can't really decide how I feel. 
 I learned a lot. It challenged me a lot and I left it with a better understanding of some of the history of my country. But I did not really like it. And it made me sad. And uncomfortable. But sometimes that is what a book is supposed to do. Challenge you. 
 I feel like it was a big effort. 
 A huge effort that might have fallen a little bit too short. 
 I discussed with a friend on Twitter that we had hoped the female characters were a little bit more drawn out. They felt a bit flat, not fully rounded out and I wanted a little bit more from them. 
 I wanted them to be heroes, to come out happy and on their own. I wanted more from Gosling the whole time, she fascinated me. 
 I wanted a little bit more about how these people felt, their emotions the inside of them. 
 All in all, I thought it was a heavy book but a book people should read. 
 I don't remember learning any of this in the history I studied in school. 
 And we all need to learn this story.

So my teeth ache after reading this. In had to clench them so often to be able to navigate through the horror in this novel. I really enjoyed it. I would actually give it a 4.5 only because it was a tough start for me. But once I was in, I was hooked. It was great book. I feel things stirring in me now that I'm done.

Fictionalized version of the first Catholic mission in Ontario, and the dispersal of the Wendat (or Huron) peoples during the Huron-Iroquois wars, which culminated with the sacking of the Sainte Marie mission located near what is now Midland Ontario (a reconstuction of the mission is now a "living history" tour site which I visited as a child). 
 The novel is narrated (irritatingly) in the present tense by three voices, the Crow (Christophe), a fictionalized version of the leader of the mission, Jean de Brebeuf; Bird, leader of the Wendat/Huron: and his adopted Iroquois/Haudenosaunee daughter, Snow Falls (who early in the novel pees in her adoptive father's bed and cuts off one of his fingers--and one of her own, by mistake, at the same time--ah, family!). I say "irritatingly" because, first off, I tend to find present tense narrative disengaging, but in this instance even more so because the conceit is that each figure is apparently narrating his or her experience inside his or her head to some other figure: God for Crow, his dead wife for Bird (note the nomenclature, btw), her dead parents--killed by Bird--for Snow Falls. I just don't buy people carrying out their daily life in constant internal monologue to some imagined auditor. Two of the three first-person present-tensers are dead by the end, by the way. 
 Anyway, that said, Boyden seems to be aiming for a relatively fair representation of the historical reality. Notoriously, he does not spare details about the tortures inflicted by the First Nations peoples, though people complaining about this violence in the book seem to me both rather to miss the point and to have selective vision when it comes to media violence. The novel is primarily about culture clash, after all, and about the inherently violent (even if the violence is implicit rather than explicit) process of cultural erasure. Boyden is fair-minded in that the three narrative prespectives show that the issue is not merely European vs FN, but also clashes among FN groups, though obviously the European incursion into North America is central, as it exacerbates the internecine warfare. Boyden perhaps overgilds the lily by not only giving us Europeans providing FN people with alcohol and anally raping a young boy but also by making the Eucharist literally toxic when one missionary poisons it in order to perform what he conceives of as compassionate euthanasia on his flock, to spare them capture and torture. I also wasn't overly thrilled by the novel's intimations of genuine mysticism; it's one thing for people to believe in magic, another for a supposedly historical novel to, if not actually endorse, at least strongly imply its reality. 
 Even linguistically, the novel comments on cultural erasure. For instance, only Crow uses the terms "Huron" and "Iroquois"; the peoples themselves use "Wendat" and "Haudenosaunee." Somewhat oddly on this front, though Crow's actual French is represented in English, he is always represented as using the French word "sauvages" rather than its English equivalent "savages" to describe the FN peoples--perhaps to play punningly on the verb "sauver" "to save" as well: the "savages" are those he wishes to save, but it clunked a bit for me. Indeed, Boyden's prose is not overall exceptional. Infelicities like referring to "stragglers" "straggling" in are relatively rare, but his prose is not, in general, particularly impressive. However, as a work of historical fiction, this is overall a worthwhile read.

THE ORENDA by Joseph Boyden was on the ScotiaBank Giller Prize Longlist. It was a Finalist for the Canadian Council for the Arts Governor General's Literary Awards and is a 2014 CBC Radio One Canada Reads Selection. 
 All these awards sound impressive, but in reality they mean very little. The proof of the author's prowess does not come from receiving awards, it comes from the enjoyment of the person reading the book. Often the people giving out awards (in my opinion) get it wrong. This time, however, they definitely got it right. The Orenda is a superb read. 
 The book begins with the kidnapping of a young Iroquois girl named Snow Falls, and with the murder of her family. The kidnapper/killer is a Huron indian named Bird who was acting in retaliation of the murders of his wife and daughters a few years previously. 
 Bird, Snow Falls, the Huron war party and a Jesuit Missionary named Christophe are returning to the Huron settlement. 
 Christophe views the Indians as savages and believes they practice witchcraft. 
 Bird hopes to take on Snow Falls as a daughter to replace the ones he lost. 
 The many Indian nations are warring amongst themselves and are all but oblivious to the fact that the settlers are actually the bigger threat. They see only the opportunity for profit through trade. The few who do see the Jesuits (or Crows as the Huron call them) as a threat are overruled by the Elders. 
 The Jesuits seek to change the Indians to be more like "civilized" Europeans. Christophe says, "If there is one thing I will never grow accustomed to, it's the sauvages' (sic) inability to chastise their children. In all my years here I have never seen an adult even raise a hand in anger toward a child." 
 You would think this would be a quality he admires in the Huron, however, that is not the case, as is proved by the next sentence he writes: "Indeed, this should be one of the first behaviors we must try to modify." 
 This book is an informative and engrossing read. The storyline is compelling and I found myself not wanting to put the book down, even to go to sleep. 
 What I began to read as pure entertainment quickly became more; much more. This is a timeless tale that is rich with historical detail. The characters of Bird, Gosling, Fox, Christophe and Snow Falls are so well written and painstakingly detailed that I felt each of their fates keenly. I fretted with them in times of difficulty, mourned with them in times of sadness and shared their happiness and contentment in times of joy. 
 There are very few novels that Si would designate as "Must Read" but THE ORENDA is exactly that. Anyone and everyone who reads this book will not be disappointed. My expectations of this book were very high and I am thrilled to say that not only did it meet these expectations, it surpassed them. Simply put, if you do not read THE ORENDA, you are missing out. 
 I give this book 6 stars out of 5. I know this makes no sense mathematically, but it is just that good.
Easily Boyden's weakest, and derivative of Brian Moore's Black Robe.

This story got more and more brutal as it went along, a crude yet seemingly accurate depiction of the life that was lived by first nations, especially the Huron-Wendat, with their own wars to wage against the Iroquois while Europeans settlers were arriving in their lands and trying to assimilate them. 
 It wasn't always easy to stay invested since I didnt find any of the characters that likeable and since the pace was slow for more than half the book. Still, this style of narration, with the 3 different point of views (a Huron war chief, a young captured Iroquois girl and a French Jesuit priest) gave the reader a very wide view and understanding of the story, which ended up being pretty devastating, to be honest. 
 Overall a very poignant historical account, even fictionalized, of a time when the country that is my home was a very different place.

This book tells the history of interactions among the Huron, Iroquois and Jesuits in Canada during the 1600s. The author relates this history through the perspectives of three main characters, each told in first person, of a young Iroquois female (Snow Falls), a Huron warrior (Bird) and a Jesuit missionary (Christophe). I thought the author did an excellent job of showing how differences in perspective can lead to misunderstandings. I enjoyed the descriptions of the physical beauty of the country and the way in which the people lived. The characters were well-developed, and they evolved over time. 
 I found the book well-written, engrossing, and educational. I recommend this book to those who enjoy historical fiction, or who want to learn more about Canadian history or the lives of native peoples of North America. WARNING: It is EXTREMELY graphic in describing torture of captives of the warring tribes. It depicts a brutality that will likely be disturbing to many readers.
Wow. Just, wow.

A very impressive piece of writing which contains a heap of character and flavour. The mean, bitter (and mostly ostracized) cynic in me was kind of wary in the sense of 'Oh hey another CanLit book about the early colonial era of North America, listed for prizes, Jesuits (there's a surprise), clash of cultures, First Nations depictions sure to rankle and enchant the critics in equal measure, recall Brebeuf, oh well let's go...' - the usual unworthy response. The book was at hand and I decided it would fit the bill nicely, though at some point I might regret not reading Doctor Zhivago when I had the chance. 
 That said, this book is incredibly, even amazingly well-written. It practically reeks of craft. I found that the passages sped by feverishly and there was no real slack in the plot at all. It touched upon a few familiar notes, sure, but I am beginning to think they are unavoidable (hence the cynic). Obviously it's not the happiest tale around, most people ought to know full well what's going to go down, but it reads sublimely at points and that alone recommends this book to those who would enjoy it most. I found it to be rather bittersweet, all in all, with a lot of cool detail. 
 The characters are all interesting and most of them are deep, though some of the most promising ones only ever exist in the margins. If the setting interests you, take a chance on this one: I've never read one entirely like it and I suspect parts of it will stay with me for some time. At this point in time it's so easy to forget the history of North America thanks to the tireless efforts of the historical taxidermists to turn it into a stuffy tale that won't offend too many people. The truth is almost always offensive, not to mention horrifying. All of which makes this book pretty important, even if it is flawed.
Amazing book.

reference_books.title: Women in Love (Brangwen Family, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Oh my. It is a book about people who have too much time on their hands - or how else wopuld they have time to ramble about the very minute details of life. 
 Long rambling about love (between a man and a woman and two men) and hate. There are many love triangles in the book. And a lot of philosophy on living and death. But so long and over verbose. And for me lacking an overall idea. 
 A truly boring book and I was really happy once I had finished it.

reference_books.title: The Restaurant at the End of the Universe (Hitchhiker's Guide, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Oh my. Just as good as the first one. I really love the scrabble part of it. 
 Just big smiles.

reference_books.title: The White Tiger
reference_books.review_text:
The good thing about this book is that at least it is readable and I finished it fast. 
 Other than that it was not a good book. There were no characters in the book - just self-centred unmoral corrupt figures - all the same and without any depth. There was no story, things just happened. And as there were no characters there also was no character evolution - which you would expect at least when talking about the murder (how a person can be lead that far). 
 It is also a rather dark book about India - not one good person, not one good thing about India in the entire book. Just dark and angry.

reference_books.title: Tarzan of the Apes (Tarzan, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
The story is enthralling even though I knew the outlines before I started (it is hard not do know anything about Tarzan). 
 However the inaccuracy of the book left me a little appalled (though some of it was thought to be correct at the time of writing). I guess I expected more from this book, but in the end it was just a fantastic story.

reference_books.title: Jazz
reference_books.review_text: Not at all what I expected after the first couple of pages. I kept looking for the brilliance of the beginning and in the end felt disappointed in the book.

book_a.title: Unless
book_a.user_review: A story about all the little things in life. About ordinary people and tragedy. About women.

sample_reviews.review_text: Kept trying to force myself through the book, but, finally, at page 76, I just couldn't do it. Protagonists seems a bit narcissistic, and Shields couldn't really get to the point. Wanted the emotion and depth connected to her (homeless) daughter, but this was too buried in exposition.
It was a great story idea but I didn't love the main character.
Such a long hard slow. I hate give no up on books so I finished it.

Unless spoke directly to me as a parent and I suppose as a feminist, as a person who has experienced the terror of a "lost" child and the frustration of a world that sets limits on my children. As a reader, there were times that I wondered if Shields would get beyond the angst and the dreaming to something that resembled plot. Without realizing it, however, I found myself hooked on the mystery surrounding Reta's oldest daughter. Sometimes irritated by the mundane and the philosophical, the whimsy and the whining, I soldiered on and was rewarded in the end for my patience. In the end, the pieces fit rather nicely into a story. In the end, what seemed at first like fat, was indeed muscle.

I don't have a whole lot to say about this book. The central premise, that a normal young woman, raised in a normal loving suburban family, would suddenly abandon her life and become a panhandler on the streets of Toronto, is compelling. The concept of having the story told from the perspective of her mother, who has no idea why her daughter has made such a bizarre choice, seems to offer a lot of possibilities for psychological examination. But somehow the whole book seemed to fall a little flat. 
 The speaker in the book, the mother mentioned above, is a writer, and she is always reflecting on her writing process and the way a novel should be constructed. She mentions her habit of reading obituaries because the idiosyncratic personal details that they include are the sort of perfect little traits a writer can include to make characters more relatable, realistic, and appealing. And then she fills her novel (and the novel that her novel-writing protagonist is working on) with just these sort of quirky traits-- we get an elderly, well-respected and serious writer who always wears cheap, ugly cardigans and gets weekly manicures to keep her nails immaculate; a physician who spends hours researching trilobytes; and a professional trombonist with a passionate desire to reconnect with his Albanian heritage. I guess I felt the author constantly referring to herself and her own writing process and it seemed as if she was pointing out how clever and observant she was, which I found a little annoying. This is particularly irritating because all of the characters came equipt with cute foibles but seemed to lack real psychological depth. Even the eventual explanation for her daughter's break with society, though touchingly written, seemed tacked on and wasn't fully explored. 
 There was also this running thread about the exclusion of women from the literary canon that kept getting on my nerves. It just seemed like a shallow feminism, maybe just another quirk culled from someone's obituary-- "She was a life-long feminist intellectual, passionate about promoting the work of underrated female writers." 
 This book kept me reading, but ultimately, it wasn't very satisfying.

Did I tell you I just clocked up a count of just over 500 novels read, according to my GR novels shelf? Hey, how about that. It must make me some kind of authority now. I can dish out advice, start up a helpline, I know which novel to attach to the St Bernard dog to take to the fallen climber in the Alps. 
 Except, I'm actually getting worse at picking novels to read. I just checked, and 13 out of 27 novels read so far this year have got a 1 or 2 star rating, i.e. I hated them & felt they were a blight on my life. Why is that? 
 Part of the problem is that when I find an author I like I never read anything else by them, it would be too obvious (recent exceptions : Edward St Aubyn and Jean Rhys). Also, I think I'm easily led by reviewer enthusiasm. This explains The Shock of the Fall, Gone Girl, Little Big and Her. But glorious reviews also led me to Life After Life, Animals and The Death of Bees, three recent books which delighted my very left ventricle. 
 You can't even rely on a novel's "classic" status, whatever that consists of. I Capture the Castle and The Man Who Loved Children turned out to be insufferable and worthy of forceful defenestration, but Lucky Jim, Where Angels Fear to Tread and The Talented Mr Ripley were all ripping good fun. 
 This present volume, Unless, winged its way to me garlanded with shortlists (2003 Booker & Orange) & dripping with critical fluids. But they were all wrong. It was dire. 
 A comfortable late 40s doctors' wife in Ontario has three lovely daughters. The eldest, 19 year old Norah, drops out of university to become a street person. Sits on the pavement in Toronto with a begging bowl holding a sign saying GOODNESS. This is not an uninteresting circumstance - Philip the Roth had a similar thing going on in American Pastoral. But it's not what you do, it's the way that you do it, and Carol Shields does a Lionel Shriver by mentioning the awful horror briefly then spending 100 plus pages maundering over every last possible detail of her comfortable middle-class-translating-wise-feminist-books-from-the-French-growing-old-gracefully-but-now-wondering-what-the-point-of-it-all-is-cutesy-artsy Canadian life. After p 120 I knew what the daughter was up to. The front of her sign said GOODNESS but the back said ME, MOTHER, PUT A SOCK IN IT.

I liked Carol Shields' book Stone Diaries, but this one didn't measure up. The narrator just did a lot of thinking during most of the book, and nothing really happened. Just like real life? There were parts that didn't make sense to me, that I thought would be resolved, like the man who asked the elderly mother-in-law to "tell him all about herself." This somehow gave the main character a clue, but I remained clueless. The denouement was a disappointment to me too. Well written, but meandering.
Just couldn't get into this book. Gave up.

Unless runs almost along a similar vein to the narrative in "The Gathering," where a mother loses her daughter to a cause that no one understands, and has to deal with the situation both practically and emotionally. In Unless though, as opposed to The Gathering, this process is dealt with with a vast amount more insight, more positivity, and depth of feeling. As with life, there are comic moments in the dark, there are strong relationships, idiotic bosses, and funny friends to get you through. A quick but worthy read, I really enjoyed this one.

I was bored by this book - I didn't care about any of the characters and since it was the first Carol Shields book I had read I haven't read her since ... I need to try another one of her books and see how I feel about her.

book_b.title: A Clockwork Orange
book_b.user_review: A horrible story written in a hard to follow language.

sample_reviews.review_text: Couldn't get through the whole thing.

I had somewhat high expectations for this book, as it is so well known... 
 I hated it. 
 Don't get me wrong, the writing was good, often poetic, to the extent that even though I didn't understand a lot of the words, you could still get the gist, which makes for a clever author. 
 But the STORY, urgh. Yes, themes are all there, I understand the moral, but the story? It was grim. It was hard not to wince at some parts of this book. Maybe it's my gender speaking for me, but it was so uncomfortable to read. 
 I forced myself to the end of this book in the hopes that there would be some light at the end of the tunnel but I was wrong. I just felt empty, angry and deflated. 
 Would I put this book in my top 100? No. Would I recommend it to someone else? Probably. Just because I feel liked it was a learning curve for me. 
 However, I would not ever read it again and I most definitely won't be watching the film.

Not sure how I feel about this book. The vocabulary made it quite hard to understand, although easier to stomach some of the super violent scenes, especially early on. I would agree that the last chapter, omitted in the American version, ends on a note of optimism that I don't think the story ever merits. 
 Alex's remorse under reconditioning is not true remorse; it's merely classical conditioning at its finest. As the chaplain put it, "a man who cannot choose ceases to be a man." And when he can choose, he chooses violence again, which says a lot about the human condition. Others in the story show little or no remorse either, as his victims turn around to brutalize him just as easily. 
 There were some salient points about the government however, especially regarding the cycle of violence and power and how violence maintains power. Still mulling over the story though. Might be good for a revisit later.

What can I say...this was one of the strangest books I have ever read. I was a little nervous to read it considering I had heard about the movie when I was in college and all that was entailed in it...but I was curious and wanted to know more. Boy...I'm glad they have an introduction to this book to help explain what in the heck is going on here. The language is something else..."nasdat".....the talk of teenagers at that time. It does help to soften the reading of the gross violence that Alex bestows upon his many victims by sounding it out in "nasdat talk"...but it is still so strange and foreign. I could not entirely enjoy this book...I suppose it kept my interest...I did not find it boring...but I did not find myself wanting to race through my daily routine to get back to it. But hey...now I can finally say I actually read it!

There is only one thought that comes to mind after reading this book: 
 Jesus wept.
I get why this book is a classic but I hated it so there you go!
Amazing.

I had to watch the Kubrick film of Clockwork several times for a couple of film studies classes I took, and every time I did I hated it. There was always an eye roll and a "oh not this again!" mental note. So when we got around to writing papers I completely ignored this film. 
 So now.. approximately 2 years later, I am going back and actually reading the books to the films we studied (it wasn't encouraged in class to avoid comparisons or bias, the film should stand alone we were told). At any rate, I am so very glad I read this, and so very glad I read it after I saw the movie! My mental scenes were so vivid, it was like watching a better and more intricate version of the film. Also I was surprised at how easily I could pick up on his language and the meanings to the words. 
 I also noticed that the book was very efficient at removing the reader from the violence through the use of the Nadsat slang language of the droogs. I kept commenting to myself repeatedly throughout the book, how much reading the violent passages in plain talk would have been highly disturbing to me, and yet reading it in Nadsat, it wasn't. The film did not have this effect at all. The weird language did nothing to alter the sharpness of the violence. 
 I also very much love the 21st chapter. Perhaps one of the reasons I hated the film so much is because Alex did not learn or grow, it was as if his whole crazy journey was pointless because nothing changed in the end. I was pleased and surprised to see that Burgess actually wrote a last chapter that the US publishers had removed. It gave me a closure that the film could not. 
 And lastly, of course, the unavoidable philosophical questions that repeatedly surface throughout the book. The age old question of free will. If free will is what ultimately makes us human, and distinguishes us from machines, robots, or AI, then conditioning free will out of someone would whittle them down to just a machine, or a puppet. So although Alex is really quite an awful person, the reader cannot help but to subtly root for him, and hope for a cure to his conditioning. 
 I really have no critiques for this book. I thought it was excellently composed for all of the reasons stated above.

Excellent book. There was a period where the last chapter was actually edited out and banned in the 60's but rereleased in the 80's if I remember correctly. Get the unedited version and you'll laugh at why it was banned. There is a version that also has the slang dictionary, after reading this book, I had to catch myself from saying some of these terms. This is one of those books that is epic and has a cult following, I highly recommend it.

I was kind of worried that I was going to find this boring or hard to understand but it ended up being a very interesting read. I listened to the audiobook narrated by Tom Hollander and it was a great experience. His performance of Alex was spot on and he nailed the voices each and every character. There's quite a bit of made up language in this book but listening to the audio helped me catch on quickly. I eventually found myself thinking with Nadsat words, haha. 
 I really appreciated the brevity of this book - it was just long enough to explore the theme of good vs. evil. It was extremely interesting (and kind of horrifying) to read from the perspective of a completely immoral narrator. I wasn't sold on what happens in the last chapter but I kind of liked the conclusion anyway. 
 ...I wish I could write a more insightful review about this classic, but I'm terrible at Goodreads reviews.

reference_books.title: Gotham Academy, Vol. 1: Welcome to Gotham Academy
reference_books.review_text: That was a fun read, but...I feel like I'm missing something. It could just be that Olive Silverlock's mysterious summer will be revealed in a future issue/book, or (what I suspect) it's revealed in an issue/book in overall Gotham/DC universe which is irritating. I'm giving it 4 stars in spite of my irritation. It's a school story a la Harry Potter. Gotham Academy is a prestigious boarding school, Olive Silverlock (our protagonist) is a sophomore there on a scholarship provided by the Wayne Foundation. She's assigned to mentor the younger sister of her erstwhile boyfriend, a girl nicknamed Maps (because she draws maps of everything). There's some problem with the North Hall (it's unstable as a result of a fire that occurred during the summer), there may be a ghost, and Olive doesn't remember her summer. I decided to read this because there is going to be a mashup of this with Lumberjanes (which I really like) and it's 2016 Hugo eligible.

reference_books.title: Uprooted
reference_books.review_text: Novik is best known for her Napoleonic dragon books featuring Temeraire. This is quite a departure from those! In a way it's a re-telling of the Baba Yaga mythos, minus the chicken-legged house. The setting is deliberately Slavic (names, towns, etc.), and there is a book of magic that Agniewska finds and uses that is by the witch Jaga. It's a bit more though. There's a wizard called the Dragon who takes a girl every 10 years from one of the villages of the valley of the Spindle; she's not killed and eaten but she never returns home - instead she heads off into the wide world after her decade of service. The Dragon lives in a tower in the valley rather than being at court like the other wizards. He's there to fight the evil that is the Wood which wants to take over the villages. Agniewska is one of the taken girls. I gave this book 5 stars, but really feel it's more a 4.5 or 4.75 because I think that it went on maybe 100 pages too long. I read this for my 2016 Hugo nominations.

reference_books.title: The Dream-Quest of Vellitt Boe
reference_books.review_text: This novella is an homage or commentary on "The Dream Quest of the Unknown Kadath" by HP Lovecraft -which I have not read. Maybe if I were more familiar with the world I would give it a higher rating. As it is it's a travel tale of a professor from a women's university in the Dreamlands, the home of the Elder Gods, who is seeking a student who has wandered off with a dreamer from our own world. Vellitt Boe was a far traveler in her youth until settling in Ulthnar which slowly became her home. This journey takes across her world, across seas inhabited by kraken, and even in the underworld home of ghouls, ghasts, and gugs. I read this as part of my Hugo nominating process and also for my 2017 Reading Challenge.

reference_books.title: The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel
reference_books.review_text: Ok. I loved the movie. Seriously it was the best movie I've seen in ages. I thought, well, maybe I'll read the book. I read an excerpt and it bore no relation to the movie I had seen. I should have stopped there. I purchased the e-book. The movie was wonderful. The book wasn't. Oh, it was well written, but the characters that I loved in the movie were barely present to totally absent in the book. The ones that did double up were 90-100% different. It was jarring. The story was about 25% the same. I know this happens when adapting a book to a movie, but the disconnect for me is usually in the other direction, that the book is better than the movie, or rather, I liked the book better than the movie. Not this time. I read the book. It had none of the atmosphere that the movie had. The movie made India seem enchanting, a place I might want to visit (it made me nostalgic for Egypt!). The book made me want to stay as far from India as possible and awakened the memories of Egypt that I tried to repress. The movie was hope and happiness. The book had only hints of that. There were more characters in the book, but the ones in the movie were more developed. Sonny (hotel proprietor) in the movie was wonderful, Sonny in the book gave me the skeeves. Graham, the former lawyer, was relegated to a few pages in the book and in the movie he was one of the major characters. Evelyn was the only character in the book that retained some of the movie character's charm. If I hadn't seen the movie I would never have picked this book up. Having picked it up and read it, I now need to see the movie again to overwrite the bad taste that the book gave me.

reference_books.title: The Peculiar (The Peculiar, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I read this for the PopSugar 2015 reading challenge. It ticked the box "book written by an author under 30 yrs old". 
 It has an intriguing premise: Faerie has entered the world. There are Changelings aka Peculiars who are the children of Faerie and Humans. The Sidhe and the other Faerie are as nasty as they should be, and so are most of the Humans. Characterization is weak and didn't stand up to the interesting world.

book_a.title: Rat Queens, Vol. 1: Sass & Sorcery
book_a.user_review: I read this as one of the 2015 Hugo nominees for Graphic Novel. Fairly standard sword and sorcery with lots of gore. Interestingly it ties in a bit with Dungeons & Dragons.

sample_reviews.review_text: Zingy, witty with a lot of fun characters. I wanted the plot to have a little bit more direction/mystery about it, which I think will happen in the second volume.
I love the concept, but found the story to fall a little flat.
First five issues were pretty solid! Excited to see where this series goes....
OMG. I super enjoyed this. Butt-kicking, hard drinking, swearing and take want they want mercenaries who happen to be women. Very fun.

"This modern spin on an old school genre is a violent monster-killing epic that is like Buffy meets Tank Girl in a Lord of the Rings world on crack!" this tagline sums up Rat Queens well. It had everything that I thought I would like but somehow it just wasn't for me.

*3.5 stars* 
 My first genuine reaction after finishing this: 
 I'm slowly realising that I'm giving a lot of 3.5 as ratings. For me it means: "Meh, okay. Good. I liked it but nothing I would recommend even to my grandma right away". 
 Oh God, imagine my grandma reading this. WTF. 
 The cast of characters was what made this first volume epic and fucked up at the same time. I don't even know how to describe it. High five for diversity. 
 The art was truly amazing and epic too. 
 I want to continue on with this series but it's not going to be a priority.

This could be called a feminist fantasy adventure. The cliches of fantasy are there, but the authors twist them in such a way as to seem unique and interesting for most of the tale. Occasionally the book teeters into the usual fantasy tropes, but not enough that a reader will be bored.
Freakin' hilarious, nice art. Looking forward to the next one.
Muy original, una vision feminista y humorista del mundo de la fantasia Duungeons & Dragons. Gran dibujo y buen guion.

Beautiful art, creative swearing and an all around twisted look at the typical D&D world. The characters were amusing, but a lot of their dialogue didn't differentiate them from each other well enough to build characters. But still a really charming and amusing read!

book_b.title: Ready Player One
book_b.user_review: Wade/Parzival lives in the near future of 2044. Climate change is real. Much of the world (although we really only hear about the US) is poverty stricken and fighting for dwindling resources. But there is OASIS, a virtual world in which it's possible to escape the realities of life. Wade is a senior in high school, attending online via OASIS; he's an orphan, living in the stacks (trailers and rvs stacked vertically to maximize space), but most importantly he's a "gunter", one of millions searching for the keys of obtaining the fortune of Halliday, the man who designed OASIS. Halliday grew up in the 1980s and was obsessed with it. The way to his fortune is by solving several riddles & quests based in 1980s trivia. Wade has been working on it for 5 years before he cracks the first clue and tops the leader board. As universe building goes, this hangs together a little better than that in some nonSF dystopias (Hunger Games), but it has definite issues (for instance I'm not sure where the food is coming from given the supposed state of the US outside of the cities). There were lots of info dumps and lots of extraneous detail added just because it was cool. Wade was an ok character, but it was still a white male POV. Some of the other characters were more interesting. That this novel was written in the first person bothered me less that first person stories normally do - I'm not sure how you'd it from any other POV. I read this for my 2016 Reading Challenge "read a book recommended by a friend" (PopSugar 2015).

sample_reviews.review_text:
07/01/12 
 Things I like so far: 
 -It's fun. 
 -I like how, even within a semi-dystopian cyberpunk setting, it highlights some of the positive, world-expanding aspects of tech. Free education for all, for instance. 
 Things I don't like so far: 
 -Reminds me of Little Brother. On the one hand, it is less annoying than LB on a number of fronts. OTOH, the difference is (so far) a quantitative, not qualitative, difference. It's still a novel about a (presumably) white het geek guy and his pursuit to get the prize and the girl, and I have yet to see any sign of more profound social commentary lying underneath that. Will wait to the end to see, though. 
 (-Seriously, dude, STOP SAYING SHE DUMPED YOU. YOU WERE NEVER DATING. THAT IS RAPE CULTURE RIGHT THERE.) 
 ETA: Forgot to add another thing I don't like so far: Literally every time Daito and Shoto show up, one of them has to say something about honor. Cool! Totally not a massive stereotype! 
 *** 
 Thoughts upon finishing the book: Overall, I really enjoyed it. It's possible that I'm more inclined to like it just because it reminds me of Little Brother and is SO MUCH BETTER at a lot of things, though. I was so annoyed by LB that I was ready to give this book an A+ just for not being terrible about race and gender.

(Minor spoilers) 
 Wow! I would give this more stars if I could. Ready Player One is easily one of the best books I've ever read! The premise is amazing, the polt twists incredible and I really enjoyed watching Wade turn from a chubby and spotty teenager into a badass. And, oh my goodness, the ending! It was both epic and incredibly satisfying! I don't think I've ever read another book which kept me on the edge of my seat and holding my breath as much as this! I absolutely loved this book!! :D

DNF at 16%. Because this is the most annoying book I've ever read. Life is too short. And yes, I'm rating it 1 star after only having read 16%. I know for sure that I read somewhere that goodreads encourage you to use the rating system in any way you want to, so for all they care you can rate books before you even read them, so I am in no way abusing their rating system. 
 There was nothing not annoying about this book. Wade was annoying. The OASIS was annoying and made no sense. The worldbuilding made no sense. So many actual problems that would be so interesting to deal with in this world are barely touched upon. The 80s pop culture references were annoying. It's not that I didn't get them, but there were so many references that it started to get on my nerves by page 15. It just read like some big circle jerk/glorification of the 80s in the United States. Maybe it's because I'm European (/not American), but it did not sit well with me. 
 (And before anyone says I can't complain about so and so because I didn't finish the book, I read the full plot summary and several reviews. I know what happens and it's not great. For further reading, I will do the lazy thing and link two of my favorite reviews, here (I agree with everything they say, but not their rating) and here. Happy reading.)

I don't quite see what all the fuss is about. 
 I'm a geek-child of the 80's, squarely in the target demographic, so I definitely enjoyed the extensive video game / movie / anime nostalgia. And the use of immersive VR in a dystopian future had me predisposed to love it (Snow Crash and Neuromancer and Ender's Game are among my all-time favorites). But as a sci-fi story, it didn't impress me at all. The writing was mostly flat and functional. The plot alternated between long periods of stasis that were used to describe the setting and technology in detail, and sudden resolutions when some external character takes action at random times, or through the introduction of an item or location with just the right properties to allow the plot to advance. 
 It was a fun read, and the impressive depth of the 80's pop culture references deserves some accolades. I'll happily pay to see the movie when it comes out, but I'm not sure why it became such a sensation. Presumably its many fans are getting something from it that I didn't.

Narrated by eighteen year old Wade Watts, Cline's plot is set in 2044, a dystopian 
 future, where the majority of the population is immersed within an on-line game. 
 Another book with a similar theme is the graphic novel: 
 In Real Life.
Just as good the third time around. Not writing a review this time. Just going to bask in the awesomeness.
I DID NOT THINK I WAS GOING TO LOVE THIS AS MUCH AS I DID

James Halliday is the creator of the OASIS. In all immersive MMO that allows everyone on Earth to escape the horrors of what has become of the world in the near future and go to school, party, or just explore and level their avatar. Halliday was the biggest geek there was and he wanted his passions to be your passions, and his main passion was the 1980s, the time when he was a teenager. When he died he left no heirs and created a treasure hunt within the OASIS to decide who would be worthy of being his successor. His Willy Wonka test was neigh on indecipherable with a little video he made which ended up being nicknamed Anorak's Invitation, after his Avatar, Anorak. Soon a culture of hunters, called gunters, form with the sole purpose of memorizing the minutiae of Halliday and the 80s and finding Halliday's fortune. 
 Wade Watts is a gunter with the handle Parzival. He has spent five years of his life learning everything there is to know about James Halliday. For five long years no one has made the least bit of headway with the quest until Parzival stumbles on the answer while sitting in his virtual classroom. Within hours two people have passed through the first of three gates that lead to Halliday's egg. It soon becomes clear to Parzival that this is going to end sooner then anyone thought, with more dangers then he could imagine. Now that the first hurtle is passed, it won't be long before things come to a head. While Parzival has troubles trusting the other gunters he's come to view as his friends, the real danger is IOI, a rival organization who wants to win the game, not to win, but to control the OASIS. 
 As many people have started their review with "this book was written just for my generation and me in particular," well, I figure, I will reiterate that sentiment. Yes, this book was written for me. I was born in 1978, so a little younger then Halliday, and Cline himself, but of the same generation, so to speak. I will not go on and then say that this book is just wonderful and marvelous and just spoke to me, because, well, it just didn't. You know, it actually kind of enrages me that this book is so well regarded and lauded. It isn't the book itself you can be in love with, it just can't be, with it's bland prose riddled with errors, and it's dry clinical writing style, making it almost like a history book, though written by someone with an ego who is very self impressed that they have all this knowledge at their fingertips. 
 You're in love with the memories this book evokes, the connection it forges using emotional cues from your past. You say "Pac-Man" and I'm a little kid again down at the Brat and Brau feeding quarters into their "Ms. Pac-Man" machine in the few spare minutes I had before the food arrived and my grandmother started piling the A-1 on her dinner. That dark and dingy little restaurant that had the cliched wooden panelling that my basement had and made the restaurant part rathskeller, part sports bar. Side note, I didn't need to read a whole chapter on every level of "Pac-Man" and how the final screen is only half there, I knew that, move on. Cline has taped into the zeitgeist of an era and has just info dumped on us, using touchstones like the Whedonverse to make little geeks and wannabes sqwee with joy. There is nothing that it makes me think of more then the episode of Community "Regional Holiday Music" which they did as a skewering of Glee. One of the songs, to entice Pierce to enter into the singing spirit, was called "Baby Boomer Santa." As Annie said in the episode "Pierce, they're just trying to pander to your demographics documented historical vanity. Resist!" The song is nothing more then a list of things that would appeal to Pierce, from Coca-Cola to The Beatles, Woodstock to Vietnam. This is what Ready Player One does! It just lists things from the 80s that we connect to from Galaga to WarGames and all the hipsters and 80s geeks and everyone is sucked in. To that I echo Annie Edison! RESIST! 
 This info dump mentality makes the book like the carrion of literature displaying the largest lack of imagination I have seen in a book. Ready Player One is part Willy Wonka, part Ender's Game with John Hughes doing the adaptation. I defy you to find something actually original in this book. All the humor and originality is directly lifted from other sources. Why is the final battle Parzival faces so funny? Because he's in Monty Python and the Holy Grail! The entire action, the entire everything is Monty Python's genius, NOT Ernest Cline's! This happens again and again throughout the book. And then there's Halliday and Morrow. Let's talk about James Halliday and Ogden Morrow, or as they really are, Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak. Even if Cline hadn't laboriously pointed that the "fictitious characters" had been compared to these two real men, there is no grey area here. They are 100% these two men. Halliday even dies! Add to that the fact that Ready Player One goes into Phone Phreaking a lot, and Wozniak was part of this phenomenon, and they just get more and more similar. Then, in the, really, you really had to do that, bash my head against the wall, make me want to light the book on fire, there's the fact that the Wozniak character, Ogden, had the nickname Og, like Wozniak with Woz. Seriously? I mean seriously? It's not funny, it's a joke that is flat. Also, let's keep in mind that everyone knows that Woz is the one who was more, how shall I say, fun and relaxed of the two, so he wouldn't be litigious, even though he's spinning tunes as a DJ in a glass bubble before shooting lightning out of his fingers (yes, this seriously happens, and if it was me, I'd have my lawyer on speed dial). This is just degrading to me and in my mind to him, a man I very much admire. Sure he was on Dancing with the Stars, but you know what, he had a choice in that. I have a strong feeling, that while Halliday is never depicted negatively, if Jobs hadn't been on his deathbed, there might have been some serious legal action on this book. 
 If I where to just talk about Cline's writing, I would have to go back to the major flaw in this book in that Cline NEVER sticks to his own internal rules he has created. One minute there's never been a game like the WarGames simulation in the first gate, the next second Wade is on a date with Art3mis and they're in a Goonies rendition that is exactly like the simulation no one had ever thought of. When he's getting ready to clear the first gate, it's a Thursday night, clearly stated as Thursday, because he says he only has one more day of school before the weekend. Because of clearing the gate he sleeps through school, but then gets up bright and early the next day and goes to school... on a Saturday? Then the stupid Fyndoro whatever can only be used once in 24 hours, and then they use it like 6 hours later? Um,if you're going to phone in half your book by ripping other, better, people off, the least, the very very least you could do is get your own writing right. To step further away from all the things that are like or ripped off from other sources, let's talk about the part of the book that is Cline's. It's like he doesn't know what he wants his world to be. Is it dystopian, well yes, but then he drastically shifts away from this interesting study of the poor Wade and his living in "the stacks" and goes 180 and it becomes about this "affluent" kid that Wade has become, lured by the gadgets money has bought him. Which takes the soul out of the book. And then it just becomes the typical "Big Brother" story about a company trying to take control of the OASIS at any cost, deaths allowed. So, now the book is a thriller with corporate espionage? Really, Cline, you needed to keep a similar feel and a through line through this book. Instead you made Wade a douche and then I almost wanted the bad guys to win. And in the end, what was the moral? Stop playing games and get a real life? Because, Halliday just had these gunters waste SIX YEARS of their lives to learn that lesson. Douche Halliday. Also, you kind of made me never want to go near a computer again. And what fantasy world is this where a company would actually keep your information private, cause it's not ours? Now that is pure fiction. 
 To finalize what I refer to now as my ranty rant. There are just so many books and movies and music that Cline has mined, all of which are more original and better, so just go and give credit to the original, not the wannabe. Also, if you want something that actually captures the feeling I think Cline was aiming for, go read or watch Scott Pilgrim. As I read in another review among those fellow haters, I think Sissyneck on goodreads summed it up perfectly. "In a nice manifestation of the novel's lack of self-awareness, Cline at one point derides the villains of the book for simply using "Johnny 5" style robots from Short Circuit instead [of] coming up with their own design. This appropriation, he explains, demonstrates "a lack of imagination," a valid criticism that only too accurately applies to the ostensible heroes of the book, as well as to Cline himself." Right on Sissyneck! And here's a little Pierce Hawthrone to sing us out... 
 The Last Word: "OASIS"

This is probably one of my favorite books I've read for a while. It's fun and entertaining, and full of wonderful pop-culture and 80s references. What I loved most about the book though, is that even though the book is all about gaming and a massive VR world, you don't have to be a gamer to really appreciate it. I rarely play video games but I really enjoyed this book.

reference_books.title: This Shattered World (Starbound, #2)
reference_books.review_text: I enjoyed this one even more than its predecessor - more action, more characters (none of that claustrophobic feel of only having 2 characters) and more worldbuilding (three cheers for the Space Irish!).

reference_books.title: Crossed (Matched, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Book #1 of this series sucked me in with a pretty writing style (despite a fairly ho-hum dystopian YA setting). At first, the focus on forbidden poetry was cute and romantic. 
 Matched, however, lost me completely. The poetry focus grew too intense for the story - it was irritating, unrealistic, and felt grossly mismatched with a dystopian setting. Plot felt aimless. Abandoned this series for good.

reference_books.title: The Alchemist
reference_books.review_text:
I think The Alchemist is a vapid, saccharine-sweet, steaming pile of crap. 
 I'm not sure why this book is so widely beloved. It beats you over the head with a simplistic and incredibly trite message of "follow your heart." No subtlety, no nuance. The book is sprinkled liberally with a bunch of mystical and quasi-religious elements that don't quite fit together - meant, I suppose, to appeal to readers across cultural bounds... I got really sick of hearing about one's "Personal Legend" (yes, capitalized, as though a copyright symbol should follow). And despite my personal love for (well-done) magical, mysterious worlds, I didn't find the world invented here to be especially beautiful or interesting. 
 Don't get me wrong: I'd be all for a touching, motivational fable that transcends cultural bounds to embrace and uplift the millions. The Alchemist, however, fell flat.

reference_books.title: These Broken Stars (Starbound, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
(3.5 stars) Great writing and character psychology, but it feels a little aimless. The entire book rests on the interactions between two characters, which begins strongly but eventually gets a bit claustrophobic. The story drags a little in the middle: once the characters are ejected from the spaceship, it becomes "teens on the camping trip from hell," which didn't quite feel like it needed the awesome sci-fi beginning to work. 
 Minor side note: I'm disappointed that we never hear the full story behind Tarver's status as a war hero...! 
 For those of you who have watched Farscape... 
 ...the "perfect replica of my lover" story rings a bell.

reference_books.title: Sex Criminals, Vol. 1: One Weird Trick
reference_books.review_text:
Suzie and Jon can stop time when they have sex. They use this power to rob banks. 
 It's cute. Hilarious in its absurdity. Raunchy, as you might imagine - but not distasteful or overly explicit. It's worth reading this in some kind of digital edition which allows you to zoom in - every single tinily-lettered imaginary porn title/poster/...device is gloriously nonsensical! 
 Downsides: 
 - Sometimes a touch difficult to follow, given the main character's many asides to the fourth wall, wearing different outfits - but that might just be my inexperience with graphic novels as a category (or maybe Saga was just especially easy to follow). 
 - I'm not so sure the library plot is necessary. Can't these be actual criminals who rob banks for profit, rather than wishy-washy-Robin-Hood shenanigans using ill-gotten gains to save a public utility? Maybe I watch too many heist films, but I think actual criminality would have been a lot more fun.

book_a.title: The Moor's Account
book_a.user_review:
The Moor's Account tells the tale of early European conquest of the New World from a new perspective: that of Estebanico, a black Moorish slave on the doomed Narvaez expedition. While fighting for survival among new lands and peoples, Estebanico navigates ambivalent relationships with the Spaniards, leading a precarious journey from slave to conquistadors' comrade. 
 Rapacious greed is the villain in in this story: the Spaniards (as well as Estebanico himself) fluctuate variously between a hunger for gold and a respect for universal human dignity. Estebanico emphasizes the power of storytelling, narrative, and names to wield power or to heal. 
 I had the pleasure of reading this book alongside its source text, Cabeza de Vaca's Adventures in the Unknown Interior of America - so I got to see what parts of Cabeza de Vaca's narrative were challenged, omitted, or embellished by Lalami's fictionalized Estebanico. Very well done, and very much in keeping with the tone of Cabeza de Vaca's account (which is to say: a little bit dry, with constant acknowledgement of the reader).

sample_reviews.review_text: This was so boring! There characters were one dimensional and the story read like a list of 'and thens'. Even the cannibalism was boring! Not sure when this has gotten such good reviews. AVOID!
A refreshing take on the disturbing history of the brutal conquest of the Americas, through an inside-oriented outsider's perspective. Beautifully written, tightly drawn yet sweeping in scope.

A young Moor from the Mideast has to sell himself into slavery to save his family. He is boght by a Spanish Conquistador who travels to La Florida in the time after Cortes found fabulous wealth in Mexico. His struggles with redefining his life in the New world.

Ugh. This book was unbelievably boring. I don't how it made its way onto so many "best of" lists. It makes no sense to me. Maybe 1.5 stars because it picked up a bit around the end when the survivors travel to Spanish Mexico. 
 What's so ironically awful about this book is that storytelling is a central theme. And yet quality of storytelling is exactly what this book is lacking. It sort of just plods along with no sense of momentum or suspense, meandering in a manner as lost as the main characters, and with mind-numbingly simplistic prose. It's like reading an encyclopedia. There's not a single beautiful or profound line in the whole darn thing. 
 And the characters are all really monochromatic, especially the Spaniards and Native Americans, but even Estebanico/Mustafa is sort of one-dimensional. Oh, and boring. Omg is he boring. 
 The whole thing. Boring boring boring.
I guess I missed the boat yet again on another Booker prize. Great premise, but I couldn't get interested.
Just could not get into it.

I really wish this had a map, but then that gave it the extended feeling of being a parable, of being a myth. Excellent consequence since it is based on true events, however fictionalized or hypothesized. 
 Plus, I ended up pulling out my own map and determining for myself the track of the expedition and survivors... The sparse, clear storytelling makes that almost straightforward to figure out. 
 Still. A map would be nice. But the heart aching story was enough. This narrative questions what is humanity, what is authority in the face of equalizing hardship? And should force us to consider every single bit of history we learn and try to relearn it. It isn't enough to say history belongs to the victor.

Review: The Moor's Account (aka A Literary Sleep Aid) 
 You know what? Forget this. 
 This is so boring I can't put it into words. I could hardly stay awake. I had to reread several pages because I would zone out. The only part I was interested in was Mustafa's past. I gave zero craps for the genocidal Castilians. They got what they deserved, the greedy, stealing fucks.
Brilliant! I am overwhelmed by the novel's monumental power and grace.

The Moor's Account - Owning the Story 
 The narrator of Leila Lalami's THE MOOR'S ACCOUNT, the Moroccan slave Mustafa (or as the Spanish rename him, Estebanico) is a lover of stories. As a boy he listens to his mother's stories and when he is older they come back to him as a source of comfort. As a man he learns to tell stories, first those of his mother and later his own. Lalami's novel is Mustafa's attempt to set the record straight and tell the true story of the Spanish expedition to "La Florida" in search of gold and to spread the King's empire as well as Catholicism. 
 In the beginning, chapters describing the expedition alternate with chapters about Mustafa's history starting with his birth. Eventually the two tales merge into the present. Mustafa wants to tell his version of the events because as a slave his account was not sought when the official record was drawn up. Only the three Castilian gentlemen, Dorantes, Castillo and Cabeza de Vaca, were required to make the Joint Report for the King. But as Mustafa listens to the story they tell, he notes all they omit and how they misrepresent certain aspects of their time among the Indians. Mustafa says, "What each of us wants, in the end, whether he is black or white, master or slave, rich or poor, man or woman, is to be remembered after his death." And so he sets down his account, hopefully for posterity, of "truth in the guise of entertainment." Here Lalami looks at the very nature of storytelling; its motivation and purpose. 
 A bit slow to start, the narration soon becomes riveting. The adventures that befall Mustafa are at once appalling and spell-binding. The reader witnesses the follies of the Spanish would-be conquerors who carelessly commit atrocities against the Indians whom they consider inferior savages and give "new names to everything around them, as though they were the All-knowing God in the Garden of Eden." One cannot help but draw parallels to the experiences of other attempts, both historical and current, of conquering nations. Mustapha says, "How strange, I remember thinking, how utterly strange were the ways of the Castilians - just by saying that something was so, they believed that it was. I know now that these conquerors, like many others before them, and no doubt like others after, gave speeches not to voice the truth, but to create it." 
 Lalami also looks at religion and identity. Mustafa, a Muslim, is forced to "convert" to Catholicism when he is enslaved and summarily christened and given a new name. Although the others now call him Estebanico, he never truly relinquishes his name as he says, "A name is precious; it carries inside it a language, a history, a set of traditions, a particular way of looking at the world." To the reader, he will always be Mustafa ibn Muhammad ibn Abdussalam al-Zamori. In the same respect, he never truly converts, keeping true to his faith throughout even if he cannot practice it openly. He muses, "Standing in that half-finished church, surrounded by statues of prophets and saints, I wondered why God created so many varieties of faiths in the world if He intended all of us to worship Him in the same fashion. This thought had never occurred to me when I was a young boy memorizing the Holy Qur'an, but as I spent time with the Indians I came to see how limiting the notion of one true faith really was. Was the diversity in our beliefs, not their unity, the lesson God wanted to impart? Surely it would have been in His power to make us of one faith if that had been His wish. Now the idea there was only one set of stories for all of mankind seemed strange to me." There is much food for thought in that one paragraph. 
 The writing is full of beautiful metaphors such as, "To overcome my fear, I shackled myself with hope, its links heavier than any metal known to man." And describing the feeling of finally being able to quench his thirst after days without water: "It was the same kind of pain I used to get when I broke the fast on the first night of Ramadan, a feeling of being at once satiated and yet still thirsty." The descriptions of nature and the Indians are also lovely. The reader is transported to these strange, exotic scenes, experiencing them through all the senses. 
 One of my favorite metaphors and one which exemplifies the novel's theme of storytelling is: "Telling a story is like sowing a seed - you always hope to see it become a beautiful tree, with firm roots and branches that soar up in the sky. But it is a peculiar sowing, for you will never know whether your seed sprouts or dies." For this reader, the seed that Lalami has sown blooms magnificently. 
 P.S. Here is a link to an interview with the author: 
 https://www.moroccoworldnews.com/2016...

book_b.title: Pride and Prejudice
book_b.user_review:
I read Pride and Prejudice for class in high school, and its tedium (sadly!) put me off of reading 19th-century literature altogether for a couple of years. I remember it as a long-winded will-they-won't-they set amongst frilly aristocracy, in which characters' deepest interests lay in social climbing through marriage (yuck). 
 I rather enjoyed (and agreed with) Charlotte Bronte's opinion of Jane Austen, taken from a letter to a friend: 
 "Why do you like Miss Austen so very much? I am puzzled on that point... And what did I find? An accurate, daguerreotyped portrait of a commonplace face; a carefully-fenced, high-cultivated garden with neat borders and delicate flowers; but no glance of a bright, vivid physiognomy, no open country, no fresh air, no blue hill, no bonny beck. I should hardly like to live with her ladies and gentlemen in their elegant but confined houses." 
 And from another of Bronte's letters to a friend: 
 "[A]nything like warmth or enthusiasm, anything energetic, poignant, heartfelt, is utterly out of place in commending these works: all such demonstrations the authoress would have met with a well-bred sneer, would have calmly scorned as outre or extravagant. She does her business of delineating the surface of the lives of genteel English people curiously well... [But] She no more, with her mind's eye, beholds the heart of her race than each man, with bodily vision, sees the heart in his heaving breast. Jane Austen was a complete and most sensible lady, but a very incomplete and rather insensible (not senseless) woman." 
 ....Eh. Maybe I'll give it another go someday... but there are so many other books waiting on my to-read list!

sample_reviews.review_text:
"I haven't any right to criticize books, and I don't do it except when I hate them. I often want to criticize Jane Austen, but her books madden me so that I can't conceal my frenzy from the reader; and therefore I have to stop every time I begin. Every time I read Pride and Prejudice I want to dig her up and beat her over the skull with her own shin-bone." 
 -- Mark Twain 
 I'm sorry. Truly. I wanted to love this. Couldn't. And I feel really bad about you guys liking my status updates... I've just never read more mind-numbing book. 
 I thought it would get more interesting... imagine my surprise. It took me ten years to finish this. I wanted to abandon it countless times. Now I get why. Plot is non-existent, absolutely meaningless. I felt like Austen threw around a lot of big words just for the sake of it. Just because she'd been to her father's library and learned some fancy words. Not that she actually knew how to write a beautiful sentence. Is this what "novel of manners" are like? 
 Mr. Darcy and Elizabeth. Prideful Darcy and prejudiced Elizabeth. I don't know. They made me think of these really snobbish couples you see on Facebook whom everyone hates but they do have cool pictures. And because they're so annoying to everyone else, you think they're probably good match for each other.
das beste Buch ever! :)
I'm sad to say I really didn't like it. i thought it was too trivial and couldn't feel anuthing for the characters. Oh well, at least I tried!
I tried I really did.

I loved it! So much that I just couldn't get away from the book. 
 Setting aside the fact that the ideas of the time about the attitude of a "proper" lady should be are completely opposite to what I believe, I liked the way Austen portrays the society of that era. I specially loved Elizabeth's wit. 
 Favorite character: Lizzie, hands down. 
 Least favorite character: Collins, although I should say Mrs. Bennet was a close second here.

The audio book made this somewhat enjoyable to listen to - although 10 hours long. 
 But, having the flue and nothing else better to do (hey that rhymed gY~%0) I flew through it in under two days. 
 Would recommend the reader of the audio book as it is the best one I have ever listened to however, I found the story quite plain and dull on its own as well as hard to read.

I somehow managed to not read this until now, and then I finally did read it and felt like a jerk because it was so great. This was so much more insidious than I expected it to be. That Jane Austen was snarky, timeless, brilliant.

'Jonathan Livingston Seagull' is a unique little book: a self development story written from the viewpoint of a non-conforming seagull. It is about his passion to fly like no other seagull, his self growth and how he breaks through the restraints of family, friends and community to live his dream. 
 The book appears to be more than the life of one seagull. It is a fable about self empowerment and the importance of seeking a higher purpose in life, even if the people around you find your goals threatening or ridiculous. He shows that you can do anything and be anything you want if you just believe in yourself. It is also about the struggle to find the answers about life itself. 
 It is also a good fable for children as it stimulates discussions on the various meanings of the story. The ending is slightly puzzling but on viewing the DVD which, though very lengthy (2 hrs) did offer some explanations. The film also shed light on why the book had numerous black and white, grainy photographs of gulls. (All the music and songs are by Neil Diamond)

Do I just not get it or am I reading this book out of context (30 years too late)? I don't understand why people like this book. The apparent "messages" are so blatant that I find it somewhat insulting.

What's the deal with people raving about what an inspiring and life-changing book Jonathan Livingston Seagull is? When I've brought up books from my youth in conversation, I've had several people tell me before that I absolutely need to read this one, and not reading it in school when I was younger meant I was missing out. Except now that I have read it I realize I wasn't missing out at all; in fact, I'm probably going to forget all about this book by the time I wake up tomorrow morning. Jonathan Livingston Seagull was supposed to be some inspiring tale about an outcast seagull who follows his passions to become the best he can be without the crushing conformity and judgement that the rest of his flock burdens him with, but instead it was some pseudo-religious, self-help, motivational speaker crap. I don't get the hype. The entire story was boring (not to mention it's about seagulls. seagulls! of all animals to write about!) and I kept waiting for some turn to take place that never happened. It took me maybe an hour to read this book--thanks to the ugly, grainy photos of seagulls that took up a good chunk of the book for some reason--but even that time wasn't worth the investment.

reference_books.title: The Orenda
reference_books.review_text:
This story got more and more brutal as it went along, a crude yet seemingly accurate depiction of the life that was lived by first nations, especially the Huron-Wendat, with their own wars to wage against the Iroquois while Europeans settlers were arriving in their lands and trying to assimilate them. 
 It wasn't always easy to stay invested since I didnt find any of the characters that likeable and since the pace was slow for more than half the book. Still, this style of narration, with the 3 different point of views (a Huron war chief, a young captured Iroquois girl and a French Jesuit priest) gave the reader a very wide view and understanding of the story, which ended up being pretty devastating, to be honest. 
 Overall a very poignant historical account, even fictionalized, of a time when the country that is my home was a very different place.
