sample_reviews.review_text:
Mild Spoilers.... 
 This book kind of disappointed me. I don't really see what the hype is about. This book just irritates me... 
 First, the worst part about this book is the writing style. At some point, I got used to it, but dear god, how frustrating it was... See, the story is mostly about Clay Jensen listening to a set of tapes that were made as a suicide story that explains why Hannah took her life to those she blames the most. So, as you read this book, you are reading what is said on the tape and Clay's reactions. But see, the writing about the tape would continue even when Clay was thinking completely random thoughts that are being interrupted by the tape. It seriously bugged because why in the world would you just go back and forth between the two and expect me to continue two completely different lines of thought? 
 Then, we get to the characters. So this set of tapes is passed to multiple different people who Hannah blames for causing her to just give up on life. She threatens to send a second set of tapes out to someone random if they don't pass on the tapes till the very end. The reader never really meets the other characters on the tape which is a bit disappointing because I wanted to see their reactions, not hear about the rumours and whatever Hannah tells us. 
 The narrator of the book is one of the guys who is on the tapes, his name is Clay (I've never met a Clay, have you?). Clay seemed to like Hannah when she was alive but was afraid to act on his feelings. Clay gets really upset over these tapes as he misses Hannah and wishes that she reached out for him. But honestly, he barely really expressed himself and I never really felt any emotions that were described in this book. Like, he seems really overwhelmed with this idea of Hannah's death because of those people when he seemed to barely know this girl. Oh and his contribution to her death? Completely Lame... Not what you're expecting so prepare to be like, seriously?!?!?! 
 I could see the snowball effect throughout the story and I was only really reading the book for the tapes, I couldn't care less about Clay's inner monologues that interrupted the tapes. I was a little disappointed with how the whole book ended because it kinda just jumped to a completely random conclusion. 
 I don't know, maybe this book isn't my type or something but this wasn't my cup of tea.

 If you are subjected to bully "emotionally, physically.. etc", you call for help, if not found, you stand up for yourself.

 -----------------

 ------------------ 
 Switching the dialogue between Hannah's voice over the tape and Clay's thoughts was annoying. 
 ------------------

This book was a drag to read (or listen to in my case). A girl, Hannah, kills herself, but before she does she creates audio recordings of why she killed herself. She also has a list of people who she wants to listen to the tapes after she's gone, and the people who should listen are all the people she blames for her death. Suicide is not a light subject, and readers will not find this to be an uplifting book. 
 Hannah is obviously depressed. I don't find depression to be a rational disease, and I realize that a small problem for some people may become an unsurmountable obstacle for someone who is depressed. With that said, the reasons she gave for killing herself were so trivial that it made me sick. 
 The writing in this book is not too bad. However, the content really turned me off, and I didn't care much for Hannah. This is classified as a young adult book which is troubling to me. I think it's possible that teens who may be troubled in one way or another who read this book may find they have problems that are more serious than what the main character is going through. I would worry that young, impressionable readers could be inspired to try to harm or kill themselves after reading this. I wouldn't recommend this book to anyone.

reference_books.title: Aristotle and Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universe (Aristotle and Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universe, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Das Buch zu bewerten, fallt mir ehrlich gesagt gar nicht so leicht. Bis zur Mitte fand ich es wahnsinnig gut und alles, was danach kam war einfach uberhaupt nicht mehr Meins. Den Anfang mochte ich soooo gerne, weil man dort eine Menge uber Ari und Dante erfahrt und uber die Art und Weise, wie ihre Freundschaft mit jedem Tag wachst. Ari ist auf den ersten Blick ein ziemlich witziger Junge. Die Dialoge, die er mit anderen fuhrt, fand ich immer sehr witzig und schon geschrieben. Allgemein hat mein schnell ein Gefuhl dafur bekommen, was fur ein Mensch der Protagonist ist, welcher die Geschichte erzahlt. Ich fand ihn vom Fleck weg sympathisch und mit Dante ging es mir da nicht anders. Sie sind beide etwas speziellere Figuren, die mit dem normalen sozialen Gefuge nicht so gut zurecht kommen. Umso genialer hat der Autor beschrieben, wie sich die Jungs anfreunden und sich ihre Beziehung weiter entwickelt. Es gab so tolle Momente, in denen ich immer dachte: So etwas ist wahre Freundschaft. 
 Mir wurde aber auch durch die vielen Hinweise rasch klar, in welche Richtung alles gehen wurde. Daher fand ich es auch extrem gut gemacht, dass Ari und Dante's Wege sich schnell wieder trennen. Man sieht wie Ari auf einmal den wichtigsten Menschen in seinem Leben verliert und allein klar kommen muss. Das eine Jahr ohne Dante (welcher aufgrund des Jobs seines Vater fur diese Zeit weg ist) war wie eine Art Selbstfindungstripp. Das war dann auch der Zeitpunkt zu dem sich alles fur mich gekippt hat. Aris Schulleben war echt ode und immer, wenn es zu langweilig wurde, passierten merkwurdige Unfalle. Nach dem ersten dachte ich noch: OK, aber irgendwann wurde es mir echt zu bunt. Es kam so ruber, als wolle der Autor zwanghaft Ungluck heraufbeschworen. Auch die ganze Abwicklung gegen Ende war mir personlich zu uberzogen und dramatisch und es hatte nur weniger Satze und ein bisschen Ehrlichkeit bedarf, hier klare Verhaltnisse zu schaffen.

reference_books.title: The Faerie Ring (The Faerie Ring, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
THE FAERIE RING konnte mich am Anfang besonders dank des Settings uberzeugen. Im 18. Jahrhundert spielen ja so einige Jugendbucher und hier hat das richtig gut gepasst, weil es in Kombination mit dem Fantasyelement mal wieder etwas aus der Reihe getanzt ist. Ich bin auch Fan von solchen alt historisch angehauchten Geschichten, weil das Leben und die Gepflogenheiten nun einmal anders waren als sie es zur heutigen Gegenwart sind. Die Sache mit der Kinderbande hat mich etwas an Cornelia Funkes Herr der Diebe erinnert und das Buch mochte ich eigentlich. Kiki Hamilton hat sich viel Muhe gegeben die Dynamik der Charaktere wie eine Familie zu beschreiben und das war schon. Es war allerdings so, dass man die Figuren sehr schwer auseinander halten konnte, da sie nur namentlich erwahnt wurden und nicht wirklich eine Rolle gespielt haben. Auch die ganze Sache mit dem Diebstahl von Tiki fand ich sehr unglaubwurdig gemacht. Leider war es auch sie als Protagonistin, die mir gar nicht gefallen hat. Ich habe eine Zeit lang versucht mit ihr klar zu kommen, aber im Grossen und Ganzen ging mir ihre Art gegen den Strich. Tiki hat mir immer zu viel um den heissen Brei herum geredet, anstatt, dass die Gute auch mal etwas tut. Man konnte fast sagen, dass sie sich gerne reden gehort hat, ohne zu erkennen, wie die Lage/Realitat eigentlich aussieht und wie viel Gluck sie bei vielen Dinge hatte. Ausserdem war sie einfach schrecklich undankbar und zickig. 
 Die Sache mit den Feen war dann schon wieder cooler. Es ist zwar nichts Neues, was die Autorin sich hier zusammengebastelt hat, aber gerade wegen dem Setting waren die Ereignisse oder eben die magischen Wesen noch einmal mehr gezwungen sich anderen Dingen anzupassen. Teilweise war es auch recht spannend, wenn es an das Entdecken der Geheimnisse ging. Die Liebesgeschichte hat der Handlung dann aber wieder den Wind aus den Segeln genommen. Man hatte hier so schon eine Hass-Liebe einbauen konnen, aber, nein, immer wieder gabs diese zweideutigen Bemerkungen und das fast-Dreieck.

reference_books.title: The Mark (The Mark, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Buchgestaltung... 
 Das Cover ist ganz nett. Irgendwie symbolisiert es die Botschaft des Buches. Alles ist verganglich, wenn der Anstoss erst einmal gegeben ist. Der Titel ist ja so einfallsreich. Ja. Aber passt halt zum Inhalt des Buches. Ich wette ein dt Titel wurde besser klingen. Ich habe aber auch keinen Plan wie genau man The Mark ubersetzen wurde, sodass es gut klingen kann! xD 
 Meinung 
 Die ersten 30 Seiten des Buches sind wirklich ein super Anfang. Danach folgten so in etwa 100 Seiten bei denen ich mir vorkam als wurde ich KEIN Fantasybuch lesen. Nicht, das dies etwas Schlechtes ware. Ich habe in letzter Zeit solche Bucher wirklich gerne gelesen, aber hier hat es einfach nicht hinein gepasst. Es war gut geschrieben und eine Zeit lang echt unterhaltsam, aber nach 80 Seiten in denen das alltagliche Leben so vor sich hinplatschert hat es angefangen mich zu nerven. Das gute ist, das genau eine Seite nachdem ich dachte: ich hor jetzt auf zu lesen! Endlich Action ins Spiel kam. Ein kurzer Hohepunkt und danach geht das Buch besser weiter. Es passieren viele Dinge, die Dialoge steigern sich und das Ende hat mir gut gefallen. 
 Ich wurde das Buch trotzdem nicht als YA Fantasy bezeichnen, sondern eher, als ein Buch mit einem Fanatsyelement. Cassies Gabe steht zwar im Vordergrund der Geschichte, aber erst auf den letzten Seiten bekommt man Hintergrundinfos geliefert und einige Sachen werden endlich mal aufgedeckt. Ich habe mir das Buch wirklich so ganz anders vorgestellt und war auch etwas enttauscht. Cassie ist ein glaubwurdiger Hauptcharakter, der seine eigenen Werte und Vorstellungen hat. Da diese aber teilweise nicht mit meinen eigenen ubereingestimmt haben, war ich zwischenzeitlich sehr oft nah dran sie zu verfluchen. Die ganze verdammte Zeit uber lauft sie durch die Gegend und sieht Menschen sterben und sie unternimmt rein gar nichts. Wahrscheinlich ware es ewig so weiter gegangen, wenn sie Lukas nicht kennen gelernt hatte. Er war die Stimme der Vernunft und hat Cassie zur Besinnung gebracht. Ich finde auch, das Lukas das halbe Buch uber der Charakter ist, der die Geschichte des Buches vorantreibt indem er sich mit den Dingen auseinandersetzt die Cassie sich von Anfang an mal hatte fragen sollen. 
 Das Buch hat mir trotzdem gefallen, weil es viele so richtig gute Aspekte gab, die ich mochte. Zum einen ware da der moralische Konflikt. Der Tod als Hauptthema und die Frage, was man tun wurde, wenn man weiss, dass man sterben muss. Ich fand die ganzen Kapitel in denen Cassie in den Philosophie Vorlesungen geht einfach super. Die Diskussionen die sie dort fuhrt, die Theorien bekannter Philosophen die mit eingebracht wurden und ihre Gedanken dazu waren einfach nur clever eingeflochten. Die Beziehung zwischen Cassie und Lukas war ein Pluspunkt des Buches, weil sie realistisch dargestellt wurde und das Ende war kein Happy End, was hervorragend die Botschaft des Buches weiter aufrecht hielt. Zum Ende hin passieren viele Dinge, es wird spannend und man erfahrt, was es mit Cassie Gabe auf sich hat, eine Idee, die wirklich mal neu war. 
 Fazit 
 Ein Buch mit starker Botschaft, unterhaltsamer Geschichte, aber doch zu langem Mittelteil und viel zu wenig Fantasyelementen und Spannungsbogen.

book_a.title: The Iron Legends (The Iron Fey, #1.5, 3.5, 4.5)
book_a.user_review:
Buchgestaltung 
 Dass das deutsche Cover so wunderbar zu ganzen Reihe passt, finde ich echt super und auch, dass es trotz der etwas ,,gestreckten" Lange als HC erschienen ist, denn so sieht die Reihe komplett im Regal einfach toll aus! Mir personlich gefallt dieses Cover hier von allen auch am Besten, weil ich das Motiv sehr gelungen finde. Die englische Ausgabe finde ich auch nicht schlecht, obwohl die Charaktere darauf, nicht meiner Vorstellung entsprechen, so ist die Idee mal alle die abzubilden echt nett. 
 Was ich allerdings etwas blod gemacht finde ist, dass einem dieses Buch, als der 5 Band der Plotzlich Fee Reihe verkauft wird, wobei es das eben nicht ist, da die Kurzgeschichten, zwischen den Buchern spielen und oft auch Geschichten von Charakteren erzahlen, die in den eigentlichen Buchern kaum vorkamen. 
 Meinung 
 Ich hab ehrlich gesagt mehr schlechtes, als Gutes uber die Kurzgeschichten der Reihe gehort. Viele Leser waren enttauscht, hatten sich mehr erwartet, aber ich denke, dass diese Leute ganz falsch an das Buch heran gegangen sind. Man sollte es als das sehen, was es ist: eine Kurzgeschichtensammlung als Erganzung zu den Buchern! 
 Wie alle Fans der Reihe, habe ich mich sehr darauf gefreut noch einmal einen, wenn auch kurzen, Abstecher in die wundersame Welt des Nimmernie zu unternehmen. Genau, wie in den Buchern sind die Orte, an denen die kleinen Abenteuer stattfinden einzigartig beschrieben und aufregend kennen zu lernen (wobei man die meisten schon kennt, das aber wirklich egal ist) Die erste Geschichte wird aus der Sicht von Meghan beschrieben und bezieht sich auf den Teil der Buchreihe, in der es um den geschlossenen Handel mit Ash geht, indem Meghan ihn zuruck zum Winterhof begleiten soll. Was ich hier besonders mochte, war noch einmal zu der Zeit zuruck zu reisen, in der die beiden sich nicht geliebt haben und den lustigen, aber auch ernsten Dialogen zu folgen, die Band eins damals so interessant gemacht haben. Hier gab es auch eine kleine spannende Wende und alles in allem, fand ich die Geschichte echt gut und sie hat perfekt als ,,Fullmaterial" fur nach Teil eins gepasst. 
 Eine weitere Geschichte wird von Puck erzahlt, in der es hauptsachlich um ihn und Ash geht und ein Versprechen, das der junge Prinz einzuhalten versucht, wenn man dass denn so nennen kann...diese Geschichte war sehr abenteuerlich geschrieben und hier kommt Pucks Charme und Humor mal wieder sehr gut durch. Die letzte Geschichte setzt nachdem vierten Band an und hat bei mir so einen kleinen Nachgeschmack hinterlassen, was die Zukunft der Charaktere hinterlasst. Einerseits hat sie meine Neugier geweckt, mich aber anderseits auch enttauscht, weil sie viel zu schnell zu Ende war. Aber eines ist gewiss: die Zukunft wird kommen! :P 
 Ich fand den Roman insgesamt betrachtet wirklich schon zu lesen. All das, was man an Julie Kagawas Bucher bisher so mochte, kommt hier noch einmal durch, auch, wenn die Kurze der Geschichten irgendwie ernuchternd wird, aber dass sind Kurzgeschichten eben: KURZ! Man sieht wieder Meghans altes, naives und tollpatschiges Ich, man lacht uber Pucks sorgenloses Alter-Ego und wird bei Ash daran erinnert, dass man eine Zeit lang nicht wusste, ob er es verdient hat gemocht zu werden. Geschrieben ist das Ganze genauso gut, wie eh und je. Die kleinen Episoden enthalten Witz, Spannung und jede Menge Magie und schaffen es sicher, das Herz eines jeden Fans zu verzaubern. Ich glaube, ich werde ebenfalls die komplette Reihe in chronologischer Reihenfolge noch einmal lesen :P 
 Was mir auch gut gefallen hat (wenn man es auch schon kennt) war, dass in diesem Buch das ,,Handbuch" zur Buchreihe abgedruckt wurde, welches wirklich richtig schone und ausfuhrliche Beschreibungen, zu allem und jeden enthalt 
 Fazit 
 Eine kleine Praline :P fur alle Fans, die traurig nach dem Ende der Reihe waren und noch etwas mehr von Meghan und ihren Freunden haben mochten. Zwischenzeitlich kommt man jedoch um die ein oder andere Enttauschung nicht herum. Sei es nun wegen der Kurze der Geschichten oder der Tatsache, dass wir uns nun (fast) endgultig von all dem verabschieden mussen...

sample_reviews.review_text: Beautiful.
I loved these these novellas. But makes me want more and more of these stories!!

If you want answers to the questions you had when reading the storyline, well, here they are. There were so many loose ends the stimulates didn't clear up, and then this book came into my life. Now, don't get ne wrong, I still have more questions that this book didn't clear up, but at least I won't have to go crazy thinking about them.

Winter's Passage- 3.5 stars 
 Ok, well, this novella did not have much to rate on. I read it from my copy of The Iron Legends, and it only takes up 62 pages, making it very short. I did enjoy it, although it had no substance for the series watsoever. 
 So basically, in this book, Ash is bringing Meghan to the Unseelie Court, due to his Oath he made with Meghan. Not much happens, they visit Puck momentarily, who is still in a coma of sorts, and they run into The Big Bad Wolf. And of course theres the hot and cold romance between Ash and Meghan. Sigh. Why can't they just get together officially already?!?! 
 Once again, I loved the setting in this novella. Julie Kagawa's scenes are desribed beyond perfection. I was surprised I liked it in this one though. In The Iron King, I enjoyed the descriptions of the Summer lands, but I didn't really get into the Winter ones. I did in this book though, and I was very happy for it. 
 Overall, I mostly gave this novella a 3.5 because it lacked substance to the series(which is good for people who didn't read it, they missed nothing) and it was just too short to give it a higher rating. 
 Summer's Crossing- 5 stars 
 I never thought the first 5 star rating from me fo the Iron Fey series would be from a novella, but shockingly it was. And I totally take back what I said in my review for Winter's Passage about it being too short to be ranked high. 
 Overall, I loved this novella. I finished it in one night(not surprising since it's not very long), and I loved every second of it. 
 So, this story begins with Puck and Ash, setting out to find a way for Ash to be with Meghan. Their first step in this plan: find Grimalkin. Which as we all know: is going to be very difficult. 
 Right before they can begin the search, however, Leansidhe shows up and asks for a favor from Ash that he owed her. Queen Titianna has stolen one of her "violins" and she wanted him and Puck to retrieve it. 
 By far, the best part about this novella was that it was from Puck's point of view. It made the story amazing, and that earned the novella two whole stars. I loved how we could see how Puck really feels about Meghan, and his relationship with Ash. At one point, I was worried he had sold over Ash to Queen Titianna to get Meghan, but thankfully no. 
 So, ya. If you are Team Puck, DO NOT MISS OUT ON THIS NOVELLA. DO NOT, DO NOT, DO NOT. 
 The Iron Prophecy- 5 stars 
 If they ever make this series into movies(they HAVE to), then this should be it's own movie. Basically, in this novella, Meghan and Ash are together and married when they learn that Meghan is pregnant, and that their child could destroy the Nevernever. That's all I'm saying on this book though ;)
I loved this book so much!! My favorite story was Iron's Prophecy. Loved all the new knowledge we got. Julie Kagawa is my favorite female author!! Can't wait for The Lost Prince!!!!!!!!!!!
Well these little novellas are great for those clamoring for a little more in between the pages of the series. Plus, a guide to the iron fey verse

Instead of having put these out individually between the other novels, I really think that it just would've made more damn sense to ADD THEM TO THEIR RESPECTIVE INSTALLMENTS. 
 Holy beejeezus, stop torturing everyone just to make money.

Loved this book. The three short stories in it really helped expand the Iron Fey story and tie up some loose ends. I always enjoy it when authors write these little snippets of scenes that wouldn't otherwise fit into a whole novel or part of the story line already established.
Great extra novels to Iron Fey series. It fills the story of charcters from books of Iron Fey series.
Cute, entertaining, short reads. i love reading about Ash and Puck and Grimelkin and these stories gave me a sweet little fix.

book_b.title: Isla and the Happily Ever After (Anna and the French Kiss, #3)
book_b.user_review:
Buchgestaltung 
 Ich finde, dass der Coverwechsel der englischen Motive wirklich eine Verbesserung war. Die neuen Cover sind schlicht und farblich gut abgestimmt und daher mag ich das von Isla auch sehr gerne. Der Titel passt auch wie die Faust aufs Auge. Die deutsche Aufmachung finde ich aber auch nicht schlecht. Leider sehen die Figuren darauf mal wieder gar nicht so aus, wie die Charaktere. 
 Meinung 
 Ich weiss, dass viele Fans von Anna und Lola jetzt horen wollen, wie gut ich das Buch fand, aber in der Reihenfolge, in der die Bucher erschienen, genau so, ware auch mein Rating fur alle: 1) Anna, 2) Lola 3) Isla. 
 Stephanie Perkins hat bisher mehr als einmal bewiesen, dass sie wunderschone Liebesgeschichten schreiben kann, die einem ans Herz gehen. Anna war wundervoll, Lola war einzigartig, aber Isla? Tja, das Buch erzahlt die Geschichte eines Madchen, dass BESESSEN von einem Kerl ist, den es nicht kennt und dann am Ende genau das bekommt, was es wollte: Ein Happy End. Ich weiss gar nicht so genau, ob mich die Tatsache gestort hat, dass das einfach so mega unrealistisch war oder eher, dass es schon eine krankhafte Idee ist, die hinter dem Roman steckt. Was ich immer sehr zu schatzen wusste war, dass man die Figuren kennenlernt und MITERLEBT, wie sie sich verlieben...ja VERLIEBEN...und das war einfach immer soooo klasse! Bei Anna hab ich mitgefiebert, bei Lola gelacht und Isla...die habe ich einfach bemitleidet. 
 Dabei fing es so gut an. Die ersten Kapitel lag ich lachend auf dem Boden, weil es so suss war, wie Isla vollig benebelt, nach dem sie die Weisheitszahne raus bekommen hat, Josh voll gelabbert hat. Die erste (wenn man das so nennen kann) Begegnung war einfach ZUCKER. Und danach ging es dann los. Mehr und mehr taucht der Leser in Islas besessene Gedankenwelt ab. Josh ist heiss. Josh ist perfekt. Josh, Josh, Josh... 
 Und ganz ehrlich? Ich weiss selbst nach dem Lesen noch nicht, WER Josh eigentlich ist! Er hatte eine Ex-Freundin und kann zeichen. Wow...und was ist mit dem Rest? Was macht ihn aus? Das selbe Problem hatte ich aber noch viel starker bei Isla, denn bis auf ihre Stalker-Qualitaten bekommt man einfach kaum etwas mit. Die Autorin hat hier wieder versucht, die Nebenfiguren einzubringen, aber VERSUCHT ist eben das richtige Wort. Mich hat keiner von ihnen wirklich interessiert und so lebendig und authentisch, wie es Freunde und Familie in den anderen Buchern waren, war hier keiner. Bei Anna und Lola hatte ich immer das Gefuhl, dass andere Charaktere WICHTIG sind, aber hier? Fehlanzeige. 
 Und dann der Plot...WO war der Plot eigentlich? Es gab Konflikte, die keine Konflikte waren und oh so much drama, das ich gegen Ende kaum noch ertragen konnte! Die Sache mit Josh und seinen Eltern hatte man einfach mal in einem vernunftigen Gesprach klaren konnen. Ebenso wie die Probleme zwischen Isla und ihrer Schwester. Das war alles reinster Kindergarten und gerade die Entwicklung der Charaktere blieb auf der Strecke. 
 Und der Kitsch! BAH! Alle der Kitsch. Anna und Lola hatten auch kitschige Stellen...ja, STELLEN, aber nicht so viel Gebrabbel und Gesabber auf einem Haufen. Diese ganzen Liebesbekundungen und Geschmachte und diese sexy-Szenen, in denen Isla noch mal heftiger uber Josh hergefallen ist...urg. URG!!!!!!!! Das war einfach over the top. Ich meine, BARCELONA?! WTF! "Wir benahmen uns wie die Tiere, die wir waren" <--- Steht so im Buch. Und jetzt lasst mal euren Gedanken freien Lauf. Und das obwohl Isla ja so schuchtern am Anfang war, aber sicher, jemand wie Josh, fur den tut man eben ALLES. 
 Ich will auch gar nicht sagen, dass ich das Buch nicht mochte. Es bekommt gute 2 Sterne von mir. Besonders der Anfang war einfach toll und es gab auch einige Dialoge, die ich gut fand. Aber zusammenfassend war Isla enttauschend und nicht wirklich eine Empfehlung (zumindest meinerseits) wert. 
 Fazit 
 ISLA war eine grosse Enttauschung fur mich. Ich weiss, dass Stephanie Perkins es besser kann und der Overload an Kitsch war einfach furchtbar. Ausserdem fiel es schwer mit den Figuren zu sympathisieren, da man sie leider nicht gut genug kennenlernt. Auch von der Handlung her ging alles viel zu schnell und besonders das unnotige Drama hat mich den letzten Nerv gekostet. Fans der Reihe sollten es sich trotzdem mal anschauen. Wer weiss, vielleicht gefallt es auch ja besser als mir?

sample_reviews.review_text: I thought this was a perfect reminder of what it's like to me a high school aged girl. I had the same insecurities and doubts about myself as Isla deals with. Josh's devotion was so sweet. Of course I loved the appearance from the characters in the first two novels.

Isla and the Happily Ever after isn't as charming as Lola and the Boy Next Door nor as magical as Anna and The French Kiss but the story has its own beauty. Maybe because the story itself is an art, and arts aren't supposed to be nice, nor charming,it's supposed to make you feel something. (and yes, I am definitely quoting Eleanor & Park here) 
 So the story started when a disoriented Isla Martin met her long-time crush Josh Wassertein at a cafe. They had their very first real conversation that time because Isla isn't her low self-esteemed, shy self; she even had Josh draw her and walk her home. She woke up the next day trying to remember what exactly happened and felt a gush of embarrassment once she had recalled everything. So she tried to talk to Josh again but can't find the willpower to do so. But then fate itself made its way and finally they had a chance to talk. Josh admitted that at first, he thought Isla and her bestfriend, Kurt, were romantically involved so he tried to not to be involved with Isla even though he's kinda interested in her. But then they started talking, the little chit chats became riveting conversations and then they started dating. 
 But as for someone like Isla who lacks self confidence, her insecurities start to fill her up, especially when her boyfriend got kicked out of school and was grounded from using his phone. Will Isla let her insecurities get in the way of their love or will Josh find more ways to show his true feelings to her? 
 I actually expected Josh and Rashmi to fall apart once I've heard about this book but assumed that it would be more about Josh moving on from his failed relationship with Rashmi and Isla being there to comfort him or something close to that to be honest. Stephanie Perkins knew the right plot and the right words and that's what made this a very wonderful book. I love this book (specially the ending! love the cameos! )
*3.5 Stars*

2.5/5 
 Como mencione no paso ni mejor momento en la lectura y probablemente este no era el tipo de libro que necesitaba para adentrarme de nuevo. 
 Siento que las cosas pasaban demasiado rapido y al contrario del primer libro hubo cosas que no se me hicieron muy reales. 
 Ya para el final mejoro un poco, creo que fue mas agil.
I love Stephanie Perkins and her wonderfully happy endings, and this book is no different. I also love how all of her books subtly tie into one another.

No va mas. 
 Trate de terminarlo, llegue hasta un poco mas de la mitad y no puedo seguir de tan malo que me parece. 
 No me sobra el tiempo y ultimamente estoy siendo bastante selectiva con los libros, y no voy a gastar tiempo que no tengo con un libro que me hace rodar los ojos dos veces por pagina. 
 Trate de darle una oportunidad mas a la saga, lei Anna, y no me fascino, la sinopsis de Lola no me llamaba la atencion y la pase e intente con este. Craso error. 
 Las historias en las que un nene y una nena con plata se enamoran en UN mes, que por lo que vivieron en UN mes, de repente no importa nada mas en el mundo, y los planes de repente giran en torno al chico porque blablabla por UN mes de haber estado juntos, me hacen querer recrear la escena de Bradley Cooper tirando el libro por la ventana. Excepto que lo lei en la computadora y no me puedo dar ese lujo. 
 El chico artista, timido, egocentrico, que '''''casualmente''''' le sugiere a la chica dulce y tonta, que tiene que hacer de ahora en mas para estar juntos onda ir a una facultad pesima, me violenta. 
 Oh que gran problema que los reten por IRSE DEL PAIS, pucha che, como no lo pudieron pensar antes? 
 Y el tema de estar separados despues de UN mes de amor intenso? WOW totalmente me deja sin palabras. 
 Nunca mas con esta autora.

I just want to start by saying that I have truly enjoyed Stephanie Perkins' other books immensely. Unfortunately, this installment was just blah. You'd think the premise of an artsy boy and a bookish girl would be plot-gold but the characters are expected to be madly in love after years of far-away infatuation and one month, yes that's right, one month of actually being in a relationship. I found their romance a little hard to root for. This book was also raunchier than the other two which I just thought of as frustrating. The characters are in flippin high school. I mean, some of this crap shouldn't be happening at this point. I also felt like every step in their relationship they just took way too seriously for what was actually happening...extreme teenage drama I guess but it was just over the top. Although, since it is a Perkins book, the actual writing was well-done. I also liked that the characters from the other books show up at the end. I almost didn't want to finish but I'm glad I muddled through. However, if you liked "Anna and the French Kiss" and "Lola and the Boy Next Door", just stick with those. Don't indulge you're curiosity by trudging through this one.

Ughhhhhh....oh my goodness!!!! I abso-freaking-lutely LOVED Isla and the Happily Ever After!!!!! It was more than worth the wait and I already can't wait to read it again!!! Maybe after rereading Anna's and Lola's books, too! ;) Isla and Josh were fantastic and I love them so much!!!! :D okay...I'll stop this gush-feat for now, and I should have a full review coming in a bit! ;) 
 Thanks again for borrowing me your ARC, Mandy! I'm glad I could read Isla's story before going on my holiday. :)

**I borrowed an ARC from a friend** 
 SO SO SO BEAUTIFUL. Stephanie Perkins is brilliant. I love how she brings the characters to life. I feel like I've read this book at the right time. I related to Isla the most out of the three girls (Anna, Lola, and Isla). This book made me realize things and actually gave me things to ponder upon as well. I can't wait to buy a finished copy and reread it again.

Quite honestly, it was torture seeing everyone reading this back when it came out since I decided to wait for the US paperback to match my set. I'm very glad I did though, since for the most part I enjoyed Isla a lot. I loved everything that was related to art, traveling, falling in love, the old gang get-together, the family parts with the Martins etc. I loved a lot and there was major swooning okay. Also, I loved that it was pro-sex and very mature in exploring young adult's sexuality. It's not like it doesn't exist irl, on the opposite, but YA books often don't do this, so it was a pleasant surprise. 
 Howeveeerrrr, I didn't like how Isla blamed everyone else for her own actions. (I note that she grew by the end of the novel though and took responsibility instead of putting blame on other people.) I also got tired of the melodrama with the separation of Josh and Isla . Ugh. I know that for a teen this is hella intense and upsetting, but seriously just.. no. From the moment this happened the book started dragging and I wasn't on great terms with Isla until she got her act together. 
 As a whole though I enjoyed it and have fond memories, so all's good. If it hadn't been this dramatic, it would have been a decent 4, but it's more like 3.5 so 3 stars it is. 
 Overall rating: 3.5 out of 5.0

reference_books.title: The Shepherd's Tale (Serenity, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 SHINY!!! technically i just had my pupils dilated sx i can't actually read this for several hours but i'm so ruttin' excited i had to get it out there!!! i also cant see wht i'm typing clearly.

book_a.title: Howl's Moving Castle (Howl's Moving Castle, #1)
book_a.user_review: I loved this book! Whenever I had to put it down I couldn't wait to pick it back up again. I enjoyed that nothing was ever wholly as it seemed and even though I guessed a few of the mysteries before they were revealed I feel like it was part of the experience. Loved the transformations of the characters as they developed and how the concept of appearances figured in. I can't wait to watch the movie now, though I know it takes a different turn.

sample_reviews.review_text: Once the pages ended I wanted to start it all over again. Fantastic story. :)

I'm really not one for the fantasy genre, but I do love YA/J fiction so I thought I'd give it a shot. I thought the concept and the story was fascinating, and to be honest, that's the only reason I kept reading. That, and the fact that Jones totally had me in the beginning with her witty and sarcastic tone. 
 The book begins really strong with Sophie, the eldest of three daughters sent into the world to make their fortunes, and this interesting world of moving buildings owned by wizards. The book took a downward spike for me when I started to realize how much I actually disliked Sophie, who carries the entire book on her back. She starts out meek and timid, then moves on to pushy and rude, and then ends with completely clueless. I absolutely hate it when I'm reading a book and feel smarter than the main character. I actually put the book down in disgust a few times because I was so annoyed with the way things were going. 
 The book felt a little like an extended Grimm's Fairy Tale, and I'm not talking about the Disney version. If you like this sort of thing, you will like this book. 
 Then we get to the ending, and if you're going to read this book, skip this paragraph. I really, really did not want Sophie to be with Howl. I wanted her to walk away, strong on her own- I hated how the whole book moved in the direction of tricking her into being in love with him. Then when she realizes it, they both live happily ever after. What the? There was no moment in the book for me where Howl really redeemed himself, so why would I want him with Sophie(even if I do find her annoying)? 
 My only other big issue was a completely personal one. I don't read the fantasy genre, so a lot of the terms were really confusing to me. It was also difficult for me to keep up with the confusion of a world where scarecrows stalk people, magic just suddenly reveals itself, and pieces(literally) of people and dogs and men are confusingly intertwined. Basically the book wasn't "commercial" enough for me; it didn't stretch itself to include those of us that just want a quick fantasy fix. 
 It absolutely made me realize why this genre is just not for me. 
 I am going to include the link to Amazon's reviews and description though, since I seem to be fighting a tidal wave of love for this one.
We watched the movie and I couldn't figure out what was going on, so I had to read the book! The book was much more comprehensible than the movie.

I read this after seeing the Studio Gihbli film. I was surprised at how much it resembled the movie throughout nearly half of the novel. Toward the end, it DID branch off quite a bit. But the overall story was bubbling with the most endearing humor, and heartwarming characters. The relationship between Sophie and Calcifer wormed it's way straight to my heart... And Howl, though a bit much at times, won me over in the end, just as he did Sophie. It is just pure gold.

What a charming book! I had been told that the Miyazaki film called "Howl's Moving Castle" was based on a book and that the book was better than the movie. So, I finally got around to checking it out. I enjoyed every page. I love Miyazaki's animations. Rather than move the story with every second of action, he creates atmosphere the way art films frequently do. In "My Neighbor Totoro" there is a sequence when sisters are standing holding hands at a bus stop. One drop of rain falls, then we zoom into a puddle and slowly the rain multiplies into a down-pour. Taking a minute to show a hypnotic sequence for the purpose of creating atmosphere can really take a viewer into the scene making them forget they are watching a children's animation. There is real love in Miyazaki's work and Jone's book has a similar sensibility. 
 The story is of a pretty young woman who is made a very old woman by the Witch of the Waste. Sophie, the young woman, goes to the enchanted castle of a wizard named Howl despite his reputation for mischief. Most of the twists and turns of the story are amusing, charming and atmospheric. It appears that the Witch of the Waste has been busy casting spells and mixing and matching people who've been trying to stop her. Howl and his household which includes a demons, an apprentice and Sophie, end up straightening everything out. 
 This is not high adventure, just a fantasy set in Victorian England with a Welch wizard, an evil witch and enchanted young maidens in disguise. So, if you are charmed by Miyazaki, the book has the same charm. While Miyazaki takes liberty both with the story and the cast, he captures the feel. The book is better in so far as it is more complex and has a more satisfying ending. However, having seen the film, I had a visual impression while I was reading which I enjoyed. I would recommend the movie and the book quite highly - absolutely enchanting and intended for young adult and adults young at heart!

Movie was better than the book. 
 I didn't like the depressed howl- the movie made him much more endearing.
I enjoyed this version of the story. I had seen the movie first and wasn't sure what I would get, but this was a pleasant read. Very British story telling that I really enjoyed.

I watched the movie first. I know, I know, shame on me. But it's not my fault, I didn't even know the book existed before I watched Studio Ghibli's take on Howl's Moving Castle. 
 I absolutely loved the movie, and when I read there was a book I was thrilled! The books always better right? 
 Wrong. 
 Well let me explain. 
 Howl's moving Castle is about a a girl named Sophie Hatter, the eldest of three. She works in a hat shop living a very simple and boring life, until.... The notorious Witch of The Waste comes in and turns her into a old lady. Sophie runs away and meets the handsome (but a little rude) Wizard Howl. That's all I can say without giving away too much. 
 Back to the movie: 
 It left out A LOT and got A LOT wrong. But for some reason I liked the movie better than the book. 
 *gasp* 
 I'm not sure why, maybe it's just my obsession with Hayao Miyazaki's films, or just the way it was portrayed. 
 But the book wasn't bad. Not at all! The writing was good (Though very confusing towards the end) and the characters were very likeable, though I liked the more mysterious and charming Howl from the film over the original Howl in the book. And I really liked Sophie, because she reminds me a lot of myself, and relatable characters are always a joy to have in books. 
 It's an magical fantasy story that I highly enjoyed, even though for the first time in my life, I liked the film better.

A recent re-read, and a book I wish I would have found as a child or teenager. I love Diana Wynne Jones, and how she treads the line between employing and shirking fairytale logic for what happens in her stories. I'm actually glad I saw the Ghibli movie before I read this book, because I think if I hadn't, I might not have enjoyed the film as much, as it departs so much. As it is I think they both are great tellings of a similar story, though I prefer the route the book takes. 
 The book gives us deeper portraits of the characters, I love how Sophie's own power is explored, and also the role her family has to play. Howl's character seems bigger in the book as well, he's both more and also less vain and cowardly in different ways, I loved how the book bares more of his past and life to the reader while at the same time keeping his motivations and humour a bit mysterious as we go along. 
 My favourite books are the ones where I'm almost angry they're not real cause I want to go and just live inside. This counts as one, I'm so sad there's no Ingary!

sample_reviews.review_text: This was one of my favorite books of all time.

Don't get me wrong, it's wondrously well written. The story took over my brain for the whole of the time it took me to read it - and at nearly 900 pages, that was quite some time. The settings are alive and real; I can see rocky Tintagel, green Wales, misty Avalon with its standing stones. The characters are well-executed and believable. 
 They're also rat bastards. Not one person anywhere in nearly 900 pages is anything but cruel, small-minded, self-righteous; not one has a shred of human decency, or honest courage. If just once, anyone had stopped to tell the truth - well, that would never happen. Instead, they try to do what their gods want them to do; but their gods condone betrayal, falsehood, cowardice and murder. Religion fails again. 
 I've never been a fan of Arthurian legend, and I don't know more of the story than has been presented by Disney or Monty Python. But I don't see how that could make a difference. People being rotten to each other sucks, and at every turn in the story it only got worse. It's a hell of a thing to put up with for 900 pages. I can't honestly recommend this book to anyone who isn't a masochist.

Thank god that is over! What an interminably long book. Was it entertaining? Yes.. maybe.. I don't know. I couldn't tell you much about it. It was way to long for me. Or maybe I wasn't ready for such a tome. I felt the female characters were complainers and whiny. They were always so full of guilt and doubt. I would have liked them to seem a bit stronger in personal character, especially since this was a book about the women surrounding King Arthur. 
 I felt it was overblown with the religious topic. It was repetitive. I was tired with it very early on. A lot of the details were repetitive as well and felt like filler. I don't think this book needed to be so fleshed out. Towards the end, it felt rushed.

The magic surrounding Avalon enchants all, but like time and men, it passes into the dark mists and becomes a blurry memory. Here is an encompassing tale about the adventures and upheavals of Camelot's court through the eyes and lives of the women behind the throne. Based on the Arthurian legend most loved by all, we follow the story of the characters, as told by Morgaine, from their childhoods through the fulfillment of their destinies and their search for spirituality. 
 The present king of Great Britain is dying and the kingdom is wrought with struggles, from the heirs vying for the throne and the invading Saxons to the spreading of the new religion. In the distant shore is the Isle of Avalon, the lair of the old magic of the Goddess, where the Merlin of Britain and the Lady of the Lake wield power. It was said that a child born from the blood of the Goddess and of the land will unite the old world and the new. But some things aren't always set in stone and even now Avalon is fading farther into the mists... 
 In the beginning I was enamored by the book cover (of a fairy priestess atop a horse), the nostalgic melancholy of the prologue and the fact that it was about the Arthurian legend that I've always been fascinated of but the epic proportions of the book might be daunting to some. The portrayal of the familiar characters didn't really follow the original saga but it has its own unique perspective and the bulk of that relies on its figures of strong, albeit rock stubborn, women; their sacrifices and pain to keep forever what they hold dear. 
 There's a coat of sadness breathing on its pages. It's not without surprises and unrelieved angst of why fates sway this way or that way. It is only a matter of succumbing to each of the character's beliefs and you can't help yourself rooting for a few of them even if you feel a foreboding on their fortunes. 
 Marion Zimmer Bradley took to exploring elements and concepts that are quite debatable to some but it is done with good research. Others may claim it is a feminist take on the old legend (but don't really expect too much on this). There are times that I find myself frustrated, still on a fence on how things pan out, but what exactly am I talking about? This is not my story but theirs. One must step back and look at things in a certain light especially with the spiritual and religious contexts (which I am not sure if some would agree). And if you look closely, you find them as much as human as we are in our present world. 
 In the end, it is about the magic in the world, war and peace, power and beliefs, destiny and salvation; a good fantasy book that lingers in your mind as if Morgaine's voice still echoes out of the sky. Even more, I found myself secretly wishing I have a blue crescent moon painted on my forehead.

I seem to remember really loving this book the first time I read it, probably as in my teens. I re-read as an adult and could barely get through it. I'm only keeping it on my shelf to read again down the road a bit to see what I think.

There were moments where I hated this book. There were moments when I loved this book. Most of the time, though, I just didn't care. 
 This is a "feminist" telling of Arthurian legend, if your version of feminism is women who never really get along, constantly try to shame each other, and only experience character development of any sort when it involves the man that she fell in love with after knowing for five whole minutes. Seriously this is a nearly 800 page book all about women, entirely in the point of view of women, and if you told me that it didn't pass the Bechdel test, I would believe you. 
 I might not have had as much of a problem with it if the book wasn't paraded as a feminist novel. I might have passed it over as dated fantasy tropes. Regardless of the ideology though, the characters are so frustrating. All of them go through this constant cycle of close-mindedness to slight character growth and hope for change to regressing to the same close-minded person they were at the beginning of the last chapter. I could not make myself care much for characters that were just this static. 
 Literally the only way I would suggest this book to anyone is if they specifically were looking for books on Arthurian legend. I wanted to like this book, but I don't. I can't even say that I hate it. I just don't care about it. Don't waste your time.
Good telling of the story of Avalon.

It's the summer of Arthurian retellings! The Mists of Avalon was probably at a bit of a disadvantage from the start, as I read it right after T.H. White's The Once and Future King. White's work is one of my favorite things I've read in recent memory, so Zimmer Bradley's had a tough standard to live up to. Though to be fair, they are drastically different books in tone and intent, and I think most of my problems with The Mists of Avalon would have existed regardless of when I had read it. And sorry in advance: this is a long review for a long book. 
 There were a lot of things that I did like about The Mists of Avalon. I very much appreciate the idea of re-writing the Arthurian legend from a female perspective. That's a great narrative idea, filled with potential. I thought that it was very nicely written, with passages that really effectively evoke the sense of 'Englishness' that's wrapped up in the Arthurian mythos (or, perhaps, what American readers think of when they think of Englishness). There's loads of mist, moors, and a sense of drastically open space that gives the book a very good sense of place. I also didn't mind the pacing: the book meanders, and often won't have a definitively identifiable plot line. It probably could have worked just as well if it topped out at 600 pages instead of 875. But the slowness of the pacing sort of works for it, since so much of the work is about people growing old, and carefully laid plans, worked out over years, failing abysmally. 
 Despite this, though, I wasn't able to say in the end that I really enjoyed it. I think there are two central problems that permeate the book: its preachiness and its characters. 
 The first problem is the dichotomy that drives the book, and propels most of its characters: the worldview of Avalon vs. the worldview of Christianity. Despite nominal attempts to give credence to both sides, Zimmer Bradley clearly prefers the older Celtic religion and portrays it as a kind of matriarchal, sex-positive paradise that's constantly under threat from the narrow-minded and misogynistic zealot priests of Christianity. It's frustrating, predominantly because in a lot of ways I can see where she's coming from. Christianity absolutely does have some very questionable tenets in terms of women, gender, and sexuality. They deserve to be questioned and critiqued, and this is a potentially great venue in which to do it. But the origin and reasons for these tenets are also very complicated, and derive from an intricate mixture of social, political, and cultural features that existed during the period. All of these are essentially ignored, and the Christians in the book range from actively cruel to well-meaning-but-stupid. On the other side, the idealized faith of Avalon remains exasperatingly vague, particularly because it makes no attempt to deal with what it means to the vast majority of its believers who don't happen to belong to the royal priestess line. I'm not convinced, for example, that the Beltane Fires were all that great for women who didn't get to be priestesses. 
 With these things defined over-simply or not at all, the reader is left with a black-white split that lacks the substance to support the endless discussions that characters have about it. Zimmer Bradley just sets up Christianity and all its practitioners as simplified and oppressive straw men to stand against her overly-rosy view of paganism, and refuses to engage in the issues she introduces with any depth. It's frustrating, because there are loads of interesting things to explore here, and The Mists of Avalon seems content to bash away at the same pinata in the same way for 900 pages. Individual characters will have the exact same conversation about the arrival of Christianity eight to ten times over the course of the novel, without adding anything new or introducing any complexity to the question, like they're some kind of didactic record that's stuck on a loop. It's a huge narrative turn-off. 
 The other problem, very wrapped up in the one that I just mentioned, is the book's characters. The men remain almost entirely one-dimensional and unexplored (with the possible exception of Lancelet). I understand that this is a course-correction after centuries of one-dimensional Arthurian women, but I'm not sure it's terribly helpful to simply put the other gender on the backburner as a response. The female characters are a more complicated problem. I think that the central issue is that the vast majority of women in the story function as mouthpieces for the previously mentioned theological discussions more than as real people. And because the theological question is so simplified, it makes the characters feel weak and lacking in depth or dynamism. There are smaller problems as well. Almost all of the women tend to argue and compete incessantly over the men in their lives, and they had the tendency to be terribly mean and petty to each other, a big pet peeve of mine. The vast majority of them at some point hate another woman just because she's prettier than them, and Morgaine spends most of her time thinking about how stupid and petty all of the women who aren't Avalon priestesses must be. This is certainly something that happens sometimes, and I would not complain if it were an occasional occurrence. But it's frustrating when it's a perpetual characteristic of every single woman in the novel, with the occasional exception of Morgause (who everyone continually disdains for no discernable reason). 
 The concept of a "strong female character" in modern story-telling is talked about a lot, but I think it's still rarely done well. In most cases, a strong female character is interpreted as a woman who possesses a strong will (and often the physical skills to back it up) and who can come back with a witty rejoinder whenever someone questions her ability or worth. There's nothing wrong with that archetype. But it doesn't equate to a good character. I think what's needed more in fiction isn't strong female characters, but interesting, distinctive, or dynamic ones. These are mostly absent from The Mists of Avalon. Despite a long list of female characters, nearly every one fits solidly into an ideological box: the priestess woman or the Christian woman. Vivaine is the same person as Morgaine, and neither changes much in the course of the story: they are both ideologically fixated, unafraid to use the people around them to enact their will and worldview, and punctuated by moments of loneliness or self-doubt. Christian women are simpering, submissive, lacking in intelligence, and occasionally dogmatic. The only person who doesn't fit into these boxes is Morgause, who is given very little attention and is mostly vilified by everyone else. The only person who changes at all from the beginning of the book to the end is Gwenhwyfar, and the change is abrupt and unearned after long sections of ambivalent and waffling characterization. 
 I think the book is too wrapped up in its own message to function simply as a story, and the message is too overly-simplified to be of much interest or use. It's a really good idea for a book, but the potential of its premise is only occasionally reached in the execution.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I really enjoyed this book, and it was the first book that I have read from Kody Keplinger. The narrator, Bianca, is hilarious and spunky, something you don't see a lot from a female protagonist. I like how realistic she is, and how cynical she can be sometimes. Despite her seeing the glass as half empty, she wasn't whinny and I am sure that her and I would be great friends if she wasn't a fictional character. I also liked her relationship with Wesley, and how comfortable they are around each other. Their romance isn't a typical one, and I like that it is still cute without being overly cheesy. 
 There wasn't anything particularly wrong with the story or the characters, it just didn't reach out to me the way some contemporary books do-I didn't find this book partially touching or memorable. The plot line was a bit predictable, and everything kind of ended way too conveniently. The climax was a bit of a let down, and there wasn't that much character development in my opinion. 
 This was a funny, quick, and light read but I didn't view it as anything special; however, I am interested in reading more books by this author.

Starting this book, I thought I was in for a Teenager's-journey-through-low-self-esteem-and-self-loathing-until-she-gradually-learns-to-love-herself-and-with-the-support-of-her-family-and-friends-becomes-a-better-person type novel. I'm not sure why I thought that, looking back on it. Most of the inside cover is about romance, and none of the quotes from other authors on the back say anything about the moving aspects of the book. 
 Turns out that is because there are none. This book barely touches on--whatsherface--Bianca's view of herself. Sure they mention it a few times in passing. "Oh no, I'm the Duff! Look there! A conveniently placed mirror, so we can bring it up again: Oh no! I am the Duff! Now where is Wesley..." Seriously. Every other scene is a sex scene. 
 To be fair, I finished the book in less than 24 hours. Something about the writing style is addicting, I think. It's certainly not the characters. Wesley is a complete Complex Bad Boy stereotype, and we barely find out anything about Bianca's friends other than they're really good friends for sticking by her because she's REALLY FREAKING ANNOYING. Why do all the characters love her?? Ooh, I know. Because she's special and cool and rebellious, right? Oooooh, she doesn't approve of prom? She hates nightclubs? What an original character! Really though, she's just not like other girls! 
 Also, did the whole "maybe we're all the Duff" realization make anyone else gag? Wait, let me quote what the book actually says. "So, maybe, every girl felt like the Duff, too?" HOW DID THAT GET PUBLISHED. That sounds like the end of a claymation Christmas special! 
 Honestly, I hated this book. It was just dumb. I heard so many great things about it, so it was really a disappointment.

Well. I must say that this is the first book I've ever slammed against a table and thrown across the room. I hated it. I don't even know where to begin. 
 Perhaps with the main character, Bianca. I can sum her up in one word: toxic. This is exactly the kind of person you don't want in your life. I've known a few Bianca's in my time, been friends with a few - I know this from experience. This is a person who is constantly looking down her nose at others, constantly judging them. This is a person who thinks they're so incredibly intelligent when they really don't know anything at all. This is a person who will constantly take people for granted and great them horribly. This is a person you always have to walk on eggshells around so you don't set them off. This is a person who thinks they're do enlightened and mature, when the truth is that they're one of the most immature people out there. Toxic. I didn't like her at all. 
 It's ludicrous that Jessica and Casey would want to be friends with her - she doesn't deserve them. For all the talk about how horrible a person Wesley was, Bianca treated him so much worse than he treated her. Yeah, he was arrogant and obnoxious a lot of the time, but nowhere near as vile as he'd been made out to be. 
 I think what frustrated me the most about this book was that it could have been so interesting. The basic idea was an intriguing one. For all the talk about how much it hurt to be the Duff, it was never really explored. This book could have had a strong message about looking for the inner beauty and others, but instead we're left with this lame spiel about how we're all the Duff. The word is supposedly so hurtful and yet in the end it's being used as a joke. Such a terrible message. Actually there were a ton on awful messages in this book. 
 For instance, forget about things like dignity and self-respect because those things are for losers! If a guy calls you a hurtful name that cause you to have serious insecurities, forget about, I don't know, ignoring him. No, way better to jump into bed with him at every available opportunity. Meanwhile, sex addiction is a thing and it would have been something worth addressing. But of course, we didn't. The idea was touched on a couple of times but never explored. 
 I can totally see people using sex as a distraction. People do it all the time. That part was realistic - would've been a lot more so if Bianca had started sleeping with someone else. Anyone else. But going with someone she hated who labeled her the Duff? No. Here's a hint: if you feel dirty and ashamed after having sex with someone than you shouldn't be having sex with that person. If it feels wrong to you, it is wrong. Me, I'm old fashioned. I think sex should be reserved for people you love who love you. But that's me; maybe it's not the same for you. And you know what? That's okay. I'm not telling anyone not to have sex, but pay attention to how you feel afterwards. Have enough respect for yourself to not continue to sleep with someone if you hate the way you feel after. I don't care how amazing the sex is. Speaking of, sex is always going to be better with someone you like and respect and vice versa. It just is. Again: if it feels wrong, it feels wrong for a reason. Don't ignore that. 
 I do commend the author for having Bianca and Wesley use condoms and for having her on the pill. Especially considering how much Wesley was said to sleep around. Though that said, to Bianca, if you tell your friend that you've been having sex for months and you call her early in the morning to pick you up and you tell her your life sucks so much more now, it is perfectly valid for her to ask if you're pregnant. It did get mentioned briefly in the book but condoms fail. Birth control is not 100% effective. Using them both is the way to do it, but you have to realize that there's still an amount of risk. Albeit a much smaller one than if you didn't use anything at all. 
 Meanwhile, assuming that someone is actually a man whore - you know, if they actually sleep around as much as they're rumored to - you might want to have them get tested before you sleep with them. I understand getting caught up in the moment and things going too far, but it's still worse mentioning. 
 Now onto the next point, teenagers of the world, if you have a parent struggling with addiction you need to tell someone. In this case, Bianca really needed to tell her mom. Addiction doesn't just go away. It doesn't get better. I really hated that whole subplot in this book because it was handled so poorly. You don't fall off the wagon and then have everything magically be okay because you started going to meetings again. Don't get me wrong: that's a fantastic first step. But you have to realize that it's a struggle. I wish there'd been some mention of Bianca talking to someone too. If nothing else, her mom should've brought it up. 
 Man, I had so many problems with this book! Could've done without all the political comments - either build it up more or leave them out all together. How did I know that Wuthering Heights would come into play? Major eye rolling moment when it was first mentioned because of course. Of course it would. Another eye roll inducing moment? When Wesley called Bianca compassionate. Nope. Not even a little. 
 And now, the nickname. Duffy. I never believed that Wesley was using that term In a negative way. I totally get Bianca hating to be called that, but I don't get why it took her so long to say anything. People talk about how strong she is, how she's not a pushover and yet, she never said anything! I couldn't blame him for being surprised when she finally did. 
 I've seen people gush over the Wesley/Bianca relationship and honestly, I think he was far too good for her. Maybe not in the beginning but certainly as it neared the end. Wesley got to grow some, but she didn't. She was the same person she was in the beginning and evidently going to stay that way. Couldn't root for her at all. I seriously regret spending money on this. Maybe it's because it's been a while since I was in high school and not only that, but my high school experience was pretty different. But I didn't enjoy this at all and I wouldn't recommend it. I know I certainly won't be reading it again.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Let me preface this review by saying that I adore Kody Keplinger, and she's an "instant buy" for me whenever she releases a new book. I'll speak on this more later... 
 But The DUFF. I absolutely disliked this book. I was so excited for it because at the time, I was querying and drowning in the world of traditional YA books. I'd heard so, so much about this book. The hype was huge. The reviews were glowing. Other agents raved about it. So of course, as someone who wanted publication, I had to read this book and see what was so perfect about it. The premise was outstanding. The idea was huge. The title itself had spunk and just sounded like it was a book that was pushing boundaries. 
 However, it fell so very flat. It took me months to finish it, at snail's pace. It was so unrealistic. I can suspend belief and go along with most books because "it's fiction, so just play along." I even write books that are a little "play along" types. But Bianca was an outright biatch. I was never once rooting for her. She was rude to her friends. She wasn't "snarky and witty." She was mean. Rude. A bitch, to be very blunt. Wesley was an ass, but he knew it, and everyone else knew it, and he owned it. I could tolerate that. Bianca's friends lacked personality. They were names. They were flat characters. And I don't know why they put up w/her because she treated them like dirt. 
 The sex was...eh. It just didn't feel right or work for me. The parental relationships were ugh. There were so many awesome ideas here that just didn't work. 
 However, Kody can write well. The book wasn't terrible. It felt like a teenager wrote it (which she was 17 at the time). It lacked a lot of the depth I prefer in a book. I did enjoy the Xbox scene, where Bianca and Wesley were just hanging out like normal teens. That felt real. Sadly that was the only part. 
 I think I'm in the minority, though, which is good for Kody's sake and The DUFF's sake. So many people LOVED this book. I hesitated to read Shut Out after this one, but the premise sucked me in, and I LOVED it. I loved A Midsummer's Nightmare even more. I think Kody really does touch some deeper subjects, and I like that about her. I've thoroughly enjoyed her other books, and I look forward to more from her. This book just didn't do it for me. Maybe it will for you...?

This book did well depicting social norms of beauty, but not very well at depicting the consequences of casual teen sex - there is a pregnancy scare, but not really. Sort of thrown in as if to say, 'now your parents will let you read this book.' Lots of language. (Read: too much.) Also, Bianca turns into sort of a jerk at the end (you know the part, where she's talking to Wesley about the future of their relationship. "I'm gonna throw things at you, do what I want, insult you, etc." If he had said that, it would have been a red flag for an abusive relationship! But the girl says it and it's okay? Equality? This part came across to me like Megan Trainor's 'Dear Future Husband.' Eughh. *shivers*) 2.5 stars.

I've been drawn to this book since last year, because who DOESN'T want to read about the makings of this mysterious stone giant? Doesn't it remind you of that movie, The Iron Giant? Well it did for me, and I really loved that movie, so of course I had to pick this up at one point or another. 
 The prologue introduces us to a young girl who discovers the an enormous stone hand, illuminated by glowing carvings. Fast forward to the future, and this girl, Rose, is now a well known physicist. By luck, she's been asked to lead the project on researching the hand, and also finding the rest of the pieces. And putting it together, and seeing how it works, or whether it works for that matter. 
 Sleeping Giants is told through interviews, a couple of journal entries, and recorded phone conversations between the mysterious interviewer, and a number of other characters. Although I loved how everything came together, and we got to know more about the events that were taking place, I felt that I would have liked it better as prose? There were a countless number of times where I felt left in the dark, and I wouldn't find out what happened until it was reported or the interviewer asked about it. This led to a weird pacing, as there were many time jumps between certain events. 
 Like I mentioned before, there were many characters. Although there were the main four, a couple more were introduced to put everything in perspective. But I just couldn't wrap my mind around all these characters. 
 But other than that, the plot completely pulled me into the story. Where the heck did this giant come from? How is it so powerful? What sort of technology is it? And more importantly, what the heck happened at the end there? I'm going to need that second book, because I need all my answers. 
 Overall, I enjoyed Sleeping Giants, even though it doesn't live up to other adult science fiction novels I have read in the past. It definitely satisfied my "Iron Giant" feels.

Thoroughly enjoyable and creative sci-fi novel. Interesting concept and characters but a bit hard to follow occasionally. 4.5 stars.

The premise of this story is that we get informed, in a series of case files, the events that led to the United States finding a giant alien robot which had been buried underneath the earth thousands upon thousands of years ago. They put the robot together and thus begins political pandemonium as you can imagine seeing as humans see anything as a weapon. I had previously read dossier-style books before - they seem to be the 'letter writing' style of the late 1800s (The Time Machine, Dracula, etc) as many authors today choose to do their books as such however despite some succeeding (Illuminae is a great example), Sleeping Giants missed the mark by a mile. This book is a quick read as it feels like you're reading a movie script, if you've ever read a script or a play you understand the general gist. We are presented with a series of interviews done by an unnamed man who seems to be the puppet master of the rest of the group. 
 The main issue that I had with this book was the utter lack of the human element. The point of a book is usually a connection between the reader and the writer; the writer attempts to make the reader feel something and the reader accepts this and internalizes it. However this book was so disconnected, the format made it even worse given that the characters were so stereotypical and lacking in dimension. The bad people were all bad, the clever people were always clever and you do not get to understand the why behind the decisions. There needs to be a balance between characters and plot and here the scale tipped drastically. 
 So we follow 2 pilots of the giant statue/weapon and these characters were absolutely painful to read. The plot of this book is ridiculous, which is fine, this is sci-fi, plots are meant to be ridiculous but it was all plot, plot, plot, the entire time and the human element was not woven throughout the novel which left the reader alienated. I cannot tell you how incredibly let down I felt, the disappointment was palpable because the premise held such promise and I was so excited to read this. I believe this is a debut novel so I can see how Mr. Neuvel will grow, he knows how to do plots, he just needs to learn to bring the reader to his characters. I also think this format does him no favors; this is truly better suited for a big blockbuster script than a piece of literature.

This book is so fucking boring. It took sheer determination to finish it.

Are we alone? A lot of Sci-Fi deals with this main question. Some would make you directly jump into an ongoing human-alien society, others build up the meeting of civilizations. 
 Sleeping Giants is in the second category and it builds up the anticipation really well. You have mysterious robots, cryptic texts, unexplained metallurgy, questionable energy laws and genetics thrown in. It is probably not that well thought out that modern science nerds would go gaga over it but it serves as a good book for generating mass interest in Sci-Fi. I believe there are way too many readers enamored with Vampires, Werewolves, and Zombies; much more then those books really merit. A book such as this can generate the needed interest. 
 One good thing about the book was that even though the scope of such a discovery is huge, the human angle is sufficiently present. Asimov used the human angle very well while in Kevin J. Anderson's (Saga of Seven Suns) books make the individual character rather blurry. Sleeping Giants falls between the two. To start with, the kind of profile provided for each character is interesting but in the second half the book devolves into squabbles and mush. Even the attempts at justification for the events are boring. That's the main reason why I reduced my rating. 
 A note on the format: This is the first book that I have read which is in the form of interviews, although I see that there are other, more popular books, that have used this format. It is surely a very interesting format. Initially, I was put off by what I felt was a broken narrative. You especially see this in Indian Authors such as Amish, Ashwin Sanghi etc. who sometimes have parts of chapters that last 6 lines! However, the case here was not so. After the first few pages itself I was gripped by the book and the narrative style turned out to be quite pleasing.

I feel like this book was mostly setting up for a sequel because I kept waiting for something to happen or something to be explained. The premise of discovering parts of an ancient robot built by aliens intrigued me, but after a while, the interesting science bits decreased and were replaced by character development. That's fine - I love a good character-driven story - but I couldn't help but question why the nameless interviewer/someone with clearly massive amounts of power was interested whether two people were sleeping together? 
 Again, this all might be explained in the next book. The epilogue made me widen my eyes quite a bit. Despite some of my issues with this book, my curiosity will definitely make me pick up its sequel!

** spoiler alert ** 
 this was a quick, zippy book that i raced through, in no small part because calling it a "book" is a bit of an overstatement. at best, this is a teleplay (so i was excited to see there's a full cast audio production of it, even if i didn't love the story). everything is in dialogue, and at times this works beautifully -- but it also leaves the door wide open for egregious telling-not-showing, confusing action scenes, and only ever hearing about events after the fact. it puts distance between the story and the reader, and in a story that is already so heavily science-oriented (i see it compared a lot to the martian, and for good reason), you kind of want to avoid pushing the reader any further back? imo, anyway. it also allowed for very, very limited characterization of the main cast, who struggled to rise beyond vague scifi action flick stereotypes (the hero who Goes Bad, the Action Girl Too Tough For Love, the female scientist who is an apparent genius in multiple unrelated fields but also not old or ugly because ew). 
 the first two thirds of the book were really interesting and entertaining, and it was such a quick read i was ready to overlook its flaws. it felt like it was building up to something really massive and grand-scheme. i was into the science, the evolving mystery, the possible conspiracies, even the stunning decision made by one of the characters about halfway through (although i did think the motivation for it was...thin, at best). but then about two-thirds in, they pretty much...explained everything? and it was deeply hackneyed and dissatisfying in a way that felt almost a disservice to what had been a cool and interesting story. the alien love story in particular was just. so bad. so trite! you have a whole universe -- literally -- at your fingertips, and you choose some bland tristan and isolde nonsense? you could make an argument that maybe the old man was lying or making some inexplicable metaphor, but nothing in the text really supports that. again, when we're just reading transcriptions of dialog, it's difficult to convey dramatic irony. also: alyssa. what? 
 all in all i don't really regret reading this, but i doubt i'll be picking up the sequel. the first 2/3 is so enjoyable that the sheer badness of the last third seems even worse by comparison. also, if i never have to read about a tough lady pilot who's mad about being sad and drinks/fucks/fights the pain away, it will be TOO SOON.

reference_books.title: Don't Let's Go to the Dogs Tonight
reference_books.review_text:
A quick and compelling read with some insights into the experiences of white colonists. However, Fuller's desire to narrate her experiences--rather than reflect on them, or ask hard questions of herself and others--leaves the overall impression that colonialism was a fun, somewhat dangerous adventure instead of a profoundly brutal and oppressive system. 
 Additionally, while Fuller's descriptions of the smells and sights and sounds of her childhood are marvelous, they're undone somewhat by her repeated claim that they are the "smells of Africa" and that's a big part of why she feels at home in Africa and loves Africa so much. Africa is a huge continent made up of over 50 countries, only three of which Fuller actually lived in. Her constant use of "Africa" as a descriptor is problematic, essentialist, and irritating. It could be an insight into the blinkers and assumptions she grew up with as part of the colonial project, or it could be a cheap way to attract U.S. readers (would "A Zambian Childhood" have sold as well as "An African Childhood"?), but either way, it's disappointing.

reference_books.title: The Lacuna
reference_books.review_text:
I liked parts of this novel, written mostly as the journal and letters of Kingsolver's fictionalized main character who holds many jobs, but most interestingly as a cook and confidant for Frida Kahlo in Mexico while Trotsky is staying with them. There are early chapters that are gorgeous and thrilling in their political, sexual and artistic intrigue. I particularly liked a chapter in which the narrator, a teenager at the time, is sent back to the U.S. and falls in love with another student at his all-male boarding school. The political discontent in D.C. at the time (something about veterans camping out on the Mall for their benefits and getting teargassed? I hadn't learned about this and wanted to learn more) makes a surprisingly graceful, exciting and thematically resonant backdrop. 
 However, the book overall, and in particular its back half, felt cumbersome. The epistolary structure felt increasingly clunky as the book continued to hammer away at heavy-handed themes about art and politics and stilted incorporation of not very interesting tropes and slang from the 40's and 50's. An ending that should have been mysterious and ambiguous, was made painfully, wincingly obvious, which is more or less a metaphor for the problems with the book overall.

reference_books.title: Dreams from My Father: A Story of Race and Inheritance
reference_books.review_text:
It's probably safe to say that, had I read this while swept up in the hope (yes i said it), optimism and excitement of his 2008 campaign, I would have loved it. And even now, as glum as I am about national politics, there is still something thrilling and inspiring to me about reading a young voice that is so authentically struggling with and reflecting on identity, race, privilege, and power and knowing that he is now the president. But I also recognize that part of that thrill is deeply personal, because of the ways in which his experiences resonate with my own--the grueling self-reflection that comes with making a boatload of mistakes as a young organizer, the gap between the idealization and reality of relationships with far-away family. 
 I generally thought that the book was too long, and I suspect that without the personal resonance that I felt to his experiences in both Chicago and Kenya, I would have found it a bit of a slog. I had especially mixed feelings about Obama's narrative voice, finding it to be thoughtful but also verbose and overdramatic, self-aware but also self-important. Still, the book is an intimate look at how one person's sense of self and racial identity developed, an interesting topic imbued with even greater gravity when the person in question happens to be our president.
