reference_books.review_text: Ugh! I really wanted to like this, but instead I found it a real slog: a dull religious allegory narrated by my least favorite device, the precocious child narrator.

reference_books.title: When You Reach Me
reference_books.review_text:
Ahh! So good! I really loved the mystery component to this, and will say nothing more about the puzzle that moves the plot forward, because I think part of what I enjoyed so much was how the mystery unfolded and added so many complexities and twists to what I originally thought was your standard coming-of-age-and-learning-things-about-self-and-others young adult novel. 
 I will say, though, that even though the mystery's resolution was what really struck me at the end, I thought the character development and narrative voice felt really rich and true throughout the book, which is part of what made the mystery of it so satisfying and moving. The "learning-things-about-self-and-others" felt particularly well done, with more subtlety and authenticity than that found in many other books for young readers. 
 Highly recommended for those looking for a quick, high-quality read that is both suspenseful and emotionally resonant.

book_a.title: The Underground Railroad
book_a.user_review: I'm probably in the minority in being underwhelmed by this book. I generally find Colson Whitehead's writing plotty, with thin characterization (an exception might be Sag Harbor, still my favorite of his, though I read it a while ago)--which sometimes works very well for highly symbolic subject matter (like Apex Hides the Hurt, for example). But I think that really didn't work for The Underground Railroad. As a reader, I thought all the bells and whistles of the plot distracted from the trauma and horror of the subject matter.

sample_reviews.review_text: Excellent!

The Underground Railroad by Colson Whitehead tells the story of Cora, a slave in a Georgia cotton plantation. Abandoned by her mother, Cora eventually decides to make a run for freedom with a fellow slave, Caesar. They escape to South Carolina by riding on a literal Underground Railroad, a network of tracks and tunnels under the ground, built and operated by former slaves and their sympathizers. Eventually they are hunted down by a ruthless slave catcher. Cora manages to escape and flees from one state to the next in search of freedom. The novel ends on an optimistic note in that it appears as if Cora is well on her way to finding the freedom she has long sought. 
 The novel begins on a strong note. We meet Cora as a young girl trying to survive in a brutal environment. We witness the horrors of slavery, and we see the impact of institutionalized oppression both on the oppressor and the oppressed. The descriptions are vivid and graphic and cause one to recoil in horror. 
 After Cora's escape to South Carolina, however, the novel seems to lose focus. We are introduced to a host of new characters, which is understandable. But we are also given fairly extensive background on each of the characters, even the minor ones--their families, their upbringing, why they are the way they are, etc. etc. All of this tertiary information is problematic, redundant, and detracts from the main narrative. Why give us so much background information on a minor character, especially since such material slows the pace of the narrative and interrupts its progression? 
 None of the main characters are fully developed. They are portrayed in a detached, clinical manner, so we never become emotionally invested in any of them, not even in Cora. We should feel immersed in her experiences and see what she sees, hear what she hears, and feel what she feels. Instead, we observe her from a distance, which prevents us from forging a connection with her. 
 The absence of a cohesive structure in a narrative that jerked from one event to the next with little to no transitions coupled with a lackluster character portrayal made this a somewhat disappointing read. It is certainly not up to the level of previous Pulitzer Prize winners. But it is worth reading if, for no other reason, because of its depiction of the horrors and dehumanizing impact of slavery in its opening sections. 
 Recommended with reservations.

Brutal and beautiful.
I tried to get into this, but just couldn't focus on the story. Gave up and didn't finish. I think the story itself had potential, but I wasn't a fan of the writing style.

I wanted to like this book, and, happily, it was not a long and arduous read, but the characters and plot are made secondary to the moral--not ideal for a novel. The writers of some of the professional reviews sounded as though they were praising who wrote it instead of what he wrote. 
 The book starts out good, as long as he sticks with the plantation and history. But then it seems the author doesn't trust history, bad as it is, to be bad enough; he has to change it to make things worse, make unchanging white-on-black racism the predominant factor in man's inhumanity to man, everywhere and in every age, and to make the hate and greed of individuals the drivers of racism. Paradoxically, that could weaken his effort. 
 I know I'm equating what his characters are saying with what he's saying. 
 I am not complaining about the underground railroad image itself. That isn't a problem--although in that connection the author has characters rhetorically ask at least twice who has built everything in this country, while the railroads of America were not built primarily by black people. Too, we have engineers driving big old steam engines but without firemen to stoke the furnaces. 
 Now, in retrospect, I see we may be primarily concerned chiefly with the process of conducting, in a sort of reverse-River Styx journey with Charon moving from death to life, slavery to freedom--if only we ever could get there in this endlessly repeating saga. 
 At this point I went into a reverie to see if there was some other mythology going on: Orpheus? Eurydice and Persephone mixed? Circles of Hell? But, no, I don't think so. That isn't working for me. After all, it's a woman, and she's trying to get out, not in, maybe with no way out. And without a clear just-so story telling why things are the way they are. 
 The characters are fleshed out but pretty much good guy or bad guy at heart, with someone sometimes going over to the other side, but still good or bad and without much nuance. So I think maybe what we have is a book about slavery times, but written in these times and pertaining to confusions inside the head as well as to our external situation. And so, for that purpose, we get good guy-bad guy: useful in untangling inner confusions, but then so easy to take as we-good, they-bad, and so ultimately to be doing just what they did. 
 Two wrongs don't make a right, as my mother used to say (and now my husband says it to me). But don't they? Don't the people who did it deserve it to be done back to them? In other words, bad guys getting what they deserve (or promulgation of attitudes pointing that way)--the old, old justice: vendetta, Kanun, feud, redemption of the blood, revenge. 
 Ever so slowly, what we call civilization kicked in, over the eons separating deliberate from accidental harm and taking justice further out of the hands of interested parties. It's where that did not happen, or or can be perceived as having not happened, or happened insufficiently, that the old ways threaten to rear up again. 
 The basis for that old-time justice, then, is the condemnation of America for what it has done, is doing, and presumably will always do, racist world without end. As always, those on the receiving end of retribution must deserve it, so that the story must be about their evil. The more retribution sought, the more evil must the perpetrators be portrayed. 
 From that developing angle it appears what's needed is repentance and confession and atonement, that that is what would make allies and bring satisfaction. 
 Until it doesn't. Until they, or some of them, or their descendants repent of their repentance. 
 I am the veteran of a long marriage. And I went through a huge chunk of it convinced that my husband was a male chauvinist pig. He was, of course.* So I wanted him to repent and reform and do right. Meantime, also of course, I was treating him as I didn't want to be treated. We invested money and time in shrinks, but it was our wallets and patience that shrank--followed then by a long stalemate--broken in the long run not by him but by me. I saw the light, and it was I who behaved differently. 
 [*And I'm the one talking about nuance; the devil truly is in the details. Just about any pejorative can be shown to be true, whether that be 'male chauvinist pig,' 'Crooked Hillary,' or any others that we can think of. I'm not saying there's no raw material. We never lack for dirt (and in some cases there's more than in others) since things aren't perfect, but we ourselves also have a hand in shaping what we see and then firing it into seeming permanence in the kiln of our accusations.] 
 Yes, others are sometimes holding you back, and down. Sometimes it's the others in your head, though. Both. You may die, yes, but, more likely (and here I have to be grateful) you may be suppressed. If you have to go, I say take with you as little of your confusion as possible. 
 The kind of society we have depends greatly on its getting inside you and controlling you from inside. Whatever you call that, some of it we call good: conscience, we call it. Fear of God is an--the?--idiom for conscience in both the Hebrew bible and Christian New Testament. There can't be a parent, elder, or policeman around all the time, so we instill self-control--but it comes warts and all. For example, Isabel Wilkerson in The Warmth of Other Suns: The Epic Story of America's Great Migration on black parents in the Jim Crow south having to beat the sassiness out of their children lest it surface at the wrong time and get them killed. 
 Most likely we'd opt for self-control, though--with improvements--since it beats the alternative. 
 Then, there's speaking truth to power. 
 When liberals do it, it may not be power we're addressing, if, as Steve Coll wrote, liberals get weak-kneed in the face of potential violence ("Talk of the Town," New Yorker Magazine, October 1, 2012). 
 Beyond that, there seems to be a power component to morality. Those toward whom we are at pains to behave well seem to be those who have the power to hurt us (or harm us in the eyes of our social group); those who do not wield such power over us, not so much. But I digress...further.... 
 I think we've got to decide what we want. Do we want vindication? Or, do we want change? 
 If we want vindication, just keep on blaming: in this case, let's say our political foes and the government of the US. Look what can happen. If what we wanted was to 'be right,' well, we got that now. Somehow we aimed at what we didn't want instead of what we did. 
 In this martial-arts sort of thinking, we must watch out for strengthening the opponent. 
 But condemnation feels so good, so right! 
 I am thinking about the US, the government, maligned by Left and Right alike. Speaking here as what in America we call a liberal (that's center left, I guess), I say the government is what we have to rely on to 'do something.' 
 And now look. 
 These have been my thoughts, perhaps a sermon (which I consider a step up from a 'diatribe'), provoked yet again, this time by Colson Whitehead's The Underground Railroad.

https://booksnooks.wordpress.com/2016... 
 The beginning was like a typical story of life on a plantation, but then it picked up!

Wow! What a terrific book and a wonderful read. Whitehead creates not only unforgettable characters (especially Cora) but an unforgettable story that makes us all think...and try just a little to understand a lot more about ourselves. Brilliant! I highly recommend it to all.

Pffff... that took me quite some time to finish and I really had to force myself to do it. 
 Cora is a slave on a plantation. When a newly arrived slave, Ceaser, tells her about the Underground Railroad and proposes an escape, she is hesitant at first, but ultimately decides to go with him. 
 The subject is totally interesting, but I can't get past the writing style. It's rather boring and drags a lot. I felt the characters were underdeveloped and I just couldn't get on board with the railroad being depicted as an actual railroad. 
 I wanted to dive fully in the history of slavery while reading this book, I wanted to feel happy, angry, sad, hurt... anything... but I found this book to be cold and devoid of any feeling. It didn't make me feel connected to Cora in any way, shape or form unfortunately. 
 It did give me more insight in slavery, but this book was not for me

I had high expectations for this book and for the most part I believe they were met. I loved the concept of the book, with the Underground railroad being a tangible thing, it was brilliant actually. I also fell into Cora's story, her journey. The words were riveting and the writing was smooth like a good Whiskey. That's how I would describe the feel of this story, like sipping on really nice whisky on the rocks. 
 A lot of people felt more rigorously about the story, in terms of the events that happened to Cora and all the things she encountered on that journey. For some reason I was not jolted by those events, I didn't feel the fear or pressure other felt. I was invested don''t get me wrong, I just didn't get a fear factor. Perhaps I've been desensitized to the runaway as I was working on an audition for a TV with the same subject matter. So I had been researching the underground and Harriet Tubman ad nauseam.

book_b.user_review:
I find in general on the left an overly optimistic point of view of our political moment, and specifically people engaging in some wishful thinking that "deep down" a majority of working class people hold left political views. I don't think this is true, and I appreciated Hochschild taking her subject's disagreements and complaints at face value, and seeking to understand through empathy and curiosity. 
 That said, I sort of wish she would take the same approach to her liberal-left readership...I thought some of her assumptions about those who she believes to share her political views were off-base. Also, a minor complaint, but reading this after Payne's book about the Civil Rights Movement, but I was annoyed by the centrality of part of the Civil Rights Movement that she personally participated in (Freedom Summer) in her analysis of the lingering political effects of the CRM for white voters in the south.

sample_reviews.review_text: Good reading, some new insights but still no sympathy for the lifestyle of tea-party supporters that denies plain facts, fears diversity and is blind for the dire consequences.

This book was readable as heck. It was simply the maddening content it presented that took me so long to finish it. I needed to read this in small doses so I could really process what was being handed to me. In the end, I was left frustrated, not due to the book itself but because I don't see any solutions to bridging the vast ideological gap between conservative and liberal politics. 
 To be clear, Hochschild never claimed she'd discovered any answers. Her research was entirely exploratory and anecdotal in nature, which went a long way in making the content engaging. Over the course of nearly a decade, Hochschild visited various locations in rural Louisiana and got to know the residents (mostly white). She stepped into their lives and let them do most of the talking, only occasionally stepping in to ask a polite counter (which was either brushed off as unimportant or itself countered with a fine example of mental gymnastics to avoid having to address in any genuine sense, imo; The book's Appendix C addresses many of these claims and provides sources as to their veracity). 
 Most of the focus was on capitalism, on economics, environmental regulation, and government services, as well as the role of evangelical religion in political decision-making. Occasionally, immigration, asylum-seekers/refugees, welfare recipients, the disabled, and LGBT people got brought up (usually as a conservative complaint about how these types of people cut the line that straight, white, Christian individuals had been waiting in since time immemorial on the path to the American Dream), but they certainly weren't the book's focus. 
 I found this book enlightening, but was left more than a little frustrated. Because it's great to know that rural Tea Party conservatives have different priorities, but as an autistic LGBT person in an interracial relationship myself, all I keep coming back to is wondering why I should cut the "moral majority" a break over ableism, xenophobia, homophobia, and other so-called liberal issues that they deem unimportant. 
 Hochschild comes to the conclusion that liberals are more socially-focused and public welfare-oriented while conservatives are personally aspirational, looking up at the 1% not with mistrust but with the aim of, somehow, someday becoming one of them (the poor be damned, seems to be the underlying sentiment; if they don't become rich themselves, they're not working hard enough/not religiously devout enough). Once in awhile, there'll be a story in the news about how some evangelical Christian decided to support their transgender child despite being shunned by their religious community, or realized the need for social welfare programs like universal healthcare when their spouse is diagnosed with an illness that otherwise might have bankrupted them or precluded them from even being eligible for health insurance. Great. Awesome. Yet I can't help but feel a bit cynical in thinking that conservatives only realize the need to expand their own boundaries for activism when they are personally affected by such matters (which fits in perfectly with Hochschild's own conclusions in this book, truth be told). 
 So while I appreciated this book and found it enlightening in some respects to delve into the Tea Party conservative mindset, I come away feeling a little dissatisfied, in knowing that the people I've begun to empathize with in this book's pages are still voting against their own self-interests, as much as in realizing that the likelihood a conservative would be willing to pick up a book that explores liberal thinking seems next to nil (speaking as someone who grew up in a conservative, upper-middle-class family that lived in both the rural Midwest and Bible Belt South, I can't even conceive of my conservative family members reading a book about social progressivism). Therein lies another distinction, one that Hochschild doesn't touch upon - if so-called coastal liberal elites are so out of touch with "real America", why is it these individuals who've been devouring books on just that subject since the election while those in the rural Midwest and South seem to be getting a pass on understanding their coastal counterparts? To say the least, it's troubling. 
 At any rate, this book did what I believe it was intended to do. It made me angry, but it also made me think and consider the lives of people outside of my own relatively homogeneous social and political bubble. I'd love to know if any of the individuals portrayed in its pages have read this book and, if they have, what they thought about how they were depicted by a Berkeley academic. I guess that means I vote for a follow-up (perhaps an add-on epilogue in later editions).
Repetitive and boring

Strangers in Their Own Land: Anger and Mourning on the American Right by Arlie Russell Horchschild is a 2016 New Press publication. 
 Recently, there has been a rash of books published that highlight the 'angry white American' movement, that attempts to explain the cultural and class divisions our country is experiencing, which are designed to give us insight into the mindset of those who voted for the republican candidate. 
 I feel like this book, written by someone about as far removed from this culture as one could be, is a telling and insightful look at how the country came to be so divided. The author keeps her mind as open as possible, genuinely likes the subjects she has chosen to spotlight, and works very hard to understand their point of view without bias. 
 It's always difficult to write personal reviews, especially when my online friends come from such diverse backgrounds. I know I risk offending someone along the way, so I apologize in advance if my political views do not match up with yours. 
 I tend to call 'em like I see 'em- so here goes: 
 Axiall - A chemical company located in St. Charles, Louisiana had an enormous explosion in 2013 and again in 2014. A safety inspector for Axiall had the job of trying to reduce the risk of accidents. The young man climbed the towers and squeezed under machines to check pipes and valves and attach small red flags to pipes that needed replacing or valves tightening. Operators didn't like him coming around because each red flag meant extra work, he said. Some waved him away, "No, not today." 
 Then he said, "They would gang up. I'd have to call their boss, and they hated that. So, when they saw me, they'd say, 'Here comes Big Brother." It was a stressful job. 
 On hearing this story, a man hired as a corporate industrial hygienist, tasked with sampling acid mist in the battery-charging area in a Ford battery plant, recounted this: 
 "To set up the air monitors, I had to wear a respirator. The staff asked me to take it off since it might make workers who saw me with it to worry about the ill effect of the air on them. But, they needn't have worried. Some of the guys started to taunt me, the corporate sissy who couldn't tough it out like they did. But when they laughed at me, I could see their teeth were visibly eroded by exposure to sulfuric acid mist." 
 For those living in Louisiana, people make sacrifices, expose themselves to toxic dumping, harmful chemicals, and devastating effects to the environment for various reasons. Some, believe they must learn to cope because of the jobs it provides, some think of it as the sacrifice made for capitalism, and some consider it respect for bravery. No one considers themselves a victim. In fact, they are critical of liberal sounding talk of victimhood. 
 And, so it goes- What the author refers to as the great paradox. 
 If you are looking for a way to understand why the conservative right is so angry, why they voted the way they did, what issues they face, this book will put you in their shoes, and give you an up close and personal view of their concerns, where they form their opinions and ideals, and why they are so important to them. 
 The state has a strong Christian population and their faith, church, and the Bible is the cornerstone of their lives. They don't have a large Hispanic population or Muslim population, but, they get their world view from Fox news, and have a strong contempt for the 'liberal' media. 
 The most important thing for the residents of this state, next to their faith, is jobs. Many are quite aware of the health and environmental risks involved. But, they also hate the EPA and the government poking their nose in. 
 It's no secret that our country is deeply divided. For at least eight years, folks like these felt frustrated by welfare recipients, immigrants, refugees, all getting special opportunities they would love to have come their way. They felt betrayed. They felt like Obama was 'their' president not 'our' president. 
 Now, the tides have shifted, with the feelings reversed. But, before the country can come together, we must take a long look at our history, to be sure mistakes aren't repeated, to understand the situation from another angle, which is why I think this book is so important. For people, like those featured in this book, Trump's win feels like winning the jackpot, while those who oppose the new president, feel like it's been a reversal of fortune. 
 While, liberals feel compassion for those who are fleeing persecution, for the 'slaves' of society, these folks don't share that sympathy, and resent the implication that they should, because their situation is just as poor and downtrodden, and their livelihood is at stake, which stretches their limits of compassion. Often their point of view is quite harsh. 
 Looking at things through their eyes will most assuredly give you some perspective if you happen to walk on the liberal side and are having a hard time understanding why, even knowing the environmental risks, these proud, hardworking, loyal people, still voted for the republican candidate. 
 I'm not a sociologist, just a patriotic American, wishing and hoping, against insurmountable odds that this country can decrease the gap that has only widened after the election. I may be one of the few people who understands both sides of the spectrum. While my personal upbringing was strictly conservative, and those values are deeply ingrained, and I live in a very conservative leaning small town in Texas, my politics tend to lean to the left, and yes, my heart bleeds- (insert 'snowflake' insult here) Sorry, not sorry. But, my heart doesn't just bleed for Syrian refugees, or immigrants, or for women who struggle for equal pay, for the ill effects of oil, coal, and chemicals on our environment and on the health and quality of life of those who will suffer from it, but for those like the people featured in this book. People who are struggling to keep their heads above water, who want to work, need to work, struggle with educational funding, and see their values and way of life slowly disappearing, or even reviled. 
 While, I may not be all that skilled at multitasking, I am capable of feeling compassion for more than one group of people or feel passionate towards more than one 'cause'. That compassion alone separates me from some of the people in this book, who seem to think feelings are overrated and they don't much care for them. 
 However, attempting to understand the whys and the wherefores can at least bring about the possibility of open dialogue, although I think the ability to communicate reasonably is still a long way down the pike, and despite my openness and willingness to understand the plight of those living right here in America who could use a little of that liberal compassion we are so willing to extend to other people, my cynicism, my skepticism, and activism, and realism, doesn't leave much room for hope that things will work out quite the way these folks were hoping and of course the divide is stronger than ever, at least for now, and I think compassion has to work both ways. At the moment, neither side seems to be willing to budge, even a little. A little 'do unto others' might go a long way towards bridging the 'great divide", and Christian values can be interpreted in a variety of ways. Remember, Jesus was very compassionate. So, there is that. 
 But, this book did help me tamp down on some of my frustrations, did give me a different view of what some of my fellow Americans are going through, and provided me with enough information to consider possible solutions other than just lashing out at those who are holding fast and hard to their way of life, while the other half of the country are progressing, adapting, and hoping to move forward with their vision of what America should be like. 
 It's a kind of flip flop that I see taking place now, where the left is feeling as though they are strangers in their own country and they too have come out swinging. 
 I think this is a must read for those still struggling with our current political climate. I pray for our country and hope that at the very least, we can begin speaking to one another again, in calm, reasonable voices, in order to bring about the solutions and compromises that must take place if we ever hope to bridge the gap that is keeping us separated. This is something that bothers me a lot. I worry constantly, and feel uneasy about our future as a country the longer we continue to fight against one another's vision of what America stands for. 
 Overall, I felt the author did a very fine job with this book. She allows the voice of the people to be heard, she works very hard to understand the psychology, and is fair to the subject and the people. She does have to work at it pretty hard, at times, and I did pick up on her frustration at times, a feeling I also had to work to keep under control. Her liberal convictions never wavered, no one convinced her that the future should revert to the past, but she does come away with a better understanding, and with a new -found respect for the people she studied. This book is very thought provoking, no matter which side you come down on politically and is definitely worth looking into and strongly recommend it! 
 4.5 stars

Still no closer to understanding what happened, and have less respect for conservatives now. Probably deserves a higher rating but I'm just disappointed that after all the hype things still don't make sense.

I am a liberal who was not surprised by President Trump's election victory. Sad and angry, yes, but I always knew it was a possibility because I do not live in the "bubble" that the media placed many of us blue-state people in. I am as equally aware of the economic situations in the Midwest and South as I am of the poverty-line populations in cities such as New York and Los Angeles. 
 Dr. Hochschild focuses on the Tea Party supporters around Lake Charles, Louisiana. The oil industry has destroyed the environment, people's health, and ways of life for at least a generation. Yet the residents of these areas continue to support it because they believe oil brings in jobs. Dr. Hochschild provides research to show that that is not actually the case yet people continue to vote for oil and against regulation. One statistic she brings up over and over again is that Louisiana receives 44% of its budget from the federal government yet everyone she talked to wanted less federal government intervention. Governor Jindal gave away money from the education budget as incentives to oil companies but that investment was never returned in any significant way. They bring in foreign workers who don't spend money on the local economy. Much of the the company makes money goes back to a corporate headquarters in another state rather than investments in Louisiana. Tourism is sinking because it's not safe to go into most of the water. No one wants to eat the fish. Yet people persist on believing in oil. 
 I want to tell people that the American Dream we were sold a generation ago, two generations ago, has changed. One of the great things about Americans is that we adapt. However, this segment of people refuse to do so. And with President Trump's revoking of environmental regulations today -- I literally got the news alert as I was typing this review -- we get to regress instead of grow. 
 As I skimmed the other reviews for this book, however, I felt like I was joining a tide of like-minded people, and it's Trump supporters who might actually benefit from reading this book and opening their minds to some facts rather than going along with ideology. (At least read Appendix C, if nothing else. It will only take about fifteen minutes.) 
 This book is clearly well-researched. Dr. Hochschild considers many of the people she interviewed and visited with friends even though they are about as far apart ideologically as can be, because as humans there are more things that bring us together than tear us apart, ultimately.

Layla has decided that for the rest of her life she will focus on her teenage daughter and making up for what she put her through by staying with her abusive husband. As much as she thought she has shielded her, she soon realises that Elle may have been more aware of what was going on than she thought. It does not take long until she comes face to face with Blake the Snake, who is instantly attracted to Layla, a single mum who is obviously fighting to overcome issues from her past, and give her daughter a better life. Blake's protector instincts kick in, and he is adamant that he is the one who will look after Layla and Axelle. 
 The journey of watching both Layla and Blake heal individually and then together is beautiful. Both having been through traumatic times in their lives are afraid to let go and love, but when they do it is beautiful. They compliment each other so well, and it is so lovely to read how Blake and Elle's relationship develops. It does not take Elle long to realise that Blake is the type of man she should look up to and learn from. I was so happy watching Layla coming out of her shell and bonding with Raven and Eve, learning that she is worthwhile and is worthy of love and affection. It is so wonderful watching Layla and Elle's relationship heal and recover. 
 I loved everything about this book, from the prologue to the epilogue. I am so happy that this is another winner for me, and I can not wait to read the 3rd book in the series about Rex. If you like alpha fighters, who are really deep down sweethearts and reading about people who are dealing with genuine real life issues, and resolving them in real life situations they read these books as you will not be disappointed. 
 "Torture. Being so close. Smelling you all over with the taste of your kiss still on my tongue. standing by while mother fuckers check you out. Knowing that they're dreaming about what I know to be better than anything their wildest fantasies could come up with. Fuck, it's killin' me."

I was really looking forward to this book ever since I finished fighting for flight, somewhat so because I wanted to see what was happening with Jonah and raven. Really enjoyed this book, Blake was his typical cocky self but this is what we love about him right ladies?! sexual tension was off the charts. can't wait for book 3!!!

LOVED.THIS.BOOK~LOVE.BLAKE 
 This book was definitely worth the wait! It's Blake and Layla's story and it was excellent. We know Blake and his horn dog habits from Fighting for Flight. I honestly didn't think another character from this series could top Jonah, but I was wrong. I loved Blake!!! He was a jerk to Layla at first but the way he is with her and her daughter is so sweet. I totally didn't see him being that way, but I loved every bit of it. The story kept me interested throughout the entire book, the connection between Blake and Layla was amazing and Mrs. Salsbury has me anxious to read Rex's story. This is series is fantastic and I'd recommend it a thousand times over! I won't forget Blake and his story any time soon... it's definitely one that will stick with me :-)
I love this Series!! I am so excited to start Rex's Book next!!

sample_reviews.review_text:
Do you like turkey sandwiches? I do. In fact I LOVE turkey sandwiches. And while it is true that all turkey sandwiches have the same components (turkey, bread, and optional toppings/sauces) not all turkey sandwiches are the same. I could eat a turkey sandwich just about every day and be happy. Toasted turkey and gruyere on sourdough with cranberry chutney, oven roasted turkey on farm white with lettuce and bacon, thinly sliced deli pepper turkey with Hawiian ham and pepperjack, are all good choices. Do you know what I don't like? MUSTARD! A tiny bit of spicy brown mustard is okay on some things but yellow mustard is without any redeeming qualities (besides as an ingredient used sparingly). Do not ruin a good sandwich with mustard! 
 I know what you're thinking, 'Nobody cares about your dietary preferences Jim.' or even 'No sandwich is complete without mustard.' My point is that there are things that can ruin things we like. 
 I like romances. Crazy Little Thing is a cookie cutter romance. It has all the parts in the right order. The writing is not completely to my taste but is not bad either. The humor is good. The hero is likable with a good backstory and completely believable reason for being there. That's all straight 3 star territory. Some of the humor and the hero are even possible 4 star candidates. So what's the problem? The heroine (our narrator) is PURE MUSTARD. 
 She is bitter, judgmental, and whinier than a middle school goth wannabe. She's just plain old unpleasant. And as far as I can see, she never really recovers throughout the book. 
 Would I read another Bell Harbor book? Probably - after all I like turkey sandwiches. But if this author spreads any more mustard on it she's dead to me.

sample_reviews.review_text: If I had to choose one word to describe this book it would be: disappointing. The Lovely Bones is one of my favorite books. I also appreciated Sebold's memoir, Lucky. My first attempt to read The Almost Moon failed. I put it down in frustration. My second attempt was successful, but only because I kept expecting it to get better. It didn't. Don't waste your time; there are far too many good books out there to waste time on this one.

I always try to finish books I start. I finished this book, but it was excruciating. The first-person narrator is among the most stupid characters ever. Usually, I can find something to like about a character who does a bad thing. Not this one. So if, like me, you feel compelled to finish a book--don't even start The Almost Moon.

Tengo la impresion de que con este hay mucha menos controversia a la hora de puntuar que con el mas conocido "The Lovely Bones"... y, la verdad sea dicha, no me extrana, porque se trata de una novela bastante mala, quiza no tanto por su calidad narrativa como por la trama en si, y, sobre todo, la forma en que esta se desarrolla. 
 Empieza esta historia de la dificil relacion entre una madre y una hija con el asesinato de la primera a manos de la segunda... pero ni siquiera se puede decir que tal circunstancia aporte un toque especialmente interesante al conjunto, y creo que solo eso ya dice mucho del tono de esta novela. Bastante mas introspeccion que accion, mucho dar vueltas en torno al mismo tema y una conclusion bastante poco satisfactoria; ni siquiera puede decirse que los personajes tengan el suficiente carisma o profundidad como para redimir el conjunto. 
 Asi pues, una lectura bastante intrascendente que probablemente no recomendaria a nadie. Mas cerca del 1 1/2 que del 2.
Oh my god. This was one of the most depressing and wierd books I have ever read! Don't bother.

There is a line people do not cross. Helen Knightly, middle-aged divorced mother of two and caretaker of her chronically mentally-ill elderly mother, Clair, crosses it more than once in this unnerving and haunting twenty-four hour narrative. In effort to clean away the acrid scent of her mother soiling herself, Helen wraps Clair in blankets, sickly thinking, "Super Giant Mother Burrito," takes her out on the porch and instead smothers her with a towel. 
 Alice Sebold, author of reader-acclaimed novel, The Lovely Bones, writes another unforgettable book, despite how much one wishes to forget the latest. The story darkly weaves back and forth in time detailing their awful family life. Narcissistic and agoraphobic, Clair behaved cruelly to her husband and only child. Helen's father, mentally and physically exhausted, committed suicide several years earlier, and she is left alone to deal with her aging, demented and difficult mother. A less self-focused narrator might have elicited sympathy and suspended harsh judgment. I eagerly awaited the release of Sebold's latest novel since I enjoyed her first. But she fails to give any reason to like or feel compassion for Helen and offers no clear story's end beyond the crime scene line.

This is by no means an easy read. The opening line is heavy in the most unimaginable of ways and making it past the first chapter is difficult. Yet, Sebold manages to take this impossible, unthinkable act and write a gripping story surrounding it. Do I by any means support what Helen did to her mother? Heck no. Do I understand why she did it? No. 
 What gets me with this book is that Helen was compelled to do something so impossible for me to understand, something so morally wrong, and likely for reasons she can't even understand. Every character in this book is not without issues - Helen's past from the very moment she was born impacted who she became. Those little moments where her mother failed to show her love or her father told her a lie or she had to become an adult when she shouldn't have been shaped her into who she is. She tried to escape it, but couldn't and in the end sought a horrific way out. 
 Alice Sebold isn't afraid to go places in her writing. Look at her other novels. She tackles difficult subjects and you have to be willing to step outside of yourself - your morals, your values, etc. - and go on the journey with her or else you'll never be able to enjoy her work. A good novel, book, literature - whatever fancy word you want to throw on it - should be willing to go places that others aren't and Sebold is.

1.5 STARS 
 "For years Helen Knightly has given her life to others: to her haunted mother, to her enigmatic father, to her husband and now grown children. When she finally crosses a terrible boundary, her life comes rushing in at her in a way she never could have imagined. Unfolding over the next twenty-four hours, this searing, fast-paced novel explores the complex ties between mothers and daughters, wives and lovers, the meaning of devotion, and the line between love and hate." (From Amazon) 
 Maybe I like my mom too much but I could not get into this story at all and only finished it because it was written by Alice Sebold.

I loved The Lovely Bones but this is disturbing. I finished the book even though I was completely uncomfortable with what the character was doing and thinking. I mean... 
 Aside from her killing her own mother her freaking mom here's another one. 
 "This was not the first time I had been face-to-face with my mother's genitalia." 
 oh, those are just two of the many discomforting things I've read. 
 Unfathomable. WOW. 
 Sorry. But this book isn't for me, no, no, no.
This book was sick. Twisted. Disgusting. I felt physically sick after reading it.

Many don't like the plot. The prose is very poetic and I enjoyed it. Sebold took a chance on a dark subject. People don't want to connect emotionally to a murderer; especially an unrepentant daughter. The author went into that deep dark place where most of us (should never) are scared to go. I think it was bold book. At its core it is a tale about mental illness. The daughter, who apparently suffered a psychotic episode, killed her mentally ill mother. Everyone in the novel was mentally ill and the author showed the journey through the complexities of the human brain.

reference_books.title: Heaven is for Real: A Little Boy's Astounding Story of His Trip to Heaven and Back
reference_books.review_text: "Heaven is for Real: A Little Boy's Astounding Story of His Trip to Heaven and Back" - written by Todd Burpo with Lynn Vincent, and published in 2010 by Thomas Nelson. My copy of this book was cataloged in the Dewey Decimal Classification of 133.9013, which is described as "Personal survival, nature of spiritual world and life after death." Our book group had a discussion on how to rate the book, whether purely on how you liked it, or on how well it was written. Anything can be written in a readable style as this was, so my rating reflects my own personal impression. I believe most of the recounted conversations were fabricated or manipulated for the purpose of writing a book. The topic does not interest me but I think it's important to recognize cultures with strong beliefs like this - everyone has their own way of approaching life and death.

reference_books.title: Now You See Me (Lacey Flint, #1)
reference_books.review_text: "Now You See Me" - written by S J Bolton and published in 2011 by St Martin's Press. Bolton's thriller is packed with flashbacks and asides that cause the reader to question both the identity of a serial killer and of our main character, Lacey Flint, who happens upon the first murder victim. [Trigger warning - there is a lot of violence to women described in the book.] Lacey is drawn into the investigation both as a witness and as a member of the police force, but there's a whole lot more going on, as the short chapters reveal piecemeal. From start to finish, this was a headlong rush through some inventive plot turns, and the shocking ending was cause for careful review to put all the pieces together. Lacey's adventures continue in several more books and now that we know her unconventional back story, it will be interesting to see how her character evolves.

reference_books.title: The Girl Who Circumnavigated Fairyland in a Ship of Her Own Making (Fairyland, #1)
reference_books.review_text: "Once upon a time, a girl named September grew very tired indeed of her parents' house, where she washed the same pink-and-yellow teacups and matching gravy boats every day, slept on the same embroidered pillow, and played with the same small and amiable dog." What a great fantasy to begin a new year of reading with! September is gathered up from her kitchen in Omaha, Nebraska, by the Green Wind, astride the Leopard of Little Breezes, and thereupon encounters many wonderful and absurd creatures as she moves her way across Fairyland. The rules are simple as well as nonsensical and September approaches each situation with a sense of adventure and a tender heart. Especially enjoyable were the lush, intensely colorful descriptions of Fairyland. "Squeeze your eyes closed, as tight as you can, and think of all your favorite autumns, crisp and perfect, all bound up together like a stack of cards. That is what it is like, the awful, wonderful brightness of Fairy colors." Author Valente intends this to be a series, with the second book just out this past October, and I look forward to more vibrant writing from her.

Let me start off by saying that I'm not a very religious person in the world, and normally I do not read books that deal with religion and God, but this one, for some reason, caught my attention right from the start and I just couldn't help but read it. I went into this book with very low expectations and a lot of prejudice, but while reading it I changed my mind and added two more stars to it, thus giving it three in total. It wasn't that great, but it wasn't bad either. The thing that really stood out for me was Mack's "conversation" with the Trinity that I found very inspirational, insightful and very much relieving. I can see how these shack conversations could really change one's whole concept of God and the way they percieve God and Jesus! However, I also found the book to be overly didactic in tone in certain scenes and emotionally manipulative, which was rather annoying. So, I wouldn't call this book the best one about God I have ever read, but it sure did rock my little world a bit. Hard to wrap your mind around this one but interesting, thought-provoking and well-written.

book_b.title: The Expats
book_b.user_review: "The Expats" - written by Chris Pavone and published in 2012 by Crown Publishers. This spy novel with a domestic foundation has a lot of nice blurbs on the cover from the likes of John Grisham, Patricia Cornwell and John Connolly but I didn't feel the clever, compelling or accomplished vibes as strongly as they did. Kate's husband Dexter, a computer security expert, has been suddenly transferred to Luxembourg, so she quits her operative job with the CIA (a secret to him) and they pack up the household goods and their two little boys to start new lives in Europe. What follows is a jumble of spy-related goings on, heavily peppered with Kate's household duties, picking up the kids at school and learning how to deal with an unfamiliar language and culture. At one point she wonders, "Maybe her family could be her mission." Secrets between Kate and Dexter threaten to overwhelm their relationship and her confusion and apprehension about them permeate the story. "The fundamental truth was that she didn't want to understand Dexter's world, because she didn't want him to understand hers." While all the parts of a good spy novel were incorporated into this debut novel, the journey to reach the unwinding of the secrets at the end, and the domestic component were a bit tedious and made this a ho-hum read for me.

sample_reviews.review_text: Review to come!

When Kate Moore's husband is transferred to Luxembourg for work, she relishes the opportunity to start over, quit her job and become a full-time mother to their 2 young sons. It turns out that Kate has never told her husband what her real job is and with the move, it seems she won't ever have to. However, old habits die hard and once the family is relocated in Europe, Kate can't stop looking over her shoulder, wondering if her past is catching up with her and wondering if while she was keeping secrets from her husband, he was also keeping secrets from her. 
 I really was looking forward to reading this, hoping for a satisfying, twisty thriller. However, despite the intriguing premise, the story came off as contrived and I never really believed Kate's connection to her husband or vice versa.

I have never read any spy fiction before, so this genre was new to me. To be honest, it caught my attention because of the whole mother/family take and I thought the book worked overall. Some of the reviews on here are critical because it didn't work as spy fiction, but as a book about a mother who has to make some tough decisions, it was interesting enough.

The Expats is the story of Katherine, aka Kate, an ex-CIA agent with two small children whose husband, Dexter, has decided to take a lucrative short-term position in Luxembourg. Dexter's specialty is IT security for the banking industry. So Kate quits the CIA, packs up the family, and the Moores move to Lux where Kate begins a new life as an Expat Stay-at-Home-Mom. While she adjusts to shuttling the kids to/from school, coffee meets with other moms, and the repetitive nature of home life (clean, cook, clean, sleep), her CIA agent radar starts to suspect something weird in a couple (Julia and Bill) who have befriended them. 
 The beginning of The Expats is a fun play on the old working mom vs. SAHM controversy with the intrigue of European living thrown in. But stylistically, the book flips back and forth between present day (random confrontation between Kate and Julia) and the build to how we get to the present day with the Moore's transition to Luxembourg. There are way too many breadcrumbs in this light spy novel to really give it a serious level of intrigue, and if you haven't figured it out by mid-way through the book, well, you're probably better suited for a desk job than field work. So while I found myself enjoying the beginning, the book just didn't stay compelling enough through the finish.

I had stopped reading spy thrillers or any kind of thrillers in my late teens. I find them formulaic and depressing, though I still enjoy over-the-top, psycho-sociopath Bond as written by Ian Fleming and the crazy adventures in Alistair Maclean's novels. The latter I treat with respect; some of his books made me cry crazy buckets (say, Guns of Navarone or HMS Ulysses). 
 When I read the review of this book in The Sunday Star, I was intrigued. A former spy female protagonist in a thriller? Bring it to mama, sugar. 
 Sadly, as a reader who favours characters over plots, I don't find Mr Pavone's characterisation of Kate convincing. I am willing to forgive clunky story telling if I love the characters (I'm looking at you, Laurell K Hamilton). Somehow, I don't think a female former spy would let matters of trust and privacy to stop her from finding things out about her husband when she sniffed something suspicious about his new job. 
 Also, as the story was near totally from her POV, I find that Kate I is ... boring. I get that she has to make a huge transition from being a CIA analyst to being an expatriate hausfrau, but her desperation at the banality of her life is so ... meh. Perhaps she's not a larger-than-life character as I am used to reading in other genres, but seriously, it's hard to want to root for her. Or her husband. Or the antagonist characters. They're all so meh. You expect some unexpected jalapenos somewhere when you read about spies (they have licence to kill!) but this is like consuming a huge bowl of oatmeal pudding. Bland and never ending. 
 The timeline jumps did not help matters. It's a bit disorienting because the flashes are disjointed; what does it have to do with what's currently going on? Perhaps if I re-read the book I can pick up the pattern of the chronological leaps, but I really cannot be bothered to re-read this. 
 However, I will admit that Mr Pavone has a gift for describing scenes that really makes you feel like you're a part of the scenery, even smell the coffee served at the corner boulangerie. For instance: 
 "She can see past the woman to the bright, leafy courtyard at the other end of the dark breeezeway whose walls are filled with mailboxes and electrical junctions and rubbish bins and loose wires and chained-up bicycles. Her own building has a similar passage; there are thousands of them in Paris. All competing for the best-place-to-kill-someone award." 
 It was an interesting foray into the genre, but I don't think I'll be picking up another sample anytime soon.

Consiglio generale: Non compratelo se siete iscritti su Pottermore. Nonostante quello che dice il sommario, c'e poco - o forse nulla - di nuovo rispetto ai contenuti speciali del sito. Nel complesso e stata una delusione. "Storie brevi" per me significa novelle. Leggendo il sommario pensavo di trovare si i contenuti speciali di Pottermore ma anche, appunto, nuovi racconti inediti. I contenuti invece non sono ne piu ne meno che schede dei personaggi o creature magiche. Il genere di biografia che si potrebbe trovare su Wikipedia, anziche delle vere e proprie "short stories". 
 Ho trovato interessanti alcune parti, specialmente quelle sugli Animagus e i Name Seers, che mi sono giunte nuove, ma non entro su Pottermore da una vita, quindi e probabile che siano semplicemente contenuti speciali che non ho mai scoperto. Mi e parso che ci fosse qualcosa di piu sulla vita della McGonagall (niente di nuovo invece su Lupin e la Trelawney) ma non ci metterei la mano sul fuoco, perche non leggo quel particolare extra da molto tempo.

A must read for anyone who is a fan of the Harry Potter stories. It has a lot of spoilers so you definitely want to read this after you read the rest of the books. 
 It gives the backstory and sometimes the conclusions of Minerva McGonagall, Remus Lupin, Sybill Trelawney, and Silvanus Kettleburn (the Care of Magical Creatures teacher before Hagrid). These are in-depth descriptions of their parents meeting, and their childhoods and how they came to be involved in Hogwarts and their relationship with Harry and where they were during the Battle of Hogwarts and finally what they did after the battle (if they survived). Then J.K. Rowling tells a little about how she came up with the character or how she decided what their fate would be. Some of them are very emotional. 
 Again, I am shocked at just how much thought Rowling puts into her characters. She really is an amazing author.

"After all, you don't have to be a sword-wielding Gryffindor to be a hero; sometimes, all it takes is having your heart in the right place." 
 One of three eBooks released comprising exclusive Pottermore content, this volume includes detailed backstory on Hogwarts professors Minerva McGonagall and Remus Lupin - Lupin's history was the most interesting and heartbreaking (though many of the details had been drip fed by Rowling in interviews over the years). There are also smatterings of information about teachers Sybill Trelawney and Silvanus Kettleburn, allowing for an interesting insight into two background characters. 
 Alongside the character profiles are comments made by J.K. Rowling, but these are short and generally vague. Whilst this is a short and absorbing read, it felt as though something was missing with this volume.

reference_books.title: Last Chance Saloon
reference_books.review_text: I've read all of Marian Keyes' novels now, and I have to say that this might be her best yet. Watermelon was great, Lucy Sullivan Is Getting Married a bit disappointing, Rachel's Holiday mildly depressing and frustrating, but Last Chance Saloon had me hooked. I very much enjoyed the cast of characters, each very well sketched out. The book really is a clever look at how easily one can become complacent, how easy it is to settle or simply float through life. The novel was a perfect mix of having something worthwhile to say about life and being immensely readable -- I oftentimes have the feeling that most books make me choose between substance and pleasure. Tara, Katherine, and Fintan will make you laugh and cry with their lives. Most definitely recommended.

reference_books.title: Soulless (Parasol Protectorate, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I finished Soulless late last night and I'm still kind of cheesed off about it this morning. You know a book's got to be pretty bad when you find yourself thinking, "Well, that was absolutely ridiculous" in a trope-heavy genre full of sassy virgins and alpha males, werewolves, vampires, and the obligatory quivering loin or two. I don't mind all the cliches, I can suspend disbelief for a few hours of reading enjoyment. But the problem with Soulless was that the author didn't pick and choose -- she just stuffed 'em all in there. Vampires! Werewolves! Victorian-era historical romance! Steampunk! Jane-Austen-style vapid family! Old-timey speech patterns! Modern speech patterns! Sure, why not?! Let's just throw it all in there and see what happens! And don't even get me started on the ridiculously contrived scenarios the author dreamed up to get the sexy ladytimes going. (And again, this in a genre of ridiculously contrived scenarios.) The deflowering scene was downright insulting. 
 I'm giving the book a charitable two stars because it did have some clever turns of phrasing peppered throughout. But ... ungh.

reference_books.title: The Dress Lodger
reference_books.review_text:
I've recently embarked on a historical novel kick -- a satisfying read with the added bonus of learning a little chunk of history, what could be better? I came across Sheri Holman's novel on the "paperback favorites" table when I was browsing in a local bookstore. It looked intriguing, so I thought that I'd give it a try. The book is about a 19th century cholera epidemic in an English town, and features Gustine, a poor girl with a very ill child who works as a potter's assistant by day and a prostitute by night -- she is provided with a fancy blue dress to attract higher-end clientele (hence the title). Also featured is Henry Chivers, a young doctor who is trying to escape a grisly past. It's really the secondary characters that make the book though -- Eye, the old woman who follows Gustine around to make sure she doesn't abscond with the dress; Pink, the daughter of Gustine's conspiracy-theory crazed landlord who is desperate for a little love; and Mike, the landlord's prize ferret, treasured above all, and much above Pink. 
 The novel is not a cheery one; death lurks around every corner and loathsome characters abound. Even each of the main characters is deeply flawed in some way, and the reader is left without anyone to truly cheer for. Dr. Chivers, especially, is hardly the hero the reader might have initially expected him to be. Holman employs an interesting technique to tidily wrap up the plot, leaving open the possibility that it doesn't get tidily wrapped up. She is a gifted writer; the novel is darkly humorous at times, and very well researched. Also recommended is A Conspiracy of Paper by David Liss.

reference_books.title: You're Never Weird on the Internet
reference_books.review_text:
Really great read, written in a super-engaging conversational tone. I've been a fan of Felicia's work since The Guild (and I am not a gamer), and I've dug the hell out of Dr. Horrible, The Flog, Co-Optitude, and particularly Vaginal Fantasy. I eagerly pre-ordered Never Weird back when it was announced, but approached it with some trepidation. Would it live up to the hype? In a word, yes. Felicia's memoir is funny, endearing, smart, and interesting. Yay! 
 And Felicia, I'm really sorry for screeching, "Oh! HI!" at you that one time I opened my bathroom stall at Dragon*Con and you were standing there.

reference_books.title: Guilty Pleasures (Anita Blake, Vampire Hunter, #1)
reference_books.review_text: For some reason unknown to me, genre fiction seems to be the "naughty" release for the sheltered and devout (see: Stephenie Meyer). I'm sure someone somewhere is writing an overly-earnest scholarly paper on the topic as I type. Anyway. While I am willing to put up with a lot for a fun escapist read (I really enjoyed Karen Marie Moning's Fever series, for example), what I am not willing to put up with is painfully clunky prose coupled with thinly-veiled backwoods proselytizing. That being said, I gave Guilty Pleasures three chapters before I promptly returned the Kindle book to my public library. Alcohol? BAD. Atheists? BAD. (I'm made to understand from other reviews that writing and reading about all manner of sexcapade, however, is a-ok. Awesome.)

book_a.title: Sloppy Firsts (Jessica Darling, #1)
book_a.user_review: Young adult fiction is my secret vice. I admit it! Every now and then there's nothing better than a re-read of a childhood favorite, or, as in the case of Sloppy Firsts, the discovery of something new and wonderful. Quite truthfully, I expected Sloppy Firsts to be nothing more than a pleasant romp. I was surprised to find that though the book was immensely easy to read, it was also thoughtful and substantive. Ms. McCafferty manages to touch on so many of the universal strains and pains of adolescence; it seems like one would be hard pressed to find a woman or girl who can't in some small (or large!) way relate to the misunderstood Jessica Darling. If I had to criticize the book in any way, it would perhaps be that it's _too_ perceptive and well-written. As the novel is written as excerpts from Jessica's diary, it's a bit of a stretch to believe that a high-school sophomore would be quite so eloquent and insightful. That tiny little peeve aside, I highly recommend Sloppy Firsts to anyone who has ever been a teenage girl.

 I started out reading Sloppy Firsts very bored. But then I began paying attention and found in Jessica someone that I recognized. I found it interesting how the author could present Jessica as smart and athletic and yet totally alone. How the people around her were shallow and flighty. There's a lot of teenager drama. Lots. Some parts of the book are downright depressing. Jessica thinks a lot, and worries neurotically. Her observations can be boring, funny, thought-provoking and a little sad. When her relationship develops with Marcus, it feels like the author is trying too hard. Here we've got the intelligent, but quirky, messed up boy who shows the heroine a whole new world, but it's forced. The two go into all these philosophical sharings that Jessica just goes, "Wow" and kind of goes gaga.
Unexpectly good. Expect teenage drama and a very, VERY slow burning romance.

The Backstreet Boys, the WB, Trading Spaces, WWF and Stone Cold Steve Austin, etc. Overall, I just think it was so great. There are too many YA books that focus on chaste and virtuous young girls.  Awww, I love Jessica Darling. I loved this book. Because most of it felt so true. Jessica's world is set in a small high school, and she's in the same grades in the same years that I was. The parents, the friends, the cliques, the teachers, the dramas, the boys, even the music they listen to (hello, Backstreet Boys), just felt like my high school experience. But told from a smarter, funnier girl than I ever was at that age. 
 (**SPOILER**Even when Jessica finds out her big crush is gay, I thought, Omigod, this is me. Except I didn't find out until college. Whoops.) 
 Thank God I actually liked my friends in high school (aww, miss you girls) because Jessica's got it pretty rough. All of her friends are horrible, even/especially Hy. Thank goodness there's a cute boy for her to have odd encounters with throughout the year. Except he has dreadlocks? That's...unexpected. And not any of the boys I had crushes on. Whatever. Once they get too close, though, **SPOILER** what do you think happens? Jessica screws it up. I would have felt like, Wow, this boy's been paying attention to me even before I knew he existed, and so he talked about all of things I like to get closer to me, cool. Instead she sees this as some sort of trick and betrayal. Am I missing something? Well, it's drama that sucked me into the second book right away.

book_b.title: Everything I Never Told You
book_b.user_review: Very well-written, but quite possibly the most depressing book I've ever read, with every character marinating in misery throughout. The book took me ages to finish because it felt heavy and toxic.

sample_reviews.review_text: This book was heavy with missed opportunities and misunderstandings. Imagine being born on the cusp of acceptability: of women achieving career goals and not having to quit pursuits when pregnant, of mixed-race marriages, of being open about sexual preference. All these undercurrents drive this book while the main plot on the surface stirs them into a tempest. It is the late 1950s and Marilyn is a bright, studious young woman at Radcliffe, determined to be a doctor, despite her mother's pressure to be a wife and homemaker. When she meets James Lee, a Chinese-American professor and falls in love, she initially believes he understands her goals, but when she becomes pregnant, they marry and she quickly falls into a traditional role. He is passed over for a professorship at Harvard because of his race, and is able to get a job at a small Ohio college. Soon there are 3 children to look after and Marilyn's hopes for achievement get transferred to her middle daughter, Lydia. All this back story explodes to the surface when Lydia is missing one morning and turns up dead in the town lake. It is an apparent suicide -- Lydia could not handle the burden of all the misplaced hopes of her parents. Her older brother Nath is convinced a neighbor boy, Jack is responsible in some way, but Jack had merely befriended her to feel closer to Nath. The loneliness in the story is palpable because each character feels so utterly "other" but is not able to articulate that to anyone. It's a well-written study of the effects of suppression and isolation, despite the ability to interact with others in the conventional expected, accepted ways.
The story was attracting however I had sensed a slight contempt towards audience's intelligence while reading.

 the characters are so complex and at first you dislike them, but what I found at the heart of my dislike was a sadness of their deep humanity, their abilities to make awful mistakes, to say hurtful things, and I found that what I disliked was how easily I could be in their shoes.

I find it hard to enjoy books where the characters don't grow or learn from their experiences. This book was focused on very selfish people who punished their children for their own issues instead of dealing with them themselves. They completely ignored one child, bullied another, and set unreasonable expectations on the third. It was just sad and unsatisfying. 
 Ng is a good writer, but I can't say I enjoyed the book. I liked the pacing of the story. But for a book driven by character instead of plot, I would have preferred for the characters to show some self-reflection. I find stories where the majority of problems could be solved if people just talked to each other really frustrating. 
 I feel like I have a reading hangover.

I finished this book, and basically... 
 Yeah. 
 This is an excellent book, but it is extremely emotionally taxing. 
 Everything I Never Told You is the story of a family recovering from a tragic loss. It moves back and forth in time, so that you can experience what led up to the tragedy, and fall through the canyons of grief alongside them afterwards. 
 One day, Lydia walked to the lake next to the family house. She unmoored the rowboat from the dock and rowed out into the center. She vanished. 
 "There is nowhere to go but on. Still, part of her longs to go back for one instant--not to change anything, not even to speak to Lydia, not to tell her anything at all. Just to open the door and see her daughter there, asleep, one more time, and know all was well." 
 Something has happened that should never happen. A family lost a child. She was a teenager, on the brink of a brilliant life. Or, maybe not so brilliant. She was exactly who her mother dreamed of being herself as a teenager. Or, maybe not so much. She was her father's popular golden child. Or, she wasn't. She was her brother's keeper, nagger, responsibility. Or, maybe she didn't want to be. Lydia was the middle child of three, All-American mother, Chinese father, suburban middle-class household during an era of changing times in the United States. And this book is as much about the struggle to be yourself and to not be drawn into the roles expected of you as it is about loss and grief. 
 "How had it begun? Like everything: with mothers and fathers. Because of Lydia's mother and father, because of her mother's and father's mothers and fathers." 
 This book is beautifully written. I can't possibly say enough about the incredible, lyrical prose. It is heart-wrenching in places, it is so lovely. The simplest of moments are so eloquently expressed. 
 "Morning sun fills the house, creamy as lemon chiffon, lighting the insides of cupboards and empty closets and clean, bare floors." 
 Beyond that, the characters are amazing, and honest, and raw, and real. Their journey is so personal, yet so universal. The struggles to fit in, to be accepted, to please your parents, to honor your family, to have someone to understand you, to be yourself. Every single person in this book is struggling with the same issues in completely different ways. 
 This book is a gorgeous work of art. It's emotional. It made me cry. It made me very angry. It made me smile. I even laughed a time or two, when I wasn't busy swooning over the amazing writing. It touched me in a way few books have, and will forever be one of my favourites. 
 Oh, Lydia. I wish I could have been your friend.
