reference_books.title: The Windup Girl
reference_books.review_text:
Good Steampunk novel. Set in the future when oil has been depleted. Story of Thailand where Environment and Trade ministries are in conflict with eath other while the royalty is largely a figurehead. 
 Companies manufacture seed for food that produces sterile crops so that nations must continue to purchase from the 'Calories Companies'. 
 Enjoyed this enough that I'll read the author's short story collection. Based on some of the titles it sounds like they'll provide some back-story to the novel.

reference_books.title: All the Birds in the Sky
reference_books.review_text: An interesting story setting, science versus magic with a nice love story wrapped around it all.

reference_books.title: The Shining Girls
reference_books.review_text:
This is a fast and thoroughly enjoyable read. It was slightly different than I expected. Whereas I thought that there was going to be a time-traveling investigator and serial killer chasing around through time, it's really just the serial killer that does so. 
 I'm not disappointed however. Beukes also does a very good job of helping you keep the POV character and the time-period straight through the chapter titles. There's a nice little ouroboros piece to the story that's a good touch for the time-travel geeks but the book is pretty light on the overall mechanics of the time travel. It is something that isn't explained, just presented as fact. 
 One thing I noticed when I read this book is that I was far more affected by the scene where a dog is hurt than I was by the scenes where humans are hurt. Its not a fault of the writing, I think its a comment on the desensitizing impact of today's movies, T.V. and other media. 
 Strongly recommended for anyone that likes a crime book or some light time-travel tales.

reference_books.title: Golden Son (Red Rising, #2)
reference_books.review_text: A good continuation of the series. Looking forward to the final one next week.

reference_books.title: Infomocracy (The Centenal Cycle, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Corrupt elections, fake news, splintered society. It was a thought-provoking read this close to the end of our own Presidential election. Good fun as well.

book_a.title: Radiance
book_a.user_review: This is a very strange, interesting and beautiful book. It's part noir-detective, part golden-age Sci-Fi, presented in very differently-voice pastiches. The main plot is a bit hard to follow through this presentation but I found myself amazed at the different voices that Caherynne Valente manages within a single book.

sample_reviews.review_text: I loved this book! Would recommend to anyone however the reason I've given it 4 stars instead of 5 is because some parts were hard to understand. Other than that this is so far one of my favourite books this year, just below the Red Rising Trilogy. It seems I'm very much into space this year!
Da fuq did I just read?

Huh... 
 This is a difficult book to review. It's a difficult book to read, jumping between genres as quickly as the characters jump between planets and times. I do a lot of my reading in the little waiting spots of life, during commercial breaks or in restaurants. I couldn't really do that with this book as it required all of my attention to keep pace with what was going on and even giving it all my attention didn't guarantee I was going to understand anything. 
 The book is billed as a modern take on sci-fi classics where the whole solar system is habitable and mankind sprawls across it the way we so often do when we find some extra room and consequences be damned. It's also about movies, set in a future where Edison hung on to talking film patents thus never really graduating us from silent films and the style they embodied. There's a found girl lost and a lost boy found. There's murder, drugs, and all that jazz. More than anything, I feel like it's about Story and humans' persistance in writing ourselves in as the stars without fully understanding the plot. 
 At first, I felt the tropes were gimmicky and hard to follow, but as I kept reading, I found myself enjoying it more, trying to put the pieces together. There's a Rashamon element of hearing the same story again and again, not just from a different perspective but through a different lens (see what I did there?). Valente really understands what it's like to be on camera, and she casts her story with characters who are always on camera, even in their most unguarded moments, always posing, always quipping, always trying to make something that is both real and right. 
 I'd recommend the book if you like mysteries, David Lynch films, and golden age sci-fi. Also if you have time on your hands to sit and devote to the story.

I think this book is far better than I was able to appreciate. It's exquisitely written and constructed, and rich in ideas, and needed my full attention. I just wasn't able to give it that, and as bedtime reading for a very tired Woollythinker, it was kind of hard going. If you're ready to dive in and immerse yourself in this beautiful world and lyrical language, though, you should totally do that. I'll come back to it again some day.

Did not like this book at all, although I have to recognize that it was well crafted. Just not to my liking. 
 I found it very difficult to read and the world she created felt too fantastical. Great for fantasy, but not so much for Sci Fi.
I'm not really sure what to say about this one. It just never clicked for me. There a few passages here or there that amused me, but in general it just fell well flat for me.

This book is stunning. Valente has a way with words that you don't see much today. She is wholly original while at the same time reading like a classic. Her books speak on a number of levels and this one especially goes from telling the story of a girl to solving a mystery to dealing with the meaning of life and the universe. It is funny, tragic and thrilling. It takes old school Hollywood to the stars in a way that makes you feel like it's always been there. Then it looks back on our world and says, "Oh, how lonely it must be to only be on one planet and not amongst the stars." Read this book for something different. Read this book even if sci-fi isn't normally your thing because it's not just sci-fi. Read this book if you want a story to do more than entertain. Read this book.

Things I loved about Radiance: 
 1. Valente's prose is always gorgeous. The descriptions of places and creatures and foods are vivid and sumptuous. 
 2. I love stories told through artifacts (in this case, film footage, interviews, scripts and script revisions). 
 3. The whole concept. Every single bit of the fact that she unstitched the last century and a half - all of time and space, really - and replaced it with a science fiction of the fantastic, with space travel and colonies and unknowable creatures: fish that are not fish and horses that are not horses. 
 If the plot never quite fired for me, if I had trouble keeping track of some of the characters, if I fell in love with the language and the ideas but not the story built on that frame, I'm okay with that in this case.

Radiance is a complicated book. It is a science fiction story set in an alternate universe, where mankind populated all planets, moons and others significant in the Solar system, from the early XX century. Paradoxically, movie making is mostly focused on silent movies - not because sound movies have not been invented, but because the Edison family has the patent over it, and charge vast royalties over its right. Most film makes simply gave up trying, and keep it mute. The Moon is the Hollywood of this universe. 
 Percival Unck is a famous director, and Severin Unck is his daughter, raised from birth to be a star and a movie maker as well. But during the making of a documentary across the system, an "event" happened in Venus. Severin died, or disappeared (it is not clear), and several of her crew die. For the rest of his life, Percival would try to write the script telling the story Severin's disappearance, at the same time, trying to cope with it. 
 This description of setting and plot do not grasp what Radiance is, really. Its most significant aspect is the narrative. It is composed of bits and pieces of scripts. Parts of the rewritings Percival did. Some of his homemade footages of Severin as a kid. Some debriefing interviews. Radio shows. Advertising pieces. Bits and pieces, out of chronological order. Someone mentioned it feels like browsing through case files, instead of reading a book. I didn't had the same feeling, but it illustrated the experience well enough. 
 It could have been a very clever book, but I didn't like the end result. Catherynne Valente is very bright, and has a rich writing style, but the end result is too confusing - too "artistic". 
 The first third of the book was dreadful to go through I simply could not understand what was going on. There wasn't enough to grasp the plot or the main characters. Everyone had the same affected manner of speaking - as if I had crashed by mistake on a Hollywood party, and what the guests discussed had no relevance or meaning to me. Gradually, too slowly, things start to make sense, and the reader starts to get slightly interested in finding out what happened to Severin. 
 There are several things that dissatisfied me reading the story. The narrative is confuse. The way the characters talked (at least those working on movie making) bothered me. The actual plot wasn't that interesting. The ending was a bit of Deus Ex Machina. 
 There's depth on this work, though. One can clearly notice that he's not reading the story as it happened, but versions of it - as one of the characters mention: "if it is not on tape, it didn't happen." How a story is told sets how people will remember it. And that is strongly present in this story. 
 I was also very touched by Percival Unck, from the early pages. From his early relationship with his daughter, to trying to cope with the pain of not knowing what happened to her. That was someone I could relate with. The only one, in fact. 
 One reviewer said: "I liked the book, but I felt it was too smart for me." I don't think so. I think too many words were used to transmit a message that wasn't that profound. It was a pain, more than a pleasure, to read its pages. But there are merits on the book, certainly. If you find other reviews, more positive than mine and decide to try it, be my guest. It is an unusual book, no doubt. But I don't think it was worth my time.

I confess I started to read this book and could not understand the writing style or content. Totally not for me and I would never recommend this to anyone. If you like abstract near impossible to understand content... this might be for you.

Really enjoyed this book. Set in Post WWII Stalin era Soviet Union. Obvious comparisons to Gorky Park.

sample_reviews.review_text: Smith does an excellent job portraying a bleak Stalinist Russia in the early 1950's, which is quite reminiscent of Nazi Germany, complete with cattle cars packed with prisoners and the constant fear of denouncement by neighbors or loved ones. The heart of this novel is Leo, a complex and superbly written character. He begins as a successful and highly respected government agent, and by the end he is a desperate fugitive whose only goal is to hunt down a child killer. The transformation of Leo is very compelling as he is forced to adapt to his circumstances. The plot contains so many different facets that contribute to the outcome: Leo's own personal history, his wife's motives, his colleague's jealousy, the dangers of the regime, and the pursuit of a serial killer in a country that denies the existence of crime unless it is against the State. All components are woven together so effectively to create this engaging novel. It is a mystery and thriller, a character study, and a history lesson. Smith was greatly successful in portraying this totalitarian society and how it affected its citizens, and I look forward to reading the sequel and witnessing Leo and Russia evolve.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Quite readable, but just too sad. I have so many other books that I really want to read - didn't feel in the mood to be dragged down into Russian prisons and children's deaths.

It is fitting to find the works of Tom Rob Smith right next to the works of Martin Cruz Smith on library and bookstore shelves. Tom Rob Smith is carrying on in a genre that Martin Cruz Smith practically invented: the detective story featuring a beleaguered, Soviet-era Moscow investigator. Yet I don't think MC Smith's Arkady Renko ever had it as rough as Leo Demidov, the hero of TR Smith's debut thriller, Child 44. 
 It is early 1953, shortly before the death of Joseph Stalin. Demidov is a loyal officer of the MGB (forerunner of the KGB) with unswerving faith in the Soviet system and the strength of his marriage. His faith in both institutions is shaken early on in Child 44, as he catches his superiors in a lie and then discovers his wife, Raisa, has never loved him. 
 Child 44 opens as an espionage novel, with Demidov chasing a suspected spy across a snowy field. We suspect the spy will get away and Demidov will spend the rest of the novel hunting him down. But this sequences turns out to be a feint that foreshadows the betrayals Demidov will face. 
 For reasons relating to this suspected spy, Demidov is demoted, fired from the MGB, exiled from Moscow and forced to join the militia in the rural outpost of Voualsk. There Demidov discovers a child murder similar to one he was instructed to cover up in Moscow, and Child 44 becomes a serial killer story, but one unlike any other I have read. 
 Officially, the Soviet Union of 1953 is a society without crime. Crime is a symptom of the decadent, capitalist West. In the Soviet worker's paradise, everyone has what he wants so there can be no crime. Especially not murder. By suggesting a man is traveling the country murdering children, Demidov is guilty of treason. If he persists in his investigation, he could be sent to the gulags. 
 Smith's plot takes many sharp, unexpected turns into fearful new directions. A reader's expectations, based on years of reading detective novels, are constantly confounded. Demidov becomes obsessed with the case, determined to find the murderer even if it kills him. And the odds of that are high. 
 During his travails, Demidov rebuilds a marriage that had turned to ash. Raisa hated him because he represented the oppression of the state. The more of an outcast Demidov becomes, the more she finally respects him. 
 Child 44 is built upon the paranoia of Soviet life, where betrayals by close friends and spouses are routine. This is a Looking-glass Land as Demidov investigates a series of horrific crimes the state insist never occurred. The story builds toward a climax that may be infuriating, depending on how you receive it. I've gone back and forth. Demidov learns of a connection to his past that is either a jaw-dropping coincidence or, as one character argues, fate. 
 The characterization and humanity that Smith weaves into his tumultuous plot elevates Child 44 above most modern thrillers. I look forward to reading the subsequent books in the series. I just hope the endings aren't quite as bonkers.

I am giving up reading this book. It upsets me too much to read the way people have to mistrust people, report friends and family, and accept untruths as truth. BECAUSE it evoked strong emotion, I gave this book 1 star. Otherwise, it would be no stars. 
 I read to around page 100, or to where Leo was interrogating an innocent vet. I skimmed to about page 140, not wanting to read the cruel details, to when Leo was 'called on' to investigate his wife. Then I jumped back and forth through the book hoping to find some redeeming qualities to the 'story'. It appears that Leo finally accepts what his heart was telling him, that the vet, his wife are innocent and small children are being victimized. 
 My need to know the solution to the mystery about WHO was victimizing children, is not strong enough to allow me to read the horrors that may surface in the rest of the book. So I have stopped reading it.

How do you take a story of Chikatillo and make it somehow the government's fault? 
 Why take the serial crimes happening in 1978-1990s and place these in 1960s? 
 A get all about the artistic licence. And I'm no fan of USSR as well. But I'm no fan of blatant misrepresentation of widely-known facts. 
 You don't really make it seem like people can be forced to make allegations against their neighbours. When there was a slew of denunciations during the Stalin's terror yet, oh wonder!, there were people who did not do any. Imagine that? What, did they live in a different country from the ones who did? The bottomline is that it is always people who make the ultimate choices. 
 I think this will be a DNF. Will give it a try sometime later. Maybe I'll get it better in a more appropriate mood.
Serial killer mystery set in 1950s USSR - a country that thinks murder is obsolete. Claustrophobic... in a good way. Got me more and more engrossed throughout.

I STRUGGLED with this book. I really didn't connect to any of the characters, and although there were promising parts of the plot, it was so slow. The murder mystery that the description highlights didn't even start until page 230. Blurgh. Not a summer winner.

This book had just small passage in it interesting. In about 70-90% of the book I was just interested what will come out of it. For a little while I thought it might after all turn to something interesting. 
 But most of the other stuff I just hated it. The flat description of the Soviet state, The stupidity of the main character, who has been a leading officer in MGB/KGB, but acted as a 17 year old, end up in a position where no "officer" would most likely end up and got out of the situation with enormous luck. Once the common people were fearful to death because KGB and then all of a sudden we're helping this fugitive without any resources. Than this fugitive travels across whole Russia without any support and just by miracle find the killer who happens to be his long lost ".............." (among 100mil people?? Really??). Just ridiculous, nonsense. 
 The writer knows how to write, but the setting is totally wrong and selected most likely for an appeal about something which has a good potential to raise interests for PR stories in news or film rights, but which sounds ludicrous from a person (author) who did not lived through that era.
If you only do 1001 things in your lifetime, don't make reading this book one of them.

Reading Child 44 by Tom Rom Smith is almost like reading Kafka's The Trial. The whole judicial apparatus was alien to me. While I could kind of understand the logic (such as it was) behind it all, I found the process of accusation, arrest, confession, trial, and punishment to be surreal and frightening. When I picked this book up, I knew there was going to be a political element. How can you write a book set in Russia in 1953 and not address the political element? When I picked it up, I was expecting a book predominately about the mystery. But after finishing it, I think this book is really more about the Soviet criminal and judicial system than it was about the mystery... 
 Read the rest of my review at A Bookish Type.

reference_books.title: The Maze Runner (Maze Runner, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
3.5 of 5 stars 
 This book. THIS book. Sigh. It was something else. Where do I begin? 
 I heard a lot of good hype about this book. When I heard that it was being turned into a movie, I knew I had to read it. After a good friend of mine finished it and gave it a 5 star rating I knew it was time to pick it up. 
 I would be lying if I said I wasn't a tad disappointed in it. It was slow to start. I felt frustrated for the longest time to not be fed information to the the story moving. The reader is in the dark, which numerous questions right along with Thomas. There were ups and downs once the ball started rolling. I thought certain parts were awkward. Around half way, maybe a little further in, the story started getting going and moving fast. The ending really threw me for a loop. I did not expect any of it. The epilogue threw me and even bigger curve ball. It left me thinking "Are you for real?? You guys. I hate you." 
 There are currently two more primary books to this series and a few in between books (I don't know what these books are called. help?). I do not think I will go out of my way to read the rest of the series in the too near future but I will want to read them before I see the films.

book_a.title: The Scorch Trials (Maze Runner, #2)
book_a.user_review:
The Scorch Trials is a roller coaster of a book. I felt so many different things while reading it but the major theme running through my head was...man, these guys have just the worst luck ever. I feel like the story was just one thing after another the entire story. At times I felt like I couldn't catch a break just like the characters. I became really annoyed with the story line toward the end of the book. Like Thomas, my trust and loyalties are broken with certain characters. You don't mistreat friends like that, no matter what, even if authority figures tell you you have no choice. You find a way around it. Needless to say I am completely miffed by this turn of events in the story line. I can't trust any of them anymore. At the end, just like the ending to The Maze Runner(book 1 in the series), I was left with an Are you freaking kidding me?! feeling. 
 No matter how annoyed I am at certain events and characters in this book, I have to admit that I was sucked in from page one. It is a definite page-turner. The visuals that I got while reading were exquisite. If I had to compare this series to another series, I would have to say that it has a slight Hunger Games feel to it, though nothing can compete with my love of The Hunger Games series. This book has fighting for one's life, death, and a high-octane need for rebellion. 
 The Scorch Trials may trigger some people to have psychological grief. It contains violence, blood, death, betrayal, hunger, and disease.

sample_reviews.review_text: Wat een boek. Van de ene plot twist naar de andere. Denk je te weten wat er gaande is, gebeurt er weer wat onverwachts
This series is not written well..
It was okay.....

The Maze Runner series is truly among one of the worst series I've ever read (but not THE worst). Still, I want to read the third installment of the series, and I've reserved a copy at the library. What can I say in my defense? Something about Thomas's travails is drawing me on. 
 This is not a stand-alone book, by the way. Read the first one before this book. 
 Would I recommend this book to mature teens? Absolutely. I'm more fascinated the more I read, even while laughing at the unbelievably wretched so-called 'typical' dialogue of teen slang and the manufactured and misplaced 'swearing' of every other word, and at how these teens can waste their time to despise and hate each other so much even though at any moment they could be tormented, tortured, be severely hurt or maimed, go insane or die. They work together most of the time, which is a complete mystery to me. Why do they make plans on how to proceed when they have no respect for each other, besides hating each other to the point of complete lack of sympathy if one of them dies? The author, James Dashner, has not laid down any story background or provided any emotional development between his characters which would lead to their helping each other, except that which occurs between Thomas and a couple of friends. Indeed, they obviously hate each other so much I'm surprised the 'team' aren't murdering each other. 
 However, I am very curious what these mind-game tests are all about. Are they really racing through the Scorch (a supposed area on earth burnt by a solar flare from the Equator to Mexico), or is it an induced vision? Are they really dying, or is it all imaginary scenarios? Is all of earth really contaminated by a disease called 'Flare'? If you've read the first book, 'The Maze Runner' you have these questions in your mind already, so I'm not revealing any spoilers in asking them. 
 The characters are one-dimensional, and the conversational interchanges are excruciatingly awful, but unlike the first book in the series, this one has so much continuous action I didn't mind that very little else was explored. Instead of a maze, which they had to run in the first book, our frenemies have to run a more typical race from the laboratory to a finish line, where the winners will get to live if they are able to survive the burning atmosphere and the infected zombie-like humans roaming about. I felt like I was watching a bunch of scenes from action movies pasted together. It's very eye-catching and interesting to the brain. Who will survive? By the end I STILL knew almost nothing more about why WICKED was torturing and killing these kids. But who cares? I was enjoying this as much as I did the 'Sharknado' movie on the Syfy channel. 
 Parents, sometimes you simply have to let your kids enjoy something which will not enlighten, teach, or introduce anything meaningful. Do not stand in anyone's way if they want to read this modern penny dreadful. The key here is they will WANT to read it.
Not as good as the first, but I enjoyed the extent and the twist of the storyline that comes from this book.

Changed my rating down to 2 stars instead of 3 because the more I think about it, the more annoying I found it. Which is disappointing because i loved The Maze Runner.

So there are 2 girls in this book and they are both attracted to the same person? YEAH OK. Especially since that person is the most boring piece of shit asshole in the world? Why isn't Minho the protagonist? I would enjoy that much more. At least he has a personality.

You're left in this book knowing virtually no more about the situation than the first book. It was a bit frustrating. Hoping some answers will be revealed in the 3rd book.

I will start by saying I did not enjoy Maze Runner. The only reason I read this was in hopes of getting some answers about the maze. I got none. What I did get was the same characters that I have established no connection with interacting with some new characters that are equally not to my liking in a less interesting environment. 
 At the halfway point I was determined to not read book three even if I still had questions. My problem is I am not a fan of quitting in the middle of a story. Unfortunately I have read some pretty bad books because of this and have a feeling this series is going to end up in that category. But at this point I think it would be more irritating to give up than to waste a another few days and figure out what I want to know.

if only 0.5 stars were possible

 Challenges: 
 2017 Goodreads Challenge 
 2017 Reading Quest Challenge - The first book in a series

Before I begin my review I would like to say that this children's story infuriated me :) 
 Violet, Klaus and Sunny become orphans after their parents die in a fire. Their parents' Will instructed that the children must live with a relative preferably in the city. Unfortunately, the only known relative in the vicinity was a Count Olaf and he was an awful despicable man. 
 I told me 9 year old son to read these book, unknowing, the content within. I don't think he is too young for the series, but at the same time, I can't believe how dreadful they are. There is some intense moments and ugly situations happen. As an adult, I was disgusted by Count Olaf's actions and my heart pounded in fear for the children. 
 I'm pretty sure what the end is suggesting, and in the next books, I will at least know what I'm getting myself into. Poor, poor orphans.

So I started reading this series since it is going to be a show on Netflix and wanted to read about it before getting in to the tv series. What a horrible first book everything that could go wrong did go wrong. Though it did make for an interesting read and did keep me wanting to know more, just when I thought it would turn around it even told me to stop reading if I wanted it to be a happy ending. Of course I didn't listen and had to know the true ending. I do want to know more and do plan on continuing on shortly. They are very quick reads so that helps a lot. Perhaps this will make the children stronger for all of it.

As the first in a series, it does what it's supposed to do. I'm not saying it's amazing, but it's worth it to get to the better books. We're introduced to the Baudelaire children (soon to be orphans), their "relative" Count Olaf and the basic plot that the following books would resemble. The world this is set in is bizarre, unique and interesting, This sort of helps lighten the mood when Count Olaf puts a baby in a cage & tries to marry one of the orphans. The only real problem I had with this book was the ending. I mean, a contract is a contract what a ridiculous loophole to make up. But again, this is just introducing us to the ASOUE world, so I kind of forgive it for that. The characters are all so interesting & fun to root for/against that you kind of don't care about the plot. The plots become more convoluted (in a good way) later, so I appreciated this basic rundown of everything.

This book is awful. Thank God it was only 176 pages. It had awful writing, a bad plotline, unrealistic events, and stupid explainers for basic words. 
 If you look at my books you'll see that I don't hate sad endings. I don't hate it when bad things happen to characters I love, I don't angry when everything is full of despair. But only as long as it's realistic despair. The things that happened to these kids are just stupid. They're things that would never happen and it's dumb to write about them. 
 I almost ripped my hair out from Snicket explaining words. I get that this book is aimed at younger kids, so it's fine to explain what a word means; it would be good for young readers. But it explain such basic words it was ridiculous. 
 The writing wasn't exactly bad quality, but it was a style I didn't like. I won't say people shouldn't like it, I'm just saying it wasn't for me. 
 If you liked this book... well, I don't really get it, but kudos to you. Doesn't make sense to me, but other people can have opinions, too. This wasn't a very low-quality book, just not my style. I'll probably read more books in the series just because I hate to start and not finish one, but I probably won't like those, either.
I have seen the movie and now had a chance to read a wonderful book. I love how he creates vocabulary for readers. Going go enjoy the series.

An interesting reversal of typical storytelling, but I found the mini-vocab lessons distracting and annoying. The story felt flat and while I can see its appeal to some audiences, I was unimpressed. Although it was a very quick read, I won't be spending my time on any of the others.

book_a.title: Loving Frank
book_a.user_review: I was interested to read this as I'm heading to Chicago soon and viewing a number of FLW buildings. This book fictionalised the relationship between FLW and Mamah Borthwick. While the book was interesting it didn't paint FLW in the best light. A flawed genius I would say. I did find the book interesting but wouldn't rate it as a brilliant book.

sample_reviews.review_text: I found the book interesting on one level - it provided details about architect Frank Lloyd Wright. The reader gets to see how architects work and deal with the realities of creating and building. But, I was also appalled at how awful Frank and Mameh were as just plain human beings. He was a narcissist of the first order. She cashed in her devoted husband and young children to be with Frank. In other words, a lot of innocent people suffered (greatly - the end of the story is horrific!) because these two entitled jerks had to have their own way!! I'm halfway through Z by Therese Anne Fowler, and I'm seeing some parallels between the two couples. I hate how some so-called 'geniuses' or 'stars' seem to think that the rules of life/society just don't apply to them. I have found that the folks who are truly worthy of attention and praise are ordinary people who live decent, thoughtful lives every day, make appropriate choices, give to others, and treat their fellow man with respect. Of course, that's considered boring, so we end up reading about skanks and scumballs!

This book was a book club book for me last month and stirred up some controversy. One person thought Mamah was justified in leaving her children in her path to self-realization, (I have always thought that self- realization was a more acceptable term for self-absorption). A couple of us understood her reluctance to stay in her marriage, but still thought her decision was wrong--I think morally wrong. One thought Frank genuinely loved Mamah, I felt he never grew beyond the narcissism and denial which enabled him to rationalize leaving a wife and six children to miss their husband and father and to struggle to pay the bills. I felt he was arrogant and selfish. He was horrid to his wife, and not much better to Mamah: I mean, three grand pianos! I think the author tries to be fair but really wants the reader to empathize with Mamah's choices, but I could never reach that point, though the book is admittedly seductively written. What disturbed me most was statements like this one: "At moments she could even imagine that everyone involved--Edwin, Catherine, the children--would someday be happy." (p. 138) And a few days later: "Somehow she would turn this terrible mess into a blessing for the children. She believed it was possible that they could someday feel enlarged by the love all around them. People with children got divorced and remarried; it wasn't the end of the world for them. Martha and John [Mamah's children:] could actually end up better off, with four happy parents." (p. 140) I realize that my reading of the book is colored heavily by my own experience and that of my own children, but those statements seem so deluded and self-serving that I lost all sympathy for her from that point. And as any reader of the book knows, things did not turn out so well for the children.

I had wanted to read this book because I like Frank Lloyd Wright. I did not like this book as much as I thought I would. I believe it has more to do with my inability to comprehend how someone could make the decisions made in this book. I have read it and do not have to read it again.

I enjoyed the book. It was a good read. I was so shocked with the ending that I had to google Mamah Borthwick it to find out if this was in fact true. 
 She gave up her children and used so many people in the process of loving Frank. I wonder, "Was he worth it?"

Mamah is not my cup of tea. Her rousing independence and passion are too frequently tempered with guilt, confusion, and regret. Frank seems like a player. I am glad to have spent some time in Oak Park, but my household cleaves to Louis Sullivan. I consider this a worthwhile book, and Mamah is an interesting figure. Yet the end is grisly, sudden, and unexamined. I'm left cold as the book ends.

Our book club read this book. The story was interesting, but I didn't. like the characters 
 Mamah Cheney came off as selfish and self-centered. Had a great discussion on this book.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Painful. I assume that Nancy Horan, on learning about the tragic story of Mamah Borthwick and Frank Lloyd Wright sought to put together a novel that described this relationship and brought compassion and some level of enlightenment to the situation. However, while the first few chapters of their relationship and building the house in Oak Park are interesting, the remainder is quite banal, until the end, which is tragic. It's tragic but no more emotionally draining than reading the actual story out of the NYT archives, because this novel didn't build any affinity towards either Mamah or FLW. In fact, it served the opposite effect. I'm really confused as to why it's so highly reviewed.
A fascinating, heart-wrenching story full of interesting facts about FLW. LOVED this book!

Loving Frank is a treasure. This book is more than the story of Frank Lloyd Wright and his mistress, Mamah Borthwick, it is the story of a woman, who could be any one of us, trying to make her peace with her life, her surroundings, and her relationships. The text is beautifully written, there is not a word written that does not have a reason for being there. 
 I found both lead characters completely believable and sympathetic. It gives me tremendous hope that a contemporary writer, Horan, can write so generously on the subject of a woman's struggle with the role of motherhood. For those of the reviewers who dare to suggest that Mamah, in her time, would not have felt what Horan portrays her as feeling, I say, "hogwash." Don't think for a minute that the women of every generation have had and continue to have the feelings expressed by Mamah Borthwick. It was the women from her generation, thinking outside their roles as mothers, that got women the vote for goodness sake?! 
 Agree with Mamah's decisions or not, you can clearly understand the reasons she does what she does as well as her torment over the results of her choices. Mamah makes no apologies to society for her choices nor does she ask for any sympathy, she clearly just wants to BE. She's even enlightened enough to know that although she aches for her children, it is best to leave them to their daily life without her. She will have them in her life as they allow and will not place her own needs above theirs. Truly enlightened, if you ask me. 
 Do not this miss the beautifully written, thought-provoking triumph.

sample_reviews.review_text:
There are three 'VanRipper' sisters, Aubrey, Bitty and Meggie. Bitty had just returned home, and home is also known as The Stitchery. Bitty had just left her husband and brought with her her two children, her daughter, Nessa, and her son, Carson. Bitty did NOT want her children knowing about ANY references to 'magic' in their home. Hmmm? Probably because of the talk of the town as these girls grew up. Unfortunately, the girls had been living with and was raised by their Aunt Mariah. She passes away and leaves them the only home they know, along with the home also being known to the public and as the girls source of income, The Stitchery. They all continue to live together, while everything still pretty much stays the same, especially with Aubrey, having given up on love pretty much, as she feels more complete as she knits what she believes are the townspeople's dreams and wishes into their clothing, all the while giving up on having her own life. Is what she does considered magic? 
 Meggie is a restless soul, and is only back so they girls can decide what to do with the house/store Aunt Mariah left them. 
 Not only are these girls trying to decide what to do, but the town also has plans of it's own, too, that affected their home/The Stitchery. 
 The story was a little slow for the most part for me. It was not one that I ended up diving into and couldn't stop reading. There are a few unusual things that happened, and I found many things about this story intriguing, at least! One of the town's names intriguing, Sleepy Hollow! (The Headless Horseman! Oooo!) The VanRipper sisters! More references to magic! 
 What interested me the most about reading this book were the references to the girls sewing/knitting, actually, secrets and perhaps spells that fit whom the article of clothing was meant for. My mother was a woman who was never without a knitting needle in her hand, and she belonged to a knitting prayer shawl group who while they stitched, they prayed for the person for whom they were making the shawl for, and whatever that person needed in life. That really got me thinking about her (I lost her back in 2010) this book, and what the girls did, why they did it, and was this magic after all? 
 This cover sure is beautiful, isn't it! I want to thank Random House/Ballantine Books and NetGalley for giving me the opportunity to read and review this book in exchange for a review. Thank you!

The Stitchery is not just a regular yarn shop: it's also a place where townsfolk can come, and - in exchange for a sacrifice they determine, something they feel is very meaningful to themselves - ask for a spell. Sometimes the spells work, sometimes they don't. Of the three Van Ripper sisters, only Aubrey (the middle sister) still lives in The Stitchery when the book begins. Her older sister Bitty moved out, got married, and now has two children and problems at home. Her youngest sister, Meggie, ran away and has been wandering the world searching for clues about their mother - who may have died, or may just have disappeared. 
 Aubrey is the one who still believes in the magic of knitting, and who is destined to take over The Stitchery when the girls' aunt dies. But complications arise when the sisters discover what their aunt wrote in her will, and it seems like they will never be able to agree on the fate of The Stitchery. 
 There is an easygoing, small-town atmosphere to the book- it really takes you into the town and immerses you in their quiet ways.A romance also crops up in the story, for added interest. I least enjoyed the part of the plot based around the town council meetings. Honestly I cared about the characters, but I wasn't all that invested in the whole land battle. I'd recommend this book to others who love knitting. If you don't care for knitting, you may become slightly bored throughout some parts. 
 Thank you to the publishers who, via NetGalley, provided me with an e-copy for review!

 I have been thinking about my review for this book. I enjoyed to read but nothing really happened to me reading it. I had expected more mystery surrounding the knitting but as the rules limited the way the knitting was supposed to be used that did not happen enough. I received an advance copy of this book via NetGalley from Random House Publishing Group - Ballantine Books. 
 You know the legend of Sleepy Hollow. You've heard the stories about Tarrytown, Ichabod Crane, and the Headless Horseman. But you've probably never heard of the Stitchery - a three hundred year old house in the middle of a rundown development in Tarrytown that is home to the Van Ripper women and a legacy of secrets and magic. For generations, the Van Ripper women have been working spells into items they knit for customers, and they live on the fringes of respectable society. Aubrey Van Ripper has always been content living apart from the townsfolk and quietly working her magic, but she is forced out of her comfort zone when her aunt Mariah, guardian of the Stitchery and Van Ripper matriarch, dies unexpectedly. Suddenly, Aubrey has to contend with the return of her estranged sisters, the stirrings of a romance with her long-time crush Vic, and the complexities of becoming the Stitchery's new guardian. Perhaps Aubrey's most pressing problem, however, is the uncertain fate of the Stitchery itself. Tarrytown's town council wants to raze the Stitchery and all the other buildings in its neighborhood to build a new shopping mall. Aubrey has to figure out a way to unite her sisters and the other residents to save the neighborhood. She has always had faith in the ability of the Stitchery to make extraordinary things happen, but magic requires a sacrifice, and nobody knows that better than Aubrey. 
 Lisa Van Allen's writing can be beautiful. Her descriptions tend to have a dreamy quality to them, like when Meggie Van Ripper says Spanish moss looks "the way music might look if it were a tangible thing and could get caught in the branches of trees." All the chapter titles for the book are knitting instructions: "Drop a Stitch," "Check Gauge," etc. The conclusion of the book felt a bit rushed to me, and I do wish that more time could have been devoted to the backstories for Bitty and Meggie Van Ripper. But I thought this was a good debut novel, and I would read another by Lisa Van Allen.

book_a.title: Along for the Ride
book_a.user_review:
As always, Sarah Dessen is capable of drawing a smile on my face every time I finish one of her books. As a reader I always grow up with Dessen's characters emotionally. 
 Auden, the main character, can't sleep at night. She spends her time reading in a cafe at night. She's not really girly, if I have to describe her, she is more of a tomboy. I loved how Auden is always engrossed in one of her books; zoning out from the world's problems. Auden is also different and complicated character. She doesn't know that of course, but as a reader you notice that right away. I liked how Auden was not flawless ...just like everybody else. She's not perfect. 
 Eli, the main male character, was different from any other Dessen's characters. It was so easy to picture him because Auden couldn't stop from describing him( thinking of him). 
 The pacing of the book was normal. Not too face or too slow. Auden was fun to follow anyways. 
 Overall, this book had taught me that my love for Dessen's work should increase every time I read her books. Along for the ride was a fun, edgy, summery, sad book that will make you bite your lower lip for being so proud that you had joined Auden's adventure from the first page.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Even more than John Green, Sarah Dessen repeats the same plot elements over and over again: 
 1. ONE SUMMER, 
 2. AN OLDER TEENAGE GIRL WHO IS REPRESSED IN SOME WAY -- family secrets, personal secrets, others' expectations, her own cynicism or need for control 
 3. MEETS A WACKY GROUP OF PEOPLE -- long-distant family, a rock band, coworkers, a new group of friends 
 4. INCLUDING ONE UNUSUAL BOY -- usually artistic in some way 
 5. SHE DOES SOMETHING UNCHARACTERISTIC OF HER THAT STARTS OR DEEPENS HER RELATIONSHIP WITH THEM -- like confess a secret, or kiss the boy, or take on a job -- something that exposes her for a moment 
 6. AND THINGS GO ALONG SWIMMINGLY FOR A WHILE as she gets to know the boy and has her original assumptions about the people challenged and develops new skills through her association with them 
 7. But then, about 1/3 to 1/4 of the way from the end, SOMETHING HAPPENS TO SCREW THINGS UP, usually causing the girl's retreating for some reason into her original repressions/assumptions 
 8. A CONFRONTATION INVOLVING/REGARDING THE CAUSE OF THE GIRL'S REPRESSION OCCURS. 
 9. GIRL REUNITES WITH BOY; HAPPINESS INTO FORESEEABLE FUTURE. 
 There is no doubt Ms. Dessen works and reworks this material very, very well -- she has wonderful, fully developed image systems (in this one, the idea of what being a girl means, and riding a bike); the prose flows gorgeously; her supporting characters are consistently marvelous; the dialogue is terrific and realistic, particularly when it's teenagers sitting around b.s.'ing; every i is dotted and t crossed writingwise. I love the way she weaves all her characters into one large world. And I adored this plot the first time I read it, in THIS LULLABY, and also greatly enjoyed THE TRUTH ABOUT FOREVER and JUST LISTEN. 
 (Also, she creates great store names -- someone should hire her as a brander.) 
 But by this one, I was feeling a bit of diminishing returns in the familiarity of everything, chiefly in the fact that all her narrators sound the same, the same hiddenness, the same neatness. I'd love to see her do a book from the point of view of one of the supporting characters, or the boy . . . someone a little more scattered, more unpredictable and passionate, where the voice and the story wouldn't tie up in a neat bow. I do not know that this wish is fair to Ms. Dessen; when you know your material, you should own it and work it, and she's doing that, and I'm delighted that it's paying off for her. (Such a pleasure to see a GOOD writer of teenage romances on the Times bestseller list!) But all the supporting characters here felt more interesting than Auden to me, and the few changes she rung here just too familiar; and I'd love for Ms. Dessen to break some new ground in both structure and protagonist.

It's exactly what the author said- "It's not only a story, but an experience as well." 
 Along for the Ride is quite a long read. I started reading it August 29 (6 days ago) and finished it just now. 
 *** 
 'I told you', I said, 'I was a social failure.' 
 He took another turn, tossing a couple more papers as we cruised down a dark street. 'You didn't try to be homecoming queen and lose, though.' 
 'Well', I said, 'I never wanted to be homecoming queen. Or any of that stuff.' 
 'Then you didn't fail. You just opted out. There's a difference.' 
 *** 
 *** 
 'It all counts,' Adam said again. 'And the bottom line is, what defines you isn't how many times you crash, but the number of times you get back on the bike. As long as it's one more, you're all good.' 
 *** 
 *** 
 'So you believe in second chances now,' he said, clarifying. 
 'I believe,' I said, 'in however many you might need to get it right.' 
 *** 
 On a personal note, I loved that Auden has formed a special bond with her stepsister. I cried over the end part where she describes her affection for Isby. It's something I wish that I have (the bond) with my own stepsisters. But as the novel says, as long as we live, there's still an infinite number of chances that we can take. 
 Also, I'm now a believer of reading books by fate. Books like these are meant to touch people's hearts (mine included).
Quick and light- a weekend stress relief book. Main character's parents are a little flat (both total jerks) and the plot isn't super complex.

Auden West has missed out on much of her childhood, including riding a bike. She is the younger daughter of her divorced parents, and has always felt pressured to be an adult. Her older brother Hollis is the irresponsible one, but Auden has always been studious and dependable, which has left her to miss out on much of growing up. Since her parent's divorce she has been unable to sleep at night, which leaves her wandering to all night diners and shopping centers alone, until she goes to stay with her father, his new wife Heidi and their newborn daughter Thisbe, in the beach town of Colby. There she meets another insomniac loner, Eli, who encourages her on her quest to reclaim her childhood. 
 Dessen has created another realistic and interesting heroine in Auden. At first she is difficult to like because she is so distant, but as the novel progresses we see more and more we like about Auden. As always Dessen has great supporting characters and depicts realistic teen issues. 
 I definitely recommend this book to fans of Sarah Dessen, she has written another hit! 
 Cautions for sensitive readers: There are some mentions of sex, but nothing is described in the book. There is no violence, and only mild language.

I found this book to be bland and pointless. The only reason why I continued with this book was because I was listening to it on an audio book while doing other tasks. The characters were awful unless you like bland, annoying, or just uninteresting characters. The only characters that I kinda liked were Maggie and, for the most part, Heidi. I found myself not liking the main girl or boy and their "romance," if you can call it that, was not cute or moving and had no impact. It was supposed to be Eli that would teach her how to ride a bike and I kept on anticipating that moment...which never came. Maggie ended up teaching her. The dad and mom were complete jerks. The mom and dad redeemed themselves at the end but I was still incredibly upset and annoyed by the dad. What kind of father acts like that?!? He was a selfish jerk! The book also skipped over details or events and then would eventually rewind and explain what the heck happened which was really annoying. The one thing that was good about this book was the writing. The writing was good. But story line, plot, characters and development sucked massively. This book was a waste of my time and would not recommend it to anyone that I like.

I've been wondering if my opionion of this title suffers from having read it around the same time I read Catching Fire and When You Reach Me. But I think not. 
 Pleasant, formulaic, and forgettable. Dessen is skilled at what she does, but it doesn't linger.

I think Auden and the other teens are presented a bit too maturely. For example instead of hating Auden for unwittingly hooking up with her boyfriend like most teen girls wood, Maggie realizes Auden probably did her a favor and the two become good friends. Also, most of the boys seem to have lived on their own for years yet they just graduated high school. How many teen do you know move out of the house early in their high school years? 
 If you can look past this short-coming, which I could, this is a fascinating journey of self discovery. Auden saves Eli from the life halting depression that has gripped him since Adam's death while Eli teaches Auden, the child born at 30, how to be a kid. Two insomniacs on a quest to have a life time of childhood experiences in one short summer break. Throw in an uptight mother, a not quite as flaky as she first appeared second wife for dad and a very colic-y newborn baby girl and Auden has the summer experience of a life time, including a second chance at prom, just in time to head off to college. Join her on this mostly realistic, gently paced journey; you won't regret it.

Like many of Dessen's novels the story is much more character focused than plot focused. Similarly to Macy in The Truth about Forever, Auden faces resistance from her mother when she begins to loosen up and change. Unlike Macy's mother, Auden's mom does not try force her daughter back except for a few verbal remarks. While this may be due to the difference in the characters ages and proximity, it makes Auden's regression more high stakes, as it is internally motivated.

I don't even know why I bother with Sarah Dessen books. It is all the same thing. Girl with a problem, absent parents, overbearing/controlling mother, a boy who is also troubled and understands her pain and finally a rushed resolution to whatever the conflict is. This one was no different. I think I am done with her books. I don't think I will be reading any more.
I liked this book, it was just a little too slow paced for me.

book_b.title: The Vampire Stalker
book_b.user_review:
A different take into the vampire world. 
 Amy is obsessed with a vampire series. Her favorite character becomes reality. Now the plot of the book is doubled. All the time I am left wondering what will happen in the main story (Amy's story) and the vampire's story (Alexander Banks). And I did like that. However, at the same time, I felt the pacing was slow. I felt like there wasn't much action going on but there was. I mean, there was enough action but I still felt it slow. 
 The concept of the story was so original and new to me. And of course it's a dream come to true to many of us. But, I didn't like Alexander Banks. He is not one of the characters who I might love. He just didn't get made to the list of my favorite character. Maybe because of how he spoke. I don't know really. 
 I liked Amy, though. We had a lot in common. And if you are a bookish, you will like Amy too. She stands in line for books and author signings. She writes fan fiction too. I mean, WOW.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Review from www.bookflame.blogspot.com 
 The Vampire stalker had potential...a lot of potential but it just didn't quite hit it. 
 There have been plenty of times I've wished one of the fictional characters I've read about actually were real. And thanks to a very creative theory called literary physics, Alexander Banks is able to cross over into the dimension in which Amy lives in. Seriously literary physics is a genius of an idea. I loved it, especially since I was curious about how Van Diepen was going to bring Alexander into Amy's world. 
 Now as far as the characters are concerned I was able to relate to Amy's bookworm personality, but that was about it. As far as her feelings for Alexander, her anger towards her dad, and her annoyance towards her sister, it just all fell flat. I couldn't feel any of her emotions. When it comes down to it all the characters in the novel could have been more fleshed out. The relationship between Alexander and Amy also happened way to fast for my likes. Maybe if the novel wasn't so short their relationship could have developed in a more deeper and meaningful level. 
 Then their was Vigo the antagonist. He just wasn't something to be fearful of, not to the extent Amy and Alexander made him out to be in the novel. Maybe it's just that I've read way to many novels with far worse villains than Vigo, the ones that actually get under my skin and make me worry about the protagonist. 
 I also have to admit I wanted to know more about the story within the story. Alexander Banks Otherworld Chicago sounded so much more intriguing and I hope Van Diepen decides to write about that world someday soon. 
 Overall don't let the cover or the name fool you. Vampire Stalker was in the end a fun, quick, and very light read. But it had the potential to be so much more.

This is the second books with vampires I read this year and it's definitely not the best, but it was cute. I loved the idea of a fictional character coming in our world and fighting off vampires from his dimension while trying to stay under the radar. 
 FULL REVIEW COMING SOON!

So I was at my local indie bookstore talking with two of the booksellers, when one of them stopped and said, "Oh, I have a book you have to read. You'll appreciate it." She then picked up The Vampire Stalker and said, "Ignore the title, and the cover," and then explained the book to me. 
 It was a quick fun read, and is good for anyone who likes fanfiction or has ever been too into a fictional character. 
 Amy and her friends are excited to get their hands on the next book in the popular Otherworld Vampire trilogy. While her two best friends are in love with the book's James character, Amy has always loved Alexander, the dark brooding vampire hunter, the best. Imagine her surprise when after a school dance she is attacked by a vampire, and the real Alexander saves her. 
 It turns out that the Otherworld books are the product of what is called 'literary physics', which is the idea that there are multiple different demensions, and that some books are the product of authors who can simply see into other demensions. 
 Now Amy and Alexander have to team up to save Chicago from one of the Otherworld vampires that is terrorizing the city.

This book was a short and easy read, but had right to the point detail which I liked. I really enjoyed it. I enjoyed the buildup from Alexander and Amy. I enjoyed the idea of the author bringing a book to life inside a book. Hmm, if only I could find a portal to some of the books I've read, lol. It was fast paced and nothing dragged. I enjoyed the characters and the plot. I look forward to reading more from this author.

I REALLY wanted to love this book! I was so excited to read it, but it was disappointing. :( It started out so slow that I had to push myself through most of it. Even then I ended up skimming through some chapters just to finish the book. I wouldnt purchase this book.

So when I read the description I got really excited.Amy the main Character is a total book lover and is in love with the smart and sexy Alexander Banks.the only problem? Alex doesn't exist, he is a Character in the book she and her friends are reading. Soon Amy finds herself mix up in a war between Alex and his worst enemy Vigo,and is willing to help Alex stop him. 
 I liked this book and I didn't,it had a really good story line but not a whole lot of action or romance,I was a little disappointed.Also there was to much unnecessary detailing.The book kept you guessing the whole time thinking that something really great was going to happen but in the end Nothing did.
Quick, fun read about a girl who meets her favorite character from a popular vampire novel.

You know the kinds of book series that you are thinking about constantly? The ones that you would not mind at all waiting in a line forever to be the first to get the new installment or to get your book signed? Series like The Twilight Saga, Harry Potter, The Mortal Instruments, The Hunger Games (which I still have yet to read...). Now imagine Edward Cullen (because Jacob is a sorry excuse for a point on a love triangle), Harry Potter, Jace Wayland, or your favorite Hunger Games character appeared in the real world. The Vampire Stalker is the story of what happens. 
 Amy is utterly obsessed with the Otherworld trilogy and wouldn't mind marrying it's tortured protagonist, the vampire hunter Alexander Banks. When Amy comes face to face with Alexander, her whole world changes. Not only is the extremely good-looking Alexander Banks talking to her, but she also has to come to terms with either she's crazy, Alexander is a fake, or there is some weird science going into novel writing. Oh, and Alexander's existence also means that the villain, evil vampire Vigo is also in town. And that is bad. Really bad. 
 I really enjoyed this book. With the influx of fandoms surrounding book series, The Vampire Stalker is being released at prime time. So many people can relate to Amy, and it is actually kind of funny to see your own obsession from the outside, see how ridiculous you seem (but still wouldn't change a thing). 
 Another thing that I really appreciated was the science behind Alexander's existence in modern day Chicago. It isn't just explained as "magic", it is explained in a way that seems somewhat possible. No, I'm not expecting Edward to appear down the block any time soon, but Allison Van Diepen makes it seem less impossible. 
 This book is pretty straight forward, but I would recommend it. it is a really fun, quick read that any book obsessed person would enjoy. It is your secret dream come true - until your realize that is just might not be what you thought it was. reference_books.title: Lost Memory of Skin
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 If you want a book that you can get lost in the prose (in a good way) and challenge your perceptions of people outside of your everday reality, you might like Lost Memory of Skin. I think this book suffers from the same issues Mr. Banks has in his other works, namely fuzzy plot and horrible endings. 
 I'd say about 3/4ths of the book was engaging and I couldn't put it down, but then the plot took a turn that didn't make a lot of sense, wasn't fully developed, and never came to anything even closely resembling a conclusion. I understand that in life there are rarely satisfying and complete endings, but sometimes I feel a reader is owed that. The text states several times something to the effect of real life not being like a novel in that things can't be wrapped up nicely. I was not a fan of such repeated meta comments. 
 I felt like this book would've been much better had it been written from the main character's point of view. The third person voice that Mr. Banks chose was often intrusive, offering opinions that came from nowhere. I'm not going to assume that these statements are Mr. Banks' personal views, but I feel like they should be attributed to someone, otherwise what are we supposed to make of them? What is this outside voice? Why should we listen to it? 
 In the end, the book is well written in the sense that the imagery is vivid and the dialogue is believable. But overall the plot was underwhelming when the premise seemed ripe with possibilities.

reference_books.title: Less Than Zero
reference_books.review_text: Sorry, but I hated this book the entire way through. I've always been fascinated by the 80s but this book was a total dissapointment. The main character (who narrates the novel) is unappealing to say the least. I could not identify with any of the characters as none of them had any depth. Nothing really happened in the book. There was no progression or tension. We get it, teenagers do drugs and have sex. This story could've been a paragraph long. Really can't recommend it at all.

reference_books.title: The Bone Garden
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I enjoyed this book because the characters were strong, but it really didn't meet any of my expectations for a thriller- and especially for a Tess Gerritsen thriller. If her name wasn't on the cover I wouldn't have a clue that this is the same author of the Rizzoli & Isles series (which I've read all of). 
 What captivated me was how effortlessly Ms. Gerritsen transports the reader back in time to 1830. I live in Boston so I got a real kick out of the descriptions of streets and neighborhoods that I'm familiar with, and what they were like in the past. 
 This book is heavy into the medical side of things. Many human dissections are discussed in great detail and I would warn you NOT to eat while you are reading this! I consider myself to have a strong stomach and I was forced to dry heave a few times. The descriptions are not grotesque or gratuitious persay, but I feel like the average person would be adversely affected by the language. 
 If you like stories set in the past and you also enjoy a little murder mystery, you will probably like this book. I really felt that the murder mystery was a subplot and I would've liked it if the suspense around the killer's identity was built up more. I found myself distracted by the horrors of everyday living in the 1830s and didn't care much about the "West End Reaper". 
 I also felt like the side story of the woman in "present day" was forced and unnecessary. The frame story technique didn't add anything to the overall story and things should've just stayed in the past. I found myself skimming the short "present day" chapters so I could get back to the real story. The "present day" woman was too unbelievable in her sensitivity and I didn't appreciate the cheap love story ending and implied psychic connection between her and the historical story's heroine. 
 So not the best thriller, not the best Tess Gerritsen book by a long shot, but worth a read if you enjoy some historical fiction with class warfare thrown in.

reference_books.title: Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas
reference_books.review_text: This book made me want to do drugs. I'm not sure that was the author's intention but I have to give Mr. Thompson credit for making this straight edge girl question her morals. It's not that drugs were glamorized in the text, far from it, but the strong first person point of view made me want to take the same risks as Duke. I found myself relating to him and the attorney and this both terrified and excited me. I was able to experience a world completely foreign to me in an era before my birth. For this reason alone I will recommend this book to anyone who asks my opinion. I was transported by both the subject matter and the intense writing style and that's more than enough to get my stamp of approval.

book_a.title: Haunted
book_a.user_review: Yes, the book is disgusting and graphic- but that's what you get with Chuck Palahniuk. If you force yourself to get over some of the shock value, you will find that this is really a huge satire of our materialistic society. This isn't a happy book that you can lose yourself in. You have to work hard to navigate it.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I'm not a squeamish reader. I actively seek out books that get labelled as "disgusting" and "horrific". And I have a great deal of respect for Chuck Palahniuk. 
 But. 
 But. 
 But I did not enjoy "Haunted" in the least. I lost count of how many readers recommended this title to me. I actually think that's why it took me so long to get around to reading it--I had very high expectations. 
 The framing structure of the work is clever. And the words crackle. 
 But. 
 But. 
 But I don't think the stories are very good. There. I typed it. 
 The one that starts the book off is infamous. I found it plain silly. It didn't shock me because I didn't believe any of it. I'm sure the author can reference real pool incidents where creative masturbators severally damaged their insides. But that just means it happened. It doesn't make it believable or interesting. 
 The stories that followed didn't do much better. Overall the title reads like a literary "Saw" but the individual bits felt like leftovers from one of Palahniuk's good books like "Fight Club" or "Snuff" or "Survivor". 
 Carac

DNF. The premise is interesting. But the several first chapters is just... no. 
 Maybe things will escalate. Maybe it will be a great ride. But I just don't have the patience, so... dropped it.

This book was a huge waste of my life. 
 Through all the tryhardery and gross out tactics employed by Palahniuk, I was painfully bored the entire time. Haunted seemed less a creative outlet than a meandering collection of incoherent musings and reflections on a number of topics buried within the husks of stories. 
 Yes there was indeed cleverness throughout and several of the short stories were quite good. Overall, though, I am disappointed. I don't know that I expected Haunted to be a classic but the bar was certainly set higher than what was achieved.

Not one of Chuck's best books. It really started to drag in the middle but I powered through it to a somehwat interesting ending. I would recommend reading it only if you really are a fan and have nothing else to read.

I just couldn't do it. I've liked the other books I've read by him so I tried. I tried very hard. In his other books the gross stuff was sprinkled in and you could get past it because the stories were good. This book seems to be all about the gore and it was just too much. I could only read a few chapters before I had to give up.
Messed up, cryptic, cynical, worthwhile. Not as good as Fight Club.

After reading the blurb I thought this sounded like it could be an interesting novel, and I'd wanted to try something by Palahniuk for a while. However, I soon got very tired of his shock tactics and the constant attempts to stimulate my gag reflex rather than just my mind. I dropped it about a third of the way through, and won't ever bother trying to finish. 
 Read more reviews on my blog Violin in a Void

Well, one thing you can say is that this book will definitely stay with you. I was very excited to read this at first and sped through the beginning of the book. Loved the gross out factor of some of the early stories. But by the end, as it got to be more and more reality show absurdity, I was turned off. Was actually glad to be done with it when I finished the book.

Picked up this book because it was suggested as something similar to House of Leaves by Mark Z. Danielewski. It is not like that at all. While I can appreciate the cynical outlook on Society Today, I guess I just can't appreciate gratuitous grossness. House of Leaves made me think; Haunted just made me turn my nose.

Actual rate: 3,65. 
 Well, to be honest I'm sort of disappointed by the ending because I expected something more spectacular. But anyhow come to think of it again, maybe it is the most coherent ending for a very messed up situation. What else could you expect from people who already lost their ratios and consciences? 
 Anyway, in spite of its ending I still like this book so much. The gross and sad--almost pathetic--parts are very entertaining, and so are the insane mental conflicts happened between the characters. Palahniuk also put some philosophical(?) wisdoms through the tragedies, i.e, "don't we only know the present reality that we know?", or "This is just what human beings do--turn objects into people, people into objects." 
 Would I recommend this book? Yes and no. Just like another work of Palahniuk's this one is not everyone's cup of tea, but everyone who loves dark humour/satire will simply love this.

 "We kiss a lot. And Gabriel takes me to one of the bedrooms and we kiss more, undress each other and do stuff, nice stuff, making-love stuff. And it's good. Very good. Very sweaty. And then we sleep together. Naked, sweaty-type sleeping. We wake in the night and start kissing again and more making love. Then he kisses my scars, kisses me everywhere, and I fall asleep."

sample_reviews.review_text: Yikes.

I really wanted to love this book, it does after all have a bi Asian main character. Maybe I was just too old for it? 
 Not Your Sidekick is one cliche after another. The writing is terrible, it was so repetitive I almost quit several times. The characters are badly written and like I said earlier, the plot a massive cliche. 
 First we have Jess, who is a normal girl in a family of superheroes. She's trying to find her way in life and ends up getting an internship. But through a turn of events she realizes that the internship is with a company run by her town's ''villains''. Why didn't she stop then you ask? Since her parents are rivals with the villains. Or at least why didn't she tell her parents who she was working for and maybe get information on the bad guys? I don't know. The character literally never thought about any of that. She never told her parents who she was working for, and what's worse, she didn't even seem to care? 
 Then we had every other character being obvious about who they were, or what was going on. Obviously Jess' sister was being brainwashed. Obviously Abby was the daughter of the villains. But did Jess notice? Nope. Not at all. 
 And third I had a huge problem with the ending. Basically, without giving the spoilers away, there are no stakes. Nothing matters. Could have been fixed by people actually thinking. Oh and on top of that it literally took them no effort whatsoever to be the heroes in the end. It made no sense at all. 
 I think Not Your Sidekick had a lot of potential. Jess could have been a great character in a slightly older book. The story could have been entertaining if the plot had been better. It could have been a fantastic story. It has all of the right diversity parts, it just fell flat everywhere else. I am very disappointed. I gave it 1 star on Goodreads.

An enjoyable, if predictable, super hero story. The dialogue was a little stilted in a few places, and there were no real surprises, but it was still a nice story, and I liked the multiple facets of diversity represented in a genre that is traditionally white and straight (though that has been changing a lot in the last few years. Maybe it's just the books I have access to, but almost all of the OC superhero novels I've seen lately have featured characters on at least one of the diversity axes.)
I really wanted to like this but it felt a little too YA for my tastes. Probably those who regularly read the genre would find more interest in it.

I didn't like Not Your Sidekick that much, but it was cute. I saw the twist about M coming from a mile away, but I thought the romantic dynamic between Jess and Abby was cute. Maybe it was because this book is intended for a younger audience, or because I had high expectations for it, but it just wasn't much of a pleasure to read.
Surprised by how much I liked this.
THIS WAS THE CUTEST THING, I'M SO HAPPY I READ THIS, TOO ADORABLE FOR WORDS OH MY GOODNESS. *continues gushing unintelligibly*

I loved every reading moment, every chapter. 
 The main character is very captivating and made me excited by her quest to be her own person. 
 I'm very excited about the next volume!

On paper, Not Your Sidekick seems like a fairly standard YA superhero book. Girl daughter of two fairly well known superheroes, girl not born with powers, girl feels substandard compared to her "special" siblings and parents. Jess is resigned to the fact that she's going to live a life of doing paperwork and otherwise have a boring, normal life, when she applies for an internship position at Monroe Industries, a larger tech company. It turns out, however, that Monroe Industries is just a cover for Master and Mistress Mischief, her parents two arch enemies. From there, Jess begins her journey of self discovery and acceptance, while also uncovering dangerous plots that threaten the entire superhero/supervillain dynamic that the world has in place. 
 However, where this book really shines is in how wonderfully diverse the world is, and how easily that diversity fits in place. Jess comes from Asian parentage (I believe Vietnamese) and the area they live in is full of Southern and Eastern Asian cultural influences. Jess is also bisexual, and a very large portion of the book had to do with her crushing on her coworker Abby, volleyball captain at their local high school. We have characters who are on all ranges of the LGBT spectrum (including a ftm trans character who I believe is becoming the focal point in the sequel, which I'm looking forward to). Due to the futuristic world C.B. Lee has set up, harassment and persecution over what gender you identify as or who you're attracted to has taken a back seat compared to the near constant threat of super villains undergoing their devious machinations. It was refreshing to read a book with LGBT+ characters and not have one get beaten up due to their sexuality (granted, they do get beaten up but that's moreso due to the aforementioned superhero/supervillian fights than who they enjoy kissing) 
 Potential plot twists in this book are fairly obvious, although guessing the twists in advance did not lessen my enjoyment of the book. These are teenagers we're primarily dealing with and as such, they will make some stupid decisions and be quite dense when it comes to picking up on social cues that someone likes them. This book is also most definitely primarily set up for upcoming sequels. Although most of the character subplots (which were my favorite part of the book anyway) are resolved by the end of Not Your Sidekick, superhero related plots have been busted wide open and shown to be a much greater scope than the characters initially thought. I do hope that we get some famial resolution in book 2 regarding Jess and certain family members, though. 
 All in all, I really liked this book. It was cute, light hearted, superhero fun times that didn't take itself too seriously but had well fleshed out characters that I loved to be around. I am eagerly awaiting book 2's release in October.
