I didn't realize that the tile was referring to the quality of the book - I would have saved myself from reading this mess. Because it's bad. Bad on so many levels it doesn't deserve wasting more time with it. I'll just outline a few 
 1. Characters - I have read some characters in the NA that I just couldn't connect with but these two were just ridiculous. The guy was a douche and abusive for no good reason. The girl was over the top dramatic and a doormat with self esteem issues. 
 2. Relationship - one word to describe it: toxic. Actually if you read the story with the idea that it's not a romance novel but a study of a toxic and unsatisfying abusive relationship, you will be definitely right. This is the most unromantic romance I've had the misfortune to come upon lately. Ironically, the use of Romeo and Juliette is even less flattering for the premise since it creates a stark contrast between what a romance is and what isn't. Heads up, this book doesn't even exist in the same universe as Shakespeare's timeless tale. 
 3. Writing style - in order to be objective, there were some fun and original moments throughout the book but the whole concept of flashbacks and present time was poorly executed and in need of heavy editing. I am more and more certain that the editors for the so called NA genre are either sloppy or incompetent. So many books can benefit from better structure and critical approach. Here, the jumps between the two timelines were not organic and felt strained and random. At times I was wondering whether there were originally two books that were randomly meshed together. 
 4. Ending - worst cliffhanger ever. Seriously, I can understand wanting to draw your readers into the second book but this is ridiculous. If you do not want to give some sense of closure, at least you shouldn't make them check if they are not missing part of the book. I totally did and reading some of the comments I find I am not alone. Such a poor device to sell your next book. It's almost as if the author didn't believe enough in the story itself. But then again, I understand why one wouldn't.
Nothing says romance like sexual harassment and emotional abuse.

reference_books.review_text: My rating for this is somewhere between 2 and 3 stars. I was suggested this book by a coworker because "it is just so amazing", and she thought I would relate to it since my son was recently the object of some bullying at school. While the style had you really wondering about the who and what happened, I felt as if I were sitting at a table listening to a bunch of women gossip. Perhaps this was the author's intent, but as someone who hates gossip, I did not enjoy it. sample_reviews.review_text:
I'm not sure about how to review this novel. I always feel terrible when I have to give a novel or book less than three stars. I'm too empathetic in that sense; I just think about all the effort the author must've put in their novel, like coordinating and constructing the proper structure for their plot, how to arrange the dialogues and finding the proper words to express what they want their characters to say, finding ways to develop their emotions and conveying a believable synergy to the reader among other things. When I think about all these things I feel both bad and amazed, the prime because I didn't like the novel and the author put effort into it and I feel bad for disliking it, the latter because, well, the effort must've been big. However, I cannot force myself to like a novel, and I just didn't like this one. 
 The spiritual and metaphysical basis of "The Alchemist" seems to be a combination of Christianity, Pantheism, Mysticism and every speech any public motivator would want to deliver an audience. The novel sums up in the following words: " 
 Follow your dreams and do not give up, no matter what the circumstances are. 
 " 
 I almost feel as if Darth Vader was trying to say in the most polite and protracted way possible: " 
 Use the force, Luke! 
 " 
 Unfortunately, I consider this novel to be filled with the trite, over-used and hypersensitive phrases we have all heard before: "Don't give up!" "Follow your dreams!" "You can do anything you want!", and that's simply not my cup of tea. I like cold, hard truths and different point of views, not recycled phrases I can read on-line. Now, with all that being said, I'm not certain if Coelho's objective was to help his readers grow and feel more confident about themselves, or if he simply wanted to use demagogy at its finest to win his readers and have a larger audience for his next novels. Quite frankly, this novel is both demagogic and boringly trite, so in short words: I didn't like this novel. One star.
that's so stupid. sure not "everything is one"!!

The Alchemist is a story about a boy who was a shepherd, found out his Personal Fortune was to find a treasure in Egypt, and had to decide whether to follow this Personal Fortune or stay where he was comfortable. The book was written like a YA book with simple language, proselytizing, and mercifully short. Everyone except for one character was unnamed, the main character was "the boy", which made me wonder how old he was. No character is fully developed, everyone is rather flat. The section with the boy and the alchemist was the worst part. It was boring, drawn out, and the "God" talk and "turning yourself into the wind" was ridiculous. The ending was okay, but the rest of the book was so bad, it didn't shore up.

0.5 stars 
 It's a fucking sad excuse for a book. 
 It's tedious. It's a drag. It's annoying. It's full of an incredulous amount of statements that just made me roll my eyes and say "ugh, duh??". It's taken (I would use the term stolen but I'm trying to be a little polite here) several stories from everywhere else that it lacks originality. It's basically another version of the Bible, with less blabs and a more modernized tone to it. 
 This book is just so goddamn awful that I don't understand why several people (peers included) liked it a lot. This isn't a self-help book. If anything, it's preachy and leads people into thinking that if they want something hard enough, the universe will fucking conspire for them to get it. And all that without lifting a finger. 
 Also, what is up with this only think about and focus on your present shit?? Why are you telling me to forget about my past or not worry about my future?? What the hell is the fucking matter with you?? 
 I don't understand. I just cannot. I wouldn't recommend this book to anyone. With all the hype around it, I'm seriously disappointed.

sample_reviews.review_text: This book was at times incredibly tedious with her recollections of a childhood obsessed by cleaning. Towards the end some of her instructions were feeling ridiculous, like her opinion that whenever I enter my home I should be thanking it for providing shelter .... ok whatever. I managed to get about 9 post it notes worth of information from this entire book that will help me declutter my house

This was an audio book which I kind of tandem read with the book alongside me from time to time. As a consequence of reading this book I have thrown away 3 large bags of stuff from my home and a heap of papers out of my office, and that is just the beginning. That said, I think it is completely and utterly weird to speak to your belongings, to kneel down in the middle of your house upon getting home and say thank you out loud to your house. It is completely strange to talk to your clothing! There is often a condescending tone in the book, and I can imagine that Marie Kondo just despairs of people like me who actually like their overstuffed houses. The book, however, does have some great ideas for culling your belongings and for storing things. I will definitely revisit the book for inspiration to cull more things. I'm not going to buy into the whole Konmarie system, that is just a bit too far for me, but I have definitely taken some of it on board.
Some good ideas but also a lot of crazy ones.

The author uses unconventional methods of decluttering. I feel there is wisdom in much of what she says. I don't agree with the declaration that tidying one's house and everything in it can be done quickly, thoroughly, and "all in one go". It does make me want to try to do better though.

Fairly interesting premise, but could have been shorter. The gist is essentially to unload all of your belongings by systematic themes, then touch each item with your hands and ask your intuition whether or not it sparks joy. If it doesn't then get rid of it. Period. Don't second guess. 
 She also had a section on how to organize and fold clothing that I found to be refreshingly new and interesting. I also found her idea of talking to your belongings and home intriguing but could see how many would be put off by this idea. 
 One of her wisest concepts was when discussing the various reasons why we keep our belongings, especially when they no longer serve a regular utilitarian purpose. 
 Overall, I found this book worthwhile and would recommend it to everyone since we could all use a refresher on how to organize our homes and refine our skills of discernment when it comes to pitching things out.

The gist of the book is: throw away stuff and tidy up by category. 
 I believe most of the content in this book can be abbreviated into a blog post. 
 It is a waste of time to write a book, as well as to read it.
It is hard to rate until I have tried her method. It seems very logical. I am hoping it works for me.

I took my time reading this book - on the recommendation of a friend and as part of an online book club. 
 I love some of the ideas and hate others so I feel conflicted in giving a clear review. 
 I think the book contains a lot of clever ideas, motivational energy and clear guidelines on how to get hold of your belongings and therefore your life. 
 I don't think a lot of the ideas are completely novel to me and I don't agree with some of the ideas. 
 I did use the magical method of joy to go through my clothes and i threw out a lot of stuff. 
 I went through my papers and very few gave me joy but they were essential to keep for tax purposes. 
 I love my books and whilst I regularly weed some out and donate to the library or school, the majority stay and do get Reread - often in fact! 
 So some good ideas but I took it with a big grain of salt and used what worked and left the rest hanging. It has made me look at things I own in a different light and I do try to have a home for everything but that has been a longer work in progress than reading this book.

I have come to the conclusion that with today's world as it is, that if a person can juggle 2 or 3 things, then they have life down pretty pat. Anything more on your plate than that is too much to handle and because we all think we can do everything in life, that now it leaves many of us scrambling around, trying to find time to clean the house just to maintain order when life is so much more stressful in many ways than it used to be (ie. If you have a really demanding job, have to take care of a kid or two, are single, and have to do the merry dance of shuffling everything around that, taking care of a sick or elderly parent, barely having any time to yourself, then good Gods, who has the time to clean?). We all think we're superman or superwoman anymore and where have all the relatives/family support/community gone? We've taken on too much and that is why so many of us have dirty/messy houses... not that things can be perfect, of course, but no one person can do everything. 
 Oh, and this author has some major OCD. No wonder she can do this. She has all the time in the world. This IS what she does. It is her whole life. 
 Getting ready to pitch this book in the garbage. I already figured out what was wrong and why my house was a mess. My house was a mess because my life was a mess (and I've been reading a bunch of psychology and self help books in the mean time that did a munch better job at acknowledging this than this damn book ever did) and my life was on perpetual pause... and living with my sister made it worse, in some ways, because she adds to the mess and has really bad depression... but it's more than depression. She's lazy. She always has been, even when she used to be neater (she was never really neat to begin with, but she was manageable in her earlier years). She just doesn't care and I've given up on trying to make her change. I can't make her change. You can't make anyone change, even when you try to be positive about it and stop badgering her about it. She doesn't want to and she sees no need to. She will always be a pig... but I don't have to keep living with her. For now, it's yoga and meditation until I can move out and find a new job. She's stuck, too, but unlike her, I haven't given up on my dreams or myself. She doesn't want to deal with her baggage, but I do. I'm tired of feeling miserable and tired all the time. I don't want to be this way and I don't have to. 
 The only way I got out of my mess was by going to therapy, reading books on situations pertaining to myself, and taking some much needed time off so I could sit down and actually go through my stuff. 
 It didn't hurt that I went through a long bout of mania during this period of time, either. Hypomania. It actually helped. With everything, including cleaning my house. It was like doing a complete 180. I wanted to change and it's like my body just knew what to do. 
 How else am I going to grow up? And move on? 
 I wish I could offer advise on this, but I have little to give. I know my situation doesn't pertain to everyone and not everyone is naturally neat. I'm not "naturally" neat either, but I do have my moments.
Waste of time.

Poor Mortimer is just a lonesome zombie looking for love. He tries everything he can think of with no results. Then he puts an ad in the paper (sung to the pina colada song) to meet at the Cupid's Ball. The love of his life comes in the room right at midnight! 
 Okay for preschool storytimes.

I fell head over heels in love with Mortimer, the lonely zombie who couldn't get a date for the Cupid's Ball. This is such a clever book - not really for young children but a delight for geek parents to use to indoctrinate their older, soon to be geek kids. I love the maggots that almost steal the show on several pages, playing poker, baseball, in their little bowties; I love the brain pie Mortimer shares with his sweetie in the end, I love the diamond ring - with finger still attached - he tries to give the waitress in the diner. I love the hands coming out of graves as Mortimer and Mildred share a picnic in the graveyard, two holding eyeballs and one giving a thumbs up! I adore the ad Mortimer places - it can be sung to the tune of the old Pina Colada song by Rupert Holmes. Am I gushing? Yes, I am. I was so impressed with this I actually bought it, and I haven't bought a children's picture book in years (my daughter is 19 - but being a geek kid, she will love it!). My husband loved it too, and he isn't easily impresed with children's books. I sure hope to see more of Mortimer... and more by Kelly DiPucchio.

Rating: 1.5 Stars 
 If you were thinking about whether or not to continue this series, let me tell you now: walk away. Seriously, Fifty Shades Freed isn't worth it. It's by far the worst book in this series. Ironically, it isn't even because of the sensual scenes (even though there are plenty of those), it's simply because this novel had no plot whatsoever! Christian and Ana are now married and...that's it. This is a story of their married life. The first quarter is all about their honeymoon, Ana complaining about having so much money, and her inner goddess looking up from her copy of The Complete Stories of Charles Dickens to make a face or some snide comment. The novel progresses in a similar manner: Ana and Christian buying a house, getting adjusted to being married, Ana's inner goddess appearing every so often, etc. The last quarter of this story was the only interesting bit and the last aspect of Christian's character growth that needed to occur finally happened. Still, after finishing this series I am unable to see why it has made such a huge splash in the book community. 
 I am constantly befuddled by why a woman would write this series and furthermore, why other women are extolling its virtues (non-existent virtues more like it). I understand that every woman probably has some crazy fantasy of seducing a man who can't be seduced by other women, of having a man be jealous of you and possessive, and even having a man who is romantic and completely besotted with you. Christian Grey is an extreme version of this Mr. Perfect though. He doesn't give Ana any freedom, any issues they have are resolved by sex, and they only seem to do what suits him. Of course, this is supposed to have changed by the end of the book, leaving you with an impression that their married life is all hunky-dory and that Ana and Christian have reached a state of equilibrium, balancing normalcy with their messed-up qualities, but that still doesn't explain Ana's characterization. Erotic content aside, this series could have been a lot better than it was if Ana showed more backbone. If she had stood up to Christian a little bit more, if she had had normal and realistic reactions to many of the uncommon situations she found herself in, if she had simply grown a backbone, this book would have been infinitely better. I know what you die-hard Fifty Shades Fans are going to say - Ana does stand up for herself! She's always fighting with Christian! That's why he loves her and not any of his ex-submissives! Yes, Ana brings up ideas that she disagrees with and argues with Christian, but none of these arguments are ever seen to their completion. Ana walks away in a puff of anger, she resolves not to talk to Christian, she finally sees him and then can't help but melt into his arms and do anything he asks of her. That isn't woman empowerment! It isn't even standing up for yourself! It's like starting an argument with a bully and then deciding half-way through it isn't worth it and giving in. E.L. James characterizes Ana in this same fashion and ultimately, the messages it's sending out to woman of today are bad. If James wanted to write Ana the way she did, she should have made this novel set in the 1800s or a little later. The fact that she didn't only fuels my anger towards this series. 
 I have to admit though that I did find one aspect of this novel interesting: the story with Ana's ex-boss and his connection with Christian. James explores the psychological situations that makes men revert to becoming Dominatrix's in the last few chapters of this novel, and that was extremely thought-provoking. Either than that though, this series simply is not worth the time and energy. 
 Unless you like mature, erotica content, this series is not for you. It will make you pull out your hair in frustration and bang your head against the wall - repeatedly! The only redeeming quality about this series is the fascinating psychological impact that these types of Dom-Sub relationships have on people. Either than that though, this series isn't worth spending time or money on. In some ways, I'm disappointed with the book community for giving a story like this so much popularity when there are dozens of literary gems which never get the recognition they deserve. Anyway, I won't be buying into the hype anymore - Twilight was bad, but this was just a nightmare. I don't think I've ever been this happy to finish a series and never have to read it again, but I am so glad I will never have to read about Ana or Christian again! There is only one thing I feel now: liberated.

I started reading about Anne's antics when I was a young girl, not yet a teenager, and had an imagination to rival even this beautiful, darling red-headed girl. As you can imagine (and like so many other girls), I fell promptly in love with Anne after reading the first book and hungrily devoured every book in the series. I felt both the "flying high with anticipation" and the "thud" that came after finishing each book, knowing that I was one step closer to having to put Anne away. 
 It's those thuds I sadly remember the most clearly. I've gotten my Anne fix over the years by watching the wonderful PBS movies that go under the same names.. but they just aren't the same - and this book is a good example of why. 
 So many beautiful characters are left out of the stories. Mr. Harrison and his rascally parrot (who's Jersey cow is the one sold, NOT Mrs. Rachel Lynde's). The adorable Paul Irving, his American father and... not Anne who is the romantic interest, but the lovely Miss Lavender and her house of echoes. sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 "Do you understand, sir, do you understand what it means when you have absolutely nowhere to turn?" Marmeladov's question came suddenly into his mind, "for every man must have somewhere to turn. . . ." 
 A bit heavy in Philosophy at times. But so far a good read. It made me ask Had the world been better off without Ioseb Besarionis dze Jughashvili? 
 It begins with the decision of an impoverished student, Raskolnikov, to rob and kill a pawnbroker, having justified his decision with the argument that her death will do the world more good than harm, both because she cheats her clients and because the money from the robbery will give him the start he needs to become a great man and ultimately benefit humanity. 
 The action of the novel is confined to the day of the murder and a few days following it, during which time, in addition to dealing with a murder investigation led by a clever and intriguing detective who suspects him, Raskolnikov spends time with his mother and sister, who have just come to visit, and with the tragic Marmeladov family, consisting of a drunken father, a consumptive mother, three young children, and an eighteen-year old girl who is forced into prostitution in order to support the family. 
 There are reasons that this book is considered one of the most celebrated books in Russian literature. And you need to find that out by getting a copy of this dang lit! 
 Can someone lend me a copy of the Idiot please?

Okay, so I'm glad I read it, but I was not impressed. Maybe it was the translation (I read the free Kindle copy, so that's a serious possibility) but it was pretty slow in my opinion. Maybe someday I'll have to read it again since Matt gave it four stars and Mom gave it five stars (really, Mom? You though it was amazing?).

There were two books in my school career that I didn't finish because the experience of reading them was just too awful. This was one of them. (Something by Faulkner was the other - Light in August, maybe?) Oh, how I hated this book.

So many great quotes I saved but here's the best: 
 A special little theory came in too--a theory of a sort--dividing mankind, you see, into material and superior persons, that is persons to whom the law does not apply owing to their superiority, who make laws for the rest of mankind. 
 Make sure to vote for your congressional candidates.
Hard work!

This book put me into a funk so deep that there was almost no returning. 
 I had to stop reading it, and change to something bright and happy (such as 1984) or cut my wrists and end it all.

There were definitely some things to like with this. The first dream sequence was rather effective horror, and has been used effectively for to elicit dread by a number of horror authors. It resonates with Lovecraft's Dream Cycle. Additionally the murder scene was far more brutal and gory than what I was expecting of something from this era. 
 That said, the pacing was deadly dull. It wasn't the remnants of the serialized format that bothered me, but the endless moping. I find that sometimes drunk people who I like rambling on and on tedious. Strangers who do that are pretty unbearable. I might have hated it less if things had been woven together at a tighter pace. I made a valiant attempt, but gave up during Part 2.

I liked this book a lot. It certainly provides readers with a different way of looking at things, which is great. Often times too many people think "inside the box" and this promotes them to look outside as well. In fact, the author originally left this book with an open ending. The publishers however, decided the book wouldn't sell because people can't handle uncertainty, which is where the epilouge came from. 
 In my opinion the epilouge RUINED the book. Perhaps it's because I'm an atheist and don't believe in the religious rebirth he goes through after getting sick over lent and getting better over Easter. This book would've been better off the way the author wanted it to be and I certainly would've enjoyed it more.
Took me forever, but what a great book!
I read this in my Russian phase ... don't know that I would tackle it now, 30 years down the track, renowned classic tho' it may be.

reference_books.title: Forever . . .
reference_books.review_text:
High school senior Katherine Danziger is a typical teenage girl. She enjoys spending time with friends and playing tennis, has a part-time job, and looks forward to graduation. When Katherine meets Michael Wagner at a New Year's party, she immediately falls for him. As their relationship progresses, Katherine finds herself being confronted with the realities of her and Michael's physical relationship. Torn between the hormonal reactions of her teenage self and her desire for romantic perfection, Katherine soon begins to cross the lines she created for herself. Michael is charming and devoted, and before too much time has passed, the two are deep in the sometimes murky waters of young love and intimacy. Told in an upfront, straightforward style, Katherine and Michael's story is resonant through the decades since it was written. Its themes are still extremely relative to the situations of today's young adults. Forever tells an honest tale of young love, first experiences, and the emotional repercussions of one's choices. Judy Blume does a remarkable job of crafting the young adult voice in this realistic novel. 
 A warning, however, to readers who are sensitive to graphic sexuality: the intimate scenes in this book are candidly narrated, which may be too intense for some readers, especially those of a younger age. This somewhat uninhibited quality is beneficial to the novel; it allows the reader to create a deeper connection to the reasons behind Katherine's choices, and to the distress she experiences when her expectations are broken down. All in all, this novel has a variety of relevant themes, realistic characters, and redeeming qualities. 
 This book is recommended, but once again, with consideration of the open quality of the sexual scenes.

sample_reviews.review_text: Amazing, romantic, funny, heartbreaking and oh so compelling. READ THIS SERIES!

Only in London a short time, Tessa Gray's world has already been turned upside by her brother's betrayal and the discovery of her own strange ability. With the help of her unlikely Shadowhunter friends, Tessa has managed to make some order from the chaos of lies and mystery that surrounds her. 
 That order proves tenuous when rival Shadowhunters seek to displace Charlotte and her husband as heads of the London Institute. With Charlotte's position in doubt, so too is Tessa's place in the only home she has known since leaving New York City. If Charlotte can find the Magister, the villain cloaked in secrecy who wants to use Tessa's powers in his mission to destroy all Shadowhunters, her position will be secured. But what if she can't? 
 As Tessa helps in the search for the Magister, her future place in London is not the only dilemma presented to her. Why is Jessamine sneaking off so often? What madness leads Will to move so violently between passion and cruelty? Why does her heart still ache so much just to see him? And what of Jem, Tessa's quiet, steadfast companion in all of this chaos? 
 With so many secrets, it is unclear which truths should be told and which should remain hidden in Clockwork Prince (2011) by Cassandra Clare. 
 Clockwork Prince is the second book in Clare's Infernal Devices series, preceded by Clockwork Angel. This trilogy is a companion to Clare's Mortal Instruments series which begins with City of Bones. 
 It's hard to review books that are part of a series because, particularly in the case of this book, you cannot read just one book. Things are even more complicated when the series ties back to a completely different, longer, series. 
 That said, if the idea of a quasi-steampunk Victorian London where the descendants of angels fight monsters (even while befriending one of those "monsters" who happens to be a warlock) this is the series for you. But don't start here. Go read Clockwork Angel first then come back to read this review. 
 Clockwork Prince is simultaneously compelling and painfully frustrating. Many questions from the first book (particularly about Will's . . . affliction) are answered. Some of the answers are satisfying and add to the story. Some of them add to the general annoyance I had while reading the book. 
 Neither being or knowing the author, I'm not really qualified to say what each character would or would not do. BUT, for this one reader, it felt a lot like every single character walked through the book doing the wrong things. Worse, they seemed to be doing them for all the wrong reasons. Will all be resolved to my satisfaction in book three? Maybe. Then again, maybe not. Finding the answer to that question (aside from my genuine fondness for these characters and this series) is enough to guarantee I will eagerly await the release of Clockwork Princess in 2013. 
 Clare's writing remains top-notch here. While the larger plot does take a back seat to character development, Clockwork Prince sets readers up for what is sure to be a stunning conclusion to a clever trilogy. 
 Possible Pairings: Jane Eyre by Charlotte Bronte, City of Bones by Cassandra Clare, A Tale of Two Cities by Charles Dickens, Incarceron by Catherine Fisher, Sabriel by Garth Nix, Snowfall by K. M. Peyton, The Amulet of Samarkand by Jonathan Stroud

Cassandra Clare once again weaves a fantastic tale of the Shadowhunter world. Tessa has found refuge with the Shadowhunters even though she still is not quite sure what she is. The seach for Mortmain continues and Tessa must use her power to Change in order to help with the search. Along the way, Tessa struggles with emotions of whom she thinks she should be with and whom she is destined to be with. Seeing Jem and Will grow as characters, and Tessaa's love interests, was exciting and heartbreaking! I can't wait for Clockwork Princess.

<3 Jem... It's been a while since I read the Mortal Instruments series, but I believe I prefer The Infernal Devices even more, simply because James Castairs is in it. I could never fall in love with Jace, and he and Will are much of the same, but Jem is awesome on a whole new level. I am giving this 4.5* only because Tessa's behavior annoys me a bit (Jem or Will, seriously?) and the twists and turns were predictable, compared to those in Clockwork Angel. I still enjoyed every page and wish I had all day to start reading Clockwork Princess... but I'll have to wait till tonight. Already missing the characters. xx

reference_books.review_text: "The Strain" Series is probably one of the most unique of its kind. It manages to describe the fall of humanity (in terms of this evil vampire plague), the fall of humanity in terms of personal demons (for some characters), and the RISE of humanity (where you can see growth and the desire to remain something unspoiled by gluttony and evil). This is done with precision and finesse that master of horror Guillermo del Toro is known for in his films. He's a one of a kind artist and I hope dearly that he'll be able to give more books to us while he continues his filmography. (My personal scale this book receives a 8.5 out of 10).

This one falls right in the middle where I was so bored for the first 3/4 of the book, but the last 1/4 was interesting and I'm glad I knew what happened... Basically, I will say that the only reason you should read this book is if you've read the other two and want to know what happens at the end. If you haven't started the series, don't! If you didn't like the first book, just stop! I mean, even though a lot of the other books have disappointing final pieces (The Hunger Games, Divergent, and some others), they at least kept me entertained. The Last Star was just plain boring.

2.5 stars 
 I have a lot to say about this book. But, at the same time, I have no idea how I feel about it as a whole. There are some things I like, some I hated and some I don't even understand properly. 
 Mostly, I like to develop a organised way to write a review. But this time, I don't know how to do that. So, I'm just gonna wing it and then add bold titles. 
 Lack of information 
 First thing I felt about the book was that it had a very bad beginning. I wasn't at all exited to read the rest of it when I read the first 2-3 chapters. That was mainly because I had no idea what anyone was talking about. They were yapping about moroi, dhampirs, strigoi and a bunch of shit that didn't make sense. 
 I once read a review about a book from 'The Mortal Instruments' series that said that Cassie, the author, told us everything we could be curious about regarding the aspects of the world she'd created and that that was a bad thing. I found it stupid that anyone would take information as a bad thing and, reading this, proved me right because, Rachelle, didn't tell us a thing. She didn't offer any information until about halfway through the book. 
 The Big Secret 
 Many times in the book, there were referenced made to THE incident that made Rose and Lissa leave the Academy in the first place. It was made so improtant that I soon began to dread finding out the reason because I was afrid it wouldn't be good enough. And I was right to dread it because the reason sucked! 
 I understood that Rose felt the need to protect Lissa but none of what happened proved that running away would be a good solution. There was no reason for them to hide everything from the grown-up, sensible people who could help them. Who did actually help them in the end. The entire mystery thing was stupid and just there because the author needed them to not be at the academy in the beginning. 
 The Damned line 
 There was a line in the book when Rose found out that a character Mason has a crush on her. There line was: 
 "He's crazy about me." 
 Who do I blame for that? 
 Do I blame the so modest character.(NOTE. SARCASM.) or do I blame the writer for phrasing it in the worst possible way? I just... 
 The Characters 
 The only character I like in the entire book was Christian. I'll tell you why. 
 Rose- She was a horrible character in the beginning. The kind that thought that she knew everything, that she could fix everything and that other people were just a bunch of idiots who were getting in the way. In reality, she couldn't do a thing. She wasn't capable of protecting Lissa, she didn't know how to make good, smart decisions (she tried to protect Lissa by taking her away to a world full of monsters and her way to stop Lissa from using her poweres was to make her use her powers in the human world.) and she did absolutely nothing productive the entire time they were on the run. 
 Other than being the only person to have a connection with Lissa, she did nothing productive 90% of the book. She lied, manipulated, made bad decisions, made selfish decisions, fought with a bunch of people, argued for no reason and... you get the point. The only positive point she has is that she became smarter later on in the book. 
 Lissa- Lissa was such a weak character. The entire time, all she did was, 'I'm in trouble, Save me!' or 'I'm sad, help me!' I tried to understand her, accept her. There was a reason given for her fragile state but it wasn't good enough. She was just too pathetic for me to care. 
 Dimitri- He didn't have much of a role. He was there for many parts but we got to know very little about him. So, because of that, I neither like nor dislike him. He's just like a piece of necessary furniture that only come in one design. If I had to decribe him in short, it would be: 
 'Me strong. Me protect.' 
 These are the only characters that I care to mention. So, you can understand why I only liked Christian, who seems to be the only one with a personaly ( good one too) and a proper functioning brain. 
 The going-into-head thing 
 I strongly believe that the only reason for the going-into-head thing to be there was so that we could see what was going on with Lissa. The emotions thing I understood, but not that. It was just for convenience. I would have preferred for the author to either go with third person or multiple POVs. The multiple POVs would have been refreshing because usually the two poeple are one male and one female, this would have been different. 
 Then there the fact that it's a huge invasion of privacy. It's one thing to not be able to control it, but to do it deliberately? It's just wrong. And, to me, disturbing. I mean, what if Lissa was having sex. Or what if, instead of Rose, it was a guy? He could be a perv who would get a strip show every time she changed her clothes. 
 Overall 
 The plot was okay, the characters I just explained, the writing was a 3-3.5 out of 5 (but it's forgivable since it's one of the authors earlier works.) But the book was mess in so many ways and definitely need some more structure and planning. 
 So, this one gets a 2.5. I' gonna read the next book. If I like it, I will select 3 stars and if not, then 2. (Update: Did like book 2 but not that much so I'm going with 2) 
 Last thing, there was a line: 
 "Aaron would never make up something like that!" 
 It made no sense to me because I doubt it had any sense at all. I think it was written wrong or something. If anyone got it, what it was referring to that Aaron made up, please explain.
