reference_books.title: The Magicians (The Magicians #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I hated this book the first time I read it, but when it was chosen for book club I decided to try to give it a second chance and try to be more objective. It didn't work. I still hate it. 
 When I first read it I thought I only hated it because of the way it completely twisted some of my favorite novels from childhood (The Narnia Chronicles) but I realize now it's much more than that. This novel has been described as being "Harry Potter for adults" but that statement couldn't be more wrong. This is Harry Potter for adults who have become completely disillusioned by books about magic. There's nothing even magical about this book - Grossman turns magic into science and takes away everything that's magical about magic. The book feels completely sterile and antiseptic, with no heart or imagination at all; instead of the creativity and color Harry Potter inspires in my imagination, I pictured this whole world dreary and grey. The style and tone of the book made the narration feel toneless, and uninterested, which made it hard for me to care about what was happening or get into the story. I didn't like any of the characters in this novel - not because they were unlikable, but because I simply didn't care about them at all. 
 And I haven't even gotten into the minor things that bugged me, like the fact that the school's calendar is randomly 2 months off from the rest of the world for no apparent reason. I've discussed this book with some other people who defended it based on the fact that the tone is intentional and the author is trying to make a statement on these types of novels, but even if this is the case it just put me off the book entirely. If you're looking for Harry Potter for adults, do not read this book. Check out Jim Butcher's Dresden Files instead.

reference_books.title: Ready Player One
reference_books.review_text: This is probably one of my favorite books I've read for a while. It's fun and entertaining, and full of wonderful pop-culture and 80s references. What I loved most about the book though, is that even though the book is all about gaming and a massive VR world, you don't have to be a gamer to really appreciate it. I rarely play video games but I really enjoyed this book.

reference_books.title: The Girl on the Train
reference_books.review_text:
This novel just did not live up to the hype. I feel like Hawkins was trying to hard to make it the next Gone Girl, and she just did not succeed. The style and mystery is similar to a Gillian Flynn novel, but Flynn's novels are far superior to this one. I figured out the murderer/twist before I was even halfway through the book. There isn't a single likable character in the book - all the women are weak and sad, and the men are manipulative and abusive. Everyone seems like some sort of stereotype. The women are also indistinguishable from eachother - there are three female narrators and their voices are almost identical, to the point that I had to keep reminding myself which chapter I was reading. 
 It's a quick read, so those curious won't waste a lot of time on it, fortunately. But it you're looking for a good mystery, stick to Flynn or Tana French.

reference_books.title: Touch of Power (Healer, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I love every book of Maria's that I read, but this may be my new favorite. Or, most likely second behind Poison Study. I've always been more of a fantasy over sci-fi fan, which is probably why I enjoyed her Study and Glass series more than the Inside series (though I still love the Inside books as well). This book reminded me a lot of the Study books, which is probably one of the reasons I loved it so much. If you're a fan of Maria's books I'm sure you'll love this one. And if you haven't read anything of hers yet, Touch of Power is the start of a new series, so it would be a great place to start!

book_a.title: In the Unlikely Event
book_a.user_review: I liked this book, but didn't love it. You can read my full review on my blog.

sample_reviews.review_text: Too many characters to keep track of and truthfully, even though it was an easy read, nothing compelled me to keep reading. About three quarters of the way through, I finally got the cast of characters straight, I think, but with so many it's almost impossible to develop them. I was thrilled to have Lehigh University mentioned several times. Go Engineers/Mountainhawks! Judy Blume has always been one of my favorites, wish I could say the same for this book.

Best to just stick with Judy Blume's classics. As excited as I was to read this one, it did not read like a modern novel. The characters, plot & drama all have a very 1970's feel which is great if the book is some fabulous nostalgia from the 1970's. As it is, I won't be re-visiting this one.

I have always loved Judy Blume books so I was excited to read her new one. I found it interesting that she lived in the town that was the setting and during the time period of the book. That three planes really crashed in one town in the span of eight weeks boggles the mind. The characters were so real and relateable. Some reviewers have complained that there were too many points of view but I loved how she interwove so many characters into each others lives.

Oh, Judy! No teen was a bigger fan than I was/am!!! Your books were my bibles in adolescence. As I have grown into an adult and a high school English teacher, I am only more and more amazed at the skill and empathy and raw honesty with which you can engage a teen reader. So, it breaks my heart to say that, even though I did a little jig of joy when I saw this book in the bookstore, I did not enjoy it. Too many characters, sections were too short, newspaper extracts were boring, characters too young, repetitive plot. The premise of the novel was really interesting and actually happened, but this novel read like a romance. It was very Blume - mentions of pads, descriptions of outfits, worrying how 'far' to go with a boyfriend - sadly, the stuff I loved two decades ago just bores me now. I'll always love you, Judy Blume, but I would only recommend this to readers who are after an easy, quick, holiday-style read.

I wanted to love this book. I'm a huge fan of Judy Blume, having cut my teeth on Are you there God? It's Me, Margaret and all of her other books for adolescents. I remember reading Wifey and thinking she would forever be my friend, someone who shared secrets with me that like no one ever had. I struggled with this book and wouldn't have finished it if I hadn't had the encouragement of other readers on Book Riot and The Reading Room. They promised me things would come together during the last third of the book. I'll admit, that part was where it picked up for me but most of the book felt like I was in the middle of a soap opera. I realize the era was the '50's and it was suburban New Jersey but there were so many extraneous characters that I got bogged down trying to remember who all of them were. Maybe this is what she was going for but for me, it didn't work. The last third of the book was like she was trying to wrap it all up, make the connections and tie it into a nice neat package. The "30 Years Later" epilogue made me feel cheated, like there was more of the story that could have been told if so much time hadn't been devoted to minor characters and minute details. I hope this isn't her last book. I'd like to see her go out with a bang. For me, this just wasn't what I'd hoped for.
Interesting that this was based on real events. I enjoyed the read, but the book didn't do much for me. I enjoyed Miri's character and Henry.

"In the Unlikely Event" is a slice of life novel about real life events that colored Judy Blume's childhood - three plane crashes that happened within roughly two months of each other in Elizabeth, New Jersey in the 1950s - and how they affected the community. 
 I read this for a book club and, like many, I remember loving Judy Blume books as a pre-teen. I did see some glimpses of what drew me to her books back in the day - the expert way she captures women's inner lives and relationships with each other and, in the case of this book, how ridiculous it was to be a woman in the '50s. 
 But overall this book bored me, and I struggled to finish. Like other reviewers said, I felt there were way too many characters/alternating points of view to keep track of, and no one's story was delved into deeply enough to really connect with or care about. Everyone's "voice" kind of sounds the same with maybe one or two exceptions (a 7-year-old girl and an immigrant speaking in broken English). 
 If you're gonna do multiple points of view, I would've appreciated throwing in some characters who helped contribute to a bigger picture view to help us understand the events. Perhaps someone outside the town's white upper middle class community such as someone in charge of working on the planes or approving the planes to fly in the first place, rather than yet another wife complaining about her husband or high school senior wondering where to go to college. What really happened with the plane crashes is handled in an info-dump fashion in the form of brief newspaper clippings at the beginning of each chapter. 
 I think simply focusing on a handful of people who lost immediate family members would've worked, too, rather than this endless parade of barely distinguishable folks trading horror stories about their cousin's best friend's girlfriend or whatever. 
 Ultimately, "In the Unlikely Event" really lacked focus. I guess I was hoping for something more epic and/or more emotionally immediate rather than a meandering tale of personal melodramas that aren't that interesting and don't really have anything to do with the plane crashes.

Judy Blume is now writing "adult" books, but I think she should stick to the "coming of age" young adult novels that lead her to fame and acclaim. I did not... could not.... finish this book, due to the boredom that ensued.
Slow to start, but a good reminder of why I like Blume so much.
I just couldn't get into the flow of the writing style

book_b.title: Seeker (Seeker, #1)
book_b.user_review: The plot and location of the this novel intrigued me, (how can I resist anything set in Scotland?) yet didn't live up to my expectations. The plot was slow and the structure was weird. The multi-narration didn't bother me, it was more the weird part 2 that was all flashback; why couldn't that have been inserted more organically throughout the book? Then there's the fact that half the book (at least it felt like it) was just two characters trying to avoid their problems, one by doing lots of drugs and the other by actually succumbing to voluntary amnesia. Something about that just bugged me, because it comes just as we're getting to know who the characters are and this made them feel less heroic. The antagonist is equally frustrating as he's not truly evil, he's conflicted and constantly feeling guilty and hiding behind the men that he sends to do his dirty work for him, so he doesn't have to personally beat up the girl he supposedly loves. The whole story felt kind of meh to me; there was no urgency to get it finished. Though I am curious enough to probably read the next one when it comes out, so I guess the author was successful after all?

sample_reviews.review_text:
Seeker is set up in three sections. Present. Past. Present 
 Each chapter focuses on a specific character while remaining in 3rd POV. 
 It's choppy...But I kind of liked it that way. 
 The structure is similar to 'Infinite Sea' by Rick Warren or even 'Cress' by Marissa Meyer. 
 The author presents little bits of details at a time. This is done on purpose. If you knew at the beginning what being a true Seeker actually was it would make the story flat. 
 My favorite character, surprisingly, is Maud...I found myself wanting to learn the most about her. Which is good, because I think she will play a big role in the next book of the series. 
 One thing I didn't like, which I will try to get across without relying spoilers...At the end of the book, I found a character not acting in how I thought they should. Rather in the way the author needed the story to go. Sure, did the author give me hints as to what was going to happen, YES! More than enough actually. I knew where it was going from early on--but I didn't feel as the reader as to really WHY this character all the sudden changes their mind. I might have accepted the change of heart, because believable circumstances arise, but not to have been the first one 'admit it.' 
 As a whole: interesting story. I felt attached to the characters...However, some of the weapons reminded me of power ranger swords, but that is neither here nor there. Worth the read and I will be giving the next book in the series a chance.

DNF 37% 
 I was so excited about this book when I first got approved for it on Netgalley, but it was actually quite a disappointment. Most of the time I had no clue what was going on. I see this book as appealing to some and confusing to others. If you are interested in this book and happen to see my review, do not let that discourage you from attempting to read this book. You may find yourself falling in love with it or you might find yourself hating it.

I had high hopes for Seeker but I ended up having to DNF the book at 21%. The book was just not for me, I tried to keep reading but it soon became a chore to even pick it up instead of something I looked forward to reading. 
 I had some serious issues with the world building in this case the lack of it. I found myself confused trying to figure out what day and age this book was set in. At first I thought it was in the medieval days but then there is a mention of a gun and then later on one of the characters is watching t.v. I just found it frustrating. Also what is a seeker? I still don't really know. 
 I figured I would stick with it until Quinn takes her oath, hoping that after that things will make sense and pick up but I felt cheated. During the oath ceremony Quinn goes through a portal where they come across a home and she is pretty scared. Then right after that it jumps to the next chapter with Quinn back from where ever she went covered in blood. We have no idea what happened at that house, to me that is a pretty important scene to leave out and I don't know the characters well enough or their world to be able to figure it out on my own. 
 Also I didn't connect with any of the characters and their dialogue did not feel natural.

I'll start by getting to the point right away- this was not the right book for me. But, that doesn't mean it won't be the right book for you. 
 Now, I'll explain. First off, the writing is good. It drew me in right away, and I love when a book does that. At first I was so interested, and then, all the s*** hit the fan and I was not so thrilled. John's character did so many deplorable things out of his desperation that I came to loathe him. I think the biggest problem for me is, when you're reading an adventure/fantasy, you should want the adventure fantasy to continue. But, I ended up, like Quin, just wanting the whole sorry story to be over. I felt myself thinking, "Nope, I don't need this. Where Quin is at right now is great. Let's just forget all this other crap and move on." But, of course, that is not what happened. 
 I became so disillusioned, that I actually stopped reading right at about the 60% mark. Actually, the only reason I decided to finish the book was because, I was behind on my Goodreads goal, and that was totally bugging me, with only 40% left, it would be easier to finish this book and get the credit for a book read. And, I'm also doing another reading challenge for 2016, where you read books for other reasons (like your BFF recommended it to you). One of the categories was, read a book you previously abandoned. So, finishing this book a few weeks after I abandoned it was really killing two birds with one stone for me. 
 So, obviously I wasn't a huge fan of the book. But, I think a lot of that comes down to my own sensitivity to various things and what I expect out of my reading. I became too disillusioned. While I found the storyline interesting, it just wasn't the right book for me. I am ambivalent about whether or not to read the sequel, Traveler, when it comes out in 2016. I think it will depend on how hopeful I am feeling at the time. 
 I was given a free ebook from NetGalley in exchange for an honest review.

Nope. Do not pass go, do not collect $200, go straight to jail. That's how I feel about this whole book. What's this book about? I HAVE NO CLUE. I know it's about Seekers... but what are Seekers, besides such a secret society it's kept hidden from even the readers. I know it's about revenge and killing people. Other than that not sure. I can't even... at this point I just want 3 hours back, I would reread it if it was done differently, if the author could just have a clue to give us in better understanding the world they built. The characters didn't even make me want to be part of this confusing world, sometimes the story is the best and sometimes it's the characters... both fall flat in this case. 
 I am sorry, because I do appreciate someone writing a book, putting themselves out there, and doing something that most of use just rip to shreds. 
 1 star. Thanks Edelweiss.
I got about 26% through and I just can't read anymore. So unfortunately I'm marking my first DNF of 2015 :(

I received an arc copy of this book from Netgalley in exchange for an honest review. 
 Story / Inhalt 
 The night Quin Kincaid takes her Oath, she will become what she has trained to be her entire life. She will become a Seeker. This is her legacy, and it is an honor. As a Seeker, Quin will fight beside her two closest companions, Shinobu and John, to protect the weak and the wronged. Together they will stand for light in a shadowy world. And she'll be with the boy she loves--who's also her best friend. 
 But the night Quin takes her Oath, everything changes. Being a Seeker is not what she thought. Her family is not what she thought. Even the boy she loves is not who she thought. 
 And now it's too late to walk away. 
 In der Nacht, in der Quin Kincaid ihren Schwur ablegt, wird sie endlich zu dem, wofur sie ihr gesamtes Leben lang trainiert hat - ein Seeker. Dies ist ihr Vermachtnis und eine grosse Ehre. Als Seeker wird sie zusammen mit ihren beiden Freunden Shinobu und John die Armen und Schwachen beschutzen. Zusammen werden sie das Licht in einer Welt voller Schatten darstellen. 
 Ihre grosse Liebe, die zudem ihr bester Freund ist, wird sie auch auf ihrer Reise begleiten. 
 Doch in der Nacht, in der Quin ihren Schwur ablegt, verandert sich alles. Das, was sie uber Seeker wusste, stellt sich als falsch heraus und sogar ihre grosse Liebe scheint nicht der zu sein, fur den sie ihn gehalten hat. 
 Doch nun ist es zu spat zum wegzulaufen... 
 My Thoughts / Meine Meinung 
 I received this arc copy of the book on netgalley after I got approved for this title. I was really happy about it because it was one of the books most requested and the storyline sounded pretty interesting and good. However, after the first chapters, I was a bit bored and not that intrigued to go on. The characters were simply without any depth just like the description of the natural surroundings. I couldn't connect to any of it. Another thing that bugged me were the time jumps. First it felt very medieval but then again they had some advices that were more than modern. After the oath-taking scene there was a time jump to the past and just some chapters later back to the present. I can tell you that this was very confusing. The mix of times and places together with the scarce information about the lifes and thinking of the characters was a bit disappointing. 
 Overall, this book is aimed at Young Adults starting from the age of twelve that like an action-filled read. It might be interesting for many readers - just not for me. 
 Ich hab dieses Leseexemplar bei Netgalley bekommen, nachdem der Titel fur mich freigeschalten wurde. Ich hatte mich sehr daruber gefreut, da das Buch am meisten gefragt war und auch die Geschichte sehr interessant klang. Nach den ersten Kapiteln war ich allerdings schon etwas gelangweilt und habe mich nur sehr schwer dazu aufraffen konnen weiterzulesen. Den Charakteren haben mir an Tiefe gefehlt, ebenso wie die Beschreibung der Umgebung und der Welt in der sie leben. Aus dem Grund konnte ich auch keine Verbindung zu ihnen aufbauen. Was mich auch geargert hat, waren die Zeitsprunge. Am Anfang kam die Welt sehr mittelalterlich heruber, aber die modernen Gerate haben dieses Gefuhl gestort. Nach dem Ablegen des Schwures gibt es einen Zeitprung in die Vergangenheit und nur wenige Kapitel spater zuruck in die Gegenwart. Fur mich war das sehr verwirrend. Diese standige Vermischung von Zeiten und Schauplatzen zusammen mit den kaum vorhandenen Informationen uber das Leben und Denken der Charaktere hat mich etwas enttauscht zuruckgelassen. 
 Insgesamt lasst sich sagen, dass das Buch fur junge Erwachsene ab 12 Jahren gedacht ist, die auf actionreiche Geschichten stehen. Fur manche mag es vielleicht interessant sein - fur mich leider nicht.

*** I received an ARC from Delacorte Books for Young Readers through NetGalley for an honest review. Expected publication date: 2/10/2015 *** 
 My feelings towards this book are all over the place, and unlike many, I did actually finish the book. I was intrigued by the premiss of it and thought that it would be a great ride to be on, but that ride ended up being drawn out and jumbled. The very beginning starts of at a great pace, then it slows down, especially because this story is told from four separate POV's, and I found myself mired in a lot of unknowns: What is a Seeker? We get a vague definition but not the true purpose of the Seeker, but not what that person's true purpose is. Who are they protecting and how are they supposed to do it? The world is a mish mash of eras. Scotland feels like it's back in feudal times. Hong Kong, though touted as futuristic feels more like present day and London has a futuristic feel to it. There isn't a cohesive feel to it at all. 
 I couldn't really connect with Quin, John or Shinobu and the only one that really interested me was the Young Dread. Quin is the idealistic girl who wants to do good but when she finds out what being a Seeker is she wants to escape but can't due to her oath and when she is finally given a choice she chooses to forget. Shinobu is another idealist who follows a similar path as Quin but instead of a full mental wipe he chooses to self medicate to forget. John is trying to do right by his family but constantly goes about it in the wrong way. Of the three I did feel for what he had been though, but soon found myself rolling my eyes at what he was doing to make things "right" because it was the same approach over and over, and it never yielded what he wanted, in fact it went against what he said he wanted. The Young Dread was the only one that had a any depth of character and whose purpose in the world had any solid ground to stand on. 
 The Quin/John/Shinobu love triangle. Some may find it distressing, but it didn't move me. Quin is pretty oblivious to it and while there is posturing between John and Shinobu, that's all it is throughout most of the book. 
 There is potential for this series to take off, but it just isn't for me.

Ik heb lang uitgekeken naar het lezen van dit boek. De verhaallijn was goed, en het vond deels plaats in Schotland (yeah) en Londen, wat ik altijd leuk vind. Het was op de een of andere manier wel lastig om te lezen. Ik deed er veel langer over dan dat ik over normale boeken doe. De karakters waren allemaal interessant, vooral Maud, mijn favoriete karakter uit het boek. Ik vond het erg leuk om langzamerhand de geschiedenis van de Seekers en het verhaal van de families te ontdekken. Toch werd ik snel afgeleid bij het lezen en het was zeker geen boek wat ik het liefst in 1 keer uit wil lezen. Desondanks ben ik erg benieuwd naar het vervolg, Traveler (:
couldn't finish

reference_books.title: Tony and Susan
reference_books.review_text:
My first thought after reading this book can be summed up by a single sentence: 
 A HUGE DISAPPOINTMENT!!! 
 I hate giving a negative review, which is why I feel the need to explain my reaction. First of all, it was only when I saw a trailer for a recent movie, "Nocturnal Animals", which is described as a thriller based on a successful book called "Tony and Susan" by Austin Wright, that I became aware of this book. I wanted to read the book before watching the film at some point in the future. 
 The premise of the story is quite simple and interesting, a woman receives a manuscript to read for a novel called "Nocturnal Animals". This manuscript has been sent to her by her ex of many years ago. So, this book basically consists of two stories: 1) The woman's life before her separation with her ex and then her subsequent marriage and family life; and 2) The story contained within the manuscript, which follows the life of a meek mathematics professor whose life is turned upside down after the brutal rape and murder of both his wife and daughter. 
 So, when one thinks of a story which contains another story within it, our first thought is that the two stories must be connected somehow. Now, unless I lack the sufficient mental capacity to comprehend simple things, by the end of this book I failed to see any real link between the two stories. Secondly, I'm not sure why, or how, this book is described as a "thriller", I failed to spot any "thrilling" moments, or anything one might associate with a thriller, in the whole of this book. The story of a woman reading a manuscript and reflecting on her own life is not particularly interesting, especially when she comes across as a constant winger who is never happy with anything. Would it have been better had the manuscript within the story been published as a book in its own right? Possibly not, there just isn't even substance in it to make it an interesting read. 
 In short, this was a highly frustrating reading experience where I was waiting for something to happen which never materialised, whether it be a thrilling moment or for the two stories to come together. 
 In all honesty, I can't understand why anyone would think this book is a good read, let alone worthy of basing a film on. There is no way I could possibly recommend this book to anyone else.

reference_books.title: Disgrace
reference_books.review_text:
Until I began reading this book I had never read anything by Coetzee, although I had heard a great deal about him, in fact, it was for this reason, I decided to read this book. 
 Over the years, Coetzee's work has generated all kinds of praise, so, as I expected, Disgrace, is a book which is really well-written with all kinds of wonderful prose. However, the subject matter of the book does not make for a pleasant read, the difficulties of life in post-Apartheid South Africa. Coetzee is a great writer and handles the difficult subject matter really well. Unfortunately, what spoilt it for me was the main character, Lurie, an aging university professor. No matter how hard I tried, I just couldn't see him in any other light than that of a sleazy old man, preying on younger women. As a result, Lurie is just not a likeable character, I didn't really care what happened to him. I suspect Coetzee deliberately made Lurie so unlikeable, a way of representing the unpleasant face of the old South Africa. This raises an important question, in the post-Apartheid era, how should we treat those who were closely associated with Apartheid? Whilst I think this is an interesting, and important, question, I found it very hard to feel sorry for a sleazy old man, especially one who sees nothing wrong with his actions. 
 I'm sure many readers out there will enjoy Coetzee's writing, and anyone interested in South Africa will definitely enjoy this book.

reference_books.title: The Dry (Aaron Falk, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I decided to read The Dry by Jane Harper because it was highly recommended on Twitter. Apart from the praise heaped on the book, I knew nothing else about it. It was only when I downloaded a copy that I learnt that this is a crime novel set in rural Australia. The setting of the story immediately got my interest as I haven't come across many stories set in such a location. It's nice to read a story set in a very different part of the world; some aspects of life out there will be very different, while some will seem familiar. 
 It's not easy writing about a crime novel without giving the story away, so I will have to be brief. 
 The story is quite simple, Aaron Falk, an Australian Federal Agent, who returns to his hometown to attend the funeral of an old friend of his, Luke Hadler, who killed his family before taking his own life. Luke's father wants Falk to look into the deaths just to make sure there are no doubts about Luke's guilt. However, as Falk begins asking questions, we learn the real reason why Falk left his hometown many years ago, a friend of his and Luke's, Ellie Deacon, was found dead in the river, and Falk was suspected of being involved. A number of residents of the small town blame Falk for the death of Ellie Deacon and want him to leave town, just like they did many years ago. 
 As Falk begins to look into the murder-suicide carried out by his friend, he begins to notice the story isn't quite as straightforward as he was led to believe. And as Falk revisits his past, we slowly learn the truth behind the death of Ellie Deacon. All this leads to a great climax. 
 As this story is set in a small town in rural Australia, as one would expect, this is not a story full of lots of fast-paced action. If I were to criticise this book, I would say the pace was a little slow in parts, especially near the beginning. 
 The book is well-written and I am sure even people who don't normally read crime fiction will enjoy it.

reference_books.title: Finders Keepers (Bill Hodges Trilogy, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
As Stephen King is my favourite author, it pains me to award two stars to this book, especially since the book is an enjoyable read. 
 I think my disappointment is due the fact that in my opinion this book could have been, probably should have been, better. I really like the idea of a criminal who hides his loot before he gets sent to prison; on his release he wants what he believes is his; however, someone has already found his hidden stash. Even more interesting is the fact that the loot consists of a series of notebooks by a famous author which contain some of his unpublished works. Apparently, many people who read this author's works become obsessed by them, just like the main villain of this book. 
 This book is described as the second of the Bill Hodges trilogy, however, I don't think the character of Bill Hodges - a retired police officer now working as a private detective - is even necessary. I agree with another review on Goodreads that, at times, Bill Hodges and his colleagues rushing around trying to catch the villain sounds similar to an episode of Scooby Doo. 
 I think the inclusion of Bill Hodges and Team to resolve things was a little lazy. This is a shame for a book which promised so much but failed to deliver.

reference_books.title: If on a Winter's Night a Traveler
reference_books.review_text:
I first heard of Italo Calvino, a highly respected Italian author, a few years ago, but it wasn't until recently I came across one of his novels and decided to read it. As the novel, If on a Winter's Night a Traveler, has received many glowing reviews since it was published, my hopes were high. However, having read the novel, I can honestly say that I can't remember the last time I read such a frustrating book. 
 So what about all the positive reviews it has received? Well, it's possible I read a different version of the book from everyone else; maybe I lack sufficent intelligence to understand a book like this properly; or, as I suspect is more likely the case, because this book has received huge amounts of praise from many intellectuals, many average readers will be hesitant to criticise it fearing the conclusion people may make about their intelligence. 
 The premise of the book is quite interesting, it raises a number of important questions such as: What is a book? Should a story always have a beginning, middle, and an end? What is the role of the reader? Does the reader influence the story? 
 These sorts of questions could be answered in a straightforward manner, maybe in some kind of a literary essay. Calvino's approach to address these questions is one which I certainly don't agree with. The overall story is quite simple, someone begins reading a story which abruptly ends; this story has been incorrectly printed in the wrong book; the reader then looks for the book this story originally came from; but it turns out the next book also contains an error as it has part of a story from another book; and so we move from one unfinished story to another one, all the way to the end. If reading a series of unfinished stories isn't frustrating enough, Calvino has a very strange writing style, it's as if he were deliberately trying to make his work hard to be understood by any reader, for example, the narrative frequently switches between the First, Second, and Third Person. At times, it becomes very difficult to figure out what is going on. I continued reading the book hoping things would slowly become clearer, however, the more I read, the less I found myself caring, and if the book had been much longer I'm sure I would have given up on it long before I reached the end. 
 Final thoughts, a book like this is only worth reading if you can get a free copy. I'm sure most people who spend money to buy a copy will quickly regret their decision.

book_a.title: The Year of the Runaways
book_a.user_review: If I had come across this book by chance then I'm sure I would have enjoyed it a lot more. However, this book has been nominated for the Man Booker Prize and has received rave reviews from many people, including Salman Rushdie. So, when I began reading this book I was expecting something great. This isn't a bad book, it's well written and the story is interesting, however, this is something which could be said about many books. At best, I would say this book is "okay". I'm not sure why this book has been singled out for so much praise. Surely, there must be other books out there more deserving of such praise?

sample_reviews.review_text:
This book tells about young people trying to make their way in a world determined to value them based on their caste. 
 You know how Latinos come to the U.S. thinking they will make a better life for their family, only to find that society is dead-set against them? Well, Indians go to England, hoping to make a better life, only to fight the same thing. 
 This book is heartbreaking and beautiful; for all you readers out there who stubbornly stuck to what they believed in, even if it meant you would never be successful in the conforming world, this book is for you.

This book centers on a year in the lives of a group of young people of Indian extraction, most of them Indian in nationality and one British. During this year they are mainly located in Sheffield, but we are also told in detail of their previous lives in India and in London. 
 I found this book thought-provoking, both in the present-day portions of the book (virtual slaves in Sheffield - I live in Sheffield! - really? Who knew!) and in the portions set in India. I was only vaguely aware of the problems illegal (and in one case, legal) immigrants faced, and can only say that if the jobs these young men did are the jobs so many British people complain immigrants are taking from them, I really don't think you would see British people queuing up to do them! The young men certainly are not rolling in wealth as a result, and the working conditions are awful to the point where I am sure they are illegal. I was also only vaguely aware of how badly those at the bottom of the caste system are still treated in India. 
 It's quite a sad book, in a way, as no easy solutions come to light for any of the problems the young people involved encounter, either in India or in the UK. I'm very glad I read it. Not only is it a good story, but I feel I understand the problems they faced much better than I did before, even if I am no closer than they were to finding solutions.

So obtuse as to be useless. There was some great potential in this - both in the story and in the writing - and it probably deserves more than a one star review, but I was maddened by the deliberate vagueness and obfuscation. Literary fiction often seems to suggest a thing is better hinted at than described but it's not: if something is worth writing about, then write about it - FFS!

My second Booker-2015 book : 
 First of all this was very fast pace book with story running with speed of train. 
 "All you can do is surrender, happily, to its power," commented by Sir Salman Rushdie for this book. And this is why I was attracted towards this. 
 The entire book was based on three Sikkh lives: Avtar, Randeep, Narinder and one low caste person from Bihar : Tarlochan. The main issues concerned with this book was : Low-caste differentiation, poverty, illegal immigrants, condescending nature of jobs but more than everything solitude. 
 Avtar and Randeep, were two characters belonging from middle class Punjabi families. And later circumstances migrate both of them to England for search of Job. The entire episodes like: going through multitudes of Jobs, their memories back home, the subversion of money-less situation etc. were weaved in their stories. 
 The most likable character of book was Narinder, Girl from God, whose mission of life was to give sacrifice, like Sikkh Gurus, to fulfill happiness in at-least one life. She lived in England and every year went to AnandPur Sahib in India to provide service (Seva) for God. She had got married with Randeep to take him to Europe and helping him to get marraige visa and all. 
 Last was Tarlochan: An auto-rickshaw driver from Bihar who later lost his entire happy family in one riot and later went to Europe to search for Job. 
 The writing was brilliantly refreshing. Fast Pace. But what I liked most is the, the description of Sikkhs. Being a Sindhi, I am accustomed during my childhood to go at Gurudwara near my home every week and attend Ardass, though with growing age this thing Vanished. I lived my entire childhood and its memories in those descriptions. 
 A good book. But I felt not Booker type material again due to fast pace narration and ORIGINATLITY which Booker book contains was missing that I felt.

DNF : the mix of Indian swearwords (I presume) and English, soon got on my nerves as I dislike books which attempt to portray accents and speech patterns.. 
 I read the last ten pages, and was glad I hadn't waded through the rest. 
 Not for me. Is another Man Booker Nominee , disappointment...
Just couldn't get into it or bring myself to finish it...

What kept putting me off is the language style, which I think is very essential for the spirit of a book. I heard that this book has an amazing plot and that it has received praise from Rushdie. Unfortunately, I wasn't able to make myself read beyond a hundred pages no matter how hard I tried to and then I had to eventually face it and give up.

This is an outstanding novel of the Indian, specifically the Sikh, experience of the UK, seen from the view point of the illegal or semi legal new arrivals. The lives of quiet desperation that result from the need to find work and somewhere to live while navigating a hostile, alien environment, are horribly fascinating. The drive to earn, support family back home, pay off debts and evade the authorities, leads to some pretty raw choices for these young people, adrift in the UK. 
 The writing is a challenge at times and to fully understand some of the language I turned to Sikhwiki for clarification. This has the effect of slowing the reader down, turning the novel into a careful, contemplative experience. This will stay with me, and impact on my thinking. Thank you Sunjeev Sahota, for a challenging and rewarding view into an unknown world.

Edna O'Brien once complained, "There is hardly any distinction between a writer and a journalist - indeed most writers are journalists." I couldn't help thinking of this as I read The Year of the Runaways by Sunjeev Sahota, one of the books shortlisted for the Booker this year. This is a closely-observed account of the lives of young Indian men trying to make a life for themselves in Britain, working illegally in the guise of students, contracting fake marriages to qualify for a visa, being exploited by employers without conscience, and living in conditions that would break anyone's spirit. It is, of course, a comment on the dog-eat-dog culture of modern Britain and the cruel caste system of India. There's no doubt that it's a realistic picture of the lives of illegal Indian immigrants to Britain, and we do sympathise with the young men who are its subject. 
 But it's a fact that should be universally acknowledged, though it isn't, that serious material, moving material, doesn't make a great novel. The Year of the Runaways is interesting in the way that a documentary is interesting; but there's no transformation through exceptional skill in the writing or psychological depth of characterisation. That's what makes it so surprising to me that it made it to the Man Booker shortlist. 
 It's a big, generous, social-realist novel about young Indians escaping the subcontinent for a perilous existence in Sheffield, trying to wrangle a new life in Britain through student visas and sham marriages, or taking a life-or-death risk with people smugglers, says The Guardian's article on the shortlist. Yes, it is, but its interest depends entirely on those themes and not their handling. 
 The young men, Randeep, Avdar and Tochi (Tarlochan), are representative of aspects of modern India. The early part of the book, after showing us the three at work in Britain, tells us the individual stories that have brought them there. Middle-class Randeep's government-employed father has had a nervous breakdown and he finds himself carrying the burden of his entire family, who face destitution if the father cannot work; Avdar, a struggling shopkeeper's son, needs to earn some money if he is to marry his middle-class girlfriend (Randeep's sister); and the Untouchable Tarlochan has lost his entire family in a caste-based massacre. Randeep has contracted a fake marriage with Narinder, a British girl whose Sikh faith inspires her to help him gain residency in Britain; Randeep hopes Narinder will come to feel something more for him, but it is Tarlochan she falls in love with. 
 Hammering us with the details of the characters' experiences, as Sahota does, doesn't convey their inner life. Their ages and backgrounds apart, Randeep and Avdar are almost indistinguishable from each other, and even the stronger, darker character Tarlochan is largely defined by the cruelty and injustice of the treatment of Untouchables. Narinder is the character with most light and shade, but it was not clear to me what we are to make of the change in her, other than the way it plays into the general theme of loss of innocence as the young characters learn the price of their naive dreams of life in Britain - as we always know they will, pretty much in the way it turns out in the book. 
 Sahota's prose is workmanlike, often pedestrian: 
 At lunchtime, they found their backpacks and joined the others sitting astride a large tunnel of aluminium tubing, newly exposed for the dig. Beside them, a tarpaulin acted as a windbreak. They slid off their helmets. Their hair was sopping. 
 Afterwards one or two turned up their collars and sank into a sleep. The rest decided on a cricket match to stay warm. They found a plank of wood for a bat and several had tennis balls handy. They divided into Sikhs and Muslins, three overs each. Gurpreet elected himself captain and won the toss. He put the Muslims in to bat. 
 There's a lot of writing like this; it's as if Sahota has decided that realism demands minute attention to detail, no matter how uninteresting the detail. Yes, the lives of the young men are a grind, often boring, repetitive and exhausting, but the detailing of it puts a serious drag on the book's momentum. 
 The narrative reels out a series of events that earnestly demonstrate different angles of the illegal immigrant problem: the dodgy employers, the swaggering British-born Indian thugs who act as standover men, the apparently sympathetic Indian shopkeepers who like and trust Tochi and then turn feral when they realise he's an Untouchable, the difficulty of getting medical care when you live in fear of deportation. I come back to Edna O'Brien's comment. Sahota is not a bad writer, and his story is a strong one in terms of human interest. It's a perfectly OK read. But shouldn't a novel be more than a group of moving stories, relevant to the problems of our time, bolted together into a narrative? Shouldn't the whole be more than the sum of the parts? What exactly it is that makes a novel more than the sum of the parts is the question; but you recognise it when you see it. I didn't find it here. If it wins the Booker it will be further evidence of the fashion for social-realist books in which what you write about is more important than how you write.

A moving but gruelling read. It took me a little time to get into the story and to really begin to feel for the different characters, but I'm glad I stuck with it. The story tells of illegal migrants from Indian trying to find work in the UK, but their stories are universal. They want what we all want - to be able to afford a roof over our heads, put food on the table for ourselves and our families, and to live our lives in security, without fearing our neighbours or our government.

book_b.title: Silence
book_b.user_review:
The story of this book is quite straightforward, in 17th century Japan Christians face persecution, two Jesuit priests head for Japan to find out what has happened to their mentor who, according to rumours, has apostatised and given up Christianity. Unless it had been for the film based on the book (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence...) made by my favourite director, Martin Scorcese, then I would never have been interested in reading this book. I am somewhat uncomfortable with subject of missionary activities; I don't like how some people think they are superior to others and have the moral right to go to other parts of the world to inform the locals that their ways are wrong, and they should give these beliefs and convert to a foreign faith. So, if a missionary goes to a foreign land where he finds he is not welcome by locals and is instead persecuted, this isn't something to be surprised about, and stories about such persecutions end up sounding like propaganda to promote the work of missionaries. 
 What makes this story stand out for me is that it raises a number of interesting questions, at the top of the list is: how a devoutly religious person, someone who has devoted their life's work to promoting their faith, can apostatise and turn again that faith? Another interesting question is: what makes anyone give up the faith they have been raised with and adopt a belief system which has arrived from abroad? And looking at things from the opposite point of view: how to go about de-converting those who have adopted a foreign faith? What I find so interesting about this story, something which may also explain its appeal to many other readers, is despite raising so many questions, the book doesn't seek to provide any answers to them, allowing the reader to do so instead, as a result, this book can have many interpretations and appeal to many different people. 
 I highly recommend this book as I'm sure everyone will find something of interest.

sample_reviews.review_text: One of the most compelling books on faith ever written and one of the most difficult to read.

I had been looking forward to reading this book for some time. I had high expectations going into it. While I liked it, I was not blown away by it as so many others were. The meat of the story is certainly one to be explored and I feel the author did it well. Maybe it was the translation that threw me off. I'm not sure. It will be one that I will read again - just to give it another chance. I do feel that it is something to be slowly digested and not rushed through. 
 I can say that it had me thinking about it days after I finished reading it.
Very bleak yet powerful book about underground Christian missionaries in medieval Japan.Soon to be a movie by Scorcese.

Endo writes well, and the book is memorable and sad. I gave it three stars based on how I "feel" about it, which is I'm glad I don't have to read it again. I was expecting the book to be pretty bloody but it isn't really. It's dismal though. Questions it raises include: what is faith? What does it mean to have faith or lose it? What good does it do people to believe? Is it worth it to be a missionary in a land that tortures new believers? What good is it to give people hope of an afterlife if their current life is miserable? Is God silent?
I tried really hard to get into this book but I just couldn't.

Ugh. I'll never get those hours back. 
 Some good moments, but plot never went anywhere. Protagonist: not my cup of tea.
Review will (possibly) follow after I have a chance to process this book. It wasn't an easy read.

I honestly expected to cry, I think I did the first time I read this. Maybe I've grown jaded in my old age. 
 Silence tells the story of Father Rodrigues, a Portuguese Jesuit missionary, as he goes to Japan to minister to the Christian population there after the official persecutions have begun and, more personally to Father Rodrigues, after Cristovao Ferriera has apostatized (real person, by the way). 
 And then he goes to Japan, suffers a lot, watches his flock suffer and wonders where God is in all this. It's a little soul crushing. Not that I know what soul crushing is seeing as I've never been hung upside down over a pit full of feces until I renounced my faith. 
 And about the ending: Father Rodrigues is captured but not tortured. Instead, some Japanese peasants who have already renounced the faith are tortured while Father is kept in a room next door so he can listen. Father Rodrigues agrees to apostatize if the others will be set free. In a similar situation, I'd like to think I'd do differently but what do I know of suffering? (Sighs dramatically) Now I need to go do something happy and life affirming.

This book is fictional but inspired by the lives of two Catholic priests who travelled to Japan in the 1600s to attempt to encourage secret believers in a country where Christianity was outlawed and Christians put to death when they refused to apostatize. I enjoyed reading about this time in history but this book troubled me on a number of levels and left me feeling like it was all wrong -- probably mostly because I don't feel that the God I love was represented in it at all. 
 I was troubled by the attitude of Rodrigues -- one of the priests from Portugal -- who believed he was the only hope for Japanese Christians and that they would be lost without him. Is God so small that he can't foster a growing faith in a community of people apart from the help of formal clergy? 
 Rodrigues seemed to me not to possess any true faith at all. He seemed rather to be on the mission for the adventure of it all, for the thrill of the challenge and to be seen as a hero and savior himself. 
 The common Japanese people and persecuted Christians in this story were treated like props. The priests nor the author seemed to find them worthy of exploration and knowing. And that broke my heart, for it is a prerequisite of mission that people are known and loved. 
 And the ending of this book was so disappointing. I don't believe Christ, as Rodrigues "heard", would trample to save the apostate believers. That view is so short-sighted and assumes that God does not have a greater purpose and a bigger story that he is writing that we get to be a part of. 
 This book did make me think about persecution more. I know of people today, in other countries where Christianity is outlawed, who are being tortured and are imprisoned for their faith. This issue is not isolated to the middle ages. It is very real and very current. I like to think that I would die for Christ before renouncing my faith. But it's very easy to say that from my comfortable, relatively secure life. Reading this book brought me closer to the realities of persecution and helped me to realize that I can't judge others who are in the arena, facing the pain and torture head on, from my position in the stands. 
 This book makes much of the silence of God. It's true that God doesn't immediately swoop in when his children go through hard times or are persecuted for him. But that doesn't mean he's not loving and good. And it doesn't mean he's not with them. I know that if I am ever in the position to be persecuted for my faith, God WILL be with me. I won't have to face it alone. And I believe he will strengthen me to endure. Because there is a greater purpose and a greater story than my life and whatever immediate pain or suffering I might face. 
 I hope that people who read this book know that Christianity and God are not well-represented in its pages. It is interesting for it's historical context, but apart from that, leaves much to be desired.

For whatever reason, I get very uncomfortable reading on the topic of religion, and this one was no different. But my uncomfortableness was a far cry from the shock and awe apparently felt by other reviewers of this book, which is about Portuguese Jesuit priests who, in the 1640s, travel to Japan on a mission to help the oppressed Japanese Christians and face religious persecutions. Perhaps my lackluster response is due to my Catholic school upbringing during which I heard such stories of martyrdom, persecution, and crucifixion daily in my religion classes. The only real surprise in the book for me was Father Rodriguez's arrogance and grandiosity. It put me off when he would wonder why his capture and "torture" weren't worse, like he needed the fan-fare and wanted the re-enactment of Christ himself if he were to be martyred. The priests of my upbringing were unassuming, soft-spoken, almost "silent." It also surprised me that the priests questioned why God was the silent one during these tragic times. This seems like a basic tenement of our faith to assume that apparent silence. It's called faith. That's not easy to embrace, but it shouldn't be a surprise to a priest. While I understand this book was a translation from Japanese, I also found the writing redundant and monotone. I'm clearly in the minority in my perceptions of this book, but it just wasn't for me.

reference_books.title: The Dog Stars
reference_books.review_text: Post-apocalypse novel where almost all remaining humans seem to be sadistic rapist/killers. Narrated by a nice-guy survivor who is holed up at a small airport in mountainous Colorado, maintaining a perimeter for nine years with a hard-ass tactician who has a big stockpile of weapons. Despite the description, it's thoughtful and doesn't focus on action but rather daily living and thoughts of the way things used to be. Kind of a sweet post-apocalypse novel. I liked it and at certain points thought about buying it as a present for a couple of relatives who've lived in that area of Colorado but it's not quite compelling enough to give as a gift. Better than "The Road," though.

reference_books.title: Testimony
reference_books.review_text: Three older star basketball players at a fancy private high school have sex with a drunken 14-year-old girl. A video recording surfaces. Lives are destroyed. The book sucked me in and held my attention. But two major problems made me dislike it. The event that triggered the "good" boy to participate in the gang rape certainly could have been believable, but the author never established why it would send him off the deep end. More problematic was the victim. Having her be a shallow "slut" -- there's no better way to describe how she's portrayed -- could've been an interesting jumping off point for discussions of consent, pressures on girls to be sexy but virginal, etc. But the author does nothing with the character except, from the very beginning, make the reader hate her for destroying the lives of these boys who had so much potential. (The author seems to be channeling a misogynist here. Another female character also gives into her lust and destroys everyone around her, too. And a third main female character is ball-busting nag.) Perhaps I could've lived with the victim being stupid and materialistic but then when the plot needed her to be, she was cunning and manipulative. The book did help me understand why schools rally around rapists, though. It's all about protecting tuition fees and alumni donations. Bechdel test: fail.

reference_books.title: Handle with Care
reference_books.review_text: People tend to hate Picoult's endings but I tend to like them so I ignored all the negative reviews of this one because Stephen King liked it. The story's good -- about a family having difficulties under the weight of a kid with brittle bone disease so her bones are always breaking, and the mom learns she can sue the obstetrician for "wrongful birth" for not alerting her to the disease at her 18-week ultrasound. But there's a subplot that could've been handled without a really absurd coincidence and the ending -- no spoilers here -- but let's just say it wouldn't have happened that way. Sure, there's a literary quality to it but at the expense of anything plausible. That said, I did race through the book and it brought up a lot of interesting ideas. Bechdel test: Pass.

reference_books.title: Reconstructing Amelia
reference_books.review_text: A teen girl dies at her school and her mother reconstructs the last days of her life by going through her emails and text messages. Generic writing. Decent plot but too many scenes where someone is about to reveal everything but then gets interrupted, as well as too many scenes where people must explain at length why they did something because no one would believe they could be so dumb. Bechdel test: pass.

reference_books.title: End of Watch (Bill Hodges Trilogy, #3)
reference_books.review_text: It's very good but it didn't top the first two, and that has to be the goal of the third book in a trilogy. I would've liked to see the mind-transfer plot taken further. There were no crazy memorable scenes that I'll remember a year from now (like the opening scene of the first book). That said, I'd read some good fan fiction about the surviving characters because they definitely are memorable. Bechdel test: Pass. Grade: B+

book_a.title: Tomboy: A Graphic Memoir
book_a.user_review: Graphic novel where Liz tells about her growing up preferring boy things and to literally be a boy and all the challenges not conforming to gender stereotypes presented in school. She perfectly captures what grade school and high school were like. Older women are key in her learning that she can still be a girl without liking the stuff society says girls should like. Bechdel test: Pass. Grade: A-

sample_reviews.review_text: A great graphic novel memoir. The author's exploration of the complexities of gender self expression as a kid-teen are mixed in to a coming of age story complete with fracturing friendships and first crushes.
Sweet quick graphic novel of a straight girl tom boy growing up in the 1990's.
Found the handwritten text and black/white drawings pretty jarring... Couldn't finish.

Sweet, funny, and poignant. This autobiographical comic tells Liz's story without pandering or over-explaining. This book was so good that I wanted to flip a table and run down the street pumping my arms in victory after I finished it.
Good stuff. I am not now nor have I ever been a tomboy, but--as with all good memoirs--you don't have to identify with this one to enjoy it.

If you can hang in there to page 240, where the book quickly wraps up and redeems itself in some ways, there are some gems of snark and storytelling througout. As someone who somewhat relates, and felt more "boylike" as a child, but never labeled myself a tomboy or anything else, it irks me when those who think they are challenging gender "norms" are perpetuating caricaturish stereotypes further by enforcing "girl things" and "boy things." Girl things being make up, dresses, shopping, pink, and boy things as reptiles, video games, tanks, etc. Here's my version of a culturally conventional "girl thing": having two x chromosomes. A culturally conventional "boy thing" is holding your penis in your hand while you pee. I do wish the revelation could have come sooner for the author, and am naively still surprised/disappointed these attitudes persisted among people 30 years ago, much less today. An easy choice that opens itself for a book club discussion.
A positive message about gender norms, but overall not that interesting. Just didn't engage me.

Prince reminded me so much of a dear friend, it was a bit difficult to read. I often wonder if she struggled the way Prince did, and I just didn't see it. 
 I'm glad that Prince was able to learn to understand that there is so much more to making up your gender, your life, and your experiences than the fact you refuse to wear dresses.
This pretty sharply touched my middle school soul in the most sincere, relatable way.

This was really fun to read. Anyone that grew up with a complicated gender identity (so really, anyone, if we're being honest) can likely find something in here to appreciate. Think John Porcellino drawing style meets Julia Wertz confusion/life angst. Good for growing girls especially.

book_b.title: One Kick (Kick Lannigan, #1)
book_b.user_review: This book is definitely more interesting to describe than read. The star of the world's most-downloaded child porn videos -- made between the ages of 5 and 10 -- grows up to be a beautiful weapons and martial arts expert. Soon after her 21st birthday, she is tapped by a mysterious man, who flies around in a private helicopter, to find a kidnapped boy and his pedophile abductor. This is a world where pedophiles have secret off-shore bank accounts and make 10s of millions of dollars selling video downloads of children being raped. The FBI has a giant screen TV with a global map covered with hundreds of lighted points showing in real-time where someone is downloading images of our heroine being raped as a girl. The book is horrendous -- and I know Cheryl Strayed only gave it a stellar blurb on the cover because she's BFFs with the author -- but one part that intrigued me were the alternating chapters told from the perspective of the heroine when she was a child remembering the good times with her abductor, in between being raped and locked in a dark cabinet. One of the stranger books I've finished. No social commentary, just bloodless (and bloody) angst and a racing plot. Bechdel test: pass.

sample_reviews.review_text:
A new series by Chelsea Cain, and another fantastically satisfying beginning to a mystery/thriller series. This story is a little more main-stream crime involving kidnapping, but the uniqueness of the story comes from the uniqueness of Kick as a protagonist. Her past puts her directly involved with this case, and her character development really propels this story forward in an exciting and intriguing way. I am very interested to see where this story goes next! 
 Just one more year! *sigh*

I recieved this book as a Goodreads Giveaway.This was a fantastic book, about a woman that is abducted as a child.She ends up returning to her family but the emotional toll the abduction takes on her gets channeled into positive/negative avenues.This is the first story in what appears to be numerous books to follow.Great Job Chelsea Cain

Kick has been through a lot...but her past horrors only add to her determination to prevent the same harm from happening to others. It seems she will do almost anything to save a life, even if it puts her own mind and body in jeopardy. 
 I loved Chelsea Cain's Archie & Gretchen series....and I was worried that a new series may not hold my interest. Although this novel has toned down some of the "gore" found in the A&G series, there is still plenty...and it's all centered around a truly awful subject, which this author handled very well. The characters are complex, and the ending promises more to come. 
 A good, fast read !
Excellent book! I read the book over one day and didn't want to put it down.

I love Ms. Cain's other series with Gretchen and Archie. This wasn't bad, but not as amazing as her other series. I found the writing in this one more simple, if that makes sense. I will try another Kick Lannigan book to check out how it is evolving.

I obtained this ARC at BEA14, in exchange for an honest review. 
 Cain's latest novel (thankfully the first in a new series) was high octane, unputdownable, darkly suspenseful fun. Kick is a prickly but empathetic character, a young woman who is wise beyond her years due to her horrible childhood history. Instead of wallowing in her nightmarish past, she uses what she learned about the darkness men are capable of as motivation to save other children from being subjected to her fate. A fast read, I hated getting to the end because I really, really, really wanted more Kick, more Bishop, more triumph over evil.

Well, I like Kick and James and eventually Bishop! I think Bishop's introduction was wrong but he is a damaged soul too but not believable at the first meeting. I enjoyed the book, not as much as the "heart" series but I look forward to the character development in the next one. Very well written and a difficult subject matter so I applaud Chelsea for writing about it and making survivors kick-asses!

Eh, this book was okay at best. My largest problem was two-fold, and with the main character. First of all I didn't really like her. I didn't connect with her and found her a bit annoying. Second, as someone who is supposed to be kind of kick butt - as in she's good with a gun and knows self defense and martial arts - she sure seems to need a man to save her quite a bit. Seriously??? 
 The plot was okay, the characters kind of flat and need more life.
A pure adrenaline rush. A book I couldn't put down. Kick Lannigan is superb and someone you would want on your side. I cried many times reading this book and it truly is one book I will never forget.
Just not very good at all

reference_books.title: The Looming Tower: Al-Qaeda and the Road to 9/11
reference_books.review_text: 4 stars= liked it alot, but I did not LIKE it...I was informed by it.

reference_books.title: What I Saw and How I Lied
reference_books.review_text: Really liked how the book shows how a young, trusting girl comes to see the adult world through her experiences in this book. Except possibly for one scene on the beach, the content is appropriate for middle school readers. I think most YA fiction is really attractive to adult female readers because of the emotional and observant nature of the characters. This book is a good of example of YA that adult females would like.

reference_books.title: The Maytrees
reference_books.review_text: Observant, objective, and quiet. Sneaks up on you.

reference_books.title: The Handmaid's Tale
reference_books.review_text: Brilliant!!! Perched carefully in the future which is our past, Atwood's terrifying look at religious government in America is startling and insightful.

reference_books.title: Divergent (Divergent, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Liked it and thought I would read the sequel, but have not yet. Good YA novel that appeals to general market.msharesmthemes with HUNGER GAMES and other dystopia. Set in Chicago, it is fun to identify locations like Navy Pier and the great marsh (Lake Michigan). Female protagonist always appeals to me.

book_a.title: James Potter and the Hall of Elders' Crossing (James Potter, #1)
book_a.user_review: Tails is on my to-read list. Spin-off city & hallelujah ! Now can someone write about Harry's father, James? Or the Weasley's or...endless possibilities.

sample_reviews.review_text: i think i put too much faith into this guy to make another harry potter book and it just wasnt the same...i didnt finish it

Vse pak chovek't si e napravil truda da ia napishe. S tova komentar't mi prikliuchva. Dobre de, shche 
 dobavia, che se chete lesno i b'rzo. Da niama ochakvaniia, che shche se nauchi neshcho ot neia. Spokoino bikh 
 mogla da mina i bez neia.

Even now, I wish that there was a half-star system on Goodreads. This book was well written and it was wonderful to step back into the wizarding world, but the original series will always be better, in my heart. I still loved this book though, so it deserves the 5 stars I gave it.
I loved it! I know JK didn't write it, but it feels just like she continued where she left off. It is excellent and perfect. Can't wait to read the others...

As a piece of fan fiction, this is an extremely impressive book. As a continuation of Harry Potter, I feel that it fell short of my expectations. Most of the novel followed Rowling's original descriptions of the magical world and Hogwarts. There were some instances that didn't quite fit. For example in the description of one of the classes it was said that there was a fifth year, in the same class as James... Which I find highly unlikely. But in general I enjoyed the overall story. For me the story, even though it was interesting, didn't really pick up until halfway through.

I was skeptical of how another author might be able to extend the adventures of Harry Potter. These are big shoes to fill, after all. But someone on Twitter recommended the book/series so I thought I'd give it a try. 
 I loved the way the book began. Lippert immediately grabbed my attention and began reeling me in. He imaginatively introduced changes to Hogwarts that allowed the story to be believable and go in many new directions. 
 I loved part of the new plot with explaining how magic works, weaving that in to the resolution. I was a tiny disbelieving having first years and fifth years in the same class, but that was a minor criticism. 
 My biggest disappointment was Mr. Dolohov. That part comes out of left field and was not an effective element of the story. Yes, it explains how that part happened, but I'd rather have seen the author resolve it more coherently with the rest of the book. It just felt tacked on to an already great story.

It's books like this that make me wish I wasn't so stubborn about finishing things that I have started. 
 I used to read a LOT of fan fiction. And I mean a LOT. All the big ones - the Draco Trilogy, A Year Like None Other, maya's stuff... So, then I came across this on GoodReads and saw the huge number of downloads and the millions of positive reviews and thought: why not? It's been a while, but I still love Harry Potter, and this could be a nice bit of fun. 
 How wrong I was. 
 It has taken me so long to get through because I had to force myself to read it. It was so disappointing. I feel mean writing such a negative review, but I always strive to be honest. This felt like the sort of fan fiction written by quite young American teens, wanting to insert lots of their own stuff into JK's world in a way that doesn't really fit. Why did we have to have the American exchange thing? It didn't fit. Why were James and co, as first years, so incredibly powerful? (accepting the part about Ralph's ridiculous wand). Why were they suddenly learning arithmancy and divination in first year? 
 It just didn't sit right. If you're going to write fan fiction, you have to strike a balance. It is your story, but it is not your world. Don't mess with what works. And JK's world works. 
 The writing was mediocre at best, cringey at worst. The characters were mostly one-dimensional. But it was mostly the STORY that got me: it was so unrealistic, and just did NOT hang together. These are 11 year olds we're talking about! For crying out loud, why did such huge and drastic stuff happen in what is meant to be the FIRST book in a series of seven? Where to go? And why was James involved in so much of the big decision making? Just because his father is Harry Potter? 
 I apologise to the author for my negativity; I do feel guilty. The best part about this book was the illustrations on the chapter pages. Those, and the relief I feel that I have finally finished it and don't have to read it anymore.

book_b.title: Sarah's Key
book_b.user_review: Really made me think about how the personal events of history can be lost and forgotten. Wish the author would have been a better writer though.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I appreciated the info about the Vel' d'Hiv' roundup during WWII, but I didn't care for the simplistic, chick-lit romance style of writing. 
 Edited to add: Romance chick-lit is my least favorite genre so that no doubt affected my opinion. I would have preferred to novel to focus entirely on Sarah's story.

This book was about an American woman who has lived 20 years in France. She's assigned an article about the Vel' d'Hiv that occurred during WWII, where the French police arrested more than 13,000 Jewish residents that were eventually sent to concentration camps. The other half of the story was told by a young Jewish girl who was part of the "roundup." 
 The portion told by the young girl was very touching and thought provoking. However, I found that the part told in current times felt a little like chick lit. Obviously, their stories intertwine throughout the novel, but I just couldn't get over the writing style. 
 Overall, I'm glad I read the book, as I was totally unfamiliar with the Vel' d'Hiv. It still amazes me how little we know about the events that surround one of the most horrific atrocities that has ever occurred.
very well done.

Wow. What an incredible story about such a terrible event, which most people have never even heard of. Beware reading this in public--you will cry! 
 I was lucky enough to read this book while visiting Paris on a school trip, and we were staying mere blocks from where the Vel d'Hiv stood as well as the current memorial. I finished the book sitting in the grass behind it, which was incredibly surreal. I was also able to walk down the street fictional Sarah lived on in Le Marais (Jewish Quarter), which was also crazy. Definitely recommend this!!!
I appreciated learning about another atrocity that occurred during the Nazi occupation o Paris. Sarah's story was gut-wrenching.

I am clearly in the minority, but I simply can't understand what people loved about this book. The writing was terrible, the story (which should have been fascinating, terrifying, moving, and filled with tension) was dull, and the whole novel was incredibly predictable. I only stuck it out because I was listening to the audiobook (and therefore could not skim to the end), and because I couldn't believe it wouldn't improve. The reader didn't help--she did the text no favors with her slow and whiny narration.
Sad and predictable.

I thoroughly enjoyed this book. It's set in two different time periods in the same apartment in France. In 1942 a Jewish family is forced out of their apartment by the French Police. Left behind, hiding in a wall in the youngest child. Fast forward to present day where a young family is about to remodel their apartment. 
 The book switches back to each family. Amazing and incredibly sad story.

This story alternates between a horrific incident in 1942 (France WWII)and the present. Thousands of Jews were rounded up and imprisoned in the Velodrome d'Hiver before being sent to Auschwitz. Yes, in France, from France, and by French authorities. The incident in the past is told through the eyes of a ten-year old Jewish girl who locks her little brother in a hidden cupboard, promising to return for him when it's safe. This part of the story is riveting, horrific, and poignant. Sixty years later, an American journalist becomes obsessed with the story and sets out to uncover what happened. This part of the book isn't nearly as interesting/well-written. But if you are drawn to Holocaust stories, incredibly moving. It's a story that should be told and remembered.
Meh.
