reference_books.title: Magic Breaks (Kate Daniels, #7)
reference_books.review_text:
4.5 stars 
 Magic Breaks is what we have all been waiting for, finally coming face to face with Roland. Everything has been leading us here this whole time. I was so pleasantly surprised with the way everything went down. All I'm really going to say about it here though is that, everything we have learned of him thus far did not fully prepare me for this first meeting. He is maybe even more a mystery to me than he was before! And I have a feeling I'm going to love figuring him out. 
 The way Kate handled him was a true testament to just how far she has grown throughout this series. She has found herself having to deal with certain things in different ways now that she isn't alone anymore. We've seen that for a few books now, but the way she handled finally seeing her father, the one person most of her life was centered around destroying at any cost, that was the true test of just how far she has come. I was impressed. 
 This book has the same sarcastic humor that we love and expect from this series. There wasn't as much Curran in this one, but it was ok. It made sense that Kate go through some of these things on her own, just knowing he would be there was enough. Also, when Curran was there, HOLLY HELL did things get interesting. I was completely shocked at the end with his big announcement! 
 That's what I love about this series, and the construction of it. This somehow caught me off guard, I wasn't expecting this at all, but it totally made sense once it happened. I could go back 3-4 books and see the seeds of this decision being planted. There were quite a few things that happened spanning over multiple books in this series that lead to this huge thing. It's glorious. These authors know how to lay down some serious ground work. I've come to see just how much even all the seemingly little things all mean something here. They are all working towards something big. 
 I really look forward to seeing what happens next. I honestly have no idea what to expect. So many big changes in this addition to the series, if you haven't picked it up yet, do yourself a favor and get on that! You won't be disappointed.

reference_books.title: Beautiful Disaster (Beautiful, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Wow. I have to start of by saying I started this book with some pretty low expectations. I have read a bunch of friend reviews on it, and it was pretty much split down the middle with people either loving it or hating it, there wasn't really any middle ground. I don't know what it was, but I couldn't put this down! I started Beautiful Disaster in the afternoon and I was not able to sleep until I finished it....which ultimately resulted in me being up until 4:45am devouring this. Any book that keeps me enthralled like that is well deserving of 5 stars. 
 The thing that really has me flummoxed is why so many people thought Travis was such a douche. Was he possessive and overly jealous...definitely. But that's about all I can fault him for. I felt like, although he didn't come right out and say it, it was apparent how much he cared for Abby from pretty much the very beginning. And I'm sorry but in my opinion, him sleeping with all the girls in the beginning.....who cares?! He's an adult, and he made it clear he had no intentions of being in a relationship with these women. They were consenting adults that knew his reputation and still threw themselves, spread eagle, on his couch! I feel no sympathy for them. Travis wasn't perfect, it was apparent all along that he had some issues, but the love he had for Abby was truly undeniable. I just don't get it, I have read plenty if other books with male characters with these same possessive traits, and everyone thought they were amazing, I really don't feel like Travis was any worse than these guys! And I have to say, I felt bad for him through a good portion of this book. Abby was infuriating! I will admit that when he got the tattoos, I was a little like....whoa there.....pump the brakes! Too soon, Travis, too soon. 
 Abby...oh Abby. I wanted to shake you so many times! She fained ignorance so many times, just so she wouldn't have to come to terms with the fact that she did truly want Travis. She knew how he felt! She just didn't want to admit it because she thought she needed some boring, cookie cutter, preppy boy, so she could pretend that her past never happened and that she was a good girl. No man makes a bet with the hopes of winning a month of you living with him because you're such a good friend. You don't sleep in the same bed as a man continuously, cuddle with him, grind on him, and spend every free minute together because you want to be each others friend. It was so frustrating! Every time she would go on a date with Parker and come home to a waiting, and pissy Travis, she just couldn't figure out what was bothering him....WHAT?! Are you serious?! Ummm, he's jealous dumbass! Because he wants you....in ways that are definitely beyond friendly. Ohhhhh and then at the end of the bet, when she finally acts on her true feelings and then leaves him without a word!!!!!!! What a hypocrite!! She was so disgusted with the way he treated women in the beginning and then she pulls that garbage?! Knowing that he wanted more....she was worse than him! Ok....now that I have that out of my system lol. Really though,the last half of the book, Abby wasn't so bad, there were a few more times I wanted to shake some sense into her, but it wasn't as bad as the beginning of the book.....mostly. 
 Sheply and America were both great secondary characters. They added a little balance to the extremity of Abby and Travis. America was a prertty great friend to Abby. She held her tongue a lot and was supportive, but she also told Abby some hard truths, and that's not a fun task but it is what a real friend does. Sometimes you need to hear the truth, even when it's not pretty. Sheply was also a wonderful person. He put up with a lot from Travis over the years, and still had the guy's back. I also LOVED the Maddox boys! How could you not fall for those ruffians?! They were like the lost boys and Abby was their Wendy. She was this young girl who swooped in and was strong enough to take some of their shit and sweet enough to give them some of the mothering that they so desperately longed for. I also enjoyed Abby's past, it was a lot more colorfull than I could have even imagined! It was an exciting twist for sure! 
 This is probably one of the longest reviews I have ever wrote, but I just had to get it all out!! This book had its hooks in me from start to finish, and I really enjoyed every minute. It was worth being up until 5am and being exhausted today!! And that's really saying something! I will definitely be looking into other books by Jamie McGuire!

At the end of the day I'm just glad that this book was free and I didn't invest anything more than my time into it.

Originally posted at http://smexybooks.com/2012/10/review-... 
 Favorite Quote: "I had a price to pay for my choices." 
 In Low Town, where elves, fairies, trolls, werewolves, and vampires are happily walking among humanity, everything has its price. Gage just wants to run his tattoo parlor and live a quiet fuss free life, but this former warlock is finding out that what he wants and what he'll get are two very different things. Leaving the Ivory Tower, where the warlocks and witches of the world rule with an iron fist, has left Gage with a huge target on his back as no one EVER leaves the Ivory Tower alive. Gage was allowed to leave only if he never uses his magic for anything but self defense, however, circumstances cause Gage to break this rule on many different occasions. When Gage finds himself hunted by his former mentor, the grim reaper, a mob boss, and a werewolf, Gage hopes that with a little help from his friends, he may just live to see tomorrow. 
 Angel's Ink is the first installment in a new urban fantasy series by bestselling author Jocelyn Drake. I adored Ms. Drakes Nightwalker series and was excited to see her penning a new and obviously different type of series. Angel's Ink has an interesting premise and introduces us to a supernatural world where everything and everyone lives together; though not necessarily in harmony. As this is heavily character driven, I found the world building suffers as it tries to complete against the overwhelming and convoluted amount of subplots presented. I would have enjoyed learning more about the world presented, the war that brought this world to where it's at now, and more about the various groups of supernaturals that we are introduced to. 
 Told in the first person, our main protagonist, Gage, the sole proprietor of the Asylum Tattoo Parlor, has a huge secret. A former apprentice warlock who didn't agree with the cruel indicts of the warlock/witch community, he left that world only to find himself under a death sentence. His life is contingent upon his promise to never use his magic in any shape or form except for self defense. As Gage struggles to remain under the Ivory Tower's radar, his altruistic nature places him on the path of no return when he fulfills a young girl's dying wish with a tattoo. Gage inks the tattoo with a special ink mixture that he hopes will make her last few days comfortable. Only, the ingredients he uses have a catastrophic effect and suddenly Gage has to find this girl before he finds himself on the chopping block. 
 Gage is an interesting protagonist. His backstory and characterization reminds me of calmer, younger, Harry Dresden. Gage is a loner. His history requires him to not form lasting attachments to anyone yet he is fiercely loyal to his friends, regardless of the outcome. A former warlock who is at the mercy of a council deadset on erasing him, he has a natural altruistic nature that constantly pits him against various opposing factions. He only wants to be left alone, but Gage's inability to say no to anyone, conflicts with his own agenda. While it goes a long way to building Gage's character, it is also a cause for concern concerning the storyline. We are given multiple conflicts that sends us into various directions as Gage's decisions set off chain reactions, causing him even further problems. I did have some problems connecting to him. While I enjoyed his thoughts and actions, there was a small part of me that felt like he was ambiguous. I did enjoy that in dealing with a male protagonist, we aren't made to suffer through overly emotional angst or breakdowns. Gage deals with things in a forthright manner and that is blessing these days when emotional bloodletting and closed off protagonists are the main ingredient of most genres. 
 There is the beginning of a romance between Gage and Trixie that progresses slowly throughout the storyline. Enjoyable in that I like seeing Gage with someone, but in some ways it feels forced. I would have liked to have waited longer in the series to build up the tension for the readers. You may get the feeling that you're missing something but there is a novella before this installment that actually sets this storyline up. 
 A strong personable secondary cast adds depth and understanding to the plotlines and Gage's life. Trixie, an elf, and Bronx, a troll, are both employees of Gage's and fast becoming his best friends. Both Bronx and Trixie have what I suspect are complicated back stories, though only Trixie's is revealed in depth. Gideon, Gage's handler from the Ivory Tower, is an enigma. His constant threats and bullying Gage over using magic outside of self defense are in line with his job but we are given hints that lead us to believe there is more to all of this than we or Gage think. 
 Plenty of dry humor and wit is sprinkled throughout the book as we learn more about vampire OCD, and a certain werewolf conflict presents itself in a unique and funny manner. As stated earlier, there is a plethora of subplots in here that cascades over you as you try and sort out exactly what the main conflict is. I enjoyed the various subplots though we aren't allowed to spend much time with any of them as Drake keeps Gage jumping, trying to stay alive and one step ahead of everyone. Various one scene characters are introduced that clue us into future storylines, which only adds to the confusion in my opinion. Some conflict(s) which intertwine and play off each other towards the end, are somewhat resolved, all in predictable manners. I really can't say more without spoiling but needless to say, this book is a set up book all the way, though more in characterization and storylines rather than the usual world building aspect. 
 Regardless of my feelings of misgiving, I did find the overall presentation and introduction interesting and engaging enough to warrant a continuation when book two releases. There are two novellas that predate this release and a third novella that happens after this book. The first two novellas introduce us to Trixie and Bronx and tell us how they came to work for Gage. In the anthology, Blood By Moonlight (releases Oct 23, 2012), we get a small but action packed story after Angel's Ink. 
 Overall Rating: C+

Angel's Ink is a story about Gage, the former warlock, living in hiding from the tyrannical witches and warlocks that rule over all from the Ivory Towers. Gage owns a tattoo parlor, where he and his two employees, an imposing troll and a gorgeous elf, ink all sorts of humans and magical creatures. 
 This is a fast paced urban fantasy, unfortunately it is so fast paced that it's difficult to keep up with all the times our main character is being threatened, beaten half to death, or experiences something so extraordinary that the plot takes yet another turn. 
 I had very little time to make up my own ideas about where the story would go before yet another thing happened and I am hoping, for the story's sake, that the loose ends and that many of characters will reappear and clear things up in the following books of the series. 
 I will probably not read the rest of the series, as I failed to be captured by any of the characters and can not find it in me to wonder what will happen to them. 
 Not a complete waste of space but nothing I would recommend.

I got an uncorrected proof version at San Diego Comic Con a couple of years back, recently found it in my huge to read pile. 
 There are some spoilers below, nothing too blatant I hope, but beware. 
 Overall I enjoyed the book, the writing was fluid, the action was pretty much non-stop and the author did a good job of wrapping in some humor. It was an extremely quick read at 338pgs, and was compelling enough to return to immediately after having to put it down so I could get my standard 8 hours of sleep. 
 Despite the interesting take of magic application through tattooing, the structure felt entirely too much like other well known urban fantasy novels. Synopsis: Wizard has personal issues/interpersonal issues, has warden to keep him in line, wizard is being manipulated by everyone in the known world, wizard does something he said he would never do only to find his ass in a sling, etc etc etc. I appreciate that there is a mould for urban fantasy and that there are authors that have blazed that trail prior (Harrison, Armstrong, Butcher, etc). And I really do not like reading reviews that reference comparisons of these previous authors, yet here I am doing that exact comparison. I just don't feel like this story is enough to stand up on it's own against those that have come before it, there are just way too many parallels. 
 Was it entertaining? Yes. (Thus the three stars) 
 Was the magic usage new and fresh? New application, fresh not so much. There was a lack of development into the magical world other than slight knowledge as to who can and cannot sense (feel and/or smell) magic. Basic background into the Warlocks and Witches, but nothing much for any of the other magic users. 
 Was the overall story line fresh - No. Here I have to maintain that it was not, and I wanted much more from this novel than what it gave. 
 Character development - this was decent, none of the characters feel flat. At times they were hard to picture some of them, specifically Simon. Initially he started out much younger in my mind which conflicted with later prose where the author was referring to him as an old man. 
 Story Arc - decent webbing of character arcs and the over all story arc, this is actually built well that it flows easily, and sets the author up nicely for more novels. However this is where I nit pick and say that this feels entirely too ripped from previously published novels, that the author cut and pasted here. Nothing feels new. 
 Prose - this reads more like YA than I think it should; given the sex scene. 
 The other problem that I have is that the some of the character names at way too similar to others already in the urban fantasy genre specifically the use Atticus and Simon. If I had been the publisher I would have pushed for those to be changed.

This book is not badly written, and the characters all feel real and have realistic motivations. The the plot... 
 He gets in trouble/involved with 
 1. the wizards 
 2. death 
 3. the tattoo board 
 4. the elven king 
 5. the mob 
 6. lilith 
 7. an underground sect of wizards 
 8. a dragon collector 
 9. a witch turned into an animal 
 and more! 
 It seems like the author was trying to set up every single sequel she could imagine, whilst giving us as little to go with, plot-wise, in this book. 
 For example the romance: he works with this elf chick. He likes her, she likes him, they flirt. At least, we're told they've been flirting for the last few years. Then, suddenly, they have sex! I was super surprised that there was nothing major leading up to it, no awkward talks. They almost sorta kiss once, and then BAM! 
 I will not be picking up the next ones, which have been so obviously telegraphed in there.

It's always exciting when a favorite author starts a new series, but also a bit worrisome. There was no need for worry though because Angel's Ink blew me away. I loved the characters, the world and the writing from the first page. Jocelynn Drake brought this new world to life for me. The characters are complex, witty, and smart. She didn't hold back in this first full length story of the series. Sometimes an introduction to a new series will tease the reader to the point of frustration, but Angel's Ink gives us insight into the characters and their situations without leaving us hanging. It's solid urban fantasy much like The Dresden Files, but fans of paranormal romance will love it too. If you like Kim Harrison, Vicki Pettersson and Karen Chance I think you'll truly enjoy Angel's Ink.

Mediocre at best. The plot line was interesting as was the world but things felt rushed and far from masterfully written. The surprise sex scene in the middle felt unneeded, sudden and out of place. Got this in a humble bundle and glad I didn't pay full price. I won't be looking for the other books.

book_b.title: Brightest Kind of Darkness (Brightest Kind of Darkness, #1)
book_b.user_review:
3.5 Stars 
 That was an interesting book. It reminded me a lot of that movie, Final Destination. The first one though, when everything was fresh and surprising and totally original. That's how I felt after reading Brightest Kind of Darkness. It was a super interesting story line, with some pretty interesting characters. 
 I liked Nara, she seemed like a brave and kind person. I think her family is made up of some colorful people and I think a lot more about them will be revealed in the following books. Ethan was super cool. He was all dark, mysterious and tortured. I really liked that he was really never an ass, he might have been quiet or reserved but he didn't follow the typical male chauvinist bad boy mold that so many books put out there now. He was always sweet, caring and genuine, he just didn't let everyone know it all the time. I can't wait to find out more about what Ethan's powers are and where they come from! He was super interesting and Some of the stuff he saw was chilling. It makes me want to start reading the next book immediately!

sample_reviews.review_text:
4.5 Stars 
 "You know that feeling of deja vu people talk about? I live it. Every. Single. Day." 
 This book is about a 16 year-old girl who can predict her next day through dreams. Nara Collins lives her day twice and she finds it boring. One night before she went to sleep she wished for just one "surprising" day... she woke up the next day regretting her wish and decided to do something to prevent her dream to happen. 
 I read this book for a reading challenge that I joined and I wasn't expecting much about it. I thought it was just another YA paranormal book, but I was wrong! I had a hard time putting it down. It sucked me in after reading a couple of chapters. I loved the plot, the writing style, the pacing, the characters... I think I liked almost everything about it, LOL! 
 Nara isn't your typical YA heroine. She's tough, independent and athletic. She's not perfect though. When she stopped dreaming her future we learned that she's misusing her gift...she started failing her classes, not performing well as a soccer goalie, and to top it off, her relationship with her best friend became shaky. Through all of that stuff, there's one guy who unexpectedly became her ally. Ethan Harris is a mystery to everyone. He has a bad reputation and keeps to himself until she met Nara. They became good friends and later developed into something more. The chemistry between this two is undeniable, they are just perfect for each other! *sigh* As they get to know each other, their secrets are revealed one by one. 
 The mystery is one of the best things in this book...*note: AVOID READING SPOILERS!* it will make you want to read more. Also, the twists in the plot and the action will keep you on the edge of your seat! There's one thing I didn't like on this book though --- Nara's friends, including Lainey. I think I'm more hurt and annoyed than Nara when Lainey believed Sophia about the whole Jared thing. The way they turned their backs on her when she wasn't performing well on their soccer games made my blood boil. And the pranks...arrgh, thank God for Ethan Harris! 
 Anyway, I am so glad that I have a copy of book 2 handy because the book ended abruptly, there were a lot of questions left unanswered. I immediately jumped to Lucid as soon as I hit the last page of The Brightest Kind of Darkness. I had to find out what happens next! If you plan on reading this, make sure you buy Lucid too. =) 
 This book is highly recommended to readers who like action romance and mystery on their YA books. =)

This was pretty good. I liked that the main'ers had seperate issues. There are no vampires and garbage. The male lead isn't freaky possessive and threatening. It felt really complete, not too short or too long. probably a little dark for the tweenagers. Not a lot o laughs. K, maybe none laughs.

I promise to be brutally honest with my opinion, but it should not be taken as fact. Any reader should read it for themselves, before they decide if this book has any merit or not. Do not judge this book biased solely on my opinion. If you do, you might miss out on a great read. You never know. It could happen. 
 1. Strong Main Character/ Female Heroine: Nara was just your average girl, until she started seeing her immediate future in her dreams. Her life really changes in a big way, when she interferes and that is when the fun truly begins. Nara is a caring, loving person and I cannot imagine a teenager like her in the real world. No one can be that selfless all of the time. She is always concerned about other people more than herself. This aspect of her personality makes her unbelievable at times, because you would aspect her to be a little selfish at times. I mean, we are all just a little and having daddy issues does not count as being selfish. It counts as being emotionally hurt by someone who was close to you at some point in your life and now you are questioning that person's motives for contacting you after so much time has passed. I can truly relate to that and I had a great guy like Nora does to help me keep my life in one piece. She also has a friend who has her back. Well, most of the time, but what real friendship does not have its dramas. Nara is strong, but weak. A perfect Bella Swan, but unlike Bella, Nara fights for herself and her Fate. She does not allow herself to lose anything, including her dreams. She fights for the people she loves and the things she wants out of life. She is not going to be cheated by a man, this Fate. She stole my heart with her relate-ability and her strong human connection to life. 4 out of 5 stars 
 2. Strong Minor Characters: Ethan is the best hawt minor character in the world with problems his own to discover in the next installment. [Which I definitely will be reading, because this author has captured two characters so perfectly while keeping one the lead and the other the supporting actor; however I believe that this author has also made it so that readers would feel a strong connection to both of the characters. At least, I felt it.] He is mysterious and intriguing. He excites my fancy, but somehow makes the reader feel a bit distanced from him, like how he distances himself from Nara. His personality and character demand my attention. Lainey is Nara's best friend. She is funny and cool, although she was really selfish. It's like Nara was too selfless and Lainey is too selfish. The author could have balanced the two better than she had seeming as how this whole book is about keeping the balance. They go through hardships and are reunited. I just wish that the reader would have known more about her at the end of the book. For Nara and Lainey to meet up at least after the whole thing with Ethan, would have resolved some underlining issues for me, but hopefully they are resolved when the next book begins. 4 out of 5 stars 
 3. The Setting: I found the setting to be very interesting, especially when Nara experiences the darker dreams. The whole scenes are so vivid. I know how hard it is to write really emotional, heart stopping scenes and this author did a terrific job at it. All the places were believable. I also had a sense of deja vu like I had been to these places before. It is a weird feeling, but I think, the author wants you to experience these weird feelings to better understand the book. Although, I wish there was a little less school, but that's just me. 4 out of 5 stars 
 4. The Plot: I love the plot of this whole story. This whole story is based on this girl and her dreams. She has a natural gift to alter Fate and uses her gift. Fate does not like this and fights back, which is really ironic and humorous. In Greek tragedies, no one can escape their fate or fight it. Fate always wins in the end, but this time...Maybe, it won't. Nara fights against her fate and is unwilling to back down from the fight, even when the person she loves most tells her to stop interfering. Interfering maybe the best thing Nara can do to protect herself and save her own life. I also like how this plot leads into an entirely new one about Ethan. I just wish that Nara's life and her secrets were not so tidied up at the end. 4 out of 5 stars 
 5. The Artwork: The cover is very beautiful and eye-catching. It was the reason why I started reading the book; however, I have seen more beautiful covers, but this one caught my attention as well. 4 out of 5 stars 
 6. The Writing: There is not a lot of annoying grammar or editing mistakes in the book, so I can really concentrate on the writing style of the author, which is very unique and distinct. The author has a distinctive writing style that allows the reader to sympathize and feel close to not one, but two characters simultaneously. The reader can feel close to Nara and to Ethan. At times, the reader may even detect the mysteriousness of Ethan's actions that signify that he has been keeping something significant from Nara all throughout the book and in the end, still does not tell her. The mystery and darkness that this author creates is effortless and beautiful. She gives a whole new meaning to the Brightest Kind of Darkness. 5 out of 5 stars 
 7. The Dialogue: I find the dialogue a little disbelieving, forced, stilted, and phony at times, but in the whole, it seems to flow with how real teenagers act and talk. Certain scenes in the book had me laughing because of how stilted the dialogue was, especially with Sophia and Jared. This situation, I felt, was the worst dialogue between all the characters in the history of books. It was awkward and not well scripted. It did not seem especially real to me, just something that took up valuable space in the novel. If these scenes were omitted, yeah, there would be less crazy drama, but the novel would have the perfect dialogue. 3 out of 5 stars 
 This novel gets a perfect 4, for being just so ah-mazing! It was a really great book that was very unique, but did not let you down or make you feel disappointed. It leaves you with a craving in your mind for the second book and I need to score the second book before I detox from the high this novel has left me in.
Very cliched with cliched romance and damsel in distress bah:{ {starts vomiting and gagging} Quite painful took me four days to read.

Originally reviewed on Hello, Chelly. 
 The good: What drew me to the book was the concept - the idea that this girl knows her entire day ahead of time and how she deals with it. It was interesting to read how Nara used that knowledge to her advantage with school, sports, relationships and how that same knowledge also crippled her at times. 
 (Major) reservations: Aside from the concept, I just didn't like the book or the protagonist very much. The concept was great; the execution was not. There was so much to explore and instead the author focused too much on a romance that felt extremely rushed. It was a bad case of instant "falling in love" and overly dramatized moments of professing their feelings, which I didn't find compelling at all (and I love a good romance!). The language also felt too juvenile and I'm pretty sure I caught some grammatical errors (it's self-published so that might explain why). 
 Do I recommend?: No. I really wanted to like this because I've seen so many positive ratings but I could not get into it. Now, that makes two books in a row that I haven't liked - wish me luck on my next one. I need something good!

Brightest Kind of Darkness is soo good! Seriously, I loved this book. The premise is fresh and such a cool idea! Plus it is more complex than it initially seemed. I still have no idea what is going on with Ethan. You get answers in layers, and I want more, more, more. All I know is that I LOVED him. I just started reading book 2, Lucid because I need to know what is going to happen next. 
 Nara dreams her whole next day. How different and awesome/scary is that? I can't decide for the life of me if I would love or hate this gift. I think I would like it, no matter how creepy it might be, because I always like knowing things over not knowing. I applaud her willpower too. She normally always stays out of things. Meaning, she lets life take its natural course. But then one day, she steps in to save some lives and that is when the book takes off from. It is action right from page 1. I was so engrossed in the story the whole time. Ethan is so freakin' perfect for Nara it is crazy. I love seeing the two of them interact. 
 The writing is excellent, the plot is so intriguing, and the characters are awesome! I had to think long and hard before even coming up with anything critical to say about Brightest Kind of Darkness because I really enjoyed the book. I got sucked in right from the start and I just kept reading until I was done. But I did finally come up with something- Lainey. She was so quick to give up and turn her back on her best friend. She eventually came around and realized how uncool and rude she was, but it still bugged me to see Nara isolated like that. 
 I can't wait to get back to Lucid and see what is going on with Ethan, Nara and the whole gang. I have a feeling that way more is going on with Ethan than even he knows about. If you are looking for a mysterious paranormal, the Brightest Kind of Darkness series is one that I would wholeheartedly recommend for you to check out! I have fallen in love with it.

Book Review: Brightest Kind Of Darkness 
 By: P.T Michelle 
 Truly a captivating mysterious paranormal book. I recommend this book to all lovers of paranormal, mystery, and love stories. This book has a creative story plot and great writing style. Which keeps the reader wanting more. 
 There are a few great life lessons in this book. Which is to appreciate what you have because you never know when or if it will be taken away. Also that true love will undergo anything together no matter what. The two main characters remind me that no matter how odd you think you are, you are perfectly normal to someone else. They also remind me that no matter how useless or unimportant you think you are, someone out there needs every bit of you. 
 Written by: Jesenia Sanabia

As I said in my review for Ethan, I had pretty high expectations going into Brightest Kind of Darkness that weren't really met. It was more the writing style than anything else as I think Michelle has likely become a stronger writer since she originally wrote Brightest Kind of Darkness. I felt like Ethan was not characterized properly and I became confused because it seemed like events in Ethan contradicted events in Brightest, like when Ethan starts at the animal shelter and what happens on his first day. 
 It was also a little more 'woo woo' than I wanted, what with personified forces of nature and whatnot. However, that might be a result of my post-BEA fatigue as Brightest Kind of Darkness encourages the reader to mull over the concept of Fate vs free will and that was more thinking than I wanted to do. 
 I'll read the next book in the series, Lucid, eventually, especially since the reviews of that title seem to support my theory that Michelle gets better with each book. Actually, I might pick it up sooner rather than later because I'm curious if you could get away with going from Ethan to Lucid and skipping Brightest all together.

Sadly, I skimmed through most of this book, so I don't remember some of it. But what do remember wasn't very good. When I read the synopsis for Brightest Kind of Darkness, I was immediately intrigued. It reminded of Final Destination and this television show I used to watch called Tru Calling. Most of the book involved Nara obsessing over Ethan or being total doormat to her best friend (I use the term "friend" loosely because no real friend would behave the way Nara's did). The supernatural bits that were there were decent, but not as exciting as I was hoping for. I don't really remember the other characters because they were all kind of bland. Overall just not what I was expecting

sample_reviews.review_text:
Still reeling from the death of his partner, Officer Nate Burke takes a job as sheriff of a small town in Alaska. Nate soon meets the colorful town's people, including Charlene, a serious man-eater who runs the town's only hotel, and her daughter Meg, a sexy pilot. Nate and Meg are soon drawn together when three college students go missing while mountain climbing. While the boys are soon found alive, Nate gets a big surprise when a frozen body was also found with an ax in chest. 
 I wasn't expecting this book to be so good. The descriptions of Alaska and the town's people are so real, you feel like you're there with them. Great story! My rating: 5 Stars.
Northern Lights is a highly recommended read! Full Review: http://thetbrpile.weebly.com/reviews/...

Nate and Meg fall for eachother while investigating the death of her father and trying to contain their own tightly bottled passions~each struggling with inner demons and small town life. 
 I lived for nearly 20 years in a town like this in Alaska, and I can assure you, it isn't easy to keep your relationship a secret in such a close knit environment. But, when your relationship is being tested, by occupational hazzards or other venues, it's even harder. 
 Nora Roberts did a great job in capturing the small town community of Lunacy, and she brought it to life through her character's actions. 
 Good read for a cold night.

Nate Burke, a Baltimore police detective, blamed himself for the death of his partner in a shootout, and the resulting anger and grief sent him into a depression so dark and deep he thought he would never climb back out. Then Nate decides to accept the position of police chief in the small town of Lunacy, Alaska, and it seems as if life is giving him one more chance. Things are certainly different in Lunacy, and Nate begins to enjoy his encounters with the town's colorful inhabitants, especially bush pilot Meg Galloway. The unexpected romance that slowly develops between Nate and Meg becomes quite complicated, however, when the body of Meg's father, who disappeared in 1988, is found in an ice cave, and Nate has to try to keep his new love safe from a cold-blooded murderer who is willing to kill again to keep old secrets safely buried.
Took too long to get to the point.

Admittedly, I didn't have high expectations for this book, but was pleasantly surprised. I don't normally read popular fiction, and had never read a book by Roberts, but it was recommended to me. For such a long book, the plot and pacing were fairly tight. The chemistry between to Nate and Meg was great. I did think the ending wrapped up a little too quickly.

ex-Baltimore homicide cop takes a job in Lunacy Alaska to recover from the death of his partner in a shooting. There he falls in love with the town, the northern lights, and a bush pilot, Meg Galloway. Solves the 16 yr old murder of Meg's father, etc. Her best novel in a couple of years. All characters were likable and well developed. Great Fun!

It has been many, many years since I read my last Nora Roberts romance. I recall them being sweet and fluffy and the hot sex scenes. Perhaps it's my maturity, the wide range of romance I've read since that time, or simply the new contemporary romance genre that has changed my perception of Roberts. This book was beyond boring; even the sex scenes barely got an interested eyebrow raise from me. The romance was practically non-existent, just a series of ill-timed sex scenes. The mystery was so dragged out that I gave up caring about halfway through the book. I couldn't wait for this to finish. 
 I listened to the audio version and I hated Gary Littman's narration. His pacing was slow and monotonous. His cadence suggested a noir book instead of a romance/mystery. And don't even get me started on the absolutely ridiculous female voices in this book. All of the voices were terrible, but especially the females'. Should have been read by a woman, even though the main protagonist was male.

I seriously loved everything about this book. First of all, it was mostly about Nate, which was AWESOME! NR NEVER writes books about the hero! And it was soooo refreshing. On top of that, I ADORED Nate. He is seriously everything I want my future husband to be. How Nate sat with the little boy for breakfast every day was sooo cute. It made me want to kiss him. I loved spending time with him as he adapted to life in Lunacy. 
 Okay. I loved the setting of Alaska, because I pretty much knew nothing about it beforehand, and found it very interesting. Plus, who doesn't love a town called "Lunacy" whose residents are called "Lunatics?" Really. All of the characters were fully developed, including the secondary ones, which I liked, because it didn't take away from the development of Nate and Meg and their relationship. 
 Another thing I loved was that it was the heroine who had a nick name for the hero. That never happens. Every time she called him "cutie," a smile would spread over my face. It was new and awesome to have people warning the hero that the heroine might break his heart. Loved that. 
 I even liked the characters that I didn't like, including Charlene. I really ended up feeling for her and her struggle with getting old and her love for the husband that left her. I didn't like Jacob either, but found him intriguing. The mayor was cool, too. Annoying, but likable. I also liked all of Nate's police team. They worked well together. It was so cute that Nate refused to shoot the moose. Could he be any more perfect? About Meg. I didn't LOVE her, but I have to say I liked her because she was so unique. She was a little cold and selfish, but she got over it in the end, so it was all right. I actually thought she and Nate worked well together. She really brought out the fire in him. :) 
 I thought the emotions of the characters were so true and real, like when one of the characters died. Very realistic reactions. 
 Following Nate as he adapted to life in Lunacy and dealt with the residents was soo fun. I wasn't bored for one second. Seeing him trying to work through the major blizzard was great, too. 
 As for the killer, I had no idea who it was. I never suspected this person. It was good, because there were so many characters and so many people it COULD have been. 
 Basically, I REALLY hope NR writes another book w/ the hero as the main character. 
 And Nate, will you marry me, please? Thank you.
Good solid mystery with some romance thrown in.

It's taken me a long time to get through this book. Not because of any lost of interest, but because it was a lot to take in. Navigating the emotions and struggles of the the unnamed protganist was a challenging and rewarding experience. The sections addressing the prejudice and manipulation he faces, while at the same time being forced into performing like a perfect gentlemen, is about the angriest I've ever felt on behalf of a character. It's an important book, and I can see why so many recommend it as "the one book every person should read." 
 Had I been strictly reading this book, I probably would have given it four stars instead of five, due to the twisted nature of the prose that skips back and forth between the protganist's reality and his fantastic interority. It's well-done; it's just a technique that I find hard to follow. But as I listen to this book, narrated by Joe Morton, I'm bumping it up to five due to his amazing performance.
I quit. This is hurting my head too much. Too many metaphors and rambling digressons from the plot for my tastes.
Another classic work that I managed to put down.

Well, I can say that I've read it. But I did have to force myself to finish it because it is one of those books that I felt like I "should." For the first half of the book, I just did not like the protagonist. If Ellison's motivation was to show the crushing effects of racism, then his character should have been less of a self-centered fool and less complacent in the events that happened to and around him. By the second half of the novel, the character has become much stronger, more community-oriented and more likeable. Unfortunately, it's at this point that the author's political agenda clouds the story. In the end, if readers do take a serious look at themselves and ask how they contribute to the invisibility of others- because I assure you, no matter who you are, there is someone in this world who you do not "see"- then it is an important contribution and should continue to be one of those classics that must be read. I simply wish that I had enjoyed the process.

Often I feel like I pick up a book at a perfect time. This one hit home. A lot of good things can be said about this novel. I'm sure other people have other feels, but if you're wondering what's the point to it all and searching for meaning in this vast wasteland of miscommunication and failure that we call life, you'll find patient and profound rhetoric in Ralph's Invisible Man.

This book I honestly can't stand. Perhaps it's a combination of the fact that I wouldn't have liked the book to begin with married to the fact that when I read it in high school we spent 3/4 of the year agonizing over EVERY SINGLE PARAGRAPH that kindled my thoughts of violence towards this novel. I don't care about the plot, I don't care about the characters, I hate that he whines and is stupid over and over and over again. I hate the fact that whole world is unlikable. I hate the writing style...ugh..I know it's supposed to be considered "artsy and deep and complex" but this just isn't any of those things for me.

This book was assigned to me as an AP English summer assignment. Reading a book over the summer for homework is daunting however I'm glad my new english teacher picked this one. 
 Invisible Man by Ralph Ellison takes place during in the early twentieth century and told by an unnamed narrator. The reader follows the narrator through his telling of what eventually led to his 'invisibility'. This novel examines numerous themes such as racism and identity (and more). This novel made me think on a different level.

Let me risk the scorn of the ages by saying that I think this may be the most overrated classic in American literature. The first couple chapters would have made compelling short stories, but the book as a whole is an incoherent mess. It's no surprise Ellison could never finish his followup, since this is barely finished. I'm baffled as to how this became part of the modernist gospel.

Amazingly up-to-date when it comes to engagement in political organizations: grassroots workers suddenly encounter criticism for choosing initiative and field work over the discipline as envisaged by "The Committee". It might also aptly reflect the relations at work places, in which all are supposed to be equal, but know your place, if you're holding a lower position. 
 Funny at times, grotesque, moving, deeply humane.

Emerson Watts is a teenager on the fringe of the school who secretly has a crush on her best friend Christopher. Their favorite things to do are play computer games and make fun of the Walking Dead (those who give up their own personality to fit in and be pretty)at their school. All that changes after an accident that leaves Emerson in the body of teen supermodel Nikki Howard. Unfortunately, Emerson now has to lead Nikki's life and learn to deal with beauty. 
 As long as you can totally suspend reality, the book is a lot of fun and also funny. Having someone come to realize that beauty isn't all you thought was an interesting take. I was just a little disappointed, though, that more didn't happen in the book. It's obviously the set-up for a new series.

New Meg Cabot YA! Squee! Okay, that's out of the way - it's the most absurd premise since the modern Arthurian Avalon High, and ends more abruptly than most of her serials, but still a fun read. I still can't not recommend a Meg Cabot book.
Didn't get interesting until the very end. What? There's a book 2??? Shocker.
First of all Meg Cabot is seriously one of my favourite authors her books are always funny and amazing and this book was so different from anything I have ever read before love it so much!

This book is about a body transfer.A tomboy called emerson has switched brains with the supermodel Nikki howard. only one is alive the other dead. With her brain stucked in a supermodels body she doesnt know what to do. All she know is if she says anythiging her parents have to pay 2 million dollars to a coorperation.With her love life mixed up between nikkis and her, shes going to find out that be4ing a supermodel is more than relaxing and easy.

Whose body would you most wish to have if you had the chance? Emerson Watts and her best friend, Christopher are not popular, they have nicknamed the popular kids "the walking dead" because they all act the same. Emerson and Christopher like to hang out and watch surgery shows especially new techniques like the whole body transplant. At the grand opening of the new Stark mega store when a freak accident happens, Emerson is in the wrong place. To save her life, Emerson is the recipient of a full body transplant. She wakes up in the body of supermodel, Nikki Howard. Not the body she would have chosen if she could have, but she had no choice. Why did it have to be Nikki Howard?

** spoiler alert ** 
 My expectations were not high for this teeny-bopper happy-go-lucky book, but Airhead did not even make them. The premise of this book is totally unrealistic. A brain transplant? What about the moral implications? 
 I was skeptical throughout the entire half of the book I somehow managed to swallow, but it got to the point where I could not even finish. The character is more obsessed with her appearance than anything, and I found it sickeningly boring. I feel like Meg Cabot wrote this book as quickly as possible, written only for the sole use of appealing to the pre-teen masses. I would not recommend this book to any self-respecting reader, that is for sure.

Well, I liked this book. But not as much as I liked the Princess Diaries and DEFINITELY not as much as The Mediator series. 
 Emerson is fine by me, even though I like her way better after she becomes Nikki. And I like Lulu. But that's about it. The story had a potential to make me forget how to breathe, but unfortunately it ended up being just okay. And the number of unnecessary characters bugs me too. For example: Brandon and the British guy who's charming when he's there but I forget him two seconds after...those two could be reduced into one character and no one would mind. 
 Christopher is great and I'm really interested in what happens with him and Em/Nikki. But I can't decide if it's worth reading the other two books.

I struggled with the free verse style of this book, to be honest. Though I knew that's what I was getting going in, I wasn't really impressed with it. I'm not sure how necessary it was. Unique, certainly, but necessary? I'm not sure. 
 The problem for me was that despite the creativity the style offers, it also kept me from being totally immersed in the story. Hopkins skimps on the details in favour of flow and visual style on the page. The challenges the characters face are very real, but I never particularly cared about any of them. Again, this was part of the disconnect I felt because of the style. 
 Anyway. An interesting read, but not one that makes me inclined to want to pick up any of Hopkins' other books.

This was one of the best books I have read from Ellen Hopkins who I adore as a writer. I think she captured the adolescent drug addled thoughts and emotions well. There were certain things I didn't like about this book but nothing worth mentioning. This is a reread for me.
terrible. just terrible--and on so many levels. how is this a bestseller? or poetry?

This book scared me on a whole new level. The topic of drugs has always been one that causes me deep unrest. I don't think anything is more terrifying than addiction. God, I wouldn't wish it on my worst enemies. 
 Also, this book scared me because I dream of being a good mother and reading this made me realise how easy it is for your baby to fall from grace. Bad mistakes are so easy to make. And they come in quick succession so you don't see the mess you're in until you've hit rock bottom. 
 I don't want my kids to go astray but look how easily they could end up there. 
 Overall this was a really eye opening book. I try to avoid books about sex and drugs but this one shed a negative light on the issues, and that's what we need our youth to see.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This book aggravated me more than anything but I did enjoy the story. This is kind of based off of the author's own daughter's story and her struggle with addiction to crystal meth a.k.a. crank. I wanted to like Kristina but I just couldn't relate to her. I found her to be really selfish and although you are getting her perspective I still didn't understand the choices she made. I felt there were some unrealistic moments or moments that happened a little too quickly such as meeting the guy and then bam I'm an addict. I did like the brief times that Kristina acted more like herself and questioned everything she did. She just seemed like a typical teenager but caught up in some heavy stuff. I thought this book was okay, I think I'm just not a fan of these kinds of stories just because addiction is a topic I personally intend to avoid. I'll be continuing the series because I want to know how her family and even Kristina deals with this addiction especially after having children.
Gut wrenching. Horrifying. Debilitating. Insightful. Promise. Waste.
Just Ok, I am Glad the author got to make something good about all this bad stuff that happened to her and her family.

I can relate to this novel from a thrid person account (one of my immediate family members is a drug addict currently seeking help) and from a first person account (being pregnant at 17). I honestly did not enjoy the writting style, the mother seemed too self absorbed, the broken sentences pissed me off to the point of rants. The story was uncaptivating, I only finished this novel because I like to follow through. I read a few pages to my husband and my mother, to justify my rants on how horrid it was and oddly enough they agreed. 
 My friends recommended this series to me, and I love them so I took the time. I do see why they liked the novel both those friends have addictions, so I take it, it makes them feel hope that they're not the only ones battling demons. Good book ... just not for me... 2 stars.

I did not like this book one bit! I would recommend it to no one! I do not understand why it was written since its basically a teens how to do drugs handbook. I want to go to half price books to sell it to them but I'm not sure I want anyone else to buy it!!
2.5 stars, I guess.

reference_books.title: Empire of Storms (Throne of Glass, #5)
reference_books.review_text:
THIS IS A FIASCO. 
 There were few the things that I truly enjoy, and a lot the ones that bother me. 
 I like the way the book starts. That first chapter with Elena was so cool. And the thing about the gods... I wasn't expecting that, and it felt weird, but I like it. I want to see more about these angry, freaking crazy gods. 
 I also like the part when Aelin finds out that she couldn't just arrive to Terrasen and claimed herself queen. That's just to easy to even happen. She has to convince others that she deserves the Throne. REALISTIC. 
 And then that attack on Rithfold... i didn't enjoy it as I wanted to. It all happen so fast that at the end of the book I had already forgotten about it. Unnecessary. 
 And Rowan saving Dorian. OH MY GOD! I'm so tired that all of Sarah's characters are beautiful and the most powerful fae in the word. Just cut the shit off with that! If they are that powerful, then why they just go to Erawan and kill him? 
 For a moment I thought Asterin was going to die, you got me there Sarah. 
 I love Manon scene with her bitch-grandma. I almost had a hearth attack when they were fighting. But... I didn't like it that now, not only we have one, but TWO lost queens that can save the world and make it a better place and whatsoever. Having two queen feels like as easy solution to the upcoming war. 
 What up with Elide and Lorcan??? I didn't give a fuck about them. And their chapters were so boring. 
 I must admit that the best part in this book was the battle in Skulls Bay. THAT WAS EPIC. Aeline being poses by this god and Lysandra as a sea dragon were the best part of that battle. 
 And after that beautiful and amazing battle. Some really stupid chapters came. Like Rowan and Aelin in flames while they are having sex in the sea! COME ON! That was so stupid. 
 I honestly can't understand Dorian and Manon relationship. For me, in QoS, they felt in love instantly. But in this book... they only seem to have sexual attraction. Like if they just wanna be fuckbuddies. They are not in love. They are just playing sexy games. I'm sure that at the end, they are gonna forget about sex, they are gonna have the healthiest of relationship and they are gonna be happy for ever and ever. Which is gonna be, of course, predictable. 
 Then we have that scene when a five hundred legion of liken are coming and Aelin, Manon and Dorian kill them all, like in three, maybe four seconds. That didn't feel real. Not at all. It was so easy. 
 Aedion. I know that Sarah has been criticized because the lack of diversity in her characters. And the thing with Aedion in this book, when he said he likes to be with women's and men's, confuse me. Why we didn't knew that since the moment Aedion was introduced in Her of Fire? Because Sarah just came up with this after the many critics she received, or at least that's how it feels to me. 
 It feels good to have a bisexual characters in the main group. 
 My main problem with this book is that the plot wasn't enough. At least for me, the plot felt weak. 
 We find out that Nehemia and Elena have been working together and that Nehemia had to die in order to break Aelin and bla, bla, bla... when I read that, I was like: Wait, I already knew this!!! Like, since book one. 
 The locket wasn't an interesting thing to the story. I mean, yeah, all can go to shit without that thing, but, someone has to die? Wait... are we talking about an horrocrux? 
 Now, that thing about Aelin and Manon jumping into that witch mirror was so Harry Potter that for a moment I thought I was reading the Deathly Hollows. I hate that part so much. It was not unique, now at all, and that's why I read SJM books, cause she is freaking unique! 
 And then of course the last part. 
 I honestly wasn't paying attention to the battle that was happening in the ocean, because even when we didn't have to much details about it, that wasn't the real good action. I was curious to see what Manon (I LOVE HER) was going to do with the rest of the group. And of course she didn't disappoint me with what she did to Aelin. God, that was cruel and sad and violent and perfect for readers who enjoy the evilness of villains. 
 The last part when everyone decides what to do and where, just left me wanting to read the last book. 
 But despite that, im not that excited for the last installment. This book just disappoint me in so many different ways. 
 For me, Empire of Storms is the book with more failures in the series.

reference_books.title: Throne of Glass (Throne of Glass, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
ONE MONTH. It took me one month to read this book. 
 This is my second time reading this book and I think that it's going to be my last. 
 As the first time I read it I hate half of this book, I just don't like the way the series start. The book doesn't have a plot, it's boring at times and there are so many unnecessary chapters. 
 But, despite that. I love the characters, I love the world and I love all the little details that I have already forgotten about Elena and the war. And I'm excited to read the other four books, that are nothing like these one. 
 I love Sarah J. Maas and it feels weird to say this, but this is the only book that she has written that I don't like.

I love this series! Its hard to give a review since I read them several years ago and jumped straight into the next one. So I'm just going to review them all together. 
 This series is great. It's got action, adventure, and a little bit of a love story(ok that's somewhat stretching it). I'm not a stickler for greek mythology so it didn't bother me how Riordan used it in the books, they are for children also. Sometimes the greek gods did get confusing since I don't know a whole lot, but it was never overwhelming. The concept of the series is very interesting and new(at least to me anyway). I honestly didn't see anything Harry Potter-ish in them. I recommend this to anyone who is interested in a fresh new take, on action and adventure.
Worth the hype. I have to read the rest of the series now.

I feel like this book killed my brain cells. 
 I realise it may have been written for 4 year olds but still. 
 This book was just so... EMPTY. Alot of "somehow I knew", "suddenly it just happened" and "supriSinglys". Like tell the story properly.. 
 Learn things where I can see it. Don't just have super super intuition it boring. 
 And also.. All the chapter names were a summary of the chapter. Why... Why... Chapter 123 would have worked for me. 
 All the missions Percy went on reminded me very much of a video game.. Every step of the way there was some pathetic obstacle, he pressed "up, down, up, up, triangle, square, circle, up, r2" and it was over. So predictable and so meh.. 
 I'm reading the second one because im determined to get through.. I have hopes it will improve.

I've seen the movies and loved them so I thought it was about time I saw where everything began for Percy, Grover and Annabeth. The Lightning Thief by Rick Riordan tells the story of how twelve year old Percy Jackson discovers he's a demigod. Son of Poseidon, Percy has never quite been like other kids. Hidden in the mortal world to protect him from those with grudges against his biological father, Percy has always known that he was different. When Zeus' lightning bolt is stolen, Percy's existence comes to light and his paternity is revealed. If Percy is to find the bolt (and consequentially save his mother and become a hero) - he needs to overcome monsters and battle gods. Not alone in his quest, his best friend Grover and one of Athena's daughters, Annabeth, tag along to give Percy the best chance against the powerful immortals. 
 For the right audience, I believe this book would be perfect. There's action and adventure. A great take on classic mythology and characters I could fall in love with. 
 The problem is - I'm not the right audience. I'm in my twenties and unlike a lot of other young adult and middle grade books I've read - this one made me feel old in a way no other book I've read before has. 
 The characters, as entertaining as they are, read a little young. I liked that they are true to their character. I believe that Percy is twelve despite him having to try and take on challenges that would terrify people many times his age. And the author is consistent with the the trio's skill levels. I just think that I'm not the right person for this book. The mythology is amazing. I love how much Riordan packed in. There's all sorts of gods met and mentioned with places and stories being inserted into the plot all over the place. Journey wise - it didn't feel very planned all the time. Like the trio were sort of stumbling upon where they were supposed to go next. But in the end they got to where they were meant to be so it all worked out for the best I suppose. 
 I'll still watch the movies (provided they make more! Fingers crossed!) but this series isn't for me.
Fun quick read. Sam and I both read it in in one day. This will be a great series for when our kids are older.

The Percy Jackson series was the first major series I had read; and I was obsessed from the very first word. Needless to say, I'm a big fan of the series. From the hilarious narration from Percy, to the wonderful combination of the modern world and Greek myths, this series was a recipe for goodness from the start. Even now, I am still reading Rick Riordan books. I just can't get enough. The characters he wrote were ( and still are ) memorable and full of heart, and that's hard to write off.
couldn't finish it

For many, these series of books are considered to be a Harry Potter rip-off but in reality they are just following the established formula of all teen/children adventures. So it is a fine book at what it's all about but hardly feels special if you have read or watched enough of the same type. 
 So, as the stereotype dictates, the hero is a boy who is treated at first as a looser before he is revealed to be the son of a God and taken to train to a special school of half-breeds just like him. Throw in some basic Greek mythology, lots of monsters, some conspiracy that can destroy the world, and there you go, you get the much familiar path Harry Potter made famous but otherwise did not establish. 
 Just like most such stories, it suffers from what I call "weakened enemies". Since he is constantly fighting monsters and rivals gods, you would expect for him to be some epic-level fighter who does all sorts of stuff but all you see is an everyday boy who can hardly manage at school. It makes all the challenges he faces to pass as pathetic if any kid can beat up a Minotaur with a few sword swings or a Hydra with a hax Medusa head. I am pretty sure most of the target audience won't notice or even care about that, as it feels very cool if a nobody can do all those cool stuff. Yeah, I wonder how many of them realize that this nobody is a demigod who is constantly aided by all sorts of people and other gods just because he was born special. 
 The second thing it suffers from is how the plot seems to drive him and not him driving the plot as it would normally be the case. He is just running from one mission to another without really deciding anything for himself, or even accomplishing anything with his own strength or cunningness. Heck, even I could rival the gods if had for free all the allies and equipment he gets. Just think of all the main events he was part of. 
 - Fending off the Fury because someone intervened. 
 - Accused of being a thief without having a saying in the whole thing. 
 - Fending off the Minotaur because of a magic sword someone else gave him. 
 - Taken to the training camp without choosing it. 
 - Finding a way to save his mother through someone else, whom he didn't even ask for help. 
 - Beating the Medusa with a pitiful excuse. 
 - Beating Hades without really fighting him. He was betrayed. 
 - Fighting the real villain with the powers his father gave him. 
 So he feels too much like a plot device instead of a boy who tries to fight his destiny or something like that. He never even questions his own status but rather runs after the more experienced ones. 
 The third problem is the villain of the book, rather easy to tell who it's going to be despite being hidden. The main conflict of the book also makes no sense at all. If the lightning bolt was so powerful and precious, how was it stolen so easily by a nobody? How can anyone blame Percy as the thief when he never went to the temple of the gods or didn't even know they exist? If the villain knew how to go to the underworld, why didn't he just go there himself? And what a classic, when revealed he just explains his plan in detail, as if it matters at all to someone he plans on killing a few minutes later. 
 The fourth problem is quite minor if you are not Greek. I am and I found all this bastardization of my country's mythology rather insulting. All of a sudden the whole realm of the gods is at some American soil and the three main gods are rivals. Oh come on! 
 But I guess it is a fine line of books for kids since the plot is rather fast and it has magic and monsters and gods and stuff happening every few pages. Cool but hardly great.

This series appealed to me when the movie was in the theater but I was busy and never got to it. When I saw that it was soon being released on DVD I decided I wanted to read the book before seeing the movie. I belong to the school of though that most of the time, the book is better than the movie and this is another story that I believe that holds true for. 
 I shared this book with my children, we read almost the entire thing aloud and then borrowed the audio book to listen to in the car on a long trip. One thing I liked about listening was hearing someone else pronounce the names for the Greek gods, I just wasn't entirely sure of the pronunciation of some of them which is no big deal when you are reading silently to yourself but becomes a bigger problem when you are reading aloud! 
 Parts of this book reminded me of Harry Potter (another series I am working through with my children this summer) and somewhat of the Spiderwick Chronicles which we have already finished. I like that this opened their minds to the idea of Greek myths because I think we are going to moving into those in a few weeks. This book was engrossing enough for adults or children and I highly recommend it. When we went to the beach last week my children were throwing shells back in telling me that they were offering for Poseidon the sea god!

I don't know if it was all the hoopla I've heard about this that built it up too much in my head, or what. I closed the book with a shrug of the shoulders and a "meh" on my lips, feeling resoundingly underwhelmed. i started reading it to my somewhat timid 9 yo son. He was too scared of the monsters and asked me to pick a different book to read to him. I had to finish it on my own. The only plus I can see from reading it is that I now have a better grasp of who some of the Greek gods are. So there's something at least! I'm still undecided if I will finish the series or not.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This was such a beautiful book. I'd heard plenty of good things from various people and sources, and it'd been on my to-read list forever. 
 "I bet you could sometimes find all the mysteries of the universe in someone's hand." 
 Picking it up, I was worried that it would be one of the popular books that had too much hype, but ultimately disappointed me. But this definitely wasn't the case! 
 Following two Mexican-American boys in a coming-of-age story in the 1980s, it's a powerful book that follows a multitude of themes: family, friendship, violence, growing up, culture, and all are merged beautifully together into one compelling story. 
 Both Ari and Dante are so wonderfully created and defined that they are full and loved characters. I empathised a lot with Ari, and his feelings of his future and his growing up. It's rare that you find such well developed characters that means you don't realise their really teenagers. Despite being popular in the YA fiction area, it's remarkably more than that, and it feels distinctly more than merely a young adult novel. 
 Their families really stuck out to me, and the focus on LGBT rights was actually far less than I expected. It has been heralded as a piece of LGBT fiction, but it does not seem forced. Instead, it is merely another facet of the boys' story. It feels very real and very well placed. 
 I just realised that there is a sequel in the works, that I will undoubtedly wait eagerly for. I'm so glad this book lived up to the hype that has surrounded it since its publication 4 years ago.

"The summer sun was not meant for boys like me. Boys like me belonged to the rain." 
 How will you discover all the secrets of the universe? -That's the sixty-four-thousand-dollar question. 
 Aristotle and Dante Discover The Secrets of the Universe became an enticing diversion from all the physical and mental torments I've experienced these past few days. It is the antithesis of reading the same old thing. Beautifully poetic indeed. 
 This is such a beautiful coming of age story. A tale about friendship, family relationship, diverse ways of growing up, acceptance, loyalty and the exploration of human sexuality exemplified by intense narration. A beautiful book that can be summed up into six words: Simple. Poetic. Lyrical. Honest. Unapologetic. Liberating. 
 Truth be told, words won't be enough to describe this book. For me, this one was definitely worth the hype. This was such a poignant story told in a sensible way. One thing that was truly remarkable was the authenticity of the book. The story had been weaved in a permeable manner with no unnecessary verbose formulations. 
 This time, I don't care whether these boys acted like pseudo-intellectuals. Those teens that sound like adults, well hey, f*ck that, this is me saying that teenagers have the ability to perceive. We couldn't belittle their intelligence and wit. I don't care if some scenarios are too good to be true. I don't give a damn if all the characters are immaculate and idealistically likable or how exceedingly unrealistic the dialogues are. I just let myself enjoy the story; like submerging oneself regardless of how deep or shallow it is. 
 THE CHARACTERS 
 The year was 1987. Everything was told from Aristotle's perspective. 
 ARISTOTLE 
 Ari had a dim notion of who he really was. He didn't know who he was in front of his friends; who he was as a son to his parents and who he was when he was with Dante. 
 Ari's life was complicated by these 4 unknown & known variables: 
 1.	Father's life robbed by bullets and war. 
 2.	Mother's distortion of reality. 
 3.	A brother in prison he knows nothing about 
 4.	An accident that turns his life upside down 
 5.	Other unfortunate Ways of Growing Up 
 He felt he was being led down the primrose path that was full of pleasure but leads to his own internal destruction. As Aristotle strives hard to live a life according to the conventional rules of the society, he failed to recognize his worth as a person and he was blindsided to the things unconditional love could offer. The ugly reality manifests itself through anger, denial and self-preservation. He never let others see his weaknesses and he acts contradictory to his will and real self. .He unconsciously acts based on his own internalized standard (how he wants to be seen) which apparently resulted in emotional discomfort 
 DANTE 
 On the other hand, Dante's only struggle is discovering what to do next when you already know the truth. 
 Will he ruin the friendship? Or will he live between hurting and healing? 
 Dante instantly became one of my most favorite fictional characters. It was only when I read that Dante didn't run away from his enemy that the penny finally dropped and I realized how admiring he really was. 
 WRITING STYLE 
 You will be blown away not only by the book's simplistic writing style but also all the deep-seated meaning it contains. You will be moved by the author's account not only of human sexuality but of healthy family relationship. There's an existence of positive interactions between family members. Other remarkable scenes in the story are the Mexican-American vibe and some touch of social and cultural narratives like societal norms and different childhood upbringing. Since I'm an Asian girl, MENUDO and TAMALES are totally relatable/nostalgic food for me! 
 The author enmeshed his readers to the painful but liberating reality of revealing oneself as one really is with no ifs, ands, or buts. It unravels the harrowing path of accepting oneself in the absence of 
 "conditions of worth." 
 The theme confronts any condition and prominence we think we must meet in order for other people to accept us as worthy of love and respect. The book strives hard against pleasing other people for approval. 
 Upon completion of this novel my heart skipped a beat. I was blown away. Everything was incredibly beautiful. All of the characters were so likable including Ari's and Dante's parents. Every single word written on this book was very raw, veracious and spontaneous. Anything will punch you right in the gut and you will just find yourself rereading every single paragraph. The sadness and authenticity therein made this book awe-inspiring. This was indeed a breathtaking must-read novel.
the only word i can think of to describe this is perfection
Fantastic. The last line left tears in my eyes.

Given all the hype, I thought it would be so much better. ...I liked it, but I had a hard time believing the chemistry between Aristotle and Dante, and their dialogue and the way they thought didn't seem realistic for two teenage boys.

Me gusto. Es una historia que nos ensena a valorarnos por lo que somos, sin importar lo que los demas piensen o digan de nosotros. Una historia que nos ensena a ver y encontrar lo que mas nos hace felices, a apreciar a los que te quieren, demostrarles tu afecto siempre que puedas y a no juzgar a otros por las apariencias. Y principalmente, nos ensena que todos tenemos nuestras propias estrellas brillando en nuestro interior. Benjamin Alire Saenz escribio un relato magico, que transmite paz y esperanza. Y si, logro tocar mi corazon. Varias partes me hicieron un nudo en la garganta.

** spoiler alert **

reference_books.title: Stepbrother Dearest
reference_books.review_text:
10 Stars! 5 is just not enough! 
 This is one of the best books I have read in a really long time. I was sucked so far in that I could not put it down. In the past few hours I have laughed, had my panties melted, my heart broken, and a huge goofy grin left on my face. I read so much that anything that can bring about these emotions in me is instantly one of my new favorite books. 
 Elec is so mercurial that I have whip lash, but yet yummy enough that you just lick your lips and smile. Tattooed, pierced, smart and gorgeous! Wickedly delicious! Wildly emotional. 
 Greta is meeting her step brother Elec for the first time. He is coming to spend the school year with his father. She is excited to finally have a sibling. She has scene pictures but seeing him in the flesh leaves her feeling everything but sisterly affection. Thus starts the tale of Elec and Greta. Push and pull. Love and Hate. It's a relationship that can never be but one that will knock the earth off its axis and send two people spiraling for years. 
 I can not recommend this book enough. I am so blown away. I did not want it to end. 
 Penelope Ward hit a grand slam with this one!

reference_books.title: Jed Had to Die
reference_books.review_text:
YAY! This book was so much fun! 
 5 Stars of PIE! 
 Would you love a great piece of blueberry pie? Well you may want to think twice if getting it in Bald Knob, KY! 
 "You know every time you say Bald Knob I picture a town square with a giant stone statue of an old guy with his dick hanging out. And people flocking to the statue to touch his 'bald knob' for good luck," 
 A fun, mysterious read with a HAWT reformed geek and lots of caffeine. 
 There's murder afoot, the town golden boy is dead...he wasn't all that golden. 
 Peyton escaped the small town drama of Bald Knob but when her best friend needs her she returns after 12 years. Saving Emma Jo is her main goal. A town full of gossip, a hot sheriff and every bad decision she ever made is brought front and center all with out being able to find a decent cup of coffee. Let the fun and angst ensue. A lot of wine and some mischief lead to a great tale! Bettie, Peyton and Emma are on a mission to solve the mystery of Jed's death.

 He's all she thinks about, all she fantasizes about, but he's not right for her. He's not right for K.C Carter! K.C.'s story is very interesting. I will not say much about her because the story explains it so much better than I ever could.
