sample_reviews.review_text:
Insider introduces us to the band, Exodus End, a sexy as hell metal band. I have read a few of the books in the Sinners on Tour series and have enjoyed my time with the Sinners. I was excited to know that this was a new series about Dare's band, but I was disappointed it was not about Dare. Hopefully that's to come later in the series. 
 Toni is a naive virgin that goes on tour with Exodus End for a month in order to gather info and material for a book. She is thrust into a world of rock stars that she is completely unfamiliar with. Logan is the bassist for Exodus End and is in a constant state of promiscuity, being a rock star and all. 
 Even though she's a virgin, Toni drops her panties for Logan within about five minutes of meeting him. I was not crazy about this aspect of Toni's character. A virgin at 25 who has no idea what goes on in the bedroom is not going to throw herself at a rock star within an hour of meeting him. While Logan thought her sexual inexperience was cute, I saw it as irritating. 
 As predicted, Toni falls for Logan, but Logan plays off the relationship as just friends with benefits. However, at every turn, Logan is either playing the crazy jealous boyfriend or the romantic and then stupidly denying they have anything more. He got on my nerves a bit when he would treat Toni like a girlfriend and then totally blow her off when she got too serious. 
 I loved the band. Of course they were hilarious. I even liked Reagan, who apparently had a backstory with Trey and Ethan. I haven't got to that book in the Sinners on Tour series, so I'd really like to read that. Bi-sexual rock stars sound like fun! 
 Overall I loved Toni and Logan's characters at times but found them annoying at other times. It was a little inconsistent. The kind of instalove thing was not my favorite. I still enjoyed this read though. I look forward to finding out more about the rest of the members of Exodus End. 
 Copy provided by Netgalley in exchange for an honest review.

3 "Inside Exodus" Stars 
 After having read, fallen in love with and adoring the leading men for the Sinner's, I was so excited to see that Exodus End (whom we meet in the Sinner's series) was getting their own series. Olivia Cunning is a master of writing steamy erotic stories that not only make your panties spontaneously combust but weaves emotion-filled tales of sexy rockers falling in love. While this story had the makings of a great rock star romance, it felt a little lacking as compared to the Sinners on Tour. 
 Logan is the bassist for Exodus End and Toni is a journalist tasked with writing a book about the band. They are complete opposites in almost every way. While Logan is outgoing, loud, silly, confident and not especially picky about his bedmates, Toni is a quiet, reserved, shy, serious virgin. As soon as these two meet, sparks fly. Literally within the hour clothes are shed and so are their inhibitions. As their time together progresses, they try to tell themselves that they're only friends. Being only friends starts to wear on Toni but she's determined that she'll take what Logan can give. Logan tries to deny his feelings and for a while doesn't even really understand his feelings toward Tori. But he does know that anytime she's working with a bandmate during an interview, jealousy eats away at him for the first time and he wants her for himself even if he doesn't think he can give her more. 
 I really enjoyed watching the banter between Toni and the band. Watching Toni come out of her shell was fun to watch. I was silly smiling through her "interviews" with each band member. Watching her struggle with her job and unintentionally learn all their dirty secrets was a highlight of the book for me. (Ms. Cunning used this plot device to create the ability to not only make drama but also let us inside the heads of the bandmates.) One of the best parts of Ms. Cunning's Sinner's on Tour series was that each rocker had a sexual niche he filled. In this book, that was fulfilled by Logan being Toni sexual teacher. It was hilarious, sweet and sexy all at the same time. 
 The reason this book was just okay for me was mostly because I felt like Logan and Toni's characters lacked depth. Because of this I wasn't really able to connect with them. I liked them well enough and I was invested in their HEA as well as the story in general, but I didn't feel the connection that I did when I read the Sinner's. I also figured out the main conflict pretty early on. That in and of itself is okay but it just didn't feel well executed. It was something that was easily fixed and really should have never existed in the first place. I mean why would Toni use that format for remembering things that she really had no need to even know. It was confusing. 
 In the end, while I did enjoy the story and will most definitely be keeping up with all the Exodus End band members and their books, this one fell a little flat. I'm hoping my second favorite Sinner, Trey and the loves his life, body guard Ethan and Exodus End guitar player Reagan, will bring back the fire I felt when I first started reading Ms. Cunning's masterpieces. 
 Arc provided by publisher via Netgalley for honest review.

Los libros de esta autora son absurdamente adictivos para mi. Las escenas de sexo siempre son lo mejor... pero todo lo demas es bastante mediocre y superficial como para que sea una historia que vayas a recordar toda la vida.

Oh THIS was deliciously dirty! I'm going to steal Logan's word and call INSIDER absolutely Sexsational! 
 WOW! It has got to be hard to live up to the hype of this book! Olivia Cunning has her work cut out for her. She has SO many die-hard fans, it's just incredible. Are you ready for the shock factor? Okay, here we go...INSIDER is the first book I've read by Ms Cunning. Did you gasp? Did you shake your head and wonder what the hell I'm thinking? I know! I know! It's crazy, but true. AND Rock Star Romances are one of my FAVES, so I can't give you a reasonable answer as to why I haven't touched her Sinners on Tour series or her One Night with Sole Regret series. Anyway, I can tell you that after finishing up INSIDER, I told myself I was a fool, and promised myself that I would remedy that right away. So stay tuned.... 
 So, INSIDER...this book...this sexy as sin book was GREAT! I loved it! I loved the characters, the plot, the unique leading lady and the yummy male lead. I enjoyed the fact that I got to know all of the members of the rock band Exodus End. It got me pumped up for the rest of the series. 
 Logan was a fantastic character. I liked him right away. He is crazy, fun, doesn't take life seriously. He is just refreshing. Toni's character was a little bit harder to connect with, but eventually I did, and the more I got to know her, the more I liked her spirit, her spunk. Together, these two were explosive. I mean talk about a first meeting! Holy Shit! That was intense and so not romantic. But don't worry folks, the romance comes later. I enjoy a romance when the main characters couldn't be more different from each other. And yet, they make it work. Ms. Cunning wove that web very nicely. 
 INSIDER is a Rock Star Romance so you better expect some drama, some angst. You should also expect some off the charts sexing going on! All together, Cunning brings us a pretty great romance with so many characters that some may already know from the SINNERS books, but new fans will appreciate the fact that INSIDER is a standalone and a chance to start fresh with Olivia's kind of writing. I'm excited. I'm anticipating the Exodus End series to have a great following and I look forward to what's next for the band. 
 *Gifted copy provided by the publisher in exchange for an honest review*

I'm unfortunately giving this book 2.5 stars. I say unfortunately because I LOVE Olivia Cunning. I love all the books she has already put out. Every. Single. One. I loved the Sinners series and I waited forever for Exodus End's books. Maybe that is the problem, I built it up and wanted so much. But really it boils down to two points that really bothered me. 
 One: The insta-love. I don't always mind insta-love. But goodness gracious it happened so fast. I was 25% into the book and it hadn't been 24 hours and already they had sex I don't know how many times and thinking about love. It might be personal, but I think a huge opportunity was missed when she crammed it in to the first two days. I wanted the tension. I wanted her on that bus for a while and to feel the build up. But it wasn't. There was just a lot of sex. A lot. It was all deliciously steamy like Olivia Cunning is amazing at doing. But a lot in the beginning. 
 Then I was reall looking forward to these delicious sexy scene that would pop up later in the book and they were skimmed over. I just wish the timing was different and the sex scenes were more spread out with more of a punch. 
 Two: Tori's character was really inconsistent. I had to keep readjusting my perception of her while reading because the way she thought and the way she talked and the way she acted kept flip-flopping. Overall I think she was supposed to come off as naive and innocent and sheltered with the silly boldness when she was with Logan, but sometimes she was naive and wouldn't know what to do and then others she would be bold and dirty and know so much. Then with the job; she was supposed to be able to prove she could do so much and that she got this job because of her hard work, but she didn't really work that hard. Her interviews were weird and unprofessional and she had sex with Logan most of the time. I just wanted her to be consistent. If she got the job on her work then show me she's a good worker. 
 Overall, the book was hot and it was a great introduction to a lot of the other characters in the book. Am I going to want to read the next book in the series ... you bet your ass I am. I can't wait. I will sit here and wait for another amazing book about Reagan and her guys. I can't wait!!! There are WAY too many books that rocked my world to let one inconsistent book to turn me off of her. I still love Olivia Cunning and I still recommend reading this book to decide for yourself and there is just too much information in it to not be able to read it but continue on in the series.

There were so many things I did not like about this book I am not sure where to begin. Don't worry, I am not going to try to cover all of them. Since my #1 rule is to actually like the main characters in the story, the most obvious place to start is the whiny, naive, insecure, and immature heroine, Toni Nichols. She was not a believable character. Seriously, she is a journalist but when she writes in her diary it reads like a middle schooler. Apparently, she dresses like one, too. Is her love of mismatched socks supposed to be cute? Yet, she frequently goes on about not fitting in and is insecure about her appearance. Not to sound harsh, but here's an easy, basic fashion tip: start with wearing matching socks so you don't look like a freak. She also has a habit of writing her notes on napkins, even though she is lugging around a large purse with a notebook. I am pretty sure professional journalists actually use a notebook...all the time. Especially when it is reiterated several times this is a chance of a lifetime. One spill, ill-timed sneeze, or swipe of the mouth and, darn, there goes that day's work. 
 Her hook up with Logan an hour within meeting him was anything but romantic. Awkward and gross would be more accurate. Especially his comment about getting blood on the sofa and her going in search of a hydrogen peroxide to remove the stain. Her naive behavior during their self-proclaimed sexual education sessions were also over the top unrealistic. Logan surprisingly seems to like her. So far he seems to be pretty much the handsome but musically gifted, man whore, air head. Yes, I know (minus the airhead part) that seems to be the typical character traits for rock band romance leading men. I'm just hoping eventually I will find something redeeming about this one. 
 Unfortunately, at 35% into the story, it is becoming painful to continue. I'm sorry folks, but I don't think I'll be able to finish it. I recall Ms. Cunning's Sinners series being better. Not sure what happened with this one. So far, it has been a big miss with this reviewer. For now, I've had to put it down and walk away. To be fair, I'll let some time slide then pick it up again. Maybe once I delve inside The Insider again, I'll view it differently. I'm not holding my breath, but I will still hold out for some hope that might happen. In which case, I will gladly revise my review and report back to you. 
 (This review is based on ARC e-book provided via NetGalley in exchange for an honest, unbiased opinion.)

 DNF @ 20% 
 I went into this book wanting to like it - I really did. There are a lot of positive review on it, and I love band books, so I thought there was a high chance of me walking away with a new author and series to fuss over. 
 I couldn't have been more wrong. 
 I don't know where to begin with the problems of this story. 
 It all starts off so well. A simple enough storyline of a journalist trying to prove herself to her business-oriented mother by going on a month long tour with the famous rock band, Exodus End. Here, she is meant to interview the band member and take photos for a digital book she will be writing and designing. 
 Then everything seems to just...take a turn. 
 The main character, Toni, is a more delicate type, if you will, which is something that doesn't really bother me - not everyone has to be a strong female personality. But seriously, she could use a few extra brain cells...or maybe a brain to begin with? 
 But that's really not what irks me the most. It's the fact that she is introduced in the first chapter as an insecure, 25 year old virgin who dresses quite conservatively due to said insecurities. She also doesn't really interact with the opposite sex much because she's an introvert who looks after her special needs sister. 
 Now, all of that just screams that 9% into the book she's obviously going to allow the bassist, Logan, to follow her back to her room in the tour bus and have sex after only knowing each other for ONE HOUR, doesn't it? Oh wait... 
 No. It doesn't. 
 The character does a complete 180 as soon as she steps on the tour bus, and for a second I wondered if I'd actually been reading an urban fantasy novel all along, where the band members were actually supernatural beings who exuded so much sex appeal women just lost all their inhibitions. 
 Seriously, what on earth happened? 
 If that's not enough, the love interest, Logan, isn't much better on the intelligence scale. There were a tonne of indications that she was a virgin from the start, and if that wasn't enough, before they'd done the deed he assumed that she was acting skittish and inexperienced in bed...as a turn on. Huh?! Even after everything was said and done, he asked if the blood was because she was on her period. *bangs head on desk repeatedly* 
 Logan, of course, runs away as soon as he finds out the truth, leaving Toni once again feeling insecure, and writing come of the following in her diary: 
 "How do I get him to like me? Maybe I should go against my promises to Dad and dress less appropriately." 
 For the first time in my life I'm labeled a slut. 
 Why am I okay with that? 
 And with that giant NOPE, I think I've probably made my point. I'm giving this book 1 star, and that's only because Dare punched Logan when he found out and that was awesome :D

This is one of my favorite books ever! 
 Liesel Meminger is only nine years old when she is taken to live with the Hubermanns, a foster family, on Himmel Street in Molching Germeny, in the lat 1930's. She arrives with a few possesions, but among them is The Grave Digger's Handbook,a book she stole from her brother's burial place. During the years Liesel lives with the Hubermanns, Hitler becomes more powerful, life on Himmel Street becomes more fearful, and Liesel becomes a full-fledged book thief. She rescues books from Nazi book-burnings and steals from the library of the mayor. Liesel is illiterate when she steals her first book, but Hans Hubermann uses her prized book to teach her to read. This is a story of courage, friendship, love, survival, death, and grief. This is Liesel's life on Himmel Street, told from Death's point of view. 
 I really enjoyed this book. Had me going from the beginning. At first, I thought this was going to be boring because it was about Nazi's, but it turned out the be one of my favorites. Definitely recommend it to anyone and everyone. At first, I though Death was a girl but it turned out it was a boy. Pages 533-539, I was crying because it was so sad! It was about (dont open spoiler if you dont want the ending spoiled because I am going to spoil it for you if you open it) Rudy died and Rosa and Hans Hubermman, well, everyone on Himmel Street died. She handled Rudy's death rather sadly and Rosa and Hans. I did not like these pages. 
 "BRILLIANT and hugely ambitious...Its the kind of book that can be LIFE CHANGING." 
 ~The New York Times 
 Read. It. Now.

In my view not as good as the Percy Jackson collection, but I would be willing to admit that might be just because I don't know the Egyptian Myths as well. 
 An interesting style of telling the tale with each of the major protagonists reading it into a tape. The Gods take a different role in this than they do in the Jackson books as well, but it makes for an interesting change and the way things are put forward is also very a nice change. I am looking forward to reading the next one in the series. 
 It certainly puts a new spin on the Stargate mythos as well. 
 Have to say though I am really looking forward to the Norse books that have been rumored.

Everything but my taste. Hard a hard time getting from one page to another. Didn't like the plot nor the writing. Had to close the book after reaching maybe page 80. I can't make myself read any further.

While this book is set in the same AU as the Percy Jackson novels, this is NOT a Percy Jackson novel. There are no Greek or even Roman gods, and there are only two off-hand mentions of that world in the entire book. I really love the way Riordan describes his characters. They come to life in handful of paragraphs. That being said, the back and forth narrative between the two siblings sometimes made it hard to keep the voices straight when I was reading (important since the sister has an English accent). I wish they had successfully made movies of the PJ novels because these books would be fun if done well on the big screen. So much action and life and personality. The mechanics for the Egyptian mythology and this story is very different from the demigods of the previous two series, but that really added to the interest here. I love the Riordan educates while racing you through to the finish line. There were just enough twists and turns to make the book interesting without being excessive. I am definitely looking forward to reading the next book in the series.
My review of the audiobook version

I loved the Percy Jackson series so I've been waiting for Riordan's latest offering impatiently. In his newest novel we meet a pair of siblings, Carter and Sadie Kane, descendants of the pharaohs and magicians just coming into their power. Carter and Sadie have grown up separately, unaware of their magical heritage or the fact that the ancient Egyptian Gods are alive, well and apparently being kept in check by a secret society of magic users. 
 In the beginning of the book there's a reference to the Gods living in Manhattan that had me smiling because it was a subtle reference to Riordan's Jackson series. There are similarities between this book and those, but I think it more closely mimics his 39 Clues Maze of Bones book. The story doesn't feel original and while it's a fun romp, filled with humor and an interesting writing style - for me it lacks the spark that the Jackson series had. I like the characters but I'm not as attached to them. I'm also not sure I like how continually the narrators, Carter & Sadie, break the 4th wall and directly address the reader. The call to action at the end of the book feels too much like a marketing gimmick and forced. Also, the ending was fairly predictable. I'll read the next book in the series but I don't think this set is going to go on my permanent book shelves. It's a fun read, but too easy to put down.

Wow. I really liked it. Really intense and smart written. It discusses a lot of serious problems amongst a fictional world of the Egyption gods. I liked the ending. I'm off to find the locker now, lol. Can't wait for the next installment. Wonder what it'll be like...
This was good, but my expectation was close to Percy Jackson the series. But it's OK for me. Some of the fight scenes not feel enough to tell they were fighting.

Good story. I don't think it was quite as well-written as the Lightning Thief series and the constantly changing author was at times confusing, as I neglected to read the "author" of each chapter when I'd start reading. I do wonder how they'll work the second book, as it seems they were trying to recruit the reader. The characters were likable, the story made good use of Egyptian legend, and the plot moved along at a fairly decent pace. I enjoyed it. Somewhere, they alluded to the Greek Gods, so I wonder if we couldn't see a merging of the two series at some point.

I enjoyed this book quite a bit. Gave me a lot of information on Egyptian mythology which I'm hoping is true--in Riordans other more Greek mythology based books the information is correct, so I've no reasong to believe he's making it up here. Already started the next one.

Another dystopian book. 
 Ive read quite a few of these kind. The Maze Runner Series, Delirium series, The Giver, some of my favorites. But The Hunger games, making it the mother of them all, gave Matched a weak and less thrilling scenario. Dont get me wrong, i liked the Matched, the idea, the premise, the characters, especially Ky! Oh Ky, ure the one thing that will make me read the rest of the series. But, im telling you, how much the beginning will intrigue and tease you, the story as it unfolds is as flat and as scarce. Yes, ive been sucked to the few sweetie moments of Cassia and Xander, the matched banquet and the kiss, then Cassia and Ky, The poems, the writings on the tissues, the stolen brushes of hands, the kiss on the cheek, the hills. But when it comes to the action part, development was quite lacking, and if there was, really in a snail's pace. The book is promising, but maybe because ive got used to those heart-jumping, brain-bombing, nerve-wracking scenes from the fave books that ive mentioned, Matched failed in that department. 
 I liked how it started, but flattened at the mid, then the supposed to be cliffhanger ending, became almost the dead end, but because the search for Ky Markham will actually begin and be setting off, im gonna try to be on board. :)
It was exactly like The Giver, except not nearly as well-written.

I am so disappointed with this book. The story sounded good .. A dystopian society where Officials control all aspects of their lives and one girl is torn between her Match and another boy.. But I feel like I have already read this book several times over. I wanted to be emotionally invested but I just couldn't get there. I don't really care to read book 2 because I couldn't care less about if Cassia finds Ky.. Ugh just so disappointed.
A little slow in the beginning, but the story brilliantly fleshes out the importance of choice in society. a strong beginning to the trilogy.

As a dystopian novel: FAIL. 
 As a YA love triangle *gag*: FAIL. 
 I just tried to plow through the nauseating wuv BS to get to the action adventure that I expect dystopian novels to have...till I got to the end and I'm throwing the book across the room like, "REALLY?!? That's it? WTF!!!" 
 There goes two days I'm never getting back. 
 Matched was basically one long-winded set-up for Crossed that could've been condensed to: 
 [SPOILERS AHEAD!] 
 ...But then again you might want to read it anyway to save yourself from wasting your time on this boring wuvfest... 
 Society controls everything, including who you marry. A whole lot of nothing happens. Cassia is matched with Xander. Cassia and Xander sittin' in a tree...K-I-S-S-I-N-G... Cassie and Ky are toyed with by Society as an experiment to see if they fall in luuurv and act on their own will despite Cassia already having a match and Ky being an Aberration. Oh, I'm sorry, was that not obvious? Insert lame poetry here. C'mon, Ally Condie could've come up with more powerful poetry to move the characters and readers, but I digress. Cassia breaks Xander's heart. Boo-fracking-hoo. Society manipulates Cassia into sending Ky away on a "project." Yeah, nobody saw that a mile away:/ A whole lot more of nothing happens. Cassia goes to look for Ky...to be continued in Crossed. 
 This is when I screamed "REALLY?!? That's it? WTF!!!" I need a green pill... 
 I was thinking for a nanosecond of reading Crossed simply to justify the time I wasted reading Matched. I was really hoping it gets better. After reading reviews for Crossed, however, I'd rather draw on the dirt with a twig.

Originally posted at: http://girlzandtheirbooks.blogspot.co... 
 I wasn't too sure about this book. I had heard and seen so many different things about this book varying from "amazing! This book is great. A favorite for sure." to "I really wanted to like this book. Unfortunately I couldn't. I was bored." But when Christmas and my birthday cam along I had all this book money....what should I buy was the question and I decided. I'll give this book a try. And so I bought book 1 and 2. And you all know...I have a huge To-Read pile and I am soo far behind on it because of school so I just got to read it. And again...I was hesitant. It wasn't until my book-sharing-cousin texted me and and told me that she absolutely loved it! So..what the heck! 
 There are so many dystopian books these days and it's hard for the greats to stand out. And even though I don't particulary agree with the "amazing! This book is great." reviews....I don't necessarily agree with the "I didn't like it all. I was bored." reviews. You can say I was in the middle...leaning a bit more towards the great reviews. I liked it. I liked it a lot! At times I felt that there was a lack of depth in the story, the Society, and the characters. Even though the world made sense...stuff was missing. A Society with no past, no reason of being. All of a sudden there was an unspeakable War. An unexpected peak of interest in an experiment..involving Ky and Cassia. A lot of questions that never got answered.... 
 Cassia was an interesting character. She was clueless. One of the Societies robots. she does what she is told and doesn't ask questions. She truly believes that the Society only wants the best for her. That is until she gets a malfunction in her microcard. Two Matches? Not normal. Heck! It shouldn't even be possible! The best way I could describe her was a candle. One spark and....she went out in flames. She started to see clearer. She got a spark of rebellion....a spark produced from her grandfather and love. True love. Ky. He was adorable! He wasn't the bad boy I was expecting. He was probably the only character...the only thing that had depth in this story. I loved him. 
 And back to no depth....Xander and Cassia...what was it? For being her match and best friend..by the end of the story. I had no freaking idea about him! She said that she never needed to look at his microcard because she already knew him so well but never gave us anything about him!! I wanted to like him but his lack of any character building...I didn't get to even know him. Which made me deeply sad. Hopefully we get to see more....I sure hope so. All I want is more depth...more insight. 
 Altogether, this book brought a unique idea to the dystopian world. I don't regret buying this book and can't wait to start the second which...btw....is told from alternating POV's ....Ky's and Cassia's!!! :D Miss. Condie did an excellent job create the guessing game and a gorgeous poetic romance that left my heart aching for the doomed couple. When it comes down to it...this book didn't disappoint. Slow at times, yes. Horribly bad and not worth the read. No. Do what I did...give it a chance. Borrow it..buy it...just read it. You might be pleasantly surprised. :) 
 ~Rating: 
 3.5 stars! :) 
 Thanks for stopping by! 
 Have a great day!! :) 
 ~Jaiden

reference_books.review_text: Love the Amazon reviewer who said: "The only reason anyone buys this series now is pure hope only a small child who still believes in the Tooth Fairy could appreciate. I loved this series. I recommended this series. Now I have to hide the book under the sleeve of my arm around the bookstore before I read it and subsequently put it back, glad that I didn't waste my hard earned $26.00 on it." Substitute library for bookstore and you have my feelings too. I keep reading them as they come out hoping that they'll revert to her earlier form. The good news is they are very quick reads!

reference_books.review_text: The parts I liked, I really liked and found incredibly funny but...like most of these types of books a lot of the humor was in the initial setup and as the book went on, it felt draggy to me. Another one that I"m glad I read but also glad I didn't purchase.

reference_books.review_text: This isn't the first time a book recommendation from skimm has let me down...it was ok, a quick read...but flat characters. All told from first person in the whole unreliable narrator approach (and that's not a spoiler...in the very first sentence the narrator cops to that. This strikes me as someone saying if you like "Girl on a Train" or if you liked "gone girl" you'll like this one....

book_a.title: The King's Curse (The Plantagenet and Tudor Novels, #7)
book_a.user_review: meh...I haven't been a fan of this series (The Cousins' War) but continued reading it because I am fascinated by the events it covers. The series was interesting because it was a POV series from the viewpoints of people not typically placed front and center--Jacquetta of Luxembourg, Margaret Beaufort, Elizabeth Woodville, Isabel and Anne Neville, Elizabeth of York and Margaret Pole--but there's always a nagging sense that the history is not quite accurate, the need for a backdrop of supernatural curse/mythology.

sample_reviews.review_text: Good to read from the view of someone whose family probably should've been on the throne.

Acting as a hinge between Gregory's Cousins' War series and her Tudor series, "The King's Curse" follows the life of Margaret Pole, the niece of Edward IV and Richard III. Through Margaret's eyes, we see Katherine of Aragon come to England, Anne Boleyn rise to power and her execution, and Jane Seymour give birth to the future Edward VI and die. We also watch in horror as Henry VIII transforms from the golden, beloved Tudor prince and king to a warped, paranoid tyrant. All the while, Margaret and the rest of the Plantagenet's must tread carefully lest they be the next on the block... 
 Anna C. / Marathon County Public Library 
 Find this book in our library catalog.

Plodder of a book. But some of her interpretations were thought provoking, such as Catherine of Aragon's decision about how to talk about her first marriage, and interestingly enough, it gave me some insight about the times, but man, is Margaret Pole an unsympathetic character! I really disliked her (although, as opposed to many other reviewers, I was not as disturbed by the various "slut" comments aimed at Anne Boleyn. I like Anne a great deal, but what do you suppose her opponents would have called her? They wouldn't be polishing her halo!) 
 But as usual, some of Gregory's historical facts are nothing like the truth and no explanation is given for tweaking them. I'm just glad the series is over.

This book was much better than the last few in the series and it read like a Tudor style soap opera! A great beach read about King Henry the VIII, his wives, his madness and a cut throat court. I liked the fact that the curse from the previous novels was carried on, it had that sense of continuation. Looking forward to the next one...these ones are so addictive!
Welcome back Philippa!

See full review for The King's Curse at: https://toomanybooksnotenoughshelves.... 
 The quickest summary of a 597-paged book ever: The King's Curse follows Margaret Pole as she recovers from her brother's death and watches as her home country of England turns from the worst to the better and back again. I think that pretty much sums it up. 
 I did not like this book one bit, which is such a shame considering I liked the time period that this book took place in.

I don't have too much to say about this book, because I feel that Gregory took a rather mild character and tried to churn out some intrigue, but instead made her even more boring. Possibly because I know the outcome of the Catholic church under Henry VIII's reign, but I was just so bored and there wasn't any real suspense present in the plot. Not what I've come to expect from her novels, definitely.

I love the rich history provided in Philippa Gregory's books. This is the story of the Tudors from Margaret Pole's perspective. The story was rich and touching. Even though I knew how Margaret's story ended, I found myself hoping for a change in history.

This is another novel of the Tudor era set in the court of King Henry VIII. It is innovative in that it is from the viewpoint of Lady Margaret Pole, a member of the former ruling family of England, the Plantagenets. It begins during the reign of Henry VII and introduces us to Arthur, Prince of Wales and his younger brother Henry, who would later become Henry VIII. What is also somewhat unique is the bitter tone of the narrative. It is so bitter in the beginning of the book that it is grating on the reader. Also grating, is author Philippa Gregory's (PG) insistence upon repeatedly emphasizing the family connections of every single character. It is as if PG assumes that her readers are too incompetent to remember (or know in the first place) who everyone is. I didn't need to read "...my cousin, the queen..." over and over again. Although I was interested in learning about Margaret Pole, Countess Salisbury, there were many reasons why I nearly put this book down and not finish it. 
 Much of PG's writing consists of long, run-on, excessively compounded sentences. One is found at the bottom of page 225: "His sister Margaret, the Dowager Queen of Scotland, now sees the husband that she chose for love has turned into her enemy, and she wants to replace him in the country, and some say in her bed, with the Duke of Albany, her rival regent." The whole book is like this which makes it fatiguing to read. 
 Some of the sentences were even more confusing and hardly befitting a "New York Times Bestselling Author," as noted on the front cover. Take this example on page 255: "She is to marry either the French king, or his second son, a little boy of seven years, the duc d'Orleans, so a completely disorganized and inadequate plan." What is inadequate in this case is the writing and the editing of this book. It appears that Simon & Schuster was in a hurry to cash in on previous popular novels by PG and the resulting Starz tv shows. 
 Other reviewers have criticized PG's portrayal of certain historical characters in the novel, of them mainly Jane, Lady Rochford. PG characterizes her as a sneaky, nasty character who "sent her husband and her sister-in-law to the gallows." I have to agree with those other reviewers that there is nothing in the historical record of which I am aware that that is accurate. I also stopped and wondered about a character named Gervais Tyndale whom Margaret Pole worries has carried tales of treason by the Pole family to Thomas Cromwell. I am aware of William Tyndale and the Tyndale Bible from a slightly earlier period; is Gervais Tyndale a real person or a made-up character? PG certainly has the right to make up a secondary character. It just put a "bump" in the road of my reading. 
 I have to note that PG's mention of terriers for hunting rabbits is accurate according to other sources, as well as her mention that one male character had a handgun. Today I looked at drawings of European handguns from earlier than the time noted in the text: a Medieval "handgun" from 1400 Hungary, a matchlock from 1450 Germany, and a wheel-lock from 1550 Italy. It is possible that a member of such a wealthy court had a handgun of some sort in his possession. 
 There are also very few descriptions in this novel. The most notable was the description of Katherine of Aragon's hair as bronze. I wish there had been a few more as the overall picture painted by the text was lacking. 
 Over all, I was interested in Margaret Pole, Countess Salisbury, but appalled by the poor writing in The King's Curse. I read this book as it was the one selected by The Tudor History Book Club on Goodreads, but I really cannot recommend it.

book_b.title: The Omen Machine (Sword of Truth, #12; Richard and Kahlan, #1)
book_b.user_review: Cheating....I didn't read this. I made a conscious decision to quit after book #11 (which was 4 too many for me). I wanted this on my list so I wouldn't accidentally pick it up!

sample_reviews.review_text:
1) Rating: 4 of 5 stars 
 2) Genre: Fantasy 
 3) Synopsis: Richard and Kahlan have just won the war. They are back home and everything should be good. However, it is not. 
 4) Feelings: I love the Sword of Truth series. It is so good to be back in this world. Although this book is on the Sword of Truth world, you really don't need to read the other 11 books to get the enjoyment from this book. Sure, you won't feel the deep connection to the characters that I did but it is still a good book. 
 5) Final recommendation: A good book. I am a fan so it might not be as good for someone who isn't a Sword of Truth fan. I highly recommend it.

As interested as I was in the continuing adventures of Richard and Kahlan and as compelling as the idea of the Omen Machine was I did just not enjoy this one. All the prophecy nonsense and Jit, oh Jit, just underwhelmed. 
 It is disappointing that the most interesting part of this story is the Omen Machine, yet it hasn't made another appearance since this book and has only been mentioned a handful of times. It seems to be a wonderful idea that never reached its full potential of entertainment value.

I can only give this two stars because of how much I liked the series up through book 6. Then it was like Goodkind decided this was just a job and not worth taking pride in. This installment is no different. The characters we came to know and love are flat and the reader just does not get them anymore or else they have changed to the point that they are not who they once were. 
 For example? Nicci. Zedd. Nicci was a badass when she first came on the scene. Now the Sister of the Dark is soft hearted and nearly has a heart attack any time Richard is in danger. She only really exists anymore to provide insight to Subtractive magic and other stuff Zedd doesn't have a clue about. Zedd has gone from wise old mentor to a device for when Richard needs to come to some revelation. 
 I think Terry Goodkind still has talent hidden somewhere deep inside of him. But he just keeps hashing out the same plots. Maybe if he decided this universe is dead (as it should be) and tried his hand at an entirely new novel or series we would see some of that talent again.
It was goooood but not as good as the first 11...
Pretty good. Goodkind is a jerk though.
This series could go on forever and I would keep right on reading!
Truly terrible. Repetitive, could have told the whole story in 1/4 of the pages.

Horrible book. The first 90% was all plot build up then it finished in 3 chapters. Really Terry, you couldn't have built up to the finale a bit better and allowed us to enjoy the ending? Felt really rushed of an ending also felt like it was the first act in a 3 part play, which we all hate.

I got suckered in by a false review on Amazon or something. The review said that Goodkind's writing had matured. It definitely has not. It was very painful getting through the Sword of Truth because Goodkind seems to think his audience is unable to remember anything that has happened in previous chapters, let alone previous books. 
 He repeats himself way too often and spends too much time re-explaining the magic of the Sword and a Confessor's power. What makes it worse is that it is the SAME explanation every time. This is the thing that frustrates me more than anything else about his books. 
 This could be a great series if only he was a better writer.
Not good. Should have just left the series alone.

book_a.title: Beautiful Creatures (Caster Chronicles, #1)
book_a.user_review:
I did enjoy this book but I think it could have been better. I found that there was a lot of I do dumping and description, I honestly thought the book could have been have the size and streamlined. 
 I haven't decided yet if I will continue on with the series.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Right.... I'm not used to giving up on books, especially if I'm 3/4 of the way through them. It feels like a waste of time to ditch something you've invested so much time on. But I'd lost the will to go on with his book. 
 First, it could have been shorter. There were too many unneeded interactions and narrations by the main character and the story was starting to drag because of them. 
 Second, the characters were getting a little annoying... Ethan was expressing way too much emotion for a boy (you could tell it was written by a woman), Lena and her pessimistic outlook on her life etc... 
 Third, it was poorly written with a couple of sentences that didn't make sense) 
 Fourth, I think this book has just tried too hard to jump on the Twilight saga/Paranormal Romance/Young Adult band wagon and completely missed it. 
 I will say though that there were a few nice scenes in the story that were written as flashbacks/visions of the past which I really enjoyed.
I'd say 2.5 - I liked the book, but if I compare it to other books I've read, I cannot give it 3 stars.

It was good I guess. Not a fan of the writing style and the fact that it took me three years to finish says something. Basically there are a lot of better books out there that I think you'd enjoy reading more. It's not awful though.

I see Beautiful Creatures as Adult Literary Fiction meets Young Adult with a heavy dose of Paranormal Romance. 
 The story is told from a male perspective (unusual for this genre) in first person by Ethan Lawson Wate who is stuck in a small southern town in the middle of nowhere, where no one moves in and no one moves out. You're born there, live there and die there. Ethan wants to be different, he wants to get out and see the world, he's tired of the small-town attitudes of his school friends and neighbours. He's been having nightmares about holding onto an unknown girl he's in love while she dangles in the air until he drops her, nightmares in which he wakes up soaked from the rain in his dream, and is haunted by a mysterious song called Sixteen Moons. 
 Everything in the town is the same until Lena Duchannes moves in with her reclusive uncle, Macon Ravenwood the town's bogeyman. Everyone tars her with the same brush automatically believing she's as "crazy" as her uncle, everyone but Ethan. He recognises her from the nightmares and sees something different in her. She's a symbol of everything he wants: she's travelled, she's well-educated, well-read and she doesn't think like the rest of the town, and when Ethan becomes her friend the town turns on them both. Ethan adores her until she reveals she's a Caster, a magic-user who will be Claimed either by the Dark (evil) or the Light (good) on her 16th birthday but she belives she will go Dark. They form an unusually strong bond especially since he's only a Mortal and together they try to find out more about the Claiming to see if they can stop it but both Macon and Ethan's housekeeper (or second mother), Amma stand in their way. 
 This is very slow-building, so slow in fact that it took me over two weeks to finish. Only bull-headed determination got me to the end. A lot of background on the town and its characters was given but there were parts that just didn't interest me, like detail on the all-important war and the repetition of certain facts that got tiresome after a while as did Lena's behaviour, constantly pushing Ethan away "for his own good" when it was clear he wasn't going anywhere and all she was doing was hurting them both. I had to skim a few times. 
 Macon Ravenwood was my favourite character, I wanted to read more about him and his life. I also wanted more on Genevieve and her life after the visions, how much did she change after she made the failed bargain? How Dark did she become? I wondered if there was something special about Boo Radley the wolf-dog other than being Macon's eyes, was his relationship with Macon symbiotic? It seemed like it. I think something more could have been made of Ethan's father, I don't know what exactly but there wasn't enough interaction with Ethan especially after the suicide incident. 
 Ethan struck me as very feminine and extremely mature until quite late in the book when he found it difficult to say the words "girlfriend" and "I love you". I waited for his thoughts to turn sexual, like every hormonal teenager but it didn't happen. His unusual bond with Lena wasn't really explained, even though there was a comparison to Ethan Carter Wate (Ethan's great, great uncle) and Genevieve's relationship, it wasn't clear on what made Ethan able to feel and communicate (via mind-speak) with Lena so easily. There was a suggestion he was a Caster and then doors were opening of their own accord for him which was later explained away as his mother's spirit helping him. Lena's father is practically glossed over, we only know that he was murdered by her mother. I didn't fully understand the extent to which Mrs Lincoln was possessed by Serafine, she said she wasn't always possessing her so I was curious to know how much of Mrs Lincoln's behaviour was due to Serafine and how much was her own nasty personality. 
 The ending was lack-lustre, rushed, not well-thought out, hodge-podge. Lena gets rid of the enemies quickly and easily, a flash of lightning was all it took. Lena isn't claimed and doesn't claim herself, she doesn't make a choice instead a wishy-washy explanation was given - suddenly there is no moon and Lena, being a powerful Natural temporarily got rid of the moon so she wouldn't have to choose (when did she have the time to do that?) until of course there is another verse of the song but instead of Sixteen Moons it's Seventeen Moons. I'm guessing this means her choice has been put off until her 17th birthday. Ugh. I'm not sure if this is right because Ethan notices Lena's eyes have changed colour, one has remained green and the other is now gold like those of Dark Casters. Shouldn't both of her eyes be gold like Genevieve's? 
 One thing that wasn't addressed was the fact that Ethan and Lena could never be together physically, it was stated and then after the drama of the climax it wasn't discussed by Lena and Ethan. I would think they'd be thinking about that as well as Macon. I can't see them staying together, especially since Lena hasn't admitted to killing the Dark Casters or even bringing Ethan back to life - which is another thing I'm not clear on. Is he truly alive? Why was his life traded for Macon's specifically. I just don't understand. 
 I know this review is quite negative but I do believe the small-town mentality was well-drawn. As a child I lived in a small English village in the country, my mother was the only black person and I was mixed race. We both felt like outsiders and the rumour-mill got so bad, led by the stay-at-home mums, that my mother sent me away while she packed our things and moved us out, back to the city. She didn't want me to be affected by their behaviour. Lena and Ethan were pretty strong not to crumble under that collective pressure. 
 I really wanted this story to finish in this book. I made an extraordinary effort to finish it due to the hype, some great lines and a few intriguing scenes, I deserved to be rewarded with a good ending. This book isn't as concise as it could have been or as clear, I believe a concerted effort was made to make the town and the many characters realistic but the ending wasn't right. The need for a sequel seemed to outweigh the need to end the book properly.

Contemporary fantasy in a small southern town, where a local boy falls for the new girl, who turns out to be a "caster" as in spell caster, and niece of the local recluse. In spite of several touches, such as a Civil War reenactment, it didn't feel really Southern to me, more researched than experienced.

Eh. 
 Was expecting better. The trailer for the movie is what sparked my interest. I was disappointed. Maybe the movie will be better?

It is definitely a YA, sci fi, love story. You know how the teenagers always seem wise and really in love, but there are moments when you know how immature they can be and how much more they have to grow. I really enjoyed it all the same. It was creative and interesting throughout the whole book. 
 I grew up learning about Salem Witch Trials and my sister taking me to Salem often (where my siblings were born), so I have always been in interested in the "Caster" world. 
 Although this plot takes place small southern town where everyone who is different is cast into the shadows, I still could relate. 
 The characters were well developed and I loved to hate the bad ones and really enjoyed rooting for the good ones. 
 I look forward to reading the books in the series and watching the movie...even though the movies are never as good as the books.

This is the first in the Beautiful Creatures Series. 
 I had a very hard time getting into this book and I didn't particularly like the writing style. I could see how young girls might find it a bit more appealing but as an adult I found this one to be lacking. You had to read half the book to even understand what was really going on. I almost gave up on it, but did finish because I looked at the reviews and they went from 1 star to 5 stars and nothing in between. It would be interesting to see if the 1 star reviewers were young adults to adults. I really don't believe this book needed to be this long, as the story could have been told in about 200 pages. The most interesting part was in the last 50 pages and that was even hard to understand at times. 
 I think some of the things about these creatures were either not explained well enough or we were expected to know. I saw where she they wrote this book in three months or at least the rough draft. Maybe it would have been better if it would have been better edited. I am not sure. 
 I am giving this 3 out of 5 as I did enjoy the premise of the book, I just had a hard time with the way the story was told.
Great fun read. Books 2 and 3 weren't as great unfortunately.
Not for me. This may be due to the fact that I was listening to the audio version and the reader was AWFUL. So might possibly pick up a physical copy of this and give it another try, but not likely

book_b.title: Burned (House of Night, #7)
book_b.user_review: When will the series end? and these poor characters be put to death? I know these books are making money, probably a lot, but still. I really want the series to come to an end with a some sort of overall conclusion.

sample_reviews.review_text: This books was really awesome. My stomach was churning and I was on the edge of my seat the whole time. I liked having more perspectives to read from although I wish there had been a little less Stevie Rae and a bit more of Stark and Aphrodite. I also can't figure out how Neferet is still able to pull the wool over most of the High Councils eyes? I mean she is clearly evil and she has that whole Darkness thing going on. I cannot wait to see who he comes back as that should be really interesting maybe he will be a vampyre in the next life. Other than that I am a bit worried about what is going to happen with Stevie Rae and Rephaim. Especially after that whole Dallas debacle, which I'm kind of glad happened because the guy was so clingy and needy, and just terribly annoying. All in all, I'm glad Zoey is back and it is going to be interesting to see how Kalona fairs with being bound to Neferet.

ok so....this is where this series ends for me...its not moving enough and it gets harder to pick up the book every time... 
 i am already that far to throw something on it to not have a bad feeling or feeling sorry for abandoning it... 
 i tried...i did...i promise...and some might not understand me but no...this is not meant for me

Tuto knihu som citala, len preto ze nemam rada nedokoncene serie. A tiez ako ostatne knihy z tejto serie ma ani tato velmi nezaujala. Aby som povedala presne vobec mi nesadla. 
 Nuz asi som prilis stara na tuto seriu.
It was so so. Not the best, I think I'm over this series, but still going to read them all. I'm hooked either way.

So damn good!! 
 I know a lot of you have given up on this series. After Hunted, I don't blame you. I almost gave up on it too. But, with Tempted (the last book) it picked up. A lot. And this book? Wow, it's as good as the first!! This book was SO good, the writing was phenomenal! So wherever you stopped in this series, just pick up Burned and give it another try. 
 You won't regret it. I have to finish this series! I ordered Awakened (the next book) as soon as I finished this! 
 I'm just shocked that a series can lose momentum this much and then bounce back SO strongly! I like that the new, or rather, old old ways were introduced. The bulls, the ancient power, all of that added a huge element to the already amazing mythology -- which is my favorite part of this series. The back story and mythology is so rich, I love that it just got better in this book! The Darkness (with a capital D) and it's smoky black tendrils, circling and waiting for an entrance...seriously? If that doesn't evoke excellent imagery...idk what does! This book played like a movie in my head. Those are my favorite kind of stories.
There's Nothing new happening!

Once again I'm left entirely disappointed by the House of Night series, I honestly believe I'm going to give up here, and believe me it takes an awful lot for me to say that, I rarely give up on a book series that I've made it this far into. Let me start by listing the reasons why I should give up on this series: 
 1. Zoey, is there really a more flat, one dimensional protagonist who uses and abuses those around her as if it is her role in life? 
 2. The writing, it is getting simply unbearable, some parts seem as though there was a lot of thought put into them, and they read well, however there are others that are riddled with grammatical errors and spelling mistakes that seem to do my head in at various points in time. 
 3. The shameless pop-culture references, they are unnecessary and in my opinion completely and totally misplaced, there is a time and a place for shameless pop-culture references, and these books are not the type, for such an interesting storyline there is a lot more that could be done without references to pop-culture on every page. 
 4. The plot, brilliant, I openly accept this. Well researched, well planned. The delivery, however falls completely short of what the plot deserves. It continues to fall down a slope as the books progress. 
 5. The number of books, there just seems to be more and more books with no end in sight. The books only progress a few weeks at the most and at the rate this is going the storyline will have completely shattered like Zoey's soul by the time we reach number twelve, although I have heard there are to be fifteen, if so I have some serious concerns for the storyline, I do not see how it could survive so many more books. 
 6. The characters, not all of them. Just most of them. They alike Zoey are flat and have very little besides a shameless stereotype to define them. It seems unfair that they all have to be entirely dedicated to Zoey when all she seems to do is use them as though they are her puppets. There are some exceptions, such as Nerefet, Stark, Repheium and Stevie Rae. The rest are just horrid. 
 7. Kalona is the worst antagonist I have ever had the misfortune to read about. Period. He's supposed to be a villain. He should act like one. 
 8. Heath. If he died why did he had to be in 85% of this book, I was glad to see him go as a character why did he have to linger behind for another whole book. 
 Now that's out of the way... Where was I again? Oh yes, will I read the next book? The answer? Most likely, let's just say my reading the rest of this series hangs in the balance of the next book, as I certainly did not like this book. It was not my cup of tea at all, and I am somewhat glad I borrowed it from the library rather than buying it. There are 8 reasons why I don't like it, and not all that many as to why I do like the series any more, and that is beginning to really get me down *cries melodramatically* oh, the waste of such potential. 
 1 Star.
This series is really treading water now.
I really liked the different view points all though out the story, especially seeing things from yummy Starks POV.

i loved the previous books in the series but this was un-interesting, boring and i just couldnt get into it. i thought it was uneventful and just kinda stupid. i tried to finish it but it was too painful.

reference_books.title: Die for Me (Revenants, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Kate just lost her parents and it feels like her whole world has ended. Her grandparents move her and her sister to Paris with the hope of giving them a new start. Kate finds it too hard to let go until she meets the mysterious and gorgeous Vincent Delacroix. He sweeps her off her feet and she lands hard on the ground when she discovers what he truly is. Kate can't lose someone she loves again. It would be too much. So should she dare fall in love with Vincent at all? 
 The strength of this book was in the romantic plot. Kate and Vincent complimented each other well, and how they dealt with the going-ons felt real. The story introduced us to an original supernatural concept. No vampires or werewolves here. We have revenants. I was excited about this, but I don't think it was explored as fully as it could've been. Too much telling instead of action. I wanted more from the paranormal part of this tale. There was also a lack of tension. Not that there wasn't a build up, but it wasn't tight enough and thus, for me, the short climax wasn't fulfilling. 
 I think the story has potential and the characters are solidly in place, but I needed something more to give it a higher rating.

reference_books.title: Notorious Nineteen (Stephanie Plum, #19)
reference_books.review_text:
Stephanie Plum gets herself in a mess again. A man missing from the hospital, a lunatic on the hunt for her, a talking Tiki, and a ghastly pink dress. 
 This has the same formula as the previous books in the series. It's a fun and easy read. I laughed out loud. Some of the jokes are getting old, and Stephanie really, REALLY just needs to choose between Morelli and Ranger. I know this is fiction because no real man can be that tolerant of her.

reference_books.title: Evermore (The Immortals, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Sixteen year old Ever Bloom only wants to be normal. She had a perfect life until her family was in a deadly car accident. Everyone died except for her, and Ever was left with psychic abilities that make being around other people horrible. She's labeled a freak at her new high school and attempts to stay that way even after gorgeous Damen Auguste transfers. He's the only one that she can't sense with her abilities. She's drawn to him, but will his secrets be too much for her to bear? 
 It's an interesting premise, and I've heard good things about this book. YA books are usually hit or miss with me, though. I didn't connect with Ever. How she acted didn't make any sense to me, even with teenage angst. Not being able to do so, it tainted the rest of the story.

reference_books.title: Fifty Shades of Grey (Fifty Shades, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Anatasia Steele is a sweet girl with a big heart, and completely clueless. She meets mysterious and irresistible billionaire Christian Grey and finds herself caught up in a relationship far more complicated than one just involving kinky sex. 
 I wasn't sure what I was expecting. I heard varying opinions, but none of them fit what I just read. Though I found much of it boring, I did read the entire thing and I can respect the ending. Though, knowing there's two more books, I know it's just a teaser cliffhanger and I don't like where the story will likely go. 
 Ana is a weak protagonist. Her inner dialogue is repetitive. Actually, the dialogue throughout the book is repetitive. I don't respect her or even like her. I don't believe a virgin is that good her first time nor do I believe she'd be capable of orgasms like that. I do realize this is a work of fiction, an escape fantasy for readers, but it isn't realistic. 
 Christian is frightening. He is a sadist no matter how much he protests the fact. And he's a stalker. He did admit to that. That's not romance. That's criminal. Sure, I know the appeal of finding a dark soul in need of rescue, but his behavior isn't appealing in any way to me. 
 The story didn't really take us anywhere. I didn't feel the intensity I know I should've been feeling. The writing lacked tautness. It lacked sizzle and spice. It was all laid out on a silver platter with the expectation the reader would be shocked and turned on by the sexual content. 
 That's another spot I expected a lot more. Supposedly this book shocked the writing world. It really wasn't shocking. A little spanking and bondage. I didn't feel it was a big deal. I've read kinkier things in other genres of romance and they didn't get this sort of attention. It would take a lot more than this to shock me. Perhaps that says more of me than the book!

reference_books.title: Norse Mythology
reference_books.review_text:
For Gaiman fans and mythology fans, this is a must read. Told elegantly staying true to the original lore, but with that Gaiman flair to it. I have a general knowledge of Norse myths, but this brought to me so many delectable details I hadn't known. 
 Beautiful cover art too. My son told me he wants a hammer just like it. I told him he needs to go on a quest and find two dwarf brothers to make it for him!

book_a.title: Dark Witch (The Cousins O'Dwyer Trilogy, #1)
book_a.user_review:
I'm a fan of Nora Roberts, and I have enjoyed several of her other books. I simply could not get into this story. I liked the premise, and I know Nora writes paranormal romances very well, but several things didn't work for me here. 
 I didn't like the protagonist, Iona. She felt too much like a child to me. There was a lot of head hopping in the narration, and sometimes I didn't know whose head I was in. The cousins connected too easily, too quickly, and jumped into the magical reasons of their meeting. I was a bit lost in parts. 
 I did like Branna, Connor, and Fin which says I might like the next books in the series more. But this first book did not start the series off strongly. A big disappointment.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Dark Witch felt off. Just completely off, and it's one of Nora Roberts' very few misses in the last years. 
 We start out with an extended prologue which sets up the trilogy. 800 years earlier, dark witch Sorcha (who's the good one here; in this series a dark witch is not one engaged in dark magic) is besieged by the evil Cabhan, who wants to take her powers. She succeeds in escaping him and passes on her powers to her 3 children and their descendants, knowing that at some point in the future, 3 dark witches of her blood will come together to fight the final battle against Cabhan. 
 In the present, Iona Sheehan has decided to up sticks and move from the US to Ireland, where her beloved Nan was born. There's something about the place that calls to her, and she somehow knows she's meant to be there. And as soon as she knocks on the door of her cousins' place, it becomes clear why. She, and her cousins, Brenna and Connor, are Sorcha's descendants and the ones who are meant to finish off Cabhan. 
 As Iona trains and develops her powers, she also finds a job that's right up her street. She's always had a connection with horses (each of the three dark witches has that; Brenna and Connor with dogs and falcons respectively), and she's hired at the local stables. There she meets the owner, Boyle McGrath, whom she's immediately attracted to. Iona's always been on the diffident side with men, but she's never wanted one like she wants Boyle. 
 Ok, so, where to start? I suppose the first thing to say is that this felt derivative. Now, Nora's books have never been unpredictable, but I usually don't care at all. Until this one. It was a bit too much, a mix and match using bits of previous series. The biggest chunk is from the Three Sisters Island trilogy. There's the witches, there's the fight against an old evil, and then there's the characters. To me, that was the most striking bit. Iona reminded me a lot of Nell, the nervous, very unsure and tentative new arrival in the island, who's taken under the wing of the established, confident Brenna/Mia (Iona does prove to be a bit more confident than Nell was, especially with Boyle, but at the beginning, she was forever apologising and babbling). Brenna/Mia is clearly being set up for a romance with a man (Fin/Sam) with whom she shares a history and quite a bit of resentment, a man with his own powers, which will be needed for the final confrontation. Meara, who works with Iona at the stables, is a sort of blander version of Ripley, with some of her experience but none of her "I don't give a shit" abruptness. I liked Meara, but Ripley was much more fabulous To all that, we add a dash of the Ireland from the Gallaghers of Ardmore trilogy, and shades of the Circle Trilogy in the nature of the evil that must be confronted and there, new trilogy. 
 Then there's the plot about fighting Cabhan, which never even began to engage me. The problem starts with the immediate coming together of the group of 6 (Iona and her cousins, Boyle, Fin and Meara) and their absolute commitment to the future fight. Iona has learnt a bit about her magic from her Nan, but had absolutely no idea of the history or that she's meant to risk her life to fight Cabhan. And yet there is no hesitation when she hears the story. She experiences no doubt or wonders why she should do this or what might happen if she doesn't. She's all "risk my life to defeat this powerful being who's done nothing to me but killed an ancestress 800 years ago? Of course, sure, let's do it." Bizarre. I kept thinking of Iolanthe, in Sherry Thomas' The Burning Sky, whose first reaction in a similar situation was, very sensibly, "the hell I will, I want to live and this is a suicide mission!", but who was convinced of the necessity of the struggle by experiencing the reality of the evil of what they're up against. 
 I think that realisation of the reality of what they're up against was precisely what was lacking here. Because you see, Cabhan is just not scary. He's nothing more than a sort of cloud of... well, I can't really say "evil", because although our protagonists think he is, he doesn't really do much here to warrant that description. He attacks them because he wants their power and because he knows they mean to destroy him. Sure, you wouldn't want him to succeed, but evil? For all we know, he seems to have spent the ensuing 800 years waiting as this disembodied force. There isn't much of a sense of menace. 
 It didn't help that the magic in this book feels silly. It's all very twee, with rhyming spells (which made me giggle uncontrollably) and floating bits of fire and stuff like that. There are some scenes where Iona is supposed to do things that are spectacular, but they didn't feel so, they felt meh. 
 The romance just wasn't great. I did like how the otherwise shy Iona basically blurts out her feelings for Boyle in front of everyone and pursues him, but then the romance develops in a bit of a frustrating way. Everything's fine, and then there's a point where they experience a crisis which felt very forced, making what to me was a lot about nothing much. I didn't particularly care whether they got back together or not, and that's the mark of a very boring romance. 
 The final thing in my litany of complaints is the way Roberts approaches her setting here. It's an area she's usually great at. Her settings, both physical and thematic (by that I mean, say, the world of smoke jumpers in Chasing Fire) are big parts of her books, and they usually come alive and are fascinating. Ireland, though, she seems to fetishise, and that's a problem. There's no shred of anything that feels real in her setting here (for instance, this is a world where every small business is thriving and doesn't seem to have experienced any issues in the previous years), but the problem is how it's all romanticised. Things like the way her Irish characters spoke felt really off. I live in Liverpool, so I have a fair few Irish friends and acquaintances. Not one of them speaks like Yoda. 
 There were some things I did like here. Iona is the child of extremely distant parents, and it's lovely to see her begin to build a family with the rest of the circle. The developing friendship between her and Meara and Fin, and the way Brenna and Connor become her family were the strong points of the book. Other than that, though, this was a bust. 
 MY GRADE: A C-.

This was a major let down, and I'm a big Roberts fan. But the hero was boring and the story was regurgitated from her other trilogies - predictable and not interesting. Had to force myself to finish this one and I doubt I'll read the rest. Hopefully her contemporary suspense novels don't go downhill too!

I know that there is a formula to writing (as a general rule), but for me, her work seems painfully obvious that she does. So why did I read this? Because someone at work pestered me to and then went so far as to lend me not just this book, but the 2nd one in the trilogy. She knew I would love it because I enjoy paranormal romance and it is set in Ireland. I didn't love it. I didn't hate it either though and that counts for something, right? This is a good book for someone who isn't me and I suppose it was decent enough for a summer read.

Maybe I've reached a time where Nora Roberts and I will part company. We've been companions for many years now but for me, especially with the PNR books, there's a staleness to the formula that I can't get past anymore. Perhaps I'd be in a more forgiving mood if I didn't feel like I paid for and read this story already as part of the Three Sisters trilogy Dance Upon the Air. This is very much a condensed version of that one. 
 Why bother with providing the MC with anymore than a cursory back story when you can skip all that and set things up in the 1200's. Then we can have your character in modern day be aware of ALL of that information (through oral history from her grandmother *insert eye roll*) and know she's a witch and come to her ancestor's home and have them all recognize that of course she's the one they've been waiting for all this time and of course we'll teach you how to control these powers that you've been manifesting. So blase...magic/shmagic. 
 There's no joy here, it's all very rote and checking ticks off in the boxes. 
 This is a fine story if you've never read any other Roberts PNR book. The shine is off for me though because I can see clearly how this trilogy will play out. I'd rather re-read the Three Sisters.

I should have liked this more - good premise, ancient curse, magical Ireland and hot Irishmen, but somehow it seemed a little bland.

ehh started out good

The first book of the cousins O'Dwyer series, Dark Witch, reminded me a lot of two other "firsts" of her trilogies- the Gallaghers of Ardmore, and the Three Sisters Island. If you've read both, you know they both involve "outsiders" coming into a life already in progress for the others, but quickly being accepted into the fold. In the Gallaghers, it's Jude going to Ireland to reevaluate herself. And in the Three Sisters Island, it's Nell fleeing an abusive husband, and unlocking her witch powers. 
 In Dark Witch, we met Iona Sheehan, who goes to Ireland to meet cousins and basically get away from her parents and her old, unfilling life, at the urgency of her grandmother. She grew up knowing she had powers, but was never able to fully explore them because of her mother's indifference and almost fear of them. 
 We meet her cousins, Branna and Conner, who open her up to her powers. We meet Boyle, who gives her a place to work at his stables, and who captures her heart pretty much immediately. And we meet Finn, who we discover has a history with not only the Dark Witch mythos, but with Branna. They had a past relationship that is still causing them heartache today. 
 The Dark Witch myth is pretty intriguing- an ancestor of Iona, Branna, and Connor was the Dark Witch, and she is being attacked by Cabhan, an evil male witch who is obsessed with the Dark Witch and wants her powers (and her body). This entire portion goes on for 40 pages, but that's not a bad thing- it was pretty interesting, and I'm hoping she touches on the history of Cabhan and the Dark Witch a little more in the next books. 
 Iona learns how to harness and control her magick through working with Branna, and she grows both in her job and relationship. I really loved hearing about her relationship with her horse, and the other's relationships with their animals as well. I really love when a story has that element. 
 Her relationship with Boyle, on the other hand, was a little lacking. I don't know if it was just that Boyle is a harder male character than I've read from Nora in awhile, or if there was little to no chemistry- I just wasn't happy when they finally got together. And I didn't care when they had their typical Nora Robert's fight to "break up". It was the typical Nora formula that I love, but I wasn't all that into the characters or their relationship. 
 What I really enjoyed about the book, and why I still gave it four stars on Good Reads, is the relationships between all the characters in general, and the history behind them. And I want to know more about the Dark Witch, and I want to see Cabhan defeated. I'm invested. 
 The second book in the Cousins O'Dwyer Trilogy, Shadow Spell, is set to release on May 6th, 2014 (as of this blog post). It looks like it is going to be Connor's story, and I'm so glad- I was hoping she would save Branna for last!

sample_reviews.review_text:
Review originally posted on Bitten Books and given 4 stars. 
 I am completely in love with the circumstances of Cassiel's character. I love that she's a djinn who's been cast out and now must learn to be not only human but to have a physical presence at all. Her annoyance and displeasure over simple things that we take for granted made me truly appreciate her as a unique character. How many other characters do you read about who go through eating food for the first time? Eating is something we all do and have likes and dislikes for but the idea that it's a hassle for Cassiel because she never had to eat before is very interesting to me. 
 Cassiel's struggle with human emotion is what makes Undone such a compelling read. Sometimes Cassiel came off as cruel and uncaring but it was such a pleasure to watch her slowly open up. Early on in the book, when Cassiel first encounters compassion when she heals someone on pure instinct, I was blown away by how much the moment affected me. From that moment on it was impossible to do anything but root for her success and happiness. Even the tiny shows of humanity that she exhibits like offering Isabel part of her cookie made me want to squee, hug her and exclaim 'yay! progress!' 
 The beginning of Undone was a lot slower than most urban fantasy novels. It was enjoyable for me to read but action junkies will probably find it boring. It wasn't until about a third of the way way through the book that the actual plot even began. I think it was necessary for the book to begin so slowly because it allowed time for Cassiel to adjust and the reader to adjust to her. I think without this, that Cassiel might have become harsher and much less likable as a character. Once the action starts though, it's a never ending roller coaster of constant loop-de-loops and ninety degree drops. There was so much going on and it was always so big. 
 I love urban fantasy as a genre. Everything about it captures my book loving heart. I can read hundreds of vampire and werewolves novels and not get sick of them. But when something new comes along, I do find that it becomes more special to me. Caine's djinns and Wardens were so interesting to read about and I'm taken aback that they're the first I've experienced in the genre considering they aren't that uncommon in older literature (as elementals and genies). I haven't read the series that Undone is a spin-off of, Weather Warden, but I was never confused or felt like I was missing information. I'm so glad that this unique take on urban fantasy has more for me to read though because I will definitely be reading the rest of Outcast Season then picking up the Weather Warden series as soon as possible. 
 My only complaint about Undone is sort of a major one. Undone is in no way a complete book. It ends on not only a major cliffhanger but there is absolutely no resolution to the plot. I want to compare it to an episode of a TV show but at least they complete the mini story in each episode while carrying on the overall story arc. Instead Undone was like only having the first half of a movie. I really, really loved this book but I don't like what was done. Now I feel forced to buy and read the next book instead of doing so because the first was so enjoyable.

Caine uses characters from her "Weather Warden" series to jumpstart a new one from the perspective of a Djinn. Cassiel--not Cassie--has been cast out by Ashan, forced to live as a human. The only way she can survive is through other Wardens. 
 Jo and David make cameo appearances and Luis Rocha, who helped Jo once, takes center stage with his brother. The Rocha family takes Cassiel in as she tries to track down a new threat to the Dijnn and Wardens. 
 Moving and engrossing to start with, it ends on a strange note with the Ranch, but Cassiel is a character I now care about, so I'll read the next one. 
 It's best if you read the first seven "Weather Warden" novels before this one, so you can understand the world, Dijnn, and the events leading up to this. It just makes it run smoother. 
 Interesting, suspense-filled, and with a strong female character and plenty of suport characters. Cassiel even fits the mold of someone not really used to the human world. Props to Rachel Caine for another promising series!
