book_b.title: Lincoln in the Bardo
book_b.user_review: A beautifully-written rendering of President Lincoln's love for his son Willie, and the unbearable grief that cloaked him in the wake of his son's death at age 11. The personification of the dead in the cemetery where young Lincoln was laid to rest is very clever and creative. However, purgatory as depicted here, with a cast of strange and sordid characters, is unsettling and weird. I found the chaotic, disjointed conversation among the spirits confusing.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I read AND listened to the audiobook simultaneously and feel like that was what made it probably one of the best pieces of literature I've ever experienced. If you're reading this, then I'm sure you know to expect the unexpected with Saunders- and especially with style. After you become accustomed to the style of the novel, (like a script without stage notes sandwiched between relevant bits and pieces of historical "facts", accounts , etc from a variety of sources surrounding Lincoln, his reaction to the death of his 11 year old son during the FIRST YEAR of his presidency (seriously, how did I never put the two together and how relevant to his administration?!), the party the White House had the night of Willies death, the funeral, and other snippets concerning that time. , then you start to get the big picture of the book. 
 That unraveling - to me at least - was beautiful and part of what this book is about: the juxtaposition of life & death, "fact" & fiction, history vs religion, beauty & ugliness. Life is all these things and more, but never easy. It's takes some time before unraveling your beautiful bits from your nasty and how THAT perspective and understanding of the incomprehensible is what becomes you. 
 There is just so much to uncover in this book; I seriously wish everyone I know would read it, just so I can get their take on it. 
 The biggest takeaway from it all is this basic idea of kindness to all because of the shared pain we experience. And the beauty of this message is that it never comes out and says this directly, but you feel it leap out of the pages: at first like a tiny heartbeat that only gets louder as the story continues. 
 God bless you George Saunders for writing such a beautiful, living piece of art that will always be relevant and relatable as long as there are humans reading it and hopefully, living a life with more kindness and empathy because of it.

Took a little while to get into, and it was easier to read when I stopped trying so hard to get it. A lot of unfolding to do in this one, but ultimately a unique take on grief and mortality. Loved the writing style here -- it was quick, and subtle, and really relied on me.

Astounding. An oral history of the dead backed by a greek chorus of historians, with a great, nuanced, humanistic, empathic answer to the question "Why do we keep going? Why do we keep living after tragedy." After this and 10th of December, Saunders is easily now one of my favorite authors.

What the heck did I just read? 
 ERIN CLEMENCE 
 The entire novel, "Lincoln in the Bardo" by George Saunders is written in this format. Similar to screenplay format, except without any cast of characters of descriptions of settings. It took me a good ten minutes into this novel to even figure out who was important, who was the main character, what was going on. 
 ERIN CLEMENCE 
 To be honest, I nearly DNF'ed this book three separate times. I really only finished it because the novel was easy to read in its screen play format and I could just skip over the boring parts (for example, two pages of descriptions of Abraham Lincoln). 
 ERIN CLEMENCE 
 Annoyed yet? So was I. "Lincoln in the Bardo" tells the tale of young Willie Lincoln, who dies from a case of typhoid fever and then is send to "the Bardo", which is a form of purgatory, where he interacts with several others who have passed on while the battle for his soul continues. Or at least that's what I think it's about. This novel had such potential, the concept was so creative, but the format was so irritating and a reader did not get any opportunities to bond with any of the characters. I was not invested in the outcome of the characters at all, even little Willie. 
 I don't know what Saunders' other books are like and if they are in a similar format, but I won't be finding out. I was disappointed in this book as I have seen many positive reviews for this novel, and I expect this review won't be very popular. But I couldn't do it folks- it just wasn't for me.

"And if you go.. chasing rabbits, 
 and you know you're.. going to fall 
 Tell 'em a hookah-smoking caterpillar 
 has given you the call." 
 The unusual format, like oddly punctuated and inverted lines of a play, was fine by me. It just took some adjustment, and then it was easy to read. 
 But the random, psychedelic-seeming thought trains were way too artsy for me, and the periodic sophomoric vulgarity struck me as stupid (sorry). I did not titter for an instant. There was definitely a plot to follow, but like from the thick main trunk of a vine, there were tendrils of offshoots that obscured the main body at times. Some of these shoots were their own little stories, but some were just weedy backdrop. I'm all for setting a mood or seeing a theme evinced in different ways, although here, I just did not care about any of it. 
 I did have empathy with Lincoln and his boy, but this story robbed me even of that. Others have complimented the depth of research that went into the accounts, primarily at the front end of the story, but using two books and Google can cough up many quotes and accounts, and for me (who is a boring and methodical scientist), quantity does not equal quality. As a reader, some of them were entertaining (like opposing descriptions of the moon's phase, Lincoln's appearance, etc), but a handful would have sufficed. Thankfully, these barrels full of quotations took up more space such that I did not have to spend too much reading time in the bardo. 
 Oops. I've gone too far perhaps and ticked my five- and four-star friends off. But I'm not the "magical realism" type. Dull, grounded, and bound with facts, this story just isn't my thing. I do love Yann Martel's work and that of Gabriel Garcia Marquez, though. Heck, I even adore reading The Master and Margarita every few years around Easter! Talk about the surreal! But this story went too far for me without a meaningful payoff. My 13 year old sister died pretty suddenly - within a week's time - many years ago, and maybe the deterioration of dead 11-year-old Willie speaking from the half-life added to my distaste. I felt a bit protective of and angry on behalf of President Lincoln, too. He was a real person - a heartbroken dad with a helluva stressful job. How dare we pull his memory and that of his little boy out and sandwich it with these absurd ghosts, ones with giant phalluses and multiple noses, just for our entertainment? Shall we next exhume Martin Luther King? 
 The recurring matterlightblooming phenomena and Mr Bevins' ever growing number of appendages were just too ridiculous for my taste. If Edward Scissorhands or the Mad Hatter or Beetle Juice thrilled you, be my guest - you'll love this. I just do not have an active enough imagination to have taken the plunge into the bardo. 
 Despite the constellations of five stars out there, this thing went dim for me at the halfway point. 2.5 bumped to 3 so I wont catch flak from my more creatively minded friends. I'd have to have eaten some sort of magic mushroom to have liked this...just not my taste.

Whaaat did I just read? I wish I hadn't forced myself to finish this. It didn't get better, just more of the same weird disconnected quotes from historical pieces and fictional voices of random ghosts. What was the plot line? I don't know. I also didn't care about any of the "characters" (can I even call them characters? They are so underdeveloped). This was one of the strangest books I've ever read (but not strange in a good way...)

Boy has this book gotten a lot of hoopla. And sure, it's kind of revolutionary in having so many voices and perspectives around one historically famous person/family. It is a fascinating unpacking of how every moment is being seen in multiple ways by multiple people. Add to that that more than half of the narrators/characters are dead (with few of them being actually aware of this fact) and things do get pretty interesting. But it's almost too clever for its own good. We lose the story amidst all the footnotes and different voices clanging over each other. I listened to the audio book, which is a true cavalcade of stars, but that still didn't quite save the story. But if you are a Lincoln history buff, you are probably going to be over the moon for this heavily researched story.

It's February 1862, and President Lincoln's nine-year-old son Willie has died. He is interred in Oak Hill Cemetery, but his spirit is still in the "bardo", a transitional state between life and whatever comes next in Tibetan Buddhist beliefs. The cemetery is full of spirits that talk about their lives, and also about President Lincoln's visits to the cemetery. 
 The President comes alone on horseback in the middle of the night to see Willie again. He opens the coffin and tenderly holds his son in grief and love. He thinks of other parents that are grieving soldiers that died in the bloody battles of the Civil War. He also is disturbed about the terrible problems of slavery. Lincoln is weighted down with sorrow about the war and the loss of Willie. Short chapters of interesting historical snippets from factual sources are also inserted into the book among the fictional chapters. 
 As a reader, I felt like I was sitting in the cemetery with a chorus of voices surrounding me. They are mostly unhappy spirits from various economic classes, some white and some black slaves. The voices had a 19th Century sensibility with dialogue that ranged from serious, concerned, and generous to comic, bawdy, and absurd. The book is unusual, creative, and thought provoking. Although I read the book in print, I imagine that listening to an audio book would be a wonderful way to experience the voices in the bardo. 4.5 stars

book_a.title: See You at Harry's
book_a.user_review: My daughter read this and really enjoyed it. I like keeping up with her books too. Good book for a child dealing with loss. Probably fairly realistic.

sample_reviews.review_text: Wow! This book works on so many levels and touches on so many topics. In See You at Harry's we get a glimpse into a flawed, real family that many readers will be able to relate to. This family is pushed apart and brought together by an unbelievable tragedy. But the characters in the book face the tragedy in their own true ways. I think that's what I liked most about this book- it was so true. The dialogue was spot on. I held my breath in certain spots, cried in others and wanted to hug each one of them. I will continue to think about the characters in this book.
A really gripping book. I really loved the whole family so much. This book touched my heart and didn't let go. That's all I can really say about it. Loved it. So wonderful and sad. Very very sad.
4.5, to be accurate.

Jo Knowles skillfully and sensitively tackles lots of "coming of age" issues in her novel: grief, loss, insecurity, and love. She shows Fern's emotions with simple yet vivid detail, and there were several passages where I had to sigh with admiration at the beauty of her writing. 
 Another great thing about the novel are the characters. Fern has a great bond with her brother Holden, but their relationship gets tested as he explores adult issues. Fern also has a wonderful best friend, Ran, a boy who was bullied in elementary school and who calms Fern with the motto "All will be well." Because of his experiences, Ran likes to figure out the "why" behind people's actions, even when they are mean. 
 More of us need to be like Ran. 
 See You at Harry's deals with some mature issues, including death and homosexuality. These were great discussion points for my daughter and I, but might not be suitable for younger readers. 
 If you liked the novel Wonder, by R.J. Palacio, I think you'll enjoy See You at Harry's. 
 The full review of this book is posted at my blog: Why I Love See You At Harry's
Very emotional...laughing, crying as we silently support this family...that all will be we'll.
Really good book! Haha just one of those cutesy little stories... Sad at the end though. Would recommend for like 10 year olds
Read this on accident after it wound up on my desk for replacement... Highly recommended.

Jo Knowles has captured the emotional turmoil of a loved-one's death. I loved this book and can't wait to read more by this author.

I'm extremely picky when it comes to Middle Grade books. Due to this, I tend to avoid them most of the time because when I do read them, I'm notoriously hard on them and my rating tends to reflect that. It's unfair, but it is what it is. However, I've been extremely busy the last couple of weeks that I thought a Middle Grade would be an easy enough, mindless, enjoyable read that I would pick up on the very few instances I wasn't so busy. My initial feelings on See You At Harry's ended up being wrong on so many levels. 
 While See You At Harry's was an enjoyable read, it was far from mindless. And while it was easy to read in a sense, it was also oh so very difficult due to the subject matter. I just found this book to be one of those books that you're not initially to impressed with and then as you keep reading, you realize exactly how many feelings you have invested in this book and that somewhere along the way, you ended up completely enthralled and impressed with it. 
 I don't want to give away any spoilers, but I will say that I had to control myself while reading See You At Harry's. Since I read a big chunk of this book in public, I had to constantly tell myself "Don't cry, don't cry, don't cry" and my throat ended up killing me with trying to hold my sobs in. I was that affected by it. 
 Overall, I found See You At Harry's to be a really great, impressive read. The characters all rang true and the book was beautifully written. It also wasn't too young for me (which tends to be my problem with most MG books) and I feel like it can resonate with readers of all ages. I do have to say that if a big chunk of MG books are this great, I'll definitely have to add more to my list.

book_b.title: Sophie's World
book_b.user_review: Ugh! I finished this book but felt like I was in school while I was reading it. Wait, I am in school and my reading for it is MUCH more enjoyable. I thought the ending would be good, but it wasn't. I guess I"m just not intellectual enough for this type of book!

sample_reviews.review_text: A great interview to philosophers and philosophy, not so great as a novel. Starting out, the premise is a little sketchy. The descriptions of the girl portray her as innocent and lovely, she is suppose to be in her teens, but acts as if she's still in elementary school. On top of this, she is receiving letters from an unknown older male who she is replying to. She listens to her parents, who undoubtedly have told her not to talk to strangers, and shows no spark of rebellion so it makes no sense at all for her to be doing this. It definitely rings of a male writer portraying what he thinks a young female would act like, and that part is a flop. The writer does have a good knowledge of philosophy and can explain complex concepts simply, which he does through the older male's letters. That part is the only portion of the book I would recommend reading.

This book read far too much like a philosophy novel for my liking. It's not that I don't like philosophy, just that I'd pretty much heard it all before. There was very little dialogue in the first 2 thirds of the book which made it horribly boring and monotonious. I can see now that the phiolosophy back ground was necessary for what the book is actually about but in my opinion it just wasn't worth it.

Sophie begins receiving enigmatic, anonymous letters addressed to herself, as well as letters directed to Hilde, whom Sophie does not know, from Hilde's father, shortly before her fifteenth birthday. They cause her to start thinking about the "big questions" - who are you, why are you here, etc., and eventually lead her into an unusual relationship with a mysterious older gentleman who becomes something of a mentor. 
 I did learn more from this book about philosophy than I knew before, which was a pitifully negligible amount; perhaps a straightforward philosophy textbook would have suited me better. reference_books.title: MaddAddam (MaddAddam, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
readathon17 book 30: a book that has been in your shelf for long time. 
 Not longer than others, but no other category to put it. 
 The trilogy is finally over. The book focuses on the life story of Zeb for the flashbacks (all of the three books have mostly flashbacks to life before the flood) and then some weeks after the day book 2 ended on. 
 I would prefer less flashbacks to be honest. The story of Zeb was interesting, but I was more interested in what will happen in the future for the human race and for the Crakers. 
 In general I liked the trilogy. It is definitely not a typical post-apocalyptic trilogy. It has more "literature" than action. Also more time is spend on the past (before the apocalypse) than the future. But I think they are worth reading.

reference_books.title: Big Little Lies
reference_books.review_text:
readathon17 book 43: a book that was adapted into a series 
 I am in a reading black hole. I can't focus on anything these days. I have 6 books on my "currently reading". So I decided to go for something like this book, an easy read. 
 And hallelujah! I read it in 4 days. 
 Story take place in Australia, a big plus for me, since I don't remember ever reading something australian. The main characters are three mothers that take their 5-years olds in the same school. The story takes place in the first months of the school year. And there is a death, but you don't know who died and how until the very last moment. 
 The story is about gossip and fighting between the mothers and family secrets in a small community. There are moments of surprise (I think I made a noise towards the end when something was revealed and I was reading it in public...). It deals with some serious matters. I did not agree with some of the opinions in the book, but generally it is ok and I especially liked how domestic violence is presented there. 
 I am watching the series now, I have already some troubles with the casting and so far the book is better...

reference_books.title: Not That Kind of Girl: A Young Woman Tells You What She's "Learned"
reference_books.review_text:
I expected more stories about how a 20-something year old girl got her own show, how is it to write, direct and star in a very popular tv-series, how weird it feels to be famous, win awards and go to parties, having to wear designer clothes when it is really not your style... 
 There is nothing about her work. 
 All you get is a 20-something year old girl talking about life... you can imagine how much you learn! 
 But there were some chapters that were nice to read, felt like having a friend tell you her childhood stories.

reference_books.title: The Perks of Being a Wallflower
reference_books.review_text:
The main character is a teenager with some psychological issues and no friends. Through his letters to an anonymous person, we learn about his family, his new friends and how he deals with his problems. 
 I found the writing very good. This is surely one of the best YA books. It doesn't feel like YA at all, since it deals with many serious issues. The "teenage love" is a minor part and even that is presented with great maturity.

sample_reviews.review_text: Beautiful, incredible, feminist art. 18 million stars.

STOP BEING SO FAT AND GROSS YOU BIG FATTY! OR maybe try not to let other people's standards of beauty and femininity or your value as a human-being dictate your self-worth. If ANY PART OF YOU has ever been jealous of anorexics or considered extra-medical hormone interjections or parasites, or used body hate to bond with girlfriends, you have bought in. It's nearly impossible not to, but maybe today TRY not to believe that your VALUE is inextricably linked to some asshat's assessment of your desirability. Fuck that dude. Fuck that CULTURE. 
 This comic is a clear case of a great idea being poorly executed! I'm all for emancipation, girl power, diversity and a big fat fuck you to sexism, and this comic has a lot to offer on that part - a diverse cast of female characters, some being women of color, others lesbian, most of them being strong and not afraid to fight back - however, the execution was horrible. I'm too lazy to write a proper review, so here's just a brief overview of my problems: 
 1. The plot was a clusterfuck 
 There was simply too much going on. Too many characters were too quickly introduced. By the end of it, I couldn't name a single character and I didn't give two shits about them. Midway in, we had an official on Earth having an epiphany of wanting to see his daughter again (who is held captive on Bitch Planet), and I was so confused, this man had no evident motivation, and his plot didn't get further developed - why include it then? 
 There was another sub-plot of the inhabitants forming a sports team and this random-ass sport (with its rules) was fully explained, and I just didn't care and didn't see how this advanced the plot. 
 2. The world (dystopia) wasn't believable 
 The premise of this comic is that there's another planet for women who are non-compliant, Bitch Planet. It functions as a jail, and these "aggressive" women are guarded by men. The husbands on Earth get clone-wives, when their original wife turned out to be a "bitch". It was way too absurd for me. Even though I enjoyed little bits which showed the daily sexism that prevails on Earth (e.g. a female news reporter being referred to as "sweetheart" by another reporter live on camera). 
 3. The message was too "in your face" 
 I like challenging reads, and I like to work out metaphors for myself, but this was way too "This is about how fucked up the patriarchy is - DO YOU GET IT? DO YOU? Hello? Did I mention that this comic makes fun of sexist people?" - Yes, I get it. No, I didn't need a reminder. 
 4. The art style was ugly af 
 Beauty in art (and in life - look at me being deep af) is subjective, so I won't bother explaining, but this retro style didn't work for me at all, and I found the panels (in their arrangements etc.) very boring and repetitive. 
 5. The dialogue was stupid (might correlate with 1.) 
 Nope, not a fan of the dialogue. The jokes didn't work for me, and I didn't think of the clap-backs as epic. My favorite parts and quotes were on the issue covers (like the quote at the beginning), so they weren't even part of the real story or dialogue. 
 Overall, I don't regret reading this, because it was super quick (20 minutes) and provided nice and easy entertainment on my train ride today! :D

First off. I'm so happy I got to read this. I'm so happy this exists. It's diverse and feminist and despite being a dystopian feels very real. The description in the synopsis saying "Think Margaret Atwood meets Inglourious Bastards" is very truthful. It met all the expectations I had for it. 
 I received an e-copy of this through Net-Galley for an honest review.

A really promising opening. A bit one note as far as the world, which is often the problem with extreme dystopias. I'm withholding any further opinion until I read more as this volume is really just the beginning and it's not yet a complete story.

They also believed their gods lived in a mountain and that trouble was caused by little men with horse dicks and pan flutes. Don't make it clever just because it's old. 
 Well, this was disappointing. I think the thing is that I read graphic novels almost entirely for the art. So when I dislike an art style, it becomes very obvious to me very quickly that the novel series is not for me. And unfortunately, the art style here is mediocre at best. I did not like the art in this comic for the first few volumes. The art gets significantly and suddenly better in three, and then goes back under. Whichever artist drew comic three needs to draw this whole comic, because wow, they're talented. 
 In terms of story, Bitch Planet is... fine? I like the intersectional feminism, but the story itself is mediocre at best. 
 I honestly only truly cared for a couple of characters. Kamau Kogo is our main protagonist, a former athlete accused of murdering inmate Marian Collins. I liked her fine, but didn't love her. There's also Penelope, who's fat and proud and maybe my favorite character. There's Fanny, a manipulative and good-at-spying lesbian with no depth whatsoever. And there's Meiko Maki, with a tragic backstory to rival the greats. 
 You know, there's nothing particularly bad about the story, but nothing amazing either. I had really high expectations and this was disappointing. If you're looking for more thoughts, maybe check out Whitney's review.

 But I feel like I ended up wanting a lot more from it than I got. Only one of the women really has much in the way of backstory so far, and even that was...confusing? And now that we come to it I think that might be my biggest complaint--I frequently got confused about what was happening. Action scenes feel muddled. Important information is cut off in the gutter of the book. And it happened multiple times that I read a page, thought, "Huh????" and read it again only to realize that you're supposed to read across a two-page spread instead of across just one page like you do in the ENTIRE REST OF THE BOOK. And that sort of thing just made it really difficult for me to stay immersed in the story. 
 I am interested in several of the main characters so far (although one's already died ), and I definitely want to find out what happens with them, so I'll read the next volume. But I'm hoping for a little more depth and a little more clarity.

This book was like reading illustrated creepypastas and I loved every moment of it. The open endings, the wordless panels, the strange realism of it all; I really hope that Emily Carroll puts out more books like this.
Wow! Just simply exquisite! This graphic novel has some of the best art work I have seen! And the chills it gives you!! Creepy to its very core. Would love to explore more of Carroll's work.
This is a tiny bit beyond my comfort zone. Scary, creepy, and not a happy ending in sight. Brrr. The art is terrific, and I think my students will love it.
Fantastic illustrations. So-so stories. "His Face All Red" and "The Nesting Place" were definitely my favorite of the 5 stories in this collection, but even then, I was a bit underwhelmed.
Creepy, creepy, creepy, original yet familiar and creepy as hell, thanks in part to the use of blacks, reds, and blues in Carroll's color palette.

Through the Woods was absolutely gorgeous, and somehow I ended up with a black and white e-book version instead of physical copy. The illustrations created a stunningly eerie atmosphere but I felt like some of the stories lacked a punch or climax. Regardless, I would be incredibly happy to add this book to my shelves so I can treat myself to Carroll's illustrations whenever I want.

reference_books.title: The Memory Keeper's Daughter
reference_books.review_text:
Overwrought on steroids. I know several families dealing with some pretty severe challenges right now - a baby girl who had to have part of her brain removed to alleviate her seizures, a father of three struggling with bone cancer - and they are dealing with all of these with WAY more resilience than these characters deal with a missing (presumed dead) infant. 
 The missing daughter haunts every aspect of their lives, creating rifts and a vortex sucking away every possible moment of joy. 
 The chapters examining the fierce parental advocacy that opened the door to an education for special needs children was interesting. I was happy that Caroline found some happiness in her life. But overall, the resolutions weren't particularly joyful. This book sat on my shelf for months before I finally picked it up during a snowstorm. It was nice to have a new book to read by the fire - but I really wish it had been better!

reference_books.title: The Buddha in the Attic
reference_books.review_text:
I wanted to love this book about the emigration of Japanese "picture brides," brought from Japan to California in the 30s and 40s for arranged marriages. The husbands pay the families and arrange passage; the women and girls sail to a new world to find a bewildering alien language and culture, roughscrabble existence, and new husbands who almost never match in picture or fact the information sent to them in their bride letters. 
 The book opens with a collective narrator, and with direct, poetic phrases, Otsuka creates a moving third person picture of their lives: "Some of us were from Hokkaido, where it was snowy and cold, and would dream of that landscape for years. Some of us were from Hiroshima, which would later explode, and were lucky to be on the boat at all though of course we did not then know it. The youngest of us was twelve, and had not yet begun to bleed." 
 After the first chapter, I found myself ready to move from the collective experience to something more direct, perhaps following 2-3 women as they enter their new lives. However, "We" remains the narrator, and the story flits like a small camera from person to person, a sentence or two, and then on to the next. The chapter of the first night with their husbands is heartbreaking, but as the book progressed, I found myself sadly detached. The book seemed like an overly-long lyric poem: I stuck it out, but often skimmed, and had no trouble putting it down. So many breathtakingly-beautiful phrases, but it just didn't touch me as a narrative; I was never allowed to engage with any character long enough. 
 I'm sure the narrative style illuminates the experience: thousands of women who made this journey, desperately scraping out a life with new husbands while blending quietly into the background of this new culture. And then, one day, they disappear into the internment camps, and the narrative shifts: now it's the collective "we" of the Americans who remained in the town, wondering what became of the Japanese people who once farmed and cleaned and tended shops. Buddha in the Attic is creative, poetic, and even, at times, haunting. Unfortunately, it just felt more like a required reading assignment than a novel that truly engaged my interest and heart.

reference_books.title: The Lotus Eaters
reference_books.review_text:
This book received such glowing reviews; I feel like I must be misguided somehow because I really did not enjoy it all that much. 
 Soli did a wonderful job immersing the reader in the experience of Saigon, frontline battles, and the lives of both the Vietnamese people and the journalists covering the war. However, I just did not ever grow to really connect with the main characters. Helen Adams arrives in Vietnam with the ambition of becoming a combat photojournalist, yet her only previous photography experience is a high school photography class? It seeemed too big a jump that she progresses from novice to cover photographer. I wished for more of an emotional connection to her motivations, something that would leave me pulling for her success. Instead, I felt frustrated at many of her decisions, especially in those crucial last chapters. 
 I wondered if female photographers were really allowed to travel into battle, but have since found online biographies of fearless, ambitious women like Catherine Leroy, whose experiences must have informed this novel. 
 I did find the backstory of Linh very moving. 
 I read Lotus Eaters on an iPad, and I'm wondering if perhaps the electronic format creates an emotional disconnect? I expected to enjoy this book much more than I did. Instead, I was skimming and flipping the virtual pages, impatient to be done with all the angst and just get to the darn resolution.

reference_books.title: The Whipping Boy
reference_books.review_text: A fanciful and humorous setup and adventure-filled plot make this a terrific choice for junior high readers.

reference_books.title: Still Alice
reference_books.review_text:
Still Alice gives a moving, first-person account of a woman coping with early-onset Alzheimer's. Harvard professor Alice Howland first begins losing things (her Blackberry), then words, then herself (suddenly, she can't find her way home from Harvard Square, a path she has traveled for 25 years). 
 Each stage of the journey is so movingly portrayed, from the shock and denial of first diagnosis, to the despair of gradually losing the ability to read, to the panic and rage of standing in your own house, unable to locate the bathroom. 
 As a reader, I especially admired the way Genova immersed me in the experience of dementia. At least twice, a paragraph is repeated, and because I was reading the book on Kindle, I double checked, thinking perhaps I had accidentally thumbed back a few pages. Then I realized that these must be intentional repeats, asking me to experience the same confusion Alice feels as she circles back to the same thoughts and anxieties. 
 The book asks excellent questions about identity and quality of life: who are we when our memories and accomplishments are stripped away? Can we find meaning in the present moments of joy, knowing we will have no ability to recall these moments? 
 I'm appalled by the mediocre review given by Publisher's Weekly. I did not find Genova's prose and dialogue the least bit clumsy or heavy handed; rather, I found myself in tears over the relationships as Alice's family members transform from husband and children to caregivers. 
 Any reader will appreciate this book, but it will be especially treasured by those coping firsthand with the disease, who will surely find empathy, understanding, and a small light for a dark and frightening journey.

book_a.title: Cutting for Stone
book_a.user_review:
Parts of the book had me mesmerized, and I am certainly fascinated by this look at Ethiopia (and suddenly have a desire to taste Injera and Wot). I loved many of the characters, particularly Hema and Ghosh, Matron and Tsige. 
 My main objections were two: first, the sort of magical POV of the narrator - he describes details that should not be available to him, with no good explanation. Without spoiling a plot point, how would you know what someone is wearing and what they say if you are, at the time, unconscious? At first I attributed this to the style of magical realism; later, it just frustrated me. 
 My second objection: the big plot twists are just SO over the top. Too much gore, too much graphic detail, too many coincidences accompanying too many turning points. 
 I was happier with the book when it focused on the everyday. This writer really has a way of making you care for certain characters. Certainly I stayed with the book through the end, and I would probably read Verghese again. Overall, the book reminds me of a television miniseries - certain episodes go too far in creating the drama, but I still enjoyed the characters and the setting and hung in there for the finale.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 This book was really uneven for me--I loved the creativity of the story, and I appreciated learning so much about Ethiopian/Eritrean modern history and some very authentic medical tidbits. The use of language during my favorite parts of the book was elegant and lyrical. For content alone, I would have given it four stars. 
 Then there were the very mystical aspects to the book, which is not something I am ever able to digest easily. And the characters, because of so many otherworldly qualities, did not seem believable to me--they lacked depth, contradictions, reality. Ghosh seemed the most real to me, like he could be an actual human being instead of a mere symbol of something. And the way sex was treated was so simplistic. Does sex have to be pure evil that kills or ruins people's lives? That aspect of Marion's character never matures, and it's tedious. I've heard so many amazing things about this book that I was nervous to pick it up--I didn't feel like it could hold up to my expectations. And at first, that's what it seemed like it would happen as I read the book, because the first 100 pages or so were just good, not great. But once I got out of the backstory and into the pages that began to develop the main character, I fell in love. 
 Everything in this book was woven together perfectly, and as one thing led to another I never knew what was coming but it always made perfect sense. And everything had a purpose in the grand scheme of the book, whether to show how the characters evolve or to further advance the plot to the perfect conclusion. 
 I really connected with Marion, the main character. Reading about events from his point of view felt like how I would have experienced them, and by the end all I wanted was for him to a happy ending (finally). 
 The medicine involved in the book also made me want to learn more about the topics being discussed--it's hard to unravel truth from fiction in a story involving fictional characters, but as I did I learned a lot about topics I never would have thought to research on my own. 
 You should read this book if you have ever enjoyed any novel, because you will enjoy this one too. Every part of it, from characters to plot to setting are fantastic and work to make this book the incredible story it is.

I'm a big Weiner (heh) fan. Loved her Carrie Shapiro series, and several others. This one...this one was...very boring to me. I had a hard time reading it and found it very slow (Kiesha informed me I'm crazy because she loved this book--to each's own!) 
 It follows three storylines: Sylvie (the mom), Lizzie (the delinquent daughter who has turned herself around) and Diana (the other daughter....the perfect one). 
 I couldn't really identify with any of the characters. There was lots of cheating involved and lots of terrible decisions (ie, not wearing a condom...it was just one time!) 
 Some characters were more complex than others. Sylvie definitely fell flat, but Diana and Lizzie were intriguing. As always, Weiner's writing was good. Again...I just wasn't feeling it. 
 If you're looking for romantic chick lit, this is not it. If you're looking for an emotional story about family of the female variety, this is your ticket. I think those who liked In Her Shoes would like this one. However, it didn't do it for me. I rated it a 2/5.

 The writing is boring. The story could have been good, but I'm just not interested enough to waste my time any further.

I think this novel really rates 3.5 stars, and I would give it four for a number of reasons. One is that Jennifer Weiner is a smart cookie and she says (her characters think and say) smart, true things. Two is that she is on the zeitgeist of the betrayed woman issue, and I have wondered much that her characters wonder: How do women deal with this kind of public betrayal? Three is that I like the way she draws characters. They are real people, in all the ways people are people. 
 But reading as a writer, Jennifer does something I've been warned against: she interrupts all of her scenes with huge chunks of flashback. Charles Baxter once told me that if I was flashing back too often, that I should "start your story earlier." I have been known to flashback within a flashback, my first readers saying to me, "When the hell are we?" 
 In almost every scene in Fly Away Home, we are cooking along, and then we go back back back to the early life of this family. It's all important, really, but what if we got it first? And not tucked into the story at hand? I found myself thinking about my own writing, and reminded myself, again, not to ever do this. 
 But it's not boring. It's not disappointing. It's a good novel, but it tuaght me again a lesson I need to keep learning.
I keep picking this up to read, but honestly, I can't get out of the first chapter! This is not typical Weiner writing and I'm so sad.

Political scandals have become commonplace in the news recently. We are actually surprised when political figures don't have secrets or skeletons in their closets. But what we don't take into consideration is the personal toll these scandals take on the innocent victims involved; the wives, daughters, mothers, and sons. Jennifer Weiner tackles political scandal and the ultimate destruction it forces on relationships in her novel, FLY AWAY HOME. Sylvie Woodruff is the ideal political wife and has been for the past 30 years. She has stood patiently by her husband's side, carrying his mints, reminding him of forgotten names and holding his business cards. Sylvie, a lawyer in her own right, has ignored her own personal passions and transformed herself into the perfect wife and mother. Which is why she is more shocked than anyone to discover that her husband has been carrying on an affair with a young legal aid half his age. When the scandal becomes public, Sylvie and her two adult daughters are unwillingly thrown into the spotlight. 
 While Sylvie's life begins to unravel, things aren't going smoothly for her daughters either. Lizzie is 24-years-old and a recovering addict still trying desperately to win back the trust and respect of her older sister, Diana. When she meets someone who could be "the one" she gets an unexpected surprise that could ruin everything she's been working towards. Diana is a successful doctor with a perfect husband and a happy son, but things are never how they appear. Diana is carrying on an affair and watching her own marriage crumble around her. 
 Each chapter is told from the point of view of one of the three female characters; Sylvie, Diana and Lizzie. Weiner has created real characters and impeccable dialogue that keeps the story entertaining, authentic and honest. The characters don't feel flat at all and their internal struggles are extremely relatable. What's wonderful about Weiner's story telling ability is that she creates enough suspense to keep you rapidly flipping the pages, while at the same time making you want to slow down and savor the pitch perfect dialogue and thought-provoking themes.

I liked this book, though not as much as I thought I would. The subject is very topical (smart women married to slimy philandering politicians)and I was interested to see how Weiner would treat the subject. The book had received very good reviews. However, the book was just as much about the daughters and their romantic problems as the mother married to the philanderer, and I felt like this storyline often got lost. I was disappointed in the ending, though given the background of the wife, I could understand it.

I love Jennifer Weiner and was excited to read her latest, but in the end it was disappointing. I saw the twists/turns from miles away and hated the ending. However, it was a nice departure from some of her other storylines and in a way a more "mature" book.

So basically, take the plot of the Good Wife but add 20 years to the age of the wife... and you've got this book. Jennifer Weiner is a talented writer. I'll give her that. The book was engrossing and thoughtful. But I also felt like the conclusion to this one was telescoped like a figure skater doing a double axel. (I'm sorry, the Olympics just finished.) 
 So, yeah. 
 The story waits until the final act to bring all three main characters together. I felt like this was a mistake. We never got a great conclusion to Lizzie's story from her perspective. And I really hated Diana through the whole book. And how does a woman who never stepped foot into a kitchen for 50 years become an amazing cook in 2 months? 
 But hey, I'll always give Jennifer Weiner another shot. She brings good writing to a genre that's often maligned for its tropes and cheesiness. Some moments in this book will stay with me for a long time.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Kicking off the Atlanta Business Trip, Read #1: In which my days are largely too exhausting to allow me to focus on a new story and so I reach instead for something old and comfortable I've read twenty times before. Okay, maybe just ten. At least five. 
 Honestly, it felt like I had five minutes of spare time at a given stretch and I was not at all in the mood to start a new book. I was more in the mood to open an old book at any random page to read for just a few minutes. Sometimes it's nice not to have the urge to stay up all night reading to the end. 
 Howl's stands as almost certainly the first of the Wynne Jones' books I've read (I came to her late as an adult reader) and remains my very favorite. Plus, it's great fun to contrast with the film adaptation. 
 Atlanta Business Trip Reading List (October 2012) 
 #1| Howl's Moving Castle

A fast read, but too confusing to be great. 
 I liked the premise of the book: a young girl is cursed into being an old woman and goes to live with a fearsome wizard in a castle that walks. How could you not have fun with that? Unfortunately, the plot gets lost in riddles and poorly executed references. I found myself turning back pages several times to figure out what the characters were talking about and why, and I couldn't always figure it out. I'm well-educated, so I wonder how this book could be aimed at children. 
 The characters are the redeeming factor. Sophie is fun to read and grow with, and Michael, Howl's apprentice, is friendly and very likable. Meeting Sophie's sisters added another dimension to her that the movie didn't have. Calcifer was brilliant. My only complaint here is the flatness of Howl. He, unlike Sophie, did not seem to develop as a character. He was only a product of circumstance. 
 The book has little in common with the movie, and I'd say the movie is better. Admittedly, Miyazaki also changed much of the plot and themes to fit his own vision, but the story was more digestible. One could delve into deeper meanings at will, but it's not necessary to enjoy the story. The book, in comparison, felt over-complicated by superficial puzzles.

Confession: Sometimes I find Diana Wynne Jones hard to read. As a light reader, sometimes I miss some of the plot threads she hides in there, and sometimes I never see why, exactly, she included an inexplicable symbol. 
 Howl's Moving Castle is a Jones book, and if you think you can skim through it, you're mistaken. But I loved the storyline, the realistic portrayal of Sophie, a girl who's bound up in her boring life making hats until an unexpected curse sends her out on a journey, and the lighthearted tone. Although I wouldn't rate the movie adaptation as high - maybe a three or four - I would recommend this to everyone.

Charming, entertaining. Diana Wynne Jones must be one the great children's fantasy writers. I never wanted to read this because I associated it with Japanese cartoons and anime which I don't like, but this is a warm, Britsh sort of fantasy about a wizard and a girl who finds her own magic.

I'm really not one for the fantasy genre, but I do love YA/J fiction so I thought I'd give it a shot. I thought the concept and the story was fascinating, and to be honest, that's the only reason I kept reading. That, and the fact that Jones totally had me in the beginning with her witty and sarcastic tone. 
 The book begins really strong with Sophie, the eldest of three daughters sent into the world to make their fortunes, and this interesting world of moving buildings owned by wizards. The book took a downward spike for me when I started to realize how much I actually disliked Sophie, who carries the entire book on her back. She starts out meek and timid, then moves on to pushy and rude, and then ends with completely clueless. I absolutely hate it when I'm reading a book and feel smarter than the main character. I actually put the book down in disgust a few times because I was so annoyed with the way things were going. 
 The book felt a little like an extended Grimm's Fairy Tale, and I'm not talking about the Disney version. If you like this sort of thing, you will like this book. 
 Then we get to the ending, and if you're going to read this book, skip this paragraph. I really, really did not want Sophie to be with Howl. I wanted her to walk away, strong on her own- I hated how the whole book moved in the direction of tricking her into being in love with him. Then when she realizes it, they both live happily ever after. What the? There was no moment in the book for me where Howl really redeemed himself, so why would I want him with Sophie(even if I do find her annoying)? 
 My only other big issue was a completely personal one. I don't read the fantasy genre, so a lot of the terms were really confusing to me. It was also difficult for me to keep up with the confusion of a world where scarecrows stalk people, magic just suddenly reveals itself, and pieces(literally) of people and dogs and men are confusingly intertwined. Basically the book wasn't "commercial" enough for me; it didn't stretch itself to include those of us that just want a quick fantasy fix. 
 It absolutely made me realize why this genre is just not for me. 
 I am going to include the link to Amazon's reviews and description though, since I seem to be fighting a tidal wave of love for this one.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I didn't realize this book had only four stories in it until I started reading. Here are the comments on each individual story: 
 1922: This is probably my favorite story in the mix, or perhaps my second favorite. The basic premise is that a farmer's wife inherits a sizable piece of land. She wants to sell the land and escape the farming life for the city; he wants to use it to double the size of the farm. The setting was interesting and King certainly evoked the time period well, but I particularly liked how the one act that started the story slowly snowballed into much more widespread ramifications and ultimately destroyed what the main character was trying to protect. My only small qualm was the twist at the ending. It felt unnecessary. The story could have ended more simply and been just as powerful. 
 Big Driver: This is the other contender for my top pick. After the initial sexual assault, I thought the character's actions were completely believable. And how she figures out who attacked her and what she does to follow through with that was great. I particularly liked the "mistaken identity" twist, which again was completely believable. I expected the plot to develop in a slightly different vein after the emphasis on the GPS system early on, but I was also expecting King's usual "supernatural" aspect to enter into the story somewhere. But the fact that there isn't a "supernatural" aspect to this story (or to 1922) is sort of the theme of this book. 
 Fair Extension: Until you get to this story, which DOES have a supernatural aspect. In fact, the premise of the story is based on the cliche "deal with the devil," and the devil is the supernatural element in the story. This isn't that cliched story though. There is a twist with the main character as the story progresses, but the ending just wasn't as satisfactory as it should have been, in my opinion. It fell a little flat for me. Which is why this was the weakest story in the book. 
 A Good Marriage: Here we return to the non-supernatural theme, with a wife who thought she knew her husband after 27 years of marriage discovers that perhaps she doesn't know her husband at all. How she handles the situation is both totally believable and completely simple. You can see this story playing out in real life. There were no twists in this story. It simply details how one woman might react if she discovered her husband had a horrible secret life. 
 Overall, the collection contained some excellent stories. Fair Extension was sort of an odd story to be included though, since it contained that supernatural bit, while the others were all more "ordinary" in nature. They all depicted how an "everyday" person might react in extreme circumstances, sometimes because of horrible situations, sometimes creating horrible situations.
Amazing. 4 compelling and terrifying novellas, especially the first one 1922. I wonder whether King is better at writing short stories or novellas.

Four stories, though one is so short it doesn't really count (and also reads too much like "Thinner," without the surprise twist ending.)  Make sure to read King's afterword. They're always good, but this one is particularly introspective, though perhaps slightly defensive. The afterword is a bit of an explanation of why darkness returned. I suppose for an author such as King, such a thing is never too far away.

Stephen King has once again proven why he is the king of short stories. King's novels often tend to ramble, and while he does a great job of setting up the story and characters, the basic plot often goes into incoherence. King is best when his narratives go in short doses. As evidenced by this book. These novellas are long enough to flesh out the characters well, but short enough to keep King from going on and on and rambling about insignificant details that distract from the story itself. I've been a fan of King's short stories for a long time, and this collection proves why. This is King at his best, and sometimes creepiest.
In my opinion, this is King's best work since the Dark Tower series ended. These stories are well told, and excellent reads!

Our dear Uncle Stevie does it again! Say what you will about Mr. King's novels (some of them are just hit and miss), but his short fiction is often simply amazing. Four well-crafted tales from the dark side that illustrate again that people are the scariest creatures walking the earth.

 Spelled is one of those books where I fell in love the first time I saw the cover. I have always loved The Wizard of Oz, and I have been loving fairy tale re-tellings, so I knew this would be a match made somewhere over the rainbow for me. And I was so right. Spelled is so much fun that I want to pick it up and read it again right now. Betsy Schow has taken a classic tale that is already so fantastical and turned everything on its' head. Who you know as good might turn bad and vice versa. And Betsy was not satisfied with just the land of Oz, so she took all kinds of fairy tale worlds and created a delightful mashup. 
 Dot, or Dorothea is a the princess of the Emerald city, and because of a curse-gone-wrong on all the major fairy tale families long long ago, she isn't allowed to leave the castle. Someone in her line of women is rumored to be more powerful than all and will burn the world to the ground. That sounds pretty serious. Dot might have a tendency to come across as a little shallow and a lot spoiled, but given her sheltered life I wasn't too surprised. But I was pleasantly surprised to meet the real Dot along the course of her journey. And the real Dot is a treat. Spunky and brave and very, very kind. I loved her. And I loved Kato and the whole gang. 
 One of my favorite parts of reading Spelled was waiting to meet new characters and see where they would fit in in this crazy rendition. Nothing was as it seemed and I learned quickly to expect the unexpected. Fans of all ages will thoroughly enjoy Betsy Schow's imaginative re-imagining of Dorothy's adventure. Dot, Kato and a few others set out to right a curse, and the adventure it takes us on had danger, familiar faces, prophecies, and all sorts of fun. I would have liked to have a seen a bit more romance, but what is there is not rushed. No insta love in this tale. I think there will be more on that front in the next book. And I was so, so excited to see that there will be another book. And the action and adventure won't die down in the second book, if the ending of this one was any indication. Spelled is a great read. One that I would recommend to all fans of Fairy Tales, Young Adult, and the Wizard of Oz. I can't wait to see more from Betsy Schow! 
 This review was originally posted on Book Briefs

'Spelled' is a fun spin on the fairy tale trend that seems to be taking over YA fiction right now. It follows Dorthea, our main character, who happens to be the princess of Emerald. Being a teenager, Dorthea loves most of the awesome perks that come with being royalty - like beautiful ball gowns and shoes to die for. What she doesn't love about being a princess? The whole idea of waiting for a prince to 'save' her and then having to marry him. Dorthea isn't the damsel-in-distress kind of girl - and she doesn't hide that at all in the story. She actually makes it really clear right from the beginning that she's sick of being wooed by all of the princes and being pressured to choose 'Prince Charming' from the mix. Dorthea just wants to live her life how she wants - free and without having to answer to anyone. She's so desperate to change her life that she actually wishes on a star. Of course, just her luck, it happens to be a cursed star - one that twists her wish around and ends up sending her parents to a strange place named 'Kansas,' and the kingdom in utter chaos. Now it's up to Dorthea to find the mysterious Wizard of Oz so she can make things right again - and she has to do it before a dangerous witch is released and causes the end of her homeland of Story. 
 I'm really loving the fairy tale retellings and trend that's been going on lately. There's something about taking an old story that we've known since we were kids and then morphing it into a tale more suited to our modern times and/or an older audience. It can be enchanting and magical - or it can completely go down in flames, which is how every book is viewed in the end. Although this novel is mixed in with the fairy tale theme, it's completely different than the majority of fiction that's available. It doesn't retell a well known fairy tale or myth, but rather takes bits and pieces from several and meshes them together to create a truly unique and entertaining story. I absolutely love how the author takes specific pieces of various tales - like the Wizard of Oz references - along with common themes found in most fairy tales, and then expertly weaves them together with her own unique writing style and imagination to create an original and exciting novel. There are a lot of different references and snippets from a wide variety of folk lore and fairy tales - and it would seriously take an enormous amount of time and space to talk about each one; why it was chosen, how it fit into the story, what it means, etc. Obviously, I don't want to ramble on all day about how each piece effects the story. What really matters is that the author did include them and was able to produce a book that was a blast to read and a breath of fresh air into the genre. 
 I adored every single aspect of this book - except for a few parts when Dorthea seems to get a bit whiny and annoying (in my opinion). All of the characters were well written and distinct - especially Dorthea and the other major characters like Kato and her parents. Since the book is written from Dorthea's point of view, we get to know her on a very personal level. It's like a peek inside of her mind - we learn of her hopes, dreams, fears, dislikes, and inner thoughts. From this point of view, we get to see the book unfold up close and personal, as if we're experiencing it alongside Dorthea. I think that this writing style gives the story a depth that wouldn't be capable otherwise, along with making it a fast and fun read. Dorthea has some attitude problems - like normal teens - and I have to admit that I loved her snarky and sarcastic attitude. Her character does grow throughout the novel though - she has to take responsibility for her actions and their consequences, which makes her more mature and understanding. Overall, this was a really enjoyable read for me - it has a quick pace and a conversational tone that helps draw the reader into the world the author created. Although I adore the darker and more serious fairy tale retellings, this was a fantastic reprieve that lightened the mood and gave the current craze a breath of fresh air. Very highly recommended for fans of fairy tales, retellings, as well those who enjoy paranormal and fantasy. 
 Disclosure: I received a copy of the book in exchange for an honest review.

reference_books.review_text:
I was looking forward to Bear's story as his character was very interesting in the first two books (King and Tyrant). This is Bear and Thia's story. 
 Bear had left his MC and was a dead man walking. He was drowning himself in booze, drugs, and whores because he was lost without his MC, family, or his late friend Preppy. All this changed when Thia went to find him for help. 
 Thia is a teen who had met a big biker many years ago. She was instantly drawn to him even as a kid and he to her (in a completely non pedophile way). The biker, Bear, promised to help her if she ever needed it. Thia came to collect on this promise which she had always cherished. Her life is in shambles with a very uncertain future. Bear was the first and only person she thought to seek out help from. When she arrives, she discovers that this help will not be as easy to come as she expected. It on starts the rollercoaster story. 
 Before you read this you need to read King and Tyrant to get the full picture. Lawless ends in a cliffhanger just as King did. 
 Again the editing is not great with grammatical errors throughout. The storyline is solid and the characters are well developed so far.

reference_books.title: The Martian
reference_books.review_text: Still an excellent read. I cannot comment on the realism given I am not an astronaut but it all seemed to flow well. It is a nail biter which keep you turning the pages even on a reread. Loved how the humor broke up the seriousness. I would read another book by this author.

reference_books.title: Forever Too Far (Rosemary Beach, #3; Too Far, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
I have generally enjoyed these books thus far but this one fell a bit flat for me. The author used "OK" what seemed liked a thousand times. Or I suppose I am so sick of seeing it now that I have hit book 3 in the series? I can't say for sure. 
 The whole whiny brat Nan drama was a bit overboard. I mean she is a grown woman. We get it. She is entitled and has some serious issues but this was just so over the top and too far in this book. 
 Then the baby. The author either had never had a baby when this book was written or it was so long ago she forgot time lines because her expectations were so off the wall. A 4 week old will not sleep through the night and not need nursed. Hello, mom's boobs will wake her up ready to burst before then because baby needs to eat often when they are that tiny. That was just one example, there were others too. 
 Anyway, this one needed work. I have this whole series, really hoping the rest pick back up.

reference_books.title: V is for Virgin (V is for Virgin, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I wasn't sure about this book going in. It sounded a bit hokey but like it could be really good if done right. Well Kelly Oram was able to pull this one off. I really enjoyed it. The characters were developed and intriguing. It does have a good message for the ya reader. This book ends with you wanting to find out what happens in book 2. It is not a major cliffhanger and you could just stop there but I am happy that A is for Abstinence is written. I am starting it now.

reference_books.title: It Ends with Us
reference_books.review_text:
My review is going to be very minimal. I went into this book without even reading the blurb. I think that is best. Go in blind. Spoilers will hinder this book experience for you. 
 This is Lily Bloom's life story. We see her from childhood to adult. Her life is not easy but you experience real life situations which evoke strong emotions as is typical of CoHo books. You will laugh, tense up, gasp, and of course cry while following Lily on her journey. 
 Another absolutely amazing novel by Colleen Hoover. A definite must read.

book_a.title: Cannon (A Step Brother Romance, #3)
book_a.user_review:
Another great "taboo" romance from Sabrina Paige. 
 This book while still being a fun and easy read seemed to have a lot more depth (read emotion and real life) than her previous books in the series. 
 Addy and Hendrix are step siblings, meeting when they were in high school. Both strongly fight their attraction and affinity for one another. Hendrix enlists with the marines while Addy continues her country music career managed by her overbearing and uncaring mother. They reunite after Hendrix leaves the military and attempts to work for his father's security firm. He just so happens to now work as Addy's security guard. The same feelings return to both along with their same hesitations. In true Sabrina Paige fashion, the sparks fly. Will they let down their protective barriers and what will happen if they reveal their true relationship? 
 Great fun, easy, a bit steamy read. This is a dual POV with scenes from the past interspersed with the present.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 This has been my favorite of Sabrina's stepbrother books! I really loved this storyline and the characters. Of course Addy is easy to love. But it took a little longer to see what a good guy Hendricks actually is. Their story really was like a fairytale...kids falling in love with each other secretly but staying apart because that's what they think they should do. Unrequited love - seven years of it! But to finally find it with each other - super sweet. But the journey was definitely anything but "sweet". It was rough and harsh and mean and dirty and full of pain and heartache. But that just makes it all the better! Loved this book!!

Super hot But with a Storyline!! that's why I love reading Sabrina Paige! She always tops it! This time we have Addy a country singer with a mother that is also her manager. You can imagine how that would work. Then you have Hendrix an ex military with some issues of his own.. Not to mention they are step brother an sister , and they share much more then just there feelings! It's sexy , emotional, and challenging all in one !
I'll never understand the popularity of some books.

As with Sabrina Paige's other 'step' books, I thoroughly enjoyed Cannon. 
 The story opens with Addison and Hendrix meeting for the first time in five years. The last time they saw one another, they were just teenagers. He'd disappeared off to join the Marines and she carried on with her successful career as a country music star. 
 Hendrix comes back into Addy's life as her new bodyguard, after returning from Afghanistan and leaving the Marines. His dad has been married to Addison's mother for seven years - and both are controlling and not the best parents in the world. 
 Addy is managed by her mother. She feels the constraints on her life and career. She's just a puppet for her record company, and her mother is manipulative and demanding. Addy never wants to be poor again but, at the same time, she's not really singing the songs that she wants to sing. 
 Hendrix has never got on with his ex-Army father, The Colonel, who is also demanding and disapproving. Hendrix spent his teens rebelling against his father and his ideals. 
 As teenagers, the two are drawn together, against Hendrix's volition. He wants to hate her perfection but he is irresistibly attracted to her. He thinks he's not good enough for her. Addy is really hurt when she overhears a cruel conversation between Hendrix and some school friends, and then when he leaves for the Marines without saying goodbye. 
 This story moves between the present and the past, showing how their friendship and relationship evolves. It illustrates their depth of feeling, the hurt and their desire for one another. This story wasn't as humorous as the first two 'step' books - it was more emotional, especially when we read about Hendrix' experience in the Middle East. 
 It was an easy, effortless read. Love this author's style!
I absolutely loved this book!!!

 On ne presente pas Sabrina Paige qui en quelques romans sans pretention a reussi a imposer sa marque dans un genre un peu tabou celui de l'amour entre des demi-frere et demi-soeur. Voila deja le troisieme roman du genre, totalement independant des precedents et presente comme plus profond que les autres et il est vrai que le resume etait allechant. Sans etre rate, c'est peut-etre le moins reussi des trois. Peut-etre que la lassitude s'installe avec des romans qui ont globalement la meme dynamique mais celui-ci laisse l'impression d'etre moins approfondi. 
 Il semblait y avoir plus qu'une simple rencontre entre un garcon et une fille dont les parents se sont maries ensemble. Cannon, le heros, est un ancien militaire rentre au pays apres une experience penible. L'heroine, Addison, est une chanteuse a succes qui a ete vaguement menacee. Pour la proteger et aussi pour la faire tenir tranquille, son beau-pere va charger Cannon de veiller sur elle, d'etre son garde du corps. 
 Une des principales deceptions est que l'auteure ne va pratiquement pas utiliser ces derniers faits. Cannon aurait pu etre absolument tout sauf un garde du corps et un ex militaire, cela n'aurait guere changer l'histoire. Ces deux elements amenaient pourtant une profondeur supplementaire, mais ils sont un peu survoles, ici, c'est dommage. 
 Il reste ce que l'auteure sait faire le mieux c'est a dire tisser une romance tres sensuelle entre deux heros qui ne doivent pas se frequenter a cause de l'interdit que cela represente mais egalement parce qu'Addison a une image a preserver. Cela, on pouvait le trouver dans les deux precedents romans et c'est bien la. 
 L'auteure a peut-etre un peu fait le tour du sujet avec ces trois romans. Elle a un vrai talent pour montrer des relations brulantes entre ses heros, il faudrait peut-etre travailler davantage sur le scenario souvent un peu faible. Mais en tous cas, ce qu'elle ecrit est prometteur.

Sabrina's books just keep getting better and better.
