Compared to Prick and Tool I consider this as 4 stars. 
 the build was great, but the ending lacked the drama I thought it had the potential to have, so that left me a little disheartened. 
 another great job by Paige!

Received an advance copy for an honest review. 
 Can you pick any hotter than hell kinda guy then Hendrix Cannon Cole. Even his name calls to you as a strong, sexy alpha male. Add in that he is a Marine with a body to die for and don't even get me started about his heart and way his feels for Addison. Swoon, gasp, gulp and just plain submerge yourself in a cold bath. The chemistry from them are just off the charts steamy, you'd think your kindle will set itself on fire. 
 Hendrix is back from his tour of duty in the Marines and his first assignment back home is to babysit his step sister that is the golden child of country music. We flash back to when they first met and have both POV which in my opinion is the best because I always want to hear what a guy has to say and what he is feeling. Hendrix comes home a changed man but his feeling for Addy is still the same if not stronger than before. Same goes for Addy, she has tried for the last five years to forget him but once your heart falls for "the one", nothing will ever change. They try their best to hide their true feelings for one another but in the end, they both give in. Now they are trying to keep it from the parents but in the end fails. All I have to say is lock the doors all the time. What a way for your parents to find out but to walk in when Hendrix in under Addy's dress. That is just how hot the book is. A must read and a must read for all the other's in Ms. Paige's line of step-brothers. Start with Prick then Tool and more over to Cannon. You will not be disappointed.

book_b.title: Rowdy (Marked Men, #5)
book_b.user_review:
Rowdy is a very artistic man with a cross between cowboy and rockabilly style. Yes it totally works and he owns it. He believes he was burned by his only true love and vows never to take his sex life seriously because there can be no other true love out there. 
 Salem walks into his life again. No not his long lost true love but his best friend from childhood. She happens to be yet another in a long list of people who abandoned him. 
 There is quite a lot of avoidance and animosity between the two until he finally gives in and starts to open up to her. At just that time his true love from the past comes to him with a freight train of baggage. 
 This book was felt like it was filled with a lot more action than the others in the series. Rowdy and Salem are the first two in the series who actually seem to be made for each other but can they make it work?

sample_reviews.review_text: Another good book. I like the books in the series that show a lot of the characters. This one centered on the new tattoo shop and the retail shop that would be opening up there as well. It was the story of Rowdy and Salem.

I am a big fan of this series filled with troubled bad boys and smart sassy women. Rowdy is the 5th book in the Marked Men series. After reading this one, I think that Rowdy is my new favorite. The best part about this book is that it is a friends to lovers story. One of my favorite types. Rowdy and Salem were best friends until she left town to get out from under her parents' strict rules. Rowdy was convinced that her sister was the only love for him. When Salem comes back into his life, he starts to question his philosophies on love. 
 I definitely liked these two together. They have a deep respect and friendship that carried well over into their romance. I was really rooting for Rowdy to figure out that Salem was the one he has loved since childhood, not her sister. Of course they both have their insecurities. Rowdy is afraid Salem will leave because she has never stayed in one place. Salem is insecure about whether or not Rowdy is still hung up on her sister. At times, I just wanted to shake these two because they were so right for each other! 
 There are changes coming for the group. I won't say what, so you'll have to read to find out the details. Asa's story is next. I am very excited to read that one. A cop and a reformed hoodlum,..what could be better?

This really is a freaking awesome series....it doesn't matter who the main characters are - everyone is mentioned. 
 This is Rowdy and Salem's story, and from the blurb, I was really afraid to read it. I am happy to say that fear was unfounded and we have another epic Marked couple ... with a Jimbo!!!! 
 With new characters being introduced here and there, I hope this series last for a few more books.

"I feel like you and the past have been chasing me down ever since you walked in to that shop, Salem. What are you going to do if I decide to let you catch me?" 
 Rowdy is the fifth book in the Marked Men series by Jay Crownover and in many ways it takes me back to the first book, Rule. Rowdy and Salem have a deep history and that history both taints and enhances all that they come to have. Despite being a couple years older than him Salem and Rowdy were best friends as kids but that is where it stopped. Feeling trapped in her small consecutive town with her preacher father who was full of judgment for his non perfect daughter, Salem quickly got out as soon as she graduated leaving orphan Rowdy there alone with just her all to perfect sister, Poppy. Rowdy desired all that Poppy stood for and soon they too become close but in the end all that Rowdy left their town with was a broken heart and the clothes on his back. 
 "I've heard you say my name in a lot of ways, Salem. Gotta say hearing you say it in bed when I'm about to eat you is probably my favorite to date." 
 When Nash calls and offers Salem a job at the new shop (per Phil's request) she cannot say no to reconnecting to the one friend she was sad to lose when she left home. But seeing him her feelings for grown up Rowdy are very very grown up! Oh yeah! These two and their tangled past broke my heart at times. You could see that they wanted each other but damn why must they fight so hard. Salem is so into him but just can't get past his past with her sister and for him Salem reminds him of all those who have left him. Can these two get past these hooks up and all their other issues to find peace with themselves and their pasts? 
 "You always made me really happy, Rowdy. I'm sort of infatuated with all the different ways you make me happy now that we're all grown up." 
 This book was oh so steamy and had me wiggling in my chair reading it! I knew that Rowdy would get me all riled up and I do love when I am right. But then again which of the Marked Men has not been sexy as hell! Once Rowdy lets loose there is no turning back and I LOVED this sexy man! 
 "I always thought it was the firsts that matter, but now I know that it's the lasts that stay with you." 
 This book is a great New Adult novel with an erotic feel. The characters are young and fun and you get peeks into the lives of all the couples from previous books which is a nice little thrill for me and a bit of story into what Asa's book will be like (come on April I am dying over here) Overall I was extremely pleased with this book and look forward to reading it again! 
 ~miranda

Ahhh....the Marked Men have hit again! 
 Let it be known that this series is one of my top fav but this particular installment, I'm not sure how to rate it...It's somewhere between 3-4 stars. 
 The 4 stars would be because it's well written and a complete story, 
 The 3 stars is because Rowdy fell a little flat for me. I truly did like Rowdy and Salem together and it's a wonderful second chance romance story for me but for whatever reason, it did not tug at my heart strings like the other guys did. 
 I usually read these installments with my heart in my hand and I can't put it down for a single second but Rowdy didn't do it for me in that way, i just liked it. 
 On a positive note - man how much do I love this story and I CANNNNNOOOTT wait for Asa and Royal's story (which I called after Nash and I'm so excited!) 
 Could we get a holiday novella for Saylor and Zeb?! pleasseee.....
I loved this book just like the others! Marked men can't be beat!!!

Rowdy's book was almost like second chance love. While I enjoyed it, I didn't overly melt with it like I did with Rule's story. I am excited for Asa's I think he has a long way to go and with the ending of Rowdy's story I'm excited to see where it ends up. I love this group of people, so I enjoyed the book because I was able to still interact with that band of characters, although not as much but still enough to excite me for their happenings in life.

This book didn't really do it for me. It felt like I was reading several different books and only one of them was interesting. It was far too slow, and the relationship between the characters just didn't click for me.
Rowdy had potential, but the story kind of went nowhere. Oh, and I see Saint is still Saint. Poor Nash.

Wow, I didn't think I would love Rowdy as much as Rule and Rome, but he was right up there! I am so invested in this series! I just love all these guys (and girls). With each book, I feel like it's a family reunion for me, catching up with all of them! 
 I loved Rowdy and Salem! They were perfect for each other! They both had their insecurities, but they were both pretty honest with each other. Oh and their sex life was more than hot, it was SIZZLING!!!!! 
 Can't wait for Asa and Royal's story!!!

reference_books.title: Lost at Sea
reference_books.review_text: An earlier work by Bryan Lee O'Malley (creator of Scott Pilgrim) that may appeal to those with a soft spot for morose, angst filled tales of soul searching - and while I typically do - this one falls short of delivering. The art, however, is stellar and in some ways superior to the styling of 'Scott Pilgrim.'

reference_books.title: Medium Raw: A Bloody Valentine to the World of Food and the People Who Cook
reference_books.review_text:
Most food celebs of Bourdain's stature would be content to rest on their laurels and take the easy road to nirvanaville - but Bourdain being Bourdain decides to crank up the volume, exceeding even the screeching levels of his incendiary 'Kitchen Confidential' in this no-holds barred diatribe of things that Bourdain finds right and (mostly) wrong in today's food scene. 
 Reading through this book is like sitting with Bourdain and his closest chums in an after-hours watering hole while he unleashes his thoughts and rips apart various culinary luminaries that are typically regarded as untouchable (Alice Waters, Alan Richman, Thomas Keller, Alain Ducasse, etc). His thoughts are extremely insidery, frank and lucid and his commentary cuts straight to the bone even if you're not familiar with most of the sacred cows in question. 
 Of course, a fair portion of the book is dedicated to things that Bourdain has deep appreciation and fondness for such as Vietnam, Fergus Henderson and David Chang - but the raw, candidness of Bourdain's head-space is really what we came for and yes, he does deliver in full yet again.

reference_books.title: Harbor
reference_books.review_text: A decent, atmospheric horror thriller set in a small, Swedish seaside town. The story is very reminiscent of vintage Stephen King but the emphasis on internal character struggle can sometimes distract from the plotting.

reference_books.title: The Walking Dead, Vol. 17: Something to Fear
reference_books.review_text: This volume compiles issues #97-102 and as of March 2013, this is the most recent compilation with volume #18 schedule for release in June '13. The story line and character arc takes a major shift from the opening pages of this volume so if you've followed the story up until now there's no reason to pass this one up.

reference_books.title: A Dance with Dragons (A Song of Ice and Fire, #5)
reference_books.review_text: I'm still every bit enamored with the series as I have been since the first book and will gobble up every bit of story George Martin throws my way but with this most recent entry I finally felt the pangs of impatience and vehemently wished that Martin could go back and capture some of that brilliant narrative pacing he pulled off in book #3 and re-inject that energy back into the series. PS - the Daenerys storyline is starting to bug!

book_a.title: Die Trying (Jack Reacher, #2)
book_a.user_review: The Jack Reacher series hits a minor Sophomore slump with this 2nd book in the series. The narrative becomes somewhat disjointed with too much switching back and forth between other characters - I estimate that around 35% of the book is told from the perspective of other characters. Still, if you're a fan all the trademarks are here - swift and brutal action and nuggets of backstory to help fill in the persona of Reacher.

sample_reviews.review_text: Jack Reacher is awesome. This book is a thrilling suspense novel.

I appreciate this is fiction, but it's so far beyond belief that it becomes stupid. And it's really rather dull. In fact for a thriller it's REALLY dull, with very little thrilling about it all. The second Reacher I've read, and I doubt they'll be a third.

The good, and there isn't much, includes the action sequences and the description of Reacher's tight squeeze, near death experience in the tunnels he must navigate to escape from a locked room. But that is it. 
 This second Jack Reacher novel was simply too full of holes and convenient circumstances and good luck in Jack Reacher's favor that by halfway through the book, I wanted it to be over. I don't mind if the hero is given a second chance by the bad guy to make a comeback, (you know, the bad guy talks too much about his plans and rather than kill the protagonist he elects to torture him, but the hero escapes...that kind of jazz) but Reacher is captured, wreaks havoc upon his captors, is given a couple chances to say he is sorry, kills some more bad guys, is told to play nice, destroys munitions and supplies, is released into the wild (yeah, RELEASED) so then he can come back and put the bad guys down. WHAT? The actions of this paramilitary group that wants to become independent of the USA are so asinine and backwards that they deserve their own country...in a mental institution. Seriously, who allows this outsider, Reacher, to do what he does then hands him a sniper rifle to show what he can do, then, upon realizing how deadly accurate he is, basically lets him go. I haven't even mentioned the incredible luck he has in figuring out the bad guys' plan based on a couple things Mr. HeadBadGuy, a 400 pound fat ass by the way, has said. With time ticking against him, Reacher correctly guesses which way the bomb was headed on a hunch. Just too unbelievable for me.
Shit load of coincidences and an uninteresting storyline. Not half as good as the first Reacher novel (Killing Floor) I read.
This is a blockbuster film type book. If go along with the ride you will really enjoy it

My first audio book... Listened at a good pace.. The best part is one can learn the exact pronunciation of words. Besides, the way speaker intones the novel, you can easily decipher different characters. 46 Chapters and you can have a beautiful experience. It will get you addicted.

 As a second novel though, it was great stuff. Very exciting.

book_b.title: The Walking Dead, Compendium 1
book_b.user_review:
Read this one a few years ago but wanted to dive in again now that I've viewed the first 3 seasons of the 'Walking Dead' television adaptation. If you've never read the books but have watched the tv show this is still very worthy of your reading time to note some of the drastic differences between the original storyline and the tv adaptation. Also, as it compiles the first 48 issues this book provides tremendous value and is an all the way riveting read that is hard to put down once you get started. 
 Another interesting bit is that Kirkman's art starts off very strong with great attention to intricate illustrative detail but going into issues 20 and on there is a noticeable degradation of overall artistic quality. This book/series would be worthy of 5-stars if Kirkman was able to sustain that artistic level on a consistent basis.

sample_reviews.review_text: WOW... I can't wait to read more.

My first foray into graphic novels in an effort to learn the canon of The Walking Dead. I Have watched the series from the beginning and am just reading the graphic novels now. While I love the story lines, the graphic part is hard for me. Lots of drawings seem exactly the same. Perhaps I just need to get into the genre more. I like that the novels don't match the series. Makes things more fun!

Um... the way this book just left me in a lurch is hardly fair. I understand that it's only volumes 1-8, and there are currently 13 volumes (78 issues total), but I wasn't expecting the ending that I got. Kirkman was on point at the end of volume 8. Ice cold.
My first introduction to comics and it's Absolutely fantastic.
Excellent collection, but nothing like the TV series!

The Walking Dead compendium 1 had me hooked from the first page. As an avid watcher of the show, I had heard countless times how different the comic is, so I was already expecting some differences before starting. I was constantly shocked or surprised by the subtle and definitely not so subtle differences. Without any spoilers...the Governor's story line was much more tame in the show, I actually like Andrea more in the comic, than the show, and I still hated Lori. I can't wait to start compendium 2 and find out what my favorite gang of survivors is up to!
At some points it was quite slow-paced but maan that ending...

I'd give this a 3.5 stars. There's a lot that was changed between the comics and the TV show, but I learned a while ago to enjoy things for their differences. Not everything has to be exactly the same. Far more brutal, this was an enjoyable read and i'd definitely recommend it to fans of TWD - just don't expect it to be the same!

*I seldom put comics in GR as it was very easy to finish and would appear like cheating on my annual book challenge.

 The characters also the most clueless type i have ever seen. When one see zombie apocalypse, one would think this is the end of the world, but not these men and women. There just seems clueless of what happened, almost as if the word 'zombie' and 'undead' never occurred to them.

I probably won't read any further because I'd prefer to be surprised when I'm watching the show but I'll definitely follow up the show with the next compendium.

reference_books.title: The Heir (The Selection, #4)

sample_reviews.review_text:
This book. THIS BOOK. AARRGHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHH! 
 Thinking about this book just makes my head hurt. 
 Mare. Mare is absolutely annoying. The plot is nonsense. The love triangle in this between the princes is the tritest, pointless, and most stupid thing ever. Good, well-written character development is absolutely nowhere to be found.

Mare Barrow is a Red, which means she is a mere human, and is destined to either work for the god-like Silvers as a laborer for the rest of her life or she is headed off to die on a battlefield. Not much to look forward to, right? But Destiny brings Mare to the Silver's playground and she discovers that there is more to her than just a thief, a soldier, or a laborer. 
 You suffer and worry for Mare and her family. You want to trust and care about the princes but are too scared to. You want to trust and rely on some of the Silvers and some of the Red servants but you're just not sure who you can trust....Red Queen takes you on an interesting ride through a very uncertain world! 
 I have heard a lot of great things about this series so when book one, Red Queen, went on sale I thought to give it a try. I wasn't sure that another dystopian type saga was something I could get into but I liked The Hunger Games so why not? 
 At first, I had a little trouble getting into the story because there were just so many people and so many different places, houses, and names to remember that I wasn't sure I could keep them straight but I shouldn't have stressed myself! The author does an excellent job of keeping you "in the loop" with everyone and their special abilities so after a chapter or two I got past this issue and was able to enjoy the story. 
 The book has a lot of twists and turns and although Mare finds people within the Reds and the Silvers that she trusts, I did not. I had a feeling about how things would end up and I was right. Normally, this would bug me, but in this instance it did not matter at all. The characters are all so intriguing and even though you may guess the end results you will still enjoy the ride getting you there. 
 This is considered a YA fantasy novel as all the main characters were teens. If you enjoyed The Hunger Games or the Divergent series this is in a similar vein. I liked The Hunger Games but wasn't that into Divergent as much and in my opinion, Red Queen is better.

Red Queen is a book that's not the easiest, nor will it ever be, but the discussions and the feelings in this book definitely deserve the praise. It is fantastic, and reading it was (literally) a rollercoaster, and one I do not regret going on. Just read it. No need for an introduction or any form of details about it. All you need to know is that it's awesome and that it's waiting for you in the nearest bookstore.

This book was, well, bland. I am so freaking unimpressed right now. 
 I mean I get it there are some fixed tropes for each genre that authors exploit...tried and tested formulas that will work with the audience but even then they throw in something of their own to the mix, something original, Aveyard went ahead picked pieces from all the popular YA hits and compiled a big ass book of derivative plotlines and single dimensional characters. 
 I won't lie the premise of the book, the blurb at the back of the novel and the stunning cover art are all so solid that they will reel you in but that is where the magnetic force of this book stops. You are thrown into a world where you have arenas and broadcastings of brutal nature intended to keep the subdued population threatened and well subdued (let's take a pause and give a nod to the Hunger Games series, shall we?) Here in this world we are introduced to our 'heroine', someone who steals things to provide for her family and has a male best friend who hates the current government (let's wave to Katniss and Gale *waves frantically*). Now her life gets entangled in the bigger frame of things when her power of being able to control lightning comes in to public view (oh look! there are Katniss and president Snow and they are joined by Juliette from shatter me and the Storm fron X-men as well). 
 The whole book felt stretched, the writing was ineffectual. I literally didn't feel a thing right from the beginning to the end and that's a pretty massive feat to acomplish since I am someone who feels every single thing that a character goes through. 
 The ending, the action sequences, the romance all felt in a dire need of originality. 
 The gaurd was so much like the rebels in divergent or what we saw in hunger games and the characters associated Farley, Kilorn, Will whistle well let's just say i wont remember even their names by tomorrow morning. 
 Every character was so unidimensional. Cal was the only one that I found remotely interesting. 
 Mare was downright annoying. I mean for fuck's sake get real, use your own head and do something concrete for once! anyone can manipulate her, steer her in the direction they want and she will go with it. She barely misses her family or thinks about them. We have no profound insight as to what she is like as a person even after being in her head for about 400 pages. Even she barely knows what she feels. 
 Queen Elara well I have just one question was I suppose to be afraid of her? 
 And Maven. Oh god where do I start with him. I can see that he is that one character the author typically pins their hope upon. The character meant to get majority of the readers hooked. But that just didn't happen for me. Don't get me wrong I liked him, the whole good boy turned bad and shades of grey thing is my addiction which is why it was even more surprising for me that I felt zero pull towards him. 
 The love triangle was downright pathetic and I am being mild when i say that. 
 I didn't care one bit about who ended up with who which defies the only thing that a love triangle intends to do, make you invested and root for someone. I couldn't picture the guys in my head because there was no concrete decription of their appearance and call me shallow but i need to have a picture in my mind to get my imagination going. There was no building up of relationships, no tender exchange of emotions or actions. There were barely any personal dialogues between the three! How does this even qualify as a romance I don't know. 
 Lastly the plot twist, the plot twist I have seen so many people rave about, it was so predictable. I refuse to believe that I am the only one who saw it coming from a million miles away. Glaringly obvious and unimpressive is what it was. 
 This book has done for me what no book before has done and that is make me give up on a series just after the first book. I have OCD when it comes to stories. I just have to know the end, read the whole damn thing even if its bad only because I have started it but this book...well no such need there.

A sci-fi version of the hunger games. It wasn't intellectually stimulating, but it was DEFINITELY a page turner. I read it in a single day and am looking forward to reading the next one. This book SCREAMS movie adaptation.
WOW! Such a magnificent first book in a series! SO GOOD! Also makes me want to keep reading Shadow and Bone!

Man, that ending! I was expecting a lot from this book, I will be honest with all the hype and that aboslutely beautiful cover. I was hoping to LOVE this book. I did like this book, I really liked the twist at the end that was in my peripheral vision- then right there in front of me I had to cover my mouth from the excitement/horror. But, yes there is a but...I was expecting more going into it. 
 Mare was a good mostly likable, but typical YA heroine. That was my main issue I believe, is that it is another dystopian like all other dystopians before it. You know, two types of people against each other, an oppressive government, and a group of rebels trying to change the world and we all know that most likely in the end of what I assume is a trilogy or series, they will. 
 "The truth is what I make it. I could set this world on fire and call it rain." 
 I did like how the rebellion had a name though (and a motto). The Scarlet Guard. Rise red as dawn. 
 Against the silver blooded powerful rulers who have really cool powers. Powers I am always up for especially when I can see what our main character can do with it. 
 And Mare did well, just not great with what she was giving. I liked her slight temper though I thought we could have went further. When you are a Red with a gift, I don't know, I think that I would practice until I was exhausted and the best there was. Mare didn't give me that feeling that she wanted to be there in the story the whole time and when she finally did at the end, it was almost too late. 
 "In the fairy tales, the poor girl smiles when she becomes a princess. Right now, I don't know if I'll ever smile again." 
 The romances though that pretty much try and revolve around this story between the two slightly feuding brothers Cal, and Maven who is living in his older brother and soon King's shadow. I didn't think either had full chemistry though I did lean one way or another the entire story. As of now after reading I want both of them gone and Mare to become the first Red Queen or badass, or whatever she wants to be while figuring this messed up world out. 
 VERDICT: 
 I did really like this book. The ending with a major plot twist really did it for me and saved the book from me just liking it. It has such an interesting concept and I really hope that in the next books the author makes it her own with more characters and the bit of Game of Thrones type killing possible? I can see some ruthless tendencies that could be in there by the end. 
 I want to know what happens next with so much left to unveil and figure out in the next books. 
 If You Liked... 
 -The Selection by Kiera Cass 
 -Shadow and Bone by Leigh Bardugo 
 3 stars

I wanted so bad to love this book. And yet, despite trying to read it three times with full determination, it continues to bore me tears. 
 Everything from the plot to the characters felt flat, forced, and typical. 
 That said, I know many who love the series. It simply didn't work for me. I will not give this novel a fourth chance.

The Red Queen is not a good story if you are looking for a strong heroine lead in a fantasy series. If you are looking for a series like The Hunger Games, a tale about a female (Mary Sue) becoming the leader of a revolution, then this series and this novel will be great for you. If you enjoyed the love triangle and push-pull romance in the Hunger Games, the romance in the novels will be enjoyable for you. 
 If you can stomach a perfect character for whom all the main male characters fall in love, has a rare and powerful ability, and is as emotionally mature as a middle schooler, the background characters are interesting and the story about the revolt is intriguing. It does require reading the entire series and suffering through the point of view of the main character before this part of the story is resolved. 
 I enjoyed this novel because I enjoy stories. I wanted Maven to be a twisted, psychopath and finishing the book let me know if I was correct. I wanted to see if Cal was a kind-hearted character as I suspected. I wanted to see if the Reds would rise against the Silvers. To resolve these background tales and inquiries, I pushed on from the otherwise obnoxious point of view. 
 To be fair, I am about 100 pages into the second book and the character seems to have grown a bit. Yet, the growth seems very focused on vengeance and still lacking any emotional depth. 
 I guess I learned that you can enjoy a novel while disliking the main character and their point of view simultaneously. 
 -A Bookish Girl

sample_reviews.review_text:
I stayed up all night reading this. I just couldn't put it down. A perfect ending. More thoughts when I'm not sleep deprived! 
 Winter was everything I wanted. Action, heart, romance, REVOLUTION. Shit gets real, and it's scary but you just can't look away. The pacing was fantastic, and honestly this book could not be any better. 
 Also, Winter as a WOC means a lot to me and I'm sure it will mean a lot to many WOC who read this book and this series. Winter is strong, smart, and above all kind. She's compassionate. She helps those who need it, and even if she basically gives herself schizophrenia because she refuses to use her Lunar powers, that doesn't change how wonderful she is. It takes real strength of will to refuse to use something she was born with. Her and Jacin also have an amazing dynamic, it's so cute. Her friendship with Scarlet was also great. They may have clashing personalities, but they truly care for each other. Also, when she first saw Cinder, broke my heart. 
 Speaking of Cinder, I was so proud of her. She's grown so much since the first book. She's a true leader, and she had the charisma to convince the outer sectors to rebel. Her and Kai are still the cutest. They're both my babies <3 
 Cress and Thorne are hilarious and adorable. I love them both. 
 Scarlet and Wolf probably had the hardest journey in getting back to each other. Both went through the worst things, but their love for each other is what kept them going and brought them back. I just want to give them a hug. 
 *sigh* I know I still have Stars Above to look forward to, but I'm really going to miss my babies. The Lunar Chronicles is one of my favorite series of all time, and I'm really going to miss this world and these characters. 
 Also, ALL OF MY SHIPS SURVIVED!!!! BLESSSS!!!! 
 Truly a happily ever after.

A story in which fairy tale princesses and their respective prince charmings unite to form a galactic rebellion against the most evil of wicked witches. 
 I don't know what it is, but the charm of the first story just didn't translate well with the rest of the series. Meyer is weaving a lot of threads for all the plots and sub-plots and myriad of characters to come through, which is quite a challenge, and for the most part she is successful in the technical aspects. That complexity came with a price though. With each additional fairy story, the retellings further spiral off towards a cumbersome plot in which the individual nuances of a reinterpretation are lost. Winter's story doesn't feel like her story. Instead she's the delusional but idealistic princess to further the other characters' stories. As the titular character, it's sad to see her reduced to a sub-plot. 
 I can understand why people loved these books, but ultimately I left disappointed considering the series had such a great start.

Is it really over??? :( 
 I was one of the lucky few who received my paperback copy early last Friday. I was so thrilled to jump right in to Keira and Kellan all over again... But I didn't. I decided to take it back to the beginning and re-read the series straight through. I am so glad I did that!! First off, I've re-read the books in the past but it was different this time. I was so caught up in the Kellan tunnel the first time I read it, that I think I missed some things. Don't get me wrong, I am still seriously, over the top, in a completely unhealthy obsessive relationship with Kellan Kyle. But rereading the series with a "if I knew then what I know now" perspective allowed for a greater appreciation for the entire story. First, I was so much more devastated for Denny this time around. He truly represented all that is good and my heart broke for him. I better appreciated how his friendship with Keira rebuilt in Effortless and the crucial piece he played in the grand finale, reckless! I could understand her inability to decide what to do because there was really no better choice. And I could sympathize with the pain that she and Denny will always feel for what happened. When I first read it, I just got annoyed with her for not getting on with things, but I have a clearer picture this time around and a greater respect for how difficult this road really was. 
 I went through such a range of emotions while reading this book. Truly, I think I held my breath the entire time and fought the urge to throw up. I don't want there to be an end to this journey... yes, we are left in a wonderful place, but an end is still an end, and for that, I am sad!! I still found myself laughing uncontrollably at times (usually wherever Griffin appeared.) I felt the painful heart tugs with all of the drama thrown out their, (the sex tape, the music video, the constant obstacles thrown between Keira and Kellan) I also found myself in tears (Kellan crying at his parents grave.) It's the best kind of emotional roller coaster and I never wanted to get off! 
 I was so happy with a number of things in this story. First off, I loved what the author did by having Keira write her "story" of her love triangle. I loved that she almost sort of made fun of herself or her writing, anyway, in Thoughtless. The way all of us loyal readers initially had described Keira as whiney, wishy washy and at times, annoying, was thrown back at us in Reckless and I couldn't help but find the humor in that. I, at times, found it hard to connect "rock star Kellan" to "Seattle small-town singing in Pete's bar Kellan" because the dynamic in this story was so vastly different from the other books, that revisiting their early relationship while Keira wrote her"book" really helped me to reconnect where they came from to where they are now. I also love the closure that Keira' s book gave to Denny. I don't think I ever really considered that not having all the facts, Denny probably had a considerably different version of the situation in his head. I also loved what Kellan got from her story, seeing it all from Keira' s view was critical for them. 
 I knew going in that this book would be different from the others, knowing it was the last book, there probably wouldn't be that underlying threat of a breakup like there was in Thoughtless and Effortless, the fear that at any minute the bottom could do out. Or at least I assumed so. I assumed that we'd be getting our happily ever after, but still S.C. Stephens did not disappoint when it came to angst and drama. I thought the Joey sex tape was enough to push me over the edge...And right out of the gate no less. But the controversy stirred up with Siena Sexton just about drove me to drink. I was literally expecting Keira to pack up and head home. I wasn't even sure what the title 'Reckless' even meant for this story until the radio interview that set the world straight, when Kellan and Keira went rogue and went public with their relationship. Then, I GOT IT!! 
 I thought the author did such an amazing job, no surprise there, of wrapping up all the loose ends, no stone was left unturned. Over the course of the first two books and then a chunk of the third, Keira never once embraced the fact that she was beautiful. She never looked at herself as worthy of Kellan' s perfection and I always knew that this was her own projection and not reality... so with that said, I consistently asked myself over the course of the entire series "Why does Keira never get hit on???" It was always Kellan garnering unwanted attention and Keira sitting by catching dirty looks from his admirers. We all know she must be gorgeous, regardless of her unwillingness to believe it, so where are the guys that would undoubtedly be checking her out in the midst of all of this? And then it happened!!! I was so glad the author gave that to Keira... And to us, the readers!! I felt that was a crucial aspect of the story. I also loved that several times it was emphasized how beautiful Keira really was in this story... when she finally admitted it to herself, when Denny acknowledged it and through her being hit on finally hit that nail on the head. 
 I could really just go on and on about how satisfied I was with this ending. I loved all the characters met along the way coming together for this finale. I loved getting the insight into where they are now, Keira' s group of friends, the other bandmates, Kellan' s family, the Pete's bar crew... I loved that we got to meet them again and see them off in the end. New marriages, babies, engagements, jobs... it was a satisfying end for everyone. 
 I'll admit this book made me tremendously sad. The entire time I was reading I wanted the D-bags to pack it in and go back home. I missed them just living somewhat simple existences back home, playing at Pete's, with Keira waitressing there. I missed the little house that started it all, I hated the idea of Keira essentially sharing Kellan and the D-Bags with the world. I know... I know... this story showed that despite the fame and notoriety that came along, Kellan and Keira could survive it all. Selfishly, I just missed the Kellan that played his guitar on his grungy couch, ran in the park and had beers at the local bar. I missed Keira coming home to him and their quiet conversations over coffee. But such is life, things change and with all that changed, I felt what Keira felt... the fear that she'd lose Kellan to the world. I think I felt that same fear, thus hating change, wanting it to all to stay the same. But despite my sadness, I still adored it, and this will always be my favorite series.

reference_books.title: Lord of the Vampires (Royal House of Shadows, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
A good Gena Showalter book is one that has all of the following: 
 -humor 
 -a strong and determined heroine 
 -a non-angsty hero aka THE alpha male 
 If one is missing, especially the third, I find her novels to be a bit painful to read. When I first started reading Gena books, I noticed a lot of humor and alpha male heroes. I was instantly smitten. She knows how to write her alphas extra sexy and commanding. 
 Fast forward to her LOTU series post Gideon's book and all her heroes are emo and angsty now. I can't read them anymore because all the Lords are like this. Where did my beloved alpha male go? Goodbye grunts and sexiness, hello "I am not worthy, woe is me, we can't be together." There also seems to be a lot less humor in these instances, too. 
 I'm wary of new releases now because of the shift, and I was reluctant to open this book in particular. I hoped against hope that the hero wouldn't be angsty, and thank goodness, I was spared. LORD OF THE VAMPIRES seems to be a flashback to Gena's brilliance when it came to her novels, and reminded me of what had me falling in love with her writing in the first place. 
 Now, is this the best book she's written? In my opinion, no. I don't think the romance was rushed, but it felt like the ending was. The characters were good, but they don't stand out in my mind like some of her other characters do. There were funny moments, but they didn't have me crying from laughter like some of her other books have. I was a bit unclear about the teleporting aspects, and the villains in this books were lackluster...but to be honest, I've never found Gena's villains to be very intimidating anyway. 
 All in all, this novel is worth reading, but it wasn't my favorite. It does give me hope that maybe some of her other releases outside of her LOTU universe may still maintain that spark that I find myself missing in her books, but I won't be holding my breath.

reference_books.title: Black Wings (Black Wings, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
So I just finished reading BLACK WINGS, an urban fantasy that I was extremely excited for. I've had enough of vampires right now, and I've always wanted to read a story about a grim reaper. Maybe it's just me, but I always thought the idea of death being personified was exciting. The English major-dork in me loved reading about/the concept of the Danza Macabra (aka The Dance of Death) during the middle ages. Perhaps I found it so interesting because I always wondered what death would think, how she/he would react, and if death would have a love life. How could he/she, if whenever death touched someone, they died? Or perhaps the busy work schedule deterred any love life? Would there be multiple deaths, collecting souls? There's just so many possibilities, and now I got a story about it! 
 Unfortunately, I did not enjoy this novel as much as I had hoped. The writing is accessible and I believe that many will enjoy Christina's writing style. There are bits and pieces of humor that will make you laugh out loud while reading this story, which is definitely something I can appreciate in a novel. One cannot laugh enough while reading a book. 
 Then, there is the world Christina created, which is what kept me reading this book. Like I said earlier, I love the concept of a good grim reaper story and I believe there are not enough books out there right now that focus on that sort of character (this will probably change soon). Fallen angels, nephilim, and Christina's take on Lucifer were also unique and refreshing. There is no actual hell. Who would have thought of that one? It definitely makes Lucifer's minions seem more modern and... well, I thought it was amusing that they would be living alongside humanity. Oh, and the gargoyle sidekick/comical relief? Priceless. Give me more gargoyles! 
 Alas, that is where my adoration for this book ends, because we are ultimately forced to learn more about Maddy, the heroine in our story. If I love the heroine in a UF, you can believe that I will probably love the book. If I don't, then even if the world is unique, I probably will not love the book. Guess which side of the spectrum I'm on? 
 When it comes to Maddy, our 32 year old heroine, let's just say she has more temper tantrums than I did when I was 12. I said to a friend of mine when I reached the midpoint of the book: "Maddy is bipolar x10." Almost every single encounter contains a moment where Maddy seems to overreact and act childish. She vents and complains so early on in the story that I found it hard to like her since it made her come off as whiny and dramatic. Granted, there were three encounters that had occurred beforehand, but I couldn't even recall one because it was so brief. Heroines having mental breakdowns and rant-fests within the first 100 pages of a book do not earn my sympathy. 
 I will give Maddy the benefit of the doubt though, because her emotional state of mind did serve a purpose to the story. Alas, fights are one thing; how the heroine interacts with the allies around her (read: when she isn't fighting) is entirely different. I hope that Maddy's character vastly improves in book two. 
 Speaking of ranting, parts of the dialogue felt too condensed for my tastes. Instead of flowing naturally, the venting scenes were repetitive and long winded. I would have appreciated some lines cut, simplified, or explained via Maddy's thoughts (ex: I then began to explain to so-and-so about how I felt. How I was tired of getting my ass kicked, how I was tired of being left in the dark) I feel that flows more naturally than some of the things actually said, but that's just me being nitpicky. 
 Moving on to the love interests: I loved Gabriel. I loved the attraction (later on in the story) between Maddy and Gabriel. But the initial attraction between them? I wasn't buying it. For me, the pacing was off at that point and it went from Maddy dealing with struggling for her life to suddenly crushing on this man. There were no bonding moments between the two early on. Hell, she was mad at him. Despite her anger, he saves her life by kissing her and she's suddenly drooling over the man. For me, this felt too abrupt and unrealistic. 
 JB was another character I took issue with. He's an asshole at the start. Maddy thinks he's an asshole, albeit, an attractive one. Yet once Gabriel enters Maddy's life, JB transforms from jerk to attracted man. There were no other signs during earlier interactions that would hint at any sort of attraction on his end, which is why I struggled with the initial unveiling of him as a love interest. I liked JB as one, but I would have enjoyed that element developed further so that it was more convincing. 
 I think the problem that I had most was Maddy's emotions being everywhere and the pacing. There was a lot of action in this story, which is not bad, but it can hurt a book at times too. I had no opportunity to become intimate with Maddy's character because I felt like I was always on edge, expecting her to get her ass kicked at any second (or, having her discover ANOTHER new skill that will conveniently save her life and kick the bad guy's butt). I wanted to get to know Patrick and Maddy and Beezle more before everything started to become undone. Patrick's fate did not phase me because I did not know him as a character. I also wanted Maddy and Gabriel to interact more and get to know each other before all the drama began. Same with JB. 
 I also had a few technical problems with the book, but those are nitpicky and can probably be overlooked by most readers. Primarily, how did JB know Gabriel was a paranormal creature and not just some human? Did humanity know about vampires and demons and whatnot? I might have missed the latter question at some point, but if not, that should have been addressed. 
 Aside from all those complaints, I thought BLACK WINGS was a decent debut. Not my favorite, but I enjoyed it enough that I am looking forward to reading the next book in the series. Hopefully, Maddy's character will act a bit more maturely and the pacing will improve, now that Christina's a more experienced writer. I suggest reading this book if you enjoy action-packed UFs combined with a bit of humor, or if you want to read about a grim reaper-filled world. I believe that most will be able to look over the pacing and romance issues I had, just like I believe some will detest Maddy's emotional state of being. I also believe that despite how emotional Maddy is, those readers will look forward to book two also.

reference_books.title: Zodiac (Zodiac, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This was okay. It started off strong and had me hooked, but then experienced typical middle book syndrome of a debuting author. You know--where the plot slows down and characters seem to run around in circles? Yeah. That. 
 There's a love triangle in this series. And to be honest, it feels forced. But I think that's because the characters fall a bit flat for me. Two dimensional and their motives are....murky. Emotional reactions sometimes came out of the blue and surprised me. There was no smooth lead up. 
 What this heroine experiences. What she becomes....it felt over the top. Too much all squished into one book. 
 But the world building is great. I loved the approach and the idea behind this. I'll be anticipating book 2, despite my reservations from book 1.

reference_books.title: Mercy Blade (Jane Yellowrock, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
Once again, Faith Hunter has completely wowed me with another amazing story in the Jane Yellowrock series. Fans familiar with the series will be thrilled to discover that all established characters in the past two books make some sort of appearance in MERCY BLADE. That means we finally discover some unanswered questions, we witness new and blooming relationships, and we figure out whether or not Leo is actually batshit crazy. 
 A recent relationship in Jane's life, while brief in the beginning, adds a new, complicated element to our heroine's persona. On one hand, the young woman struggles with physical wants and desires, but then on the other, she struggles with a guilt that surfaces, reminding her that she is a bad Christian. At some points, the religious and political commentary seemed like it was a little overdone, but I felt that I could easily overlook that tiny bit. 
 There is so much sexual tension in this book. I admit that I was not a fan of Bruiser in SKINWAKER, however, he slowly grew on me in BLOOD CROSS. Now, in MERCY BLADE, I was begging my book for him and Jane to hook up. The chemistry and attraction between these two characters had me wanting to fan myself, while also feeling guilty because of Rick. When the heck has a book made me feel GUILTY about the heroine lusting after guys? Never. I think it has to do with the fact that Jane kept reflecting back on her guilt, which in turn, made me feel guilty. I'm still in shock that I felt bad! Nevertheless, I love the interactions between them now. I adore how flirty they are and how pushy Beast is when Jane and Bruiser are alone together. It just... was perfect. 
 Speaking of Beast, once again, I was not disappointed with our furry friend. I think that the relationship evolving between Beast and Jane has evolved to hilarious levels. I felt the comfortable bond the two share now, which made me smile. Looking back on this series, our lovable duo has come a long way. 
 The attention to detail is spot on in this book. I don't know anything about motocycles, guns, and weapons in general, but after reading MERCY BLADE, I feel like I can name a few facts. While I thought that all of this information provided was interesting, and reveals the author did her homework, I also felt that some description scenes went into a little too much detail for my tastes. I'm not into weapons or crime scenes, which is why I felt the need to skim over a paragraph or two regarding these points. For those who are interested, I believe these descriptions will impress the reader and draw them into the Jane Yellowrock world. As for me, it made the beginning in particular a little more difficult to get into. However, once the action in the story picks up, the detail gives way to heart-thumping action and the pages are no longer bogged down with pages of descriptions. 
 Too much description was actually my only complaint with this story. I almost cried by the end because I felt as emotionally exhausted as Jane did. I wanted to kick and scream and punch that stupid were-bitch early on. I wanted Jane to finally be happy...but I won't know until book four because of the cruel (okay I'm exaggerating a little bit) cliffhanger at the end. I'm hoping--no, praying--that the next book in this series will come out later this year. I don't think I could wait until 2012 for another Jane Yellowrock book. 
 MERCY BLADE, like I've stated earlier, does not disappoint. It is solid proof that Faith's writing continues to improve with each book published. I find that this is one universe chock full of characters that I fondly remember whenever discussing this series to a fellow reader. If you're looking for a dark, gritty tale where vampires are psychotic and not lovey dovey, where werewolves aren't sexy beasts, and where there is sexual tension up the wazoo, then MERCY BLADE and the Jane Yellowrock series is the series for you. Highly suggest buying this book today, and reading the prior novels ASAP!

reference_books.title: Dreams of a Dark Warrior (Immortals After Dark #11)
reference_books.review_text:
1 sexy, angsty hero + 1 outspoken, kick-ass heroine = my IAD addiction has been sated. For now. 
 After the previous events in DEMON FROM THE DARK, I was curious to see how Kresley would incorporate past events to influence this new novel. Due to the prior knowledge of Regin's fate in the Order's facilities, a guessing game (of sorts) began for me. When would she be mistreated? How would that affect the relationship? Would it happen early on? Later? A nice addition to keep me on my toes. 
 There's less sex in this book, but sex does not always equate to a successful romance. The sex that was there was hot. Also, to compensate for the lack of sexytime, readers are gifted with lots of action, violence, and fun. I hope Kresley continues to make each of her books filled with that much heart pumping action. 
 Also, Lothaire. Enough said. I loved the scenes where that crazy vampire--literally!--led us around on some wild chases. Definitely looking forward to his book now in 2012. 
 Like many of Kresley's books, DREAMS OF A DARK WARRIOR satisfied my hunger for witty humor, heartbreaking romances, and sexy heroes, while also leaving me desolate in my angst-filled wait for the next book in the series. I would be stupid not to recommend this book or series to any fan of paranormal novels--especially romances. If you're new to the Immortals After Dark series, then you should hurry the hell up already and start reading! Any fan can attest to the sheer genius Kresley Cole is. 
 I wish I had her writing skills.

book_a.title: Gulliver's Travels
book_a.user_review: Had to read this for my Satire class.... Interesting premise, but I am not a fan of Swift's writing.

sample_reviews.review_text: As a huge fan of 18th century British Literature, this book never fails to give me a few chuckles. Swift satirizes the British and their habits so well; he was a master.

Swift is such a snarky cynic. Honestly, it's no wonder from what I read about his life that he was so miserable and everyone hated him. He really was one of the least likable authors of his time. I only had to read half of this as a school assignment and thankfully I was not expected to finish it because the entire thing is absolutely ludicrous. I love fantasy and imaginative books, but this entire story was just so bizarre it makes me wonder about Swift's sanity. Surely all that isolation was not good for him?! I also read his famous essay "A Modest Proposal" as well and found this much better despite the disturbing questions it raises about the cheapness of human life. Here his cynicism actually works for him instead of against him, but honestly Swift will always leave a bad taste in my mouth. What can I say? I am a romantic at heart and Swift's stark view of the world doesn't jive with me.

Parts of this were tiring and a little too descriptive but I liked most the satire parts about how silly classes and government and other things can be. In the end though I did feel he went a little crazy thinking he was a yahoo though it did make me feel kind of lame myself compared to the higher race of horses.

At the risk of coming off like an un-intellectual simpleton, I'm giving this work of classic literature one star out of sheer boredom. I understand and appreciate the historical importance of this book. However, I think you need to have a lot more background in 1700's England to appreciate the political satire. I almost gave it two stars due to Swift's incredible way with words. But in the end, the endless descriptions of room dimensions, etc., didn't speak to me on an entertainment or intellectual level.
Not for me.
I loved Gulliver's Travels and the different chapters. This was a very good read.
I managed to get to the halfway mark until I got utterly bored.

So at a whim I decided that I should read all of those classics I dodged while I was in school. And I had heard this book is a classic. Full of humor, fantasy and political satire. Unfortunately for me I found it was full of a lot of things, but in general the aforementioned weren't a part of it. And as far as it being a classic...well. My understanding of what makes something classic is that in spite of everything it survives the test of time and it is read and remembered now as it had been previously. So in that regard Gulliver's Travels is as much a classic as To Kill a Mockingbird or Don Quixote. I don't mean to compare it to those books on literary merit, just the fact that people remember parts of it, and exclude the rest. This could be due to Hollywood picking pieces of these books to put on display. 
 In the case of Gulliver's Travels this means that the opening with the Lilliputians is what is remembers while the rest of the book is mostly forgotten, ignored or unknown by anyone not committed enough (or forced to by an English Teacher with a large sense of sadism) to read all the way through. 
 As far as the Political Satire, well the version I had didn't have any notes in regards to that so it was no longer current and therefore not all that relevant to any real issue. So what the book ended up being was a fantasy trip through other worlds, albeit all on Earth (no space flights here) and a pretty dang nasty one at that. If I hadn't committed to finishing the book from the start I would have stopped reading it about the second or third new group of peoples he came across. Each time he found a new race he sank even deeper into caustic assertions and sometimes amazingly nasty descriptions that were sometimes distracting from the flow of the story itself. 
 By the end of the book, after he has reviled that the only descent intelligent race on the Planet are some Superior Horses, you find that the author has a self loathing that borders on the obsessive, and considers the whole of the human race to be nasty, filthy and not worth the effort to mingle with. While this may have had some deep underlying meaning at the time it was written to me it just made me wonder why he didn't just end himself and all his misery. It certainly would have been in keeping with the nihilistic style of dissertation he took up towards the end of the book. 
 A classic, it may be, but for myself it is destined for the scrap heap of history.
awful

book_b.title: A Local Habitation (October Daye, #2)
book_b.user_review:
A LOCAL HABITATION is an improvement in comparison to its predecessor, ROSEMARY AND RUE, because Tybalt shows up a lot more. In fact, he's in the very first chapter, and is so incredibly kind to Toby I wanted to jump into the book and give him a huge hug. That, in itself, was a huge improvement for me; I'm quite partial to the cat. But aside from Tybalt? I had mixed feelings about this story. However, first, I'm going to talk about Tybalt/Toby and their "relationship." 
 The beauty with urban fantasy is that sometimes, one doesn't want any romance. Sometimes, it's better to be teased and left guessing who the possible love interest will be instead of being guaranteed a happily ever after. And then you have other times where you wish the heroine--or hero--would stop being so dense and realize that they might have a willing lover sitting right under their noses. 
 Toby falls into the latter category for me. 
 A LOCAL HABITATION's love interests are almost like a game. Will Toby and Tybalt hook up? What about Toby and Alex? Or maybe it'll be Toby and Connor? Oh the possibilities! 
 I will admit that this floundering about frustrated me, despite the obvious relief I felt from not being guaranteed a HEA. Tybalt gave Toby his jacket, and Toby wore it throughout the entire novel. She commented on his comforting scent multiple times. Hell, Tybalt dropped everything to come make sure Toby was okay numerous times. 
 Toby seems to be attracted to Tybalt too, and the two acted like a couple on more than one occasion. She's leaned against him for support, turns to him for help, and trusts him. How the hell she's oblivious to his obvious signs of jealousy (which made me cackle with glee) during the confrontation with Alex is beyond me. She's ignoring the fact that the damn King of Cats touches her at almost every opportunity and follows her silly commands. And he doesn't get mad at said commands either--he teases her. I'm pretty sure if Tybalt hated Toby, he wouldn't have followed her around like a lovesick puppy dog. 
 Yet still, despite all of that, she's convincing herself that the two are enemies--EVEN THOUGH the vision she had of Tybalt in the first book and him taking care of her more than once in A LOCAL HABITATION says otherwise. *head desk* 
 That's my complaint about the love interest. I think this book would have been more interesting if the duo followed through on their obvious attraction. It would have definitely made me more excited for book 3. 
 In regards to Alex, I thought that was a creative approach to introducing a new species of the fey, while also making me so incredibly wary at the same time. I had my suspicions about the culprit, and was ultimately right in the end, but I still wondered if there was a possible second villain. At one point, halfway through the book, I was convinced Alex was guilty. But then things weren't making sense; why would he be guilty instead of the other person I suspected? 
 So the mystery in this was good, but I think it was also a bit obvious after a while. That didn't bother me like it clearly has some other people. I was still interested to see what Seanan would have happen next. 
 Thankfully, Toby doesn't get her ass kicked as much in A LOCAL HABITATION. Instead, I feel like there are a lot more of the mental mind games, which is good enough for me. It's nice to have someone else--even if they are a fictional character--who's ready to rip their hair out because of the stress (instead of it being me). I also felt emotionally connected at the end--though not so much in the beginning or middle. Toby's not a very good... umm... detective. The ending at the funeral pyre actually made me tear up. 
 I love how all the relationships were strengthened in this book, though I will admit that it was a bit strange to see Toby so happy at the start. I'd grown accustomed to her angst--and of her being convinced she could do everything alone--that it came off as strange and almost out of character. How bad am I for saying that? I don't want Toby miserable, but I truly couldn't see her being that cheerful. 
 Unique story, cool characters, and a hot King of Cats; what more could you look for in a book? A LOCAL HABITATION is a must read if you're salivating for an urban fantasy read.

sample_reviews.review_text: When the main character is as stupid about a MAJOR plot point as Toby is.. well, I spent almost the entire novel frustrated and angry. The first book was bloated with exposition and this one was worse. I'll read the rest of the series because it's not that long, but so far I'm not impressed at all. The secondary characters are interesting, though, so I'll give it that.
Engrossing murder mystery, clearly building into a larger fictional universe than is depicted just in this book.

October Daye is a changeling. Her mother is Amandine of the Daoine Sidhe, and her father was a mortal man. She works as a private investigator but she also a knight for her liege lord. And he has asked her to go check up on his niece. She is the Lady of a small Country known as Tamed Lightning, which makes this a politically sensitive job. Small countries don't tend to do too well in faerie, bigger and more powerful entities usually gobble them up, and Lord Sylvester doesn't want to provoke a diplomatic incident with Dreamer's Glass. 
 This is the second book in the series, and while it certainly does help to have read the first I think you probably could read this without getting too confused. Toby did learn lessons in the first book, and there is a background story that a reader might like to know, but it isn't essential. 
 This is easily as good as the first, if not better, as I said after reading Rosemary and rue, Toby is just a great character. 
 Of course she makes mistakes, and I am sure there is at least one character who may as well be flashing giant warning "Stay Away" signals at the reader, a fact that Toby doesn't seem to pick up on until too late, but usually her flaws and mistakes are understandable and human and fit the character. This is an important thing as she is the narrator as well as the protagonist, so if you don't identify at least a little with her I would guess the story will fall a little flat. 
 The first book in the series dealt with Toby reacquainting herself with the world after being absent for 14 years. Now, while she still has some adjusting to do she seems to have found her niche again. This book is more of a straight-forward detective case, albeit one with faery and magic and the like. 
 I'm very tempted to dive straight into book 3 of the series, because I have it here on my bookshelf waiting for me. But I don't want to overdose on Toby, I like the anticipation of knowing that I have a good read coming up, so I think I'll leave it for a book or two :)

This book was an incredibly frustrating sequel to Rosemary and Rue. Toby (October Daye), is sent by her liege, Sylvester, to check on his niece January. January is Countess of a small county (County of Tamed Lightening) between Sylvester's lands and a rival neighbor, and January hasn't been returning any of Sylvester's calls. 
 Sylvester asks Toby to bring along Quentin, a young pure-blood Daoine Sidhe, as an assistant/trainee. The plot started to unravel for me the moment Toby arrives at Tamed Lightening. Toby quickly learns that the situation is bad: January runs a tech company called ALH, and two of her subjects/employees have died under mysterious circumstances. January has been calling Sylvester but thinks Sylvester hasn't been returning her calls. 
 Stop. Right. There. Toby knows Sylvester has been calling January, then learns that January has been calling Sylvester, but neither has been receiving the other's calls. Toby is supposed to be an investigator, but this little fact doesn't set alarm bells ringing in her head. 
 The rest of the book is Toby missing obvious clues and making decisions that don't make any sense. An example is when, after telling the remaining ALH employees to stick together in groups, she learns that someone (Gordon) has gone off alone. She's concerned enough immediately to go after Gordon to make sure Gordon is ok, but on the way discovers the office of one of the murder victims, and stops to search the office thoroughly. What? 
 The main mysteries (what's the deal with Alex?, who is the murderer? what is the motive? what is really going on at ALH?) were blatantly obvious to me, the reader, but Toby blunders through, missing every clue. I chalk this up to bad writing. What we get, instead of a well-crafted mystery, is a lot of bloat in the story: Toby runs about talking to January and various ALH employees, Toby gets lost in the building, Toby drinks coffee, Toby tries to protect Quentin, Toby calls/tries to call Sylvester, etc. 
 I would be finished with the series here, if a lot of other readers didn't say the next book is a significant improvement. I still like the world and Toby herself.

Oh, I'll just pick this book up to have something to read while I eat dinner! SIX HOURS LATER: Welp, I guess I finished the book. 
 Yes, this book telegraphed its twists from miles away. I figured out what was up with Alex and Terrie the moment Terrie showed up, and I was pretty sure I knew how the murders had happened, even though I didn't know why. But this book still kept me up way past my bedtime reading it. It's like a bottle episode/locked-room mystery/horror movie, where the characters are all trapped in one place and you know one of them must be the killer, because they keep dying, one by one... 
 In the previous book, Toby was convinced she had very few friends, and it took a long time for her to realize that people cared about her. So the friendships in this book are particularly refreshing. I love her interactions with the Luidaeg, but the real treat is getting to spend more time with Quentin. I like that Toby doesn't pull any punches with him, letting him see exactly what her investigative work entails, even when it's horrific. He feels like her apprentice, and I hope later books expand on that relationship. 
 I think maybe the plot of this book would have worked better for me if I had never seen a certain Doctor Who episode, but the world of Faerie keeps getting more intriguing, and I'll definitely be picking up the next book in the series.

Reading this book was so infuriating. There are spoilers ahead so anyone interested in reading the book should stop now. As many people mentioned Toby is damn annoying, she sucks at being investigator of any kind. She makes so many mistakes, and she drives me crazy (you got angry when you learned HE TRIED TO SEDUCE YOU WITH MAGIC, killing people wasn't enough? She got angry when it got personal? I.. I'm just speechless). The thing is, she had potential, and it's sad to see it wasted, completely. I wasn't that into first book but it was okay, I thought it will get better. No, it didn't. I already read few reviews of following volumes and it's supposed to get better so I will try reading next few ones but this book was a serious blow to the series. There's something not letting me just throw it away and forget though. I dare guess this thing is actually Tybalt... Yeah, we OH SO DON'T suspect they will get together. Which worries me. Is she really as old as she's supposed to be? Her actions doesn't make any sense, her conversations doesn't make any sense. I don't understand why so many people love her so much. I'm disgusted by how she handles herself since her pond accident. Already forgot about her family, failing once again to protect the lives of people she was asked to protect. Way to go... Why do people trust her on this anyway? I see no logical reason for that, she doesn't seem to have any abilities making her useful. If she at least could fight with her magic, but no. Every time someone saves her ass and it gets to be Tybalt quite often. What does he sees in her? He seems to have hots for her from the very beginning. Capricious leader like him shouldn't just stalk out of pure malice...? Or am I too naive? Sigh, it hurts to see the world with so many interesting things and such crappy heroine. I do hope it will get better later on. For now I'm switching to books with heroines with more backbone.

The only reason I read this book is because I heard the third (and fourth) books are awesome. I read the first book, "Rosemary & Rue" a long time ago, at least two years ago, and was intrigued by the premise, delighted with Ms. McGuire's imagination, horrified by the shoddy world-building, and saddened by the lack of side character development... also annoyed at figuring out the mystery long before Toby did. When I read the reviews for the second book and saw many complaints about how clueless Toby is and how much of the book is spent meandering around in a knowe, I was not impressed. 
 But! I will do lots of things to get to a good book, including reading the crappy ones that come before it. So I went into this book with the knowledge that I was probably going to be frustrated with Toby's lack of investigative skills and lots of running around. That probably helped a lot, actually - otherwise this might have been a one star review. Which would be awful, because the worldbuilding is getting better and Ms. McGuire writes quite well. The multiple plot holes are big enough to run a truck through, the abrupt character changes with no explanation (only acknowledgement) are annoying, the events that were supposed to be horrific and moving were sappy and boring... yea. But it's ok! Because the next one is supposed to be better! 
 And if the Goodreads rating for the next book is inflated (due to the majority of people stopping with this book, because people were so relieved to read something actually interesting) I will be very upset.

I ended up enjoying this book a lot even with a few gripes. Like whether the author intended to hint about it or not, I knew who the killer was almost towards the beginning of the book. And in my opinion that was mean of the author to have Tybalt in the beginning and then he's gone until the end of the book. I wanted more Tybalt and less Connor. Meh. But anyways, this is definitely becoming and new favorite urban fantasy of mine. Both the characters and world building are excellent.

sample_reviews.review_text: Nicholas Sparks released a book about two teenagers who fall in love with each other despite their different personalities. A Walk to Remember was a book I never wanted to put down because of the all the emotions and descriptions. This romance novel made me think about real life and death.

Alweer een schrijver waarvan ik niet eerder een boek had gelezen. En opnieuw een goede kennismaking. Sparks schrijft levendig. Het is alsof hij het verhaal aan je staat te vertellen. Het speelt zich af in de Carolina's, SE USA. Ik hoorde ook het accent uit die streek. Alhoewel ik een boek met een te hoog "Lord" gehalte snel aan me voorbij laat gaan, stoorde het hier niet. Het past helemaal bij een van de hoofdpersonen. Door de opzet een verhaal dat vraagt om door te lezen. Tranen. Dat ook. Moet er bij zeggen dat ik daar snel last van heb. Goed geschreven.

This book is rather short but entertaining. 
 It's sweet and romantic and follows the same heartbreaking course that every Nicholas Sparks book seems to follow. Boy and girl meet. They fall in love. One of them dies. The other one lives on to see another day. 
 But it's the journey rather than the destination that's important. 
 I liked the characters of Landon and Jamie. And I liked how this book was set in the past - unlike the movie which was modern day.

I watched the movie years ago and cried like a baby. Even though I was conscious of the fact that everything in the movie was sculptured to emotionally manipulate me, I fell for it. Fortunately, the book did not have the same effect on me. Reading A Walk To Remember was like eating a whole tub of chocolate ice cream by yourself - it feels good while you do it, but after you just feel awful and annoyed with yourself. 
 A Walk To Remember is, without a doubt, the most emotionally manipulative book I have read to date. Which came as no surprise to me, because even though this is my first Nicholas Sparks book (and probably my last), I am very familiar with his criticisms - that he writes predictable, sappy, saccharine loves stories that will make you cry. (Please refer to this Cracked.com article written 5 years ago but remains relevant today.) 
 Allow me to elaborate on that last point: the problem with Sparks's novels isn't that his books make you cry, but it's the fact that he tries extremely hard to make you cry. There are topics that are inherently sensitive for many people, such as young love, love that is separated, terminal illnesses, unexpected accidents and tragedies, death and dying, and so on. 
 These issues are not off-limits, but given the nature of these topics, they should be written with sensitivity and with dignity. Sparks does neither; instead he unashamedly, unapologetically reminds you of the very tragic, very sad, very horrible circumstances of his characters. This is no exception in The Walk To Remember; all of his characters aren't human beings, they are accessories to further Sparks's goal to write his super sad stories. To drive my point home, this line is within the first chapter: 
 First you will smile, and then you will cry - don't say you haven't been warned. 
 Only writers who try to make you cry would ever say such a thing. Or just really bad writers. Or both. (Both.) 
 Needless to say, the writing left me speechless at times. If you're wondering what sort of speechless, consider these lines: 
 Wishing someone luck before a play is supposed to be bad luck. That's why everyone tells you to "break a leg". 
 Gee, Sparks. It's a little insulting to assume your target audience is incapable of understanding idioms that are prevalent within Western society and culture. 
 "It happened so fast, Mom, the car came out of nowhere. It just darted out in front of me, and I couldn't stop in time." Now, everyone knows cows don't exactly dart anywhere, but his mother believed him. She used to be a head cheerleader too, by the way. 
 What sort of insulting, stereotypical, sexist drivel is this? 
 ... I'd come to realize that drama was just the most boring class ever invented. 
 How is this man a bestselling author? No wonder people feel sad after reading his books; it's the end of good literature as we know it. 
 Rating: 1/5 
 - 
 Review can also be found on my book blog, Read, Think, Ponder!
