reference_books.review_text: Wow I really liked this book. There was more language in it than I prefer but otherwise I really enjoyed it. Typically you think about how hard Nazi Germany would have been on the Jews, but this really gave another perspective on how hard it would be to be German (with a conscience) in Nazi Germany. It was very sad, but how could a book set during WW2 not be sad? Definitely some great insight.

book_a.title: Life on the Refrigerator Door
book_a.user_review: Reeeally sad and a very quick read, but makes you appreciate your mom.

sample_reviews.review_text:
It was an interesting enough book, and a unique take on the epistolary novel form. I thought it was somewhat light on substance, however, but given the medium she chooses (fridge notes), that may have been intended (or unintended but unavoidable??). It was a reasonably good presentation of a sad event, but I was not moved to tears the way (perhaps) the author intended (and certainly other readers were). 
 My biggest complaint about the book is that I thought both the mother and daughter, though they obviously loved each other, were incredibly selfish individuals. Both put their work, school, friends, etc. before each other for the greater part of the novel, and when it finally REALLY WAS too late (the mother was dying), all of a sudden it becomes important to make each other a priority. Granted, the girl was 15, but still... She had a poor role model (in my opinion) for learning how to put loved ones before herself...mom certainly didn't.
Unusual construct, the premise is a mother and daughter leaving each other notes to tell the story. I enjoyed the story and the writing style.

read this book in a hour, it was written through a series of notes left on a refrigerator door, that are written between a teenage daughter and her mother. I liked the way the story was written, it is a tear jerker, so be sure and have a hankie handy!
It was a really quick read- I think it took me about an hour. I wish there was a little bit more to the notes at some points but overall I enjoyed it.

I've read a few other books in similar format (all done as correspondence via emails, letters, and in this book through refrigerator notes) and much preferred the others. I thought the subject matter was too heavy for notes on a refrigerator. It seemed really forced. It was a very quick read, but the quick nature made it hard for me to believe the relationships or feel any kind of connection or emotion.
Enjoy and love every time, every moment you have with your love ones.
Clever set-up, quick read, a bit melodramatic.

If you read any of my reviews you may know that I will be meeting this author next week for a one on one session for my English creative writing class, so I wanted to get familiar with her writing style and her books. I actually really liked this book. It was very interesting. The whole book was formed of letters which kind of reminded me of The Perks of Being A Wallflower. I had no idea what the story was gonna be about and when I found out it kind of shocked me, but in a way you could see it coming. The end was pretty predictable. But what I really enjoyed was the way Alice wrote the mother and Claire's characters. They reacted the way anyone in the real world would, real issues and decisions. It was a simple and light read yet a little emotional and intense.

I had mixed feelings about this one. I had a hard time not feeling frustrated with the mother. I have a teenage daughter and I cant imagine being so busy where I had to leave notes on everything from being dianosed with breast cancer to what boys she is dating. The mother was the won suffering with the cancer but I felt more sympathetic towards the daughter who I felt was neglected. The ending was very sad and it did bring tears to my eyes. The good thing about the book is it is a reminder to slow down and enjoy each day and the people that are in it despite how busy things get.
you can probably read this book in about 20-30 minutes easy. that said, it gets right to the truth of the matter and is a good reminder to slow down. a very clever style here.

book_b.title: The Walk (The Walk, #1)
book_b.user_review: I'd say 3.5 stars ... same formula as all his other books: devastating loss followed by lots of soul-searching. However, I enjoy reading his books because they are such a quick read and usually help me to reflect on what's important in life. So I'll probably read the sequel.

sample_reviews.review_text: Probably won't read the next in the series. He was great at description, but the story can't stand on that alone. I kept waiting for more substance to the plot...for the story to take me from here to there...but I just stayed in the same frame of mind. I thought he was a funny writer and I loved the name McKale. I wanted to punch Kyle...that little weasel! He was the best character! I liked it enough to finish and I appreciated that it was clean.

Easy, quick read. It is a compelling story, and he has some fabulous one liners but over all not a fan of the writing of the story. The first part of the book should have been way longer, in my opinion and the second half should have been way shorter. How you can cut out details about the love of a lifetime but then go into detail about each and every single thing this man eats for a week is mind boggling to me. However, do to the wonderful characters he is meeting along his journey and the life lessons they share I will most certainly be reading on to the next book.

I wanted to like this book for the simple reason that I heard Mr. Evans speak at the SC Book Festival, and he was such a nice person. I thought Alan and McKale deserving of pity but uninteresting. I wasn't surprised by Kyle's behavior. The people Alan meets on his walk are not especially interesting, either. It's the first in a series, and I own the set, but I doubt I'll bother to finish it.

I couldn't put this book down! Personally, having lived in the Seattle/Tacoma area of Washington and driven cross country to Key West, I felt a connection to this story from the very beginning. It was like a trip down memory lane for me since I actually know of several of the places he mentions. 
 The story is very well written and you can feel his pain. I actually started to cry while reading the book; I gave it to my husband to read. He said he had to stop reading it because he started to cry and didn't want to cry while he was at work. It is a very emotional journey of one man's struggle to escape his past while walking towards an unknown future. I can't wait to read the rest of this series!

I absolutely loved this! Not only can you relate to it because everyone experiences loss, but it also is humbling to see that everybody struggles with things and finding out things about life! It's a quick read and truly touches your heart!
Fast read, enjoyable story. Excited to read #2 in the series.

Alan Christoffersen is a former ad executive with the magical ability to walk for days without showering and somehow not stink up any of the tiny roadside diners he frequents, and a dead wife named after some kind of lettuce-y fast food sandwich. He traverses a fantastical land in which waitresses he met five minutes ago will come to his cheap motel room with free food and foot massages (ew), good people are all beautiful, mean people are all ugly, and every single person on the planet and their (unfailingly Christian) life experiences revolve around Al and his hat. 
 I didn't choose this book for myself, as you can probably imagine. But I promised a friend I'd finish it in order to expand my literary horizons, and so I did, with a new appreciation for the books I normally read and their wonderfully coherent plots. I can see why people get sick of traveling for work because if I have to read one more description of diner food or a crappy motel room, I will lose my mind. And to add insult to injury, the author has such a hard-on for his own trite aphorisms that he gives you bonus twee at the beginning of every single chapter. The only joy this book brings me is the knowledge that I won't be shelling out any money for the multitude of inexplicable sequels. Okay, and writing this review. That felt pretty good.
Nice story.

Another great book by Richard Paul Evans. All of his books that I have read so far have really been feel good books with great story lines and wonderful lessons! 
 This is a super quick read, and one that I think that most people would enjoy.

Like most of Evans' books this is a feel good (well except the part that you cry), inspirational (or superficially inspirational) novel. It was a quick read (1 day) and I enjoyed it. One part I did NOT enjoy was the fact that this is going to be a series book (which I didn't find out until the last page). Not because I won't read the series (because I really enjoyed the style and main character) but because I like to read series only after they are completed. 
 --------------------------------------- 
 I could have put many quotes here but I chose only one. 
 "We can spend our days bemoaning our losses, or we can grow from them. Ultimately the choice is ours. We can be victims of circumstance or masters of our own fate, but make no mistake, we cannot be both." 
 And although the main character seems to be becoming a master of his own fate, I do not necessarily approve of walking away from everything - like he does at the beginning of his journey. Yes, we would all like to walk away from the things that cause us pain but I think real people learn to face them.

reference_books.title: The Glass Castle
reference_books.review_text:
The book held my interest from the first page straight through to the end. But, like many reviewers, I struggled with issues of believability. The fact that she could remember conversations she'd heard when she was three years old - nuanced conversations she wouldn't have been able to understand even - left me with a skeptic's view of the rest of the book. 
 Even though she wasn't openly self-pitying, the very selection of memories that compose the collection seemed emotionally manipulative. The whole book seemed to scream "Look what happened to me, and look how stoic I've been. I need you to feel sorry for me since I'm above self-pity." 
 And I know that's not fair. It's not fair to any memoirist. But this was the book that made me see why I couldn't write memoir. I too would be exploiting my readers' emotions. 
 To the extent this book is true, she did have a childhood worthy of a book. I felt sorriest for her and her sibs when they lived with her grandmother. She really brought that woman to life, with the perpetual bottle of hooch in her apron pocket. Up until that point, I kept wanting the family to settle down, but when they got to that godforsaken place, I wanted them to do the skedaddle right out of there. Drove me crazy that that was the one place her parents couldn't leave.

reference_books.title: Icy Sparks
reference_books.review_text:
Appalachian orphan girl growing up with undiagnosed Tourette's Syndrome in the 1950s. 
 The first three-quarters of the book wasn't too bad, apart from the flagrant abuse of adverbs. But then (spoiler alert) she discovers religion. (Not just any old religion either, but the kind where tics, spasms, contortions and speaking in tongues is considered an asset.) 
 Hallelujah, praise the Lord, I got through this book!

reference_books.title: Unbroken: A World War II Story of Survival, Resilience, and Redemption
reference_books.review_text:
The first half of this book captivated me. It's quite the adventure story, and it's supposedly true. But eventually - somewhere in the Japanese POW camps - it started breaking down for me. It became repetitive, exaggerated and a bit too hero-worshippy. And the ending left me feeling manipulated, like I'd been brought here under false pretenses. How could this man, who had survived so much, finally be brought to his knees by [caution: spoiler alert] evangelist Billy Graham?? 
 Given the sheer number of endnotes and footnotes, I'm sure it was extensively researched. But it came across as somewhat propaganda-ish in places. The American soldiers were all so honourable, and the enemy was so despicable. Most of the characters came across as caricatures. And our hero? Louie Zamperini? I liked him very much in the first half of the book - by the end, I thought he was an egomaniac with an adoring biographer.

reference_books.title: The Elegance of the Hedgehog
reference_books.review_text:
I found it difficult to care about the protagonists, who were both such intellectual snobs and pretending to be less intelligent than they were, because omg what if someone were to find out that the concierge can read?? 
 The book annoyed me. I liked the title though.

reference_books.title: Complications: A Surgeon's Notes on an Imperfect Science
reference_books.review_text:
This is a collection of essays in the memoir genre, as opposed to a true memoir. It consists of interesting true tales from the world of medicine, and is written by a surgical resident. In some ways this book reminded me of some of Oliver Sachs' writing. The stories range from medical oddities to medical ethics and doctors gone bad. 
 Among other things, these stories explore the reality that people make mistakes and doctors are people so doctors make mistakes - and they're basically practicing on us. 
 Routine procedures are often not as routine as we might think, especially when the doctor is doing one of their first few of any particular surgery. Or when the doctor has become complacent and thinks they can do this surgery with their eyes closed. It occurred to me that I spent more time researching my plumber's qualifications and reputation than my doctor's. 
 Anyway, it was an interesting read, and well written. I have no idea where Gawande gets the time to write, being a doctor and the father of three little kids, but I'm glad he does.

book_a.title: Let's Pretend This Never Happened: A Mostly True Memoir
book_a.user_review:
This book would never have found a publisher if Jenny Lawson, AKA The Blogess, wasn't already a wildly popular blogger. 
 Her writing style and sense of humour work very well on her blog, where you consume it in 500-word doses. But I found her very difficult to take for 300 pages. She is at times screechy, manic, repetitive, rambly and tedious. 
 We all have inner dialogues, imaginings and random thoughts. But Lawson seems to believe that the unfiltered contents of her brain are endlessly amusing and worth preserving for posterity. The ones that aren't really detract from the ones that are. At times it felt like she was screaming "LOOK AT ME! I'M HILARIOUS!" 
 I read the whole thing because that's what I do. Even if a book irritates me, I finish it. (I blame Mrs. Stevenson, the librarian at my elementary school, who frowned upon unfinished library books.) 
 There were parts that I liked. For example, I did enjoy the metal chicken story (though I'd already read it on her blog). And I enjoyed the bonus chapter at the end. And there was the odd quieter chapter in the middle that worked. Overall, though? No.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** This book review, as well as many more, can also be found on my blog, The Baking Bookworm (www.thebakingbookworm.blogspot.ca). ** 
 My Review: I picked up this book recently from my local library right before a job interview. Trying to distract my nerves I sat there reading the book jacket I was quietly chuckling to myself and it honestly helped to reduce my nerves. I like funny reads. I do. But I also feel that they're really hard to write well. What is deemed "funny" means different things to different people and while I think that Jenny has a great sense of humour I don't necessarily think it came through well in this book. 
 There were some great, hilarious gems in this book but the overall feeling of chaos in her writing stifled those funny bits. It felt very disjointed -- like you were talking to a overly caffeinated person who would shoot out random stories that didn't necessarily have anything to do with each other. It often felt like she was just babbling and not caring about what she was talking about and after awhile that got frustrating. And don't get me started about the overused and excessively annoying footnotes! Gah! Enough already! I know you're funny Jenny! Show me! 
 Don't get me wrong, there were certain parts of stories where I did actually laugh out loud because Jenny is funny. But then she'd take too long to get to the end of the story and start to lose me. Or the story seemed much too unrealistic to be true and ... she'd start to lose me. Overall, I guess I just felt really lost. I read over half of the book before I finally called it quits because I just couldn't take any more of the rambling bedlam that is her memoire. 
 I think Jenny excels at writing funny little snippets (like on her blog, The Bloggess) but this full-fledged book didn't showcase her best comedic assets. With better editing and a more polished feel I think this could have been amazing. Unfortunately her frantic way of storytelling just isn't for me, I guess. I'll stick to reading her blog. 
 My Rating: 0 (didn't finish it)

The read was definitely a train-wreck. I good train wreck at times definitely, but a train-wreck nonetheless. The funny thing is that Jenny would probably take this as a compliment. It was great to hear Jenny's story and it gave so much honest perspective on the most interesting experiences. Throughout the book, I wondered if she would still be with her husband by the end. She must have guessed that because she addressed in the epilogue and made it clear that sometimes what people perceive as imperfection or "weird" is actually just a fraction of the silent majority's reality.
I bought it because Jen Lancaster wrote on her blog that it's funny. Meh. It was an ok, quick and easy read for a hot and lazy summer weekend but it did not make me laugh.

This is an incredible book. Its "laugh out loud while rolling on the floor" funny. The author is vulgar, opinionated and offensive, but she is never condescending to the reader. Her writing reminds me of Lewis Grizzard, who was a brilliant storyteller. 
 If you are offended by profanity or overt references to reproductive organs in contexts you would never dream of, stay away from the book. 
 If you want to read writing that is heartfelt and can make you laugh at things the would normally have you crying, this book is well worth the cost and time.
Hilarious. The author narrates herself and is very funny. Anyone looking for a light listen (but who is not offended by strong language) should try this.

I was unfamiliar with The Bloggess before this book started popping up in all the summer "Must Read" lists, but the buzz surrounding this one was enough to convince me to give Jenny Lawson a shot. In the end, I'm kind of underwhelmed. She started out strong; her childhood stories were flat-out hysterical. Reading about her father waking Jenny up with a puppet fashioned out of a dead squirrel had me laughing so hard I couldn't barely breathe. It's not necessarily new territory - the wacky parents are a staple of the humor memoir - but Lawson related the antics with a wry tone that killed me. 
 And then she grew up, and the stories became less funny than "Look at how weird I am, you guys. Ohmigosh, I'm so weird." Maybe I'm being a little cynical but once the perspective shifted to her life as a wife, mother, HR specialist and socially awkward blogger, I got bored. I didn't feel like there was anything particularly unique about Lawson's story and the tales of her arguments with her husband and her inability to moderate her anxiety as she met with other bloggers for a spa weekend weren't amusing. It struck me as someone trying too hard to be funny and quirky without any idea of the point she was trying to make.

Jenny Lawson is a blogger. This book consists of stories of her life. Her family did not have much money as she was growing up in Texas. She has an... unusual... father. She and her sister grew up with lots of animals around, wild and domestic, dead and alive (her father is a taxidermist). She suffers from social anxiety. Her husband's family has money and is quite different from her own, so she struggles a little bit to fit in with them. 
 I had no idea who she was, but I saw some good reviews for the book, so I thought I'd give it a try. I found this so funny! I laughed out loud plenty of times, and the one chapter that had me laughing so hard I was crying and it was hard to breathe, and I couldn't stop for some time, was the one that described the 5 foot tall metal chicken she brought home. In particular, it was her husband's reaction that got me going. It was the best 15th anniversary ever! Oh, and there are photos to go with the stories, so you know they really happened!

I couldn't/didn't finish this. Who ever said this was up there with Tina Fey and David Sedaris is smoking crack; or has never read either of them. She is in serious need of an editor. It's over written and she's trying way to hard which just made it terribly annoying. I'm baffled how this became a best seller.

If you want to laugh so hard you cry or pee your pants then this is your book. I have never in my life enjoyed a "funny" book as much as this one. It never bores you, or makes you wish you hadn't bought it. It was a hysterical, tear jerking, pee your pants, not for the faint at heart or the easily offended kind of person. I think Jenny and I are related somewhere in our family tree because this book made me think of my own family and childhood and makes me happy to see there are other families like mine. Be proud of yourself and your abnormal family and enjoy more than a wee chuckle.

Hysterically funny, laugh out loud hilarious!! 
 5 out of 5, no question! 
 Love her blog and her book was just wonderful...! 
 Rude, crass, un-explainable at times but truly wonderful.

book_b.title: The Hour I First Believed
book_b.user_review: Hmm. I didn't really care about his characters in this book, and the story lacked energy and momentum. I think it would have been better if he'd pared it down to 350 pages instead of 700+. He could have left out all that history thesis stuff, for example. Bottom line? It was okay...but certainly not his best work.

sample_reviews.review_text: Interesting and well written but longer than necessary and so very depressing.
The concept was great, but the book did not keep me interested. I read a number of beeks in between this book to keep sane.

Caelum Quirk's wife Maureen endures the Columbine school shooting while he's out of state because his beloved aunt has fallen ill. Maureen suffers an extreme case of PTSD which becomes chronic. To alleviate her misery, they move back to the Quirk farm in Connecticut. Maureen's troubles aren't over and Caelum involuntarily stumbles accross his family's literally buried secrets. 
 This book spans several years in Caelum's life and several generations of his family. It tries to cover most American ills: school shootings, hurricanes, the war in Iraq. It is simply too much, the story breaks under its own weight. Caelum never becomes the least bit sympathetic and his simperly wife manages to rise above "pathetic" just before she dies. After "I know this much is true", this is a disappointment. More like "she's come undone", another unpalatable book about mental illness by the same author. "The hour I first believed" would have been an excellent book if it had been less verbose, the topic narrower and if some emotional strings had been pulled. What is "art" in any form: sculpture, poetry or prose if it does not evoke emotion? Pointless.

Well he tackled on a lot. I think he had about three books in here at least. I can't say I enjoyed the meandering story lines and waiting for them to come together. Saw shades of other characters from another of his books to further gum up the plot. He brought in characters and then just dumped them and then made other characters important at the end that had little or nothing to do in the whole book. Too much going on for me.
just like his other book I reviewed, total waste of time. This one, I didn't even finish.

** spoiler alert ** 
 ebook. 
 i am somewhat disappointed in this book. perhaps that's why it took me so long to get through. after devouring I Know This Much Is True, i felt that this novel fell short of the amazing talent that Wally Lamb has exhibited in the past. 
 though Caelum's voice is admirably sharp and caustic, the story he tells leaves something to be desired. i honestly didn't appreciate the plotline of this story until about 300 pages in...when Maureen went to jail and the story of Caelum's ancestors began. 
 i do appreciate wally lamb's ability to weave in other texts which open up an entirely new storyline...he did it in I Know This Much Is True also...this time, through letters, diary entries and a Janis' paper, he reveals Caelum's ancestry and the mystery of who and where he comes from. 
 it was extremely difficult for me to find any redeeming qualities in Caulum's wife, Mo..and i found myself waiting until her story reached some sort of arc that would turn my feelings around. again, this didn't happen until well after the half-way point in the novel. i honestly disliked the entire Columbine aspect to this novel...finding it trite and actually rather boring. i actually found it disrespectful in a way...and i know he didn't intend that. 
 i also disliked the character of Velvet...finding no use for her in the storyline. i felt that the relationship that developed between she and Caelum so late in the novel was forced and rather unbelievable. her relationship with Maureen was just another reason why i disliked Mo in the story. again, i felt that the choices Mo made regarding Velvet were unrealistic and rather annoying. i can honestly say that the novel would not have suffered if Lamb had cut Velvet out of it all together. in fact, the pacing may have been a bit more readable. i felt like she was an unnecessary character. 
 the overlying theme of the novel...the absurdity and malevolence of violence....the quest for identity and redemption, the search for the meaning of life and misery were solid, and definitely well represented. i just didn't find the storytelling as compelling as i had hoped. 
 i wish i had just reread I Know This Much is True instead of fighting my way through this novel.

The book seemed to be a vehicle for the author to show-off his knowledge of such vastly different topics as the Civil War, mythology, and Post Traumatic Stress Disorder. 
 I skipped over large chunks of pages, mostly those involving letters from the narrator's great-great-great grandmother. I didn't miss anything by skipping those parts. Clearly, some parring down could have been done without risking the clarity of the story. 
 I found the narrator highly unlikable and his attempts at being a "tough guy" laughable. I also found it confusing to keep track of his family tree, especially when I found a few discrepancies throughout the book from one story to the next. 
 The use of questions to begin a paragraph was irritating, i.e. "Those first weeks? God, they were hideous." It was a tool used over and over again, I suppose to sound more conversational, but it just seemed unintelligent. 
 The concept was interesting, and the idea of stringing the story together with current events that we call all relate to (Columbine, 9/11, Hurricane Katrina) was interesting. The problem was, he was also trying to string the story together with about 10 other themes that didn't work or were just overkill.

I'm at a loss as to if I ended up liking this book or not. The language is terrible. The subject matter depressing. And it is really long. I got tired of reading the paper that Janis wrote about Caleum's ancestor. Boring. I didn't like all the adultery. It was well written, the author is a very good writer. But it wasn't a good book for me to read.
A LONG book that I wouldn't recommend but also would discourage someone from reading.

After reading the notes at the end of this book, I feel guilty about my negative feelings toward it... I wish I'd just read Wally Lamb's 10 pages of reflections and thank-yous and not read the 700+ pages of the book itself. I was fascinated by the Columbine plot and thought his characters were quite well-drawn. (Throughout the whole book, I kept remembering an insult the main character uses in the first few chapters of the book, that a woman on the phone's "voice sounded fat" -- given "She's Come Undone," I'm assuming Lamb did that very consciously. Caelum was supposed to be flawed and complicated but ultimately likable, and I'm not sure he ever got to that last one for me.) 
 Anyway, I stuck with Lamb through Columbine and Maureen's PTSD and the other subplots, but once he hit Hurricane Katrina, he lost me. He just gets so off-track with the dissertation proposal and academic paper at the end... it didn't ring true at all, and the ending was far too neat and tidy. Somehow, I couldn't stop reading this book, but I also couldn't wait for it to be over.

reference_books.title: The Second Life of Nick Mason (Nick Mason, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I would give this book a 3.5 rating...nearly a 4. It is a simply told, well written "sell your soul to the devil" story. To cut his very long prison sentence short, Nick Mason agrees to do whatever a fellow prisoner ( and a very powerful one) orders him to do when he gets out. I found it to be a very good read.

reference_books.title: Dead Simple (Roy Grace, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Although this was an "easy read" and doesn't particularly insult the reader's intelligence, it was still a rather predictable story. I bought this from a limited selection of books while away, and it passed the time and was bearable. It's about a stag night prank gone terribly wrong (the groom is buried alive as a "joke"...already they've lost me) and also major betrayals between the main characters. It does move right along, so for that reason, I'd give it a 2.5/5stars.

reference_books.title: Defending Jacob
reference_books.review_text:
I would give this book 3.5 stars. I thought it would be 4 stars as I found it to be real page-turner while reading it. But it was the ending that dragged it down for me. 
 I found it to be very reminiscent of Scott Turow's Presumed Innocent. The manner in which Andy Barber, father of accused murderer Jacob, narrates this story is sensitive and knowing (just like the narrator in Turow's book). We like our narrator, and want everything to turn out OK. I really did enjoy reading this book, and perhaps others would like or accept how it is resolved. 
 But I was left unsettled, as a reader, by the ending. Although we are led to believe it was probably Jacob who committed this murder and possibly another, we are not completely sure. And, to me, this is not a twist, it is just muddy water. I also didn't buy that the parents couldn't get the "truth" out of Jacob in a stronger way. And after that chilling report by the psychiatrist they hired for the defense, why not immediately get him some help after the trial was over?

reference_books.title: The Tourist (The Tourist, #1)
reference_books.review_text: This was a dry read for me. It had a twisty plot that seemed twisty just for the sake of being so. I found the plot incomprehensible and the characters very one-dimensional. I wouldn't read Steinhauer again. Though I'm admittedly not spy novel fan, I have read books in this genre that I've liked better

reference_books.title: The Lock Artist
reference_books.review_text: This novel has an interesting conceit...a mute young man who has a natural gift for opening locks is the protagonist. This gift leads him into dubious company, where various people want to use his gifts to complete their criminal heists. I found the two threads of the story somewhat confusing, as they are both set in different timelines with a lot of the same characters. I also found this shift back and forth an interruption and somewhat annoying. Michael's inability to speak also has a background story. I expected more from this novel due to the excellent reviews, and was left underwhelmed after reading it. I think I'd give it a 2.5/5 rating.

book_a.title: Live by Night (Coughlin, #2)
book_a.user_review: I thought the first half of this (overlong) book was quite good. The story is set during Prohibition, and tells of Joe Coughlin, son of a Boston police captain, who is following a life of crime. Joe ends up in prison, and some of the descriptions of his struggle to survive in there, and the depiction of his relationship with his father are quite good. But the second half of the book, which describes Joe's journey up the ladder of organized crime, became tedious, and dragged for me. I have enjoyed some of Dennis Lehane's other novels a great deal. But this novel was not one of them.

sample_reviews.review_text:
ARC received through the Goodreads First Reads program. 
 Dennis Lehane's Live By Night takes place during the prohibition era--through the latter half of the roaring Twenties into the Great Depression. The story chronicles the rise of Joe Coughlin through the criminal world as his career takes him from the streets of Boston to the high life in Tampa. at its core, this novel is about the politics and power at play in the shadows during a time when alcohol was illegal in this country. 
 The pages are peopled with people of all different stripes, from underworld kings to fugitive Cuban revolutionaries.The dialogue is very well-written, with each major character having a distinct voice. It is amazing how rarely this is pulled off in fiction, and I always greatly appreciate it when characters do indeed sound like different people! I have learned that this book is a sequel. It more than stands up on its own, but I think I will have to read The Given Day because I really really liked this story and I want more.
Sort of like reading Boardwalk Empire + Magic City. I had no idea this was the second in a three-part Coughlin family series, but it worked well as a standalone.

As much as I liked 'Live by Night' - and there's a cracking story here, expertly put together by a superb story-teller - I couldn't help thinking that I'd seen it all before. "Seen" is the operative word, as in this post-'Sopranos' age (and post-'Boardwalk Empire' age), there's a hell of a lot that's really familiar. I enjoyed the various ups and downs of the young, prohibition-era, Irish-American gangster at its centre, following his path from grim violent Boston to sunny violent Florida. But even though I enjoyed it, my thoughts found themselves wandering frequently to 'Scarface' or 'The Shawshank Redemption' or 'Carlito's Way' or 'The Roaring Twenties'. Okay, this is at the top-end, quality-wise, of gangster novels; but no matter how much I enjoyed it, all the plot points and characters beats I have already seen at least once at the movies and on television. And I guess that puts 'Live by Night' in an odd position, as the people who will want to read this are no doubt fans of the gangster genre, who will thus be frighteningly au fait with the ins and outs of tough guys in spats making threats. So although these people may enjoy it a lot, they'll probably come away thinking, like I did: "Entertaining read - but is there anything actually new here?"

I really liked this book. Not my favorite Dennis Lehane book, but still very good. Every time I read one of his books, I ask myself why I haven't read them ALL yet! My only real criticism would be that while I love gangster movies, I felt a little like Lehane was writing the book with the movie already in his mind. It seemed almost screenplay-ish. Otherwise, fun read.

Very disappointing sequel to The Given Day. More like a trip to the bank for Lehane rather than a serious effort. Written with an eye toward a movie sale - and a mediocre genre film at that. He's capable of good and interesting work when he feels like it.

I was really excited about this since I liked The Given Day so much. Unfortunately, this story follows the other brother, Joe, who ends up being a gangster. As it turns out, I enjoy (some) gangster movies but can't stand to read a book about gangsters. Now I know.

"I don't understand," Danny said softly. 
 "I know you don't," Joe said. "You, you buy into all this stuff about good guys and bad guys in the world. A loan shark breaks a guy's leg for not paying his debt, a banker throws a guy out of his home for the same reason, and you think there's a difference, like the banker's just doing his job but the loan shark's a criminal. I like the loan shark because he doesn't pretend to be anything else, and I think the banker should be sitting where I'm sitting right now. I'm not going to live some life where I pay my fucking taxes and fetch the boss a lemonade at the company picnic and buy life insurance. Get older, get fatter, so I can join a men's club in Back Bay, smoke cigars with a bunch of assholes in a back room somewhere, talk about my squash game and my kid's grades. Die at my desk, and they'll already have scraped my name off the office door before the dirt's hit the coffin." 
 "But that's life," Danny said. 
 "That's A life. You want to play by their rules? Go ahead. But I say their rules are bullshit. I say there are no rules but the ones a man makes for himself." 
 Little Joe Coughlin is all grown-up in this sequel to The Given Day. He has grown up to become a criminal. He calls himself an outlaw, but everyone else calls him a gangster. In Prohibition America, it's a good time to be a rum-runner. 
 You've got everything in here: love, sex, murder, back-stabbing, double-crossing, betrayal, despair, hope, and lots and lots of money. 
 Lehane is a great writer. I mean, I'm not going to screw around and try to pretend that Lehane is anything less than a great writer. Sometimes you see this in his long passages: 
 ...and he wondered what his father could see right now and what Emma could see. Could they see him? Could they see the past and the future or vast worlds far beyond his imaginings? Or could they see nothing? Because they were nothing. They were dead, they were dust, bones in a box and Emma's not even attached. 
 He feared this was all there was. Didn't just fear it. Sitting in that ridiculous chair, looking out the window at the yellow windows canted in the black water, he knew it. You didn't die and go to a better place; this was the better place because you weren't dead. Heaven wasn't in the clouds; it was the air in your lungs. 
 Sometimes he hits you with little short passages: 
 The sun flung itself against the windshield and breathed fire through the glass. 
 Either way, what I'm saying is that I am not debating Lehane's status as a master of his craft. 
 But I do want to address some things. 
 One, if you want to write romance or erotica, just do it. There ain't no shame in it! Lehane is joining my ever growing list of male authors who on some level desperately want to write romance novels or perhaps erotica novellas, but can't bring themselves to do it. (Paolo Bacigalupi is another one.) 
 A woman had been serving drinks to the table. She put the tray aside, lifted her cigarette out of an ashtray and took a drag, looked about to yawn with three guns pointed at her. Like she might ask to see something more impressive for an encore. 
 The entire first part of the novel, in which Joe holds up a poker game and meets a firebrand of a woman, is like reading an erotica in itself. 
 Joe said, "Everyone but the girl, get on your knees."... 
 He took the sack and dangled the set of cuffs from his finger. "Turn around." 
 "Yes, sir. Right away, sir." She turned her back to him and crossed her arms behind her. Her knuckles pressed against the small of her back, the fingertips dangling over her ass, Joe realizing the last thing he should be doing was concentrating on anyone's ass, period. 
 He snapped the first cuff around her wrist. "I'll be gentle." 
 "Don't put yourself out on my account." She looked back over her shoulder at him. "Just try not to leave marks." 
 Jesus. 
 "What's your name?" 
 "Emma Gould," she said. "What's yours?" 
 "Wanted." 
 "By all the girls or just the law?" 
 I mean, sheesh. I'm not complaining, but considering the way the rest of the novel goes, I can tell Mr. Lehane has a lot to say on the topics of romance and sex and I want to inform him that if he wants to stretch his legs a bit in a less confining space than historical fiction, the gates of romance and erotica are wide open to him. :) 
 When Joe tracks her down to a bar weeks later, 
 "If I tug this earlobe? You won't make the stairs." 
 He looked at the earlobe she'd indicated with a flick of her pale eyes. The right one. It looked like a chickpea, but softer. He wondered what it would taste like first thing in the morning. 
 There's a really adorable part later in the book where Joe teaches himself how to give his woman oral sex and it's very cute and sweet. His insistence on eating her out five times a day is what eventually leads her to admit that she's in love with him, which is highly probable and realistic in this reader's opinion, LOL. Lehane should start penning romantic fiction as soon as is physically possible, IMO. 
 Lehane also uses the historical context to examine racism a lot, as he did in The Given Day. 
 Albert leaned into Joe. He looked around them. "I don't want this. Who wants THIS? I just want to feel like I felt when I made her laugh of when she threw an ashtray at my head. I don't even care about the fucking, I just want to watch her drink coffee in a hotel bathrobe. You HAVE that, I hear. With the spic woman?" 
 "Yeah," Joe said, "I do." 
 "What is she by the way? Nigger or spic?" 
 "Both," said Joe. 
 "And that doesn't bother you?" 
 "Albert," Joe said, "why on earth would that bother me?" 
 Joe is not exactly a "good guy," but he's pretty good for a mob boss. And we know that because he loves and respects his women, he isn't a racist, and he doesn't murder innocents. 
 He'd killed for this woman. Killed for himself too. But if there was one question he hadn't been able to answer all day, it was why he'd shot the sailor in the face. You didn't do that to a man unless you were angry. You shot him in the chest. But Joe had blown his face up. That was personal. And that, he realized as he lost himself in the sway of her, was because he'd seen clearly in the sailor's eyes that the man held Graciela in contempt. Because she was brown, raping her wasn't a sin; it was just indulging in the spoils of war. Whether she'd been alive or dead when he did it would have made little difference to Cyrus. 
 Joe is very attracted to strong, hard women. I rather enjoyed the relationships he had in this book. It's strange (or perhaps not so strange) that Joe adores dangerous, kickass women when his own mother was such a chickenshit coward. From Emma, who gets sexually excited from him pulling a gun on her, to Graciela - a spitfire Cuban revolutionary who knows her way around guns and bombs, Joe always admires and lusts after and eventually loves the most strong-headed, dangerous, and forceful women he can find. I thought this was very realistic and never questioned why Joe was falling in love with whomever he was falling in love with at the time. Lehane NEVER made me beat my head against a wall questioning WHY Joe was being such an idiot and questioning his good sense and/or his taste in women. Another reason Lehane should go into romance novels, IMO. 
 That being said, there are missteps occasionally: 
 At the bar, Joe sat down at the end closest to the door, where a woman with fat that hung off her arms like pregnant bellies... 
 Lehane is either ignorant of women's arm fat or he's ignorant of what pregnant bellies are like because these two things are COMPLETELY different. But laughable lines like this are rare. 
 Another problem I have with Lehane is the same problem I end up having with another excellent author, Joe Abercrombie, which is that both men are convinced that the world is populated with pieces of shit instead of human beings. Both men have a rather dark and grim view of life and humanity, which - true or not - is not something I enjoy in my fiction. Bad things are going to happen in Lehane's books. Very bad things. Now, whether you are okay with this or not is up to you. Obviously, I finished it, which tells you that there is no graphic on-page rape or graphic on-page torture in this (plenty off-page, though), but don't think that means this book isn't grim. It's grim. And unlike his first book in this trilogy, The Given Day, this doesn't leave us on a hopeful note. Therefore I cannot give it the five stars that Lehane's writing deserves from a technical standpoint. I'm not into grim. 
 Tl;dr - I would treat you to more beautiful writing, but I don't want to spoil you on any key plot points. I just want to let you know that this is an excellent book. Playing masterfully on very dark themes, Lehane brings alive Boston 1926-1929, Florida 1929- 1933, and Cuba 1934 - 1935. It's wonderful, it's vivid, and Lehane's talents are in full-force here. He doesn't turn away from the darkness of criminal life, however, so proceed with caution. Highly recommended after you've finished The Given Day. This IS a sequel, I would advise reading and enjoying the amazing The Given Day first.
guess I wasn't in the mood for a gangster story

Dennis Lehane has long been on my list of authors I really should try, given the near universal praise for his work and many recommendations from my friends here on Goodreads. But I've been a little afraid to do so at the same time, for fear he might be a little too "literary" for my usual fare. After all, if the critics like him so much, his work must be "engagingly profound" or "both disarmingly poetic and serious" or just pick your own over-the-top cover blurb. So when I had the chance to read an advanced copy, I decided to take the plunge. 
 In short, this novel was serious fun. No doubt it will win critical praise as it does have all those things that make for a well-written novel: in depth characterization, nice pacing, strong themes, an unpredictable plot, etc. But while I recognize the abilities of a great writer here, that is all overcome by becoming lost in a great read. That's when I know I'm really on to something. It's like watching a baseball game, when you're not even a baseball fan, and getting lost in the drama of a tie game in the bottom of the ninth. You lose sight of the professional skill of the players and simply get swallowed up by the moment itself. 
 This novel stands alone and can be completely enjoyed on its own. However, I understand it shares some characters with Lehane's novel. "The Given Day". In particular, this novel's protagonist is Joe Coughlin, the brother of The Given Day's protagonist, Danny Coughlin. This novel is essentially, a gangster novel, although Joe prefers the term "outlaw" to gangster. It takes place during the rise of the organized crime era at the start of prohibition and runs through the mid-1930s. But, as opposed to most gangster novels you might run across, this does not take place in Chicago or New York but rather begins in Boston and moves to Tampa, Florida and even Cuba. Rum is the source of the action through most of the novel. We get to follow Joe's rise through the world of crime but I can't give many details for fear of spoilers. Rest assured, there is lots of violence, much of it coming as a complete surprise. The characters are multi-dimensional, not just the hard-edged men but the women they interact with. And the settings...just fantastic, each one almost another major character. 
 So yes, I am so glad to have finally taken the Lehane plunge. I plan to go back and read all of his previous work, starting with "The Given Day" and hoping for another companion novel with the third son as the protagonist. Highly recommended.

book_b.title: And When She Was Good
book_b.user_review: I have never read anything by Laura Lippman, and was pleasantly surprised to find what a clear, intelligent writer she is. This is more of a character-built novel than a mystery or suspense one. It is kind of static, and in that rather still, plodding way, Lippman does let us know a lot about her main character, Heloise Lewis (nee Helen). Heloise is a madame, and she is raising her young son in a suburban area, keeping her background and her occupation a secret. Some of this is believable, some of it stretches the imagination a bit. But Heloise is a pretty well-fleshed out character, and I liked the first half of this book. I felt it started dragging a bit during the second half, and I kept waiting for it to pick up and become somewhat suspenseful. Although that does not really happen, I kind of liked the way Lippman ties up the ending,even though I stongly suspected the character who causes the turn of events at the end.

sample_reviews.review_text: I usually love Laura Lippmann's books. This one didn't work well for me for two reasons: I did not find myself able to develop sympathy for the protagonist, and I found the ending too contrived and almost by-the-numbers in execution. The protagonist is a single mother who is also a madam running her prostitution ring from her home in an upscale suburban neighbourhood. Given that Lippmann has written many novels with characters who are not automatically sympathetic, I'd expect that she could create someone whose life choices and outlook would be compelling, but from the start of the book, she just left me cold. Usually, I tear through mysteries, but I wasn't invested enough in this character to reach for the book very often. Lippmann is as always a competent writer, but this one doesn't work for me.
Bizarrely uninvolving, from a usually very engaging author. What a shame!

Got through disc 3 of this on CD and just didn't have any desire to start disc 4. I have really enjoyed the other Lippman books I've read, but this one is just not interesting enough for me. I need more bite and intrigue and action.

This book is kind of difficult to categorize. I enjoyed the read and Lippman's writing is always eloquent, but I kept wondering what kind of a story it was. I had a hard time sympathizing with the character of a modern madam, and the suspense element didn't come into play until the last half of the book. I enjoy Laura Lippman's books enough that I will always read them, but this was not my favorite. I miss her mystery series.

This was a waste of time! I listened to the audio at work and that is the only reason I finished this one! It was more like a bad first draft. It jumped all over the place. I didn't feel anything for any of the characters.

"SUBURBAN MADAM DEAD IN APPARENT SUICIDE." 
 With this startling opening line, we are plunged into the world of Heloise. A world of secrets, fear, a son to protect, and a long history that led to this place in her life. 
 Once upon a time she was Helen with a "nothing face." Or so that's what her father told her. His verbal abuse set her up for a whole chain of events leading to this moment, this life. 
 Narrated in alternate chapters in the voices of "Heloise" and "Helen," "And When She Was Good: A Novel" held my interest from the first page to the end. Just when I thought I knew what would happen next, Lippman would surprise me. 
 How can one feel such a strong connection to a character like Helen/Heloise? Certainly many might argue that Helen made wrong choices and kept making them until it was too late. But is there a chance for someone like Heloise to redeem herself? Can we feel for her plight? 
 I certainly did, because the author reveals the inner thoughts of a woman who, like all women, has felt the pain of betrayal and the insecurity of not belonging. A woman who feels the need to be in control when life doesn't often offer the opportunity to control things. 
 This was definitely a story about finding oneself and learning from the past. It's a story about forgiveness and second chances. It is unforgettable, and thus earned five stars from me.

Lippman presents an interesting story about a "madam" and how she became a madam. The story does not go into vivid description of the murder scenes, or into Helen/Heloise's fall from grace. The story follows Helen's life in all the sadness and triumph. The story misses the depth of degradation and hopelessness that is shown in the books of Tess Gerritsen. Lippmann presents a Technicolor movie version minus the grit.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I was unsure as to whether I would finish this book. On the one hand, the Internet absolutely raves about this series and I've heard very few bad things, but on the other hand, the first half of this book was just such a typical "special-snowflake-boarding-school" type of story - complete with our female lead slobbering all over some unattainably hot magical man and discovering her "true" super magically hot self after accepting her powers. All of that being said, though, the last third-or-so of this book really redeemed it and I am looking forward to reading the second. 
 Unfortunately, I'll be starting off on a negative note because the first good chunk of this book was so boring and annoying to me. Alina Starkov is a petulant child; an orphan, yes, but a petulant child all the same. She complains about everyyythinnngggg and is always in a sourpuss mood - which can be super-interesting for a character, but even when she's found to be a special snowwwflaaaake and Alina's living conditions skyrocket she still can't admit that it's not so bad being Grisha. She also falls head-over-heels for the most powerful Grisha (the Darkling) and even though she loves to point out to the reader how plain she is and how she doesn't deserve anything because she's so hiiiiideeeeouussssss, she never wonders why he falls for her so completely and so quickly. This annoyed me. Greatly. Their makeout scene in the castle made me just about roll my eyes out of my head. 
 Alina also had a fixation on beauty that was about to grate on my last nerve. The author works as a makeup artist (as per the author's blurb on the back flap) and, being a connoisseur of beauty enhancements myself, I was interested as to how she would weave beauty in with her story - especially after Alina mentioned her supposed plainness the first few times. There was a scene with Genya the magical makeup-makeover-artist that impressed me; where she explained to Alina that her makeover powers were temporary and didn't need to be abused to make people lovely. But Alinaaaaa omggggggg. There is more to a person than how beautiful they/you areeeeeeeee. Well, let me amend that statement: there is more to women than how beautiful they/you areeeeeee. Because Alina only ever commented on beauty when it had to do with women or the Darkling. Also Alina's only reason as to why she couldn't be a special-snowflake Grisha wasn't that she didn't have magical powers it was because omgggggg she's not prettyyyyyyyyyyyy. 
 Also also the prettiest Grisha, Zoya, was the bitchiest Grisha. Of course she was. 
 Let's move on to when I started to enjoy this story: PLOT TWIST TIME. 
 It wasn't one of those plot twists that made me go "OMG HOW DID I NEVER SEE THAT COMING MIND BLOWN OMGGGG", but it was more of "Omg I'm really glad the author also thought of this twist now everything is less annoying thank you". The Darkling is a manipulative, ruthless, greedy, power-hungry dick. Yes. Thank you, Leigh Bardugo. Thank you. This makes everything so much more interesting and makes the annoying parts relevant - the Darkling fooled Alina in to thinking that he cared for her, and as we are seeing this unfold through her POV we also believed him. 
 I also really liked Alina's childhood friend Mal and his confession of love to her. 
 One more flaw before I go, because it needs to be mentioned: even with my extremely limited knowledge of Russian culture and language, I could notice some blatant flaws in the author's interpretation of things like character names and especially kvas. And with a simple Google search I easily was able to double-check the rest of the cultural terms. So that was pretty irksome for me - I can only imagine how a Russian reader would feel! 
 I will continue with this series.

Catching Fire is the second installment of the Hunger Games trilogy. 
 An action-packed book. This book showcased the nation of Panem under the cruel hands of the Capitol through the eyes of sixteen-year old Katniss Everdeen, who after winning the 74th Hunger Games together with fellow tribute Peeta Mellark, found herself inside the Games once more for the Quarter Quell (75th Hunger Games).

The book took a deeper look on existing characters for book one, particularly Gale whose relationship with Katniss became clearer throughout the plot, and also present new characters which are as fascinating as the ones on the first installment. Excellent second book-- it flew by for me, and I honestly didn't see many of the plot twists coming. I have to admit that the end baffled me.... I was there before I realized it-- and with so many questions (as I'm sure Collins would have hoped!). All I can say is that I'm really glad I'm reading these AFTER all three have been published. If I had to wait for Mockingjay to be released, I would be ticked off! 
 Having said all this... let me address it from my "teacher hat" standpoint. I began reading these books because I teach some 10 year-olds who were reading them. After The Hunger Games, I could honestly say that I felt some of those kids could handle the book IF they had an adult to discuss it with. I don't keep the books in my classroom library, because I believe they honestly need to be something a parent makes a decision about for kids the ages I teach. I would have to say that this second book was darker, more violent, and harder to stomach-- and I really would NOT recommend it for the kids in my school. Middle school age seems to be about right for these books, and if a parent of one of my 4th or 5th graders asked my opinion, I think I'd suggest they try to hold out for at least another year....
Thus far my favorite, though there are only 3 books and I've only read 2. But I really enjoyed Catching Fire.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This was a brilliant book, exciting and imaginative. I have thoroughly enjoyed reading this book and look forward to reading more books in the series. 
 The main character is Ceony, an apprentice magician hoping to become a smelder but instead gets a placement as a folder. She doesn't have the highest of hope for her apprenticeship with Magician Thane, but enjoys the basic tasks that she does to start off on her path as a folder. But then a magician comes back into the life of magician Thane, stealing his heart and trying to use it for bad. Ceony sets off to get it back entering Thane's heart and learning more about him. 
 The most noteworthy secondary character is Magician Thane, he's a paper magician and Ceony's mentor while she learns the craft. We learn a lot more about this character than we normally would with a secondary character and that is because of Ceony's journey through his heart. 
 The storyline was original and excitingly imaginitive, honestly I wouldn't mind being a folder because the imagery of that house. The pacing was good and I look forward to reading more books in the series to see where the characters go next. 
 4 stars a great book

The Paper Magician is a whimsical fantasy set in Victorian London that features a delightful and creative magic system, a strong female heroine and a little touch of romance. 
 The magic system is established within the very first chapter. Magic can only manipulate man-made objects, like glass, paper, metal, and rubber. A magician must 'bond' to a certain type of object and then are able to manipulate it in a variety of different, interesting ways. It was such a treat to read about the different ways magicians manipulated paper. Two of my favorites were when Ceony learned how to make a scene from a book come to life just from reading aloud and when Magician Thane animated a little paper dog for Ceony that acted just like a real one. Ceony called him 'Fennel' and he became one of my favorite characters in this series. 
 I wasn't just fond of Fennel, though. I love the main character, Ceony, and you know why? Because she is a strong female character who is able to think for herself and take action - while remaining feminine! Ceony has many traditionally feminine traits like modesty, a sense of decorum, and she knows her way around the kitchen. Yet, she is still able to speak her mind and rescue the guy in the end by relying on her wits and her gut instinct. This is so refreshing to see because sometimes I feel like too many people who write strong female characters (both in books and on screen) think that strength = masculine so they just give a female character masculine traits and call it a day. It's the 'Dude in a Dress' trope and it's getting a little tiresome. So I love that Ceony is an example of a strong, yet feminine, female character. 
 The plot was interesting and moved along at a rapid pace (which is understandable considering the book is only 222 pages.) I liked the developing relationship between Thane and Ceony. I, personally, love student-teacher romances although the one in The Paper Magician is very chaste indeed. There's only a small hint of a romance developing later in the series. No kissing, no nothing - which is totally fine as it suited the story. 
 The Paper Magician is great for readers of all ages looking for a light, whimsical fantasy.

This book was very fast paced and moved quickly. I have some caveats. There were times when I was uncertain about the time period and level of technology. There was some world building that was missed because most of the novel is concentrated on the action sequences. Also, I have some knee jerk reactions to some of the things the heroine does and her suddenly falling in love with the hero, who we know little about.
This book had all of the ingredients I love - magic, a female heroine, a historical bent, a mystery - but it just never grabbed my attention and I ended up abandoning it halfway through.
The relationships were unrealistic. The characters were flat. The concept was interesting but it just didn't go anywhere.

DNF. 
 Wanted to like it, but couldn't get into it at all. I found the descriptions really bogged the book down. I didn't mind that it wasn't historical accurate in any way, but the attempt to make it both modern and not really wasn't meshing for me. 
 Really disappointed that I didn't like it, because the idea was really cool.

I was very excited for The Paper Magician and highly disappointed. 
 I will start off by saying that the concept and a few explanations of the magic in the book were exactly what I was hoping for (paper magicians can animate images from stories mid-air, genius!) and I enjoyed these aspects of the story. I was hoping the first book, knowing the novel was the first in a series, would focus more on the different types of magic and the history behind this universe, as well as how the magic shaped it, before moving on to a far-fetched adventure. There was not nearly enough background to the story. 
 When it comes to the "action" in this novel I strongly disliked the turn the story took. First and foremost, I did not like that the memories, hopes, dreams, regrets, etc. were actually "located" in the magician's physical heart. There is too much overlap between the anatomical description of the heart earlier in the novel and where memories are stored, I thought it took away from what could have been a great concept of being inside someone's mind or thoughts. I also did not enjoy the descriptions of the heart as a muscle: Ceony moving through the valves was much too bizarre and graphic. 
 Again, as I was excited by the concept, I was disappointed by the poor writing. First, the author uses descriptions that are much too overdramatic and take away from the image she is trying to portray. She descriptions the main character feeling like a moment was "raking her brain with needles" - too much! This is just physically painful and does not really conjure an image of emotional pain or anxiety. Second, in a scene where the male magician is protecting a female magician from the police so she is not jailed the author says "he couldn't even deny her a prison cell" when in fact he made sure she did NOT go to prison as she was trying to avoid it. The author's sentence would make since if the female magician had WANTED to go to prison and the male magician had allowed it, knowing it wasn't a good idea. The fact that this story was published with an error like this is concerning. 
 Overall, interesting concept but poorly excuted.

sample_reviews.review_text: Short read about a Pakistani man relating to an American his time in the US before & after 911. I enjoyed it because it moved fast and told how his outlook was changed because of the event.
Although i was a bit confused at the end but still I loved this book <3, Mohsin Hamid is truly a blessed writer!

I'd heard good things about this book and it was a very quick read. I liked it quite a bit- it offers a perspective that I hadn't considered and which will resonate in my mind for awhile. The way in which it was told- a Pakistani man sharing a meal with an American in Lahore without ever knowing who the American is or getting his story- was compelling and intriguing. I have a growing interest in reading non-American authors and this was a good book.

Unbelievable writing. It was so tense and easy to fall into (I read it in 3 days) but still explored complex ideas- phenomenal. 
 The Ups: This book has pushed at so many boundaries of the novel form and I loved it. The entire story is one side of a conversation between Changez, a Pakistani man who studied and worked in America, and an unnamed American veteran visiting Pakistan. We hear everything Changez is saying as he tells his story, and even though that could be boring or unrealistic, it is compelling and reveals so much about both characters- it's incredible. 
 Changez's voice is so distinct and perfectly maintained throughout the course of the book- which is quite short, 175 pages- that whenever he referenced another character's speech, I could actually hear another voice speaking the words because the voices were so well-characterized. Changez has a formal and polite way of speaking that hints at his foreignness, but his sophistication doesn't bore the reader. His life could also seem boring or over-dramatized, but he discloses just enough emotion explicitly and implicitly to create so much tension and suspense. 
 He also sometimes feels like an unreliable narrator, and acknowledges this in his interaction with the American. He says things like, "I see you don't believe me," or "You, sir...seem ready to bolt." There is a clear barrier between the two men and the subtle suspicion escalates, following the change in Changez's story. 
 The slow change that Changez's world and emotional state goes through after September 11th is depicted extraordinarily. Slowly as the nation he lives in (America) and its people treat him and his country differently, he begins to feel more alienated and feels called back to his native country. After more thought and after leaving a place that has caused him a lot of success but also a lot of discomfort and hurt, Changez returns to Pakistan. He finds himself becoming increasingly critical of America and its exploitation of the rest of the world for its own success. He speaks openly against American policies- he has never wanted to become, or fitted into the mold for, a fundamentalist, but finds himself changing in response to the world's treatment of his country. 
 It is amazing how succinct the prose is, and how much it covers and expresses. There is a simultaneous calling to America and its promises and dreams alongside a revulsion of its imposing "superiority" and ignorance. As an immigrant myself, I greatly enjoyed the depiction of Changez's dilemma and difficulty with identity. 
 The Downs: I was a little detached to the romantic relationship with Erica. I do see how it contributed to Changez's overall experience with America and how her denial and appeal was almost a metaphor of America in general to him. Nevertheless, I wasn't very invested in the actual relationship and didn't feel its importance. Maybe that was the point, though. 
 Overall: An amazingly written, brief novel exploring one man's transformation in a hostile America.

Yes, despicable as it may sound, my initial reaction was to be remarkably pleased......I was caught up in the symbolism of it all, the fact that someone had so visibly brought America to her knees."

I picked up this book under somewhat false pretenses. It's currently being packaged as a five book series, of what would ostensibly be new novellas by Ian McEwan. So, you could imagine my surprise when I learned that this was actually Mr. McEwan's first novel, which is now being repackaged and sold with his other older books as a result of his current success. Apparently, someone also went and made a movie out of this book a while back. Go figure. 
 On one hand, having read a number of Mr. McEwan's more recent books, it was interesting to view his origins as a writer. The writing style of The Cement Garden is a bit more straight forward, and a bit less flowery and affected, than that included in say Atonement, The Children's Act or Saturday. And yet, I enjoyed all of those books to varying extents, and really just can't recommend this one. 
 Having read the reviews, I knew a bit about what I was getting into here. The death, the sadness, the dysfunction, the incest. This was by no means touted as a "feel-good" story. What I didn't count on was how unpleasant the book was to read. All of the characters were just so distinctly unlikable. Jack, the narrator, is selfish, antisocial, and aggressively unhygienic (i.e. he refuses to shower for three-quarters of the book). Julie is a manipulative, self-absorbed siren. Her boyfriend Derek is a total douchebag. Even little Tommy is a whiny needy, possibly severely troubled, child. Neither of the deceased parents seemed particularly likeable either, in their cameo roles at the start of the novel. I think I actually would have been less bothered by the incest aspect of the story, if I could understand at all why any of these characters would want to spend more than a few minutes with one another, let alone sleep together. 
 And don't get me started on the smells that pervaded this book. So much of the book's 154-page run time was focused on bad stenches: Jack's body odor, rotting food, decaying bodies, a house fallen into disrepair. I get the idea that this was meant to be a Lord of the Flies type story, where the characters went "wild" without parental supervision. But the characters in Lord of the Flies were no older than 12 and 13. Jack and Julie are in their mid to late teens and should have known better. 
 I don't know. Looking at some of the other more positive reviews of this novel, maybe I'm in the minority here. And I'd still recommend Ian McEwan's other writing to anyone interested in a solid, well-crafted read. I may even try some other novels in this five-book series. But this one was a thumbs down for me.

So before writing it off altogether I decided to skip around and see how it was written. Oh My Goodness! I was absolutely astonished at this man's talent! I read the book in 2 sittings. His writing manages to cut out all the fluff that most authors seem privy too. He goes writing comes across as honest, he cuts right to the point and draws and very poignant picture in the process. He gives so much depth to the characters and does an amazing job at making this tough subject palpable. I also respected him for not romanticizing this situation which I feel that many authors do. 
 I can't get over what he did with such an unsavory stroy but I must admit I think I enjoyed how he wrote it more then the story itself. I am still absolutely in awe! I will be searching out more of his work based on his ability alone, topic be damned!
