In November last year, as I walked by the British Library, my eyes were drawn to a large poster advertising an exhibition entitled Terror and Wonder: The Gothic imagination. I first discovered Gothic literature as a teenager when I read French writer Jules Verne's novel The Carpathian casle, and like many other readers, I quickly fell in love with the sublime scenery and the dark mysteries of medieval castles perched atop lonely and perilous mountains that are so frequent in Gothic fiction (and for those of you who might not know it, the Transylvanian castle in Jules Vernes' novel actually served as the model of Dracula's castle in Bram Stoker's novel). Since then, I have read a few other books belonging to this particular genre, and become quite a fan of Gothic, so the poster at the British Library immediately roused my interest. 
 In November last year, as I walked by the British Library, my eyes were drawn to a large poster advertising an exhibition entitled 
 The exhibition started with The Castle of Otranto, the novel which is generally considered as the precursor of the Gothic literary genre. Originally published in 1764 under the guise of a translation of an old Italian text printed at Naples in 1529, and supposedly discovered in the library of "an ancient Catholic family in the north of England", the novel is set in the Middle Ages and tells the story of Manfred, prince of Otranto. Hoping to avert an ancient prophecy according to which his dynasty would come to an end, Manfred plans to marry his son Conrad, heir to the house of Otranto, to Isabel, the daughter of the marquis of Vicenza. However, on the day of the wedding, his son is mysteriously crushed to death beneath a gigantic helmet adorned with black feathers. The vile , cruel and scheming Manfred accuses a young peasant of having murdered his son, and he determines to divorce his current wife Hippolita and marry his son's bride himself to perpetuate his bloodline. This unnatural union is cursed, and soon a series of supernatural omens threaten the doomed marriage... 
 I enjoyed reading this eigtheenth-century classic because it helped me understand the origin of the tropes of Gothic fiction: the settings, which usually include ancient medieval castles or houses standing in a remote and desolate landscape with an uncanny and supernatural feeling; the characters, which typically involve a confrontation between a vulnerable virgin and an obscene, aristocratic patriarchal figure full of lust; and finally the dominant theme of a male sexual desire perceived as overwhelming and threatening, from which the heroin must flee to save her life, and which ultimately destabilizes the world order and causes a tragedy that was announced by disruptive supernatural forces from the afterlife. 
 The exhibition at the British Library quite rightly established and described the filiation between The Castle of Otranto and other works of literary fiction (Count Dracula and Dr Frankenstein's creature, in a way, are but later incarnations of Manfred), but also other types of media in contemporary popular culture, such as the more recent Twilight and The Walking Dead movies and TV shows. Without consciously knowing it, quite a few of us are actually indirectly readers of Horace Walpole's classic novel.
I could not finish this book. I was trying to read it for background when I read "Nothanger Abbey". It was just too over the top. But from what I've read about Gothic Romance, that's the whole point.

Loved this. 
 Completely melodramatic. Pure gothic. Those poor women!

The only reason I picked this book up to read was because it was the first Gothic novel ever. But it is an utterly disappointing read. In short, this book has pretty much all the Gothic elements which are held miserably by a really sorry story line. 
 Compared to Edgar Allen Poe, this book could be said to be written by some teenager who dabbled with a little bit of Gothic research. 
 Pathetic read.

book_b.title: The Girl Who Played With Fire (Millennium #2)
book_b.user_review: I loved the way this book started and the way it ended, but the middle moved a little slowly for me. I didn't like this one as much as the first because it seemed that Lisbeth played a less frequent role. She is what makes the story interesting and when she's not present, the book captivates me less.

sample_reviews.review_text: I tried to read this twice and couldn't get past the violence.

A really good sequel to The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo. This one picked up a lot quicker in the beginning and held my interest throughout. I can't wait to see what happens with Lisbeth & Blomkvist in The Girl Who Kicked The Hornet's Nest!
This thrillers moves like gangbusters. Loved it! It is better than the first book in the series, however, it is imperative that you read the first book to understand what's going on in the second.

This book was extremely painful to get through. Everyone told me how great it was, and I was very excited to start reading. Unfortunately I was bored from the start. I find that Stieg Larsson puts too much extra information into his stories. While i was reading, I kept thinking to myself "why will I need to know this?". Turns out, I did not need to know, nor was I interested. I also did not think that the book was very climatic. I did try to guess what would happen, but I eventually stopped caring. Now I need to decide if I want to read the third book of the trilogy.

This was an okay follow-up to The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo. One of the things I really liked about the first book was the subtle mystery and build-up, and The Girl Who Played with Fire lacked that. Also, I like Blomkvist's character markedly more than Salander's, and while the first book seemed more Blomkvist's story, the second definitely belonged to Salander. Honestly, Salander just creeps me out a bit. While her back story is given in this book and that explains much of her personality, her inability to trust can be maddening, especially when it comes to Blomkvist. 
 I found the events in the last chapter to be highly improbable, but perhaps that improbable drama is what made this book an exciting read. While I'll admit to this book falling short of the expectations Dragon Tattoo established for me, this second installment is compelling. And I already started the third one. Obviously.

I didn't enjoy this one as much as the first. It didn't hook me nearly as fast or as hard. But I did like learning about lisbeth's past. And I always love cliff hanger endings.. Especially when I already have the next book in my possession haha 
 Maybe the first one was just so good that this one just didn't stand a chance, but I'm really hoping the last book will make up for my disappointment in this one.
Wow! In the second book of the Millennium series, we are not lacking in suspense and intrigue. I couldn't put this book down once it got started. I can't wait to read the final installment.

Here's the thing about Stieg Larsson's Millennium trilogy - the characters are well-formed and the plots are engaging and suspenseful, but the execution is terrible. Larsson's writing in The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo was unnecessarily specific, something which not only completely grated my nerves but also forced me out of the story (if just to form a "UGH. WTF." reaction). In writing The Girl Who Played with Fire, however, Larsson either stopped with the incessant descriptions or else I stopped noticing - because, again, engaging and suspenseful plot. Does this mean Larsson got better at writing? That someone like an editor stepped in and said, "Hey, you kind of need to stop"? Did he just overly explain everything he needed to (overly) explain in The Girl Who Played with Fire? 
 I don't know - and, frankly, don't really care. To me, the Millennium trilogy is a great, fun three-part read but not necessarily something I'm going to love years down the road or even re-visit. I've seen the Swedish adaptation of the trilogy - so I totally knew what was really happening or going to happen, both within one book but also throughout the series - but I was still so unbelievably engrossed in the novel's plot and read the last fourth or so in one sitting. Even if Larsson has his quirks, there's something to be said for nail-biting suspense and engaged reading. It's very hard to go into a horror flick or thriller knowing where the scares or adrenaline-pumping sequences are going to be and STILL jump out of your seat or have your heart race. That takes considerable talent - and, as I keep mentioning, Larsson has that talent - I just wish he could have perfected it a bit before he passed away. 
 All in all, The Girl Who Played with Fire is a fantastic example of a psychological suspense-thriller (with some good old mystery thrown in). As much as I complain, it has way less annoying quirks than The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, and, in effect, you can read the former without reading the latter, but I would highly recommend you don't. You learn things in Millennium's first installment that you're expected to know in its second, and, like J.R.R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings, Larsson's books (including the trilogy's conclusion, The Girl Who Kicked the Hornet's Nest) are stand-alone stories but fit snugly within a larger narrative, exploring the lives and relationships of the same characters over multiple years. The Girl Who Played with Fire is worth a looksie - but remember to do your homework.

This book is so good! I think I liked it more than the first book. There was some stuff early in the book that I kept waiting to be important later, but it didn't really come back up. That being said, I excited to read the last book.

Somewhere in the middle, the book becomes more boring compared to the previous due to the lack of Lisbeth Salander. It is apparent how powerful Lisbeth is as a character that when she went missing for a number of chapters, I already felt less motivated to finish this book. However, after Lisbeth returns, it all becomes worth it. More of her emotional turmoil is exposed and readers like me genuinely feel sympathy for her. Blomkvist however is more or less a static character, making no character development whatsoever though he remains essential to solving the mystery. Inclusion of more investigator perspectives (the police, and Milton Security) is very much welcome due to the complexity of the problem in this saga. 
 Once again, plot twists are aplenty nearing the end, making the last few steps of the journey impossible to stop when the resolution is oh so near. Expect to be surprised a couple of times and I promise you, these moments are pleasant. The cliffhanger ending isn't very satisfying though. If you LOVED the first book, do not hesitate to grab this book and trust me when I say that though the middle part is boring, it will all be worth it as you approach the end. Then after you reach the jarring conclusion.... Grab the last book.

reference_books.title: Allegiant (Divergent, #3)
reference_books.review_text: My least favorite of the series. I can't fault the author for not doing the totally expected with it, but that doesn't mean I have to like the way it ended. overall, "meh"

reference_books.title: Daemon (Daemon, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I wasn't too impressed with this one. Seemed unnecessarily technical (and I'm a technical person by trade). Seemed written targeted for 13-25 great old males. No good story arch. There didn't seem to be a closure to this story at all.

reference_books.title: The BFG
reference_books.review_text: This book came highly recommended from a friend... We were reading it with my 5 year old as one of his first few chapter books (we had already done a few others including Charlie and the Chocolate Factory). I really struggled with it. I didn't like the story particularly. It wasn't bad, but it wasn't necessarily all that great either. And I would also say that for a child I find it inappropriate as a "reading aloud" book - because the abundance of made-up words results in more effort trying to explain what words are to a child that is still working on their own vocabulary. (Not to mention its hard on the adult in order to pronounce things incorrectly on purpose). While my child had no issues with it, I found that the premise of giants that eat people might be a little disturbing to children. Again, my child didn't, but I would suggest reading this first before just starting it with your child. I would have skipped reading it with him had I done that.

reference_books.title: The Secret (The Secret, #1)
reference_books.review_text: ugh - my cousin's wife highly recommended and even bought it for me. I couldn't really stomach it at all. Hated the writing style and I got nothing out of it.

reference_books.title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Eh - being a self-professed geek I am supposed to like it... but it was just "eh". Don't judge

book_a.title: The Magicians (The Magicians #1)
book_a.user_review: ugh - I barely made it through. I just wanted to slap the main character and tell him to grow a pair and DO SOMETHING!

sample_reviews.review_text: I had a really difficult time connecting with the main character, which made it difficult for me to become invested in the story. This was probably more of a 2.5 star read for me than just 2, and I will end up reading the other two books since I have them, but overall the book didn't really do it for me.
Hated it. Finished it, but hated it

I'm still not entirely sure how I feel about this book. The structure is unusual in a way that might be flawed, or it might just be different from what I'm used to. There isn't a conventional story arc, but it's not arranged as a series of interludes connected by a device, either. Normally, a story with school at its center will be structured around the school time frame, but this isn't. Sometimes a lot of time passes with the narrative just skimming and skipping over things, then other times we stop and zoom in on things that don't necessarily move the plot or develop the characters, although they aren't really objectionable to read. And then the whole school thing turns out to be not so important, in a way. 
 I think the protagonist is problematic for me. I don't really like Quentin, but then he is an anti-hero and I'm not really supposed to like him. It's more that, while Quentin may be more realistic than a conventional hero, he doesn't feel real to me as a fully developed character. After everything he experiences, I still don't feel like I know him or understand what makes him tick. In some cases, I might say that was the desired effect, or I was just not connecting to that particular character, but in this case I'm afraid it's because the character isn't whole. 
 Overall, I still enjoyed the book to a reasonable extent, and I'm looking forward to seeing how the second book picks up the story and pushes the characters in hopefully new directions. I guess I'm supposed to talk about how the book is and is not like Harry Potter, or how Fillory is or is not like Narnia, but really, that's tiresome. It's refreshing to see the Hogwarts-like situation given such a different treatment, and the Narnia stuff seems like perfectly acceptable and somewhat traditional literary signifying.
Fantastic read. Can not wait to start the next book in the trilogy.

A mash-up of Harry Potter+The Chronicles of Narnia+The Lord of the Rings+A Secret History, that really didn't work for me. It was interesting at times, but the main protagonist, Quentin Coldwater was not a very likeable character.
Instinct told me to stop reading early on and I should have listened.

Quentin is sort of the lovechild of Harry Potter and Holden Caulfield; this is his magical "coming of age." Q is self-centered, petty, insecure, and awkward...in short, your average teenager. This is a novel of his dreams and fuck ups, both spectacular. I really liked it, tho the pacing was a little off for me, and most of the time you want to strangle the protagonist. I'm not running out to devour book 2, but I'll get to it eventually.

I hated this book. I really struggled to even complete it. It was fairly boring until the very end when it finally picked up. But for the most part nothing of any importance really happened. The book covered about 5 years total and it was so fast that I couldn't really get to know the characters at all as they grew. This is not Harry Potter for adults but it is not even a good book.

As other reviewers have said, equal parts Harry Potter, Narnia and Catcher in the Rye -- without the depth of any of them. Intriguing concept and there were moments I wanted to love this, but it's too rushed to get truly invested and that's to say nothing of your childhood hopes and dreams getting crushed by the biggest Eeyore of all protagonists imaginable . I'm not sure what Grossman was gunning for with the oppressive negativity, but his characters' collective lack of wonder, motivation and compassion doomed this book.
While I stuck it out and finished this book, I really didn't enjoy it. I can't really put my finger on what or why.

book_b.title: Why Not Me?
book_b.user_review: Kaling is surprisingly a good read. Both witty and capable of dishing out reality with good advice. I can see why she jokes about people always wanting to be her friend.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Awhile ago I read "Is Everyone Hanging Out Without Me?" by Mindy Kaling. I never knew her as a writer/actor on The Office - that show never drew me in. But I am a fan of The Mindy Project, which she also writes and stars in. That book was hilarious. She's a really funny person and full of personality. 
 This book, "Why Not Me?" is more of Mindy's musings. You get to know her a lot better. I wasn't in love with this book at first. It wasn't making me laugh as much, but at the same time I kept picking it up again. 
 It read like hanging out with a good friend. She's witty, charming, and as crazy as anyone I've ever met. She knows that she suffers from anxiety, she's overly competitive, she works her ass off, and she's a great friend and daughter. 
 My favorite part of the book was a little story she made up that was staring her if she'd stayed in Manhattan and become a Latin teacher at a rich kids school. It plays out via e-mails and some texts. Honestly, she needs to write a book (yes, I see what I did there!). But seriously, Mindy, write some fiction - that was a fine little story. 
 It was funny in its places, but more to the point, it was real. This was an honest look at the real Mindy Kaling. What her day looks like, and it will make you want a nap! What she worries about. What she still wants out for her life.

Oh Mindy, you are so funny! 
 Both of her books are just so enjoyable to read.

I tried this before and quit after 10 minutes because I could NOT bring myself to care about Mindy's spray tan. Then Susan exhorted me to try it again, and so I did. I'm glad I pushed past the spray tan part, and I enjoyed a lot of this book. There is definitely fluff in here, but there are a few cool nuggets. My absolute favorite part was the story about BJ Novak and the theater, and I really liked the titular essay at the end. Those were worth the time for me.

Why Not Me? is not nearly as charming as Kaling's first book. She spends the first half talking about what life is like now that she's a "star." If it's meant to read as tongue-in-cheek, it doesn't. Kaling does have some very sweet things to say about her family and BJ Novak, but this one fell much flatter to me than the previous book.
Not as good/funny as her first. Lost interest less than a quarter through.
I have always thought Mindy Kaling was charming and hilarious and adorable. I didn't read her first memoir but I really enjoyed this one.

3.5 
 Not as funny as her first book, but had some really awesome anecdotes. The one with Edward Albee made my jaw drop and burst out laughing. Loved reading about her experience with President Obama. So cool! Every little girl should read the last essay about confidence.

I enjoyed this little book. Didn't laugh out loud, but chuckled. I liked some of the insights, and MK seems like such a nice person, with a slightly warped mind. I enjoy insider glimpses of famous peoples' lives, attended exclusive events, meeting the rich and famous. Ok, yeah . . . gossip. I hope a few things she revealed were exaggerations. Some felt like filler, but not much. I suspect younger women, perhaps, will get the most out of it, not us old grumpy guys, but it actually made me smile. I have a friend, also Indian American, who she reminds me of: smart, funny, nice, who also dreams of being a comedian (though she is a MIT trained physicist and computer geek).
I simply could not get into this book. I had high hopes but just didn't find it funny, interesting, or insightful.

reference_books.title: Bared to You (Crossfire, #1)
reference_books.review_text: sexy romance, not much to it.

reference_books.title: Sarah's Key
reference_books.review_text: I read this book in 5 days, (which is impressive for me). It was hard to read since it was painfully sad at times, intriguing and disturbing as it describes the journey of ten year old Sarah, during the Velodrome d'Hiver roundup in July of 1942, in Paris. She and the rest of her jewish family was arrested by the French police in the middle of the night and she locked her younger brother in a secret cabinet, in order to protect him. This was a educational piece of history for me of a true event that occurred on July 16th, 1942.

reference_books.title: Don't Blink
reference_books.review_text: Not a typical James Patterson but, He didn't let me down with this suspense thriller that kept me up late each night. Action packed.

reference_books.title: Worst Case (Michael Bennett, #3)
reference_books.review_text: There hasn't been a James Patterson book that I didn't like. I could of easily given this book a 3 1/2 star but, it doesn't allow me to do it... This is still very good and kept me interested and wanting to read every chance I had but, I can't putt this psychotic murder thriller up there with my 4-5 star books. It was a great fast read while on vacation.

reference_books.title: Suzanne's Diary for Nicholas
reference_books.review_text: one of my VERY favorites. Not a usual mystery/thriller from Patterson, this is a love story.

book_a.title: The Declaration (The Declaration, #1)
book_a.user_review: Another fabulous book on cd which made me want to sit in my car to finish. It was about the future during a time that people could live forever but, they weren't allowed to have children. The children who were born were considered "surplus" and sent off to prison/orphanage. Let's hope that day never comes!

sample_reviews.review_text:
This teen novel is set in the mid-twenty-second century, in a world where they've managed to control disease and stop aging. Over-population has meant that people are not allowed to have children unless the Opt Out of the anti-aging drugs, but of course some people are involved in a movement against this and therefore institutions have been created to deal with the illegal children (Surplus) that are found. 
 In these institutions, children are indoctrinated to believe that the parents who created them are evil, and that there lives must be spent atoning for their parents sin. 
 Anna lives in a surplus institution and is almost finished her training to be useful. When a new child arrives, almost her age, he tries to change her outlook and save her from her fate. 
 This tale covers a lot of interesting ethical issues and would be an interesting choice for a book club. The teen characters are interesting, with Anna having some depth to her.
Good if you like dystopic type books. This was only readable because I wanted to see how it would end. Not the best story I've read - a little slow in spots.

I'm not sure how to review this book! 
 I honestly hated the writing style. We get it. She's been brainwashed. We get it. 
 Also, unnecessary diary entries to information dump. 
 However- the story was great and the concept was incredible so I overall really enjoyed it. 
 Keen for the next two!

Me encanto este libro, lastima que se puso interesante mas alla de la mitad porque las primeras paginas son realmente pesadas y aburridas! pero luego de pasada la mitad se pone super interesante. Un tema diferente que ademas de que te pone en constante intriga te deja un mensaje! Definitivamente es una lectura obligada si te gustan las distopias y yo soy fanatica!

I normally love dystopian teen fic. And the premise of this one sounded fairly interesting. I just assumed I would really enjoy it. But right off the bat I was annoyed by the beginning--a nine-page-long diary entry. Such a lazy (and boring) way to give background information! I mean, diary entries CAN be done well, and written in a believable way. The ones in this book are not. A lot of times it's a case of telling instead of showing, which always makes events feel flat and not quite believable. Other times, the journal entries repeat things that just happened in the story, only with the main character giving her (very immature) opinions on things as well ("stupid" seems to be one of her favorite words). The diary entries really irritated me. 
 But they aren't the only parts I found frustrating about this book. The characters don't feel real at ALL to me--a sterotypical evil headmistress, a naive, brainwashed girl who is suddenly UN-brainwashed without any real conflict of conscience after overhearing ONE conversation, a traditional mean girl/bully type, a heroic, overly patient boy who has all the answers...blergh. None of them have any depth whatsoever. On top of that, the overcapitalization! 
 The entire thing just feels really immature and unoriginal to me. I'm quitting to read something more compelling.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This book sounded so promising at the outset. A scientific break through that allows people to live far beyond their natural life span! A society facing the moral conundrum of population control! New class systems! An escape story! 
 Nah. All the intriguing moral stuff is pushed aside by a rambling teen romance that doesn't feel real at all. The characters seem stereotypical and uninteresting. There is little to no character development - Anna just goes through a 180 degree turn in opinion overnight. And apparently hiding in a shed together is all it takes to believably fall in love. It's a shame, because what with Anna's guilt for being alive, their tenuous friendship, and the tension of their escape, there was the potential for some serious swoon. 
 I'm just saying, if you're going to sideline everything for the romantic plot line, at least make it good.
If you haven't read the Declaration by Gemma Malley HIGHLY recommend it. I just finished the book and it was so good! Such an underrated book it's a shame.

For most of this book, I kept stumbling over WHY if the rebels didn't agree with the policy of no children, wouldn't they just opt out and then have a child. Most of the book, I felt this way, thinking, "So Opt Out! Why do you need to live forever if having a child is so important to you?" And I could even get why the policy was in place. It made sense, though the execution with the Surplus seemed needlessly cruel. It turns out there was a small fact of WHY they couldn't do this. It wasn't a big jaw-dropping reveal and was treated more like a throw-away line. But it was an important rule and had it been explained earlier in the book, I wouldn't have spent the entire thing, yelling at the stupid characters in the book. 
 Overall, I did enjoy this one and I passed it on to my daughter because I think she'll like it too. But I don't think I'm interested in reading more of the series. This one was fine as a stand-alone for me.
I've heard this book is excellent--fingers crossed it will someday be available in ebook form.

You know that saying, "Life is too short to finish a bad book" ? This is how it turned out. I didn't make it past 100 pages. 
 The plot was really interesting, but I couldn't stand the writing. It was very amateurish and unimpressive. I couldn't even make myself want to read it.

book_b.title: Fifty Shades of Grey (Fifty Shades, #1)
book_b.user_review: I decided to join the majority and read this book and see what the big fuss was about. I actually enjoyed the story line and was drawn into the romance between the main characters Ana and Christian. Yes, there is a lot of sex in this book and the storyline is a little far fetched but, I had a tough time putting it down and will be starting the 2nd one soon.

sample_reviews.review_text: Okay, so I knew the book was going to be about sex. "Fifty Shades of Grey" I hoped that meant an older woman with grey hair was going to have great sex. But no, I was disappointed. Anyway, there was lots of sex but I would have told Mr. Grey to go F*** himself from the beginning and then there would be no story.
Utter drivel.

The success of Fifty Shades of Grey is the very definition of viral marketing. A book that was originally self-published as an eBook and a print-on-demand paperback, it somehow caught the imagination of women everywhere and it's said that a copy now sells every sixty seconds. Amazing. There are three books in the series and they are numbers 1, 2 and 3 on the New York Times best seller list, and have been for months. 
 I have three words for this phenomenon: WTF?? I mean really...have you read this thing? 
 I bought a Kindle version ($9.99), just to see what all the hoopla was about, and got through about 1/3 of it (31% according to my Kindle), rolling my eyes and saying, "Oh, please," on every other page. With one exception (from Jessica Reaves of the Chicago Tribune) it seems to be immune to criticism of any kind (because it's made a boatload of money?), and as an author it's probably bad form to say this (you know that won't stop me), but it's crap. I don't mind the concept of it or the genre of eroticism itself, but something that's selling like the latest iPad release should at least be...well, good. 
 Fifty Shades of Grey is not good. That's not hurting sales in the least. It doesn't seem to matter that the writing stinks, the characters are unappealing and not engaging, the storyline is non-existent and, worst of all, the sex isn't even good, just lots of murmuring and moaning and gasping, and heartbeats quickening and racing. Kinda trite. At least be original. 
 The protagonist, Anastasia Steele, is a 21 year old virgin, and the narrative (told from her point of view) is sprinkled with lots of italics: holy crap! holy fuck! holy shit! jeez! and so on. And her inner goddess talks to her, and does "merengue with some salsa moves." Need I say more? Now, you can't argue with that kind of success - it's phenomenal - and good for E.L. James. She seems as amazed by this as everyone else. But seriously...what are you people thinking? Whatever it is, could you please transfer it to my book? And when mine becomes a runaway best seller it won't bother me a bit when E.L. James trashes it on her blog.

The author will be the first to tell you she isn't a great writer, and it's evident in Fifty Shades. The gratuitous sex scenes got ridiculous and tired very quickly, the language used was very asinine, especially in the everyday conversations of the characters, and the main character's thought process was like a balloon with the helium slowly leaking out. 
 At first the sex scenes were fun and thrilling, and then they never stopped happening and I began skimming through them in order to get to more of the story-- which was, sadly, lacking. There isn't much to this book other than a whole lot of sex. 
 If you've never read a sexually explicit romance novel before, then this might float your boat. I've read my share of romance novels (ones that actually had characters you could care about and plots with mysterious twists that make you want to keep reading), and this one was so ridiculously bad, in my opinion, that it was hard to finish reading.
Did not finish.

Everyone probably knows what this fan-fiction novel is about already, but I'll just summarize it briefly. One day when Ana's friend falls ill and calls in a favour, requesting Ana to interview one of the richest, successful men in Seattle in her place. Although it should it was indeed a formal interview, Christian and Ana both realize that this encounter was anything but ordinary. They start to form a curiosity and fatal attraction for one another. But as all businessmen know, sometimes the only way to keep something is by signing a contract... 
 I read this book because there were so many people raving about it, and of course it was also because it made it onto the top 20 list of best sellers on Indigo etc. If you ever watch or read the Vampire Diaries, Twilight or any other similar television shows or books, it is a definite possibility that you will enjoy this novel. I think the most captivating part about this novel is Mr. Grey himself. What kind of girl does not have an attraction to a bad boy? A handsome bruting one? A mysterious, rich, powerful and charming one? When you combine all of these aspects into one character, it becomes irresistible to desire more information, and the only way to gain more information is by blazing through the pages! 
 So why do I give this three stars? As explicit as the sexual content in the novel is, there is quite a bit of repetition. Not only in vocabulary, but also events in the story. The higher the predictability, the less enjoyable it is (excluding fairy tales, the ones where we watch because we expect the feel-good happy endings).

Muy mala, aburridisima, una historia tonta y predecible, y la escritura es tan repetitiva y superficial que me queria suicidar. 
 Es un crepusculo mil veces peor y ademas es tan cliche que me aburri un monton.
disturbing.

I'm about as confused as much as Miss Steel about this book. I really hated this book....I loathed it, and 1/2 way through it I set it down and didn't pick it back up for months, but I wanted it cleared off my night stand so I finished, and ...........I hate, hate, hate to admit......I liked the ending. It went from a 1 star to a 3....Just for the ending.

I don't get what the fuss is about! 
 Fifty Shades of Grey is poorly written, has no actual plot, the characters are extrimely uncredible and annoying, and all the sex scenes get pretty boring after 100 pages (the book has a total of 500!). This story could have been told in 100 pages MAX, without the boring repeated considerations of the narrator, without the millions of "Jeez", "Oh my", He's so sexy", "It's so erotic" and without alle the cliches. 
 The only thing that I liked in this book was the e-mail exchange between Ana and Christian, which was quite funny and to the point. 
 I read somewhere that the book was about to be made into a movie - maybe this interpretation will be more interesting, even though I don't see how you can make a movie out of this book without making it an adult movie - it's all about sex!

reference_books.title: The Walking Dead, Vol. 15: We Find Ourselves
reference_books.review_text: I have wasted countless hours talking about WHEN the zombies come and how I am going to survive, so I try to get my favorite zombie "novel" as soon as it is released. Not as good as some of the others in the series, but still gave me the creeps -- and I learned some good survival ideas for THAT day.

reference_books.title: Blackout: Remembering the Things I Drank to Forget
reference_books.review_text: This fantastic memoir from fellow Texan Sarah Hepola, doesn't pull many punches. Both tragically funny and tragically sad, this Salon writer (editor?) bravely takes us along on her journey of drunken one night stands, work trips to Paris and the uncomfortable unraveling of close friendships. You root for her to get better. Spoiler Alert -- she does. Plus, she's friends with one of the actors on Law and Order so you know I gotta like her.

reference_books.title: Brooklyn
reference_books.review_text: A heartbreaking, beautifully written story about a young Irish woman coming to American and where her life takes her. So quiet in tone, and yet, you will be thinking about the main character for a long time. Beautiful.

reference_books.title: When Breath Becomes Air
reference_books.review_text: A beautifully written memoir about the brief life of a brilliant neurosurgeon. It is truly sad that such a young doctor, whose love of literature had such a huge impact on his practice was taken from life so early. I said it once, I'll say it again a thousand times -- Fuck Cancer.

reference_books.title: Let's Explore Diabetes with Owls
reference_books.review_text: Probably not his best book, but he has so many stellar ones, that isn't a diss. Great for reading on a plane.

book_a.title: Lies That Chelsea Handler Told Me
book_a.user_review: Another good beach read -- it would be fun to be a part of Chelsea's lies.

sample_reviews.review_text: Huge Chelsea Handler fan, so it was great to hear what she's like off the air (not a whole lot different than she is on the air, hahah). I enjoyed all of the stories, and it was great to hear how generous and loyal she is, even though she lies to everyone!

I think the funniest part of this book is just how much people are willing to put up with. I am really not sure that I could be around someone like Chelsea, but it is pretty funny hearing the stories of what she comes up with just to mess with people.
A decent read, but not nearly as good as Chelsea Handler's other books.
Such a disappointment - well, I guess they can't all be winners

This book has absolutely no socially redeeming feature, so naturally, I really liked it. Chelsea Handler spends much of her time creating practical jokes with which to bedevil her friends. The rule seems to be that if she decides to make you a victim of her demonic humor, it's a sign of her love and respect. Unfortunately, I share this worldview which might be the reason that Chelsea Handler is one of my guilty pleasures. If I like you, I'm all over you, if I don't like you, I can't be bothered. Some of the jokes were truly funny and some were truly vicious. But I tended to laugh at both. I think that my favorite was when Chelsea convinced one of her fellow bridesmaids at a wedding that the bride was afraid to sing a song to her new husband and needed someone to sing with her. It was only after the "duet" started--to the surprise of the bride--that the extent of the joke was realized. And, of course, it's captured on the video, forever. Thank goodness that Chelsea Handler spends so much time working to embarass and humiliate her friends. If she wasn't so engaged, the rest of us would be in trouble.
Good for beach reading, but I wasn't on a beach so just mildly entertaining.
I've never disliked a book so much. Had to stop listening to it.
Not near as good as the last book, but still had some really funny stories. If you are a Chelsey fan then it is a fun read.

Chelsea's adventures, when told from her point of view, are reckless and fun. 
 When told from the point of view of her "victims" (this word is written on the cover), it's, well, kind of traumatizing. She pulls mean-spirited pranks and lies constantly, and it really seems to mess up other people's lives. Seeing the other side of the coin takes Chelsea from a drunk, self-deprecating prankster to a sociopath, which saddens me, since I really like reading her memoirs. 
 Also, these chapters are hit and miss. Each one's by a different "victim," some of whom are funnier than others. I had a few good laughs here and there, but not enough to keep me going.
God, I loved her other books so much but this one just lists all the horrible mean things she does to her family and friends. I really started to dislike her while reading this.

book_b.title: In a Dark, Dark Wood
book_b.user_review: What the hell was that? A (bad) YA novel or a novelization of a Lifetime (Network for Women) movie? Either way, it wasn't good. The only reason I finished it was I thought zombies would finally show up (sadly, no) and because I haven't finished a book in awhile because I keep reading books as thick as my (very) thick head, and it's messing with my 2016 Reading Challenge results. Sorry, book. The cover is nice.

sample_reviews.review_text: Are all adults this immature?

Although In a Dark, Dark Wood started off with a nice hook, this book turned into a quest to see if I was right; Much to predictable for my liking. However it was an easy and quick enough read that I did finish it. Unfortunately I don't have much else to say other than that.
DNF @ 73%

I really liked this book. The characters were right on point for a creepy who'd done it kind of plot. The setting of a glass sided cabin in the middle of no where definitely leveled up the creep-o-meter. There were a few instances where I was genuinely scared! I will definitely be reading Ruth Ware's next book, "The Woman in Cabin Ten"

I have been listening to audio-books like crazy this year. I actually found a favorite narrator in Imogen Church and sought this out because she was reading it. While Church was, once again, fantastic, I felt like the book was very lacking in character development, pacing, and plot. I think my biggest issue is that I thought we were going to get a twist through a certain character, and I got extremely excited for that possibility, only for it to take a twist in a much less sinister direction. I think Ware ignored the characters she was writing up until the twist and decided she needed to fit the new trend of constantly making characters evil to attempt to shock the reader, rather than let something happen organically. I found myself losing interest after the twist, to the point of not really caring what happened to the characters, because it just started to get outlandish and asked for too much suspension of belief. 
 Overall it isn't a terrible novel, but I think that Ruth Ware's The Girl in Cabin 10 was much better. Keep your eyes open for a review of that! She seems to have improved after this novel so there are some nice, creepy moments to be had if you want a tale in the woods. 
 FictionForesight

The blurb on the cover said, "Prepare to be scared...really scared!" --Reese Witherspoon 
 So I prepared myself, and waited. And read more. And waited to be "really, really scared." And it never happened. 
 It was pretty good, though. From the beginning I thought I knew who the perp was, but the author was skilled at making me have my doubts. But then, when the shite hit the fan, I came back to my original suspicions. 
 Still, I can see this becoming a pretty good movie. It might even be better as a movie than as a book, since the setting is really the scariest part of the story.

God, what is there to say about this piece of garbage? 
 I wanted to like this. I checked and rechecked myself at so many points in this book, trying to accepts its cliches and its faults, hoping there would be a pay off. 
 I rolled my eyes from paragraph 1 with some totally expected scene of a girl running through the woods and pining for some guy we don't even know. I continued not to care about the love-interest as the romance never existed on the page. I get that she was supposed to be an unreliable character (as every single one of them was) but my god was she horrible to listen to for the duration of the narration. I couldn't feel sorry for her (with maybe the exception of the awkward car quiz). There were also gaping plot holes that felt like the writing lacked research, or plot points that were never resolved. Why did we never discuss those weird forest hillbillies ever again? That would have been a better plot. 
 Overall: cliche, trite, and equivalent to reading the Jersey Shore: Horror Edition
Ugh, bye.

Un thriller psicologico trepidante que juega con tu cabeza en todo momento. Es sugerente, bastante escalofriante, y sobre todo, imposible de soltar. Hubiera deseado que la protagonista no hiciera tanto hincapie en cierto asunto de su pasado, creo que es lo unico que no me termino de agradar del todo. Si bien es importante para la trama, creo que fue algo que hizo que se tornara bastante monotono y hasta irritante. La rapidez con la que se resuelve el nudo tambien me dejo algo pendiente, pero aun asi, creo que fue un final digno de un buen thriller. 
 Si gustan ver una resena mas extensa los invito a ver mi video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eURjb...

2.5 [?]'S 
 I've been trying to read this book since last summer and for some reason I could never get myself in the right frame of mind to read it...... it kept getting put back into my tbr pile. This summer, I vowed to finish reading this book, no matter what. 
 I was on chapter 23 and still I couldn't get my head into this book. I think there are some books out there that you just need to be "in the mood " to read before it can become a good read. For me, this is one of those books, and obviously I mustn't have been in the "right mood". I'm sure this could have been a very interesting storyline, however, not the right book or fit for me at this time. 
 For those of you reading this, please do not let this review be the deciding factor as to whether or not to read this book. Unfortunately, this book wasn't right for me this time around, maybe it will need to be a reread in the future.

reference_books.title: And I Darken (The Conqueror's Saga, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Holy crap! This book was good! I loved every character, even the despicable ones (and most of them were pretty despicable), but Lada was my favorite. She might be one of my favorite Young Adult heroines ever. I can't wait to see her continued transformation into the female Vlad the Impaler. The wait for the next book is going to be super difficult.

reference_books.title: The Selection (The Selection, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I have a pretty high tolerance for the light and fluffy and I especially like the books with a little or a lot of romance in them, so I thought this book would be good. But there was no fluff and there was no swoony romance. Instead there was a love triangle of epic I could not care less proportions, lame tension provided by a couple of bullies and a group of "rebels", and a dystopian society with a very cringey background and caste system. But despite all that I hate to only read the first book in a series. Curiosity is going to get the better of me and one day I'll read the next book, but today is not that day.

reference_books.review_text: This was kind of boring.

reference_books.review_text: Why did I continue with this series? Ugh

reference_books.review_text: I couldn't resist rereading the next one.

book_a.title: Shopaholic Ties the Knot (Shopaholic, #3)
book_a.user_review: I was going to stop my reread of the Shopaholic series with this book, but now I'm not so sure. I still love Becky and Luke!

sample_reviews.review_text: These books are so funny! Definitely recommend the series!

This was another great installment on the Shopaholic series. It's somewhat anxiety-causing to read these books. Becky gets so deep into intractable situations that you just get very impatient for her to find a way out. But it is terribly entertaining, and ultimately her adventures are very funny and warm.
This is is just as good as the first "shopaholic" story..Funny,quirky, and enjoyable to read..

I do not know why I keep picking up books from this series. I think the main character is overly silly. The messes she gets herself into are completely unreal. Her thought processes are totally unbelievable. I think the writing style is slow and in some spots, rather tedious. I think I will try one of the Domestic Goddess books and if I feel the same way I will be done with this author.
Becky really is a stupid bint who did not deserve to have everything work out.

3.5! 
 (Allow me to eat before vomiting a review (; )

My least favourable Shopoholic book so far. 
 Becky is stuck having 2 weddings and she have to decide which one she want the most and still manage to make everyone happy. 
 It is an ok read but the story wasn't as funny as the previous ones and throughout the whole book Becky just keep avoiding confrontation and whining. Very little plot material for this one. 
 I still can't get the chemistry between Luke and Brandon. They are vastly different. Yeah u can say opposite attract but I still can't see how they fit in each other's life
I liked this one better than the second one but they're kind of getting old. She never really learns her lesson and then she gets out of the bind she's in WAY to easily.

These books continue to give me a stomach ache. This girl gets herself into more problems by lying. I also saw the ending coming from the very first mention of a wedding in England and a wedding in New York :)

Full review is here 
 I prefer the second book than this one. It is also less hilarious compared to it, however still a decent read.

book_b.title: The Princess Saves Herself in this One
book_b.user_review: This could have ben very relatable and enjoyable. She talks about a lot of relatable topics, you see. But I couldn't get past the angsty, simplistic writing and format. Too much tumblr. Not for me.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Normal, 
 sentences 
 with 
 a lot 
 of 
 spaces 
 is not 
 poetry. 
 If you like stuff like this (cough cough Milk and Honey cough) then be my guest, give it a read. I know tons of people who were deeply affected and moved by this collection. I was not one of them. Though I don't read much poetry, when I do enjoy it is because the worlds create atmosphere or vibrant imagery that provokes thought and/or deep emotion. That is what I expect from poetry, how one can creatively string words together in a way that touches people. I certainly don't hate this book by any means, nor do I want to disrespect the writer because you could feel her vulnerability and the genuine nature of her words. But to me they were only that, words. They didn't have the flow and melody that the poetry I enjoy carries. 
 That's all I have to say about it. I didn't like it.

 poetry! 
 read review HERE

Wow, I really wasn't expecting to like this. I generally don't care for this style of poetry, I prefer more traditional poems and poets, but this book was so cathartic. 
 I cried during the first and second parts. I found the third part a little lackluster, although happy poems tend to be harder to pin down, and then the fourth part felt more like advice than poetry, but it was good advice so at least there's that! 
 It took maybe 30 minutes to read this, so if you ever have some free time to yourself, I recommend giving this a go!

I enjoy poetry. It's not that I'm only a stickler for classic poetry or the conservative rule-bound poetry. Using different techniques and literary devices to make poetry more fun, modern, new or different: I'm all for it. I think experimenting with effects and techniques is a great thing. But it has to have a point to it. And here I think it just fails. Flat out. Using pauses and orthography as a way of adding to the power of text is something I enjoy experimenting with myself. How can you emphasise or add meaning, power or feelings to the text by breaking it up in different ways? But here it's almost like a joke! As if hitting enter enough times makes something poetic and deeper. To me all it does is annoy me and make me question how so many people can look beyond that stylistic ginormous flaw. 
 The writer is not bad with words. And some of the things she writes about touches me. It's meaningful and put in a way that makes me moved. The words would've been poetic and poetry on their own, if she had stopped hitting enter all the time. Because even these parts are ruined by the exaggeration of pauses. I ended up reading it as a whole, and giving it my own breaks and pauses, and I was constantly thinking of how I could've done it better. NOT the text, the content or way with words, but the phrasing! 
 It almost makes me sad that someone can look at this as good poetry. If it had been redone without all the linebreaks I could've ended up giving it 3 stars, but the writer ruined this for herself. (Though I guess not really since so many enjoyed it.)
Sorry, this was just a miss for me. I just didn't connect with it. I feel like I have seen all of this already all over the Internet from other writers.

Whatever the opposite of subtle is, this is it. 
 I mean, *eye roll*: 
 everyone i love leaves -----> This is not a poem, this a 13-year-old's msn status from 2004.

I felt like I was reading someone's personal diary with this book. And that's not a bad thing. I truly felt like I was right next to the author when she was experiencing all the traumatic events that happened to her. I felt her pain, her anger, her sadness as if it were my own. I only gave it 4 stars because yes, at some points it didn't feel like poetry. I felt like I could write some of those myself. Some were only one short sentence that I could have come up with. However, the book is still emotionally raw and moving. My favorite parts were the queen and you (the second half of the book). While the whole thing could be relatable to certain people that experienced the same things, I felt that these 2 parts were relatable to everyone. Every girl and every woman should read them. It was inspiring and uplifting and I feel that everyone needs a little bit of encouragement at some point. That's what this book is for.

This book was AMAZING. Poetry is not my main reading fair (despite being an English teacher), but I absolutely LOVED this book of poetry. It was funny, heart-wrenching, and immensely identifiable. When I saw that it won the 2016 Choice Award I thought "Good. It f*cking deserves it". I also snap chatted 20% of this to friends (and had some screenshots) and will be buying a copy (which is my main proof of how good a book is) and I am planning on hanging up multiple poems from this collection in my classroom. 
 Seriously, just read these poems.

2.5 stars? I don't know. I find it difficult to rate poetry collections, as it feels like grading someone on the content of their soul. 
 I'm not going to debate what is and isn't poetry when it comes to form. But I do believe for something to be considered poetry, it has to have emotion. It has to make you feel, make you think. There were a handful of powerful images in this collection, and one of them even made me cry. The reason for my low rating is how few of them there were. Most of the poems in this book are shallow, like this one: 
 please 
 believe me 
 when i say 
 revenge 
 was 
 never 
 my intention. 
 Using bad grammar and odd formatting doesn't make this profound, just pretentious. This book has pages and pages of this sort of poetry. It's like cotton candy. It might look nice, but it's mostly artificial and provides little nourishment for the soul. I just wish it were deeper. The author has clearly been through a lot and learned a great deal because of it, but with the exception of a few powerful pages, there isn't much revelation in her words.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This review from my blog: http://lostinstory.weebly.com/home/re... 
 Summary (spoilers, if that can be said of poetry books?): 
 This is a collection of poems that is grouped into three "chapters": Princess, Damsel, Queen, and You. Princess focuses on the author's experiences with an abusive mother, sexual abuse, eating disorders, self-harm, and youth of loving books. Damsel focuses on the death of her mother and her sister and her relationships with abusive men. Queen focuses on her growing up and realizing the errors in so much of her previous thinking as well as meeting a man who treats her well and validates her worth. You consists of pieces of advice, encouragement, and empowerment from the author to the reader. 
 What I liked: 
 I though this anthology was really well done. No section stood out as being weaker than any of the others as well. 
 This anthology has a clear feminist focus and message that was really encouraging and uplifting. The movements show a progression from needing to be rescued to rescuing oneself. 
 Along those lines, I loved that the author finds someone who makes her happy but that he doesn't "save her" or complete her. He simply helps her and supports her as she finds her way to a healthy form of self-love. 
 The poems where she talks about her love of literature and words were my favorites. They definitely spoke to me in ways that many of the others did not, as someone who has never struggled with these issues in general. 
 I think this would be a really solid collection to gift to others and would really be meaningful to people who struggle or have struggled with the effects of abuse or self-harm. Lovelace is writing very much to that reader and takes the role of a mentor, especially in the section You. 
 What I didn't like: 
 Some of the poems were very vague but seemed to refer to something very specific the author had been going through. While this isn't a huge issue, I'm just not sure what the point of publishing them in a collection would be.

reference_books.title: Covet (Covet, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Last year I read On the Island which really surprised me and I enjoyed so when this showed up in my mailbox I thought I'd give it a try, even though I normally shy away from women's fiction. I will say it definitely has romance tones in it. 
 Chris and Claire have been married for years but after Chris lost his job, he went into a depression. A year later, he finds a job but the void in their marriage is large. He travels constantly, leaving Claire home with the kids. They stop communication, stop being intimate etc... 
 Claire randomly meets a police officer and they start spending time together. They don't physically cheat but there is definitely emotional cheating. 
 I read this in one sitting and it kept me engaged. I really do like this author's voice. And I liked this book. It was emotional and I like it when authors give us an already established marriage in trouble. 
 So why three stars? We spend pages and pages (which translates to months and months) of Claire and Chris struggling. Of Claire and police officer building a relationship. And then when all is said and done, and Claire and Chris reunite, it is sooo rushed. I needed Claire and Chris to come together happily and examine their issues with more depth. It was this really slow build up of emotions between these three people to have it all end with a HEA very abruptly. Otherwise I liked this one. But the rushed ending definitely frustrated me.

reference_books.title: Undeniable (Undeniable, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Have you ever read a book that you secretly guilty-pleasure loved, that you want everyone to read yet at the same time you don't want everyone to read? This is me with Undeniable by Madeline Sheehan. This book came out last year and I remember general buzz - some loving, some hating - but all saying "whoa, this book has some crazy in it." Last night my hair dresser went on and on about this book so I came home and thought I'd read the first chapter or so just to get a feel. But it was so cracky, I had to read the whole thing. 
 My definition of a "cracky" book is one that contains scenes or a trope or just a behavior by a character that would usually turn me off. But for whatever reason, the way this author writes it, makes it work for me. 
 Undeniable has A LOT of stuff in it that should have made me throw my kindle and turn me off. There is rape, there is derogatory behavior towards women, there is extreme violence, there are characters who do horrible things, there are no sweet, romantic scenes really. The hero makes out with the heroine for the first time when she is sixteen and he is 34. I KNOW I KNOW. Sounds great, yes? LOL 
 But. I couldn't look away. I just couldn't do it. This author somehow makes it work..... for me - I know there are a lot of you out there that it didn't work at all. 
 Deuce is our hero. He is much older than the heroine, Eva. The first time they have sex, she is 18 and he is 36. Her dad is the president of a Motorcycle Club (MC). Deuce is the president of a different MC club. They have a fragile truce between them, and of course daddy does NOT want his baby daughter anywhere near Deuce. (he actually shoots him after he catches her at 16 making out with Deuce.) 
 Anyway - The book progresses through the years. Deuce and Eva have explosive passion. They come together hard, and then leave on a bad note. The book will jump forward a few years and they come together again with more drama and even more passion. This worked for me. I didn't mind the jumping ahead. I didn't mind them leaving miserable. Their lifestyle is very dark and gritty and rough. And their romance is that way too. 
 I should also note - Eva has an adopted brother who falls in love with her. He is truly certifiably crazy and becomes obsessed with her. Eva is abused by him - mentally and physically - and while for some time I think she realizes this, she also falls into his crazy weird psycho stuff. It's hard to read at some points. Eva also has a best friend who is crazy and just kind of weird. (did I mention there is a lot of crazy in this book? *wink*) 
 So yes - I was horrified at times, I was amused at times. It's not like Kristen Ashley where she can write an asshole hero but by the end he is romantic and lovable. Deuce is hardcore rough. But overall it was a book I enjoyed reading. I didn't want to stop reading it. It's not a book though I can easily recommend because it will offend some people. And that's okay if you hate it. And some, like me, will really enjoy it. And that's okay too. 
 There is a second book out which I'll probably read tonight featuring Deuce's daughter and Ripper (you meet Ripper in this book - he has a very scarred face...yes..totally reading this one tonight).

reference_books.title: Crux (Southern Arcana, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Mackenzie Brooks is scared. She has been running from her ex-boyfriend, Marcus through five states, and no matter how many times she dumps her car or hides out, his people always seem to track her down. She has ended up in New Orleans, and has taken employment at the local bar, in desperate need of money. While working, she craves normalcy and desperately just wants to fit in. However, she is so scared of the men chasing her and their crazy ideas about magic and other unbelievable things that she can not allow herself to let her guard down. She does her best to be a flirty, carefree bartender but she is not fooling the patrons especially her boss Nick. Although she is on edge, she can't help but notice the hunky guy that hangs out, Jackson Holt. 
 Worried she is in trouble, Nick sends Jackson, a private investigator, to follow Mackenize home one night. Mackenzie, who is used to being followed and totally on edge, realizes Jackson is following her and has to make a decision right there whether she is going to fight and flee, or fight to stay. Making the very hard decision that Nick probably wouldn't try to hurt her, she decides to trust these people. She ends up moving into the apartment above the bar. 
 Nick, Jackson, and his partner Alec all know something is a little off with Mackenzie, and it is not just her fear. They have a feeling she is a shapeshifter, but not a wolf like Nick and Alec, nor a wizard like Jackson and they are stumped. Jackson decides there is something special about Mackenzie is he is not going to let her run off. When Marcus' men track her down again, Jackson uses his magic to fend them off. Now Mackenzie must believe magic and supernatural beings exist and trust those around her to keep her safe. 
 The writing team of Moira Rogers, aka Bree and Donna, really impressed me with Crux. It is one of those books where you sit down and are immediately at ease with the pages. They have a really great smooth, witty writing style and some of the most engaging characters I have read. 
 Jackson describes himself as a "charming bastard," and that sums him up well. He very alpha in his protectiveness but over all a really nice guy. He is not cocky, or arrogant, just a man you definitely would want to take home to your mother. He is also built, tall and as Mackenzie tells him, "unfairly sexy." 
 I loved Mackenize too. At the beginning of the book she is terrified and on the run, but once she trusts Jackson and the events happening to her and around her, the true Mackenize opens up and she embraces life and is carefree. What I truly love about this heroine is when she is in trouble, she accepts help. She listens when they tell her what to do - she knows they know more about this magic then she does. She never puts herself in a TSTL (too stupid to live) situation, which I often find heroines who just discover magic fall into. 
 The love scenes, while not abundant in quantity, make up for in in quality. My favorite part is the amount of talking during the scenes. These two never stop the chatter, and it really is a turn on during these scenes. 
 My absolute favorite part of the book are the supporting characters. We get introduced to so many, yet as the reader you will definitely come to know all of them, and quite well. There is Alec (ladies I've already claimed him so move along) who is Jackson's partner and very quiet, very alpha, very mysterious (he will be the hero in book three, Deadloc). Kat, the secretary who is more of a computer whiz and like a kid sister to Jackson and Alec. 
 There is also Nick, who owns the bar and her father just happens to be head alpha wolf, although she wants nothing to do with the politics that status brings her family. Nick becomes a great friend to Mackenize, making sure the boys keep themselves in line. Nick is the heroine in the next book, Crossroads, which I am starting very soon! 
 I absolutely recommend Crux and I am very eager to try more from Moira Rogers.

reference_books.title: Lover Unleashed (Black Dagger Brotherhood, #9)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 Lover Unleashed, book nine in my beloved Black Dagger Brotherhood series is Manny and Payne's book - or so we were told. But honestly, this book is Vishous's. True? Vishous steals the show. Manny and Payne have a romance, but their story is nothing compared to V's. Nothing. There is also no way this one can be read as a stand alone - you need V's backstory throughout the entire series to get anything from this book. 
 I was definitely disappointed with the ending of V's book Lover Unbound, when Jane was turned into a ghost. Not only with the ghost aspect, but I just wanted more of a closure with V and Jane but we get it in this book. V is not in a good place. Payne comes to his side, paralyzed from a sparring session with Wrath. Vishous has had no idea in the 300 years he has been alive that he even had a twin sister. The Scribe Virgin, their mother (who is not in this book which is a shame), has had Payne imprisoned. Now she is here, in his life, and the protectiveness V feels for her is out of control. 
 When Jane calls Manny in to help operate on her, there is that instant "mine" between them (even though Manny is a human). This does not go over well with V, as Butch and the other brothers struggle to keep him from killing Manny. As time goes on, V goes into an even deeper downward spiral. Payne doesn't heal as she should, and when Jane attempts something shocking, he walks away - from Jane. This scene is very moving and well done. What we really get is V coming to terms with his abusive father, his negligent mother, and his role as a hellren. Yes he loves Jane, but can he overcome his past, and his current broken self to give her what she needs? Can he fulfill the new role as a brother to Payne? 
 Butch plays a very important role in "saving" V. I won't go into specifics as to not spoil too much, but this issue had to be addressed. He is in love with Butch as we all know. We finally get a little more exploration into this relationship - the one we were teased with in Lover Unbound. 
 As the other continued fighting, the pair of them just stared at each other against the audio backdrop of grunts and metal-to-metal strikes and inventive cursing. There should be something said between them, V thought. There was just so much...to be said. 
 "I want it from you," V bit out. "I need it." 
 Butch nodded. "I know." 
 And just to note - the "it" is not exactly what you think. Also *Mandi dies* 
 Before I started the book I thought how in the world will anything happen between V and Butch with both of them mated (to Jane and Marissa). But it works out totally fine. And it is not the actual scene that fulfilled me, but a scene with them later - a very quiet peaceful moment that to me, lets me breathe a sigh of contentment for these two males. I still don't know if JR Ward gives Butch and V a fair shot - the big scene with V and Butch is kind of short. But I'm glad she does what she does. 
 And I have to say, I actually liked Jane in this book - crazy, right? I think JR Ward does a nice job with the emotional turmoil between these two. There is one scene where V just walks away from her - and it is heartbreaking. But I get her more. I understand her more. I like her with V now. I'm content with their relationship. And we get several dirty sex scenes with them: 
 "Vishous..." 
 "What" 
 His gloved hand dipped under the black satin, and she didn't have to see where it went to be well aware he'd gripped himself. The fact that he arched back told her everything she needed to know. That and the way he bit down on his lower lip. 
 "Jane..." 
 "What." 
 "Are you just going to watch, true?" 
 We also get some classic V and Butch moments that make me smile: 
 Butch clapped him on the shoulder. "Listen to me. You have the fashion sense of a park bench and the interpersonal skills of a meat cleaver - " 
 "Is this suppose to be helping?" 
 "Let me finish-" 
 "What's next? The size of my cock?" 
 "Hey, even pencils can get the job done - I've heard the moaning from your room to prove it." 
 Let's move onto Blay and Qhuinn, or as they are called "Qhuay." They had such a presence in Lover Mine I am disappointed with the lack of progress in their relationship. I hear a novella might be in the works for them so maybe JR Ward is saving up for that - but still, there is no Qhuay in this book. We get a tiny bit with Blay and Saxton. And we get a little more than that with Qhuinn and Layla (OMG - I can't even go there right now). We get a big reveal with Qhuinn - something that will happen in the future. We need to discuss this my friends....soon. 
 No Lassiter or Tohr in this one. No Murhder, which surprised me since we were introduced to him in Lover Mine. There is also an odd side story of a serial murderer. Now in it, we are introduced to Jose de la Cruz's new partner Thomas DelVecchio Jr, or Veck. I can only hope Veck plays some kind of role in the next book because otherwise I have no idea why this storyline is in it. Unless I missed something. Veck does have some strange...ways, so I assume there is more to come of him. I'm very intrigued. 
 We meet some new vampires, not necessarily brothers, but six men (although we really only meet three) that fight lessors. They fought under the Bloodletter until he died, and the Xcor took over. Along with Throe and Zypher, they are a secret band of "brothers" - I use that term loosely because they are not necessarily like The Brothers. They fight together -killing lessors, or humans. They are much more violent without as many morals. They have been living in the old country, but have realized, most of the lessors have moved to where the Brotherhood now reside. Xcor wants one thing - to be king. So they move near Caldwell and start to set things in motion. So, yes they fight lessors, but they are not necessarily friendly with the brotherhood. I am interested to see how this plays out. The brotherhood is aware of Xcor, but we don't get any details of the how or why. It looks like the new conflict might be moving away from the lessors and more towards a fight with Xcor for the King. 
 I suppose I can't leave Payne and Manny out. Honestly, they did nothing for me. If I had to hear Payne say "Verily" one more time I might have thrown the book. For some reason I thought Payne was going to be similar to Xhex, but she ends up more like Layla. She has a few kick ass moments towards the end but I didn't feel like she was a warrior or a brother like Xhex is. There was just nothing that stood out about them. I like Manny - he had nice interactions with Jane. And I liked out he stood up to Vishous and his interactions with Butch are fun. But for the actual romance between these two - it did nothing for me, which makes it really hard to rate this book. Also - the way Payne ends up healing is so corny. I'm sorry - but I just didn't get it. 
 While Lover Mine really took us back to the romance, away from the UF feel after book 3, this one takes us right back. In a way, I don't want to complain because the spotlight is on Vishous. And I LOVE Vishous. Before I started this book, my one hope was that we got a lot of Vishous material. Little did I know he would be the entire book. He even announces at the end that he is officially mating with Jane (tattoo on his back etc). Seriously, this is his book. 
 Bottom line is - I have very mixed feelings. The book entertained me. I read it in one day. I love this series, I love the brothers, I really enjoy JR Ward's style of writing. I love that we get tons of stuff with Vishous. I think Vishous's story needed to be continued, but it was at the expense of the main characters. Honestly, I wasn't invested at all in Payne and Manny, so not getting a full story from them isn't all that heartbreaking to me. But - this is their book. And they get jipped. With the lack of Blay and Qhuinn after such a build-up in the previous book, I can't help but be a little disappointed. 
 I also want to note that no one is really set up to be next in the series - and that is driving me crazy!!! I'm very curious to see who it is!!!! 
 Rating: C+ maybe a B-

I didn't have high expectations coming into this book. Book one, Backstage Pass was fun and really dirty, but the story line was just okay. I also want to note that although this is the third book published in this series, it is actually the fifth book. By that I mean, band members Eric and Jace already have their HEAs in this book, although their books are not out yet. I don't like that this book is out of order and I don't know why the publisher decided to do this (we get Jace's book in January and I assume Eric's book after that) but there you go. 
 Trey has been in love with his best friend and fellow band member Brian, for a very long time. As teenagers, they share some intimate moments, but Brian is now very happily married to a woman, and he has just become a new father. While Trey never wants to lose his friendship with him, he has to deal with the fact that that is all they will ever have together. Trey is bisexual, and enjoys the very nuemerous hook-ups he has in every city The Sinners tour in. Trey's brother is also in a band, and Trey helps them audition a new guitar player. The one that blows them out of the water is Reagan. She works at a coffee shop but has some mad skills at playing the guitar. They have an immediate connection (total insta-lust but it worked okay for me). Trey decides it is time for him to have a steady girlfriend (After 24 hours of knowing her.....a little fast) and Reagan feels the same about him.

But Trey can't hold off his urge to have sex with another man, and eventually Ethan comes into the relationship, as he loves Reagan and is very attracted to Trey.
