book_b.title: Eleven Scandals to Start to Win a Duke's Heart (Love By Numbers, #3)
book_b.user_review:
Favorite Quote: "You are a scandal waiting to happen. 
 Although this is the third book in the trilogy, it's the first I read and it works perfectly as a stand alone. This book is so well written, I don't see how it won't capture your heart. 
 Simon, Duke of Leighton or nicknamed the "Duke of Disdain" made my insides flutter. He is the cold, impenetrable duke who lives his life as he was raised - emotionless and bred for his title. His lineage is perfect and he portrays the perfect duke. But he has a secret (one I'm not going to spoil)- and because of this, he must marry the perfect duchess before this secret comes out to the ton. So he sets his eyes upon Lady Penelope, who has an unblemished reputation although there is no romance between them. 
 But there is a vibrant force in his world that refuses to go away. Juliana Fiori has no title, only a marquess for a brother. From Italy, her mother is a former marchioness who left her titled English husband and two sons and married an Italian merchant, resulting in Juliana. Then, her mother ran out on her, leaving her with her father. Now that her father has passed, she is forced to seek out her half brothers back in England for guardianship. All of this has resulted in a great scandal surrounding Juliana. She is invited to ton events because of her brothers, but the gossip mill is running in full force. She also doesn't have the proper etiquette of the English ton and speaks her mind quite loudly. When she first meets Simon, he is led to believe she is titled, and a proper lady and he is immediately enamored. But when he finds out who she really is, the daughter of a runaway Marchioness, he is offended. He can't be seen with the likes of her. But she won't go away. 
 He is drawn to her. Attracted to her. And little by little, she breaks down his facade. Juliana is just a fabulous heroine. She has a slight language barrier that has her using the wrong words in certain situations which is very charming. 
 "He called me a pie!" She announced, defensively. There was a pause. "Wait. That's not right." 
 "A tart?" 
 "Yes! That's it!" She registered her brother's fists and looked to Simon. "I see that it is not a compliment." 
 It was hard for him to hear over the roaring in his ears. He'd like to take a fist to the man himself. "No. It is not." 
 She keeps finding herself thrown into these situations that embarrass her, and keep her the talk of the season which is humorous. Simon wants to ignore her and pretend she doesn't exist, but by chance and a little planning on Juliana's part, she becomes part of his life. And we are treated to these little tidbits from their conscious throughout the book that I love: 
 Desire slammed through him hard and fast, and he stiffened at the blinding emotion. He did not want her. She was a madwoman. 
 A stunning, goddess of a madwoman. 
 He cleared his throat. 
 Nevertheless. 
 What I love is that both Simon and Juliana become so frustrated with their station in life. As they are reminded endlessly, "Reputation triumphs." Simon has a duty, not only being an esteemed duke but to hide this family secret from the public. And Juliana was born into a scandal and that leaves her no leeway in the eyes of the public. She is terrified of becoming her mother, and lives her life finding herself in endless scandals that exhaust her. They both have accepted their fate, but this yearning for the other starts to take over their lives. It is done with such an exquisite, sensual tone by Sarah MacLean - to the point you are not going to want to put down this book. You have to keep reading to see how these two overcome society to be together. Plus you have to read for the very smexy love scenes: 
 This kiss was an exploration. 
 It sought and found, chased and captured. It was a kiss that suggested they had an eternity during which to learn each other, and when his tongue ran roughsmooth across her bottom lip, sending wave after wave of sensation rocketing through her, she hoped they did have an eternity. Surely it would take that long for her to tire of this. Of him. She gasped at the feel of him, so powerful, so wicked. 
 The dialog is fast and witty, the romance is intense and the characters are vibrant and sexy. One of the best romances I have read this year. 
 Rating: A

I keep loving her more and more :) 
 Check out my full review at http://generalconfessions.weebly.com/...

** spoiler alert ** 
 Eleven ways to 'tell' versus 'show' a Duke 
 Eleven scandals taught me how important well-rounded characters are towards a romance, particularly if one (or more) of your characters is not likable from the start. 
 Juliana is a wonderful heroine! She is trapped by English society's rules and traditions and readers sympathize with her right from the beginning. Some readers thought she was too immature and her 'scandals' too unrealistic, but let's not forget she was 20 years old and from Italy. With the critical eye of every member of the ton on you, she'd either have to revolt or cave under the tremendous pressure. I admired Juliana's adventurous spirit and bravery towards the tonnish vice-like grip, but her anxiety about being like her mother grew boring and her refusal to marry Simon because she wasn't good enough? Pul-leeze 
 But Simon? A number of reviewers have exclaimed that Simon is one of the worst heroes they've ever read. He insults Juliana, does not treat her as his equal, and gets engaged to another woman. Readers are introduced to a cold, passionless man determined to enter into a cold, passionless marriage and he does not thaw until the ending. We are offered very few reasons for WHY Simon is this way, but we're sure his mother (and maybe his father who no one talks about) has something to do with it. I wasn't sure whether Maclean had not thought about Simon's motivation or personality or whether she decided not to include it in her story? I thought some familiar justification of his character would have provided some additional sympathy from readers, but it never materialized. Simon's mother is in several scenes, but only to increase conflict between Juliana and Simon. I felt Maclean was 'telling' me how bad Simon was without 'showing' me with his past and experiences. I wanted some stories from his past woven in to make me like him, but they never materialized. One author who does this very well is Lisa Kleypas in "It Happened One Autumn" - Lord Marcus Westcliff is snobby and arrogant, but the pieces of his past woven into the story make us sympathize and cheer the romance between him and Lilian. Readers are 'shown' evidence to why Lord Marcus is the way he is - he becomes three-dimensional character while Simon still felt two-dimensional. 
 Another strike against Simon was that his sister, Georgiana, was truly the hero in the book. She sacrifices her reputation (and shockingly enough, her DAUGHTER'S reputation!) to give her brother a happy ending. "Thank you, mom for telling English society that I'm a bastard, so Uncle Simon can get his girl. What?!" - any critique partner worth her salt would have called for a plot time-out to discuss that maneuver. 
 Pacing was slow in the beginning and middle and I felt there was some repetition about her scandalous nature, being like her mother, her thinking that she wasn't good enough for Simon, and his aversion to scandal. It became a broken record. The writing is excellent and I admire Maclean's versatility with words. I also thought the sexual tension between Simon and Juliana was paced more appropriately than "9 Rules" and each love scene was necessary towards the plot.

Oh, it's been too long since I've read something by Sarah MacLean. This is a delightful romp with the delightful St. John family. Nick and Gabriel found love matches, now can their half sister Juliana do the same? 
 Of course she can! 
 Ah, the games the titled play. The value of name, legacy and reputation. The dangers in social ruin. 
 I do wish some loose ends had been taken care of here. Who is Caroline's father?? I know there isn't another book in the series so it just won't be answered, but I need to know! So I'm going to go ahead and assume that it's no one we've actually met and therefore it doesn't matter. 
 With this series being finished, I'm going to have to find another by the same author. I truly enjoyed reading this.

4.5 stars 
 This is, without a doubt, my favorite Sarah Maclean book. I loved both Leighton and Juliana immediately, something I was really worried about. In Nine Rules to Break When Romancing a Rake (my review)I liked Juliana, but I worried she might be too much character and issue for her own book. Leighton in both Nine Rules to Break When Romancing a Rake and Ten Ways to Be Adored When Landing a Lord (my review) just comes off as so awful (I mean, he's called the Duke of Disdain) that I didn't know if I could envision him as a leading man. 
 But I could! For both of them, and I loved it. For me this was the perfect mix of more experienced, closed off man and more naive, open woman. I could go back and re-read pretty much every scene between Leighton and Juliana over and over again. Their chemistry was amazing and I just wanted to get them together ASAP. 
 There's quite a bit of Ralston and Callie in this book, which I appreciated since I always like to think characters live on and are very happy once a book ends. There was less of Nick and Isabel, but they were still there and I also was happy to see what happened to them. I almost wish there was more time between books so there would be even more to know. 
 I highly recommend the Love By Numbers series overall, but I also think this could work as a stand alone novel, you just wouldn't know as much of the background for the supporting characters.

2.5. Sarah MacLean's work keeps getting such great press, but I have to say that I'm not a big fan. At CT Fiction Fest yesterday, romance authors Diana Holquist and Ellen Hartman gave a workshop on common cliches in romance writing, and it seemed to me that quite a few of the cliches they mentioned appear in MacLean's work. 
 And I felt that this book didn't stand alone well -- the first meetings of the hero/heroine take place in earlier books, and are mentioned rather than remembered in much detail in this book, so if you hadn't read the earlier books you'd have a hard time understanding why these two were so invested in one another, or what motivated them emotionally. BUT on the other hand, she had revealed the hero's big secret to the reader, but in this book, the heroine didn't know it, so the narrative kept it secret from the reader here, too. This became annoying if you as reader already KNEW the secret from having read the earlier book. Would have been better, I think, if the author had acknowledged the reader's knowledge of the secret by showing the hero's reactions to its potential revelation, even while keeping it a secret from the heroine. 
 I wonder if the editors at Avon spend much time editing their authors? Seems that the problems here could have been easily fixed by an editor who was paying attention... (Ah, can you tell I used to be an editor??)

This is the best of the three books. 
 The first two were lukewarm, but this one really connected with me. 
 Both the H/h were passionate and flawed and stubborn and imperfect. 
 That was the appeal I guess.

Eleven Scandals is the third book in the Love by Numbers series and it features Juliana Fiori and Simon Pearson, Duke of Leighton (we know him as the fiance of Lady Penelope in A Rogue by Any Other Name). 
 Ridiculously Short Plot 
 Juliana Fiori and Simon Pearson try to fight their attraction for each other but fail. Simon ends up rescuing Juliana from all sorts of scandalous behavior and the two fall in love in the process. 
 Main Characters 
 Juliana Fiori - Italian half sister of the Marquess of Ralston (their mother ran off and married an Italian merchant) 
 Simon Pearson - Duke of Leighton AKA The Duke of Disdain is a stickler for propriety and hates scandals with a vengeance 
 Themes 
 Love/Hate 
 different social class 
 Thoughts 
 I enjoyed reading this book but it isn't one of my favorites. I like Simon but Juliana, however, is another story. I love the chemistry between Juliana and Simon. Despite there being not much s-e-x going on, every meeting with these two had sparks flying all over the page. Their witty banter is awesome and totally Sarah MacLean. 
 Overall, the plot moved pretty fast for me and it was enjoyable. 
 Recommendations 
 I recommend reading Nine Rules to Break when Romancing A Rake, the first book in the series.

Perhaps that's because my personal preference is for action, and not romance, but I would have liked to see the action fleshed out a bit more and the relational drama tightened up."

book_a.title: The Snow Child
book_a.user_review:

 Read the rest of Ann's review on the library's blog.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I really loved this book and even sent my mom a copy of it after reading it. 
 The writing style is lovely and describes the beauty and wilderness of Alaska in a romantic yet realistic way.
Such a lovely, magical novel! Full review (including some of my favorite quotes) here: http://jennakunc.hubpages.com/hub/The...
beautifully written

This book is a clear echo of a pattern that I have seen in a lot of modern fiction where the beginning third of the novel is full of robust themes, characters, and potential only to be weighed down by a subsequent couple hundred pages of dull, meaningless, confused, and underdeveloped story and set of characters. By the last 20 pages of this book, I was so disappointed at where the author took this story. 
 At first, this is a tale about two struggling and depressed people longing for a child to raise on their own bleeding with themes of loss, longing, and love marked by the introduction of the titled character who offers life, love, joy, and sorrow to the plot. The story is full of all sorts of fantasy and mystery and growth for all the characters involved. It was truly a beautiful build into what ultimately was a hugely missed opportunity. Around the halfway point, the novel morphed into a lame and rushed love story between two young adults, completely ignorant of the previous characters and themes that were so wonderfully built up. It almost seemed like the two halves of the novel were two different books...the latter of which being so shallow and empty that I almost forgot about the wonder of the first. 
 Luckily, the ending of the book reverts back to the initial protagonists and re-emits the beauty of the themes and substance that the first half of the novel had presented. If only that second act's nonsense hadn't been in there vying to be the majority mass of the story, this book could've been a real favorite of mine. 
 The first half and the ending were great enough to warrant a worthwhile reading experience and a three-star rating. But with that mess in the middle-to-late parts of the book, I can't give it any more than that, though I wish it had been more.
I've got to think about this one a little more before I write a review. I may come back and give it a five.

The story tended to drag a bit. I got tired of waiting for the next reveal. At first,I was disappointed at the ending, but after I thought about it for a while, it intrigued me and I started wondering just what the snow child really was. In the begining, you were led to believe that she was spirit, but spirits don't have babys. Over all I have a hard time getting through the story because it was so sad and a bit different. The protagonist (Mable) had no antagonist to fight, nor any conflicts to resolve. 
 Surprisingly I enjoyed reading about the Author's life more than the book. I can really relate to her.
A beautiful story.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I loved the first half of this book. A middle aged childless couple in 1920's Alaska build a snow girl one stormy night and soon after, Faina comes into their lives wearing the snow girl's mittens and hat. The scenes of the snowball fight, the chicken plucking, the evolving friendship with the Benson's and the setting of building a life in the harsh wilderness were all wonderful. The is-she-or-isn't-she-real-ness of Faina was intriguing and I found myself as happy as Mabel with the little life they built. 
 Then several years go by and I found myself really struggling with the path the story takes. Mabel and Jack are getting old and so is Faina. Then Faina and the Benson's son fall in love and the story no longer seems magical. The fact that Faina gets really feverish when she is inside isn't enough to keep me believing in her. And frankly, if she isn't magic, then the story loses much of its appeal for me. Now of course, in the end, I can't say she wasn't magical. Ivey brings us back to the magic in the end but in a way that didn't seem especially climactic. In fact, I found myself asking, "That's it??" I wonder if she just didn't know how to bring this lovely world to closure.
Loved this book. It was like a fairy tale for big people. It was absorbing and joyful. Loved every page.

I didn't think I liked magical realism, but it turns out I just hadn't found the right book to pull me in, ground me in a reality, then sprinkle magic in a way that is wondrous and enchanting, and leaves you puzzling throughout - is it magic or is it real? The Snow Child was this book for me. 
 Set in the wilderness of 1920s interior Alaska, The Snow Child is the story of a aging couple who have moved west from Pennsylvania to homestead in Alaska in an effort to escape an emptiness left by their stillborn child. A two hour horse ride to the nearest "town" and then a train ride away from Anchorage, Mabel and Jack become isolated even from each other, grieving while they labor separately to make workable land from wilderness. One night, they succumb to the magic of a snowfall, and in laughter and joy, they build a child from snow. The next morning, the snow figure is gone, and a wildling girl appears in the forest. 
 The Snow Child chronicles the growing affection between Faina (the wildling) and the elderly couple, who over the years grow to think of her as their own, though she comes and goes without notice, and though they live with opposing stories of her flesh-and-blood father who Jack buried and the idea that Faina is a snow maiden of their creation, as Mabel read about in a Russian Fairy Tale. A tale that never ends well. 
 The magic in this book isn't just the obvious fairy tale quality of it. The magic is in the crystalline descriptions of Alaska in winter. Author Eowyn Ivey may not be Eskimo, but I would argue she has a thousand words for snow. Her descriptions are like snowflakes on the tongue - delicate, feathery crystals that sting with loveliness: 
 "The December days had a certain luminosity and sparkle, like frost on bare branches, alight in the morning just before it melts." 
 "Dawn broke silver over the snowdrifts and spruce trees." 
 "The child was dusted in crystals of ice, as if she had just walked through a snowstorm or spent a brilliantly cold night outdoors." 
 "The cranberries were tiny red rubies against the white snow." 
 "Around the curve the valley opened up, and in the distance spires of blue ice glowed. 
 This is a biting and beautiful book of love: love for neighbors, of husband and wife, for children, and love for the wild pull of the land, the forest, the snow, and the wilderness. It is one I will come back to when I want the magic of a winter landscape.

book_b.title: The Engagements
book_b.user_review:
"Some reviewers complain that The Engagements develops too slowly. I think this was part of the book's charm. It is not static; the story keeps progressing, I just wasn't sure where it was going. Most chapters end suspensefully, and the following chapter might move to a different set of characters, so I wanted to keep listening to learn how each story played out. Some books with complicated plots leave loose ends. The Engagements does not." 
 Check out the rest of Michelle's review on the library's blog: http://carnegiestout.blogspot.com/201...

sample_reviews.review_text:
Evelyn has been married to her husband for forty years--forty years since he slipped off her first wedding ring and put his own in its place. Delphine has seen both sides of love--the ecstatic, glorious highs of seduction, and the bitter, spiteful fury that descends when it's over. James, a paramedic who works the night shift, knows his wife's family thinks she could have done better; while Kate, partnered with Dan for a decade, has seen every kind of wedding--beach weddings, backyard weddings, castle weddings--and has vowed never, ever, to have one of her own. 
 As these lives and marriages unfold in surprising ways, we meet Frances Gerety, a young advertising copywriter in 1947. Frances is working on the De Beers campaign and she needs a signature line, so, one night before bed, she scribbles a phrase on a scrap of paper: "A Diamond Is Forever." And that line changes everything. 
 As I read each of the vignettes that seemingly had nothing in common with each other, especially since we skipped ahead years to focus on the characters in each of the spotlighted times, this tale felt a little like a collection of short stories. The common element: diamonds. And specifically, engagement rings. 
 Some of the characters and their lives were more enjoyable than others....and at times, I was weary of trying to remember the characters from the previous stories about them. But gradually, as more details surfaced with each leap in time, and as more backstory was revealed, I started to feel connected to them. 
 In the end, many loose ends seemingly converged to reveal the mysterious connections between them all. "The Engagements" is an intriguing story that I would have enjoyed more if it hadn't "sprawled" quite so much. Nevertheless, a book I'd recommend to Sullivan fans...and those who like to think of how much "serendipity" plays a role in our lives. 3.5 stars.

I read Maine, which I found entertaining, while at the same time, the book rung with such truth and realistic characters. I feel the same about this novel. I love the various storylines Sullivan creates and then her ability to weave them together subtly left me wanting more. Often, I've found, when other authors attempt this style, the details feel absurd and the meeting of stories forced. Anyway, this one has inspired me to read her first novel, Commencement.

I thoroughly enjoyed this novel even though it had multiple narrators. I thought the author did an excellent job at developing all the characters and capturing the time periods she placed them in. At the end she acknowledges her friends who helped aide in her research and who assisted her. I highly recommend thus book.

An interesting look at the concepts of love, commitment, engagement, marriage, and relationships in general. Five stories - one factual, the rest fiction - weave together in interesting ways. Not all of the characters are loveable, but neither are they completely abhorrent; the dichotomy keeps the reader interested.

I was excited for this book because J. Courtney Sullivan's Commencement is one of my favorite books, but this was not good. Most of the characters in this story were annoying or unsympathetic, like the French lady who cheats on her husband and leaves him to go to America then relentlessly complains about it and goes nuts when he cheats on her. It was so bad I never even actually read the endings to most of the storylines. I'll still read her next book but bleh.

I enjoyed reading this book and was saddened when one of my book podcasts unintentionally gave away a spoiler that I don't think they realized was a spoiler. Reese Witherspoon supposedly has acquired the rights to make this into a movie and I believe it could turn out great. I can easily see this book being adapted into a screenplay.
I was surprised by how much I liked this book- the characters were fantastic.

Really wasn't crazy about this book, which surprised me because I adored Commencement. Perhaps reading it on a Kindle was a mistake, because with such a large cast of independent characters and plot lines, referring back to previous chapters is almost a necessity. I was also bored by some sections of the book that read more like middle school book reports on the history of diamonds, Nazi war crimes, etc. 
 There were parts of the book that I enjoyed - and I certainly stuck around to figure out how all of the story lines would intersect at the end - but this is not a book that I would recommend to others.

What I Liked: 1) My favorite part of this story was following the timeline. What the summary doesn't tell you is that at the very core, this story is about a ring, one diamond engagement ring and how it follows these different couples over the span of about 80 years. The story itself covers about 100 years. It begins with the initial inception of the De Beers campaign slogan "A Diamond is Forever," and then through the progression of the different generations of couples, it proves how true that statement is. Sometimes I have trouble following a story with a lot of characters. But this one is done very well, and because they are from different generations, it is easy to follow. It examines how the concept of relationships, engagements, and marriage has changed throughout the years. I loved this part of it, it was beautifully written and thoroughly explained. 2) The characters. This is the part of the review where I typically choose a favorite character and talk about what I liked about them. It's really hard to pick a favorite in this book because they were all so wonderfully different. They were all developed themselves, but also as a part of a couple, and it was their relationships that created the majority of the story lines. There was so much complexity involved in this story but it did not hinder the book in the slightest. Instead, it only made it richer. 
 What I Didn't Like: Nothing! 
 Overall Thoughts: I'm actually having a hard time putting into words what exactly I loved about this book. I'm sure part of it was that it was so different that what I'm usually reading, and it's always refreshing to step outside the norm. But The Engagements was a lovely and fulfilling novel without being fluffy. It also never crossed the line into dark either. Have y'all noticed that in YA fiction it seems to be one or the other? Fluffy or dark? Maybe that's what is so great about branching out into adult fiction, at least every once in a while. This is the second book I've picked up after seeing it in Entertainment Weekly and really enjoyed (the other being Crazy Rich Asians). I'm going to have to start checking out more books EW recommends! The Engagements is one of my favorite books I've read recently. The plot itself comes alive as you travel through the life of a diamond and how it represents love to many couple throughout the years. It's beautiful, complex, and very rich and I think that EVERYONE will enjoy it! 
 My Rating: 5 shots 
 See this and other reviews at Fuzzy.Coffee.Books!
A little confusing .

reference_books.title: Guess How Much I Love You
reference_books.review_text: Saccharine. This is the kind of book that is popular with book buyers (parents, grandparents, godparents) not children. What kind of loving parent would try to one-up his or her child in this way. Icky. Gave it away, which is very rare for me.

reference_books.title: A Year Down Yonder (A Long Way from Chicago, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
I thoroughly enjoyed this book. A few of the situations felt a little contrived, and the ending was rather pat. However, the larger-than-life characters made up for these shortcomings. 
 I do wonder about the appeal of this book to today's young readers. It reminded me of the sorts of books I devoured when I was a tween. What do generations Y and Z think about teenaged girls who admire their grandmas? Someone drop me a line if they have an opinion about this.

reference_books.title: Jeremy Fink and the Meaning of Life
reference_books.review_text:
Jeremy Fink is a slightly eccentric boy trying to come to terms with his father's untimely death. His partner in crime is an equally misfit Lizzy. The two of them together have a safe adventure involving a mysterious locked box and the quest for the keys to unlock it. 
 The tale is reminiscent of The Westing Game. 
 My son, who usually will only read fantasy, read and enjoyed Jeremy Fink. The story is sweet, but not sentimental or cloying. It would be a good book for a precocious reader; although it does deal with the subject of grieving, it is not "raw."

reference_books.title: Born Standing Up: A Comic's Life
reference_books.review_text: This is a provocative book about the creative process and professionalizing the creative process. It was not as humorous as I thought it would be.

reference_books.title: Speak
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 Nearly perfect novel. Poignant without being overwritten. The terrible thing that happened to narrator Melinda at the party where she called the cops is not the subject of a lot of false suspense, but there is a satisfying twist at the end. The friendship-of-convenience between her and the new girl at school rang particularly true.

book_a.title: The Historian
book_a.user_review: Could not even finish this dreck.

sample_reviews.review_text: At times, this book held my interest, but too often I was frustrated with the pace and the shifting points of view. Perhaps my expectations were simply too high?

Although this story got a little slow in parts, I still loved it. I listened to this one and the narration was superb. If you are looking for blood, guts, and gore, this story is not what you're looking for. This is a tale of Dracula told from a more scholarly standpoint. In actuality, I would probably rate this 4 1/2 stars. I am going to bump it up to 5 stars because the narration was that good. I loved it.

Peripherally about the hunt for Vlad the Impaler, king of the vampires who still stalks the earth, this novel is really a heartfelt ode to scholarly research and travel. If you are not interested in research, books or travel, this book is not for you. I enjoyed doing side research on the fascinating places and historical details Kostova uses to create her book. Amazing scholarship, well-developed characters and a slow-moving, but intriguing nest of stories which span from the 1400s to the present with just enough vampire horror to bring an edge. A very unique reading experience.

I've been quite unexcited and neutral to it until - of course - the vampire turns out to be a book collector (as if there was nothing else) AND gets killed by a few so largely incomentent and harmless people. And there's more: the usual medieval brotherhood. I quite liked the first half though. 
 A very positive thing to say about it is that it helps you to sleep quickly and reliably, and that you won't get addicted.

This was a really un satisfying book for me. It's a story about a woman who is hunting down Dracula. It was not scary nor thrilling at any point. Really long descriptions of cities and buildings and probably the most disappointing ending ever. Didn't develop a relationship with any of the character either, although I'm not sure why that was.

I enjoyed the first half of this book and although some people said it was slow I enjoyed the suspense, it just seemed to drag on forever though towards the end and I really got bored with it which is a shame because I did enjoy the mystery of this book. So initially I would have give it an 8/10 but because of the slowness I give it a 6/10

Akhirnya selesai juga baca buku ini. 1.5 bulan. Lamaa yaa hehe. Mood2an bacanya, to gak mau di skip juga. 
 Jadi ini cerita ttg folklore vampire, asal mulanya dr Transyvlania, Romania. 
 Vlad Tepes III dari Wallachia adalah Dracula. Dracula itu legenda banget buat negara Eropa Timur. Kenapa muncul Dracula? Gak lain buat membunuh pasukan Ottoman. Eng ing eng. jd ceritanya Ottoman meluaskan daerah kekuasaannya, selain merebut Byzantium. Raja Mehmet membutuhkan banyak pasukan untuk berperang, jadi mengambil dan menculik anak2 dr beberapa daerah jajahannya. Dibawa ke Byzantium, dilatih kemudian dijadikan tentara Ottoman. 
 Di buku ini sih menceritakan Raja Mehmet itu kejam, tukang perang, jahat, intonasi negatif lah. Kemenangan atas constatinopel itu dianggap the greatest tragedy in history. Bias banget. Kayak Ottoman itu jelek bener, padahal dimana2 yg namanya perang dan penaklukan pasti melakukan hal2 tersebut. 
 Nah si Vlad Tepes ini melawan pasukan ottoman dengan menjadi vampire, the undead. Dracula itu artinya anak dr dragon, semacam garis keturunan gitu. 
 Ceritanya seru, cuma sedikit kecewa dgn endingnya. 
 Paul, seorang ahli sejarah, menemukan buku yg aneh bgt, kayak dikasih ke dia dgn cara yg aneh. Ternyata buku itu juga ditemukan oleh beberapa ahli sejarah lainnya, lintas negara. Buku itu menggambarkan naga, lambang keluarga Dracula. Dan petualangan di mulai, ke Hungaria, Bulgaria, Romania, Perancis dan Amerika. Dracula ini masih hidup, ternyata Dracula itulah yg memberika buku2 mIsterius itu kepada beberapa ahli sejarah-the historian. Mengapa? Spoiler bgt deh

I like history and vampires, so I was excited when I received this for Christmas. First of all, let me say that I did like the book, but was dancing for joy when I was done. The book is interesting, but way too long. It is not a hard read, but I felt the author just added information to give the book substance. The information she added was interesting(would be even more interesting if it was true), but definitely not needed. The author also constantly changed the narrator; this threw me at first, but I eventually got the hang of it.

Being one of the fledgling librarians and vampire enthusiasts of this world, I could hardly resist a hefty novel in which Dracula preys on scholars throughout history in order to staff his rare and incredible hidden library - the product of centuries of careful selection. What a beauty of an idea! Unfortunately executed, however. The characters are a little flat, the plot driven by coincidence and there are certain screamingly obvious (to me) themes that are totally ignored - for instance, some sort of incredulity about the fact that Vlad Tepes is still wandering about? The numerous historians of the story are indeed horrified about the prospect of meeting the undead but seem to be able to accept it willingly enough, which seems a little odd for academics dedicated to discerning the truth. And wouldn't part of any historian be secretly (or openly) delighted to meet the legendary Vlad Tepes in the (dubious) flesh? Particularly when he turns out to be such an ardent scholar. I found him rather endearing. Anyway, for all that, it is quite a nice read (lots of descriptive meandering passages through Europe, in and out churches etc) and I'm glad I got through all of it.

Well... That was not what I expected. At all. 
 I am so disappointed this book didn't work for me. It has Dracula in it. FREAKIN' DRACULA! Who doesn't love the undead?! 
 But somehow this book is so effing boring. I honestly didn't think it would end. And if it hadn't been recommended by my mom, I would have given up on it early on... 
 This book gave me some Goldfinch vibes. Not in content, but both are relatively well rated, over 700 pages, and bring-tears-to-my-eyes boring.

book_b.title: Pictures of Hollis Woods
book_b.user_review: Very enjoyable story about a girl in foster care. Another take on the Gilly Hopkins situation, in other words. I felt like Giff was a too easy on her main character--there was no price to pay for her mistakes. Moreover, the portrait of Hollis was somewhat unbelievable, in that she is supposed to be such a "mountain of trouble" who has been in the foster care system for all ten years of her life, and yet all we ever see from her is care and consideration for others. However, the characters are well-drawn and likeable and the plot is engaging.

sample_reviews.review_text: It was a good book. But I did got confused from here to there.

Vaguely, I recall reading Pictures of Hollis Woods when I was young, but as it often is, adulthood puts a different spin on youthful memories. Hollis is a young orphan, and a self-proclaimed "mountain of trouble." Only she makes most of those troubles for herself. After a while, it's frustrating that she doesn't see this. While the subject matter is right up my alley--foster care, specifically--I felt the narrative dragged on too long. I will say that Giff is a master of showing, rather than telling. The book is all aching, breathing feeling.

This book may be for young readers but it is better written than some adult novels that I have read. 
 Never heard of the author or the book until it surfaced in a box of books given to me. Quick easy read that didn't feel as if I had wasted 2hours of my life.
This was a great book. I think I want to own it. And read it again.

Eah. This is a some-what popular book in our school, and honestly, I didn't like it. I read it in two sittings, and yeah, no. The writing is really hard to follow, and I didn't like how it was done. The story line was simple, but truthful, and I think something most of my students can relate to on some level- wanting the perfect family. 
 However, it seems a bit low for my students, but I think the writing style would be too confusing for our students who are at that reading level.
This was a very touching book of hope. It was a quick read.

Considering this was a middle grade book, this was an excellent story about a young girl its 13 in the foster system who finds a family that loves her. There was some struggles to overcome and some story about her finding herself basically.
This book was very touching.

Hollis Woods is a place. A lonely place. Dumped on a corner as a baby, Hollis' only wish is for a family of her own. After so many mistakes she finally finds one, only to mess it up. Or so it seems...

This was a really great book about the foster care system told from a child's perspective. Hollis is a sweet little girl who just can't catch a break and then when she does she can't believe that a family can actually love her for herself.

reference_books.title: All the Birds in the Sky
reference_books.review_text:
I was sadly disappointed by All the Birds in the Sky. 
 It has a very strange premise and I felt the writing styled paired really well with this weird narrative. 
 My biggest pet peeve was the story itself. There was a clear point to this story and it felt like the characters got lost in the midst. I loved the beginning when we followed our main characters through their childhood, but once they reach adulthood their story lines are rushed to fulfill this ulterior purpose. 
 The book was pretty short, just over 300 pages. Maybe if it was longer, that story could be hashed out a little better. 
 Overall I'm happy I read it, but it's not one of my better reads for the year.

reference_books.title: 100 Sideways Miles
reference_books.review_text: Hilarious

reference_books.title: Sweet Evil (Sweet, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I did enjoy this book; but aside for the authors take on angels & demons I feel like I've read this story before. Oh well, I'll still read the other books, lets be real.

reference_books.title: Illuminae (The Illuminae Files, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I knew going in that I was either going to love or hate this given the unique way this story is told, and it definitely felt like a miss for me. I had a hard time connecting to the characters and the plot with how broken the story telling felt. At around page 400 I got more invested, but it was a drag up until then. This just was not for me. I dont think I'll be picking up the other books.

reference_books.title: The Strange Library
reference_books.review_text: This was enjoyable but very odd...

book_a.title: Hidden Bodies (You, #2)
book_a.user_review:
'Hidden Bodies' is the greatly anticipated sequel to the chilling thriller, 'You'. We pick up right where we left off with everyone's favorite psychopathic killer, Joe, though this time around the thrill factor was just a little on the low side. 
 'You' felt very fresh and inventive, but 'Hidden Bodies' lacked that with the change from second person and what felt like an aimless plot. 
 The first fourth of the book had so much promise but the rest was just all over the place... I don't know what happened to Joe, but all his antics just lost meaning and felt quite repetitive. 
 If you haven't read it yet, I would highly recommend 'You' but 'Hidden Bodies'... not so much.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I enjoyed the prequel to this book, "You" and was interested in seeing what would happen between Joe and Amy, as he chases her to L.A. to continue his psychopathic stalking. There he finds a completely different world and a new set of challenges - as well as a new surrogate family to insert himself into but he continues to be himself - a narcissistic serial killer stalker who thinks he's being a perfectly rational person. It's well written and Joe is still an intelligent and likeable guy (considering what we now know about him!) but it didn't have as many pop culture / literary references in it, it focused more on the life of the Hollywood elite. 
 Sadly I didn't feel that this book had quite the same level of originality and believability as the first book. Everything just seems to fall into Joe's lap, and his relationship with Love always had a too-good-to-be-true feel to it for me, even more so as the book progressed towards the finale. In the spirit of keeping this spoiler free, I'll simply say that that the lack of believability in their relationship removed most of the tension and suspense for me, but I did enjoy the ending, and would still recommend it for those who want to continue following Joe's journey - but definitely read "You" first.
This was so underwhelming and You was so much better.
Joe is just as fascinating as he was in "You." He's just as hopelessly romantic as he is poetically dangerous. I'm officially hooked. I'm looking forward to Caroline Kepnes' next book.

Not as good as the first book but still original and compelling. The whole story is so simple yet so complex, plus I just love Joe, what a charming Psychopath! I feel a bit creepy for loving this books so much though, thanks for that Ms Kepnes :D

And sometimes I really don't get the hype. 
 American Psycho meet Fifty Shades of Grey meets Popculture meets bullshit. 
 I really just listened to it beacuse the reader is doing such a fantasic job.

The first part in this series is one of my favorite books so I can't deny I had high hopes for this one. Not that I ever expect a part two to be as good as part one but I have looked forward to this one thinking it would be a nice read given how spellbound I was by the first. But this did not thrill me, I did not connect to or feel for the characters and the book quickly became repetetive and way to much. The first one was a lot to take in but nothing even near this one. 
 If you are considering the series my recommendation would be: read the first book only. It works well on its own and you don't need this one.
For me, this lacked the magic of the first book. The Love & Joe storyline grew tiresome.

It's official, Caroline Kepnes is now one of my favorite authors. Her writing is simply brilliant! From her pop culture references and beyond. It is no easy feat to make a deranged serial killer likable. I found Joe enduring and oddly sweet at times.. Don't get me wrong, the dude is still beyond, beyond insane with the way he uses murder to fix his problems and inconveniences, but you can't help but root for him. 
 "A book lets you choose how much of the blood you want to see. A book gives you the permission to see the story as you want, as your mind directs. You interpret. Your Alexander Portnoy doesn't look like mine because we all have our own unique view. When you finish a movie you leave the theater with your friend and talk about the movie right away. When you finish a book you think." 
 I mean, my word.. the truth in this quote, as well as the many truths with respect to modern culture. The flow of this book, the feeling and thoughts that were provoked.. I'm going to stop here and I've avoided speaking on the story line as I do not want to give any spoilers on either book. This series, these characters, this author.. yes, yes, YES! I need a third book ASAP!

DNF at page 84 
 I wasn't kidding when I said this is the worst book I've ever read. This is seriously the worst book I've ever read. Every other book I actually finished and awarded one star and every other book I never finished because it sucked... all of those books are a million times better than this garbage that masquerades itself as a book. 
 Caroline Kepnes has to be a pseudonym for a thirteen year old boy who just learned about sex from his friend and spends his days watching porn and eating Cheetos. This is the most poorly written excuse for a book ever, and Kepnes can't put a sentence together without something explicit, sexual or otherwise. There are so many more deserving authors who could benefit from a glimmer of the spotlight she has somehow drunkenly staggered herself into these days. 
 There is not one redeeming quality about this book. It's pretentious, disgusting, uninspired, juvenile, immature, pathetic, and sad. It deserves no place in any bookstore or library, and all copies of this book should be burned or buried somewhere so we can all forget it was ever written.

Our favorite psycho killer is back in this one and is even creepier. I think what is so creepy is how I find myself liking Joe. I find myself relating to Joe. What the hell does that say about me? 
 Joe is back with a whole new slew of bodies adding up. He takes off after Amy his current girlfriend, but in the process of locating her, he meets Love. But the question is, is Love enough? Can Joe change his crazy ways? 
 I feel like Joe grows in this book. Granted he is still batshit crazy, but still he matures. There were things I didn't expect in this book and things I was able to figure out quickly. Either way I really enjoyed this book and being in Joe's demented mind. Once again I also loved the way this was written. It does take a minute to adjust to it again, but it just works so well. 
 3.5 stars! 
 ***ARC provided from the Publisher via Netgalley in exchange for an HONEST review. Thank you!***

book_b.title: A Monster Calls
book_b.user_review: That was beautiful and haunting. My heart is breaking.

sample_reviews.review_text: If you've ever lost someone you love, perhaps to a long, drawn-out illness, then please, please, read this book. It is heart-breaking, gut-wrenching, healing and possibly life-changing, all at the same time, and you'll be glad to have read it at the end.

I mean, it was good. It got me out of my reading slump, but like I didn't really have any emotional attachment to this story? Like I know sooo many people who cried while reading it but for some reason I didn't?

Like wow. This book had been on my radar when it first was published about five years ago with rave reviews. And then I saw the cover and thought "Nah, I'm not ready for a horror book right now." So so wrong. Talk about judging a book by its cover! Sheesh. Thankfully, I saw the trailer for the movie recently and moved the book up on my priority list. You know that you have to read the book before you see the movie, right? Back to wow. Written by Patrick Ness but based on a story idea started by Siobhan Dowd before she died, this is a story of a young man shouldering the burdens of fear, guilt, anger, and social instability and who needs help from a monster. It is wise and sensitive. And the characters very real. Yes, even with a monster in the story. I'd say more but you should have all the details for yourself as you read. Cleverly written and a true gem. Loved it!
This was fine. I understand why so many people found this very emotional and moving, but other than tearing up a little on the very last page, I didn't really connect with this.
Gut-wrenching. Do not read this unless you're ready to cry.

What a beautiful, heartbreaking book. 
 I think a regular live action movie will still manage to capture the book, the whole time I was reading it I was imagining it in the style of a Studio Laika film, and I'm a bit disappointed that that's not what it's going to be.

"Stories were wild, wild animals and went off in directions you couldn't expect." 
 Never has a sentence from a book been more fitting for the book itself! Wowza! This book was amazing! I had times where I was just crying-sometimes it was just because it was lyrically beautiful! It was so sad and yet full of courage and human spirit. It's about speaking the truth and acceptance. It's about fighting to be seen and heard. The illustrations are amazing! I found myself studying them because they were so cool! I cried when the tenderness of the mom was displayed. She was beautiful. Her love for her son was beautiful. I think my mind is still reeling a little bit from it all! Sorry if the review is a bit jumbled-I tend to get that way after a book that I REALLY REALLY liked! :D 
 "Because humans are complicated beasts, the monster said. How can a queen be both a good witch and a bad witch? How can a prince be a murderer and a saviour? How can an apothecary be evil-tempered but right-thinking? How can a parson be wrong-thinking but good-hearted? How can invisible men make themselves more lonely by being seen? The answer is that it does not matter what you think, the monster said, because your mind will contradict itself a hundred time each day. Your mind will believe comforting lies while also knowing the painful truths that make those lies necessary. And your mind will punish you for believing both. 
 "But how do you fight it?" Connor asked, his voice rough. "How do you fight all the different stuff inside?" 
 By speaking the truth, the monster said. As you spoke it just now. Stop this, Conor O'Malley, the monster said, gently. This is why I came walking, to tell you this so that you may heal. You must listen. 
 Conor swallowed again. "I'm listening." 
 You do not write your life with words, the monster said. You write it with actions. What you think is not important. It is only important what you do."

My 11-year-old read this book and after reading Patrick Ness' Chaos trilogy I thought it would be interesting to sample something else by him. Bleh. The prose was fine, but every narrative move was utterly predictable. Even my 11-year-old thought so. It's main redeeming quality was listening to the audio performance by Jason Isaacs (of Lucius Malfoy fame). That man can act.

In both style and content, this book is reminiscent of Neil Gaiman's books for young readers, a very favorable comparison. The illustration style highlights the narrative rather than distracting from it. The main character and his emotions are very relatable, regardless of the reader's age or life circumstances. While the story was very short, it was moving enough to bring tears to my eyes at the end.
Such an amazing story!

book_a.title: Left Neglected
book_a.user_review: Different than Still Alice but still good. A little bit repetative at times but interesting

sample_reviews.review_text: As much as I loved Stil Alice, I disliked this book. Why is it always a fast-paced life of a Harvard super-achiever versus a part-time job for a mom of three kids. So predictable it hurts.

Busy professional mom has severe brain damage - can't 'see' or orient to the left. Difficulty with acceptance of her limitations and the changing dynamic of her family and relationships. 
 Acceptance is hard won: 
 I laugh, releasing all fear and vengeful emotion from my heart, replacing it with an open-armed acceptance and empathy that extends first to Charlie... then it reaches Ms. Gavin in her ugly shoes.. And then it stretches to include myself.

While the topic was interesting, the main character was self absorbed, self important, immature, and obnoxious. She set herself up for her accident because of these traits. She could have injured or killed others with her driving style. This is chick lit with a brain injury.

Full disclosure... I did not finish this book, after reading a little over half I skipped to the end, read the last chapter and called it good. 
 I hated the main character from the start, she was not appealing or likable at all (playing rock paper scissors so you don't have to drive your kids to school and then being mad that you lost? leaving your baby in the car because his car seat is too heavy? seriously, I hated this woman). The weird dream things at the beginning of the early chapters were distracting and pointless. I get that the book is about left neglect and not recognizing left as a concept, but when every 10th word is left and every third sentence is "I can't see my left" I was ready to scream. The constant brand dropping(Cartier watch, Jimmy Choo heels, Harvard education)were unnecessary, it felt like every single thing had to have a name brand in front, it could never be "my car" or "my bag". When I skipped to the last chapter of course she had figured out that family is the most important, but I wasn't willing to read how she got there.

Sarah is a very career oriented woman who is left with a traumatic brain injury that completely changes the world as she knows it. 
 First of all, I have to say that I kept checking the little library tag to make sure this wasn't an autobiography. It's told in first person and the details, thoughts, and feelings shared with the reader, both before the accident and afterwards, were very real. Not only is Sarah dealing with a very demanding job, but she's also trying to juggle the many hats of a wife and mother and the accident couldn't have happened at a worse time. 
 Secondly, I thought, because of the nature of the story, this would be a very dark and depressing book, but it really wasn't. It was told in a very matter-of-fact way and there were always little glimpses of hope that became reality. 
 I liked the message, intended or not, that family is what truly matters--not a big house, vacation home, nanny, money, etc. It's kind of sad that it took this accident for Sarah to realize this. I love how things ended up, although the ending felt a little rushed to me, given how much detail was spent on the first 95% of the book. 
 Content: there are a handful of cuss words; there are two mentions of intimate moments (or lack of), with the second being a little more straightforward (not erotic, by any means) and fades to black before details are given--it is between a married couple.

Sarah's life left me fatigued, just reading about it. A Harvard Business School graduate, she had a high powered executive job with a company that considers forty hours a week to be a parttime schedule. She also has three kids, a husband, a second home in Vermont, and a desire to have anything else that she was possibly missing in life. I admit that I had very little sympathy for her until some misfortune entered her life. Lisa Genova's writing immediately connected me to all of her characters. They jumped out of the page like people I actually knew. I zipped through this book, eager to find out what happened next and it never disappointed me.
I loved this book! The whole story is centered around a woman who has a horrific car accident and ends up with TBI. Her injury doesn't defeat her and her struggles and life changes are inspiring!
Heartfelt and really makes you think about how you live your life. Only problem is that it dragged a bit and the kids' personalities were a bit one-dimensional.

3.5 rounded up. There's no comparison (content-wise) to Still Alice because in that case, it's a disease that was slowly crippling Alice with no recovery and this situation was the cause of an accident with a possible recovery. To me Alzheimer's is a much more scary disease even though both these have to do with mental capacities. 
 The writing was very good in both cases (although this ending was too good-to-be-true). I sympathized greatly with the grandmother. Can you imagine being in your 60s-70s and suddenly taking care of a whole household, 3 small children and helping with physical therapy? 
 Just as in Still Alice, this family really had no money worries, lack of insurance or lack of help. Yes, the physical therapy ended when the insurance carrier said it did, but at least their insurance included physical therapy. They had some money pressure but hey, selling off one of your houses is a dream most people wish they had. 
 I can see why they didn't make a movie of this because most adults would squirm when seeing Sarah's actions that caused the accident. But put the shoe on the other foot--have the main character be a teen and it would be made and shown at all high schools.
A good story but a slow paced book. Honestly I couldn't wait to finish the book. Just not my cup of tea.

book_b.title: The Unlikely Pilgrimage of Harold Fry (Harold Fry, #1)
book_b.user_review: I wanted to like this book more than I did. Harold sets off one day to mail a letter to an old friend who is dying of cancer and just keeps walking. The first part of his walk where he is alone and reflecting on his life are good and then other people join and it just gets bit silly. It seemed a little drawn out in the last 100 pages and somewhat unlikely.

sample_reviews.review_text: This is a great book. A book that makes you feel things. A book that makes you want things. I am familiar with these emotions as someone who most always wants something or other. But I was unprepared for the heartbreaking beauty of the story. Harold Fry walked straight into my heart. As a fan of any book, movie, play, or piece of music about the need to go - wander - explore - this book called to me. And I wasn't disappointed. If you're looking for something in your life you have not yet found, this book may become something of a guide for you. You'll remember it when you're not sure about taking that next step or when you have to decide how far you're willing to go to know yourself, and be happy. The eclectic cast and descriptive landscape enhance every part of Harold's journey. As we walk with him, and stay home with Maureen, we're given access to a rare insight. That of what time and disappointment can do to a relationship. But we also see the hope there. We root for them to succeed and find one another again because we all need that hope of a happy ending. It's what drives us forward. Belief that we can change things if only we try hard enough. That's what Harold believed and it turns out, he was right.
A wonderful sweet story ..loved it..

This little book turned out be positively delightful. Harold goes off on this unplanned pilgrimage to see a old friend who did something for him years ago, and to whom he feels eternally grateful. She writes to say that she is dying, and that is the first that he has heard from her in years. 
 Along the way, Harold reflects on his life - his job, his relationship with his wife, and his relationship with his son. He makes some amends. He has some epiphanies. These are the things that you would generally expect from the premise. 
 The beauty of this book, is in things that you don't expect. (Or, in any case, I didn't.) The way other people become a part of his journey - either by motivating him, supporting him, or joining him for their own reasons. That was the heart of this book, for me: the way other people take inspiration from Harold's journey to make changes in their own lives. The essential human nature in the way people band together to support him - or quite the opposite. 
 This book turned out to be an unexpected gem.
Amazing....please, please read this amazing story of a man and mission.

Yawnnnnnn 
 Should have just walked away. 
 Again, I am out of step with the Reading Public. I found this was a bore and a disappointing read. 
 If it was meant to be "quirky", I found it cliched. If it was meant to be philosophical, I found it shallow. If it was meant to be endearing, I found it dreary and uninspiring. 
 And more than that, I found it poorly written. It ended abruptly. Character development was minimal and superficial. The sense of place, which could have been a real feature, was lacking, due to the poor use of descriptive devices. With a chance to paint a vivid picture, the author used a monotone palate.
Good book. Enjoyed it a lot.
Beautiful. Moving. Touching.

I'd probably give this 3 to 3.5 stars. I liked it, and there were a few parts that I really loved, but I didn't LOVE the entire story overall. 
 I did enjoy Harold, and being taken on his journey. I really enjoyed the way the story of his and Maureen's past slowly unfolded throughout the course of the story. It built a little bit of suspense, and felt like a puzzle that you were slowly piecing together. 
 I especially enjoyed Harold's walk during the early days of it, and while he was alone. I enjoyed encountering new people with him, and trying to figure things out along with him -- why was he going on this walk? What in his life led him to make this decision, and NOW? I also liked the mystery of why Queenie was so important to him. 
 Even more than Harold, though, I really enjoyed watching Maureen's transformation throughout the course of the book. Her relationship with Harold is so cold and non-existent at the outset of the story, and I liked that Maureen came more alive and appreciated Harold more once he was gone, and despite the fact that she didn't know if Harold actually left because he no longer cared for HER. I loved how her story unfolded, and how sympathetic I became to her by the end. 
 There were parts I didn't love, too -- the pacing was very slow for me, and this took me a lot longer to get through than most books. The band of travellers Harold finds himself with in the 2nd half of the book drove me crazy -- I know they were supposed to, but I still didn't like them. 
 Also, of the two main reveals in the book, one I actually (sort of) realized almost from the outset, while the other I felt like I should have seen coming, but didn't actually. Neither of them seemed particularly shocking or exciting in the end, I suppose, but it also wasn't that type of book. 
 One thing I will say is that I absolutely LOVED the final pages of the book. I thought they were so sweet, and such a perfect end to the journey that both Harold and Maureen had been on throughout the course of the telling.
My favourite book of all time. An endearing story about love and reconnecting

One line from this quirky little book that has stayed with me ever since I finished reading it- "But maybe it's what the world needs. A little less sense, and a little more faith". The book traces Harold Fry's trek from one end of England to the other, all in the belief that this will save his friend, Queenie Hennesey, whose cancer is slowly killing her. Through the journey, we are taken through Harold's life, and as he walks, we meet numerous other characters, all having their own fears, hopes, and worries. As Joyce so endearingly writes, "Harold could no longer pass a stranger without acknowledging the truth that everyone was the same, and also unique; and that this was the dilemma of being human." 
 A lovely heart warming read. I cannot wait to read the parallel story to this book, told from Queenie's point of view. Highly recommended :)

reference_books.title: Mockingjay (The Hunger Games, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
Read me and cry. Dis-app-oin-ted. 
 Spoilers Alert! 
 Catching Fire, maybe with slow beginning, but promising conclusion, leaved readers gasping and thinking. Mockingjay couldn't be bad, it just couldn't, how epic war between vicious Capitol and Rebells from long-forgotten lands can go bad, especially under a quill of Collins? 
 Impossible things happen, book is digestible, you can read it alright, kept me focused from time to time and had some great scenes. But this can't cover up actual badness (?) of novel. 
 First, begging, Katniss feels guilty, cool scene, good beginning, but Katniss... Isn't Katniss anymore, she barely thinks, get mind is influenced by others (Snow and Coin), she's weak and that makes her annoying, she starts to act like Bella, oh no! 
 District 13 is boring, vicious and grey, like everything in world of Panem, but reading about Seam or Capitol seemed interesting, while 13, not. 
 Katniss is mortal, we know it, but why does Collin make her suffer so much? She had survived fire, water, knives and guns; in Mockingjay she gets injured and faints a lot, I really mean it, good 70% of book is about Katniss sitting in hospital and recovering from attack. So, book is: 2 pages of mare action, 10 pages of pointless talking, page for character development and 20 pages for sitting in hospital (divide it by five to get entire book). 
 Collins also includes new characters which seem alright, plot is new, we are no longer in games, bad, Collins opens a lot of new stuff (e.g sneaky Coin, 13) they aren't interesting, but still, they are there, and Collins ends them, concludes new stuff, but what about old stuff, Districts and Capitol, Gale and Peeta, the answers for events we were waiting for since first book! Well, Collins seemed to forgot about them, and started to conclude boring stuff. 
 Did she have forgotten that this book is about Hunger Games, and we want to see how actual games end? But here we have, nothing about districts, about life after games, why did Katniss picked Peeta? Also Finnick, Collins treats him as a background character, while new character like Boggs gets more attention when dies. Collins, stop adding new and Finish old, we want it, that's the reason of conclusion!!! 
 I will give it 36/100, but I gave it one star because of real hater.

sample_reviews.review_text: It's a reading kind of night and I forgot how irresistible this kind of writing is.

DNF'd at 100(ish) pages. 
 I hate, hate, hated this book. I wanted to punch Tessa in the throat (and that's being kind) and Hardin was the biggest douche bag ever. There was nothing redeeming about the characters and their relationship was a giant cesspool of manipulation and abuse (and that after reading only 100 pages). 
 This book was awful. 
 If you're going to insist on reading a fan fiction to book adaptation, do yourself a favor and read 50 Shades. Yeah, I said it. Do something. 
 In conclusion, this book sucked. Do NOT waste your time on it, do NOT waste your money on it. I hated it.

** spoiler alert ** 
 When a book is recommended to you, you would think it to be good, eh? Wrong. So wrong. Never jump to conclusions. I just wasted a whole night reading this and could not even finish it. 
 Such a disappointment; when you start reading a book are unable to finish it. 
 I mean, don't get me wrong - I TRIED to finish it, hence why I got more than half of it done, but I honestly could not take it anymore. 
 She wants him, they kiss, he says mean things, they fight, she runs away etc. etc. it all goes back and forth. I'm just too tired of these females that don't know what they want and males that are just down to the point RUDE. That is not sexy, nor is it attractive, heck it's jot even feisty anymore. It's simply annoying. 
 Women don't want emotionally unavailable men that scream at you and treat you like sh*t, or am I totally in the dark with this one? 
 The worst part though, is when they are such bad characters that they can't even keep to their own characteristics! I mean, all those "shy smiles" and "blushes" coming from him creeped me out more than his screaming. And sure, it's understandable that these small reactions are thanks to Tessa but COME ON!!!! How on earth could he develop such strong feelings for her when he's known her for merely a month - during which he's only called her names and treated her like dirt. 
 And Tessa? No, I can not even go there, I mean the girl is more inexperienced and innocent than an actual saint, but given the opportunity she would just about jump Hardin's bones. Somewhat unrealistic. She gives in so easily and apparently seems to know what she is doing. Not to mention how much she thrives on the bad mouth if his, absolutely LOVING his crude language. 
 I don't know, I just found it really hard to enjoy this book. Perhaps the ending will be just about wonderful, not that it would make up for an otherwise awful book. I could not finish it. 
 It's hard to find a really good Wattpad book, but they do exist. Therefore it's just so sad seeing this one being published, translated into several languages and having so many reads. Wattpad is more that this! 
 No, sorry, but this is SO not my cup of tea. I rather like it when I can avoid rolling my eyes after every third sentence.
Why!?!!!?! Shame on me, but I have to know what happens next.

Did I really stay up 'til six. 
 I'm so crazy, oh god.

Book review moment of honesty - I have read some really embarrassing things in my life. This is one of them. I bought all three of the Fifty Shades books, paying in cash and buying in a book store so there is no digital record of my trashy book reading habits. I own all of the Twlight books, in hard cover. I have no shame when it comes to actually reading something, but plenty of shame when it comes to admitting that I've read it. Picture me while I'm writing this review wearing a bag on my head with eye holes cut out like the Unknown Comic from the "Gong Show" tv series from the 1970s. This is fan fiction, which, yes, I've read before. And fan fiction about a boy band that I have no particular interest in (One Direction - I'm old enough to be any of their moms). But, it was in the bargain bin at Barnes & Nobles (it was $4.95 less the B&N store membership discount). And, I'd heard of it and was looking for a light romance as we approach Valentine's Day. So, why not. Warning - this is kind of gross, so if you don't actually know what this book is about (the methodical deflowering of an innocent), you might want to take a pass on this review. This means you, Mom. 
 Then I read the description on the back, and it is exactly the premise that my husband hates. The "good girl" is bored with decent guys and wants to be with the guy who treats her like garbage. And she loves him for it. Only she can fix him with her love. Yes, it is insanely frustrating. My husband is a genuinely nice guy. And he's also hot and smart and funny and reads lot of books (mostly sci-fi, but he did just finish A Man Named Ove to appease me). He is a catch, and when I met him over a decade ago, he was 36 years old and had never been in a relationship that lasted "a whole year." So yeah, he has now. He was single a long time before that though, and saw a lot of disastrous relationships. And he hates it when women ignore it when a guy flat out tells her that he is bad news. I think one of his mottos is: "When someone tells you that they are a train wreck and you shouldn't date them, you should believe them." Whenever we see this in a movie or book, he just shakes his head at the stupidity. And he is right. If you date someone who says that they will treat you poorly, and then who does in fact treat you poorly, you have given them permission to treat you poorly. Value yourself more, ladies (and guys who also put up with entirely too much crap in the name of "love"). He is not a fan of relationship power games, and this book was nothing but head games. He shook his head all day Sunday when I was reading it (during the Superbowl when Atlanta laid an egg and lost in OT after a commanding early lead). But, I didn't care, I was reading this book, despite how dumb it was. 
 This is smack your head with your hand level of stupid when it comes to Tessa's "attraction" to Hardin. And, I can't even type that name. Good lord, Anna Todd, you are naming your fake Harry Styles, Mr. Perma-boner whenever he is around Tessa character Hardin Scott? I'm surprised she didn't go with the surname Richard, or one of its nicknames, but then it wouldn't be H.S. like Harry Styles. I can't say Hardin, or even type it, so I'm going to call him Hayden as it close, and it reminds me of Hayden Fox on the old tv show "Coach" (and that character was named after iconic Iowa Football coach Hayden Fry). These are names, people, but Hardin is a condition; one that was explored thoroughly in this book. Ewww. Or maybe I'll just call him H. Which reminds me of Preparation H, as he was a complete pain in the a$$. I was mentally comparing H. to the protagonist Fred, in The Utterly Uninteresting and Unadventurous Tales of Fred, the Vampire Accountant and Fred is the clear winner, despite being undead. He's a nice guy. Seriously, that is a funny book (I got the audiobook) and the contrast between Fred, who treats people with respect and can't believe that his former classmate might actually be asking him out, vs. H. who thinks he is God's gift to women, is stark. 
 I don't think that Tessa should have stayed with Noah, though, as it was obvious that they weren't actually attracted to each other. I'm picturing Noah as a young Pat Boone. Tessa was actually quite cruel to Noah with how long she strung him along, ignoring his texts and calls, and inviting him up and then ditching him in her dorm room while taking his car for an entire night. Nice. But, Noah was a tool who was ratting her out to her mom about everything - wow. And why the mom thought Noah was some catch, this still in high school guy. No-one in college should be dating a high schooler. That isn't a thing that works out with someone who isn't living with their parents and commuting to school just for classes. I don't know why Tessa was surprised about this development, as she had allegedly done her homework about what college life would be like and wrote up a detailed schedule for every minute of her 4 years there in advance. This was dumb. And didn't give me warm feelings for Tessa. Why did I keep reading this? 
 I know why. I am strangely drawn to romances that feature the loss of innocence, thus the aforementioned Fifty Shades. My favorite of the "Black Dagger Brotherhood" books is the one featuring Butch and Marissa. OMG, did I just admit that I've read almost all of the BDB books? When will this series of embarrassing book confessions end? I stayed up until midnight last night finishing this book. On a work night. Midnight. Dang, that is late. And now I think I'm starting to sound like Tessa and all her whining about staying up late on school nights. Which is a thing, people. You should sleep at night. Unless you are a vampire. And then you can just hang out all night and watch the person you've got a huge crush on sleep. Because that isn't creepy and weird or anything. Oh, there is plenty of sneaking into your room and watching you sleep in this book, so if you are a fan of home security, this isn't your book. 
 Or boundaries. Fans of boundaries should also avoid this book. No seriously, this is not a feminist manifesto, shockingly. Trigger warnings abound in this book, where "no" means "maybe" and driving drunk is cool and stomping away angry after 1 million fights is sexy and all sorts of other immaturity that is passed off as "passion". This is also not a realistic portrayal of college life, as Tessa reminded us 1 million times that she is "getting a 4.0 GPA" despite the fact that she is still in her first semester of school, so she hasn't even received any grades yet, and she seems to be missing all of her classes after getting her internship. And let's spend one minute on her classes, as she is an English major (which I did too, albeit many years ago), and I never had a class called "Literature." Seriously, the class is named "Literature" like they are supposed to cover all of literature in one class that meets three times a week for one semester, a class with both first year students and upper class students? Intro to Lit? Nope. Literature. And we're talking about Pride and Prejudice and Wuthering Heights and Jane Eyre? Really? And the professor is letting H. add and drop his class on a weekly basis for months, and Tessa is somehow in it despite the fact that she is also working every day at the completely impossible internship. You know the one, where you get an office with a window (and a door that locks - seriously, locking doors in an office building), they let you out early every day, just because, that is how offices work?, and you get paid, while also getting school credit (for what class, mind you, doesn't matter, as you know the Dean - whee!) to read a manuscript and write notes. Um, cool? And she got it because she's getting a 4.0, and she knows this because during the first week of school she went to her classes. Ok, it is realistic that if the Dean put in a word for her, that she would get an internship, but everything beyond that is incomprehensible to anyone who has ever worked in an office, and seems to draw on Ana's "job" in Fifty Shades as the source of what work is actually like. 
 Ok, enough ranting. I kept reading, and at a ferocious pace, because I wanted to see the train wreck. I would say I wanted to know what would happen, but you and I both know what was going to happen. It was pre-ordained. This plot was not even slightly original. And, I don't need to actually read the second and third books to know what they are about. But, I might anyways. I'm still deciding. Anyone who is old and cynical like me but who enjoys the cheese (and this is quite cheesy) and who has read these other two books who wants to give me any indication of whether they are worth it, please, chime in. 
 In the meantime, while I decide whether to continue this series, please let me give the alternate universe version of how I think Tessa should have responded to H's rebuffs. 
 T:	Hey, why weren't you around last night? 
 H:	Don't ask me anything, you nosy uptight prude. 
 T:	Um, ok, that was rude. I think I'll go now. 
 H:	But I love you. 
 T:	Well, you sure have a funny way of showing it. [exit scene left and never go back.] 
 [scene]
