When I first bought this book, I was very excited to read it. I'd heard very good things about this book, and had been wanting to read it for a while. I thought that when I read the first book, I was going to be totally engrossed in the story and never want to put it down until I finished the last book. 
 I was totally wrong. I hated it. I thought it was poorly written, had awful plot points, and I thought the main character, Tessa, was a pathetic and naive little girl. 
 For those of you that don't already know, After was originally written on Wattpad as a Harry Styles fanfiction. It become so popular that the story was slightly altered so every "Harry" became "Hardin" and the story was published as an actual four-book series. I knew this when I started reading it, but I didn't realize just how immature the author's writing was especially since the story was originally written as a fanfiction. 
 Anyways, the story of After is of a new freshmen named Tessa Young, at Washington State University. She is a petite, pretty, intelligent girl who always has everything planned out for herself, and always wants things to go well. She wants to focus on her studies, her boyfriend, and staying out of trouble. However, this doesn't go as planned when she meets her dorm roommate's group of friends, one of them being the (predictably) mysterious, tattooed and pierced Hardin Scott. 
 Obviously, despite Tessa trying her best to fight it, Tessa and Hardin fall in love. Of course, just like every other fucking novel I have read, Hardin is not one for relationships, besides (literally) screwing around and being a manwhore, but of course he falls in love with Tessa after they meet and she "changes" him. Lots of shit goes down, betrayal, and devastation. 
 Ok, that was just a run-down summary, and I could've probably done a better job, but to be completely honest I hated this book with a burning passion so I could care less about the summary. I thought Tessa Young was pathetic, too trusting, too naive, and honestly annoying. She thought she was so much better than she actually was. And don't even get me started on her and Hardin's toxic relationship. The only time they weren't fighting was when they were naked. 
 I probably would've enjoyed this book more if I read it like two years ago, but unfortunately I just read it now. I'm probably going to read the rest of the series, just to see what happen.

book_a.title: Tweak: Growing Up On Methamphetamines
book_a.user_review:

 Moral of the story...do NOT expose your kids to drugs and sex; ESPECIALLY at a very young age!!

sample_reviews.review_text:
I've never been one to delve into drugs beyond the occasional experimental joint. And though I'm not obtuse or blind to what drug abuse and addiction can do to someone, I found it fascinating just how far down the well an addict will fall before they even being start trying to claw their way out. 
 Nic Scheff is one who fell to the bottom and continues his struggle to get out of and stay out of that well. 
 Scheff's depictions of his life are brutal and disturbing....not only the drugs, but the obvious mental illness(es) he has that exacerbate the problem even more. 
 Though I feel Scheff was pretty honest throughout the book, I think he also chose not to delve into some elements that caused him to take the turn he did--his father's lifestyle, where he lived, his tenuous relationship with his mother, his obviously resentful relationship with his step-father, and his blatant objectification and idolization of many women in his life. He mentions these elements, but doesn't really push to let the reader in on how deeply seated these things were and how the contributed to his addiction to far more than Crystal Meth. 
 Overall, it was a really good book and I'm looking forward to reading Beautiful Boy by his father, David Scheff to see what the view of this story is from the other side.

I actually give this a 4.5~~~~ 
 I went into this book thinking it would be about him discovering drugs and stuff but it actually starts as he relapses, and as it goes on, he recovers, relapses and finally recovers again. But anyway, I thought this was wonderfully written and relatable but it didn't get 5 stars because some things irked me. Little things like me not remembering who some people were, were the only thing that wasn't my opinon of the book that I didn't like. Basically I wasn't a fan of Zelda from the beginning of the book and she made me so angry, and she made me angry for Nic, too. I actually enjoyed Gack and Spencer the most. And some of the things I was like "oh my god no you didn't", getting mad at Nic; and then I was like, "that line/passage/etc was so beautiful". So I'm so conflicted on this book, because I would myself relating to Nic and understanding why he did things, and then really not liking how he did some things, and then getting angry, and then feeling so sorry for him, and wash rinse repeat the circle continues. I also totally imagined him as looking like someone I know but that's beside the point. 
 But alas, I liked and enjoyed this book alot, going on the rollercoaster of a year or so of a recovering addicts life, I loved how he went into such detail with what he did and when and who was there and what they were doing and when, and how he described surroundings and people was something I also liked, even if usually it was in a negative way. And, to end this review: I recommend this book to anyone looking for a good memior, or at least the kind of memiors I like. Or just anyone looking for a read you will NOT put down, no seriously, I read the last 200 pages in one sitting. 
 EDIT: Looking at the other reviews, this is either a book you will LOVE or you will HATE. So, take that as you will.

Raw, honest, depressing, graphic. Started the audiobook, listened for an hour, and just had to stop. I don't want to be in an addict's life, even virtually. Tried it out because one of my students borrowed it from our hs library, and she loved it. Not for me.

I read somebody's review that said they tried three times to get through this book and could not. That was my experience. I wanted to read this as my daughter did and I wanted to know what knowledge she gained from this. I really really hope it scared her enough not to ever try this. However, I just could not get through all the graphic parts it contained. I realize this is what he went through but I guess I'm at a point in my life where I just don't understand the utter selfishness this drug brings and why people continue to start doing it.

I found myself going between being annoyed with Nic and feeling sorry for him. I intentionally chose to read his story before reading "Beautiful Boy" (written about his father's experiences in dealing with Nic's addiction). A little more than a year has pasted since I read this and I am almost ready to read the other side of this story.

What I really liked about this book was the raw and honest account of the author's journey through drug addiction. Nic Sheff didn't hide much of it, which made it painful and frustrating to get through at times. It was compelling to read through the thought processes that Nic had during the times of his many highs and his logic while he was under the influence. During "Part Two" of the novel, I was really getting bored with the recovery process because it was all fine and dandy, but I knew that there was a foreboding event about to happen or else the book would have ended shortly. That was what got me frustrated. It is easy to become frustrated with Nic, but the reader has to realize that Nic, at the time of his addiction is in an entirely different state of mind. The frustration stems from the fact that Nic's account is entirely honest. He admits that what he did in the past was wrong and during his rehab, even related his own frustration and annoyance at being confined to the facility, not realizing it was for his own good and initially, his own willingness to change. 
 While reading the book, I was taken into an entirely different world. It is crazy to realize that this entire drug infested community thrives in the same neighborhoods that we live in and that every single day, people on the street are living Nic's story and not getting help or never realizing what the world can be like outside of drug addiction.

Nic Sheff was drunk for the first time at age eleven. In the years that followed, he would regularly smoke pot, do cocaine and Ecstasy, and develop addictions to crystal meth and heroin. Even so, he felt like he would always be able to quit and put his life together whenever he needed to. It took a violent relapse one summer in California to convince him otherwise. 
 I am going to start out by saying I do not care for the genre of memoir. I feel that it is a cheap shot at biographies or autobiographies. It is a "hazy recollection of what really happened." It allows the author to put a his spin on the story. I only read this book due to the fact that a friend of mine at book club wanted to read this and she reads all the books I have brought up to the book club so I felt I owed it to her to read this book. 
 I could not empathize with Nic Sheff. Yes, he is an addict. He was honest in his recollection of what he did and how he got there. He will always have these cravings and every day of his life he will be in recovery due to his choices in life. It made me mad that he grew up with so many advantages and blew them all. He continues to write about addiction since it is the only thing he knows and can share with people. He has written other books about this as well as writing for the San Francisco Chronicle. Good for him that he is trying to put his life together. I wish I would have not picked up this book and read many of the countless others that I really want to read.
Very very sad:/

So, like, this book originally started out like, pretty rad, y'know? But then like, it went downhill, man, cuz there were so many things wrong with, like, all of it, like. word. Y'know? Amazing. (if you read the book, you would understand that the above sentence is sarcasm). 
 In all seriousness I love books about addictions because it provides me with a reality check into other people's lives who are struggling with worse demons than myself. I picked up this book because it was really popular back in high school with a friend of mine so I thought I would give it a go. It was a mistake and I am kind of disappointed I spent money on this. 
 The way in which this man talks is utterly annoying. I have never seen the words "y'know", "word", "like" and "amazing" used so many times in a novel. I can not describe in how much this annoyed me. I kind of want to provide him with a dictionary so he can browse for some word choices, y'know? *sarcastic sigh* 
 The story, in itself, is bad. Spelling errors and in need of editing aside, the character was the biggest disappointment of all time. I understand that drugs are not easy. I understand that addiction is not easy. But what irritated me was how many times this man got help, had the support of his family just to turn around and smash it in their faces...then wonder why no one trusts him. I've noticed other commenters have labeled him as a straight up douche bag and honestly, I think it fits. I've read books about addiction before where the person describes how evil and down right low the drugs make a person act. But in every single one of these books, there is always a shining light. Or perhaps a light bulb that will go off in their head and eventually provoke positive change in themselves. This book basically begins how it ends. Nothing really happened. The ending enraged me considering how he talked about his loved ones and at the time, his girlfriend. There was and is no respect and I honestly feel no sympathy for him whatsoever. 
 Just honestly, do not read this. There are FAR better novels about overcoming addiction than this.

I'm currently reading this book and I'm not sure I'm going to finish it. I have a hard time feeling any sensitivity toward the author who is a basic train wreck. It's so incredibly obvious (after reading Beautiful Boy) that his many problems start out with his parent's divorce, his dad having an affair and his mother abandoning him to move far away. How hard could it be to figure out the kid was going to end up on drugs? I think there has to be a point when someone has to take responsibility for their life and stop playing the blame game. 
 I finished the book last night and was not impressed. The book isn't well written - more like a 15 year would write. I feel incredibly sorry for the author that he sacrificed his body and soul for drugs. I just closed the book thinking, "blah."

sample_reviews.review_text: This author doesn't disappoint but neither does she absolutely thrill. As always, my beef with a lot of books is the page count. When a book is this long, don't go throwing hints around that I am expected to put together MORE than 150 pages later! I had to return to the first third of the book quite often to remind myself of a few of the things that had been foreshadowed. I really appreciate those authors out there that can "get 'er done" with many fewer pages but really fit in enough nuance and details without having to resort to complicated plots. I will say that while everything gets tied up almost too perfectly in the end, I can appreciate why many readers enjoy that. I can honestly say this would be a rather excellent British miniseries--quite possibly better than the book.

The Distant Hours ate up way too many hours and was relentlessly bad. When the final secrets were told we were even blessed with a horrible storm. I'm only upset that I didn't give myself permission to just stop partially through. Enjoyed the two earlier Morton novels, but I'm not going to trust her with my reading hours for quite some time.

I had trouble getting into the narrator, (I couldn't seem to care about her and her feelings or motivations). She was essentially the main character,although the book wasn't about her at all... perhaps if it was written in 3rd person instead of first....but that being said, 
 I stuck with it and was rewarded with a great suspenseful ending! My favorite line - I have to share... 
 "Nighttime is different. things are otherwise when the world is black. Insecurities and hurts, anxieties and fears grow teeth at night." 
 How true! Excellent line. 
 I'm glad I finished this book, though at times it seemed too slow and I almost gave up on it. Someone else mentioned that the author was striving for atmosphere but fell short. I have to agree that something was off with the pacing.

However, by page 110 when nothing had happened to pique my interest or attention and the first person POV was boring me to death plus dialogue was ominous by its absence - I decided to move on. The whole premise of this book seems very tame compared to her earlier work. 
 Begs the question - Had this been her first would it have been published? I seriously doubt it.

Morton's books are always a pleasing diversion. A nice thunderstorming-out-but-I've-got-a-cuppa-and-a-page-turner distraction from reality. This is my personal favorite of hers thus far. More than her earlier books, this is a true mystery (the others were a bit more obvious with where the plot was going). There are more layers with the characters and a more grounded reality in the setting than I've gotten from her other works. I found the history and varying perspectives of WWII-period Britain fascinating. You get to hear about that period (or at least get strong hints of it) from the point of view of adults on the homefront, a returned soldier, and a child who is removed from her family for her own safety. Lots of empathy all around for all of these characters on the author's behalf; a true labor of love.

Poppy Wyatt seems to have everything going in her favor - she is about to marry the ideal man - successful Magnus Tavish whose parents are even more successful university professors. But on the very day Magnus' parents are visiting, Poppy loses her engagement ring, which is also a family heirloom. On top of it, she also lost her phone and while she anxiously tries to ponder missing the one message saying her ring has been found, she finds another phone in the bin. Happy to find a functional discarded phone, she quickly tells everyone to text/call her at this number, only to get a call from someone named Sam Roxton asking for the phone back since it belongs to his company. 
 Sophie Kinsella has done it again. She made me laugh from the first page without making me roll my eyes or feel ridiculous or cry 'cheesy'. I stopped reading light women fiction years ago, but Kinsella is the only author that I still happily read, knowing she won't disappoint me. 
 I've Got My Number rolls along standard Kinsella lines - the plot is pretty much predictable, the protagonist has low self-esteem, there is a hot guy who we know she will end up with but she is totally clueless about the guy, the guy is some high flying corporate guy with plenty of influence and moolah, things go wrong and then wronger and then even wronger than possible from the first page, there are plenty of laughs and deja-vu moments, and most significantly, the central character knows how to stand on her feet when it matters. 
 That pretty much sums up any Sophie Kinsella book, and while I typically hate formulaic plots and predictability, there is just something about these books that make me enjoy them more than feel pulled away. I find her novels set well in environments that I can relate to, and not something that feels more of a historic before-my-days past. 
 I enjoyed the addition of technology in this book - it was fun reading all the texting that went on and on between Poppy and Sam. Poppy's overuse of X's and O's made me snort - I have a few friends who speak mostly in X's and O's and that annoys me, ha! True, some of the events that happen were a little too convenient, but I knew what I was getting into, so that was fine with me. I didn't really like where Magnus' character ended up - I thought that could have been done better, and the introduction of a corporate scandal towards the end kind of sprung up on me, but otherwise, I've Got My Number was a truly delightful read.
A fun, light summer read!

reference_books.title: An Ember in the Ashes (An Ember in the Ashes, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Recommended for fans of: 
 * Fantasy worlds that are dark but not graphic 
 * Female friendship in difficult circumstances 
 * Casual Roman history mixed into a fantasy world 
 * Complex relationships to read as friends OR romance 
 A Roman-inspired world 
 An Ember in the Ashes is a YA fantasy inspired by the Roman empire. As a Greek/Roman history nerd, I went into this book with a mix of dread and hyperactive glee. The Roman influences are obvious and not as deep as I would have liked, and I felt disappointed. At first. Then, I let go of my hunger for Roman history, and just let this be a fantasy story. 
 The characters swept me away. After a slow start, the intricate demands of friendship, obligation, and survival pull Laia and Elias in all directions. The characters keep the focus, while the world is left more as an impression than a concrete setting. Soon, my brain started to fill in whatever background details it needed, and I settled in for the ride. 
 An Ember in the Ashes also brings in mythological creatures from the lands conquered or colonized by the Martial Empire. Thus we get jinn and ifrits, from Islamic mythologies, instead of rehashed Greek creatures that sometimes pop up in Roman stories. The world building would be shallow for an original fantasy novel, but the historical inspiration allowed me to pull in enough details to make it feel complete. 
 As should be expected in a novel inspired by Ancient Rome, An Ember in the Ashes does contain slavery and brutality. The threat of rape is a constant, and one scene contains an assault that avoids rape only at the last moment. If that is a trigger for you, avoid this book. But the threat is not realized, and there are no graphic descriptions to endure. Likewise, there is violence, both as torture and in combat. 
 Complex relationships 
 Laia and Elias are at the center of a complex web of relationships. Many characters play an important role in their stories, and each is well developed. Their enemies are layered and interesting, and their allies even more so. 
 For Laia, there's Keenan, who serves as her contact to the rebels. There's Izzi, the kitchen girl, who risks her life for the sake of Laia's friendship. And there's Elias, the son of her tormentor, who shows her that not all Martials are evil. 
 For Elias, there's Helene, his best friend and the only female warrior at the Academy. There are several fellow soldiers, trapped in the same system but without the vision to see another way. And there's Laia, a slave who has yet to be broken. Elias can't watch her suffer and do nothing. 
 Some readers treat those ally relationships as love triangles (squares?). To me, they felt like strong friendships. Sometimes circumstance reminds them that there could be more, and there's a moment of confused awareness. But there doesn't need to be a romance to be willing to put yourself at risk for someone else. It doesn't have to be love to share a moment of attraction. 
 An Ember in the Ashes features a complex network of developing relationships and conflicting loyalties. I enjoyed watching both viewpoint characters weigh difficult decisions. No matter the choice, someone they care about is endangered by their actions. There is a moral weight to every decision, and consequences are painful. 
 In such a brutal world, it is a risk to care about someone, a risk to feel. That's what makes An Ember in the Ashes well worth reading. 
 Reviewed on Come Hither Books

She has 1 magical ability at the beginning of the book and keeps gaining new ones until she has about 8 by the end - a little overboard and a little cliched, aspects I noticed a lot throughout the book. I have a feeling you are either going to love this book if what you want is something trashy + erotic + pure fluff, otherwise you may not like this.

book_b.title: A Confusion of Princes
book_b.user_review:
Disappointing, after how awesome the Abhorsen trilogy is. My bias is for fantasy over space scifi though, so I'm not sure how much is due to genre preference rather than story quality. Regardless, Confusion of Princes was much less satisfying than Nix's fantasy books. Parts of the world building were cohesive, others seemed random and poorly thought out. Few of the characters were sympathetic enough to root for. The main character's journey away from his mind-programmed culture drives the plot, and therefore makes some of its worst offenses forgiveable in context, but it still makes him so unlikeable as to be a hard sell for a protagonist. 
 Also, the dominant culture's attitude toward sex makes this book a hard fit into YA for me. Yes, he grows out of it and starts to realize it's wrong, but sentences like "if she were one of my mind-programmed courtesans I'd just tell her to lie down and prepare to receive her lord and master" do not belong in a teen book. Yikes. It's rare for me to have a gatekeeper moment, but that was a little too far over the line. 
 So yes, my recommendation: go read Sabriel instead. Confusion of Princes is not the worst book I've ever read, but neither does it manage to rise very high in the ranks. There's better out there, including by the same author, so start elsewhere.

sample_reviews.review_text: A terrible book, the main character had the personality of a shoe, and the little 'oh look, a girl who isn't under mind control, I guess I'll fall in love and give up everything' just came out of nowhere.

This is proving a lot harder to get through than my love for Nix's other books (namely his Sabriel trilogy) would have indicated. Khemri is an extremely difficult protagonist to root for, although he at least does you a favor and acknowledges his own dickishness like, 75% of the time. Also, I'm probably just not cut out for hard sci-fi, but some sentences with too much ~lingo~ just read like word vomit to me. Almost done though, so we'll see if the ending redeems the novel. 
 Update: Finished. The ending is okay. Er... a bit disappointing from Nix, but I do appreciate his effort writing in different genres.

I started out not particularly liking this; the character of Khemir is difficult to like, as he's immature, ignorant, and arrogant, and that's a difficult combination with which to identify. However, life and his situation end up knocking him into a much more likeable character, and I ended up liking the book. Khemir grows in a largely believable (and appealing) way, though perhaps the transformational power of love is a bit overdone; and the plot is interesting and imaginative enough, though there are some aspects of the ending's construction that aren't necessarily logically consistent with the overall structure of the Empire/characters.

Ever since I read the Abhorsen Trilogy, I have held Nix's works in generally high esteem. "A Confusion of Princes" however did not manage to meet the mark. 
 There is not much I can say that others have not said before me. The pacing is awkward, slow where it need not be and fast where a little more elaboration would help greatly; Khemri's about-face mid story is not adequately justified, something which I suppose is lampshaded with all the "I don't know why I did the thing, but I did it anyway" narration which follows. There was little suspense as the whole book reads rather like a memoir and therefore means that the protagonist exists beyond the story, even if he has died three times to get to that point. 
 Khemri is the only one with much personality, and, though this is sometimes the case with first person novels, the lack of much personality in the rest of the cast seems particularly glaring in this case. 
 I did enjoy the arena fight, but I found that it smacked of The Hunger Games - weapons all in the middle of the arena, fighting each other to the death, tridents (Seriously, who other than Aquaman or Finnick Odair uses a trident? Why was that a weapon available in this sci-fi world? Why such low tech weapon choices for the final battle at all?), and of course the Katniss ultimatum of "Give me what I want or your last two contestants die and there will be no winner to this contest" which Khemri pulls at the end. 
 All in all, I would concede that "A Confusion of Princes" has an interesting concept, but suffers from awkward execution and is unable to meet the fullest potential.
Too much tell, not enough show. Might've benefited from being expanded into two books, but I'm not sure if there was enough plot for that. Still, I read the whole thing without needing to.

This book left me terribly conflicted. On the one hand, I love Garth Nix's writing, and I love the worlds and ideas he comes up with. This one is no exception. Much as Prince Khemri's arrogance and selfishness is obnoxious, it's also justified by the world he lives in, and ultimately he overcomes it enough to be someone you can cheer for. Khemri's adventures take him through many different places and cultures, all of which interested me (I think inventing new cultures is something Nix is consistently good at). And I was especially fond of Khemri's priest/assassin/babysitter Haddad, who truly has the patience of a saint and a genuine affection for Khemri all out of proportion to how much he deserves it. 
 So why only two stars? Because so much of the rest of the book dissatisfies me. My general complaint is that I don't feel this has the same polish, the same unity, that has distinguished Nix's other books. The plot seems disjointed, as though individual moments (Khemri's military service, his time in the training habitats, etc.) are connected the way a set of independently-published stories might be fitted into a frame novel; they're related, but they don't flow together. Also, the narrative is Khemri's first-person story, something he's telling after all the events of the novel have passed, and it often slips into a dull "here's what happened, and then this happened" voice that kept me somewhat alienated from the novel. 
 More specifically, while I could see that Khemri's personality at the end was a possible outgrowth of his personality at the beginning, he didn't always learn from his experiences the lessons he should have. Example: Khemri's sent to a set of four artificial environments to learn important survival skills, including humility. He quickly discovers that his arrogant assumptions of privilege will get his teeth kicked in by regular folks. It's *stated* in his narrative that he learned that ordinary humans (Princes are genetically enhanced for strength, intelligence, what have you) are deserving of respect and aren't just inferiors to be ordered around. Yet in his very next "mission," he goes back to acting as though he'd never learned that lesson. (It apparently takes the magic of sex to make this lesson permanent.) Ultimately, I liked the Khemri at the end of the book despite his character transformation and not because of it. 
 But this is just nit-picking by comparison to what really bugged me: Am I the only person who was seriously disturbed at the idea of mind-programmed humans serving the Princes? They're mentioned only briefly near the beginning, something Khemri takes for granted, so my first thought was that their introduction was to show Khemri being a self-absorbed jerk. The next time, I wondered if these were people who'd volunteered for the position, and thus they'd chosen to give up their free will. But no, when Khemri starts considering bringing someone he cares about back to the Empire so they can stay together, he remembers that she'd have to be mind-programmed for obedience and that this would be required of her. And yeah, it turns them into slaves with no will of their own, effectively killing the person they once were. At no time is it ever suggested that turning people into robots--robots who, among other things, may become sex toys for Princes--is a bad thing on a universal scale; it's wrong only so far as individuals Khemri cares about are concerned. Khemri's newfound respect for non-augmented people doesn't seem to extend far enough to even wonder where mind-programmed servants come from. While I'm not faulting the book for not being about Khemri freeing the slaves, I am faulting it for not even subtextually suggesting that this practice is evil. 
 Two stars, and that makes me sad.

reference_books.title: Red Country (First Law World, #6)
reference_books.review_text:
I liked Red Country more than Best Served Cold, but less than The Heroes and the First Law Trilogy. I think Red Country's plot felt less urgent than Abercrombie's other books--less incipient mayhem, less immediate peril (for example, the fencing match between Jezal and the guy with the girly voice in the First Law trilogy? Edge of my seat. It felt like there was so much at stake. The Northman brawl over the ownership of Crease ? Meh). 
 Sometimes I think I wish that he'd do less scenes from other viewpoints, because that destroys the surprise when one of the characters does a 180 and sells the others out. On the other hand, it allows him to flesh out many minor characters in a way that would be impossible otherwise. You see, one of the things I like about Abercrombie's novels is that the characters are all so clearly existing in their own heads. It would be difficult to get a good sense of the more minor characters' motivations and feelings if we had to be dependent on what was going on in the major characters' solipsistic craniums. 
 I love Logan. My relationship to ice cream is rather like his relationship to violence, so I can relate! Once I start eating ice cream, it's difficult to stop no matter how much I should. Once Logan starts creating mayhem, it's difficult to stop until all the noisy fleshy things stop moving. 
 Ok. Not equivalent. But still, I have a warm place in my heart for the poor bastard.

reference_books.title: Three Parts Dead (Craft Sequence, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I really wanted to like Three Parts Dead. The world is so bizarre--it kept me off balance (and that's a good thing). Combining magic and legal agreements is such a perfect idea. Here. This is a small detail, but it can serve as a illustration of the larger whole. 
 A club bouncer is under a magic legal contract. He is granted strength and protection, but only as long as he follows the club rules. He breaks a rule, lets someone in who he shouldn't? There goes his protection. 
 Awesome. A few other things: 
 As part of the investigation, the characters went to a library and did a bit of forensic accounting. 
 One main character wanted to question a witness before anyone else (and prevent him from being identified or detained). She had only a minute or two to think of a plan and execute it. What does she do? 
 She stole his face. 
 This is a world where ripping out a person's spine and arranging it around him (accompanied by magic sigils, of course) counts as a valid medical procedure for preserving his life. 
 This is a world where a legal contract can kill a god, especially if the god has not been particularly up front with the priests. 
 This is a world where resurrecting said god is totally doable. The real problem is in proving he wasn't negligent because if he was, his creditors would get more control over the resurrection process. 
 These are the sort of details I loved, and the reason I forced myself to finish it. 
 Yes, forced. 
 I couldn't read more than a few pages without wanting to put the book down and do something else. I think it was due to two things, mainly. First, I didn't connect with any of the characters. Ah, well. What can you do about that? Second, though, was because the viewpoint would shift between characters more than necessary. It felt like every time one viewpoint gathered momentum it would switch to a different one and the process would have to start all over. It really irks me when books dump momentum like this. It only works when I care about the characters, because that gives the plot a certain amount of inertia. 
 Therefore! Despite how freaking awesome the worldbuilding was, I will not be reading the sequels. It took me a bit over one week to finish this 300 page book, and I only got through it that quickly because it was overdue with no renewals left (oops).

reference_books.title: I Am the Cheese
reference_books.review_text:
I can't really call myself a connoisseur of the unreliable narrator genre, but I'm not unfamiliar with it, either. 
 I Am the Cheese is too simplistic for my tastes. It does its best to wrap everything up neatly at the end. If I wanted a neat ending I'd be reading...well, pretty much any other book. I suspect it was pretty mind-blowing back in the 70s, but I was not impressed. 
 On the plus side, it was an easy and quick read. Plus, I did get a kick out of the reveal that the purpose of the interviews was to establish whether or not Grey should be allowed back at his job .

reference_books.title: The Warded Man (Demon Cycle, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I have a problem with this book. I am going to attempt to explain my problem clearly and calmly. My previous attempts at writing a review have all lapsed into inarticulate rage. I will admit that, as I did not finish reading the book, it is possible that Peter V. Brett redeems himself later on. I do not consider this likely. 
 Here is the problem: 
 The sun goes down, and demons overrun the earth. Protection is provided by defensive wards which get drawn on houses, barns, fence posts, etc. If a living creature is outside of these protections when night falls, that creature will be ripped apart and eaten. There is no way to fight the demons. 
 Eleven-year-old Arlen lives in a village with his parents. A messenger from the city shows up, carrying mail and salt. Arlen gets the job of showing this man around, and during the tour the man tells Arlen about a country far away in which young men train to fight and then go out at night in the hope of finding a way to defeat the demons. They all die, but the point is that it is not in man's nature to cower in safety while demons walk the earth. Men want to fight, and when deprived of that opportunity they become weak, depressed, and suicidal. The messenger's argument is supported when, during the tour, they come across a man from a nearby town who has hanged himself to death from a tree limb. 
 So Arlen takes this putrid idea to heart, and starts haranguing his father about how cowardly it is to stay safely inside the wards when there are demons to fight. I think this is very stupid, because if every man took Arlen's advice humans would have died out long ago. At this point, though, I am willing to give the author the benefit of the doubt. Arlen is only eleven, so it would be a bit much for me to expect him to act sensibly for the entire book. Perhaps he will learn the error of his ways. 
 Arlen is living with his mother, father, and a woman who recently lost her family in a demon attack. One afternoon, the sun sets more quickly than they were expecting because some clouds moved in. The adults and Arlen scramble to move the animals to safety. They run back to the porch, and then realize that the dog is still chained to a post in the back yard. Demons are about to start sprouting from the earth, and the dog will suffer a horrible, agonizing death. The guest runs out and unchains the dog, which bolts to the porch. The woman moves more slowly, and as a result gets a chunk ripped out of her leg by one of the first demons to spawn. Seeing this, Arlen's mother runs out into the yard to help the woman back to the house. Demons start attacking the mother, and drag the guest away to be eaten. 
 Arlen looks at his father. He realizes with disgust that his father is too afraid to move, so he jumps off the porch, beans a couple demons over the head with a nearby bucket, and drags his mother to the safety of the pigpen. They hang there till morning, when Arlen's father comes out to help them. Arlen gives his father a cold shoulder, and goes on and on about how cowardly he was, etc, etc. 
 I was filled with disgust, and stopped reading soon after. Why? 
 Because it became obvious that the author agreed with everything Arlen was saying. Not only that, but in his pursuit of setting Arlen up as The One (or whatever), he had to stack the deck in the kid's favor and kill/injure a few women to make the point. 
 Problem one: 
 A preteen farm kid should not have had any more success at fighting/surviving/staging a rescue from demons than two grown women. 
 Problem two: 
 Who demonstrated the most courage during the demon attack: the woman who risked death to save a dog, the mother who risked her life to save a woman who wasn't even part of her family, or the kid who risked his life only when his own mother was in danger? I think the answer is obvious. 
 Who demonstrated the most common sense during the demon attack: the kid who ran out into a yard full of hungry sprites to attempt a rescue that two adults had just failed at, or the father who stayed on the porch instead of running out there and leaving his kid an orphan? Also obvious. 
 Arlen is the loser by both metrics. If the author treated him the same as everyone else, he should have been eaten. And yet he lives so that he might make his father's life miserable. He lives, but not once does he say, Father, why couldn't you have been brave like Mom? 
 After that, I was afraid of what bits of blindness and idiocy the rest of the book might contain.

book_a.title: The Drowning Girl
book_a.user_review:
I bounced off this one hard, and I have no idea why. I love unreliable protagonists, and I've happily devoured other books which meander around talking about random details that don't necessarily have anything to do with the plot. 
 But I've gotten pretty far in, and I still have to force myself to not put it down every few minutes.

sample_reviews.review_text:
The quirkiness of this story grabbed my interest right from the start. About 20% into the book it started to get on my nerves. After about 50% or so, I started to hate it. There may be a bit of genius in here somewhere that I lack the intelligence or creativity to appreciate but in any case I was disappointed. 
 If this is worthy of any award this year, the Bram Stoker is the wrong venue. It has some dark elements but doesn't quite fit the horror genre.

At times breathtakingly beautiful, at others frustratingly tedious, THE DROWNING GIRL is India (Imp) Phelps' attempt to write down and perhaps exorcise the ghosts not only of her past, but also those of her present. The ones of her past (the suicides of her mentally ill grandmother and mother) are surely factual, but is the ghost of Eva Canning real? Imaginary? A product of Imp's schizophrenic brain off medication? A combination of all of the above? 
 Not a book for those invested in plot, especially plot with a neat resolution. But one likely to haunt your dreams (or more likely, your nightmares).

I'll admit it: I don't understand this book. I couldn't tell who was speaking sometimes, I don't understand how the Evas fit (or their relationship to Imp), and I don't understand even whether there WAS a narrative arc, let alone whether it was good. The nonlinear structure didn't help in this regard. 
 The reason I gave the book 2 stars is because of the writing. Kiernan gets across brilliantly what a disordered mind might be like, and I want to root for Imp because of it. She also conveys a sense of place very, very well. It might simply be the nature of the mental illness that I couldn't find a hook to hang my hat on. 
 As I said, I don't know what to think about this one. Sorry if this review isn't much help.

I wish I had the words to convince everyone to go out and BUY a copy of this RIGHT NOW. (It's a wonderful study of mental illness.) Unfortunately, the book's brilliance has rendered me mute. Yesterday, I sat outside in a different town--a city, in fact--at a gigantic market where hundreds of people went in and out, where I saw their purchases and smelled so many different kinds of food from all over the world--and all I could do was read this book. There was nothing else. It's that good. I hope to read it again before the year's out.
I was bored out of my mind.

Superb writing style. The book was presented to me as sci fi/fantasy which probably accounts for only 3 stars, as I saw it as more of reading about the dream world of a schizophrenic. At times a little too disjointed in plot structure, compensated by the incredible backstory the author invents regarding a painter and author.
Tor.com gave this book a stellar review....now starting....

The germ of this review comes from a discussion thread about it. I don't think I've borrowed anyone else's insights, but I'll freely confess I was confused for much of this book and therefore very probably suggestible. I just finished it -- I stayed away from the thread entirely until I got chance to read The Drowning Girl, because I knew from reading The Red Tree that I'd find it frustrating, but ultimately rewarding, to go it alone. I had wikipedia and google open, fact-checking the allusions made, whether they were fact or just a part of Kiernan's truth (and that often led to other things as fascinating as Kiernan's writing). I always like doing that kind of detective work. 
 I still don't know what to think about it at all, until I take in pieces. Like, in reaction to a discussion of the genre, I realised I don't care for pinning it down to one genre; that would be to choose one of Imp's truths over the others, to designate for her which one is fact. People often do that with mentally ill people -- act like their truth, what they (as in the "sane" person) see as fact, is more important than the truth as the mentally ill person experiences it. Actually, you see that with transgendered people as well; although that parallel isn't made explicit, it's implicit in the form of Abalyn. The truth of Abalyn is that she is, and always was, female. The facts, for some people, are that she was born a boy and transitioned to become a girl. But it remains equally true that she was always a woman. 
 Anyway, I'm going to file this under a whole bunch of genres, but none of them is necessarily true for you...

 Yazarin kitabin basinda uyardigi gibi beklediginiz gibi bir kitap olmayabilir. Yani en azindan benim icin oyle oldu. Arka kapak yazilarini okumadigim icin kapagina bakarak herhalde bir genc yetiskin romanidir diye dusunmustum ama degil. Daha karanlik ve bol bol psikolojik ogelerin oldugu bir kitap. Haliyle bu guzel kapaga bayilsam da biraz daha karanlik bir kitap icerigini daha iyi yansitirdi diye dusunuyorum. Sadece kapaga bakip benim gibi hareketli bir kitap beklentisi icerisine girmeyin...

I moved into a new place at the end of last year. The bare walls are dotted throughout with picture hooks, so I've been keeping an eye out for things to hang on them. However, thus far I've only bought one piece of art - a framed print of a painting by Olga Noes titled 'Gently Lain Down'. 
 It's a picture of a drowning girl. Or a mermaid. Or siren. All of the above or neither. She has long blonde hair and calm, pale eyes, staring out from the bottom of a pond, the water of which is so still it's invisible. Fish swim in ignorant circles around her, while a dragonfly hovers overhead, as though her presence is the most natural thing in the world. 
 This painting hung over my shoulder as I read The Drowning Girl, insane young Imps's account of a life haunted by a woman who may be a ghost, a mermaid, a wolf, all or neither. 
 The purchase of the painting and the book had nothing to do with one another. I read the book after setting out to read all the nominees for this year's Bram Stoker award for best novel. 
 The Drowning Girl ultimately won and is a deserving, if unusual choice. It's a poetic, literary read, far, FAR removed from the average horror novel. There are a few creepy moments, but the overall sense of unease comes from reading a troubled woman's descent into suicidal psychosis, rather from anything more overtly supernatural. 
 It's a fascinating, though difficult and occasionally frustrating read. I wouldn't go so far as to call Imp an 'unreliable narrator', since she's recounting her own very personal haunting as she remembers it. Whether or not certain events happened is irrelevant. She remembers them, they're real to her and the emotional toil it takes is VERY real (the difference between 'truth' and 'fact'). 
 However, her admitted habit of procrastinating and digressing from the subject is off-putting in the early going. It takes a while before you realize how little story there is. So much is implication, allusion, a crazy person joining the dots between coincidences to find crucial connections that don't exist - except when they do. 
 Underlying all this are the author's efforts to tell a new kind of ghost story - one in which a person can be haunted most of their lives without realizing it, failing to see the patterns in the pernicious meme, reaching out to them through old songs, books and paintings... Not till it's too late. 
 At one point Imp worries herself that the book she's writing might only succeed in spreading her ghost - like a virus - onto whoever should be unlucky enough to pick it up. 
 How effective you find this concept will depend entirely on your own proclivity for attaching meaning to coincidence. 
 Me? I have a painting of a drowning girl on my wall. 
 I bought it before I'd even heard of the book. 
 I'm pretty sure about that...

book_b.title: Discord's Apple
book_b.user_review: I read this because I liked After the Golden Age, but it wasn't as good. It's an apocalypse-with-gods sort of book. Evie writes comic books about a military squad. This isn't too surprising, as the world she lives in is wracked with war. Her mother was killed by an attack from a suicide bomber. It's impossible to travel through small towns (let alone major cities) without running into checkpoints to search your car for weapons and explosives. Evie becomes intimately caught up in the apocalypse-with-gods when she visits her dying father and learns (rather unwillingly) of her family legacy. I had two major problems with this book. Well, one major, one minor. The minor problem is that the romance bit felt forced. The major problem has a few parts: A) if this is the apocalypse-with-gods, where are all the gods? (There's really only one god, plus several magical or mythological people. Don't expect me to assume they all died. The fate of the Greek pantheon is the only one truly discussed) and B) was the apocalypse supposed to succeed? By which I mean, why the hell were a couple people from Arthurian legend called back up if they weren't actually supposed to accomplish something? Who or what is responsible for resurrecting them, anyway? If the gods are dead or weak, who's left pulling these strings? The plot didn't make much sense to me. If the other bits are sufficiently good, I can overlook that failing. In this case, they weren't.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Good idea, but it just doesn't work. 
 I like Carrie Vaughn, but I don't like this book. At times, this book is trying to weave together too many plot threads - immortals, gods, Arthur, Troy, end-of-the-world, comic books, and a secret room. It's just too much and nothing really seems to gel. The characters are shadows. Even the comic book plot, which is supposed to stand in for Evie's development and be homage to an old sci-fi show from the 1980s. (Honestly, it wasn't that bad of a show, but Jessica Steen's best sci-fi show was Earth 2) - though it was nice to see homage to the show, even if it made the comic book plot too predictable. 
 I have to give Vaughn credit for trying to branch out, but I must ask, what is wrong with writing funny with serious mixed in? This is what makes the Kitty books so fun, and there is nothing wrong with that. This book is all serious, but it doesn't work because there is waaay too much going on. It almost seemed like Vaughn wants to write a "grown up" fantasy book, but that is what the Kitty books are. You can do funny and be taken seriously (think Terry Pratchett). Serious is fine, but serious is not mixing too much, too quickly.

I was so disappointed with this book. I love Carrie Vaughn's Kitty Norville series, so I was sure I'd love this. I didn't. I think the theme of gods interacting with the world is interesting - I love Sherrilyn Kenyon's series that does that - but this book was choppy & unclear. It wasn't very clear why the world was in such turmoil and the going back and forth between times and characters just didn't work for me. It was confusing. 
 Also, I thought this was supposed to be a young adult book but there was a lot of sex in it for a YA novel.

I'm angry at this book. I wanted to like it so much. It sounded right up my alley, I loved the concept (a "Warehouse 13" guarded by a family), as the characters were introduced I got more and more excited (Merlin! Greek gods!)...and then WOW what a let-down. 
 I can't give only 1 star as it provided some mild amusement, but even 2 stars feels high. I want to give it a 1.5 stars for "Ehhh, could've been worse"

Evie Walker is the heir to the Storeroom in her family home, which holds (as we discover) magical artifacts - like Arthur's sword, Pandora's box, and Discord's apple - the apple labelled "To the Fairest" that started the Trojan War. And now it seems like the end of the world is coming, and Hera wants the apple back. 
 Discord's Apple jumps around a fair bit - we get snippets of Evie's family's past (as being the keeper of the Storeroom moves from generation to generation); bits of the Trojan war through the eyes of Sinon, a Greek warrior; parts of Evie's comic book that she's writing (a bit too much of the comic story, I thought); and then Evie's story itself. I thought this movement within the story worked well - as we're getting to know the characters better, we find out more about their pasts. 
 This novel gets pretty chaotic towards the end - a little incoherently so, perhaps - but after all, it is called Discord's Apple. I'm a sucker for Greek mythology, so I loved all those aspects of it - Evie grappling with the fact that she has the golden fleece in her basement. I didn't particularly like the ending, but it didn't spoil the book for me - it's still a great read.

Fantastic story-telling. I love Carrie's ability to combine the present world with "other" worlds (be it Greek gods or werewolves and vampires). There is such a good thread to the story that, even though there are fantasy elements, it would keep a non-fantasy fan interested. The overall theme of society and the direction the world can go in... loved it. This is my first venture outside of Carrie's Kitty books, which I love, and I'm very glad I read it. Look forward to reading more of her work.

Interesting premise to work "mythological" gods into the near future (?), I can't say it grabbed me and really pulled me in. I was intrigued to see where the story went, but I'm not rushing out to read the next in the series.
Her werewolf books are better.

Someone recommended this for my science fiction/fantasy book club. I wanted to like it more than I did. It was okay. I was hoping more of the magical objects would come into play. I'm also not a big fan of the Greek gods, which no doubt colored my opinion (although I enjoy Rick Riordan's Percy Jackson series).
I tried to get into this book but i couldn't.

This is my first time reading one of Carrie Vaughn's books, and it wasn't a bad start either. It wasn't what I expected, but then, I didn't know what to expect so I was bound to be surprised. 
 Evie Walker leaves the city - which, like all the other cities in America, has been divvied up by local militias who have started fighting each other instead of terrorists - to go home to her family's house in the country, to be with her dad who's dying of cancer. From the moment she arrives, she detects something odd about the place - or, rather, something odd about the random people who appear at the door, asking for something or other from the basement. 
 All her life, Evie has never stepped foot in the basement. Off-limits when she was a child, she now learns that the basement has a storeroom where all the magical and mythical artefacts of the world have slowly piled up over the years - and her family are the guardians. Now, with her father dying, knowledge is beginning to pass down to Evie, and the storeroom seems to speak to her, or at least, to her gut instinct. 
 So when a beautiful woman knocks on the door wanting something from the basement, Evie tells her there is nothing for her there. But this woman is no mortal woman: she is Hera, a Goddess and once wife to Zeus, and the object she seeks is Discord's Apple, a magical golden apple that has the potential to sow chaos and destroy the world. And Hera isn't about to let Evie get in her way. 
 There was plenty to enjoy in this short, deft novel: the premise, for one, and the execution, for another. If you heard that this is a novel about fairy tale and warring gods and magical attacks, you probably wouldn't be all that impressed. You may even roll your eyes. But even though Vaughn writes like a pulp writer - with her background in Urban Fantasy, which is often just one step sideways from Romance with the lower standard of writing inherent in that dismissive statement, this is hardly surprising. But she writes with cheerful confidence, knows exactly where she's going with the plot, and doesn't have the kind of authorial ticks commonly found in Romance and Urban Fantasy that drive me crazy. 
 Before I get ahead of myself, though, I have to mention the other side of the plot. One of the unsavoury characters hanging around her dad's house is Alex, whose story is quite interesting as it is revealed, alternating chapters with Evie's in the present. Alex was once Sinon, the Greek who tricked the city of Troy into opening it's gates and letting the giant wooden horse in. Yes we're all familiar with that story. How he comes to be stranded in modern times - or slightly in the future, as the case may be with Discord's Apple - I'll leave that for you to find out. It wouldn't really be spoiling things if I told you, but I don't want to overdo it. 
 It does present some variety to the structure and pacing of the story, though. There aren't really any surprises in Sinon/Alex's story, but since the present-ish-day side of the story is told only from Evie's perspective, it gives us a chance to get to know Alex, understand him, and care about him. I really liked him a lot, the most of all the characters. 
 I do wish for more detail in genre fiction (Fantasy comes in the detailed form, but the other genres, not so much), but it was easy to get swept up in the telling. Perhaps it's because I've been reading similar books in the space of the last couple of weeks, but the apocalyptic edge was very noticeable. This is one of the things I love about genre fiction, how it can take current events and play out a hypothesis, or follow the path of our fears (either collective or individual) to an imminent conclusion. Here, Vaughn takes the current climate prevalent not just in the US but globally, exaggerates it only a little, and follows through - leading to a situation where global war is imminent and countries are doing deals with each other. 
 While the "real life" situation is downplayed in the story, Evie's career as the writer of a comic book series called Eagle Eyes Commandos allows for it to be fleshed-out: her comic book characters and stories reflect current events and play out scenarios - just as Fantasy and Science Fiction and other genres do. So the story-within-the-story adds another layer, and in the end we actually have four interwoven stories in Discord's Apple: Evie's, Sinon's, the Eagle Eyes Commandos, and the snippets going backwards in history that detail the passing down of the storeroom in Evie's family. Without these extra layers, the main storyline would have been flat and unoriginal, and it would have been harder to invest in the characters. 
 There were a few points where the story lagged a touch, but it soon rallied. Hera was no megalomaniac villain, and there was plenty of humour in the story - especially with a sprite named Robin around, who we remember more familiarly as Puck in A Midsummer Night's Dream. The story of Troy and Odysseus made me want to try reading The Odyssey again (I didn't get far with it in First Year Ancient Civs, I confess). I balked a bit at Arthur and Merlin, but actually the hint of cheese made it quite palatable ;) Vaughn obviously loves mythology, the classics and fairy tales and she's clearly well-read. 
 Overall, while this was an easy, even light read in terms of writing style, the story itself is fun, entertaining, well-written and did give me a little something to chew on.

reference_books.title: Eat, Pray, Love
reference_books.review_text: I feel almost anti-American not liking this book. It was (is?) on the bestseller list for ages and will soon be a movie starring none other than Julia Roberts. But I hated this book. A memoir that reads more like a diary, this whiney, self-indulgent woman feels sorry for herself, delves deep into introspection, and flits to three different parts of the world to "find herself." Truth be told, I couldn't get through the whole book.

reference_books.title: All We Ever Wanted Was Everything
reference_books.review_text: This was a trite yet readable book. It was well written and it seemed to me that the author was striving for that Jennifer Weiner crowd who were looking for a quick chick lit read. Brown is too literate for that. She claims her book is a satire but it doesn't work as that. You can't straddle genres is the message here.

reference_books.title: Water for Elephants
reference_books.review_text: I resisted reading this for a long time (not a huge fan of the circus). I was surprised. I ended up liking it for its originality of story and odd assortment of characters.

reference_books.title: South of Broad
reference_books.review_text: In the tradition of southern writers, Pat Conroy has a lovely way with words and a gift for storytelling. Any book by Conroy is better than most books by most other writers. The characters are larger than life, but seduce you into believing their stories even though they are implausible. The book was too graphic in spots for my taste, but it's entertaining and enjoyable. The setting and scenery made me long for a sunset on the water.

reference_books.title: Three Junes
reference_books.review_text:
This is the first book I've read by Glass and it won the National Book Award. Overall, I liked it. Glass tell three distinct stories, all somewhat related. The second is the strongest with the most riveting main character. I am disappointed in the secondary characters, though. A few pop in out seemingly of nowhere and are quite flat and not nearly as interesting or believable as her main character. But 
 Glass is quite readable and I'll read others by her, I'm sure.

book_a.title: Wolf Hall (Thomas Cromwell, #1)
book_a.user_review: Since I'm a huge fan of historical fiction, I loved this detailed story of how Thomas Cromwell helped King Henry rationalize getting rid of Queen Catherine. Because it's told from the point of view of Cromwell, it puts a fresh spin on this slice of Henry's often told story. There are tons of characters and a meandering path that is not for everyone, but I love a long and winding narrative. I can't wait to start Part 2.

sample_reviews.review_text: Utterly boring. I tried, I really did, I almost made it to page 500, but I couldn't see the point.
Brilliant concept and tightly plotted. Somewhat disconcerting writing style at first, but I quickly adapted to it. Well worth Book of the Year.
Not ever going to finish......

tedious is the perfect word to describe this book, but before I get into that, there is something I would like to explain. 
 When I read a book, I have two purposes in mind - to enjoy it, to be gripped by it and the other to be uplifted by it, to learn something. 
 This was my second attempt at reading wolf hall and I really wanted to finish it and genuinely say in liked it, but unfortunately I have failed at both. not only have I given up on the book half way, I also haven't liked it. 
 That's not to say there was nothing likeable about it. Cromwell's character is a masterpiece, built up and revealed layer by layer. Each person in the book is superbly painted, coming truly alive. to make such a wonderful story out of bare minimum facts is a feat of the imagination rarely seen. 
 but the writing is annoying. it took me a while that the 'he' in the book is Cromwell resulting in me having to read some of the paragraphs twice. it never became clear to me who was speaking and the dispensation of the quotes has never been more confusing. Mantel has moulded English according to her convenience and while it is something laudable, it just makes the book impossible to get through for readers like me. 
 coming back to the motives that drive the will to read a book. I will often put aside my wish to read something gripping for a book that is more literary and gives a sense of accomplishment. but wolf hall falls smack dab in the middle of the second category with so little fun aspect that I simply had to give up on it. and mind you, I am a person really taken in by Tudor history. 
 Bye bye Wolf Hall and Hilary Mantel. There are other books I'd rather spend my time and energy with.

Boring; slow-paced; confusing pronouns. Every time something starts happening, we're back to enumerating spoons and tapestries. Finally gave up 1/3 of the way through. 
 I also found this one really hard to read, due to the author's insistence on using pronouns only -- no names -- for the protagonist, unless in a serious syntactic bind. Totally confusing. 
 Too bad; I had high hopes.

Ugh. A painful slog through impenetrable prose. The pronoun "he" is used in the most confusing fashion possible, and it is often completely unclear who is speaking. I was so looking forward to this novel, and it was a disappointment.

I was a huge fan of the tudors, which is why I was excited to read this book and it did not disappoint. It made an interesting time in history and made it rooted in the common (in a good way). It takes a time far back in history and makes it relatable. I definitely find myself intrigued by this fictionalized tale of Henry, Anne, and company. If I didn't know how it would end I would be shocked.
I must be a bit of a moron when it comes to literary fiction. I found reading this was like wading through mud - way too much detail, and I couldn't connect with the characters at all.
not a page turner
HORRIBLE! I love historical fiction but when you make Thomas Cromwell and Tudor England dry and boring then I don't have time for to finish the book.

book_b.title: Half of a Yellow Sun
book_b.user_review: Compare it to The Kite Runner only this is set in Nigeria in the 1960s. Story is character driven with the war as a background. Some is hard to read but a great book.

sample_reviews.review_text: When reading this book, you are there with each character understanding what they know and feeling what they each feel. It makes me want to know more about this revolution.

A wonderful introduction into a new world (for me) of Nigeria in the 1960's. The characters, and particularly the two sisters, are wonderfully done, as are each of their relationships with the men they love. The book combines the politics of the day with the feelings of people who are living through the times in a way that puts the reader right into the young Biafra nation fighting for its survival and compels the previously uninformed to care deeply. I am so glad I read this book.

A wonderful book! I instantly fell in love with Ugwu and was charmed by Olanna and her twin sister. It's always interesting reading about civil wars. It was very sad at times, however, it does make you reflect on things in life we take for granted. 
 I look forward to discussing this in my local book club.
A MUST READ -- loved it.

I cannot say enough good things about this book. The characters felt real, rounded, warm. I cared about each and every one of them, and it was heartbreaking to see them suffer - and also make mistakes and do terrible things. This is my second book by Ms. Adichie (the first was Americanah, which I absolutely loved), so I think it's safe to say I will be reading everything she's ever written or will write. Excellent.

This is a great tale of love, loss, war and family relationships. It increased my knowledge of Nigeria. I loved the writing and lack of sentimentality. Adichie really has a way of writing strong female characters, although her young boy is great, too. Good read!

I read this through a book club and liked it a lot more than I thought I would. The characters were very well developed and the story kept my interest. At first the multiple viewpoints were distracting but then I got used to it and ultimately enjoyed the way that each first-person account contributed to the story as a whole. 
 Another good thing about this book is it taught me something about the Nigerian/Biafran civil war, which I knew nothing about. 
 Ultimately some terrible things happen in this book, but the excellent quality of the author's writing really sucked me in. I'd recommend this book to just about anyone.

really great for learning a bit more about the biafran/nigerian civil war, of which i was totally, and embarrassingly, unaware. there's a lot going on in this book though, and it gets somewhat overwhelming. but all in all worth it.

I have wanted to read Adichie's work every since I watched her TED talk 'The Danger of a Single Story'. Having picked up Half of a Yellow Sun recently with great anticipation, I must say I was underwhelmed. It certainly doesn't live up to the accolades on the blurb ('... exquisitely written, ... a literary masterpiece ...) or the great reviews it has received here on goodreads. 
 The novel is set in Nigeria during the 60s around the lives of five very distinct central characters. The story begins a few years before the onset of the Nigeria-Biafra war. The novel recounts the events surrounding the lives of the five characters before and during the war. The Nigeria-Biafra war was a momentous event and Adichie certainly deserves credit for attempting something very ambitious. 
 The novel is well-written in parts -- especially the war stories in the later part of the novel are tragic and intense without being melodramatic. But overall I found the writing somewhat tedious. Adichie seems to have a tendency to overwrite -- a tendency to not stop writing even after what needs to be said has been said. At many places, I found myself thinking that a good editor wouldn't have allowed that superfluous sentence. 
 Another major problem I have with the novel is that I found the characters lacking depth. One of the characters is Odenigbo, a mathematician, whose house is a meeting place for his other intellectual friends. They are supposedly an integral part of the Biafran movement, especially Odenigbo, who is often referred to by others as a 'radical' and 'revolutionary'. But it's hard to believe that. Except for an occasional, and mostly disconnected, statement somebody makes, after dinner and brandy, the characters mostly don't seem to say or do anything remarkable about the cause of Biafra. Perhaps the strongest character in the novel is that of Kainene. Adichie has done well there quite consistently throughout. 
 The author uses the device of non-linearity, switching between early and late sixties. It doesn't add much value and could have been avoided IMO. 
 Half of a Yellow Sunrise is a good novel about the love, loyalty, and aspirations of some of the characters that livid through a period of great turmoil in Nigeria. It gives a good perspective on the civil war for people like me who aren't aware of the history of the country. It also does well to highlight the Biafran aspiration (which seems to be alive even to this day). As a literary piece, I found it just okay. I didn't find the prose strong enough to affect me.
