book_b.title: The Girl with the Lower Back Tattoo
book_b.user_review:
I'm never really sure how I feel about Amy Schumer. One minute she's so sharp and witty, the next she is performing a sketch that misses my humour bone by a mile. 
 Her rise to the top has been nothing short of meteoric. 
 Now I know this will anger her (and probably many other females) but is it due to her being a woman? And a hot one at that. A lot of her humour is about sex and this book is no exception, going into great detail about her exploits. But after a time it becomes obvious she is playing to the lowest common denominator. Once the shock factor wore off I started skipping pages to see if the next chapter was any better. 
 She actually comes across as ungrateful at times. Ungrateful to her parents; ungrateful to her friends; ungrateful to her exes. The old saying tells us to be nice on the way up, maybe she could remember that.

sample_reviews.review_text:
My reading of this book coincided with the election, and in part complemented my anger, despair and frustration. There's an entire chapter on the sexism she faced on the promotional tour she did for Trainwreck, with one reporter starting an interview with "So your character's a skank...". I re-watched the movie. She kinda sorta hooks up with 1 guy and then has a hilariously awful on and off with John Cena, and then ends up with Bill Hader. Apparently that makes her character a skank. 
 I wasn't that familiar with Amy Schumer, but had had the impression that she was some kind of anthropological sexual explorer, like she could report back all genetic variations of penises in the world. I suppose she has her reputation because she talks openly about her experiences. Reading the book, I related to her awkward adolescence, bad diary entries, wanting guys to like you, your 20s, wearing Bebe, and terrible relationships. In short, her experiences were and are not exceptional or atypical to most of our experiences. She had a few serious boyfriends, some semi-bad to awful encounters, and lots of unrequited love. So I guess we are all skanks. 
 That is not what the entire book is about, and it's funny. Of course, her experiences in sex and love are not the most interesting thing about her.

For those of you who are living under a rock, or perhaps in a country in which self-confident, successful women are, like, banned by law, Amy Schumer is a VERY successful writer, producer, actor, and comedian. She's made quite a name for herself in recent years not only through her work and work ethic, but for the candor, fearlessness, and humor with which she speaks. Needless to say, her very existence incenses many people who are disturbed by the fact that she is proof females no longer need to rely on the approval or validation of society's absurd standards in general, or the attention or approval of men in particular. 
 What's that you say? Yeah, she's pretty frickin awesome. She owns her body, her sexuality, her mistakes, her successes, and her strengths, and she has no problems sharing them with us on stage, and on the page. So if you haven't seen her in Inside Amy Schumer or Trainwreck, but want to know more about Ms. Schumer, go right on ahead and read this book, for it's very much like how I think she is in person: honest, funny, and unabashedly true to herself, and thus, to her fans.
Meh. Not really funny, and not very enlightening either. I did like the ending but that was just about it...
shit!! tabloid shit!! this is hardly a book!! I wonder how this book won goodreads best book in humour category!! utter wastage of time!! I literally skipped paras, pages and chapters too!!

I was very surprised by this book. I expected myself to think it was only "okay" or to not enjoy it. I have been reading a lot of comedy books and not loving them, but I really enjoyed this book. 
 Amy Schumer is someone that I knew very little about. I had seen her act in a couple of movies (less than a handful). However, when I saw that she wrote a book and saw how extremely popular it was, I had to read it. I had this book on hold at the library forever. They had 35 copies of it and it still took me months and months to get it. But I am glad I requested and read it :) It was well worth my time. 
 The title of the book: The Girl with the Lower Back Tattoo, comes from when Amy got a terrible lower back tattoo in high school. It is crooked and too deep. But instead of being embarrassed by it, Amy wears it proudly. She wears her mistakes for everyone to see and I think this is a good matto for life. We shouldn't be embarrassed or ashamed of our past decisions, instead we should learn from them and move on. Just like Amy did. 
 This book covered more than that. For everyone that knows Amy knows that she does not hold anything back from her fans. She is completely open and honest and so was her book. She talked about her own personal sexual experiences (a lot), but she also covered much deeper topics. She talked about being a female in the comedy and movie director fields. She talked about her body and the struggles she used to go through to star in movies. She shared her personal story of being sexually molested and how no one should ever feel ashamed or like it was their fault. She shared how her dad has MS and all the struggles that he goes through and she witnesses. She shared how both of her parents have been married three times and she lost a best friend in middle school because her mom had an affair with that girl's father. And lastly, she shared her point of view on gun violence and how she is trying to stop it. Two women were killed at a movie theatre watching Train Wreck (a movie that Amy directed and starred in). The women were killed by a man that purposely targeted a movie that helped empower women. 
 This book was not only funny, but really deep and personal. I loved reading about Amy's life and I hope she writes a second book.

These essays are not what I imagined or expected from Amy Schumer. She is honest, raw, serious, and occasionally, funny and/or vulgar. I started this book many months before I finished it. It was easy to sit aside. 
 I appreciate Amy Schumer more as a celebrity and person, but ultimately I think this would've made a better listen than read. Perhaps I'll give it a listen later this year.
This was a lot less funny than I thought it would be, but entertaining nonetheless. If you like her stand up you will enjoy this book.

Hard to say anything that hasn't already been said, but here goes. Ms. Schumer's recollections of her youth and her drive to make it in the standup business are nothing short of amazing. She's a modern woman who has experienced much of the same crap that other women do (assault, violence, caring for a loved one with long-term illness, parental strife and manipulation). The fact that a woman talks about this openly is, unfortunately, very rare. The fact that Amy Schumer maintains her amazing sense of humor in the face of this is amazing - she speaks openly, admitting her own flaws without letting them negate everything that is grand and amazing and special about herself. I admire that, and I admire her. 
 If you can, I do recommend listening to her on audiobook. What makes you giggle quietly when reading the book in public will make you guffaw openly when you hear it spoken in your car on the way to work.

Heartbreakingly, poetically, fantastically, gloriously, absolutely some of the best shit (I think Amy would be okay with me saying shit in a positive way) I have read in years. I want to meet Amy. I want to be a mutual foodie with Amy. And I really wish this could all happen so that we'll wind up being lifelong friends. Did that sound creepy? Only just a little? Okay. We're good.
I thought it would be more like Chelsea Handler's book. But it was certainly more serious and did not reflect her on screen persona.

reference_books.title: We Were Liars
reference_books.review_text:
I stayed up all night reading this book. 
 I hated it at first. I didn't care for any of the characters, I had no idea where the plot was going, I honestly thought it was sort of stupid. But everyone was talking about it right? So I decided to do what I never do and skip to the end just so that I can make sure I'm not missing out on anything. And I'm glad I did. After that glimpse I went back and finished it and the next day I went to read it again. 
 This book is complex and surprising and meaningful and heart-wrenching and not at all what you would expect. It is dark and you need to pay attention. This book creeps me out and yet I can't stop thinking about it and I can't take my eyes away when I see it or start reading it. It's like the flame that draws the moth: deadly yet beautiful. The writing was wonderful as well. I love this book and yet I feel like it might invade my nightmares one day. It's one you HAVE to read all the way through to understand, and I highly recommend that you do. :)

reference_books.title: Orlando
reference_books.review_text: This is a book literally just to include all of the inside jokes between Virginia and her secret lover. This story wasn't written or meant to be understandable or enjoyed by anyone other than the two of them.... so WHY should we study it or read it is my question... I really hated having to read it... If I could give it 0 stars I would.

reference_books.title: Anil's Ghost
reference_books.review_text: I think that the reason I really hated this book was because I had to read it for class but our teacher didn't tell us ANYTHING about it beforehand. I had never even heard of Sri Lanka before this novel (which makes me feel horribly ignorant honestly). I didn't even know what genre it was supposed to be going into it so the entire time I was reading it I just felt lost and confused and unsure of what was supposed to be going on. I really hated every second of it and honestly I can't even remember if I had bothered to finish it in the end. If you do your research before reading this then I recommend it as I'm sure it would (hopefully) make more sense to you. If you don't want to research and learn about Sri Lanka and its history before reading this though, then I don't recommend it as it won't make any sense to you.

reference_books.title: A Kiss in Time
reference_books.review_text:
DNF. I could barely make it through chapter one though I skimmed through later sections of the book to make sure I wasn't missing out on anything. I wasn't. This was my first Alex Flinn novel and I must say, I don't think I will ever be reading anything by him again. 
 The main characters are both despicable. For being magically blessed with intelligence she is one of the dumbest characters I have ever met. Not only that, but she was prideful and self-absorbed and inconsiderate. I really, really hated her. As for the guy, he was just as bad. And that's without the blessing of intelligence. So you'd expect him to be worse but he was actually about the same. They were well-matched in that respect. 
 I hated both of them. 
 The writing style was very simple and immature. The word choices were obnoxious, especially for her and her "old world" terms. 
 I enjoy fairy tale retellings (this one was for Sleeping Beauty), so I thought that there was promise where the plot was concerned, but as it's sleeping beauty, you're really relying on the characters to pull you through. The characters failed tremendously at this. 
 A friend had warned me about this book but I didn't listen... I was taken in by the pretty cover. Don't give in to the pretty cover and listen to your friends when they warn you about horrible books.

book_a.title: Bewitching Season (Leland Sisters, #1)
book_a.user_review:
I got through a fourth to a third of this book before I had to start skipping ahead and skimming through. I think maybe ten to fifteen years ago I would've really enjoyed this book. It had simple writing, immature characters/relationships, and a stereotypical plot line. Back when I was ignorant of how things were in the early 1800's and back when I was immature myself, I would've liked the cliche situations and relatable characters. However, now that I know better and am (hopefully) no longer as immature, I just found this book incredibly ridiculous. As I said before, the writing style was incredibly simple though not stinted and jumping around all over the place, which was good, and I recognize that this book is aimed at girls about ten years my junior, but still. Girls ten years my junior can handle more complex writing styles than this. It was a little TOO simple. 
 As for the characters, I didn't believe a single one of them. Except MAYBE Pen. The author seemed to think that people in the early 1800's would think and act exactly how we do in the modern age. They didn't. They had a different set of rules to live by and were raised in a different kind of society. That changes how you view things and how you act. No one in this story acted as if they were from the 1800's and that killed me. These are high born ladies, sitting on tables, and calling their governess Ally. I'm sorry but that would NEVER happen. EVER. Also it was hard to tell them apart as their nicknames for each other were Pen and Persy. It took a few chapters to successfully know which was which and even then there would be occurrences of me mixing them up. Plus I really hated Persy. I liked the idea of her, but she really annoyed me in the end. Here she is constantly talking about how her sister is so much prettier, and so much more interesting, and has such greater hair than she does.... when THEY ARE IDENTICAL. And when the love interest is interested in the same things she is and tries talking about them with her, she just sits silently and thinks to herself how happy he looks sitting next to her gorgeous sister who is carrying on a great conversation with him (but only because Persy refuses to talk or answer his questions. So in order to not appear rude and to cover up Persy's awkard silence, she talks to the guy instead. Which is really quite considerate of her really). It's just obnoxious. 
 They never take the magic thing seriously. None of them. Except perhaps Ally. It made me annoyed and nervous the entire time that they were going to get themselves exposed (and maybe that happens later.. I didn't actually finish reading this so I don't know for sure). 
 Then there's the plot. It was so cliche and predictable. Half of the events weren't necessary, they were just there for over the top drama. Which I find annoying and unrealistic. 
 The only slightly redeeming quality was the love interest but after two chapters of that I was fed up already. So it wasn't redeeming enough. The reason I got fed up with that situation was because of Persy's handling of the situation (which was always in terribly immature ways - and she's supposed to be the intelligent one) and the love interest himself. I didn't believe him. I didn't believe that he would go from being what sounded like the worst little boy that walked the earth, to the most charming, handsome, gentlemanly 18 year old in just one summer and to just continue getting better from there when they finally see him again at 21. I just didn't believe it. You don't tease someone for your entire life and then just suddenly turn into a different person who's in love with them instead. I can see being an immature little boy and teasing because it's funny and they're girls and whatever, but to do it until you're 17 and then suddenly decide that you're going to stop and have a normal conversation with them which leads to love when the girl is 13.... I don't know... Seemed forced and fake. Again, unnecessary drama that was added to complicate things. 
 I know I'm railing on this book pretty hard, especially when I didn't even read the whole thing. And my main problem is just that I waited too long to read it because now I'm too old for it. But this is my honest opinion on it at this moment. 
 I recommend this for a really young audience....like 10-13 maybe. But nothing higher than that. Unless you're SUPER into the immature fluff of historical inaccuracy. Your call :)

sample_reviews.review_text: This was such a great book. And it's in one of my favorite genres, gaslamp! (Magic and Victorian England. Fantastic!) I loved all of the characters, including the main one, Persephone Leland, but sometimes you just wanted to punch her. She was basically the epitome of shy, nervous girl around a handsome man. And she seemed to love making the man she truly loved insanely jealous! But overall, a great book.

Maybe I was just in the mood for a fun, lighthearted read - but I really liked this book! It was kind of like Harry Potter meets historical fiction meets regency romance for young adults. 
 Sure the plot was predictable. Sure the main characters could get whiny. Sure sometimes I wondered if they could really be as clueless as they were in the choices that they make (but then again...I was 17 once upon a time). But still, it was an enjoyable read - one that I didn't want to put down! I loved that it was clean, and good-natured, and fun. 
 I didn't give it five stars for some of the above reasons, but mostly because of a sub-plot love story where the kidnapped falls in love with the kidnapper. It just seemed too easy, too obvious, and, well....disappointing. 
 I'm going to be reading the next one in the series without a doubt!

I read the first 100 or so pages and then read the last 10 pages. I don't feel like I missed anything. I guess I can't really say I READ the book, but since I probably didn't miss anything, I'm calling it a "read". I grew tired of Percy's constant, "I'm not good enough," diatribe. Blah blah blah. While one reviewer said that it's exactly like a teenager feels, I think it's more appropriate for a new teenager...like 13...not someone who is almost 18 and "coming out". It was tiresome.

It gives me back my faith in this genre. This charming mix of magic in nineteenth century England. One can't take it for serious. But as a light, enjoyable story it was worth my time. 
 It was funny. I laughed reading banter between siblings. And who wouldn't want to have Charles as a brother? ;-) 
 A love story was sweet, clean and with a little spark. 
 I didn't mind that was totally predictable, (I knew very soon that Lochinvar was a wizard. ) that the world here was black and white (each character was utterly good or bad) and that the whole novel was evidently for young adult (teenagers). It was written in a way that everyone who is open to such genre can enjoy it. 
 Nonetheless, I give only 3 stars because I think that Marissa Doyle should give us here also a love story for Pen or make the book a little shorter. I felt sometimes that she was pushing too hard. But perhaps it was just my adult voice that thought so ;-) 
 Still, I think I will try another Doyle's book in the future.
A moderately enjoyable book that combined girlish gossip and drama with more in-depth magical story lines. Nothing too amazing, but worth a read for entertainment's sake.

I love historical fiction. I love the manners, the balls, the dresses, the courtesy... it all feels so romantic (No, don't touch me with reality)... fueled by the likes of Jane Austen's works. 
 I wanted to love Bewitching Season. I've been waiting to read this and when I finally bought it and read it... 
 I love the manners, the balls, the dresses and the courtesy well enough but they couldn't detract for the utter silliness of one Persephone Leland. She may be a bluestocking but that didn't help her at all from being over-anxious, over-thinking things and at times pretty stupid. I rather think that Penelope was the more level-headed of the two even if she was, uhm, more inclined towards the balls and meeting eligible men. But I was reading the book from Persy's point of view so I couldn't say much of Penelope. I still say she's more level-headed. Both were impulsive. I like Charles though. 
 Full review at Whatever You Can Still Betray.

Decent effort for a first time author. I have great hopes that her next book will be much better. I enjoyed her setting and her characters, and the mystery kernel of the plot could have been really spectacular, if she had done more with it. Instead, the characters seemed to have the same conversations and interactions over and over, while the plot languished in the background.
a beautifully done and addictive book!

Bewitching Season by Marissa Doyle is a fun YA historical fiction of twins and magic set in pre-Victorian England. The twins, Persy and Pen are about to have their first season, which basically means they go to balls in pretty dresses and try to look for somebody to propose to them. The problem? Their governess who taught them how to use their magic gets kidnapped by this evil Irish dude. 
 Read the rest of my review here

I bought this because it seemed kind of like Harry Potter and was set during the 1800s in London. It's a little juvenile, but I think I'll stick with it, because so was the first Harry Potter. (First couple, really.) 
 It's about twin sisters Persephone and Penelope (okay, seriously, is it now be a rule that every historical fiction YA book have a character named Penelope--The Luxe series, this and The Season?), who have the ability to do magic. (Their governess gives them magic lessons on the downlow, but she cautions them to never do magic where anyone can see (because the time when witches were killed isn't so far in the past). So when she (governess) disappears suddenly, they decide to find her. 
 And, of course, they do magic all over the place, with no regard for who can see them. 
 Fun book.

book_b.title: A Storm of Swords (A Song of Ice and Fire, #3)
book_b.user_review:
By far the best in the series so far. IT WAS SO GOOD!!! 
 Read this series, just for this book. It was fantastic. One of my all-time favorites. 
 There's not much else you can say without giving things away... so... just read it!

sample_reviews.review_text:
God! I was expecting anything but this. Storm of Swords has more blood and gore than the other two books. And you might just end up feeling sorry for a character that you had loved to hate. 
 Jaimie Lannister has a POV (Point of view) chapters in this book. And the author takes us into minds of one of the most complex characters in this series. If you felt like killing him in the first two books, then you would feel sorry for him in this one. The chapters where he loses his hand and yet manages to save the maid of Tarth, will make him your hero. Yet he loves his sister and dreams of marrying her in a la Targereyan fashion. He also makes us to pause and question about a knight's duty and honour and understand why he had to become the kingslayer. 
 Catelyn Stark is one worried woman in this book. Her son is furious when he learns that she has freed the Kingslayer, Jaimie Lannister. And he has another bombshell for her. He gets married to Jeyne Westerling effectively putting their alliance with the House of Frey at jeopardy. Robb pardons her but she is aghast at the turn of events and is frightened of the outcome. 
 Arya is on her way to Riverrun along with Gendry and Hot Pie. I read her progress in this book with my heart in the mouth. 
 Tyrion wakes up in the King's Landing to find himself bereft of the Hand's position. His father Tywin Lannister is back along with the Tyrells. Tyrion finds himself shunted out of the council as his father takes control. And Joffery has a new bride, much to Sansa Stark's relief. 
 Sansa may not be as resourceful as Arya but she is still wary enough of people around her. But sadly her romantic sensibilities still leads her to believe her Florian (Ser Dontas) who promises to take her home. Margery Tyrell (widow of Renly Baratheon) is to marry Joffery now. And her grandmother the Queen of Thorns tries to find out all about their prospective groom from Sansa. Even while they plot to get Sansa married to Margery's brother (who is a cripple) Tywin arranges a match for her; Tyrion Lannister. There can't be a worse nightmare for Sansa than this one and Tyrion is torn between doing his duty and yet being gentle with his new wife. 
 The Red Wedding 
 A mind blowing chapter when you least expect it. And it reads very scary especially since it is shown from the perspective of a heartbroken mother. Catelyn Stark, Edmure Tully (Cat's brother), Robb Stark and all their bannersmen arrive at the Frey House to wed one of his daughters. Since Robb is already married, Edmure Tully becomes the replacement groom to bind their houses. Yet Catelyn is scared and nervous. And the carnage begins once Edmure Tully and Roslin are sent for the bedding ceremony. Robb Stark dies at Roose Bolton's hands and Catelyn claws her own face in desperation, helpless even as her first born is killed in front of her. Thankfully she too is put out of misery. 
 Dubbed as the 'Red Wedding', the gory horrific event was apparently inspired by Black Dinner from Scottish history. Personally it was traumatic to read this chapter yet you are addicted to the story that you can't help turning the pages. What is worse than this chapter was the next one where Arya is on her way to rejoin her mother and brother? Even as she nears the place, you feel so sorry for the poor child. (More than family honour, palace and sword, these Starks really need a family song. If this was a hindi movie directed by Manmohan Desai, Arya would have found her brother and mother with the help of one :) and Robb and Catelyn might have escaped the Red Wedding. Just kidding!) 
 Close on the heels of Red Wedding, Joffery's wedding is also celebrated. Apart from the betrothed couple, it is Sansa who is looking forward to this event. That would be the day when she makes her escape from the King's Landing. Tyrion is at his best during this event. He has become the new master of the coin, since Little Finger is out of town and finds it difficult to churn out the money needed for the gala affair that Cersai plans for her son. Joffery's death at the banquet was a small redeeming factor that gave some poetic justice to the Starks. 
 Sadly it is Tyrion who is blamed for Joffery's murder and Sansa escapes unscathed with her fool of a knight. Spirited away to a ship, she finds that the escape was orchestrated by Little Finger who kills Ser Dontas. Will this girl ever learn that there are no true knights in this realm? Well the eternal optimist in me hopes that the author brings her back to her husband after she learns to distinguish between appearance and character. 
 In the meanwhile, Danearys is on her way to buy herself an army; the unsullied. In this book, one will find her becoming more and more comfortable with her queenship and the role of command. With clever manipulations she gets herself an army of eunuchs. She forges ahead to capture yet another city, supposedly impregnable and discovers that Ser Barriston had been lying to her about his identity. To her dismay she also finds out that Ser Jorah used to spy on her. Furious she sends them both on a suicide mission to capture the city for her. 
 On the wall, Jon Snow is with the Wildings now. He breaks his vows with Yigrrette a Wilding girl with whom he falls in love. With the wights and Mance Rayder threatening the wall, the Brother's watch is desperately sending messages to the King(s) which is ignored by all. Thankfully Onion Knight has sense enough to convince Stannis Baratheon to come to the wall. 
 Bran is on his way to meet the three eyed crow, who has been coming in this dreams. He is able to merge his consciousness with his wolf Summer and explore freely. Sadly he misses meeting his brother Jon when they both take refuge at the same castle. (They really need that family song). 
 The book wraps up when Jaimie allows Tyrion to escape the prison but not without drama. Jaimie's confession about Tyrion's first wife breaks Tyrion's heart. Furious, he escapes and emerges in his father's chamber and kills him ingloriously while he sits in the privy. 
 All through the book, the author makes us ponder about the oaths that men take to uphold and circumstances that lead them to break it; case in point being Jaimie Lannister and Jon Snow. Juxtaposing it with the Red Wedding, where the House of Frey breaks the age-old adage of offering safety and succor to their guests one has a lot of food for thought. 
 The last chapter is mind blowing. I won't reveal it now. But trust me, it is explosive enough for you to buy the next book.

Far, far too long, but I've read the whole thing, and it's absorbing I'll admit. 
 Read on an iPad.

I enjoyed the first 2 entries in the series, but this book was the point at which I got fed up. It's not even that this book is necessarily worse than the other two, this was just the point at which I got tired of the GRRM formula of 3/4 of the book being exposition, with the last 1/4 or so being actual action. There are chapters (Aria's chapters in particular) in which the reader follows a character around for a time, and by the end of the chapter nothing consequential has really happened. 
 Another downside of this book is the sheer number of characters and houses. GRRM will introduce some minor character, and then 20 pages later mention him as if he's a well-established fixture in the story. Even some of the major characters got jumbled up for me. Reading on a Kindle was a definite plus, because I could search for character names when I forgot who they were. However, the labor involved was not worth the pages and pages of relative inaction, which is hard to tolerate in any novel, but especially one with a medieval/fantasy setting.
Bloody brilliant.

The thing that really bugs me is how everyone wants a fake medieval kingdom with elves and some kind of zombie. Why not put some effort into it and write about a real medieval kingdom or come up with a genuinely new fantasy landscape? The fake Mongolians in the first book showed promise, but then they just became henchmen to the dragon girl. LAME. Here's what I'd like to see: a faux-Ghengis Khan laying waste to every kingdom ever ripped off from Tolkien! 
 Also, what's up with literally every single non-princess woman being labelled a whore? I'm hoping that Martin's big reveal in the last book is that they're mostly just regular women trying to get by and they're only called whores because every single viewpoint character is a noble with no regard for the peasantry.

To say that I've been sucked into the universe would not be enough to express how I feel about this series. I am leaving town for the weekend and the fact that I won't get to start book #4 until Monday makes me eternally sad.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Martin periodically entertains me and enrages me. While he's created some compelling characters (most notably for me are Arya, Dany and Jon Snow), I dislike many of his plot contrivances. Too often, he relies on the same twists to extend his plot - I suspect that he may need a firmer treatment by an editor. Admittedly, the last quarter of the book was what saved this one, as much of the plot in the book's middle annoyed me - Martin's tendency to kill characters without reason grates on me.
Another review described this as a gritty, clever take on fantasy. That sums it up for me.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I had been meaning to read this for a long time, and finally did amidst growing controversy about the veracity of Mortenson's claims and his business practices. I heard about Jon Krakauer's Three Cups of Deceit, and since I read everything Krakauer writes, I knew I had to read Three Cups of Tea so I could get to Three Cups of Deceit. 
 Well, the story is pretty neat and inspiring and all that, but I thought the writing was cheesy and over-dramatic. I liked to hear about the mountaineering stuff and the cultures and peoples of Pakistan and Afganistan, so it wasn't torturous...but it wasn't great either.

I got this book hoping to use it in the classroom. While I love his story, and what he has done is nothing short of amazing, this was a hard read. Slow going, lots and lots of wandering narration, chapters that didn't hang well together, and yet were not really separate either. I think this is a good story, and I think that the co-author did the best he could with a difficult subject. The last 3-4 chapters are what made this a 2 star--otherwise I would have given it a 1 star. I think this would be much better as a long article/short novella.

A dull, dull required reading from high school. I couldn't bear to finish. Several years later and I still look back on this book with disdain. I actually smiled when I saw an article proving that the story was fabricated! I'm all for the causes Mortenson supposedly believed in, but I'm more supportive of people who are genuinely making a difference. Someone send me their stories please.

Read for book club. they loved it, I found it tedious at times. Although the premise was good, the story could have been told in a simple magazine article. Too much self serving and when did the guy have time to spend with his own family. His wife was much nicer than I would have been.
I love what this man did for Afghanistan and Pakistan. But the book was painful to read. He should of cut it short and stuck with a shorty story for a magazine.
I struggled to finish this one. I can't say I enjoyed it. I found the writing not really keeping my attention and after viewing the 60 minutes report on Greg M. I was questioning a lot of the book .

This book about Greg Mortenson building schools all over Pakistan and Afghanistan, has good intentions. I am convinced that Greg is truly a good person, aspiring to make good change throughout the Middle East. However, this book, destroys a lot of the message. 
 At the beginning Relin, the narrator, wrote, "I choose to side with Greg Mortenson. Not because he doesn't have his flaws," insinuating he's not trying to glorify Greg. That's exactly what he does though. He glorified him. He made him this more human than human through his storytelling. It was more of a story of one man's worship (Relin's) of another (Greg). Much more could have been enjoyable if I was not told how to think about Greg and his actions throughout the book. There was no criticism, nor objectivity; nothing left open-ended for the reader to form opinions about. The whole book was an advertisement for how great Greg is (and less about what his achievements have accomplished). 
 The writing, was indeed terrible. Relin had some pretty awful sentences and descriptions. It makes the reading difficult to endure. There were sentences that were just so sappy that it made me want to put the book down altogether. It was awful. 
 Also, I feel there was this underlying theme of, "we have so much to learn from the Afghans/Pakistanis, we should be learning from them." An example is when Greg sat with the nurmadhar of Korphe, "He taught me that I had more to learn from the people I work with (the Pakistanis) than I could ever hope to teach them." Anyone who travels to a foreign culture for the first time, gets this euphoric feeling at first. Going back time and time again makes one realize that there could be something learned from anywhere you travel, and more often that thought becomes that they have something to learn from American culture as well. It read like some one who has just arrived in and is enamored with another society, rather than some one who has lived both societies. 
 Progressing farther towards the end of the book, Relin slipped in more and criticism of America. There was so much of putting America down and pushing the flaws of it. I don't think the push should have been to look at how much America has done wrong, but to push how much we could still do to help. So it annoyed me to read the part where Greg went to DC to fight for aid in Afghanistan, and the government agreed to give him $2.2 million! So he got government approval to delegate its money as he argued to, and then told it, after all that fuss, "no thanks." He scoffed at the money, saying he would lose all credibility. What a mixed message. He got what he wanted and then just spit on it. $2.2 million to use in a good helpful way (which was just a starting point). How could he criticize the government when he turns his back on his own advice? That money would have funded so much, as he wished, and he turned it down? That doesn't make sense and it's not really fair to put down the government after that. 
 Furthermore, I cannot see the Taliban as anything but a bad force. Greg said at one point, talking about their "ingenuity" against our "sophisticated technology", "I didn't have much sympathy for the Taliban, and I didn't have any for Al Qaeda, but I had to admit that what they were doing was brilliant{...}I realized that if we were counting on our military technology alone to win the war on terror, we had a lot of lessons to learn." Brilliant? Really? And you have some sympathy? And again slights America, admires the Taliban, by inducing that we are less intelligent than the Taliban in warfare. Plus, he just watched all this on an airplane, and had no sympathetic thought toward the Americans who were possibly getting killed below? Hm. 
 Relin scoffed at the "danger" of being over there after 9/11. He wrote about the American Embassy leaving many messages warning Greg of his security as an American, making it seem like the Embassy exaggerated. It makes me think of Grizzly Man, the documentary of the man living with grizzlies, laughing at the fact that so many call them "dangerous," and then he is destroyed by a grizzly. No, not all Middle Easterners are dangerous, and there are many who are good people, but there are still extremists populating those areas, searching for and specifically targeting people from Western areas. It's nothing to play down. And it certainly doesn't make him heroic, I think it makes him somewhat naive. What makes him safer than any other Westerner? 
 I agree with the overall idea of building schools, water suppliers, and health centers. I think it is an excellent idea of how to promote peace. It could really do good throughout the Middle East. On the grand scale, what Greg is doing is fantastic, but this book doesn't do a good job of illustrating it. I agree with others that this book could have been better as a much shorter, less biased, more factual article in something like Rolling Stone. This book could have been used more to focus on the students and communities and how they've benefited, rather than criticizing America. It could also tremendously benefit from having a different author. Oh, and some more photos would be nice too. 
 *UPDATE 12OCT11* 
 It makes me thoroughly disgusted to find out that most of this book is a work of fiction. There is a lot that is just not true, and is written about in Jon Krakauer's book Three Cups of Deceit. I still like that the books gets some people to think, but the fact that Mortenson is ripping off his readers and believers is just plain wrong.
Honestly, some problematic orientalist stuff in here despite the good intentions.

I'm only giving it two stars because I'd feel awful giving one. The story itself is quite beautiful and inspiring, but the way it's written makes me 
 want to scream. Seriously. I want to bang my head against the wall.

Don't do it. Just don't. If you like a good story, well told, about an interesting person, look somewhere else. 
 The writer is blinded by hero worship, and while I'll admit that Mortenson has done some wonderful things, he even admits that he has less than admirable personal skills and has isolated many people. (The author tells us he almost abandoned this book due to the difficulty of working with Mortenson. And we would have been better off, let me tell you. I will never get these hours back.) 
 It is also so overwritten as to be almost unreadable. To paraphrase: Greg drank the last of his water from the canteen, but couldn't drink in enough of the beautiful mountain scenery. I should have put it down then, but that was page 12. I thought it might get better. This guy never met an adjective he didn't like. 
 I wondered what others thought about this book, so I checked Amazon. There are about 1200 reviews, and almost 1000 of them are 5 star. Apparently I am in the minority, at least in the Amazon reviewer crowd. 
 Lest anyone think I am critiquing Greg Mortenson himself, I am not. He has done great things, and, often, people who do great things for humanity are not the greatest humans. But the book needs some serious editing, and maybe another author.

"It's hard to be different," Scarborough said. "And perhaps the best answer is not to tolerate differences, not even to accept them. But to celebrate them. Maybe then those who are different would feel more loved, and less, well, tolerated." 
 There are two things you should know about this book: 
 1. Mr. Scarborough is the best character to ever exist. 
 2. It will take your beliefs apart, and question them. 
 "We're a pretty tolerant place," Steve said, an edge to his voice. 
 "Ah, interesting word. Tolerant. What does tolerant mean?" 
 "It means we tolerate," Steve said, flat. "We accept people." 
 "Actually, tolerance and acceptance are different. To tolerate seems to mean that there is something negative to tolerate, doesn't it? Acceptance, though, what's that?" 
 "Well, if you need to accept something, that means it's not like it should be, right? Like you accept something as it is. Acceptance is an affirmation you're good enough." 
 And in these two quotes, lies the crux of this novel. It doesn't tell us what to believe, the main character isn't preachy about anything. He's just trying to figure things out for himself. He's trying to understand labels, and why they're (not) important. And it's important that we, as readers, try to figure this out along with him. 
 Rafe is tired of being the gay kid. He's tired of people expecting him to be different. Tired of people expecting him to be special. When someone else crossdresses on halloween - they're a travestite. When Rafe does the same - he's a drag queen. This book left me thinking about a hell lot of things. If being gay was the "norm", would we objectify men the way we talk about women as things? (We = society in general) Or is that treatment reserved only for women? 
 Why do we have labels for everything? 
 "I'm so tired of being a type," I repeated. 
 "It's not just a black and white thing. Jock. Geek. Stoner. No one is considered just a human being, it seems like." 
 I don't have the answers. Nor does Bill Konigsberg. But it's important that we think about this.
2013 Rainbow Awards Honorable Mention (5* from at least 1 judge)

Posso dizer q ela tem q desapegar dessa serie e escrever algo novo , algo melhor , algo que faca sentido pois para mim ela entrou na lista de piores autoras de 2016 so pelos Maddox (tirando Travis) e pelo livro funeral... 
 ODIOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO !!

Siempre supe, desde que me entere de la existencia de este libro, que iba a ser una completa decepcion. Un intento desesperado de la autora por extender una serie que encontro su cierre en "A Beautiful Wedding". 
 Puedo entender por que Jamie McGuire escribio la saga "The Maddox Brothers" y por que los seguidores de esta historia siguen leyendo los libros (me incluyo) a sabiendas de que el contenido es cada vez mas absurdo y menos creible. Como lector, uno se involucra con los personajes y la constante curiosidad por saber que pasa despues, pero es gracias a libros como este, que me pregunto ?era este libro realmente necesario?. En mi opinion, en este caso en especifico, la respuesta es no. 
 COSAS QUE ME GUSTARON: 
 -- ASUNTOS FAMILIARES: el libro entrega un vistazo de la cotidianidad de las distintas parejas. La infertilidad de Camille y los problemas matrimoniales entre Taylor y Falyn le dan a la historia mayor realismo y credibilidad. 
 -- EL FINAL: el relato de Jim sobre su vida con Diane y sus cinco hijos mientras su propio funeral se lleva a cabo, le otorga a la historia la justa cantidad de emocion para un cierre que no deja interrogantes. 
 COSAS QUE NO ME GUSTARON: 
 -- LA MUERTE DE OLIVE: el nivel de irrespeto por Olive es simplemente vergonzoso. Una muerte sin sentido y sin mayor relevancia. Si la autora cree que la mencion de un supuesto funeral es suficiente, dejenme decirles que no lo es. 
 -- ABBY: gracias a este libro, Abby paso de ser uno de mis personajes preferidos a uno de los mas desagradables. Su falta de empatia para con los otros y su soberbia se me hicieron insoportables sin mencionar sus infulas de gran senora Maddox. Ugh. 
 -- CAMILLE: su incansable afan de hacer todo sobre ella y sus sentimientos, como si fuera la esposa de Thomas es agotador. Me pase todo el libro pensando: YA ESCOGISTE A TRENTON, !SUPERALO!. 
 -- TRAMA: todo este asunto del FBI es demasiado rebuscado y poco convincente. Honestamente no se si tiene que ver con la manera en que la escritora describe la situacion o el hecho de que no existe mayor desarrollo que le respalde. La actitud condescendiente y autoritaria de Thomas y Travis sobre como ellos son seres superiores (por ser del FBI) que poseen la razon y los demas deben acatarla sin preguntar es extremadamente desagradable. Aplaudi cada vez que Trenton los golpeo en la cara. 
 -- EL RITMO: este libro, como ningun otro de la serie, se me hizo extremadamente lento. Me tomo 7 dias para leer un libro de 240 paginas aproximadamente cuando mi promedio de lectura para un tomo como este es de dos o tres horas. 
 1 decepcionante y misera estrella para un libro que no logro engancharme y que definitivamente no recomiendo.

The Maddox brothers were a great family and (even if i hated some of the books) they all got their HEA... before. 
 This book, in my opinion, ruins it ALL. They will never be a family again. They will never be BROTHERS again. Not like before. 
 Guilt is gonna come between them. Resentment is gonna come between them. 
 Even if you dont see it within the story, how could it not? And even more after the last chapters. 
 Two Maddoxes are gonna live with profound guilt. One of the wives is gonna live with hate and regret. And the others (brothers & wives) will obviously take sides. 
 Sooooo sad. 
 I've decided that Im going to pretend that this book doesnt exist, because Im a writer myself, and I cannot BELIEVE J.M. cares so little about her characters to made them (and us readers) go through all this.
Demasiado drama. Arruino a la familia.

UPDATE 10/4/16: My rating went down a star because I can't stop thinking about the book's reference to the Shakespeare authorship debate. Yes, the debate bugs me that much. 
 * 
 Ehhhhhhhhhh. 
 I thought I was going to be ecstatic about this book. Then I found out that it's a comedy, and I thought I was going to be disappointed. Then I heard so many glowing reviews that I was ecstatic again. Now I've finished it and I'm disappointed. 
 I love the story of Lady Jane Grey. English nobles don't get much more tragic, do they? Married off to a social climber, set on the throne against her will, imprisoned, and beheaded. I'm kind of uncomfortable with the idea of her story being made into... this fantastic romp through English history and 21st-century pop culture. 
 It's not that I think history is off-limits for reinterpretation and imagination and comedy! I love all those things. Give me all the Hamiltons. Give me all the Dunk Histories. Give them to me! Just don't give me this. 
 My problem with My Lady Jane is that I think that this particular story is strongest for what it is: a deeply tragic tale of a girl who did the best she could under the strangest of circumstances. If you won't give me that, then why not give me a story of three interconnected women of formidable strength: Lady Jane, Queen Mary, and the future Queen Elizabeth? All three of them show up, but Bess and Mary are woefully underused. If you won't give me Mary and Elizabeth, then why not show me more of the low-born female characters? Why wasn't this book about Gracie, the shapeshifting Scottish pickpocket on the run from bandits? That would have been a cool story, and the courtly drama could have provided an excellent backdrop. 
 As it is, this book lacks the drama that the original story had. It's funny, yes, it's cute, yes, but it's so much more fluffy than I would have liked. I knew I was going to have a problem with it early on when the English Reformation was changed into a conflict between people who can turn into animals and... people who hate people who can turn into animals. It's just... not the same thing as a religious schism, is it? It simply wasn't enough to drive the plot. Why does everyone care so much about who can turn into an animal? Because religious tensions aren't fun and turning into animals is fun. I get it. But it makes for a paper-thin plot. 
 Basically, so many pages of this book might as well have "FOR FUN" scrawled across them in red ink. There's no better explanation for anything that happens. Why does everyone keep quoting Monty Python? For fun! Why is everyone so easily able to hide Edward's escape? For fun! Why do he and G have to go kill an evil bear that has never been mentioned until this point three-quarters of the way through the book? For fun! Why does G write poetry? For fun! Why do the narrators tell us that people could die in the climactic battle, even though it's obvious that everyone will live? FOR FUN! 
 Maybe my sense of humour has gone too black. Maybe I'm being too pretentious. But I'm definitely not the right person for this book. Still giving it three stars for being an entertaining read, and because OMG A BOOK ABOUT LADY JANE GREY - but I wish it had been something else entirely.

I've often thought Lady Jane Grey to be one of the more tragic figures in history, so I jumped at the chance to read this alternate version of how it should have happened by three young adult authors I admire. And I knew from the dedication page, when I read, "For everyone who knows there was enough room for Leonardo DiCaprio on that door," that this book and I were going to get along very well. 
 Sixteen-year-old King Edward VI is dying, and his biggest regret is that he's going to die a virgin. He hasn't even kissed a girl. His favorite girl is his cousin Jane, but he's just been convinced to sign off on her marriage to another boy. One from a family of unfortunate noses, but since Jane's nose is always in a book, perhaps she won't mind. Still, it sure would be nice if Edward could take a break from his nurses and councilors and just be a regular teenage boy for what little time he has left. 
 By the age of sixteen, Lady Jane Grey has been betrothed four times. None of them worked out. Now her dear cousin has gone and promised her to yet another boy of noble lineage, but she's pretty sure this one won't work out either. At least she hopes so since the as-yet-unseen groom's father and brother have the largest noses in the kingdom, and her betrothed is rumored to be quite the ladies' man. And he probably doesn't even like books. But alas, it figures this is the wedding that will actually take place, and wonder of wonders, her new husband turns out to be quite the handsome stud! Literally. 
 Gifford Dudley--call him G--is cursed. Every morning as the sun rises, he turns into a horse. Every evening as the sun sets, he turns back into a boy. Thus his conspicuous absence from court, even though his father is Lord Protector of the realm. He spends his days frolicking through the countryside and his nights dallying with every tavern wench and village maid he can get his hands on. If you believe the stories, that is. The truth is that while G is supposed to be making his father proud by "dalliancing," he's really off attending . . . poetry readings?! This whole getting married thing is really going to put a damper on his lifestyle. 
 I'm going to avoid any further description of what happens when these three get together since most of you already know what happened to Edward VI, Jane Grey, and Guildford Dudley, and I don't want to spoil any surprises as these writers turn history on its ear and give them the story they should have had. This book is just such a delight to read. And it throws all the rules of writing historical fiction out the window. For example, modern expressions and behavior in historical fiction have long been no-nos. But here, the authors never let the reader forget that they are writing in the 21st century, and it works. Oh, how it works! It works because it's hilarious. The authors occasionally insert their own opinions on anachronisms and some of the more outlandish historical details, modern expressions are sprinkled throughout with a Tudor twist, and if you're paying close attention, you'll find references to The Princess Bride and Game of Thrones too. 
 Where this book may lose some readers is with the inclusion of the magical element. Some people in this story world are able to turn into animals (like G), and they are called Edians. (Henry VIII often turned into a lion and ate people who displeased him. Doesn't that explain a lot?) Then there is a group who believes Edians are abominations that should be eradicated, and they are called Verities. Needless to say, there is a lot of contention between them, and this spills over into politics. It is set up to mirror the divide between Catholics and Protestants during this time in real history. I was able to go along with this aspect of the story because it is fun and results in some hilarity and in our heroes being able to take control of their own destinies. But in the end, I did feel the authors' attempt to pare down the European Wars of Religion to such a simplistic, look-how-silly-you-people-are portrayal showed a lack of respect for the complications of religious history and the importance of religion on a personal level for just about everybody during this time period. But I suppose they felt those topics were too deep for their target audience and didn't fit in with the lighthearted tone of their story. 
 And overall, it is a fun read. Smart, laugh-out-loud funny, romantic, and adventurous. If you've ever wished things could have turned out differently for Edward, Jane, and Guildford, who were really just young pawns in an adult struggle for power, give this merry tale of what could have been a spin.

pretty funny, just wished they were a bit older (maybe that wasn't in keeping with the time, but the book seems to revel in being anachronistic so?) b/c 19 yr old gifford with 16 yr old jane was a bit skeevy. make her 18 at least!

book_b.title: Fairest of All: A Tale of the Wicked Queen
book_b.user_review: Total disappointment...this book did not live up to its cover! The writing was terrible...too flowery, repetitive, contradictory and sometimes just incorrect- ex. Hunting foul instead of fowl. *facepalm* Sad to see such a cool idea executed so poorly.

sample_reviews.review_text: Great read, I actually felt sorry for the Queen at times. Loved the ending.

It was okay, for such a quick read. I didn't think the writing was fantastic and I was disappointed by that, and I hated the repetition of certain words and key phrases (which were done on purpose, I know, to drive the point home, but still). The best part for me was the very last three chapters. I definitely think that middle schoolers might enjoy this book.

I was pleasantly surprised to find the cover underneath the cover of this book. Didn't discover it until I was about three quarters of the way through it. The concept of the ugliness beneath the beautiful jacket was a stroke of brilliance. 
 Comparatively the rest of the book wasn't quite as catching. The characters were more than a little flat and nothing about this book really had my full attention. This is one of those fairy tale retellings that make me not like fairy tale retellings. Although, I suppose the story of the Wicked Queen isn't technically a fairy tale, but it IS meant to portray the Wicked Queen from the fairy tale of Snow White and I really don't think Valentino did the character justice. 
 More often than not I prefer the back story of a villain to that of a hero. I'm sure that most people do for the simple reason that the villain's madness is always more interesting. I'd take the Joker over Batman any day. That's the reason I picked up this book. The problem is that if you're going to take a normal, sane, perfectly lovely person and turn them into something evil, you better give me a good story there. Unfortunately, this book didn't deliver that. I felt the Queen should have had a lot more depth to her. 
 It's possible that I was just expecting a certain outcome and it's not the same one the author had. Generally when I read a book about the villain, such as Wicked, by the end of it, I'm cheering for the bad guy to be good again. I didn't even have enough feelings for the Queen to be on her side. I just wanted her to die and get it over with. 
 Not a total loss here, but I was expecting something totally different than what I got.
Everyone knows the story of Snow White but few know what happened to make the Wicked Queen so wicked. A fun but tragic retelling of the classic fairy tale through the eyes of the villain.

When I first heard about this book, I had such high expectations. There were so many places that this story could lead. Sadly, it was a book I feel was written more for children than an adult truly wishing to learn the history of one of the greatest villains in Disney history as well as faerie tales. 
 I felt as though this book was on the same level as fan fiction and perhaps even a step below. Many parts were poorly thought out and there were even typos and punctuation errors. This is from Disney Press, and, frankly, I expected more from it. 
 There were parts where the story seem to drag on so slowly where others plot points flew by. The Queen had a change of heart too often and too quickly. The ending was sudden and abrupt and I didn't feel as though there was ever a climax. 
 Personally, I would not recommend this book to anyone. If you're a reader, a fan of faerie tales, a Disney fan, or if Snow White is your favorite princess... Just steer clear of this book.
Enjoyable and easy read. The ending left me wondering what will happen next.

Aesthetically, this is a gorgeous book. But Serena Valentino is up to an impossible task in trying to make the Evil Queen sympathetic. I mean... Gregory Maguire humanized Elphaba in Wicked, but there's just not very much to work with here. The Evil Queen was jealous of Snow White (her stepdaughter's) beauty and ordered her killed. Then tried to kill her with a poison apple. Then died. So, I think the author tried her hardest, but it just doesn't really work.

Disjointed writing throughout the book. Right after a scene where the Queen is hysterical, she is described as being "even-keeled." Um... what? That doesn't make sense. Lots of ambiguous character construction, and 'telling' instead of 'showing'. So many pointless flashbacks and dreams! gah. 
 The plot meanders along, and even the action feels boring. The relationships between characters feel contrived. "Let's go on a picnic and be best friends." bleh. Just your basic story with the ending exactly mirroring the dialogue of the Disney movie, (since this book is published by Disney). There was one interesting plot twist at the end, but it didn't exactly blow my mind. 
 No real complexity or depth to the story or the characters.
YAY! I'm excited to see that Valentino is coming out with another tale called, The Beast Within, starring Beast from Beauty and the Beast!

Oh the cheese... 
 I never thought I'd find a fairytale to be "too" cheesy for my tastes, certainly not one written by Serena Valentino, the writer of Gloom Cookie -the Bible of my teens- and Nightmares & Fairy Tales -one of the best works of FSc and SLG publishing. 
 I understand that the undertaking of revamping a classic fairytale is difficult and overdone. More so when you are obliged to stick to the Disney version, which not only comes with many creative limitations but also sets the stage for your work to be compared with the rest of the retellings the Disney universe already has -not even counting the tv series Once Upon a Time which was released later than this book. I also understand that when writing for a young audience authors usually feel the need to focus on different things, use simpler words, or clarify certain feelings and situations eradicating any nuances in favor of making their work easily comprehensible. 
 I understand and I disagree. 
 I disagree that young adult books, and books for younger audiences in general, need to be one-dimensional. I don't think children and teenagers are incapable of complex thought and I certainly don't think that we can justify bad literature as "young adult" because "kids are dumb" and all that. No. Especially when we have an abundance of well written YA books that do not infantilize or patronize their readers. Some examples: Un Lun Dun, The Chocolate War, Something Wicked This Way Comes, The Catcher in the Rye, Porci con le ali, A Wizard of Earthsea, Witch Child, The Last Unicorn, Kamikaze Girls the list is endless -not even including the Harry Potter series or John Green's books. 
 It's my pet peeve when people assume children/teenagers are incapable of complex thought, simply because it's not true. 
 The first chapters of Fairest of All are an overdose of cheese and sugar. The young not-yet-evil Queen is supposed to be full of love, the picture of virtue and kind-heartedness so as to make her transformation into a villain all the more shocking. The way this is communicated to the reader, though, is by making her repeat the same phrases about how much she loves her husband and his daughter and everyone really, again and again (example: calling Snow White "my little bird") so as to bludgeon us with the knowledge that yes, she is a very-very-VERY-good-not-bad-at-all person. The effect this has when it lasts longer than 100 pages (in a 250 pages long book) is annoyance and/or laughter. Had it been played for comedic effect, even nuanced in a meta way, this book would have been brilliant. 
 The Queen is presented to be so kind in fact, that she is almost bullied and tricked into evilness by three mysterious SUPER EVIL witches. Here I was left wondering. The point of this series is to find out what made the villains of these classic tales so bitter and cruel. You can't just pretend you have explained everything and answered all our questions simply by introducing new villains who, in a way, transfer their evilness to the original bad-guy of the story. That's not a solution to any mystery. It's a kind of cop-out that shifts the mystery of "why are they so evil" to new characters we don't care much about. A vicious cycle of evilness. 
 It's not that there weren't good original thoughts in this story, or that I regret reading it. I enjoyed the idea that the Queen had a poor self image and came from an abusive household. The need for constant affirmation from an authority figure, being starved for love but at the same time feeling unworthy of it, is a very touching, very real theme that not only is a believable justification of why this woman acted the way she did, but that also resonates with many peoples' actual experiences. It's really a shame that the story lost its way in describing how beautiful and kind everyone was, instead of fleshing-out the characters more in order to make them multi-faceted and not one-dimensional. 
 I could laugh off this amateurish kind of writing if it came from a new or unknown author. I am disheartened that Serena Valentino, whose name was the only reason I bought this book, the queen of revamping fairytales, or modernizing them and giving them a dark new twist, whose work -along with that of Jhonen Vasquez and Roman Dirge- was the reason that SLG had those golden years between 1999 and 2008, the woman I have most admired in the comic industry for writing amazing stories exactly in this specific genre, wrote this mediocre cheesy mess. 
 I know it's unfair to judge someone harshly and with the utmost severity just because you claim to love their previous work and expect more from them. No-one owes you anything and it's certainly not the author's fault when you put them on a pedestal and have unrealistic expectations of excellence of them. This is why I'm putting it out there. Take this review with a grain of salt. Either I'm exaggerating or I'm right and at least some salt will balance out the spoonfuls of sugar this book forces upon you.
