 The plot looked good and it started off pretty good...but a little less than halfway through I lost interest and was never able to pick it back up again. Flipped through to the ending, and it was just blah. :/

reference_books.title: Truly Madly Guilty
reference_books.review_text:
So here's the thing. This book is too long. Way too long for its plot. What happened at the barbecue? About 30-40% into the book I stopped caring and just looked it up. And I guess I did the right thing, because what happened seems a bit anti-climatic after such a long build up. 
 I enjoyed the characters, and their problems/lives, and would have probably rated the book 4 stars or so had it been much shorter. But I don't want to spend all my time on one book that keeps dragging on and on without any major plot development. I'm moving on to another book. 
 A disappointment from Moriarty after having enjoyed Big Little Lies.

reference_books.title: A Thousand Pieces of You (Firebird, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Amazing. I've read a few intradimensional YA books, but this one was by far the best. It was well written, a real/interesting plot with twists, and the difficult concepts of traveling through dimensions were easily explained so that the reader wasn't completely lost as to what was going on. The book was full of action, super fast-paced, and had me flipping through the pages. The fact that the characters changed dimensions quite a few times (but not too much that it was overwhelming), kept the book interesting. It was so unique to see the same characters in different circumstances and living in a world that is so different than the world we know...really made me appreciate the idea of different dimensions and possible life alterations. Plus, I loved all the characters. The genius parents, the grad students, the sister, and of course the main character Marguerite...I love that they all share such a strong bond with each other and genuinely care about each other so much. The love triangle between Theo and Paul and Marguerite made me think at first that it was going to be "just another love triangle" but the three share such an interesting relationship with each other...and the whole dimension traveling makes the relationships even more complicated. But I have to appreciate that the author decided to explore such contradicting and complicated aspects of love since her characters do technically have multiple personalities. All in all, I applaud Gray for a well-written book...and I can't wait for the sequel!

reference_books.title: The Best of Me
reference_books.review_text:
Perfect. It was perfect. 
 Having read enough Nicholas Sparks books I knew I was getting into a tear-jerker from the get-go. However, a good ways into the book, I thought I knew what the tragedy was going to be and I thought I knew how it was all going to work out for Amanda and Dawson. I had liked the story, the characters, and was thinking about rating the book a good four stars. 
 But THEN near the last two or three chapters of the book, Sparks threw in something so unexpected and so tragic that I was sitting there bawling my eyes out and silently cursing Sparks for making me cry like a baby once again. And if a book that makes you feel such strong emotions doesn't deserve a five star rating then I don't know what does. 
 Nicholas Sparks had this story thought out very cleverly from the start. We meet various characters that reside in and near the town of Oriental throughout the novel. And the way all these characters end up connected to each other by the end of the novel is quite surprising. There is great character growth, some great big decisions that have to be made, and almost every range of emotion you can possibly imagine. 
 Without giving too much away, I just wanted to add that I really really liked the ending. I appreciated and respected Amanda's decision though my heart was wrenching while she was struggling to make the right choice, feeling just as conflicted as she was. And as for Dawson, since almost every character was in a way connected to him, he was the heart and soul of the book. And with no other purpose in his life left after that weekend, his ending was more than appropriate and fitting. 
 And the last line of the book...well it left me smiling :')

reference_books.title: P.S. I Still Love You (To All the Boys I've Loved Before, #2)
reference_books.review_text: I reread TO ALL THE BOYS before starting this one to refresh my memory. And while reading it, I just didn't seem to understand why I liked it so much the first time around. Had I rated it again, I definitely would have dropped the rating down to 4 stars instead of 5, but I didn't. Then I started PS I STILL LOVE YOU and unfortunately got the same feeling. I like the characters and everything, just...the whole book seemed a bit forced. If Han had just allowed Peter and Lara Jean to get together in the last book, then this whole book wasn't even really needed. The hot tub video, the "tag" game, John and Stormy, and just everything was really unnecessary, especially when you already know that Peter and Lara Jean are endgame . It took me a while to finish this book, because honestly whenever I put it down, I just didn't want to pick it back up. I don't know...I just really wasn't into this one. And that really sucks because I had so been looking forward to this book. Oh well. It was a nice read, just not the best.

book_a.title: The Moon and More
book_a.user_review:
A typical Sarah Dessen novel. So obviously I loved it. 
 I love Sarah's writing and her stories. I love that she keeps bringing back old settings and characters in her new books, and they remind me of her previous books...leading to a bit of a tug of longing for those characters that I'd read of oh-so-long ago. 
 This story, though a bit long, was quite enjoyable. I liked all the characters, the storyline, the character growths, and the way different problems in the book were tackled. Emaline and Theo weren't really working out for me...Theo was just a little too ambitious and city-driven, and during their brief relationship there were far too many awkward moments for me to really appreciate them together. I did however really like Emaline and Luke together. Even after their break-up, he was always there for her as good friend, and you could tell that he truly did care for her. The two understood each other, and being in college together...and with Dessen even hinting it a bit at the end..I would like to think that eventually they got back together. Benji was just the cutest boy and his relationship with Emaline was adorable. The side plot of Emaline's relationship with her father as well as Benji dealing with his parents' divorce were also nicely executed into the book, and kept things interesting. Clyde and Ivy were great characters, also a bit different from the usual Dessen characters, so that was a nice change...but by far my favorite part was the very end character reveal. I knew Theo was just NOT going to be getting the job he wanted from Clyde...because well he was being really over-confident and obviously he didn't really get Clyde the way he thought he did. But MORRIS getting the job as Clyde's assistant was just the Best Decision Ever, because Morris deserved it after all the lack of confidence that the rest of the world seemed to have in him. Morris started off as the character that was simply too lazy to even move the dishes from the truck to the table but ended up being the kid who snuck the most wanted job from the student who had been spending his entire summer for it. I just thought it was a bit ironic but I loved it anyways. 
 Another hit by Dessen, and of course, I can't wait to read what else she has in store for us!

sample_reviews.review_text:
Rating: 3.5 Stars 
 The Moon and More has a lot to love, but it's very different from a typical Dessen novel. I think, by now, we've all come to expect a certain type of book when we hear the name Sarah Dessen. Obviously contemporary with a heavy dose of character development, beautiful settings, and swoon. Not to mention rich secondary characters and always, always, always growth, if not self-discovery. And it's a formula that works, every time. While I am thrilled that Dessen chose to veer off from her usual this time around, I can't say I wholly enjoyed it. Nevertheless, this is perfect for those who are looking for highly realistic young-adult-on-the-cusp-of-new-adult reads. 
 Emaline is an easy character to love; motivated, kind, and with a readable narration. While she lives by the beach, helping a family business, making out with her boyfriend Luke, and generally enjoying life in a small town, she yearns for more. Emaline was conceived when her mother was only a young teen and, consequently, her family is a little different from most. While she has her mother, she also has her dad - who married her mother when Emaline was only three - and two step-sisters. And then, of course, is her father whose contact with her is still recent but already unreliable for he was unable to pay for Emaline's tuition into Columbia and refused to attend her graduation. Needless to say, the relationship between them is strained at best. In the midst of all this, though, Emaline's relationship with Luke isn't heading in the direction she planned and now her father is driving down for the summer as well. All in all, this isn't shaping up to be the summer Emaline imagined...not at all. 
 As always, Dessen excels in building family relationships. Emaline's relationship with her mother is deep and touching, the kind of bond that takes years to build but is so effectively conveyed by Dessen's writing. Furthermore, Emaline's blooming friendship with her half-brother, Benji, is simply adorable, especially as she helps him to cope with his parents - her father's - divorce. In particular, though, Emaline's relationship with her father is most intriguing. It ends on a very realistic note, bittersweet because of the sad admission that people don't always change and yet the hopeful thought that something strong still does exist between them. And their journey there, their awkward encounters through the summer and the curveball they constantly seem to throw at Emaline, are all so richly explored. Classic Dessen: she never disappoints. 
 And yet, her most compelling point, the romance, seriously fell flat. For one, it should be known that Emaline and Luke are together only for a short time before they break up and Emaline winds up dating Theo, a NYC student in Colby to film a documentary on Clyde Conaway, a local resident and past artist of great merit. On one hand, I really did like Theo - he was different, cute in a nerdy way and very insecure about himself, unable to really believe that the gorgeous Emaline would date him. At the same time, though, he's quite irritating, a pushover when it comes to listening to his boss and ambitious in a round-about manner. Personally, I was impressed that Dessen created an unlikable love interest. I mean, let's face it: most romances in life don't work out and even if they do, not all of them make you swoon. And yet, I will admit that this set-up didn't make for an interesting read. For one, the plot was slow - as is always with case with Dessen's novels but where the romance picks up when the plot lags, here the romance only slowed it down further - and secondly, Theo was just not a character I could get behind. As readers, we don't really know much about Theo beyond what we see on the surface and he remains that way, oscillating between extremes (insecurity and ambition) and generally failing to charm the crowd. 
 In addition, there was a lack of depth regarding the secondary characters. Dessen can write beautiful sibling relationships, as she proved with this installment, but I felt as if the bonds between step-sisters was forsaken in this novel in favor of the half-brother relationship Emaline sustained with Benji. Sadly, I know Dessen can write multiple sibling relationships well, as in Just Listen, but that aspect was ignored with her latest. Another issue was the fact that Emaline's father got a lot of limelight and thought in this, but not so much her dad. Cashore's Fire explores a similar father/dad situation, but both these figures are fully realized and their relationship with Fire is as well. The Moon and More lacks that clarity. 
 Nevertheless, despite the flaws this book had, its messages and themes were incredible. Emaline not only comes into her own, realizing what she wants from life, but she also comes to realize that change and disappointment go hand-in-hand with every walk of life. In this summer leading up to her first year as a college student, she grows immensely and in important ways, which was a nice change from the naive heroines whose growth seems so obvious. All in all, despite my qualms with this one, The Moon and More is a solid read and a Dessen novel I wouldn't hesitate to recommend. Only, really, The Truth About Forever and Just Listen are her best and probably will always remain that way.

*** Book Club Edit *** 
 We were hoping for a fun beach read, and came away disappointed. The only characters anybody liked were very minor (Daisy, Morris, and Benji). We didn't get the feeling of a love triangle as Emaline didn't seem particularly fond of either Luke or Theo. While we're on the topic of the boys - what was the appeal of Theo to begin with? He is so dismissive of the 'small town folk' and acts like he's superior by virtue of being from the city. Luke doesn't seem like a bad guy, but he's bland and without personality - we get the impression that he's nice to look at, but doesn't have much to add to a conversation. The father was actually kind of believable, but it would have been a lot more satisfying if Emaline blew up and gave him what for and then sent him packing. We didn't hate the step-mother either, but mum was such a flake. Grandma was entertaining. 
 The most redeeming thing about this book was that it took exactly zero mental energy to read it. Not at all a brain exercise. Would only recommend to superfans, or perhaps chick lit fans age 15 and up.

Not the best Dessen book I have read. It was a bit boring actually. I was trying to hurry and get through it most pages. The love story was kinda bland as well. I did like Benji though, the ten year old brother, he was the best part of the book I believe.

The only reason I haven't read a Sarah Dessen book before was because I'm not a huge contemporary fan, but once this was one of the selections for Razorbill Canada's blog tours, I jumped at the chance. I'm glad I did. Not only did she manage to write with a passionate teen voice, but she also brought in all the problems, worries, and drama that a teen goes through in this day and age. I did have problems with the pacing and the lack of plot. But considering the summer-y beach theme of the cover, I had assumed it would include a summer fling and a transformation of sorts. Characters always change once they graduate high school and are thrust into their first year of college. 
 I always have trouble reading a book when I dislike the character more specifically the main character because then I stop caring about the story. This was hard to get into because I knew it was about Emaline and her summer before going to college but I felt lost just as much as she did. I felt Emaline to be a little flat and whiny in the beginning, but was luckily introduced to a much more emotional and changed character at the ending. The full cast of characters added so much more meaning to the plot and I'm glad they were all included. From Emaline's entire family (I have a soft spot for Benji) to her best friends Daisy and Morris, each character had a little bit of a back-story that's revealed little by little. 
 In the end, I was happily gobbling away the final chapter. I'm glad I read my very first Sarah Dessen book and I'm sure it won't be my last. I'm looking forward to reading the rest of her back-list titles because she knows her teen audience and knows them well. Here's to more SD books in my TBR list! 
 Characters 
 Love the back-story tidbits on each of the characters. Very strong! 
 Pacing/Length 
 Slow pacing, and the length was too long for me. 
 Cover/Design 
 Very summer-y feel! Fits the setting well! 
 Plot 
 Simple story, but I was hoping for a lot more. 
 Overall, a cute beach read, perfect for vacation!

this was my first book of Sarah dessen's & it was honestly a bad read for me. The entire plot was so slow & there wasn't much happening either, yes there were character development between the main character & her father, also her half-brother, benji. But on the romance side of the story, it was slow & nothing really happened. In my point of view, Sarah created theo as an annoying character. He was too pushy during the entire relationship & his actions were somewhat immature for his age, like the whole "Best ____ date". Whereas Luke was somewhat interesting in the main character's love life, but it only lasted a split second. Overall, i disliked this book due to the slow plot & dry content.

Tengo claro ya que Sarah Dessen no es para mi. He llegado a captar la esencia de sus otras obras pero no sus sentimientos, y 0Te dare las estrellas y mucho mas0 me parece una triste cascara vacia con personajes inutiles y un trasfondo insipido. Su narracion ha sido poco convincente, sin un argumento solido, y tras recapacitar y darme cuenta de que me pase gran parte de esta lectura mirando ansiosamente cuantas paginas faltaban para poner fin, llega el momento de poner fin a una relacion. 
 Resena completa: http://nubedemariposa.blogspot.com.es...

Most of the story was okay, but it was nothing special. However the ending really made up for that. That wasn't the typical contemporary YA romance ending. The main character doesn't end up with neither of her love interests. But it is still a happy ending. I love that here the main character doesn't need a boy to be happy. I love the sweet and cute books, in which the characters end up together, but it is really refreshing to see a heroine, which realizes that a boy isn't everything and has her own ambitions and goals. Also I liked the whole father and dad thing.
I quite liked this book, but it wasn't as amazing as some of sarah Dessen's other books.

A typical Dessen novel, but this one was more...mature. The characters were less teenage-y, the writing wasn't as fast-paced, and the plot moved slowly. 
 Emaline lives in a shore town with her boyfriend (Luke) of nearly four years. She and her friends are prepping for college in the fall while still dealing with jobs and other things - such as tourists. Her biological father is estranged and often a jerk; her mother is a well-meaning woman and her stepfather is amazing (if a bit in his own world). 
 Then Theo and his boss Ivy show up to do a documentary on a local artist (whose skills were quite unknown until now). When Luke and Emaline split, Theo dives in (without even realizing the split happened). That boy (he's 21 but acts childish) is exuberant and needs to have The Big Thing for any event - first date, second date, outside date, first kiss...I swear, he'd have a Super Big Poo In the Ocean Day! anniversary if he could. 
 He also is like Ivy in ways - if he doesn't get his way, he'll push and manipulate without Emaline and her friends fully realizing it. 
 OK, her friends Daisy and Morris see it, and are the only ones not afraid to point out something is off with Theo until near the end when Emaline's parents do. 
 She also has to deal with her father and step-mother getting a divorce, which is making their son Benji (he's such an adorable 10-year-old) sad and craving positive attention. 
 I just find it ridiculous that the teens are drinking so much, and it's almost as if their parents know and don't care. When Emaline goes out with a 21-year-old NYU student who is only around for the summer/documentary, it's as if only Daisy and Morris have an issue with it. Naw, not a problem at all in a tourist town where summer hook-ups are common. 
 As another reviewer stated, it's difficult to care for the characters. They're flat and honestly, I thought there'd be a drunk driving accident, or something exploding in Emaline's house. And I'd have taken it all under stride.
I listened to maybe 10% of this and wasn't feeling it. So I moved on.

book_b.title: Gone (Gone, #1)
book_b.user_review:
*warning!! contains spoilers!* 
 Good. Great. Awesome. Wonderful. 
 New concept, great story, and well-written characters. 
 First of all, I have never read a dystopian novel with no adults. Every dystopian novel is unique in its own way, but this one was crazy creative. I loved that this entire world, "The FAYZ" is run by children under the age of fifteen. And while at times that was a bit annoying because I couldn't really picture such young kids doing half the things that these kids do, I shrugged off the irritation because this IS a strange situation and who knows how mature young kids can get when there is no adult to guide them. They would have to take everything in their own hands and learn how to survive no matter what it took...and that's precisely what these kids did. 
 I think I loved almost every character in this book. The author did a really good job telling the story through multiple characters' pov so that the readers could get attached to as many characters as possible. Each character was a genuine kid with a backstory or unique powers or a good conscience that drew me towards them. And for the first time I would have to say that I was glad that the "villain" of the novel wasn't crazy horrible. I mean the kid, Caine, is just fourteen years old. If the author had made him do some really horrible stuff just so he could be a true villain, it would have only made me mad. Not to say that Drake wasn't just as crazy...but then again you always have your psychos... 
 Speaking of Caine and Drake, I liked their little group with Diana and Jake. I was even rooting for them a couple of times ahaha. But then again who can ever turn their backs on Sam, Astrid, Edilio, and Lana? Am I sounding like Quinn yet?! ahaha And of course I loved Albert and Mary and all the other tons of kids that easily found their place in society and took over some responsibility to help establish order and stability in their crazy world. 
 And now let's speak of the plot. LOVED IT. I mean the "poof" was great. But I'm still dying to know what exactly happened to all the adults and where did they go? Little Pete may have done some permanent damage, and for a moment I was even hoping that Sam would disappear just so that we would get to see where exactly these people disappear to when they turn fifteen. But I guess that's what sequels are for. 
 I also loved the cute romantic storyline between Sam and Astrid. They were so adorable together, and I ship them 100% ahaha. Even Diana and Caine for that matter...though maybe Diana deserves a better version of Caine? Still glad that she stuck with him even after he failed though. And I also loved that they hinted a little something between Edilio and Lana. Maybe we'll get to see something between these two in the next book as well! 
 And talking of these couples brings me to the cover of the book. I mean Sam and Astrid look so perfect I don't even know what to say. Whoever the models are, they're both gorgeous and look perfect for the characters/look perfect together. And on the back I'm guessing it's Edilio and Lana but it might even be Caine and Diana. I'll keep my options open until I'm notified otherwise. 
 So wow this was long. But I just really enjoyed this book way more that I thought I would. I just wish these kids would get a little bit older in the next book, because I feel kinda silly reading a book about fourteen year olds. But hey, it was a good book, soooo...onto the sequel!!

sample_reviews.review_text: This book is not for me.

So back in my younger days a friend suggested I read this spectacular novel called 'Gone' because "apparently" it changed her life. Clearly she must have been referring to a different book or she was out of her mind. This was beyond awful. To make matters worse there are 5 other books in this series! Yes! What has the world come to?! I give up.

A post-ap type scenario where all adults and teenagers over the age of 15 suddenly disappear. Lord of the Flies meets the Fantastic Four. Engaging and quite well written but I'm not sure if the scenario itself is enough to make me read the next instalment.

This book was alright. I liked it, but at the same time, it was slightly disappointing and frustrating to read. I think part of my problem is that I'm currently experiencing some YA burnout, so read this review with that in mind... 
 I spent a good deal of time wishing that characters would put on the big girl/big boy panties and deal with things. Sam was GREAT in a crisis, but in smaller events, he ran away and didn't want to help. Although I get that that is a realistic response for a 14 year old boy to have to these events, so there's that. 
 I also have an extreme aversion to the word "retard" and all it's forms. So when the "mean kids" kept using that term or versions of it, I was ready to scream. I 100% empathized with poor Astrid when she's forced to say those things about her brother, as I have a brother with a disability as well. I know that the kids saying these things about/to Petey were meant to show how awful those kids were, but it got to a point where it was too much for me to enjoy the story further. It was distracting. 
 I was frustrated that I felt like this book set up SO many things, but accomplished nothing. I loved the premise. I thought it was intriguing. But I wanted more of a resolution. I prefer book series where each book resolves the problems within the book but keeps you interested in what else is going to happen, as opposed to a total cliffhanger ending that left me feeling like "That's it? That's all I get?". 
 I wanted to know what else happened, but I was not willing to commit to another 2500 pages to get there. I ended up reading the wikipedia explanation of the following 5 books, as well as getting the synopsis of each from my friend who read all of them. Beware that if you start this book, you're likely committing to roughly 3000 pages...... 
 So to recap...Great premise! Intriguing. Disappointing execution and ending.

I was compelled to continue reading the book because it has a good story line and the characters are likable enough. I have to say (without spoiling it for those who want to read it), I HATED the ending. It was one of those books where you find finally find out what is going on and you think, "Really?" It was almost as if Grant couldn't figure out a way to end it (and provide enough "umph" for a sequel) so he just... (you'll have to read the book yourself to find out what happened).

This book had me crying in times, pissed off at characters in others and also reminded me a lot of Under the Dome by Stephen King. I did not enjoy the book and thought the plot was pretty predictable, I found most of the characters to be not as relatable. There are some moments in this book that are graphic and probably not suited for kids younger than 10. Those were the moments the touched me. I didn't continue on with the series. 
 I give this book a 2.5 stars because 3 stars are usually books that I've enjoyed a bit but were not overall well written, consistent or captured my attention enough to be a 4 or 5 stars. 2 stars is usually the lowest I rate books, some are DNF and some I finished but would never recommend. This book is in between these two ratings. I read this book when I was around 16, perhaps too old to really enjoy this book, perhaps not. I did not detest the book, just did not think the writing was up to par, neither the characters, content, pace and flavour.
I liked it, but didn't at the same time. It was fast-paced but kind of grating and weird too.

Suffice it to say that the Gone series, perhaps by virtue of being a series, touches on pretty much everything you might expect in a post-apocalyptic adult-less world: rivalries, competition, chaos, mob mentality, hunger, and so on. Add to that a bunch o' supernatural forces, and you really come away with an all-encompassing work of socio-political science fiction. You know, for teenagers. 
 [FULL REVIEW]

Have you ever started a book without any intention of liking it and then totally falling in love with it. After finishing Gone in two days I felled relieved that I also borrowed the second book, Hunger, at the library. Now I only need to do is go back to bed and start reading. I can truly say this book is awesome, Michael Grant you just earned a place in my top ten of favourite authors. 
 The story is told trough different characters. And to tell you all about them would make this review a very long one. So I will focus on only two of them, Sam and Caine. 
 Sam is a great character. He is brave, honest and very forgiving. Caine on the other hand is the evil reincarnated, he is selfish, strong and vengeful. Both of the boys have special powers that makes them more powerful than the rest of the children. I liked both of the characters a lot and especially the relationship Sam has with Astrid. It felt real and very sweet. 
 Also I liked that some of the children got different powers. And these powers play a big role in the story! It reminded me a lot of the X-men, which I enjoyed when I was younger. 
 The story is suspenseful, action filled and intense. The mystery about the disappearing of the adults will keep you turning pages at a extreme fast paste. 
 Gone is very well written and flows easily. The writing style was excellent and Michael Grant has written an unique story with a lot of twists. There was always a surprise in for me and I love that about the story. 
 Gone is a story you must read! It's a excellent first book in this series and a unforgettable one it is. Read it, you won't be sorry!
I really enjoyed this book and would highly recommend it. It was a very strong start to a great series. A must read!

reference_books.title: On Basilisk Station (Honor Harrington, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I got a manuscript rejected because 'people talked too much' in it. Any creative writing teacher will tell you to "show, dont tell". The reason I had a tough time getting through "Foundation" by Isaac Asimov was because the charatcers talk in order to construct Asimov's future space world. Once they've finished talking, the story is over. 
 So too David Weber's book. It's a lot of talking. A Navy space captain saying things like "Make it so" and her crew saying "Aye, aye, Captain", etc. This goes on for many pages. 
 Why is she demoted? Because she got in a good shot at her superior captain ... and that was a major plot point (which happens in abotu a page or two) for the first 100 pages. There's so much talking I dont know half of what's going on in this damn story. (And apparently Weber wrote more in this series. Were these characters interesting enough to stay with them?) 
 Only until about page 310 of a 425 page book does a battle break out and then SOMETHING HAPPENS!!!! (Still, like a Greek tragedy, most of the action still happnes off stage, with characters entering to say what just happened, sprry you all missed it ... as the captain is flying her ship to engage the enemy, she's yammering on with something about what is about to happen....why not shut the hell up and just SHOW IT HAPPENING!) 
 Anyway, Im not done yet but I will finish this just cuz I'm in a sci-fi escapist mood and I always wanted to read one of these Jim Baen books. This gets accepted for publishing? Really? Good to know the right people I guess. 
 My manuscript had about fifty percent of the story taken up with people talking. This has about ninety percent. Life is not fair. 
 PS: AND WHAT THE HELL IS WITH THE DAMN CAT ON HER SHOULDER? She wears this real cat on her shoulder throughout the whole novel. Why? It does nothing! Even Lassie saved Timmy from the well, and the Chesire Cat made a point and knew when to fade away. This cat does dick all. And it stays alive when everything else is blowing up! The thing should die! (I love cats, just not this one.) It is a useless character (if thats even what it is; its really just sci-fi space furniture to show how futuristic the story is ... a CAT!!!) 
 PPS: Anyway, I finished reading this. The last 100 pages has the most action. Which means (for Weber): the characters and/or narrator is still going to talk too much about whats about to happen, what might happen, what might not happen, what should happen, and what definitely shouldn't happen. And then the bullets and lasers fly and people die. Just in time for an Aristotelian climax. If SHIT HAPPENED earlier, I might want to read another of Weber's novels, but I don't ....

reference_books.title: The Phantom of the Opera
reference_books.review_text:
Ive never seen the musical, but I assume its very serious and romantic. 
 The book, however, is kind of funny. Its a mystery and a thriller, quick to read cuz it keeps your attention and strings you along nicely. But there's a lot of comedy, slapstick, vaudeville, in it. The Phantom is a wacky character when we meet him, doing some schtick about being a ventriloquist throwing his voice -- wanna hear it over there, over here, under the geraniums, etc. Wacky stuff! All important to the plot of course. And its in the vein of the Gothic novel of course, how can it not be taking place in an opera theatre which extends below the stage for five stories to an underground lake. Thus, I thought it would be darker, more serious, but its not too much. And it follows the Ann Radcliffe tradition where everything is explained, nothing mysterious after all, the chandelier fell cuz its old and worn. Too bad it killed some people. 
 A dark comedy, this could be called. I guess Andrew Lloyd Webber removed all the funny stuff and replaced it with songs. I like the book, but still wont go and see the musical.

book_a.title: Written on the Body
book_a.user_review:
Nipples and cancer. 
 Lots of poetry written about those two things, usually in that order. First the sex, then the death. When I was in university, I cant tell you how much poetry I read of my own and others in writing class that basically conformed to these two things: sex and death. (ever read the poetry of a teenage Goth? I dare you not to laugh or puke) I love the taste of you, smell, touch, etc (all five senses mentioned) then I hate you cuz you left me, or your dying -- usually of cancer. Amazing to what extent cancer is used to kill off a character, making the character left alive turning very profound, and we should sympathize with them in their grief. I didn't like the protag in the beginning during the nipples, I aint liking them during the cancer. 
 This novel starts out like a long Hallmark card. By page 20 I knew I wouldn't like it. Seriously, if you think you're reading a card and not a Winterson novel, here you can't tell the difference. (I liked some of her other books, but now I'm thinking that I read them during my school days and figured that since they were classified as LITERATURE, I had to like them. She IS a poetic writer, absolutely. So I gave her a 2.) 
 The protagonist lists all the women she has slept with. If this was written by a guy .... he would be a sexist, misogynist, and it may not even get published. I think Winterson became a published and award-winning writer because of her poetry and cuz she was an open lesbian before many others were letting themselves be open. (1985 was her first published novel.) So, even though (I don't think) the protag's gender is specified, if you think its a girl having many lesbian affairs as a list, then you feel OK about it as opposed to a guy saying how many girls he has banged. Again, I don't care. Didn't like the protag from the start. 
 Please stop using 'fait d'accompli' and 'Lothario' in any writing. As they are used here. Plus sentences like "Beyond the door, where the river is, where the roads are, we shall be." That's from the last page (yes, I read the whole thing, and it didn't get better. The main squeeze of the protag dies of cancer and so death is the theme of the latter half -- actually, the first part, the nipples, is over half of the novel.) That sentence, especially the last part, would sound fine if it were spoken by Yoda. For some reason, George Lucas and many poetic writers think if you switch the clauses, it sounds more ethereal and wiser. It sounds like Wordsworth. He dead! 'Douche bag, you are", is much more poetic as opposed to 'You are a douche bag". 
 Anyway. Hated this one. (Again with my university writing days -- I, like everyone in my class, wrote hideous poetry, most of it love poetry, sometimes about the love for Jesus or a puppy) this novel sounded like something I would try to write in second year University. Thus, Winterson really has some clout to be able to get it published. That's power! Picasso power! Draw a picture to pay for a five-course dinner, write a piece of shit book and make a couple bucks, keep your name in people's mouths, go on vacation and never have to get a real job. 
 Anyway. It comes down to this: 
 DO NOT write a book when you are in love. 
 DO NOT write a book if you've had your heart broken. 
 Because you will write something like this. Write it for yourself (what they taught us in class), keep it at home, don't let it out into the world for people to criticize cuz then you'll hate them for not loving you. And they'll break your heart all over again. 
 Don't waste your time on this one, try the Cherry or the Orange.

sample_reviews.review_text: 2.5. moments of really beautiful things, but mostly reaaaaally disappointing! i love winterson, but this, for me was her worst book. i did not enjoy it. And the ending was just very very bad.

What a wonderful book! It is the love story of the unidentified author (I believe her to be a woman), and Louise. Louise is married, but willing to give up everything for her love. Still, tragedy soon follows, and the author is plunged into a dark night of grief and despar, so real it leaps off the page and settles heavily on the reader like a weight upon a fragile chest. "Hurry, please ler her find the return of her/his love", we beg. To comment on the ending any way would reveal too much. A wonderful book meant to be read again and again.

i don't like jeanette winterson. oh, i'm sure she's a perfectly nice person, and quite intelligent, but i just don't care for her books, and i kinda don't get why she's as well known as she is. 
 i read oranges are not the only fruit last year. all that i remember is that it didn't suck. i have this vague feeling of maybe enjoying the read, but i don't even really remember what it was about. that i didn't take anything away from it makes me feel like i wasted my time. 
 and as for written on the body being among the most notable lesbian fiction titles out there, i don't know what to say. i was a little disappointed by it, and confused as to why so many people supposedly love it. part of this is because i do believe i read more than the average person, and given my english major background, i'm sure i have read more difficult texts than the average person. winterson's writing is, i guess, poetic, and not what i would call an easy read. easy enough to understand the language, but if you really want to follow what she is saying, not so easy. some of her metaphors took me a couple times to get. 
 i think one of the things that bugs me is her lack of chapter divisions. the sections, if you will, seem to ramble, and there's never a good stopping point. not that i couldn't put it down, but rather that i could have put it down at any time; i didn't really care if i got to the end of a section. she's also not big on setting. i can't get into her books because i can't picture where they are. and where's the sex!?! oh, i'm kidding! well, sort of. there's a little in there- one of my favorite lines was about moving the bed ;) - but i wouldn't have minded a little more steam, if ya know what i mean. 
 all this being said, i did have to write down a few lines from written on the body because i liked the sound of them. a couple of my favorites: 
 "i was not so sure but too tired and too relieved to go further that night. to reach one another again had been far enough." 
 "this hole in my heart is in the shape of you and no-one else can fit it. why would i want them to?"

What an awesome final paragraph. Loved it from beginning to end. 3 for 3 with Winterson so far. 
 "This is where the story starts, in this threadbare room. The walls are exploding. The windows have turned into telescopes. Moon and stars are magnified in this room. The sun hangs over the mantelpiece. I stretch out my hand and reach the corners of the world. The world is bundled up in this room. Beyond the door, where the river is, where the roads are, we shall be. We can take the world with us when we go and sling the sun under your arm. Hurry now, it's getting late. I don't know if this is a happy ending but here we are let loose in open fields."

Having looked at the average rating for this book, and the many positive reviews, I feel like I have misunderstood this novel. Perhaps it was the time of life I was reading it, or the fact that I often read it on the Tube while being jostled about by my fellow passengers, but I just can't understand why I read it and, more importantly, why it was written. 
 I felt that the novel was self-gratuitous and served no greater purpose than to allow Winterson to get some thoughts and words down on paper. I definitely didn't feel that this was written with the reader in mind but was instead more of a therapeutic exercise. Now, there's nothing wrong with authors taking pen to paper in a therapeutic manner, but if that is the intention I feel it should be more personal and raw. This felt too distant and third person - despite the fact it was being narrated in first person. I never felt like I understood the character, had sympathy for the character, or had interest in what would happen to the character. 
 The majority of the way through the novel I wondered whether I would even be able to give the book 0 stars... what clawed it back for me was the speed and impetus involved when the character returned to London. Perhaps I'm a sucker for a narrative and simply needed some action to be taken in order to feel like there was point to me reading it, but I've read other novels about mourning the end of a relationship which have been lacking a narrative just as much but have felt much more real and less contrived.
skimmed the body section. I got it. Did enjoy the story around those chapters though.
Middle of the road. I got my one of my cat's name from this one.
i love that you never know the sex/gender/sexuality etc of the person to whom this gorgeous love letter is directed. poetry in prose.

This was beautifully written but I didn't find it interesting. I struggled to pick it up and get to the end. It didn't go anyway and the best bit about it was turning the last page and realising it was over.

Written on the Body is told in first person by an unnamed narrator who never overtly reveals her gender. While this gimmick was incredibly novel and interesting when the novel was first published, it has since been rather overdone. Having read this book long after the novelty had worn off, it just detracted from the story. This particular narrative form, I find, creates a real barrier between the character and the reader. If I don't know who is telling the story and some very basic things about her/him, then I can't care about the character. Reading creates empathy because the reader is creating the characters and their world entirely within his/her head, and having a nameless narrator of unknown sex prevents the reader from being able to fully imagine that person. Imagination can fill in an awfully lot but not every single thing. 
 I wanted to love this book because it is a book about love and being brokenhearted. The discussion of love is really powerful. I was still young enough when I read it for some of the most dramatic sentiments to resonate with me. My favorite was, "You'll get over it ... It's the cliches that cause the trouble. To lose someone you love is to alter your life for ever. You don't get over it because 'it' is the person you loved. The pain stops, there are new people, but the gap never closes. How could it? The particularness of someone who mattered enough to grieve over is not made anodyne by death. This hole in my heart is in the shape of you and no-one else can fit it. Why would I want them to?" 'There is a hole in my heart in the shape of you. Alas! I will never get over your dumping me!' To quote Dumbledore from the film adaptation of Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince, "Oh, to be young and to feel love's keen sting." 
 That being said, the real trouble I had with the book was that I couldn't sympathize with the narrator. She began by confessing that she only dates married woman. Wow! You only date people who are not only involved with other people but married to them, and you wonder why all your relationships end in horrible train wrecks. Really? Really? That shouldn't be a surprise. You should know this is doomed right from the start. I knew this wasn't going to work out, so I couldn't root for the lovers. Then I couldn't pity the vague, shadowy, undescribed, nameless character who got her heart broken when her married girlfriend called it off because the only thing I really knew about her besides that she had incredibly bad judgment when it came to dating is that she works as a translator. I just couldn't care.

book_b.title: Swan Song
book_b.user_review:
Read this months ago, but I recall it being the best post-apocalyptic novel I have ever read, even better than 'The Road' by Cormac McCarthy. Made me a fan of McCammon, so I bought another of his but havent read it yet. 
 Enjoy this. Its long, but it gets into you so you can get into it.

sample_reviews.review_text: Swan Song was a very long book. Because of that the character development was great. Everything came together well at the end and I enjoyed it.
One of my favorite end-of-the world titles. I so wish this was a made for TV series. I could not put it down.

More like a 4.5, it's awesome. I don't read horror fantasy much but this was truly well done. Will evoke comparisons to The Stand. The writer is as good if not better than the honorable Mr. King. Same goes for the story. I don't know how this even got in my queue but I'm grateful to who's ever goodreads update made me aware of it.

There's something wrong with judging books entirely by some presupposed standard of literary merit. Because it seems to me that a lot of the time the most cliche-ridden and intellectually barren books are the best. Not that cliches are all good, but they're cliches because they've managed to resonate with enough people to be deemed worthy of imitation. There's probably some Campbellian monomyth type of explanation for this, but what I'm getting at it is that they're the currency of our stories, and in good check they can be used very effectively. 
 In so many words, Swan Song is a cliche-ridden mess, and that it happens to be a very good book. Pretty much every action movie trope imaginable is utilized here, the characters are all archetypes with almost no personality, and the moral spectrum in post-apocalyptic America is pretty much relegated to black and white. We've all seen these characters and situations before. And normally, I would throw the book down in disgust and write strongly-worded letters to the author, but McCammon does something right. It's never too over-the-top and he doesn't rely of any his tropes to carry the story. It's really well-balanced. 
 And the story. It's basically The Stand with nuclear bombs instead of superviruses. The characters and plot structure are a bit too similar for this to be a coincidence. No, McCammon unabashedly borrows from The Stand, and does something that makes this totally acceptable: he improves it. Where King overwrites and overdevelops characters, McCammon writes with a remarkable subtlety. Where King makes the apocalypse out to be a minor annoyance, McCammon paints a picture of a hellish nightmare. Where King tells, McCammon shows. 
 That's another thing. McCammon is an excellent writer. The novel is ~1000 pages and there's no lag time. There was no point where I felt that I was growing tired of the book. Also, just check out the opening line: 
 "Once upon a time we had a love affair with fire, the president of the United States thought as the match that he'd just struck to light his pipe flared beneath his fingers." 
 Daaaayum. King ain't got nothin' on this guy. 
 But I think the most important this about this is just that is was a joy to read. It's dark visions regularly sent shivers down my spine. It has a really deep sense of beauty and a lot of really touching scenes. I have to admit my eyes were watering up quite a bit while reading and I even cried a bit at the ending, tropey action scenes and all. 
 Read it if apocalypses are your thing.

Swan song was a great story, why this has not been made into a movie baffles me. I can imagine the actors that would play the characters. It was long with a few plot minor plot holes. Mr McCammon is a brilliant author, his craftsmanship is fantastic. He made you care about the characters easily enough, the bleak landscape he painted with words. Left me with a mixture of fear, loathing and facination. I would say that Swan Song is akin to Stephan Kings the stand. But only in the basic premise of a Doomsday story. I like that there were fewer characters to have to remember. Which gave them a more refined personalities.

I had very high expectations going into this book. It has been compared to The Stand numerous times, and the ratings and reviews speak for themselves. That being said, Swan Song exceeded those expectations. It's a wonderful story with with a little touch of everything. It has romance, action, adventure, fantasy, supernatural, drama and horror all rolled up into this epic story. The comparisons to Stephen King's The Stand are not inaccurate, but this story is much different in so many ways. The characters are done very well too. If you like stories like this you will love this book. If you do not get into apocalyptic type books, pick this one up anyway as you will not be dissapointed.
A lot of violence and not enough hope...though it ended well. I am just glad I'm a fast reader. I would not have wanted to spend more than three days with this book.

This book has been compared to The Stand by Stephen King and has received glowing reviews from the masses for almost 20 years. At over 900 pages, I found it to be dreary in parts and if whiddled down to 500 pages perhaps I would have rated it w/ 4 stars. A Bram Stoker Award winner that never gave me any chills or frights. Stick to The Stand if you want to read about the apocolypse.

I gave up after about 200 pages. It's a generic post-apocalypse novel that's very 1980s. Child who is the chosen one -- check. Magical negro woman -- check. Evil mystery man who may be the devil -- check. The writing was filled with forced awe and mini-tragedies that unfold as if by checklist. It seemed to be basically The Stand without Stephen King's flair for characters.

I can see how it could be viewed as derivative of The Stand (also a much loved book of mine). It's a post apocalyptic book and I would imagine there are similarities in many of them. For me, there were enough differences to make it good in it's own right. 
 I noticed that the author revisited the president towards the end after only introducing him at the start of the book. Something he has done before. 
 Either way, I would happily read this book again and for me that's the litmus test.

reference_books.title: The Lone Ranger and Tonto Fistfight in Heaven
reference_books.review_text:
After really enjoying Diary Of An Indian earlier this year, I wanted to read more of Sherman Alexie. Friends recommended this as my next foray into Alexie's work and I have to say that it is definitely quite a bit different, tonally. This may have a lot to do with the fact that although humorous, "Diary" hinted at the annoyances of living on a reservation while "Tonto" showed the author's downright disgust with the Native American's lot in life. There IS humor here and several chuckles to be had, but there is more frustration and anger than anything else. A collection of short stories, I found it a bit disjointed. Not terrible, but not necessarily one of my better reads so far this year. 
 The highlights (for me) include the following; 
 "The Only Traffic Signal On The Reservation Doesn't Flash Red Anymore", a sad but humorous tale of two guys discussing who may make it out as a basketball star and who will be left to deal with alcoholism. A great blend of humor and sadness, one of the few that I thought provided a good balance. 
 "This Is What It Means To Say Phoenix, Arizona", the story that "Smoke Signals" is based off. Very witty, with two characters you can't help but enjoy reading about as they deal with the loss of one of their fathers and the trip to Phoenix. 
 "Imagining The Reservation", a hypothetical "what if" about the different ways that Native American life would/could be different if history had played out differently. Heavy, but a very interesting and well-written one. 
 One thing I noticed that I thought was very cool, was how Alexie made small word additions that turned a simple sentence into so much more. A passage mentions the dinner of macaroni and cheese, but changes the cheese to "commodity cheese", completely altering my visual of those delicious little neon orange noodles. A simple dish usually, specifying the fact that this is "government" cheese shows the disparity between the Mac and Cheese I would eat and those of Alexie's characters. Several other places discuss leaving the character's "HUD house" vs just stepping out of the house. Alexie definitely knows what he is writing about, and he does a great job of portraying the malaise inherent in reservation living.

I did enjoy the story-line of this novel; the combination of journal entries and narrative recounting run like a biography or non-fiction account of events. Stylistically, it is a clever idea. I did hope for more character development of LIncoln, though. The storyline is more action-based as if Grahame-Smith was anticipating the screenplay. It runs like a movie as opposed to a novel where an author is afforded more room for development of the characters' interior thoughts.
Well written, but weird.

I just finished this and I have to say it was good. It started out really slow and frankly, did not get really interesting until a bit before the halfway mark. I liked the author's weaving of actual history with the idea of such a wonderful man being a Vampire Hunter. Obviously, we know this is a fictional take on the battles that Lincoln did face in life. This did not take away from the story at all however. I did find that the story was a bit over the top at times such as the amount of people classified as Vampires and how Vampires helped to shield Abe on many occasions. Again, this is a fantastical look at the life of Lincoln but sometimes I had a tough time suspending my disbelief. 
 The historical information presented here was well researched and well weaved into the story. I found the pacing to be generally good, but as with many books the pacing did slow down from time to time. I did like that the author broke things into sections and even those sections down into chapters. It made the pacing a bit easier to handle. The ending was really well done tying it into someone else who was a pioneer for human rights which I will not give away due to it being a spoiler. I did enjoy this book and may read it again but I am not sure about that yet. This may be a re-read for Halloween one year as it fits the theme quite well. 3/5 stars for pacing issues and the fact it did not really pick up until, as I said halfway through the novel. I may consider this author's next work but will likely get it from the library first.

I much prefer this one to Pride and Prejudice and Zombies (which, bizarrely suffered from not enough zombies). It's a clever, if silly, take on the civil war done in a pseudo historical fashion with narrative intersperced with Lincoln's lost journal. A triffle don't get me wrong, but it's a truly enjoyable read.

I don't really care if he got some of the history wrong (I hear history buffs have that complaint), it was a fun read that got me more interested in the actual history than probably anything else would. I don't care for certain vampire stories (the romance ones), but this, I can enjoy. I'm not into violence, though, so I had to skim past a few gruesome paragraphs, but overall it wasn't too bad. I know I wouldn't want to see the movie, though.
Better than i thought it would be. Fun, it even included a bit of emotional weight here and there. Not played for camp (which was what I expected) but rather presented as alternative history.

This was a fun book to read. I learned alot about the history of Abraham Lincoln along with the fun twist of the vampire hunter. Definitely worth picking up. 
 Enjoy!!!!!!!

Like many others, I went into this expecting something tongue-and-cheek, but Grahame-Smith actually tells the tale in a completely straight-faced tone, gruesome horror and action mixed with the historical fiction. He pulls this off pretty well, but I found the book's depiction of Lincoln's earlier years more engaging than what should have been the climax, his presidency and the US Civil War. Likely because the author had more room to creatively maneuver with Lincoln's youth, whereas he has to kind of shoehorn the vampire narrative into the known facts of the Civil War (he also ends up summarizing events of those later years a bit too much). I don't know a lot of the details of Lincoln's life, so it's hard to say how clever or clumsy Grahame-Smith is being with those details. Overall, though, an interesting and blood-soaked spin on old Abe.

sample_reviews.review_text: 2.5/5 stars. Might write a real review later but right now I'm just happy I'm done with the book because I just had no motivation to get through it for the longest time.

What a cool story! Clever character development (mainly for main character Mark Watney) and a compelling, forward-moving plot made this a fun and addictive read. This was one book-to-movie scenario where I really wanted to read the book first (at the recommendation of friends). The writing is not great, however, and gets very technical at times, but it's worth trying to follow along with all the math and mundane details for they come together to paint a bigger, more impressive picture with serious consequences. This is a survival story after all, one that pushes the bounds of humanity. Another thing I really appreciated was learning about how NASA scientists and engineers solve problems: by focusing on one thing at a time and by understanding priority (and by being super smart, of course). I love the simple approach to complex situations--it's a method that can be applied in many fields. With elements of science, humor, perseverance, and don't forget the unpredictable setting of planet Mars (!), this book sets the stakes high and the rewards even higher.

reference_books.review_text: While occasionally giving a bit more background than I was interested in, this was still a very engaging account of one of the most notorious secret operations of World War II. I especially enjoyed the disection of the double- and triple-guessing that the covert services had to perform, as I had not previously appreciated the degree of fine nuance of this sort of deception involves.

reference_books.review_text:
Ah, Japanese surrealism of the 60s... Some strong imagery, a few interesting insights as to how we choose to find meaning in our lives. It was interesting to see the precedents for Murakami and makes more clear the lines of influence from Kafka and the Existentialists to Murakami by way of Abe. But as for this particular tale: Sorry Kobo Abe, it's me, not you. 
 I'll try other of Abe's works, though.

reference_books.title: Among Others
reference_books.review_text:
I'd heard mixed reviews going in, but I was pleasantly surprised by how much I enjoyed this book. This is contemporary speculative done in a way I especially enjoy, namely: it's not a "magical" person following "rules of magic", but instead, every element of the fantastical could have another plausible explanation. In this case, every supernatural happening, and many key pedestrian happenings, could be due to an unreliable / unstable narrator. Since the viewpoint is a tight focus within this character's head, scope is proportionately widened for how everyone else around the protagonist might be perceiving the same events. 
 Recommended, but be warned that this has a significant amount of content, of the type sometimes found in other coming-of-age stories.

reference_books.title: Promise of Blood (Powder Mage, #1)
reference_books.review_text: A very promising debut. I can confirm another review that said that the book felt as if there were two complete books in here, one after the other. That hiccup aside, I quite enjoyed the characterization, the setting, and the reveals and payoff. If you enjoy the premise and can prepare yourself for starting the narrative momentum all over again at the half-way mark, then I think you'll find a lot to like here. I'll be reading more of Mr McClellan's books.

book_a.title: Norwegian Wood
book_a.user_review: Atypically for Murakami, this novel contained none of what might be called "magical realism" in other authors. In spite of my hesitation, as the fantastical elements happen to be one of my favorite aspects of a Murkami work, this was still quite an interesting book. By focusing on the reactions of people to more mundane circumstances, one could see different aspects than when the author treated characters confronted by extra-ordinary happenings. Not one of his best for me, but still quite readable.

3.5 stars. 
 At first, I found it boring and dragging, but then as the story developed, I found myself immersed in Toru Watanabe's world. I found his perspective of the world very refreshing. Toru Watanabe proves that the silent ones have the loudest, and most interesting minds. This book felt like a rainy afternoon spent in solitude.

Three themes emerged in my reading of Haruki Murakami's Norwegian Wood: the impact of death particularly on young souls, how we can fall into bondage to another and loss. 
 In Human Bondage Somerset Maugham deals with being held a virtual captive to another who does not return the affection, in Philip Carey's love for Mildred with whom he had had nothing in common and who had used and mocked his love for her, certainly never returning it. This is what I saw in Toru Watanabe's obsession for Naoko, a young woman whose life had been undermined if not ruined by the inexplicable and unexpected suicide death of Kizuki, a childhood boyfriend. The difference between Carey and Watanabe was that Philip Carey was inherently strong, intelligent and deep, and his obsession with Mildred was profoundly authentic and selfless; in Norwegian Wood Toru Watanabe remains weak, superficial and selfish, and the love he and Naoko share, if that is what it is, is dysfunctional and destructive. 
 For loss, I believe in Watanabe it was more his being part of the first post-War generation, a generation that had lost anything to anchor them down, infuse their life with the meaning that it once had in Japan's position as an imperial militaristic force for almost a century (from the 1860's to 1945 when Japan was master of much of Asia and significant parts of China itself). No overriding imperialistic dreams that had motivated and unified the country for almost a century existed for Toru and his generation. There were riots but no 1960's anti-establishment revolution for students like him. Their balloon had burst long before. It was I believe even worse for the author himself: I suspect that as Haruki Murakami completed Norwegian Wood, he was aware that his country was about to lose its economic dominance as well - such a resounding success to that point that Western business schools waxed eloquent of it being a miracle - only to see the country stagnate and slide into a deflation that remains with them today. Perhaps that was the real role of the quite prominent character, Nagasawa, a University school friend of Toru Watanabe, eminently likable, memorable, rebellious in his way, alive with a fire and vision, envisioning a future for Japan that others in their despondency seemed to have given up on. Unfortunately he was also ruthlessly narcissistic. There may have been too many Nagasawas in upper-echelon Japan. In the mid-1980's as Haruki Murakami was finishing Norwegian Wood, it was beginning to dawn on critics that Japan had simply not been playing fair: its success came from adversarial trade policies, it was infested with industrial cartels, there was an entrenched oligarchy that readily sacrificed the well-being of the Japanese citizens to economic imperatives. Characters like Nagasawa were the seeds that effectively destroyed Japan a second time. 
 For his part Watanabe was a dead soul, he had been that way even before his best friend, Kizuki, committed suicide. It is no wonder that Haruki Murakami say Norwegian Wood is no autobiography. Toru Watanabe prides himself on his literary skills but calls consuming a Herman Hesse masterpiece in a day reading and yet lingers longingly over the emptiness in The Great Gatsby probably because he felt an affinity. Watanabe is a feelingless monster. 
 But of the two most attractive and engaging characters, next to Nagasawa, is Midori Kobayashi, a vibrant girl, innately good, alive and loving, and wonderful in her humanity and ability to repeatedly forgive Toru Watanabe. I cannot see Midori remaining with Watanabe, and I cannot see him being anything but alone. For me, Midori - as I suspect for the author too, who had along with Toru and Naoko's roommate in the convalescent hospital, Reiko Ishida, given her a full name - seemed heroically good (as I think had even Nagasawa, although rather bad) in the face of the despair that seemed to consume all those around them. 
 I liked Midori the best. It struck me as no surprise that Midori's father, near death awakened, fascinated with Toru Watanabe's talk of Euripides, a playwright he was studying in University whose work is notable for its strong, bright, brave and complex female characters. If Midori Kobayashi were alive today, and as young as she was in the novel, she would be one of the many Japanese women adopting a single life style, not in the way the author described in 1Q84, living an empty aimless life and trolling for men to sleep with in one-night stands, but living in the way she had in Norwegian Wood, remaining intelligent and engaged, taking care of her dying mother and then her dying father, and sitting from time to time bravely and insolently before a statue of a dead God, in this case Buddha, naked and with her legs spread wide. She was a woman no man would likely tame and few would be worthy of. 
 Edwin
a love triangle that takes place inside a completely vacant setting. murakami agrees that this is not very good. i tried to flush the book in the toilet but it got caught up in the pipes.

I'm undecided about this one. There's always something special about Murakami's writing, but I just felt too old for all this teen angst.

Patience is the most important thing. We have to go on unraveling the jumbled threads one at a time, without losing hope. 
 I have so many feelings after reading this book, but most of it was sadness, like a hole was left inside me. I can't quite put my finger into it. This book was just painstakingly beautiful and true. I found wisdom in this book, like it has summed up life itself. It is my first Haruki Murakami novel and I was not disappointed. This book was beautifully written and carefully laid out. It was not written to please the readers, it was written from what the author truly feels and I think that is amazing.

Setelah selesai membaca dua novel Murakami, Sputnik Sweetheart dan Norwegian Wood, sepertinya aku jadi tahu beliau memiliki kecenderungan untuk menulis buku yang judulnya menjurus ke judul lagu atau buku. Aku sendiri baru tahu kalau Norwegian Wood yang dimaksud dalam buku ini adalah judul lagu band legendaris The Beatles. Sedikit informasi yang mungkin gak begitu penting, aku saat ini sedang membaca Tsukuru Tazaki and His Years Pilgrimage, di mana 'His Years Pilgrimage' yang dimaksud di sini ternyata judul sebuah lagu. Ommo! 
 Toru Watanabe tiba-tiba merasa dunia melemparnya kembali ke masa lalu ketika ia mendengarkan lagu Norwegian Wood di pesawat dalam perjalanan menuju Jerman. Masa lalu itu menggambarkan tragedi cinta yang terjadi antara Naoko, Kizuki, dan dirinya. Mereka bertiga bersahabat. Naoko dan Kizuki adalah sepasang kekasih sedangkan Toru sendiri menyukai Naoko secara diam-diam. 
 Suatu hari Naoko dan Toru mendapati kenyataan bahwa Kizuki bunuh diri. Naoko terguncang hebat. Tingkah lakunya jadi aneh dan seperti orang gila. Sebenarnya ini peluang untuk Toru mendekati Naoko. Namun, sepertinya tidak semudah yang dibayangkan, Naoko ternyata masih belum bisa move on dari Kizuki. 
 Kira-kira begitulah sinopsis singkatnya. 
 Menurutku, Murakami adalah penulis sekaligus penghipnotis. Cerita yang dia tulis selalu sederhana namun karena kejeniusannya merangkai kata-kata, entah kenapa aku selalu betah baca karya-karyanya. Padahal kalau dipikir-pikir premis utamanya tidak begitu WAH. Simpel saja. 
 Karakter-karakter yang digunakan juga rata-rata sama. Tidak pernah ada laki-laki yang 80% adalah laki-laki baik. Hampir semua tokoh laki-laki yang Murakami ciptakan pendiam, pintar, cool tapi suka tidur sama perempuan. Aku gak tahu apakah hal ini adalah tradisi pergaulan di Jepang sana sehingga menjadi sesuatu yang amat biasa, atau tidak. Murakami suka sekali menulis hal-hal yang berbau seksual, kupikir. Aku hampir saja menyerahkan 100% cintaku untuk Toru Watanabe kalau saja dia gak plin plan dan gak suka tidur sama perempuan stranger, apalagi sampai tukar pasangan. Hate that I love Toru Watanabe. 
 Hal-hal seksual yang diangkat Murakami dalam setiap novelnya bukan hal-hal yang bisa dikesampingkan atau sering disebut sebagai bumbu penyedap saja. Justru sepertinya hal-hal itu menjadi hal esensial dalam setiap bukunya. 
 Seperti Naoko yang kelaminnya gak bisa 'basah' saat berhubungan seks dengan Toru (aku gak tahu ini kenapa, mungkin karena Naoko gak ada 'rasa' sama Toru). Juga kecenderungan Midori, gadis ceria yang baru dikenal Toru di sebuah kafe, yang doyan banget bahas hal-hal bokep sama Toru tanpa merasa malu atau jaim sedikitpun. Argh, this book really drives me crazy. Jadi bertanya-tanya apakah di Jepang hal-hal begitu tuh adalah hal-hal yang lumrah yah? Kalau ya, aku harus bilang "WOW". 
 Bukan berarti di Jakarta gak ada perempuan yang suka bahas hal-hal bokep sama teman laki-lakinya sih. Tapi yang dibicarakan Midori dan Toru ini adalah something yang, kalau buat aku sih, amazing. Seperti misalnya Midori pernah meminta Toru onani sambil membayangkan dirinya. Eh, ya ampyun... 
 Meskipun isinya vulgar, jujur lho aku sama sekali tidak merasa bahwa Murakami sedang berusaha membuat cerita mesum. It's just simply telling me about how 'sick' the people on this beautiful earth when it comes to love. Aku bisa membayangkan bagaimana merananya jadi Naoko yang tidak bisa merasakan cinta lagi sejak ditinggal mati Kizuki. Juga bagaimana rasanya jadi Toru yang mencintai dua orang perempuan di saat bersamaan namun dia tidak bisa memutuskan siapa yang dia pilih karena kondisinya amat sangat tidak memungkinkan. Aku paham rasanya jadi Midori yang harus sabar menghadapi Toru yang dingin. 
 Ini karena Murakami menulisnya dengan cara yang super junior, eh.. jenius. 
 Mungkin itu sih yang bikin buku ini jadi buku Murakami yang fenomenal, meskipun aku bilang mah karya-karya Murakami tipikal. Hahaha //ditoyor fansnya om murakami// 
 Membaca karya-karya Murakami tidak begitu jauh dengan mendayung di atas danau seperti adegan di film Heart ketika Acha Septriasa dan Irwansyah (cie..mantan..cie) sedang memadu kasih. Tenang dan tidak ada naik turun sama sekali. Gak ada klimaks. Jadi yang mengikat pembaca hanya misteri tentang kesehatan mental si tokoh utama yang SERINGNYA berujung absurd. //banting buku// 
 Kekuatan Murakami gak lebih adalah karena kepandaiannya menciptakan kalimat-kalimat yang bagus dalam setiap ceritanya. Juga tokoh-tokoh utama yang menarik yang doyan ngobrol. Sering juga Murakami menghadirkan satu orang yang perannya gak begitu penting, tapi obrolan-obrolan dan koneksi yang terjadi antara si-peran-gak-begitu-penting dengan si tokoh utama ternyata berperan penting pada satu titik tertentu dalam hidupnya. Misalnya, teman satu kamar Toru yang gila kebersihan. Yang akhirnya bikin Toru juga jadi gila kebersihan. Atau Nagasawa dan pacarnya (serius deh, kalaupun part ini dihilangkan, gak bakal ada masalah berarti terhadap alur cerita, kupikir). Yah, hal-hal semacam itulah, pasti bisa kau temukan dan nilai sendiri nanti setelah selesai membaca beberapa buku Murakami. Pola dan gayanya akan terbaca dari situ.

book_b.title: People of the Book
book_b.user_review: Ugh.

sample_reviews.review_text: I really enjoyed the premise of the book, and found the writing very interesting. At first, I didn't think the story would feel complete with all the switching back and forth between time periods and events. When I realized that the switching was explaining what had been found in the book, and telling it's story, I really began to enjoy it. However, as I got farther into the book, I found that the stories weren't connecting, and I was left with questions as to how the book got from one place to another, which were never answered since the book went backwards. If there had been more intertwining, this book would have been wonderful.
awesome

One of the better books I've read this year. I was really drawn into the story and wanted to know all the secrets within the life of the book. It almost felt as if the book was the stationary character and the people moved through its life instead of the book moving through the hands and lives of all the people.

If the story was interesting, I wouldn't have had a problem with it being a complete retread of The Source, a far superior slice-of-life-throughout-history dissection of how the Jewish faith has interacted with the other major religions over time. Michener's novel is more comprehensive, better-detailed, and more rewarding. But that's not the point... 
 Brooks clearly wrote this novel to capitalize on the Dan Brown phenomenon. Again, not a problem if the book was interesting, but it wasn't. The main character is a "cold fish" whose backstory does nothing to engender the reader to her. And, serving as two final nails in the coffin, the twists in the novel are as ridiculous as they are uninspired. 
 Don't bother with this book. There's far better out there. As a last note, Geraldine Brooks has won the Pulitzer Prize. The cover of this book makes it appear as if she has won for this novel, but that is fortunately not true. What is troubling is that the author bio on the jacket does not disabuse the reader of this notion by saying what she did in fact win for (an earlier novel in 2006). Disingenuous advertising on top of a lackluster novel...

Nice book. A lot of history told about a book that went through many hands. Quite moving, but I read it about 5 years ago, so can't remember any details. Think it was an illuminated manuscript or bible.

Got to page 168 and just couldn't go any further. The writing is poor, the characters are all one dimensional, with the Muslim and Jewish characters all being saints and the Christian characters are overly incredibly flawed and bad. I HATE books that demonize one religion or people or gender or color, etc. Especially when the book is pretending its goal is to be "fair" and "level headed" and to promote "equality". What Brooks does in this book is to show the horrors the Jewish people went through and thoroughly point the finger of blame at the Christians. So to make things "right" for the Jews (who did really suffer, I'm not mocking what they went through, just Brooks' poor attempt to rectify it) she persecutes the Christians. 
 The main character, Hanna, had no redeeming characteristics, other than being Australian and a graduate of Harvard with a PhD. Sorry, but Hanna was WAY too proud of those two things, which she beats you over the head with every other page or so. And her mommy issues were so juvenile. Unnecessary drama, really. Same goes with her Muslim love interest. Slock cheesy romance, also not necessary for the plot. 
 Avoid this book at all cost. It will make your head hurt as your brain cells slowly die.
Fabulous, engrossing and interesting. Loved it!!

I liked the premise of the story but it didn't unfold how I was expecting. It was great being able to reach back into the centuries and discover where this book had been as well as how it came to be but I thought it would be more of a mystery instead of it being all laid out before me. This book didn't capture me as I thought it might and it felt long at times. It was well written and well researched but some of the situations seems forced and unbelieveable. Some of the characters were well developed but others are complete contradictions. The relationships feel flat and I couldn't believe them. So, 3 stars for the premise, general history, and writing style of the book, but 2 stars for overall character and story development.

I enjoyed the idea of taking a real object (The Sarajevo Haggadah) and creating a history of its supposed provenance. Although I was assigned to lead the discussion, I enjoyed reading the book, and leading the discussion in our book group. I was able to skim over the "smut" that offended several members, although at points it became rather difficult to do so. I felt that the Haggadah's journey to the present paralleled Jewish history--oppression, difficulties, and miracles abounded. I also liked the "realism" in that much of history isn't made by the big-wigs and rulers, but of common people being at the right place at the right time. 
 The historical narrative is cut up (or held together, depending on how you look at it) by modern-day Hannah who restores and researches the book. She and her myriad problems increased in both complexity and unbelievability and got in the way of an otherwise good story. This book reminded me of "Girl in Hyacinth Blue" and, although grittier, I found it to be a more compelling read.
Excellent!
