book_a.user_review: I wanted to like it, but I thought it was boring

sample_reviews.review_text: Really enjoyed this perspective of the life of Jesus, told in a way only this author could.

This is about Jesus's life when he is about eight years old and he moves back to Nazereth with his family. This is written from a Catholic point of view since Mary, Jesus's mother had no other biological children and never had any sexual relations with Joseph after Jesus's birth. Jesus is starting to question the circumstances about his birth and even asks his step brother James about it. His father doesn't want him to ask questions about it and when he does find out about the previous Herod's slaughter of young boy babies years ago he is saddened by it. He does receive his religious instruction from the local rabbis and in this book his family is portrayed as being middle class and not struggling for their day to day survival. Overall this is a good telling of Jesus's childhood since he would be naturally curious about his true identity about this age range even though the story may not be historically accurate.

Great premise, but I just kept thinking that it could have been so much better. Rice was possibly just being careful, but since there really is no biblical basis for this story I wish she would have taken more liberties with the story.

I read the lives of the Mayfair Witches series before I read The Vampire Chronicles. Her seductively descriptive writing style got me hooked. I fell in love with Rowan and all of the family ghosts. I did not have a fancy for vampires but loved Rice's writing style so very much that I read the whole series and all of the books she added regarding the individual histories of each of the significant Vampires, and became quite a fan. her writing of late doesn't carry the same passion and thus not the same appeal as her previous series. The Life of Christ series is rather stale and short. Although, in her graceful style she researches and relates the history and culture of the traditions of the ancient Jews quite well. Her more recent work, The Songs of the Seraphim, including "Angel Time' and "Of Love an Evil" are bit better to me.

To get in the right headset to edit a novel set in biblical times, Christ the Lord seemed like a perfect short novel to read. I'm not sorry I did; it had the desired effect. And that's about all I can say. I've never been that big a fan of Rice's vampire stories, though I loved Feast of All Saints, a richly historical novel. And in the spirit of historical writing, I think she wrote the best story she could, given what we don't really know about Jesus's life and times. Other than that, I agree with the reader whose assessment was "meh."

The early years of Jesus' life are unknown to us; Ann Rice wrote a historical fiction about what may have occurred in the first 12 years of his youth. The premise of the story was good, and there were some moving scenes in the novel, .....however, I found the book a little slow reading at times.
A quick read...more history and family lineage and less characterization than i was expecting. I am curious to see where some of the themes she developed in this book will go in the next volume.
This book couldn't keep me awake. Had to give up on it.

An excellent story about Jesus returning to Israel from Egypt. This book is entirely orthodox and loaded with details about people and events of the period. The author also tells her personal faith story at the end of the book.
Boring. Not very interesting. A lot of walking and walking and walking and walking...

This series is just not for me. A bunch of my friends love this series, but I just can't seem to get in the story. There is just nothing that draws me in and there is always something that makes the story stand still for just a moment. Thought many disagree give it a try if you want.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I'm DONE! This is too stupid to live. Marking this one as DNF. 
 I *HATE* male chauvinist pig and lead character in this mess Harry Dresden. 
 And I *HATE* dense blase-about-his-own-family, I'm-too-stupid-to-know-when-not-to-disturb-someone avenging angel Michael. 
 I gave this series (nearly) 3 books to grow on me, time well wasted. 
 Book 1: Harry constant 'white knight in shining armor'-routine merely annoyed me. And his refusal to communicate with people. And Murphy's constant flipflopping (invite Harry to crime scene, proceeds to suspect him of the murder) 
 Book 2: In this book the whiteknighting and communication-block and Murphy's flipflopping were doubled, and it angered me. I rage quit the book at one point, but in the end I did finish it because people told me it would get better in book 3. 
 Book 3: Wow. well at least it's Murphy lite. But I ended up halfway chapter 28, and I just... gave... up... So here is our 'hero' and his team of 'friends', surrounded by vampires, and a pretty woman tells him that she doesn't wanna end up in the whorehouse of one of the lead vampires. And mr White Knight said: "I'm not going to let that happen" What the fuck?! You're surrounded by death with fangs... First, you can't make that promise. Second, no one in their right mind would make that promise in that situation, and thirdly ESPECIALLY not that unthinkingly. 
 Also the sexism in this novel is just rampant. All women are described by their cup-size. And the protagonist sees them all as fragile little dolls who need his protection, despite the fact that they act bad-ass and have been able to fend for themselves. 
 I can deal with a bit of "protagonist against the world" in a novel, but Dresden, 'hells bells'... It's him against everyone and their ghost and their ghost's pet dog and their ghost's pet dog's favorite firehydrant. 
 The only plus is James Marsters' narration. Too bad he picked this lousy book series to be associated with.

Good book. I liked many aspects of it: the action, the chivalry, the jokes. But I get upset at stubborn female characters but then it wouldn't be much of a story without them... It did get rather long as if some of the action scenes were added as secondary thoughts and didn't flow as well as others. But besides that, I really liked Michael and Thomas and I look forward to the next book...
Fun read, I like how the character developes and also how the author keeps the other characters in the loop.

This third installment of The Dresden Files is the one that kicks off the whole series into a development of extraordinary masiveness, and lemme say it: it us a testimony to the awesomeness that is the Paranormal Genre. 
 Lable it Action Feast, because this book is packed and full of surprises. 
 Read the full review here.

Action is great - but one big, bad, dangerous situation after another makes for an exhausting read. I really like the characters and story. I'm hoping the next book gives the reader time to "catch their breath" between Harry's numerous life threatening adventures.

Not as good as the first two books in the series. I could not shake the feeling throughout that I missed something - that there was a Book 2.5 or a short story that I was supposed to have read in between. Part of that sense might be that Butcher was trying to reveal information about the baddies bit by bit, in something of a flashback or retrospective formula, but I really could not stop thinking that I was supposed to already be familiar with Michael and Charity, and have more background knowledge of the new characters than I did. 
 By the latter half of the book, I was familiar enough with the characters for that nagging sense of "missing something" to subside, although it was still there throughout. This book was simply less satisfying than the first two, despite plenty of action and intrigue - it seemed like Dresden was being willfully stupid and reckless throughout most of it, and the side plot with his Godmother seemed tacked on to the central plot; I would've preferred one book dedicated to what was going on with his partnership with Michael, and one book dealing with his Godmother. That, in fact, might've made the sense of missing something go away, too - there was just too much backstory that it felt like I was supposed to know, that WASN'T THERE. 
 The witty banter and fascinating magic were still in place, though, which keeps this ranking as one of my favourite series, even with the let-down of this particular book. 
 I look forward to seeing what happens with Susan, too...I've been wondering when her investigative-journalist tendencies were going to get her in trouble...

Another fun read from Jim Butcher. I went from 1 to 3, skipping #2 (fool moon) because it wasn't in at the library yet. Besides the introduction of Michael (who I'm sure popped up in the previous book), I didn't feel like I was missing any major plot points of the ongoing story. Everything seems episodic to some extent, and I quite like that - I want my stories to have resolution when I get to the last page of each novel. 
 While the book was a blast to read for the most part, I agree with others that Mr. Butcher gets a little too descriptive when describing the female characters. Maybe he was sex-starved or something, but holy cow - I don't think any ladies in this book have ever heard of a bra. C'mon Jim - leave something to the imagination man. 
 Is this a mind-bending mystery thriller? No, of course not. But it is entertaining - not sure how many of these I can read before I get bored, but for now I'm having a blast. Fuego!

I think I'm in the minority on this, but I'm really struggling to get through the Dresden series. All of my friends who have read it have at least enjoyed (if not loved) the series and it's honestly all I can do to get to the end of each book. Before I get into why this was yet again a struggle for me, a short synopsis for those unfamiliar with this one. 
 In Grave Peril, Harry Dresden (shabbily dressed detective/wizard-for-hire) has teamed up with his friend Michael Carpenter (Knight of the Cross, all around bad ass devout templar dude) to try to figure out why the spirit world in Chicago has suddenly gone insane. After several rounds of ghost busting, Harry and Michael start learning that there's a wizard pulling all of the strings and they must take care of him and his allies, who have it in for Harry in particular, before they and all of their friends up in very serious trouble. 
 My biggest gripe about the Dresden series has remained the same since the first book. Harry is unforgiveably stupid. He is the definition of Too Stupid to Live. At least two thirds of the conflict in each book would never occur if Harry didn't run off to do some foolhardy shit instead of asking his friends for help. Being independent is one thing, being a complete moron is a bit different. And it's really too bad because the world building is FANTASTIC. The vampires make a major appearance in this one and it allows Butcher to really develop the concepts of the various courts and their interactions with the wizards and it was all incredibly compelling. If only Harry were a wee bit more intelligent. And even above that, his goddamned white knight complex. While I admire someone who puts himself at risk for others, Harry takes it to a ridiculous extreme. Seriously dude, stop acting like you are the sole reason people do things. If the incredibly boring love interest (seriously, name one thing about Susan beyond being a journalist and sexy) makes an incredibly foolhardy decision, that's on her for being an idiot. It's not because you didn't protect her well enough. Argh. 
 My frustration with Dresden as a character overwhelms my interest in the world that Butcher is setting up every time and it's such a shame because it could be so good and I just struggle every time. I do honestly get why people love this series, but Dresden drives me absolutely up a wall. I have never yelled at a book so many times in my life as I have with this series. Yet again though, I have promised to keep going for a few more to give it a chance. So maybe eventually I'll enjoy it as much as everyone else.

sample_reviews.review_text: Ordinarily I love Sarah MacLean, but this watered down YA version of her usual period romance was uninspired. Everything felt predictable, and the characters were dull.

One word to describe this book: Insipid. 
 The plot was uninspired and has been done many times before - and much better. The writing style was simplistic and the author had no true voice/personality. It was very bland - it was to reading what a monotone professor is to listening. The characters were completely out of line when it comes to historic accuracy. It read like a cheap knock-off of Jane Austen's books. 
 There are better books written about the Regency era. Pick one of them up and leave this on the shelf. Mediocre reading at best.

So do you ever pick up a book and know--just know--that it's going to annoy the shit out of you? And yet you put it in the basket or the cart or under your armpit or whatever and BUY IT ANYWAY? 
 Yeah. That was pretty much my entire reaction to The Season, and I was right: I did hate it. In fact, I loathed it. I despised it so much that I couldn't actually read most of it--I just skimmed it the seemingly important bits. Which were few and far between, I'm afraid. 
 So, why did I hate The Season? Well. It contained pretty much all the things that I despise in a romantic YA novel, particularly of the historical variety. Here's a list: 
 1. The heroine falls in love with someone she's known her entire life. This is annoying on two levels: first off, it's kinda gross to be all, "You were like a brother to me!" and then go off and suck face. In your heart, you know I'm right. Also, and more importantly, these situations inevitably lead to cringe-worthy, soft core porn-esque paragraphs full of rapturous descriptions like, "He wasn't the shy young boy she'd known, the one with soft blue eyes and hair the color of ripening wheat. Now his eyes were firm, his jaw was square and set with purpose, and his shoulders--the pit of her stomach fluttered when she considered his shoulders." 
 Authors, you are SORELY mistaken if you think I need that kind of TOTAL ICK in my life. 
 2. The heroine is not at all sure that the hero likes her, even when it is TOTALLY AND COMPLETELY OBVIOUS THAT THE HERO LIKES HER. I don't think I need to elaborate on why that's so irritating. 
 3. On a related note, the heroine spends most of her time whinging about whether or not said hero likes her. This is actually even more annoying than just not being sure a guy likes you when he OBVIOUSLY DOES, because I can honestly understand being a little obtuse, particularly when you're a teenage girl and you haven't quite gotten used to your new boobs and all the attention they attract yet. But the whinging? Dear God, have some pride, already! Don't you have schoolwork? Books to read? And, I don't know, FRIENDS? Jesus Christ, expend your mental energy on something other than, "Does he like me? No, of course not--he could never like me! But...he gave me a special look. Does that mean he likes me? No, of course not! But..." 
 Lather, rinse, repeat, SENDING ME FROM THE ROOM, SCREAMING. 
 4. Our Heroine is always ahead of her time. She's not just any old spoiled English upper-class crumpet! She chafes at the rigid gender restrictions of her era! She believes that women should be equal! She wants the vote! She doesn't want to get married! And onward! And etc.! 
 Don't get me wrong: it was perfectly possible for a girl of that era to have ideas like that--if it weren't, I wouldn't be sitting here right now as a married woman with my own credit rating intact and my "maiden name" still my legal name (because nowadays, you actually have to make an effort to change it). HOWEVER. To have those ideas so fully and completely articulated at the tender age of seventeen or whatever? Unlikely. Also unlikely? The support of one's family and friends. While there are plenty of stories where EBIL PEOPLE try to keep the heroine from being a full human being, there are plenty of other books where her family and friends are like, totally cool with it. They even agree with her. And it's like, I'm sorry, but that's really fucking unlikely, okay? As a reader, I'll buy one a-historical/ahead of their time character, but don't populate your entire effing book with them. Jesus. 
 In conclusion, arrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrg! Skip it.
Sometimes the books that are so easy to predict, are so fun to read!

sample_reviews.review_text: If you've ever lost someone you love, perhaps to a long, drawn-out illness, then please, please, read this book. It is heart-breaking, gut-wrenching, healing and possibly life-changing, all at the same time, and you'll be glad to have read it at the end.

Like wow. This book had been on my radar when it first was published about five years ago with rave reviews. And then I saw the cover and thought "Nah, I'm not ready for a horror book right now." So so wrong. Talk about judging a book by its cover! Sheesh. Thankfully, I saw the trailer for the movie recently and moved the book up on my priority list. You know that you have to read the book before you see the movie, right? Back to wow. Written by Patrick Ness but based on a story idea started by Siobhan Dowd before she died, this is a story of a young man shouldering the burdens of fear, guilt, anger, and social instability and who needs help from a monster. It is wise and sensitive. And the characters very real. Yes, even with a monster in the story. I'd say more but you should have all the details for yourself as you read. Cleverly written and a true gem. Loved it!

"Stories were wild, wild animals and went off in directions you couldn't expect." 
 Never has a sentence from a book been more fitting for the book itself! Wowza! This book was amazing! I had times where I was just crying-sometimes it was just because it was lyrically beautiful! It was so sad and yet full of courage and human spirit. It's about speaking the truth and acceptance. It's about fighting to be seen and heard. The illustrations are amazing! I found myself studying them because they were so cool! I cried when the tenderness of the mom was displayed. She was beautiful. Her love for her son was beautiful. I think my mind is still reeling a little bit from it all! Sorry if the review is a bit jumbled-I tend to get that way after a book that I REALLY REALLY liked! :D 
 "Because humans are complicated beasts, the monster said. How can a queen be both a good witch and a bad witch? How can a prince be a murderer and a saviour? How can an apothecary be evil-tempered but right-thinking? How can a parson be wrong-thinking but good-hearted? How can invisible men make themselves more lonely by being seen? The answer is that it does not matter what you think, the monster said, because your mind will contradict itself a hundred time each day. Your mind will believe comforting lies while also knowing the painful truths that make those lies necessary. And your mind will punish you for believing both. 
 "But how do you fight it?" Connor asked, his voice rough. "How do you fight all the different stuff inside?" 
 By speaking the truth, the monster said. As you spoke it just now. Stop this, Conor O'Malley, the monster said, gently. This is why I came walking, to tell you this so that you may heal. You must listen. 
 Conor swallowed again. "I'm listening." 
 You do not write your life with words, the monster said. You write it with actions. What you think is not important. It is only important what you do."

reference_books.title: I Am the Messenger
reference_books.review_text:
2.5 (is what I have decided on) 
 Oh I just do not know what to say about this book quite yet. So I shall type out my review and then decide on the rating. 
 Quick Plot Summary: 
 Meet Ed, 19 year-old guy, who actually seems to be in his thirties (in my opinion). He is what you can call your "typical loser:" hasn't gone to school, is a cab-driver, lives with his dog (who smells horribly and Ed is okay with that) (oh also this dog drinks coffee, eats human food, eats ice cream and somehow lives...), doesn't date because the only girl he loves so dearly (his best friend Audrey) refuses to fall in love. In his free time Ed likes to play cards with Audrey, Marv and Ritchie, his best friends. At the beginning of this novel, Ed intercepts a bank robbery and shortly after, starts receiving Ace cards that have names or addresses on them. He then goes on to accomplish missions that he gleans from observing the people at the addresses (or the names he found). He doesn't know who is behind this, but Ed accomplishes everything dutifully... 
 That is all I can say without giving away any major spoilers. 
 I just do not know how I feel about this book... As you may or may not know, The Book Thief is, at the moment, my all-time favorite book. Zusak's writing and story were so magnificent and amazing, that I could not wait to read I am the Messenger. OF COURSE I wasn't going into this expecting it to be anything like The Book Thief; however, I had high expectations in Zusak. I know that he can write what in my book is seen as perfection, so why wouldn't he repeat that in this book? 
 So I can safely say that I was let down. It was nothing like what I expected, but then again, I cannot say that I hated this book because I didn't. Let me be more specific. 
 I loved the message (ha-ha get it?!) behind this book. I get what Zusak was trying to teach, and I think that he did a good job with that. I also think that he did a good job with keeping me interested. I don't usually DNF books (I am too curious for that), but I knew all along that I had (!!) to finish this novel. I really wanted to know what happened at the end. So I also liked that about this story. But those two things are pretty much it. Oh and maybe the feel of the book. I don't really know how to describe it, but the feeling I did get when reading was very particular and I enjoyed it. I guess I am saying that I liked that it made me feel something, because that doesn't always happen (hello Howl's Moving Castle). So I really liked those three things. 
 But then I disliked that Ed just seemed so old to me. What 19 year-old is a cab-driver and would do all this? What 19 year-old has the life of a guy in a mid-life crisis? 
 Then the romantic relationship was just a little off... Ed is in love (as in she is the only one he ever wants - again the kid is 19?) with Audrey. He admits at being a little lousy at everything that has to do with sex, but knows that with Audrey things could be different because of the strong feelings he has for her. But Audrey does not want to date Ed. She doesn't want to ruin their friendship, but more than anything, she does not want to get attached to anyone in this life. She gets into relationships for the sex, without the commitment. And this is okay, if it weren't that at some moments it feels like Audrey is an object to Ed (who claims to love her so much). He thinks he deserves a reward for all the good things he is doing, and guess what he imagines to be the best reward of all? You guessed it! She is a human being, not some sort of prize. I know what he means, but the execution is done poorly. I won't spoil what happens to them though... 
 I must say that I was a little bit disappointed with the ending as well. I really hoped for something else, and this left me wanting for more, for a different reality... 
 I also want to warn that there is a lot of profanity in this book, in case that bothers anyone. 
 All in all I think it was an okay book. Not amazing, not something I will re-read (at least not soon, that's for sure); but something unlike any book I have ever read before with a good message in the end.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I first encountered this book during one of the classes in my Master's program. I was fascinated by it then, but now, as I read it with my own students, I find it even more impressive. 
 This isn't the easiest topic to cover. I've had to read--and have chosen to read--more than my share of Holocaust narratives. They're always disturbing, but this version was a little more...palatable than most. The author is so careful about what he includes,and though there are times when he chooses not to shield the reader from the horrors--and always to great impact--my students were able to analyze without shutting the entire thing out. 
 There's also something to be said for a Holocaust narrative that emphasizes the person over the victim. This story focused so much on Vladek's relationship with Art, on the consequences of what had happened to him, on the impact this has had on future generations. It wasn't just a tale of horror after horror. It had so much more meaning this way. 
 I will admit that some of my students were a little confused by the whole narrative-as-a-construct thing, but even that led to some interesting discussions. I've never had a group so into a work. 
 The fact that it's a graphic novel probably didn't hurt, either, of course. When I told them what we were reading, most of their jaws dropped. I was criticized a bit by some of my co-workers for using this, but I have to say, it's been a hit. 
 That said, this isn't just ideal for a class. Though I'm not sure individuals would get as much from it without the analysis, it's a fascinating piece in its own right. I wouldn't categorize it as pleasure reading, but it's enlightening. 
 Very highly recommended.

This is a dark but stirring story of the Holocaust told in graphic form in which Jews are mice, Nazis cats, Poles pigs, and Americans dogs.The Author is recording his Dad's story which is also told in the story so in addition to experiencing the powerful story of Spiegelman during the war and Holocaust we are constantly reminded of how damaging it was in the long run. I couldn't put Maus down, it was a very gripping and intense story. 9/10.
Humorous in parts, but largely dull.
Very, very good. Not often we run across graphic novels that are non-fiction.

I can't say I liked this book. I mean it wasn't horrible, but it didn't want me to read the next one. I thought, since it was apart of my school work, that it would be a bit more kid friendly. I certainly didn't expect to turn the page and see a naked woman in a bath tub after committing suicide, I could understand seeing it once, but twice is way too much for me. I don't want to read it again.

I'm afraid I don't have anything to say about his book that hasn't already been said, but I definitely agree with all the praise and positive reviews! It's a worthwhile read for anyone, including those who don't read comics because it's more of a biography in the form of a comic strip (something I've never experienced before). If you're interested in WWII history or the effects of war, this is definitely a must-read story =] 5/5

I feel like I am really going to always have both parts associated together, so writing a review on just the first half, especially when I have already started the second half, feels awkward. 
 First of all, I find what the author is doing really interesting. The use of the animals standing in for people may in some ways soften it, and certainly adds a uniformity which is kind of interesting, but at the same time, it is not soft, and it just keeps getting harder. 
 Also very interesting to me are the elements outside of the Holocaust. That is the main story, but the depiction of the parent child relationship, and guilt and love and frustration, is ultimately very human, and no matter how much your parents may have suffered, and you may admire them and love them, it does not erase their faults or make them easy.

Well I don't really get the point of the "graphic novel." I mean... if I wanted to read a comic book, I would date someone from the Big Bang Theory. So, of course, I love the postmodern themes and how the book approaches the topic of the Holocaust. All fine and dandy. But, I just couldn't get into the book with all these pictures and mice jumping from place to place. It confused me and the words sort of lost their meaning. Though I suppose this is postmodernism...they probably had little meaning to begin with since language is ultimately useless in expressing our meaningless and absurd existences. 
 But I'm just getting sentimental now. It's definitely worth trying, because the book is undeniably groundbreaking. I rated it three star because it isn't my taste. But I am sure a lot of you, and you being probably no one because I doubt anyone is reading this, just may be a more enlightened and open-minded person. OR you really like pictures. Either works.
Fucking gut wrenching and absolutely phenomenal. I won't say more. Just read it.

Now there's a genre you don't come across very often: holocaust comics. Darkness and human misery I thought I got plenty of with Tardi's It Was the War of the Trenches but this graphic novel pushes the envelope a tad further. While Maus' core strength is the story told in the personal idiom of the father who had to live through the ordeal -- you soon learn to respect the creative way that Spiegelman arranges his images to make the whole thing work. Jews are mice; Poles are pigs and Nazis are cats...all in a sort of Animal Farm telling of history which at the end of Part I takes us to the gates of Auschwitz. 
 So simple really when you think about it -- a simple story you'd tell the offspring -- a once upon a time horror that happened before you were born. 
 ["And just quietly, son, I can't help myself as I still live through it day in day day out..."] 
 As a recollection offered as an oral account it would have had a sort of talking head interest -- just another voice from among those who survived the 'Final Solution'. Even a pictorial would pass master as historical research...But as a comic? Well, it takes off into a totally different dimension. And while I don't make a habit of reading such literature I did seek out and read this graphic work only because it was a comic... 
 And it is so deceptive. The voices engage with your head and demand to take you back to the ghettoes and the pogroms: to the time when these human beings had to survive being hunted down like mice. 
 But it wasn't for me saddening to read Maus. Despite the horrors they had to experience -- yes even before the gates of Auschwitz -- I learnt to respect these people for the way they fought to survive. Maus regrettably is a survival manual even for those who became Jewish police or informants or chose to look after themselves than others...Surviving, that is, in the context of massive Barbarism and our own frailties and indecisions. 
 I mean: if you were in their shoes, what would you do?

sample_reviews.review_text: My daughter got this out of the library and decided on this as the latest read-aloud bedtime story book. It's a fantasy about a girl in a kingdom that prizes singing ability. And it's sortuva preteen romance-y type thing and really geared towards younger girls. So... it was okay for my daughter but OMG this did nothing for me. I thought it pretty clunky and slow and just, well, dull. Maybe it's okay for you, though.

This is just a really cute kinda story. Aza is a 16 year old girl, in the kingdom next to Ella's I believe, and it is a kingdom of song. Singing is very important to these people, and because Aza has such a beautifully talented singing voice, people tend to forgive her for being so darn ugly. Yup, that's her problem, she is utterly ugly, the ugliest around. But she can throw her voice and mimic other people without anyone being able to tell, and no one else can. This is how she has come from inn keeper's daughter to lady in waiting to the brand new queen, Ivi. Ivi, beautiful and young and in love, can't sing. So she pleads with and, when refused, threatens Aza until she agrees to sing for her, and lie to the entire kingdom. But then the king is injured saving Ivi, and during his unconsciousness (basically the whole story) Ivi become power hungry in her rule. 
 I had a good time reading this. There were plenty of parts that were funny, and what girl doesn't at least understand the battle Aza has with wanting to be beautiful, and both Aza and Ivi's struggle to fit in. The characters are wonderful, with depth, good and bad to them all. Unlike with most annoying characters, I still enjoyed reading about Ivi, who for once is not the stereotypical villain, if you could even classify her as such. Then again, maybe her decisions are not entirely made on her own.. 
 Just like the magical world of "Ella Enchanted" (my judgement that based from the wonderful movie not the book yet), "Fairest" feels modern in its telling and classic in its setting. The magic is fun, and there are even some gnomes (probably my favorite part). Throw in the love side plot with the sweet Prince and you've got the full story, right on to the fairytale happy ending. 
 Like I said, it's a cute story. It's light, short, and easy to read. Definitely a worthy companion in the Ella universe!

Fairest attempts to bring song to print and lost me in the translation. 
 This is one of those books that I wanted to like but was unable to involve myself in the story because of the entanglement of songs written into the plot. Trying to imagine the songs being sung and creating a melody from nothing brought me out of the story and into my head. This bothered me especially because song is such a major element of the world that Levine is trying to build that this disturbance is ever present throughout the book. 
 In the moments I was truly involved in the story I found the plot, the characters and the message being told to be intriguing and well written. It was these sections that made me read on to finish the entire book, but my problems with the incorporated music is what stayed with me in the end. 
 Overall I do want to return to Fairest at some point and give it a second chance, only this time it will have to be an audio book instead.
As this is a fantasy genre for Young Adults, I had a higher expectation. Sadly, I was disappointed. It's more of a novel directed at young teenagers. I honestly found the piece childish and a cliche.
Liked Ella Enchanted much better.

In the same universe but not a sequel to Ella Enchanted. 
 It was a nice touch that Aza always hated apples and refused to eat them if she had a choice. She only ate the apple offered to her because she was tired of gnome food

** spoiler alert ** 
 The only elements I liked about this book were the magic mirror she could go inside, the scene in the library where she is trying to find out about the mirror, and the gnomes that represented the dwarfs in this tale. I was really excited that FINALLY much less emphasis was placed on the concept of the seven dwarfs, because that aspect of Snow White always seemed much less important to me. The gnomes were absolutely adorable and lived in an underground cave; their world was really interesting. They spoke their own language and the protagonist finds out she is actually part gnome. 
 It was really disappointing how the "Snow White" aspects didn't show up until a 100 pages and then really not until the last 100. I kept wondering "when is this story going to turn into Snow White?" The entire singing concept was silly; a musical does not transfer well to a book, but I did enjoy the lighter passages that were just song and not text (lazy reader). It just seemed like the author wanted to expand the world of Ella Enchanted (which I haven't read in well over a decade, but I probably should read again because it has fantastic reviews and I remember really enjoying it) and have the singing aspect, AND cram in Snow White. Like in Mirror, Mirror, it was too ambitious and came off as cluttered rather than seamless. 
 This story was pretty irritating until the very end when it finally got interesting. All of the names of both the places and the characters were strange and almost all alike, starting with the letter "A" and ending with "A" as well. I'm all for authors inventing their own character names but it gets really confusing when they sound all alike. I couldn't even tell you the name of the country they were from, it was just that memorable. 
 I wish the story had been more of a straight up Snow White retelling rather than all the other stupid things it included because that would have been much more enjoyable for me. The evil queen is actually the main character's age and doesn't hate her because she is prettier than her, but because she has a better singing voice than she does, but she does try to kill her via the huntsman and then later poison her. I thought the message of "accept yourself as you are" was poorly done and it didn't resonate with me as it did with some of the other readers, which is a shame because it is a good concept for young adult literature. I wouldn't suggest anyone go out of their way to read this one.

My friend who lent me this book said it was better than "Ella Enchanted." 
 No way! 
 While I applaud Levine for making the heroine "ugly", I didn't like the story that much. It didn't seem as strong as "Ella" and was basically a watered down version. And the singing...Ugh.

Kind of disappointing after Ella Enchanted. Ok, I guess, but it was a little too heavy on the PC "empowerment" message and too light on the character development and quirky magic confusing life. The plot was a little too similar to Shrek at times.
Cute story. Good life lessons about beauty. I reccommend it as a quick, fun read. I am definitely going to reccommend it for my 13 year old niece.

Richelle Mead has written these novels in a unique way in that one does not have to have read the first novel to be able to join the adventure described in the book "The Glittering Court". The first novel is centered around a young woman that is known as Adelaide, an Osfridian Countess who faces an arranged marriage to an itching, boorish, boring Baron. (I HATE it when that happens...!) The attractive opportunity to switch places with her servant to escape to a new life in Adoria the New world, is too much for her not to. She will attend a type of finishing school, that will train young ladies in class; it is both a school and business venture. As she is leaving she meets two girls who are sharing her carriage. Tamsin, fiery of hair and personality, and Mira, caramel skinned and shy Sirminican. and they are joined by Cedric Thorn, her sponsor, and his father Jasper. Cedric notices immediately he has a countess and not a servant, but... his sponsorship's on the line... (whispers) and...he... says nothing.... 
 The girls are at Blue Spring Manor, one of three, where they are to learn under the tutelage of Mistress Masterson, and she teaches them all etiquette, grace, how to eat, to dress, style, and to know current politics. After a few months the girls are rewarded by visits by their families; Ada received an actor hired by Cedric who got into the booze! Jasper announced that they were going to Astoria two months early for economic reasons although it was still winter storm season. 
 Outside at night, Ada discovers Cedric doing an Alanzan ritual. Alanzan has been outlawed, mostly due to rampant ignorance, and she agrees not to say anything. If he could pay for a stake in a town of Westhaven in the New World where he would have the freedom to practice his religion without persecution, he would go. She starts to think of ways she can get money to pay for it. Number One on the list: Make sure she gets a great commission for herself! She retakes her tests and gets a perfect score! Of course, she is after all, already a Countess! She earns a Diamond theme. Amazing and unheard of at the Glittering Court! 
 The Court sail for the New World aboard two ships, uneventful until a thrashing storm, and they make it through. The morning shows massive debris and Cape Triumph, Adoria. They made it! They locate a large piece of wood, the "Grey Gull's" figurehead; their sister ship is gone, and so is their beloved friend, Tamsin. 
 At Cape Triumph, the governor's son and also impending governor himself, Warren Doyle doggedly wants Ada and will pay incredible amounts of money just to secure her for his very own, even before the girls attend the Ball. She is repelled by this behavior as is Cedric, She feels as there is something inherently wrong. She gets to be presented at the Ball, a beautiful party with gown, jewels, and hopeful gents. She meets Warren's mother, who can be likened to a spider; so eager for her son's match. While with Warren, she overhears his intent to attack Alanzans gathered at ritual; she knows that Cedric is there and she races to save him and others, just in time. 
 She faces the fact that she is caring for Cedric deeply. But, on the other hand the Doyles have her in their web and are pulling her in deeper. They are also actually likening her to a piece of meat. The mom has the information of her nobility and threatens her with exposure--Clara catches Cedric and Ada kissing in their secret room--Cedric arranges to marry Ada by morning. 
 Warren and his mother are furious about the news of the couples' romantic arrangement, initially. Warren, for some reason offers them a gold claim in the town of Hadison in the area he will be governor. Cedric accepts, needing funds to pay for a stake in Westhaven after being cut off by his angry father Jasper, for marrying the prize jewel Diamond, and removing its commission. She lives with a hard working family, teaching the kids, working, and Cedric works the claim and rebuilds a shanty house. They accidentally find a massive lode in a huge rock! Of course, Warren and the Weasels try to take it.... First, by giving Cedric tampered climbing equipment, hoping he would splat off the rock, but Ada helps to save him. Next, they sabotage the explosives; and when it backfires and he is still alive, they try to blame him for it, although Ada has seen the whole thing. His Weasels grab Cedric and he molests Ada, and she fights back with the first thing she finds, and Alanzan knife, and plunges it into his thigh. 
 Silas Garrett, a lawman who has been working to seek the Countess by her mother has miraculously showed at this time, although to have any item of an Alanzan nature is a punishable offense, usually by death. The Weasels know this and make sure that Cedric is taken. The Countess' honor may have been saved but Cedric has been taken before the law at Cape Triumph, and Aiana helps Ada there. She finds her lawyer friend and the ones at Westhaven to accept her "backdated" shares bought for their permissive town. This is the shining gold that she needs to save Cedric's life, and she races to save her beloved from the waiting noose. She shows at his hanging just as the native Icori attack!! Their leader speaks of soldiers attacking their villages, and of their doing so under the direction of Warren Doyle. They are here for justice. Ada is amazed to see her friend Tamsin at the side of the leader, as she fits in so wonderfully with their colorful kilts a carefree and wild nature, and her wild red hair. Needless to say, they removed Doyle from power. 
 They all enjoyed a lush and larger wedding than the first one they had! 
 I really liked this book a lot, and I am looking forward to reading about Tamsin and the Icori! It sounds a lot similar to Scottish, with kilts and plaids and colors and wildness! I was pretty invested early on with the Countess character, and it caused a book inhalation to occur, when I voraciously read wanting to find out what happens!! Her name as we find out, after many clues: is Elizabeth! I give it a four and a half out of five. Love the characters, love the cover. A definite must read...!

I should have known from the blurb that this wasn't going to work for me. 
 The Selection meets Reign in this dazzling trilogy of interwoven novels about three girls on a quest for freedom and true love. 
 Really. This is my own fault. What did I think this book was going to be? I couldn't bear the aching stupidity of The Selection. Reign, the TV show, was abominably dumb, and more a parade of pretty prom dresses than anything resembling historical fact. And for once, the book was true to the blurb, sadly so. And in fact, this book is more an homage to fashion than a book with an actual plot. 
 Some of the dresses, particularly the daytime ones, were of purest white, made of delicate fabrics that rivaled those I'd worn in my former life. The evening and ball gowns were radiant confections of velvet and satin, done in gleaming white and glittering silver, embellished with jewels and metallic lace. 
 This hurts. It really does. Richelle Mead was one of my favorite authors, but her previous few books have done nothing for me (and let's not even mention the bullshittery ending of the Bloodlines series) and I have regretfully knocked her off my favorite author list. 
 This book is about a noblewoman who runs away to escape an arranged marriage - only she's kind of dumb, because in running away to escape that marriage, she ends up in a place where the "men outnumber women three to one." These men are fucking desperate for pretty wives that they're willing to take servant girls and My Fair Lady them into perfection. 
 "...the Glittering Court has taken it upon itself to create a cohort of young women willing to transform. We take lovely girls like Ada here, girls of common birth, girls with no family--or maybe too much family--and we train them up to greatness." 
 So running away from one marriage into another. Out of the pot and into the fire, as they would say. Not the brightest girl, our Adelaide. Even so, she finds herself the object of desire. The "diamond." 
 "I don't want to risk losing her to someone who might woo her with a lot of flash and no substance. I'll put out a price to make it worth your while for removing her early--one I might not be willing to match if I have to wait. One thousand gold if you do the deal right now." 
 Some of the girls near me gasped. There'd never been a sum like that offered in the Glittering Court's history. It was double my starting fee. 
 Wow. Much expensive. Very special. 
 The book is as boring as it sounds. It is 416 excruciating pages full of proper girly training, dressing up, and checking out cute rich guys. I could include quotes, but there are no notable quotes. The writing was dull and uninspired. The setting is left unbuild, it's a pseudo-historical setting with some made-up religious stuff and that's it. No effort is made to give this world a sense of reality. The romance was dull, the love interest completely lackluster. It wasn't even one of those so bad it's good books, it was just plain old boring.

I just can't...where do I even begin to describe this book? I have no idea. I am disappointed because I liked Vampire Academy, so I thought hey let's read her other series it looks like it could be awesome; the cover art is beautiful! But no...no no no...I was disappointed a lot! 
 Basically these girls are "bought", they are maids or poor women, whatever, they get bought from the families they work for and shipped to the new world (which is basically America and they live in basically England). Once they are there, and even before, they are taught to be ladies of the high court. They learn etiquette, music, dancing, art, etc. Once they are in the new world they are paraded around like high class prostitutes and they are sold to the highest bidder. These women are all for it because duh they get to live that high life that they never had before. But seriously it just reminded me of high class prostitutes... 
 But then there is Adelaide...aka Lady whatever...a royal who ran away from marrying her itchy cousin and took the place of her maid, who she sent packing back home. The guy who creates these contracts and finds these women knows who she is, and he's like well wtf now you have to pretend you can't do any of this so we don't get caught. Which she does until she finds out he needs money and if she is the diamond girl then he will get a high commission. So she aces all of her tests, becomes the diamond, and then low and behold the governor's son wants to marry her in the new world, and better yet he knows who she really is as does his mom, who's like you marry my son or I turn you in. So she freaks out because duh, she likes the guy but she's in love with the heretic dude who discovered her. Drama drama drama, they go to the governor's son's land to pan for gold, I shit you not...and they live like pioneers in this shanty little shack with a dirt floor. 
 That's where I just couldn't do it anymore, I was already bored and struggling to get through this book, and when they just start panning for gold and what not, I was like no I am done...I don't care if I have 30% left I'm done. Maybe one day I will finish it...when I have nothing better to do. But I just couldn't do it, and really I don't think I'm missing out on much.

I loved this book! I don't believe because it mentions Heaven that it is a holier than thou account of anything and it doesn't shove any religiousness down your throat. I thought the theory if this book was wonderful and it was written so that the ending is not discoverable by the middle of the book. 
 Following the life of Eddy who is, at 83, a maintenance worker at a pier amusement park, this story takes you to Heaven. Eddy dies this day, not knowing if he saved the little girl he intended to save before his life ends and he is swept into a totally new adventure. 
 When he gets to Heaven, he is told that he will meet 5 people and their explanations of why they are part of his lessons to learn about his life. Who will they be? What part did they play in the way that Eddy lived and died? How he lived? Why he suffered or rejoiced? 
 This book makes you wonder at who would be your own 5 people and shows that everyone is connected to some thread of existance even if we don't personally cross paths. What minute change did someone make in your life just by existing generations before you and what trace do you leave behind for someone yet to come?

You can read the full review and more on my blog.(: 
 I'm having difficulty putting my thoughts into words on this one. It just IS. It defys opinions. It's pure storytelling, with no problems or special features. It's just a story, Eddie's story. And eventually all of ours. 
 The plotline is original and fascinating- an idea of heaven that's very different from the various religions' views of it. It kind of gives you hope - that one day, you'll understand. It shows you the difference you made on others' lives, and them on yours. 
 I liked the writing more in this book than in Tuesdays with Morrie. I think it has to do with the quotation things he did in the above. What can I say, it really bothered me. Or maybe it's the fact that this is a work of fiction, as opposed to the former which is a memoir. Either way, The Five People You Meet in Heaven reads quickly, and touched more heartstrings for me. It really made for a beautiful read, good for all ages.

 If I need a reminder as to how screwed up our country is, I'll turn on the news or check out the latest stock quotes or talk with the countless number of friend and neighbors who are out of work.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Julie Klassen is on my must read list; she is just one of those authors that when I find she has written and released a new book I am all over it! This book did not let me down. It will be placed right alongside her other books on my shelf. This story is told from the point of view of three different characters: Alec Valcourt, the dancing master, Julia Midwinter, and her mother Amelia Midwinter. When Alec moves to the small town of Devonshire, in hopes of finding new employment, he is shocked and completely dismayed to learn that dancing, his profession, is outlawed in this small town. Alec is soon hired on, to work in their lovely estate, by Mrs. Amelia Midwinter, the woman who is responsible for the outlawing of dancing. Alec quickly becomes introduced to Julia, and together these two break the rules and devise a plan to bring life and magic back to the lonely little town. 
 I was so glad that Klassen incorporated so much of Alec's life, background, and point of view in the story. I did appreciate him more as a character than Julia. I found myself thinking how selfish she came off at times, but I knew that Alec would be just the person to soften her. The way that Alec was written made me cling to his character and root for his ambitions and dreams all throughout the book. I liked seeing him interact with the Midwinters and I especially loved his reaction to the law of "No Dancing." I thought he was a noble man for taking such good care of his mother and sister. Small actions like these say more for a character than words do. 
 Do not worry. Change came over Julia and her mother, Amelia in more ways than one. From the start of the book I was hoping for a change for both of their hearts, and of course Klassen doesn't disappoint. Julia did a lot of maturing and growing up by the end of the book and that was very refreshing to see. Amelia Midwinter is full of hurt and anguish and this is apparent very early on in the book. It was so nice to see the thick layer of ice around her heart melted away! 
 ***A copy of this book was provided to me by the publishers at Bethany House and Litfuse in exchange for my honest review***

To put it quite simply, I have loved every book that I've read by Julie Klassen, and The Dancing Master is no exception. Julie's prose is beautiful and the descriptions of village life are excellent. Her research must have been extensive and the historical quotes at the beginning of each chapter are a great touch. 
 The Dancing Master might seem long to some - and while there's mystery, the action is not fast paced - but I savored every moment spent in its pages. The setting is Devonshire, England in 1816, and the Prologue sets the stage for what's to come with this beautiful picture: 
 "From behind the market hall, an old man hobbled into view. He tossed aside his apron and bowed before the woman. And she in turn curtsied. She gave him a girlish smile, and decades flew from her face."

reference_books.title: Tandem (Many-Worlds, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
When a book is the start of the series, I find it difficult to give it a rating based on its own merits. I've read some that started out well only to crash and burn before the end and had others with mediocre starts only to pick up steam in later installments. 
 What's important to me is that it gives me characters that are interesting to some degree and for fantasy/futuristic series, that it gives me a concept and world where I would like to return. 
 This succeeds on both fronts. I like the parallel world concept that they used here and I liked Thomas and some of the other characters, though Sasha could stand some improvement (but hey, it's not like there is normal behavior for this situation). I'll track down the sequel when it comes out, which is the best endorsement I can give.

reference_books.title: Laura Lamont's Life in Pictures
reference_books.review_text:
50 years of the life of Elsa Emerson, aka Laura Lamott, as she moves from Wisconsin country girl to Hollywood star and beyond. I generally like character driven books and while this is, Laura's inner life is not explored as much as you would think. An early death affects her throughout, but she still remains fairly shallow as events around her transpire. The depiction of Hollywood as it might have been in the 30's and forward might be accurate, but is is certainly not the draw either. 
 However, I found the book oddly compelling wanting to know what happened to Laura and the people around her. This is the type of book I normally find dull, but the story hopped from period to period, marking the changes in her life and I couldn't stop reading, Not the best, but not a waste of my time either.

reference_books.title: Life After Life
reference_books.review_text:
Probably a 4 1/2 stars. The basic genre of this book is historical fiction, with much of it taking place between 1910 and 1945 mostly in England. However, the twist (and it's not giving away anything to say since it happens in the first few pages) is that Ursala Todd is in a loop - a years long, in most cases, Groundhog Day. She is born, things happen, she dies, and then she starts again at the beginning. Things change that are out of her control and sometimes because she remembers a previous iteration. 
 You will either love this book or drop it quickly depending on whether you buy into the premise, which obviously I did. The time period covers 2 world wars, which makes the background events a major player. However it's the little things that change,and the implications, that pulled me in - that and Ursala herself. Well written, interesting characters, and a chance for introspection and questioning. If you w ant something different, this might be the right one to try.

book_a.title: Harriet the Invincible (Hamster Princess, #1)
book_a.user_review: Turns sleeping beauty story upside down. Cute book for maybe grades 2-4. Found it a bit brash and not as funny as I would have hoped.

sample_reviews.review_text:
First sentence: Once upon a time, in a distant land, there was a beautiful princess named Harriet Hamsterbone, who, as her name indicated, was a hamster. she was brave and intelligent and excelled in traditional hamster skills, like checkers and fractions. 
 Premise/plot: When Harriet was born her parents forgot to invite the evil fairy god-mouse Ratshade which resulted in a curse--a sleeping curse via enchanted hamster wheel on her twelfth birthday. When Harriet is old enough to learn of it, she rejoices in the fact that she is invincible for a few more years yet. She leaves the safety of her home and packs each day with wild, crazy, dangerous adventures. But her twelfth birthday is approaching... 
 My thoughts: I really loved, loved, loved this one. I loved Harriet and I came to enjoy her friendship with Prince Wilbur. This chapter book features illustrations, speech bubbles, and traditional text packed with adventure and humor!
I liked that the princess wasn't dainty and that there wasn't a predictable ending.

In most ways, Harriet Hamsterbone is not your typical princess. She'd rather go cliff diving than take deportment lessons, and dreams of slaying dragons atop her trusty steed quail, Mumfrey. She does have one princessly quality though: she was cursed by an evil fairy to fall into a deep sleep on her 12th birthday and to stay asleep unless a prince wakes her with a kiss. When her parents tell her of the curse, Harriet looks on the bright side: if she will definitely fall asleep on her 12th birthday no matter what, that means until then, she's INVINCIBLE! 
 With its cute art, fast-paced story, and funny characters, this would be good for younger girls who aren't quite ready for the Enchanted Forest Chronicles by Patricia Wrede.
Will kids really get it if they haven't been steeped in versions of Sleeping Beauty? Also the vocabulary is pretty advanced. I feel like it's geared towards ironic adults v. kids.
Funny, spry and satisfying adventure.
What an awesome book! A cross between Disney's Brave and Sleeping Beauty, this book will appeal to girls who like adventure and reluctant readers who like a good story.

Woooow okay where do I even begin with this godawful book? Its weird and unhealthy portrayal of "friendship"? The inconsistent characters? The muddy, confusing plot line? The poor, lazy writing? The complete lack of context and setting? The creepy sexualization of twelve-year-olds? The nonsensical magic system? "Clumps"??? 
 1) Friendship: Friendship is seemingly one of the most important themes of this book. We keep being TOLD repeatedly from the beginning of the story to the very end that Sophie and Agatha are best friends despite how different they are. Best friends, best friends, over and over. The author TELLS us they're friends, but nothing that happens in the story even remotely supports this description. From beginning to end, all these two characters do is mistreat each other and USE each other to achieve their own ends. There is nothing about their friendship, or their relationship in general, that rings true to me. They're basically both just horrible, selfish people who only care about their own desires, and never once consider the aspirations of their so-called "friend." 
 2) Inconsistent characters: never in my life have I read a book where the characters switch personalities so much as this cast. One minute Sophie's roommates are evil psychos, then suddenly they're nice, but then they're evil psychos again, but wait then they're nice again! One minute Tedros is an air-headed jerk, but then he's actually a deep guy, but then he's just a shallow user, but then he's a gallant prince, and then he loves this girl, but no now he loves this other girl, and oh look now he's in love with another girl! What?? These characters make no sense. Furthermore, the only characters with even remotely distinct personalities are Sophie and Agatha. Beyond them, all the characters kind of just blur together into a gray mass of boring inconsistency. I couldn't tell any of the teachers apart because they all seemed to have the same personality, I couldn't tell the Evers or Nevers apart for the same reason. And might I also say that not a single character in this entire book is even remotely likable? I seriously just couldn't stand any of them. 
 3) Muddy, confusing plot: I spent about half the book thinking, "wait, what is happening right now? But why??" The series of events that the plot follows is just so incredibly random. There was no sense of cause or effect in the plotline. One thing never clearly led to another. The plot was basically just random event! Random event! Random event! with no flow whatsoever. Speaking of the lack of cause and effect, can I just point out how cartoonish the writing was? We're talking, like, a character will get brutally injured, and then literally five seconds later they're absolutely fine as if nothing happened. Falling from high heights, getting knocked out, stabbed...apparently none of these things are actually damaging according to the accountability in Chainani's writing. 
 4) Poor, lazy writing: Don't even get me started. On how annoying it was. That Chainani kept writing like this. To try and make things more dramatic. It didn't. Work. Furthermore, I never would have expected that an action-and-dialogue heavy book could be so bad. Action and dialogue tend to be what makes a story fast-paced and exciting. This story had a fast pace, yes, but the excitement fell flat because it was so hard to tell what was happening or why it was happening. Which leads me to my next point... 
 5) Lack of context and setting: this book is so action and dialogue heavy that it completely lacks context. Chainani has apparently never heard of "descriptive writing" because most scenes in the story completely lack description, or the descriptions are weak at best. Descriptive writing tends to have a bad name I think, because too much description can of course make a book dense and dull. But this book really reminded me why description is so important. Since the writing is so vague, the setting has absolutely zero personality, which is very disappointing when you're reading a fantasy novel. The writing is vague even to the point that the reader has no idea how much time is passing. From the beginning of the novel to the end, it's unclear whether all this has taken place over the course of a few weeks, months, or even years. There's just no way of telling due to the lack of descriptive writing. The lack of description also made the cast of characters all seem like caricatures, and made them very flat, because we knew little to nothing about most of their motivations and inner thoughts/feelings. 
 6) Creepy sexualization of 12-year-olds: Let's not forget that Sophie and Agatha are supposed to be quite young. It is eluded that they are 12 years old (another vague part of the writing that I hated--we barely even know basic information about the main characters). The story also states that the School Master only takes children ages 12-16, which would imply that all the first year characters are between those ages. So why are these characters so sexualized? Why is being naked in front of other people a running joke? Why is Sophie, A FUCKING TWELVE YEAR OLD, described as "provocative" and "seductive" on multiple occasions? Why are there so many sexual jokes throughout the story? This is supposed to be a fucking kids book! A book where immature fart jokes are a big thing should not be the same book where jokes about sex are as well. It just made me feel like Chainani is a pervy pedo or something. 
 7) Nonsense magic system: I found it just a bit unrealistic that first year students could perform such advanced magic as being able to transfigure objects, TURN THEMSELVES INTO FUCKING ANIMALS, use magical weapons, and pretty much everything else they did. How did they master all these things so well, despite never having used (or in Agatha's case, even BELIEVED in) magic in their entire lives? It makes no sense. There is no sense of them actually learning their powers (only adding to the cartoony feel of the novel). 
 8) WHAT THE FUCK ARE CLUMPS???: Chainani referenced Agatha's "clumps" about a hundred fucking times in this stupid book, but he never once explained what a clump actually is. This fanned my hatred for the book even more intensely. 
 Bottom line: this book was just stupid in general. I can't believe I forced myself through it. If I could have, I would have given it 0 stars because frankly, I don't think it even deserves one. To say the least, I won't be continuing with this series.
Started very promising but found it went on too long with overdone language better served by nuance or inference. Still, an entertaining read.

Didn't realize this was a kiddie book, despite the cover. Also somehow overlooked the giant J the library placed on the spine. In my defense, I had put a hold on it, so I didn't have to go into the Juvenile section to look for it. 
 About a quarter of the way through, I was looking at the Amazon description and realized it was for kids. I liked it, though. The School for Good and Evil has its problems, but I'm letting Rabbit (who is 11) read my copy, because she's been bugging me about it since she saw the cover. I have a few issues with the story, including one big one that I'll get into in a minute, but first: this is a REALLY long book. That's part of the reason I didn't realize it was a middle-grade novel at first. Kids like mine will not have an issue with this, though; Rabbit loves nothing more than a long book. Well, except a series, she MIGHT love those a little more. Double points for this one, then. 
 But like I was saying, there is at least one turn-off for me: I have a big problem with the way (current) conventional beauty is shorthand for "good" and "ugliness" is used to indicate evilness. At first, it seemed like the story was trying to flip that around, turn it on its head, whatever, but as the book went on I became more disappointed in the author's reinforcement of this trope. It almost reads like Chainani STARTED the book with the intent to skewer the more grating fairy tale blather but got lost along the way. 
 Okay, I'm going to quickly spin through the rest of my gripes. Like Rabbit, I love long books, but the reality is that this one did not NEED to be so long. There are twists and turns that end up being both confusing and pointless. A character who is so terrible at her lessons that she has to cheat to pass classes somehow becomes one of the most powerful people in the book. Agatha and Sophie's friendship is ostensibly the focus of this novel, but in reality it's a one-sided relationship for most of the 450+ pages -- I wouldn't call it a friendship -- that somehow ends up being a magical rainbow kind of thing in the end. There are pieces of the story that are coded as "mysterious" that don't make sense and are never fully explained. The prince we're supposed to like (I think) is a toolbox who mopes about only being liked for his looks and then judges female students by their appearances. I'll stop there. 
 The writing is serviceable, simple and clear without being dumb, but as I read The School for Good and Evil I felt like it was written with the hopes of being chosen as the Next Big Movie. Wasn't surprised to find out it's already being made into one. Harry Potter Lite + fairytale tropes -- it sells itself. 
 But I gave it three stars, despite all that, because I love the potential in this story. There are some great secondary characters, like Hort (the frog pajamas were one of the most touching things in the whole book) and Hester. And it was engaging; I finished it in a couple of days and put a hold on the sequel. 
 I'm a sucker for retellings of fairy tales, so I'm an easy mark for this kind of thing and it isn't aggressively bad, just irritating at times, while still being enjoyable enough for me to continue reading. That's kind of fun every once in a while, you know? I don't mind being a little righteously irritated every now and then. But I do feel like the story that was promised in the first quarter of the book just faded away as I got further into the story. I'm hoping the sequel makes up for some of that. Not holding my breath, but hoping.

...First, tell me I'm not the only person who picked up on the sexual tension between our heroines? There were a few very thinly veiled homosexual references smattering throughout the novel, but it really amped up at the end there. Not that it's bad...but unexpected for what is being (in my library system) cataloged as a Middle Reader. Honestly...I don't think I'd let anyone under the age of 13 read this, slating it pretty firmly in the YA section for me. 
 There is murder, mayhem, transformations, backstabbing, and all other sorts of mischief. 
 Which I like. 
 Something about the stringing on the story wasn't quite right though. It felt like a jerky read. A book so large should flow better. I hated Sophie almost immediately. Agatha was pretty decent though with her creepy-cute vibe. 
 Over all, I just feel like more could have been done to make this a smoother tale.
Hmm...3.5 stars...

It's come up a lot in my life recently. There's the musical... There's the sequel... Rebs bought it and despised the beginning so heartily she took it back to her bookstore... Di liked it enough to IM an endorsement. And I've been listening to a podcast version of The Road to Oz over the course of the last few months. 
 If your only experience with Oz is the movie, you may not enjoy the book as much as if you have read some of the Frank L. Baum stories the movie is based on. But having said that, I thought that most of the book was very clever, thorougly drawing on Baum's world as it does -- from the characteristics of the various inhabitants of the nation to the types of characters he peopled his books with to the small details that changed between the book and the movie (those slippers aren't really ruby in the stories, for instance). 
 Maguire enjoys playing with language and includes a number of Word Wealth words. My friend Amani was so taken with his vocabulary she started writing down words she wanted to learn. 
 Maguire also began an interesting discussion on the role and/or nature of evil. Is there such a thing? If so, what makes a character evil or makes them do evil things -- free will, destiny, some combination? Is collateral worth the price of eliminating evil? Is it cut-and-dried? And are there always two legitimate sides or perspectives to things? 
 Unfortunately, something happened toward the end of the novel and for whatever reason he rushed around trying to squeeze the end of the story in before the book got too long. My head reeled as he bounced from one scene to another and as he tried to wrap Elphaba's (the witch's real name) story up as neatly as possible. But in his hurry to close the curtain, he undermined the importance of the questions he raised earlier, leaving me a little disappointed in what was otherwise a terrific novel.

reference_books.title: Peter Darling
reference_books.review_text:
[I got an eARC of this book through NetGalley. All the fangirling is mine. Peter Darling will be published the 15th of February] 
 Captain Hook is bored. Neverland isn't nearly as exciting since his old rival Peter Pan left; even the Lost Boys are rather tame without their fearless leader. But when he comes back and the truce with the pirates is broken, things don't go quite as expected. 
 This is the Peter Pan retelling I didn't know I needed and sure as hell didn't deserve. It's both a retelling and a sequel of sorts, in which the original story of Peter Pan we all know and love but with a twist: Peter was the older of the Darling children and ran away to Neverland because he didn't want to grow up in a world that didn't understand he was a boy, but went back because he missed his family. 
 After ten years he has grown up and returns to Neverland, and he is still the same selfish, cunning and ruthless boy he used to be. Of course the first thing he does is resume the war against his old enemy, Captain Hook. 
 Both characters are amazing; although Peter keeps the classic qualities he goes through an amazing development where we see his more vulnerable and empathetic side. And Hook. OH, HOOK. I wasn't a huge fan of the villain in the Disney movie but this book has turned me. He is painfully aware of his part in the story, of how he is supposed to play the villain because Peter Pan needs someone to fight. Hook delivers some of the best plot twists in the book, has a flair for the dramatic and is more compassionate that anyone imagines. Instead of making him just ruthless and evil, Chant turns him into an explorer, not so different from Peter himself, who just went to Neverland to have adventures. (Also his obsession with clothes is an amazing detail. I loved it). 
 The relationship between them had me hooked since moment one (first and only hook pun, promise!). Their dynamic somehow paces the book: at first their rivalry means a lot of sword fighting scenes, Peter flying all over the place and ambushes in the woods. But somewhere in the 40% mark the narrative slows down a bit to show us more insightful and vulnerable scenes. And there is where I absolutely fell in love with this book. What starts with the expected rivalry turns into so much more. No spoilers but SO MUCH MORE. The fact that they are so vital to each other plays a huge part, but they don't stray from their parts right away: the teasing and mischief and fighting are still there. 
 This is coming out too lengthy but I love these two and the scenes of introspection and opening up to each other killed me. And then the slow burn buried me. Their relationship evolves very naturally and doesn't seem forced or rushed. 
 The writing was very fitting to the setting and mood. The description of the places in Neverland made them cruel and magical at the same time, just like their inhabitants. I loved all the fantastic creatures, from the kraken to the mermaids, and of course the fairies. The fact that we got to explore more of Neverland and learn about the places and customs of the magical creatures was one of my favorite parts. 
 My only complaint would be that it focuses so much in the main characters that the secondary ones lack a bit of depth. It makes sense for both the pirates and the Lost Boys, but I would have loved more character development for Ernest and Tinkerbell. 
 The theme about growing up is different than the original story, here is more of a struggle of not wanting to live in the real world. Peter Pan is the ultimate escapist; he was unhappy with the Darlings, who didn't accept he was a boy, and his only way of being treated like one was playing pretend. That's how he came up with Peter Pan. His gender identity was the reason he ran away to Neverland, and there are some traumatic moments in the flashbacks, which include misgendering and deadnaming. (Also when he is about to fly away there are some thoughts that could be considered suicidal, but Chant doesn't dwell too much on them. Just be warned when you read about his past in London). The idea of leaving toxic family and being yourself were implied. 
 I honestly devoured this and now can't get it out of my head. I can feel the reading slump approaching after such an amazing read.
