 This was a book I had walked past in the library for weeks, but had never picked up. I had high hopes, though - the cover was beautiful, and the blurb seemed interesting (although it was a little like every other YA novel out there). But now that I've read it, I don't think I feel anything but underwhelmed. 
 The book is written from two perspectives. 
 Rhiannon, or Rhee, is the last living member of her royal family. Her parents and sister were killed years ago, and Rhee is out for revenge; what she learns, however, is that half of the galaxy wants her dead. 
 Alyosha is a Wraetan and is looked down upon, but he is also the star of a DroneVision show. But being a star doesn't mean he is free from the prejudices. 
 When Rhee is attacked and incorrectly presumed dead, Aly becomes the scapegoat for her supposed murder. But there's more to the story. There's always more to the story. 
 First of all, the blurb is very misleading. Rhee and Aly are never really "together". They have their stories at the same time, but the most their plotlines intertwine is one scene where they make eye contact. I kept waiting for them to meet each other, but it never happened. 
 Several reviews have mentioned that this book was boring, and I really just have to agree. It began well, and I was interested in the premise and the history, but then Aly and Rhee began their individual journeys, and the story just became very messy. I still had a basic idea of what was going on, but it wasn't quite cohesive enough. 
 The characters were hard for me to relate to. I felt like I just didn't quite care for either one, and at the same time, so many secondary characters were introduced that it was hard to keep up and hard to associate them to the correct main character when there was so little screentime and personality. 
 The one character I honestly loved was introduced at the beginning: Rhee's best friend Julian. But he appears only for a few pages, and I realized I spent the rest of the book wanting to know more about him. (He does appear in some memories and flashbacks, but it's just not the same.) 
 The writing style was okay. Nothing really stood out to me, which I think definitely contributed to my disinterest. The world-building had a lot of potential, but I feel as though the writing style made it difficult for me to understand just exactly what everything was, considering how many technical terms there were. 
 Overall, I wouldn't say that this was a good read, and I don't think I'd really recommend it to anyone. It does seem to be geared towards a YA audience, but it didn't work well for me, and I don't even think I care enough to read the second book.

Wow. I received an ARC of this, and (almost) instantly started reading it. I love how Rhoda develops the characters, and even though the plot may not be the originalest (not a word but you know what I mean), the characters and dialogue certainly made up for it. I like how there's little to no romance, and the book focused mostly on the main problem without becoming distracted and fixated on a subplot. Great read, would recommend 12/10 can't wait for book 2

I did not know why but I enjoyed reading Alyosha part than Rhee part and the plot of the story's pretty easy to predict. Overall, this book's had thrilling journey of the main characters and good world building.

This book bored me to death. Ugh. Scifi could be a very tricky to write, it can get too serious too quickly, flooding the reader with weird names of people, planets, races or places and that is exactly what happened. 
 Few things I liked: 
 - diversity 
 - there was a space reality show! - why oh why wasn't entire story line dedicated to this? Adventures of two boys in a spaceship, brought to you live... I would so watch it IRL... but again, it was described on few pages and that was it... such a wasted potential! 
 - there was no romance - refreshing to see 
 Things I didn't like: 
 - names - Alyosha, Pavel... weird weird names, but that is just mine personal pet peeve 
 - characters - I haven't connected to them at all, their behavior didn't make sense all the time, they were flat and there was nothing special about them... you can take any other YA scifi or fantasy and find exactly the same characters (and with less weird names probably) 
 - plot - it was just all over the place, boring, not surprising and over-used...there were chapters were literaly nothing happened. NOTHING 
 - it was too serious - what happened to obligatory funny character? there was no fun in this book, it took itself too seriously and I hate when scifi does that

Absolutely NOTHING new or even that interesting in this book. Very slightly reminded me of the Lunar Chronicles, but not nearly as interesting. I'd pass on this one and read something with a little more imagination.

EMPRESS OF A THOUSAND SKIES by Rhoda Belleza is one of the best sci-fi novels I've ever read. Strong writing, compelling characters and action-packed scenes are combined to create an all-around fantastic debut. Not only does the author introduce themes of racism and prejudice but unpacks them through her characters, their actions and the world-building. Whether or not you're a fan of space opera, this is one book not to be missed. Belleza is sure to bring you to the dark side. 
 Just to add: I think I misinterpreted the synopsis. I pretty much expected Rhee and Aly to meet at some point and was a little disappointed when this didn't happen. I would be waiting for something to happen because of the way the synopsis was written. I still enjoyed the novel and liked how the author showed the ways two people's lives can intersect without actually meeting. This is a dual POV and because the two characters don't actually meet it's almost like getting two books in one (a good thing for me). The reader gets to see Rhee and Aly unravel the plot in different ways. I actually think this fits more with some adult SFF books - you could have several main characters but they don't always meet or they don't meet right away. 
 The POV changed every other chapter and the transitions were pretty smooth. The end of each chapter had that perfect sort of cliffhanger - you want to continue with Rhee's POV but are still excited to start Aly's.

There is a reason why I'm giving just one star. 
 As a reader, I have to find a book not only interesting (it's not enough), but it has to make me feel something . It can be hartred as well as fear, joy, happiness. As a reader I enjoy feeling emotions while I'm reading. It's one of the reasons why I read. If it wasn't for the emotions I feel while I'm reading a book, I probably wouldn't have ever read so much in my life so far. 
 This emotions are connected to situations, but also to the characters involved in them. This book didn't give me anything on this. I didn't feel anything about the girl killing her best friend's dad(I'm not even sure if he is her best friend but whatever). I didn'feel anything for nothing. It was just...dull. A dull reading I couldn't finish because it became just too much. 
 To really enjoy a book you must feel connected with what is happening and with the characters, but when you don't for some reason, it means the book isn't just for you.

I'm on the fence with this one! I loved it but some parts were just all right. There just needed an extra push to be a four star or five star. Something along the lines of twists and turns and maybe more action? Also if the plot had a more direct way of telling the story than being broken up into parts. The writing is just lovely and easy to digest. This was a political sci-fi space opera, so deeply similar to our society today. Told in alternate point of views from Rhee and Aly, the story plays out well, without really converging together. Did I mention that there isn't really a romance? And that it was wholly refreshing? Only a smidge at the end, but you were rooting for them anyway so it was nice to read! 
 I liked the parallels of everyone's cubes that are so similar to our cellphones. Maintaining a news feed of one's memories *cough cough Facebook* that are recorded at will. And how the government is using the cube to spy on everyone. Even the dark skinned Wratens being committed for a crime he didn't commit because he was just a scapegoat. I enjoyed all of those parts immensely. What it lacked was the emotional depth of the characters and their missions. I just needed to care more about them and I wasn't able to get it. The back and forth of their memories were a little jolting because I like pacing where everything is moving forward instead of backward, but I fully understand why the author did that. I just found it a little too disorganized for my taste. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed her writing I will continue on with the series because I'd like to see what happens with Rhee and Julian. 
 RATING 3/5

 Was there so much hatred in the universe, so much prejudice, even among people who claimed to be unbiased? (200) 
 People always measured war in terms of the numbers dead. Maybe they should measure it in terms of the people left behind. (206)

book_b.title: The Upside of Unrequited
book_b.user_review:
I requested this on Netgalley because I loved Simon vs. The Homo Sapiens agenda and wanted to read what Becky Albertalli would do next. Sadly, it has fallen a bit short for me. 
 After giving it some thought, I have pinpointed the reasons I didn't enjoy this so much: it's lacking a strong plot, besides the whole "getting Molly a boyfriend" thing, which couple would be endgame felt too obvious for me, and the main topic about the character isn't as developed and doesn't have a clear conclusion (in Simon it would be his homosexuality, in Molly is her self-image issues and consequent avoidance of romance). Still, this theme was very important and was handled carefully and with a lot of sensitivity. 
 On the bright side, I loved Molly. She is sweet and slightly awkward, and her relationship with her family was amazing. I feel like Becky Albertalli is amazing at writing family dynamics and loved the topics they brought up, like drifting apart from your family when you get a partner, or still being siblings although they have different parents (this is a bit tricky, they share a sperm donor, but Molly and her twin are from one of their moms, and their little brother is from the other). 
 The secondary characters were lovable but not very interesting. The same way that we saw how in Simon vs. everyone had their own issues and secrets going on, this was a bit lacking in that sense. And the two boys who were potential romantic interests felt boring to me. 
 Also there was a line in her first book that sit wrong with me, something about lesbian and bisexual women "having it easier" because men think it's hot. And in The upside of nurequited there is a lot of queer female characters, and the representation is perfect. Something that I appreciated a lot personally is the rebuttal of biphobia. I'm glad the author notices what readers might feel uncomfortable with and makes an effort to correct it. 
 So overall it was an entertaining read with some great themes, and the writing and teenage voices were perfect, but the romance and plot were slightly underwhelming. 
 The whole review in Spanish + review of Simon vs. the Homo Sapiens agenda here: https://sparsireads.blogspot.com.es/2...

*Disclaimer: An ARC of The Upside Of Unrequited by Becky Albertalli was provided to me by Indigo Books & Music in exchange for an honest review. This does not effect my opinion in any way. 
 Actual Rating: 4.75 Stars Rated Up! 
 -- 
 Initial Post Reading Thoughts 
 I know, I'm so behind in reading this book...but I'm kind of glad I waited for the hype to die down a little before finally picking this one up. It was one of my most anticipated of the year and it definitely did not disappoint! I loved the story, the characters and everything in between! 
 -- 
 What I Liked 
 The diverse characters. All of the characters were pretty great within this story and all for their own reasons. I loved both Molly & Cassie and their twin sisterly relationship. This story explores both of them as they come of age and start discovering who they are as separate people. It shows how this can put a strain on a relationship, but also how it can further strengthen it. I loved all of the side characters and how diverse all of them were. We were blessed with multiple lesbian/gay/bisexual characters as well as characters that come from different cultural backgrounds. Honestly, the diversity of characters was fantastic! 
 The mention of anxiety. Our main character Molly deals with anxiety and it is mentioned throughout the novel. It is even stated that Molly takes Zoloft to help her deal with her anxiety. What I really loved though was that no one made a big deal about it. It was just something that was a part of Molly and that everyone accepted as normal. No one made a big deal about it and it definitely did not become the focal point of the overall story. 
 The pacing. The Upside Of Unrequited was really fast paced and in the best way possible. The story was constantly moving and it never had a dull or boring moment. I read through this book quite quickly and I was always completely engaged! 
 Reid. Who DOESN'T love Reid after reading this novel? Honestly, he was adorable. His friendship/relationship with Molly was adorable. I just loved Reid so much okay. 
 The tone & feel. Sure, there were some dramatic and heartfelt moments, but for the most part this book was completely upbeat and positive the entire time which was wonderful! I tend to prefer darker and more serious contemporary novels, but I think it's great to read a happier book every once in a while and The Upside Of Unrequited was exactly that. 
 The little easter egg! All I'm saying is if you've read Simon Vs. The Homo Sapiens Agenda, you may have noticed a quick appearance by a few characters from that book in The Upside To Unrequited. I loved this quick little small connection! 
 -- 
 What I Didn't Like 
 The hype? It's not that I really disliked anything about this novel, because I really did love everything about it. It's just that, even though I waited for the hype surrounding this novel to die down before I read it, my standards were still maybe set a little too high. When I read Simon vs. The Homo Sapiens Agenda, the hype was real and I was left feeling a little underwhelmed. This time around, I waited a few months and I definitely wasn't as underwhelmed this time around, I still felt like I was missing out on something. Honestly, I barely took any points off for this though. This book was really solid. 
 -- 
 Overall, The Upside Of Unrequited was everything that I needed at the moment. It was a fast-paced, fun and upbeat contemporary read and I absolutely adored it!

Current rating: 2 stars (Original rating was 3.5) (was 2.5, went down to 2 as the review kept getting longer) 
 (This review is semi-spoiler filled? Legit spoilers will be hidden as per usual, but I feel like this has a lot of mini reviews) 
 As always, my reviews are a tad messy, because I'm still getting used to doing legit reviews and not rambling to my friends about how good or bad a book is. 
 "And no one warns you about this. No one tells you how hard it is, because, yay, love! And we're so happy for them! But there's this sharp edge to it, right? Because yeah, you're happy for them. But you've also lost them." 
 Let's write a book about how you can feel good about yourself if you have a man! 
 This book. 
 Honestly. 
 I have so many thoughts on this book, I don't know where to begin. 
 Let's start on a positive note; 
 This book was hilarious I loved, the author's sense of humor, I feel like the only reason why I finished the whole thing was because I just kept laughing over and over and over again. 
 I enjoyed the slightly, more "childish" narrative about this book, because it felt like I was in the mind of a seventeen-year-old girl. Sometimes authors write this book and the character are 12, 14, 16, etc.... But they sound like they're in their mid-twenties, so this was a pretty refreshing take on this. 
 It's the end of the world and the beginning of the world and we're seventeen. 
 I'd like to start off by saying that I originally loved this book. The first 150 pages felt like a 5-star book for me, but the more and more I read it, the less and less it was sitting well for me. 
 Honestly, I feel like the biggest disappoint of this whole book was the tittle itself. 
 The Upside of Unrequited. 
 What is the upside of unrequited love? Because based on this book there is no upside of unrequited, this book was essentially about a girl that all she wanted was a boyfriend. But she didn't want to put herself out there (fun fact; if you don't lay it all out there and see what bites, you're never going to catch anything). She fell into this stigma that people that aren't a size 2 can't have a significant other and that's such a shitty thing to do. 
 I originally thought that this book was going to be a strong, hilarious story about this overweight girl with a diverse family, talking to us about all her crushes and why they never worked out. (The insta love this main character has is so strong, if you listen to her talk about some of her crushes it kind of leaves you like????? How is that a crush???? It just sounds like you were briefly attracted to them. I've met dudes and girls that I thought were hella fine, was genuinely into them, never saw them again though, and I wouldn't call them crushes. But apparently, Molly does.) 
 This book to me just sounded like it was going to be such a phenomenal story, I'm disappointed that it just wasn't that. I'm genuinely so sad about this, I really, really loved the book in the very beginning, but god dammit it just had such a massive drop for me. 
 Diversity 
 It's 2017. You don't get brownie points for diversity anymore, I feel like the #1 thing this book has gotten praised for is how diverse it is. But honestly, that's such bs. That's not a reason to praise a book, diversity should just be a thing. It's not 2002-2010, when we were all tip-toeing around being gay and being astound that TV shows and books have LGBTQIA characters in them or people of color. It should just be a thing, you know? 
 Another reason why I think this was praised so much was because of the overweight main character. honestly, if Molly would've been a skinny girl, I'm about 60% certain people would say "it's just another story about how this beautiful girl (btw Molly got called beautiful quite a bit in this story) with no self-esteem, it's nothing special.". 
 But no one would point out this trope, because of the big ass stereo type that e v e r y o n e that's over weight is insecure. 
 Guess what? 
 They're not. 
 Writing style 
 The writing style of this at times was really, good, I enjoyed it, I enjoyed the young take on this book, but it was so awkward a lot of the times. 
 The number of sentences that start with "Okay," 
 new drinking game 
 Take a shot every time a sentence starts with "okay" in this book 
 Lmao, don't u dare, you'll die. 
 Judgmental 
 "Sorry, but this guy is literally choosing to advertise Lord of the Rings on his body. I don't think there's going to be a whole lot of common ground." 
 I'm sorry, but who the fuck allowed you to be such a judgmental ass over someone's clothes?? 
 This is a recurring theme in the book, Molly pretty much bashes this boy's clothes for being dorky t-shirts or for his "sneakers being electric white" (something that makes no fucking sense to me). 
 You'd think that someone that's overweight, that understands what it's like to have someone look at you up and down and judge how you look 24/7, would never do that. But no, Molly is apparently superior to Reid. (on a hypocritical note bc I'm calling her out for doing what I'm about to do, but um, home girl wore a yellow skirt with a n a v y b l u e blouse. And she's judging him for wearing lord of the ring shirts and game of throne ones) 
 Many praises for Reid though, because the boy literally give's no fucks about what people think about what he wears (Mina also made a comment about the "electric white sneakers). 
 Also, there's a lot of people that wear LotR shirts and GoT shirts and don't even know what they are, they just think the shirt is fucking cool. Your clothes don't exactly determine your taste. 
 This motherfucking line that destroyed the whole fucking book. 
 "It's the weirdest thing. My hair is un brushed. I'm wearing what may actually be one of Nadine's maternity shirts. And pajama pants. And there's a spot of toothpaste in the corner of my mouth. 
 But for the first time in maybe ever, I feel really beautiful." 
 (to add in some context, this is right after Molly got herself a boyfriend and she was texting him in the morning) 
 I don't think there will ever be words to quite describe, how fucking much I hated this line. Honestly despite a lot of the issues I had with this book it still kind of was a 3.5-star for me, but this line. 
 Your. Beauty. Is. Not. Dependent. On. Having. A. Significant. Other. 
 You are beautiful, handsome, pretty, stunning, however you want yourself to be seen. That is what you are. It does not depend on dating someone. your beauty is not defined by the person you date (or don't) Married. Single. Dating. It doesn't matter, you are a stunning individual. 
 There's so fucking much I want to say about this, but I'm just going to rage out and write like a 5k review, and we don't need so much of my thoughts. 
 I'm extremely disappointed because this is generally aimed towards younger views and I don't want young girls or boys to think that they can only "feel really beautiful" just because they're texting their boyfriend. 
 Family 
 I hate the sister relationship in this. 
 I think Cassie was honestly such a dick to her sister, I hate how their relationship progressed. I hate how passive aggressive she was towards Molly, I fucking despised the party scene. 
 I was so fucking heated up at how Cassie was pretty much shaming Molly. 
 And then how she was like "fine don't come, but don't bitch about how I'm ditching you for Mina" 
 Do us all a favor and piss the fuck off. 
 Molly and her grandma? 
 Goodbye. 
 I hate how they call their moms by thief first name though (love the moms, thought they were great characters), I feel like that's just rude honestly? Maybe it's how I was raised, but I don't know anyone that's allowed to call their parents by their names (that aren't "hippies") 
 Olivia 
 Olivia becoming single was literally the most useless thing ever. It made no sense. Other than to add some "drama". 
 Honestly though, everything Molly was feeling, I get. Like that felt so genuine to me, because I, myself, (like so many of us) have experienced this. 
 But I felt like this was just unnecessary, how Molly handled it was so poor, and it felt more like 
 something a 13-year-old would do, instead of someone that's nearly 18. It was so childish. 
 The MOST FUCKING UNNECESARY LOVE TRAINGLE EVER 
 Why was this a thing? It was always so obvious who Molly was going to go for, I feel like this is what people felt like when the whole Team Edward and Team (I forgot his name, idc, I never read Twilight) was a thing. 
 Like why? 
 Why? 
 Why throw in one of the most annoying tropes ever. 
 I don't get it. 
 Resolved (lol if u can say that this book resolved anything [spoiler; it didn't]) 
 It felt like the "resolutions" or explanations for why Cassie and her grandma acted the way they did was just, no. 
 It felt like the author slapped on a band aid on a bullet hole and honestly, no, I wasn't feeling it. I hated how she resolved this. It honestly felt like Cassie was being fake af with her "apology" and her grandmas reasoning for being a dick towards her was just such a cop out. 
 I'm done honestly, this is about to turn into a 1-star review. There's so much I left out, but this is nearly 2k, so, bye bitch, 
 ANOTHET THING TO NOTE: IT FELT LIKE MOLLY ONLY WANTED A BOYFRIEND BECAUSE ALL OF HER FRIENDS HAD BOYFRIENDS. I ALSO HATED HOW IMPORTANT THEY MADE SEX SEEM IN THIS BOOK, LIKE IT'S AN AUTOMATIC THING TO HAVE SEX JUST BECAUSE YOU'RE DATING SOMEOEN it isn't FUCK THIS WAS SO ANNOYING. 
 While I appreciate the attempt of this book, the execution was just poor. 
 "The fat kids. You're beautiful" 
 This was in the acknowledgments, and I don't know why, but this rubbed me so fucking wrong, it just heated me holy fuck y'all.

Molly, and her quest for love, is an interesting, funny read. I adored her character. Shy, body conscious and with 25 crushes, I could completely relate! 
 I really enjoyed seeing her friends, and her new 'crushes', and I felt like Molly grew massively as a character. 
 I also really enjoyed the amount of diversity. It's always great to see, and whilst I do think it shouldn't need to be celebrated, it's nice to see it more in the ya genre. 
 The only reason the book didn't get five stars from me, is because I really didn't like Cassie. I felt like she wasn't considerate of her sister at all, and although she was going through her own changes, I just felt her to be a little harsh. I also felt like I didn't learn that much about the characters, except for Reid. We learnt what Reid liked, and about his passions, but Molly? I feel like she was defined by her longing for a relationship. I would have liked to have seen more of her aside from that.

2.5 stars 
 I can't say I was disappointed in this book because I did go into it with kind of low expectations, I did relate to Molly so much and her personality is adorable and all .. and the love story is cute and fluffy, but I did have a problem with some of Molly's faulty thinking, like, this girl is so obsessed with having a boyfriend that she is desperate, who needs a boyfriend when you have a sister like Cassie and friends like Olivia and Abby ? they are really squad goals to the max .. it was a nice story but I didn't quite enjoy it, I think the diversity overload is what made this book so famous

Becky writes cute, relatable teen romance. Like Sarah Dessen for the misfits. And I LOVE IT. 
 I don't have time to write a full review, but I really appreciated: 
 -the diversity of the cast of characters 
 -anxiety rep- it was a part of Molly's character and it felt SO real, but it wasn't her defining characteristic 
 -ALL THE ROMANCES WERE SO GREAT AND SWOONY. I felt 17 again. Truly.

Okay - I have a few problems with this book. I enjoyed the ending, well the last 100 pages more than the first 3/4 of the book because cmon it was just a little to much to handle for a YA novel. I didnt expect there to be so much swearing, talk about sex and alcohol consuming. 
 I feel like these themes were made to feel like they were okay.. everyone is different and I totally understand that BUT I just felt like this book had so many negative points. 
 ONE being the way Molly was treated because she was fat.. like seriously its the 21st century don't we live in a world where beautiful comes in all shapes and sizes? 
 TWO I hated that Molly had this need to feel like she was only worthy if a guy liked her - because seriously this is not a good habit teach girls. I managed to tab a few parts in the book that I couldn't stand. 
 THREE - okay this needs its whole paragraph but Molly thinking that being called a slut was a compliment because she was having sex?! LIKE WHAT?! DID I JUST READ THAT?! I honestly had to read that segment of the book a few times to really witness what I just read. That being a slut meant you were normal. LIKE NO... please just no. I hated this book from the moment I read this. 
 FOUR - having sex doesn't mean you have become a woman.... like really? What is even going on in this book.. like why? We put so much emphasis on women being strong and not needing a man to make them a woman, like why does sex make you a woman? I feel like this is the exact reason why our society is the way it is .... seriously girls be confident enough to know your self worth. But then we have books that tell you otherwise.. and we categorise it to a YA market.. like what are we trying to do here?! Traumatised. 
 Okay so you can take it from my review that I was not overly impressed with this novel. I know so many people have rated it so highly.. and I understand these are common issues but I just couldn't relate to this and to be honest just felt a little disgusted. 
 Rant over*

reference_books.review_text:
I'm obviously no longer the fan of romance as I used to be in my YA years. It's fairly well-written for the genre, but I had high hopes that the novelist heroine would bring a creative spin (the book was recommended on a popular website). 
 Surely there were interesting possibilities here. But that whole storyline gets buried into the usual romance cut-and-paste. Unfortunate.

reference_books.title: Wild Card (Elite Ops, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Here goes, disagreeing with most reviewers. I'm French-speaking and as a teenager, I actually learned most of my English reading Harlequin romances, then historical ones. I moved on but felt like revisiting old habits and this book was on a Top 10 list I happened upon. Loved the premise, liked the beginning then it got so darn repetitive, that I almost threw it against the wall. If I had to read one more time how "his love for her tore at his soul," I was ready to have a fit... 
 The author keeps repeating herself ad nauseam like water swirling a drain. I was even skipping the sexy parts! And the final twist per the white supremacist storyline was beyond ludicrous. So I advise you to RUN from this one. Instead, pick something like Bet Me, which I'm reading right now and where even a simple kiss rings way truer and sexier. At least, Wild Card did not turn me away from romances for another decade, but it came close.

reference_books.title: After Anna
reference_books.review_text:
I wanted to like this book given the many good reviews (so many meh reviews start this way, I thought I would do my part to uphold the trend lol). Foiled, again. There were nice bits here and there, the final showdown wasn't bad, but the characters are so poorly drawn, it's hard to care. 
 (I felt the author soar a bit when she described Julia's law firm partner later in the story, and kinda went "Where were you all this time???", but it proved too little too late.) 
 To me, the worst failing of this book -- apart from the cover giving you too much notice of the daughter-returns as a plot twist, thereby gutting most of the potential suspense -- was how Lake "tells" us Julia, the mom, is destroyed, going crazy out of her mind after her daughter goes missing but.you.dont.feel.it. Don't use words to tell me how she feels, or do so with much greater affect, show me. Make me feel it. It's all very superficial and plot driven, when you KNOW the plot twist (see above for self-made spoilers, sheesh...). 
 This book needed lots more emotional writing than it gave, on a topic so heart-wrenching for parents as child abduction. I'm a mom, if somebody were to take my son, believe me, I would be bleeding my soul on the ground. Yes, we are all different, Julia gets to handle it her own way, but it was as bland a way as any writer could make it. As for the husband, don't get me started. He was supposed to be such a stand-up loving father yet comes across as whiny and weak all through. You have to be told he has redeeming qualities to believe it. 
 Alex Lake needed to be more invested to make me care. The faint glimmers of a voice were there, more grit and heart next time please.

reference_books.title: Bared to You (Crossfire, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Why do I do this to myself? The only thing Bared here were my fangs. I can't believe this is a #1 NYT best-selling author, although yes, Day writes better than most romance authors. That said, I actually started skipping the sex scenes halfway through (repetitive much, you say), then pretty much every other scene. I think this book may have broken my intermittent addiction to mindless fluff when my brain needs a rest. I'll just sip green tea and stare into a candle next time I want time out of mind. If you're looking for a modern, sexy, thoughtful romance with risque sex, hum, keep looking... I wish I had.

book_a.title: Bet Me
book_a.user_review:
This was cute. The author has a great way with dialogue that is tailor-made for the movies. I laughed out loud often. And the sexy parts avoid the overblown style that so many romances seem to adopt, which many readers love, granted, but that make me cringe and roll my eyes. 
 Loved the characters, the rhythm, the way the author didn't feel the need to edulcorate and make nice with everyone's ending. And to those reviewers who suggest a cute guy could never fall in love with a chubby girl, thereby making this a far-fetched premise, shame on you. Really.

sample_reviews.review_text:
LOLOLOLOLOLOL. 
 Okay, so this book- seems okay, right? You probably look at it and think, "ooooh, a nice hate to love story where the characters don't fall into each other the next time they meet. I could like this." 
 WELL, I HAVE NEWS FOR YOU- YOU WON'T. 
 They fucking kiss- french kiss with all the tongue and saliva in front of a fucking kid who is probably scarred for life upon seeing two fleshy tentacles colliding into each other -around the third time they meet in a public park overlooking a kids' baseball game. 
 IN WHAT UNIVERSE IS THAT ROMANTIC? WHERE DID THE STEAMING HATE GO???? OH, AND DON'T EVEN GET ME STARTED ON THE CHEESINESS THAT STARTS AFTER UPON 40% OF THE BOOK. BYE, CRUSIE, FUCKING BYE.

Amazing book. Seriously amazing. 
 I love the humor, the banter and the overall storyline.

If I could give it 2.5 stars, I would. 
 I have read other Jennifer Cruise books and this one isn't my favorite. The first half of the book was fun and lighthearted, but then the story goes nowhere after that. There was really nothing fundamentally wrong with the story, characters, or writing, the book is just about 100 pages too long. Too much of the same ground covered over and over. Would have been a better small/series romance novel.

It doesn't deserve even a single star but since I made it till the end, I would be generous to give it a little credit. I found it displayed in the section of humour/comedy books and since it had four stars out of five, I picked it up, thinking that it would prove to be a good, happy end to my hectic day. However, it proved me wrong; it was a badly written book, had a rough and a quite predictable plot and above all, it didn't make me laugh at all! Reading it was quite a waste of time

It's a fast read, I'll give you that. I literally read it in one day. It's a bit slow and I'm not too convinced I liked the plot. The characters were okay, but sometimes they were downright annoying. I would have given the book two stars if not for some very funny an redeeming moments. In general, I'd say it's an okay book which you can entertain yourself with. Other than that? Not the big deal.
I love this book. Not always a big fan of Jennifer Cruise, but this is one of my favourite romance novels. I read it whenever I am feeling a bit down and it perks me right up.

I enjoyed this book, though it is not what I usually chose in a romance novel with a contemporary setting; I typically like mine to be New Adult, laugh out loud funny (a la Sophie Kinsella), or involve a mystery where someone is murdered. Read into that what you will. This is much more of your standard "chick lit" (though I HATE that term) kind of book. Which turned out to be both a good and a bad thing. 
 Let's get the rant out of the way first. This would have been a 4 star review for me with the great scenes and witty banter. They were just so good. I loved it, except what I am going to go off on here. 
 This book was published in 2004. Because of that, it has some tropes that have (blessedly!) been mostly done away with in contemporary romance novels written for women: lots of discussion of not eating carbs, talk of diets and "good" foods (kill me now!),the "you'd look pretty if you just ditched the frumpy clothes" advice, a look of bliss on a woman's face when she allows herself to eat a "forbidden" food, etc. Basically, it's a lot of focus on the physical/superficial. 
 The book itself is at least partially about Min allowing herself to be who she is, inside and out. So I get why these things are mentioned, but I guess it just reminded me about how for awhile these types of books, it was just EVERYWHERE. These things are all part of the experience of being a woman today, and it is totally understandable/human to have insecurities about the way you look sometimes. But it being something that is the subject of so many of the conversations between the women in the this book made me sad. 
 End o' rant. 
 Now, let's talk characters: 
 Min is great! She is such a kind, smart, loyal women who will always stick up for people she cares about. (I just wish she'd turn some of that kindness inward sometimes. You are the best, girl. Remind yourself of that!) I also love that Cal will let her fight her own battles. He knows when she (like Olivia Pope) has a situation that is "handled". Her not standing up to her mother, though, drove me CRAZY for that very reason. She is also lightning fast with a quip, and I loved that. 
 I love Cal too. And though some characters tried to paint him as a player, I know me a rake when I see one, and he wasn't it. Lay off Cal, friends of Min! He really is a mensch who just made one dumb bet. Jesus! I also love that he coached his nephew's little league but would openly admit he kinda couldn't stand kids - he just loves his nephew and did it for him. I am v over the "look how good with kids he is" thing that's supposed to make women swoon in romance novels/movies, so that was refreshing as hell. 
 I wish the writer had let us get into his head a little more. Also, the physical description is basically "he's hot". I couldn't get a picture of him in my head, so that made scenes that (I guess) were supposed to be swoony less effective. As I thought back on this book after I finished it, though, my main thought was "Man, he was just great!" I just wish I had felt that AS I was reading the book. 
 This book had some GREAT quotes/witty banter. It was mostly with these deadpan reactions that just killed me. And,oh my lord, the end of the book alone makes it worth reading. 
 Normally, I LOVE me a book with a bet, but this was one kept going on so long, I was oh. my. god. It definitely lulled around the middle. Push through if you can, because the last quarter of the book was excellent. I really felt like the stakes that kept Cal and Min apart became increasingly just an excuse (plot-wise) for them to not get together until the end. 
 The way this book wraps up/how the couple gets together will totes be too cheesy for some, and that is totally cool. I love a good happy ending all around in my books though, so that was the best for me.
I loved the first 3/4 of the story, but the big the way the big misunderstanding played out in the final quarter irked my soul.
DIK

Chubby heroine stops struggling to lose weight and gets it on with a hot dude who is into her curves and her sexy shoes. 
 I love Jennifer Crusie's romance novels, and I've only read two of them. As a closer to 40-than-30-year-old mother of two, I appreciate a romance novel (or any work of fiction geared towards adults) with a female protagonist I can truly relate to. In Bet Me and Anyone But You, the leading ladies work wonderfully unglamorous jobs, have body/weight issues and have an unabashed powerful sex drive. Unlike their chick-lit counterparts, Jennifer Crusie's heroines are emotionally generous, educated, beautiful in their ordinary looks, don't obsess about the latest fashion trends, or are socially awkward neurotics. 
 They are normal women with normal quirks, and you can understand why the hunk du jour in Bet Me and 
 Anyone But You 
 fall for them and want them more than just for their looks. The ladies are witty, relevant, strong-willed without being the stereotypical bitch. The male characters are not as well drawn out as the women, but are presented as more than just two-dimensional and all-understanding eye candy that is featured in today's more contemporary female-geared fiction.

book_b.title: Yes Please
book_b.user_review:
I've usually had better things to do at 11 on a Saturday night than watch tv, so although I like SNL, I've only seen a handful of full shows over the year. These days, I just catch up on talked-about skits through YouTube. So while I know Amy Poehler, I only saw a small sampling of her SNL work. Truth is, I became a fan later in the day, through her sensitive Smart Girls advice videos (wow, a real nuanced human being, how nice), her work in movies and with Tina Fey. 
 I picked up Yes Please because I needed some light fare and read it in increments, between other books. Since the book waxes autobiographical here, comic there, social commentary or name-dropping elsewhere, this style of reading proved well-suited. 
 It's also a very uneven book for the same reasons. I laughed, and yawned too. I was entertained at times, bored by the subject matter at others. I zipped through sections and dragged almost painfully through others (looking at you UCB and Parks and Recreation). 
 At times, some of the book felt like total filler needed to fulfill a contract, hello reproducing a whole boring letter from LAX to end a book on!?!??! 
 Although it was often funny because Poehler is a smart, thoughtful storyteller, bottom line: there's a better book in there somewhere...

sample_reviews.review_text: I freakin love Amy Poehler. She's not an author; she's just someone who loves to tell stories. Her take on being in film, television and the Hollywood spotlight is refreshing, honest and straight forward.

I love Amy, but I didn't like this book. It took me ages to read it (I started way before the 10th, I just didn't update it until the 10th). 
 First of all, I thought it dragged. The stories seemed pointless and for most of it, I didn't understand why she included them in the first place. 
 Second, half of this book is just about name dropping. The amount of times she mentioned someone famous was ridiculous. I understand she's famous herself, therefore she works with famous people, but if you go back to my first point, it just seems like pointless name dropping. 
 I liked maybe two chapters out of this book and couldn't wait to finish it, to read something better. So, yeah... 2 stars.

I like Amy Poehler and this book is really just Poehler riffing on stories from her life, or random thoughts she has. I listened to it, which likely helped; I can't really imagine reading it. I realized that her rapid fire comedy, which works so well on screen, doesn't work so well in narrative. There were several sections I skipped because I just didn't care, but overall I found it an entertaining car listen.

Heard as audiobook. Patchy, with moments of hilarity, or wisdom about creating. But only parts. Too often she actually complains about how hard it is to write a book. It honestly reminded me of the trope of someone who'd cashed the advance cheque without a firm idea what to write and who stalled until the book was near deadline.

A light, fun read. I wasn't particularly familiar with Ms.Poehler's work beyond her Hilary Clinton impressions on SNL, but after reading his book, I'll say that I like her. The essays varied between personal memoirs and more straight humor, and it was a good balance.

I listened to the audio book version (yes, Amy, through my phone). I am simultaneously happy and not that Amy recorded it herself. It's always nice when a autobiographical work is told by the subject, but for an actress, I found it surprising that it was still difficult at times to know when she was joking. In particular, the chapter where she talks about how she hates being approached by strangers. I'm not the type to approach strangers on the street, celebrity or not, but the chapter rubbed me the wrong way and for the first, but not the last time, I thought that I liked Amy more before I started listening to her book. There are some genuinely funny passages, but not a lot of insight into the events of her life. It's on par with recent books by Tina Fey and Mindy Kaling.

I wanted to like this book, but I just didn't like it. Unlike Tina Fey's Bossypants, I found Yes Please wasn't funny. I expected many laughs but only had a few chuckles. From the very start, Amy Poehler went on and on about how hard it is to write a book. I found it equally hard to read her book. She was definitely candid, and I enjoyed reading about how she got her start as well as her stories about her children and her trip to Haiti, but as a whole I found the book disjointed and much too long.

The only reason I picked up this book in the first place was because my book club was reading it. I got about 1/3 of the way through, but really didn't care about what she had to say, just not interested in Amy Poehler and didn't want to waste any more of my time.
I liked the takeaways, and her insights about mothering and kids.

I hated this book. I'd say that if Amy Poehler wasn't a celebrity, this wouldn't have been published, but that isn't true. The truth is that if Tina Fey's book wasn't so successful, and she wasn't friends with Amy Poehler, than this wouldn't have been published. Bossypants was a funny, cute, and sometimes offered some decent life advice. This book is Amy Poehler talking about how wonderful she is. We get it. You think you're lower middle class, you did some drugs, you were poor in the "cool" way that liberal arts kids love to be after college to prove that they don't care about money. Whatever. I'm actually sad I read this because I love her comedy, but now I'll know what an annoying person she is in real life every time I see her :/

reference_books.title: Why Not Me?
reference_books.review_text: Her first book was a tad better but that's not saying much. I feel like she wrote a book because she's famous and she can. The book lacked substance and felt like a huge promo for her show. Not impressed or even mildly entertained.

reference_books.title: This Is Where It Ends
reference_books.review_text: I definitely did not want to put this book down. I liked the varying points of views offered for the different characters. I think some characters, like Tyler and Autumn, should have been more developed while others, Claire, were too developed.

reference_books.title: One Day
reference_books.review_text: Predictable book, but I got tired of the main characters "chasing" each other and then the cliched ending of being together (or not being together).

reference_books.title: Lily and the Octopus
reference_books.review_text: A heartwarming story that is a must-read if you've ever owned a dog!

reference_books.title: A Clockwork Orange
reference_books.review_text: The ridiculous overuse of made-up slang made this book more of a chore than an entertaining read. I get that the storyline has some moral points, but I wasn't willing to spend my time struggling through this book just because it's considered by some to be a classic.

book_a.title: Lost in Shangri-la: A True Story of Survival, Adventure, and the Most Incredible Rescue Mission of World War II
book_a.user_review: I usually love nonfiction accounts of historic events, but this one read more like a history textbook than an actual story. I was bored and essentially, didn't finish the book.

sample_reviews.review_text: This was a faithful rendition of a story that seems more fiction than fact but actually did occur in the jungles of New Guinea at the end of World War II. It is highly entertaining and packed with photographs, which really help you connect with the survivors experiences. The pacing is a bit off, especially in the 2nd half of the book and the author tried to create tension in spots where I felt that he should have just let the story continue to flow. Still, it was an engaging read overall.
Audiobook read by the author, true story of a plane that went down during WWII in the jungle of New Guinea. The rescue and survival were amazing.

The beginning was truly fascinating and I found myself wholly swept up in the story. There were a few moments with Zuckoff (who did the audio - yay for authors who read their own work!) pronounced words incorrectly and that threw me out of the story, but those were few and far between. By the halfway point, however, my attention span grew mighty thin. I wanted to know more about this handful of survivors - some of whom had gangrenous limbs. I wanted to know more about the native tribe who took them in. Sadly, as the novel progressed its intrigue lessened and by the end I was so far removed I barely noticed. Bummer.
True story of a plane crash in the jungles of New Guinea during World War II and how three people survived. Two Army Air Corp men and a WAC. This was a big story in 1945-1946

This was an absolutely gripping account of a group of soldiers who crashed on an island in the south Pacific during WWII. It tells of their crash and rescue, but the details about the natives who lived on that island and the technology available in the 1940s to rescue these soldiers was interesting. I am not a war history buff by any means, but I loved this book. Much of the account is pulled from the crash survivor's diaries so it makes it very real.

Zuckoff pulls it off: this is at the same time an adventure book, and a pure non fiction account of a plane crush and subsequent saving operation in New Guineea during World War II. As a bonus, you'll get some interesting anthropological interludes about culture crash between american soldiers and stone age warriors. Very good read.
Not bad for a historical biography. I learned a lot and it kept me thinking about the situation of the survivors.

I admit that Lost in Shangri-La caught by attention because of Shangri-La in the title. That is what Camp David used to be called and I live near there. However, once I read that cover copy that it was a survival story and rescue mission I was intrigued. 
 Near the end of WWII, a plane took off from a U.S. Army camp in New Guinea. It carried two dozen people and was supposed to be flying on sightseeing trip and giving the soldiers and WACs aboard a little rest and relaxation. That was until the plane crashed in the jungle high in the mountains. 
 Five people survived initially, though two of them died within a day. The remaining three survivors had various injuries, but they managed a three-day hike with nothing to eat but Charms candy. (This fact probably sticks with me the most from the book.) 
 Some of the tribes in the jungle were known to be cannibalistic, but the survivors were lucky enough to meet a tribe that had never seen white people but they were friendly. The two groups couldn't communicate, but were friendly and got along. 
 A rescue plane found the survivors after a few days. It couldn't land, but it was able to help two medics parachute into the area. The medics hiked to the survivors and began giving them needed medical attention. A few days later another group of paratroopers landed in the area to offer help and protection if necessary. 
 With troops now on the ground, the trick was to find a way to get them back to the camp. Planes couldn't land, helicopters couldn't operate at that altitude and it was a 150-mile hazardous march with wounded personnel back to camp. Their solution was a daring rescue that mission that I won't spoil. 
 I enjoyed the book. It was well written and it told an interesting story as a story. Though it went off on tangents to tell the background of the characters in the story, they weren't overly long or uninteresting so I didn't mind them at all. 
 I would definitely recommend this.
This is so different than any WWII story I've read, but still fantastic.
Meh. There are some interesting parts, but it bugs me that it feels like the story is constantly being drawn out with irrelevant details.

book_b.title: Eleanor & Park
book_b.user_review: Read it in one sitting and I can't remember the last time I've done that with a book. Amazing.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 This is a late review but I was thinking about this book this morning. I am aware that the book jacket has numerous references to how it perfectly describes teenage love. It does. The awkwardness and longing make you vividly remember high school. The part of the book that stays with me though is the domestic abuse portion. The fact that the mental abuse was so traumatic haunts me. That a teenager would feel so threatened merely because of verbal threats is so telling and honest. The whole family is torn apart because of abuse. So much of the story is so heartbreakingly honest, I find myself reviewing it and hurting for adults and children out there that are going through a similar trauma.
I was afraid this book would break my heart, and it SO DID. Loved the ending anyway, as much as I wanted to throw the book in the freezer.
Sweet sad YA.

No no no and no. I was very excited to read this book given the ratings and all the rave about it but I barely got through the first chapter before I about threw it across the room. No offense to the author, but to my personal opinions, I don't like books with more than 2 cuss words in one sentence. The cuss words weren't even the actual problem for me. The actual problem was that Jesus was used WITH a cuss word and then the bus number was 666.... I don't have anything against the author but that just rubbed me the wrong way.

Leave it to Rainbow Rowell and John Green to suck the fun out of YA. Even so, Eleanor & Park was so much better than Fangirl. The build up in the start was beautiful, but the open ending really ticked me off.

Totally loved this book. It was so hard to put it down, and I enjoyed almost all of it. Although, some parts were kind of hard to digest. At some points, the book comes off as really cheesy and fluffy, and its hard to believe that the point of view is appropriate for 16-year olds. Despite that, the writing style was so, so amazing! And the shifts in POV were what made the book special.

"Eleanor tenia razon. Ella nunca se veia bien. Se veia como el arte, y no se suponia que el arte se viese bien, sino que se suponia que te hiciese sentir algo." 
 Ya desde Fangirl que Rainbow Rowell me deja con un pequeno vacio que debo llenarlo con algo: helado, un libro, cafe, fotos de Logan Lerman, cualquier cosa con tal de olvidarme. 
 En este libro, tenemos a Eleanor, una chica como cualquier otra, pero a la que juzgan casi todos. Tiene el pelo rojo, enrulado y muy desordenado. Viste extrano. Es timida, y no habla con nadie. Tambien tenemos a Park, quien viste siempre de negro. No es popular pero tampoco deja que lo tomen como un marginado. Es medio asiatico y le gustan los comics. Ellos se conocen cuando, en el autobus, Eleanor no sabe donde sentarse y Park (duramente) le dice que lo haga con el. De a poco se forma una relacion, ella mirando de reojo a los comics que el lee y este, dandose cuenta de que ella lo hace, le presta alguno para que Eleanor lo lea tranquila. 
 La historia me gusto. No comparto la misma euforia al igual que a mucha gente que le encanto. Se me hizo entretenido, pero no le llegue a agarrar el hilo de la emocion por la historia. En muchos momentos, las escenas se me hacian aburridas y las leia rapido para pasar a otra cosa. Ojo, eso no quiere decir que las veia innecesarias pero, personalmente, me hubiese gustado que diera otro giro. 
 Algo que me gusto mas que la historia, fueron las frases. Hay muchas de ellas que uno puede tomar y apreciar, leerlas y memorizarlas. Tengo un algo con los libros en los que si estos traen frases hermosas, es mas probable que me gusten mas que la historia misma. 
 El final me parecio brusco, me dejo con muchas dudas. Odio eso. Pero, creo que esto es lo que caracteriza a Rainbow Rowell, ya que en Fangirl ocurrio algo similar. 
 Tengo ganas de recomendar este libro a mucha gente que todavia no lo leyo. Y es que aunque yo le haya dado tres estrellas (me gusto) no significa que no marco algo en mi. Hubo muchas escenas que me dejo boca abierta y otras que pense que eran innecesarias. Pero a simple vista se ve que es un libro lleno de significaciones que a uno luego lo va llevando a entender muchisimas cosas. 
 Una cree que si abraza a alguien con todas sus fuerzas, lo tendra mas cerca. Una cree que se puede abrazar a alguien con tanta fuerza como para seguir sintiendo su presencia, grabada en ti, cuando te separas. Cada vez que Eleanor se separaba de Park, tenia la misma sensacion de perdida irreparable. 
 Ahora realmente quiero helado. Y alguien que me abrace.

Amazing book, absolutely fantastic, buuuuutttttt HOW COULD IT POSSIBLY END THIS WAY! I now have a piece of my soul missing because of this ending! I'm assuming that I'm never going to see these character again! I will never know what happened to them after that last page! My life has no meaning and now I must deal with this book hangover in the only way I know how (by watching something stupid but happy)

So disappointed in this book. While I was expecting the likes of John Green and David Leviathan, I was instead met with unfulfilled expectations. Rowell attempted to tackle several significant and dangerous issues in her novel (insecurities, abuse, bullying, and race) and they were dealt with shallowly and selfishly. The characters were unconvincing and I found the storyline hard to follow at times. The relationship between Eleanor and Park was equally unconvincing. Their relationship developed out of nowhere and was based wholly on physical touch. I was expecting depth out of this book. I was expecting to be moved by this book. But, the book was shallow and unconvincing. I would not recommend it to anyone.
Lovely and heartbreaking... Just like love in high school always is in reality :(

reference_books.title: The Red Queen (The Plantagenet and Tudor Novels, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
Margaret Beaufort is a horrible, selfish woman who thinks of no one but herself. God she angered me so much!! I've never read a character who I have wanted to punch more than her. It is all about her, her rise, her power because she was destined for greatness and she doesn't care who gets hurt along the way. She's made me so angry!! 
 The story was pretty decent but the best bit was the battle description at the end. I loved Henry Stafford her 2nd husband who was obviously treated like crap and the relationship with her last husband was basically what she deserved; cold, calculating and simply for personal gain. In all I think it's got to be 2 stars because she's such an awful, selfish cow.

reference_books.title: Inferno (Robert Langdon, #4)
reference_books.review_text: Quite disappointed with this book, seems to be a lot of running about and describing the buildings of Florence rather than any substance. Starts off well, gets bland toward the middle then a hurried ending with not much resolution... Overall it seems to be all about the hype rather than the content itself.

reference_books.title: The Hypnotist (Joona Linna, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I'm a big fan of Scandinavian crime writing: I adore Jo Nesbo, so I thought I would give this a whirl. What a pile of crap! 
 So it starts off with this gruesome murder where the boy is the only survivor. It goes on and on where the hypnotist goes to work on him to find out what happens, he upsets the boy after 1 session! 1 session! So he's not good at his job! 
 So the story goes on, flits to his son going missing, then delves into the hypnotists past etc then the author attempts to deliver a twist... Your suspicions were wrong... The boy from the beginning was not behind the kidnapping... Shock Horror... It was this completely obscure woman who has randomly popped up in the story for no apparent purpose aside from kidnapping the son. So now you know the truth, the boy from the beginning is killed very easily and quickly. 
 Considering this kid was a stone cold killer, obviously if he's the only survivor he did it, he would know what was coming or would have carried some form of protection... But no, why would he?? It was such a dismissal of a character who was apparently an integral part of the story. It didn't get any better and I felt very cheated. 
 A big waste of time, if you want a decent Scandinavian crime books stick with nesbo

reference_books.title: Fifty Shades Darker (Fifty Shades, #2)
reference_books.review_text: I'm drained from just reading this with the up and down emotions, clinginess etc. for a man who just wants to dominate he sure comes around to the idea of marriage rather quickly! Too predictable

reference_books.title: Illuminae (The Illuminae Files, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
DNF: My first one of the year. 
 I'm sorry I tried but this really wasnt for me. The concept is a good one and I like the idea of the reports and transcripts etc but for me it completely detracted from the story. I wasn't gripped at all: the two main characters annoyed me with kady thinking she was all that and Ezra just being so immature. 
 I fully expect a witch hunt on my opinion but I tried, I really did!!

book_a.title: Madame Bovary
book_a.user_review: Got really bored. Too slow, nothing interesting happening so I gave up!

sample_reviews.review_text:
After giving it some thought, I decided that the book is a classic not because of the story and characters, but rather in spite of them. Although the characters are insipid, vain, pompous, silly, ignorant, grasping, dishonest, and self-important (yes, all of them) and the story chronicles their unintelligent flailing about into melodrama, vice, and bungling, Flaubert employed such a witty and realistically descriptive voice (and was the first writer to employ that level of realism in his descriptions, evidently) that the book is not a dime-store bodice ripper but rather a literary masterpiece. 
 {Read my full review here}

Henry James once said, "Madame Bovary has a perfection that not only stamps it, but that makes it stand almost alone; it holds itself with such a supreme unapproachable assurance as both excites and defies judgment." 
 That's right. Defies judgment. 
 I don't know... he looks kind of judgy to me... 
 Unfortunately, I had to read a translation as my French is nowhere near good enough to read the original. Though I am assured that the prose in the original French are amazing and inspiring. 
 I can certainly appreciate the characterization and story-telling ability but I personally struggled with the story as I reconciled what Flaubert seemed to be saying about society, women, women who had affairs, men and romance. 
 Now, I would like to take a moment to quote Manny's Review, since he is the one who convinced me to read this book in the first place. 
 "Flaubert makes no obvious attempt to judge Emma..." 
 No, Flaubert doesn't break up his beautiful prose at any point with, "So whilst that is a very nice tree, I would like to intrude and mention that Emma is, like, a total ho! So, now back to the tree..." 
 I feel he doesn't do this because that would be superfluous. In fact, it seems to me that he doesn't stop judging through this entire book. 
 [image error] 
 The judgement is like looking at vacation photos of a ninja family. You can't see it but you know it's there. 
 Why else would Flaubert so meticulously describe and relish in Emma's fall from grace? Every little detail is mentioned with the same eagerness as a kid dobbing in their little brother. He puts together a file of evidence for her complicity, a smoking gun as you'd say, and leaves it up to us to point the finger. 
 -She immediately decides after her wedding night that she doesn't love Charles. 
 -She then sets about creating her own misery by obsessing and romanticizing this unhappiness until it consumes her. 
 -She goes from a productive and proficient housewife to a morose, unrelenting mess. 
 -She quickly begins despising Charles and blaming him for everything while he dotes on her and grows increasingly content. 
 -Her home quickly falls into a state of shabbiness. 
 -Her daughter goes neglected. 
 -Her first romance uses her unforgivably but is eventually driven away by her incessant neediness and demands. 
 -Her second romance, whilst more earnest in his affections, is also driven away by her incessant neediness, deteriorating mental health and demands. 
 -She drives her husband into bankruptcy. 
 -Commits suicide to escape it all. 
 -Her husband falls into despair, neglects their child and quickly dies. 
 -The child ends up working in a cotton factory. 
 What would a child do working in a cotton factory, you ask? 
 Oh, just a little mill-scavenging. Their job was to crawl under the huge, spinning WHEELS OF DEATH to pick up the spare bits of cotton. They were not allowed to sit, rest, or take a break while the mill ran - which was always except for Sunday when they cleaned the huge, spinning WHEELS OF DEATH that caused these children to live in a constant state of grief and terror 
 Well, doesn't that just cheer you up! 
 The entire story arc and every unnecessary tidbit condemns Emma like one more nail in the coffin. Society is condemned, men are condemned, romantic idealism is condemned. Really, this novel thinks everyone is to blame. What is this novel's answer to it? It seems to be saying, "Well, that silly woman had so much and she threw it all away and look at her now, kids. She's dead! And poor, which is really much worse." 
 The novel seems to step back and tsk at Emma, saying that she had so much. A safe and comfortable home, a good husband who doted on her and she just couldn't be happy with that. 
 Then it looks at society and says, "Well, you created this and now you've helped destroy her too, you assholes!" 
 It shakes its head at Charles and says, "You weren't strong enough to keep her in line and then you pined over this worthless woman to the ruinment of your only child." 
 But I wonder what this book would have been if Emma hadn't been a victim to everyone and every circumstance except for Charles. I wonder what this book would have been like if it displayed a far more realistic approach to a woman having an affair and her reasons. Because, let's face it, this book's depiction of a woman and why she has extra-marital relations is very obtuse. Emma's life and situation is hardly the common for women who seek more out of life. This book makes her quest for more seem silly, unneccessary and ungrateful. 
 Most of all, I wonder what this novel would have been like if it had dealt with Emma as a real character. One who didn't need to be mostly insane to justify having an affair. One who wasn't both stupid and entitled and didn't lose all her money through a lack of self-control and ability to take five seconds to do the math. One who was capable of growing and learning from life. 
 Unfortunately all that is lost. Even in the end, Emma learnt nothing. All sound and fury. Signifying nothing. 
 Much like this novel. 
 My final criticism about this book... 
 This was a book about people gettin' it on... 
 AND THERE WAS NO SEX! 
 [image error] 
 Curse you, Flaubert! Curse you!

I just felt like I read a bullshit Soap Opera. I do not like Emma, I pitied Charles & Berthe and disliked Charles' parents completely. I guess for 1856/7 it would read as intense. Sort of. I don't know. I enjoyed the scenery, pretty flowers, but I do not care about these people.

Of course, two stars was my senior-year-of-high-school rating, for which I was one of two people - me and my best friend - who chose it over War and Peace or some such, so we just read (/talked) out in the hallway. It therefore needs a serious reread.

2.5 stars. It's unfortunate that I find such an important and influential novel to be so slow. To be sure, Flaubert's attention to detail is precise, and his writing can be brilliant. But I found these details to be as excessive as the romantic flights of fancy that he mocks in Madame Bovary's life, just excessive in a different way. That is to say, Flaubert's verbal mise-en-scene can be overwhelming at times, much in the same way that a romantic work might be overwhelming in sentiment. The plot itself was no frills: a bored middle class housewife with romantic dreams of a better life has several affairs to spice up her life. Perhaps we have Flaubert to blame for making such a plot so common? In any case, straight-forward plot combined with the droning descriptions of the details of everyday life made this a slog for me. 
 Indeed, this was the third time I had attempted reading Madame Bovary. First, as a teenager, I didn't make it past the first thirty pages. In my twenties, I didn't make it much further. This is the first time I was able to make my way through the book. What kept me reading was that occasionally Flaubert would deliver these lines that would bowl me over. Example: "When she went to confession, she invented small sins in order to stay there longer, kneeling in the shadows with her hands together and her face against the grating, beneath the whisperings of the priest. The metaphors of betrothed, spouse, heavenly lover, marriage everlasting, that recur in sermons, awoke in the depths of her soul an unlooked-for delight." Those types of brief insights and beautifully conveyed ideas would keep me turning pages, even though this was not the most enjoyable novel for me to read. Much like Sentimental Education, which I found just slightly more tolerable, I felt equal parts frustration (in the novel) and awe (in Flaubert's writing), but never much joy in the reading experience.
Is there something wrong with for not really liking this book?

This is a hard one to review. I loved Flaubert's way of describing things, but I didn't love the fact that he looks at all his characters (maybe except little Berta) with discernible irony. Well - that's the hard thing - the irony IS, on one hand, enjoyable, but on the other - how to feel sympathy for wholly ridiculous people? But, it is the most colourful sociological ouevre I've ever read.

This was an interesting idea. But sadly, there were many plot holes/issues. 
 In the beginning, when Thomas shows up at the maze, there's a phenomenon where the other Gladers won't answer Thomas' questions. It continues for days on end where they will tell him some things, but hide others. As if something bad will happen if they let Thomas know too much too soon. And this is never explained. Nothing bad happens when he discovers information on his own. So in the end, it seemed like a bad plot device to excuse the slow giving of information. 
 Other spoilery examples... 
 Then Teresa (the only girl) arrives. She and Thomas were the ones who created the maze in the first place. It's a game meant to weed out the most intelligent of the group. So it's confusing why the "Creators" would send Thomas and Teresa in the maze at all. They've already proved themselves the most intelligent, so why send them into the maze just so they'd lead the Gladers to the exit, protecting their friends most? That doesn't lead to an intelligence-based outcome, and isn't that the point? 
 Then there was an incident where Thomas killed a Griever, the creatures that hunt the Gladers, and it seemed so easy. Just hacking their saw and pincher arms off. But, in the two years when Thomas wasn't in the Glade, no one else could figure that out? Seems unlikely. 
 Then there was the death of one of the main characters. A character who was supposed to be dead (which is never explained) is actually alive and throws a knife at Thomas as a final "Variable" in the trial. Thomas' good friend takes the knife in the chest and dies. Again, no explanation. Why was Gally still alive? Why did the Creators want a last variable if it only eliminated one more player out of twenty? 
 And towards the end, they muse over what happened to the Gladers who didn't follow the group to the exit. A character says the Grievers probably got them. But hours earlier, they pushed the "Kill Maze" button, which eliminated the Grievers, so that's kind of not possible. 
 So overall, there were many plot points that were never explained. And never mentioned in one of those paragraphs where the main character is asking himself questions meant to direct the reader's attention to certain points. And from what I read in summaries and reviews I read for the sequels, these issues aren't resolved, and even more arise. I probably won't read the others.

 If you've been around my blog for a bit, you know I have a soft spot for YA dystopian novels. I've been wanting to read The Maze Runner since I first saw the preview of the movie. I refused to see the movie though, until I read the book, so I figured it was about time. Especially after my roommate read the whole series in about a week and the book is $1.99 on Amazon. Nothing to lose right? 
 This is very much a book for the intended YA audience. I don't mean that in a negative way at all either. The style, the verbiage...while I don't read a ton of YA, this is one of the first I felt was suited mainly for the age group, whereas I think Hunger Games and Potter reach beyond their intended market. Not that I didn't enjoy it, although there were a few things that irritated me (like how people initially treated Thomas), but I could notice the difference. The plot was a mix of Lord of the Flies (I blame that one the fact that all I remember about that book is there's a group of young boys surviving in a jungle, a total jerk and a sad ending of Piggy), rather gruesome deaths, an apocalyptic world, mystery of the Creators and toss on a scoop of the Dharma initiative. 
 There were some parts of the plot I figured out or expected and other twists I didn't see coming. Yet, the twists and still elusive overall plot are enough for me to pick up the rest of the series, especially after reading the epilogue. Who are these people?! If you follow my blog, this might be a good point of reference: I'm much more interested in finishing this series than Divergent. 
 I have the movie waiting for me and am looking forward to seeing it on the big screen. While no Hunger Games, if you enjoy YA dystopian, I think this will fit the bill of a quick and enjoyable read. 
 Have you read this series or seen the movies? What are your thoughts on it?

reference_books.title: The Broken Kingdoms (Inheritance, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Set ten years after the events of The Hundred Thousand Kingdoms, Broken Kingdoms follows the incidents that happen to Itemptas after he's turned mortal and later found by Oree. The world setting is still as creative as ever and it's interesting to see what changes have been wrought by the climax of the first book. Sadly though, that's pretty much as exciting as it gets. This book did not have the appeal of the previous one for me and most of my issues revolve around the MC. 
 Oree isn't particularly a great character but neither is she a terrible one, but she never asks the right questions, always seems to stumble into one trap after the other and generally just exists in a state of confusion. Perhaps the author meant to write her that way. As Oree is blind for the most part, all the scenes and dialogues in the book are written from the perspective of one who has to depend on her other senses to analyse the situation. And I can imagine how disconcerting and difficult that must be. I could even consider it a bit of genius if the author meant for us - the readers - to experience the story from that viewpoint. But either way, it was much too confusing for me. Usually we readers have an inkling of the plot ahead of it happening. We can solve some of the puzzles before the characters realise it. But that was lacking for the most part here. The feeling of being led around (for lack of a better word) blind set my teeth on edge. I could not enjoy the book at all and rushed through it so I could get to the end. And when I reached it, it was bit of a let down honestly. Nowhere near as exciting as the first book. Hopefully, the third one won't have the same issues.

However, Ms. Casey fails to inform the reader there is bullying, slut shaming, gratuitous violence, and an emotionally abusive relationship.  Similar to Beautiful Disaster in the set up-bad boy who illegally fights and is used to getting what he wants meets a good girl who is emotionally cut off from the world and rejects him and his love.

His gives voice to his attraction by calling her a phat arse (that's suppose to be a complement), slut, crazy bitch, and my personal fav...c*nt.

She makes her feelings known repeatedly that she wants nothing to do with him yet after he beats up a boy who she's friends with for the 3rd time she decides to try being his girlfriend because why fight fate. *head desk* . I think what cheesed me off more then anything is his and her family saw nothing wrong with the way they acted. They just poo pooed and brushed it off because that was just the way this couple is, ya know? No, I don't know. I don't want to know.

He was a bully, hell yes he was, it was not cool. The thing is, I know as an author, just because we write a character does not mean we condone their behavior. We're just writing a true character. Dominic is a strong-willed dumbass teenager who says dumb shit but is a really good guy underneath. He pushes it too far. He makes Bee cry. It's not cool. She calls him on his shit. She responds with physical violence back. THAT is not cool either. 
 HOWEVER. Beyond all that, these two characters seriously work. They are real, flawed characters who we are still rooting for in the end. They have wicked chemistry. They can have sweet as hell moments. It's a seriously great story. Up and down, I was with them every moment, couldn't put it down, I was deep in it. I can't wait to read the next book. He falls madly in love with her within a small time frame, and when she rejects him, he shows off his alpha male tendencies by threatening any guy in a 100 mile radius... Here's the thing... She's a bitch. I mean she's really really really a bitch. It's not the cute I-stand-up-for-myself kind of bitch... It's not even the not-a-broken-heroine-trope-again Kind of bitch...  The story feels elementary; there's not much depth to the characters, and there's no scale to their emotions -- everything is extreme anger... There's not sadness, or annoyance, or self-loathing... It's more like "you stepped on my shoe, I'm gonna fucking kill you and all your brothers." <--- who the hell acts like that? 
 I held on till the end of this book, because I hate dropping books half way through... I hate writing reviews. I hate the time it takes and the energy it wastes, but this book deserves to come with a warning label, so please, save yourself the time and energy and do not read this one.
