 I read a Maxine Kiss short story quite a while back in an anthology and remember really enjoying it,so I wasn't surprised at how engrossing The Iron Hunt is. Maxine is a Hunter,from a long line of Hunters,tasked with keeping demons in check. She's settled into tenuous comfort with her boyfriend Grant,former priest and so much more,and enjoys helping out at the soup kitchen and shelter that he runs. He veneer of normality that Maxine has cloaked herself in is shattered when she is accused of the murder of a private investigator. Her name is on a piece of paper found in the dead man's pocket,and Maxine has no idea who else could know of her identity. Her investigation will lead her to a man who may have much to do with her past and creatures that hint at the possibility of a coming apocalypse. 
 The Iron Hunt opens with this line "When I was eight,my mother lost me to zombies in a one-card draw." Sucks you right in,yes? It certainly caught my attention,and I ended up staying glued to the pages. There's trouble brewing beyond the veil,and things not of this world are pushing through to this reality. What begins with the murder of a private investigator turns into a search into Maxine's soul,and her past. Maxine is a tough girl,make no mistake,and her tattoos are,um,unusual. During the day,they are her armor. When I say armor,Maxine can get hit by a car and she'll be right as rain. That's some serious armor. At night,the tattoos come off and coalesce into five seriously rough and tumble little demons. Zee seems like the alpha guy of the group,and the only one that Maxine actually speaks with. They're a charming lot,and I found myself falling in love with them as the book goes on. I mean,these little guys can devour a baddie in seconds,like to cuddle teddy bears (well,pieces of teddy bears),eat tools and other various non-edibles (somehow the author makes this charming,seriously),and will do anything to keep Maxine safe. Ms. Liu's writing is sharp and immediate,and the action hardly lets up. I also like her concept of zombies. We're not talking the shambling undead here. "Zombie" is used to describe humans inhabited by demons. Maxine is convinced the lot of them are up to no good,but Grant is convinced they can change,and he just might have the ability to make that happen. In fact,there's way more to Grant than meets the eye. This is just another one of the stunning discoveries Maxine will make during the story. She knew Grant had some magic,but just how much remains to be seen. Her devotion to him is unshakeable,however,and her strength,tempered with an aching vulnerability are part of what make Maxine a heroine to root for. The author has a wonderful way with words,and has created a world rich in mythology,ghosts,demons,and plenty of darkness (although there is light at the end.) Her imagery is immediate and the twists and turns don't stop! I highly recommend this series to any urban fantasy fan,and can't believe I had it sitting on my shelf for so long!

reference_books.title: Magic Rises (Kate Daniels, #6)
reference_books.review_text:
You may also read my review here: http://www.sfsignal.com/archives/2013... 
 Magic Rises is the 6th book in the Kate Daniels series, and in my opinion, the best. In this outing, Kate is settled in at the Keep as the Beast Lord's Consort, which means her bond with Curran puts her in a very high position indeed. Helping to lead such a large group of shifters, of all breeds, is tough anyway, but Kate constantly feels like an outsider, because she's human. Don't let that fool you though, Kate is as tough as they come, and has some pretty powerful magic. It's a good thing too, because soon she's going to need it. When the teen daughters of a pack member succumb to loupism, always a possible side effect of the Lyc-V virus all shifters have, Kate, and Kate's young ward, Julie, are devastated, as is the rest of the pack. Loupism causes shifters to be stuck mid-transformation and also causes homicidal derangement. It can strike any shifter during puberty, and usually, once it sets in the shifter must be put down. Luckily, there is a cure, but its availability is very limited. When Curran tells Kate that they've been asked to arbitrate a dispute in Europe, with payment of the cure, Kate is all in. Unfortunately, the chances of this job being a trap are very high. Good thing Kate and Curran will have help from a few of their friends. 
 When Kate, Curran, and crew arrive at their destination, they're bombarded on all sides with hostility. After all, they're there to bodyguard Desandra, who is the pregnant daughter of an alpha that is disputing territory with the two fathers of her babies. Yep, two. She's pregnant with twins, and because of her father's machinations, she's got babies on the way that each have a different father. (Yes, this is biologically possible.) The two fathers aren't truly interested in her well-being, but they are interested in getting at her father, who's frankly a psychopath, and getting the jump on the Beast Lord could be a huge coup for just about everyone there. So, problems all the way around. Then there's Lorelei Wilson, whose father leads the Alaskan pack. Why she's there, Kate isn't really sure, but the last time Curran saw her, she was 12. She's 21 now, and has grown up into a beautiful young woman. She also seems determined to undermine Kate at every turn and monopolize Curran's attention. I wanted to slap Lorelei. Repeatedly. If you're looking for some serious tension, you'll find it here. The storyline involving Lorelei was one of the biggest reasons I enjoyed Magic Rises, and with everything else Kate has to deal with, including the identity of the gathering's host-this one's a doozy, but in my opinion, to give it away, would spoil a major part of the story-it's just adding insult to injury. Did I already mention that once they get there, they pretty much immediately have to start fielding attacks from creatures that Kate has never seen before? Really nasty ones. I also really enjoyed Kate and Co.'s interaction with Desandra, who first appears to be a spoiled brat, but is much more than she seems. The lady has hidden depths, and discovering these was another high point of the story. 
 Readers of this series are used to seeing Kate pushed to her physical limits, and she is in Magic Rises, but she's also pushed to her emotional limits (and nearly beyond.) This emotional turmoil was one of the most important parts of the story, and you'll want to see resolution so badly, you won't want to put the book down until you get some satisfaction. Don't worry, though, the fight scenes are superb, as usual, and you'll want to keep an eye out for the scene in which Kate spars with their host. Magic Rises goes to some pretty dark places, but the stakes are very high, and expect some major game changers here. Seriously, there are some stunning twists, and some tragic ones. While the majority of the narrative delves into very dark territory, the authors are always good at inserting some levity here and there. (Veteran readers will be delighted to find out who owns the ship that takes the group to their destination.) The story is made much richer by having read the previous books in the series, but I can honestly say that new readers could start with this one as well (though I would recommend starting with book 1, Magic Bites, because it's, well, awesome). 
 I have to admit, I've been stagnating a bit where urban fantasy is concerned, but Magic Rises has reawakened my love for the genre. Urban fantasy absolutely does not get much better than this.

reference_books.title: Miss Peregrine’s Home for Peculiar Children (Miss Peregrine’s Peculiar Children, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
You may also read my review here: http://www.mybookishways.com/2013/08/... 
 You've probably noticed that when I review a YA title, I usually feel the need to mention how hard I tend to be on YA. Not because there isn't plenty of wonderful YA fiction, it's just that sometimes it's way too hard for me, at my age, to identify with young protagonists who are at wildly different points in their lives. So, that said, when I do review a YA title, I consider it exceptional indeed, and Miss Peregrine's Home for Peculiar Children is about as exceptional as they get. Since it was published in 2011, it's gotten so many glowing reviews I started wondering if it really did live up to the hype, and after getting a paperback copy, finally decided to dive in. Peregrine is told in the voice of Jacob, relating the story of his muddle through his 16th year, as the child of a mother who is heir to a chain of drugstores and a father that can't seem to complete anything of substance, moving from project to project, only to abandon it. Jacob has a rather aimless, poor-little-rich-kid vibe, and he's aware of this, but when his beloved grandfather, Abe, whose health has been declining with alarming frequency, is attacked and killed outside his home, Jacob is aimless no more. In fact, it's Jacob that finds his grandfather's ravaged body, and imagines he sees a terrible face in the undergrowth, but it's only his imagination, right? 
 Jacob feels there might be more to his grandfather's story (especially after finding a very, very interesting letter), and on the advice of his therapist, he decides to visit a tiny island off the coast of Wales which supposedly houses the children's home that Abe grew up in, and that Abe left to go fight in WWII. Jacob has seen photos of many of the children that supposedly lived at the home, and many of these photos contain oddities that Abe insists are the talents and abilities of some very different, and very special children. Jacob is understandably dubious as to the photos' authenticity, but after arriving in Wales, accompanied by his father, he sets off to find the home, and among the wreckage, some very peculiar things begin to happen. 
 It's immediately obvious from the moment you pick up this gorgeous book, that you're going to have a unique experience. It's a beautifully put together book, and interspersed among the narrative are the very pictures that are described within. There are sepia photos of each of the peculiar children that make up Miss Peregrine's motley assortment, and I found myself flipping back to look at the pictures again and trying to keep myself from paging forward and spoiling the fun. What Jacob finds among the ruins of that long ago children's home is a portal to another time and place, so magical and beautiful it defies description. However, where there is light, there is also darkness, and although Jacob is content to wile away the hours with his new friends, discovering their abilities and delighting in their company (especially that of the lovely, feisty Emma), something dark is indeed coming, and it could threaten this beautiful world that Jacob has found. Miss Peregrine's Home for Peculiar Children is by turns heartbreakingly delicate and unflinching, fraught with wonder and danger, and sparkles with delightful and terrifying magic. I highly recommend this book to kids and adults alike, and have never experienced anything quite like it! Keep an eye out for the sequel, Hollow City, in January 2014.

reference_books.title: Another Little Piece
reference_books.review_text:
You may also read my review here: http://www.mybookishways.com/2013/08/... 
 When the 17 year old girl that looks like Annaliese Rose Gordon emerges from the woods, covered in a trash bag, she has no idea who she is. Soon the authorities are alerted and she finds out that indeed she is Annaliese Rose Gordon. DNA doesn't lie, and Annaliese has been missing for a year, ever since she came out of the woods covered in blood, then vanished without a trace. Her parents are ecstatic to have her home, but don't know quite how to deal with her apparent memory loss. Annaliese doesn't remember anything about her life, her parents, any of it, but one thing she does know: she is most definitely NOT Annaliese Rose Gordon. Soon, she starts having disturbing visions, visions of other lives and bloody encounters, but what does it mean? As Anna (as she now calls herself) begins to settle uneasily into Annaliese's life, she also, through the visions, discovers a horrible truth. For many years she's been jumping from one teenage girl to another, each year, in a gruesome exchange. This always happens on the girls' eighteenth birthday, and Annaliese's birthday is right around the corner. Her next door neighbor, Dex, has secrets of his own, and may hold the key to who, and what, Anna really is, and her attraction to Dex surprises no one more than Anna. 
 When I started Another Little Piece, I expected suspense, but I didn't expect the clever supernatural twist. Anna has been jumping bodies for many, many years now, and by all rights, jumping to the next girl after Annaliese should be the easy choice, but things are changing. She gets to know the real Annaliese through a series of poems the girl has written, and the fierce love "the parents" have for their daughter is something Anna has never experienced. It's obvious Anna didn't have happy beginnings, and we get a glimpse of that, and slowly, the author reveals what led to the start of this soul exchange, and the man behind it. He brings creepy and obsessive "love" to a whole different level, especially when Anna meets him for the first time in Annaliese's body. It's a standout scene in the novel, among many. Anna's narrative is tense and the story pulls you inexorably toward Anna's final choice, before she must move on to the next body, and it may not be what you expect. Creepy, suspenseful, and surprisingly tender, teens and adults will find much to love (and be chilled with) in this unique thriller, and very unusual love story.

reference_books.title: The Dragon Factory (Joe Ledger, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
You can read my review here: http://mybookishways.blogspot.com/201... 
 The second novel in Maberry's Joe Ledger series starts very soon after Patient Zero left off, with Joe visiting the gravesite of one of his oldest and dearest friends. The problem is, he's a wanted man, and the man that wants him is none other than the Vice President of the United States. He's sent his goon squad to pick up Joe, but Joe has other plans... 
 Taking off like lightning and never letting up, The Dragon Factory is a cross-genre, gritty, fun, roller coaster of a ride! I loved Patient Zero, and The Dragon Factory doesn't disappoint, in fact, I think I loved it more! Told in first person POV of Joe Ledger, my favorite tough, snarky ex-cop, (with frequent forays into third person with one of the book's star psychos, Cyrus Jacoby) it grabs you by the throat, and doesn't let you go until the last page! What's not to love? Joe and Echo Team have to deal with everything from psychotic Nazi clones, to an organization called the Cabal, which is out to achieve ethnic cleansing on a worldwide scale. Add to that DNA manipulated beasts, a race of slaves called the New Men, bio-terror on an epic scale, a pair of the creepiest, ickiest (yes, icky), twisted (had to throw that in there), albino (yes, albino) twins, and a boy hero that will break your heart and reaffirm your belief in the power of the human spirit. 
 Maberry throws all of this at you with his usual perfect pacing and style, and the depth of detail and research put into this book is, as always, impeccable. One thing that Maberry does in his novels is something that you don't see a lot of in books that are this action oriented. In the midst of all this chaos and adrenaline, in Joe Ledger he's created a character that not only kicks ass, but he has a heart and soul, and it comes across in nearly every scene that he's in. In Joe, he gives us a hero to root for, if for no other reason than he is intrinsically good. Joe is not superhuman, and he doesn't have supernatural abilities. He's an everyman with, admittedly, rather unique talents that we can all identify with in some way. In The Dragon Factory, Maberry takes topics that are complex and sometimes terrifying, and delivers them with humanity and sometimes humor. There were moments during this book (in particular one) that brought me to tears, as with Patient Zero, and Maberry shows us that humanity does not have to be sacrificed for the sake of an exciting read! 
 This series is absolutely not to be missed, and I recommend it to anyone that loves thrillers, horror, suspense, espionage, fantasy, and all of the above! I am breathlessly anticipating the third book in the Joe Ledger Series, The King of Plagues, due out March 29th!

book_a.title: Hexed (The Iron Druid Chronicles, #2)
book_a.user_review:
You may also read my review here: http://www.mybookishways.com/2011/06/... 
 Poor Atticus. After the epic battle in Hounded, he just wants to train his new apprentice and tend his Druid grove in peace, but it's just not in the cards. He's still cleaning up the demon mess left behind by that battle, and that's not all. Atticus is asked, by the local witch coven, to take down a group of Bacchants that threaten to turn their patch of Arizona into a seething den of iniquity. He's also got his Viking vamp lawyer trying to convince him to take down Thor, which he absolutely does not want to get involved with. Then there's that feisty (and nasty) coven of German witches, and they're out for his blood... 
 Hexed is just as awesome as Hounded, and some of my favorite characters are back, and getting lots more play! For example, my favorite Viking vamp Leif is enlisted to help Atticus and the Sisters of the Three Auroras fight that coven of German witches I mentioned earlier. This particular showdown is like the O.K. Corral, but with a Druid, witches, a vamp, golems, goat headed demons, and RPGs. Seriously, RPGs folks! My favorite Irish wolfhound, Oberon, is back and better than ever (I seriously love this dog), and we get a rather memorable visit by the Morrigan (remember the Morrigan?), and get to see her, um, softer side. Yes, the softer side of a death goddess is just as entertaining as it sounds. We also get to spend a bit of quality time with the lovely Brighid, which is always a singular treat! Mr. Hearne's writing is fast paced and spot on, and really, if you're like me, you'll have quite a bit of trouble putting this down in order to get other things done. Like, you know, eating and stuff. Hexed is steeped in magic and wrapped in awesome. It really doesn't get much better than this!

sample_reviews.review_text:
I was surprised at how much I enjoyed the second book in this series, given how much flak I've seen it take. This isn't a series that takes itself very seriously, and any expectations to the contrary feel like they would be unrealistic. That said, despite enjoying this book, the plotline didn't feel as important as the first book's did. It felt like the first book was a story, and this one was part of a series. 
 I'm thinking that within the next couple years, Atticus's teaching modern vernacular is going to be painfully embarrassing to read. 
 So, in summation, fun read, love Oberon, and I hope that part 3 goes back to book 1's grandeur, such as it is.

I didn't love the first book, but wanted to give him a second chance. Turns out I couldn't. 
 My problem with this book is that the author has created an anti-hero, that has no redeeming quality for me to cheer. It wouldn't matter if he were selfish and sexist if he also saved people in an interesting way. When I got to the part where the author had invented a new kind of not-zombie that could have just as easily had a way to be cured (because this is all fantasy), I had to give up. Instead of saving an entire nightclub full of people, he chose slaughter of non-monster characters. This follows up the first novel where an innocent non-evil park ranger gets nailed as a bystander and the main character feels no remorse for that beyond how it might get his dog in trouble with the law. 
 Kevin Hearne is a technically adequate writer, with a decent vocabulary but it feels like he is probably writing out his own selfish fantasies to nail goddesses and kill people without reprecussions.

With snark and banter, the Iron Druid chronicles mixes serious moments with baudy humor and a grand sense of fun. Hearne creates a riotous mix of Star Wars quotes and Lord of the Rings and Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy references, with One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest and Shakespeare. Historical eras and pantheons are mixed higgledy-piggledy in a kind of egalitarian irreverence that somehow works. Gotta say, I am looking forward to getting the scoop on Thor from the Atticus/Oberon point-of-view. Meanwhile, a few of my favorite quotes: 
 "Dropping a werewolf into a witch fight is like dropping a tank into a snake pit." 
 "I started to give chase, but I remembered my profound lack of clothes just before I leapt through the window. A naked man pursuing two curvaceous women down the street would probably be misinterpreted by the general public." 
 "In the old days, Celts used to charge into battle naked, wearing nothing but a torc around their necks. I'd fought my share of battles like that--very recently, in fact--but I'd long since found a I could run faster when my goodies weren't flapping around between my legs." 
 In this installment, we learn more of Atticus's history during the WWII era, learn about the aftermath of the battles from the last book, get to hear a lot from Oberon, and see a new side to the nosy neighbor.

The series is underpinned by a neat idea, but it is such a shame that it is so poorly developed. There is some cutesy humour in this one, but nothing to make you laugh. The characters are pretty shallow. 
 The hero is so powerful that the conflict is non-existent. He cannot die. Any challenge is waved off in the manner of schoolyard play. Something like, "they shot me with a death ray but I specially use an anti-death-ray lotion every day. It could hurt my dog, but he dodged. 'I am a good dodger,' Oberon said," would be completely in order for this book. 
 The prose is horrible. There is no tension. No beauty. No complexity. Bland. Feels written by a teenager as a creative writing assignment.

I am completely addicted to this series. First, I need to keep up with the life of Oberon -- I so fell in love with this character that I regularly regret my own dog's inability to have an in depth conversation on some subject

Probably closer to a 3.5 star. There's a fair amount of humor, and some decent action scenes--if you make yourself forget Atticus is under no REAL threat the entire book. I hear people try to compare this series to Dresden, it's not. Mainly because Harry is always punching above his weight against everything he faces. Whereas Atticus is essentially invincible. That aspect of the series takes a level of enjoyment away for me.

This was definitely as entertaining as the first one. The bad witches are evil and demented, and the good witches...well, they arr scary powerful. And, of course, as in the last book, Oberon gets the last word in the book. The last time was about french poodles, and this time was about treats. He's still my favorite character.
Book #2 in the iron druid series.

Also posted on The Procrastinator's Corner 
 Hexed was just as fun as Hounded! Atticus and Oberon were as hilarious as ever. I have to say though, my respect for the hound shot up way higher than Atticus in this book. In Hounded, I thought Oberon thought like a 5-year-old kid. He still did in Hexed sometimes, still demanding sausages and bacon. But most of the time, his intelligence beat that of Atticus. He could handle complex conversations with Atticus and could even come up with jokes that would surely crack you up. 
 In the first half of Hexed, a character we only heard about from Hounded was introduced. A trickster god, Coyote, tricked Atticus into helping him kill a fallen angel who had been causing havoc on a school where one of Coyote's people was studying. In the second half, Atticus was forced to form an agreement with a coven of Polish witches to help annihilate another coven who had become a threat to both the Polish witches and Atticus, as well as to the very few people who were close to him. 
 Just like Hounded, Hexed was also filled with heart-stopping action-packed scenes that would surely challenge your imagination. One of the things I so loved in this series is the abundance of mythologies. In book 1, we met lots of awesome gods and goddesses and strange creatures from different pantheons and here in book 2, we are introduced to more of them. There was also a lot of running and fighting around naked and the gore leveled up as well. 
 The characters were just as hilarious and more clever, and the story itself was both enjoyable and nerve-wracking at the same time. But just like Hounded, one of the drawbacks of Hexed for me was that Atticus seemed to always get his way. There were also the rare times when I felt the tediousness of the plot. Although the events were unpredictable, the results were not. But even though I knew how the fights were going to end, I can't deny that this brought me to the edge of my seat for almost the entire duration of the book. If you're looking for a read that exudes with exhilarating fight scenes and one that would also make you double over with so much laughter, you must pick up this series NOW.

These are not great books. They resemble dorritos. No nutritional value, plenty of empty calories and yet I keep stuffing myself with them. Excellent as an audiobook, I listened to this one while running mostly.

book_b.title: Three Days to Dead (Dreg City, #1)
book_b.user_review:
You may also read my review here: http://www.mybookishways.com/2011/10/... 
 Evangaline Stone is having a bad day. Can you imagine waking up on a morgue slab in someone else's body? This is what happens to Evy,after she's tortured for days and left to die,someone does a reincarnation spell,but unfortunately,it goes wrong,and she ends up in a different body with no sign of the memories of her last few days of life. Evy was a Dreg City bounty hunter,and a crack one at that,before her team was killed and she was framed for murder by her own people. Finding someone to trust is first on Evy's list,so she turns to her Handler,Wyatt,who may hold the key to what actually happened after the death of her friends. With an unheard of,but very possible,alliance between the goblins and the Bloods (vampires) looming,Evy must get to the truth of her death and stop a partnership that could threaten humanity as we know it. 
 All is not what it seems in Dreg City,though. Along with her memory loss,Evy is haunted by possible feelings and memories of her new body's former owner,Chalice Frost. Most noticeably are warm fuzzies for her Handler,Wyatt and the unmistakeable buzz of magic that she's all of a sudden able to feel. When she finally begins regaining memories of her final days,the truth of her death is worse than anything she could possibly have imagined. I really enjoyed getting to know Evy Stone and the Triads! This is another series that I've had on the shelf for a while,waiting to be discovered,and I'm so glad I started it! The author's world building is rich and original,and I liked her twist on vampires,shifters,and trolls,as well as the Fey. Three Days to Dead is quite dark and gritty,yet I really felt a connection to Evy and Wyatt,and was eager to follow them into battle and beyond. At just over 400 pages,Three Days to Dead isn't a short novel,but I blasted through it,eager to get to the next page. This was a great start to a series I'm eager to get caught up with!

sample_reviews.review_text:
I could have just not been in the mood for this type of book. I think i just came off too many 5 star books in a row and so this had a lot to prove. 
 This was one of the most boring books i have ever read in my life. to put that in perspective let me also add that 99% of the book was an action sequence. I use the term action loosely because it was actually more like a written version of Lord of the Rings. There was a lot of walking to destinations but nothing ever happened. When you got to the end it was the equivalent of dropping the ring in the volcano. 
 no thanks.

I really enjoyed the premise, but I wish there had been more character development. And I felt frustrated the entire time because absolutely nothing the main character did worked out for her. I just wanted to slap someone. All of the plot developments were made by other people.
Could not get into this book.
It was just so bad, and I had such High hopes.....but no just no. Never wanted a book to end so much.

Book #20 of 2012 
 Interesting concept and book. But it did leave me wondering why the rest of the series will be like?

Nuh-uh! This book is not very good at all. Evy is illogical and annoying (and the story of her death and torture and how she handles it? Not plausible. Just gory and stupid.) and gets on my nerves constantly. The plot is rather weak and doesn't justify a book this thick, the storytelling is all over the place... and there aren't even any great co-characters to root for. I am not impressed and won't read more from this author. Too bad. I had hopes for this book. 
 Hardly makes it to 11/2 stars.

Killing the main character off is always a good indicator of how the book will go. In this case, the book went very well as it was fast paced and revolving around who the character's killer is. Overall, a long read but worth it.

While Meding has created an interesting world in this book, I found the characters flat and unappealing. I never bonded with Evy, and I found I couldn't rejoice in her success or failure--she was too much like every other kick-butt urban fantasy girl. 
 Also, for someone that has only three days to live, she seemed to spend way too much time sleeping. It would seem to me that the better choice would be to pound espressos with a Red Bull chaser. But that's one of the problems with this book. Having established a three day deadline (in the strictest sense of the word!), Meding spends most of the book trying to find ways to pass time without advancing the plot too much. 
 Overall, this book was very much a "meh."
Yeah, well, it had potential, and I didn't HATE it...I just didn't really care for it.

It started like good urban fantasy book. The heroine was likeable, plot was interesting and there was good mystery. There also was some humor in the beginning. 
 But the more I was reading, the more depressing this book was becoming. Soon all the good thing that were in the beginning became grim and boring. 
 I also didn't like that author put in the story every mystical creature, that ever were mentioned in mythology. There were shape shifters, vampires, goblins, gremlins, gargoyles and so on.... It was confusing. And I couldn't stop wonder, how only 30 humans (10 triads) managed to keep this creatures existent from the rest of humanity? 
 I couldn't get myself finish the book. Nothing interesting there.

reference_books.title: His Majesty's Dragon (Temeraire, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I decided to give this book a try because of Orson Scott Card's excellent review. I can't say it any better than he did; if you haven't read it, I highly recommend it: 
 http://www.hatrack.com/osc/reviews/ev... 
 I've loved C.S. Forester's Hornblower books since I discovered them back in the late 70's. I've never found another historical fiction, or fiction series, to rival them - until now. The excellent plotting, the first-rate story, finely-drawn characters that make you care about them, painstaking (but not obtrusive) attention to subtle nuances of British naval and societal traditions during the Napoleonic wars, action that'll have you on the edge of your seat - it's all there and a joy to read. Plus dragons, and Ms. Novik weaves them so deftly into the fabric of the stories that you don't feel like you're reading a dragon story, you're reading a great story that happens to have dragons in it. 
 I can't recommend this book highly enough. It's been a while since it's been such an unalloyed pleasure to read through a book of this caliber. I'm looking forward eagerly to reading the other books in the series. 
 Well done, Ms. Novik.

reference_books.title: I Shall Wear Midnight (Discworld, #38; Tiffany Aching, #4)
reference_books.review_text:
Terry Pratchett's latest is excellent. Tiffany Aching is 15 (16?) now, and he very deftly balances her growth in knowledge and power as a witch, her heavy responsibilities to the community she serves, her 16-year-old longings to be just a "normal" person, and her experiences with young love. 
 And of course it's laugh-out-loud funny as always. The further adventures of the Nac Mac Feegle are particularly good. And for those who follows Terry's Discworld series, you'll be gratified to find that most of the witch characters in his previous novels turn up in this one! 
 After Terry's last novel, I was beginning to think that his advancing Alzheimer's was affecting his ability to write, but this book shows he's just as sharp as ever. 
 Highly recommended.

reference_books.title: Ross Poldark (Poldark, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Outstanding historical fiction. I'm looking forward to reading all the rest of the books in this fine series. Highly recommended.

reference_books.title: The Hundred-Foot Journey
reference_books.review_text:
Meh. Don't bother reading the book, watch the movie instead - it's much better. 
 Warning: don't read this book if you're expecting the same warm, funny, romantic story as the movie. Because the only things the book and movie have in common are the names of the characters and the very broad outlines of the story. This book is about the career of a middle-class Muslim lad from his boyhood in Mumbai to his triumphant creation of a three-star haute-cuisine restaurant in Paris. That's it. No romance, not much humor, mostly a pedestrian "boy makes good" story. I wish I could un-read this and read something better instead. 
 This was one of the few incidences of a movie made from a book where the movie is lots better. Rather disappointing, really.

reference_books.title: Ready Player One
reference_books.review_text:
Sorry, couldn't finish this one. Aside from the nihilistic doom-and-gloom "oh my gosh the whole world is gonna end up just like the Road Warrior" quick-hand-me-the-gaspipe tone, once the protagonist found the virtual key to unlock the book's version of the Chamber of Secrets, it turned into a kind of virtual "Tron". Been there, done that, multiple times. 
 Yawn. This one's in the bag for the local paperback reseller.

book_a.title: Master and Commander (Aubrey & Maturin, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Everyone recommended this to me as the heir apparent to C. S. Forester's Hornblower series. Epic fail. 
 Historically accurate? I suppose. Coherent, interesting plot? Not particularly. Characters I could care about? Zilch. 
 Sorry, but this book was boring. 
 Want to read a series of first-rate historical fiction books about the Napoleonic era, with some excellent fantasy thrown in? Read Naomi Novik's Temeraire series. For me, they're the true heirs to the Hornblower epic.

sample_reviews.review_text: I'm just not the sea faring man type, otherwise I'm sure its a great book.
liked
Just can't get through it. Aubrey has almost no sympathetic qualities. I hope that the French mock him, the Dutch fleece him, the Spanish thumbscrew him, and the Brits throw him in Newgate.

I struggled a bit with this first book in the Aubrey/Maturin series. Listening to the recorded book by Patrick Tull, I found it hard to follow while driving in the car. While I appreciated the historical details and the witty dialogue, I found it next to impossible to keep track of any plot. So I just kind of let it wash over me, and probably have a good sense of the overall picture. But now I need to go back and read the book, and then I think more of the intricacies will fall into place. Like Jane Austen, this will probably grow on me with repeated exposure. I have heard that the first book is a bit different and a bit more difficult than the rest of the series. So I have promised myself to give it at least three books... 
 Description: Master and Commander introduces Royal Navy Lieutenant Jack Aubrey and his shipboard surgeon, Stephen Maturin. Overweight, too ambitious for promotion and dangerously prone to plunder, Aubrey is an extravagant, yet likeable character. Maturin, the more cultivated of the pair, would feel right at home in a novel by Jane Austen. O'Brian writes not only of the duels, the shipboard terrors and spectacular broadsides, but includes the day-to-day experiences of his characters. He is as much concerned with these men's land-bound exploits as he is with their grander, grimmer battles at sea.

I found this in my junior high library, but it's more for high school students (if not adults)
Second time through this great opening volume--going all the way this time.
Couldn't really get into it

Great book. He really did his research on how a wooden war ship in the British Navy would have functioned. Nice technical stuff. The characters are fairly enjoyable; although, I think he develops them more further on in the series. 
 The ending was a let-down, but still left me wanting to read the next book.

Finally! I finally finished reading this book! It's excellent, but the first few chapters (especially Chapter 2) really needs willpower to go through - the nautical lingo is heavy for those who don't understand it.

I feel bad for giving this book one star since I know so many people love it, and that always leaves me with the impression that I'm just missing something. However, I found the story and dialogue improbable; the writing and plot dry; and even though I stuck through with it all the way to the end, I just couldn't get into this book. 
 I will say that the language and nautical terms didn't bother me as much as it seems they did many reviewers, but I still didn't find anything in this book that made my time listening to it worthwhile.

book_b.title: The House of Silk
book_b.user_review: First-rate canonical Sherlock Holmes thriller. I enjoyed this more than any other S.H. novel I've read in the past few years. Great story, and the character interaction between Holmes and Watson is outstanding. Highly recommended for S.H. fans.

sample_reviews.review_text: I have always been skeptical about reading a Sherlock Holmes novel that was not written by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, but when a friend let me have this book because she did not think she would have time to read it, I decided to give it a try. This is the first Holmes novel I have read outside of those originally written and I would have to say that Anthony Horowitz does a great job in presenting Holmes and Dr. Watson in a manner similar to that of Sir Conan Doyle. The subject matter is a bit sensitive, but I still thought that it was spectacular.

Finally, FINALLY a Sherlock Holmes story NOT written by Arthur Conan Doyle that didn't make me cringe. (Laurie R. King aside, most of the "new" Holmes stories make me either cringe or scream or cry or sometimes all three. What can I say, I'm a Holmes purist.) But this one from Anthony Horowitz (of Alex Rider fame) was pure delicious. He captures Conan Doyle's style perfectly and CLEARLY did his research. There are numerous reference to the original stories and he GETS THEM ALL RIGHT!!! I'm cheering, and probably Arthur Conan Doyle is somewhere smiling in the Great Beyond. Nice work, Mr. Horowitz!!
But DO NOT WASTE your time. It is Extremely Vulgar as it goes on. Certainly not for children or people who like Christie Novels

Four stars for doing what it sets out to do -- presenting a new Holmes novel, complete with twists and clues and foggy London streets -- well. Horowitz weaves two mysteries together into a sinister plot, and while I'm pleased to report that I figured out a few of the clues, the final reveal was a complete surprise. Despite some unnecessary repetition (okay, we understand the "lamentable" truth of Holmes' heroin habit) it's a quick read, great for a dark winter's night.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I will have to go back and write more at somepoint, but here is why I think this is a BAD BOOK (and I was so excited!!) 
 - Watson is rambling and nonsensical (I don't care if he's old, gah) 
 - Holmes misses stuff so obvious that I get it immediately and didn't even realise that he did (since there is NO WAY he could!) 
 - Moriarity (not named, but obvious) is either so clever that he tries to get Watson in trouble along with Holmes OR does his big crazy thing talking to Watson and it would NEVER WORK! He is WAY way way way waaaAAAAaay too smart for that crap. 
 - There are lots of places where Horowitz used Watson to apologise for what Doyle wrote. The heck? 
 - The "big thing" that will destroy British society...isn't all that big when you know about Victorian culture. it is a bad thing, but it wouldn't tear anything apart. 
 Why are these things so egregious? 
 - Horowitz is a great writer, it seems that this is just fluff. 
 - He obviously knows his Holmes...why do this? 
 - It's the FIRST APPROVED sequel (approved by the estate!) 
 - It's not FUN!

I enjoyed this book a lot - similar to originals and yet I could picture Benedict Cumberbatch as I was reading. 
 Definitely worth your time. Enjoy!

The characters, despite being engrained in our culture, were not fully fleshed in this book. I read the Conan Doyle books decades ago but this book did conjure up some of the feeling of those books as well as I can remember. As far as the plot goes, I guessed what the House of Silk was and where it was located pretty early on. Watson was a little annoying and there seemed to be too much social commentary to be a book written in the late 1800s. Also Sherlock wasn't in it nearly as much as I thought he would be. 
 I won't be reading any more of these.
sherlock holmes mystery. not impressed.

3.5 
 This series is very well done; the characters are true to form, the writing style reminiscent of Conan Doyle, and the plot well-woven. 
 The rating is probably due in part to the fact that I was listening to an audiobook. Also, while this was very well-done and well-written, I didn't enjoy it nearly as much as I enjoyed Moriarty.
This book will make you want to read all the rest of Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes stories while impatiently waiting for Anthony Horowitz to write another one.

reference_books.title: City of Bones (The Mortal Instruments, #1)
reference_books.review_text: A student recommended this. Really grabbed me from the start; am anxious to read the second book. My first (at least in recent memory) book dealing with nephilim, children of man and angel. Excellent series for kids who like to struggle between good and evil.

reference_books.title: Bones Never Lie (Temperance Brennan, #17)
reference_books.review_text:
From the start, Reichs grabbed my attention. I have read and enjoyed all the Bones books and this was no exception. I enjoy her writing style and plot development. That said, this one was a bit predictable, and it's easy to spot the killer and victim early on; however, even knowing what was coming, I enjoyed the read. 
 ***SPOILERS*** 
 I found it odd that Temp did not immediately recognize the cat sitter as a potential victim. She knew the killer was focused on her and in Charlotte, she had misgivings about the doctor being the killer, and the girl fit the type. Reichs does mention that the girl wears hats all the time. If this is supposed to be the reason why Temp doesn't recognize her as the killer's type, it's not made clear. I would have enjoyed it more if the climax weren't so obvious, but it's still a fun read.

reference_books.title: Untraceable (The Nature of Grace, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
As an avid hiker / backpacker, I really wanted to love this book. I applaud the author for focusing on a female character who loves the outdoors and activities normally associated with male characters, and for her attention to a horrific situation that exists in North Carolina. 
 For me, there were a few fundamental flaws in the novel that detracted from the story. 
 First, Grace appears to be a strong, outdoor-smart young woman. But as I read, she seemed like two very different characters depending on the moment. One minute she was standing her ground against a black bear, and the next she was a wishy-washy, girly-girl who didn't know what end of a tree pointed up. The inconsistencies in her characterization really detracted from the overall feel of the book for me. I wanted her to be a tough, head-strong young woman from beginning to end. 
 Second, as a backpacker I often found the survival / camping advice or actions of the character to be, well, just wrong. One example, Grace talks about the importance of building a fire and its uplifting feel. Well, in a dire survival situation, a fire is important, but most back country campers rarely build a fire. In the novel, Grace is trying to be inconspicuous, she's not injured, and it's a warm summer night. Yet, she builds a fire that is unnecessary and could draw attention to her. Another instance is when she decides to build a lean-to. She decides to hammer in stakes with a rock - in the woods - when she is being hunted by killers. Not a good idea. 
 Another small issue was the dialogue of the characters. In the beginning of the novel, some of the dialogue seemed very unrealistic. Kids just don't use antiquated expressions. 
 Overall, I thing the author has what could be an awesome book with some rewrites and a little more research. In it's current state, I am hesitant to recommend it.

reference_books.title: The Grimm Legacy (The Grimm Legacy, #1)
reference_books.review_text: A wonderful journey. I thoroughly enjoyed this story. More often than not, I questioned my judgment about the characters; the characterization was very well done. Magic, fairy tales and a modern day mystery. Who is stealing the items from the Grimm Collection and how are they doing it?

reference_books.title: Stitching Snow
reference_books.review_text:
Fans of the Lunar Chronicles may like this title. 
 Essie is working as a robot tech in a mining town on a miserable planet when a space craft crashes near town. She assists the injured passenger, but is cautious. Essie has a secret and will do anything to hide it. Dane is looking for someone, and Essie may just be the girl he's looking for. 
 Overall this was entertaining - lots of action and a decent plot. I really enjoyed it up until the end. 
 *** SPOILER ALERT *** 
 The end kind of spoiled the book for me. It was decently done up until the "wrap everything in a nice bow" ending. 
 Dane losing his leg was glossed over as no big deal; much more should have been done with this - at least a little angst and struggle over it. And let's face it, the bad guys fell just a bit too easily, everyone accepted Snow as their leader with no questions asked, and Dane as her fiancee even though for years they had been wary of Dane's people.

book_a.title: Clockwork Angel (The Infernal Devices, #1)
book_a.user_review: This is the prequel series to the Mortal Instruments. This one is steampunk meets Nephilim - quite an interesting mix! If you enjoyed the Mortal Instruments, this is a must read.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I've been sitting here for the past 15 minutes trying to write a review that isn't "OMG, AWESOME! PREORDER IT NOW!" I think Clockwork Angel has fried my brain. 
 It's a prequel to The Mortal Instruments series, but no, you don't need to have read those to read this (although if you haven't, what are you waiting for?!). 
 I'm not going to give any plot synopsis or spoilers, because I think it's good to enter this new series with as little advance knowledge as possible and learn about what's going on as Tessa does. There is a little crossover with the Mortal Instruments series but again, you don't need to read those books first. 
 If Clockwork Angel is any indication, I'm going to like these books even more than TMI, and that's a bold statement because I LOVED those books. :) 
 Book 2 will come out in September 2011.

Well, not horrible but - can't say I liked it. Some of it was actually good, but the periodic setting really didn't do it for me, and I had really other expectations from the love story as well.. I it started well and some of the book had good suspence, but really not all of it.

** spoiler alert ** 
 First off, im a huge Cassandra Clare fan! I absoluley loved The Mortal Instruments series and was excited to jump into this one! CLOCKWORK ANGEL was really good! I liked the humor and mystery the story had. There was a warm and happy feeling I got from the Institute and Jem saying how they were all one big family. Tessa began to become part of the family and I loved seeing that! For the first book it was good! I did enjoy City of Bones better. I know with fisry books its hard beacuse its developing a story, so i do hope/ and belive that they will get better; or the second book will be. 
 They story opens up with Tessa on the boat waiting for her brother. This scene was somewhat slow but I like how it gave us time and a backstory to get to know Tessa. As soon as she meet the Dark Sisters I knew something bad was about to take place. The "Pandemonuim Club" sighn was just icing on the cake for trouble. (If yove read THE MORTAL INSTRUMENTS, you know the Pandemonium can be the source for all kinds of trouble). Cassie did great of jumping right into the story. I thought it would be really drawn out before she meet the Shadowhunters but not at all. Tessa is immediatley pulled into the Shadowworld; which all we shadowhunters love very much. 
 From the moment Tessa arrived at the Institute and meet the gorgeuos dark haired William Herondale, I knew I was in for a spin. Sarcasm, good looks, and hard walls to break down; nothing you wouldnt expect from a Herondale. I loved how much Will reminded me of Jace. I instantley fell for him. Then we meet Jem, the caring, loving, and handsom Shadowhunter; who can't help but charm you. Two amazing, heart pulling shadowhunters? BY THE ANGEL! 
 Will or Jem. The love triangle immediatley took off and I admire Cassie for that. The story itself, the realtionship of the charecters; its destinded to be a trio. I love the banter between all three! Will's sarcasm, Jem's comedic undertone, and Tessa feircness; all together was one wild group! I look forward to the rest of their banter in later books. 
 I was so shocked when you found out that The Magister was Mortmain. THE MUNDIE!?! The minute Nathan got down on his knees, I wanted to throw the book! I didnt hate Nathan, but i didnt love him either. The way he handed Tessa over, and just didnt care about here really ticked me off. The Magister isnt all that great either. I cant wait to see them gone. Hopefully some but-kick from our adorded shadowhunters. 
 I honeslty can say i really enjoyed this book! Hats of the Cassie for another great Shadowhunter story! I cant wait to start book 2! And hey, arent all the stories true? ;)
I just don't like her books, I keep wanting to look away from the page, it's like they repel me or something.

2013 Review: 
 this book was AMAZING!!! i loved it SOOOOOO much!! It got me into the Shadowhunter world :3 I can keep reading this book and it'll never get old. Will, Jem, Gabe all the guys are so perfect. As well as the girls! 
 2016: 
 Cringing a bit at what I wrote ^^ 
 But what I said was true. The way Cassie wrote the characters and the way Will Herondale is so mysterious, its so beautiful. I could read this book over, and over again and I wouldn't get tired of it. I remember walking into Walmart towards the books and I found Will, on the cover, attractive. So I read the back then bought the book. I love books that take place in the 1800's. I don't know why, but the way they spoke and dressed made me happy. I was happy to see that Tessa was an american girl who traveled to London to see her brother. 
 The way Cassandra writes, it's beautiful. I say this in all the reviews I've done about her books 
 I recommend reading TID before TMI, that is what I did. I didn't know about City of Bones until I heard it was coming out into a movie, and when I was reading one of the TID. Or you can read them in the order they came out.

I'd read almost all of the books in The Mortal Instruments (TMI), except for the last book, City of Heavenly Fire, which is now long overdue since I cannot remember some scenes in the series. Anyway, I read this book because soon enough it will be a TV series, that a true Shadowhunter should not be missed. 
 Moving forward, for the review; I could neither say that this first book of The Infernal Devices (TID) was bad nor good. But it clearly did not blow me away like those I read in the comments and reviews; it was very average in every way. Though I must admit, this book was way better than the City of Bones. And I couldn't help but see similarities between them - a spy inside the institute, arrogant and annoying male leads, mysterious and unknown past, father issues and whatnot. And I was a bit confused about the terminologies and what they do (iratze, seraph blades, etc.) in this book, yet Clare described everything more clearly than her debut novel. 
 Additionally, the way Cassandra Clare wrote this story was very elegant. Not sure if it had something do with the Victorian settings, but regardless she still richly created a very vivid era. London in 1900s was dark and gloomy and, well, rainy. Still, I found the period setting along with Tess' abilities more interesting. (Surprisingly, London in 1900s was very gloomy and dark and rainy which was far from what I imagined! But anyway I don't really know London since I've never been there. LOL.) 
 I rated it two stars because the story was a bit dragging. Too much history, too much talking and recon. For me, it went too long. There were parts that I skipped because I could not fathom a thing Clare said. 
 Then again, there were still good things in the story. The kickass action scenes and the twist, in the end, were oh so awesome. I liked Tessa and her power to Change and how she can touch their minds, that's impressive. Yes, Clare's strategy on how to keep us going by concealing the truth about their past and backgrounds still made me want to read the second up to the last book. Also, I want to know who she ends up with. Don't we all want to? 
 So, all in all, the plot was not so bad at all. If Clare could make the narrations and storytelling short, and stop having so much drama about their past then it'll be better. 
 "One must always be careful with books and what is inside them, for words have the power to change us."

I absolutely loved this book! We get a new bit of the Shadowhunter world, and a bit of a peek into Magnus Bane's past. I actually love that he was in this book, because it takes that tie and familiarity from TMI into this new series. 
 I didn't catch the plot twists ahead of time, which was really nice. I did have one tiny bit of an issue. Will sounded a lot like Jace. It was a little distracting in the beginning, but after his character started building a bit it got a lot better. 
 I can't wait to pick up book 2! Picking up Clockwork Prince now!

** spoiler alert ** 
 2/19/2011 - So, I was a little worried about starting this book. I am deeply, deeply in lust with Cassandra Clare's Mortal Instruments series and I was afraid this book wouldn't measure up to the high standards I have set for this particular author. I am quite happy to find out that my fears were for nothing because this book is fantastic. 
 This is set in the universe of the Mortal Instruments series but is set in Victorian England and the Institute in London. The book centers around Tessa an American fresh off the boat from New York. She is searching for her brother and is taken in by some rather deplorable characters but thankfully is saved by members of the London Institute, specifically Will Herondale. 
 Throughout the book Tessa is busy trying to figure out why the bad guys want her and what they have done to her brother. She is also trying to figure out her romantic feelings towards Will and Will's best friend Jem Carstairs. On top of which is her budding new power and the knowledge that she isn't quite as human as she has been led to believe. 
 The best thing about this whole book is how the author always leaves you guessing. Never quite sure what is going to happen or what the characters' exact meanings are. I love how well developed all of the characters are and how smoothly they interact with one another. I find that as much as Jace pissed me of in City of Bones it is nothing compared to the irritating abilities of Will. I can't imagine coming across someone who was so rude to everyone all the time, no matter what his past was like. 
 I was thrilled to see Magnus Bane again. I'd kind of forgotton that he was rather old and would be appearing in this book. I also liked hearing references to families that are very important in the Mortal Insturments books. 
 I'm curious to see what happens with Tessa's brother Nathaniel. I didn't like him from the get go and I couldn't believe that Tessa kept protecting him. I have a sister and if she did even part of those things I would have completely cut her out of my life. I hope in the next book Tessa doesn't forget how many times her terrible brother has betrayed her. 
 I find that Jessamine is annoying and I'm wondering if she has any redeemable qualities. I can't figure out what part she has to play in this story? She doesn't really lend anything to the story and I don't think anyone would miss her when she's gone. I guess we'll just have to wait and see. 
 I'm very glad that the Clave decided not to kick Tessa out because who knows what would have happened to her if they had. Plus I want to see what happens with her and Will, although I'm secretly rooting for Jem. 
 Great story, great characters, great book. I'm really looking forward to the next book and am anxiously awaiting it's release.

This was just... meh. I'm not really sure why I read this, because I wasn't too crazy about the Mortal Instruments trilogy. But, whatever, I borrowed from the library, so at least all that I've wasted is time. 
 Clockwork Angel starts with Tessa on her way to London to stay with her brother, because her aunt just died, and her parents passed away when she was young. However, dun dun dunnnnnn, she is met by two strange women who say they were sent by her brother. These women are evil :O And it turns out that Tessa has strange powers and a questionable lineage :O (Clary anyone?) So, she is held captive by them for a while and is told that she is going to be given to the ominous Magister, when suddenly, she is rescued by two Shadowhunters! Yay! One of them is the completely dreamy super mega gorgeous totally ripped Jace, I mean.... wait, what was his name again? ***this is a side thought. I finished the book two days ago and I can't remember the characters' names. Ok. Nate is her brother, Jem is the sweet one, Charlotte is the head of the institute..... Ok. For all intents and purposes, this male character is the 1800s version of Jace, so we shall continue to call him Jace, because, evidently, it is too much pressure for Cassandra Clare to come up with a whole new set of characters.*** 
 Anyways, Tessa is rescued by the Shadowhunters and taken to the institute, where they are trying to figure out what evil scheme the Magister is up to. There are evil robots involved. Seriously. Evil robots. And of course, this would not be Cassandra Clare if the main character, Tessa, did not have two guys developing feelings for her. The first is the typical Jace. He is gorgeous and wonderful and oftentimes, he acts like an ass, but every now and then, there is a glimpse of a good person under that callous exterior. The second is the sweet and caring Jem, who is patient and good and, like almost every fictional character in the world, he has a special place that he likes to go when he wants to think or relax, and he takes Tessa there to be super cute. 
 And you know, just for once, I would like the main girl to pick the healthy relationship. I mean, seriously, is it that hard? Is it really so impossible for a fictional girl to choose the guy that isn't a jerk? To pick the one that is honest and doesn't jump back and forth between personalities like a mental patient.... Or even if Tessa decided that she is really overwhelmed right now, and she is vulnerable, and it isn't right for her to be jumping into a relationship with someone that she doesn't know. That would be ok too, but an author like Cassandra Clare would never have the guts to do that, because she knows that the majority of her fanbase comes from girls that just cannot wait to whip out their cell phones and tweet of fb status that they are "TEAM _________" 
 I never really intended for this to become a rant, so I think that I'm going to stop now, but I'm just getting kind of frustrated. One more thing though; the twist at the end could be seen from about a quarter into the book. Just saying.

This book was unbelievably good. I can't wait to read everything else she's written. 
 Pros: Great writing. Obviously talented writer. Good characters, and great character development. Great world building, I plan to read the entire series after this. 
 Cons: The library has the second book checked out and reserved for the next two months...so I'm going to have to wait a little while to get my next fix. I also suffered from major 'book hangover', which made it almost impossible to start any other book because I was so focused on getting my next Cassandra Clare fix. 
 I'm not ashamed to admit this: The writing on this was so good I had to take a break and go edit my own W.I.P. while reading. Because I learned a lot about the writing craft just from reading this book.

book_b.title: Dead City (Dead World, #1)
book_b.user_review: While this was a decently written novel, it was so typical, I didn't really love it. Take everything that happens in any typical zombie movie or novel, and it happens in this one in the exact order you expect it to happen. There wasn't enough about this book that was original to make it exciting. I was also disappointed with the ending. There was no explanation of how the zombies were contained/controlled; the survivors just starting going back to their lives.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This is probably one of the worst horror book that I have read. I understand that this is Joe McKinney's first novel and that he won an award in the third book for this series but this novel just sucks. There is no real purpose for the protagonist that it felt like it had been a mindless journey with a bland character who just dont know what he's doing. 
 CONTAINS SPOILER: 
 It's a story about a cop, Eddie. This guy is suppose to be a cop but he spent the entire time acting as though he didnt have any training at all. Sure, this novel really is "action-packed" if you want things like: 
 "We're surrounded." 
 "Let's get out of here." 
 "Where did they come from?" 
 and shooting the zombies over and over again. 
 He always said that he's "supposed to be looking for his family" but he wasted a lot of time reminiscing, getting a car, and then losing that car because of a really stupid thing, then the cycle of his find-a-car journey will start again.

Finally I am done with this. 
 A generic zombie book about a generic infection.

Zombies in Texas! It's like a dream come true! 
 Update: It felt like it was set more in any city, rather than my hometown. The locality was felt through the descriptions of, say, "west side barrio". It came close to feeling written-through-Google-Map. I was interested after several chapters.
Zombie apocalypse as told by Jack Webb from Dragnet. Boring. "Just the facts mam."

Not the greatest novel in the horror subgenre of zombie fiction. Plot revolves around a cop who, while on night patrol, begins to witness a zombie plague start to grow around him within his city. It has it's moments of suspense, manages to pull some tension, but it reads like a throw away George Romero script. For hard core zombie fans only, while to others who like a flesh eating tale every now & then, it's a book that will make you say: "been there, done that." 
 Best part of the book is the cop's partner who joins him in fighting off the zombie horde without a care in helping others. His selfishness provides moments where the main character has to decide should he stand by his brother of the badge or get rid of him to protect the helpless they come across. There are sequels & I'll probably read them.
2.5 stars. The character development is poor. Every female character (there are only 3 who speak) are all idiots. But it was a fun read.

Completely enjoyed this book. I stayed up late into the night to finish it because I did not want to put it down. 
 I enjoyed the fact that the author even made us think about the ethical side of zombies. What if zombies were living human beings who had caught a virus and turned into cannibalistic killers? That is the question that we are left to consider after reading this book. 
 Over all a great read and I am really looking forward to more books by this author.

Eddie Hudson is a police officer in San Antonio dealing with something his years of training and time on the streets could never prepare him for. In this story by Joe McKinney we are thrust into Eddie's world as he is just discovering that the hurricanes to the south that ravaged Houston have uncovered some sort of virus that causes the dead to walk. 
 The story is told in first person as Eddie relates the challenges he faces in not only trying to get back to his wife and infant son but just survive as he battles through the night just trying to deal with and comprehend the onslaught of the living dead that want to tear him and every other living soul to pieces. 
 This is a very fast paced read and the gore is quite vivid. This book, more so than many others I have read in the genre, lends itself to becoming a movie because we smoothly cut from one action sequence to the next and the images are bright, raw, and easy to see in your mind. At a rapid fire pace we are taken from scene to scene and Eddie is joined by different secondary characters who are detailed but never overshadow him or his goal to save his family. 
 The book strikes the right chord for a story told in first person form. We are drawn into Eddie's world and the emotions he is feeling. From the sense of helplessness he has with one co-worker who is bitten and dying to exasperation with another who seems to be almost unphased by this incredible disaster. 
 Perhaps some of the secondary characters are not tremendously complex but given what type of story this is their depth is more than adequate. We do get some nice touches, such as a small part of the story where Eddie faces off against another cop whose father (also a cop) has been turned into a zombie. The son not only refuses to kill his father, he is willing to fight off Eddie to protect someone who means so much to him. Elements such as this make zombie stories so incredibly intense for me. The author understands some of the genuine terror we feel towards zombies is because they are simply not just alien monsters, they are us. They are our families, our friends. 
 While the ending of the books slows things down to an abrupt halt I cannot say it did not necessarily work here. Certainly the author could have kept the breakneck pace until the very end but at least in this way we are granted a complete conclusion to this story, for better or for worse. 
 If this is in fact Joe McKinney's first book as some of the other reviewers have mentioned I have to say it is certainly an auspicious start to what I hope will be a long and exciting career. This was a good and fun read and I look forward to more to come from this author.

Fairly standard as far as zombie books go, Dead City is nothing if not an entertaining read. I sat down with this one to celebrate the close of my semester and ended up reading it all in one sitting. The book jumps straight into the action and stays one contnuous action sequence throughout. Beyond being fairly predictable, the book wraps up way too easily and with no real explaination. The real drama of the book is the personal story of the main character, but it could have benefitted from more detail to the conclusion of the zombie epidemic.

Wow. 3 of the last books I've read have all been 1 star ones. And each one surprised me at that fact. Especially this one. I've read this author before and liked his books. Looks like a TON of people love this book, including my brother, buuut... 
 Maybe I'm reading too much GOOD zombie novels that the bad ones are more apparent? Following up Girl With All the Gifts and a chain of Maberry with this one, probably didn't help it. But ehh...I just DID not see it. 
 I judge zombie novels on a few criteria, let's see how it ranks: 
 1) Military turning on populace. 
 Nope. Military never even showed up which was weird. Even with the disaster in Houston, they don't have a spare San Antonio National Guard? So a big fail for the military. 
 2) Saddled with plucky child. 
 Well, he gets to the baby at the end. Second book in the row with exact same incident with a newborn baby. So far no books have done what I would do with an infant in zombie invasion: would go right into a cat carrier. 
 As for being weighed down with people or dead weight, not really a problem in this book. More on that later. 
 3) Criminals taking over. 
 No time for that. This book takes place in the course of an evening--time is VERY hard to judge in this book, almost impossible actually--but probably over the course of 6 hours. That short of a time frame plus EXTREMELY repetitive idiotic actions made this book feel slim, which is odd--I know McKinney can do better. 
 4) Terrible goverment response. 
 Oh My God. I harp on bad cops a lot in zombie books--because usually authority figures go evil pretty quickly but this is the first book I've read where the main character is an evil cop. And I don't think it was intended to be read that way which is the disturbing thing about it. 
 There's also a casual misogyny nicely woven throughout too which is distracting. Both are serious accusations but I think can be handled at same time: 
 Incident A of Bad Cop/Bad Man: 2 Hours or So after first call comes in about a bunch of drunks, world apparently has gone to total hell. Mostly slow zombies, a few fast ones. I kind of wondered how there were so many zombies between the first "drunks on street" to "complete meltdown" 2 hours later, when he's carrying around a cop who has been bitten (well he makes the nervous Mexican gardeners carry his cop buddy at gunpoint), the cop turns. Now maybe some people turn RIGHT away, others turn slowly, but with the hospital ward in the church, it seems more of the slow burn kind. 
 But ok, I'll ignore the chronology (he states at the start his shift is 3 and that school just let out--so guessing outbreak at 4ish/5ish maybe?--but who the fuck knows because there were HUNDREDS of zombies for some reason in the locked school he stumbles into). Shocked, all his friends dead, gruesomeness all around, he stumbles into his old wisecrackin' partner. They spy an obese zombie coming towards them: 
 "Is she wearing a thong?" Marcus said, still laughing. "God, that is the most obscene thing I have seen all night." 
 "Shut up, Marcus." 
 ..."God, she's really fat." 
 "Forget about her, Marcus. Let's get going." 
 "Hold on, would you? I mean, look at that, I didn't know they made thongs that big...." 
 This goes on for 20+ more paragraphs. Four pages. 
 Now I get how people trapped on a roof surrounded by zombies like 3 years into the apocalypse can be cavalier about the zombies below. But this is not just asshattery of highest degree but also dumb, because in the four pages of laughing at her, she gets close enough to where they have to waste a bullet on her and almost messes up their getaway. 
 And these are also supposed to be the fine boys in blue. 
 Evidence B: Bad Cop/Bad Man 
 After he forces the gardeners and school teacher to drag his vomiting-black-grossness-moments-from-turning cop pal (horrible idea) to the firestation off the beaten path (fantastic idea). Eddie (the main character) finds a cell phone. Hooray! He calls his nag of a wife--so far all women have been scolds, nags, or evil ex-wives who hopefully are dead so no more alimony. Wife answers, they get cut off. He breaks the only working phone out of anger. Such a dick move. Maybe the dying cop in the next room would want to try and call his wife. Maybe the gardeners have loved ones they would like to call. Maybe try back in 5 minutes? Or you know, break it. When the others are understandably pissed about it, our hero "sat down in the commander's chair and simmered in rage." 
 But then, he and the school teacher decide to flee the firestation to get to his wife & baby, he hears gunshots, goes off to investigate (school teacher bounces which was best move anyone makes in the book), and through a series of mishaps where he discovers wife & baby booked it, finds his old partner. They decide to check out police HQ (also smart, though every cop inside a fool I guess because somehow they all are 100% zombies). They destroy a huge amount of cars it seems in the process of book. If they're not running through crowds of zombies while giggling, they are off to find another car to rinse/repeat. 
 Because of the cavalier and snotty attitude, it's hard to find much sympathy with the heroes. They finally find some evidence of civilization in the presence of a news reporter, a doctor from the hospital and like 70 people. Unfortunately, these people also have a bunch of bitten folks not tied down, even though they all know what happens. They escape with the leggy blonde reporter whom his friend has eyes on. When they go to push the car out of the way that's blocking the road, she somehow gets ripped to shreads inside the car by a crowd of ninja zombies. 
 Here's how this character's death is handled, her severed leg still in the backseat. "I'll pull over so we can get rid of it, I said." 
 "No," he said, and sat back down. "Don't worry about it. We're not going to have this car very much longer. Downtown's only two exits away." 
 "Okay," I said. "If you're sure." 
 "I'm sure," he said. "A pity, though. She really did have great legs." 
 There are other shitty moments. When he meets an angry black man and reminisces how before the zombie apocalypse he would put someone in the hospital for a look like that. (Really?) Then it turns out angry guy's mother just got killed by a zombie cop. 
 Just a big old eh. So besides the main characters being people I actively disliked, fairly routine plot of "trying to fight out of city", soooo many zombies--swarms always upon him, no matter where, abandoned warehouse, wooded areas?--even the characters say it doesn't make sense. 
 Hopefully the other books are better. I might try one more.
