reference_books.title: Twisted (Intertwined, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 So I suffered through this entire book and the one before it, just to find out that we're going back to the beginning. Course, I'm assuming that Aden can still go back, but I'm pretty sure he can so this just got frustrating. I hope there's only one more book, because this story just has to end! 
 I already couldn't stand Aden/Victoria. Now Mary Ann/Riley are gone and they were the reason I was reading the book. With Aden going back to the beginning in the next book, there's no telling what could change, but I want Mary Ann/Riley together and things to be great between them. 
 On a side note, I can't stand that Riley and Victoria slept together and that really bothers me. It almost makes me feel like I don't think Riley is good enough for Mary Ann. I really think that hurt the characters more than anything else could have. 
 To be honest, I skipped several pages of this book. Especially if Aden was the POV, I couldn't take him.

reference_books.title: Midnight (The Vampire Diaries: The Return, #3)
reference_books.review_text: I liked this series...then I TRIED to read this book. I couldn't get in to it. I kept finding myself more irritated with Elaina the more I read. Bonnie was also very childish--more so as the book went on and that rubbed me the wrong way. On top of that, I really thought we were going to get something more from Damon, which is what it looked like in the beginning, then Elaina showed up and that went out the window. The closer I got to the end of the book, the more I just skimmed the pages. The last chapter made me want to read the next book, which will be interesting because it's written by a ghostwriter. Maybe the ghostwriter will draw me back in to the series. LJ Smith is a great writer, I just think she had a bad book.

reference_books.title: Fifty Shades Freed (Fifty Shades, #3)
reference_books.review_text: Oh I can't begin to stress how bad this book was. I many non romantic, pointless descriptions of sex scenes can one book have? There were only like 50 pages of this book that were actually good, and that's being generous with my estimate. This book was so mindlessly boring, that I even picked up a young adult book to read in the middle and the thing was, the romance scene in the YA book were hotter than anything this book, and there was no sex! I don't want to continue on my rant, but I honestly don't see what the big fuss is about this series!

reference_books.title: Burn for Me (Hidden Legacy, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
If it were possible to go back in time and unread this book, I would - just so I could read it for the first time all over again and be again struck by the pure awesomeness that this book is. 
 I wasn't so sure when I first read the blurb about the book, since the Kate Daniels series already pushes the about of 'magic' I like in a book, I read the Kate Daniels series for the shapeshifters. I was drawn to that series for that sole reason there were shapeshifters, but I do love the series. Kate and Curran are also my all time favorite couple, but I fear that Nevada and Mad may take that spot. Ilona and Gordon Andrews know how to write a couple, they make it real. The couple is not perfect and everything is not roses (or carnations in this case) and things don't come together in one book, but the relationships develop over the series. I love it but I hate it. I hate that I have to wait until the next book comes out to find out where things go. I love that I can't stop thinking about what could happen next and how they're going to work everything out. 
 I don't want to give anything else away about the book, but trust me even if you don't like to read about magic, you will still love this book. 
 This was the best read for me this year!

reference_books.title: Fifty Shades of Grey (Fifty Shades, #1)
reference_books.review_text: The only thing that granted the 2 star rating for this book with me is the emails, which were entertaining. Other than that, this book just fell flat.

book_a.title: Touch of Frost (Mythos Academy, #1)
book_a.user_review: I wanted to rate this book higher, I really did. I just couldn't because the author can't stop repeating herself! The overall concept of the book is great, and I really enjoyed reading it. But I couldn't take reading the same sentences over and over again when it came to the Gwen and her powers and her mother.

sample_reviews.review_text:
If the book had started around 80%, I might have enjoyed it a lot more. But the beginning, UGHHH. Listening to this girl whine and moan about how "OMG THIS SCHOOL IS FILLED WITH MYTHICAL PEOPLE BUT THERE IS NO SUCH THING AS MYTHICAL ANYTHING, EVEN THOUGH I HAVE POWERS MYSELF. ALSO LOKI IS A HUGE LIE, BUT YAY FOR WONDER WOMAN." 
 I mean, really now. You don't just sit there having a ~power and yet refuse to believe that other powers exist. Or see a girl with sparks fly off her fingertips when she touches things, but refuse to understand where that comes from. 
 I also really don't understand Gwen's comic obsession, given that she so refuses to believe in myths. Really? You'd think those would be kind of compatible. Or it may just be that I love both mythology and comics. EITHER WAY, BOO. 
 Pff. Whatever. I kept reading for Loki, I admit.

Experiencing serious buyer's remorse with this one. Got about 25% in and realized I wouldn't be able to spend one more minute in Gwen Frost's whiny, repetitive head. I can think of at least two other YA series that cover the same ground, neither of which I liked much. Why'd I even bother with this one? At least I didn't pay full price.
Predictable, too detailed, boring, hot guy in love with social outcast, girl who can't lift a toothpick saves the day. Wow, YA has got tremendous standards nowadays.

Mehhh 
 Biggest complaint is that some parts felt extremely spelled out, as though the author doesn't expect the reader to be able to draw the right conclusions on their own. 
 Too much descriptions about the school that I just didn't care about. 
 Lots of repetitive phrases 
 I mean, I did enjoy the book, but the writing style could've been better
At the mid point in the book and I just don't care what happens. I don't like Gwen or any of the other characters really, they all kind of fell flat. Just couldn't bring myself to finish it.

While I really liked the characters in this book, they were put into a really bland plot with no personal stakes until the very end, in a setting with world building on the level of Xena -- which was apparently intentional. 
 And the cultural appropriation! My god, the cultural appropriation! And half-assed at that -- most of the characters are descended from heroes of some ancient war against evil, which means they're randomly assigned factions like "Spartan" "Roman," and "Valkyrie" (never mind that the first two are historic human civilizations while the latter are mythic creatures). But then there are references -- apparently to make us feel that the setting isn't a complete whitewash even though it totally is -- to Samurai and Ninja factions. Which are, like, a few thousand years after the rest. You might as well have G.I. Joes and Roundheads in there too. But worse of all is our heroine being referred to (about once per page) as a Gypsy, which Estep seems to think is another word for "fortune teller". At no point does she show the slightest knowledge of what the Roma are, their history or their culture. Nope, the heroine is pure WASP but called a "Gypsy" because it sounds cool.

This is the kind of book where you put it down for an hour or days and then go back to it thinking it wasn't that bad only to realize it is. 
 First off Spartans, Amazons, Vikings they were NOT magical warriors. You know what made them warriors that they were from Sparta or Norway or chicks from Greece who were part of a tribe! Okay, maybe Estep needed to come up with a reason why Logan Quinn was such a bad boy *eye roll* but couldn't she have done something along the lines of his family being descendent's of original Spartans that still uphold some of the traditions. Maybe not not providing clothes or food for them when they are at age 7. Or the whole making them steal and if caught beating them cause they were caught. Also, there are Amazons in the story so where are the female Sparta warriors? So Spartan women didn't go out and fight battles but at the age of 7 they too were removed from their homes and taken to a school where they were taught how to fight, gymnastics, and the like since Spartans believed a strong mother would produce strong offspring. 
 Also, the Xena references, Xena ended back in '01. I'm not too sure many teenagers will get this reference. Buffy I can see, cause Whedon is still churning out the comics. But not Xena I know my cousin who is only 7 years younger than me doesn't know how Xena is. 
 Logan Quinn is a conundrum. He's supposed to be the heroine's love interest and like all current YA love interest he's a bed-hopping jerk, who has his redeemable qualities. Ooookay. One thing I don't get, he "supposedly" (this is a rumor in the book) when he sleeps with a chick he signs her mattress as a way to keep all of the girls he's slept together straight. Wait.. what?! Do people at this school lug around their mattress' so Logan can check their mattress before hitting on somebody? Gah. 
 So yes, he's a player but Gypsy girl or Gwen is different. When he acts like a player around her, he has guilt in his eyes! *gags* Yes, this is to show he's a bad buy but underneath it all he's a big teddy bear? 
 And whenever logan is around it's an ode to his 'ice blue' eyes or his abs. I'm surprised there wasn't a haiku comparing his abs to Gerald Butlers in the 300 (speaking of which, what teacher would show that movie to a group of 16 year olds -I'm guessing Gwen is about 16? First off its Rated R and since when would a teach show that level of a movie. Plus, the sex scenes! No school would ever show that, no matter if it was mythical warrior or not). 
 Even Gwen got on my nerves most of the time. She'd complain about her psychometry abilities, she'd complain about how much she doesn't fit in at her school, she'd complain about how this is all bogus and blah blah blah blah. This is just like too many other YA books out there where a girl who has powers goes to a mythical school and its all 'normal girl in a crazy world'. Done and done. I was kind of hoping for something new and fresh. But its all old and stale. It's just one cliche after another.
Fun, readable, frothy. Aimed for a YA audience but a light enjoyable evening's read for adults.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Actual rating is 0 stars. 
 Immediately I was drawn in by the description. I mean, paranormal creatures and boarding schools, what could go wrong? It turns out a lot. 
 I was hoping to find another great teen paranormal romance series, but I was extremely disappointed. The writing was terrible and I'm usually not picky about the writing styles so that's saying a lot. It was so bad I couldn't even finish it. At the beginning, I wasn't getting into the story but I decided to try and stick it through and maybe it would eventually get better. I continued for as long as I could but I only got through to page 72. 
 The main character was so annoying. She uses her psychometric powers to help her fellow classmates find misplaced items. She is one of those characters that have no personality. She doesn't do much. All she does is help out her classmates, get a 4.0 GPA and work at the library. There's nothing wrong with that but I think Jennifer Estep could have done a better job of developing Gwen's character and personality. There's nothing different about Gwen. I couldn't stand her. 
 What really bothered me was when she found Jasmine's body. 
 "Professor Metis started to go, but she hesitated and turned to look at me once more. "I don't know if I said this before but that was very brave of you, Gwen, trying to help Jasmine like you did. Most people would have just screamed and run away." 
 I shrugged. I hadn't thought it was brave. It had just been instinct more than anything else. A foolish one, since I'd gotten knocked out and Jasmine had died anyway." 
 I don't see Gwen's actions as brave. All she did was touch the body and get knocked out. Not very brave to me. Then she plays it off like she helped out Jasmine without really thinking about it. Like she does it all the time but doesn't realize it. I don't know if it's just me but she got on my nerves so much. 
 I am definitely not reading any more books from this author and I absolutely do not recommend.
Too much inconsistency. Things are said and contradicted immediately afterwards. Main character is just plain mean. Other characters act in unrealistic ways. I couldn't keep going.

Me sorprendio que la historia mejorara, asi como la forma en como se desarrolla; es mucho mas rapida de leer que el primer libro, claro que en algunas partes en donde Anastasia me aburria demasiado me saltaba hasta donde pasara algo interesante. 
 Al termino del primer libro todo queda como en suspenso, porque las cosas no quedan muy bien entre los protagonistas y no pasa demasiado para que medio arreglen esos conflictos que se traen y darse la oportunidad de intentar otro tipo de relacion. Asi que practicamente desde el principio se puede adivinar que las practicas sexuales de Christian podrian pasar a segundo termino. 
 Siento que todo pasa muy rapido, no solo por la forma en que esta escrita la historia; sino porque creo que la autora va demasiado rapido con todo lo que pasa, no se que tan bueno o malo sea eso, de algun modo permite leer los libros bastante rapido pero hay algo que no deja disfrutarlos como se deberia. 
 De nuevo mi queja va hacia la protagonista, en serio no me agrada nada y eso no es un elemento a su favor, porque me salte algunas partes en donde de plano de aburria leerla. Christian por otro lado me agrado mas, aunque tiene algunos momentos como 3 o 4 que pense que estaba leyendo a algun personaje meloso y molesto. 
 Por fortuna este libro hizo que quisiera leer el tercero, un poco con la sensacion de saber que puede pasar pero no quiero adelantarme. 
 En definitiva mejoro bastante, aunque por momentos sea predecible no le quita el hecho de que se disfruta (sobre todo a Christian), asi que la calificacion sera mejor que la del primero.

It's not really accurate to say that I finished this book. I checked it out of the library. They asked for it back when I'd read about a quarter of it, and I was happy to return it to them. Perhaps it would have been better - more fair - to read the first book in the trilogy first, but that's something I will never know.

SPOILER ALERT. 
 THIS TELLS YOU HOW BOOK TWO ENDS AND THE SET UP FOR BOOK THREE. YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED!!!!!!!!!!!!! 
 ~~1/24/14~~ 
 I was too kind yesterday when writing this. 
 I never in all my life have read something intended for an adult audience that showed up so damned juvenile. 
 I love how Ana goes from giving a pro blow job (as a virgin no less), to giving SHY SMILES/GLANCES/GRINS/LOOKS every five fucking seconds! She's just had his junk in her mouth and her body, they've fucked every way from Sunday, and she's STILL SHY?????????????????? 
 I understand this has to be a "bad boy redeemed" story, but to castigate BDSM while you're at it is so cliche. For someone who was in to it the way Grey was to reverse himself 180 over one woman? I don't buy it. 
 It also makes me resent Ana for changing something that didn't need to be changed, and hate Grey for being so spineless. James even goes out of her way to assure her readers that sadism is not a "mental disorder" by telling us it's been removed from the DSM (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders). 
 If you're going to have the balls to assign your character the trait(s) of being into BDSM, have the balls to stick with it and not pussy out and start painting as something your character should be ashamed of. Part of Christian's early allure is his kinkiness. By this book it's starting to get watered down. 
 I've started book three and it gets worse. 
 The more I read, the more I want to tell James, if you wanted to write a billionaire romance, why didn't you? If you wanted to write a story about an innocent girl meeting a kinky guy, why didn't you? But why on earth did you combine the two and water down one to the point of insulting anyone reading it who IS kinky? 
 All right...back to the rest of the review. 
 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 
 Where do I start? 
 How many times can E.L. James tell her reader how devastatingly handsome Christian Grey is? 
 How many times can E.L. James tell her reader about Grey's gray eyes? 
 How many times can E.L. James have Anastasia bite her lip? 
 How many times can E.L. James have Anastasia roll her eyes? 
 How many times can E.L. James have Anastasia's inner goddess vaulting off/over her chaise lounge? 
 How many times can E.L. James have Anastasia's half-rim glasses/cardigan wearing subconscious scowl? 
 In a way, I almost want to keep count as I start the third book in this mess of a publishing miracle. Yes, I called it a miracle, because it's a miracle it ever saw publication. 
 The characters are made of paste board at best. 
 James must have done cursory research on BDSM. I have to wonder, the first Christmas this was out, how many beginner BDSM kits found their way under Christmas trees to hapless men whose wives had read this mess prior to the holiday? 
 This is nothing more than a mediocre billionaire finds love romance with a smattering of BDSM for spice. 
 If I dislike the series so much, why am I reading the third installment? 
 Oh, call me a sucker for punishment I suppose. 
 I wondered what lame excuse for a cliff hanger ending would bob it's way to the surface for this one? 
 In book one, it was Anastasia deciding there was no way they would ever be compatible, and running out on Christian. 
 During book two, they're only apart for a week before they get back together hotter and heavier than ever. 
 By the end, Anastasia has agreed to marry Mr. Fifty Shades of Fuckedup (her name for him), had a confrontation with "Mrs. Robinson", the older woman who introduced Christian to BDSM, and has landed her boss's job, after he makes a pass at her in the break room at the office - resulting in Anastasia twisting his pinky finger almost off and kneeing him in the groin. He is summarily let go (Christian owns the company- bought it to keep Ana safe). 
 What cliff is there left to hang off of for book three? 
 The ex-boss is in the background spoiling for revenge. 
 Lame, as what power could he possibly have to bear? 
 Can't wait to see how this peters out.

reference_books.title: Eyes Like Stars (Théâtre Illuminata, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I had an incredibly difficult time putting this one down. I want to say I didn't love it because lets face it... the plot kept pulling me in, then pushing me out, and I found the resolution sadly unfulfilling. However, I loved every bit of the characters and while I had issues with Nate and Ariel being romantic interests (as they felt so old and far away from Bertie) I also know that I wanted so badly for everything to work out with Nate at the end of the book (no further spoilers here!) 
 The writing at the very end was magnificent. While I didn't care for Bertie's overall decision, the way she "saved the day" was perfectly written and felt magical to me even as I read it. 
 I'm finding it difficult to write this review without spoilers, so bear with me. 
 The publisher and the cover struck me immediately on this book, and although it is something I won't normally comment on, I did want to just mention how visually perfect the cover was. A lot of YA fantasy these days uses photography on the cover, but the artistry used to create the cover of Eyes Like Stars and the rest of the series is just absolutely beautiful. 
 I think the one important thing to keep in mind with this series is that the characters within may have been created in a certain way within certain stories... but Mantchev does not necessarily use them as such. The Shakespearean (etc.) characters have much of their own personalities that become visible offstage, something I both loved and hated (character dependent). One should not expect the heroes of beloved plays to be quite as heroic. This is, after all, but one person's interpretation. 
 That being said, for anyone who gets excited by the idea of allusions, or is familiar with the workings of the theatre world, this book is a must-read. It is very unique, and utterly captivating.

reference_books.title: Hollowland (The Hollows, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I'm typically good for dystopias, but this was not my cup of tea. It wasn't the story - for me, it was the writing style. I know Hocking has a lot of diehard fans, and I say good for her, but I found the pacing awkward, the whole thing very wordy, and there were several times I had to stop and re-read sentences because I couldn't make out what they meant... most of the time they just seemed to be typoes. I think that with a could more runs through editing, this could be a good book, but for now, I am all set.

reference_books.title: Little Brother
reference_books.review_text:
Find more reviews like this at The Literary Phoenix. 
 UghhhA Little Brother. A How I hated you. 
 I'm not just trying to be a jerk about it, but the main character Marcus wasA exactly the type of person I despise. A IA hate reading about characters like him with their "F--- the government, don't trust anyone over 25, I do what I want" attitude. A Especially the type that turn into pathetic worms at the slightest sight of danger. A There are situations in this book - bad situations, given - that Marcus handledA so badlystill wanted Marcus & Co. to lose. A That's how unlikable they are. 
 I very rarely get so annoyed by books I yell over the narrator. A But seriously. A This kid is stupid. A I could list all the stupid things he does, but that would spoil the book? A Everything works, though. A Because this is a YA Dystopia, so hey, happily ever afters for everyone! 
 If you don't want to know every intimate detail about technology, you won't like this book. 
 Doctrow wants to tell you about cryptography. A And networking. A And MY GOD EVERYTHING. A I actually have a decent handle on computer science already - at least to the extent he explains it - so not only was thisA really, really boring, but it started to feel a bit condescending. A There were instances when something was mentioned in theA smallest frame of reference and then we'd get to sit through PAGES of explanation and back story. 
 As if I didn't care little enough about the characters already, now the WRITING is boring. 
 The plot is super unoriginal. 
 Let me know if you're heard this before: A rebel kids skip school, get in trouble, and are blamed for a terrorist plot. A No? A Me neither! A Here's a closer look at the plot: A Angsty teens go to jail after bombing, are insolent and suspicious, get out of jail and start running around and building anarchy. A Sounds a little less original now. A Throw in a bunch of naive, self-serving adults and repeated references of the main character calling himself AND his girlfriend a "horn dog" and eventually my eyes start to hurt from how much they are rolling. 
 Okay, guys, I just really didn't like this book? 
 I get the point he is trying to get across about surveillance and control via tracking... and how too much government interference can be bad. A I've seen it referred to as a toned-downA 1984... I'd disagree. A 1984 is a slice, well thought out, and you eventually want to team up with Winston but not with Marcus? A Because Marcus is an ass. 
 ALSO. A In the summary and the first couple chapters of the book, Doctrow puts SO MUCH EMPHASIS on the fact that Marcus' handle is w1n5t0n, i.e. "Winston" as inA 1984. A FUN FACT. A This is totally irrelevant to the rest of the book and he drops that handle almost immediately. 
 GAH. A Just... bleh. A I don't like this book, and I don't recommend it unless you're looking for something angry, political, sensational with REALLY AWKWARD teen sex scenes? A IF you are, enjoy. A All yours.

reference_books.title: Marked (House of Night, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I am not usually a person who flat-out hates a book... but this would be an exception. I have grown up living and breathing the vampire represented in Anne Rice and Bram Stoker... and the moment Neferet gets miffed because - Goddess forbid! - Zoey uttered Stoker's name, I was annoyed. For all intensive purposes, this is a story about immature, over dramatic witches. And yes, I meant witches. 
 As far as the description of vampire goes... the Casts decided to go with "drinks blood sometimes" and "worshippers of Night" (literally) and "burns in sunlight" as their descriptors. There is the complaint that Stoker villianizes vampires (oh, sorry, vampyres) but it's the strength and mystique that is missing. For a little while, I had hoped that it could be found in the adults...but no. Even the High Priestess gets giddy and excited over the fledglings. Zoey has a kitty cat familiar and casts circles and spells and has an affinity over the elements. Oh fantasy readers... am I the only one that aligns those gifts and traits with a typical witch... not a vampire? 
 Now lets talk about Zoey. Zoey has, like, the worst life evar. Srsly. Her mom like totally hates her and her "step-loser" is like a total brainwashed follower of the People of Faith, who are like, complete assholes. Oh, welcome to the way this book is written. Okay, I'm being a little overdramatic, but the protagonist's background is the same as any whiny teenager I could follow on Tumblr (no offense intended... everything seems worse when it's happening until you experience some more "real" life... you know what I mean?). The book starts with gossip about that cute guy at the football match. When she gets to the House of Night, it's about the Hags from Hell and omg they are so evil. No substance. It's even very dramatic when she's saving the day at the end. Zoey's family? She has an open-minded grandmother; a non-supportive, brainwashed-by-new-husband mother; goody-two-shoes siblings; and a step-father who is prejudiced. That prejudice really bothers me, actually, because over and over again the Casts bring up the "People of Faith" (oooh, that is screaming Charlaine Harris) and they talk about it like its the only religion and all religious people are blind, hateful, and controlling... which isn't a fair assessment at all. At least Harris uses a little comparison in her novels... there are different sects, and yes, some people may be like that, but the world isn't black and white. 
 Anyway. Zoey. She's an absolute Mary Sue. It's one thing to have powers. That's cool. It's another thing to be the strongest of everyone in your class. That's... okay, well, I'll keep reading. It's ANOTHER things to be the most powerful person in your school. In the world? In history? Come on. 
 But wait! There's more! 
 She also has a special mission in the school that is her mission only, a super important mission. And if THAT wasn't enough, the hottest guy in the school is falling for her, the strongest vampire in the school is her mentor, and she seems to be on the top of her classes. ... ... ... I've got no words. Lots of annoyed thoughts. Talk about excess! 
 I think the only way I'd read the second book of this series was if someone bought me the book, and paid me to review it. It made me mad. 
 I'm sure there are lots of people out there who would like it. Occasional readers, perhaps. Twilight fans? Middle school girls. That's about all I can give it. 
 I think that while it was nice that PC wrote a book with her daughter (nay, a series)... she's a better writer on her own. I read Divine by Mistake by her last year, and while I was ultimately disappointed with that book as well, it was a much better story, and a much better character. 
 Maybe the Casts just aren't for me.

reference_books.title: The Darkest Minds (The Darkest Minds, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This book has been on my TBR list forever - the way my hardcopy reading is going, I would have never gotten to it. Thank goodness for the audiobook! Although I think I really would have liked it better without the narrator.... 
 I've bounced back and forth on whether I liked the characters or not in this book, and ultimately, it really came down to the character. For a protagonist, Ruby's not bad. She definitely grows and evolves, and I love the fact she isn't awesome at everything. It's immensely frustrating when a protagonist excels at everything. The lead boy, Liam, is not my favorite, but I thought Chubs was pretty well developed. Zu was adorable. Clancy was the worst. Overall I have to say that Braken did a pretty good job with character development. 
 The Darkest Minds takes place in a crumbling world, but not a post-apocalyptic one. Especially at the beginning of the book, you get a sense of the chaos that has ensued in the ten years Ruby's been in camp. Empty houses and city blocks, looted stores, a partially exploded school - all these are nuances breaking apart what used to be a normal life. I had some issues with the calm highway miles and the complete lack of people who weren't bounty hunters, but neither of these things are enough to break the illusion of the world. 
 I kept trying to predict this book, and I kept failing. I kept waiting for things to blow up in Ruby's face, and for the most part, they didn't. I kept waiting for the worst YA cliches to bounce in and although they started to trickle from time to time... they didn't fully evolve. Thank you. The book ended differently than I expected, too. When it comes to YA, it's so important to me that I not be able to predict the book. Predictable books are boring. 
 Overall, Braken is telling a story of a generation that has developed mutant powers (five varieties only). The older generation, terrified of their children (mostly), have abandoned them to the government. The morality of this has split the country, and meanwhile, the children are tortured, tested on like lab animals, and generally neglected. It's not a great situation. It's not the most original idea, but Braken does manage to tell it in an original way. 
 Also, I kept waiting for a love triangle. I was sure it would happen. It didn't. Some bits with one of the characters near the end got pretty sappy... but it never actually became a triangle! 
 The biggest reason for the loss of a heart in this category is the narrator. Amy McFadden was not the worst narrator I've heard, but several of her voices (Liam's!) really bugged me. Ruby always sounded like she had such an attitude as well, which didn't come across in the writing at all. It just irritated me. 
 Braken made some interesting writing choice for a YA novel, including what is implied to be a rape scene. Very little of this is described as the main character is being mentally manipulated, but it may not be what some parents want their 'tweens reading. The scene that bothered me the most? Within an hour of waking after the attack, the protagonist very nearly starts making out with someone else. Not quite, but almost. I was enraged. If Braken allowed it to go from rape to teen makeout session, I was done. It didn't, but it felt really, really close. 
 Overall, I really did like this book. There were a couple things that made me mad, but the story as a whole was well-done and interesting, with characters that I became invested in. The book ended with several questions that I want answered - such as Did that character live? Did that other one reach his/her destination? WTF is Ruby's plan? and so forth. I'll be picking up the sequel at some point for sure. 
 . 
 Originally posted on The Literary Phoenix.

book_a.user_review: The book is interesting, but the writing is a little simplistic and the ending came very quickly. It read like an episode of SVU but without the detectives. A well-done crime novel, infuriating and believable, but not recommended for anyone with young children.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Reassurance if needed for potential readers is that this book is not about child sexual exploitation. 
 This book is a classic psychological thriller with a chilling undercurrent which is attention grabbing from the outset. It is really difficult to do anything else except read it. 
 The beginning of the book sets the scene explaining the relationship between parents and child leading up to the day of the event. Beth was always concerned that Carmel would go missing as she was considered to be highly intelligent but ' dream like'. 
 The reader is informed about Carmel's separation from her mother at a book fair. Carmel was a lover of the colour Red hence the red coat. Beth could see the red coat then it disappeared. The terror and desperation of her mother Beth is evident. She is searching for her young daughter with the clock ticking. Her anguish, panic and overall helplessness is evident. This is every parent's nightmare more especially as Carmel is an only child. 
 The book is told in two voices, Beth the mother and Carmel the child taking it in turns to tell the story from their individual perspective. The voice of Carmel was convincing especially the change from the child to adolescent voice. 
 The reasoning behind Carmel's kidnapping is quite original yet quite far-fetched depending on what the individual reader is prepared to believe. Some aspects stretch what is plausible. 
 Following this immediate panic the book develops into an interesting gripping read. Carmel was taken by a man reporting to be her Grandfather telling her that her mother Beth was in an accident. In essence she was tricked and isn't aware she is missing. The story moves to unexpected places. The abductors take Carmel as they think she has a gift which they want to use. Carmel is told that her mother has died and her father does not want her. 
 She is somehow smuggled to the USA. Exploration of Carmel's new surroundings ensues as well as her differing emotions. Despite encouragement and pressure from her kidnappers Carmel clings to her true identity and visions of her mother. Carmel is likeable, bright, strong willed, with spirit and does not come across as a victim. Narrating for a child in the first person can prove undoable for many but this follows well with Carmel's narrative maturing as she does. Beth is surrounded by guilt and of course self-blame. Although Beth does engage with the Police, this book does not focus on the Police investigation instead concentrating on the effects of the separation from the viewpoint of both Beth and Carmel. Beth has friends who wish to assist as well as Carmel's devastated father who is now her ex-husband. Carmel appears to cope despite low points it is Beth whose total existence is blown to shred. Beth never gives up hope that Carmel is still alive, she keeps searching, while at the same time trying to rebuild her life and taking something from her relationship with her ex-husband and his partner. 
 The writing is quiet poetic and magical ensuring that the story is not depressing. All the characters are well developed, with the descriptive passages aiding the overall story. Carmel is entertaining and it is lovely to see her innocent outlook on her new surroundings and individuals caring for her. Kate Hamer makes the story interesting from the perspective of a young child and I did miss Carmel when the story had ended. The story of the mother Beth was also believable. I didn't want the book to end yet driving the narrative from the start is whether Beth and Carmel will be reunited. I won't give any spoilers but suffice to say this book ended quicker than I would have liked. I found the closing paragraph particularly distressing and poignant. I would highly recommend this book but word of warning is that it is so difficult to put down and do anything else while reading. I would not recommend to parents of children who themselves generally have high anxiety levels.

A pre-release book from Faber given to my book group to review. Not my sort of thing at all. The only engaging character is Beth, desperate to find 8 year old Carmel who disappears at a book fair. Gramps is too spooky for words.
For me, this book was a chore to get through. Interesting at first, but I quickly lost interest. A lot of nothing in between the beginning and the end.

Clever and harrowing tale told from two perspectives - that of a mother and her abducted child. 
 Full review: https://forwinternights.wordpress.com...

Carmel is abducted by a roving preacher who pretends to be her grandpa. "Grandpa" is convinced that Carmel is a healing (which she may or may not be). This book follows several years of drifting while her mom continues to search. 
 Not the next "Gone Girl" nor is it a thriller.
A really good read. For once, you get to see two points of view. Add you're own angst (yes, that's the only way I can describe it, angst!) and you're spinning.

This book could have been more effective as a novella. Easily 100 pages shorter. I think the time jump works for the mother but not for Carmel. Carmel's dad and his girlfriend are all superfluous characters and there's not a clear degradation of Carmel's kidnapper. (Forgive me for forgetting so many names here.) The beginning is really good though. This author is known for short stories and it shows in shiny, bright colors at the start.

An exceptionally emotional read, Kate Hamer's prose is exquisite. The author brings us into an emotional and authentic world that somehow goes beyond the five senses; I am in awe of her writing. The story pulls you in, but more than that: the characters *feel* real. I lost one of my little girls for nearly an hour once and I remember the terror: Hamer evokes it so well, plus the horror of having to go on *just in case* you're reunited. Carmel's journey with "Gramps" and Dorothy, plus the colourful world of evangelists is really well drawn too. One of my favourites in recent times, was sorry to finish. Read this book!! You won't be disappointed.
Not what I was expecting, but very good. I couldn't stop reading!

Perhaps I read this at the wrong time, perhaps I wasn't letting it get to me, perhaps I simply did not understand it, but the book did not deliver the emotional punch I was expecting, and the feeling I'm left with can be best described as "lukewarm". I might need to read it again to see if I feel differently. 
 The book's take on the "missing child" story is not the usual mystery of "who did it" and the suspense of "where is she", as you have Carmel narrate her separation from her mother and the subsequent events, which takes away from the reader the anguish of not knowing. There are no intensely frustrating near-misses in the search for the child, there is, in fact, no intrigue, except for the strange mystical and religious undercurrent that is never fully resolved. Instead the focus is on the internal transformation of both, mother and child, and even though it's the first person perspective, it is told in a somewhat emotionally distant way (hence "lukewarm"). 
 *SPOILER AHEAD* 
 But what I found most unusual is how the abduction turned out to benefit the mother, who got a car, who started working, who finally settled the feud with her ex-husband and even became friends with his new partner to the point of taking their new-born for walk! This might be an author's way of saying that life goes on, but I just wasn't comfortable with it.

book_b.title: Clockwork Angel (The Infernal Devices, #1)
book_b.user_review:
Cassandra Clare's prequel to the Mortal Instruments series reminds me of the writing of Neil Gaiman - very much so, in fact. I liken her to something between Gaiman and the author of one of my favorite series - Jonathan Stroud. Clare adds her own elements to the story, and twists Victorian London around a little bit to her heart's content. And I find her London beautiful and haunting and sad and grey. I love the idea of her clockwork mechanisms and the Shadowhunters and the quirky husband who lives in the basement and invents things that do not work. I want to hear so much more about these things. 
 But I didn't. 
 Instead, Clare tells the story of Theresa Grey, a dreary mortal-who-isn't-really, who spends a great deal of time worrying that people are not behaving like perfect ladies and gentlemen, worrying about her no-good brother, and pondering her origins. After a while, her daydream like comparisons to literature I am not intimately familiar with become dreary and it is easy to find oneself skimming forward a bit. 
 I wanted desperately to like this book, and I think I would have, if I had been in anybody's mind but Tessa's. Jessamine's snobbery and secrets are equally alluring to William's, and even the small stories that do get shared are interesting of their own accord. Maybe Tessa's word be too, if it was unraveling a bit more rapidly! Clare tends to drag on a little, generally caught in a scene that - to me at least - feels mundane. Nonetheless, despite my issues with the flow of the writing and excitement of the protagonist, Clare paints such a vivid, peculiar world that one cannot help but to be intrigued. Even though I found this book a bit slow and boring, I absolutely would not toss aside Clare's work altogether, because there were many aspects of the novel I enjoyed. In fact, when my (endless) reading list starts to dwindle down, I don't doubt that I would pick up the sequel, or perhaps City of Bones. I simply became bored with this, but not so much that I couldn't push through the more tedious points

sample_reviews.review_text:
I've been sitting here for the past 15 minutes trying to write a review that isn't "OMG, AWESOME! PREORDER IT NOW!" I think Clockwork Angel has fried my brain. 
 It's a prequel to The Mortal Instruments series, but no, you don't need to have read those to read this (although if you haven't, what are you waiting for?!). 
 I'm not going to give any plot synopsis or spoilers, because I think it's good to enter this new series with as little advance knowledge as possible and learn about what's going on as Tessa does. There is a little crossover with the Mortal Instruments series but again, you don't need to read those books first. 
 If Clockwork Angel is any indication, I'm going to like these books even more than TMI, and that's a bold statement because I LOVED those books. :) 
 Book 2 will come out in September 2011.

Well, not horrible but - can't say I liked it. Some of it was actually good, but the periodic setting really didn't do it for me, and I had really other expectations from the love story as well.. I it started well and some of the book had good suspence, but really not all of it.

** spoiler alert ** 
 First off, im a huge Cassandra Clare fan! I absoluley loved The Mortal Instruments series and was excited to jump into this one! CLOCKWORK ANGEL was really good! I liked the humor and mystery the story had. There was a warm and happy feeling I got from the Institute and Jem saying how they were all one big family. Tessa began to become part of the family and I loved seeing that! For the first book it was good! I did enjoy City of Bones better. I know with fisry books its hard beacuse its developing a story, so i do hope/ and belive that they will get better; or the second book will be. 
 They story opens up with Tessa on the boat waiting for her brother. This scene was somewhat slow but I like how it gave us time and a backstory to get to know Tessa. As soon as she meet the Dark Sisters I knew something bad was about to take place. The "Pandemonuim Club" sighn was just icing on the cake for trouble. (If yove read THE MORTAL INSTRUMENTS, you know the Pandemonium can be the source for all kinds of trouble). Cassie did great of jumping right into the story. I thought it would be really drawn out before she meet the Shadowhunters but not at all. Tessa is immediatley pulled into the Shadowworld; which all we shadowhunters love very much. 
 From the moment Tessa arrived at the Institute and meet the gorgeuos dark haired William Herondale, I knew I was in for a spin. Sarcasm, good looks, and hard walls to break down; nothing you wouldnt expect from a Herondale. I loved how much Will reminded me of Jace. I instantley fell for him. Then we meet Jem, the caring, loving, and handsom Shadowhunter; who can't help but charm you. Two amazing, heart pulling shadowhunters? BY THE ANGEL! 
 Will or Jem. The love triangle immediatley took off and I admire Cassie for that. The story itself, the realtionship of the charecters; its destinded to be a trio. I love the banter between all three! Will's sarcasm, Jem's comedic undertone, and Tessa feircness; all together was one wild group! I look forward to the rest of their banter in later books. 
 I was so shocked when you found out that The Magister was Mortmain. THE MUNDIE!?! The minute Nathan got down on his knees, I wanted to throw the book! I didnt hate Nathan, but i didnt love him either. The way he handed Tessa over, and just didnt care about here really ticked me off. The Magister isnt all that great either. I cant wait to see them gone. Hopefully some but-kick from our adorded shadowhunters. 
 I honeslty can say i really enjoyed this book! Hats of the Cassie for another great Shadowhunter story! I cant wait to start book 2! And hey, arent all the stories true? ;)
I just don't like her books, I keep wanting to look away from the page, it's like they repel me or something.

2013 Review: 
 this book was AMAZING!!! i loved it SOOOOOO much!! It got me into the Shadowhunter world :3 I can keep reading this book and it'll never get old. Will, Jem, Gabe all the guys are so perfect. As well as the girls! 
 2016: 
 Cringing a bit at what I wrote ^^ 
 But what I said was true. The way Cassie wrote the characters and the way Will Herondale is so mysterious, its so beautiful. I could read this book over, and over again and I wouldn't get tired of it. I remember walking into Walmart towards the books and I found Will, on the cover, attractive. So I read the back then bought the book. I love books that take place in the 1800's. I don't know why, but the way they spoke and dressed made me happy. I was happy to see that Tessa was an american girl who traveled to London to see her brother. 
 The way Cassandra writes, it's beautiful. I say this in all the reviews I've done about her books 
 I recommend reading TID before TMI, that is what I did. I didn't know about City of Bones until I heard it was coming out into a movie, and when I was reading one of the TID. Or you can read them in the order they came out.

I'd read almost all of the books in The Mortal Instruments (TMI), except for the last book, City of Heavenly Fire, which is now long overdue since I cannot remember some scenes in the series. Anyway, I read this book because soon enough it will be a TV series, that a true Shadowhunter should not be missed. 
 Moving forward, for the review; I could neither say that this first book of The Infernal Devices (TID) was bad nor good. But it clearly did not blow me away like those I read in the comments and reviews; it was very average in every way. Though I must admit, this book was way better than the City of Bones. And I couldn't help but see similarities between them - a spy inside the institute, arrogant and annoying male leads, mysterious and unknown past, father issues and whatnot. And I was a bit confused about the terminologies and what they do (iratze, seraph blades, etc.) in this book, yet Clare described everything more clearly than her debut novel. 
 Additionally, the way Cassandra Clare wrote this story was very elegant. Not sure if it had something do with the Victorian settings, but regardless she still richly created a very vivid era. London in 1900s was dark and gloomy and, well, rainy. Still, I found the period setting along with Tess' abilities more interesting. (Surprisingly, London in 1900s was very gloomy and dark and rainy which was far from what I imagined! But anyway I don't really know London since I've never been there. LOL.) 
 I rated it two stars because the story was a bit dragging. Too much history, too much talking and recon. For me, it went too long. There were parts that I skipped because I could not fathom a thing Clare said. 
 Then again, there were still good things in the story. The kickass action scenes and the twist, in the end, were oh so awesome. I liked Tessa and her power to Change and how she can touch their minds, that's impressive. Yes, Clare's strategy on how to keep us going by concealing the truth about their past and backgrounds still made me want to read the second up to the last book. Also, I want to know who she ends up with. Don't we all want to? 
 So, all in all, the plot was not so bad at all. If Clare could make the narrations and storytelling short, and stop having so much drama about their past then it'll be better. 
 "One must always be careful with books and what is inside them, for words have the power to change us."

I absolutely loved this book! We get a new bit of the Shadowhunter world, and a bit of a peek into Magnus Bane's past. I actually love that he was in this book, because it takes that tie and familiarity from TMI into this new series. 
 I didn't catch the plot twists ahead of time, which was really nice. I did have one tiny bit of an issue. Will sounded a lot like Jace. It was a little distracting in the beginning, but after his character started building a bit it got a lot better. 
 I can't wait to pick up book 2! Picking up Clockwork Prince now!

** spoiler alert ** 
 2/19/2011 - So, I was a little worried about starting this book. I am deeply, deeply in lust with Cassandra Clare's Mortal Instruments series and I was afraid this book wouldn't measure up to the high standards I have set for this particular author. I am quite happy to find out that my fears were for nothing because this book is fantastic. 
 This is set in the universe of the Mortal Instruments series but is set in Victorian England and the Institute in London. The book centers around Tessa an American fresh off the boat from New York. She is searching for her brother and is taken in by some rather deplorable characters but thankfully is saved by members of the London Institute, specifically Will Herondale. 
 Throughout the book Tessa is busy trying to figure out why the bad guys want her and what they have done to her brother. She is also trying to figure out her romantic feelings towards Will and Will's best friend Jem Carstairs. On top of which is her budding new power and the knowledge that she isn't quite as human as she has been led to believe. 
 The best thing about this whole book is how the author always leaves you guessing. Never quite sure what is going to happen or what the characters' exact meanings are. I love how well developed all of the characters are and how smoothly they interact with one another. I find that as much as Jace pissed me of in City of Bones it is nothing compared to the irritating abilities of Will. I can't imagine coming across someone who was so rude to everyone all the time, no matter what his past was like. 
 I was thrilled to see Magnus Bane again. I'd kind of forgotton that he was rather old and would be appearing in this book. I also liked hearing references to families that are very important in the Mortal Insturments books. 
 I'm curious to see what happens with Tessa's brother Nathaniel. I didn't like him from the get go and I couldn't believe that Tessa kept protecting him. I have a sister and if she did even part of those things I would have completely cut her out of my life. I hope in the next book Tessa doesn't forget how many times her terrible brother has betrayed her. 
 I find that Jessamine is annoying and I'm wondering if she has any redeemable qualities. I can't figure out what part she has to play in this story? She doesn't really lend anything to the story and I don't think anyone would miss her when she's gone. I guess we'll just have to wait and see. 
 I'm very glad that the Clave decided not to kick Tessa out because who knows what would have happened to her if they had. Plus I want to see what happens with her and Will, although I'm secretly rooting for Jem. 
 Great story, great characters, great book. I'm really looking forward to the next book and am anxiously awaiting it's release.

This was just... meh. I'm not really sure why I read this, because I wasn't too crazy about the Mortal Instruments trilogy. But, whatever, I borrowed from the library, so at least all that I've wasted is time. 
 Clockwork Angel starts with Tessa on her way to London to stay with her brother, because her aunt just died, and her parents passed away when she was young. However, dun dun dunnnnnn, she is met by two strange women who say they were sent by her brother. These women are evil :O And it turns out that Tessa has strange powers and a questionable lineage :O (Clary anyone?) So, she is held captive by them for a while and is told that she is going to be given to the ominous Magister, when suddenly, she is rescued by two Shadowhunters! Yay! One of them is the completely dreamy super mega gorgeous totally ripped Jace, I mean.... wait, what was his name again? ***this is a side thought. I finished the book two days ago and I can't remember the characters' names. Ok. Nate is her brother, Jem is the sweet one, Charlotte is the head of the institute..... Ok. For all intents and purposes, this male character is the 1800s version of Jace, so we shall continue to call him Jace, because, evidently, it is too much pressure for Cassandra Clare to come up with a whole new set of characters.*** 
 Anyways, Tessa is rescued by the Shadowhunters and taken to the institute, where they are trying to figure out what evil scheme the Magister is up to. There are evil robots involved. Seriously. Evil robots. And of course, this would not be Cassandra Clare if the main character, Tessa, did not have two guys developing feelings for her. The first is the typical Jace. He is gorgeous and wonderful and oftentimes, he acts like an ass, but every now and then, there is a glimpse of a good person under that callous exterior. The second is the sweet and caring Jem, who is patient and good and, like almost every fictional character in the world, he has a special place that he likes to go when he wants to think or relax, and he takes Tessa there to be super cute. 
 And you know, just for once, I would like the main girl to pick the healthy relationship. I mean, seriously, is it that hard? Is it really so impossible for a fictional girl to choose the guy that isn't a jerk? To pick the one that is honest and doesn't jump back and forth between personalities like a mental patient.... Or even if Tessa decided that she is really overwhelmed right now, and she is vulnerable, and it isn't right for her to be jumping into a relationship with someone that she doesn't know. That would be ok too, but an author like Cassandra Clare would never have the guts to do that, because she knows that the majority of her fanbase comes from girls that just cannot wait to whip out their cell phones and tweet of fb status that they are "TEAM _________" 
 I never really intended for this to become a rant, so I think that I'm going to stop now, but I'm just getting kind of frustrated. One more thing though; the twist at the end could be seen from about a quarter into the book. Just saying.

This book was unbelievably good. I can't wait to read everything else she's written. 
 Pros: Great writing. Obviously talented writer. Good characters, and great character development. Great world building, I plan to read the entire series after this. 
 Cons: The library has the second book checked out and reserved for the next two months...so I'm going to have to wait a little while to get my next fix. I also suffered from major 'book hangover', which made it almost impossible to start any other book because I was so focused on getting my next Cassandra Clare fix. 
 I'm not ashamed to admit this: The writing on this was so good I had to take a break and go edit my own W.I.P. while reading. Because I learned a lot about the writing craft just from reading this book.

reference_books.title: Divergent (Divergent, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I just wrote a review on this, and then it got deleted by some unknown bug in my system. Brilliant. 
 Here is the deal about Divergent. I originally refused to read it, because I was spoiled bigtime for the ending of Allegiant. What a bummer. But then I got a great deal on the box set, and I kind of bought it anyway. Then I proceeded to read the first book in one sitting - 6 or 7 hours that is (who's counting, right?). And I must say, I'm impressed. 
 Roth introduces us to yet another dystopian universe, this one similar to The Hunger Games, although not quite as brutal (yet). I suspect it will get worse though, seeing as dystopians tend to go that way. I was very pleasantly surprised by the writing style in the book, it didn't feel like a writing style aimed for teenagers (which sadly were the case with both Legend and Shatter Me). So thumbs up for that, because I was getting really tired of authors more focused on the love story than the tragic world around them. Not that Roth doesn't have a love story, but she actually manages to provide me with an enjoyable loves tory. Please don't turn it into a love triangle, please. 
 On with the point. The characters were very enjoyable, but not quite as well-rounded as I would have preferred. Don't get me wrong, they had both depth and were generally amazing, but they lacked somethingbut it might be because they are not Lannisters, Idunno. No but really. I feel as if the character arch of Tris were kind of forced on me, with all the decisions she had to make. I didn't suddenly wake up and see a completely different character, but I could see her change being sort of forced on by the choice she made at the Ceremony. What I liked most about Tris, is that even though she was completely in love with Four, she wasn't swooning over him - because that's my problem with most YA literature. They swoon too much. Tris shows that she can manage herself without Four, but she prefers not to, and that is a very different thing than being dependent on a man looking at you, Bella Swan. 
 When it comes to the plot, I was a little confused at first. I have this issue with a lot of dystopians (except for Uglies of course) - there is no explanation as for why the world is as messed up as it is. Why are we entering a dystopian future, and why is this not happening in 201(insert number of choice). I need to know why. Was there a nuclear explosion? Were there oil-eating bugs? Did some mad political leader impose war on the world? And what about everything that is not the United States? What about Norway? Or China? No, but seriously. Even though you all think so, America is not the only country in this world. 
 But yes, the plot. There is a very nice dramaturgical arch, leading us into more and more excitement (and love) as the book progresses, and it has a nice little peak at the top. I think the ending may have been a little rushed, but not so much that I found it bothersome. All in all, a very good book, and a solid four out of five stars. I think I would have given it five out of five if I'd gotten some sort of explanation as to why.

reference_books.title: The Amazing Book is Not on Fire
reference_books.review_text: I love Dan and Phil as much as the next person, but rereading this was pretty boring. I enjoyed when I read the audiobook, and I think I would have enjoyed the physical copy much more if I'd actually read that first. The Amazing Book is Not on Fire has zero rereadability value, except for looking at pictures and maybe reading The Urge. I really enjoyed the more story-like aspects to the book, like their trip to Japan, but it fell flat against the rest of the book. If Dan could write a novel in the same voice and tone as The Urge, I suspect he would become quite successful, YouTube career or not, because he is an excellent writer, but a fanfiction about Phampires isn't enough to keep this book out of the dreaded two-star-review. Sorry.

reference_books.title: Shiver (The Wolves of Mercy Falls, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This series have always been a victim of various reviews, at best. I started this mostly because I got the whole box set for free, because of a cupon I had. So I will probably finish the rest, but I'm in no hurry to do it. 
 I have a lot to say on this first book, and I don't know where to start. 
 Okay, let's start with the plot. The plot was very simple, and I didn't care about it all that much. I realise that it is a love story, but that didn't have to be all it was about, did it? Give me some nuances, because this shit is just plain boring sometimes. It's not as bad as Twilight in describing every effing movement the other one makes, but it's still pretty annoying, seeing as it's just so unlikely. The girl, Grace, has been looking at a wolf for six years since he saved her from being eaten. And then whoopdido, the wolf turns in to a gorgeous boy her own age. Isn't that just a bit too convinient? Well, if it weren't, there wouldn't be a story, I do realise that. But then again, maybe this was a story that could have waited. If it had been done in a less sickening and clishe'd way, I would be okay with it, but right now, it was just a hot mess of convinience and clishes going all over the place, making me want to punch someone. 
 When it comes to a dramaturgical arch, I simply couldn't find one. It wasn't exactly flat, but it wasn't a very strong curve either. I could sort of see where the author wanted it to go, but she didn't get there. It just fell flat. 
 The Characters 
 Grace 
 First of all, she was very Bella Swan, there is absolutely no doubt about that. But I did like Grace a little bit better than Bella anyway, because at least Grace dodn't have a compulsion to say in every other sentence how gorgeous Sam is. The thing about Grace is that just like Bella, she can't properly function without her loved one, and that's what annoys me. I need more badass heroines in my life, who don't let the course of their lives be decided by a man. So bottom line is, she has a very boring personality, and is annoyingly dutiful, and she's the kind of person who never does anything wrong, ever. 
 What's the deal with tragic heriones being into books by the way? It happens way to often in litterature, and I'm starting to find it bloody boring. In Grace, it's not too evident though, so it's sort of okay, but I needed to get it out there. And why is it that there is never a young-adult girl who actually have had sexual encounters before? I realise that there's mostly teenagers reading YA-fiction, but there are still teenagers doing the do. It's like writers are trying to paint a rosy picture of how everything is supposed to be, and that you're not worth anything if you've already had sex. But I'm twenty, and technically, I'm an young adult. I need litterature I can recognize myself in. And I'm not going to get that from reading adult fiction where they are 35 and desperate to find a man. 
 Sam 
 First of all, no eighteen year old boy has ever acted that way. It's not humanly possible for an eighteen year old to be such a cliche. So, despite being the most annoying love interest I've seen in a long time, he was kind of okay, I guess. Except for some of the language "You went potty on yourself" I MEAN SERIOUSLY. How is it even possible for an adult writer to move her fingers so she can type that? 
 But yes, Sam. He has a very boring personality. Being the misunderstood emo-kid who writes music and plays the guitar and all. We've seen it before, we don't need it again. He's creepily obsessed with Grace, but seeing as Grace is creepily obsessed with him too, it's sort of okay. 
 Olivia and Rachel 
 Bland and boring. Both of them. I couldn't get anything out of them. It was simply utterly boring. When a character in a book series has best friends, I want to know why she is friends with them. Why are they so important to the main character? We never find out, except that they've been friends for a long time. She avoids them pretty much all the book, except in the end and at school, and that doesn't give me a reason to love them. As soon as the boy (Sam) shows up, Grace is completely engulfed in him, and can't seem to remember that she has any friends at all. 
 Isabel and Jack 
 Isabel was one of the few characters I actually enjoyed in this book. She was very strong and dependant on herself, and wouldn't deal with any bullshit. I would have liked the book if it had been from her point of view. She seems much more badass than Grace (not that that's saying a lot, but you know). Jack on the other hand, I didn't get much of a feel for. It was like he was the thing that was dragging the plot along, without really being there. He wasn't really exciting, he was just angry. And angry characters are more often than not, boring. 
 All in all, I didn't hate this book, but there's a lot of mistakes in it, and I would have liked it if Stiefvater had fixed them before they were published. Made a believable main character and a not-so-stupid love interest, and I would have greatly enjoyed it. Because the plot isn't bad, it's just a bit too much focus on the love story instead of the wolves and their lives. I would love to see more of the action, and not just the making out. Another year of editing and thinking through what the message should be, and I would have been a very happy reader. But right now I'm at the "meh" point.

book_a.title: The Book Thief
book_a.user_review:
For a long time I didn't want to read the Book Thief. Not because I was afraid that I would cry, but because I thought it was too popular. When I saw that the movie was supposed to come out, I thought, why not. So I bought it in June/July. It stood on my shelf for a long time, before I took it down and opened it. I shouldn't have. 
 Not because it was bad. But because it was absolutely breathtaking. It was beautiful and sad and everything at the same time. I laughed, cried and smiled my way through this book. But I should never have read it. Because I want to read it again, for the first time. For me, it was the kind of book that made me want to read it all at once, but at the same time savour it for as long as possible. I've read in it every evening for about a week, because I wanted to read through it. But never in the days, never on the bus, because I wanted it to last. 
 But this is also the kind of book that makes me never want to read another word again. This, of course, is because it is beautiful. It is beautifully written, it has a good plot line, and it has believable characters. And it has soul. I really hope the author poured his heart and soul into this as much as I think he did. I hope it ripped him appart to write those last few words, and that Liesel, Hans, Rosa and Rudy still haunts him in the nights. Because they will haunt me.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Honestly, I don't think I could do justice by reviewing this book. 
 All I can say is that I cried. really. hard. And I'm sure that this book would haunt me as long as my memory serves.

This isn't the book I usually reed, but yet it's one of the best I've ever read.

Een aantal jaar geleden toen ik voor het eerst echt in contact kwam met de boekgemeenschap op internet was dit boek een rage. Iedereen had hem gelezen of was hem aan het lezen en ik hoorde alleen maar lovende recensies. Op dat moment had ik dit boek niet in mijn bezit en was het er eigenlijk bij ingeschoten. Deze zomervakantie was ik naar het festival Sziget in Hongarije (Budapest) en daar stond een biebkast. Waar je een boek kon lenen of ruilen voor een ander boek die je al in je bezit had. Natuurlijk als boekenliefhebber moest ik hier een kijkje nemen. 
 Al snel viel mijn oog op The Boek Thief omdat ik er zoveel van had gehoord en besloot deze te lenen. Bij het zwembad op een luie middag (het festival duurde 7 dagen en met 42 graden heb je soms echt behoefte aan een ochtend/middag zwembad) begon ik met lezen. In het vliegtuig naar huis een paar dagen later had ik hem alweer uit. 
 Het boek was goed, niet vreselijk -mijn wereld is op slag veranderd iedereen moet hem lezen- maar gewoon goed. Helaas viel dit dan weer tegen. Ik had er zoveel over gehoord dat ik een soort meesterwerk had verwacht. Het was zo'n zelfde 'rageboek' als The Fault in Our Stars (die overigens alle fame waard is) maar deze was niet zo mind blowing als ik had verwacht. Daarentegen moet ik wel zeggen dat het een van de betere boeken van dit jaar is en zeker het lezen waard. 
 Het leukste is dat het boek wordt geschreven vanuit het perspectief van de dood. Dit klinkt heel cru, maar de dood heeft ook gevoelens en verteld puur het verhaal van het meisje Liesl en zijn aanrakingen met het meisje maar ook alles wat er tussendoor in haar leven gebeurt. Erg leuk verzonnen en origineel. Helaas kwam ik er zelf pas na een paar hoofdstukken achter (traag van begrip?) omdat ik niet de achterkant had gelezen waardoor het nogal verwarrend overkwam. 
 Ik wil heel erg veel over het verhaal zelf vertellen maar om eerlijk te zijn zou dat het voor toekomstige lezers verpesten. Het verhaal is mooi en niet heel erg extreem. Gewoon wat je zou verwachten wat mensen in de tweede wereldoorlog die in Duitsland wonen zouden hebben meegemaakt. Niet extremer gemaakt dan dat het is, en dat maakt het verhaal krachtig. Het mooiste is de schrijfstijl van Markus Zusak het is een vloeiend verhaal en kan op veel momenten zelfs licht poetisch worden genoemd. De karakters zijn goed beschreven en hebben een goede sterke persoonlijkheid. 
 The Book Thief is het lezen waard als je eraan toekomt en is erg origineel. Ik heb geen tranen moeten laten zoals bij veel verhalen over dit onderwerp maar dat maakt het des te krachtiger. Het is een heel menselijk boek met een donkere twist en krijgt van mij 3,5/5 sterren.

This book broke me once and it took the journey with it until that point to earn my tears. 
 Death has a horrible, relentless job and, as he reflects, World War II kept him busy. His purpose is to take us through his experience with the story of one little German girl, Liesel Meminger, and a slice of her life from 1939-1943. 
 You don't need anyone to tell you what was happening in Europe during this time. What The Book Thief does right, however, is keep the story focused on the lives of the common German citizens Liesel interacts with: neighbors, nuns, foster parents, shop keepers, best friends.The violence, brutality, and slow-suffocating oppression of being a German citizen under the Nazi party is of course apparent. There's an entire abandoned street of gutted, slur-smeared Jewish homes. People suffer under rationing and for falling out of favor with the local Nazi officers. But shrink the experience to Lisel Meminger's level, and the story is about these things, yes, sinking their fingers progressively deeper into her life, but also of a little girl and the people she loves and how they find ways to maintain their humanity and love one another while the war plays out in microcosm in their everyday lives. 
 Enough tragedy and simple human warmth happens in The Book Thief to make anyone misty eyed. But it took the slow layers of story and emotion to build up for me to tip over, just a little, when Death himself has to take a moment to collect himself while gathering souls from the death camps. That scene is part of his objective in telling the story--not to make the reader cry (though, I mean, it worked)--but that scene, followed shortly by his reflection on the residents of Himmel Street huddled together in a basement during an air raid: 
 "As is often the case with humans, when I read about them in the book thief's words, I pitied them, though not as much as I felt for the ones I scoped up from the various camps at the time. The Germans in basements were pitiable, surely, but at least they had a chance. That basement was not a washroom. They were not sent there for a shower. For those people, life was still achievable." 
 And his final statement at the book's end. 
 Those cornerstone moments need the rest of the story to be effective: the layering of the humanity and brutality, simplicity and hypocrisy of people just trying to be people in an uniquely difficult period of history. That process is where The Book Thief shines. 
 Death isn't human, but he has a heart. So his narration is often as alien as it is tender. My complaints with him are pretty small: he can't help himself when it comes to irony, and sometimes that and his propensity to jump ahead of himself and cap off a scene with a cliffhanger glimpse of doom can be a little much. 
 There's also a scene involving a teddy bear that I found a little too saccharine. Its purpose in highlighting a quiet moment of humanity was apparent but, nonetheless, in a book filled with moments that were handled with more subtlety, I found it a bit too on the nose. 
 Otherwise, this book is beautifully done. 
 4 stars.

Ok, let's try this. I hope my keyboard stays dry and I will somehow sob through this review. 
 I always tend to start with the cover, so I'll stick to that routine. I like a simple cover that somehow resembles the key element of the book. This cover does just that. It's simply perfect. Death is dancing with Liesel. 
 The layout of the whole book, the quotes and the drawings are refreshing and made the whole story unique. 
 The most amazing and unique thing? 
 The story is told from Death's perspective. I admit, first I wasn't too sure if I liked the idea of Death narrating the whole story but after reading a few pages I just couldn't get enough of this particular writing style. 
 The most most amazing and unique thing? 
 Death has a personality. He likes colours. He is kind enough to warn you ahead of time of someone's death. From the very start Death will tell you something about the ending that they will all die, so he somehow spoils his own story. I liked Death's snarky side comments, as well as his wish to grasp the human mind. 
 The most most most amazing and unique thing? 
 The characters. Liesel, Max, Hans, Rudy and even Rosa. They went directly to my heart, and never left. The development of the relationship between Liesel and her foster parents (especially with Hans) was heartwrenching and oh so sweet. The friendship/lovestory between Liesel and Rudy was so freaking cute and I always smiled whenever I've read Rudy saying "How about a kiss?". The relationship of Max and Liesel is one of the rarest and purest kind of friendship. Neither did they share blood, nor were they of same age. They were bounded to each other by the power of words and their love for books. But the most amazing character was definitely Hans Hubermann. The wise man with the Accordion. Liesel's fosterfather with silver eyes. He occupies a special little corner in my heart. 
 A few words on the german. Markus Zusak did an amazing job in using the bavarian language, and it was quite entertaining to read his translations. I can understand that to some readers, these phrases and translations can be irrelevant, bothersome or even frustrating, but for me it was quite funny, entertaining and hilarious. There is nothing more frustrating when authors misuse certain languages by not knowing them or by using google translator for their translations. For me, it was refreshing to spot german words and sentences while reading The Book Thief. 
 The Book Thief is a wonderful book, full of beauty and pain. It's heartwarming and heartbreaking at the same time. 
 "The juggling comes to an end now, but the struggling does not. I have Liesel Meminger in one hand, Max Vandenburg in the other. Soon I will clap them together. Just give me a few pages." p. 175 
 "Even death has a heart." p. 252 
 "They say that war is death's best friend, but I must offer you a different point of view on that one. To me, war is like the new boss who expects the impossible. He stands over your shoulder repeating one thing, incessantly.'Get it done, get it done.' So you work harder. You get the job done. The boss, however, does not thank you. He asks for more." p. 319
