book_b.user_review: I'm not going to review this properly. I'm just going to say that I read this for school, and I have to write a paper on it, so I've read a couple of articles as well. The text deals with feminism and patriarchy (which I barely know how to spell by the way). It can't really be called a book, seeing as it is very short, but I'm going to count it anyway, because why not.

sample_reviews.review_text: Oh my this is such a great great story! it is a true classic everyone should read at least once, the narrator is so insiteful on the woman experience and the lack of creative outlets they had at the time and how those who wanted to be creative and do such things as write were seen as sick and were told they were much to fragile and needed rest and no stimulation, and how this fact drove most really crazy! and the ending is awesome and morbid and twisted! I loved it!

An excellent short story that explores a woman's mental breakdown as she is denied any kind of creative outlet or independence. I couldn't help thinking of the song The Ballad of Lucy Jordan as I was reading it. I was surprised to discover the story was written in 1892 as it seems much more modern in its style and themes.

A quick read since it is a short story and thus gets into the nitty-gritty very fast. I'd have to say this is a rather sad story in that watching a character such as watching someone descend into madness is truly heartbreaking. Some say that her husband is controlling, but I'm not so sure he's controlling in an abusive sense, but rather more so because he truly doesn't understand her. Mental health is to this day still such a highly misunderstood area and that's with today's advances and discoveries, but when this was written, I don't believe even the best doctor's truly knew how to handle it. So I do think her husband was controlling yes, but I believe it was because he truly thought that that was best for her. Was it? I'm not sure. I wonder, had she not been kept to herself and so isolated would she have descended to utterly into madness without hope of returning or would it have simply prolonged the inevitable. I guess we'll never know, but either way, I found it to be fascinating.
A lot was packed in this one little story. It's sad, creepy, horrific. I'm reading it a second time.

What a interesting book! It is so fascinating to observe her behavior as she slips further and further into insanity. The more insane she becomes, the more clearly she sees the woman in the wallpaper until she eventually sees it as being herself!

I absolutely loved this story! It's engrossing all the way through and masterly written. The style seems so modern, and despite its devices not being the summit of innovation, they are wonderfully effective and well done. It's creepy, fun, and brilliant. Totally worth re-reading.
I think I'm one of the very few who found this completely boring and a waste of time.

Classmates and professors have been urging me to read this short story for years - and so finally I caved and downloaded a copy on my phone. Though it certainly does touch on a topic I enjoy - mental illness and women - somehow I couldn't connect with it. 
 Perhaps it was because the narrator was a mother, and older than I am. I think ultimately I just didn't like the writing style. Of course I recognize the importance of including this kind of text in the discourse on gender, mental health, and history - but I just didn't really enjoy it (like most books I encountered in academia).
Good at describing the creeping in of madness (very disturbing) but a bit flat.

reference_books.title: Thor, Volume 1: The Goddess of Thunder
reference_books.review_text: While suuuuper heavy handed at times, it's kind of interesting how exactly real-life controversy about "omg, lady Thor!" is written in here. Still, I'd rather the focus be elsewhere, because I think this is a super interesting story--Thor dealing with self-doubt, the mystery of who the new Thor is, the strife between Thor's parents, and strife between old Thor and new Thor...it's cool and fun and I'm looking forward to more.

reference_books.title: Un Lun Dun
reference_books.review_text:
I ended up really enjoying the end of this book, but it took a reeeeally long time to get there, and I never once forgot that I was reading a book or felt terribly involved in the story. Mieville is certainly very clever, but it felt like either the cleverness got in the way of the story he was trying to tell, or else the story was just an excuse for the cleverness, if that makes sense. I found myself wanting just ONE THING to not be a pun or pithy word combination. That said, once I made it about halfway through the book, I got used to the way UnLondon worked and it stopped being quite so jarring (unlike Deeba's very erratic speech habits). 
 Having finished it, I really like what Mieville is saying--the cleverness of the general plotline I DO admire. But as a whole, the book is choppy and there are pacing issues, and loose ends, and inconsistencies, and cliches, and those things made it hard for me to really LOVE it. I definitely think it's worth a try though--there are certainly some funny moments and some characters that will really grow on you...

reference_books.title: The Dispatcher
reference_books.review_text:
I will admit it, I listened to this mostly because Zachary Quinto is purty and I like his face. I also like his voice, and I feel like he did a really excellent job of narrating, and can he please just narrate all the John Scalzi books now? Sorry, Wil Wheaton, guess I'm ready for a change. 
 Anyway, the actual story. I found the premise really interesting, and was actually totally okay with the fact that we never really find much out about the mechanics. At first. But then towards the end we start to see how the mechanics can be...worked around, and then I realized that I didn't really find the mystery very compelling, and that instead I wanted to learn more about why this was happening and more about how it could be exploited or controlled. I think really I wanted it to be a much longer book, and for that to be the focus instead of the disappearance of some dude we don't really have any reason to care about. 
 Five stars for Quinto! But three for the book as a whole.

reference_books.title: North of Beautiful
reference_books.review_text:
I liked this, but it took me almost half the book to actually get interested in the story. Luckily it was semi-fluffy, so I was able to stick with it long enough to get to the good parts (China). I had a hard time connecting with Terra, and even at the end of the story I wasn't sure how much I liked her--some of the decisions she made just really bothered me. But I loved the way her relationship with her mother changes over the course of the book, and the way her mother's relationship with Terra's abusive father changes, and, heck, even the way Terra herself changes in the second half of the story, though part of me wonders how permanent that will be for her. And, of course, I really liked Jacob. Jacob was great. The cartography references worked well in some parts, but were pretty cheesy in others; they got much more tolerable the further in I got. And I actually did really enjoy the geocaching, and how that connected back to Terra's family history in a neat way. 
 A good story, but I'm not sure it really warrants all the rave reviews I'm seeing on here. That's just me though.

book_a.title: Golden
book_a.user_review:
On the surface, this is a really compelling story about choices made and opportunities passed by, with mystery and romance and poetry thrown in for good measure. I liked the characters well enough, and I found the writing engaging and I stayed interested enough to read a large part of it in one sitting. Though I knew where the story was headed early on, there were a couple of small twists I didn't see coming. 
 But... 
 I guess I find myself disappointed in the ending. Because those twists? They didn't stick, and Kirby sort of goes back and erases them and we end up with the ending I expected all along, where everyone finds love and main character Parker decides not to follow the path she's been set on all her life. And while part of me can respect the decision she makes about her future at the end, part of me is also really bothered by it, and I think it's probably because I'm an adult and have totally gotten over the whole "follow your dreams and do what you're passionate about" idea that so seldom works out for people in real life and am now more about the whole "let's mostly be practical but still have some fun along the way" idea. And I guess it sort of feels like some of what is being said in this book is: a) having goals and studying hard and following the rules is bad, and being a free spirit is good, and b) if you make some really bad decisions they can always be fixed in the end, and c) love at first sight 4-eva! 
 I might be taking this all too seriously, but I wanted a little more reality here, I think. The whole mystery aspect is certainly intriguing and fun and tragic, but I couldn't buy it. Nicholas Sparks is mentioned a number of times, and yes, in a lot of ways this book is like that, and I just...wish it wasn't. 
 So yeah. I mostly enjoyed it while I was reading it, but the way it all ends just really bothers me and kind of ruined a lot of the book for me. Maybe it's because I was totally that kid that didn't really do much crazy in high school and I still feel like my life has turned out just fine. 
 *Shrug*

sample_reviews.review_text:
A fairly easy read, and that includes the conflict, romance & resolution within the story, which for me was a bit of a let-down. I would have preferred it to have gone a bit deeper and darker, considering the subject matter (missing, possibly dead girl & guy; infidelity; stealing property; lying; running away from overbearing parents, etc). I felt like the writing style sort of skimmed along the surface of this book's dark potential without ever getting too challenging or realistic. The characters were enjoyable, but they felt very safe - even "wild" best friend Kat. And the few uses of profanity were carefully measured out and apologised for, and didn't feel like authentic teenagers speaking. 
 But it did have a Judy Blume Tiger Eyes kind of vibe to it, making it an enjoyable, easy read. Fun and lovely and sad, with an 80's feel to the writing style. A great beach book.

I liked the first 75%!!!! As such, lots of spoilers under the cut. 
 NO YOU DON'T JUST WALK AWAY AND LET EVERYTHING THINK YOU'RE DEAD. How awful. And implausible. It also felt like somewhat of a cop out to have her be alive at all. (And she and Orion hung out, what, three times? I am not feeling the epic romance here.) 
 You also don't walk away from a four year scholarship to the college of your choice? I mean, Parker's mom was awful, but I didn't get the sense Parker didn't want college at all. TAKE THE MONEY. You don't have to use it to be a doctor!

This review and more at Sab The Book Eater 
 There really isn't anything I could say to encapsulate just how breathtaking this book is. It was heartbreaking yet beautiful, powerful but in a subtle way. It's a story about self discovery and the choices that define us. It follows Parker and her journey to finding answers to a town mystery and, along the way, finding herself. 
 Golden is probably one of the most well written Young Adult contemporaries I've read thus far. The story was told in a steady pace with a cast of relatable and well written characters. What made me fall in love with Jessi Kirby's writing was how Julianna's journal was written. There's something about the insightful way in which she tried to describe herself by describing the love of her life, Shane. But as Parker went deeper into Julianna's story, we're given a view of how her life took a turn by just one momentous meeting. I wasn't prepared for the rush of emotions I felt with every journal entry. Perhaps it was the idea of reading the words of someone who has passed or it was simply Kirby's impeccable writing (or both) that made something so simple stunning. And it isn't simply about a journal anymore because everything that takes place in the book, every choice that Parker made from the moment she decided to take Julianna's journal, is anchored on it. 
 I loved Parker's transformation throughout the book. She wasn't the kind who took chances on anything because she already had her life mapped out for her. But as the story pushed forward, she learned that chance is everywhere and it's also what life is made of. She learned from the words written in Julianna's journal and lived it. Parker took more risks and did what she just knew she had to do. I think the only thing I didn't like so much about her was how strongly she fought for love and fate towards. She got so caught up in how she wanted things to turn out that she refused to see the implications of what she wanted to happen. But in the end, I still like her. She grew up and made choices that she wasn't sure of but hoped that in ten years or so, would matter. 
 This book had its fair share of cheese though. Names like Orion and Hope, and repeating the Mary Oliver quote 'Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?' over over again ticked me off a little bit (just a little). But after having read everything, I guess it mixed perfectly with the story that I couldn't rate the book less than 5 stars. 
 Golden is a compelling story that leaves the readers something to ponder on, dares the readers to make a life altering decision no matter how scary it seems. It's a perfect coming of age novel that says so much without saying a lot and undeniably leaves a lasting impression. 
 (I received an ARC in exchange for an honest review. This review is based solely on my opinion.)

"What will you do with your one wild and precious life?" 
 People talk a lot about "#YOLO" but I think more people should live like that. There's no reason to box oneself in and repeatedly do the same things. Do something outrageous. Don't be a homebody every day. Be happy.

We can thank Harry Potter, Twilight and The Hunger Games for the current trend of adults devouring YA and New Adult novels. But, not all YA/NA crosses over well. Golden is firmly targeted to teens, with hardly a parent or adult being represented. The one parent that is given a few pages is overbearing and controlling. Of course. I can't imagine any adult, let alone a parent, even less a parent of a teenager who is constantly trying to teach their teen about responsibility and taking charge of their future would like Golden very much. But, teens will eat the message up with a spoon. The message being, as far as I can tell, that 1) a parent that wants the best for you is wrong and 2) making spur of the moment decisions that will negatively impact your future is okay as long as you have a hot snowboarder boyfriend you can fall back on. 
 Hey, I get it. I'm definitely not the target audience for this book. And, I don't think all YA, New Adult or whatever you want to call it, should have a message that is "parent approved." But, to have a "message" book that so clearly disregards both perspectives - the adult responsible one and the YA impulsive one - does a disservice to the target audience. In Golden, the author didn't do a good enough job of showing why the MC's decision was the right one. As a result, Golden will be one of those books that teens love but, when they revisit it as adults, they will wonder what the hell they were thinking.

This review first appeared on my blog: http://www.knittingandsundries.com/20... 
 From the opening: . . . our worlds are sometimes balanced on choices we make and the secrets we keep. 
 Parker Frost is 17-years-old, a girl who has always done what was expected of her and at the beginning of this novel, it is all starting to pay off. She has been chosen as a finalist for the Cruz-Farnetti scholarship, which will give her a free ride to the Stanford pre-med program. Her father, a writer and professor, has always insisted that they are distant relatives of Robert Frost, and excerpts of his poetry appear throughout the novel. Her mother, disappointed in her own life, has been the main force in Parker's life so far. She wants her daughter to make better, more logical, choices than she herself made, and she takes no pains to hide her disappointment whenever she feels Parker isn't measuring up. 
 The Cruz-Farnetti scholarship was founded after the death of a "golden couple" - Julianna Farnetti and Shane Cruz - in a car accident ten years before. Although their bodies were never found, the Jeep they were in was found half-submerged and they are presumed dead. 
 Parker works a teaching assistant for a well-liked teacher named Mr. Kinney. One of Mr. Kinney's senior projects calls for the students to keep a journal of their life, hopes, and ambitions, and hand it in to him at the end of the year. He then seals the unread journals to send back to the students ten years later. 
 When Parker goes through the lot of journals to be sent back this year, she comes across Julianna's journal. Against her normal nature, she decides to keep the journal for a while and to read it herself. As she reads, she comes across quite a few surprises. Her friend Kat has been urging her to do "something bold" just once before she goes off to college, and the journal provides the impetus for her. When she finally shares the journal with Kat, they both decide to find answers. When Kat shares the discovery with Trevor, the boy who has had a crush on Kat since forever, all three find themselves on a road trip that may change not only their own destinies, but others as well. 
 I don't know how to sum up this story. The synopsis does not do it justice, although the title does. This book IS golden - it shimmers with emotion, and hopes, and longings. As I opened the pages and began reading, I was totally immersed in Parker's story. She is a reflection of all of us who strived to do our best to succeed in high school and beyond. She's like all soon-to-be-adults - seeking and questioning and wondering. Coupled with Julianna's tragic story, the reader is rooting and hoping and sometimes even finding a tear or two rolling down as they continue to read. I'm not a huge Nicholas Sparks fan, but this story pulled those kinds of emotional heartstrings without being overly dramatic or sentimental. 
 This is a perfect read for any age. I believe it's billed as "New Adult", but this older adult loved it. An emotional, heart-tugging read with a bit of mystery and romance. Highly recommended. 
 QUOTES: 
 Kat will end up staying here because the mess that is her mom will make her feel like she has to. Where my mom drives me insane with her never-ending sermons on how important it is that I achieve more and do better than she did, Kat's seems to wonder why her daughter should ever want or deserve anything beyond a job that barely pays the bills, an endless string of guys she hopes will, and the resulting need to find comfort in a bottle when they don't. 
 She meant I should do something unexpected that would leave me with something I could keep and remember. An experience instead of a goal. And I get what she means. She's right about me not having very many of those to show for four years of high school. But it seems to me that the experiences that stay with you, the things you'll always remember, aren't the ones you can force, or go looking for. I've always thought of those things as the ones that somehow find you. 
 True love, meant to be, fate, destiny, serendipity, kismet. They're all his romantic words. Words saved for movies and books and fiction. Not for real life. In real life parents get divorced and people live unfulfilled lives and love goes unrequited and there are no second chances or do-overs or perfect moments. 
 BLOGGERS: Have you reviewed this book? If so, please feel free to leave a link to your review in the comments section; I will also add your link to the body of my review. 
 Writing: 4.5 out of 5 stars 
 Plot: 4 out of 5 stars 
 Characters: 4 out of 5 stars 
 Reading Immersion: 5 out 5 stars 
 BOOK RATING: 4.4 out of 5 stars

"Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?"* 
 Where do I start with this review? Jessi Kirby's latest is full of surprises, mix-matching contemporary with a mystery that's darker than one would have expected. Golden made me feel so many things at once, it's hard to describe just how much I felt for this book. It's a wonderful read that deserves all the hype and more! 
 Parker Frost is the model student, the daughter every parent longs for: smart, hardworking, and obedient. But she's about to graduate from high school without ever doing something adventurous or risky - something which her best friend has strived to change from day one. Her wish comes true when Parker stumbles across Julianna Farnetti's journal... and decides to take a look, discovering things that no one had ever known, or would've guessed. 
 I have to thank Blythe for convincing me to read this book. Despite the fact that I would much rather curl up with a good science-fiction/post-apocalyptic read, something about her review just made me want to pick the book up. So I did. And I have absolutely no regrets. Golden is the kind of book that will hook you, tear you apart, and yet, you'll still come back for more. Jessi Kirby pulls you in with smooth and easy writing that demands all your attention; I just couldn't stop reading. 
 Rarely have I read a book where both the plot and characters are practically flawless, but Golden was - is - one of them. It was so easy to fall into Parker's shoes and connect with her. Cheering her on became second nature as she struggled to piece together the mystery surrounding Julianna and Shane's death, ten years ago. I loved how real the characters felt to me, though I have to say that Kat is my favorite so far! Impulsive and fun, she brings a lightness to what could've easily been a much darker story. 
 This brings me to the plot, the heart of the book. I loved how Kirby combined contemporary and mystery together, because they worked brilliantly with each other. Unexpectedly, too, there were two love stories here: one that could end happily (I'm not telling you), while the other was tragic and surprising at the same time, because everything, everything, was shrouded in mystery and suspense. I was kept guessing until the very end. 
 abbreviated. 
 PROS: The characters; story and plot; emotional; brought tears to my eyes; full of surprises 
 CONS: None! 
 OVERALL: Golden is, without a doubt, one of the best contemporary reads of 2013 so far. In fact, Blythe managed to sum up my very long and boring review with two words: "Read Golden." A must-read for all those contemporary lovers who are tired of the same-old stories, and who're looking for something that will sweep them off their feet. 
 *Quote from poet Mary Oliver, also mentioned in the book.

book_b.title: The Hound of Rowan (The Tapestry, #1)
book_b.user_review:
I haven't gotten too far in this one, but I'm already really annoyed with it. Most people seem to dislike it because they think it's a Harry Potter rip-off. I just don't like how it's written. 
 I read the first book in Neff's most recent series, Impyrium, not too long ago and really enjoyed it, so I was looking forward to visiting the same world in a previous time. But I feel like Neff's majorly grown as a writer since this one came out. 
 The Hound of Rowan seems aimed at a way younger audience, and so far everything just feels extremely forced and awkward to me. The humor is dumb, the decisions people make seem nonsensical, and I already kind of hate the main character's dad. 
 I just don't have the patience to push through this and get to the (maybe) good stuff, at least not right now. I'll stick with the more recent series for the time being, but I'm abandoning this one.

sample_reviews.review_text: This book is basically a Harry Potter rip-off. While it has some differences (for example, technology is embraced not eschewed; the kids have animals that they care for; the kids come from across the world, not just the UK), it's pretty similar - ie: the kids have untapped powers, the kids are specially selected, the kids go through a process similar to the sorting, there is a school sport (soccer-esque), there is a powerful yet charming headmistress, quirky teachers, and a villainous group that seeks to thwart them. Basically Harry Potter. The story follows Max as he starts his new life at his new school, has some adventures, figures out a mystery, saves the day, etc. I could see why kids would enjoy the book, but for me, it was too similar to Harry, and no where near as good.

I had really high hopes for this book based on reviews. Unfortunately, I was not able to finish it. Struggling to get through it, I managed to read approximately 100 pages before giving up. 
 The story line in many ways was similar to Harry Potter and although there were differences The Hound of Rowan just fell short.

Si extranabas Harry Potter, entonces ya hay una solucion, claro esta que es la solucion si lo que quieres es volver a leer Harry Potter escrito por otro autor y con los nombres de los personajes algo cambiados. 
 Y es que me parecio terriblemente familiar todo lo que iba leyendo, desde la academia de magia, el metodo de seleccion, el mentor que va a buscar a nuestro protagonista, el personaje paternal que es medio inutil, el hogar incompleto del protagonista, la imposibilidad de abandonar la academia aun en temporadas vacacionales, el pueblo magico fuera de la academia, el enemigo innombrable ... y podria seguir colocando similitudes a lo large de hojas y hojas. 
 Sin embargo me parecio entretenido. Sigo esperando el segundo titulo para volver a vivir mis aventuras magicas.
I really like it..... very much dY~S

Wonderful--I loved the main character. I loved the initial Chicago setting because I was familiar with exactly what was described. I loved the world of fantasy that was created at Rowan Academy particularly the animals. I liked how fast the plot kept moving. I liked how there are so many questions left unanswered in anticipation of the next book. Thank you to my fifth grade patron, Lauren, who did an amazing book talk to me about it. She was right!

Max McDaniels ist auf den ersten Blick ein ganz normaler Junge, der mit seinem Vater glucklich zusammenwohnt und ein bodenstandiges Leben fuhrt. Es gibt aber auch eine andere Seite von Max McDaniels: Er entdeckt bei einem Museumsbesuch einen Raum, der gar nicht existieren sollte. Dadurch wird er fur das Internat Rowan entdeckt und angeworben. Rowan ist ein Internat fur Magier, indem Kinder fur sechs Jahre lang ausgebildet werden. 
 Nur mit schwerem Herzen lasst sein Vater ihn ziehen und Max lernt auf seiner neuen Schule, dass Magie nicht unbedingt das ist, was er sich vorgestellt hat. Und dazu gehen unheimliche Dinge in Rowan vor, denn fur die Sicherheit der Schuler kann nicht mehr garantiert werden... 
 "Das geheime Portal" ist der erste Band der "Schule der Magier"-Reihe. Vor ca. zwei Jahren habe ich bereits das Buch gelesen, jedoch bei der Halfte abgebrochen, weil ich mich nicht auf die Geschichte einlassen konnte. Da ich aber immer wieder mit diesem Buch konfrontiert wurde, wurde es nun hochste Zeit, dass ich dem Buch eine zweite Chance gebe. 
 Henry H. Neff hat mit "Das geheime Portal" eine kurzweilige, magische Geschichte geschrieben, die doch sehr stark an Harry Potter erinnert. Trotz des Vergleichs hat die Geschichte aber durchaus ihren Charme und kann durch Spannung, Charaktere und einem interessanten Ort uberzeugen. 
 Max McDaniels ist ein mutiger, schlauer Junge, der in den letzten zwei Jahren durch ds Verschwinden seiner Mutter einiges durchmachen musste. Dementsprechend anhanglich ist er, was seinen Vater angeht. Das Einleben in Rowan ist kompliziert, aber kommt mit den Schulern in seinem Jahrgang und den Unterrichtsstunden gut zurecht. So gerne ich Max auch habe, so musste ich auch immer an Harry Potter denken, denn die Gemeinsamkeiten konnen sich nicht leugnen lassen. 
 So haben beide mindestens einen Elternteil verloren, haben auf der Schule einen Erzfeind, bekommen ein Haustier zugeteilt, sind eher schmachtig, sind die Lieblinge der Direktoren und werden ahnlich heldenhaft dargestellt. 
 Auch Rowan weist gewisse Ahnlichkeiten zu Hogwarts auf. Beide Orte stehen nicht auf einer normalen Landkarte, sowohl Harry als auch Max wurden per Brief in die Schule eingeladen, die Unterrichtsfacher sind ahnlich gestaltet. Bei den Bosewichten in der Geschichte sieht es leider genauso aus. Sie sind zunachst nicht sichtbar und es wird viel spekuliert, ob diese noch am leben sind. Hier mochte ich jedoch nicht zu viel verraten. 
 Allerdings ist die Geschichte trotz der ganzen Ahnlichkeiten nicht schlecht. Der Autor hat sich bemuht, etwas eigenstandiges zu schaffen, was ihm mehr oder weniger gut gelungen ist. Ein wenig mehr Henry H. Neff und weniger Joanne K. Rowling hatten dieser Geschichte mehr als gut getan. 
 Stefan Kaminski ist ein unglaublich toller Sprecher, dem ich immer wieder gerne zuhore. Die Art und Weise, wie er die Charaktere zum Leben erweckt ist grossartig. Vor allem bei den Tieren und dem Kuchenpersonal hat er eine absolute Glanzleistung vollbracht. Auch die jeweiligen Akzente sind toll umgesetzt und ich wurde bestens unterhalten. 
 Mit einer Lange von sieben Stunden handelt es sich um die gekurzte Horbuchfassung. 
 Insgesamt konnte mich Henry H. Neff mit dem ersten Band der "Schule der Magier"-Reihe beim zweiten Anlauf einigermassen uberzeugen. Zwar hat die Geschichte hier und da noch einige Schwachen, aber diese werden hoffentlich in den anderen Banden ausgebessert. Wer mal eine etwas andere Internatsgeschichte lesen, bzw. horen mochte, ist hier bestens aufgehoben.

I reead the entire Harry Potter series in May. I see review after review comparing this to Harry Potter, but to me it felt like a combination of a lot of middle grade series like Fablehaven, Percy Jackson, The Magisterium series, with a little tiny bit of science fiction mixed with the fantasy. In other words, the only real comparison to HP is that he receives a letter in the mail to get an evaluation and there is a magic school. And there is references to a chosen one. If that's plagarism, then J.K. Rowling plagiarized as well (that's me being sarcastic). Overall, I think this book diverged from being a Harry Potter replica early on, and had it's on take on the classic chosen one story. 
 While I did enjoy the book, I do think that some chapters could have been longer with greater explanation and description of what was happening. Usually, I complain about books being too wordy, but there were some scenes in this story that felt too abrupt. I really liked Max, and he reminded me more of Callum Hunt from the Magisterium series than Harry Potter. He's a little darker, more angry, and has less control of his power than most heroes. This recklessness will likely lead to interesting future plots (yes I know this book came before the Magisterium series). I do wish some characters, for instance Alex would have been further explored, but as this is the first book in a series, I might find that this is dealt with in the sequel books. 
 Anyway, this was a solid start to a series. I have plans to continue on with the 2nd book.
Enjoyed it, but it skipped over certain scenes that could have been very interesting and fun to read. I'm sure this was done to save space, but at the same time it was disappointing.

If you liked Harry Potter, you will like this book. 
 The Hound of Rowan is essentially about a young boy named Max who happens upon a rather mysterious tapestry. After his discovery, many strange things begin to happen; people begin to follow him, and he also learns that he has special abilities. 
 Max is whisked off to the Rowan Academy where he is introduced to a world of magic and mythology. All of the students at Rowan Academy are just like him, and some of the staff there are out of this world. But then terrible things begin happening at Rowan Academy, and Max finds himself sucked into a mystery far bigger than he ever imagined. 
 Had I not seen so many similarities between this book and Harry Potter, I may have been able to enjoy it for what it was. It's not a terrible read, and is quite entertaining. However, by the end of the book I found myself completely uninterested in finding out what happens next. I don't think I will be reading the second book in the series any time soon, though my tendancy to want to see something through once I've begun it may win me over yet.
i enjoyed this book quite a bit. Kind of along a similar storyline as Harry Potter, but it has it's own uniqueness to it. I would recommend this to many friends.

reference_books.title: The Reformed Vampire Support Group
reference_books.review_text: This is an interesting look at vampire myth. Lots of times the down side to being a vampire is explored - not being in the sun, no garlic and the like - but this is the first time that I've seen a story where it is all downside. There is no compensation for what is lost. And that makes for a rather angry and sad group of vampires who wish they weren't. Nina is forever fifteen and everything is always the same. And every Tuesday she meets with the same group of rather sullen and depressed vampires who never change either. Until one of them is killed and after about 50 years she finally has to grow up. It's a nice change from the other vampire stories I've read. I think it's interesting how it can somehow have a coming-of-age feel to it when the youngest person there is 50 years old. And I like how it is about overcoming people's low expectations of you and the low expectations you have of yourself. The vampires are a group of interesting characters and the story is familiar in some ways but still new. And the mystery and suspense, along with the bickering of people who have been stuck with each other a long time, keep things going at a good pace. It's not the best young adult novel I've ever read, nor is it the best vampire book I've read but it is fun, the characters compelling, and the plot enjoyable.

reference_books.title: Halting State (Halting State, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I liked the premise of this book. I liked the idea of a virtual bank robbery. I liked how it took place in the not so far off future so you had interesting new technologies but they were in a world you still recognized. I liked the changing point of view. I even liked the way it all wrapped up. So I really wished I had enjoyed actually reading the book more. Maybe it was because I am not the target audience for this book. Or maybe I just needed to concentrate a lot harder. But I found myself reading and getting just the gist of the story without ever fully understanding what people were saying. I didn't have trouble with the Scottish accent or the changing point of view but as soon as anyone started to explain how something worked everything went hazy. It was worth reading and I was able to follow the plot but a lot of the finer points were lost on me. Although maybe someone who is more into virtual reality and online gaming would not have this problem.

reference_books.title: Shades of Grey
reference_books.review_text: The world has become a place where seeing in color is becoming a thing of the past and no one knows why. Something terrible happened in the past and no one knows what that was either. There are rules you must follow and conventions you are expected to conform to but no one knows where they came from. Fforde throws you right into this new world without any warning. I like the fact that he does not feel the need to take us by the hand and carefully explain every little thing. But it does mean that you have to give the book a chance. At first there are a few things that just don't make much sense but as you move along things start to fall into place. Some things at least. Some things continue to elude you as they do for the characters themselves. Why is no one allowed to make spoons? It is a rule and must be obeyed but no one knows why. Why can't poor Eddie make suggestions for a better queuing system? Well, it just isn't done. People have been following the rules so rigidly for so long that no one can remember what they were made for in the first place. The lack of colored sight has made color so important that is rules everything. And everyone lives under the constant fear of Reboot, this vague punishment that you know is bad but are uncertain of the specifics. It is a depressing place if you think about it. But Fforde manages to work his wit and humor into the book so that it is not all depression. He tells you that librarians draw circles around their eyes and connect them with a line cross the bride of their nose as a sign of their job but no one can remember what it means. The people have to be on the look out for killer swans. And the characters are fun and entertaining. But it all happens in a world where people who can't see any color are treated as inferior. Where strict conformity to the rules is expected and enforced. Where curiosity and questions will get you in trouble. Where Eddie is forced to find out cold, hard things that there will be no turning back from. Where he will have to decide what is the greater good and how much he is willing to give up for it so he can make life and death decisions. So it isn't that Fforde does not address serious issues in the book but they are blended with a subtle lightheartedness that stops the entire tone of the book from being depressing and at the same time manages to make the ugly parts of the society stand out and still look ugly. And in with the humor there is a slight sense of dread always hanging over everything. It is an oddly fun book for one that deals with issues that are not traditionally funny like prejudice, the dangers of asking no questions and trying to eliminate the past, the consequences of finding truth and figuring out what to do with it, and making hard choices about what is truly important. It is the first book in a trilogy so there are many things that are left unexplained and unresolved at the end of the book but it did come to a nice place to take a pause before the next book which you will want to read to see how everything works out.

reference_books.title: The Penelopiad
reference_books.review_text: I guess you have to give points for the idea of putting in a Greek chorus but after the first few had so many silly rhymes I was put off by the whole thing. As for the rest? Well, Penelope does tend to go on. Maybe I would be bitter too after her life and then how ever many years in the underworld. But I hope not because it turned Penelope into a terrible bore.

reference_books.title: Mistress of the Art of Death (Mistress of the Art of Death, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Franklin does a wonderful job of bringing the setting to life. It is filled with suspicion and hate, intolerance and superstition. It is a dark dangerous place but you also get to see the hope and the good of the people who Adelia meets along the way. The acts committed against the children are bloody and horrid and they are often described in detail. And Adelia, being a doctor and trying to be impersonal, talks about the things that were done in cold scientific facts that gives both the crimes and her a hard edge. Adelia is a woman in a field where women are not accepted and she has had to learn not only to deal with the hard facts of her profession but also with working under the constraints placed upon her by society. To do that she thinks of herself not as a woman but as a doctor and sometimes I think she pushed the point too hard and too often and her constant reminders of who she is and what she knows makes her come off as pompous. A romance develops that you can see coming and I don't know that it adds much to the story but it doesn't detract from it either. The ending is rather sensational and dramatic as compared to the rest of the book. And maybe it is not completely historically accurate but any faults I found in the story I was able to overlook because it was enjoyable to read. Adelia and the characters around her, including the dog, are interesting and well drawn. The reader is provided with a good picture of the world of the time and the thoughts and politics of the people. There are enough suspects and danger and clues to make the mystery fun to follow. And it is even alright if you can figure out a few things before you are told because you will still want to read through to the end.

book_a.title: Godmother: The Secret Cinderella Story
book_a.user_review: A dark twist on the Cinderella story. Poor Lil, once Cinderella's godmother, has been banished from her fairy home to a life among mortals and the story switches between her two lives. You get to see her life as a fairy and the events that led to her banishment parallel to her life as a human and her efforts to get back to her fairy home. Lil is likeable and you feel for her as she aches for what she has lost and you wonder what she could have possibly done to be banished from her home. It is a sometimes heartbreaking story about loss and the search for redemption. Although based on the Cinderella story this is a unique story all of Turgeon's own and I enjoyed the small things about the fairies, living under water, the fact that they have different kinds of wings, that made them different then ones I had read about before. In both story lines you can feel something coming. You are aware from the beginning that something goes wrong with Cinderella and in the human world you can see Lil start to fall apart. It fills them with tension and foreboding, almost dread, of the crash you know is coming. It grabs your attention and pulls you along to the stunning conclusions to both, conclusions that you anticipate but somehow still don't see coming. I really enjoyed the book but it is not to be read if you are looking for happily ever after.

sample_reviews.review_text: This is the story of Cinderella's godmother, post-fairy tale. I didn't read the other reviews here but I'm sure that others are more than happy to provide a synopsis, so I won't bother. This book brought me to tears. I felt such sympathy for the protagonist, beginning to end, and I hoped for a happy ending for her. I don't want to say much more than that because I don't want to give anything away at all. I highly recommend it, however!

I expected when I picked up this novel to enjoy a light hearted quick read. There is a story within a story here. After you finish the book you will gasp at the sub context of this book. Sure Cinderella is here , and faeries too but the under lined story is Lil and her blocked out memory of a tragedy from long ago. 
 I did like this book but felt the darkness coming the more I read. Other reviewers stuck with the Godmother theme of Cinderella but it is so much more than that. 
 Lil the main character is in love with old copies of Fairies and childhood happiness. In her life a major twist of fate left her without her sister. She places herself in the role of Fairy Godmother and functions near enough to work, live and hide at her apartment. 
 The book has several revolving flashbacks that manage to hold the story plot together. Expect to be shocked when you finish this book.

I thought this would be a good twist on the fairy tale, but I only got 100 pages into it. The Godmother just moaned about how miserable she was. I'm pretty sure how the whole thing ends, so I didn't feel compelled to finish it...

Lil, an old woman who works in a bookstore has a secret--she was the fairy godmother who was supposed to get Cinderella to the ball to fall in love with the Prince. Lil breaks the rules by falling for the Prince herself and is banished to the human world, living her days hiding her past and her white fairy wings. Lil thinks that if she can find love for a girl that wanders into the shop, she can return to her sister, friends and fairy life. 
 I was sent a free proof of this book and it sat around for quite a while as I didn't think it was something I would like but I actually found it to be engaging and fun. Liked the book, hated the ending though.
It's weird and the fairy/godmother turned woman kills herself in the end. Only she thinks she is returning to her fairy world.
Oh what a waste of 9 hours of reading and made the airplane rides that much longer!!!!! Horrible and such a letdown.

Do you like fairy tales? Godmother: The Secret Cinderella Story is a fascinating read by Carolyn Turgeon. The main character is Lil, a fairy godmother who was cast out from her kingdom and forced to live as a human because she fell in love with the Prince. 
 The author weaves a mesmerizing tale of overwhelming desire, heartbreaking loss and the search for redemption. Her storytelling evokes images of those long-ago days where, at least on the surface, right and wrong seemed so obvious. It was place where princes were good and a time where choices were clear. While this is what makes the protagonist's decision is so blindingly wrong, it is also what makes us empathize with Lil. 
 Presently, Lil works in a very dusty old bookstore in Manhattan; Lil is a little dusty herself, having been living her human existence close to 300 years. She misses her fairy world, her sister and friends with a deep and painful sadness. She knows she does not belong to the human world, but failing as Cinderella's fairy godmother leaves her banished, old and alone. The only vestige of her previous life are her glorious white wings that she must keep hidden. 
 She is employed by George, the handsome son of a wealthy New York family. George spends his days buying collections of old books and nursing his wounds from a recent divorce. Lil longs to help him find someone so he can love and be happy again. After meeting Veronica, a beauty with wounds of her own, Lil realizes that in order to get back to the world she loves, she needs to be the fairy godmother that brings George and Veronica together. 
 Lil begins to see that by aiding the couple, she will be redeemed and returned to her fairy self, sister and kingdom. She becomes aware of the presence of fairies all around her in a series of signs that give her hope and strength, for she believes "What occurs in the world of faerie will become manifest in the world of men." 
 Though there is a twist that makes you re-think all that you've read before, the book is well-written and one I am glad I read. Is Lil who she thinks she is? Or is her mind masking the reality of what happened to save her from even more pain and sadness? Who is Lil, really? I am now more interested in reading the author's next book Mermaid to see if it will follow a similar trajectory. Now if only they would stop putting those annoying book club questions at the end. They make me feel like I have to read Silas Marner next. 
 Published 2009 by Three Rivers Press, an imprint of the Crown Publishing Group, a division of Random House, Inc., New York 
 Read more book reviews at http://inkandpage.me

Well, at first, I really loved this book - the beauty and romance of it all was initially intoxicating. But the crushing reality of its ending ruined the whole book for me. It really did. Too many questions were left hanging... and for all that magic to be stomped away, it really left a reader wanting to read something else. I wouldn't recommend this to anyone who wanted to be disappointed. This one retold fairy tale that really lost the magic of its medium.

Godmother was a cute but sad story. You really feel for the godmother and hope she makes it home. This is not a normal telling of Cinderella and it really make you think out the tales we were told as kids. It is not your grandmothers bedtime story.

This book was a retelling of Cinderella from the Fairy Godmother's point of view. It takes some liberties with the original Cinderella story. In this book's version, the Fairy Godmother was young and beautiful like Cinderella. She majorly screwed up when trying to help Cinderella get to the ball and was banished to live as a human on earth as punishment. 
 The beginning and middle of this book was so slow I had trouble maintaining interest. The last twenty pages were exciting - I would have expanded this section and fleshed it out more. I spent most of the book waiting for something to happen and when it finally did, it was over in a flash.

book_b.title: Just One Look
book_b.user_review: This book has a quick start right out of the gate. You don't have to wait a long time for something to happen. And it never stops for long. The suspense starts right away and Coben manages to keep it going. There are enough twists and turns and false leads and partial answers that lead to new questions that you don't lose the tension along the way. There is a lot going on here. You jump from scene to scene and have to keep track of a lot of characters (some of whom you never actually meet) in a complex plot. A very complex plot. There are people who are not who they appear to be, pasts that come back to haunt people, memory loss, creepy killers and just about anything else you can think of. They are all pieces in a puzzle you don't have the picture for so it is a surprise when you finally see how they all fit together. And the surprises keep coming to the very last page. There are some points that are a bit of a stretch and push you almost to the point of unbelief and it also stops just short of being too convoluted and becoming confusing. But it is written well enough that it never really loses you. It's a good fast paced thriller.

I found the blend of violence and ordinary suburbia a bit too raw for my taste.[return][return]Coben certain created engaging characters.[return][return]Some quotes;[return][return]'I'm a swarm of useless facts.'[return][return]Being a mother, Grace thought, was a lot like being an artist -- you are always insecure, you always feel like a phony, you know that everybody else is better at it than you. The mothers who doted obsessively on their offspring, the ones who performed the numbing tasks with that Stepford-ready smile and supernatural patience -- you know, those mothers, always, have the right supplies for the ideal after-school craft ... Grace suspected that these women were profoundly disturbed.

The usual excellant page-tuner from Coban. Great characters, suspense, huge plot twists and much action make this a tough book to put down. His stand-alone novels have been better than his most recent Myron Bolitar novels.

A few pages in, the killer manages to pull out a spinal nerve of someone with his fingers. This paralyzes the victim from the chest down and he is laid in a tub to be tortured. Once I read that, I was sufficiently grossed out that I skipped to the end to figure out what happened in the end.
Like all Coben's books, this one was very compelling and also ridiculously convoluted.

It's easy to forget how highly improbable the whole scenario is as you tear along at breakneck speed. I did like the bit at the end where Scott Duncan is speculating about who might have distracted the security guard at the concert, no need for Grace to feel smug nor sanctimonious. Very entertaining - just what a thriller should be.
Fast moving and suspenseful - I enjoyed this.

Although it was still a decent read much like his other novels, it could be time for Coben to change a little of his formulaic writing. The plot in this novel is so confusing that the last two to three chapters were devoted to explaining it all. It almost felt like the rest of the novel were just fillers.

reference_books.title: Fried Green Tomatoes at the Whistle Stop Cafe

book_a.title: Official Book Club Selection: A Memoir According to Kathy Griffin
book_a.user_review: I'm a big fan of Kathy Griffin, so I figured I would enjoy this book. I expected it to be comical, which it is. However, I did not expect Kathy to lay bare the ugly part of her life. But, she did, and she did so with a flair peculiar to only Kathy.

sample_reviews.review_text: Hilarious tell-all with funny insights into Seinfeld, Oprah, Andy Dick, and more. Kathy's own obstacles of a drug addict borther and thieving husband balance the memoir well. Don't even try to compare Chelsea Handler with Griffin - Kathy actually has a brain....

This is a better book than some might give it credit for. Yes, it's humorous. Yes, there are bitchy celebrity run-ins, and yes, there are odes to mom and dad. 
 But there's also a lot of heart here, and Kathy gets "real" in many chapters. She doesn't hold back, even when she's detailing sexual abuse from her own brother, her eating disorders, and her lack of self-esteem. If you didn't already love Kathy, this will get you there.

Okay, I really, really enjoyed that! 
 I don't know much about Kathy Griffin. Sure I watched Suddenly Susan, and I've I know her face, but I don't watch My Life On the D-List (though I've always meant to), but maybe it's because I don't know anything about her that I really enjoyed this book. She's so candid, outspoken and frankly one-step from crazy; it really makes it a fun read. A nice way to start the new year.

While I love switching to biographies in between a good love story but I was absolutely shocked with this book and the language content! Every other word was a 4-letter word which totally turned me off! It was so bad I got dis-interested, quick! When I think biography, this is NOT the book I had in mind!
Fun, super fast read. Even the index was funny.

this gets two stars instead of one because I azs able to finish. The whole book in a sentence: who has Kathy Griffin screwed, and how she got there. There are other parts, but most of the book is just name dropping. What someone would expect from this author, nothing more.

Hilarious, laugh out loud, at times touching book. I was surprised by how deeply personal some of the chapters were, and it was great to see how the tough parts of her life made her who she is today. Excellent, highly recommended. Don't read on any sort of public transportation vehicle if you're easily embarrassed by chuckling to yourself.

Though there were a few laugh-out-loud funny parts, there were only a few. I found most of this book a bit dull and/or spiteful. Believe me, I'm just as game for some bitchy gossip as the next woman, but there just wasn't enough of interest in this so-called-comic memoir.

book_b.title: Beauty's Punishment (Sleeping Beauty, #2)
book_b.user_review: Just not what I expected.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I liked this one much more than the first book, or maybe I should say I liked Beauty much more in this one. Here, we see her exhibit some spirit, occasionally rebelling in order to be given harsher punishments. I could relate more to this side of her. She decided not to always be obedient, perhaps knowing that by pushing back she would reach a greater level of submission than if she meekly obeyed every order. This fascinated me as much as it disturbed me, yet ultimately made me adore her more for it. 
 We also get to see the pov of male slave Tristan, who was also disobedient, but for very different reasons: Tristan longed for a firmer hand, the guidance of someone who could and would truly master him with decisiveness and confidence. Once he found what he sought, he began to find peace and contentment in his position as a slave. 
 Overall this story was more fulfilling, and I found a deeper understanding of the mind and soul of a true submissive. No less whimsical than the first book, it nevertheless told a more in-depth and revealing story. And at times, it was also extremely arousing and thrilling. Though again, I did not wish to be Beauty, there were moments in which I truly envied her. 
 The ending of this story leads to another adventure for both Beauty & Tristan. And I'm glad I already have the book - the last in the series - so I can go on this journey with them.
just as good as the first one! a must buy!

This book is so utterly ridiculous. The series as a whole, actually. I am not so naive to think that pleasure and sex doesn't exist - but those aren't the reasons why I am not keen on this read. Let's begin, shall we? 
 First of all, Beauty has sex with a lot of men. She is NOT on birth control. They are NOT using condoms. How is she not pregnant yet? How does no one in this BDSM-driven world not have any STDs yet? 
 Second, how can rape be glorified so much? This is downright shameful. Beauty doesn't even hesitate in welcoming whatever penis decides to enter her. How is that even 'real'? 
 Third, who gets an orgasm from EVERY organ that enters her vagina? Are we really supposed to believe that every object/finger/penis/etc. that enters Beauty sets her off every time no matter who is subjecting her to sure pleasure-torture? 
 Not to mention, some of these people might be inexperienced and yet Beauty still seems to have mind-blowing orgasms from them all. Hard.to.believe. 
 I don't mind erotically written stories. I also don't mind BDSM. However, I do mind when the sole woman protagonist is nothing but a pillow princess who is as helpless as a virgin in a whorehouse. Where's the strong women? Why do all the men have to have such power? 
 Lame. For such a strong female writer to succumb to such a dumb broad as a protagonist is rather disappointing.

The first installation on the series, The Claiming Of Sleeping Beauty, was very good. It was novel and captivating. It also ends in such a way that the I couldn't wait to start Beauty's Punishment, the next installment. 
 I should have waited, or put it off all together. 
 The best summary I can manage without wasting too much of my time is to say this: the continuation is trite, boring, uninspired at best, infuriatingly incompetent at worst. 
 Beauty being a petulant twit in the first book is understandable- she's new and used to being treated like a princess. How she manages to not wise up and quit the babe in the woods routine is beyond me. It's certainly not sexy, just ridiculous. 
 Do yourself a favor and stop with the first book.

I should have really been finished with this book alot sooner but I had to take a break from it. I could throughly handle all the subject matter but at times it just became tedious with all the beatings and sex. Knowing about some of the aspects of the BDSM lifestyle made me think like are you really serious? But then I had to remember that this was a book and it was entertainment purposes. I didn't become interested in the story until the very ending and now I am considering reading the third book in the future because before I was dead set against it.
I was intrigued by the story, but still am not a fan of the sexual torture. Pleasure and pain are even more explained in this book.
Please tell me there is more to this genre. I thought Ann Rice would bring it, but no. Same old stuff.

I like what Anne Rice did with this; it could be simply a retelling starring smut and porn - and that would be fine too, that would be what most might expect to find, but no. 
 She made Beauty into a character, gave her a personality beyond the shadow of a sleeping "Princess", blonde and bland; instead this Beauty is full of subduction and sins, that she discovers as she makes her way in this world where what could be simply submission works to be more, it has a purpose, this book shows the flaws in humanity, in all it's sexual appetites and "kinks"; the driving force of need and beauty.
Same complaints as the first book but more so. I'll read the third to finish the story. Or should I say, what little story there is.
O.O

reference_books.title: The Bourbon Thief
reference_books.review_text:
I received and ARC in exchange for an honest review. 
 The Bourbon Thief is about you guessed it bourbon. Our male lead owns a bourbon bar and a bottle of bourbon worth over a million dollars. Our female lead comes from a family that used to make some of the best bourbon in the world and she likes to drink it also. To sum it up our mc's are obsessed with bourbon but ultimately this story is about what happened to the Red Thread Distillery and people in the past. 
 "Women considered him handsome, and even if they didn't, they considered him rich, which was usually enough to close the deal" 
 Cooper McQueen is handsome, extremely rich, a playboy, and very arrogant. The fastest way to send a man like this off kilter and to wrap him around your finger is to not be overly impressed with him and just show mild interest; Paris expertly deploys this tactic to steal the million dollar bottle of bourbon she feels is rightfully hers. Paris still gets caught and to try and get out of the mess she has got herself into she tells Cooper a story of why the bottle belongs to her. 
 "By the time I'm done telling you the story, you'll hand over that bottle with your compliments and an apology." 
 I'm going to have the unpopular opinion about this book it seems. I think this is a book that like Fifty Shades of Grey is going to be more popular among Baby Boomers then with younger generations. Women in this book seem to have a complex that they need a man in charge of them; they all seem to want an older man that is controlling and that is just a huge turn off to me. Older husbands telling their wives "now do what you're told" just ticks me off, women are not chattel, or property or the lesser sex. 
 "Sit down, Tamara, Levi ordered. He did that sometimes, gave her orders. And she loved it. He was her teacher and her lord." 
 The Bourbon Thief also seemed to be a check list of social issues and I think the author was trying to fit in every social issue she could think of in this story. 
 Gay guy kills himself ....Check 
 Bi-racial character....Check 
 Loads of racial tension in the South.... Check 
 Underage teen girl marries older guy in the South....Check 
 Pedophilia....Check 
 Attempted incest rape....Check 
 Murder....Check 
 Wife having sex with the father in law....Check 
 All women having sex with much older men....Check 
 Rich people getting away with whatever they want....Check 
 Brother and sister unknowingly getting married...Check 
 Brother and sister conceive child...Check 
 Lots of drinking....Check, although that should be expected in a book with a bourbon theme. 
 The southern brother and sister getting married and staying married after they learned the truth seems like a bad stereotype, made even worse that she was an underage teen bride. I kinda felt that the author took every southern stereotype she's ever heard and threw them altogether for the shock value. 
 While there is compelling parts to this story ultimately it's about a family that is sick; it's not romantic, it's not sexy, it's not cool just disturbing and sad. I also didn't find it believable that the billionaire listened to her story and gave her a million dollar one of a kind bottle of bourbon for it. The Bourbon Thief just isn't a story I can like.

reference_books.title: My Sister's Grave (Tracy Crosswhite, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I've only made it to chapter 7 of My Sister's Grave; some things are really annoying right from the start. It might be better if I was not from Washington State and spent had my life living west of the Cascade Mountains. There really isn't anything in the Puget Sound region that is old westy in feel, especially not our state capitol, even in 1990. That is a stereotype one can overlook but the actual beginning police work is horrid. For starters Sheriffs are the head of a county police force, not of a town. Bones found anywhere in the state isn't actually a cause for concern here. It actually happens often that human remains are found and turn out to be old Native American bones that have surfaced or been unearthed somehow. Bones found in the woods would not be cause for any sheriff to be recalled from a vacation immediately and it certainly would not be enough for that sheriff's office to call the family of someone that went missing 20 years ago before the bones even are looked at by the anthropologist. It takes time for an anthropologist to date a set of bones, even if there was any clothing or other items left with the bones to hint of them being more recent it would still take time. Next on my hit list is the lovely word murder... When it comes to skeletal remains they may not even be able to determine a cause of death let along know from looking at a femur a dog dug up that and saying it must be murder. Here someone could have just injured hiking, or got lost and died, murder isn't something that gets tossed around as a fact before they even have found all the bones. These elements have annoyed so much in the first 7 chapters of the book I don't think I will continue.

reference_books.title: Darkness of Light (Darkness, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Darkness of Light is off to a rough start and I don't feel like I'm going to go past the first 25% of this book. I find it annoying when YA books make adults over the top unreasonable. In this case a school principle and a sheriff harassing a girl for what appear to be electrical problems at the school. They have no proof she is involved in any sort of sabotage and the problems apparently show no sign of foul play. The principle and the sheriff are just certain she is behind it though and are blaming her and are making her to go a school for troubled kids anyway or she won't get to graduate and will be expelled... It just doesn't work for me, and many parents would hire a lawyer by this point, but the author needed this to happen to make her plot work out. 
 Another thing that is not working for me is that the story is placed in Olympia Washington, a small city with the population of 50,000 and the author is treating it like it is a really small town. Olympia has 9 high schools and the Thurston county sheriff does not have time to harass one kid over and over again based on something so flimsy and unrealistic. I went and look at the author's bio and see she is not from Washington State and I have my doubts she's actually been to Olympia before. 
 I'll be telling my teen to skip this one.

book_a.title: Monster Hunter International (Monster Hunter International, #1)
book_a.user_review: I like the idea of this book but the writing is really over the top, forced and doesn't make a lot of sense.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Monster Hunter International is like the Twilight series -- through the looking glass. You get to meet every class of monster; but instead of emoting over them, why not just blow them up? 
 With its good humor, cartoon violence, and uncomplicated plot, the book should appeal to adolescent boys. But really it's just a vehicle for Larry Correia to share gun lore. And repeatedly stick it in the eye of vampire lovers. 
 Unfortunately, the book is about 2X too long. The schtick runs thin, and the yucks dry up long before the monster juices do.

I was a bit torn on if I should give this one or two stars, maybe I should have gone with two but decided on one. I think I would have enjoyed this book more if I had known nothing about Larry Correia or his politics but as I have read a bit about the man. This was the first thing that bothered me about the book. I think the best way to describe this book is "gun porn" - there is so much gun porn that the whole thing should be rated NC-17. 
 The plot is pretty straight forward. Man finds out there is a hidden world and that monsters are real. He then joins organization to battle the monsters only to uncover a plot that will destroy the world. There is nothing new here but it is not bad. I would even say that the book is ok in many parts, just filled with so many cliches. 
 I found the characters to be rather unbelievable especially the protagonists love interest, but maybe that's me. I've never lived in rural America and don't know the people there. I found the main protagonist to be cruel, judgmental and almost savage in his behavior. The author's hate of government was silly, as were his prejudices against people who don't share his political views. The tone of the whole thing just bothered me from start to finish. It is like mr. Correia thinks his opinions are right and everyone else is just an idiot, which is a little juvenile in my opinion. But like I said I'm just a European moderate so I'm very far from Correia's world. 
 Also I found the whole set up to be childish. Again maybe I know too much about the author. The main protagonist is an accountant and a loves guns. Larry Corrie was an accountant and loves guns. So the book sometimes feels like the author's dream, like he wishes this would happen to him. There are just too many things that point to this. All the good guys are southern conservatives, everyone that works for the government is an idiot, gun laws are stupid and should be ignored, privet industry is the best (even for monster haunting) and the love interest was something that a 13 year old dreams about (basically a man with tits). 
 So why did I read this? I liked mr. Corriea's Grim-noir book, especially the first one which I thought was great. Why did I finish it? Well even though the story is cliched it is entertaining in parts and there are good scenes (like the one with the elves). But the whole tone of the thing just got to me and I found it just so childish. When I was 12 years old I would have loved this and not even thought about the politics. Problem is, I'm not 12 years old. So I say skip this one.

Free on Amazon Kindle. 
 Dude shoots monsters and blows stuff up. If you're looking for sheer number and variety of shooting-monsters events, this book pretty much has you covered. 
 This book contains some real-world conservative political content. There wasn't actually that much of it. It was still kind of grating.

I wanted to like this book. As a regular reader it's not terrible, but as a writer myself, I couldn't shut off that part of me and the problems just kept piling up. 
 - doesn't really pay attention to "show, don't tell" very well. 
 - Choppy sentences, too many of which start with "I". Many of them could be saved by semicolons. 
 - It's generally suggested to use the word "said" prior to/after dialogue and convey volume or stutters, etc. within the dialogue itself. Using other words (muttered, yelled, commanded) more than sparingly just doesn't flow well. 
 - Z says "Groovy" a few times. He's 24 years old. Since he doesn't seem to throw out any other pop culture references, I doubt he's quoting Evil Dead, so this sticks out. Poorly. 
 - There's so much specific gun info that it gets confusing. So many names and calibers and types that I'm sure other gun nuts get, but as a lay person it's just too much. 
 - For a bunch of hardened monster hunters, many of whom are former military (and many also special forces) there is a weird dearth of cussing. Every time Sam Haven said "Fricking" I rolled my eyes. I'm not saying I need the F bomb every five words but it's weird to see things like "heck" and "darn it" and " oh my gosh" amongst grown men. 
 - Aside from Z's brother, there is no mention of the rest of the Pitt family after his parents leave following the werewolf incident. No "I'll have to figure out a cover story" or anything. Strange. 
 - At the end: they're leaving the artifact to the Feds? After an entire book of people saying how incompetent they are? WTF? 
 - A lot of weird sentences where words that should be contracted aren't. Thy make the sentences read poorly and stiffly. 
 Lastly... Characters can be amazing bad asses without becoming Mary Sues. Z? Mary Sue with a gun fetish. Top of his classes, expert in guns, expert in hand-to-hand combat, trivia whiz, top of the MHI Newbies who becomes part of the elite squad by the end, quite literally a 'chosen one'... Hard to swallow. 
 And even aside from all that, the writing is rough and packed full of cliches and unnecessary repetitions (in one paragraph, he's described as first falling to the floor, and then two sentences later is mentioned falling off his chair). I kept wondering if anyone had thoroughly edited this beyond spelling and punctuation errors. 
 It's crack, I get it. The author even says its meant to be the literary equivelent of a B movie. But that doesn't mean he can't also write it well. Interesting story, poor execution.

This one did not do it for me at all. I didn't mind the underlying story, which was decent urban fantasy fair but the way it was delivered was nearly unbearable. Correia's writing style is so verbose, it felt like every single scene took three to four times as long as it should have to play out. At first I didn't mind to much but as the book goes on it really started to grate on me, to the point where I actually stopped reading it on a few different occasions.

It's books like this one that restore my belief that there's always something else out there you're going to love reading. I'm reviewed over 1,100 books so far on Goodreads, most of them in some sort of fantasy sub-genre. I've been pretty jaded recently, feeling like the creative brainpower behind good fantasy has been lured away towards dystopian fiction. The urban fantasy heyday post-Twilight couldn't last, but it's still my literary love, and when I read this, I fell in love anew. 
 This is a great book: irreverent, quirky, slightly political but not overly so, bloody violent, and wildly creative. Great story line that I've never heard before, and boy were these characters developed - over 700 tightly packed pages of development. I loved how the author turned my urban fantasy expectations on their head. Refreshing and really well done. The orcs and elves are particularly entertaining. Bravo! 
 The premise of the story is that the government keeps monsters under wraps from the public and that private companies hunt the monsters for bounties. Owen is recruited into one such company after fighting off a werewolf. The job suits him, and his boss is H-O-T. Eventually, it comes down to his team to save the world from destruction.

MHI is a fast and loose. Its like the A-Team crashed its van into Sam and Dean from Supernatural, and splattered gore on a bunch of frat-house girls crossing the street, and the whole lot of them stopped to laugh at the scene. 
 Seriously - Great book. Larry has a great style. Yeah, he's known for describing the hardware, but, well, that's awesome. 
 The plot is solid, the humor is good, and there were even some nice twists salt and peppered throughout the novel. I'll certainly be picking up the next book in the series. 
 If I had to sum it all up, I'd say this is pure entertainment. 
 Also, I've had the pleasure of attending some conferences in which Larry spoke. He's a great guy, and I saw the same fun spirit with which he writes come out in person. 
 Good times.

Contrary to the opinion of many others who read this book, my biggest question is whether Larry Correia was attempting a satire of the modern-fantasy genre, or if his love of B-movies made sure that his book was the literary equivalent thereof. Combining a mostly-unlikable cast with the most egregious misuses of action tropes, this book would have been a bigger disappointment had it ever encouraged my expectations to rise above the hope of 'it's so bad it's good.'
A fun read. Good ole shoot em up with a side of apocalypse.
