Und ausgerechnet der attraktivste von allen, Reed Royal, ist besonders gemein zu ihr. Trotzdem fA1/4hlt sie sich zu ihm hingezogen, denn es knistert gewaltig zwischen ihnen. Und Ella ist klar: Wenn sie ihre Zeit bei den Royals A1/4berleben will, muss sie ihre eigenen Regeln aufstellen aEUR| 
 Meine Meinung

I loved Paper Princess by Erin Watt, the pen name for a collaboration between Elle Kennedy and Jen Fredrick. This book had me hooked from the very first page, and I read it in one sitting. 
 Ella is strong & resilient, she's lost her mother, never knew her father. I loved Ella she's such a strong character who does what she needs to in order to survive and support herself. When Callum Royal, appears and takes Ella in as his ward, to live with himself and his five sons, she is thrown from destitution to a world of the opulently rich. Ella struggles being the new girl in town, school and within the Royal family. The book mainly revolves around a high school setting with a group of malicious, snobby rich kids who endeavor to make her life hell. I totally loved her best friend Val, and how two kindred spirits found each other within such an image driven group. 
 "I still believe that there's something good out there for me. I just have to keep going until my time comes, because surely, surely, none of this would happen if there wasn't a reward down the line." 
 Whilst Callum Royal is sweet, awkward and rich. Callum's sons are quite different and give the story depth, fun, tension. Reed Royal, is used to being in control, being in charge of not only his siblings, but his peers within the school. Reed and Ella have this complex, evolving love/hate relationship that keeps you on the edge of your seat for much of the book. The boys are mysterious and all seem to be harboring secrets. 
 "You should know whatever game you're playing, you can't win. Not against all of us.If you leave now, you won't be hurt. If you stay, we'll break you so bad that you'll be crawling away." 
 The characters are not only likable, interesting and believable, they are incredibly fascinating, much like the world of opulence Ella is thrown into. The interactions between the characters keep you enthralled and engaged with this book, there are just so many twists and turns. 
 This book has a bit of everything romance, suspense, mystery, drama and forbidden relationships. In saying that this book is not a traditional romance, there is a potential for a love story between Reed and Ella but it wasn't what the main focus for this story. 
 You won't be disappointed in this book. Although this book ends in a huge cliffhanger, and I really can't wait to read Broken Prince. There are so many ideas rolling around in my head of what will take place in the next one, I can't wait to see what the authors have in store for us. If you can't wait for the next book in this series, maybe wait til they are both available to read them together.

Paper Princess as a novel is a total candy bar: it's wish fulfilment in the extreme, as teenage protagonist Ella (orphaned, working as a stripper) suddenly finds out she's an heiress. Oh, and btw, her brand new stepbrothers (who, conveniently, are not blood-related to her) are all suuuuper hot. 
 There are a few dropped plot lines along the way and it ends on an annoying cliffhanger, but the pace of Princess is zippy, the OMGZ factor is high, and the author(s) mostly pull off what even they admit is a cracktastic story. 
 What's more interesting to me is the self-published Princess as a publishing case study. Because ... oh boy ... this is not your mother's YA fiction. The authors, already established in the romance genre, transplant many of the tenants of "romance" into Princess: there's the hyper-masculine Alpha hero; the wealth porn; the no-imagination-needed sex scenes. 
 The result, of course, is a novel that no YA publishing house in their right flipping mind would publish. The backlash from parents would be incredible. 
 (I'm no prude, but I'll admit that the idea of squishy-brained young people reading Princess makes me feel slightly queasy. I remember how I practically imprinted on YA fiction as a teen. It worries me that young readers would take Princess too much to heart, especially in light of the prevalent theme of "ohhh I just want to be overpowered by a big strong man". This is par for the course in romance novels, but in this context ... eh.) 
 Of course, Princess taps into a reality of the YA genre, which is that some 55% of it is read by adults. As one of those adult-type persons, I am more than happy to read frank sex scenes, prolific cursing, casual drug use, etc. etc. (In fact, I'd argue that any teen novel that doesn't include reference to those things is unrealistic as fuck.) 
 This is the new world of publishing: where authors can bypass squeamish publishing houses and go directly to readers with exactly what those readers want. (And The Royals books have been riding high in the Kindle charts ever since their release, so they must be hitting the spot for readers.) Is it a good thing? A bad thing? IDK, but it's happening. 
 As a hilarious postscript, I see that HarperTeen has now scooped up these authors for a new traditionally-published book. I wonder what that will look like ... 
 A few more notes on the novel itself: 
 - I think the one downer for me in Princess was the thin characterization. There are SO MANY brothers (five, for bewilderingly little reason) and they blur together for much of the novel. Easton gets a bit of a personality, but Reed, who finally emerges as the Love Interest, remains a total cypher. 
 - This is basically a step-sibling romance, but like, that's barely mentioned???? 
 - Speaking of weird subtext, there's a lot of it between Ella and her new stepdaddy Callum. Like ... she does a strip tease for him in the beginning? And he's basically her knight in shining armour? And all the brothers think the two of them are fucking? But then, near the end, Ella's all, "me and Callum? ew, so gross". Like. Meh. C'mon, authors. Don't piss on my leg and tell me it's raining. (Ella/Callum OTP 4eva!!!! ... ahaha, I'm kidding ... OR AM I.)
Train wreck of a book. And yet I'll read the rest of the series. I hope the next books are edited. And I really hope (but doubt) that there is less creepy abusive teen romance...

Seriously, what kind of story is this. 
 I read the first book because I was curious. I read the second book because I didn't want to judge a series by the first book. I read the third because I wanted to see how bad it could get. I read the fourth because the mindfuck had officially drawn me in and I couldn't help myself. It's like a car accident, you know you shouldn't look, but you can't help it. I don't even want to remember the things I've read.

This book just didn't have the right feel to it. It's obviously rushed. Book 1 & 2 are flawless, but the last part of book three and much of book four were full of typos such as missing words, inconsistent verb tenses, and the overuse of the words guffawed and ghosted. I usually don't mind typos. Nobody is perfect, but there were enough to annoy me and take me out of the story, and this isn't some small press book. You would think with such a huge release as this, Meyer would insist on a better editor. Moreover, what was up with the half-assed chromosome explanation for the supernatural creatures? I'm not a biologist, but that just didn't make any sense. Leave it vague or hire a consultant, but don't have your medical doctor sound like an idiot. Beyond the technicalities, this story just feels all wrong. The sexual tension between Jacob & Bella, which served as a powerful catalyst in the first three books, quickly flat lines. Bella was set up for some serious heartbreak and agony in book four. She was going to have to make some serious sacrifices to join the vampire family, but Meyer gives her a pass on all this by granting her a superpower, which comes off as a total copout. Many of the characters seem to be reduced to two dimensional fashion accessories with no real emotions, motivations, or purpose. And the absolute worst thing about this book is that with the forbidden love aspect gone and the entire mystique of the vampire family removed, the romance and passion is nonexistent. Sure Edward & Bella finally get to go the distance, but so what. The love, emotion, and devotion felt between the two in the previous novels is more akin to the love shared by a long married, child-wearied couple of fuddy-duddies. It's hard to think of Edward as a badass vampire when he is changing poopie diapers. (And don't tell me that baby don't shit. If Edward shoots jizz, then that baby fucking shits!) The scene when Edward changes Bella into a vampire, man I was waiting for that since book one, and it was a let down. That scene should have been the orgasm of the book, and it didn't even start to get me off. Overall, it just wasn't the story I wanted and unlike the first three books, I could put this one down.

I'm having a hard time rating this book. Scheeres' story and prose really pulled me in, and her relationship with her brother David, with all of its unlikely turns and challenges, was complex, profound, and well-wrought. 
 With the multiple abuses and struggles in the memoir, it felt like watching a car wreck at times. Despite the dismal retelling of multiple disasters, I feel that the book ultimately succeeded. I came away encouraged by the siblings' persevering friendship and the strength of the human spirit, and intrigued by the religious culture that can allow such abuse to thrive. 
 Unfortunately, Scheeres doesn't explore the larger picture of how religious fundamentalism can create and contribute to racism, sexism, and abusive environments. The book is constricted to a simple, narrow narrative: "here are bad things that happened to me and my brother, perpetrated by bad people." Scheeres dwells on a very two-dimensional cast of supporting characters: the abusive teachers, the violent father, the selfish mother, the fun sister, the stupid hicks, the subversive friends. 
 Especially compared to the rich, nuanced exploration of David and Julia's relationship, these supporting characters all fell flat into tired stereotypes. I hope that, in her journalistic work, Scheeres continues writing on the topics of race, gender, fundamentalism, and abuse. Her story could prove a good jumping off point for a deeper exploration of how these themes intertwine.
I didn't like it because it was disturbing to me.

After reading some of the exaggerated reviews, I expected this book to have details of abuse so horrid that I would have to avoid reading them. But it didn't, Julia told her story of survival and how the love she had for her brother gave her light in the darkest of hours. I was glad to know that she found her "Florida" in the end
competent. not earth-shattering. (it was pretty good. a story worth telling and told with competence.)

i wanted to love this book - but the way the story is told kind of threw me. i think this would have made a great novella, but not a full length memoir.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Scheeres' depiction of her brother David did not sit well with me throughout the book and it made sense once I got to the last chapter and learned he had died in an accident and she had possession of the journal where he'd been writing his life story. She essentially co-opted his story for herself. As I was reading, I couldn't figure out if her casual racism was intentional- was this how she was as a child? was this what she really believed now? It would be one thing to fairly and honestly depict how people, Scheeres included, responded to her adopted black brothers. It's another thing for her to write memoir and not check her privilege. Yes, she survived many messed up things and I'm sure she and David did have a mostly good relationship but it is clear she profoundly misunderstood his experience.

This book seemed less about freaky religion than it was a repulsive story of abuse. This may be good for those that like to read harrowing and detailed accounts of abuse (think along the lines of A Child Called It) but it wasn't to my taste at all.

Jasmine is a national scholar, cheerleading champion, and extemporary student. Her life is on track to go to a top college and become something great, but when she gets the awards letter for being a national scholar her parents drop the bomb that the whole family is in the country illegally. They don't have green cards. With no documentation Jasmine can't accept the free ride to her top choice college. Plus, if anyone in the family does anything wrong the whole family could be deported. All this is happening just as her relationship with Royce, a congressman's son, is starting to take off. With the fear of deportation looming and Royce's dad against undocumented immigrants staying in the country, Royce and Jasmine may not get to stay together and Jasmine's whole family may be sent back to the Philippines, where she and her two younger brothers don't even know the language.

Jasmine is a Dreamer, a child of illegal immigrants- one who has been brought up on the Dream. Work hard, excel, do better than your best and succeed in America, the land of opportunity. She thought she was a legal resident and when she got the National Scholarship Award letter she was elated. Wow! A chance to meet the President and go to college without money worries. She cannot take the scholarship though and her family may be deported. 
 This is the story of Jasmine's senior year as she struggles with this uncertainty.

"Life isn't only about figuring out what we need. We need to figure out how to help others too. We have to ask ourselves: what can we do to better ourselves and our country? What can we do to be remembered? Who do we want to be? " Good story, YA but also an impactful message to contemplate

I was sent a copy of Something in Between by MB Communications in exchange for an honest review. 
 Something in Between is the incredibly delightful story of Jasmine and her family on their journey to become American citizens. For most of her life, Jasmine de los Santos believed she was an American citizen. But when she receives a prestigious scholarship straight from the federal government, her parents are forced to admit that no one in their family has green cards, and so she cannot accept the scholarship. Worse yet, she may not even be able to go to college at all, since they cannot apply for financial aid. Not to mention that if they are discovered, the entire family could be deported at any time. 
 First of all, I absolutely adored this story. After reading so many books with dark themes and tones, this was a breath of fresh air. Jasmine de los Santos is such a great character. She is so positive and driven, sometimes to the point of being competitive, and filled with so much love for her family. If I ever met her in real life, I know I'd probably roll my eyes at the way she gets so worked up about things or is so over-focused on school and the need to succeed. But those parts of her personality added to her character and made her perfect for the story. It was refreshing to see such a go-getter character like Jasmine in young adult. I can't remember the last time I found a character with such an unbreakable drive. Of course, Jasmine wasn't the only character that delighted me. From Royce, to Jasmine's parents, to her friends Kayla and Lo, all were wonderfully balanced. I especially found myself impressed with Jasmine's parents. In contemporary, it's very common for writers to skim over the parents' personality and thus make them background robots. As this novel is very family-focused, it was essential to have the rest of her family as vivid as Jasmine herself, which the author pulled off perfectly. 
 Overall, this novel is very much a romance. From the first few chapters we get a glimpse of Royce Blakely, the handsome congressman's son who keeps popping up in Jasmine's life. Jasmine, however, has always been very focused on school, and has never kissed a boy much less had a boyfriend. Still, when she begins shyly texting Royce and they strike up an awkward friendship, she can't deny how attracted she is to him. I really loved Royce, and felt he was nicely developed. A lot of time romance can gloss over the love interest, so it was nice to see him be as human as Jasmine was. As well, the relationship is not all kissing and holding hands. I loved all the ups and downs that these two have together-- from breaking up and getting back together, to fighting about family issues, and so on. It felt so real because the romance wasn't just the fairy tale lead up to how these two got together. The book showed how their relationship evolved and grew, which was really awesome to see. The only issue I took with the book--- and it's another thing I find common in romance-- is that the guy will do back flips, pull down the moon, run a mile and then go further, all to impress the girl. And the girl, often, does little to nothing in return. No huge romantic gestures or efforts made. Royce states in the book that Jasmine gives him the courage to be himself and follow his dreams, but it would have been nice to see Jasmine put a bit more effort into the relationship to make it seem more balanced. 
 The writing in this book is smooth and even, and with no swearing or any mature content (Jasmine and Royce don't make it past heavy kissing), I could see this very much appealing to younger audiences of young adult. Aside from the looming threat of deportation, there isn't a whole lot of tension. A lot of action takes place between every page but unless you're engaged in the characters and their day to day life, it can start to drag. That said, there is a lot of meat to the story, so those that fall in love with the characters will be delighted at all the adventures they get to enjoy. 
 The heart of this story comes down to Jasmine's story of immigration. It is an incredibly empathetic story and really allows readers who may be so far removed from situations like this to understand what's it's like to be an immigrant in America. I really believe this book will do a lot of good in helping young people build empathy for those in this kind of situation. Not only was the glimpse into Filipino culture delightful and enlightening, but the points the book raises on what it means to be American are especially pertinent in this day and age. I'd strongly encourage librarians to sneak this book into the hands of those looking for romance, as they will get all that and so much more. 
 The only issue that I had with the book comes down to how it all ends up resolved. No spoilers, but I found that the solution felt a little too simple, and like it was an option right from the beginning. There was a lot of work the characters put into achieving that end, but the way it was actually achieved-- with a single phone call-- made all that effort feel pointless. It made it feel like the book could have been half its size, if that was all it took to resolve the conflict. 
 All in all, 3/5 stars. A culturally delightful story that builds empathy for immigrant struggles.

2.5 STARS FOR "SOMETHING IN BETWEEN" BY MELISSA DE LA CRUZ 
 I feel bad for not really liking a story that the author holds so closely to her heart. I don't think I've read very many books centered around the topic of immigration, as well as the identity crisis that goes along with belonging to two different cultures, so I did find it refreshing to get to see into the mind of someone who was at the risk of deportation. However, I couldn't connect to the main character, Jasmine, at all. I didn't like her. I know how eighteen year olds talk - I am 18 years old - and her voice just wasn't convincing for me. She acted and sounded more like what I think a fifteen year old would. 
 The dialogue and conversations in the book felt very forced, and as much as I found Royce to be sweet, the constant misunderstandings and arguments over the smallest things got on my nerves. Jasmine projected so many of her own insecurities onto him that it was ridiculous. You know that couple that breaks up and makes up all in the same day? That's Jasmine and Royce. 
 I guess it just wasn't for me. I felt pretty bored throughout the 400+ pages, and the voices of the characters just didn't resonate with me. They all acted and sounded too young to be convincing.

I'd put this in the same category that some LGBTQ books are in on my list, which is that they're necessary books, but that they're not well-written enough to be "the best". Essentially they're tolerated on the YA market because there isn't anything else and because the voices and characters are needed to be the voice of youth, but that doesn't mean that they're all good. I'd put de la Cruz's book in this category. It's needed, oh so very needed like Ask Me No Questions, Shine, Coconut Moon, Touching Snow, but that this bloated story with its cheesy romance isn't the kind of book I'd like to read. 
 Jasmine is a Filipino immigrant whose family enjoys their California life. Both parents have a good, menial labor jobs while they support their children, including Jasmine, who works her tail off ("Youre so perfect, Jasmine. You do everything right. You were junior class president. Cheer captain. Honor Roll. Volunteering. Don't you ever get tired? Never, I say with a smile. Except the truth is I'm always tired, but I can never admit it, not to my friends, especially not to my family.") She continues on this path and receives a national scholarship that would allow her to attend a reception at the White House and then a full-ride to a four-year college of her choice. Yet her dreams are dashed when her parents admit that they came her on a work visa that expired and don't have green cards/citizenship of any kind and that accepting this scholarship wouldn't be possible, especially since it would open them up to questions. What unfolds is 400 pages of too much stuff. There's a insta-love interest, her fight against legislation to get rid of illegal immigrants, her identity crisis, helping her family while still trying to get the scholarship, and probably some other stuff that I missed because it was all just a little too much.

 I initially put off reading this book, because I wanted to savor it - I tend to inhale these books the day they come out. I actually forgot about it (!) jntil a friend asked if we could read it together. I don't know if she finished it yet or not, but... if I wait too much longer to put in my review, it won't happen. 
 This series focuses on the LA Shadowhunter Institute, Emma Carstairs, and Julian Blackthorn. It's set in 2016 (I believe), and is approximatley 5 years after TMI ended. We left these two when they were all of 12 years old, but already experienced in the war with Sebastian and his army of anti-Shadowhunters. In a horrifying and heartbreadking moment, Julian had to choose between saving his younger siblings and killing his father (turned into an anti-Shadowhunter by Sebastian). 
 It is a NEW, FRESH, INVENTIVE, IMAGINATIVE tale - not quite as epic as TMI or TID, but full of the richness, twists, turns, and just plain good storytelling that we've come to expect from it's Author. 
 Don't get me started on the rants about the Author... If you don't like the book or feel as if the Author is milking readers for all they've got, then DON'T READ THE BOOK! If you leave a review, at least don't make it a ranting flame of hate. At least attempt to leave an objective or critical thinking type of review. Sheesh! 
 So much has changed for Julian after the war and in these 5 years. Helen, his half-sister, has been banished for being half-Fae; his brother, Mark - Helen's brother and also half-Fae, has been abandoned to the Fae's Wild Hunt - both political moves that also reflect the Shadowhunter attitude towards the Fae, who sided with Sebastian in the war. 
 Julian has had to carry much on his shoulders these past 5 years - sole caretaker and guardian to his younger siblings and so much more, while trying to deal with the guilt of killing his own father. One of the things I really love about this book is that the Author doesn't forget the history. There's a particularly poignant moment between Julian and one of his brothers that provies another POV - another eyewitness account of that horrific moment. I like that Julian was able to find some closure and some peace by the end of this book. 
 Emma, too, has unfinished business - answers regarding her parents' death 5 years ago. Were they really murdered by Sebastian, and if so, why didn't he just turn them? Are these answers what I expected? No. You see, while this book is still in the Shadowhunter world, it's no longer Jace-Clary-Sebastian... YAY! It's a new story in the world post-all of that. Its still about Good and Evil and how the lines can be blurred..how perceptions affect how we view and treat others..how everyone is a combination of both Good and Evil - no one is all one thing. 
 This book might not be the sweeping epic, but it's storytelling at it's best. It builds upon the familiar to sereis fans, and yet takes us to new places - literally - where we meet all new characters. I'm impressed by how the Author took a well-known poem and managed to weave it into a new, fresh, completely different story. 
 The book engaged me and still gave me something new - something to build on. There are still things, places, and characters to explore. Perhaps some things seem "convenient" but they still fall within the world we know. The Author has the right to withhold information until she feels the time is right and if we already knew all of this, who'd care? And remember, we've been told not to believe anything or any POV in this world 100% anyway. Who's truth is it - Shadowhunter? Fae? Werewolf? Warlock? 
 I look forward to the next book, hoping that we learn more about Diana and continue to follow Emma and Julian.

 T H O U G H T S: 
 shadowhunters. a universe that captured hearts and stole breaths. this is my first book by cassandra clare, but i don't know if it will be my last. since i did not read any other shadowhunter books, it makes sense that i wouldn't be able to appreciate all that lady midnight has to offer. as much as i loved the cover {yes, i judge a book by its cover} and hate how much cassandra clare feels like a one-trick pony, here i am. 
 from the reviews i read and whispers i heard, lady midnight is some of cassandra clare's best work. i don't know what possessed me to pick it up before the mortal instruments series, but i think my entrance into the shadowhunter universe would have been similar either way. i don't understand the hype. the plot and writing is generic, mundane, and cliche. despite the supernatural world of demons and ley lines and fae, the story is stereotypical and cluttered with the usual tropes of the urban fantasy genre, from love triangle to an absence of adults. nothing surprised me. nothing captivated me. nothing took my breath away. 
 lady midnight feels like fan faction. like it would be a gem to an obsessive fan, and something generic - if not repellent - to the average reader. what is there to love here, other than another dip into a fan's beloved universe? the writing style is simplistic. the characters are bland. the romance is cheap. the plot is weak and only involved in about 200/698 pages. the detailed, atmospheric world-building and dynamic character relationships are the only elements that intrigue me. still, i struggled to connect to characters and a world so foreign to me. also, it was hella, hella long. 
 still, there is something alluring about the love fans have for the shadowhunter universe, something i want to taste too, however overhyped it is. lady midnight is not, by far, the worst book i've read. it just wasn't compelling and fresh enough to be my cup of tea.

reference_books.review_text:
Actual rating: 1.5 stars 
 I really enjoyed the Trylle Trilogy, so I was very excited for this new spin-off series. But, honestly? I was very disappointed by it. 
 I just kept waiting for something to happen after the big event right in the first chapter, but nothing really did. The romance was unrealistic and flat. reference_books.title: Ruin and Rising (The Grisha, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
Review originally posted on my blog, Turning Pages. 
 You may or may not know this by now, but I didn't love Shadow and Bone - or even Siege and Storm - like a lot of people did. I found the plot and characters inconsistent, and found some frankly problematic views present within the stories. But I got that far in the series, and I wanted to see it through. By no means did I love the conclusion to this popular trilogy, but I did enjoy it more than I thought I would. 
 To begin, the plot in this book is almost always moving. There's always action, and if there isn't there's comedy and drama to keep readers interested. While the first book in the series (and probably the second, too) had it's fair share of slow moments, Ruin and Rising didn't. I was hooked to the story, and I felt satisfaction at the ending. I think the resolution for Alina felt right because as a character she finally had a say in her life. 
 Alina has always been a tricky character for me. I never particularly liked her, and some of that had to do with the serious and near-constant girl-hate she felt. But, thankfully, the girl hate is toned down more in this book which made it easier to stomach. I can't stand girl hate being present without being addressed as problematic somewhere in the book. At the beginning Alina does something and blames the Apparat, which is stupid but at least she admits it was her own choice later. Just a few inconsistencies. But otherwise the character was strong. Alina learned it's okay to cry, it's okay to need others for support. It's okay to not be feeling 100% all the time. 
 The other characters each added flavour to the novel that I enjoyed, whether it be emotion with their love and support of one another which was beautiful, or the banter they exchanged so the novel wasn't all doom and gloom. Having some distance from the first two books in the series made me appreciate the characters. 
 I've never been a fan of Mal, Mal who shamed Alina and yet also took her for granted. I never saw a romance between them as realistic. But if you can ignore the first two books, the romance Bardugo crafts in this book is actually more believable. And Mal wasn't annoying in this book, thankfully. Though whenever there's a 'romantic rival', Bardugo either had them hurt or killed so Alina and Mal could be together. It's a shame Mal was such a jerk in the first books (another inconsistency). 
 I know there's some debate about the resolution to the novel, but as much as I feel for the Darkling, he wasn't a good person anymore. It did seem maybe too easy and quick. Perhaps it could have gone a different way, but the way it went freed people from his darkness and pain; he was killing people without a second thought . As a villain, he was well written. Bardugo made us almost like him at first, and she made us understand him. Bravo. 
 I wasn't blown away by this series like a lot of people were, but I actually quite liked Ruin and Rising. The issues present in the first two books are less of a problem in this book. The characters are sweet and strong and go through a lot together. The ending was bittersweet, but hopeful. The story isn't easy to read, but the ending is worth it. Maybe this book will make me appreciate the rest of the series more.

book_a.title: Carry On
book_a.user_review:

 I liked Carry On, Rainbow Rowell's first full fantasy novel, but I didn't love it. Simon and Baz are adorable, but I wish their relationship was a bit more developed. The pacing is quite slow, and some readers may struggle to stick with it until things pick up. There are also some inconsistencies and plot holes. But like every Rowell book, it's also charming, enjoyable, and funny. If you can look past its issues, then you'll really enjoy Carry On.

sample_reviews.review_text: Fanfic, this book is pure 100% fanfiction. And not even GOOD fanfiction which is why I loved it so much. It was just enough to keep me reading (I love reading bad fanfic) and just good enough to keep me loving it. I've always been a sucker for Harry/Draco stories and this just led right into it. I'd kill to know what fandom name Rainbow Rowell wrote under, because there is no way she wasn't one of us!

I'd give this a 2.5-3 It was...ok....I'm just disappointed. 
 I really wanted to like this book because it has so many things I normally enjoy. Vampires, Wizards, romance & LGBT romance to boot. The book starts off strange like I picked it up in the middle of a series and I am supposed to really care about these characters already. I spent the whole book telling myself to care about these characters but it just felt forced. I think maybe if this was the 3rd book in a series and there was some kind of build up and back story I might care...or not. As it was all these characters felt as empty as a bag of potato chips. 
 I struggled to get past the heavy Harry Potter influence and had trouble not seeing these characters as Harry Potter characters. I think I started thinking of them as Harry Potter characters to help me get through the book easier. 
 On the topic of the romance let me start by saying I am a romance sap, I love romance in books, movies, TV even ultra sappy romance. The romance in this book felt so ???? unfounded and forced like it felt like it was just a romance to have 2 hot guys make out woohoo!!! I feel like I might of bought the romance if there was more build up to it but there wasn't. One day Simon wants to murder Baz for going after "his girl" then the next minute it's like oh hey they are kissing & now they are in love ok yeah that makes sense. 
 The characters really needed more fleshing out. Simon is total boring jerk with like no redeeming qualities. However to be fair to Simon there was no connection for me to any of the characters, at all. They were all just so boring. This book just came off as flat which is a shame because it had so much potential to be a book I could totally love. I managed to get through it fairly easily and quickly which was nice. It wasn't the worst book I've ever read but it wasn't good. It was just ok. 
 P.S. I'm thinking about it more & did this book have a plot? like did it? Where was the plot??? Who fucking knows!! the plot was was a mess. I've read better one shot fanfictions than this entire book. That was mean I'm sorry but it's true!! 
 P.P.S All of this is really a shame because I really enjoy Rainbow's books and I think she is a good writer this just wasn't what I was expecting.

Again, like Fangirl, I just don't see it. This one was overhyped and was too overhyped by booktuber katytastic. It was interesting enough for me to power through it (the harry potter x fanfic similarities we're gripping) but it just didn't wow or intrigue me at all.

** spoiler alert ** 
 What happened to Rainbow Rowell? Don't get me wrong the story was cute and I got heart warming moments, but what happened to that thing that made her books so damn amazing?! No I'm not bothered by the gay thing or the cheese spells or the weird world that is a copy of Harry Potter and Vampire Academy. Honestly this book read more like Carth's fanfiction than a Rainbow Rowell book. Where was the depth in the characters? Where were the unique moments that made her book so heart warming? Where was the author that wrote Fangirl and Eleanor and Park? This characters are flat and boring and, my god, could they be any more corny? Disappointed in this book. There are a handful of reasons why I did not enjoy this book: 
 1. I read it as I was rereading Half-Blood Prince and it helped highlight what a pale imitation of the world created by J. K. Rowling this is. 
 2. Having just finished Jodi Picoult's Small Great Things, the idea of creating a superior being--which I compared to race--made me uncomfortable. 
 3. I did not appreciate being parachuted onto the end of a saga. 
 4. I read other things to escape, but I look for substance in my YA and I found it lacking. 
 5. It was not good writing.
Did not like it at all. I did finish hoping something original would happen. It reminded me of Eregon where the author cherry picked from other books.

Carry On is a Harry Potter-style spin off. It's an expansion of the book series first referenced in Rowell's novel about fanfiction, Fangirl. It's basically, give or take a lot of worldbuilding and character development, a Harry/Draco Seventh Year fic. This is a very similar concept to A HERO AT THE END OF THE WORLD, which was one of my favourite books of last year. I personally enjoyed that more, but this was a very fun read. 
 It picked up a lot of speed near the end - the start had a little too much info-dumping for my taste. I did come to love Simon and Baz by the end, and found Baz's candidness about his sexuality particularly refreshing for a fantasy novel ("Are you gay?" "Completely."). His queerness is a huge part of his self expression in a way that's never usually seen in fantasy and science fiction. 
 In fact, Simon and Baz are a brilliant pairing, above and beyond the Harry Potter connection. It's a very long book, but I flew through it, and would happily read more about this world. Penelope in particular was a really great character, and I want to read a sequel about her and Micah. 
 Huge kudos for Rainbow Rowell for writing and publishing a straight up Harry/Draco fic though (life goals right there.)

After reading and loving Fangirl, this book was everything I wanted it to be. The story of Simon Snow was fun and snarky with characters who acted and spoke like real teenagers (with the addition of magic).

This book was so much fun !!! I will definetely read it again someday. 
 The only thing is... I was a bit surprised by some of the elements at the end, more than any other Rainbow Rowel's books. The last few pages reminded me that it's supposed to be a fanfiction, which I had completely forgotten

 Characters were rather drab. And the writing could have been better
read 50% so far: main character, boring and plain. Unable to connect with her. No signs of plot speeding up. I get easily distracted.

3.5 stars; 
 I really loved the idea of this story and for the most part it was pretty action packed and engaging. The story is correctly promoted as X-Men meets Ocean's Eleven. With the MK virus and therefore vaccination of it, it resulted in the "Immune", those who gained super powers (powers may vary) as a result of the vaccination. Similar to X-men, there's a power struggle between the immune and their freedom versus the government and their desire to control the immune. The part Ocean's Eleven comes from the groups of Immune (who managed to avoid the government) who use their powers for "evil" or rather just criminal activities. The story follows two teenagers, Ciere and Daniel, and their crew and their lives as immunes and as criminals. 
 But for the moment, none of the matters. 
 They are young. They are criminals. They are glorious. 
 They are immune. 
 The story is told from both POVs of Ciere and Daniel and how they intertwine. It starts off as a any normal heist, steal a will from an attorney, but of course it turns out to be way bigger than it seems with the secrets to the vaccination on the line. I loved the story, it was fast pace and intense and unforgiving (talk about drama). And I really enjoyed most the characters. Kit Copperfield is the leader of the crew, and quite brilliant. There's Mangus, who is totally freakin' awesome ( mostly because he's an extremely interesting criminal with a moral code). Together they're fascinating duo. I enjoyed Ciere's friend Devon, who is part part-time criminal, part rich boy and part comic relief, I like to think there's more to Devon than meets the eye. 
 Daniel was an interesting character, though we didn't get to see as much of him, or know a great deal about him. I'm hoping the next book will expand and dig deeper into Daniel for us. And there's Ciere. Oh Ciere, how I wanted to like you so badly. She started off as a pretty cool character, as illusionist, she was rare and could do pretty cool things making her talent valuable to the criminal lifestyle. But time after time she just kept doing really stupid things. 
 "She's a lunatic", says Conrad. 
 "Absolutely insane," says Gunthram. 
 "Either completely fearless or utterly stupid," says Conrad. 
 Seems like people think she's fearless, I personally think she's utterly stupid because most of the problems that she gets herself into that requires complete fearlessness could have easily been avoided if she didn't do those stupid things. For example, after a botched attempt to retrieve "the prize" with the crew, why in the devil, would you think you could do it yourself, andddddd to use it to save your own ass (from something stupid you did earlier). Yeeeaah. This was the downfall of the book. 
 Overall, it was a really enjoyable read despite it not living up to the mind-blowing expectations I had (which couldn't really be helped because, the idea/concept just had so much potential for awesome). It's still a worthwhile read, especially for fans of the sci-fi/superpower genre and the idea around the power struggle between government and the "gifted". 
 PS. Oh the romance! It's pretty subtle, if almost not-existent. Or rather, it's kind of hard to know where the (potential) romance(s) might go. I wasn't too impressed by the pretty stereotypical (prospective) OTP, but there's potential for a lot of cuteness.

Ugh, you can't say things like it's X-Men meets Ocean's Eleven and not follow through on that. You get me all excited and leave me so unsatisfied. I realize the job of the marketing department is to say things like this to get you to buy the book because that is their job but, damn, it's one of my biggest pet peeves. I cannot stand it when the book doesn't deliver on the promise. 
 So, yeah, it had super powers. And heists. And cons. But, that's about it on the similarities... It lacked the depth and ambition of X-Men. It lacked the wit and charm of Ocean's Eleven. It lacked a whole lot of things when you get down to it. The book follows a rag tag band of criminals who use their powers to their advantage and try to avoid run ins with government officials who are none to keen about their being differently able. They attempt to find the formula for the vaccination that birthed these super abilities. It had all the promise of a good story, but it never happened. If the characters don't pop, the book is a flop (for me at least). 
 Ciere, our protagonist, is a borderline unlikable sort of anti-hero that goes around constantly mucking everything up. She's hard to sympathize with. Add a dash of throw away supporting characters, dismal character development, shoddy world building, and unmemorable dialogue... voila a two star review is born! It gets an extra star because I enjoyed Devon as a character and, yeah, I definitely appreciated that the author didn't try to fix them up in some horrid love triangle (as is so common in YA these days). 
 All in all, like I said, unsatisfying. Unmemorable. Disappointing. I think I was hoping for a different book. Maybe I had unrealistic expectations? I feel like when you bill a book as a cross between X-Men and Ocean's Eleven you're inviting the comparison and the book just never took off for me.

This is probably a 2.5 star read for me. It's not horrible, I've just lost interest. 
 The first issue for me was that it is written in present tense. This probably will be a non-issue for most, but I just am not a fan of present tense. 
 The actual issues are the fact that this story is incredibly flat. The characters are flat and the plot doesn't seem to exist. The story just has no spark. Ciere has no personality and she's rather boring to read about. All the other characters are incredibly two dimensional. And I really don't know where the plot is. It showed up in the beginning but then took a back seat so Ciere could go do something else and sort of forget about the plot. 
 Other people might love this but it just hasn't held my interest and I have other things to read.

When the MK virus swept across the planet, a vaccine was created to stop the epidemic, but it came with some unexpected side effects. A small percentage of the population developed superhero-like powers. Seventeen-year-old Ciere Giba has the handy ability to change her appearance at will. She's what's known as an illusionist. She's also a thief. After a robbery goes awry, Ciere must team up with a group of fellow super-powered criminals on another job that most would consider too reckless. The formula for the vaccine that gave them their abilities was supposedly destroyed years ago. But what if it wasn't? The lines between good and bad, us and them, and freedom and entrapment are blurred as Ciere and the rest of her crew become embroiled in a deadly race against the government that could cost them their lives. 
 Illusive is an intense thriller, an action-packed adventure, a series of events and car wrecks that come together over and over in a battle between cops, criminals, and a secret that could change the world if it falls into the wrong hands. 
 One of the first things about Ciere that I like is she's an illusionist, she can create any kind of illusion, can trick anyone into seeing someone or something that is or isn't there, but she's bad at it. Just because you have superpowers doesn't mean you're perfectly skilled. Because she's not, she's foolish and reckless, she's frightened and frail and useless in a fight. She's jumpy and impulsive. But she's still trying to fix her problems. 
 Ciere's world is a curious one. So familiar because it's Earth, but because time has passed, because of the MK virus and its vaccine, it's not exactly the same. And so there are some differences, some advances in technology. Some new groups and new crimes. New labels and reasons to fear people. 
 What's interesting about books with thieves and crime syndicates and government agents, books like this, is that the lines between good and evil are blurred beyond all recognition. It's not about good and evil anymore, not about right or wrong. Instead, it's a fight for survival, for freedom. Ciere has committed crimes, and she's done that in order to survive. She was pushed to the edge of the cliff and found the only escape route that guaranteed her living one more day. Technically, almost every character has committed one crime or another, but would all of them be considered evil? And what about the FBI agents? They don't exactly have the best motives when it comes to people like Ciere. 
 A book like this certainly humanizes thieves and criminals. There is always a reason why crimes are committed, why a person steals priceless works of art or robs a bank. Why a person works as a bodyguard for a crime boss. It's certainly an interesting look into a different world, one where you're constantly looking over your shoulder, constantly running, constantly hiding. A world where safety is just an illusion. 
 This book has a lot in it. Criminals and superpowers, running scams and schemes, government agents, truth and lies, plots and plans, secrets and suffering. And it all works together. There's a high level of tension running throughout the book, spiking when things go wrong and bullets start flying. A fair amount of the dialogue from Ciere and her group was witty and clever. I can see where there would be a sequel, where there are questions left unanswered and secrets still waiting to be unleashed, and I can see where this story as a whole ends. Knowing there will be a sequel makes me excited.
