 I thought this was going to be amazing...it wasn't. 
 Don't waste your time on this book.

Illusive had the potential to become one of my favorite books of 2014. The premise was unique and amazing (well to me at least) and I thought that it'd be the perfect thing to read after the many contemporaries I've been reading lately. Illusive wasn't bad per say, but it was a let-down. 
 Illusive is set in a world where people with powers exist but instead of making them superheroes, Jones chose to make them the "villains" instead. In Ciere's world, those that are "immune" are regarded as dangerous weapons. They are brutally imprisoned if found and constantly are on the run to avoid it. It's a really cool idea and I was hoping that it'd be just as amazing as it sounded. Unfortunately, there were two major things that brought the book down. 
 Firstly, the characters are flat as a board. They had so much potential and could have become some of my favorite book characters if not for the crappy characterization. I know I would have loved Ciere, Magnus, Devon, Kit, the whole lot of them if they had been more deep. They were each unique and had extremely rough character sketches. Evidence that the personalities were considered were definitely present, but the rest of it was all in the author's head. I can take a wild, educated guess that Devon was sarcastic and that Magnus was a grudge-holder but Illusive lacked the deep characterization that would have brought the crew to life. 
 Secondly, Illusive had a great premise but the plot itself wasn't. It doesn't ever really pick up and if I could draw a line graph that showed the amount of action and suspense, it would be a straight line from the exposition to the conclusion with the exception of one teensy, tiny bump at the end that hits a record high of 0.02 excitement points. It's a really slow read with no end in sight. When the "climax" is finally there, it falls flat. 
 I will give some praise to Jones for that twist in Part 3. I never saw that coming. And the action scene at the end in Part 4 was really cool. And I ship two couples in this book. For the first couple, I don't want to spoil anything so I'll just say that he and Ciere are adorbs together even if it's a seriously bad case of insta-love. The lack of development is so terrible but I still kind of ship them regardless. In fact, I think part of the reason I ship them is because the nonexistent character development makes the nonexistent romantic development slightly better (which is kind of sad). I love Kit and Magnus's banter. At this point, I'm not sure if they're gay or if they've just had some really messed up history but I'll be reading the second book to find out. I really wish that the characterization had been better because then I'd be shipping these characters even harder together. But alas, obviously it can't happen. 
 Illusive is a solid book that didn't illicit any particularly strong opinions. It was disappointing to say the least but I will be picking up the sequel and hoping that these issues improve.

a new take on a theme I've read before. 
 I don't know what it was - perfect timing? good writing? fun characters and a plot that sucks you in? YES YES & YES! 
 This one just had me hooked from the first chapter. I like the characters and the way the story played out. I liked the way things were told and the sequence of events. I loved the twists and turns, even if I saw them coming - and I definitely love the set up for the next book 
 I will definitely read more of this series!
Great read, decent plot and no stupid love triangle. What else can I ask for :)

reference_books.title: Say You're One of Them
reference_books.review_text: To be fair, I stopped reading this book after the first two stories. Waaaay too dark and depressing for me. I cannot tolerate stories involving any form of child or animal abuse. These stories center on the horrific, dismal lives of African children. My own life is depressing enough. I just cannot read a story that haunts me and makes me want to cry for hours afterward. I stopped reading Oprah's picks a looooong time ago for this very reason. She does not seem to think a book is good unless it involves the most depressing and horrid cicumstances.

reference_books.title: The Devil's Punchbowl (Penn Cage #3)
reference_books.review_text: Although a huge fan of Greg Iles, and especially enjoying the previous novels with the character of Penn Cage, had I known this book was about dogfighting I would never have bothered to pick it up. I found this book to be disturbing, disgusting and stomach churning. I had to skim over several passages because I knew if I had read them, these invoked images would have haunted me for a very long time. An avid animal lover, I just found this subject far to revolting to ever be able to consider it entertainment in any way, shape or form. The characters in the book barely had their feathers ruffled either when confronted by this disgusting "sport" and I found that to be equally disturbing. Definitely not for me. I am not sure I will ever be looking forward to a new release from Greg Iles again.

reference_books.title: The Vacationers
reference_books.review_text: Everything about this book was, in my opinion, dull.The plot, the characters, even the location. None of the characters was even likable enough for me to care what became of them.

reference_books.title: The Postcard Killers
reference_books.review_text: Whatever has happened to James Patterson ? I used to devour his books in one sitting. This book bored me to tears and I actually just quit wasting my time halfway through and quit reading it. I think he has become so compelled to impress us with pumping out a new book as fast as a toaster can pop out a toasted piece of bread, that he no longer cares at all about the quality of his work. I, for one, am not impressed. PLEASE bring back the quality to your work Mr. Patterson.You've become predictable and boring........

reference_books.title: The Middlesteins
reference_books.review_text: I read a few reviews stating that this was a great book, so when I spotted it at my Library, could not resist picking it up. I certainly do not see what all the fuss was about. This book had ZERO character development and when the author doesn't give me that, I could not care less what happens to them. The characters, like the plot, were pointless and empty, leading to the inevitable ending, but oh so boring getting there. A complete waste of my time. The only thing I got out of this book was a sudden urge for Chinese take-out. My fortune cookie insert should have said "stop wasting your time".

book_a.title: The Lincoln Lawyer (Mickey Haller, #1; Harry Bosch Universe, #17)
book_a.user_review: One of my favorite things to do is read a book that has been turned into a movie, and then go see the movie. Having already been a fan of Michael Connelly's, I could not wait to get my hands on this book when the movie hit my local theater. This was my favorite Connelly book, even outdoing The Poet and The Scarecrow. Great characters, great plot, full of surprises. I am anxious to read more books involving the charater of Mickey Haller. I felt much more of a connection to him than I did to Connelly's other protaganist character, Harry Bosch.

sample_reviews.review_text: Best audio book I listened to this year! The narrator is wonderful. The novel is amazingly well written, for a legal procedural, and gives you a wonderful sense for the life of a defense attorney. This had all the things I enjoy in a mystery, great characters, fast plot and sinister villain. I mostly don't read mysteries because the ending is usually predictable, but this one had me till the end. My only quibble is that, as an attorney myself, I just couldn't buy how he runs his practice from the back seat of his "Lincoln." I know it would bog down the story to explain how Mickey Haller actually compiled/conducted all the depositions,drafted petitions, researched jury selection, and basically prepared for trial without an office (aside from the one in his home.) I don't think his ex-wife answering the phone is enough of a back-up...but, I'm willing to suspend belief because the story was so damn good!

Mickey Haller is a lawyer on the move, a criminal defender whose clients are so numerous and widespread that he conducts business from the backseat of his Lincoln Towncar. For him, the law isn't a calling. It's a business, and the entire legal apparatus is a machine that he manipulates as best he can to the advantage of his clients. He is a charmer, a hustler -- and when a big ticket comes along, he jumps. Who wouldn't want a case to milk for a couple of years? But Louis Roulet, a Hollywood real estate mogul who is accused of beating and attempting to rape a call girl, will be more than he bargained for. While Haller maintains his greatest fear is an innocent client, one who presents real consequences for failure, in Roulet he will find something worse: genuine evil. The Lincoln Lawyer mark's Connelly's stunningly successful swift from writing cops to writing law, introducing a new character to his grimy Los Angeles. 
 I heard of this book because reviews for Grisham's Rogue Lawyer described it as a pale imitation of The Lincoln Lawyer. Those reviews are dead-on, because while both use similar elements -- starring a cynical lawyer who works from his car, arguing with his ex-wife and being driven around by a client-turned-bodyguard -- Connelly is far superior in both plotting and story. Haller may be cynical about the machine he operates, but he isn't a character who inspires despair. His relationship with both of his ex-wives is cordial, even sweet; his friends are genuine, and he, true to them. Ultimately, Haller is defiant of evil, not resigned to it. The mechanics of the novel are far better, too. Connelly's usual pace is fast, perilous, and unpredictable, like a sprint through dark city streets, weaving through alleys and dodging blows from sinister corners. Haller soon realizes he is in over his head, as the nature of his client becomes obvious, but even while he is being dragged into unknown territory, he's crafting a possible escape that is hid from the reader. In the later courtroom scenes, when Haller steps into a testimonial minefield, it isn't know whether he saw the danger and tempted it, or planned the provocation. The action doesn't conclude until the very last couple of pages, but Connelly's skill at keeping the reader engaged means there's no dramatic exhaustion. I didn't expect Connelly to write law as well as he did law enforcement, but...wow, Harry Bosch has met his match. (Harry's taste in music is far superior to Halley's, though.) 
 The Mickey Haller series is definitely one I'll be looking to for future legal thrills.
God, how boring! It is very wordy, you get tangled in words and just want to get through a long paragraph. No interest in characters whatsoever.

Mickey Haller is a Los Angeles defense attorney. He's been at the job long enough to qualify as a real pro. Along the way he's acquired two ex-wives, a daughter, a free-lance investigator, a host of clients and ex-clients, a driver, and three Lincoln Town cars wherein he spends a great deal of time. Hence the title of the novel. 
 Connelly is an experienced crime novelist with some serious recognition in hand. He's a fine writer and that's a good thing. If he was any less talented, this over-long novel would really weigh you down. Compelling is an overused term, but in an odd way it applies. The novel is a long and twisting trail to a stunning conclusion in a way that almost forces the reader to deal with many of Haller's shibboleths. His slide into near depression as he dissects and excoriates himself over the growing venality of those who try to enforce the law and those who try to manipulate the machine to preserve the lives and rights of the citizens caught up in our adversarial legal system, provides us with a disturbing inside look at the workings of our justice system. The legal system is a machine and the people in it are gears and levers and wheels. About the only people in the machine he treats lightly are the judges. Everyone else come in for some well-aimed cudgels. 
 Haller is the son of a famous defense lawyer who echoes his father's concern. He is afraid he won't recognize true innocence when he hears and sees it. Indeed, it is Connolly's contention, as expressed in this novel, that that is exactly what happens all too often. One might wonder if real defense lawyers around the world have this same concern. 
 Connelly can be counted on to deliver a well-thought-out, strong and realistic novel, which in the fantasy world of Crime Fiction is a real accomplishment.
Not impressive as a work of literature, mostly enjoyable as a beach read.
Lots of "f bombs," otherwise I'd give it a 4.25. If you can look past the language, good story!

I would give this book 3.5 stars. On the positive side, it was a very interesting story. The author had me guessing about nearly every facet of the story throughout, and it kept my attention. The main character, despite his position toward legal aspects of the law, was likeable, but realistic. 
 The primary reason for the lower rating was simply the language. There were a lot of swear words and crude language. Yes, I understand that this isn't a YA book, and I know what language is like in LA having grown up there (and having worked in a law firm). However, that doesn't mean it was crucial to the novel. The story would have been just as good, and just as realistic, without all the language. There were other things I didn't much care for, such as the lawyer's belief that the guilt or innocence of his client was irrelevant, and his lack of concern that he was putting drug dealers and gang members back onto the streets by finding loopholes in the law or flaws in the cops' procedures. But, I am able to believe that there are plenty of attorneys who think similarly. 
 So, overall, good story, but be aware that there is some very adult language in there. If that bothers you, don't read this book.

Read this for a book club. Good read, can see why they made it into a movie. 
 Not the type of book I normally read, but I recommend it if you're into not-too-scary law-related thrillers.
It was just ok. Very predictable but not awful.
Loved this one - one of his best. If I ever get around to bumping off someone, I want Micky Haller as my defence lawyer.

book_b.title: While My Sister Sleeps
book_b.user_review: Heartwrenching, thought provoking plotline about a family faced with the decision of whether or not to pull the plug. Surprising secrets come to light making the story much more interesting, but overall, I was a bit bored by this book, especially toward the end. None of the characters were very likable, which for me, made it hard to really care how they felt, or what action was to be taken. Also, the ending was just a little to pat for me. I would have given it only 2 1/2 stars if I could have.

sample_reviews.review_text: Couldn't do it. I haven't read any of Delinksy's other books, but the dramatic flair was way over the top and I couldn't stand the italicized words for extra emphasis. I wanted to know how it ended, but I could only get 60 pages in before quitting. Not a fan, too dramatically over the top. Will probably not look for any of Delinsky's other books either.

What I liked: 
 The side love story was very nice, not lust driven- just very respectable. I loved all the honorable characters (but they all weren't that way). 
 What I didn't like: 
 The grief. It seemed to go on for months when, in reality, the timeline of the book lasts one week. I'm sure that is what it really feels like, but that doesn't mean I want to read about it.

These books where something tragic happens and family secrets are dramatically revealed are not really my thing. That said, my book club will like it I think. So...there's that. I'm just glad to be done with it.

Blah. I had to literally push to finish it and it pained me. I feel sorry for anyone in this position with a family member, but I just spent more time being irritated than anything else. There were some pointless sub-plots and I just didn't see the purpose in the "big surprise" with the character in the coma.

I would have liked to give this 3.5 stars. I really enjoyed this story of sibling rivalry between the star and Miss Dependable, and the family dynamics we all seem to get stuck with. It was heart wrenching to read about the struggles this family had to endure after a tragic accident and the choices and decisions the family needs to face during a medical crisis.

I didn't start listening to this book with high hopes. I checked this book out on impulse from the library because the story is about 2 sisters...one a runner, and one a horticulturist. Considering I am an avid runner, and my sister has a Ph D in plant physilogy, I couldn't pass it up. The book did also have "women's lit" posted on it, so I knew this book really wouldn't be my style. The drama seemed silly, and everything wrapped up a little too neatly in the end. 
 Not a horrible book, just not my style.

This was the second book that I have read by Barbara Delinsky. I like her writing style. It is easy to be drawn into the story. 
 This is a story about the Snow family. There is Kathryn (mom), Charlie (dad), Robin (oldest), Chris, and Molly. Robin is a marathon runner and star of the family. She collapses on a run and is found by a man running behind her. He starts CPR and gets her heart going again. Robin has had a heart attack. She is 32 years old. While she is unconscious in the hospital, her family learns to deal with losing Robin. They find out things about her that no one ever knew. It is hard to come to terms with finding out someone you thought you knew was entirely different that what you thought. 
 Everyone comes to terms with Robin's issue in different ways, but soon everyone sees what needs to be done in order to make sure that Robin's wishes are granted. The family learn a lot about each other along the way and Robin has left the most precious gift that she could have: understanding in a family.
Slow start but once it got moving it was good.

Meh. *Slight spoilers.* Not my genre. Flipped through it on a two or three hour flight. Not bad, but very family drama where it all ends up improbably well in the end, tied up in a neat little bow. The mother character was a witch on wheels in the beginning, with no concept of common sense or decency in how she treated others, which is what turned me off in the beginning. Also the brother was pretty much an ineffectual male. Very namby pamby, letting other people do the heavy emotional lifting. Most of the characters just wanted to avoid conflict rather than straighten things out, but again, the HEA reigns supreme. Well, as happy as a book with this subject matter can get. Which is pretty darn happy considering. Not my cup of tea.

I was ready to pull the plug on page 50. I could not connect with any characters and there were way to many topics going on in one book. This family had more problems then an entire town in a soap opera. Just way to much for one book to allow the reader to connect to the characters.

reference_books.title: Black Ice
reference_books.review_text: It was just interesting enough that I finished it, though I thought about putting it down several times. I'm not in love with the author's writing it's very lack luster to me. That being said I'm not really into thriller novels, I got an advance copy at Bookcon for free or I probably would have never picked it up to begin with so take what you will from my experience.

reference_books.title: Outlander (Outlander #1)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 This book started out okay, potentially interesting, and then it just got more and more rape-y (I know not a real word but it is what it is) and weird. 
 There were lots of strange unnecessary moments, things that did nothing to build the story or the characters and which actually took away from the book because I had to sit there going why did you just tell me that, and that ruins the momentum (not that there was very much momentum to begin with), speaking of momentum I felt so many times in the book like I must had missed a page, usually because Claire was contemplating some situation and then she would have an epiphany that she wouldn't explain and then she run off and do something that supposedly was the answer to her problem but made no sense to me because no one told me what she was thinking. This book is a great example of the meme 'well that escalated quickly' 
 For an spoiler example.. 
 Claire : my husband was raped and has PTSD and doesn't want to see me, now he's dying of a blood infection induced fever, I know what will save him! I'll drug him and reenact his rape while he's half dead and high, sweet he's all better now we can back to have strange sex scenes like any happy married couple...(read with heavy sarcasm because it's crazy) 
 What the hell was that...really what the hell? 
 I can say with 100% certainty I will not be reading anymore of these books...and I'm going to stop taking book recommendations from people because this getting old.

reference_books.title: Betrayed (Rosato & DiNunzio, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
So I picked up an advanced reader copy of this at Book Con. Now it's the first time I've ever had an opportunity to acquire advanced copies so I grabbed everything I could without thinking about it to much. I mention this because after getting home and having a moment to go through the books I realized this was a genre I didn't really care for and it wasn't the first book in the series. That being said I felt there was an unwritten agreement that by taking the free advanced copy I agreed to read, so I figured I ought to give a go. 
 Now some of my problems with this story I feel stem from jumping into the middle of the series, I'm not attached to these characters, I don't really understand their feelings, and if it was a stand alone book I would find that unacceptable, however I forgive it here because there is the chance that that wouldn't be the case if I read all the books. 
 However, I can't forgive the poor writing. The pacing was terrible which was a serious disservice to the main character. It made her seem impulsive and fickle. She's suppose to be this intelligent talented lawyer but she behaves more like a teenage girl who doesn't understand cause and effect or how the law works. Honestly if it weren't for the occasional vague mention of her job I would never know she was a lawyer and quite frequently forgot that fact. 
 It almost read like entries in a diary, each event seemed separated from the other events, only tied together because the people were the same. 
 I also felt that the author's writing lacked something, there were multiple moments when I thought oh that's kind of repetitive, read it again, decided that it wasn't really repetitive but merely worded strangely. 
 I slugged through it because I felt obligated as I mentioned above, but if it weren't for that feeling I would have put it down quite fast and I definitely won't be picking up any of the other books.

reference_books.title: The Scorpio Races
reference_books.review_text:
This book was magic, I'm madly in love. It is both wonderful and terrible that it's the first book I read this year because the bar for everything has been set very high now. 
 Maggie Stiefvater's writing is like a spell she's woven and I cried when I reach the end because it was just the right one. 
 Puck is fantastic, just about everything I want out of a female lead character, she faces many things in this book but she doesn't act as though it doesn't bother her but she also doesn't let it stop her. 
 Sean is great too, another dreamer not willing to go down without a fight, not willing to quit. 
 And the way they with each other interact is both fantastical and believable, I so don't have the right words.

reference_books.title: The Iron Trial (Magisterium, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I got a copy of the uncorrected proof and there are definitely things in here that remind me of Harry Potter but every time so far that I've felt it was getting to close to the HP verse they've veered off and done something different enough that it manages to stand on its own, at least at page 130. 
 Also for the record the blond boy on the cover is not the main character though he is a significant character... 
 Edit 
 I officially finished my uncorrected proof, and there are quite a few similarities to HP, I feel that they are on a very fine line between being influenced by and being a rip off of HP. I liked it quite a bit though I look forward to book two. 
 It's a light read, the pace is rather brisk, but interesting enough that it didn't bother me too much. It is meant for grades 3-7 so with that in mind I think it is a great book for the age group. 
 I was surprised by the twist at the end, which was cool because it's become harder and harder to find a book that surprises me like that. I think they did a good job at planting red herrings. 
 Basically it's a fun, quick read for people into fantasy.

book_a.title: Sinner (The Wolves of Mercy Falls, #4)
book_a.user_review:
I was going to try and review this book all serious like but I don't know how to do that with all the feelings I have right now. This is the first book I've read by Maggie, I got the uncorrected proof at Bookcon and figured I give it a go and I need to read Shiver so badly now. Basically the book left me with this... 
 I have an overwhelming urge right now to be someplace entirely different from my every day life. It's not an unhappy or angry urge just a kind of burning excited need to see something else, to be someplace else. To get in the car with nothing, no supplies, no plans, and just go out into the world. To be on the road with open air, someplace where I could see the stars when it grew dark, where the sky would just stretch out in front of me and I could feel wild. 
 It has been so long since a book left me this way it's the only way I can phrase it... I posted this that paragraph on tumblr after finish the book and then was just that's it that is my review.

sample_reviews.review_text: 500 gold stars. If you truly want to connect with a character(s) read these books.

It took me about 30 pages in before I started falling in love with it, but then I did. Cole and Isobel are characters that I feel you're either going to really really hate, or end up really really loving. I really love them. This book was honest and open even to the point of being mean, just like them. It definitely took the fact that nobody is perfect, deconstructed it, and showed us possible legitimate reasons that's sometimes the case. I certainly don't agree with half the things either of these main characters do throughout the book, but I understand where they're coming from. In the end, I'm very glad I didn't give up on this series and I made it all the way to the last book, because it was have been really sad for me to have passed on this one and never know how good it actually is.

I've been trying to finish this book since July. I kept abandoning it because it was so horrible, but I felt like I should finish it since it's a signed copy and I met the author. Not a good enough reason. I really enjoyed the Wolves of Mercy Falls trilogy, but this one is beyond pointless. The wolf part of it is just an afterthought. It's basically two self-absorbed young people saying overly dramatic things to themselves in their heads. I wanted to tell them both to go volunteer at a soup kitchen and get some perspective. The author spends an inordinate number of sentences on Isabel wondering whether her white dress is leather or vinyl, for example. What a waste of time.

This book was just as great as I was hoping it would be! I love Cole and Isabel and I'm so glad they got their own book and a conclusion to their story. It was a rollercoaster ride with lots lots of highs and lows and anything less from Cole and Isabel would have been disappointing. Plus, Maggie Stiefvater's writing is on point, as always. 
 ------------------------------- 
 Cole St. Clair is getting his own book!!!!! WHAT!? 
 "Is this the real life? Or is this just fantasy?" 
 I can't even handle this knowledge right now!
Wow I expected so much more. Loved the Shiver trilogy and Raven boys but this just did not do it for me.

4.5 stars bc I did sometimes get annoyed with Isabelle. However, I absolutely loved the character development from both of these incredible characters. They grow so much and come so far and I was so proud of both of them. Ironically this was my favorite book in the series. I ship Cole and Isabelle way more than Sam and Grace.
Too much angst and not enough wolf. But let's face it. There weren't enough Ravens in this book either.
Ok that was a whole lot of nothing other than it took till the epilogue to find out they are together and that took 10 seconds. I would not recommend this series at all

I love anything written by Maggie Stiefvater: she is just that good. What I really loved was the huge contrast of Isabel and Cole from Grace and Sam. Seeing a different road in life and what can happen on a road no matter the choices made was very eye opening and sobering. Basically, you can do anything you really set your mind to as long as you have a good support ssystem.and someone who knows you. At least, that is my take on the book.

Actual Rating: 2.5 
 I really liked Cole in the origional trilogy and was hopeful for this book but it really fell flat for me. 
 The first three books weren't really well written in my opinion and this book didn;t even have the paranormal draw of warewolves that the other books had. It was mentioned a few time but this book read much more and just another YA contemporary teenagers trying to figure out love. There were fuinny aspects and soe of the ssecondary characters- like leo- were very enjoyable. 
 the premise of Cole being on a reality TV show was a decent idea but came off as pretty superficial when the author was trying to expose deeper emotions in cole as he is growing up, going straight edge (giving up drugs and acohol) but it just didnt pan out very well. 
 I'm not upset that I read the book, but overall this isn;t a series I'd recommend often.

book_b.title: City of Glass (The Mortal Instruments, #3)
book_b.user_review:
My biggest problem with Clare is that she doesn't do detail well, I have no idea how much time was suppose to have past. I feel like she continues to use the same tools to make things happen or to explain things. Someone just magically shows up in time to fill in some story real quick. 
 I realize she's well know for her fanfiction so I get that's where she started but these book read like fanfiction everything is rush rush rush one dramatic moment to the next without any real downtime. I want to know the characters I want to really care about them. By book three I am starting to like them all a bit more but I don't know I she's gotten better at writing them or if it's just because it's book three... 
 To me these are quick somewhat interesting books that I've enjoyed reading but I'm glad to say I borrowed them from a friend instead of buying my own set.

sample_reviews.review_text:
What an amazing end to the trilogy. Jace and Clary's relationship goes on yet another rollercoaster ride. Simon's character develops massively. There's a bit just after the middle of the book that made me cry. The end made me cry too. I love Alec and Magnus!!! OMG they're so brilliant (in want of a better word). If you loved the other 2 books you won't be disappointed. 
 Cassandra Clare what an author!

** spoiler alert ** 
 Wowza! That was a whirlwind of crazy and exciting and nerve racking and amazing! 
 I absolutely loved Jace and Clary's relationship. I loved finding out that they aren't truly siblings and the way that found out. And their last scene alone together, I agree with everyone else even though Cassandra Clare refuses, was totally leading to sex! I just absolutely loved their time with one another and the love they had. Definitely my favorite couple in this series and Jace still stands as my favorite character. 
 Seeing Jocelyn again was shocking because I definitely wasn't expecting and and the reaction coming out of Clary was not how I thought it would go. Finally having Jocelyn and Luke be together was nice though. 
 Max's death was definitely probably the biggest surprise. I wasn't expecting that at all. I didn't really feel the sorrow since we didn't get much connection to him as a character but I felt the sorrow when Isabelle would talk about him. And I hope Isabelle and Simon do end up together in the later books. And the way Alec showed everyone of his relationship with Magnus. Just out in the open in front of all those Shadowhunters and Downworlders. 
 Overall, the story was great! I just hope that Clary and Jace's relationship isn't bothering throughout the other half of the series.

As these books can keep me reading/skimming, I know they'll never be added to my favorites. They're fluffed and mediocre, that being said... It has been the best out of the three. Although, I felt like it was full of fluff, and could have been just as powerful in half the word count. There was a character who died that I felt the author literally just created to die. No character development, nothing and as such it invoked very little emotion for me and actually annoyed me that the author would add the person and death at all. I felt like everything was wrapped in a nice little bow and think the story was intended and should have stopped there. Which makes it that much harder to even want to finish the series, but, I hate leaving series' unfinished. So, here we go...
OMG OMG OMG OMG OMG

so i didnt exactly give this book a high rating. but i did enormously enjoy a large chunk of this book in the mid section where we first arrive in alicante and things start really brimming up. the last half i kind of felt to be repetetive from the ending of the last two books. in fact i wouldnt really be able to tell apart between the endings of the three books. its almost like each ending has too MUCH climax, too MUCH action. ofcourse the books are meant to stand alone by themselves but id also like to see a gradual growing in momentum as the series progresses. instead i felt like i was given this ultimate climax in the first book then twice again in the next two books without a sense of excalation. 
 but that wasnt ultimately why i gave only two stars to this book. there was something at the very end of the book that was personally not to my taste. but regarding this (which i will keep to myself because its personal), i DO see hope for improvement in future books because i AM able to see Clary develop slowly as the series progresses, even if she does manage to annoy me big time at the moment. but i mean noone's perfect, right? what an annoying character I would be if i were a character in a book :) 
 which is why i plan to continue on with the series despite its being a beastly long series. plus i have to get through the infernal devices series before i can return to this one! oh the pain and sorrows of a booklover..
Technically, I didn't read all of this (but there's no option for that). I just gave up. I didn't like it at all. Bored out of my mind. The first two were okay...but yeah, nada.

Like the the first two books I really enjoyed this one. Unlike the first two books I could not give it 5 stars. 
 Although I have never really loved the POV or the character Simon it was not those things that lost the extra star. You see, a few chapters in this book were boring. I almost considered skipping them but was worried I would miss vital information- but as it turned out I would not have. 
 However I do still love there world building and most of the characters. Also when it was good it was very, very, good. It really got the emotions stirring.

Way more entertaining than the last book, there was more speed, more story and it was less whining. I think I enjoyed this story the most from the books I read in this serie. Why do I give it less stars than the first book? With a first book I'm more foregiving with things like character growth and a lot of predictability. Cassandra Clare is a queen in writing a predictible story, she gives clues away that are so obvious, it makes me roll my eyes. And letting a character die that at the end only seemed to be written there to let him/her die, just irritated me a lot. 
 Even though I liked that we didn't only read in Clary's mind, the POV changes where a little too often for me, which pulled me out the story sometimes.

reference_books.title: Beautiful Disaster (Beautiful, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 Very poor writing and a sad example of what has happened to a whole facet of popular 21st Century writing (thank you Fifty Shades of Grey). There is barely a plot in Beautiful Disaster, though it could be said to have more of one than Twilight. The main character is dull and uninteresting, as seem to be SO MANY female protagonists in these new young adult and "erotica" books. Travis, the love interest, is quite the jerk. I know they say girls are attracted to bad boys, but I think overly-jealous, I'll-smash-everything-up-because-you-won't-talk-to-me types are really not that appealing at all. Well at least he didn't break the engine in her car so she couldn't go and visit her best friend! *coughcough*Edward*cough* 
 It's quite funny when you get to that part about 3/4 of the way through with the casino and the gambling thing. It seemed to me like Jamie McGuire suddenly realised she had no plot and no suspense and quickly had to add something in to give the book a bit more "depth". 
 To be fair, I've read worse than this, but it's really not that good. I just don't feel right wasting my time reading a book that gives me nothing to think about. I'd rather waste 1.5 hours on a Judd Apatow movie for that.

reference_books.title: Divergent (Divergent, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 Divergent is like one of those Hollywood films where the character sees something that the audience could probably figure out on their own, but still feels the need to announce it out loud, like a weirdo. We, as the audience, have usually put two and two together along with the character and them telling us, "oh, this means THAT!" is patronizing and boring. I guess what I'm getting at is the writing really lets this book down. Tris is perceptive and good at figuring things out, but only because the author doesn't seem to trust the reader enough to figure these things out alone. Everything had to be explained by Tris, even her feelings about Four. For me, good writing is when I am left to ponder the characters and the situations without much direction. 
 A lot of this book is just unconvincing. Tris is more like a robot than an actual person, Four's characterization seems a bit weak and almost inconsistent at times, they fall in love way too quickly, and many parts of this seemed like a Hunger Games rip off. I was bothered by the logic of these "factions". I don't believe that a world like that could ever exist. People CHOOSE their factions at the age of sixteen -- so they're not really being oppressed. This is something I was also unclear on -- they take the test and are given a result of which faction they are suited to, but they can still choose whichever one they want? And the consequences of being factionless don't seem that bleak or terrifying to me... You end up as a 
 bus driver or cleaner. Well, I guess it's nice to know what Veronica Roth thinks of those jobs, given that in the world of Divergent being factionless is scarier than death. It's kind of offensive. The Erudite (ie, the intelligent) are viewed as inherently suspicious and cunning. Sounds a little like old world Christian thinking! 
 I thought at times there were glimpses of an attempt at imagining Plato's Republic, as his ideal polis was one in which people were organized into areas of society or jobs they were "best" at. That could have been kind of brilliant, but no. I don't think that's what Roth was thinking. I heard she wrote this in a month, and I totally believe it. 
 I know this is a novel for teenagers and perhaps it doesn't deserve to be critiqued as much as books written for adults, but with series like Harry Potter, The Hunger Games and His Dark Materials I feel like there's no excuse. Those series have proved that writing for teenagers can be just as amazing, convincing and philosophical as anything else. Ah well.

It came as no surprise that the author based him on Cocteau's beast from 'La Belle et le Bete'. That's still my favourite version of the fairy tale. There were a few moments I thought were exceptionally nice -- mainly when the beast is describing how he cuts the roses before they die to prevent their 'suffering' and wishes someone would do that for him. I found the author's use of the roses as various metaphors to be the most effective part of the novel, and it surprisingly didn't seem entirely cliche. However, I still can't give this more than two stars, because a lot of the dialogue was pretty mediocre and unconvincing, and the chat room parts... Seriously, WTF.

book_b.user_review:

beautiful art. smart dialogue. can't wait to see where it goes

Awesomely good graphic novel that is as much a character study of the human condition under life-and-death stress as it is about survival in zombie-infested lands. Not to beat you over the head with it or anything, but "walking dead" refers to the survivors.

I don't get all the hype over this. I enjoy the TV show a great deal, but don't understand what all the hype is over the comics and how it got picked up to be a TV show in the first place. The show is 100 times better than the comics.

It has been a while since I read graphic novels. However, after several of my friends who do suggested this series, I've found myself enjoying it. It diverges quickly from the AMC TV Series, however that makes it more enjoyable in my opinion. 
 It appears to me this series is being written on the fly and is attempting to investigate what people will do/are capable of doing when society breaks down. This has been an area of writing I have been interested in. I have a strong opinion that our hold on humanity is possibly an illusion Books like "The Road" have been brilliant at investigating this question. Results usually do come out that someone who decides to not give into the chaos shows that humanity can survive. I feel this series is attempting to probe that question as well and is doing it in a thought proving manor. 
 Very enjoyable, great artwork and I look forward to reading more of the series.

reference_books.review_text: 2,5 stars. I don't think I should've read this book this year because I truly think I would have enjoyed it more if I was older.

reference_books.title: All the Bright Places
reference_books.review_text:
*exhales slowly* So, All the Bright Places... this was a hard one to get through. I almost quit reading it several times and maybe pushing myself to read it wasn't the best choice but I did it, I did it! 
 "The Fault in Our Stars meets Eleanor and Park" apparently every new contemporary release is going to be compared to John Green and Rainbow Rowell novels. Do they have similarities? Yes, quite a lot but I felt that it tried too hard and overall this book was just a big no for me. 
 Talking about the characters, I didn't understand Finch at all. Sometimes he didn't even seem like a true character but just fragments of ideas that didn't work out. He was so judgemental and half the time I wanted to punch his face and I didn't really sympathize with Violet's character too. 
 The book had enjoyable parts and presented some nice facts and ideas but it didn't do anything particularly new, and didn't really make me think about something I'd never thought about before. To be honest it actually made me feel very sad (and not the good kind of sad) and really angry (as I read things like "Note to self: Suicide is not a laughing matter" and "The thing I know about bipolar disorder is that it's a label. One you give crazy people." I actually wanted to throw my digital copy across the room.) 
 I saw a lot of people who loved this book and that's okay but this one just didn't work out for me.

reference_books.title: Saving Francesca
reference_books.review_text: 3.5 stars. This was a great book but also a little bit dry.

reference_books.title: 100 Sideways Miles
reference_books.review_text:
3.5 stars. 
 I read Andrew Smith's other novel, Grasshopper Jungle, some time last year and didn't particularly like it, but I think that a lot of the things that went wrong with Grasshopper Jungle actually worked really well with this book. If you're acquainted with Andrew Smith's books, you know that they're pretty weird, and 100 Sideways Miles is not an exclusion, it is awkward, uncomfortable and it had the kind of humour of a sixteen year old boy, but it was such a nice story. 
 A little bit hard to explain why I enjoyed it so much but it was such a poignant coming of age story, and it wasn't so much the characters I liked but the themes explored. I would've rated it higher but the last chapters, excluding the last two, were so uninteresting.

reference_books.title: Ugly Love

book_a.user_review:

Although it is a very fast read this was one of the least exciting books I've read in my life, I may be speaking for the work of a translator but I wasn't such a big fan of the writing and for the exception of a few chapters, I didn't think this was a creepy novel at all. 
 I just couldn't get into the author's idea of a horror novel, the only 'scarier' parts were towards the end but still... everything felt so juvenile and the characters were so annoying. Conversations between characters were so random(I know the book was first published in Norwegian, so maybe it got lost in translation? But I find it hard to believe it got that messed up by translation), a ton of stuff with the plot was random and then I didn't even get to be scared by some awesome aliens. 
 The book was definitely dark and had the creepy factor. But what made it dark is that Harstad went in thinking I'm just going to kill everyone off in space(on the moon!) and then give a massively nonsensical ending. WTF ending? WTF? 
 I picked this book up because a few reviewers I follow and love had just finished reading it and gave it 5*, saying "it's intense, dark, creepy and mind blowing." Yea, I don't know what book they read, but it must have had a different story under the cover. Oh, there's a positive; the cover makes sense with the story. Absurd idea, sorry can't even finish.

What an interesting horror story - and one with very little chance of a sequel (I hope!). 
 NASA, for various reasons, has decided to go back to the moon but they need an excuse and a way to gin up public interest. The excuse is a search for a mineral that would give America the edge in nanotechnology, the public interest angle is that three teens (between the ages of 14-18, of a certain height, in good physical and psychological health) will be chosen as passengers. In reality they're gong back to activate DARLAH 2, a Top Secret lunar base set up in the 1970s. 
 Mia only wants to play in her punk band, possibly cut an album and go on tour before moving to an artists loft with her band mates; her parents, rather that recognizing that she's nearly an adult treat her the same as they treat her 6-year-old brother and cannot believe she isn't eager to be one of the teens, so they enter her into the contest. Midori is a disaffected Japanese teen who only fits in when she's at Harajuku, spending all her money on items for her outlandish costumes; entering the contest is a way for her to escape and gain fame to spur her move to New York. Antoine has just been dumped by his girlfriend, stalking her by using the telescopes on the Eiffel Tower to peer into her bedroom; the contest is the perfect way for him to change his life (and possibly get her back). 
 The three join the NASA trained astronauts on the trip, which goes very, very wrong indeed. There's a reason why the moon trips stopped, but the people who were involved were sworn to silence or - like Oleg Himmelfarb - suffering from Alzheimers. Or dead. Mr. Himmelfarb, sitting in his nursing home, has flashes of memories but can't do anything about them. 
 There are some logic issues with this book (for example, wouldn't NASA have tested the three, or had a cadre of teens from which to ultimately choose, like some reality show?) but the subtle horror will render them unimportant. This is horror like that in Let Me In, with a higher psychological component than most American writers allow for. 
 ARC provided by publisher.

book_b.title: This One Summer
book_b.user_review: Beautiful art, nice summer setting and the story was entertaining, but while it tackled a lot of issues, I don't feel it dealt with them in the right way. I understand that Rose was still a really young character that is dealing with a lot of stuff at the moment, but she had such awful views and a bad attitude. The only part I truly liked was the moment when Rose's friend, Windy, called her out for sex-shaming, but at the ending of the book I'm not sure there were any character developments or if any of the issues were resolved.

sample_reviews.review_text: Slow pacing evokes the mood of summer, and realistically brings together the twin dramas occurring in Rose's life as she observes the teenage townie drama between the "duds" and "sluts" and the pervasive sadness in her own family whose roots lead back to the previous summer.
It's a good graphic novel but it does have a little bit of language in it.

I wanted to like this so very much. The illustrations are absolutely beautiful, and it won a Caldecott honor. But I found the text to be devoid of any beauty whatsoever. It's simply filled with vulgarity, profanity, ugliness, glorified horror. Yes, teens are exposed to this stuff (language, sexual content, family issues). When I bought for a high school library, I bought books with plenty of strong language and mature issues, but the content seemed appropriate for the purpose of the book and for what was to be gained by reading it. I could have felt very differently about this if it simply gave me SOMETHING to make exposing myself to all the vulgarity worth it. I took nothing good away from it. It was ugly and seemed to be shocking for the sake of being shocking. It seemed to bank itself that kids will like it (and buy it) just because it can cram 10 offensive things into a double-page spread. No great truths, no lessons learned, no nugget of beauty...just ugly. It's not the world I want to live in and not the kind of stuff I want to fill myself (or my teenage daughter or my students) with. And at some point, we as a society need to make decisions about the world we want and what we want to fill our kids up with. This is not it. I can't believe it was given a Caldecott honor! The Caldecott is for children's books, and this is absolutely NOT for children. And I certainly don't find it honorable.
Boooring! 2 stars only for nice graphics.

I read this book because I love Mariko Tamaki's work on the current run of Hulk. While there many great things in this graphic novel, it just wasn't for me. 
 I liked the sense of temporality built throughout, and I appreciate anything that focuses on the weird, liminal experience of being a 12 year-old girl. This plot was simple and well done, but didn't grab me particularly. I just personally don't feel compelled by overhearing marital conflict and teenage pregnancies. I thought the perspective in relation to these conflicts was interesting, but in the end, I didn't come away feeling as wow-ed by this as I was by Hulk. 
 The art is lovely, beautiful, and really contributes to the pacing of the book in a masterful way. 
 A good book and worth a read.
I enjoyed this graphic novel but it din't blow me away. The artwork was great but the story was just ok. I felt like they could have done more.
2,5 stars
Such a beautifully done graphic novel both story wise and detail in art. I'm glad I finally got to read this from my backlog.

This is one of the loveliest graphic novels I've seen in years. The perfect summer read; you can smell the sea salt, taste the smores on your tongue, feel the forest leaves crunch beneath your feet, and feel the wind as it whips through the trees. Take this one to the cabin for the weekend, share it with friends, and enjoy.

November 2- Honestly, the story didn't resonate with me in any sort of way. I was more drawn in by the art and the color palette of the book, which is a new experience for me. I haven't read too many graphic novels but I was just so absorbed by the art of this one. The movement and the characterization and the emotion and just -- it was spectacular. reference_books.title: I Capture the Castle
reference_books.review_text: Loved it, the British are so damned charming. Why couldn't I have grown up in a crumbling English castle? reference_books.title: The Buried Giant
reference_books.review_text: I really wanted to like this since Never Let Me Go is one of my favorite books. And I like that Ishiguro isn't afraid to jump genres. But the story didn't have enough tension and (spoiler alert!) the dragon was so easily slain that it was ridiculous. And by the end where the real meaning of the book came to the fore I just felt kinda manipulated by the pathos. Maybe it would have had better effect as a short story so that the metaphor could sustain the whole thing.

reference_books.title: Wicked Bugs: The Louse That Conquered Napoleon's Army & Other Diabolical Insects
reference_books.review_text: Interesting, quick read. If you're a fan of Mary Roach you'll like Amy Stewart and I'll definitely read her other book about plants. And the actor of this audiobook was really good.

reference_books.title: The Count of Monte Cristo
reference_books.review_text: I can't believe I'm going to say this but I liked movie better. It was more tightly plotted and dramatic so more enjoyable from a modern perspective. And the ending! Jeez. Still great even when Dumas writes twenty words where one will do. Also, just modern taste and for some reason 30+ CDs are harder to get through than actual pages. The audio version was very good. Are they always better when read by a British actor? I think I am beginning to have that prejudice.

reference_books.title: The Amityville Horror
reference_books.review_text: You gotta respect it as a trailblazer and an icon but even still it's not a great piece of "non-fiction." No surprises after all the movies. The real story behind the DeFeo murders is far more interesting and probably written better. An interesting perspective I heard in a podcast is that the demon panic caused by this and The Exorcist in the seventies was an impetus for the resurgence of fundamentalism we see today... food for thought.

book_a.title: Coraline
book_a.user_review: Freaked me the eff out! And I read it when I was 22 years old!

sample_reviews.review_text: Great book, I saw the movie first but no biggie, still a marvelous book!

Coraline and her family moved to a new building with neighbors that just don't get her name. The guy upstairs who plays with mice and the ladies downstairs who still are living in their acting days call her Caroline. Oh, and her parents are always busy...working and never having time for little Coraline. So Coraline has to find ways to entertain herself in this weird building and its raining outside. 
 Coraline's dad suggests that she go explore the place and count all the doors and windows in their new home. The thing is, she finds this one mysterious door that is locked and her mom says its nothing but a brick wall behind it. But curiosity gets the better of Coraline and she unlocks it to find an odd, different world. Here she finds her "other" parents that want to entertain her and feed her everything that she loves. 
 At first, it seems perfect, but when she wants to return back to her real home and parents, the "other" mother doesn't want her to. Will Coraline escape this "other" world? 
 I'm not quite sure if I had more expectations for this book or if it's too much of a children's book. But I felt as if this one was an okay book (maybe I shouldn't have bought it). However, I'm sure I can pass it on to my nephews when they're a little bit older because it seems like the kind of a book boys would like to read (even if the main character is a girl). I think it's because this book has that scary edge to it. And even good lessons about appreciating your parents. 
 But for me, I think the book could have had better character development (that could just be the fact that I love character based books). The weird neighbors were interesting, but I liked the children in the "other" world. Their story was the most interesting for me and I wished it was more developed. On the bright side, the descriptions were wonderful and the theater scenes were fun to imagine. 
 This is a book that elementary teachers can definitely recommend to their young students. But as an adult, I found parts of it kind of creepy and too weird for me.
Loved it.

This audiobook, made by Harper Audio, is a real treat. Not only is the author Neil Gaiman reading it, in its entirety, but HE SINGS in it. Just a tad bit, but still...! ".....you are not my mother.......and I want to go home.....!" Is still ringing through my head. 
 The book is somewhat like the movie, for the most part. There are some small differences, here and there. The similarities and sameness kept, are wonderful. It's still brilliantly done. 
 I sincerely wish I'd had this novel available to me when I was a young girl, instead of (or maybe along with?) the Nancy Drew series my mother bought me, in nearly it's entirety. (We were missing one or two books). It was not scary at all, just a little creepy. And not in a bad way at all. I enjoyed it all, very much, especially since I'd made sure to watch my copy of the movie, the day before reading this novel. 
 I have found that the movie version of Coraline is a bit more bratty, a bit more sarcastic, and a bit more snotty to her parents. I'm betting this is so that it will appeal to kids these days, maybe. The omission of Wybee (or however you spell his name) and his grandmother was strange, but ok. (This just meant that Coraline's parents bought the part of the huge house they lived in, instead of renting it.). The weird 'actress' ladies downstairs didn't have tons of Scotty terriers, just a few. (And they didn't make angel outfits for them, and stuff them and keep them, thankfully). There were no dolls made, with black button eyes, and left on people's doorsteps. The Other Mother didn't turn into a spider-like lady at all, and there was no web. There was a garden, but it played no part in the movie what-so-ever. I don't think it was even mentioned what Coraline's parents did, much more than they worked on computers, somehow. And Coraline only visited the Other Mother's house, through the passageway once, before things turned bad. 
 All in all, I enjoyed this novel a lot. I wish there was more of it. I will buy it one day, so I can listen to Gaiman sing softly, and slightly embarrassed-ly, some day soon. 5 stars.

Coraline's story has been an inspiring one for me since I first watched the movie many years ago. This fall, I decided it was about time I read the original story. Essentially, there is no need to read the book if you have seen the movie -- which I almost never say, being a devout bibliophile. However, in this case, for most of the book I was reading the dialogue in the voices of the characters from the movie. It nearly word for word, and the plot is generally followed all the way through. The only noticeable differences were those that the movie added for better scene transitions and for visual affects. The most important, and sadly disappointing, difference, was the lack of my second favorite character (after Coraline, of course), Wybie. He was a crucial character in the movie, having appeared and influenced many of the important moments in the film, including the climax at the end. 
 Speaking of which, the book's climax was far less dramatic than it was in the movie, unfortunately. I also thought that the movie wrapped everything up a little bit better (more positively as well) than the book. 
 Also, if you pick up this book, make sure you acknowledge the quotes it exhibits. There are quite a few inspirational ones in there. 
 'Coraline' was one of my top to-reads for the fall, and I must say it is sort of the perfect book to read all cozied up alongside a cup of tea or hot cocoa! I will be putting up a list of great fall novels to read for the fall on my book blog: www.umbrellabooks.blogspot.com 
 Did you imagine the movie characters while reading the book, or did you read this before seeing the movie? And most importantly, which was best? Too close to call? 
 I would love to know what you thought!

sample_reviews.review_text: Sepertinya kurang meyakinkan. Trus, cerita cintanya kurang menarik, bukan karena ceritanya sedang di dunia zombie, tapi memang kurang aja.

The Forest of Hands and Teeth is a cross between M. Night Shyamalan's The Village and Day of the Dead. Yep, it's another zombie story. 
 Zombies are surfing high on zeitgeist, why we're not sure of exactly, their enduring popularity baffles, and all the weaknesses of the zombie genre are apparent in The Forest. 
 Set well after your typical plague-of-undead, survivors persist in a handful of fenced-off enclaves, living like pioneers. It's the timescales that are the problem here: Where do the zombies come from, if people are so few? This illogicality is par for the course in a book that too often tries to have it both ways, like she writes often of putrefaction, but then specifically tells us her 'Unconsecrated' do not decay; protagonist Mary is breathtakingly selfish for a woman brought up in a village that relies on self-sacrifice, and the plot depends on complete isolation for the village, yet still having fenced paths linking it to others. 
 The book trips on the narrative problems posed by these paths - it says the chain link fences are maintained, but where do the raw materials come from? Why do maintenance crews from different villages not meet when out repairing the path fences? If, on the other hand, they only maintain them sporadically, why do the fences not rust away or get breached by falling trees? There are other unanswered questions: Why don't the villagers hunt the zombies out? If they have access to supplies of wire, why don't they make armour? Why do the characters not get other infectious diseases after being raked by rotting fingernails? Details are iffy too: crossbows fire bolts, not arrows; arrows are nocked, not notched; and a scythe - taken up by the heroes instead of a couple of handy swords - is next to useless as a weapon. Ryan is replaying magpie-gathered bits of popular culture here, she's not bringing any fresh flesh to the dining table. 
 For all that, The Forest... is diverting, its mixing of romance and zom-conventions oddly engaging. Expect sequels.

I really wanted to love this book for many reasons. First of all it was my first zombie read,second the cover was amazing and 3rd the synopsis sounded great. I will say the first quarter of the book had me riveted but as I got to know Mary more ans see the love triangle(if you can even all it that) develop it just all fell flat for me. I really started to loathe Mary and her thought process as well. I always try to put myself in every characters shoes and try to understand their thoughts and choices, Mary's lost me and kept me frustrated. It has been a year since I have read this book and since the other 2 are not from Mary's point of view, I might read them at a later date.

Ryan's first novel in the Forest of Hands and Teeth series is gripping. Mary lives in the future when the world has been overrun by zombies, called the Unconsecrated. Her town is the only safe bastion left. Surrounded by a chain-link fence that no one ever goes beyond, her world is small and simple. You marry for commitment and to have children, not love. You listen to the governing body, the religious Sisterhood and never question them. Life within the fence is safe, there hasn't been a breach in years. But Mary's father is missing, assumed to be one of the Unconsecrated now. Mary's story is about love, following dreams, and trying to make it in a world that is dangerous and oftentimes depressing. I can't wait to pick up the second novel.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I like books about zombies. I like that zombies are an enemy you can't negotiate with, win over or sexualize (unless you're into really, really weird stuff) but are still disturbingly human. Zombies are not the problem in this book. In fact, the zombie world Carrie Ryan has created is very interesting to me: the intricately linked yet isolated villages; the Sisterhood and the extent /limits of their influence; and the seemingly human-made fast zombies. The problem is the protagonist, Mary. I don't know if I've ever hated a main character like I hate Mary. I dislike her for two reasons: 1- Everything she does has the same emotional intensity. Everything from her mother dying to Harry grabbing her hand in the river to her choosing to be the one that decapitates Travis has a shrill, one-note panic that just becomes maddening over 300 pages. Every book needs to have an arch in plot and emotion to make the story truly satisfying. "The Forest of Hands and Teeth" has neither, it's just Mary freaking out the whole time. 2- Mary has no gumption. She stumbling into situations blindly, led only by emotion and when things go wrong she curls up and wishes she can rewind time or just gives up and waits for death. Then, she's miraculously saved. . .
Absolute drivel. This book is exactly why YA(fantasy) has such a bad name.

I had seen this book many times in the bookstore, but the above description sounded like the story was some clone of 'The Village'. 
 Imagine my surprise when I read in another review that it was about zombies! So I decided to pick it up 
 This book has lots of things that make a good zombie story, zombie mayhem being one of them. The story is quite good: dark and disturbing at times. So I should LOVE this book and I wanted to, but instead it fell short of that and I thought it was ok. Why is that? 
 It has to do with two things. 
 First: Present tense! 
 I have mentioned before I'm no fan of stories written in present tense. Once in a while there's an author who can handle present tense and write in such a way I don't even notice the present tense being used, but most authors fail in this and Ryan is among them. I kept getting pulled out of the story by the use of present tense. It just didn't feel natural. 
 Second: The viewpoint! 
 I read a lot of stories that use one person as the focus of the story and let him/her tell the story to you. Usually I do not have a problem with this and even love it as it gives you a great deal of insight in the workings of the lead character's mind. 
 In this book however I really missed the viewpoint of other characters besides Mary. This has to do with the fact I kept thinking Mary was not being honest in how she viewed the other characters. I felt like there should be more to the other characters than only Mary's view of them. This too kept me from losing myself in the story. 
 And lastly (ok, I said two things, but this one isn't really about me not loving the book, but just a pet peeve): Did you see the cover?! Again no zombies!! 
 All in all I'm really on the fence about this book and I'm not sure I'll read the next book 'The Dead-Tossed Waves'.

sample_reviews.review_text: I thought this would be disturbing and upsetting but it was written so beautifully that I was carried along and just went with it. Another beautiful book by a talented writer.

I finished this book and I thought. I thought about people and lives, about the things we don't see, the things we don't normally stop to think about.

I picked this book up purely because it was about conjoined twins and I had never read a book about conjoined twins before. I didn't realise it was written in verse until I got onto the bus and opened the first page. I'm not sure if that would have made a difference concerning me buying this book or not but I am glad that I bought it. 
 It was so so interesting and the poetic layout just added so much to the story. The story was well thought out and, in my opinion, well explained. Conjoined twins are not something I often think about. I am aware that they exist of course but I have never personally encountered any so I don't think about them at all really. This story was so important because it explored the way that people perceive these twins and I realised that yes, I too would feel sorry for them or hate to be like that. Because I can't imagine being tied together with another person, I would feel suffocated, I would feel trapped. But of course, if that is all you ever knew, you wouldn't feel that way. 
 I read the whole thing in like two hours. I just really loved this story.
Such a good book, would recommend to anyone.

DNF at 74% 
 It was a mistake to read One after I read Wonder. I couldn't help but comparing the two books and I just keep disappointed with One. 
 I have two main reasons as to why I didn't like the book: 
 1. Annoying main characters (especially Grace) 
 I know, I know. I should've been at least a bit sympathetic toward them but to be perfectly honest, I didn't. Grace was too deep in self-pity, in my opinion. And as much as I tried to tolerate her and Tippi, I think they did so many disappointing things that would threaten their health, like no. No. No. No. 
 2. The writing style 
 It was written in verses which sounded like a good idea until I realized what a huge mess it was. I didn't get enough of the messages and information, I didn't feel engaged with the characters, and so on and so forth. This was probably the main reason why I didn't like this book. If only it could be told in a different and better way, then perhaps, I could like this book more.

This was an awesome read. I like variety and I also like publishers/authors/books that include many facets and experiences... and this book did just that. For once we are given a YA book about conjoined twins. I am not sure how accurately it depicts growing up as a conjoined twin, but the effort alone is great. Another note worthy point is that I never felt as though this book was making fun of conjoined twins or even exploit such a situation. 
 Besides its originality the main character, Grace, has a remarkably insightful voice, but of course that is something you would expect from someone who has lived on the outskirts of the norm. While she is the relaxed and quiet one, Tippi is the loud and usually dominate one. They have 4 arms, 2 heads, 2 hearts, 2 legs, and fused intestines (and lady parts). Her parents have homeschooled them since they were little, but times are changing, and they will soon be in a regular high school with regular kids, like their little sister "Dragon". 
 Unfortunately for the twins, life is just getting started and it's getting harder. Now they will navigate the outside world, alone (obviously together), meet new friends, feel the stirrings of first loves, and eventually have to deal with the health complications that come with being a conjoined twin. The characters are endearing, the laughter is great, and the pain is just bittersweet. 
 4 stars. Thanks Edelweiss.

This was fantastic. As the first book I've ever read written in verse, I wasn't sure what to expect but I enjoyed this so much. Since this was written in verse, I flew through it in just over an hour. One is beautifully written and utterly heartbreaking. I thoroughly enjoyed this (despite my emotions being taken on a total rollercoaster!!!) Highly recommend if you're looking for something unique in both writing style and plot. 
 I have a full review for this on my blog here... http://girlreading.co.uk/bookreviews/...

4.5 stars 
 One is a novel written in free verse, emotionally charged, sad and touching about two conjoined twin sisters. This is the first novel I've read that is written in verse, so that part was new for me and I really really enjoyed it tremendously. 
 Tippi and Grace are two 16 year old girls that all their lives have been home schooled, attended regularly to the doctor for check ups about their health, and visit often the psychologist, all of these have affected the economy of her family and for the first time in their life they're going to public school, where they will make friends but also be mocked and misunderstood by their peers. Besides that one of the girls begins to have romantic feelings for one of her classmates, something she never saw as a possibility, due to the isolation in which they grew up, aside from their family, doctors and people they crossed paths on the street, they had no friends of their own age. 
 An also for the first time Tippi and Grace are forced to really contemplate the idea of separation surgery because if they didn't undertake such surgery it would have a great impact on their health. 
 The story is told in verse, from the viewpoint of Grace, which is the most friendly twin, which accepts the decisions of their parents and sister, without causing problems and is carried away by his Tippi, the twin with more character dominant. 
 One is beautifully written, it's a sad, touching, poignant, bittersweet novel, is one of those books that once you finish reading it you can not get it out of your head by the roller coaster of emotions that provoke on you. I highly recommended this contemporary novel.
