What a horrendously boring book. This was unexpectedly the only other book that I'd rank alongside Twilight. Like Twilight, I actually just skimmed through the entire second half of the book and couldn't wait to finish it just because it dragged on and on, I just wanted to go straight to the end. 
 It had so much promise in the beginning. I'm a sucker for stories of different women from varied walks of life, backgrounds and ages coming together and traversing the journey of life. I like exploring the depth of each character and looking at them from the lenses of a reader vicariously experiencing someone else's life for a few hours. 
 But the characters in this book were at best, mediocre and lackluster. 
 WARNING: SPOILERS AHEAD 
 The main character Georgia, I found to be quite annoying. While I appreciate her struggles from the point-of-view of a woman, I disliked the ambiguity of her character. I couldn't understand if she was strong or weak, a whiner or a warrior. She spent the better part of the book whining about being abandoned by a man who cheated on her, who walked out on their daughter too. He attempted contact, tried to make amends, to no avail. And after that build-up about her refusal to take him back, all it took to get her to relent was a night in Scotland. I know fiction often mirrors real life, but this is just preposterous. 
 The frustration I felt at her character led me not even feeling a smidgen of emotion at her death. And don't even get me started about the manner of her death, and how abruptly it was introduced in the story. Nothing about the whole book even led to this plot possibility. While I appreciate unexpected endings, this one just came from left field. Her death did not add any value to the story's end. I got even more frustrated that she died without really having any form of resolution or at least a version of a happy ever after. 
 The secondary characters Anita, Cat, Lucie, KC and Darwin were merely women who were lost struggling to find their place in the world. However, I felt that the tension that brought them to where they are today were feeble attempts at even creating some sort of tension. In my mind, they just seemed weak and tentative. 
 The only characters I actually responded well to were James and Dakota -- and yet, when THEY could finally have their "ever after", their Georgia died. 
 It was quite a disappointing book - character-wise and plot-wise. I wish I could say that there's a redeeming quality in the book, but even the writing style and story build-up was disappointing. It was slow, went too much into the nitty-gritty details of the mundane everyday. Maybe my unfamiliarity with knitting was a contributory factor, but I've somehow managed to enjoy books before that also had parallelisms to things foreign to me -- even something as technical as coal mining. 
 All in all, I guess this is the last of Kate Jacobs that I'll ever read.
I think this is a 3.5 star book. I liked it a lot better till I got to the end. Hopefully the 2nd one will be good!

** spoiler alert ** 
 This book threw me for a loop. I'm reading along, falling in love with the cast of characters and empathizing with their struggles, when all of a sudden Georgia has cancer	! And then she DIES. Who said the main character can die? I don't think I approve of this development... Especially since I can't figure out a reason for it to happen. I mean, sure, in life sometimes people get cancer and it's totally random, but this is a work of FICTION. Character deaths are supposed to make sense for the plot, or for other characters' development. But for a novel to be a joyful read centering on a strong single mom & businesswoman who learns to trust again through her close friendships with other women for 300 pages, and then she fights cancer for 50 pages, and then dies 16 pages before the end? That's not long enough to show how the other characters react to her death. 
 To be fair, one of the main themes is that life is unpredictable; characters are faced again and again with the ways in which their lives aren't going according to plan. Georgia's estranged high school best friend, Cat/Cathy, returns to her life rich and glamourous, but deeply unhappy in her marriage. Despite Georgia's long-nurtured hurt, they become close again. Anita, second in command at the yarn store and 10 years a widow, finds the courage to accept the advances of the delightful Marty (who runs the deli in the same building) and they fall in love. Grad-school Darwin's dissertations suffers a roadblock when she miscarries; her guilt over losing the baby and loneliness while her husband's doing his residency in California lead her to cheat on him. Lucie decides at 42 to have a baby, regardless of the fact that she's single and not earning a lot of money, because she wants to be a mother. K.C. is laid off of her job in publishing and decides to go to law school at age 50. 
 But the plot mainly revolves around Georgia and Dakota, her daugher. When Dakota's father, James, turned up on the scene after 12 years of silence, an angst-filled slow-burn romance was added to the mix. Georgia eventually acknowledged her feelings and they worked through the betrayal of his leaving while she was pregnant; everyone was happy. 
 Everyone was happy. They fought their fights and shared their lives, and found joy together. So it felt sloppy to suddenly introduce a major character death so soon before the end of the novel; what character can rediscover happiness in a mere 16 pages after a loved one's death? If it had been halfway through, I don't think it would have bothered me this much. I would have been sad, because the writing is so good I really cared about the characters. But the other characters, the Friday Night Knitting Club, would've had space to heal and incorporate the absence of her into their lives. The grief process could've gotten a fair treatment, not several throw-away paragraphs per character. They all are inspired by her, and heal enough to continue on with their lives, but I am not satisfied with how abridged that process is.

 i got this for a dollar at borders. it's not like i was super pumped to read it, friends giving it only a medium rating. i'm really just too tired at home to read anything too taxing. i think it's related to how much brain power i use at work. i'm still pretty busy and doing big, new projects, so my ability to read novels that do more than skim the surface is lacking. but the pendulum will swing the other way soon, i'm sure.

book_b.title: Codex
book_b.user_review: I picked this book up at a tag sale a while back. I'm really not sure why I bothered finishing it, because it was pretty sucky. The characters were not just flat, they didn't even make sense. Why did the duchess hire an investment banker to catalog her rare book collection? Why would the investment banker do it? Why does this dude act like he's melting down when the whole story takes place over like three weeks? I don't know it was like everything annoying about Dan Brown but worse.

sample_reviews.review_text: Meh.

I really love The Magicians and The Magician King by the same author, so I decided to read this one, knowing it wouldn't be as good. I think he really came into his own with The Magicians (apparently his first book wasn't much good). Still, it was an interesting read. It has a distinctive style, in syntax, plot, and mood that is very similar to his other works. Further, though I may just be reading into it, the book seems to provide some insight into the life of the author, and the kind of place he was in at the time of writing it. I didn't like it as much as his other two books I've read, which are among my favorites, but it was a good read, and I don't regret the purchase.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I'm hiding this review because it's impossible for me to review this without discussing the ending. 
 Codex was a book that I really, really wanted to love. 
 I'm a lover of literary mystery and of medieval history, so the premise began as enticing and quickly became irresistible. It presented a mystery so big and so ancient, that I couldn't wait to see where the author was going. It seemed like an incredible story for anyone who is fascinated by the mysteries of the past. 
 Throughout the book, it seemed like we were moving closer and closer to some kind of answer, or at least some information. 
 And then the end came. 
 Out of nowhere, with more confusion than it began with, Codex came to a close. The mystery wasn't solved - it had only gotten bigger. If there were some kind of other focus - if, for example, the characters had been incredibly deep and faced incredible growth throughout their efforts - I might say that Codex was worth my time reading. The first half or three quarters of the book was incredibly enjoyable, regardless of believability. In the end, Codex just left far too much unknown. If I wanted nothing more than a hugely intriguing mystery that I would never know the answers to, I could have found plenty in the real world instead of being disappointed by a novel.
This book was a bit slow to captivate me at first, but by the end I was wondering when I could sneak off and read. Train delayed a half hour? No worries! I have a good book!
I loved this book, but the ending is so frustrating, and screeches to a halt.

The storyline started off strongly and felt like the story

Tried to be too much, there were hints of a good story here, but it got lost in the shuffle of a convoluted plot.

There seemed to be very little direction for most of this book. The motivations of the characters were weak at best, and if they were present, were not very believable or compelling. The two storylines of searching for the codex and playing the computer game were completely disjointed until the very end of the book, and the way they connected was not particularly satisfying. This book was not a pageturner and it often seemed that I looked forward to the end of a chapter so that I could put it down or even stopped in the middle of chapters. I did not miss the characters when I finished the book, nor did I want to find out what happened to them after the story ended. All in all, I was happy to be finished with this book so that I could move on to something else.

reference_books.title: The Gate House
reference_books.review_text:
If you haven't read Gold Coast -- read it first. 
 You definitely don't need to leave your brain at the door -- but this is NOT a cerebral jaunt. It's a book written by an intelligent man for fun. 
 I like DeMille's style -- he sort of lurks around mystery, but this one has a lot of character development based on the Gold Coast.

reference_books.title: To Have and Have Not
reference_books.review_text:
Meh. 
 It starts very strongly -- good character development, definite Hemingway commentary tone -- lots of Hemingway Southern Hemisphere fun in Cuba. 
 But midway -- he just sort of wanders off and starts pointing his Hemingway at anything that moves. He introduces secondary and tertiary characters with incredible detail, but with no discernible purpose. 
 It's not one of his better books, and ends leaving you wondering how much better it would have been if the writing from about the second third on was more substantially interconnected. 
 What's great about this book, if you want to enjoy it/study it/comment on it -- is that he really does scatter shot his Hemingway. You could tear out just about any page of this book, and it's pure him. His meaningless meandering details are done with true depth and edge ... but they really never imbue the reader with any concern for the characters that he sort of follows randomly. 
 It would be the equivalent of going to a train station, closing your eyes, opening them, writing something about the first person you see, closing them for another hour, opening them again, writing about the first person you see and so on ... but meanwhile, there's a CRITICAL character standing off to the side smoking a cigarette doing absolutely nothing. 
 Go read The Old Man and the Sea -- or "For Whom the Bell Tolls" ... leave this for the poor sots at school who are forced to read everything by him.

reference_books.title: The Third Option (Mitch Rapp, #4)
reference_books.review_text:
I did not finish this book. I wanted to enjoy it, but the main problem I had with this book was that it was attempting to address terrorism as if 9/11 hadn't happened ... from what I can tell, it is set after 9/11 would have happened, but creates a fictional future that just clanged too hard in my ear to enjoy. 
 This specialist, who works for an anti-terrorist group and is trying to interfere with the possible weapons trade to Iraq while working for a fictional president ... it's too distracting. So I stopped reading it. I couldn't care about a character that can't exist. 
 It just clanked is all.

reference_books.title: Buried Secrets (Nick Heller, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
This is a decent character piece. The plot line is much the same as many "hired expert" books, and the tension methods are also not completely uncommon either. 
 As I read this book, I found myself watching an author write a book about a character that the author knows very well, that we know to some depth, but not as much as I would have liked. I made the mistake of reading this second book in the "Nick Heller series" before reading the first. But I also noticed that there were many suppositions about the original character that seemed to have been repaired in this second book (the author mentions newly hired people, old relationships that are different, etc.). 
 The visual descriptions in the book are well done, and Finder doesn't wander far from the premise and direction of the story -- but there are some secondary story arcs that, while related to the completion of the book, tend to be given very short resolution at the end. 
 All in all, this book is likely Finder's intended attempt to develop the Nick Heller character more completely in the hopes of starting a potential series. I would say, as far as character development goes, Finder has started the process well -- I'm just sad that he had to be dropped into an interesting, but somewhat common story arc. 
 I'll be reading more of Finder's books -- but I'll be expecting more surprises than I found on the stage around this strong character.

book_a.title: Calico Joe
book_a.user_review:
The place where this book failed was at the beginning. 
 Grisham, a gifted writer of course, made a choice to write in the point of view of a boy whose father is a baseball player, and has since grown up. Much of the book is this man looking back about events and decisions that happened around his father -- especially one event inside baseball. 
 The problem with choosing this point of view is that everything the boy saw and remembered later was from the outside -- from the stands, from far away. I already know what professional baseball looks like from far away, I wanted to see it up close. 
 This is not a spoiler, the son's relationship with his father is highly estranged (outlined on page 1). Since it is so distant, all of the feelings and motivations of his father are also removed from our view. The one professional baseball player close enough to touch is distant and cold -- not really what I was hoping to find in a Grisham novel about baseball. 
 My hopes had been to go with Grisham and stand on second base, to hear the jokes in the dugout, to sweat over the 3-2 count while gripping the ball behind my back as I prepared for my next pitch. I wanted to see that a player's relationship with his wife had affected his swing because I'm inside his head ... instead, I get pages and pages of fake statistics and artificial results of games that didn't happen ... all tracked from the viewpoint of a boy who would have liked to idolize his dad, but couldn't. 
 Finally, I think Grisham gave up. Often his characters would break with their original descriptions. Some players would be defined as highly protective, and then turn around with open arms to the seeming threat, other characters would be written as surly and unreachable, but they would arbitrarily change their minds and "do the right thing" with no further explanation necessary. 
 It could have been a great game on the field with Grisham, but instead it was a tired conversation, sitting in the stands, years after the game was over.

sample_reviews.review_text: Great book--a touching and lyrical story about a young man who seeks redemption for the sins of his father and forgiveness from a man whose life was destroyed in one venial act.

Haven't read a Grisham in I don't know when. Got tired of variations on it's- all- about- the- billable- hours. This is a departure and I liked it. A baseball story but more about redemption and the relationship between a father and son. A short but powerful read.

I had a hard time putting this book down. Unfortunately, I had to come to work. :( 
 A great book for Grisham! It's a baseball story that reads like a biography. It's about Calico Joe Castle, a baseball star for a brief time in the summer of 1973, but it's also about Paul Tracey -- an 11-year old boy and his father, Warren, another baseball player. 
 The story is told from Paul's adult point-of-view as he looks back to the summer where it looked like the Cubs might just win the pennant. 
 I highly recommend this book to anyone who loves baseball! I would also recommend this to anyone who likes historical or realistic fiction.

'Baseball is a game of failure...' 
 In a departure from his usual legal thrillers, Grisham here gives us a book about the world of baseball. The first person narrator is Paul Tracey, whose father, Warren, was a pitcher for the Mets in 1973 in the same season as Joe Castle, the Calico Joe of the title, was breaking all records as a rookie player with the Cubs. Warren is now dying and as Paul travels to see him, he tells us about his childhood, his hero-worship for Joe and why his relationship with Warren reached breaking point. 
 Normally I am a big fan of Grisham but really, there are limits. Firstly it is very short and yet the plot, such as it is, is so slight as to barely maintain interest to the end. Instead the book is filled with extremely detailed descriptions of imaginary baseball games, so detailed that Grisham felt it necessary to give what he calls a summary of the basics of the game. This 'summary' runs to 13% of the entire Kindle book and was so dull that I gave up halfway through, deciding to trust that the book would make sense even if I didn't know what a drag bunt or a pick-off might be. By about the fourth chapter, I was so bored that I was speed-reading through the innings by innings match descriptions that fill easily half the book dropping back in whenever it looked like the plot might move along a little. However, the plot was so uninteresting and cliched and the characterisation so superficial that it did not make up for all the rest. 
 I would have given this book 1 stars but I recognise some people will be more interested in baseball and perhaps in interminable scoring statistics, even imaginary ones, than I and so have upped it to an extremely generous 2. Grisham says in his introduction 'Baseball is a game of failures'. Unfortunately I feel this self-indulgent book is an example of that. Here's hoping Grisham returns to form (and the legal world) in his next novel.

A good story. If you're a baseball fan I think you'll enjoy it more. I liked the intertwining of the present day stuff and the flashbacks.

The author is a pretty big baseball fan and it shows in this story, part coming of age and part reconciliation. Told in two eras, this is the story of a rookie hitter and a veteran pitcher in 1973 coupled with the story of an aging, distant and difficult father and his son. 
 I found the baseball credible (though the rookie accomplishments cross the line to in-credible) and the story believable. Both the characters and small town America are well fleshed out. This is the first John Grisham novel I have read, though it won't be the last.

This was my first John Grisham book, and despite my favorable rating it will probably be my last. He's not as bad of a writer as I had expected, but he certainly has his limitations. Fortunately, they don't come to fore very often. This book is simply a lot of fun, especially for a guy who became a Cubs fan in the seventies. 
 (Spoiler alert). 
 Calico Joe is a Bryce Harper-esque youngster from Arkansas who gets called up to the Chicago Cubs in 1973 and sets the National League on fire. But a month later he suffers from a bean ball that ends his career and leaves him disfigured for life. 
 Grisham uses a complicated frame to tell this story. The story is told in first person from the son of the pitcher who beaned Joe. His dad, whom he loathes, is dying of cancer. The narrator decides that he's going to make his dad go to Arkansas to apologize to Joe for beaning him. He tries to blackmail him by telling him that he'll publish a story on the inside story of the beaning if his dad doesn't agree to apologize. His dad still refuses, but as he gets closer to death, he changes his mind, goes to Arkansas, and apologizes to Joe. His dad, Joe, everybody wants the narrator to publish story anyway, and presumably, the book Calico Joe is the product. 
 If that were it, then there wouldn't be much to like in this very short novel (four and a half hours in audiobook form). But the novel's flashbacks to Calico Joe's heroics, and the narrator's avid following thereof, are a heck of a lot of fun. Grisham does a marvelous job of getting into the head and heart of an eleven-year-old hero-worshipping boy. He's masterful on the baseball stuff. The narrator jokes that the final story will be like a longish Sports Illustrated story. But there's not a doubt in my mind that Grisham would make a hell of a sports writer. 
 Grisham shows a lot of wisdom in the specific heroics that Joe performs. He doesn't have him hit six home runs in a game, doesn't have him throw out a runner four hundred feet away. He chooses obscure records such as consecutive hits in a row - not Joe DiMaggio's 56-game streak, but an at-bat streak. Joe's feats are stupendous, but not unbelievable. 
 But if Grisham isn't writing about sports, I don't want to read him. I don't need to have people eat and drink random stuff to act as filler for the dialog. He even goes so far as to describe what a waffle looks like in case there are some space aliens reading and don't know that it's "a thick dessert-like creation smothered in whipping cream." I'd love to have seen the editor notes on that one. Maybe he or she deleted it, but then got direction from the publisher that they needed to thicken the book. Actually, now that I think about it, "a thick dessert-like creation smothered in whipping cream" is a perfect description of this book. I read a lot of broccoli, so I guess a treat like this is good every once in a while. Not something I want to read every day, though.

book_b.title: Seveneves
book_b.user_review:
Wow ... this book is both wonderful and a bag of garbage. 
 The first half of the book is truly captivating and a well-written and thought out "pseudo realistic" science examination of a cataclysmic event that affects the entire earth. In painstaking detail, Stephenson goes over what it means, how it happens, who it affects, why we react the way we do and so forth. 
 We get to know the characters, dig DEEPLY into their lives, minds, approaches, experiences -- it's rich and wonderful and meaningful and severe and -- 
 The second half of the book just happens and then it's over. Whatever. 
 Hope you enjoyed my review. That's how the book feels.

sample_reviews.review_text: It's quite possible that there's a great story in here, but it is so dense, and there is so much unnecessary detail to wade through, that I lost my patience trying to find it.
Great science fiction spanning 5000 years! The writing could be friendlier but it was very entertaining and interesting. What would become of us if an agent came to be?
I liked the story. The book is a little to long, and a little too many scientific details.

I found myself zoning in and out of this book, taking the words in without digesting them at times. There would be parts and bits that would hold my attention, but then it would revert to droning on and on about details that would turn out to be irrelevant to any plot development. I would say that *too* much care was given to descriptions - to the point that it was monotonous and cumbersome - without much purpose behind it, or connection to the individual being described. As has been mentioned, character development was severely lacking. The only characters I found myself caring about, even slightly, were Dinah and maybe Sonar Taxlaw. 
 I was fascinated by Neal's knowledge of hard science and found these core nuggets to be truly interesting. Unfortunately, they're surrounded by layers and layers of unnecessary fluff. Was this Stephenson going Jan Brady on us? "Rothfuss! Rothfuss! Rothfuss...!" 
 As has also been mentioned, there are also two connected but separate stories in this book. Had he split them into two, maybe that would have helped; or trimmed the gratuitous rambling down to a minimum (thusly reducing the word count by half).

** spoiler alert ** 
 Some great ideas but let down by absurd flaws that couldn't even be avoided by a 'I'm going with the flow this is a sci-fi' attitude. 
 I did go with the flow as there was enough of a storyline to keep me reading, but the flow killing techno explanatory roadbumps and 'I'm drinking a hidden stash of liqueur on a spaceship' roadbumps then the later 'everyone is race pigeonholed' roadbumps - were all just too much. I was irritated on a regular basis. 
 Seveneves is really two stories or books joined together, perhaps there should have been two separate books? The first half genuinely had potential to be a thriller page-turner with characters you cared about, but the second half left me a bit cold and eventually fizzled out, after such an epic the whole thing groaned to a slow end. 
 A bit disappointed to be honest and absolutely nowhere near Ian M Banks, Culture series, which I guess is my sci-fi 'benchmark'.

I have mixed feelings about this book. 
 I started off not quite buying the characters and the technology, but slowly got more and more into it. Once I was finally enjoying it, it jumped forward in time and for a while it was terrible again, until I got used to the characters and new supertech. It feels like two novels stuck together. The reveal of the title was disappointing, my imagined explanation of the title and the direction of the plot seemed better to me than what it turned out to be. 
 I read this right after finishing Kim Stanley Robinson's "Aurora". In a way they are very similar, but I kept thinking "Aurora" was better. If they were not so close in my mind I might be judging it as harshly. 
 Huh, I thought I liked it, but as I write this I realize that I was really not a fan. I am not sure if it is objectively bad, or just not to my taste.

I read this book in large part because I've liked most of the other Stephenson books I've read, and besides, Bill Gates recommended it. It turned out to be one of those rare books that make me wish I belonged to a book club so I could talk to other people about it. 
 First sentence: "The moon blew up without warning and for no apparent reason." Honestly, that didn't strike me as a sentence that boded well for the accuracy of the science in a book. But that assessment was wrong. The book is just as full of good science as The Martianis (though not nearly as much snark). And the science is just as well handled - it isn't just thrown on the page, it is explained, often by characters within the story. And is it mostly broken into digestible chunks. And there is plenty of plot and good characterization so even if you aren't really into the science, there is plenty of drama and action and suspense to keep you turning pages. 
 At the end of part two was a scene that didn't really work for me in terms of my own experience with human nature. Then in part three, results of that scene also didn't ring true to me. But as the book progressed and the author explained his reasoning, he won me over somewhat. This is what I wish I could discuss with others! But I decided that overall the book is so wonderful that this disagreement over human nature is just theory & a difference in our expectations. I have certainly read many books with which I disagreed more about human nature and how people would act in certain circumstances!

** spoiler alert ** 
 I cannot imagine how much research this book took to write. I didn't always agree or like where the plot went, but I trusted the author enough to know that the story would still be worth reading. I love science fiction and this was exactly to my taste. The massive size of this book allows the reader to sink into the story and read with your heart in your throat. 
 I had one tiny beef...if you knew you were one of a handful of male humans left, wouldn't you set aside some sperm? Just sayin'.

 With that said, I didn't hate this book. After everything is said and done, I like the premise and think it's a decent read if you have the patience to get through it.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This book was the best case of "Tumblr made me do it." Contemporary romances are generally not my first pick, or something that generally interests me. But alas, I succumbed. That, combined with the fact that I am a. asexual and b. kind allergic to alcohol, left me with characters that I couldn't really relate to. And for me, contemporaries work best when I can at least relate in some level to the characters. There's no world building, magic, or politics like in fantasy to distract me. The characters make up the book. And suffice to say, not only can I not identify with any of the main characters, they were annoying as fuck. 
 Lily... I think this book's first error was choosing to narrate from her point of view. It might have benefited from switching points of view, or a third person point of view. Her constantly whining about everything, and thinking about sex every two words got old after two pages. And the way the author wrote her addiction felt really forced. Some books can make an addiction, mental illness, whatever feel real, whereas some sound like the author has no fucking clue what they are talking about. I don't really know if this author has a clue about what they are talking about, but it certainly doesn't seem like it. I didn't feel it in Lily's character. I felt like I was just being reminded again, and again, and again by the author that yes, Lily has a sex addiction. And she has a terrible throbbing between her legs. Yes. I get it. Can you not repeat the same phrase over, and over, and over? 
 Now for Loren and Lily's relationship... It felt forced. There was absolutely no chemistry between them. Just because its a friends to lovers novel, doesn't mean that the characters can be forced together without any build up. And Lily constantly lusting after him doesn't really count as build up, because there was no fucking connection between them. No spark. Nothing. I was never rooting for them, and I hoped that they would stay friends. Alas, I was disappointed in that regard too. 
 Loren wasn't as bad as Lily, but he wasn't that captivating either. No offense Loren, but if you have been slumping at home, over drinking etc. and barely exercised until Connor came into the picture (I doubt you ran every day, and even still, it takes more than running, honey), there's no way you will have a killer body. I'm not liking this trend in adult romances where the love interest is this big buff guy who gets there without any working out. If the guy doesn't put in a few hours a day at the gym, I'm sorry, but STOP GIVING HIM MASSIVE MUSCLES!!! It ain't that easy to get killer muscles. Why do you think people spend so much time working out? 
 This book peaked when Connor entered, but even he wasn't enough to save me from the ever constant whining of lily Calloway. Ryke was okay too, but Connor still takes the title of my favourite.
Fucking good is such an understatement. Wow. This. Book. I. Can't. Even.
*3.5 stars

damn these two are messed up...and each of them feed off of each others addictions while covering for each other. Loren pissed me of so many times...but then so did Lily! Such a mess...couldn't put the book down! this was a freebie...and i'm hooked...heading to next!

2.5/5 
 This started out good and interesting but in the middle dragged so much. I know they were trying to show their battles with addiction but uggh, get to the story already. The ending really picked up and redeemed it for me. I'm still undecided if I'll go on with the series.

Wow. I'm so mad I waited until now to read ADDICTED TO YOU. I'm amazed at how different Lily's perspective was from Rose's in KISS THE SKY. I shouldn't be; Rose and Lily are as different as two sisters can be. I guess I assumed that because it was written by the same authors, it would sound somewhat similar. But where KISS THE SKY came across witty and intelligent just like Rose, ADDICTED TO YOU is so much darker and full of self-doubt (just like Lily). Krista and Becca Ritchie truly captured the voice of their characters and told the story exactly as the character would have told it. 
 Lily and Lo have created the perfect system to hide their addictions from the world. They use each other as their alibi to hide the parts of themselves that no one else wants to see. Lo is able to continue drinking without letting on just how dangerous his drinking has become and Lily can have as many one night stands as she needs without anyone calling her a slut or knowing how addicted she is to sex. Lily and Lo have carried on their pretend relationship for so long that the lines between pretending and real have started to blur and Lily isn't sure she still wants the relationship to be pretend. 
 When Lily and Lo begin to add people to their inner circle, complications arise and the chance for discovery becomes much more likely. They must question if the crutch they provide for each other truly benefits the other person or if they are enabling themselves right into a shallow grave. 
 Just as I loved Rose and Connor's perspective in KISS THE SKY and Daisy AND Ryke's in HOTHOUSE FLOWER, I truly adored getting to know Lily and Lo in ADDICTED TO YOU. I quickly came to understand the depth of love and devotion they have for each other. Lily and Lo are in such a low, dark place in ADDICTED TO YOU and yet I can't help but see just how beautiful they could be if only they could find a way to conquer their addictions. I'm so impressed with the three books I've read by Krista and Becca Ritchie and I can't wait to read more. I'm really grateful that not onl as well to indulge in my new Ritchie addiction!

I think 'read' is a generous term for what went down here. Merciful skipping and skimming. 
 I was eye rolls and exhaustion and boredom. Such boredom. Fires extinguished by the breadth of my yawns. 
 I can see why young adult audiences would thrive on this writing--it's overly effusive, sentimental, and dripping with soul mate love stories. The author attempts, I think, a kind of stream of consciousness approach, but it fails for a more .... self aware audience, I think. This book really could have been half as long. Limitless descriptions of every single thought do not make for enjoyable experience. Because the reader does not experience! We only hear, we are told over and over and over again from every single perspective about the magnitude of every single second. 
 That bores me. 
 Not to mention all my problems from the earlier novels: the recovery from a more or less genocide (even if souls can be refurbished) was too clean and simple; the instant love that is love for the sake of love being there (whenever their eyes meet!!!!) is meaningless--she tries to recover that by showing their discovery of each other's character in this novel, but it rings false all the way through; the storyline is convoluted, and the ending is just talking (not the epilogue); the idea that ripping through worlds creates traumas is straight out of Pullman (the idea of tithing it is unremarkable); akiva's all consuming and amazing powers again are made I think to try and make up for the fact that these people are all killers. They find a happy ending. Good for them. Abandon earth, and all is well. 
 Sigh. I didn't really read it halfway through. I found the prose too burdensome, especially with the constant longing and sexual tension that is dumped on us like a merciless avalanche. For me, the first half of the first book is stellar. The second book angers me bc of Karou's characterization, and this book was just unbearable to get through. 
 I am surely in the minority, but these are my thoughts.

More reviews available at my blog, Beauty and the Bookworm. 
 I was so excited to dive in to the last book of this trilogy, but also apprehensive, because the second book was not as magical as the first, and I was concerned about the third following in that path. And there's the rub: I was right to be apprehensive. 
 With seraphim invading the human world, our heroine Karou and hero Akiva find themselves trying to force the remaining Misbegotten seraphim and a paltry bunch of chimaera to get along long enough to save both Earth and Eretz. But here's the thing...Taylor can't seem to be satisfied with that as a plot. Instead, she starts throwing in new ones, like a looming cataclysm and a backstory that hasn't been mentioned until now and worlds-threatening monsters that don't ever actually end up getting resolved. And while some of this is cushioned by another burgeoning romance between Liraz and Ziri (THANK GOD, because I couldn't put up with any more of his pining) and of course Karou and Akiva trying to come together once again, it just felt like too much, especially because the story didn't really just end, it just kind of trailed off. 
 I'm not really sure there's that much more to say about this. There were some excellent moments in here--the confrontation in the Vatican comes to mind, Eliza's return to her true self, Mik and Zuze and the stormhunters as well--but overall I'm not sure they could really redeem a book that felt kind of scattered. It definitely didn't have the magic of the first book, the snap and sizzle and all of the tropes made over and new again; instead, it felt much more like a generic fantasy story, and one that didn't come to a soaring or even a crashing conclusion, but instead just sort of petered out. While Karou and Akiva were wonderful and even Liraz got some redemption (but what the heck was up with Haxaya? Something else that was never explained) there were just too many holes and dropped strings here to make me really like it as a book. Ultimately, the first book was the best of this series, and it was a bit of a downhill slide from there. I'm interested in Taylor's more recent book, but this series ultimately didn't deliver what I had really hoped it would. It read a lot like the upwards-of-a-million-word-long RP a friend and I have had going off and on for years--and while it might be fun to write your own melodrama and jump from plot to plot and have things dropped, there's the potential of it all coming back together again later. I kept hoping things would come together here, but they never did, and that was a disappointment. 
 2 stars out of 5.

Oh. Wow. This third book is the best of all. Well, no it isn't. All three are so good! But Taylor finished up her magnificent trilogy PERFECTLY. 
 I can't go into detail because, in all honesty, it would take me forever because there are SO many details to address! Let's just say that every doggone plot thread was brought to a clean and satisfying end, which is no small feat. This trilogy has ended up with a huge cast, and Taylor developed personal plot lines for, what, at least ten of them. I will say that the last fifth of the book starts to feel a little like somebody ticking items off a list: "Okay, this plot line is done, that one's done, this one's done," etc. But again, there's no other way to do it, really. It's THE END, and each character's personal adventure has to be addressed. 
 POSSIBLE SPOILER ALERT! 
 And Taylor had fun at the end. When Karou and Akiva can finally FINALLY get together, she throws in a monkey wrench that drives them apart again, just for a little while longer. It's perfectly logical, so even though I wanted to scream I couldn't really complain. The monkey wrench got worked out, and ta-dah! Our main heroes came together. 
 I can't wait for enough time to go by so that I can read them again!
I absolutely loved this series! I highly recommend it.

I was so looking forward to this book...and I wasn't disappointed! Darynda Jones's zany, at times corny but always funny humour is back. I found myself at times groaning, laughing out loud and overall just smiling. It isn't too often a book can wring all this emotion but Charley, Cookie, Reyes and all sure take you on a roller coaster. I was almost in tears at one point with Charley's relationship with her Dad hurting her so much. I could feel her pain. 
 I enjoyed how Reyes's story unfolded and gave him a more fleshed out back ground. Most of what we learned was alluded to in previous books but it was nice to have it confirmed. We go from highs to lows back to highs and then drop us down to the lowest low and then she twists us up again with a surprise ending. Her secondary characters also jump off the pages at you. Cookie, Ubie, Garrett, and the Davidson family all bring a unique humour and help move the story ahead. 
 I love this author she is innovative, and in a field that at times you feel you keep reading the same story over and over Charley Davidson is definitely unique. I can't wait for the Fourth book in this series! I know Charley is going to get up to no good...and what the heck is happening with her and Reyes...I need to know!!! 
 A solid 5 stars for this fantastic tale with side splitting laughs...oh...and where does Charley get her tshirts and bumper stickers..I need to get me some of them!

Read this book in one night! Holey smokes!! Once again Charley gets in deeper than she should and Reyes just might be free after this. I'm so happy I have the next book sitting on my bedside table calling to me.

Have you ever read a series that leaves you emotionally hung-over afterwards? There have only been a few for me, and this series is one of the top 3. Whew! What a ride. We go from ROFLMAO (with tears) banter between Charley and Cookie, to several near death experiences (with tears) only Charley can get her self into (and out of) on a daily basis, to the emotional extremes of sadness, loss and betrayal. This book has them all. Plus, we get a few new characters introduced (one who seems quite yummy). And in true Darynda Jones fashion, she throws us off the ride scratching our heads wishing we had the next book in our hands because I HAVE TO KNOW WHAT'S GOING TO HAPPEN NEXT! A complete emotional rollercoaster for me. 3 books into this series, and I can't think of ever putting them down. So without giving away any spoilers, I would tell everyone, give this series a chance. Start at the beginning, you won't regret it. 
 And I'm still on team Reyes.......

 "Sometimes that light at the end of the tunnel is a train." 
 Charley and Reyes are back, and as hot as ever. In Third Grave Dead Ahead Charley accepts a case of a missing woman. She has suspicions about the woman's husband, however, and chooses to not accept any payment from him until she knows exactly what is going on. While in the midst of working her case, she is kidnapped by Reyes, who has recently broken out of jail. Apparently he believes that his "father", Earl Walker, the man he has spent 10 years in jail for supposedly killing, is still alive. 
 He hires Charley to find out if Earl is still alive, and basically uses her as bait to draw Earl out. It works beautifully, especially when Earl breaks into Charley's apartment where Amber is sleeping on the sofa, puts a gun to Amber's head and threatens her life and Cookie's life if Charley doesn't do what Earl wants. After Charley takes a sleeping Amber home, Earl then proceeds to torture her for hours, almost killing her. While attempting to save Charley, one of her friends gets shot and dies. The entire experience leaves Charley feeling betrayed and shell shocked, but not bad as the betrayal she faces from the man she loves the most. That was more than harsh. 
 Once again, I sing the praises of this series. Charley and Cookie's dialogue is just the best! When I'm not laughing out loud, I'm snickering under my breath. Uncle Bob is my hero. He is there for Charley, no matter what. And her gives as good as he gets. He's always threatening to arrest her, but he never really would. Love Ubie! And Reyes...his betrayal, and lack of communication almost cost Charley her life, and she is not happy about it. Then there's the hot ass biker dude, Dominick, and his adorable pup, Artemis.  Like the others before it, Third Grave Dead Ahead is not to be missed. It is sexy, funny, witty, and entertaining enough to make you miss out on much needed sleep...ok maybe that's just me. Still, this is a kickass

Tumultuous! Intense! Third Grave Dead Ahead is a caffeine laced journey into a world only Charley can lay claim to. Non stop intrigue and detective work drives Charley as she tries to unravel the multitude of cases before her, in order to save lives. As always you will find her trusted friend, Cookie, by her side, doing what she does best. Once again we are gifted the with the presence of Reyes. His anger and need for Charley to set him free will send this ongoing story into a completely different direction. We will finally be able to place a face to those elusive characters we've only heard about and could not wait to meet. Warnings of an impending war and torture will be foretold by the unexpected. As events unfold, Charley will unearth secrets long ago buried, yet still powerful enough to destroy lives. Yet, to make matters worse Charley will face a predator, a monster, that must be vanquished. 
 Just when thought you knew all there was, TGDA throws you for a loop! 
 Darynda's power in manifesting Charley's grief was superbly done. We watched in dismal awe as Charley experienced anger, guilt, helplessness, sadness, shock, numbing, yearning, and self-blame. Betrayal will violate Charley, and it will wear many names. All I could do was shout, "Reyes, do something, make her see reason, she didn't trust you either, fix this!" The writing was so well done, the anguish was palpable. We've been on this caffeine induced madness with her since the beginning, we went from 100 to 0 and were left reeling. Third Grave Dead Ahead was brilliant, and at the same traumatizing. It has left us marked, by way of questions and fear. Will we see Reyes and Charley unite, or will their suffering and pain be for not?

I have dreaded reviewing this book. Dragged my feet, avoided sharing my disappointment....sigh. All of it. I LOVE Harry Potter. I love the book, I love how it is written....the characters, the magical world, how it is a gateway to get kids to fall in love with reading....LOVE IT. I have taught the first two books in class numerous times and melted every time I see my students bitten by the HP bug....but I was not as excited to read this book....it isn't written by Rowling, it isn't her characters....it isn't a novel....it isn't Harry Potter. It isn't. I don't care how you try to explain it....it didn't feel the same and it kills me that this book is now part of the Harry legacy. Gah. I tried my best to go into this book without any pretenses, but it is hard...I was excited to see the play write's interpretation...but the deeper I got into the play the more annoyed I became. 
 1) I don't feel like the play write truly understood JK's characters....I hated his interpretation of Hermione and Ron. Hermione is not that annoying....and Ron isn't the dumb guy that all the jokes are made on....I mean maybe in the movie? But not the characters I fell in love with! 
 2) The play write does NOT know teenagers....no teenager I have hung out with would hug his friend ESPECIALLY when no one is around...that's not how teens act. Nor how they talk....it really bothered me. 
 3) The end was obvious....the villain was obvious....JK is never obvious. 
 4) Just don't touch what is good. Please. I feel very protective of this world....write your own play about your own characters. 
 So....in the end....should you read it? Sure. Should you gush and love every second? No. It is not the same as the original books. This is a whole different world--- I shall pretend this is fan fiction that got published because he knew the right people....but it isn't the same and I am not inspired to go see the play....I prefer to let the characters live on in my imagination without being clouded by someone else's point of view.

Muddled thoughts on this one, what can I truly say except for what is in my heart? Tbh, it reads like a piece of simple fanfic, and that's the bottom line. I could add that I think Rowling might have sold out but that is speculation on my part. I have my reasons to think it however. 
 So, I give it two stars - It was ok.
Good if you want Doctor Who-ish meets Harry Potter fan fiction but don't want to search for it.

Gaah I never thought I'd ever give anything related to Harry Potter 1 star and yet here I am. 
 SPOILERS BELOW 
 Now if you go in expecting another Harry Potter book, you will be sorely disappointed. If you go in expecting a play which borrows your favourite characters for a story, you'll probably still be disappointed considering JK Rowling's name is attached to this and you expect a certain level of clever writing from her. Alright so she didn't write the whole thing, she did give her stamp of approval. 
 Firstly, no one is in character. Yeah, sure 19 years have passed but there is so much incongruence it's just making my head hurt. I love Ron. I have always loved Ron. But it seems like they forgot how to write Ron. It reads like movie Ron and not book Ron. Do you not remember Ron Weasley who shared his family and home with Harry after only a year of knowing him? Do you not remember Ron who told Sirius that he would have to go through him before killing Harry, when he thought Sirius was a mass murderer? Do you not remember Ron who Hermione fell in love with because he remembered the house elves and went to warn them during the Battle of Hogwarts? But you know, whatever. Let's have Ron only for comic relief, who only thought about food and wore a gravy-stained napkin when his best friend's son went missing. Fuck you. 
 I get Albus. I get it, it can't have been easy being Harry Potter's son and living up to his name. I can understand his frustration and his anger. What I can't get is Harry's reaction to his son. Really, you really think Harry is going to tell him he wished Albus wasn't his son?? Are we basing Harry on his 5th year when he got mad at everything? It's so out of character for him. And don't give me the bullshit that JK Rowling obviously knows her own characters better, because if she did, no way would she treat Cedric like that. 
 Which brings me to Cedric. Cedric Diggory, the boy who was kind above all, became a Death Eater because he was humiliated during the Triwizard Tournament? Is this the same Cedric Diggory we are talking about who wanted a rematch because Hufflepuff won only because Harry fell off his broom? The one who wanted to be fair so told Harry about the Second Task? The one who wanted Harry to take the cup because he felt Harry deserved it more?? Okay, as long as we're clear. This is especially shitty, considering Hufflepuff has almost no other heroes. 
 What about how the only reason Ron and Hermione are together is because Ron got jealous about Krum?? What are you even on about?? 
 Yes, completely murder Draco's character, why don't you?? 
 The worst of all was the plot. The really weird bizzaro plot. Time- Turner? Is this even a plot? It sounds like those memes where people keep suggesting why didn't they just go kill Voldemort when he was a kid? The wacky plot had so many loopholes it'll make you laugh. 
 The only good thing was Harry confronting Dumbledore about leaving him in an abusive household for ten years. 
 Scorpius as a character was really good. He was funny and smart. 
 But the plot. Ugh. 
 My head hurts from all the bullshit. 
 tl;dr I've read fanfics by 15 years old with tighter plots and better characterisation.

I love this book. It didn't take me a long time to read it. For one, it is a relatively short book. I think it is only a hundred pages long. More importantly though, it is due to the flow of the story. His words, his words are lyrical, flows easily; it has rhythm. His words are pure and simple, yet it is those words that take you deep into the heart of it. 
 If you look at the novel, you will find many aspects of the story you can focus on. Seeing as this is me, of course the main theme I took with me was that of love. Unrequited love, was it? No, it was much more than that, deeper than that. The protagonist [Herve Joncour] falls hard for a Japanese concubine. They do not touch. They do not speak. Yet, something undeniable exists there. It is not without its complications though, as the girl is from a different country, a different culture, who belongs to someone else. Herve, on the other hand, has a wife, Helene. It is the interplay among these three characters that break my heart. How strong is their love for one another, how much courage will they display, how much sacrifice do they have to offer up, how long do they have to endure - all for this so called love? The last few chapters of the books truly captivate me. It is sensual. Oh, that letter given to him. How much passion can you gleam from it? How bold and firm and passionate, powerful and unmistakable? Only towards the end do you realize that, man, oh man. After that discovery, you go back and reread the whole thing and you see it in such a different light now. 
 Actually, I wanted to go back and reread this story right away. It is the kind of book that gets better every time you read it. You read it once, get a message from it; you read it again, and get somehing else altogether. Going back to his words, so simple and pure, you realize the depth of it, how he pieced it all together, how he picked these select words and combined them to affect the reader so, so much. 
 It is a strange grief. To die of nostalgia for something you will never live.

reference_books.title: The Way You Look Tonight (Seattle Sullivans, #2; The Sullivans, #10)
reference_books.review_text:
4.5 stars 
 I just checked my library and it seems despite owning the whole series, I've only really read just one other Sullivan book (Which I really loved and gave 5 stars to. See: Let Me Be The One) 
 There's something about Bella Andre's writing that makes me come back for more. I guess it's the way I'm able to emotionally connect with both her heroes and heroines and the rest of the lovable, sympathetic, and crazy bunch of characters that make up the Sullivan Family. It happened again with Brooke and Rafe; thoroughly enjoyed the all the push/pull, the anticipation, the coming together, the healing and the love. I also fell in love with the setting, this time, the entire time I was reading it, I was wishing I was somewhere lakeside too. Hee. I'm definitely looking forward to reading the four follow-up books, and in the meantime, I know I'm going to have a great time going back to the beginning, reading about the rest of the Sullivans.

reference_books.title: Beauty and the Blacksmith  (Spindle Cove, #3.5)
reference_books.review_text:
Tessa Dare is a master at writing scenes that would cause you to have a permanent grin, leave you breathless with excitement, make your heart melt, and definitely leave you craving for more. Beauty and The Blacksmith is no exception, as it is chock-full of moments that left me sighing, chortling, fanning myself (oh, so hot!) and clutching my heart, all at once. 
 We first met Diana and Aaron in the first book of the Spindle Cove series, A Night To Surrender, and it's such a treat to finally get to know these two amazing individuals on a much deeper level. Aaron is an exceptional man; it's difficult not to fall for this loyal, hardworking, kindhearted and passionate person. Diana is equally outstanding; a woman, who has so much to give, firmly resolved to live her life and be happy. These two complement each other, and every so often, I hear myself sighing because of how perfectly they fit. They don't always have perfect moments, goodness knows how many times I died laughing because of one mishap or another, but in each moment, even the ones that left a twinge in my heart, it was very clear how much love these two have for each other. 
 It was such a joy to see more of the crazy cast of characters in Spindle Cove (reading this seriously felt like coming home!). Loved reading more of Charlotte, that very spirited and unrestrained youngest Miss Highwood. She is such a force to reckon with. Love, love, love her. Very touching, that moment with Aaron. 
 Watch out for the revelations, pay attention to the powerful words and savor the expressiveness in each statement. So beautiful. Beauty and the Blacksmith is such a decidedly sweet and deliciously sizzling story. Definitely a must read! 
 ARC provided via Edelweiss. :)

book_b.user_review:
Read it last night as soon as my Nook let me download it and finished it in one sitting. Ooooh, so, so good. Everything so delish. I'm already planning on re-reading as soon as I get home from work, hahaha.

The writing is crisp and refreshing, the banter always sparkling, the UST always palpable, the love scenes so hot and sizzling (and did I mention HOT??), the characters so unforgettable, and no matter what, you end up falling in love with them and their journey, (and the setting too! The community!) and you know they'll just forever inhabit a space in your heart. 
 I can't even write a proper review, I'm still basking in all the love, but suffice it to say that I'm going to be talking to everyone about this book (and probably end up buying it for all my friends again, lol). 
 Oh, so much love!!

sample_reviews.review_text:
Mallory Quinn is a good girls, who is a little bit tired of being so good. But she can't stop herself. Ty Garrisson is a special forces man, who is recovering from an injury in Lucky Harbour. On night, they have what's supposed to be a booty call, but that to good, old Mallory, feels like more. 
 He kind of feels attracted to her like a moth to a flame (I really kind of felt it was because she was the "motherly" type), while she is attracted to him because no woman could not be alive and not attracted to him. 
 I'm not really sure, but I didn't bought the love story. Furthermore, the plot bored me close to tears and Mallory kind of disappointed me (the only thing she changes about herself are her heels and a little bit of backbone in the end). It was so predictable, so sugar-coated, and definitely too cheesy to me. 
 In any case it's a good book for sunny afternoons when all you want is an uncomplicated, conventional romance story about good-girl meets hunk.

Jill Shalvis writes the heck out of Contemporary Romance and I love her Lucky Harbor series about three sisters who find love in this small Washington town. I was thrilled when I saw she'd come up with three new books set in the same town; this trilogy focuses on three friends who live and work in the quirky little town of Lucky Harbor. 
 Lucky in Love spotlights Mallory Quinn - nurse, town good girl, and kind of a pushover. She's reliable, focused, and can't say no to a request for help. Her friends decie Mallory's problem is she's looking for "Mr. Right" and she needs to take a spin with a "Mr. Wrong". 
 Ty Garrison, aka "Mysterious Cute Guy" is a former SEAL and medic - he'd been in a horrible accident that left his friends dead; he was badly injured and pulled off duty until he recuperates. Ty is temporarily living in Lucky Harbor in a house a friend is letting him use while he recovers, both physically and psychologically. 
 Mallory is trying to start a health clinic to care for the underpriviledged, and is facing an uphill battle. She's got her own reasons for wanting to succeed and help people who might otherwise fall through the cracks. Her budding relationship with Ty becomes a complication to achieving her goal. 
 Ty couldn't be more wrong for Mallory, and both of them know it, but when they're together it's all passion and hot sex. Mallory knows she's going to get hurt when Ty leaves, but she can't seem to stay away. Ty knows he's going to hurt her, but she brings out feelings he didn't know he possessed, and he can't make himself turn her away. 
 It took me awhile to figure out what about Lucky in Love didn't work for me. The writing is good, the setting is one of my favorites and the characters I love from the first book make appearances here. There are two problems for me: The first is that Mallory and Ty both kept telling themselves that Ty was going to leave and break Mallory's heart. The second is that Lucky in Love tackles some serious issues facing society today - health care, drug abuse, PTSD and lack of facilities for veterans, suicide. Both of these issues led to me having a hard time keeping focused on the book because I would have to put it down and "step away" so that I didn't get depressed. I have a tendency to feel the emotions of the characters as I'm reading and in this case I was just kind of bummed through a lot of the book. That's not to say there weren't any funny parts, or sexy parts, because there were. I absolutely love Lucille, the elderly resident who puts all the town gossip on facebook, and Mallory's friends Amy and Grace were fun characters who seem to have interesting stories; I've already purchased the next book, At Last, and plan to start reading as soon as I can. 
 Recommendations 
 You do not need to have read the first three books in this series to enjoy Lucky in Love, it's the first in a 'second trilogy' set in Lucky Harbor.

Finally got to Mallory & Ty's story. Read Amy & Matt first. Then Grace & Josh. Finally Mallory & Ty. 
 As usual, another great Lucky Harbor story!

Mallory Quinn has always played it safe. Tired of looking for Mr. Right, and with the encouragement of her friends, she decides to take a chance with Mr. All-Wrong. Ty is only passing through Lucky Harbor until the doctor clears him for active duty. Never wanting to stay in one place, he now finds himself with a reason to do just that. 
 I've loved these Lucky Harbor novels from page one. This didn't disappoint. If you haven't followed them, these are stand alone reads, but I recommend reading them all in order. I love these bad boy/good girl stories when done right. Love that Mallory is a nurse too. The way these two meet was beyond hilarious, and the story never dragged. And as before, the secondary characters rocked. A must read!
full review to come but I absolutely loved Mallory and Ty! This series has so much heart (and lots of smexy times!)

If you like Alpha Males, you'll love this book. Ty defines it in his sexy suit and his dark expressions that make you want to pull him out of the book for yourself. Do yourself a favor and read this book!
I think this is my favorite Lucky Harbor book so far!!!

For real, like I'd do anything but love the hell out of this book. Jill did it again, and this time, she did it even better. I can't seem to put her books down, and I'm completely head over heels in love with her characters. 
 She's got the touch, folks. The one that grips you and doesn't let go.

I was a really big fan of the main character. It was nice to read about a strong, independent woman who was confident and not a helpless, whiny female. The characters in the book were fun and I got a really strong visual of them. I think this would be a fun movie to watch. 
 ONe of my biggest grievances with the book, however, is being told every detail of what the characters are feeling. Shalvis misses in the main rule I like to be followed; "Show, don't tell." 
 She told us exactly what Ty and Mallory (the two main love interests) were always thinking at all times, even switching perspectives to do that. It really took away from the whole experience and left very little to the unfolding of the story. The story was easy to follow and was a very basic and extremely predictable plot, but I find that to be the norm in this genre. 
 I think she was also a chapter short on the book. It needed one more closing chapter to really wrap it up. It still worked, but I would've preferred a cleaner ending. 
 If you're looking for an easy read with no surprises and lovable characters, this is your book. If you want a little more, then skip this. 
 No regrets in reading this 
 ** SPOILER ALERT ** 
 there's only one discrepancy that bugs me. How did Ty get the charm bracelet? She was sitting next to him when the bidding was happening and he didn't bid on it. So how did he get it? This could have easily been explained.

reference_books.title: Sheepfarmer's Daughter (The Deed of Paksenarrion, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
A slow-paced, unexciting preface to the much better sequel, Divided Allegiance. The story never hit full-speed; it's not compelling. There's not enough character development, so I didn't care much about them, even Paks. There are a few battles, but the descriptions aren't detailed enough to make them page-turning sections. 
 I did like the unique perspective of Paks' membership in a mercenary company, which is different than many fantasy books which feature soldiers in traditional armies or independent heroic bands. There are brief mentions and glimpses of the larger world, including elves, dwarves, gnomes, and magic, but this book doesn't explore them. It feels like foreshadowing, as if the story is leading up to more.

reference_books.title: What If?: Serious Scientific Answers to Absurd Hypothetical Questions
reference_books.review_text:
This is entertaining in an intellectual way; it's full of science, math, and stats. As you'd expect from xkcd author Munroe, it also contains some morbid humor and plenty of geeky references to movies, comic books, and games. I laughed out loud a few times, but I was disappointed that I didn't find it as funny or interesting as many xkcd comics. 
 If you like xkcd, you'll enjoy this to some degree. It's fairly impractical (it's not intended to be), but I did pick up some trivia. 
 I received this as a gift from a marketing agency that my web design company, OptimWise, works with. I'm nerdy and something of an xkcd fan. 
 Notes 
 * The ISS experiences about 90% of gravity we feel on Earth's surface. 
 * Water is good for radiation shielding. 
 * Energy density (MJ/kg): coal: 24; gasoline: 46; uranium: 76 million. 
 * For most human-carrying spacecraft, the problem is keeping cool, not staying warm. That's because although you lose heat by radiation faster in space, you don't lose much heat by convection. 
 * It is dangerous to swim, shower, or bathe during a thunderstorm.

reference_books.title: Revenge of the Sith
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I was disappointed by this book. I would have thought with all the hype surrounding this final episode of Star Wars that they'd have found a better author. I've seen the movie a few times, but even so, I didn't find this book at all engaging. I felt little motivation to keep reading it. I did finish it, just because it does have some additional information and explanation beyond what's in the movie. 
 The first one-third of the book follows Anakin and Obi-Wan aboard General Grevious' ship, The Invisible Hand. The battle over Coruscant takes only a few minutes in the movie, but the book dedicates about 150 of its total 400 pages to it! It definitely wasn't time well spent, because I just kept wishing that the story would move along. 
 The book contains much more dialog than the movie, which was pretty action-focused. Like all the Star Wars novelizations, there's more exploration of the characters' hopes, fears, and intentions. Discussions of the Jedi Council are recorded, including discussions between Mace Windu and Yoda. The first seeds of the Rebellion are sown by Bail Organa, Mon Mothma, and Padme Amidala. There are many conversations between Anakin Skywalker and Chancellor Palpatine/Darth Sidious in which Sidious tempts Anakin to join the Dark Side. Near the end, Qui-Gon Jinn converses with Yoda through the Force, and offers to teach him the secret to maintaining consciousness in the Force after death. 
 Only recommended for Star Wars fans.

reference_books.title: The God Delusion
reference_books.review_text:
Richard Dawkins, a British evolutionary biologist, makes the case that religion is not only a foolish relic of the pre-scientific past, but an outright evil because of its closed-mindedness. He says religion prevents rational, critical thinking and blames it for intolerance, slowing scientific progress, and causing unnecessary bloodshed throughout history. If you're religious, I recommend this book for understanding the atheist arguments and motivation against religion. 
 Dawkins lumps all religions together as delusional; "major" religions such as Christianity, Judaism, and Islam, minor faiths such as Mormonism and various tribal religions, and even extinct religions such as those of the ancient Greeks. He sees no difference between extremists and moderates. Christians in the United States draw his condescending ire the most. 
 Dawkins says that religion was an early human invention for coping in a pre-scientific world. As a Christian, I believe that all religions are a perversion of the true religion, Christianity (with its Old Testament, Jewish roots), which mixed with human myths over millennia. I don't have the time in this review to explain my reasons for believing that only one religion in all history is truly legitimate, but an atheist would probably find them preposterous anyway. 
 Dawkins makes several good points about many illogical defenses of religion and embarrassing attempts to reconcile faith and science. This is warning to Christians that we must be consistent in our beliefs. Many people practice selective faith, choosing which parts of the Bible are historical, which miracles really occurred, and which of God's commands to obey. It can be difficult to determine in all cases if a text is to be interpreted literally or figuratively, but we must try. When Christians treat their faith as a la carte religion, atheists understandably smell blood in the water. 
 The book addresses the roles of religion: explanation (how things work), exhortation (morality), consolation (comfort), and inspiration (purpose). According to Dawkins, science can fill all these roles, eliminating the need for religion. He says there's no evidence or need for a Creator because science reveals the origin of the universe and life. He claims that morality and altruism have no supernatural origins, but arose from natural selection, and persist because of society and culture. 
 I disagree with Dawkins that creationists are lazily ignorant and don't research. Admittedly, I'm a layman, but I've found that creationist organizations like the Institute for Creation Research and Answers in Genesis embrace modern scientific tools and techniques in their studies. Yes, they have a different worldview than their secular counterparts, but I don't agree that it invalidates their scientific work. 
 The book contains many interesting statistics, such as the inverse relationship between education and intelligence levels and religious beliefs; in general, the higher a person's education and IQ, the lower their self-professed level of faith. Also, there's no statistical difference in morality between atheists and theists. In the US, "red" or conservative states tend to have higher crime rates than the "blue" liberal ones. Dawkins admits that there may be additional factors at play, and that such relationships may point more to correlation than strict causation. 
 I liked the book's final chapter, which includes an interesting discussion of matter and energy, the unfathomable scale of the universe from the quantum up to the astronomical.

book_a.title: Eragon (The Inheritance Cycle, #1)
book_a.user_review:
There's nothing novel here; the characters, places, and plot felt formulaic. I was reminded at many times of Star Wars, The Hobbit (my review), The Lord of the Rings (my review), Harry Potter (my review), and other fiction. It contains the usual fantasy fare: magic, elves, dwarves, dragons, swordplay, a quest, and desire for revenge. The vocabulary and plot are relatively simple, but that's unsurprising because Paolini published it at age 15. The scale is small; more like The Hobbit than The Lord of the Rings. I'm sure I would've liked it more as a teen than at 27. 
 The character development is decent, and I sympathized with Eragon's misfortunes. Dragons being forces for good made for an interesting departure from most fantasy. Eragon's telepathic link with Saphira was entertaining, but was a plot device used too frequently and conveniently. I liked the description of the underground city Tronjheim. 
 The final battle isn't described in as much detail as I would've liked. The focus is on Eragon's duel, so the battle felt anticlimactic. The book ends with slight suspense, but probably not enough to make me read the sequel, Eldest. 
 The audiobook by Listening Library is pretty good, but the way the narrator lowers his voice for Saphira's lines grated my ears.
