book_b.title: Mostly Harmless (Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, #5)
book_b.user_review: This book isn't nearly as funny as the first four Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy books; especially the first two (see my reviews). The characters aren't particularly interesting, and Random is quite annoying.

sample_reviews.review_text: This was probably my least favorite of the Hitchhiker trilogy (of five books. Yes, it's a five book trilogy). That's not to say you shouldn't read it (especially if you've gotten this far already) but it's a rather depressing book. To be fair, it does have one of my favorite scenes ever written by Adams (the Sandwich Maker), but other than that, it's a bleak book. Granted, Adams agrees with me, so I don't feel too bad about my opinion, but still. I would have liked a happy ending.
Lol. Well that's one way to end a trilogy. Though I do think this book probably read the worst out of the five.
Somehow this turned to be one big 'meah'

Kinda like the last one, but less so. This one is weirder and more depressing. I never was certain if Arthur was lost in an alternate universe or if he was traveling between universes and didn't know it. Also a big plot hole between the last two books... what happened to the love of Arthur's life? Is she the only survivor from Earth? I guess we will never know.

I am done. 
 I started with THGTG in May, I have dwelled in the universe of Adams - which is not child's play - for 2 months now and though I won't be reading him for a while, I won't come out of the trance-madness-obsession. Seriously Adams, you have me wrapped around your finger. 
 I will not stop using using words like Zarquon or froody . 
 I will not forget how satire changed my frame of mind. 
 Mostly Harmless is the fifth book of the Trilogy(Aren't you piqued?)and it has disappointed many. It wasn't bewitching because Adams set the bar high in his first 2 books. I would say Mostly Harmless was not even 1/5th as awesome as THGTG but it has to be read. All things that have begun must end. I am quoting because I am really not sure how to convince you to read Mostly Harmless. Maybe with revealing a secret. 
 'Psst! The Vogons accomplish what they were born for!' 
 "A common mistake that people make when trying to design something completely foolproof is to underestimate the ingenuity of complete fools."

Well, when I started reading the Hitchhiker's Guide series, an acquaintance who had recently finished it said it had wholly underwhelmed her. Sure, the majority of the series is an exercise in pure whimsy, but I had enjoyed the first three books and thought her a bit off-base. 
 But in the fourth and fifth book of the series, I found my interest lagging and the end of Mostly Harmless caught me somewhat off guard. I sat there with the finished book in my hands, feeling rather put out. 
 I like and laughed numerous sections of the Hitchiker series--from cows convincing you to eat them, to the idea of a Perfectly Normal Beast sandwich and "the King" singing in an intergalactic bar with a gaudy pink spaceship.And I don't think I'll look at dolphins in quite the same way. Adams is a clever and witty writer who certainly knows how to turn a phrase. 
 But at the end of Mostly Harmless, I felt as if I hadn't really gotten much more than that. I think if I had read this when I was around 13-15, I would've loved this series a bit more than I did. 
 As is, I found the Mostly Harmless to be the weakest of the series and the first two books to be the strongest. Overall, it's an alright series with a few good laughs and an interesting take on life millions of lightyears from Earth. 
 So long and thanks for the read.

Well, to the credit of Douglas, I would've guessed an ending of quite the different kind. 
 Especially with the claims about linearity in the beginning of this fifth installment in the Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy's trilogy. 
 What I expected was that after the fifth installment, part four would've made sense. How on earth did Arthur end up on earth? Especially since it's been hinted at that he ended up on the real earth, opposed to the other versions he ended up visiting in this fifth installment. And whatever happened to Fenchurch? 
 I admit, I wrote my own version of how the series would've ended. 
 And Douglas didn't do anything like that at all. 
 Usually, when an author manages to surprise me, that's a really good thing. An author who tickles and entices is an author I would hold very dearly. 
 Unfortunately, Douglas didn't overwhelm me. He underwhelmed me. 
 The ending seems somewhat forced and rather easy. 
 It disregards all the different threads Douglas weaved in the previous books, and now fails to tie them together in any kind of way. 
 It's ok if an author leaves some questions unanswered. Always good to keep the reader figuring out some things of his own. But Douglas ended this novel quite conclusively, leaving little room for the reader to add some ideas or insights. It's a very easy ending indeed. It feels to me like Douglas had enough of it. The fifth book in the trilogy was the book where he lost his motivation to make something out of it. Quite a disappointing ending to a very fun series.
I've tried to like these books, but they are so silly and pompous that I just can't.
A little step up from the terrible horrible sadness that was novel four. The second half of this was particularly better. Still not as good as the initial trilogy by a long shot.

reference_books.title: The Lost Girls
reference_books.review_text: What a great read! Told from alternating persons between the past and the present. Justine's great aunt Lucy died and left her the house by the lake along with a diary of some sorts. Although Lucy only met Justine once as a 9 year old girl she knew it would be her to uncover the truth about what happened to Justine's 6 year old sister Emily all those years ago. Emily went missing the day her family was supposed to leave their summer house by the lake. As a result of her disappearance, Emily's mother as well as her 2 sisters Lucy and Lilith wind up living the remainder of their lives at this lake house. You don't really understand why they chose to stay there all those years until the very end of the book. As I read through this book I had a mixture of emotions about several of the characters not really knowing exactly who was safe and who wasn't. In the end Lucy's secret is revealed and so is Emily's!

reference_books.title: All the Missing Girls
reference_books.review_text: This was my first time reading a book by Megan Miranda and she did not disappoint. I wasn't sure how I was going to like this story for the sole reason that it was being told backwards. However, the way Megan Miranda used her words to create a story starting from the end to the beginning was truly amazing and shows what talent she has. Nicolette ran away from home, her missing best friend, and her boyfriend a decade ago. But her brother Daniel's phone call finally brings her home. Daniel and Nic need to sell the house in order to continue to pay for their fathers care, but their father is refusing. He's disoriented and somewhat delusional but he insists they keep the house for it holds secrets and skeletons. The more Nic uncovers, the more mystery remains and you really don't find the answers until the very end!

reference_books.title: Mud Vein
reference_books.review_text: Okay so this review is totally out of the blue since I read this so long ago. But I actually just thought about this book and realized I really needed to change my rating from a 4 to a 5. I originally rated it a 4 ONLY because this book left me reeling with questions. Many questions were not answered and it honestly annoyed the shit out of me. Having said that, I could not get this book out of my head! I joined groups about it and asked questions there only to have my questions answered with new questions. Tarryn is an EXCEPTIONAL writer and both this and Marrow left me in a daze. Because of that I have to be fair and give this a 5. The story was amazing and I had no idea what was going on. I'm still not sure what went on but I could tell you this, I truly didn't want to put the book down. Every story of hers I've loved but I'm always scared to read her stories because they stay with me for days, even weeks. But that's the sign of a truly talented author and that she is!

I just want to express that my deepest regret is that I even read this book. It's not like the prequel novella, Dirty Filthy Rich Boys, wasn't without its problems. I wanted that book to be a fluke and for this book to be better. But alas, this book truly is just as terrible, if not worse, than the novella. I will say that Laurelin Paige writes an addictive story and I flew through this book. However, reading Dirty Filthy Rich Men is more akin to watching a train wreck. I knew nothing good was going to come out of reading this the further along I got, and yet, it was impossible to put down. 
 I would like to start off with a recap of all the problematic stuff that happened in the novella that I reviewed here. Our cast of characters primarily consists of Sabrina, Donovan, and Weston. In the prequel, Sabrina was 17-years-old attending Harvard on a scholarship, was sexually assaulted at a college party, was rescued by her TA, Donovan, who then practically forced her to have sex with him (then 22-years-old) in order for him to change her grade in her class. There's definitely an illegal age difference here that I was already not comfortable with. And all these events lead up to this book, Dirty Filthy Rich Men, set 10 years after the events in the prequel. 
 If you, like me, thought this story couldn't get any worse, you would be so wrong. 
 Sabrina happens upon Weston, a boy who she had a crush on back in college and Donovan's best friend, in LA. They have dinner and hooked up a weekend before Weston decides he wants Sabrina to quit her job and join his and Donovan's company in New York. She says no, and a few months goes by before Weston makes her an offer she couldn't refuse and now she's off to NYC, thinking that Donovan is still working overseas and that she won't have to see him. Well, he's back in the US and he spends every opportunity to make sexist, misogynistic comments and sexually harass her. Sabrina constantly tells herself that she's a strong woman and she deserves respect. Then, she throws all common sense out the window to have sex with Donovan. 
 The plot is thin and vague. The only thing driving this story is how many times Sabrina will throw common sense out the window and sleep with someone who doesn't respect her and harasses her at every turn. Donovan is jealous Sabrina and Weston might have a thing going on, and Donovan is manipulative and absolutely awful. He's also the love interest we're all supposed to fall for? This book is a good example of an unhealthy, toxic relationship and Sabrina needs to get out of it. 
 I'm just going to pull a lot of quotes now (and if anyone tries to argue with me that these are taken out of context, there's no amount of context in the world that could make these okay): 
 "Seriously, Sabrina. What were you thinking coming out here alone? If you wanted to get raped, you could have just called me." Even with the dark, teasing words, his delivery was a lecture. 
 SPOILERS AHEAD 
 The plot twist is disgusting and unless the endgame is for Sabrina to love herself, see a therapist for the trauma she's carried around since college, and for Donovan to get thrown in jail, I am not here for the next book. Let the quotes tell you all you need to know about Donovan's relationship with his ex-fiance: 
 "When I fall in love, I become so consumed, so preoccupied with the person I'm in love with that I do things I shouldn't. I get involved. I intervene. [...] I was so obsessed with her that I hired a private detective to follow her. I needed to know where she was - always. She found out, and we fought. She told me she'd call off the wedding if I didn't stop. But I couldn't stop. For no other reason except that I was addicted to her. I was addicted to knowing everything about her." 
 So, we find out Donovan is a stalker. Was Sabrina terrified that the manipulative asshole is a stalker? No. She just feels bad that he feels bad for what he's done. 
 And even though Donovan had been overzealous in his passion, he hadn't killed Amanda. 
 Maybe no one had ever told him that before. 
 When she finds out that Donovan kept 10 years worth of documents, pictures, and had an entire FILE on her, was she terrified then? 
 But, as messed up and confused as I felt, there were two things I now understood without a double about Donovan Kincaid. 
 Number one - this was what he meant when he said he got obsessed with the women he loved. 
 Number two - Donovan was in love with me. 
 This is not romantic. I don't know in what universe you would find this romantic. Donovan Kincaid is another Christian Grey. Sabrina is not as naive as Ana, but she is not using her head and thinking things through. 
 Just because that's not enough, here are some other WTF moments where Sabrina questions people's ethnicity (please note that instead of saying someone's "Asian", the author should have clarified instead of lumping everyone together *rolls eyes*): 
 I follow his gaze to an elegant Asian woman sitting near the bar chatting with a few other people. 
 I walked up to his secretary's desk. She was an attractive woman with black hair and dark skin, but her ethnicity wasn't immediately recognizable. 
 "You're welcome to wait in the bar," the hostess suggested, a pale young woman who looked one hundred percent like she'd some from East Asia but talked like she'd lived one hundred percent of her life in the Bronx. 
 This book was a mess. I can't even say this was a hot mess, because that would imply that Sabrina and Donovan's relationship was hot, and it's anything but. I would not recommend this series. It doesn't seem likely at this point that single Sabrina is the endgame, so this book will be my last for this series.

OMG this book was amazing. All I can say is I NEED BOOK 2 now. Donovan and Weston are great. Sabrina was made for Donovan. There are times when I wanted to strangle Donovan. Always sending mixed signals to Sabrina. Just when you think he is going to open up to her with his feelings he "shuts the door" So frustrating. But soooooo goooood. What a story. Ending so good. Makes me wish for the Fall when Book 2 is being released. Donovan is so complex. But with good reason. He tells her it is just sex but she can't help but fall for him. He always has an excuse for his good deeds regarding her, but Sabrina is so afraid to hope that maybe he does have feelings for her. Killer tan.' Of course I lusted after him like nobody's business. This man could drive a nun to sin - he's that fuckin drool worthy and scrumptious. Head to toe, he is perfection personified. And of course you can't have all those muscles without the rest of the package being equally complimentary. Spikey black hair, gorgeous blue eyes, dimples *swoon* The body of a god, boyish good looks and all wrapped up in a deceptively insecure little package. My love for Remy is fierce...he's just so amazing, the fact that he's drop dead gorgeous to boot is the icing on a delicious cake that I can't wait to eat. 
 'There he is, a woman's living, breathing fantasy, doing his slow, cocky turn, spiky black hair, darkly tanned chest, dimpled smile - killer smile - all in the package of Remington Tate. He's perfection itself, and a new surge of hormones sweeps through me as I do what the rest of the crowd dows and take in his visual, so blatantly on display in those low riding boxing shorts and so strikingly sexy, he becomes the center of my attention.

 You jump in head first with Remy and Brooke, they meet on page one and there is no question about their connection or their chemistry. It's tangible. I felt like it reached thru my kindle and grabbed my by the throat. I loved it. But of course it's never that easy. So while I knew what they had and secretly, they knew what they had...I was taken on this painstakingly fabulous journey of them denying what they had. O.M.G. but was it the best and sweetest torture ever. All the while you're craving them, begging for the moment when they can finally be together...but all the while it's just building and building. The reasons are there though...just because we're not in Remy's head, doesn't mean he doesn't get his point across. And don't get me wrong...I liked his point - I just also liked Brooke's too! :-) What else did I love about Remy and Brooke...the way they communicated through music. The way they communicated with just a look in their eyes. Their connection was way more than just physical...obviously it's a huge part of what drew them together...but their like magnets, just drawn together. I always love it when I fall for a BBF, but when I fall for the couple...that's when I know I'm done for - and they made me fall. Hard. 
 'Now just the tiniest look from him swells me up. When he glances at my lips. When he tucks a loose strand of hair behind my ear. I know we're just sending our adrenals to hell, doing this. Keeping the output of this lust is just not healthy, but I can't stop him. In fact I want more. I want him to stop because we're suffering and I want him to go on until I lie dead in his arms, burnt to ashes from my want of him. 
 I want him. Every hour, minute, and second.' 
 The book is entirely from Brooke's POV...which sometimes it would have been nice to have been in Remy's head. There are a few scenes when knowing his thoughts and seeing things from his eyes would have helped - but logically, you can't just throw a couple of scenes in a different POV, so I get it. But there is Remy, Book #3 to look forward to for all that goodness. (Can't lie...pretty sure Remy is going to be my fav - just a prediction!). And the book is not all Remy and Brooke and the insane rollercoaster that is there relationship. I liked the secondary characters, Mel, Pete, Riley, and the rest of them - they all felt very genuine and real and they all played their crucial part in the story. My heart twisted a little bit for Brooke and the drama with her sister, Nora and Scorpion, the closest thing to a 'villain' in this story...well...he's just flat out a disgusting piece of shit. Excuse me while I vomit *gag* 
 'I feel like Beauty and the Beast, except I willingly locked myself in with my beast so he could kiss me senseless, and he's the beautiful creature who tortures me with wanting him.' 
 Remy is a different kind of creature. From the way he is portrayed, I didn't expect the kind of discipline and control that he has with Brooke...maybe that's why I was a little frustrated. It was the good frustrated, but still...I had a lot of those grrr... moments. Remy is also a very different kind of alpha...he's not like any other BBF that I have ever read, and that's a compliment. He says and does things that are classically all his own. He's very animalistic and some things if any other guy did, I would laugh or roll my eyes - but on Remy...it just works. And it works like a charm. But unfortunately Remy has a lot of demons. You feel Remy's confliction because while he cannot live without Brooke, he still wants to protect her from what he is. My poor Remy... The pinnacle scene at the end...where he just completely rips my heart from my body...after I got past that...when I'm bawling...and then I find out the truth and I'm bawling even more...that's the moment when I knew Remy was permanently etched onto my soul. He. Is. Perfect. 
 "You tie me up in knots." He presses my mouth with his. Briefly. Then he withdraws, breathing hard, and looks at me with heavy -lidded eyes. "I want to play you a thousand different songs so you get a clue of what...I feel inside me..." 
 Oh-MY-Angsty-Goodness. Angsty books are my bread and butter. They are what sucked me into this genre...this book is one of the best. All that tension and desire and hormones just about killed me. So you see, there's a lot to love about this book besides the scrumdiddlyumptious piece of man candy! He just makes it more...fun. A lot more fun. All that angst is totally worth it because Remy and Brooke together equals magic. Hot, panty melting, holy bejesus, leaves you drooling, can't-get-enough-of-it magic. Fireworks. Just...W.O.W. So...yeah...it's worth it. ;-) 
 'He's my beast. My dark and my light. Mine. 
 There's just no other option for me except ending up with him.' 
 This is another one of those books that I felt devoured me rather than the other way around. It grabbed my heart and soul, I felt every single emotion through the entire book and I was breathless when I finished it. And...it's...a....SERIES!!! SQUEEEEE!!!!! 
 Mine 
 comes out November 12th, just in time for my birthday, thank you very much Ms. Evans! :-) I cannot wait for the next part of Remy and Brooke and if Real is any indication of what we can expect for the rest of the books, we're in for an awesome ride. :-)

reference_books.title: Between the World and Me
reference_books.review_text:
A powerful testament to the ongoing legacy of American imperialism and the myths that sustain it. Brief, intimate, and convicting. As long as we are satisfied with sterilized history that exonerates white Americans of the violence that carved out the country we call the land of liberty we will be blind to the violence around us today. In particular, this passage struck me as a potent truth: 
 At this moment the phrase "police reform" has come into vogue, and the actions of our publicly appointed guardians have attracted attention presidential and pedestrian. You may have heard the talk of diversity, sensitivity training, and body cameras. These are all fine and applicable, but they understate the task and allow the citizens of this country to pretend that there is real distance between their own attitudes and those of the ones appointed to protect them. The truth is that the police reflect America in all of its will and fear, and whatever we might make of this country's criminal justice policy, it cannot be said that it was imposed by a repressive minority. The abuses that have followed from these policies - the sprawling carceral state, the random detention of black people, the torture of suspects - are the product of democratic will. And so to challenge the police is to challenge the American people who send them into the ghettos armed with the same self-generated fears that compelled the people who think they are white to flee the cities and into the Dream. The problem with the police is not that they are fascist pigs but that our country is ruled by majoritarian pigs. (78-9)

reference_books.review_text: I wanted a good story, and having just finished "Chronicle of a Death Foretold" I was looking for some more Magical Realism. Unfortunately, "Alchemist" just didn't measure up. There were definitely some great things about it - fun style, interesting world, and a few concepts that were worth playing with, but all of its good qualities were continually exploded by the constant reminder that it was all an allegory. The story wasn't crafted to explore its own world - the possibilities opening up into unexplored space - but only to point a finger back at our own. I really wanted to like it, and in a few places I did, but in the end it's not a piece of art meant to stand on its own, it's an allegory, making its fantastic elements simply teaching tools, and it's plot grounded only in the basic ideas that were trying to be communicated to the reader. Even where this not actually the case, the fact that it is indicated as such is distracting enough to render simple enjoyment of the story minimal. If you're going to skip simple enjoyment, why write a story?

reference_books.title: Orientalism
reference_books.review_text:
Powerful cultural theory with a beating heart. Love it. 
 Definitely need to read around the issues he addresses and to get other perspectives on the cultural production he criticizes (not to mention reading through the whole work) in order to get a sense of the validity of his arguments, but a first read is both startling and satisfying. The introduction alone puts forth a serious challenge to the way we think about and represent our place in the world.

reference_books.title: Gone Girl
reference_books.review_text:
This came to me highly, highly recommended, and I understand why - it is very narratively clever. 
 Over and over again the direction of the story is thrown on its head. Almost with every chapter. New revelations constantly open up new possibilities. My friend put this in my hand and said "I will be surprised if you predict anything in this book." While I don't pride myself on being able to guess what's coming next in the stories I read, I was still, repeatedly, almost constantly surprised by how easily my expectations were overturned. 
 Unfortunately, one of those expectations was that I would like the book. While narratively clever, it put me off on a very basic level: there wasn't anyone in the story who was really likable and there were no real, good human connections. Taken academically, it might be interesting to reflect on how this story treats our ideas of what "likability" is - why we are attracted to or allured by some people but not by others, why some things turn us off and others turn us on. That's certainly, thematically, at the center of the narrative. But I wasn't approaching this academically, really. I was hoping to jump in for some fun, go for a ride, see something new. Honestly, I'm not quite sure why I expected that other than the recommendation. With a title like Gone Girl this was bound to be a rough ride. But even the rough stories, at least, the ones that I like, offer something to the reader, leave some glimpse of hope, balance the sordid with a measure of something good. Some anchor of sympathy or human connection in the world. Some acknowledgement that it's not all bad. 
 Didn't really get that here. And after about fifty pages of people I would never, ever want to actually meet in real life, well... I kinda felt done. I pressed on, and read the whole thing, but the majority of the time I was just hoping it would end quickly. I just got tired of all the nastiness without any nice. 
 In the end, I came away impressed by the cleverness that it took to write this, it just wasn't fun to read.

 But aside from that this book is just a great, wonderful read! 
 There is always a place in me for children's books and even more so now that I can look at them from a slightly different point of view then when I was younger. Here we have a perfect combination of the silliness and wonder of childhood thoughts and stories and yet there's this tone of satire, of growing up to know different that makes reading this book even more interesting. 
 Whenever I read poetry especially the silly and nonsensical, I always end up wondering about the poet. The process of how that one poem came to be, how they came up with their idea and what they were thinking while writing it, what exactly compelled them to write down something that can only truly be appreciated by a child? I don't know why this happens but for me it adds that little bit of amazement in reading this sort of book. 
 You will probably notice by this point that I don't really have anything critical to say about the poetry itself but in my defence this inner narration is making forming thoughts really hard.

It is astonishing to think that Minneapolis was the center of the Faerie world in 1987. Who would of thought?!? 
 And yet, Emma Bull's absorbing novel provides eloquent testimony to the centrality of the City of Lakes to the Fey World. 
 Undoubtedly there is some important event that transpired in the next decade, since by 2000 the Dresden Files are evidence that Chicago is the place to be. 
 * * * 
 I didn't realize for a while that this book was written so long ago. I was enjoying the retro nature of the bands mentioned and the clothing styles, but then suddenly realized a character had just ducked into a phone booth. How quaint! Oh: no cell phones, no computers, and despite this being a rock 'n' roll band story, somehow the whole grunge movement never got mentioned? Finally, I looked at the publication date and realized why half the references were to punk and the other half to the new romantics. (But no Adam and the Ants. Quite surprising.) All the male faeries are described like they stepped out of a Prince music video, and the lead character apparently dresses like Stevie Nicks. 
 In any event, 
 War for the Oaks 
 is an excellent urban fantasy. 
 Strongly recommended.

I don't read a lot of urban fantasy, but this is an exception, a guilty pleasure I read every year or two. The premise is so grand you have to go along, and Bull sweeps you right in from page 1. It seems the fae want to have a war, but the only way to make it meaningful is to have a mortal on the battlefield on each side, for then the fae themselves can die. Eddi, our heroine, just wants to play her songs in a good rock band, not the one her sulky ex-boyfriend put together, now defunct. But then a phouka follows her home and informs her she has been chosen as one of the mortals, and life gets very weird. But oh, the band she gets out of it! 
 If you like rock and roll, or even if you don't, you will love watching Eddi fight to put her band together, to keep it together through battles that get bloodier and scarier as the summer progresses, and ultimately against the bitch queen herself. The Queen of Air and Darkness makes the stakes of the final battle so very personal, and so very high, that even though Eddi is fighting with her own weapons the outcome is not at all a sure thing. 
 Bull does a great job of weaving poignancy and loss and triumph and bittersweet victories all together into an excellent brew. I have read other books by her. Though not bad reads, none of them come up to this one, in my opinion. Highly recommended.

You can read my review of Emma Bull's "War for the Oaks" here: 
 http://www.conradzero.com/book-review... 
 -Conrad Zero

reference_books.title: The Perks of Being a Wallflower
reference_books.review_text:
The Perks of Being a Wallflower is a strange mix of heartbreak, annoyance and tediousness. There were certain enjoyable parts of the novel, but the bad far outweighed the good in this case. 
 The novel follows Charlie, painfully shy, introspective, highly intelligent and socially awkward. He is a wallflower, watching on the outskirts while people live their lives. On the advice of his teacher, he starts putting himself in new situations, and what follows is one of the best years of his life. Charlie is introduced to a world of dating, music, drama, new friends; a world of sex, drugs, musicals and books. Charlie was content to life his life on the fringes, but now is the time for him to see what life is really all about. 
 As we all know, Perks is a hype book as it became extremely popular in 2012 when the movie, also written by the author, was released. I remember watching every second person read this book, but I was not a part of that majority. At that time, I had sworn off YA fiction, not deliberately of course, just because I get into moods for reading a particular genre. When the #DAReadAThon came up, I knew it was the perfect opportunity to give this highly popular, and long overdue, novel a try. 
 Charlie was a average and elusive character. His frank discourse so often reminded me of a child, which evoked deep endearing feelings from me, at least at the beginning of the novel. The book is set from Charlie's perspective and, considering how painfully awkward he is, the style of writing reflected that: it was astonishingly simple and the were sentences rigidly structured. It was always "This happened, and then this, and then this and now I am sad." It is suggested that Charlies has some sort of disability, but it is never specified, so I understood the need for this particular style of writing in order to get into Charlie's head. 
 It worked, at least for a while. And then it began to feel like reading this book was a chore, rather than a pleasure. The writing style grew dry very quickly and achieved the opposite desired effect. I could not connect with Charlie because I began to find him repetitive and artless. It is a shame, because I so very much wanted to like him. 
 Patrick and Sam felt greatly removed from the novel, despite them being Charlie's best friends. They were present in scenes, but at the same time they were transparent characters. Sam was the cliched next-door-neighbour type of girl that the protagonist can't help but fall for, while Patrick was a stereotypical gay boy. They did not feel like fully-fleshed out characters, but rather like poor attempts at one. This greatly confused me, as I so enjoyed their characters in the companion film. Chbosky actually wrote the screenplay so I don't understand how his characters could be so different. Perhaps this is also a testament to the elementary writing style. 
 The plot was, frankly, all over the place. It felt like there was just too much happening: sexual and domestic abuse, homosexuality, drug issues, paedophilia, suicide, racism, and sexual discovery. I personally felt that there was a mix of too many issues and I think the book could have greatly profited from a narrow look at one or two of these issues, rather than a dozen. The result would have been a cleaner novel that would have allowed more people to emotionally connect to. It was almost like Chbosky sat down and wrote a list of all the things a stereotypical teenager from an American movie would do and included every single one of them in his novel. It was also incredibly awkward to read about these issues as Charlie, while fifteen years old, reminded me of a child. Just look at his description of masturbation. He asks the reader if they know what it is, defines it, and then says, "Wow!" I got second-hand embarrassment from that scene. 
 Perhaps one of the reasons I did not enjoy this novel as much as I thought I would have was because I expected it to be exactly like the film. While the film was accurate with certain events and scenes, there were many new scenes that were included which positively affected the movie. Unfortunately, because I had watched the film, I also knew what the big reveal at the end of the novel was going to be and I was not as shocked or disturbed as I ought to have been. 
 Overall, I was disappointed in this novel. I expected a well-written coming-of-age novel about a socially awkward teen, but received a superficial look at teenagers and their issues instead. I can certainly see elements of a good novel in this book, and understand why many other people loved it, but I am just not part of that group. 
 Check out my blog and other reviews here

reference_books.title: Paper Princess (The Royals, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
1.5 stars - previously 3 stars, but writing this review made me realise how much I hated the book. 
 Paper Princess had been stalking me for many months. It felt like almost all of my Goodreads friends had read, devoured, and fallen in love with this novel and the subsequent series. This book was recommended to me by several people, so I went out and borrowed it immediately. What followed was two days of confusion, occasional interest, boredom and antagonism. 
 The novel follows Ella Harper, who has spent her entire life flitting from town to town with her unreliable mother. Struggling to make ends meet, and determined to climb out of the gutter, Ella is fiercely resolute and wants nothing more than to make something of herself, especially after the death of her mother. But then Callum Royal appears, a man who says he was best friends with her unknown, and now late, father. Ella is then plucked from poverty and strip clubs and sent to live with Callum in his remarkable mansion. Callum promises to see her through to college and pay for anything she wants or desires, if only she will live with him and allow him to care for her. This should be a dream come true for Ella; the only problem is Callum's five sons, who all hate Ella the second she walks through the door. Each Royal boy tries to make her life a living hell, but Ella can't help but feel drawn to one of them: Reed Royal, who is determined to send her back to the streets where she belongs. 
 I don't often read romance novels, but last year I fell in love with Colleen Hoover's contemporary romances and wanted to further expand into this genre. I picked up Paper Princess, because the novel had been generating a lot of press for months. Admittedly, I enjoyed the first few chapters of the novel. Ella was a captivating protagonist whose survival instincts were impressive. When we first met Ella, she was stripping, despite the fact that she was underage, because she needed the money. Obviously, I don't condone this, but it was interesting to see a main character have such a pragmatic and slightly pessimistic view of the world. She does what needs to be done. 
 But then, Ella moved into the Royal Mansion and the intriguing, unique independent was suddenly reduced to a lovesick, heart-on-her-sleeve dupe. She was introduced to the five Royal Boys - all of who hated her with a passion - and quickly fell in love with Reed, the brother who seemed to despise her the most. I usually adore enemies-to-lovers stories, but here there was absolutely no chemistry and scarcely any development between the love interests. I honestly could not comprehend why Ella was attracted to Reed: perhaps it was the blatant sexism that he constantly spouted, or the fact that he told his brothers not to have sex with her because she was probably diseased. I know I can't help but fall in love with a guy when he calls me a slut to my face. 
 Reed was a contradiction - so much so, that if you look up the definition of contradiction in the dictionary, you will see Reed Royal's name there. He continually stated how much he hated Ella and wanted her to stay away from his brothers, but then told her: "If I have to fuck you so you don't ruin my family, I'll do it." 
 ????????????????????????? 
 What? WHAT?? Not only does that make zero sense, he basically told her he would assault her. I feel like the authors attempted to purposely make the reader dislike Reed at the beginning of the novel, but then as Ella fell for him, we would too, but with scenes such as this, that did not happen. At all. 
 Reed wasn't even the worst brother. There was Easton, who groped himself in front of Ella and insinuated that he would force himself on her; then there were the twins, who swapped identities so they could each sleep with one of their girlfriends, without her knowledge. The boys were just as bad as their father, who encouraged their bad behaviour by providing a ridiculous amount of money and never punishing them if they did anything wrong. Easton had a genuine gambling and drug addiction, but his father was oblivious and only concerned himself with his mistress, whom he treated like an actual piece of meat and kicked her out of the house when she wanted to take their relationship further. Gee, I wonder why his sons turned out to be such assholes. 
 It honestly feels as though the authors wrote down their most titillating fantasies and tried to write a book about them, but failed. Like, five guys? Ella just had to have five guys falling over her and have sexual tension with. Are they overcompensating for something? 
 Excluding the abusive and problematic male characters, the novel had absolutely no plot. It was literally just Ella moving into the Royal mansion and trying to befriend the brothers while they made her exceedingly uncomfortable by talking about blowjobs in front of her, and refusing to believe she was a virgin. Which brings me to my biggest peeve: the fact that the female protagonist always has to be this untouched and pure virgin while her love interest has so much experience. And then Reed made fun of her for it! I can't deal. 
 The strong Ella at the beginning of the novel had been stabbed, stomped on and burned to death: in her place, was a submissive and, frankly, pathetic child. I could no longer connect with her and just wanted to yell at her for not standing up for herself - not once in the entire novel. She was such a disappointing female character, especially because teenage girls might read this novel and accept the way the male characters treat women as normal behaviour. FYI, it's not. 
 Paper Princess had so much potential and it truly astounds me that a YA novel written by two women could pen such sexism and obvious abuse. I never tell people to not read a specific book, but I really don't want people to even touch this novel. It will only make you angry. 
 Check out my blog and other reviews: thebookcorps.wordpress.com

book_b.title: The Alchemist
book_b.user_review: Great book.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I'm not sure about how to review this novel. I always feel terrible when I have to give a novel or book less than three stars. I'm too empathetic in that sense; I just think about all the effort the author must've put in their novel, like coordinating and constructing the proper structure for their plot, how to arrange the dialogues and finding the proper words to express what they want their characters to say, finding ways to develop their emotions and conveying a believable synergy to the reader among other things. When I think about all these things I feel both bad and amazed, the prime because I didn't like the novel and the author put effort into it and I feel bad for disliking it, the latter because, well, the effort must've been big. However, I cannot force myself to like a novel, and I just didn't like this one. 
 The spiritual and metaphysical basis of "The Alchemist" seems to be a combination of Christianity, Pantheism, Mysticism and every speech any public motivator would want to deliver an audience. The novel sums up in the following words: " 
 Follow your dreams and do not give up, no matter what the circumstances are. 
 " 
 I almost feel as if Darth Vader was trying to say in the most polite and protracted way possible: " 
 Use the force, Luke! 
 " 
 Unfortunately, I consider this novel to be filled with the trite, over-used and hypersensitive phrases we have all heard before: "Don't give up!" "Follow your dreams!" "You can do anything you want!", and that's simply not my cup of tea. I like cold, hard truths and different point of views, not recycled phrases I can read on-line. Now, with all that being said, I'm not certain if Coelho's objective was to help his readers grow and feel more confident about themselves, or if he simply wanted to use demagogy at its finest to win his readers and have a larger audience for his next novels. Quite frankly, this novel is both demagogic and boringly trite, so in short words: I didn't like this novel. One star.

While I could see some pockets of humour it seemed more like short comedy bits that were put together to try to support a story behind the scenes i.e. the comedy bits didn't make sense with the story. The discussion of the website religious content just didn't make sense and was rather boring. The first time Paul talked to Betsey in that one-sided conversation way was funny but when it was repeated it lost its appeal. This one was just not for me.
This book joins the short list of books (less than 5) I couldn't finish.

I didn't actually finish this book. I don't waste my time on mediocre novels. I could not connect with the main character and I was put off by the crude language, which at times seemed nothing more than gratuitous. It added nothing to the story.

I guess I just don't appreciate "literary" fiction by American men. Or what I expected to be a funny look at the perils of everything being online turning into a treatise on a bizarre religion. Stopped at the halfway mark.

Well, I got through this, hoping that somehow the slog would be worth it, but it in the end it was not. Our hero is beyond grating, whining his way through pages and pages and pages. His identity has been stolen and misrepresented "on the Internet" in order to reveal an elaborate conspiracy theory around a "lost tribe" of free-spirited utopians. We spend the ENTIRE book with our "hero" flinging himself around and screaming at everybody, because he is not in control of his life. When he finally finds his way to this lost spiritual community, it's literally the epilogue. So we have spent over 300 pages watching/listening to him whine, be nasty and judgmental about everyone around him and being completely miserable. WHY?
Protagonist--unlikable. Weird storyline that just did not hold my interest. I'm not at all intrigued by weird variations on religions.

I read Then We Came to the End earlier this year, and between that book and this one, I've come to really like the cut of Joshua Ferris's jib. He's irreverent without resorting to being snarky and twee, and he can definitely write his way around the mind of a neurotic upper middle-class American. To Rise Again at a Decent Hour explores the distance a man can unintentionally put between himself and the world through his own choices and all the attempts he can make at closing that gap again--and how cringe-worthy those can be.

This just made me sad, because I liked Joshua Ferris' Then We Came to the End a lot, and I really loathed this book. Paul, the protagonist, didn't have a single redeeming factor, as far as I could tell. He was obsessive, obsequious and creepy. And the whole religious plotline just lost me, but it was probably because I had no interest in it whatsoever. It's really sad because I know Ferris is capable of being clever and funny, but there was no evidence of it here.

This seemed like a great book in the first few pages, but as I kept on reading, I got more and more disinterested. I did not enjoy the dialogues at all. The characters were a little better but I could not care less about the negative tone of the narrator/protagonist. The website "mystery" was also a weird addition to the plot in my opinion. On top of that I did not enjoy the heavy religious undertone in this book.

sample_reviews.review_text: This book is heavy, and covers a whole lot of tough subject matter, but the writing was simply fantastic. Omerzitel'no, gadko, otvratitel'no. Ia kak budto izvalialas' v griazi. Kniga ogromnaia, i ia vse vremia pytalas' vynyrnut' i podyshat' chistym vozdukhom, no mne snova prikhodilos' v nee pogruzhat'sia. 
 Nesmotria na to, chto eta kniga - samoe otvratitel'noe, chto ia kogda-libo chitala, stil', osobennosti i iazyk avtora ochen' interesny. Oni napomnili moi liubimye knigi, takie kak: Making Faces by Amy Harmon i The Strange and Beautiful Sorrows of Ava Lavender by Leslye Walton. Povestvovanie vedetsia ot pervogo litsa, no glavy mogut byt' ot litsa kogo ugodno (prichem ot litsa geroev ne tak uzh chasto), chut' li ni mimo prokhodiashchikh liudei: kuziny Veivi, podrugi iz kolledzha, sherifa, malen'kogo brata geroin i t.d. Istoriia nachinaetsia s rannego detstva geroini, tak skazat', izdaleka. Iazyk neplokhoi, avtor pishet khorosho, i ia mogu poniat', pochemu kniga poluchila nagradu ot Goodreads, no siuzhet nastol'ko omerzitelen, protiven i nevynosimo zatianut, chto ia ne smogla po dostoinstvu otsenit' eto proizvedenie. 
 Sobytiia razvivaiutsia v 70-80-ykh gg XXv. v Oklakhome. 
 Vot i khotelos' by otnestis' k personazham s ponimaniem, pozhalet' ikh, no ne mogu. Prosto ne mogu sebia zastavit'. Chto on, chto ona... chto okruzhaiushchie... Ia ni za chto by ne zakhotela, chtoby eti liudi okazalis' so mnoi riadom. Navernoe, nuzhno otdat' avtoru dolzhnoe: ona dostatochno khorosho propisala personazhei, chtoby vyzvat' u menia takuiu nenavist'. No dlia menia seichas eto ochen' slozhno. 
 Personazhei million, u vsekh svoia istoriia, korotko (ili ne korotko) rasskazannaia nam avtorom. I ia takoe obychno ochen' liubliu, no tochno ne v etom sluchae. 
 Ia daleko ne khanzha, vot uzh tochno, no dazhe mne eto vse bylo nastol'ko protivno... Avtor pokazyvaet nedalekimi idiotami okruzhaiushchikh geroev, kotorye ne ponimaiut i vystupaiut protiv otnoshenii 13-letnei devochki i 25-letnego ogromnogo baikera. I da, eti okruzhaiushchie i menia vyvodili iz sebia (tam uzh oni chereschur lezli ne v svoe delo), no ia tozhe ne mogu etogo poniat'. Ia ne veriu v <<liubov'>> s pervogo vzgliada (20-letnego parnia v 8-letniuiu devochku), o kotoroi vsiu knigu taldychit avtor. S chego by vdrug? My vidim vsiu ikh istoriiu, i ona deistvitel'no gadkaia. Bednaia devochka, kotoroi i tak v zhizni ne povezlo, eshche i takogo parnia poluchila. Da, soglasna, on ei mnogo pomogal, oberegal, no odnovremenno i razvrashchal (delaia vid, chto eto ne tak, no eto vran'e, on prosto uspokaival svoiu sovest', on nikak ee ne ostanavlival). 
 Vozmozhno, mne ochen' povezlo v zhizni s sem'ei (ne vozmozhno, a sovershenno tochno), i ia prosto ne mogu iz-za togo, chto ne videla nichego podobnogo v real'nosti, poniat' geroev... nu, togda prosto skazhu: eta kniga opredelenno ne dlia menia. Vse eti podrobnye opisaniia seksa, kak ona s nog do golovy byla v ego sperme, bezzastenchivo rasskazannye trinadtsatiletnei devochkoi, sovershenno tochno ne dlia menia. Nichego ne imeiu protiv opisaniia seksa v knigakh, no ne v etom sluchae. 
 Ia videla sotni takikh <<porno>>-knig o baikerakh, zapadavshikh na dochek bossa, no ia nikogda ikh ne chitala, schitaia musorom. Gliadia na reiting i priznanie etoi knigi na Goodreads, ia dumala, ona o chem-to drugom. Vozmozhno, tak i est', potomu chto pisat', kak ia uzhe govorila, avtor umeet bessporno, no siuzhet... Br... Dlia menia odnoi iz samykh bol'shikh zagadok v mire stal reiting etoi knigi na Goodreads. Ona ogromnaia, i ia ele ee dochitala, i prazdnovala neskol'ko chasov, kogda ona konchilas'. 
 Bol'she vsego menia razozlilo to, chto khot' geroi i dumal o tom, chto vse, chto on tvorit s trinadtsatiletnei devochkoi kak by nepravil'no, avtor polnost'iu opravdyvala vse ego postupki <<liubov'iu>>. A vse neodobrenie i nakazanie, kotoroe prishlos' ponesti geroiu, ob'iasnila nedalekost'iu okruzhaiushchikh, tem, chto oni ne znali, chto on ee po-nastoiashchemu liubit. Nu, ia vot vrode kak <<znala>>, no vse ravno ne poniala. 
 V obshchem, etakaia ocherednaia istoriia <<Lolity>>, no Nabokov khotia by ne opravdyval geroev i ne ustroil im kheppi-end>>.

4.5 stars 
 This was touted as a "meth lab romance" when it was chosen as an August BOTM pick, and that's really what drew me in- 
 Wavy is a young girl living with two abusive, good for nothing, drug addicted parents. She is often neglected and left to her own devices, and is befriended by an adult man Kellen, who works as a drug runner for Wavy's father. 
 Wavy is very introverted, to the point where she doesn't even talk. She is obviously a very intelligent girl, but people don't know what to make of her. Over the years, as Kellen becomes her rock and the one person she knows she can rely on, Wavy slowly emerges from herself and finds her footing in the world. 
 Meanwhile, you still have the very seedy setting of a trailer compound where everyone fawns over Wavy's father. No one seems at all fazed that Kellen is spending such an inordinate amount of time with a minor child, driving her around on his motorcycle and showing up at her house at all hours. It sounds creepy as hell I'm sure, and yet I found myself rooting for Wavy and Kellen. 
 All the Ugly and Wonderful Things spans over ten years, starting when Wavy was 8. {SPOILERS} And as time wore on and Wavy's relationship with Kellen turned sexual, it almost seemed natural. And their relationship certainly didn't feel sinister or wrong. And I began to wonder wtf was wrong with me that I wasn't totally disgusted by their relationship. 
 I read some other reviews and chatter about this book as I finished it because I wanted to know whether I was alone in my feelings or not and I was relieved to see that I wasn't. That was part of the reason I loved this book. It was one of those books that turned all my preconceived notions on their head and made me question how I truly felt. And it showed me that maybe everything isn't as black and white as it appears. And I am still uncomfortable with how I feel.

This was actually a 3.5 stars for me. Pretty good. 
 Going in I knew the story enough to be thinking about Nabokov's Lolita. 
 Overall the story about a young girl and older guy who helps her out, she makes him feel special, they begin to enjoy each others company. You can't help to think this can be bad. She is 10yrs old and he is 24 when they meet. 
 Kellen(guy) works for wavy,s(girl) dad, helping out with the family meth lab. 
 Wavy and her younger brother are pretty much left on their own. 
 Kellen almost runs over wavy with motorcycle and wipes out. Wavy get help for him. He then begins to help out around the house after he sees how bad off they are. Wavys parents are a mess. The father is not only a drug dealer but has multiple girlfriends around the house and rarely is home. The mom is on drugs and is rarely awake. Kellen begins Cleaning, making food, taking wavy to school. 
 The wavy and kellen relationship develops. Wavy begins to trust kellen and they spend a lot of time together. The uh-oh factor is climbing very quickly. 
 Wavy wants to make a real relationship. She is 13 almost 14 by now. She wants to get married and Kellen finally agrees. He knows this is wrong in the world of the law but he can't help what his heart is telling him. They get engaged. 
 The story did get erotic at times, but definitely in a love story way. 
 The law finally catches up. I was starting to wonder how their relationship was not getting questioned. Him and wavy are out buying an engagement ring and wavy was telling people she is engaged. Small town talk and school gossip didn't catch up with them, not a big deal. I just started to get a feeling they were headed for trouble. 
 I liked the way things turn out for them. But it took a little too long for me. I lost the emotional high that the story had built.

reference_books.title: Seating Arrangements
reference_books.review_text:
When scrolling through others' reviews, I picked up on the words "satire" and "light" and "WASP wedding" and while, yes this book is about a WASP wedding, it is not light. And it might not be very good satire because I was left feeling depressed by the sad, unfulfilled lives of these people. 
 Also sad and depressing? The lack of action in a 300-page novel. There are few things that "happen" other than general drunkenness and douchbaggery. The action, as it is, is mostly in the form of flashbacks and what-coulda-beens. Oh, and there's a washed-up whale. Woohoo, excitement! 
 This being said, the novel is well-written, a character study down to the very last sentence, which, unfortunately led me to my lukewarm review. The denouement is bland and practically nonexistent. Blah. A labored read with little payoff in the end.

book_a.title: All the Bright Places
book_a.user_review:
"Mad Love" for a new generation. But not as good. 
 I enjoyed reading this as an adult, but I can't help but feel as though the notion of suicide was too poetically rendered. Teenagers reading this, especially troubled or mentally ill teens? Hmm. Not so wise. 
 Also, probably a product of being YA, but the imagery was so heavy handed I felt like I were being repeatedly hit over the head with metaphor. Boy named Finch watches a bird ramming itself into a glass door. Girl named Violet acts like a delicate flower, then tries to say she's not a delicate flower. The constant references to holding breath under water, and the weightless feeling of the Jovian-Plutonian gravitational effect. 
 Also, and this is a product of me reading way too much fiction, but I know of approximately no one at ANY age who can quote random poetry or passages from Virginia Woolf's suicide note. Give me a break with this stuff.

sample_reviews.review_text: Oh, this book! I loved Holding Up the Universe by Jennifer Niven and this was the perfect opportunity to push her YA debut up on my TBR. I'm SO glad I did. I adore Niven's writing and I'm easily sucked right into her stories. I've heard before (SPOILER) that this book does not have a happy ending, so I was kind of just waiting for it. I think considering that this was the third somewhat gloomy book I read in a row, I was glad I had a heads up. It didn't take away from the story for me, but potentially saved me from an emotional breakdown. I can't tell you enough how much I loved the characters. Finch and Violet were both lovely, unique, and powerful when it comes to what they had to offer the readers. This is another book focused on mental health, death, grief, love, and friendship-with a little bit of high school struggles thrown in. This is a must read for everyone, but especially for someone who has someone close to them who struggles with depression, bipolar disorder, or thoughts of suicide.

o que dizer deste livro... tantas emocoes! estou sem palavras... 
 2 personagens que se encontram no inicio do livro, quando ambas estao prestes a cometer suicidio, a historia desenvolve-se com a relacao deles, de amizade e amor, quando ambos se apoiam um no outro para sobreviver. 
 A historia e narrada por 2 pontos de vista, ele e ela. Sentimos a evolucao dos dois, como eles lidam com tudo o que se esta a passar. 
 Ao inicio nao me cativou tanto, penso que por estar numa fase que ja me aborrece ler tanto 'YA'... mas quando dei por mim estava completamente agarrada a historia, a autora puxou-me para este seio e eu nem dei por isso. Dei por mim a sentir-me sugada, a viver com estas personagens, a beber cada pensamento/atitude do Finch (que personagem estupenda!!!!) e a certa altura doia tanto a leitura, que tive que parar, porque era de tal intensidade que eu deixava de respirar... 
 A autora, Jennifer Niven conta-nos no final, que esta historia de ficcao tem um paralelismo com acontecimentos do seu passado, por isso sentimos vida neste livro, sentimos que as coisas, as personagens, os acontecimentos nao sao levianos ou nao sao tratados como um simples livro para adolescentes... Nao sou de chorar em livros, mas este despedacou-me o coracao e vai ficar no meu pensamento durante bastante tempo...

Parents turn their backs and refuse to acknowledge it, peers find a way to make fun of and encourage harmful behavior, and meanwhile, the child/adolescent drowns in their own illness. And let me be clear: books that romanticize symptoms of serious mental illness as cute little quirks are not my kind of books. 
 Good intentions, bad delivery.

 *** 
 I have struggled with mental disorder for 8 years (BPD) and none of the books about mental illness I've read so far have really stuck with me. So when I found out about this book and read all these amazing reviews, I thought I would LOVE it and unfortunately I didn't. I did enjoy it while I was reading it but I just couldn't ignore all the issues I had with this book despite its entertaining value. 
 The thing is, yes it entertained me but I think that a book dealing with a subject like this one has to do MORE than entertain. I wanted it to help me in some way, make me feel better. It didn't. It made me feel even more isolated and misunderstood. Because Finch isn't me. In fact Finch is nobody. Finch knows everything about everything, he can do anything he wants. Oh except when he's "asleep". I'm sorry but things aren't that simple. And it's not even about it being unrealistic because I know It's fiction and it has never bothered me before. Honestly, the thing is I couldn't feel anything about Finch most of the time. He was just a character, he didn't feel real to me even though I'm going through similar things. I felt like it was some kind of cliche "tumblr-users-will-like-it-bc-my-book-is-so-dark-and-quotable" novel and I hated it for it. Hated. 
 Being suicidal is not fun, it's not cool and it shouldn't be glamorized. 
 It's ugly and scary and alienating. 
 (Oh and the dialogue in this book is ridiculous. : 
 "- Finch, honey, how are you ? 
 - The stars are so bright tonight, I want to thank the universe for being the way it is and I met the most beautiful girl in the world and I'm so thankful for that, so thankful. The world is a strange place but the planets are ..." 
 JUST SHUT UP AND GET SOME HELP SON.

"SOmetimes, things feel true to us, even if they're not." - finch 
 Depressing. :-(

reference_books.title: The Old Man and the Sea
reference_books.review_text:
Such beautiful, beautiful prose! The book could be summarised in about two lines! But it's amazing how Hemingway took such simple a plot and turned it into this amazing piece of writing. I guess you don't really need a 'great' story for a book to be great! This would last rank if you'd want a book in terms of a fast-paced suspenseful storyline.. But that's an escape most authors use to get people's minds racing. But can people really write about the vastness of sea, of its harsh unforgiving nature, of its beauty, of its gore? Well Hemingway can! People today have too short an attention span to appreciate a book like this. Every story needs to be running in all sorts of directions to keep a reader's attention. 
 In spite of that, the old man and the sea stands out to be the best novella I've read in a long time. It's succinct, no shorter or longer than it needed to be and a book that I will think a lot about in days to come.. 
 It's a 100 pages.. So come on already

Review originally posted on my blog at http://fun-with-books.blogspot.com/20... 
 Lately, I've been reading a great deal of literature that is categorized by the publisher as "Young Adult", but this is the first book I've read that falls into my pre-conceived notion of what that is. Before I started reading so much of it, I thought that the category dealt with teenagers and growing up, or at least functioned as a tool to help them do so... sort of a public service announcement or an "After School Special". Although, I've been rethinking the definition (this would be a great book club discussion topic, Christine), this book is NOT the reason. Please, don't take that as a dis of this book, cuz it certainly isn't meant that way. "After School Specials" can be very touching and generally have a good message to impart. Lock and Key is certainly both of those things. 
 Although she has published a number of books, this is the first Sarah Dessen book I have read. It won't be the last (in fact, I have another queued in my MP3 player right now) although I must confess that it was not love at first sight. I had to warm up to this book, but thaw, I did. I have a number of criticisms that I'm mostly willing to forgive at this point. Although set in reality, there's an element of unlikeliness that can easily be picked at. Like many Nora Roberts books, the events in this story COULD happen, but most likely wouldn't happen the way they've been written. 
 In Lock and Key, 17 year old Ruby is taken in, by her older sister Cora, after being abandoned by her alcoholic mother. Ruby has been forced to rely on herself for the past 10 years (after Cora left for college) and consequently become leary of people in general, as well as fiercely self reliant. 
 Both a strength and a weakness of this book is its meticulous construction. For me, it didn't feel as organic as other books I've read, but at the same time it was marvelously well "built". The "lock and key" theme is used effectively, if not subtley, as a metaphor throughout. Events portrayed in the book have specific reasons for being there and efficiently facilitate the growth of our protagonist. Sarah is another straight forward writer. The book is not heavy on prose or intricate description, but the dialogue felt natural and she's good at characterization. 
 My major knock on this book is the change in pacing. Sarah takes her time developing her characters and getting them from point A to point B, but at the end there is a mad rush to tie things up. It's like she was limited to a certain word count and suddenly realized she was going to exceed it if she didn't sum things up. 
 I've seen a couple reviews where people have complained about the language (which i totally missed) and the use of drugs and alcohol. Personally, I think these are elements that were under utilized given the subject matter of the book, but I guess you should be warned if this kind of thing offends your sensibility. 
 -Chris

reference_books.review_text:
I fell in love with this book, long before I ever read it. A friend was reading it and each day she would come to work and tell me what she had read the night before. She told me the tale, bit by bit, as she made her way through the book. I never knew the name of the book, nor the author, as I always forgot to ask. It wasn't until years later that I picked up the book and started reading it on my own, only to find out that I knew what it was. 
 There are so many characters, leading such different lives, yet all intertwine in such an amazing way. Martin writes beautifully and the story unfolds smoothly, as he introduces each person. The description makes it easy to picture the world that he created. It is a novel that keeps the reader turning the pages and always wanting to know what will happen next. 
 I've read the book several times as well as listened to the audiobook. I will continue to do so over the years as this series will never get old to me.

The other part of this masterpiece is the journey of Katniss' awakening, she is not born a revolutionary, nor should she be, because no one is. Okay, so I may have said, multiple times, that I would never read this book. Well, never, say never. I finally broke down and read this for work; I DO work in a library, after all. And it really wasn't as bad as I thought it would be, you know, for a book with such a twisted plot. I mean, a dystopian future society in which children are annually forced to hunt and kill one another, as a permanent reminder that "the Capitol" is in charge and that there is supposedly nothing that they can do about it. It is just all so contrived. The only apparent threat is that "the Capitol" would kill everyone if they didn't participate. Well, apparently the citizens of "the Districts" have forgotten that some things are worse than death. Like, the sick, twisted "Hunger Games" that they have gone along with for the past 70+ years. Sometimes you HAVE to die for what you believe in, instead of giving the enemy what they want--scared citizens, going along with whatever absurd demands they make. Anyway, the characters and writing are interesting. The arena is never fully explained, but whatever. Apparently, this alternate future is so high-tech that anything is possible. Oh yeah, except for living ethically, and morally, and actually respecting your fellow human beings. But, anyway, I listened to the audiobook edition. With stories like this, I welcome the bit of distance that it places between the reader and the story, and the narration was actually pretty good. I would have rated it just okay, but it was the type of story that keeps you interested, even when you're not reading it. You always want to know what happens next, and can't wait to finish it. I will be reading/listening to the rest of the series, assuming that it doesn't become too gruesome. For anyone that is interested, this first book takes place when Katniss is 16 years old and chronicles the entire Hunger Games from start to finish; relevant backstory is told throughout.

book_b.title: The Moon is a Harsh Mistress
book_b.user_review: Sometimes it's fun throwing rocks but this takes it to a whole new level. This is the first Heinlein book that I've read and I quite enjoyed it. I do believe I will have to read some more.

sample_reviews.review_text: This here is my favorite book. I suppose The Road meant more to me, but when I'm taking my entrance test for heaven, and they ask me what my favorite book was and why, I'll say this one. And it'll be because of the amazing world Heinlein created, and the amazing characters he had populate it, and the ideas, which aren't always new -- in fact, certain of them are awfully old, and crusty from disuse -- those characters have, and the story, oh!, the amazing story of the liberation of the moon. I have a tattoo with a brass cannon over a field or stars with a red bar sinister and the acronym TANSTAAFL on my left arm. This is my favorite book.

The novel leaves a strong impression of being much older than it really is, with the lazily thought-out AI, the barely credible daily lives of the 'Loonies' and the flat cliche female characters. 
 The author clearly improved on the ideological front (compared with 'Starship Troopers', that is): while the whole pseudo-anarchic society on the Moon is still a fuzzy ball of porcupine bollocks - the judicial 'system' alone is worth convicting to some education for - it manages to keep to the background, and doesn't excessively annoy the reader with pompous musings about the nobility of the former criminals - heh, in the place and conditions that in reality would turn out to be such a fertile compost heap for organised crime and gang violence that 'Mad Max' and 'Judge Dredd' combined would still look like a peaceful utopia. 
 I also find the ending to be quite poor. I'm fine with the 'Loonies' winning (although I did wish that they should have got some thermonuclear belt on their cheeky buttocks at times), but the deaths of Prof and Mike are just oh-so-convenient and pathetic. I see that you could read a bit of cheap 'now, that the parents are gone, you children have to get by on your own' symbolism, but it is what it is: cheap. It reeks of the author's just not caring enough to make up something interesting for two crucial characters. 
 However, I do have enjoyed the preparations for the revolution and the amusing propaganda games against the Warden and the Earth. The war itself was mostly great - although I think that the hidden catapult construction, and also the rather silly military responses from the Earth, are a big stretch.

This is from Heinlein's later production when he had gotten more chatty. And in the first three hundred pages there was plenty of "talk-talk" as the narrator would have said. Being a computer technologist he finds this trying. I don't know if Heinlein himself found it trying or if it was his subconscious telling him to move along. I found it trying. 
 I enjoyed the fact that the moon being a destination for convict transportation from all the nations on earth there was some language variation. Calling one another "gospodin", for example - when not calling one another "cobber". Language otherwise spare for taste. Pronouns in short-supply on moon. Narrator talk-talk easy understand, but unimproved reading pleasure. 
 I like Heinlein's take on race. The narrator's name is Manuel Garcia O'Kelly. He may be mostly Hispanic, but nobody cares. Other people may be black, may be white, not important. 
 But with a title like this one, I would expect a little more bounding across the surface, falling down craters, being scorched by radiation or frozen by shadow. Here people hang out in tunnels all the time. Well, they do get outside on occasion, but briefly and without any real danger. I suppose it is earth who finds her a harsh mistress when their grain supply world starts throwing rocks. 
 Heinlein has cogent ideas on revolution, rather far-out ideas on government and pretty wild ideas on family but with less lecturing they would have been more fun. 
 But being Heinlein, brighter and more far-seeing than most he hits the mark on more than one occasion. As, for example, on the current situation in Syria: "Correctly organized and properly timed it (revolution) is a bloodless coup. Done clumsily or prematurely and the result is civil war, mob violence, purges, terror." 
 There is too little humor, but now and again he throws us a bone... "Wyoh recruited Sidris; Sidris started own cell by recruiting her other assistant and Bon Ton Beaute Shoppe became hotbed of subversion." 
 There are some other good bits, prophetic? "Wyoh" is named after "Wyoming" where she was born. The chatty AI "Mike" fills her in on her birth place: "It is a region of high plains and of mountains, having limited fertility but esteemed for natural beauty. Its population was sparse until augmented through the relocation subplan of the Great New York Urban Renewal Program, A.D. twenty-twenty-five through twenty-thirty". Hmmm. Brooklyn-West south of Ten Sleep? Lost Springs swelling from a population of four to forty? Interesting times await.

**Hugo/Nebula Awards Reading Challenge - 38 of 93** 
 Without a doubt, this was one of the best books I've ever had the pleasure of reading. Five stars seem insufficient to do it justice. A wonderful mash up of an early stage sci fi lunar penal colony (with laughably old-school but cool tech) and an important treatise on how to conduct a revolution and the necessity of human freedom from over-government. 
 The matriarchal, polygamous, anarchist/communist colony, where debts seem to be best written off by gambling and badly behaved individuals make discreet trips outside airlocks without wearing a pressure suit, is the very best and most realistic of the utopias I've discovered. I'm impressed that a sci fi written back in '66 still stands impressive over 50 years later, where so many of its cohort seem so awfully outdated. The sexism apparent in the earlier Heinlein books I've read (Stranger in Strange Land and Starship Troopers) was a little toned down in this one, and certainly made me appreciate the value of the novel more without sparking my righteous feminist indignation with every unnecessary bottom slap. 
 As an Australian, and descendant of a harsh a penal colony I feel a special connection with the characters sent to the moon to work themselves to death, or survive and thrive. This novel reminds me of another favourite, The Dispossessed, although I imagine it should be the other way around, as The Dispossessed was written some eights years later. 
 The highest possible praise I can give a novel - this one should be required reading for all. Go forth and spread the love!

I have to admit I have struggled with this book for a long time, and not to be disrespectful to an acknowledged master in the SF genre or to his many devoted fans, I am inclined to bestow on it what noted SF writer and critic Thomas M. Disch might call a St. Bradbury. 
 The feast of St. Bradbury, Disch says, is when critics, readers, and reviewers gather up all the books they've been "unable, despite their best intentions and firmest resolves, to read all the way to the end," and ceremoniously dispose of them. Disch puts it a bit more caustically, but like I said I don't want to be disrespectful, since, despite what for me is a difficult roadblock on the Heinlein highway, I acknowledge there must be something good to account for Heinlein's amassed critical and popular following. 
 So what's my problem? Let's just say that with The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress, considered by most critics and many readers to be Heinlein's finest, the gender issue once again raises its ugly head. Not half a dozen pages can pass in this avowedly political novel, without the male characters' lengthy verbal and visual ogling of the female characters, and the female characters then simpering, giggling, and cooing their appreciation of the men's appreciation. And this is generally DURING any of said political and philosophical conversations, although fortunately not so much during the action sequences, comprised so far in my reading of political rallies meeting with government reprisal, strongly flavored by the novel's 1960's origins. 
 All of this "he looked her up and down, and whistled"--followed by four or five paragraphs of extraneous flirtation--wouldn't be so bad if Heinlein didn't seem so bent on generalizing about what women think (and, believe me, Heinlein has NO problem writing with paranormal authority on what women think) and how women are different-which so far in my reading mostly seems to involve a propensity for intuition and girlish gossip, occasional short-lived and inexplicable (yet adorable) flirtatious huffs, and an abiding love of compliments. 
 Now, don't mistake me, Heinlein may be a product of his times, but he is no misogynist. To quote Disch once again, Heinlein is more than eager to grant women "equal wages and equal fun" and a certain naive amount of mental acuity. To cite another of Heinlein's well-loved novels, Stranger in a Strange Land presents a passel of female character, all of them nurses and secretaries, but at least he gives a few of them eidetic memories, plenty of smarts, and great job skills. Conveniently, as we are at length informed, they are also extremely attractive. But then, as Heinlein says in Moon, there are no ugly women. 
 The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress is the story of political dissent and government rebellion at a former penal colony on the moon; it is also the story of a computer achieving consciousness. Is the computer "Mike" really a Michelle? Heinlein's characters must, of course, dicker about this, since they have crystal clear ideas about gender differences, even when talking about banks of electronic controls. For myself, I will continue to struggle with both the book and its ideas, at least until the traditional date set for the feast of St. Bradbury, August 22 ("the great man's birthday," as Disch reminds us), or until someone or something pushes me to read past my roadblocks. I am hoping with an idealistic postmodern gusto that our hero and heroine will finally realize that Mike/Michelle's identity changes depending on his/her audience and that that in itself is an indication of the social constructs of gender reflected in the novel and its characters. Then, at last, I will be able to pitch my tent in Heinlein's camp. 
 I am not holding out strong hopes for this eventuality. Still, if there are any readers out there who have read The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress and are up for debate, I am honestly open for discussion and ready to hear about the novel's finer points, which I will then respectfully blog about to set the record straight. Push me to read a little faster. I am ready. 
 All quotes from Disch are from On SF (University of Michigan Press, 2005). Quote from The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress is from the Orb Edition (Tom Doherty Associates, 1997, copyright 1966), and appears on p. 71, among other pages.
