I felt like something science fiction. I always liked the title of this book. I thought I would give it ago. 
 Despite getting my interest from the get-go with an intelligent computer, the book is slow and wasn't terribly exciting, even in the midst of a riot. But okay, I'm patient. However, the sexism in this book is painful. It wasn't actually enough to stop me from reading it until about 60 pages in when the only real woman character in the book says that the protagonist insulted her by not raping her--or at the very least, making aggressive sexual advances on her when she had already made clear several times that she did not want to have sex with him. When the guy demurs, Heinlein has her say, "Michelle would understand," referring to the computer with AI. Sooo... 
 Sigh. :\ I hopped online to check out other reviews of the book. It has an amazing 4.17 star rating on Goodreads, but many of my friends on the site gave it 2 stars or below. I'm not saying that all books with high ratings on Goodreads are necessarily bad, but I am saying that often I am suspicious of books with ratings over 4--especially if they're 4.1+ and "classics" in any genre--because it seems like people who might have read a book and enjoyed it as a child just think, "oh yeah, warm fuzzies for that one--5 stars." 
 Luckily there are some great reviews of this book out there. I'll leave you with my two favorites, after the reading of which I was assured that the book would not get any better, would in fact get worse, and decided to DNF it: 
 "Joint Review: The Moon is a Harsh Mistress by Robert A. Heinlein" at The Book Smugglers 
 "The Moon Is a Harsh Mansplainer (1966) by Robert A. Heinlein" at From Couch to Moon

reference_books.title: The German Girl
reference_books.review_text:
Mixed feelings. 
 1, I think I am very different with this book because the S.S. St. Louis is a part of my family's history. My grandma was 16 when she and her family left their home in Berlin for Cuba on a ship called the S.S. St Louis. They were lucky enough to go to England and eventually emigrate to the USA. 
 2, I was hoping to learn more about the ship or life before the ship but the narration of this time period was very quick, and most of the book focused on Cuba in the 1940's and 1950's (which WAS interesting...but not what I was expecting). In addition, many subplots felt rushed to me and I wanted to truly see things unfold but wasn't able to. 
 3, I'm not sure if it was the translation or the writing but I found the characters to be two-dimensional and some of the thoughts not always true to character. I never quite connected to Anna (2014), but I did like Hannah (1939). 
 OVERALL: I think this would be a good read for those who are interested in learning more about the time period and the ship as well as Cuba later on.

reference_books.title: The Distance from A to Z
reference_books.review_text:
Dear Bloggers Who May Read This Review: 
 This book is MORE than the fluffy romance the blurb makes it seem to be. It deals with secrets, lies, anxiety, taking medication for your problems and being A-OK and proud of it, kissing, flirting/banter, and realizing you judge people even when you don't mean to. 
 I was lucky enough to read an early copy of Natalie's THE DISTANCE FROM A TO Z and I couldn't put it down. The voice and story and setting were so different. I grew up going to gifted & talented camps, which while this is not exactly the same, had a similar feel here. Abby distrusts baseball players because of a family drama. She has two older brothers who are goofy and silly and let her be a little tomboy-ish and also girly. She has a roommate at this camp, Alice, who is great. Man, I love Alice. And Zeke? What can I say about Zeke? I think that we often judge people on what we think we know of them, but it's when we learn who they really are = what matters. 
 Trust me when I say you want this book. 
 Love, 
 Rachel

reference_books.title: Small Great Things
reference_books.review_text: Wow. I loved so much of this because it made *me* acknowledge I'm privileged, I suffer from "white lady racism" (in which I don't think I'm racist but I benefit from certain things etc). I applaud Jodi Picoult for putting that on the page and for this book. 4.5 stars 
 A feminist, surrealist YA title in shades of Vonnegut. Ostensibly the story of a 16yo girl calling out her family on its toxicity and lies, TORNADO is really a bold invitation for women to welcome, love, and nurture of all our different selves. 
 An invitation to tell ourselves and those around us the truth. 
 An invitation do the work we love even when other undermine it--or us. 
 In the present, Sarah is avoiding school and art, following a homeless man in her neighborhood, and frequently bumping into her 10yo, 23yo, and 40yo selves. She hasn't seen her brother Bruce since the family took a trip to Mexico when she was 10. Interspersed with modern day chapters are short monologues from her mother's point of view as well as chapters for each of the days of the Mexico trip. 
 But what makes this book go beyond an issue book is King's mastery of motif. For example, on the Mexico trip, the ocean is so churned up that it's not clear or blue but dull brown and full of churned up seaweed, like a toilet bowl full of diarrhea, according to Sarah. 
 Later, as she learns the truth of her family, she talks about living in a toxic stew of lies and ruin...but the images of the ocean in Mexico so well established that it creates echoes seamlessly. 
 The book has hundreds of layers like that, overlapping images and phrases and ideas that come back again & again to create new light, new energy, new meaning. 
 TORNADO is an impressive feat from a leading literary writer. 
 Disclaimer: I moved this book up on my TBR after King told me and my students recently on a Skype visit that this book "hit too close to home" because she'd stayed in an abusive marriage herself. 
 Post Script: I hate star ratings. I went back and forth between 4 and 5, but I usually reserve 5 for books that are not only fabulous, but I'll also re-read. As much as I love this book, it's not one I'm going to re-read. So 4.5 is my compromise.

book_b.user_review:
I love love love loved this memoir so much I'm going to go out and buy a copy. This is a literary knockout mixed with science.

sample_reviews.review_text: As a "wish I was a" scientist, Lab Girl was a beautiful tribute to botany and a fierce argument for what it takes to make it, especially as a woman, in science. Jahren's writing was exquisite, though her lab practices seemed a touch harsh at times.

I am deeply conflicted about what to say about this book. On the one hand, I strongly disliked the first half of the book. On the other hand, I realized that by about 75% of the way through, I'd frown attached to Hope and Bill. Moreover, the book had started to feel Important for the honest and plain spoken way it portrayed scientists, mental illness, and women in science. I feel like it is a book I would recommend to someone... but I'm not sure who that someone is yet!

I really wanted to like this book. I should have liked this book. 
 I love non-fiction about science, I love learning about plant biology, I am inspired by women who are passionate about their path in life. I am moved by how people transcend outside challenges and personal difficulties to reach fulfillment. 
 But I didn't really like this book, at least not the memoir part of it. Most members of our book group liked this book so I was an outlier with my reaction. 
 Lab Girl felt oddly dispassionate to me. In alternating chapters, Hope Jahren writes about interesting tidbits of plant biology, each followed by chapters of a memoir of her life as a scientist and creating her lab along with an intense work relationship/friendship with her brilliant and anti-social colleague, Bill. 
 I thought her most engaging writing was when she delved into aspects of plant biology and her love of the natural world: How particular trees become important to us as individuals; how improbable it is that a seed will become a tree; the risk a root takes as it pushes forth and exhausts the last reserves of a seed. Here Jahren shows her passion about the natural world. 
 The chapters about her personal life, on the other hand, left me cold. She seems to be determined to show us that all the stereotypes of the odd scientist are true. She bounces from one anecdotal incident to another that reveal a messy personal life with unhappy interactions. We finally learn that this is a result of her manic-depression. 
 The story of the multi-day trip driving through a blizzard with lab assistants to go to a conference was disturbing to me. It shocked me to think that a scientist, who ostensibly takes great care with the details of experiments, chose to drive over a mountain pass in a blizzard without paying attention to weather, road conditions, or the safety of those to whom she is entrusted. And then we don't even get to find out what happened at the conference that supposedly made taking all those chances worthwhile. 
 Jahren alludes to an aloof coldness in her family growing up that must have affected her life deeply, but she doesn't ever really explore in depth (at least in her writing) what that meant and means to her. She "tells" us short details, but I didn't feel the pain it must have brought her. 
 Instead of the memoir part of her book being enlightening, it felt more anecdotal and aimless. I finished the book feeling unmoved. 
 To be fair, Jahren is often quite eloquent when she wrote about plants and trees. And I appreciated the metaphors of the struggle of plants to survive were carried forth in the subsequent memoir chapters. 
 This is from Chapter 3 which was followed by a chapter about her first job in a laboratory at age nineteen at a university hospital pharmacy: 
 "A SEED KNOWS how to wait. Most seeds wait for at least a year before starting to grow; a cherry seed can wait for a hundred years with no problem. What exactly each seed is waiting for is known only to that seed. Some unique trigger-combination of temperature-moisture-light and many other things is required to convince a seed to jump off the deep end and take its chance--to take its one and only chance to grow." 
 "Something so hard can be so easy if you just have a little help. In the right place, under the right conditions, you can finally stretch out into what you're supposed to be." 
 "Each beginning is the end of a waiting. We are each given exactly one chance to be. Each of us is both impossible and inevitable. Every replete tree was first a seed that waited."

While I didn't like this, I appreciated it. I thought the structure of the personal chapters alternating with the scientific chapters was really smart. However, the science chapters weren't for me, it's just not where my interests lie. The writing is wonderful and I think this is a book that would be excellent reading for any young woman interested in science.

I enjoyed listening to the audiobook, read by the author. 
 LabGirl is an emotional yet pragmatic look at a woman's life in scientific academia, of the sad state of science in America and the sad state of our diminishing natural world. With a gift for conveying the sheer wonder of nature, the miracle of the plant world and the many mysteries of it, Jahren offers a truly unique scientific memoir, unlike any I've read. Brutally honest about her own problems, she offers indictments of the scientific funding for research in the US, and of the continual uphill battle women face in the tenured academic world, all while shimmering with delight over the science itself. Truly a wonderful book by a unique author.

This book made me look at plants and tress on a whole new level, and its the awesomeness of the writing on the way how the author interspersed her views and knowledge of the plant kingdom with her everyday life as a scientist, a mother, a wife , a friend, and to live with bipolar disorder on a day to day basis, this made me think on how the natural world really operates and gives meaning to life! But the overall thing that i like about this memoir is the friendship between Bill and Hope. Its their camaraderie and selflessness, that no matter what happens, even you are worlds apart , there is always something to look forward to when you see each other again, its their comforting ways of respecting each other's mindfulness and personalities that exude in the narratives that really captures the essence of this book! 5 stars !

Because I read 50% and skipped to the ending I'm considering this DNF. I did appreciate and relate to her observations of the Scandinavian culture! (Certainly true in my childhood home!)..... 
 "We had long since established the habit of not speaking as we walked the two miles home; silent togetherness is what Scandinavian families do naturally, and it may be what they do best. 
 The vast emotional distances between the individual members of a Scandinavian family are forged early and reinforced daily. Can you imagine growing up in a culture where you can never ask anyone anything about themselves? Where "How are you?" is considered a personal question that one is not obligated to answer? Where you are trained to always wait for others to first mention what is troubling them, even as you are trained to never mention what is troubling you? I saw this book on NetGalley and instantly LOVED the cover. How gorgeous. Then the description pulled me into reading it. Billie Flannigan went out for a hike in the wilderness and never made it back home. Now a year later, her husband Jonathan and daughter Olive are having trouble adjusting to life without Billie and their new normal. Then Olive starts seeing her mother in hallucinations - is she psychic? - and is convinced that her mother is still alive. 
 The further you read, the more the onion peels back on Billie's character, and the lies she told her family. Jonathan begins to wonder if Billie really died in those woods, or if she just left her family for good. The Billie he knew wouldn't do that. But the new Billie he's learning about just might. 
 Overall this is a page-turner and a fun summer read. 
 Visit Hidden Staircase to see my full review.

Billie, both a wife & mother, goes missing on a hiking trip and disappears. The assumption is that she is dead; they find her car in the parking lot of the trail head and one of her hiking boots, but they never find a body. Her husband, Jonathan and her daughter, Olive struggle to move on with their lives; Jonathan begins drinking and Olive pulls away from her father. Around the 1 year anniversary of Billie's disappearance, Jonathan is awaiting the death certificate for his wife from the court, however his daughter seems to not be entirely sure her mother is really dead. Olive decides to start searching for her mother herself and eventually her father agrees to help. 
 This book sounds really interesting to me when I read the synopsis, however it fell a little flat for me. Basically, as you would expect, once they start searching for Billie, they discover that she has been lying and things aren't exactly as they seemed to be. I never really connected with any of the characters and generally when that occurs, I don't find myself as interested in the actual story. I did find the second half of the book a bit more interesting when Jonathan starts digging into his wife's past. The writing is alright, but nothing that really grabbed me and pulled me into the story. The story is told mostly in the present, with some flashbacks to the past. I do have to say I found the ending to be pretty impressive, it wasn't what I expected after we find out everything else. I know that is a bit vague, but I don't want to give anything away. An interesting story, just never really grabbed my attention the way I expected it to. 
 Thank you to the publisher for sending me an ARC.

See all my twisted reviews at https://booksbejeweled.com 
 Janelle Brown, the author of Watch Me Disappear, says in her Goodreads author profile that her books "tend to be page-turners with dysfunctional family relationships at their hearts." I couldn't have said that better myself. Throw in a compelling mystery and this book exceeds that description. 
 Watch Me Disappear tugged at my own heart from the beginning with a beautifully described scene of a family of three --lying on their backs watching hundreds of butterflies cling to the eucalyptus trees during the monarch migration through Northern California. We soon find out that one member of this family has gone missing and the book takes us on a truth finding mission that had me quickly turning the pages until the twisted end. 
 Janelle Brown is an effortless writer. She is so good, you won't even notice the writing, and she expertly gives an authentic voice to husband Jonathan and his teenage daughter, Olive. Between these two character's roles we are left to our own speculation of what happened to missing mom, Billie. In the Prologue, the reader hears Billie's thoughts for the first time. We find out exactly what may or may not have happened to her. 
 I loved the California setting of the book; the mountains, deserts and beaches of the West Coast are colorfully drawn. The story mostly takes place in the small city of Berkeley, with coffee shops and neighborhoods brightly depicted. There are some mean girls and high school angst issues that may appeal to the YA crowd, but the marital secrets and lies are the subjects that create the uneasy suspense in the book. 
 The book is quick to read but the one slow wordy area is the Prologue itself. I imagine the author wanted Billie to answer every possible question the reader might still have. This last chapter was a bit too tedious for me. 
 Many thanks to NetGalley and Random House for an advance copy of the book.

book_b.user_review: This book is a poetic recounting of the diversity of the Japanese citizens who were rounded up into the concentration camps during WWII. It is not a story as such but a melting pot of stories. It left me wanting to read more about this topic.

sample_reviews.review_text: Wasn't for me. Read 40 or so pages and no real characters.

The book is a very short one--an account of the fates of a group of Japanese picture brides who came to the U.S. during the early 20th century and settled in California. The voice used is a collective first person: "we worked in the fields. Some of us had babies in the fields. Some of us married well." I've never before read a book written with that point of view. For the most part it worked, although after a while I found the constant use of "we did this", "we did that" became a bit tedious. Then in the last two chapters, the story moves to the internment of the Japanese in camps during WWII. That was told in a very low key, but it is heartbreaking, especially in view of the things that are now being said about Muslim immigrants and even citizens. I read this author's earlier book, "When the Emperor Was Divine" and found it even more effective than this one in covering that tragedy.

I think I would have liked this much more if it were written differently. I really got bored as there was not much of a story. I think it would have been a better read if it were about a specific woman or short stories about several of the women that came over on the boat.

A collective, composite history of Japanese women who came to U.S. West Coast in early 20th century to wed Japanese laborers already there, from their voyage and arrival, through marriages, work, family life, etc., up until forced relocations after Pearl Harbor. No single individual characters or story lines, but simply descriptions of group and personal experiences. Very detailed and nicely written, but often repetitive (I suppose for a cumulative effect), which can get tiresome at times.

If not for the overused tedious and monotonous style, I could have really loved this book for its content and insight. The repetitive "some of us...one of us..." killed the ability to connect or even get to know any character and quite frankly became tiresome after the first few pages. Were the book any longer I would not have pushed through.

I loved the style of this book. There is no one main character but a collective main character. This subject is a very painful one for many Americans and still something for which this country should be ashamed.

It's fascinating. And sobering, if you're, like me, a person who too often takes things for granted. But as a work of fiction? Sooooooooooooo boring. 
 read more...

This is really more of an epic poem than a novel, and to be honest, it just wasn't to my taste. 
 The use of the group over individual is an interesting concept, but I find it more off-putting than anything else. I Just don't like the idea of grouping such a large and varied group of people as a single unit like that... it feels weird.

Ekhontas molis diabasei to "Phantastika Zoa Kai Pou Briskontai", etan skhedon adunaton na men xekineso amesos na diabazo to biblio, "To Kouintits Ana Tous Aiones". Os gnesia fan tou Harry Potter, toso sten logotekhnike tou ekdose, oso kai sten kinematographike, panta goeteuomoun apo ena kalo paikhnidi Kouintits, esto ki an den eikha anarotethei pote pragmatika, okhi toulakhiston mekhri semera, gia ten proeleuse kai ten katagoge tou. An kai e Rowling, me ton diko tes tropo, eikhe katastesei saphes oti to sugkekrimeno athlema, einai ston kosmo ton magon tes, kati san to podosphairo ston diko mas, thneto kosmo, to antilambanomoun os ena akoma paikhnidi pou se kapoia alle diastase, eikhe megale, isos kai terastia semasia. 
 Domemeno kai pali me ten morphe ekpaideutikou, skholikou egkheiridiou, me ten upographe tou phantastikou Kenilgouorthi Gouisp, to sugkekrimeno biblio, mas milaei gia polu perissotera apo to Kouintits. An anekete se ekeinous pou anarotiountai, pos e skoupa, proekupse na einai to magiko meson metaphoras kathe magou, to sugkekrimeno biblio, ekhei mia polu euphantaste apantese na sas dosei e opoia, phantazei olos diolou logike ki endiapherousa. Epises, endiapheron ekhei kai e parousiase tes exelixes tou mesou ana tous aiones kai pos auto prosarmosteke stis agonistikes anagkes ton paikton tou athlematos. Parallela, ekhoume mia plere katagraphe gegonoton pou odegesan to Kouintits, apo ten arkhike, tukhaia tou emphanise, se auto to opoio einai semera kai pou gnorisame mesa apo ten pena tes suggrapheos. 
 Ousiastika, to en logo biblio, mas boethaei na katalaboume, okhi mono ten spoudaioteta kai ton sumbolismo tou athlematos autou, alla kai ten exelixe ton magon kai ten diamorphose diaphoron kanonon tous, pou mporei na eikhan os apheteria to sugkekrimeno athlema, ostoso, pegazoun apo polu bathutera gegonota. Kata mia ennoia, mporoume na rixoume mia matia sten koinonike, alla kai ten politike diamorphose kai diarruthmise tes koinonias ton magon, pou opos kathe anthropino sunolo, ekhei ten anagke na thesei orous kai oria, prokeimenou na diaterethei e taxe, e armonia, e dikaiosune, alla kai bathuteres axies, pou kathe noemon on, opheilei na ekhei. Ekho ten aisthese pos eidika to antriko koino, tha eukharistethei idiaiteros to sugkekrimeno bibliaraki, khoris auto na semainei pos oi gunaikes, den tha to broun exisou endiapheron.

book_b.title: The Light Between Oceans
book_b.user_review:
So good so so so good -that is all 
 (Ending was far better than I thought it would be)

sample_reviews.review_text:
In the commentary for the movie, "Little Miss Sunshine," the director states that Olive's scream of delight at the beginning motivates the action for the rest of the movie. If you don't believe that moment, then "Sunshine" isn't for you. While that movie relies on the actress to scream her little lungs out (check!), Light Between Oceans relies more on the personal experience and preferences of the reader. 
 If your life's single, overwhelming mission is to have children, then Light Between Oceans will sweep you into a magical world and you won't be able to put it down. This book is masterfully written and full of beauty and drama. On the other hand, if you like children fine, but also like when someone else takes them home, this book may not capture your imagination. 
 I had trouble suspending my disbelief at the pivotal moment near the beginning that propels the drama for the rest of the book. Then there were many "baby" details to wade through before making it to the more adult-oriented drama at the end (which was excellent). Two stars are all this book meant to me, but it has all the makings of a 5-star book if children are your primary passion.

Excellent book. Well written with excellent descriptions of places I've never been. The story/plot unfolds in a way that keeps you reading. Even when you think you have it, you're never sure. Uses a crisis of moral decision points and you can follow how one decision leads to another, even when you know it is going in the wrong direction. Good read. Recommended.

The characters were written beautifully. It says something that I was rooting for characters whose interests were in complete conflict. Parts of the plot were like watching a train wreck - you knew what was going to happen but you still felt compelled to keep reading.

This book was tough for me to get through and the only reason I finished it was for my book club. It was dull and dragged on and on. It picked up a little by part three, but not enough to redeem the book for me.

This book was predictable, boring and melodramatic. Unfortunately, it starts off very strong and thus tricks you into reading further, with Tom being an interesting and mysterious character, Isabel tough and a little unorthodox, and Janus' secluded and hostile setting. If you're entering this book hoping to read about two people surviving on the island, dealing with the issues that arise and overcoming them, you've picked up the wrong book. This novel is 5% about living on a secluded island and 95% melodramatic boring drivel. 
 The last hundred pages are near insufferable. The only "heartbreaking" thing about it was that I read to the end, and that's only because I had to read this book for a Book Club. Honestly, not only did I want to wring everyone character's neck, but the author insisted on giving Lucy dialogue, which was utterly painful to read. 
 Maybe this novel just isn't for me, because I found it insulting how it suggests that women go completely bonkers regarding children and conception. There are many many women/couples who can't conceive and they don't go around stealing babies. But apparently all Isabel can think about is having a kid so she loses it. Granted, she was stuck on that island so maybe that drove her a little crazy, but then in the same novel you have Hannah, another women who, when faced with the presumed death of her child, becomes a mentally unstable women who is basically unable to function in society. Give me a break.

The Light Between Oceans was a good book. I think, for me, though, it paled because I read it immediately after Gone Girl. That one was so riveting and well paced, that this one just seemed slow in comparison. I think I might have rated it higher if I hadn't read Gone Girl first.

When I reached a certain point in this book, I was not sure I could finish it....too sad and tragic. I had to keep reading, however, to decide if the author could redeem the awful decisions made by the main characters.

I enjoyed reading this book, even though the topic was not an easy one to deal with. The plot was well developed, as were the characters. The metaphor of the child's name "Lucy" meaning light did not dawn on me until the end of the book. It was one of those books that I will still be thinking about long after I have finished reading it!

My heart is still in my throat and tears are still drying in the corners of my eyes. 
 I wanted to stop reading several times. I only kept on because of the encouragement of my friends, whose judgement I trusted. I know why I needed to now. 
 Life is definitely not easy after a war. Love can come so unexpectedly. That is what happened to Tom. Isabel was the love of his life and Tom never allowed himself to give that up, no matter what else happened. 
 The fairy existence of living on a small island 100 miles off the coast of Australia and being a Lighthouse Keeper was such an enormous attraction for wanting to read this story for me. I wanted to know what it was like. I found out. 
 Life and death and love and loss and love. That is what I found out.

This was a hard book to read. It was to me so sad. It did raise a lot of questions and things to think about. It was hard to decide who was right and who was wrong, what was selfish and what was not. There is a lot of pain around motherhood and what it means in these pages. It was interesting to think about what I might have done under similar circumstances. If you have experienced pregnancy loss, you might find the beginning of the story triggering.

reference_books.review_text:

 I already thought Issa Rae was awesome, based on what I'd seen from her in her interviews and the shows she's in - so I had to listen to her book. She's so much more than I even expected. 
 The book is hilarious. I was snorting with laughter for much of it. She's a brilliant comedian, especially catering to the socially awkward. 
 There's a lot more than jokes in this book. It gets pretty personal - which only helps me relate to her more than I already did. 
 So, she's got a lot of stuff in here that I totally get. And then she's got even more stuff that make me think she's way too awesome for me ever thinking I could be on the same level as her. 
 I totally have a girl crush on Issa Rae. 
 The book has a lot of amusing stories with some pretty personal ones mixed in. I highly recommend it. She's an amazing woman. I wish I could put into better words how much I appreciate the stuff she does.

book_a.title: Off to Be the Wizard (Magic 2.0, #1)
book_a.user_review:
http://www.platypire.com/j-hooligan/o... 
 This book was recommended to me about a year ago by Sofia. I should have read it then, but I was such a fool in my youth. I bought the audio earlier this year for whispersync purposes, before I had kindle unlimited. 
 Anyway, this is one of the most fantastic books I have ever read. Also, the narrator... Holy plop balls! Luke Daniels was amazing! I have already been heckling/harassing/highly recommending (how ever you want to say it) it to several of my friends. 
 One thing I need to point out is, I recently watched Kung Fury - so the thought of hacking time is gloriously amazing. Throw in a gaggle of computer nerds that are also hacking a program they found to become "wizards" and I'm hooked. I'm already a fan of time traveling back to the time of King Arthur, so all this extra was a whole lot of awesome piled on top of what was already awesome. Basically, it would have been very hard for this book to not be enjoyable for me. 
 What I didn't expect was pretty much everything I read in this book. It was nothing like what I expected, and I could not even begin to guess at what was going to happen next. This was one of the more unique books I've read, and that's a major plus for me. 
 My favorite part of this book was every time I snorted with laughter, which happened quite often. (Usually something related to Phillip) It was brilliant, fantastic, glorious, and every other similar sort of word you can think of to fit right here to explain how much I loevd this book. 
 I've never finished a book and immediately wanted to go back to the beginning and reread/listen to the whole thing over again. I'm hoping to convince my husband to give in to my whims so I have an excuse. I did notice book 2 is on Kindle Unlimited, so I'll be downloaded that and listening to it soon. 
 Truly an original. I absolutely loved it. Highly recommended. One of the best books I've ever read. (I can go on if you need me to...)

sample_reviews.review_text: I really liked this! It was fun and clever and the humor felt very modern. I recomend for anyone that likes time travel, video games, tech, board games, humor, king arthur, and inventive stories. I am going to read the next book in the series!

This was a really cute story. It was a nice bit of brainless entertainment to listen to when I wanted to unwind. I listened to the audible version thanks to prime and I will say that the narrator did an excellent job voicing the characters and telling the story. 
 I didn't get too invested in the story enough to grab the next one and I don't see myself doing so unless it ends up being free too ... or I signed up for KU at some point.
I suppose if you can't bring yourself to actually write women in your story, shipping them off to a faraway place is the next best option. Loads of potential never fully realized.

3.5 stars 
 I'm torn. I LOVED the first 80% of the book, but man, it ran out of steam the last 20% and fast! Meyer's writing style is highly reminiscent of Douglas Adams, so if you are a DA fan, I highly recommend this one. If you are someone who loves computers mixed with a bit of fantasy steeped in geek humour, I highly recommend this as well. 
 In other words, just go read it already.
Giving up on this one. The premise was mildly interesting, but I couldn't get past the author's writing style and the fact that I hated the protagonist, who is an idiot.

Felicia Day and Kristina Horner both recommended and loved this book, and I have a massive nerdy-girl-crush on both those wonderful ladies, so I used an audible credit to grab this. Unfortunately, I was just a bit [okay, I was a lot] bored with the plot. I think it had a neat concept, and it had a lot of interesting ideas, but there actually wasn't very much story to this... a LOT of world building and character building, but it didn't really have a direction. There weren't a ton of problems, and in some places I felt like things were going a bit too fast and in some places it dragged along. I just couldn't get into this. The humor was sometimes great, but other times it seemed completely immature for a story involving grown men. And the lack of female characters was not necessarily *bad*, but it definitely wasn't a bonus... I need strong female characters in my books to be fully satisfied!

Well, not quite Ready Player One, but I actually enjoyed it thoroughly. The basic premise of the book is that the entire world is a computer simulation, and everyone in it is the result of a few lines of computer code. With slight modifications to the code, almost anything can be modified by someone who knows how to access "the file". As intriguing as this is, in itself, the book is elevated to the next level by introducing the idea that magic is just the result of computer geeks (I mean wizards) being able to modify code and alter reality. 
 What a fun book. Since I'm on a series challenge this year and trying to clean out my TBR/TBL lists, I'll move right on to the next 2 books in the series, the last of which was just released this week. Luke Daniels, the narrator of the Audible edition of this book, did an amazing job differentiating the characters and giving each a distinct personality.

No. Just no. I know this is a silly book with a silly premise. I get that. You can have your computer program reality and time travel. But if you're going to send someone back to actual 7th century actual England then you need to do enough research at the very least to grasp that the people would have been speaking a completely different language from modern English. Not some ye olde version thereof - might get away with that a thousand years later - but a different, completely incomprehensible language. England being an actual place with an actual history rather than your generic Fantasyland. Probably some people are going to read this review and say "you accept the computer program premise and historical accuracy breaks your suspension of disbelief?" This is exactly the kind of book where historical accuracy matters the most, BECAUSE suspension of disbelief is already stretched. Besides, it's just lazy.

This was the best book I had not read! Just imagine, if the world is a computer simulation -- which the book doesn't really say it is -- take a moment to think all those things that could be done when you find the config file? Macros! Shell scripts! If you understood at least one term and/or find the cover at least a tiny bit of intriguing then read it! 
 ...Or on a second thought, you should probably listen it. The audio version is hilarious - written in letters the size of the Hollywood sign. Your preference of humour might vary, though. 
 This is all I got the time for. I'm off to listen the second book!

What I liked 
 It is a fun, mostly light hearted story of a modern boy being dropped into medieval times. To really enjoy the novel, the reader must go with numerous twists without asking questions or you will hate this story. Personally, I decided to just go with it and really ended up enjoying the novel. 
 For me, the two central characters, Martin and Phillip, are what make the story so engaging. Most of the story involves Phillip "teaching" Martin how to be Wizard and the rules of their secret society. I really enjoyed the interaction between the two as they began to grow into a big brother, little brother type of relationship. 
 Also, if you remember the dark ages of computers in the 80's then you will get a kick out of the some inside jokes (except the slam against the Commodore Vic-20, which was my first real computer). 
 What I didn't like 
 If you let the twist of how Martin ends up in medieval England or some strange logic used during the story then you will absolutely dislike this novel as it goes on. Basically, the author uses what I like to call "Video Game" storytelling, which means, throw some outrageous plot points at the reader and then just move forward. Even with all the weird stuff going on around the characters, they have no time to ask basic "what the" questions. For me, when Martin accuses Phillip of a horrific act, it just did not ring true and just a dumb plot device to get into Phillip's secret area. 
 Plus, the discovery and battle against the "bad guy" feels a bit tacked on and rushed. 
 Last word 
 A mostly compelling novel that meshes plot of The Matrix with A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court yet sprinkles strange and unnecessary plot twists to form a different type of story that eventually boils down to an enjoyable read.

I thoroughly, thoroughly enjoyed this book. Without spoiling anything I find this book to be worthy of a movie. It brought me back to my childhood, my teen years and beyond. It has brought me the desire to watch all the wonderful movies talked about, listen to all the referenced music and die to find an Atari 2600 so I can go back and play all its games.  Onward to your next book.
Fanfreakingtastic!

Ready Player One is the most referential book I have ever read. Its pages drip with 80s pop culture references, some of them obvious, many of them not. It's entertaining at first, especially when you understand the reference, but then it becomes a bit obnoxious and excessive. This, in fact, is a good analogue to the book itself. Its beginning is much stronger than its conclusion, and the aspects of the book which were its most entertaining element at the start become tired and worn-out by the end. 
 The book is on the whole enjoyable. I described it to a co-worker as "aggressively okay." The narrative pulls you along at a steady pace, interesting things happen, the mystery of the "Easter Egg" is sufficiently compelling, but it's the finer details that start to nag. As mentioned, the references, the worship of 80s culture, although explained through the narrative, becomes irritating. The details of the story are impressive, and the author's passion for the subject matter screams on every page. The writing and dialogue serves the story fine and provides only a few moments of profundity. 
 Sadly, the author, Ernest Cline, commits one of the most grievous mistakes of any science fiction or fantasy story, which I call "The Magic Wand." Essentially "The Magic Wand" is a narrative tool to magically fix the story's most perplexing problems. (Did you know reversing the Earth's orbit reverses time itself!? Thank you, Superman). Often times authors use this Wand when they've painted themselves into a corner. "Oh, look, now the main character can fly!" or "travel through time!" or some such thing. Ready Player One's Magic Wand is the main character's outlandish sudden ability to perfectly plan and execute a plan of such devious and conniving genius it leaves both the characters in the book and the reader of the book completely stunned. Furthermore, throughout the book, there are far too many instances of the character needing to know some obscure or obtuse fact about 80s pop culture and the main character conveniently notifies the reader: "Good thing I've watched this film exactly 175 times." Good thing, indeed. 
 Having said all of this, I enjoyed Ready Player One for what it was. I was especially interested in the possible and entirely plausible future of virtual reality that the book showcases. It's both exciting and dismaying. Although the messaging of the book is muddled, which is too bad, the fiction aspect of it was very interesting. (It's worth mentioning that according to an article in Businessweek, each new Oculus Rift employee--a company which has created a virtual reality headset--is issued a copy of Ready Player One). A few years ago I was extremely skeptical of virtual reality's ability to be adopted by the mainstream. Although that hasn't happened in a significant way yet, I do believe it will; in addition, I believe it very well could herald a massive shift in how we consume and participate in entertainment, education, business, commerce, and even how we interact with and make sense of reality itself. Ready Player One shows a world that is either terrifying or exhilarating depending on your worldview. I'm not convinced the author knows exactly which one it is. 
 Ready Player One is being adapted into a film by Steven Spielberg, and I think it might have a better chance being a great story as a film than a book. I think the story needs to be trimmed, sliced and diced a bit, and leave behind many of the arcane details meant to be enjoyed by only a few. There is definitely a fun adventure to be found here, but it might take some other storytellers to tell it a bit better.

This was just what I needed to zone out while traveling in Vegas. It filled up all the waiting time (like waiting for the taxi, the plane, the Miss Asian Pageant -- you know what I mean). Definitely a children's dystopia book for Gen X gaming nerds -- no social commentary, implicit reliance on the ultimate justice and protection of the legal system, and straight-up D&D.
Well, I pushed through it, even though I didn't like it. There was barely any action, and the romance between P and A was boring. The ending was boring, too.

Not especially dynamic in terms of character development, and the writing tended to be a lot of "I did this, then this happened, then I did this, and oh-by-the-way, here's a historical summary of what this thing is all about," etc.. But that makes it sound like I didn't like it, which isn't true! It actually was a lot of fun. I think the writing style is probably strongly informed by the fact that most of the story takes place in virtual reality, and our narrator was pretty much alone most of the time. So it makes sense, but still wasn't my favorite writing. Anyway, the premise and the plot were interesting and the end was satisfying, so definitely a solid read.

LOVED this. Started out with the audiobook (highly recommended - Wil Wheaton is a GREAT narrator), got about halfway through, and then switched over to print so i could finish faster -- and read the rest in an evening. Such an imaginative, genre-bending, addictive read.

I liked but didn't love this straight-ahead adventure story clothed in an unreasoning, nostalgic love for 80s geek culture. I am just a little too old to remember the 80s so fondly. I did laugh aloud numerous times, and the story was involving and plotted well. It's pure summer/escapist/goofy fiction, and it's a lot of fun if you have even a passing familiarity with the 80s. I suspect there's a generation for whom this one is as evocative as Among Others was for me.

I really liked this book! Chock-full of pop culture and pop culture references - and anyone who knows me well, knows that I love that kind of stuff - there was even a "Heathers" reference, which is one of my favorite movies! So needless to say, I was hooked right from the beginning. 
 However, there was one particular thing that bothered me, while reading "Ready Player One", and it ultimately keeps me from rating it four stars. Cline seems to tell, instead of show, what happens, A LOT of the time. I realize that sometimes it's easier to simply describe what's going on, versus show it, but the saying "Good authors show, and don' tell!" kept popping into my head, at various times. Sure, this is his first published book, (plus, he's a screenwriter, which I find extremely cool!)...so combine the two, and I'll let it slide. :) 
 One star for the cool, unique premise, one star for the awesome (and incredibly detailed) 80's material (this guy knows his stuff!) and one for the fact that he is a screenwriter. I just love the idea of being a screenwriter!!

A helluva of a nostalgic and high energy/stakes competition through the 1980s and geek/nerd culture. Yes, it's a whole lot of fun but there's a sobering message here too about where the world could be headed. Even though the message is that reality is always better than fantasy, in this world, it's hard to argue for that point. Being plugged is better than the reality of Ready Player One unless you are one of the priviledged few. 
 Fun read.

reference_books.title: Ethereal (Celestra, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Woohoo, I'm finished! Thank goodness for that. Although admittedly I won't get that time back again the thought that I won't have to read another page consoles me. 
 I have read quite a lot of Young Adult books and have been pleasantly surprised by a lot of them. This one, however, is memorable for all the wrong reasons. 
 You should be able to relate in some form to the main character(s) but with the main female in this book I just wanted to turn to a page where she wasn't on it. She whinges, she whines, she's rude and obnoxious (and that's to her friends, let alone her family), she's pathetic and does nothing apart from complain or be bitchy. She thinks nothing of leaving her two sisters at the mall whilst she goes off with her boyfriend, even though she's already only being let out on "good behaviour". 
 And speaking of boyfriends, do try to keep up over which one she is locking lips with as it changes quite frequently, although the fact that she is a virgin is brought up quite frequently too. It's almost as if the author was having to remind herself of this. Ellis is a dopehead but a good looking one ... obviously! Logan is described as an Adonis and also seems to think the same way himself and Gage has eyes like a cobalt sea and stunning features. Yeuch! Of them all, Gage shows the most promise but is the one that you hear the least about. He seems to be permanently saving their asses and getting no thanks for it! 
 I can't actually think of anything about this book that pleased me apart from when I realised that it was over and I didn't have to read anymore. 
 This book has been described as spiritual - I'm sorry, I just don't get that!!!! 
 Book's finished, series is finished - the thought of reading 9 more books like this one .... I just can't do it.

reference_books.title: Beautiful Demons (The Shadow Demons Saga #1; Peachville High Demons #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This short book starts with 16 year old Harper moving to Stepford, sorry, I mean Peachville, because she has powers that she can't control that no one wants to admit they know about. 
 She moves there and quickly finds out that the town is split between the perfect and beautiful ... and the rest of them. She doesn't fit in as she lives in the Shadowford home, until some magic mojo is performed which suddenly affects her memory and her whole ability to judge people on who they are. 
 This book was ok but I'm not sure whether the jocks and the cheerleaders are actually the good guys or bad (I'm going with bad based on this book) and I'm certainly wishing to have known more about Jackson as he was the character with the most oomph about him. 
 This book will leave you with a lot of questions that remain unanswered which is supposed to make you buy the rest of the books to find out the answers. However, for me, I really couldn't care less what happens to 99% of the characters. 
 A very quick read and not enough hooks to get me to buy the rest FIVE in the series!!!

reference_books.title: Prince of Wolves (The Grey Wolves, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
After seeing some of the reviews already listed for this book, I knew it was going to be a Marmite book so it was with some trepidation that I started reading it. I am glad to say that I am firmly in the "Love It" half! So much so that I've downloaded and am currently halfway through the second book with the others on my wishlist so I don't lose any of them! 
 The characters are all well-rounded and the relationship between the 3 girls is exceedingly well written. Everyone should have friends like this during their lifetime! The leading male is an Alpha in every sense of the word and his family are to die for. 
 Basically, if you are content to let the story take you for a ride, then sit back and enjoy.

reference_books.title: Without Regret (Pyte/Sentinel, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Chris has had it tough. Not only was his childhood nothing to write home about but when a Master attacks their home in Book 1, it is Chris who ends up being shot and severely wounded. Through sheer grit and determination, he has made it back to full health. But along the way he has lost that cheekiness that I loved about him. The responsibility he feels towards his family and making sure that no one can hurt them again is what makes him get up in the morning. His mate is still out there and he imagines she will be just like him. Isabella is the perfect partner for Chris. He needs someone to bring laughter back into his life and she manages to do this even when she doesn't mean to. Isabella shows Chris that you don't always need physical strength. Yes, she is the helpless and hapless female on more than one occasion but she also has a mind and isn't afraid to use it. Her wit is rapier sharp too and once she sets her mind on something, it takes a very good reason for her to change it. 
 This book is the second in the series and doesn't disappoint. The plot moves along swiftly and we reconnect with characters from book 1 which too often isn't the case. This book is once again filled with action and humour. We get some depth in the lives of all the characters too which is also good to read. Absolutely brilliant with lots of spicy moments. Recommended!

reference_books.title: Her Mad Hatter (Kingdom, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I really enjoyed this book and it appears that I really liked the differences that other readers have hated! I LIKED the fact that the Mad Hatter was ........ well,.......... mad! I LIKED the fact that he was hot and sexual. I LIKED that Alice was already a fan of Wonderland and I really LIKED the fact that this wonderland was crazy, psychedelic, magic and NOT like the Disney film! 
 If you want a fairy godmother then I would ask for Danika as she has attitude. One of my favourite quotes in this book comes from her when she is thinking about her boys and Cinderella - "Why any self-respecting fairy godmother would pass them over for an inane twit who relied on animals to do her housecleaning was beyond her." 
 This story is crazy, fun, hot and makes reference to Johnny Depp which is never a bad thing! If you want a bit of madness in your life then read this short novella. Recommended for fans of Mercedes' Lackey's Five Hundred Kingdoms series.

book_a.title: Reckless Magic (Star-Crossed, #1)
book_a.user_review: I love a book that I can pick up and not want to put down; a book that engrosses me and keeps me turning the pages; I love a book that makes me laugh and forget about the world outside. This book does all this and more. It is a book out of the YA genre that is not just for YA's!!! As you might have guessed from the name of the series, think Romeo and Juliet but with magic and high school angst. A thoroughly enjoyable read and looking forward to reading the next 3 in the series.

3.5 stars...

R: Reckless Magic by Rachel Higginson 3.5 Stars 
 Finished 10/8 
 I wanted to absolutely adore this book, especially since it came so highly recommended to me by a friend. And don't get me wrong, I liked it quite a bit. I just didn't love it. Something about the writing really bothered me...the author seemed to conveniently shove things under the rug to explain later even though it really would have been fine and much less irritating to just explain then. And there were a lot of arbitrary things going on, like, "hey, this is how such and such works with the monarchy, and there are absolutely zero decent people who would fight against this." Reckless Magic is also really verbose...and not necessarily in a good way. There were pages where I was like...60% of that was unnecessary. It didn't happen a lot, but it happened some. 
 All of that being said, I did really enjoy reading this book. I've already started the sequel. Here's a summary: "16 year old Eden Matthews has been in and out of private schools for the last two years. Kingsley is her last chance to finish high school and she is determined to simply do that. But when she meets Kiran Kendrick and her world opens to something she thought only existed in fairy tales, she's unsure what her future will hold. Suddenly she is captivated by a boy who seems to be the source of all of her problems and struggling to rescue her best friend from a foreign prison. When attempts are made on Kiran's life, Eden alone must save him. Thrust into a world that is more make-believe than reality, Eden has to find her own destiny without losing those she loves most. Reckless is an intricate story of mystery, adventure, magic and love. Eden Matthews is an unlikely heroine set on a path to save the world and her loved ones before its too late." 
 I really liked Kiran; although it got annoying trying to figure out if he really cared about Eden or if he was just using her. I REALLY liked him by the end though, so that was good. Some of the explanations for things were actually quite interesting and well-thought out. I'm interested where Rachel Higginson takes the sequels.

I liked the story and thought the original mythology was cool and developed some new concepts. But the main character was stubborn to the point where she was illogical. Kirian even says at one point that she has to have things spelled out, that she can't figure anything out for herself. If a normal person would hear the hoofbeats, and not think zebra. She would ignore the hoofbeats entirely and get trampled by the stampede.

book_b.title: Bah, Humbug! (A Christmas Street, #1)
book_b.user_review: A mellow, feel good book about Christmas, children, decorating, cooking and the pain of losing a loved one. It shows how sometimes the ones that don't celebrate Christmas have a reason for it, instead of just being grinch-like.

sample_reviews.review_text: This was my first Heather read and I loved it. I will be reading more by her. Warning: this book is G rated but so much fun. I know some ladies like it steamier but you should give this story a chance.
A short Christmas story. I great length for reading during the holidays. I wouldn't read it again.

Who reads a Christmas love story in summer? 
 Me! 
 Nice and enjoyable Amazon freebie. It's a dreamy "hallmark-ish" love story. Although the fact that they fall in love in a matter of days was too much for me. I'm a hopeless romantic but I would've liked for them to have at least a date. Yes they spend a whole holliday together but not as a couple. I wouldn't have minded a little more romance between them...no, not sex but a little more spark than family ties between them. It's romantic that they knew they were made for each other right away, but it just felt too right away...too perfect. 
 The cover didn't blow me away, would've preferred a snowman on it instead of the cookie, something more relatable to the story. 
 Anyway, I have the whole summer to wonder and imagine what became of Lexi and Kyle...and I can't wait for this year's Christmas, who knows, maybe I can have a love story like Lexi's! Ha!

Even though I read this during the non-holiday season, that snow does not fall here, and that I don't really like 'homemaker shows' (the comparisons with my own abode is frightening!) I truly enjoyed this. 
 Things happened very rapidly (but that wasn't a bad thing) and I suppose I see this as more of an interlude in the protagonists lives. They may well develop something permanent and wonderful and this is the first stage of their journey i.e. I personally think their engagement after knowing each other for a week was way too soon and I hope it's a REALLY long engagement) . 
 Bssically this was a nice quick bedtime read.

There were typos and that drove me a bit nutty, but that isn't why I'm only giving it two stars. It was sweet enough, but the characters fell a little flat to me. They know each other for less than a week, have never even had a date or even kissed! He proposes in this wonderful grand gesture, she says yes. You have kids, woman, use your head.

Published: 09/09/2011 
 Author: Heather Horrocks 
 Recommended for: fan's of romcom stories and novellas 
 Edition: Kindle 
 This is a romantic comedy book written by Heather Horrocks, I found this novella on the Kindle Store for free and so I thought I would give it a go. I thought that this was incredibly well written and is a fun and lighthearted read. It was the type of story that was slightly predictable and with it been a short story the ending (a quick proposal) made it seem like the whole thing was rushed and rather unrealistic. Also with it being a Kindle book there was rather alot of spelling mistakes and grammer problems which lost it a star as it was rather frustrating. It didn't do a very good job at keeping your attention but it was a fun story to read.

Really sweet story 
 I really enjoyed this feel-good holiday story. Light little read for anyone wanting a happy romantic happy ending type tale. It wasn't very comedic but exceptionally sweet with a dose of punches to the emotional feels. 
 My only possibly complaint if I had to pick one is that it wasn't as comedic as I expected or hoped for but still fun and enjoyable. I really liked it!

This is an author I have never read before but I really enjoyed this and plan on reading more of these stories in the future. The characters were all likeable and easy to relate to. There was a lightness and sweetness to the story that made it feel like the holiday and not just a title. 
 Lexi Anderson and her children move onto Christmas Street and they fit right in. Lexi has been touted as the next Martha Stewart and has the television show to prove it. Kyle Miller is an author of a successful series of books who unfortunately finds himself with writers block. When he destroys the snowman of the people next door, thinking it is for him, he finds himself getting in deeper than e expected with his new neighbors. 
 I just found this to be a quick, fun read that had me from the first page. I could not put it down until I finished!
Not my kind of book. Tried it as a quick foray into novellas, will not be doing so again, not enjoyable personally.

I'm glad it was free- I mean, come on. Their first kiss happens after they get engaged? And they don't even date? The day before the proposal she didn't even want to start a family with anyone else? Give me a break.

sample_reviews.review_text:
A delicious romp! 
 finally, a story where the mom doesn't die before the action gets started (a bothersome trope that implies nothing exciting ever happens when moms are around)!

** spoiler alert ** 
 Honestly what spurred me to read this awesome book was getting to meet Cherie Priest at Dragon Con in 2010. That was my first fully submersive experience with Steampunk. So getting to meet someone who not only writes within the genre but truly seems to enjoy it herself made me want to read her books. 
 I have to say that the beginning of the book was a little slow. I had to push myself to continue through the first six chapters or so. The disjointed timeline had a lot to do with that. Jumping from Briar to Zeke and vice-versa made the story hard to follow until I actually figured out that their time-lines don't actually line up. 
 After I figured that out I began to truly enjoy the book. I love Priest's creative restructuring of Seattle's past. The Alternate Antebellum/Civil War time line. I also loved the technology. Some times it feels like Steampunk lit can pull too much from fantasy, but Priest's tinker toys seemed plausible. 
 All-in-all I have to say that I enjoyed this book. I can't wait to read Clementine!

Sixteen years after Leviticus Blue reputedly robbed a string of banks and released the Blight using his drilling machine, the Boneshaker, his son Ezekiel goes back into the walled remains of Seattle, braving rotters and Doornails, to clear his name. His mother, Briar Wilkes, goes into the walled wasteland to bring him out. Can she find Zeke before Dr. Minnericht finds him? 
 I've got mixed feelings about this one. For one thing, the writing doesn't tickle my innards and the characters are all pretty weak. It also feels like it could have been 70 or 80 pages shorter. A steampunk book with zombies and airships shouldn't have so many dull spots. Also, there was a 35 page block missing from my copy but I don't think I missed a whole lot due to the aforementioned pacing issues. Furthermore, Boneshaker is a misleading title since the Boneshaker doesn't make an appearance until the very end. 
 However, I did manage to enjoy myself while reading it. I love the idea of a walled up city infested by zombies as well as the culture of those that stayed behind to live off of what was left, the Doornails. The concept of zombies being created by subterranean pockets of gas was interesting, as was lemon sap, the drug made from said gas. The steampunk tech was nicely done, complete with artificial limbs and a sound cannon. The airships were also good, even if under-utilized. Zeke and Briar's struggle to find one another was well done, even if it dragged for my tastes. Dr. Minnericht was a Darth Vader-ish enemy but the reveal of his identity was pretty good, as was his death. 
 I wouldn't exactly say I'd recommend buying this but if you could find someone to lend it to you, I don't think you'll be very disappointed.

I read this book after watching this Steampunk panel that was hosted by Cory Doctorow, and featured authors Scott Westerfeld and Cherie Priest. I already read (and loved) Westerfeld's Leviathan, so I figured I would give Priest's Boneshaker a read. 
 Although I am glad I read it, because you can never have enough post-apocalyptic/steampunk/zombie books, I did not love it nearly as much as Leviathan, and am unsure whether I will read the next book in this series.
It started a little slow but it was nice to see zombies and steampunk together.

There were a lot of things I liked about the novel. The brown typeface wasn't one of them. 
 It's a big, thick book, and yet each time I sat down to read, I flew through it. Sadly, I was out of town and busy so it appears as if it took me weeks to finish. It's really a surprisingly fast read. 
 I picked it up because it had a lot of components that I intend to put in my own next series. Luckily, the two will be quite different. 
 I liked it. The book wraps up nicely. I'm unclear if it's the start of a series. I'd read on if it were.

Well, I did finish this book so that does bump it up into the two-star range. The story, as predictable as it might be, at least interested me enough to see it through to the end. I found the dialog to be really rather contrived, silly, and downright simplistic at times. I get that these are hard-bitten, simple, rough people living on the frontier, faced with deadly gas and zombies... but really, the dialog could have seen a better effort. Nice to see more books showing up in the Steampunk genre, but this is a poor entry.

The story was very bland for me. The progression was obvious and I didn't like any of the characters. I couldn't connect with them so it was difficult to care what happened to them. It felt like I was reading a bad soap opera. The world building was surprisingly good, but that's about it.

I don't know if it's quite the "steampunk magnum opus" that the author was intending, but it's at least a "good work" (does anyone know the Latin for that?). It's a more realistic take on the genre, which probably makes it easier for critics to look at it as serious literature, but I'm not sure that serious literature is what I want from my steampunk. 
 Boneshaker is set in a world where a mad scientist built a steampunk digging machine (called the "boneshaker") that somehow released a bunch of zombie gas into central Seattle. The good people of Seattle walled off those neighborhoods, and mostly ignore it. Mostly. There are determined blimp captains who mine the gas, there are some desperate scavengers who are still sifting through the rubble, and there are some stubborn survivors who never left. 
 ...and then there's Ezikiel Blue, the scientists son, who enters the area is search of clues about his father. 
 ...and Biar Wilkes, his mother, who sets off to rescue her son. 
 The point-of-view shifts between Ezikiel and Blue. Both of them have realistic personalities (by which I mean they both do believably stupid things) and it's fun to read about their interactions with the various colourful inhabitants of the "Blight". 
 It's less fun to read about them running from zombies and fiddling with gas masks, which they do a lot. They're probably running through interesting parts of Seattle, but I don't know Seattle well enough to appreciate this. Still, it's a pretty good novel, overall, and I'll check out the sequels one of these days.

Due to a test of a machine that has gone horribly wrong, Seattle of the 1880s has become a walled city because of a gas that turns people into zombies. The wife of the inventor of the machine fights to get back into the city, because her teen-aged son has broken in to find proof that his father is innocent. 
 Really had trouble with this book, since I didn't buy into the central conceit of the story, that a mysterious gas called The Blight has been released that turns those who breathe it into zombies, and that it shows no signs of ever abating. Not only am I not interested in the current fad of zombies, but the whole idea is totally unlikely and given no context. I am totally able to suspend disbelief given the right situation, but this didn't work for me. Since that was most of the motivation throughout the story, it was extremely hard to get into the overall adventure as well. Would have worked better if there was some other motivating story device. (Tho, this is one of the most cited of the SteamPunk genre, and is highly recommended by professional writers and such, so what do I know.)

book_b.title: Trapped (The Iron Druid Chronicles, #5)
book_b.user_review: I was super excited and very impatient for the newest Iron Druid book Trapped by Kevin Hearne to come out, and I wasn't disappointed. It gave us even more back story and mythos of the world, along with new mythological groups and lots of action. I did not mind the 12 year break between the last one, though it is hard to put it that far in the future, as the daily lives of your average person does not seem that different than now, and 12 years is a lot of advancement in the modern world, IMO. But loved it anyway.

sample_reviews.review_text: Another winner starring druid Atticus, his faithful canine companion, Oberon (who gets all the best lines), and Atticus's apprentice, Granuaile. Loki the mischief-maker has escaped his prison, Ragnanok is about to break loose, and the Roman god Bacchus wants revenge - there's never a dull moment.

I did like this one. It seemed a little over the top at times, mashing Irish, Slavic, Norse, and now Greco-Roman mythologies into one. Everyone seems to want this guy dead, and sometimes I agree with them. He's really annoying at times. Doesn't quite pull off Harry Dresden's smart alecky style with awesome capability. I felt there were far too many story lines to follow, maybe because I missed a story in there somewhere, but the whole part at the end could have been in a different book. It seemed rather rushed. 
 But as I said, I liked it; it was entertaining. Oberon the Irish Wolfhound is my favorite character, but I'm starting to like Granuwaile (or however you spell her name) a lot too. I'm glad that she's now a Druid, so maybe she can give Atticus what-for when he needs it now. 
 Still disagree that this is in the same league as Butcher and the Dresden series--that bar is pretty high--but it's not bad for what it is. I do enjoy learning more about myths that I'm less familiar with, too.

Still a fun read, but this book had less focus and far more meandering around for not very clear reasons then previous installments. After twelve years of relatively peaceful existence, Atticus and friends are once again thrown into a situation where it seems that everyone wants to kill him. Unlike previous books, here I felt no really clear picture of what the plot for this particular book wanted to be. I am also getting a little bit frustrated with the lack of in depth characterization of people other then Atticus. It may be difficult to add much new background and character to the multitude of Gods who show up, but Grainne at least deserves some personal details other then "hot red head who wants to be a druid." I will keep reading the series but I admit that I had to struggle a bit to wade through the middle sections of this particular book and I hope that the series ultimately returns to more tightly plot driven narratives.
Yes!! *fistpumps* Atticus finally admits he loves Granuille in this one. So far I think this is my favorite in the series.
While I enjoy Attic us, the Iron Druid series is just getting a bit too gonzo. So maybe a bit less on him besting gods, and a but more Oberon.

Wish I could give these books more than 5 stars. Such a great writer! I have learned so much mythology. I read a lot, so when I have to do some research of my own to enjoy these books more deeply. They have opened me up to more art; music, dance, photography and paintings. I've always said, 'read everything, explore a variety of subjects, and keep up with pop-culture (watch tv and movies), then you will understand the references and get the joke.'
A worthwhile read, taking place just over a decade after the first book, this installment offers the comeuppance readers hoped for after the Iron Druid tore apart the Norse pantheon.
Another brilliant book by Kevin Hearne.

Everything has consequences! That is what Atticus keeps being reminded of in the 5th volume of the Iron Druid series. He is trying to finish the training of his apprentice, but keeps running into roadblocks. He works his way out of one problem only to have two others smack him in the face. The book does not end so much as flow into the next volume which I will have to wait for. An enjoyable update to the series. Finished it on St. Patrick's Day (sort of appropriate).

Trapped left me rather disappointed. It felt less a novel and more two short stories woven together, without complete success. The end of the book came as a surprise, as the climax wasn't exactly as climactic as I would have expected. Ultimately, the book seems a couple stepping stones to the next that might have been done better independently.

reference_books.review_text: A man with little to live for in one part of London decides to become one with a fantastical part of London. I found Fortunately the Milk and The Graveyard Book more enthralling.

reference_books.review_text: Reading the first chapter, it felt like a good albeit interesting start. By the time I got to chapter six, I skipped to the end. Yep, I'm not missing a whole lot.

Seriously though, you almost think the author wants you to make this into a movie, but no screenwriter would dare try to wade through all the nonsense.
