You can have pretentious and unlikeable characters, but I hoped to like them more at the end of the story.

reference_books.title: The Language of Flowers
reference_books.review_text: It wasn't bad, but it wasn't exactly compelling either. I could only get to page 20 before I had to skip to the end section. Thank goodness, I was tired of the mess of this focusing more on flowers than her actual life.

book_a.title: My Lady Jane (The Lady Janies, #1)
book_a.user_review: I don't know what to say with all the references. You need all your fingers and toes, and your friend's hands and toes, for the comical references. Nothing completely hilarious, but there was genuine interesting parts.

sample_reviews.review_text: This book was pretty good, and I did enjoy parts of it. I really felt the Princess Bride vibe that it gave off, but I wasn't really loving the characters. I found myself caring about everyone else more than Jane. Overall, it was a pretty good read, just a little lacking in my opinion.

This is a hard book to review because it really is strange. I read this while in London, which made things extra interesting, and really did enjoy it. 
 That said, I was very disappointed with how one-dimensional the portrayal of Mary Tudor was, as it just reinforces the shallow view of Mary = the worst, Elizabeth I = the best, which I am not a fan of. Both women had their good and bad points and Mary deserved better than this book gave her. As such, what could have been a 4 star review has been dropped to 3. 
 But I still recommend it for anyone who thinks they would enjoy a good defenestration experiment with historical fact going mostly out the window.

I read this for book club and sort of hated it. 
 A narration that absolutely jarred me out of the...well, narrative. 
 Poorly explained anachronisms that did same. 
 Trying to break the 4th wall. Books suck at that. 
 Nutshell: If you're going to write a historical fantasy (totally my type of genre), maybe plot it to fit the timeline.

This book had a little of everything in it. History, fantasy, a good bit of humor, however I feel let down. I wanted to love this story, with it having a good plot and a satisfying ending, but yet I feel conflicted about giving it a higher rating! I'm chalking it up to the sometimes annoying narration. Maybe, my expectation for this book were too high, but I feel it could've been better.

UPDATE 10/4/16: My rating went down a star because I can't stop thinking about the book's reference to the Shakespeare authorship debate. Yes, the debate bugs me that much. 
 * 
 Ehhhhhhhhhh. 
 I thought I was going to be ecstatic about this book. Then I found out that it's a comedy, and I thought I was going to be disappointed. Then I heard so many glowing reviews that I was ecstatic again. Now I've finished it and I'm disappointed. 
 I love the story of Lady Jane Grey. English nobles don't get much more tragic, do they? Married off to a social climber, set on the throne against her will, imprisoned, and beheaded. I'm kind of uncomfortable with the idea of her story being made into... this fantastic romp through English history and 21st-century pop culture. 
 It's not that I think history is off-limits for reinterpretation and imagination and comedy! I love all those things. Give me all the Hamiltons. Give me all the Dunk Histories. Give them to me! Just don't give me this. 
 My problem with My Lady Jane is that I think that this particular story is strongest for what it is: a deeply tragic tale of a girl who did the best she could under the strangest of circumstances. If you won't give me that, then why not give me a story of three interconnected women of formidable strength: Lady Jane, Queen Mary, and the future Queen Elizabeth? All three of them show up, but Bess and Mary are woefully underused. If you won't give me Mary and Elizabeth, then why not show me more of the low-born female characters? Why wasn't this book about Gracie, the shapeshifting Scottish pickpocket on the run from bandits? That would have been a cool story, and the courtly drama could have provided an excellent backdrop. 
 As it is, this book lacks the drama that the original story had. It's funny, yes, it's cute, yes, but it's so much more fluffy than I would have liked. I knew I was going to have a problem with it early on when the English Reformation was changed into a conflict between people who can turn into animals and... people who hate people who can turn into animals. It's just... not the same thing as a religious schism, is it? It simply wasn't enough to drive the plot. Why does everyone care so much about who can turn into an animal? Because religious tensions aren't fun and turning into animals is fun. I get it. But it makes for a paper-thin plot. 
 Basically, so many pages of this book might as well have "FOR FUN" scrawled across them in red ink. There's no better explanation for anything that happens. Why does everyone keep quoting Monty Python? For fun! Why is everyone so easily able to hide Edward's escape? For fun! Why do he and G have to go kill an evil bear that has never been mentioned until this point three-quarters of the way through the book? For fun! Why does G write poetry? For fun! Why do the narrators tell us that people could die in the climactic battle, even though it's obvious that everyone will live? FOR FUN! 
 Maybe my sense of humour has gone too black. Maybe I'm being too pretentious. But I'm definitely not the right person for this book. Still giving it three stars for being an entertaining read, and because OMG A BOOK ABOUT LADY JANE GREY - but I wish it had been something else entirely.

"Dedication: 
 For everyone who knows there was enough room for Leonardo DiCaprio on that door. 
 And for England. We're really sorry for what we're about to do to your history." 
 Fav quote: 
 "Armies aren't very good about carrying libraries with them. I can't imagine why. We'd fight so much less if everyone would just sit down and read" 
 This (not) entirely true story of Lady Jane Grey that, co-authors Cynthia Hand, Brodi Ashton, and Jodi Meadows have created is seriously a one-of-a-kind fantasy. 
 I had just come out of reading a contemporary and I was in the mood for something historical but that would be light hearted and this hit just the spot. 
 Honestly My Lady Jane was not what I expected but was also pleasantly surprised by this amazing twist on historical facts. 
 I mean if you were sixteen and about to be married off to a stranger and caught up in a conspiracy to rob your cousin, THE KING, of his throne and on top of that about to become the Queen of England. I mean I would probably be having anxiety attacks every 5 seconds. 
 That's why I loved about Jane's character she's so smart and knows so much about the world through her books and that's the point, she's smart and knows so much about the world but she's never actually experienced it and it was lovely to see her realization of that through Guildford and how he started to realize things through her and even if their relationship started off a bit rocky you could always see how much they cared and it was adorable. 
 The different POV's were so fun and I was laughing throughout the whole book and I loved how these 3 authors blended so well together to create this story where they just you know, throw history out the window and tell the story they would of wanted to see; at that point in time while at the same time giving us actual facts, information and anecdotes on the pages to let the reader know what the hell is going on during that period in time and in their fictional story as well. 
 The fantasy aspect of the story was the part I wasn't expecting and I don't usually read fantasy but this so entertaining and well thought out The Edians (eth-y-un) who have two different forms, human and animal and henceforth should enjoy the same rights and privileges as Verities who don't. I kind of got the whole Protestants and Catholics feel from the tension between the two groups. It didn't feel forced and I would love to imagine that as what actually happens in history. 
 Overall I really enjoyed this and if these 3 authors ever wrote another book I would love to read it.

I have read a ton of historical fiction set in this time period, but this is up there with my favorites. book_b.title: Will Grayson, Will Grayson
book_b.user_review:
Figuring that it took me nearly two months to complete, I want to give it a solid One and a half stars. It doesn't really draw me in, and the lowercase Will Grayson constant deprecating left little to be desired. If you read the book out loud, you would notice how often "I say" or "I ask" pops up in reference to a statement or question. Throwing dialogue around doesn't give any indication of depth in character; furthermore, I doubt teenagers would seriously be educated enough to understand Schoedinger's cat even if it is on Wikipedia. 
 There is also too much general philosophical statements being stated by the characters. Lowercase Will Grayson's mom wanting to talk, suggesting prescriptions in lieu of talking, and not having a grip of her son's social behavior are seriously why I want to question what the authors think is the purpose of parents in a story. I could have stopped at anytime reading the book after my initial stop on page 11 and gathered that the end would be how it ends. 
 No, I would not recommend this book to anyone because it doesn't inspire me. It is a very deadpan book, and I don't want anyone getting their hopes up.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I hope that both of these Will Graysons died shortly after. 
 One thing this book has taught me: Stay away from anything written by David Levithan. He doesn't know what a capital letter is.

Will Grayson, Will Grayson happens to be a book. I thoroughly enjoyed because of all the comical aspects. It gives a great message to lgbt youth; as well as, those who are shy. It gives both sides. One Will is gay and the other Will is straight. One is off the radar and the other wants to be off the radar. I love how their personality's are very stagnant until once they meet at Frenchys. I love the ending when Tiny finally gets the recognition he deserves from everyone.

I've had Will Grayson, Will Grayson sitting on my bookshelf for about 2 years. I finally decided to read it. The description looked interesting, two boys with the same name meeting. The book is written by two different authors. They each write as their own Will Grayson. David Levithan's WG is the depressed teenage who hates the world. I feel Levithan went a little overboard when he wrote this character. That WG is too moody, and has an 'I hate the world attitude.' We've all been teens and have gone through that phase. I read Nick & Norah's Infinite Playlist, also by Levithan, and parts of Will Grayson, Will Grayson resembled that book. For example, when Jane, Tiny, and WG attend a secret concert of their favorite band (turns out to be a different band), that was so much like Nick & Norah's Infinite Playlist. I noticed a small slip up in the book. Levithan's WG has his friend Maura come to his home. He says they go to the garage to talk and he lets her out through the garage door. A few chapters later, Tiny visits Levithan's WG and WG makes the comment that he's ashamed to have Tiny see that he lives in an apartment. I live in Texas and our apartments do not have garages, except the expensive luxury ones. 
 Green's WG started dating this girl Jane, but the romance just feels forced throughout the whole book. The ending of the book was okay. I didn't get that great feeling of having finished it, but I did.
I found it disappointing, to be honest. The storyline didn't appeal to me much... It was really boring.

While this novel was a bit frustrating at times, I have to admit that it was frustrating in a good way. There was a lot of teen angst in the mix which was occasionally annoying, but Green and Levithan use it to allow the characters to have epiphanies about themselves and life in general which did resonate with me. I have quite a few quotations from the book written down, which is always a good thing! Overall, not stellar, but not a waste of time.

I liked this book. I thought it was good and written very well, but for some reason I just personally couldn't get into it. I felt like I kept waiting for me to be super interested in it, and before I knew it the book was over. I do have to admit, though, that it is a bit hard to get used to reading every other chapter in all lower case letters. It's definitely a good read, and I recommend it to anyone looking for a John Green fix, but it just wasn't quite the right book for me.

I really liked this novel. I found that I really enjoyed John Green. I've heard a lot about him and I figured I'd give him a try, the fact that I found a novel by him and my favorite author was simply icing on the cake. I'm always nervous to start a David Levithan novel because you never know if it going to change your life. This book was not earth shattering but it was still an extremely interesting read and made me smile. 
 The characters were outrageous. Tiny was hilarious and irritating at the same time. I wanted to hug him and punch him. Will Grayson (1st Will Grayson) was an interesting guy. I found him annoying yet lovable and realistic. will grayson(2nd Will Grayson) was an interesting read. You don't get the characters when they are in the middle of everything. You get a character who is struggling with the onset of depression but never the character who has it and is just living with it. 
 I found myself really entertained with this novel. I am definitely glad that I read this novel and I will definitely look into John Green.

Cuando uno lee a John Green y a David Levithan por separado lo ultimo en lo que piensa es que dos estilos tan diferentes puedan coexistir en una misma novela sin que esta sea un desastre. Pero ambos autores encontraron la formula perfecta (la formula que utiliza siempre Levithan en sus novelas a cuatro manos), que consiste en que cada uno de los autores da voz a un personaje. De este modo, la historia es explicada por dos narradores en primera persona con dos voces tan diferentes como sus propias personalidades. 
 WILL GRAYSON, WILL GRAYSON me ha sorprendido sobre todo por el trasfondo de la historia. Al principio me parecio que iba a ser una historia de dos adolescentes que casualmente comparten nombre y apellido y que llegan a juntarse gracias a un amigo en comun. Cual fue mi sorpresa al comprender que los dos Will casi no coinciden en la historia, y que el verdadero protagonista iba a ser Tiny Cooper, ese personaje tan excentrico y que tantas risas -y sonrisas- consiguio arrancarme. 
 Sin duda, recomiendo la lectura de WILL GRAYSON, WILL GRAYSON a todo aquel que quiera una historia sobre la amistad y como la valora cada uno. Escrita por los que son, en mi opinion, dos de los mejores escritores de literatura juvenil de hoy en dia, la novela ahonda en dos personajes que, a pesar de compartir nombre, no podrian ser mas diferentes.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I finished this book because it was a quick read and I was interested in the mystery of what happened to the main character's sister and husband. I enjoyed Where'd You Go Bernadette, except for a couple of timing pieces in the plot that I couldn't get over. I enjoyed the writing style and thought this one might be enjoyable as well (and might not have the flaws). I was wrong. The main character is annoying and the mystery turned out blah for me. 
 I don't think I will look for another of her books.

I enjoyed this, largely because Semple has a way of playing with words or ways we see the world that turns them on their head so they can be seen a new way. That's an incredible skill. I also appreciate a self aware, self-deprecating protagonist/narrator. However, this story goes a little off the rails partway through, gets very complicated with multiple timelines, and the self-aware meta critique of the narrator disappears as she gets more and more reckless. I have to meditate some more on whether this was intentional, but for me it made the second half of the book a bit let enjoyable and messier.
I have found myself saying "smell the soup, cool the soup" the past week! :)
I enjoyed Where'd You Go Bernadette, so I was expecting something in the same vein. This was random, erratic, and a complete snooze.

This book felt like a whirlwind! Definitely worth a read, but lacking some of the humor/charm of Semple's "Where'd You Go Bernadette?" In particular, I think one of Semple's comedic strengths is crafting absolutely ridiculous wealthy people. Selfishly, I hope her next novel has more of them.

I really enjoyed this novel and found it to be fast paced and engaging. Maria Semple has a bold writing style and takes her quirky cast of characters in unexpected directions. 
 I recommend reading this one in print, as it contains a graphic novel that I do not believe could translate well into the audio version.

My mistake was having high expectations for another Maria Semple novel. I adored Where'd You Go, Bernadette and was hoping for another great story to that same caliber. Today Will Be Different was terrible. It was like a knock off version of Bernadette but none of the characters were endearing or quirky in a good way. I definitely do not recommend this book and will make today and every other day different by pretending it was never written.

I found this book by serendipitous happenstance. I was out for a run on a route that has a Tiny Library. I stopped to look inside--as I usually do--and lo and behold, I found a brand new copy of a book by one of my favorite authors. Hallah! 
 Semple has this way of writing characters that really speak to my own thought processes, insecurities, and anxieties. I loved the characters in this book--so quirky and written in a way that I connected with. The story line was a bit convoluted that calls for a reread now that I know where the story goes.

Maria Semple (who was a writer for Arrested Development, which certainly comes through in quirky funniness) has a lock on the middle-aged dis-likable Seattle mother who pines for more elsewhere. 
 While not as solid throughout as her previous novel, Where'd You Go Bernadette?, there's still a lot of awkward interactions, self doubt, comedic mystery, and groan-inducing cringe moments in TWBD. 
 It's a mom who used to be defined by her career, then derailed by internal family strife, now lacking in identity, who sets out to try to change things in her life and we follow her through that day - far from what she had expected at the start. It's slapstick and painful and easy enough to read, just don't be looking for much and you'll enjoy it.

DNF on page 87. 
 "Today will be different," declares Eleanor Flood. She wakes up and decides to be polite: spend time with her son, have sex with her husband. Of course you know that today won't be different, but anyway, so begins this book. 
 Zzzzz... 
 It's interesting that even the author calls this book what it really is on page 7: "a normal day of white people problems." It helps to know that even the author knows her character is complete bullshit: a rich doctor's wife with too much time on her hands, grudging time with her son, her dog, her husband, pretty much everyone around her. It begins somewhat funny, but it declines into one a really bad joke. A book trying to be witty when it isn't. Bleh. 
 And oh yeah, the plot is all over the place. Between learning about the main character's long lost sister, her husband's secret, her dysfunctional childhood, her former career as an artist--you just don't care about what else is going to be thrown in during the course of one day in poor, rich Eleanor Flood's life. I wouldn't mind this clusterfuck so much if it were not for the fact that she's not even a likable person--she's ridiculously self absorbed, uninteresting, and obnoxious while pretending to be friends with people. 
 Perhaps other people find this book amusing, which is why it's on the NYT Bestseller list. I normally don't read books on the list though. I'd feed this book to wolves.

sample_reviews.review_text: I tend to like books written by strong women, but I struggled to get into this one. I got through the first few chapters and then it became more work than enjoyment to finish reading it. I'm not sure what they want the takeaway to be? If you decide to crack it open you can expect lots of real and unfiltered stories, but no real point or conclusion to any of the conversations that are started.

I was really disappointed by "Not That Kind of Girl". I loved books like "Bossypants", and I enjoy Dunham's HBO show "Girls", so I thought this would be a funny, interesting window into her life, creativity, and success. It ends up Dunham is either exactly like the main character of her show, Hannah Horvath, or she's not really ready to let down the curtain between her persona and her true person. The memoir's writing feels very contrived and studied, and yet at the same time the organization of the book makes no sense at all. She has it separated into parts like "Love & Sex", "Friendship", etc. but everything sort of seems to meld together, repeat, and ultimately make its way back to sex or bodily functions. If someone who did not know Dunham's real-life story read this memoir, they would assume she was a lazy, neurotic hipster who was self-indulgent and spoiled by her parents, and most likely still occupying her childhood bedroom and working at a coffee shop. They would not assume she was a successful young woman with her own popular TV show, feature films, multiple Emmys, and two Golden Globes. Dunham hardly mentions any of those parts of her and only flippantly mentions ambition once or twice. It's ultimately a puzzle to me why she would rather discuss her tonsil stones than, perhaps, her creative goals or development as a filmmaker and writer or really anything besides a bunch of stories that paint her in a fairly negative light. It's almost like she likes putting a certain group of people off, like there's a security in coming off as always self-deprecating and slightly inept. Read more at www.iwantmichikosjob.com.

SUCH A DISSAPOINTMENT! I love Lena Dunham and her show "Girls" so I had high hopes for this book. Unfortunately, it was a total let down. I couldn't even finish it because I could no longer stand her trivial essays. One essay, recalling her online relationship with a Russian boy named Igor was particularly dreadful. Most of her essays seemed to have no real impact her life, just non-funny experiences she had growing up. I could not relate to anything Lena had to say, which is sad because I look up to her as a feminist. But this book was just no good in my eyes. 
 Again, I am so sad to give this book such a poor review. Maybe one day I'll give it another shot... But for now, 1 star :/

I had to change my review to "2" stars after I asked myself: if I had no prior knowledge of a Lena Dunham, never watched Girls, and picked up this book purely as a book to read, what would I think? While this book fits nicely into the Lena Dunham brand that I appreciate: quirky, wry and narcissistic, as a stand alone piece of literature it doesn't really add up. 
 The author has no real struggle beyond the issues in her own head. She even says as one point, if she had been molested as a child it would explain all her mental health problems. She was raised in privilege. So, for me, I don't understand or sympathise with her on that level. It's like her persona had to make up mental health issues because she was dealt such an easy life and she needed something to set her apart. 
 When she describes wild nights out and thrift shop clothes I like it. Her nerdy obsessions with music and books are relatable. Her very brief insights to people in Hollywood were entertaining, as was most of the sexual encounters she describes. Her voice is amusing, but as I said, is it funny because I read her as Hannah in Girls, or funny because it's an original voice in literature? 
 Miss Dunham is only three years younger than I and maybe I'm a narcissist but I think I could put a spin on my own life's adventures just as well as her. There is nothing unique about her life as described in this book, despite having a TV show, which she doesn't really detail getting or working on. 
 As much as I like her, I have realised in the future when someone picks up this book with no prior knowledge of who she was, they won't find this book particularly illuminating in any way. Unless you grew up privileged in Manhattan with artist parents and attended private schools and summer camps, the vast majority of people will not be able relate.

I just don't get it. 
 I know I've seen this book everywhere with everyone reading it. 
 I thought I was going to pull the hairs out on my arm for more entertainment than this. 
 Let's just say that I get it - I'm a totally different person than Lena Dunham. We have different up bringing, we have different ways to approach life situations - & apparently we have different outlooks & values in life. Maybe I'm just a prude. Half of the book, I'm shaking my head at the language & the stories & the other half, I was just sort of bored. 
 I don't get what all the huff is about. 
 I'm totally disappointed.
I'm quitting 60% through. Nothing so far has been interesting or even funny. If fact it's been pretty gross or depressing even though se doesn't seem to want it to be.

PLEASE DO NOT READ THIS BOOK. 
 Okay, I got that out of the way. 
 Lena Dunham is a smart chick. She knows how to spin a good story and make people laugh. However, this is the most self-indulgent piece of garbage I have ever read. I disliked almost every one of her anecdotes. She isn't old enough (and hasn't experienced enough) to write something of substance. While she has had a few struggles in her life--the account of her rape had chills running down my spine, and was the only thing in the entire book that struck a chord with me--for the most part, she comes off as a whiney, narcissistic, upper-middle-class, privileged girl (yes, EXACTLY THAT KIND OF GIRL). Reading this was like watching a train wreck; I couldn't put it down because I was waiting to see what new horror was around the next corner. 
 In retrospect, I am not surprised that everyone who recommended this book to me was under the age of 21. I am not knocking the younger generation; they just haven't had the life experience to know that this kind of "memoir" doesn't have much to it.
I don't get it
I liked the last chapter...THAT... IS...IT!

I am saddened that I can't give this book a -100 star rating. It's horrible. Lena Dunham sounds like a horrible human being who tortured her parents from the time she learned to speak, and sexually abused her sister. I now understand why hamsters sometimes eat their babies. If Dunham was a hamster her mother's instincts would have kicked in and she would have realized that there was something terribly wrong with her baby and chomped her head off immediately. Aside from being a sexual predator, she slept with any man that would have her, pretended to sleep with some who wouldn't (like her imaginary internet boyfriend who had to fake death to get away from her.), she is a hypochondriac...or the most sickly person in the world..., and an obsessive compulsive. I am a number one Margaret Atwood fan, and I was so excited to hear that she had a new novel coming out. Well, to say that I'm extremely disappointed would be an understatement to say the least. I just couldn't get into this uneven novel -- I didn't care for the characters and I just didn't get the plot (was it farce? was it parody? I have no idea). Perhaps I want another Handmaid's Tale. I don't know.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This is a hard book to get into. Obviously it was written as a series of shorter stories, so there are clear demarcations between each section, and it can get hard to keep tabs on the passage of time. I can't really say I enjoyed this much. I liked the premise, that the recession of 2008 was much worse than it actually was, and resulted in some sort of semi-apocalyptic United States. But it was hard to connect with any of the characters. Stan is clearly the more sympathetic of the two main characters. Charmaine is written with a vaguely sociopathic bent. She's clearly had some sort of trauma in her past, and her recurring theme of Grandma Win provides intriguing monologue, but she's shallow, and admits as much. Side characters are fairly one-dimensional, with the exception of Aurora, who gets a nice backstory. I think The Heart Goes Last suffers from being too many things, with the main story not being the interesting one. I wanted to learn more about the Positron/Consilience program, the outrageous things happening there. By the end of the book, I really didn't care if Stan and Charmaine found their way back to each other, despite it being clear that they would. And after building up Stan as a fairly good guy, Atwood ruins it by making it seem like he was ok with Charmaine getting the surgery to implant on him. And then that random twist at the end, what was the point of that? It's so unsatisfactory. 
 tl;dr: good premise, shallow characters, frustrating ending.
I'm sad to say I got about 50 pages though this book and gave up. I just couldn't get into it. So disappointed.

This one reminds me of it, with the speculative science fiction and weird sexual overtones. So if you liked that series you will probably like this. I loved it. I thought it was hilarious and it makes you think about social implications and ethics in sciences and technology. Reminded me of "More Happy than Not, but I won't say why to avoid spoilers. 
 The first Atwood book I read was "The Handmaids Tale" I didn't really like it at the time, but I think I now want to read it again now that I "get " her writing.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Oh lord below, just let me survive the slog through this book so I can eventually get to the next one (which Goodreads people *promise* me is good - or at least tolerable). Maybe less rape, dick-talk from Negan and hand-wringing from the generic fools who populate this world. 
 Seriously, you've survived *years* among the walkers, biters and moaners, and you *still* don't have sense enough to keep your head down and one eye over your shoulder EVERY DAMNED WAKING MOMENT? You *deserve* to die, Stupid Nameless Background Character #473 - there is no zombie-apocalypse earth on which you earned the right to eat the last of the organic carrots. 
 There are plenty of Dramatic Moments of Culmination - at least, that's the way they're played, even though I couldn't be bothered to even try to remember who any of these extras are. Deathbed hand-wringing, stand-up speechifying, meaningful glares and sidelong glances...it's all sturm und drang with no cliff walls from which to echo balefully. 
 The inevitable stand-off and stand-down occurs (Because Rick), and then this book just takes a leap of writer's ego and terror that I CANNOT condone: Rick spares Negan's life, because "we're better than that". 
 Here's the deal: murderous pieces of shit need to die, to preserve the herd. You leave a diseased fish in the tank, they all gonna perish. Spoiled apple, there goes the barrel o' monkeys. Ripe banana? Separate it from the others, lest you have ten pounds of black cigars on your hands. 
 What. The. Fuck. Does Kirkman think he's pulling, keeping that turd in play? There is only one reason to keep a character like that - not because the readers like him, or he's necessary for some dramatic outcome later on. No, he's alive only because Kirkman is too lazy to come up with a *novel* threat to the humans. Every other scene where this kind of outcome is threatened, we get rid of the rot. This dude lives so that Kirkman can pull him out later and get a cheap jump scare, and some lazy drama. 
 Fuuuuuck that. I see you coming Kirkman, and I will continue to read your shitty books for free whenever they show up at the library shelves. (Oh sure, I'll keep reading this - it's a sport for me to crap on Kirkman twice a year. Like one of my favourite holidays.)

Rick is pissing me off. And it feels like I've read this volume before because it's so repetitive. 
 SPOILERS BELOW 
 What is the fucking point of this war if it's not to kill Negan? Rick finally has the perfect opportunity to kill this monster and he decides now it's time to be civilized? What the fuck Rick? I can't believe Rick thinks Negan will be reasonable. Hasn't he learned based off his experiences with The Governor and the cannibals and every other shitty cruel person that sometimes people can't be reasoned with? They need to die in order for Rick and his people to be safe.... I just can't believe Rick would ever let someone as terrible as Negan go. They way he killed Glenn... He deserves to die for that alone. Rick is becoming too soft and I hate to say it but I agree with Carl. They need to kill Negan to stay alive. At the end when Rick says he wants to watch him rot in a jail cell.. Like what's the difference? Killing him would be better than letting him rot in a jail cell and wasting food and resources on him. I just can't! I don't know what's happening to Rick... 
 I gave this one 2 stars because I did like how Negan's people covered their weapons in zombie blood so that everyone who got injured gets infected and dies. That's brilliant and I don't know why nobody ever thought of doing that before.
Stupid ass decision Rick made in the end. I have a feeling it will come back to bite him. For once I was on Carl's side. This was decent. Can't wait to see what the next one holds.

The Walking Dead has become so repetitive and mundane that after I finished reading this volume I realized I hadn't actually read All Out War, Part I and it made no difference whatsoever. I read this mindless, lumbering series out of habit but I should really stop.

I think I'm done. It's a shame, I keep kicking at the dirt, trying to make this series do something for me again, but it's gotten tedious. I thought the events of this one, once they finally came, would perk the series back up, but we've sunk even further into stupidity now. 
 Which is a real shame. because coating the weaponry with zombie nastiness in order to infect people faster was a really brilliant plan. I can't wait to tell my friend Mike, who watches the show but hasn't read the comics. He's going to totally dig it. 
 But Negan, this big bad motherfucker who we have been waiting to die for so. damn. long. god. get on with it. We finally get him down on the ground, this murderer, rapist, everythinger. And we're going to be fluffy kittens about it? 
 Really? 
 REALLY RICK?! ARE YOU FUCKING KIDDING ME. 
 I'm not going to stick around and wait for this idiotic plan to fall apart. I'm just not. I'm done.

I read volumes 18 - 21 back to back and really enjoyed this section of the story. Negan is a disgusting villain and I hated reading his scenes. But you're supposed to hate the villain so that just made me more anxious to see how things would play out. 
 I loved how old characters were pushed to their limits and stepped into new roles. I loved how new characters shook things up. I can't wait to see this play out on the show. It was a great end to this story arc and sets up the next. It's not about zombies anymore. I'm so interested to see where the survivors can go from here and if they will restore some semblance of civilization.

*2.5-ish* 
 As another reader pointed out, Kirkman painted himself into a corner with Negan. Too smart, too vicious, and too well-organized, Negan is a formidable adversary for Rick's people. That's why we have so many issues of him repeatedly getting the upper-hand. 
 But Rick is the hero and must succeed, so... 
 But does the core group ::coughRickcough:: always need to be in the spotlight? Can't we give some of the new people a moment to shine? It would've been more satisfying and believable to have Dwight step forward, assassinate Negan, and take over. Instead, Rick convinces Negan with the powers of Optimism! and Logic! that working together would be The Bestest Thing Ever. What. I...huh? Like Negan would switch philosophies on a dime? As if he would suddenly abandon his hatred for Rick? And then we slice him and yell WAR'S OVER! So. Much. No. 
 Kirkman's chosen fix is weak. It's illogical. It's done for drama and tension, yet inevitably falls flat. There was another option available that - while perhaps equally anti-climactic - would've made much more sense in the context of the story. Not to mention it would've been truer to the characters involved. 
 The next volume needs to be captivating, because this one has me seriously wondering if Kirkman has any long-term plan in mind.

Oh Rick. When the bad guys plan is better than yours, I smack my head. But this... The war happens and it ends with me thinking, "Really? Because every possible conclusion does not point to this bullshit ending. It's not possible. What is Rick's real plan?!" Then, it's over. 
 Oh Jesus.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Can't give this a full 5 stars because Negan wasn't killed. I think its a huge mistake that will come back to bite them in the ass later on. I get that Rick wants to be civil and all. But I still think it's a bad idea to let Negan live. I still love Rick more than anything, but haven't we been here before? Let a bad guy live, and they will most definitely be a problem again sooner or later.

So much action in this volume and I am happy with the end of this sequence. Of course, this is The Walking Dead so it's not going to stay peaceful for long. 
 5 out of 5 stars!

Life is just to short to be finishing bad books. What. Great start to 2015.

So this is the first book in a new series by Evanovich that follows Wulf and Diesel. As people may remember these characters were seen in the "in between numbers" Stephanie Plum books. But there are no other people that are seen in Wicked Appetite. 
 The premise of the book, Diesel is trying to stop his evil cousin Wulf from doing naughty things. Wulf's new scheme is to find what are called "The Stones" (no joke lol), and they represent the Seven Deadly Sins. Diesel is trying to stop Wulf from acquiring the stone of Gluttony. The other main character is named Lizzie. And she is also an unmentionable (like Diesel and Wulf). She's not sure what her ability is and when she first encounters both cousins she is suspicious of both. There's also a cast of animal characters and rather amusing side characters with strange behaviors and "collections". You just have to read it to understand. 
 I gave this one three stars, but in reality it does not compare to the Plum series. The characters, while funny, felt very similar to many characters that are seen in Stephanie's world. Lizzie seemed like a lesser replica of Steph and Diesel was Morelli and Wulf was a badder version of Ranger. It was a nice read that can hold me over while waiting for the next Plum book but it wasn't fantastic. 
 I'll still read the next book, but this is a series I won't be investing in financially.

Writing was flat, reading was sluggish and I often found myself pushing to keep reading, and story had no sense of mystery but instead demonstrated how this literary Dexter was SO much smarter than everyone. Speaking of Dexter, if I had to single out one thing that made me quit this book, it was his inner monologues. Jeez can you get any more obnoxious? What, with the unnecessary capitalization and describing your whole "Dark Passenger" business?Totally campy. How the crew of the TV series made their Dexter better than the source material is simply amazing - thanks Michael C. Hall for improving on the original Dexter. His Dexter will be the one I choose to follow.
I think maybe the TV series ruined me for the book but I'm willing to give the next book in the series a shot.

I'll be honest and say that I watched seasons 1 & 2 of Dexter on Showtime before reading this book. That said, this is the first time I've ever read a book and preferred the on-screen adaptation. Darkly Dreaming Dexter is a short and a very quick read. The writing style is a bit unusual because of all the witty internal monologue from the first person main character, and might I say, Jeff Lindsay loves his alliteration! The ending screeched to a halt and I think another 20 pages could have sufficiently wrapped up this story. If you want to start this book (and series), I would suggest watching at least season 1 of Dexter, that way you are already familiar with the characters, and more importantly, Dexter's unique character. I'd give the book 4 stars... and the show 5.

DNF 
 As a mystery book, this is pretty droll. As a supernatural thriller, it might be better? As it is, I have been having the hardest time trying to read this and it is simply getting worse and worse. I have had people tell me I'd love the TV show. I'd never watch it if I had to continue torturing myself with this one.
This was a present from Nathan.
I agree with Kathi, its much more fun to watch the actor who plays Dexter then to read him.

Seeing murders from the points of view of serial killers is nothing new; Dean Koontz has been doing that for years. But I expected something more from a novel that had a cable series based on it. 
 On the surface, Dexter seems like a nice, normal person. But he's completely lacking in human emotions, like someone with Asperger's. In spite of this, he manages to hold down a job and have a girlfriend (although when he finally has sex with her, due more to her instigation than his own inclination, he experiences such inner horror and disgust, it's nearly laughable). 
 This admits to more amusement than the rest of the novel affords. Dexter is so lacking in emotional affect that he comes off as being far less interesting than his menacing alter ego, a character he names the Dark Passenger. It's indicative of poor characterization when the main character is so boring, the other aspect of a split personality is more engaging to read. 
 There isn't enough else going on in the novel to inspire interest, which would save it from the ennui it elicits. (After all, "Perfume" had a similarly emotionally disconnected character but it managed to move me because of the wonders of the French countryside and the detailed description of a vanished age that the author managed to capture).

reference_books.review_text: I just finished this book and all I can say is no one does it better the Abbi Glines. She has ruined me for all other authors. I loved Della and Woods from the minute they met at the gas station. Their love was real, raw heartbreaking. From their first encounter I was routing for their happily ever after. I am trying not to include spoilers in this so everyone can read my review and know how much I loved this story. The sudden twist left me heart broken and confused. Abbi somehow has a way of making you feel every emotion as if you were one of the characters in this book. I only wish there was an epilogue but I know that we will be seeing glimpses of Della, Woods and the rest of the Rosemary beach gang in her next book (which cannot come soon enough). I had incredibly high expectations for the Della and Woods saga and I was not disappointed...it was perfection. My only complaint is that it's been an hour and I am already experiencing a Woods hangover.

reference_books.review_text: Wow. I wasn't really sure how much better hopeless could get but this book went above and beyond my expectations. Losing hope was completely different for me. I got lost in holders raw emotion and got utterly swept away. I loved him in the fit book but this added so much depth to his character that I almost found it hard to breathe while reading parts of this. I am hoping there is somehow another sequel to hope and holders story because I am just not ready to let go of them yet.

2.5/5 Stars 
 I really wish I liked this one more. Rockstar romance books are a serious guilty pleasure of mine and it always breaks my heart when I don't enjoy them. This is the fourth book in the With Me in Seattle series and follows the story of Sam (Luke's sister) and Leo (Meg's brother). 
 Sam -- who we were introduced to in Luke and Nat's story -- is known by many as a bitch. She's been hurt before and to protect herself she puts up very high walls which have proved to be unbreachable... Until Leo Nash. Sam has an undeniable attraction to the world famous rocker Leo, although she tries to deny it because she's been hurt by a celebrity before. Sam throws all her attitude at Leo but he doesn't stop trying to break down her walls and start a relationship with her. 
 I don't have too much to say about this book, I certainly didn't hate it...I just found it to be extremely underwhelming. I knew it was a lighthearted, easy read when I started but instead of being enjoyably simple, I found it awfully boring. Nothing exciting happened! There was no major plot points, no excitement and no great character development or growth. I wasn't looking for an epic read, but I was looking for something enjoyable and entertaining, this wasn't it. 
 On top of it being very boring, the characters and the relationship didn't really develop throughout the book. Leo and Sam got together very early in the novel and their beginning relationship was the same as their finial relationship. They were unbelievably close and familiar at the start which meant that they couldn't develop much as a couple from that point. The love scenes were pretty much the same from start to finish which added to my loss of interest in the story. I just wanted something exciting or swoon worthy to happen. 
 I also didn't like Sam as a character. She had been labeled a bitch earlier in this series which was due to her past experiences. This is all fine, but I didn't really believe her as a character. If would have been fine if she was attitudinal at the start and slowly opened up to Leo, but that didn't happen. Instead, she was a bitch and then she was nice and then she was a bitch again, she was a very inconsistent character. I felt as if the author forgot to make her bitchy at some points and so she randomly made mer mean and nasty throughout the story. She also had a lot of negative characteristics which made her seem like she just got all the bad traits from the first three heroines in this series. She was jealous, vindictive, unforgiving and very hateful towards Leo's career (the last one is kind of understandable due to her past experiences). 
 There were two things that I loved about this book: 
 1. Leo Nash!! The hero in this book was absolutely hot, swoon-worthy and everything I could want from a male lead. I loved him from the first time he was introduced, he was a humorous and very alpha male character. 
 "You are everything I've ever wanted, Sam. More than music. More than anything." 
 "I don't ever want you to run until your legs give out on you like this gain. The only time your legs will shake like this is if I'm inside you." 
 I could write a whole review based off the sweet and sexy things that this man says! He is definitely one of my favourite heroes! 
 2. I also loved the family dynamic and large friendship camaraderie in this book. All the characters from previous books and this book have great banter together and a genuine family feeling! I really enjoyed the scenes where everyone was together and interacting! 
 Something to take into account about my feelings for this book is the fact that all the books I've read this year (excluding this one) have been five or four star reads. I've had great luck with books so far and the brilliant books I've read definitely make others look a lot worse, which is wha happened here. Perhaps if I'd this book at a different time I'd have rated it higher (probably a 3 or 3.5).

Well it's come down to this. Lexi had to make a choice. 
 It's wasn't an easy choice. It's wasn't a cut and dry choice. It was a soul searching and gut wrenching choice. It doesn't matter if you went into this book as Team Ramsey, Team Jack, Team John or Team Run Lexi Run... at the end of this book you will be, or maybe I should say "should" be, happy with the choice she made... because she made the only one that made sense for her. 
 None of these characters were the same people they were when we started this journey with them. They all grew and changed. Lexi the most. She had to take a good long look at herself. Oh she didn't want to. She tried so hard to make what she thought she should want "fit". To be who she thought she was supposed to be. How many times have we done the same thing? Went through the door everyone else thought we should and ignored our heart? There was one scene where Chyna (God I love Chyna) has a "Come To Jesus" meeting with Lexi. It was exactly what Lexi needed to hear. It's what I was screaming at her. 
 I am not going to lie this book will destroy you. It will rip you open and make you bleed. I coyote ugly cried. The author took me through every emotion with every character and I loved the ending. Did Lexi end up with the guy of my choosing. She may have... or she may have chosen opposite. The point is K.A. Linde convinced me beyond the shadow of a doubt that she made the right choice and she did it without demonizing one or the other. She didn't tear anyone down to make the choice easy. It was painful and hearts had to break. Good hearts. Love is messy like that. Did Lexi get her Happily Ever After? She absolutely did and it was her story afterall... 
 Now I am going to open a bottle of wine and re-read now that I can breath <3

After rereading the entire Harry Potter series this summer, I was looking for a continuation of the magic. I'm sorry to say that this book doesn't deliver. If I wasn't expecting the Harry Potter series' style or storytelling or characterization or even set-up, I might have enjoyed the book more, but from most of the reviews, you would think that this book was close. It's not. 
 Let's start off by pointing out that this book is, in fact, fanfiction. It's set in the Harry Potter world, shares some characters with the original series, but was not written by J.K. Rowling. As with all slush, fanfiction consists of a lot of dreck and then occasional gems. When I read fanfiction before (at least 10 years ago), it was almost exclusively recommended to me by other people that I trusted, and that has always served me well. I forget where I first heard about James Potter, but so many reviews talked about being so close to HP that I wanted to give it a try. I wanted to continue the way I felt when I read HP. 
 The prologue starts well enough (although a character from HP didn't seem much like himself), but as soon as we're with James, I began finding little things that irked me. We start with him on the train heading to Hogwarts. Obviously, he's not Harry and his story isn't going to start out with finding out about the wizarding world the way Harry's did. But even past the first book, JKR always found ways to make Diagon Alley interesting (and how interesting would it be to see how it's changed in 17-18 years?) and no matter what setting Harry was in before Hogwarts, we were always intrigued. Why wouldn't we want to know what James's (and therefore Harry's) homelife was like before James went to Hogwarts? So right off the bat, the set-up seems off. We meet other kids on the train, both Muggle-born but neither quite as inquisitive as Hermoine, who came across as if she knew more about the wizarding world than the Muggle world actually. So instead we had a lot of introduction of James to Muggle stuff. It feels very fanfiction to do so. "Hee hee, let me insert stuff from my world into the author's world and have characters react to it." With the technomancy (actually less technological than it sounds) and technology suddenly able to work in Hogwarts, this is not just a cute exchange between the boys, but an initiation into what we can expect for the book. 
 As is Zane. I like Zane. But Zane introduces the American element. Remember when witches and wizards came to Hogwarts for the Triwizard Cup. It didn't suddenly change the atmosphere of the book to match with those countries (whatever they were). HP was very British. JP is very American. It's in the writing style, it's in the new American characters, it's in the way the classes are taught (kids of all grades in some classes), it's in the type of classes taught (let's explain the magic scientifically), it's in the type of pranks the kids play (Doctor Who aside, aliens are so American), and so on. I was unsurprised to look up the author and find out he was American. 
 Unlike most, I felt the book picked up a little after the first quarter. We actually visited a few classes (just a few) and all these strange things that we've been wondering why we got introduced to begin to make sense. The storytelling, otoh, is nowhere near as smooth as JKR's. The moment the staff is mentioned it's pretty obvious where it is. We're told a character has an "evil-looking" wand, and, lo and behold, that character is evil. James correctly jumps to conclusions about what was stolen in the prologue pretty much the second he starts wondering where the three relics are and then it's just taken as fact from then on out. When we get to the climax, I'm still not sure whether it was supposed to be the baddies trying to resurrect Merlin, because that felt like a climax but ended up rather anti-climatic, or when the Muggles visit the school, because that was just humorous. But everything we'd been worrying about for the entirety of the book was just sort of fixed with the, well, wave of a wand, figuratively-speaking. Seriously, we spend the whole book worrying that Merlin is going to come back and be the next Voldemort, and then he comes and is like, "Hey, I think I'm a good guy, and I totally want to be a good guy," and we make him the new Dumbledore. I also liked Merlin quite a lot, and I think he'd probably be a very fun character if I were to read the future books, but that's not how to end a conflict. While fooling the Muggles was amusing, it still didn't feel like a Harry Potter ending. It was just fun. 
 Despite the fact that it seemed like the author was trying to avoid many constants from the original series, except in exposition form ("Let me tell you about Charms class"), there were times when we did see characters from the original series. It's always hard to age characters for the next generation, and so it's hard to say if Harry felt Harry enough, if Neville felt Neville enough. But the original adults are a different manner. After the very short Mundungus incident, where I didn't feel like it was him--but then again, how well do we know Dung?--I noticed in short order that McGonagall and Filch were a little off. The one character I think was nailed was Severus Snape's portrait, but all you need is Alan Rickman in your ear to pull him off ;) 
 So, you've had the long of it, here's the short of it: If you're looking for a story set in the HP world and you're not looking for JKR's storytelling and worldbuilding, and especially if you're a reader of fanfic who is used to these kind of detours from the original source, you'll probably enjoy this book. But if you want to feel the magic of the original series again, the only advice I have for you is to pick up Sorceror's/Philosopher's Stone and begin rereading once again.

I was skeptical of how another author might be able to extend the adventures of Harry Potter. These are big shoes to fill, after all. But someone on Twitter recommended the book/series so I thought I'd give it a try. 
 I loved the way the book began. Lippert immediately grabbed my attention and began reeling me in. He imaginatively introduced changes to Hogwarts that allowed the story to be believable and go in many new directions. 
 I loved part of the new plot with explaining how magic works, weaving that in to the resolution. I was a tiny disbelieving having first years and fifth years in the same class, but that was a minor criticism. 
 My biggest disappointment was Mr. Dolohov. That part comes out of left field and was not an effective element of the story. Yes, it explains how that part happened, but I'd rather have seen the author resolve it more coherently with the rest of the book. It just felt tacked on to an already great story.

It's books like this that make me wish I wasn't so stubborn about finishing things that I have started. 
 I used to read a LOT of fan fiction. And I mean a LOT. All the big ones - the Draco Trilogy, A Year Like None Other, maya's stuff... So, then I came across this on GoodReads and saw the huge number of downloads and the millions of positive reviews and thought: why not? It's been a while, but I still love Harry Potter, and this could be a nice bit of fun. 
 How wrong I was. 
 It has taken me so long to get through because I had to force myself to read it. It was so disappointing. I feel mean writing such a negative review, but I always strive to be honest. This felt like the sort of fan fiction written by quite young American teens, wanting to insert lots of their own stuff into JK's world in a way that doesn't really fit. Why did we have to have the American exchange thing? It didn't fit. Why were James and co, as first years, so incredibly powerful? (accepting the part about Ralph's ridiculous wand). Why were they suddenly learning arithmancy and divination in first year? 
 It just didn't sit right. If you're going to write fan fiction, you have to strike a balance. It is your story, but it is not your world. Don't mess with what works. And JK's world works. 
 The writing was mediocre at best, cringey at worst. The characters were mostly one-dimensional. But it was mostly the STORY that got me: it was so unrealistic, and just did NOT hang together. These are 11 year olds we're talking about! For crying out loud, why did such huge and drastic stuff happen in what is meant to be the FIRST book in a series of seven? Where to go? And why was James involved in so much of the big decision making? Just because his father is Harry Potter? 
 I apologise to the author for my negativity; I do feel guilty. The best part about this book was the illustrations on the chapter pages. Those, and the relief I feel that I have finally finished it and don't have to read it anymore.

This is the first book by John green I've ever read. I was hesitant to read it because I try to stay away from hyped books and best sellers, and also because I knew it was YA and its not really my genre. However I enjoyed this book. It is fast paced, easy to read, funny and sad, and very complete. I liked the characters, they were very real and relatable. But the thing I enjoyed most in this book was the approach of cancer and death and life. It does not turn the characters into victims, it does not make you feel sorry or pity any of the characters. It celebrates life and the message of living the life you are dealt comes across very strongly. 
 It's pretty deep for a YA book. And although I did find the whole romance thing a bit cheesy, It made me be very grateful for being healthy and alive, and also I think that people who have struggled or are currently fighting cancer would appreciate it, I people treated them like regular people, and see far beyond their illness, because cancer does not define you. 
 I recommend it widely and I'm also curious to read more of this author.

reference_books.title: Prodigal Son (Dean Koontz's Frankenstein, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
A horrifying and fun modern retelling of the original text, Frankenstein Prodigal Son brings us to a near future world where a conglomeration led by a mysterious scientist turns out to be more than it appears on the surface. Murders, mystery, and horrific disembodied parts squiggling along on their own, all contribute to the larger action/adventure/mystery novel that this very genre-based piece is a part of. It is a classic mystery with bodies piled high and an application of the airport-bookstore staple in original, albeit predictable ways. 
 I am a very big fan and teacher of the original novel, so reading this text was really an experiment in finding some outside material with which to use as fun, supplementary material for my courses while being exposed to new iterations of our scientist in literary pop culture. Koontz has not been part of my bookshelf since I was probably twelve years old, and after having read this book I was reminded why. 
 I enjoyed the story, the interesting and novel ways that he has found to contextualize our scientist and his creature(s) in a modern setting, however the writing was very difficult to get through. It is what it is, however - an everyman's exciting, thrilling, and driven narrative that speeds along, slipping in blood and gore while we have new iterations of the plot, twists, and a colorful cast of characters all out for their own profit and worldwide domination. At times, however, I found myself unsure of even where the setting was, overshadowed by the speed and colloquial language that the book relies on. Will this sell millions of copies to a wide, general audience? Absolutely. Is it an interesting new twist on the text? Certainly. Is it a worthwhile, well-written read? I am not sure about that. I can only say that I only read this first book, and will not be finishing the rest.

reference_books.title: Mort(e) (War with No Name, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This was one of the most unique books I have ever read - mashing up a dystopian war with the philosophical anthropomorphic avatars of the animal kingdom post-human apocalypse. It is a mix between The Road, Starship Troopers, Homeward Bound, Watership Down, and maybe a little Redwall. 
 I really enjoyed the book, and the book design is really sexy and sold me on wanting to pick it up. As someone who only occasionally enters the science-fiction and fantasy world, the reading did occasionally lose my attention span, but I really enjoyed the message and the excitement that the book provoked in me. It was well written for what it was, and the various complications to the plot contrasted with the evolution of the animal behavior and social workings was an interesting speculative angle to the text. 
 Mort(e) was an enjoyable text with intriguing characters, and its most notable characteristic was in its originality in concept and execution. It is rare that I read a book that truly makes me reflect that I have never read anything like it before.

reference_books.title: Fun Home: A Family Tragicomic
reference_books.review_text: Decided to pick this book up after purchasing season tickets to a theater and knowing it was on the bill. I knew little about the source material, even though I did know about the author. This book was a fantastic autobiographical six-feet-under-esque story about a variety of family dynamics at play after a death. It explores a variety of themes that touch upon the global experiences of sexual awakening, friendships, queer exploration and growth, family secrets, aging, and death. The artwork is beautiful, and the manner in which the story is presented is not only effective, but genius. The author manages to weave many elements of existence into a masterful application of perspective and narrative order. Every chapter not only carries the audience along at an effective and energetic pace, but the book also manages to present the story with the drive of delicious visual, plot, and narrative discovery on just about every page. A great graphic novel. Gorgeous, true, and touching for any reader. Very much looking forward to the play.

reference_books.title: Hillbilly Elegy: A Memoir of a Family and Culture in Crisis
reference_books.review_text:
I have read many books that I have thought spoke to me as a human being and seemed to figuratively reflect my difficult childhood. 
 While I don't share many of the specific geographic issues in this book, I certainly found every anecdotal situation Vance presents as being a part of my development. He presents the various socioeconomic conditions present that have not only stifled generations of young Americans who are struggling with the disease of indifference, but more realistically, have been caused by decades of poor political, economic, geographic, social, communal, and other choices that have led to the current lost generation of young people struggling to make choices that promote moving up the social ladder. There are some elements that they have control over that they don't know they do, while others they have no control over but can change their circumstances in order to do it. They key central concept underlying all of it is to have mentors and adults to help them make the proactive, healthy, and productive emotional and executive intelligence choices to move forward. 
 Vance is clear that this is an anecdotal memoir that is only partially supported by generalized data, however, it is a memoir that I can attest to being absolutely connected to my own experience as to how I have grown into a functioning, successful adult despite the odds stacked against both of us. This is certainly what happened, and what is perhaps most helpful about Vance's piece is how clearly he has outlined A. How my previous life continues to affect my current life and life choices despite emancipating myself from it decades ago, and B. How I can help others to find their way despite politics and policy, family, upbringing, race, indifference, and the drive to make the same choices of our parents. 
 This book should be a required text to understand exactly what is happening in our country right now, and what actions need to be taken in order to change it. It is precisely why we are in the political situation we are right now - education is the key, not the enemy, and as a community and a country, we need to make drastic and deliberate changes to remain relevant in the twenty-first century. Vance's successes came from a distinct set of choices he made, the same ones I did that were difficult, expensive, and oftentimes against what my body and family history told me to make, and the skills and coping mechanisms that were necessary to navigate them are teachable. 
 The only issue that I see as standing out in the book - one he was very clear about in the intro - is that this book is strictly from his perspective. It is a memoir, after all, and while it was easy to think in terms of his experience as similar to mine in many ways and differentiate it from my geographic one (where his rural Appalachian community of production was suffering the fallout of our country's transition to an idea economy), there is no question to me that race plays a huge role in our opportunity and privilege. But, in many ways the issues poverty raises are the same, and like Vance I had to work very hard in very low paying jobs to move away and survive, and it took learning, adapting, and navigating many emotional and executive skills AND a decade of literally working from 6AM to the following 2AM almost every day of the week in order to make college and the apartment and everything happen in the midst of my own independent poverty. I also recognize Vance's story, along with mine, are strictly anecdotal, so one can argue about what the book is not, or recognize what it is - something the author stresses is mainly a memoir. Everyone's experience is different, and I wonder what changes we need to make on the macro level in order to impact as many people as possible in these same circumstances regardless of, and perhaps specifically paying special attention to, race. In the case of this book, it is simple to recognize that whoever is in circumstances where substance abuse, emotional abuse, bad choices, and poverty culminate, there is a lot of suffering that that affects many generations. 
 A book that is excellent for what it is, however, and I will be recommending it to just about everyone around me. Additionally, it is a book that I wish my parents would read...but that I know they will not.

reference_books.title: The Unwritten, Vol. 1: Tommy Taylor and the Bogus Identity
reference_books.review_text:
This is a review that I have duplicated to both Volumes 1 and 2 of THE UNWRITTEN since I read them concurrently. 
 I was recommended this graphic novel by a friend who knew of my penchant for books, and what I really love in books - tongue-in-cheek referencing to other works of art. I like graphic novels if they are done well, and I am currently finishing up one of my favorite forays into the genre, The Sandman series. 
 The Unwritten is a story about a man who comes from a literary family with an uncertain past. When his father becomes a huge success because of his Harry-Potter-like book series, Tommy finds himself embroiled in the success as he resembles and is a part of the mythos that goes along with the book (as much as he would like to deny it). When a murder is committed and he is the only possible perpetrator, he is on the run from a fan base that is absolutely horrified that he could have betrayed their trust (even though he is a real person and the character is fictional). It is then that the world between reality and magic become blurred, and all of the places where it happens are completely based on consciousness and literary meaning within the construction of a story. 
 I liked this series, but there is a lot it is trying to do in less pages than I think it takes to be done well. My favorite part is the literary-winks that happen throughout the books that are a direct address to the readers who are knowledgeable about history and authors that the books nod to. From Mary Shelley to Mark Twain to Rudyard Kipling to A.A.Milne to Nazi propagandists, everything in the first two books great a really cool, literary world of danger that blur the lines between fact, fiction, and the purpose of narratives in our lives. It is a lot of fun, and I just wish it was somewhat longer (but I understand the constraints that exist in the one-offs prior to being collected in these omnibus volumes). I really liked the ending of the second volume and the tribute to the "Beatrix Potter" type narrative (without giving much away - but it was awesome). 
 The thing about graphic novels that stinks is also part of the things that make them great - it is the perfect blend of the literary and the visual, allowing you to take in the art at the same time that you are taking in the narrative, thereby allowing for "whole picture" visualization of the piece that one can study and look at for five minutes and study, but promoting and providing the same wonder and meta-analysis in the text that it presents. Of course, the thing that makes it great is also the thing that makes it difficult for the people like me who want to stretch out what I am doing to the end of time, evidently. 
 Unwritten was not one of my favorite graphic novels, but I surely think that the execution and in-jokes among readers of great literature that it presents is well worth the price of admission. I do wonder what the piece would have looked like if it pandered to a little more of an intellectual audience and not so much of a more general audience overall, but at the same rate it is enjoyable. I am tempted to read the rest to see more of the intellectual jokes, but I am not sure that the main conflict storyline is something that would particularly engage me for ten volumes. I will probably give it a shot.

book_a.title: Jonathan Livingston Seagull
book_a.user_review: This book was kind of a disappointment, especially considering it has such a deep reputation that spans decades throughout its history. I took it out of the library, and I had to have it shipped from another library because all of the copies, so very appropriately, were never returned. The text itself is nothing special, and could be written by anyone, and the philosophy is seemingly an oversimplification of a lot of great ideas that are much better expressed in classic and modern literature. There are moments of nice sentences and phrases, but it is much too simple, much too short, and much too much of a disappointment for me when I was done reading it. I thought it was sort of funny when I read something that said that Bach was unhappy with the film version of the text - which I haven't seen - but I honestly don't think that anyone could make a good movie, or a movie in general about this book. I guess there are just better books than this one that ask / answer the same questions in a better way.

'Jonathan Livingston Seagull' is a unique little book: a self development story written from the viewpoint of a non-conforming seagull. It is about his passion to fly like no other seagull, his self growth and how he breaks through the restraints of family, friends and community to live his dream. 
 The book appears to be more than the life of one seagull. It is a fable about self empowerment and the importance of seeking a higher purpose in life, even if the people around you find your goals threatening or ridiculous. He shows that you can do anything and be anything you want if you just believe in yourself. It is also about the struggle to find the answers about life itself. 
 It is also a good fable for children as it stimulates discussions on the various meanings of the story. The ending is slightly puzzling but on viewing the DVD which, though very lengthy (2 hrs) did offer some explanations. The film also shed light on why the book had numerous black and white, grainy photographs of gulls. (All the music and songs are by Neil Diamond)

book_b.title: Factotum
book_b.user_review:
So, I love Bukowski, but Factotum was not one of my favorites. 
 To clarify, if I had read it earlier than I had I would have enjoyed it a lot more. I read Ham On Rye, Women, and Post Office in order before picking up Factotum, and there is something about the structure and execution of the first three that seemed to have more of a linear and structured point to them. Of course, Factotum totally met my expectations in his voice, attitude, happenings, and events throughout the piece - as a matter of point, I don't think a book could be any more Charles Bukowski than this one - but this book is really just a series of disjointed vignettes that are pieced together in a chronological job-based format that was not as good as the others as far as I am concerned. I think the chief reason behind that all comes down to Chianski's motivation - and there doesn't feel like there is a payoff by the end of the book. 
 It is the author's job to convince us of his character's agency and narrative direction. As his work surround the same autofiction characters, events, and motivations, this one ultimately is not as good as the ones I have experienced so far. Had I not read the others before this one, I would have enjoyed it a lot more because of its earnest and striking voice - but save for its moments of brutal bodily imagery (including a triple crown toilet symphony) that occur more strikingly than the others and some great interpersonal moments and statements on writing, Factotum left me disappointed. Bukowski's other work is more effective than this one.

 Nao acontece nada. Absolutamente nada. Nao existe narrativa para se discutir. Nao e que seja mal escrito - o estilo e minimalista e preciso, sem firulas. Mas nao ha simplesmente o que dizer. E a vida vazia de uma pessoa vazia, desmotivada e hedonista por pura preguica de ser qualquer outra coisa alem de vazia, desmotivada e hedonista. 
 Se e para ler nada por nada, muito melhor ler Sterne, que e pelo menos o nada mais divertido que existe.
Interesting enough.

I probably need to read more books of the author to understand the purpose of his writing... 
 My friend rec me this book I need to ask him again why he did.

Just as the descriptions of jobs he couldn't hold down was getting unbearably tedious, the book was over. I now do know what people who like Bukowski mean and I can infer more than a little about those people.

Meet Henry Chinaski. Henry is a twenty-something L.A. man who loves to drink. Wine, port wine, cheap wine, expensive wine, gin with water, whisky, beer, you name it. He also likes to have sex with prostitutes. Oh, and he keeps getting hired from countless jobs before getting sacked because he is either too drunk to do the work properly or because he has sex on the job. And he does this all throughout the book. All 205 pages of it. Oh, but guess what? Henry Chinaski likes to write. He wants to be a writer one day. 
 Yes, as much as I wanted to give this novel a go, mainly because of Bukowski's popularity and because I really liked "Roll the Dice" (one of his most famous poems), I had a really hard time enjoying it. While reading it, I ended up giggling at Chinaski's misfortunes, scorning at the way he treats women, and being just plain bored at how he got sacked by his countless jobs. Seriously, I lost count of all the sackings, because at one point I didn't care anymore. I decided to hang on to the novel because all in all it wasn't written in a complex way, and I had already guessed how it was going to end (spoiler: there is no ending), so I just thought, 'you know, might as well get this over and done with'. 
 I definitely didn't feel sorry for Chinaski, and I don't think Bukowski's intention was that the reader should feel sorry for him. But then again: why simply list down all of the things Chinaski does and thinks, like a shopping list? Is it just a matter-of-fact thing, or does the reader have to find meaning/poetry in what is written here? Also, if Chinaski was Bukowski's alter ego did he ever feel guilty about all the drinking and all the mistreating of women? Sure, his drinking problem was a way to channel his anger towards his father: but seriously, was he trying to rid of that self just by making this list? And also, why didn't his character write more about the act of writing on this novel? Oh, of course, he was too busy getting drunk. Why am I even wondering. 
 I don't want to come across as being insensitive towards alcoholism, but I just thought that maybe, just maybe, it would have made sense to try and write about it differently, with more pathos, nuances and so on and so forth. But then again I'm no writer, so who am I to judge? 
 Don't read this novel if you are easily impressionable. Luckily for me, I just got bored by all the misfortunes, alcohol, vulgarity and sackings. I will easily avoid Bukowski's novels in the future. I'm sure he'd probably want to spit at me from heaven because of this, but I don't care.
Could the life of Charles Bukowski, I mean Chinaski, get any lower? Read this and find out how low he can go. His life is like a train wreck; you can't bear to watch, but you can't look away.
Blunt, harsh and vulgar. Bukowski could weave stories that stay with you.
