sample_reviews.review_text:
Mr. Panda is cute. But he's also a meanie. 
 Maybe I just don't get it. I think this is supposed to be a message book, teaching kids to say please when they want something. But I find Mr. Panda more rude than all the animals who forget to say the secret word. 
 To get specific: (I'm about to spoil the book, fair warning if you haven't read it) Mr. Panda goes around offering animals doughnuts. When they don't say they want one PLEASE, he takes back his offer and tells them they may not have any doughnuts. What?!? 
 I guess it's okay to be a jerk if others don't live up to your high standards. Or maybe it's a modern tale illustrating how arbitrary life can be. But I think Mr. Panda should do a little self-examination before he goes around judging everyone else. That's the real lesson I'm hoping kids can take from this book.

I'm super sad that I didn't enjoy this book, especially because it's about doughnuts and Pandas - two things I enjoy. I have no idea what happened in this story. Maybe I need to go back and read it a few times?!?

This one's a bit confusing. Mr. Panda offers other animals a doughnut, which is a very polite thing to do. But, when they don't say "please," he denies them, and walks away. 
 Now, with the way the interactions go, the panda seems like a huge jerk-- when you offer something, typically you're expecting a "thank you." If the animals were approaching the panda, then yes, a "please" would be in order. 
 Maybe that's just the way interactions around here go, but on the whole I felt there are better books to teach little ones about manners.
After reading this my daughter will correct people how to ask for something properly. Thank you for this book! Pretty sure this will be the first book she reads!

 Last spring I went on a Life As We Knew It binge and read the first three books in just a few days, ever since I have been anxiously awaiting the fourth book. It was unique to see that the book was from Jon's perspective, but I was completely disheartened to see that he had been sucked into the snobbery that is prevalent in Sexton. There were many, many times that I was almost disgusted with not only Sexton, but Jon as well. There was an event (don't want to give away too much) that finally shook Jon out of his comfort zone and he started to realize that the way things were wasn't right. I will say that it was nice to "see" familiar characters and see how they were doing in their "new normal". It also challenged me to think about what I would do in that kind of scenario. Oh, and the author definitely left it open for another book and I sure hope that she follows through, I love these books! 
 Bottom line, loyal fans of the Life As We Knew It will not be disappointed with the fourth book in the series. You may get a bit discouraged at first with what is happening in Sexton & White Birch, but you must stick with it until the end. I promise, you will not be disappointed!

reference_books.title: The Middlesteins
reference_books.review_text:
http://charlotteswebofbooks.blogspot.... 
 The Middlesteins is told from all different angles in all different periods of Edie's life and at the start of each chapter from Edie's perspective is her weight at that moment in time. (nice, huh?) But the underlying theme in each chapter is Edie's weight. And while her family would LIKE you to believe that they are concerned about Edie's weight because of her health, the feeling I got was that they were concerned for more selfish reasons. Like being embarrassed by her size. It was especially interesting to me to see all of the reactions when she brought a date to the big party. In fact it even made me mad on her behalf that they were so shocked that she actually had a date. 
 Bottom line, The Middlesteins is not just another ordinary book about family dynamics. Well it is, but when you factor in Edie's weight and all of the family's perceptions (and realities) that go with it, you have a pretty exceptional book. Let me know what you think!

I wanted to really like it but i just didn't! All the way through the book Gretchen Rubin spoke of her extensive reading and research and yet it read more like a series of 'what I did today' blog posts strung together. It felt like she had lost all sense of audience in her writing and was being overly self-indulgent...this something she also continually worries about during the book and rightly so! The extensive reading didn't really filter down...after reading I felt like I had been forced to view every photo album of a stranger without really being given access to anything useful! Also at times i simply had to laugh at the many digs at her husband in the 'i know i should let that go to be happy and i really did.....even if he should have acted differently!' way! What a great way to have the last word in a fight...write a book! I ended up not knowing if i had to applaud her for her honesty in showing how human she was or really disliking her for her lack of self awareness within what was effectively a totally self-absorbed project. 
 also there was a part of the book that killed me to read...in August she began to contemplate eternity in a challenge to become more grateful! To do this she read 'memoirs of catastrophe' in order to try to be more grateful about her 'ordinary existence'. She laughingly jokes about her holiday reading, her husband being aghast at what she chooses to read on vacation.... 
 ''is that really what you want to be reading while we're away? he said doubtfully as he scanned the book jackets. Stan Mack on cancer, gene O'Kelly on brain tumors and Martha Beck on having a baby with down syndrome''. 
 As a mother of a child with a syndrome in many ways similar to Down Syndrome this little nugget really pissed me off! Like my life and my daughter is an affliction or a disaster to make others more grateful for their lot! (This the woman who decided to buy 3 magazines every Monday with her eyes shut to ensure she was exploring new things....like who has the spare cash or need for that...really!) Seeing her basically link my own beautiful and wondrous child who is a total gift, in the same boat as cancer and brain tumours in a self absorbed and ghoulish project on catastrophe to make her own lot seem better like i said pissed me right off! 
 A further project on empathy and tact may be a good idea for a follow up!

Self-help is a new genre before, one I hadn't needed and didn't particularly want to try. However, the buzz generated over this book captured me. I read reviews and interviews with people who said the book changed their way in some profound and meaningful way. 
 I have one question to ask those people: How? 
 The book is divided into 12 different chapters, one for each month of the year whereby the author dedicates that month to changing something in her life: career, marriage, children etc. Overall, it sounds like a great idea. However, the "advice" generated in the book is alarming. Her big marriage advice was to treat her husband "nicer". If you are shallow enough to not already treat your spouse nicely, I doubt your marriage will be saved by the book. As for children...apparently, the lesson is don't let their whining annoy you. As a mother of two, good luck with that and that came with the program, so suck it up. The whole book just seemed so ridiculous to me. I can't think of one piece of advice I gleaned that wouldn't be so obviously apparent for anyone with an ounce of self-reflection. 
 What bothered me most of all about this book is the obvious attempt just to sell. The author is very clear about her purpose in writing to be just to sell books. So, in this book, she gathered all her blog entries from other readers and tacked them in. Not all the entries were relevant or interesting and it just felt like an attempt to make the book thicker. There are also lots of quotes and "studies" about happiness, more obvious attempts to fill the pages with something relevant. The title kind of got my goat, too. A year trying to fight right? Can't recall an instance where the author was really focused on anything other than her own selfish pursuits. Read Aristotle? Not a chapter in the book so I'm not sure how it made it to the title other than to make the book seem more worthy. 
 You want some happiness? Save the money you would normally spend on this book and look elsewhere. Buy yourself a latte, a bouquet of flowers, take your spouse or boyfriend out for a hot dog, buy a stranger some balloons...

It was a bit long but Gretchen did inspire to think about things I'd like to do and encouraged me to start some new projects. I only read the first third and then skimmed the rest of the book. It wasn't amazing but it was effective in that it got me thinking and I did make a point of writing a whole bunch of friends that I hadn't stayed in touch with as well as I'd like.

This was a book that many of my friends have read and enjoyed so I was eager to read it myself. I really liked the author's Twelve Commandments and her Rules of Adulthood. My favorite part was her allowing us little glimpses into her private life. All married couples have little sayings and things they do together and it was interesting to read about the things she and her husband do together. I didn't enjoy the comments from her blog readers and tended to skim those sections.

The Happiness Project has some good thought provoking points, even with the "in a year" idea that has been done before. Gretchen Rubin braves revealing her weaknesses and personal flaws to help the reader improve their lives and to learn to live happier...overall it was worth the time and a good read.

This book chronicles the author's self-challenge of having a focused year of happiness. Each month is a different theme/challenge towards that goal. Along the way the author started a blog which gives others a chance to join the project. 
 It's nice to read a book by an author who clearly loves words (and has built up a nice vocabulary). I can relate to being self-motivated by earning little gold stars, whatever form they come in. Other reviewers disliked the entire concept but that seems strange to me -- the author is very up-front and honest about her intentions, personality, and methods. This project seems like the kind of project she personally wanted to do for herself. 
 But that's actually where the book loses a few points in my eyes. This seems like a personal project and it's less about committing fully to an experiment (by strictly following certain rules or reaching certain goals) and more about personally journaling through a general topic.

I enjoyed the first half of this book much more so than the second half, when reading it began to feel like a chore. The premise of the book is enticing- is it possible to make yourself happier via goals, resolutions, checklists based on research on happiness? The answer, according to the author would likely be "yes", but according to this reader, the answer seems closer to "sort of, depending on how you look at it". As the book dragged on in the second half, and particularly the last third, I could almost feel the topic becoming more mundane, less novel, less interesting to not just myself, but the author. I admire her fortitude, and I liked being reminded of certain things that we all need reminders for at times- hug people more, forgive more easily, try to smile, complain less, stay in the moment, be mindful-- all good lessons, none unique to this book, but feel-good topics in general. On the other hand, the last few chapters, I found myself consistently checking how many pages I had left to go, wondering how much longer I was going to have to keep reading to finish it, and when it would end. It lost my attention. Rubin is a solid writer, but this book could have used some serious editing down- would have been better as a book half as long. Two stars.

I'm possibly too cynical for a book like this. The author was already happy to begin with, so really her happiness project didn't do much apart from help her to exercise self-care more effectively. Towards the end I was beginning to feel like the whole book was just a bit of a cash grab, especially since the author has a habit of using comments from her blog to pad the pages. In terms of useful guidance, the sections were often short and didn't really get in-depth into techniques used. In terms of an interesting personal narrative, there wasn't one because the author had nothing to lose even if her project failed. So really the book didn't do much for me. Funnily enough the book ends with reading lists that contain books of actual use.
I enjoyed this one all the way through; I also found many of her ideas, quotes, and experiences to be inspiring.

I thought I would enjoy reading something light. Unfortunately, it is also boring.

This is light (to the point of air-heady) southern chick-lit. From its popularity at my local library (it was always on reserve and there was a long wait), you'd think this must be a winner. I've enjoyed other efforts by Mary Kay Andrews, and I was drawn to the fixer upper part of the story. (Anyone who knows me can attest that I'm a house person.) While her descriptions of renovating and decorating show that M.K.A. is really into it (check out her blog for pics of her adorable re-done beach house), they were too idealistic. What novice can master floor sanding and staining, cabinet refinishing, tiling, and wallpaper removal with the veritable snap of her fingers? But that was perhaps the most believable part of the story. The main character is a twenty-something lawyer who worked for a lobbyist involved in buying votes from a congressman. For being near the top of her class in law school, she is ridiculously naive. She is fired from her job and her boss tries to implicate her in the scandal. She flees Washington to a small Georgia town where her father has inherited a once grand but now old and dilapidated house from a distant relative. He wants her to fix it up just enough so that he can flip it for a nice profit. There's the usual big city girl in a small town set-up with a young handsome lawyer ready to escort her to the country club dance. He's charming, sexy, and too perfect to be believed - even his flaws that he lists are more endearing than maddening. And after seeing her for maybe a dozen times, if that, and maybe two of them actual dates, he's ready to spend his life with her if only she could decide to give up the big city life. Pleez. Not only cliched, but totally unrealistic. (My thirty-something sons were with their girlfriends for seven and nine years before they got around to proposing.) The plot sounds more like some movie from the forties with Jimmy Stewart playing the romantic lead. It's old-fashioned, despite the modern trappings, but not in a good way. In fact, I think Andrews had a harder time with such a young protagonist. Usually her characters are a bit older and been around a few times. In an attempt to give her character suitably young tastes, she has her juking out to Thriller on her iPod playlist. That didn't seem to really fit for a twenty-eight-year-old, and when she dances the shag to beach music at the country club, the author's real tastes - and age - becomes evident. To round out the supporting cast, there's the crotchety old biddy who won't leave the house who is supposed to end up being endearing somehow, but doesn't. Andrews usually writes with her trademark southern sass and wit, but it's lacking here. I had a hard time finishing it. There's nothing much to drive the plot - the end is a foregone conclusion, and there are no surprises. I'm not really sure why it's so popular here; it's not one I'd recommend. But maybe it's just me.

reference_books.title: The Things We Wish Were True
reference_books.review_text:
Audible version : similar to Picolut, Moraiatry, Scottoline etc but not nearly as developed unless I somehow missed entire sections, but I rewound it over and over and couldn't find an unheard section. It had great potential with a multi-view story told through various females crossing generations all from Sycamore Glen and its community pool. 
 Started strong with me excited to find out the secrets hinted about the past of the "mom's" and then the blurb had also mentioned how one incident at the pool changed a community forever, so I thought I was in for a real treat of a story. And boy was I wrong. 
 The "incident " wasn't what brought all the women together and felt like a strange event to focus on when the author had so many more past and present events with each character that should've been expanded on. Their was a missing girl that would only be mentioned when convenient, a husband who was in prison for what can only be inferred as money related, a single mother who was never home because she was working (?), an oddball neighbor who isn't even introduced until 3/4 of the book, a son who had a penchant for stalking, etc and never did we get the back story or explainations on that when all were extremely relevant to the plot 
 the author spent so much time building the suspense over exposing these "secrets"- a whole other list of events, btw- that she failed to create any sense of cohesion and when said secrets were exposed , they fell flat on account of the other more dramatic events she had thrown in. Not only that, the secrets became obvious for the most part. 
 I could go on and on about my issues with this book, but I don't have the time to generate that much work into a book so shoddily written. To sum it up, the author spent too much time on events less interesting and/or not as relevant to the plot and not enough on events, characters or descriptions that were absolutely relevant and what I continued to listen to in the first place. 
 I did enjoy the narrator's rendition of the women with their southern drawls, but that wasn't enough to salvage this book.

reference_books.title: Saving Grace
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 It's summertime and for me that means indulging in literary dessert- aka ChickLit. Saving Grace was the first of my - hopefully- many books in this genre to read for the summer, and I'll say it was quite delicious and whet my appetite for more! That being said, I did have some qualms with the book that kept this from being rated higher for this specific genre. 
 SUMMARY: Grace - the middle-aged wife of best-selling author Ted (a pompous, narcissistic, and abusive jerk) thought she had built a charmed life and was living her dream. Her passion is food (hence the reason for my cheesy food metaphors) and his is writing, but his career has taken a nosedive and he'll need a best-seller to save his career. To really put the "cherry on top", they recently lost his assistant who was always able to manage everything from appointments to his moods. Grace finds herself overwhelmed and in desperate need of an assistant; enter the "too good to be true" Beth. She instantly begins making herself indispensable to the family, overtly thrilled to do any little thing to make them happy. It doesn't take long for Beth to become one of my most hated antagonist of all time. She expertly weasels her way into Grace's life and before long, Grace is the only one to see that Beth doesn't just want to help Grace; she wants to be Grace. She sets out to ruin Grace's life and does it in a way that is only apparent to Grace. Before long, Grace finds herself sleeping on a park bench, doped up on copious amounts of anti-psychotics, broke, and alone. Grace is determined to get her life back, but is side-tracked when she finds herself suddenly happy without her husband, big fancy house, and engaged in a romantic relationship with an old childhood pal. 
 MY TAKE: So, great storyline, characters, and overall good book. But, there were some problems for me with the book. My first "complaint" was that Green really focuses on Ted's abusive behavior towards Grace in the beginning of the book - even though the word "abuse" is never mentioned. I'm pretty sure that was intentional since Grace works at a women's shelter for abused women. I really thought Green was going to make the association and bring the abuse to light - not only to Grace, but also for the readers. No, Grace is not physically beaten, but she lives in fear of this man whose mood swings dominate her life. This is only touched upon in the first part of the book and it seems strange that it's not mentioned later. He is clearly abusive and it seems Green has made this a character "trait" rather than a theme to be dealt with. Grace also was clearly abused throughout her childhood by her bi-polar mother, but only feels guilt for "abandoning" her and shame for her mother's mental illness. I'm not saying that she needed to make this book about abuse, but I just think the abuse was more central to why Grace accepted the betrayal of Beth, her husband, and her friends. When she finally gets the right help she needs, it never involves confronting the abuse Grace endured her entire life. 
 A theme Green did spend a lot of time on was mental illness, and at times, I wanted to scream at the book when characters would regard those suffering from bi-polar as "crazy". I also was offended that Grace was ashamed of her mother's illness to the point she hadn't even told her husband of twenty years. Unfortunately, many sufferers of this disease deal with shame and they can't help it anymore than someone suffering from cancer. This is a major reason many don't pursue long-term treatment, and the outdated misconception that someone with bi-polar is "crazy" has to be stopped. I felt like Green tiptoed around that notion, but never resolved Grace's own misconception of the disease. There were definitely times when Green got it right in regards to mental illness especially when it came to the doctor who jammed every type of pharmaceutical down Grace's throat. But even that I found hard to believe because he was "supposedly" the best of the best when it came to psychiatry and that behavior is more typical of a GP who knows little on properly treating long-term mental illness. And I found it disconcerting that when Grace was told she didn't have bi-polar, poof... It was gone. She was weaned of the drugs and that was it. Even though she didn't have it, didn't mean she didn't need therapy to deal with the trauma she had endured her entire life. 
 And my last complaint - the ending! I wanted a satisfying end with Beth, the assistant and was so upset to not get it. This was where I really felt Green was going to tie in the mental illness since it was obvious that Beth was the one with a mental illness (and maybe even Ted, her husband). I think she could have really made this book more than just ChickLit by exploring more of Beth's motivations and especially explaining how Beth was able to do what she did. She uses the word "sociopath" at the end in regards to Beth, and I was close to believing it, but again, I wanted more on her - whether it demonized her or simply explains her behavior, we needed that to believe the entire story. 
 In the end, I just felt that Green introduced some fairly heavy themes and failed to do them justice by "Disney-fying" them. I realize that, yes, this is Chick Lit, but that doesn't mean that it has to be dummied down. There is a reason the word "lit" is in the genre's title and Green should've put a little more into the "lit" rather than just the "chick".

reference_books.title: Sworn to Silence (Kate Burkholder, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
For this genre (psy/thriller), this book is 100% 5 stars! I read it in one sitting if that tells you anything! I don't think a book of this type has ever had such a grip on me like this. A former Amish, female detective of a small town takes on a gruesome serial killer that is killing young girls in a way that I still can't shake. To boot, the detective has secrets of her own that ***might*** be the key to solving the murder, but can she take a chance at ruining her career by telling? 
 This book will have you guessing "whodunit" & as soon as you think you've, figured it out...BAM! Another twist in the plot! If you're a fan of Gillian Flynn's, DARK PLACES, you're sure to love this!

reference_books.title: And When She Was Good
reference_books.review_text:
An upscale madam, Heloise, has enjoyed the fruits of her labor for many years. She's came a long way from being the poor, "forgettable face" of an abusive father & neglectful mother to running a high-end escort service, living in a McMansion, and allowing her son to have the best that life can offer. She finds a balance between her life as a typical suburban soccer mom and not only running the secret escort service, but being a high paid escort herself. That was until "now" when she begins to fear her cushy life may be at jeopardy when her past comes back to haunt her. 
 Overall, this book was fun to listen to, but it was fairly forgettable. The main character was hard to like and if it weren't for her son, I wouldn't have "rooted" for her.

reference_books.title: Every Fifteen Minutes
reference_books.review_text:
For the genre, I'd give this book a 3.75. I really liked the author's choice of pov: shifting from the protagonist & the mystery antagonist in 1st person. It kept you guessing who it was throughout the entire book with several red herrings along the way; not to mention the fact the antagonist is a self-proclaimed "psychopath" & when it is his/her pov, he/she only discusses his/her answers on the psychopath test used in psychoanalytical settings, giving subtle hints to the identity of this person. I loved that! 
 I do feel this book (considering the genre) did a fantastic job at realistically portraying all sides of mental illness: from the scope of the severity of several disorders, to the inner workings of a psych ward, all the way to the character portrayals of those suffering from mental illness and to the characters' actions & reactions to the mentally ill. That did seem to honestly reflect the myriad of societal perspectives when it comes to the topic of mental illness in todays's world. It seemed that Scottoline was trying to voice the desperate need for society to start to listen and take action when it comes to the mentally ill. 
 All of that aside, again, I'd consider this a "roller coaster book" for me: fast, fun, twists & turns, but once the ride was over, it soon is forgotten. I think she could have delved a little more into the "mind of a psychopath" to have made the ending cleaner. I don't know any other way to really say it; the ending was just too messy for me. Overall, fun read, worth the "ride," but if the topic of psychopathy interests you in any way, I must recommend Jon Ronson's nonfiction best seller, "The Psychopath Test." Now that book really stays with you.

book_a.title: Gone Missing (Kate Burkholder, #4)
book_a.user_review:
After reading the third book, I worried that this series was at it's end of life for me because of the lack of evolution of the personality of Kate - the main character - in the series. Being a former Amish, Kate is emotionally torn between the two worlds as she leads the town as Chief of Police. The first two novels really brought that tension out along with creating new tension, but the third seemed to only reiterate her thoughts, feelings, etc. But in the latest book in the series, we finally see Kate evolve into a more confident, less alcoholic human being who isn't dwelling on the past, but has miles to go until she can live in the present. Her relationship with BCI detective "Tomasetti" isn't quite as stagnant as it's been, but Kate is still hesitant to commit. (I don't mind this at all because I'm not a huge fan of "romantic suspense", but I am getting a little tedious of their over-done relationship that doesn't even qualify as a relationship in their terms. Just move in together and get on with it!) 
 As far as the story goes, it did lack a sense of creativity like the others had. Basically, several Amish teens have gone missing over the past few years, and Kate is called in to help Ohio's BCI because of her background (and relationship to Tomasetti). Because of this, we are taken away from the small town of Painter's Mill and this is when I missed some of the other characters -especially Pickles and Mona! I had a hard time believing that Kate didn't figure out the "connection" sooner, making the first half a little slow because I guessed what "the connection" was (and I'm sure you will too). After she does figure it out, the book picks back up and once again we are taken on a wild ride where Kate puts herself in danger to defend and protect. 
 Overall, if you enjoy her other books, you'll like this one too. If you generally like suspense novels or cop dramas, you'll probably like this series.

sample_reviews.review_text: excellent series

"Gone Missing" by Linda Castillo was a fantastic read. I'm now hooked; I HAVE to read more of this author's novels. The story moves along at a swift pace and the characters, especially the main character, Kate, are authentic and likeable. I hated to close the book when I finished reading the last page!
Repetative, forced and memtioned past cases to many times.

GONE MISSING is the fourth book in the Chief of Police Kate Burkholder series. A complex series that should be read in order and one that once again finds deep rooted evil hiding behind the pastoral beauty of Ohio's Amish country. Long before she was Police of Chief of Painters Mill, Kate knew first hand that evil was present and could do horrible things. She knows that a missing child could mean several very bad things. 
 Agent John Tomasetti with the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation also knows what evil can do from direct personal experience. He knows what it usually means when a child goes missing. Tomasetti also knows that when the missing kids are Amish, he needs Kate's help. 
 This two missing kids are not the only ones. As Burkholder and Tomasetti work to keep their relationship secret and stop the abductions, a nightmare is continuing to unfold for the missing and their families. Because of the secrecy of the Amish, the nightmare has been going on for years and only now is starting to come to light. 
 This latest in the series from Texas author Linda Castillo is another hard hitting mystery featuring a complex case, depravity at its worst, and the ongoing complex relationship between Burkholder and Tomasetti. These characters have been fleshed out in great detail over the preceding three books which leads to an obvious turning point in their relationship. That detail as well as the current ever widening case is handled well and with a skillful touch. 
 This has been a powerful series since it began with Sworn to Silence. While Texas author Linda Castillo may have stepped away from the "silence" aspect of her titles, everything else readers of this series know and love remains fully present. Furthermore, this book continues the slow evolution of the Kate Burkholder character as she begins to feel a little more confident not just in her job, but as a woman who can have a real and positive relationship with a man. The bottom line is GONE MISSING is a complex, often very dark and extremely graphic mystery, that pulls no punches and will mess with your mind long after the last page.

Another good read in this series about a former Amish woman who is now the chief of police in a small town. Although the end felt muddled and the relationship between Kate and her beau just dragged on.

Castillo develops great characters and a wonderful storyline in her newest novel. The mystery is complex and almost unguessable until the end. Castillo's stories revolve around the Amish community and provide much interesting information about their life. A great page-turner.

Hmmm I'm really on the fence about this one. It was good but not great. And a 288 page hardcover? ReallY??? I have big issues with that ($$$) but I realize that's not on the author but the publisher. 
 1. The writing, all in first person this time, wasn't stellar (In previous it was a mix of first/prsent and third person which worked real well). I know 1st person is difficult but I also know what well done 1st person is and I'm SUPER PICKY about reading it. All the 'I see' or 'I saw' and 'I smelled' got old fast. 
 2. I know this is the fourth book in a series but the backstory felt forced as did the character descriptions of her team (really? Lady Gaga'esque was the best you could do for a character as great as Mona? Come on!! Plus...that's how you described her in book 3 also.) 
 3. How many times did we need to be told what Rumspringa is? It was in the book description AND in the book itself at least three times. We get it. 
 4. Without going back to look I'm pretty sure someone mentioned that farm used to be part of the Underground Railroad...so how did the main characters forget? 
 5. The whole thing with the suicide not ever really being figured out kinda bugged me. I hope there's another book because it felt very much like a loose thread. I know in real life we don't always get justice but that was SAD on so many levels. 
 That said there was enough to like to keep me going--and I guess I felt I had a vested interest after three books to see how this one played out. Glad Kate isn't drinking as much and really glad to see her relationship with Tomasetti is going places (at a nice pace I might add). 
 Maybe I had high expectations because I enjoyed the other books so much. None of these are deal breakers but I can see myself waiting for the trade paperback of her next book rather than shelling out for the hardcover.
Would actually give this 3 and a half stars. It was a good book just not as good as others in the series

Another good book in the series. This was better than the third book, so the author is still going strong in the series. 
 I liked this crime and the ending of it. It was finished but with the option to continue on in another book down the road. 
 What makes these books good is the characters in them. I love the building romance between Kate and Tomasetti. There relationship is getting stronger. I've said it before in another book review, but I love the pace of there building relationship. It wasn't fast with I love you's or let's live together. It feels natural. 
 We didn't get much of the usual characters or town this book but that didn't take away from the feel of the books. 
 I'm not on to read the next book in the series.
Not nearly as good as the first 3 but I plan to continue the series.

book_b.title: Find Me
book_b.user_review: This book had me at "hello" starting with a world destroyed by an incurable virus, a 19 year old, cough syrup sipping girl scouted out mysteriously because of her inexplicable immunity and an off-the-grid hospital where she is "lucky" enough to be shuttled to in hopes of "finding a cure." How could it go wrong? Oh but it does, way, way wrong. It felt like the author had developed this really great plot with a developed protagonist, but failed to put much thought into everything else...and I mean everything else from her interactions and relationships with the other characters, the actual other characters themselves, even the style of writing is inconsistent throughout the book. I kept my fingers crossed through part one, just waiting for all of "it" to come together, but by part 2, the whole story fell apart from there. It seriously felt like the author had put a lot of time & effort into the beginning and then threw together some haphazard middle and end, as if the idea of the book could make up for the book itself. Highly, highly disappointed. I want a re-write!( and the hours back I wasted reading it)

sample_reviews.review_text: I went from a 4 star to a 3 star because of the ending
Interesting at the start, but increasingly hard to follow.

Find Me is a dystopian novel set in the future after an illness wipes out most of the population. The writing is good, but the story feels unfinished. The novel ended with the main character on the brink of discovering something important about her past. I think the author hoped readers would feel the suspense of not knowing, but there were too many unanswered questions. The book ended so abruptly, I thought part of the story was missing. I listened to the ending twice to see if I had missed something important that would explain what happened. Without an ending to tie everything together the story fell apart. I feel like I had a better idea of what the author tried to achieve by reading the book's synopsis then I did from actually reading the book itself. I don't think this book reached it's full potential.
A strange dystopian novel along the lines of Station Eleven, Margaret Atwood, and Cormac McCarthy.

The story revolves around nineteen-year-old Joy and begins in a hospital where she is being held with seventy-four others. A plague only known as 'the sickness' has swept the world and killed hundreds and thousands. 
 My only problem with this novel is that it feels a bit aimless. There are a lot of questions without any answers or sense of closure. I do enjoy reading about dystopian worlds, as it's what seems to be popular at the moment, but this, unfortunately, didn't really cut it for me. I feel like the first half was eerie and exciting, but the second half just dragged out and by the end, it just felt like it was rushed. 
 I would like to thank NetGalley and Random House for providing me with an ARC in exchange for an honest review.

Laura van den Berg's debut novel Find Me is an engaging story about memory, forgetting, and the search for identity, set against the sciencefictional background of a mysterious plague (which apparently only affects the United States). Joy, the narrator, is a woman who was abandoned as an infant, grew up in a series of foster and group homes, and is working retail (where she steals cough syrup which she uses as a drug). When the plague strikes, she is contacted by a dying woman who gives her some clues about her birth mother, including a photograph. 
 Not long afterward she is contacted by an organisation conducting research on the plague. As Joy was exposed to the plague early on but has not developed symptoms, it is possible that she is immune. She agrees to participate in the research, and is taken, with 149 other possible immunes, to an isolated hospital in rural Kansas. 
 There is an odd, almost dream-like quality to Joy's experiences before, during and after her time in what she refers to as "The Hospital," a quality accentuated by the non-linear narrative. Events seem fraught with symbolism, and the plague is itself a metaphoric sort of apocalypse that reflects Joy's own issues with memory and traumatic amnesia. 
 Interesting but ultimately unsatisfying, largely because of the author's choice to use sciencefictional tropes but not fully engage with them.

I am a sucker for a dystopian novel. I enjoy a quirky protagonist. I love road trips. So I was primed to lodge this book. I save my one star ratings for those books I would never recommend and wish I could retrieve the time I wasted reading. 
 The book was divided into two parts:. Time spent in an experimental hospital and a road trip to find the mother she never knew. Part one started off interestingly but teetered on the edge of monotony as the days in the hospital varied little in its routine. The protagonist, Joy, almost does things several times. . . Almost. She ta!is about memory in short declarative statements with minimal introspection. Paer II we entirely aimless. She travels via bus and hitch hiking WITH A MAP and goes from Kansas to Pittsburgh to Charleston West VA to Memphis to Birmingham AL and on and on to get to KEY WEST! Few observations about any of these places and no emotional response. 
 There are major flaws in the book. Big hunks are spent on areas with no payoff such as the amount of time devoted to researching the person who may or may not be her mother and the non sensual stay at The Mansion. The end of the book just fades away with no resolution. The worst sin was the tone of the book. I think this is one of the most emotionless books I have ever read. No passion, no purpose, no drive. I reLly have no idea what the author was trying to say.
DNFed it at page 104. This is the second time I've tried to read it and it's just not happening.

I picked this up because I saw it on at least one Best of 2015 list (and I believe a strong review in a print magazine) but I had to force myself to finish it. The first half was pretty interesting, but the second was not only almost completely unrelated to the first, it became disjointed, inconsistent, tedious, self-conscious and contrived. It is a dire collapse of civilization indeed when some bathrooms in open, operating fast food restaurants continue to be well-stocked with paper towels, and SOME DO NOT. From other Goodreads reviews it looks like it's pretty polarizing. Wasn't the right book for me.

Every character seems to be mentally challenged - and many of them have drug addictions that make the reader distrust the story line. The story wanders, pointlessly, and never achieves any resolution.

reference_books.title: Small as an Elephant
reference_books.review_text: A well written book, although I did want to throw it at the wall a lot.

reference_books.title: The Eighth Day (Eighth Day, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Great book. Good ending. Ready for more!

reference_books.title: Ghost Hawk
reference_books.review_text: Historical fiction that feels episodic. At multiple times throughout the book I had to ask myself "What ending is this working towards?" While I like Susan Cooper's Dark Is Rising series and wish a movie with similar landscape and time feel to Lord of the Rings would be made, I can't seem to get into her historical fiction. This was okay, but nowhere near the top of my list for this year.

reference_books.title: Creepy Carrots!
reference_books.review_text: An okay but unusual book. Be careful not to read to any youngsters prone to irrational fears. Yet, it was funny for maybe first and second graders.

reference_books.title: The Island of Dr. Libris
reference_books.review_text:
Billy's summer adventure starts quickly as he finds a book to read. In the distance he hears sounds that seem like they are coming from the story. Then he sees the creatures from the book on a distance island--the island of Dr. Libris. 
 This fun story brings characters from classic stories to life. Modern characters get to interact with the classic characters and the results are hilarious!

book_a.title: Messenger (The Giver, #3)
book_a.user_review: My least favorite of the original Give trilogy. I felt like there was less for the reader to infer on his or her own. Also, I didn't like the ending much and didn't understand why Matty could not have used his gift earlier. It will be interesting to see what Lowry does with the fourth installment due out in fall of 2012.

sample_reviews.review_text: Not as well developed as the first two. And I didn't like the ending! There was so much more that could have been developed.
AAAAAAAAAHHH! The woods are alive!

This was the second time I read this book - although I didn't remember reading it before because of how underdeveloped it is. 
 In this book, Lowry tries to tie in the beauty of The Giver with the story of Gathering Blue. I say she tries because you can tell the whole book that is the only purpose of this book. It is extremely shallow compared to The Giver and disappointing. She tries too hard to add allusions and fails to develop these past the shallow mention of them. 
 ----------------------- 
 "'And so we would give up - or maybe even trade away - reading, and music, in exchange for the extreme excitement of pulling a handle and watching sourballs spit forth from a mechanical device?'" 
 He saw Forest and understood what Seer had meant. It was an illusion. It was a tangled knot of fears and deceits and dark struggles for power that had disguised itself and almost destroyed everything. Now it was unfolding, like a flower coming into bloom, radiant with possibility."

What do i think about this book? Too short for thorough comprehension. Just when you are about discovering things and people, the author had to end it. Yes, the ending was inevitable but as much dramatic as it was, i felt it did not explain most of the things needed explaining. Hence, the 4th book? Okay, let us give it the benefit of the doubt. Ill read Son soon. But to sum this all up, Matty is still my saving grace here while im glad to re unite some previous characters like Jonas and Kira. It breeds familiarity and relatable situations. This is an okay book for me.

This boy has been through a lot and is going on a big mission. He gets help a long the way. The ending wasn't what I thought it would be but the girl from Gathering Blue comes back in this outstanding book.

Starts pretty solid, starts to get silly when you realize how the "Trademaster" works. Not a fan of the whole "Trademaster" idea-it's pretty ridiculous and silly. I have to admit, for all the hype I was hearing, I was expecting more.

I am glad that I have finished the series. Finally everything was tied up in a neat bow. I loved this series and am glad I read it. I hope the make the rest of the books into movies but I feel that they could combine the last three books into a single movie.

Messenger almost completes The Giver and Gathering Blue. That really sums up Messenger. I wonder if Lois Lowry heard the lament of her readers about unresolved plot issues in both The Giver and Gathering Blue and wrote this, the shortest of the three books, in an attempt to resolve those issues. If so, she did not entirely succeed. 
 Messenger takes place several years after the end of Gathering Blue. The protagonist is Matty from that second novel. He is the Messenger of a rather enlightened village set in a dystopian world. Matty lives with Seer, the blind father of Kira, the protagonist of Gathering Blue. The head of Village is named Leader and is clearly Jonas, the protagonist from The Giver. 
 Lowry never lets the laws of physics get in the way of her story. There is an element of fantasy and magic in all three books and it is very strong in Messenger. While it is clear that the books occur on our world, the planet has changed in weird ways. The forest is alive in an almost conscious way, people have powerful psychic gifts and there is a strange magic going on with the Trademaster at the Trade Mart that is never fully explained. 
 The Trademaster is built up as some evil manipulator or, as another reviewer noted, a Satan like person stealing parts of people's souls. However, this great subplot is just dropped. Another plot problem is that in Gathering Blue we are told repeatedly that there is nothing dangerous in the forest but in chapter two of Messenger, someone is literally killed by the malevolent forest. The darkening forest becomes the core of the plot in Messenger. Lowry clearly has a problem with loose ends and problematic endings in her writing. 
 If you have read The Giver and Gathering Blue read Messenger, it will be an enjoyable addition but it does not stand up well alone. Only as the last of the three books does Messenger become an enjoyable adolescent or young adult novel.

I didn't have a big problem with this book, but as it's part of the series I expected it to feel like part of the series. 
 I adored the Giver and what I wanted to read was more about the community, how they dealt with the memories after Jonas left; I wanted to learn more about the committee and other people living in the community. 
 Instead we see Jonas as The Leader and using his seeing Beyond talents in a way that never truly made sense to me in terms of how it was revealed in The Giver. 
 The Giver series ended up being about magic and strange talents, rather than the amazing community created in the first novel, and that makes me so sad. 
 It wasn't the worst book ever, I did enjoy reading it, I just wish it hadn't been a part of the Giver series.

book_b.title: One for the Murphys
book_b.user_review:
A good solid book, but I was a little disappointed with the ending. I didn't think the state should have let her back with her mother after everything Carley had told the readers, but maybe the state didn't know all of that stuff. Still, I would have assumed that her mother would have had to have housing and a job, or welfare lined up before she took Carley back in. 
 A few times the conversations Carley was having with Mrs. Murphy about feelings were a little much and it was hard to imagine actual kids saying those things. 
 Still, I did like the book and stayed up really late to finish the second half of the book.

sample_reviews.review_text: A moving story about a young girl growing up in the foster care system. Hunt's writing grasps the complexities of puberty quite well. Carley Connors is a likable and quite believable character, whose vulnerability and courage will move you. For middle school readers that desire to read more realistic fiction, it's a winner.

I read this book in one evening. I cried several times. There were a few silly errors in this book but I still give it five stars because I think it can really give new perspective to some people and it really moved me. I loved Carly, I understood Carly and I rooted for her throughout. This is one of those books that, upon completion, makes me feel "full." I'm not looking to read another book immediately upon finishing this one because I just want to let this one sit for a little while. It's been awhile since I've read a book that I truly wanted to just reflect on and...honor a bit, before moving on.
I enjoyed this book because I don't often find ya fiction that centers on foster care.
Definitely a contender for the Newbery as well. So good. I kind of want to run out and sign up as a foster parent now.

Carley is a foster child. Her life before being assigned to the Murphy family was unpredictable and violent at times, including the latest episode that landed her in the hospital. She learned to look out for herself. So she doesn't quite understand the affection she sees between the members of the Murphy clan, nor does she feel worthy of that kind of love herself. She does not belong to this clean, ordered world...until she kind of does. Little by little, she's able to let her guard down and let the Murphys into her heart. But foster situations change often, and this one is no exception. 
 I tend to search out books about foster children, and I was happy to see this offering by Hunt. Carley, for all her tough outer persona, was sweet and a bit fragile inside. The Murphys weren't perfect, but they tried. It left me with a hopeful feeling for Carley. 
 I have to admit, this felt like the rose-colored glasses version of foster care. That's not necessarily a bad thing. Carley eventually wins everyone over in the Murphy family, she and Mrs. Murphy connect on a deeper level, and Mrs. Murphy is able to give her a much-needed boost of self-confidence to change her own future. I closed the book thinking, "I hope that's really what happens for Carley." 
 My experience with foster care (admittedly quite limited) made this book seem a bit syrupy. While we had many of those sweet moments of connection (our boy was with us for 4 years,) we also experienced rage, defiance, and complete disregard for us and our house rules. So. Carley's biggest angry moment was mouthing off to a waiter her own age in a restaurant. One time. Carley, you can come live at my house anytime! 
 It was hopeful and encouraging. Not so realistic, but maybe that's okay too. Hopeful is good.
Heartwarming. Filled with lots of little moments of lovely writing.
All the children's librarians in my department have been reading this one. I read in one day and did not want it to end. The author creates wonderful characters and dialogue.
Every east side Osseo school needs several copies of this book. It is real, honest and ultimately uplifting.
Good book. Hit a few sensitive spots for me. But love it.

I hadn't heard of this book until a friend recommended it to me, and I'm so very glad she did. I needed to read this book. The longer I teach the more I realize what a sheltered life I've led, and books like this help me begin to understand a bit better what lives other people lead. What we see on the outside isn't always what's going on on the inside, and sometimes we need to listen in a different way. 
 One for the Murphys will definitely be a part of my classroom book collection. 
 First read: July 2014 
 Re-read: December 2015

reference_books.title: Bite Me If You Can (Argeneau #6)
reference_books.review_text: An excellent - and often entertaining - addition to the series, which fans of vampire themed romance novels will love.

reference_books.title: Poughkeepsie (Poughkeepsie Brotherhood, #1)
reference_books.review_text: The characters were well developed, and the plot was pretty good in general. However, the constant head-hopping made it difficult for me to connect with any given character so as to really get in to the book, and the excessive use of curse words spoiled the story for me.

reference_books.title: Vampire Most Wanted (Argeneau, #20)
reference_books.review_text: The descriptions of the violence of one character described to another by a thirdd near the end of the book - while thankfully not as detailed as they might have been - were unpleasant to read. In fact, some would say the entire last few chapters are a bit disturbing as the truth is revealed. However, I did take some comfort from the fact it's made clear that this sort of behaviour is not considered acceptable, so I was able to push past those things and focus on enjoying the rest of the book. Still, those things make me feel I can't give this book the full five stars.

reference_books.title: The Long Winter (Little House, #6)
reference_books.review_text: I think this is my favourite of the series so far. The book itself is an enjoyable read, and reading about how people coped through the long Winter was fascinating.

reference_books.title: Little House on the Prairie (Little House, #2)
reference_books.review_text: A fascinating and enjoyable read for all ages.

book_a.title: Angel Evolution (The Evolution Trilogy, #1)
book_a.user_review: This is a reasonably good read; not amazing, but pretty good. The plot is interesting and the way angels and demons are portrayed is unusual.

sample_reviews.review_text:
As the one star rating proclaims: I didn't like it. 
 It has the standard YA formula and offers nothing new really. 
 The characters are confusing, it's either they have some sort of complex especially the protagonist Taylor. 
 Why I had to shelve this book as DNF 
 Page 137 
 "She knew then that she was in love with an angel. 
 Abruptly, her life had meaning. She knew that this boy--this 
 angel!--had something to do with her purpose in life." <<<---- Taylor had this revelation/epiphany and they were just on their 2nd date and according to Gabriel's POV he was testing Taylor is she is indeed "The One" 
 Yep, totally shelving this one.

Dnf. 
 It started of good with a lot of potential and then it turned into something similar to twilight.

I tried to like this book, I really did! I just couldn't... 
 It was so similar to other stories I had read, I groaned inwardly when I finished the first part of the book. 
 It's not just the book, it's what it was about, that made me feel so negatively towards the entire novel. Maybe if it was the first time I had encountered this plot and idea of the book, 
 I would have felt differently but no such luck :( 
 I have read similar book to this, and because of that, I can't say I liked it. I twas just so...ordinary. 
 The Plot: 
 This is ALL you need to know: 
 There's this pretty, "special" girl who just doesn't know it. In addition, she has no idea she is pretty. Both of these factors lead to her low self esteem. (And she's socially awkward, but that's a given lately in YA fiction.) 
 Then comes the guy. He's hawt, of course, but he has a secret agenda! He has a mission. It involves her and it isn't good... 
 Not that she knows that! Yet... 
 But when he's with her, she feels so special! 
 But what will happen when she finds out his secret? 
 And what will happen to him when he fails his mission and falls in love with the target? (Or does he?........) 
 The Protagonist: 
 Taylor: 
 She was like a brick, no personality at all. It didn't even seem like she loved her family. She was happy to get away from her dad and had no connection to her brother. Her brother, she claimed didn't care about her, well how is that? There is no evidence to support that and how can you not love your sibling? No matter what, even if you hate them you still FEEL something towards them, have some sort of a connection. It's simply not possible to feel NOTHING towards your bro or sis! 
 Also, when meeting Gabriel, she didn't change out of her sweatpants or put makeup on because "that's the kinda girl she is". 
 Wow! You're sooooo deep bella, I mean Taylor! Hehehe 
 I think the author was trying to make her come across as deep or so sophisticated and mature by making her the atypical girl but the effect was that she seemed like she was trying TOO hard to be "different" which makes her seem no different than anyone else. 
 Overall Impression: 
 This book was a hard read for me because it was so dull and uninteresting. By page 43, I had had enough of this book. I wanted to put it down, but because of the deadline, I plunged on. If I could have abandoned this book, I would have. There was nothing that struck out to me about the book, neither the characters or plot nor the writing style. Everything seemed...average. 
 The plot was not engaging, especially in the beginning and it continued to drag on. The characters were mediocre and I felt no real connection to any of the half-developed characters. Taylor, the protagonist who was a college student, seemed like such a brick head sometimes, I felt hatred towards her. She was another faceless girl who fell deeply in love with the hawt guy, who just so happened to be evil. There was nothing about that made me even remotely interested in her, if she fell of a cliff, I would wouldn't even blink my eyes. Maybe I would cheer if I bothered to pay attention...

4.5 stars 
 So, "Angel Evolution" is like a big tasty looking slice of pizza that you don't know what the ingrediens are, but it confuses your senses with the yummy smell and once you get a bite you cannot do anything but eat it all...(sry for the food analogy) 
 First of all, I must properly appologise to the author and to myself(i had a guilty conscience) for not finishing this book earlier. It's not because I didn't like it(Oh My Gabriel! -it was amazing), it's just because time was not on my side. 
 The author, David Estes is such a nice guy that if you ask him what's the book about, he will tell with such passion that you'll feel captivated before you even start reading it. 
 As you can see from the pretty cover and the title: "Angel Evolution", this is a story bout angels and where there are angels, there are demons. Well, one thing I got to say: FORGET THE BIBLE's view on these creatures and prepare yourself for this book to rock your world. 
 I won't say any details because I'm afraid I'll spoil all the fun. 
 The game between good and evil, dark vs light, was so much fun that it made me confused sometimes. One of the greatest gifts of a brilliant book is to make you feel confused. 
 I love the romance/game between Taylor and Gabriel, because it brought out memories of another couple(the sexy, mischievous angel Patch from "Hush Hush") and because it kept me on edge: is he toying with her? does he love her? does he want to harm her? ...and many other questions... On the other hand, I also love Sam and Chris...imagine the cute easy-going cheerleader and a friendly...well demon...one word: ORIGINAL. 
 Fav. Quotes: 
 "Two guys asking me out in two days, now that is a record, Taylor thought. But neither of them human, she laughed to herself. Just her luck." 
 "I am shocked that I didn't wake up. It's a bit disappointing that I didn't get to experience another trip on the greatest amusement park ride around." 
 "Taylor continued to stare at David, marveling at his resemblance to her boyfriend. Interrupting the brothers' conversation she said, "You look so much like your brother, David." "Yeah, sadly it's a curse I will just have to live with," David joked. Taylor laughed and said, "Yeah, true. Gabriel is a bit awkward looking. But I bet you still have girls lining up for you."" 
 "One time Sampson was supposed to be marching with the 4th Quadrant of ground soldiers, but he was so tired that he fell asleep just outside the battle doors with his head against a rock. Despite the epic battle that occurred that day, he slept through the entire thing. He almost got kicked out of the army because of it." 
 I might be wrong, but I feel that Gabriel's little brother David is the author's alter-ego. We all know that every book blooms from a single idea and then characters start to live, breathe by themselves...I think the "David" character is an inside joke of this amazing author so that he can keep a close eye on the charcters' real personalities so he can better describe it to his readers. 
 All in all, the "Angel Evolution" was an EPIC WIN...I really loved it and I hope I'll read the next books soon..

I really enjoyed reading this book. I rather enjoyed the fact that the angels and demons were not based on religious/biblical aspects. Every character played a perfect role in the events that were presented. Talk about emotional rollercoaster! 
 Quick little summary: 
 Taylor is a laid back non-attention seeker heading to her first semester of college. And while at college her world changes. She meets a gorgeous boy who comes in and sweeps her off her feet. Gabriel, who happens to be an angel and rather quickly becomes her boyfriend. Gabriel tells her about his heritage but everything he tells her are lies. That the angels want to protect the humans from the demons and that they need her help. 
 She not only falls for him but her for her. And even though she really cares for him deep down she senses something is off. All the lies Gabriel tells soon catch up with him and he doesn't know how to get out of the jam they are in. 
 There is way more to this story then what I have written and I highly recommend you give it chance. 
 Over all this was a very unique story and im glad I gave it a chance, now on to book 2!
Review coming soon...

This novel certainly kept me interested. It was an entertaining read and one that had me wanting to continue turning page after page to work out where it was going and what would happen in the end. It was brilliantly executed and I am glad that I got the chance to read it. I also cannot wait to continue reading the second book in the trilogy and look forward to finding out what will happen next! This was an easy, steady and well-flowing story that kept me curious right up until the very last page. 
 One of the things that I liked most about this novel was the concept of angels and demons. I, for one, haven't read all that many angel novels but I can tell that this is an extremely original storyline. This isn't a novel about the angels from heaven or the demons from hell, but instead their history is a little different. I loved to read how they came about, but especially loved how as a reader, you weren't entirely convinced by the story due to it being explained in first person by an unreliable narrator. I found that this was a curious device used by David Estes and I have to admit, it definitely kept me hooked! 
 This was the same throughout the novel. It is told in switching POVs throughout the novel but instead of being frustrating or hard to keep concentration, this was a nice touch. I liked that we were able to see how all the different people within the novel were feeling during the most climatic moments. David really managed to become the omniscient narrator without it becoming confusing or irritating. If anything, these ever-changing POVs actually captured my attention more as I flicked through the pages waiting for certain things to happen or watching to see how certain things would play out. It was definitely an intriguing style. 
 I really liked Taylor and Samantha and their relationship with each other. It was totally noticeable that they had been friends since childhood and I loved that they were almost complete opposites and yet still got along really well. I liked how strong Taylor was, how she wasn't going to just back down just because someone said she should. But I also liked that, despite this, she let her love for a boy overcome her. While it is something we all aim to never let happen, it is just one of those things that happens and I like how believable she makes it feel by trying to remind herself that she is independent... and then he says or does something that makes her feel weak at the knees. She has the all-knowing weakness that really manages to bring out her character. 
 I liked Gabriel to an extent, but I also found him quite hard to get along with. I'm not entirely sure where I stand with him. At first I didn't like him at all, but mainly because of his POV. Then, I started to like him slightly as I realised that he felt slightly conflicted but then I just sort of lost that for a bit. I guess I just didn't really connect with his character. I didn't feel sorry for him at the ending, I just felt sorry for Taylor. There was no rooting for him, or hoping that it would work out for him. I guess, in a way, I felt slightly betrayed by his character and it was hard to believe that his last act really changed everything else he had done until that point. But then, maybe that's because he was really meant to be the antagonist of this novel. 
 Christopher, on the other hand, I absolutely adored. He was so caring and kind and only ever had Taylor's (and Sam's) best interests at heart and I just loved that in him. I loved the contradiction that came along with him as well and truly adored it when he explained to Sam about who and what he was and what he could do. He was so patient and admiring and yet, at the same time, there was a hint of something else behind his eyes as well. He knows that his race isn't perfect, but he's just glad that Sam didn't run a mile upon finding out what he was. Yes, I did like Chris. 
 In fact, I think I probably preferred Chris and Sam's relationship to Gabe and Tay. I just found the romance flowed better between them and felt more realistic. I believed that Tay and Gabe did love each other, but I also felt it was a little forward and you didn't really get to see why they did. Although, there was one scene, one look that Gabe gave Tay that stole my heart from my chest but then there was even more of those from Sam and Chris. Either way, this novel has enough romance and couples to satisfy most readers and is just another thing that makes it a good novel to read. 
 All in all this was a lovely novel to read. There was nothing spectacular about it that made me truly inspired by its words but it also wasn't a bad novel. I would read it again easily and I am most certainly interested in reading the rest of the trilogy. I have heard that it gets better in the next books and cannot wait to see why. I look forward to finding out what happens in the next leg of the story and hope that my thoughts about Gabe can be transformed. I also hope to see lots more of Chris. This was a good starting novel to this trilogy and I would recommend it to anyone that wants something that is slightly different and truly unique. 
 I received this novel for review from the Goodreads 'Shut up and Read' group as part of their Read it and Reap program. I am extremely glad that I got the opportunity to read this and hope that I will inspire others to pick it up as well. It is currently only $0.99 from Smashwords!

Everything you think you know about angels is turned on its head in David Estes' Angel Evolution. 
 This fast-paced story grabs your attention with Taylor's dream of two strangers and a snake, and just takes off. The plot moves quickly as Taylor enters high school and establishes a group of friends, which includes her high school best friend, Sam, Gabriel, and Christopher. The story is set up so that it appears that the boys and Taylor will end up in your typical love triangle, but you quickly see that little about the world Estes has created is as it seems. The interactions between Taylor, Gabriel, and Christopher are defined by the author's new take on angel and demon lore that even removes God from the equation. It is difficult to know who Taylor can trust, since everyone seems to want something from her. 
 Angel Evolution also features an atypical heroine. Taylor is written how female leads should be written-she's offbeat, possesses great inner strength, and is completely likeable. Like most teenagers, Taylor is still finding herself and sometimes doubts her inner voice and intuition, but that is part of growing up and even when she makes mistakes Taylor tries to ensure that she is staying true to herself as much as possible. 
 Gabriel starts out as very mysterious, but I also thought he was kind of a jerk. Many "bad boys" do unlikeable things, but secretly have a heart of gold. Gabriel, however, isn't introduced through unkind actions or words, but his intentions toward Taylor are clearly not in her best interest. It's a nice spin on the typical strong girl meets bad boy story line we've come to expect. 
 Readers who do not appreciate the second male in a triangle will likely not take to Christopher, who comes into the story later. The plot is not set up for the reader to like him initially, but I found myself flip flopping between routing for Gabriel and routing for Christopher. This pair provides an interesting reversal over the black and white/good and bad/angel and demon dichotomy that has become a cliche in our culture. 
 If you're looking for a novel packed with action and a fresh spin on angels, Angel Evolution should be on your to-be-read list.

I don't know what to think anymore. This trilogy drove me crazy. I couldn't stop reading it since the moment I picked up the first book. But, if I had a physical copy of 'Acceptance', I would have tossed it across the room the moment I have finished, due to sheer frustration. 
 The momentum builds up so much at certain moments just to get dissipated without amounting to anything. It's as if someone was filling-up a balloon and stopping short of bursting it, only to start letting the air out slowly. 
 Although the biologist's character managed to be salvaged, I have issue with the rest. Just as I have suspected, Control's character is absolutely and utterly irrelevant to the plot. The whole of the second book could have been told from the perspective of Grace, which would have been more interesting. If any answers were provided concerning the Severances' implication in the genesis and/or maintenance of Area X, it would have justified the need for a one dimensional character like Control. Unfortunately, none were provided and the bitterness of having to endure 'Authority' washes over you in waves. 
 Overall, the Southern Reach trilogy was a hell of a ride. Read the first book, I wouldn't recommend the rest.

I started this book and was confused immediately. I actually don't know why it was on my kindle if it's the third in a series, but I would strongly recommend watching the first two, but from what I read I couldn't really say that it would be any better.

Glancing at other reviews, there seems to be a divide between those disappointed by the lack of answers, or by the over-resolution of the answers. Because there's a bit of both here. Vandermeer has a lot of pieces on the board by the end of book 2, then introduces several more early in the one, but in the end it rather feels like a post-hoc answer, rather unconvincingly delivered via a flash of understanding or vision, is left to smooth over various other discarded plot pieces or lines of progress that eventually lead nowhere. There's a strength and weakness in that this volume is Acceptance as well: in some ways the story takes an unexpectedly gentler path of easing-out, which perhaps is tied to broader, possibly quite well-chosen themes, but which also robs the story of its early atmosphere and intensity. I'm left with rather a rather non-specific sense of underwelm, which perhaps is inevitable after a beginning so perfectly calibrated for fascination. Do I want more explanation, or less? Perhaps just something different. Different from what we already knew or felt from the earlier volumes. The new aspect, I suppose, is exactly this kind of elegaic slow-fade of acceptance of the world as it is and now must be, which may be the stronger ending in some way than something more climactic, but it is hampered in this by the other attempts at resolution, at climax, that flicker in and out here, as if Vandermeer lacked full commitment to the course he'd set, or never fully chose between several.
You needed a 3rd book for that? Jeeze.

I am glad to have finished this series, even though there are few enough answers for all the questions raised throughout the series. I think I enjoyed this one best - I liked that the story was presented through several different points of view. It made the story seem more satisfying in spite of the gaps in answers. I did not really appreciate that one of those points of view was second-person - it strikes me as affected. But overall the tone of this book seems to nail the sort of creepy suspense that the previous books lacked.

I made it to the end, though I skimmed that last quarter. I figured what could be said that wasn't already said a dozen times or more. 
 So many characters, so many names, and each person telling the same story over and over. No answers, only questions, and dull boring people, or people pretending to be people, or other things pretending to be people. 
 My favorite quote, "There was a comet dripping fire through his head, trailing flame down his back". It means nothing but they are great words. 
 This sums up the whole series: "You could know the what of something forever and never discover the why". I should have stopped there and read something else.
Per the directive of the title, I've accepted I've wasted my time. Enough said.

I was not overwhelmed with the final segment of this series, unfortunately. I loved Annihilation, I enjoyed Authority, but I found Acceptance to be... well... acceptable but not as entrancing as the first novel. The prose was just as mesmerizing as the other two, but certain things seemed to drop off for me. Ghost Bird becomes quite uninteresting when you find out what she is; there is nothing to know about her anymore (what I enjoyed about the first novel was how much you stayed inside the Biologist's head). And Control went from being an interesting and intriguing main character to a near-useless sidekick; all he does is follow Ghost Bird around, but we don't get nearly enough of his internal monologue or feelings or input (and they don't even get together! ). He might as well have just been left behind in book 2. The same with Grace - I found her completely useless. It's like both Grace and Control were there to fulfill one purpose at the end and other than that their presence was superfluous. Given how much they contributed to the plot, tone, and everything else, it might have been more interesting to just follow Ghost Bird around, as boring as she turned out to be in the end. 
 The only part I really liked was the sections with the Lighthouse Keeper, though I still am not 100% sure I understand what the heck happened there regarding certain matters (Why did the initial organism land in the lighthouse lens? Why were the S&S people even there in the first place before the alien transformation happened? Why can't we just bomb the shit out of Area X if it's going to take over everything? I'm pretty sure fire kills a lot of things. Especially biological things. ). I also thought the second person perspective with the Director was well done (because second person is hard to pull off without alienating your reader) but also less-than-fulfilling in terms of resolving mysteries. We learn nothing else about Lowry, Control's mother or Central from the Director. Instead of Gloria's perspective, why not Control's mother or Lowry's? They could have told the Gloria story but also answered other questions. 
 Overall, I give the series 4/5, but this one gets a 3. Kind of a buzzkill, really.

..huh? 
 I'm not sure why I bothered to finish this series all the way through. The first book was.. weird. There's no other way I can think to describe it right now. And I'm usually ok with weird but the writing style didn't do it for me. But it went by fast and I thought it was a setup for something more compelling. I think I wanted to like it more than I did. I keep changing my rating because I don't really know how I felt about it. I'm letting its potential dictate my feelings towards it. 
 The second book was exhausting. I was completely indifferent to the characters and it was kind of boring. For something so high concept, I am not sure how it could be so uninteresting. But I stuck it out to the bitter end because I had stupidly already purchased the third book. I was able to finish it faster than the second book, thankfully, because I was just so determined to be done with it. And for what? I still don't really understand what happened. I mean, I do in the most basic sense. But there was so little payoff. So little point to any of it. There was too much going on.. and yet it was still kind of boring. 
 Now I'm afraid to start something new. I feel like so much brain power was used deciphering this that I need a break from reading altogether.
