sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 Mark Kurlansky is currently a New Yorker who worked for several years as a doc worker and as a cook and pastry chef. His degree was in theater, but he turned to journalism not long after graduating. His journalistic resume boasts of a number of different books, magazine contributions and articles published around the world. He's received numerous rewards for his exceptional narration, philosophical substance and tongue-in-cheek observations of the global evolution of fishing. I agree with one of these things; he does, in fact, talk about the global evolution of fishing. 
 Any fish enthusiast around the world could easily find their attachment to Mr. Kurlansky's book. Included in his number of geographical mentions are New England and the US in general, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, Canada in general, Latin America and the Americas in general, Iceland, Norway, Denmark, Germany, Holland and the Netherlands in general, Scotland and Britain in general, France, Belgium, Portugal and Spain, West Africa, Japan and Asia in general. Almost anyone, regardless of their country of origin, could find a connection with this book-so long as they are really, really, really a die hard, relentless fan of...cod. And who of us isn't? 
 Mr. Kurlansky knows his literature, music, newspaper headlines and extremely old school cookbooks, as he takes quotes and recipes from these sources and makes them the introduction to every chapter. Occasionally, he throws a fish ball or fish head recipe (or three) in the middle of the chapter, just in case we were bored of reading his endless facts about fish and the progressive methods in which they've been caught. 
 This is not your typical book. There is no love affair, no resolution, and no story line. While Kurlansky does attempt to walk you through the history of fishing, he occasionally jumps years, so it's difficult to say that the book even follows a strict chronological order. While you can predict that you will be taken from early 1900's to late 1900's, there's nothing that stops him from taking you from 1960 back to 1940 and on to 1980. Instead of a story, this book is 276 pages of facts. The only tale that is spoken of here is the kind that gets thrown in bouillabaisse. However, if you are preparing to be a contender on Jeopardy, this is definitely a helpful piece to familiarize yourself with. 
 For a history buff, particularly one who has an interest in maritime and or the discovery of new countries, this is a great book. It's also a great book for anyone who has ever been curious about the method of trawling, or what vegetable should be served with fish tongue. Since I often lie in bed awake at night pondering the correlation between fish and the French and Indian war or why I always have to ask for the mysteriously fluctuating "market price" when I'm considering seafood for dinner, the fishy facts that I have learned from reading "Cod" have helped me sleep better at night. 
 For those who have not had a chance to read this, I've decided to condense the part two of this uniquely structured book from page 112-125. With the exception of small words and repetitive sentences this is what a reader can expect to hear. 
 There are harsh conditions of icy water. Fishermen commonly lose fingers from frostbite, line snags or machinery. A fisherman is forced into retirement when he looses too many fingers. Fishermen have a sense of the elite brotherhood "like combat veterans." No Social benefits go to fisherman; as they are self-employed and struggle economically. The max age for fisherman is typically 50. The number of Gloucester fisherman lost at sea between 1830 an 1900 was 3,800. That number is 70% grater than all American casualties in the war of 1812. Many vessels are lost by high winds and large waves. Fishermen have the highest fatal accident rate of any type of worker in North Atlantic countries. The Canadian and French have an agenda to get government to financially support their fishing industry. Once frozen food idea came along, the entire nature of commercial fishing would change. 
 Environmental tragedy and impending sense of doom due to the evolution of industry and nations at war for over-fished cod is the tone that the book ended on. For instance, Kurlansky tells of the financial hardship of his former industry. 
 "In 1989, a study by the UN food and Agricultural organization estimated that it costs $92b to operate global fishing. Revenue was only $72b." 
 Kurlansky also tells us that out of work fisherman resort to becoming the skippers of tourism. This is apparently a huge insult that requires much swallowing of pride to the men who once risked their lives at sea. These statements are meant to evoke sympathy for these men and their line of work in the reader. While it is difficult to see anyone have to take what they consider a downward move in their career, I imagine these moves are typical in any industry and it's difficult for me to sympathize more with these characters than with anyone else who has ever been demoted or lost their job. 
 The best summary of this book is probably given in the quote Kurlansky uses on page 158 of his tribute to Cod. It is simply a quote from 20th century Icelandic novelist Halldor Laxness, who states, " Life is saltfish." 
 Fin.

Rating: 3.75* of five 
 Victorian scientists said that cod was the fish in the miracle of the loaves and fishes because there were so darn many of them.... 
 Yeah, late to the party yet again...13 years late. I read this book, I would swear, when it came out; I recognized a few of the anecdotes, and I remember the jacket design very clearly. But a lot had slipped from my memory, and I now wonder if I actually read it, or had enough conversations about it to think I had. 
 Well, whatever, if it was a re-read it was a fun one. I like Kurlansky's informative-yet-chatty style, and I love the angle of view in the book...what's cod done for us as a species? So what? What's cod made possible in the world? The rise of an independent America. The agrarian horrors of African chattel slavery. The Industrial Revolution. Little stuff like that was built on the white-fleshed back of a formerly abundant fish. 
 I like cod. Salted, dried, fresh-frozen, the tongues, the cheeks...it's all good, as my daughter's generation says with monotonous regularity (and questionable factual basis). I never once thought about Cod, the deliverer from hunger, until the Cod Wars of the early 1970s. I remember the world reaction to Iceland going to a 200-mile fishing limit with a teenager's detached bemusement: "So? Little teeny place like that, let 'em have it, big whoop." For rhetorical effect, let's assume I was sitting in front of the TV eating Gorton's fish sticks at the time I said this, though I spent little time with the TV and less eating fish sticks as a kid. 
 It caused such trouble because of cod's enormous significance even now as an agribusiness output. Iceland's post-colonial economy was built on cod; Canada's Maritime provinces relied on it in those days (and on unemployment payments from the rest of Canada now that cod's commercially extinct); Norway and the UK want all there is to have so their fisheries industries don't wither away and leave them hungry as well as sailor-less. 
 Kurlansky wrote a very enjoyable read about a very important food-source and industrial product. I recommend it to anyone even marginally interested in the world around them, to science browsers, and to policy wonks of a scientific bent. You won't regret it.

Fascinating account of the importance of cod to the nations bordering the North Atlantic and the part that cod and fishing for cod has played in their history and economies. The text is interspersed with historical recipes on how to cook cod and the different ways different nationalities like to eat it. From the heyday of cod fishing when huge catches were possible to more recently when over-fishing has drastically reduced cod stocks this is an unusual look at an unexpectedly important fish. An interesting read.

This book gets a lot of love. I've never understood why, except perhaps because Kurlansky's choice of a non-traditional subject for 'historical' analysis (a pattern he is now milking shamelessly) seemed 'innovative'. I found most of the early chapters completely sensationalist and unbelievable, at least for their historical plausibility. As a pop-history he eschews detailed sources, and so pretty wild claims about Basques and others are left hanging ... Ultimately in such a short work the big picture ends up being impressionistic and unconvincing. Nice idea, but poor execution.

This book was published in 1999 and changed how people thought about the seafood that they eat. It tells the story of man's relationship to cod, a species once so prolific in the Atlantic that it was said that you could walk across the ocean on the backs of cod. But, through overfishing the species has been decimated, forever changing the working life of many communities on the eastern seaboard. Cod is integral to the life and culture of communities in Newfoundland, Iceland and Massachuesetts and in the kitchens of England, Spain, and France. 
 The most moving part of the storyline (this book truly is narrative non-fiction) is how fisherman in one country blame the fisherman in another country for the overfishing. The Canadian's blame the Massachusetts fisherman, the English blame the Spanish, and the Icelanders blame the English. No one fully acknowledges their own countries rule in the problem. The book also discusses how Iceland changed international law regarding territorial waters pushing it out 200 miles from their coast - the little country that could in terms of cod preservation. 
 The book also discussed how the Basque found the fertile Northern Banks but told no one else about their discovery and failed to claim the land as their own. What a difference that would have made in the geography of the new world. This is just one of the many interesting historical facts this book has to offer. 
 About 40% of the book is cod recipes - something that I did not anticipate. Normally, I like a good recipe, but after reading this book, eating cod was not something that I was inspired to do - saving a few thousand - not eat one. So, I found this to be a bit of an odd choice by the author. 
 Foodies, history buffs, and fans of books like Outliers that connect miscellaneous facts into a strong narrative line will like this book. But, codfish is a bit of an obscure of the average reader so I think the readership may be a bit limited. This is also a good choice for college students taking classes in food sustainability (my son had such a class at his university so I know that these classes are offered).

I love micro-histories. And this book is an excellent example of the genre. Going back to the Vikings, Kurlansky explores the entire commercial history of cod. From its involvement in colonizing and enriching New England, to its roles in the slave trade and the American Revolution, to the national and economic battles now fought over the few remaining cod. If you've ever wondered why cod is so popular or how it became the poster child for overfishing, this book has the answers. Kurlansky's writing is Easy to read and understand, but packed with knowledge. And the pages are enriched with beautiful pictures and illustrations of the people and places profiled in cod's biography. The end of each chapter also includes a historic recipe for cod. These extra elements, especially the pictures, added to the reading experience. Highly recommend for other history buffs and fish fans.
Finally!!!!

If you enjoy popular nonfiction such as The Perfect Storm, Longitude, or A Walk in the Woods, you'll enjoy this book. The connecting thread is that in each of these, the author uses an interesting narrative angle to describe historical trends and scientific facts without being overly pedantic or dry.

Great historical book about humankind's history of fishing Cod. It takes us from Vikings, through the middle Ages in Europe to early North American Settlers up to present day. It shows how much of Northern Europe and North American development and wealth was initially founded on the Cod industry. Also goes into today's overfishing of Cod in New England and political battles over North Atlantic Cod fishing rights. If you like history this book is great.

This is a real favourite of mine and Mark Kurlansky is a favourite writer. Who would have thought a single species of fish could tell such a story? Kurlansky's history of New York, told through the oyster (really!), and '1968' are also highly recommended.

reference_books.review_text:
One star for the Malfoys. One star for Harry's (long overdue) character development. One star for the bit with the "wibbly-wobbly timey-wimey" that allowed me to enjoy my favorite character (albeit horribly mischaracterized) even for a while again. 
 One star because two feels too generous. This has nothing to do with the fact that this is a script. I know scripts. I know the format and how it works. I'm not judging that here. I'm judging content. And this content was pretty insulting to what this story's history is/represents. This had so many flaws, so much disregard for actual canon that I can't help but be convinced that Jo didn't really get an active role in the making of. Her name here is just a hook. She may have authorized this (although I can't figure out her train of thought at doing so) but this is not her story. This book just killed me! 3 But i loved every twist and feels it gave out.

Percy and Annabeth 
 Well, the two heroes that I like best are back (they get their storyline). They go through the depths of the evilest place in the world and happen to make a few friends while they're at it also. The other heroes all go through their quests with their quirks and their powers beginning to show. We also learn of Nico and what is vital to him (why he does everything he does). It feels like there are too many characters in this series. I don't know about you, but I'm getting exhausted switching between so many characters and trying to keep the stories intact. 
 Thoughts 
 I feel like I read this book ages ago. I've started writing again so my mornings for reading have gotten shorter. I read this on a plane from Munich to Edinburgh and back again. So, this book has travelled quite a bit with me. I find it nice to read on aeroplanes, it's relaxing and gives you something to do for the shorter (1-4 hour) flights to do. 
 Themes 
 Now, I like to mention themes in all my new reviews. Obviously, since Percy and Annabeth survive in the worst place possible, through impossible odds, one theme I believe prevalent here is the idea of good v. evil. That there is inherently evil people in this world (monsters), and there are good people in this world (heroes). That good will overcome all obstacles. We almost see Percy turn evil at one point of the story, but Annabeth saves him from himself and talks Percy out of the act of evilness. I believe this also plays into the theme of good v. evil, but in another way, in that, there are good and bad sides to everyone. We also see this (spoiler alert) with one of the Titans, who should be an evil creation, but he turns out to be a really good guy. 
 I guess another theme in this book would also be courage. As with a lot of Riordan's books in the Percy Saga, courage is something all heroes need. They need the courage to face their worst fears. They need the courage to overcome their greatest weakness. They need the courage to be a hero. 
 Recommendation 
 Well, I think if you have liked all the earlier books, you'll definitely continue to like this book. There is quite a lot of character building in this book, but it still feels like I am watching too many characters in the spotlight. Riordan keeps track of the seven heroes throughout the story, but it can feel overwhelming at times. 
 Originally published at www.amaitken.com/book-review/the-house-of-hades-review/ on September 17, 2016

reference_books.title: The Shack
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 The Shack has become a very popular read of late. It's about a man, Mack, whose daughter is murdered during a camping trip. After his daughter death, Mack loses his faith and the entire novel becomes about Mack regaining his faith. 
 The concept of the novel is very interesting. The ideas and philosophies behind the novel are worth debating about. However, the character development in the novel is a little lacking and the miracle in the shack...well, it's didn't seem very miraculous to me. 
 The book is surrounding in mystery and the marketing behind it does not want to reveal what happens at the shack...which I understand, but also find it a bit misleading. What happens at the shack is a conversation between Mack and God. That's the miracle. I was waiting for something a bit more challenging to the character and less acceptance from Mack...more anger, maybe some yelling - then maybe I could've believed his character. 
 Also, the beginning of the novel, I just didn't find it well written. It seemed horribly cliche. 
 I was expecting a little more from this novel and not some Christian diatribe. However, saying all that, I do think it would be an excellent read for a book club and/or a Christian group.

reference_books.title: The Poisonwood Bible
reference_books.review_text:
The Poisonwood Bible is one of the most heart-wrenching books that I've read in a long time. The southern women's voices were so clear to me and even though the story is told through 4 different voices, I could differentiate between the 4 women clearly. I loved how these southern women were plopped in the middle of the congo and the reader's first thought is how different they would be from the Congolese, but in the end, you realize how similar they are to the people there if the characters allow themselves to see it. 
 A tragedy occurs in the middle of the novel and I love how Kingsolver keeps the story going after the tragedy. I love how she doesn't leave the story with "and these women were forever changed" but show us how they are changed and how each woman copes with the tragedy. 
 I loved this book and found myself crying at several points in the novel. Mostly because I am a mother and I can't help be feel for any mother's pain, whether she's fiction or real.

book_a.user_review:

 The one aspect of this book that I really liked was Mattie's relationship with Royal. Royal is handsome and for the most part has good intentions towards Mattie. As an outsider, you can easily tell how little Mattie and Royal have in common, but I love how Mattie's awakening hormones guide her with her relationship with Royal, which is a very realistic emotion, especially as a teenager. 
 I loved this book. Although the plot and ending where very common, the method of the story and the lovable character of Mattie made this a very good book to read.

Well written book. I enjoyed the fact that it took place in the Adirondacks. It was based on true events at the turn of the century on Moose Lake. Not your typical YA book. There was a lot of realism. Donnelly did a great job in capturing the essence of the early 20th century.
She made a promise to her dying mother and she didn't keep it. She felt it was more important to follow her dream of attending college and becoming a writer. So sad.

Very readable, with a main character that will be compelling to girls that like to read and write, less so to boys that don't. Mattie Gokey has to decide whether to leave her farming life in 1906 northern New York to study at a college or stay with her family. A parallel to this is a young woman who has mysteriously drowned near the Glenmore Hotel where Mattie works. Overall, a bit predictable, based on an actual incident.

A lovely, well-written bildungsroman that must serve as inspiration for a whole bunch of young adult readers, and those of us who were there a few years back. In following the life of a gifted young farm girl in Upstate NY, the novel also manages to address lingering issues of class and racial prejudice, misogyny, the hardships of rural life, and a historical murder mystery. All of this is woven together with the bonds of love, friendship, and self-trust.

I loved reading Revolution, so once I discovered Jennifer Donnelly's other books, I knew that I was about to embark on a historical fiction detour. Once again, she wowed me. Maybe it's just because I have so much trouble writing contemporary, slightly fantastical fiction, but I can't imagine how much research Donnelly must put into these novels. Her depictions feel so complete and intricate, and you definitely start to appreciate the complexity and struggles of living in a rural area in 1906. Mattie shows us how much work went into making a meal or taking care of sick relatives, what a luxury a book was, and what exactly can go wrong when you don't milk the cows everyday. I know, when I say it like that the cow thing sounds a little trivial. Having been a city girl for most of my life, I was a little confused as to why Mattie was freaking out during a particularly stressful portion of the book about the cows not having been milked recently. She then promptly explains that if the cows aren't milked an infection in their udders can set in, they will have to be killed and the family will be out of its primary source of income, as they usually sell milk to the local resorts. Watching all of these struggles was amazingly enlightening for me, and made me aware of my modern blessings. I mean, I start to get punchy if I haven't been on the internet in a few days. And by "few" I may mean one. 
 It's not all about the struggles in this book, however. The primary conflict is a pretty standard tale: should Mattie defy her family (and her mother's dying wishes) and go study writing at college in New York? Or should she stay and marry the boy next door? Does she even love the boy next door? Does he even love her? And while we're at it, what does love even mean? 
 Do not let what I am about to say put you off of reading this book, especially if you like historical fiction. The book is fantastic and superbly researched, Mattie has a strong and believable voice, especially as she doesn't really know what she wants a lot of the time. The following is primarily an analysis from my standpoint as an apprentice-writer (aka Writer Wannabe): I was not a fan of the pacing of the last third of the book. There is an intense conflict, and then there are a few anecdotal scenes that seem a little out of place to me. Maybe it's because I have been trained to expect that the conflict spurs the main transformation of the character immediately. Instead, Mattie goes through the intense struggle and then goes about her life as normal until she fully processes the drowning of Grace Brown. To me, this just left the plot feeling stymied. However, I also think that I am mentally comparing this book with Revolution, which was brilliantly structured and had action continually interspersed with the inner conflict. As I am more of a plot-reader than a character-development-reader, I can see why I would feel like Revolution was a bit more of my cup of tea.

Full review to come... 
 But, this book was beautifully written with wonderfully crafted characters. It felt like more than just a story. These people were almost real, and I love them. Mattie is one of the greatest heroines I've come across in a long time.

In a word? Overrated. I don't read THAT many "thriller" or mystery books, but on occasion. The first half of the book was exceedingly dull. Yes, it got much better in the second, but compared to, say, The Silence of the Lambs, it wasn't even close, tension-wise. And the "Girl" character... of course the 25-year-old bisexual can't resist the mid-forties protagonist who kept saying "I just want to be your friend!"

My motivation for buying this book stemmed mostly from seeing it on bestseller shelves for a year or so. I was a sucker and fell for the brilliantly applied title. I love mystery books, let's just start with that. I think that the fact that this book centered around an unsolved murder was a great way for Larsson to address his larger theme: men hating women, essentially. The way Larsson frames his story is what made the book for me. I love that he uses the main character Mikael Blomkvist as being the investigatory journalist. Though Mikael is morally ambiguous about many things, Larsson lets the reader see that even Mikael is disgusted with the sexual assaults on these women. What I disliked about this book was its tendency to drag on; I think he could have made an even stronger case for the story in about 100 pages less. Another thing I didn't quite like is the explicit detail of the acts of sexual violence. I do, however, understand that this detail was put in precisely for people to feel bleak and disgusted that such acts are occurring in our world, which is justifiable and understandable. That being said, this book is not for the weak of heart or the weak of stomach. I think this book was well-written with an excellent plot, but did not cater to my style of taste.

If not for you, my Goodreads pals, I would feel like the only person on the planet who didn't love this book - left standing in a public square, gaping and utterly alone, while legions of Larsson fans point at me and shriek in an alien, unified voice. That might have been an exaggeration. But it's hard, I tell you, to be a bookseller who doesn't love whatever publishing darling is huge at the moment. You'd think I'd be good at it by now, having hated my way through Dan Brown, 'The Secret', and the collected works of Stephenie Meyer. And really, it's unfair to lump Larsson in with any of the above, because this book didn't completely suck - it just wasn't great, veering between boring and distasteful, like sitting through a lame documentary into which a snuff film has been spliced.

I love all the hash tag series books.

Lyrik West, guitarist for Sunder, is a notorious partier and womanizer, but he has his reasons for keeping relationships impersonal. His entire focus has been on the band's success and the sacrifices he's made over the years have shaped his entire outlook on life. 
 Tamar King slings drinks and attitude at Charlie's bar, but she has crafted an illusion. She lives under the radar, projecting the image she wants those around her to see. Though she is lonely at times, she is finally safe. 
 When Lyrik walks into Charlie's, he is immediately attracted to the red headed bartender. He wants one night with her, but she rebuffs him. 
 The spark between them is immense. Though they both feel it, Tamar fights her attraction, preferring to maintain the status quo and avoid the attention Sunder brings with them. This is the kind of couple that keeps me reading a book simply to discover what makes them tick as individuals and what draws them together. 
 There was so much running, but it is so well planned that it complimented the drama rather than fueled it. Every time Lyrik purposefully holds himself back, or Tamar turns from her past these characters ask why rather than react or do something rash. I was glued to this book from start to finish with the level of angst and drama that flowed between these two. 
 The pain was matched only by the loneliness of the other. Lyrik and Tamar are each holding on to or trying to forget a past that is eating away at the present. Tamar's carefully crafted safety is eroding, while Lyrik has to face his past if he wants to have a future with Tamar. But when the story reaches that point where each must face the things holding Lyrik and Tamar back as individuals, that is where things book sings. I loved the treatment of those particular plot points and what the resolution says about Tamar and Lyrik as individuals and as a couple. 
 I thought I knew what was coming -- the secrets Lyrik was keeping, the past Tamar was running from. But thinking and knowing are two different things and what I though was surpassed by the reality. I had been anticipating this book and once again I am floored by A.L. Jackson's storytelling. Her broken characters pull me into the story and I can't put it down until they have put themselves back together again. This sent me on an emotional roller coaster of fear, desire, sadness, and hope. 
 ARC provided by author in exchange for an honest review. This review will be posted at Reviews by Tammy and Kim.

**4.5 Stars** 
 AL Jackson's lyrical prose will captivate every reader with this story. It had a delicious push/pull between Lyrik and Tamar that instantly sucked you in and wouldn't let go. And that sweet, slow burn of a romance with characters who fought so dang hard to resist one another created an explosive chemistry that flew off of the pages. Jackson has a magical, poetic way with words and it gives life to every story, and you'll find WHERE LIGHTNING STRIKES to be no different. 
 Lyrik and Tamar have both created a barrier to others out of necessity. They've suffered things in the past that have forced them to be closed off, thus creating a stubborn willpower that inhibit's them from changing. They don't want to want the other, and yet they do with everything in them for reasons that neither can understand. Each is scarred in their own painful way, and Jackson writes this story so beautifully that you come to know, slowly, how each of them has suffered. In doing this, she makes it feel incredibly gratifying to achieve how deep we come to know the characters, and how far our hearts reach out to them. 
 WHERE LIGHTNING STRIKES was an incredibly beautiful novel filled with deeply fleshed-out characters that will reach deep into your soul and demand a reaction. Their connection will fuel turning the pages, and bring you right into the story with them. You won't want to put the story down, except, maybe, to take a deep breath. Jackson did another fantastic job in bringing these characters to life, and you'll fall right in love with them.

A.L. Jackson is a new author to me, but she has made me a huge fan by just this one book. The way she is with simple one word to describe something happening simply was captivating. I could not put this raw and electric book. 
 Tamar Gibson is a tattooed bartender with a horrid past that she was running from. So many unspeakable things happened to her as a young woman. It caused her to leave home and her family, change her identity completely and hide. She gave up her passion for photography because of a monster that shook her fragile soul so bad. Lyric West is a tattooed guitar player for the band Sunder. He is also living with walls built so high up on his heart that he doesn't know what to do when he meets Tamar. In book they have already met prior and the band is back for Shea and Baz's (lead singer) wedding in Savannah. 
 The chemistry between these two is hot, rare, and earth shattering. They both have so much gIve to each other. Lyric sees something had happened to Tamar and he wants to "fix" her. Tamar can sense Lyric is not fully giving himself when they do have their time together. They discover so much of each other and slowly, piece by piece those walls break down. 
 Can lightning strike so hard and you survive? Will love overcome demons or will it destroy something with the potential to be so beautiful? This story will grip you and take you into a raw world where nothing is perfect. I can't not wait for book 2 in the series.

5 Stars 
 A.L. Jackson somehow has a way of completely obliterating whatever expectations I have for a book of hers. The way she writes is beyond compare. The way she describes things paint the perfect picture that I can clearly envision in my head. 
 I thought I was ready for Lyrik's story. What I didn't expect was the way my heart would break for him and all that he's gone through. The men of Sunder have always had a bevy of women that would kill for one night with them. While it has always been great, Lyrik has had his eye set on one girl. The red-headed beauty at Charlie's bar. "Red", as he calls her, doesn't give him the time of day. She has up this front and dishes out sarcasm that usually keeps the boys at bay. Only, Lyrik isn't like most. He feels he should keep his distance, but he simply can't. 
 Tamar has a very hard exterior. She only lets a few select people see parts of her. She's been hidden behind her wall so long that she thought she was safe. She thought she was unbreakable. What she didn't expect was for Lyrik West to pick away at her until she broke. She reveals parts of herself that no one else knows about. He slowly becomes everything to her. Only, he's just as closed off as she is. 
 "And there you were, breaking up all the broken, brittle parts and making room for something different. For something better. Waking me up from the dead. Making me realize what it's like to feel again. Making me feel things I've never felt before. You were making room for you." 
 They both have this hard outer shell that they use as a shield. To shield themselves from getting to close to anyone, but when they find someone who is just as broken as they are, their souls seem to call out to each other. 
 The build-up that led up to the storm was palpable. It was as if I was standing in the middle of the storm itself. I felt the electricity building, the storm growing, and I knew that when the lightning struck, it would decimate me. Both of their stories are tragic, but Lyrik's past prevents him from allowing himself to feel, to even think "more" is possible. He helped Tamar overcome her fears and be brave. Now he just has to see that he too can be just as brave. 
 I cried because I was sad. I cried because I felt the gut-twisting pain that can cripple you. Last of all, I cried out of pure happiness. By the time all of Sunder has told their story, I feel like I'm going to be a complete wreck. When it comes to book boyfriends, it's hard to pick favorites for me, but these boys are making it easy. Lyrik is up high on that list with Baz. When it's all said and done, I have a feeling those first four spots will be reserved for all of the Sunder boys.

Right.... I'm not used to giving up on books, especially if I'm 3/4 of the way through them. It feels like a waste of time to ditch something you've invested so much time on. But I'd lost the will to go on with his book. 
 First, it could have been shorter. There were too many unneeded interactions and narrations by the main character and the story was starting to drag because of them. 
 Second, the characters were getting a little annoying... Ethan was expressing way too much emotion for a boy (you could tell it was written by a woman), Lena and her pessimistic outlook on her life etc... 
 Third, it was poorly written with a couple of sentences that didn't make sense) 
 Fourth, I think this book has just tried too hard to jump on the Twilight saga/Paranormal Romance/Young Adult band wagon and completely missed it. 
 I will say though that there were a few nice scenes in the story that were written as flashbacks/visions of the past which I really enjoyed.

 It was one of those types of books that you like a lot, but they seem too short because it doesn't get really good until like the middle of the book, and there should have been more romance between lena and ethan...you didn't get that vibe between the two of them until probably the end of the book

I see Beautiful Creatures as Adult Literary Fiction meets Young Adult with a heavy dose of Paranormal Romance. 
 The story is told from a male perspective (unusual for this genre) in first person by Ethan Lawson Wate who is stuck in a small southern town in the middle of nowhere, where no one moves in and no one moves out. You're born there, live there and die there. Ethan wants to be different, he wants to get out and see the world, he's tired of the small-town attitudes of his school friends and neighbours. He's been having nightmares about holding onto an unknown girl he's in love while she dangles in the air until he drops her, nightmares in which he wakes up soaked from the rain in his dream, and is haunted by a mysterious song called Sixteen Moons. 
 Everything in the town is the same until Lena Duchannes moves in with her reclusive uncle, Macon Ravenwood the town's bogeyman. Everyone tars her with the same brush automatically believing she's as "crazy" as her uncle, everyone but Ethan. He recognises her from the nightmares and sees something different in her. She's a symbol of everything he wants: she's travelled, she's well-educated, well-read and she doesn't think like the rest of the town, and when Ethan becomes her friend the town turns on them both. Ethan adores her until she reveals she's a Caster, a magic-user who will be Claimed either by the Dark (evil) or the Light (good) on her 16th birthday but she belives she will go Dark. They form an unusually strong bond especially since he's only a Mortal and together they try to find out more about the Claiming to see if they can stop it but both Macon and Ethan's housekeeper (or second mother), Amma stand in their way. 
 This is very slow-building, so slow in fact that it took me over two weeks to finish. Only bull-headed determination got me to the end. A lot of background on the town and its characters was given but there were parts that just didn't interest me, like detail on the all-important war and the repetition of certain facts that got tiresome after a while as did Lena's behaviour, constantly pushing Ethan away "for his own good" when it was clear he wasn't going anywhere and all she was doing was hurting them both. I had to skim a few times. 
 Macon Ravenwood was my favourite character, I wanted to read more about him and his life. I also wanted more on Genevieve and her life after the visions, how much did she change after she made the failed bargain? How Dark did she become? I wondered if there was something special about Boo Radley the wolf-dog other than being Macon's eyes, was his relationship with Macon symbiotic? It seemed like it. I think something more could have been made of Ethan's father, I don't know what exactly but there wasn't enough interaction with Ethan especially after the suicide incident. 
 Ethan struck me as very feminine and extremely mature until quite late in the book when he found it difficult to say the words "girlfriend" and "I love you". I waited for his thoughts to turn sexual, like every hormonal teenager but it didn't happen. His unusual bond with Lena wasn't really explained, even though there was a comparison to Ethan Carter Wate (Ethan's great, great uncle) and Genevieve's relationship, it wasn't clear on what made Ethan able to feel and communicate (via mind-speak) with Lena so easily. There was a suggestion he was a Caster and then doors were opening of their own accord for him which was later explained away as his mother's spirit helping him. Lena's father is practically glossed over, we only know that he was murdered by her mother. I didn't fully understand the extent to which Mrs Lincoln was possessed by Serafine, she said she wasn't always possessing her so I was curious to know how much of Mrs Lincoln's behaviour was due to Serafine and how much was her own nasty personality. 
 The ending was lack-lustre, rushed, not well-thought out, hodge-podge. Lena gets rid of the enemies quickly and easily, a flash of lightning was all it took. Lena isn't claimed and doesn't claim herself, she doesn't make a choice instead a wishy-washy explanation was given - suddenly there is no moon and Lena, being a powerful Natural temporarily got rid of the moon so she wouldn't have to choose (when did she have the time to do that?) until of course there is another verse of the song but instead of Sixteen Moons it's Seventeen Moons. I'm guessing this means her choice has been put off until her 17th birthday. Ugh. I'm not sure if this is right because Ethan notices Lena's eyes have changed colour, one has remained green and the other is now gold like those of Dark Casters. Shouldn't both of her eyes be gold like Genevieve's? 
 One thing that wasn't addressed was the fact that Ethan and Lena could never be together physically, it was stated and then after the drama of the climax it wasn't discussed by Lena and Ethan. I would think they'd be thinking about that as well as Macon. I can't see them staying together, especially since Lena hasn't admitted to killing the Dark Casters or even bringing Ethan back to life - which is another thing I'm not clear on. Is he truly alive? Why was his life traded for Macon's specifically. I just don't understand. 
 I know this review is quite negative but I do believe the small-town mentality was well-drawn. As a child I lived in a small English village in the country, my mother was the only black person and I was mixed race. We both felt like outsiders and the rumour-mill got so bad, led by the stay-at-home mums, that my mother sent me away while she packed our things and moved us out, back to the city. She didn't want me to be affected by their behaviour. Lena and Ethan were pretty strong not to crumble under that collective pressure. 
 I really wanted this story to finish in this book. I made an extraordinary effort to finish it due to the hype, some great lines and a few intriguing scenes, I deserved to be rewarded with a good ending. This book isn't as concise as it could have been or as clear, I believe a concerted effort was made to make the town and the many characters realistic but the ending wasn't right. The need for a sequel seemed to outweigh the need to end the book properly.

Initial Impressions 9/10/17: Either this book was shorter than I thought or time just flew by as I was listening! That felt so quick!! Which I guess it a good thing. 
 I really enjoyed WARCROSS! It was a fun, futuristic read that reminded me of READY PLAYER ONE meets THE HUNGER GAMES but still in its own original way. I loved the game aspect behind it and I think games within a story really pull me into the action! I also liked the different friendships and relationships that Emika made and how they all shaped the book. 
 One thing I really enjoyed was a nice set of twists that Marie Lu incorporated into the plot. I was all, "Oh yeah, I guessed that one and saw that one coming" and then BAM something else I did not see coming, so that was really fun! 
 It ended on a cliffhanger which in this case WHYYYY I need to know! Because it went by so quickly that I didn't even realize it was ending... But I'm definitely picking up the next book! I'm excited to see what's next! 
 Review as posted on The Book Addict's Guide 9/18/17: WARCROSS is only my second Marie Lu book (I've only read LEGEND. I know, how horrible am I? I loved it too...) and I'm so glad I had the chance to get back into her writing! Every since READY PLAYER ONE, I've been dying for more video game/virtual reality-type adventures and I know there are others out there but WARCROSS was one that really caught my eye, both because of author and concept. 
 Either this book was shorter than I thought or time just flew by as I was listening! I listened to the audiobook (thanks, Listening Library!) while I worked and it seemed like this story just flew by, which I guess means that I was really enjoying it! I really enjoyed WARCROSS! It was a fun, futuristic read that reminded me of READY PLAYER ONE meets THE HUNGER GAMES but still in its own original way. I loved the game aspect behind it and I think games within a story really pull me into the action! There were plenty of action-packed moments, especially during the games themselves, which were not at all like Quidditch but reminded me of the action breaks that Harry Potter took to play out a Quidditch game. It brought some fast-paced scenes to the book and added more the the character relationships, meanwhile adding a dash of plot all at the same time. The game sequences also really added to the world-building, showing exactly how Warcross worked and why everyone was so excited for these competitions. It's essentially like everyone playing sports and then the tournaments featured here are like the Olympics. 
 I really enjoyed all of the different relationships throughout the book! Emika is kind of a loner to start and as the book progresses, she learns how to work on a team and finally starts to let people back in. She also lets go of her heart a little bit and ends up with an unexpected relationship (or at least more than friends) with a prominent figure in the book and the romance was sweet and exciting all at the same time! I really liked the team aspect and how that really brought Emika in, as much as she didn't want or expect that, and I always love gangs of characters who might not have otherwise been friends coming together like that. 
 I've only read one Marie Lu book but I feel like she's good at keeping readers on their toes! One thing I really enjoyed was a nice set of twists that she incorporated into the plot. I totally saw one twist coming and was like, "Oh yeah, predictable..." and then BAM! A totally different twist caught me by surprise. I'm not sure if I was supposed to see the one coming but I definitely appreciate that it threw me off for the other one, thinking I had already caught the "twist". 
 The book ended before I knew it and I was so engrossed in the audiobook that I didn't even realize it was coming to a close! Marie Lu left us on a hell of a cliffhanger which I loved but also whyyyyy! I'm so anxious to read the next book and as much as it sucks to be left on a cliffhanger sometimes, I'm definitely left wanting more as soon as possible!
That story did not go where I thought it would, and I am intrigued enough by the set-up to wait with a gently-tapping foot for the next one.

2.5. 
 I'm sad, because everyone loves this book and I really didn't. My main problem was that I didn't feel like things were explained properly in this book. Like, I found the world really intriguing, but not the world building . It didn't feel substantial, it just felt like a collection of cool technology just thrown together to be cool technology without explanation (even by characters who are supposed to understand.) I don't want to say too much, because maybe minor spoilers, but I just thought this felt really insubstantial and poorly developed. 
 Emika is a hacker and bounty-hunter. She hunts down people who have illegally gambled on the game Warcross, a game that literally everyone plays. Emika needs more money than she's earning, so she hacks into, just for a moment, the opening game of the Warcross championships. But she makes a mistake, and suddenly everyone watching and playing can see her. Soon, instead of getting arrested, she gets a phone call from the young creator of Warcross, offering her a job as a spy competing in the Warcross championships. She accepts. 
 Spoilers Discussion! 
 So, I get that when writing about technology and coding, or another similarly advanced and complicated field, you can't give a lot of details, because your average reader won't understand what's going on. But , all of the technology here was incredibly advanced, and not explained at all, or grounded in things the average reader could understand. And if we hadn't been reading from the perspective of an apparent hacking prodigy, that'd be fine, but Emika knows what's going on, and we just don't get to know. I think the author probably thought that understanding more of the tech would be boring, but I think there's a way to do it that really develops the world, instead of just asking us to trust in this huge element of the story. I want to know how Warcross works, I want to know how Emika is so smart she can hack into everyone's everything but no one else can (besides her "look at the whole and see what's wrong" thing). 
 Also, how did Emika even learn to hack? She had that moment of discovery, sure, but then she had to actually develop the skills to become the first person to hack into Warcross. Again, this felt like a really essential part of the novel and important for understanding Emika as a person, and we just didn't get that opportunity to have that development of her character. And maybe we're going to get it later, but I didn't like this book so I might not read the next one... 
 And then I didn't like the relationships, they all felt shallow. The romance felt like it just... happened. Why are they attracted to each other so much, why does he just trust her... it just felt like total insta-love to me. 
 We are also supposed to kind of take for granted her friendship with her team, and how she got close to them all, but we didn't get to see that. I would've loved way less description of the cool technology, and way more time spent on her actually developing relationships with the other characters and building those up. It just felt secondary to me, and I don't think it should be. 
 The twist was just not for me. Like, while I can buy Hideo turning kind of evil and wanting to mind-control people, I'm in for that, I don't understand how his brother could possibly be Zero. I get that we're supposed to be shocked, and that's kind of the point, but I need for there to be some thread to follow if there's going to be such a huge twist, and there absolutely wasn't here. Also, why couldn't he just tell her earlier if he was eventually going to confess anyway... like he assumes that she's going to agree with him that what Hideo is doing is bad, so why not just tell her and get her on your side before everything goes wrong? And also... just how. What happened to him, why is he partial to all this information, why was this the only solution he could think of, just why. 
 I will read more of Ms. Lu's work in the future, this particular book was just a total bust for me. I think it'd be a much better movie than book, to be honest.

sample_reviews.review_text: These books used to be my favourite Spring/Summer read but no. Too repetitive and if the killer is who I've guessed it as since book 2 I'd be very disappointed, too obvious and boring. This book was just one too far for me. The rest have been great though so will probably read on to find out if this book was boring just because I know the structure or what.

If you want to know who killed Sutton, just skip to the last book. The first five are a complete waste of time. Here is a synopsis that will apply to each one: 1. Follow Emma as she chooses a suspect and follows them around for the entire book. 2. Suffer through random flashbacks with Sutton that incriminate Emma's suspect and make them appear hella guilty. 3. Rip your hair out and throw fits about Emma and Sutton ignoring every suspicious thing about Ethan, including his anger problems, reluctance to introduce his family and hints that he knew Sutton more than he lets on. 4. Encounter Sutton's last flashback which proves the suspect completely innocent and we are back to square one. I don't know who killed Sutton but I am so relieved that this will be revealed in the last book. Sara Shepard has an annoying habit of dragging these series out for way longer than need be. I have complete faith that the last book will be amazing and shocking, judging by the thrilling ending of Cross my Heart. Finally, something interesting happened! It would have been preferable to leave this series at four books but UH COURSE she has to drag it out and I will succumb to buying & reading. Oh well. I'm excited to finally get this series over with.

Emma (and ghost Sutton) learns that their birth mother, Becky, was actually the Mercer's first daughter. How no matter how nice and willing the Mercer's were, their daughter Becky just seemed troubled. Running away, showing back up pregnant, and then left them, to what they assumed, was the only child Becky had. Not knowing that Becky thought she could take care of one twin, and gave Sutton to her parents, while keeping Emma to herself. Yet it was Becky, Emma soon finds out, who met Sutton late at night on the 31st, and as Emma knows as of now, was the also one last to see Sutton alive. Yet their mother couldn't kill her own daughter? Emma has to face up to her biggest problem yet, as it was time to dwell into the past of a women Emma used to idolize. 
 Sutton, tied to Emma like a puppet, is forced to see Emma dress up and pretend to be her, each and every day. Watching Thayer, a boy who still holds Sutton heart, be rejected by Emma, while Emma is kissing a boy Sutton use to bully. Even watching as Emma crack the frozen hearts of her best friends, who hearts were frozen by Sutton to begin with. Sutton realizes that now she's dead, how good she had it. How instead of pinning her friends against each other, she should have come clean for them, and maybe is she was a little nicer, she wouldn't have been murdered. 
 Sara Shepard is close to wrapping this series up. With only one book left to go, and a few hours left on the 31st, the murderer is coming into focus. Emma and Ethan's relationship grows, but hits some bumps as Emma discover something that Ethan never told her about. As Emma is dedicated to Ethan, Thayer still thinks he can win her back, causing even more bumps as Ethan and Thayer square off. The writing is the same as the other books, and it kept its fast pace going. By this point the whole "each book has a new suspect" thing is getting old, but push on though there is only one book left. With a surprise ending, sure to leave you feeling unease, the murderer makes it known that he (or she) is always one step ahead of you.

 Out of all of the books in the series so far, I'd have to say this one is my least favorite. Now, it's not a bad read or anything. I just wasn't able to immerse myself into it like I could the rest of the books in the series. But before I talk about why I didn't enjoy this book as much as the rest of the series, I'd like to mention what I did enjoy with Cross My Heart, Hope to Die. 
 One of the aspects of this series I continue to enjoy is how Shepard develops her characters. In this book in particular, Emma has become close to Sutton's family. She's repaired Sutton's relationship with Laurel to the point where they aren't arguing anymore. The Mercer family is finally acting like a normal happy family, somewhat. Yes, there are some secrets and lies being told. But they are doing a whole lot better than before. I think the family's development is important in this book in particular because this book is heavily focused on their family, which is something I do like. When Becky comes to town, you know there's going to be some trouble. You as the reader just don't realize how much. 
 Along with her character development with regards to Sutton's family, her friendships also continue to grow and be tested. When Emma allows her twin's rival to help with a prank, she befriends another person her sister wouldn't have thought of giving a chance. You're also introduced to a new girl to the school named Celeste whose character is pretty strange in some ways. She supposedly is very in tune spiritually and warns Emma several times throughout that she's in serious danger. I really like her character because despite her odd personality, I honestly believe she cares about people even those she's not friends with. I have a feeling Celeste is going to play a significant role in the final book, though I don't yet know how that's going to take shape. 
 One of my favorite parts of this book is how it ends. Emma is having a really happy moment with her family when she receives some really bad news, the type of news nobody wants to get. Then the story ends with you wondering how Emma and her family are going to react and how this all plays into what's going to happen next in the story. I love it because you're reminded that Sutton's killer is still out there watching Emma's every move and that the killer is far from being done with her. 
 What I don't like with Cross My Heart, Hope to Die is that I feel like the plot is really slowing down. Out of all the books in this series, the pace in this book moved too slow for me. It was like Shepard put brakes on this book so that the story wouldn't move too far along. I didn't like it because it made me not want to finish this book, even though I really want to know how this all will end. 
 But even though the pace was slow, it's not my least favorite thing in this book. I absolutely hated how mental illness was portrayed through Becky in this book. It's pretty obvious that she has mental health issues with the way Emma was raised by Becky before she abandoned her. But I feel like the way Becky's illness is portrayed is really terrible. What made it so awful to me is that she's never given the help she really needs. In the book, she escapes from the hospital only to find Emma so she can tell her she's leaving Tucson. She apparently also finds Mr. Mercer to tell him the same thing, yet they are both completely okay with her leaving them despite that she really needs help. Yes, Emma does show more concern for her well-being, but it's very obvious that neither of them are trying to get her any help. I get with Mr. Mercer that he doesn't want his wife to know Becky is back, but to me it just seems like he doesn't care about his daughter's well-being. He knows she's very sick, but does very little to really give her the help she needs. 
 I also find the portrayal of mental health in this book to be awful because Emma does suspect her mother of killing Sutton at one point. This brings up the stigma that only really sick people with mental health issues are the only ones capable of killing someone, though there's no way her mother was capable of the crime Emma was suspicious of her committing. And it also uses mental health as an excuse for why people do terrible things, which makes it even harder for people with mental health issues to actually want to get help. This is pretty apparent when Emma finds out Ethan has a file at the hospital and wonders why he kept it secret from her. While I appreciate Shepard writing about mental health, I don't necessarily think she portrayed it properly. Or in a way where the reader could really sympathize with Becky and understand what she's going through. 
 But despite these problems with Cross My Heart, Hope to Die, I'm still planning on reading the last book in the series. Since the next book in this series is the last one, I'm planning on talking about the series as a whole and give you my thoughts on who I thought could've killed Sutton and why. I have a couple people I suspected and really can't wait to share with you my thoughts on this series as a whole.

sample_reviews.review_text: I loved McKinley's style in this book. It was written in first person, with a character (Sunshine) that was intelligent, sarcastic, and confused. That sounds strange, but you are revealed to Sunshine's inner struggle to find both identity and a moral compass. The book is so funny that I started laughing out loud just from the first page. I don't generally show emotion while reading. Sunshine was brillantly written, and in turn helped inspire my own style of writing.

I read McKinley's Beauty many years ago and remember enjoying it, so I was curious to read her take on vampires. Unfortunately, the vampire in question suffered from a case of one-dimensionality. I wanted to learn more about him, and there were so many hints of what we could learn, but we never did. The book itself seemed cluttered with inconsequential tangents, and the author's train-of-thought style of writing was very distracting. In addition, some readers may be offended by some strong language at times and one brief questionable scene, so potential reader beware. Mildly recommended for those who enjoy the vampire genre.

I only really read about 30 pages. However, it read just enough like a sequel to be annoying. You feel like you're missing something that everyone else knows but there's enough information being given out to make you realize it's it's the first one. I'm not sure if that makes sense, but that's how I thought about it. I usually like Robin McKinley, but this one was just not up to her usual standards.

What I liked most about this novel was that it was NOT yet another tired re-worked supernatural romance. This is a realistic telling of a world which goes on daily, coping with its supernatural aspects just as with taxes and other inconveniences. We don't get -- or need -- a lengthy exposition of where the Other Stuff comes from or how humans should fear it; we just get a story that is fresh. 
 We're left wanting more -- that's a good thing. Better to wonder what the "different ways of being what we are" might be than to beat it to death in minute detail and choke the reader. We don't know where the magic comes from, or how it works, or why Constantine is who he is, or any of a number of things -- but we know enough. We know that the story works, and we know that the story hasn't ended, as stories don't just "end" in real life. I liked that.

You know how sometimes you can zone out while reading without actually absorbing what's written? Somehow I managed to do that for this whole book, it was that boring. I picked it up because vampires are my thing and I was seduced by the pretty cover. And it had quotes from two of my favorite people on it, Neil Gaiman and Amber Benson. Unfortunately we didn't see eye to eye on this one. I think YA vamps are more my speed.
Is it over yet?

I've heard so many good things about this book, but I just couldn't connect. There are moments if humor in this dark world and the writing is smart, so I think people that like minor horror and quirky characters should give Sunshine a shot. I'm sorry that I didn't enjoy it, maybe with a second read another time in my life.

sample_reviews.review_text:
The newest release from Roxane Gay, famed for her memoir Hunger and collection of essays Bad Feminist, is a short story collection focused on the difficult and often tumultuous relationships experienced by women. These stories standout in their ability to show a diverse set of women, but sewn together by a very apparent theme, one of sex, but not only of just sex, but abuse. A story of two young girls, abducted and abused, relying on only each other when they finally escape their captor. A woman working at a strip club is stalked by a customer to her home and raped, her reluctance to call the police due to her devastating claim that it was an expected "occupational hazard." Though there are stories of love or of insular drama in female friendships in this collection, it is clear there is a focus that centers on the horror of sexual violence. 
 I brought up this prevalence with a friend, and the question of if it was hyperbolic to have the majority of these stories with the title presenting that these were just themed as stories about women, but reflected mainly on unhealthy sexual relationships, or if that was simply the heartbreaking reality of women today? This brought me to reading one of Gay's earlier essays, The Careless Language of Sexual Violence, where she explores the idea that: 
 "We cannot separate violence in fiction from violence in the world no matter how hard we try... I also feel committed to telling the truth, to saying these violences happen even if bearing such witness contributes to a spectacle of sexual violence... These are difficult topics where we need to be vigilant not only in what we say but how we express ourselves. That same care, I would suggest, has to be extended to how we write about violence, and sexual violence in particular." 
 In this collection Gay's stories do make a spectacle of this horror, but in a responsible and careful way. Her ability to be frank about this situations and not shy away from all aspects of the stories, especially the subsequent trauma, exemplify her ability as an expert and perceptive storyteller. I found this collection to be best paired with her essays to gain perspective on her methods. More of Roxane Gay's fictional work can be read in her 2014 novel Untamed State, where she takes on similar themes in a longer format. 
 Get Difficult Women from the Denver Public Library 
 - Hana

A pick, but with a qualifier: it's dark. Really dark. These stories reminded me about what I loved about Breaking Bad: superb writing, complex and well developed characters, and completely engrossing, but so incredibly dark. I'd read another of Gay's work any day.

CW: I think every story in this is about either sexual assault or miscarriage...maybe not every but definitely most of them 
 Roxane Gay is a wonderful, powerful writer, of course, and I was so looking forward to reading this book! I...won't say I enjoyed reading this, exactly, since most of the stories are pretty heavy. But I appreciated the weight of her words and the resonance I felt with these fictional difficult women, for all their struggles and small victories (and large ones) 
 ps I know not to judge a book by what I wish it was, rather than what it actually is, but also....I hope she does another essay collection soon b/c that is my true jam

"She asks me how I got so lucky and I am at a loss until I consider the sequence of events bringing Gus into my life. I explain I got so lucky because of a lifelong dedication to slutty and inappropriate behavior and my ability to drink tequila straight."

I am a huge fan of Roxane gay's writing technique. It feels powerful and direct, yet poetic. 
 The themes in her compilations of stories are very similar, so at times it felt repetitive when I was expecting a new theme (as is the case with most short story compilations I've read). However the tone and substance of each story held its own flavor, which was enough to keep me engaged and engrossed by each one. 
 What makes a woman difficult? How does it shape her relationships with others? I loved her exploration of the relationships between men and women, as well as the relationships that women have with other women. She seems to argue that theyre fundamentally different, which didn't come across as good or bad. 
 Reading Roxane gay's works always leaves me emotionally raw. One may argue she is too over-the-top, but I completely disagree. I think that her writing forces us to face harsh subjects and realities- you can't dance around her explicit use of topics such as rape, miscarriage, abuse, Etc. I appreciate her strength and forthrightness in her writing.

What I love about short story collections is that often times I can enjoy different stories for many different reasons. For example, there were stories in this collection that spoke to the social worker side of me; many of them (of course!) spoke to the feminist in me; and even some of them spoke to the side of me that loves shows like Criminal Minds and overall enjoys criminology (which I wasn't expecting, but honestly this may be due to the fact that I just binged 2.5 seasons of the show). I loved the diversity within the different stories and I loved how each story was different even if it did have similar aspects and details. 
 I recommend this to all my feminist friends, as well as anyone looking for books written by diverse authors!

I give the final story "Strange Gods" 5 stars because I imagine it was terribly difficult to write considering Roxane Gay's personal story. Ms. Gay is a brilliant writer. From real to dubious, the stories in this collection have a common theme, emotional trauma. A bit too much in here for me.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This is a well-written collection and I really wanted to like it but it wasn't for me. While the styles and details differed story to story, they all seemed to revolve around women being abused, being downtrodden. And there was only one or two stories where I felt the protagonist was able to move forward by the end. Truthfully, I would have given up on the book halfway through but I felt like I had to finish it.

Along with the ones dealing with outright rape, almost every story in this collection is filled with violent sex and features female characters who allow or even beg men to sexually hurt, abuse, and degrade them. This is feminism?
This book will cut you open, but it will also sew you back up. The takeaways are worth it.

reference_books.title: The Iron Witch (The Iron Witch, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Ich habe mir das Buch vor einigen Wochen recht gunstig als Mangelexemplar erworben. Der Klappentext horte sich interessant an und das Cover hat mir sehr gut gefallen. 
 Donna hat ein Geheimnis: Sie hat silberne Tattoos und ist Mitglied im Orden des Drachens. 
 Sie wird von ihren ehemaligen Mitschulern als Freak bezeichnet. Seit einem Vorfall in der Schule wird Donna zuhause unterrichten. Ihr einziger Freund ist Narvin. 
 Nach einem Angriff der Dunkelelfen in ihrer Kindheit besitzt Donna eisen silberne Tattoos an ihren Handen, die sie grundsatzlich mit Handschuhen bedeckt bzw. versteckt. 
 Fruh lernt Donna Xan kennen, zu dem sie sich sofort hingezogen fuhlt und Donna erfahrt, dass nicht nur sie ein Geheimnis mit sich tragt. 
 Doch als die Dunkelelfen in die Stadt zuruckehren und Narvin in ihre Gewalt gerat muss Donna eine Entscheidung treffen: Narvin retten oder das Geheimnis ihres Ordens zu bewahren. 
 Von der Handlung habe ich mir wesentlich mehr versprochen, nachdem ich den Klappentext gelesen habe. 
 Wahrend des Lesens habe ich mir erhofft das 'sowas in der Art' oder 'sowas' passiert, aber leider war das nie der Fall. Vielleicht habe ich mir selbst zu viel von 'Iron Witch' versprochen. Dennoch finde ich ist die Geschichte ausbaufahig gewesen. Durch detailliertere Beschreibungen (besonders bei den Personen) oder auch durch ein etwas langsameres Voranschreiten der Geschichte (denn es war immer Handlung nach Handlung, es gab nie eine 'Erholungspause') ware die Geschichte wahrscheinlich 'vollkommener'. 
 Mit dem Schreibstil der Autorin (oder war es nur die Ubersetzung?) konnte ich mich nur langsam anfreunden. Der oft verwendeten Sarkasmus war, meiner Meinung nach, unangebracht und wie bereits beschrieben verlief die Handlung zu schnell. Dies ist mir besonders am Anfang der Geschichte aufgefallen: Donna geht auf eine Party, sie trifft den 'mysteriosen' Xan und fuhlt sich sofort zu ihm hingezogen. Am folgenden Tag treffen sie sich und die jahrelang gehuteten Geheimnisse werden beiderseits ausgeplaudern. ...ich weiss ja nicht... 
 Trotz der Mangel habe ich das Buch nicht gehasst und ich habe mir auch nicht gedacht: "Man ist das Buch langweilig". Die Geschichte war okay, jedoch werde ich nicht den zweiten/dritten Teil lesen.

reference_books.title: The Sun Is Also a Star
reference_books.review_text:
Ich habe das erste Buch der Autorin "Du neben mir und zwischen uns die ganze Welt" letztes Jahr gelesen und das Buch hat mir gut gefallen. Als ich dann erfahren habe, dass die Autorin ein weiteres Buch herausbringt, war mir klar, dass ich dieses ebenfalls lesen mochte. 
 Meine Meinung: 
 Eine Sache, die mir sehr an Nicola Yoons Buchern gefallt sind die langen der Kapitel. Ihre Kapitel variieren zwischen 1 und 6 Seiten und sind daher eher kurz, was ich wesentlich angenehmer finde als lange Kapitel. 
 Auch ihr Schreibstil ist besonders. Auch wenn einige Kapitel kurz sind, macht Yoon etwas mit ihren Worten, dass auch kurze Kapitel genug fur eine jeweilige Szene aussagen. 
 Ausserdem ist das Buch in verschiedenen Sichtweisen geschrieben. Haufig wechselt es zwischen den beiden Hauptprotagonisten, Natasha und Daniel, doch manchmal erfahrt der Leser kulturelle Geschichten aus deren Vergangenheit bzw. Leben. Natasha kommt namlich ursprunglich aus Jamaika und Daniel aus Sudkorea. Ausserdem kommen manche Nebencharaktere auch zur Sprache, sodass der Leser auch noch andere Eindrucke bekommt. 
 Die Geschichte von Natasha und Daniel hat mir im Grossen und Ganzen gut gefallen. Die beiden Hauptprotagonisten waren gut ausgearbeitet. Und auch wenn beide sehr verschieden waren, empfand ich beide von Anfang an als sympathisch. Anders war es leider mit ihren Familien... diese haben mich meistens sehr genervt. Das war durchaus von der Autorin gewollt, allerdings hat es mich manchmal dazu gebracht das Buch zur Seite zu legen. 
 In den meisten Buchern finden wir 'weisse' Hauptprotagonisten mit wenig Vielfalt. In diesem Buch ist es anders, was mir sehr gut gefallen hat. In diesem Buch sind die Hauptprotagonisten Jamaikaner und Asiaten. 
 Die Geschichte selbst, ist gut durchgearbeitet worden. Allerdings wirkt sie auf Grund der sogenannten "Instalove"-Geschichte etwas unglaubwurdig. Auch wenn die Autorin es versucht realistisch zu gestalten, dass man sich innerhalb weniger Stunden verliebt, ist es in der 'realen' Welt immer noch sehr unrealistisch und vermittelt eventuell ein falsches Bild von Liebe an ein jungeres Publikum. Auf der anderen Seite thematisiert das Buch "Schicksal" und "Zufalle" in einem besonderen Licht, was manchmal zum Nachdenken anregt und man sich wirklich fragt, ob das Leben eine Kette aus zufalligen Geschehnissen besteht. 
 Nichtsdestotrotz hat mich das Buch unterhalten und ich habe mit Natasha mitgefuhlt und immer gehofft, dass sie nicht abgeschoben wird. (Ihre Geschichte hat mir besser gefallen als die Liebesgeschichte zwischen ihr und Daniel). 
 Insgesamt hat mir das Buch gut gefallen. Die verschiedenen Sichtweisen machen das Buch interessant. Yoons Schreibstil wirkt sich poetisch auf die "Instalove"-Geschichte aus, sodass sie nicht allzu kitschig und unrealistisch ist. 
 4*

Enter a world, no THREE worlds each with their own version of London. The only ones with the ability to move between worlds are the Antari, or those born with the strongest form of magic. Kell is one of the few with the ability to move between worlds. There are four Londons: Red London, Grey London, White London, and Black London (but no one ever talks about that one). When Kell is tricked into smuggling an old relic into his world he finds himself inadvertently setting loose a dark and powerful force into his world. In his quest to rid the worlds of the darkness he runs into a pickpocket and thief named Lila. She is fierce and desperate with nothing to lose. Despite being magicless her quick wits and determination end up helping Kell in more ways than he could have imagined. When she forces him to let her help he is left with no choice but to accept, and together the two struggle to bring balance to the power hungry worlds. 
 This story was a shade darker than the stories I typically read. (Yes, I know its called A Darker Shade of Magic). The story contains some inappropriate content and swearing, so it is definitely geared towards an older audience. Still, I found it good enough to finish so that says something. Honestly I finished this book in two days. I was about to return it to the library, but I wanted to know what happened to Kell and I ended up staying up until to 2am to finish it. 
 Pros: 
 The characters are entertaining. They do not grow or change significantly throughout the book, however I loved the characters to begin with so this was not as much of a problem. I was just thinking to myself the other day about how the guy characters are always the ones who are witty, one-step ahead and think of the awesome comebacks. I asked myself -why aren't there any girl characters as sassy and hilarious as say, Eugenides from the Thief? Lila is almost like a girl version of Eugenides....but different. She is smart, sassy and just a little too weapon crazy. Her desperation drives her, yet beneath her cutthroat bravado she genuinely cares about the people around her. 
 Kell on the other hand has a very intense, wry personality. He struggles with his loyalties and identity throughout the story but never comes to a conclusion on who he is necessarily. The book is written as a trilogy and so I assume the following two books explore both Kell and Lila's characters in greater depth. 
 The storytelling is excellent. I enjoyed Schwab's descriptions immensely and the plot was compelling and full of twists and turns. 
 Cons: 
 The story claims that magic = power. The story further claims that either too much or too little power is bad. While the story does an excellent job of showing how too much power is bad, I never felt convinced that too little power was bad. In the story, one of the characters Rhy doesn't have much power and yet he is a wonderful ruler. This theme wasn't explored enough for me. I wish the pros and cons of power would have been talked about more in depth. 
 The darkness is pervasive. This book left me with an eery, oppressive feeling. However I will say that I'm glad I finished it. There are a few lighthearted moments as well as dark ones, but it ultimately ended on a good note. 
 A Darker Shade of Magic is captivating. Literally. Read it and you'll understand why I chose that word specifically.
Loved this book even more than I loved Vicious, I cannot wait of the next one. The world is unbelievable.

 Listened to this one on audiobook. Loved Stephen Crossley's narration. 
 My favorite aspects of the novel: the fascinating concepts surrounding multiple Londons and magic itself, which must be handled with utmost care; a focus on male-female friendship; a stalwart hero who is genuinely good, despite the temptations he faces; an unpredictable anti-heroine with a striking personality, a kind of female character we don't get to see much of. 
 Yet I had problems. First, as much as I loved Lila, I couldn't help being disappointed by how little she contributes once she leaves Gray London, though she's so strong in the personality department it may escape notice. She tells Kell she'll save his life, but she doesn't. Instead, Kell does pretty much everything. He saves the prince. He kills Athos. He kills Holland. He kills Astrid (which particularly rankles, since he'd earlier told Lila she hasn't the strength to take on Astrid and she's denied the chance to prove him wrong). He dispels the stone. All Lila really does at the climax is a bit of "I know you're in there" stuff more befitting a sidekick than a co-hero. I can only pray she gets more genuine Moments of Awesome in later volumes. 
 Another thing: in this book, if you're a woman and your name isn't Lila, you suck. 
 You're either evil (Astrid) or you're a barely-there nonentity (all the other women, who appear only briefly and leave no impact). There are no female friends, no female mentors, no sisters, and the only "mother," the Queen, is less than nothing to the plot and to the characters therein. Couldn't we have seen at least ONE substantial sympathetic female character other than Lila? Schwab is too gifted a writer to cling so regrettably to the Smurfette Principle. 
 Still, I'm up for the sequels.
