"I am a weapon made of flesh, a sword covered in skin. I was born to kill a king, to end a reign of terror before it can truly begin." 
 My review for Red Queen here. 
 I am so disappointed. It breaks my heart to say this considering that I loved Red Queen, but I didn't enjoy Glass Sword as much as I thought I was going to. 
 After reading Red Queen in February, I went to get the next book soon after it was released. I was so excited to read it. With an ending like that and the gorgeous cover, I had high expectations. Sadly, they were not met. 
 When I first got this book, I tried multiple times to start it. I would only get past chapter 1 and then quit. This month, I told myself that I was finally going to finish this. I was tired of having to avoid spoilers. I desperately needed to see why this triggered so many emotions out of everyone. 
 This book has suffered Second Book Syndrome. The first half of this book was so boring. Nothing really interesting happened. After each chapter, I was ready to put it down. 
 Mare irritated me so many times in this book. I didn't find her annoying at all in the first book. I really liked her, so I was confused as to why others were annoyed by her. Now, I understand why. 
 Her thoughts are so conflicting. One moment she thinks about how she's the most powerful being, acting like she did when she was pretending to be Mareena Titanos. The next, she's broken and alone. Throughout the book, all she does is go on about how powerful she is, how she's worth more than other people, and how she's the little lightning girl. She thinks/says either of those things in basically every chapter. 
 Mare is also quite rude towards some of the characters. I think she sometimes forgets that they have feeling just like she has, and that they have suffered just as much, if not worse, than her. She's stuck-up. She views herself being above everyone else, noting multiple times that they aren't as strong as her, and they never will be. She pushes people away from her, gets upset that they're not taking, and comes back to them when they apologize to her. 
 There were a lot of new characters in this book. It was kind of hard to keep track of who each person is and what they do. 
 Regarding the second half of the book, I was glad that things started to pick up. I was also upset at the turn of events. I was so sad that Shade died. I was in shock.  I tried reading Glass Sword as a palate cleanser. 
 When I studied English Literature in college, I would frequently be reading five works of literature at one time. Occasionally, I would have a night where I ignored all of my school work/reading and would blaze through a YA novel in one night. I'm not sure if it's because I'm not reading classic literature as much or because this one just wasn't that good, but Glass Sword just didn't do it for me. 
 The whole book felt uninspired. It is a lesser version of The Hunger Games. Instead of having a clear vision like Katniss (who just wants her family to be safe), Mare bounces around between her own self-interest, guilt, and a supposed goal of trying to save the newbloods (who are dropped in as a plot point that isn't even fully realized). 
 This book is truly a testament to aggressive YA PR campaigns. It lacks even the most basic elements that make a good YA palate cleanser. Instead of having a clear romance plot (a love triangle would even be acceptable!), Glass Sword has a messy square with no payoff. Mare loves Cal, but Cal doesn't love her (something that is an obvious lie). Kiliorn loves Mare, but she doesn't love him (which feels thrown in for shock value). Finally, Mare still loves Maven, the boy who betrayed her and continues to kill her people. This part of the wonky love square could have been interesting if it had any real consequences. Instead, it just softens the blow of the fake cliff-hanger ending. 
 The whole book, Mare is an uninteresting and selfish narrator. She is constantly focused on her pain, which could have been at least mildly compelling. But instead of showing us the consequences of the trauma that Mare experienced, Aveyard instead tells us everything. She must have no trust in her readers at all. Either that, or she completely lacks the ability to write well. I know I've never written and published a novel and I might not have room to talk. But I learned that the first rule of writing was to show, not tell. 
 Another way Aveyard's lack of decent writing shines through is in her treatment of the newbloods. At the end of Red Queen, the hint of meeting all of the new and complex characters thrown into danger that they are unaware of was one of the elements that made me want to read Glass Sword. Instead, they got a combined few pages of characterization between all of them. The majority of them only had their power listed and maybe their home, a detail that doesn't matter one bit to the story or anyone's characterization. Aveyard missed the chance to round out her books with some complex characters. 
 Glass Sword is an apt title for this book. If crafted properly, it could have struck a deadly blow to the reader's heart. Instead, it's pretty exterior is the best part about it and the lack of substance just leaves one feeling like they experienced the most mundane instead of extraordinary.

I read this book with the understanding that this would be a good read if I'm looking for something post-Potter. Yes, I am one of those Potterheads. And everything seemed to be perfect.  One very good point about the writing, though, is that the descriptions are lush. Morgenstern certainly knows how to paint a vivid picture with words (though it feels like she uses thousands and thousands of words to achieve this). I really did feel like I was in that circus. The only thing is, I couldn't care too much about the story itself...which is really the important thing, isn't it? 
 Overall, I was quite disappointed. The book was horrendously slow and didn't hold my interest long enough for me to care about what happened to Celia and Marco in the end. I didn't even care to look at the last page.

reference_books.title: Divergent (Divergent, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This book was good, but not phenomenal. Perhaps if time had allowed this to precede a certain dystopian trilogy, it might have garnered more attention. Caution: review may contain SPOILERS. 
 Unfortunately, for me, it was difficult to read without comparison. It has something like a Sorting Hat; some of the cheesy and completely needless romance aspects reminiscent of Twilight; and the death-desperation and government issues of The Hunger Games. I will say that it was written well; you will definitely find yourself turning the pages with ease. Random neurology references will probably sound astounding, especially to someone who doesn't know much about the brain. (But I do, so it sort of made me just roll my eyes.) There are a few interesting parts of the book that I wish were expanded upon, but since this is a trilogy, I'm sure Roth is saving it for later. 
 I found it very difficult to relate to any of the characters. I was not particularly attached to anyone (though I'm not sure if this is a fault that had developed after reading book after book where everyone basically dies). It could have done without the romance. And my biggest problem was simply not caring about any of the characters and rolling my eyes at the awkward dialogues. A small detail about body image also disturbed me; I mean, really? More fat antagonizing? That's a low blow. 
 In any case, this would be a good selection for its age-appropriate group. I would personally rate it 2/5, but this review will hopefully help people pick out a book for their angsty teenager. As a bookseller, I figure that's part of the job.

reference_books.title: A Discovery of Witches (All Souls Trilogy, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Alas...here's a book that I really expected to enjoy. I was looking forward to it so much that I neglected to read the little summary at the back. Witches! How wonderful! When I was in high school, witches were still popular...up until Twilight. Had I known that this was going to be another vampire romance novel, I would have elected not to read it. But it was too late. I read it anyway. It had gotten past my 100-page mark and by that point I thought, "I don't like this book, but I've already gone this far, so I may as well finish it." It's a good enough page-turner, I'll give you that. 
 The first thing I realized I disliked was how annoying the main character was. Never a good sign. The protagonists were special snowflakes and acted like it, especially Diana. Oh, look at me, I'm so smart, I'm a genius, I just so happen to have an Eidetic memory, and I went to this and that university and by the way I'm a witch and my parents are dead and I don't know why BUT I don't use my powers because I'M SO MUCH BETTER THAN THAT and being a witch SO doesn't defined my LIFE I MEAN GAWD -- also please note that I love tea and all I eat are eggs but I'll say my favorite food in the entire world is pizza and have a look at all my comfortable leggings... 
 Whew, that's most of that out of my system. And that's just the witch. The vampire is your typical vampire, physical attributes aside (this one doesn't sparkle, nor does he burn in the sun). Why, he's so classy that he uses his excellent sense of smell for determining what wines are good, AND he does yoga! Fancy. Real fancy. And really annoying. 
 As I read, I couldn't get past the sense that the author must have read Twilight some time ago and thought, "You know, I could write a better version of Twilight," and set out to do so. Except instead of useless Bella, she made Diana, who is supposedly much cooler because she actually does stuff -- and as we all know, it isn't that difficult to make a better protagonist than Bella. But it seemed like she was trying much too hard. At the very surface level it's quite similar, even down to the vampire family in the fancy home and the congregation that's out to destroy them because of their forbidden love (no kids yet). Yes, Twilight, but mix in witches and daemons and vampires. Oh, and vampires are all biologists because what else would they do with their time? 
 There's another thing that bugged me. Aside from being pseudo-history, it was also pseudo-science. The strange descriptions of chromosomes really annoyed me. Mutations in chromosomes? Yes, that I can understand. But saying that it's a whole new pair of chromosomes or one...um, that's a chromosomal disorder in our world. I figure this is the sort of book where you're supposed to feel like you could actually be there. And yes, I know, there are witches and daemons and vampires, and that's unrealistic as is (but the narrative really tries to make it seem realistic -- we only notice them when they're all gathered together, for instance), but now you're going into so-called science and trying to mess with it in a way that doesn't even make any sense. So as I read it, I really had to remind myself every time they started getting into the science journals: this isn't our world. At all. 
 In fact, I had to remind myself of several things as I read. 
 "Okay, she's...she's a witch but won't use her powers. Okay. That's why she's so...perfect. Right. Sure." 
 "Okay, he's a vampire that does yoga and is basically Edward with several science degrees instead of high school and he just wants to know who he is. Got it." 
 "All right, yes, sure, please spend a whole chapter that looks as if it's written, 'He kissed me, I kissed him, and his lips were on mine as we kissed, oh, that kiss, so good that kiss was, I kissed him more and he pulled me closer to deepen the kiss, OH THE KISSING' -- I mean, that must mean they dig each other. And not just because she smells good or because she's super-powerful. Yeah." 
 "Yes...chromosome...extra pairs...and that...doesn't mean trisomy or...dammit. This book is ridiculous." 
 I couldn't stand it for long. I don't want to have to keep reminding myself that the character is like this and try to force myself to enjoy the characters. Here was yet another story where EVERYONE ELSE is a thousand times more interesting than the protagonists, and although we went into the other characters' histories for a bit, it was still about Diana and Matthew getting it on (after knowing each other for three weeks). I finished it, and it took me a long, agonizing time to do so. I just couldn't care for the characters. The plot was interesting enough and it ended in a way that obviously said, "GET THE NEXT BOOK LOL"...it felt like the romance was systematically injected into the middle of the story to make it longer. I had to wonder if she had this fantastic plot set out, and perhaps her editor wanted more lovin', and so the terrible romance parts happened. It just felt like it should have been one book, not a trilogy, and all the extra stuff was siphoned into the writing to make sure it would be a trilogy based on size alone. 
 Too many times I'd hoped there would be a SparkNotes version, because that's all I really need. One more damned line about Diana's stretchy pants and how great she is at EVERYTHING THAT COMES HER WAY or how Matthew smells like cinnamon and cloves and is OH-SO-POSSESSIVE and I'll go on a witch hunt myself.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 Rating 2.5 Stars 
 This book was very much on the meh spectrum to me. Helen is not a memorable or strong willed protagonist and Lord Carlston seemed like the author was trying to make him like Mr. Darcy but failed. 
 Besides, no one can be as dashing and brooding as Mr. Darcy. 
 Me: 
 *Ahem* well moving on... 
 The only character I can really praise is Darby, Lady Helen's lady's maid. She was so faithful to Helen and was put in so many situations that would have got her fired if she was caught. Yet she did everything in her power to help Helen, even getting a blow to the face by Mr. Benchley in order for Helen to escape. She was a brave woman who was afraid but still stared it in the face and carried through it I would want her to be my friend. 
 As for the antagonists they certainly made my blood boil. Her Uncle was a henious bastard that thought a woman was supposed to be submissive to men and to secure a good husband to also control her while she was to run the household and produce airs. I know this is not unusual since this is the regency era when men was thought superior instead of equal to women (Frankly, misogyny is still rife today but I'm not going to go on a feminist rampage). But I still wanted Helen to just knock him into his place with her reclaimer strength. But no she was submissive, only using her strength against him at the very end when he was losing her mind, calling her a whore and all horrible names for being discovered in her bedroom with Lord Carlston. Seriously he grabbed her by her shoulder and forced her to her knees. No man should lay a hand on a woman without their permission and no woman should either. As well as no woman or man should lay their hand on a man as well. Helen was too submissive to her Uncle for too long, only showing some resistance to her brother who was being as close-minded as her Uncle. 
 The only thing I liked about Helen was her good-natured heart. She gave the Duke a way out from their marriage when she thought he would not want to marry her after her powers were stripped from her. If I were in her shoes I would have just accepted his hand on the his word of him being my equal so I could be married to a decent rich guy and get away from my terrible uncle and spineless aunt. But no she was too caught in her feelings for lord carlston. Which segways into another problem I had with this novel: the romance. 
 It seemed to come out of the blue. Lord Carlston did nothing that was particularly dashing or nice he was evasive and cold. But yet Helen started having feelings for him and 
 I was sitting there completely confused as to where the hell it came from she didn't seem to be that fond of him. And then he also had feelings for her too but continues to be evasive what the fuck. That's totally husband material there with a personality of a rock, and not to mention his secretive past of his wife going missing. There was just so much wrong when it came to this romance I'm getting really tired of books with romance honestly because they are either instalove, a triangle, or this out of the blue nonsense with no slow burn or context. 
 Anyway the only reason this book didn't just go down the tubes in terms of stars was the paranormal element to it. It was an interesting concept of these super human men and women called Reclaimers that are built to fight and protect their comrades from the deceivers. The deceivers are really fascinating, a creature that hides in plain sight and sucks the energy from unsuspecting innocents with their tentacles. Only Reclaimers can see them with a lens if they have gorged themselves on energy. There was also Helen's mothers minature that held the ultimate power against deceivers and could strip away a Reclaimers powers. There is also the part of a Reclaimers job that is to absorb the energy from these creatures and to also learn to control their own erratic energy that could cause violent outbursts. Theres' also the Dark Days Club that seemed too shrouded in mystery for me to really get its purpose and who is or was a part of the club but i would like to know more about it. 
 I also have to give credit to the narrator of the audio of this book she was really good and that is not always the case with narrators. 
 I will read the sequel to see if this gets better but eventually I have other books to finish or start.

I didn't like this book - it pains me to say this because I really loved Eon and Eona, and for the sake of the good old times I had reading them, I'm adding an extra star. 
 It wasn't the writing that put me off - Allison's writing is still decent, even if it's not as captivating as Eon. 
 It was everything else! 
 This book also made me realise I'm really, really sick to death of olden day England. I've read enough regency/Victorian books that they all sound the same to me these days. 
 And I swear if I see the word 'propriety' one more time, I'm gonna smash something. 
 This novel should've been an interesting, unique, fresh read... but really, it was boring. 
 Some lady called Helen whose mother betrayed England (she didn't actually betray England, just so know, it turned out to be an boring plot line), inherits her mother's power - the ability to do all kinds of stunts, as well as having the strength of two men, and extra hearing, and heightened senses, basically your typical superman shit. 
 Then that Duke guy Carlton comes and tells her she's a 'Reclaimer'... which means they hunt down devils or whatnot, and so begins the story of her adjusting to the idea of becoming a Reclaimer, or deciding not to. It's a really deadly, dangerous job and she refused it at first - but in end she was forced to join... 
 I thought that it was really contrite. I would've have preferred if Helen didn't have to lose 'the best aspects of her personality, such as her adventurous spirit or quick wit' if she got rid of her powers. 
 Btw, whaaaat. Didn't see her so called 'wit' ONCE throughout the whole book. And she didn't seem very adventurous until her speshul powers started kicking in. She seemed like a typical Victorian female, which is totally understandable because of it's setting. But puh-lease, let's NOT pretend she was some *profound* character. 
 Everything was always so convenient. The author tried starting up a love triangle - ffs, leave that shit in the past - PLEASE! - and it's obvious she wanted Helen (the main girl) to end up with baaad sexy handsome chiseled all-male Carlton. Btw, Carlton was boring as fuck. This guy is trying to be the new Mr Darcy or some shit - but he failin bad. 
 The pace was SO SLOW. Instead of reading it quickly like I do most books, it took me almost a week to finish. I kept putting down, and leaving it - my attention span wore off to the point where I had to force myself to finish this: 'One more chapter, come on, you can do this Elle Faye!' 
 Oh, and speaking of which - WHY were the chapters so long!! It drove me nuts... 
 I won't be reading the rest of the books. 
 Will she get rid of this 'Grand Demon?' who is a treat to their land? Will she - 
 Eh. 
 I just don't care enough to want to know what will happen next, which is so disappointing considering the fact that I ate up both EON and EONA in a couple of days.
I tried getting into this book many times... I just couldn't. I didn't care at all for the characters, the world, or the story.
What a bore this was. Don't know why I consist on buying novels that people hype up cause they always suck!
That was such fun! I would like the next book, yes?
It's like pride and prejudice meets Buffy the vampire slayer! Loads of fun! Very different from Eon/Eona.
Beautifully written and researched, a lot of fun to read also. I felt like I had moved back in time into a secret London. Loved it!

I was really enjoying this...until I wasn't. 
 As Clementine says in their review, the plot is "Will she [Helen, the MC] or will she not be the only woman to fight demons or will she merely become a housewife?" 
 Listen, I like Regencies. I wouldn't want them to be all I read, but I enjoy them here and there. I like finding out about our two main characters, and how different everyone thinks they are, but how perfect they really are for each other. 
 I also really like Regencies that have "something else" going on--the Parasol Protectorate is frothy fun, I thought Garth Nix's Newt's Emerald was surprisingly fun, too, and I occasionally enjoy partaking in a Georgette Heyer. 
 Part of the reason for my fondness for Regencies? Well--romance. This is supposedly a 'romance' novel, along with other genres, but there's none so far, at page 295. Yes, there's a bit of a love triangle, but it consists of "mean (but attractive) guy who may or may not have killed his wife" and "brother's friend who is probably still in love with the wife mean guy killed". 
 There's a bunch of classism, sexism, and sizeism in here. I get that it's part of the era, but if you've got DEMONS in your book, you could also fudge the other historical bits, just a touch? Why not make Helen into someone with a bit more mobility, like making Helen the lady's maid who got kidnapped? (Also, that's literally the only question I have at this point in the novel, which is the main reason why I'm DNF'ing--what happened to Berta? I don't know. It's dropped as a plotline except to occasionally remind the reader that mean guy may have kidnapped her.) 
 Another character who would have been more interesting to read about: Helen's mother. 
 Helen is tall and thin, but it's not in style when this book takes place, so that means she's "unattractive". Uh... 
 Finally, the demons in this book are trying to hard to be original. 
 DNF'd at p295. (62.5%) 
 Edited to add: Screw it, I'm adding it to my reading challenge. I read 295 pages of this book!

Originally posted on Sleepless Reads (http://sleeplessreadsreviews.blogspot.ca) on January 22nd, 2016: 
 In all honesty, the Dark Days Club was everything that I was looking for in a book. Filled with supernatural creatures, secret societies, mysterious heroes, and of course, set in Regency England, this book is exactly what every historical YA bookworm will want! 
 The story revolves around Lady Helen, who's about to be presented in front of Queen Charlotte and is having a hard time coming to terms with her season. The pressure is on for her, since her mother (despite her being deceased) and her reputation still cast a huge shadow over her. After a series of unfortunate events, Helen finds herself entangled in a world of demon hunting and secret societies, causing her to realize that being a lady isn't the hardest job in the world: but being a demon-hunting lady is. 
 I loved this story very much, although I will have to say, it is a slow burn. This book was very big, and although I felt in the beginning that it seemed to go on forever, at the end of it, I found it fitting to be as long as it was, otherwise we wouldn't have gotten the story as it is now (well, I don't know how much has changed in the final copies, since I got this book way before it was published). 
 What I loved about Helen was that she was smart and unlike so many other YA heroines thought things through (which is probably why this book was as long as it was, but for her to not jump to conclusions, it was fine by me). She's really protective, and will do anything to save those she loves. She's also a very proper lady (who discovers she inherits a lot from her mother), and I felt really bad for her because she was so intelligent and her own character, but her environment and livelihood didn't really understand that. I felt that Good man did an amazing job representing the repression of a lady during the 1800s- no matter how much Pride and Prejudice got us swoon, being a lady before the 21st century sucked, for the lack of a better word. 
 Also, on the topic of Pride and Prejudice, I really got a PPZ (Pride, Prejudice and Zombies) feel from the book. I know they weren't hunting demons in PPZ, but the fact that it's regency era and they're hunting demons got me thinking more of PPZ than Shadowhunter (it's probably due to the amount of movie trailers I see). 
 But what really made this novel for me? THERE WAS NO LOVE TRIANGLE! There's a bit of romance, but it doesn't really distract from the fact that you know, Helen ends up entangled in a world where people hunt demons. In terms of the men in her life, her brother bothers me because he doesn't know how easy he has it, his friend Selburn is hiding something (in my eyes), and Lord Carlston... Oh Carlston, you misunderstood man. We get to know him, but he has more secrets that are not revealed in this book. 
 Overall, this book is awesome, and I really recommend on getting it!

Lady Helen is the first YA heroine I've come across whose special magical destiny makes her less interesting. 
 The Dark Days Club is about whether she'll risk becoming a monster-fighting Regency superhero or stifle her nature and talents for the sake of luxurious mediocrity. If she's a protagonist actually worth basing a series on, the choice should be obvious. But instead of getting the hell on with meatier topics, we get a whole book of Helen's dithering followed by a climax that skips the entire central question of the novel. 
 For the sake of some of the characters, I could have forgiven the draggy pacing. I could have forgiven the info dumps of supernatural lore and historical detail. I could even have forgiven my most hated of historical novel sins: peppering scenes with Byron and Beau Brummell and any Patroness of Alamack's. (I should know by now to quietly consign a book to my "didn't-finish" shelf the instant Prinny shows up at a party.) But a heroine who wrestles with a very specific dilemma and then has that choice taken out of her hands? I guess that's my breaking point.

Wow. I had such mixed feelings about this. I plan to review it soon but for now... like for real how did you guys tolerate Mac for that long? I kept going because y'all smart people told me to but jeez oh man it took until the last 40 pages or so before I could stand her.

Synopsis: Mackayla Lane is a typical 20-something girl. She lives in the small town of Ashford, Georgia, with her parents. She works part time as a bartender and enjoys working on her tan and spending time with her family. But Mackayla's world is changed forever when her elder sister, Alina, who is studying abroad in Dublin, is murdered. The Lane family is stunned and shaken by the experience. More troubling is the fact that the Dublin police have no clues about Alina's murderer. Mackayla refuses to see her sister's death go unsolved, so she goes to Dublin herself in the hopes of lighting a fire under the investigators or possibly turning up new evidence herself. 
 Alina's murder takes on an entirely new and sinister view when Mackayla finally listens to her voicemail and discovers that Alina left her a desperate and puzzling message several hours before she was murdered. Mackayla plays the message for investigators but gets nowhere. When she asks a local bookseller about a Gaelic word Alina mentioned in the voicemail, Mackayla is told to go back to Georgia and forget she ever heard the word. Unwilling to take no for an answer, Mackayla continues to dig, but what she discovers terrifies her. Mackayla is a sidhe seer. She can see faeries. 
 Desperate for help and not understanding how she sees what she sees and if her ability has something to do with Alina's death, Mackayla returns to the bookseller, Jericho Barrons, for help. Uncertain if Barrons is using her or helping her, Mackayla has no one else to trust in learning about being a sidhe seer or the death of her sister. 
 Review: I tend to avoid books that generate an insane amount of hype. Sometimes, I should have stuck to my instincts (Twilight. I just don't get those books). Other times, my instincts were totally wrong (Harry Potter, The Hunger Games) and I am glad I went against them. Darkfever is another example of me being glad I went against my instincts. 
 I almost don't even know where to start with this review. This story was complicated (in a good way). 
 Mackayla is a great character. I enjoyed her Southern charm, which wasn't over-the-top, thankfully. Despite her supernatural powers, she was really normal. She was a normal girl trying to get justice for her sister. I enjoyed Mackayla as a whole. 
 Moning creates an interesting paranormal world. I like the power with which she imbued Mackayla. I really enjoyed her faery structure and hierarchy. Moning created a tantalizing world for her story to operate within. 
 The plot was quickly paced and kept me interested and entertained. 
 I checked this book out from the library, because I was skeptical. I ended up liking it so much I went out and bought the entire series, including this book. 
 I would like to point out that most booksellers have this series categorized as "romance." It is definitely not romance. It is hard core Urban Fantasy with some racy sexual scenes. If the "romance" label has kept you from this book, don't let it. 
 Overall, I enjoyed this book immensely and cannot wait to read the next installment!
try as I might I just couldn't finish this book
A disbelieving Southern Belle thrust into the paranormal urban fantasy. I kept wavering back and forth between relating to the main character and wanting to smack her.

Oh, yawn. Definitely not my cup of tea at all. A beautiful young Georgia woman travels to Dublin to look into the mysterious murder of her sister. Then we get into a world of vampires and evil fairies and all sorts of supernatural bad guys with Gaelic names. And, of course, our heroine is also part of this clan, only one of the few good ones who can counter all that evil. this book surprised me I hadn't really been a fan of moning's highlander series and was hesitant to check out this book but a friend recommended to me and I must admit I rather enjoyed it. there wasn't much a climax in the plot but I suspect this is because the story line is much bigger then one book and this book left me wanting more I can't wait to see what mac and barrons face in the next book.

Find all of my reviews at: http://52bookminimum.blogspot.com/ 
 Ahhhhh, stop yelling at me already and let me explain. 
 It seems everyone liked this book. I'm talking everyone. EVERYONE. Except me. I. Just. Don't. Get. It. 
 Okay, not really. This is obviously a case of it's not you, it's me. Maybe I'm too mature for stories of the supernat . . . BWAHAHAHAHA! I couldn't even type that without laughing. I don't really know what went wrong, so I'm gonna play it safe and blame it on Sookie Stackhouse . . . 
 After riding out the horribleness which became the Southern Vampire series, I just wasn't prepared to deal with yet another vapid waitress and her otherwordly interactions. 
 You see, Mac is a simple waitress from a simple small Southern town whose simple life gets flipped upside down when her sister gets murdered. Annnnnnnd of course Mac has to take it upon herself to travel halfway across the world in order to become an amateur Sherlock Holmes and find out "whodunit." The problem? Well, Mac is an idiot. I mean, she made Sookie seem like a real braintrust, which is simply terrifying. Mac spends most of her time coordinating her ensembles with her nails, and don't you know . . . 
 Yep, Mac referenced pink so much I thought I was going to barf Pepto Bismol. 
 Along the way, Mac meets a mysterious alpha male named Barrons who (like me) finds her insufferable, but (unlike me) somehow doesn't follow his instincts to step aside and let her be murdered. Turns out that's a good thing as Mac has some special powers of her own. Powers that detect the hidden Fae that walk amongst the normies as well as the ability to sense hidden Fae Objects of Power (OOPs for short). 
 Sidenote: My brain insisted on replacing OOP with O.P.P. - which is a VERY different thing. That song is still playing in my head. Are any of you even old enough to remember Naughty by Nature? Probably not *insert sad face* so here's a little image that will show you how the song goes . . . 
 Okay, back on topic. Barrons recruits Mac in order to find the Sinsar Dubh - the most powerful of all of OOPs that can destroy the world as we know it. Talk about some serious pressure. 
 Get it? Anyone? Bueller? Under Pressure - Queen and David Bowie??? Hilarious! 
 Alright, so this book didn't work for me and I didn't like it, but I didn't completely hate it either. Some things I enjoyed? 
 1. The writing wasn't horrible and although I really don't like first person narrative, I did like that Mac's voice was well aware of the fact that she was telling a story that already happened. Seriously authors, if you are writing from first person it's pretty obvious that person ISN'T DEAD, so don't try to bullshit the reader into getting all nervous about whether they're going to make it out alive. 
 2. Mac admits she's a useless Barbie in times of crisis. 
 3. The setting. Although the world building was pretty lame for me, I'm assuming it gets better since there are a crapton more books in this series. However . . . Dublin???? That's good - assuming Mac and Barrons ever leave the f-ing bookstore. 
 4. Mac's superpower of detecting bad guys? She vomits. LOLOLOLOL. I got a kick out of that. 
 5. And last, but obviously not least, BARRONS. Duh, right? I haven't yet read any reviews of this series, but I'm assuming there's a lot of Joe Manganiello gifs to be had. For me, though? It was all about this dude . . . 
 and anytime I can't get the image of Oded Fehr out of my head is a good time. 
 To all my homegirls out there who have read/are currently reading/or are re-reading this series - I'm sorry it didn't work for me. I'm always the oddball : (

 this series was awesome. I do wish you could make more of mac and barrons they made these books with their steamy romance. would like to know if they are still together,are they still living in dublin????????????????????????????????????????

I don't know if I was reading a different book than everyone else, or what. 
 Positives: It was a fairly quick read. Which was probably the only thing that kept me from Lemming it. 
 Negatives: 
 The main character - was not someone I could get behind. This may just be me, as I can be a tom-boy sometimes, but her fussing over clothes and nails was totally lost on me. She was also a strange combination of whiney and get-along-go-along (by that I mean she was willing to just blase go along without any answers). 
 The side characters - were totally unlikable. I wanted to like Jericho, but there was never a thaw in his rude behavior. As for the other characters, the author barely brush pasted them and the attention they get showed them in a very negative/annoying light. 
 The world building - was not there. Having Jericho be so aloof with his answers means that I know more about Mac's fashion sense than the world. 
 The writing - felt very repetitive and time-skip narration was a total distraction. 
 Oh well, turns out I am in the minority disliking this book, but to each his/her own.

reference_books.title: The Iron Queen (The Iron Fey, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
original post here 
 The Iron Queen marks the epic conclusion of Meaghan Chase's battle with the Iron Feys. All she wanted was to be normal. Even though she knows she can't have the "normal" life she wants, at least she wanted the bit of what her being a half-human, half-fey can offer her. With the threat of the false Iron King still hounding her, she knows she cannot go back to her family, and her only choice is to confront her battles head on. Her only consolation is having Ash by her side and they are determined to fight for their love no matter what happens. 
 As the threat of the Iron Kingdom spread like wildfire across the Nevernever, Meaghan, being the only one to withstand iron, is called to stop the false Iron King. Together with Ash and Puck, they are thrust into the faery war, knowing that with everything at stake, they have to win this war or bring the false Iron King down with them. Meaghan and Ash knows that the future is bleak for them. The only thing that keeps them going is their love for them and a promise of a possible future for them to finally have a life together. 
 Expect that this journey will be perilous, merciless, and heart-wrenching. If you think that the first two books gave you a mighty ride, then hold on tight and prepare something to console you because The Iron Queen is a heart-stopper until the very last page. 
 Julie Kagawa delivers once again in this much anticipated third book in the Iron Fey series. There's a fine balance of humor, ardor, pain, and love in the time of war and crossroads. I found it very hard to write a review for this one and at the same time a strong nudge to write about it. It's like reading/seeing Lord of the Rings: Return of the King again, where war have torn friends, demanded sacrifices, and living knowing it could very be your last. But it was certainly worth every tear I shed after closing the book - tears out of the mixed emotions flooding in, but mostly out of hope for a love that will endure.

You know the feeling that you don't want something to end? Well, I got that feeling after reading City of Glass. I badly wanted the story to go on, not fearing it will disappoint readers. Because after the three books, you know that it's THAT good. 
 So looking forward to City of Fallen Angels!

reference_books.title: The Demon's Surrender (The Demon's Lexicon, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
I have said this before and I will say this again. Everybody can have Nick. I'm keeping Alan. 
 I really would love to hug Sarah and thank her for a beautiful trilogy. It's so wonderfully complicated and twisted that will make you ache, but she still managed to get away with it smiling and have you loving a demon (or a compulsive liar in my case). 
 It is not just a story of a battle between good and evil, but rather those who are the lesser evil. And above all the stuffs about demons and the Goblin Market, is the story about family - of how two brothers fight for each other, a brother and sister who are there for each other no matter what, and someone who is willing to sacrifice everything she had just to be with her sister. It is about love, that you are willing to hurt, lie, and betray for the sake of it. 
 I'm really a sucker for stories about siblings. It was the story of the brothers, Nick and Alan, who captivated me in the first book. There was something between them that transcend blood that defines their brotherhood. And in this last book just proves how beautifully dark their brotherhood is that it is heartbreaking. I cried after the reading the book. It was not out of relief or sadness about the end of the story. The experience of it just made a storm of emotion in me that well, cracked the dam so to speak. 
 This is one book I would dance the Goblin Market for. A feverish conclusion to a beautifully twisted trilogy. Sarah Rees Brennan, you are my Goblin Market Queen. (Belated Happy Birthday!)

reference_books.title: Darkness Becomes Her (Gods & Monsters, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
original post here 
 Ari always felt different. She's been in foster care for as long as she can remember and looking quite different does not help her case. But she didn't expected that she is that different. After discovering what happened to her mother, Ari had to run to the last place she wanted to be. New 2 in New Orleans. Though she can't quite shake the feeling that she belong in the place, and that something lurks in the dark corners that will finally shed light to the darkness that hounds her past. 
 I loved the book despite the darkness that trails behind every page you turn. I had no idea what the story was all about aside from the blurb that was provided. I was not quite sure at first how the mythology aspect would come in the story since there are certainly an array of supernatural beings depicted in the story. Only later in the story would it all dawn to you and the tragedy that is the story behind Ari's history. 
 I love how Ari was depicted as a strong-willed character, despite her past experiences in foster care, she used it for empowering herself and not as a sad part of herself to wallow on. It is lovely to see that in a town full of people and creatures that can be looked as different, they created a home for themselves and welcome others just like them. When the government cannot do anything for them, they took it upon themselves to do something for their own. 
 This is a fitting modern tale of how mythology gods turn on each other and destroy themselves, battling supernatural beings for power and the latter for survival. The truth about Ari is shrouded in darkness and despair, but can she own it like she did of her past? Or will it terrify her as well as the other is terrified of her?

reference_books.title: The Poison Eaters and Other Stories
reference_books.review_text:
original post here 
 Holly Black delivers wicked good stories in bite size fun in her collection of short stories. Starting off with the stark-dark vampire story, The Coldest Girl in Coldtown, and ending off with the story of The Poison Eaters. 
 I can't really pick favorites because all of them are particularly good! Though I would particularly mention the story of Paper Cut Scissors because it is a smart story about books coming to life. Then I was surprised by the story, Night Market because it was about one of the folklores in the Philippines, and a good one about it. I haven't read Ironside yet but this is a side story of Roiben and Kaye, but mostly about a situation about Roiben and Corny, Kaye's friend. 
 Whether you're in the mood for some play with the demon, the occult, or even otherworld entities, Holly Black got it covered for you. They are all beautifully twisted stories that would entice you, leave you off guard, and wanting more.

 This is an enthralling first novel from Andrea Cremer about supernatural teenagers, plagued by hormonal surge, issues on identity, friends and family, and being responsible for the choices one makes. You'll fall in-love with the strong will of Calla, the dynamics of the packs, and pick a team between Ren and Shay. And there's also the mystery behind the history of Calla's world, the danger that threatens everyone and hidden truths that can shatter everything they believe in. 
 I personally fell in-love with this book. It was definitely a big book to chomp on but I devoured it like I was one of the pack. It wasn't hard to fall for Shay's charm and also feel for Ren on the other hand. Every chapter will have you holding your breath wishing wicked creatures out of the way, or the boys are just so freakishly hot they will make you skip a heartbeat. Though Ren is never short on hotness, I'm on Team Shay and is cheering for the team. And, sorry Drew (Patch) but I think I'm also crushing on Will (Shay).

I have the ARC for the fourth book in the series, so I figured I'd better get a move on. There may be some mild kissing spoilers. 
 Nightshade by Andrea Cremer is a book about teenaged werewolves. It stars the stuffy Calla, who is the alpha of her pack. She's destined to mate with Ren, the alpha of another pack. And these two packs stroll the halls as the most popular kids. During the very first pages, Calla rescues a mere human, named Shay, and introduces him as the third wheel in the love triangle. With Shay, Calla teaches him the background of her people, the Guardians, and he shows her that not all is how it seems. Will Calla be able to become the individual that she's always dreamed of becoming? 
 I can see why people like this book. It's pretty fast paced, and there's some interesting world building. I like the ideas that stem with the mythology of the Guardians, Keepers, and whatnot. I also liked how Cremer shows us a lot of this as Calla is explaining her world to Shay. There are some pretty good twists that develop throughout the plot, and leaves me interested enough to stick around for the sequel. 
 That said, I had a ton of issues with this book. I wonder if I'd have liked it better three years ago when it first came out. The dialogue is so stuffy and stilted-- all of the characters sound middle aged, especially Calla. And she is way too easy with her lips. She very frequently kisses different boys right after one another. Sorry if that's a spoiler, but if you don't know there's a love triangle by page 5, shame on you! Also, I don't understand why these kids are taking some high brow college courses in high school. Are they in a magnet school or something? Organic Chemistry? Some other crazy philosophical course? Most kids would be lucky to be in a school like that separating caffeine from tea. I'm rather jealous actually. Both of the boys seem pretty pushy, so I'm not really digging either one of them. I wish Calla would just tell them both to take a hike and go on a girly vacation with Bryn or something. 
 Overall, good world building and some interesting twists, but I'm not yet convinced by the characters, how they talk, or where this is going. We'll see how the next 3 books go.

I'm one of those people whom if a book starts out slow or doesn't really interest me at first, I'll give it a while to pick up in case it gets better. However if a book immediately starts with a writing style that drives me crazy, I can only go about two chapters. I'd heard good things about this book and I'm always up for anything to do with werewolves. But the author here has decided to throw you into this universe and all it's people without any explanation whatsoever. From the reviews I've been reading by people who even liked the book it doesn't really get explained until the middle of the book. I know some people don't mind that kind of writing or even prefer it. And I'm not saying an author has to spoon feed you everything going on in a book, but that just drives me up the wall. Utter confusion is not what I want to feel after reading the first chapter. Maybe it's up other people's alley, but it's not for me.

Book blurb: Calla is the alpha female of a shape-shifting wolf pack. She is destined to marry Ren Laroche, the pack's alpha male. Together, they would rule their pack together, guarding sacred sites for the Keepers. But then, Calla saves a beautiful human boy, who captures her heart. Calla begins to question everything - her fate, her existence, and her world and the orders the Keepers have asked her to follow. She will have to make a choice. But will she follow her heart if it means losing everything, including her own life? 
 Let me start by saying this: if there are ANY names that are different, I'm apologizing straight away. I've read this book in Danish (a gift from a friend), and they're not always very good at remembering to keep the true names when they translate - they're getting better though. 
 Calla is not an ordinary 18 year old girl. She's a wolf, destined to be a part of a new pack formed by the young ones from two different packs; Nightshades and Ravens. Calla is from the Nightshade pack and her chosen mate is Ren from the Ravens. None of them chose this reunion, but are proud to be a part of the new pack. 
 Every pack is ruled by a pair of alphas. Everyone in the pack (including the alphas) are ruled by a Keeper. The Nightshades are ruled by Lumine and the Ravens are ruled by Efron. The new pack will be formed when Calla and Ren are married and will be ruled by Logan, Efron's son. 
 One day when Calla is running patrol through the forest as a wolf, she runs across a young boy who's been badly hurt by a bear. She saves him, without knowing who he is. It is forbidden to interact with humans, to save them -and especially to tell them ANYTHING about the packs, the Keepers and the Searchers, but Calla can't just leave him to die. Something about him draws her. 
 Calla finds out the next day, when he shows up as the nephew of a Keeper, starting school. His name is Shay. Calla is scared frightened her secret will be revealed. If her pack finds out she helped Shay, the consequences would be bad. 
 Calla is ordered to look after Shay, help him settle in by the Keepers. Calla is already drawn towards him, and the extra time she spends with him doesn't make it easier to control the attraction. When Shay shows Calla a book that is forbidden to read and tells her about it, her entire existence starts to tumble. Calla starts to wonder about a lot of the rules she has been living by her entire life. She starts to question things about the Warriors (the packs), the Keepers and the Searchers. Life is not black and white - it's full of grey shades, and Calla is about to find out in a bad way that every choice has consequences, not only for herself, but for everybody else too. 
 This book felt like a "starter" story. It shows us the dilemma, the different characters - kind of... like the first book in Lord of the Rings. It shows us the background, the reason for the story to take place, but the "true action" really doesn't begin until the very end of the book. But when it happens - it explodes! 
 There is plenty of action before, but more on an emotional level. Calla is going up against ancient laws, expectations and everything she knows for love. She struggles to find a foothold in the things she thought she knew, the things that are shown to her and the things she wants and needs to do. 
 The book left me wanting to know what will happen next, and I can't wait to read Wolfsbane, the second book in this trilogy. Bloodrose is the third and was released January this year.
a virgin constantly in heat. I was not impressed with main character at all who though was a virgin and said no seemed to get hot and bothered for two different men.

I was very excited to get this book, sure I bought the e-book myself even though I much prefer print copies, I just could not wait. It was the cover art that first drew me in, the picture was just absolutely stunning and lucky for me, the story turned out to be as well. 
 The character's in the novel are very well thought through, each of them strong and rounded, perhaps one of my favorite that shows just how realistic the characters were created, was the fact that there was a gay couple within the pack's, and as you might imagine, not everyone agreed with it. Despite being told by the Alpha, that they needed to suck it up and deal with it because they were in full support of the relationship, words were exchanged as well as a couple of punches and instead of it rolling through as if it was no big deal. The alpha's actually punished those who were in the wrong. 
 That was another thing that I liked about this book. I have noticed a lot of the time, author's forget the wolf hierarchy that comes with werewolves,this one was obviously not one of those cases. To me they seemed to follow the wolf hierarchy pretty close, even to the point on who eats first. 
 I did have a little bit of mixed feelings when it came to the main character Calla, I liked her personality, and the fact that it seemed well balanced, not to sweet so everyone loves her and not to witchy so everyone hates her. What really disappointed me was Calla's reaction to Shay. I felt that she was practically engaged and arranged marriage or not, she had been serious with it and Ren definitely drew some sort of emotion out of her but she still seemed to not act as if she were engaged and that bothered me. 
 The big fight scene at the end also seemed a little rushed for my taste but it left off in a way that I immediately went and bout the sequel so it could have possibly been the point. 
 Favorite Charrie: Ren. He is one fine piece of beef cake and his actions in the end sealed the deal where I am concerned. 
 Quotes: 
 1. " I swallowed a groan, searching for any clothes I particularly wanted to protect, and sat on top of my Republicans for Voldermort hoodie." 
 2. "I've got a bottle full of hydrochloric acid in my hand, Ren. Don't piss me off." 
 3. " I didn't have these boobs until you cinched it up.

This was an interesting story. The mythology is quite unique, though a bit confusing at first, and I really liked the themes of feminism and slavery running throughout. Also, it did a great job of showing the difficulties around doing what is expected of you versus doing what you really want to do. The writing is strong as well, and painted vivid images. 
 I liked Ren a lot. He is a complex character with a rough exterior and a softer, understanding side to him. He's a good leader and a good listener, and acts according to what he believes is right, as well as how he's been brought up. I didn't like Shay or Calla, though. They're both pretty selfish, and they seriously mistreated Ren many times. 
 Shay professes to be better than Ren because he wants to treat Calla as an equal and not a possession. But he contradicts that every single time he kisses her, because she has repeatedly told him not to. I found that very disrespectful. Shay treats Calla as an object more than Ren ever does, because Ren actually listens when Calla tells him to stop, and also lets her set the pace with their upcoming union. If she'd told him to never touch her again, he'd have listened and respected her wishes. But she never says that. Instead, she encourages him. 
 At the beginning of the story, Calla is a strong alpha and a good leader. She starts out saying that she and Ren are both alphas and would run the pack together after their union, but then she willingly gives up control of the wolves in her own pack and we're not told why. We're just given her assumption that she's supposed to submit to Ren. 
 It bothered me that Calla just let's Ren take over like this without talking to him about her own wishes first. Ren has proven himself to be a good leader and listener over and over, so it made me mad that she didn't even try to talk to him. This undermined some of the feminist themes running throughout the story. 
 Calla's transformation wasn't a positive one in this story. She starts out strong, but then kind of melts into a puddle. In the beginning, she's a strong alpha and demonstrates inherent qualities of decision making and decisive action. It doesn't make sense that she'd fall to pieces because of a simple attraction to someone she's not supposed to be with. Instead, an alpha would weigh the possibilities and then make a firm decision one way or another. And, she'd enforce that decision with strength and confidence, because that's what an alpha would do. Instead, she slowly turns wishy-washy. 
 The mythology was interesting and unique, though, and I would have liked to see more of it. I was a bit confused by the ending, and the way it unfolded didn't ring true to the characters or the situation. But I am hoping that will be cleared up in the next book. And, I'm hoping Calla's spine will be back and intact.

** spoiler alert ** 
 1 1/2 
 So, where to start? 
 I've heard a lot about how this book is a rip-off of Twilight and Sookie Stackhouse. I haven't read either of those series, yet (well, I have no intention of reading Twilight, but I am interested in the Southern Vampires), but from what I know of both, I can definitely see the comparisons. It also initially reminded me of Midnighters, with the obligatory group of outsiders/freaks who hang out together, and you could even throw in little Harry Potter reference, if you count using the Elixir of Life (which, of course, is a historical thing, but I doubt most people nowadays know of it and the Philosopher's Stone or anything alchemical except through Harry Potter). 
 It really was rather cliche, right from the start. Normal, popular, cheerleader girl turns freak by getting in a car crash which kills her family and becomming psychic. (Though, after what we learn, it wasn't the crash but the elixir, imo). Hangs out with troubled goth girl and gay guy friend. Of course. (Btw, I was part of the freak/geek crowd in my high school. There are other variations. Or maybe it's just the 30 year-old demi-goth in me which is tired of seeing goth as just a teenage fad, but I digress.) 
 So in comes ubermensch, in all his glory. How boring is Damen, honestly? Ok, so I tend to go for the dark and brooding types, or the rough and rugged types, and the California beauty thing doesn't really do it for me - but he had no real mystery. The reader knows exactly what and who he is from the outset, and there's nothing which makes him at all interesting or conflicted or anything. 
 And, for the love of all things holy, I would like - even in a trashy romance novel - for the girl to learn a little something about the guys personality, his beliefs, his ideas, and not just fall desperately in lust 'cause he's just oh so hot... (I also wouldn't mind a hot chick knowing she's hot.) 
 And since when does beng psychic mean you can touch a book and know everything in it? 
 Oh, and of course she can't tell anyone about her psychic abilities 'cause they'll think she's a freak. Hello - one of your best friends is a goth chick. She would probably think it's the coolest damn thing about you. Admittedly, she'd probably be a bit freaked that you could read her thoughts - but you could tell her some of it, if not all of it. Us freaks just love freaky things - get it? Ugh. 
 And then comes the kindly psychic who could help you. But you're dismissive - lying about it, firstly, then saying she's a phony. Of course she can see your dead sister and read your thoughts, but clearly she's a phony. 
 But then we learn it's not that, really, it's your guilt for "causing the accident". It's your punishement, and you don't want help... you just want to wallow. Ok, I can dig that - for awhile. I remember my own moments of wallowing in angst - though I always turned to someone to confide in, to trust. I mean, you don't even trust your dead little sister with some of your burden? That's right - because you're punishing yourself. 
 But wait - what's this? You find that alcohol shuts out the noise, so you become a raging alcholic... overnight! Not just a nip here and there to take the edge of, no, of course not. That won't do. 
 So you're whiny and annoying AND a hypocrit, because if it was about punishing yourself you wouldn't jump at the first - no, sorry, second - chance to turn it off. 
 And even then, when you're desperate to turn it off, you still won't just pony up and go to the goddamn psychic! 
 Ok, anyway... 
 And then there's Drina. Drina - so obvious. Of course even she's so drop-dead gorgeous that even while she's trying to kill you you're struck by her beauty. Obviously the elixir not only keeps people alive, and heals them, (and gives them other super powers, apparently) - but it makes them drop dead gorgeous. Except it didn't seem to have the same effect on Ever. Maybe it only happens after the first 100 years... who knows, they never explain anything. 
 I have to pause to say the first half of the book was ok. Yes, it was cliche and annoying, but it was readable, in that teenage trashy romance kinda way - but then we get to the end where Drina "reveals" herself as the killer, and we discover she's a complete and utter cartoon villian. "It was I who killed your family... muahahaha!" "Oh, you mortals... so boring, so obvious." I kept thinking of Voldemort at his cheesiest ('cause, let's admit it, Voldemort was cheesy, especially in the movie version of GoF). She might as well have said "I'll get you my pretty, and your little dead sister, too" - afterall, she practically died like the Wicked Witch. "I'm melting... I'm melting... " 
 And Damen the clueless. Never figuring out that Ever, in her various incarnations, kept being killed? Never putting together that it kept seeming to happen in sort of the same way, according to Drina. 
 So I guess Mr. Perfect does have a flaw - it's sheer and utter stupidity. 
 And half of the drama between Damen and Ever could've been resolved by just talking to each other, instead of playing mind games half the time. I mean, really, Ever - why do you love him, besides the fact he's hot? Ok, so you recognize him on some level. (Did anyone not know it was Damen that saved her from the car accident from the first moment you meet him and their eyes meet? Really?) 
 But, of course, Ever doesn't seem to learn much in her various incarnations, either. Yes, Damen says part of the journey is forgetting, but he also mentions that souls are meant to evolve. Of course, I guess she never gets past 17, so that might explain a lot. 
 And the ending was just so saccharine. 
 And if Ever "pressed her lips together" one more time I think I was gonna scream. I really hope the author discovers some more descriptive phrases for the next book. 
 But, I must admit, despite all it's various flaws, I did get the tinglies once or twice. I guess I'm a sucker for romance, no matter how badly portrayed. *sighs* That's more a failing of mine than a credit to the author, though. 
 I'm glad I didn't buy it. And, ok, I might read the next one. Then again, I read the first couple of pages that were previewed at the end of this book, and I found them even more annoying than the horrible ending I'd just read. So maybe not. I certainly won't pay for it.

this book totally ripped off twilight saga's idea. it added different things in the mix. it has potential to be different. author needs to also learn to suck readers in a bit more. i want the feeling that i dont/cant want to stop reading. this didnt have it for me.

The first half of the book seems like a mashup of random other paranormal books and goes on way too long. I think it could have been condensed down to half the pages and been much better. I would have given the first half of the book two stars. 
 The last half of the book really improved though. It got much more original and interesting and started moving much quicker. I would have given the last half four stars. 
 So I split the difference and ended up with 3 stars. I'm really looking forward to the next in the series though and hope that it keeps the originality and fast pace.

I don't read many YA books, but when i do i want the story to hook me in right from the get go, If i get bored im pretty sure to dump the book unread. But Evermore by Alyson Noel The first book in The Immortals series was a real page turner. 
 Getting to know Ever, Damen, Haven, Miles and Riley was a pleasure. For any teenager or adult that's lost loved ones you'll empathise with Ever as she struggles with her grief when her family are killed, and you'll go along for the ride as she struggles to contain her new ability of hearing thoughts, seeing auras and just knowing things by touching them. It's only when the new student cute boy Damen joins her school she feels normal when being around him quietens everything around her. 
 Even though it's a million and one years ago since i was a teenager i smiled at the flow of Ever's relationships with her two school friends Haven and Miles, the "Dibs i saw the cute boy first" rule that was just absolute amongst friends, and it's only in stories you get the funny gay friend who i would have killed to have back in school, Miles was so funny to read i loved him instantly. 
 Since the accident that killed her family, Ever had been visited by her dead sister, and although i did like these sections of the book i felt Riley spoke older than her 12 years, since it wasn't that long ago they died im assuming she'd still speak as a kid, and i just felt she was more sassy young adult than annoying little sister...although she was that too. But that didn't take away my enjoyment of her, she was kooky and sassy and a pain in the butt, but she loved her sister enough to not let her be left behind...and there's a part near the end i don't mind saying i had a little sniffle at. ( I read Riley is getting her own spin off series too) 
 People have said Evermore has a tinge of Twilight, and yes if you mean theres a teenage girl and an older guy pretending to be 17 and in love with the girl, there is that similarity, but Damen is no Edward Cullen, he doesn't sparkle for one, but he also doesn't hide from his feelings for Evermore, he's waited for her lifetime after lifetime and he's determined to get the girl this time. I loved watching them fall in love...and it's not all easy going, there's twists and turns, intrigued, death threats. 
 Like i said a real page turner. A must read for anyone who loves YA books or who just wants something different to the genres they usually read.

So I bought the first two books to give this series a try and well no offense to the fans but it was a waist of money. When I first started reading this I felt like it was Twilight all over again. reference_books.review_text:

And i really liked the idea of the main character losing her memory and then becoming a new person (and how she couldn't understand why she used to hang out with horrible people who were such jerks).

book_a.title: The Maze Runner (Maze Runner, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Let me start by saying that the first 100 pages were completely gripping, and it was a real fun ride trying to figure out what was going on with Thomas and this new crazy world he was in. It was really fun. 
 There were some little touches about things he could only vaguely remember, like when he feels that he 'must' be a runner even though he can't understand why. Stuff like that was really cool, and it's hard to pull off without becoming annoying. 
 But after a while, i got the feeling that although things needed to be explained during the book, after all Thomas doesn't know where the hell he is, so how should the reader know either?-the writer kept doing this annoying thing of describing something, and then describing it again, in the same paragraph, as if we weren't around or didn't hear it the first time. Lots of times there were things like 'Thomas walked around feeling nervous' and then in the next sentence, 'he was nervous but he couldn't understand why he was nervous.' Maybe i'm the only one who noticed this, but it started to really bother me. 
 Anyway, the book really slowed in the middle and the end was actually pretty great, right until the last page. I won't spoil it, but when an author does something like that, it makes me feel a little cheated somehow. 
 Over all, it was a bit disappointing, and i don't think i'll read the others in the series. Although i heard that it will be made into a movie next year, and i guess that would be interesting to see, especially with some of the action scenes in the maze.

This was an interesting idea. But sadly, there were many plot holes/issues. 
 In the beginning, when Thomas shows up at the maze, there's a phenomenon where the other Gladers won't answer Thomas' questions. It continues for days on end where they will tell him some things, but hide others. As if something bad will happen if they let Thomas know too much too soon. And this is never explained. Nothing bad happens when he discovers information on his own. So in the end, it seemed like a bad plot device to excuse the slow giving of information. 
 Other spoilery examples... 
 Then Teresa (the only girl) arrives. She and Thomas were the ones who created the maze in the first place. It's a game meant to weed out the most intelligent of the group. So it's confusing why the "Creators" would send Thomas and Teresa in the maze at all. They've already proved themselves the most intelligent, so why send them into the maze just so they'd lead the Gladers to the exit, protecting their friends most? That doesn't lead to an intelligence-based outcome, and isn't that the point? 
 Then there was an incident where Thomas killed a Griever, the creatures that hunt the Gladers, and it seemed so easy. Just hacking their saw and pincher arms off. But, in the two years when Thomas wasn't in the Glade, no one else could figure that out? Seems unlikely. 
 Then there was the death of one of the main characters. A character who was supposed to be dead (which is never explained) is actually alive and throws a knife at Thomas as a final "Variable" in the trial. Thomas' good friend takes the knife in the chest and dies. Again, no explanation. Why was Gally still alive? Why did the Creators want a last variable if it only eliminated one more player out of twenty? 
 And towards the end, they muse over what happened to the Gladers who didn't follow the group to the exit. A character says the Grievers probably got them. But hours earlier, they pushed the "Kill Maze" button, which eliminated the Grievers, so that's kind of not possible. 
 So overall, there were many plot points that were never explained. And never mentioned in one of those paragraphs where the main character is asking himself questions meant to direct the reader's attention to certain points. And from what I read in summaries and reviews I read for the sequels, these issues aren't resolved, and even more arise. I probably won't read the others.

I could not get through this book. Normally I love dystopia fiction but it was hard for me to read a book that was completely male centric and was basically just a retelling of Lord of the Flies. If you liked Lord of the Flies you will like this book. If you hated Lord of the Flies, like I did, I would skip it.

Kind of an interesting concept - Thomas wakes up with no memories and finds himself trapped in a deadly, ever-changing labyrinth in a sort of Lord-of-the-Flies meets Theseus situation. None of the other inhabitants ("Gladers", people who live in the Glade, which is a little oasis in the middle of the maze where they can farm and stuff) have memories either, or understand why they've all been put into this place. But they've cobbled together a complex community to keep order, keep their minds occupied, and try to find an exit. 
 I have always liked stories where the protagonist is thrown into a chaotic, dangerous world with no memory or information and we as the readers have to uncover the information at the same pace as the protagonist(s). I also liked the Grievers (labyrinth monsters), once we finally got a description of them; very grotesque and Lovecraftian. 
 There were some definite flaws in this book, though. The book obviously banks on us being curious and seeking answers to the many, many questions posed (where/when is this taking place; who is behind it; who designed the maze; why does nobody have memories; etc.). But so often when Thomas asks a question, the Gladers shut him down fast - "Stop asking questions! Do what you're told!" Also, some people who have been affected by the Grievers' poison and survived have regained some of their memories -- but they are never willing to talk about it to the others! At that point, it starts to feel like the mystery is being artificially drawn out, like a magician milking his stage act with a lot of unnecessary swooping hand gestures. 
 Also, dear god, the kids' jargon and slang gets old REALLY fast, though. I guess it's in line with the trope of sci-fi stories using made-up words as curse substitutes, but the dialogue is absolutely saturated with it. "Hey, you shucking slinthead, what kind of klunk are you trying to pull? Tell that greenie to slim it before the Grievers find us!" (Not a direct quote, but very much in line with some of the dialogue). Oh, and don't forget the Random Capitalization of Many Things, another sci-fi writing trope. Grievers, Grief Serum, the Maze, the Glade, the Changing, the Flare, etc. It grates after awhile. 
 Despite the flaws and stylistic things that aren't my cup of tea, I'm likely to check out the next book because I want to know where the story is going. We're introduced to a few new characters and concepts at the very end that have caught my imagination.

 If you've been around my blog for a bit, you know I have a soft spot for YA dystopian novels. I've been wanting to read The Maze Runner since I first saw the preview of the movie. I refused to see the movie though, until I read the book, so I figured it was about time. Especially after my roommate read the whole series in about a week and the book is $1.99 on Amazon. Nothing to lose right? 
 This is very much a book for the intended YA audience. I don't mean that in a negative way at all either. The style, the verbiage...while I don't read a ton of YA, this is one of the first I felt was suited mainly for the age group, whereas I think Hunger Games and Potter reach beyond their intended market. Not that I didn't enjoy it, although there were a few things that irritated me (like how people initially treated Thomas), but I could notice the difference. The plot was a mix of Lord of the Flies (I blame that one the fact that all I remember about that book is there's a group of young boys surviving in a jungle, a total jerk and a sad ending of Piggy), rather gruesome deaths, an apocalyptic world, mystery of the Creators and toss on a scoop of the Dharma initiative. 
 There were some parts of the plot I figured out or expected and other twists I didn't see coming. Yet, the twists and still elusive overall plot are enough for me to pick up the rest of the series, especially after reading the epilogue. Who are these people?! If you follow my blog, this might be a good point of reference: I'm much more interested in finishing this series than Divergent. 
 I have the movie waiting for me and am looking forward to seeing it on the big screen. While no Hunger Games, if you enjoy YA dystopian, I think this will fit the bill of a quick and enjoyable read. 
 Have you read this series or seen the movies? What are your thoughts on it?

 I don't really know what to say about this book. I didn't like it that much, but I didn't hate it either.. 
 The bad: 
 For the most part of the story I didn't really care about Tessa, about her illness and her strange wishes (as I never got attached to her). I understand the desire to have a boyfriend, to be kissed and have sex, probably at her age this would be an important part of her life, but the other 'wishes' were kind of stupid and not the ones that someone would like to think about before dying. I just expected something else from her and I was disappointed by all this. 
 More than this I hated her dumb friend who reminded her every 5 minutes that she's gonna die and who was NEVER there for her (and when she tried to help Tessa with her stupid wishes I just wanted to punch her for being such an idiot and not being a good friend at all), I hated her little brother telling her that he can't wait for her to be gone (sometimes he seemed to be 5 years old even if we've been told he was older), I hated her mother who seemed not to care about her at all. Ok, so there were lots of things I didn't like in this book. 
 The good: 
 The only character that I liked was Adam. I don't know why he fell in love with Tessa because she didn't even deserved it (and didn't deserve him) and because this happened so suddenly, but he was really nice and caring. There were some scenes with him being there for her and giving her all his love that made me like him more. I felt sad for him, really, because Tessa was going to die and that was the end for her, but he will remember her all his life, he will lose a part of him forever.. so he was the only character in this book that made me care. There were times that Tessa wanted him close, and there were times when she told him to get away and never come back, but he was always there for her, never disappointing her. 
 'I love you,' he whispers angrily into my neck. 'It hurts more than anything ever has, but I do. So don't you dare tell me I don't. Don't you ever say it again!' 
 The best part of this book is of course the ending. All those dreams mixed with reality and thoughts, the notes for the ones she was letting behind, the people that cared for her being finally there for her, that was the only part that touched my heart, that was the only part that made me care, because death is hard even if only written in the books, death makes you cry, death makes you think about all the thing that you want to do while still alive.. 
 SO, what's on your list? 
 You never know how much time you have.. so, how many items on your list did you check so far, and how many are still waiting to be done?

 Anna Dressed in Blood is one of the horror book I can't put down. I read the book at night, and it give me chill but I still can't put it down. I really, really, really love the book. Today she is just a night time story in slumber parties even though her brutal acts continue and the rational minds choose to find alternative explanations. 
 I went into the book not knowing anything but the title and the cover gave me some idea of what I was getting into..lots of creep and blood..and I was NOT disappointed! This book was such an amazing ride of creep and yet the author manages to keep it light with the narrator's wit.. boy oh boy.. I loved Cas! Cas may be a ghost hunter with a lineage, very certainly not an average boy, but I loved how vulnerable and soft he was when needed. Afterall he was just a 17 year old kid, a smartass witty one at that! And Anna.. Too bad I can't reveal much of her without revealing the story, but I sure can give a glimpse of her.. 
 "Anna is like nothing I've ever seen before. Her strength seems limitless, along with her bag of tricks. She's not some shuffling phantom, pissed off about being shot to death. She's death itself, gruesome and senseless, and even when she's dressed in blood and veins I can't help but stare." 
 The way Kendare Blake manages to strike a balance amongst all he elements in the story is truly commendable. This book creeped me out, made me laugh (thanks to Cas's comments), made me sad, happy and full of anticipation. It has been a while that I had been sucked into a book this way. I just couldn't stop reading.. A definite 4.5 stars! So if you haven't read it yet.. GO READ IT NOW!!!!
