I was not even sure I should write a review for this book. But considering that the reviews that hyped me into buying it... well, maybe a few words will convince a poor soul into reading something else - something better, and that will be worth it. 
 I am easily scared. Truly. Once I rented The Ring (back in my time kids, we used to rent movies...). The scenes that played while you were selecting the subtitles and the language were enough to scare me, and I returned the DVD that same day. 
 When I was a kid I watched Hollow Men on a open TV channel. It's a movie about some scientists that discover how to make people invisible, and one scientist tests it on himself, becomes an invisible psychopath and start killing everybody. Well, how did I cope with an invisible threat? I convinced myself that if I used my glasses (i'm nearsighted), I would be able to see thru his invisibility. (Back then I HATED using glasses). Well, it worked. I use them till this day (for different reasons). But that got me started. 
 So if I am so easily scared, why I picked a supposedly horror book? 
 I love romance. Pride and Prejudice, Jane Eyre and even the more atual books such as Red Queen and The Bird and the Sword. And I was really attracted to the idea: a ghost hunter falling in love with a ghost. How would it happen? How would he gain her trust? Would he kill her? That feeling, that hope, made me face my fears and buy the book. 
 Of course none of that happens. Not even the dreaded scary part. They just fall in love like that. Puff. No development. No teenager doubts. 
 I mean, when i was young I was never SURE somebody loved me or even liked me properly (I'm not even sure nowadays). Yet, they simple knew... The ghost hunter and the ghost trapped for 100 years in a house alone killing people instantly in love. HOW PRETTY. 
 Well... besides that: 
 (i) none of the characters were likable. I would honestly like Cas (main character) more if he died some epic way. The 'supporting' characters were plain. (Seriously, read The Name of the Wind, even the doorman will have dept.) 
 (ii) He says "Anna Dressed in Blood" a hundred times. I feel like listening to "Bond. James Bond." but without the hottie actor saying it. 
 "I'm going there to kill her. Anna. Anna Korlov. Anna Dressed in Blood." 
 "I thing of her again. Anna. Anna Dressed in Blood. I wonder what tricks she'll try." 
 "Anna Korlov. Anna Dressed in Blood. Her name moves through the dark like a dancer." 
 (iii) IT WAS JUST TOO EASY. If Amy Harmon was not giving romance or something scary to read, AT LEAST she could've given us some action. Some fight. Damn. Within less than 24 hours of preparation they killed the strongest ghost/voodoo thing ever and it was DONE. Honestly. Want to know what happens? Read the chapter 33. With 20-something pages you can get all done and solved. 
 Nothing happens in the between. No skills developed. No drama. Nothing. 
 So if you find yourself needing some romance/action/horror - go find other book. Watch some Netflix. Eat. Just don't spend your hard earned money in this book.

I picked this up because of the cover and title. While the story wasn't terrible, it wasn't quite unique enough. Ok, so there's a kid who can kill ghosts. But his method of killing ghosts is.... lame. Really, a knife? No special description is given, no special powers, it's just... a knife. Wow. Not. The kid has no special fighting skills, took no classes on fighting or self-defense. He is described as trying to land clumsy and desperate knife lunges during fight scenes. Yet later he declares he has killed something like 200+ ghosts in three years. I find it very hard to believe he would have survived the first battle. Granted, his father was also a ghost slayer, but there is no mention of him training his son. As far as Anna goes, boring. Here you have a girl murdered and wearing a dress dripping blood, strong character right? Wrong. We are TOLD how terrible and beautiful she is but I never really feel it. The description of her is so minimal and even her dialogue is lacking. Again, one of those sad cases of good elements but a bad writer who didn't know how to harness them or flesh them out. sample_reviews.review_text: I don't know where to begin...this book was one of those books that begins great then something crazy happens. I was like oh my gosh...then it kind of slows down you want something to happen but it doesn't but you just can't seem to put the book down because you just want to know what's going to happen next. So you keep reading and oh my...it don't disappoint I absolutely loved it. It was just such a sad but wonderful story about life. Very touchy.

This book was just ok. Candace was not necessarily likable, although Ryan, of course, was (doesn't it seem like the male characters always are?). The big conflict in this book was a serious one, but I don't think it was portrayed well or in a realistic way. Like, despite the seriousness of it, I was rolling my eyes at Candace almost the whole time. The resulting conflicts and tension throughout the book were also stupid, unrealistic, and avoidable. So even though Candace is a victim, you just get annoyed with her because she's acting stupid. That was enough to kinda kill the book. But add to that that although this book is about a powerful topic, there is nothing interesting about it. Nothing memorable. It just slightly registers as you read it. And the ending was rushed. I wanted more. Well, that's a lie. I didn't want more because by the end I really didn't care and I just wanted to finish. But I registered the way it was written enough to feel like I should have wanted more. I read this book because I liked ek blair's book "Bang." I appreciated the dark and powerful subject matter from that book and it was really interesting, daring and different. But this one doesn't even come close. I wouldn't recommended it. It was pretty much a waste of time.

Being a bookaholic, I have a hard time remembering books. But this one will stay with me for a while. What an incredible story of pain and growth to overcome such a devasting tragedy. This journey of Candance & Ryan is awesome. Every emotion is felt.

*I was gifted this book for an honest review. 
 Fading is about a girl that is raped and how she heals from this horrible experience. To begin with, this reviewer knows and understands that rape is not something that a person can easily recover from overnight. With this in mind, I found Candace's character to be whiny and needy throughout the entire story. Her inability to do anything alone was a huge disappointment to me. Candace was surrounded by coddling friends that would give in to her every whim. They thought they were helping her recover from the rape, but instead they were helping her to stay the victim of it. The one character that stands out the most is Donna; she was just want Candace needed in order to stop playing the victim. 
 I was able to figure out how the story was going to end before I was a quarter of the way through it. The supporting characters helped make the story more interesting and helped move it along. I gave this book a rating of 3 stars.

This was a pretty emotional story. I enjoyed the basic theme of it, but I had a hard time with several issues. First off, I have a hard time understanding why people do not report tape. I realize that I can not even begin to imagine what that would be like, but I also don't believe anyone can heal and move on until the person is held accountable. So, that aspect of the story was hard to get past. I also hated how Candace hid and pushed Kimber away. Those two points in the story were troubling to me and made it hard to get fully invested in this book. I loved Jase and Mark, and how they supported Candace. I appreciated the fact that they tried to push her to move on, and they were the ones who brought Ryan in closer. He was the saving grace for this story. I loved him and his family. What they did for Candace was heartwarming, and it broke my heart when she so easily cast him aside after learning his secret. I was thrilled that she finally got help, which should have happened earlier. I did think she was a little codependent on everyone else, and she needed to learn to grow and move on by herself. So, I was encouraged by her decision in that regard. I did feel like there was a lot of filler. A lot of random musings about nothing related to the plot. I could have done without that. Overall, I'm glad I read the book and look forward to reading about Jase and Mark next.

Fading - EK Blair 
 5 big fat emotional stars!! 
 This book was just WOW!! Totes AMAZEBALLS!! 
 Emotional, passionate, sensitive, poignant....I could go on and on and on but it was beautifully written. This is by no means a hearts and flowers romance, it is dark and covers the horrible topic of date rape. Candace was not only date raped but she was brutally beaten too and probably would have ended up dead had it not been for a stranger that interrupted the assault and beat her attacker away. 
 Candace is a brilliantly talented ballet dancer at Uni studying ballet and dance before her life is cruelly destroyed, this book covers the before, during and after and some of it is not pretty. Rape is not often covered in books and the author has covered this subject sensitively and compassionately. It centres around Candace coping, surviving and trying to recover from this terrible ordeal and learning to trust and love again. 
 This book had me hooked, I could not put it down, I didn't want to put it down. The first thing that had me drawn in was the cover, it was simple and alluring yet it spoke to me and I didn't fully appreciate it till after I had read the book. Once I had read it, the cover spoke volumes, pure genius!! I loved Candace, she was not some 22 year old tart with a heart, but she studied hard, worked hard and just did all she could to be better, she had her aspirations and was working solidly to achieve them despite zero emotional support from her parents. Kimber was Candace's room mate, she was encouraging Candace to go out a bit more, experience a bit of life, Candace's parents encouraged her to go out with Jack, they were friends of his family, he was of good stock blah blah blah. Candace had zero experience and her first was brutally taken from her. 
 Candace turns to her BFF Jase (who is gay), he has got to be the best BFF ever...he knows exactly what Candace wants and needs and is always there for her, eventually his partner Mark is let in and they make a formidable trio. Candace shuts out Kimber as she is too embarrassed about what has happened and does not want to have to explain to anybody about what she has been through, she shuts herself off from everyone apart from Jase. Slowly but surely, the dark place that she sinks too affects her dancing, something that normally manages to bring her out of any funk, her tutor notices but still she does not let anyone in. 
 Jase and Mark introduce Candace to Ryan, he is the bar owner of a bar that Mark's band play in....he finds Candace instantly alluring and can't help but want to get to know her better. He tries to befriend her but Candace is still shut off...he perseveres....but as with any book is he as good as he seems, does he have an ulterior motive, is he really that perfect. 
 I must admit, I loved Ryan and I adored his mum, she was the mum that Candace never had and I am glad that she saw through Candace and worked hard at breaking her walls down. Ryan comes from a loving family, something that Candace never had. Her parents whilst supporting her financially are embarrassed at her chosen profession and feel that their money is wasted on a pie in the sky vocation. They cannot see that Candace lives, eats and breathes dance and most days it is her reason for even getting up in the morning. Only lawyers, doctors etc are suitable enough to uphold the family appearances not anything artsy fartsy and they are willing to lose their daughter over this. God, her parents, I could have nutted them!! 
 I was so glad that Ryan was 28, being that bit older he was more sensitive, more worldly wise and knew that he couldn't push too far. He was very accepting of Candace's relationship with Jase to a point and being so mature he realised that she was never going to heal quickly and he gave her that time. I can see why he did what he did and I could see it coming but I was willing him on to be more open, I knew it was going to end up biting him on the bum. 
 "I promise you, nothing will change the way I look at you. Nothing will change what you do to me when you are next to me. You make my heart beat in a completely different way - nothing will ever change that" 
 All I can say is I highly recommend this book, I feel EK Blair can hold her head up high and pat herself on the back for a brilliant approach to a more or less taboo subject. She has dealt with it amazingly and you cannot help being moved whilst reading and feeling every ounce of pain and heartbreak that Candace goes through. 
 "This doesn't define you" 
 I can't wait to read more from this author and hearing there is more to come in this series...I can't wait!!

I don't remember specific criticisms as it was over 10 years ago, but this is making me want to reread it now and compare, especially cause so many loved it. 
 (Please note: I am going through all of my read books with an attempt to star and review, at some point, all of these books will have a decent review, I promise.)

My taste in humor has changed greatly over the years. In my younger years I found Mark Twain very funny. I picked Mark Twain as the author and subject of a high school paper. I read about five books of Twain's at that time, and several others later. 
 I remember reading that several school boards had banned this book, because it was offensive to blacks. I couldn't see that point of view at the time. Now I find several things offensive about this book. Twain writes about Tom and Huckleberry as young boys, who like to have adventures. The boys make things more complicated than necessary, and make stupid mistakes. Whites could be just as offended by this book as blacks. 
 Twain leads Huck to a white family, who have been feuding for generations, with another family. It was so long ago, that the families don't know what the feud is about. The families hunt and kill each other, and then they go to church on Sunday. There is some insight and truth in this, but I no longer think it's funny. There are too many countries and people doing the same things today. 
 Huck takes his black slave friend, Jim down the river on an adventure. He makes Jim think he is freeing him from slavery, knowing that the old lady who owned him, has set him free in her will. I don't find this humorous either. Huck gets shot in the leg for his efforts, and Jim is a true friend, and stays behind to help and protect Huck.
This is where it all started. A great read.

Rubbish - even YA literature must assume that the reader isn't stupid and has a basic idea of science, especially when reading a story set in a dystopian alternate universe. There's enough plot holes in this short story to sink a battleship, even without the shoddy science and plotting. 
 It gets one star for the inadvertent comedy of the Scrabble-tastic names of the countries and the idiotic names of the "Others".

I'm being generous when I give this book two stars.Edit: After some thought I've changed my rating to a one star. I really don't where to begin with this one. I guess I should start with the beginning of the book. We have this young girl named Rachel who lives with her mother and this old woman named Ms. Moore who is Rachel's mother's employer. My first problem with this was the characters. They weren't well developed at all. I didn't know how old our main character - can you even call her that? - was. My first thought was that she was about ten or eleven years old given her temperate and her mentality in the beginning of the book but it wasn't until a mid way though the book that we find out that Rachel is actually a teenager. We don't know if she's 13 or 19 though. I'm assuming she's under the age of 18 because she's preparing for college, but many of us prepare for college at 15 or 16. So I genuinely have no idea how old Rachel is. My mental image of her is blurry at best. I can't see her in my mind, I have no clue what she looks like. For the longest time I was imagining her as a child because that's how she was portrayed. As for the other characters I feel the same way. The only thing I know about Ms. Moore is that she's old-ish and wears here hair in a bun and that Vivian, Rachel's mom, has chestnut hair. That's pretty much it for character development and painting a picture of the characters. By the time Hall tries to create a back story for her characters it's too late. The character's stories are filled with plot holes and simply don't flow well. There was one particular scene that literally made cringe - it was about 75% in - and Hall was trying to create this witty banter between the characters but it was painfully awkward because the characters had no support or bases to behave as such. I would say it was out of character but there was simply no character. 
 Another issue with this is the world they live in. There is a line that divides the Unified States. It's not just a line, but an impenetrable, clear, border. How was it made? How much area does it cover? Explanation is given to why this divider exists but the explanation isn't clear and it doesn't make much sense. On the other side of this border is a place where people have been bombed and left behind, thus possibly leaving them with magical powers. The potential to tell this story is amazing but such a big let down. Another issue with this world is that you don't get to see much of it. It basically takes place in a house for the entirety of the book. We learn a little bit about this world but nothing too specific. There is special terminology that suggests this takes place in the future (creds, digmas) but there is also a lot that makes me think that it doesn't. It's clear that this place was once the United States but I'm still not sure how we got from here to there and in most dystopian books this is clarified. The only explanation we got was, "The government said so". 
 The plot could have been wonderful. There is a great story here but it can't be found in this book. This book is filled with one dimensional characters and poor world building. The writing didn't flow well and was confusing and juvenile at times. A huge portion of this book was about gardening, which really had nothing to do with the story at hand. I felt like I knew more about orchids by the end of this book then anything about the world or the characters. I was bored and couldn't wait for it to be over. I will say that the writing got a tad better by the end of the book but not enough. 
 I feel honestly terribly for this harsh review and I feel bad for the author but I need to be honest to my own readers. I'm just not sure how this book got published.

reference_books.title: Sweet Evil (Sweet, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
When I first read the first chapter of this book, the main thing that kept running in my head was "Why is this book 400+ pages?". Now why would an avid reader question such a thing like that? Well, because in my opinion most of the book was utter nonsense and inessential banter between stereotypical characters. 
 The main character, Anna, is a completely naive, childish, sheltered girl who borders almost into stupidity. (If your drink tastes funny don't freakin drink it!) Having been born as a Nephilim (half demon and angel) she finds herself in a unique and lonely position because of her odd personality and abilities. She is incredibly, sickeningly sweet. Now I'm not advocating bad behavior at all, I'm fine that she's as sweet as sugar but its almost too much. She's a lovely kind girl with no faults. But that's exactly what I couldn't stand; she's so damn perfect that it's entirely easy to relate her to a Mary Sue. 
 Then there's Kaiden, an incredibly unappealing character. His brooding personality creates that aura of mysterious sexiness about him but he's also a cruel, unpredictable boy with occasional bouts of anger. Plus... Ugh. I know this might be a spoiler so please avert your eyes! Kaiden is basically a male prostitute. Every night he says he's going to "work" but he actually has sex with a different girl each night. 
 Oh but it doesn't matter at all to Anna! Why??? Well now, he's an extremely handsome guy that's why. So beautiful with his British accent that Anna completely ignores the fact that he fucks every girl he sees. What the fuck???? I completely understand that books are supposed to be an escape to everyday life and all; I understand that certain things in books are what-ifs and made up situations but I can't accept this. I hate that this promiscuous cruel boy is being romanticized as a tender-hearted young man with a heart of gold! It's not a comforting thought that girls fantasize about bad boys treating them like utter garbage all because they secretly harbor a sickening idea that they can change the boy/man. 
 I mean, you're judged based on your actions and Kaiden screwing different girls while telling her continuously that he's a non-committal guy doesn't exactly equate to love. But Anna is so naive that she keeps treading on dangerous ground. And please don't get me started on Anna's foster mother Patti. It's entirely, completely, stupid to let your young naive daughter go on a roadtrip with a teenage boy who happens to be the son of a demon of lust. Knowing that they'll be in hotels alone together and be totally fine with that is just plain ridiculous. 
 Oh and another thing. An unnecessary love triangle is inserted in the book, adding more evidence that Anna is indeed a coveted and perfectly special human girl. 
 Of course this is my opinion so don't let this ranting review discourage you. It has a rather high rating so maybe I'm just one of those occasional oddballs that don't get the hype of the book.

reference_books.title: Die for Me (Revenants, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I thought this book had so much potential in the beginning. I was pleased because they didn't speak in that terrible slang that some YA authors usually use in these type of books. They spoke normal, yes normal English without the use of dumb trying-too-hard words. 
 The protagonist is a teen named Kate who describes herself as nothing like her beautiful sister and with lifeless hair but of course, of course she ends up being so damn beautiful to everyone else around her. What is it with these type of characters? Why can't they for once just have an ounce of self-confidence with them? It makes me feel terrible for teenagers who read crap like this. Girls, you can admit that you're beautiful! You don't have to dumb yourself down and be reluctant of your looks. I feel like if you admit that you're attractive that people will regard you as conceited or shallow. NO, dammit! You can be beautiful, and humble at the same time. I don't understand why authors continuously write characters like this. Why is it such a bad thing to recognize or acknowledge your own looks? Why are girls continuously oblivious of their beauty and have such terrible confidence. 
 Anyway, yes so there's Kate, the average but beautiful girl who also happens to attract the impossibly beautiful... I don't even remember his name. 
 All right I had to go back to the book because he was so forgettable that i forgot his name. Vincent. Oh Vincent. So beautiful, and perfect, and romantic, and beautiful, and gorgeous and yes, that one guy that can only exist in books. I'm happy he exists only in books because he's a creepy stalker! Once again, what is with this type of characterization? Are people seriously romanticized by the idea of a man following you? ugh no, not for me. I don't care how beautiful you are, don't follow me home. 
 So it's a book about a group of people in a grand, rich home. They are basically undead but they save lives and become obsessed with the people they saved. It's creepy, and strange and although i'm a fan of that I just did not like this. It was cheesy and unrealistic! I still don't understand why they fell in love. God, I just want to read a book where they actually fall in love for the right reasons, not because of looks and beauty. 
 Oh yeah, nothing happens till the damn end! The antagonist is introduced at end chapters and all of a sudden he wants to kill everyone! What the heck, it doesn't even make sense. 
 I will add that the setting was lovely. It's in Paris, and most people will probably cringe because it's the type of cliche setting perfect for love and romance but no, it's actually very beautiful to read. It isn't just the Eiffel tower; it's the cafes and the museums and the bridges that make it a tangible atmosphere to lose yourself in. Other than that, I didn't like this book. 
 This is more like a rant than a review so I'll just stop here.

reference_books.title: Waterfall (River of Time, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Warning: very long review with spoilers. 
 I do not understand how this book has such high reviews. People truly do have different tastes. 
 This book is about two teens -17 yr. Gabi and 15 yr. old Lia - who spend their summer vacations hiking along excavation sites with their archaeologist parents. One day on a sudden bout of boredom, they decide to explore their mother's newly found archaeological tombsite. They end up time-travelling to an ancient life of medieval Italy where they are caught up in a feud between two warring sides. 
 Told from the perspective of Gabi - the older sister- I found the book unrealistic and quite frankly, foolish. 
 You see when she does the whole time traveling business, she comes out of the tombsite and sees a full-out battle in front of her. Instead of being traumatized or shocked mentally by what she's seen, she instead locks eyes on a handsome, no scratch that, HOT knight. 
 Here is the opening introduction of our love interest as told by Gabi herself: 
 "I wanted to look away from him, but I couldn't. He was the most handsome guy I'd ever seen, with a model's physique and a face to match. Big, chocolate-brown eyes, square jaw, aristocratic nose, pronounced cheekbones...a serious hottie. 
 I've never encountered such Italian hotness outside of Roma." 
 I regard myself a varying mix of a tomboy and a girly-girl but let me tell you if I was to suddenly time-travel and see a battle in front of me, I will not pay attention to a handsome knight. I will see blood, guts and soldiers screaming in pain. I would want to get away from this confusion as fast as possible, not check out some armored man! 
 I hate this type of language. It seems silly but I can't stand talk like this. I absolutely loathe it when adult authors try to imitate the way younger people speak by the means of adding slang words. I'm quite young and let me tell you I hate it so much when I read sentences like this. I read books to escape from this world; I want to read things that will feed my mind and enhance my vocabulary, not dumb it down! 
 There are words like "Whatever, totally, loser, hottie, hotness, hot". I can't stand it! Speak proper English damnit! 
 Then there's the fact that she's immediately fluent in old Italian all because she read Dante's Divine Comedy in it's old italian dialect. What??? I've read about 5 Spanish books and studied the language (all to communicate properly with my bf's parents) and I still need to inquire a dictionary from time to time. 
 I liked that she was brave and she never let boring love interest "Marcello" tell her what to do but sometimes she could just be a bit too much! She did things that would have appalled the men in those times; realistically she would have been looked down upon but instead she was praised! Don't get me wrong, I'm all for strong female warriors but you can't reward them so heartily for disobeying society's norms at those times. I mean, if it was such a big deal and men were truly against a woman riding a horse bareback, why would you praise it? I'm not saying she needed to be punished, but some type of acknowledgement that this wasn't right for that time would have been realistic. I want to be told it isn't right and I want our heroine to rebel and say, "No! I do what I want!" not "Oh, fair Gabriella, we are taken by you." 
 Oh and the love story, goodness... It wasn't love! There was no other reason for them to like each other. Marcello was clearly bored and trying to rebel, while Gabi was naive and taken by his "hotness". 
 It's lust. Not some epic romance that the author made it try to be. 
 Everyone has different tastes so please don't let my rant ruin your chances of enjoying this book. You might like it considering so many people did. But as for me I' going to say no thanks to the second book. This was too silly.

reference_books.title: Bitterblue (Graceling Realm, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
I didn't really like this. I felt like it was too long and some parts just dragged. There were too many characters that kept popping out of nowhere and Bitterblue herself didn't seem real enough. I understand she was a young inexperienced queen, but it was just the way it was written that I didn't particularly enjoy. A shock considering Graceling is one my favorite books. 
 The romantic aspect of the book seemed pointless, and the overuse of the term "Lady Queen" irritated me to no end. 
 I did like that Po was evident throughout the book. He was sweet and brotherly towards Bitterblue and I found it quite endearing. Although he and Katsa seemed different from the first book. I guess it makes sense, considering it's been eight years. I also enjoyed Giddon's presence; it was nice to have a man that thoroughly cared for her as a friend and nothing more-- basically I was happy there was no love triangle. 
 I found myself skipping a few passages every now and then. I'm disappointed since I really enjoyed the first one.

reference_books.title: Obsidian (Lux, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This will be the shortest review ever because I have never been so frustrated with a series in my life. 
 I don't know what compelled me to read this book. Actually, I don't know what compelled me to keep reading the whole series! I thought the premise was interesting enough. Aliens on planet earth that have somehow managed to live amongst us in peace? Sure, why not. 
 But here is what I could not stand about these books. 
 It is sooooo cheesy. Every minute or so, these two "lovers" will suddenly lust after each other at the most inappropriate times. There are passages and passages droning about their eternal love for each other and how much they are both willing to sacrifice in order to keep their loved ones safe. I'm sorry but I just cannot stand it. I think this is the only time I've read something, and my eyes will literally roll in annoyance over the stupidity of the protagonists. 
 Not only that but the writing... oh dear god. See, i love to read because I want my writing to get better. Because I want my brain to still be somehow educated even if i'm reading something for fun. I want to escape this world full of "WTF's" or any sort of ridiculous slang. Why? I don't understand. The language they use is so ridiculous I cannot fathom any teenager speaking this way. "Sweet baby jesus" or "Holy alien babies" or quite simply, "Crap." Why??? 
 Prepare to read every character mentioning how they have no choice, many mentions of rocking back and forth in a corner in order to regain sanity, hormonal teenagers, and just overall cheesiness. 
 Can you tell I didn't quite like this book? I won't even review the rest because it's all pretty much the same. I read all of them but I stopped at the last chapter of the final book. I just couldn't anymore. How ridiculous of me to read all of them but abandon at the last chapter.

book_a.title: Tyger Tyger (Goblin Wars, #1)
book_a.user_review:
I hate giving one star ratings to any type of book. I think it's terrible since so much work and imagination goes into a single book and there I am giving this hard-earned thing one star. 
 Still, there's times when I just have to. This is one of those times. 
 Teagan Wylttson has a perfect life. She's smart, has a good job working with what she loves, a good family, a devoted best friend, and is on track to attend a good university. Until handsome Finn Mac Cumhaill enters her life and informs her that her little world is actually populated by goblins an magic. 
 Filled with mostly dialogue, inane chatter, and unnecessary passages -- the book is plainly dull. The characters lack definitive qualities which makes if difficult to tell one from the other. I don't know how the protagonist looks and I don't necessarily know what makes her special and interesting and because of that I'm a bit detached from her. In fact, the only person who's described is Finn himself who is supposed to be a "beautiful boy". But instead of describing that beauty, the author instead describes him as a "young Brad Pitt". It's just such a cheap way to describe a character, in my opinion (but of course I do think Brad Pitt is beautiful). 
 I just think that the book is written poorly. Characters weren't memorable, the pacing was strange, and the constant modern references didn't blend well with the folklore of the book. One part of the book dealt with a loss, and just when I thought I'd see something special about the characters -- the author decides to skip a few months ahead, making the death seem entirely unimportant. 
 Obviously, I didn't like this book at all.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Teagan has a plan for next few years of her life. After high school comes college. No boys, no excitement until after college. Life has another plan for Teagan. One day after finishing her shift at the zoo, her friend Abby calls her frantic. Abby has had a horrible dream of goblins and evil shadows...and they were after Teagan. 
 Teagan's brother, Aiden, has the remarkable talent of being able to learn songs immediately after hearing them and singing them back perfectly. He also never gets lost. 
 The strangeness continues when Finn arrives bringing with him the unimaginable, the goblins from Abby's dreams. But don't worry too much, Finn was born to fight them, and he will need all his skills to help get not only himself, but Teagan's family out of trouble. 
 A story full of twists and turns, interesting characters (human and otherwise), and fantastic places that are brought to life. I had a hard time putting this down and picked it up again as soon as I could. Teagan is a bright girl who knows how to use her brains, which helps them out of many tricky situations. 
 I hope Hamilton writes more about the goblin world we visit here. I'd read them all in a heartbeat.
Hey! That was pretty good.

God awful fluf. The term "Fantasy" as a genre is far too broad of a category and I swear authors an publishers use it to their advantage. Im not saying the the genre should be rigid to any persons particular view mine included, but there is a vast difference between Tolkein fantasy and works like this that are catered to 12 year old girls.

This is almost a 2.5. As a paranormal adventure it works but the romance subplot is a bit flat. I was thrilled though that Teagan had plans for the future that didn't include boys because she wanted to concentrate on getting into the best vet school in the country. I applaud that. However, when the romance does start there isn't much to it. I'm not even sure Teagan would have considered it if her grandmother hadn't said hey by the way Finn's in love with you. It's not bad but I didn't connect with the characters like I would have hoped.
Great potential, but very unpolished. Review coming 12/12.

Eh. That's my summary of the book, eh. It wasn't awful but it certainly wasn't great. It jumped all over the place and the celtic myths and legends got super confusing after a while. 
 The story follows Teagen and her brother as they discover their world is not as it seems. It turns out their Irish heritage is based more on legend than normal history. Goblins, angels, and shadow men are real and it's up to Teagen and her brother Aiden to team up with their cousin, Finn, (and soon to be love interest... weird) to defeat the Goblins and save their dad. 
 It's an alright book, but I was not intrigued enough to pick up any of the other books in the series. The characters all act waay older than their age and hardly seemed surprised when their world is turned upside down, totally not believable. Then again neither is anything in this story. It's a great idea but it needed more development or something. The only redeeming thing is the fact that their dad is a kickass librarian. But even that still couldn't save the story. Oh well.
Urban paranormal folklore fantasy? Could have been less gritty; and accordingly I would have enjoyed it more. "Far too pedestrian" is one of my gripes with this book, admittedly!
LOVED IT!!!!! Soaked in the Irish legends likea sponge! Cannot wait for another one!
review to come

book_b.title: The Lost Hero (The Heroes of Olympus, #1)
book_b.user_review:
I read the Percy Jackson series prior to this but wasn't exactly in love with it. I liked it well enough, mostly because the narration depicted Percy's sense of humor and Annabel's wit. On the other hand, I didn't quite enjoy the way this was written. It was very straightforward and simple -- almost too simple. I know, I know, it's meant for younger audiences but it was too simplistic. I felt like the tone of the book was somehow sarcastic in a way, like the quests that the characters had to endure they always greeted it with a "Wow, this is soooo amazing, lets just tackle someone way stronger than us." I just didn't like it. 
 The humour was forced, and the characters were in a way, almost too... Perfect? Special snowflakes who (as usual) had troubled pasts even though they were merely sixteen. Then there's Jason who had the "I forgot my past" trope going on, (not a big fan of that at all. For any other book) but when it came down to it he did in fact remember certain things. It's just pointless in my opinion. Why even write him as a person who suffers from amnesia but suddenly make him remember important facts? Why not just stick with either amnesia Jason, or Jason who does remembers. 
 I know I should enjoy this book, particularly because I am extremely in love with mythology and ancient civilization. I love Greek and Roman gods, and it fascinates me that to this day, these imaginary deities still influence our way of story-telling. Sadly, I just did not like this. I didn't like coach Hedge either! He was just so pointless and irritating, it was as if he was inserted there to provide comic relief which failed because I simply didn't find him humorous. I'm clearly in the minority here since everyone gave glowing reviews of the book. It happens, so don't let this review dissuade you from reading this. You might like it after all. I did like the little cliffhanger in the end and that alone is enough to persuade me to continue to the next book. So, hopefully it gets better.

sample_reviews.review_text: I loved the Percy Jackson series, and I probably would have loved this book had it not been for Piper. I was reading and rereading this book and I just wished Riordan killed her in the middle. She was plain annoying, and her constant whining and lack of self-confidence pissed even my brother off. Seriously, just because she's a daughter of Aphrodite doesn't mean she can't be useful. All she thinks about is getting Jason and that's just stupid. This review is turning into an anti-Piper rant, but it's only because I loved how Riordan portrayed girls as strong and confident in the original series and then he suddenly made such an annoying character. Seriously. The only reason why the book isn't a one-star or a two-star is because Riordan's still pretty awesome when it comes to Leo and Jason. The story's also pretty interesting. But other than that, Piper just brings down this book to a blah.
I'm sure this is a great book if you're into this sort of thing. Turns out, I am not. I wanted to try it because it is so highly rated but I just can't get into it. I gave up on page 32.

First read: November, 2010 
 Second read: January 29th, 2012 
 Third read: December 19th, 2013
This book was okay. A little predictable but I'll read the rest of the series I'm sure.

I'm really so disappointed in this book. I had loved the Percy Jackson series and had such high hopes for this series, but, sadly, after reading this book, I'm not sure I'm going to continue reading the series. 
 The Lost Hero changes perspective between the three main characters: Jason, Piper, and Leo. Normally, this doesn't bother me, but Riordan does this in such a systematic and tedious fashion. Literally, it two chapters of Jason, two of Piper, and two more chapters of Leo, repeat. Often,these sections aren't even progressing but offering the perspective of each character on a single event, therefore creating a plot that is dragged on chapter by chapter. 
 Speaking of the plot, it takes almost half the book for anything to really happen. They're just sitting around at Camp Half-blood for eons. The book is not engaging in the slightest. I remember bemoaning the task of finishing the book to my mom who kept insisting I just shut the book and move on, but I had hoped that once I got to the quest,it would pick up and be great. False. After 400 plus pages of filler, when you finally reach the final confrontation it lasts about a page. And then there's more chapters after the resolution. 
 Although, the Greek-vs.-Roman mix is fascinating and interesting,it can't make up for all faults of this book. Ultimately,the characters are not memorable constantly complaining about their situation, gifts, etc, and the plot is so stretched-out that reading the 500 page novel is more of a task than an enjoyable vacation.

I felt like this took too long to really get going, and a lot of the book was unnecessarily drawn out. It could have been shorter, and that probably would have helped me to like it more. I was also getting a little frustrated about how no one would simply tell anyone else anything, and I didn't like the new characters quite as much. Still, I'll continue with the series and see where it goes.

I am rating this book NOT having read Percy Jackson, so take it with a grain of salt. I could not get into the tone of the narrative. The story is simple enough. Think Harry Potter only they're demigods instead of wizards and at camp instead of Hogwarts. But the casual, American, and juvenile writing style really threw me. I guess I like higher fantasy, but that is purely preference. I also think there should be some distinction between "teen lit" and "young adult lit", and that this would fall into the former.
Another great book! As always, Rick didn't disappoint, all the Olympus books are great. I really like the new guys, Jason is awesome!! Looking forward for the next book... Son of Neptune.

Los libros de Percy Jackson me agradaron. Son libros que les puedo presentar a mis hijos o futuros alumnos o que puedo tener en una biblioteca de primaria o de secundaria porque de ahi pueden aprender. Te presentan a los dioses tal cual, sin taparlos como Disney, y eso es bastante enriquecedor. Otra forma de atraer personas a empaparse de la mitologia griega y latina. Sin embargo, este libro falla de manera estrepitosa. Es aburrido, los personajes son aburridos, la historia se vuelve repetitiva (si de por si, ya tenia mucho de eso) y lo unico que quieres es que todo acabe y alguien salga muy lastimaod, de preferencia Rick Riordan por no llevar a sus personajes a un nuevo nivel y por hacerlos aun mas estereotipados. Anda, que eso es lo que me choca: los estereotipos. Uy, idea.

I loved the Percy Jackson books, but this just read like repetitive overkill. Just mountains of confusing hints leading up to a pretty stale ending. The new gods are not very interesting and I would have preferred more interaction with the old ones. I don't see the appeal of the weather gods. I did like some of the traits of the new characters, but the set-up of two boys/one girl as the main characters with similar traits is just getting old. I don't know if I want to continue the series right now. Things are predictable and I don't really care what happens, which is a shame. I'm still interested in checking out Riordan's other series besides Percy Jackson, but I think PJ's story should just have been let go. (This, by the way, is exactly why I never want to see a Harry Potter book 8. Some stories reach their natural ends and just need to stop there before they're reduced to meaningless drivel.)

sample_reviews.review_text:
Actual rating: 3.5 stars. I really hope this review makes some sense, it's hard to explain my train of though 
 I've had this book sitting on my bookcase since the summer so I'm glad I finally gave it a chance. I really like the premise behind this book. This plot takes place in a world where every soul is reincarnated into new bodies with memories intact about their past lives. Suddenly, Ana is born and when she is put into a soul scanner (they still need farming and other medieval means of survival yet they have soul scanners?!) they find that Ana can't be identified. She's a Nosoul and her birth is seemingly connected to the disappearance of an already pre-existing soul. This obviously makes Ana an outcast and her "mother" is trurely evil and terrible to her. The beginning of the book had a lot of info-dumping that mixed with Ana's self doubt, sometimes get confusing but I can see why it is necessary. 
 Although this book was in first person point of view, it felt very disconnected. Instead of seeing the world through Ana's eyes, I seemed to see it from outside of her body. I felt that the first person point of view was very disconnected and that everything Ana was feeling, felt too fake. Despite the detachedness I felt, I think Ana was an alright main character. I felt that there was nothing really special about her but she was likeable. It was interesting to see how she saw herself as a disgrace because of her upbringing but other people *cough cough* Sam *cough cough* didn't. 
 To discuss the love interest, I need to talk about the romance. So when Sam and Ana first meet, I immediately shipped them. I am a shipper through and through and I saw them together but as time went on, I started to doubt it. You know those parts of the book where something shocking happens and then all the characters are like "Don't trust *insert love interest name here*, he/she is actually evil/using you/being a jerkface!" and the main character is like "I can't believe it!" and then the main character becomes very very skeptical. In this book, the opposite happened. When said shocking thing happened, the main character was like "NO NEVER HE WOULD NEVER" and I was like "WAIT HE TOTALLY WOULD" (inner monologue is the best). So then I doubted Sam and I still do. How can we trust him? And to be honest, before this happened, he was semi-swoon worthy. I liked their romance but honestly, like Ana, Sam was nothing special. 
 Overall, I think that Incarnate was cute with an interesting setting and unique world building. I liked the romance but I am still a little dubiuos of the love interest, Sam. I also felt that Ana, the main character, is nothing special and easily tolerable unlike in most books. I might read the sequel sometime in the future, but not anytime soon because I feel no urgency to.

Incarnate's plot was so unique to me that even though I didn't love the book, I still had to finish it to find out where it was going. I've often wondered about past lives and if we have been here before as another person at another place in time, that's what originally drew me to this book. As well as the very striking cover. In my mind I never imagined that you would always remember you past and the people who you've known. That's where Incarnate went with this idea though and I found that to be so intriguing. 
 The first half of the book was definitely my favorite part. This is where we meet Ana. Ana is uncommon because she is a new soul, meaning that this is her first life. In the world that Meadows has created, a new soul is a rare and terrifying event for the rest of the people. Typically a person dies only to be reincarnated into another body where they remember everything and everyone from their past life. Something went wrong for one soul though and that soul didn't return. Instead Ana was born. 
 Ana sets out on her own, leaving her abusive "mother" behind to find more people and to try and figure out why she is here. Along the way she meets Sam. While I liked Sam there was something about the way that he was SO old (in a hot young bod) that was just a little creepy for me. Then during the second half of the book things took a weird turn and I began making those weird huh? faces. So while I didn't love Incarnate I did find it interesting and I've found myself thinking back on parts of the story again and again. If you like fantasy a lot or even a little you will probably enjoy this one more than I did.
DNF. I was excited to read this but it wasn't for me.

Read this review and more like it at Written Permission 
 I really wanted to like Incarnate. And for a while, I did. I mean, just look at that cover. It is absolutely stunning. But the cover is not the only thing that matters. 
 The blurb is deceiving. About 75% of Incarnate is Ana and Sam and their romance. 15% is music related. And then there is a mere 10% that is related to plot, worldbuilding, Ana trying to find out who she is, etc. 
 The romance read a lot like Twilight to me. Ana and Sam are so in love, but there is something keeping them apart. Yet we are never really sure what it is. He seems to like her well enough from the start, as in he doesn't treat her like garbage because of what she is. And then he completely backs away from most romantic advances. For no real reason. It was very frustrating. 
 I felt like Incarnate had so much potential, but focused too much on the romance, and therefore left too many holes. Why do the dragons go for the temple every time? Why does Sam leave the house every night? What happened to Ciana? Why was Ana born? These are all questions that go unanswered for the sake of awkward teen romance. 
 For that matter, Ana and Sam are both eighteen. Should their romance not be a little less awkward? Especially in a society where kids are considered grown at fifteen? 
 I found Ana to be very angsty for an eighteen year old, and every time Meadows wrote a reminder of her age, I was taken aback. I thought I was reading about a sixteen year old a lot of the time. She is impulse driven, she is angsty, and she didn't read like someone who would be desperate to show she knew how to take care of herself at three years past the "normal" age for striking out. 
 If Ana was the first of her kind, where did the term "nosoul" come from? This was a big sticking point for me throughout the entirety of Incarnate. I can see coining the term "newsoul" for Ana, because she is new. But what about "nosoul"? Where did it come from and why? There is no precedent for the term "nosoul". 
 The ending showed promise, and then descended into wtf-ery. I just, don't know. 
 Bottom Line: I would be interested in seeing some of the questions answered, but I am not confident that they will be. So I may read book two, but I won't be rushing out for it. This book didn't deliver what I hoped it would.
This book was so different and my head is still reeling from trying to figure it out, but I really liked it

I liked the premise for the book but in the end, I felt that there was more romance than I had anticipated. I thought with dragons and sylph, the world would be more fantastical. 
 I think what kept me going was to figure out what happened at the end and still now, I have so many questions. I am debating whether or not to read this to the end...but as of right now, I don't think I will. Maybe in the future though.

This book makes me wish I could play an instrument. The way Jodi writes about music is just beautiful. 
 I really love the world. I can't really picture it though. The fantastical element of having mythical creatures and a city and woods and almost a whole uncharted world really pushes my into an RPG styled world, but it's dystopian? I'm just going to think of Final Fantasy and stick with that :P 
 Ana starts off as super overprotective of herself- with good reason. Having a crappy mum and growing up in exile has made her construct a pretty high wall. 
 But then Sam comes along. Sweet, Sam who brings her to Heart- The major city everyone lives in. He's really such a great character, such a drastic difference compared to most of the bad assery boys we typically see in YA novels. 
 My first thought going into reading this was "We better find out some sort of answer to why she's new and stuff." 
 And I wasn't let down. It wasn't ALL the answers, But it answered the major question of why and how she came to be.

What an interesting and creative concept for a series. In this world when a person dies, their soul is reincarnated in a different body. This tradition has been going on for five thousand years. That is until one day Ana is born, a new soul, who has never lived before. It's up to Ana to find out why she was born and the secrets of the town that she lives in, Heart. I really enjoyed Ana and Sam's relationship. Sam was so loving and protective over Ana and I enjoyed reading her journey to allow herself to love. The world building is great and I enjoyed the element of fantasy creatures, such as dragons. My pet peeve is that at times, it could be slow and I found myself wishing for more story advancement. 4 out of 5 stars

Incarnate was not what I was expecting, really. When I read the synopsis, I was really enthralled by the society Ana, the nosoul, lived in and then there were the dragons mentioned and basically the entire concept of souls and reincarnation had me excited. I wasn't exactly disappointed but it's not what I was expecting. The story seemed to focus on the romance between Ana and Sam, and her figuring out where she belonged and if she even belonged was a background occurance. The action scenes were well-described and as intense as it could have been. It was a bit slow for me but it does get good later on in the book!

This book had an awesome premise and a beautiful cover, but in the end, it was just another tacky paranormal romance about two people who fall INSTANTLY IN LOVE within days of meeting each other and any hope of plot is tossed out the window as we are shown scene after scene of these two falling all over each other. 
 The supposed "plot" of the book is that this girl wants to find out why she was born and whether it can happen again. Except all she does by way of "uncovering the mystery!" is going to the library. And even then, she gets distracted by the pictures and journals of her love interests' past lives, and spends all her time poring over these instead of researching her own condition. 
 The characters and their relationship are pretty poorly written and kind of gross. Examples: 
 - The main character has (supposedly) been abused her entire life, which makes her fearful of strangers and skittish during the first few chapters, but by the 1/3 mark of the book that is all completely forgotten. It's not that her character grows or develops, but she starts acting like a totally different person. 
 - When the protagonist was born, she "replaced" a woman who had been reincarnated over and over again, and who the love interest had previously been in love with. Instead of exploring this complicated and delicate situation, the author has a "big romantic moment" where the love interest says that if he had been given the choice to kill his girlfriend's soul so he could meet this new chick, he would've chosen the new chick in a heartbeat. I'M SORRY BUT THAT IS NOT SEXY OR ROMANTIC. "I totally would've killed off the woman I love if it meant I got to meet you." What???? 
 And this is just because I'm a queer lady, but the author talks about how these souls are reincarnated into different bodies and are not the same gender every time around. This is a perfect opportunity to explore how love can transcend gender, and yet every single couple presented in the book is heterosexual. The protagonist has some weird feelings about the fact that she's wearing a dress that belongs to her (now male) love interest, but that's about as far as it goes. 
 Overall - great concept, EXTREMELY poorly executed. How much longer do I have to wait before the effects of Twilight fade and we stop being force-fed this horrible "paranormal romance" crap. It cannot happen soon enough.

book_b.title: Not That Kind of Girl: A Young Woman Tells You What She's "Learned"
book_b.user_review: I got this book out of the library. Glad I didn't pay for it. I like to give books a fair go but by page 42 I couldn't go on. I was bothered. sample_reviews.review_text: I tend to like books written by strong women, but I struggled to get into this one. I got through the first few chapters and then it became more work than enjoyment to finish reading it. I'm not sure what they want the takeaway to be? Nope. Got about 70 pages in and gave up. Picked this up because I like her show, but this is self-indulgent p.o.s. is pretty worthless despite its myriad attempts to seem self-aware or insightful. Could do it. Abandoned.

SUCH A DISSAPOINTMENT! I love Lena Dunham and her show "Girls" so I had high hopes for this book. Unfortunately, it was a total let down. I couldn't even finish it because I could no longer stand her trivial essays. One essay, recalling her online relationship with a Russian boy named Igor was particularly dreadful. Most of her essays seemed to have no real impact her life, just non-funny experiences she had growing up. I could not relate to anything Lena had to say, which is sad because I look up to her as a feminist. But this book was just no good in my eyes. 
 Again, I am so sad to give this book such a poor review. Maybe one day I'll give it another shot... But for now, 1 star :/

I had to change my review to "2" stars after I asked myself: if I had no prior knowledge of a Lena Dunham, never watched Girls, and picked up this book purely as a book to read, what would I think? While this book fits nicely into the Lena Dunham brand that I appreciate: quirky, wry and narcissistic, as a stand alone piece of literature it doesn't really add up. 
 The author has no real struggle beyond the issues in her own head. She even says as one point, if she had been molested as a child it would explain all her mental health problems. She was raised in privilege. So, for me, I don't understand or sympathise with her on that level. It's like her persona had to make up mental health issues because she was dealt such an easy life and she needed something to set her apart. 
 When she describes wild nights out and thrift shop clothes I like it. Her nerdy obsessions with music and books are relatable. Her very brief insights to people in Hollywood were entertaining, as was most of the sexual encounters she describes. Her voice is amusing, but as I said, is it funny because I read her as Hannah in Girls, or funny because it's an original voice in literature? 
 Miss Dunham is only three years younger than I and maybe I'm a narcissist but I think I could put a spin on my own life's adventures just as well as her. There is nothing unique about her life as described in this book, despite having a TV show, which she doesn't really detail getting or working on. 
 As much as I like her, I have realised in the future when someone picks up this book with no prior knowledge of who she was, they won't find this book particularly illuminating in any way. Unless you grew up privileged in Manhattan with artist parents and attended private schools and summer camps, the vast majority of people will not be able relate.

Bad. Just really bad. Written by a self-important, self-absorbed woman who loves drama and does everything in her power to surround herself with it. A lot of strange stories, about her sexual experiences and her weird family, that go nowhere and seem to have no purpose or meaning other than to illustrate her own lack of proper upbringing, confidence and self-respect. Really, really bad.

Review 
 If you have ever been bullied, the title of the book Bully can make you cringe. I still remember the bully in my high school who used to pick on certain kids. I always tried to stay away from him to avoid being a target. Here I am many decades later and I still remember what he did to his victims. So can a victim forgive the boy bullying her and fall in love with him? 
 In Bully, the answer is "yes". Tate is a high school girl who is starting her last year of high school. Jared lives next door and growing up the two of them were best friends. However, Jared changed freshmen year and instead of loving Tate he started bullying her. Tate has no clue what she did to deserve this treatment and Jared won't tell her. The sweet boy is gone and an angry mean teen has replaced him. 
 Tate spent her junior year in Europe and has returned confident and ready to have a good senior year. This year she plans to stand up to Jared and no longer be the victim. But Tate is confused how she should fight back. Should she bully him or just tell him how she feels and let it go? Tate finally decides on the latter and her words shake up Jared causing him to change. 
 Pros 
 Douglas took a chance on this storyline, especially since bullying drives some teens to suicide. Instead, she showed how someone can fight back. Tate decided enough was enough, and you have to admire her strength of character to fight back. 
 Cons 
 I had many issues with this book. First, the fact that Tate was left alone for so long is difficult for me to believe. A good parent wouldn't leave their teenage daughter alone for months. And if he did, it could be considered child neglect. 
 Second, the characters in the book are not engaging or three-dimensional. Tate is a difficult heroine to like. She's critical of others and schemes to payback Jared for the years of abusive. At the end, she almost turns into a bully herself. 
 Third, Jared's sudden changes in behavior are not believable. In the beginning, Jared experienced horrible abuse and then channeled all his rage towards Tate. Realistically, I think he would be angry but why decide to start bullying Tate? Why not his mother? 
 At the end of the book, Jared changes again. We are to believe that Tate's speech to the class affects him so much, he loses all his anger and stops the bullying. People don't change their emotions that quickly. 
 Conclusion 
 Readers who are interested in bad bullying boys will like this book. I didn't enjoy it.

This is a negative star review as one star is too generous. A portion of one-star is too generous. Goodreads won't let me roast this thing without tossing it some kind of bone, so here we are. 
 The premise of this book was interesting: an emotionally abused boy reconnects with his former best friend who he'd treated terribly. Enemies-to-lovers is my kryptonite and I consider myself a pretty easy lay when it comes to that type of fiction. Just have the characters undergo the bare minimum of the most cliche development -- grow a backbone, grow a heart -- and I'm in. Sadly, the writer just didn't have the chops to put together any kind of emotionally rewarding -- hell, or even interesting -- way. 
 First of all, The characters are all assholes, including our ridiculously named main character/bullied "victim" Tate. She has the hots for a boy who has supposedly been abusive to her for the past four years, but she'll let him feel her up because he so hawt. Jared, the bully, apparently only treats her that way because he's soooooo in love with her. Seriously, this relationship reads like it was written by a 12-year-old with no understanding of relationships, sex or romantic love. 
 All of the characters act like they're 23 instead of 17. Which itself is another big problem. I'm not perverted enough to want to read about some teenager losing it on the night of her Homecoming dance. WTF? I thought NA meant college aged at least. There's a revenge porn subplot that's not treated with anywhere near the seriousness it deserves. 
 No one has any involved family members making sure they don't do ridiculous shit like run around in the rain half naked or get involved in illegal drag racing tournaments. Everything is told to us. Nothing is shown. It's like I'm reliving This Could Be Us But You Playin' all over again. 
 Ugh. Don't read this book. And if you do, sure as hell don't pay for it.

This book has often caught my eye and I've heard that David Sedaris is funny so I finally picked it up from the library for some light reading. I can't honestly say that I found his essays about his somewhat dysfuntional family particularly entertaining or funny for the most part.
A year ago I couldn't put it down - but now I can't remember one thing in it.

I actually completely forgot that I even read this book. 
 I had high expectations for this book, esp after Me Talk Pretty One Day had me laughing out loud. This book was a lot darker. I think it was supposed to be funny, and it WAS sometimes, but then it would take a sudden tragic turn and I'd just feel sorry David. I don't know what Sedaris was going through when he wrote this. Was he depressed? Did something happen? They were a collection of anecdotes, and at most they were interesting--strange snapshots of a life gone by, of moments that were stark and grim, and I have no idea what to feel. I don't understand what the purpose was. It was like watching one of those movies that really isn't anything--not funny, not overtly dramatic, not anything except just a series of snapshots of stuff that has happened to someone else. Me Talk Pretty One Day had a purpose; it was funny, and I think it was nostalgic, and if there were any grim bits I really don't remember. But this book... I just felt sad for him. I want to reach out, and make sure he's fine. 
 It explored familial themes and if you forget that he's talking about real people, then you can take a step back and snort I guess, but then somewhere in the middle of the book, he talks about how he DOES write about real people (well, not him. His sister, actually) and it just kind of hit me then and struck me for the rest of the book. These are real people. This is sad. 
 But I also get why he jokes about it. I think anyone one would. There are not too many ways you can cope with this otherwise. His family (in the book) isn't dysfunctional in an Arrested-Development way, they're... broken sometimes. And I think he was trying to say that it's okay. Maybe that's what the readers are supposed to take away from this, that it's okay to be broken and that you need to be a little broken to be functional sometimes. Well, still. I'm giving two stars because I signed up for comedy and what I got was just. Not entirely comedy. 
 For the record: I respect him and his life and his family. I don't want to seem like I'm giving THESE things 2 stars. I'm giving the BOOK 2 stars. Okay. Bye.

Another terrific slew of non-fiction essays by Mr. NPR himself, David Sedaris. Unlike his last book, "Me Talk Pretty One Day" -- which only spent half the book on his family (the other half on Paris and his boyfriend Hugh) -- this one is almost all about the Sedaris family, from Mom & Pop to Paul, Amy, Lisa, Gretchen and Tiffany. Culled from his contributions to Esquire, GQ, The New Yorker and "This American Life," the collection of 22 essays is a quick, satisfying read. 
 The first two pieces, "Us & Them" & "Let It Snow" get the raucous laughter flowing immediately. "Full House" is pervy but fun, reminding me a bit of A.M. Homes's style of writing and subject matter. "Slumus Lordicus" & "The Girl Next Door" are both serious departures for the writer, and they both strike a somber, unforgettable note. "The End of the Affair" is a sweet little morsel of a tale about Hugh & David seeing the Neil Jordan film in Paris. 
 A few of the siblings get starring roles in a few of the stories, all of which are very fun and tell us a lot about why Sedaris possesses that particular temperament and twisted sense of humor -- Lisa in "Repeat After Me"; Paul in 2 stories, "Rooster at the Hitchin' Post" & "Baby Einstein"; and his completely wacked out younger sister Tiffany in "Put a Lid On It." 
 A definite recommend and a summer fave.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Every Last Word takes a commonly misunderstood mental illness, in my opinion, and reorganizes it into a refreshingly realistic story that explores therapy, friendship, and eternal support. Our main character, Sam McAllister, suffers from the purely obsessional form of OCD. As in, her anxiety-inducing obsessions are strictly in her mind. 
 "But every once in a while, I'd glance down at the odometer, fascinated by the way the numbers changed. I felt this strange charge whenever the last digit hit the number three. 
 When I finally pulled into the driveway that evening, the last digit was resting on a six, so I backed out again and drove around the block a few times until the odometer stopped where it belonged. And now I have to do that every time I park." 
 Every Last Word is an emotionally powerful book. Without getting too personal here, I found myself connecting with Sam on a certain level. There were moments while reading that forced me to take a pause. Every Last Word placed me in the mind of Sam so well that I started feeling her emotions internally. It was like being transported into her brain. Experiencing her obsessive thoughts caused my heart to physically beat faster in my chest. Yes, I've experienced connections to characters before. But, this was unexplainably a whole new familiarity. The fact that Tamara Ireland Stone was able to write this character with such conviction has me flabbergasted. 
 The character development that Sam goes through is perfection. It is, honestly, one of the best I have read. I only wish it was executed differently. In the beginning, Sam is trapped in this terrible group of friends, who are basically the spawns of Satan, with the exception of Hailey. They are the definition of mean girls. Because of this, Sam works extremely hard to hide her mental illness from them. When Caroline Madsen, a girl from school, presents a secret poetry club, Sam starts to discover a feeling of normality and comfort. 
 What happens in Poet's Corner, stays in Poet's Corner. 
 And of course, a love interest is introduced while in Poet's Corner. AJ was a perfect male character, in a perfectly unconventional way. He is not muscular. He is not flawless. Basically, he is not the typical love interest so commonly seen in YA. He was, however, thoughtful, kind-hearted, and sympathetic. He unknowingly acts as a positive influence throughout Sam's journey. 
 When Sam is not in therapy, Caroline acts as her encouraging support system. Their friendship was so uplifting and acts as the perfect push for Sam to slowly remove herself from her toxic friends. I didn't enjoy, however, where the friendship transitioned in the end. Unfortunately, I need to be vague in my reasoning due to spoilers. To put it simply, it was a little bit of a disappointment. I do think what their relationship signified was beautiful, purposeful, and necessary. But, on the other hand, I can't quite understand the relation to the overall story. Honestly, it left me a little confused. 
 The relationships that develop in Every Last Word are a really strong aspect to the story. I found at times, however, that while some were explored so well, such as with her therapist, others were left dwindling in the background. Sam's mother, for instance, was such a lovely woman. She was so supportive, understanding, and, overall, a positive presence in Sam's life. Aside from a few moments, there is hardly any family involvement. This is just a personal preference, but I would have liked to see more of the family dynamic side of Sam's mental illness. 
 And then there is Hailey. Similar to Sam in the beginning, Hailey is treated terribly by their group of friends. I expected there to be some sort of big moment with their friendship, but nothing really happens. More or less, Hailey is a character that is just there in the sidelines to provide Sam with a purpose to stand up for herself. I wanted more involvement with her. 
 Keep in mind, this is just me being nitpicky. Every Last Word is a book that I think everyone can appreciate, whether you experience a mental illness or not. Although there are plenty of areas with Sam's life that I can't specifically relate to, it was still easy to feel entwined with her situations and struggles. Sam's improvement from the beginning of Every Last Word to the final pages is very moving, and I'm happy I was able to experience it. 
 Thank you to Kassidy Voinche for hosting the giveaway that allowed me to receive this copy.

DNF @ 30% 
 Your mental illness does not define you. 
 Say it with me: Your mental illness does not define you. 
 Samantha McAllister is a popular girl with a secret. She has OCD, which she was diagnosed with when she was ten, and also gets occasional panic attacks. She has successfully (or rather, miraculously) managed to keep these secrets hidden from her mean-girl clique, whom she hates with passion, and soon meets Caroline, who helps sneak her into the Poet's Corner where she finds her true people. 
 In retrospect, I guess this does sound like a fantastic idea but it didn't work for me. It's a shame, really, because I've seen mostly rave reviews and I'll get to the reasoning behind this decision, well...now. 
 This is a terrible representation of mental illness. I can say the same about bullying. The depiction of bullying in this novel, which is never a subject to play with, is watered-down. Samantha's friends are the very definition of shitty but she blends in with them so perfectly, I couldn't see why she hated them so much. 
 There are three tropes I hate more than watery iced-coffee. Cheating, couples boning when the actual apocalypse is happening outside their window, and loooooooove curing mental illness. (I'll come up with trope names later.) Take a guess which was included in this YA. 
 I expected to care more for this. It's about mental illness. They are usually the books close to my heart. Samantha is only half-realistic, though. Although, I sympathized with her insomniac issues, I just have a hard time believing how she could hide a full illness from her troupe of gals and they'd never notice. YA has been truly outstanding this year but this just couldn't win me over. 
 Tamara Ireland Stone is an author with promise, so I may check out what she has planned next. Tell me what you think, bumblebees!
I loved this book. The mental health aspect was great and I loved all of the characters so much!

I want to barf. 
 It's like the popular, unknowingly pretentious, but earnestly sincere, Mary Sue type girl watched her less emotionally fortunate friend go through something like this and then decided to write a book about it. You know, because she was right there in the thick of it. And sooo sympathetic. She practically experienced it herself! She totally gets it. 
 Except she doesn't. 
 She knows the details, but she doesn't know how it feels. She just doesn't comprehend the depth of it. She's playing at tragedy, playing at being a tortured artsy kid. Ooh, look, I can be creative and angsty, too. 
 Ugh, it's disgusting. 
 It's awful that so many people like this book. It paints such a horribly skewed picture of mental illness; that rather than raising awareness (at the very least), it romanticizes it (as in, makes it idealistic and unrealistic)!! 
 If anything, it characterizes teenagers who get all self-pitying and wrapped up in some legitimate issue, but also kind of milk it for the various forms of attention it creates. They allow themselves to be victimized by their issues so they aren't so accountable for their words/actions/behaviors. It's needy and immature. 
 I want to be clear that I'm not talking about the characters or events in this story--I'm generalizing about the feeling it gives me. 
 It probably didn't help that the audio narrator channeled Paris Hilton for the entire book.
