 The time frame and the mixed marriage scenario, the way people who do not conform are treated all add to a deeply troubling picture of our world. 
 Worth reading although the characters are not engaging.

formal review to follow but.. 
 the characters are so complex and at first you dislike them, but what I found at the heart of my dislike was a sadness of their deep humanity, their abilities to make awful mistakes, to say hurtful things, and I found that what I disliked was how easily I could be in their shoes.

I find it hard to enjoy books where the characters don't grow or learn from their experiences. This book was focused on very selfish people who punished their children for their own issues instead of dealing with them themselves. They completely ignored one child, bullied another, and set unreasonable expectations on the third. It was just sad and unsatisfying. 
 Ng is a good writer, but I can't say I enjoyed the book. I liked the pacing of the story. But for a book driven by character instead of plot, I would have preferred for the characters to show some self-reflection. I find stories where the majority of problems could be solved if people just talked to each other really frustrating. 
 I feel like I have a reading hangover.
seriously one of the best debut novels I have read in a very, very long time. The plotting is sad, so I will probably end up teaching it.
Wonderful book!

This book was well-written but it was hard for me to enjoy it. Too realistic, it made me a little bit depressed. Honestly, I don't know if i would've finished it had it not been a book club selection. I do think it will make for good discussion though, so in that way, it was good. It could very well be that it is winter and we've had many snow days with everyone home that added to my downer impression of it.

The first chapter was great. I was expecting an exciting mystery/thriller. I was anxious to find out how Lydia disappeared. 
 Then, the rest of the book happened. 
 I hated all of the characters. I hated the perfectly executed sentences. I hated the story. I hated the ending. 
 Oh, and I really hated how half of the book was written in italics. I would usually insert something sarcastic or witty here about the use of italics in the book, but I just can't do it. But, man, I hated her overuse of slanting letters to the right and writing choppy sentence fragments to attempt to make me care more about this stupid book. 
 First, it was The Martian 
 Then, it was The Girl on the Train 
 And now it's this horrible, lifeless book with wooden characters that no one cares about and hundreds of wasted pages on the past of the stupid characters that no one cares about. 
 I'm done with popular, overhyped books like this. There are too many great books out there, and I refuse to waste my time on something like this again. 
 Hey, was I clear on how much I hated this book? 
 Just wanted to be sure.

I finished this book, and basically... 
 Yeah. 
 This is an excellent book, but it is extremely emotionally taxing. 
 Everything I Never Told You is the story of a family recovering from a tragic loss. It moves back and forth in time, so that you can experience what led up to the tragedy, and fall through the canyons of grief alongside them afterwards. 
 One day, Lydia walked to the lake next to the family house. She unmoored the rowboat from the dock and rowed out into the center. She vanished. 
 "There is nowhere to go but on. Still, part of her longs to go back for one instant--not to change anything, not even to speak to Lydia, not to tell her anything at all. Just to open the door and see her daughter there, asleep, one more time, and know all was well." 
 Something has happened that should never happen. A family lost a child. She was a teenager, on the brink of a brilliant life. Or, maybe not so brilliant. She was exactly who her mother dreamed of being herself as a teenager. Or, maybe not so much. She was her father's popular golden child. Or, she wasn't. She was her brother's keeper, nagger, responsibility. Or, maybe she didn't want to be. Lydia was the middle child of three, All-American mother, Chinese father, suburban middle-class household during an era of changing times in the United States. And this book is as much about the struggle to be yourself and to not be drawn into the roles expected of you as it is about loss and grief. 
 "How had it begun? Like everything: with mothers and fathers. Because of Lydia's mother and father, because of her mother's and father's mothers and fathers." 
 This book is beautifully written. I can't possibly say enough about the incredible, lyrical prose. It is heart-wrenching in places, it is so lovely. The simplest of moments are so eloquently expressed. 
 "Morning sun fills the house, creamy as lemon chiffon, lighting the insides of cupboards and empty closets and clean, bare floors." 
 Beyond that, the characters are amazing, and honest, and raw, and real. Their journey is so personal, yet so universal. The struggles to fit in, to be accepted, to please your parents, to honor your family, to have someone to understand you, to be yourself. Every single person in this book is struggling with the same issues in completely different ways. 
 This book is a gorgeous work of art. It's emotional. It made me cry. It made me very angry. It made me smile. I even laughed a time or two, when I wasn't busy swooning over the amazing writing. It touched me in a way few books have, and will forever be one of my favourites. 
 Oh, Lydia. I wish I could have been your friend.

This was a beautifully written book. I particularly liked the interweaving narratives from each character from both present and past perspectives. It all culminates in the second to last chapter in which you start to understand the impetus for the event that is listed in the first sentence of the book. Our actions affect those around us in ways we never intend or fully understand until those relationships unravel.

reference_books.title: Sunny Side Up
reference_books.review_text: My young patrons at the public library LOVE Jennifer Holm, so I flipped through this when it came across my desk. I had heard an interview of Jennifer and Matt talking about the book on a podcast, and it didn't sound that fascinating then, but I figured I'd give it a shot. Overall, I was just not so impressed. The illustrations are very good, and I think the format will appeal to some readers (though it's more comic strip than graphic novel), but overall I though it was dull. The stories are snippets from the character's life (it's semi-autobiographical), and some of them were amusing but they didn't seem to follow much of a story arc. I think readers who are used to Holm's other work will be disappointed by the lack of plot in this book. To be honest, I read about half of it and then just skipped to the end because I lost interest.

reference_books.title: In the Unlikely Event
reference_books.review_text: I wanted to love this but I got about 50 pages in and gave up. Maybe it was listening to it as an audiobook, but there were way too many characters to keep track of, and looking ahead, there were still way too many more. I guess this is sort of a family saga book, but all the different POVs and back stories were confusing. Upon reading some other reviews, it sounded like one of those books where nothing actually ends up happening, so I gave up and moved on. I love Judy Blume's kids books, but maybe her adult books just aren't for me.

reference_books.title: Hello, Goodbye, and Everything in Between
reference_books.review_text:
Ho hum. 
 In the interest of full disclosure, I labored through 100 pages and then just skipped to the last chapter to see what happened. This book reminds me of movies like Before Sunset, where the characters talk and nothing actually happens. I liked the premise of this--a high school couple who are deciding the fate of their relationship the night before leaving for college. I think it's a somewhat realistic problem, though these days it seems most couples would tough it out, since they have snapchat, facetime, etc. I just didn't feel all that attached to the characters and didn't really understand why they were together in the first place. The book goes through different stops of importance in their relationship (which Aidan doesn't remember any of--typical guy) which Clare arranged, even though she's pushing for them to break up. The whole thing is just remembering when this or that happened, and after 100 pages, I was b-o-r-e-d. I had read The Statistical Probability of Love at First Sight by this author as well, and though I finished that, I thought it was similarly overhyped for what it was. The ending was pretty predictable and leaves room for a sequel which, if it happens, I'll be skipping. 
 I received an e-galley of this title from NetGalley, as well as an ARC from Hachette. Thank you to NetGalley and Hatchette!

reference_books.title: Dead Until Dark (Sookie Stackhouse, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I really like this first in the series that True Blood is based upon (though I haven't actually seen any episodes of True Blood yet). I'll probably get some slack for saying so, but it's like a darker, sexier Twilight. I can't wait to read the rest of the series!!

reference_books.title: Dumplin' (Dumplin', #1)
reference_books.review_text:
TL;DR: A really fun, funny book about underdogs standing up for themselves and rocking their confidence. 
 I'd been hearing about Dumplin' everywhere recently and was thrilled to get the opportunity to read an e-galley from Edelweiss. This novel is the fight song of all teen "misfits". The characters are lovable, even the ones who are a little jerky. Even the main love interest has a past of not being the greatest guy in the world, but he recognizes that and doesn't come off as a jerk in the present. The characters seemed very realistic, like the asshole bully who will always be an asshole bully. The insights about friendship are so true and really important for teens to hear; people change, and sometimes the friendships survive, but sometimes they don't. What made me fall in love with this novel the most, though, is that Willowdean really never even considers dieting to make herself a better pageant contestant. Rather than treating being overweight as a problem to be fixed in 200-300 pages, Julie Murphy creates a character who has flaws and moments of insecurity but has overall come to terms with her present self and is going to rock it out. While it may not be the most realistic situation (true life: kids can be incredibly mean and sometimes high school is just hell for certain kids), it sure is empowering. The novel had a few laugh-out-loud moments and was a fun, quick read. My only issue and the cause of losing that 5th star is that the ending just felt abrupt. There's always a fine line between wrapping up a story satisfactorily and tying it up TOO neatly, but I kept switching back on my Kindle to make sure that I hadn't missed the last page. I just needed a little, maybe one more sentence, to make me feel totally happy about the ending. Overall, though, I think this is a special book that will resonate with anyone who has ever felt like a misfit. 
 Many thanks to Edelweiss and Harper Collins/Balzer + Bray for the opportunity to review this e-galley.

book_a.title: Crenshaw
book_a.user_review:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I received an e-galley of Crenshaw from NetGalley. 
 I really liked this book, and I think the young patrons at my library will, too. Crenshaw is a wonderful novel that is mostly realistic but with a hint of magic. I was, admittedly, skeptical when I heard Applegate's newest book was about homelessness, but it's handled in a way that makes the issue not very traumatic, and the aspect of Crenshaw being an imaginary friend helps lighten the mood at any intense parts. However, I can see the argument that the novel may handle the issue of homelessness (which in this case, mostly manifests itself in the family not always having enough to eat and generally doing without extras, as well as a stint of living out of their minivan in the past) a little too lightly. Overall, though, I think it's a good way to introduce the issue to young children, especially those who have never had to worry about their family's stability. 
 Much of the novel is a flashback, and as such, there's not a great deal of action. I think the emphasis on flashbacks may deter some readers. I found myself getting near the end and wondering when something big would actually happen and how it would wrap up so quickly. However, there are a few very suspenseful pages towards the end. Also, I thought I knew exactly what would become of Crenshaw at the end, but I surprised, pleasantly so, and it's a twist that I think kids will especially love. Overall, a quick (less than 90 minutes!) read about some serious issues handled with respect and humor, if not complete realism.

sample_reviews.review_text: No es el mejor libro del mundo, pero estuvo bien. Muy duro y realista.

Stories about families in financial crisis need to be told more often. I am grateful to Applegate for taking on the task. This book is a fast read and Jackson, along with the people he loves, is an endaering and authentic character. Great read-aloud for upper elementary.

I wished I have my own Crenshaw. Yep, it's a cool name for a cat. I don't think I've ever had an imaginary friend. 
 This book reveal a social issue that is seldom being talked about. The issue about homelessness. On the outside Jackson's family looked fine, but they struggled to make ends meet after several setbacks like his father's sickness and the lost of jobs. His parents had to hold several part-time jobs and every month they were in danger of eviction from their rental apartment. They are hardworking, but life just threw them some curveballs that hit them hard. Readers can feel how humiliating it was to be homeless. The uncertainty, the shame, and the fear. 
 Jackson's family became homeless for a few months when he was in first grade. It seemed that it will happen again. And then, Crenshaw appears.

This book was tricky to rate because of the subject matter. It's definitely well written, but homelessness isn't a subject I'd choose for entertainment. Even as an adult, I found the book to be depressing, lending a sense of anxiety. I recommend that parents read with their children and explain anything they don't understand. The story deals with telling children the truth about every situation, which the book exemplifies, but I would have to disagree that trying to protect one's child is always bad. It's what parents do, and each situation is different as well as the child's ability to comprehend. I did like the author's use of the imaginary friend to help the protagonist with his issues and the fact that the ending wasn't predictable or too Pollyanna in it's conclusion.

This was an amazing book, so relevant to so many of our kids today. This is this years Bluebonnet book that hits you on a deep meaningful level, one that sticks with you long after you finish reading it!

** spoiler alert ** 
 Hmm.. I bought this book for a 9 year old. Her mom read it to her and then she told me to read it so we could discuss. After I finished, my first thought was to apologize. I said, "wow. I'm sorry I accidentally bought your daughter this terribly depressing book." 
 She said she thought it was important for kids to read these kinds of things, to appreciate what they have. 
 But the discussion she wanted to have was over how frustrating books like this can be. It's one thing for kids to understand their parents are human and make mistakes but this seemed... different. 
 -*** SPOILERS ***- 
 I wanted Jackson to go live with Marisol. He would've been happier there, but, at the ripe old age of 11 he felt obligated to stay and look after his little sister. It felt wrong. I wasn't happy at the ending, either. Maybe it wasn't supposed to, but it didn't feel hopeful at all. It was very depressing.

I was disappointed in aspects of this story. I really don't understand why the Invisible cat friend was necessary in this story (although books featuring invisible friends seem to be popping up everywhere at the moment). The story depicting homelessness and helplessness from a child's perspective made for empathy inducing reading and most of my readers in Y5-6 that like this genre would enjoy the story very much - but Crenshaw - somehow adding the unsubtle invisible friend was too much in my opinion and makes for a 'harder sell' to my student community.
Excellent for upper elementary! I loved when Crenshaw compared the waiting room for invisible friends with a teacher's lounge!

First line: I noticed several weird things about the surfboarding cat. 
 I loved The One and Only Ivan I cared deeply about the characters, so I assumed that these new characters, Jackson a boy who is dealing with his parents' money problems and Crenshaw an imaginary cat, I would also love. But, I didn't. 
 I did enjoy the book, and my heart ached for Jackson and children like him, but I didn't love him as much as I did Ivan, Ruby, or Stella. And Crenshaw was a character whom I just did not like. I think he was suppose to come across as a "real" cat would, aloof and arrogant, but I didn't like it. I wanted him to be more caring towards Jackson and his situation. 
 If you have a student or kiddo who liked How to Steal a Dog or Hope is a Ferris wheel then they'll probably like this one. If you have an older student or kiddo who's dealing with a difficult issue and struggles with addressing the issue honestly like Jackson then I'd recommend When a Monster Calls. 
 Check out the great book trailer and resources about hunger at: 
 http://www.mackidsbooks.com/crenshaw/...

As I read this book, I wondered about Applegate's intentions in writing it. I found it to be a gentle way to introduce some students to the idea of homelessness, and to also show some understanding to those who might have experienced it. I found the somewhat-sudden ending a little jarring. I liked the fact that Applegate wrote about a family with two parents and that even they can strugggle, included helpful librarians and teachers, and some humor. However, I would have liked to know a little more about Crenshaw. The imaginary friend idea could lead to some interesting conversations with students. Ironically, I read this book just a few hours after Mac Barnett's Leo: A Ghost Story. In both cases, who does or doesn't see the ghost/imaginary friend, and what physical presence could they actually have? (None in reality, questionable in the books.)

book_b.title: Vanishing Girls
book_b.user_review: I began listening to this as an audiobook and got to the 3rd disc when it started skipping. I realized then that I wasn't that interested in it and decided to abandon it altogether. I didn't find the characters likable or interesting and thought the plot was taking too long to develop.

sample_reviews.review_text:
"Sometimes people stop loving you. And that's the kind of darkness that never gets fixed, no matter how many moons rise again." 
 I just, I'm sort of speechless. This is one of the best books i've ever read, the smartest, most unpredictable and favorite thriller I've ever read. 
 Lauren Oliver's writing is invincible, uplifting and truly unique. Her description jumps into your mind and pulls at your imagination, the images she creats enter your mind ans stay there. 
 It was so interesting to see the differences and similarities between the two sisters. Small things like the description of Parker's eyes let you know how different yet similar they really were. I felt so many emotions while reading this, I couldn't put this down, it definitely got me out of a reading slump that I was about to start having. 
 That ending is by far the craziest craziest ending I will ever read. I kept going back and seeing things now that the truth was revealed. I felt like my brain was unfolding and adapting to the truth behind everything. It's so crazy, just so so crazy. Don't spoil this, pleased don't. I was nowhere close to predicting it, I am mind-blown. 
 I loved Nicole & Dara "Dara" (the Dara Nicole took the role of and the Dara from the journal. In retrospect, I can see Nicole In the "Dara" we thought we were reading and everything makes so much sense, the events rolled in an infinite stream, Parker's kiss, the party at the drink, the reporter..... so so much, the characters were so intricately woven, the writing beautiful, the craziness authentic. 
 Thank you Lauren Oliver for reminding me of how much I truly love you for the beautiful and unforgettable books that you write. Thank you.

I had trouble getting into this book from the beginning and when I figured out the plot twist a third of the way into the book I almost gave up on it. The author uses a ridiculous amount of awkward similes so that instead of being immersed in story, you are always aware that you are reading a book.

"That's the thing about Dara and me: we're both similar and worlds apart" 
 This was a mindf*ck, but not exactly in the good way. This is my second Lauren Oliver book, and I don't know if she's an author for me. 
 This book is about sisters Dara and Nick, who are very close. One day, they are in a car accident, and their relationship falls apart. Months after the accident, Nick comes back to live with her mom and Dara, and tries to connect with her sister. At the same time, a young girl goes missing, and Dara soon is nowhere to be found. Nick decides to look for her sister and bring her home. 
 I think Lauren Oliver is a great author who writes crappy books. This was boring and it felt so long. The first two thirds were a bore, and nothing was happening. What I really liked was the fact that there were two points of view, pictures and transcripts from articles in the internet and text messages. But there was a problem in the dual POV, and it was the fact that Dara and Nick sounded the same And maybe that was intentional, all things considered? 
 Dara and Nick were also very annoying, proclaiming love and friendship from each other, and then being very jealous and petty Also, the love triangle... WHY? And Parker, such an idiot, playing with both girls. Why would he start dating Dara if he was interested in Nick? Such a douchebag . I don't think this was a very healthy relationship. Also there were some weird things, like this Ariana chick seemed to be only friends with Dara and tolerating Nick. Nick had some friends, but they never appeared. Also, the were a lot of things that happened "off screen" (like the accident) and that felt a bit off in my opinion. 
 I saw the ending coming from a mile away (maybe because I read a lot of thrillers?). The plot twist at the end is waaaaaay overused. Dara being dead and Nick having a double personality kinda thing. Which seemed so stupid because NOBODY REALISED THAT NICK WAS ACTING WEIRD?? . I can't buy that plot twist, sorry. 
 Maybe somebody who doesn't read many thrillers would have found this book enjoyable, but to me, Vanishing Girls was flat, boring and very predictable. 
 "	How convenient if you could see what was wrong with people right away, if they wore their sicknesses and crimes on their skin like tattoos."
I am fairly annoyed that I read the book description and guessed the content shortly after I began because of a comparison to another book. It was still very enjoyable, and overall a good read.

Another reading struggle... Why? (Sobs) 
 This book frustrated me the entire time I was reading it. I didn't felt the mystery vibe until I was near the end of the book. For me, it only covered sibling rivalry, insecurities and selfishness. 
 Then when I read the plot twist, I wasn't impressed. I really think it was forced and it did not lifted the terrible scenes in the first and a half part of the book. 
 I am a psychology major student but I didn't felt the impact of Nick's illness. It was so fast paced and not detailed at all which confused me (big time). One moment she was normal, then she's not then she's already back to normal. And I'm like Whaaaat???!!! 
 I saw that the reviews with this book were high, which confuses the hell out of me. What is wrong with me? Why did I not like the book when everybody did? But I guess we do have different taste and point of views. This book wasn't for me. Nope.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This was really horrible. I would say that it is her worse novel. It's too bad as her Delirium series is quite fun. 
 ***************SPOILERS*************** 
 My biggest problem with this story is that it has been done better by other YA authors. There's We Were Liars, Loud Awake and Lost, and the books that are most similar, The Perfectionist Series. All use unreliable narrators to tell a story, some of the above are good, some bad. 
 Aside from that the writing is just atrocious... And the cliches. Don't bother with this one.

I think I'm done with YA fiction for a while. This book was so frustrating, not only because the "twist" was so incredibly obvious from the first few chapters that it was embarrassing; but because the events that happen are so sensationalized, the whole story in unbelievable. 
 It's a book about teens. Normal teens going through life and hard times. And that's cool, that's okay. There are so many good books written about this very thing, with no super-extra-dramatic-unbelievable things happening around ever corner. 
 But it can't just be about a teen going through one thing. She has to also be dealing with: 
 Divorced parents, 
 Estranged sister, 
 Love triangle, 
 Missing girl, 
 Paedophile website, 
 "Trouble" always drunk/high teen, 
 Solving mysteries all by yourself, 
 Being chased by random leather wearing dude, 
 Infiltrating underground societies on a whim. 
 Honestly it's just too much. I mean... Come on. Pick one of these things. Just one, and write a book about it. Write a really thorough, insightful book about it. Don't just throw a bunch of exciting things together, stir and hope no one notices that the pieces don't fit. The ya books that I love are simple and heart wrenching (the perks of being a wallflower, the fault in our stars, the curious incident of a dog in the nighttime etc) but too often ya books try to outdo all the other by doing this kind of over the top crap. I'm done with it for a while. 
 Ps- Am I the only one who picked up on the fact that this book is supposed to be about her sister going missing but the "before" and "after" chapters are referring to the car accident where Dara only received minor scarring and a bad wrist? I can't be the only person who thought that was odd!
Well, I saw that coming from early on.

Sisters share many things... but a boy shouldn't be one of them. 
 After a traumatic car crash, Nicole (Nick) wants to get close to her sister Dara again. But it won't be easy. Dara is not accepting any of her invitations, even framing Nick for a party faux-pas. If only Dara would understand how much Nick cares for her. If only Nick could remember what happened that crazy night of the crash. 
 Told in a dual point-of-view between Dara and Nick, as well as with after and before the accident chapters (yes, this gets confusing at times), we get a glimpse at both sides of the coin. Dara comes out as an extrovert and makes it easy to relate to her emotions. But Nick is the opposite. She hides her true feelings from Parker (her crush), Dara, and even her parents. Therefore, Oliver focused more chapters on Nick, piercing the mystery even more. Add a case of a 
 missing nine-year-old neighborhood girl and you get a thriller. The book includes emails, photographs and diary entries to serve as clues. 
 Although, some of the ending revelations were too coincidental, the book left me guessing until the end.

Das Buch hat mich ziemlich enttauscht; das kenne ich von Lauren Oliver viel besser. 
 Zum einen hab ich (leider) den plot twist schon relativ fruh von Weitem gerochen. Klar, es ist letztlich ein Jugendbuch und - ohne das arrogant zu meinen - fur weniger erfahrene LeserInnen geschrieben. Trotzdem hatte ich mir eine bessere Tauschung und nicht so viele hints gewunscht. 
 Dann: Wie oll ist bitte der plot mit zwei 'rivalisierenden' Schwestern, die von der jeweils anderen glauben, sie sei der (Eltern-)Favorit? Und dann sind noch beide in den gleichen Jungen verliebt - ugh. Nee danke, Frau Oliver; das konnen Sie besser.

reference_books.title: The Heretic's Daughter
reference_books.review_text:
I tend to lean toward 3.5 stars, but since you can't give half stars I went with four. Mostly because I have an ancestor executed in the Salem Witch Trials and had a personal interest. 
 The story was really great, but got slow at some points and I felt like the characters could have been developed a lot better. I would have liked to get to know her parents better, there was so much history and story there that were ignored.

reference_books.title: The Hunger Games (The Hunger Games, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I've heard great things about this book for a while now, but the wait list at the library has always been incredibly long. I finally put my name on the list and I am so glad I did. This book was incredible. From the moment I started it, I couldn't put it down. I think I finished it in about a day and a half. My only regret is now I'm going to have to wait a couple of weeks before I'm able to read the second one as it has an even longer wait list than this one. Sigh.

reference_books.title: Frankenstein
reference_books.review_text:
This book was incredibly good. I decided to read it because I'm going to be the Bride of Frankenstein for Halloween, and being the neurotic person I am, thought it would be important to have read before then. Yes, I know, I'm insane. 
 I have delved into the classics over the last couple of years and prepared myself for a tough read with this one, but it was actually a very fast read. It had such a great flow to it. And throughout the book I kept thinking about Wuthering Heights, I think it was how similar the two are in their dark, gothic settings. Although I do have to admit, because of the language, I kind of felt like I was reading some fantastic, Shakespearean play at some points. Lots of drama. 
 Also, and this isn't too surprising given how twisted I can be, I felt really sorry for the monster most of the time. He just wanted to be loved. Weep. Sob. Heh. Poor monster.

reference_books.title: Lamb: The Gospel According to Biff, Christ's Childhood Pal
reference_books.review_text:
This book made me want to go back and read the bible again. I've read it a bajillion times, but it's been ages and after reading this book I want to fill in the blanks. I'm not big on religion, but this book was awesome. I mean, of course it was, it's Christopher Moore and the man is brilliant. 
 OK, so the backdrop for this story. Levi bar Alphaeus, also known as Biff, is best friends with Jesus throughout their childhoods and adult lives. Present day, Biff is resurrected to write a gospel of his life with Jesus and the missing 30 years of Jesus' life. The book goes back and forth between Biff's experiences in present day and his time with Jesus. 
 The present day accounts are hilarious, he discovers the hotel room bible and "new" chapters which he secretly reads to see how accurate they are. He and his angel companion are introduced to the world of soap operas, professional wrestling and the Wizard of Oz movie. 
 The recollections of times past are mostly funny and entertaining, but can get slow at some points. Usually Biff's unique voice and point of view make them a lot of fun. I have to say that if Jesus is the Christ, Biff is most certainly the anti-Christ, but not in an evil, end of days kind of way, just his polar opposite. 
 All in all, another fantastic book by Christopher Moore. I continue to be his biggest fan.

reference_books.title: Marley and Me: Life and Love With the World's Worst Dog
reference_books.review_text:
I borrowed this book from the library last week with the intention of reading it before I saw the movie. But I was still reading another book and some friends were going to see the movie and I went anyway. I loved the movie, it made me sob unattractively in the theater, which I hate doing, but it was so good. 
 I started the book a few days later and got through half of it in the first sitting. I couldn't stop reading it. I finished it this afternoon. Again I cried, but again it was worth it. Such a great story and such an incredible writer. 
 I loved that this book made me laugh and sympathize with both Marley and his owners. I loved that almost everything he did reminded me of the dogs I have, have had and know. I loved that I could relate. I can't count how many times, when Bailey was still young, how many times I would break down crying and wonder what on earth I had done to deserve such a terrible dog. He was SO naughty! It was great to read this book and know that it wasn't just me, many people go through that with their dogs, especially when they are lab mixes.

book_a.title: Prozac Nation
book_a.user_review: I couldn't finish this book. I never got into it.

sample_reviews.review_text:
It was ok. 
 Harrowing? Lame.

book_b.user_review:
I kept going back and forth between rating this book two or three stars. I finally went with two stars because it was a doggie snuff novel and I have no patience for those. (OK, so it was only ONE dog, but still, completely unneccessary.) 
 This was my first Vonnegut book (I finally read him because so many friends recommended him) and one thing I have to hand him is that he is a truly gifted writer. I read through this book in about a day and a half, it has such a great flow to it and really beautiful writing. But the book kind of reminded me of those suspense movies where you have no idea what is going on in the beginning and as the movie proceeds, more and more pieces of the puzzle come together. Just when you think you know what's going on, they throw you a curveball right at the end. Except there was no curveball. The ending felt anticlimatic to me. 
 The story is this: World War III breaks out in 1985 and what is left of humanity is shipwrecked on one of the Galapagos Islands. The story is told the ghost of a shipbuilder a million years later. There is much discussion about evolution and too-big brains (AKA the crazy things people do in today's day and age with perhaps too much time and not enough to do). Like I said, interesting, but not too exciting. 
 In spite of my lackluster experience with Galapagos, and because of the great writing style of Vonnegut, I plan to give him another go. But I'm going to try one of his earlier novels, like Slaughterhouse Five or Cat's Cradle.

However, I felt the ending was a little rushed and parts of it were dumb. I know some of that is his writing style, but really? people turning into otters? I know that its fiction but I felt he could have done better than that.

Also typical of the other Vonnegut books I've read, while the plotline is utterly bizarre, you get sucked in and see yourself in a parallel reality being pushed to consider the philosophical, political, and scientific commentary he weaves throughout. 
 Especially relevant today in relation to the economic downturn; but eternally relevant as long as we continue getting it into our heads that we know best about something.

They say a statue is made when a sculptor sees a statue in the air and then just fills the form with substance, and a writer sees the story itn the blank sheet of paper and then just fills it with ink. 
 If 'Galapagos' was a sculpture, then it was made when Vonegut shaped it very roughly, then instead of polishing it began to slap handfulls of clay until the original shape was all but gone. The end result isn't pretty. 
 For a start, you'll know the entire plot within the first 20 pages. He just keeps throwing spoilers at you, at times repeating himself untill it gets so repetative that you say 'Yes, I already read that, like a dozen times before!'. So you know what happens, you might just want to see HOW it happens, but it doesn't help that the story is not very interesting by itself. 
 The story of the book do not follow any logic. Many writers are frowned upon for introducing 'deus ex machina' unexpected illogical events as plot fixing. Well, 'Galapagos' is made entirely by such occurrences. You can't predict them. I have no problem feeling helpless when introduced to an unknown system of cause and consequence, like the first half of 'Gardens of the Moon', as long as there is any indication such a system exists. Being thrown random events is not what I call fun. 
 But there were some good things in there, and they won't let me put one just star and feel good about it. The main storytelling style, of telling the skeleton of the story and then gradually filling the details is original, and could work well with a better story. The idea that big brains are an evolutionary handicap is interesting, the symbolism of the human evolution taking place on a Galapagos island is touching. Vonegut advertises evolution back to a seal-like appearance, but admits that it has its drawbacks. He says wars, pollution and slavery are gone, and people do not need dentists anymore, but admits that the latter is not because their teeth are better, but because they die before their teeth start falling. 
 In the end, I do not regret I read this book. But I will not read any more from Vonegut, that's for sure.

sample_reviews.review_text: Probably closer to a 3.5. I enjoyed this book as I found the character of Chris Knight, a "hermit" who essentally walked into the woods with his backpack and didn't emerge for 27 years. He is a controversial figure, as he sustained himself by stealing thousands of times from local homes and cottages. However, I was so curious to understand how this individual seemed to have no drive for connection, relationships, and contact, which are the very things that I feel give life its meaning. I also enjoyed some of Finkel's reflections on solitude, other famous recluses and hermits, and what it means to be alone. Definitely an interesting read.

The Last True Hermit? This is a sensational and unnecessary by-line as even the author includes information on many present-day hermits. That put aside, a very good listen (read), well-written and very engaging. I wish there had been more detail about Christopher's Knight's day-to-day existence and less psychology. I found it heartbreaking that this man was forced to return to a society/life that he felt so alienated from. Also put off by the author's continued insistence on making contact with Knight when he so clearly did not want it. I understand and empathize with Finkel's commitment and concerns about Knight, but the poor guy had to beg and plead to be left alone. 
 Excellent bibliography for other works on solitude included. 
 As always, superbly read by Mark Bramhall. (I would listen to anything that this man narrates.)

Not my favorite book. Unfortunately I had to forward through several of the pages due to the writing style employed. Finkel writes this like a term paper, as if he is proving a thesis through research. What I wanted was the story of Christopher Knight. It was difficult to sustain close reading through the drudgery of philosophic and psychologic references. 
 Just OK.
This book was very interesting. I learned more about the history of Hermits than I ever knew existed!

I have mixed feelings about this book about a man who lived in the woods for 25 years in Maine. On one hand, it is excellently written and a good investigation on what it means to live a solitary and isolated existence. On the other hand, Chris Knight, the hermit, is so disillusioned when he re-enters society that it's really disheartening. He also, despite one tearful moment, seems genuinely annoyed by the author's persistent interviews and repeatedly tells him to stop bothering him and wait until he's dead to publish anything. Well, the author didn't wait, which made my annoyed! Very interesting, though, and I can't believe Chris didn't light one fire that whole time, for fear of being caught.

Very straightforward and readable without making more a myth out of the man than needed. I particularly liked the well researched medical interpretations as well as the appropriately placed quotes about silence. If you are even marginally introverted I highly recommend this book.

This felt very exploitative, particularly when you learn how much this family and Chris did not want to talk to this reporter. 
 The only parts I really enjoyed were the sections on the history of hermits. I'm interested in further reading in the future on isolation and hermits throughout history.

I didn't expect to like this book, but I loved it. It is very interesting, honest, and well researched. It is the story of Christopher Knight, the "hermit" discovered and arrested in Maine after 27 years living in the woods without any human contact.

This book was well researched and fairly well written, but the pacing was on the slower side for my tastes. The actual story of Chris Knight was padded with so many factoids from literature, psychologists, scientists, and history that I at times forgot what I was even reading. The extra information was necessary to make this a full book length piece (and some of it was genuinely interesting), but the fascinating and bizarre story of the actual hermit got lost in all the extraneous info.

sample_reviews.review_text: At first I would have given this 3 stars, but then I read To Say Nothing of the Dog (finally!) and realized just how much of a rip-off of TSNotD this is. Jesus, come up with your own freaking ideas, Jodi.
Very fun book for me. The audio narrator was fantastic!

The title unfortunately describes the way this book is plotted. Things happen, and they are sort of loosely slung-together, with very little sense of time passing (at one point the protagonist notes she's known another character for five years, and I genuinely thought only a single year had passed since their meeting at the beginning of the novel) and with absolutely no character development. No characters at all, really: Taylor's creations seem to turn on a dime, depending on whatever the plot ("plot"?) dictates. Out of nowhere, one character is suddenly revealed to be a sexual predator, because Taylor needs the reader to hate him now. The love interest up and screams at the protagonist, also out of nowhere, for...angst I guess? Oh and some rando background character suddenly calls the protagonist a slut and...sexually attacks her. Of course. I see more of a pattern here than to the plot and it's gross. 
 The main character has no personality except to be perfect at everything and drive evil people to fits of revealing rage -- classic Mary Sue stuff. I get annoyed with the overuse and misuse of that term, but it really applies here. Max feels like a self-insert. She, her love interest, and the innumerable interchangeable secondary characters are all amazingly under-characterized and flatly written: I couldn't describe a single one of them to you, nor could I tell them apart much of the time. (Which one was Markham and which was Murdoch again?) Early in the book, Max notes that she often does not react to things in a "normal" way, but this is never used to make a point about her history or to develop her character as the story progresses; instead, it feels like Taylor simply did not know how to write realistic reactions to situations and was using this as an excuse. 
 And nothing else makes sense either! You have a secret -- but not all that secret if it's known by a major university and receives "assignments" -- time travel organization, which for some reason is severely understaffed. At one point they only have four historians (a.k.a. time travelers) working for them, and don't hire more -- but no real qualification seems necessary? Like Max makes a big deal about how rigorous the training is, but without actually conveying that in any way, and it's also not explained why they can't just recruit more people for the training in the first place. Max's "specialty" as a historian is brought up, but then she never works on anything related to it. They send her back to study dinosaurs when her speciality was ancient Greek and Roman civ. You guys couldn't recruit some paleontologists? 
 As a time travel book, this novel makes poor use of its subject. In fact, nearly no use: the main conceit of historians using time travel in their studies was done better many times over by Connie Willis; the big "twist" is the starting point for many other time travel narratives, and seemed so obvious that the characters not figuring it out sooner just makes them look dumb. On the most basic level, St. Mary's does not seem like a fun or exciting organization to work for, so why would I want to read about it? This book was baffling for me from start to finish; I kept waiting for it to get going, then to get better. It didn't. Now I wish I could go back in time and not bother.

This book and I got along well; it has many of the elements that I love in storytellingaEUR"aspects of historical fiction, time-skips, sci-fi, strong lead female, relationships that build vs insta-love, a plot with twists and turns and a good pace. 
 Do not expect a deep book, because it is notaEUR"it is a quick, easy and engaging read that is satisfying. There is suspense; I did not know what was going to happen, and at one point, the storyline made mush out of my emotions. It has witty dialogue with characters that are well played and nicely developed (for the first book in a series). The plot is clever and amusing but I will admit the time-skips may frustrate some due to the lack of explanation/rules. I had no issues there because it didn't feel chaotic nor at the author's whim. The ability to time travel just simply existed plus they used the same device and reason for the travel. 
 Most important to me, One Damn Thing After Another was a super fun reading adventure. The story was mesmerizing.

I give this book 2.0 stars for the writing and 0.5 stars for my enjoyment of the story. Obviously, the latter mark is the far more subjective and many will disagree. The plot unfolds in a secret historical academy which has developed the technology to transport people back in time. Although the historians who make the journey are sent to observe, never to alter events, things do not go as intended and all sorts of mayhem ensue. At first I thought I had stumbled into a young adolescent novel with its setting reflective of a boarding school and the dynamics between trainee historians and the administration reflective of stogy old teacher and mischievous student. The idea of traveling back in time to various historical moments to watch and report felt like those educational afterschool programs. But, the addition of attempted rapes, passionate sex scenes, adult power grabs and a miscarriage made it clear that an adult reader was intended without ever shifting the dialogue, character behavior or plausibility to indicate maturity in the characters or the reader. Had this not been a book group pick, I would never have picked it up and not have read past the first 50 pages had I stumbled on it.

I wanted to like this more than I actually did...mostly because I feel like a ton of people that I work with have read it and enjoyed it. I mean, it was mostly enjoyable, but it could've been WAY better. 
 It was a fine, somewhat funny time travel novel, but there were a few glaring inadequacies, most notably in the absent of a larger plot. I mean, there was a bit about trying to save the agency, but it was too little, too late, and didn't make a ton of sense. Hopefully that plot point (which was like the overarching plot point) will be more developed in the subsequent novels. Otherwise, it was just kind of random and often gory time travel adventures, which were kind of fun, but the book definitely suffered from absence of a larger plot. 
 There was also a spontaneous abortion subplot that was unnecessary and made me really hate a character that was pretty likable up until he had a SERIOUSLY terrible reaction to the whole thing. 
 So yeah, it was ok. I don't know that I'll be reading the other entries in the series, although I think with a few improvements (more plot and character development, less action! action! action!) that this could be a very cute series. 2 stars.

They've been dating for like 5 years. 
 Which of course makes the next man who hears that tale, try to rape her, because might as well, she's slept with everyone since Farrell said so. She once again handily fights him off, depressed waif and all. The make up scene made me even madder. He never apologizes at all for accusing her or his reaction, just makes it all about him like the whole book: "Ashamed. I broke the thing I loved most in the world. And I can never get that back." Her response is to go all no no! you still have me! hugs! Bleh. The characters all just do extreme things each scene--she's either drunk, or whooping it up, or placidly drinking tea. 
 I think also if you want to do time travel, yay, I like time travel novels. But the rules to how it works seemed to change chapter by chapter. Sometimes it seems like there was decontamination procedures, other times off to party right afterwards. I know it seems like a nerdy thing to bitch about, but there didn't seem to be much consistency in how the world worked. It didn't help that almost everyone was terrible in communication. I might read the second one, since I already read the sample chapters included in this one, and seems Victorianish, and since there is like 7 more of these, maybe they get better.

I think my expectations were a bit too high with this one. I love history (that's what my undergrad degree is in), time travel, and female lead characters, but this book just did not do it for me. The main character was mostly annoying and drunk almost all the time, so her rare moments of brilliance/coherence just did not make any sense. I have also never cared less about characters dying than I have while reading this book...most of the time once the random character was announced dead I responded with "Who?" because none of the characters were discernible from one another. Plus, ending every other chapter with some kind of "We had no idea we would never see them alive again" nonsense pretty much tips you off that some rando side character was gonna die in a few pages. 
 Also, for a book whose characters are described as 'historians' there's little to no history whatsoever. I don't know a single historian who would care about visiting dinosaurs (shouldn't they bring scientists along for that kind of mission??) and the few visits to the past don't contain any description or historical events other than a fleeting mention of why they are there. Most of the book is dialog (which I barely understood; the author has a habit of using a pronoun without establishing who that pronoun belongs to), descriptions of what the character are eating/when they make tea, and technical descriptions about how they prepare for the missions. Then the mission itself is basically "We showed up there. We did some stuff. We drank." The casual rape scenarios were also disturbing to me. It just seemed inconceivable that Max, the lead heroine, would be so upset about the death of a man who tried to rape her and then KILL her, yet was completely unforgiving of the female she hated, Izzie. Then the man that she's in love with basically accuses her of hooking up with her attempted rapist, but she's like "It's fine, I still love you." That does not say strong female character to me. Overall, I wish this book delivered what it seemed to promise, and I won't be reading the rest of the series.

I felt like this series had a lot of potential. Ideas that were squandered by the mediocre execution. The first book in the series, Divergent, is the most fully realised of the series. It's clear that the necessary time and care was taken with that book to improve it before it went to print. It feels like after the success of Divergent, the other books in the trilogy were rushed onto the market and their quality really suffers for the haste. 
 The biggest problem is the completely one-dimensional and forgettable characters. Looking back I don't think there is a single fully-realised character in the series. The lack of development was ok in Divergent, because the first book in a series should obviously set up questions to be answered in later volumes. Satisfying answers never came. The lack of development was most obvious in Allegiant, as the perspective switches back and forth between Tris and Tobias, but their narration is indistinguishable. Sometimes my mind would wander, bored, and when I dragged my attention back and reread the page I'd have to flip back to the start of the chapter to remind me who was supposed to be talking. They both sound totally the same, and they both sound like characters in the first draft of a dystopian young adult novel: mere simulations. They seemed to be robotically reciting whatever messages the author wanted to get across. Sometimes they spoke in soundbites of fortune cookie wisdom. 
 My indifference to one of the major storylines, the romance between Tris and Tobias, was the inevitable result of my general indifference to the characters. While the first book did a good job of setting up their romance, the follow through was completely lacking. The later books somehow simultaneously overplayed the romance and undersold it: Tris and Tobias are constantly making out and having melodramatic arguments / making up, but apart from that they never really seem to spend any time with each other unless they're facing some kind of oncoming doom. They never hang out just for fun. The narrative tries to make out that it's just because they're ~so busy~ but they both seem to have time to spend with other people, and there are plenty of opportunities to spend time together that they don't bother seizing. Without that kind of evidence of their genuine attachment to each other, all their romantic melodrama is completely meaningless. 
 The underlying message of the trilogy is seriously underwhelming, in part because of the lacklustre worldbuilding. An effective dystopia should tell us truths about the world we already live in, or the world we might inhabit if we don't change our ways. Otherwise, what is the point? If the Divergent trilogy was supposed to be critiquing some aspect of our civilisation, I'm still not entirely sure what it was. It felt like even the book didn't understand its own metaphor. Halfway through the trilogy it got bored of its first allegory and set up and entirely new one. 
 It probably doesn't help that I read this trilogy immediately after rereading the Harry Potter series from start to finish, as all of the severe deficiencies of Divergent are strengths of HP: characterisation, worldbuilding, and those little details that turn an abstract and distant reality into something that grabs your heart in its mighty fist and squeezes.
Why...? And if you read the book then you know why I've asked this question

*2.5 stars. Yes...I'm rounding down--for the second time. Because, it's probably a bit lower than 2.5. 
 Yep. This was a step down from the first book... Probably because the coolest part of the first book was Tris becoming Dauntless. This book seemed to be spiraling, looking for a plot, and it wasn't until the end that one was found.

 Another problem, which is probably just me, there was totally way to much kissing in this book. Yuck. The love was one of the parts of this book I couldn't stand. Four and Tris were going back and forth and back and fourth (maybe a pun?) with loving each other and being angry with each other. 
 There were some really good parts, but the bad parts really got on my nerves. And the good parts were outnumbered, and sometimes senseless. 
 One last thing to mention. At some point in the book, Four made the effort to remind us that he was only eighteen. He told Tris (I'm paraphrasing) that if she didn't quit endangering her life, they were off. That made me laugh... Four you immature teenager. 
 Overall, it wasn't too bad. I read it in a matter of days. Certainly keeps the interest (if you can get past the first several chapters, and the dozens of names thrown at you). Let's just say: It won't kill your brain.

So I re-read Divergent and enjoyed it again (it is one of my fav books). BUT at about 30% into Insurgent, I lost interest. Maybe I was in a bad mood or something, but I didn't like it.

This book is heartbreaking and frustrating and real. The writing is perfect. The characters felt real, like those scenes flash before your eyes or like a movie in your mind. The worse part was when Tris' parents died. Honestly, I think it is unfair for them to die just like that and Will, no matter how it breaks my heart I know that one or another he will kill Tris because he is under a simulation and we can't have Tris dying only in book 2. 
 Jeanine Matthews, just hearing her name makes me want to wring her neck. The book is confusing, there are characters who become traitors and some acts as a spy; I can no longer pin point which is which. I don't know whom to place my trust even Tobias. Every thing is messed up. The factions too, turns out against each other; it is so sad to see. The Erudite is the most confusing faction. Some of them are innocent because they are ignorant, some are bad because they are protecting a secret that only them knows. I really don't know, it feels like I am Tris so confused with what's happening around here. I guess that is what Roth wants her reader to feel.

"Killing you is not the worst thing they can do to you. Controlling you is." 
 Insurgent lost the best thing about the first book: the action and entertainment. I get this one is more political and less Dauntless jumping out of trains, but damn. When I picked up this book, I didn't have high expectations. I remembered reading it years ago and thinking this had to be one of the most disappointing sequels. Yep, still is. 
 The world building in this gets really...weak. The first book had a very well-explained world that the reader could easily picture and understand. Things are explained poorly, leaving me confused. Maybe this is because I skimmed a bit due to boredom, but honestly. I just didn't care enough to connect the dots and understand this world that Roth created. Basically, here were some additions to the world that I liked but some that I didn't. 
 Then we have Tris and Four. The swoon-worthy love interest that will probably go down in history from what I can see. I don't get it. Their relationship gets so unhealthy in this book. They break each other's promises. Four tells Tris he doesn't love her when she's "reckless", yet she's just trying to save the freaking world. They fight for a solid chapter then the next chapter they're making out in an elevator. Tris is still scared of intimacy with Four, which is in absolutely no way healthy. I don't know why an author would make it seem like a romantic thing. Nope, nope, nope. Might be my number one NOTP. 
 This book could have easily been shorter. The first half of this book is stretched so long and the problem is this: nothing happens. I guess when the second half hits we start to figure out things about Jeannine and her evil mind, but the first half is just the Dauntless hiding out in the Candor headquarters. 
 I can't believe I actually trudged through this 525 page book. I'd say I'm pretty proud of myself. I wanted to DNF it so bad as I was reading it, but a new goal of mine this year is to finish series. I'm really bad at finishing series, so I just want to finish the Divergent trilogy and get rid of it in any way possible. Sounds harsh, but I don't have enough room on my shelves for books that I don't enjoy.

reference_books.title: Holy Bible: King James Version
reference_books.review_text: A little background: I grew up in a basically non-religious home. My mother is Catholic and my father is Anglican. While my mother has a nebulous belief in a higher power and heaven, I literally can not remember my father ever mentioning religion at all for good or ill. On the other hand, 3 of my 4 grandparents worked at a convent as housekeeper, cook, and maintenance man respectively, and I spent a lot of time hanging out in the convent kitchen with my Nan. The Sisters in the convent were always lovely to me and I loved visiting with them up until we moved away. I went to an elementary school that had religion classes (separated into Catholics, Protestants and 'Values' which worked as a catch all for anyone not of the first 2 or if your parents didn't want you take the class.) Every morning we sang Oh, Canada and then said the lord's prayer. My grade 4 teacher was Sister MacNeil and that was one awesome lady. Until I was 13 or 14 I had a vague belief in God, wherein I occasionally prayed every other month for random things, but I never really shook the thought that I was just talking to myself. If the topic came up, I claimed I was Agnostic because I just didn't know. Finally, probably around my last year of high school I admitted it, I did not believe in God. Not even a little bit. I wasn't the only one either. Both of my sisters, one older and one younger also don't believe in God. We went from moderately religious grandparents, to vaguely religious or at least neutral parents, to 3 non-believers. All of this to say: I grew up reading the bible, I had almost all positive experiences in my contact with any kind of church clergy, I had parents open to letting me make up my own mind, and I don't believe one word of it. Because I don't think any of it is true, I believe it to be a work of fiction, and as a work of fiction it fails across the board. It's clunky, long winded and derivative. It contradicts itself in numerous places. And though I do find some parts beautiful (mostly in Psalms and Corinthians) I cannot forgive the utter shitstorm this book provokes in the world.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Damn. Looks like this is an uncredited rip-off of the Movie Shelter, hell the movie blurb is pretty much the book blurb. *sigh* I have waffled back and forth on this, because I've not seen the movie, but the blurb is just too close for MY comfort, so I'm keeping the 3 stars I originally gave it along with this caveat. 
 So... Bear, Otter and the Kid. One of the most popular books of the past year. Everyone loved it. Well, I kinda wish we had the ability to award half stars, because this at times was a 3 1/2 star book for me. Young love, gay for you, love conquers all - it was all here. 
 Of the title characters, I loved Otter and I loved the Kid - Bear, not so much. I wanted to smack him far too many times for me to love him. Good Lord, talk about getting in your own way! Sheesh! I think he was just a little TOO ... whatever he was supposed to be - neurotic, damaged, paranoid. And a lot of it was the same stuff over and over. Not a great student, our Bear. :) In retrospect, maybe giving a couple of Bear's flaws to Otter might have been a good thing. 
 I found myself wishing that Bear would pick one metaphor for his inner feelings and stick with it - be it the ocean or the earthquakes. (I really liked the whole bathtub for safety thing.) I also wished he'd stop hitting us over the head with them so often. Introspection is good, but too much of it just makes the character seem selfish, self-absorbed and not sympathetic at all - at least to me. 
 That being said, I did enjoy the actual scenes between the characters. Bear and Otter were sweetly sexy and hot. Bear and Tyson were adorable and made me laugh out loud more than once. Creed, Anna, Mrs. Paquin - I enjoyed their appearances as well. I think that was the strongest part of the book for me - the characters interacting. 
 The huge stumbling block that was thrown in for the last quarter of the book seemed unnecessary to me. I think the conflict between the characters could have carried us through to the end and the 'twist' felt a little like 'deus ex machina' to me. I still don't get the motivation behind that one character's actions. 
 I did enjoy the choice to write the book using the 1st person POV and present tense. It was different and refreshing for the most part and the author did it quite well. :) 
 If I'm honest, Bear, Otter and the Kid felt like to me as if the author was trying to write their own story in Amy Lane's Promises series and for me, it doesn't quite measure up. 
 Would I recommend it? Yes, I would. Would I read something else by T.J. Klune? Yes, I would. 
 **review edited after discussion about the plagiarism issue**

For the past three years Derrick McKenna--"Bear" to his friends--has been raising his 9-yo prodigy brother with the help of his friend Creed and off-and-on girlfriend in the 3 years since his mother abandoned them. But now Otter, Creed's older brother, has returned to town, and Bear must work through the awkwardness between them and face the feelings that lie underneath--but just as everything seems possible, events conspire to threaten it all. 
 Remarkably good m/m romance, with some themes that seem more YA (Bear is 18-21 during the events of the book). The characters are fully fleshed out, including the female characters. The Kid's quirks are interesting--he's vegetarian, a PETA activist wannabe, but also insightful about human emotions--and impatient with teacher mistakes in a way that seems very typical for gifted children. The dialogue is often cracking, and the prose is entertaining as hell, with many giggle-out-loud moments. On the other hand, Bear's excessive internal agonizing about his life and sexuality, along with a extensive use of flashbacks, broke the flow of the story somewhat. 
 I finished this book and then I sat down and read it again, which only happens when a book touches me deeply. This is apparently Klune's first novel, and I look forward to reading his other work.

The love story was cliche, unrealistic, melodramatic, and the main protagonists had the intelligence and emotional awareness of rocks. But I've come to expect that when reading romance. What I found really puzzling was the characterization of the kid, who was completely unbelievable, to the extent that I was almost expecting a -- he is actually YODA pretending to be a 9 year old! -- type reveal. Not only that, but it was very inconsistent, too, how he was the ~wisest yenta evah~ at times, and at others, even more clueless than an average 9yr old would be. I'm still quite puzzled by this! Perhaps it is a setup for a scifi sequel that will explain it all!

** spoiler alert ** 
 dY~,dY~,dY~, 
 The story was predictable, but the execution was absolutely phenomenal. Instead of getting bored, I was looking forward to every upcoming event (i.e. the inevitable return of the runaway mother, Jonah vs. Bear, Bear's coming out to Anna and Creed, Anna+Creed). The writing was comedic, heartfelt, and expressive. I wish I could write like TJ Klune... 
 Ty had the best reactions and lines, hands down. I think I need to re-read this book just to highlight his lines. But combine Ty and Bear's dynamic together? Hilarious. 
 I had gotten as far as to pick up my phone and was about to press in Otter's number when Ty grabbed the phone out of my hand and threatened to tell Otter that I liked to be spanked during sex. This proceeded to lead us on a long tangent where I had to have him explain to me how he knows about stuff like people getting spanked during sex.

If there's one thing I love most about books, it's stories about people who come together to form a family, loving each other for more reasons than any blood relatives could even understand. 
 This book is about family. Kids who have stuck with each other through the good, but mostly the bad. They love each other. And I bloody love it. 
 I could criticise a couple things. 
 Mostly, a couple of decisions taken in the last 10% which I found a little ridiculous if I'm honest. 
 But all in all, I cried my eyes out because I cared so much. I cared so much because the characters cared. That's all that matters.

Original Blog Post: http://www.multitaskingmommas.com/201... 
 My Series Rating: 5 of 5 Stars 
 I think I had the good sense to read this series when all three were all already out and I had the misfortune of having power outages. I took to the first book and fell in love, inhaled the second and grinned myself silly, then broke my heart on the third. The past two days have been a roller coaster ride of emotions coupled with the heat of anticipated storms and ended up dreaming of Bear, Otter and Kid. 
 Bear, Otter, and the Kid is a story of abandonment, heartbreak, making it out there in the world and learning to accept that not all family are genetically connected. It is a story of survival and enduring strength based on love and acceptance. 
 It all begins with Bear. He was handed a bad hand early on in life and ended up having to raise his younger brother, Kid, all by himself. First with his mother around but not much and finally all on his own when said mother disappeared with his savings. He had a girlfriend who was a very good friend, he had a best friend who had a brother and whose parents loved them all. And then there was Mrs. Paquinn. As his world fell apart around him, this non-related family rallied around him and gave him the boost to make it through. It gets complicated when his best friend's brother, Otter, that older and hunky brother, gives him a kiss then disappears for three years. When they reunite, his relationship with this new family is threatened. His love affair with Otter may just be the key to give him that family life he always wanted, but it could also be the same one that would make him loose everybody else, excepting Kid. And what about his girlfriend, Anna? 
 The second book opens to Bear and Otter raising Kid on their own, but of course the rest of the unrelated family members are all there, ready to lend a helping hand and thought, solicited and unsolicited. Complications had risen with the reappearance of the un-mother so not only are they both stressed from life itself, they have to be stressed out dealing with things like lawyers, therapists, judges (the one sitting and the those who know nothing but everything), and all other things. Bear is nearly losing it, but thanks to Otter and Kid, he does make it. He gets his strength from the two men in his life and no one, not even a sexy teacher ex-anything of Otter can get in his way. Life is as it should be for this incredible three complete with all the panic attacks, hilarious misconceptions and imagery that can be a bit incredible in their lack of logic. All in all a fun book that gives readers that feeling they are reading a fairy tale and the dragon is sure to be slain. 
 As the third book begins, the point of view shifts and instead of Bear on the forefront, we have Kid. He is a young man now who dares to dream. And to love. We go through his heartaches, his earthquakes and his misconceptions. For all his logic and knowledge, he is truly an immature young man who can fall victim to his own lack of wisdom. We are shown a story of how he slowly matures into that promise we were hinted to in the first two books and we are also shown how his future will look like, especially with Dom and Ben at his side. Is his story parallel to Bear's and Otter's? In some ways it does but mostly it does not. It is Kid's story and it is an incredible journey seeing him grow in so many ways. 
 Bear, Otter, and the Kid, the series, is a beautiful read, especially the way I read it, back to back. There was no chance of losing track to what was going on and it was truly an incredible journey. If I had read this as they were released, I would probably have been confused and made it a point to read the first two again just to keep track. It is quite a verbose work and can be confusing. Read the way I did, and it is enjoyable, heartbreaking, real and yet fairy tale like and simply a must read. Now I know what the hype was all about.

The jacket description is so horrifically misleading. The first chapter is fantastic and sucked me in immediately. 
 Harriet is a wonderful character; while I was doubtful early on that we would ever find Robin's killer, the ending was so abrupt that I didn't know what to do with myself. There was no resolution, no inkling as to what would become of Harriet or Danny Ratliff or Edie or Hely. 
 I generally enjoy stories that are a snapshot of a person in a place at a certain time - I don't demand a tidy ending wrapped up in a bow. But I despise getting to the end of a book as I did here and being confused as to whether my copy was missing a few final chapters, because certainly it couldn't have just ended like that. 
 But...it did.

I am SO SO glad I read The Goldfinch first, instead of this book - otherwise I would have missed out on The Goldfinch. The Little Friend was just far far too boring and ponderous to get into and I have it a good go given I had fallen in love with the writing style of this author.

Had a hard time deciding between 2 and 3 stars. Some parts had the same kind of compelling darkness that I enjoyed about The Secret History, but other parts should really have been edited down. Having heard such great things about Donna Tartt, I was so disappointed and would love to hear other opinions on this book.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This novel could have been so great if Tartt had used the same calculation she did in the Goldfinch. In many interviews she mentions eight months of writing that she threw away in order to change direction. In my opinion that should have happened maybe 150 pages into this book. sample_reviews.review_text: All my favorite elements combined in one book: space, survival, mystery, relationship, post-apocalyptic setting. The plot is probably unrealistic, but the idea of humans escaping the perils of earth by living in a giant spaceship has been explored by several authors - this one is among the better takes on the idea, IMHO. I read this in tandem with watching the CW show online, so it was nice to have a visual comparison. Rating disclaimer: the tv show is far more violent and sexual than the book, both of which are potential turn-offs for me, and therefore those downfalls of the tv show probably improved my overall impression of the book.
