Wow, just wow! Had I known this would be a romantic book instead of the promised post-apocalyptic survival story, I would have never started reading it. Perhaps I should have read the reviews that would have warned me beforehand. 
 Anyway, this was a complete waste of time. I like the series for what it is: a goddamn survival story. But instead of creating tension, this book was only about stupid characters going through puberty and being in love when the focus should be on surviving on Earth. Honestly, I don't have a problem with some romance being included, but almost 90% was about that. 
 In addition to that, I didn't understand what this character with the ridiculous name of Glass contributed to this story other than desperately trying to get back the love of her life. 
 I actually lost count of how often I laughed about the ridiculousness of this story. Even after reading about 20%, I struggled to finish it. Frankly, I only did so because I abhor not reading a book to its end. I know that it's a premise to the whole story, but without including any bit of tension, you cannot expect anyone to enjoy this. The actual story started right at the end. I'm sorry, but this is just utterly weak. Please, watch the series, it's great, but DO NOT waste your time reading this book.

I really wanted to like this book. I love the television series. For some reason, the writing style is so dry that I had attempted to read the book twice - once three years ago, and a year ago, and I couldn't bring myself to finish it. For whatever reason, I decided to give it one last chance. I ended up finishing the book while feeling utterly dissatisfied. 
 The novel is told through multiple perspectives. Each character's perspective has very little distinction between them that it wasn't necessary to focus on one particular character. Also, the characters are so bland and uninteresting, I couldn't fully emphasize with them. They didn't feel very real to me. 
 The television series, in contrast, is excellent.

Plot: In the future, humans live in space on a ship because earth is too harsh to live on. When life is threatened on the ship (unknown to those not in power), 100 teen juvenile delinquents are sent to Earth to recolonize. 
 Such potential for an awesome sci-fi, but wasted on a romance-drenched, heavily angsty story that lacked any world-building whatsoever. What a shame! While I liked that it was told from 4 different points of view (2 guys, 2 girls) and that one of those took place on the ship in space, the characters (especially Wells) were too worried about their love lives to get anything accomplished. It seemed like only Clarke and Bellamy could do anything helpful while trying to survive on earth. Wouldn't you think that the author would write about the conditions on earth and getting these teens to maybe even set up a camp and explore the area instead of giving us largely flashbacks to moments in the main characters lives that of course all revolved around romance (except Bellamy!)? 
 While I liked that it was a quick read and I could read it in a couple hours, I would have preferred an origin story type of book that used crazy world-building in order to fully submerge the reader in this new world. It could have even dragged a bit on long descriptions and I wouldn't have hated it. All we know about earth is that radiation affected the animals, because deer have 2 heads. That's literally it. 
 Sidenote: Wells is a terrible person. I couldn't find anything redeeming in his character and could not believe the crazy things he did for his supposed love of Clarke. He's going to have to really step it up in the next book, or make him the evil villain because I'm over him.

I'm usually pretty good at separating books from their adaptations, but this one was harder for me. I picked up this one because I like the TV show so much. The show is excellent, and I'd recommend it to anybody. The book is a lot different. It's a quick read, and I like that we got more into the backgrounds of the POV characters through the use of flashbacks. Octavia's backstory especially surprised me. 
 However, it just didn't live up to the promise of the premise. A hundred delinquent kids get sent to Earth to see if it's inhabitable and save humanity! That's awesome. It lends itself so easily to a gritty survival story. Instead, the description and world-building are thin, and we hardly see much of the kids setting up camp and learning how to survive on earth in favor of focusing on the romances. Glass's story in particular is romance-heavy, and yet the romance feels too shallow for her ending to resonate. 
 There's not a lot to increase the tension, and not much actually happens. The whole book probably could have been condensed into 50 pages and used as a jumping-off point for a more complex story. The most interesting development happens on the very last page! Considering that, maybe I'll like book two better.
Way to much drama and overdid on romance. The POV's were randomized and not my taste and just plain annoying. I like the plot of the book but the characters themselves were aggravating.

I'm reminded now of why classics become must-read classics after having re-read this, A Tale of Two Cities, Les Miserables lately. 
 I don't think there is a point in trying to compare great art. That said, I found this novel even more chilling than 1984. I believe that's because it is more believable and more immediate. 
 It is obviously a metaphor for human society and the "Beast" enclosed within us with a patina of civilization that is ever so fragile. F.A. Hayek, in his treatise, "The Constitution of Liberty," states that when individual liberty is forsaken the only possible results are anarchy or dictatorship. In this extraordinary novel, we have both: Jack is the narcissistic dictator that rules by force and eventually by terror and torture to ensure obedience. 
 Ralph (I assume pronounced "Rafe", since all the children are British--perhaps considered the most civilized and civilizing nation)represents civilization, representative government, reason, etc. Without the civilizing force of society, brute force in the form of Jack banishes him, and with him, rationality and humanity. The "id," the "heart of darkness," and bestiality are the inevitable result. 
 We also have "Piggy" the scientist and rationalist advisor to Ralph and Simon, who I see as the philosopher who in Plato's Allegory of the Sun sees reality, where "truth and beauty shine resplendent." As a consequence of being the one being who can bring down Jack by identifying the "Beast" as really a man (and, consequently, the real Beast hiding in all of us beneath a veneer of civilization) he is therefore slaughtered. 
 Although there were parts that seemed a little slow, the payoff came only as a result of those parts and was overwhelming for me. 
 ...A truly extraordinary piece.

I really liked this book, especially the flashbacks to 1830 Boston and the medical school. Combined mystery, historical fiction, and present day research. Tracking down a serial killer from clues found in old letters. This was the first book I had read by Tess Gerritsen, author of the Risoli and Isles series. I will definitely be reading more.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I enjoyed this book because the characters were strong, but it really didn't meet any of my expectations for a thriller- and especially for a Tess Gerritsen thriller. If her name wasn't on the cover I wouldn't have a clue that this is the same author of the Rizzoli & Isles series (which I've read all of). 
 What captivated me was how effortlessly Ms. Gerritsen transports the reader back in time to 1830. I live in Boston so I got a real kick out of the descriptions of streets and neighborhoods that I'm familiar with, and what they were like in the past. 
 This book is heavy into the medical side of things. Many human dissections are discussed in great detail and I would warn you NOT to eat while you are reading this! I consider myself to have a strong stomach and I was forced to dry heave a few times. The descriptions are not grotesque or gratuitious persay, but I feel like the average person would be adversely affected by the language. 
 If you like stories set in the past and you also enjoy a little murder mystery, you will probably like this book. I really felt that the murder mystery was a subplot and I would've liked it if the suspense around the killer's identity was built up more. I found myself distracted by the horrors of everyday living in the 1830s and didn't care much about the "West End Reaper". 
 I also felt like the side story of the woman in "present day" was forced and unnecessary. The frame story technique didn't add anything to the overall story and things should've just stayed in the past. I found myself skimming the short "present day" chapters so I could get back to the real story. The "present day" woman was too unbelievable in her sensitivity and I didn't appreciate the cheap love story ending and implied psychic connection between her and the historical story's heroine. 
 So not the best thriller, not the best Tess Gerritsen book by a long shot, but worth a read if you enjoy some historical fiction with class warfare thrown in.

Though the book started with a promising mystery the protagonist in the current-day plot line was a namby-pamby and hard to identify with. The storyline in the past was more interesting but the contrast between the two left the book off-balance. 
 It was OK until nine-tenths of the way through it took a turn toward romantic drivel in the past plot line which soon ended tragically. I don't have a problem with the tragic end but it was tempered by the intimation that the romance continued reincarnated in the modern day plot which was just lame. There was a plot twist that had me moderately interested for a short time but when the evildoer was finally revealed the mystery seemed to lose interest in itself. There was no final answer given as to whether that person committed the Ripper-style murders or was only behind them. Characters actually considered not telling the public which strained credulity. To have limped through the entire book and have this be the payoff felt like a punishment for making a poor choice!

I have loved other books by this author, but this one wasn't my favorite. The historical storytelling is fantastic, but the present-day portion seemed contrived. Still super fascinating, well researched, and definitely a page-turner.

The Bone Garden by Tess Gerritsen. 
 The story begins with the discovery of a skull in the soon to be garden of Julia Hamill. Maura Isles, medical examiner, is called in to make her estimations on this discovery. Isles reports the skull to be that of a female that has been murdered. 
 The next scene brings the reader back to Boston in the 1930's. A callous doctor glides by the tables of women in various stages of labor. This monstrous excuse for a doctor holds no empathy for the women in agony some for days on end. The author chose to continue on and on with this grotesque scene which I found abhorrent. Totally unnecessary in any good mystery in my opinion. 
 There was no mention of Rizzoli & Isles anywhere in this book, which is the reason why I checked this book out to begin with. This book is something to avoid if you're looking for a mystery with substance.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I really like Sarah Addison Allen. I've read almost all of her other books and I have liked every one of them! They are mostly just normal fiction but there is always a little element of magic in them that I love. She makes magic seem possible in the real world, which is my opinion it is. The Sugar Queen is about a woman named Josey who is dealing with a lot of difficult issues. She lives at home as a servant to her mother, basically, and tries to make up for being a terrible child. To cope with her mother's smothering influence on her life she hides sweets, novels, and travelling magazines inside of her closet. She is stuck in her sad life until one morning she finds a woman in her closet and her entire world starts to change. 
 This book is a great one and has a good message too. It is all about being who you are and not being ashamed of it. I know it made me think about how I was living my life.

I'm a sucker for magical realism and those aspects of The Sugar Queen were my favorite parts of this book. I would love it if just the right book would appear for me at just the right time. It would make readers' advisory so much easier, that's for sure. 
 This might not be a negative for some readers, but I hate cheating and it seemed like everyone and his brother was cheating or had cheated on someone in the past, and for the most part they didn't see it as a horrible thing. That definitely took away from my enjoyment of the book a bit.

 Like Sarah's book, Garden Spells, this story has a bit of magic in it making it a fairytale for adults. The characters are each from a different level of society and come together to form form friendships that bring out the best in each other. This is a feel good book :)

I loved it. Loved the characters. Wasn't crazy about the ending.

I really enjoyed all four of Sarah Addison Allen's novels. If I were to rank them according to preference, I'd probably go with: The Peach Keeper, The Girl Who Chased the Moon, Garden Spells, and the Sugar Queen, but I did like them all pretty equally. 
 I'm very interested that every book -- save for perhaps Girl/Moon? -- incorporates a story of man against woman violence. It's very much part of the story in Garden Spells (her first) and much less part of the story in the Peach Keeper (where it happened in the past). Given this fairly constant element in her stories, it makes me wonder what Sarah Addison Allen's past experience with such violence has been. 
 She really is a very pretty writer (in terms of her language, not her physical person, though I'm sure she's that, too) and I have thoroughly enjoyed all of these books and wish there were more to consume!

It took me two weeks to finish this small book. I was continually being distracted by other things. I can't say if that was completely due to the book's not holding my interest or that I subconsciously wanted a break from reading or I simply assigned a higher priority to those other things. It's not like I don't find some fantasy intriguing but I seemed to have more difficulty with the quirky "magic" the characters in The Sugar Queen had versus the other two Sarah Addison Allen books I read: Garden Spells and The Girl Who Chased the Moon. I'm not going to offer any spoilers I just feel these mystical occurrences distracted me from the human emotions and kept me from feeling a strong literary attachment to the characters. I did find the story imaginative and original, just not enough to rate it any higher.

I love Sarah Addison Allen's novels. In The Sugar Queen, the follow-up to Garden Spells, we follow Josie Cirrini as she gains the courage to stand up to her mother's dominance, face her fears, learn who she is and take chances. Sarah Addison Allen always interweaves more than one plot into the story and you can always expect a strong sense of community and a bit of the romantic and mystical (reminiscent of stories such as Practical Magic by Alice Hoffman). Sarah creates such wonderful characters and each must overcome obstacles, awaken to their potential, gain courage to face their fears, and have faith, The Sugar Queen is a heartwarming story about hope, courage, forgiveness and redemption.

book_a.user_review: Loved it! So so funny and so so touching and insightful.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Wow. This book is an absolute roller coaster. Trevor Noah gives us a glimpse of what life was like growing up in South Africa at the tale end of apartheid. Some crazy things happened. Some hilarious things happened. I had no idea (and still don't, really) how things are in South Africa. 
 Don't get me started on his mom. Absolutely amazing person! 
 I highly recommend this book, especially the audio book read by the author. Warning: language and violence.

Trevor filled this book with his essence, which is made of sterner stuff than what comprises most Americans. I'm a fan, I like his comedy and I like him as the Daily Show host, and I feel like I finally understand why he was tapped to replace Stewart. 
 Jon had the political background for Crossfire and to defang Ailes' ilk, Trevor has the depth of perspective to steer us through the boomers' last blows. Nothing he encounters in today's America can hold a candle to what he has made it through. 
 I also admire and find edifying how Trevor steers us deftly through his faith and worldview, and yet he doesn't expend a single word in this book trying to sell the reader any of it. Not one iota. Many might read his memoir and be able to shrug, cluck about what an experience he's had, and move on. Many more, I think, might be able to adopt or adapt Noah's experiences into our worldview and be richer for it.

This is one of those books you read when you think you have it bad and then you read this and decide you'll just be grateful for what you have. 
 This book is solely about Trevor Noah's childhood and young life in South Africa, nothing about his career rise in the US. Trevor Noah has lived ten lifetimes already, and at least that many nightmares. The book is not a comedy, there is absolutely nothing funny about any of his early life. The horrors he experienced daily are beyond what we can imagine, and the book ends on one of the worst real life events I can think of. It's a dark story about a boy who grew up with unimaginable horrors just an expected part of daily life. 
 But throughout the book you can feel Trevor's strength, which he got from his mother, and his ability to look on the bright side of life, which he also got from his mother. 
 It's an extraordinary book about an extraordinary life.

I read the audiobook and it's absolutely brilliant ! At the beginning I felt it was hard to concentrate because everything was going upside down, with no chronology, yet Trevor caught me after about 40mn of listening. From then on I could not stop listening. And at the end I shed up some tears. As an African girl with a really close relationship with her mom, that really talked to me, even though I never lived under Apartheid. For that the story was enlightening and for everything that looked my own life in Africa it was refreshing and funny. Well, Trevor, thanks for that piece of brilliance. I loved it.

Trevor Noah is a South African comic. I have seen his funny segment comparing Trump to an African dictator, but haven't seen much else of his (maybe nothing). As a result, I probably came to his memoir of his childhood growing up in South Africa, Born a Crime, from a different vantage than most readers (having only heard him interviewed on NPR). His memoir is sometimes funny, but if that's what you're looking for - I wasn't - you probably want to look elsewhere. 
 Noah's memoir is an often-insightful exploration of the relationship between a mother and son, love, domestic violence and physical abuse, racism and color in South Africa, the effects of poverty on the impoverished, and more. I have friends who are "colored" in South Africa who have in the past attempted to explain the color system and their place in it - and I didn't get it. It makes sense now - as much as their system makes sense. (When my friends visited last summer, they asked for Trump stickers so as to put their own government's problems in context.) Noah's descriptions of the decisions one might make when poor - from my perspective, desperately poor - explains why he and others flagrantly skirted the law (e.g., often because that was the only available option). 
 Noah named people, some of whom probably would have preferred to not be named. For example, his stepfather attempted to kill his mother, saying, "You've stolen my life... You've taken everything away from me. Now I'm going to kill all of you (Loc. 4015). His mother was at risk before, but probably even more so now. Noah was as brutally honest about himself, describing a range of embarrassing behaviors and illegal acts, as well as smart and savvy ones. 
 Noah offered nuanced views of his world: You want to live in a world where someone is good or bad, where you either hate them or love them, but that's not how people are (Loc. 3868). He described the good in his abusive stepfather. He saw his mother's "hidings" as coming from a place of love (Loc. 3808). He allows his world to be as complicated as it is. 
 This is a man to watch.
Fabulous!!! And eye opening biography about his life in South Africa, from Apartheid to stardom!

This was a very powerful book that touched base with so many important and challenging issues of our time: such as colonialism, racism, domestic violence, hate and hypocrisy... 
 The book tells us about the life in South Africa under apartheid and after.. Life Trevor Noah had as a child; not fitting in any community. Even basic human necessities like food, running water and electricity were denied of him most of the time. He didn't grow up in a loving and nurturing home with dependable parents. Danger, violence and fear were a part of his daily life. 
 Yet he tells his story with such humor and through such humanistic/existentialist perspective that one is left with awe and inspiration and deep respect for him. He is a fighter and a survivor. He is also a wonderful writer/story-teller.
This may be my favorite memoir ever.

I found Born a Crime to be an interesting and informative read. Trevor Noah is a good storyteller. This book gave a deeper understanding of the complexities or race and class, by looking through the perspective of a boy trying to figure out his own identity.

DNFed at 60%. 
 This book is much loved so I'll be swimming against the current, but that's never stopped me from being honest with my thoughts so here goes: 
 Let me first start by saying that I was a huge fan of The Daily Show with Jon Stewart, and when Trevor Noah joined I gave it six weeks before deciding he was just not for me. Something about him rubs me the wrong way, so I wasn't planning on picking up this book, especially since it was a memoir. Then my local book club selected it for this month and I decided to at least try, maybe I would be pleasantly surprised. That did not happen. 
 I did not know going in that this was a collection of "eighteen personal essays" which explains some of the somewhat disjointed style of this book. It was interesting to hear about this mother and the decisions she made, and this is clearly an ode to his Mom, but why would I care about any of this? While I did smile at some of the humor, I found myself mostly annoyed both with him personally and how he talked about his experiences. Was this a difficult childhood, sure, but so what? As someone who grew up in Kenya, there wasn't much he described that was new to me, and the fact that he talks about his "mischievous" acts where there were no consequences without a sense of regret was something I found deeply disturbing. The longer I listened the more unlikable he become, and when I got the section of his Matric dance when it suddenly occured to him that he and his date didn't even share a common language I called it quits. 
 I was completely blown away when almost half of the book club members "didn't know about Apartheid." How is that even possible? The group had a mixed reaction to the book, with many feeling that he left out significant bits about how he got to host the Daily Show for example. However, given that this book might be a way to introduce people to some of what happened in South Africa I'm glad Noah wrote it. I'm just clearly not the target audience. 
 I listened to the audiobook which is well narrated by the author. I did enjoy listening to his various accents as he switches back and forth between South African languages. I would not have read this far if I'd read it in print, but if you're a Trevor Noah fan, or somehow who doesn't know anything about Apartheid this might work better for you.

book_b.title: Fifty Shades of Grey (Fifty Shades, #1)
book_b.user_review: Not a fan. I felt like I was reading a script for a low-budget porn movie. The characters had no real depth and I failed to see any underlying themes in the book. The whole thing felt cheap, kinky and dirty. Or maybe it's just not for me...

sample_reviews.review_text: Okay, so I knew the book was going to be about sex. "Fifty Shades of Grey" I hoped that meant an older woman with grey hair was going to have great sex. But no, I was disappointed. Anyway, there was lots of sex but I would have told Mr. Grey to go F*** himself from the beginning and then there would be no story.
Utter drivel.

The success of Fifty Shades of Grey is the very definition of viral marketing. A book that was originally self-published as an eBook and a print-on-demand paperback, it somehow caught the imagination of women everywhere and it's said that a copy now sells every sixty seconds. Amazing. There are three books in the series and they are numbers 1, 2 and 3 on the New York Times best seller list, and have been for months. 
 I have three words for this phenomenon: WTF?? I mean really...have you read this thing? 
 I bought a Kindle version ($9.99), just to see what all the hoopla was about, and got through about 1/3 of it (31% according to my Kindle), rolling my eyes and saying, "Oh, please," on every other page. With one exception (from Jessica Reaves of the Chicago Tribune) it seems to be immune to criticism of any kind (because it's made a boatload of money?), and as an author it's probably bad form to say this (you know that won't stop me), but it's crap. I don't mind the concept of it or the genre of eroticism itself, but something that's selling like the latest iPad release should at least be...well, good. 
 Fifty Shades of Grey is not good. That's not hurting sales in the least. It doesn't seem to matter that the writing stinks, the characters are unappealing and not engaging, the storyline is non-existent and, worst of all, the sex isn't even good, just lots of murmuring and moaning and gasping, and heartbeats quickening and racing. Kinda trite. At least be original. 
 The protagonist, Anastasia Steele, is a 21 year old virgin, and the narrative (told from her point of view) is sprinkled with lots of italics: holy crap! holy fuck! holy shit! jeez! and so on. And her inner goddess talks to her, and does "merengue with some salsa moves." Need I say more? Now, you can't argue with that kind of success - it's phenomenal - and good for E.L. James. She seems as amazed by this as everyone else. But seriously...what are you people thinking? Whatever it is, could you please transfer it to my book? And when mine becomes a runaway best seller it won't bother me a bit when E.L. James trashes it on her blog.

The author will be the first to tell you she isn't a great writer, and it's evident in Fifty Shades. The gratuitous sex scenes got ridiculous and tired very quickly, the language used was very asinine, especially in the everyday conversations of the characters, and the main character's thought process was like a balloon with the helium slowly leaking out. 
 At first the sex scenes were fun and thrilling, and then they never stopped happening and I began skimming through them in order to get to more of the story-- which was, sadly, lacking. There isn't much to this book other than a whole lot of sex. 
 If you've never read a sexually explicit romance novel before, then this might float your boat. I've read my share of romance novels (ones that actually had characters you could care about and plots with mysterious twists that make you want to keep reading), and this one was so ridiculously bad, in my opinion, that it was hard to finish reading.
Did not finish.

Everyone probably knows what this fan-fiction novel is about already, but I'll just summarize it briefly. One day when Ana's friend falls ill and calls in a favour, requesting Ana to interview one of the richest, successful men in Seattle in her place. Although it should it was indeed a formal interview, Christian and Ana both realize that this encounter was anything but ordinary. They start to form a curiosity and fatal attraction for one another. But as all businessmen know, sometimes the only way to keep something is by signing a contract... 
 I read this book because there were so many people raving about it, and of course it was also because it made it onto the top 20 list of best sellers on Indigo etc. If you ever watch or read the Vampire Diaries, Twilight or any other similar television shows or books, it is a definite possibility that you will enjoy this novel. I think the most captivating part about this novel is Mr. Grey himself. What kind of girl does not have an attraction to a bad boy? A handsome bruting one? A mysterious, rich, powerful and charming one? When you combine all of these aspects into one character, it becomes irresistible to desire more information, and the only way to gain more information is by blazing through the pages! 
 So why do I give this three stars? As explicit as the sexual content in the novel is, there is quite a bit of repetition. Not only in vocabulary, but also events in the story. The higher the predictability, the less enjoyable it is (excluding fairy tales, the ones where we watch because we expect the feel-good happy endings).

Muy mala, aburridisima, una historia tonta y predecible, y la escritura es tan repetitiva y superficial que me queria suicidar. 
 Es un crepusculo mil veces peor y ademas es tan cliche que me aburri un monton.
disturbing.

I'm about as confused as much as Miss Steel about this book. I really hated this book....I loathed it, and 1/2 way through it I set it down and didn't pick it back up for months, but I wanted it cleared off my night stand so I finished, and ...........I hate, hate, hate to admit......I liked the ending. It went from a 1 star to a 3....Just for the ending.

I don't get what the fuss is about! 
 Fifty Shades of Grey is poorly written, has no actual plot, the characters are extrimely uncredible and annoying, and all the sex scenes get pretty boring after 100 pages (the book has a total of 500!). This story could have been told in 100 pages MAX, without the boring repeated considerations of the narrator, without the millions of "Jeez", "Oh my", He's so sexy", "It's so erotic" and without alle the cliches. 
 The only thing that I liked in this book was the e-mail exchange between Ana and Christian, which was quite funny and to the point. 
 I read somewhere that the book was about to be made into a movie - maybe this interpretation will be more interesting, even though I don't see how you can make a movie out of this book without making it an adult movie - it's all about sex!

reference_books.title: Egomaniac
reference_books.review_text:
Steamy 
 Writing: I enjoyed Vi Keeland's writing style. From the onset she sucked me in to the book. 1St person narration. 2 POV. 
 Characters: Emerie and Drew are the MCs. I enjoyed the maturity of both characters. Fault acceptance and working through problems was a huge plus for their personalities. These characters fit together so well. They played off of each other's strengths and weaknesses beautifully. 
 Storyline: Emerie was swindled into buying an office that was not available. This unfortunate event sparked the relationship between Emerie and Drew. Drew allowed Emerie to continue to use the space while she was searching for a new office in exchange for secretarial services. 
 The banter between Emerie and Drew was hilarious. Captain Prolactinator had me laughing for about 5 minutes. And Emerie's white board...that was wrong and brilliant. Throughout the book Drew was crass and upfront and although Emerie was not used to it, she realized that she loved it and needed it. This caused her to come out of her shell a bit. Drew helped Emerie to stand up for herself and Emerie helped Drew to become less cynical. 
 There were a few things about the book that I didn't like or I wanted a little more information on. Such as, Emerie talked about her parents and how wonderful they are, but they had a very insignificant role in the book. 
 What bothered me the most was Emerie moving for the men in her life. When was she going to be important enough for someone to make a sacrifice for her? 
 Intimacy Scenes: Dirty talking alert. Drew lit this section on fire all by himself. You could delete all of the sex scenes from this book and it would still be steamy just because of his mouth. 
 Overall: This was a quick fun read. Vi is a funny author and was able to produce a great story line and some heartfelt angst. I really enjoyed the chemistry between the characters and look forward to reading more from this author. By the way, what is up with the bow tie on the cover? Drew didn't wear bow-ties, his nemesis did.

reference_books.title: The Edge of Never (The Edge of Never, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Writing:J.A. Redmerski is a great writer. She gave me enough history that I felt like I knew the MCs and their thought processes. 
 HOWEVER, she also gave entirely too much. Why is this book over 400 pages? There was no reason for it to be this long. Some of the narratives went on and on. 
 Characters: I had issues with the MCs. Camryn has been through so much in life. Nobody understands her. Her family & friends do her wrong. She is always so forgiving and never judgmental. She is wise beyond her years. And let's face it, her brother going to prison WAS ALL ABOUT HER! 
 Andrew is the perfect, tatted up, muscled, beautiful face, hair & eyes Hero. He is deep and understands everything. His words make you brave. His touch makes you crave. He is the quintessential bad boy. Nobody is better than him. 
 Okay I'm done being facetious. 
 Storyline: The story was interesting. I've never read a road trip novel before. How do you make a road trip interesting to read about? Redmarski did it. I would have enjoyed a few more stops along the way, however I guess the long narratives ate up any more potential stops. 
 Last facetious moment for real. 
 I know you can't tell by my sarcasm, but there were moments of this book that I really enjoyed. The event that triggered Camryn's road trip was intriguing. The way the MCs met was believable and fun. I even enjoyed the talks on the bus and in the car. And many other things, however some of it was overshadowed by the long narratives and the unrealistic MCs. 
 Intimacy Scenes: Camryn's favorite word is slut. But wait let's not forget, she is not judgmental. But their first intimate moment, I was definitely thinking- 
 Then their sex talks in the car and the subsequent sex scenes- 
 Overall: It was interesting. I'm not sure if I will continue with this series. I'm all for secrets, but Andrew's secret came out of left field. But I would like to read something else by Redmarski.

reference_books.title: Exclusively Yours (Kowalski Family, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Writing: I enjoyed Shannon Stacey's writing style. There were 3 POVs. I prefer no more than two, but it wasn't so bad. 3rd person narration. 
 Characters: Keri, Joe and Terri are the MCs. This is not a love triangle. Joe and Terri are siblings. I wanted a little more history on the event that caused the riff between Terri and Keri. 
 storyline: Keri and Joe were high school sweethearts, but Keri left to pursue her dreams. Keri's job is demanding something that puts her in close quarters with the man she has not seen in 20 years. It takes no time for sparks to fly. 
 Parallel to Joe and Keri's story, Terri is suffering from a dying marriage. She loves her husband and wants him back, but she is hurt. 
 My biggest issue with this story is that it mentioned the 20 years that Keri had not seen the Kowalski's several times, BUT the actions of the characters did not portray a 20 year break. It was very strange. 
 Intimacy Scenes: A little steamy, but there is a lot of tension and build up. 
 Overall: This was good. I enjoyed the Kowalski family. I hope Kevin is next because his backstory was very intriguing.

reference_books.title: Fear Me (Broken Love, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
MY FIRST DNF! 
 I have a sick obsession of finishing things. It may even border a little on OCD. BUT THIS BOOK! 
 I had to stop. I couldn't endure it any longer. I struggled to even make it to 50%. It was too much. 
 I've been vocal about by issues with masochists. But this went beyond the pale. Why? What was the purpose? I don't understand.

reference_books.title: All About the D
reference_books.review_text:
I'm not sure what I feel towards this book. I liked it, but 
 The beginning of the story was slow. Around 60-70% it picked up and I started getting into it. 
 So, Josh was kind of soft. I'm not sure if this was on purpose or if the authors need to work on writing male interactions and dialog. I think it might be somewhere in between. But I really liked Josh's quirk. It encouraged a deeper attachment to him. 
 I liked Evie, although I was confused about her a little bit. For instance, the author stated that Josh was over 6 feet, but Evie was average height. So, how is this possible while they are both standing- 
 I press my chest to his back and wrap my arms around his neck 
 She should not, even with heels, be able to do this or if she did, he would be choking. 
 There were also gaps. I'm still trying to figure out who leaked the information. The authors never said. There were speculations, but never a clear answer. And there was a big deal about Drew losing weight, but nothing came of it. Is he sick? Why keep mentioning he's losing weight, but then not address it. 
 What made me uncomfortable is that I'm not a fan of love triangles and granted there wasn't one in this book per se, but it felt like it. I can't explain why, but there was this invisible third entity in their relationship and it bothered me. 
 I liked the book. It was cute and it made me laugh, but there was just something missing and I didn't really become invested into the story until closer to the end.

book_a.title: The Hurricane (The Hurricane, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Decimatingly Delicious! (Yes, I'm aware that decimatingly is not a word, but nothing else fit) 
 Writing: I love books that are based in the United Kingdom. I have an accent while reading the book and several days after. When done right, I feel a part of a world that I desperately want to visit. R.J. Prescott did a great job of introducing her world/culture to her readers. 
 The prologue and epilogue are written from Cormac's POV. The rest of the book is from Emily's POV. 
 There are a couple of errors. There is one part where Danny loses his Irish-ness and there are a couple of wrong words such as 'though' instead of 'through.' 
 Characters: The main characters are Cormac "The Hurricane" O'Connell aka Con and Emily aka Sunshine. R.J. Prescott did a great job of revealing the personality and history of Con and Emily that it sucked me in and I felt invested in the success of both characters. R.J. created a slow build of chemistry between them and set it to simmer for a little while. I was cheering very hard for Con to keep it together and felt disappointed when I thought he ruined it at the party. There are a boatload of supporting characters in this book and they add a special piece to the story. If one of them was missing from the story it would not have been the same. Besides the main characters, I can't really say who my favorite is because R.J. did a fantastic job of creating characters that were different, but integral to the story. The only character that confused me was Frank. I didn't understand the purpose of his obsession with Emily. Even though I hated Emily's mother, her behavior made sense. Unfortunately, death can trigger a psychotic breakdown. So, I understood the mother (I hated her behavior), but was left bewildered with Frank. 
 Storyline: Con and Emily both come from a past that left deep scars. Con's past is cyclical and he didn't know how to get off of the hamster wheel until he met Emily. Emily's past is haunting and she uses invisibility to remain safe. A patient, cantankerous old man (Danny) was the beginning of a new life for Emily. Along with Danny came a bunch of misfits that rocked the foundation of Emily's well-constructed protective barriers. One in particular, Con, stealthily makes his way into Emily's heart. He took her polite rejections and made her crave him. 
 This book shows the struggles of those living in poverty. Emily talked about her embarrassment of her living conditions, not having a phone, her clothing, etc. I remember Emily heavily contemplating which was needed more with winter around the corner. Should she save for a coat or should she make do with the one she had and buy gloves? Given her location and how cold it gets both are needed. R.J gave us real insight into poverty. Despite their poverty stricken conditions, a heartfelt love story was still constructed. Con was smooth with his pursuit that neither of them having a phone actually worked in his favor. Those handwritten love notes were genius. 
 There were also moments where I laughed really hard and loud. Every book needs a Kieran personality. I was always excited when Kieran's or Tommy's name appeared. I think I smiled every time they were in a scene. These light-hearted scenes were needed to break-up some of the despondency of Emily and Con's situation. 
 R.J. also gave a lot of words of wisdom in this book. There were moments where I had to stop and allow the wisdom to work through me. I did quite a bit of introspection. R.J. could probably be a motivational speaker if this book writing stuff doesn't pan out. She really did her homework for this book. Even Emily's unconscious responses to her new life was on point. There are books with characters who are struggling with some serious stuff and the hero comes along and with one touch or look it all goes away. That's not real life. But R.J. said it best in this book - 
 "Confidence is not the absence of fear" 
 Erotic Scenes: There is one scene that I wish was skimmed over. However, after reading it I developed the necessary hatred for Frank. I did have to put the book down for a little while after that scene. Cormac and Emily's love scenes are sweet. Con begins with setting Emily's body on fire and making her crave his touch and beg for it. I thought this was perfect after what she endured. He was still dominant in the bedroom, but also gave her a voice. 
 Overall, this book was fantastic. I will definitely be reading the next installment. Great Job R.J. Prescott!

sample_reviews.review_text:
Although I enjoyed this, I can't give it four stars and influence someone's reading style....because there were SO many grammatical errors, lost commas, misplaced paragraphs, and sometimes I was not quite sure which character was speaking. 
 C'mon, editors, help out your writers!!!! 
 The hero and heroine were characters worth rooting for; their love felt genuine and sweet. 
 I have to say that despite the technical errors I'm complaining about.....I just downloaded the second book in the series!!

3.5 stars... 
 I'm torn because while I didn't love the writing style (way too much he's-perfect-she's-perfect type narrative) and the plot seemed to repeat itself more often than not...I didn't hate it. I think I would have enjoyed it a lot more if I hadn't read similar stories (it reminded me of Fighting to Forgive a little bit), especially when the similar stories were written better IMO. 
 I think if you're debating, it's worth giving it a shot. But if you can't get through the first 25% or so...don't expect it to change because like I said, it's a lot of the same plot just in slightly different scenarios.
4 1/2 stars!! Great read!!

It was the beautiful hard body on the cover that caught my attention. I'm not a much of fighter-trope gal, but that label "New York Times Best Selling Author" scrawled across the cover gave me that little extra push, assuring me I wouldn't be sorry if I read it. 
 It wasn't love at first read, but it flowed easily enough, and I thought it OK to continue after chapter testing. The main character Emily is a nervous introvert who had an abusive father. She changed her name and escaped to London to go to school. 
 Red flags waved early on, but trying to give the book a fair shake, I batted them down and continued. until there were just too many to be ignored. 
 The first red flag came with the hero's blithe declaration at first sight of Em. He thinks to himself, "She's hot, but then again, every girl I fucked was hot." That just so rubs me the wrong way, and is the worst possible way to ruin the hero of the story for me. Pompous ass is what I thought. And that was only the Prologue! 
 This was a DNF for me mainly because there was a discrepancy between the main character's supposed issues and her behavior. It was completely, off-the-charts unrealistic. Maybe it's my problem, but try as I might, I simply cannot get into a book when stuff doesn't add up, yo. 
 Red flags that an author didn't do her homework to make her character convincing enough: 
 Red flag 1: In high school, while Emily is being abused by dad, she faults the teacher for not reporting the situation to social services. If she was so cognizant of her situation, why didn't she get help herself? 
 Red flag 2: Author goes to great lengths to show us Em is a chick who avoids people and is basically afraid of her own shadow, but suddenly befriended by an outgoing girl in her class, she is dressing up sexy and going to frat party. She goes because hot fighter O'Connell said he was going to be there. At the party, said friend trots off, leaving her alone in the crowd for a long time, and Em doesn't lose her shit! Isn't even angry with the friend when she reappears! For real? Major red flag. A crow bar could not get a savagely abused young woman in hiding to suddenly jump out of her comfort zone. It would take many years of therapy for that. 
 Red flag 3: Emily seems quite comfortable dropping f-bombs, in her thoughts and conversation but when in the boxing gym around the fighters, she claims, "I was a little overwhelmed by the cursing." Apparently she's quite the delicate flower when it's convenient for the author. 
 At 21% an obvious scapegoat, the obnoxious villainous 'frat party slut,' starts a fight with Em over O'Connell sending the trite and ridiculous meter whirling. That's when I officially called it quits. 
 There were many other things that annoyed me in this story, like mind-numbing dialogue tags, such as 
 He asked, dangerously. 
 Ugh. Just how does someone ask dangerously? 
 But by far, the most annoying thing this author did was make Emily a woman-basher without justification. In just the 20 percent I read, she repeatedly called other young women 'sluts' though she knew none of them. I don't know where all the venom towards women came from, it felt so out of left field. 
 He practically shoved the slut aside to get to Nikki. 
 [Here I was]...pretending that the first man I'd been attracted to for years wasn't banging some slut in a bathroom like a street corner prostitute. (WTF does that make him? Fuckin' McDreamy?) 
 Yes, there are women out there who hate on other women, and their hatred might even be justifiable, but damn it to hell authors - then show me! Give me a reason why your character is a hater of women! What happened to her that made her mistrustful of women and think all women are sluts?! R.J. Prescott doesn't provide any reasoning for this slight, so I can only assume she is a hater herself, and therefore nominating her as a honorary member of the She-Women Haters Club. 
 Sukey's take away: Don't put too much faith in a book whose cover boasts a best-selling author.
The book was a bit lacking in the conversation department at times and I would've liked to see a bit more action but overall it was O.K>

first this cover is just eat them up luscious. Really pulls you in. the story is a good one. there are areas that things are drawn out a wee bit much but it doesn't take away the concept of the story or what it is you take away from it. 
 Emily is from a abusive past and ran away from it. More like escaped. She allows it to bog her every waking moment. That is until cormac o'connell. this is a man that can lit up candles with one look. He and his best friend Kieren are the quintessential bad boy fighters. Kieren is a little more tame than cormac or con as everyone calls him. Tame as in more refined and temper wise. Con has had a rough time and it was kieran's family and danny that has kept him going. He meets Emily and wants to change. He wants to be the man she deserves in his mind. He wants to turn his life around and become her everything. He is gobsmacked by love. this rough and tumble guy becomes a tumbleweed for her. He takes fighting seriously and goes about proving to her he loves her. 
 Here is where a little bit of the drawn out starts to come into play. Emily's constant we are just friends line just doesn't cut it and gets old. They go beyond that but he plays along with it until she feels comfortable. Emily is definitely suffering from PTSD but it isn't something she acknowledges. Con helps her alot but seriously it should be looked at more. Another area that is more angst is Con's mom. that woman should just give up. Her snide remarks do her no good and the first moments she was there it helped to show con's life before and what he wants but over time you wanted to smack her upside the head. 
 the side characters like Danny, the father patrick (a hoot for a priest), tommy and kieren helped give this book more ooomph. They were great and helped these two feel loved and safe along the way. They helped Emily to see that she was loved and had a family even if they were blood related. 
 Overall the book and its premise was good. A different twist on the take of bad boy turning a new leaf with the angst of Emily's stepdad at the end, the fighting that was almost lost due to guilt, and the crazy mom. These two characters made for a cute couple and I hope that we see a book with Kieren falling head over heels as well for he was awesome throughout this sweet romance of bad boy gone good and winning the girl and a better way of life.

Recently I have been reading some good books (stories that I like) and Hurricane is one of them. 
 I like obsessed hero's and the one in this is definitely obsessed at the start. 
 But this story is not all about obsessive love, it grows into sweet, caring and strong love. 
 I love how different the h and the H are to begin with, but how they support and compliment each other as the story progresses. 
 The H is a fighter by profession and the h has undergone trauma She was raped by her step-father. He is still trying to find her and she is in hiding . The problem's the h faces and her inner strength she shows makes her the real fighter. 
 I would like to read more books by this author.
As much as I found this a little slow in part I did actually enjoy it. There was hints of another book coming out soon? I hope so as I wouldn't mind reading that.

Romance isn't a genre that I commonly read, so when I was asked to beta read by the author I will admit that I was hesitant. To my surprise, the story sucked me in from the very beginning. I found myself instantly adoring the main character, Emily, who when we first meet her, has managed to pull herself out of a horrific life event, and is working her butt off to get her life back together. As a reader you can see how strong she is, but she still hasn't realised it for herself, and that's what makes her journey such an interesting and rewarding read. 
 Because of her background, you would think that Emily would run a mile from a man like Cromac O'Connell, an up-and-coming boxing champ. He epitomises everything she should fear: he's a mountain of muscle, and could squash her with his little finger. She wouldn't stand a chance if he ever came after her in a violent way. But something draws her to this broody hulk of a man. He's like the oasis she never thought she would find wandering the dessert all alone. The feelings between them are mutual, and it sparks off a charming friendship that develops into something more. 
 There were some darker moments in the book, which the author interwove with specific scenes to highlight just how much Emily's life had changed. But the scenes also reminded me that her dark past could surface again at any time, and that created an undercurrent of suspense. That said, the book is filled with lighthearted and funny moments that had me giggling out loud, particularly the interactions with the brilliantly written supporting characters. 
 I look forward to reading more of R. J. Prescott's work. This is an outstanding debut. 
 I was provided an ARC of The Hurricane for an honest review.

book_b.title: Rusty Nailed (Cocktail, #2)
book_b.user_review:
Writing: Still witty. Still funny. Buuuut, there was too much recap in the beginning. I read book 1, I don't need a retelling of the story. 
 I realized from this series and the Hudson Valley Series, that Alice Clayton is a big foodie. I liked it in this novel, but in Book 1 in Hudson Valley it felt overwhelming. 
 Characters: I really like Caroline's character. She ascribes to the eccentric creative personality. But Simon...There's not much of him. He is supposed to be an MC but he is more in the background. 
 At the end of Book 1, I liked how Simon was able to calm Caroline when she was worked up, but we don't really get that in this book until the end again. 
 Storyline: What happened? I was excited to continue this series, but... 
 This book was more like THE CAROLINE SHOW. We spent more time in Caroline's head than anything else. I hate to say it because I enjoyed book 1 a lot, but I didn't enjoy this one that much.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I adored Wallbanger. Loved it. It's easily my number one favorite guilty pleasure book. As you can imagine, I was thrilled to find a sequel and snatched it up. Finished it in less than a day. Was terribly disappointed. 
 Where did the characters in the first book go? It was so real, but the good kind of real, where this was just work drama, relationship drama, and friend drama. Frankly, I deal with enough of that in real life! I don't want to read a jumble of unpleasant "real life" crap when I read. I don't. I read for pleasure, and to be honest the characters this go around gave me a headache. 
 Caroline is all over the place, and lost her fun and vivacious edge. Simon, God love him, isn't the confidant, arrogant and sexy man he used to be. The smut scenes are "eh" compared to the first book. I feel like the two did a total 180 from their personalities in Wallbanger. Very, very disappointed.

No one knows how to make me laugh as well as Alice Clayton. Her writing style is like no other. 
 I can so totally share a drink or two with her and know I would be wetting my pants before long. 
 In Wallbanger we meet world traveling photographer Simon...the actual Wallbanger, who shares a very active wall next door to Caroline. Caroline is an Interior Designer, please do not call her a decorator, who loves to bake. Simon falls head over heels for Caroline's...ehhmmm , baked goods and a romance has begun. 
 Rusty Nailed brings us into the future of their relationship and the changes that occur in both their careers and living arrangements. Let's see how these two crazy kids navigate the obstacles of love and all things pussy....cat , did I mention they have a cat called Clive who needs a stage, a mike and a cigarette. 
 Simon and Caroline venture back to Phillie where Simon originates from and we share a very touching lunch date with his childhood neighbors. Probably the only time I felt sad reading this book. At Simon's class re-union we meet some old friends and one in particular that I am sure we will see more of in the next book ScrewDrivered. 
 Back in San Fran, their present day friends are always at it. We share some hilarious moments with Sophie and Neil trying to get their act together. Mimi continues to organize lives, closets and drinking stations. Jillian is away on her extended honeymoon leaving Caroline in charge of work and the stress that comes with owning a company. Simon is taking his own sabbatical of sorts and not traveling as much but just plain enjoying his new relationships both with Caroline and Clive. 
 Life is good ...so why does Caroline feel so "pickled" about it?? 
 I anticipated this sequel for so long and I loved this book. I am so not done with Caroline and Simon and I do hope that Alice Clayton is not done with them either. 
 Will Simon and Caroline ever need that nursery?? Will Clive and his harem fill the house up with a bunch of hangnailed kittens? Will Neil and Sophie ever come out of that coat room? Can I have that white convertable Benz Simon bought Caroline?? 
 More please.

1/2 
 Some of the books in Alice Clayton's Cocktail series feature different couples and different storylines, but Rusty Nailed is a direct sequel to the first installment: Wallbanger and continues following lead characters Caroline and Simon. After the hilarity of Wallbanger, this sequel was fairly disappointing in comparison, but the newness of the characters' romance has passed and watching relationships progress can get a bit rocky at times. I love this series and had previously skipped over this sequel but after watching a friend recently meet Caroline and Simon for the first time, I thought it was about time to finish their story. If you are a fan of this series, make sure to include this one in the mix. 
 My favorite quote: 
 "...sometimes you have to pretend to be feeling better to actually feel better. It's why new workout clothes make you feel like you want to work out. I was still waiting for that one to turn out to be true..."
Utter shit

I gotta be honest, this was slightly disappointing. I thought the first book was much better, and I had a hard time caring about the story. 
 Maybe it was just me, but while I loved Simon, Caroline and Co. in Wallbanger, this time I thought they were very childish sometimes, and quite annoying. 
 The main thing I disliked about this book was the drama surrounding Neil and Sophia. They could have solved the situation like adults, but no, they just acted like five-year olds everytime they got together, not to mention the huge amount of time everyone spent talking about them. 
 I don't think Simon and Caroline's story needed a sequel but, overall, it was a fun read.

The Wallbanger books will forever be some of my favorite ones ever written. And, as I expected, Alice Clayton delivers a whole slew of laughs and ridiculousness in the sequel to Wallbanger. 
 Rusty Nailed is the perfect sequel to Wallbanger. The story picks up shortly after where the first book left off, with Simon and Caroline banging walls, Clive seeking Purina, and the giggle worthy circle of friends in ... a transition of sorts. Some relationships are flourishing while others aren't doing so well, but Clayton keeps the focus of the book on Simon and Caroline and the progression of their relationship. 
 I really enjoyed the development of Simon's character in this book. He comes so far from where he was at the beginning of Wallbanger, and Clayton writes this transition in a way that's realistic. His changes are very natural and what I would expect from a man of his age living in the situation he is living in. Nothing felt forced, and this to me is proof of how well Clayton knows her characters and in the end, knows what's best for them (which any author should). 
 Caroline evolves too, and I like the way things played out with her career choices and how she manages to find a good balance for everything in the end. 
 The chemistry between these two is palpable, as it was in the first book, and when they come together it's hot, hot, hot! 
 I can't wait to dive into the third book and see what kind of ending Clayton will give these two. 
 I definitely give this one five stars. There are a ton of laughs, some moments that will make you get a bit teary eyed, and plenty of sexy scenes woven in.
DNF. Just couldn't connect, maybe next time :)

2.5 eh stars

** spoiler alert ** 
 Jerry football tryout. Weird culty Archie, punishment. Jerry philosophizing on sexuality/hippies. Some shady back room deal about chocolate sales. Super-secret prank meeting. Sadistic teacher plays cheating mind games. Mean Emile siphons gas, is muscle. Prank carried out. Jerry and dad deal w/grief. Chocolate sale begins, prank takes effect. Football practice. Jerry refuses to sell chocolates. What's the big deal w/this chocolate sale? Archie blackmails Emile jerkin it. Jerry continues to refuse to sell. Other kids start refusing. Psychological torture. Important to sell chocolate caz school's in debt to this bad sale, so Jerry's refusal is fueling that fire and makes the Vigils look bad. Vigils threaten Jerry, then debate on what to do w/him-nothing. Vigils start messing w/his head. Also start padding sales numbers. Some sort of metaphor for society going on. Vigils beat him unconscious after ruining his rep. Archie sets up Jerry to box Emile to make up for not participating in that fight, to ensure no one else refuses to sell ever again. Is everyone evil deep down? Some metaphor for pacification? Kids are betting on the fight. Jerry lost. School authority/sadistic teacher comes down on side of Vigils, Jerry's carted off to the hospital. School full of sociopaths.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I wish I could give 0 stars. The Vigils run the school, even when Brother Leon likes to pretend that he does. And Archie runs the Vigils. On the surface, the Vigils just like to cause mischief and pull off impossible stunts. But they're really into humiliation and power. Jerry accepts an assignment from them--don't sell chocolates in the school fundraiser for a week. But when he continues not to sell them, the Vigils turn against him. And they turn the entire student body as well. He gets kicked till he can't even get up (literally and metaphorically). The story ends with the Vigils in just as much power as ever.
My favorite 8th grade teacher said I'd love this book. She was sadly, fatally, wrong.
A good book, but not my favorite book.

** spoiler alert ** 
 One of the things that makes this really groundbreaking in young adult literature is that it shows a gritty, dark side of being a teenager. The novel brought in not only peer pressure, with Archie and his Vigils assignments, but also pressure from authority, such as when Brother Leon threatens a student with an F for information. The plot also deals with issues of morality and ethics. For a moment it seemed like despite all of the bad things that were happening, the Vigils might be defeated and "good" would overcome. Jerry almost starts a revolution, with other students not selling chocolates, but the Vigils quickly squash it. It just goes to show the power a group of teens can have, especially when they are cruel and don't care about consequences. 
 The ending of the book is particularly disturbing. All of the boys in the school were like wild animals, screaming for blood. It reminded me of the novel Lord of the Flies, in that it showed how boys could deteriorate into beasts and be so un-humanlike. The fighting is awful, and no one stands up for it or really tries to do something about it. This was an interesting parallel to the scene where Brother Leon called out Bailey in front of the class and accuses him of cheating, mercilessly taunting him, and no one says anything. In the end, Goober tries to say something but just like in the classroom, it is too little, too late. This also further cemented the parallels between Brother Leon and Archie. 
 I do wonder about the tone of the ending, though. There were a few times when it seemed like a little hope might be restored, but hope was absolutely destroyed, with Jerry declaring that it's better not to disturb the universe. I'm all for showing teenagers in a realistic light, and even all of the horrible details about what can happen, but is ending the book in this way really the message we want to send to teenagers? It seems to tell teens that it's better to lie down and take whatever the bullies give you, or else you'll end up a bloody pulp like Jerry, wishing he had never tried to be different. I think this book could have still been very effective but also thrown in at least a small glimmer of hope or redemption at the end. Of course, it may just be that I'm a sucker for a least a somewhat happy ending, and perhaps most teens prefer this sort of ending. 
 Overall I found the writing style to be really good, and I appreciate the fact that Cormier was trying to show teens in a different light. However, the book was downright disturbing, but beyond that it was also implausible much of the time. The fact that boys can be cruel I buy. But for a teacher to be as horrible as Brother Leon is, and nothing done about it, I don't understand. Not one single boy tells a parent what's going on? None of the other teachers try to do something? And after the whole ending Archie doesn't get punished in any way whatsoever? At the very least, I think Jerry's dad would have called the police after all of the creepy phone calls!
Sickening. Good.

"He hated to think of his own life stretching ahead of him that way, a long succession of days and nights that were fine - not good, not bad, not great, not lousy, not exciting, not anything." 
 "A Controversial book" was one of the categories for my 2016 Reading Challenge. I wasn't entirely sure how this different from the "Banned/Challenged Book" category, so I just googled it, and this was the top result across multiple websites. It seems people either love this book and teach it in high school curriculums, or abhor it for it's violence and ban it in their school. On both sides, people have really, really strong feelings, which does earn it the controversial label. I assumed I'd have really strong feelings too! 
 But... 
 I was sure this book would bring all the feels! I'd be angry! I'd be upset about the bullying! I'd be ready to make a change in the world! I would want to spread the word of the book! 
 But... 
 So this book is about an all-boys prep school in the 1970's. There exists within a "secret" society (hush hush nod nod, the administration know all about it and sort of control it). One boy defies them, sort of. Not even outwardly, because he isn't sure if/why he cares either. It creates a "war" that all takes place in the last few pages and involves a bit of bullying and violence and no real resolution at the end. 
 I just didn't care about or relate to any of the characters. Maybe because they were mostly high school football players in the 70's. I don't know. But I felt I had no investment in anything that happened to them. There was a lot of build-up but not much payoff. 
 I totally don't understand why this book is a big deal. I found it almost excruciatingly boring. I resorted to forcing myself to read only a few pages at a time several times a day because I just hated it. I would have DNF'ed it but if this was any indication of how I'd feel about "controversial" books, I didn't want to have to deal with another one for my challenge slot! 
 This is the first book I've picked up only because of the challenge and hated. I guess it had to happen sooner or later. Most I've adored.

Even though I marked it a 4, I really think this is more a 3.5 book. But I liked it enough to round up. 
 I checked this out from my library because it came in on the new books cart, and because I'd seen a lot of buzz about it. I flipped it open, read the first few pages, and was hooked. I down half the book in a day, roughly to the 200 page mark. It was at that point the book lost interest to me, and I didn't struggle, but didn't engulf the remaining 200 plus pages. 
 I liked Rossi's style at first. I loved how she threw us into this world with no explanation with these neat terms and slangs. I loved how natural the speech was, and how the action picked right up. 
 Somewhere around page 200, I lost that freshness. I noticed the slang was dropped, the world was being explained, though honestly, I didn't need it to be. I'd figured it out. Plus, the romance became the central plot. 
 I love a good romance, but I only love it if it's a subplot. Somehow the romantic subplot of this book overtook the main plot for the majority of the story. Though I liked it, I was a little sick of Perry and Aria's sudden intense devotion to each other. 
 There was a turning point in the book that I found felt forced. Aria and Perry seemed to undergo a huge personality shift very suddenly. I think it was this point that the romance overwhelmed the main plot, of Aria getting home and Perry getting his nephew back. I also realized at this point that this had to be the 1st in a series, something I didn't know when picking up the book. 
 The world drew me in, and that's probably why I started reading the book. I found the two cultures interesting. That being said, I got mad when the technology "culture" became vilanized. I'm just not a barbaric kind of girl. I don't like surviving in the woods and tribal systems. And why do the two have to be separate? There was a great chance to merge Aria's techosavvy and Perry's ruggedness, and it just doesn't really happen. 
 Overall an interesting read, but not one I'm going to be running out and telling everyone to read. Though I will be reading the sequel when it comes out.

What I Liked: The world Veronica Rossi created. It wasn't just a dystopian young adult novel, but there was such underlining science fiction aspects to it, and it was an interesting telling of the world after great disaster. Such as the world of Reverie and how everyone who lived there could go anywhere they wanted in the world, create realms filled with the things the love most, do what they wanted most, just with a thought. It's a world that seems almost perfect on the surface, a paradise that the people who run Reverie want others to crave. Then we have the world of the outsiders, a world aptly named The Death Shop. It's a place of many dangerous things, and stories are past around Reverie about what lives out there. Cannibals, Savages, and the deadly Aether Storms that are feared by all in the pods. And the outsiders aren't the same as those in Reverie, biologically. This was a really interesting aspect of the story, especially when it comes to Perry and his sense of smell descriptions of Aria and the others from Reverie. 
 Perry. Oh Perry. From the moment he was introduced I was intrigued by him, even if Aria wasn't quite fond of him. He's the complete opposite of Aria in the way he grew up and the life he's used to. It's a lot harsher, and he's learned to survive danger in a way only Aria has been able to imagine. There's not much to condemn when it comes to how Perry and his village has had to survive (outside the certain events). I couldn't help but feel for him either when you get to know him and his full story. Outside the circumstances of where he lives, he's not had an easy life emotionally. And the way his feelings of distaste for Aria gradually changes, had my heart going soft big time. 
 Roar. This character was a delightful surprise to find in Under The Never Sky. He's the kind of charming character who makes you smile when things get tough, and provides the laughs when you need him to. But he's not just a comic relief, he's a character that I fell for just as much as I did for Perry, especially when you get to see what's under the funny and charm he exudes constantly. His fondness for Perry and eventually Aria evolved so nicely. I don't think I can even fully describe the evolution of feelings that built for this character, he was just there in my heart by the end of it. All of his scenes in the book were some of the best. 
 What I didn't really like: The lack of world building. Rossi creates a universe that's pretty amazing but there isn't enough descriptors when it comes to making sense of things for the reader. You have to pretty much assume what certain things mean or how certain things look like. When it comes to dystopian/fantasy novels there should be more building for the setting to pull the reader into your story. Reverie was just brushed on, as well as the Death Shop and the extent of the world outside the pods. This part of the novel could have been added to. 
 Lastly, I wasn't too fond of Aria. At least, in the beginning. It was very annoying to see her prejudices and emotions over her situation being pushed onto Perry. I couldn't sympathize for very much until she finally quit it with her preconceived ideas and thoughts to see what was really in front of her. That's when I began to see how things changed between her and Perry, and her relationships with Roar and the others along the way in the novel. 
 However, it was an enjoyable novel overall and there were plenty of things I enjoyed enough that the weak points didn't greatly impact how I felt about the story. I will definitely be continuing the series and most of what I see from others say that it gets even better in the next book of the trilogy.

This book could have gotten a better rating but the beginning was really, really slow. It didn't pick up until about a third of the way into the story. There was a big action sequence in the beginning followed by some dramatic bits and lots of character and world building. It wasn't poorly written or unsatisfactory.. just a little dull at first. 
 This is a take on the traditional "Civilians" vs. "Savages", but the world and the storyline take on a life of their own. I really do love the world Veronica Rossi created. She's got an eye for detail and uses a lot of great description. 
 The world is slowly being destroyed by Aether-- some sort of fiery chemical lightning from hell-- so most of the remaining population loves in indoor Pods to stay safe. After being present for a scandalous incident involving the son of a high-powered society leader, Aria is blamed in his place and abandoned in the middle of what her Pod lovingly refers to as "The Death Shop". It's there that she's discovered by Peregrine, a savage who isn't all too found of Aria but desperately needs her insider knowledge. 
 If I have one complaint about the book, it's that there's a weird problem with Perry. He goes from unpleasant to wonderful way too quickly. Don't get me wrong! I love Charming!Perry, but there needed to be some more moments where we see hm transition from one state to the other.

sample_reviews.review_text: Five word review: Bonfire of Miami police vanities
couldn't get into this story.

I don't even know what I just read (technically listened to as it was an audiobook). 
 I hated how Magdalena didn't know what certain phrases meant. She is a nurse which implies medical training. Pretty sure she would know what a metaphor is. 
 And what happened to some of the characters? They just disappeared! No explanation. 
 I almost lost my mind during the early boat scene when the narrator shouted SMACK a million times.

I listened to the hachette audio version, and almost gave up after two hours of Lou Diamond Phillips. In retrospect the enjoyment of the story overcame the quality of narration that put me off, and I end up giving it three stars as a compromise. Wolfe comes through as a great storyteller, and although I've spent almost no time in Miami I feel as though he's given me a good overview of life there. What is it about Phillips? He almost does a reasonable job with making me believe he's is voicing a Cuban, or Black English, or Russian speaker - but that seems the limit. It was difficult at times to sense the switch from dialog to narration.

What an ordeal!!!! BAM!!! POW!!! WHAMMO!!!! Annoyed yet? This is just a tiny taste of what Back to Blood was like to read. Tom Wolfe's first novel in 8 years looks at Miami the same way that Bonfire of the Vanities addressed Manhattan, and A Man in Full explored Atlanta. Wolfe repeats his usual formula of a vast array of characters, satiric tone, and paragraphs full of irritating onomatopoeic devices, over-punctuated with caps on steroids and exclamation points. At 704 pages, Wolfe could easily have accomplished the same effect with a mere 500 pages just by eliminating the verbal histrionics. I finished the book just so I could say that Wolfe didn't defeat me, but it was a tough go. If my own writing students had handed in similar pieces, I would've returned them with one word: EDIT!!!!!
I will have to try this one again, maybe in the summer.

As much as I wanted to believe this book would be better than the reviews, it was a huge disappointment. Could not get into the story or like any of the characters, and the funky punctuation and sentence structure was really grating.

Unless you are considering relocating to Miami, or live in Miami I cannot recommend this book. It makes me want to crawl back into the loving embrace of the 19th c.--Jane Austen, Henry James, Dickens, Edith Wharton "time machine take me away." I have had it with the genre of Jonathan Franzian existential ethnology of modern 21st alientation and ADD. If I want to feel bad, I don't need to shell out $23.00 in hardcover and slog through 700 unentertaining pages, all I gotta do is get on the Miami Dade Metrorail and schlep my post millenial Anglo ass to work in this city "where everyone hates everyone" (which is the most quoted and patently hyperbolic excerpt from this well-written "feel bad" read).

An interesting look into the country that is Miami, focusing on Art Basel, the Miami PD, the struggle that some Cubans face as they try to fit in, and the struggle that other races have in relation to the high Cuban population. 
 Fast paced, thrilling, and insightful. I dug it.
Just hated the writing. The conversations between the characters are terrible. He's trying too hard to sound young and hip which just makes the book irritating to read.

An awesome read combining all the elements that make a James Rollins roller-coaster "tick", namely: exotic locales, an emotional story at the centre, terrifying and tantalising secrets being hinted at from the corners of the eyes, colourful villains, natives under siege and reverse, exotic flora & fauna, and super-fast pace. Yes, the expression "suspension of disbelief" assumes whole new meaning in these works, but since you go through the pages often suspending the process of breath itself (and going quite blue in the process), nobody minds it. Epitome of techno-thrillers, and highly recommended for sleepy afternoons if you wish to keep yourself not just sharp, but razor-sharp.
