Review 
 Plot: I was happy to find this book in the library. I saw the cover of Hades and knew after two good covers, I needed to know if the story was good as well. We instantly meet Bethany, Gabriel, and Ivy who are on Earth to help get rid of the Dark Forces. Unlike her siblings, Bethany seems a need to know the human race and make connections with them. Her siblings try to warn her about this, but Bethany can not help herself. Soon, she meets Xavier who surprisingly consumes her thoughts and diverts her focus on why she's here on Earth. As they grow closer, it seems that someone is trying to keep them apart. With the rules in heaven and the people on Earth, Bethany is trying to find a way to stay with the one she could possibly love. 
 Characters: Bethany - At first, it was hard to read Bethany's perspective because everything was new for her. She just came on Earth and was not used to living like a human yet. This took some time in the first half of the book because every situation and experience was so new to her. However, you could see her develop courage to stand up for herself and a personality of those of a human teenager, which I would like to see if it lasts. 
 Xavier - He was surprisingly more understanding with things than I would have thought. It seemed like he was shocked and decided it's OK. Obviously, it is different because she's not a vampire or werewolf but an angel. So, I could see his acceptance. He is a good guy and shows Bethany more of himself as the book progresses. 
 Cover: Like I said before, I love the Halo series covers. Each one seems to fit the plot line of that installment and is so beautifully crafted. I loved this cover since I saw it earlier this year and a large part of why I wanted to read this. 
 Overall Rating: I loved this book and am giving it a three out of four. It is a slow start and seemed pretty cookie cutter but with problems that still needed to be resolved. There were some questions I had throughout the book like how are Gabriel, Ivy, and Bethany siblings and why are the Dark Forces a problem now. But, this book brings a different take on angels and a romance that's sure to have it's problems.

I hated it. Really boring; predictable plot with major holes; dodgy basic premise; narrowminded, stereotped characters and so preachy. Ugg. I threw it away in disgust. How did it get published when there are so many new authors out there with fantastic books trying to hook a publisher?

Bethany is, like, a teenage angel. She's young for an angel, where as her brother and sister have thousands of years on her, experience wise as well as in age. When they are sent down to earth to help thwart the dark forces, Bethany enrolls in the nearby high school, her task: to change the views of the teenagers there to look up to God and to support Him. Basically, to make everyone truly believe again. As she prepares for her task, she falls in love with a mortal boy. Though her siblings are wary of her utter, almost pure, humanity, she goes for it, following her gut feeling. Waiting for her powers to develop, she and the mortal connect, date, and she begins to fall in love. As the Dark Forces make their way to their small city, will Bethany be ready for them? Or will she be trapped? 
 An interesting read, though a little cheesy and cliche, but good. For me, it was kind of like 'The Devil's Kiss' by Sarwat Chadda, a book that I had detested the moment I began reading (I still regret buying it), mixed with 'Hush, Hush' by Becca Fitzpatrick, which I had loved. A mix between those two books would result in one like this; not amazing, but still not bad. 
 Plot: 4/5 
 Characters: 3/5 
 World Building: 3/5 
 Cover: 5/5 
 Overall: 3.5/5 
 GoodReads Rating: 3.70/5 
 -review by Between Printed Pages

book_b.title: Fourth Grave Beneath My Feet (Charley Davidson, #4)
book_b.user_review:
Hi. My name is Brie, and I love Garrett Swopes. I don't love that there wasn't a solitary mention of the man until around chapter 12. The man was only SHOT and FINALLY believed that Charley wasn't a complete crazy person. But no, lets not mention him until a third of the book is over. It's cool. (sarcasm) 
 Also, if I have to continue to read about how OH-MY-FREAKING-GOD-REYES-IS-SO-HOT-BUT-DUH-HE'S-THE-SON-OF-SATAN I may punch myself in the face. Lets face it, if you've not understood from the previous 3 installments of this series that Reyes Farrow is a Dark God of Hotness and Sex Appeal, then you've not been paying attention. And you're wasting your own time. But for those of us who have this detail on lock, it's annoying to read about it. It makes Charley unsympathetic and just seem pathetic because she can't manage to stop thinking about how much she wants to rip her clothes off when she's near him. That and how pissed off and mean he always is. Just...ugh. 
 Whilst writing this I found myself nearly incapable of remembering what the subplot of the book was. It has something to do with a poor girl being stalked by someone. I can't remember her name. Yes, it was that interesting. 
 Moving on... 
 Charley was still funny as ever, if not a bit....damaged, to put it mildly. Her new hobby of haunting home shopping networks brings about some hilarity. Her relationship with her father is still sad and we don't see as much of Ubie in this one as the others, much to the detriment of the book. 
 Overall: I felt this book was strained and unfocused. While the main story was propelled further and the subplot was neatly wrapped up, I felt apathetic about this book in general.

sample_reviews.review_text: LOVED this one!

En cada libro la historia mejora. Eso si,Charley cada vez es mas loca y sus hormonas estan mas revueltas que las de un adolescente.Me hubiera gustado que sus jueguitos amorosos fueran con Garrett y no con el motero.Pero en fin. Tambien pienso que ese viajecito de Garrett,lo va a hacer cambiar y no precisamente para bien y seria una lastima,porque el me encanta. 
 Lo mejor del libro es que al fin Charley tiene mas interaccion con el Malo Malisimo.Que bueno que comence con la saga cuando ya hay varios libros publicados,porque todos nos dejan con deseos de mas.

Oh, Charley, how I adore your antics. You may be having a hard time coping with the events from the last book, but once things start happening, you have a knack for ending up right in the middle of things. Often with a quip on your lips and a solution brewing in your head. 
 Similar to previous books, this one had several plotlines criss-crossing and intersecting, with Charley being the focal point. Everything builds to exciting resolutions, with several new threads being spun out to come into play in the next book. Charley's main case in this story involves a woman who has been terrorized since she was a child, and you won't believe some of the reveals that happen. There was one that just blew me away! It had me flipping back to see if I could or should have guessed it because I definitely didn't. 
 Looking at the known characters, I was slightly disappointed by both the biker gang and Garrett. Mainly that neither got more page time. After the events of the last book, I was hoping to see them more in this one, but alas, it was not to be. Hopefully Garrett has a bigger role in the next book because he really is my favourite character next to Charley. 
 Overall, this series cements itself in my heart with every book I read. This volume had us seeing Charley in a vulnerable position, and it just made me love her more. As usual, the humour was on point and fabulous. This is definitely a series I'd highly recommend.

Very good book. Lots of excitement and mystery. Should have realized sooner that the one woman was dead to begin with but I didn't get it till the end. I love Reyes. He is a definite bad boy. So hot! The biker Donovan isn't bad either. Charley is hysterical. She always cracks me up. This series just gets better and better.

Loved this one! We finally got some real answers! And the hole harper thing shocked the hell outa me! I really fell for her. As for the new neighbor I SO CALLED IT! Reyes and charleys relationship is so disfunctuonal, i wish they would just sit and talk to each other like adults but then again that woudnt be any fun. I really like that we're actually getting somehwere with the hole mystical side of the story, Darynda does a wonderful job balancing both aspect and juggling complex plots in such a pleasing manner.
Shit is getting real, yikes!!!

Genuinely did not expect this series to get better. 
 But it did. 
 Four books in and it up and got better. 
 Dayum. 
 So no nice easy transition here. I've been looking back and it's really astonishing the transition of the first three books. Most series like this would have spans during or between books of months to years. But not this series. The first three books took place in what- about a month? It was bam! bam! bam! with only minor processing changes between. 
 Well, much like another series I know, book four now brought it. Everything that happened in the other books has accumulated and caught up with the characters. Two months have passed and things are different. 
 Reyes: out of prison. The courts processed, the case was re-evaluated, he's been released. But he's not right up at Charley's side. Nope. As ever, there relationship is anything but easy, but this time there is some real weight behind it between Charley's feeling of betrayal and Reyes' anger at that. 
 Gemma: seriously in her sister's life. Like, really an important character now. And super important because... 
 Charley: for the first time feeling the effects of the last case. PTSD. Big ole' case of it. We're talking hoarding, agoraphobia, lethargy, depression...the full shebang. For once we see that everything that's gone on has effected her. It takes a case to bring her to start to realize this though really, that should have tipped me off. She finally decides to leave her apartment because of a case? A case that where a client mysteriously finds her? And the safe house she stays in doesn't even have food? Girl was a ghost the whole time and I had no clue. Geez, She sees dead people, it was laid right out. Anyhow that is the job she's had as long as she can remember and Charley is finally leaving the house. But she's not magically better. For the first time ever she is dealing with this and it's effecting her relationships with everyone. 
 Really, this book has thoroughly invested me in the series. Demons. Apocalypse. Hot sex. 
 And on top of it all characters I care about with major emotional developments? 
 I am so in.

After the big events in the last book, our girl Charley is going through some rough times. She is not sleeping, barely coherent, and spending most of her money buying random stuff from the home shopping network. Thank goodness Cookie, Charley's best friend, and for a new client to come snap Charley out of her funk. 
 Like the other books in the series, there are many story lines happening at the same time. I'm always amazed on how Darynda can keep these events straight when she's writing! Some of the mysteries are easy to solve while the questions surrounding Reyes, the sexy and insufferable love interest, always has me puzzled. I was surprised a few times in this book and was happy to come upon a couple of nice twists too. 
 Fourth Grave Beneath My Feet gives us a little more insight to the relationship and personalities of Charley and Reyes. The tension and sexual chemistry is what makes us turn the pages faster. While they do snap, crackle, and pop, the huge cloud of doom that lingers above them when the key of darkness is inserted into the locket of light is pretty frightening. We finally get to know the meaning behind Reyes's nickname for Charley, Dutch, even though it was a bit of a let down. 
 Reyes still has me frustrated and confused. He was a major jerk for most of this book, but there are moments when he's sweet and vulnerable. I enjoyed the parts where the green monster reared its ugly head for both Charley and Reyes. It was nice spending time with the secondary characters, but I was a bit sad that we didn't get much time with Swopes and Ubie as much as I would have liked. We also got to meet a new character named Quentin which I liked and am looking forward to more of him in future books. Of course I would be remiss if I didn't mention the special addition of a lovable yet ferocious dog named Artemis. I can't wait to make some time in my busy schedule to revisit Charley and company in her latest adventures.

Loved it! Super great addition to the Charley Davidson series, I don't know what i will do while waiting for the next book! Reyes was so hot in this book, and I am over the moon about learning more about everything! I was a bit bummed that Swopes wasn't in the book more, but we did get to 'see' Artemis and that is great. reference_books.title: The Unfinished Life of Addison Stone
reference_books.review_text:
I've never read a book like THE UNFINISHED LIFE OF ADDISON STONE. And I've read many other books by the author, Adele Griffin, who, by the way, is amazing. ADDISON STONE has been pitched as a "docu-novel." It's set up as somewhat of a biography of the fictional title character, Addison Stone, a young artist who left small-town New England for big-city New York only to end up dead at eighteen. Her death becomes scandal. Some say it's an accident. Some say one or even both of her boyfriends could be involved. Some think that her history of mental health problems points to suicide. 
 But everyone agrees: Addison Stone was a prodigy, one of a kind. And there will never be another like her. 
 THE UNFINISHED LIFE OF ADDISON STONE is a unique reading experience. With visual art -- pieces by Addison, discussed in the book -- mixed in, along with portraits and snapshots of Addison, the book is narrated not only by the people Addison knew (from childhood besties to boyfriends to frenemies and teachers and family and the press) but her body of work. It's easy to forget that this is a fictional account, that Addison is a character, and not a real girl. That these paintings and illustrations are work commissioned by Adele Griffin for her book, that the girl in the photos is not Addison, but a model. 
 In short? Read this book. Read it now. It's beautiful and intense and the kind of book that stays with you, that makes your world both bigger and smaller. Meet Addison Stone, and hold her close to your heart.

reference_books.title: Catching Jordan
reference_books.review_text:
For those of you thinking that this is just a book about football, you're quite mistaken. And for those of you thinking this is just another YA love story, well, you've got a lovely surprise waiting for you as well. CATCHING JORDAN, Miranda Kenneally's debut novel, is the perfect mix of steamy romance, family drama, strong characters, and action both on and off the field. 
 Jordan Woods is the quarterback of her high school football team. That's right -- her. And she's one of the best players in Tennessee. In order to play with the boys, she has to keep up appearances as a tough girl -- a girl who doesn't cry, get crushes on team mates, or write in a journal. 
 Except she does all of those things. Especially after Ty comes into the picture. Just moving to town from Texas, Ty is the apple of every cheerleader's eye -- and for good reason. He's smokin' hot, and sweet to boot. What Jordan doesn't expect is that Ty thinks she's pretty cute, too. But things aren't as simple as they should be. If Jordan wants to be with Ty, it could cost her respect on the football team. And rumors are spreading int he girls' locker room, too. About her and her best friend, Sam Henry, a fellow football player who recently broke up with his girlfriend -- and he won't even tell Jordan what happened. To make matters worse, it seems like at every possible opportunity, Jordan's father -- the great NFL player Donovan Woods -- is trying to hold her back, supporting her friends and her brother but discouraging her from playing college ball. 
 CATCHING JORDAN has so much going for it. Characters you fall in love with, swoon-worthy romance, and an accidental education in football (I think I might be able to follow a game on TV after reading Miranda's book). Plus, Jordan Woods is not only a strong narrator, but a strong girl that you absolutely want to root for. You want her to get what she wants and deserves, rather than siding with one of the romantic leads. You're not on team Ty or team Henry -- you're on team Jordan. And as a member of team Jordan, you can bet I'll be recommending this book to anyone who will listen -- football fan or not. Keep your eyes peeled for CATCHING JORDAN, which I'm sure will be popping up on recommended reading lists from both the ALA and state organizations. It's just that good!

reference_books.title: Deadly Little Secret (Touch, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Camelia's life changed in an instant when she was almost hit by a car - and saved by a handsome stranger. She can't stop thinking about him, or the way it felt when he touched her before he jumped on his bike and fled the scene. When the new kid at school, Ben, appears to be Camelia's knight in shining armor, she confronts him only to be told she's mistaken. Meanwhile rumors are spreading - Ben is a murderer, there was an accident, he killed his last girlfriend. Camelia is getting closer and closer to Ben, though, despite pleas from her friends. When she starts to receive scary messages and gifts, and even suspects someone is watching her, she isn't sure where to turn. Could Ben be who everyone says he is? Or is he telling her the truth when he says he wants to protect her? Stolarz' latest is gripping from page one, exploring ideas of psychic abilities and teen drama in a compelling, original way. Though I found the ending a little unlikely, this is a page turner whose characters speak for themselves. Deadly Little Secret holds promise for a fresh, new series.

reference_books.title: Cracked (Soul Eaters, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I love a novel narrated by the bad guy. And that's what Meda is -- she's the bad guy. She's not really sure what kind of bad guy she is, but she knows that if it wasn't for her love for her mother, she'd be way badder. She eats souls. And she's doing her best to keep her menu limited to souls that deserve it. But everything changes on the night she mets Chi and his Templar friends. 
 The Templar are an order of men and women dedicated to one thing -- taking out demons. And it seems like they might have answers to all of Meda's questions -- what she is, where she comes from, who her father might have been. And if she can convince her new pals that she needs their protection, maybe those answers can be hers. Of course, plans don't really pan out, and it's not long before Meda, Chi, and crew are in way over their heads. 
 CRACKED is a fast and furious action novel, narrated by a snarky delinquent that readers are sure to get a kick out of. With a little bit of Catholic mythology and a dash of conspiracy theory, Eliza Crewe has whipped up a debut that, even without vampires, is sure to make fans of authors like Richelle Mead and Lili St. Crow salivate for the next book in this exciting series.

reference_books.title: When the Sea Is Rising Red (Hobverse #1)
reference_books.review_text:
One word: Atmosphere. 
 Cat Hellisen's debut is so delightfully thick with atmosphere, with magic, and with character. In Felicita's world, magic is a luxury, allowed only to Pelimburg's wealthy houses -- the houses in power. But when Felicita's best friend Ilven commits suicide to avoid marrying a man that she doesn't love, Felicita runs away, taking a lower class name and squatting in the slums with a small band of vagrants. Soon, Felicita is torn between Dash, the secretive but charismatic leader of their troupe, and Jannik, the vampire royalty whose interest in Felicita is just as mysterious as Jannik himself. But it's not easy to live in hiding. And, worse, the recent high house suicides have awoken a dangerous, dark magic to rise from the seas -- a magic that threatens all of Pelimburg. 
 WHEN THE SEA IS RISING RED is a gorgeous, exciting, and refreshingly new novel. Pelimburg is a world that the reader is completely immersed in, and even after the book's last page is turned, I found myself wondering about Felicita and her friends. I'm looking forward to future works from Cat Hellisen, featuring her lyric prose.

book_a.title: Everneath (Everneath, #1)
book_a.user_review:
When I picked this book up, I had no idea that EVERNEATH was entangled in Greek mythology. The rich world built by Brodi Ashton was a pleasant surprise to me, as it unfolded piece by piece, revealing the secrets of a new imagining of the underworld. And it was super fun to read about. 
 The story of EVERNEATH is told both in the present tense and in flashbacks to the past -- to before Nikki Becker consented to be a part of the Feed that drained her of every single emotion, feeding her Everliving host Cole for one hundred years. And while she was away for a century in the Everneath, in Nikki's world, it was only six months that passed. And in that time, rumors have piled up. She left her boyfriend and longtime friend Jack in the lurch. Everyone thinks she's some strung-out druggie now, talks about her like she's destroyed Jack's life. Even her father, the mayor, is having her drug tested regularly and has signed her up to volunteer at a soup kitchen to help save face for the upcoming election. 
 But none of that really matters. Nikki is going to have to return to the Everneath -- to the Tunnels where she'll be used as a battery to power the Everliving. It's her debt to pay. Even if Cole -- guised in this world as the singer and guitarist for a popular local band -- says there's another way, that she is special, that she could be with him, make a bid for the throne, change the Everneath forever. But Nikki doesn't want that. She'd have to feed off of people the way Cole fed off her. All she wants in these next six months is to be able to say proper goodbyes, to make up for hurting her friends and family when she disappeared without a trace for the Feed. 
 It's not so simple, though. There's a woman named Mary at the soup kitchen who talks about the daughters of Persephone -- and while everyone tells Nikki that she's just an old lady with dementia, Nikki knows there's more to her crazy stories than senility. And there's the conversations Nikki has overheard at the convenience store, between Cole and members of his band. Perhaps she can find a way to subvert the system she won't have to go, and she and Jack can go back to the way they were before the event that sent her running to Cole, to the Feed, in the first place. 
 Written with a delicate hand, EVERNEATH has the perfect blend of mystery, romance, and suspense. If you want a good love story, pick this one up.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I don't really know why I liked this book so much, but I really enjoyed it! I think maybe it was a combination of a few things: 
 -Every time Nikki started to get whiny, she stopped. 
 -Even though she blamed Cole for what happened, she also took responsibility for her actions in it. 
 -I'm quite partial to stories where the first guy {ie- boyfriend, long time best friend, guy with a forever crush on the girl} gets the girl. Pleasantly happy when the paranormal new guy doesn't get the girl, and I think that's what will happen here. I hope.

The writing was fine, and the world even better, but felt no connection towards the characters at all. I really wanted to like this book but by the end I just wanted it to be over. I wanted to care about the characters, to care if they lived or died, but I just didn't. Sad. The cover's pretty though.

This book is stunningly beautiful.From the writing and characters to the flawless blending of myth and reality, it is perfect. Not to mention the gorgeous cover, I mean, really, what girl doesn't dream of a dress like that? 
 What caught me most was the writing. It was dramatic and completely character-centric. No unnecessary words or long, rambling paragraphs. Yet it never felt rushed and flowed naturally throughout. I loved how the author managed to portray such intense emotions with such subtlety. I also truly love what she did with two of my favorite myths, Orpheus and Eurydics and Hades and Persephone. 
 Nikki is wonderful. She's so quiet that you don't always notice, but she has a will of steel. Knowing that she has little time before she is lost to torment and death, her greatest wish is to make it easier on the people she leaves behind. Especially for Jack. 
 Ah, Jack. My favorite character. He's a really, really nice guy with hints of a rebel that sneak out with an eyebrow piercing. He doesn't know where Nikki has been for so long, but he knows that she's been hurt. So he is what she needs most; a friend. He never pushes too hard, but he never gives up. He may take a step back at certain revelations, but never for more than a moment. 
 Cole is an entirely different kettle of fish. He's dark through and through, and has undoubtedly done terrible things, but is he completely irredeemable? Perhaps, perhaps not. It should be...interesting. 
 I would recommend this book to just about anyone, but especially lovers of mythology and beautiful, beautiful romance. And to people who don't mind shedding a few tears over a magnificent ending. 
 I received an advance copy of this book through the author in exchange for a fair and honest review.
This is a textbook example of a book that is not necessarily terrible, just terrible for me. I gave it 10 pages.
I really like this book. It was light read but a good story. Loved the ending, and look forward to more.

What worked: 
 Greek Mythology is a one way ticket to Fangirl Kingdom. It's not like I know a lot about the different myths and legends but there's something about them that I just can't get enough of. Brodi Ashton's new twist on the Persephone myth (which is something I've read a LOT of) is very intriguing and I liked the hierarchy of the Greek system. 
 What irked: 
 Have I been reading the same book as everybody else? My good friend, Brooke, really enjoyed it and normally our taste in books is spot on but with Everneath it wasn't happening. I actually did a buddy read with Hollie from Music, Books and Tea and the only thing that kept me sane is that she felt the same way about it. Everything about it was a disappointment. 
 Nikki is so frustrating and drab in a way that reminded me of Bella Swann. The whole reason she fought so hard to come back home was so she could put things right when actually she spends her time ignoring issues and focusing on the stupidest of tasks instead of the people she cares about. She jumps to conclusions and as for her pathetic excuse for going to the Everneath with Cole, don't get me started. I don't even see the appeal for this leading man. He's boring, he's kinda obsessive and he's a bit creepy and as for the other part of the "love triangle", I'm reserving judgement on Jack for now. He's a forgettable character to me and actually I have a question. Nikki creeps into his room at night (because obviously some YA characters have a blindspot for the creep factor) and he puts on some glasses. Hold on, did he already have glasses? Does he wear contacts the rest of the time? Because right now the image in my head is changing drastically with this sudden piece of information. Before she'd even climbed through his window I was already wondering about the logistics of it because Nikki looks through his window. It's 2am people, does he have blinds? Does he have curtains? If so, why aren't they CLOSED?! If I had a bedroom on the ground floor at the front of the house, I'd be gripping onto every bit of privacy I could, especially with riff raff clambering through my window when I'm sleeping.

I had high hopes but unfortunately they were not met. Some things felt like they were never properly explained. And I don't think I ever fully understood what had happened in the Everneath. It was a good idea and I am sure I will (eventually) read the sequel, but its not a high priority for me. That said Nikki was an excellent character, although the other characters felt undeveloped as though all the authors energy went into her.
Just found the worst, dumbest, most passive protagonist in the history of literature. Absolute shit. Love triangle with most-popular-boy-in-school quarterback and handsome rock god demon... kill me.
3 Es un libro entretenido por un rato pero nada especial, sin embargo mi amor a la mitologia griega me hace querer leer el segundo, espero volver a ver a Jacke pronto :)

This is a book that had the potential to be wonderfully amazing. I'm not one to obsess over covers because I really honestly don't care, but the cover for this was gorgeous. The main factor in my picking this up though was the premise. I read the back of the book and I was digging the whole Everneath concept. I'm a sucker for mythology and I was interested to see what kind of spin the author would take on the Persephone tale. Sadly, I have to say that I was super disappointed. It had all the components to be a fun book, but I felt a little let down. The characters were bland and I didn't connect to any of them. It also seemed liked nothing much happened, which was surprising for a book where the main character is on a time limit to save her soul. It was pretty much Nikki hanging out knitting and awkwardly staring at her ex, Jack. It wasn't until a great deal in the book where things started happening and even then, it was a lot of back and forth. Of course, the whole time Nikki was determined to damn her soul to the Tunnels of the Everneath. I was like, 'Is she serious?!'. Sure, Cole's kind of freaky, but the guy is nowhere bad enough for her to be so resistant to his offer. I'm sorry but if I had the choice between eternal life and being buried alive in hell, I'd for sure be running off with Cole. Just saying. Her doing what she was doing was just stubborn and stupid. The longer I read, I just wanted her to throw herself into the Tunnels already and end the book. The ending itself was a little lackluster. I have a feeling I was supposed to be heartbroken by how things played out, but I wasn't. 
 The main character Nikki was boring personified. Gahh, I swear that she had no personality whatsoever. I could get through a slightly underwhelming book plot if the characters are realistic and have some life to them. Nikki was the type of protagonist I hate reading about. She came off as a lethargic blob of a person who wandered about wasting time. Not that every protagonist has to be a kickass pillar of strength, but at least make them have some kind of spark. I have no clue what Nikki even looks like, which shouldn't be such a big deal, but I also have no insight whatsoever into her as a person. Looking back, I honestly have no clue what things she likes or dislikes, what she wants to do in her life, etc. Aside from the car accident thing, I virtually knew nothing about her. She was just some cardboard person bumbling about the storyline. 
 As for the two guys Jack and Cole, I didn't feel either of them. They didn't have much of a personality either. I'll admit I kind of liked the two of them in the flashbacks Nikki had, but any life the characters had were thrown out in the present part of the book. Nikki had these two guys fighting over her and I couldn't understand it. Cole I could kind of love because he had ulterior motives for the things he was saying and doing. He's not a nice guy really. I mean, the guy feeds off people's souls. However, the author had to ruin things by making Cole some obsessive, love-struck boy. I would much rather Cole didn't like Nikki and was just using her for his whole power ploy. Jack also was a bit cardboard. He was just there. I didn't feel the connection between him and Nikki either. All the words were being said, but it didn't feel real to me. The two of them were made to seem 'so in love', whirlwind romance or whatever and it wasn't to me. Jack and Jules should have hooked up because they seemed better together than him and Nikki. 
 Overall, I didn't really like this at all. I don't want to bash because it wasn't even close to being the worst thing I've ever read. That goes to 'Personal Demons' by Lisa Desrochers. However, it was sort of disappointing. The premise itself sounded interesting, but the execution was kind of terrible. I hate to be mean, but I feel like this would have been a lot better if someone other than the author would have written it. The concept was there, but the characters needed to developed more and just in general I wanted more depth. I want to read a book that makes me fall in love with all the characters, both good and bad. I want to care about what's happening and this book was lacking all that for me. It seems like a ton of people are in love with this book and good for them, but it just wasn't for me and I'm defintely not going to read the next one.

book_b.title: Across the Universe (Across the Universe, #1)
book_b.user_review: I was lucky enough to get an early review copy of ACROSS THE UNIVERSE. I read it so quickly, entranced by Amy and Elder, two very different teens from different worlds together on a space ship that is meant to be a sustainable environment until the entire crew (and population) get to a new planet. Amy isn't even supposed to be awake. She was cryogenically frozen back on Earth, with her parents, and meant to be awoken upon arrival. But someone unfroze her, perhaps attempting to kill her. And she and Elder are starting to realize that something very wrong is going on on the ship that Elder had previously thought was a fairly Utopian society, despite his regular tiffs with his mentor, Eldest. Part mystery, part space western, part romance, this is a book that is going to blow you away, too.

This book was really inappropriate an should be rated R.

Review 7 out of 5 
 Seventeen-year-old Amy and her family leave Earth to colonise a planet which is 300 years away. But she is brutally woken fifty years before she was supposed to be. Amy feels so alone, but there is someone who wants to protect her. Elder is sixteen, but he is to be the new leader of "Godspeed" when it's his time. 
 Can Amy and Elder unravel the secrets and lies and get to the truth? Can they find the killer before more lives are lost? 
 I absolutely LOVED this book! Those who know me know I very rarely, if ever, swear. BUT - O.M.G. - This book is fantastic! 
 I had heard on the review grapevine that it was good, but to me it's an understatement! This is one of the most exciting science fiction novels I have read in a long time! The characters are so life-like, that I couldn't believe that they only existed in the author's imagination. This book is told from both Amy's and Elder's point of view. 
 Amy is a typical teen, but she has to make a hard decision whether or not to join her parents on a 300 year journey to a new planet. She is very brave, because if I was in her position, I don't think I would go through with it. After being woken, she has to cope with her new reality. 
 Elder is a not so typical teen. He has been raised on ship to be the next leader. When Amy is woken up, he takes her under his wing, trying to protect her from an unknown murderer. 
 There are some other great characters in this book too. I especially liked Harley, Elder's friend. There are some disturbing issues brought up in this book, but I think that they (the issues) need to be examined and are quite relevant today, as I'm sure they were in the past and will be in the future. After I finished reading, I sat for a bit thinking "WOW, that's some story!". 
 Beth Revis has found a new fan in me, and I'm now looking forward to reading the sequel, A Million Suns. I highly recommend this book if you love YA/science fiction/adventure/action/mystery.

Actual rating 1.5 stars. 
 This was poorly written but the worst part was that she was a seven year old, not a teenager. It creeped me out, how can someone miss so bad in targeting the age?

Liked the premise, didn't care for the structure. Was engaged in the initial story, but lost interest after the jump ahead. 
 First in a trilogy I won't be reading.

This was an okay book. For my first YA Sci-Fi Novel, I was really expecting more... 
 Not to spoil it for anyone else, but I saw EVERYTHING that happened at the end of the book within the first half of the book. All of it. The revelations, the secrets, the reasons everything. It was kinda disappointing. 
 CHARACTERS: 
 Amy and Elder are the main characters and the novel jumps back and forth from their perspectives. Honestly, I didn't see much difference between their viewpoints. Both of them had the same narrative style, they just had better insight into some area of the story (which is fine, it just made it a little confusing resuming the read half-way through a chapter). 
 I was more than a little disappointed that neither character showed much development or change by the end of the story. Amy was still upset, and Elder was still confused and torn. The romance felt a little one-sided to me, and forced. 
 STORY: 
 A really novel (ha-ha) idea. I was really expecting more of a star-trek feel to the book, but was surprised when it kept reminding me of the Giver (dystopian, a ban on emotions and free thought, a single individual chosen to carry on duties as ruler, love interest with flaming red hair, etc.). The Giver freaked me out, but still, I pressed on. 
 There's a few moments that made me antsy in reguards to the sci-fi/YA world. The whole 'season' thing, I could have done without and I don't think the story would have suffered for it. And for those of you who have read it, i don' think Amy needed to go through what she did in the cornfield for the novel. I really didn't see the point. You traumatized her, and them moved on. Not realistic. 
 Finally, I should mention that there's and awful lot of characters talking about death and suicide. I mean, a lot. There's at least two characters who were referenced as having killed themselves, and it plays a big part in the story in two places. 
 OVERALL: 
 Worth it, but know what you're getting into. It's a good read. I'd say it's the giver in space. It's definitely not for the younger YA readers. I'd say 17+ for some of the subjects in it... I might read the next book. I haven't decided yet.

Buddy read with Elizaveta.. Mission complete! 
 Across the Universe is so much more than a Sci-Fi Dystopian book. It has tragedy, romance, action, and even a faction of depression that's usually found in Contemporary novels. The story itself blows your mind and as you discover more secrets about the ship, it draws you in more and more. 
 Story begins with Amy and her parents saying goodbye to each other. Giving an opportunity of a lifetime, they have to be frozen, only to arrive 300 years later at a planet that was recently discovered. But Amy's dad gives her a choice: either to leave her whole life behind and get frozen or stay on Earth. What I loved the most is that she chose family. 
 When she gets unfrozen, she realizes that someone tried to kill her just like they have been doing with several other members. The mystery remains while noone is trying to do anything about it. Amy realizes that the ship itself is a huge mystery and Earth's history may be forgotten a long time ago. 
 With all the mystery and secrets, it usually pretty obvious what happens at the end. But definitely not in Across The Universe. I did not see that coming. At all. And I'm pretty good with freaking things like that. So BRAVO to the author who made me be in the dark until everything was revealed. Definitely recommended for anyone who likes Sci-Fi and doesn't mind the world-building in the ship.

Spoilers btw. 
 So I found this story overwhelmingly frustrating. I was actually sucked in right away. The first description the author used when explaining what a young girl who had been drugged was seeing ended up being an incredibly imaginative and beautiful piece of writing. Then we moved on to the actual story, and dear lord was it 80 leaps and bounds backwards for feminism everywhere. 
 I decided I hated the main character the moment she was complaining about not wanting her hands to smell like gas if she had to fill up her car by herself. However, I shrugged that off and expected that as this story continued, she would learn to be more self-reliant and less shallow. The sad thing is, I think the author really thinks that she accomplished this. I don't know in what universe girls make out with their kidnappers in the middle of the woods, good intentioned ones or no, but I just couldn't believe that was even included. I also couldn't believe she was supposedly in love with him in the end. I really wanted Britt to just become a bad ass, but that never happened. As a matter of fact, she bases her perception of herself on what men think of her. She's supposed to have gotten over this by the end, but it's still based on what her love interests see her as, and has nothing to do with being strong herself. And there was the whole grizzly bear story line that just kind of... went away. I really wanted the bear to eat the bad guy in the end. Instead it just stopped existing and everyone went about their business. Over all it's got some nice descriptions, but the story isn't really worth it.

I am utterly disappointed in this novel... 
 I'm not sure why but something about this story was off for me and it may be the unrealistic characters or love triangle. The characters annoyed me to no end in this novel and while the love story shored between Britt and Jude is fantastic the context in which it is set throws me for two. In a hellish scenario I couldn't imagine someone becoming romantically involved with one of their kidnappers, no matter their motives. 
 Overall this novel is sadly not going to become a favorite of mine.

I'd give 5 stars to the concept of the story and the design of the book, but unfortunately, the story disappointed me a little 
 bit. I'd say it's written in a very unrealistic way, (which is obvious because it's horror) since the story line was just weird. It was still entertaining though but sadly not scary at all.

Hey, Ikea stores are funny and weird right? Wouldn't it be funny to tell a horror story set in an Ikea, 'cause the contrast would be so funny and weird, right? Right...? 
 Make no mistake, this novel is a one trick pony -- once you've absorbed the premise, there's not a whole lot there. Basically, an Ikea-knockoff chain store is built on top of an old prison site and some strange stuff starts to happen. The story covers what happens one night when a peppy assistant manager decides to get to the bottom of things by keeping slacker Amy and upbeat Sue Ann after hours to see if they can catch the overnight intruder/vandal. 
 About halfway through the book, the horror is unleashed: insane homeless dude, waves of rats, hidden passages, slime, grasping hands, restraints, etc. All pretty typical stuff, if effectively rendered. The characters all types, not real characters, and the only reason I read all the way to the end is just to see how it was wrapped up. As a satire of consumer culture, corporate culture, and the modern workplace, it's pretty tame stuff. 
 I will say that the design (size and look of an Ikea catalog) is quite good. Each character opens with a simple Ikea-style diagram of a home furnishing, with item #, etc. and as the book goes on, these get creepier. But ultimately the book is a mildly amusing joke that wears thing pretty quickly.

I would score this book as 4.5/5. 
 I really enjoyed this book. I had high hopes going into this one. Horror elements + an Ikea? Yes please. And though I was a bit worried that I would be disappointed, this book did not let me down. 
 1. Character Development- 
 The character development is quite good. The main character has a pretty solid arc, though for some it may be a little bit too classic. She finds her strength, in many ways, and I think the author did a great job of making that common arc feel genuine. The other characters don't have as much of an arc, but they do have pretty good development. There were one or two instances where it felt like a character's backstory was spoon-fed, but I could certainly overlook it. All-in-all I felt sympathy and understanding for each character. 
 2. Plot- 
 The plot in this story is perfect for me. I don't think it would capture every reader's attention quite like it captured mine, but I'm a sucker for changing ideas, twists, horror, and humor. The reason behind the ~haunted happenings~ is a touch generic, but the author handles it well. I've certainly read and seen the subject matter touched on in this book handled much worse, and much more insensitively. 
 3. Ending- 
 The ending is solid. I'm fond of the way the author wrapped up the storylines, and took the opportunity to stuff in a little more character development. I'm very happy with the character's decisions in the end. 
 4. The Scares??- 
 It's honestly hard for me to judge how good or bad the scares were in this book. Going into it, I was expecting to have exactly 0 scares, mainly because the plot seemed so silly. But there are genuinely scary moments. I found the seance scene to be particularly spooky, though for the most part I was not scared. If you're scared of rats, water, or tight spaces, you may have more of a terrifying time. 
 5. Diversity- 
 I'm quite pleased to say that I was happy with the diversity in this book. For me, it's important to have a diverse range of characters in a book. The main character is female, and her supporting character is an African-American male. The three other characters in the book consist of a racially unspecified older woman, a racially unspecified young woman, and a racially unspecified young man. It could have been a touch more diverse for my liking, but I was happy to be reading a normal story with a female character. If I think deeply about it, each character may be enabling a certain stereotype, but this analyzation could take up an entire essay so I'll leave it at "I'm happy that the characters were diverse".

reference_books.title: Till We Have Faces
reference_books.review_text:
Not quite sure how I feel about this. It's the story of Cupid and Psyche, retold from the sister's point of view with some minor changes. I am assuming the changes are why he wrote the book (otherwise, why write it?) The good stuff comes at the end - really the whole book is just a set up for the last 20 pages of brilliance. 
 Some themes were clear: reason and logic, love and jealousy... Beauty and ugliness, though? That can't be right. I definitely can understand how being ugly translates to loving and fighting for others, but somehow I feel like that wasn't the message. I'm going to be thinking about this one for a while.

reference_books.title: The Other Queen (The Plantagenet and Tudor Novels, #16)
reference_books.review_text: Not my favorite but really interesting nonetheless. There are three narrators: Mary Queen of Scots, and her two "jailers" Bess and George. book_a.title: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child - Parts One and Two (Harry Potter, #8)
book_a.user_review:

 So, I give it two stars - It was ok.

Gaah I never thought I'd ever give anything related to Harry Potter 1 star and yet here I am. 
 SPOILERS BELOW 
 Now if you go in expecting another Harry Potter book, you will be sorely disappointed. If you go in expecting a play which borrows your favourite characters for a story, you'll probably still be disappointed considering JK Rowling's name is attached to this and you expect a certain level of clever writing from her. Alright so she didn't write the whole thing, she did give her stamp of approval. 
 Firstly, no one is in character. Yeah, sure 19 years have passed but there is so much incongruence it's just making my head hurt. I love Ron. I have always loved Ron. But it seems like they forgot how to write Ron. It reads like movie Ron and not book Ron. Do you not remember Ron Weasley who shared his family and home with Harry after only a year of knowing him? Do you not remember Ron who told Sirius that he would have to go through him before killing Harry, when he thought Sirius was a mass murderer? Do you not remember Ron who Hermione fell in love with because he remembered the house elves and went to warn them during the Battle of Hogwarts? But you know, whatever. Let's have Ron only for comic relief, who only thought about food and wore a gravy-stained napkin when his best friend's son went missing. Fuck you. 
 I get Albus. I get it, it can't have been easy being Harry Potter's son and living up to his name. I can understand his frustration and his anger. What I can't get is Harry's reaction to his son. Really, you really think Harry is going to tell him he wished Albus wasn't his son?? Are we basing Harry on his 5th year when he got mad at everything? It's so out of character for him. And don't give me the bullshit that JK Rowling obviously knows her own characters better, because if she did, no way would she treat Cedric like that. 
 Which brings me to Cedric. Cedric Diggory, the boy who was kind above all, became a Death Eater because he was humiliated during the Triwizard Tournament? Is this the same Cedric Diggory we are talking about who wanted a rematch because Hufflepuff won only because Harry fell off his broom? The one who wanted to be fair so told Harry about the Second Task? The one who wanted Harry to take the cup because he felt Harry deserved it more?? Okay, as long as we're clear. This is especially shitty, considering Hufflepuff has almost no other heroes. 
 What about how the only reason Ron and Hermione are together is because Ron got jealous about Krum?? What are you even on about?? 
 Yes, completely murder Draco's character, why don't you?? 
 The worst of all was the plot. The really weird bizzaro plot. Time- Turner? Is this even a plot? It sounds like those memes where people keep suggesting why didn't they just go kill Voldemort when he was a kid? The wacky plot had so many loopholes it'll make you laugh. 
 The only good thing was Harry confronting Dumbledore about leaving him in an abusive household for ten years. 
 Scorpius as a character was really good. He was funny and smart. 
 But the plot. Ugh. 
 My head hurts from all the bullshit. 
 tl;dr I've read fanfics by 15 years old with tighter plots and better characterisation.

I don't even know how to begin. The whole story seamed very far-fetched and cheesy and I think I understand what all the people out there mean when they say it's better to watch the play. It all seemed a little more justified when I was imagining it happening on stage, but it's the script we're talking about and I can't rate it higher than 2/5. 
 The characters - some of them I loved, most of them I felt sorry for. Their dialogues ruined them, made them simple and easy to understand while the originals were much more complicated and that made them truly magical. On the other hand, I just adored Scorpius, Draco and Rose. 
 The plot is something I will never come to terms with. While I think I would love to see it happen live on stage, I will never accept it as an official 8th story. I can't consider it canon, just nope. Some scenes seemed so unreal that even magic couldn't explain them (the trolley witch, cough cough). 
 All in all, I guess I had been prepared for this. I hadn't expected this story to match the previous 7 books. I'm kind of glad I got to know more about Scorpius and some other characters but I will never be able to accept the plot as more than a "what if?" sort of thing.

book_b.title: Bad Feminist
book_b.user_review:
I have a lot to say because this book made me so angry. I had such high expectations, too, which made things worse. 
 Gay's theses are shallow and vapid, and her writing is completely void of cadence, rendering this book both intellectually dry as well as physically difficult to read. I understand that writing for the Internet is different than writing for print in that it is shorter in length and usually rushed to be published, but that seems like a poor excuse for an English professor. Calling this a book of essays is a bit of a stretch; this was a collection of blog posts. Or more accurately, a collection of transcribed rants posted on a blog and then printed in book form. 
 The book starts out with Gay saying that she is a fallible human with contradictions. As I got further in, this retroactively struck me as somewhat manipulative. I would read something stupid and then think, "Oh, but it's okay, she told us she would say stupid things." It's like the literary equivalent of saying "No offense, but..." and then being really offensive. She would also constantly embrace stereotypes that she claimed to reject. But this is allowed, right, because she told us she's full of contradictions!!! 
 I got particularly frustrated after reading few chapters where she said white people in Hollywood shouldn't be allowed to create movies about black people, and then followed it up with a few chapters complaining about the black people who make movies about black people. Nobody wins in this book. Every time I came across a sentence that I thought was inspiring, it turned out to be her quoting somebody else. I read the whole thing because I kept searching for something to show me why people love her so much, but I got to the end empty-handed.

sample_reviews.review_text: Meh.

I wanted to like this book, as I really enjoy Roxanne Gay's point-of-view when I hear her speak. Although I enjoyed some chapters, I did not love that the book was full of critiques of women in pop culture. Probably because I'm not familiar with many of the references. Couldn't finish.

I feel like Bad Feminist in a lot of ways, has always been the voice inside of me, trying to make sense of how I can be me but feminist at the same time. 
 Roxane Gay's collection of essays is a mixture of topics, most notably race, but everything seems to connect itself in ways you may have subconsciously pieced together before but never really took the time to think out. I think she is a breath of fresh air because she is rational. She recognizes both sides of the story in many of her essays, and points out how damn difficult it is to be any one thing. How can we demonize the black kid just walking down the street, and blame him for his own murder, but creepily empathize with the "boy next door" kid responsible for the Boston bombings? These questions and points she makes are so well thought out in how she presents them. It's equal parts awe-inspiring and frustrating. 
 Parts of this book were not written for me. They were not written for the average, white privilege, white girl from the midwest. They weren't meant to speak to me on a personal level, because they are not me. But they did teach me a lot. 
 Because they point out the ludicriousy of white people and our failings to black people and how we marginalize in the smallest ways, ways we don't even realize, but happens to have big consequences. All these little thoughts people have about race, and how they're shared and presented, further perpetuates how we can literally put a black kid on trial for his own death, Gay points out. 
 At times these essays are baffling. You don't want to think of The Help as being detrimental, but quite frankly, now that I've read her perspective on this story, I can't help think it over and realize shes right. But it makes me a bad feminist because I still think its a good movie and a good book. 
 I like that she realizes shes a feminist but a bad one. It gives me hope, somehow. And, it's a relief.
2/5 stars. Some of it is interesting but she is really annoying so half of it I really couldn't handle.
