I think that some points of her essays were great but other points were disjointed and made little to no sense. Several essays could have been left out (that whole thing about green girls was not necessary and made no sense even when I read the essay 3 times to try and get it) and several of them needed something more to them and several needed some editing. I think some of what she talked about was too superficial and didn't go in too deep. However I do like that she brought up certain pieces in feminist literature not being all too great and calling them out for it because we know that certain literature should not be lauded as the end all be all of certain things.

This feels so disconnected to the introduction and title! The pop culture references is grating and I feel like she misses the point of so much.. but that is just my opinion. Not what I was expecting and wouldn't recommend it, if you don't like scrabble..

These essays are incredible. Not because they necessarily shine light upon new ideas and ways of thinking that I've never thought about before but because they are written so well! I can't find any fault. Roxane Gay is open and vulnerable with the reader and everything she says (in my opinion) is smack on - without offending anyone. She justifies herself but really it's just an enjoyable experience to read something that flows so well and includes current popular issues. It makes me sad that in 20 years time these essays will be harder to relate to because the popular culture references will be out of date. But the writing will remain the same at least. The essays are structured well! I've really enjoyed the essays on homosexuality and celebrity culture, race and tv, we need more female directors, art-makers from culturally diverse backgrounds. I believe this so much. Fuck Hollywood and their 7% female directors. 
 equality is not where it needs to be. Gives the feeling that we need to work harder to get things moving forward. But she doesn't shout and make you feel guilty or anything like that. She simply lays down the facts and her opinion and that in itself makes me want to actively change where we're at today with feminism, racism, homosexuality, inequality in every form. 
 I don't necessarily agree with the title of 'bad feminist'. I think she is too hard on herself, in many parts of the book, but this especially. I've never been ashamed to call myself a feminist even if I enjoy 'girly' stuff and can't wait to have children or whatever. That's not what feminism is about for me and I think that's where it goes wrong if it makes people feel like they can't call themselves a feminist because they don't fit into its rigid rules or stereotypes. Every woman should be a feminist without changing who she is or what she enjoys. There's no such thing as a bad feminist. If you believe men and women should be treated equal - you're a goddamn feminist and I hope the title of the book doesn't deter anyone from labelling themselves feminist. 
 Only negative thing would be that the structure of explaining thoroughly in the first couple paragraphs of every essay what the plot of the book, film, tv show, news item etc. got repetitive for me. Also she ruined Gone Girl for me hahah. No spoiler alert or nothin. Shocked and horrified

My review from Stories with Stephanie: 
 I wish everyone would read this book. I'd quote the whole thing at you if I could--I practically did over at my tumblr. Reading these essays was like sitting down with my best friend and having casual but heartfelt discussions about the problematic nature of pop culture and politics, or like delving into a series of the best blog posts ever written about feminism and entertainment. 
 But I don't want to put Gay on a "Feminist Pedestal," a position she intentionally tries to avoid by preemptively labelling herself as a bad feminist: "People who are placed on pedestals are expected to pose, perfectly. Then they get knocked off when they fuck it up. I regularly fuck it up. Consider me already knocked off." 
 Regardless, Gay has a lot to say--about more than just feminism--and she says it well. In 38 essays about gender, sexuality, race, politics, entertainment, and her own life, Gay covers topics ranging from Scrabble to The Hunger Games to Chris Brown to The Help. She's unapologetically candid in sharing her thoughts and experiences, even when it comes to opinions that might not be popular with all her readers (the chapter on trigger warnings comes to mind). 
 I'm sometimes nervous about reading nonfiction essays because I worry they'll be tediously academic or filled with technical jargon, but the beautiful thing about Bad Feminist is that it's so accessible. I hate to use such a cliche word, but it fits here. A lot of feminist texts might be daunting or turn readers off because they address the complex history of feminism and issues of sex and gender in such dry, scholarly language. That's not to say those writers aren't doing important work, but Gay shares her knowledge and experience in a way that turns a feminist text into an intimate reflection and conversation that anyone can join. 
 Part of the reason I loved Bad Feminist so much is because Gay puts into words everything I've felt about sexism in media and politics (see the chapters on 50 Shades of Gray, rape jokes, Chris Brown, and women's reproductive rights). And at the same time, she opened my eyes to so many other issues I'd been ignorant to, often because of my privilege; the essays on race and entertainment were especially enlightening. 
 I only had one issue with Bad Feminist. In her last essay, Gay says she is "failing as a feminist," and as proof she points to her desire to be taken care of, her affinity for the color pink, her appreciation for music with lyrics that degrade women, and so on. "If I take issue with the unrealistic standards of beauty women are held to, I shouldn't have a secret fondness for fashion and smooth calves, right?" Wrong. I think this is one of the biggest misconceptions about feminism (and feminists are, admittedly, partly to blame). 
 It's OK to shave your legs and like makeup, as long as you're doing it for yourself and not because the beauty industry tells you you should. It's OK to like movies or books that are problematic, as long as you understand and acknowledge why they're problematic. Being a "good feminist" doesn't mean hating men and babies, being totally independent, and not shaving your legs. 
 Being a good feminist means advocating for equal rights for men and women, calling out sexism when you see it, and being critical of media that promotes misogyny, rape culture, or domestic violence. In this sense, Roxane Gay is not a bad feminist--in fact, she's the complete opposite--and I think she knows that. But good or bad, she's still a feminist, and that's a wonderful thing to be.
REVIEW TO COME

3.6 stars 
 I couldn't help but compare this book to Lena Dunham's (Not that Kind of Girl). Is that fair? No. But the pink, black, and white covers were begging for it. 
 Though annoyingly repetitive, the intro had me psyched. Especially compared to Lena's intro. Roxane Gay, thank you for not claiming to be perfect. For not claiming to know it all. 
 I struggled a bit as I read this, anticipating how I would talk about it with other people. I wanted to love it. But no one gets a free pass. Though they are arranged loosely by topic, the essays have a haphazard nature (I was entertained by the Scrabble one, but it definitely should have been cut!) and are often overstuffed with similar and repeated ideas. 
 And though I was on board for a more modest and grounded style of writing, I still often found myself confronted by a viewpoint that felt offensively narrow. It's okay and even laudatory (if not solipsistic) to write about your own experiences, but I was surprised to see how many times Roxane Gay discounted perspectives that differed from her own. (Skinny girls have body issues, too, please. And it's not just men who are guilty of reading almost only books written by men, and on and on). 
 So I'm conflicted... but that's okay. What's important is that we have these conversations.

reference_books.title: The Time Keeper
reference_books.review_text:
Mitch Albom always had a way to make the readers think. This time, he used a mythical figure, a legend of Father Time, and retold the story in such a beautiful way. I loved how he described the way time was invented in a very touching story, and combined it with two different stories from modern times. The only complaint I have is about the climax near the end of the book - a bit Disney's fairy tale for my taste =) anyway, a very good read to remind us why does God give us a limit time in the world. 
 ps: my rating is actually 3,5 stars. I blamed Goodreads for the inaccuracy of the rating!

reference_books.title: Inferno (Robert Langdon, #4)
reference_books.review_text: Aww... I don't know, I think I just got bored with Dan Brown. Probably if I read this book before I read all of Brown's previous ones, I would like it better. But the formula is too predictable for me now, nothing new (except of course the exotic new cities), and there's this amnesia plot that for me is just a bit dull. Langdon is confused as usual - I really hope Brown creates another hero/heroine in his next book. I love the description of the cities and museums but the repetitive explanation about Dante's Inferno is a bit much for me. I don't know. Maybe next book will be more fun?

reference_books.title: A Thousand Splendid Suns
reference_books.review_text: another masterpiece from one of my fave authors...

reference_books.title: Have a Little Faith: a True Story
reference_books.review_text: In the beginning, this book reminds me too much of the beloved Tuesdays with Morrie - only more like a copycat. But in the middle of the book, I fell in love with the way Mitch Albom described his Reb. Genuine, very human and oh so lovable, this book is so much more than just a story about religion and faith. And again, I was reminded of why I love Albom's writings since I read them for the first time, many many years ago.

reference_books.title: The Sixty-Eight Rooms (Sixty-Eight Rooms, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Interesting story about Jack and Ruthie, who found a magic key that could shrink and bring them to the miniature houses in Chicago Art Institute, living in the small rooms and meeting many historical figures. Combining adventures, mystery and history, this is a very cozy book for middle grade booklovers =)

book_a.title: Americanah
book_a.user_review: I like all the references about culture (especially race) in America, since I've been working with Americans for quite some time and I feel the stories are relevant. I can connect well with many references in this book. But I don't really like Ifemelu the main character- her self righteousness and judgmental tendency made me dislike her even more. I also don't like the ending- the romance part sucks in my opinion, and not necessary. Too bad though. I love the idea of this book and the importance of its the theme. Hence the generous 4 stars!

sample_reviews.review_text: A beautiful romance novel about race and culture but also a satirical coming of age tale. The core themes are identity and choice, or lack of. The focus on the importance of hairstyles for African women seemed a bit odd at first but makes complete sense by the end. Clever stuff.

Flawless. Suffering from a book hanger upon completion of this. I'm still to engrossed in Ifem and Obinze's world to move onto another book. 
 My only complaint (and this has nothing to do with the content): this edition daunted me, so it took me awhile to get into this book, a book that otherwise would've grabbed me immediately. The font was small and the line spacing was very small, and that made it a bit difficult to read. I would've much preferred a longer book with manageable type (which, I realise, would've cost the publishers more).
Love the writing style but just didn't excite me at all! Super Disappointing!

I loved this book. Adichie is a writer in the classic sense - an observer who directs the reader's gaze to give insight into lives we might otherwise know nothing about. I found this book to be wholly current and absorbing. I will be reading more of her work.
It was such a pleasure to read this book. Didn't want it to end.

One of the best novels I've read recently! At first, I really didn't know what to expect, I thought the story would revolve around Ifemelu--which I couldn't tell the gender of--and her returning from America. However, the story turned into this bittersweet nostalgia of her childhood and adolescence in Lagos, her youthful love life with Obinze and, ultimately, what drove them apart. This book encompasses everything I need to know about Africa, specifically Nigeria, and breaks every myths about African countries that I know thus far. It teaches me the difference between an African-American (or 'black people') and African people. I've always felt like there is this thick cultural difference between them two--like, would an African-American know of their ancestors and their family history before they came to the USA?--and to have it so eloquently put in the form of fiction, bordering reality, is something close to an enlightenment. More over, it answers the confusion about race and its different meanings to different cultures. In Indonesia, we don't talk about race much either, despite there being so many races and tribes among us. Yes, there are conflicts sometimes, but we don't turn it into a political agenda. 
 The way that it is written is simply beautiful. I love seeing the development of all the characters, most especially Ifemelu and Obinze. And how, though subtle, every little moment seems to lead up to something bigger; to have an entirely more solid meaning. There are times in the book when Ifemelu and Obinze's relationship seems like a faraway memory in sepia colour, asking to be remembered in a melancholic sense. I root for them and it breaks my heart that they drifted apart when Ifemelu was in America. I think their relationship symbolises something other than their difference, but also their innocence, because when it ended, they both had to face the hardships of the world and realise they can no longer hide behind the curtain called youth. And that day Ifemelu decided to go to the US, she was taking a step into a life she can never change back.

Americanah is the story of Ifemelu and Obinze, two Nigerian people who have very different experiences of immigration. Ifemelu leaves Nigeria as a young woman to complete her studies in America. Thirteen years later she is still there, having established a successful career for herself as a blogger, but she has now made the decision to go home. Before she returns to Lagos, Ifemelu goes to an African hair salon in Trenton, New Jersey, to have her hair braided - a process which takes six hours, giving her time to reflect on all the things she has learned and observed during her years in America. 
 Obinze, who was Ifemelu's boyfriend before she left Nigeria, also has dreams of going to America but is unable to obtain a visa and ends up working in London as an illegal immigrant. Obinze and Ifemelu are eventually reunited in Lagos, but will their love have survived so many years of separation? 
 As promised on the book cover, there is a love story to be found in Americanah, but this is not the main focus of the novel. The focus is on Ifemelu and her life in America, with several chapters following Obinze and his experiences in England. On arriving in the country that will be her home for the next thirteen years, Ifemelu faces a lot of challenges and difficulties, ranging from finding a job to learning how to cook hot dogs! She has many encounters with examples of racism (sometimes very subtle and sometimes much more obvious) and at the other end of the scale, people who are trying too hard to avoid talking about race because they're afraid that they might cause offence. All of this gives Ifemelu plenty of material for her blog, which she calls "Raceteenth, or Various Observations About American Blacks (Those Formerly Known as Negroes)" by a Non-American Black. 
 Some excerpts from Ifemelu's blog posts are included in the book and are fascinating to read, particularly when she writes about the differences between being a black American and a non-American black person. Something I found interesting was Ifemelu's comment that "I came from a country where race was not an issue; I did not think of myself as black and I only became black when I came to America." This is in contrast to her cousin, Dike, who leaves Nigeria with his mother as a very young child and so has a very different perspective on life. 
 While I didn't love Americanah quite as much as I'd hoped to, it was full of insightful observations and it's a book that I would recommend to everyone, whatever your race, nationality or skin colour. As a white person, I confess that many of the aspects of race discussed in the novel are things that have never even occurred to me. So, as a commentary on race and immigration, I thought this book was excellent - the best I've read on these subjects. The various devices Adichie uses (blog posts, discussions at dinner parties, the conversations of the women working in the hair salon) give her an opportunity to explore important issues in an interesting and often witty way rather than just lecturing the reader. 
 Purely as a novel, though, I thought Americanah was less successful. It felt a lot longer than it really needed to be, considering the plot is not a particularly complex one, and while I was interested in following Ifemelu's and Obinze's separate storylines, I found I didn't really care whether they got back together at the end of the book or not. I think for me personally this is a book I enjoyed on an intellectual level rather than an emotional one, which is not necessarily a negative thing, but probably the reason why, of the two books I've now read by Adichie, I prefer Half of a Yellow Sun to this one.

Finished this book in two days...at first I was excited because of the many recommendations from my friends and the high expectations I had from reading Chimamanda's previous novels. This, of all her works, disappointed me a lot. really. There were so man characters...it was almost impossible to keep up with them and the very many scenes and sketchy sketchy scenes. Also, there was so much negative energy in it. I did not like it. I almost regretted buying it but...meh! At least I have one more book in my library that I do not like.

This book was given to me by a friend and I am very much obliged to her. I would probably not have read it otherwise. When I was young I was very much into books about other cultures and about tragic real life or historical events. The more personal, the better. Today I tend to avoid books that make me sad or are devoid of hope. And this book isn't one of those ;-) It is full of life and people that feel real to me. The story and the writing made the reading a joyful experience, and it has many, many eye opening moments. The book may also have changed some of my perspectives on life and politics. Not bad, eh?

I really liked it, but I had some problems. One thing is that it was very slowly. The second thing that bothered me was that the topics were discussed over and over again. That much that in the end I was kind of tired about it. The ending was also kind of obvious. Most people also wished that there was more character development and a plot; I agree only a little bit. I wasn't bothered with it so much. I still highly recommend this book, because I do like the blog aspect, some of the topics that were discussed, the love story and that it's about a Nigerian who moves to America. But if you haven't read anything by Adichie yet, I recommend to read Purple Hibiscus first. I still haven't read Half of The Yellow Sun yet, so I can't say which of hers is my favorite (but I think it's going to be Purple Hibiscus).

book_b.title: The Secret History
book_b.user_review: Okay. Where should I start? Honestly I expected more on this book. I love Special Topics (Marisha Pessl) and so many people recommended this book when they know about my feeling toward Pessl's book. But turned out, it's too much lagging for my taste - big language and too serious convos, even though there are several great jokes and witty characters inside (I love Francis the most, he's so comical). There are no mystery - only some puzzling philosophical and psychological stuff, with lots and lots reference to Greek, even the tragedy theme of this book is referred to the Greek stories. I love the campus part - a new England college with many kinds of students. But to tell you the truth, I expected more.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This is about a group of college students who are so jaded, so filled with ennui, that they are driven to fill their spare time with incest and murder. Please. I find it hard to believe that this group of soul-less, limp, uninterested and uninteresting fops would put the effort into either of those endeavors. 
 Donna Tartt is actually capable of great writing, but for a better story, try "The Little Friend".

A compelling cast of characters (all of whom I found completely loathsome and fascinating at the same time...I'm still grappling with it), an interesting setting of a New England college, and the absolutely brilliant way that the author instantly pulls the reader into this story of murder. Right from the first chapter, you find out who was killed and by whom. The rest of the book pieces together the events that lead up to the horrific act and then the aftermath. 
 I found the book interesting and it kept me reading, though at times I thought the writing to be a bit long-winded. Much like Tartt's recent novel "The Goldfinch," cutting some of it down would have been beneficial for keeping more interest and keeping the plot intact...in my opinion. Warning for lots of drugs and language within these pages, not to mention the dark subject matter.

Jag ar personligen inte sa fortjust i laskiga eller alltfor spannande bocker, men for en nagot ovan deckarlasare ar denna perfekt. Den hemliga historien ar valdigt spannande, men den innehaller ocksa valdigt tydliga och starka karaktarer och det kanns som att lasaren ar en i ganget, och darfor blir spanningen mindre laskig och mer trovardig. Tartts bok innehaller flera overraskningar och blir aldrig trakig, trots att den ar 703 sidor lang. 
 Den hemliga historien lamnar lasaren med en valdigt mysig kansla, men ocksa ett behov av eftertanke och en langtan efter att fa umgas mer med karaktarerna.

I have finally given up on this book. I know it is supposed to be like Carol Goodman, but it defiantly is not. The story dragged until the point I finally gave up reading it. As a person who reads several books a week, this book took me almost 2 months to get through and I never finished. I would not recommend this book.

This books was good. Really good. But, but all it's beautiful prose and realistic characterization, the plot did not move forward swiftly enough to captivate me. I feel the plot was sacrificed -very deliberately- to the exploration of the characters and their inner selves. The story was about the people, not about the events. And much like in real life you spend all this time getting to know the characters, but unable to rally articulate what they are about, or who they truly are.

Oh my goodness, I am sure that Donna Tartt is a lovely person, but man oh man I found this book pretentious. I was so bored, I couldn't wait to get through listening to these self obsessed people with no moral conscience. I almost quit reading halfway through but as I hate not finishing a book if I start, I slogged through and finished. I wish I could say that the end perked up but for me, the ending seemed out of character and rushed after 500 pages of draggieness.Can't say that I will be reading this one again really soon, not sure why it is on so many must read lists...

There is more that I don't like about this book than there is that I do like. I like the idea that studying ancient literature can be transformative. Certainly the Victorians thought so. But I don't care for the main character; I don't understand why he has no history and no personality. I also think the whole Separate-Peace-Lord-of-the-Flies plot about a group all betraying one another has been done to death and is boring. And while I appreciate the fact that the hidden roots of magic and psychology within one another are pointed out, the idea that failing to avoid transformative catharsis leads to crime and death is a gross overstatement. Generally I disagree with the apparent premise of the book and dislike all the characters, so there is little left to enjoy.

I enjoyed this book, and I don't know if my reservations about it are enough for me to discourage anyone from reading it. 
 I sometimes felt that the book was too focused on being a tragedy -- it is by no means a happy book. I can't really say more without spoiling the book, but if the author had cranked back the dial on the drama-rama, I probably would have enjoyed the book more.

It could have been a great book for me - had the writer kept the language and tone a little less morose and simpler - it was too much effort to keep myself in the flow of the thriller. 
 The concept of a murder mystery in reverse is great, and so are the seven main characters with their shades of grey ...! Disturbing

I've been meaning to read this book for almost 20 years, since its original publication. Strangely, I think I would have absolutely loved it had I read it back then. Tartt is an extraordinarily gifted writer - one of the best out there at creating a moody, unsettling environment for her troubled characters. Having said that, I found myself putting the book down time and time again. Leaving aside the murder at the heart of the story, The Secret History reminded me unpleasantly of all the things I don't miss about university: aimless blocks of time, unworthy mentors, unreliable friends, existential anxiety and bad weather. But maybe that explains the book's perennial popularity - it captures a period of life that is unquestionably formative but, thankfully, fleeting.

reference_books.title: Changes (The Dresden Files, #12)
reference_books.review_text: Holy Cliffhanger, Batman!!!!!!!!

reference_books.title: Open Minds (Mindjack Series, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I figured I should do a review of this book, since I read it recently and I guess I am still thinking about it. You must be thinking, "Wow Sam, you're still thinking about this book. It must be good!" Then you see my two star rating and you're confused. Well don't be. Yes, I'm thinking about this book, but hardly in any way that is positive. In fact, the more I think about it the more I kind of dislike it. But I'll try to get this out of me before, the rating drops any more. 
 As with all of my reviews to come, I will do my best to not include any spoilers. 
 I'll start out with the positive. The writing is good. The general idea of the novel is pretty decent. Most of the world is now operating free of speech and solely with their thoughts. The technology reflects that and it is used well throughout the book. I liked it. I didn't love it, but I liked it. Our main character, Kira, is not capable of this mind to mind communication and is labeled a Zero. Zeros can't have their minds read and therefore she is branded as untrustworthy. 
 Again, I like the idea of this. It seems pretty realistic, that people who can't have their minds read would be treated harshly when everyone else must have their minds out in the open for everyone to judge and whatnot. So sixteen year old Kira is dealing with things a sixteen year old girl would probably be dealing with if they were her. I'm guessing. You'll have to forgive me for being a guy and not being certain. SO that's pretty much the positive I can give you. Everything else is... well, not positive. 
 The story from here is basically this. "I'm special, but that's sooooooo scary. Oh you're special too, we should totally date. Screw that other guy who's not special and has been like totally awesome to me my whole life. Oh there's a special group of these special people who want me to join, so I can do some special things. These special people are bad, but they're not, but they are, but maybe, oh well. Then enter the government baddies, who know about us special people and they want us to be in special camps. It turns out that now I'm even more special, so I should use my special specialness to get out of here and save special people who are put into this special camp only to be taken out of the camp, three seconds later." I could continue, but I think you get the point. 
 The whole progression of this story completely relies on people who are bad or worst and Kira being one of the only good people, besides her family, alive apparently. The bad and worst people are simply dumb. They're all adults who have been living as one of these special people for a long time, but Kira is so special that she can out-special them all. It's just not a very good story. It feels like everything just kind of happens without much sense to it. It doesn't feel natural. Just forced story mechanic upon forced story mechanic. Then it's explained in a non-satisfying way. 
 I hate to say bad things about anybody's story because I know it takes a lot to write one, but jeez this just was not a good book. I just didn't care about any of the characters. When one of them died, I was literally just like, "cool, that happened." 
 I also really wish that the "fighting" was cooler. This book definitely needed something to spice it up a bit. Needless to say, but I don't think I'll be continuing with the series. This book's ending, like most of the book, just felt flat. 
 Of course, I am but a humble reader and this is only my opinion. Please take that into consideration :D

reference_books.title: The Butterfly Garden (The Collector #1)
reference_books.review_text: 3.5 Stars

reference_books.title: The Magicians (The Magicians #1)
reference_books.review_text: I tried to finish this book. Really I did. Maybe someday... Maybe. Oh but if you want my brief opinion on what I did read I shall tell you. It is like if a friend called you up and said "hey man/lady dude you want to come over and have a pizza with all your favorite things on it?" Then you're like "ill be right there" and you go over for pizza and the pizza has everything you hate on it and then your friend implores you to stay for an episode of the jewelry channel. . That's what this book is. A big ole boring disappointment. I know this is not a very helpful 'review' so by all means please go read the book if you think you might like it but I just could not get into it.

reference_books.title: Wool
reference_books.review_text:
Hmm... So Wool. This book. This bloody book.... sigh. 
 Hugh Howey is a indie-author phenomenon. And that is surprising to me.. Not to say he is bad. He's not. He's just middle of the road. Mediocre in all ways except for his success which is by all means amazing. But what do I know... I am just a human with his humble little opinion. 
 Wool definitely had its moments, but other parts of it were just a drag, making the story just fall flat. People are living in a post-apocalypse wasteland where they are only safe inside a giant silo that extends far into the earth. I mean like hundreds of feet into the earth. Like skyscrapers except down. Lots of floors. I mean LOTS. So as you can imagine there are lots of stairs that are used frequently. But that's okay, if you get tired there are also elevators. Wait. No, there are not. There are zero elevators. Only walking is allowed. Even if you're old and dying and dead already. That's rough, buddy. You walk. 
 And that's most of the story. Walking. It gets to feeling like every step is being described. (I exaggerate, but still!) Walking and walking. Thinking and thinking. More walking, more thinking. Then talking. Then walking... 
 It gets tiring... Like all that walking. I'm tired. Sigh..... 
 Up then down. Drink some water. MEMORY TIME. Someone's dead. Repeat. Plot moves forward, the pawns die, the story continues! Then there is a love story thrown somewhat randomly into the mix. It should not have been... 
 Hugh Howey is not a bad writer. He has some characters that are okay. I just never really cared about anyone. And this was a story that seriously needed you to care about the characters... I don't know. Maybe I'm being a bit tough on this book. I don't mean to be. It just really didn't leave much of an impression on me. I was expecting more and I was just let down. 
 But hey I guess it's unique. I, myself have never come across a story that was quite like this one. Whether that is because my "Read" list is pitiful or because of its uniqueness might be up for debate, though. 
 Still some parts held my attention, keeping me interested through this easy read.

book_a.title: Best Served Cold
book_a.user_review:
This was hard to get through. I loved The First Law Trilogy. Loved it. The Shattered Sea Trilogy fell apart in my opinion, but it was still okay. This. This was just a mess. Boring for more than most of it. A lack of cleverness throughout. And most characters were so meaninglessly selfish and asshole-ish, that you couldn't be bothered with caring about them, even slightly. So who cares when they die? I don't. 
 Sigh. That being said Abercrombie can still write well. And though I said that I didn't care about his characters, they weren't all that bad. It's a shame they were forced into this boring story of revenge that is mixed with a side story of revenge and topped off with some more finely grated revenge. Also, for now till forever, it's served with a cold glass of revenge. Salt lightly for enhanced flavor. 
 The world which was interesting and mystical in the First Law Trilogy only has specks of that kind of wonder here and it is mostly disregarded so we could follow some dumb lady's revenge for hundreds of pages. (Or a couple dozen hours in my case as I listened to the audio book. The Narrator was fantastic and likely the only reason I finished this book.) 
 Maybe it wouldn't have been all that bad, but I was saving this book, hoarding it away and expecting it to be a treat once I finally decided to devour it. Because surely the world of the First Law Trilogy would surely be worth revisiting no matter the story it was paired with, yeah? Nope. Just nope. 
 Wish it weren't so. Really, I do.

sample_reviews.review_text:
After devouring Abercrombie's First Law Trilogy, I was keen to jump into his next bit of fiction, also set in the same world that Logan Nine Fingers calls home. Like his first books, this one is full of colorful characters doing interesting things, with clever dialogue and internal monologues - although nothing along the line of 'you have to be realistic'. 
 Alas, although the cast of Best Served Cold is cut from the same dark cloth Abercrombie used so ably before, here it quickly bleeds to blackest black. This is revenge fantasy, sure, and it shouldn't be surprising that cold-blooded murder is the only thing on the menu. Everybody has their reasons, good ones too. That said, I put the book aside three-quarters finished for some 6 months after the story's lone moral compass becomes more of a monster than his deplorable comrades. 
 This slide is handled realistically, but when you trash the only likable character so ably, you leave no one to root for, and that is a problem. Fiction grants the chance to look inside a person, to understand his motives. In this way, even the darkest of characters can become sympathetic. But for the final part of this book, I couldn't empathize with any of the characters. I was emotionally disconnected, although Abercrombie still won the rare smile with a clever bit of dialogue. 
 I forced myself to finish the story recently. It is interesting to the last, and I've already started the next book - 'The Heroes', also set in this same universe, but thankfully centered on some different characters. But I'm unlikely to ever revisit this book.

Short review: a woman kills seven men. 
 Set in the same world as his previous books, a rather nice addition if you've read those, I don't think it stands by itself very well. 
 The book is divided in 7 parts, each one a kind of "Ocean's 11" type deal, which often leads to unexpected results. The characters are well written and it's occasionally very funny. Bloody, but funny.

This was a good book, set in the same universe and slightly after the events in Joe Abercrombie's First Law series. It is an independent story, but does involve some of the minor characters from that previous series. I would recommend the original trilogy over this book; but if you would like to see more of that universe this is a decent continuation. The plot revolves, as the title suggests, around revenge and one woman's quest for it. This is not an uplifting book.

Real close to putting a three star review on this one but only due to a couple scenes I didn't care for. In no way am I a prude but the sex scenes were a little too much for me. Overall the story was very good to me though, reminded of Oceans Eleven with murder instead of burglary.

I'm gonna be honest: I got 75% of the way through this, then I just googled the plot. It took me THREE WEEKS to get that far. I had absolutely ZERO CLUE which of the characters I was supposed to like, and there was so much pointlessly descriptive prose that I had bugger all desire to see how it all turned out. 
 I really enjoyed the Blade Itself trilogy, and I've no doubt I'll read more of Joe's stuff, but this just meandered with little of interest going on, as though it was concerned more with getting a huge page count than a driven plot. Like it's title, it left me cold. 
 EDIT: I forced myself and skim read to the end. Nothing above has changed.

I wanted this book to be better than it was. I'm not sure what was missing for me but it was something...perhaps a decent editor? Maybe it was the fact that I had no comassion for the main character...I liked the roguish Nicomo Costas but he was the only truly interesting character in the whole story. I kept thinking the book was going to get better but it just never manifested.
I loved it so much and hated it in equal parts. 4 stars because the end frustrated me a lot, but if I hadn't loved the story - and Shivers - I wouldn't have cared.
Not a children's book. You got to love battle and revenge. I love how Abercrombie's characters have character.

What a great read. This was a dark fantasy novel that was very graphic and barbaric...never a dull moment that's for sure! Too bad this wasn't a series. I look forward to his new book Heroes when it comes out.

I always pay close attention to the first sentence in any book. A tone is being set, if nothing else, but often, the focus of what follows is revealed in just a few words. So when I began "Best Served Cold" (Orbit, $24.99, 512 pages), and read "The sunrise was the colour of bad blood," I figured Joe Abercrombie was going to be taking me on a bloody, dark ride. 
 Sadly, I was correct, and "Best Served Cold" is 500 pages of blood, betrayal, bones, agony, betrayal, blood, bones and more agony. And really, this isn't even fantasy, as it's basically a historical pastiche of the 15th and 16th centuries with made-up countries. But, for example, the heroine is named Monza Murcatto, and the man who sets her on a trail of revenge is Duke Orso. There's no magic (though one character is basically superhuman), no dragons (for which small mercy many thanks) and nothing but swords, knives and poison. 
 Abercrombie is a good writer (he does a wonderful job getting inside the head of a mentally unbalanced character obsessed with numbers) and he has things to say about vengeance and life, but after about 300 pages of swords slipping through bodies, and red froth bubbling from characters' mouths, I confess I began to tire. There's some explicit sex (in a ratio of about one to five hundred in terms of explicit violence) and plenty of words the FCC would ban, but in general, this is a book about violence and the costs of revenge, both physical and spiritual. For what it is, it's pretty good, but, as perceptive readers have noticed, I'm not that excited about reading a long book that focuses on the color of bad blood.

book_b.title: The Body Reader
book_b.user_review: 3.5 Stars

sample_reviews.review_text: I didn't want to put this one down. It started with a bang and didn't slow down. I did have a willful suspension of disbelief moment or two with regard to our main character's quick return to the police department, not once, but twice, but was more than willing to let that go in light of seeing how this story would unfold. Lived the characters and hope this is only the first if many adventures for the Body Reader. Read a NetGalley version of this ebook.

"One day she stopped screaming." With these chilling words, the reader is plunged into the nightmare world of Jude Fontaine. For three hellish years, Jude Fontaine has been the prisoner of a sadistic captor. Filthy, starved, and beaten, she barely clings to her sense of self. Then for one moment, she has an opportunity to escape. But freedom is difficult. Her boyfriend has moved on. Her partner on the police force doesn't think Jude is mentally fit for police duty. Just maintaining an aura of normalcy can be a challenge for Jude. 
 Then the body of a missing teen is found. What looks like a drowning accident is murder. Then another teen girl is found dead. Someone from Jude's past is connected to the murders. The investigation will bring Jude face to face with old demons and challenge her sanity. 
 Author Anne Fraiser has created the most believable story about the mental and physical torment of a kidnap victim. Jude Fontaine is a mesmerizing heroine. Despite the physical and emotional abuse of her kidnapper, she struggles to survive. After escaping, she fights to take control of her life. But she is no victim. She is a kickass heroine. She is the best female character since The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo. 
 However, this novel is much better written than Stieg Larrson's debut novel. As with all of Fraiser's novels, there is amazing depth to the secondary characters. In particular, the mother of a missing teen girl resonates with humanity. The plot twists and turns. There are betrayals. In the end, I was left wanting to read more about Jude and her partner, Uriah Ashby.

So you're seeing everyone else's 4 and 5 star ratings, and you're probably wondering why I've rated it one star. I just can't think of anything to like about this books: 
 The characters - flat and unsympathetic. A few years ago I read a Jussi Adler Olson book about a woman kept prisoner for years. That book made me cry and feel so much empathy with the characters. This made me feel the opposite - I didn't like Jude. She was completely one dimensional to me. 
 The plot - completely unbelievable. I don't mind thrillers are far-fetched. I'd say that most thrillers do need to stretch credibility to be exciting, but this was just plain ridiculous. 
 The baddies (every thriller needs them) were so bloomin' obvious a blind mole could have spotted them. 
 This bad book was made worse by the dreadful narration of the audiobook. Worst narrator I have ever heard. It sounded like a robot was reading - urgh!

Kidnapped, held hostage for three long years, abuse victim Jude Fontaine gained her freedom. After that, she went back to being a homicide detective. 
 Jude is not a fluffy air-head. She is strong in so many ways. She freed herself from her rich but less than ideal family at the young age of sixteen. That takes some doing, because a judge had to agree with that. 
 Lots of changes happened in the world while she was a captive, and many of them are devastating to Jude. She has a new skill, one she will need. She learned to "read" her captor. Now, a girl is dead and it's so much like her entire case that her years of captivity are starting to get confused with her current reality, or are they? 
 Uriah Ashby is her ally. He is on the force and his wife is dead. He becomes more important in Jude's life and I think we might see more of them together in another book. However, it will be a challenge because this book dove deep, and hard. It covers abuse and rape as well as a page turning mental thriller. 
 My copy came from Net Galley in exchange for my honest review and nothing more.

2 Stars. I wanted to like this book. For a while it looked like it was going to be a really good book but things never came together for me. Jude was abducted and manages to escape 3 years later. Four months after her escape she gets her job back as a homicide detective. I was willing to over look this unrealistic bit but things got more ridiculous. Her first case is a major murder case and her father is a high up politician. She has nothing to do with her family because she believes her father murdered her mother. Jude then links her case with some old ones. Loses her job puts around the house then manages to solve the case. Her partner wasn't really supportive and dismissed her theories. Mostly treating her like she's crazy. 
 The big sell for me to even pick up with book was the skill she picked up while kidnapped. She was supposed to be this great body language reader. However her skills were so/so and not used well. 
 I don't normally read these kinds of books but I am a fan of Agatha Christie. In the end I guess I know too much about psychology and police to find this book realistic or believable. If I was going to set up this book in one word it would be disappointed.

After three years of captivity and sensory deprevation, Jude Fontaine returns to work in Minneapolis as a homicide detective. She quickly becomes involved in a case of murdered and missing girls that comes too close to home. 
 I really enjoyed this book. Jude is a very interesting character, who, despite her often incomprehensible behavior is right on course, even if everyone else is not. And her partner has his own personal beasts to battle. The story was engaging and I really got involved with it. I think the writing was very good for this sort of book. I could see the places and almost smell the smells. I plan to read more Anne Frasier and hope to see more of Jude in the future.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Ranting ahead.... 
 when i started this, i was expecting the h to be somewhat of a better cop after undergoing some type of torture.... what I didn't expect was the story of how she was tortured,escaped, badly handling it with equally badly handling wifes death of a partner, who doesn't trust her and a shit load of personal issues with her father ... AND I absolutely did NOT expect the whole story to be revolving around her...even the crimes... I mean, seriously, her father is involved, her brother is involved and everyone ends up dead. I f this was a series starter... it was epic fail. 
 why couldn't she have established herself as a good cop, better after troubled past, solving cases uniquely and then after few books introduce how her family is involved with a crime and she solves it...NOOO ... what she gets is powerful father,hated family and gets accused of being mad...since she was a kid... and really!! was it necessary for us to read how badly she was tortured pages and pages??

I went into this book pretty sure of what I was getting. A fast, trashy read with murder and obsessive cops. It started out well. A woman held captive for three years escapes, killing her abductor. We later find out she's a homicide detective. So the first thing she does, starving, abused, and turned into an animal? Buy a motorcycle of course! A couple months later, she's back on the beat! 
 *Audible groan* 
 Okay, all that is good, clean trashy fun. The parts that took me out of it were the bits about Jude's senator father who *gasp* probably killed her mother. They didn't fit and seemed like a lot of filler. I don't know if the plotline came to anything, but the constant reminder that Jude is just another rich girl with a tortured past totally turned me off. And every time it was mentioned, it felt like I was being pulled out of the story. 
 Granted, this was a DNF for me because, you guys, I just couldn't. Usually I'm all for these creepy formulaic things. They're like trashy television or cop shows. They're like a warm blanket to snuggle up to when I'm feeling stressed. But not this time, sadly. Luckily I only paid 1.99 for this. I don't usually write bad reviews, but this was a bad one, and I thought a warning was appropriate.

5 Mind Blowing Stars 
 Take a chance on a new author if you haven't read any of Ms. Frasier work this would be a great one to pick but hold your breath it is going to be a bumpy ride. Ms. Frasier will blow you away with another read you won't be able to put down. Just when I thought I had a handle on the outcome the author sent me on another spin that let me saying WOW. I was hooked from the first page to the last this was not an easy book to lay down. This is one author that has fast become one of my all time favorites that I can't wait until another book is published. If this isn't on your TRB list it should be. If you love mystery, thrills and suspense you do not want to miss reading this. I promise you don't know what you are missing as the author hooks you from start to finish. I have read and listened to the audio I am really having a hard time picking which I like the best. Both have good points but both are outstanding. 
 Emily Sutton-Smith does an outstanding job of narration. She pulls you in giving you wonderful character voices with outstanding emotions never leaving you guessing how each characters feels. Her tones are right on the money for each emotion that each characters has. She gives you a very rich and clear audio that you get lost in and do not want to put down. Her character voice for Jude is flat like it should be with all this poor women has gone through is there any wonder she shows very little emotion. Emily hits it right on the money. Her male voices are just a wonderful as her female ones giving you an even tone clear listen you get lost in. There are no background noises or any places where the volume is higher or lower that the other. There are no repeats of words, if a break was taken you cannot tell it. This is the first I have listen to this narrator but it will not be the last. She really brought this audio to life for me. 
 As the story opens you have a lady who is and has been kept in a basement nude, alone with only one person who feeds her and abuses her over and over again. As you turn the pages to start this story your mind will hold a picture of each scene once you close your eyes your mind will replay it over and over again. You will become Jude and feel her pain, you understand her as she takes on a life of hunted to being the hunter looking for her prey at every turn. She can tell what you are thinking by your body language. There are those that think she is crazy but we know her and me that she is most likely the sanest of all. Three years of living this nightmare over and over again each day and night you would think she would have gone crazy but you are very much wrong. When you have nothing but time on your hands for years you watch, look and read before long you know what people are thinking just by the way they hold their head, turn their body or let out a breath. She pulls her inner strength knowing one day somehow some way she will make it out of this alive and when she does someone is going to die. It is kill or be killed so she sets, waits, listen, waiting for the right time to make her move to set herself free. That day is today when the lights go out she makes her move running for her life she is out she is free but for how long and what waits for her on the other side. 
 I really loved Jude she is so strong yet so cool taking it all in moving around watching reading everyone's body knowing who is lying and who is hiding things. The author has an outstanding way of making the words flow easy before your eyes taking you in and making you part of the story. Before you know it you are so hooked you can't put the book down. This is not a story I would want to start at night you really need to start it early so you can give it the time it deserves. As you are drawn in the author will take over and blow your mind again and again. Just when you think you have the answers the author will change it leaving you with your mouth wide open looking back over what your eyes just took in. 
 The author switches back and forth from today to the past as you learn all that this remarkable lady has went through to become the lovely lady she is today. There is no doubt you will cheer for Jude as you feel the pain she has and must go through to find the answers to so many questions. The ending will blow you out of the water there are so many twist and turns you won't see coming. Just as you think you have a handle on it Jude takes you down a different road you never saw coming. This is one author who knows how to get control of her readers leaving them handing on asking for more. I so enjoyed the many twist and turns each character adds so much to the read. Some you will like others you will not but by the time you have read the last page you will have relooked at each one over and over again seeing each from a different light. 
 From the first page you will find you heart beating faster as you turn to the next it is running over time by the time you have finished and turned the last page your find your heart rate is still beating as fast as it was from the start. Leaving your mind in a state of WOW not being able to forget what you just read you play each scene over again and again in your mind as you regroup and close your eyes for the night hoping you never have to life the nightmare this author has given her characters. If you are looking for your next mystery, thriller, suspense read you can stop looking you have found it. This is one book and one author you do not want to miss. I promise this will be your next favorite read!

The Body Reader by Anne Frasier features Jude Fontaine, a detective who was kidnapped and held captive for three years before managing to escape. 
 Learning to read her captor's body language helped her survive, and even though she comes back to a world a changed person, Jude is determined to get her job back. 
 Maybe she has something to offer that she didn't have before. 
 This quote from Publishers Weekly sums up my take: "... Jude persists on her own as connections between cases old and new lead to results both surprising and unlikely." I added the italics. 
 NetGalley/Thomas & Mercer 
 Crime/Suspense. June 21, 2016. Print length: 289 pages.

reference_books.title: Nightshade (Nightshade #1; Nightshade World #4)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 A werewolf book that includes topics such as gender roles, sexuality, arranged marriage, and slavery? Yes, that would be this book. 
 Those are all ambitious topics to take on in one book, so the author has added a healthy dose of almost-but-not-quite bodice ripper romance to lighten the mood. The love triangle reeks of Bella-Edward-Jacob in it's indecisiveness, danger, forbidden-ness, and guys-fighting-over-the-girl-ness. I had sort of enough of the swooning, pining, kiss-me-don't-kiss me, and "twining of fingers." (I could have made it a drinking game every time "twining" was used.) 
 It's long and takes a while to get to the point, but when it does, it has a strong plot, lots of action, and interesting characters. To me, it felt like a mash-up of Twilight, The Mortal Instruments series, and Shiver. Not to mention a giant spider that could only make me think of Aragog from Harry Potter. 
 The main character, Calla, is the alpha female of her pack. Most of the time - when she isn't letting her hormones rage while in the arms of one of the boys (eye roll) - she is the leader she's supposed to be: brave, decisive, protective, and confident. BUTTTTTT, there are times when she's none of those things and is the submissive. And dumb. She makes a lot of bad decisions. It's a bit of a contradiction for Calla. The author creates her wolf pack behavior and hierarchy based on natural wolf packs where the alpha male is the highest member followed by his mate, the alpha female. Calla and all the other women - wolf or not - are submissive to the males. Her mother stocks Calla's closet with what she thinks is more appropriately lady-like clothing in order to be more attractive to her predetermined mate. Yeah. 
 I assume the author is challenging the roles in which women, men, and therefor society, have cast themselves, but it just really hard to read and annoyed me a bit. What annoyed me is that no one really questions this "arrangement." Calla does rebel, but not without a lot of internal and emotional back-and-forth. And she never directly questions why the boys have the power, or why they are allowed to sleep around when the women are expected to be chaste and faithful. That's just the way it is in her world. Some of the male characters even use some of the subordinate characters (male & female) for their own sexual blackmail. A way to keep others from misbehaving and fearful. This sexual abuse is never challenged although the subordinates know it's wrong. 
 This is the start of yet another ya paranormal fantasy series. There was no real conclusion at the end of this book since it is meant to keep going. Very few questions are answered. For those of you who can't wait for the next book in a series to come out, perhaps you should wait until they are all written before starting. If you loved Twilight (and still love it), you'll probably like this book. It has more meat than Twilight, and that's what made it redeemable for me.

reference_books.title: The Beginning of Everything
reference_books.review_text:
This book has received three starred reviews (PW, Kirkus, Booklist), and for good reason. It is a solidly written realistic teen story. There are no fairies, zombies, or anything even remotely resembling a dsytopian world. There is a glittery vampire, but only as a Halloween costume. This is a down-to-earth honest story about a boy and a girl dealing with their identities, flaws, demons, love, and of course, high school. 
 I found a couple points of the plot to be a tad contrived, but acceptable. Overally, the book is well-written and the voices of the teen characters are spot on. It feels like high school through and through - from the "where to sit" dilemma at lunch and AP classes, to extra-curricular activities and hotel shennigans when said extra-curriculars travel overnight. The friendships also feel real and are relatable. The ending is realistic and appropriate for the story. It's a good ending. 
 A recommended read for fans who liked Rainbow Rowell's ELEANOR & PARK.

reference_books.title: The Casual Vacancy
reference_books.review_text:
UPDATE: 
 I finished it. The ellipses showed up. 
 It got a little better. After all the characters and conflicts were introduced, the middle flowed and I found it entertaining. I did like how she linked all the characters and how their actions had a domino effect on others (sort of like Crash). She jumped around from POV to POV in a way that almost felt natural. I thought the teen characters were good, especially Krystal. But overall, I found this rather dull. Reading about small-town local politics isn't my favorite topic and it does get rather talky about that. I also had a hard time reading a story where none - absolutely NONE - of the characters are happy. The only character who may have actually been happy is dead. There are little things that make each character happy, but those aren't enough to offset the negative aspects of each of their lives or situations. The happy things for each of them are escapes. The other thing that is strong in this book is the location. Rowling's description of the town is very good and makes it so easy to imagine not only it's physical appearance, but it's community and attitude. 
 Is it worth reading? Well . . . I would say it's an optional read. It's not a must read for this year, but it isn't necessarily a skip either. 
 Earlier post: 
 Reading this out of curiosity and to see how she does with something non-Harry. I'm about 60 pages in and I'm bored. So, so bored. She has also introduced what feels like two dozen characters in those 60 pages, and has not done so in an artful way. Bam! New chapter, new character. Bam! Another new chapter, another new character. Or two or three. And they are connected in some way to the 18 you've already met. Once again, she loves those adverbs, and seems to be using 10 words where two will do, but I haven't noticed an ellipses yet. As with Harry's world, the setting is coming along nicely and I'm getting a handle on the sort of place it is.
