sample_reviews.review_text: I just could NOT get into this book! It just started, with nary an introduction, and it felt confusing. I gave up around page 30.

So this book was pretty messed up overall. I think everyone was messed up in it and the situation was messed up. While it was really weird, I loved it. Honestly, the first half was kinda boring, but the second half basically blew my mind. It was amazing and I just love it. Marchetta, you are a master.

3.5. I struggled through the first 150 pages, but it got better. The characters were enjoyayble, though I had trouble connecting with them. Judging by the first half of the book I would've given it less than 3.5 stars, but the way it developed and revealed some 'secrets' hooked me.

** spoiler alert ** 
 specifics to this book: I figured out all the supposed mystery very close to the beginning, and figured out who the corresponding characters in the story were and how they related to Taylor by 1/4 of the way through the book.

This is an emotional overload. ;( 
 Affects me in such a way that somehow changes how I perceive and act towards things and events. 
 Your past is a significant part of you, but you're here in the present, you might as well do what you really want and show how you truly feel.

*2.75* 
 Honestly, I was disappointed by this book. I had heard that it was such an emotional, moving and beautiful contemporary, which are my favorite kind, (like The Sea of Tranquility and Hopeless) Alas, this was not the case for me. I could see where people would get that, and I could tell that the author was trying to make it be like that, but I was just never invested. 
 Plot- The plot for this is very simple, yet very complicated all at once. The base plot is simple- Taylor's mother abandoned her a long time ago, and now she wants to discover her past. There's a lot more than that though, and at time it was very confusing. There were two parts to this story, the past and the present. At first, you're meant to not know how they connect, and then later it's revealed in a "shocking" twist, but I knew from the start how it all went together. This was a disappointment for me, because I wasn't shocked at any point in this book. I didn't like how nothing was really explained until over 100 pages in, I understand trying to keep "an air of mystery" but I think this one crossed the line a little too much. There was an interesting aspect of "territory wars," which I liked, but that's pretty much the only time I was really interested in the story. I found it quite boring most the time, and I was never really caring what was going to happen next, thus making me not want to pick it back up whenever I put it down. I wasn't invested into the emotional side of the story either. I felt like it could have been done very well, but I wasn't attached. I liked what she tried to do however, and I appreciated how well it all connected, I just wish it was executed differently. 
 Writing- This was definitely the book's strongest point. Marchetta has amazing writing. It's all very lyrical, and a lot of the time there are paragraphs where it feels like you're floating in a dream. At times, this can make the story hard to understand, but overall I really enjoyed this author's writing. I thought the dialogue had some humor to it a midst this darker plotline. I want to read more of her work, just to experience the writing again. It does my favorite thing: it's lyrical, but still feels real. It's not so poetic that it takes you away from reality, there's still some feel of the narrator's personality, and it's still believable. 
 Characters- I also had major issues with the characters. I was not attached to any of them. I didn't really care for any of them at all, not even the main love interest, which usually I'll harbor some feelings for by the end of the book. I can acknowledge that the author didn't make them all the same, but none of them stood out to me, nor did I really like any of them, especially the characters from "the past." It took me nearly until the end of the book to finally get it straight for who was related/in a relationship with who. I didn't care enough to pay attention to them, and they weren't memorable at all. I don't have much to say about them because I don't really remember them and it's only been one day. I do like that our main character got some type of character growth, and I really hold a lot of stock in that, so that did appease me. Even though separately I don't remember much about the characters, as a whole, I like how they were written. I liked their dialogue's with each other, and I liked how they interacted. Another major issue I had was there was really no descriptions on their physical appearance I can honestly say that besides Jonah, and Santangelo, I have no idea at all what any of the character's look like. That really bothered me, and it made me have a hard time getting into the story because I couldn't really picture any of the characters. 
 Overall- Sadly, I don't think this was the book for me. I thought it was average in terms of an "emotional contemporary." I appreciate what the author was trying to do, and I liked some of the unique things about it, but it just wasn't really my cup of tea. I didn't not like reading it, but just when I wasn't reading it, I didn't have any drive to get back into it. I don't think I will be recommending it to my friends, but I won't be swaying people away from reading it either. I'm still very interested to read her other works though because the writing was great, and I have faith that she can do much better.

And life goes on, which seems kind of strange and cruel when you're watching someone die. 
 It's a teen fiction and it explains the font and the color they're using at the cover. My sister is on training at the Australian ambassador and she borrowed a book from its library as a task for the training. I happened to read it. 
 Jellicoe Road is one of those book I won't be picking in the bookstore because of its (personally) unimpressive cover and synopsis. But the Printz Award gold stamp said it all, the book is incredible. Just as what the other reviews said, I was confused for the first part of the book, but it's an easy read so I continue. 
 I think the subject of the book is petty: the territory war. And they are 17. But let's say somewhere there in Australia it's really matter for the school kid; I don't know but the writer did a good job to make it appeared substantial. Anyway, this territory war thing was taken seriously by them and this made an interesting story for the Taylor, Raffy, Jonah, Chaz and Jessa. 
 Well that was my first impression, because as I read further, the author was getting friendlier and the war thing getting more and more trivial, as it should be. The book itself wasted no paper for nothing that's not contributing to the story, which I love. Melina Marchetta has this witty, thoughtful and delighting story to tell. I think she is writing for fun. She's writing for her high school memory. She's writing for what a lovely school memory should be. She explored Australia, the land and the people, blended into the plot of the story. 
 Placing Raffaela in the path of an oncoming car becomes one of the major priorities of the next ten seconds of my life. 
 It's not that I miss my mother. It's just that I miss the idea of what one would be. 
 These people have history and I crave history. I crave someone knowing me so well that they can tell what I'm thinking. 
 Teens should have Taylor Markham as someone they can look up to, along with Potter, Granger and Weasley. Forget Bella Swan and her vampire pedophile boyfriend; because through Taylor, we learn forgiveness, toughness, love and triump above all condition from the heroine. After all, what's more important than hope for lifeline? 
 "What are you so sad about?" Santangelo says to me, "We're going to know him for the rest of our lives."

This is one of the weirdest books I've ever read, but it's also absolutely beautiful. When I started reading, I had no idea about what I should expect. The story was really uninteresting for the first 150 pages, since it made zero sense to me, but then I started to piece it all together, and ...wow. This book is something extraordinary. Every word is carefully chosen and has a special purpose for the story. Melina Marchetta is a super talented storyteller, and I'm looking forward to reading more books by her. 
 My main issue with Jellicoe Road is that you have to be extremely focused while reading, because every detail is important. It might not seem like a big deal while reading it, but then 150 pages later it's suddenly of great significance for the story. Such as the postman being the serial killer. This also makes me want to re-read this book, because I'm interested in discovering details I must've missed while reading it for the first time. 
 Overall, this is an amazing book (with a crazy but really impressing plot). If you start reading and nothing makes sense to you, don't fret - just keep reading! Sadly, there are too many pages of plain confusion and boredom for me to give this novel five stars, although, in most ways, it's a five-star book. 
 I feel like I should write a longer review, but I don't know what else to say. Just read and let the story affect you. Embrace the emotions. Bye.
I read almost half of this (160 pages) and gave up. I really tried to get into it, but I just found it so confusing. I still don't really know what it was about/where it was heading.

2.5/5. 
 I really thought I would love this book. I still think Melina Marchetta is a brilliant author and I loved her Lumatere series but to be honest, I never could get into this book. I couldn't even tell you what it's really about because I feel so disconnected to it.

book_b.title: The Rithmatist (Rithmatist, #1)
book_b.user_review:
Fascinating premise and unlike any other magical/fantasy stories I've read, but at the core, it follows the formulas of so many that we already know - school story, underdog character, fiesty (red-headed)sidekick, older mentor, battle great evil, overcome obstacles, one dead parent, etc. The world building was weak, too. 
 I have started reading Sanderson's other 2013 release, STEELHEART, and I've noticed that I don't like how he writes female characters. Having never read any of his novels for adults, I have no idea if he writes women like this all the time or not. Girls in THE RITHMATIST are described as annoying, weird, gossip-y, weak, lacking talent, and needing remedial instruction. There are no female teachers, talented Rithmatists (other than one student who is kidnapped but the readers never know anything about her so she hardly qualifies as a character), and no women in law enforcement. The main character's mother is a cleaning woman. The sidekick is a girl and she is brave, and does contribute to solving the case & catching the big baddie, but she can only do Rithmatics with the help of a non-Rithamtic boy. 
 In STEELHEART, which I haven't read much of yet, one of the main female characters uses her sexuality to lure a target into a trap and then the male main character has to remind himeself several times not to stare at her chest. Granted, he is 18 and this is a typical reaction for a hetero male teenager, but still. She is a brave, guns-a-blazing girl, but I hope the author gives her a few other tactics besides wearing sexy clothes and making out with bad-guys on street corners. 
 Back to THE RITHMATIST. I do like how he paces the story and teases out clues. The drawing that are within and between the chapters are very useful and I'm glad they were included otherwise I think I would have had a hard time grasping the Rithmatics. As a whole, it is a good story that moves along quickly.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Sorry, Brandon Sanderson -- I've loved everything else of yours that I've read, but this one couldn't even inspire me to finish it. 
 And that's despite the fact that it's a middle-grade* novel that would only take a couple hours of dedicated reading to get through. 
 The characters are all flat and predictable -- naively enthused protagonist, endearingly-cluttered professor mentor, irritable and artsy female foil, snidely aloof professor red herring, militant investigator... Not a one is all that memorable. The mystery element might be intriguing, if readers had any reason at all to care about the Rithmatists-in-training who have been killed, or about any of those at risk of being targeted next, but none of them is shown in any detail. Our protagonist, in fact, is notable mainly because he doesn't fit the killer's profile -- not very conducive to raising the tension. 
 The one highlight of the book is, as in so many of Sanderson's books, the worldbuilding. Both the altered history and the magic system have heaps of intriguing potential -- but not nearly enough to get me to keep reading when none of the other elements inspire anything but yawns. 
 So I'm throwing in the towel. One star, and I'm clearing it from my currently-reading shelf. Better luck next time. 
 *I consider this book middle-grade, despite its marketing as YA, because there's really nothing even remotely teenagerly about it -- no hormones, no feel of being on the brink of adulthood. Without any of those themes, there's no reason for it to be any less appropriate for a ten-year-old than for a member of the supposedly-intended age group.

This is the first Brandon Sanderson book that I have not loved. I'm disappointed I can't give it five stars, but in all honesty, I can't. The magic system (while supremely well-thought-out as always) is kinda...boring, the characters are two-dimensional, and the 'steampunk' is limited to an off-hand mention of a few clockwork pieces. It's perilously close to 'gluing a few few gears on it'. 
 That said, I *am* intrigued by the mentions of the Tower, and its contents, so perhaps I'll pick up the sequel and give this series a second chance. Just because it's Brandon Sanderson. If it were anyone else, I wouldn't have even finished the first book.

Kun lukee englanninkielisia nuortenromaaneja, ei aina tule kiinnitettya huomiota kieleen. Tarkeinta on ymmartaa lukemansa ja nauttia tarinasta. Mutta taman The Rithmatist-romaanin kanssa kavi niin, etta jo heti alusta suorastaan nautin kirjan kielesta. En osaa sanoa, mika teki eron, mutta taman lukeminen oli erittain miellyttavaa. 
 Rithmatist sijoittuu jonnekin noin sadan vuoden taakse ja on tyyliltaan hieman steampunkmainen. Mukana on rattaita, kellopelihevosia ja kellokoneistoja ja maailma muodostuu erilaisista saarista, jotka hieman muistuttavat Yhdysvaltain osavaltioita, on mukana kylla Euroopankin saaret. Mutta tama kaikki on vain ikaankuin taustatarinaa paajuonelle, joka sijoittuu Armedius Academyyn. Academyssa opiskelee niin rithmatisteja, kuin rikkaiden perheiden vesoja, joilla ei ole taikavoimia saada liidun jalki elamaan. Rithmatisti on kahdeksan vuoden iassa siirtymariitissa saanut voiman, jolla han voi piirtaa liidun avulla tiettyja kuvioita, jotka alkavat elamaan. Tata taitoa tarvitaan villien liitukuvioiden, "liidukkaiden" (chalklings) hyokkayksia vastaan. Nebraskin saarella on jatkuva sotatila, jossa rithmatistit taistelevat liitukuvioillaan villeja, henkea uhkaavia liidukkaita vastaan. Siksi rithmatisteja taytyy kouluttaa koko ajan lisaa. 
 Joel on paassyt Academyn oppilaaksi, vaikkei ole rikas eika rithmatisti. Joelin isa oli aikoinaan toissa Academyssa liiduntekijana ja hanen kuolemansa jalkeen Joel oli saanut vapaaoppilaspaikan. Joel on erittain kiinnostunut rithmatisteista ja han luikahtelee aina salaa kuuntelemaan rithmatistien oppitunteja. Tasta ei aina hyvaa seuraa. Kesaksi Joelin pitaisi ottaa jotain opiskeltavaa, silla han ei lahde kotiin (kun asuu aitinsa kanssa akatemialla) kuten muut opiskelijat. Joelilla on kuningasajatus, etta han reputtaa sopivan aineen, jotta paasisi rithmatistiprofessorin kesaoppilaaksi. Monen mutkan kautta Joelin kesa jarjestyy, tosi ei ehka aivan sellaiseksi kuin han oli ajatellut. Sitten rithmatistioppilaita alkaa katoamaan ja rikospaikalta loytyy outoja liitukuvioita. Joel paasee aivan kuin vahingossa mukaan tutkimuksiin ja tutustuu toiseen kesaoppilaaseen, rithmatisti-Melodyyn. Melody on rithmatisti-hylkio, joka ei osaa ympyroiden piirtamista kovin hyvin, eika hanesta pideta noin ylipaansa. Kieltamatta Melody on vahan omalaatuinen tytto. 
 Tasta kaikesta kehkeytyy jannittava tarina, jossa liitukuviot voivat ottaa ihmisia hengilta, ihmiset kayttaytyvat epailyttavasti ja mikaan ei oikeastaan ole lukijalle ennalta itsestaan selvaa. 
 Tama kirja oli taas jotain aivan muuta. Liitupedot, liitukuviot ja koko asetelma oli hauskasti erilainen. Tata voi hyvin suositella fantasian ystaville. Maltan tuskin odottaa sarjan toista osaa! Ja taytyneepa tutustua kirjoittajan muihinkin teoksiin. Sanderson on muuten kirjoittanut lopun Ajan pyora -sarjaankin.
I think the author has an amazing imagination and novel plots, but his writing is a bit sparse. His only female character appeared to have some sort of personality disorder and was quite off putting.

The Rithmatist is an absolutely amazing Young Adult Fantasy that doesn't read like Young Adult because the world building and characters are extremely fleshed out. 
 The magic system is easily the best part of this novel. Not because of how intricate and detailed it is, but because of its uniqueness and entertainment. I've never read a magic system that's so fun and relies heavily on a person's mental capacities rather than their physical attributes. The ability to draw perfect circles and lines is difficult to perfect, but definitely more possible than Pushing and Pulling (Mistborn). Admittedly, it can be hard to imagine some of the defense strategies outlined throughout the novel, so I was pleased to see detailed images following each chapter about the different strategies. 
 The characters are a little on the absurd side of the spectrum of realistic characters, however they work within this novel. They reminded of characters Rick Riordan would write; relatable, good senses of humor, and extremely intelligent for their ages. 
 Joel is an overlooked genius dreaming of things he'll never attain. He's resourceful and a little stubborn, which makes him a character I was able to identify with immediately. 
 Melody is sassy, dramatic, and, is also, dreaming of things she'll never attain. Melody and Joel are almost mirror images of each other, which creates an interesting dichotomy between the two. 
 What makes The Rithmatist such an amazing novel is that it doesn't treat its reader differently because it's a Young Adult novel. There is no slowing down to make sure the reader understands what happening or what just happened. There is no dumbing down of concepts related to the world building or magic system. Sanderson assumes the reader understands what's happening as the story progresses and continues to add layer upon layer of intricate world building while also expanding on the magic system. 
 Overall, The Rithmatist is an amazing fantasy novel with a unique magic system that will keep you reading well into the night. Sanderson is a phenomenal writer with a crazy imagination that I can't get enough of! 
 Apparently the sequel, The Aztlanian, is scheduled to release in 2017, according to Sanderson's assistant on Reddit, so be on the lookout because it's story you won't want to

This was a quick read for me--I had a hard time putting it down once I started. :) The illustrations definitely enhanced the story. I think the one thing that bothered me was the level of predictability. Not in the culprit behind the crimes but the development in the relationship between Joel and Melody. I probably shouldn't be very bothered by it--it is YA, after all. An excellent blend of fantasy, mystery, alternative history, and gears!

Really good, quick read. Took me about 3 hours to finish. Not up to Sanderson's usual standard of worldbuilding, but really good for a YA book. Plot was great and magic system was really fun. Hoping there'll be more to the series eventually. Whenever he gets around to it lol.

Brandon Sanderson is becoming one of my favourite writers at present. This is the first book in a series for young adults, but that shouldn't put you off. This was a light read before I stated Sanderson's Words of Radiance - which i am expecting to be a fairly heavy read. 
 The magic system used within this book is genius - Chalk drawings. It was nice to have details of the magic system described a little after every chapter. This allowed the reader to get up to speed with the magic system without a massive info dump at the beginning. 
 The story follows Joel, a student at a Rithmatist school. Even though he is not a Rithmatist himself, he is assigned to a professor to look into a number of recent incidents. Of course, no YA novel is complete unless it has a quirky opposite sex person, and this was filled in by Melody. 
 Together they work through a number of missions for their professor, sometimes getting into trouble while others finding the convenient clues that adults failed to notice. This is exactly what i would expect from this type of book. 
 I listened to the audiobook version and Michael Kramer did another sterling job. The only complaint is Michael's voices are very similar to his other audio records. 
 I will most certainly be on the lookout for the next book in this series.

Amazing! Yet another incredibly detailed and completly original magical world created by Branden Sanderson. Who would have thought that chalk drawings could be interesting as a magical ability, let alone scary and compelling? Mr. Sanderson, that's who. "The Rithmatist" is my new "Harry Potter". Can't wait for the next installment!
3.5. Interesting and good beginning to a new YA magic series. Harry Potter-like but different, thankfully not a lot of love interest or clunky exposition.

reference_books.title: Allegiant (Divergent, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
I'm being generous with the four stars here. If I applied my normal level of critical-reading-thinking to adolescent lit, a lot of my reviews would be lower. But that's not how I read these so take the stars with a grain of salt. 
 I liked the philosophy behind the story: we try to control what we fear or what is different, and no matter what, we will always create a system of superiority and inferiority. Call it what you will, systemic categorization is inescapable. And frightfully easy to explain away. I thought Nita was stupid, though, and their plans for change flawed and rash. Because they are so young? Because those are the only options? 
 Otherwise, there were a few really poignant lines that I actually highlighted on my kindle (which is a first for me). For example, when she sees David in the wheelchair after she shot him, and her reflection in his humanity and fragility juxtaposed with his evil. Or when Tris realizes here her true loyalties should lie (with those she loves) despite her conviction for the bigger cause. 
 I also connect with the distrust of the government here, and the ease with which government can control things. Some of their actions hit pretty close to home with what I've learned governments can and have done to maintain power. I think I've written about this before but I am always happy when someone identifies and fights against those holding ignorant others under their thumb. 
 And then there is the ending. I liked (and hated!) the ending and what Tris stands for. Yet she makes me so angry. She's stupid and brash...and 16? I didn't expect her to die. I reread it a few times to be sure...I kept thinking it was a serum or something. But being a dauntless she had to have a way to disarm the disabled dude. It felt a little cheap to kill her this way. (And challenging to my suspension of disbelief that so many things went right for her just because...) without question: 
 Deus ex machina was never in short supply. 
 I also think there were a few timeline confusions which added to my struggling suspending my disbelief that anyone could endure all this in so little time. How much time had passed since Caleb tried to kill her and her choice to sacrifice herself for him? 
 I also found Tris and Four's relationship to be unrealistic in its easy I-forgive-you-and-deeply-love-you moments. But again, who knows how the mind works under the duress they suffered. 
 And Evelyn just giving in? And it being ok to wipe the bureau's memory? If it's not ok it's not ok...right? 
 Bottom line is the book made me think and question. And cry :) So I'll leave my four generous stars and be grateful I got to finish the series.

I fear my students believe Tana is actually a strong character when in fact she is not. Everything she does is for a boy. WHY?!? Think of yourself girl. Or Pearl. Or Pauline. book_a.title: Life of Pi
book_a.user_review: One of the most thought-provoking reads in a long time, everyone should check this out. Note that the premise may seem far-fetched - a boy marooned in a life raft with a Bengal tiger - and that at first the plot may seem disconnected, but I promise the final outcome is worth continuing. Enjoy!

sample_reviews.review_text:
Am beginning to think something is wrong with me that I am not liking books that others seem to enjoy....this book just made me feel gross. I was interested in the zoo life in the beginning; the boy's religious exploration interested me. The whole boat ride then "oooooooohhhhhhh did that really happen?" trip was not working for me. I also couldn't really stomach many more of the various methods of killing things followed by "oh, and I was a vegetarian." 
 I did love the intro and think all writers should read the way he thinks about writing as a process... 
 Maybe I am getting too cynical in my readings.
Listened via audible. Such a fantasy. Enjoyable. Would recommend to anyone who likes fantasy.

The boy get dumped in the ocean, alone with the tiger in a tiny boat. 
 Pi is a boy who have high interest to religion and spirituality. He got anxious because he hold almost all religions. He doesn't see the point, why he has to hold only one and why the Priest from those religions try so hard to "get" him into their religion. 
 The struggle to living. 
 How we have to be the Alpha instead of Omega. Not to be rude to the Omega, just simply to get respect and live. 
 How the hope came and gone... And how to lift-up the spirit. 
 I read this book, and easily get into the story. Just like I observe by myself the story. And it is easy to compare the story to my daily life.

This is a difficult book to review, because it is in some ways, a difficult book to understand....did these things really happen as told by the narrator? WAS there an ACTUAL tiger in this book with him? Was this story all a metaphor? Was he delirious? As it says at the end of the book--- which story do you prefer? I prefer parts of all of it!

I felt it could be an awesome book but needs more refining. First 1/3 book was painfully slow for me. I almost lost interest. It's not that it was irrelevant or unnecessary for the story...but the flow of the entire story isn't as smooth as I'd like it to be. A good finished book to me is a story that cannot be told any other way. This book to me was, "I see that you took this approach to tell the story, I get why you took this way...but it could be told in other way" kinda feeling...all over the place. 
 It's a good draft but I don't know if I like it as a finished book.
Still trying to digest this book. I picked it up more than 5 times and only ever got through 50 pages each time. I finally finished it after having it on my bookshelf for over 8 years!
The eloquent writing and last two chapters decided my 4 star rating. I am still reeling from this...

I liked the story at first - it was pretty slow, but I found it interesting how Pi engrossed himself in so many different religions. Once the boat sank (which in my mind I was like "finally!" ) I liked this book a lot less. 
 Once I realized it wasn't even chronological any more - just rambling on and on, and when Pi started talking about handling and trying to eat the tigers feces - I decided I've had enough. 
 I'm not finishing this book - it's too weird, I'm not getting anything out of it (even the entertainment aspect is gone), and I have no clue how this author came up with such a bizarre story (let alone drag it out for how many hundred pages).

This book took ages to finish but it was worth it in the end! So many have talked about a certain island he passes by as he is lost at the Atlantic Sea, and I have to join them with "Holy crap, that is freaking weird!" The island is full of sweet algae at day and not a single fly lives on the island, but somehow it lures fish into the freshwater it contains, which kills them, so the island can survive. Patel even found a tree with beautiful fruits, as he is tempted to eat one, he peels one and the core of the fruit turns out to be a tooth!! 
 It's an incredible book, very vivid and quite an eyeopener. It must be a horrible experience, so surreal. I actually haven't watched the movie but I definitely like the book, it was just too long drawn, which I why I'm giving it 4 stars. The plot is truly fascinating. 
 I like the idea of a boy Pi Patel, whose father is an owner of a big, and popular zoo in India. This boy is very religious and practices all three religion, Hinduism, Islam, and Christianity. Patel has this great view of life, that there's so much more than what the eye can see. As India goes through a change of the regime, the family, including mother and brother, decides to sail to Canada in hope for a better future, even though life was pretty great in India. 
 The ship wreaks on the way to India and he ends up alone with animals on this lifeboat. That's when part two starts and the adventure goes on, which is pretty amazing.

I only made it about halfway through this book before I couldn't take it anymore. It's so incredibly slow-paced and wordy that it's easy to lose track of what's going on. For the record, I can't stand the movies for the same reason. 
 I have no idea what the appeal of these stories are for people because the actual storylines are so masked behind all the wordy narration that it's difficult to track with the actual story arc. By the time they move on in a scene, you've fallen asleep through the descriptions and meanderings that the author gives about everything. 
 For me, I will stick with C. S. Lewis and George MacDonald (who incidentally, were friends with Tolkien - maybe he should've learned from their more fast-paced writing styles).

No soy de los que dice que un libro es malo solo porque no le gusto, y menos este del cual he visto muy buenos comentarios, mas bien prefiero pensar que no era para mi o no era el momento correcto para leerlo. Ugh...I hated this book. It was so boring and tiresome that it took me months to slog through, hoping it was going to eventually become, at the very least, interesting. Never happened for me. It wasn't the writing....obviously Nabokov is a brilliant author. It wasn't the subject matter.....very little offends my sensibilities. All of the reviewers I follow gave this book high ratings. Thousands of Goodreads members sang its' praises. It made it into the top 100 works of 20th century fiction. So, it has to be me. I am struggling to understand why this is considered to be "classic" literature. Highly overrated in my opinion. 
 This review is dedicated to my new friend DJ
Incredible. The main feeling I had throughout this novel is I wanted to know, I wanted to see things play out. Nabokov's masterpiece.

I can't say I'm glad that I've read this book. I can say that I'm glad to be able to mark it off as read, both here and on my mental 'to-read' list. But I wish I had never read it. 
 Oh sweet Jesus. I absolutely loathed this book. 
 The subject matter was, of course, vile. I feel like I need to go and have a bath in disinfectant, bleach my brain - anything to get this filth off me. But, subject matter aside, this was the most pretentious piece of crap I've read in a long time. Long-winded, at times completely pointless, and God, the parts in French - enough already! The narration style was (to me) absolutely irritating - his incessant talking of himself in the third person (Humbert Humbert), as well as his ridiculous nicknames for *himself*. 
 It was obvious that he was a complete lunatic. He really did not appear to have any remorse for what he had done, or indeed any real acknowledgement that he had done anything 'wrong'. He was obviously trying to endear himself to his 'readers'. Nabokov was obviously very skilled - he's an incredibly memorable character, and quite possibly the only character I despise even more than Joffrey from Game of Thrones. Absolutely no redeeming features or qualities whatsoever. 
 I can't remember a book ever making me feel like this before. That in itself is worth something, I suppose, but I just don't know how to rate this book. I am wavering between one star - because I truly detested it like nothing else - and five stars, because it's clearly a masterful piece of literature. 
 So three stars it is - I'll split the difference. And I would never, never, never recommend this book to anyone. Ever. 
 Edited on 30th June 2015 - down to one star. I hate this book more & more as time passes.

book_b.user_review: http://randommuzings.wordpress.com/20...

sample_reviews.review_text: More of a novella than a novel. Capote starts well and proves he can write, then gets bored and dies off. Breakfast at Tiffany's shows how a movie with a huge star can turn a forgettable book into a memorable one.

I was a bit underwhelmed with this to be honest. It wasn't bad, obviously - it's a classic for a reason, but it just lacked the charm that I think the film adaptation went to lengths to add in. 
 It was a quick read and was quite sharp with some good lines in it and I'm glad I read it, but it just wasn't really for me, I don't think.

I did not finish this book, but what I read irritated me and I kind of wanted to shake Holly Golightly. The movie is definitely a softer, more "romantic" version of this story and I don't feel depicts the emptiness of Holly's character or the lack of discernment in her "friends" in this book.

Holly this, Holly that, everyone likes Holly. Holly has no friends. Holly is messed up. End. 
 I really wanted to like this book. I had a good impression going in because I enjoyed the movie and I even liked the first few pages. But as I continued reading, I just became increasingly bored and disappointed. 
 My instinct was to give this book 1 star, but I gave it 2 stars, because 1 stars are reserved for bad writing. 
 I dont sympathize with any characters in this book. Holly is hopeless. I hoped for some sort of redemption, but she remains f**ked up, with no desire to change. But I guess this sort of story is also worthwhile in explaining life. Because probably more often than not; people never change. I just can't but help find it depressing. I wished for more of a conclusion, even if it wasn't all happily wrapped up as I would have liked.

Holly Golightly is a girl that I both pity and admire. She's glamorous and witty, she can be both honest and deceitful. She is a fascinating character and it is no wonder she has made her stamp on American literature. Breakfast at Tiffany's is a worthy read.
There's short and there is short. Not a great deal happens.

Never having read this book before I had high expectations for it due to the film, Audrey Hepburn etc. I did find Holly Golightly a fascinating character but have to say I enjoyed the other stories in the collection a lot more. I feel the writing is a kind which will stay with you long after the book is finished.
This was the first book I read on my Amazon Kindle. I enjoyed it. It was a quick read but pretty absorbing with an interesting cast of characters. Now I'll have to finally see the movie.

Although I love Truman Capote's style and especially his short stories, Breakfast at Tiffany's has never been on my radar. I haven't watched the film, either, of course. For some reason, knowing the subject matter, I knew this wouldn't be my cup of tea. I started reading it a few days ago, because of a group discussion, and the conclusion I came to was the same all along. The prose flows naturally, Holly Golightly is an interesting character with her ''joie de vivre'' attitude in life, and the narrator -called ''Fred'' by our heroine, is a voice of reason and sympathy. However, I still fail to see the appeal of the novella, as the plot is nothing special. Perhaps this is exactly why people are fascinated by it. Perhaps it is the way of simplicity with which Capote wants to pass his message to the reader. It is an entertaining story, but not something I would read again. 
 The three stories that are included in Breakfast at Tiffany's 50th anniversary edition are House of Flowers, A Diamond Guitar and the moving, beautiful A Christmas Memory.
Me gusto mucho mas la pelicula

reference_books.review_text:
Find this review and more at 
 kimberlyfaye reads. 
 Some things in life are just certain. Me falling in love with Lauren Layne's characters is one of them. Another would be me loving Lauren's latest release. When I learned the Oxford series was going to continue with I Knew You Were Trouble, I was all geeked out. I loved the Stiletto ladies. I loved the Oxford guys. Any time I can get more of any of them, I'm all in. 
 One of the reasons I probably enjoyed this book so much is that I dig a good slow burn romance. That's definitely what Lauren delivered with Taylor and Nick's story. These two had tons of chemistry, but as often happens in real life, the timing wasn't quite right at first. And for awhile thereafter. That made it all the more realistic to me. Who hasn't met someone and realized the timing was off? Thankfully, for these two, the universe had a way of making things right and they wound up with another opportunity. Which was great because, even with their differences and their tendency to pick at each other, they were great together. 
 I loved watching both Taylor and Nick grow over the course of this book. I also enjoyed seeing them come to terms with their individual pasts so they could move forward together. And, as always, it was great to see some of my past favorite characters make appearances here. 
 Long story short, Lauren delivered the laughs, swoons, feels and sexy times I've come to expect from her books. 
 I received a copy of this book for free in exchange for an honest review. This does not affect my opinion of the book or the content of my review. 
 FAVORITE QUOTES 
 She liked men. Liked their size, the way they kissed, the way the male body felt above her, below her, whatever. But not for keeps. Never for keeps. 
 "I think you underestimate just how badly you and Nick Ballantine have been giving the rest of us who have to be in your orbit blue balls."
