This is how change happens on the local level.

reference_books.title: The Road
reference_books.review_text:
Relentlessly stark, and at many times insightfully distressing, this book may take some time to get through. The backdrop pushes the strain of single parent struggle into extreme relief, while displaying both the best and the worst of what lies within humanity. 
 One thing that is interesting is McCarthy's oddly detailed choice of vocabulary. If nothing else, there are quite a few entertaining, although quite dark, prosaic arrangements, many of which use words that are a bit hard to track down, but are ultimately just the right fit. 
 Overall, if you feel there's just a bit too much happiness in your life, this may be the novel for you. :p

reference_books.title: Next
reference_books.review_text: It is obvious Crichton was trying to introduce a lot of problems with current genetic law using one character per problem that would mesh together in the final conclusion. Unfortunately, he does not successfully interest us in any of the large amount of disconnected storylines. Characterization, background, and empathy in the human characters is completely absent; we empathize much more with the non-human characters of Gerard and Dave, but we never get much of a POV with them as they are sidelined by too many other issues being thrown at the reader.

reference_books.title: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, Parts 1 & 2 (Harry Potter, #8)
reference_books.review_text: A faithful continuation of the story right from where the epilogue to the previous book left off. Although others disagree, I find the characters, both new and familiar, to be just as fully fleshed out and engaging as in the previous adventures. It also fleshes out a vital little part of the prior story that gives a little more dimension to some of the characters that we only encountered briefly in the past.

reference_books.title: Orange Is the New Black
reference_books.review_text: While it is told from a relatively privileged viewpoint, the author makes no excuses about her crime and the people in the story are all palpably real. There are many interesting parts in the evolution of the author's viewpoint that make the text independent of prison life as well. Well worth the read, and written in a good, realistic style.

This was described as the best fantasy series since Lord of the Rings. Well that is something to live up to. It certainly creates a world that is as believable as middle earth and characters that you really do come to care about. Martin has crafted a story that builds throughout this first volume and leaves you counting the days until you can get hold of volume two. The story is set in a feudal society that has lasted for hundreds if not thousands of years. At the beginning of the tale we meet Lord Stark and his family - with an array of children. But even though the children form a clear focus for some chapters, the violence can be quite graphic and the sex is explicit in language and form. Surprisingly, this makes for an engrossing read. Some of the situations are really original; for example, the way prisoners are kept in the Eerie is an image that has stuck in my mind - you will know it when you get there. 
 Highly recommended.

Ein Land, in dem Jahreszeiten Jahre dauern konnen. Ein Konig, der seinen Vorganger mit Gewalt vom Thron stiess - allerdings aus guten Grunden. Die Nachkommen dieses fruheren Konigs im Exil. Der Lokalherr des Nordens und enge Freund des aktuellen Konigs und seine ganze Familie. Die Frau des Konigs und ihre Familie. Und viele weitere adlige Strippenzieher, die uber das ganze Land verteilt sind. Eine hohe Mauer im Norden, die das Land vor dem schutzt, was nordlich davon haust - und das mit dem kommenden Winter immer bedrohlicher wird. 
 Das sind die Zutaten des ersten Teils dieses epochalen Fantasy-Werks von George R. R. Martin. Erzahlt wird die Geschichte aus vielen verschiedenen Perspektiven - jedes Kapitel ist mit dem Namen eines Protagonisten uberschrieben und wird auch aus dessen Sicht erzahlt. Das ist ein Erzahlmodus, der es dem Leser erlaubt, die Personen wirklich gut kennenzulernen, und der daruber hinaus auch fur sehr viel Abwechslung sorgt. Der Hauptakzent liegt dabei auf den Mitgliedern der Familie Stark, die im Norden des Landes lebt und dort die lokale Machtbasis bildet. Es dauert ein bisschen, bis man einen Uberblick uber die vielen Figuren und Konstellationen hat, doch spatestens dann zieht einen die Geschichte in ihren Bann, sie nimmt auch etwa nach der Halfte deutlich an Fahrt auf. In diesem Buch geht es viel um politische Verstrickungen und naturlich um die Frage nach Gut oder Bose. Doch im Gegensatz zu den meisten Werken des Genres wird diese Frage nicht klar beantwortet. Denn alle Seiten haben sowohl positive als auch negative Elemente, es gibt kein reines Schwarz oder Weiss, sondern viele Grauschattierungen. So ist mir etwa Tyrion, der kleinwuchsige Spross der als "Bosewichte" zu identifzierenden Familie, sehr sympathisch, es hat sich bald abgezeichnet, dass er meine Lieblingsfigur werden wurde. Einzelne Personen kann man durchaus gleich als eindeutig positiv oder negativ sehen, bei einigen hangt es jedoch in der Schwebe. Es kann sein, dass sich das in den folgenden Buchern andert, doch an diesem ersten Band hat mich gerade dieser Aspekt fasziniert. Denn dadurch kann ich gar nicht voraussagen, wie sich die Geschichte in Band 2 entwickelt. Romantik ist in diesem ersten Teil kaum zu finden, was mir aber durchaus passt. Kann ja ausserdem in den weiteren Teilen noch kommen. Das Buch bietet beste Unterhaltung auf hohem Niveau, meine Erwartungen wurden nicht enttauscht. Die absolute Begeisterung ist bei mir noch nicht aufgekommen, aber das Potenzial dafur ist auf jeden Fall vorhanden. Vier von funf moglichen Sternen.

Stunningly well-written fantasy novel with a deep understanding of character. Every character is interesting--some we hate and some we root for, but character motivations are eventually revealed and are always interesting. As a disadvantage, lots of characters are sometimes dumped on you all at once, but I found that not knowing who's who is rarely a problem. Those characters who are important are mentioned frequently and rounded out, and even minor characters are mentioned enough times once they become significant that you can follow the action. A must-read for fantasy lovers.

First and foremost A Game of Thrones is a very long fantasy novel and so it suffers from some of the same pitfalls as other novels in the genre. For example, nothing is really and truly resolved at the end of A Game of Thrones and readers are left teased sufficiently that they'll want to (hopefully) pick up the next instalment in the series. However, although this novel is long, its strength is also that the world that has been created, and the rules (thus far) established are well thought out and sufficiently intriguing. 
 A Game of Thrones is a fantasy novel with hints of horror and macabre thrown in for good measure. At times it can be a very fun read. At other times it is a chore, with Martin sometimes waxing repetitive and sometimes veering into stiflingly boring prose--not too much, but enough for me to notice that the novel could have been shorter by about 200 pages. I understand that epic fiction requires extra effort to flesh everything out, but when an author belabours the non-points and writes trivial dialogue, my patience gets tested. A lot of the characters are also pretty wooden, with wooden dialogue that left me wondering about who's who at times. 
 I will give Martin, credit, however: A Game of Thrones was way more interesting than Jordan's first foray, The Eye of the World. Also, the ending is awesome.

book_b.title: Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality
book_b.user_review: Although fanfiction, it manages to inject quite a lot of new dramatic angles and a healthy dose of rationalistic viewpoint into J.K. Rowling's universe. It also has a creative and relatively unique ending, which is definitely worth the extremely long buildup. Worth a read for anyone who is a fan of the universe, and who would also be interested in what a slightly different type of naivete in the protagonist, a person with the analytic strength of the typical college fan to deconstruct the fantasy world around him, but lacking the experience necessary to make certain value judgements, would have brought to the story.

 Of course, HPMOR is not flawless. There are embarassing episodes, like the first meeting of Harry and Dumbledore, or some other strange dialogues, which make sense only if you recall that you're reading a fanfic.  Battle Magic classes and armies... well, they ROCK. I couldn't just not mention it.

ok, so I'll give this one 2.5 over the last book since it was slightly better. I think I figured out why I'm having a hard time really getting into these. It has to do with the lore. There are good and bad vampires. The good ones are just like people, they feed off people who willingly get bitten, and they use magic every now and then, but not often. There's nothing dangerous about them. In fact, they're so nice and helpless that they need guardians to watch over and protect them. The bad vampires are what you typically think of as a vampire, bloodthirsty killers who go after the innocent. The guardians are trained to kill these guys because they also kill the good vamps. It's a very convenient system with some royalty and class woes thrown in the mix. 
 In this book, our main character, Rose, finally gets a chance to prove herself by pulling a stupid stunt with some friends and chasing after some Strigoi (bad vamps). reference_books.title: The Selfish Gene
reference_books.review_text: I hate to do this, but I gave this one up after about five chapters. I enjoyed the book initially, and Dawkins does an admirable job of trying to keep his point decipherable by laymen, but I still felt my brain getting overwhelmed by the material. As much as I support the theory of evolution, my mind is just not equipped to understand the science behind it! It's all so abstract, and mathematical when you get right down to it, and math has *never* been my strong suit. Sorry, Professor Dawkins - for what it's worth, I loved "The God Delusion".

reference_books.title: Three Cups of Tea: One Man's Mission to Promote Peace ... One School at a Time
reference_books.review_text:
Egads, what an awful book. I don't even know where to begin... I picked up this book at work, because it is often requested for school reading lists, and I was curious about it. Plus, I could always stand to learn more about the Middle East, as my opinion of that region has never been particularly glowing. 
 First of all, the writing by David Oliver Relin is atrocious. I've proofread vampire/human love stories from my college creative writing that were better than this. Relin's style of writing is so over-the-top and flowery, it'd take him an entire chapter just to describe what I had for breakfast this morning. Here are just a few examples of some of the more ridiculous, groan inducing sentences: 
 "Mortenson sat on a boulder and drank from his water bottle until it was empty. But he couldn't drink in enough of this setting." 
 "As they drove past the scale model of the mountain where Pakistan had detonated its `Muslim Bomb,' Mortenson told his friend and fixer about the explosion of support Americans had provided for the CAI." 
 "The widely spaced streams of tracers leaped across the road like ellipses. But to Mortenson, who wouldn't learn his friends had survived until the following week, when he returned to Kabul, they looked more like question marks." 
 I can't find it now, but there was one I read that made me want to slam my head against the wall. I paraphrase, but it went something like: "The jagged peaks of the mountain assaulted the inoffensive blue sky." Blegh. If Relin's prose doesn't get you, his hero worship of Mortenson will. Don't get me wrong, what Greg Mortenson is doing is great, and he definitely deserves the title of "hero" - but Relin makes him look more like a saint or the next Messiah. I'm surprised Relin didn't just rip off the Bible story of Jesus protecting the prostitute from being stoned to death, and replaced "Jesus" with "Greg Mortenson". When Relin isn't busy making "Dr. Greg" into a saint, he's portraying the Korphe mountain people like blessed, enlightened beings. 
 My grievances about Relin aside, Mortenson's story *is* an interesting one, and certainly worthy of being published into a book. There were times I actually enjoyed reading the book, especially after 9/11 happened and things begin to get even more dangerous for Greg's work. Nevetheless, the prose was just so awful, it was as disservice to the story that needed to be told, and made reading the book into more of a chore than it ought to be. I feel bad for kids in school who have to read this shit for an assignment - good luck!

reference_books.title: Insurgent (Divergent, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
I hate to give such a harsh critique, but I honestly hated the hell out of this book. I rarely ever leave a book unfinished, but I quit this one. The plot seemed like it was all over the place. Roth does a poor job of fleshing out this world of hers. I can never pin down where any of the characters are at times. This society that Roth has fashioned just doesn't seem functional at all, if only because we never really get to see it function in the first place. The characters are poorly defined and I could never remember who anyone was (except for the principle characters of Tobias and Jeanine - other than them, other characters were all just names on a page). The worst part of the book of all, though, is the main character Tris. My god... what a whiny ass protagonist. Yes, yes, she goes through a lot of terrible events, but how they affect her feelings could have been conveyed more succinctly without breaking up the narrative of the story constantly. I swear to god, Tris is doing one of four things: 1.) Sobbing uncontrollably, 2.) feeling sorry for herself, 3.) pining for Tobias, or 4.) all of the above. It's insufferable. It's okay for a protagonist to have flaws and vulnerabilities, it's what connects the reader to their plight, but when the main character does nothing but bitch-bitch-bitch or cry-cry-cry over their perceived weakness, it becomes incredibly redundant and frustrating, especially considering Tris is *supposed* to have a natural acumen for being a warrior (hence why she chose Dauntless in the first damn place). 
 I will not be reading the rest of this trilogy as it feels like a severe waste of my time.

reference_books.title: Smoke and Mirrors: Short Fiction and Illusions
reference_books.review_text:
I'll start off by saying I've never liked short story anthologies. I prefer longer narratives, where I can leisurely adjust to the characters and the worlds they live in, as opposed to the jolt of being dropped off via helicopter into the middle of the unknown, with only 10-30 pages of story to fill me in on what's happening. 
 That being said, I have managed to enjoy a handful of short stories by the likes of Harlan Ellison and Clive Barker. Now I can officially add Neil Gaiman to that exclusive list! 
 Smoke and Mirrors is not only a collection short stories though - there are also a few... ugh... poems as well. Don't get me wrong - the distaste I just exhibited isn't for Gaiman's poems in particular so much as the genre. My fondness for poetry never grew out of the works of Shel Silverstein and Dr. Suess, so I'm not going to comment on the ones written in this book, since my opinion will amount to "I hate poems, therefor, I hate these poems". I'm someone with more enthusiasm for poetry will find them lovely. 
 The short stories, on the other hand, are good, and the reason I can say that with any confidence is because I can remember my favorites offhand without referring to the book! "Troll Bridge" is a sobering story about how, as one grows up and makes horrible mistakes in their life, the magic of the world starts to fade away. "The Goldfish Pool" is a semi-autobiographical account of a novel writer's experience in the Hollywood system whilst staying in an ancient (for LA) hotel where John Belushi may or may not have died. This story kind of reminded me of the movie Barton Fink, which is not a bad thing. "We Can Get Them For You Wholesale" is a nice, short, but haunting piece about a man who casually looks into hiring assassins to take out his ex and the man from work she cheated on him with, and when he finds a remarkably good deal, he goes a little too far. Finally, there's Gaiman's twisted version of Snow White titled "Snow, Glass, Apple", which is a retelling of the classic story from the "evil" queen's perspective. 
 Overall, I think fans of Gaiman's work will find this a fun read.

reference_books.title: The Prince and the Pauper
reference_books.review_text:
I thoroughly enjoyed this book. Although I've always been familiar with this story (thanks largely, in part, by the Mickey Mouse film), I've never actually read the story - and I certainly didn't realize Mark Twain wrote it (though he claims to have wrote it based on a tale he heard). It certainly had Twain's distinct, irreverent wit, and there were many laugh-out-loud moments (my favorite being towards the end, when Tom reveals the location of the Royal Seal and, entirely ignorant to its purpose, what he had been using it for up to that point). 
 The story makes an interesting commentary about class, and how the grass is always greener. Tom Canty, the titular "pauper", has always dreamed of being royalty, while the Prince has a romantic notion as to what life is like as a peasant. Both boys receive jarring reality checks. Tom has difficulty adjusting to the absurdly privileged, yet rigid, life of a king, while Prince Edward gets the worst of it, seeing how rough and unmerciful life can be when poor. I found it interesting how Tom Canty had a much easier time adjusting to his situation and adapting than the Prince, who would constantly get into trouble by his unrelenting insistence that he is the king, which would, of course, fall onto deaf ears. You'd think, after awhile, he'd be smart enough to realize nobody will believe him and it'd be better just to keep quiet - but then again, his loud mouth, assertive nature is part of his charm, especially when juxtaposed with people not used to such behavior by a boy of his age. 
 Anyway, this was a great read, I thoroughly enjoyed it from beginning to end!

book_a.title: god is Not Great: How Religion Poisons Everything
book_a.user_review:
I probably would have given this a higher score had I read it a long time ago, before I was already well versed in why religion "poisons everything". As it is, this book was kind of redundant, however, unlike the books of Richard Dawkins (an evolutionary biologist) or Sam Harris (a neuroscientist), Hitchens approaches religion from a journalistic point-of-view. As such, Hitchens makes an obvious show of effort to support his views with solid facts, as would befit a journalist of integrity. The book is also rife with sarcasm and the British trademark dry wit, which helps prevent it from taking itself too seriously and becoming bogged down with rhetoric. 
 Still, in the end, it's well worth a read. Hitchens' position is very clear, concise, and most important of all, reasonable. While he isn't very sensitive, the point of his book, and all of the books by Dawkins and/or Harris, is that we NEEDN'T be sensitive. None of these writers are deluded enough to call for an end of religion, but their end goal is no less important, and far more realistic: an end to the SANCTITY of religion. As I paraphrase from Hitchens' book, it's not important that people shouldn't be allowed to have faith - it's that we should be allowed to choose NOT to have it, without legal, social, or mortal consequence. Obviously, I could rant away on the subject, so I'll just wrap up my review - thoroughly compelling read, I recommend it to fellow atheists such as myself, but I recommend it even more to the faithful.

sample_reviews.review_text:
There are books where you can honestly say, "it changed my life," and god is not Great is one of those books for me. I grew up in the Episcopal church ("Catholic light" as Robin Williams so brilliantly put it once) and I attended a private Christian School. I'd like to say I always resisted, and that my being an atheist was there from the beginning, but I'm a terrible liar. I think I always was a skeptic, I just didn't have the language and emotional maturity to really just come out and say what I was. When I discovered Hitchens through the Daily Show I eventually bought a copy of god is not Great, and read it over the summer after I graduated high school. I don't remember it being a pleasant experience, in fact I often had to put the book down and cry or just breath because I had finally found the voice that made sense. 
 This was my fourth time reading this book, and having grown older (and I hope wiser), I'm mature enough now to realize what this book is: the first real effort for a public atheist to speak his ground. As Hitchens notes in the book, atheists and non-believers often suffered publicly for their non-belief and this book then is an attempt to publish the position of atheism without fear of severe public reprisal. That doesn't I don't have conflicts with this book. Reading it again there were plenty of times I felt that Hitchens was pushing his position to far, or else engaged in some generalization and "othering," but I still defend this book because of it's station. 
 god is not Great is a book that will give young, and old, atheists their first real argument against belief and faith in the divine. And from this reading they'll hopefully experience other books which will help them figure out what their own personal position is. Every atheist should read this book because it's a jumping point from which a deeper more mature atheism can develop. 
 At the moment I'm working on a chapter by chapter analysis of god is not Great for my site White Tower Musings, and as soon as I have the up I'll update this review. If the reader is interested though they can read the first post I ever wrote for WTM, which was about Hitchens and god is not Great and Letters to a Young Contrarian. 
 https://jsjammersmith.wordpress.com/2...

I just finished reading Christopher Hitchens' exhaustive catalog of the violence and oppression perpetrated by the great religions from antiquity to the present day, God Is Not Great. 
 The book's subtitle, How Religion Poisons Everything, would have been a more fitting title. 
 Hitchens was a well-read atheist, a free-thinker and a good man, I think. In his book, he made the case that morality does not depend on religion -- just look at how religion itself has endorsed all manner of evil from genocide to slavery. 
 Too true. 
 If only Hitchens were still alive. I would have loved to see him give the same treatment to politics, which is becoming more and more like a religion and is proving to be just a divisive with so many all-or-nothing, no-compromise players in the game. (He was certainly aware of how cynical politicians have always known how to use religion -- and the religious -- to their advantage.) 
 Hitchens' book rightly promotes free inquiry and the scientific method. To him, the explanations offered by science were far more satisfying than those offered by religion. To me, science is great with the what and how of life but not so good with its ultimate meaning. 
 But there, I must admit, the explanations of the great religions aren't very satisfying either.

Ugh... just awful

I don't know if I can write a review fitting for this book. It is not so much an argument against religion as it is a rant against it. As a collection of sins, it is a great collection. It is a starting point for an endless and perhaps pointless study of theism. 
 Do not read this as an argument against religion. It is one-sided, bombastic, and incisive, but it is not an examination of pros and cons, not in a traditional sense. Politics produces atrocities; do we do away with it altogether? Do we ban politicians? Males have a very long history of abusing women and children. Do we lock all males away for life? Yes, religion has been shameful, but does that mean it is all invalid? The author does not touch on its good points in any meaningful way. He does not acknowledge that schools and hospitals exist because of religion. He does not concede that charitable organizations exist largely because of religion. This is a rant, a justified and moving rant, but it is not a complete argument. 
 Hitchens' concept that religion is a fossilized philosophy is interesting. It is the point that hit me the hardest. Religion is philosophy with the questioning left out, and that bothers me the most. I question everything. 
 It is a difficult read. He makes obscure references with no backfill, makes multiple references per paragraph, sometimes seemingly unrelated, and he leaves lines of cause and effect open ended but states them as fact. As a university essay it probably fails miserably, but as a weekend read, it is powerful and staggering. Have Google open always.

Again, what is your argument? You don't like religion therefore there is no god? Like Dawkins, this author makes the argument from silence. Obviously (given current stats on religion in the developed world), there are few people that continue to be delighted with the impact of religion and religious authority throughout history but what has any of that to do with the god question? Clearly all the references to religion are much more damning of humanity. Using this logic we should also reject quantum physics because we cannot understand Descartes earliest impression of animals. I love the question but I simply cannot abide the simplistic and unintelligent arguments.

To find truth, I expect the use of logic, examination of the opposing view's strongest point, and as much objectivity as possible. We find none of this in the book. 
 Atheists and scientists are described as intelligent and anyone religious (Christian, Muslim or others) gets the most derogative adjective possible. This sheds no light on truth. 
 All religions and sects are considered much the same. This is not because Hitchens did not have a thorough knowledge of history, the Bible, church history and religions. He does. But by blurring the lines, he is able to paint a very negative picture of religion. Even the atrocities of atheistic regimes are traced back to religion. This is done by highlighting the interaction between religious leaders and the totalitarian systems; Hitler's Third Reich and others. 
 Why read this book? It is worth reading to get an understanding of the New Atheists propaganda and methods, but don't expect to reliable information on God's existence or goodness.

Frankly, if you are looking for a thoughtful book on atheism and/or religion, this is not it. If you are a 12 year old boy and really pissed off at religion, this is the book for you.

book_b.title: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, Parts 1 & 2 (Harry Potter, #8)
book_b.user_review:
Several years after the Battle of Hogwarts, Harry Potter's youngest child, Albus, attends the famous School for Witchcraft and Wizardry. Albus isn't very outgoing, and his year doesn't go well when, bucking the Potter trend, he gets sorted into Slytherin instead of Gryffindor. However, he finds solace in a new friend, Scorpious Malfoy, son of Harry's former rival Draco Malfoy. Together the two young wizards embark on a journey through time to set right a terrible tragedy that happened during Harry's time at Hogwarts, but their meddling might create worse tragedies still. 
 This book, or rather play to be more precise, has garnered quite a lot of infamy, and for good reason. Despite being approved by Rowling herself, a lot of the play comes across like fan fiction. It's difficult to imagine Harry, Hermione, and Ron as adults, because they still talk and behave much like they did as children. Draco seems to be the only one who has grown and changed as a person. 
 Nevertheless, all of this would have been fine if only there had been one major change: the main character. We mostly followed Albus Potter through his ordeal trying to fit in at Hogwarts while having a famous wizard for a father. Through most of this, Albus comes off like a petulant brat, completely unable or unwilling to come to terms with his family heritage and using it as an excuse for his own failings. Meanwhile, Scorpious is going through a similar situation, except from the other end of the spectrum. The Malfoy family name has become toxic and Scorpious' parentage is steeped in controversy. Arguably Scorpious should have more of a chip on his shoulder, but he handles his problems with more grace and humor than Albus. So what I'm getting at is simple: Scorpious should have been the main character. It would have been much more interesting to follow a story from a Malfoy's point-of-view. Harry Potter's story is done and he came out on top - meanwhile Draco came out rock bottom and his son must reap the consequences of this. Scorpious simply has a much more engaging character arc than Albus and is the only character that keeps this play remotely interesting. 
 It's difficult to say if this story will work well as a play. On the surface, it seems ridiculous, but perhaps when acted out it becomes more palatable. There were moments that, despite the fan fiction feel, were pretty neat, especially involving the unexpected return of certain characters. It also felt a bit like cheap fan service at times.

sample_reviews.review_text: I read the book in just over one sitting, so it was an enjoyable read. I quickly settled into the world of Hogwarts again and I enjoyed a new generation of characters. It wasn't as masterful a story as I would have liked and was a bit predictable in some ways, but I was definitely entertained.

This book was not as I expected it to be. It was a huge disappointment. What the Harry Potter fans were really looking for was a Jk Rowling book, but this did not feel like her writing at all. I know that the book wasn't written by her but I had expected it to match her writing at least. The script was not very entertaining to read and Jk Rowling's writing is never so bland and boring. The story in all just felt unreal. The characters did not feel as the ones we already know and love. This book actually wasn't needed. Overall, I didn't really like this book and Harry Potter fans just don't need to waste their time reading it.

My expectations were pretty low going into this, and I was still underwhelmed. The story was juvenile and the dialogue so cheesy. Perhaps the actors delivered the lines in such a way that they came off as profound and meaningful. But, I felt like I was reading a children's book about the value of friendship. 
 By using time travel and dream sequences, the writers brought back so many characters from the books that it was too much. Do I really need to see Umbridge, Cedric Diggory, Moaning Myrtle, and Aunt Pentunia again? Not really. This kind of story manipulation in order to mention as many Harry Potter things as possible reminded me of Ready Player One and its overuse of 80's references. I hated that book. 
 There were several moments that had me thinking, "WTF?" but I will focus on just two here. First off, I'm still not over the fact that VOLDEMORT PROCREATED. Let that sink in for a second...okay, so Voldemort allegedly had sex with Bellatrix Lestrange, knocked her up, and has a daughter that the entire Wizarding World knew nothing about. Not only does the concept of Voldemort having sex carry a major ick factor, it makes zero sense. Voldemort was a villain and a monster. An elaborate spell/potion was required for him to even return to a somewhat human form. And he emerged from that cauldron with his fertility? Really? Plus, Voldemort didn't respect anyone but himself. You could argue that Lestrange had romantic feelings for Voldemort, but I'm pretty sure that Voldemort would have viewed relations with Lestrange, or anyone really, beneath him. Plus, he believed he could make himself immortal and rule over the entire wizarding world, so why would he have any desire to have a baby? Voldemort doesn't need a sidekick. And if he's immortal, he doesn't need someone to take over for him when he's dead. So...how does this make any sense at all? Secondly, Ron was so drunk when he married Hermione, that he doesn't remember their wedding? Really? Ok, wait, maybe I can't stop at just two things...I was also really bothered by the fact that Albus, Scorpius and Delphi were able to get into Hermione's office using Alohomora. Hermione would have used more protective spells. Also, the trolly witch randomly sprouting talons from her hands was creepy and weird. I am sighing, shaking my head, and choosing to believe that nothing in this play is canon. 
 Overall, I think the most disappointing part for me was finding out what happened to Harry, Ron and Hermione after the seventh book ended. A large part of me would rather have remained ignorant. We Harry Potter fans got seven wonderful books with a happy ending. I have closure. I don't need to read a story about a 40-year old Harry and his tumultuous relationship with his son. And if I ever get an inkling to revisit the Wizarding World, I have so many options. I can re-read the books, re-watch the movies, visit the theme park in Orlando, try to make butterbeer at home, listen to the movie soundtracks, visit Pottermore, etc. This play is fan-fiction. And fan-fiction is probably the only part of the Harry Potter fandom that I have not explored, and don't have a desire to. 
 Rowling should have just left Harry alone with All was well. 
 Further Reading: 
 1. Initial Reactions to "Harry Potter and the Cursed Child": A Rage Filled Catharsis 
 2. Top Five "Cursed Child" Plot Holes 
 3. Why It's Important Albus and Scorpius Aren't In Love 
 4. Top Five Random "Cursed Child" Moments 
 5. Why I Was Able to Enjoy "Cursed Child"

I really wanted to give 2.5 stars to this, but I can't, so I am constrained by the laws of mathematical rounding to give it three. I wanted it to be a home run, but it was a double, because of a bad throw from the outfield. 
 The first half of the play was not very well written, it seemed hackneyed and contrived. None of the characters, as I know them from the books, were acting or speaking in ways consistent with their development over 7 novels. It was frustrating. 
 The second half was better, but was not good enough to pull the 1 star I was prepared to give the book--based on the reading of the first half--a higher rating. 
 If you are a fan of the novels, you will find this screenplay passable, but I don't think you will enjoy it any more than I did and you will reach the end of the book wishing there were more to give praise about.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I'm not going to go super into this, but this read like bad fanfiction. 
 I felt like it undermined the characters and the message of the original books. The fact that Harry, Ron, and hermione supposedly taught their kids to hate Malfoy doesn't make sense and I don't see that actually happening after all they went through. 
 The second act is a slight against Hermione and her wonderful character. She did not need to marry Ron in order to be a successful and kind person. She was all that and more before Ron even had a slight clue that he liked her. Absolute garbage. 
 In general though, the story doesn't make much sense and I don't feel like it should have even been written. I'm sure seeing the play is a bit of a different experience, but the story and the characters are the same so I don't think it would change my opinion much.
Oh. Oh dear God. Oh, that just wasn't fair, making me feel all the feels again!!

After seeing the heavily mixed reviews for Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, I went in with low expectations but a forgiving attitude (J.K. Rowling can do no wrong, after all). However, I don't accept this story as canon. It's good fanfiction, but it's not gospel. 
 Although there are touches of the magical whimsy that never failed to fill my heart with giddiness, the play format ultimately robs the reader of any true emotional connection. There's simply not enough time to provide the characterization and depth that the Harry Potter universe deserves. Some of the dialogue was hilarious and poignant; at other times, it felt cheesy and forced. Even so, it's clear that the story has good intentions, and I appreciated the complex father-son relationship between Harry and Albus. The conflict between the two of them was what felt most authentic and interesting to me. In addition, the plot provides a lot of fan service in terms of referencing past characters and events, which made this a fitting tribute to the series. 
 Some readers hate Albus for being whiny and imperfect, but I think that's the point--he's a misfit. Still, I doubt anyone would disagree when I say Scorpius is the real MVP. Many fans tend to view Draco Malfoy through an idealized lens, one that Rowling didn't intend for a villain, and Scorpius is a reflection of Draco's soft caramel center. I'm cutting the writers some slack for giving certain characters more stage time than others; it's impossible to involve everyone in the action when you have time constraints. 
 The plot surprised me in a good way, at least for the first third. I would've never thought of that concept, and the narrative arc itself was very tightly constructed. Buuuut...the deus ex machina moments and one-dimensional villain ruined it for me. They felt like cheap solutions to complex problems. Plus, all the logistical issues involving time travel and government security made it difficult to suspend disbelief. The ending was kind of interesting, though, with the parallels between Albus and Harry when it came to both of them feeling responsible for the death of an innocent. 
 Despite the story's flaws, I can't wait until this play makes it to the States.

This book was an amazing instalment to the Harry Potter collection. You follow Harry, Ginny and his three children through their own experiences of Hogwarts, in particular, Albus. Albus feels as though he has some big boots to fill following his dad's heroic legacy. However, we find that through the ups and downs of Albus' experiences, friendship still wins over anything else. 
 The way in which this is written is so magical, even as a scripted piece, however, it would have been nicer to have experienced this in the form of a novel instead. I truly would love to see how the theatre transforms the magic in the book onto the stage, something which would probably still baffle me! The main love that I had for this book was the relationship between Scorpius Malfoy and Albus Dumbledore, it was something that I felt as though was weaved into this plot very well, and it should be emphasised more in literature. Overall, it pacified my need for magic and the world of Harry and his friends as they complete another task, but this time to protect their own children. I would highly recommend this to anyone who has a profound love for the magic of Harry Potter.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Drivel. Pure drivel. The only reason this gets two stars is for Harry Potter-based nostalgia. I think the characters of Albus and Scorpius were interesting, and I'd have liked to read more about them, but the horrid, fanfiction-y plot made this an unbearable read. What an utter disappointment.

sample_reviews.review_text: Kind of a three-star ending, but it was a fun, fast read. The main character started out feeling older than he really was, but he grew on me. There were a few predictable scenes, but there were also a few surprises.

 There is more to this story and Zevin seemed to come near the end, tire of the characters and wrapped it up rather quickly - that was a little disappointing. 
 Worth pondering: "No one who travels without purpose. Those who are lost wish to be lost."

"No Man is an Island; Every Book is a World" 
 So reads the motto on the sign of Island Books. Owner A. J. Fikry, a recent widower, is the owner of Island Books on Alice Island. Slow sales, few friends and grief are taking a toll on A. J.'s enjoyment of life and love of books. After the theft of one of his prized possessions and a mysterious appearance of a small but important gift, A. J.'s life begins to change but not in a way that he would ever have expected. 
 Each chapter begins with a reference to a short story and becomes a sort of love letter to his daughter, Maya. We see how books, reading them and writing them can change your life and transform what you expect the future has in store for you. 
 This is a must read.
Just didn't connect with this one. I can see why people liked it though.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Why, Goodreads, why can't I give a book zero stars?! Because this garbage book certainly deserves zero stars. 
 Sometimes, the library opens my eyes to enjoyable books with the book club selections (not specific group, just a title which is segregated into an area where many copies are available for patron's consumption). "Fikry," which sounds a bit like a swear and which I may begin using as such given the increase in my bile due to reading this waste of paper, however, is not one of those books. Have you guessed that I didn't find the novel "a page-turning delight," "marvelously optimistic," or "a reader's paradise of the first order?" The only delight in turning pages was to finish this heap of trash. 
 Let me explain why before continuing with further metaphors. The characterization is nowhere; there are just cardboard cutouts propped up everywhere. 
 And the plot. My Lord, what a mess. The "charming" device of using a memoir about a widower to eventually connect the curmudgeonly middle-aged bookstore owner and publisher's rep was soooo ham-fisted. And what's the name of the publishing house of this magical tome? KNIGHTLEY. Good gravy, save me from bad Jane Austen allusions. Let's just tack a bunch of stories together about a stolen, prized book, an unfaithful author husband, a surprise baby, adoption, and suicide. Of course, the baby transforms the curmudgeon (who, let's face it, is unsurprisingly falling apart after the sudden death of his beloved wife). And he suddenly becomes beloved by the entire town. OF COURSE. Mind you, I love old movies, but this Fikry thing is like a really bad movie from the '30s or '40s, all saccharin and nonsense. I'm surprised the author didn't throw in a dance number or something. 
 This book doesn't even have decent writing to tie together the mess of a plot. Goodreads won't let me quote the exact problems with the book BECAUSE I'D HAVE TO TYPE IN THE ENTIRE CONTENTS. I will state that the chapter intros describing short stories to Maya were soooo stupid. 
 Okay, I'm all worked up. It's time for wine to cleanse my pallet of this terrible taste.

This is the story of one man. His life is the life of an ordinary man. At the same time it is a remarkable book about a remarkable life. Like George Bailey, A J Fikrey influences more than he knows in ways he doesn't recognize. Loved the book

A true testament to the bibliophile. For what other reason do we gather not just to talk about but to at times dissect books? The author wove the story together so subtly I hardly noticed where it was really headed. I started out not caring much for Mr. Fikry only to realize, at some indistinguishable point, that I'd totally fallen in love with him, mourning the fact that he of all people wound up at such an incredulous end. I loved Maya for her unique "nerdy" mind and Amelia for her fortitude and total love for the bookseller. 
 Just a lovely, lovely read.

sample_reviews.review_text: I decided this year that if I did like a book by page 50-75 that I was quitting. I stopped at page 68. I am not sure what went wrong but I was sooooooo bored. Based on the ratings from others I am assuming it gets better but I could not wait for it to get there.

I had real trouble getting through this. I found the book annoying in places, confusing in other places, and downright dull in yet other places. The style of writing ranged from lifestyle descriptions, which I found monotonous, to clever memory plays on previous events, which I tended to find grating. 
 The characters seemed to have no fixed qualities, reflecting the constant change in their lives. I found this hard to grasp, as I prefer to believe we all have some innate qualities. Particularly Ursula who lived many lifetimes became a product of society and her surroundings. While events in our life do help to shape us, we all have things that are essentially us. I guess these things can be torn from us, but Ursula's character ranges too far for me to empathise with. 
 The story also seemed to go nowhere, and seemed rather pointless. Is Ursula caught in an everlasting cycle of birth and rebirth, or did she break out? Did she fulfill a destiny or was there really no destiny to fulfill? These are questions that I found difficult to answer from reading the novel, and as such I'm at a loss to understand what the point of the novel was,

This is the first book I read by Kate Atkinson. It is an incredible romp through one person's reincarnations. I could not put it down. It shows how the smallest decisions can change you life in major ways.
I liked the idea of this novel of what are the possibilities that could happen in the main character's life. It felt a little long at times.

Just not my cuppa'. . . 
 All the repeats of Ursula's lives--drove me crazy. 
 Could not finish the novel, but got through the first third of the book, and feel I read enough to make a few comments. 
 Felt so jerky, starting and stopping and starting again. 
 Disruptive. 
 Perhaps I am old-fashioned, and just want my straightforward story in a novel--a beginning, a middle, a problem to be solved, a resolution. 
 On the plus side--appreciated the humor and wit in these pages. Also, have learned that Kate Atkinson was the creator of one of my very favorite detectives--Jackson Brodie--of Case Histories (which I watched in a BBC series). 
 I will look for the next book by this author, and I acknowledge the quality of her writing. But every author has hits or misses. In many readers' minds, this was one of her hits. In mine, it's a miss. 
 As I read all the repeats, I wondered to myself--why do this to the reader? Make the reader struggle, make the reader scratch his or her head? Forgive me if this is unfair to suggest, but the skeptic in me wondered if Kate wanted a gimmick, something new and different to give to the world, to grab people's attention. I could not help but think of a modern painting of a blank canvas with one orange circle in it, framed and hanging in some museum, with people oo-ing and aweing. But to me--the emperor has no clothes. 
 Some readers like the challenge of trying to figure out what the author was trying to say by his or her gimmick. To this kind of reader, the challenge makes the reading more exciting and clever. 
 I don't want that excitement. Or rather, I prefer to be excited by the story line, by my identifying with the characters and getting caught up in their lives, but not by a writing device. To have to struggle with reading goes against my reason for reading--to escape. How can I escape if I feel irritated or frustrated while I read?

A good Miss Marple mystery with lots of suspects and red herrings. Quite enjoyable.

This is what happens when one reds too much Agatha Christie. It seems as though I know most of her tricks. I was convinced of the culprit the moment the murder occurred and deduced 80% of the plot - the means and motive. As pages turned, my convictions strengthened. The beauty of Agatha Christie is that everyone in the murder mystery is open to suspicion (even including the narrator sometimes) except for the sleuth in action. Here though the story is different. There are no plausible scenarios that can seduce a reader to think 'could this be so and so?'. 
 And there comes the reason for the low rating. Not so much because I foresaw the truth. But because the initial explanations for the murder by all the characters were so much improbable. The brazenness with which the idea was conceived-that of announcing a murder beforehand- must be appreciated. But the execution of the same falls below the standards Christie herself have put up. Still I did enjoy being proved right. Whatever small surprise I had at the end [spoiler] of Phillipa being Pip [/spoiler] didn't affect the plot at all. Also, she forgot to explain [spoiler] what was curious about the Colonel's wife [/spoiler], though it has nothing to o with the plot. 
 I think i will not read another Agatha Christie book for some time. The magic is too familiar for me to see through the tricks.
Miss Marple is apparently everyone's Aunt Jane. This time she is called on to find out who is trying to kill a kind woman. But the killer keeps missing and killing everyone around her.

Just re-read my first Agatha Christie in years and years. Margaret is reading a "Miss Marple" for her Destination Imagination team. I read every single book of hers when I was younger, and she has stood the test of time.

This is the first Agatha Christie book I ever figured out the solution to all on my own. (This was the first time I read it, many years ago.) Re-reading now, I remembered the key question I asked myself, so I had a good idea of how to get at the solution, and I very quickly remembered what was going on. What made that all interesting was that I could see how cleverly Christie built in the clues that make the solution absolutely clear--IF you are reading carefully! She plays fair! If you don't figure out the puzzles, it's your own fault!

I enjoyed this, the first Miss Marple I've read, and it was quite clever. But I had suspected I wouldn't be able to get much attached to Marple, and I found that, sadly, to be the case. I have a limited capacity for enjoying the dialogue of old English ladies - who describe everything in italics (e.g., "simply delightful," "absolutely horrid"), and those seem to make up the majority of the minor characters. (Though Marple, of course, possesses an acute sense of observation, a formidable sleuth with a disarming costume of woolen shawls and knitting needles.) 
 Maybe I'm just burnt out on mysteries right now.

A Murder is Announced was, as I'm finding usual with Agatha Christie, quite fun and reasonably absorbing. One could tire of it very easily, since the writing isn't anything special -- although I generally like the characters in the background quite a lot. When I like them a lot, it's a three-star read; when no one particularly caught my attention, only two-star. (The difference between "it was ok" and "liked it".) 
 The plot of this one is very torturous, and very... unlikely. Okay, okay, most of these books are, but the way that two imposters show up, but neither of them are actually doing anything wrong, although both keep their identity hidden, and then suddenly at the end a third imposter is revealed... 
 Still, fun and easy, which is what I expect from these books.

I really enjoyed A Murder is Announced, and would rank it as one of Christie's best, although I've read less than half of her novels. What I liked about this particular story was that the plot and characters are relatively easy to keep up with. Several of the earlier Miss Marple series had me back reading and confusing some characters. This was very well done and has a great plot. Looking forward to the rest of the Ms Marple series.
The plot seemed a little jerry-rigged but Christie is always a charming read.

I reread SPEAK in honor of Banned Book Week. More than ever, this book has a place in every high school. I would even go so far as it belongs in middle school because current middle schools have students who have experienced the same experience as Melinda. The book describes Melinda's experience at her first high school party. She spends her 9th grade year suffering inside when she needed to voice her disgust and find the necessary help she needed. Her suffering exposed itself in her attitude, her grades, her lack of friends, her feelings of poor self esteem, in other words, her entire life. The reader goes with her through that ninth grade year.

LAURIE HALSE ANDERSON, PRINTZ HONOR BOOK 
 Anderson's Printz Honor Book explores Melinda Sordino's freshman year of high school as she deals with the aftermath of being raped at a summer party. Because her peers believe that she called the cops about the party (and not about the rape) she becomes completely ostracized. The title of the book hearkens to Melinda's inability to reach out to her parents, peers, best friend, teachers, etc. to get help. Depression, anxiety, self-harm, abuse, and relationships are all themes explored throughout Anderson's book. I absolutely loved this book. I felt that Melinda's voice was so authentic, the problems in the book were so applicable to young adults, and the tie-in of Melinda's art class and teacher helping her to come to terms with her experience was so significant. In her art class, Melinda is assigned 'tree' as her year-long subject--she is supposed to master the image of the tree. This assignment comes full circle as, at the end of the novel, one of the trees outside of Melinda's home rots, and a man comes to cut the rotten branches away. The reader learns that by cutting away at the rotten parts of a tree, the tree is able to flourish--and similarly, by the end of the novel Melinda learns to cut the rotten pieces of her life away. I would absolutely recommend this book to any upper level junior high school or any high school student.
I've read it 4 times now. This book is one of my all-time favorites.
