reference_books.title: As a Man Thinketh
reference_books.review_text: While going through a box of miscellany the other day, I came across this book. Intrigued, I flipped through the pages and started reading it. Though this appears to be a sort of philosophical work, the pictures and Internet-mimicking (making each page look like an Internet website) throughout the pages greatly distracts from its intent, thereby negating any seriousness and confirming its cartoonish presentation. In a positive vein, the Old Masters type reproductions ion the pages are pleasing to look at; they don't belong in this sort of book if it's to be taken seriously. This book isn't my cup of tea, and it's in my "To Donate" box.

reference_books.title: Men Are from Mars, Women Are from Venus
reference_books.review_text: Insipid, sexist, and condescending. I got a well-worn copy from someone who swore that when I read it, I would understand my spouse so much better -- because she "finally understood " her husband due to this book. Plus, "everyone is reading it!" (So?) This book turned out to be a laughable stereotype-promoting manual. I did read the book in its entirety, laughed, then returned it to its owner. It really was a waste of my time.

reference_books.title: Life of Pi
reference_books.review_text: Not sure what this book is supposed to convey. It's like "The Little Prince" meets "The Jungle Book" meets "The Emerald Forest" and takes a wrong turn at Albuquerque. I found it tedious and the writing a bit stilted. It isn't for me. I'll stick with "Siddhartha" for life's revelations.

reference_books.title: Daddy-Long-Legs (Daddy-Long-Legs, #1)
reference_books.review_text: The premise of this story of a rich man paying for the college education of an orphaned girl sounds intriguing at first, but as I kept turning the pages, it became a disturbing tale at best. As part of his gift of paying for her tuition, subsistence, and niceties, he directs her to write him letters on her progress, and she does -- plus more. She nicknames him "Daddy-Long-Legs" from the shadowy glimpse she got of him once, and addresses her letters to him as such, but she eventually calls him with an abbreviated nomenclature, "Daddy," and professes her interest in him, and that's where the story became even more weird for my taste. This tale didn't work for me, and outcome was fantasy. The author's writing style is good for adolescents. I watched the 1919 Mary Pickford film version of this story, and it was more palatable, but still, it's a disturbing story of socially twisted characters.

book_a.title: A Certain Age
book_a.user_review:
I purchased this book based on the reviews and the setting of the novel in the 1920s. I was greatly disappointed. 
 The writing is disjointed, the storyline weak, and a character named "Patty Cake" made this whole project insipid. Really. This one is a bomb. It wasn't for me. 
 The book's cover is beautiful, so all is not lost.

sample_reviews.review_text: A definite page turner! There is an underlying love story in this book that really touched me, a connection between two characters that ran deep. I was frustrated at times with Octavian, the male lead, the type of man who wants to do the right thing, even if it's the wrong thing, even if it will bring a different kind of suffering. But it also makes him more human, a man who wants to keep to his word. Of the two female leads, Sophie was my favorite. She began very innocent, as though the entire world had just been revealed to her and she was trying to figure it out, and it didn't take her long at all to realize how complicated it actually was and how much her heart could hurt in it. But she also realized how strong she was and didn't fear having to stand in the world on her own if she had to. I wasn't overly fond of Theresa, the married socialite who'd been bedding Octavian for the last two years, the way in which she called him her Boy, how I think she wanted to have her cake and eat it too. There was scheming, but not over the top. Theresa is still likeable, a woman you can understand why she does what she does and who deserves happiness. There is a mystery involving Sophie's family here too, a trial that is told through a social column, and a climax that is quite intense, but I kept turning pages for the love triangle, to find out who would end up with who.

I enjoyed this historical read inspired by an opera set in NYC in the 1920s. Beatriz Williams writes such great books and this one didn't disappoint. Murder, scandal, romance,mystery--what's not to like? I highly recommend reading this one.

I tried real hard to like this book and just couldn't. The characters were annoying, the language of the book was hard to read. The problem with this author is she comes up with great story ideas but doesn't execute them well.
I've enjoyed all of Beatriz Williams books and this was no exception. It's a great mystery that takes place in New York City and the Hamptons during the Jazz Age.

2.5 stars. I am not entirely sure Williams' attempt to adapt a 19th-Century opera into a novel set in 1920's New York was successful. I usually feel very connected to her characters and really enjoy her writing, this was the first book of hers that felt somewhat stilted and strange. Mind you, I must have liked it somewhat because I have every intention of reading the follow up novel, Cocoa Beach.

Not only did I read this book, I re-started reading this book because I felt that I had missed critical points at the beginning. Why? Yes Williams did address the roaring 1920s between youth and age, tradition and modernism and old and new money. From the beginning of this book I saw Mrs. Theresa Marshall being played on the big screen by Cate Blanchette. Williams re-interpreted the comic opera of Richard Strauss's Der Rosenkavalier and set it against the roaring 1920s in New York City. A very poor way I feel to interpret the opera. Secondly Williams structure of writing became a little problematic especially on how the characters in her story were referred to as Mr and Mrs instead of a first name basic. Then refer to the same Mr or Mrs on a first name basic. This is shown constantly between Theresa brother Ox and her lover Octavian. The reader could become disjointed with the lack of structure in the story line. 
 Further complicating the story line was Williams invention of a murder mystery. Why oh why bother did Williams try this? The murder mystery just added to the lacklustre story line and it was totally and absolutely unbelievable to me. 
 The best part of this book was how Williams structured Helen Rowland's "Reflections of a Bachelor Girl" in the New York World newspaper. What a fabulous and accurate reflection of how really men and women have not changed even though a hundred years have passed. 
 What happened to Sophie's friend Julie? Who knows, she just gets dropped from the story line and frankly, to quote Rhett Butler in Gone with the Wind, "Frankly my dear, I don't give a damn". 
 From the beginning of this book to the end I have fluctuated between viewing the read as the greatest bore I have ever read to being the most interesting book I have ever read. As you can see from my rating a 1.5 you get a sense where I finally took a stand.

Terrible! I can't even say that this book wasn't a good fit, 1920's New York with 2 leading ladies is exactly what I love. Unfortunately the boring story telling made this a big flop. 
 1 star is harsh but I couldn't think of any redeeming qualities and I want all my friends to pass on it.

Oh, how I loved this book. After a spate of novels that ranged from awful to almost-not-bad, it was such a joy to come across a book I genuinely adored. 
 I loved the writing style, the era, and the characters. In fact, I think it was the characters that made this for me, especially Theresa. The (not so) inner romantic in me adored Sophie and Octavian - I confess every interaction made me want to find a Victorian fainting couch for the express purpose of swooning. But it is easy to make those characters likable - they are young, they are innocent and intense, they have principles. 
 But to make me like Theresa and wish her happiness is a lot more complicated. Objectively, she should not be likable - a woman engaging in adultery with a "boy" literally half her age (and trying to keep the young lovers apart for a large portion of the book, to boot). But she is so witty, so surprisingly self-aware (ironic for a character who is uncomfortable going beneath the surface with anyone else), and so very human - her affair is driven more by her desire to cling to her lost youth and to feel something than it is by pure lust or boredom. She is a desperate, unfulfilled woman underneath the charm, who can be occasionally kind (when it ultimately matters), and possibly the most magnetic character in the novel.

I liked the story, but there were a few things that kept me from loving it. I didn't like that we found out so much information from the reporter sections, and some of the characters felt two dimensional. 
 The writing was good and the relationships were interesting. All and all, I definitely liked it. I'm glad that I won it from GoodReads. Thank you!

I wish I had known at the start that the plot for this novel is based on an opera by Strauss. I feel like that may have further enhanced my experience (and perhaps made me read it more rapidly). It is about the struggle between old and new. In the author's own words, "the angsty rivalry between a beautiful young ingenue and a lady of a certain age." If google doesn't think angsty is a word, it needs to get with it (it's telling me I have a spelling error). This is the second novel I have read by the author (The Secret Life of Violet Grant is the other) and I look forward to reading her others. I definitely recommend this.

book_b.title: Anthem
book_b.user_review: This was, to my great surprise, an outstanding novella with a solid storyline about a dystopian society and the movement towards the realization of the self as individual. Ayn Rand's writing style grabs the reader and moves from one scene and/or thought to the next so smoothly that one feels a part of the plot and nothing else in the world exists. The characters are well-developed. Some portions of the story reminded me of Orwell's "Nineteen Eighty-four" and Noland and Johnson's "Logan's Run." This is not to say these three works are alike, but rather, there are scenes that are reminiscent. Indeed, all three are unique as a whole, but share the same grey dystopian milieu. Because this is a novella, I read it in one evening. It's a brilliant work, and I highly recommend it as part of a well-rounded literary and political education.

sample_reviews.review_text: This book was very well written and also through provoking for someone like me who has always taken individuality for granted, and even at times seen it in a negative light. Definitely worth reading.

Give her credit. Rand was an effective spokesperson for the libertarian branch of conservatism for a time, before her eccentricities caused people to stop taking her seriously and others had to step up to defend libertarianism. 
 The defense is ongoing, but doomed, I suspect. Libertarianism feels too much like a utopian scheme that will fail in actual practice. It is too narrow, focusing on only a few things that make human lives valuable while ignoring a host of others. 
 I am not qualified to speak on behalf of conservatives, but it is clear that many of them sense this narrowness and that's why libertarianism has had only limited impact in influencing conservative thinking. Even among conservatives, it seems that most outgrow Rand eventually, though she will always enjoy some popularity among undergraduates who are just beginning to experience the real world. 
 It may be the maturing influence of meeting life's struggles that leads most adults to acquire that sense of citizenship that balances gratitude for what we have with responsibility for service to others. Young people have not had that experience yet, and can be forgiven for an incomplete view of what makes a happy and productive life. 
 But more to the point of GoodReads is that Rand is not a talented writer. Her prose is like a bludgeon. It is mind-numbing. There is no subtlety or nuance. Nothing to excite your aesthetic sensibility. Even if you think her ideas are interesting, her books are not good art. Anthem has the saving grace of being short, but it exhibits little in the way of interesting writing.
amazing

There's not really a story in this book. Sure there's something about a light bulb, and a street cleaner and other odds and ends that unfold in a Spartan like world similar to what Plato laid out in his Republic. The story is only there to bring out Rand's absolutist (Objectivism) worldview. 
 Love at first sight is the only love she seems to recognize, equality is bad and liberty (freedom) is the only pure good, the ego rules supreme, our lives must have work in order to be happy, and a variation of the Galtism "I swear by my life and love of it, that I will never sacrifice for another and neither expect some one to do the same for me". All of Rand's themes that pop up in her other books, pop up within this short book. At first one loves that kind of talk, but then one realizes she really means it. Freedom as a goal in itself for just the sake of freedom is sort of silly. Sometimes equality matters sometimes we feel like hugging that horse when it gets beaten (Nietzsche's last sane act). To think otherwise is to always remain a fifth grader. 
 This book was Nietzsche on steroids. Their premises are different but their conclusions definitely overlap. Both clearly have a post-modern and anti-humanist take on the world and each dislike major aspects of the Enlightenment. Nietzsche, of course, is not an absolutist, but his 'will to power' is a primal scream returning us to our true instincts for the value of the individual over the group and Rand would embrace that part of his philosophy as well as a lot of other things within Nietzsche's philosophy. 
 The nicest thing about this book was that it was mercifully short.

I'll be honest: when my 11th-grade student pulled this out of her backpack and showed it to me, I recoiled like a vampire in sunlight. 
 Well, not literally. 
 But I was definitely less than thrilled: politically, objectivism is the polar opposite of my jam. And I didn't warm up to it in the reading, either - not so much because of the philosophy, but because I just don't enjoy stories without any room for interpretation. There is only one way to view the hero (the avatar of all that is right and good), and only one way to view his society (the craven, rotten epitome of collectivist evil), and absolutely nothing approaching nuance or subtlety to be found - no meaning or credible conclusion save the one the author intends. We have a name for stories like these. 
 Here is the interesting thing, though: my student warmed up to this book more than any other. Not because she necessarily agrees with the whole message (in fact, she is pretty big on charity, social programs, etc.), but I think because this was the first book where the characters and symbols were transparent enough that she could see through them to the author's main message. It was kind of an exciting lightbulb moment for her, not to be made to guess or sit back and be told that the the optician's billboard in The Great Gatsby represents such-and-such, but to actually notice symbols and big ideas all on her own. It was cool to see her actually excited about taking a book apart and talking about it, and having a genuinely good discussion about its ideas ("Where else in our world do people have to give up some freedoms and live/work in groups?" "Well, in school, and in the military, for example..." "Why is that considered okay? Like, how is that different than the world in the book?" "Well...") 
 Anyway - two stars from me, four stars from her, and at the end of the day, I'm glad we read this one. I think it's important to remember that it's okay if the books students attach to at the beginning of their reading careers aren't the same ones we would want them to enjoy as mature readers, and good for all of us to spend some time reading things we don't agree with. 
 Oh, and we made this cool diorama, too. 
 The quote is, "I am done with the monster of We, the word of serfdom, of plunder, of misery, falsehood and shame." So our shirtless ubermensch there is fighting the Monster of We with his sword (the letter I) and all his colorful, newly-individualized buddies, to save the blank ones still stuck in collectivist hell. Not bad, if we do say so ourselves!

Derivative, unimaginative, didactic crap. I respected Atlas Shrugged without being converted to objectivism, but this was a lazy effort at preaching the gospel of ego. I guess she got better at it; Anthem was the first draft. 
 Also, it's ironic that a book devoted to the power and value of the self still has its female character belong to a man.
The female lead was frustratingly stupid. I didn't like what Rand had to say about gender.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I hated this book. I had two problems. As I said when I was reading, she is verbose. Why use one word when five will do. I prefer a clean story, not one that calls attention to its language in a negative way. 
 But the story is the bigger issue. There really wasn't one, to speak of. She definitely doesn't go for the concept of Utopia. That's fine. But she's created a world that is so horrible that death is preferable. There is absolutely no reason that anyone should live in this society. It has no redeeming value. So the character should have killed himself and ended the story there. 
 Instead, we suffer through this fate worse than death until he finally escapes. And when he escapes, when he discovers the I of ego, he becomes a sexist megalomaniac. The woman he loves serves only to bear his children and his "chosen friends" will be apostles as he creates a new world in the image he's determined is best. 
 Now, the concept of Utopia being worth the cost is worthy of exploration. And a MUCH better vehicle for that exploration is the YA novel, The Giver, by Lois Lowery. Because Utopia certainly would never be worth the cost if you didn't get something back from it. 
 And with Ayn Rand's attempt the reader just wishes to be done.

"The first blow of the lash felt as if our spine had been cut in two. The second blow stopped the first, and for a second we felt nothing, then pain struck us in our throat and fire ran in our lungs without air. But we did not cry out." -- Equality 7-2521, ch.6I wrote this quote down just because how intense that whole chapter was or maybe just that part that struck me the most out of the whole story. 
 "Through all the darkness, through all the shame of which men are capable, the spirit of man will remain alive on this earth. It may sleep, but it will awaken. It may wear chains, but it will break through." -- Equality 7-2521, ch.12 
 collectivism to individualism 
 The author sends a message to those fighting for individualism with Equality 7-2521's remarks on how he wishes he could carry a message to those past generations that suffered during the transition period. Rand wanted to warn those who believed in collectivism about its dangers and to aid those who are still holding up the resistance in the name of the individual. For this reason Equality 7-2521 tells them that no matter how stark things may be, the individual will survive. Well thats how I interpret the story anyway
hahahahahahaha *in zoolander voice* what is this? a divergent for toddlers?

reference_books.title: Afterwards
reference_books.review_text: This was mostly enjoyable, but the technique of having the narrator address her husband throughout the story as 'you' turned me off after awhile. Also, the story is told from her having an out of body experience while lying in a coma which naturally has some limitations in terms of the scope of plot, and I don't really think it's sustainable fora full length novel.

reference_books.title: A Prisoner of Birth
reference_books.review_text:
So I read this book last summer at my parents' cottage, and then read it again this summer, forgetting that I'd read it before until the very end. I have a pretty good memory for books, so that says it all, doesn't it? 
 And clearly Jeffrey Archer has not heard of the show-don't-tell rule of writing. I'm all for breaking that rule on occasion, but not on every page. Not so the reader feels like they are in a sixth grade English class.

reference_books.title: The Husband's Secret
reference_books.review_text: This is a tough book. I loved it, loved the characters, but in the end I wondered how they really could go on. It is, I suppose, an as-happy-as-you-can-be kind of ending. Love this author!

reference_books.title: Wreckage
reference_books.review_text: The cover of this book makes it look like it's going to be a deep, psychoanalytical study of what happens when people try to covers something up but no, it was a ridiculous, over-the-top soap opera. Disappointing, I'm sorry to say.

reference_books.title: Alone in Berlin
reference_books.review_text: Kind of slow

book_a.title: The Chaperone
book_a.user_review: This book was disappointing. It went really slowly and then sped through fifty years in about as many pages--and felt rather preachy at times--not to mention the whole end setup with the heroine, her husband, and their SOs being unrealistic and dishonest. If they really felt strongly about it, shouldn't they have taken a public stand?

sample_reviews.review_text: Essentially chick lit, but with an historical twist. Such fun!

So many people enjoyed this book and I thought it was just OK. I have read so much better but then I have read a lot worse too. 
 I never did feel a connection with any of the characters. Cora the main character didn't really seem to have a spine, and I felt she lacked depth. Some of the story was well written but I felt it faltered in places and just never really worked.

I read this book in two days, which either shows it was great or it was easy reading. I really enjoyed this book until the end. Basically, the plot is that Cora travels with a young 15 year old, Louise Brooks, to New York, for dance. The book takes place during the 1920s and highlights women's vote, clothing changes, prohibition, great depression, etc. Cora is a married women with two grown sons. She participates in society functions and follows all the 'rules' such as morals and how someone should dress. She travels to New York, in order to discover more about her past. Louise doesn't enjoy following Cora's rules and often tries to break free. 
 Cora discovers herself more than just being the society woman, wife, and mother. Her spirit is almost awakened as she sees Louise act certain ways. 
 I almost give the book 4 stars, but I really wasn't pleased with the ending. Yes, Cora discovered herself more in New York, but I think it was too drastic than what probably would actually happen. There wasn't too much character depth. The author seemed to need to include all details from this time period. Did I enjoy the book? Yes, but I didn't love the book.

In June 2012, this was the first book I ever put on my list of books to read. It was the time period of the 1920s that was so intriguing, and I thought it interesting to see the controversies and changes in our country throughout Cora's long life, and particularly watching how her own morals and biases changed through life experience. While I thought the author paced the 100 years well, I didn't love the book, most likely because Louise Brooks was such an entirely unlikable human being. I oftentimes wished I could reach into the book and slap her pretty face. How depressing to know she actually lived and wrote a book about her sorry life. I figured the story would end with Cora finding her family, so the latter part of the book was a surprise. I have always been enamored with the flapper era, but this book made it seem sad. I'm not sure I would have enjoyed a time of so much scrutiny and high expectations, not to mention the risks of a tarnished reputation and all the gossip the follows.

** spoiler alert ** 
 the Chaperone held my attention and I enjoyed many aspects of the story although I disagreed with the social aspects of the story. I was pleased that the story was not predictable or cheesy. 
 At times I thought the author was using foreshadowing and nothing would come of it and other times I saw the next thing coming before it happened. I didn't enjoy the fact that there were homosexual relationships as well as adulterous relationships normalized in the story. The fact that these were best option for the main character is contrary to the Bible and encourages the reader in the belief that there are no other options. For Cora there were no other options, but Cora is a fictional character. It is easy for readers to confuse the two and believe that a real life individual would be equally trapped. I did appreciate the kindness that Cora continued to show Louise despite her awful behavior toward Cora throughout their experiences together. Cora showed immense grace and recognized that Louise's early childhood had a great deal to do with her behavior as an adult. As far as Myra goes, some people should not have children! I read this because the author is coming to our library for an event and I wanted to have read the book.

I received this book via FirstReads. 
 This story is the fictional telling of a trip silent film star Louise Brooks and her chaperone, Cora, made to New York City when Louise was 15. Louise is attending a Denishawn dance academy, hoping to win a part in their troupe. Cora, a 36 year old mother of 2 college age boys, comes along to try to keep Louise in line with the morals of the day. However, she has her own reasons from the past to want to visit New York City. 
 I enjoyed this story; it made me want to learn more about Louise Brooks and read her memoir. Cora's character became much more likeable as her backstory was revealed. While I was glad we got to learn what became of the characters after the time in New York ended, I felt that the conclusion was longer than it needed to be. Still, I would recommend this book to anyone who likes historical fiction.

Cora Carlisle is hired to escort Louise Brooks, a minor, to NY from Wichita, Kansas. Louise is auditioning for a famous dance troupe and Cora, the responsible adult, finds this to be a perfect opportunity to investigate her own past. The story is set in the 1920s and continues through 50 years of Cora's life. 
 Louise Brooks was actually a real silent film star, and it was interesting to learn about details of her career as well. Louise certainly needed a chaperone because she was a wild and reckless teen who liked to flirt with older men with a disregard to laws of prohibition. Cora, a proper married, woman was tested by Louise and tempted when she finds herself sneaking off with a maintenance man who works in the boarding house where they are staying. 
 Cora's ulterior motive for taking the job as Louise's chaperone was to search for information about her birth parents. She was raised by nuns in NY as a very young girl before being sent away on an orphan train bound for Kansas to live with her adoptive family. Her husband is a well-liked attorney, but he has secrets himself ... his longtime friend is also his lover. It seems his marriage to Cora is a cover-up for his homosexuality. Although theirs is a kind and caring relationship it lacks passion and is more likely compared to a brother/sister kinship. 
 There are many twists and turns throughout the story as the lives of these women unfold. It was a hard book to put down and quite shocking in parts. I won't spoil too much by the set-up and insight into the secret motives and past lives of the characters, but I will say that there is much to learn, ponder, and discuss after reading this book. It touches on many historical highlights about rights of women and taboos of the time.
Enjoyable but pacing was off. Fascinating research about the 1920s, the orphan train and more than a few other storylines. Wished more info on some events, less info on other situations....

So part of the reason I liked this book so much was the time period - the flappers, the jazz music, the scandalous skirt lengths (showing the knee? oh my!). But also, it's a great book. 
 The Chaperone is mostly about Cora Carlisle. Cora is an orphan, sent out from The School for Friendless Girls on a train from New York City to be picked over by the childless masses of the mid-west. Some of the childless couples truly wanted a child - others had worse fates in mind. Cora was adopted by a family that loved her, but she's always been curious about her birth parents. When she hears that an uppity neighbor requested that one of the neighborhood women chaperone her daughter to NYC to attend a dance class, Cora jumps at the opportunity. She's hoping to learn more about her parentage and this is her chance. 
 Moriarty did a great job peeling the layers of Cora away so that the Cora you started with is not the same Cora in the end. Cora is discovering herself as you the reader are discovering her, too. Through flashbacks you learn of her parentage and why her relationship with her extremely handsome husband is strained. In the future, you agonize with her when the nuns won't give her any information on where she came from, and cheer when she's able to get it through the kindness of a handyman. 
 Cora's charge, Louise Brooks, is so annoying you wish you could reach through the book and slap her silly. But again, Moriarty did an amazing job creating a character that you absolutely can't stand, but also pity. Louise is selfish and rude, mean-spirited and manipulative. She's also gorgeous, a wonderful dancer, and a world-class teenager, believing the world to be her oyster. You also know a different Louise by the end, and you understand a little of what contributed to make her the way she was. 
 Highly recommend, I truly enjoyed the book very much. I am looking with much anticipation towards reading Moriarty's next book!

This book started out good, but the last half was boring and unnecessary. It was as if the author just gave up. I did enjoy learning more about the drastic change in women's thoughts and dress in the twenties.

book_b.title: After You (Me Before You, #2)
book_b.user_review: I absolutely love Jojo Moyes' books, but this one didn't really do it for me. Me Before You was complete, and I liked the way that book ended, on a note of hope for Louisa. This book wasn't necessary, and didn't add anything to Louisa's story, at least that I wanted to know. I would have rather imagined Louisa's life after Will on my own.

sample_reviews.review_text: Not always a fan of sequels, but this was a good one.
I wish I hadn't read this. Me Before You was a great book but this sequel, unnecessary.
Loved it. I still miss Will.
Still an enjoyable read but nothing compare to "Me Before You"
I rarely if ever quit on a book, but this was so disappointing after reading Me Before You. And, I do love this author.

I read more than half-way through this novel (sorry, listened to more than half of this novel) before I decided that, actually, I didn't like, care about, or even want to know anything more about Lily. I picked up After You primarily because it's a book my mom adored. She was stuck on a long waiting list for Me Before You at our local library and picked up this companion novel in the meantime and, to put it quite simply, she couldn't stop talking about it. 
 Needless to say, my mom and I have very different tastes. Not to mention, my mom is a significantly nicer person than I am so she sympathized with Lily while I ranted about this selfish, spoiled, and highly irritating sixteen-year-old girl. There is a LOT to love about After You. I enjoyed Louisa's family immensely, especially her relationship with her sister. I admired Jojo Moyes for writing a companion novel that isn't perfect. Louisa is still grieving and though she tries to be everything Will ever wanted her to be, she falls short and fails spectacularly at doing the one thing he asked: live. And I appreciated this messy, imperfect life of Louisa and the mistakes that she made along her journey. 
 But while Me Before You tackles a sad, depressing subject, it feels light, buoyant, and hopeful. It moves quickly, makes you smile often, and leaves a lasting and resounding message, not to mention impact. In comparison, After You is slow. It introduces new characters who don't do much for me (*ahem* the aforementioned Lily) and I felt as if the overall themes of this novel weren't felt as strongly as they were in its predecessor. Perhaps most importantly, though, while After You is meant to be a hopeful tale of moving on, it feels sad and depressing, unlike Me Before You ever did. 
 I'm sure ardent fans of Me Before You will find a lot to love in this sequel and, if you're half the nice and sympathetic person my mom is, probably you'll feel for these characters and their tricky situations. If you have a heart of ice, impenetrable, it may be harder to care, really, when it comes to this companion novel. Not bad, but clearly not for me. 
 On the Audiobook: I thought the narration of this was excellent! Everything, from the accent to the pacing and the voices were really well-done. I will say, though, that since this is a slow novel to begin with, I don't recommend picking up the audiobook of this one unless you enjoy a slow start. It made it much more difficult for me to get into this story, despite the wonderful narration.

In the interest of full disclosure, I rarely like sequels as much as the original. That being said, I liked "After You," just not as much as "Me Before You." 
 The second book in the series (the ending makes me think a third book is on the way...) focuses on Louisa's life after Will's death. It's a subject worth exploring, but many of the plot conventions Moyes uses are unbelievable and seem to exist just for laughs. Lily's story was my least favorite, but I did like Sam's character :)

As a stand alone book/story it was good. As a so called sequel I was disappointed. I guess it's really hard to follow the first one, especially given how it ended. So I guess I'm asking why bother. Why try to connect this to that. Just write a new book.

Initial Reaction: 
 Holy crap. 
 Do I want to read about Lou's life without Will ? 
 Who am I kidding? We all know the answer to that, and that is why I must stock up on ice cream (because screw tissues, right?)

2.5 but rounding up. I read this quickly and it was okay, but contrived and forgettable. I missed the spark of the first book and chemistry between characters that made Me Before You so real and special.

reference_books.title: The Strain (The Strain Trilogy, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Why did I read this book? Well, I am one of the people who really liked Blade II and it happens that the author directed it. I can understand why people hate that movie but there was something about its style and the way the vampires were depicted that I found really exciting. I also really like one of the soundtrack songs called I Against I by Massive Attack and Mos Def. 
 All in all, this book was a little bit of a disappointment. Mainly because the hero of this book was a little bit of a prick and all characters were completely underdeveloped. You get a character and you immediately know what his role in this book is going to be because they are all the same in the mainstream books or movies. Oh, there's for example the thug who is living a tough life hustling and doing all kinds of shit but it's mainly because of the environment and actually he is just trying to help his suffering mother. Sounds familiar right? 
 The writing was alright I guess and I have to say that there were a couple of bloody scenes which were very captivating but as a whole it didn't really work out in my opinion.

reference_books.title: The White Lioness (Kurt Wallander, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
I hesitated a long time before reading the third Wallander story. That's mainly because I knew that this book would be much different than the first two since it is a lot more ambitious. It deals with Mandela... hence with world politics. Uuuughhh... is this really what I want to read in a proper noir/crime novel? Nah... I read the papers for that kinda stuff. 
 The first two books had many flaws but they were also interesting in a certain way because they mainly focused on the characters and the crime. This story is about Mandela and I think that this territory is way too big and grand to properly deal with when it is put into a crime novel. I obviously get the point, Mankell had good intentions but when I pick up a crime novel I enjoy reading about the most simple characters in their daily surroundings, it is absolutely enough for an exciting story. This book is simply aaaaall ooover the place! There is nooooo character development whatsoever. There were too many plotlines, too many flat characters, the villains were only bad and nearly completely one-dimensional, there were also many plotholes and moments when I wanted to shout "Ooooh pleeeeasseeee... really now?" while rolling my eyes as hard as I could. 
 I don't want to hate on Mankell because he wanted to do something good and had the right intentions but in my opinion it didn't work out at all. If you want to write a proper book about politics or about Mandela then that's fine.

reference_books.title: The Hunger Games (The Hunger Games, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Sometimes it is so obvious that the author just wants to write a stupid bestseller and not a good book. This is like a well-calculated plan to make money. 
 1. Take Running Man and Battle Royale, mix them together! 
 2. Let the main character to be as one dimensional as possible, always purely good and never really in conflict with her emotions. 
 3. Go even further and make all characters less complex than in the source material. 
 4. Cut out most of the satiric social commentary. 
 5. Add as many stupid twists to lead the reader astray just for suspense. 
 6. Do not forget to add a love triangle. 
 7. Make EVERYTHING less serious, simplify it in order to please everybody and to entertain. 
 8. End on a cliffhanger. 
 It was always so clear what the author wanted the reader to think at what moments. That is just bad writing. The funniest thing about it was that at the end of the book there was even an explanation about how the author got the idea for the book. Boy does it sound made up!

reference_books.title: Fever Pitch
reference_books.review_text:
Nick Hornby... what can you say about this guy? He's really a brilliant narrator. Sometimes he's talking nonsense and you don't agree at all, but you still enjoy reading it. The way he sees things is just so funny! 
 I'll be honest and let you know that A Long Way Down and High Fidelity were much better. Fever Pitch is a very good book nevertheless.

reference_books.title: Invisible Monsters
reference_books.review_text:
I've never read anything by Palahniuk before but I've read a lot about him and his works. Palahniuk is notorious for his shock value and his in your face kind of social criticism. Critics often argue that his style can get too straight forward, that it is too plain and that he can sound like an annoying school teacher. Most of the time it turns out that the actual work itself is much different than what others write or say about it. That is why I gave this book a try. 
 It is about a young girl who has to start a new life with a disfigured face. She used to be a model and then has to hide half of her face in order to not be called a monster by children in public. There is a lot of black humour, a loooooooot of social criticism and some clever passages. But all in all it was a very weird read and not in a good way. The language and the narrative are so annoying at times. Palahniuk often describes unnecessary aspects, skips through time and topics. It was not really a fluent read. The characters are caricatures, they are only there to help the author ramble and moan about how bad Western societies are. That lecturing tone is something you should be prepared for. All in all I wouldn't say that I regret reading this book but it could have been better.

book_a.title: The Chemistry of Death (David Hunter, #1)
book_a.user_review:
This used to be a bestseller. I am very sceptical about bestsellers, because they were written for the masses. And if it's written for everybody to understand, it's usually stupid, generic and predictable. But even though this books had many flaws I actually enjoyed it, because it was written really well. The idea, the setting and the characters were shallow to be honest, but the atmosphere of the book was its major quality. Whenever you opened the book, you could dive in into Manham, the place where the story takes place. It also drew some important influence from Arthur Miller's The Crucible which is another positive aspect. 
 Now let me come back to the characters. When you think about it, could you really describe Dr. Hunter? What kind of character is he and how does he behave? In my opinion we don't even know that. He's such a flat character it's almost criminal. Even if you compare him to other characters from bestseller crime novels like Kurt Wallander he's nowhere on the same level. The girl he meets isn't a recognizable character either. I also didn't like the ending at all, it reminded me of a Hollywood script. Those last pages were awfully boring in my opinion. 
 All in all the atmosphere of Manham and the great prose makes this book a very fast and easy read. Don't expect anything extraordinary, though.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Wow, so I might be a little late to the table as this was released in 2006, however it is superb! By the way, it's currently on special and promoted through Dead Good Reads on all e-book platforms for PS1.99, my recommendation is to buy it, now! 
 So I rarely give 5 stars, particularly to crime/thriller fiction, however this is a beautifully written crime novel. I can understand why this author is popular in Germany and Scandinavia! Usually I rush into chapters because it's all about the action and getting to who the culprit is. However this time I had to consciously stop myself and just take in the beauty of the writing. In one word, its evocative.... 
 "The grass cracked underfoot like broken glass. The early morning frost bleached the colour from the landscape, turning into a monochrome wilderness.. 
 "the blood..smeared her skin in an abstract pattern of cruelty" 
 "After centuries of self containment, of knowing it could always rely on its own no matter what, Manham could no longer trust itself" 
 You are literally transported into the local landscape, seeing everything as if you were there. I couldn't help but feel the conjuring of Agatha Christie. This is the quintessential whodunnit in a local country village, with all the personalities, parochialism and politics that go along for the ride - just set in more modern times. Where local sleuthing meets forensic pathology/anthropology. It has all the suspense, twists and turns of an enjoyable thriller, however these are actually understated because it's the strength of the writing that drives the momentum of the story, making this a great read. An absolute pleasure in fact, 5 stars.

Is there anyway I can give this series more than 5 stars ??!! 
 I love Simon's story and his writing style and I love David Hunter!! 
 Once you started reading this book, you'll be drawn into the scene instantly. 
 You'll forget the real world...really! 
 Simon will make you feel you're with David but invisible along the story. 
 I think you even feel you are able to smell and touch something!! 
 The most wonderful crime novel I've ever read.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Abosolute tripe. I knew who the killer was after merely reading barely a quarter of the book. 'HMMMM who is the only person who smokes (the smell of pipe smoke lingering) who would immediately be devoid of blame, (the disabled person)and has a dead woman character in his background'. 
 God, when i read that this has won all these awards and such i was genuinely shocked. I am not by any means a Sherlock Holmes, but this was appalling. It was like trudging through treacle to read. If your cogs are going this slow, they must be going backwards!

I loved this book, I literally could not put this down a real page turner which had me gripped from start to finish. 
 I wont spoil it for those of you who have not read this fantastic book but I was so very shocked by the ending, a twist in the story line doesnt even cut it I was wide mouthed with the element of suprise. 
 A beautifully written book that is wonderfully wrote in such description that you can almost smell the decay running through the pages. 
 A must read! 5*
the ending was a little to contrived for me, but I will definitely be reading more of the series.

http://avadhutrecommends.wordpress.com/ 
 Summary - 
 Dr. David Hunter arrives as a GP in Manham, a small village in Norfolk. But he has a secret to hide and a tragedy that he is trying to forget. Three years later his past catches up with him as horrifying things begin to happen in the quintessential English village and Dr. Hunter is forced to reveal his secret. 
 Review - 
 I always like mysteries set in quaint little places where a murder seems to be the last thing that can happen. But once things become murky, the skeletons start coming out of closets and the darker side of human nature reveals its ugly face. The Chemistry of Death delivers just that. Set in a picturesque little English village in the middle of nowhere, women start to disappear and their mutilated dead bodies are found in the woods around the village. 
 As a relative newcomer, Dr. Hunter is a suspect till he is forced to reveal to the Police that he was a forensic anthropologist before becoming a GP and an expert in the field of study of dead bodies. Hunter reluctantly joins the investigation as his new girlfriend becomes the latest target of a demented serial killer. 
 It is a captivating novel with a mystery that is beguiling. It kept throwing red herrings at every turn and there were twists and a big twist in the end and an even bigger one after that. I tried my best to fathom the mystery beforehand using all the possible clues that Dr. Hunter left in his narration and yet could only partially unravel it. 
 But I liked this novel more for Beckett's knack of turning the gory subject of forensic anthropology into an interesting one. There are descriptions that are sometimes graphic and macabre but overall Beckett has kept them to the bare minimum. He describes the process of analysing human remains in an interesting fashion thus creating a genuine curiosity about this uncommon specialised field. 
 Dr. Hunter as a grieving young widower is a strong central character. Forced into his earlier profession, one that he was trying to run away from, he rediscovers himself and emerges as a revived man. I am now hooked to the series and will like to read how Beckett further gives shape to his personality.

This is my first Simon Beckett read. I liked it a bit, but not enough to give it three stars. The resolution of the mystery was a bit unbelievable to me, a bit too contrived. It seemed to go against the grain of how people would behave. But I like the central character, so will probably give him another try sometime.

I have the feeling I already read this exact same story about 20 times. Middle-aged man has retired from being a cop, journalist, medical examiner, etc , after a trauma -usually dead wife and/or child - when suddenly people start dying. As he is drawn into the investigation someone close to him disappears. Gee, giant surprise there. And then it's all about elaborate ways in which the killer tortures the new girlfriend. whatever. But particularly annoying about this one is that the reason for why the killer turned into a killer is so stupid and not credible that I actually rolled my eyes. 
 So I continue my search for good UK mysteries/thrillers.

Loved this book about a doctor who comes to a village in Norfolk to get away from his tragic past and who leaves behind the big city (London) and his previous career as a Forensic Anthropology. He takes up a post as a G.P., in partnership with a doctor who has had a car accident, that has left him wheelchair bound. Soon, a body is found and the police ask for his help to establish a time of death, on a badly decomposed corpse. He gets drawn in, against his intentions of keeping his past life from the locals, and then, a second woman goes missing. A whodunnit, which I really enjoy can't wait to read the next one.

A bit heavy-handed in parts--the suspense of last reveal of who does/doesn't survive was over-contrived and forced to say the least--but generally a good read. Nothing spectacularly good, but nothing spectacularly bad either.

book_b.title: Mockingjay (The Hunger Games, #3)
book_b.user_review: lol

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 Its hard not to talk about this book without spoilers, so I am going to be a little more vague as I realize I am an early bird reader on this. I admire Suzanne Collins for where she decided to go with this book and what she gives a young adult audience credit for being able to handle. The book pulled no punches, she let it get really dark, and acknowledged that sometimes damage is permanent. Fantastic series.
Ending was confusing

The third book in the Hunger Games trilogy, Mockingjay brings the story of Katniss Everdeen's struggles to a conclusion. This book explores the end of the civil war and the life after the Hunger Games. A perfectly serviceable book, this, too, lacked the spark of the first book in the trilogy. Perhaps the tired tone was appropriate to reflect the exhaustion that comes from war, but the book just did not feel as fresh or optimistic as the first book. Enjoyable, if only to conclude the series and see how everyone ends up

this trilogy was a downhill. mockingjay was entertaining and a fast read, but its main character instead of developing was regressing. my dislike is not due to the book being too dark or too real (which it isn't, at least not in my opinion), but because it's not consistent with the previous books. katniss unraveling at the end is possible, especially after essentially losing all she holds dear, but not for the entire book. not when she had so much to fight for. and that ending? it's been a while since I last read something so forced and fake.

I had to read this after watching "Catching Fire". I haven't read any of the other books. I know, I know, it was a stupid thing to do, but I just HAD to know what would happen next. I don't know what to say... I am not speechless, but am slightly... traumatized. Some of the things that happened were quite predictable, some others I was sure they were bound to happen, but there were others... I just... I don't know. Is it just me, or raw is now a word we might use when referring to The Hunger Games trilogy? There's so much emotion, so much going on. I just hope they don't screw things up with the adaptation, or I will never forgive myself for having read the book before the last two films came out.
The best series ever... No matter how many times I read it! Real or Not Real... real

The last book in the Hunger Games trilogy and it doesn't disappoint. 
 Katniss, her mother, sister, Gale and a few others from District 12 are in District 13 where everything is regimented, down to when to eat, when to exercise and when to sleep. 
 A revolution is happening and the leaders of the rebels need Katniss to become 'The Mockingjay'. However she doesn't feel up to being the spokeswoman for the revolution, until she sees Peeta alive and being paraded by President Snow on TV. 
 A rescue attempt is made and an assault on the Capitol is planned. 
 The ending seemed to be a little rushed to me, but I didn't want this story to end. 
 Warning: There are a lot more deaths in this book, each more vivid than the other.
This book was just boring and did we really need that ending?

Not as good as the first two. I was bored most of the way through the book, till towards the end I couldn't put it down. Another reviewer said Katniss was so strong in the other books and now she is just going along for the ride ... really that's how she was through the entire series. She was basically just a pawn. I don't think she lost her strength in the last book. She was using her strength even though she was being used herself.
The heaviest and darkest installment of the trilogy. Unsettling.

reference_books.title: Night Owls
reference_books.review_text:
The Journey quote on the back about strangers in the night was enough to make me want to read this book. The cover art is gorgeous and this links in with the story. Descriptions of San Francisco were really good and made me desperate to visit. I liked the love story too although was unsure about how younger readers would react to the sex scene (topic handled very well up to this point but this part felt a bit rushed). The latter half of the book was not as good. 
 Characters were great, definitely not one-dimensional. I liked that they had real world problems to contend with which meant you could identify with them. There was a diversity to them although her brother Noah was a bit of a token gay character at times and I would have loved for Beatrix to have had some freinds of her own in the book. 
 I liked that the book dealt with mental problems but had a bit of a problem with the sister as a 'mad woman in the attic' type and the issues with the Dad did not ring true. I wondered how the book would have evolved if it had been Jack or Beatrix who suffered from schizophrenia. I think this could have made the story really, really strong. 
 I liked how the main characters were from different economic backgrounds and this was done well. 
 All in all, this book kept me reading, is a sensitively written love story and is enjoyable but could have been a lot tighter. I would read Jen Bennett again and will recommend her as an older read.

reference_books.title: The God of Small Things
reference_books.review_text:
Some well-known, prize winning books are overrated. This is definitely not one of them! It is perfect. Gorgeous, evocative, masterfully written book about love, the tragedies of love and loss and transgressions in society that literally ripped my heart out of my chest. A book about Kerala, star crossed lovers, the loss of childhood innocence, colonial legacy, twentieth century communism, caste system in india.. It is just so multi-faceted. The novel is structured in a clever way, you find out a key character dies tragically in the beginning and the story teases you, revealing bits and pieces of what happen as it brings you through time and place, like a human memory as it cascades towards heartbreaking tragedy, precipitated by small, trivial events. The final chapter of this book is one of the most romantic I've ever read and is so rewarding as I was fascinated by Velutha and Ammu. 
 Arundhati Roy is a magician with the English language . Her rich, poetic descriptions adds another layer of beauty to this book.

reference_books.title: The Remains of the Day
reference_books.review_text: I feel like this book filled in some details of the British class system that I didn't know. There were so many devastating, quiet moments.

reference_books.title: The Melancholy Death of Oyster Boy and Other Stories
reference_books.review_text: I liked that Tim Burton brought his dark comedic and quirky touch to this volume but I felt it was slightly lacking. This may be as I am not a huge fan of nonsense poetry. However the illustrations and the poems made me giggle lots. I feel that kids would love it. I wonder why he didn't call it 'The Melancholy Death of Oyster Boy and other poems'?

reference_books.title: Harvest
reference_books.review_text: Reading this was a torturous experience and the shame is it shouldn't have been. Had this tile lingering on my e-reader and decided to read it when I saw it mentioned at the British lib Gothic exhibition. The premise is great, the description is beautiful, the characters (except narrator) are great but the story didn't work at all. Although there were great moments I expected something much more haunting. Felt like 600 rather than 200 pages!

book_a.title: We Are All Completely Beside Ourselves
book_a.user_review:
This book was like a hybrid of John Green's quirky YA Paper Towns and the chimp documentary Project Nim, but unlike these touching works it left me cold. I enjoyed the narrator for the first half of the book.. Rosemary is quirky, intelligent, odd and I really wanted to find out how she got to this place. As the story unravelled, I enjoyed meeting other characters such as her parents, Harlow, Lowell and Fern and I yearned to hear their perspective on events. The story is supposed to be about Rosemary's childhood and relationship to these characters but apart from jumbled up memories and non sequential events, she doesn't seem to come across as caring about them. Every other character seems.so passionate in comparison. I feel like I never got to know Rosemary despite 300pages of first person narration. 
 I did enjoy how science was worked into the story.. All in all, a different read and I learned from reading it but I don't think this warranted the literary attention it received.

sample_reviews.review_text:
There is much promise in the premise, but it didn't prove out. 
 The plot: family raises a chimp alongside their daughter until she is 5. Father is a psychologist and grad students live with them. Unfortunately we don't get any of this in the story, it starts when the chimp is returned, having been removed from the family. The family is now dysfunctional - mother has taken to her bed, father is not around, teen age son leaves to live with friends' families, the 5 year old is confused because no one tells her what's going on. 
 I couldn't relate to any of the characters; all we know about the 5 year old is that she talks too much. 
 Told from the perspective of the 5 year old.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I feel bad not loving this book as I picked it up in a bookstore following a rave review by a colleague who devours a book a week. I don't know, it just didn't gel with me. There was one sentence I loved where the protagonist, Rosemary, just separated from her "twin" is playing a ball game by throwing a ball against a wall and catching it, "because thats how you play catch when there is only one of you" - as an only child and a keen player of catch for one as a kid I loved this moment. The facts that unravel are powerful and do resonate strongly, and some scenes are beautifully crafted but I found the characters too self-absorbed yet at the same time just out of reach to really root for.

This is possibly a 3.5 for me. I grabbed it in a rush with barely a glance at it. Only knowing it didn't have a genre sticker and was something about family and recommended by a friend. Best way to read it I think. A fictionalisation inspired by true events, the reveal partway in is important, I think, to help develop the significance of the events to the narrator rather than dismissing its importance. Think the title seems to refer to how we put aside parts of ourselves to fit ideals of others and the image of ourself we create. Edited to add. Actually I think it gets the full 4 stars. I am still thinking of the book, but now less about its animal ethics than the ways humans try to distinguish ourselves from them, and the way we think about ourselves.

We Are All Completely Up Ourselves: Some good ideas absolutely drowned in meandering drivel that not only does not add to the storyline but totally distracts from it. I really cant understand the good reviews for this book, but at least the reviews give some clue as what 'it' was supposed to be all about as the storyline was completely lost in the noise. A precis down to under 100 pages would have done this novel a world of good. The author clearly loves the sound of her own written voice, but I'd had enough of it after a while and bailed out half way through, this is actually quite a commitment waiting for a book to get going that was never going to get going. Thank goodness it's gone!
This book did not grab me because I found it difficult to like the characters. Finished it for book club.
Sorry...not my cuppa. I could not get into the characters of the plot.

I particularly enjoyed the actual research presented, though it was vexing to then not be sure what was true (e.g., about UC Davis). at first this seemed like a flighty college book a la Monsters of Templeton, but it is actually much better, with more emotion and much more to deliberate, especially in re: ethics of animal research. And I laughed out loud a few times. Audiobook narrator was perfect.
Thought provoking, heartbreaking, and compulsively readable.
I honestly don't know how I felt about this book or how to rate it. No clue.

A moving and wryly funny book and a delightful surprise to me as I wasn't expecting much. It could have easily kiltered into farce or become maudlin. The less one knows about the plot, the better, so I will just say it is a heartbreaking yet witty story about memory, loss and family.

book_b.title: The Little Stranger
book_b.user_review: A little bit of Stephen King, a little bit of Downton abbey, the tension of Jane Austen and similar in atmosphere to The Turn of the Screw this book was a complulsive read. Description of the ruins of the house and the unravelling of the well-drawn characters was brilliant. The horror and haunting in it was quite subtle but it did chill me and I am glad I did not read it when I was living in an old crumbling house last year. I am now waiting patiently for a TV adaptation!

sample_reviews.review_text:
Waters is much improved as a writer (no blatant Mary Sue here - first time!). But the plot is slow and jumpy, the descriptions masquerade as plot, and what plot, anyway? I'm perfectly all right with good character-driven stories and I'm perfectly all right with good ambiguity, but this book is 566 pages long. After that sort of long-winded nervy anticipation, I expect some conclusion - or a really riveting conclusion. Waters just isn't good enough to deliver. 
 Also? Shades of The Haunting of Hill House, almost certainly unintentional, but I just hate petty theft. Even the unintentional sort.
Hallelujah I'm finished! What a terribly boring book with a serious identity crisis... bah.

** spoiler alert ** 
 The novel succeeded in communicating an image of the post-war decline of the landed class. This would be a great book for a reader that wants to get a sense for that setting. 
 The language was fluid, easy to read, and pulled me forward. I read the ~500 pages in very little time. 
 The story is intentionally ambiguous. There are several possible explanations for the events in the book. This of course prompts a lot of speculation in some readers or groups. If you like speculating on how things might have actually played out, this is a good book for you. 
 One of the problems I have with the novel is that it failed to make me feel invested in the possible interpretations of events. I don't care if "the little stranger" actually existed and if so which character was responsible for its existence. I would have felt more invested if the novel had done a better job evoking the Uncanny. I think it tries to do it but it falls short of the great stories that do so successfully, e.g. The Turn of the Screw or for Spanish readers the stories written by QUIROGA HORACIO or Maria Luisa Bombal. Or, instead of going for the Uncanny, it could have aligned the reader with a character that actively struggled with the conflicting possibilities. The character Caroline did struggle with the question of what was actually happening in the house but the story wasn't focalized through her. Instead we saw things through the perspective of a character (Dr. Faraday) that nearly always opted for the rational explanation and was not personally experiencing the strange/ambiguous phenomena. Because Pynchon's The Crying of Lot 49 focuses its story through a character that is heavily invested in the correct interpretation of events, I also found meself trying to figure out what was really going on. 
 I consider Dr. Faraday's first person narrative to be a weakness as well. A lot of the story depends on the experiences of other characters. Having those events told by Dr. Faraday was distracting. I think three alternatives could have been better in these situations: a switch to a third person narrator, multiple first person narrators, or some clue or reason to believe that Faraday might have had first had knowledge of the events (through supernatural means).

** spoiler alert ** 
 Extremely well written, if a bit slow paced, Gothic novel set in postwar England. Is it a ghost story? Maybe. By the time I got to the end, I wondered if the narrator was any more reliable than Nabakov's Humbert Humbert. Waters does not spell it all out, which I think only makes the book that much better, and a bit harder to shake. Creepy book: glad I read it.
I thought that the writing was excellent, but the story dragged on and on. I did not like the protagonist, either. He seemed weirdly obsessed with the Ayers' family and their house...

Very slow starting. I was told this was a great horror story but I found it to be more of a love story. I was frustrated throughout because Waters spent the majority of the time trying to have the main narrator rationalize the activities of the house and this was a relevant theme. It was redundant. 
 I think it had potential but it never quite got there for me.

The setting in the book is overwhelming, with the house becoming its own leading character. The plot builds with a steady creeping intensity so that it is hard to put down once you hit the midpoint. It was well written overall, but the characters lacked depth and this made them difficult to empathize with. Although I'm sure this will become a gothic cult classic, I wasn't a huge fan and actually pulled another of Waters' books off my 'to read' list after pushing through this one.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I finished reading the book yesterday and was so disappointed with the ending for two reasons. 
 1. That Caroline Died and 2. The Little Stranger was not revealed! 
 After I read other reviews, they shed some light on a new possibility that I didn't consider which was "Betty", but I'm still not convinced. I think it's the dead child S or mostly Dr Farady with his unconscious spirit because the writer hints at the end that all he saw was the reflection of his face. Plus, he wanted the house so bad which what made me hate him at the end because if he really loved Caroline; he should have taken her away from Hundreds. Plus, the evil stuff didn't happen until he showed up! 
 A similar book with a puzzling ending would be In The Woods by French!

I really enjoyed this one, for its engrossing psychological suspense. I read it in two sittings. It's one of those books that stays with you for a while after you're finished reading. Made me think of REBECCA by Daphne Du Maurier, especially the intro, and the pacing and buildup of suspense that creeps up on the reader. Highly recommended.
I really tried to get into this book, but in the end, I gave up.

reference_books.title: Second Chance Summer
reference_books.review_text:
Very Dessen-esque writing. In fact, I had to remind myself a few times while reading that it WASN'T a Sarah Dessen book. That's a compliment, by the way. 
 A little overlong and predictable, but otherwise a very sweet and touching story. There was definitely something in both my eyes during the last few chapters. 
 Also, a good option for those looking for a clean YA.

reference_books.title: Amy & Roger's Epic Detour
reference_books.review_text:

sample_reviews.review_text: Here is my spoiler free review!

I still have a lot of feelings that I need to sort out, but I will be (hopefully) writing a review for this soon. But for now, I can safely say that this is a very cute book that I enjoyed a bit more than expected.

I've been debating to give Becky Albertalli's debut novel Simon vs. the Homo Sapiens Agenda either 4 or 5 stars (or even my unofficial 4.5 stars), but I am just going to go with the latter. 
 This is the book I wish I could time travel back to give my high school self. This is the book that would have my Judy Blume, or since the advent of YA literature my The Fault in Our Stars or Eleanor & Park. It is a novel that brought made me relive my younger years, made my heart palpitate and swoon. 
 Even some 30 years removed from my high school experience, I still related to the title character who is (thankfully) living in a much different world. He is gay and he knows it and, more importantly, knows there's nothing wrong with it or that he's the "only one." What has not changed is still feeling different and alone and still having to come out and it being a pretty big deal. 
 Simon's life is thrown into chaos at the open of the novel as his emails with "Blue," a fellow (and closeted) student at his high school, are threatening to be exposed. So, yes another thing that has not changed: the fear of being outed. Unless you are famous and do it in one fell swoop, I've learned you never stop coming out. And likewise the fear/anxiety of being outed unexpectedly or not on your own timeline/doing is a constant as well. Having accidentally outed myself (in almost sitcom fashion) to my own brother, I could relate to all the stomach sinking, scrambling, "what will I do?," "not ready to deal with it right now" feelings. 
 But this plot line, is nicely contrasted with sweetness (and quite adorkable) burgeoning romance between the two young men via their email exchanges. The sharing of their own hopes and fears, their daily lives, and themselves. 
 It's not all gay tho, Simon's hetero friends who can't quite figure out who to date or not to date themselves are also part of the picture and there is all sorts of drama (literal!) as Simon and his classmates put on a production of Oliver!. Albertalli, who is child/teenage psychologist, seems to totally captures the mind and voice of high schoolers. One of my pesky issues with YA lit, is that often the teens seem so wise and well-beyond their years. But here it all rang very true and again, kudos to Albertalli (and likely thanks to her day job) for so capturing all the internal workings of coming to terms with being gay and coming out. 
 While I was in my mid-20s and it was the early days of the Internet (landline/baud modems, no digital photography, etc.), my own first real romance started in an online chat room and via email exchanges. Much like Simon and Blue them we fell in love "from the inside out." and it took us a long time at least 6 months)to meet in-person. 
 I'd love a sequel to this novel, but perhaps it is best to leave it as it is. For me, I had my happy ending. A few weeks ago and some 20 years after our first email, just celebrated my first wedding anniversary married to what was tantamount to my own high school crush.

Some books are perfect little slices of reading pie that you should just gobble up in on sitting. This book is one such slice. I put this book down once today. And I stayed up until 5am to finish it. Because I couldn't stop. 
 I don't know which I did more while reading this: laugh or cry--the good kind mostly. I loved Simon's voice. I adored him; he's freaking precious. The honesty and emotions and thoughts... I'm not a gay 16yo boy but, while I read this, it felt like I was. That's how ingrained into the narrator I was. And it was perfect. 
 If a book could be a cinnamon roll, it would be this one. Just such a joyful resounding yes.

This was so cute! I'm not much of a fan of contemporary fiction but I still pick it up now and then because of books like this that are honestly so refreshing and fun that I can't help but read them in practically one sitting. 
 Now to wipe this stupid grin off my face and think about what to read next. :) :) :)
Oh my god, this was so great. I had a huge smile on my face at the end of it. Literally, I could not stop smiling.

I love this book! I love Simon! I love Leah, Nick, Abby! I love the dog, Bieber! Okay, I love a lot of people in the book. Oh and I love Blue :-) 
 I have said it once and I will say it again, I love when I finally read books that I have had for awhile and they just make my day! I was smiling and laughing and crying through this whole book. 
 And there are so many excerpts from the book I want to add but I would have to write the whole book so I will just add one or two. lol. Anyway! This book is about Simon obviously. He's gay but hasn't told any one. He has a secret online gay friend that he talks to every day and slowing they are falling in love. But... they don't know who the other one is, they are keeping it a secret for now. They do go to the same school and are really close to each other, that is all they know. It is really sweet reading them email back and forth to each other and see what forms. 
 Then one fateful day Simon just has to log onto his email at school and forgets to sign out of his gmail account. Yeah! This little dude named Martin reads it and saves it and blackmails Simon into getting him together with Simon's friend Abby. Of course Simon is speechless and hating on himself that he did not close his email. So a bunch of stuff goes on in that regard. 
 Simon is in a drama class with some of his friends and they have rehearsals and stuff every day. They have so much fun. I want to have them all as best friends! Simon thinks one of the guys in the group is Blue but he's not for sure. Can you imagine going around school looking at people and wondering if that is YOUR person. I might add I was thinking it was one of two different people at one time but something happens, a brief moment and then I knew who Blue was and I was right! Woot! 
 Moving on. I love how Simon and his friends are together. Nick he has known all of his life and Leah for several years, but he's only known Abby a few months but they get on so perfect together. 
 --->EXCERPT<--- 
 "Watching videos," I say. 
 "Oh man. Perfect. I've got this song in my head." 
 "If it's by the Who," I inform him, "or Def Skynard or anyone like that, then no freaking way." 
 "I'm going to pretend you didn't just say "Def Skynard." 
 I love messing with Nick. 
 At one point it get out that Simon is gay and he is so upset as you can imagine. I mean, he really wanted to be able to come out when he was ready and to tell his family and friends on his own time. So he has to tell them a little earlier. He does get some jerks at school that start teasing him but some of the teachers and his friends shut that down real quick. I absolutely loved how they all came to his defense. You shouldn't have to be bullied anywhere no matter what it is but unfortunately, that is life. 
 There are some sweet little revelations about each person in the book. I loved every one of them. I loved when Leah and Nora have their moment. I won't what they did but it was awesome. I was invested in each one of these characters. I loved the authors writing style. Simon had a way of talking that I understood. 
 --->EXCERPTS<--- 
 "Okay, well, I'm taking over your bathroom now. Time for the transformation." 
 "Sounds good," I say. "I'll transform in here." 
 Nora looks up from her book. "Simon. Eww." 
 "It's a dementor robe over my clothes. I think you'll survive." 
 "What's a dementor?" 
 I mean, I can't even. "Nora, you are no longer my sister." 
 "So it's some Harry Potter thing," she says. 
 ****** 
 It's chilly and unnaturally quiet---if Abby weren't with me, I would have to drown out the silence with music. It feels like we're the last survivors of a zombie apocalypse. Wonder Woman and a gay dementor. It doesn't bode well for the survival of the species. 
 ******* 
 I ignore her. 
 "I'm not leaving, bub. Because you're going to wallow. You're going to put on that playlist. What's it called?" 
 "The Great Depression," I mutter. It's like all Elliott Smith and Nick Drake and the Smiths. I already have it cued up. 
 "Right," she says. "The Great Depression. That romp. No way." 
 "Why are you here?" 
 "Because I'm your big sister and you need me." 
 "I need to be left alone." 
 "No way. Talk to me, bub!" she says. She slides toward me, squeezing in between my body and the wall. "This is exciting. We can talk about guys." 
 I just couldn't help adding a few more! So in the end we find out who Blue is and I was so excited for Simon. And so were his family and friends when they found out he had a boyfriend now. How sweet. 
 I love you Simon. Your my book best friend. :-D
