I experienced minimal enjoyment in reading this and a lot of agony. I wanted to love it so much! #unpopularopinion

In the span of just a few days, Etta Spencer's life has been thrown into turmoil, as she's gone from aspiring concert violinist to time traveler, determined to save her mother from a despot determined to seize an astrolabe that allows one to control time and rewrite history. But when her mission with Nicholas Carter, the handsome privateer -- and grandson of her family's greatest enemy, Cyrus Ironwood -- goes sideways, Etta is ripped from Nicholas's side and left orphaned from her natural timeline. Thrust into a world she doesn't recognize, Etta is captured by the rogue Thorn family. It is among the Thorns that Etta discovers shocking secrets about her own parentage, calling into question everything she once held to be true and rocking her fledgling faith in her mother to her core. As Etta learns about her familial heritage, she discovers that traveling is a sacred trust, and every decision she makes has the potential to transform not only her future, but the entire world's, forever. And her dream of a future with Nicholas may be the price she is forced to pay in order to prevent Ironwood's quest for power. 
 With Etta lost to time, Nicholas is left trapped with his hostile cousin Sophia as his best ally in his quest to find Etta and break his grandfather's hold on his life forever. As Etta discovers the secrets of the Thorns, Nicholas and Sophia discover the truth behind the travelers' powers -- a terrifying, ancient, age-old battle between long-hidden forces with the power to not just rewrite the timeline, but to destroy the world as they know it. Desperate to reunite with Etta, Nicholas makes a dangerous bargain that leaves him with no choice -- to become that which he hates most, or die, either option promising to compromise every honorable precept he's fought his heritage to claim as his own. As his path converges with Etta's in their race to find the astrolabe, he must find the strength to resist the siren song of the one thing he wants most -- a future with Etta, a dream that, if claimed, could cost their world everything they know and hold dear. 
 After finally reading 
 Passenger 
 last month, I immediately dove into Wayfarer, as the thought of delaying the discovery of Nicholas and Etta's fate was simply unthinkable. I was somewhat surprised by the change in tone and the core dynamic of the Wayfarer narrative, as Passenger was tightly focused on Etta's point-of-view, interspersed with Nicholas's perspective, whereas this installment is more evenly divided, and in my opinion heavily weighted to Nicholas's viewpoint. In Passenger, through Etta, Bracken introduces her gloriously absorbing take on the mechanics of time travel and the heady reality of not only seeing history, but the chance to live it. The first installment in this duology is a non-stop adventure with a highly romantic focus, as Nicholas and Etta discover not only each other but seek to reconcile their wildly disparate views and navigate their respective experiences vis-a-vis race relations within the reality of the time periods in which they travel. 
 With Wayfarer, Bracken sacrifices some of the heady flush of new romance in favor of raising the stakes in regards to the time travel/adventure element of the storyline, diving deep into the history and potential of the travelers' virtually limitless potential. By separating Nicholas and Etta for the bulk of the narrative, each is forced to come to terms with their identity as a traveler and the responsibility such a life entails -- should they seek to use their gift wisely. Accepting their shared inheritance comes at a cost, and in order to do so Bracken forces both Nicholas and Etta to confront the prejudice and privilege of their respective time periods. The tumultuous history at the root of the conflict between the traveling families was a deliciously dark surprise, cementing Bracken as not just another YA fantasy author, but a master wordsmith capable of spinning a heady web of thought-provoking fantasy, never hesitating to address the twin dark plagues of prejudice and unchecked evil that have colored mankind's experience throughout history. 
 If Passenger is a romantic journey of self-discovery, Wayfarer is a journey of purpose. Within the pages of each installment, Bracken has reimagined and refreshed the tropes of the hero's journey. In Etta and Nicholas, readers are given two heroes to not only cheer for but who inspire, as they realistically confront the twin capacity for good and evil within themselves and each, inspired by the other, strive to give their better angels sway. While I adored everything about this story, from Bracken's world-building and globe-spanning plot to her breathtakingly human characterizations, I perhaps love most how she subverted my expectations as to the story's outcome. The heavy emphasis on Etta's point-of-view in Passenger lulled me into a false expectation as to Etta's importance relative to Nicholas in the overall arc of the story -- but what I didn't stop to consider was that Passenger and Wayfarer are, essentially, two halves of one giant whole. 
 Over the course of this breathtakingly original tale, this becomes as much Nicholas's story as Etta's, if not arguably moreso his, as he becomes a man who confronts both age-old prejudice and the temptation of his familial heritage -- from a family who very nearly always grossly underestimated his potential. If Etta is the reader's entree into history, Nicholas is a powerful reminder of how the forgotten and overlooked throughout history possessed stories worth writing and potential worth exploring, not by virtue of their social position but by virtue of their very existence. For while history is writ large by the victors and socially dominant, it is often those everyday men and women who have the greatest lessons of sacrifice and honor to teach us, if, like Etta, we can learn to see beyond the color of one's skin or social antecedents to the humanity common to us all. 
 Wayfarer brings Nicholas and Etta's time-traveling thrill ride to a stunning conclusion. These novels have been a reading experience like no other. Romantic, thrilling, and wholly absorbing, this was a story I never wanted to end. I adored Bracken's world-building and carefully-crafted characters, each organic to the time of their origin. That, perhaps, is one of this duology's more stunning feats, as Bracken never sacrifices historical reality for fictional expediency. For every moment of breath-taking, time-travel wish fulfillment, the harsh truths of history that Etta and Nicholas cope with are never diminished for fictional expediency. Wayfarer is that rare treat, a gorgeously-rendered conclusion to a tale that exemplifies intelligent, wildly creative storytelling, and taken as a whole this set of novels marks one of the most wholly satisfying reading experiences of recent memory. Nicholas and Etta and their vibrantly-realized world have taken up permanent residence in my heart, for theirs is a story that has stayed with me long after finishing Wayfarer's final pages, and is one I know I shall be tempted to revisit often.

3.5 Stars - I was happy with this one, the ending was perfect and I totally cried... but at the same time it just didn't "captivate" me like the first one did. It moves very slow and didn't seem to have as much history mixed in as the first one did. I do love the amazing diversity in this and how Bracken addresses issues of oppression throughout history and highlights ways things have changed throughout time. It's really great and I actually learned a few things. I did feel that the character and relationship development in this one was much weaker than the first. We miss out on a lot of the emotional draw that she had in the first. For me that's the biggest motivator in keeping me reading so I struggled a lot finishing this one for that reason. However I LOVED the overall plot! When you combine all the moving parts of this story; the technicalities of time traveling, keeping family histories, alternate time lines and other things historically accurate - it was all so complex and really well done. I feel really torn because I love and appreciate so much of this duology but at the same time wasn't that invested in the characters. It's best for fans of time travel and slow moving historical fiction with lots of details. 
 Note: If you haven't read Passenger recently, you need a review before diving into this one. Big Time. When I went into this the first time, I really needed to go back and refresh several times. I highly recommend marathon reading these two books (back-to-back) because there's so many moving parts and little things you'll miss if you wait in between.

I'm a massive fan of Alex Bracken's writing and fell in love with The Darkest Minds trilogy. I was nervous when starting "Passenger" because I wasn't sure how the new duology would win me over, but Bracken knocked it out of the park. I ended "Passenger" anxiously waiting to know what was going to happen next for Etta and Nicholas. 
 Full disclosure, Etta and Nicholas spend the majority of this novel separated. Although it sucked, I honestly didn't mind this because they were both doing so much! I loved the jumps through times and cities, especially when Etta and Henry land in Russia (poor Tsar Nicholas). Some of the explanations around how travelling works went a bit over my head, but I was fine with it because I was hooked in trying to find out what would happen to these guys. 
 For those who haven't read Passenger, you need to do so immediately. Otherwise, the changes we see in Sophia, Nick, Etta, and Henry become meaningless. I mean, who would have thought that I'd actually care about Sophia?! 
 "Wayfarer" definitely has a different ending then what I might have been expecting but Bracken doesn't disappoint. I'm a huge fan of how she finds ways to tie up loose ends up leaves openings for readers to continue hoping that we'll get a few more short stories (**wink** pleasseeee!!!) about what's happening with these characters following the series. (hey, she did it for TDM, why not for Passenger??!!) 
 Bracken has yet to let me down and I'd highly recommend these books to any interested readers.

I received a free copy of this book from the publisher via NetGalley in exchange for an honest review. 
 Summary 
 As the second book in a duology, Wayfarer continues to explore the world of time travel initially established in Passenger. It expands on what we discovered in the first book, escalating the conflict and putting the characters through all sorts of difficulties, and then wraps up the duology perfectly. 
 I thoroughly enjoyed reading this book and thought the series as a whole was brilliant as a whole, especially given how difficult time travel is to get right. As this is a sequel, there will be spoilers for the first book, however I shall try to keep them to a minimum. 
 Plot 
 The majority of this book follows two threads. On one side, Nicholas searches for Etta, who has been forced through the timelines. On the other, Etta finds herself mixed up with the mysterious Thorns on their quest for the astrolabe. Ironwood is hot on the heels of both, but another enemy emerges from the shadows and things get a lot more dangerous. 
 If I'm honest, I really wasn't sure how Alexandra Bracken was going to build on the previous book, but the introduction of a new party really gave Wayfarer an added depth and threat. It also allowed for further exploration of the world's lore, something which I particularly loved. The addition of a few extra side-plots on top of the original story-line from the first book kept the story enjoyable and the plot was fascinating in itself. 
 I did find the story did feel a bit slow-paced in times and the book was, perhaps, a little too long. I found myself enjoying Etta's story a lot more than Nicholas' and a lot of that was due to the fact that Nicholas' did come across as repetitive in places and was often where the slow parts occurred. That being said, the book is regularly punctuated by conflict and confrontation, character development and the odd twist to really keep your interest throughout. 
 Characters 
 For me, it was the secondary characters that really made this book. Thinking back on it, it felt a lot like Nicholas and Etta were there to keep the story moving, but it was the other characters that really got the most development and focus. This made the book come alive for me. Having strong side characters allowed the world to feel rooted and allowed me to get fully invested in the story. 
 That's not to say that Nicholas and Etta felt flat or unrealistic in any way; Etta, in particular, found her feet in this book. My only problem was that I found Nicholas boring. I really enjoyed his character in Passenger but very little of that substance seemed to have made its way into Wayfarer. On a plus side though, Wayfarer does include two LGBT characters whose relationship received the most focus and development throughout the novel. 
 World/Setting 
 As I've said, Wayfarer goes deeper into expanding the world we see in Passenger. Not only do we get more time travel, but we also meet more of the families and central players in their feud and discover more about how the whole time travel works. This was probably one of my more favourite parts of this book as it really made the more fantastical elements feel tangible and an integral feature to the story. Exploring the effects of timeline changes was particularly interesting, especially if you enjoy history as I do, and once it crossed into questions of ethics and morality, it really got me thinking. 
 Final thoughts 
 I thought Wayfarer was a brilliant conclusion to the Passenger duology. It did a good job of rounding up the story to a conclusion that felt right while also building on the story in the previous book and making it an entertaining read. My main gripe with the novel was that it probably could have done with being a tad shorter, not to mention that Nicholas did not really work as a character for me in this book. Really, though, I would recommend this duology to anyone who likes a good bit of time travel and feuding families.

What an absolute mess. I feel like I should be handed an award for finishing this. 
 512 pages for a book that probably still would've moved forward at a snail's pace if it had been half that. And it honestly should have been at least half that amount of pages, because both main characters spend the entire middle section of the book just running from one place to another in search of the same thing. 
 This book bored me to tears. 
 I liked Passenger well enough, though I was by no means enchanted by it. Here, though, I could only be disappointed with this lackluster sequel. The things that bothered me in the first book were still very much present here. The time travel still does not make even a little bit of sense and the pacing of the story is incredibly slow. It was slow in the first book as well, but at least I was intrigued enough to want to keep reading, which wasn't the case here. 
 The entire first half of the book is just so dull. Book 1 ended with a pretty big cliffhanger, but instead of picking up where they left off with the exact pace and sense of suspense, it all falls flat. 
 There's Etta and Henry on one side and Sophia/Nicholas on the other side trying to achieve the exact same thing, but it took far too long for Etta and Nicholas to be reunited. And I say this as someone who didn't even ship them. I didn't mind the romance either, but I wasn't actively involved that much. The Nicholas & Sophie chapters didn't manage to hold my attention in any way; I found myself skimming huge sections of their chapters to keep it moving and even when doing that, I didn't think I was missing much. I liked Nicholas in the first book quite a bit, but his inner narration now, and how whiny it was, made me want to cry. Though, come to think of it, both main characters spend a good amount of the book simply pining for the other, which made me want to tear my hair out. 
 Julian, by contrast, amused me much more and I was actually glad he was around, in all his useless glory. There was not enough Julian. Or Rose and Henry; theirs was a story I would've been more interested in reading. 
 I'm not even going to mention the whole fantasy element that suddenly popped up towards the middle of this, because that was a disaster all around. I honestly thought about quitting a half dozen times, but eventually kept on going to the end. I'm not sorry I read these books (well, maybe a little), but had I known that the blurb would turn out to be more exciting than the actual book, I never would have bothered. 
 To end on a somewhat positive note: this duology has the best covers. I could blow them up, frame them and then just stare at them for a while.

book_b.title: The Heart Goes Last
book_b.user_review:
SO. 
 Sex robots. 
 Maybe not the best way to start reading Atwood....

sample_reviews.review_text: A really interesting concept, but it became oddly predictable and heavy-handed toward the end. However, solid writing as always, and quite entertaining in a pulpy sort of way.

Although a good read, a dead cert for any book of Atwood's, I did not find the material nearly so inspiring, nor gripping as her previous books. Whilst slightly eye opening, especially in regards to the world of capitalism, I found the ending a little bit of a letdown.

Margaret Atwood is one of my favorite authors. The Handmaid's Tale and Oryx and Crake are some of my favorite novels of all time. Atwood's books are usually beautifully written and thought provoking. Usually. I've been struggling with some of her recent releases. Angel Catbird made me cringe so hard that I'm surprised my face isn't stuck in a permanent cringe. Unfortunately, The Heart Goes Last also left me thinking WTF? 
 Fun fact: I actually put off reading this book for a strange reason. Two of the characters have the same names as my grandparents, and they have tons of graphic sex. The characters, I mean. Not my grandparents. I know nothing about my grandparents' sex lives. I was worried that I'd picture my grandparents as the characters during the sex scenes, and that's just . . . *shudder* 
 This review is only two paragraphs long, and it's already awkward. 
 Okay. Moving on. The Heart Goes Last is a dystopia set in a world with rampant crime, joblessness, and homelessness. The main characters, Stan and Charmaine, are living in their car when Charmaine sees an advertisement for an experimental community. The people in the community would get everything they need: food, homes, money, hobbies. However, every other month, they'd have to give up their freedom and become "prisoners." They'd live in a prison and do all the hard, unpleasant jobs it takes to keep a community running. Stan and Charmaine eagerly sign up for the experiment. When they get to the community, they notice that things are not as great as they seem from the outside. There are mysterious disappearances and a strange factory that makes lifelike celebrity sex robots. Stan and Charmaine get roped into the deadly job of uncovering the community's secrets and smuggling them to the press. 
 "That was the original idea, but once you've got a controlled population with a wall around it and no oversight, you can do anything you want." - The Heart Goes Last 
 I felt very hot-and-cold about this book. There are some plot points that I loved and really got into, and other plot points that just seem . . . silly. 
 The mystery is the best part of The Heart Goes Last. What is going on in this utopia, and who are Stan and Charmaine's "Alternates"? The Alternates are the people who live in Stan and Charmaine's house while they're in prison. Stan and Charmaine aren't supposed to have any contact with the Alternates, but they start learning things about them based on what they leave in the house. Stan and Charmaine also have their own secret ideas (and sexual fantasies) about the Alternates' identities. I enjoyed watching all the pieces come together. 
 Like all of Margaret Atwood's books, this one raises some interesting questions. I don't want to give away spoilers, but would you rather be free or happy? The characters are forced to make some tough choices about that. 
 "Oblivion is increasingly attractive to the young, and even to the middle-aged, since why retain your brain when no amount of thinking can even begin to solve the problem?" - The Heart Goes Last 
 "If you do bad things for reasons you've been told are good, does it make you a bad person?" - The Heart Goes Last 
 My biggest problem with this book is that it doesn't feel like a Margaret Atwood novel to me. I love her work because she's phenomenal at developing characters, but the characters in The Heart Goes Last are shallow. I never felt like I understood their motives. They mostly seem like pawns that the author is forcing through a silly sequence of events. 
 That brings me to the next issue: The characters come up with this bizarre, convoluted plan to smuggle information out of the community, and it all seems very unnecessary. Why did the plan have to be so silly? Why did we need all those details about sex robots and gay Elvis impersonators? It feels like there's a metafictional joke somewhere in here that I didn't understand. Maybe Margaret Atwood is just much smarter than me. My brain can't keep up with her. 
 I didn't hate this book. There are some aspects of it that I appreciate. I'll continue to read Margaret Atwood's work. But, I don't think this is one of Atwood's stronger novels.

I am a number one Margaret Atwood fan, and I was so excited to hear that she had a new novel coming out. Well, to say that I'm extremely disappointed would be an understatement to say the least. I just couldn't get into this uneven novel -- I didn't care for the characters and I just didn't get the plot (was it farce? was it parody? I have no idea). Perhaps I want another Handmaid's Tale. I don't know.

There were a couple times when I breezed through 50+ pages in one sitting but mostly, it felt forced to the point where I could only read a chapter at a time. I felt absolutely no connection to the main characters and their sex-obsessed lifestyle. Every single character was extremely one-dimensional. I'd still recommend this book, but I wouldn't go into it expecting something life-changing.
I'm sad to say I got about 50 pages though this book and gave up. I just couldn't get into it. So disappointed.

I can see why everyone might not like this book, if you don't like Margaret Atwoods satiric humor. I fell in love with the author's writing with the Oryx and Crake series. This one reminds me of it, with the speculative science fiction and weird sexual overtones. So if you liked that series you will probably like this. I loved it. I thought it was hilarious and it makes you think about social implications and ethics in sciences and technology. Reminded me of "More Happy than Not, but I won't say why to avoid spoilers. 
 The first Atwood book I read was "The Handmaids Tale" I didn't really like it at the time, but I think I now want to read it again now that I "get " her writing.
The premise was interesting but the plot and the characters failed to convince me. Pity!

2.5 stars. I prefer my Atwood a little more serious, with a dash of humor. This was the opposite. It started promising, but quickly turned into a very ridiculous set of situations and I don't feel it really held together well. I've read this was originally published as a serial, and it might have worked better in that format, but I also just didn't care for this one.

I do love Margaret Atwood. Perhaps I was expecting The Handmaid's Tale, v2 and so I was quite disappointed. The book started strongly and there were definitely thought provoking parts to the tale; but ultimately I didn't really care for the two main characters and it didn't feel as immersive as her other work has.

reference_books.title: Heir Untamed (Latvala Royals, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I'm going to try to be gentle on this one since the genre was totally out of my usual comfort zone. Though the book takes place in modern day, it definitely had the feel of a historical romance which is really not my thing. 
 The book was actually pretty good. Chey is a photographer who (out of nowhere and very unrealistically) is invited to photograph the royal family of Latvala. She accepts because she is low on money and thus her adventure begins. 
 From the beginning, it is a mystery as to which guy Chey is falling for. The mysterious prince, Matthias, or the rugged head of security, Sander. There is also a bit of action, which maybe made the historical monarchical theme a bit more tolerable. Chey's life is clearly being threatened, and it adds some umph to the book. 
 The book actually reads pretty fast and is well written. I enjoyed the descriptions and the characterization. However, there was the occasional redundant passage in which three paragraphs would basically repeat themselves - basically unnecessary filler. This is a pet peeve of mine - but I made it through. 
 The most redeeming part of this book is the twist at the end. I didn't see it coming - which maybe I should have. But I think it was more unexpected than most plot twists would be. I certainly enjoyed the ending of the book, though I believe it could have ended in a slightly better way. I understand leaving the cliffhanger so the reader wants to read the sequel, but the ending didn't seem quite complete. 
 I recommend this book more so to readers of historical romances than contemporary romances. The book is more reminiscent of books my mom would read, no offense Mom, than what I have currently been reading. The sex scenes are tame and very vague - so I guess if sex scenes scare you off, this book might be alright for you. But if you like a little raunchy bedroom action, which the characters in this book could have provided, I don't recommend it. Overall a well-written book, just not quite up my alley.

 Had my heart beating faster:Olivia and Alex go to his hometown and Olivia gets to meet not only his family but Jamie and Anne too. 
 Gave me a heart attack,a stroke and had me screaming:Except from the fact that Alex,Jamie and Anne are back together in the same place with Olivia there?!That only made my heart beat faster.Well here is what made me have a strongest reaction in the whole book.Anne and Jamies son,Cam,is almost 3 years old and has gray eyes,like Alex has and Olivia says Cam looks like Jamie but also that Jamie and Alex look alike . 
 And then I knew. 
 It was in what she hadn't said.In how she hadn't touched him,not even a handshake earlier.It was in how she'd watched Alex with her husband,both men being boys,and how she'd been so kind to me.And suddenly,sickeningly,it was in a pair of big gray eyes in a toddler's face. 
 In the kitchen,everything stopped. 
 It was a very quiet showdown,and I wasn't sure whether to draw or hold my fire.I wished desperately for my camera,which I'd left behind in the hotel room.Behind the lens this all might have seemed like just another party.Just another group of people Anne and James might have been an average married couple.Their son might not have looked like my lover. .The second spoiler is a quote from Olivia.

sample_reviews.review_text: OMG! This is a cute story that just keeps developing and developing! Great characters, and I am wondering who will win the affection of our lovely Carlotta.

First off, these are NOT like the Janet Evanovich Stephanie Plum novels. Plum is more hardcore than this woman, whom I don't even think took a swing at a guy. Plum is also a bounty hunter, and Carlotta sells clothing. Plum has a reason to investigate things, whereas this woman? Hardly. If you want a series with more meat on its bone, go with Plum. Want something fluffy and light that you can read while multitasking? Here ya go. 
 Not that this series is boring; it's just...there. You can read it and feel like the consequences aren't going to be serious. Wesley won't be dismembered, his sister raped, nobody dies but the bad guys. It's a stress-free series, so far. Well, nobody dies if you ignore the bodies that Wesley and Coop pick up. 
 Lively characters, and Carlotta's plight is very well described. I'm still not sure why she wasted $300, or why she actually trusted her brother not to waste his paycheck, but hey, without that kind of stupid, the book would be shorter. Hannah is annoying - her constant flirting got old, really quick. I want to see more of this...uh, forgot her name, the other friend that's happy with the dude overseas. And more of Moody - she seemed like someone Carlotta should hang out, someone who has her head on straight. 
 I haven't been reading chick lit mysteries very long, but they share common elements. A woman starts investigating something she likely shouldn't be investigating, ends up in trouble, and usually has one or two potential love interests, one of which will save her. It happened in this series, the Wollie Shelley series by Harley Jane Kozak, and in pretty much every Mary Higgins Clark book ever. (For those who care, that's why I stopped reading MHC. The plots were tired and worn-out.) 
 Why keep reading? Eh, I'm bored and why not. As long as the book doesn't actively piss me off, I'll give it a shot. I just wish some of these women made smarter decisions.
Damn cliffhanger endings!

Well this book was ok, but a bit disappointing. I had read another novel by Stephanie Bond and it made me laugh much more than this one. I couldn't identify with the characters or at least find them beliveable enough. And though there were twists in the story, there was not enough suspens for me to want to know what would happen. I still read it until the end and the teasing at the very end (since it is the first book of a series) almost attracted me, but I'm not sure I'll give a chance to the following novels.

Poor Stephanie Bond. I finished reading her book Body Movers at the same time I finished listening to Mark Kay Andrew's book Deep Dish . I now get the warning sides that will produce a formulaic yawn. The following elements are required in the almost-a-beach-book category. If you find some / all of them in the book you are starting be prepared to bang your head against the wall in frustration at some point(s) in your journey from cover to cover. 
 1. Start with a cute / beautiful heroine. Extra points if the woman is blond; blue eyes are expected. She must be slim and at least a little hapless. 
 2. Add in a grown / nearly grown sibling the character is responsible for tending to (sister for Deep Dish's "Reggie", brother for Carlotta) 
 3. At least half the characters must have a cute name - witness Carlotta and Regina 
 4. All animals must have cute names (Moonpie...really ? And who wouldn't name their pet snake Einstein...) 
 5. An extra 10 points for either a body (Body Movers excels at this) or a natural disaster. In either case the heroine must be directly threatened and rescued 
 6. There has to be a sleazy ex-boyfriend 
 7. There will not be parents on the scene - dead parents are preferable to just missing / absent ones and luckily both Andrews and Bond neatly cavort throughout the editions noted above without more than a sibling or aunt. 
 8. Financial implosion must be imminent for the main character so that there is a required note of "if I wasn't so desperate I wouldn't be an idiot" surrounding the plot 
 9. There should be a plot device that gives the a reader a crisis to pin all this nonsense around 
 10 There is always love in the air..that is the real plot to any of the books in this category. Forget the murder mystery or fake animosity (the old hate at first sight routine)

reference_books.title: Miss Peregrine’s Home for Peculiar Children (Miss Peregrine’s Peculiar Children, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I have a lot of mixed feelings about this book. I want to like it but there was so much about it that I just didn't care for. 
 The beginning of the book was impossible to get through. I would purposely distract myself just so I wouldn't keep forcing myself to read. I'm not even joking. I went as far as bringing out my old DS and playing on it for a good two hours before pushing myself to read more. But even then I'd just stare at the pages until my boredom put me to sleep. 
 I wanted, so badly, to put this book away and just be done. It wasn't until Jacob finally found the "portal" to Ms. Peregrine and the kids that I started to get interested in the story. When i say "interested" I'm using that word very loosely. When Ms. Peregrine started explaining how they're all still alive and that whole world, I was having an extremely difficult time understanding the words coming out of her mouth. I'm still not 100% sure what she was talking about. 
 Then there came Emma and Jacob's relationship. For starters I didn't like it. I thought it was weird that he was coming on to his grandfather's ex lover. Even after he found out she was almost 90 years old he still pursued her. Emma seemed really taken away with him also and I can't figure out why. They have one conversation and suddenly their sexual hormones are running rampant and they can stop thinking about each other and have several kissing scenes that where very very hard to read. 
 The only other problem I had was when the scary shadow people started attacking and then there was that whole chapter at the light house. I have absolutely no idea what the hell I was reading. I'm guessing it was so we get to see Jacob's ability.....and I'm boring myself just talking about it. 
 I'm giving this book two stars because there were pictures and they were fun to look at. As for continuing on this series...Nahhhhhhhh.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I hate to say that I had to DNF this book, but I did. I was super excited to read Allegiant when it first released and I got it the day it came out I believe. But as time went on, I kept putting off reading it because of school and sort of lost that excitement for the book. I was also doing my best to avoid reading reviews because I didn't want to be spoiled and I was doing good until on a random blog post or goodreads or something, the spoiler came. I was sort of ticked off about it, but I still wanted to read the book and give it a try. 
 I started the book and was completely bored. When I went into reading Allegiant, I went into it with an open mind even though I already knew what happened. The entire time I was reading it I felt disconnected from both Tris and Four. I had no feelings towards either of the characters and that bothered me. So I decided to put the book down for the day and try again the next and it still happened. I felt absolutely nothing. No emotions, no excitement to be back in the world, NO NOTHING! Maybe it was because I was bored and felt like nothing was going on within the story besides talking. There wasn't any action going on or anything like that. By this point, I was fed up and figured since I already knew what happened I might as well DNF it because the book wasn't doing anything for me and I knew I wouldn't make through the rest. 
 So then I decided to read a bunch of spoiler filled reviews just to no more of what happened. I still wanted to know something since I made it through books one and two. I read good reviews and bad reviews. I found out about the government and Tris and Four and everything that happened in the book. After that, I went and talked to my mom because she read the book and finished it and I asked her what she thought of it. She didn't like it that much. I asked her what she'd rate it and she said either 2 or 3 stars. She thought the trilogy went downhill after the first book to some it up. 
 Overall, I don't know why I was so disconnected from the story. Maybe it was time or the fact that I was spoiled early on, I honestly don't know. But I do now know what happens from all the spoiler filled review (good and bad) that I read and I also went and read like the last ten chapters to see how Four dealt with everything. It sucks that I couldn't finish this, but I'm not sorry that I started the trilogy. I did enjoy both Divergent and Insurgent.

Two stars because I really couldn't connect with any of it and I just wished it would end already. The first book, Divergent, was really good and it made me want to continue on in the series. The second book, Insurgent, was where I started losing interest. This book...sorry to say but I'm glad it's a trilogy.

While I liked Allegiant it was not without problems. The ending didn't bother me, nor did the lack of science knowledge. I liked that the plot took us outside of the city to what was further beyond, which was bleak and disturbing. 
 I had two major issues with Allegiant. I couldn't stand all the bickering and arguing between Tris and Four. We had enough of that in Insurgent and there was already so much going on in Allegiant that it detracted from everything else that was going on. 
 Over the last couple of years I have come to love dual narrated books, but it didn't work at all in Allegiant. Their voices weren't distinct and I couldn't always tell who was narrating. A fact that was made worse because it didn't always alternate with each chapter. There were a couple of times that I got pulled out of the story a bit when I realized I had the wrong narrator.

Hmm. Hmm! What to think? I have so many mixed emotions about this book. While I agree that the plot was idiotically planned (and therefore a bit hard to follow at times because of its ridiculousness, but not NEARLY as bad as in Mockingjay, God save me on that one) something about the writing (particularly at the end) well, worked. 
 I will say this. Writers are not known for their ability to use logic. Creative people are generally not the most scientific bunch out there. The two coincide occasionally, but realistically speaking, one is either right or left brained. I understand this is a science fiction novel and therefore the plot SHOULD be rooted in scientific fact backed by research rhe author has done, but frankly, as a reader, I don't really care. There. I said it. 
 Readers are so quick to judge authors and criticize every last attempt, but if some of them would try writing their own story, they would see how tedious and ghastly research actually is and have a bit more respect for the CREATIVE LICENSE authors are ALLOWED to take. Writing is an art, and should be appreciated as such. Who cares if all the facts were 100% correct? Historical fiction is one thing, but accuracy shouldn't matter as much in a world that is not and never was our own IMO. 
 Anyway, that being said, the author left me with a feeling of "woah" when I put the book down. That doesn't happen often. The intense emotion at the end and impact all the events had make the story well-done in my opinion. I understand why the author chose the ending she did, even though I am not happy about it. Sometimes authors "realize" the ending instead of inventing it, and that's just the way it must be. Stories have lives of their own in that way. 
 Improvement over Insurgent was, as I said in the previous paragraph, the impact the events had. Less people died, so each death was more meaningful. Significant degradation was the switching points of view between Tris and Tobias, and boy am I relieved I was not the only one flipping back to the beginning of the chapter to see who was speaking (and reading entire chapters thinking one character was speaking only to discover at the end it was the other character...) 
 One irritation I must wholeheartedly agree with is Four's complete personality change. I am going to assume the author had a reason for doing this, perhaps exposing a side of him we had not yet seen, but the change was out of context and made no sense. 
 One last thing thing that surprisingly no one else has commented on: the overuse of interjections of the author's own opinions and views of things. I will provide examples when I am more coherent and less tired, but boy, once I noticed that, did it get annoying. Obviously an author's work reflects their personal opinions, but never should they be so bluntly stated. Keep it discreet. Make the readers believe what you believe by showing, not telling, always.

So this happened. 
 I put off writing this review for about two days after I finished the book because I couldn't formulate coherent thoughts about what had happened. 
 I still kind of can''t. 
 I'm not sure what this review will end up being. Probably kind of short, probably kind of rambly, but I did want to write something about this conclusion to the Divergent trilogy. 
 I've heard a lot of negative things being said about Allegiant as people have finished the book, some of it justified, some of it completely unwarranted hate. And what I will say is that yes, Allegiant was unexpected. The concept of the GP's and the GD's was definitely different; honestly, I wasn't expecting the genetic war and general explosion of science and post-apocalyptic-ness that occurred, and yes, the story was slower than that of the other books. I won't deny that there were times when I was wishing for something to happen, or wishing that something would happen differently than it did. There were times (Four's involvement with Nita's rebellion? REALLY?) when I seriously questioned actions that the characters made. Was Allegiant perfect? No. Were there aspects of the book that I didn't like? Absolutely yes. 
 But did I hate it? 
 Absolutely, one hundred percent no. 
 I didn't hate it because of the brilliant characters that brought so much life to this story. I didn't hate it because Tris was brave and selfless and brilliant in every way; because she managed to one up the other characters every time and prove that yes, she might only be sixteen but she knows what she's doing. Four might have made some VERY rash decisions, and yes, he was a little bit harder to love in this book, but he was still brave, still flawed, still gloriously unsure of his place in the world and so relatable because of that. Veronica Roth does an excellent job of creating very realistic, flawed characters that can be frustrating at times, yes, but who we can all connect with. Christina and Uriah were right up there with beloved characters; they've always been two of my favorites, but I grew to love them even more in this book- they were so lovable, and I adored their relationship with each other. They both had lost so much, and even though they got a short amount of time together (I can't even express how distraught I am over Uriah's death) their friendship was beautiful. 
 Veronica Roth is a brilliant, brilliant writer. You can say whatever you want, but you can't deny that she's extremely talented. Which is why I can't say anything bad about her for the ending- because yes, the ending was emotional, and yes, it killed me, and yes, I sat on my bed sobbing for twenty minutes after finishing the book because I literally couldn't calm down, but if I can be bold for a minute, killing Tris was a genius move. 
 It seems to be kind of a trend in YA literature to have happy, sugar-coated endings to war stories. And that's what Divergent is, it's a story of war, and so casualties can only be expected, but for some reason, the concept of a protagonist's death is never one that is really dwelt upon. Sure, I had considered that Four might die, but I never in a million years expected Tris, and that's why I was panicking so much when she died, because I held out the hope that she was alive until the very, very last page. 
 And then she didn't come back. 
 I was crying before then; I cried as she died, I absolutely lost it when Four was thinking about the first time he saw her, and the epilogue killed me, but when I finished that last page and knew that Tris Prior was good and truly dead, I completely and utterly started to bawl. 
 But like I said, it was a genius move. It was a genius move because nobody saw it coming and as much as I cried and wanted to die, it was realistic. And when war happens, it doesn't just magically skim over main characters. 
 And not only that, but Tris didn't die in vain. She died saving her city, she died saving her brother and the other people that she cared about, and she died being selfless and brave. 
 Having said that, I'm going to miss Tris Prior more than I can say. 
 I'm going to miss how she was brave enough to leave Abnegation and her family behind, how she left and went to Dauntless because that was what she genuinely wanted. I'm going to miss how she was the first jumper, the first initiate brave enough to make the jump. I have no idea how I will sit through that scene in the movie without sobbing. 
 I'm going to miss her wit and outspokenness, how she was never afraid to say what she thought, how she always stepped in when she disagreed with the way that something was being done. I'll miss her protectiveness, I'll miss her selflessness and bravery, I'll miss how she loved deeply and cherished the people close to her. Honestly, I'm just really going to miss Tris. 
 I don't know what to do with myself now. I finished the book two days ago and I'm still reeling; I genuinely don't know when I'm going to come to terms with this. But for now, thank you, Veronica Roth, for such an incredible series.

This book kinda fell flat. It didn't fall as flat as Mockingjay, in my opinion, mainly because the female lead didn't try to shirk her responsibility. I will say that this book, with its flaws, was okay. It would have been better of it wasn't such an info-dump. I feel it should have been made into two books instead of being one. book_b.title: Throne of Glass (Throne of Glass, #1)
book_b.user_review:
** spoiler alert ** 
 This book was good. The reason I gave it 4 stars is because I'm extremely disappointed about the action scenes. I mean since Celaena Sardothien is known by everyone in Erilea as Adarlan's Assassin, I expected some absolute bad ass woman power. I wanted blood. I wanted daggers embedded in chest cavities. I wanted fancy ninja cartwheels that she used to avoid an attacker right before she beheaded him with her Steele sword. I wanted risk taking, daredevil, action packed scenes. But instead I got someone who talked like she was the shit but never proved her title once. Someone who kept saying how and what she would use to kill anyone who threatens her but would never, NEVER ONCE, act on it. The most disappointing scene has have to be the final duel between her and Cain. I was so pissed that Kaltain was able to poison her. I didn't understand the whole Elena coming in and saving the day scene. I had to read that part twice. The most and I mean the MOST infuriating part was that even after Celaena was able to over come the poison and still kick Cain's cheating ass, she didn't fucking kill him. Like all that work and energy and you're not going to kill that asshole. 
 Something I wasn't expecting was how emotional Adarlan's Assassin was. Not in a PMS kind of way. But she showed her affectionate, and lovable side a whole lot more than what I was expecting from a deadly, ruthless killer. It was overwhelming. As much as I was anticipating, it was actually a really awesome book. This book focused more on Celaena's actions and personality persuading Dorian and Chaol that she isn't the emotionless murderer that they presumed she would be. Every chapter was written well and had just the right length. No one chapter was too long or too short. I'm extremely impressed that no characters got on my nerves. I loved her relationships with everyone and her sarcastic, smart mouth. The mystery of Elena, The First Queen of Adarlan, who has been awakened after a thousand years and the whole concept of Wyrdmarks is very intriguing. The loss of Sam and not knowing anything about Celaena before Endovier is still unsolved. The best part is now that Celaena is The King's Champion there should be a lot more blood and gore and, hopefully, we will finally get to see if she lives up to her title. I'm excited for Crown of Midnight and I hope that I will be more impressed with the sequel.

sample_reviews.review_text: I listened to this on audio and made myself finish, but I really didn't care about the characters or the plot. I've heard many people say this series is great so it must just be me.
3.5 stars

3.5 stars. An interesting start to a series. Didn't like the talk about appearances and dresses etc being so important ( this improves in the next book) Did like the mysterious wyrd keys and hint of magic.

Throne of Glass by Sarah J. Maas is the first in a series about an assassin who is thrown into a competition to become the king's Champion. Not only has the king destroyed and conquered most of the land, but he has also extinguished all magic.. or so he thinks. 
 Celaena Sardothien has spent the last year in one of the deadiest death camps. Few have survived the Salt Mine, but she has somehow managed a year. When two surprising visitors come for her, she wonders if this is the end. But, she may be given a second chance to make it out of her lifelong sentence of torture. Being the greatest assassin ever feared, she is asked to join a competition that could ultimately lead to her freedom. 
 We follow as she journeys to the last place she would have found herself: the king's castle made out of stone and glass. Celaena has to keep her identity a secret from those around her while trying to fight over thirty other assassins, thieves, and mercenaries over the course of a few months to prove her ability. But, Champions begin to go missing and found half eaten. Who could be behind this? 
 I give this book 4 out of 5 stars. I personally did not find the plot to be predictable. There were a lot of twists and turns to the story that made it very interesting to continue reading. I had just spent the entire day finishing the book, so definitely an easy read. There were a few times that I found myself a little dragging which is why I didn't give it 5 stars, but I enjoyed it none the less. The character development was very good. You could tell their differences between the beginning and the ending of this first book. I cannot wait to continue the story with Crown of Midnight. I first plan on buying the bind-up of novellas that recently came out a few months ago called the Assassin's Blade, and then continue on with the next three books. The fourth installment is coming out 1 September 2015, so I am excited for that. 
 I can definitely see myself getting engrossed in more of Sarah J. Maas's writing. She has an enticing writing style which I hope gets better as I read more of her books. This was the first book that I have read from her. Sarah also kept the romance to a point where it was not a majority of the story which I also thought made the me want to read more. As readers, we weren't stuck in long scenes where we would have felt stuck in. Sarah also makes the main character an assassin who is also kind of a girly-girl which is very rare to see. She was not just your typical hardcore strong girl. This, I think, gave her more of a relatable feature. Definitely a lot of fun characters in this series so far.

After having sat for a couple of days I think I am going to give this a 3.5. While I did enjoy it I think the hype got to me a little bit. 
 I really do enjoy Maas's writing. It's compelling and descriptive but I could definitely see a difference in her writing in this book and in her writing in her later work A Court of Thorns and Roses. While that book was slow but completely kept my attention, I felt like this book was slow and left my mind wandering, not focused on what was going on. Much of the book was focused on the everyday tasks of the castle and not the mystery behind the competitor's deaths or the king's competition. 
 Celaena was an extremely confident heroine. Almost to a fault. She was so prideful and by the end of the book it started to get on my nerves. There is only so many times I want to hear her talk about how she could kill every person in the room, and not show that she actually can, or how pretty she is. I did enjoy the relationships that grew between her and Chaol and her and Dorian. Not gonna lie... totally team Chaol right now. He was strong and silent and I loved that he didn't jump on the Celaena bandwagon. They got to know each other, learning about their pasts, slowly learning to trust each other. Dorian. Oh Dorian. He was funny and brought a light hearted edge to the book that I liked but he was such a stock character. Typical prince trying to break free of the role he was born into. I hope that he will show a little more depth later in the series and will play a larger role in the politics of his kingdom. 
 The world building could have been stronger. By the end of the book I didn't really know anything about where it took place, the kind of people that lived there, the type of trade or economy they have. The king was virtually non-existent so there was no kind of political intrigue to help understand the court or policies happening. The book pretty much exists within the entirety of Calaena's room and nothing really penetrates that. I can see so much potential in what she has created and I hope that the world expands in the next books. 
 I have heard many people say that the series gets better as it goes and I do plan on continuing on to see how the story expands. While my entire review sounds somewhat negative, overall I enjoyed what Maas was doing and the story that she was setting up.

Celaena Sardothien is the most infamous assassin. Though when she is retrieved out of the mines where she has spent her last year she is a mere shadow of herself. She is given a proposition by the Crown Prince to compete to be the King's Champion. Given the option of going back to her torture or possibly working for a King she despises she chooses to go into the competition. Once she arrives to a place she only remembers from a year ago before her capture she realizes things may be more challenging than she anticipated. She is forced to train with the Captain of the Guard and fend off the advances of a very attractive Crown Prince. But, these aren't her only worries. Once the competition begins other competitors begin being killed off. She must figure out who is behind the killings and maintain her standing in the competition. Though Celaena came for a chance at her freedom she doesn't anticipate gaining a friend and two admirers vying for her heart. Will the best assassin win or will the shadows and her past catch up with her? 
 I was blown away by this book. This book opened up a new world, new adventure and a phenomenal heroine. Celaena is tough, strong and yet has a gentle and intelligent side. You truly find yourself forgetting that she is well-known for killing people for money. I adored the imagery within the story. The glass castle and her opinions of it and its ruler felt natural and honest for the character. It wasn't just the pretty imagery that really paints a grand picture. The descriptions of the mines and dungeons would make anyone fear being a rebel in this story. I would also be remiss if I didn't at least address the love triangle between the Crown Prince, Celaena and the Captain of the Guard. It's technically not a standard triangle but there are definitely three hearts and love in the air. Overall, this book has drawn me in hook line and sinker. Sarah Maas has just got a huge fan in me and I will be finishing this series in no time. I have truly fallen for Celaena and her world. I need more!
I absolutely loved this book! Beautiful writing, interesting characters and kept wanting more! Who doesn't love a female assassin! I can't wait to read the rest of the series!

This book pissed me off in so many places that even my genuine interest in the world and some of the characters couldn't drag the rating up from a 2 star. 
 Right off the bat the main character was painfully obviously a Mary Sue; The eighteen year old assassin who could handles swords, knives and arrows, kill ruthlessly but still has impeccable court manners and like frilly, pretty things, loves books and reads voraciously, plays the piano masterfully and of course charms everyone she meets with her stunning good looks. 
 Books like this don't need legions of devotees writing them fanfiction. They are their own fanfiction. 
 People flock to her as if mesmerized. Except for women, of course. They hate her. Because why would a woman ever be friends with someone she thought was prettier than her, right? As if women only existed to compete for the attention of men. 
 I can't believe the author dared to use the "I don't have any female friends and don't know why trope". She even had her main character say it in so many words. She said that she no longer befriended or trusted girls. 
 Pet peeve number two: The dreaded love triangle. If I had known this novel contained a love triangle I wouldn't have picked it up. Groan. 
 Pet peeve number three: The dialogue was so confusing that I often had to run my eyes backwards across the page just to figure out who said what. 
 Whatever happened to using plain old "he said, she said" and putting spaces between different peoples' lines? 
 Not to mention the use of prepackaged descriptions like"he said softly but not weekly" and "she breathed a long sigh through her nose" 
 I realize this is a minor inconvenience but this stuff just leaps out me as I read. They just bug me to no end. 
 Pet peeve number four: and this is the whopper that dragged the rating down to a two star; in the end the author describes a fight scene between the main character and Cain. 
 Imagine being punched in the spine by someone who at least twice your size, Someone who had been killing people and magically absorbing their strength for the past twelve weeks. 
 Imagine being punched in the jaw by that same person. 
 Imagine being punched in the ribs by him. 
 Now imagine having that person slam your face into a stone wall. Twice. 
 Now tell me if you think you can come out of that with nothing but a single fractured rib, a cut on your thigh and assorted bruises. 
 It would take a person the better part of a year to recover from that kind of damage to their body, assuming they were fortunate enough to survive and endure the agony of recovery. 
 Our main character was up and at 'em within a week. A week, I tell you!. 
 Smh. 
 Here's another thing I should add to this review: When you look at religions in terms of the principle deity worshiped, you can determine the society's approach to gender equality (or lack thereof) through the gender of that principle deity. 
 In this book, people worship a main goddess. There are other gods, yes but principally, their deity is female. here's my problem: 
 Wouldn't that society be then considered decidedly matriarchal? if people believe their god is a woman and go to temples to listen to high priestesses chant and Chanel said goddess, I'd have to think that they would be pretty comfortable with the idea of women in power. and if so where is all this sexism coming from? 
 How could a matriarchal society believe a girl can't compete in a contest and become the king's assassin simply because she's a girl?
This was an ok book there were some flaws to the book, but overall it was an enjoyable read and look forward to the next book.

This was one of those books that takes a bit of patience as it is slow going at first but well worth the wait. Kevin, of the title, is a school shooter and the novel details his life as seen through his mother's eyes. The "talking" is something Kevin's mother wanted to do throughout his life but it always seemed as if she could not find an audience for her concerns. Add to that, she was a reluctant mother to begin with so many folks brushed off her insights into her child as unfounded. It is interesting how the author chose to tell the story through letters, a convention that was very popular during the Victorian and Romantic periods. Perhaps this was one way Kevin's mother could "talk" without being brushed off. The subject matter is disturbing but handled very well by Lionel Shriver. A well written book that uses black humour, insights into the world of parenting, and the all too familiar tale of a child who leaves his mark on the world through violence.

I've started marathon training again, and with the increase in kilometres comes an increase in books I listen to instead of reading. M. suggested I might like "We Need to Talk About Kevin" (well, maybe not "like" so much as be-interested-in) and she was right. It's hard to separate out liking the book from liking the audio recording - a lot of background and supplemental sounds to keep this running reader engaged - but whatever the cause I did enjoy this story. 
 I'm not sure the book is about Kevin so much as it is about the narrator and wife Eva, and not so much about what makes for a sociopath as it is about what makes a mother (the plot, in brief, is that Kevin massacres 12 people at his high school, goes to prison, Eva and Franklin's marriage falls apart). My friend C. recently asked what it might mean to be a woman and not be a mother in terms of the values we hold. She asked because she'd been thinking about Idle No More and the explanation many of the women gave for their participation as a result of their concern for their children and grandchildren. What shapes our values - or justifies them - if we don't have children through whom to explain our actions? This narrative asks a slightly different - but related question - in that it wonders how women become complicit or implicated in the successes of failures of their children. It wonders whether mothers are nothing more than extensions of their children, or hold ultimate responsibility for their actions - as if they are always-already accountable for what the child does or doesn't do (and in a manner different from that of the father). And what of those mothers who do not "do" maternity well? Those who dislike their children, who experience post-partum depression, who make egregious and conscious errors in parenting? These sorts of obvious "failures" of maternity are contrasted with the unspoken but assumed failures that attach to childless mothers, barren women, women who abort or miscarry, women who do not "take" to mothering with the seamless ease supposedly innate and natural. And in all of these questions the reader is left to ask what happens to Eva as a person - someone who wanted particular things from and for her life in and beyond maternity - if all she is becomes subsumed by her actions and failings as a mother. And this is, I think, where C.'s question comes back into it - if we allow femininity or womanhood to be unilaterally attached or drawn to our propensity or success as a mother, what do we leave women for themselves? If our values are tied to preservation and protection of our children, our identities wedded to our success as mothers, our purpose and meaning derived from our children... well it seems an awfully oppressive kind of maternity. A sexist one that says that women must identify themselves first and always as mothers (while men might have identities far beyond or in addition to paternity) and that any inclination toward a separate life is selfish or unnatural. And one that casts doubt or suspicion on those women for whom maternity is not possible, desirable or suitable. 
 The book is supposedly about what makes for a sociopathic killer, but it is, I think, far more interesting in the ways it grapples with what makes for a woman, a wife and a mother.

Mild Spoilers.... 
 This book kind of disappointed me. I don't really see what the hype is about. This book just irritates me... 
 First, the worst part about this book is the writing style. At some point, I got used to it, but dear god, how frustrating it was... See, the story is mostly about Clay Jensen listening to a set of tapes that were made as a suicide story that explains why Hannah took her life to those she blames the most. So, as you read this book, you are reading what is said on the tape and Clay's reactions. But see, the writing about the tape would continue even when Clay was thinking completely random thoughts that are being interrupted by the tape. It seriously bugged because why in the world would you just go back and forth between the two and expect me to continue two completely different lines of thought? 
 Then, we get to the characters. So this set of tapes is passed to multiple different people who Hannah blames for causing her to just give up on life. She threatens to send a second set of tapes out to someone random if they don't pass on the tapes till the very end. The reader never really meets the other characters on the tape which is a bit disappointing because I wanted to see their reactions, not hear about the rumours and whatever Hannah tells us. 
 The narrator of the book is one of the guys who is on the tapes, his name is Clay (I've never met a Clay, have you?). Clay seemed to like Hannah when she was alive but was afraid to act on his feelings. Clay gets really upset over these tapes as he misses Hannah and wishes that she reached out for him. But honestly, he barely really expressed himself and I never really felt any emotions that were described in this book. Like, he seems really overwhelmed with this idea of Hannah's death because of those people when he seemed to barely know this girl. Oh and his contribution to her death? Completely Lame... Not what you're expecting so prepare to be like, seriously?!?!?! 
 I could see the snowball effect throughout the story and I was only really reading the book for the tapes, I couldn't care less about Clay's inner monologues that interrupted the tapes. I was a little disappointed with how the whole book ended because it kinda just jumped to a completely random conclusion. 
 I don't know, maybe this book isn't my type or something but this wasn't my cup of tea.

reference_books.review_text:
Blown away by this story, this is a book I love to hate ... 
 Quintessentially Q is the next book in the series Monsters in the Dark. I first read Tears of Tess which opened my eyes to a new genre of book that I was not familiar with - a totally twisted dark romance. I battled with Tears of Tess in a way that I have never felt before when reading a book of this calibre. The battle raged inside me for most of the read and at times I just had to put it down and have a rest from the rollercoaster ride of feelings, emotions and resentment at the characters and the storyline. That being said, I also couldn't stop reading it. It was awesome and a must read, but beware you may find yourself reading until the small hours of the morning and having a mighty fine book hangover. 
 This story continues with Tess as the esclave and Q the dominating master or as Tess calls him her monster in the dark. This book has everything, it was hauntingly good, it gripped me from the beginning to the end, even if I did have to have a rest occasionally, it broke my heart and shattered it into a million pieces and then put it back together again only for it to shatter again, it was as passionate as it was disturbing, it was cringe worthy but mostly it was unforgettable. I am totally speechless and I really am finding it hard to put into words how I feel about this book and the writer. I loved these books, I would give them more than five stars if I could and I was obsessed with devouring this book as quickly as my brain could absorb the words. 
 While I am still trying to get my emotions back into the state they were before I finished this book, and the fact that this book has plunged me into a world of darkness that I never saw coming, I am grateful to Pepper Winters for writing such a fantastic sequel to an awesome series of books. To say I am looking forward to the next book in the series would be an understatement.

sample_reviews.review_text: I will come back one day and try to formulate my thoughts into words, but today is not that day.

** spoiler alert ** 
 To begin with, I am not a new reader to alpha male romance/erotica. I also have not read any other books in this series, nor will I be reading any other books in this series. 
 The main characters of this novel were so abhorrent to me on so many levels that I had a hard time finishing the novel. I made myself finish it thinking there had to be a positive ending. How wrong I was! 
 Sophie, a young woman who makes a poor decision and ends up pregnant at 17, tells her son she'll protect him/love him forever when he's born. When she makes a bad decision of babysitters in desperation one night, her son makes an emergency call to "Uncle Ruger" to save him. He and his associate show up and scare Sophie (to make her feel unsafe and like a bad mother) and then terrorize and brutalize the "bad babysitters." Ruger then moves Sophie and her son, Noah, from Washington to Idaho to live with him. 
 Ruger is an unapologetic motorcycle gang member. He is always telling Sophie how great the guys in his gang are and that not everything in the gang is illegal...how comforting for a mother of a young boy. For all Ruger's talk, it seems they are always doing illegal things. Their parties are free-for-alls where women are expected to do whatever the men want. Ruger has sex in the open at a party to "claim" Sophie as his property, and the author expects us all to believe that being "property" is an honor because those women are protected above all others. Then she is practically raped because she takes the party garbage out for the "pigs" and the girl she is with for safety is hauled off over the shoulder of her man saying "I want sex, woman!" Ruger tells her he expects her to be true to him, but he isn't willing to give up other woman. His concession is that he won't bring the other women home. How noble. 
 All through the novel, Sophie keeps agonizing over her desire to create a safe life for her son and her incessant tingling-for-Ruger vagina. I was disgusted. The child should always be first and Ruger is obviously a piss-poor choice for a role model for her son. 
 Then the plot gets really stupid. Sophie and another gang member's daughter get kidnapped by a rival gang--nearly raped/killed. But nobody calls the cops because that would go against the code. Here is where I thought she would finally get it, and she did for a few seconds. But then Ruger shows up on her date with a normal guy and scares the guy off. Then Ruger tells her how awful her date was for running off. 
 Finally, the ex-husband/Ruger's half brother, Zach, sneaks back to Idaho and traps Sophie alone in her apartment. Although she has a restraining order, that doesn't stop Zach from showing up. (Finally, something that is real!) Sophie then kills Zach which causes her to call Ruger to clean up her mess. Love blooms, and all is well. 
 Some of the reasons this novel was so offensive, abhorrent, and repulsive are: 
 1) Alpha males should be good at heart. I never felt this from Ruger. All I got from him is that he was an arrogant, male chauvinist, entitled asshole. Using violence and control tactics are not sexy. 
 2) Outlaw, illegal, gang, mob, whatever you call it--isn't sexy. Kidnapping, rape, murder, etc.--isn't sexy. 
 3) Sophie's unwillingness to put the safety and best interests ahead of her vagina repulsed me.

Well, because I think the heroine is stupid. I mean, where in the hell do you find someone whose independence meant more to her than getting help from anyone else? Especially if the help was offered by someone she used to always depend on and is very good to her son? And especially, too, if her son benefits from all the help? I would have enjoyed Reaper's Legacy more if the hero and the heroine didn't dance around each other for a huge part of the book. 
 Okay, so they had a history. But, come on, whatever happened between Sophie and Zach when he saw her and Ruger is hugely her fault, as she herself admitted, because she deliberately set herself up.  So when she finally killed Zach, who does she call? Yep. Ruger. And who fixes the whole mess, so she doesn't get into trouble? Yep, him and the MC. Because Drew's bestfriend and roommate us no other than Travis Fucking King. Viola and Travis are soon to find out that these 2 weeks will be harder than either of them will want to admit.

Can this book be classified as a romance, even? 
 I got this book for free on iBooks during a sale, but I had heard about it from a few people. 
 I tend to love the 'enemies to lovers' trope, but this one was just... not my thing. Usually in these kinds of stories there's a lot of underlying care for each other and they gradually begin to realize that the other is not as bad as they originally thought. 
 In this book, they just hate each other. A lot. Viola says it like every chapter. 
 Also Travis was a grade A asshole. He was controlling, possessive, and a massive hypocrite for getting all hyped up whenever Viola showed any level of interest in other men, when he was literally still sleeping with other women after he and Viola had started... whatever they were doing. 
 Viola was a doormat, constantly thinking about how much she hated Travis in one moment and then tripping over herself for him in the next. The first time they did anything, it was after Travis had just been with another woman (and Viola knew this) and she was still putty in his hands. 
 Also Travis ALWAYS had the upper hand, which felt slimy to me. Another thing I like about the enemies-to-lovers trope is that the characters usually balance each other out or are constantly one-upping each other. There usually isn't just one being a constant asshole to the other while the other just sits there and lets it happen. 
 I've also seen it pointed out that this book was full of double standards when it came to Travis vs Viola. Viola wasn't a virgin heroine, but she might as well have been, the one time she goes on a date, there's a huge fuss made about how he's not attractive. Like literally every guy she kind of sees is described as unattractive because god forbid she have any sort of sexual action with someone else while Travis is going from girl to girl. 
 We got almost excruciating detail of Travis's day-to-day life at work, but nothing about how Viola spends her time and her days, which made her come off as really bland. 
 The inciting incident for her all-consuming hatred of Travis was very lame and would have been easily cleared up if she had just confronted him at some point. 
 It got really tedious and a little disgusting having to read about all of Travis's sexcapades with women who weren't the heroine. Which continue even after he and Viola begin doing things. Would have been much appreciated if these were more of a fade-to-black thing. 
 Which brings me to the writing. It was overly simplistic and the dialogue wasn't clever in the slightest. The name being Checkmate, I was expecting witty banter and intelligent characters, but the characters were childish and petty and the dialogue was just... meh. There were quite a few times where the writing made me cringe. 
 My favorite sentence being: 
 "I enter the building, taking the stairs two at a time because I want to feel my body being pushed to the edge."
