reference_books.title: Love's Reckoning (The Ballantyne Legacy, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Title: Love's Reckoning 
 Author: Laura Frantz 
 Pages: 407 
 Year: 2012 
 Publisher: Revell 
 Note: I received a complimentary copy for an honest review of this book. The opinions shared in this review are solely my responsibility. Other reviews can be read at http://seekingwithallyurheart.blogspo.... Also follow me on Twitter @lcjohnson1988 
 Love's Reckoning is the beginning of a new historical romantic series written by Laura Frantz titled "The Ballantyne Legacy". This story is set in 1784 in Pennsylvania. Liege Lee has been thrown out of the Quaker Society and has shunned all religion. There is no Bible in the house and no one is allowed to attend church. However, in the name of courtship, he will allow one of his daughters to attend church with Silas. Liege is greedy, selfish, and a tyrant. 
 Silas Ballantyne has left his homeland of Scotland to make a new life in America. His past is has many painful memories, and he is hoping to start anew in America. He is an apprentice iron worker and has agreed to take a position in York County, Pennsylvania. He is a Christian, trusting in God to protect and guide him. He has a dream to go further west in Pennsylvania to Fort Pitt. He must complete his apprenticeship before realizing his dream. He arrives in York at the home of Liege Lee, his new boss. Liege has two beautiful daughters, Elspeth and Eden. Unbeknownst to Silas, Liege is planning to follow a tradition whereby the apprentice is "encouraged" to marry one of the employer's daughters in order to keep the business in the family. Will Silas be forced to wed? What about his dreams of the west? 
 Elspeth Lee is unwed and pregnant. She has been confined to the house during her "illness". She won't say who the father is and doesn't regret her choices. She has spent most of her life in the shop with her father learning the ins and outs of iron working. She does the bookkeeping for her father. She often uses that as an excuse to get out of helping around the house. Her father has made a proposal that if Silas arrives before the baby is born, he will marry Eden. If he arrives after the baby is born, then he will marry Elspeth. Once the baby is born, she shows completely no interest, leaving the care of the baby to Eden and their mother. She is not a nice young woman. She plots and schemes to get her way and will do anything to get what she wants and she wants Silas. She finds church tiresome and tedious. 
 Eden Lee is a gentle, obedient and dependable daughter. She pretty much runs the household. She does not want to marry anyone. She has plans to leave for Philadelphia and work at an orphanage, but no one knows her secret. Marriage wound ruin her dream. She meets Silas and they form a friendship. He reads to her from his Gaelic Bible and gives her verses of Scripture on scraps of paper to feed her hungry heart God's word. Her sweet innocence and heart draw Silas as no other has ever done. Soon their friendship grows to love. They must always be on the lookout for Elspeth's nasty schemes. 
 Can they ever be together as they each have their own dreams? How can God allow events to happen that might separate them forever? Will Eden find the love she is searching for and give her heart to God? I could tell you the answers to these questions, but that would spoil the enjoyment of reading the book for yourself. Pick up a copy and discover the answers. 
 My rating is 3.5 stars.

reference_books.title: Full Disclosure
reference_books.review_text:
Title: Full Disclosure 
 Author: Dee Henderson 
 Pages: 373 
 Year: 2012 
 Publisher: Bethany House 
 Note: I received a complimentary copy for an honest review of this book. The opinions shared in this review are solely my responsibility. Other reviews can be read at http://seekingwithallyurheart.blogspo.... Also follow me on Twitter @lcjohnson1988 
 Full Disclosure is the latest novel from Dee Henderson, her first in several years. She continues in the genre of romantic suspense that she is so well-known for via her O'Malley Series and Uncommon Heroes series. The main characters in this book are involved in law enforcement with a multitude of family, friends, and co-workers as a supporting cast. 
 Paul is the head of an FBI team that profiles, tracks, and captures murderers. He is the oldest son of a wealthy businessman. He is adopted, but treated as the firstborn son. He will inherit his father's businesses when he dies so he is well-versed in business, finances, as well as the law due to his being a cop. He is a Christian and has a strong relationship with the Lord. He has a large family and they are close. He has decided that he wants to settle down, get married, and have his own family. Is Ann the right woman for him? Can he overcome her need for solitude? Can he earn her trust and her heart? They begin to contact each other more and more as Paul works on a case that has been on the books for over 10 years. A female assassin with 30 kills credited to her. Will Paul finally catch this criminal and succeed where his former boss failed? 
 Ann is the Midwest Homicide Investigator (MHI). She is called in when a case gets too difficult for the local law enforcement agency to solve. She has a case that she doesn't want and realizes it is linked to a federal investigation so she meets Paul and gives him clues that jump starts his stalled investigation. She doesn't like being in the limelight and downplays her accomplishments. She has many friends who have valuable connections; she even has a friendship with the Vice President of the United States. She loves to fly small airplanes, write stories about her friends, and take long walks where she talks to God. She never feels alone because she always has God. She isn't looking to settle down. She is very cautious in her relationships and won't risk making the first move to initiate anything more than cordiality. After meeting Paul and working with him on a case, her thoughts turn to him more and more. Is he the one she might risk giving her heart to? She has been burned in the past, so is very wary. 
 While there is action in the book at various points, there is a lot of time spent on the development of the relationship between Ann and Paul. In my opinion, there were too many pages of this slowly developing relationship that could have been filled with action instead or eliminated altogether. This makes for some slow reading. The romance between the two characters is good just too much video chatting. It is good to see strong family and friend support, protectiveness, and love. The characters have a willingness to go the extra mile for a friend without expecting anything in return. 
 My rating is 3 stars.

reference_books.title: The Traitor's Wife: The Woman Behind Benedict Arnold and the Plan to Betray America
reference_books.review_text:
Title: The Traitor's Wife 
 Author: Allison Pataki 
 Pages: 496 
 Year: 2014 
 Publisher: Howard Books 
 What a riveting, suspenseful and thoroughly entertaining novel! When I approach a historical novel of this magnitude, I usually read the author's notes on the research that sometimes details which characters are from reality and those which are purely fiction. One reason I do that is so as I am reading, I can savor the richness of both the history shared along with the imagination of the writer. While I remember that Benedict Arnold was a traitor who was willing to hand over West Point to the British, there is more to the facts than I recalled. 
 Another reason I read the notes first is to attempt to glean the depth of the story based on the length the writer goes to in order to unearth fact. Finally, the last reason I read the back first is to see if there are other notable books I might desire to obtain on the subject matter. What Allison Pataki writes in the back is for the audience to read on their own time the knowledge and sources shared by Allison. 
 While many may approach this tale with more knowledge than I or less will in no way make the reading of the book less enjoyable. I spent hours just turning pages, trying to imagine what life was like in the past for both the servants and those of means. What was it like to have war on this soil in this country that I love with all my heart? What would it be like to be the maid in service of a self-absorbed woman who cared only for herself and not a whit about the men she claimed to love or the cost of freedom? 
 Part of the novel was just entrancing as I felt like an observer watching the main antagonist work cunningly to maneuver people to do the bidding necessary to bring to her what she wanted without care of family or friends. Then, I would come upon a scene and realize just how far removed the servants were thought to be from their masters and the many things they observed, heard or witnessed. Servants were treated as if they were property or merely shadows to do the master's bidding. In this tale, Clara, the maid servant is becoming entangled in the treachery of her mistress. 
 The ending of the novel is bittersweet. For a debut novel, this author truly did her homework and took painstaking time paying attention to details of all different sorts related to this period of history. The details help the audience picture in their minds the setting and mannerisms of the era. It would indeed be a shame if anyone passed up reading a wonderful novel that reminds us all of how our choices not only affect the moment, but can have rippling consequences decades down the road. 
 My rating is 5 stars.

reference_books.review_text:
Title: No Man's Land (John Puller Series #4) 
 Author: David Baldacci 
 Pages: 432 
 Year: 2016 
 Publisher: Grand Central Publishing 
 My rating is 3 out of 5 stars. 
 In what I assume to be the last novel of the series, the missing mother shared with us in the first novel of the series is found. John Puller, Sr. is a suspect in the disappearance of his wife and John Puller, Jr. is bucking the Army's orders all the way while still looking to figure out what happened 30 years ago. It's more than just his mother's vanishing that he wants to solve as around the same time that his mother disappeared four other women were murdered in a town not too far away. 
 Until recently, the unsolved cold case of the four women and the missing Puller mother were quietly buried. Now, John hopes to finally have closure and though his older brother Robert wants him to let it go, John doesn't. John's investigation gets entwined in intrigue, political and military issues maybe even espionage. All John wants to know about is his mother, but what he uncovers are experiments that turn people into possible super soldiers. 
 While the other three novels were my favorites in the series, this one had just too much of the cussing with f-bombs. Plus, there wasn't as much depth to the novel that is evident in the other stories. The author took lots of time to build the Puller family characters and their history, but this just fell flat. It was enjoyable, but not as suspense filled as other novels by the author. 
 Also, there were a few sexual references and such that didn't add anything to the story, just people using people. While I appreciate the lack of detail the author gives to those scenes, again they were distracting to the story. I know that writers can't get five stars all the time and for the most part I really enjoyed each book, even with the last one ending without the adrenaline rush the other tales gave me. I hope in future books the author refrains from sexual stuff and the f-bomb so it doesn't detract from the stories that are published.

book_a.title: Lady Maybe
book_a.user_review:
Title: Lady Maybe 
 Author: Julie Klassen 
 Pages: 400 
 Year: 2015 
 Publisher: Berkley Books 
 Hannah Rogers is desperate to get her son back. She was forced to live in a home for unwed mothers and after giving birth, her son was basically held hostage until she could afford to pay for his care. The landlord, however, keeps raising the rates. Hannah is forced to go back to the Mayfield home and ask for her job back to earn the necessary money to retrieve her son. While on a journey to the country with the Mayfields, they are in a carriage accident. While recovering from injuries, mistakes are made entrapping Hannah. She knows she is doing wrong, but how else can she get her son back? While contemplating that situation, she is also trying to sort out her feelings for two men. She might set one free only to discover the other man holds no love for her. 
 Negatives: Please be aware that the publisher for this book is not Bethany House, who has previously published some of this author's books. This is not a Christian publisher and that is evident in some of the content of the story. The intimate scenes are more descriptive than in her other novels and add nothing to the storyline. The infidelity of characters in the book is just too much. There are a few brief references to God by Hannah, but not like in the author's other stories where faith is more evident in the main characters. 
 Positives: The description of this time period seemed spot on to me, and it is a period I enjoy reading about. I liked the writing style of the author. I also liked the one character who did speak of God the most, the housekeeper, Mrs. Turrill. She speaks of God's ability to forgive any sin; there is no sin that is so great that He cannot forgive. She also shows the love of God to Hannah and Becky. She tells them that God loves them and that they are valuable in His sight. The author's next book will be published by Bethany House, so I am hoping there will be more of a faith focus. 
 My rating is 3 stars.

Title: The Mapmaker's Children (A Novel) 
 Author: Sarah McCoy 
 Pages: 336 
 Year: 2016 
 Publisher: Broadway Books 
 My rating is 4 stars. 
 The Civil War era is a personal favorite of mine to read about either in fiction or nonfiction. For me, this is the first of Sarah McCoy's books to read. Here she takes readers between two time periods. One is at the time of the Civil War, John Brown and the Underground Railroad. The other is the present day where a married couple is wrestling with infertility and find out the home they now own was once a part of the Underground Railroad. 
 Both Sarah, who is John Brown's daughter and Eden are trying to find their place in life as women who are unable to bear children. Children are usually expected or desired in marriage and depending on culture, it's a sign the marriage is successful. Eden's character is very different by the time the reader reaches the end of the book, which is captivating. 
 Sarah's story for me was more interesting as it was full of historical scenes and time is taken to develop her story. Eden's tale happens within a shorter time frame and perhaps because it is more present day I didn't find it as interesting or captivating. Either the author could have written two separate novels in order to develop Eden's story better or just shared with reader's Sarah's journey. So much more could have been included about the Underground Railroad, John Brown's life and Sarah's artistic gift. Overall though the novel was enjoyable and interesting, I will be watching for what the author decides to share with us next! At the end of the book the author shares her pictures and interesting notes from her research.

The Mapmaker's Children by Sarah McCoy follows two women - Sarah Brown in the 1850s and Eden Anderson in 2014. Sarah's story is personal and global - the story of slavery, abolition and the time leading up to the Civil War in the United States. Eden's story is about personal sorrow, a house, and a doll. Sarah's story is the more compelling one, but Eden's story feels more "alive." 
 Read my complete review at: http://www.memoriesfrombooks.com/2015... 
 Reviewed based on a copy received through a publisher's giveaway

An integral part of being a woman is the potential to bear children, to nurture and watch the lifelong joys and sorrows of those children's lives. Two women separated by decades, whose inability to have children affects their lives, are brought to vivid life in Sarah M. McCoy's The Mapmaker's Children. 
 In the present, Eden has a good life. She and her storybook prince of a husband have just bought a beautiful old home. But nothing matters to her because years of trying to conceive a child, including fertility treatments, have not worked. Eden can't get past it. 
 In the past, Sarah Brown overhears that the fever that nearly took her life has taken her ability to have children. She grows into womanhood never forgetting what her mother said: "Who will love her now?" 
 When your worth as a woman depends on the marriage market, that's a big drawback. When your father is the infamous John Brown, it may be even more significant, depending on the kindness of other abolitionists. 
 Sarah is not the kind of person to look at things that way though. If one avenue to living is closed, she's going to find another. Her artistic ability helps her father's work with the Underground Railroad, depicting maps as artwork. Even if it's supposed to be a secret, Sarah knows she is helping. 
 After her father's death, she is the only child to not give up on the cause or fall into despair. She grabs any educational opportunities possible and the attention of the son of a southern family that believes in their cause of abolishing slavery. 
 Back in the present, Eden would just as soon spend the day in bed. But her husband gives her a puppy, then leaves for business trips. He also enlist the help of the neighbor girl who is resilient and handy in ways Eden can only marvel at. Finding the head of an antique doll in the house and the arrival of Eden's musician brother add to the world not allowing her to pull the covers over her head. 
 Whether it's the onset of the Civil War and its hardships on families in the path of the battles or the ways in which a modern small town struggles to keep up with the times yet not lose its heart and soul, McCoy weaves the tales of Eden and Sarah into their times. But the times do not take over the women's stories. The focus remains on their hearts and how they are shaped by the ways they make families. 
 Although many novels currently use multiple storylines, McCoy shows how it should be done -- to serve a storytelling purpose that has great heart and uses great skill. The MapMaker's Children is a novel that is about love in various forms and how one creates a legacy by being true to oneself and what one holds dear. McCoy's research into Sarah Brown pays off well by bringing this artist and maternal figure back to vivid life.

In the current story, set in 2010, a young wife named Eden is struggling with her own infertility and the path her life is taking leads her to the mystery of the ancient doll head. Summary: 
 America Singer is chosen to be one of the Selected, a handful of teenage girls who will compete to win the affections of the crown prince and become his future Queen. America, whose "true love" is from a lower cast, has no interest in gaining the affections of the prince, but eventually the two start to become friends as the competition is narrowed down. 
 Review: 
 Not every book is for every reader, and that is probably why I put off reading this one. This was a book group pick so I felt obligated to read it. I know how popular this book is, but it never held much appeal for me--just not my thing. 
 Essentially this book is "The Bachelor" for teens. I think my biggest problem with the book is the predictability--it is all so cliche. Of course America doesn't want to be chosen to be the future queen, she has no interest in that. Of course the prince would be intrigued by American who just wants to be his friend. Of course they will begin to fall in love. Sorry, but there is nothing original here--it is very stereotypical. 
 Despite that teens love these books, and apparently quite a few adults do too (judging from the reactions of most of the members of my book group). I think the appeal is that the everyday girl gets the unattainable and then there is the happily ever after. Entertaining fluff, but that is sometimes what people want. I may pick up book two someday when I am looking for something light and entertaining, but that's for another day. 
 Overall: 
 Light and entertaining, but lacking depth. Perhaps the sequels will have more meat to them, but this didn't really hook me. It was okay, but it wasn't a favorite. Still, I might pick up book two someday should I feel the need for something light. 
 Cautions for Sensitive Readers: 
 Language: Mild--I don't remember anything graphic. 
 Violence: Some, though mostly off in another part of the palace from the narrator. 
 Sex: Some kissing and groping, but nothing explicit. She is informed that she must be a virgin to compete in the Selection and that the prince may ask anything of her. 
 Drugs/Alcohol: Some alcohol consumption.

Hi, I'm baack! And here's my first book finished in 2015. The first book in The Selection series which I finally start due to curiosity and I'm a sucker for long pretty dresses I could never wear nor own, not a good reason to start a book, but it's something. 
 Anyway, The Selection is about a selection, thirty-five girls competing to win the heart of seventeen year old Prince Maxon of Illea. The heroine, America Singer, is, yes, a singer. And here are a few things I thought of the book: 
 The start of the book is slow, I'm so close to give it up, but I held on and finished it. Entertaining read, yes, but it left me with a lot of unaswered questions. 
 Like, I still fail to see the need of a monarchy heir to marry a true daughter of the country, as it was put in the book, unless there was a written agreement to do as such or else the people will overthrow the crown. It seems like Illea is a weak, developing kingdom, unsettled in their international relation (past princesses sent off to marry foreigners) and also its own internal matters, I mean, weekly televised report? 
 And the rebel attacks. While, Maxon's theory on North and South rebels is interesting and I expect it to be explored more, I still wonder, how the rebels even get past the gate? I mean, this is the royal palace, the king and the royal family live there, the current king is not its first monarch, so I assume the palace has been around for a long time, and rebels get past the gate and into the property. HOW in the world? What are the guards doing? The rebels got in to their bedrooms, for god's sake. While the purpose might be to emphasis the danger and threats these rebels posses, that's plain ridiculous. I expect a much, much better security measure for a royal palace. Like, invest in a impenetrable wall as high as you can build, a strong, defendable gate, a new security head. It doesn't matter how many of them are, they should be well prepared. People like these rebels just can't be allowed to go waltz into a royal palace like it's a freaking open-for-all shopping mall. 
 And on the second attack, the king himself was also in the safe room along with the Selection ladies. Oh my God. And Maxon was also there. As the palace was attacked. Perhapts Kiera Cass was trying to be unconventional, the monarch's life is important, I know, but having him in that safety room looks even more ridiculous. (I thought the king, and the prince, would be out there leading the fight back? His kingdom needs a more than an administrative, doing-office-works king in its current state, it needs a king and heir who could also defend it in actual fights.) 
 And our dear girl America saw this situation as the king defending the palace like a ship captain. Then she just kind of remind me of Bella Swan. Average, but kind of okay, wanted by two men, uncertain whom she wanted to be with. (The start of The Elite has even got me disliking her character.) 
 Oh and the whole China invading USA and got labor instead... wait, China actually needs more labor force? Their population is much bigger than USA's, unless it declined drastically for some unknown reason, they don't need any more people to do anything for them. And the American State of China, what kind of a state was that? Is it like the Dutch East Indies? 
 What I'm trying to say is while the story idea is good, its base is not. For a universe to be believable, it needs a strong base for the whole thing to grow on. This lack of strong base might be due to America Singer's own lack of knowledge regarding her own country's history and current affair. But, still, when you dig deeper as reading the book, there is nothing much. 
 As I previously said, it's an enough entertaining read, but nothing more. I don't expect much as I begin reading, but even it still fell short of what I expect to find. 
 I'm not sure if I'll finish the second book, I'll give it a few more chapters.

No one told me this is "Hunger Games and Tiaras".

The Red Pyramid is about estranged siblings Carter and Sadie, two vastly different individuals brought together to fight for their father's safety. On their journey they run into many mythological creatures and Gods and Goddesses of Egypt, encounter magical artifacts, and learn profound things about each other. 
 Fun, fast-paced, and claiming to be based on fact - this beginning novel of what seems to be a new series by Rick Riordan will please fans of Percy Jackson and the Olympians. I would recommend this especially to kids and teens interested in Egyptian mythology or a book filled with action.
My review of the audiobook version

I loved the Percy Jackson series so I've been waiting for Riordan's latest offering impatiently. In his newest novel we meet a pair of siblings, Carter and Sadie Kane, descendants of the pharaohs and magicians just coming into their power. Carter and Sadie have grown up separately, unaware of their magical heritage or the fact that the ancient Egyptian Gods are alive, well and apparently being kept in check by a secret society of magic users. 
 In the beginning of the book there's a reference to the Gods living in Manhattan that had me smiling because it was a subtle reference to Riordan's Jackson series. There are similarities between this book and those, but I think it more closely mimics his 39 Clues Maze of Bones book. The story doesn't feel original and while it's a fun romp, filled with humor and an interesting writing style - for me it lacks the spark that the Jackson series had. I like the characters but I'm not as attached to them. I'm also not sure I like how continually the narrators, Carter & Sadie, break the 4th wall and directly address the reader. The call to action at the end of the book feels too much like a marketing gimmick and forced. Also, the ending was fairly predictable. I'll read the next book in the series but I don't think this set is going to go on my permanent book shelves. It's a fun read, but too easy to put down.

This was a beautifully written (and narrated) book. 
 I just love what Henriquez did with this book. She gave us two characters (Alma and Mayor) who allowed us great insight into the specific family lives of two hispanic families living in the US, while also providing glimpses of the many other lives and experiences of their neighbors. 
 I think it can be easy to group people who are different from us all into one group, assuming everyone in that "other" group has more similarities than differences. Henriquez showed that this is not at all the case. All brown skinned people do not come from Mexico, and have not had the same life experiences. One of the best moments in the book is a scene on Christmas, when the heat goes out and many of the apartment building's tenants gather together in the Rivera's apartment, discussing their various Christmas traditions, which are just as wide and varied as each of their backgrounds are. Sharing a language doesn't necessarily mean they all share the same culture and traditions, and that scene illustrated that so beautifully and with such a light touch. 
 I don't think that I am doing a good job of articulating what was so great about this book so far. But I will say that, aside from the obvious message Henriquez is sending about not judging a person by their skin color, she also writes a beautiful story about two families. Alma's constant worry about her family is touching and, I think, universal. She just wants a better life for her daughter, and for her husband to be happy and feel fulfilled. And I really loved the relationship between Mayor and Maribel. Even though Mayor was obviously attracted to Maribel, their relationship was so innocent and sweet, and I loved the way he cared about her, and how she slowly became a different person than she was when she first arrived in Delaware with her parents. What made both of these stories even more interesting is that Alma and Mayor, while both caring very deeply for Maribel, were at odds in terms of how to show that care. It made for an interesting conflict, where the reader could easily see where each of those characters was coming from, and yet be frustrated that they couldn't communicate those things to one another. 
 This is definitely worth a read, and one I'll be thinking about for awhile.
A noble goal, but man -- so simplistic. The characters were more like caricatures.
amazing story of the immigrant experience in u.s. heartfelt, real and exhilarating. heartbreaking, but hopeful.

Although this book hit some of my check boxes-- marginalized characters, POC author, heavy subject matter-- it was a quick read, and ultimately didn't feel substantial. Some of the super dramatic plot line was too predictable, and several of the characters didn't come off as more than charicatures.

The Book of Unknown Americans centres on the intertwining lives of immigrants living in the same apartment complex in Delaware. The immigrants are a mix of new arrivals to the US along with second generation citizens, those who arrived illegally and legally and whose countries of origin are all very different. 
 The overarching story is both tragic and sweet. It touches on a lot of themes such as poverty, racism, disabilities and forgiveness and each chapter is written from a different character's perspective. 
 I found the writing a bit too simplistic at times. The characters felt a bit one dimensional and I wonder if the need to represent certain types of stories and characters may have taken priority over fleshing out those stories and characters so that they felt real. 
 At the same time the story is a welcome reminder of the struggle that many immigrants have with things like missing their home country or being underestimated and misunderstood. Based on my knowledge of the American political landscape it seems like these kinds of stories definitely need to find a place in this genre of novel and among its target audience. 
 Overall, it's a pleasant enough book but I expected a bit more from it.

For some reason, Mirabel's realization that "school french fries suck!" was the moment when I knew The Book of Unknown Americans would twist my heart in a million different directions. Henriquez handles big disclosures and plot twists with subtle beauty, and she unfolds the worlds of her "unknown Americans" in powerful ways so that each character seems fully realized.

This won the Pulitzer fiction prize last year and comes with four pages of dazzling reviews. Sorry to say, it did not dazzle me. It's very weird, a series of episodic chapters centred around a New York record producer and one of his artists, their families, friends, lovers and kids. All these lives, hedonistic and self-absorbed, criss-cross over several decades. One chapter, supposedly by a child, is laid out like a PowerPoint presentation. A VISIT FROM THE GOON SQUAD seems to be the literary equivalent of Installation Art: Hirst's pickled sharks or Tracey Emin's famous unmade bed. 
 I'm very resistant to experimental writing unless it's broadly linear in construction like, say, Catch 22 or The Ginger Man. A couple of Jennifer Egan's characters have the off-the-wall appeal of Salinger's FRANNY AND ZOOEY. There's a wickedly funny chapter when a PR lady stages a photo-op with a blonde bimbo filmstar for a South American dictator with image problems similar to Qaddafi's; and a chapter involving a teenage runaway in Naples has some pleasing moments. Egan writes crisply and economically (bearable at 350 pages, 700 would be torture!), but overall this disconnected kaleidoscope seems to me another egregious example of that recurring cultural phenomenon: The Emperor's New Clothes. In literature it probably started with Virginia Woolf and, yes, I am afraid of her!

This is not an inner-monologue any man in the history of the world has ever had. 
 Fortunately, Egan front-loaded the 2 worst chapters. As the story progresses, she manages to create a fascinating world full of interrelated characters that only occasionally feels overwrought. It is definitely not the work of a master satirist, as the jacket copy implies ... but it is a well-written, engaging novel that offers plenty of surprises and a lot of memorable moments.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I wasn't too impressed with how the characters or plot developed in this story. The dialogue and descriptions were quite wooden, and I didn't feel that I entered Blanche's mind at any point, even though it was from her perspective. While the plot was exciting on paper, in practice it was very formulaic. I also didn't experience the setting very much at all--and it would have been an intense setting! 
 And a small critique: the audiobook narrator's singing voice irked me.

Siiiiigh. I tried. Alas, Frog Music is too often clunky, repetitive, and contradictory. And also waaaaaay too long. Someone's editor was asleep on this job. I liked Blanche, but she is a bit stupid, and it's painful to read her thought process as she tries to figure out the "mystery" of who killed Jenny. Most of the supporting cast of characters are irritating, and even Jenny eventually had me rolling my eyes despite having liked her at first. What is nice about Frog Music is Donoghue's descriptions of historical San Francisco, but it isn't enough to carry the novel. Go elsewhere for your historical fiction this summer.

Frog Music is the new gold standard for historical fiction. Donoghue takes a real incident for San Francisco's early history, researches the heck out of it, then turns to fiction to fill in the blanks and make the characters leap off the page. This is just a fascinating story very well told.

I have an hour or so left on the audiobook- This is barely a 3 star book for me. If it weren't for Donoghue's obvious talent as a writer and the research she did it would be less. I agree with a lot of the negative reviews on Goodreads, although the jumping between time periods was not as much a source of contention for me as others (although I did find that she overused that device at times). I also do not find Blanche to be as unsympathetic or irritating as other authors. But I am seriously over listening to her interior monologue. Also Jenny is kind of a knock off Idgie Threadgoode, just saying. I think this book would have probably been better if it were significantly shorter.

As a San Franciscan & local history buff, I had high hopes for this book. It's set in & around the city--mostly Chinatown & the Barbary Coast--in the 1870s. Impressive research has gone into it, but not much heart. 
 The book starts with French songs & a bloody murder in a remote outpost, then jumps back in time while it continues forward, a double timeline which makes the fairly simple plot harder to follow. I enjoyed the afterword, re the real events & people fictionalized here, more than the book. 
 My biggest frustration was finding so little to like or admire in any of the characters, or the setting. Emma Donoghue (who apparently hasn't spent much time here) depicts early San Francisco as unrelievedly grim & grubby; only in 1 or 2 scenes do we glimpse its vital & delightful spheres. That's partly because the real events that inspired the book took place during a heat wave & a smallpox epidemic, & the characters are mostly poor. Everybody hates, suspects, &/or resents everybody else (usually for good reason). Still, we do occasionally catch sight of people enjoying themselves offstage; we just never see enjoyment, except when someone's getting his or her rocks off with Blanche, the prostitute main character. 
 There is a lot of singing, = song lyrics, mostly unfamiliar (often French) songs of the period, which helps slow the pace. 
 I was about to quit reading this exceptionally depressing book when I realized I only had a few pages to go.

3.5 stars. This book was not at all what I expected, but that isn't necessarily a bad thing. I thought the writing was beautiful and such an interesting setting. I had a few issues with characterization, just some things I felt were contrived, or "off". That being said, a wonderful historical fiction piece with beautiful prose.

After reading Room, I was intrigued to dive into this one. It definitely has a different feel from the aforementioned book. I guess this is more in tune with Emma Donoghue's works, since apparently she writes a lot of historical fictions in the past as well. Somehow, at first, I got the impression that this was a children-friendly book or even something that has anything to do with children at all. Boy, was I wrong. It showed the dreary and glum parts of the late 19th century San Francisco. The way the story was told in a back and forth of flashbacks, it became a bit confusing at first. I swear I couldn't quite get what happened in the first chapter, except that Jenny was already dead. The way the city was described made me think of 1870s San Francisco to be quite downtrodden, dirty and decrepit. I love how Emma matches old folk songs with the theme of the chapter, relating it to the current storyline, and how much research went into creating this story, making it have way more depths in its symbolism. Although Blanche isn't a favourite character of mine, to be honest, and it made the book less enjoyable to read. Lastly, I love how the story was also a little bit about feminism even though it was set way back when, surrounded by prejudice and societal dysfunction.
I'm on a bad streak of reading books I really don't like. I did enjoy the San Francisco setting and the last chapter was written well, but otherwise blehhhhh. I recommend skipping this one.

 Y la moraleja es: 
 Que aunque no me gusto la historia original esta me encanto jajaja nonsense ^-^ 
 OFF WITH HIS HEAD

I really liked this...and I have to add at least an extra half-star for the fact that it's a stand alone. 
 This is...not exactly a retelling. It's more of a Gregory Maguire-style prequel. And Meyer actually credits Maguire as her inspiration in the author's note -- which, sidebar, I love when authors do. I think Meyer and Maguire could actually combine forces for the perfect prequel. I loved Wicked the first time I read it, but it didn't exactly hold up to rereadings. The setting is amazing, but the characters are kind of flat. Here, the characters are great, but the setting, while more fully realized than the Lunar chronicles, is still sort of just...there. I had sort of a vague image of the cartoon in my head, but she could use a dash of Maguire's flair for setting (and he could use a whole heap of her flair for character!). 
 Anyway, this is the story of the Queen of Hearts before she was all obsessed with beheading. When she was just Lady Catherine Pinkerton, all she wanted to do was open a bakery with her best friend. Romance wasn't even on her mind, especially since the only person interested is the ridiculous King of Hearts. I like that Cath is an independent, career-minded lady, but of course that all goes out the window the moment she lays eyes on the King's new court Joker, Jest. On the one hand it's a typical annoying case of insta-love, but I'm almost willing to chalk it up to small-town syndrome (which is a condition I just made up). You know, when you've lived in the same small town, with the same group of people, for your entire life and then suddenly this ~*~new~*~ person arrives, all shiny and unfamiliar! It's hard NOT to immediately be drawn to them, for no other reason than the fact that they're different. Still an overused trope though! 
 There's another "queen of hearts" series floating around out there -- I think it was either self-published, or just some kind of ebook independent published, and then got picked up by a major publishing house? Either way, the first two books were out there, and the 3rd was imminent...and then they all just disappeared. I follow the author, and apparently the whole series is being repackaged and re-released in sequence, so the 3rd book is supposed to come out sometime around 2018. I really liked the first book of that series (I think it's called The Crown), but the second book went off the rails a bit. So far, it's implied that the reason the Queen of Hearts became a villain is because she was rejected by a boy. Barf. Be a badass lady in your own right, but don't make your badass lady a bitter old crone with no heart. I was concerned that Meyer was going to go that route here too, but thankfully she saves it. Also this is NOT a series starter! Which is good because even as it is, this book could stand to be a little shorter. 
 Anyway, Cath and Jest fall in love, and she dreams of opening her own bakery, and her mother is basically every terrible Victorian mother who only cares about her daughter getting married (and the fact that she has the attention of the king is even better). But like so many spunky girls who came before, Cath wants to live her own life. I feel like this sounds dismissive -- it's not! I actually really liked Cath - spunky, insta-love and all. And her descent into villainy is well done. It's not because Jest leaves her...although he does reveal that he's part of a plot to steal her heart to end the war in Chess between the Red and White Queens (sidebar: why is there a Red Queen AND a Queen of Hearts? If they're in the land of Chess, why isn't it the Black Queen and the White Queen?). But he really does love her! (Meh) Anyway, there's a whole thing with pumpkins and the Jabberwocky and basically the pumpkins were cursed, the farmer's wife ate them and became a monster, but he still loves her because it's his wife, so when Cath and co try to kill the monster, he kills Jest. Which turns Cath into a scary revenge monster. Then she makes a deal with these three wraiths who live in a well that they can have her heart in exchange for...something (still not clear on that. Were they giving it to Chess? Or just using it for themselves?). So they take her heart and then she makes with the chopping, and the book ends with those familiar words: "Off with his head." 
 I really liked what Meyer did with all of the characters -- we see, not modified, but younger versions of the Mad Hatter, the White Rabbit, the Cheshire Cat, and more that I'm probably ignoring. I'll admit that I was never much of a fan of the original story -- I've seen the Disney movie (or maybe just the parts of it that were on those old school Disney Sing-Along videos...), and I think I read bits and pieces of the story at some point. But it's just never appealed to me. And also Lewis Carroll is kind of a big creep. But you don't have to be super-familiar with the original in order for this to make sense. Of course I'm sure there were references that I missed, but I thought Meyer's version was clever. I also loved the Poe-esque Raven who accompanies Jest everywhere. He speaks in rhymes, mostly lifted from Poe's poem. And that has always been one of my favorites. 
 This isn't a happy story, but you also kind of know that going in -- the ending has been predetermined. But it is, for the most part, a fun story, whether you like the original or not.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I. Should. Have. Known! You know how sometimes you pick up a book knowing it's a retelling, but you want to think its a retelling that twists the ending to be a "happily ever after"? That was my hope for this book. As a kid I had an extreme dislike for the Queen of Hearts, and while reading this I just knew there was absolutely no way Cath could ever be that horrid creature from Alice In Wonderland. No. Way. Marissa Meyer has a knack for taking things that have me going "there is just no way" and turning it so I'm saying that same phrase with a bit of awe in my voice. Because there is. And she always finds it. 
 Catherine {or Cath} is the daughter of one of the upperclass titled families, the only daughter of a Marquess and his wife. She is full of life and joy, loving to pour her heart and time into baking, dreaming of a day when her and her lady's maid. Her desire, passion and just joy made me look at her and say "there is just no way she's going to be the angry Queen of Hearts. No way." Oh, I should have known. 
 The secondary characters bring out so many different aspects of Cath, and, one by one, we see how each could bloom or shatter. Maryanne, Jest, The King, and even Hatta bring out the different sides to Cath - friend, lover, subject, and ruler {sorry if I'm spelling anything wrong, I listened to the audiobook}. I don't want to say too much, because it really could give the book away, but its amazing what actually happens - what Cath actively does and what she stands back and allows to happen. 
 Meyer takes this story and makes it so beautifully her own, but it's also apparant what inspired this story. Much like her Lunar Chronicles, Meyer doesn't really re-tell the story, but takes elements from it and makes it her own unique masterpiece. Any time I thought it was going to turn more towards the most recent Alice in Wonderland live-action film {you know, the one with Johnny Depp} or a little like the classic Disney film {honestly, one of my least favorite films}, it never did. 
 This book gave me a serious book hangover. When I finished I just couldn't gather the words to describe the feeling, over than heartbroken. This left me shattered and unable to really say anything other than "I should have known!!" My husband nonchalantly said that to me as well when he was wondering why I should have known what was going to happen. And, guys, I really should have known. I should have. But I still can't believe it. 
 Original thoughts: 
 Ugh. Okay, I think this is going to seriously give me a book hangover. It filled my heart to overflowing, then crushed it beneath the weight of a might white rose tree... I just can't...
The Marissa Meyer/Rebecca Soler combination is just as great here as it was in the Lunar Chronicles. I couldn't stop listening.

Fantastic! I wasn't even too sure I wanted to read this because I was never a big fan of Alice in Wonderland, but the voice acting in this is incredible! And it is acting, not just reading.  It kind of lost steam for me like 75% through. It was just a bit too long if you ask me.

The story was clever, very cheesy :/, but still fun and Wonderland-esc, although Cath was a bit stupid at times. Like the Peter Peter poem... she really didn't catch that the first time??? Come on. However, I enjoyed reading it, but definitely think it was geared towards a younger audience. I don't understand why some readers say they cried at the end. But then again, maybe I'm just as Heartless. ;)

** spoiler alert ** 
 I love Ruth Reichl's memoirs, but this book was complete miss for me. The protagonist was the worst kind of author surrogate Mary Sue; her only flaw being that she found herself too flawed. 
 Billy (Wilhelmina) has a tragic, undisclosed past! She has a perfect, remarkable palate, but also has panic attacks when she steps into the kitchen! She's awkward, plain, and untalented, but everyone who meets her loves her and wants to be her friend! She wants to be a writer, but has no ideas about what to write, except for the one thing she can't write about, and finds it unbelievable that her magazine editor boss would be put out with her about this! Why can't he just UNDERSTAND?! Midway through the book, after she undergoes a glasses to contacts transformation, turns out she is beautiful, and a fashion prodigy to boot! Then her tragic past is revealed - her beloved sister, who she found perfect at everything but no one else thought that much of, died in a tragic cake delivery accident! This is her fault! But wait, no, her sister was on drugs! It was no one's fault! 
 The book took way too long to get to the story within the story, the tale of Lulu, a girl in World War II who carried on a correspondence with James Beard. I found myself wishing we could we could just have Lulu's story, free of Billy's nonsense and the love story to New York and food. 
 Don't get me wrong, I understand the deep and abiding love you can have for a place, and for the food and people that populate it, and I have read a number of love stories to cities and food. But the tone, and the annoying protagonist, completely ruined this one for me.
Like a piece of Billie's gingerbread this delightful, beautiful, tasty, and delicious book was perfect and unforgettable.
I love Ruth Reichl's nonfiction, but this attempt at a novel was so juvenile and poorly written that I couldn't make it past the second chapter.

 Reaching the second half of the book, I realized how similar it is to Somerset Maugham's "The Painted Veil". A marriage of convenience. A young couple living in an far, exotic land. The husband is a physician/researcher. The wife is beautiful and bored. She is involved in marital infidelity (though the degree of involvement differ greatly). The husband realizes this and reacts. And colorful descriptions of the land and the people. 
 These similarities, once realized, are discouraging for this book lacks the intensity of the Painted Veil. The tone is also flavorless and flat. Never have I read a book taking Africa as its backdrop yet missing all the passion, intrigue, and magic of the Dark Continent. 
 Margaret is a confusing character. Childish is the word that come to mind. But I have nothing but respect and admiration for Patrick. He is a man on a mission. reference_books.title: The Racketeer
reference_books.review_text:
In many ways, it feels as if this is a first draft of a novel. 
 Many elements from previous novels such as The Partner and The Broker can be detected in The Racketeer. Outsmarting the government, orchestrating a complicated and intricate plan, having a lady to help the protagonist in executing it, and many other similarities bind Grisham's novels. And don't forget the necessary addition of a South American country or a Caribbean island. 
 This novel, however, is the one I hated the most. although I hated The Appeal and The Associate before it, but this one takes the prize because it has the potential to be a great novel but it was ruined by the dispiriting lack of emotions and the the overly enigmatic chain of events. 
 Spoiler Alert: 
 I think it should have been divided into two parts within the same book while keeping the time frame. The first part is about getting out of prison and in the Witness Protection Program and the second part is about after the escape. 
 This novel lacks a great deal of significant emotions that it feels like I am reading a report; so many names of places or dates and tracking of movement and travel! I think that Grisham's intent was to keep us at the edge of our seats, but there comes a point when i was so frustrated that I wanted to jump to the last page. I wanted to sympathize with Malcolm in prison. I wanted to be glad that he got a ticket out of it. I wanted to be angry because the FBI failed in protecting him. But I felt none of that because Grisham didn't bother in communicating those to me. 
 Grisham's writing is usually devoid of emotions and descriptions and stuff (which I love), but here, it was really annoying. 
 *If this is all planned from the beginning, why did not Malcolm reunite with Vanessa earlier? Is it that he wanted the FBI off his back first? 
 *I believe that no matter how honorable and decent a government agency is, it wouldn't let some one fool them like this without any repercussions! The deputy director even begged him not to speak to a reporter!! 
 *Malcolm got out of prison, and got a literal pot of gold, yet never made an attempt to contact his family? Not even his son? 
 At first, i thought that he wouldn't contact them because he was afraid of the drug gang. But now we now that is bogus, so what the hell!! 
 I truly love Grisham and think he is brilliant, but this novel... is not

book_a.title: Gray Mountain
book_a.user_review:
** spoiler alert ** 
 So disappointing. 
 Let's first start with Samantha. She is honestly no one special. All Grisham's previous characters are distinguished in one way or another. Big shot lawyers or brilliant novices. But Samantha is neither. And this fact doesn't help me as a reader in engaging in the narrative. She hasn't "grown" along with the story. The old Samantha who lost her job and ran to her parents is the same new Samantha who ran to her parents when things got heated. Even professionally, I don't think winning the Booker case is her win. The judge practically did all the work. Although I realize that not all cases need to have a big day of litigation and testimonies in court. But still. 
 People keep telling her how brilliant and brave she is, that she is the best lawyer. But I kept thinking: why? She barely did anything. Donovan trusted her and told her confidential information. Again, why? 
 Grisham has a way in presenting the theme in every novel in a way that makes you feel that you are reading a report written by a journalist, and frankly this is the boring bits in his novels. The thrill of the espionage and the court drama are what make these "non-fictional" bits somehow tolerable. Not in this novel, though. Long-winded passages about coal mining and the evil companies. It's almost mind-numbing. 
 And how stupid is she for leaving the cabin towards the fucking gunshots in the dark in an unmarked trail, instead of locking herself inside with a gun glued to her hand like a normal person?!!!! 
 I suspected that she was a corporate spy sent by her father on behalf of the coal companies to infiltrate Donovan's team and find out what dirt he has on them. And maybe that they killed him without her knowledge and things got outta hand. Wouldn't that be cool? I realize that would mean making the protagonist a bad person, but why not? It's a great twist. 
 I guess I had a hunch that the novel would be disappointing when I learned that the hero is a she. It reminded me of The Pelican Brief. It just feels that Grisham doesn't know how to write from a female perspective.

sample_reviews.review_text: There were some really good parts to this story but a lot of so-so parts. I'm a little disappointed in it because I usually LOVE Grisham books. I feel like after all of the length of the story, the ending was a little abrupt. I'm just super torn on my feelings about the book. However, read it for yourself. You may enjoy it more than I did

Preachy. His agenda was hammered too much and got in the way of the story, instead of using the story to advance his agenda. Not so crazy about books that purport to be fiction but seem more like propaganda. I am concerned about the environment and what goes on in West Virginia is astonishing, but make the point within the story.
One of Grisham's worst. Boring plot, no investment in character development.

Samantha is working a dream job in a large firm in New York....suddenly she is booted due to the financial world. She accepts a challenge from the firm to volunteer for a year in a legal aid clinic. She chooses a clinic in the Appalachian mountains - discovers the world of BIG coal companies and the injustices suffered by their workers. Good story but felt the ending was very lacking.

With the financial crisis of 2008, Samantha Kofer gets downsized. However, she is given the chance to return to her Wall Street Firm after working for a non profit. 
 Her company had a list of companies to choose from and Samantha decides to work for the Mountain Legal Aid Clinic, in Brady, Va. 
 The type of cases that go through her office is made up of miners who have lost their jobs due to black lung disease and their company refusing their compensation demands. She also works on creating wills and with a woman who was dismissed from her job illegally. 
 The people in Appalachia are definitely a group that would create sympathy but Samantha seems to be just fulfilling the requirement before she can return to New York and a high income salary. I didn't feel that she was emotionally involved with her clients. 
 She does meet another attorney who has taken the minor's plight to heart but she doesn't commit to help in the long run. She returns to New York to speak about her old job and speaks to her father in trying to decide her future but I didn't feel an empathy for her or that she had the guts to help those desperately in need. 
 There were many greedy characters in the book, from debt collectors, to coal mine companies or to FBI agents under the influence of the coal mine companies themselves. 
 The best part of the novel was the description of what strip mining does to the community, to the natural landscape and to the will to live of some of the depressed former miners. 
 I'm a fan of Grisham's writing but I expected more from this story.

I was a big Grisham fan back in his Pelican Brief days, but somewhere along the line I fell away. So when I saw Gray Mountain on the shelf I thought it was a easy win. 
 Not so much. I don't know if my tastes have changed, or if Mr. Grisham's writing has, but this book was a significant disappointment. 
 Gone were the gripping drama, the complex legal conundrums, even the compelling characters. In their place we get treated to a book-length screed against the evils of coal mining, told by a set of characters that are barely sketched out. The most fully developed character, the protagonist, is notable for her inability to cope with her own life and her complete dependence on circumstances to set her course and direction. I found little to appreciate in her. 
 Not at all a work up to Mr. Grisham's early glory days. Such a disappointment.
I liked it and hope Samantha will be back in another book.

Audiobook Review 
 2 1/2 Stars 
 John Grisham, I am sorely disappointed. A book about a female character, Samantha Kofer, a spoiled NYC 'climber' in corporate law, daughter of a disbarred wheeler-dealer dad and a DOJ attorney mom, who is unceremoniously dumped by her company in the 2008 hysteria. She can keep her health benefits if she does an unpaid intern gig at a non-profit. She ends up in Brady, Virginia, at a free legal clinic that provides a plethora of services to the many poor of the small community. But there are cases that involve Big Coal and their victims. And then there's a guy. And murders. And conspiracies. And more spectacular murders. 
 Grisham plays readers by pulling at every emotional string he can find: 
 -- people decimated by poverty, domestic violence, and family dysfunction 
 -- small town lawyers fighting the honorable and sometimes dishonorable fight against wrong 
 -- love interests 
 -- the protagonist's longing for a return to NYC and civilization 
 -- big Coal's abuse of power and rape of the environment 
 -- fear 
 -- murder 
 -- conspiracy 
 There is no one big case that gets followed start to finish. There are a few biggies, but they are not resolved. 
 I did not like 'Samantha' from the beginning. She's a whiny 29 year old brat who thinks the world owes her. Even after her experiences in rural VA, she's still a whiny brat and an unlikeable protagonist. I'm not sure what Grisham was trying to do, other than writing something that is a deviation from the 'one big law case' while featuring a female protagonist, but it didn't work. 
 In audio, Catherine Taber is a whiny narrator, so she probably matches the lead character very well. It was absolute torture listening to her for 15 hours. 
 There was a story to be told here. In fact, there were many. But Grisham did the greatest disservice to the victims of the Coal Industry by using them as pawns in a disjointed, poorly executed work.

The most bizarre book from John Grisham I've ever read. It was preachy about the coal industry and I kept wondering when the in court room legal battles would begin. Instead, the entire time we followed a whiney young lawyer around with no real action. Very disappointed.

"The horror was in the waiting--the unknown, the insomnia, the ulcers." 
 It is September 2008. Ten days after the fall of Lehman Brothers. 
 Samantha Kofer is a privileged 29-year-old midlevel associate at a huge New York City law firm, where she puts in 100+ hours of work per week doing the legal grunt work necessary to be made partner by age 35. However, her plans come to a grinding halt when the US economy takes the plunge, and Big Law firms-- including Samantha's--begin to purge themselves of their associates. 
 Samantha, newly furloughed, agrees to intern for one year without pay for a nonprofit organization in an impoverished Virginia town in order to (a) hold on to her health care and (b) possibly get her job back in the event that the economic climate rebounds. Samantha's work at the Mountain Legal Aid Clinic goes from helping a woman in desperate need of separation from an abusive, crystal meth-dealing husband to engaging in a lackluster war with Big Coal. 
 The fight against strip mining, a coal extraction tactic which causes black lung disease in miners, echoes the timely political battles common to Grisham's canon. However, Grisham's messages frequently consume his stories, and unfortunately this is no exception. The message should always be secondary. Plot and character must come first, otherwise both suffer. For long stretches of the story, the issue of Big Coal upstages the character of Big Coal, which renders the novel preachy and demotes it to a soapbox. 
 Another problem with the novel is the "heroine" Samantha Kofer, who is boring and ambivalent, two contemptible qualities for a hero. Samantha does nothing noble or notable early on to persuade readers to admire and follow her. She simply goes from leading a posh, entitled life to...not. Grisham assumes that readers will automatically sympathize with her and agree to go along for the ride no questions asked. And she hardly develops as the story unfolds, more or less remaining the same from start to end. 
 All in all, Gray Mountain is an unremarkable novel. With an uninteresting protagonist and a muddled story, this Grisham novel is one that I would not recommend.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Book review: 
 Overall, I'm a little confused. Part of this is because I'm trying to listen to it at work, and surprisingly enough, work does occasionally require my brain to focus, and I'm missing stuff. But I think mostly it's because there's no real coherent storyline. There's sort of an "ultimate goal" looming in the background, but mostly Mac and Jericho are just getting themselves into little (or big) messes and then trying to get out of them again. I'm not sure they've made any progress toward their main goal at all. I'm not quite sure what the plot of this book was. However, it's an entertaining ride, if only because the tension between Mac and Jericho is thick and I really want to know what his deal is. 
 And I'll just warn you, there's lots of "Ewwww!" in this book. Lots. 
 And there's also some sizzle. (One scene in particular sticks out in my mind... Whew!) But I'm ready to flick Mac in the nose and yell, "Uh, hello, moron! Jericho Barrons is completely ape-shit crazy about you. Wake up." And he could not possibly be any more jealous of V'lane... 
 Also, Mac seems to wax maybe a bit too poetic at times. I'm not reading this series for any deep revelations about life, Karen. It's an adventure story. I'm all about character growth, believe me. But there were definitely some parts that rambled on too long and made me roll my eyes. 
 Audiobook review: 
 As far as the problems with the reader that I had with the first book (namely horrible accents), it came and went. Sometimes it bugged me a lot but most of the time I was able to think past it and it was okay. I think she may have toned it down a little.

 I would say that this book series is the perfect example of an author and a publisher trying to drag out a series. This was the s-l-o-w-e-s-t progressing story that I have ever read. I cannot fathom sitting through anymore of these books.

I liked this one much more than I liked the first installment in the series. It's still more like a 2.5 for me but definitely fun and different.

Originally read in November 2012 
 Re-read in January 2015 
 Original rating of 3 stars revised to 4 stars. 
 Review below was written after my re-read: 
 So in this book the search for the Sinsar Dubh continues, the Lord Master is continuing his dastardly plan to bring down the wall, and his minion Malluce is still out to get Mac. 
 Mac gets darker in this book, and Barrons is so badass. He always seems to be appearing out of nowhere, voice preceding him. He's still his unreadable self, but you do get hints of possessiveness/jealousy from him when Mac interacts with others like Derek O'Bannion and Christian MacKelter. Ahh he's so snarky. It's great. 
 For those trying to remember what happened in this book: 
 The major event in this book is when Mac gets kidnapped by Malluce. He convinces her that Barrons won't be there to save her, so she gives up hope and incites him into beating and breaking her so badly that she almost dies (she wants to die). sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 Everything comes down to this and KMM made this so epic, so unbelievably good that I knew I had to take my time reading this. I don't think I've spent so much time with a book in my life. Knowing that this was the end, I wanted to savour every word on each page and I still don't think it's enough in the end! I NEED more Fever! 
 MacKayla Lane is one of my favourites UF heroines! Her narration is so unique and distinctly hers that I find any other changes in the POV to be annoying (No offence, Dani). I just get so into Mac's head that reading from another POV throws me off. I adore her courage and her resiliency. Despite the fact that who she thought she was in the past was all wrong, she still stays true to herself in the most important ways. And I couldn't ask for more in a heroine. Mac kicks ass! 
 Barrons, you infuriating man! Sometimes I just want to maul him for being so incredibly secretive, but then later I always find myself giving in and loving him despite his mysterious ways. His beast explains his animal magnetism and makes him that much more irresistible. How Mac can keep her hands off him is a mystery to me! And his secret? I didn't see that coming AT ALL. It's no wonder he kept it all under wraps this entire time! 
 And my girl Dani! I fecking lost it when I found out that she was Alina's murderer! What the hell. A murderer. At thirteen. 
 All because of that stupid bitch, Rowena. I've always hated this old hag. Manipulating Dani was the last straw for me. Die, bitch Die! What KMM does is crazy! You think Mac is talking to Isla, her "MOTHER" but no, she's Ro - ha! Gotcha! It's the Sinsar Dubh! My head is still reeling from all this. I couldn't possibly understand this world even if I wanted to. 
 Then all this time I hated LM for all the shit that he caused. For Mac's rape, for supposedly killing Alina. But he really did love Alina, didn't he? That was another thing I loved about this book. There was heart and hope even through all the dark times. Mac's grief in the beginning is enough to bring on the tears. 
 Then there's V'lane /Cruce - *rubs temples* 
 And Christian - I wouldn't be surprised if we see him again in the new series. Please let it be about him! PLEASE! Lots of unanswered questions with him... 
 But most of all, the Fever world is what captivated me from the beginning. So intensely mysterious and alluring, I found myself mesmerized by KMM's worldbuilding. I would say I'd love to live in this world, but I really don't. I'm way too chickenshit to live a second in Mac's shoes. 
 Nevertheless, I'm saddened to have Mac's journey end...for now. But I will definitely be picking up this series again and again! 
 STAY TO THE LIGHTS!

I DIEDDDDDDDDD a little bit reading this book. COULD NOT put it down!!!!! SO MANY EMOTIONS!!!! SO MUCH....STUFF!!!! JUST SO MUCH...AHHHHHHHHHH I COULD NOT HANDLE IT ALL!!!!!!! So anyways...I LOVE Mac and Barrons. The wrenches that KMM puts in their way just MAKES ME LOVE THEM MORE!!!!!! This book had a beautiful beginning, middle, and end, and all parts in between. I loved Mac and Barrons from the VERY beginning and I will now patiently for their story to continue. I know it's not over, that would be TOO EASY!!!! I took my time in reviewing Shadowfever. I wanted to be certain that I wouldn't regret my words upon further reflection. Afterall, I had devoured the previous books in this series and I couldn't give the final installment a low rating lightly. Truth be told, I devoured Shadowfever in the same manner that I speed through its predecessors. The only difference is that I enjoyed my time spent with the others. Books 1-4 gave me the fever, and book 5 simply burnt me up. 
 Here's the crux of the matter. I try not to be a hypocrite when I review books. If I dock one book for containing certain written faux paus, I'm going to dock others for it. There are exceptions to the rule for sure, but I also usually preface my review by saying as much. You see, this isn't the first series that enthralled me and let me down at the final hour. Breaking Dawn anyone? I'm not ashamed to admit I was a twi-hard until all things went astray in the final installment. I even still enjoy books 1-3. But I have no love for the final book. Why? Because it was illogical and seemed to be thrown together at the last minute, yet it was so freakin long. I still scratch my head at that one. None of the events or clues that I thought would be important amounted to anything in the end. It was underwhelming. The characters stagnated, some reverted to all new lows, and that hefting bow crushed my heart. So what does any of this have to do with Shadowfever? 
 *Spoilers ahead* 
 *Seriously, there will be spoilers* 
 The plotting was bullshit. It went on and on and on and felt like an altogether different series. I read nearly a hundred pages about a white mansion that was never mentioned prior to this book. Why? The only reason I can think of was that Moning needed a way to mention that Mac had dreamed of previously mentioned mansion since her childhood, so that Moning could somehow tie Mac to the Unseelie King and to also inform us that Mac had thought she was bi-polar most of her life because she had homicidal urges. Um, where did that come from? That might have been something to mention in book one, only I think it took Moning five books to think of it. I wanted this book to answer my burning questions, and I did get them, sort of. I wanted to know what Mac was, how she got her powers, where she came from. And I got those answers, they just came straight from crazy town. She's human, but has super powers because the book possessed her pregnant mother and uploaded its evil into fetus Mac. *pauses for a moment of silence*. How is that any better than demon spawn from Breaking Dawn? More questions that I wanted answers for included the identity of Alina's killer. Guess who, Dani. WTF? Dani? Really? Why did her character have to get chucked under a bus? I wanted to know what Barrons was, and sadly, I still don't have an answer for that. But mostly, I wanted to know who the Unseelie King was and I wanted the book to be stopped. I'll admit, Moning did a great job with the King's hidden identity, she even throws in an additional wrench that was truly top notch, but neither of those things could trump the stupidity of that wretched book. All I'm going to say is that at some point, Mac gets whisked away to outer space along with the Unseelie King and one other in order to talk about the pending epic battle. Yes you read that right, outer space and talking about an epic battle. Nothing epic ever actually happens. Just as nothing epic actually happened in Breaking Dawn. And guess what, we readers also getting a nice big bow tied to the end as no one important dies, nor are any fan favorite relationships ruined and cruxes of all cruxes, there is even a demon child. 
 So, imo Shadowfever was a big honking let down. I expected more from Moning.

So I finally finished reading it...I had been taking my time and savoring...phooey! I loved it of course...but I had to say I was expecting a much bigger BANG to the whole thing. I don't know why? Maybe I was expecting to much...but I still loved it! There were lots of shocking moments when secrets started to come out. I almost felt saddened when I found out that some of my favorite characters were not what they seemed. All in all though, it was another great book by Ms. Moning. 
 Now I'm moving on to her Highlander series. I've read one or two in the series but plan on starting it from the beginning because I LOVE me some Highlanders
By far, the most amazing book of the series! I read it twice because I was so sad to see it end! I hope KMM writes more about Mac & Barrons...fantastic series!

reference_books.title: A Monster Calls
reference_books.review_text:
This was a simple, beautiful tale that managed to capture an enormous spectrum of feeling in a very small number of words. I can honestly say that I have never faced anything as harrowing as what Conor faced, and for that I know how tremendously blessed I am. What astonished me most about this book was how well Mr. Ness seems to have stepped into the mindset of a teenager beset by more problems than anyone should ever have to face at such a young age and relay the emotions of that teenager perfectly. This entire story felt true, and this is exceptional in a world where some writers feel the need to twist events or characters to get to a certain place they expect the story to be. More than anything, I think that word describes this book: truth. And given what Mr. Ness was trying to accomplish, I have to imagine that to be high praise indeed. 
 I enjoyed that it was difficult to understand where the monster's tales were going until close to the end. Without spoiling at all, I felt the moral behind them, or perhaps the reason for them, was both complex and fitting. I also appreciated in circumstances such as these that there was no easy ending, but just a resolution. 
 A word on the illustrations: the book is replete with them, and they always seem to work in perfect concert with the book's message. In the proper context words and pictures can convey an emotion effectively, and in this book each are excellent at this.

reference_books.title: Case Histories (Jackson Brodie #1)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 This book was a fine escape, and I felt the character development was excellent. Particularly the characters of Jackson and Amelia I felt were well fleshed out, and I truly cared about what happened to them. I think the moment I realized that Atkinson had made a likable character in Jackson was when he found out his 8-year old daughter was being moved to New Zealand; I distinctly remember being angry for Jackson at the seeming callousness of his ex-wife. 
 With that said, the plot could have used a bit of work in my opinion. In none of the three cases did Jackson really do all that much to solve the crime. In Olivia's case, he essentially did what should have been done 34 years earlier: interview the family and push when he had to. Now clearly the discovery of Blue Mouse (Olivia's stuffed animal) changed the equation from when the case was investigated earlier, but Jackson didn't have to do much to find out what happened to Olivia. Similarly, in Laura's case, all he did was interview a friend of Laura's, which led him to another interview, followed by another until there you have it, the killer. And in Caroline/Michelle/Shirley/Tanya's case, he did absolutely nothing. I understand that this book was not intended to be simply another mystery novel, and I can certainly appreciate that, but a little more, ahem, mystery would have been excellent. 
 But this book was quite enjoyable merely because of the characters. The dynamic between Julia and Amelia was captured perfectly, and the "dance" between Jackson and Julia was interesting as well. For a book that I more or less just picked up on the fly, I was happy to have lost myself in it for a few weeks.

reference_books.title: Black Hole
reference_books.review_text:
This is a graphic novel where it's hard for me to rate it. On the one hand, I can see it as an incredible piece of art with excellent storytelling, but on the other hand I didn't "like it" insofar as the narrative is exceptionally dark, hard to handle, and thematically bleak. On the "important as a graphic novel" scale, it gets a 5, on the "did I actually enjoy reading this" it probably gets a 2. In any event, a 3 sounds about right. 
 It's the 1970s, and teenagers are doing what they have done since the beginning of time - drugs, sex, rebellion and angst. The only problem is that the sex part of things has led to the transmission of a viral strain that causes all sorts of mutations to crop up - some have uncontrollable hair growth, others shed their skins, and still other grow tails. As you can imagine, the mutations are somewhat horrifying, and have led to alienation from society and a questioning of self-worth (which of course is typical teenage behavior anyway). This is truly the theme of Black Hole, I suspect - the mutations seem to be a signifier for growing up and how a period of awkwardness and wanting to disappear is a hallmark of the teenage experience. Of course, another phase of this is that everyone grows out of this awkwardness, where in Black Hole it does not appear that any of the teenagers ever lose their mutation. Also interesting, the adults here seem to be more or less completely absent, which only adds to the tension and terror of the teens who seem to have no one to try and help them besides each other. I will say that the murder storyline that also crops up here I think is particularly important in a culture now where we seem to have more and more violence appearing in our youths. 
 The art is grotesque and horrifying - more or less exactly what you would expect. It's all black and white as well, which to me definitely lent a significant creepy factor. As I said, it's a wonderful graphic novel, but I just didn't enjoy my experience here.
