reference_books.title: The Angel's Game (The Cemetery of Forgotten Books, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 First off, the translator of this book did a masterful job. I found that the prose was simply magnificent, and that's a credit to both the author and the translator...there were many turns of phrases that were exceptional. Perhaps it's because it was written in a different language, but the analogies in particular struck me as perfect and never cliched. 
 I also really enjoyed the David Martin character. I felt as if I really was inside his head for about 4/5 of this book. His conversations with Isabella were likewise priceless and often hilarious. I remember thinking around page 100 or so that I felt a connection with the character, and I often don't feel that way when I'm reading a book. I also really enjoyed the plot for again about 4/5 of the book, and I was looking forward to where it was headed. 
 But the reason this gets 3 stars from me is the last 100 pages. The rest of this book was so strong that I'm going to chalk up my dislike of the ending and general confusion at those last 100 pages to me not understanding Zafon's genius. Even after I read the epilogue I simply did not get it. Was Martin Correlli? Did Correlli exist at all? Whose soul, exactly, did Marlasca steal, and why was he so intent on having one in the first place? I understand the witch had told him that death would pass him by if he offered a soul in exchange, but why did Marlasca want to escape death? As I understood it, he missed his dead son, and it would seem he would want to bring him back, rather than live forever. And what was going on with Correlli bringing Cristina back to Martin in the end? I just didn't understand, and I said, I assume this is my failure, not Zafon's. Nevertheless, it can't get a higher rating from me as a result. 
 I really did enjoy the first 430 or so pages, and I probably will try Shadow of the Wind at some point, as others have said they liked that better. But my enjoyment was tempered by my disappointment in those last 100 pages.

book_a.title: Nick & Norah's Infinite Playlist
book_a.user_review:
This story started with such energy that I was disappointed when it lost that drive about halfway through. I will candidly admit that the film version of the novel is a guilty pleasure of mine, and perhaps I was hoping that the novel would simply mirror it, but this is a different animal altogether. I liked the idea of the alternating perspectives between Nick and Norah with the different chapters, and I also enjoy the concept of two teenagers "falling in love" over the course of one night while also understanding that this feeling may be fleeting. 
 But as I said, I felt like the second half of this book just fell flat. Once the two main characters had overcome some of their mutual insecurities, I just didn't feel like there was much urgency to the narrative. I don't even know if I could reasonably pinpoint a climactic point here, and that's a significant problem when you're dealing with a novel. All in all, if they had improved upon the second half it would have been a pretty great YA novel.

book_b.title: Stay Awake
book_b.user_review:
In a word: unsettling. It's interesting, I remember liking Await Your Reply and thinking that it was full of characters with bad decisions to make, but man, those characters have NOTHING on the poor saps that populate this collection. I read a review where someone mentioned that it took them a few stories before they realized that Chaon had created a collection of horror stories, and I definitely had the same experience. It should of course be said that these stories are not horror in the traditional sense, but rather horror in the "ordinary burdens and things that overwhelm us and can very well destroy us" sense. 
 As always for short story collections, highlights for me - Thinking of You In Your Time of Sorrow (quite possibly my favorite short story of my 2013 reading), Long Delayed Always Expected, Patrick Lane Flabbergasted, I Wake Up, Shepherdess. The others were decent enough, but they just didn't hit me in the same way (and I'm quite certain I didn't even GET the last story, "The Farm, the gold, the lily-white hands"). Chaon explores varying levels of grief and loss in these stories, with nearly everyone to be found in pain over a recent death and trying to find a way to survive. 
 Chaon is clearly a very talented writer, but I think that next time I will have to have my guard up and expect a darker narrative than I was anticipating when I first cracked this open. True horror, I suppose, is not found in the bogeymen and vampires of our imagination, but rather in the terrible things that could actually happen to us, and Chaon is able to see this in spades and describe the WORST POSSIBLE outcome of these terrible things occurring.

sample_reviews.review_text: Some really strange short stories............
I liked the open-endedness. But it barely compensates for the sections that crossover into mawkish self-pity or sentimentality.

I actually saw this book at Barnes & Noble and it looked so intriguing, I snapped a picture and put it on my to-read list. Stay Awake is a collection of short stories by Dan Chaon. The stories are depressing, creepy and a little haunting. They could definitely make one 'stay awake' at night... Unfortunately, I found through reading these stories that I really don't enjoy short stories as much as I do a longer book. Once I finally start getting into the characters and story, it ends...which is so disappointing to an avid book reader. 
 Each story left me a little confused and lost at the end. Were they supposed to leave questions in the air? The characters in each story were all dealing with deeply emotional issues - loss of a loved one mostly, which led them into a downward spiral. At the end I was often wondering if it was all just a dream or were they imagining the events that took place. 
 Overall, all though the short stories grip you and are intriguing, I was left with this empty feeling of not quite understanding what just happened. I believe I will stay away from short story collections for awhile...
3.5 stars. I liked the stories. I plan on reading more of his work.
I am generally not a big fan of short stories. I didn't realize it was a book of short stories when I picked it up at the library. Most of the stories are just plain sad and depressing.
Excellent before bed read! Great short stories reminisce of the Twilight Zone, I would definitely recommend this book!

Lovely. A collection of short stories based on increasingly familiar people. What a wonderfully written little book. The reading experience could probably be enhanced by listening to the soundtrack of Twin Peaks at the same time. Also, what a very fitting cover.

The stories in this collection are downright creepy, though not in a horror movie kind of way. Many of the characters are dealing with the death of loved ones, and the atmosphere and psychological toll of loss is fascinating and uncomfortable. If you're okay with stories that don't wrap up nicely and linger gloomily in your mind, definitely read these!

How creepy is this collection of short stories? So creepy that, when I finished the last short story (reading late at night in a cabin in the woods, by myself) I hopped out of bed and carried the book to another room so that I wouldn't accidentally spot the cover of the book if I woke in the night. Consider yourself forewarned.

This was a book of short stories that were very, very dark in tone--all of them. Which I liked because it was kind of different and almost fun to revel in the gruesomeness and in the dark aspects of the human spirit. These were unapologetically negative people and situations--car crashes, deformed babies, abandoned children, coffins, suicides, etc. Don't read this book after you've had a bad day! But in the right mood, it was interesting. 
 I did not, however, think it was very compelling or any kind of pageturner. If it wasn't such a quick read I probably would have stopped. Also, I hated the affected writing technique in some of the stories, particularly the last one. It was a bunch of e e cumming B.S.--uncapitalized beginnings of sentences, half-finished sentences, large amounts of space between words on a page. Give me a break! Pretentious and added nothing to the telling, I thought.

reference_books.title: The Marriage Plot
reference_books.review_text:
I wanted to like this book given all the reviews and awards it received, but I didn't. I slogged through it, and it was just downright depressing at times. Not to mention frustrating. I just kept wanting to shake madeleine and tell her to wake up and get away from Leonard. I'm sure there are probably parallels and metaphors and meanings in the book that I haven't thought about that make it richer, but I can't even be bothered to think about them because I'm just so glad to be done with this book. 
 Here's a good review that sums up my thoughts much more elegantly and with much more insight into why this book misses the mark. http://www.guardian.co.uk/books/2011/...

reference_books.title: Fall of Giants (The Century Trilogy, #1)
reference_books.review_text: As a huge fan of pillars of the earth and world without end, I had high expectations for this book. And I liked it but didn't love it like I loved pillars of the earth. And I think thats because I liked the time period of pillars of the earth and world without end more so than the time period of fall of the giants. Which is odd, because I would expect that the time period that is closer to me would perhaps capture my interest more, but apparently not. And perhaps fall of the giants is less intriguing because you know what's ultimately going to happen historically, whereas with pillars of the earth and world without end you, nothing is a foregone conclusion unless you really know those time periods, which I don't. I mist say, I still think follett did a great job, precisely because you know what's coming historically, which I think makes it harder to build suspense and create story lines. I listened to this book rather than reading it and I'm glad I did because I'm not sure if I would have stuck with it had I been reading. But all in all, worth the read--or listen.

reference_books.title: The Valley of Amazement
reference_books.review_text: I wanted to like this book more than I did. It's fine, but a bit of a slog at times. It's written well, and towards the end you really see (and recall) a number of literary devices (parallelism, foreshadowing, etc.) Tan employs, but The Joy Luck Club it is not. (Which is the only book I've read by Amy Tan, and it was in high school, but I remember loving it.) So my feelings on this book are meh, it's fine. If you're a huge Amy Tan fan, then go for it, but if not, perhaps skip it.

book_a.title: Gone with the Wind
book_a.user_review: I never had a huge desire to read this book, probably because I tried to watch the movie three times when I was younger and could never get past the first 20 minutes. But when one of my friends suggested we read it for book club, I thought why not? And after reading it, I now understand why people love it so much. Scarlett is such a great character, and I love how the book ended. It took me a long time to get through it though. One fourth of the way through I thought what else can happen in this book besides the obvious historical events? But I was pleasantly surprised. And now I can't believe that it took me until I was 30 to read this book. And now I'm determined to get through the movie when it arrives from Netflix. I definitely recommend this book.

sample_reviews.review_text:
To explain why I only gave this one star, the book is probably a really good book, but when this was "required reading" at school, it was a bit much. I grew up in the south, all you learned about in history class was the Civil War. Everything before it was just a prelude and everything after was just a result from it. We barely finished studying WWII and that was because we rushed it. 
 Now another reason I don't like this book: if you grew up in Atlanta as I did, Gone With the Wind was an almost every week discussion. There is a whole culture surrounding the book and the movie. I guess I just grew too tired of it to appreciate the work itself. 
 Now, having said all that, I do rather admire Margaret Mitchell. She seemed to be a bit of a "trailblazer" for southern women of the time. Flounting conventialities (sp)and expectations of "proper" women of the time. Plus she defied expectations and never wrote a sequel, when she was pressured to do so. 
 But truly, to never hear of Scarlett O'Hara and Rhett Butler again would be so very peaceful.

Almost a year later, and I finally finished Gone With The Wind. While I can see why it's a classic, there's another part of me that thinks it's vastly overrated. I don't see why people would want to read it more than once. Margaret did a great job making Scarlett a spoiled brat. She ended up having four kids, but only one mattered. For the second half of the book I kept wondering what about the other kids? It was only about Bonnie. There wasn't any characters that I found myself attached to. It was meh.
Another one of my favorite books ever. Good to have a different perspective of the Civil War. Second time reading.

Thinking about race tends to turn Gone With the Wind inside-out; the good guys are the bad guys, those Union soldiers look like liberators--and the black characters seem not like marginal players, but like the focal point, even if the novel is too filled with racism to really look at them.
About the Civil War

Didn't like the prose - too slow and boring. Scarlett got on my nerves from the start. There was so much overt racism and nastiness from characters who thought nothing of killing black people. I did not like it at all and cannot understand the fuss.

Gone With the Wind is pretty cool, except for all the racism! 
 Of course, you could say that about the Old South in general, and look where that got them. Spoiler, it got their asses kicked because they were hateful fucks who absolutely refused to stop enslaving millions of people and 70 years later in 1936 here's Margaret Mitchell whining about it for a thousand pages. If you'd like to hear why slavery was terrific and black people are inferior to whites and they liked being slaves, here is your epic. If that sounds unpleasant, you're not going to like Gone With the Wind. 
 A non-racist book can have racist characters, and all the characters in this book are racist. Is the book itself necessarily racist? Yes. It has an omniscient narrator, and many long, racist passages that are clearly not from any character's perspective; they feel like the nonfiction interludes in War & Peace. Is it possible Mitchell means for us to disagree with her omniscient narrator? No. There's no evidence whatsoever of that, and the passages that defend the South and slavery are written with passion and supported by racist scenes in the story. This book intends to be racist; Margaret Mitchell believes what she says; she was a racist person who wrote a hateful book. I can prove it and I'm about to. 
 We start off in the glory days of the Old South, as a young, callow, beautiful Scarlett O'Hara flirts with everyone's boyfriends. Happy slaves bustle around: 
 "The house negroes of the County considered themselves superior to white trash...they were well-fed, well-clothed and looked after in sickness and old age. They were proud of the good names of their owners and, for the most part, proud to belong to people who were quality." 
 We meet some of them, Scarlett's "small white hand disappearing into their huge black paws and the four capered with delight at the meeting and with pride at displaying before their comrades what a pretty Young Miss they had." 
 Faithful slave Mammy is introduced, with her "kind face, sad with the uncomprehending sadness of a monkey's face" - "the mottled wise old eyes saw deeply, saw clearly, with the directness of the savage and the child, undeterred by conscience when danger threatened her pet." Mammy is one of the few morally pure characters in the book, but it's always that noble savage quality. 
 Luckily Scarlett stays away from the slave quarters, where "the faint niggery smell which crept from the cabin increased her nausea." 
 But then war comes. Here's noble and boring Ashley, the limpest point of the oncoming love triangle, describing what the war is about. Notice that his vision of the South is indivisible from slavery: 
 I hear the darkies coming home across the fields at dusk, tired and singing and ready for supper, and the sound of the windlass as the bucket goes down into the cool well. And there's the long view down the road to the river, across the cotton fields, and the mist rising from the bottom lands in the twilight. And that is why I'm here who have no love of death or misery or glory and no hatred for anyone. Perhaps that is what is called patriotism. 
 After the War and during Reconstruction, things get really dark (get it? lol) as Northerners ruin black people: "Some of the free negroes were getting quite insolent. This last [Scarlett] could hardly believe, for she had never seen an insolent negro in her life." 
 But "The [Freedmen's] Bureau fed them while they loafed and poisoned their minds against their former masters." And here's much more from the omniscient narrator: 
 [They] furthermore told the negroes they were as good as the whites in every way and soon white and negro marriages would be permitted, soon the estates of their former owners would be divided and every negro would be given forty acres and a mule for his own. They kept the negroes stirred up with tales of cruelty perpetrated by the whites and, in a section long famed for the affectionate relations between slaves and slave owners, hate and suspicion began to grow. 
 [Now Southerners] were looking on the state they loved, seeing it trampled by the enemy, rascals making a mock of the law, their former slaves a menace, their men disenfranchised, their women insulted. 
 This eventually leads to the formation of the noble Ku Klux Klan, who merely attempt to protect Southern women from being raped by uppity former slaves. Here's a Klan member now: 
 "'Wilkerson had gone a bit too far with his nigger-equality business. Oh yes, he talks it to those black fools by the hour. He had the gall - the - ' Tony sputtered helplessly, 'to say niggers had a right to - to - white women.'" 
 "The negroes were on top and behind them were the Yankee bayonets," thinks Scarlett: "She could be killed, she could be raped and, very probably, nothing would ever be done about it." 
 And here's the omniscient narrator summing it up: 
 It was the large number of outrages on women and the ever-present fear for the safety of their wives and daughters that drove Southern men to cold and trembling fury and caused the Ku Klux Klan to spring up overnight. And it was against this nocturnal organization that the newspapers of the North cried out most loudly, never realizing the tragic necessity that brought it into being. 
 This is all demonstrated in the action. Scarlett O'Hara's headstrong ways nearly get every man in town hung. Her foolish habit of driving alone through the worst parts of town almost gets her raped by a freed slave, forcing the Klan to take action and lynch him, and they all almost get caught. Her second husband is killed. Divorced from its context, this is a brilliant scene. It's done entirely from Scarlett's point of view, so the actual gun fight is totally off page. What we see instead is the wives, with Northern soldiers in their living rooms waiting for the men to return - surrounded by enemies, their faces frozen into nonchalant expressions, desperately and silently scheming to save their husbands' lives. It's great stuff, as long as you can forget that you're being asked to root for the KKK to get away with lynching a man. 
 And here's a pretty long series of quotes. Again, they're all from the omniscient narrator - that is, from the book itself. 
 The South had been tilted as by a giant malicious hand, and those who had once ruled were now more helpless than their former slaves had ever been. 
 The former slaves were now the lords of creation and, with the aid of the Yankees, the lowest and most ignorant ones were on top. The better class of them, scorning freedom, were suffering as severely as their white masters...Many loyal field hands also refused to avail themselves of the new freedom, but the hordes of 'trashy free issue niggers,' who were causing most of the trouble, were drawn largely from the field-hand class. 
 In slave days, these lowly blacks had been despised by the house negroes and yard negroes as creatures of small worth...Plantation mistresses had put the pickaninnies through courses of training and elimination to select the best of them for the positions of greater responsibility. Those consigned to the fields were the ones least willing or able to learn, the least energetic, the least honest and trustworthy, the most vicious and brutish...[but now] the former field hands found themselves suddenly elevated to the seats of the mighty. There they conducted themselves as creatures of small intelligence might naturally be expected to do. Like monkeys or small children turned loose among treasured objects whose value is beyond their comprehension, they ran wild - either from perverse pleasure in destruction or simply because of their ignorance. 
 To the credit of the negroes, including the least intelligent of them, few were actuated by malice and those few had usually been "mean niggers" even in slave days. But they were, as a class, childlike in mentality, easily led and from long habit accustomed to taking orders. 
 ... 
 Here was the astonishing spectacle of half a nation attempting, at the point of bayonet, to force upon the other half the rule of negroes, many of them scarcely one generation out of the African jungles. 
 ... 
 Thanks to the negro vote, the Republicans and their allies were firmly entrenched and they were riding roughshod over the powerless but still protesting minority. 
 Man, just read that last sentence again. Wow. 
 Anyway, this is all very difficult for poor Scarlett: "The more I see of emancipation the more criminal I think it is. It's just ruined the darkies. Thousands of them aren't working at all and the ones we can get to work at the mill are so lazy and shiftless they aren't worth having. and if you so much as swear at them, much less hit them a few licks for the good of their souls, the Freedmen's Bureau is down on you like a duck on a June bug." 
 She complains that Northerners "Did not know that negroes had to be handled gently, as though they were children, directed, praised, petted, scolded...How could anyone get any work done with free niggers quitting all the time?...[It's] too dear a homeland to be turned over to ignorant negroes drunk with whiskey and freedom." 
 And with the final word, here's a former slave himself, Big Sam, who "galloped over to the buggy,his eyes rolling with joy and his white teeth flashing, and clutched her outsretched hand with two big hands as big as hams. His watermelon-pink tongue lapped out, his whole body wiggled and his joyful contortions were as ludicrous as the gambolings of a mastiff. ... 'Ah done had nuff freedom. Ah wants somebody ter eed me good vittles reg'lar, and tell me whut ter do an' whut not ter do.'" 
 Okay, is that enough? That was gross to type out. And don't think I'm cherry-picking the only racist passages; this book is soaked in racism. God's nightgown, this book is fuckin' racist. Pat Conroy, in a despicably fawning introduction, sees fit to mention that "No black man or woman can read this book and be sorry that this particular wind is gone," and what the hell kind of thing is that to say? "White people, on the other hand...you gotta be a little bummed out, right?" Is that what you meant, Pat? 
 And look, yes, it's too bad that this book has destroyed itself with hatred, because it's got a lot going for it. It certainly has Scarlett O'Hara going for it. She's fuckin' terrific, a towering antiheroine, amoral, selfish and brave - somewhat like the South itself. Rhett Butler, her swarthy and cynical love interest, is pretty good too, although he can't stop mansplaining amorality and he might have some kind of social learning disability. (He's also a murderer, by the way: "I did kill the nigger. He was uppity to a lady, and what else could a Southern gentleman do?") They have sortof a proto-50 Shades thing going on, including a fairly kinky love scene that's not explicitly described but Scarlett was definitely into it. Third love triangle corner Ashley sucks, no one cares about him. 
 It also taught me the phrase "God's nightgown!" which is certainly a great thing to yell. 
 But it is totally, irredeemably ruined by its racism. Look, I'm not trying to be "politically correct" here. That's not even a thing; it's a term made up by haters to excuse hate. Gone With The Wind angered me. I don't like hearing black people described as stupid monkeys over and over again. I didn't enjoy reading the book because I was constantly pissed off by how ignorant and hateful it is. 
 Books matter. We use stories to describe and define society. If we allow this book to become part of the foundation of our past - if we call it a classic, as some people have - we're basing our past on a terrible lie. And it is a terrible lie, in case we need to say that out loud: Slavery was bad, black people didn't like it, almost everyone else didn't either, and the South were the bad guys in the Civil War. 
 And books are also our companions. When we choose to read, we're spending significant amounts of time - hours and hours - deep in their worlds. This companion is full of hate. These hours and hours will be spent listening to her yell about insolent niggers. If you find it unpleasant to hang out with viciously hateful racists, you won't like this book. It's the most racist book I've ever read. I didn't like it.

I like the book a lot better then the movie. You get a much better picture of how it was to live in the south during the civil war and also Scarlett is a much less sympathetic character (if you can imagine that) just in the way she treats her older children.

I'm giving it three stars though, because at times, I felt like she was using this book to explain / justify some of the things people have said about her in the media. Which she has every right to do--it's her book. There were just times during the book in which that aspect turned me off. I also felt like the book started off strong, but towards the end I was ready for it to end. But I think that was partly due to the fact that the advice in the beginning of the book applied more to me than the advice at the end of the book. I could see how a couple of years from now the latter half of the book might resonate more strongly with me. All in all, it was a good book and a quick read (well, listen, since I bought the audiobook). If you're contemplating reading it, it's worth it. I appreciated her willingness to tackle hard issues head on and in a frank manner. But I didn't think, oh, I loved this book.

sample_reviews.review_text: So Sandberg's white privilege definitely peaks through but generally, a good read. There's a lot to chew on, stats-wise, in here and I appreciated how well-researched it was.

Read for GSK WLI book club (kindle version). Overall, I liked the book but there were some chapters that I thought were a lot more applicable to my life/job. 
 I really thought the chapter on a career as a jungle gym was very good, as was "are you my mentor". 
 However, I did think that the book and some specific chapters bounced around a bit from topic to topic. As a non-fiction book, I would expect a more linear approach.

All very reasonable, one of those books if you take the time to read you realize that the critics haven't. Speaking as an entrepreneur and manager who has employed countless women, Sandberg's advice is pretty spot on. It's not controversial, and most male managers would welcome women taking the advice. 
 Of note this quote: "In a perfect meritocracy, tiaras would be doled out to the deserving, but I have yet to see one floating around an office." I feel bad for Google. I have seen many Tiaras in offices. My office currently has three. 
 And this: "Larry and Sergey came to my baby shower and each gave me a certificate that entitled me to one hour of babysitting. (I never used the certificates, and if I could find them, I bet I could auction them off for charity, like lunch with Warren Buffett.)" Collectors rev your engines. 
 I know, I know, it's an important book and I'm picking little things. I apologize. In reading overly-discussed books, I often tend to look for the little anecdotes not discussed in the press. 
 But I'll leave you with this one, because I think it sums up the success and importance of this book: 
 "Talking can transform minds, which can transform behaviors, which can transform institutions."

Though I think she focuses a lot on how to balance family life and work life, I liked how Sandberg reminds women to not feel guilty about success or to feel like we haven't worked hard enough to earn it. 
 This book reminded me of a more readable version of the Beauty Myth. She uses real life experience and stories to get her point across, along with various studies without making the book to dry or academic. 
 I was prepared to give this four stars, but I was expecting the book to be a bit longer (the kindle version is a bit misleading due to her acknowledgments and foot notes) and my favorite part was the last section where she mentioned the "Queen Bee" mentality and I wish she would've elaborated on that more.

Four stars just for the fact that Sheryl Sandberg wrote this book. It's a quick and easy read and a great reminder to all about the continued inequality between men and women. There are a few misleading bits, especially about FMLA, and she recognizes she doesn't have an answer to the larger problem but does offer great family and career advice for the individual, male and female.

reference_books.title: Go Set a Watchman
reference_books.review_text:
So this book shatters some myths, primarily the myth that Atticus was a lone voice of tolerance and justice in a deeply racist and unjust Deep South. Many people refuse to read this book for this reason, which I don't agree with because he was after all, a fictional character. Even if Harper Lee modelled Atticus after her own father, I always assumed there was a lot of artistic license. Besides, I was just too curious to find out what else she had to say. 
 The reality is that racism is a deeply complex issue. At the time the story of To Kill a Mockingbird takes place, the 1930s, the Southern Way of Life was not under threat, everyone knew their place, so maybe Atticus really could be considered a tolerant and just man in that context. Twenty years later, that way of life was definitely changing, so maybe his reactions and his views should not be so shocking to the reader. 
 Even Jean Louise, who considers herself "color blind", a term attributed to her several times in this book, makes some pretty racist statements. 
 It is quite obvious that this book was published "as is" without any much-needed editing. As I was reading it, I could understand why it was rejected in the first place, for the quality of the writing alone. Also, the story does not seem to have much of a point besides her shock and horror that her father is a segregationist. 
 For all its faults, this book is still worth a read. I enjoyed the theme of a young woman coming home and finding out that the world she grew up has changed or wasn't ever as idyllic as she thought it was growing up. I wish she had done more with this theme, I found the way she reacts to this all is pretty unsatisfying. I am happy to report Jean Louise is still Scout. She is still rebellious and tomboyish and Aunt Alexandra is still trying to turn her into a Southern Belle. And yes, the quality of the writing is very uneven, downright bad in some parts, but I actually found this aspect quite interesting because it gave you a little bit of insight into the writing process and how an initial idea for a novel can turn into something completely different. 
 Should this book have been published or should it have stayed in the safety deposit box where it was "found"? I am not sure. On the one hand maybe not because many people will be upset to learn that Atticus was not the saint and the national treasure that the world has grown to worship. But on the other hand, it gives a more balanced and perhaps realistic view of that time and place and of the author herself. 
 If the reports are true, maybe it should not have been published simply because she didn't want it to be. When her sister, who managed all her affairs died, the publishers did what they wanted with the manuscript. A few years ago, when asked why she never wrote or published another book she replied "Because I have nothing more to say" or "Because I have said what I had to say" or something like that.

reference_books.review_text:
This was a very poorly written book, which didn't even provide much information on the subject. There was way too much irrelevant detail about the author herself and mundane aspects of Harper Lee's daily life (ie trips to McDonalds and the laundromat). After over a year of recorded conversations with Nelle Harper and her sister Alice I was expecting much more. The most interesting passages are where she clears up many misundertandings and distortions of her relationship with Truman Capote. Also, I liked their housekeeper, Julia, who was really a modern day Calpurnia, straight out of her novel. 
 I basically skimmed over the last 
 When this book came out, there was some controversy over whether the Lee sisters authorized the book. I have no doubt they did. It is sad that the realease of this book and Go set a watchman are clouded in controversy. reference_books.title: The Dinner
reference_books.review_text:
Overall I was disappointed by this book. It was not very suspenseful and apart from the revelations about the main character's wife, not many surprises at all. I did not have a problem with the unlikable and unreliable narrator, I love a book with a really odious villain actually. 
 There were quite a few holes in the whole story and some bits that were not very believable (the choice of a popular restaurant where a public figure would meet with his family to discuss how to deal with horrible crimes committed by their children, the amniocentesis test revealing mental illness, the main character's violence not resulting in any criminal charges). The last couple of pages in particular were a bit confusing and didn't quite fit with the rest of the story. 
 Paul, the narrator, several times refers to the quote from Anna Karanina "All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way". Except that he turned it completely on its head since this story basically deals with a happy family of sociopaths that brag about their fascist views to anyone who will listen. A bit of irony which unfortunately in the end makes you not take this book seriously.

book_a.title: The Satanic Verses
book_a.user_review:
A fascinating book but I must admit I struggled through parts of it. I especially found the beginning very difficult to follow and almost gave up a couple of times. At first, the writing style was very chaotic and jumbled and I just couldn't get into it. It also helps to have some knowledge of Islam and I did have to go and look up a few things as I went along. Once I overcame these issues, I thoroughly enjoyed this book and am very glad I read it. 
 It is the story of 2 Indian expatriates, one a famous actor and the other an expat living in London, who fall from the sky when terrorists blow up the plane they are travelling on. When they miraculously land on the English shore, Gibreel (the actor) is surrounded by a glow like a halo and Saladin grows horns. As you can imagine just by this introduction to the story there is a lot of magical realism throughout the book and a lot of Rushdie's biting wit and satire. 
 I was drawn to this book because of the controversy and as I also want to read Rushdie's memoir Joseph Anton, I decided to read this first to see for myself what the fuss was about. When it was first published, the Ayatollah Khomeini put a fatwa (an order to kill) on Rushdie because of its portrayal of the Prophet Mohammed. I can see why. It is definitely blasphemous as it depicts Mohammed in a very negative light and Islam in general. There is also a chapter on an exiled Imam in London who wants to destroy clocks. This no doubt made the Ayatollah furious as well and contributed to the proclamation of the fatwa. 
 However, this book is so much more than that and in the end that is what won me over. It also delves into the themes of good and evil, angels and devils, envy, jealousy, the tyranny of religion. It also covers race relations in the UK, immigrants, the return to your home country. While a lot of the themes are still very modern, it is definitely set in Thatcher's England. At one point the story turns into a variation on Othello based on the two main characters Gibreel and Saladin and Gibreel's lover Allelulia Cone. While the "Satanic verses" of the title refers to the religious theme, they also play a role in this part of the story. 
 So there is A Lot going on in this book and although I struggled through the beginning I really enjoyed it. Rushdie is definitely a brilliant writer, and there were even some laugh out loud moments. I do think that if you are not familiar with his work, Midnight's Children is a better introduction. If I hadn't read Midnight's Children first I probably would not have appreciated Satanic Verses as much.

I read this in high school to look cool. I thought I was such a rebel for reading a 600pg book with such a controversial plot. The footnotes were so difficult to get through. Had I lived in Rushdie's time, I could appreciate the subtle pop cultural references. When I took a World Literature class in college I could really appreciate the magical realism in the dream sequences and the powerful metamorphosis of the main character.

I avoided this book for a while because of the controversy surrounding it. I guess I prefer to read books on their own terms. I finally decided to read it just because I remember enjoying Midnight's Children so much and wanted to experience some of that Rushdie magic again. 
 It's important to know that religion is not the primary focus of this book, though it is most famous for having been offensive to some Muslims. The primary focus is emigration, and what it does to the identities of the emigrants and the cultures of the countries involved -- in this case mostly India as the country left behind and England as the country that is adopted. Rushdie attacks this subject from so many angles, and with such imagination, that it's easy to see this book as a jumble of stories, some presented as dreams and/or hallucinations, without focus. For me the word that keeps popping in my head when I try to describe this book is "kaleidoscopic". The plot, or plots, are at turns dreamlike, twisting, fragmentary, and colorful. There is method to the madness, though, if not answers. 
 To be fair, religion does play an important part in the book. All of the stories related to the history of Islam are presented as dreams, with the names of places and people changed, which provides some distance (but apparently not enough for some). The questions Rushdie raises about religion, however, are the same that he raises about his emigrants. The main question is "What kind of idea are you?" Are you an idea that admits no compromise, that risks shattering rather than giving up on rigidity? Or are you flexible, accommodating, willing to compromise? 
 The first kind of idea is a kind of insanity, fragile but brilliant. The second is practical but dull. This struggle for identity is universal and, maybe, unifying.

reference_books.title: Divergent (Divergent, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Really fun, really easy read. I love the main character, Tris, and her narration, dare I say even more than Katniss Everdeen. I liked the concept of the factions, their history and development, but also the details about their focus, behavior, dress, speech, etc. It was fun to imagine which faction I would grow up in or want to join, and where my friends would fall. At the same time, it makes clear statements about the direction that our society is heading in and what we need to do to make it the best possible environment for every kind of person. 
 I thought the pace of the book was great, not too rushed at the end as I found the second and third Hunger Games. It definitely made me want to read the second one, which luckily I had and started the same day. 
 I didn't mind the violence, especially because she was in the Dauntless compound for most of the first book, but I wish we had gotten more of a sense of the other factions' daily lives before the second book when their worst facets were the only things highlighted. I liked Four and thought he played a necessary role. I sort of skipped over their typical YA love story pages -- heart racing, fingertips touching, can't breathe, space between us nonsense. Maybe that makes me an old woman with no fire left, but it was a little more than I cared to indulge at times. 
 Details like the fear landscape, the science behind the serums and the concept of divergence were all really well explained and added a cool science-fiction layer to the story. 
 Overall I think its a worthwhile series for teens, but also a fun read for anyone -- especially because of the portrayal of women as strong (mentally, physically and emotionally) leaders who are self-reliant and can work through their fears.

reference_books.title: The Book Thief
reference_books.review_text:
This book was beautiful and I loved reading it, although I would not recommend it for everyone. 
 The Book Thief takes place in a small town on the outskirts of Munich in the late 1930s and early 1940s. The pivotal character is a young girl who is given up by her mother, who can no longer take care of her. What occurs next is her entry into the family life of a very complicated but loving couple, Hans and Rosa Hubermann. Rosa and Hans could not be more different in their approach, but their love for their foster daughter is tangible. Enter Hitler, a mysterious Jew from Hans' past and an onslaught of bombs, all told from the point of view of Death, and you have quite the moving tale. 
 I personally enjoyed the stylistic narration, including excerpts from characters' notebooks/sketchpads, bolded updates/previews from Death and ten parts divided into chapters, but I can see how others would not. Furthermore, this is a book that you really need to be in the right mindset for -- it's certainly no beach read. I attempted to start reading it earlier in the year and stopped after a few pages.

reference_books.title: Slammerkin
reference_books.review_text:
Here's the thing: Slammerkin could easily be written off as a typical tale set in 1700s London detailing all the hardships that people experienced. However, the more you read, the more you see Donoghue's clear talent for developing her characters into multi-faceted, relatable beings, all the while weaving in side stories and complex thematic elements. This book started out as simply interesting (the title is what initially grabbed me, as did its double meaning..), but I ended up hooked. 
 Let's just say that I read this book while traveling around Japan, and at times even the promise of cherry blossoms and fresh fish couldn't tear me away from fifteen-year-old Mary Saunders and her choices.

reference_books.title: The Lowland
reference_books.review_text:
Lahiri is, without a doubt, my favorite author. Her books are my favorite books. Lowland took a fourth place out of four. That being said, it is still an engaging and strikingly well-written book that any Lahiri fan (or any fan of Indian fiction) should read. 
 The Lowland tells the story of two brothers growing up in a small, poor suburb in India. One brother becomes entangled in revolutionary idealism, eventually landing himself in trouble with the government. The other brother, only fifteen months younger, prizes being a good son and provider for his family, and moves to Rhode Island to study oceanography. 
 That is sort of where I got lost for a little while. Having spent a lot of time on the East Coast myself, I was reluctant to spend a portion of this book out of India and in Rhode Island. I love Lahiri for her interpretation of what it means to be an Indian transplant in America, but I don't want to read about the shore birds of Naragansett. Sorry. 
 Once the climax occurs, actually pretty early on, things get moving again, characters make shocking choices, your emotions rev up and again I felt like I was back with the true Lahiri. Bouncing back and forth from the past to the present to the future. Focusing intensely on the development of only a few main characters and letting them carry the story. And her writing -- to put it plainly, there were more than a handful of times my jaw actually dropped reading and rereading a single, beautiful sentence. 
 Overall, Lowlands was excellent. It was historically interesting, as I didn't know a lot about the Naxalites and their rebellion. It was emotionally accessible, and the characters surprise you. I can't wait until her next one.

reference_books.title: Around the World in Eighty Days (Extraordinary Voyages, #11)
reference_books.review_text:
Lately, I have been challenging myself to read more of what are considered "old classics." Since this one comes for free on the iPad (its just that old), I thought I would give it a whirl. I was not too disappointed. First of all, to hold a book written in 1872 to the standards of American literature today is not fair. So I will not. I will take it for what it was: at the time, a very compelling, adventurous book about blasting through obstacles to achieve goals in the "new world." 
 However, it has to be said that Jules Verne was writing at a time where it was acceptable to call people "coolies" and describe Japanese people as having large heads and tight-looking eyes. That, I wasn't so amped about. He also describes the western part of America as "infested by Indians." There is no female character in the book who is anything but a damsel in distress or a "lady of the night." But, again, 1872. So, if we can look past that (and his spelling of the country Chile as Chili), it is an interesting look into the past. It gives a great perspective on travel back then, just how long it took, but how shockingly fast that felt compared to the early-1800s. I enjoyed the relationship between Fogg, his "manservant," and the traveling detective, and it made me laugh a few times. In the end, it simply made me appreciate that I was not born in 1872, and wonder if, in 143 years, people will be reading our current novels and laughing.

book_b.title: Secret Daughter
book_b.user_review:
This book was engaging, warm and well-written from start to finish. It was written in short chapters, each told by a different, alternating character, which contributed to its pace and flow. Gowda's narrators were multi-faceted and easy to connect with, even when you perceived their weaknesses, disagreed with their choices or flat out despised their actions. She told the story slowly and with beautiful imagery, unfolding the layers as she went along. The basic plot line -- Indian daughter adopted to an American family, trying to find her way home -- has been told before, but not in such a dynamic way, exploring the issue from all angles and from the perspective of all major players. 
 I also appreciated the descriptions of India, as I think they are written in a way I would write about Cambodia: contrasting and at times painful, but always brutally honest, admitting the bad along with the good. Finally, I appreciated Gowda's ability to skillfully delve into many of the issues currently plaguing India (overpopulation, rampant crime, overflowing slums and obscene treatment of women) without allowing them to detract from or overshadow her story. 
 I am a sucker for Indian-American fiction and this book (which I read in two days) left me satisfied on all fronts.

A moving story about two families--one in California, one in India--with a daughter in common. Click here for my full review.
Nice story, a lot to talk about in book club.

In India, Kavita Merchants gives birth to a daughter. Her husband feels they can only afford one child, and it must be a boy to help him in the fields. So Kavita brings her baby to an orphanage to save the newborn's life. 
 In California, Somer and Krishnan Thakkar decide to adopt a baby since they are unable to have a child. They are thrilled to learn they can adopt a beautiful Indian baby girl, and name her Asha. 
 The author tells the story of Asha growing up, her adoptive parents, and Asha's search for her birth parents when she lives with Krishnan's family in Mumbai for a year. It explores the challenge of a bicultural family, and the difficulty of being an Indian child in a Caucasian community. 
 The book is full of the sights, smells, and sounds of Mumbai ranging from the poverty in a slum, to an over-the-top wedding of family friends, to the descriptions of the wonderful spicy Indian food. The story shows that love can come from both birth and adoptive parents, and what being a family really means.
Gave up on this one. Couldn't do it. Something about the writing just wasn't right...

This book is written in a simple style, at times, overstating the emotion involved in this heartwrenching tale of gendercide and survival as Asha searches to find the meaning of family. I once took a class on culture and literature and my insight was that fighting for gender equity isn't going to go away until we tackle class disparity. This is very much represented in Secret Daughter. I was very relieved to see that there are no simple answers in this book, and there is a lot of grey area between culture and human rights as these are complex issues. I will recommend this book to anyone interested in the plight of female children in poverty and it will fit nicely into many of the literature studies in my secondary school library.

reference_books.title: The Girl Who Played with Fire (Millennium, #2)
reference_books.review_text: This is a sequel to the book, "The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo" and fell into the typical sequel curse for me; the concept (murder mystery-ish), characters, etc aren't new so it just can't be as good as the original. I still enjoyed the characters and story but felt it dragged in some places and could have have used some editing to maintain the suspense. It did seem to have more plot twists and it kept me guessing longer than the original. Part of why I liked the first book so much was because I thought the characters are so well developed and that was continued in this book, especially as the reader is given so much background in Lisbeth Salander's life. There is a third book due out and I will definitely pick that up when it's published in the US.

reference_books.title: The Lost City of Z: A Tale of Deadly Obsession in the Amazon
reference_books.review_text: This book was fascinating. Fawcett was an explorer back in the early 1900s and he explored and mapped extensively throughout the Amazon. He was renowned for his personal strength and his apparent inability to get sick. David did an excellent job of weaving the history behind Fawcett the explorer and David's current interest in the story. He used Fawcett's diaries, letters, interviews, and press releases to provide a complete picture of Fawcett the man, husband, and explorer. It was well written and researched and I loved/was disgusted by the descriptions of the Amazon conditions. Descriptions of skin literally peeling off and having actual maggots under your skin and being able to see them put it over the top. Exploring the Amazon without any of the modern conveniences of maleria tablets, GPS, bug spray, is pretty amazing and more amazing that he kept on going back and doing it when members of his party (and other exploration parties) were routinely dying of disease or disappearing. It was all put into perspective when David and I went to a baseball game on Monday night and it was rainy and 50 degrees and I was cold and miserable. I'm a wuss.

reference_books.title: American Wife
reference_books.review_text: For the most part I don't like reading the inside jacket blurb about the plot of books. It's almost always way to informative and ruins it for me. So I was late figuring out exactly what this way about. I enjoyed the first 3/4 of the book talking about growing up and figuring out what to do in life and then how their life started together. How it was fun and frustrating and hard (shock-marriage is hard?) but I liked how intimate, how intruding I felt pulled into the character's relationship. Then the last section started and I just read it to finish the book, I wasn't interested anymore because it seemed to completely be about justification of behavior in a well, boys-will-be-boys sort of way. However, I did significantly like this over the more popular "Prep" and would recommend it. I just couldn't get past that last section of the book, that to me, was just whining.

reference_books.title: The Story of Edgar Sawtelle
reference_books.review_text: I don't think this is a book for everyone but I LOVED it and was surprised it was a debut novel. My husband would say it's a book where nothing happens which translates into it's a story about a person's life and there are no car chases or explosions. It's primarily told from Edgar's point of view though occasional chapters are told from the prespective of his mom, his uncle and even his dog Almondine. This is a book that's a little slow to get to the "meat" of the story but I thought it was a needed leadup and wasn't bored or annoyed at the detail, descriptions, and gradual buildup. Edgar's father unexpectedly dies and the book is about Edgar and his mom's handling of that, the dog business, their relationship and how it changes as well as the relationships with uncle and how that changes. My favorite passage is from a chapter from Almondine and it's right after Edgar's father passes away. "And so she searched. She'd watched his casket lowered into the ground, a box, man-made, no more like him than the trees that swayed under the winter wind. To assign him an identify outside the world was not in her thinking. The fence line where he walked and where he slept-that was where he lived and they remembered him"

The book starts off with a murder and a note was left on the victim. What the note says isn't revealed into several chapters in and with good reason. As soon as I found out what it said, I figured out the book and didn't hold my interest after that. Sometimes that works because finding out the "how" or "why" is still fascinating but in this case I was mostly bored. book_a.title: Loving Frank
book_a.user_review: This book is the story of Frank Lloyd Wright and the relationship with his mistress, Mamah. Mistress isn't quite the right word as she was so much more than a fleeting interest or the "other woman". It takes place in the early 1900s when Wright's career was taking off and ideas about marriage, children, divorce and obligation were different than today. Both Frank and Mamah faced condemnation from clients, friends, family and the press about their relationship though their romantic relationship lasted almost a decade. Mamah was a fascinating woman though little is known about her personal life. She spoke many languages, was a firm believer in women's rights, and worked to translate feminist texts. The relationship was real and the author did her best to piece together what is known with what she imagined and I love that combination to produce engaging historical fiction.

sample_reviews.review_text: I found the book interesting on one level - it provided details about architect Frank Lloyd Wright. The reader gets to see how architects work and deal with the realities of creating and building. But, I was also appalled at how awful Frank and Mameh were as just plain human beings. He was a narcissist of the first order. She cashed in her devoted husband and young children to be with Frank. In other words, a lot of innocent people suffered (greatly - the end of the story is horrific!) because these two entitled jerks had to have their own way!! I'm halfway through Z by Therese Anne Fowler, and I'm seeing some parallels between the two couples. I hate how some so-called 'geniuses' or 'stars' seem to think that the rules of life/society just don't apply to them. I have found that the folks who are truly worthy of attention and praise are ordinary people who live decent, thoughtful lives every day, make appropriate choices, give to others, and treat their fellow man with respect. Of course, that's considered boring, so we end up reading about skanks and scumballs!

This book was a book club book for me last month and stirred up some controversy. One person thought Mamah was justified in leaving her children in her path to self-realization, (I have always thought that self- realization was a more acceptable term for self-absorption). A couple of us understood her reluctance to stay in her marriage, but still thought her decision was wrong--I think morally wrong. One thought Frank genuinely loved Mamah, I felt he never grew beyond the narcissism and denial which enabled him to rationalize leaving a wife and six children to miss their husband and father and to struggle to pay the bills. I felt he was arrogant and selfish. He was horrid to his wife, and not much better to Mamah: I mean, three grand pianos! I think the author tries to be fair but really wants the reader to empathize with Mamah's choices, but I could never reach that point, though the book is admittedly seductively written. What disturbed me most was statements like this one: "At moments she could even imagine that everyone involved--Edwin, Catherine, the children--would someday be happy." (p. 138) And a few days later: "Somehow she would turn this terrible mess into a blessing for the children. She believed it was possible that they could someday feel enlarged by the love all around them. People with children got divorced and remarried; it wasn't the end of the world for them. Martha and John [Mamah's children:] could actually end up better off, with four happy parents." (p. 140) I realize that my reading of the book is colored heavily by my own experience and that of my own children, but those statements seem so deluded and self-serving that I lost all sympathy for her from that point. And as any reader of the book knows, things did not turn out so well for the children.

I had wanted to read this book because I like Frank Lloyd Wright. I did not like this book as much as I thought I would. I believe it has more to do with my inability to comprehend how someone could make the decisions made in this book. I have read it and do not have to read it again.

I enjoyed the book. It was a good read. I was so shocked with the ending that I had to google Mamah Borthwick it to find out if this was in fact true. 
 She gave up her children and used so many people in the process of loving Frank. I wonder, "Was he worth it?"

Mamah is not my cup of tea. Her rousing independence and passion are too frequently tempered with guilt, confusion, and regret. Frank seems like a player. I am glad to have spent some time in Oak Park, but my household cleaves to Louis Sullivan. I consider this a worthwhile book, and Mamah is an interesting figure. Yet the end is grisly, sudden, and unexamined. I'm left cold as the book ends.

I agree with another review I read on goodreads that the book was good-but-not-great...it moved a little too slowly, and I definitely had a hard time seeing FLW's architecture through the metaphoric poetry employed in the literature. 
 Still, any book about feminism in any form is going to be a winner with me, and the narrative surrounding Mamah's incredible struggle with the choices she made was wonderfully urgent and engaging. Mostly I'm still reeling from the ending...I knew NOTHING about what was going to happen and it hit me like a ton of bricks.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Painful. I assume that Nancy Horan, on learning about the tragic story of Mamah Borthwick and Frank Lloyd Wright sought to put together a novel that described this relationship and brought compassion and some level of enlightenment to the situation. However, while the first few chapters of their relationship and building the house in Oak Park are interesting, the remainder is quite banal, until the end, which is tragic. It's tragic but no more emotionally draining than reading the actual story out of the NYT archives, because this novel didn't build any affinity towards either Mamah or FLW. In fact, it served the opposite effect. I'm really confused as to why it's so highly reviewed.
A fascinating, heart-wrenching story full of interesting facts about FLW. LOVED this book!

Loving Frank is a treasure. This book is more than the story of Frank Lloyd Wright and his mistress, Mamah Borthwick, it is the story of a woman, who could be any one of us, trying to make her peace with her life, her surroundings, and her relationships. The text is beautifully written, there is not a word written that does not have a reason for being there. 
 I found both lead characters completely believable and sympathetic. It gives me tremendous hope that a contemporary writer, Horan, can write so generously on the subject of a woman's struggle with the role of motherhood. For those of the reviewers who dare to suggest that Mamah, in her time, would not have felt what Horan portrays her as feeling, I say, "hogwash." Don't think for a minute that the women of every generation have had and continue to have the feelings expressed by Mamah Borthwick. It was the women from her generation, thinking outside their roles as mothers, that got women the vote for goodness sake?! 
 Agree with Mamah's decisions or not, you can clearly understand the reasons she does what she does as well as her torment over the results of her choices. Mamah makes no apologies to society for her choices nor does she ask for any sympathy, she clearly just wants to BE. She's even enlightened enough to know that although she aches for her children, it is best to leave them to their daily life without her. She will have them in her life as they allow and will not place her own needs above theirs. Truly enlightened, if you ask me. 
 Do not this miss the beautifully written, thought-provoking triumph.

book_b.user_review: Great seat of your pants, keep you guessing thriller

sample_reviews.review_text:
Fractured by Karin Slaughter is a 2008 publication. 
 This second book in the Will Trent series, is a complicated case involving the death of an unpopular girl, and the kidnapping of her affluent friend, Emma. 
 Will finds himself feeling a little off his game when it comes to light that he and Emma's father have a shared history and Will must work on this case with a partner, Faith Williams, a woman who holds a grudge against him. 
 This crime story is complicated, sordid, and pretty lurid. The police procedural is interwoven into a complex family drama. Once more the devil is in the details, and Will eventually locks all the pieces together, to open a Pandora's box of evil. 
 This second installment was not quite as strong as the first, but it is still a very absorbing story, one that made me cringe on more than one occasion. I love how the story is cleverly woven together, piece by piece, connecting everything so seamlessly. 
 I also like the attention the author gives to learning disorders and the difficulties those who live with these issues face. Will, of course, is a prime example, and his expertise in these matters actually comes in handy. 
 I did kind of enjoy Will's discomfiture at times, since he seems so smooth outwardly, at least, most of the time. He is certainly an enigma, and hard to figure out. I thought Faith really gave him a run for his money and kept him on his toes, which is good for him. 
 Angie is not prominently featured in this installment and I am curious about the future of her relationship with Will. 
 I found the family dramas added a layer of angst to the tense situation, as the inevitable blame game began, and marital discord became public knowledge. It is also a little bit of a character study, not so much on one particular person, but on a class of people, who have become accustomed to having their way, controlling situations, and making demands. Emma's parents have no control over the investigation, but attempt to manipulate it, bully the investigators and pull strings, thinking they can handle this situation like they do everything else... with money, power and influence. Suffice it say, that when all is said and done, none of those things will help when dealing with depraved individuals. 
 In the end, this is a pretty dark and twisted tale, and a compelling crime drama. 
 4 stars

book_a.user_review: Didn't even finish this one. One word: BORING! Enough said.

sample_reviews.review_text: There is more that I don't like about this book than there is that I do like. I like the idea that studying ancient literature can be transformative. Certainly the Victorians thought so. But I don't care for the main character; I don't understand why he has no history and no personality. I also think the whole Separate-Peace-Lord-of-the-Flies plot about a group all betraying one another has been done to death and is boring. And while I appreciate the fact that the hidden roots of magic and psychology within one another are pointed out, the idea that failing to avoid transformative catharsis leads to crime and death is a gross overstatement. Generally I disagree with the apparent premise of the book and dislike all the characters, so there is little left to enjoy.

** spoiler alert ** 
 The first sentence is brilliant. 
 "The snow in the mountains was melting and Bunny had been dead for several weeks before we came to understand the gravity of our situation." 
 I had high hopes for this book-- it looked challenging, with terrific language, and marvelous imagery. The plot was also intriguing. The personalities of the characters were well-drawn and interesting. 
 However, that said, the language had a certain haughtiness. Despite the main character's scholarship, I didn't think anybody transplanted to a hoity-toity East Coast school from California would speak quite that eloquently, all the time. Even when he's talking about drinking like a fish or doing lines of coke. 
 He completely lost me toward the end of the book when, having been "the good guy" during all this, he displayed a misogynistic quality that completely turned my stomach. Telling Camilla to return to a situation where she had been abused, simply because her brother had become a loose cannon. For someone he purported to be so in love with? Nope, didn't buy it. 
 Add to that, it was at least 100 pages too long. It took me forever to finish, due to the tiny typeface and the number of pages (over 500). Also, the ending left me completely cold. If I could have given it two and half stars, I would have.

Jag ar personligen inte sa fortjust i laskiga eller alltfor spannande bocker, men for en nagot ovan deckarlasare ar denna perfekt. Den hemliga historien ar valdigt spannande, men den innehaller ocksa valdigt tydliga och starka karaktarer och det kanns som att lasaren ar en i ganget, och darfor blir spanningen mindre laskig och mer trovardig. Tartts bok innehaller flera overraskningar och blir aldrig trakig, trots att den ar 703 sidor lang. 
 Den hemliga historien lamnar lasaren med en valdigt mysig kansla, men ocksa ett behov av eftertanke och en langtan efter att fa umgas mer med karaktarerna.

I enjoyed this book, and I don't know if my reservations about it are enough for me to discourage anyone from reading it. 
 I sometimes felt that the book was too focused on being a tragedy -- it is by no means a happy book. I can't really say more without spoiling the book, but if the author had cranked back the dial on the drama-rama, I probably would have enjoyed the book more.

The experience of reading this book was odd. The characters were hateful. I was mostly bored. (Is it me or were all the juicy bits purposely skipped over while the mundane crap was expounded on in excruciating detail?) But for some reason I kept reading. The writing itself was pretty decent? I kept expecting something to happen that I could care about? It's a mystery.

I've been meaning to read this book for almost 20 years, since its original publication. Strangely, I think I would have absolutely loved it had I read it back then. Tartt is an extraordinarily gifted writer - one of the best out there at creating a moody, unsettling environment for her troubled characters. Having said that, I found myself putting the book down time and time again. Leaving aside the murder at the heart of the story, The Secret History reminded me unpleasantly of all the things I don't miss about university: aimless blocks of time, unworthy mentors, unreliable friends, existential anxiety and bad weather. But maybe that explains the book's perennial popularity - it captures a period of life that is unquestionably formative but, thankfully, fleeting.
