reference_books.title: When It Happens
reference_books.review_text: This book was horrible. I gave a summer reading discussion on this book and all my students basically said the same thing. It is predictable and I didn't like the book. I have to agree with them. First off, I had a hard time believing the main characters were in high school. They way they acted, you think it was seventh or eighth grade, not a bunch of seniors. The romance was too rushed for me. A boy who barely noticed this girl suddenly finds her attractive and then next minute is in love with her. Granted I will give the guy A for effort. Also, there was some teen issues that could have been touched on a little more than a brief mention. The main character's best friend's parents were at the brink of a divorce and it only scratched the surface. None of the parent-teen relationships were all that developed either. Lastly, what bothered me the mist was how the author wrote some of the teen age dialogue. Instead of I said, she said, etc or I say, it was I go, "So what like are you like doing this weekend." I asked the high school students and not one teenager talks like these kids talked in the book. It was a waste of my time.

book_a.title: The Tea Girl of Hummingbird Lane
book_a.user_review:
I enjoyed reading this book. I learned about an ethnic minority I never heard about called the Akha who live in China. They have an interesting culture and way of life. Lin Yan is an Akha, part of an ethic hill tribe in China. The book starts out when she is ten years old and goes into her adulthood. She falls in love with a boy and gets married but he isn't what she thought. She had a baby with him out of wedlock which is taboo in their culture. She doesn't want to disgrace her people so she leaves her baby at an orphanage in a city three days away. When Lin Yan is released from her marriage, she goes out to establish a tea shop. Eventually she finds love again but she has never forgotten the baby she gave up. 
 The other part of the story is about her daughter Yan Yah. She is adopted by an American couple. Her American name is Haley. I like how Haley takes an interest in her Chinese roots and becomes interested in the origins of Chinese tea. It was a connection to her birth mother.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I'm a little disappointed with this. I love a good family saga! But this was a let down! 
 My main issue is that its really slow. The middle was super hard to get through. 
 And, quite frankly, I do not care this much about tea. I was expecting some human drama, some character-driven fiction. What I got was 385 pages of tea trees, tea growing, tea benefits, running a tea business. 
 I enjoyed A-ma a lot (more of her please) Especially when she took off with the tea cake and forced Haley to chase her! 
 And I really enjoyed the look in to the Akha culture. I've read quite a few books set in Asia, but I believe this is my first book set in China specifically. It was definitely fascinating.

The book was good but it got slow there in the middle, like at some points I was totally into it and then it would just get tedious. There were just parts of it that felt superfluous and they didn't add much to the story. Also I thought that maybe the growth in the characters could have been more subtle and developed over the course of the book and it would have added more depth. And just what was the thing with her ending up married to some rich guy and then life is perfect, the ending was a little too much for me with everyone being great but it's fiction I guess. 
 I did enjoy the characters and the immersive writing that let me experience the culture and values vividly. The topic is such a relevant one of changing cultures and commodification through globalization and trade. The story circled back around in the end which was great and unexpected because I didn't think they'd end up meeting. I mean until like the last chapter by then you know it's obvious. 
 I would read it if you enjoy fiction relevant to the cultural and societal changes in the present. Narratives have a way of making us understand things more empathetically than we would otherwise.

Lisa See does it again with a fascinating look at the adoption of Chinese girls by American families and the industry of tea. I had no idea of the value of certain teas picked from ancient trees in some areas of China. And really did not look at the trauma experienced by some adoptees from China in the past 20+ years. I was hooked from the first to the last page.

I love all of Lisa See's books. I really appreciate all of the research she does beforehand so that the novel can be viewed as historical fiction. (At the end of the book, she details out all of the people she worked with that helped form the story). The beginning has some difficult "scenes" dealing with babies but if you can get beyond that, it is an incredible book looking at all angles of modern Chinese, Native Tribal Chinese and Chinese American lives (interconnecting at some point). :)

2.5 stars. A book about tea and adoption from China to the US. While I enjoyed learning about the culture and practices of the Chinese ethnic minority group described in this book, the adoptive parents and the adoptive daughters seemed like stereotypes. Also the Hollywood ending was too much, regardless of how much the author professes that without coincidences there is no story.

Lisa See does it again, another beautifully written story, this time about a mountain village steeped in tradition and superstitions. Li-Yen is a very intelligent young girl who lives in the village and goes to school. They usually finish that schooling then move on to picking tea leaves and helping their families make a living. Li-Yen's teacher talks her parents into letting her continue her schooling but she will still learn her A-ma's trade of being a healer. 
 This is a coming of age story and follows Li-Yen to adulthood. See writes her characters with such depth that I am sorry I've finished the book, I want it to continue. There are a lot of details about the tea industry also that I found interesting. This book will stay with me for a while.

Lisa See introduces us to the Akha people of Yunnan province in this story of mothers and daughters. Li-yan grows up in a tea growing family, in a village whose ways have not changed in thousands of years. When she becomes pregnant out of wedlock, Li-yan, with the help of her mother the village midwife, manages to get her baby to an orphanage to be placed for adoption. Her child, Hailey, grows up in a life of privilege in California. Li-yan leaves the village, educates herself, and manages to carve out a life of accomplishment, but never forgets the daughter she gave up.

Apparently, I have not read anything by Lisa See since I started keeping track of my reading. See is another author that I just haven't been able to keep up with. I know she has written several books in the last nine years and I like her writing. I just don't have time to read everything. 
 Thanks to the loan of an ebook from her publisher and Jellybooks, I was able to read the novel See is publishing in March 2017. I was happy to try a new story by See and I was intrigued by Jellybooks's notion of tracking reading. I hope I didn't throw their statistics off. I so enjoyed the book that I read it very quickly. 
 The novels I have read by Lisa See have all had a basis in Chinese history. I don't know how many liberties she might take and I don't actually care about the historical accuracy. As always, I am looking for a good story, well told and something new to learn. See provided all of that. I found her story about Li-Yan, her family and their tea to be fascinating. Although I drink tea regularly, there was a lot to learn in this tale. 
 I don't know if I will manage to get back to See's novels. There really are too many books out there that I want to read. In the meantime, I highly recommend this novel to readers of historical fiction, family tales and those who read to learn new things. See has done a good job telling an interesting story. 
 Thank you again to Scribner and Jelly Books.

I thoroughly enjoyed this book. It not only tells the story of an ethnic minority in China, the Ahka, but also the story of Pu'er tea which is an exceptional variety that originated with this tribe. Their lifestyle seems very similar to that of the pre-war Hmong, a more well-known minority. 
 The narrator, Lin-ya, is a young child at the start of the book. She learns about the tea trees as she learns many skills - from her mother, a midwife and cultural leader in the village. Her mother shares the secret of some special tea trees. 
 A plot complication is the very traditional way that the Akha desire boy children. They are also following Chinese law that says that couples may only have one child. This causes many problems.
I was shocked by the opening story of the twins born and killed. Beyond that, I couldn't bring myself to read so I didn't finish it.

book_b.title: Pride and Prejudice
book_b.user_review: It was difficult to get through the language but once i got used to that the story was okay. I didn't find it as great as it was supposed to be and I felt the relationship between Mr Darcy and Elizabeth was brought on too quickly. She suddenly decided that she loved him after despising him for so long and I felt the marriage was rushed. I felt all the marriages were rushed. I liked Mrs. Bennett least of all because I felt she was pressuring her daughters to marry and more or less taking whatever man proposed marriage to her daughters first. Some of you might argue, well it is the time period. Yes, the times were vastly different but I still feel there could have been more time for the feelings between the couples to develop.

sample_reviews.review_text: Alright .. I think I can safely say that I am not a fan of Jane Austen. This book is all about style. It's "delightfully" written. There's also quite a bit of humor and wit in the dialogue and the way the characters are presented. And, perhaps, back in Austen's days, this was a means to show the plight of well-to-do ladies (though there is e.g. Charlotte Bronte whose work is filled with so much more). In the end, it's a chick lit novel about girls falling in love with a mysterious stranger. Beautifully arranged like a lovely bouquet of flowers .. without any depth or actual content. Pointless and so utterly boring. I honestly hated reading this book and only finished it as it was part of a challenge. I also don't do modern romantic comedies/dramas etc ... I read books not for their style (or if I do it has to be more than cute witty conversation), but for their content. Something real and beyond silly infatuations. A pretty package with absolutely nothing in it.
And people enjoy this?

book_a.title: We Love You, Charlie Freeman
book_a.user_review: I had the privilege of seeing this author at two separate author events. Once in conversation with another author and once reading from her own work. So I could hear her "voice" when I was reading this book. The description of the storyline does not begin to fully identify the themes explored in this book; family, race, coming of age, and dreams deferred. sample_reviews.review_text:
2 1/2-stars, i think. for now. 
 the freeman family - parents, laurel and charles, and daughters, charlotte (14) and callie (9) - accept an offer to live at a research institute, integrating a young male chimpanzee (charlie) into their family with the goal of teaching him communication through the use of sign language. the freemans are an african-american family. all of the employees of the research centre are white, and the town they relocate to is predominantly white. charles is given a job outside of the centre, teaching at the local high school (which charlotte attends), while laurel becomes the primary caregiver and teacher to charlie. though none of the freemans are deaf, they are fluent in ASL - language charlotte learned as a younger child as she grew to distrust spoken language, and spent time refusing to speak. woven into the alternating perspectives of the freemans' stories in 1990 is the voice of a woman in 1929 who served as one of the first 'specimens' for the institute's first director. the institute's unethical and racist studies come to light in both timeframes. 
 so there is a lot going on in this debut novel. greenidge covers some big issues: racism, language and communication, history, sexuality, family dynamics, science and religion. in so many ways this is a very timely book and it was a mostly interesting read. i liked greenidge's style very much and was pretty well all in for the story until i hit the open letter from julia toneybee-leroy, founder of the toneybee institute. this open letter totally bisected the story for me and nearly lost me. i understand its purpose, and the voice was certainly distinct... but it completely took away from the flow of the reading for me. i also felt for all the importance language and communication were given in the book they hung as loose threads by the end (unlike, say, Embassytown). i found myself thinking a lot about the ending of The Grapes of Wrath while reading WLYCF. psychologically, morally and socially, there is a lot to think about and unpack in we love you charlie freeman. 
 i've become a fan of greenidge's in 2016 - google her to read some of the wonderful essays she's had published online this year! she is a very thoughtful, smart, and sensitive writer. i look forward to her next novel and so wish i loved WLYCF more. though, perhaps it will stick with me - i am actually hoping that will happen, as it does sometimes with reads: the more distance from the book, the better it gets. maybe you've had that happen in your own reading too?
This book had so much potential, I was pretty disappointed.

This is a tough one for me. The ideas presented in We Love You, Charlie Freeman are ones that don't get explored much in fiction and definitely need to - we need to see more novels explore race in complex ways, to look at how racism has, and continues to be, such a huge part of the culture, but a part that we don't want to talk about, we don't want to examine, especially within our own hearts and minds. I love that this book does that. I love that this book takes racism and throws it in the readers' faces - and the characters' faces - and says, "look at me! I'm here! I'm a problem! You must figure out a way to talk about and address and maybe attempt to resolve me!". While I love all of that, I didn't love how the novel itself came together in a lot of ways. 
 Part of the issue for me was the chimp stuff was really, truly dark. I was expecting the family/chimp dynamic to be similar to a few other novels I've read on the subject, novels that portray this relationship as that of a family - perhaps the chimp becomes like a sibling to the kids in the family, or at the very least like a beloved family dog, part of the family in a very concrete way. That didn't happen here. I get why it couldn't happen, not just for the animal research part of the story but also for the greater arc of the story Greenidge was telling about this family, but it just was not fun to read about. This chimp, Charlie, did not like anyone in the family except for the mother, who he was of course obsessed with. This led to there being this level of tension just under the surface, in every single interaction between any two members of this family. It just felt so uncomfortable, and dangerous, because who knows what Charlie was capable of. I can also say that this feeling shows how talented of a writer Greenidge is, but in my case I just didn't enjoy feeling that way throughout almost the entire book. 
 I did like how we saw this story from multiple points of view, and multiple time periods. I also liked how Charlotte's sexuality was explored, but not in a showy way or like the author was trying to make a point, it was just part of her coming of age and growing up and figuring out who she is, what she likes, etc. 
 Like I said, We Love You Charlie Freeman is really a difficult one for me to "review". Greenidge tried to do a lot with the book and I think she was successful in some areas, in others, not so much. I do plan to keep an eye out for her as an author, because I think she's got excellent ideas and will continue to write smart, interesting books that push the envelope.

This book was so good. It has had so many great reviews and I love when I can get on board with something so many people love. I love characters that get in my head and stick with me and this book's characters all were brought to life in a way that was palpable.

I really liked the pacing of the story, changing POV, different voices, all good. This book got bumped to the top of my to-read list as a finalist in The Morning News Tournament of Books. Several of the books' central themes concern the history of racism in the US. Compared to Homegoing and The Underground Railroad, both of which are favored to win the tournament (and both of which have been much more widely recognized), all of the characters in We Love You Charlie Freeman called out to me, felt fresh to me, and moved me. To me, that's what makes a book. I love you, Kaitlyn Greenidge.

I reeealllly liked this, its characters make bad decisions and hurt each other in ways that are not contrived for the story. I could have used more of the 1929 story and more of Callie's inner life, just more of things, because I wanted more of this brutal and delicate world.

3.5. Not a big fan of chimps in fiction, but this was compelling, had interesting themes, was easy to read if slightly ominous in tone, and had a great ending I did not expect. I enjoyed it more than the recent novel by Karen Joy Fowler.

Finally digging into my Tournament of Books 2017 stack. 
 Charlie is a monkey who lives with the Freeman family at the Toneybee Institute for vague science experiment reasons that are never fully explained. 
 With this premise, my mind immediately went to "We are All Completely Beside Ourselves." Didn't I just read a monkey sibling book for this tournament? Instead of an exploration of human-animal relationships, though, Charlie serves as a catalyst for the dissolution of the Freeman family unit. His incessant needs expose and exacerbate the Freemans' problems. 
 The family's daughters, Charlotte and Callie, serve as the point-of-view narrators, taking opposing positions toward their unruly new housemate. Charlotte struggles to make friends as one of the few black students in a mostly white school, and unearths the racist history of the institute. 
 I was impressed by how many moving pieces and complex themes that Greenidge pulled together here. The book also flashes back in time to the institute's early years, as Charlotte gradually learns more secrets. This thread added a lot of complexity to what otherwise would have been a more straightforward family drama, but the pieces didn't always come together neatly.

I liked the sound of this book more than I liked the actual book. I wanted to like it much more, as I very much enjoy the parsing out of race relations and ways that people deal with that legacy, and I really liked the premise of a 90s family teaching sign language to a chimpanzee, especially from the linguistic end of things. But the end result focused very little on language, every major character seemed hopelessly harmed (rightfully so, but oi!) by the traumatic experience, and I felt that the blending of the two stories only ended up resolving one of those stories. There was much unfulfilled promise and I felt a little left behind, not quite understanding some of the praise heaped upon the book. I would read more by Greenidge, as her development of characters and pacing is solid, but her resolutions were unclear to me, lacking resonance.

I thoroughly enjoyed this book--smashed it in one weekend. There are clear nods to Beloved and Gloria Naylor's work, but it's such a unique story and plot. The writing was lovely--Greenidge might be my new favorite author next to Jesmyn Ward. I got it from the library but I think I want it in my standing collection. It was that good.

book_b.user_review:

sample_reviews.review_text: There is a definite disconnect between the title and the story if there is one. Since it is about one black dress, I figured it would be like "Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants." Not so much. I do know that the first two chapters are about men, the one who designed the dress and then some actor. Finally, we get to one of the apparently nine women that wear the infamous dress but by this point, I simply don't care anymore. There is no flow to the story at all. The Prologue and Chapter 1 seem out of order. As is, I struggled to finish.

Full disclosure: I received this novel as a Goodreads First Reads giveaway, but that in no way affected this review (although I am so glad I had this opportunity to be one of its first readers as I loved it and its subject matter). 
 The "IT" dress...the little black dress that is magic. This IS the story. And the women who get to wear it and how it affects their life (or feel it does). Although titled "Nine Women, One Dress" (and nine women do appear in the story), interwoven between these women, are the tales of three women: Felicia, Andie, and Natalie, and how this LBD really affects them. Their lives are forever changed in this story as this dress passes through their hands in some manner. 
 Yet, it is also the story of Morris Siegel, the designer of this Max Hammer dress, and it is his story that provides some of the more poignant moments of the book (at least for this reader). 
 Throughout the novel, there are moments of humor, poignancy, and more as each woman is transformed as is appropriate to their situation. Friends, family, business associates, and acquaintances all play into these stories as well making for a wonderful reading experience. 
 Quotes to remember: "A beautiful dress holds a little bit of magic in it." (p. 256) 
 "What is important in a dress is the woman who is wearing it." (from Yves Saint Laurent...the epigraph) 
 As an aside, I understand the power of a LBD. I had the perfect one (not unlike the one (except with three-quarter length sleeves) pictured on the book jacket) until it disappeared over thirty years ago. I still mourn its loss despite the fact that my closet contains at least eight black dresses, all different. 
 Although I read giveaway books in the order received, I must admit I jumped this one ahead of a few others because of the description about the story line of this one perfect little black dress and the women who experience the magic...thanks to the publisher for the novel.

3.5. I picked this up at World Book Night and was spurred to read it after seeing Didi's 4 star review. It's very well-written (and presumably well translated). Schlink's style verges on floral, foregrounding emotion without slipping into sheer nostalgia. 
 Something I assumed early on (the "deep secret" of the blurb) turned out to be the big reveal, which dampened my enjoyment somewhat. Schlink is great at undercutting tension of plot point reveals in favour of the characters' emotions and actions that follow, which I liked. At times, though, it wound up feeling a tad predictable. 
 What it lacks in plot it makes up for in fantastic use of metaphor and in raising ethical questions on a personal level. 
 With a few reservations, it's a great, short read, and definitely one of those good books for the bookish.

reference_books.title: Our Man in Havana
reference_books.review_text:
I am loathe to disagree with Christopher Hitchens, who wrote the introduction to this book, but as difficult as it is to denounce the opinion of a man who most certainly knows better than me -- I'll do it. 
 Our Man in Havana centres around British expatriate and vacuum salesman Mr Wormold - seldom referred to as Jim, even his nearest and dearest. Struggling to care for his 17 year-old, devout Catholic daughter, Wormold is head-hunted by the British secret service. In order to maximize his earnings, Wormold, rather than hiring agents, invents some. 
 The story is overrun with dialogue, which is often unmarked and therefore difficult to follow. Though there are some interesting characters, their emotional distance is palpable and demonstrated by their formal addresses. The story centres on Wormold but is narrated in third-person, which is often confusing. 
 Most exposition on the storyline is delayed, leaving that disgruntled, anti-climactic moment where you feel like you might have missed something. While this probably works perfectly in the film, the big reveals are sidelined; dulling the effect of the big give-away instead of enhancing it. At many points I felt that I could almost have skimmed over some of the most important moments. 
 Intriguing, but never quite entertaining, Our Man in Havana is a sleepy espionage tale for dads.

book_a.user_review:

sample_reviews.review_text: Hm. I finished this a few weeks ago, and thought it sort of eh. Maybe I shouldn't have read it so close to The Outliers, because it is sort of more of the same. Tipping Point is about trends that take off...sort of. There are some fascinating points to this book, but it seems like each chapter would make a better stand alone article than the sum of a whole book. I will probably read Blink at some point, but not anytime soon.
It was good food for thought.

Little things make big differences. What causes Hush Puppies shoes to make a come back, crime reduction on New York subways, the success of an obscure children's television shoe with muppets - little things. 
 This book has given me several ideas of implementing little things to market my book. Napoleon Hill preached the Mastermind Group. Gladwell has given me a description of three people I need to add to my group: the Connector, the Maven, and the Salesman. 
 Recommend this book to anyone who wants to make a difference. Figure out what are the little things and do those.
This was a well written book with a good balance of science, explanation and anecdote. I especially benefitted from the analysis of Sesame Street & Blues Clues since there is a 2 year old in my life.

Part of me thinks that because more people will read this post (being driven, no doubt, by their search lust for 'bestsellers,' and not for 'Malcolm Gladwell') that I ought to spend a good deal of time crafting a thoughtful and reasoned response so as to fuel my relentless hunger for more readers. But given that I'm not particularly concerned with how many readers I have, I'll write my review with as little care as, I suspect, Malcolm Gladwell researched his book. 
 Much like Freakonomics, Gladwell has written a book that could benefit from a combination of research, peer-review, and a good editor. Unlike Freakonomics, The Tipping Point does have a unifying thesis (and a remarkably logical, and hence dull, organization with repeated transition sentences and maddeningly precise topic sentences - really, if you're trying to teach essay writing this is the book for you), just not a terribly inspired one: some things become popular while others do not. 
 That's about it. The book's exploration of why this is the case falls into three neat categories (again, good for teaching essay writing): context, 'stickiness' and 'the law of the few.' Each category is "explained" through particular case studies. So arises my beef (as it were): particular, however compelling, case studies does not a proven point make. Case studies that illuminate research are engaging ways of accessing complex research findings. Case studies that serve as a platform for sweeping generalizations give the merits of academic study a poor showing. 
 I'm sure Gladwell had a difficult time in writing his 'afterword' not including the gleeful observation that his own book reached something of a tipping point by becoming an international best seller. Such restraint. Would that I were a maven, salesman or connector myself I might here begin a global word-of-mouth campaign defaming the book. As it is, it's just you and me. And while I know that my lack-of-mavenness means you may not take this recommendation seriously, I'll give it anyway: don't read The Tipping Point.
Would never have read on my own...but it was actually a nice little break from my usual fantasy reading.

I quite liked The Tipping Point. But it's not a masterpiece, as many people claim by rating it 5 stars. Far from that. 
 I think it's a nice read and Malcolm Gladwell certainly makes very good points about certain aspects of how epidemics are created and expanded. He uses good examples from both history and everyday life, but at the same time some of the situations the author mentions stretch it a bit. 
 Some stories, like the one about NYC's underground or the one about suicide in Micronesia, are amusing and interesting to read about; others, like the one about Blue's Clues are inexplicably long and could easily use half the amount of pages and the point would be equally clear. 
 In general terms, I would say that Gladwell documents some arguments very well and with examples that are easy to follow and to agree with; but some others are a stretch and they clear impact the quality of the book. 
 I'm not surprised that this became a bestseller. It has many of the ingredients; but it is not a masterpiece. It is a good book and I enjoyed reading it; it was time well spent. But in my opinion Outliers (from the same author) is more interesting.
This was a second quick read. I enjoyed the research and the ideas once again, though this time it seemed more dated. Imagine writing about this concept before facebook, twitter, et al!
While this book had some interesting points to make, the historical references about Paul Revere were inaccurate which therefore blew a hole into the point the author was trying to make.

Malcolm Gladwell interests me for one reason only. I wonder how it is that this man's book spent many many weeks on top of the new york times best seller list?(But then again look at the new york times best sellers list.) What struck me the most about this book is its total lack of in depth analysis. The question which lead to the writing of this book has to do with how fads start. He explains the process of what takes place in order for a fad to happen with the implication that if these steps are not met then the fad will not happen. This to a certain point is interesting, where the book disappoints is that he never gets into why one fad is started presumably at the expense of another. Suppose we have two things in the possession of a connector/maven, why does this maven/connector choose one thing over the other. Presumably these types of people also own other things and wear more than one pair of shoes or pants. Why the Levi's instead of the Dockers or the Nike's instead of the Reeboks?

sample_reviews.review_text: I listened to this book on CD during a road trip with my parents, and although I slept through a few parts, what I heard I strongly disliked. Although it's a coming of age story, I can only bear to watch a main character make so many mistakes in one novel.

I did not like this book at all. It sounded like it could be interesting, but it was not at all. There was no plot, no character development, no imagery or descriptive detail, and no purpose. I was particularly annoyed by the fact that the main character has no name. This may not be a problem for some, but personally, I find it pointless to read an entire book without ever knowing the character's name. This book had no effect on me whatsoever and I found it boring and tedious. It was obvious that the narrator was trying to get across certain points, but these themes were difficult to pick out.

Unique piece of period fiction. For a writer or a literary reader (or, specifically, devotees of Frost, Hemingway, and Ayn Rand), the book is a gem (at least in part). In many ways, very nicely done. The prose, at least to my mind, was artful and pleasing. My only gripe was that the book felt like three or four vignettes or short stories about a place and time, each well worth the time and well executed. But the whole didn't feel like a "novel" or a fully evolved "story" to me. Having said that, each relatively self-contained event was nicely crafted, and, more often than not, the conclusions were extremely gratifying (but not in the "happy ending" syrupy sort of way).

Fantastic book about growing up and accepting that your identity isn't as special as you thought. And with a far more interesting protagonist than Holden bloody Caulfield. 
 Seriously, I wanted to have gone to this school even though they would have flunked me out: my inner class warrior (never far from the surface, it seems) sneers at the rich boys of this novel and their petty rebellions but I love the environment that these students are in: it's a school that values learning and knowledge (the two don't always go together) but also places some high standards of behaviour upon their students. 
 There's also the lesson, repeatedly given in this book, that sacrifices and compromises to your principles often have consequences that you might not want or expect. It also begs the question, "Is the fall worth it?" Mr Wolff doesn't appear to know either, but he seems to have a better idea of what form an answer might take than a lot of other people.
I really enjoyed this one. Loved his style and reading about young boys in an all boys school. Definitely would recommend this one.

At Donald Hall's house, he talked quite a bit about formalism and style in literary traditions. He told me that a person can't really move into the contemporary unless they have read pre-1800's writing and beyond. In Charles Simic's classes, he taught a more delicate, elegant modern aesthetic. his approach was more arachnid, mysterious, dark and removed. his writing is about the hidden and therefore, he admires any approach used to unleash what one can usually only whisper about. while Billy Collins wrote to me about the meat and potatos of prose and the birds that are poetry. each man took a seperate approach to his literary style that i wanted to understand because i felt like they were different ways to speak the truth. i was curious about truth, what was my truth, how to use my voice in society; what is that voice, what is a voice? Kierkegaard, who I read and reviewed in 2009, said that a poet is an "unhappy man who hides deep anguish in his heart, but whose lips are so formed that when the sigh and cry pass through them, it sounds like lovely music.... And people flock around the poet and say: 'Sing again soon' - that is, 'May new sufferings torment your soul but your lips be fashioned as before, for the cry would only frighten us, but the music, that is blissful." This mirrors an essay I wrote in 2005 called Poetic Injustice, Learning to Undo the Poetic to Find the Truth of Suffering. 
 I understand the stereotype often listed of the poet whose drive to write started from this place of suffering. the critique is that eventually, the sweetness of their own words, they way the describe this pain through poetry is so fine that it masks the horror that they actually feel, trapping it behind a veil that sounds romantic and stirring. Pain, underneath it all becomes, unconsciously, the muse the muse that drives your work. Without that pain, there is no poem and this is eventually intuited by the writer. Being tortured becomes romanticized because when the poet is tortured, the poet writes. This discourages the poet from seeking health or offering hope. This falls in line with what Plato warned: Be careful of the poet, they can make anything seem beautiful but is that beauty Just? What he meant by justice was: is it good for you? good for others? 
 Well....What if you don't want to feel pain to appreciate beauty? What if life is hard enough, you feel plenty of pain every time you watch the news, worry about sending your kids to school, how your mother is doing, etc. What if you want to heal from past hurts? What if you want to find a voice to promote that healing process? What if you want that voice to be strong, interesting, nuanced enough to assure people you are not close-minded, friendly without being corny, smart without being condescending. What if after healing, you want to write poetry that can comment on both pain or beauty? what if you want that poetry to have depth not because it hides your pain but because you came to understand and empathize with those who suffer and in subtle ways want to share the lessons you found. 
 On the way to the airport on two separate occasions Billy Collins told me to remember that poetry is a bird. He says this because during his early twenties, he attempted suicide and he found that poetry was an antidote to suffering. I studied this idea for a while and found ways to implement it into my life (which sounds vague but I don't want to go into detail right now). but while Donald and I shared a cigarette ("80 sucks," he said. "Don't tell anyone I bummed a smoke from you," I said)...he told me that structure provides freedom. For Charles Simic's class, I wrote an essay called No Ideas But In Things, Formalism in Postmodern Art to challenge some of the ideas of the formalists. Charles Simic took offense to some of the angles I was working on while using Robert Bly as the voice to work out these angles and he wrote a poem about Robert Bly, honesty and suffering. Simic was kind enought to give me his Kenneth Koch book and drove me to the airport to meet Billy Collins for the first time. I still wonder about it all, though. Donald Hall talked about Robert Frost quite a bit. Because I have failed to find a voice that works as evidenced by feeling still alienated, I turn once again to the formalists. Those who play by the rules. I couldn't help but quote this passage from Tobias Wolff's book. 
 Quoted from the text: 
 "Your work sir," Mr. Ramsey said, "follows a certain tradition. Not the tradition of Whitman, that most American of poets, but a more constrained, shall we say formal tradition, as in that last poem you read, "Stopping in the Woods." I wonder--" 
 " 'Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening,' " Frost said. He put both hands on the pulpit and peered at Ramsey. 
 "Yes, sir. Now that particular poem is not unusual in your work for being written in stanza form, with iambic lines connected by rhyme." 
 "Good for you," Frost said. "They must be teaching you boys something here." 
 There was a great eruption of laughter, more caustic than jolly. Mr. Ramsey waited it out as Frost looked slyly around the chapel, the lord of misrule. He was not displeased by the havoc his mistake had caused, you could see that, and you had to wonder if it was a mistake at all. Finally he said, "You had a question?" 
 "Yes, sir. The question is whether such a rigidly formal arrangement of language is adequate to express the modern consciousness. That is, should form give way to more spontaneous modes of expression, even at the cost of a certain disorder?" 
 "Modern consciousness," Frost said. "What's that?" 
 "Ah! Good question, sir. Well--very roughly speaking, I would describe it as the mind's response to industrialization, the saturation of propaganda of governments and advertisers, two world wars, the concentration camps, the dimming of faith by science, and of course the constant threat of nuclear annihilation. Surely these things have had an effect on us. Surely they have changed our thinking." 
 "Surely nothing." Frost stared down at Mr. Ramsey. 
 If this had been Last Judgement, Mr. Ramsey and his modern conciousness would've been in for a hot time of it. He couldn't have looked more alone, standing there. 
 "Don't tell me about science," Frost said. "I'm something of a scientist myself. Bet you didn't know that. Botany. You boys know what tropism is, it's what makes a plant grow toward the light. Everything aspires to the light. You don't have to chase down a fly to get rid of it--you just darken the room, leave a crack of light in a window, and out he goes. Works every time. We all have that instinct, that aspiration. Science can't--what was your word? dim?--science can't dim that. All science can do is turn out the false lights so that the true can get us home." 
 Mr. Ramsey began to say something, but Frost kept going. 
 "So, don't tell me about science, and don't tell me about war. I lost my nearest friend in the one they call the Great War. So did Achilles lose his friend in war, and Homer did no injustice to his grief by writing about it in dactylic hexameters. There've always been wars, and they've always been as foul as we could make them. It is very fine and pleasant to think of ourselves as the most put upon folk in history--but then everyone has thought that from the beginning. It makes a grand excuse for all manner of laziness. But about my friend. I wrote a poem for him. I still write poems for him. Would you honor your own friend by putting words down anyhow, just as they come to you--with no thought for the sound they make, the meaning of their sound, the sound of their meaning? Would that give a true account of the loss?" 
 Frost had been looking right at Mr. Ramsey as he spoke. Now he broke off and let his eyes roam over the room. 
 "I am thinking of Achilles' grief, he said. That famous, terrible, grief. Let me tell you something boys. Such grief can only be told in form. Maybe it only really exists in form. Form is everything. Without it you've got nothing but a stubbed-toe cry--sincere, maybe, for what it's worth, but with no depth or carry. No echo. You may have a grievance but you do not have grief, and grievances are for petitions, not poetry. Does that answer you question?" 
 "I'm not sure, but thank you for having a go at it. "

This book reads so much like a memoir, that I was surprised to find it wasn't. The story follows a young man in his senior year, at a private boarding school, somewhere in New England. It is 1960. He is part of the "scribblers", a group that reveres writing, "book drunk boys". 
 Several renowned authors visit the school and in preparation to Ayn Rands visit, the narrator reads The Fountainhead and becomes infatuated with her radical ideas. This changes quickly, as she makes her appearance, along with her thuggish entourage and her Fascist presentation. It's both funny and scary. 
 The story takes a dramatic turn, when Hemingway is scheduled to appear and a contest is put in motion, for a short story contest to be submitted by the students and judged by Hem himself. Here our narrator makes a crucial error, a mistake that could have serious repercussions, in both his academic and adult life. 
 I loved Wolff's memoir This Boy's Life and look forward to reading his short story collections. This is his first novel and it was a pleasure to read.

A brilliantly written novel and a deeply thoughtful one. I loved the intertwining of the two stories of protagonist and teacher, both living their lives and basing their careers on the falsehoods others believe about them.

I finally picked this one back up after I gave up on the mystery. For some reason, I was in a much different mood and just loved the second half. 
 It was a little pretentious with all the conversation and comparison with famous authors of the day (Hemingway, Rand, etc.) Since I haven't read any of these authors since high school, and don't even remember what I read, that went mostly over my head. 
 I was a little puzzled by the wrap-up at the end, since it seemed a little detached from the rest of the book, and the fact that Wolff doesn't even really give much follow-up on the main character left a lot of room for speculation. 
 The last line of the book, though, made it all worth it. It was pulled straight from Jesus' parable about the prodigal son. 
 I did enjoy his writing style.

A story about a working-class boy that attends a New England preperatory school in the early 1960s; he has a great passion for literature, and aspires to be a writer himself. Wolff has created a sort of memoir, as well as a coming-of-age novel. 
 Honestly, I was expecting a little more... this was my first book to read by Wolff, I heard many good things about him, and read a review that highly praised it... yet, I thought there were many unanswered questions.

The Maze Runner series is truly among one of the worst series I've ever read (but not THE worst). Still, I want to read the third installment of the series, and I've reserved a copy at the library. What can I say in my defense? Something about Thomas's travails is drawing me on. 
 This is not a stand-alone book, by the way. Read the first one before this book. 
 Would I recommend this book to mature teens? Absolutely. I'm more fascinated the more I read, even while laughing at the unbelievably wretched so-called 'typical' dialogue of teen slang and the manufactured and misplaced 'swearing' of every other word, and at how these teens can waste their time to despise and hate each other so much even though at any moment they could be tormented, tortured, be severely hurt or maimed, go insane or die. They work together most of the time, which is a complete mystery to me. Why do they make plans on how to proceed when they have no respect for each other, besides hating each other to the point of complete lack of sympathy if one of them dies? The author, James Dashner, has not laid down any story background or provided any emotional development between his characters which would lead to their helping each other, except that which occurs between Thomas and a couple of friends. Indeed, they obviously hate each other so much I'm surprised the 'team' aren't murdering each other. 
 However, I am very curious what these mind-game tests are all about. Are they really racing through the Scorch (a supposed area on earth burnt by a solar flare from the Equator to Mexico), or is it an induced vision? Are they really dying, or is it all imaginary scenarios? Is all of earth really contaminated by a disease called 'Flare'? If you've read the first book, 'The Maze Runner' you have these questions in your mind already, so I'm not revealing any spoilers in asking them. 
 The characters are one-dimensional, and the conversational interchanges are excruciatingly awful, but unlike the first book in the series, this one has so much continuous action I didn't mind that very little else was explored. Instead of a maze, which they had to run in the first book, our frenemies have to run a more typical race from the laboratory to a finish line, where the winners will get to live if they are able to survive the burning atmosphere and the infected zombie-like humans roaming about. I felt like I was watching a bunch of scenes from action movies pasted together. It's very eye-catching and interesting to the brain. Who will survive? By the end I STILL knew almost nothing more about why WICKED was torturing and killing these kids. But who cares? I was enjoying this as much as I did the 'Sharknado' movie on the Syfy channel. 
 Parents, sometimes you simply have to let your kids enjoy something which will not enlighten, teach, or introduce anything meaningful. Do not stand in anyone's way if they want to read this modern penny dreadful. The key here is they will WANT to read it.

sample_reviews.review_text:
It almost reduced me to tear, and not in the good kind. 
 Scatterbrain fallen angel met scatterbrain woman. They're probably attracted to each other, but they denied it. They had sex. They found out that they're soul mate. Shit happened. End.

I wanted to like this book, but it was just way too slow for me. No action until the very end of the book, and the first three quarters there is very little plot line at all. The premise of the book is that fallen angel Raziel pulls Allie, a human, back from the fires of hell because he believes she doesn't deserve it. 
 The next 250 pages of this book are basically 'we are so hot for each other but must deny deny deny'. There's nothing else. It's just Raziel and Allie going back and forth denying their attraction to each other. Now, don't get me wrong, I enjoy a little anticipation and characters who are stubborn. But there was NOTHING else! No other plot at all! 
 Finally, 258 pages into the book, the Fallen's home is attacked by the evil Nephilim and we get some action in the book. Having said that, it was fairly predictable (even me, who can guess NOTHING usually, had figured out who the traitor was before we were told). 
 Overall, two stars. The writing was fine and I didn't mind Allie and Raziel as narrators. I struggled mostly with the plot - nothing was happening! I definitely think others might enjoy this book, but I need a little more adventure and action in my stories ;)

Have you ever had the experience of reading a book where you flip back and forth between too much background and not enough background? This book was full of that issue so it was definitely not in my favorite books. If we could have evened these random moments of too much/too little out, it would have done extremely well. Or at least better, hhmmmm. 
 Writing style notwithstanding, I did like the story and the overall concept of how the fallen angels live currently, how they came to be, and who the 'bad guy' is was interesting. Also the transition to the next book was smoothly done and I look forward to the next installment as well. 
 Alli was pretty much a bimbo in all regards, so the author obviously did something right so that I came away liking the story and not wanting to rant about dim-witted female leads and how they all need to be burned off the page. Scumps to Ms. Douglas for that. Although others didn't like Raziel's character, I thought he was exactly as he should be given the circumstances. That doesn't make him great, but definitely right for the part. :) 
 Overall an enjoyable story but has some weak moments in the writing. I am looking forward to seeing if the writer can mature in the next installment and really 'wow' me.

 Once again, Jill Shalvis worked her magic. This is the first book of hers that I have read that did not take place in Lucky Harbor and I have to admit, I may need a vacation home in Sunshine, Idaho. Especially if all of the male residents are like Dell Connelly. The sexual tension and chemistry between Dell and Jade was amazing and I found that the attraction they had for one another was completely believable. I read and enjoyed Slow Heat by Shalvis, and this was instantly available as a library ebook, so I thought I'd give it a try. It wasn't as good as Slow Heat, but it wasn't terrible either. The good: a St. Bernard named Gertie and a kitten named Beans! That is the best name for a cat. Also? No one gets kidnapped! The medium: The main characters were ok. I didn't love them but they weren't awful either, just sort of boring. Jade wasn't oversexualized, which happens in a weirdly hight number of romance books and Dell was your average brawny vet with a heart of gold (because of course). The setting in the Bitterroot Mountains could have been better, but for a contemporary cozy, at least it wasn't conservative either. The bad: The conflict was sort of dumb and boring (just two people having regular misgivings). But the worst was that in the beginning of the book, the two main characters already know each other and are already flirty. I like the meet-cute and the build up to the flirting with banter and the getting to know you bits. Starting where this did seemed like a let down. Beans! :)

Dell's and Jade's story. Jade a victim of a violent crime escaped to Sunshine, Idaho. Dell hired her as the receptionist/office manager for his animal clinic despite her giving no references. When they finally succumb to their mutual attraction it is with the knowledge that it is only a brief fling because Dell doesn't do relationships and Jade is leaving Sunshine to go back to her parents and previous life. 
 Probably a 3.5, because of the animals, but a bit too much on the denial for me.

We met Dell and Jade in the previous book, teasing us with their flirty banters, that's why I couldn't wait to reread this one right after I finished the first one. 
 Dell is the oh so popular vet of Belle Haven's clinic (or I should say of the whole town) and Jade is the receptionist. She arrived in Sunshine, Idaho, one year and a half ago, trying to forget a traumatic event that happened to her. She made friends but she closed off about this part of her life and didn't reveal much about her past. She's well organised and neat. She act tough but she's not as in control as she appear. 
 Dell is the man all women dream about and want for themselves or just for a night of fun. He's easygoing, playful and protective of the ones he love. It's funny because he said to one of his brothers he doesn't connect with others but he doesn't either. He interacts with others, but as long as it stay superficial and doesn't become serious. 
 Dell flirt with Jade all the time. Their verbal jousting is like foreplay and there's so much chemistry between them. Since he's the most eligible man in town and all the women are after him, she's determined to resist him. And she knows that she's only there temporarily. But try not falling for a charming and generous guy who save animals lives and ooze sex appeal. With the help of Dell, she will learn to face her demons and he'll finally take a chance at love. It was interesting to see Jade regain control of her life and discover who she really is and what she wants. 
 Careful what you say in front of a parrot is probably an other lesson our heroine had to learn :) 
 Of the forty and so books I read from Mrs. Shalvis, this book is one of my favorite, and sweet and sexy Dr. Dell Connelly is one of the best hero she wrote. There's so much more I could say about him, but no matter what I will say, I can't do justice to the character. You have to read the story to see what an incredible man he is.

Still really enjoyed this book, but not as much as Animal Magnetism. Dell and Jade have some great chemistry, and he is a real sweetie, but for some reason I didn't like Jade as much. I understand how she was traumatized by the robbery in her former life, but she seemed to hold onto it a bit too long. Also, I think if she was going to home in the end (until she decides to return to Dell) she should have been there longer. I wanted her to go back to the office and face her fears, but she doesn't, so her choosing Dell seems almost an escape from having to face her troubles.

 Nearly Boswell used to have money. Then her father disappeared; her mother became a strip-tease dancer; they moved into a trailer park. Now Nearly reads the personals in the local paper. At first, it was because she saw an ad that seemed like her dad was trying to get in touch with her. Later it was just something that seemed to express her own loneliness. 
 She still has a friend from those former days, wealthy Jeremy, and a friend in science class, Anh Bui, who is also trying for the same scholarship Nearly needs to go to college. And one other thing about Nearly- she can sense feelings when she touches someone - so she avoids touching anyone. 
 Add to all this, the fact that every Friday, a personal ad now appears in the paper. One that leaves a clue about a murder. All science clues. The class Nearly needs and excels in. The class that is studying Shroediger's cat. All ads that Nearly must solve. At first it is a hurt cheerleader. Then a dead cat. Then a string of murders. 
 Of course, in steps a new boy- Reece, who is the stereotypical bad boy; hangs out with the drug dealer in her trailer park; has a police record; and attracts Nearly to an extent she doesn't understand. Makes her want to touch him. 
 Science geeks take note! This is one story that will leave you sweating, looking for clues, wanting to throw things, but definitely engaged. Can you guess the killer before the last person is killed? I doubt it. 
 One last thing- who names their child Nearly and why???

I feel as though I have two different standards when it comes to fantasy. Either it must be fun and funny (in which case I will voluntarily overlook any number of plot holes - see: Croak, for sci-fi, Stitching Snow), or it must be serious, and of the absolute highest quality. I'm not saying that a book can't be both excellent and fun (after all: Unspoken), I'm just saying that there's a strange dichotomy in my head that awards high marks to books that make me laugh. All that to say... I like my thoughtful fantasy nearly flawless. Know what? Marie Rutkoski's The Winner's Curse met and exceeded those expectations. 
 Kestrel is a privileged young scion in a society where there are two paths open to any young woman: military enlistment or marriage. Luckily, she has a few years until she will be forced to make that despised choice - despised, because her true passion is music. But as the daughter of a famous General living in a recently-colonized land, her options seem few and poor. When she breaks her own rules and buys a slave at auction, Kestrel begins to see bits and pieces of the larger game she's playing (cheating?), and she's determined to win - but at what cost? 
 Oh, this book! It's smart and beautifully-written, and engaging, and... emotion-filled. When I finished it I felt like I need to sit still and breathe deeply, to calm my racing heart. That is talent. In Kestrel, Rutkoski has created an intelligent, resourceful and caring heroine who has been steeped in strategy from birth and trained by the finest fighters on offer. And yet, this is not a "fighting book" (by which I mean, a series of action sequences/battles described in great detail one after another)(though there are fights. the knife on the cover doesn't lie). No, this is a story about a good person weighing the odds, calculating the outcome, and making impossible choices. Kestrell is a badas$. No qualification needed. I love complex heroines! 
 This paragraph is where I usually summarize the plot. Just, NOPE. I can't spoil this book for future readers. If you want to know more, read it. It's flipping good, and you won't be sorry. What I will talk about is world-building. This is non-magical fantasy. What does that mean? It's set in an alternate world, and is vaguely historical in nature (no mention of electricity, no science that isn't present on Earth). There's a sprawling empire, omnipresent military, and a barbaric stance on subjugated peoples. Think Rome, but forwarded into at least the Renaissance era. And what makes it all hold together? Politics! I can't believe I'm saying this (because I'm an outspoken proponent of standalones), but I'm glad Rutkoski is writing this as a trilogy. There's so much to play with: economics, societal hierarchy, gender norms and expectations, and of course star-crossed love. 
 One comment on "love" - I was so, so pleased that there wasn't instant adoration in this story. I feel that in young adult lit romance is often forced on the reader, even if it seems to go against the natural inclinations or morals of the characters (and in this case it would have: there's a master/slave dynamic, differing nationalities, and opposing goals in life). I also appreciated the fact that the reader is never asked to fawn over the beautiful main characters. Kestrel and Arin are described by their thoughts, actions and conflicts before their pretty faces are mentioned. Maybe it's just me, but that made the characterization sing just a little bit more. Kestrel and Arin's growing understanding ended up punching me in the gut (in a good way), and a large part of that reaction was due to the complex sentiment that Rutkoski built between the two main characters. 
 In all, this is an intricate, intelligent book, and it knocked my socks off. Oh, and it's fantastic entertainment - I couldn't put it down. 
 Recommended for: fans of the fantasy and politics of authors Kristen Cashore and Sharon Shinn, those who appreciated the intrigue of Elizabeth Wein's Code Name Verity, and anyone who likes their fantasy magic-less and full of plot twists.

The Winner's Curse is so much better than I could have ever imagined! I have seen this title all across "Bookstagram," and when BookBub showed that it was on Kindle sale for $2.99, I figured I might as well see what all the hubbub was about. I also bought the audio version because the price was very reasonable with my Audible discount, which is how I ended up taking my journey through the book. My thought was if I didn't like it, at least it wouldn't have cost so much that I regretted the buy. I'm pleased to say that I don't regret a single cent spent, and now I just want a hardback edition. 
 That said, while I had seen The Winner's Curse on Instagram accounts all over the world, I had not seen anything that the book was about. From the cover (with the lovely blonde in the pink gown), I suspected it would be a high-society novel, remiscent of the Luxe series, dripping romance and scandal. That... is not what The Winner's Curse turned out to be, and I am a bit thankful, honestly. There is high society - Kestrel is a general's daughter living a very cushy lifestyle. There is a bit of scandal and a be-all-end-all romance, but there is also political intrigue and subterfuge and war. The romance, which could be annoying, is well actually played. 
 With some hesitance, I have to wonder if Marie Rutoski sat down and thought, "I want to write the Big Kids' Meal version of Game of Thrones." I hesitate to say that because I'm sure there are people who would verbally slaughter me for comparing anything to such an excellent fantasy series, but really... This book would be a great way to set young adults on the path to adult-adult political intrigue driven high fantasy. The story is far less complicated than Game of Thrones, and there is no magical element, but it is enthralling and captivating regardless. Seriously, this book was such a pleasant surprise.

While I did give this a two, I didn't hate it. I just didn't care for it. Honestly, I really don't have any serious opinions on it. Granted, I finished this in basically a day, because it's short and easy to read, but I also wanted to get it over with. 
 The world was sort of interesting in that the women were treated rather equally, at least militarily. The main character's father was a bit disappointed that she didn't enlist (granted, he's a general, so it makes sense). So that was kind of cool to see a world where the women are seen as competent fighters, and equals to their male-counterparts. 
 My main problem, really, is that I didn't get attached to either of the two main characters. I was just very neutral about both of them. I didn't dislike them, but I didn't like them either. They just were there. 
 After a while I did start to groan a bit. The romance got really annoying. It's just another forbidden love cliche. And I will admit, sometimes cliches are great; sometimes they work well. It just didn't seem to work for me. 
 I can get why this is popular. There's probably going to be a lot of people who will absolutely love this book. I just didn't connect with it at all. 
 Also, this is supposed to be trilogy? Honestly, the ending was adequate for me, but that might just be because I'm done with this story. I won't be picking up the next book. 
 However, I strongly recommend others try it and form their own opinion.

In a story of another world, of wars, slavery, and deception, Kestrel is a woman living in a culture that prizes itself on its military aptitude and strength. She is the daughter of a military general, lives life in luxury, attending balls and galas, in the recently acquired Valorian territory, conquered by her father's army. She is quick-witted and sharp, more of a military strategist than a warrior. She has power to be ruthless to some and compassionate to others. With her position and with her will she has the potential to change the tide in the battle between her past and her future. 
 In the beginning of "The Winner's Curse," Kestrel purchases a slave, Arin, at a local auction. An action out-of-character for Kestrel, she is tempted by the auctioneer because of the slave's boasted musical talents, something she also pursues and desires. Kestrel, conflicted by her purchase, attempts to ignore the blacksmith-singer slave on her father's plantation property. On the other hand, Arin works hard to not be ignored. Kestrel tries to redefine their relationship, perhaps as friends, and Arin aims to continue with his own agenda. They are on two sides of a war, fighting against preconceived notions of who they are and the groups they represent. Kestrel does not agree with the idea that Herrani's, the peoples the Valorians so recently crushed, are in fact an inferior race or deserve to be slaves, but she is also the general's daughter, in a race of people born to fight and win at all costs. A tale of intrigue and deception, of lies and truths, unfolds as a slave turns out to be more than he appears, and Kestrel begins to find out the true meaning of her own power. 
 Rutkoski begins her trilogy with a fantastical story, following a simple, but effective plot line that has rich surprises in her characters. Each character is thought out, has depth, and changes within the context of the story. Where some authors would fail in showing the complexity of Kestrel's life choices, she succeeds in additionally surprising the reader throughout the novel with great dialogue from Kestrel, wonderful thoughts and ideas, while also surrounding her with helpful supporting characters. Love is a main theme for Kestrel's character, but it is not only romantic love that exists in this story. She has great love for her best friend Jess, a great example of a female relationship that is hard to come by in some young adult stories, where the romantic love interest story is paramount to all. Additionally, Kestrel deeply cares for her father and he reciprocates this affections towards his daughter who is different from who he wants her to be. A huge sub-plot for this story is Kestrel's inner struggle between wanting to please her father, but while also wanting to pursue her own dreams. Rutkoski's strength in her characters comes from their own inner-conflicts. The characters are simple, but they are not overdone or underdone. 
 It is a great addition to the Young Adult genre, a shocking kick-off to a new series. We will have to see if Kestrel's ingenuity will keep the reader's on their toes and if Rutkoski's second installment can keep the plot twists coming.

I loved this book! At first I didn't really care to read it but then I saw someone compare it to eternal sunshine, which is one of my fav movies. I loved how weird this book was. The dreams were so vivid and fun! And alice was such an awesome Mc. She reminded me a bit of me :). With all her quirkiness. This was a really fun and fast read! I loved all the characters too!

Alice has something that make her different from the other girls of her age. Some people may think of her as crazy. She's in love with a boy callaed Max. But Max lives only in her dreams. 
 Or so she belives. When her life starts in Boston, things will change. 
 I hate to say that but Dreamology disappointed me. At first I was quite sure to give it an average score, but day after day and thought after thought, I decided that this book doesn't deserve it. 
 The premises of the dreams, the difference between a dream-guy and a real-guy, sleep and vigil, were all interisting points of start for a book. Alice is also a bit clumsy protagonist - even if the authore could have worked a little bit more on her - and can also led the reader quite well inside the book. 
 So, actually there are all the premises for a good, but page after page, reaching the end, the lack of logic became quite clear. 
 If you're not really interested in the romance parts, or at least you're more concerned about the dreams, probably you will not enjoy that book so much, but if you're a lover of fluffy romance I may suggest this book for you. But if you're searching for a complex romance, well, then the answer is: no.

book_a.user_review:
Fucking hell. Absolutely amazing. Mesmerising. Pure Awesomeness. Genius. Loved every little piece of it.

 This review is going to be an ode to this book and the author. I absolutely adore A Court of Mist and Fury. It was my favourite read of 2016, and I can't count how many times I've read it and enjoyed it immensely. 
 This book is everything. It encompasses passion, action, twists, guilt, sadness, love, a lot of trips, and loyalty. And really good sexy scenes. 
 Feyre is different in this instalment. The good girl who wanted safety over everything else has died Under the mountain. Now we are faced with a Feyre who is struggling to overcome the guilt she feels about the events that took place Under the mountain. It's not an easy journey. But it's written so beautifully that the emotions will take over you and you will be full of feels. And omg the feels. 
 Rhysand. There are no words to describe how slowly and deeply I fell in love with Rhys in this book. He is the most complex and beautiful character of all times. The dynamics and the journey of Feyre and Rhysand's relationship is stunning, and wonderful, and so so magnificent. 
 There is so much action. This book is such a roller-coaster of emotions and sometimes you are going to have to stop for a second to take it all in. 
 The romance is very, very good. I'm honestly telling you, if you are a romance fan then you need to read this book. The sexy scenes are one of the best scenes I ever read, and believe me I read a lot of them. 
 A Court of Mist and Fury is the winner of the Goodreads Choice Award for Young Adult Fantasy and Science Fiction 2016. That alone should tell you something, too. 
 All in all, A Court of Mist and Fury is one of the best fantasy reads out there if not one of the best reads out there in general. It has action, great romance, a lot of adventures, great freindships, loyalty, and two beautiful main character that you won't be able to help yourself but grow to love them with everything you have.

Rating: 2 Stars 
 That Boy, upon reading the blurb, will catch the attention of anyone looking for a sweet contemporary romance about a girl torn between two guys. It centers around the lives of three very close friends who grew up together. As time came and went, JJ (the girl) slowly realizes how her two guy friends changed from scrawny little boys to gorgeous young men. Then, the story begins. 
 The story was very disappointing. I was expecting something delightful, fun and worthwhile to read. But the sweetness, the tingles on the skin, and the knots in the belly I was hoping to feel was not there. The supposed love triangle was bland and boring. The story seemed to drag on due to the wide time frame it covers. To be honest, I felt it was too long because of some of the insignificant moments or parts in the story. 
 The characters, especially JJ, was unappealing. She was quite annoying, confusing and hard to relate to. And there's not much character development with her. With the guys, I was hoping to read something about a healthy brotherly/friendly competition to win the girl's heart. But none of the interesting and exciting parts of the sappy 'ol love story was present. They were okay for me, but crush-worthy? I think not so. They are tolerable. 
 I don't usually comment on the writing style because I'm not good at judging those kinds of things. But truth be told, this was not the greatest on the planet. It wasn't that good. It felt too conversational and informal. Not my kind of style, though I don't have any specific preference with the writing. 
 To sum up, I did not like it very much. But like I said, it was tolerable. But sweet, fun, dramatic and entertaining? No, not really. Well, not for me.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Ok, let me explain my rationale for this low rating .... I am a huge Oliver Jeffers fan (despite his odd method of drawing human noses)in fact Erin loved "How to Catch a Star" so much that we bought a copy! 
 I rated this one low because it seems to be a picture book marketed to adults (this is true for a majority of things) but would a young child really understand the message "of a broken heart and locking it away in a bottle!!!?" Granted some kids wouldesp Maurice Sendak as a kid but most kids would be puzzled. I made the mistake of testing it on my children ... Erin (4 1/2)was really curious about taking one's heart out of the human body and then she had countless questions about where to put it once it was out!! Eghads, what a nightmare! Jordan (13) just looked at me like "what the heck?!" I would by it as an adult as a gift book for adults indeed the message is beautiful and powerful.

This book was beautiful and would be a lovely story for adults but is obviously supposed to be a children's story. My daughter (3) didn't enjoy the story and thought it was "spooky" (her words). I feel bad about giving this book a low rating but my daughter did not find it enjoyable and it wasn't easy for her to understand the whole heart in a bottle thing.

Having read Oliver Jeffers to our boy for his entire life now, I was very surprised by the emotional moment in this sweet book about life and loss. Let's just say I was unprepared for the empty chair image, and was completely caught off guard reading the book for the first time last night. I ended up in a wet, weepy puddle at bedtime reading because of my own empty chair (my mother). Thankfully, I do not need to keep my heart in a bottle because it's so thoroughly owned by my son and my husband who consistently open up the wonder of the world to me. Oh, this book. THIS BOOK. We read it through three times and I just cried every time.
Very interesting. Not sure kids would get it, but I adore it. great illustrations, as always. I like that the girl was a main character in this one.

Wow. This book came along just at the right time. I have a little girl in my life who is going through something terrible. I will have to keep this book handy. This would be a great book to read when you have a child who has something difficult to deal with. It might be a great way to start a conversation. It could be read to children who have a friend who has suffered a loss to encourage them to know how to help their friend. Donalyn Miller says this is a deceptively simple book with a great message. She hit the nail on the head. 
 The little girl likes to read with her grandpa in a big red chair. One day the chair is empty. The story doesn't say he died, but you can infer that. She is sad and stops doing the things she used to love until someone comes along and helps her enjoy that again. 
 The author illustrates his own books. They're beautiful. I ran across his books by chance when we read one in class.
This beautiful little picture book will bring tears to your eyes.

I love Oliver Jeffers. The beautiful artwork and the simple yet heartfelt story make for another winner. I love to recommend his books for read-alouds, especially in that 1st-3rd grade crowd. Although a picture book, there is nothing babyish about this story.

A perfect example of the power of a picture book to tell a story that can be as concrete as a two-year-old and as philosophical as a guru, all the while entertaining and engaging. The end papers tell fantastic stories on their own.
Is it our heart that makes the world magically for us as a child but do we listen to our heart as we become adults?
I don't use the term "stunning" often, but that is exactly what this book is. Absolutely stunning.

sample_reviews.review_text: it's very different from Austen's other novels...much shorter and much more scandalous ...

Jane Austen gets her snark on. The epistolary style gets stale pretty fast, but Austen's biting humor and sarcasm elevates the novella to hilarious levels. Austen is never so darkly witty in her later novels, which is a shame because she does evil irony really well.

I had read this epistolary novel before, about 20 years ago. For some reason, Lady Susan did not entertain. I gave the short complete novel a 2nd chance. I enjoyed it. I made myself break it up into 2 readings. 
 A change for Austen. This time her main character is not sympathetic. That may be the reason I did not like it all that time ago. 
 Because the novel is short term, the pace picks up rather quickly. The novel held my attention, encouraged me to make big eyes at the main character, and to almost laugh out loud, andnthe writer is Austen, I will likely be returning to this short novel.

I had never even heard of this particular Jane Austen book before I went looking on my Kindle for free classics. What a delight to come upon it!! It was so much fun and so clever! I thoroughly enjoyed the epistolary style it was written in. The letters back and forth from the various characters in the book were so entertaining. It was tremendous fun to read about the dastardly doings of the coquettish and scheming Lady Susan and her equally awful friend, Mrs. Johnson. I loved the fretting and disgust of her sister-in-law, Mrs. Vernon. It was a fun and very quick read. I also just found...today in fact...that the movie Love and Friendship is in fact the movie version of Lady Susan. Perfect timing! Can't wait to see it. 
 My Rating: Fun!

I love Jane Austen, and if you do, too, you'll like LADY SUSAN. Be warned, however; this is an epistolary novel, and I'm sorry to say that Jane took the easy way out by finishing the story with her own comments. It really doesn't matter, though. I think Jane grew tired of Lady Susan, and just wanted to end her part of the story. I enjoyed the story that was there, but I, too, grew tired of Lady Susan.
#AustenNeverFails
Una novela epistolar muy cortita y divertida. Me ha encantado odiar a Lady Susan y a la Senora Johnson. Muero de ganas por ver la adaptacion que creo a ver leido por ahi que llevaron al cine en 2016.

Before Holly's Inbox and Bridget Jones's Diary, Austen wrote this thin little book of imagined letters to, from, and about Lady Susan. A quick read, it felt like I was getting a little glimpse into Austen's writing process as she defined and developed a character.
I loved this book. It's a strange read in that it's a series of letters but you'll get it as you go. Austen at her satirical best.

My last of Austen's novels. Had I known about this one prior to the end of the year, I would've attempted to squeeze it in in 2010 so I could say I have read all of her finished works! A very short epistolary novel and is her third work, but one of the last to be published for some dispute with a publisher. 
 I enjoyed this work, it was a different reading format from her other novels, and sometimes I felt like I could be reading a very modern book, not something written in the late 18th, early 19th century (except that we rarely receive hand-written letters anymore). Lady Susan is quite the vixen and her faults are great, but I like how Austen added a female character with questionable repute and moved away from the meek,mild,child-like attributes that typically come from Austen's pen.
