She was meant to be a cruel assassin, possibly the best in the Land, but for the entire book she just sat in her room reading. (boooriiing) and she continued to pass through the competition just because all the other champions were slowly being killed one by one ( not by her). 
 What about the romance? well, did you actually believe that a cruel assassin couldn't be involved in a love triangle? hah mistake. from the first chapters I could see that damn love triangle coming. 
 Everything was just so obvious. 
 A part from the fairies. I can't really remember much about that part - but I can recall that at one point Caeleaennnee (I'm sorry I'll never get her name right) starts to think about magic fairies folklore.... don't ask me why.

sample_reviews.review_text: I didn't read the entire book, so the label "read" is not quite correct, but it's definitely neither a "to-read" or a "currently-reading." There ought to be a label for "not-worth-finishing," although this is the only book I've ever started that would deserve it. I'm not sure if it counts to have ATTEMPTED to read this book. I am not sure I was able to finish a single chapter, no matter which one I attempted. The writing was an atrocity, and the story was false but published as non-fiction. I could have possibly accepted one or the other, but not both. Can I give negative stars? This is the only book in which, if someone asked me, "Well, could you do better?," my answer would be, "Unequivocally YES."

I am not sure why I like reading about people with completely screwed up lives but I do. This is James Frey's true story about addiction and recovery. Although, I have heard that this story may not completely be true but embellished to be a crazier story. Either way- entertaining read.

I liked this book for the same reasons I didn't like this book. The protagonist (the author) is very stubborn throughout the book and doesn't like to listen to other people. I liked that he holds onto his beliefs because for a second I thought he was going to give in and it was going to turn into a religious book, which I totally would have been disappointed with. However, at the same time he doesn't open himself up to any of the ideas of the rehab center. Basically, he is saying "I am supreme over any 12 steps of rehab and you should just have enough will power to overcome addiction." I wouldn't recommend this book to someone who is an addict for that reason. Also I felt like the author kind of brags about how he was tougher than everyone else in this rehab place, and although it's a memoir some of it I have a hard time believing. I have never had any real experience with addicts, so I really have no idea how that life is, but I still felt like it was overflufffed a bit. The other thing I did not like was the way it was written. Here is an example of how I felt a sentence would be "I read the book. I liked it and didn't like it. I wrote a review and hit enter. The review went off into the universe for everyone to read." There were just took many words and it was very simple. It took a long time to read because there were just too many unnecessary sentences. It was like he literally just wrote down everything he thought and it was too much for me. That being said, the way it was written also made me feel like he was just a normal person going through a very hard thing which made me feel more connected to it. Overall, I guess what I am saying is that I am on the fence about this book which is why it gets 3 starts from me. Happy reading!

A friend's sister recommended this to me as she knew I loved to read and she claimed this book had really helped her through some difficult times and she really connected with the narrator and the tough things he was going through. As I was reading, it wasn't terrible at first. Then it got annoying. Then I found out it was fake, and I got mad. How can you write a book about this experience, when you didn't even live the experience yourself? Here this girl is recommending this book to me because the main character helped her through so much, and he is a phony! He also was a pain, trying to be some tough guy when he really doesn't have many options. I'm sorry princess, but suck it up and live with it. He tries to be a tough guy in this facility, but all I see is a whiny, stuck up brat. You want to be seen like a man? Admit you need help and take it, not complain about it through an entire book. I put it down for a long time with no desire to finish it, but I felt like I owed it to this girl to finish what had helped her through a dark time in her life. Needless to say, I skimmed the last 100 pages because I felt more sympathy for the characters he met more than I did the main character. I'd rather read more about them and their stories.

Crushing, devastating, underscores the absolute futility of everything. I want to like the guy and I do, but I hate him as well. It is a sickening book and I never even want to look at the cover again. The pain in this one is a sledgehammer. It has a happy ending in that he has not relapsed, but I don't trust that it will stay that way, and I've asked the G-d he doesn't believe in to help him.

I picked up this book from a Goodwill for a quarter, I think. Given all of the controversy surrounding it, I bet that's all that most people would pay. Certainly, if I had read it along with Oprah's book club, I would be furious to learn that James Frey made up or exaggerated much of it. 
 I already knew about all of the controversy, though, and I practically devoured it. I thoroughly enjoyed the stream-of-consciousness writing style and plot. I suppose you can tell by now that I read it as a novel. It's a good novel. My question now is, why did he or the publisher try to market it as a memoir? Is it really that hard to break into fiction these days? Or is he just a jerk who wanted money, and was unwilling to place an "Inspired by actual events" line at the beginning of his book? I'm not sure what happened, but I still enjoyed the book. It's exciting, touching, and inspiring, even if it didn't really happen. I just wish James Frey had let the James in the book be a character, instead of claiming that it was really him.

This was a re-read in conjunction with reading Go Set a Watchman. Like many others, I think Mockingbird is the far superior novel. 
 The writing of To Kill a Mockingbird is nothing special overall. It doesn't require a graduate level English course or Cliffs Notes to decipher. But the beauty is certainly in the simplicity. It's a quaint novel, telling the childhood of the Finch kids and the various characters who inhabit their world - small town Maycomb, Alabama. 
 Much of the story is typical kids stuff - fisticuffs on the playground and sibling dynamics. But things take a turn when their father has to defend a black man accused of raping a white woman. Scout and her brother Jem must contend with heavy issues that force them to grow up and see their world in a new - and not better - way. 
 I appreciated the story from Scout's point of view. It lent so much color and humor to the the book. I also liked the world that Harper Lee created. It felt real, from the descriptions of the town square to the townspeople's varied personalities. And its message of kindness and justice for all is necessary and accessible to both young people and adults. I think it's a must read for everyone.

to kill a mockingbird is the kind of books that look so little and innocent but once the concept of the book settles in your mind it expands and takes over your surrounding, it compels you inside and repels you of the outside the story line was in escalating state of events were you start with a simple story of a little girl with her brother and father but you end up finding yourself holding a book about racism, female empowerment and the struggle of social classes from rich to poor and how they get along all of them in one small village the character's presence is so powerful that you can't help but get engaged to all the conversations in there, their individuality is so admiring especially 'scout' the little girl whose so brave and wise that you'd notice how unfair that age is being to her the way she kept standing up and out among the kids in her age and even among adults is what makes her the best character in the book moving on to another awesome character is her father the assertive decisive knowledgeable lawyer i envied her for having such father who is so responsible and reliable and that's not the only thing, he also understands kids i think all of us need such stillness and stable ground like atticus in their childhood and let's not forget about jem who incarnated the perfect idea of brotherhood he was such a protective adorable escort to scout in their adventures, all the characters worth mentioning and i have a lot to say and admire about them. the progress of events was very smooth and quick that i suddenly found myself a couple of chapters away from the ending then there was a taste of bitterness crawling into my mouth as i reached the last page of the book i felt sad for i will no longer read about scout,jem and dill adventures i will no longer learn from atticus or unravel the mysteries of maycomb county. they were good people i will miss them a lot.

I was fifteen or sixteen when I first read To Kill a Mockingbird. It was high school, that great bastion of superficial drama that I still can't seem to rid myself of eighteen years after graduation, where I first heard of Harper Lee's novel. I was much closer to Jem and Scout's age then than I am now. I can't truthfully recall, but I was much less jaded back in the tenth grade than I am now. I probably would have believed then that Tom Robinson wouldn't be convicted. Ah, the delusions of the young. Now if you will permit me one quick Harry Potter quote: "Fear of a name increases fear of the thing itself." While we cannot take Dumbledore at his literal word, for Lord Voldemort does not exist in Maycomb, Alabama, we can still extrapolate from it: that which is avoided, is that which is feared even more. That, dear readers, is applicable to Mockingbird. That being said, I think that this is still a novel of hope. It if were not for the children, there would be no hope for anything. 
 Classical novels are classic for a reason. They are well written and usually quite accessible (though I would argue the contrary point if we're discussing Russian literature). Mockingbird is an easy, if uncomfortable, read, told from the point of view of Scout Finch, a young girl. If newspapers are still to be believed, this is a prequel to Lee's recently published Go Set A Watchman. If true, it makes Mockingbird all the more remarkable. Such a powerful novel written on request? Impressive. 
 The children are the key to this story because of their lack of cynicism and hypocrisy. Why, poor Dill got physically sick at now the prosecutor was treating Tom Robinson. None of the adults, except perhaps his own neighbours, even batted an eye at Tom's treatment. They shunned Mr. Raymond, with his alcohol filled coke bottle, him and his 'nigger-wife.' What did Dill do when he discovered Raymond's secret? Not faint. He laughed. He and Scout did not run crazily up and down the streets when they learned the truth that Mr. Raymond put on an act that he was drunk to help the townspeople accept that he chose to be with a coloured woman. What a perfect example of the occupational malleability of children, and that hate is a learned and not innate response to difference. 
 I have only yesterday started reading Go Set a Watchman, and will have comments on that later, but I have read that Atticus is depicted as a racist. This is disappointing on the surface, however it made me wonder about how he was not depicted as a racist in this novel. Assuming this wasn't an error, and I have confidence in Lee as a writer that it was not, I can see one of two reasons for this apparent discrepancy, and they could each be true in part. Atticus was a man of great character and morals. Perhaps he was racist, but when called on to defend Tom Robinson, he did it to the best of his ability because he knew no other means. Setting a good example for his children would come of that. The other option, and certainly could overlap, was that he chose to act the way he did to help better his children. Kids learn by example, if he realized that his own beliefs were wrong but could not change them, he at least had the ability to show his children a better way to act. They say you can't teach an old dog new tricks, but a puppy is no problem. Atticus at one point tells his children that he got started late, perhaps too late to change his ways, but still able to provide a better path for the kids? 
 Way back in 1935 they could feel that change was coming, with the jury being out as long as it was, and not just convicting right away. We also see that it does not come only with the ebb and flow of the tide. We are able to effect change. When the mob shows up at the jail to kill Tom, Atticus is there to fend them off, but so are his children. Jem refuses to leave. Scout, for her part, singles out someone she knew and started talking to him, eventually breaking mob mentality and sending everyone home. Perhaps she is a psychologist in her adult life, because she certainly got through the anonymity thing. 
 I wrote elsewhere about fear, and repeat myself enough already to not want to do it again, but I think the same thing applies here. There is a reason they say fearful dogs are the most dangerous: fear is a great motivator but can cause us to act rashly and irrationally. And in the deep south, circa mid-20th century, fear of the 'coloureds' was high. Fear and hatred. The black people were great scapegoats for all manner of crimes. They were looked down on as savages, inhuman, trash, animals, you name it, what happened when Tom Robinson made the mistake of saying he felt sorry for Mayella Ewell? Outrage. How dare a nigger feel sorry for his betters, even if that white woman entrapped him? Disgusting. 
 Robinson represents the African American people as a whole, and the unjust system that they had to endure, are still having to endure. it is disgusting to think that fifty, nearly sixty years on from To Kill A Mockingbird, progress in many respects is going backwards. #blacklivesmatter is an important and sadly necessary movement. I am even more revolted by the ignorant asses who start the while lives matter, too whine. Not the point at all, you arrogant fucking pricks. Millenia of history have shown that white lives matter, and we still live it every minute of every day. Perhaps if we would take our heads out of our asses long enough to look around we would see that we are not the only people on this earth. 
 Unfortunately, justice for the likes of Tom Robinson and Boo Radley only come in fiction. 
 What angers me most is the total, TOTAL hypocrisy of the Maycomb residents. Scout's teacher in one scene is lamenting the terrible fate of the Jews who were being persecuted by Hitler, but could not recognize just as bad an injustice in her own town? The Ewells were only white trash when they were talked about by other white folk. If a colored even 'felt sorry' for her, he was guilty. 
 'Mr. Underwood simply figured it was a sin to kill cripples, be they standing, sitting or escaping. he likened Tom's death to the senseless slaughter of songbirds by hunters and children . . . " (p. 275). 
 And it is. It really is!

Read this for English literature class in high school. I'd say its an eye opening classic at the time because racial discrimination wasn't a commonly talked about issue from where I lived. It existed but it was always something everyone just swept under the rug. I particularly won't read it again for entertainment purposes but I wouldn't pick any other book to study if I were to go back in time. This was a great pick for a class study.

reference_books.title: Playing Patience (Blow Hole Boys, #1)
reference_books.review_text: There are several major plus factors for this book. First and foremost, the realism of Patience our lead. I felt like I totally got her her up until she caved to sleep with Zeke so soon after another moment. But still got her and her dialogue. Even though I didn't like Zeke objectifying women, I still got his motives as an escape of his life and home turmoil. I loved that this wasn't an insta love book but the characters showed development throughout the book. There were also some really great one liners that I loved. One example, "she was the sense of peace I'd been searching for in all the wrong places." Love that. The big negatives for me included there was no recourse for either dad and the time lapse between the last chapter and epilogue. I'm very very glad I have 1.5 already because I'm sure it's covered in there. I enjoyed the author's easy writing style and conversation development. I do however wish some of the grammar and probably autocorrect mistakes would have been caught prior to print such as "hole" instead of "whole" or "gas hand" instead of "gas tank", even one character's name was misspelled. In addition, I don't think it was until the end drive to Florida that I even knew the setting was in South Carolina. Because of the Spanish outside of the trailer park in the beginning, I just thought this was set in a large city in Texas or Cali. Regardless, a solid rock star romance read.

reference_books.review_text: Fun YA read with some elements to totally interest adults. Could see many political themes in this writing that would make an excellent English class discussion novel.

reference_books.title: Pulse (Collide, #2)
reference_books.review_text: Redeemed. Wow. so glad I waited to read Collide until Pulse came out. Whew! Gavin is redeemed. Hell, Emily is too. I don't want to give too much away but honor...that is the word for this book. Love, loyalty and honor in choices and commit to said choices. I love Gavin's dad. Love the line. "Honor isn't found in victory. It's found within the wounded reason that need you from the start." Love his final chat with Gavin too. "But whatever you do, never question the decisions the heavens make for us. Again, there's a reason behind everything. All that matters is what you do with those decisions. You can let them break you or mold you." After reading BOTH of the books, I rate this a four. As a stand alone, for either of them, not so much. But the plot building and randomness I saw in Collide concluded nicely in Pulse.

reference_books.title: Finding Cinderella (Hopeless, #2.5)
reference_books.review_text: Hoover really is in a class of her own. This might be a novella but it has all the trappings; a quick start into captivating characters, laugh out loud lines, memorable-I need to use that in real life lines, plot twists, strong emotions and a conclusion that ties up loose ends. Love it. Thank you for the gift Mrs. Hoover.

book_a.title: The Trouble with Goodbye (Fairhope, #1)
book_a.user_review: Have you ever wondered "How can something so monumental not leave any noticeable scars?" In The Trouble with Goodbye, Sarra Cannon presents the story of Leigh Anne and Knox who both have battle scars from life. This book develops really well rounded characters, beautiful settings and the strength found both in our own hearts but also the hearts of those we allow around us. In the end, "We're all somewhat the sum of our experiences, you know? But each individual event can only define us if we let it." I loved how two very different people from very different backgrounds trusted their hearts to open up to eachother without shame. The author had some very memorable lines that readers can find applicable to their own life as bits of nuggets to chew on without being preachy. She deals with very real circumstances and shows how life after monumental moments can change us both for the worse or better if we allow it. Being that this is the first book in a series, I was pleasantly surprised that a lot of loose ends were tied up and this could be a stand alone however, I really hope to learn what happens next for some of the friends Cannon created and hopefully tidbits of Leigh Anne and Knox after facing life head on together. Very good read with a powerful point.

sample_reviews.review_text: I think this book had some charm. Not one of my favorites, but I liked it. I feel like the love connection between Leigh Anne and Knox was sort of sudden but again, I liked it. (:

Publisher synopsis: One night can change everything... 
 Two years ago, Leigh Anne Davis shocked everyone in tiny Fairhope, Georgia when she broke up with her wealthy boyfriend to attend an Ivy League university a thousand miles away. At school, she finds a happiness and independence she's never known. 
 Until one terrifying night takes it all away from her. 
 With no place else to go, Leigh Anne heads home to reclaim her old life. A life she worked so hard to escape. On the outside, she seems like the same girl everyone has always known. But deep inside, she's hiding a terrible secret. 
 That's when she meets Knox Warner, a troubled newcomer to Fairhope. His eyes have the same haunted look she sees every day in the mirror, and when she's near him, the rest of the world fades away. But being with Knox would mean disappointing everyone all over again. If she wants to save what's left of her old life, she has no choice but to say goodbye to him forever. 
 Only, the trouble with goodbye is that sometimes it's about courage and sometimes it's about fear. And sometimes you're too broken to know the difference until it's too late. 
 The Trouble with Goodbye is a very good novel. It deals with A Lot of different issues, and does it with flare. Rape, Family Negligence, Stereotypes, Instant connections. This book runs over the gam-met. I really liked Leigh Anne's character. I liked that she was self sufficient and even though she was "broken" in her words, she was still able to love, trust and hope. She redefined herself and stood for what she believed in. 
 Awesome book. 
 ** Book contains some violence, talk of rape.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I really wanted to like this book, but at page 29 out of 233, I've lost interest. I always find myself looking up Sarra and following her on twitter, because I admire the amount of novels she has written and her work-ethic is amazing 
 But I'm afraid, The Trouble with Goodbye has missed the mark. 
 From the very first line of the story, had me confused. It shouldn't have me confused. I should get 
 grabbed by the world and character from the get-go, but it was like us, the readers, were plonked into this scene where we know nothing about the character or what we're supposed to be looking at. I was left completely blind, which isn't a good starting point. All we got was 'a gravel road'...what gravel road? What's around? What time of day is it? I like my setting to be set up before going into the details of the characters grumbling stomach, because all I saw was a stomach. 
 Still on the same page, the author's wording could come off a bit better. For example, when she's about the crash, to give the speed and action, the words cut have been chopped off and give it a much better rhythm. 
 The way the character thinks is not normal, because doubt anyone would think like that just after crashing her car. This is when the two characters meet for the first time, with "But it's his eyes that capture me." - Really? Really now? I mean, you've just crashed your car, hurt your shoulder and meet this complete stranger, and this is the first thing that comes to mind? 
 I stIll pushed on, but we just get her blushing on the next page because the stranger smiles....-sigh- 
 Sarra tends to info dump quiet a lot with unnecessary thoughts from the MC, thoughts that wouldn't necessarily happen at that moment in time, but just for the sake of the reader. On this front, it could do with another round of editing. 
 I'm still only on the second chapter, and the emotions from the MC are over-dramatic, I have a feeling its supposed to get a reaction from the reader but it just too in-your-face and unrealistic to be pulled off. 
 Another of my pet-peeves is not being told what characters look like, so all I'm left with is a body-shaped person with no features or face. I would like to have some details of the character so I am able to imagine them. 
 Also, one-page chapters? Really? 
 I think I may have to call it quits. 
 There was too many things wrong with the first four chapters to keep me reading.

I almost didn't read this book because of some of the reviews, but I decided to give it a shot. I enjoyed the book. I have to say that I didn't like Leigh Ann very much at first. I thought she was a puppet doing what her parents and friends wanted her to do and to be. I liked her just fine when she wasn't around those people. Knox, now he's a sweetie. He has had a life full of hard knocks. Leigh Ann is trying to outrun her past. One review that I read said that Leigh Ann didn't handle her problems very well. I have to agree to a degree. If we were faced with the trouble that Leigh Ann was, would we react any differently? We never know how we would react to a situation unless we are in that situation. We have to remember that Leigh Ann didn't have supportive parents. Knox is the person who makes her become stronger. I would have liked to have had Knox's point of view. I wanted to know what he thought. I felt that even though he was the book's hero, we didn't really get to know him. I wanted more of him because he was such a strong influence in her life. No cliffhanger.

*Received book in exchange for honest review* 
 Leigh Ann comes from the small town of Fairhope where everyone knows everyone and their business to boot. She left for college in Boston and hasn't returned until now, mostly by her parents decision. She meets a stranger her first night there after she aptly totals her car by hitting a tree and ever since that meeting she can't get him out of her mind. But she has family to deal with, friends that try to pick up where they left off (which leaves Leigh Ann feeling bored as her lifestyle had changed) and not to mention an ordeal that happened at school she had been trying to forget for the past year and a half. Only now what happened is being blasted in her face daily by the news and she's forced to make a decision; speak up for herself or follow everyone else's plans for her. 
 I liked this book. It was a quick read (I read the whole thing in almost one night) but it didn't particularly stand out all too much. I hated her mother. Like, couldn't stand her and I'm glad Leigh finally got a backbone and stood up to her for herself. Preston and the rest of her old friends reminded me of just pampered rich people and that kind of was off putting to me and I'm glad that she decided to go out on her own and get a job and make friends with other people that are making their own way and are individuals. I liked the relationship she had with Knox, he seemed very sweet and caring towards her. I will say that the girl that accused him and took it back, I thought it was Molly and it would be a tangled web. All in all, it was an enjoyable read and I appreciated how the subject matter was dealt with as schools actually do that and sweep things under the rug and it's absolutely not right. And I also like how she had to battle herself to decide to speak up or not; too often people just expect survivors to tell authorities and they don't for reasons cited in this book. So I really liked the thought put into that whole story and how it played out. I would totally read the next book on this series

I have to say, I feel quite disappointed after reading this book. 
 Sarra Cannon's Beautiful Demons was the first book I ever read on a kindle, and I remember falling in love with her writing and the story. Each subsequent book was just as captivating, so when I heard she had written an NA novel, I was thrilled. 
 Unfortunately, this story was not as captivating. While Sarra Cannon chose to write about a very sensitive and underrated topic, it lacked the emotional punch I can only imagine comes from the actual experience. Is it terrible that I want to feel the emotions of the victim? Maybe. But I'm assuming the point in writing is to submerse your readers into your world, and the point of reading is to submerse yourself into a different life, and I found it almost impossible to feel anything but mild sympathy towards Leigh Anne. Even Knox. 
 The whole thing read clinically, with large info dumps throughout. We meet a friend of Leigh Anne's and get her whole backstory. Leigh Anne and Knox open up to each other, and there's paragraphs upon paragraphs of their past stories. 
 As a whole, it wasn't a terrible book. Maybe the lack of heart-wrenching moments was on my part and my inability to relate to a character who has gone through such a traumatic experience. As far as content, it was written well enough to keep me reading, ignoring the fact that a large number of sentences began with "I" and "He." There weren't any grammatical errors that I caught, and the dialogue was mostly believable. All I know is that if I was her, I would have slapped my mother twenty seven times and walked away without a backward glance. Just sayin.

reference_books.title: From Ashes (From Ashes, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
When I started the book I was thinking - very similar to Because of Low by Abbi Glines which I loved. I thought the book had so much potential. 
 Cassi is an abused wreck taken care of by her best friend Tyler. Tyler - who protects her from everything and is the only person since her Dad died when she was 6 to care for her. So when Tyler leaves to school in Texas he takes Cassi with him. 
 Cassi is drawn to Gage who is Tyler's cousin and their new roommate. Cassi and Gage have an undeniable chemistry - though they barely interact and don't even really talk. 
 Some of the weird things for me - Cassi and Jackie are all of a sudden besties. Cassi has never let anyone in and I didn't really get the progression of the friendship. 
 Tyler's weird stalkerish ways - going from being so respectful to an ass in 15 seconds flat. 
 If Cassi was hurt so bad that she was unable to walk at times and needed to be stitched up - how did she have such a close relationship with Tyler's mom? 
 The thing that bothered me most in the book so far is the storylines that went nowhere. For example - Cassi's alcoholic Mom has access to $100K for 12 years and hasn't spent a dime but the week before Cassi turns 18 she takes all the money? And Cassi doesn't argue it at all? Another example is - Cassi is so sick and Gage takes her to the hospital and then it is 6 days later and he is happy his Mom is there but they aren't even at the hospital. What happened in those 6 days? 
 I found the jump aheads in time odd. I would have to go back and read it again because I was confused. 
 I liked the Isabelle and Jesse storyline. However, Jesse checking Cassi out and feeling attracted to her was a useless storyline. It added nothing to the story. They should have just hit it off as good friends. 
 Connor - a wasted storyline, could have had a meaningful conversation as concerned officer and a case that he didn't follow up (address the guilt) and as two victims and left it there. The rest was just junk. 
 The scorpion - a wasted storyline - totally and completely 
 The epilogue - we really just needed the synopsis on HEA, the rest was a wasted storyline. 
 This story covered 2.5 years but could have been written in 8 chapters if all the junk was left out.

book_a.title: When Women Were Birds: Fifty-four Variations on Voice
book_a.user_review:
This is a gem of a book, so small it can fit in the palm of your hand. But the size is deceptive, given the depth and power of its words. 
 Written by Terry Tempest Williams at age 54, the age her mother was when she died, the book was prompted by a single statement: "I'm leaving you my journals - but don't read them until after I'm gone." In Mormon culture, it was mandatory to keep a journal. I'm not sure why - perhaps writing was seen as a form of religious experience? But Williams' mother was a renegade because - get this - she left every single one of her journals blank. 
 As Williams turns blank page after blank page, she struggles to understand what her mother meant by it. After all it's not just one journal in question but shelves of them! She stares at the books, spines facing out, devoid of words, and begins to deliberate the possibilities. Her soulful meditation on the subject is a rhapsody of prose - some of it stream of consciousness, some of it blunt and deliberate statements, all of leading back to the mystery of her mother's intent. 
 In these pages you will find thoughts on womanhood, autonomy, motherhood, feminism, democracy, writing, love, marriage - yes, the entirety of our life experience. In some parts the author does seem to come on a little strong - part of me feels like she never emerged from 1960s feminism, still as militant and resentful as ever. And it was off-putting. Not because I didn't agree with her views but because her opinion reads as fact. Still this is a book about voice, so it's no surprise that Williams overly asserts hers. And if it empowers other women to reach inside themselves and live more purposeful lives, then in fact this book has made a difference. 
 I know for a fact that it made a raw and lasting impression on one reader - who was so awed by the book she read it three times in a row! The woman is Rebecca Schinsky of Book Riot, on the power of whose recommendation I read the book myself. Click here to read about her transcendental experience with When Women Were Birds. Her eloquent, deeply felt words will send you to the bookstore! 
 ~Kelly Massry 
 www.readlately.com

sample_reviews.review_text: Her prose is like poetry, and we share the journey from finding her mother's journals to filling her own pages. Soft, like a summer rain.
Loved it, it was a bit slow at times, but by the end I loved it.
This book was horrible!

Beautifully written, poetic meditations on voice. 
 What I learned: 
 A voice may refuse to speak. 
 Listen. 
 A voice may save your life. 
 Williams shares several personal stories about her marriage, her mother, her mother's family, and herself. I understood voice to be agency. It also includes all the invisible threads connecting us to each other and to life. And life speaks back to us in diverse ways. Williams is a master at probing beneath surfaces to find the pulse of the divine within the events she shares. She also makes an effective case for the value of silence. Both storyteller and poet, Williams is a gifted spiritual writer who never turns her gaze away from life here now on earth. 
 I have one complaint. When Williams is not writing about experiences specific to women (in particular, I enjoyed her meditation about the way women must find out from their bodies whether a sexual experience has led to pregnancy or not), I found her constant references to "she" and "women" distracting. Many men have sensibilities similar to those of women concerning spiritual power, the environment, and the longing for justice. As someone familiar with voices who limit their worldviews to women, I was surprised that it grated on me here. My wonderful, feminist son has changed me. Patriarchy is something apart from individual men. Some men may also have been birds.

I can understand why some people find this book deeply moving, spiritual and rhapsodic, but sadly I am not one of those people. I would never have been able to find meaning out of blank journals the way she does.
Really good passages about nature etc. But some parts too introspective.

If it hadn't been picked for August by the book club, I would never have read Terry Tempest Williams' When Women Were Birds. The memoir is poetry masquerading as prose. I felt lost during most of it, to be honest. I'm not used to diving that deeply into a real person's psyche... 
 Read the rest of my review at A Bookish Type.

I get it. But I didn't like it. I needed more. 
 read more...

I love everything that Terry Tempest Williams write, and this book was no exception. I loved reading about some personal stories in her life, but also about the voice of women and the absent voice, and the native power of women.

This is a very satisfying read as the lives of three members of a family are interwoven in a saga on the order of 'Giant'. Each family member is a standout in his or her own era. The research on this book has to be awe inspiring and it brought to mind the saga of my fourth great aunts who made that same danger ridden journey to Texas, which wasn't Texas yet, in 1836. Their families also went through the pioneering days among the Indians fighting to maintain their domain and their way of life, only to prosper because of oil and not cattle.

This book started off incredibly. And more than halfway through, I would've scoffed at giving this any lower than a "4-star" rating. But, for some reason or another, the last 200 pages sort of let me down. 
 Eli's story is the most consistently entertaining, and quite honestly is what makes the book worth reading. The chapters where he is Tiehteti are all awesome, interesting and I LOVED them. Like the other characters, the last 200 pages sort of slow down. It turns into him just summarizing large chunks of his life and going through real historical events, and it isn't very fun and lacks the heart of his early chapters. And although it isn't something I approve of, I could appreciate that if it was intentional--because it would make sense for the character. 
 Jeannie's chapters start slow, but are interesting. Then they hit a stride sometime near the middle, but eventually slow down again and never pick up. She is debatably the most complex character, but that is wasted on a lackluster story. Her arc goes nowhere and every chapter of hers is basically her complaining and doing nothing to get over her grievances, which got really tired and frustrating for me, as the reader. How can I cheer for such a complainer? Peter is also very whiney and complains a ton; he's sort of a wimp--and I'm not quite sure that was what I was supposed to get, but it's what I got. But at least he has a clear arc. 
 The ending, like the last 20 or so pages, was pretty good though. And for a second, I thought about picking the rating back up to a 4, but the promise of the early chapters was too much to give a pity-4. Meyer is in my eyes an incredible talent and can write beautifully when he is focused, but it seems to me the farther in he got, the lazier-- or at least more rushed. 
 Having said all this, I will definitely give his first book a read and I also look forward to future releases, because he shows tons of promise. And when he is at his best, he is one of the best I've ever read.
An amazing read. Epic and unforgettable. Told from three different viewpoints unfolding in three different eras, the story unfolds full of violence and hope, anger and love. I loved this book.

This book debuted with much fanfare and reviews that gushed with rare superlatives. The author was a James Michener Fellow at the University of Texas, so I looked forward to an epic Michener-like saga. Many readers claim the book delivers just that, but it did not for me. 
 When I saw that confusing family tree in the front, I knew that I would need a guide to follow the characters. That works sometimes, but not this time. It seemed to me that Meyer went out of his way to make things confusing in an attempt to be literary with the constant shifts between the diaries of various characters combined with forward and back time shifts. 
 There is quite a bit of revisionist Texas history here, too, the usual kind that makes most whites appear as racists, murderers and plunderers. I enjoyed Meyer's take on Comanche history, gritty social structure and superb horsemanship, but I have serious doubts about the modern day gutter language he puts into their mouths. I made it through this book and there are fascinating parts, but get ready to pay very, very close attention because the author will try to lose you. It's literary to do that, you know.

To begin, let me get this out of the way: I won a copy of The Son through a giveaway here on Goodreads. Despite that, this review has not been bought and paid for, nor is it in any way anyone's opinion but my own. 
 Well. That gets the nitty-gritty out of the way. So let's get down to business, shall we? 
 Welcome to The Son: historical fiction at its finest. A vibrant picture not only of characterization, but of the history and personification of the Lone Star state itself, this work is an engaging saga that carries across generations, and through them, unveils the cultures and people that helped to form the true uniqueness of the American south. 
 Our guides are four-fold: Colonel Eli McCullough, patriarch of the McCullough clan and the first male child born in the Republic of Texas; his son, Peter, in which morality finds a foothold; and Peter's granddaughter, Jeanne, whom expands the McCullough empire to new heights. No, that is not a mathematical error, by the way--there is a fourth character, but unveiling them would in turn prod too deeply into the plot for a review. Apologies. 
 This book is not your average Western. If you go in expecting that, you will be sadly disappointed. There is violence, tragedy, and unsettling portrayals of family--but it is captured in an authentically real voice and narrative; one will find cowboys, but they're not roaming the prairie with the easy heroism of "The Duke." 
 It also delivers what is, in truth, a captivating portrayal of the Comanche Indians, from the height of their dominion to the devastating about-face a flip of luck's coin can bring. The effect this tribe would have on the generations to come, and viewed through the eyes of Eli McCullough, a white man raised in this world, positively resonates through the soul of the book. 
 Each character has a unique voice, fraught with its own foibles and virtues; yet the book itself shines through Philipp Meyer's own voice, originally rendered to us in the equally powerful novel, American Rust. Here, it captures the untamed wild and brings it under modern inspection; he breathes emotion into history and shows why it is so important we should never let the past die. In some ways, it can come back to haunt you; yet, in others, the peril is so much greater for those that turn aside. 
 It can be jarring initially. If you go in without any foreknowledge of what you're getting into, the character shifts and settings might leave you a little off-balance--but once you settle in, you won't be able to put it down. There is power in the voice, humanity (in all its shades of grey) in the characters, beauty and terror in the setting, and a sweeping breadth of life in the cultures and landscape it covers. And the dialogue is none-too-shabby either--a fact that is paired with enough twists and turns to keep even the most suspicious fellow on their toes.

I find it interesting that I could listen to a book that has everything I dislike in the world, manifest destiny, racism, white supremacy, oil dynasties, excessive violence, corruption of those in power and greed. I do not know about Comanche history but I would be interested to know how much of their oral history is true to the book. My guess, not so accurate. How settlers perceived Indians is different from how Indians were, that's the way I've always known it, so would the Comanche be any different. 
 One thing, the word "fuck", in my traditional language there is no word for that. Intercourse, yes but not used in the context that was written. 
 I could go on but will not bother, I will let this go as another of those stories told by those that really "don't know".

There's plenty to not like about this book: the length, the cardboard-like characters and seemingly never-ending explicit description of unimportant details in the lives of these people. Then there's Meyer's insistence on perpetrating the age-old no-no among writers: telling versus showing. If you have read the book you'll know what I mean. 
 However, there is an undercurrent that runs throughout this Texas-sized tome that reverberates the timeless traditions and stereotypical hard-headedness of Texans since the rough-cutting of the state. It is steeped in the traditions of taking what's not yours just because it was there and someone else took it from others before. The more interesting chapters deal with Eli's captivity and Stockholm-syndrome like experience with the Comanche. Indeed, there's familiarity here with those who have read other works like Empire of the Summer Moon or Captured! or those who are familiar with the story of Cynthia Ann Parker and Quanah Parker. Intertwined with Eli's story are those of his descendants, namely Jeannie and Peter McCullogh. One can't help but wonder how in the name of Sam Hill did these people come from the same genetic pool as Eli. But I believe that is what Meyer wants us to think. It's the age-old paradox of the unfit and undeserving benefitting from the work of others gone before. 
 Overall, I really didn't care much for these characters, but I think that's what Meyer intended. And to that end, I'd say he has Texas-sized succeeded.

I tried; I really tried to finish this one but had to bail. I made it halfway through but there are too many other potentially good ones on my to-read list that I would rather get to. 
 This is another one of those books that nearly everyone likes. I thought I would too as both the style (multi-generational) and the topic (the old southwest) are among my favorites. Thanks to other reviews, I knew going in about the violence and sex. That didn't detract from my opinion as again that is the way it was and is to be expected in this storyline. I knew the main character's family was killed by the Comanche while he is taken captive and adopted by the tribe. It's tough to listen to and although fiction, it is historically correct. His story during his time with the Comanche is what I most enjoyed. The stories involving the other generations of the family had me wondering who was who. I could not figure it out. Nor did I care because the story perspective seeming bounced randomly between the three. To me, multi-generational stories need to be told sequentially in order to make sense. I understand this is a personal weakness. In the end, although this was not my style, I would still feel comfortable recommending it. 
 I am disappointed though, that I won't know the outcome of Eli's story. I loved the narration from his point of view by Will Patton, narrator extraordinaire.
The only appropriate word to describe this book is epic. I'd heard a lot of hype about this and I usually consider that a bad thing as the story rarely holds up. This one did not disappoint.

reference_books.review_text:
I initially intended to give this book 2 stars but hell, it doesn't deserve it and I decided to stop rating books too generously. And Hitched is bad. Plain bad. It has no real plot whatsoever and the story does not evolve one bit and having read the synopsis of the second book, I doubt it ever will. 
 The idea of this book was truly appealing to me but what I got was just...nothing. The author did nothing of her ideas and nothing of her characters. Everything is just superficial and centered around sex, which wouldn't have been so bad if it was handled in a better way but nay, it was all about the main guy's huge cock and the fact that the girl hadn't had sex in forever. I've always begged for book that didn't involve characters with a heavy past of abuse but this...this was way too shallow. The characters were supposed to have known each other for their entire lives and yet, it felt as though they were merely acquaintances and we never truly get to know anything about any of them. 
 This story is literally so uninteresting I don't even remember the characters' name. Read it or don't, it's your business but in my case, this book was a waste of time. I don't even have the energy to review it properly even though I had highlighted quotes to show you... I'm actually surprised this book got so many good ratings for what it is.

reference_books.title: All the Bright Places
reference_books.review_text:
It's time for me to write a review. 
 I read this book 4 days ago and I still remember how incredible it was. I don't think I'll ever forget. This book literally killed me. I, not for one second, thought about The Fault in Our Stars or about Finch as Augustus Waters. For me, it was totally different. As deep as TFiOS but with a different meaning: 
 TFiOS was about living. 
 AtBP was about dying. 
 Finch was such a mysterious character with a beautiful soul. He was different. The definition of different. I did not fall in love with him but I admired him. I loved him because he was precious and so, so, achingly different. He was beautiful. Glowing. And yet, so damn broken. 
 This book, these words, everything about it made me weak. it wasn't original, it wasn't even actually sad but there was something heartbreakingly beautiful about the words, about Finch. I fell in love with the book. And I kept hoping for the end to be different. I kept hoping that, somehow, Finch would win this. But he didn't. And that, my friends, is what hold the sadness and the beauty of the entire story. 
 I'd like to live in a world designed by Theodore Finch.

I think it was the worst story of the series? And it's the last one so I consider it a really bad thing. It wasn't horrible. Some parts, mostly when Simon wasn't thinking alone, were good but the whole remembering, nostalgic thing was boring. And the last bit, after the ceremony, was so extremely cheesy and predictable. I don't know if it's CC or Robin Wasserman but this story wasn't well put and pretty disappointing for a final.

book_a.title: November 9
book_a.user_review:
I loved the idea of having two characters only meeting once in a year every November 9. I found it refreshing somehow. It allowed us to see those characters, that we get attach to, grow, learn and slowly fall in love with each other. It avoids us the ridiculously annoying and unnecessary stops in their lives and brings us directly to what the readers are interested in. 
 I also adored the fact that the protagonist wasn't perfect. She wasn't physically flawless but she was yet, so incredibly beautiful. She had her "meh" moments and I couldn't entirely relate to her on a personal level but I loved her nonetheless. 
 And the sort of mirror effect with books in themselves was genius. It is very common for authors to create characters that also happen to be bookworms. But it is so rare to have them actually acknowledge the books, the plots and the cliches they read. It is so rare for an author to point out the flaws in their own books so they could write another. And to me, it is genius. Although the book finds itself in yet another sort of cliche schema, Colleen Hoover, as usual, managed to make it amazingly pleasant and worthy. 
 P.S.: The little Ugly Love references will make you smile like an idiot.

sample_reviews.review_text: Oh my god soooooo good!!!

Okay, I've heard so many good things about Colleen Hoover's books so I wanted to pick up something of hers and see how I like it. This definitely really disappointed me. 
 From what I've heard about her writing, I expected a dramatic new-adult romance that I would be able to fly through but I didn't get that at all. There was just so much unnecessary drama and so many eye-roll worthy moments I was beginning to grow so frustrated while I was reading this. I really didn't like this book. It took me forever to read and I had no motivation to pick it up at all. It's not even like it's a long book. It's literally only 300 pages and it took me like 2 weeks to read which I rarely do because I can usually read a 600 pages book in less time than that. Reading this just left a bad taste in my mouth every time I put it down and I didn't look forward to getting back into it. 
 I didn't like the characters. They were just so super uneccisarily cheesy and I felt like it was trying to hard to be 'every book-lovers dream story.' Every time I read about Ben and Fallon getting together it was like there was a neon sign flashing over their heads. I just couldn't take it. 
 Also, I've heard a few negative reviews about this book because of Ben's actions and sexual harassment and whatnot and I have to say that I 100% agree with those reviews. I didn't like Ben at all. He just wasn't appealing at all as a character and the dumb things he'd say that were supposed to be oh so romantic just made my blood boil. I couldn't stand him and Fallon and the way he'd treat Fallon and just their whole relationship in general was toxic and I don't like it at all. So I caution you about that if you're thinking of picking this up. 
 Honestly, I thought the premise was interesting and unique but there was nothing outstanding about this book. I was hoping to really enjoy it because of how many people rave about Colleen Hoover's writing and I know I have an unpopular opinion here when I say I just really didn't notice anything special or dare I say (gasp!) enjoyable about it. It was bland and I didn't like the style of writing much either. The writing and dialogue just felt stilted and I wasn't particularly enjoying any of it. 
 I appreciate that Fallon had scars because it isn't seen much in books (at least the ones I read) so I thought that'd be an interesting factor in the book but it was literally only used as a plot device and gave Ben another reason to tell Fallon how "f****** beautiful" she is every 5 fricking minutes. Gag me with a spoon. It's nice and all, but she shouldn't need a boy to tell her she's beautiful in order to realize that she IS beautiful. Whatever. Ugh. I'm done with this issue. 
 Honestly, I don't think there was really anything I enjoyed about this book. Some parts made me angry and some were just meh. I hope Hoover's other books aren't like this because I was really looking forward to devouring a cute, cheesy new adult romance. I don't even know if I want to give any of her other ones a shot now if this is what her writing style is like. 
 Overall, I didn't like this book and I personally don't recommend it. There were just too many things that happened in this that I don't support or couldn't stomach, but that's just my opinion. If you liked this book I am in no way trying to belittle you or your opinion, this was just my experience while I read the book. And I am aware that Hoover released a video after the allegations about the issues in this book but that doesn't make me enjoy it anymore than I did. It was nice she made the effort to speak about it and I can appreciate that as a reader. Welp. Those are my thoughts. A bit disappointing.

book_b.title: The Crown (The Selection, #5)
book_b.user_review:
NON-SPOILERY SECTION: 
 When I heard that Kiera Cass was to write a sequel series to The Selection, I was thrilled to say the least. I'm aware that this book series doesn't have the best plot ever created and that the writing isn't phenomenal but it has something. It made me go places and I loved the first three books. 
 Reading The Heir made me reconsider everything I felt reading the first trilogy but it didn't disappoint me as much as The Crown. Jesus. That book made little sense to me. It felt like Kiera Cass just wanted a sequel series and didn't think twice about how to put it out there. The two books were extremely short, which is good because it allowed me to get it over with faster than expected but they should have been longer for two simple reasons: BACKGROUND STORIES AND BETTER DEVELOPMENT! 
 None of the Selection boys had an impact on me whatsoever. They were all sweet and lovely. I liked them, at best but I didn't care for them at all. Not even Kile, not even Erik, not even Henri. None of them was outstanding in my opinion because Kiera Cass didn't care enough for them, didn't introduce them properly enough for the readers to get attached, to love them. Everything felt rushed and packed in one place. The only thing we got over and over again was Eadlyn, Eadlyn, Eadlyn and Eadlyn. For fuck's sake, I know she's the main character but you cannot write a good book if you're solely going to focus on one person. Not with a plot like that. Not when there's a Selection and certainly not when it's a sequel series. 
 We barely got anything of the secondary characters: 
 - Josie's character development fell from the sky at the last second and I couldn't even start liking her that the book was already over. She deserved a proper development. 
 - Neena was barely present even though she seemed like a strong female character that could have been a better help than she was in the book. 
 - Marid, although suspicious from the start, was just fucking dull. The guy appeared twice and disappeared right after and his charisma dropped from 10 to 0 real quick. 
 - Lady Brice could have been soooooooooooo interesting, she made me doubt of who she really was from the start and that could have been exploited but no, Kiera Cass just dropped her secret on our ass and left it at that. 
 - Ahren, baby Ahren...why couldn't he be used a little more? He's Eadlyn's twin after all. They have this superb amazing connection and Kiera Cass did nothing of it. This whole eloping-story-thing with Camille had no other purpose than to make my sweet baby America have a heart attack and I'm annoyed at that. 
 - Kaden and Osten should have been more present in a way, or at least, they deserve their own short story because the end left a good window for Kaden. Meanwhile, Osten is just funny so I'd love to have more of him. 
 It's like this whole book was made out of drafts barely worked on. And for that, I am so...so disappointed. I wanted to like this book more than I did and it broke my heart to face such a downfall. Although I cheer up at the thought that the last 20 pages made me smile more than the rest of the book. I'll talk more about those pages in the following SPOILERY section. 
 SPOILERY SECTION: 
 In all honesty, I didn't like the way everything seemed to unfold exactly the way Eadlyn wanted to. Like, the fact that all the boys had a solid reason to leave at some point even though 5 minutes earlier, they were all front-runners and ready to fight for her love. 
 - Hale and Ean being gay and falling for each other fell out of nowhere. I'm all for representation but Kiera Cass wrote this as if she just needed gay characters in her story + that would help to get rid of two characters who were in the way of her happy ending. 
 - Kile being banished was OK, I guess. I loved that Eadlyn made that selfless decision and that she allowed him to be happy. However, he was pretty much indifferent to her rejection even though he'd been eager to marry her, which doesn't add up. 
 - Fox was irrelevant from start to finish and the fact that he left angry was a good thing, it added to the reality of the situation. 
 - Henri was so sweet and adorable but he could never be her husband, they had no real chemistry because they couldn't communicate. I loved how mature he was at the end, pushing Eadlyn and Erik to each other. It was an amazing thing to witness. I wish it could have been him, I guess he was the only one I was sort-of rooting for but it was obviously impossible. 
 - Eadlyn being all infatuated with Erik just...it just...why so suddenly? They were never real signs that she loved him more than she loved Henri or Kile... so WHY? I know it must have been decided from the start but pulling such a move 50 pages towards the end was random to me. There was no real development to their relationship. They went from friends to lovers in a matter of minutes with a strong connection pulled out of the void. So forgive me for not buying into that. I like them both and I like them together but I don't like the way they got together. 
 I loved that Eadlyn announced a constitutional monarchy instead of a democracy like most would expect, it's a big step but a realistic one so it can work and I liked that idea. 
 OVERALL, the words I'd use to describe The Crown are flat, fast-paced but not developed enough. Cute at times and extremely boring for most of it. Most obstacles Eadlyn faced were pretty random and not necessarily important while the big stuff were totally ignored by the author, who could've done much better. 
 I can't believe I'm about to say that but I think those two sequel books were unnecessary. God, I was happy just knowing America and Maxon had kids.

sample_reviews.review_text: 3.5 stars

I am sadly disappointed in this book. I had loved the Heir and thought that Eadlyn's story would be so much better than her mother's. But this book felt rushed, as though the author had run out of conflicts to work with. Which is upsetting because the girl is the next Queen, there should be lots of conflict. And in the Heir, there was. But instead of maturing and being a Queen the country needs, the end basically says, "Forget what you should do, just make snap decisions based on what makes you happy. If you do, everything will turn out fine." 
 I know there is a bit of truth in needing to find what makes you happy, but not at the cost of entire kingdoms well being.

Well, I can't say that I really enjoyed the story of Eadlyn as much as the one of her parents. I'm not even half pleased if I want to be honest. But it was a pretty decent ending overall and I have to give it credits for that. If I could turn the time back I would have stopped at ''The one'', so I suggest you do the same thing ;)

Actual rating 3.75 stars. 
 This book is by far the my most favorited of the Selection series. Though the story is not as complex as the initial trilogy, 'The Crown' pulled more emotion from me than I expected. It is a guilty pleasure, a soppy romance, and was great escapism. 
 Its predecessor 'The Heir' left me a little despondent, I did not entirely like Eadlyn. She was cold, stuck-up, and a part from moments of a childish temper, fairly flat and boring in nature. But her journey through 'The Crown' made her endearing to me. It brought out her caring and compassionate side. The suitors (or bachelors) managed to drag emotions out of her and open her eyes up to the society she is slated to rule. 
 I was in a little disbelief at the ease in which the men vying for her hand left the competition towards the end, with little theatrics or heartbreak... it felt manufactured. I applaud the inclusion of Ean and Hale's fate. It came out of left field but added another dynamic and commentary on Illean society. 
 There are a few expected plot twists, and many unexpected. It was a nice surprise. As I've said about the entire Selection anthology, much of it feels derivative and trope-driven. But if you like a large helping of sugar with your reading this will go down smoothly. Like a B-grade horror film, or a cheesy Hallmark movie, 'The Crown' is entertaining and hits the bullseye for its intended market. There's a heavy dollop of girlie fashion, food, and cute boys to gush over. 
 I read the book in a day and it was easy to get swept into, especially with storylines and characters we've known throughout the series getting involved in the culmination. A fun snippet of nostalgia. It was an effortless read, and only something I'd recommend to staunch fans of this series.
It took me two days to finish this book because I FORCED myself to put it down to make the story last longer. I loved Kiera Cass' conclusion and I hope she writes more soon!

sample_reviews.review_text: Can't stand Dylan.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Madre de Dios! Yes, that gets thought a lot by our hero. Sadly, after a really good installment with Midnight Awakening, Lara Adrian slipped up a bit with Rio's story. 
 I did like the leads, but there were some major, unnecessary logic blips that bugged me throughout. Mainly -- how could Dylan not tell Rio immediately that her mom had told Gordon Fasso about the crypt? Bizarre. And she even thought about Fasso in the context of hearing about other people getting their memories scrubbed. It wasn't necessary to make her TSTL to keep the plot moving. 
 That and Rio getting the brainstorm that maybe Dragos's hidden offspring was keeping the ancient and breeding it. Huh? What caused you to come to that conclusion with absolutely nothing pointing in that direction whatsoever? Madre de Dios, Rio, you're a genius! Again, not necessary. Give 'em a clue to go on and I'll be happy to follow and believe. 
 And what dunderheads would leave the guy who's more than half out of his mind with grief, betrayal, brain injury ... inside a mountain cave with a bunch of C4 and expect him to come home when he's through? 
 While I'm complaining, why do ghosts have to be so cryptic? Is it in the job description of the spectral visitor? You must not say anything beyond that which will drive your visitation target insane. Except for that moment when we're getting kind of close to the end and we don't have time for ambiguity, in which case you can be as specific as it takes to skip over all that dreary deciphering and save the day. 
 That said, I did like the couple's chemistry, and I'll move on to the next book. I thought it might have been the wrong choice for Adrian to do Rio's book so soon, actually. It felt rushed to me and I thought we could have seen Niko or Chase before we got to Rio. After I read on, maybe I'll see how it was important to do it this way, but right now I feel like there wasn't enough time from when the betrayal and injury occurred for him to be ready for a romance. 
 I appreciated the emotion -- I did get choked up a few times -- but I got the icky feeling that Mom was sacrificed so Dylan could go to the Order unattached sooner rather than later. In fact, I'd though it was a lovely thing that Rio was going to stay with Dylan for her mother's last days (or I'd thought they might bring her to the compound where she could get hospice care but they'd be together and safe, too), and then he'd go back to work. But no, she was dispensed with rather quickly -- another plot point that felt rushed. 
 At this point I'm rambling and I'll stop, but Madre de Dios, Rio deserved better!

** spoiler alert ** 
 I don't know what happened...Lara was on a roll. But don't despair for that one lost star. I think the others will overshadow this little mishap. Overall, I think Dylan just bugged the hell out of me. She may be smart, but her attitude was annoying. The one thing that did make me continue forth in reading book 4, was our poor...sad...mentally messed up Rio. He's a great character and I think Lara kind of messed up in the way she told his story. Hey, maybe it's just me who thinks this way. 
 Our sexy warrior talks about his past, major tear jerking here. Then we get to learn more about his torment in trying to deal with the painful betrayal of his dead wife - lots of self hatred going on. Now we are onto Dylan's special ability. Wow, a ghost whisperer...really? I guess it seems to come in very handy - she can see dead breeds. 
 I do like the darker side of this book. In a bigger scheme of things, a very old breed -- the original and true monster of vampires was found. Notice here: Dylan's ability comes in handy. The breed warriors are finding dead mutilated breed mates and the ghosts leads Dylan to the secret lab. The realization here is that the kidnapped breeds are being used to harvest a new army of breeds. Talk about one sick plan...Dragos is EVIL. 
 Okay, book 5...I am ready for ya!
Was fur eine Zeitverschwendung. Alien-Vampire und Frauen, die eine alien-kompatible DNA haben, sind nicht wirklich mein Ding.

Rio is a Breed Warrior ready to give up on everything and everyone, including himself, after over a year of futile attempts to recover from severe injuries to his body and mind after a betrayal that hurt not only him but also the entire Order of Breed Warriors he once embraced as his family. He is suicidal and full of self-hatred and doesn't care about anything anymore except for ending his sufferable life. But then a journalist stumbles into the assignment his fellow Warriors left him to handle, he has been dragging on for months and now because of her discovery he has to go after her to secure the secrets of the entire Breed. His life has purpose again. 
 Dylan Alexander is an unknowing Breedmate, Her reporter curiosity and Breedmate gift lead her to a story that will change her life forever. Having known rejection and solitude in her life she has learned to be independent and cares only about her mother whose weak health is threatening the fairly decent life she has managed to build. Until on a tour of Europe, the discovery of a cave and an extraordinary man starts a string of events she could never have dreamed up for the newspaper she works for. 
 Dylan is curious, cynical, smart and stubborn. She is used to handling everything on her own and taking care of her mother. But then she meets Rio, a man who fascinates her while she should feel revulsion, if not for his physical appearance then for his emotional deficiencies. Slowly Dylan starts to accept what she is, the world she belongs to and her feelings for Rio. 
 Rio is a broken man, both emotional and physical. Betrayal has left scars on both his mind and body and his past and present both touched me deeply. We met Rio in the first book of the series and he's been appearing in every following book. The disclosures of little bits of information on his recovery (to know from what I recommend reading the previous books in the series) held me until I could read his own story and have a chance to get the whole picture on Rio. I knew Rio was damaged from reading the previous books but it wasn't until reading his own story that I realized to what extent. 
 Both Dylan and Rio are proud and defiant and their story is set up gradually and carefully, which I found perfect because especially Rio had some issues to deal with before he could commit to his feelings for Dylan. 
 Despite the fact that the story is set up gradually and carefully, it's still written in a pace that kept me going back to the book every minute I could. 
 Again the secondary characters play their perfect roles, enhancing the story with their appearances and actions. Two new warriors who were briefly mentioned in MIDNIGHT AWAKENING were fleshed out a little bit more and prove to be some interesting characters. I hope Lara Adrian will write their stories too. Sterling Chase remains an enigma, and a very intriguing enigma too. For me he and Nikolai are the warriors whose stories I anticipate with the most eagerness. The agony of waiting for Niko's book (VEIL OF MIDNIGHT, Dec 08) has begun with the glimpses of Niko I had in this book, they only made me crave his book more! 
 I can imagine some readers will find this story the least of the books up until now and I don't agree with that. I think this book has the purpose of setting up a twist in the ongoing plot and Lara Adrian did a great job with it, without taking the focus away from Dylan, Rio and their feelings. For me the balance between romance, plot, action and characters was flawless and provided a fluent, fast-paced and captivating story as a result. 
 After reading MIDNIGHT AWAKENING I thought I knew where Lara Adrian was heading with the ongoing plot of the Rogues and other enemies of the Order but she again she has managed to surprise me at the end with some mind-blowing disclosures en I'm certainly curious as to where she is taking us next in this mesmerizing world she has created in this series. 
 In my eyes with the Midnight Breed Series, Lara Adrian has created an amazing world within the vampire romance genre that really stands out in the plot department. With every book more information is disclosed, more elements and characters are added and you get better acquainted with the existing characters. Each book is unique in plot, intensity and character development, despite the similarities that glue the series together and each main couple has their own issues and Lara Adrian provides each hero and heroine ways of coping with these issues and each other. The perfect mix of all these elements is what makes this series a keeper for me 
 Book 4 of the Midnight Breed was everything I expected it to be! Lara Adrian has been on my auto-buy list since the 2nd book in this series and with MIDNIGHT RISING she has only secured that spot more. With her fluent and accessible writing style and the fascinating ongoing storyline Lara Adrian pulled me deep into this enthralling world with its unique band of vampires, their mates, their allies and their enemies.

Nice little quandary to start of the story: Dylan (the girl, yes I know) is a reporter who takes pics of Rio and a super secret cave. Rio can't have those pics come out and now since Rio messed up he has to keep Dylan with him when all he wants to do is off himself (in the previous books he is betrayed by his breedmate and scared horribly from an explosion). 
 Their relationship happens/progressing at warp speed, not sure why they are in "luv". 
 This story is just kind of more of the same. The tone and set-up felt the same, the characters just have different names. Rio and Dylan didn't make a lasting impression on me or anything. 
 Once again the author finishes strong with an ending that was fast paced and exciting. Liking the continuation storyline of the Ancient (original gansta', sorry, Vampire) being alive and breeding new Gen Ones. 
 C
Loved it!

Closer to a 4 star, really. I don't know why these books aren't doing more for me. The stories are good, the characters are good. I just don't find them compelling. I loved Rio, and I thought his getting over his 1st wife/mate was well handled. His heroine didn't do much for me. She was likeable enough, but she was kinda boring. I automatically dislike reporters, cause they usually come with a stupid action factor, but this one didn't. So she wasn't stupid, but she wasn't really much of anything else, either. And her "superpower" I thought was a little lame, though necessary to bring in certain aspects (whom shall remain nameless for spoiler reasons). Now, forgettable heroines don't usually bother me either, cause I usually just substitute myself anyway :), but maybe there wasn't enough action to make up for her forgettableness. Still, I enjoyed the read, though not exactly a page turner, and will continue on with the series.

This book was two things for me. 
 FIRST: 
 SECOND: 
 Okay, so Dylan's powers were a really cheap and lazy plot device that I had to force myself to endure -- it's so incredibly stupid and inane (that is, a vampire has been stealing breed mates and killing them off in suicidal breeding sessions and oh, look! Dylan's talent is to see dead ... breed mates. Adrian must've really plunged her depths for that one!) I liked Rio's character, though, so whatever. 
 So, at the end there, we dramatically see like 10 dead breed mates and they're all imploring her to help the others not yet dead. She get's captured, meant for the same fate, but she's saved. 
 AND THEN THE DEAD GIRLS AND THE GIRLS STILL NOT DEAD ARE NEVER MENTIONED AGAIN! WTF? I just... can't. I'm taking a break from this series for a while.
What can I say about this book? Well.. it was OK, I wasn`t very into it. Yes, I read it but it was very hard to finish this book.

sample_reviews.review_text: Please, Jace and Clary, you have to get together, you're my OTP! T~T

After reading the first book, I already wanted so much to read the second. It just caught me off-guard with its extraordinary story. 
 Cassandra Clare's The Mortal Instruments Series is very modern and grand. From the places to the events.

. 
 Here is my problem with this book... Here is why I read the first chapter and then put it down - on to the next book. 
 ok, first, I just finished reading "Absolute Brightness" by James Lecesne - it is poignant and stunning and an amazing read. It is intelligent and thoughtful and well-crafted. 
 This is how "City Of Ashes" starts: 
 The formidable glass-and-steel structure rose from it's position on front street like a glittering needle threading the sky. 
 so... needles don't thread things... they pierce, they poke, they prod, they prick, penetrate, inoculate, puncture, pop, they draw blood... needles don't thread things... they get threaded... 
 .... 
 further down... 
 in describing the penthouse... 
 The window glass was perfectly translucent, providing such a complete illusion that there was nothing between the viewer and the view that it had been know to induce vertigo even in those unafraid of heights. 
 Transparent = Clear - both light and views are completely unobscured. 
 Translucent = Light passes through but not views - like Frosted glass. 
 Opaque = Light does not pass through at all. 
 Why is this important in this story... these are such minor issues in the grand sceme of the whole story, of the whole book...? 
 Because, words are important. I don't look at the Mortal Instruments series a Grand Literary Tome - but... lets at least respect the reader's intelligence enough to use the right words and get our metaphors worked out. 
 but then you think... what if the excuse for this sloppiness is... "whatever, these are only Young Adult readers, we don't have to hold up to the same level of expectation as Normal or Regular books". 
 In my opinion this kind of disrespect and sloppiness is completely dishonorable... and unforgivable... 
 The author wrote it, and the editors let it slide... 
 .

Three thirty something childhood friends meet in Nags Head for the month of August. Recently unemployed and anal Ellis, supermodel Julia hiding bruises on her arm, and newlywed Dorie whose husband didn't make the trip as planned. To save money, they rent the fourth bedroom to Maryn/Madison, who they don't realize is running from her husband with the money she's taken from him (which he stole). 
 SUMMER RENTAL is a lighthearted beach read that tackles some serious topics, though not well. In my opinion, if a writer is going to tackle serious issues, she should give those topics proper attention and not gloss over them as items to make boring characters more interesting. I was particularly turned off by the stereotypical manner the characters acted upon realizing someone was gay. People don't act like that in 2013 (I know the book was written a few years before, but still), and the use of words like "swishy" seemed unnecessary. 
 I'd have rated the book higher if better attention was paid to the serious matters. I'm not sure I'd read this author again, though I suppose I would if someone gave me a free copy and I had nothing else to read.

sample_reviews.review_text: This book started out with high expectations but did not meet them. The book read like a nonfiction book but is historical fiction. I kept having to remind myself that it wasn't all true which frustrated me because I didn't know what was fictionalized and what wasn't.
