sample_reviews.review_text:
Source: Received an ARC from Amazon Vine in exchange for an honest review. 
 After enjoying Mr. Churchill's Secretary and being completely blown away by Princess Elizabeth's Spy, of course I knew I would be reading the third book in what has rapidly become one of my favorite mystery series. This book promised more adventure and deepening threats but ultimately was less satisfying to me than the previous outings although I'm not entirely sure why. 
 The premise is very promising as Maggie is finally getting an opportunity to flex her espionage muscle, becoming the first woman to be dropped in the field on a mission to Berlin, Germany. This expands when Maggie picks up some clues and expands her directives even further to fight Nazism. Meanwhile her own personal life implodes with family and romantic relationship troubles. 
 Maggie is, as always, intrepid and very daring; not bloodthirsty but committed to seeing through her cause. She faces some tough moments in this book and handles them with aplomb. The previous books have been building toward certain events and those payoff here while also setting up further events for the next book. 
 I think part of the reason for my enjoying this book less is due to the more somber tone because this book highlights Operation Compassionate Death aka the Nazi program to euthanize thousands of mentally ill and physically deformed children, those who were deemed unworthy of being part of the pure master race. This hangs over the entire book and Maggie part of a group who gathers evidence to expose these disgusting acts. I guess I felt like the first two books were a little cozier and I preferred that style but I should have known that a story set during World War II will have to address this at some point. Of course, since this book is set in Germany, we're also seeing the persecution of Jews in particular the forced deportation. 
 A subplot I did love concerns Maggie's friend David who is gay and may have found the one to his parents' dismay. Though it does not take up much page-time, I enjoyed whenever the book shifted back to him. Something I did not enjoy was Maggie's love life, which ends very unsettled but which I will not discuss for fear of spoilers. Let's just say that I was a big fan of John in book one. 
 Overall: Mix of tones is a bit confusing: we have the darkness of euthanasia and Nazi evil balanced against some lighter scenes and mixed with very addictive writing that led me to finish this much faster than I had anticipated. If you've liked the previous books in the series, you'll probably want to continue. 
 Cover: Love this cover-the glamor of her dress plus the menacing Nazi swastika in the faint background are just excellent and so appealing to me.
Things are getting darker - more intense for Maggie, her friends and Britain in this third book of the series. I look forever to seeing what comes next for Maggie, the (retired?) spy.

I don't know why I keep reading these, except that I get such a perverse pleasure from getting annoyed about them. This was no exception. I can only recommend the Clara Vine series by Jane Thynne if you want a better British-spy-in-Germany hit.

It is obvious Ms. MacNeal does her homework when it comes to the historical background. I have as much fun reading her notes at the of the book as I do reading the actual book. 
 I think this is the best of the series so far. Characters are interesting as ever. She sets the story in Berlin and shows a bit of Germany that a lot of people don't think about (like the country was a virtual police state under Hitler, that not every citizen was a Nazi, etc...) 
 Time for new one please!

2013 321 pages 
 fun to read a new author. takes place in Berlin WW11 main female character is a British spy.

I read this hoping for intrigue and mystery. It's there--but the prose is utilitarian and I found my attention drifting. The author tries hard to impress the reader with the historical details but they don't seem organic to the plot. I just couldn't get into it and gave up halfway. Maybe it gets better, but I guess I'll never find out.
Pedestrian writing and obvious, transparent setups that made me groan with disappointment. Could not finish.

His Majesty's Hope is the third book in the Maggie Hope mystery series set join the dark days of World War Two. 
 In this book, Maggie's assignment is more dangerous than ever. After being recruited by the SOE she is to be dropped into Nazi occupied Europe. This alone is extremely dangerous but Maggie's mission has her being dropped in the heart of Germany with her needing to infiltrate the highest ranks of the Nazi party. 
 This fast paced thriller keeps you hooked until the very ending, twisting and turning so you as the reader have no idea what will happen next. As with the previous 2 books this was an excellent and very enjoyable read - calling it a 'mystery' does not do the book justice.....far too fast paced and exhilarating for a 'mystery'.

This excellent historical novel is, of course, fiction all the way, although it is set during one of the world's greatest real upheavals. It should appeal to readers interested in World War II, in spy and espionage stories, and those who like solid thrillers. It also provides some interesting insight into how the great evil that was Adolph Hitler and the Nazi empire, evolved in the early years of the European war before the entry of the United States. 
 The novel owes a good deal of its strength and interest to the closely personal stories of Maggie Hope, the central character and her colleagues, her loves and those around her at greater distance. On one level readers are treated to a well-researched look at the maneuverings of intelligence gathering efforts on both sides of the English Channel, and the way in which British spymasters recruited and ruthlessly used any human resources to help them win the war. And even though these people have the reader sympathies, being on the side of the angels, their attitudes and actions were not much different from those of the enemy. 
 Maggie Hope, an American, recruited for and working in British Secret Service, is dropped into Berlin to deliver communications devices. And because she's an independent sort, opportunities arise that keep her in-country far beyond the scope of the original mission. As a character, Maggie is exactly the kind of heroic figure we want in these stories, yet she is far from perfect, beset by doubts, and ineptitude from colleagues, she manages with appropriate derring-do and a lot of help from family, to get out of Germany just ahead of the Gestapo. 
 There are coincidences in life. That's a recognizable fact. There are multiplicities of events going on in the lives of those around us. Another accepted fact. Too much activity and too many coincidental happenings might cause an undercover agent to become seriously paranoid. If this novel were not so well written, so replete with high emotion, if the main character was other than a bright, independent accomplished woman of the nineteen forties, I might have set the novel down unfinished. As it is, "His Majesty's Hope" is better than three, but doesn't quite rate a four star review.

Another marvelous World War Two thriller / adventure / espionage / romance wonderful book. This one sees our heroine go on her first, indeed Britain's first oversee mission as a spy. Lots of nice and accurate historical detail as well as lots of fun adventures, twists, subplots and some true horror. 
 A great book - ready for the next!!

1.5 stars. 
 I am a little bit disappointed. 
 Sentinel is the last book of the Convenant Series and it should have been the best book of the series. 
 In my opinion, it could have been better. I'm not talking about the writing. The book was a little bit slowed paced for me. I know I've said that the action started quite fast, but that died down pretty fast. It was just a small battle. I feel like some stuff could've be left out, like the pregnancy scare. What was the point of that, especially since a few pages later we found out that what was happening with Alex had nothing to do with babies?! 
 The battle and Ares death was a little bit rushed. It was like one or two chapters. I wasn't expecting a Titan to help them. That was a nice surprised. I would've like to see more of him, thou. To know more about the character, more about his history. 
 Olivia dies. I think she was killed of so she can be reunited with Caleb. I'm not sure how I fill about it right now. :D 
 Seth. Poor Seth. :( 
 Seth turns against Ares and goes back to Alex and helps her fight and win the battle against Ares. I was surprised and at the same time I was not.I had two theories: 1. Seth goes evil and tries to kill Alex or 2. Seth snaps out of it and goes back to Alex. I thought it would be the first one, but I liked the fact that I was wrong. Nice twist. 
 I would've liked to see more of Seth and Alex, thou. Not necessarily them going back together, but hanging out, talking and catching up. 
 Also, I don't like how Seth ended up. Ok, he didn't end up with Alex, but it was necessary for him to end up all alone and to give up his soul to Hades when he dies? I would've liked to see him happy with someone. Aiden was suppose to give up his should to Hades in order to free the titan from Tartarus, but Seth took his place so that Alex can be happy with Aide. He did loved Alex after all, didn't he? 
 I think it was obvious that Alex would choose Aiden. I would have liked to see her with Seth. Aiden is fine, but for me he is too feminine. 
 I didn't understand much of the end, it seemed rushed. Alex dies and then she is a demigod. She has to stay 6 months in the underworld and 6 months on earth. But why? It is explained, but very briefly.More details would have been wonderful. 
 While Alex is in Paradises, Aiden and the others are changing the law, killing the Breed Order, releasing the salves, Seth is giving up his future for Alex and Aide. Aiden, Marcus etc. are mourning for Alex. Aiden sets a building on fire. We don't see any of this. We found out about it in one small paragraph, when Apollo tells Alex for short what had happened while she was in the Underworld. It would have been nice to read about all that stuff, from Aiden's point of view or something. 
 I expected more from this book. More action, more details on important stuff and less fill ins and pointless dialogs.. 
 PS. I'm sorry if my English is not perfect. It is not my first language, I'm still learning. Writing reviews on books I've read seems like a good practice. If I made mistakes, you can tell me, nicely. :)

 I'm finding it difficult to sum up my feelings for this book. At first I was bored, then mid-way it was okay, but then it just got silly and I sat there contemplating what my rating would actually be. I settled on a good 2 stars. 
 I got this book with RavenPost with the theme 'Isolation', and it's a book I've definitely seen around but never really considered picking it up. Still, it was an interesting read. I've not read a story of someone who has to stay inside and never leave their house due to terrible allergies, so it was quite new to me. I just the story lacking in some areas. 
 Firstly, it was a bit slow. Maddy was inside and basically just reading and spending time with her mum or nurse, all the while pining for the normality of a regular teenage girl. Of course that's to be expected, she's isolated. But then her neighbours move in. And one of them a handsome young man called Olly who takes her fancy. From there, this book is mostly just Maddy wanting to be with Olly and cursing her illness for trapping her in her home. Which leads to my other issue with the book overall - romance. 
 Maddy and Olly speak a few times online, meet face to face twice and then THEY'RE IN LOVE. It's instalove, and it's too unrealistic for my liking. Not only that, but Maddy makes some terrible decisions and does pretty questionable things just to be with him, right up to risking her life. It's pretty careless of her. Literally risking everything just for a boy she's just met. Instalove isn't a seller, I don't know many people who like it, so I wish authors would stop writing that in. I, for sure, am not a fan of it 
 Also, there is a plot twist in this book. Sadly, I kind of suspected that there would be one. The book was a little too slow for there to not be. When it happened, I wasn't that surprised. I did have a reaction along the lines of 'WHAT' because I wasn't sure that would even be an option. If you know what it is, you'd think 'surely this can't be after everything that's happened.' Yet it did. It's not easy trying to explain without spoiling, so go read the book and let us know what you thought about the twist! 
 There was also a part of the story which I really didn't like (can't say due to it being a spoiler), but I felt that Maddy was really stupid and acted on impulse without thinking. It ended up being extremely bad for her and others around her. I was reading it thinking 'Why do this, and what made you think this was a good idea?' 
 She learnt the hard way. 
 With the characters, I wasn't a fan of Maddy. Her bad decisions, dramatic nature (mostly near the end of the book, crying over such a small issue), and her slight lack of consideration for others. As soon as she saw Olly outside from her window, she was obsessed. I got bored of that very quickly. 
 Near the end though, she was just so emotional and crying so much (for about an hour - maybe longer!) over something and I was like 'what is she even crying about?'. I know she's a teenager, but I was genuinely not sure what was wrong. If it's about Olly, it's honestly her own fault for making silly decisions, getting people in trouble and nearly dying for her reckless attitude. 
 Speaking of Olly... he was alright actually. He was quite patient with her, and he wasn't pressuring in any way. His penchant for climbing on everything and stuff was a little strange, but it's not really a bad trait. He was quite a nice guy. I do think he should have knocked some sense into Maddy, though. Sometimes it felt like he should say 'Alright, stop now. You need to be careful', if he really cares about her. He was just as reckless as Maddy in the end, and should have been a bit more decisive in some cases. 
 The other characters were interesting, but didn't really stick out much. I quite liked Carla - she was a warm and caring character, a bit more lenient and sometimes funny. There aren't many characters in this book, but considering the type of story it is, you don't need too many. The number itself was enough. I just wished that some were fleshed out a bit more. There was time, for sure. 
 Olly's family was quite interesting to read about. His overall story and what was going on in his life was sad and I wish we learnt more about that. Of course, the male lead as well as the female lead needs a sob story. We had quite a bit of pagetime with Olly, so again, more fleshing out of his life would have been good. Ultimately, it was all about Maddy. 
 I did like that the main character was half-Japanese and half-African American. It certainly makes a change. I'm all for diversity, especially in YA. I just wish I enjoyed the story more, considering it was a kind I'd never read before. I haven't read many books revolving around isolation and it's one of those rare ones that I read that's about sickness. As a hypochondriac, I tend to avoid them. 
 I'm not entirely sure how I feel about this book. I forced myself to read it, I did get into it but then I was left feeling like it was lacking something. Hence my 2 star rating.

reference_books.title: Red Hook Road
reference_books.review_text:
This novel starts with a tragedy of almost unbearable magnitude, which I found made it hard to like the book. The characters move on from the tragedy -- and I really liked the structure of seeing them at the same point in the year for each of the first few years after the tragedy. You see how they pick up their lives and how the grief becomes more bearable with time. That felt very real. But for the reader, the tragedy was just a few pages ago. It's still fresh and hard to get past, and I struggled with that. 
 Some of the characters and plot points felt broadly drawn or cliched. I liked the novel enough to stick with it, but I probably wouldn't suggest it to others.

reference_books.title: May We Be Forgiven
reference_books.review_text: I started out intensely disliking this book -- every character seemed depraved. People sleeping with their sister-in-laws and picking up strangers in the supermarket, students having lesbian affairs with their teachers, husbands inviting their wives' lovers over for a barbeque, relatives handing a child over to the people involved in the death of the child's parents, daughters abandoning their parents to near-strangers, and so on ... ewwww. No character seemed likable and they were all just so morally repugnant. And the main character seemed wooden, numb, or just flatly drawn ... does he feel anything, ever, or does he just roll along with what others are pushing on him? But as the book went on he and the other characters became more real, more sympathetic, and if not likable, at least bearable. I had to make a conscious effort to appreciate this novel's dark comic humor though. I chuckled sometimes but most of the time it didn't come easily.

reference_books.title: Stiff: The Curious Lives of Human Cadavers
reference_books.review_text:
I had two big problems with this book, and one thing I loved: 
 1) This is going to sound ridiculous because obviously the subject of the book is morbid ... but I found it so morbid and gruesome that I could hardly stand to read it. It was depressing and upsetting at times. I expected to read about burial vs. cremation vs. other newer methods that are coming along, and there was that -- but there was also figuring out how the passengers on TWA Flight 800 died (horrifically) and how a crucifixion actually happens, and cannibalism, and all these side-roads that are more about dying than death and are really just awful. I KNOW that's what I signed up for, but it was worse than I expected. Especially ... 
 2) All the medical experimentation on animals. I did NOT sign up to read about that, but the book flows from "this happened to cadavers" to "this also happened to live animals" in every chapter, and goes into terrible detail. What made it worse is the author's detachment, and sometimes what seems almost like amusement, about the animals being decapitated or hurled into hard surface to see "what happens to the lungs" or having one puppy's head sewn onto another puppy's body ... blehk. I actually liked how the author roams off-topic into related channels but she roams into the world's long history of animal abuse much, much too much. 
 3) The thing I loved, and that kept me reading, was her fabulous, wry writing style. Despite the subject matter, I laughed out loud at times. If you like a writer who stays on topic, don't read her, because she goes way, way down side roads, but she's funny and engaging and just wonderful to read. 
 I am looking forward to reading her other books, assuming that animal experimentation won't be a major topic in them (I hope).

Great House is not a great novel, not even a good collection of short stories. The book has some beautiful writing, the trouble being the good parts seem to be floating like icebergs in a muddy sea. The reader who invests time in reading the book will come away (after heroically trying to make a story by linking together the random icebergs) covered in mud, feeling cold and tricked. 
 I read the book on my Kindle and at first I thought there must have been a serious screw-up with the formatting resulting in unrelated paragraphs turning up in odd spaces. But, then I noticed that the narrators (often unnamed well into the book) would indulge in tangents completely unrelated to anything, certainly not the story. It wasn't a Kindle formatting problem. 
 Many contemporary writers skip around in time, point of view and narrators successfully (A Visit from The Goon Squad, The Impressionists are two of my favorites). But those novels have intersecting stories that are linked together. Krauss doesn't bother with that. A desk is supposed to be the link in the stories, but that obviously wasn't enough. I was going to reread the book, because I couldn't make sense of the plot. But when I came to the rambling asides I couldn't make myself persist. One sleepless night I resorted to mentally flow charting the characters' connections. I think I put more effort into that than did Ms. Krauss. 
 There are passages in the book that are beautifully written. There are interesting observations on the life of a writer. There are thought-provoking ideas about loss. But an editor would (or should) have cut away huge sections of text that merely distract from the worthwhil

"We search for patterns, you see, only to find where the patterns break. And it's there, in that fissure, that we pitch our tents and wait." I was pleasantly surprised by this book. 4 different stories are connected, but remotely, by an object that carries through all stories. I often struggled to recall who was who and how they related to the previous story. And all of them leave holes, are open-ended. Nevertheless, the writing is excellent. The content is exciting and interesting. Characters come to life, each one of them. "After my marriage had ended I'd stopped seeing her, having slowly given up on the idea of undertaking vast renovations of my self in order to make myself more suitable for social life." The themes are interesting too ... Jewish characters, spanning several generations, their lives uniquely affected by what we all know is a tragic history. Difficult topics are discussed - life and death, being a parent and the effect that certain mistakes can have on children, marriage and secrets discovered too late to act upon. And throughout, little wisdoms that demonstrate the author's closeness to life. "There are times when the kindness of strangers only makes matters worse because one realizes how badly one is in need of kindness and that the only source is a stranger." Would have really liked this book to continue on some more, another 100 pages or so, to close some of the gaps that for me were left open. As I began to become acquainted to these characters, I felt left hanging, wanted to read more about them. "In other words, sometimes politeness is all that stands between oneself and madness."
Amazing writing and sprawling story of a desk but so much more. While I didn't love any of the characters, I was so in awe of the words that I didn't care.
I both loved and hated this book simultaneously. I think the word which best describes it is 'tedious'. It didn't come together for me until the last two stories.

This book started off really good. I thought I was going to love it. But it disappointed in the end. The writing is lovely, especially in the early chapters, and I loved getting to intimate with the characters' inner lives. But not enough actually happened, so the language and the intense inner lives started getting tedious. And the ending left too many mysteries unsolved. I know it isn't fashionable, in literary fiction, to tie things up too neatly, and I'm fine with little ambiguity and some respect for the reader's imagination, but this story had way too many loose ends and so I found it ultimately unsatisfying. 
 I did find intriguing the theme of how much people hide from each other, how little we really know each other, and how private writers are in particular. I have often thought that I'd have more intimacy with other human beings if I didn't keep a personal journal. I confide in my journal and that's often enough for me. Even the people closest to me probably feel shut out sometimes, just as Arthur and "S" did.
I get where this is going. This desk is the string that connects all the people. But I don't really like the people. So I abandoned the book.

sample_reviews.review_text: It was very difficult to get started. The first 50 pages really dragged for me. However, once I got to know the characters, they were quite endearing!
An aspect of WWII history that I was not familiar with - war brides, and their journeys to England and the US after the war ended. A good story with mostly likable and relatable characters.

This is a wonderful, memorable story and a fascinating glimpse into a part of history of which I was not aware. 
 In July 1946, the British aircraft carrier HMS Victorious traveled from Sydney to take 655 Australian war brides of British servicemen to Britain where their husbands awaited them. More than 1100 men also were on board. These young women had married British servicemen serving in Australia during the war. When the author discovered that her grandmother had actually been one of these brides on the HMS Victorious, she resolved to create a story from it. She envisioned four young women from very different backgrounds who were thrown together in a small cabin for the journey. 
 Avice is a wealthy society girl, and "desperately disappointed" that her bunk mates have a lower social standing than her own. Maggie is heavily pregnant, and charming. She worries she won't be a good mother, because her own mother abandoned her. Frances is a nurse, very quiet, and seems to be carrying a secret. And Jean is only sixteen, and probably married too young: she is wild, indiscreet, and not immune to the flirtations of the sailors. 
 The girls are guarded in the their bunks at night, and Frances becomes friends with the marine, Henry, who stands nightly in front of their door. Henry has received a devastating letter from his wife back home. But neither Frances nor Henry confide their secrets to one another. 
 As the story progresses, we become familiar with the tensions between everyone cooped up together on the ship. Some of the tension was among the brides, with Moyes especially picking up upon the class snobbery that prevailed at the time. There was also a sexual tension between the brides and the men. Many of these girls hadn't seen their husbands since the night they wed them - in some cases several years before. And the men of course had been deprived of the company of women for quite some time. There was also tension coming from the husbands back in Britain: upon receiving word that their wives would be coming, some sent telegrams to the ship succinctly advising: "Not Wanted Don't Come." A woman about whom the message was directed was dropped off at the next port, where a representative of the Australian government would make arrangements for her to go back home. All the brides dreaded getting the call to the Captain's office. 
 The Captain is close to retirement age, and "at sea" about what he is to do next. He is also plagued by a war wound that he dare not admit bothers him, but it has gotten so bad he fears for his survival. And now he has do deal with all these women, with their lingerie hanging to dry on lines around the ship, having to come up with entertainments for them, and the occasional trysting, and so on. Moyes limns him so well you can almost hear his heavy sighing as you read the book. 
 Although the voyage only lasts less than six weeks, some of the lives of those on board go through radical changes. Matters come to a head for the protagonists just as the ship nears the port of Plymouth. 
 Evaluation: The characters are so good - I felt sad at the end not to be able to hear more about them, especially Maggie and Frances. Moyes always makes me care about characters and think about them long after I finish a book by her. In addition, another of the ways in which Moyes is so excellent is that she always manages to throw complete surprises into what you assumed was a predictable plot. And finally, the exceptionally skilled way in which Moyes takes readers into that aircraft carrier so that we feel we too are experiencing every aspect of the trip is so rewarding - as Emily Dickens said, "There is no frigate like a book...." What a happy double entendre for this reading experience. 
 Highly recommended! 
 Rating: 4.5/5

Another fantastic Moyes read! She's definitely my new favorite contemporary writer of fiction. I was blown away by the fact that this novel is based on a true historical incident, and so very few people seem to know about it! It should really be made into a film.... hint, hint ;)

During WWII, many British servicemen married Australian women, leaving them until the war ended. Then the Royal Navy shipped some women from Australia to England. The Ship of Brides by Jojo Moyes is the story of the women and men aboard one of these ships, the HMS Victorious in 1946. It happened to be an aircraft carrier. 
 We learn the story of four bunk mates thrown together: Avice, the social snob; Margaret, the friendly (and pregnant) farm girl; Jean, the exceedingly immature 15 year old; and Frances, the introverted nurse with secrets. We also get glimpses of a few of the men, but mostly the captain and Nicol who is a marine. 
 Jojo Moyes has written an interesting and often gripping story. I didn't feel as invested in the characters as I do in some novels, but my thoughts would linger to the story when I wasn't reading. I liked the historical snippets at the beginning of each chapter and the lecture topics which would probably horrify many women today. I'm not sure how well researched this novel is, but it sounds realistic. 
 Overall, a good book.

3.5 stars. I will start by saying that love Jojo Moyes writing. This book was well-written and a pleasure to read, but I just thought there were too many characters to keep straight. The narrative is told from the perspective of several brides on a ship to England to reunite with their soldier husbands after World War II. It's also told from the perspective of the soldiers on active duty on that ship. The main characters were wonderful and easy to warm up to, but the minor characters, who would flit in and out of the narrative, clogged up the plot for me and made it tougher to follow the storyline. I wish Moyes would have edited some of these passages out to allow for more clarity. It's still a good read, but it definitely took me longer to finish on account of the choppiness.
I usually like JoJo Moyes, but just couldn't get into this one.

The third book was okay, again not as good as the second one, and it put me in a small reading slump. Though I think I was reading during a complicated time in my life, so I wasn't as invested in it as I could have been. 
 I wished there were more Ronan chapters because he's my bae. And I wish it had a bit of a faster moving plot. Though I think many MANY YA books rush with their story lines, I feel like sometimes The Raven Cycle slows it down too much. But maybe it's just me, and the weather outside. 
 Still, a really enjoyable book and can't wait to read the final one!

Apparently I was so discombobulated by this book that it took me five days to mark it "finished." Because I did not feel finished when I got to the end. I want more! This book is definitely my favorite of the trilogy so far, and I know that book 4 is going to knock it out of the park. It's nice when a series grows and deepens over the course of three books rather than sort of just chugging along for the sake of more plot.

I think when it comes to "Blue Lily, Lily Blue" I'm in the minority for the number of stars rated. I think that this book is essentially filler and nothing of note occurred until the last 30 pages or so. I felt that it was along the similar vein of book one, but not as captivating. I ended up skimming the book, but then I made myself go back and reread it.

sample_reviews.review_text: I couldn't get into this story which surprised the hell out of me since I love Janet Evanovich's 'Stephanie Plum series. Definitely not for me but read if you haven't read One for the Money or any of those series.

I couldn't finish the book. I had to skip to the end to read the last two chapters because I am a chronic finisher. 
 I'm just not vested in the outcome of the characters. The sexual tension between Lizzy and Diesel was too forced. 
 Clara cannot be a real employer. She just can't be. I don't know of any boss who would regular let their employees run off to save the world or do not care that she is bringing dangerous people to her store. I know its fiction. But this is not science fiction. It's just not believable. 
 The part I enjoyed was the photos in the end of the Boston/Cambridge area.

I don't know what I think of this series...too unrealistic for me. I will continue to read the series as it is an quick read and they are comical. I am so curious if Lizzie and Diesel will end up together once they finish saving the world.
The picture was great. The story line was crazy. I was not please.
Argh. Less "___ was ____" and "he cut his eyes to her" (yay) but in the end, the main character was stupid. I hate stupid main characters. :\
I had this teed up for my vacation as an e book. A fun silly little story. Evanovich is very easy to read. A shorty, you can bust through it in a day. Lizzu & Diesel are fun.

This series has all the things all like vampires, magic, cupcakes...and yet I don't like it. I thought I ought to give the second book a chance as I liked all the elements but in the end it is just too over the top for me to care about the characters.

Whimsically comical book. Absolutely no literary value but has "great" entertainment quotient. Potpourri of fantasy, action, chase and romance. A Friday evening read that is not intellectually demanding. I guess Harry Potter fans will love this book.
No more Lizzy and Diesel books for me. Not interested in stupid monkeys and supernatural characters.

Not the most interesting start to this year's reading. I like Evanovich's Stephanie Plum novels - although that series has probably run a little long - and this book is pretty much in the same vein but I just didn't like it. I basically cannot remember most of the plot despite reading the whole thing in the last 24 hours. Likeable enough characters, a fluffy storyline, but just not me.

reference_books.title: Lover Unleashed (Black Dagger Brotherhood, #9)
reference_books.review_text:
Reviewed at http://anotherlookbookreviews.blogspo... 
 V is my favourite brother, true. So on that mention, I loved Lover Unleashed. Since the fifth book Lover Unbound I had always felt that Vishous' story hadn't been told completely. I wanted more. I felt like there was still some unresolved issues. I wasn't a fan of Jane being a ghost and I felt like V got the short end of the stick for his shellan. I liked Jane well enough it's just the whole ghost thing and were they really happy with that ending. Lover Unleashed was a perfect resolve for me. 
 Manny and Payne's story was great. Their chemistry was a bit to immediate for me though. I couldn't understand how Manny had been pinning for Jane for an entire year and then he walks into the hospital room, sees Payne and BAM he's in love and Jane is all but a distant memory. I'm glad he got over Jane but the instant "MINE" gave me whiplash it was so fast. 
 I liked Payne. I loved her speech and I loved how she went after the Bloodletter for all that he had done to V. She is a good sister. I especially loved that even though Payne is a kick ass chick, she can still be a soft, warm and a loving woman. It was good to see that not all tough women like Xhex need to be so butchy. 
 Manny was a good guy and I liked how he stood up to the Brothers. He knew they could easily kill him but that didn't stop him from standing his ground. Very interesting story ending on a way to link Manny to the Brothers. J.R. Ward set it up so that it could be elaborated or just left well enough alone. Smart writing. 
 I loved that Lover Unleashed had lots of Butch and V scenes. I adore reading about those two together. I love their talks and how close they are. Lover Unleashed offers many squee moments and one particular pivotal moment that completely demonstrates just how tight their friendship really is. 
 A new group of vampires were introduced and I am dying to know where J.R. Ward is going to take us with them. Another great set up for future books. All I know is that I am super interested in that story line. 
 Poor Layla. She needs a life. I have no idea what is going on with Blay and Quinn and how Layla fits into all of this. Vampires aren't keen on sharing so I don't think a vampire menage is in their cards but something is definitely up with all of them. I want to keep reading the series just to see how that all plays out. 
 So all in all, excellent book. I loved it. In fact I devoured it so I may have to re-read it shortly so that I can enjoy it a bit more and I won't be in such a rush to get to the end. Lover Unleashed was so good I didn't want to put it down. 
 Teasers: steamy shower, return of V's penthouse, waxed leathers, distant relative

reference_books.title: The Darkest Night (Lords of the Underworld #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Still on fence about my feelings regarding this series. 
 http://anotherlookbookreviews.blogspo... 
 The Darkest Night was way better than the prequel story, The Darkest Fire but still a long way off what I would describe as an addictive series. 
 Maddox and Ashlyn were a great couple to read about but (and a big but here) there was so much that ended up being a head scratcher for me. For instance, there never really was an explanation offered on what caused their electric chemistry as clearly it was more than just an attraction. Their chemistry was described time and time again as literally being shocking with electric jolts. Why did the voices in Ashlyn head go quiet around Maddox? What was so special about their connection as I believe the reader was lead to understand that it was more than just a mutual attraction? I kept waiting for some sort of back-story to emerge to explain all of this information but nothing was shared. 
 It drives me nuts in a story when the male protagonist (that has been living for thousands of years) becomes so in love and protective of the female that in less than 24 hours from meeting her, he'd be willing to kill his best friends (that he has had for thousands of years) if they tried to harm her. It just didn't jive. 
 I still wasn't a fan of the writing style or the how the voices were written and I totally thought that Ashlyn's self sacrifice storyline was way out there on the ridiculous side. I fully admit to rolling my eyes. 
 One more thing that I didn't care for were the amount of characters that The Darkest Night introduced. Wholly smokes my head was spinning and I had started to take notes. I am going to list the characters after this review so I can refer back to them. 
 There are a lot of reference in this series to the Greek Gods & Titans. I found that part all very interesting and I still like the idea about searching for Pandora's box. I am going to continue on reading the series for now. It is an easy read that I can put down without hesitation. 
 Torin - Lord of Disease 
 Lucien - Lord of Death 
 Reyes - Lord of Pain 
 Aeron - Lord of Wrath 
 Paris - Lord of Promiscuity 
 Sabin - Lord of Doubt 
 Gideon - Lord of Lies 
 Kane - Lord of Disaster 
 Strider - Lord of Defeat 
 Cameo - Misery 
 Amun - Lord of Secrets 
 Anya - Goddess of Anarchy 
 Maddox - Lord of Violence 
 Ashlyn - when standing at a spot, she can hear any conversation that has taken place at the spot from the pass no matter how long time has passed.

reference_books.title: Bound by Blood (Bound, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Really didn't like Bound by Blood. 
 http://anotherlookbookreviews.blogspo... 
 I totally was not feeling this book. Bound by Blood's storyline and character development made no sense to me. Going with the premise of the story, Wolfman and Vamplady marry to solidify and unite forces in order to battle the Demons. 
 She was to marry to save the vamp nest. How many years long do you think a marriage would last in the paranormal realm? Hundreds of years maybe? That was my guess. Then imagine my surprise when this bit of information is shared, 
 "She wasn't supposed to have sex with him. The Council has been adamant about that. Drink him, yes, take his power, give him hers, but sex? Forbidden." 
 Now come on. Does that even make sense? The Council agrees to marry off their precious Vamp Princess for unity sake but then no sex? It is so, well, dumb. Who would insist on a marriage to take place but no sex. I swear you could hear my eyes roll. 
 Then in the course of one day, she loves him. Morgan didn't know Jace previously. She was bartered away for the good of her people and it only took one day. Yep. He stalked her for years behind the scenes so I can imagine that his lust level was high and he claimed to have loved her from afar but it was all way way waaaaay to quick for me. Also, I don't know but the whole "love from afar" thing was just creepy to me. 
 Then I got confused once again. A trusted council member traps her inside a burning house. Supposedly this action was to see if she could or would burn badly after she had a chance to drink Jace's blood. But you see, why the hell would he take a chance on that if that same Council member planned on (and needed to) setting Morgan up as a sacrifice to the demons in hell? Talk about a complete contradiction. 
 Once again, my confusion ensured regarding the plans of each of the Wolf and Vamp groups. The Alpha and Council members never figured out each other's evil plans toward one another. They never considered their opposition schemes? Not very good leaders if you ask me. How do you lead people you are suppose to protect if you don't consider your enemies strategies? 
 So basically, the story, the pace, the characters were all just a big fat turn off for me. Paranormal or not, the story has got to make sense to me. Good thing Bound by Blood was only a $1 purchase on Amazon.

book_a.title: When You Dare (Men Who Walk the Edge of Honor, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Sorry. Disappointed. 
 http://anotherlookbookreviews.blogspo... 
 I had been looking forward to reading this "Men Who Walk the Edge of Honor" series since last June/11. In June I went out and bought the first three books but with such a huge TBR pile, I only just got to it now. As proof of how badly I wanted to read this series, here is me with a couple of the men. 
 <> 
 I think I also held back a bit because Romance Suspense isn't a favourite genre of mine. I can't handle suspense and angst. I know this fact about me so I have to be a mood to have my heart pumping and my hands all sweaty. I can only take that in doses. 
 After reading When You Dare, I have to admit my true disappointment with the lack of suspense. Last night as I was reading it, I was at the half way mark of my book and I said to myself, 'when is anything going to happen!?!' When You Dare was a yawner when it came to suspense because there is none. Nada, nothing, zip. So if you are looking for a romance suspense, pass on When You Dare. 
 As for the character development, it was very easy to like Dare and Molly. Dare has a killer body, rich, smart and very good at his job. Now to be clear, I'm not quite 100% what his job was. He rescues people in peril...I think. He is for hire but I am not sure what job title that would say on his business card. 
 As for Molly the one thing that really struck me odd was her name. I like the name, Molly well enough but it just didn't suit this character. Nothing against the Molly's of the world but the name just needed to have a stronger representation of the protagonist. The character, Molly was such a tower of strength and bravery that her character's name just conflicted with the personality. Molly would have been better suited as a Dana, Anne, Jean or Lisa. 
 Out the gate When You Dare was powerful. The book starts just at the conclusion of a daring rescue (you do not read about the rescue itself) where young women were kidnapped for sex slavery. You read about the abhorrent conditions the women were kept in and a shiver goes up your spine. Dare is the sole man that goes into a Tijuana lair, kills the bad guys and single handily rescues about eight women. His best friend's sister was the reason he took on the mission and he saves Molly as she was one of the chained up females. I felt the save was a bit of a reach and not realistic. I understand it is fiction but it was hard to even imagine that one man could have done all of that the rescue alone plus then set the women free. 
 What I found frustrating over and over again was the lame reasoning for not bringing the police or FBI in on the case. I would have thought Molly and the other women would want to protect any more females from suffering the brutal kidnapping and have the slavery ring shut down. 
 As Molly and Dare get to know and trust each other, the reader is then treated to chapters and chapters of Molly wanting Dare to sleep with her and Dare (being the gentleman that he is) holding off on his sexual urges because he wants Molly to heal from her cuts and bruises. Literally chapters. Molly wants to feel again, Molly wants to move on, Molly wants her hair to look nice so that maybe Dare will want her, Molly wishes she had her makeup and clothes so she will be desirable for Dare...oh boy enough already. 
 I would have made When You Dare a one star except that I will admit that the actual writing was good. It was just the story line and plot holes that I serious problems with. I could list all my dissensions but it would be full of spoilers and it would just turn into a rant. Even though I have the next two books sitting on my shelf, I am not sure if I'll bother reading them. 
 Teasers: great hair untangling scene, awesome doggie personalities, dysfunctional family, clean freak

sample_reviews.review_text: I have read this book before, but I didn't remember how it ended. The book starts out well, but Dare becomes very patronizing toward the end, and Molly is a little too accepting of his faults. The book is total fantasy.
good strong characters, interesting plot twists, keeps you on your toes! very detailed!

DNF @ 20% 
 I seriously thought this would be my new KGI series replacement, no such luck! 
 There were so many things wrong with this novel, that kinda just kept popping up and I thought I could brush it aside but I just could not handle. So let's break it down shall we? (Yes be warned from this point on it IS a RANT!) 
 1. The novel opens up with Dare rescuing a family friend's sister from a human trafficking port, he returns her to her brother, and is left with an American female named Molly who was also in the cell with the woman he was supposed to rescue, and obviously he could not leave her behind. When Molly comes too, she is instantly on alert and attack mode, she fight's Dare, and when he explains the situation she calms down and ask's to be taken to a hotel... 
 PROBLEM How do you know he is not lying? He has no proof that he is the "good guy" as you did not see him because you were unconscious when he rescued you, how do you know your captors are simply just not transporting you to another location, or selling you? 
 SOLUTION What the author should have done was make Molly come too in the presences of the other woman who was held captive with her, that way she could vouch for Dare and Molly would know that she was safe and could trust him. 
 2. Once they get to the hotel Dare is left to take care of Molly and Molly is forced to depend on him... the two share a room, in the predicament that they are in they both realize their attraction for each other... 
 PROBLEM Dare should be solely focused on Molly's health in a very professional matter, not noticing that she has a "nice rack" or "voluptuous curves." Yes men are men, I understand, but Dare does this rescue and retrieve thing for a living you think he would be more professional about the whole matter. Molly darling please explain to me how you feel safe and are attracted to this big man when you have spent nine days being tortured, abused, and held captive by a bunch of men, you would think she would be a bit more wary, especially by strange men. 
 3. In the night Molly wakes from a nightmare and Dare ends up cuddling and sleeping next to her... 
 BIG PROBLEM I'm sorry if Molly is taken back subconsciously to a place where she was held captive and tortured by men why on earth would she find comfort in the arms of a man who is a stranger to her? 
 Solution The conversation that the two did have was a very good one, and probably did a lot to comfort her. What the author should have done, was keep the conversation, but just have Dare in his bed and Molly in her's, because they are in a hotel room, there beds are in the same room only separated by a night table, and this would have made more sense to the rational readers in the world. 
 4. Molly is attacked, Dare rescues her, and in order to calm her down and get her out of the shock and hysteria she is feeling Dare kisses her, and this ain't no chaste kiss folks... 
 YES YOU CAN BET YOUR ASS I HAVE A PROBLEM WITH THAT WHY ON EARTH ARE YOU KISSING HER AFTER SHE JUST GOT ATTACKED, SHE DOES NOT KNOW YOU?! How on earth would that calm her down I would be sacred and shocked shitless, like how selfish are you I just got attacked and your trying to kiss me? Like WTF you are either selfish or stupid. You would think Dare would know more in order to calm a woman down considering he does this for a living, I'm sorry Dare if I was ever in need you would not get my business. 
 So with that last scene I had had enough of Dare, Molly, and "When you Dare." This is not it for me and Lori Foster, I hear she is a great author, and there are actually two more books that I want to check out from her, so fingers crossed those go well.

I really loved this series. I love strong men who are very protective. This series is very well written and I really connected with characters. If strong protective men make you melt, kick back and enjoy. This series is well worth your time.

I started like, 5 books in the last 24 hours and this was the only one I could finish. I wasn't expecting much, partly due to the previous 4 failures of literature and partly because I just don't have high expectations for a book with man-candy on the cover. Don't get me wrong, I'd totally wash my panties on that washboard, but I don't read a book with a cover like this thinking I'll be finding the next NYT bestseller. 
 So color me surprised when I read the whole book during work (it's not like they actually have work for me to do). Let me first say that, although I didn't hate the heroine, I felt she was contradictory in the sense that she would refuse to show weakness over her kidnapping/abuse, but she was meek and unsure of herself around the hero. He was toootally into her and she just wouldn't accept it. I admit I skimmed over some of her fretting because I'd rather her be the brave, tough, independent heroine than the awkwardly unassuming, 'oh no, don't trouble yourself over little ole me' heroine. 
 The hero is what kept me from putting this book down. Dare (hero) and Chris (bff & personal assistant to Dare) were great characters that I legitimately cared for. I liked how Dare wasn't running through the "I'll just have sex with her once and get her out of my system, then ditch her" hamster wheel. He knew he felt something more for the heroine and never tried to deny it or push her away in an effort to give her freedom to find somebody that truly 'deserved her'... I hate that excuse. 
 If Chris ever gets his own book, I'll read it even though I tend to avoid M/M romance novels since I can't really identify with the characters. He was a delight, not taking away too much attention from the story, but making a lasting impression as I feel secondary characters (especially one of the good guys) should. 
 The villain... Can we say 'batshit crazy'? I picked up on who the bad guy was a little sooner than I think I should have. But I blame that more on the fact that I've got backstabbers and schemers on the brain than on any misstep the author may have made in foreshadowing too soon. 
 I would have enjoyed an epilogue with a little familial closure, but since most of what would be in an epilogue was briefly wrapped up in the final paragraphs of the last chapter, I guess I can't complain. It would have been nice to have the wrap up explained a little more. 
 So all in all, I enjoyed the book quite a bit. I would definitely recommend it to people that enjoy romantic suspense, but not to those who like it a little steamier. This was fairly tame on the sex. While I have a few minor complaints, they weren't enough to make me put the book down (and anyone who reads my reviews will know I DNF a lot of books because it doesn't take much to put me off a story).

This book was...ok at best. No depth to the heroine and Dare was an ass most of the time. This book was an "I am bored and have nothing else to read at the moment" story for me. Not sure if I will pick up the rest of the series anytime soon.

3.5 stars 
 This was an okay intro to this series. I think I had my expectations bar set a little high, so that may have affected my rating. I just wasn't wow'ed by anything, but there was nothing wrong with the book. 
 At the very beginning of the book, Dare is involved in a one man rescue mission getting a friend's sister out of her place of captivity. He rescues the rest of the women that are being held with her, and Molly is one of those women. He soon realizes that he can't just send the broken and battered Molly back to the loving arms of her family because she those loving arms are quite possibly responsible for her situation in the first place. 
 So there's the setup for this couple being thrown and held together by some funkified circumstances. Of course, sexual tension is readily apparent and they both try to fight it. Dare doesn't get involved with clients, and Molly doesn't feel as if she and Dare match up well. (He's REALLY HOT!) I can relate to that! And sometimes that trope gets old...the "I'm not good enough for Mr. Beautiful" complex. But Molly isn't self deprecating. She just accepts that Dare is out of her league and therefore never imagines to flirt and simper like a teenager. Not that she doesn't look and drool. 
 I think this was a nice romantic suspense if you're looking for something that isn't off the charts crazy suspenseful or so steamy you're squirming in your favorite reading spot. It was a good story, well planned and executed, but just didn't hit any of my "amazing" buttons.

I decided to get this book because somewhere (can't remember - Goodreads, I think) someone (can't remember) said that Dare is the ultimate hero (or something). Haha! So, I guess it was a moment of flakiness. Anyway, I've been looking for a new hero - I mean, who hasn't; right? Unfortunately, for me, Dare did not exactly fit the bill. I can't say why, but he just didn't really excite me. There was nothing there. All in all though, the story was okay. It kept me distracted from life. That's always nice. I have to say though (and this is, of course, my own opinion), but I totally hate names like Dare, Jett, Trace. Maybe I'm just too old fashioned! :-S

Before my love of YA took over, I was obsessed with romance books. All kinds of them. Mystery romance, historical romance, contemporary, you name it and I loved it! Although I have been reading a ton of awesome YA books lately, I decided that it was time for me to throw in an adult book. It wasn't hard to decide which one because A. I love Lori Foster's books, B. This is a new series and C. Look at that cover! Holy swoon! 
 Dare Macintosh is a mercenary and out to help a friend. When his friend Trace's little sister gets kidnapped and is about to be sold in Tijuana, Dare is there to rescue her. He also finds that she is not the only one. After several of the girls get away he is left with Molly Alexander and this turns into a not so simple job after all. 
 I so loved this book. Not only because it was a romance, because I would have loved it for that alone, but there was action and mystery. Besides the romance we are brought into the mystery of finding out who had Molly kidnapped and why. There are still people out to get her and Dare will do whatever he can to make sure that she is safe. All the while, of course, completely falling for her and she with him. 
 There were some way HOT scences in this book! Like literally take my breath away hotness! Foster can tell such an amazing story and have the perfect amount of swoonworthy romance. It wasn't hard to fall in love with Dare just a few pages in. He's not only a big, tough mercenary, but he is also sweet and gentle when the time calls for it. 
 I always enjoy how the characters from one of Fosters books flow into the next. The follow up to When You Dare is Trace of Fever, which features Trace from this book. Along with getting to learn more about a supporting character from When You Dare, we still get little tidbits of the current characters lives. 
 Overall this book was insanely good! It makes me miss all those romances that I had been reading prior to my obsession with YA! This book kept me up late into the night. I seriously ate it right up and I could not put it down! It was that good. If you are looking for an excellent romance with a little toss of mystery and action then this book is totally for you!

Story follows Dare, a military man turned mercenary. He breaks up a human trafficking ring after they abduct Alani Rivers, his friend Traces' sister. One of the women rescued is Molly Alexander, a romance author. She was treated differently during captivity which leads him to believe it was a paid abduction instead of it being a snatch and grab at random. Dare takes over her protection and plans on cracking the case of who wants Molly out of the way. 
 Lets start with the characters. Dare is a sweetheart. He is always doting on Molly and worrying about every little thing. Even before he develops more than lusty feelings for her he plans on protecting her at no expense. He agrees to charge her only to get her to accept his help. Molly was an okay character. Kind of quiet. On the fence about her. Together they have great chemistry. 
 What turned me off was not the story, but the pacing of it & possibly the writing. Nothing ever happened. The reader was told of experiences, but we never get the birds eye view of what happened. I was bored through most of it. If it wasn't in audio I would have quit about 30 pages in. 
 I do like my romance parallel to my action so keep that in mind. Looks like i'm an exception looking at the rating of this book. The who-dun-it was pretty ridiculous also. Will not continue this series.

More like 3 1/2 stars.... 
 Another good installment from Lauren Dane. This was a nice friends to lovers books. Very adult and low key. Tatto artist Brody is the older brother to Erin (whose book Laid Bare was a nice eroic m/f/m read) and Adrian. He lives a good comfortable life. Although he looks like some mean, tattooed biker, he is a really a nice solid citizen who loves his family and has a good business. 
 Elise, a former prima ballerina, moves in across the street from him. She has a lovely daughter and a harrowing past. The two strike up a friendship and then decide to become friends with benefits. It is all nice and civilized. They heat up the sheets (and the tables and the stairwells and the desk...) while holding the party line that they are just friends. 
 But that fiction becomes harder and harder to maintain as Elise becomes good friends with his family and friends, he becomes hopelessly in love with her charming daughter and they find themselves more entwined with each other's lives. 
 Really enjoyed the book with the very little drama between the two principals. The drama was amply supplied by people outside the couple. There is a plot point where the parents of Elise's dead husband are trying to take custody of the daughter. And one of Bordy's exes suddenly realizes what she let go and tries to stir trouble.
Fair. A lot of heat, I like the protags well enough. I was wishing for more story and less sex, though. Probably my own attitude. I probably shouldn't read romance when I want story.

What did I think. I have only read a couple of Lauren Dane books and they have always been good. This one I don't know if it was because I really connected to the characters or what. I love Brody he looks like a bad boy with the motorcycle and tattoo's but he's really a good guy. Raising his younger sister and brother after their parents deaths. Then he meets his next door neighbor. Elise is a single Mum with a 7 year old daughter, she has baggage. They meet and fairly quickly start a friends with benefits relationship. I liked how it didn't happen just over a couple of weeks it took over a year for this relationship to develop. I loved the interaction with Erin and her two men and brother Adrian how they want what is best for their big brother. I loved Rennie and how she is a happy go lucky kid that is willing to embrace most people but how she hates talking to paternal grandparents. Raven another character well she came off to me as a lonely woman that doesn't know what she wants other than she does want a family but she's scared somethings happened in her past that they don't know about and she hasn't dealt with it yet. 
 I have kinda read this series out of order starting with Adrian book and now Brody. I will be reading Erin's once I get it, she sounds like she has been through a lot. 
 I would say if you like well written, solid characters with some good sex thrown in then this book is for you.
Awesome and smoking hot!!! I'm a dancer and loved this one!!

I absolutely love Elise, she talked in poetry when she described someone. I have never read a character that spoke like that. I love it!. Rennie she was so cute , there isn't much else one could say about her. I am happy Brody got his HEA he has done a lot for his family and deserves for someone to take care of him

Loved this book, how could you not love Brody? He is my second favorite character in the series (Ben is my first). He has the body of a "Bad-boy" but the heart and soul of a good guy. Elise is very lovable as well and definitely a good match for Brody and her daughter Rennie is so sweet and funny I can't help but laugh whenever she is in the scene. 
 A great followup to the series!

I was a little disappointed by this one, it just didn't grab me as much as Erin's story did. 
 But I could have had too high a expectations, as I adored the first book so much. I was also a little peeved by the direction a secondary character went in, who I had found interesting in first book. *pout* 
 Some parts of this book just seemed a like I was being preached at, (definitions of 'good' peoples etc) which kind of bugged me and pulled me out of the book.

reference_books.review_text: Meh. I expected more, actually, than this book was able to give. It was penned by the father of the boy, and frankly, I felt that the father was all, me, me me, instead of telling what his son felt and went through. book_a.title: The Wednesday Letters
book_a.user_review: This book was enthralling, touching and wonderful. It wove love, heartbreak, friendship and love between families and those involved in their bed and breakfast. Upon the deaths of the parents, the grown children find letters written by their parents to each other, that reveal a family secret. I loved this book and found it very hard to put down.

sample_reviews.review_text: A book club selection. I tried to look past the sticky-sweet Christian fiction fluff and get to the meat of the story but really had a hard time. I didn't even feel bad for Malcolm. A couple, one sick, both die in the same night. The kids gather for the funeral and find letters written to the mother from the father over 30 some odd years of marriage. The letters (too few) were the best part. Nice little twist at the end that made me say OMG, but it wasn't enough. Eh.

Disappointed in this one. Compared to the Notebook by Nicholas Sparks so I had high expectations. The writing was choppy and hard to follow in some places. Characters appeared without any introductions or lead ins. Neatly wrapped up at the end with one somewhat surprise that I found unbelievable. I would not recommend it. 
 In fact the only reason I finished it was because it was the choice for book club this month.
predictable, didn't really get going, too blatantly pro-choice

I think the thing that kept me reading this book (which is a very fast, 5th grade level book, by the way) was the way the book never fully explains itself until the last page. And even then, upon finishing, I didn't even feel like it had been worth my time. Really over dramatic, little character development (surprising since all the characters deal with more than a few serious matters in their lives), very cheesy (fit for a Hallmark or Lifetime movie) and not at all what I was expecting from a book that seems to advertise it is an epistolary novel.

Great book, quick read, a few suprises along the way. 
 I thought, at first, this book was all the love letters the husband wrote to his wife every week for their whole marriage. I thought I would then think my marriage is poop since my husband doesn't write me love letters every week. And it was actually phyically painful to read in places because it was so poorly written. 
 The dialog between the characters seemed very unrealistic, simplistic and just plain bad. And the author's attempts at description. Well, an example, from p 147 - "Matthew watched the scene unfold like the night's last, blurry dream before the sun wakes the house and its dreamers."
