sample_reviews.review_text:
** This book review, as well as many more, can also be found on my blog, The Baking Bookworm (www.thebakingbookworm.blogspot.ca). ** 
 My Review: I picked up this book recently from my local library right before a job interview. Trying to distract my nerves I sat there reading the book jacket I was quietly chuckling to myself and it honestly helped to reduce my nerves. I like funny reads. I do. But I also feel that they're really hard to write well. What is deemed "funny" means different things to different people and while I think that Jenny has a great sense of humour I don't necessarily think it came through well in this book. 
 There were some great, hilarious gems in this book but the overall feeling of chaos in her writing stifled those funny bits. It felt very disjointed -- like you were talking to a overly caffeinated person who would shoot out random stories that didn't necessarily have anything to do with each other. It often felt like she was just babbling and not caring about what she was talking about and after awhile that got frustrating. And don't get me started about the overused and excessively annoying footnotes! Gah! Enough already! I know you're funny Jenny! Show me! 
 Don't get me wrong, there were certain parts of stories where I did actually laugh out loud because Jenny is funny. But then she'd take too long to get to the end of the story and start to lose me. Or the story seemed much too unrealistic to be true and ... she'd start to lose me. Overall, I guess I just felt really lost. I read over half of the book before I finally called it quits because I just couldn't take any more of the rambling bedlam that is her memoire. 
 I think Jenny excels at writing funny little snippets (like on her blog, The Bloggess) but this full-fledged book didn't showcase her best comedic assets. With better editing and a more polished feel I think this could have been amazing. Unfortunately her frantic way of storytelling just isn't for me, I guess. I'll stick to reading her blog. 
 My Rating: 0 (didn't finish it)

The read was definitely a train-wreck. I good train wreck at times definitely, but a train-wreck nonetheless. The funny thing is that Jenny would probably take this as a compliment. It was great to hear Jenny's story and it gave so much honest perspective on the most interesting experiences. Throughout the book, I wondered if she would still be with her husband by the end. She must have guessed that because she addressed in the epilogue and made it clear that sometimes what people perceive as imperfection or "weird" is actually just a fraction of the silent majority's reality.

I think this book would be hilarious as a stand up routine. The stories are wacky, but something about the narration just didn't work for me in written form. It was funny (maybe not funny haha), but didn't make me laugh, if that makes sense. I'd give the audiobook a try. I share this review as a very personal take on this book. It obviously worked for some folks!

This is an incredible book. Its "laugh out loud while rolling on the floor" funny. The author is vulgar, opinionated and offensive, but she is never condescending to the reader. Her writing reminds me of Lewis Grizzard, who was a brilliant storyteller. 
 If you are offended by profanity or overt references to reproductive organs in contexts you would never dream of, stay away from the book. 
 If you want to read writing that is heartfelt and can make you laugh at things the would normally have you crying, this book is well worth the cost and time.
Hilarious. The author narrates herself and is very funny. Anyone looking for a light listen (but who is not offended by strong language) should try this.

I was unfamiliar with The Bloggess before this book started popping up in all the summer "Must Read" lists, but the buzz surrounding this one was enough to convince me to give Jenny Lawson a shot. In the end, I'm kind of underwhelmed. She started out strong; her childhood stories were flat-out hysterical. Reading about her father waking Jenny up with a puppet fashioned out of a dead squirrel had me laughing so hard I couldn't barely breathe. It's not necessarily new territory - the wacky parents are a staple of the humor memoir - but Lawson related the antics with a wry tone that killed me. 
 And then she grew up, and the stories became less funny than "Look at how weird I am, you guys. Ohmigosh, I'm so weird." Maybe I'm being a little cynical but once the perspective shifted to her life as a wife, mother, HR specialist and socially awkward blogger, I got bored. I didn't feel like there was anything particularly unique about Lawson's story and the tales of her arguments with her husband and her inability to moderate her anxiety as she met with other bloggers for a spa weekend weren't amusing. It struck me as someone trying too hard to be funny and quirky without any idea of the point she was trying to make.

Jenny Lawson is a blogger. This book consists of stories of her life. Her family did not have much money as she was growing up in Texas. She has an... unusual... father. She and her sister grew up with lots of animals around, wild and domestic, dead and alive (her father is a taxidermist). She suffers from social anxiety. Her husband's family has money and is quite different from her own, so she struggles a little bit to fit in with them. 
 I had no idea who she was, but I saw some good reviews for the book, so I thought I'd give it a try. I found this so funny! I laughed out loud plenty of times, and the one chapter that had me laughing so hard I was crying and it was hard to breathe, and I couldn't stop for some time, was the one that described the 5 foot tall metal chicken she brought home. In particular, it was her husband's reaction that got me going. It was the best 15th anniversary ever! Oh, and there are photos to go with the stories, so you know they really happened!

I couldn't/didn't finish this. Who ever said this was up there with Tina Fey and David Sedaris is smoking crack; or has never read either of them. She is in serious need of an editor. It's over written and she's trying way to hard which just made it terribly annoying. I'm baffled how this became a best seller.

If you want to laugh so hard you cry or pee your pants then this is your book. I have never in my life enjoyed a "funny" book as much as this one. It never bores you, or makes you wish you hadn't bought it. It was a hysterical, tear jerking, pee your pants, not for the faint at heart or the easily offended kind of person. I think Jenny and I are related somewhere in our family tree because this book made me think of my own family and childhood and makes me happy to see there are other families like mine. Be proud of yourself and your abnormal family and enjoy more than a wee chuckle.

Hysterically funny, laugh out loud hilarious!! 
 5 out of 5, no question! 
 Love her blog and her book was just wonderful...! 
 Rude, crass, un-explainable at times but truly wonderful.

reference_books.title: One Plus One
reference_books.review_text:
Ditched by her husband, living on the breadline in a housing association estate, 27 year old Jessica Thomas finds providing for her family to be a constant battle. She tries her best, she sees herself as a glass half full person, but she never stops working - or worrying. In her job as a cleaner alongside her friend Nathalie, and her second job as a barmaid, she gets glimpses into other peoples' lives and they never match up to her own. Daughter Tanzie, 10 and a maths prodigy, has the opportunity to go to public school via a scholarship. Goth stepson Nicky, a sulky 16, is bullied at school by the local hooligans and finds it hard to cope, seeking solace in cannabis. The scholarship will remove Tanzie from the bullies' orbit, but how will Jess ever find the money? 
 Moyes has a knack of putting together "damaged" individuals who would ordinarily never have a relationship with each other. One of them is always "out of the other's league" and this person has to go through a humbling, life-changing experience to effectively "bring them down" before a relationship can blossom. Enter Ed Nicholls. He's a wealthy computer nerd with a massive problem; he's facing jail for insider trading. Their worlds collide when Jess cleans his South Coast holiday retreat, setting off a chain of events that are quite unbelievable. Ed's good deed is indeed very odd. However, he has been a victim of his own weakness with a former university crush, driven, I think, by his determination to finally win "the one that got away". 
 Faced with finding the contribution to the scholarship, Jess finds out that all Tanzie has to do is to win a maths competition. Small problem - it's in Aberdeen and how will they get there? Somehow Jess persuades Ed to drive them there - the whole family, including Norman the dog. This seemed unbelievable to me, although without it there would be no story. All kinds of madness then ensue as a bonkers road trip gets under way. 
 I think we fall into the trap of thinking authors are always sympathetic to their main protagonist. Were we meant to like Jess? I'm not sure that I did. Having persuaded Ed to drive them heaven knows how many miles, she hides from him the fact she has pocketed PS800 that dropped out of his wallet when drunk, proceeds to sit with her feet up on the dashboard of his car (that image is horrid) and gets them all into so many scrapes we think she's bonkers. A lot happens in these four days; Jess comes face to face with her ex-husband Marty, a completely ridiculous and unsympathetic individual who was only included to complete the story arc, allowing Jess to move on. The best storyline belonged to Nicky. It was great to see him come out of his shell under Ed's influence and out of his usual environment. But, my most favourite character of all was Norman the dog. 
 This was an amusing read, and on the whole kept my interest, but it worked better for me as a funny road trip than a romance. I thought the love element happened far too quickly, and felt it quite irresponsible and selfish of Jess as a parent to sleep with a complete stranger in front of her children. (Not literally, but they knew what was going on). I thought it took the theme of the kindness of strangers just a little TOO far and I really didn't like it. This author seems to have a theme of pitching together characters who wouldn't touch each other with a bargepole without some cataclysmic event happening to make them "in each other's league". In his "Me Before You" life, Ed wouldn't have looked twice at Jess. It was also completely morally wrong of Jess to have stolen from Ed. His reaction was reasonably justified, but I think the old Ed wouldn't have forgiven her; she wouldn't even have been on his radar. 
 It was our book club read and I felt it well worth reading, though somewhat unrealistic in the romance stakes.

reference_books.title: I Let You Go
reference_books.review_text:
Right from the beginning, this psychological thriller is not at all what it seems. It is a very cleverly crafted tale of the consequences of a hit and run. The driver fails to stop when 5 year old Jacob is killed on a dark, wet November night in Bristol, and his mother's life will never be the same again. 
 Unable to cope, Jenna moves away from her home in the aftermath of the accident and seeks sanctuary in remote South Wales. Alongside this we read about the police procedural following the investigation into the accident. The two officers involved are dogged and determined to find the person who mowed Jacob down, against the instructions of their superiors and this uncovers a series of massive shocks. We also learn quite a lot about the lives of the investigating officers, a little cliched here, a mid-life crisis and a marriage that's running none too smoothly, 
 It begins with a shocking prologue describing the accident. This sets the scene for everything that is to happen (and has already happened), following on with chapters alternately narrated by Jenna and omniscient narration going into detail about the investigation. It's full of twists, and you end up wondering how you ever thought something was reality when something else pops up and surprises you. Jenna attempts to put the past behind her in Wales, slowly piecing her life together and starting a tentative romantic relationship with the local vet. There is a shock at the end of Part One, included to highlight the irony of Jenna's relationship with a guy who is seriously in the business of saving lives as he's not only a vet, but a part time lifeboat crew member. 
 Part Two comes as a shock too. There is a third narrator - possibly one of the rottenest characters I have ever come across in a book - and the descriptions of Jenna as a vibrant, lively 21 year old are in stark contrast to her narration in Part One which invoke a dismal, dreary, pathetic character, struggling to exist. From then on you are never sure about her, about her new love, about her life, and who is wrong and who is right. The ending is far too swift, too unbelievable and too rushed, and this brings down the overall rating, I'm afraid.

reference_books.title: The Girl on the Train
reference_books.review_text:
Rachel Watson is no different from the rest of the characters in this book - every one of them is seriously messed up. Rather than a whodunit or a thriller, this book is more of a character study of flawed individuals, what makes them as they are and what effect their interaction has had on them over time. 
 We first meet Rachel when she gets the train to work every morning - or does she? What can we believe about what Rachel tells us? Is she telling lies to us, does she think her narration is true, or does she even know the truth herself? This is the most fascinating aspect of this story. Rachel's train stops at a signal every day, she looks out of the window and constructs a fantasy about a couple who live in a house just over the tracks. In her mind she knows their names, their lifestyle and their jobs. The story is told from the points of view of three women - Rachel, Anna who has married Rachel's ex-husband Tom and who Rachel sees as a thief and a cuckoo in her own nest, and Megan, the perfect woman in the perfect house. But absolutely nothing is as it seems in this story. Rachel's turned to drink, has lost almost everything and is very open to suggestion. Daydreaming about the lives of the couple in the house meets this need and distracts her from the hot mess that is her own life. And the surprising scene she witnesses one day provides her with a reason to be a part of something again, but will she be taken seriously? Many of us people-watch and imagine fleetingly about those we see on our daily commute, but Rachel takes this to extremes because of the emptiness in her own soul. 
 The narration is meant to lead the reader in certain directions and make assumptions about Rachel, her husband, and the basis for the break-up of her marriage. For this reason she is an unreliable narrator, but not in the traditional sense. In fact, she is not aware of the truth herself, which adds to the central mystery for the reader. We see her as a nuisance, a threat to her husband and his new family, and a danger to herself. But that is what we are meant to see and the author has skilfully woven the interlinking lives of these characters together to keep our curiosity. 
 One issue I had with the three narrators is that their voices seemed almost identical. All female, about the same age, same demographic, probably similar level of education, and all are morally flawed. They had no distinguishing features and this made the narration somewhat bland and samey. Also, none of them are particularly likeable (although by the end you have developed empathy with one of them) so it's hard to care what happens to them. 
 For me, the least interesting thing was unmasking the murderer (though I kept changing my mind about who that was as I read on) as opposed to finding out why they did it. None of the characters are trustworthy, and none can be trusted to make informed decisions about others, either. 
 Another real issue I had was that all these women define themselves in relation to men in their life. Rachel felt nothing without Tom, Anna felt superior because she was able to prise Tom away from Rachel and Megan, well, she was a manipulator, but it was all about relationships with men, being a mother (or not as the case may be) and very little about being an independent woman. 
 The book brilliantly handles the perceptions we make about other people, and particularly those perceptions in relation to ourselves. One realisation, one awakened memory, as one of the characters finds out, changes everything - our whole life, our memories and our reasons for doing things. 
 The ending wasn't satisfying enough for me as I thought it too predictable and unsubtle though I can highly recommend this as an excellent (4.5) read.

reference_books.title: I Found You
reference_books.review_text:
I picked this up immediately after finishing a 10 year old book by the same author in a different genre both for curiosity and comparisons. This is a very different book in both plot and construction, but the similarity I noticed is that this author is excellent at characterisation. In both books I was able to really visualise the characters, their mannerisms and motivations and this really drives the story along. 
 On reading the back cover, I thought the plot was obvious (so many books give the game away on the back) but it isn't, and though there are connections, they aren't immediately apparent. The narrative unwinds at a good pace but there are still shocks in store. 
 The immediate focus is on two very different women; single mother of three children all with different fathers, Alice, who has moved from London to a North Yorkshire seaside town that could be Robin Hood's Bay, could be Whitby ...... and Ukrainian Lily, married to Carl for three weeks after knowing him only a few short weeks before that. What does she really know about her husband, twice her age, who has failed to return from work and who she has reported missing to the police? Meanwhile, on a wet and miserable day Alice spots a man sitting on the beach outside her house, who appears to have lost his memory and who she takes into her house to try to help, though she is warned by her best mate not to get involved. The story starts to come together when the dual timeframe element is employed which harks back to a holiday from hell in the 90s, which is truly dark and disturbing. The present and the past tense is used in the current and the 1993 segments, which works to give a sense of immediacy and distance respectively as well as contrast. 
 Out of all the characters, I felt the most empathy and connection with Gray, though I liked Alice's get on with it attitude and Lily's adjustment to living in a foreign country although not living the life she had anticipated. 
 I love Lisa's writing and will be seeking out all her back catalogue. But be warned - the last few pages, whilst wrapping it all up, are heart rending and poignant. I've given 4.5 stars because I couldn't put the book down (was told off for being antisocial!) but I felt that it relied too heavily on coincidence - the chance meeting in the street in London, the coffee shop gathering - and Kitty's appalling behaviour, the results of which almost made me cry. 
 But please tell me, someone found and fed Brenda! 4.5.

reference_books.title: The Widow
reference_books.review_text:
Is this one of those unreliable narrator books, where you are never quite sure just what is going on? The cover mentions The Girl on the Train, another review has it as the next Gone Girl (how I wish these tiresome comparisons would stop!) I found it was nothing like either of those books and an interesting read all on its own. I am surprised that this is Fiona's first book as it is very accomplished. Jean Taylor is a mousy housewife, barely 40 years old which came as a shock, as the way she was presented led me to believe she was in her 60s. 
 Written from various points of view - Jean, the widow of the title, Kate, the reporter, Bob, the detective, and Glen, the "monster" - do we ever really know what is the truth, what has gone on and if we are being led up the garden path along with Jean? She's a definite unreliable. She's either trying to convince us, or herself, or all of us that she loves Glen, the control freak who she was lucky to bag, and has been happy with him all this time. Once Glen has fallen under a bus, all the journalists come out of the woodwork to get the "real story". This is where the back story unravels through flashbacks and we come to learn more about the disappearance of two year old Bella, about Jean, Glen, their relationship and the police/journalistic procedural aspect. Jean, I could not work out at all, but I did like the journalist, Kate and the detective, good old Bob, who was like a terrier and wouldn't let go until he found the answers. 
 But here is where we don't know the answers; it was interesting, disturbing and covers some frankly sick territory, but who actually did what?

book_a.title: Defending Jacob
book_a.user_review:
This was our August book group choice, and I'm glad I waited until after the group discussion to write a review as talking about the book brought up many interesting issues. The book is a family drama as much as a crime novel and though at first I thought it would be full of Americanisms I couldn't understand, I found it drew me in to the point I couldn't stop reading it. 
 Andy Barber is an Assistant DA with a 14-year-old son Jacob, who is standing trial for the murder of one of his classmates, Ben, who was found stabbed in the local park. The skill of the writer meant that I could never work out if Jacob was guilty or not and my mind kept changing; indeed by the end I still wasn't totally sure. Many things come out of the woodwork that seem as if Jacob committed the crime; he's found in possession of a knife, he was bullied by the deceased boy, his Facebook page features questionable posts and he writes a detailed description of the killing. It is not just Jacob on trial, it is his whole family. 
 Taken off the case owing to the conflict of interest, and driven by unconditional love for his son, Andy never seems to once consider that Jacob is guilty and goes to great lengths to prove his innocence. He seems blinkered and obtuse, unwilling to consider he isn't acknowledging Jacob's real character. Jacob seems a detached, strange boy although Andy views him as nothing but the normal son of a very happy couple. Andy's marriage to his wife Laurie, who he has known for 33 years, seems strong and unbreakable. But here too there are omissions. Laurie doesn't know Andy's family history but I think she does have a clue about her son. 
 In an absolutely fascinating chapter, Andy tells us about the Barber gene. His father is in prison for murder. His grandfather and great-grandfather did time for violence. Andy has led a blameless, upstanding life. Do the sins of the fathers pass on through the generations? Is there a murder gene that is passed from father to son? Did Andy avoid it? Or did Andy choose his profession to keep himself in check, knowing there was no margin for error, thinking that the family traits may come back to haunt him? And did Jacob inherit this? 
 You're on the qui vive all the way through the book for clues, and the ending is shocking and heartbreaking. I was left wondering how Andy could go on, but all of us are still left to work out who actually killed Ben. We think we know, because of Laurie's actions in the twist ending, but do we really? It was left open to interpretation and I am still thinking about it now, three weeks after reading it. We're all left to draw our own conclusions. 
 5 stars for this compelling page turner.

This book was good! Kinda all over the place and I wish it would have actually gone into if Jacob did the crime or not! The end was sad and a complete twist! Overall I enjoyed reading it just would not be on my top five list!

The scenes at the witness stand bored me until Derek was called. Laurie was insane. I never ever imagined she would do that. I was excited at first then boredom was mounting up at the middle then disappointed at Laurie. What she did was inconceivable and deplorable. 
 I was confused at this statement. "Mr. Logiudice: Well, you didn't report it. Witness: I was slow to realize--in hindsight, I admit-- Mr. Logiudice: Mr. Barber, how could you be slow to realize when, in fact, you'd been waiting for this moment for fourteen years, from the day your son was born?- huh?? What moment?

 3.5 Stars - Interesting novel to be reading at the same time that a young man actually shoots innocent movie goers in Aurora, CO. I couldn't help draw parallels in my mind between the fictional young man in the story and the disturbed shooter in Colorado. Both accounts made me wonder why...what went wrong? Finally, is there really such a thing as a "murder gene?" If you enjoy a courtroom drama and a surprise ending, this is a good read.

Full of twists and turns, this legal thriller will definitely keep your attention from beginning to end. 
 What would you if you are the assistant DA, and a boy from your son's school is dead? What would you do if your son becomes the prime suspect? What would you do if you think he just might be guilty? 
 This book asks and answers all of these questions and several more in a well written story that uses court transcripts from a witness deposition as a jumping off point. Just when you think you have a grip on the situation something else is revealed, making this book very difficult to put down, and to forget about once you are finished
Great, compelling courtroom drama. Hard to resist. Tight and well written.

book_b.title: The Versions of Us
book_b.user_review:
This book has been compared to One Day - I fail to understand why, as the concept is not the same at all and Sliding Doors - which it has more resonance with, though this story has yet one more variation. It's an absolutely fascinating and intriguing hypothesis and has inspired me to do something similar with my own diary that I wrote at 16, for curiosity and creativity - what would have happened if I had done this, or that, or not as the case may be, or stayed in on that evening? I find it a really interesting hypothesis to play around with. 
 However, I found it confusing to follow by reading from page one right through - so I read the whole of Version 1, then the whole of Version 2 and 3 and then the 2014 section that I'd purposely left until last. Perhaps I could have read the ending(s) at the end of each version too rather than all together because by that time I had totally forgotten about Jennifer, Carl, Daniel .......... 
 I've always thought "what if" about my own life - and not just thought it but tried to extrapolate it - so was excited to read this. I think the writing was very good particularly for a debut novel, but each version of the story was rather mundane and quite depressing. Were any of the characters truly happy or just making the best of what happened to them because of the decisions they made? 
 The main characters are Eva and Jim, who meet (or don't, depending on the version you are reading) in 1958 in Cambridge. Depending on what happens next, their stories play out very differently. 
 I was annoyed at Jim in Version 1, being such a wet muffler, jealous and resentful of his wife's success and expressing that through his inability to keep it in his pants so I wasn't surprised when it came back to bite him on the backside. I could see exactly how Version 2 would play out with the awful mother in law (though liked how she was treated at the end) and David being such a self-centred luvvie. In Version 3, Jim again came across as somewhat selfish but I had more sympathy with him in this life. 
 Which did I prefer? It had the same outcome for poor old Jim, whatever (maybe smoking all that grass did for him?) though I think the second version is preferable for me. They had a happy ending as such towards the end of their lives, without having gone through all the trauma with Sophie. Yes I think that is the best one. They had nothing to regret about each other and their relationship, short as it was, would have been more real and "pure". 
 Also, is the message that you can't have it all? In Version 3, Jim has a much more successful career, but he's not happy with his personal life. Eva's career is less stellar than in Version 1, but she has an unhappy marriage to a narcissist and though her second marriage is happy, there is a personal cost to that relating to her husband Ted. Jim has the most diverse career - in one he actually becomes a solicitor, in others he's an artist. The solicitor role was forced on him, clearly, by his sense of responsibility to his mother. Eva is clearly the strongest character in the book, with more moral fibre and back bone than selfish David (who is consistently selfish in every version), Jim in version 1, etc. I wasn't sure what shaped Jim - he was unfaithful in the first version, owing to his immaturity and inability to handle his wife's career being more successful than his. But a friend remarks "like father like son" when he leaves Helena for Eva, but this is the only aberration in this part. I don't think he was like his father in reality. 
 It shows us three different lives, not versions of the same one, because they are all unique. I liked how it treated the idea that there is no such thing as fate (because there isn't). Or a perfect life. If the same problems don't occur in one life, others do. Also, there is probably no Mr/Miss Right, either! I don't think we got to know the characters in enough depth, though, because each segment was only a snapshot and with a good few years in between each one made it feel sketchy, just a snapshot rather than a portrait. 
 What didn't work, and I don't think the author thought of it nor any proof reader, was that in the version (3??) where Eva chucks Jim because she is already pregnant by David, surely she would have been already pregnant in both other versions too - because the only constant point of reference is Jim and Eva's first meeting on the Cambridge Backs. Following from whatever decision happens then, their lives veer off in other ways. So that didn't work at all. Or is this the version where she didn't fall off the bike?? Hmmm .......... 
 I liked the Cambridge setting at first, because I know Cambridge fairly well, and could visualise the places - I know the Backs, Market Square, Clare College. Also I went to Broadway in the Cotswolds and know the pub they mentioned too so that was interesting. I just knew that a T S Eliot quote from Four Quartets Burnt Norton would be included - "Time present and time past are both perhaps present in time future, and time future contained in time past." - as soon as it was mentioned Eva had an assignment on Eliot to hand in. 
 Very interesting concept on the whole I enjoyed it. But the outcome for Jim at the end of each version was the same. So how much could we have controlled by changing one thing? To what extent does the butterfly effect really influence our lives? Read this and decide.

sample_reviews.review_text: I didn't mind this too much at first but the last 100 or so pages dragged really badly. Also it was SO hetero and the only LGBTQ character was a cliched lesbian who a wife fell in love with but it was written from the perspective of the husband so nope.

** spoiler alert ** 
 A clever concept, nicely explored. I raced through this book in a day - possibly why I didn't have the problems with confusion between the different stories that other reviewers had. 
 My two problems with the book are really the same problem: Jim is so thoroughly unlikeable that the only story I really enjoyed was Version 2, where Eva doesn't get involved with him until very late on; also I expected to be deeply emotionally invested and cry at the end, but as the end focuses on Jim's death I didn't find it sad - if it was Eva's death, it would have been much more emotionally affecting. 
 Still, I enjoyed this a lot, and will be reading Laura Barnett's future books.

Perhaps because I read this on an e-reader, the pattern of the "versions" of the story were not immediately obvious because I didn't see the words "version one" (or two and three) at the top of the chapter. I assume that's easier to see on a print version. 
 In the end, I really enjoyed the stories of Eva and Jim- the ways in which their lives intertwined in each version of the story. Eva and Jim meet one afternoon in college and then their blossoming romance is tested by circumstances that lead to choices that give us three versions of their two lives. Familiar faces populate each version- Eva's parents and brother, friends they have known since college or soon there after- all providing continuity to these stories no matter how the relationship of Eva and Jim varies. 
 The novel takes the reader from Jim's and Eva's college years to their later years and as a result, the book has an emotional resonance and the natural bittersweet reality that comes with love and loss of loved ones and friends over the course of a lifetime.

I received a copy of this from the publisher via NetGalley in exchange for an honest review. 
 Review also appears on my blog The Book Brief 
 The Versions Of Us is a thought-provoking, elegantly written debut which takes inspiration from both The Time Traveller's Wife and One Day, two of my favourite novels of recent years. This clever novel - which has already been snapped up for television - tells the story of Eva and Jim, three different ways. 
 "A young woman with a broken bicycle. The man she might, so easily, have missed cycling past, not stopping, carrying with him a whole life, a life that might never have been hers to share." 
 In 1958, the two Cambridge students almost collide when Eva has to swerve suddenly while riding her bicycle to class. Or, what if Eva doesn't swerve? Or ignores Jim's offer for help? This is the entire concept behind the book; as three different versions of events unfold, each revolving around Eva and Jim - either together or separately - at its centre. 
 I don't want to go into details about the storyline of this book - firstly, because it would spoil it, and you should read it for yourself. But secondly, because the story feels so vast and all-encompassing, it's impossible to contain in one review. The writer somehow effortlessly covers not just one lifetime but three alternative ones with all their complexities and ups and downs, and packs it into just over 400 pages without it ever feeling rushed. Admittedly, things do feel a little difficult to keep track of at times - it's not just their relationship you need to follow, but their varying careers, children and lifestyles - but I think this is to be expected considering the vast ambition of this book. The way Barnett captures a lifetime among her pages; following Eva and Jim from student life into old age; it felt almost surreal and emphasised to me how insignificant and yet conversely meaningful one life can be. This isn't just a love story, but a life story too. 
 The characters were realistic and imperfect, but I have to admit they did border a little on irritating at times. In all versions Eva feels very wise, dignified and self-sacrificing, while Jim is artistic and impulsive bordering on downright insensitive and cruel - the situation began to grate a little. I did begin to wonder if the novel was a little skewed towards the woman being the righteous character, and I got so wound up with Jim there were times when I was no longer rooting for the two of them to end up together. 
 But my small niggles about the characters didn't matter by the end, as I was still an emotional wreck as I entered the moving final few chapters. What I had realised at that point is that there is no perfect version. This book is posed as asking What if? but the answer I came away with was that it doesn't matter. There is no perfect life based on making all the right decisions. All lives will be peppered with good and bad, and what life is really about is holding on and making the most of the good times, and not lingering on the negatives; "Because he is old enough now to know happiness for what it is; brief and fleeting, not a state to strive for, to seek to live in, but to catch when it comes, and to hold on to for as long as you can." A deep, thought-provoking tearjerker which I won't forget in a hurry and I look forward to re-reading.

I just didn't like it - three underwritten stories instead of one properly developed one. This was hard work to read because of the gimmicky structure - there's no joy of reading to be had here. 
 Avoid unless you want to grind your teeth to bored, irritated stumps. Oh, and for this conceit to be logically accurate, Eva should have been pregnant when she meets/doesn't meet Jim in EVERY version
Slightly confusing at times keeping up with three versions of two people but well worth the read. Really loved the main characters and all the heart strings were tugged. so many feels.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I loved the premise, the sliding doors idea of how our lives can take different paths based on one moment, one decision. I enjoyed the characters, the backstories and following them over the course of their different possible lives. 
 That said I really found it hard to follow, jumping from version 1 to 2, then 3 and back again in any variation. It was just a bit frustrating. It would have been better to read in one sitting to get the continuity of each story. Eventually I stopped worrying and let it wash over me. This seemed to work and by the end I'd worked out different 'versions' enough to enjoy the final chapters and the stories being wrapped up. 
 I suppose what strikes me now as I reflect on it is that the book is fatalistic- regardless which version there is a destiny for Jim and Eva and the author really creates that sense of 2 people having that connection in life. She explores how the path we might believe to be the best may not play out as you'd expect and I like that. 'The best laid plans...' and all that.

3.5 stars- 3 stars for the book, 4 for the conversation it sparked at book club. Three different versions of the same couple showing that we are the sum of our choices. Different choices lead to different outcomes in who we are, who we become, and who we have in our lives.

reference_books.review_text:
I won the third book in this series, so I needed to make sure I checked out the first two and get them finished before the third arrived. I will say that I am giving this book a lower rating for reasons below. BUT, I want to say that I am about 50 pages in on the second and many of the issues I had seem to be fixed in the second. So! Read the first as an introduction.

reference_books.title: Those Girls
reference_books.review_text:
I'm sorry to say, but I just wasn't all that impressed with this book. Stevens' writing is simple and easy to speed read. I was expecting more thrills and chills given the cover and the synopsis, but now that I'm finished, I'm totally underwhelmed by the story telling. It was fine, but it wasn't great. It wasn't memorable, and there wasn't much that stood out to me. I think it would make a great lifetime movie . . . if it's not already one. 
 Dani, Courtney and Jess live on a farm with their abusive father. One night he tries to kill Courtney for having an affair with a married man. Jess (the youngest) ends up shooting and killing him to save her sister's life. This was an open and shut self-defense case. But, of course they buried the body, got rid of his truck and ran away. While fleeing their truck breaks down in another small farm town. Two boys offer to help repair the truck, but they turn out to be sick, twisted sociopaths. The kidnap the sisters and rape them. They escape after five days and a local bar/restaurant owner helps them escape to Vancouver where a friend helps them start a new life, and they change their names - Dallas, Crystal and Jamie. Crystal can't really cope with what's happened to her. Jamie ends up being pregnant from the sexual assault and not being able to give up the baby. Crystal goes back to the small town to try to kill their attackers, 17 years after. Her niece, Skyler, is the only one who realizes that Crystal has gone to do this and follows her. They both get captured and tortured by one of the original two boys. Eventually they free themselves, because the police are useless to do anything. Crystal and attacker two end up killed in the end. 
 I felt that the characters were very flat, especially the "bad boys" from the second small town. What drove them to be such sick-os? Did they do it to anyone else? If not, why those girls? Surely they would have had a reputation, surely the police force in that small town would be aware of their tendency towards sadistic acts or hurting women. In a town as small as Stevens depicts this one, people usually don't have too many secrets. Again, the book was OK. It wasn't the worst, but it certainly could have been better. I had predicted the ending almost right away. There wasn't anything creepy or surprising or new said here.

reference_books.title: The Little Paris Bookshop
reference_books.review_text:
Picked this book up from a local little free library. I'm not sure what I was expecting, but this wasn't it. I could not wait for this book to be over. I wished that I could have skimmed it faster, but almost every time I picked it up I was bored to sleep. 
 It's about a bookseller who claims to be a literary apothecary - can prescribe books to heal your soul, etc. But he rarely ever does that and spends more time just floating (literally) around France looking at silly shit and have basically meaningless experiences that all somehow help him get over the love of his life, who left him some twenty years ago and he NEVER got over it. I mean never opened the letter she left him, never loved another woman or was open to anyone else ever again. Never slept with another woman or had any affection from anyone. Really it's quite pathetic. I can't believe that someone can be that locked down emotionally and yet somehow be able to make a living sensing what other people need and reading their souls. It just really wasn't my cup of tea. There was very little action and when something did happen I was excited. . . for a second, but then almost immediately bored again. I'm not sure if the authors writing was lost when the book was translated, I just found it very childish and did not find the characters to be very deep or well developed, as they would need to be to make a story that relies so heavily on characterization and the transformation of characters successful. When Perdu does open the letter his lover left, he finds out she had cancer and was dying! What kind of ass doesn't read the woman he loves letter. She could have written anything in there. How childish to assume the worst and then not read it for years. He wasted his life, and in all honesty I felt like I was wasting mine reading this book. 
 I would not recommend this to anyone and I will be returning it to the little free library for someone else to find. Perhaps they will enjoy it more than I did.

reference_books.title: Wolfsbane (Nightshade #2; Nightshade World #5)
reference_books.review_text:
I liked this book better than the first, because you learn a lot more about world of the Searchers, and I thought about giving it four stars. . . buttt I just couldn't commit because Calla disappointed me yet again by not choosing Ren. UGH. I know it's never going to happen now, but I can't help myself. 
 Calla and Shay find themselves with the Searchers, and given an opportunity for a new alliance that promises to help not only themselves but also their pack. Saving the pack was the most exciting part of the book, as well as all of the new Searcher characters. Shay continued to annoy me the majority of the book. I'm sorry Cremer! You just made him SO unlikable. 
 "His wolf instincts were taking over, and they were threatening something he considered to his territory . . . me. He was acting like I was his mate. His alpha counterpart. And that meant I was the only one who could intervene," (58). - So much for this being a book about a girl who wants to be free and make her own choices. She was the property of one man, only to become the property of another. Shay is so possessive, selfish and insensitive. 
 Calla's brother Ansel arrives close to death after a Searcher shoots him with arrows. He is no longer a Guardian, no longer a wolf and he tells a gruesome story of the torture the pack has had to go through since Calla left. Her pack held prisoner and being tortured by wraiths, her father having to watch her mother be murdered by a rival alpha because she failed as a mother, and Ren being tortured worst of all because he loves her and is protecting her. So the small team of Searchers decides to go in and rescue the pack, and Shay just wants to chalk it up to casualties of war. He is OK with letting the whole pack die just to make sure that there is no chance of Calla changing her mind to be with Ren, when he had clearly sacrificed so much so that she could be happy with another man . . . really sick. I mean if he truly loves her he would know how deeply this affects her and not say such cold things to try to get her to let it go. 
 When they finally make the rescue attempt half the pack helps Calla and the other half has chosen to submit to Emile. Ren is angry and broken and goes after Calla, but he still loves her and wants to be with her. He just can't seem to see any other way than the through the confines of what's allowed by the Keepers. We also find out that my assumption that Monroe is Ren's father was correct. We can assume that he is now dead. Calla chooses Shay as her new alpha. Gosh I'm just so shocked at the consistently shitty lot that Ren has received in this book. PLUS I was reading reviews and I already know what happens in the last book. I almost don't want to read it. A man who lost the woman he loves and submitted himself to heinous torture to protect her while she ran away with another man, finds out his mother was murdered, his father isn't who he thought he was and then his real father is murdered in front of him. He must be completely broken. But, his real father did care about him and his dying wish to his daughter was "Save him." So that's where we leave off. Calla is going to try to save him from himself . . . too bad she couldn't have saved him from herself. He's honestly the most compelling character in the book in my opinion. What it would be like to know what's going through his mind and to have grown up with Emile. How different his life could have been if he had grown up with his mother and/or his father. Perhaps that's why Calla was so conflicted for so much of this book, because she knows there is more than meets the eye and that she was actually in love with him. 
 I said it in my last review and I'll say it again . . . Calla and Ren would be together under different circumstances and if Shay would leave Calla alone long enough with her thoughts perhaps she would have chosen Ren over him. But, he did not let that happen.

book_a.title: Cruel Beauty (Cruel Beauty Universe, #1)
book_a.user_review:
I really did not like this book, and I'm pretty disappointed, but it was so weird and confusing and hard to follow and yet still pretty boring. . . I'm sorry I rarely ever give a one star rating but I just couldn't wait for it to be over. 
 A retelling of the classic Beauty & the Beast. Nyx is promised to the Gentile Lord (aka Demon Lord) in marriage, even before she is born. Her mother couldn't have a baby, so her father struck a deal with the Gentile Lord to marry him one of his daughters at 17, so long as his wife would have a child. She had twin daughters, but died in childbirth. Nyx is supposed to kill the "beast" with some Hermetic magic bullshit. Honestly, it really doesn't make much sense to me. And, neither does Nyx's relationship with her sister; she hates her guts, but she loves her, but she really hates her. Make up your mind. You either love your sister because she's your sister and it's not her fault your dad is a prick, or you hate her . . . simple. 
 I read on Hodge's author page that she loves mythology. I think that she has so much of Greek mythology in this book that the story itself is drowning and not standing on it's own merits. Not to mention the fact that most people probably don't have such a deep knowledge of Greek Mythology to know what a Hermetic lamp is nor what the symbols are, nor how they could be used to stop a demon king. Is that even what is going on? I'm not sure. It's just not really grounded in something that one can easily understand. 
 Several times I felt bored AF! Then! Nyx falls in love with the Demon Lord. . . and his shadow. But then promises to kill him, even though he's really not in control. Yikes . . . it's just a mess. I would not recommend it. Sorry people that liked it!

I just finished this book. I had high hopes since it's a re-telling of beauty and the beast, which is my favorite fairy tale. But I did have some issues with it. I found the world extremely confusing (even being someone who does know quite a bit about mythology)I didn't fully understand the ending or what happened and I found myself lost very often in the book, having to go back and re read certain parts to better grasp what was going on. I had trouble feeling sorry for the world or relating to the world that Nyx was trying to save because I felt I knew so little about it. 
 I did enjoy the characters (for the most part) and the twist (which I won't give away) but my confusion overruled any attachment I could have for the book. I spent more time trying to figure out what the author meant than I did enjoying what I was reading and every time I started to get engrossed, I'd stumble upon yet another part where I found myself lost. 
 Although I actually enjoyed her writing and I didn't feel the book was poorly written I couldn't give it a higher rating since the majority of this book was over my head. I gave it overall a 2.5 rating.

Disjointed, scattered, horribly edited. too much happening at once: ancient Greek gods, pagan traditions, science based wizards, demons, romances, beauty and the beast fairy tale. this book was all over the place trying to be more than it could in 342 pages.

Que diablos? ... 
 Creo que no se que paso realmente en esta historia no comprendi la mayor parte de ella y eso realmente es frustrante. 
 Creo que la autora sabia tanto, tenia tanto conocimiento que se extralimito al momento de tejer la historia. 
 Nyx, cielos la odie y por mas sacrificios que hiciera me parecieron nefasta.

I love fairytales and folklore, so I was excited to read this fairy/folktale mashup. It was a bit of Beauty and the Beast, Rumplestiltskin, The Two Sisters, East of the Sun and West of the Moon, Blackbeard, etc.. Cool combinations, right? To add to that, it delved into ancient mythology. Such a fun idea for a book! 
 Unfortunately, Cruel Beauty wasn't good enough to warrant 4 or 5 stars. The execution of the plot was a bit flimsy, and the majority of the story seemed to focus on the romance (as YA books are known to do). Yet it was still an enjoyable read. I also liked that everything wrapped up sufficiently for me so I don't feel driven or compelled to read the next book. I'm tired of trilogies and series, so I appreciate when such books can also act as standalones.

Maybe I'm starting to become jaded when it comes to YA fantasy/romance. I really wanted to like this story, but it just felt old and tired to me. A love triangle, a bad-boy love interest that's clever and witty, an impossible puzzle (that disappointed me), winning in the end through the power of twue wuv. (Though I did appreciate that the author tried hard to make it seem like the two of them save themselves in part because they are both wicked (ie, human). But it was still ultimately Love with a capital L that compels Nyx to sacrifice herself at the end, essentially pointlessly. She has no way of knowing that things will work out okay, so basically she agrees to eternal torment simply out of love. Ummm? No thanks?) 
 It was a very readable book, and I enjoyed it for the most part. Maybe I just didn't like it as much as I thought I should?

That was good. Not sure I can put it into words beyond that right now.

 After reading Uprooted and Heart's Blood, I wanted another Beauty and the Beast retelling and so I finally picked up Cruel Beauty. 
 Unfortunately, Cruel Beauty didn't live up to the other two for me. It didn't have the depth and coherence of the other two and there was something that kept me from really sinking into the story, though I can't totally put my finger on it. 
 The characters didn't quite do it for me. Nyx kept pushing everyone away, and that worked on me, too. I couldn't get close to her and as much as I wanted to warm up to her, I had a hard time connecting. She was so down on herself all the time for being cruel, but her actions didn't really line up with this. It all worked together to create a vague character that I couldn't ever really connect with or even remember clearly. 
 Her romantic interests also suffered from this vague personality and, like Nyx, while I wanted to like them they too kept pushing me away. I could never fully settle in with trusting them or even knowing who they really were. When everything was finally revealed, it felt more destabilizing instead of less. 
 I'm also not sure how I feel about the ending, but I won't say anything more on that. 
 Then there was the story, and this I did really like. The magic was evocative and gave me just what I was looking for when I wanted more Uprooted. Exploring the house and unraveling the mystery gave me what I was looking for when I wanted more Heart's Blood. This is the kind of story where once everything is revealed I can spend a lot of time thinking over it all and savoring how all the pieces fit together. 
 Bottom line 
 Cruel Beauty came very close to being a great book for me. The structure is good and a few tweaks and a little more fleshing out and I think I would have easily loved it. I think I will enjoy it as a reread, now that I know what to expect out of the characters. I'm wavering between a 3.5 and a 4, but I think a re-read could bump it to a four.

After reading the first book, I already wanted so much to read the second. It just caught me off-guard with its extraordinary story. 
 Cassandra Clare's The Mortal Instruments Series is very modern and grand. From the places to the events.

 Here is my problem with this book... Here is why I read the first chapter and then put it down - on to the next book.

 The formidable glass-and-steel structure rose from it's position on front street like a glittering needle threading the sky. 
 so... needles don't thread things... they pierce, they poke, they prod, they prick, penetrate, inoculate, puncture, pop, they draw blood... needles don't thread things... they get threaded...

 further down... 
 in describing the penthouse... 
 The window glass was perfectly translucent, providing such a complete illusion that there was nothing between the viewer and the view that it had been know to induce vertigo even in those unafraid of heights. 
 Transparent = Clear - both light and views are completely unobscured. 
 Translucent = Light passes through but not views - like Frosted glass. 
 Opaque = Light does not pass through at all. 
 Why is this important in this story... these are such minor issues in the grand sceme of the whole story, of the whole book...? 
 Because, words are important. I don't look at the Mortal Instruments series a Grand Literary Tome - but... lets at least respect the reader's intelligence enough to use the right words and get our metaphors worked out. 
 but then you think... what if the excuse for this sloppiness is... "whatever, these are only Young Adult readers, we don't have to hold up to the same level of expectation as Normal or Regular books".

book_b.title: Traffic: Why We Drive the Way We Do
book_b.user_review: Too rambling for my taste.

sample_reviews.review_text: I didn't finish this book. It didn't grab my attention the way I thought it might and was long enough that I decided I didn't feel compelled to read the rest after a few chapter.

Confession: I couldn't take more than three chapters. 
 Tom Vanderbilt should sue his editor. Mr. Vanderbilt obviously has voluminous knowledge on this subject but this is an endless ramble of facts, studies, insights and observations that not once; really, not one single time; is boiled up to a conclusion, an important trend or even a clear summary. 
 Believe me; I was eager to read this book. I drive ALL THE TIME and am very interested in why and how we perceive things on the road and what motivates me to make the good - and often the extremely embarrassing - judgments I make. But this was a ramble, a directionless stroll through everything there is to know which, unfortunately, leads the reader nowhere. 
 For a comparison, take a reading of "The Flamingo's Smile," by Stephen Jay Gould, where you wade through very detailed scientific explanations and descriptions of biological phenomena. This stuff inundated me with details on subjects about which I knew very few generalities. But, it was great reading (and great writing). All along the way, Professor Gould tells you why what you are reading is important and how it all ties together at a higher level. 
 No, not everyone is a writer of the caliber of Mr. Gould but Mr. Vanderbilt doesn't even come close - and doesn't seem to try. He just goes on and on, slipping from one potentially interesting topic to another, from one isolated study to another. 
 I couldn't take it. I got off the first exit and headed to a more rewarding reading experience.

I really liked this book the first night. 
 After that I realized I had enough of it. 
 It's an interesting book, but I'm not into analyzing traffic to death.

As someone who drives a whole heck of a lot (about an hour and a half to two hours commute every work day), I find myself thinking a bit about traffic and its general rules. Traffic the book seemed like an interesting take on the subject, so I gave it a whirl. 
 Traffic is a lot about human psychology. One thing that Tom Vanderbilt does is drive home how much of an unnatural activity driving is. Humans did not evolve to control these vehicles traveling 3-4 times as fast as we are. So, we as drivers have used a bunch of shortcuts to allow us to drive. 
 Another thing is about how cars tend to isolate us from other people on the road, especially pedestrians and bike riders. We behave in ways on the road, a distinctly foreign place, than we would in social settings. 
 While the book has some of the basics of traffic management like how cities have vast command centers that can alter traffic patterns for the better by tweaking traffic light timings (a fact that I learned when that system went down for my county and ended up destroying traffic flow for a good week) and how traffic engineers use things like speed humps to "calm traffic". One of the more compelling parts of the book was when Vanderbilt talked to one of the traffic engineers who advocated using less signs, barriers, medians to regulate traffic. By forcing drivers to pay more attention, use social cues rather than mechanical cues, it improved traffic flow and traffic safety. It was eye-opening. 
 Traffic is a book that discusses what we generally take for granted, traffic, in ways that were interesting. I'd recommend it as both for learning more about psychology and exploring a topic that's often not explored.

OK, I am a traffic and engineering geek, so I was pre-disposed to like this. But I think Vanderbilt does a good job of explaining the science to laymen, and getting into all the psychological stuff which you wouldn't normally think about associated with traffic. 
 And, I've been driving way more carefully in my local streets -- it's a complete eye-opener in that sense.
It was interesting, but I always end up feeling a bit hopeless when it comes to the car society. It is, it kills people, I don't know what else to do about it.
Common sense seems to have left the byways and highways.

This really was an immensely fascinating book. It really highlights the fact that driving is not a natural thing for humans to do. Most of us think we're great drivers, when really we're just lucky all the time. Until we're not, that is. It's not just teenagers who engage in risky behavior while driving (though they are way worse). People of all ages fiddle with the phone or radio, read papers, eat, and do many other things that we think we can handle, but which reduce our ability to pair full attention to the road. But we've done it a hundred times before, so we know it'll be fine. Taking your eyes of the road to find a radio station seems trivial, but it can take a few seconds, during which you can travel hundreds of feet. That's a lot. But even beyond that, basic aspects of driving are harder for us to do properly than we think. Think of being lulled to sleep by long, straight interstate, for instance. 
 Vanderbilt is very thorough in his analysis of traffic/human interaction. He looks at numerous places around the world for interesting points, and talks to lots of traffic engineers (who are more interesting than you might think). He describes lots of different traffic situations, from a discussion of roundabouts to traffic calming schemes to the impact of signage. 
 Overall, I'm not sure why I liked the book quite as much as I did--I just found it hugely entertaining. Probably I liked it because I was constantly being taken totally by surprise by completely new and unexpected information. Lots of "Oh, I never even thought of that as a problem!" moments. Which I really enjoy. I kept thinking, "This is awesome! I know, I can become a traffic engineer!" But I always do this when I read an interesting book on a new topic, so it's not going to happen.

reference_books.review_text:
This is originally posted on my blog, Bibliophile Mystery: http://bibliophilemystery.blogspot.ro/ 
 It took me a while to post this, but I wanted it to be special. I hope I made it. 
 I don't know what you're going to think about me after I tell you this, but it's true, and it's all me, therefore I'm not ashamed: I have always hated school books and forced reading, so I did everything I could to get away from it. "The Divine Comedy" was a mandatory read for my junior year of high school, so of course I didn't read it. The same happened to "Pride and Prejudice", "Jane Eyre", "Wuthering Heights" and many other classics. I've eventually read some of them a few years ago, just because I finally wanted to. 
 "Gabriel's Inferno" made me WANT to find and read Dante's work as soon as possible. All the quotes, the poetry, the artful style Sylvain Reynard used to write the story, left me aching to know more about the basic tale. As a matter of fact, I didn't even have to search that much: it stared back at me from the middle of my living room bookcase. Front row. 
 "I was thinking about how I waited for you. I waited and waited, and you never came." He smiled at her sadly. 
 "I'm sorry, Gabriel." 
 "You're here now. Apparuit iam beatitudo vestra." 
 "I don't know what that means." She sounded shy. 
 "It means now your blessedness appears. But really, it should be now my blessedness appears. Now that you're here." 
 I can't think of this novel as a story about forbidden love, well...it is, but I left this aspect somewhere in the back of my mind. Julia and Gabriel are both adults, and get to know each other in the most fascinating way. But it's not at all a story about sex. You won't find any explicit sexual content in its pages, just an artful, amazing and unique love story, sometimes heartbreaking, sometimes very sweet, but all so subtle and intelligently written. Every touch, every word and every look the characters give each other has a deeper meaning. You'll definitely fall in love with the author's style! 
 "Have you ever fallen asleep in the arms of a boy before, Beatrice?" 
 She shook her head. 
 "Then I'm glad I'm your first." 
 "Look at me. Look into my eyes." His eyes fixed on hers as they fluttered open. 
 "I'll give you anything. My body, my soul, Take them. Take everything." 
 "You are hot like the sun but far more lovely." 
 The mystery of their pasts is also a big part of the story that will keep you turning pages and enjoying every minute of it. Both Gabriel and Julia have their light and dark sides, and you can see it even if they don't. Get ready to be left breathless while discovering the reasons they act the way they do. 
 "Why not think that sometimes--just sometimes--you can overcome evil with silence? And let people hear their hatefulness in their own ears, without distraction. Maybe goodness is enough to expose evil for what it really is, sometimes." 
 "Well, you scratched me deeply today, my kitten. You drew blood with every word. Are you happy now?" 
 "You begged me to come after you - to look for you in Hell. That's exactly where I found you. And you can stay there forever, for all I care." 
 The supporting characters, especially Rachel, Gabriel's sister and Grace, his mother, have an important part in the story as well. Grace isn't there, but you can always feel her presence. Her kindness and love for her children guide them through life even after she's left. 
 Rachel can see through Gabriel's darkness when no one else can. She loves him and always hopes for him, not letting herself be intimidated by his Professor vibe. 
 Rachel narrowed her eyes. "He's Gabriel, Julia. What's wrong with you two?" 
 "She's my student. There are rules." Gabriel's tone began to grow increasingly cool and unfriendly. 
 "She's my friend, Gabriel. And I say screw the rules!" 
 "Gabriel, get Julia a drink, would you? And stop boring her with your antique crap!" 
 This is one of the few slow paced books I truly loved. In fact I wished it could've been even slower, because I didn't want to finish it. Sylvain's ability to describe feelings, touches, emotions and last but not least places, turns this book into a real work of art. 
 "When I am an old man and I can remember nothing else, I will remember this moment. The first time my eyes beheld an angel in the flesh." [...]I will remember your scent and your touch and how it felt to love you. But most of all, I will remember how it felt to gaze at true beauty, both inside and out. For you are fair, my beloved, in soul and in body, generous of spirit and generous of heart. And I will never see anything this side of heaven more beautiful than you." 
 Happy reading!

Four & Half Stars 
 I got hooked by this book from the very start, the first time I read the blurb, It's not something I would usually read but why not give it a try? And I don't regret reading it, not a little bit. 
 We all have something we regret, and for Christian it is the day he left Elizabeth when she told him she's pregnant. Christian had a plan laid out for his life, and that plan didn't include a child to take care of. He couldn't afford to lose his chance to be an attorney so he left the only woman he loved, Elizabeth. 
 It's been five years, Elizabeth had struggled very hard to provide for her child, to give her a safe, comfortable life. But when Christian sees a little five-year-old girl in a supermarket, he just knows that she is his child. And now, Christian wants his family back. Although he admits he has caused much harm, he still wants Elizabeth and her child, Lizzie, back. 
 But will Elizabeth let him back into her lives? Will she allow Christian to cause the same heartache for her daughter? And will Elizabeth be able to forgive the unforgivable? Find out much more in this breath-taking, astonishing contemporary romance novel, Take This Regret... 
 Take This Regret, revolves around Christian and Elizabeth. Describing their lives through their point of views, it was a very refreshing experience to be able to read both of their POVs. I sometimes don't like to read more than one point of view, I feel like it spoils the book, but for this novel, I think it was required to be two POVs so we can understand the characters better. 
 A. L. Jackson has written an unforgettable novel, the pace is pretty quick, and the characters are captivating. Elizabeth had been through too much, but she still loves Christian very much, she is so loyal. Christian is so regretful and lovable, he melted my heart. And Lizzie, the little girl who wrapped both of her parents around her finger, she is amazingly adorable and sweet. 
 The description is pretty good, A. L. Jackson doesn't describe the setting very much, she gives room to your imagination. The plot and the idea are very strong, real love can overcome anything. The hard work of the author is obvious on the book. If you want an enjoyable, romantic, read then Take This Regret is definitely the one for you!

 What a sad disappointment! I thought I would love Take This Regret. The blurb sounded great and I wanted to read something different ( I read a lot of fantasy). 
 So let me start with the part I liked: 
 The First Chapters- I loved the first 5 chapters or so. It had me crying and I was a blubbering mess. I felt the heartbreak Elizabeth went through and the struggle within Christian. It was written so well. The writing style is engaging and I was able to read it in one sitting. 
 But it went downhill from there: 
 1)The characters got annoying- 
 Elizabeth: I sympathized with her. She was strong and I liked her. But she turns weak. I like my MC's strong. Not perfect, but strong. Here's an example: When Christian, after 5 years of no contact, appears out of the blue and demands for visitation rights to see Lizzie(their daughter), what does Elizabeth do? She runs to the bathroom (this takes place in her office) and starts crying. She should have given him an earful and kicked him in the balls! I know she is sad, but shouldn't she be angrier? But what annoyed me most was how easily she lets Christian back into her life. 
 Christian: Now what bothered me most was how suddenly he becomes Mr. Goody goody pants. He had no contact with Elizabeth for 5 years. He did think about them but never felt the need to contact them. Then he sees Lizzie and suddenly he wants his family back! He wanting to see more of his daughter is okay. But wanting his whole 'family' back? He got on my nerves. A lot. 
 2) The plot: I felt the plot was feeble and too predictable. Any problems that arose, disappeared conveniently. It was so easy to guess. 
 The Writing: The writing was really good. Yes, I hated the characters and the plot. But I kept turning the pages because the style of writing was so engaging. I never felt bored. 
 I know I'm in the minority here. So many people seem to love it. Guess it was not my cup of tea.
