4.5 stars 
 Apres ma lecture du tome 3.5, Elixir, je ne pouvais pas faire autrement que de lire ce 4e tome de la serie. Si je devais le decrire, je dirais que c'est un tome de revelations et de preparation en vue du tome final de la serie. Il y a de l'action, quelques bonnes batailles, mais ce n'est pas le point central de ce roman. 
 Il va sans dire qu'Alex est mise a rude epreuve du debut a la fin et ca a ete un vrai plaisir de la voir grandir a travers toutes ces epreuves. Elle a beaucoup change depuis le 1er tome de la serie. Elle est plus mature et reflechie. Elle n'agit plus sur un coup de tete. Maintenant, elle analyse la situation, pese le pour et le contre et surtout, elle reflechie aux repercussions que pourraient avoir ses actes sur les personnes de son entourage. Bien evidemment, elle n'est pas encore parfaite et elle a besoin d'aide pour y voir clair. Et je dois dire qu'elle est tres bien entouree. 
 Comme je l'ai deja dit, oui il y a de l'action dans ce tome, mais on y revele aussi beaucoup de nouveaux elements. L'affrontement final approche et meme si nos personnages ont trouve de l'aide, c'est Alex qui au bout du compte devra faire le plus gros du travail. Tout est donc en place pour un dernier tome enlevant. 
 Je n'ai pas mis un 5 etoiles a ce tome pour la simple et bonne raison que j'ai trouve que le rythme n'etait pas assez soutenu. Oui, il s'y passe beaucoup de chose, mais j'ai trouve le tout un peu trop saccade. J'ai donc eu du mal a certains moments a rester accrochee a l'histoire. J'ai adore le debut et la fin, mais un peu moins les 200 pages entre les deux. 
 Il y a toujours un cliffhanger a la fin de ce 4e tome et c'est encore une fois insoutenable. J'aurais pu imaginer bien des scenarios, mais pas celui-la. Je suis donc impatiente de connaitre la fin de cette merveilleuse histoire.

book_b.title: Longbourn
book_b.user_review:
"I would ask if you miss me like I miss you, so that there is not another spot in all the world that seems to mean anything at all, but where you are." 
 I did give this 2 stars, but on reflection I think that was bit generous. I would give it 1.5 probably. 
 Initially I read this because I love Pride and Prejudice and I love Downton Abbey, and this, apparently, is a mixture of the two. Instead of focusing on the Bennet family, Baker used the downstairs servants as her book's main characters. This was an interesting take on Pride and Prejudice, and I'm a sucker for reading/watching stuff when they're about servants from before the mid-2oth century. However, I felt it really lacked. To me, there wasn't much of a story. What were we to learn from this? or take away from this? 
 I really didn't like Sarah (this was the book's protagonist) - she was miserable, judgemental, listened to no one, and was just really annoying. Mrs Hill was interesting, but her part of the story ran dry. I didn't like the idea of her having a child with Mr Bennet - when reading P&P, I never imagined him to look anywhere but his wife. Yes, Mrs Bennet is extremely annoying, but I think he secretly liked that about her. Speaking of their son, James was decent character, but he wasn't given enough attention. I would have much preferred for him to have joint narration with Sarah, rather than focusing mainly on the latter. It was just so random I feel. 
 I found it hard to give my full attention to this. At time it felt tedious to read - I was simply reading because I wanted to finish it. I just don't think Baker executed it very well, which is a disappointment because I've been looking forward to reading this for a few years now. It didn't live up to my expectations. She didn't do justice to any of the existing characters - Elizabeth didn't seem to care for Sarah's worry about James, which I felt was out of character. Mr Darcy was just a bore - to be honest, he hardly appeared, but when he did he gave off his awful vibe which I didn't get when reading P&P. Maybe I'll prefer the movie.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This review and others posted over at 
 my blog. 
 While the Bennet family worries about who will marry whom and how their estate will be entailed, should Mr. Bennet pass away, the running of the household is left to Mrs. Hill and the young maids, Polly and Sarah. The washing, the cooking, the cleaning, all go unnoticed throughout Pride and Prejudice, but realistically those who lived to serve did not have an easy life. 
 From page one of this book, where Baker is disgustingly describes laundry day, I was interested. This book sheds a new light on the life of one of my favorite heroines, Elizabeth Bennet, and that of her family. Never once did I think about the work involved in running the Bennet household or preparing their many daughters for the ball. While they are portrayed as "poor" (especially in comparison to the Bingleys and Darcys), they still employ several servants to cook and clean for them and tend to their whims. While Hill and Sarah and Polly are not abused or starved, they do not live free, comfortable lives. Sarah chafes against her lifestyle - no moment of the day is her own. 
 I especially enjoyed how Baker fleshed out Mary and Mr. and Mrs. Bennet. The love story between Elizabeth and Darcy and Jane and Bingley takes a backseat, while readers are given insight into the daily lives of a family of their station. Mary is given a bit more of a personality, and Mr. Bennet has quite a backstory. 
 I certainly see one of my favorite books in a new light after reading this book. It was thoroughly engrossing and an excellent companion novel for fans of Pride and Prejudice. If you've never read the novel, the plot does contain some spoilers, but the story does focus on the life the servants, and if you're interested in historical fiction, I would recommend this.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I honestly considered giving this just one star, but there were some really beautiful bits so, it earned one back. 
 The first half of Longbourn was really enjoyable. I loved seeing the play between upstairs/downstairs in a story I love so much. But after about that first half, the book takes a big departure. It goes back in time, explains back stories and relationships and... I think I wouldn't have minded that so much if it'd been introduced sooner. I felt like the book went from being Sarah's story to being a lot less focused. I REALLY wish the flashbacks to pre-Pride And Prejudice storyline had started waaaay earlier in the book. They felt like a departure from the tone/style of the first half. 
 The ending was enormously unsatisfying, and actually pretty hard for me to buy in to. 
 It's unfair to compare any author to Jane Austen - but if you're going to set your book in the world of a Jane Austen book, it would make sense to me to at least try and capture some of the tone and humor of her world. The occasions when the servants of Longbourn interact with any of the Bennet sisters feels *shrug* kind of fake. Like, THESE aren't the characters I know and love. Who are these people? I didn't feel like many of Austen's characters were captured accurately here. Mr. Bennet's wry humor/annoyance wasn't there. Lizzy's spirit was boiled down to "she's really pretty". 
 There was also just TOO much information. The slave trade? The war in spain? Mr. Bennet's dallyings with the housekeeper? Illegitimate Bennets? It was all over the place. 
 I also failed to understand Sarah's motivations towards the end. She definitely grows as a character - you see her go from sort of punky late teen to decisive woman. That's great. But, (and here be spoilers) I did NOT understand why she decided to leave Pemberley at the end. It would have been so dangerous and foolish to just be a woman living on the road with a knapsack at that time. Like... unimaginable. And she just walks away from a comfortable, safe situation and then just happens to track James down on a road? I just... gah. It doesn't make sense in the time and place.

Loved every single second of this book, fully, completely. Found it to be a brilliant, and well written, counterpoint to the many Austen "fandom" titles. Longbourn is a rich tapestry of the life beneath the pages of the beloved Pride and Prejudice, where the ladies have monthlies, laundry must be done weekly, and the business of the bathroom must be disposed with in the morning. Highly recommended.

I'm a huge Austen fan and I am always open to trying tributes/retellings/sequels. I am usually disappointed. 
 Not so in the case of Longbourn. The premise is interesting (although I must also admit that I love alternate viewpoints) and it seemed to be well researched. 
 I felt the author fit the major P&P plot points into the story well. Some fan favorite characters suffer from their plotlines and one undergoes a last-chapter personality change but the book is not really about them. 
 The two main quibbles I have with the book are: 
 -The lengthy and tedious detailing of James' back story. Yawn. 
 -Random cursing that seemed out of place and threw me out of the story to wonder if that was a phrase commonly used at that time. 
 I received an advanced reader copy of this book from the publisher in exchange for my honest review.

I love Jane Austin and find myself compelled to read every deriviative book that comes down the pike. Most of this copycat genre are really bad books - poorly written and trying to hard to capture Austin's magic. Jo Baker's book is an exception. She did a nice job of creating unique characters you care about, while successfully incorporating the original Pride and Prejudice characters we all know love. She created interesting story lines. Further, she obviously did her homework in regards to what life of servants would be like during this time period - her attention to detail was remarkable. 
 So why the 3 stars? Beware of spoilers*** 
 I really did not buy her two main plot twists. First, it seems inconceivalbe that Mr. Bennet would continue to hide a male heir after having five daughters. Surely, he would have had enough residual care for his wife and single daughters than to leave them to the whims of Mr. Collins. Second, when Sarah was departing from Elizabeth, I find it hard to beleive that neither Darcy asked Sarah why she was leaving. With Mr. Darcy's resources, it would be a simple matter to track down James. This contrivance really took away from the overall novel.

Just couldn't get through this one. The gimmick is clever enough as far as it goes, but 50 pages in the whole thing is utterly predictable and rather tiresome. For a much more interesting look at servants in Austen's work, read John Mullan's What Matters in Jane Austen".

Read for our book club. I enjoyed what it added to the Pride and Prejudice story, though I felt like the it took sometime for the novel to hit it's stride. It was honest and a little graphic, and because of that I was a little disappointed by it's clean ending. The romance didn't do a lot for me, though I did enjoy that the love triangle was never a full out brawl that other media tends to make those situations.

For starters I really liked the premise of this book, it offered a different perspective on a story anyone interested in Austen already knows intimately. Unfortunately there were a few thnigs I believe could have been sorted out better. 
 I liked that Longbourne has its own narrative- It doesn't waste time repeating events from Pride (except for a phrase or two at the beginning of each chapter, so as to guide the reader on what was happening with the Bennets) and instead focuses solely on what happens to its own characters, which I really appreciated since I wasn't really looking for a recycled version of the novel. 
 Characterization-wise, some were more interesting than others, although to me the main couple happened to be the blandest during most of the story. I found it difficult to connect with Sarah and had the same issue with James, although that changed by the second half. On the other hand, Mrs. Hill was one of the most interesting, tragic creatures I have read in a while. I loved how the author managed to develop a storyline for her that felt as believable as it was compelling. 
 As to the plot, there were some things I found quite refreshing but didn't feel completely necessary for the storyline. The main couple's development felt quite modern as to pacing and while that usually has consequences, in this case nothing changed because for their actions. Because I was expecting those events to happen, I found it odd but fresh when they did not, although the lack of events made the general pacing in the second half feel a bit slower. 
 There were a few wasted opportunities as well: the whole chain of events that lead to James discovery at the end seemed a bit too luck-dependant for my taste. I would have preferred Sarah to get on with it and make some detective work instead of sitting on her hands and expecting some information to fall on her lap (which it did, eventually). There was little character development as well on her part during the final stretch- no self-discovery or catharsis-, which I found disappointing because I felt that there could have been a more evident maturing process for her, some change in her after what she lived through. 
 All in all, it is intended to be viewed as a 'b side' of the original novel and it delivers perfectly on that part, but on a personal level I think it wasted a chance to go a bit further and offer the reader some development of its own characters, especially during the final chapters which are set after Austen's ending and are a point in which the reader is already emotionally invested in most of the characters.

It's a charming idea - a look at the harsh realities behind the gilded lives of the Bennetts (no matter how badly done by they may think they are, they are of course remarkably privileged) and the prose is quite lovely. It does sometimes get bogged down in the detail - you feel the author has done so much research she's keen to show it off - so it's slightly more slow moving than it could be. Definitely worth reading though.

The title Pride and Prejudice could literally translate to "Rich People Problems." If you find your hand reaching up to clutch your pearls at that statement, please go re-read "Darcy and Lizzie Make Out In a Barouche, vol. 152." Because Jo Baker is a badass, and not for you. 
 Listened to the audiobook, mostly while preparing for Thanksgiving. Good company while dealing with domestic concerns, especially if you want to feel thankful for indoor plumbing and recognizable meat products. I would love to see this made into a Downton Abbeyesque mini-series, because it deals so beautifully with characters who tend not to get their due in adaptations - Mary Bennett, Mrs. Bennett, and Mr. Collins in particular. Perfect antidote to all of the cloying Jane Austen fanfic out there, and a good reminder that it takes an army of servants, a ton of beauty privilege, and the mother-effin' slave trade to create the world Austen fans have so romanticized.

reference_books.title: Portrait of a Spy (Gabriel Allon, #11)
reference_books.review_text: This is the first Daniel Silva novel I've read in a while. It was my return to the series after a lengthy hiatus. I found it timely, thought provoking, and very well written. The author shows a lot of class with this book. It that sense the novels just keep getting better. The book even gave me some new perspective on the war on terrorism, the art world, and the complex relationship between America and Saudi Arabia. It was a quick, interesting, and entertaining read. Although it kept my interest, not a lot happens in the course of the novel. After three incidents of horrific violence to set up the story, there is very little action, and it all comes at the climax of the book. Some readers might call this a "thinking person's" spy novel, which is not necessarily accurate. It is suspenseful, but just wasn't quite as thrilling as earlier books in the series. I will definitely read more from Daniel Silva, and more in this series. I was just hoping for a little more from this volume.

reference_books.title: Firestarter
reference_books.review_text: "Tried to start this three times. Read some and dropped it all three times."

First the good: We meet a couple of King's strongest characters. Their love story is one of King's best. He provides an accurate and entertaining look at life in the 1950's, and nicely contrasts this with life in 2011. There are a number of well-placed references to other King novels throughout this book. There are also some interesting parallels drawn between the real world city of Dallas and King's fictional town of Derry. The setup is pretty good, but science fictional aspects are ignored. The idea seems like a natural, if not too original. In the sixth grade, a couple of friends and I thought it would be cool to build a time machine and go back and save President Kennedy...just sixth graders daydreaming. Also, there is a very interesting episode of "The New Twilight Zone" you might want to check out, starring Lane Smith and Andrew Robinson. 
 (See this article at A.V. Club about other alternative versions - but not until after you read this book, if you are interested - SPOILERS!! - http://www.avclub.com/article/back-an...) 
 Now, the not-so-good (in my humble opinion): According to his afterword, King seems to want this to be a Jack Finney style time travel story, and he doesn't quite pull it off (Finney was the master of the time travel story - you should read some of his work). King's book seems to me like maybe a mash up of two novels he had lying around: a pretty good slice of life novel about a school teacher and a school librarian falling in love in the 1950's; and an average novel about a man who goes back in time to prevent the assassination of JFK. In this mash up the school teacher and the time traveler are one and the same. 
 This novel will in no way illuminate any facts about the JFK assassination for the reader (especially for a novel titled with the date of the assassination). King doesn't even try to do so. Conspiracy theorists will find little grist for the mill. Late in the book is a glimpse at a dark science fictional future which King also doesn't quite pull off. 
 My main complaint is this novel is too long. This book is way too long. Pages and pages go by where the main story is not advanced. I found much of this book depressing, and this goes on for pages and pages, as well. I actually did not care for this book very much, and would be unlikely to recommend it, even though it was highly recommended to me by two friends. I would not read it again, and therefore I can really only give it two stars. 
 Your mileage may vary.

You remember that Family Guy bit where Stephen King is pitching ideas to a book editor, grasping at straws ("this couple gets attacked...by the scary lamp-monster!") The weary editor tells him, "You're not even trying anymore, are you?" then asks him when he can have it. This novel is the punchline to that joke. It feels like a parody of a Stephen King novel, with all his worst tendencies blown up over 700 pages. It's not surprising this was written at the peak of King's substance abuse; what is surprising is that his editor didn't demand he cut at least half of it. Just an unmitigated disaster. For completists only.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Mummoja alligaattorien ruoaksi 
 Carl Hiaasenin postomoderni kioskiviihdedekkari sijoittuu Floridaan ja lahemmin Miamiin seka enimmakseen lahiseuduille. 
 Paahenkiloina ovat marlowemainen yksityisetsiva Brian Keyes, Sunin toimittaja Skip Wiley seka jalkimmaisen terrorijarjeston "La Noche di Deciembren" ydinjoukko eli futaaja Wilson, intiaani seka kuubalainen pakolainen. Kolmiodraamaa on saatu aikaiseksi, silla Keyesin entinen naisystava majailee Skipin luona. 
 Kirjan junnaavat ja ylipitkilla dialogeilla pilatut tapahtumat nykivat liikkeelle, kun eraan Shirer-jarjeston jasenia aletaan tappaa. Toimittaja-terroristin jengi haluaa iskea turismiin ja paikallisiin kihoihin. Huomiota saadaan myos rajayttelemalla pommeja siella sun taalla. 
 Vaikka sivullisetkin tuntuvat tietavan, ketka ovat murhien ja rajaytysten takana, poliiseja ei tunnu olevan missaan, joten mummojen pelastajaksi ilmaantuva Keyes joutuu ottamaan vastuun. Han lahtee Bermudaa myoten nokittamaan vinksahtanutta kohutoimittajaa. Valilla piipahdetaan Sunin toimituksessa, psykiatrin luona ja sairaalassa lemmiskelemassa, muttei tapahtumiin tunnu saavan millaan otetta. 
 Eipa hyvin alkanut kirjavuosi 2011.

This is my least favorite Carl Hiaasen book so far. I've loved most of the other others. I had trouble connecting with the characters & there wasn't as much wit and charm and irony as his other books have. At the end I found myself skimming huge paragraphs. I really wanted to know how it ended. And I did like the ending. Overall, not a horrible waste of time, but he has plenty of other books to choose from and that's what I would recommend you check out. Star Island is awesome.

It works...to a degree. Hiaasen works to a formula: single/separated/divorced male stuck with an adventure/challenge is forced to assert himself during difficult times. Potentially there is always something more there but Hiaasen is obsessed with a sort of libertarian solution that , in this case, warps the novel . If things are so bad, why not destory it and begin again? 
 It's as American as apple pie. Iraq, Vietnam, Afghanistan...offers a sort of logic that is played out in Florida.

reference_books.review_text:
I just finished, I'm kind of enraged so before I rate and review this I need to calm down. 
 So I slept on it, and I'm still enraged. So 2 stars it is. Longer review to follow. 
 My Real Review: Also posted on my Blog, I'll Tumble for YA 
 I'm having a bit of difficulty thinking about how I want to write this review. The end of the book is of course the most important part, discussing that, which I really want to do, would spoil the whole thing. 
 First things first: if you haven't read any of these books go away. No seriously, if you have any plans to read this series, I'm going to spoil the heck out of books 1 & 2. If you don't mind being spoiled, please join me. 
 Let's start by talking about book one, Delirium. I actually thought it was really well done. I didn't love it as much as Before I Fall, but I was willing to keep going with the series. The ending had me at the edge of my seat, and I couldn't wait for book 2. 
 I really enjoyed Pandemonium, book 2 and I liked getting to know Lena as she had to change to accommodate her new life. Although I really liked Alex, Julian kind of grew on me and I learned to appreciate him. When Pandemonium ended I was kind of annoyed, and didn't understand why there needed to be an actual love triangle introduced into the story at all. Alex was always part of the story even when he wasn't in the story. The triangle already existed without bringing Alex back from the dead in order to further complicate things. Even with the end, I thought the book was well done and I was looking forward to final installment. 
 Now we're at book 3, Requiem. I received this ARC in January, and held off reading it because I'm really bad about finishing series. But I just had to find out how it ended. 
 I want to start by saying some positive things. 
 I really thought that both Lena and Hanna's characters were really well written, I left this series really feeling like I knew them. I didn't read Hanna's short story, and even without it, I thought she was really fleshed out. I actually like all the characters. I wish I knew more about some of them, but they're all really likable. 
 I like the world building that happens in Requiem, and in the series. It's a really interesting concept. 
 I like the pacing. I read the vast majority of this in one day, and it flew by. 
 What I didn't like. 
 Everything else. Seriously. And it wasn't that I didn't like it, I HATED it. I finished the book and I was actually enraged by the ending. If the ending had been better I might have given it a meh, but the ending was so infuriating that it made me hate the book. 
 Nothing happened in this book. I didn't see much character growth, they're still walking, they're still fighting, and they're still just moving from place to place. 
 The triangle that never should have been was one of the worst parts of this book. I know there are a lot of mixed feelings about love triangles in books but I don't really a have an opinion on them either way. I've read some that I thought were really well done, and others that were horrible. This one definitely falls into the horrible category. It was utterly and completely pointless. It didn't add anything to the story and didn't add to any kind of character growth for anybody. It was ultimately a waste of time. Do you know what would have made a better story? Killing Alex for real in the last book. If he had died in the Crypts or been killed when he was captured it would have made for a better story. While Pandemonium focuses on Lena getting over Alex and becoming independent, Requiem would have been better with her really coming to terms with it and finding a different type of love with Julian. The way this one was handled was a complete and utter cop-out. 
 I won't even get into how the story ends. Let's just say it was really poorly done. I've read other books that had similar endings, and were really well done. This was just crap. 
 And finally I must discuss the very last few paragraphs. Did the author really have the audacity to tell me how I should feel about the story and what lessons I should have learned? Oh yes. Thank you Ms. Oliver, but I'm pretty sure I'm a big girl and don't need a lecture on how I'm supposed to feel, what I was supposed to learn from these books, or how I'm supposed to live my life. 
 "Awe, Hell NO!"--Direct quote from me when the book ended. 
 2 footballs out of 5

sample_reviews.review_text:
If you're looking for a well-done contemporary look no further because I'll Meet You There hits all the right marks. Fifty pages in and I knew I was going to love this story and I loved it even more by the end. It takes a lot for me to enjoy a contemporary but this one just showed the right amount of dept and dimension to still be Summer-friendly yet tugs at the heart strings. 
 Our main character is Skylar 'Sky', a girl from a very poor town where she lives in a dilapidated trailer with her depressed Mom. Our story begins with us learning about Creek View, CA. A tiny blink-and-you'll-miss-it town where everyone is poor as dirt and hardly anyone gets out of the town. Sky however wants something more, she wants her full scholarship to San Francisco and just get the hell out of dodge and be an artist. That's when things start to unravel. Her old co-worker and friend, Josh comes back from Afghanistan. At age 19 he's lost his leg and suffering from PTSD at the same time her Mom looses her job and falls into a depression leaving all responsibility on Sky's shoulders. With hardly any money for rent and no money for food Sky spends the Summer trying to make extra money and growing closer to the Marine who is a shadow of the carefree ladies man he used to be. 
 I have to say that I loved LOVED this story. This story is filled with social critique but it's also beautiful and rich, I can almost see this as a artsy movie with fantastic cinematography of the California desert. 
 The relationship between Sky and Josh develops slowly, blooming with time and really pulls you in and I just love when books take their time showing how love grows from friendship. Yet it's not only about love it's about Josh's experiences in the war and the people he has lost, how alone and adrift he is. Sky's life falling apart and Demetrios doesn't pull any punches with poverty. There's days Sky doesn't have food to eat, there's days when she wonders what it would be like to be a middle-class kid who has cars with air condition. In Joshua's side his trauma is not swept under the rug, it's actually not cured at all by the end of the book and it's realistic because PTSD doesn't go away over a Summer. 
 I don't want to say more because it is a rare treat to read a well done contemporary. I highly recommend it. Also, this reads like New Adult rather than YA but it's very YA friendly with serious hard-hitting subjects that adults will also appreciate. A very enjoyable read.

It features a character who lost his leg as a soldier in Afghanistan, our main character is living in poverty (an underrepresented group in YA), and is, on the whole, pretty relatable. I'm really not a contemporary fan but I'll occasionally reach for one if it's been getting a lot of rave reviews. I'm definitely the black sheep on this one though and I just wasn't impressed by this book. I really wanted to love this one, especially because I absolutely adored Heather Demetrios' Exquisite Captive but unfortunately, I was bored for the majority of this book and I couldn't engage with the characters. 
 I'll Meet You There tells the story of Skylar (Sky) and Josh, two teenagers who live in a middle of nowhere town and are each facing different struggles. Sky is tired of her town and cannot wait to escape to her art college in San Francisco. Josh has just returned from serving as a Marine in Afghanistan and has been wounded during the war. Both characters deal with quite traumatic experiences and it's easy for readers to sympathize with them. As one might expect, this book is mainly about the romance between the two characters and how they slowly grow to care for each other. 
 I thought Heather Demetrios did a wonderful job writing about dark issues (PTSD, psychological issues, poverty, etc.) in a very realistic manner. Including POVs from both Josh and Sky really helped me get inside each of their heads and see how they were truly struggling with their problems. Here's the thing, even though I was able to sympathize with the struggles that Josh and Sky were going through, I just didn't love them as characters. 
 For most of the book, I wasn't intrigued by Sky's POV and only became interested in her story when her problems with her mom escalated. Even though Josh is a much more complex character and is suffering from post-war trauma, I really couldn't get over how much of a douche-bag he was at times. Josh is so incredibly sexist: he loves using the words faggot and gay in a derogative way and he constantly states that he doesn't want to be viewed as a "pussy" when he shows emotions. Additionally, he is such a womanizer and really doesn't change until towards the end of the book. For most of the book, I was so frustrated with Josh and his notions of masculinity. I get that Josh probably represents the typical teenage male but nothing about him, other than his war related suffering, appealed to me. For that reason, I just couldn't get into the romance and didn't really ship the characters. 
 Although this book was well-written and told a powerful story, it just wasn't for me. I found that the book dragged and I didn't really start liking the characters until the last 30%, which honestly saved the book for me (my rating would have been much lower). Additionally, I had some major issues with the romance but that could also be due to the fact that I'm not really a fan of contemporaries in general. If you're usually a fan of romance contemporaries, you might want to try this book out.

I'll Meet You There is one of the many books that have been sitting, unread, on my shelf for months. I was reading another book (trying to, really) when I noticed I'll Meet You There, and decided to glance through it. Of course, glancing turned to reading, and there was no turning back. 
 Skylar, a recent high school graduate, cannot wait to leave the backwater town in which she resides. She's poor, so her only ticket out of there is a scholarship into college- which she already has. When her mum starts slipping into some old bad habits, Skylar has to rethink her decision to leave. Josh, an old acquaintance of Skylar's, has just returned from his service in Afghanistan where he lost parts of himself, including his leg. During the summer, Skylar and Josh discover a deep, unexpected friendship, despite their huge differences. 
 I like Skylar; if she were an actual person, we'd get along pretty well. She's not from a very privileged background, but she doesn't blame anyone for her situation. She doesn't go around whining or acting like a victim of circumstance (even though she kind of is). She's smart, sensible, and sometimes too caring for her own good. She's real. 
 The thing I like best about this book is the fact that everything is just so realistic. There are some things that should be cliche, but somehow end up not being cliche. The interactions between the characters are real, and the circumstances surrounding everything that happens in the story are things that are likely to happen in real life. 
 I also like the romance aspect of the story. I like how their relationship doesn't seem to appear out of nowhere; there is a gradual process that starts with friendship and ends with something far deeper. I did feel a bit irritated when Skylar and Josh were in denial about their feelings for each other, but oh well... 
 There are alternating perspectives, which gave me insight to the workings of not only Skylar's mind, but Josh's mind as well. The author clearly took time to portray Josh's thoughts, as I was able to better understand his struggle with his memories from the war. There is real character development, and there is a mixture of all kinds of characters (both annoying and otherwise). 
 This might seem weird, but I also love the fact that I did not cry when I was reading this book. With all the intensity of the story, I was totally expecting to have to lock my room door with a box of tissues in hand, but I didn't need to. The story did touch my heart in more ways than one, and it did make me admire people who serve their countries even more than I already did, but I did not cry. And for that reason, I am glad J 
 After I read the author's note, I realised that she has quite a personal experience with the military. Not as a veteran, but as someone who is knows what it's like to be surrounded by people in the military. It's also very clear that Heather Demetrios conducted some major research in the course of writing I'll Meet You There, which makes it even more real. 
 Overall, I'll Meet You There is one deep story. It has all the right features of an excellent read, and is very realistic. Hopefully, I'll be reading more of Heather Demetrios in the near future.

 I've been scared for weeks that I had outgrown YA contemporaries. For days I've been looking at my shelves, afraid of picking up a YA I wanted to read badly but would end up despicing it. 
 I took a breath and did it. I picked up I'll meet you there by Heather Demetrios, which proved one thing: it's not about the genre; it's about how great and touching a book can be. 
 Skylar and Josh have lived there whole life in Creek View, a blink town in the middle of nowhere, California, and they both need out. While Josh joined the US Army two years ago, Skylar has just graduated and will go to a college in San Francisco to study art, after spending the summer working her part-time job at the Paradise Motel. 
 But lives is full of unexpected events. Josh comes back from Afghanistan because he lost a leg in an explosion and has to deal with PTSD and the guilt of being responsible for a friend's death on the front. Skylar's mom loses her job and can't get over her husband's death, which makes her fall into alcoholism and depression. 
 They need out but can they? They only have one summer to figure out, together, what their future will hold and how to find themselves before it's too late. 
 This is one of those cases where you can say without a hint of hesitation: the author did her research. There are spanish words for latino people; you get Skylar's contemplations on art, some history of painters and the motives behind their works. 
 But, most important of all, the war. She undoubtedly spoke to soldiers, veterans, survivors who had lost something or someone while fighting. You can clearly see the extreme respect and gratitude in her words, in the way she portrays the military world. Those brief but heartbreakingly intense chapters from Josh's PoV were traumatic, filled with pain and confusion, grief, strenght and hope. It was real. Real and raw and beautiful. 
 Skylar and Josh had the perfect chemistry. Their story is more about finding themselves together and overcome the ghosts of their pasts than the actual romance, and I believe I wouldn't have liked it, had it been done differently. They can confide in each other, trust each other with secrets and confessions and understanding free of judgement, as well as crack jokes about Josh having one leg because yes, it sucks, but he's alive and breathing and that was their way of accepting and dealing with that awful and unfair truth. 
 The cast of characters was impressive, all of them were realistic due to their flaws and mistakes, but they all redeem themselves in the ending. 
 Last but not least, the Paradise Motel. It's an eccentric and kitsch, with its rusty sign, scraped paint and themed rooms and it was the perfect setting. It had an attitude that almost made it a character and not just a place without meaning. 
 I'll meet you there left its mark. It's a heartfelt story that made me more aware of what I can do, it made me appreciate everything I own and everything I am and it's definitely one of my favorite comtemporaries of the year, if not of all times. 
 I can't wait to read all the other books Heather Demetrios wrote and will write, because if they are just half as good as this one.. hell yes. 
 Ps. I will say, though, that the letter Heather Demetrios wrote around Valentine's Day from Josh's PoV and sent to some readers should be part of the book because THAT for me was the absolutely perfect ending.

This was a brilliant book, exciting and imaginative. I have thoroughly enjoyed reading this book and look forward to reading more books in the series. 
 The main character is Ceony, an apprentice magician hoping to become a smelder but instead gets a placement as a folder. She doesn't have the highest of hope for her apprenticeship with Magician Thane, but enjoys the basic tasks that she does to start off on her path as a folder.  The most noteworthy secondary character is Magician Thane, he's a paper magician and Ceony's mentor while she learns the craft. We learn a lot more about this character than we normally would with a secondary character and that is because of Ceony's journey through his heart.

 4 stars a great book

The Paper Magician is a whimsical fantasy set in Victorian London that features a delightful and creative magic system, a strong female heroine and a little touch of romance. 
 The magic system is established within the very first chapter. Magic can only manipulate man-made objects, like glass, paper, metal, and rubber. A magician must 'bond' to a certain type of object and then are able to manipulate it in a variety of different, interesting ways. It was such a treat to read about the different ways magicians manipulated paper. Two of my favorites were when Ceony learned how to make a scene from a book come to life just from reading aloud and when Magician Thane animated a little paper dog for Ceony that acted just like a real one. Ceony called him 'Fennel' and he became one of my favorite characters in this series. 
 I wasn't just fond of Fennel, though. I love the main character, Ceony, and you know why? Because she is a strong female character who is able to think for herself and take action - while remaining feminine! Ceony has many traditionally feminine traits like modesty, a sense of decorum, and she knows her way around the kitchen. Yet, she is still able to speak her mind and rescue the guy in the end by relying on her wits and her gut instinct. This is so refreshing to see because sometimes I feel like too many people who write strong female characters (both in books and on screen) think that strength = masculine so they just give a female character masculine traits and call it a day. It's the 'Dude in a Dress' trope and it's getting a little tiresome. So I love that Ceony is an example of a strong, yet feminine, female character. 
 The plot was interesting and moved along at a rapid pace (which is understandable considering the book is only 222 pages.) I liked the developing relationship between Thane and Ceony. I, personally, love student-teacher romances although the one in The Paper Magician is very chaste indeed. There's only a small hint of a romance developing later in the series. No kissing, no nothing - which is totally fine as it suited the story. 
 The Paper Magician is great for readers of all ages looking for a light, whimsical fantasy.

I probably would have given it 2 & 1/2 stars if there had been an option to do so. 
 Parts of this book just dragged and the characters are one dimensional. 
 But there are some new ideas in this book, such as being bonded to specific forms of magic. And part of me was curious as to how paper magic could be used.

I wanted so badly to like this book. It wasn't a bad book, but it could have been a great book. There just wasn't enough detail. The characters weren't fleshed out enough, their relationship was rushed, the plot rushed along into the action with a few cleaning/cooking scenes in between, the magic system wasn't well explained, I had no idea what the purpose of the magical school the Ceony went to actually was because it didn't seem like she actually knew anything about magic at the beginning of the book. This read more like a skeletal draft of a book. There was a good concept, some good conceptual characters, but no depth. I've heard in writing classes that world building for fantasy books should be like an ice berg: the part above water is what appears in the book, while the even bigger part under water is everything that the author knows about the book. The Paper Magician's world building wasn't even an ice berg, it was a chunk that had fallen off of the ice berg. 
 Also, I don't think the author did much in the way of research. The book was supposed to be set in Victorian London, or at least a version of Victorian London, but based on the contextual clues I didn't figure that out until an actual date was expressly mentioned. 
 This book could have been fabulous if the author had been more rigorous in the writing and researching of it. The actual prose of the book was very good and the story had the spark of a good story hidden at it's center, but that spark was not fanned into the glorious blaze it had the potential to be. Maybe the next books in the series are better, maybe they're more in depth and developed, but I won't be continuing to read this series.
This book reminded me of the magic school bus..... it was not that great. I had such great hope for this book but it was just disappointing. It is pretty short though so it is a fast read.

DNF. 
 Wanted to like it, but couldn't get into it at all. I found the descriptions really bogged the book down. I didn't mind that it wasn't historical accurate in any way, but the attempt to make it both modern and not really wasn't meshing for me. 
 Really disappointed that I didn't like it, because the idea was really cool.

I was very excited for The Paper Magician and highly disappointed. 
 I will start off by saying that the concept and a few explanations of the magic in the book were exactly what I was hoping for (paper magicians can animate images from stories mid-air, genius!) and I enjoyed these aspects of the story. I was hoping the first book, knowing the novel was the first in a series, would focus more on the different types of magic and the history behind this universe, as well as how the magic shaped it, before moving on to a far-fetched adventure. There was not nearly enough background to the story. 
 When it comes to the "action" in this novel I strongly disliked the turn the story took. First and foremost, I did not like that the memories, hopes, dreams, regrets, etc. were actually "located" in the magician's physical heart. There is too much overlap between the anatomical description of the heart earlier in the novel and where memories are stored, I thought it took away from what could have been a great concept of being inside someone's mind or thoughts. I also did not enjoy the descriptions of the heart as a muscle: Ceony moving through the valves was much too bizarre and graphic. 
 Again, as I was excited by the concept, I was disappointed by the poor writing. First, the author uses descriptions that are much too overdramatic and take away from the image she is trying to portray. She descriptions the main character feeling like a moment was "raking her brain with needles" - too much! This is just physically painful and does not really conjure an image of emotional pain or anxiety. Second, in a scene where the male magician is protecting a female magician from the police so she is not jailed the author says "he couldn't even deny her a prison cell" when in fact he made sure she did NOT go to prison as she was trying to avoid it. The author's sentence would make since if the female magician had WANTED to go to prison and the male magician had allowed it, knowing it wasn't a good idea. The fact that this story was published with an error like this is concerning. 
 Overall, interesting concept but poorly excuted.
Couldn't finish it ...
Creep, weird, and good.
I enjoyed this book. It was a rather unique magic system and just a fun read.

book_b.title: The Last Girl (The Dominion Trilogy, #1)
book_b.user_review: Handmaid's Tale meets Mad Max. The main character Zoey was boring and typical and most of the the book made little sense.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 This was a struggle to get through. It starts out slow, picks up and then fizzles out by about 60% through. The beginning is all a build up where there are so many possibilities of what could happen next. I kept thinking that something insane was going on, come to realize it's basically the most plain and obvious answer. By about 80% I had to force myself to stay awake and pay attention in order to finish it. The ending was a disappointment, although it's probably the most interesting and unpredictable part of the book. I really wanted to like it. That's why I saw it out until the end, in hopes that it would have some turn. But really the only surprising things that happened were unnecessary deaths throughout the entire story and the fact that Zoe managed to miraculously escape EVERY situation she was put into. I won't be reading the sequel. This just wasn't my cup of tea I suppose.

2.5 stars. Pretty cliched, not really as interesting as it should have been. Could have been an interesting counterpart to The Handmaid's Tale with some similar plot points but it got way away from that. A bit of a shame.

I wanted to like it.... 
 Just too many details that didn't make sense. Maybe it is resolved in future books in the series, but I doubt it.

I don't know. 
 This whole thing feels like the set up for something better. 
 Q: Why punish the last remaining girls who are the last hope of birthing more girls? Lock them in completely dark box? To scare them? Because they had an altercation with another girl? What is the point if that? 
 For me, it wasn't until I was 75% in that this stared getting interesting. 
 I'll read the next installment if only to see if it lives up to the potential. 
 Chicago: the pres was aware of all the killings in the Chi...wait that's real life stuff.

This book should be marketed as adult erotica. 
 There is very little plot development and the main theme of the story seems to be the degradation and raping of women. 
 Not recommended.

For some reason, there is a common dystopian trend of there being a shortage of females. Women become a commodity and in this case, the last remaining females are locked up in a prison-like environment until they are 21. At the magical age of 21, they are given a ceremony and released to live in a utopian paradise with their parents. I'm just wondering, in this world, what color is the sky? The girls who have survived, are they also somehow missing the capacity to smell a load of bullshit when it is being handed to her? 
 This book made absolutely no sense. I can allow room for imagination, I don't need perfect "science" to buy a book's premise, but this one.... 
 Here are some of the problems: 
 The girls are stolen as babies and raised in a prison, treated like animals, punished cruelly, and yet told that they are "special and important" to society. What's the point of treating them so badly? If they are the "hope of the world", why not treat them well? Then, they may not only want to actually live, but they might be happy to help the world out with their magic ovaries. 
 The whole bit about them being reunited with their parents and living in a wonderful "safe zone" at the age of 21. Why not come up with a more believable story? You can say they will get to pick a husband, that they will donate eggs and then go free, that they will get to board a spaceship and travel to the planet of endless chocolate. Any of those would be better stories than the idiotic one being told. 
 The idea that the cause of the shortage of female births is somehow related to the females themselves. Um... biology 101: the sperm determines the sex of the child. Why don't they lock up the men and experiment on their sperm instead? It would be more productive than their current plan. 
 Why wait until the girl's are 21 at all? Once later revelations come out, there is absolutely no reason for this. None. 
 There were a total of six girls at this facility. With tons of guards, sniper towers, walls and cameras, special forces, and tons of technology to keep them in place. It seems like a lot of over-kill. They could have probably housed these girls in a nice condo in Boca. It was the equivalent of housing a hamster in a penthouse apartment in Manhattan. Just... too much... 
 But, even if you can somehow wrap your mind around the world, be prepared to just feel depressed. Our 20 yr old girl is as angsty as a pubescent teen. 
 In other words, if you haven't read it - don't bother.

Epic! 
 I loved this story. I started loving it more and more as I got into it! It's not what I usually expect from Joe Hart but wow! Well worth the read !
Round up to 3.5 stars. Pretty good, but not as engaging as I hoped.

reference_books.title: Gone for Good
reference_books.review_text: Twists and turns right through to the end......

reference_books.title: The Shock of the Fall
reference_books.review_text: An amazing book which I almost gave up on to begin with. This was a slow start book for me, but it really picked up momentum and as I neared the end I was turning pages at a rapid pace. Matt is the central character and the story is told from his perspective. It is clear that there are struggles within his family and with his relationships but I initially wasn't clear where the story would lead, however, as it unfolded it became clear that Matt was suffering with mental health issues. The story was told in a way which wasn't self-pitying but which captured fabulously the feelings of turmoil being experienced by Matt. At times it felt almost as though there wasn't 'flow' - a lurch here or there - but this left me, as the reader ,feeling as though I was sharing the confusion and disconnection that Matt was experiencing. It dealt honestly and sensitively without being overwhelmingly sentimental. I enjoyed this book and believe it would be a good book club choice with lots of discussion points.

reference_books.title: Dreams from My Father: A Story of Race and Inheritance
reference_books.review_text: An interesting read. A seemingly honest account of the internal struggles to understand heritage, opportunities and choices as well as the external forces at play in an increasingly complex society. In this autobiography the obstacles to equality are still presented as essentially a battle between black and white which felt a little simplistic in this day and age but I guess that's the value of an autobiographical account.

reference_books.title: Perfect
reference_books.review_text: Dull,dull,dull. I'm astounded by the rave reviews that this book has received. The only positive thing that I have to say about it is that the descriptive writing was interesting although it did have the effect of making the book feel as though it were someone's descriptive writing homework. I just failed to make any real connections with the characters.

book_a.title: Oh Dear Silvia
book_a.user_review: Gave up (and I don't ever fail to finish a book. ...ever) The concept of the book had potential - Sylvia is in a Coma in hospital having been subject of an accident, the details of which are not apparent from the outset. Sylvia is visited by a series of famil, friends and hospital workers each of whom narrates their chapter, and from whom we, the readers build up a picture of Sylvia. I'm afraid I found Sylvia a character I disliked early on which contributed to my failure to finish the book. I wasn't really interested in how she came to be in the coma -her story was on the point of putting me in one! My book club pals told me what had happened and, perhaps harshly in the view of some, I decided karma took hold. The housekeeper was my favourite character bringing humour to an otherwise dull read which included an annoying editorial feature of underlining words for emphasis. Petty I know, but I found it distracting. Wouldn't recommend it.

sample_reviews.review_text: My first Dawn French read, and definitely the last. Populated by bizarre, extreme caricatures, it is difficult to have a shred of empathy with any of the characters as they visit Sylvia, their wife/mother/sister/lover/ patient/ employer who lies in an ITU in a coma. The style is clumsy, much of the narrative is overwritten and the attempts at using devices such as letters and dialect lack any subtlety. Difficult to grasp why some critics describe it as hilarious. Immature and clunky..yes; hilarious..no!

Oh dear, Silvia. I really did not enjoy this much at all. The plot was barely there; it felt like 300 pages of blathering on. The writing style itself felt incredibly amateur, and maybe it's because I was writing my own novel at the same time, but it just seemed so cringeworthy and I could spot exactly the same tactics I was using to increase my word count without writing anything of quality. The concept of a person being multi-faceted was interesting, but it just didn't come across well in the book. Add to that the fact that Winnie and Tia are both written in phonetic Jamaican and Asian accents, which comes across terribly. It may not necessarily be racist, but the idea of white middle class Dawn French sitting and typing out how she thinks a Jamaican lady will say things. Please, no. 
 Also, this was meant to be funny???? There is literally nothing in it that I even thought was meant to be a joke. 
 It's not very often I rate a book less than 3 stars, but... this one earned it. Sorry. 
 If you want a good Dawn French book, read A Tiny Bit Marvelous. 
 {Read 08/10/2015-28/11/2015}
Couldn't finish.
I have an issue whereby I cannot leave a book u finished even if it's boring me. I put this book down at about the fourth chapter and haven't picked it up since. So glad I picked up a free copy!

I found the book just a little bit to predictable, the reader never really got to know any of the characters in any detail, for instance Silvia herself we never learned what her actual occupation in life was, the same being true of her ex-husband Ed, who all we knew had recently purchased a wood. The character of Winnie, was completely ruined in my opinion by having all her dialogue written down in dialect, a very dangerous exercise for even the most accomplished authors, and definitely did not work in this book! On the whole very average.
Read over 100 pages so boring can't take no more maybe one I go back. Very disappointed as I love dawn french on tv but first time read her book felt like hanging myself like Ed in book

I had a bit of trouble deciding on a star rating for this book. Some aspects I would rate very highly, and towards the end of the book, I was shouting internally that it couldn't possibly end satisfactorily (but it actually did, sort of, I think). Then, there were other aspects which really irritated me, such as the VERY OVERUSED dialect of Winnie. It's just so hard to read, and you really don't need that much of it to understand that the character has a thick Jamaican accent. We get it, alright! Okay, so I was clearly irritated by that. Other parts were heartbreakingly sad. I did not, however, think that the book was 'side-splitting' or 'hilarious', which were terms used on the front cover to describe the book. Yes, there was a bit of dark humour, and I smiled at a couple of things (mainly concerned with Tia) but I think there was a bit of false advertising at work here. Okay, so overall, I enjoyed reading the book and would probably give it 3.75 so I'll round it up to 4.

I really want to like Dawn French's books but always feel so disappointed. I love the storyline but find I'm just not gripped and don't love the characters. 
 Loved the storyline in this - lady in a coma whose family come to visit and talk to her with secrets being revealed etc etc blah blah! 
 The execution the storyline just doesn't hit the spot for me. 
 Sorry Dawn not one I'd recommend
Terrible.

I started this book with little expectation regarding the execution but with high hopes. I knew that the novel was supposed to be quite morbid but I imagined that with Dawn French behind the keyboard, there was sure to be level of humour, and in this I suppose I wasn't wrong. 
 Though there was the underlying sense of morality there was a level of humour through the events that occured within Suite 5. Unfortunately I just felt it was all too forced. 
 Basically, Silvia Shute is in a coma and her life is revealed through her many visitors. Most of these visitors are absolutely bloody nuts and should be in some kind of institute themselves. The schemes of her sister Jo to wake her up were just unbelievable. I spent the majority thinking, well this isn't funny, she'd never be allowed to light candles in a real hospital because the alarms would go off and she'd be chucked out on her ear by security... 
 I'm not sure I had any real expectation regarding Silvia as a character but within the first few chapters we found out that she was a bit of a bitch towards her ex-husband and she'd effectively kicked her own children out on the street. Did this develop further in the book? Maybe, but I didn't get that far because by then I didn't care whether she lived or died. 
 I did stop reading quite early on, so maybe it did improve, but it wasn't my cup of tea!

book_b.title: The Complaints
book_b.user_review:
A story of the police policing the police, that's what this is basically about. As the plot unfolds the reader is left wondering who can be trusted, if anyone? A murder, child sexual exploitation, domestic violence and internal police corruption. 
 This was fine but I didn't enjoy it as much as other Rankin books. The characters were well formed and the plot moved at a steady pace but I just struggled to identify or empathise with the main police characters. With the heavy subjects ad plot material this ought to have been much better than it turned out to be. A moderately paced read.

sample_reviews.review_text: This book ticked me off. I thought the main character started acting in ways that were completely inexplicable for the character -- and that were much more in line with the behavior of this author's other, prolifically written-about main character...

The narrator of the audio book was fantastic--too bad the book wasn't in the same league. 
 After reading Rankin's Watchman, I had huge hopes for this. Don't get me wrong. The book wasn't a waste of time. It wasn't bad. It just wasn't anything special. 
 What had me excited to read it is that it's from the point of view of a detective in the Complaints (or Internal Affairs). How great was it going to be to see things from the other side so to speak? Unfortunately, that didn't happen. 
 When other policemen--the ones he was investigating--would ask "Why do you hate policemen?" Fox had no answer. He never really managed to come up with any justification for why he worked so hard investigating fellow policemen, other than it was just his job. Now this it's just my job may suffice in real life, but when I'm reading a book, I want a bit more. I want a character who has some reason for what he's doing--something along the lines of Harry Bosch's mission. 
 Another disappointment was that the plot diverged so far away from complaint investigation that it wound up being a more or less standard who dunnit with very little to do specifically with the Complaints Department. 
 (I've just finished listening to the second The Impossible Dead and unfortunately it's even weaker.)

I love Rankin's Rebus books, not just as crime fiction but as fiction, so I was eager to read this post-Rebus novel. 
 It was nicely set-up but then it just got messy and quite frankly boring: too many characters, too many threads, and a protagonist who has neither passion for his job nor for anything else. It's that last things that spoils the book... I don't have to like Fox or too admire him but he can't be boring. 
 I might read the next book in the series to see if it picks up, but I won;t be doing it in a hurry.
Well written but dullsville.

Being a big fan of this author's John Rebus series I was more than a little trepidatious when I picked up this book. The Complaints introduces us to a new protagonist, Malcolm Fox, a member of the Police Complaints and Conduct Dept, aka Internal Affairs of all things, a department and an individual that Rebus would loathe. I needn't have worried, for although I miss Rebus as much as the next reader, I thoroughly enjoyed this book. 
 There are some stark differences between our new hero and our old one. Fox has weathered some hand to bottle combat and when our book opens he's been on the wagon for five years. Fox's listening pleasures are also minimal unlike Rebus'. He recognizes classical "tunes", but can't place the composer, and he likes nothing more than tuning his radio dial to the Birdsong channel which plays nothing but - well - birds singing. Fox broods, but again not like Rebus - and he's not quite as funny - although Malcolm does have his quipster moments. 
 On the other hand, Fox like Rebus is not real good at following rules and protocol. (Fox's two co-workers and boss - none of them Siobhan Clark - make for a very good supporting cast.) In The Complaints Malcolm, who seems a pretty steady and focused copper, soon finds himself embroiled in a very tangled web after he begins investigating a peer on alleged internet porn charges and the seemingly coincidental murder of his sister's boyfriend. To add to the mix Fox is put on "suspension" - a not so pleasant irony for someone from the Complaints Dept - which only incents Malcolm to investigate further and contrary to his "instructions". 
 These continual twists and turns of the story, multiple plots and sub-plots and double-crosses, as well as who's investigating whom, also differentiate Fox's world from Rebus' - this a much more convoluted and complicated case than Rankin's previous books. So there are a lot of characters to keep track of. I read most of this is in a "single sitting" - albeit in a cramped seat on a plane. This possibly alleviated any confusion I may have encountered keeping all the characters straight if I had to put this book down several times over several days. 
 Still I very much enjoyed Malcolm Fox's first adventure and look forward to his next one.
Love the character development. Good back story, not too much but just enough. I will be reading much more of this author.

The Complaints is the first Ian Rankin novel that I have read, and I enjoyed it. It is an easy read, packed full of action and strong characters, along with good dialogue. There are a few recurrent themes in the novel which don't lead anywhere, which I found frustrating. For example, the protagonist, Malcolm Fox, has a history of alcohol problems, but this never impacts on the plot in any way, which leads me to wonder why Rankin included it. Presumably it is just to add extra colour to the character. Similarly, there are frequent mentions of Edinburgh's traffic problems, leading me to expect that this would be a contributing factor in the plot, but it wasn't. 
 One aspect of the plot struck me as being slightly unbelievable - a police officer engineering the removal of a subordinate from by placing under surveillance another police officer whom she had never met. This aside, the plot is good and takes more twists and turns than a slinky factory. Overall, The Complaints is an enjoyable novel that places few demands on the reader.
Good mystery set in the environs of Edinburg. Ian Rankin is a very interesting storyteller so his novels are quick reading.

If it has one star I liked it a lot 
 If it has two stars I liked it a lot and would recommend it 
 If it has three stars I really really liked it a lot 
 If it has four stars I insist you read it 
 If it has five stars it was life changing

Reading this made me ponder the difference between crime fiction and mysteries. While there is certainly a mystery that is central to the book, the nuts and bolts of this book had to do with the daily grind of police life in Edinburgh. Corruption, intrigue, and a lot of after-work pub sessions. Enjoyed it enough to keep reading, but not exactly mind-blowing.

reference_books.title: The Rose Society (The Young Elites, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Sign me up as scared. 
 I've had this book since it came out, I'm very proud of myself for lasting this long without reading it. Busy and expectant, not a good combination, so I wanted to wait for when I had the time and was a little bit more calm to read it. 
 This book was as dark and interesting as I'd hoped, and Adelina's journey was sad to witness as well as powerful. For some reason I still find myself alined to Adelina, she is broken, sad and angry but in all her evilness I can't help but be on her side. Her rapid descend into madness made me realize that I still think she can turn back; Magiano's introduction proved at least that she still has some light inside her. I'm scared for what the next book will bring because, I want her to recover but there is still so much about her darkness that has not been fully developed and that I hope we get to see unfold. 
 This book, though not perfect, was so interesting to read. I honestly kept thinking that at some point I would get bored but I never did, which just proves the power of Marie Lu's writing. The world she has created is so complex, I'm almost sure we are not going to be able to completely understand it even if we get more than 3 books. As for the plot, it was never boring but it was also always predictable and that is both good and bad; good because there is always a sense of accomplishment when you know what is going to happen, bad because I also love being surprised by something unexpected. 
 As for the character's I still feel like I don't know them at all, which is also good and bad. As I've stated above I'm on team Adelina, so obviously, I love her. I still don't know how I feel about Violetta though she has proven that she cares about Adelina and that puts her on my you're good for now -list. Sergio is a complete mystery to me so hopefully we will get to see more of him in the next book. As for super-sweet-and cuddly Magiano, I just love him, I think there is so much more to him and I just want to know it all. Stepping away from The Rose Society there is pain in the neck -Teren who, though wicked as he is, I still find to be an awesome character, and the Dagger's who I still love and hate, but I guess that's the point. 
 This book is dark but, is not as dark as I think the next book will be. So I'll hold on to my reins very tightly. 
 If you've read The Young Elites and haven't read The Rose Society: What are you doing with your life? and if you haven't read The Young Elites: What are you doing with your life? just read this book and/or the previous one. Do it. You'll like it, trust me.

reference_books.review_text:

Anyway, I freaking love this book: dystopian , lovable main character , friendship , diversity , mind blowing plot and finally, pain? .

reference_books.review_text:
2.5

reference_books.title: Demonglass (Hex Hall, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
This book was a complete disappointment, I really wanted to LOVE it but I couldn't and I'm so sad because I loved Hex Hall it was so funny, sarcastic and snarky with a world I wanted to know so much more about. 
 But , Demonglass failed to be as interesting as its predecesor and turned a great main character into a naive girl with horrible decision making skills.

reference_books.title: The Horse and His Boy (Chronicles of Narnia, #5)
reference_books.review_text:
3.5 
 The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion the Witch and the Wardrobe was one of the first books I read for enjoyment which for me as a child was really a big deal specially if you become a bookworm later in life like me. I feel like this series has a special place in my heart, although I've never read the entire series, so I decided that it was about time I read the ones I hadn't and this one was at the top of my list.

book_a.title: A Conjuring of Light (Shades of Magic, #3)
book_a.user_review:
There comes a time, in every devoted reader's life when a book you think is going to be perfection, does not meet your expectations, and you are left in the verge of: Do I chose to overlook certain things that did not work for me because of my love for everything else in this book or, do I lean on the faults of this book, even though I still kinda loved it? 
 this is that moment for me... 
 *Takes deep breath* 
 I DO NOT FEEL LIKE THIS BOOK GAVE ME A FULFILLING CONCLUSION TO THE EPICNESS THIS TRILOGY HAS BEEN! I am upset and not entirely sure why it just didn't work for me... 
 As many movie critics and movie watchers say: "It is difficult to nail the third act" 
 and as many book reviewers and writers say: "The final book in a series is the most challenging piece of the puzzle" ... I may be paraphrasing... 
 I think this book suffers from the third act syndrome (I don't know if thats an actual thing). It has the potential, the storyline threads were there, waiting to be woven together to perfection, but for some reason the results fell short. It was so close to working and making me happy, and making this review just a lot more flailing and less bitterness. But although I enjoyed the trip, I was not satisfied with the solution. 
 I think it was just too convenient and I am disappointed. 
 HOWEVER! 
 As I said, the ride to get to the conclusion was so good, that it kinda made up for the things I didn't love. Like, stavyness, thievery, magic, banter and just my beautiful loveable cast of characters that I just drool over every time they so much as breath. 
 ... 
 Please check out my blog for more on this review: *Jazz Hands*

sample_reviews.review_text: So. I LOVED ADSOM. I was really let down by AGOS but wanted to finish out the series. I barely got through this book and I only did bc I had read 300 pgs already and damn that's a lot of pages. the first 300-400 pgs could have been a lot shorter and perhaps I wouldn't have gotten so utterly bored and stopped caring. There's not enough substance to span 300 pgs in my opinion. and then I started getting tired of the writing-- the short truncated sentences that are supposed to make it all sound more epic but end up just starting to grate on me. The last 200-300 pages was when it finally started to captivate me more. I'm really overall sad about this series and also confused because I have never been more of a black sheep. I'm sad because this world has so much potential and I really liked the magic in ADSOM. I thought AGOS was just a second book slump but unfortunately this one missed its mark too.

Much like my review of A Gathering of Shadows, I suspect A Conjuring of Light would be an excellent book for most adventure/fantasy readers. 
 I had challenges with it because I didn't realize how tightly interconnected the books in this series were/are. Much like the advice I was given about The Hobbit and Lord of the Rings, the Shades of Magic series doesn't seem like stories set in a similar universe so much as three chapters of a much larger work. 
 I'd've started with book 1 in the series if I'd known that and such is my advice to others interested in Schwab's books; start with the first in the series.

I LOVED this. Schwab's writing is just so damn gorgeous. Everything I've read by her has been wonderful but if feels like this has raised the bar. 
 This book should have felt too long with so much going on and so many subplots but instead it just worked. Plus, I found myself craving even more! I still have so many questions! Who are Kell's parents? How did Lila lose her eye? What favour will Lila have to perform? I want more back story on Emira! 
 All in all, this was the perfect end to a wonderful series.

It's been a while since I stayed up so late to finish a book, but this one was especially difficult to put down. I also hugely regret not having any kleenex at hand because that ending--the second last chapter in particular--destroyed me. I love this series, and I'm sad it's over, but V.E. Schwab ended it brilliantly. 
 As well, I always know a book is good when it makes me want to write myself. And I wanted to pick up a pen, open up a word doc within the first twenty pages. So thanks for the inspiration, Victoria.
I FINALLY got my library lend back, re-listened and I AM DED. D-E-D.

4 
 Second half was DEFINITELY better. 1 star subtracted due to Lila (same old culprit, hu?) and the first half, which I found a little slow. 
 First of, I love Kell. He and Kaz Brekker are now my two book boyfriends. KELL IS SO PERFECT. his frown, his coat, his courage. All of it. 
 Second, Holland made this book what it was. He was definitely THE best character. He was simply... not perfect, because he's so broken, but... there just aren't words. He made me sad. He made me cry. He made me laugh, and frown. He was the Someday King. And it was heart breaking. 
 And that burn he gave Lila? Just perfect. Take a look: 
 "No, I did not hesitate. I cut his throat, and added his death to the ones I count every day when I wake." His eyes hardened on her. "Now tell me, Delilah, how many lives have you ended? Do you know the number?" 
 Lila started to answer, then stopped. 
 The truth-- the infuriating, maddening, sickening truth-- was that she didn't. 
 AND BAM. D'you know why, Lila? Because you kill people for STUPID, selfish reasons, and you forget about them as easily as your last meal. 
 Third, I'm so happy for all the little snippets of backstory here. Made the book more rich and well rounded. 
 Fourth, the floating market is just the COOLEST THING EVER. 
 Lastly, the negatives were, obviously, Lila (you are simply infuriating). 
 Here, take a look at a quote by her: 
 " She'd never been one for moderation. Not when she was just a street rat with a quick temper and a quicker knife, and certainly not now that she'd struck flint against the magic in her veins. She knew this about herself, she LIKED it, was convinced it had kept her alive. " 
 Being a kleptomaniac, rash idiot who has 0 consideration for others may keep you alive, dearie, but I certainly hope it will also be your death. The thing that bothered me though, is why the hell she is an ANTARI. Wtf? Why? Now we had to hear even MORE "I'm Delilah Bard, special-fucking-snowflake, who magically has a bunch of power for no apparent reason, along with a knife fetish I try to remind the audience of all. the. time, along with how badass I am." 
 Just ugh. Also, I didn't find Osaron very interesting. He made me mad in the first half, but not really in the second. Sure, he irked me, but he didn't infuriate me like an antagonist should. Though this might just be me. 
 Finally, Grey London's end was just depressing. It made Red London's end just seem weak. 
 Sigh. I'm sad this series is over. I'll miss Kell, so much. And Rhy. And this amazing world. To you, Lila, I say good riddance, but to Tieren and Emira, Alucard, Maxim, Maris, and HOLLAND, well, I'll miss you all. Terribly. 
 Happy reading. ;(
