reference_books.title: As I Wake
reference_books.review_text:
I checked this book out from the library because I really like Elizabeth Scott's books. I've read a few, and they were great. This said, I expected As I Wake to be good, too. I was soooo wrong. To be perfectly honest, this book gave me a headache. 
 This book begins in a huge state of confusion. Which makes sense, right, because that's the story. I thought if I kept reading things would make more sense and I'd understand better. NOPE. Everything was so scrambled and made very little sense. I barely had any clue what was happening for a good portion of this book. 
 It WAS nice to guess a little what would happen and why. For a bit it was all good and fine with me, but then I kept reading and nothing continued to make sense. We would be given a little information, but very little is ever really explained. I'm usually good with figuring things out, but when I'm not given enough info to figure it out, I'm not a happy camper. 
 Character Rundown: Ava. I know very little about Ava, therefore don't really have an opinion on her. As far as I can tell, she seems all right. Focused. Shy. Then there's Morgan. I liiiiiked him. We don't know all that much about him either, other than that he honestly and truly loves Ava. Which makes him awesome in my book. Yeah, that's the way I am. Ah, Morgan. 
 The ending. Have you ever seen Shutter Island? The ending of this book made me feel like I did when I finshed watching that movie. And before you ask--no, she's not just crazy amd imagining things. I'm comparing the FEELING I had, not the actual events I saw. This said, the ending gave me even more of a headache. 
 Overall, I didn't really like this book. I didn't feel very connected to he book except for when Morgan was around, and that situation frustrated me even more. If you really like books that are completely puzzling, I guess you could try this book. You may like it. I did not, though.

reference_books.title: Passion (Fallen, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
Passion was one of those books that I read because I had to to get to the next book in the series. I really liked the first book, despite the boring beginning, and I truly enjoyed the second book, even though there was so much petty arguing that really got too repetitive. So I decided to read this book because I seriously want to read this whole series. I was SO excited to read this book. I think I expected too much. Either way, I have to admit I was disappointed by this book. 
 The thing about this book was that it was so boring, in my opinion. There were some parts that caught and held my attention, yes, but those were not as often as I would have liked them to be. Another thing about this story was that a lot of it was very scattered. We just kept on getting sent to random places at random times and I couldn't understand why. I mean, yeah, Luce wanted to see "proof" of her and Daniel's love, but that doesn't seem a good enough reason to jump through time repeatedly. For most of this book, I didn't feel like there was a main plot holding everything together. My point here: we had to wait too long for explanations. Being confused or half of the book - more or less - is not the way to hold my attention. 
 All that said, this book was not COMPLETELY horrible. I did like seeing into some of Luce's past lives and learning about Cam's past. I liked to see Daniel's past self, too, because I DID have some serious doubt as to their "love" until I read this book. Before it seemed very much like lust misconstrued as love. I'm pretty confident in the love now, though. (I just want to point out that even though I was doubtful, I wasn't really questioning the love between Daniel and Luce becasue I thought this concept was sweet and I tend to be an optimist when it comes to these kinds of things.) Also, there were some completely heartfelt moments in here that I loved. Not as much as I'd like, but still, some were there. 
 Character rundown: Luce. I. Do. Not. Like. Her. At. All. I really really really do not. She just grates on my nerves. So whiny, and ignorant, and DOUBTFUL. I mean, I'm allowed to have doubts about Daniel; it's my job as a reader to do so. But Luce should have been 100% sure of him the whole way through. I don't see any reason for her to really not be. I find it almost amusing how skeptical Luce is about Daniel, and yet she trusted Bill so completely in this book. Grr. Daniel. OH DANIEL. I really like Daniel. I don't know why, but I do. It's probably because of his strong love for Luce. That kind of thing always gets me. Cam - OH CAM. I swear, this book is so incredibly hard for me to pick a team for because Cam is so amazing, yet Daniel just has the feeling that I wish Cam did. Cam never fails to make me laugh, either. Never a bad thing, that. 
 Lastly, Bill. The whole Bill situation really disappointed me for Luce's sake. How could she be so unintelligent? You'd think she'd have grown some common sense in her brain and not be so quick to take a random being for his word. Plus, I wonder if Luce realizes that a WINK is NOT a yes, or even an answer for that matter. And "sure" isn't exactly a yes either. I knew who Bill was from the moment he showed up, at page 82 or something. I did like Bill, though. He was a good comedic relief in all of Luce's irritating-ness. I'm glad he was in this book, because otherwise, I may have taken FOREVER to read this book. 
 All in all, I'm just glad I got through this book so I can read the next one when it comes out in June. I'm going to a Lauren Kate book signing, so I needed to get this out of the way. I have high hopes for the next book, though, especially now that we get to see all the characters again. I missed them in this book. Honestly, the only way I even read this book as fast as I did was the motivation to just finish it so I could move on with my life. Well, that and because I don't want to keep Monica's book for TOO long.

book_a.title: Hallowed (Unearthly, #2)
book_a.user_review:
The second book of the Unearthly series did not disappoint. 
 I've told you before how second books are usually either hit or miss, good or bad. This book exceeds good. It was such a great bridge to the next book (which I CANNOT wait to read, when it comes out, which will be I-don't-know-when). Hallowed was so many things. I laughed, I cried, I slapped people. (Just kidding about the slapping thing. Kind of.) 
 Something I really liked about this sequel was that there weren't any new characters forced on us. What I mean is that in a lot of sequels, there are new characters (to be honest, usually of the bad-boy variety, but not always) thrown on us to add to the story or something. Don't get me wrong, I can end up loving these guys along with everyone else, but in Hallowed, it was nice that the story didn't use characters that were thrown in for controversy. Yes, we will meet new characters - (none of which will be included in the character rundown because telling you about some of them could seem spoiler-like and I don't spoil. Plus, I like to stick to the very most main characters and the boys. Yeah, I'm such a teen girl) -we WILL meet new characters, but they are added naturally. They are very comfortable additions to our beautiful Unearthly world. 
 Another thing that was great about this sequel: it was sentimental. Now you're thinking WHAT? What ever do you mean, you LIKED how sentimantal it was? That makes no sense! But actually, my friend, it makes perfect sense. The last book was based around Clara's purpose. In this book, we are still wondering about what her purpose could be, but it isn't in the forefront of everything. This book is hugely about family. I was being honest when I said I cried. I seriously cried a bit. I didn't ball my eyes out or anything, but there were some sweet moments. 
 I always comment on the romance, and it was still present in Hallowed, but not the center of everything, and that was perfectly okay. The whole Tucker-or-Christian thing wasn't overbearing, but more of something that happened on the sidelines. 
 I am aware that I'm not going very in depth on much, but I really don't want to give anything important away. Because you must read this book. It is a beautiful piece of paranormal YA fiction, and I just know you will enjoy it as much as I did. 
 Character rundown! Clara, the main girl. An angel who is about to find out some things about herself that we never would have guessed. I like Clara, I really do. She is very ideal - beautiful, smart, an angel. But she has her faults, too: can be a little self-centered during crucial times (you'll understand when you read), indecisive in moments where it's not helpful. . . But I like her anyway. Now, to Tucker. Ah, Tucker. I feel so much for Tucker. The human who loves this angel and wants so much to keep her, to not be seperated by their differences. Plus, he's gorgeous and macho. But then we have Christian - OH CHRISTIAN. The perfect boy for Clara. An angel-blood. Determined to do what he was meant to do, what he knows in his heart is right. And again, he's gorgeous too! Seriously, Clara hit the jackpot in the guy department, that lucky girl. 
 In case you hadn't noticed, I am TEAM CHRISTIAN. I love Tuck, but I'm rooting for Christian all the way, folks. ;) 
 The ending. The ending gave us all a sense of closure about a very important event in this book. Which was good. But it also left us wanting to find out what happens next. Was Clara's decision for good, will she stand by it? What's going on with the Black Wings? And Jeffrey? And, dude, WHAT is going on with their purposes? So many questions, and no answers. But that's a great thing, because there will be another book! So my only problem here is that the next book isn't out yet. Nor will it be our for some time. So I shall sit here and twiddle my thumbs anxiously until I can get my answers. 
 My rating: 5 stars. I was leaning toward 4 stars for a while, but then I realized that there is nothing wrong with this book, in my opinion, to make me take it down a star. So a full 5-star rating it is! Which means you should most definitely read this book! It's amazing, it's funny, it's HEARTFELT. Oh, yes it's heartfelt. That is the word I have been searching for in my mind as I write this review. Heartfelt. That is the perfect word for this book. You should totally go figure out what I mean and READ THIS BOOK. Okay?

I just finished Hallowed and I absolutely, positively adored it!!!!!!!! Again, I'm not really into YA that much because usually it's too sappy. This book for me re-defines YA. The love that the Characters feel for each other is so pure and realistic. Hand writes so well that I feel like I AM Clara, and not just reading about her. Every time I thought I had something figured out, I was completely wrong. I liked that. Sometimes even when a book is really good, it's predictable. Not this one. I'm broken. Shattered into pieces. 
 Okay let's start this review with some of the quotes that I liked in this book: 
 "There's nothing more inspiring than the complexity and beauty of the human heart." 
 "I've learned that a storm isn't always just bad weather, and a fire can be the start of something. I've found out that there are a lot more shades of gray in this world than I ever knew about. I've learned that sometimes, when you're afraid but you keep on moving forward, that's the biggest kind of courage there is. And finally, I've learned that life isn't really about failure and success. It's about being present, in the moment when big things happen, when everything changes, including myself." 
 "You have made my life into something so extraordinary, you can't even know." 
 "I've learned that sometimes, when you're afraid but you keep on moving forward, that's the biggest kind of courage there is." 
 Okaaayy.. now, to what I think of this book. Honestly, I loved Unearthly more. I do love this book too but I think that the first book is just better. The first book made me feel more excited and thrilled. Although this one really sad and heartbreaking in the end. But sometimes, this book gets a little too slow for my taste. 
 I like though that the conflicting emotions inside Clara felt so real to me. The part in the book where she said that she finally understand love triangles is also the moment when I finally understood love triangles from reading her relationship and feelings towards Tucker and Christian. 
 Another thing I liked about this book is that it explained more about the angel stuff and talked more or paid more attention to the story of Christian, Clara's mom, and Jeffrey. We all needed to hear more about them. 
 I was broken in the end though. Because well, of the sad things that happened in the book and to Clara. And of course, I was totally depressed and frustrated to the result of Clara's relationship and whom she kind of chose in the end. That is what's making me cry the most. hahaha! 
 Anyway, I am very much looking forward to the next book! ;D

4 of 5 stars 
 This was a heart warming and heart breaking book. I didn't expect that this would be really emotional but I guess everything that happened this time contributed a lot for the development of each characters. But I was still definitely stunned and surprised by all the unexpected twists and revelations. The writing was really good that I was so consumed I finished it in one sitting. I was awed and devoured on how everything turned out this time but the ending left me really sad and with a big "what now?" question in my head 'cause I don't have any idea on what's gonna happen next. 
 To be honest, I was pretty annoyed to Clara during the first parts with all the "Tucker is my future", "I love Tucker", "I own't let him die, I'll fight my purpose" thing. And I guess I was just reacting like that because I'm on team Christian. Yeah, it was silly of me to feel like but that's just what really happens to me if I liked the other guy in a love triangle that's why I really avoid them, it affects my freaking judgement to the heroine. But anyway, it was only during the first parts. As the story progressed, I saw Clara's character developed too. She was confused between the things she wanted and her purpose. But as things started to get thrown in her she was able to handle them strongly, especially the situation with her family - her mom and Jeffrey. 
 I love Clara's relationship with her mom. And her mom was definitely the coolest mom I've ever met in the YA world. That it was really devastating when we realized what Clara's vision really was. In Unearthly, I was very amused with Jeffrey and Clara. I love their sibling fights and love but I have really no idea what's happening with Jeffrey. He was one of my favorite characters in this book and it was just sad seeing that their family looks like falling apart. I just wish that Jeffrey wouldn't go in the wrong side and direction. 
 Even though I've been on team Christian since the beginning it doesn't mean that I wouldn't feel heartbroken on how things ended between Clara and Tucker. It was just so sad during the last part especially when Clara read his emotions. I saw how much he loves Clara and how Clara loves him as well. And I know even it was really heart breaking Clara did the right choice. Loving someone doesn't mean staying with them forever but learning to sacrifice and letting them go to keep them safe and better. 
 I learned a lot about Christian here and it just really made me pretty happy. I was actually surprised with all the revelations about him and that made me love him more. lol. He's smart and mature and I love how he explained why he broke up with Kay even if he loved her. He was very supportive of Clara and was always at her side every time. You might have think that I might be celebrating right now since Christian was pretty leaning forward but no, not really. Yes, I was happy I saw a lot of him now and I still want him for Clara but I also felt Clara's lost and sacrifice that it was just hard to be totally happy about it. 
 This was a story of acceptance and letting go. And it was inspiring in many ways. I really don't know what's gonna happen next but I am really looking forward for the next book. 
 *And yeah, I heard there will be TV series adaptation of this book? Wow, that was just awesome! Let's hope it sticks with the original story. :)) 
 This review is also posted at Book Overdose

I gave it 2 stars just because I loved the first book. 
 But this one, I couldn't even finish it. I came to the 100 page, because I wanted to give it a chance, but I was so bored. I just wanted it to end. As soon as possible.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Hallowed is the second book in the series and let me say, that I have a lot to say about this book! In book one, Clara didn't fulfill her purpose; she chose to save tucker, her boyfriend because she couldn't let him die! (Yet she blames Christian for driving "Kay" home on prom night, knowing fully well Kay was upset and heart broken)! How is that different from Clara choosing to save tucker? How. Sweet! 
 In book two, Clara is having new dreams; she didn't know what it meant... soon she finds out that her dream is trying to tell her that someone she loves is going to die. Clara concludes that its Tucker and she will fight her purpose by saving Tucker again. So she started stalking tucker by hanging out on his window and playing bodyguard. She chose not to tell her mother about this dream because she didn't want to see the look in her mother's eyes, which led to little white lies to her mom. She is still avoiding Christian not wanting to talk about the fire! (Coward!)Worst she is oblivious to anything around how but Tucker! 
 Meanwhile Clara's mother is getting sick and very weak, but Clara doesn't see this, she is focused on Tucker. 
 As for Christian he just supports Clara, wanting to be friends letting her set the pace. They haven't really had a chance to get to know each other. They are drawn together yes, but what else is there? 
 Then Clara finds out that her mother is the one dying not Tucker! How she deals with it? She got upset at her mother for keeping it a secret, then and blames God for taking her mommy's life. (Isn't 120years enough? How long does humans live? Isn't she keeping secrets from her mother, by not telling her mom about the dream?) 
 Jeffrey on the other hand is taking it harder than his sister, plus for some reason he hates Clara now! why? Wait for it... secrets time! 
 Lots of secrets were spilled in this book... 
 1.	Clara should have gone to Christian, but she chose to save Tucker Avery in book 1... the ripple effect? 
 2.	 Tucker was Jeffrey's purpose not Clara's Jeffrey was supposed to save Tucker from the fire! But by Clara's interference she not only ruined her purpose, but she messed up Jeffery's and Christian's as well! (Stupid isn't it)? 
 3.	 Clara's dad is a full angel not human making Clara and Jeffery More Angelic than the human. Which means Clara and Jeffery are supposed to be super powerful. 
 4.	 Christian and Clara are the same, meaning they have the same amount of angel blood in them! They are more angelic than human. Which mean that they are supposed to be perfect for each other. 
 5.	 Clara's mother fought her purpose too just like Clara for about 60 years. 
 Conclusions? 
 Even though Cynthia Hand is a good writer she is inconsistent and her heroine is just selfish and dumb! Not an attractive quality you want in a Human or an angel! 
 1st off, there are times to be stubborn and there are times to take a step back and think! Clara is not logical, she is impulsive and thoughtless worst off all she is very judgmental. Case in point? In book 1, Clara chose to go after tucker, choosing to save tucker. How is that different from Christian when he chose to take " Kay" home on prom night, yet Clara condemns Christian for a choice that she might have made! After all she did choose to save Tuck, didn't she? Worst Tucker, wasn't hers to save. It was Jeffery's! Clara also hates her mother for keeping secrets, yet she keeps secrets of her own. Plus Clara tells everything! She can't seem to shut up! Spilling angel business to Tucker, even secrets that isn't hers to tell! If she likes to be that open, be open to Wendy too... not just tucker! Hypocrisy? Roger that! (And Christian thought her brave? He must be blind or Daft!) Seriously! 
 In book 2, Clara chose to let Tucker "go" because she believes he deserves to have a normal human life, yet this is the same girl who is trying to fight Purpose and still fighting her purpose because she wants to choose! (Is my life) she says, all the time, yet she chose for Tuck! Deciding for him (How inconsistent is that?). WOW! What was Cynthia Hand thinking? I mean I know people like conflict, but there is a difference between conflict and page feelers and this writing, this book is the epitome of Plain Rubbish! I continued reading this book because I thought Clara might become sensible, but she gets dumber and self absorb by the second! The deal breaker for me was the parts were Clara was considering giving up college to stay with Tucker. It doesn't fit; the message is confusing! What is Cynthia Hand trying to convey? Free will? Choices? Love wins all? What's is meant to be will be? Because I CAN point out all the inconsistencies with all four from her writing so far! What else is there? What am I missing? 1 star!!! ... And a waste of my time.

reference_books.title: This Book Is Full of Spiders (John Dies at the End, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
"How did we screw this all up so badly, John?" 
 He shook his head. "We always find a way." 
 This Review is Full of Spoilers 
 Warning: Opinions are of a childless hardcore dog lover. 
 For 394 pages this book was the crazed, hilarious, thought provoking, action packed tale I expected. 
 Then that blackguard Wong killed off Molly. Molly was my favorite fictional animal after Rowl from The Aeronaut's Windless. 
 I understand why they did it. 
 I understand that in a way it was a compliment both to the character and the value of dogs in society. 
 I understand how well it wrapped up the story. 
 I don't care. I did not read a drunken meta spider crawling zombie apocalypse novel by David Wong in order to ugly cry. 
 Ugly. Cry. 
 So how do I rate 394 pages at 4.5 stars when it goes on to 404 and fuck you? I guess I'll take off one star and round down to three. 
 This book was included in the August 2017 Infested/Infected Nocturnal Readers Box. My first subscription book box!

reference_books.title: Beloved
reference_books.review_text:
To be fair I knew this wasn't going to be an enjoyable book. You don't run up to your friends and say, "Hey guys let's get ice cream and watch Schindler's List!" 
 I read this out of curiosity? 
 To be moved? 
 To understand history better? 
 No, let's be real, I read it to check a box. 
 Still, I was expecting to enjoy the writing. 
 I didn't. 
 It started out immediately with disorienting POV jumps of character and time. I prefer it when authors give a damn about readers and label chapters Debra 1845 or Charles 1950 Tokyo, etc. There are few books written well enough to engage the reader while doing inter chapter POV time/character shifts. Lonesome Dove is the finest, that writing is like butter. 
 The heavy torture/murder/rape aspects I was afraid of coming into this book were only lightly touched upon. It was the discussions of freedom and PTSD that I found more effective in evoking the pain of slavery - to a point. Morrison lets her characters do the talking without filling in third person eloquence. I wish she had helped them out a little, they were illiterate. 
 Much of this story is indigestible poetry and madness. I'll leave you with a taste... 
 I am Beloved and she is mine. 
 I give flowers and eat lobster 
 Blue like the sky, flowers, water 
 I see his teeth 
 They are my teeth 
 I eat ice cream with teeth 
 I hate ice cream 
 I eat ice cream 
 Did you forget ice cream? 
 No I laugh 
 I laugh so hard it hurts 
 I cry for ice 
 I weep for cream 
 I have forgotten nothing 
 Beloved is mine 
 Ice cream is mine 
 Blood is mine 
 This is not a story to pass on 
 Good 
 Because I'm eating ice cream 
 And 
 Never 
 Reading 
 This 
 Again

I don't even know why I ended up reading Call Me Daddy so I cannot recommend this book to just anyone. LOL. But the prose is good and the psychological part of the story was to my liking. I also like how this book is not just erotica bordering to porn but also about the journey of two lost and lonely souls that found each other through a string of fate. Okay, so I got 37% through the book. I tried so hard to like it but it was to taboo for me. To dirty daddy stuff. It actually grossed me out from time to time. 
 just the thought of some little 18 year old girl calling some 40 year old daddy in bed is just wrong.

Call me Daddy is one forbidden and kinky taboo naughty taboo read. The author Jade West does put a warning at the start of the book, letting readers know this may not be their cup of tea just by the title of the book. But I have to say this was definitely up my alley and I completely enjoyed the tale this author wrote. 
 Laine is a virgin on her 18th birthday who was left along by her mother so she went out with her friend Kelly-Anne to celebrate. And then that "friend" ends up leaving her alone too out where they were celebrating. That is the story of her young life. Abandoned and left alone. So here she is is, alone with no funds and no way to get home when she is rescued by Nick, this older man who is like a knight in shining amour. Now Nick is this older, more seductive man who has seem more of the world and what he sees of Laine, he likes yet he wants to protect her and this all starts with him just wanting to save her and get her home. He ends up taking her to his home for the night until he can get her back to her friend the next day. His best intentions are what he sticks with and in the morning he plans to return her to her safe and normal world yet due to events beyond the MC control, that doesn't happen exactly. 
 The story progresses from there and what we get is this dirty, yummy, Daddy-kink story that I totally loved. There is a plot, good story line, action, oh yes and a lot of smut but it wasn't written to just be written. This is a good story that tells the story of a naive Laine and her older white knight Nick and how true love can be found when it was least expected. Oh and expect some betrayals to come to the forefront in this story when the MC least expected it. I loved how it was handled and how growth came from it. This is not so much a HEA but a HFN storyline. I would love to read a followup on how Nick and Laine are doing. I loved reading a daddy-kink storyline and hope the author writes more storylines like this. 
 My Rating: 4.6 stars ***** 
 "I voluntarily reviewed an Advance Reader Copy of this book in exchange for an honest review***

I received a copy of this book in exchange for an honest review for Stephanie's Book Reports. 
 I am not even sure where to start, I've read every book Jade West has written. She pushes my boundaries and imagination every time. I've even had to google things to learn what they were. I by no means consider myself a prude. I've read fetish book before. With that said I had to stop and at that point I told Stephanie it was a DNF for me. I do not not finish books. It drives me crazy to lay one down and not finish it. I ended up picking the book back up and did finish it. I think I'd have been ok with her calling him daddy during their private times together. I'd probably have not thought much about it. However that is not the case. It's more than a fetish of call me daddy it's a man who wants a child. A sweet innocent girl he can take care of and honestly I felt like he looked at her like a child and that's where I started to freak out. I am a pretty open minded reader but this was just disturbing on a level that had my skin crawling. 
 No doubt Jade West writes some really good books that I've enjoyed reading. Call Me Daddy just wasn't for me.

book_b.title: Wolves of the Calla
book_b.user_review:
This is going to be quick review because it's been a few months, the library digitally reclaimed my copy, and I'm almost done with the next book, Song of Susannah. I'll fix it up the next time I read the series - yes I'm already sure there will be a next time. 
 Now DT5 was my favorite of the series when I read it but being almost done with DT6 I think that will be the new favorite. Damn fine thing in a series when books get better as you go. 
 So what did I enjoy? I loved the inclusion of a character from a previous work of King. 
 The more you read of King the more you enjoy any allusion to another work of King. 
 I loved the badass Women of Oriza who defended Calla Bryn Sturgis. 
 I loved the way King knit together so many fantasy references with ease.

Great Instalment In The Dark Tower Series. 
 Wolves of the Calla was a fantastic entry into what is stacking up to be one of my favourite fantasy series. We join our ka-tet as they journey into Calla Byrn Sturgis, a village blighted by the mysterious Wolves. I'm hesitant to say much else as I don't want to spoil any of the discovery. 
 I thoroughly enjoyed the mystery woven through this book, and the tension ramped steadily throughout as the climax drew closer. The new characters were varied and interesting as ever (I even found myself wanting to mimic their way of speaking, if it do ya). I also found myself drawn even closer to our ka-tet as, page by page, they seemed to become more human. 
 It goes without saying that if you've enjoyed the series so far, this entry won't disappoint.

Out of the five I've read thus far, this one gets 3rd place (though close behind second place). Well, I made it through The Wolves of the Calla. Let me start off by saying, I highly enjoyed the first four books of the Dark Tower series. 
 This one, not so much. 
 The story begins with Tian, a local rice farmer, plowing his Son of a Bitch field, using his roont sister like a mule, when an automaton named Andy comes to inform him that the Wolves are coming. Tian holds a town meeting at the gathering hall with all the men (no women allowed, of course) and tells them they must not allow the Wolves to take their children this time. Take them away before bringing them back as thoughtless roonts that eventually grow painfully into giants. There is some disagreement, but it's a priest from our world, Pere Callahan, who sides with Tian. At this time, Roland and his ka-tet are passing by, still following the Path of the Beam leading to the Dark Tower. We learn Susannah Dean has inherited another person to her list of personalities who calls herself Mia, meaning Mother. Poor Susannah had gotten herself knocked up supposedly by a demon when she allowed one to have sex with her to keep her husband, Eddie, safe while he was bringing Jack Chambers into their world. Now in the dead of night, Mia comes out and feasts on any raw meat she can find in order to feed her chap, believing she's in a grand dining hall munching on gourmet foods. 
 Callahan approaches the gunslingers' camp and asks if they will help defeat the Wolves. While reading through two-hundred plus pages of talking about whether or not the gunslingers would help stand against the Wolves, we go into story time with Tian's father-in-law, Gran-pere about how in his much younger days, he and a handful of others fought the Wolves, and we going into more story time into Callahan's past and about his troubled days in New York City as an alcoholic, traveling across the country killing vampires. 
 Anyway, there's also some evil ball, called Black Thirteen that Callahan has and wants to pass it on to Roland, and todash, which allows the characters to journey back to 1977, New York City for a little while, to which Eddie spots his old drug boss, Enrico Balazar. There's a whole thing about the number nineteen that kept getting brought up and it became irritating quick and a Cave of Voices where there's a suspended door like the ones in the book The Drawing of the Three. All the while I was waiting for this to get good. Instead, there was a whole lotta explaining, palavers and side stories. There were constant mentions of things that didn't seem to go anywhere, and if they did, I missed it, like the number nineteen and Elton John's song, Someone Saved My Life Tonight. 
 The writing was good, but not as delicious as the previous Dark Tower books and the show don't tell violations near the very end just before the battle with the Wolves irked the hell outta me. 
 After reading this book's synopsis, I'd expected more drama and action, like Eddie having to go head to head with Balazar in order to protect Calvin Tower, the bookstore owner, who also owns property that houses a very important flower rose. And as I read the book, I thought the characters would go investigate where the Wolves came from and discover what they really are instead of it just being TOLD to them. 
 The Wolves of the Calla wasn't a bad book. The story kept my interests enough to finish it and continue on with this journey. I'm now on Song of Susannah.

reference_books.title: Reading in the Wild
reference_books.review_text: I ordered this book when it first came out, and now I have finally gotten to read it. When I read The Book Whisperer, I was really moved to help my teachers at the elementary school where I worked get kids to finish books. (I had noticed that my kids were constantly returning books with a bookmark on page 25.) It turns out that they were only reading to fulfill their reading logs, or they were reading a book when they needed to read at school, but they didn't really care if they finished it or not. The reading teachers and I worked together to build a great system to help our kids finish books. It worked! And the kids became a community of readers , which is the most important thing. One of the greatest things that happened outside of that, was that their reading levels rose much faster and higher than they did before, and that also showed on their state testing. I'm happy to read this book and see that many of the things that Donnalyn recommends as a teacher, I did as a librarian. Mostly I'm happy for the kids who get the joy and benefits of being a member of a reading community :-) This book can help you take the concepts of The Book Whisperer and make them work for you.

reference_books.title: Butter
reference_books.review_text:
This is a book about wanting to fit in, literally and figuratively. Butter is an obese teen who wants desperately to be friends with others, to talk to the girl he thinks is cute, and to be able to be a part of life apart from his computer screen. When he makes a rash decision to go online with his "last meal" and let everyone watch him eat himself to death, he alters the dynamics of his whole life and changes begin to happen. 
 Give this to realistic fiction fans, those who "live behind a screen", and anyone who has ever really wanted to fit in. 
 There is a little bit of "language" in this book, and teen-age drinking. 
 Spoiler alert below... 
 He does not die. And the ending is pretty much a happy one.

reference_books.title: Popular: Vintage Wisdom for a Modern Geek
reference_books.review_text:
Dear Maya Van Wegenen, 
 I saw you speak at TLA in the spring and I really liked you. I wanted to like your book, but I do not. I am in the minority, and I do not mean to hurt your feelings (like many authors talked about at TLA), but I found your language inappropriate in many cases, your references to life in your high school random and unconnected, and your character development flat. But I think your voice in teen literature can be a valuable one (as evidenced by the many positive reviews from teens and adults on this site) and I hope you continue to write. I think your premise was great. 
 Lone Star 2015 
 I cannot recommend this book to anyone. The characters are flat, the strong language use is inappropriate in context, and several references to high school life are random and, at least to me, superficial and meaningless. I am puzzled as to how it landed on the Lone Star list for this coming school year. 
 Example, introduction "...your life becomes a series of brutal and painful encounters: being called a dick by the football player who sits next to you in science..." 
 Example, when the main character will not come out of the bathroom after trying makeup for the first time: "I look like a clown-whore." 
 Example, in the locker room: "...every time I turn my head, I see your giant ass in my face. I don't know what the hell you think it looks like, but it's not pretty so MOVE!" 
 Example-- while in class, there is a disturbance in the hallway. Two pregnant girls fighting. Never referred to again. Really? 
 I am usually not one to point out specific uses of language, because in general I feel like it makes sense in the context of the work, but in this work many instances really jumped out to me as attention-seeking and out of place. I will not be recommending this book to my students.

book_b.title: Stolen Innocence: My Story of Growing Up in a Polygamous Sect, Becoming a Teenage Bride, and Breaking Free of Warren Jeffs
book_b.user_review:
Absolute power corrupts absolutely. 
 This story of Elissa Wall's life during and post life as an FLDS child married against her will to her first cousin at 14 is interesting, but about 100 pages too long, but otherwise inserting and a worthwhile read.

sample_reviews.review_text: This book is amazing! It definately made me see what a wonderful life I have. Freedom is something that sadly not everyone has and sometimes we don't realize how good we have it. Elissa Wall was a teenage bride (forced in marriage to her cousin, whom raped her many times) Asking for help made her a "rebel" and instead of receiving the wanted help she was asked to "keep sweet". Elissa Wall was in court to testify against Warren Jeff and thanks to her and her suffering he is now in jail where he shall remain. God Bless her! I COULDN'T PUT IT DOWN!! I 100% recommend you read it...!

I feel slightly odd about reading this book. I think, living in Utah, that on many levels polygamists don't hold the fascination that they do for people who haven't lived near or worked with polygamists. All the same I'm curious to read the author's description of the lifestyle. I'm enjoying that while she talks about the difficulties she's had, she also talks about her love for her family and good times they had. It doesn't feel as one-sided as I'd expected. 
 I ended up just scanning through. The story telling was choppy and felt a little one-sided. I certainly don't want to say that some horrible things happened to her and that she had a hard life, but I felt like there wasn't one sentence in the book that was anything other than her making her point, and by 6 chapters in I felt like I got it. Polygamy=bad. Okay. 
 That said, it sounds like the has a much happier life now, and I'm very glad to see that.

This is a pretty decent book but it is a long read. There are parts that kind of drag on but the necessity of the detail is important to remind us that these are actual events that happened to an actual person. Some of the material is extremely controversial but that's because it has to be. It is an interesting read and worth finishing.
Heartbreaking

I became riveted with this story about halfway through when the author really started struggling with getting out of her marriage and eventually the FLDS. Although I ended up staying glued to it for the last half, it was just very hard to read as she described her life from the beginning to the time right up to her marriage, which is why I didn't give it 4 stars( more like 3.5). Since this is considered to be in the true crime genre, it read like an evidence-ridden novel rather than a story. I'm not exactly into these types of books and can't seem to get into them enough to enjoy them as I try to sift through the facts and information. If I were to recommend a book about the FLDS and polygamist lifestyle, I would much prefer the story "Shattered Dreams" about another woman's struggle with being a polygamous wife and dealing with the horrible poverty that came along with it.

If you look up 'tough cookie' in the urban dictionary, I have no doubt you'd see a picture of Elissa Wall listed as a shining example. This girl was forced to marry her creepy cousin when she was fourteen, despite totally lacking the language or knowledge to be in an adult relationship. After being trained her entire life that guys were creepy reptiles, she was expected to suddenly give up an entire lifetime of programming, and be happy to make babies with her snake-like cousin. 
 When you go to the leader of your church for help because your husband/cousin is raping you, and he tells you to get back in line and "keep sweet," when you continually miscarry in private to keep the whole situation from your blind-to-the-situation mother who refuses to talk to you about sex, when you look at your younger sisters and fear for their lives because you know you can't keep them safe from the things you've experienced, and you still survive and testify against that man who put you in that marriage, even when the feds can't find ANYONE ELSE to testify against him. That is when you know you've crossed into the seriously, insanely tough cookie territory. 
 I have a special interest in FLDS stuff because I grew up in Salt Lake--in high school I drove up to a polygamist compound with my friends to check it out, surrounded by high gates, and some kids in full polygamist garb, covered head to toe, came out and started throwing rocks at our car. You'd see women and kids with the fully-poufed hair and the tights/socks with tennis shoes and very long prairie dresses occasionally, at the store or out somewhere. It was just part of life growing up in Utah. Although I've read other books on the FLDS religion, like the dark cloud 'Under the Banner of Heaven' by Jon Krakauer, and Prophet's Prey by Sam Brower, this was the first I've read from a woman's perspective and it made things astonishingly more emotional. Wall looked to Jeffs as a spiritual and community leader, and he told her continuously to stay in a relationship where she was being abused. To have that little support for your own well-being in your community is mind-boggling to me. 
 I'm hesitant of parts of the book that describe the FLDS religion as okay before Warren Jeffs came into power. Although things became dramatically worse, I don't think that makes what life was like before Warren Jeffs okay. I started thinking this myself, that I lived in Utah before Warren Jeffs was in charge (and I was young myself), so it was okay we were all turning a blind eye to this and not being more concerned about what was going on behind these gated communities. But I don't think this culture was okay before Warren Jeffs, he just made the abuse so blatant and insane that we would all be participants if we were ignoring it.

I found this book so interesting..I'm beginning to think most women from my background are fascinated by FLDS and Warren Jeffs . I was first out off by how long this book was but it was interesting to learn the background of this off-shoot of the. Mormon church...and completely understanding why the LDS church wants no part of them! Elissa Walls' story was interesting and often harrowing . I know some Good Reads reviewers have said that she comes off as self-serving and overplays the victim rifle but to me, anyone who is forced to marry their first cousin at 14 has a right to act out. I hope the fiesta of her life is peaceful.

Disturbing and true story of a polygamous clan. The story made me angry in many ways: the parents allow their children to be abused, married off young, moved around from place to place, taken from family, etc. all because of their "faith". I have always thought polygamy to be creepy, this book reinforced that notion several times over. As a practicing member of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, I am very upset that many confuse our church with this group. The FLDS teachings bear no resemblance to the things I have been taught my whole life. The only thing that kept me going was knowing that Elissa Wall broke free from this cult. Good for her, not only for the escape, but also for being brave enough to confront Warren Jeffs in court and for writing this book.

This is a train-wreck book -- not in the sense that it's bad (although it's not exactly good) but in the sense that's it's so horrifying, you can't stop reading. It's a harrowing story and made me feel a little voyeuristic for finding it so compelling. But the information about life in the FDLS (the fundamentalist branch of Mormons) was really interesting, and though the author broke away from the church and that life, it's a more sympathetic portrait than you might expect.

I liked this book, but at the same time, I felt like the story could have been told with a bit more pacing. I hate to say that because it makes me feel like I am used to fiction, and this is non-fiction, but hey, she co-wrote it with an experienced author. Why does it drag a bit? 
 I have always been fascinated by the FLDS. It was interesting to have the perspective she provides in the Epilogue about the Texas raids that separated families. 
 I hope her foundation and story can help girls who want to get out to get out of the community. It really is necessary that help exists, since these girls have no network, no knowledge of available resources, and no funds. Scary stuff.

reference_books.title: A Tale for the Time Being
reference_books.review_text:
This work is an inspiration, beginning to end. It comforts and agitates, at the same time. It came to me in a timely manner, because I am lately struggling not to hate: according to Zen, you hurt your karma even by thinking bad thoughts. I have a lot of bad thoughts, mostly of revenge: against a person who lost$10K and, afraid she would lose her rich husband if he found out, let him assume I stole it while working for their business; against people who refuse to see the face that had a family and community, on their plate. These are just thoughts: I never acted on them because I'm a civilized human. Ruth Ozeki, a Zen Buddhist priest, helped me realize that I was hurting myself by just imagining this revenge. 
 Memorable moments of the book: learning about ocean gyres; learning about what suicide means in Japanese culture (it's not shameful, like it is here--this is comforting to me because my older sister committed suicide by jumping off a roof); Nick Drake and his song "Day is Done"; the prayer you give to the toilet you take a dump in; (p.180) "I believe That in the deepest places in their hearts, People are violent and take pleasure in hurting each other"; instructions on zazen; the World Rectifying Catfish; supapawa--(I believe my superpower is being Spanish English bilingual, which allows me to help people with my understanding/privilege of white culture). 
 One last word: ReadThisBook.

reference_books.title: The Year of the Runaways
reference_books.review_text:
This book tells about young people trying to make their way in a world determined to value them based on their caste. 
 You know how Latinos come to the U.S. thinking they will make a better life for their family, only to find that society is dead-set against them? Well, Indians go to England, hoping to make a better life, only to fight the same thing. 
 This book is heartbreaking and beautiful; for all you readers out there who stubbornly stuck to what they believed in, even if it meant you would never be successful in the conforming world, this book is for you.

sample_reviews.review_text: Late October 2016. Abandoned after 174 pages. I just couldn't take it anymore. Self absorbed blathering that didn't have insight or a point, that I could discern. The essays were quite long. If I'd based the rating just on "Matricide," maybe I would have given it three stars.

What an unpleasant woman. The writing wasn't terrible and I expect a certain level of self-absorption in a book of personal essays, but this lady is ridiculous. I don't know how she expected to come off based on this book, but I'm pretty sure it wasn't as a privileged, self-absorbed, vaguely misogynistic, culture appropriating bitch. Big fail.

3.5 stars -- I just can't commit to whole numbers! This book of essays is very well-written, but I would be lying if the subject matter didn't rub me the wrong way on occasion. In one (less enchanting) essay about Joni Mitchell, Daum credits her with teaching "that if you didn't 'write from a place of excruciating candor, you've written nothing." Daum does just that. Some of her confessions are painfully honest, especially her reasons for not wanting children, and her involvement in and understanding of the foster care system. She does warn readers in her intro that "this book recounts some pretty unflattering behavior" and in that regard it is refreshing. She is not afraid to tackle tough topics (mother-daughter relationships, marriage) with honesty and candor. And she is good at letting the reader in on the joke. None of it is meant to be self-aggrandizing or preachy. Instead she is just sharing some observations and experiences and widening the reader's world view (micro-view, in some instances) just a little. Best of the lot was "On Not Being a Foodie" and "Diary of a Coma."

This is an exquisite book, full of pathos (especially "Matricide," arguably--and deservedly so--the most widely-known essay from the collection) and humor ("On Not Being a Foodie" comes to mind). She has an amazing eye and her prose is filled with vitality, even when she's talking about her own brush with death, though I found the concluding piece to be the weakest in the collection. Regardless, I love this collection. It's absolutely one of my favorites. 
 Also, for what it's worth...for as much controversy as it has elicited, I found "Honorary Dyke" rather respectful. Perhaps some are thrown off by her self-proclamation as an "honorary dyke?" Or the way that the subject matter is broached head-on? With Daum, I think that's the point. These aren't pieces that are meant to make us comfortable (hence the title); she wants us to think. And have some fun while doing so.

I really struggled over whether to give this three or four stars, but ultimately I went with the higher rating because when Daum embraces her theme she shines. And mostly I wanted to give it three stars for two pieces: the one about how cool Joni Mitchell is (don't care) and how amazing it was to meet her (still don't care) and how can you believe I lost her phone number and address?! (sorry, I drifted off there. Oh, right, still don't care.) and the following essay which was about her dog (all the eye rolls). Those aside--and yes I understand that writing about one's musical heroes (and pets) is perfectly legitimate, but that doesn't make it any less of a turn-off for me--the ideas in The Unspeakable were generally strong, approaching brave. 
 I picked this up after reading Rebecca Solnit's The Faraway Nearby hoping for more of the same. Sadly, Daum is no Solnit, which is not to say she's not a skilled essayist in her own right. Her real strength lies in her ability to cut through the schmaltz. With a couple of exceptions (see above), Daum never settles for the sentimental, and even in those weaker pieces she's capable of pulling out some smart observations. In the dog one she says something to the effect of losing a pet hurts more than losing a loved human person, and she backs it up. That's the kind of thing I wanted from this book. I wanted the "unspeakable," the unvarnished truth. The final essay, the one about her nearly dying from a rare bacterial infection, is an excellent example of this kind of thing. You expect some kind of lesson, some kind of building out of the mythos of passing, but Daum delivers just the opposite. For me, she says, in that instance, dying would've been easy, as simple as flipping a light switch. What's more, the experience didn't necessarily lend gravitas to those big ticket parts of life (family, friends, etc.), nor did they undercut the importance we place on the "unimportant" things cluttering our life. The event was merely that, an event. I appreciate this world view and the candor Daum brings to it. I just wish she went further and more often to that territory. 
 Now that I've read Solnit and Daum, I'm going to round out my female essayists trio by finally reading Slouching Toward Bethlehem. Stay tuned for my thoughts on this classic Didion text. 
 If you liked this, make sure to follow me on Goodreads for more reviews!

I thoroughly enjoyed The Unspeakable and feel as though there were parts of it I could easily have written myself. Daum's theme is the degree to which she finds much of adult life to be a performance, the way that we're all expected to play certain emotions around the subjects of death, parenthood, pets, food, and more. Daum isn't interested in pretending and she doesn't care who knows it. The opening essay, 'Matricide", concerns the Daum's complicated feelings over the death of her mother and it will resonate with anyone who has ever helped care for a parent during a terminal illness. In other pieces Daum discusses the fact that she doesn't want children and the strain that the decision put on her marriage and her half-baked entry into lesbian culture as a single writer in New York. There are also pieces about Daum's own near-fatal illness, her identity as a Californian, and her distaste for those who dismiss out of hand the music of Joni Mitchell. Daum is unsparing in describing her own shortcomings and in putting forth opinions that others might consider unpopular, and its the bracing quality of her self-deprecation that separates The Unspeakable from other books working the same ground. To put it another way: This book is not funny, and Daum doesn't care if that's a problem for you. (Nora Ephron appears in one essay, and I can't help thinking Ephron would have liked this book's tone very much.) I'll be going back to Daum's earlier writing - I can't remember if I've read her novel - and I expect to be impressed.
3.5 Some wonderful essays are contained within this book. The interesting part for me was the author's commitment to write her truth, even if it was raw and unflinchingly honest.
Very understated and very moving. These essays feel coherent and personal; I really enjoyed them, and several of them (particularly the one about her near death) will stick with me for a long time.

this novel seems to be of the love-it-or-hate-it variety, judging by others' reviews of it. personally, i loved it. in fact, i loved it much more than both on beauty by zadie smith and never let me go by kazuo ishiguro, both of which it beat out to win the 2005 booker prize. this novel is told in stream-of-consciousness format by an aging irishman whose wife has recently died; he skips around through memories of various stages of his life, primarily a summer he spent at the sea when he was eleven. all the while he muses on the infirmity of memory, love and loss, and his own mortality. there's no denying that banville's prose is exquisite. it's almost baroque in its usage of circuitous sentences and its proliferation of sensual imagery. and what a vocabulary this man has! this novel introduced me to words like "effulgence," "maenad," "catafalque," "ichor," "casuistry," and "assegai." i think some people are put off by all these masturbatory verbal fireworks, arguing that they take the focus away from the story and the emotion (see: michiko kakutani's review in the new york times), but i'm a word nerd, and i thoroughly enjoyed both the language of the text and its underlying message - so much so that i read the entire book in one sitting. (to be fair, it's only 200 pages long.) i for one am glad that banville got his booker prize, and i plan on seeking out more of his work in the future.

What do you say about a book and author that has won the Man Booker prize, has managed some beautiful sentences and turns of thought, but is a book describing a character who is sullen, near morose, and who avoids warmth and friendship, hates his parents, and believes that everyone is inherently selfish? Some reviewers describe Banville as "mesmerizing" and "heir to Nabakov." Poppycock. Banville says, "the greater part of my energies was always given over to the simple search for shelter, for comfort...for coziness." In some cases that is understandable, but there is no warmth about Banville; he'd do better on an island. He meets a family with children his age who disappear in front of his eyes; his wife dies (and leaves him all her money), and he repeatedly drinks himself almost to death out of boredom. In the end, I don't really think we should applaud a caustic ne're do well, but then maybe I'm just too American...I do miss the point. Granted, we catch him here at a low point, and perhaps end of his life. I give this two stars since the prose is beautiful, but the plot is wasted--reminiscent of slowly chewing a rotten apple.

Having looked at other reviews this does appear to be a marmite book you either love it or you hate it, as you may have guessed I fell into the hated it category. 
 I really enjoyed the beginning of the story the poetical descriptions the use of repetition to emphasize things and the feelings of loss expressed by the narrator. 
 The middle of the book in my view was a mishmash of 2 past events blended in with the present and skipping from one to the other with little warning or cohesion. 
 The end of the book at least made an effort to tie up the loose ends and give the reader some clarity but the understated way the climatical revelations were made for me made them lose impact it was almost a case of blink and you miss it. 
 While in parts beautifully written I found this overall a dull book.

sample_reviews.review_text: This one was clearly not for me. I'm sure I'm in the minority here, but I just couldn't get into the story, although I really wanted to like it. Several things kept annoying me, but my main problem was simply boredom.

Actually, I think the first 1/4 and the last 1/3 of the book should have a 5 star rating, and the middle section about a 2-3 star rating. I got kind of bored in the middle of the book, because it seemed like there was nothing really happening, and I started to lose interest in any of the characters. I read just a little further, and when it got to the last 1/3 of the book (heading into the jungle), the book picked back up and I really wanted to know what happened. There were parts of the ending I didn't like. But there were enough loose ends left that the reader can imagine any number of happy or unhappy endings post-book as he or she wishes. 
 Overall, I'm glad I powered through and read it. I would recommend it to others. However, I warn you that this book is denser than the average book and accordingly, it may take more time to read than another book of the same size.

2.5. After a slow start and a passive narrator I disliked, by the end I was, as they say, entranced. But the story's implausibility overshadowed the beautiful writing.
This was very disappointing.
This was a wonderful read. Enjoyed every minute.

A happy ending overall, but I didn't like so many of the plot twists that happened in order to get to that ending. The scientists came off as very calloused towards the indigenous people they were studying. I don't think I'd recommend this book to anyone unless they were specifically looking for a novel about fertility and pharmaceutical research based in the Amazon.

I am in a state of wonder that Ann Patchett is able to write like this. When I read an earlier work, Bel Canto, I found myself living in the world of the book, a terrifying and fascinating place. In State of Wonder, I was in a different place, at once terrifying and fascinating, and when I emerged, I did so with the blinking eyes of one who is a bit surprised to be in her own living room, under her own lamp. 
 Marina is a doctor, a lab rat. She is precise and detailed, perhaps a bit shy. Her work is her life, and, when she is asked to follow a colleague to Brazil to find out what, exactly, had happened to him, she is compelled by her loyalty to work to do so. This excursion is about as far from Marina's life as it is possible to be: she is used to the sterility of the lab; a jungle is just not in her universe. 
 As she travels, I went with her, shedding the various parts of my American life slowly, almost unconsciously. While neither of us completely "went native," we both found ourselves thinking in alien ways and, in her case, doing alien things. I was right there with her. 
 No spoilers here. I have lived my week out of contact with the world that I know, and Patchett took me there. Not to be missed.

So, I stopped reading and recommend you never start. Unless you like stupid books in which an author who writes well writes a vacuous novel.

reference_books.title: Snow White: A Graphic Novel
reference_books.review_text:
A unique take on Snow White: this version of the fairytale takes place in the 1920s, Snow is a young woman named Samantha, her father is King of Wall Street, and the Evil Queen is a famous dancer/showgirl. What I found very interesting is the fact that this is less fairytale and more fantasy realism since it has are subtle elements of magic in our world. 
 The art is simple and lovely and with a single brushstroke you know exactly what a character is feeling or thinking. I think the beauty of this story is in its simplicity; it's a well-known story, so it needs little introduction or dialogue for you to know what's happening. I love that the Evil Queen became a beauty- and financial-obsessed showgirl in this! It works so well for the time period! 
 This graphic novel is super short though. It took me less than ten minutes to read. I do wish it was longer since it was such a joy to read. 
 *Received a copy from NetGalley.

reference_books.title: Lock & Mori (Lock & Mori, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
If you like your Sherlock Holmes with a side of romance then this is for you. Sherlock and Mori make an interesting pair because they're both highly intelligent, complicated, and socially awkward. I think they are good together (and in some ways good for each other and in other ways not), but for two people who are so awkward it wasn't entirely believable how quickly they got together. But I let it slide because the characters feel very real. 
 The first half of this novel focuses heavily on the romance and moves a little slowly, but the second half is ALL about the murder mystery, so the pace picks up and the book gets a whole lot more interesting. BUT I had one big issue with the murder mystery: it wasn't a mystery at all who was killing all those people! ITS SO FREAKING OBVIOUS WHO'S DOING IT! Like come on! How does no one see this?! How does Sherlock, who's so good at deducing, not see it? It boggles the mind. Despite that, the book is a solid-ish read.

The romance between Simon and Baz goes from hate to love and you root for them the whole time. My main problem with the novel was the magic. book_a.user_review:
So this wasn't horrible, but I found everything about this book annoying. None of the characters are likable, the story feels unemotional and choppy, and it just falls flat for me. Kate bothered me so much. She's an intelligent person and yet she keeps getting in trouble at work because she doesn't know how to talk to the kids or their parents. I get that she's honest and a bit coarse, but nowhere else does she seem obtuse except for at work. I don't get it. Pyotr is the only one I found moderately interesting, but most of the time he's a jerk and verges on being completely sexist. And Kate, who is supposed to be brutally honest, for some reason just goes along which this. Really? And Bunny was so infuriating I wish I could reach into the pages and slap her. 
 I'll grant that this book has a bit of humor and the characters do get better by the end...a bit, but the story has no depth or emotion, so it didn't feel like that much changed. Which makes the story feel almost useless. 
 And the fact that Anne Tyler hates Shakespeare, especially The Taming of the Shrew angers me so much. Why would you redo a story you hate? (Obviously in her eyes to make it better.) But I feel to truly create a good retelling you should appreciate (and like!) the original tale. 
 Sorry but this was a dud for me. *goes off to watch 10 Things I Hate About You because it's a better retelling*

sample_reviews.review_text: Loved the Shakespeare play. Loved 10 things I hate about you. This is probably the worst adaptation I've experienced as it seems to celebrate all that is chauvinistic about the source material while missing out on some of the fun of it.

For many women, The Taming of the Shrew is just not amusing, even when wrapped up in the gossamer gloss of an MGM musical. What damn fool of a man thinks he will humiliate a headstrong woman and, as a consequence, make her think he's wonderful? 
 There is an interpretation of the play -- that instead of being played as a comedy, this is supposed to be an example of what women were expected to be in Shakespeare's time and, as such, is a portrayal that champions women's rights. That doesn't explain Kate's turnabout. Her long speech at the end advising wives to be gentle with their husbands does not speak of women's rights or an individual's rights, a speech given for her husband to win a wager about whose wife is most obedient. 
 There also is an interpretation that Petruchio doesn't know how to handle the attraction he feels for Kate any more than he understands how to fit into society. It still doesn't explain the cruelty. Inept and boorish are not synonyms. And if he is lashing out at her because she stands up to him, out of pride, how can that be a character worth falling for? 
 The latest version of the play is Anne Tyler's Vinegar Girl, part of the Hogarth series of novelizations of the plays. 
 In this modern-day setting, Kate's research scientist father is still the one who decides she will marry. But this time it's his Russian orphan assistant whose visa is running out. So now we've got both The Taming of the Shrew and the old marriage of convenience plot. 
 Her father is clumsy going about this. He's so obvious that Kate is at first oblivious, then aghast, at the idea. Pyotr is no better. He's introduced as a well-meaning, hapless sort, more the secondary male lead that Cary Grant gets the better of. No one except Kate even pronounces his name correctly. But Pyotr believes in her father's work and wants to stay there. 
 Kate decides might as well marry Pyotr so he can get a green card. She's not doing much beyond running her father's house as he wishes (including the weekly making of a meat mash that is served for the entire week) and working as a preschool assistant (where she tells the four-year-olds that the tomato sauce and pasta lunch smells like wet dog). She's prickly and unfulfilled. 
 The plot takes on screwball comedy tropes, including little sister's endless stream of tutors and her habit of ending sentences with question marks when men are near. The end goes full would-be Preston Sturges. 
 The tack Tyler takes is that this Kate is a "vinegar girl", that instead of trying to attract more flies with honey than vinegar, she doesn't know why anyone would want to attract flies. Her Kate also has an "aha" moment about her husband-to-be when she decides he is trying to fit in, just like she is trying to fit in, and neither one has been very good about it until they try to fit together. 
 That could be a nice enough sentiment, but it's a hard slog to get there with the green card marriage of convenience, a daft father who thinks he can control others' lives -- and then gets away with it, and a would-be hero who remains unformed. 
 Other titles in the Hogarth series include The Gap of Time by Jeanette Winterson, a retelling of The Winter's Tale, and My Name is Shylock by Howard Jacobson, who has co-written Shakespeare's Magnanimity: Four Tragic Heroes, Their Friends and Families. Margaret Atwood is contributing Hag-seed, a retelling of The Tempest. 
 Vinegar Girl doesn't work. Its source material has a great deal to do with that. Even the ad campaign for this novel that asks "if a thoroughly modern woman like Kate can ever be tamed", which shows that no matter how a story gets updated, if its core is rotten it remains rotten.

This a charming, bingeable romance, great for reading all at once while on vacation when exhausted from sightseeing (one could imagine). Often falls short in its examination of gender politics and social norms around marriage, which is really all I want from a Taming of the Shrew retelling, but truly a sweet story nonetheless!
Wonderful retelling.

Oh my, I think I hated almost every minute of this book? I did not like the main character and I found the plot to be insanely mundane and dull. I've never read The Taming of the Shrew so possible could be something that took away from my reading experience. I found Kate to be an incredibly unlikeable character. Pyotr is honestly the only character that I enjoyed because had some funny lines. Most of the characters were extremely one dimensional and almost like caricatures of real people. Ugh, I was so annoyed the. whole. time. For some reason I thought this was going to be a thought provoking read and it was essentially lame chick lit. If anything, I think it was the opposite of thoughtful and relied on a lot of gender stereotyping. Ugh, I want a refund on the time I spent on this book.
This is supposed to be a modern interpretation of The Taming of the Shrew. I didn't really enjoy it. The plot seemed thin and the characters - and character development - unbelievable.

I was really excited to read this title, as I love Shakespeare and had not read any Anne Tyler and was looking forward to reading my first. However, Vinegar Girl was somewhat disappointing - it felt unsatisfying and unfinished, as if Anne Tyler had gotten the commission and then just phoned it in. I understand that Anne Tyler is purported to be a master of the internal and middle-class family tension, and indeed, a lot of Kate's internal monologues were stellar; however, in the rest of the book, it seemed like she was bogged down by the framework of Taming of the Shrew, and was more focused on preserving those parallels than crafting her own interpretation of the story. The ending in particularly came completely out of left field and fell flat (it can be argued that the ending of Shrew does the same thing, but isn't the point of adaptation to make the story your own?) I am still looking forward to the rest of the Hogarth Shakespeare series, but this one in particular was just not for me - although I am sure that Anne Tyler fans will find a lot to love in it.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Cute book, expected the ending

Intelligent young woman goes from being controlled by her father to being controlled by some goofball she marries in order for him to get a green card and continue working for her father. After her initial resistance, she ends up in love with him. Faithful-ish to the Shakespeare, I guess, but is this really a theme for the twenty-first century?

I normally adore Anne Tyler but this one just didn't do it for me. The book was plot-driven and thus lacked Tyler's usual wonderful character development. Bunny and the father were just annoying, and I didn't really care for Kate--she seemed malleable for someone who was supposed to be strong-willed. Her last minute speech on how hard things are for men was a little abrupt and off-putting too. I did like Pyotr, and the symbolism of Kate and Pyotr standing side-by-side in the end was nice, but I was disappointed that those warm, interesting moments were few and far between.

The multiple POVs are okay and I even had fun reading thoughts from a Squirrel! but it's just a bit hard to believe that all of these people are conspiring and secretly shipping this particular couple. It's all kinds of weird and cute at the same time. I'm really sorry.

'A Little Something Different' was a fun, cute book. It's not super clever or all that different, despite the title, but it's really NICE. If you're looking for a sweet holiday or weekend read that's lightweight and throwaway, then this is for you. If not, you'll probably find this book somewhat glib and contrived. I enjoyed it for what it is; it's very much a 3-star read.

I read the description for this book and I was really anticipating it, it sounded like a unique and very interesting way to tell a romance! 
 Nope. I made it through Chapter one by sheer dint of will. Chapter one consists of no less than ten different, first person POV, including the fucking park bench. And frankly all the voices sounded so much alike, it was hard to tell who the hell "I" was without going back up to decipher the name from the curly font (whoever picked that typography...). 
 I was expecting each chapter to be a different -- and for the love of all that's wordy, there are mechanics to writing! -- third person POV on the love story, which would have been cool.

 If you want a cheesy, so cute it makes you squeal with giddy glee book, you need to read this book. 
 If you want a great relaxing beach read, you need to read this book. 
 I kid you not y'all, I read this book in three hours. Yes, I was on vacation and yes, I was on the beach but this book is a ridiculous, over the top cute book. 
 My friend, Liz, was the one who gifted this book to me and I was interested by how this book would read. It's not once told from the POV of the main characters but everyone else involved in their lives. From friends to baristas at the local Starbucks, to a love obsessed college professor to a squirrel (yes, a squirrel). The best thing I can say about this book is it's a feel good book. It makes you smile and squirm because you want Gabe and Lea to end up together but there's always something in their way. This book will have you standing on your feet cheering for them. I also threw the book across the room from frustration with them as well.
