reference_books.title: Taken by Storm (Raised by Wolves, #3)
reference_books.review_text: OK so I'm only giving this one three stars. Not because I didn't like it, not because I don't like the characters (cause I love Bryn and Chase, and everybody), and not because I didn't like the plot. It's because the book didn't really matter as far as the progression of the series goes. Sure Bryn continues to learn to be alpha. She faces tough choices with dier consequences. This one truly tore at my heart strings and I cried like a baby. However Bryn still doesn't become a werewolf. We were left thinking at the end of book two that it was coming. It was really disappointing that she stayed human this whole book. I also wanted to see more of her and Chase together in this book. I mean he's her mate but I feel like hes hardly in the book at all. I mean he'll get mentioned in a sentence that was in the room but thats it. Then when Bryn starts thinking about all these moments they've shared together I keep thinking when did this happen? Why don't we hear about how he still sneaks in her room at night? Overall I've loved this series this book was one of the ones I was most looking forward too this year. And if theres another one I will be buying it the day it comes out just like this one cause I do love these characters. I can't wait to get to know werewolf Bryn cause I have a feeling she going to be amazingly bad ass.

book_a.title: Touch (Denazen, #1)
book_a.user_review: Good plot, good characters, altogether entertaining. I was a little disappointed in the synopsis of book two though debating reading it.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I'm not going to lie...I totally picked this book for the cover. Have any of you out there ever watched the television series Roswell? Well if you have you might have noticed the same thing I did... 
 That's right...Max! (Played by Jason Behr.) I seriously believe that if a movie deal is made for this book that Jason Behr should play Kale. I would definitely pay to see that! So yeah...there's my confession...laugh at me if you will. 
 Now on to the review! 
 This book was absolutely amazing! If it wasn't for Divergent already stealing that place in my heart, I think Touch would be my top read of 2011. But it still has the much honoured place of runner-up (as far as I am concerned). 
 The story kind of reminded me up a mash-up between X-Men and Heroes (a television series I adore). In fact...if you know the series at all then you might understand my next comment. There is a neat character in Touch that seriously reminds me of Sylar from Heroes. If you have watched the series, and have read the book, tell me if you thought the same thing. 
 This book had some fabulous characters, both main and supporting. I cared about almost each and every one of them. I didn't want anything bad to happen to any of them (except those one or two really nasty ones of course). I fell in love with Kale instantaneously. His naivety and tenderness shine through despite everything he has been trained to believe and do. This provides the appropriate direct opposite to the female lead, Dez, who is a fiery young woman hell-bent on making her father's life a living Hell as much as possible. At first Dez annoyed me a bit with her out-of-control attitude and constant use of foul language. Over time I discovered the reasons behind her actions and was able to grow and mature along with here throughout each and every page, and it was a journey well worth taking. (And I'd do it again in a heartbeat.) 
 I also appreciate that the authour didn't feel it necessary to hold us hostage with a nasty cliffhanger to get us to read the next book in the series. To tell you the truth, I give way more credit to the authors who can make me want to read the next book(s) in their series without leaving me in a gut-wrenching "Oh my God what next!" kind of spot. So kudos to Jus Accardo. She is one of the few who have gotten this right!

This review is also posted at http://sychofaeriesbookobsession.blog... 
 Maybe it's just because I have been watching the show recently, but in a way it reminded me of the show Heroes. Certain people have a genetic mutation of a certain chromosome which gives them an ability. There are ones who can mimic people and things, have a touch of death, control elements, tell when you are lying, telekinesis, soul jumpers, etc. There are the ones who were born that way and the ones who were amped up by doctors when they were infants or before they were born. So yeah, if you have ever watched Heroes you can see why they remind me of each other. With all that being said, I still really liked the book. Dez and Kale made a good couple, there is just the right about of back-stabbing to keep you from guessing exactly what is going to happen next. Then you are left at the end, wondering if Dez is going to go crazy in the next couple of months. I will be reading and reviewing book 2 'Toxic' soon.

"TOUCH" BY JUS ACCARDO 
 Amazing! This book, start to finish was one of the finest pieces of young adult genre literature that I have had the honor of reading in quite some time. To be quite honest I have been constantly disappointed in some of the more popular writers abilities at conveying the truth of teenage emotion. A lot of times the realities of how they would act in certain situations, the moods that are so viable at this time in their lives were never really shown as if the author had a disconnection with the characters and couldn't describe them properly. More importantly this book had me saying "pfft, X-Men who?" The "Sixes" are an obscure group of mutant teenagers that are being captured by the Denazen group in order to use their abilities in negative ways. When Kale meets the daughter of the ring leader by accident, Dez learns that her father is not who he seems to be at all and really the enemy. 
 This is only the beginning of one of the most exciting adventures I've read in quite a while and I simply could not stop reading. I felt like E.T. following that seemingly never-ending trail of Reese's Pieces to get to the large bag of chocolate, peanut butter filled goodness at the end! So my analysis' are somewhat crazy, I know but my point is that Jus Accardo is definitely going to go far with her writing. 
 For an older woman that loves YA fiction of all types, even Stephenie Meyers "Twilight" Series did not have me near as impressed nor as excited to read more as this book does. That was another thing I loved about this book, the relationship between Dez and Kale had far more passion than so many other couples in other YA books I've read. The intense emotional draw was real, not something designed by societies acceptance of "how to go far without going too far." 
 Keep writing Jus! I'm waiting patiently for the next one! 
 Kitty Bullard / Great Minds Think Aloud / http://www.greatmindsliterarycommunit... 
 Read more: http://www.greatmindsthinkaloud.probo...

The concept and plot were both a bit cliche',there I said it.Pretty much the same abilities and character backgrounds are used in paranormal movies.But,I enjoyed it as hell so I'm gonna give it 4 stars. 
 Dez...that girl is an awesome bitch till the very end,though a bit gullible at times but I think i'll make the same choices in her shoes. 
 Kale is an innocent yet strong character whose view of normal world is amusing and sweet.The romance in this book is hands down adorable,an added perk to all the action and suspense.

There are a lot of things to admire about TOUCH, the first book in Accardo's Denazen books. Our main character, Deznee Cross is a sassy, quick-witted girl who takes no gruff and gives (almost) as good as she gets. Dez is brassy and just this side of reckless, just mature enough to make you believe (most of) her actions, but still with that hint of vulnerability that teenagers often have. Dez wants everything the world is offering, that's pretty much how you can sum up her character. She has her problems with it, but by in large she wants to experience everything life has to offer with very little worry about the future. 
 Kale, the catalyst for everything, by comparison was very inexperienced. He didn't understand some pretty common sense things and genuinely found interest in the ordinary, everyday things we take for granted (DVD's, pictures, music). Their juxtaposed ideas about life make for an intriguing and engaging way to understand the book's world. 
 Action is never in short supply either. Accardo gives a definite feeling of energy and urgency, though there comes a point when I started feel exhausted and wondered where Dez and Kale got their energy from. Every stumbling block they overcome is hiding an even bigger one which inevitably is hiding an even bigger one. Dez's judgement at times also seemed atypical for her. Not quite out of character or extraordinarily weird, but definitely worth pausing over and wondering if given a bit more time she would have come to a better solution. The tense pace of the plot also left me sometimes overwhelmed trying to keep up. During a scene between Dez and her father I swept right by it without really seeing it. It was only after I re-read it I realized how important the interaction was the central plot of the series. 
 I appreciated that Accardo kept the romance age-appropriate, especially given Dez's experience vs. Kale's inexperience. This never strays into the squick area or tries to emulate the bodice-ripper romances without the explicitness; the romance feels genuine, feels like a natural progression. There's a little competition for Dez's affection, but Accardo makes it pretty obvious how things are meant to end up. 
 In the end I enjoyed the novel and I'm looking forward to reading the next adventure Dez goes through, though I sincerely hope that the intensity of the novel dials down a bit. I'm not used to having to catch my mental breath at the end of a novel. 
 (originally this review appeared on Night Owl Teen)

Plenty of people have written what's on my mind when it comes to this book.So I'll try and make this quick. 
 I wasn't expecting great life changing literature. I knew I'd be in an awkward situation today (Yeah Passover) and I wanted something nice and entertaining to read. That's about what I got so I can not really complain. That's not going to stop me. 
 The plot is weak. It's a series of unrelated events. Things just happen with no logic behind them. It's so predictable. Of course, there's also insta love and an attempt at a love triangle. Lovely young adult. 
 The characters are ok, I guess. I liked how Kale was written. Dez was ok. I didn't really connect with her. She felt forced, like the author was trying too hard to make her quirky, cute, and rebellious. Not my type of character. Pretty flat too. 
 I recommend this book for entertainment. It's cute and doesn't really require much thinking. Next to some of the other books in the paranormal romance ya world it's pretty good.

AH-MAY-ZEEE-ING!!! I want more!! :) 
 See my review at Two Chicks On Books 
 I was intrigued by the idea of this book. It reminds me a bit of the X-Men and that's cool with me. I found out about this book one day by stalking Net Galley and it sounded interesting so I requested it and was delighted to be approved. 
 On to my thoughts about this debut novel: I have to say that it was one of my favorites this year. The plot is fast moving and action-packed. The characters were likeable, some are loveable and sometimes they even have that love-to-hate quality about them. I also loved that it didn't leave me in one of those pull-out-my-hair-scream-'til-I'm-deaf cliffhangers. Ms. Accardo ties things up nicely but still leaves you wanting more. 
 I really love the names that were chosen for the characters, too: Dez, Kale, Dax and Alex. Not only do they have brilliant names but these characters were full of awesomesauce. 
 Let's start with Dez, she's one kick-ass chick. She's not afraid to do what she wants when she wants to, no matter that it drives her father crazy. I loved her for it. I like a little rebellion in my heroines and no one does it better than Dez. She totally stands up for what she believes is right. 
 Kale is super HAWT, super sweet, super amazing guy. The thing that I love about him so much is his innocence and his primal desire to protect Dez. I don't want to say too much and spoil the book for you but believe me...he's so worth the praise. 
 Alex and Dax were awesome supporting characters and I am looking forward to getting to know them better in the next couple of books. I hear that we'll definitely be seeing more of Dax. YAY!! 
 There are also a few very nasty, very despicable villains that you'll just love to hate. I've seen some wicked villains but the ones in this novel are as atrocious and evil as they come. 
 Here's a little sample of the awesomeness that is TOUCH: 
 "He sat up straight, eyes wide, and touched the tip of his index finger to his cheek. "What was that?" 
 I blushed. "A kiss." 
 "That's what a kiss feels like?" 
 "Well, technically. There are a lot of different types of--" 
 "Show me." 
 "Show you what?" 
 "Show me some other kinds." 
 "You're asking me to kiss you?" 
 So don't delay any longer, go buy TOUCH now. You can find it at Amazon, Barnes & Noble or ask for it at your local bookstore.

The first thing that was very noticeable about this story was the voice of the main character. She is very spunky, active and strong spoken. There was nothing about her that I didn't like. She meets the male love interest within the first couple of pages. Kale has just escaped from Denazen where he was being used by the company for the powers that his touch has on others. Since Kale has been raised in the facility and it is all he knows, the outside world is completely new and his character is very naive and because of his powers he is tip toed around like a ticking bomb. The contrast between the two and the relationship that they build together was as much based on friendship as it was companionship. Sure, there are some pretty heavy and hot make out scenes but no complaints here! 
 The story is action packed and takes on from the first chapter. Deznee is very much a dare-devil and emotional button pusher. ( I mean she does things on purpose to get a reaction from people.) She speaks her mind and does whatever she wants. Kale is her opposite, although he has the power to kill, because of where he was raised his emotions are very guarded scared. I got the feeling that Kale felt more emotionally as the protector in the relationship, even though Dez acted more like it. Hope that makes sense, Kale was guarded because of his past, but Dez is more carefree and willing to make sacrifices for what she believes in. 
 After Dez saves Kale she takes him home and he tells her a story about her father that Dez although thinks it's far-fetched believes him without too much convincing. Her father has been putting on a charade of being a lawyer but the firm that he is running has nothing to do with what she always assumed. When her father comes home armed with a gun ready to kill Kale, the two run. 
 This is one of those books where I used the term "I could not put it down" there were amazing weaved plot twists, unforseen adventures and something everyone wishes for in a series, no cliffhanger. 
 This is one of the most unique stories I have read in a long time. The idea of the Sixes (people with powers) and the abilities they have were very imaginative and well blended, they just seemed to make sense and really belonged in the story. I have read books this year with teens that have powers (White Cat by Holly Black) but it's a spin on the old concept of superhumans/superheros/villans etc. One that I think the Young Adult world could use more of. 
 Just when you think that the story is going to go one way, it goes another. Right when you think they are going to get away, they don't. Right when you think that they are onto something, they got stumped. And the best part of all, nobody is who you think they are. 
 I think this story was told masterfully and it's over long before your ready for it to be.
it was good. everything was happening so fast, maybe too fast, bt it was also filled with action which was great.

There are some great reviews of this book, which is why I decided to read it in the first place. This is not one of those. 
 The summary of Touch pretty much summarizes the first few pages of the book. The plot moves way to fast to make up for lack of everything else. There was no character development, no setting description, just action action action. This got confusing at times cause there were not many transition movements. Characters could be in one place, then suddenly another or a random person could suddenly appear- and did, frequently. 
 I couldn't stand Dez, the main character. She was supposed to be this tough skateboard girl, but instead of tough she came off and reckless and incredibly stupid. Even tough skateboard girls can know when to be sweet to get what they want. Dez obviously did not. 
 The love interest,Kale, was like a child. He didn't understand anything about the world (vase, DVD, candy) but also didn't understand anything philosophical (justice, love). Some things Dez would attribute to Kale's obliviousness that were just Kale being inconsiderate or stupid. (Take telling Alex about the relationship) . 
 Interesting (though overused) idea, but I won't be reading the rest of the series.

sample_reviews.review_text: WTF?

Warning: It contains minor spoilers 
 I read Taking Chances by Molly McAdams as a recommendation and I have to say is the only book this year that I have to give a one star review to. The story synopsis was interesting enough to have me opening the book and although it had some bumps along the way it kept me going until 3/4 down the book. After my disappointment I read some others reviews to see if anybody share my concerns and what I found was interesting. Let's take this review by parts shall we: 
 The main population complaint is the main character pregnancy body type and while I most say is something not commonly view is plausible, in the other hand that military brat status is a joke. There is not decent military unit out there that would allow a kid to be on daddy's office all day, everyday there are regulations against that. Moving on to the money issues there is no, I repeat NO minimum wage job that after working it for six years even if you do not spend any of it will allow you to be "loaded". Taking care of those fantasy issues I will move to the actual story. 
 Most of the characters seem immature, conceited, full of themselves, unreal with unrealistic attitude towards situations and underdeveloped. Then when you think the story is finally going somewhere she goes ahead and kills the one character she bother to develop enough for the reader to connect with. If you were going for shock value maybe just kill one you didn't invest so much into while ignoring the ones you did left alive. To top it off the situations the characters are put in seem force and totally unnatural. I couldn't even stomach to completely read the book. I scheme the last couple of chapters. I felt disconnected from the story and an effort to just keep going. In my opinion save you the heartache and don't read the book.

What happened? Seriously. Gawd sorry but this book is awful. It's too good to be true. I just flip through pages just so I can finish the damn thing. Coz I can't not finish a book again! Not going there again. My patience really was tested with this book. It feels like my time was wasted. The story is like a beaded rubber bracelet stretched so hard it snapped and the beads are all over the place. It's too shallow and it's like the author didn't gave her full effort writing it. I'm sorry for saying that but that was just what I think. 
 I still gave it 2 stars since I'm a sucker for understanding guys like Brandon. He's every girl's dream guy. I don't think what he did can happen in real life. I dunno. Every time you will look to that child it will be a living reminder of what the bitch did. I just don't get her. It's just too damn impossible. I don't get it. Ugh

I would give Taking Chances 4.5 stars, I would of gave it 5 stars but some things did not play out the way I wanted them to. As others stated in their reviews, this was a roller coaster ride for your emotions. You go from happy, sad, angry and shocked throughout the book.  It was a page turner and I read through it pretty fast. There was some things that were unrealistic but also some really tough things that Harper had to go through. Holy cow!! This was an emotional roller-coaster! It could have been two books, it was mix of Beautiful Disaster, Thoughtless and Effortless, but it had its own twist. Wow! I almost stopped reading, it ripped my heart out! Glad I kept going!!
I loved this book so much in thw beginning!! However, towards the end of the book it was very unrealistic... how could ever think work out soo perfectly with little to no problem.
I really enjoyed this book. Good characters, it was a fast read. The drama just kept coming at you though, but written in a way to carry the emotions.

While entertaining, light, and generally fun, this book rates pretty low for me. Harper wasn't always a likable protagonist. In times of stress, her reactions were irrational and immature. Her reaction to seeing the pictures Amanda sent Brandon was childish, and I found myself silently screaming at her to think things through. Instead, Harper's childish reaction was to run away. This happened nearly every time she got upset, which was frustrating for me as a reader. 
 I found it really difficult to relate to Harper's financial situation too. It was far-fetched and idealistic. I fought for where I am now. I went to college with the intention of receiving a degree I could use to establish a career. Even now, I can't just have everything I want to have. I can't go out and pay cash for a brand-new Expedition. I don't know many people who can. This made it really hard to believe Harper's lifestyle. 
 The relationships in this story are a little too perfect. Brandon is about as perfect as a person can be. He's gorgeous, strong, sweet, and kind. He's flawless. The only time he makes a mistake is near the end when he fights after Harper asks him not to. This isn't real. I was rooting for Chase the whole time.

reference_books.title: The Rosie Project (Don Tillman, #1)
reference_books.review_text: This was an easy read, some giggling when you recognize someone from your entourage but certainly not a classic or book to generate thoughtful discussion. It is the book for my book club in April, not sure what we will talk about.

reference_books.title: Left Neglected
reference_books.review_text:
This is a selection for my Muse & Views Book Club . I will admit that I had a hard time putting the book down (closing my e-book to be precise) so it certainly interested me. However, I found that the only character that was well developed is Sarah. I would have enjoyed reading about her husband's and mother's thoughts and more about how they coped with Sarah's brain damage effects. We get a little insight into her mother's but little about her husband's. It would also have been interesting to read about Sarah's interaction with other patients at the rehab centre. 
 I might pick up Still Alice to compare the writing style from her first novel and this one.

reference_books.title: Testimony
reference_books.review_text: I have read several of Anita Shreve's novels and this is definitely not my favourite. The style she chose of writing each chapter from one of the character's perspective, sometimes in the first person, sometimes in the third person didn't work for me. I found it choppy and sometimes it took me a few sentences to figure out what character was present in a chapter. I have to admit the storyline was not particularly appealing to me either and I can't say I warmed up to any of the characters, not even Silas or Anna. It won't keep me from reading other Anita Shreve novels but this one is not a winner.

reference_books.title: Notes from a Small Island
reference_books.review_text: This was a book club read. I enjoyed the first 25% but then to me, it got repetitive. Not my cup of tea as an interesting book. Maybe if I had spent a year or so in Great Britain some of the people and places he described would have been more interesting for me.

reference_books.title: Orphan Train
reference_books.review_text: Easy read. I enjoyed the book and learned about Orphan trains that I did not know existed. Everything is tied up in a nice ribbon at the end, no loose ends. Several members of my Book Club will enjoy that.

book_a.title: The 100 Year-Old Man Who Climbed Out the Window and Disappeared
book_a.user_review: Waste of time.

sample_reviews.review_text: As much as it was meant to be farcical it was equal parts monotonous and long! Thought it would never end! Much repetition, and the writing was at times simplistic if not tedious. I don't understand why it became such a big hit.

By all the rules of the life I live, and maybe most of us, Allan Karsson should have lived a stunted life instead of the fascinating one he did live. The story seemed most improbable but in spite of that it was one that I read slowly, enjoying it immensely throughout and laughed much more at the antics of the characters that I have for a long time. What a great book I thought to read when one's spirit needs a little tender loving care, and thus the read was good medicine too. 
 I also liked the interplay between the serious (e.g. Stalin) and the comedic, it was interesting how Jonas Jonasson, perhaps as the well-read and seasoned journalist that he is, took his readers through an unusual journey through a modern history of the world.. I am convinced that the book though could easily entertain a child as a bedtime story as much as The Neverending Story might, because the story was so well and so simply told and was great fun throughout: it is twenty-nine chapters, most of which are short followed by an epilogue, with the first and last chapter being near-duplicates of one another. 
 On the serious side, we are getting older, on average, and yet we have outstanding seniors everywhere, such as Hazel McCallion, who's been the mayor of Mississauga, a large suburb west of Toronto, for thirty-four years and is going strong. Perhaps in a way, as light-hearted as the story was, it was an ode to all things old and new. 
 Edwin

So many good reviews! 
 Which is why got my money back. 
 I never do that. 
 Sometimes you just know after 30 pages...

Hilarious book about a 100-year-old man who crawls out of the Nursing Home window and goes on many adventures involving, but not limited to: murder, elephants, and robbery. 
 The chapters about what's going on with Allan (the old man) now, at age 100, are interspersed with chapters about his many adventures in the past as an explosives expert. In his extensive worldwide travels he meets and befriends Franco, Stalin, Mao Tse-Tung, Presidents Truman and Johnson, Churchill, etc. etc. 
 I love the bare-bones style Jonasson uses in this book, which reminds me of my beloved Karin Fossum. 
 I also admire Allan's constant laissez-faire attitude about everything. He just goes with the flow and it usually works out to his advantage. I adore chill men, and I loved reading about this guy - he was like the epitome of chill. 
 I laughed while reading this book. 
 This book is sort of a fairytale for adults - it reminded me of THE MOUSE THAT ROARED, which is also a sort of adult fairytale in my opinion. 
 June 2014: The REAL 100-year-old man who climbed out the window and disappeared: Link in Spanish: http://www.bbc.co.uk/mundo/ultimas_no... 
 Link in English: http://abcnews.go.com/International/b...

(3.5/5) 
 The very best description of this book I have heard was a Swedish version of Forrest Gump (I will add, with a lot more Vodka). One-hundred-year-old Allen disappears from his retirement home on what most people would call the adventure of a life-time - but Allen has had many adventures, ones that have had significant impacts on world events throughout the last 100 (or so) years. 
 This story is the final response to a boring (and Vodka-less) life in 'piss-covered slippers'. Allen is enduring and kind of annoying at the same time. He is oblivious to the world around him and always tries to do the right thing, or at least the polite thing. His entire life is seeking comfort and friends - which is the one thing he finds at the end of his life. 
 This book is a cute, light read - I spent a lot of it smiling.
Is there a worse plot device than the coincidence?

Full disclosure--I read this on a cruise with a drink package that allowed me to have (I'm not kidding) 15 drinks a day. All with parasols if I wanted! And I'm no Swede or Finn (who allegedly in this book can hold their liquor the best). 
 So I must admit, I couldn't really follow most of Allen's life and just read everything at face value. I got some of the "Bucket" and "Bolt" characters mixed up, but since they come to the same fate at the end that didn't take away anything. Taken that way it was a fun read, although the Swedes were so dry in their humor it seemed British. 
 I loved the typo in the Bible! And Allen really did live happily ever after. (I can't believe a nursing home director would forbid booze--really, what other pleasures do you have at that point. Is this usual? Maybe that explains all the old seniors on cruises!)

I so wanted to love this book. Look at how cute the cover is! And the title! But...that's as far as the cute goes. I did not like the main character, the 100-year-old man. It's hard to enjoy a novel about a 100-year-old man if you do not like said centenarian. Especially if he goes about cavalierly mucking up other peoples' lives, not to mention accidentally murdering a few. What fun! (Sarcasm; I can't help it). 
 The book shifts from the present to the 100-year-old man's past, which I found as tedious to read about as the present circumstances. I didn't care what would happen to the characters, and I cared even less about what had happened to them in the past. 
 The title says it all. You just read the story, and the mystery of what happens after he disappears will be much better in your imagination than what actually happens.

I don't know about you, but every once in a while I crave a book that's a bit, well, ridiculous. Not in the I-can't-believe-this-got-published sense, but rather in the Ha!-I-can't-believe-someone-thought-of-that sense. 
 I have some novels on my bookshelves that can satisfy that craving, but I'm always on the lookout for something new. Then, one day, I came across The 100-Year-Old Man Who Climbed Out the Window and Disappeared. Honestly, the title alone had me thinking this was probably a novel I would enjoy. And once I read the summary, I knew that I had found a book I needed to read. 
 The 100-Year-Old Man starts with an introduction to Allan Karlsson, a man who, as you may have guessed, has recently turned 100 years old. The old folks' home Allan lives in is preparing for his birthday party, but Allan wants no part of it. His solution to the problem is to climb out his window, leading to a journey filled with criminals, an elephant, and a whole lot of money. 
 But a major aspect of the novel is also Allan's past. You see, Allan hasn't lead any ordinary life. He's an explosions expert - a career that has led him to experience life in just about every corner of the globe. And Jonasson describes these events in such an interesting way, too; they way he mixes Allan's life with actual pieces of history makes the stories almost believable. 
 Although the novel took a bit of getting used to (the format is a bit different than most), I ended up loving The 100-Year-Old Man. The voice, in particular, was extremely entertaining. The way it casually discusses some of what happens (for example, certain deaths and Allan's encounters with some rather historical figures) is fantastic. 
 Speaking of which, I have to take a moment to talk about the characters. While they are, in some ways, completely outlandish, they also have a lot of very real, very relatable personality traits.  Finally, the "Halloween"-like resurrection of the evildoer, is just a ploy to drag us all along to part 2. Disappointing. As is the male character's mental breakdown at the end. Cliche. 
 Where was the father in all this? He had no clue what was happening in his own house? For nearly a decade? What about her friends, teachers, coworkers, neighbors, mailmen, etc? It is all too tidy.

This was better than the third book, but filled with a lot more adult themes than the first three. This is, essentially, because the girls have left high school and separated and moved on to start their lives as adults. The book is different from the others at the start. The Pants ritual is no longer as sacred and official as it's been in previous books, and is missing Carmen. The girls are in college. Carmen is helping with set design in the theater and is no longer as glamorous and attention-seeking as she was a year ago. She accompanies a "friend" to a theater in Vermont and ends up being interested in acting. Tibby's trademark sarcasm is set to full force throughout most of this book, particularly at her job. However, much of the book delves into her thoughts about Brian and about the situation she's in. Lena finds a new love interest in her art class and gets involved with that. Bridget goes to a archaological dig in Turkey and becomes interested in an older married man. 
 Carmen is usually the most likeable character, and sometimes the most realistic one. I think she should have had an interest in acting way before this fourth book, though, because it felt a little out of the blue. Also she never seemed to have a specific interest like the other girls did. I liked that the main interest of her story didn't have to do with her getting together with someone. Tibby's story was interesting too. I wanted to shake her during most of the book, but at the same time her situation is understandable. It showed a pretty dark side of college life. Bee was sort of funny. It was refreshing for her to have a new love interest besides Eric, however the whole time the relationship felt weird and skeevy. Sometimes it seems like the older these girls get, the younger Bee seems compared to the rest of them. She's still a mental teenager around the 30 year old love interest. Lena! She too finds a new love interest, in an art class, but of course Kostos has to come marching in and I am thinking, Enough, please! It's the fourth book! I feel like all the readers are tired of Kostos and it would be nice to have just one book where he doesn't appear, physically or in Lena's mind. this book was a great conclusion to this emotional and deep series of girl friendship books.

reference_books.title: Such a Pretty Fat: One Narcissist's Quest to Discover If Her Life Makes Her Ass Look Big, or Why Pie Is Not the Answer
reference_books.review_text:
The WORST book I have ever read, without exception. What a slog. It was like being tortured. The only reason I continued to read to the end is because I was completely incredulous that the book could actually get continually worse (& it did, OH how it did). 
 I stand in awe that Jen Lancaster could actually have gotten published. I have lost faith in American publishing if this manure could be published by any respectable publishing house. 
 I usually don't buy books, but I'd been recommended this one on amazon & later saw it on the bookshelf at Barnes & Noble & snagged it on impulse. Oh my goodness! I gave this woman my money! I am sick to my stomach. 
 The writer (book is written in the first person) is completely unlikeable with no redeemable qualities. Just goes to show you, ladies, ANYONE can get a guy, no matter how odious her personality. For that matter, ANYONE can have a bestseller if this drivel can get published. So get out there & WRITE! 
 I should have known I would have a problem with this author's opinions when she said she wears Crocs. ALL THE TIME. Hold my head somebody. 
 She curses all the time. I believe that people who curse are too ignorant to know the proper words to use, so they just spew obscenities. Jen Lancaster is a perfect example of my theory. 
 She writes about being in shock that she actually sold a book. SHE SHOULD BE! Here's an excerpt: 
 "I know I've done this a couple of times before, but each time a book sells, it feels like a miracle." 
 Yeah! Because it is! A horrible, nightmarish miracle! 
 "I want to call my publisher and ask, 'Are you sure? You're really interested in what I have to say? And you're willing to write me a check to do so? And then you'll put these thoughts - asinine as they may be - and put them in a format that will live on in the Library of Congress forever?' Unbelievable." 
 Yes, Jen! Truly unbelievable! Because this book is garbage. As my dear mother would say, its only use is to line the birdcage. Thank goodness those birds don't know how to read. 
 At one point, the author says she didn't like a personal trainer because she had no sense of humor, which Jen Lancaster defines as someone who doesn't find her funny. All I can say is, she must run into people with no sense of humor A LOT. 
 She also uses words that are not words. My kingdom for an editor! She actually used the non-word "orientated." Oh my goodness! This woman is getting paid for being illiterate. 
 Also, at one point she referred to being on a Caribbean vacation & hearing a "tin drum." She meant a STEEL drum. So not only is the author getting paid for manure, the publisher & editor are, too! 
 I have so much more to say. Just please: Don't read this book. Life is too short to waste on this rubbish.

reference_books.title: What to Expect When You're Expecting
reference_books.review_text: This series of books has to be the biggest "Emperor's New Clothes" swindle in publishing history. They are trash & nothing more. If you're pregnant, get the book The Womanly Art of Breastfeeding. It doesn't just deal with breastfeeding. The "What To Expect" book is just awful, redundant, dumbed-down, & insulting to one's intelligence.

reference_books.title: The Return of the Native
reference_books.review_text: I bailed on this book, the first of Thomas Hardy's I've tried to read. I found it lugubrious & fidgety. I made it to the second part but gave up on it because I was ill & I knew that reading this book when I was well would just remind me of being sick.

reference_books.title: A Most Wanted Man
reference_books.review_text: I would bet that this was a collaboration. Some (few) parts were classic David Cornwell; others are not his style. Not one fully-developed character nor a likeable character. I gave him an extra star because he's John le Carre.

reference_books.title: To Have and Have Not
reference_books.review_text: I'm not a Hemingway girl. I just don't get him. Is he more of a man's writer? I find his writing dated. All the male characters are drunk & hate women. All the women are portrayed as whores. I'm trying to think of one of his characters that I've ever been able to identify with or cheer on. I don't understand why he's considered one of the greatest writers of the 20th century. I think he was made into a martyr after he committed suicide in such a dramatic way.

book_a.title: Murder Past Due (Cat in the Stacks, #1)
book_a.user_review: I can't believe I paid for the Audible version of this book. The word "brandished" is overused.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Man OH Man can a protagonist be more boring then this Charlie Harris??? I think I know who-dunnit.. but seriously: I'm not even going to finish this book to see if I'm right. Total waste of time. 
 Further more+- making a "dog" out of a MainCoon by letting it walk on a leash and making it larger then life is almost insulting. So even the one star is too much.
How can you not love this cat and the librarian he owns?

Diesel makes me want to own a Maine Coon. My Mira would be very jealous if she suspected as she is just an ordinary cat. Diesel is a very sympathetic cat to a troubled boy getting buffeted around by adults closing old accounts with each other in this book. 
 Justin wants to finish college. He is trying to move out from under his doting mother. 
 Julia sees an opportunity to get back at an old lover plus gain a fortune for her son. 
 Except the lover, a famous author, ends up murdered. 
 Except the famous author isn't really who he said he was. 
 And somehow the tangled threads must be unraveled. 
 This is an enjoyable cozy mystery. It is a fast and easy read.
Although this might be to the taste of some it was, for me, unbearably slow and with little real detection at all.

I actually read "Classified as Murder" (the 2nd novel in the A Cat in the Stacks Mystery series) and then read "Murder Past Due" (the 1st novel in the series). 
 This new series is a delight! I love the librarian jargon! 
 Main character Charlie Harris has a wonderful schedule - Working three (3) days a week as a cataloger of the rare book collection at the college library and also answering various reference questions if they are related to a historical aspect of the college or the library's archives and rare books. Charlie also volunteers at the local public library. Another special joy is to read of Charlie's patronage of the town's independent bookstore. 
 As the introduction to the new series characters begins, we also meet Diesel, a Maine Coon cat, originally discovered as a shivering kitten and rescued by Charlie two (2) years ago from the parking lot of the public library. Now everyone in town recognizes Charlie and Diesel as when the two (2) are out walking together, Charlie walks Diesel on a leash and it is rare to see one without the other. 
 They know each other's habits and talk with one another particularly when they are alone. Without a doubt, the descriptions of man and cat convey the unconditional love that comes to one life's after rescuing a kitten. That is not to say that Charlie is master of the house as every cat owner knows that "Dogs have owners" and "Cats have staff". Diesel is no exception and has his needs addressed by favorite friends at various locations in town to his purring bliss. 
 A charming new series and I can't wait to read more of the adventures of Charlie and Diesel! 
 My lower star rating is due to copy edit errors that are distracting to me as a reader. I am hopeful for improvement as the series continues.

Saying that I read this book is a real stretch. I wanted to find out who did it and much to my dismay I had guessed it in the first 82 pages. I read to 101 and just gave up and went to the end. I didn't know why the murdered committed the crime and when I read the end, I didn't care. The main character did not sound like a 50 year old man. He sounded much older and flat. I wanted to read a book about a library and a cat and this didn't deliver either. The premise hooked me and I will 'look' at later books to see if the writing gets any better and see if there are any plots that take place in a library. However, this is not the worst book that I almost read. 
 Bottom line, don't waste your time on this one.

Murder Past Due by Miranda James is a cozy cat mystery that isn't just "too much" as so many of 
 them can be. Diesel is a Maine coon cat with a human named Charlie Harris. Diesel doesn't solve mysteries--he's just a big, lovable cat whose most extraordinary habits is walking around town on a leash, warbling and chirping instead of meowing as other cats do. The mystery solver is Charlie--college librarian and first-time amateur sleuth. Since everyone in Athena, Mississippi knows Charlie, they are more apt to gossip with him than spill what they know to the law. 
 When former classmate, now bestselling novelist Godfrey Priest returns home for an honorary dinner and to donate his papers to his alma mater, he stirs up more trouble than good feelings and someone decides perform a killing review on the author and end his days on the bestseller list for good. There is no shortage of suspects--from Charlie's boss who lost his wife to Godfrey's womanizing ways to Godfrey's half-brother who could have used financial help in the worst way to a possible ghost writer to the bookshop owner who lost a great deal of business when the famous author cancelled a couple of book-signing to an old flame who wound up pregnant years ago and now it looks like Godfrey wants to steal her son's affection. 
 Charlie spends his time in the library's archives and it looks like he'll need to dig in the town's past history to find all the clues necessary to help the sheriff's office solve the mystery of the cancelled author. 
 This is a pleasant cozy mystery. There are a fair amount of clues and enough suspects to distract, although I did pick the culprit out. The plot was still enjoyable and it was interesting meeting the regulars for what looks to be a good series. It's nice to have a "cat mystery" where the the cat is just a cat. He doesn't find the clues; he doesn't point them out to his owner. But he is a lovely addition to the cast. Charlie is an interesting character, but I think I like Diesel even more. 
 First posted on my blog My Reader's Block. Please request permission before reposting. Thanks.

Murder Past Due is a reasonably fun but unremarkable cosy mystery. The main draws would be the cat, Diesel, who is a main character, and the fact that it's set partially in a library. But the cat isn't the detective and isn't the main character, and the library is just where the main character works, so it's not that niche. I didn't find any of the characters or their relationships particularly compelling, though the small-town USA atmosphere was kind of interesting -- I kept being surprised when there were computers and email, because it seemed more old-fashioned than that in terms of the way people related. More Agatha Christie than Val McDermid et al. 
 I was not, however, surprised by the resolution of the mystery. 
 Overall, this was fun brain candy, but I'm in no hurry to read more of the series, and I wouldn't particularly recommend it unless you're a connoisseur of cosy mysteries. 
 Originally posted here.

A great beginning for a new series. Featured are Charlie Harris and his Maine Coon cat, Diesel. Both are well known around the small Mississippi town and the college campus where Charlie works. Will be looking forward to reading more.

Really like this mystery! 
 A while ago, I had tried to read a book with an older (50-ish) main character, and had a VERY hard time getting into the story. But then I started this book, and had no issue with the age of the character. As I read, I figured out why: Charlie Harris is a archivist who lost his wife not to long ago, owns a Maine coon cat, has a young man boarding at his house while going to college, and volunteers at his local library. While he has no immediate family near, he is engaged in his community, has someone to care about (even if it's a cat), and is connected to the world around him. The other character had been so disconnected, the reader could not connect with him. Much more preferable style! 
 The mystery part was fairly good, as well. Lots of potential suspects presented. While there was no 'gasp of surprise' moment, still had enough twists that I enjoyed reading it, and wanted to finish. I will probably find the next book or two and continue reading the series!

sample_reviews.review_text:
It's been a really long time since I've read Stephen King, and I was a huge fanboy in my teens. My "breakthrough" in critical writing was a paper on him my junior year of high school. 
 Anyway, this is an interesting collection of stories. Make no mistake these are disturbing and dark. He even warns you of that...as long as you read the afterword first. But it was very hard to put the book down.

Man, do I love Stephen King! It was refreshing to read a collection of stories by him rather than a 900 page novel for once. His work is always amazingly chilling with characters that haunt you long after you've finished reading.

I bought Full Dark, No Stars at the airport, while waiting for my cross-country red-eye to board. As soon as I got settled on the plane, and those around me began to doze, I turned on my little overhead light and began to read. I didn't stop reading until I had read every short story. I felt like I had just crawled through a dark cave filled with all manner of sludge and slime. The quote "When it came to the dark fuckery of the human heart, there seemed to be no limit." rang like a mantra in my mind. I put the book down in my lap. I didn't want to be inside my head anymore after the dark journey I had just taken. I opened up my window shutter. But the sun hadn't risen yet and all I could see was my own reflection looking back at me like a mirror. My own dark eyes, my own dark thoughts battling to be heard. I quickly closed the shutter. There was nothing out there that could help me. No, not at all. 
 So, I looked around the cabin for some sort of interaction. All of my fellow passengers were still sleeping and there wasn't a flight attendant in sight. I needed something. I was feeling sad and lonely and like I wanted to cry. I blinked back a film of tears and picked the book back up off of my lap. Even though I had read all the stories, there were some pages after that I hadn't read. Maybe something I could use to help me find a way out of this, I thought. I needed help. And Stephen King knew that. Because guess what I found at the end of that book? It was a note, that felt like it had been written just for me. It said: "All right I think we've been down here in the dark long enough. There's a whole other world upstairs. Take my hand Constant Reader and I'll be happy to lead you back into the sunshine. I'm happy to go there because I believe most people are essentially good. I know that I am. It's you I'm not entirely sure of." I read that, and more, and it was in that way that he helped me navigate my way back to the light. 
 I put the book back in my lap and opened the window shutter again. This time the sun was rising. It was just a little golden sliver on the horizon. I couldn't see the ground yet, but the blanket of clouds below me were all silver and pink. The sky was turning from black to a dusky blue. Proving that the sun will always rise, the light will always return, the darkness will always recede. 
 This book took me on a journey through the darkness of the human hear and back that winter night and you have an invitation to take that same journey, if you dare. I'll give you the road sign: Full Dark, No Stars
I thought it lacked originality and could careless about any of the characters. It felt as if Mr. King (which I am a big fan of) either needed a paycheck or was bored and wanted to publish a book.

Anything is good coming from Stephen King, but this collection of short stories is tepid at best. "1922" was VERY long but failed to capture my interest; the others were interesting and had some feeble moments of the King-factor (to give it a name). Yet throughout each story there is lacking that essential jolt you'd expect from King. The "horror" within these pages seems like recycled material and was unsurprising; much of it hinged on violent acts that test the will of the characters involved, leaving me wondering why King didn't take the opportunity to terrify that was offered by this collection. Unfortunately, while I enjoyed reading these stories, they are for the most part forgettable.
Yummy - violent, dark - typical King. If you like him, you will like this. If you get nightmares, steer clear.
grose!!

Stephen King is amazing. I tried to read him way back when in the 70s and 80s when he was becoming popular, but just couldn't do it. I have no idea why. Perhaps if I go back and read his early works, that will explain. This one was so good, and I listen to the audiobook. I drive about 100 miles on average/day for work, so I blow through books like nothing. 
 I like his short stories. During this time, my husband was gone, taking our sailboat south, and when I would drive home after dark (I live in New England, so this time of year, the sun sets at 4:15 p.m.), I'm literally afraid to get out of the car, he has me so entwined in his grip. This is success, as far as I'm concerned. Also, I feel as if I never know where he is going. Especially good was "1922". I loved the character development of all the main characters, and how the story progressed throughout. He's a real master in that regard. The one that scared me the most was "Big Driver." The huge rapist. Sends shudders up my spine. "A Good Marriage" is a nail biter, too. Bravo, Stephen. How does he come up with these things?

While "Different Seasons" was probably better overall, the novella format is where King does some of his best work. Each of the four stories is more than capable of holding their own as a separate work, there's no "weak" story being carried by the others in the collection.

Our dear Uncle Stevie does it again! Say what you will about Mr. King's novels (some of them are just hit and miss), but his short fiction is often simply amazing. Once I decided to finally take the plunge and start this one (it's actually been lurking on my nook since December) it was very difficult for me to put it down. Four well-crafted tales from the dark side that illustrate again that people are the scariest creatures walking the earth.

reference_books.title: New Moon (Twilight, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I'd heard the subsequent books are better than the first. So far: yes and no. 
 Bella is upset at growing older since Edward, the vampire she loves, will never age. Fine. But her actions range far beyond immature. Edward leaves her, which is very obviously to protect her, though only Bella doesn't get this as it was dead obvious to the reader. So, Bella goes on a reckless spree: motorcycles and cliff jumping. Even though she was supposedly more mature than other teens her age, she is entirely selfish and petty. Her "love" for Edward is more obsession. 
 Edward is supposed to be about a hundred years old, however, he's no more emotionally mature than Bella, for he turns to the same suicidal tendencies as does she, after learning of her supposed death. The correllation to Romeo and Juliet is overt, and in your face. But the sickness of these characters kills any emotional reaction on the reader's part. 
 I thought one characterization in this second installment was better - and far more engaging - and that was Jacob. The book did begin to get interesting to me as Bella's relationship with Jacob grew. It gave the story an interesting twist, and his character was intriguing. He did act like a teenager. But this too was ruined by the werewolf subplot. 
 It's stretching the reader's ability to suspend disbelief to have vampires as it is, but to add werewolves to the mix? Who just happen to live in the same area? And Bella just happens to befriend? This aspect was too over-the-top and came off as cartoonish, which was really disappointing because I'd started to enjoy Jacob as a character. He was the best part since Bella was so mentally unstable and ill. Does anyone really find suicide and obsession akin to love? Ugh. 
 The ending was the worst part: Edward goes on a suicide mission to a troupe of more powerful vampires in Italy. Alice and Bella just happen to get there in the nick of time to save him only for them to be taken into the inner sanctum of the Italian vampires - who simply opt to let them all go as long as Edward and Alice agree that Bella will become one of them. Why would they agree to this if they are opposing factions? This made no sense and made for a very weak ending.

book_a.title: The Old Man and the Sea
book_a.user_review:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I've read two Hemingway books, and I've never seen what everyone else sees. I find his stories uninteresting and slow... at least the two I've read were, including this one.

sample_reviews.review_text: I have to admit the middle of the book nearly bored the hell out of me, but in the end I came to appreciate Hemingway's style of writing, the concept of man versus nature, and the emphasis of human relationships.

Ernest Hemingway published his novella The Old Man and the Sea in 1952, but it still reads well today, owing to that terse style that won him many a prestigious award. I'm not a big fan of fishing and that kind of lifestyle, so reading this one was a bit of a trudge. However, the book was short, so I'd be damned if I wasn't going to see it through. 
 Which is kind of the point of The Old Man and the Sea. 
 Thematically and symbolically, the book is a goldmine. First, it deals with life as an endurance test, overcoming obstacles. (DiMaggio's bone spur, anyone?) If you don't catch a fish for months, the other fisherman deem you too old to be in the game any longer. But the human spirit can defy these declarations. He is not just the "old man," but rather the great fisherman and arm-wrestling champion Santiago, and he aims to conquer the age discrimination against him by capturing a truly great fish in the sea. 
 The Old Man and The Sea also describes the loneliness endured in this quest for survival, not just physical survival but the survival of one's dignity in the face of these judgments. Above all, though, perseverance is king, and Hemingway expertly demonstrates that, if at first you don't succeed, try again. You are never too old to do so. 
 So, while I didn't like the book all that much, its brevity was a plus, and it can be interpreted widely and greatly. I wouldn't recommend it, but if any of the above interests you, then maybe it's the book for you.
It's a classic piece of literature, but it's also incredibly lengthy. I'd add it to my list of classic literatures to read.
Boring man and the sea.

Okay, I know my fellow readers are going to hate me when I say this...but I just couldn't get into this book. Now, I realize that Hemingway is a huge icon in American Literature but his novel didn't grab my attention like Salinger's or Steinbeck's did. (At least I'm honest)

Very well written, but I did not like it too much. Though I appreciate the fact that Hemingway is a very good writer, it just didn't appeal to me that much. I thought it was rather slow, and it didn't really draw me in. Then again, I don't really like boats and I don't like fishing, so maybe this just isn't my thing.
Hemingway at his best. Old man and the sea is a story of grace under fire, life's little struggle, and dealing with loss all in one novella. Old man is a story that I will read time and time again.

The Old Man and the Sea is about an unnamed old fisherman in Cuba who sets one day to catch fish in the Gulf Stream and hooks a large tuna that he decides to chase until he can catch it. 
 Very good prose and a philosophical tone and mood. Quite sad though in the end. Reminded me a lot of The Stranger since it gave me the same kind of hopelessness feeling. A nice introduction to Hemingway for me, but I hope to get more out of his novels than this.

This is such a short novel and I had been exposed to it so many times that it's surprising that I didn't read it until I was 30. What do I say? I've been trying to like Hemingway since my Dad fell in love with him when I was 13 or 14. I do like him, but I don't love him. 
 I did enjoy this story. A lovely and tragic victory and defeat of a devoted young boy and an old fisherman.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This was quite possibly the WORST book I have ever read. It was all about a man..... going fishing..... getting the fish...... losing the fish...... then sleeping..... NO

 I considered rating this with two stars; I liked it the least of all the Potter books. It dragged quite a bit in the beginning.  That said, two of the most emotional scenes for me of the series were in this book, so bonus points for Neville's gum wrappers and Molly's boggart.

sample_reviews.review_text: This book is amazing! It seriously keeps you involved the whole time and there are several different villains to keep your eye on!

** spoiler alert ** 
 **This review is for personal purposes only** 
 This is my least favorite of the HP novels. It takes what I didn't not like about Chamber of Secrets (all the unfair doubt of Harry when he knows the truth)and magnifies it with teenage angst. I thought the plot concept was the weakest of any of the books so far - at least the twist of Ginny being controlled by Voldemort in the Chamber of Secrets was fun and unexpected. It was sad that Sirius died, but I didn't feel much of a connection to him in this book as when he showed up at the end of the 3rd book. I didn't like that he was so focused on just being Harry's friend. I also disliked the plot-line of finding out how cruel Sirius and James were - it ended up ruining their characters for me. Even Lily did not come off great in this novel seeing as she married James after seeing his former behavior. I thought the Occlumency could have been better used, instead of just having Harry give up on closing off his mind and that is what leads him to the Ministry. He should have been tested with it when Voldemort showed up and learned to overcome it. Instead (as you find out in the 6th) Voldemort just blocks him off instead and all those lessons were pointless. 
 One of the few things I did like about this book were the women. Hermione handles Harry so well by being both understanding and firm with him. Ginny also blossomed into a real character this time, instead of just being Ron's shy sister who has a crush on Harry. You find out that she is both funny and fiery, taking notes from both the twins and Ron. And finally, Luna is introduced, who I love. I feel like she really adds a special element to the series. 
 The other part I love about the Order of the Phoenix is Dumbledore's Army. I wish this group would have continued into the 6th book, instead of putting the pressure back on Harry to do all the work. 
 Overall, I hate reading this book. It makes me feel tense from all the anger and angst Harry feels and the plot-line does not feel satisfying. I'll probably skip over it in the future.

I am baffled that this series is so popular. While I think the character qualities have some merit, it is just so terribly written, drawn out, and boring. There are some interesting imaginary things, but what happens with all of them--that is, the plot--stinks. Not to mention, each book is successively darker and sadder than the one which came before. For me, that indicates a dark supernatural power in it far more than the witchcraft and sorcery. Perhaps it is merely the power of good advertising. That is the only reason we know about Jackson Pollack, after all.
:D
Re-read this after finishing Half-Blood Prince, it's one star better than I originally ranked it.
Not a reread!! Still amazing!! Loved all the humor and the spells!! Only two books left!! :(

Malfoy always taunts Harry, Ron, and Hermione. Snape always hates Harry and the Griffyndors for no apparent reason, and his bias is never questioned. Lee Jordan always swears at the Quidditch matches and gets scolded by McGonnogal. Harry always manages to barely catch the snitch just in time to win a Quidditch match for Gryffindor. Harry and Ron always suck at classes while Hermione gets shamed for doing well. 
 See how I revealed no spoilers there? 
 There's only so much of the same thing you can read over and over again before it all blends together into a boring mess. Five books of this?! With the plot drawn out for hundreds of useless pages? Why would I want to endure three ignorant teenagers complaining about not being told anything, while they whisper secrets in the open and lazily sit by watching the action go on around them? Why can't I be in on the big-kids' table, and help the adults put things together? While reading this I constantly had to ask myself... How are these good characters again? There's something wrong when the two-dimensional side characters are more intriguing than your three musketeers. 
 Hmm, I wonder why it's so hard to ignore the school bully long enough, so you can keep playing your favorite sport, Harry? 
 Hmm, it must be hard to control a conversation long enough to say what you want to your own godfather, Harry. 
 Hmm, so you want to "burn" the useful gift your brilliant friend gave you for help, Harry? You and your best friend pay no attention when Hermione, the successful student, tries to help your study schedule (never thought that might help you become an Auror, did you, Harry?). That must have something to do with the fact that you haven't yet realized how reading actually helps in real life, dear Harry. 
 Hmm, I wonder why it's a bad idea your mind is linked with Voldemort's, Harry. 
 Hmm, could it be a good idea to guard your mind from your worst enemy, Harry? 
 Hmm, how about you stop complaining and learn from the people you envy or criticize, Harry? 
 Please tell me why anyone would like reading 600 pages of dull plot surrounding this guy's attitude problems? I don't get it. 
 The only new material in this one is Umbridge's infernal presence, which was entertaining. But Rowling took 800+ pages to retell the same story she's done four times before, inserting maybe 20% new material, while boring me with the rest of the useless rambling junk. Stop killing so many trees and use less of my time. Stop asking so many questions, and make something actually happen. Stop writing about hormonal teenager problems, and give me morality and suspense. Give fewer homework troubles to your idiot main character, and describe more of the legacy behind everything actually driving this plot. Stop feeding me the same patronizing slop... I can see through it. 
 At least the last 200 pages are interesting. 
 Why are all the side characters seemingly more interesting than the protagonist? It's because Rowling refuses to actually use the entire 800 pages for character development. Instead she crams all the good action into the last 5-7 chapters (making me guilty for feeling happy, after struggling through the slothful 600 previous pages). 
 This book earns 3 stars only for Rowling's inventive creations in the wizarding world, and the last 7 chapters which made the whole 800+ pages of drudgery somewhat worth it. But when the environment is more interesting than the plot... Errrrr... There's a problem. 
 I'm sorry, but if you've failed to make your hero interesting by the fifth book, just stop... stop using your international fame to put me through this mediocre excuse for a saga... It was interesting in book one, Rowling, because that one was 200 pages. And maybe you could pass it by me again in book two. But no more... Please no eighth book... Please, I'm begging you... 
 *sigh* Now on to book six: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince. I'm gonna guess that the next 800+ pages have more of the same idiotic lines from Ron that pass for quality children's literature...

So much of the expert advice on writing is about advancing the plot, moving the story ahead, cutting out unnecessary detail. Harry Potter 5 breaks those rules, and it's a better book for it. 
 All this is old news, but I re-read most of The Order of The Phoenix over the holidays, just because I like it so much. And also because I appreciate its brief but gentle treatment of mental illness. 
 My absolute favorite scene is when Neville, a minor character, realizes his friends know that his parents are mentally ill. His bossy grandmother is there, and she tells him what to do and how to feel. But Neville takes his own approach, which is shyer, sweeter and in the end much more courageous. 
 Another wonderful minor character was the socially awkward Luna Lovegood. My favorite scene with her is at the very end of the book, when Harry stumbles onto Luna in the hall on the last day of the term. At first he wants to hide from her. Then, when he realizes that she knows how odd she seems to everyone else, he feels sorry for her. By the time he walks away, he is very glad to have talked to her. 
 I thought it was sad when Luna told Harry that their schoolmates played tricks on her. Bret disagreed. "She wasn't sad about it," he said. "She was handling it just fine." 
 And she was--which may explain why her strangeness is so likable. 
 She and the clumsy but determined Neville are the reasons I've read Harry Potter 5 more than once.

Let me start by saying this has to be the lowest score I have ever given to such a well written book. The author does a fantastic job of putting us into the setting of 19th century France and then America. If it weren't for a couple of issues involving the main character, and then the story as a whole, I would rate this a 4.5 to 5 star effort. The characterization was excellent, even if the main character sometimes frustrated the hell out of me. 
 The thing is that I realize the author was working within constraints that caused the following two issues, but they remain issues nonetheless. 
 First of all is the main character herself. That she was talented, pretty, and clairvoyant works. But what starts to grate after a while is her passivity in the face of machinations from a hostile aunt that only gets worse as the book goes on. Yes, I know it was the nineteenth century, but it was at the turn of the twentieth century and at some point even girls back then would show some sign of standing up for themselves, even if it were to ultimately fail. But Adrienne simply suffers without complaint to the point the reader wants to yell at her to grow a freaking spine. Show some gumption. DO SOMETHING! 
 The other part that left me cold was the conclusion and how that affected the nature of the story in it's totality. Once finished, I found I had just read a book that was pretty much about nothing. And it was only once I started reading the afterward that I realized why that was. 
 The author had woven this story based on real historical events, and the character of Adrienne was the witness who tied them together. That's all well and good, but it left the reader with a character reduced to witnessing and passively enduring events as opposed to really acting as her own agent in the story. And when the author concludes things so that the book follows the real life events, it leaves the character behind in a way that leaves the reader going "HUH? THAT'S IT?", because in reality the story was never really about her. And since the story was told from this fictional characters point of view with the real characters being antagonists of unknown motives through most of the story, it wasn't really about them either. The reader is just left hanging wondering if what s/he just read really counts as a story in the classic sense. 
 So I'm left conflicted, faced with a superior piece of writing that left me feeling slightly robbed in the story department.

I'm reminded now of why classics become must-read classics after having re-read this, A Tale of Two Cities, Les Miserables lately. 
 I don't think there is a point in trying to compare great art. That said, I found this novel even more chilling than 1984. I believe that's because it is more believable and more immediate. 
 It is obviously a metaphor for human society and the "Beast" enclosed within us with a patina of civilization that is ever so fragile. F.A. Hayek, in his treatise, "The Constitution of Liberty," states that when individual liberty is forsaken the only possible results are anarchy or dictatorship. In this extraordinary novel, we have both: Jack is the narcissistic dictator that rules by force and eventually by terror and torture to ensure obedience. 
 Ralph (I assume pronounced "Rafe", since all the children are British--perhaps considered the most civilized and civilizing nation)represents civilization, representative government, reason, etc. Without the civilizing force of society, brute force in the form of Jack banishes him, and with him, rationality and humanity. The "id," the "heart of darkness," and bestiality are the inevitable result. 
 We also have "Piggy" the scientist and rationalist advisor to Ralph and Simon, who I see as the philosopher who in Plato's Allegory of the Sun sees reality, where "truth and beauty shine resplendent." As a consequence of being the one being who can bring down Jack by identifying the "Beast" as really a man (and, consequently, the real Beast hiding in all of us beneath a veneer of civilization) he is therefore slaughtered. 
 Although there were parts that seemed a little slow, the payoff came only as a result of those parts and was overwhelming for me. 
 ...A truly extraordinary piece.

reference_books.title: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
reference_books.review_text:
I'll make this brief. Portrait is a simple story. a boy grows up to be a man, drops out of university to follow his dreams and in the process lets go of his religion. Sounds simple enough. It's been told several hundred times in any number of bildenstrums. Except one difference: none of those other stories have been written by James Joyce: literary giant, writer extraordinaire, artiste of the highest order. 
 I admit that much of the descriptive melodies drifted straight over my head. I confess the Catholic sermons and religious metaphors, Dantes allusions were way too complex for this simple Jewish student of literature. Ill freely tell you that I found Stephen Dedalus a bit of a dandy, his father a weak spirited alcoholic and his friends a bit too spoilt and self-important (well aren't all liberal arts university students?). 
 However I am more of a man for reading Portrait. I think I have gained a better understanding of what religion can do to us if we let it (take that however you wish), a more thorough belief in my own visions for a happy life and a clearer concept of what beauty is or can be. 
 Finally I am now in a position to say that to write a book which will out live all of us and then some is perhaps one of the most challenging and difficult things a person could do. To ensure each word is grouped to form perfect sentences, to form perfect structure and perfect phrases. Joyce did just that. It's a difficult read. A really difficult read, but one I'm glad I slogged through. And for that I'm grateful.

OH MY GOD 
 This book has wrecked me. Literally wrecked me. I spent the last 100 pages crying non stop. 
 I am never reading this again.

For me, two words capture this book: relentless and cumulative. I'm sure I've never read another book that so relentlessly takes the reader through a character's troubled life--day after day after day--for decades. Though there are four primary characters in A Little Life and dozens of well-drawn supporting characters, all of the focus, really, is on Jude. After finishing this book, I now feel like I know Jude personally. I've been there in his office with him as he pulls all-nighters on so many occasions that I know what the sunrise looks like as it comes in his office windows. I've sat through all those meals he struggled to eat despite lacking an appetite. I know where he goes for Thanksgiving and for his summer vacations, and I know what his body looks and feels like. The cumulative effect of 700+ pages of close observation is truly astounding. It's also truly exhausting, in an emotional sense, to make the journey that A Little Life demands of its readers. If you decide to make that journey, be prepared. 5 stars for being unlike anything I've read before and also something I'll never forget.
Jesus fucking christ. I have no words. This book..... fuck.

I want to acknowledge that this novel means a great deal to a lot of people, many of whom are trauma survivors who find their experiences echoed in Jude's(1), and I've cited Jeff Chu's essay from Vox here as a particularly evocative example(2). Also listening to Yanagihara's interview on the Lit Up podcast helped illuminate some choices I found really distancing--the New York City devoid of politics or technology. 
 But I, I LOATHED, LOATHED, LOATHED this book. I was traumatized by this torture porn, seduced by the misleading intro in the mediocre restaurant, thinking I was embarking on a delightful journey of four friends over time along the lines of "The Group." I sincerely hope I am not suffering from a lack of empathy, as some of the book's detractors are considered to be, but the amount of unrelenting trauma that Jude experiences alienated me, while less would have drawn me closer. 
 Many have written about what they found problematic about "A Little Life" better than I ever could, so I'm just going to link(4). 
 Citations

 https://www.instagram.com/alittlelife... 
 2. Essay from a trauma survivor who found A Little Life to align with his experiences and to be very meaningful 
 http://www.vox.com/2015/10/14/9519855...

 http://thelitupshow.com/episode-2-han... 
 4. Interesting critical reviews of "A Little Life" 
 http://www.nybooks.com/articles/2015/... 
 "In the end, her novel is little more than a machine designed to produce negative emotions for the reader to wallow in--unsurprisingly, the very emotions that, in her Kirkus Reviews interview, she listed as the ones she was interested in, the ones she felt men were incapable of expressing: fear, shame, vulnerability. Both the tediousness of A Little Life and, you imagine, the guilty pleasures it holds for some readers are those of a teenaged rap session, that adolescent social ritual par excellence, in which the same crises and hurts are constantly rehearsed. 
 .... 
 If anything, you could argue that this female writer's vision of male bonding revives a pre-Stonewall plot type in which gay characters are desexed, miserable, and eventually punished for finding happiness--a story that looks less like the expression of "queer" aesthetics than like the projection of a regressive and repressive cultural fantasy from the middle of the last century."
