reference_books.title: Fallout (Lois Lane, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Fallout is a fun read with mystery and great characters. I loved this! 
 Lois Lane is a character I never felt a connection with in the movies or the TV shows. But with Fallout I finally get to see what she's all about and I love her! A teenage Lois Lane is smart, spunky and wants to save the world (or at least the teens around her). She can't turn a blind eye when she knows an injustice is happening. In Fallout we see her in action as she transfers to a new school. On her first day of school 
 Lois hears the cry of a troubled student and is determined to help her out. She meets Perry White, the editor of The Daily Planet, and lands a part-time job at the newspaper. For her first assignment she focuses on the trouble at school but in turn gets in trouble herself. Lois has the best intentions but her plans don't always go that great. But with the help of her new friends and a special online friend (known only as SmallvilleGuy) a plan to save the day is forged. 
 Fallout is a perfect combination of mystery and fun moments so I couldn't put this down. Author Gwenda Bond is a creative storyteller and I loved everything about this book. I can't wait to read the next book Double Down and go on another adventure with Lois and her pals. 
 Visit my blog for more of my Book Looks! 
 Lois Lane: Fallout by Gwenda Bond by katsnook featuring high-waisted skinny jeans

reference_books.title: Serafina and the Black Cloak (Serafina, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Serafina and the Black Cloak is a magical story. This was just what I needed to add adventure to my reading list. 
 Serafina and the Black Cloak is a middle grade series that people of all ages will enjoy. Serafina has been secretly living in the basement of the Vanderbilts estate with her Pa. Her Pa has been employed as the estate's maintenance man by the Vanderbilts for many years but has been keeping his daughters existence a secret. Fear of being discovered and becoming homeless Pa has strict rules for Serafina to follow: stay hidden and stay away from the deep parts of the forest. Serafina has always obeyed her Pa but longs for a friend her age. But when children start disappearing and Serafina is a witness she knows she has to do something to solve the mystery. Thus begins an adventure filled with mystery and paranormal twists that kept me entertained and intrigued. 
 Serafina is a great character. Despite the danger she knows she has to help solve the case. I loved her curiosity and her thirst for knowledge. Along the way she finally makes a friend and learns the truth of her past. 
 The story has a paranormal twist to it that is creepy and makes this a fun read (it's always fun to be scared). I did think this was predictable but I still enjoyed the suspense. This is a great adventure that readers of all ages will enjoy. 
 Audiobook Review 
 This is the first time I listened to Cassandra Campbell and I enjoyed her performance. I was amazed to have discovered she has narrated nearly 200 audiobooks. I loved her voice for Serafina which had a touch of a southern accent. Her performance was solid and kept me engaged. I look forward to listening to her in the next book.

reference_books.title: A Court of Mist and Fury (A Court of Thorns and Roses, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
3.5 Stars for A Court of Mist and Fury 
 A Court of Mist and Fury is the second book in the A Court of Thorns and Roses series. This was a good sequel but I thought the pace was slow. I also was frustrated with Feyre. Feyre is recovering from the events in book one. Her experience Under the Mountain was horrific but instead of trying to heal Feyre and Tamlin acted like nothing had happened. Their lack of communication causes a rift in their relationship. It was repetitive how Feyre felt "damaged" but didn't seek help on how to heal. This part of the book was boring until Rhysand becomes a key player in the story. I loved Rhysand and the Night Court! Rhysand and his family (Mor, Cassian, Azriel, and Amren) brought excitement, humor and surprising twists to the story. Despite the slow pace I am starting the next book now. The final chapters were worth the slow build up and I can't wait to find out what happens next. 
 As a side note - this series is labelled as Young Adult but with the explicit sex scenes this is more appropriate for readers 18 years and older.

reference_books.title: Splintered (Splintered, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Splintered is a dark and wild ride down the rabbit hole. I'm so glad I finally made time to read this. 
 Splintered is a unique and gothic version of Alice in Wonderland. The main character Alyssa Victoria Gardner is a descendant of Alice Liddell, the real-life inspiration of Lewis Carroll's classic tale. Alyssa's mother has been in a mental institute for most of her life, suffering from the family curse of hearing the whispers of bugs and flowers. But Alyssa has also been hearing the voices and the only way to save her and her mother is to take a dangerous trip to Wonderland. 
 What did I like? 
 I enjoyed how the author took the classic tale and made it her own. You still meet the Wonderland characters we have grown up with but their roles are surprisingly twisted. 
 What stands out is the imagery. The setting, characters and scenes were so well described I was able to visualize them clearly. The authors' writing is amazing and the story is the perfect mix of romance, suspense and action. 
 I also liked Alyssa. She is a strong female character who wants to protect everyone she cares about. But her Dad and best friend Jeb treat her as if she is a fragile little girl. Alyssa takes action in her own hands but her best friend Jeb gets mixed in with her journey. Jeb is a great guy but overprotective. And while in Wonderland they meet Morpheus, the sexy and suspicious hookah-smoking caterpillar. A love triangle develops between these characters but it doesn't take away the focus of Alyssa's mission to save her mother. The triangle does add some tensions between the characters but I thought it worked well with the story. 
 What didn't I like? 
 At times I thought the story dragged. There is so much going on that I felt them more an interruptions instead of vital events for the story. 
 Overall I thought this is an impressive debut for author A.G. Howard. It is written well and very creative. For me this wasn't a retelling of the classic but more an extension of the Lewis Carroll's series. I can't wait to start the next book. 
 Audiobook review 
 This is my first time listening to narrator Rebecca Gibel and she did a great job at bringing this book to life. Her voices for all the characters were distinctive and had the right emotion. Since Splintered is a dark story she gave the Wonderland characters a creepy feel to them. And her voice for Morpheus was so sexy I completely understood why Alyssa couldn't ignore her attraction to him. A great performance and I can't wait to listen to the next book!

book_a.title: The Young Elites (The Young Elites, #1)
book_a.user_review:
This is my first time reading a book by Marie Lu and I am so mad at myself for waiting so long. I now know why this author is so popular among Young Adult fans. I was really impressed with her creativity. The Young Elites is a fantasy story takes place in the fictional land of Kenettra. A deadly illness, called the blood fever, swept the land killing the people, mainly adults. The children that survived the illness are called Malfetto because they were left with strange markings - scars and a change in the color of their hair and eyes. Some of the Malfettos have also acquired mysterious and powerful gifts. Their identities are secret but they are known as the Young Elites. 
 Adelina is the main character and one of the survivors, a Malfetto. It is too soon to say that I like this character. Adelina has been physically and emotionally abused by her father. He blames her being a Malfetto as the cause for all their hardships. When Adelina discovers her new powers she fights the urge to be dark. All the years she's been abused has built up pain and anger so it is a constant battle to be good. Plus she must learn to control her power. Adelina makes some deadly choices so she isn't a character that I have made a real connection with. I'm not sure if she is a character I would cheer for but I am curious to see how this character will develop. 
 Overall I really enjoyed this book. The Young Elites is an exciting story about good vs evil. There are supporting characters whom I loved (Enzo and Raffaele) and hated (Teren). And the world building was well done. This is a fantasy so there was the right amount of details without being overwhelmed. The scenes were vivid and exciting. There were times when the story did drag but then the last part of the book is full of non-stop action. I can't wait to read the next book! Also I plan to read Marie Lu's Legend series.

"Tell me, little wolf. Do you want to punish those who have wronged you?" 
 3,5 stars. Now this is a story you don't read every day! How many writers can write about a protagonist who slowly turns into an anti-hero-possible-villain and still make the reader sympathize with her. Too bad the writing style wasn't as refreshing and the plot contained a lot of YA-fantasy cliches, but reading about a main character as unique as Adelina made up for a lot of things. 
 Let's start with that pesky first half, where you find a lot of familiar YA-tropes: we meet a teenage female protagonist who has had a hard childhood, one dead parent, and a younger sibling that she loves very much (well, not really...it's complicated). When the protagonist finds out she has mysterious powers she gets targeted by a hot villain, but luckily she gets saved by an equally hot hero and his cool band of misfits. Together they plan to overthrown the government, and...you can fill in the rest. 
 So although the second half gets a lot better, the overall plot is pretty average, the writing not anything special - fast paced without plenty of details - and for some reason the author decided to base the world on the Italian Renaissance (because it's romantic, I guess?). 
 However, the whole story has this dangerous atmosphere that always keeps you on your toes. This is because every character is this book is morally grey: you can't trust anyone to do the right thing. Not even our protagonist. 
 As I said, I found Adelina the most interesting thing of this book. Thanks to surviving a deadly fever that swept through the land of Kenterra, Adelina now has silver hair, only one eye, and powers that make her able to conjure dark illusions. Due to being raised by her abusive father kindness and trust don't come easy, but you can see that Adelina wants to be good - she's just constantly surrounded by people who rather want her to be ruthless and deadly. 
 How she struggled with her moral compass was fascinating and very tense, which made the ending of this book so heartbreaking. (I almost threw my book against the wall, I was so shocked). I had hoped for something more happy, but maybe this ending was inevitable. 
 The other characters sadly didn't have half the strength that Adelina had. Enzo was the mysterious handsome hero with fire-powers and a wish for revenge (oh how coool~! not) and most members of the Dagger Society never become more than a name. Also: what is it with gorgeous people having to wear masks? First ACOTAR and now this series. 
 Teren had more going for him - with his twisted mindset concerning the malfetto - but in this book he acted mostly as the Queen's doormat. Hopefully he becomes more his own person in the future. 
 There is some romance in this book, but I was the most invested in the friendship between Rafaelle and Adelina, and Adelina's relationship with her younger sister Violetta. The latter's time to shine came pretty late (at the end of the book) but Violetta's secret revealed a whole new side to her sister-bond with Adelina. I'm very curious to see how their relationship develops in the next book. 
 So even though the plot of this book isn't very original, the threatening mood of the story and its unpredictable (main) characters kept me reading until the shocking end. That wicked epilogue gave the final push, so I'll definitely pick up The Rose Society soon. I can't wait to see how things will get better...or worse. 
 Read here my other reviews of The Young Elites trilogy: 
 #2 The Rose Society | #3 The Midnight Star

I received The Young Elites by Marie Lu from Penguin's First to Read program. Adelina Amouteru survived a blood fever that ravaged the people of hers and surrounding cities. As a result of the fever, several survivors are forever marked with visible scars or differences, setting them apart from "normal" people. Some of the survivors even possess powers, making them "Young Elites". After escaping death not only once from the fever, but again from being burned at the stake, Adelina must decide whether to join Enzo Valenciano and The Daggers, a band of Young Elites, or to side with Teren Santoro and the Inquisition Axis, the King's effort to search out and destroy all Young Elites. Who will Adelina choose? Will she be blinded by the dark vengeance brewing inside her? 
 Let me say, I really enjoyed this book. If you follow my reviews, I don't think you'll find many fantasy novels in my repertoire. I like the occasional fantasy read, but it has to keep me interested. This book did just that. It kept me guessing. Just when I thought I knew what was going to happen, here comes another twist. Sometimes I wanted to cheer for Adelina, and other times I wanted to slap some sense into her. 
 The characters were developed very well. They were realistic and each had their own qualities that made them believable. Some I liked, some I didn't, but it's the same in life. The descriptions were very thorough and helped me bring the characters to life in my imagination. I could picture their costumes and the scenes clearly. All in all, a very entertaining read. My first Marie Lu book, and probably not my last. I give this book 4 out of 5 stars and recommend it to anyone who is a fan of Marie Lu, or likes a suspenseful fantasy novel with twists and turns at every page.

Ah, well. That was quite a read. 
 First I'll start with the things that I loved: 
 - I loved the world building. I've read some of the reviews before reading the book so that I can at least gain some insights, and I saw that some people thought the world that Adelina resided in was practically an alternative history for the years of the black plague. I saw that it rung true in the book, and while some got irked by that fact, I liked it. 
 - Their powers. Adelina's power reminded me of The Night Circus, seeing as the main protagonists and her have almost the same powers--Illusion to all the senses and shit. And it's imposing. So are the abilities of the others, like Enzos, Michael's and Lucent's, and Teren's. They were impressive. 
 - Teren and Enzo. I ship them. I know that it's unreasonable, that they practically stand on different sides of the court, that they're probably one another's enemies, and that Teren killed Enzo, BUT. I ship them. Yeah. Ain't nobody sinking my ship. 
 Now, the things that I half-liked: 
 - Adelina. I was waiting for the apparently strong as hell and bad ass anti-heroine that everyone talked about in their reviews. Alas, she never showed up. Or even if she did, it was only half-assed. I suppose she disappointed me, in a way. Some of her scenes in the book also reminded me of Cruel Beauty (I'm currently reading that book, and I'm on like, chapter two, and yet I've literally already cringed and banged my head on my desk a lot of times. So obviously, this fact was a minus for me), especially the beginning with her unnecessary resentment towards her little sister. And I might've expected something more from her. Oh well. 
 Aaaand. That's it. 
 This book didn't really disappoint me, except for Adelina's part, and yet I somewhat still liked her. The other characters were good enough. The multiple point of views was tolerable. And the plot was executed nicely. (I felt that it could've been better though. I'm sorry) The characters were also complex--they weren't sorted into the good and bad stereotype, and I loved that. That's what I want to see in books, because that's a sense of realism. Showing that people are neither good nor bad--they're merely in between. 
 So all in all, I liked the book. It interested me enough to want to read the next one. I give this three and a half stars.

book_b.title: Ready Player One
book_b.user_review:
Ready Player One is an exciting adventure. I loved this book and I didn't want this to end! 
 It's the year 2044 and Earth is a big mess. Most of humanity "live" in a virtual world, called the OASIS, where they can go to school, play and fall in love on any of the ten thousand planets. The OASIS creator James Halliday was a teen of the 1980's so his virtual worlds paid homage to his favorite 80's pop culture. At the time of his death Halliday leaves his fortune and the rights to the OASIS to the winner of a quest, the ultimate virtual hunt for his Easter egg. Wade Watts is a "gunter" (a virtual gamer) teenager living in a trailer park (called the stacks). Wade has spent years learning about Halliday, not just for the quest but because he is a devoted fan. His devotion pays off when he becomes the first gamer to solve the first puzzle, beginning his exciting and dangerous quest to win the ultimate prize. 
 I loved everything about this book. The characters, storyline, and twists kept me glued to this book. This is an entertaining trip into the future. Wade Watts (online known as Parzival) is your normal teenager, going through the motions of surviving day by day. The OASIS is his escape from the poverty he lives in and he meets other gunters Aech, Art3mis, Daito and Shoto. They are his competition for his quest but as time passes they develop a friendship because of their love for everything Halliday and how they are each a social outcast. The OASIS is a place where people can hide behind an avatar and be anyone they want. But in reality they struggle with insecurities. This book focuses mostly on the quest but we do get a small glimpse of each character. I would have liked a little more time on developing the characters but it was enough for me to feel that I didn't want to say goodbye to them. The 80's references were a fun trip down memory lane. I was a teenager of the 80's so I was giddy and geeking out at all my favorite TV shows, music, video games and movies. Throughout the story there is a lot of information given, which I felt a mix of too much but interesting, so I hope this doesn't discourage you to read this book. All the information is necessary to understand the mind of Halliday and you don't want to miss how it all connects! 
 I was on my library's waiting list for 2 months for this audiobook, and it was worth the wait. Now I need to buy the paperback and audiobook edition. I know I will be listening/reading this book over and over again. Wil Wheaton was amazing as the narrator and the perfect fit for this book. He himself is an 80's icon (Stand by Me, Star Trek: The Next Generation) and I felt his and the characters honest passion of that decade through his performance. I wore a smile the moment I pressed play for this audiobook. 
 I highly recommend this book to everyone looking for a fun and exciting adventure. I can't wait to see the movie in March 2018!

 The world building in this is phenomenal. Only thing I didn't like was the romance.

Narrated by eighteen year old Wade Watts, Cline's plot is set in 2044, a dystopian 
 future, where the majority of the population is immersed within an on-line game. 
 Another book with a similar theme is the graphic novel: 
 In Real Life.
Just as good the third time around. Not writing a review this time. Just going to bask in the awesomeness.
AAAAAAHHHHH!!! HOW DARE THIS BOOK BE FINISHED???

James Halliday is the creator of the OASIS. In all immersive MMO that allows everyone on Earth to escape the horrors of what has become of the world in the near future and go to school, party, or just explore and level their avatar. Halliday was the biggest geek there was and he wanted his passions to be your passions, and his main passion was the 1980s, the time when he was a teenager. When he died he left no heirs and created a treasure hunt within the OASIS to decide who would be worthy of being his successor. His Willy Wonka test was neigh on indecipherable with a little video he made which ended up being nicknamed Anorak's Invitation, after his Avatar, Anorak. Soon a culture of hunters, called gunters, form with the sole purpose of memorizing the minutiae of Halliday and the 80s and finding Halliday's fortune. 
 Wade Watts is a gunter with the handle Parzival. He has spent five years of his life learning everything there is to know about James Halliday. For five long years no one has made the least bit of headway with the quest until Parzival stumbles on the answer while sitting in his virtual classroom. Within hours two people have passed through the first of three gates that lead to Halliday's egg. It soon becomes clear to Parzival that this is going to end sooner then anyone thought, with more dangers then he could imagine. Now that the first hurtle is passed, it won't be long before things come to a head. While Parzival has troubles trusting the other gunters he's come to view as his friends, the real danger is IOI, a rival organization who wants to win the game, not to win, but to control the OASIS. 
 As many people have started their review with "this book was written just for my generation and me in particular," well, I figure, I will reiterate that sentiment. Yes, this book was written for me. I was born in 1978, so a little younger then Halliday, and Cline himself, but of the same generation, so to speak. I will not go on and then say that this book is just wonderful and marvelous and just spoke to me, because, well, it just didn't. You know, it actually kind of enrages me that this book is so well regarded and lauded. It isn't the book itself you can be in love with, it just can't be, with it's bland prose riddled with errors, and it's dry clinical writing style, making it almost like a history book, though written by someone with an ego who is very self impressed that they have all this knowledge at their fingertips. 
 You're in love with the memories this book evokes, the connection it forges using emotional cues from your past. You say "Pac-Man" and I'm a little kid again down at the Brat and Brau feeding quarters into their "Ms. Pac-Man" machine in the few spare minutes I had before the food arrived and my grandmother started piling the A-1 on her dinner. That dark and dingy little restaurant that had the cliched wooden panelling that my basement had and made the restaurant part rathskeller, part sports bar. Side note, I didn't need to read a whole chapter on every level of "Pac-Man" and how the final screen is only half there, I knew that, move on. Cline has taped into the zeitgeist of an era and has just info dumped on us, using touchstones like the Whedonverse to make little geeks and wannabes sqwee with joy. There is nothing that it makes me think of more then the episode of Community "Regional Holiday Music" which they did as a skewering of Glee. One of the songs, to entice Pierce to enter into the singing spirit, was called "Baby Boomer Santa." As Annie said in the episode "Pierce, they're just trying to pander to your demographics documented historical vanity. Resist!" The song is nothing more then a list of things that would appeal to Pierce, from Coca-Cola to The Beatles, Woodstock to Vietnam. This is what Ready Player One does! It just lists things from the 80s that we connect to from Galaga to WarGames and all the hipsters and 80s geeks and everyone is sucked in. To that I echo Annie Edison! RESIST! 
 This info dump mentality makes the book like the carrion of literature displaying the largest lack of imagination I have seen in a book. Ready Player One is part Willy Wonka, part Ender's Game with John Hughes doing the adaptation. I defy you to find something actually original in this book. All the humor and originality is directly lifted from other sources. Why is the final battle Parzival faces so funny? Because he's in Monty Python and the Holy Grail! The entire action, the entire everything is Monty Python's genius, NOT Ernest Cline's! This happens again and again throughout the book. And then there's Halliday and Morrow. Let's talk about James Halliday and Ogden Morrow, or as they really are, Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak. Even if Cline hadn't laboriously pointed that the "fictitious characters" had been compared to these two real men, there is no grey area here. They are 100% these two men. Halliday even dies! Add to that the fact that Ready Player One goes into Phone Phreaking a lot, and Wozniak was part of this phenomenon, and they just get more and more similar. Then, in the, really, you really had to do that, bash my head against the wall, make me want to light the book on fire, there's the fact that the Wozniak character, Ogden, had the nickname Og, like Wozniak with Woz. Seriously? I mean seriously? It's not funny, it's a joke that is flat. Also, let's keep in mind that everyone knows that Woz is the one who was more, how shall I say, fun and relaxed of the two, so he wouldn't be litigious, even though he's spinning tunes as a DJ in a glass bubble before shooting lightning out of his fingers (yes, this seriously happens, and if it was me, I'd have my lawyer on speed dial). This is just degrading to me and in my mind to him, a man I very much admire. Sure he was on Dancing with the Stars, but you know what, he had a choice in that. I have a strong feeling, that while Halliday is never depicted negatively, if Jobs hadn't been on his deathbed, there might have been some serious legal action on this book. 
 If I where to just talk about Cline's writing, I would have to go back to the major flaw in this book in that Cline NEVER sticks to his own internal rules he has created. One minute there's never been a game like the WarGames simulation in the first gate, the next second Wade is on a date with Art3mis and they're in a Goonies rendition that is exactly like the simulation no one had ever thought of. When he's getting ready to clear the first gate, it's a Thursday night, clearly stated as Thursday, because he says he only has one more day of school before the weekend. Because of clearing the gate he sleeps through school, but then gets up bright and early the next day and goes to school... on a Saturday? Then the stupid Fyndoro whatever can only be used once in 24 hours, and then they use it like 6 hours later? Um,if you're going to phone in half your book by ripping other, better, people off, the least, the very very least you could do is get your own writing right. To step further away from all the things that are like or ripped off from other sources, let's talk about the part of the book that is Cline's. It's like he doesn't know what he wants his world to be. Is it dystopian, well yes, but then he drastically shifts away from this interesting study of the poor Wade and his living in "the stacks" and goes 180 and it becomes about this "affluent" kid that Wade has become, lured by the gadgets money has bought him. Which takes the soul out of the book. And then it just becomes the typical "Big Brother" story about a company trying to take control of the OASIS at any cost, deaths allowed. So, now the book is a thriller with corporate espionage? Really, Cline, you needed to keep a similar feel and a through line through this book. Instead you made Wade a douche and then I almost wanted the bad guys to win. And in the end, what was the moral? Stop playing games and get a real life? Because, Halliday just had these gunters waste SIX YEARS of their lives to learn that lesson. Douche Halliday. Also, you kind of made me never want to go near a computer again. And what fantasy world is this where a company would actually keep your information private, cause it's not ours? Now that is pure fiction. 
 To finalize what I refer to now as my ranty rant. There are just so many books and movies and music that Cline has mined, all of which are more original and better, so just go and give credit to the original, not the wannabe. Also, if you want something that actually captures the feeling I think Cline was aiming for, go read or watch Scott Pilgrim. As I read in another review among those fellow haters, I think Sissyneck on goodreads summed it up perfectly. "In a nice manifestation of the novel's lack of self-awareness, Cline at one point derides the villains of the book for simply using "Johnny 5" style robots from Short Circuit instead [of] coming up with their own design. This appropriation, he explains, demonstrates "a lack of imagination," a valid criticism that only too accurately applies to the ostensible heroes of the book, as well as to Cline himself." Right on Sissyneck! And here's a little Pierce Hawthrone to sing us out... 
 The Last Word: "OASIS"

This is probably one of my favorite books I've read for a while. It's fun and entertaining, and full of wonderful pop-culture and 80s references. What I loved most about the book though, is that even though the book is all about gaming and a massive VR world, you don't have to be a gamer to really appreciate it. I rarely play video games but I really enjoyed this book.

Ready Player One is honestly a book I hadn't heard of, until I was gifted it in a swap. I randomly picked it up when going downtown Chicago - I didn't want to bring a library book - and was on my way to the Beercade ironically enough. Wade is the protagonist of the book, he's a high school student who has a rough home life, his parents are both dead and his aunt and her multitude of boyfriends share part of a trailer. In order to login to OASIS, where he attends school, he hides in an abandoned van in a junkyard where he has everything he needs to hook into the virtual world. 
 Beyond that, Wade is a gunter, one of the many hunting for the creator's - Jim Halliday - idea of the ultimate lottery, a key to everything he owns. The only problem is that ever since he died and the quest unlocked, no one has gotten even close to figuring out the first clue. This scavenger hunt includes a lot of pop culture, including old gaming references and even old arcade games that Jim loved growing up. Wade has always been obsessed with the hunt, there's only one problem - he's too poor to leave the world his school is on to go anywhere to investigate. Yet he manages to be the first one to unlock the first gate, only he manages to also meet the girl he has had a cybercrush on for a while now and he can't help but give her a hint to help her out. 
 Thus begins the real adventure. Wade has to deal with the instant news that his avatar has unlocked the first Gate and cleared it. Now everyone wants to know who he really is. He finds sponsors willing to give him money and now he can really start to hunt. The only problem is there is a corporate group out there trying to spoil everything and they are after Wade. 
 I fell in love with Ready Player One, which had references to some things from my childhood and others a bit older. I love the budding romance, the mystery behind Jim Halliday himself and the action, even though most of it technically is in a virtual world. I even cried at the end of the book, I really loved how it ended and what message it sends to readers. Cline creates a world within a world that is so creative and imaginative I loved seeing the different places and games that Wade would have to play through to get further in the quest. 
 Verdict: 
 An amazing story, with science fiction elements but a human element that overrides everything.

book_a.user_review: Sorry, friends, I wasn't a fan. If you care to know why, contact me.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Oh man - I wanted to love this book. It was a gift from a dear friend who has great taste in books. She hadn't read it though and bought it because the book has a fantastic premise. It is a story that explains how the beloved children's classic "Good Night Moon" came to be - it's a story about books, authors, and friends. It has a great setting - I couldn't love Seattle more. It has letters - I love stories that have letters. BUT - it is so predictable and painfully formulaic. There are glimpses of greatness, but it felt too much like a Hallmark movie...which is a great fit for some, but for me, life is too short to read books like this. 
 Too harsh? :/
Sweet, sweet story.

This book was truly a disappointment. I literally would give it no stars if I could. It was like reading the story of a Hallmark Original Movie that was too cheesy for even them to make. It was so predictable. The characters fell in 'love' in about a day. The frantic work-a-holic business woman had her heart melted by the old-fashioned book shop full of memories and even more by the handsome lawyer turned baker in the shop next door. The Goodnight Moon back story was blasphemous at best. Bleh. 
 Bleh bleh bleh.

I confess: I am a book snob, I read literary books & non-fiction. I LOVED this jewel of a book, couldn't put it down. It taught me that sometimes we all need a good, charming and heartwarming book to heal us from the grief and pain that happens in life.
You will enjoy this if you love Margaret Wise Brown and Goodnight Moon! A lovely read with a satisfying ending.

Light and fun, quick read. It started off well, and had some interesting ideas (especially the fictional correspondence between the aunt and her best friend, author Margaret Wise Brown) but ended up being more Harlequinesque than literary novel. Not bad, but lighter weight and more predictable than I was hoping for when I first started reading the book.
Read this in almost one sitting. Loved it and had tears in my eyes at several points during the book. Would definitely recommend this to anyone.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I'll start out by saying that it really isn't fair to be the author of book reviewed after Flight Behavior. Anything looks like amateur hour after Barbara Kingsolver is your opener. I tried to take this into consideration with this review, but Wow! This book is a stinker. 
 June, the eponymously named protagonist, maybe the least likable protagonist I have run across in a book. She is selfish, self-centered and hypocritical. 
 The main plot of the book surrounds her career change from a -- 
 -- evil banker who thoughtlessly forcloses on businesses without giving them terms or second chances, needing them to pay their own way, 
 --finds herself in this situation with her own bank, and begs for the exception, 
 --tries to extort money from a ninety-ish demented woman, 
 --decides to hold a fundraiser for other people to pay the bill, 
 --is told that selling her first editions could pay the bill, 
 --allows someone to pay the bill for her anyway. 
 --being, I guess, the only exception at Chase Bank. Forclosures on people who need money will continue, while her boss's largess goes to her bookstore. 
 Her background and education is in Finance, and she does a complete reversal from businesses needing to be self-sustaining, all the way to businesses need not chip in any assets to maintain itself. Since when does a bookstore need first editions? 
 Maybe you could sell those first editions. 
 "And sell the soul of the bookstore? It wouldn't be right!" 
 The next line... "I guess this is it. We tried and we failed!" 
 Because you won't sell the first editions? 
 But accepting huge financial outlays from friends, ex-bosses and acquaintances seems just fine. Business 101. 
 Her other behavior antics include pouring out declarations of how much she forgives her sister! "I forgive you Amy! for everything!" Really? How about asking Amy to forgive you for being such a jerk to her, from breaking off with your sister over a GUY, all the way down to ignoring her pleas for help when she was dying? Unbelievable. 
 The romantic interest with Gavin is stilted and contrived, following in no way the course of a usual romance. In retrospect, I guess his only reason for existing was to direct suspicion on the identity of the missing child. He sheds his fiance and gives all his money, business and life to June after just a few weeks of knowing each other. Wow. 
 I did finish the book, but just barely.

LOVED this book. I don't know anyone who hasn't read 'Goodnight Moon' and this charming novel gives us one possible explanation for how that iconic children's book came about. June, the main character, struggles to overcome fear and learn how to trust again, she has to face past hurts and really decide what is important in her life, and her great Aunt Ruby helps her accomplish this through a scavenger hunt of sorts in the bookstore she leaves for June in her will. Sentimental at times, this story is sweet and charming and a wonderful read for anyone who grew up loving children's books.
Ridiculous and completely implausible! I like a nice light read from time to time but this book was so stupid. Everything ended up perfect and all the "mysteries" were obvious.

book_b.user_review: Agh, I couldn't put it down even as I sobbed through the end.

sample_reviews.review_text: I loved this book and it opened my eyes to many things I previously thought impossible. I predicted the ending halfway through and I worried that would take away from my enjoyment, but it didn't. I enjoyed this book to the very last page.

In the time that I have spent reading this book it has become sort of a comfort to me. I fell in love with the characters, especially Lou and Will, and it's sort of a bittersweet feeling to finish it. It was a 4/5 star read for me, and I'll definitely be picking up After You soon, along with more of Jojo Moyes's books! (full review will be up on my channel soon: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCsIc...)
Review here: https://angryangelbooks.com/2017/04/2...

In the hands of anyone else, this story might have turned maudlin or simply fallen out of its wheelchair and flat on its face. Moyes, however, strikes the perfect balance between offering us hope and threatening us with despair. If terrible, heart-wrenching things must happen, then they happen for all the right reasons. We hope. The suspense in these pages is as real and vivid as the characters themselves. Throw in some British wit, and some excellent physical comedy, and you have a fabulous story. Don't miss this one.

Books with romance are not my favorite genre but the biggest problem I had with this book is that the book is very long for the story that tells, you have over 200 pages that should not have been in this book. 
 The book has an interesting story but is full of romantic cliches that we have already seen in other books, movies, TV series, etc. Another problem is that most of the characters are very annoying and I could not connect with almost none, especially the sister of the male protagonist whose only presence brings nothing to the story. 
 Now I do not know if I give this author another chance because "One plus one" I liked it a lot but "Me Before You" is a very forgettable book. 
 Los libros con romance no son mi genero favorito pero el mayor problema que tuve con este libro, es que el libro es muy largo para la historia que cuenta, le sobran como 200 paginas que no debieron estar. 
 El libro cuenta con una historia interesante pero la autora la lleno de cliches romanticos que ya hemos visto en otros libros, peliculas, series de television, etc. Otro problema es que la mayoria de los personajes son muy molestos y no pude conectar con casi ninguno, en especial la hermana del protagonista masculino que su solo presencia no aporta nada a la historia. 
 Ahora no se si darle otra oportunidad a esta autora porque "Uno mas uno" me gusto mucho pero "Yo antes de ti" es un libro muy olvidable.

E-mail conversation with my friend, Lori, about Me Before You 
 Me: I read Me Before You and enjoyed it thoroughly up until just before the end! I'll tell you why I didn't like the end when we talk. 
 Lori: I'm now thinking why you didn't like the ending of Me Before You. One is supposed to wait until your life has really ended. 
 Me: Yes, that's the problem I had with it. If there is no afterlife, and this life is all there is, and the only thing worthwhile is being able to enjoy this life while it lasts (like Will Traynor so compassionately wants Louisa to do, and like he so sadly can't do anymore), then it's a beautiful story. 
 But if there were a Creator, there would be a different meaning for this life other than just enjoying the temporary adventures. The Creator would be the one who has the right to determine that meaning, and the Creator (of life) would be the only one who has the wisdom to decide when that meaning has been fulfilled, and so when life should end. If there were a Creator then Will Traynor's life does not belong to him. 
 So if there is a Creator and an afterlife, then this story is tragic, because both Louisa Clark and Will Trayonr missed the whole point. As you know from my novel (Zinovy's Journey), I think the whole point of this life is to become acquainted with the Creator, in preparation for the afterlife. Forgive the sermonizing! But I just feel it's so important to really know the truth about these things--life and death, purpose and meaning, and the temporal and the eternal. 
 I know it's just a novel, but as is usually the case, there is a philosophical base to the story that determines the theme, and for me it's a very tragic one. 
 BUT, having said that, I loved the book except for the ending. Even if it made me cry quite a bit. I really felt Will Traynor's dilemma. The author made a good case of explaining and justifying every character's dilemma, in fact. That was so impressive. And so gut-wrenching! Thank you for recommending it to me. It is a worthwhile read.

What an emotional wreck I am. This heartwarming and heartbreaking story reels you in, makes you feel like part of the family and then rips everything away from you in the end. I feel deflated now, but so pleased to have read this. Thinking about the characters and how their lives have panned out is on my mind right now, and surely that's a sign of a good book? 10/10

Ultimately this book gets very preachy and all "HOW COULD HE DO THAT TO HIMSELF ITS SO SELFISH?" Filled with judgey characters. Who are they to judge when they are not in his shoes? Who are they to say what is right or wrong? I also don't see the basis of Will and Lou's connection. Because its her job to spend all day with him and he encourages her to be a normal person and do things? That's not really enough of a love story for me. Maybe the movie will depict their connection a lot better....

I only read this book because of the movie and I truly expected more, I'm kind of disappointed in the story, but its not all bad, It has good and funny parts too, but I suggest you read this book without expectations.

Outstanding story brushed with romance, fear, jealousy, and anxiety.

I will NOT spoil anything here, but I was ambivalent about the ending....I saw it going both ways but liked the way the last Epilogue completed the story for me. 
 I highly recommend this book to anyone looking for a real tear-jerker of a story.

book_a.title: Flowers for Algernon
book_a.user_review: What a heartbreaking story. Amazingly built with a neat progress of event. Unconventional Sci-fi.

sample_reviews.review_text: I cried like four or five times, but this book will be something I think about hopefully for a very long time.

****** SPOILERS ****** 
 I know that I am expected to love this book because it's a Classic, and my rating of only 2 stars out of 5 may appear as an act of resistance, but I really did not like this book. 
 There was not a single character whom I found likable, and there were moments which caused a lot of eye-rolling on my part. I just think it's ridiculous that the only two females who our character meets - and who he is not related to - are both gagging to have sex with him. And that one of them just happens to be a petite, slender blonde who introduces herself to him wearing nothing but pink underwear. Come on, Keyes, you don't have to always think with your penis. 
 I'm going to sound like a total idiot now, and like a very angry person, but I was glad when our protagonist lost all of his intelligence because his constant scientific wittering was boring the hell out of me. What a dull, dull man. 
 I can't wait to discuss the book at my local book club and watch all the other members gush over it for fear of appearing unintelligent.

In a story as heartwarming as it is heartwrenching, 37 year-old illiterate Charlie Gordon goes from living a life with a 68 IQ to living a life of extraordinary intelligence. The differences in what he does and how people treat him throughout his changes makes this story a strong commentary for how so many disadvantaged people are unfairly judged and treated. As Charlie's intelligence grows, he's able to decipher ill-treatments he previously took for normal or friendship.

4.5/5 
 Fascinating. Thought provoking. Emotional. Heart wrenching at times. Brilliant book all around. 
 -late review- 
 Keyes's heartbreaking story of Charlie Gordon and his path from blissful ignorance to an artificially induced intelligence (and back again) perhaps had the biggest emotional effect of anything I read this year. Keyes's ability to make you empathise with the character he creates is truly one of a kind - the book will take you on a roller coaster ride of emotions, but it's definitely worth the ride. Although this is generally categorised as a SF book I really feel like it should be a must-read for even the biggest sci-fi critics. 
 --- 
 EDIT: Don't know why I gave this 4 stars. Goodreads ratings are annoying. Definitely deserves 5.

what's funny is that i didn't even know this was classified as sf. go figure. 
 what i think it did well, and what made a curious incident of a dog in the night so good, is that it looks at a mentally handicapped person and tells the story from their POV - bad punction, poor grammar, weird sequencing and all.
I didn't like the format it was written. by about a quarter of the way into the book,I started hate - reading it. not what I thought it was.

Born with mental retardation, Charlie Gordon has struggled all his life to be smart, mainly as a way to earn his parents' love. He is given a chance to participate in an experiment in which scientists artificially increase his intelligence, boosting him up to genius level. Algernon, a lab mouse, has already undergone the same procedure, apparently with great success. Charlie recounts his progress in a series of journal entries, which evidence how his language skills evolve as his intelligence soars. As he becomes smarter he changes, and so do the people around him, and the way they treat him. The more he knows, the lonelier he becomes. 
 His journey of self-discovery takes him through a maze of understanding himself and his past, to looking ahead and realizing that he will inevitably follow the mouse's path. At the height of his genius, Charlie reaches a point of mysticism where he concludes that ultimately love and the relationships we build are what bring us true fulfillment as human beings. 
 "Intelligence is one of the greatest human gifts. But all too often a search for knowledge drives out the search for love. This is something else I've discovered for myself very recently. I present it to you as a hypothesis: Intelligence without the ability to give and receive affection leads to mental and moral breakdown, to neurosis, and possibly even psychosis. And I say that the mind absorbed in and involved in itself as a self-centered end, to the exclusion of human relationships, can only lead to violence and pain." 
 I first read this book in high school, and I am glad I picked it up again, because I was now able to understand much more of its beauty and depth. Riveting and heart wrenching, this is a story not to be missed.

This is an amazing sci-fi, I can't even describe the emotions that I felt when reading it. I absolutely loved the way that this is written, the spelling and grammar mistakes that convey Charlie's (the main character) lack of ability when reading and writing, are really subtle and effective. I flew through this book very quickly and found it very easy to read as well, highly recommend giving this book a read if you have time :)

When I picked up this book a few years ago, I'd heard only good things about it and, as such, didn't even fathom that I would dislike it. Oh, how ill-prepared I was. 
 Now, it has been years since I read this and I am nowhere near willing to pick it up again, so I apologize for not going into specifics. The writing did nothing for me. I could tell the author was going for something pretty and poetic with her descriptions, but often, it just came across nonsensical. Even though I was privy to Susie's most intimate thoughts, I found myself uncaring towards her. She didn't hook me, she didn't interest me, and that is the kiss of death for a book. reference_books.title: The Girl with the Iron Touch (Steampunk Chronicles, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
I've read the two previous books in the Steampunk Chronicles series and really enjoyed both of them, so I was especially excited to read the last book in the trilogy. Unfortunately, I ended up not enjoying the conclusion as much as I hoped I would. 
 Things were told mainly from Emily's and Finley's point of views. I found myself not liking Finley very much, although I did think Emily was a great character. Another problem that I found myself struggling with was I didn't like either love interest too much. I wasn't really concerned over who Finley would end up with. Both guys, Griffin and Jack, weren't too appealing to me. 
 However, the plot was great. I really liked the way everything went and more importantly, the way things ended up. The ending was pretty realistic, considering what happened in the book. Also, I don't think I can get tired of the world that Kady Cross created, with all it's steampunk inventions. 
 I've found myself really enjoying the steampunk genre, and this series helped me discover it. Although I didn't enjoy The Girl With The Iron Touch as much as the previous books, I'm still looking forward to reading any other books Kady Cross writes. I'll definitely have to check out some of her adult novels, too. I'd give The Girl With The Iron Touch 3 out of 5 flowers :)

reference_books.title: The Indigo Spell (Bloodlines, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
I've been so excited to read The Indigo Spell, so I was super happy when it finally came out. It was an amazing book and I loved the romance! 
 One of the things that I've loved about all the Richelle Mead books I've read are how likable the main characters are. Sydney was awesome, and I liked how she makes rational decisions and takes the time to think both different things and the consequences they will have through. I think it makes her an even smarter protagonist. For Adrian, I could seriously probably write a whole paper about how amazing he is. Although he's not perfect, he has an amazing heart. The Sydney and Adrian scenes in The Indigo Spell also ended up being completely amazing :) 
 The plot moved really fast in this book, and Sydney and Adrian worked together to prevent some dangerous things from occurring. I could have definitely done without the witch stuff in the plot, but everything else was super enjoyable. Also, Sydney started to doubt the Alchemists more in this book. The pacing was great, as well. 
 Overall, I loved The Indigo Spell so, so much. I'm so happy for the next book in the series. The ending definitely opens up some possibilities of what may happen in the next book ;) I'd give The Indigo Spell 4 1/2 out of 5 flowers. 
 * This review is also posted at http://www.thebookbelles.blogspot.com :)

reference_books.title: Golden
reference_books.review_text:
I really enjoyed both of Jessi Kirby's previous novels, so I was so happy to get the chance to read Golden! It told two amazing intertwined stories. 
 The main character, Parker, is one that has pretty much played it safe throughout all of high school. I liked her a lot, and I love when I'm able to relate to a main character really easily. In Golden, Parker ends up discovering the journal of one of the people in the a tragic accident from the past, she finds out both that the tragedy wasn't what it was thought to be and herself along the way. 
 I loved both the romance and how much Parker grew over the course of the story. Jessi Kirby always manages to infuse just the right of romance, so it doesn't overwhelm the rest of the story. The relationship between her and Trevor was so awesome, too. He was such a great guy, and helped Parker out so much. On the other hand, her best friend Kat was such a great foil to her. She was the opposite of Parker, but they had such a great friendship. 
 The plot was awesome, especially with the mystery element it involved. The details of the tragic event were led up to with quite a bit of suspense. I was constantly trying to piece together what really happened. When it was finally revealed, I was really surprised, but I also found the outcome to be realistic. All the excerpts from the journal are in the book, so it's as if you're understanding them at the same time Parker is. The events that led up the ending were all great. 
 Golden by Jessi Kirby is definitely my favorite book by her. Both the plot and the characters were incredible and it's an amazing contemporary. I'm so excited to see what she writes next! I'd give Golden 4 1/2 out of 5 flowers. 
 Review to be posted closer to release at http://www.thebookbelles.blogspot.com

reference_books.title: Ignite Me (Shatter Me #3)
reference_books.review_text:
I've been counting down the days until Ignite Me would finally release. The first two books in the series are two of my all time favorite books and I wanted to know how everything would finally end. I started Ignite Me the second I received it and couldn't stop reading until I finished. It's the most amazing series conclusion I've ever read and I couldn't have asked for a better one! 
 This is one of those books that I wish I could go back and reread. The writing is as beautiful as ever and some of the metaphors throughout are crazy (in a good way). Juliette has changed so much from who she was in the beginning of the series. She's stronger, smarter, and more determined that ever. She's one of the best main characters I've read about in a while and the way her character developed was done really well. 
 In terms of the love triangle, although I was initially Team Adam in Shatter Me, Unravel Me switched me over to Team Warner (it might have had something to do with chapter 62 ;) There are scenes with both guys in this book, and I loved all of them. I was so happy Juliette made a definite decision of who she wanted to be with. There were several parts where I cried. There's also some super sweet scenes, along with some steamier ones. I went through pretty much every emotion possible while reading Ignite Me. 
 The ending was, by far, the best ending I've ever read for a series, especially a trilogy. I was completely satisfied by the ending, although I'm definitely sad to say goodbye to all of my favorite characters. It'd be so cool if Kenji ended up getting his own book! 
 This is one of the first YA book series I ever started, and it holds a place in my heart. I'm hoping to reread it sometime in the near future. I'm already tempted to go back and reread all of my favorite parts. There are some seriously amazing quotes throughout the book. If you haven't yet read this series, you definitely should! Each book is better than the last one, and I'd give Ignite Me 5 out of 5 flowers. I can't say enough good things about it :) 
 *This review was also posted at The Book Belles

reference_books.title: Everything That Makes You
reference_books.review_text:
Although there aren't too many of them, I always seem to love books that feature "what if?" scenarios (such as Just Like Fate and Pivot Point). Everything That Makes You was no different, with it being a highly enjoyable read that puts in perspective just how much the smallest things can impact your life. 
 The story follows two different versions of Fiona- one with a scar on half her face (from a childhood accident) and the other- if she had never had the scar. It was fascinating to read about how much that changed her personality. One version of Fiona had a passion for music, and was too timid to share it with the world. The other version, Fi, was both amazing at and very confident about lacrosse until she got injured while playing. Both versions each had their own flaws, but extremely different ones. 
 Despite the differences between Fi and Fiona, I was so impressed with the way the author managed to weave different aspects of each character's story together. Certain aspects of Fiona's life remained unchanged in both versions, while others drastically differed. It made me wonder about my own life and how some things naturally fall together. I love books that can make you think, and this one definitely succeeded in doing so. 
 There were certain parts of this book that tore my emotions apart. I don't want to give too much away, but it definitely gives you a new perspective on which life for Fiona is really better. They each have their pros and cons, and there wasn't a clear choice for me. Both lives had different love interests and I was surprised that I actually liked all of them. There's not necessarily a love triangle, just different guys who fit into Fiona's life in their own way. 
 Fiona's relationship with her brother, Ryan, was especially awesome to read about. I feel like not enough YA books feature strong sibling relationships, so I really enjoyed reading the ups and downs of theirs. Ryan was such an amazing brother and I loved how Fiona and him were both siblings and friends. 
 One complaint I do have is that Everything That Makes You ends very abruptly. Although there's a time jump, the story ends almost immediately after the conflict does. I wanted to see how things would work out and what would happen, so I was disappointed at the ending. In a sense, it's realistic to life and the fact that you're never sure what will happen. However, from a reader standpoint, I wish the author had written more to the story. 
 Overall, Everything That Makes You is a stand out debut, and one which I'd recommend to anyone who has ever wondered "what if?". The writing style and the way that different aspects of each character's story are weaved together is incredible! I'd give it 4 out of 5 flowers.

book_b.title: Masque of the Red Death (Masque of the Red Death, #1)
book_b.user_review:
I haven't read Edgar Allen Poe's poem of Masque of the Red Death, but the idea of a story based on the poem was so intriguing to me! Masque of The Red Death told a fascinating story, although it did get off to a slow start. 
 The story starts in the middle of a terrible plague, where it isn't even safe to inhale the outside air. People wear masks to prevent the illness from affecting them, but only the rich are able to afford them. The setting struck me as being so eerie. It's crazy to think about a world where the air you breathe could be deadly. 
 Masque of the Red Death had a slow start, mainly because of the fact that I didn't like the narrator, Araby. In the beginning, she came across as both arrogant and selfish. She did progress throughout the story, and some of her more frustrating qualities did go away. I liked how she grew so much stronger over the course of the story. 
 There is a definite love triangle to the story. Neither guy stood out to me, but as the story went on, I grew to like both of them a lot more. Will was a nice guy, and everything he did for his family was very sweet. Although I liked both guys, I definitely liked Elliot more ;) I thought his relationship with Araby ran deeper and he did some really swoon-worthy things. 
 The ending wrapped things up well and I'm excited to see if a cure for the Red Death will ever be found. I'd give Masque of the Red Death 3 out of 5 flowers. 
 *This review was also posted at http://www.thebookbelles.blogspot.com

sample_reviews.review_text:
It's possible that Bethany Griffin is TOO good at what she does. I came into Masque of the Red Death expecting a dark, twisted novel about a girl whose emotions were worn down to nothing...emotionally incapacitated. And that is exactly what I got. 
 Araby Worth is living a rich life, literally. Her father is a scientist who invented the life-saving masks society wears to protect them from the plague that swept the world and killed many. This has provided Araby's family, previously poor, with wealth and plenty of food in a city where the lower echelons of society kill for even less. But her life is still empty of heart and warmth because she feels alone, though she has her parents, her friend, April, and two men who may be interested in her (although for the life of me, I can't think of why). 
 I wanted to love Masque of the Red Death. It sounded like such an emotionally raw and intriguing book. But it just...wasn't. Based on the synopsis, I expected the lack of emotion from Araby, but as the main character, she was too apathetic for me. I couldn't abide by her decisions; she made a lot of stupid ones and I often found myself questioning her judgement - and not in the good way that makes a book interesting. She also wasn't a very strong character; it seemed as though anyone could manipulate her to do as they wanted. It's as though she existed in this fog of disregard for everything around her, and while I know a lot of that has to do with the drugs and her past, I just can't imagine caring that little. While Araby drove me crazy, I did like Griffin's other characters, April, Elliot and Will. All three were very interesting people, each with their own agendas and surprises. So it's not that Griffin didn't write Araby well; I think she wrote her too well. 
 The world-building in Masque of the Red Death is elaborate and great: it's Dystopian-meets-Steampunk and I had a good time getting to know the streets, nightclubs and the people who lived there. It's supposedly a cross between Louisiana and Paris, however, I couldn't get Baltimore out of my head, probably because of the reference to Edgar Allen Poe. Plus, Baltimore is kind of crummy. It seemed to fit into my imagination well. Griffin's writing is fluid and engaging, as well, and the pace is steady throughout the story, so it was very easy to read without putting down. 
 In summary, this isn't a terrible book, and I think a lot of people will like it. I fought with myself over a rating; it's really hard to rate a book you did enjoy reading. The apathy is really what did me in with this book, though. I just can't get past that. I want to connect to the characters and especially, the main character. I didn't connect at all in Masque of the Red Death and without that, the author has lost me. So it gets a 2 1/2: it's not a "Meh" book, but I didn't exactly like it.

Oh, let us count the ways this is an epic fail. Shall we start the heroine being a drug addict? Or one of her love interests being her sociopathic dealer? Or perhaps that there's an invisible crocodile which helps to neatly settle the plot in a way that just screams Deus ex reptilia? 
 Perhaps it's the curse of Poe, as the only other teen novel I've read that tried to capitalize on the Master of the Macabre, Creagh's Nevermore, was equally crap. I sense a worrisome trend, and would seriously recommend the Poe estate take out some kind of restraining order against authors of teen fiction unless and until they prove they can do better. 
 Griffin seems to have come to this novel with little more than one admittedly excellent visual image - that of steampunk'd teens in creepy porcelain masks - and a half-assed remembrance of a lesson on Edgar Allan P. she got back in high school. Little things like cohesive plot or thoughtful characterization are beneath her grand vision, and apparently not something the editors at Harpercollins insist upon as long as the art department can come up with an awesome cover design. My ARC came with a note from this book's editor, and I considered naming her here, but frankly I figure the private shame of having let this go to press in this state is punishment enough.

I remember reading The Masque of the Red Death in second grade. It was in our classroom's little library. I thought "masque" was a fancy way to spell "mask" and while I suppose I was not wrong, the skull on the cover of the book scared me enough to check out the book to try to conquer my fear. 
 Bad idea. 
 I thought the story was about a masked serial killer that stalked Prince Prospero and his friends through brightly colored chambers at a costume party. I think it was in high school that we read it in class and the teacher explained that it was a metaphor for the bubonic plague. Still scares me. 
 Anyhoo, I was excited to read this book because novelizations of Poe stories seem to be an untapped or at least unexplored subgenre. The book started off strongly with a steampunk, dystopian setting of haves and have-nots, all fearing a deadly plague. Aside from the ridiculously emo writing and drippy heroine, it held promise. 
 Sadly, it went downhill at warp speed about 25% of the way in. That plague they all fear? It's not the actual red death. Instead of letting the reader get immersed into this intriguing world, the author went the usual route of "hey, let's overthrow the oppressive government!" that YA dystopia always chooses. Araby and her friends spend their days at a neo-Victorian club, yet there is no mention of education or jobs? Where exactly do the rich get their money? Even poor families sent their children to school once they got masks, but the rich don't? Also, WTF was up with sewer crocodiles? I thought perhaps the book was set in Manhattan. 
 The book was also really boring. It was a constant lather, rinse, repeat of Araby doing something stupid, spending the night with Will, then being led around the city going to clubs and apartments. To what end? Suddenly she's key to the revolution and smack in the middle of a battle her brother's friend takes her for a joyride in a hot air balloon? Are you serious? 
 Perhaps most unforgivable is that this book - which I will again remind you is based on a very well known Poe story that has thrilled millions of readers since the 1850s - features no red death, no ball, and no colored rooms. Did the author even read the original story? 
 There's a breeze blowing as I write this, which I am certain is from Mr. Poe's body spinning in his grave.

N-da, nu i debil'naia zhe kniga. Drugikh slov net. Geroi prosto sovershenno neadekvatny, mir vrode kak dolzhen byt' interesnym, no on absoliutno ne propisan, poetomu tozhe kazhetsia idiotskim. 
 Voobshche vsia kniga mne napominala kakoe-to deshevoe uporotoe anime. 
 Geroi... eto nechto. 
 Devushka i dva parnia, znaiut drug druga bukval'no 1-2 dnia. Para situatsii: 
 1-yi paren' (Eliot): 
 - Nam nuzhna eta kniga, no slishkom riskovanno brat' ee samomu, poetomu poidesh' ty. 
 Geroinia: 
 - Khorosho. 
 I pro sebia dumaet: <<Ia ne pokazhu emu svoi slabosti, pust' dumaet, chto ia sil'naia i smelaia>>. 
 Chto, prostite? 
 Pro to, kak geroi poznakomilis' s geroinei, dazhe govorit' strashno. 
 Vtoroi (bolee adekvatnyi paren' po imeni Uill) privodit geroiniu na ulitsu, chtoby pokazat', kak on vyrastil tsvetok v etom uzhasnom bol'nom mire, kak on dlia nego vazhen: simvol togo, chto ne vse poteriano. 
 Geroinia: "Eto prekrasno". 
 No tipa na samom dele ne pro tsvetok, a pro samogo parnia. Nu ladno. 
 Paren' derzhit ee za ruku (geroinia znaet ego okolo 10 chasov, esli ne schitat', chto ona ego videla kazhdyi den' ran'she, chisto vizual'no on ei nravilsia). Geroinia: "Kak zhe ia khochu, chtoby on menia potseloval". 
 I tut ona nachinaet vydirat'sia iz ego ruk. Priamo na etoi mysli. Vnezapno. Paren' v shoke, ne otpustil ee... ona ego tolknula, tot poterial ravnovesie i zatsepil gorshok s tsvetkom. Razbil. Stol'ko vremeni ego vyrashchival... 
 No bol'she vsego reaktsiia geroini ubila. Paren' stoit, smotrit na slomannyi tsvetok. Geroinia s nevozmutimym vidom: "Ia ne mogu ni s kem za ruki derzhat'sia". 
 Ia by na meste parnia s krikom: "Dura nenormal'naia" sbezhala by. Paren' tol'ko prosheptal: "Pozhalui, mne pora otvesti tebia obratno k tvoemu drugu". 
 Pravil'no, sdai ee obratno takomu zhe sumasshedshemu, kak ona. 
 Dal'she snova 1-yi paren'. 
 Znakomy 2 dnia s geroinei. 
 On derzhit ee nad vodoemom s krokodilami 
 -- Ia vliubilsia v tebia, -- prosheptal on. -- No ia broshu tebia v vodu i budu nabliudat', kak tebia terzaiut krokodily, esli podumaiu, chto eto pomozhet mne dostich' moikh tselei. 
 -- Da chto s toboi ne tak? -- zadykhaius' ia. 
 -- Ia ne znaiu, -- ego chestnost' pugaet dazhe bol'she, chem chto-libo eshche. 
 Menia bol'she volnuet vopros, chto ne tak s avtorom i chto ona pokurivaet. Eto prosto polnyi bred. 
 Ne budu zabivat' vam dal'she golovy etoi erundoi, skazhu tol'ko, chto pod konets vse stalo prosto... kak budto i avtor, i geroi, i chitateli druzhno sidiat v durke i raspevaiut patrioticheskie pesni pod akkompanement ruchnoi obez'ianki, igraiushchei na kontrabase. 
 Avtor, sozhgi svoe tvorenie i vstan' sam v etot koster. Po-drugomu eto nikak ne opisat'. 
 Kniga poradovala tol'ko tem, chto ona otnositel'no korotkaia.

I was going to rate this book 3, but that implies that I enjoyed something about it, which I did not. Well no, I do, I like the main character's name. 
 It's not badly written or anything, but just not for me. I might be over dystopia, and while I think steampunk is cool in theory, I don't enjoy actually reading about it that much. 
 To me the story fell a little flat. Araby Worth is running from survivor's guilt, right into the arms of alcohol and a serious drug problem. Her twin brother is dead, and her actions as a child might have sped along the process. So she takes a vow that she will never experience the things that her brother died before experiencing. Only the vow only seems to kick in when convenient. To amp up romantic tension, mostly. 
 Araby thinks her parents would rather she be the dead one, and her brother alive in her place. She has a best friend who leads her deeper into self destruction. Why not? Why not take enjoyment where you can when any moment can be your last? When people are dropping like flies from the plague, the ruler of the city is killing people on a whim, and thugs are roaming the street. 
 By rights this should be something that hits me in the feels. It doesn't. I had trouble caring about any of the characters. Our heroine, Araby, is incredibly disconnected. The love interests feel like cookie cutter versions of every other love interest ever written. I actually don't even remember what they look like. One has tattoos and the other light eyebrows? Also, love triangle, not my thing. The best friend, April, is the kind of person I'd want to slap, if I cared more about any of them. 
 I don't understand. I saw so many high ratings for this book. Why didn't I like it more? I pretty much had to force myself to keep reading until the end. *sadface*

Severely disappointed by this book. 
 Araby Worth (my gosh, what a ridiculous name to begin with - last name Worth to hint at her apparent usefulness despite her lackluster in life?) is a suicidal poet girl who languishes in a post-apocalyptic world where the air isn't safe to breathe. She finds it hard to muster up the will to do anything except go to a club called Debauchery and immerse herself in oblivion. Her claim to fame is that she is the daughter of the man who made masks - which help filter the air. 
 The plot takes her to meet up with Elliot, the nephew of the villain Prince Prospero who has a tyrannical control over the entire city. She is quickly brought into the folds of a conspiracy and has to assume the guise of his fiance, all while harboring feelings for another boy. Oh, and of course she doesn't like being touched. But it's fine if it's a boy kissing her, naturally. 
 Cliche teen romance without any spunk from the protagonist. And what's more, boys fall in love for her being beautiful with vacant eyes. Ridiculous. No depth. Dull except for the world building. 
 So much potential in the world though! Ceramic masks and lovely images of a broken world with the rich draped in whale bone corsets and long flowing skirts and streaks of violet in the hair. A tyrant villain with a masquerade party. Ah what wasted potential. Poor execution, characters that I have no sympathy for, scenes that drag on, and way too many unnecessary kissing scenes. I love romance and kisses as much as the next girl, but ones that are thrown in there just to show that she's attracted to two guys, hmm not for me. 
 One star because I couldn't even bear to fully read the second half of the story. Read only if you feel like reading about a fairly dimwitted protagonist and can stomach a sappy romance against a beautiful backdrop.
So dark and goth, loved it:)

This book was outstandingly awful. It reads like a first draft--one thing happens after another, so quickly that the reader has no emotional investment in the story or any of the characters. Often I had to go back and re-read, because I was confused that the characters were in a carriage at one point, and then they were walking around in some room. I kind of hated the protagonist and the clunky, nonsensical half-hearted love triangle that has to be present, apparently, because it's a YA book. The only reason I kept reading was that I hoped it would get better. It didn't. 
 I'd like to add that I am particularly disgusted with the fact that this is supposed to be based on Poe's short story. One of Poe's greatest feats was how vivid he made his surroundings. Even though the original story was one of the shortest he wrote, the reader has a vivid, almost hallucinatory experience of the setting. The setting in this sad attempt at a re-write was such a wasted opportunity. It could have been great--crumbling city! Alligator infested waters! Debauchery club! Sumptuous but decrepit apartment at the top of a tower! Castle! However, even with all these elements, I never got a sense of what the character's surroundings looked like. Whoever wrote this needs a lesson in showing, and whoever the editor was needs a new job.

I tried really hard, but I couldn't get far in the book. I couldn't find myself interested. It sounded interesting (with Poe and the masque ideas) but I couldn't care less about Araby or her friend or Elliot. I'm sorry, but just no. I might retry but do not care right now.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I got to chapter 11. I didn't understand this world, I didn't get a clear impression of any character (though from other reviews I gather that the dad is a time-traveling something or other - he might be ok) and I wasn't excited about renewing it, finishing it, or heaven forbid, reading more of the series.

If I had to sum this book up in one word it would be "fun". Wittily written with a great central character in Thursday Next, the literary detective, and a strangely believable alternative version of the UK this book was a joy to read. It also helps that it features one of my favourite books ,Jane Eyre, as part of the plot, when her future is threatened by a master criminal who has stolen technology which allows him to enter fictional worlds and kidnap the characters. Full of word play, and with plenty of action, I highly recommend it and intend to read more of the series as soon as I can get my hands on them.

This was another book I feel had extreme potential yet ultimately failed to deliver. I don't feel that the back story was developed enough for the reader to truly understand why it impacted the present storyline and there were too many subplots that were,in my opinion, underdeveloped and unexplained for them to all weave together smoothly.

Confession Time: I've never read Jane Eyre. I've also never read anything else by Bronte either. It's not really because I don't want to, it's because I've never really made those novels a priority when there's so much else to read out there. 
 I don't think my lack of reading Bronte impeded my enjoyment of this book though. The Eyre Affair is a well-written mystery story where wit and love of literature abound. It's set in an alternate universe where the dodo is the pet of choice, an aunt can get caught inside a poem, fictional characters can be kidnapped, and Shakespeare's Richard III is treated like the Rocky Horror Picture Show. 
 I'm not sure I would agree with the critic who compared Thursday Next to Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Harry Potter. But it was still a decent, albeit slow-paced, read.

Enjoyable and quite clever, this book reminds me a bit of Douglas Adams' "Hitchhiker's Guide" series. I wasn't blown away, but was intrigued enough to probably read more of Fforde's "Tuesday Next" books. Unfortunately, it also reminded me that I've never read any Charlotte Bronte (or, for that matter, Jane Austen). Might have liked it more if I knew all the references (I did love all the Shakespearean stuff in it)!
Una montana rusa de emociones. Viajes en el tiempo, mucha literatura, hombres lobo, asesinatos, guerra... Lo tiene todo. Thursday Next esta convirtiendose en mi siguiente heroina.

Vampires that sparkle? What about exploding into flame in sunlight? And if you can live forever, why the hell would you choose to be in high school, which most of us hated? I rate this book a huge yawn.

Im going to give it two stars because, out of the four books, this one is the best. This one has the original story and, well, if youre into young love and that sort of stuff, this will keep you interested. Also, the vampire is quite a gentleman, thats a plus. Its an OK book.

I don't like romances, and the whole idea of a vampire being totally un-dangerous being the PLOT of the story is just boring. Perhaps if Edward was a more classic vampire that eats flesh and pounces on anything and everything, then perhaps I would have enjoyed this better. One star. Could have done better, Stephenie Meyer...

EUGH. 
 there is no end to how much bad I can say about this book, but what I hated the most was just how badly written it was. 
 I understand that it's YA, but there's no excuse for how simplistic this book is. 
 The characters are obtuse and Bella's only personality traits are "clumsy" and "in love with Edward." She is a perfect example of a Mary Sue protagonist. 
 I just... 
 I can't even think about this book long enough to review it properly.

Didn't love it but I didn't hate it either. 
 The Cursed Child is one of those in-between books for me. I really enjoyed reading it but it just didn't blow me away. I've never read anything formatted this way before so it took some getting used to but after a while it didn't bother me. 
 What bothered me was that the plot kind of felt like it was all over the place and at times, I really didn't care much for some of the characters. Loved Scorpius though!
