reference_books.review_text:
The Rosie Project was a cute, quick read. 
 I liked it but didn't love it. I can see why so many people loved this book but I found that while I really liked Don's character I wasn't truly invested in the story. 
 I am interested in reading the sequel though!

reference_books.review_text:
3-3.5 Stars 
 Dark. Seductive. Poetic. Magical. 
 There are a lot of words that could be used to describe this book but above all else, it's bittersweet. 
 I had trouble rating this because I really enjoyed the first half. Sadly, the second half didn't hold up as well. 
 Wintersong is a beautifully written, slow-burn story with a slightly rushed ending. I wasn't a huge fan of the romance nor did I care too much for the main character after a while. 
 I've heard this was originally supposed to be an adult novel and I can't help but feel like that would have suited the second half of the story much better.

reference_books.title: Ghost Gifts (Ghost Gifts #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This was my Kindle First pick for February. It was good despite being a bit slow to start and predictable. I liked the flashbacks and mystery surrounding Missy's death..even though I figured out who her killer was early on. 
 I found the suspense lacking and the romance left much to be desired but Ghost Gifts was still an enjoyable read.

reference_books.title: Pines (Wayward Pines, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This is certainly a page-turner however, in the end it's nothing special. I think my problem was that I had watched the first 3 or 4 episodes of the show last year and while there are some differences, I didn't care about Ethan wandering around (while constantly being beat up) trying to figure out what was wrong with the town. I just wanted to get to the action. Had I not seen part of the show I probably would have been hooked from the start. Thankfully, once I got about halfway through I became more invested in the story. 
 I wasn't a huge fan of the writing style and there is a lot that just doesn't add up. 
 The ending was a bit far-fetched but good enough to consider continuing the series. I'm going to be optimistic and hope that it can only get better from here.

book_a.title: Sleeping Giants (Themis Files, #1)
book_a.user_review:
4.5 Stars 
 I can't even articulate how much I enjoyed this book. And after that epilogue well, I need more. Going into this I wasn't aware it was the start of a series (I probably should have known but...) and by the last page I was desperately hoping that there was more to come. 
 I have to say what I loved most about Sleeping Giants is that the book is told through interviews, journal entries and the occasional news article. Now, this isn't something I'd normally go for but it worked spectacularly well here. 
 The interviewer is never named so you really have no idea who he is or what his intentions really are which adds a nice flare of mystery and (at times) a bit of apprehension. 
 If you've been eyeing Sleeping Giants but have yet to pick it up, you really should. It's an engrossing book with such an interesting concept. I mean...giant robot parts are being unearthed that are presumably of alien origin due to being thousands of years old and far too technologically advanced for that time period let alone right now. Need I say more? 
 Side note..the hardcover is beautiful both with and (definitely) without the dust jacket. 
 April 2017 please hurry up!

sample_reviews.review_text:
this book was fuckin LIT thank u book of the month i am forever indebted 
 it was a wild ride start 2 finish and the EPILOGUE SLAYED LIKE WTF
I liked this, and feel like it may end up a five star book when I let it sit for awhile.
Thoroughly enjoyable and creative sci-fi novel. Interesting concept and characters but a bit hard to follow occasionally. 4.5 stars.

The premise of this story is that we get informed, in a series of case files, the events that led to the United States finding a giant alien robot which had been buried underneath the earth thousands upon thousands of years ago. They put the robot together and thus begins political pandemonium as you can imagine seeing as humans see anything as a weapon. I had previously read dossier-style books before - they seem to be the 'letter writing' style of the late 1800s (The Time Machine, Dracula, etc) as many authors today choose to do their books as such however despite some succeeding (Illuminae is a great example), Sleeping Giants missed the mark by a mile. This book is a quick read as it feels like you're reading a movie script, if you've ever read a script or a play you understand the general gist. We are presented with a series of interviews done by an unnamed man who seems to be the puppet master of the rest of the group. 
 The main issue that I had with this book was the utter lack of the human element. The point of a book is usually a connection between the reader and the writer; the writer attempts to make the reader feel something and the reader accepts this and internalizes it. However this book was so disconnected, the format made it even worse given that the characters were so stereotypical and lacking in dimension. The bad people were all bad, the clever people were always clever and you do not get to understand the why behind the decisions. There needs to be a balance between characters and plot and here the scale tipped drastically. 
 So we follow 2 pilots of the giant statue/weapon and these characters were absolutely painful to read. The plot of this book is ridiculous, which is fine, this is sci-fi, plots are meant to be ridiculous but it was all plot, plot, plot, the entire time and the human element was not woven throughout the novel which left the reader alienated. I cannot tell you how incredibly let down I felt, the disappointment was palpable because the premise held such promise and I was so excited to read this. I believe this is a debut novel so I can see how Mr. Neuvel will grow, he knows how to do plots, he just needs to learn to bring the reader to his characters. I also think this format does him no favors; this is truly better suited for a big blockbuster script than a piece of literature.

This was exactly the sci-Fi book that I have been waiting for! 
 Normally I loathe stories told from alternating viewpoints. AND add in interview style!? Oh hell no. I am glad I didn't know that before I ordered it as my BOTM, because then I would have missed out on reading an amazing book! 
 Young Rose gets into a bicycle accident and wakes up in the palm of a giant hand. Intrigued, she becomes a physicist when she grows up and is tasked with cracking the hands " code." More alien/robot body parts begin to be found all over the world. What are the parts for? Who left them here? 
 I still have sooo many questions after reading this book and can't wait to read the sequel! The biggest question being WHO IS THE NARRATOR?!!!
This book is so fucking boring. It took sheer determination to finish it.

I just am not the biggest fan of these stories told through files and written or audio records. They lack the suspense and drama of the more traditional narrative. It's harder to engage with the characters. So even though I found the subject really interesting, I found the reading experience a little dull.

I feel like this book was mostly setting up for a sequel because I kept waiting for something to happen or something to be explained. The premise of discovering parts of an ancient robot built by aliens intrigued me, but after a while, the interesting science bits decreased and were replaced by character development. That's fine - I love a good character-driven story - but I couldn't help but question why the nameless interviewer/someone with clearly massive amounts of power was interested whether two people were sleeping together? 
 Again, this all might be explained in the next book. The epilogue made me widen my eyes quite a bit. Despite some of my issues with this book, my curiosity will definitely make me pick up its sequel!
Very imaginative. The writing style of all interviews was interesting and unique.

Terrible! Narrative style fails massively in most sections but the major problem is the absence of substance. Once the first chapter is over, everything else is useless fluff. Characters are weak caricatures with no depth and the repetitive narrative just gets more annoying as the book progresses. Only hope was that there'd be a surprise twist where all the whiny 'heroes' would be killed off! Disappointingly, that didn't happen. Instead the ending was a generic, cliche crapfest.

book_b.title: Long May She Reign
book_b.user_review:
3-3.5 Stars 
 Long May She Reign is an enjoyable standalone fantasy with minor romance, a murder mystery and a gorgeous cover! 
 Freya - twenty third in line for the throne - was never meant to be queen. She's never quite fit in with the royals in court and would much rather experiment in her laboratory than attend any court functions. When the King hosts a fancy banquet for his birthday Freya and her friend slip away to her lab with every intention of returning before the party's end. Time manages to get away from them and the next thing they know Freya's father comes barging in with guards looking for her with some very unfortunate news - Freya is now queen. 
 What I liked: 
 Aside from Fitzroy? SCIENCE. 
 There isn't much romance which is usually one of the main plot points in fantasy novels. While I'm all for a good romance, the lack of it in this case was refreshing. 
 I loved that Freya has social anxiety and for the most part I like how it was portrayed. When she becomes Queen, it doesn't just disappear. She still struggles with it but eventually - and with the help of her best friend Naomi - she is able to overcome it, bit by bit. 
 Despite not knowing who she can trust and with advisors who steamroll over any idea she may have, Freya loves her people and despises the way the royals treat them. She strives to becomes the type of Queen her people need. 
 What I didn't: 
 Lack of world-building. 
 Not much action until the end. 
 The big reveal - it felt anticlimactic and I wasn't a fan of how it came to be. 
 Was expecting something darker considering...mass murder. 
 While Freya's refusal to listen to anyone is both a pro and a con, it was quite frustrating at times. 
 *ARC provided by Edelweiss in exchange for an honest review.

sample_reviews.review_text: Summary: this one is not for me. A stand alone YA is a lovely oddity and there are some things in here that folks will love. I'm not one of them - the world building was too thin and too many questions kept pulling me out of the story.

See my full review and much more on my blog 
 KissinBlueKaren 
 Oh I wanted to love LONG MAY SHE REIGN. I honestly saw the cover and thought I needed this book. The cover is quite gorgeous. Then I saw the author and remembered that I have read Rhiannon Thomas's 
 A WICKED THING 
 . She writes good YA but it is a bit more like young YA. Reading the synopsis made me think maybe this book would be more mature. I was right and wrong about that. Although parts of this story felt fantasy book familiar it was well written and had me really absorbed in the story. It is a stand-alone, so right away I made two assumptions. 
 1. There won't be a ton of world building. It's okay because there was just enough to set the scene for me. 
 2. There will be a super happy ending that ties up all the loose ends. That didn't happen but the last line had a big impact on me. Maybe the best last line I have ever read. 
 I had grown quite attached to all the characters and there was this major issue not resolved, at least not in the way I was hoping it would be. I will say that I really enjoyed reading it. In fact I was a little sad when it was over because I wanted more. 
 I didn't like Freya right away. I didn't like her to have social anxiety and I didn't like her to be so science-y. I can't remember the last time I read about a character with social anxiety. There just isn't enough of this topic in YA. I was wrong in my initial assessments of her. The social anxiety was well handled in my opinion, and the science really came in handy. I know some would argue that the social anxiety seems t just go away, but I think in growing into her role Freya found ways to handle it.I do wish the author would have explored how she did it a bit more. 
 Freya also has this super chill cat which at first I didn't like but he grew on me. Freya also has a good female fiend that I was automatically suspicious of. While I am happy to say that my suspicion was unfounded, I know exactly why I felt that way. It is rare to see a genuine female friendship without ulterior motives. I came to realize that this book was full of surprises for me. Freya grows up a lot throughout this story and her transformation is pretty significant. There is so much I loved about her by the end of this story that it was hard to let her go. I do like how everything ended up, and that it was a bit open ended. 
 I am not even going to touch upon the love interest. I have very mixed feelings about it. I enjoyed reading this enough to recommend it. The mystery of who-done-it felt second to seeing this girl succeed in ruling the kingdom. Although the mystery didn't hook me, the surprises about Freya herself were enough to keep me interested.

At one point, main character thinks to herself something along the lines of "The killer must have a motive"! And then she thinks this realization is so brilliant that she then feels the need to write that sentence down. 
 This is when I decided that I no longer felt a need to continue reading this book. DNF at 20%.

3.5-4 stars. 
 I enjoyed it more than I thought. My only problem is that it felt too slow. It was easy to skip some pages and I didn't miss anything important.

This was a surprisingly acceptable offering from this author (I didn't like her other books). I would rate this 2.5 stars. I liked the emphasis on science - that's fresh, although I did wonder how much she could have learned since it was self-taught. But that's fine. I liked the Court intrigues - MC realising that she's out of her depth. But more could have been done with just the awareness of Court intrigues! Finding out more about her fellow nobles, talking to them, especially if you want the MC to be seen as just. And the ending was just... it was ok, but it doesn't stand up to consideration/close scrutiny.

Actual rating: 2.5 
 First line: "A hundred doves burst out of the pie." 
 The premise of Long May She Reign is an awesome one, but the execution was... not good. This story was just SO. BORING. There was almost zero action, and when it looked like there would be some, everything was handled so diplomatically and nicely and with words. The antagonist was storming the palace and was basically brought down with a light show 
 I really liked Freya at the beginning. She is super into science and logical reasoning, which is honestly, quite refreshing, but then she got caught up in the dullness that snatched the rest of the book, and made some dumb assumptions along the way. Also, the romance, if you can really call it that, didn't need to be in the story at all. 
 Despite the heavy focus on female friendships (which is ALWAYS a plus), the premise of an entire court being killed off and a girl 23rd in line for the throne becoming a sudden queen, was anticlimactic and uninteresting. I love political fantasies, but this one wasn't done very well.

There's nothing wrong with this book other than the fact that it was mind-numbingly dull. The characters, the plot, the setting, everything is okay, but I just didn't care. I got half-way through and skimmed through the rest because nothing was happening. 
 A few murder attempts here, some subtle flirting here and there, a couple of obvious betrayals, blah, blah,meh-ish ending.

How the book sounded: 
 What it felt like: 
 I had so much faith in this book... but, long story short, it let me down. Long May She Reign sounded as if it were going to be a mind boggling journey of medieval political warfare. The book, however, was completely off its rocker when it came to pacing, world building, and the characters themselves. I could bite at the premise. The 23rd in line getting the throne? I wanted to know why and how and how it was possibly going to work. Instead, I was given a long trek through a tar pit with minimal character development as a life line. It wasn't worth it. Opps.

Reader thoughts: I liked most things about this book. 
 The premise reminds me of The Goblin Emperor, except that this book is better. Here are my reasons. 
 1st, Freya is a human girl, not a male half-goblin. So, she's automatically easier for me to identify with. 
 2nd, Freya is in the middle of the danger, not sitting and listening to everyone else talk about danger. She does her own investigating, not just send a spy master to search it out for her. 
 3rd, Freya knew a bunch of the people who died and was grieving for them in the middle of trying to take the throne, which makes her job that much harder. 
 4th, the romance was better. 
 I still think this book fell short of where it could have been, though. Freya treated Queenship like a part-time job rather than a lifestyle. She naively (and immaturely) got mad at her councilors when they didn't explain an extra tax to her before putting it in place, but she never asked! 
 She has short meetings where they say, "And we'll plan those funerals." Then end. Freya's only input is that she wants the funeral to include all 400 people who died rather than doing 400 individual funerals. (It sounds cost-efficient to me, but the councilors complained. Stupid councilors.) Freya didn't ask who was planning which part or what her duties were. She didn't ask when or who was invited or anything else. She just let them all plan it on their own. Yes, this is her first week being a queen, but you can't get angry with others for your own faults. 
 Freya should have been overseeing more. Did she ever meet with the palace head cook or head groom or head guard or anyone? Did she meet her staff or know how much money was in her treasury or know where her food came from? She kept running to her lab to experiment (later proven to be very important, true) without telling anyone. She should have had guards following her everywhere, and she didn't. No one told her where to be or gave her an agenda 12 hours long. The only queenly things she did were attending council meetings and giving a speech. 
 She also (2 or 3 times) said something like, "I'm queen, and so I get to do what I want!" or "I'm queen, and so you have to do what I say!" This is not a valid argument. Somebody fire her. Grr. 
 Other than that, she was good with science and actually learned things. She didn't get too goo-goo eyed over Fitz. She had anxiety attacks but managed them to her best ability. She suspected everyone but didn't let that keep her from working with them. She was merciful but not lenient (still banished the poisoner in the end). 
 Writer thoughts: RT emphasizes certain details by explaining what the characters are NOT doing. When Freya walks past a crowd, once she notes that "they didn't bow." Other times it is, "They didn't laugh at me," or even, "They didn't attack." It's a great way to show the readers what the MC (or pov character) is looking for and noticing without explicitly stating thoughts. It was used well.

For a member of a royal court, no matter how far down the food chain, Freya seems to be pretty slow. Making the same mistakes, getting herself in trouble and on purpose being a disappointment. Unfortunately it is that way. No actual sense of responsibility, only insolence and selfishness of wanting to figure it out. Couldn't finish this one. Freya in my eyes sounded more like a daughter of a peasant, that was not taught anything in life (other than chemistry obviously).

book_a.title: Jayber Crow
book_a.user_review: Started slow, just like their lives. Ultimately, I'm glad I stuck with it.

sample_reviews.review_text: An absolutely stunning book. Fictional and epic, this work describes life on the grand scale from the eyes of a "balding, bachelor, barber" from the turn of the century until the 1970's. Must read! He grasp of small town life and how it intersects with the larger world, the passing of time, farming, families, war, love, the economy, and all things that are American is astounding.
Beautifully written story of the life of jayber crow, barber of port William, Ky.
It starts out to be hopeful and contemplative but by the middle it gets to be tedious and philosophical. I didn't finish it.

Jayber Crow; you reprehensible little worm. STFU and MYOB. 
 "Thou Shalt Not Bare False Witness" 
 All you had to do was cut hair. No one expected much from you and that's what they got. That is, with the exception of two people you stabbed in the back. . 
 Your mentor. You walked out on the man who taught you your craft, gave you a start, treated you like a man. Not a word goodbye. Well, ain't you the master of your own fate? Just a clean walk down the road. 
 You take your gal on a date and decide you have to climb out the bathroom window rather than asking/ telling her "I've seen something I don't like. Can we leave?" Instead you disappear leaving her to wonder "Where the F--K did he go?" You leave her in a bar for Christ's sake. How long do you think it would take her to worry; to even take your car; and in her mind, abandon your sorry ass? Her not knowing if you were laid out in some ditch beaten to a bloody pulp. 
 Knowing these things about you, my skin would crawl to sit in your chair and have your hands touch me. You are a user. 
 This unrequited love is a pile of crap. You are no better than the other town gossips. What do you know about what happens behind Mattie and Troy's closed doors? They did go on to have another child, presumably consensual. "Thou Shalt Not Covet Thy Neighbor's Wife" 
 There was a chance to stick with the gal who showed you the most attention. The one you almost said you loved. (Remember her?) However you decided to yearn over an unattainable, 10 to 15 yr younger married woman, that you fell in love with while she was in high school. Fortunately you didn't act on those whims. People in your neck of the woods get shot over that kind of stuff. 
 You give Troy the shaft. What ever his faults, he is a hard working man, His desires are to provide. He is a product of the post-war economy and the Judaeo-Christian ethic of the world existing for the use of man? (Does Trump vs The Antiquities Act ring a bell?) 
 Following the Depression and WWII it was time for the good life. The banking and manufacturing industry was not about to revert to an agrarian economy. Thinking it was the smart thing to do many farmers bought into the idea of accumulation, debt, and the industrialization of farming. Family farms died or were bought out. We are still engaged in that struggle. No excuses for his running around, but one can only imagine the internal stresses of being married to Mattie. She wasn't strong enough to be his wife. They were not a good match. It can't all be laid on him. 
 I come to wonder what some connections may be to Christian legend and mythology? 
 Moses among the reeds more than the Noah story. Not a baby, but lost and adrift. 
 The wandering J.C. returns home. 
 The laying of hands. A shave and a haircut. A splash of holy water. A man feels reborn. 
 Is Mattie the Mary Magdalena figure only reversed, with J.C. standing at her death bed as she becomes the embodiment of virtue. 
 J.C. forgoing any meaningful relationship with a woman. Basking in his illusions of love for the whore that married the devil. How could she? Doesn't she realize he's no good for her? What does she see in him? He forgives her. 
 The Devil destroys Eden. 
 Isn't it odd that Berry would put these two out of character events into the story? Jayber never really returned to them as a catalyst for further comment or change. I wonder what the point was. Young man indiscretions? Wild oats? 
 Referring to Mattie as a whore may be over the top but I wanted to drive home the consideration she had fallen from grace and separated herself from the nosy, interfering, small town morality around her. That she wasn't pure as driven snow. 
 I do look at Jayber as having a positive impact on the community. In many cases he gave a moment of pause before events spiraled out of control. The barber shop transforming into a cathedral. A place for men to take respite from the rigors of labor around them. 
 Virgil, my dad's barber, and contemporary, watched us three boys grow up for awhile. (I guess Dad and Virgil went to high school together,) Flat tops all around. Butch Wax. A flip in the front. A slap of smell good juice before we were let go. Driving home in the Phoenix heat in our 56 Chevy Bel Air with the windows rolled down. If Mom didn't like 'em, back we'd go for a redo. There was Hell to Pay and embarrassment for Dad. Virgil was a fast learner. Late 50's Peoria AZ. I think the bldg still stands.

This probably deserves more stars. It's the life story of a man from childhood to late in life, living in Appalachia and observing how the world changes over the course of his life. There are some really beautiful insights, the writing is excellent. But it was just. So. Slow. It's definitely a book you have to take the time to slowly digest. I think I'm just in the wrong stage of life for it right now.
Couldn't finish it!

I know Berry is a hero to many and practically a demi-god where I work, but he completely lost me toward the end of the novel. As a Christian I like the subtle working in of faith issues early in the novel, but the last section (15% of the book or so) just gets preachy, annoying, and predictable. While I'll agree with him on favoring small farms over industrialized farms, his version gives this "moral right will win" idea which is simply not the reality we see. Immoral industrialization of our food and farms will not stop if we think good intentions alone will overcome them. Yes, people suffer because of them. But the industry does not care, so what do we learn from this? Nothing.
A gem of a book. A balm to the soul and a lesson on the failings of man and the beauty of life at the same time. I know I will want to read Jayber Crow more than once.

3.5 
 Read it in AP English.
I took my time reading this, savoring and re reading passages. Wendell Berry weaves beautiful stories .

book_b.title: The Silver Linings Playbook
book_b.user_review: I have to say I liked the movie better. I did appreciate that everything wrapped up nicely.

sample_reviews.review_text: I never leave books unfinished, but I read the first half and just can't go any further. Why is it narrated in that voice?

Not my cup of tea... perhaps because I cannot see Jennifer Lawrence as Tiffany at all - far too young - and I cannot escape the image of the characters from the movie and create those images in my mind for myself. I also do not like this family. They have so many unresolved issues - the mother needs to leave the father and admit he is an alcoholic, etc... I also do not think that this story ends well down the road. How can Pat ever learn to behave properly when his father behaves so badly? How can Pat expect to improve when the family covers and shushes and brushes aside all the problems them have? That is the big lesson from literature, isn't it - that lies and deceit, within yourself or your family, is a corrosive aspect which destroys lives - from Hester and Chillingworth to Gatsby, right? 
 Beyond that, I do not like the narrative style. I am at a loss why this would be chosen to be made into a film... Finished but disappointed.

I thought Quick did a brilliant job of voicing his characters, but my favorite librarian thought it was just sloppy writing. I saw the movie first and don't think it really took anything away from the reading experience.

It was sweet, not as much information given than in the film, but an overall good read. 
 I really liked Pat, the narrator, and was rooting for him throughout.

I can't believe I'm saying this, but I actually liked the movie better??? Very strange. 
 The biggest differences between the book and movie was: 
 1) The fact that the characters' personalities seemed bigger, more vibrant, more like caricatures in the movie. Which I really liked. 
 2) In the book, Pat was not aware that he had been in a neural institution for four years. He was convinced only a few months had passed. This is a significant plot point to change and changes the conversation on the way he copes with his past and mental illness. I don't know whether this change is good, bad or neutral, but it definitely needs pointed out. 
 Also I feel like I've cheated and have to confess that I listened to most of this on audiobook. Is that fine??? I feel dirty.

This is one of those books that gets all sorts acclaim and people love. While I didn't hate the book I sure didn't love it either. My first issues were the charactets. I didn't feel anything for them. not love or hate. nothing. I had no vested interest in the outcome in their lives. I had a hard time following their motivations. I didn't believe they would or act the way they did. Even when given disclosure I felt disatisfied. who I did like was cliff therapist. He is an ideal for a therapist I would want to have. Matt's use of the ambiguity of time was probably the most interesting part of the book. How long was Pat in the bad place? The revelation was a bit of a surprise. I will read more of Matt's books as I do respect the guy and think as he grows as a writer his novels will appeal to me more

This is a bittersweet story about people and relationships, friends and family, and connections. It is a story packed with the many different ways humans can love. There are laugh out loud moments, yet others so sobering it feels grave. 
 Pat Peoples is as captivating to read as Holden Caulfield.
A fun, easy read! Emotion evoking and though provoking..definitely appealing to a wide audience.

A book and movie review will be up on my YouTube channel. 
 http://www.youtube.com/user/jordanmon...

I loved this book it was moving and funny, a very heartfelt read. You fall in love with the characters and learn to have compassion for those who struggle with mental illness. If you've seen the movie the book is still a worthwhile read.

reference_books.title: Fight Club
reference_books.review_text:
Ho deciso di dare un'altra possibilita a Palahniuk, mi sembrava impossibile che mi avesse fatto una cosi brutta impressione, quindi ho letto il suo libro d'esordio. 
 Fight Club mantiene, anzi dovrei dire preannuncia, lo stile che ho trovato in "Gang Bang", e che continua a non piacermi: secco, crudo, un lessico molto spesso basso, ed estremamente ripetitivo. 
 La trama l'ho affrontata con molto meno entusiasmo rispetto a "Gang Bang", e come sospettavo mi e risultata ancora piu estranea e lontana, estremamente irreale. 
 Pero e stata gestita meglio, e il colpo di scena finale (ma e un cliche di Palahniuk, cercare di farti rimanere a bocca aperta alla fine?) meno immaginabile ancora rispetto a "Gang Bang", quindi darei una stellina in piu. 
 Rimango comunque molto delusa da quello che pensavo mi colpisse.

reference_books.title: The Giver (The Giver, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
The giver e il primo capitolo di una quadrilogia distopica: come tutte le serie distopiche, siamo in un futuro non ben definito, in un mondo che ha perso qualcosa rispetto al nostro, con la popolazione ordinatamente suddivisa e catalogata, e con il necessario protagonista che e diverso dagli altri. Dopo un po' le distopie si assomigliano tutte, eppure questa mi ha preso abbastanza da farmi proseguire nella lettura: ho fumato The giver in un pomeriggio, e subito ho letto Gathering blue, e per questo la consiglio anche ai poco amanti del genere. 
 In questo caso, abbiamo una comunita resa insensibile per scelta di comodo, e un ragazzino, Jonas, che e diverso dagli altri, e tutti lo sanno. Si adattera al futuro a cui la comunita e la sua diversita lo hanno destinato, o si ribellera?

reference_books.title: La ragazza del treno
reference_books.review_text:
Ho letto questo giallo sull'onda del successo che aveva avuto, e come ogni volta in cui leggo un libro a causa del successo presso il pubblico rimango delusa. 
 Incentrato su tre donne, non saprei dire quale delle tre e meno negativa come personaggio. Le figure maschili sono parimenti deboli e grette. Oltre a personaggi che meritano giudizi impietosi, non ho trovato alcun elemento che possa ascrivere il libro al rango di bel giallo. 
 La storia e piatta, pervasa della sciatteria della protagonista, priva di significato: mi aspettavo un'atmosfera completamente diversa, malinconica e sognante, dato il titolo, pensavo che il treno acquisisse un significato particolare e invece niente, semplicemente una debole ubriacona svogliata che va avanti e indietro per fingere una vita ormai distrutta che non e capace di ricostruire. 
 Due stelline ampiamente meritate, non comprendo minimamente il motivo di tanto successo.

reference_books.title: Shatter Me (Shatter Me, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Prima puntata di una trilogia distopica, Shatter Me si apre su una Juliette Ferrars quasi amebica, uno zombie ridotto all'apatia all'interno di una cella. Juliette non entra in contatto con un essere umano da giorni, mesi, anni: non ha mai conosciuto il sapore del tocco di un altro essere. Anzi, una volta si, e sarebbe stato meglio non le fosse successo. 
 Come tutti i primi capitoli dei distopici che ho letto, si dipana attraverso tappe fisse: il mondo in rovina, il rapimento, un dominatore che intende utilizzare la protagonista come arma per i suoi scopi, una protagonista inizialmente inerme e inerte che acquista consapevolezza di se pian piano, il complice casualmente immune ai suoi poteri, la fuga, il combattimento, e l'arrivo nell'oasi, con il complice in fin di vita, in cui scopre un mondo sotterraneo di gente come lei. Un'oasi molto molto simile alla scuola per X-Men di Charles. 
 Per quando riguarda lo stile, non ho apprezzato le ripetizioni e l'assenza di punteggiatura, nonostante abbiano ampiamente adempiuto al loro intento consistente nel far sentire la confusione e il baratro provati da Juliette. 
 Credo che provero a leggere anche il seguito, principalmente per capire come va a finire il triangolo amoroso lasciato presagire dall'autrice.

reference_books.title: Twilight / Life and Death (Twilight, #1, 1.75)
reference_books.review_text:
Mmmmmmmhhhhh. Mhm. Diciamo che, avendo amato Twilight, ed avendo in mente Bella ed Edward, e stato abbastanza difficile leggere la stessa identica storia, la storia di Bella ed Edward, recitata da Beau ed Edythe, primo perche appunto avevo in mente loro due e questi due invece erano per forza di cose diversi, e secondo perche oltre al sesso ha cambiato pure il carattere e le dinamiche del loro rapporto, un pochino, e questo sarebbe anche un bene, ma me li rifaceva risuonare stridenti, quasi estranei alla storia. Sul finale invece e andata molto meglio, perche era un finale diverso rispetto all'originale, che era molto piu adatto a Beau ed Edythe, anche se estremamente frettoloso: avrei preferito che le cose non si svolgessero cosi precipitosamente, e sono sicura lo avrebbe preferito anche Beau. 
 Calo un velo pietoso invece su quasi tutti gli altri personaggi, a partire da Bonnie Black (la sequenza finale e da facepalm), passando per Royal, Jessamine, il povero Earnest e pure McKayla, finendo con la scena della caccia, ridicola: le tre ragazze a inseguire la tipaccia pericolosa, e i due uomini a inseguire il pivello. 
 In ogni caso, comunque, con il ribaltamento dei sessi, questo libro ha messo in luce quando Twilight sia effettivamente maschiocentrico.

book_a.title: The Left Hand of God (The Left Hand of God, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Thomas Cale e un accolito che i Redentori stanno educando al Monastero, assieme a migliaia di suoi coetanei, simili a lui. Ma lui e differente da tutti loro: e a lui che il Redentore Bosco riserva la maggior quantita di punizioni e la miglior istruzione. 
 A causa di una disgustosa scoperta, Cale fugge con un paio di suoi compagni, nemmeno lui sa se siano suoi amici o meno; dopo alcune peripezie, riesce ad entrare nelle grazie del Cancelliere Vipond e della famiglia Ferrazzi, una delle piu potenti famiglie del regno. 
 La vicenda e abbastanza banale, gia sentita: il solito ragazzo bistrattato ed educato ad essere una macchina da guerra che fugge, grazie alle sue capacita si mantiene in vita e riesce a trovare un altro posto nel mondo. Quello che e interessante e il finale, e la figura di Thomas Cale. Il finale e scontato fin dal titolo, ma e talmente aperto che e impossibile non voler sapere come prosegue la storia nel secondo volume della trilogia. Molto avvincente dunque. 
 Thomas Cale e un ossimoro ambulante, non si riesce ad inquadrarlo: e ferino, non teme la morte, e un assassino spietato e indifferente, ha una mente estremamente fredda e calcolatrice, eppure rischia la vita per una ragazza sconosciuta, e si innamora di Arbell al punto da perdere la razionalita. 
 E quindi non sono riuscita capire se la Mano Sinistra di Dio alla fine sterminera l'umanita oppure no, Cale sarebbe capace di fare entrambe le cose con la medesima probabilita.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I'm surprised that this book gets so many negative reviews. I read the entire book in one day which is a pretty good indicator that it is a really good book. If any criticism could be made it is that the book is to short. 
 The book is mainly character driven. The main character is really strong. Not the whinny powerless hero we see in some books. He is a bit fatalistic, which I like.

This has to be the strangest book I have ever read. No... that's not true nothing can beat T'is Pity She's A Whore, or the absurdest play Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead, but this came pretty close. I think what really threw me was that I could never guess what was going to happen, even when I was only a page away. And it wasn't just the major events. I didn't guess anything, not the small character developments nor the subplots. That in itself was strange. Infinitely magnified when the ending hit. I did not guess what was going to happen, I'm still not sure what did happen and I'm really not sure I liked what happened. 
 Hoffman has already written two other novels, The Wisdom of Crocodiles predicting the collapse of the world financial system and The Golden Age of Censorship a black comedy, and if I had known this before hand I don't think I would have bothered with The Left Hand of God. There was defiantly a black skepticism underlying everything. Without giving too much away I would describe this novel like a bad dream that you thought you had woken up from but find out you haven't. Continuously. 
 So, unless you like surprise ending that are more surprise than satisfying, and you can deal with twisted realities that leave you feeling lost, confused and a little bit angry then this is the book for you. Otherwise I would advice steering clear. 
 (It is a good read. I think I was expecting something else which is why the book ended up disappointing me. But I'm sure I'm sure with an open mind you will be able to enjoy the story more for what it is rather then for what it isn't. Make sense?) 
 Original review published on my blog http://mistysmess.blogspot.com/

This had an interesting use of omniscient narrator. It's been a while since I've read one, and it was... like all of the events were being reported back to me in a very dispassionate manner. It was put to good effect at times, of course, fleshing out the world, and diving into the heads of non-major characters. But the flip side is the lack of passion, I suppose. 
 It wasn't a bad read, and certainly for those that enjoy their fantasy and read ridiculously fast, I'd say this could be explored despite not being to my exact taste. With that said, any die hard fantasy fans can give this one a miss.
I like the book over all but was not entirely taken with the lead character Cale which did ditract from the book overall. So will read the second book to see if the series is going anywhere.

Well, this was pretty horrible. 
 The prose was blunt, unrefined and written badly in third perspective, something that resulted in this four hundred pages long book feeling very long indeed. It also failed miserably in conveying the characters feelings and, in general, helping us get to know them. My feelings for every character in the whole damn book ranged from a fervent wish for them to die to just plain disinterest. 
 I practically went through it thinking, "Hell, I can write better than this. Why didn't I just write a novella or something myself and save some money in the process?" 
 And then we have the sexism... 
 Every woman in the book was either as useful as a sack of sand in the desert or a narrow minded, pathetic little daughter of a biscuit eater. Hoffman's description and the male characters treatment of one "fat", beautiful, useless girl was especially painful to read. 
 Adding to this some seriously lacking world-building, weird plot, a really special fucking snowflake of a protagonist, sexism and, BAM! you have the headache pill that is "The Left Hand of God" by Paul Hoffman.
Dark Fantasy

I remember this had a very good start. Then it alternated between good and bad moments, some of which unexplainable, like the female assassin who sees the main character for 10 minutes and rushes to him declaring her love. 
 Cale also looked pretty interesting, a genius in tactical prowess and warfare, while also being able to fight on his own like nobody else. One could say the part that it's said that he makes the plans for battle on his room and then they are sent to the battlefield as insane, but Napoleon actually planned his most formidable victory for days only using maps and reports. Of course, he adjusted it as necessary as reality demanded, so I suppose the Redeemers did the same. 
 The final battle is a copy and paste, in all aspects, from the battle of Agincourt. I only found this out many years later. I actually thought there was a sense of realism in that, and now I know why. 
 However, the thing that left me a bit bewildered was the fact this was being labeled around here as the "new Harry Potter" and intended for that audience. I couldn't really understand why was that so. There's plenty of swearing and graphic violence (including an autopsy on a living girl right in the beginning), some other mutilation, sex scenes and prostitution. 
 Totally baffled me as how they marketed this book.

Truths be told, I wanted so badly to enjoy this book because folks have been singing wild praises about this.The book begins well enough, thrust right into the middle of a strange world, the dark forbidding world of the Redeemers and we are introduced to the twisted Thomas Cale, the star of the book. Midway though, the settings shift outside the walls of this world and om there on, it just nosedives. The secondary characters are too washed out, the strangeness almost seems normal and the frequent switch over of POVs right in the middle of a scene disorients. 
 Well, by the end, the twist makes it almost a 3-star but, only almost. It languishes softly in the territory of intriguing, yes but not too interesting enough. 
 Here is where I compare this book with the critically acclaimed 8-part Buddha series by Osamu Tezuka. Exploring how Thomas Cale stacks up against Buddha - http://bit.ly/157woB7

Meh. 
 Shoots right out of the gates with a creepy cult in a massive holy war, and a seductive and mysterious world beyond the Sanctuary gates. However, the characters are nothing more than stereotypes and the pacing flatlines a third of the way in. Left Hand has aspirations to be a an archetypal Hero story, but quickly deteriorates into a blander take on Jim Butcher's honor and strategy driven Alera Codex. It reads as if Hoffman signed his three book deal halfway through the first manuscript and tried desperately to stretch a 300 page novel into a trilogy. I skimmed most of the second half just to get to the end, and will not be continuing on with this boring and tired story.

"The Sanctuary of the Redeemers is a vast and desolate place without joy or hope. Most of its occupants were taken there as boys and for years have endured the brutal regime of the Lord Redeemers whose cruelty and violence have one singular purpose - to serve in the name of the One True Faith. 
 In one of the Sanctuary's vast and twisting maze of corridors stands a boy. He is perhaps fourteen or fifteen years old - he is not sure and neither is anyone else. He has long-forgotten his real name, but now they call him Thomas Cale." 
 The Left Hand of God by Paul Hoffman has been held up to be one of the great fantasy debuts of 2010 and received rave reviews from other authors as well as more conventional reviewers. It received an extensive marketing campaign and was generally hailed before its release as one of those books that everyone MUST read. Unfortunately, since its release, many people have stepped forward to list the numerous ways in which it does not live up to the hype - and I'm afraid I must join their ranks. 
 There was some part of me almost determined to like The Left Hand of God, being as so many other people had declaimed the turgid prose, the stilted characterisation and the slightly baffling plot that leaves you wondering at the end why you have bothered to read four hundred odd pages when the main protagonist finds himself back where he started. However, this is a hard book to love - or even like very much. 
 Usually when writing a negative review I like to offer the points from the book that I did, at least, enjoy. Here I'm struggling to remember anything that moved my emotions. If all else fails and I can't find any positive elements to focus on I will retreat to the comfort of mentioning the cover art - but here we have the much-derided hooded man (and I still remain childishly amused by the fact that the book is called The Left Hand of God but the character on the front is carrying that honking great sword in his right hand! Still just me? Well, alright then...) 
 My most damning comment on this book is one of apathy: I could very easily have put The Left Hand of God down at any point and not felt too dismayed at never knowing what happens at the end. Let me put this into context - I can count on one hand the books I have not finished. I feel that if the author has gone to the trouble of writing a novel, then I should respect their effort and give it a fair chance. With Paul Hoffman's book it was only pig-headed stubbornness that had me turning the last page. 
 I did not enjoy the crazy mixed-up world building that had Memphis and York right next to each other. I do not know what Hoffman was trying to achieve: was he so lazy as to not be able to make up names for his cities? Or was he going for the truly symbolic and I just missed it? My over-riding impression is that Hoffman felt he was doing something ultra clever but it just came across as pretentious. 
 There have been a couple of books in recent times that I have read, wondering if he author (while writing the novel) had half an eye on the screenplay of the movie that would be made: The Da Vinci Code and Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows spring to mind. This book can now join their ranks. There are panoramic sweeping shots of the countryside described lovingly (a la The Lord of the Rings films); some market shots that bring to mind Tatooine; and some truly awful training montages that I can hear the inspirational 80s power chords for. 
 I hated the way that Hoffman dealt with women, including one cringe-making passage: 
 "Our skin must be without flaw, our hair shiny and manageable [which sounds like a hair care advert:], we must have wide bright eyes, our cheeks pink, our breasts round and large, our buttocks large and smooth and between our legs, under our arms, nor anywhere else except our heads were we to permit the growth of a single hair. We must be always interested and charming and always smell of flowers. We must never be angry or scold or be critical of other people, but kind and affectionate and always ready with kisses and tenderness." 
 "How," asked Vipond, "did you practise your... tenderness? If you had no men?" 
 "On each other, sir." 
 Oh come on, Mr Hoffman! Let's first objectify women as sex objects and then throw in a little casual titillation. Way to go! 
 And I leave you with another quote that caught my eye: "As for smoking - it is a childish affectation: a habit loathsome to the eye, hateful to the nose, harmful to the brain, dangerous to the lungs, causes the breath to stink and makes any man who takes it for long enough effeminate." That's right, kids: smoking is BAD. Hoffman's message here is extremely clumsy and almost shoe-horned into the plot for no good reason. 
 Harry Sidebottom (author of the Warrior of Rome series of books) states on the back of The Left Hand of God: "If you do not enjoy this book something has died in your soul." Well, I'm proud to say that my soul is completely dead - and Paul Hoffman killed it. Avoid this book.

book_b.title: Messenger (The Giver, #3)
book_b.user_review: Terzo capitolo della Saga, che secondo me sarebbe stato un buon finale.

sample_reviews.review_text: WHYYYY MATTY? WHY?

Matty grows up. Matty becomes the messenger to Leader (Jonas by any other name might not smell as sweet). Matty must go through Forest to reach Kira to bring her to Seer, her father. And then there's the ending. If the ending of The Giver left you frustrated, this might as well. Grr.
AAAAAAAAAHHH! The woods are alive!

This book set an 'ok' scene, but it didn't do a great job of tying things to The Giver. It felt more that Lowry was being pushed to finish off the series and just threw something out there to satisfy the masses. Not so much. And the ending! It felt entirely tacked on and unrealistic! I think that that was my major complaint: The other two books unnerved you because you could relate them to current society, where this one was more of a pathetic fantasy with scary forests that ate you.

All the "gifts", and nouns without 'the' in front really got on my nerve. The book had great potential. But lois didn't even explain why the forest 
 Or excuse me, "forest" 
 Was decomposing. She also didn't explain why all the people after trading were mean. Maybe she did and I wasn't paying attention, but this book was a little too cheesy for me.

WHY LOIS WHY? HOW COULD YOU? 
 THE ENDING I DIDN'T EXPECT THE ENDING TO BE LIKE THAT. 
 I liked this the most, so far. I haven't started reading Son. Coming from The Giver and Gathering Blue which already established a problem within their societies at the beginning of the stories, Messenger, rather Matt's village, seemed like the perfect village out of the three before the problem started creeping in. There were so much questions that the book did not answer, which made me want to read Son immediately. 
 The ending gripped my heart, really. I wasn't expecting that kind of ending.
Not as well developed as the first two. And I didn't like the ending! There was so much more that could have been developed.

I am glad that I have finished the series. Finally everything was tied up in a neat bow. I loved this series and am glad I read it. I hope the make the rest of the books into movies but I feel that they could combine the last three books into a single movie.
#3 in Giver series

I didn't have a big problem with this book, but as it's part of the series I expected it to feel like part of the series. 
 I adored the Giver and what I wanted to read was more about the community, how they dealt with the memories after Jonas left; I wanted to learn more about the committee and other people living in the community. 
 Instead we see Jonas as The Leader and using his seeing Beyond talents in a way that never truly made sense to me in terms of how it was revealed in The Giver. 
 The Giver series ended up being about magic and strange talents, rather than the amazing community created in the first novel, and that makes me so sad. 
 It wasn't the worst book ever, I did enjoy reading it, I just wish it hadn't been a part of the Giver series.

reference_books.title: Open City
reference_books.review_text: I was liking this one until the end, when (spoilers and trigger warning) we're told that the main character raped someone when he was younger, and that's just dropped in there and not really addressed. Other than that, it's a thoughtful, interesting book, but a quiet read. There wasn't anything that really jumped out at me and felt like it was going to stick with me, and then that sour note at the end dropped it a star for me, which is a shame.

reference_books.title: Winter Town
reference_books.review_text: Was enjoying this for the most part (nothing too extraordinary, but a quick read), until I got to the sketch in the extras that is labelled "Adam's apple = tr*nny". Except without the censoring, obviously. Just needless hateful transmisogyny. It soured the whole book for me. There were other parts that I thought were questionable, like Lucy calling Evan's gay friends her "gay boyfriends", but I was giving them the benefit of the doubt. Now I'm just annoyed that this was my last read of the year.

reference_books.title: Lagoon
reference_books.review_text: A fantasy novel about an alien invasion. I loved the setting of Lagos, which I haven't read any books about before. The constantly switching narrators made this a bit of a slower read for me, but it makes for a really interesting, interweaving story that still feels personal to the three main characters while accomplishing a broader view of the event. It's alien invasion + characters with magical powers + a road that swallows people and collects their bones + various gods making cameos + animal POVs.

reference_books.title: Of Fire and Stars
reference_books.review_text: This was everything I wanted from it and more. A delight to read. I want to give it as gifts and peddle it to strangers. It warms my heart that this book is in the world for queer teen girls. Do you like Frozen but wish it was more gay? Of Fire and Stars. Perfect if you like fantasy or court politics or trying to find out who the betrayer is or magic or starcrossed lovers or grudging-friendship-turns-into-love or... Honestly, I just fell head over heels for this. All the best part of Tamora Pierce with twice the queer content. This reminds me of everything I wanted from Disney movies, but with added depth and maturity. (Maturity as in there is brief sexual content and swearing.) I can't wait to have a finished physical copy. I haven't swooned this hard for a book in years.

reference_books.title: Difficult Women
reference_books.review_text:
This was both as dark and as good as everyone has been saying it is. I feel like "Read this" just about sums it up, but here are some points I didn't see talked about before I read Difficult Women: there's a lot of magical realism! Which is great. In addition to trigger warnings for rape and violence, there is also a very detailed scene of extreme fat-shaming, so beware of that. There are some queer stories! Not the majority of the collection, but a few. 
 After the first few stories, I was steeling myself for this to be a dark and difficult read the whole way through, but there's definitely some moments of hope as well, including some romance I really got behind. Actually, one story just warmed my heart and made me sigh happily when I finished it (anyone surprised it was one of the queer stories?) 
 Not surprisingly, I highly recommend this one.

book_a.title: Georgia Peaches and Other Forbidden Fruit
book_a.user_review:
It seems like all the lesbian YA I've been waiting for is out this year. This is definitely the first time I've read an inspirational (aka Christian) YA lesbian romance. I loved the writing style, which made me laugh out loud a couple of times at Jo's observations. The premise is interesting: Jo is the out lesbian daughter of a preacher, but when they move to a conservative small town in her senior year, her dad asks her to go back in the closet. She reluctantly agrees. 
 What I found interesting was how tempting being closeted was, even for someone who was used to being out. It's torturous, but it also comes with benefits. Jo tells herself she's doing this for her dad, but it's clear that she's also reluctant to let go of the privileges that come with being part of the crowd. 
 I did have some issues with the book, but I realized that those are standard romance tropes, and this really is an inspirational romance book at heart, I think. Definitely one that I'm glad exists for teens today, especially religious ones.

sample_reviews.review_text:
[image error] 
 I had more hopes for this book

Edit 2 June 2017: I'm adding Tasha's review as a link here because she discusses the ableism in this book, which I don't really touch on. 
 (Note: all page numbers are from my hardcover edition) 
 I wanted to like this book. I'd been excited to read it for months. On a basic writing level, there's nothing wrong with it. The writing style is easy to read and the protagonist's voice is fairly strong. I also really liked the peach motif that cropped up here and there, usually tied to sumptuous descriptions that made me kinda hungry. 
 However, I find I had a lot of issues with the book in terms of structure and prejudice. I'm not an expert on racism, being a white person, but the more I think about it, the more it seems so obvious that I don't understand how so many people have missed it. 
 My first issue circulates around the one and only black character in the entire book, Gemma. As far as I can tell, the author is white, and Gemma's manner of speech was very stereotypical. I almost wanted to keep a tally of how many times she prefaced a sentence with "girl" or threw in some other awkwardly-executed AAVE grammatical mannerisms. 
 Page 70: 
 "Because, girl." Gemma growls. "Our dance parties are epic." 
 Page 140: 
 Her eyes narrow and it's like I can hear the "Oh no he didn't" loud as a bullhorn. 
 Page 150: 
 "Girl, don't you lie." Gemma is straight to the point. 
 Page 187: 
 "Girl." Gemma is attacking a slice of veggie pizza. 
 There are undoubtedly more examples. These are just the ones I noted in my Goodreads statuses. 
 I know it's not just a quirk of being southern since, with the exception of some really uncomfortable AAVE appropriation coming from Jo and her friend, Dana, she was the only character who consistently spoke like this. If the representation had been more varied (as in, Gemma wasn't the only black character in the whole book), it wouldn't have been as much of an issue. 
 EDIT: 
 Another reader also pointed out that this perpetuates the "sassy black girl" stereotype, which I should have noted originally. 
 Sidenote: we as white people need to stop saying "yaaaas" (which Dana says on page 22). Can we stop appropriating from AAVE already? Please. My crops are dying. 
 Unrelated to the racism of the dialogue, I also hated that Gemma's attempts to invade Jo's privacy by getting into her phone were treated as a silly little quirk rather than a horrible thing to do. 
 Biphobia also rears its ugly head in this book. The most blatant occasion is on PAGE THREE where Jo, the lesbian narrator, says: 
 I nod toward the late twentyish, early thirtyish bi-curious cougar Dana had been flirting with before she deigned to check up on me. 
 There's no good reason the word needs to be there as it does not impact the plot in any way. As a bisexual, this is a word I never want to see again because it is used to invalidate bi women's queerness as just a phase she'll grow out of once her so-called curiosity has been sated. 
 I also had issues with the plot, especially after the mid-point of the book. Honestly, most of the drama could've been solved with one basic conversation. Jo's internal freakout over thinking Mary Carlson would be angry to find she was lying would have been nothing compared to what ultimately transpired because she just would not communicate. Seriously. One little conversation explaining to Mary Carlson why she couldn't come out and so much of the drama would've been resolved before it began. 
 And don't get me started on Mary Carlson trying to force Jo out of the closet . That was not okay, even if Jo wasn't being entirely honest at that point. And yet Mary Carlson isn't criticised for this. Jo is the one who is forced to apologise for lying and Mary Carlson gets away with everything, even though it was horrible of her to try and force Jo to out herself before she was in a position to do so . They're living in a judgemental small town in the South, for God's sake. You'd think she'd know better. 
 Also, the rival love interest was such a flat, cardboard villain. At least give her some complexity. Come on. Just because she's an antagonist doesn't mean she has to be a horrible human being with absolutely no depth or redeeming qualities. 
 When things weren't being ridiculous between the main couple, they were pretty cute together. I also liked the development of the relationship between Jo and her stepmother, even if I didn't think the stepmother should've gotten away with as much of her low-level homophobia as she did. But all that cuteness was often punctuated by these issues so ultimately I couldn't like the book as much as I wanted to.

Georgia Peaches and Other Forbidden Fruit is not a perfect book, not by any means. In fact, it is so full of plot holes and unnecessary dilemmas that I'm surprised I managed to get through it. But Georgia Peaches and Other Forbidden Fruit shares some deeply important messages in a thoughtful manner that cannot be ignored--perhaps, especially, in wake of the Orlando tragedy. This is a story of a girl who has already come out to her friends and family in Atlanta but who is asked, by her father and new stepmother, to conceal her sexual identity in small-town Rome, Georgia where she moves for her senior year of high school. It's a ridiculous set-up because it hardly seems just that a father who supports his daughter regardless of her sexuality would ask her to change herself, but it brings up a host of fascinating points. 
 Firstly, Joanna finds that she doesn't mind being closeted. It's not quite true to herself, but in Rome no one stares at her for her outfits or for her lesbian best friend who flirts with every attractive woman she meets. In Rome she is invisible and as confusing as that is, it's also easier. It turns out that coming out isn't something that happens just once. We treat it that way and think about it as such but in reality, coming out means repeating yourself and re-introducing yourself to every community you find yourself a part of and hoping that they accept you. That if you meet their parents or grandparents that they accept you as well. It's a privilege that non-queer people take for granted and I appreciated that Brown called out the blatant heteronormative society we live in and how harmful that is to our own minds and to LGBTQIAP+ individuals around us. 
 This book calls for further suspension of disbelief since Joanna reveals her secret to a friend of hers whose parents are both lesbian but she can't trust the girl she falls in love with with the same secret. If Joanna had simply communicated better, half this novel would be unnecessary. But Joanna's journey to support a friend in coming out, making her own plan to come out again in Rome, and deal with telling the truth to the people she's become friends with is all such an important path. It's also important for her parents and those around to her to come to terms with her truth, even if they're re-coming to terms with it. Back in Atlanta, people always judged Joanna for her lesbian haircut and outfits and for once in her life, she's surrounding by people judging her for her character and then accepting other facets of her personality. 
 To add to the convoluted plot line, though, we have a hacker lesbian and a manipulative theater lesbian thrown into the mix. I don't feel great about the inclusion of these characters and their lack of depth but I did appreciate that the issues in this book were not resolved overnight and no matter how badly the plot was constructed, it was still dealt with in a realistic manner. What's more, in a strange way the fact that girlfriends can also be manipulative--not just boyfriends--and that girls can be just as jealous as boys can be is normalizing. In some way. 
 What I particularly loved about this book, though, were the relationships. Joanna's relationship with her stepmother evolved throughout the novel to a point where Mother #3 became "mom". Her anger with her father is realistic and festers throughout the story, even though her father has always accepted and supported her decisions. Joanna's new friendships, and especially her romance, are believable and heart-warming and full of swoon. It's just a shame that a host of such fabulous relationships must be against the backdrop of an unbelievable plot, but it works. 
 This book does a REALLY good job of discussing issues that plague queer teenagers and I'm a huge fan of the way that Brown approaches a lot of important topics. Unfortunately, this contains a terribly implausible plot line so if you're prepared to suspend your belief quite a bit, this is going to be a resounding hit. I'd definitely recommend this one, if only for its thoughtful nature, but it isn't stellar as a story by itself without the queer romance at its core.

Typically I love LGBTQ+ books. I enjoy reading whatever I can about the subject. I recently read Georgia Peaches and Other Forbidden Fruit, and didn't like it at all. I thought it was a poor representation of the LGBTQ+ community. It also sends a bad message to LGBTQ+ teenagers that read it, which is the book's intended audience. 
 At first, I did enjoy the book. The first couple of chapters were really good. Then the plot took a turn that I didn't like. I was not happy at all with the main character's compliance with the rules that her father set for her. It felt like the book was sending the message that you shouldn't be who you are, or tick to your values if it makes someone else uncomfortable. I thought that was a dangerous message to send to teens, most of whom are just starting to explore their own sexuality, and discover who they really are. Not cool. You should never have to hide who you really are, especially just to make someone else happy. 
 Needless to say, I didn't like Georgia Peaches and Other Forbidden Fruit at all. I thought it was a terrible representation of the LGBTQ+ community. I don't think that I will be reading any of this author's other books in the future. I do not recommend this book to anyone.

Mediocre. Very exciting... annoyingly predictable, and then mediocre again. Also by this point it became apparent that the mentally disabled character--who refers himself as 'special' and 'not smart' and yet uses complex vocabulary and demonstrates deep understanding of situations the neurotypicals miss--was really just there to make the MC look like a good person for befriending him and his sister like an angel for swearing to always look after him. The MC literally gives him a present to get his sister to talk to her again after she fucks up their relationship, and IT WORKS. Because of course if you're nice to the weird kid, you deserve a second chance no matter how much of a liar you are, right? 
 In terms of diversity and considering it takes place in a small Georgian town, this felt like the author went through a check list. There wasn't any depth to the social relations and structures enforcing all the prejudice and it was easily dismissed in a flowery 'we are all equal' handwavy resolution that didn't really deal with the obstacles that had been set up. What happened to the super scary adoptive grandmother who'd never be able to accept her being a lesbian? She was sent to the kitchen to cook by the cool grandma! This cool grandma who for some reason doesn't live with them or is related to them but follows them from Atlanta to Georgia when they move there--guessing she doesn't have a life outside of making sure they've enough leftovers? 
 Peaches is a bland, run-of-the-mill f/f romance that will be forgotten soon enough. "Keeping you a secret" did a much better job of it about 15 years earlier. Perhaps its most interesting feature is how graphic the sexy scenes are, and in the context of a novel that is nothing to write home about, that mostly felt odd to me--the scenes are hot, but I'm not sure how teenagers will actually perceive them? Not that they can't close the book if they're shocked, of course, just made me wonder about lesbian YA because gay YA is very much not this explicit.

I basically inhaled this book - I jumped into Jo's world and couldn't put it down. That said there were the occasional plot hole or odd choice of words that caused me to surface. The most bothersome to me is why at one point at the start of the story Jo refers to her lesbian identify as a choice? Or how a young many with two moms who don't attend the bible thumping local church ended up attending services on his own? No explanation is ever attempted. That said I think it's overall a great story and one that I hope will help a lot of kids (LGBTQ or not).

DNF at 100 pages. 
 I wanted to open this review by saying that this book made me legitimately consider giving up on YA, but that would be unfair to this book. This book is abysmal, don't get me wrong, but the fact that I want to move on from YA isn't solely this book's fault. This book just made me realize that over the last sixth months or so, I've hated far more YA books than I've liked, and I've hated most of them for similar reasons. Maybe the problem isn't me - maybe I'm just outgrowing this genre, and the books have always been this bad. 
 Or maybe - just maybe - I haven't changed at all, and this book is, in fact, fucking terrible. 
 I am sick to death of YA writers trying to include modern slang in their books. This is a PSA for any writers who are considering it: this never works. You are doing nothing but embarrassing yourself and making it completely transparent that an adult wrote the book. The prose in this novel is a hodgepodge of modern slang used incorrectly, slang that's completely dated (at one point, Joanna says something is 'the bomb' completely unironically), and turns of phrase that are awkward as hell. There are, in fact, ways to evoke how teenagers talk without sounding like a clueless camp counselor - just look at how authors like David Levithan and Courtney Summers use things like stream-of-consciousness and sarcasm to suggest the thought process of a teenager. Using slang is the lazy way out, and it almost invariably results in something unreadably bad. The fact that so many YA authors don't realize this is a big part of what's making me think that this genre just isn't for me anymore. Nearly every YA book I've read over the past six months or so has had some variant of this problem, and it's bad enough that I'd rather never read another YA novel than have to deal with another book this painful. 
 Apart from that, this book is just generally weak, in ways that I don't find particularly interesting. It's a shame, because if there's anything YA needed, it was a light-hearted, low-stakes gay romance. But this is just limp. I think Joanna is supposed to be quirky, but she just comes off as one-note, and most of her little winks to the audience are more painful than funny. I also find it irritating that Brown writes a protagonist who does have legitimate problems and issues in her life... and still manages to fill the novel with nothing but whining about things that don't really matter. This story pretty much fits the 'nice guy tries to win over the girl with a jerk boyfriend' archetype, except the nice guy is a girl. And that's just not something I want to read about - maybe ten years ago, before the 'nice guy' archetype became so infamous, this could've worked, but today, it's just played-out. This book isn't the worst thing I've ever read, but I'm having trouble finding anything nice to say about it. I guess it's kind of a microcosm of the dissatisfaction I've had with YA lately, and just thinking about all that makes me feel grumpy and depressed.

reference_books.title: Smoke Gets in Your Eyes: And Other Lessons from the Crematory
reference_books.review_text: For those who have read Stiff: The Curious Lives of Human Cadavers, this was very different, but probably satisfies that same part of your brain that yearns to read about corpses for some reason. The focus is narrower (death rituals and the funeral industry), the author is a professional in the field rather than a journalist and researcher, and the book is more about the author (as a memoir should be) than Stiff is about Mary Roach. The book follows Doughty's path from her first job in a crematorium through mortuary school and to the present, with detours along the way to reflect on her earliest experience with death, and her own brush with death. She's funny, and the book is written such that you feel like a friend is telling you a story.

I feel like this book deserves more 2.5 stars than 3, but I feel better leaning toward 2 stars than 3. 
 I honestly have to say that I don't see the appeal of the book and I didn't really enjoy reading it. The characters are poorly developed. You know very little of their lives barring what happens to them in those moments and you learn very little of them through the pages, aside from Montag, the main character. The setting is odd and illogical. For instance, the seeming lack of speed limits or the complete lack of the fear of death is simply seen as ordinary for no apparent reason. There's this sort of feeling of anarchy, despite the fact that the government is there with strange guidelines regarding books. Really, there seems to be no law regarding much of anything else aside from books. Many appear to think this book is a discussion about the government, but I'd argue it's a discussion on the importance of literature in the world and how a lack of such things would bring about the end of society as we know it. 
 As always, the writing style and the haunting feeling lingering behind the words is something Ray Bradbury has always done so very well. I think this book particularly is meant to haunt you, even if it does seem far fetched. 
 I assume the warning to future is what made this a classic book. Certainly, it isn't a book I would have chosen to make a classic. Most of my high school classmates had to read the book for their English classes. I feel it's a strong argument to children as a warning to the future, that books and the learning that they teach are important - that they cannot simply be replaced by movies and film. I also know that this book was written for another generation, 63 years in the past. Perhaps this book helped them to avert that future. Perhaps that future would never have come to pass. Perhaps I believe too much in the sympathetic nature of people to ever believe this could happen.

I'm not sure what I could say about this book that other folks haven't already, specifically if you were looking for literary merits or symbolism. Which, funny enough, is just a guess since I haven't actually looked up anything previously said about this book other than it's a stand against censorship, that still holds true today. 
 It was given to me by a friend, and I hadn't read it before, or seen the movie, or anything of the sort--but I read it anyway. 
 The language is beautiful. Ray Bradbury writing is poetic and intense, and full of vague symbolism while still painting a clear picture of events. It's beautiful language that still contains point and plot, and I enjoyed it immensely. 
 The story is simple, and I appreciate that. It gets to the point, and Montag is sympathetic toward the end of things. It's the story of a confused man, trying to do the right thing, while his friends are small and his wife is unavailable. His little world explodes, and in the middle of all his crisis and focus on books, there's a bigger picture with real threats that include The Hound, a fierce mechanical beast, and a looming war. It's a good story in three parts, with a man going from curiosity to full commitment. 
 If I had any cause for issue, I would maybe put it on Clarisse and Beatty. A lot of their dialogue wasn't so much dialogue, as it a method of delivery to insert a quick lecture on the state of things and where they're going. It didn't detract too much, but I did notice it was like wrapping what sounded like it wanted to be a lecture to the people inside of a fiction story. Which, it may have well been. 
 I suppose the end point, is that the book is good, I'm glad I read it--and lecture or not, I think this applies universally. Especially the Afterward and Coda where Bradbury gets angry over the editing of book. 
 Worth reading, and I suggest you pick it up if you have time.
This book is very confusing and dark. My favorite character, Clarisse, dies in like the first 10 chapters! This book was o.k. not the best, but it wasn't terrible.
For such a short book I had the hardest time getting into this. I guess it just wasn't my cup of tea.
