I read this book a long time ago, but it stays with me. In the current world of buzzwords, soundbytes and tweets, real books can be overlooked. The media draw us in and isolate us, and we react by hurrying on to the next ephemeral remark or cat video, never stopping to let an idea settle in and develop, much less read and reflect on how an idea has developed in someone else's mind, or the care that person took in expressing it for our benefit. I love Ray Bradbury's stories, and this is a favorite. What book would I memorize, to make sure it's not lost. Hmm. I've puzzled over this. How about you?

One cannot help but admire the prescience of the author, almost 70 years after he published this book. The self-indulgent and often times clunky writing, combined with some overly-expository dialogue keep this book from reaching the same heights as Nineteen Eighty-Four, but Bradbury's consideration and analysis of our society's problems is right-on. A definite must-read. Make sure you do it with an actual book.

Wasn't expecting a fridge Manic Pixie Dream Girl in this book. :P 
 This has some good ideas, but it's couched in the idea that new technology and generations are ruining the world. I couldn't help but feel I was reading the novel version of an article about how millenials are ruining everything with their trigger warnings and TV and iPods. Plus, it was very male-centric. Clarisse I barely count as a real character, as Bradbury literally writes that she is a mirror, and I disliked how the only people interested in being intellectual were men. Mildred and her friends were just silly clueless boring women. 
 Do I think it's important to have and read and digest books fully? Absolutely. Do I think books should be burned because they don't have minority representation? Of course not. I also think there's a valid point to be said that people may go towards more mindless entertainment because it's comfortable, and how that's a bad thing. But. Progress isn't bad, and that includes writing books that do strive to have better minority representation. That includes calling out views that dehumanize people due to race or gender. Those aren't the same thing as having no desire for knowledge, and the conflating of the two is what I disliked about this book.

book_b.title: World War Z: An Oral History of the Zombie War
book_b.user_review:
A friend described this book as "the most boring book about zombies," and I can see her point. It's a collection of first-hand accounts of the "zombie war" so the action is insulated by the events being in the past. Being a non-action book about zombies didn't make it a bad book, though. 
 I struggled with it for the same reason I struggle with collections of short stories. There's no hook that keeps you reading. The accounts all stand on their own. If they ever refer to each other, there are too many details to keep track of you might not even catch the reference. After all, the book itself is supposed to be the Postwar Commission Report, so it is by its very nature detailed, and a bit dry. Honestly, I think some maps or diagrams would have spiced it up, if a report is what he was going for. 
 This book appears on this BuzzFeed list of books that will change your life, but change my life it did not. Then again neither did Life of Pi, or any of the other books on that list that I've read (although David Sedaris came close), so whatever, BuzzFeed.

sample_reviews.review_text: I actually never really finished this book. I hated it. The writing style bugged me and I couldn't finish it.
Took me absolutely forever to get into & I didn't even finish it. I had to force myself to read it. While some stories I couldn't put down, others I just did not care about. Very disappointed in it.

Okay, I give up. I've been trying not to have as many "will not finish" books lately, but my God, this shit is dull and naive. At this point, hubby wants me to quit because he's sick of me yelling at him at the end of each "interview" about what's wrong with this book. So yeah, fuck it, I'm done. 
 The first part of the book is a lengthy explanation for why no one notices a zombie outbreak in our modern age. It's the cliched "what are these unknown monsters" trope that horror can't seem to get away from. And not only is the author completely wrong about the intelligence capabilities of the US, he's apparently unaware of the speed at which even the smallest incidents are reported on social media. He has to twist himself in knots to explain why no one noticed, and he's WRONG. Not just a little wrong. Completely, totally, utterly wrong. 
 *Takes deep breaths* God, what a fucking schmuck. 
 To put this in perspective, the Rakhine Buddhists can't even kill a few Muslims in Burma/Myanmar without me knowing about it. No revolt can go on for more than a day before I see it on my Twitter feed. I know when there's an earthquake, even something minor like a 2.1 on the Richter scale. But according to this doofus, NO ONE noticed a zombie apocalypse for months? Yuh-huh. And even when they did notice, they "thought it was rabies"? Seriously? Are you fucking kidding me? 
 I might forgive that, but the other problem is, I know how the book will end based on the introduction. I know that every single unlikable asshole interviewed will be fine because this is all in past tense, after the humans triumph over the zombies. And this is bullshit. Why should I feel anything for any of these people? They're mostly assholes, and none of them is capable of talking about events in such a way to inspire any emotion besides contempt. These are the people I would hope get eaten in the apocalypse. But no, they all survived, and I know that before they even start their interviews. It kills any sense of suspense, and this book should be a manual on how NOT to write a zombie novel. 
 I give World War Z 1 star and if I wasn't so opposed to burning books, I'd chuck this fucker in a fire and do the world a favor. What a crock of shit. If you want to read a good zombie book, go look up something by Brian Keene, but give this tired shit a pass.

World War Z is a wonderful piece of speculative fiction that does a great job of showing, first, man's response to a global pandemic. Secondly, I believe it to be an accurate portrayal of the governmental response of many of the key players and superpowers in the near future. 
 I'll disagree with most reviewers in that it may be a critique of the Bush administration. Actually, I'll say yes and no. Sure, the response of good ol' USA was slow in the book. Wasn't it the same for almost all the other countries? I think it's a critique of us all. 
 An interesting point to consider is what country led the way in fighting back and reclaiming the land--not necessarily the way of life. 
 Some of the responses by the countries were a little too stereotypical for me (including the US)--except for China. The outcome there was interesting. It was also shocking to note how they got there. 
 While the zombies in the book were conventional, many times the responses to them were not. I had never come across anything that approached this subject globally. Usually, in popular culture, zombie attacks are local. Sure, we see some of that here, but they are aftermath perspectives from individuals. 
 I did not stay awake at night as a result of this book. However, I was chilled at the actions of the uninfected--man. While not being too gory, this is a book I would recommend to anyone interested in global-sociology.

I started reading this book yesterday and got to the last 100 pages and just could not finish it out. normally I like things about zombies but this I did not and will NOT be finishing. Unhauling this asap

I will admit to finally getting the impetus to read the book after seeing the movie, though I knew going in that the two were very different. The book is, essentially, unfilmable, and I think the filmmakers did a good job of keeping the idea of talking to various people about what's happening while still keeping a coherent plot and some action. 
 That said, I found the structure of the book ultimately boring. A few of the stories were interesting and captivating, but most of them weren't. I also had trouble understanding the politics and such of the new world (at least until toward the end when that was a primary focus) because the interviewees tended to talk as though the audience already knew them. Which makes sense, because the interviewer would know, and I suspect Brooks was trying to dodge info-dumping and "as you know, Steve," but it still made the middle of the book a bit confusing. 
 I've seen reviews that complain that nobody talks the way the interviewees do, and I agree, but I do have to give some leeway because transcripts of people talking are just damn difficult to read. This reads like it was cleaned up a bit, which I'm okay with. However, only a few of the interviewees have distinctive voices; most of them pretty much talk the same, regardless of their economic, geographic, and cultural differences. 
 My biggest complaint, by far, is about the women. Of the dozens of stories, I counted five that were told by female characters. And each of those characters has deep issues. They are (and I may be getting the order they appear in wrong here) 1. a flighty, out-of-touch soccer mom; 2. a Russian private who turns into a baby factory at the end; 3. a developmentally challenged girl; 4. a plain, boring girl; and 5. a pilot who went slightly batshit during a stressful crash landing, escape-and-evade, and rescue. This isn't to say that there aren't men with deep problems and issues in the book, but they're much better balanced by heroes or even regular joes. The book desperately needed more women in general, but specifically more powerful, heroic women who stand up with the men. They're in the background of the men's tales occasionally, but I would have liked to hear their voices more often.
Great idea just long in the follow through. You can definitely tell Brooks is a reporter and if you enjoy that type of thing then you'll enjoy this one immensely.

While this book is frightening in its depiction of how easily everything will fall apart in the face of a zombie horde, I wasn't terribly fond of it. The Q&A format was fine by me, and I even felt it was a clever way to present the storyline, a definite departure from most zombie apocalyptic novel. My main beef is that it was just so dry. Page after page after page of discussing armament and weapons and military strategy gets numbing after a while. Sure, that's kind of the entire point of this book, that we'll have to re-work not only the entire military but also all of our weapons and body armor. But it seemed like it was just too much in this one book. I would have liked more discussions on how civilians survived or fought off the zombies, since there must have been some. I think the section that captured my attention most was the interviews with the Japanese men, the one who had been so stuck into the internet before the zombies and his mentor, who had been blinded by the flash of the atomic bomb and who had gone into nature to rid his homeland of as many zombies as he could. The rest of the "interviewees" were just too similar, and hard to keep track of as separate entities.

Howard Stern used to say (back when he could be heard on the radio for free) that ratings gold equaled one word -- LESBIANS. In the last twenty years, the publishing world has found gold with one word -- ZOMBIES. I'm not sure how the LESBIAN ZOMBIE genre is doing in the publishing world. Perhaps that's another book. 
 Anyway, back to World War Z. It was quite the disappointment. I did enjoy the Orson Wells War of the Worlds approach, but it started getting real old real fast. Things got a bit too clinical and stilted for my tastes. This is more the "tell but don't show" school or novel writing. It really slowed the pace down and made this more like reading a textbook than a novel. 
 Can you tell I'm not a fan?

just finished this for the second time around, and i gotta say, my review remains exactly the same - 5 stars - because it's still a great book, and certainly the best zombie novel i've ever read. it's the perfect blend of true horror and socio-political exploration/what-if exercise. i don't quite understand some reviewers' frustration with the fact that WWZ has no single protagonist. what has always been clear to me is that the real protagonist in WWZ is humanity itself. while an individual's story can certainly reveal and explore facets of the human experience, it seems to me that a wider cast of characters, such as that provided in WWZ, is necessary to really delve into to the wide range of emotions and reactions that people and whole governments are capable of having in the face of an imminent and horrific global disaster. brooks clearly aspired to tell a story that has a global scale. i much prefer his studs terkel approach to doing so, as opposed to, say, through the perspective of a single American (white) man who flies around the world as humanity's last great hope.* some of the voices in the novel could have perhaps been written more distinctively. but most of the voices were distinctive enough that it's a negligible complaint, if one at all. (still) highly recommended. 
 *i haven't seen the film (i plan to eventually), but this is how it certainly looks to me from the trailers. thought 1: good lord, am i over the whole summer blockbuster hero complex. thought 2: grateful for the fact that at least i know enough to expect pitt's "zombie movie" but not WWZ.

I never read the actual book, and I am sure quite a few elements were missing in the graphic novel version. To me, the plot seemed...well, lacking, to the dismay of others who enjoyed this version. I'll admit the illustrations were quite beautiful, but I could not bring myself to sympathize with the main characters half the time because I felt as if their personalities were a bit 2D, as in they felt stereotypical. Like almost every modern fantasy/sci-fi novel, you've got the oh-so-misunderstood hero, who discovers something new, whether it be a world or hidden powers, their love interest, and those playful minor characters in the background. Sound familiar? 
 There is also the cliche of black and white, good and evil, and right and wrong. However, I can understand that since the novel, for the most part, was in Jacob, the main character's perspective. We all are biased and create our own versions of good and evil in the world around us. 
 Along with the fact that the illustrations did some justice, I can surely say that the author is creative, with the little clues and foreshadowing, such as Grandpa Portman's last words. 
 Overall, I am rating the graphic novel three stars since I have no right to judge a version of a book I never read. Perhaps I am wrong in saying that there seemed to be many details left out and perhaps I am wrong when saying the characters and plot were almost typical. I'll find out soon, when I read the original novel.

Bought this today because I've been wanting to start Hollow City. Read very quickly because I forgot how great the story was. Very excited to start Hollow City now!

This book is billed as paranormal/fantasy/YA--but be warned, here there be monsters. There are definitely some haunting moments and creepy creatures illustrated in these pages, so measure your braveness accordingly. 
 When Jacob was a little boy, his grandfather told him stories--fantastical stories about a home he lived in with several other 'peculiar' children, kept safe from monsters that wanted to kill them. These children has special gifts, like super strength, or the ability to defy gravity. 
 As he got older, Jacob realized that the stories his grandfather told were just that--stories. Built on a tiny foundation of truth, but exaggerated to entertain. So he stopped asking about them. 
 Years later, Jacob discovers that perhaps the stories weren't as exaggerated as he thought. So he travels to the origin of these stories, a tiny island off the coast of Wales, where the ruins of his grandfather's childhood home remain. 
 How much of the stories were true? Jacob explores the house that was once Miss Peregrine's Home for Peculiar Children, trying to uncover its secrets. Why were the children really there? 
 And then, as Jacob is trying to discover the truth, something truly astonishing happens. 
 About the art: 
 Most of the book is done in standard graphic novel style--square panels and speech bubbles. Some panels expand beyond their dividing lines, and some pages, like those pictured above, revolve around a larger picture or a photo collage. Also interesting to me was the color choices--some sections are gray scale, some are in color. The changes in coloring--and sometimes the coloring choices themselves add to and help tell the story. 
 The sequel to the book, Hollow City, will be out in January 2014. The graphic novel version will undoubtedly follow.

book_a.title: Lily and the Octopus
book_a.user_review:
I laughed and I cried all the way through this book. My little dachshund sat in my lap and licked my eye rain. 
 A gay man lives alone with his 12-year-old dachshund. Thursdays are their days to talk about cute boys, and one Thursday, and one Thursday he notices that there is an octopus (tumor) on Lily's head. The books takes us through the emotional odyssey of Lily's last few months and her human Ted's memories of all that she has meant to him and all of the human relationship failures she has seen him through. 
 Ted drifts into fantasy land on a number of occasions, and the fantasy sequences were cute for a time but grew old for me before they were over. Despite that, the book is clever, beautifully written, and heart-wrenching. Plus, my Lucy Peanut can verify that Lily is all dachshund. Anyone who loves a sausage stealing sausage dog will be bound to love Lily and the Octopus.

I just finished reading The Absolutely True Diary of a Part-Time Indian for the third time, so, according to Gordy, I suppose I should know it by now. However, I feel just as inadequate to the task of writing a review for it as I did the first time I finished it. You see, every time I have read it, I have come away from a different book. It would be really easy to just go on and on about how often Part-Time Indian is banned, and why that is wrong or absurd, and never have to say something personal. (And yes, each of those words is its own link.) However, though I lack his humor, I will try for Arnold's honesty and explain why I think this book is so very special. 
 My first time to read The Absolutely True Diary of a Part-Time Indian was not long after it had been published. My life was full of change, and much of that change was a result of death. I didn't really know anything about Part-Time Indian, or I probably wouldn't have picked it up. Thank goodness I did! Even while reading things that resonated so deeply that I thought I would shatter all over again, Alexie made me laugh. Laugh! Because Alexie is right, "I know death is never added to death; it multiplies." (p 212) But it is also true that, "When it comes to death, we know that laughter and tears are pretty much the same thing." (p 166) After finishing, my love of Part-Time Indian was something that was just too personal to share. 
 My second reading of Part-Time Indian brought shame. Not a general sort of shame, but the very specific sort that comes from recognizing privilege you have previously ignored. I live near reservations. I have friends who are Native American. I know the very unsavory statistics of life on reservations. I thought of myself as a knowledgeable, understanding sort of ally. I could be quick to jump into a conversation with historical facts or statistics. But what a place of privilege! I could think about it or not as I chose--I don't have to live it. And a verbal 'victory' at a dinner table does precisely nothing for the people who do have to live it. I was one of those "liberal, white, vegetarian do-gooders" or "white missionary saviors" or "yet another white guy who showed up on the rez because he loved Indian people SOOOOOOOO much." You see, it took reading Part-Time Indian to realize that just 'caring' wasn't enough. Just trying to 'fix' things within the reservations isn't enough, because the problems come from outside as well. Until the Arnold's of this world are wrong when they say, "Almost all of the rich and famous brown people are artists," then we are still doing something i>wrong as a society. (p 6) I just love what Sherman Alexie said in an interview with the Progressive when he was included in the banned curriculum of the Mexican American Studies Program in Arizona: 
 "You give those brown kids some books about brown folks and what happens? Those brown kids change the world. In the effort to vanish our books, Arizona has actually given them enormous power. Arizona has made our books sacred documents now." 
 I want our world to change. But, yet again, what a personal response! Who really wants to write a review revealing just how ignorant they have been of their own privilege? 
 With this last reading, though, things changed. I realized that it wasn't the comfort it brought the first time I read it or the self awareness it provided with the second reading that brings me back again and again. It is simply this: Arnold. His frank, funny, painful, humiliating, triumphant, honest story. The way Alexie can bring you from the greatest of emotional heights to the most painful moments of sadness or shame with a single sentence--and you want to stay along for the rest of the ride because you're invested. Sherman Alexie's The Absolutely True Diary of a Part-Time Indian is a compelling story of a young boy's coming of age; it is not an issue book, but a character-driven story about a boy with a lot of issues. It is a story about finding hope when you think all hope is lost. It is about making your own hope. It is a story of learning to expect more for and from yourself than what others expect for and from you. It is about learning that where you come from does not have to define where you are going. It is about seeing the good and bad of each situation; that love can be expressed in a lot of different ways and still be real. It is about realizing that we are all a part of many different tribes, be they the tribe of poverty, small-town kids, funeral-goers, tortilla chips-and-salsa lovers, or chronic masturbators. It is about learning that "the world, even the smallest parts of it, is filled with things you don't know." (p 97) So maybe Gordy is right, maybe I do know Part-Time Indian, at least a little better than I did the first time. But that doesn't mean I won't be back again. I think there are still some things I don't know in this small part of the world, and I enjoy it here. 
 This review also appears at Chronicles of a Book Evangelist

reference_books.title: The Gunslinger
reference_books.review_text:
Seriously?! How did I miss this? This is iconic! Some books are like relationships, the timing has to be right. I remember picking this book up years (decades!) ago and thinking it was really not for me and what could Stephen King have been thinking... 
 With the benefit of hindsight I am now wondering how I could have been so dismissive...amazing what a few decades of developing your literary tastes can do to change your mind... 
 I read another book recently, The Vagrant, which I also loved. I caught myself thinking 'The Gunslinger' is like 'The Vagrant' but of course it has to be the other way round. 
 This book falls into the category of weird western for me. It is a novel of predestination, of good v. evil, of knightly quest, time travel and apocalypse. 
 Honestly, I thought I was done with Stephen King , and done a long time ago. When he started this series in the early 80s is almost exactly when I left off reading him. 
 Recently I have discovered Joe Hill and very much like his writing. And suddenly here I am back full circle, finally ready to return to his dad! The Dark Tower, the man in black, the gunslinger...genius!

reference_books.review_text:

I think the coaches reference in the title led me to believe it was historical fiction in the style of a mash up of Jamaica Inn and Jane Eyre. It was definitely reminiscent of Daphne du Maurice. Is there a film of this? I feel there might be one out there and if there isn't, maybe there should be. I very much enjoyed its gothic nature. 
 Recommended.

reference_books.title: Owl and the Japanese Circus (Adventures of Owl, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Hmmm..a low 3 stars. I enjoyed the first half of this but, despite the fact it's an action packed read, was starting to lose interest by the second half. 
 There's some good stuff in here, but it's eclipsed by the sheer precociousness and wilful recklessness of Owl. This is quite entertaining to start with and I made the mistake of thinking this was feisty assertiveness, but it turned out it was just plain (and repetitive) stupidity. 
 I feel I need to say something specific about the romance...I like a bit of romance in my paranormal fantasy, I do - as long as it's not too saccharine. No danger of that whatsoever here....the actual romance is quite sweet but do they really need to call each other what they call each other?! ( Read it for yourself if you don't know!) 
 I liked Captain, fantastic and original sidekick. I like the fact that Owl never recognises the supernaturals for what they are, even though her life is full of them. 
 That may seem like quite a lot of likes. But even combined, they can't make up for the hot mess of a convoluted plot. In the end, this book seemed far too long. Possibly I'd read the next one, but only if it was part of a kindle daily deal!

reference_books.title: Caraval (Caraval, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Hmm. I partly enjoyed this. But partly it made me cringe. I don't think it was a positive emotional template for young women. There was insta love. That's the first thing; and Scarlett our main character had a lot of Issues: constantly putting her sister first and sacrificing herself amongst them. 
 The paranoia, confusion and nightmarish qualities of Caraval were well done and the atmosphere created was well described in a sort of candy floss style suitable to the story. I don't know if a story can really be 'too YA' but this was for me. ( however I AM in fact a middle aged woman, so maybe I should just be reading more age appropriate material! Having said that, I have found there to be some excellent YA fantasy fiction out there which I have thoroughly enjoyed..) 
 So in order to be fair, I'm giving this a low 3 stars. My Inner Teenager would rate it 4 . Middle Aged Cynic would award 2.5.

book_a.title: Magic Slays (Kate Daniels, #5)
book_a.user_review: Another thumping good read, but that is not what impressed me most because I expect no less from this series. No, what impressed me was the development of the world building as the series progresses: how the long term effects of the magic and tech shifts continue to break the remains of the old world apart. In this volume, all the magical elements- witches, shapeshifter, mages, vampires have to team up to beat a common enemy. We see how Kate will sacrifice everything for Julie and how Curran would give everything up for Kate. We learn more about Kate's mother and backstory with Roland and watch Kate struggle with all her insecurities. Fab read!

sample_reviews.review_text: This series just keeps on getting better and better! Curran IS the ultimate alpha. Love Kate and Curran! :)

The world of Kate Daniels is like a vast ocean. It looks so plain and simple from the outside, but if you dive deeper it's a myriad of wonders. It is amazing that with each book (this is book 5), there is no better or worse but the story stands for itself- it gives you different emotions and excitement that it's like tasting a new dish each time. 
 What can I say? I loved it. I lapped up every word. I have never seen a female character as strong as Kate but still rational and vulnerable that cares so much for her loved ones. She is not perfect and she knows it, she admits it and faces her demons head on. Kate is like my role model for facing troubled times. I'm not saying take a sword and start a massacre, but knowing when to let things go, waiting for the right timing and persevering even when times are so tough that you want to break down. Ilona Andrews has molded Kate Daniels perfectly; she is the perfect female character- at least, to me. 
 You can also see from the writing that much research has gone into it and there were elements of both Ilona and Gordon injected into it, for example the military aspects and scientific aspects. There were no empty or boring moments and I loved the Kate and Andrea team! Ascanio is also a wonderful new introduction to the story and with each book, there are no simple "demons" or "vampires" but a whole new different concept of monsters or evil that is refreshing. 
 A small detail that bugs me is Curran. I don't advocate violence against women and not that he abuses her or anything, but some of the 'sparring' scenes made me frown. However, it is understandable that he is the pack leader and they have a different way of doing things. 
 If you couldn't already tell, this book was stellar.

This should have been titled "Magic Dives". Indeed, Kate Daniels took a deep dive, vexed me and bored me at the same time, which is an extraordinary feature albeit one, I'd rather not experience any time soon. Now I need to gobble up some credible books about terrorists to find my inner equilibrium and a will to continue with the series.

I think I prefer Seanan McGuire's non-fantasy books more - Feed (which she wrote as Mira Grant) was just incredible. Rosemary and Rue, which is the first book in an urban fantasy series about October Daye (cringe), a part-fairy. And it was fine, an enjoyable urban fantasy, and I like October, despite her name. I am just not really into books about fairies. Fairy courts and politics just bore me, and it's hard to really get into a book that centres around those things.

Usually, I don't like stories with fey elements and this book was no exception from this rule. I should just give up trying to like them, I guess. 
 Toby was as bland as any 08/15 urban-fantasy heroine. She supposedly has worked as a PI for the fairy realm many years and was super successful (even knighted), but there was very little evidence in this book supporting this claim. 
 She failed and failed and failed again in the course of events. Barely surviving attacks while following the most basic leads doesn't mean you're good at your PI job, especially if said survival solely depends upon other people saving your stupid ass. 
 That's not the worst part, though. Because Toby manages to be annoyingly stupid as well as incompetent. She never condifes in her allies and prefers to go everywhere alone, although she knows she's not equipped to deal with shit. She also has no idea how to get information and has to be clued in by everyone else. 
 Maybe I'm a little unfair with my review, but I'm really tired of tropes, that I normally like, written so sloppy. 
 If you're not imaginative enough to spin a good detecive-mystery, write something else! Toby didn't need to be a PI for this story to work. Hell, she would have been more likeable if she was an interior designer and managed to rope all these people into helping her! 
 The writing itself was okay, but repetitive and enforcing the general boring-ness. The side characters were the only aspects holding my interest, because they actually had passions and ambitions, contrary to stupid Toby. 
 Well, it seems the only emotional state Rosemary and Rue could evoke in me is 'grumpy'....

The good: wonderful world setting, nice version of the world Faerie, no gratuitous romance, no vamps or werewolves, a protagonist that experiences tragedy in a believable fashion and is definitely not over-powered. 
 The bad: Not a huge issue, but the story does seem like an opening salvo for a large story arc, so some story elements are unresolved; the ending felt rushed. 
 McGuire puts forth a very nice debut novel that takes a refreshing look at the urban fantasy seen through the lens of the Faerie world. Out protagonist October Daye is a changeling--half fairy, half human. McGuire creates a believable hero with real flaws, and real tragedy (realized in the prologue) 
 The characters were well-written, and the storyline was enjoyable. While I certainly want to read the second book, I was a bit annoyed that at times it felt that elements of the story and world were "held back" for the planned sequels. I enjoyed McGuire's interpretations of many creatures from Faerie--redcaps, selkies, and so forth. 
 In the end, Rosemary and Rue is a fine addition to the overcrowded urban fantasy field. Good stuff.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Magic Burns is the second book in the Kate Daniels series. It's no secret I hated the first, Magic Bites, but I was determined to find out what the hype is all about. I want to love them. 
 I found my eyes bled a little less this time around, but I still skipped a lot of the descriptions of the city and the mythological stuff. Boring. I did find myself not hating Kate though. I liked seeing her softer side while being on the ball and at the same time running her mouth and 'slayer'. 
 Kate lives in Atlanta in a dark and gritty time of magic flares and tech. She works for the Guild as a kind of investigator/bounty hunter, but she has a major problem with authority. She counts on no one but herself but did find herself in need of assistance by others during this installment. There were a lot of hideous mythological creatures & a psyco god out to take over the city and she had to get to the bottom of it. Kate went to the Oracle (inside a tortoise - ewwwww) for answers but instead received a mission. Lets just say, she had her hands full. If she wasn't saving a beastkin from certain death, she was dancing with a naked man in the snow, gathering blood from the goddess Morrigans hound she was fighting with Curran over the marriage of his ex consort & her ex almost boyfriend, trying to stop a girl from being attacked by sea demons or struggling to restrain her magic in the flares. 
 As Kate took her responsibilities seriously I found myself caring for her. Her relationship with both Andrea and Julia, and eventually Bran, made her more human in my eyes and also like she was fighting for people she cared about rather than just fighting for her next paycheck. I found her insecurities endearing. Seeing her devastation at the death that seems to follow her had me feeling sad right alongside her. 
 I adored all the Curran/Kate banter and will go on to the next book solely to find out when, I mean what, will happen with their love/hate relationship. I smiled each time Kate tried and failed to avoid Curran and even giggled at her bow in the room with the soup. I am also looking forward to seeing her cash in on her favor from Ghastek, more of her friendship with Andrea, Jim and Derek. 
 I have ordered Magic Slays from the library and won't wait as long to start it. Fingers crossed I like each book more than the previous one.

I typically write terse reviews. I just want to know if it is a worthwhile waste of time or just a complete waste. I like this heroine. I rarely say about paranormal fiction with female protagonists.  Kate Daniels is tough, but flawed. She screws up, usually barely stays alive, and has a myriad of social/emotional problems stemming from her childhood. She does the best she can with what she has, namely a magical sword. The writing is straightforward, unsentimental, and has a few dashes of world mythology. The stories aren't transparent or mind-numbingly stupid. Worth the waste of time.

reference_books.title: Anna Karenina
reference_books.review_text:
Synopsis: The story of several characters in 1880s High Society of Russia. Anna Karenina, the titel character, is stuck in a loveless marriage when she falls in love with another man. These are not modern times and since a divorce and remarriage are extremely complicated, drama ensues. The book also follows the life of Anna's brother, Stiva, his wife, Dolly and Dolly's younger sister, Kitty. As well as an admirer of Kitty, Levin, and several other smaller characters. That is really all I have to say. 
 Opinion: Holy crap what a long ass book (1448 pages on iPad). Don't get why it is so famous because it was incredibly dull. It was way too descriptive at a lot of parts and it was very hard to get through. I get that the character development is really good and that you can learn from the behavior of each of the characters but it was very underwhelming. I am not interested in 1880s Russian High Society. I then watched 2of the movies movies (1996 and 2013). First movie changed more of the storyline than the second movie but the second movie tried to be too artsy by filming most of it on a stage as if it was being performed in a theatre. The second movie captured the feelings better than the first.

reference_books.title: Winter's Tale
reference_books.review_text:
Synopsis: Set in a mythical New York City from the turn of the 20th Century to the turn of the 21st Century, this epic novel follows the mysterious life of Peter Lake. Sent out to sea on a floating miniature of a boat by his parents who were refused entry into the country, Peter Lake is raised by a primitive people called Baymen and later sent away on his own. He becomes a mechanic and burglar and gets involved with a dangerous Irish gang called the Short Tails. After betraying the boss of the short tails, Pearly Soames, Peter is relentlessly pursued by the gang and is rescued by an enormous white horse. When attmepting to rob the house of Isaac Penn, Peter Lake meets his daughter Beverly and she changes his life. After Peter Lake is again pursued by the Short Tails, he escapes with the white horse into the mysterious cloud wall that periodically looms around the city and when he awakens, it is almost a hundred years later and he has lost his memory. Taking ti the streets again, Peter Lake tries to find his purpose. 
 Opinion: Honestly, I was expecting the book to be a bit more mystical and enchanting with more present supernatural elements. However, the book still had some of those elements. I would recommend taking your time with this book because there are A LOT of characters and details to be remembered as you read because characters that were introduced 100 pages ago, come back around and I ended up getting a little bit lost sometimes because I was going through the book too quickly. I loved the unexplainable elements of the story and the setting of the story. I also thoroughly enjoyed the intertwining of characters and eventual links to each other's lives.

reference_books.title: The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test
reference_books.review_text:
Synopsis: A nonfiction book about Ken Kasey and his "Merry Pranksters" and the growth of the psychedelic movement in the 60s. Chronicling around the life of Ken Kasey and his influence on the movement, this book is told from the eyes of a witness as Kasey and his group travel in a Day Glo painted school bus and perform Acid Tests during which Kool-Aid is laced with LSD in the hopes of triggering group trips. 
 Opinion: Honestly, this subject does not interest me and I was just plain bored reading it. For me, this book could have been summarized into a single chapter and I would feel I read the same amount of information as I did reading the whole book. However, it was well-written and brought me as much into the chaotic psychedelic state of mind of the characters as is possible with words. The way he chronicled the psychedelic movement was well done but it simply just failed to captivate me. I am definitely off the bus.

reference_books.title: The House of the Seven Gables
reference_books.review_text:
Synopsis - Following the death of the man who commissioned the building of the house of seven gables after getting possession of the deed through questionable means, tragedy haunts the generations of the Pyncheon family who live in the house. After a beautiful young niece of the current occupants come to visit, a change is seen in the mood that surrounds the house. 
 Opinion - I have no idea why this book is a classic. In my opinion, this story would have been great as an Edgar-Allen-Poe-Like short story but it was incredibly dull as an entire novel. There was so much minute irrelevant detail that was tedious to get through. Most of the novel is also written in ridiculous run-on sentences that contain several thoughts. This probably just has to do with the style of the 1850s but I personally did not appreciate it because by the time I got through the rambling between the sentence, I almost forgot how it started so had to look back before finishing the sentence. This would be a good book to read in preparation for a GRE or other standardized test of the sort because it had a lot of world that I had never heard of. Shout out to Google for helping me out on that account. Basically, this is a tedious book that was not good reading for fun. It was not fun.

book_a.title: The No. 1 Ladies' Detective Agency  (No. 1 Ladies' Detective Agency, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Synopsis: After overcoming hardships, Mma Precious Ramotswe starts a Detective Agency as the first female private detective in Botswana. Being a tough and well-liked woman with strong morals, she sets out to fulfill her dream of running a successful detective agency and control her own destiny. I've only had two people say it didn't interest them. It's hard to say in simple terms what these books are about, but I usually sum it up with saying "it's life". There are cases to solve and I love those, but the lives of the characters, their stories, are what make the books for me.

It was ok, I just couldn't understand the hype, not much of a mystery, more like a rambling story about a nice woman in Botswana. The only aspect of the book I liked was getting glimpses of everyday life in Botswana.

Quite a fun and engaging read. I'm surprised it took me this long to get around to it!

Adored the first in the series. Warm, lovely, moving - what more could you want? Delightful characters, exotic setting, clever sleuthing. Full of charm, wisdom, and novelty (til the No. 1 Ladies' Detective Agency became a bestseller, anyway).

I say it at least ten times a year, but WHY DOES IT TAKE ME SO LONG TO READ POPULAR BOOKS? I almost always end up loving them. 
 The No. 1 Ladies' Detective Agency is no different. It was marvelous. Read it.
I didn't like how disjointed the chapters were....but I guess they did all come together at the end.

The No. 1 Ladies' Detective Agency by Alexander McCall Smith is a charming and fun book that depicts the adventures and cases of a female private detective in Botswana. The book is fascinating in the way that it captures everyday life for people in the African nation of Botswana. The reader can immerse him or herself in studying the similarities and differences between their native culture and that of the characters in this novel. The cases are also interesting little anecdotes that are throughly engaging. The main flaw of the book is that it is meandering and loosely structured. This method of telling the story defuses tension and urgency from the proceedings. It makes the events of the book feel less compelling despite the richness of many aspects of the narrative.
While I found this book perfectly pleasant I don't really get the passion the series has inspired. It seems to me that having read one I had read them all.

book_b.title: Miss Peregrine’s Home for Peculiar Children (Miss Peregrine’s Peculiar Children, #1)
book_b.user_review:
Synopsis: After his grandfather's murder by a creature no one believes Jacob saw, he goes to a Welsh island with his father to find out more about his grandfather's mysterious past. Growing up, Jacob's grandfather told him fantastical stories about escaping Nazi Germany and spending several years in an orphanage for peculiar children. Once on the island, Jacob goes on an investigation to find the old orphanage and get the answers he is looking for. 
 Opinion: I was afraid this would be too creepy for me but was not so much creepy as intriguing and mysterious. The concept of the book is very creative and offbeat. I enjoyed that many elements were unexpected and that the story staying interesting to the end. This is the first book in a trilogy so there is the option of continuing the story if you'd like. However, the book ends at a point where you do not feel obliged to, which I like.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This was a very interesting and quirky book, and I have to admit, I don't think I've ever read such a weird story. Peculiar children is putting it mildly, these kids were downright scary. The story involves time travel, WWII, and some scary otherworldly beasts, that come together on a remote fishing island off of Scotland's coast. What was pretty unique about this book, is that there are "real" photographs to go along with the story, and you find yourself studying them. I was fascinated with the story, which becomes a page-turner, and slightly surprised at the ending. 
 This is a first novel for the author, Ransom Riggs, and I can't wait to see what comes next.
It was a good book but I honestly struggled to stay engaged with it.

The hype for this book truly did not deliver for me on this book. I found Jacob to be an unreliable narrator, and the character development to be very weak. I did not attach myself to any of the characters and felt the relationships were not well-developed. The beginning was very long and drawn out. I wasn't expecting the first 100 pages to be set in Florida, and it felt like it took a really long time for anything exciting to happen. Jacob seems like a whiny and spoiled teen that became disconnected from the author. I am having a hard time explaining why I didn't particularly enjoy this book, but there was something about it that completely irked me - maybe I was just hyper-aware that I was reading a book and couldn't become fully engrossed in the book. 
 Read For: Teen Book Club, August 2016 
 Recommend For: YA/Fantasy/Time Travel/Books to Movies

As with most books that manage to gain such mass appeal, choosing to give it a try should come with a bit of a caveat: expectations might be unfairly elevated. 
 Did it reach my expectations? To be honest I still haven't decided. Admittedly I entered into Rigg's world knowing very little (likely less than most) about the actual narrative. 
 What I liked: 
 1. The use of pictures: The buzz around the book has a lot to do with its unique use of pictures. What is interesting is that this was probably the most noted element that I remained unaware of until the end of the book. I recognized that the author was using pictures to enhance the narrative of course, but it wasn't until I reached the end of the book (that contained the author's interview) that I recognized why he chose to use the pictures (namely, that they were real and not staged, and that they were lost pictures in history that he had dug up, discovered, chased after, and gotten ahold of in the name of a personal passion project). Understanding that the narrative flowed from the visuals and helped create the storyline through his imaginative take on the people behind the photographs actually changed my experience with the narrative itself. What at first had felt somewhat lacklustre writing actually ended up gaining a few interesting layers in the aftermath, helping it to linger longer than it might have otherwise. 
 2. The concept: I will address more of this in the stuff that I didn't like, but, at a grass roots level I found the theory of his concept (of peculiar children, timelines, and loops) interesting enough to hold my attention. Given that not very much happens for the first three quarters of the book, this is actually to it's credit. 
 3. Jacob: I wouldn't be surprised to hear that the story lived or died for some on how they felt about Jacob. He is the main narrator of the story after all. I actually liked the character. He plays that always difficult role of privileged child with a complex. I think the reason why this role is always particularly hard to pull off (at least well) is because it is hard to get readers to truly care about his well being. In the case of Jacob he comes from a good home with two well-meaning parents, and to top it off he also manages to have a job that he fails to care about and a best friend that he treats like crap. 
 Honestly, with that premise it would be less than surprising if people in general had a hard time connecting. But I think Riggs deserves some credit here. He could have taken the easier path and given us a poor, likable (but turmoiled) outcast. But he doesn't, and he commits wholly to trying his best to give Jacob a recognizable soul. I liked how he spends time connecting us to his relationship with the Grandfather, and I even enjoyed how he uses the relationship with the father throughout the book to examine Jacob's motivation. By the time I arrived at the end I felt like I was beginning to learn how to care about this character, and that is a difficult thing to manage for any writer. If anything I think he suffers from a weak supporting cast more than the presentation and development of the character himself. 
 4. The Cinematic presence in the story: It made complete sense to me to read the author talking about how the book was written with a film in mind. It's the feeling I had carried all through the story. I can't remember the last time I felt myself saying "this scene would work great on screen" at so many different moments. It turns out this was intentional, so I guess it's a credit to say it worked. Of course the downfall is that it sacrifices on the literary level (although that is of course subjective). But I appreciated the ability and desire to try and fuse these two worlds together. 
 What I didn't like: 
 1. The literary sacrifice that the cinematic form demands: To follow up on my last point to the positive, the negative side of this is a story that struggles immensely with flow. How a book can feel so bogged down and yet move so quickly is puzzling to me, but this was my experience. For all of the time it takes to develop nearly nothing gets developed by the time we hit the real action (a full three quarters in unfortunately). 
 I think a part of the issue here (which might be worth mentioning) is that the author can't seem to figure out which characters and which moments to sit on and let develop, and which ones are simply tools to bring the cinematic form of the story to life. It is a shame that we get to know next to nothing of the fantastical characters living in Miss Peregrine's home, as the mere mention that they all arrived at this home with tension filled past (revolving around the fact they were all peculiar children trying to find a place in a normal world) left me as a reader intrigued to know more. 
 2. Emma: If I managed to find a way to enjoy the character of Jacob, Emma found my on the other side of this coin. A character that should have been immediately likeable (and in her mysterious introduction she kind of is) derails in to all of the characteristics that I expected to hate about Jacob. I can't remember the last time I have encountered a character that was so back and forth and emotionally confused, and for no apparent (or good) reason. And again, this is a bit of a shame because there was so much good stuff there that the author could have explored (with her different personal connections to Jacob himself). Instead, she ends up so erratic and so annoying (I love you Jacob/I hate you Jacob, Please stay Jacob/You are responsible for everything Jacob) that nothing of her complicated past ends up having any real bearing on the story (at least emotionally). 
 3. The fact that it feels like a dumbed down version of the popular YA format: I need to be careful with this point, as the last thing I mean to suggest is that good, smart readers can't enjoy this story. I actually think the story has a ton of potential. My issue is in the way it meanders through its story without a really good sense of it's audience. In the beginning, I thought it was aiming for something akin to The Magicians, something a bit more mature but still in the spectrum of recognizable YA material. The entire portions given to explaining the stories dramatic and complicated theories made me think it belonged with something more along the lines of Divergent, which would be perfectly fine if I hadn't been expecting something different. And then we arrive at the book's persistent meandering in to the cliche (most notably in the eye-rolling romance of Jacob and Emma), and the ridiculous dialogue that forms the book's climatic showdown. It all seems to hamper the ability to figure out the book's core audience. 
 The book is not terrible. In-fact, there were a few moments where I didn't want to put it down. There were also a few where I was perfectly okay with putting it down. The end result left me intrigued enough to tackle the sequel, but probably more intrigued to see with Burton can do with the film. That is, after all, where I think the book truly belongs.

This book is perfection. I picked this book up after my sister gave me rave reviews. I had heard it was also becoming a movie from a random source, so I wanted to pick it up before it came out. 
 I found the novel slow to start out with a bit confusing, but once I got about one quarter into the book it was a pleasant surprise and I was hooked! I didn't want to put the book down and I adored it. The pictures hidden without the book gave a little extra boost to the story and made it easier to picture the characters. The pictures even made the characters seem somewhat real. 
 I don't have many bad things to say about the novel other than a few aspects that I found couldn't be seen as "real" in the fictional universe - such as Jacob's father not seeming to care to much about his disappearing for long amounts of time. 
 Overall, it was a good book and I can't wait to grab the next one! 
 Five out of five stars!

Eine fantastische Geschichte um ein Heim voller Kinder mit sehr ... merkwurdigen Eigenschaften. Spannend geschrieben, zieht den Leser gleich hinein und lasst nicht mehr los. Das absolute Highlight: der Roman wurde um alte Fotos herum geschrieben, die der Autor auf Flohmarkten und bei Sammlern gefunden hat. Diese Bilder verleihen der Geschichte eine zusatzliche Dimension, machen sie lebendig und beziehen den Leser in die Entdeckungsreise des Helden mit ein. 
 Lohnt sich!

Three-and-a-half stars, really. 
 The vintage black-and-white snapshots (though some have been digitally tweaked, they are authentically old photographs) peppered throughout the book really lent well and contributed to the overall creepiness of the story, however, the plot could have been slightly stronger (the action peters off a bit in the middle). I look forward to the second installment in the series, Hollow City.

Terrible. How can this book be one of the NYT's bestsellers? The dialogue is scattered, all over the place, very lame, and immature. I understand that the author tried to put imaginary characters into a fun story, instead, it came out very, very, very flat. It could have been done so much better with coherence, excitement, thrill, and good transitions, which this book lack greatly. Instead, the story is like a dish with too many ingredients and do not synchronize or go well with each other. I had such high hope for this when I saw the cover with peculiar, twisted pictures of children. I expected something psychologically twisted, instead, I ended up reading a boring story of a sixteen year-old boy and his journey to wonderland, which is not even half as astonishing as Hogwarts or Oz. Again, do not judge the book by its cover.
2 stars for the boring and haphazard plotting. Down to 1 star for co-opting some terrifically creepy photographs for such a disappointing book.

Her futuristic thriller novels have interesting plots and subplots, horrifying villains, and a superwoman police officer who is married to the richest, most handsome man in the world. My request would be for JD to leave the romance out of her thrillers.

reference_books.title: Predator (Kay Scarpetta, #14)
reference_books.review_text:
Confusing story with unlikable characters. The main character, Scarpetta, is annoyed by everyone. Her niece, Lucy, has a tumor that's making her a lunatic. Scarpetta's boyfriend is flat and bland. No wonder he annoys her. The TV star, Dr. Self, is disliked by the entire cast of characters and the reader as well. 
 From other reviews (http://www.goodreads.com/book/show/65... 
 the characters have gotten so bitter and unpleasant

 the magic of her earlier books isn't there 
 gosh darn if that wasn't a hard book to finish

 Kay Scarpetta is pretty unlikable 
 It's difficult for me to even grasp what a mess this book was.

reference_books.title: The Wrong Side of Goodbye (Harry Bosch, #21; Harry Bosch Universe, #26)
reference_books.review_text:
I tried to read slowly to make the book last as long as possible. How long until the next Bosch book or the next Amazon season of Bosch? I especially enjoy Bosch books when Harry's half-brother, the Lincoln Lawyer, shares the stage, as he did in this book. Two distinct story lines, both compelling. I was surprised at the end by "who-dun-it." I enjoy a surprise. 
 I was afraid that the "Good-bye" in the title meant we were saying good-bye to Harry Bosch. That's not the case, and I don't think saying so is any kind of spoiler. It's a happy comment that there will surely be more Bosch books in the future. Just hope we don't have to wait too long.

reference_books.title: Rough Country (Virgil Flowers, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
Good story well told. Virgil Flowers is a delightful goofball. The poor guy can't catch a break in his personal life but he is on top of things in his work life. This book was an interesting tale of lesbian musicians trying to make it big, family intrigue and of course a murder for Virgil to solve. The end was a satisfying surprise to me. 
 This is a great series. Highly recommended.

reference_books.title: Confessions of a Murder Suspect (Confessions, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I saw this book on CD at the public library. A James Patterson that I was not aware of? So I checked it out. I didn't realize at first that it's a young adult book, which mostly means that the main character is a teenager. A good story is a good story no matter who takes the lead. 
 I really liked it and, I assume because of the audience, the sex and language was toned down if not altogether eliminated. That's another plus for me. I've already purchased this book for my school library.

book_a.title: Faceoff
book_a.user_review:
This is an amazing anthology of thriller stories written by teams of two. The first title that caught my eye was RHYMES WITH PREY, Lincoln Rhyme vs. Lucas Davenport. "vs." is misleading because the characters work together to solve the situation (almost always). 
 The back story of this publication is as interesting as any of the short stories. It is explained BY David Baldacci in the introduction. 
 Don't miss this anthology if you are a fan of thriller fiction

sample_reviews.review_text: I bought this only for the stories by Sandford, Lee Child and Jeffery Deaver, but there are a lot of other great stories in here too. A lot of writers I've never read have now piqued my interest, and I'll probably be picking up books by them soon too. The aforementioned trio delivered as always, and it was great seeing Lucas and Lincoln together.
Really enjoyed the concept and the stories.

I enjoyed this book. For who are looking for a mystery author, or character to follow, these short stories are a great way to get a taste of the author and their character to find out if you connect. 
 Some of my favorites teamed up together to solve a crime, just to mention a few: 
 Dennis Lehane's Patrick Kenzie and Michael Connelly's Harry Bosch 
 Lee Child's Jack Reacher and Joseph Finder's Nick Heller. 
 I liked all the stories and discovered some new authors and characters myself.

As anthologies go, pretty good. My favorite stories were "Rhymes with Prey," by Jeffrey Deaver and John Sandford (Lincoln Rhyme working with Lucas Davenport) and "Good and Valuable Consideration," by Lee Child and Joseph Finder (Jack Reacher and Nick Heller combining forces).

I only wanted to read this for the Pendergast vs. Slappy, and that's the absolute truth. However, I had to read the other stories just so that I could review the book-and add it to my read list. Sadly, maybe two of the others were any good at all, and several of them were just god awful, and impress upon me the reason that I do not read most of the authors included. 
 Red Eye, Dennis Lehane and Michael Connelly: 2 stars 
 Before this, I had read part of a Michael Connelly book and was unimpressed, and read a short story by Lehane that was just awful, so I wasn't hopeful. And I wasn't proven wrong. I didn't like either of their main characters. I was hard pressed to find a plot that was at all meaningful, and the dialogue. The dialogue. It felt like certain famous lines were twisted around to fit the situations, and it just created a new level of tripe. And speaking of tripe? The ending. 
 In the Nick of Time, Ian Rankin and Peter James: 2 stars 
 I had never read anything by either of the authors, and am not likely to in the future. The ending just did not jive with me at all. I don't see how there was a "nick of time" in the situation at all, maybe a convenience of time, but not a deadline imminent or something. And the black and white morality and characterization is just obnoxious to me. The way the authors attempted to portray the wife as being in the wrong for trying to protect her husband. Seriously? Nah, she should have just pushed him at them and gone, "S'all cool brah." 
 Gaslighted, Douglas Preston & Lincoln Child and R.L. Stine: 4 1/4 stars 
 You. Bad story, making me want to read so much that I was willing to read all of the other bits in this collection. I mean, putting together three of my favorite literary folk in one contained story? Pretty certain that I squealed at the prospect. But to the actual review: it needed more Slappy. Or at least for Slappy to do something other than exist and be slightly menacing. That's really the reason this isn't five stars for me. If it was only meant to be a Pendergast story, it would easily have gained a five from me. I was disappointed at the lack of hilarious Slappy. But I still read the story twice. Once right off, another when I went back to read the other stories. Then there's the interesting possibilities this could open up. I mean, will this effect the series in the future, because that could get a bit crazy. No pun intended. 
 The Laughing Buddha M.J. Rose and Lisa Gardner: 3 stars 
 I have never been interested in Gardner's books, but I do have The Reincarnationist on my to-read list. Funnily enough, after reading this, my opinion of the authors is unchanged. I still don't want to read Gardner, and still have a passing interest in Rose. D.D. was boring, and I didn't get why she was supposed to be so special. She seemed to have no unique character traits at all. Malachai on the other hand...grew on me. He just was so nearly villainous in his behavior and motives that I found myself somehow actually caring about his part of the story. Overall, even that was predictable, but there was a certain wry quality in the M.J. Rose writing that made it still worth reading. 
 Surfing the Panter Steve Martini and Linda Fairstein: 2 stars 
 Firstly, author avatar is the term that I could not stop thinking throughout the story. And there was a lot of "throughout." I don't know if the story just dragged on, or if it was one of the longer ones, but it felt like it never ended. And the beginning? A waste of my time. I like law, I do, but that was just simplified, boring law. There was nothing new or interesting to discuss. The ending? About as big a waste of my time. Glad everything just managed to wrap the way everyone wanted it to. Then we all lived happily ever after. 
 Rhymes with Prey John Sandford and Jeffrey Deaver: 1 star 
 Sandford, I do not like. I read the first book of his Davenport series (because of the awesome name. I was weak) and decided that I never wanted to read another...and yet here I am. Deaver, I read a short story, but not a Rhyme one, so, I know he has a kind of old-fashioned, dry approach to writing plots. So, this ended up being a heap of dry misogyny. Yay. The misogyny was exactly what I remembered from my previous Sandford endeavor. Women are sort of portrayed as precious objects that bad men like to damage. And that's about where I start to projectile vomit. Then there was the couple/couple aspect with both of the "heroes" having their obligatory hot woman, not that they have to be hot themselves. Only women have to be attractive in any way. I freaking hate that widespread belief in books. Utterly wasted my time with this. The only thing I can say is that at least Lincoln was a stuffy jerk, and almost managed to entertain me a few times. 
 Infernal Night Heather Graham and F. Paul Wilson: 3 1/2 stars 
 I don't know anything about either author, but surprisingly this was one of the few stories I actually liked reading. It wasn't too long, got to the point quickly enough. It wasn't an overly complicated plot, but it was about the level I like for a short story. I also think the writing was more cohesive than in many of the other works. Odd, since this is inter-gender and usually women and men write differently. I suppose I should give them both credit for that. I also liked how the characters played off each other, which again, I didn't see happen as successfully in some of the other stories. 
 Pit Stop Raymond Khoury and Linwood Barclay : 2 stars 
 Okay, so never read the authors, don't want to now. I don't like the whole focus on the precocious child. I'm sorry, but I really don't like children in my books unless they're very background or are masterfully done and serve a valid purpose. The plot other than the child borefest was kind of silly and not at all creative. Oh, and the hot coffee reference...don't flippantly refer to a legitimate tort case. Alright, maybe one of my buttons got pressed there, but it does feel like the corporations are getting some free support for their belittling of tort cases in general. Done now. 
 Silent Hunt John Lescroart and T. Jefferson Parker: 1 star 
 I think that I actually liked a T. Jefferson Parker book before, but this, I hated. The meeting was just contrived. And the whining about airport security? We all do that all the time in real life, I don't need it rehashed in what I'm reading. Then there was the flatness of the characters. I got that they were like each other, and were boring people, but nothing other than that. Maybe they weren't boring, but they certainly seemed like it here. The plot was just a rehash of every "save the village" plot that ever was. And ew. So sick of that one. Fishing and impoverished Mexican villages: a recipe for making me prefer to go outside and count blades of grass rather than read another page. The "You are a slave to greed." line, that one really just encompasses my utter hatred of this story. Slave to greed...oh shut up. 
 The Devil's Bones Steve Barry and James Rollins: 1 star 
 Maybe it's not fair to Steve Barry, but I went into this already hating the way that Rollins writes, and hating his character. Overall, though, it felt like two coinciding mid-life crises. Big, rough and tumble middle-aged guys that are pulled away from their hot, much younger girlfriends to go do heroic spy stuff. Where were their Mustangs? The black and white morality and characterization, that was fun. Really tough, making your undesirable characters kitten stompers, and having your main characters the pinnacle of goodness. Speaking of self-righteous jerks... 
 Good and Valuable Consideration Lee Child and Joseph Finder: 1 star 
 All of those times I said that I never wanted to read a Jack Reacher book or anything by Lee Child? I was right to feel that way. Firstly, "lizard brain" shall be forever banned from writing forever. Then there's the part where the characters allege that they can induce amnesia just by hitting a certain part of the skull a certain way. Yep, it's the part with the unicorn horn and you have to sprinkle pixie dust before you do it. The overwhelming "simple men with simple appetites" thing I wrote in my notes while reading "KILL ME!" I suppose that sums up my feelings there. Oh, and Mr. Heller, I thought we never gave our last name when meeting someone, and yet about five minutes after that inner monologue proceeded to do the very thing. (Maybe he was instantly in love with his godfather, Reacher.) So, now I have to go make sure that I don't have any Finder books on my to-read list. This was just UGH.

Review: Faceoff Anthology Editeddata:text/mce-internal,%3Cimg%20src%3D%22http%3A//booklikes.blob.core.windows.net/post/... by David Balducci 
 Ever wondered how your favorite literary characters would fair in a Celebrity Death Match with each other? I feel like this collection of short stories was exactly that. Twenty Three of the best thriller writers set out to create unique experiences with characters that all of their fans will know. Faceoff was something I never saw coming and I am terribly happy that I agreed to read this title because I came away with some delightful reads and a few shocks along the way. 
 From Michael Connelly's detective hero Harry Bosch coming to my own backyard Boston to run into Dennis Lehane's Patrick Kenzie to the King of all horror madness R.L. Stine creating a crazy story with Lincoln Child and Douglas Preston, these aren't stereotypical stories thrown together because they just read the same. Each story was unique and interesting, while still giving you that jolt of energy and surprise that most thriller junkies have come to expect from these masters of trade. It's very clear that these are masters of their trade form page one to the end.That being said, I have to tell you that as someone who normally doesn't read a lot of this genre, I wasn't lost and confused. In fact most of these regular characters I really knew nothing about coming into this book and it never intimidated me. I could tell there were nuances about characters that I missing but I feel like a fan of an author would get it and like that incorporation, while another reader that has never read something by that same author isn't going to be scared off because they don't have prior knowledge of a character. That was the biggest part I was scared of when picking this book up and it was time wasted worrying because I didn't put it down for two days. This is exactly what I expect to find in a book with such a long list of credentials backing it up! 
 Originally posted: http://thebookblogattheendoftheuniver...

A buddy of mine at work, got this at the library and asked me if I wanted to read it. With twenty-three popular thriller writers, pairing their alter ego to work together, I thought this was a pretty cool idea. Fun and a quick read. Here are my favorites, in no particular order - 
 Rhymes With Prey - Lincoln Rhyme & Lucas Davenport 
 Infernal Night - Michael Quinn & Repairman Jack 
 In The Nick Of Time - John Rebus & Roy Grace 
 Good and Valuable Consideration - Jack Reacher & Nick Heller

This collection was a wonderful introduction to some characters and welcome reunion with others. I love the idea behind this collection - having protagonists either work with or against each other. Although not perfect, I found more of the stories entertaining than not. I will warn you though, you may notice an exponential increase in your TBR list.
Interesting premise and the little intros before each story were really fun.

 There was a bonus story included on a separate CD called MORALITY. It reminded me of that movie where a rich guy offers to pay a couple a lot of money if the wife will sleep with him. Being bad for money. In MORALITY, the bad thing the wife has to do is punch a two-year-old in the face. And for much less than a million dollars. Who cares?!? Not me.

sample_reviews.review_text: This wasn't quite what I thought it would be and it definitely felt like King just wanted to write a slightly spooky story about baseball. Meh, he has done better.

** spoiler alert ** 
 [SPOILER] 
 Fictional stand-in catcher for the New Jersey Titans during the 1957 season, Blockade Billy is the story of William Blakely, a young lad from the sticks who ends up playing with an MLB team, and what a player he is, especially on the home plate where his stopping power is the stuff of legends. A shame he turns out to be a killer, and not the real William Blakely, who it appears he murdered a few months back, along with his parents and a farm full of cows. He is Eugene Katsanis, an orphan who worked for the Blakely family, who helped young William with his throwing and catching, and who was abused by the family when his talents with a baseball outshone their son's. All told from the viewpoint of his New Jersey third base coach, George 'granny' Grantham. 
 [SPOILER] 
 For a story that took 2 weeks to write, it was gripping and unputdownable.. which was fine as it only took 35 minutes to read.

This little novella took me three evenings to read. Normally, I could consume a book this size in a couple of hours. It's 112 pages with a lot of pictures and blank pages. It's okay, but that's about it. As I was reading, I couldn't help but flashback to the Twilight Zone episode "The Mighty Casey" in which a pitcher becomes an overnight superstar but is clearly not what he appears to be. Heck, this was practically the same story. It just had a different origin for the star player. 
 Although I love mythological baseball movies like "Field of Dreams" and "The Sandlot", this book just didn't click with me.
Not so wild about this one. It had a bit of creepiness, but I wanted more of an ending.

It's a known fact that Stephen King is a big baseball fan, and possibly one of the biggest Red Sox fans (if you doubt this, just read The Girl Who Loved Tom Gordon). After the mighty tome of Under the Dome and with a four-novella book called Full Dark, No Stars due out in November, there's another little story King is releasing to keep fans occupied. Blockade Billy is a short, little book - just over a hundred pages - about baseball that is a perfect read for the start of summer and America's favorite sport. 
 Way back when, in the early days of baseball when the players weren't making much money and it was all about the rule and the game and the sport, the Titans of New Jersey had a bad start to the new season. Their everyday catcher, while driving drunk, killed a woman and is in prison, while their scrawny beanpole of a backup catcher is mowed down in a play at the plate and ends up in the hospital. Then the Titans find a young rookie from Iowa, William Blakely. 
 Blakely is strange character - in that great Stephen King way - who does an impressive job catching and hitting to boot. At his first big play at the plate, Billy tags the runner out as the man flies over the catcher and is left with a sliced Achilles heel, never play properly again. But Blakely wins the team and the fans over in that first game, as well as others to come. He starts hitting balls out of the park, doing a great job of catching, and making some great plays at the plate. The nickname - Blockade Billy - sticks and a legend is born. 
 The season continues and while the Titans don't win every game, they do well and Blockade Billy continues to wow the crowds and the team. Then a terrible secret is discovered. About Blakely. His career is over; the Titan's games are stricken from the record, and every effort is made to eradicate the name of William Blakely from history. 
 The story is told in third person to King from the former third-base coach, now in his old age, who remembers this high time of baseball and the infamous memory that was Blockade Billy. King writes it in his colloquial, easy to read style, slowly giving out the details and keeping the reader completely hooked, needing to know what the story is behind Blockade Billy. But I'm not going to give that away here; you'll have to read the book to find out. 
 For more book reviews and exclusive author interviews, go to BookBanter.

Stephen King struck the right note, that is for sure. You can tell King is a baseball fan from reading this. The atmosphere was right and the build up was perfect. The 2nd story that was included with Blockade Billy was good as well but not very memorable.

This book is written well, as are all Kings' books but I just wasn't that big a fan mainly because of the sport involved. I think it could have be a greater story if told from the side of "Billy". Still worth a read though!
