I bought this for my son because I liked the illustrations. Honestly, I wish that I hadn't. Like others have already noted, the message in this story is horrible as written. That message being that everyone should be the same and that you should give something that you hold dear to others simply because they want you to. 
 That is the exact opposite of what I want my son to learn. I want him to revel in his uniqueness and have no fear of being proud of things that others may jealously tear him apart for (modesty is good, but recognizing ways that your special is also good!). I do not want him to ever feel like he needs to give in to the demands of others. And I want him to share because he WANTS to share and not because he fears repercussions. In fact, someone who feels entitled to something he has is someone who doesn't deserve it. 
 So, since I have this book and honestly don't even want to gift it to someone else, I tell my own story using the illustrations. When the little fish gets angry that the Rainbow Fish won't give him a scale, my version is that it makes the Rainbow Fish sad and he doesn't understand why the little fish and all the other fish are being so mean to him. He seeks out the starfish and then the octopus (squid?), who tells him that sometimes people react poorly when they see that someone else has something they want and that Rainbow Fish should explore the ocean for fish who will be nicer to him. RF does this and finds a friend who admires his shiny scales and invites RF to play with his friends. The friends all have single scales and don't make demands of him and RF is no longer lonely. I don't really acknowledge how RF only has one shiny scale at the end, though I'll probably just say that he offered some of his scales to some of the other fish if it comes up. (BY CHOICE, not pressure!). Obviously, this isn't a perfect rewrite... I'd prefer the fish at the end be varied and not all fish with a shiny scale, but that's not what's drawn. 
 I really couldn't recommend this book to anyone as I really don't like what it's saying. Which is really a shame because it's pretty!

This review should have been two stars, but gets knocked down a star for disappointing me so much - Brian K. Vaughan wrote Saga! I was expecting this to be so much better than it was, especially given its acclaim. 
 1. NO WAY does the President of the United States let the last living human man travel out of her sight, let alone accompanied by a single guard. 
 2. "Believe me," says the leader of the roving gang of man-hating women, in pursuit of our rash and idiotic young hero. "I despise barking orders like a patriarch... Somewhere out there, the last of our oppressors lives!" 
 ....UGH. 
 What a nonsensical and unbelievable villain - a ham-fisted caricature of feminism imagined only by the ill-informed. I very much doubt that anybody would be able to get many followers by maligning everyone with a penis as a force of evil, fresh as the men are in their graves. It seems way more likely that women would form gangs based on any number of other things they'd have in common with surviving peers - cultural affiliation, religion, etc.
Ok... I'll read the second one to see if it looks up, but...

All men died except for one guy and his male pet monkey. Society devolves into chaos and also most women are crazy, probably because there's no men to keep them in line! 
 Reading this, I am reminded of everything I dislike about traditional American comics. The pages are blocky panels that don't naturally draw the eye along. There's little natural flow. Each panel is like looking at a movie still, the action is implied, but even in panels that are depicting action there's no movement whatsoever. And the dialogue is ridiculous--it tells the story, yes, but rarely does it flow like real dialogue should. 
 The story is mediocre. All male everything dies at the exact same time all over the globe, save for one twenty-somthing guy, Yorick, and his pet monkey. Yorick eventually ends up on a quest to help find out what happened/find his girlfriend/possibly repopulate the earth. I was interested in what happened, but not enough to even find the other books at the library (and if the Wikipedia summary is accurate, I'm not missing anything). 
 Also: of COURSE there's a giant cult of women who think all men deserved to die! What do they do when they're not trying to find the last guy on earth? Stand around and make jokes about how stupid men were and/or kill women who don't agree with them. That's a productive way to spend your precious time! Apparently they also go out and burn down sperm banks, because it hasn't occurred to them that they'll eventually start dropping like flies.

With such high marks for this series, I was eagerly anticipating it. But, I'm not seeing it. Perhaps the next few installments will change my mind. I hope so as I received the next few books in the series for Christmas.

I found this novel incredibly depressing. I chugged through it, no doubt it was well written, but if you are someone who prefers uplifting stories that don't leave you feeling hollow, avoid this book.

One of the things I like to do while reading is to sort of imagine the thought-process the author goes through while penning -in this case- her work. What most authors find most comfortable working with (and what most people consider, well, normal) is the third person; the first person voice is reserved for the occasions where the voice so irresistible that the author simply must use it; gimmicky voices - dog, child, inanima - are not encouraged. For a serious writer, then, to employ a cute and gimmicky voice isn't the easiest thing to do: to fail would plainly invite cries of 'sell-out', 'played-out-gimmick'; to do mediocrely would be to invite slams of ersatz novel, of writer out of ideas. If you care at all about your literary reputation then you know you can't afford to fail. To speak through Jack requires that small bit of courage, in other words; or as Jack would put it, scavery. 
 The best thing you can then say about Room is that it absolutely transcends the gimmick of voice: it's a thrill of a ride that pulls no punches, draws no cliches and speaks of Life and Love and Family in uniquely powerful fashions. Comparisons with Mark Haddon's Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time are both easy and inevitable but really fail to Room justice: unlike Haddon's charming cutesey novel (that ends rather with a whimper), Room isn't wholly narratocentric and feels alive and actually has a story to tell and important things to say. 
 A short synopsis here. Room is in many ways a fictional retelling and reimaging of Jaycee Dugard's 18-year-long kidnapping. In Jaycee's unfortunate place we have Ma, kidnapped by dastardly Old Nick as a freshman at college; kidnapped, raped, trapped within the 12 by 12 plexiglas-foil-cork Room with her child, Jack. Jack is the quintessence of cherubic innocence: a wide-eyed, doe-faced, long-haired 5 YO boy who knows Room not as prison but as his (the) world. Jack is a very bright boy; he loves to read, he understands far more than he lets on, and he loves his mother dearly. If there were a Medal of Valor for maternal care then Ma would qualify for it: going far and above the call of motherhood, recreating a microscopic facsimile of the World for her child, teaching him all that she knows. One episodic struggle with Old Nick after another and Ma finally breaks down. She resolves to escape. She tells Jack everything; Jack will be her Houdini. They make their escape. What follows thereafter is circa 100 pages worth of readjustment struggles (it's a lot more interesting than I'm making it sound). 
 Room is in many ways a novel of two parts; pre-Room and post-Room Room can exist as discrete, separate novels almost. The former is a cute piquant mystery novel that teases you with small details and shies from making big reveals too quickly; but when it does, it does so quickly, spectacularly. The result is a gently moving fugue that builds quickly and surprisingly into a fast and furious and loud Shostakovich finish. It's actually genuinely spine-tingling at parts. Ma and Jack are characters who grow on you quickly so you end up caring and empathizing about whether they survive. Minor gripe though: if you're someone who goes into Room unspoiled then you'll kinda pine for a reveal early on so much of the need-to-know is withheld (you can only know as much as Jack does, after all). A little of the "Yeah I get it, now move on please!" if you get what I mean. 
 Part deux of Room sees the novel make the peregrination from Curious Incident of the Dog in the night-time-esque unique-gimmick-mystery-thriller to the in-vogue observational literary novel. Mother and son, having made their great escape now face the challenge of transitioning into a world where they're very much foreign and alien (and are they not? Denizens of that 12 by 12 Room). Neither are particularly adroit when it comes to adapting: the terribly insidious but no less true accusation leveled at Ma by a journalist questioning her maternal benevolence ("Did the thought never occur to have Jack sent to an orphanage where he could have some semblance of a normal life? Was Jack raised with the intention of escape in mind?" Something to this effect.) shatters her; Jack struggles with the inundation of stimuli away from the sweet simple opiate of Room life. As they cope and grow, learn, we do, with them. 
 Here's on particularly acute observation from Jack: 
 Also, everywhere I'm looking at kids, adults mostly don't seem to like them, not even the parents do. They call the kids gorgeous and so cute, they make the kids do the thing all over again so they can take a photo, but they don't want to actually play with them, they'd rather drink coffee talking to other adults. Sometimes there's a small kid crying and the Ma of it doesn't even hear." 
 This gets into a lot more familiar territory (uniquely True observations everyone fails to see); it's pretty different from the first part and can feel rather incongruous but don't let this detract from the fact that both parts are exquisite. 
 For a story that can and should feel cliche, Room somehow doesn't. A gimmick voice; rape, kidnap and other heavily melodramatic scenes; suicide; abandonment. Yet somehow, somewhere, Emma Donogue manages to craft an amazing gestalt that filters the dregs from cliches and leaves the best stuff in. Warm, gravid with humanity, clever, true and always effervescently alive, Room really is quite extraordinary. 
 A little meta-review postscript here: I realize writing book reviews require to look at very specific things: the same way English Literature majors and Creative Writing majors can both analyze texts but in radically (or not) different ways. All the symbol/motif/intentions shenanigans I'm not really devoting enough time to even though I do want to. I rarely delve into these in my reviews unless the impulse is really strong, I'm now seeing. I'm not sure why: I do take quite a bit of notes while reading (they're the basis of my reviews) but somehow when it's time to translate them into a coherent review I neglect. Quite a shame I think. Need to think of some way to include all these in well. Maybe change my entire tact towards reviews. Hmm.

Jack, only five years old and only living life to the fullest the twelve by twelve room can provide for him. His mother, held captive by Old Nick for seven years, yearns for freedom, to see the outside again,. but as for Jack, the captivity that he's known all his life has suddenly become simply too crushing. As his mother, Ma, and him live life to the fullest they can, dependent on the courteous of Old Nick for every necessity to keep them living, Ma can only keep Jack safe for so long, hiding him within wardrobe and out of Old Nick's sight ever since he was born, after having delivered a still born daughter with the cord wrapped around her neck in the imprisonment she lived within since she was nineteen. After rehearsing the plans, she fakes her son;s death, as he escapes from the rug in the back of the truck, gaining attention and bringing help to his Mother. While at the clinic, Jack lives life quietly refusing to be separated from his mother for even a second. As he learns about the family he never knew was real, his mother overdoses and barely pulls through, before they move on to Independent Living, after Jack lived with his Grandmother and Steppa, Leo for a week. Now, as they breathe in the air, feel the sunshine on their skins, can either of them look up to the Lord's face and feel freedoms.

reference_books.review_text: Oh good lord the writing in this book is magnificent. It sweeps you up and pulls you into the world of The Winter Sea. I truly loved every character in this book. I adored Graham and John and felt that they were perfect for both Carrie and Sophia. My only small complaint with this novel is that the plot is slow. This book is not a rousing adventure that moves quicker than the speed of light. Rather it is like a beautiful stormy night that you enjoy with a cup of coffee and good conversation. It was like being wrapped in a warm blanket. I loved it. I cried at the end and was so happily surprised with where the story went. This is a book about strong women and the men they love and while slower paced it is incredibly moving and will make you want to leave for Scotland immediately. Wonderful book with great characters and with romances that I absolutely adored.

Things I never want to read about again: 
 1. Juliette's tortured soul. 
 2. Her inability to breathe. 
 3. Her breaking bones and collapsing organs.

Shatter Me was a great book. It was poetic, interesting, and I got very excited to start the second book. 
 However, I made a horrible choice. I do not know where I started to realize it. Juliet was whiny, annoying and senseless. She was also a complete Mary- Sue and waited on by man after man. Her two love interests lost all of their good qualities and the book's dystopian world remained a mystery. 
 There was no point to this book. None.

My face while reading this book: 
 I liked Shatter Me. But this book, its sequel, pounded on the things I didn't like about the first. 
 Unravel Me is essentially a soap opera trying to smush in some X-Men and dystopia (elements that only fuel the soap opera of the novel). 
 We have Juliette, who you think might take advantage of the fact that she's around people who are like her, actually stays with Adam and doesn't try to make friends. Which, you know, I can get. It's hard trying to make friends, especially if you have a history of people fearing you. But it seems to me the reason why she doesn't branch out is Adam, rather than a fear of talking to people. But you know, flaws are good. Except Juliette is also a blubber baby and likes to whine about her problems rather than trying to fix it. Things happen to her, and she rarely reacts to fix what's wrong in her life. 
 A bit of a spoiler, but something that happens within the first 80 pages: Adam fights off Juliette's deathly touch, which wears him down until her power can break through and hurt him--possibly kill him. He professes his love and desire to be with her despite this, she professes her love back, but dumps him, and they spend the remainder of the novel whining about their separation. 
 Hey Juliette, you know who else can't touch? These two: 
 And they're just about the cutest couple ever. If you two really loved each other as much as you say, you WOULD try to work something out, because you clearly both want to be around each other. Believe it or not, there's more to a relationship than kissing. Gasp! I KNOW! And if Adam is willing to give up whatever physical relationship between the two (let's face it, you don't have many options for physical relationship anyway, so it shouldn't concern you) then for the love of sanity, JUST BE TOGETHER. It works for Ned and Chuck, even if it makes the viewers weep--because we see the two of them trying so hard to work it out and loving each other despite of their difficulties. 
 But its absolute worst offense: THE LOVE TRIANGLE OF DOOM. 
 Most of the time, I don't like love triangles. Let's put that out there first. Not only do I find them unbelievable (I've never had a girlfriend or acquaintance or even known of someone who was desperately in love with two guys at the same time), most of the time they're just badly done. 
 So yes, we have a love triangle of doom. Warner comes into the picture and despite the fact that he's heartless and planned on brutally murdering Adam in book 1, Juliette can't help but feel attracted to him. Even though she points out that it's wrong, doesn't make it right. There's pathetic attempts to humanize him, but he shows no character growth in the end. 
 There are revelations that should be shocking, but they were just soap opera plot twists, which I might have dealt with if the whole feeling of the novel wasn't a soap opera. 
 Kenji was pretty awesome, and the only character with his head on straight. It was like Mafi was acknowledging the reader's criticism of Juliette through Kenji, only Juliette didn't change. Not in the fact that she would just quit whining, anyway.
I didn't finish this. I couldn't. it was torture to read more of this sorry excuse of a novel.

 I think my fundamental problem with this series is that I went into it looking for a paranormal dystopian society styled novel, when in fact it is more along the lines of Twilight paranormal romance fiction, although I will say at least the writing is a little better. 
 What I saw as an unique writing style for narrative in Shatter Me started to lose its charm somewhat with Unravel Me, especially now that we know Juliette isn't, in fact, crazy. The sentences are often changed or stop and start in mid thought, which I guess is supposed to make us connect better with Juliette as the narrative feels like you are actually hearing the story from inside her head. 
 My biggest issue with Unravel Me, and really with the series so far, is the issue of this underlying dystopian society, as I still do not really know what this whole society is about. Sure, we get a little more detail about the Reestablishment, but everything is still rather vague and I do not 100% get what the big deal with this Anderson guy is. Perhaps Mafi did explain it, but I glossed over it between all the Juliette - Adam - Warner triangle jumble. 
 If you are looking for the next series to read after The Hunger Games, the Shatter Me series is going to leave you disappointed. If you are a Twihard and are looking for something to read until the next Stephanie Meyer "novel" comes out, you will probably really enjoy Mafi's Shatter Me series. It has all the young adult romance and cliche love triangle scenarios a girl could dream for, and even attempts somewhat at a plot. The characters are interesting enough, especially Warner. At least he isn't one dimensional and is mysterious enough (he's definitely the bad boy versus Adam's good guy) to hold my attention to where his true intentions really lay. But as for an honest to goodness, keep you up all night at the edge of your bed in suspense, Unravel Me just did not deliver. 
 I already have Ignite Me on hold from the library, so when it arrives I will probably go ahead and just give it a go as well, but I honestly do not hold much hope for my interest level shooting through the roof with the next one. If Lauren Oliver's Delirium series taught me anything, it's that was a subpar series gives you a wink of hope, you are only going to wind up severely disappointed at the end. But then Ally Condie's Matched series got surprisingly more interesting the further I got into it, so you never know.

 Juliette e riuscita finalmente a scappare dalla morsa di Warner, ed ora e arrivata ad Omega Point. Grazie ad Adam e Kenji, ora si sente al sicuro, e a casa. Ma sara veramente cosi? 
 A casa si, forse. Perche ad Omega Point non e un alieno, ne un essere deforme o roba del genere. Juliette e come tutti gli altri. Si, perche ci sono degli altri. E questi altri sono uguali a lei. Poteri sovrannaturali e tutto quanto: non hanno famiglia, si sono trovati, ed hanno creato un posto per nascondersi dalla Restaurazione: Omega Point. 
 Ecco, qui inizio a storcere il naso: scusate, ma cosa sto leggendo? Unravel Me, romanzo scritto da Tahereh Mafi oppure una rivisitazione di X-men? 
 Ho visto i film di quest'ultimo, non ne vado pazza, eppure le somiglianze con Unravel Me sono tante, quasi troppe. Sono andata ad informarmi sul web, e molti hanno trovato queste somiglianze, tanto che l'autrice ha smentito il tutto: lei neanche l'ha mai visto, X-men. Figurarsi se si e ispirata da li per il suo libro 
 . 
 Chiusa questa piccola parentesi, Juliette si ambienta subito ad Omega Point. Il problema 
 Juliette alle prese con Warner ed Adam >__< 
 e che e stato tutto cosi confusionario. Non ha fatto in tempo ad arrivare, ed ecco che incontra di nuovo Warner per pochi secondi e che il suo grandissimo amore nei confronti di Adam svanisce piano piano. 
 Ho odiato Juliette, quasi di piu la persona che ha deciso di crearla. Non ha ne arte ne parte, questa ragazza. Ho iniziato a trovarla interessante negli ultimi dieci capitoli. E sono piu di sessanta capitoli, capiamoci. La sua mente e malata, non pensa razionalmente e sembra una ragazzina di dieci anni, invece che di diciassette. Il fratellino di Adam e piu maturo di lei, ed ho detto tutto. 
 Capisco la sua mentalita chiusa all'inizio, dopo aver vissuto tanto tempo in isolamento. Capisco i suoi problemi, dopo che esce da quella cella sudicia e Warner la usa immediatamente come un'arma. Capisco quasi tutto, giuro. Ma non riesco ad arrivarci a certe cose. 
 Perche Juliette non e che pensa una cosa e poi ne dice un'altra. I pensieri di Juliette con i suoi fatti sono totalmente in disaccordo. Niente, non mi ci sono proprio trovata bene con lei. E' un'amica che non vorrei, ecco. Mai. Meglio soli che male accompagnati, e Juliette sarebbe un grandissimo problema per me. 
 La trama non e per niente male, Warner e sempre piu audace e perfetto, Adam dal buono della situazione passa ad essere il cattivo psicotico di turno. Mi dispiace tantissimo, perche mi aspettavo grandi cose da questo libro. Soprattutto dopo aver letto Shatter Me e la novella Destroy Me, che ho adorato alla follia. 
 Ovvio che ve lo consiglio, se dovete continuare la saga. Se proprio non sapete se iniziarla o no, lasciate stare. Sono alle prese con Ignite Me, e che Dio mi aiuti, ma vorrei buttarlo giu dal balcone. 
 Che mi combini, Tahereh? 
 Tre stelline soltanto per un personaggio che mi ha fatto ridere come una matta, e che purtroppo non rientra neanche nei protagonisti: Kenji.

I love it when people write reviews that are EX.AC.TLY. on par with how I felt about a book. This one in particular gets it spot on. 
 I was really disappointed by Inkdeath. Not gonna lie. I finished it several days ago and have sat around trying to think of positive things to say about it but I got nothin'. This is by far the weakest book in the trilogy and should have been much shorter and much less lame. Dangit. 
 This book is not quite a total departure from Inkheart and Inkspell but it's pretty close. None of the characters feel fleshed out in Inkdeath. Farid in particular - he never gets over his weird obsession with Dustfinger. Now, having weird obsessions with father figures of my own, I feel pretty confident in saying that Farid needs to seek some serious mental help. That whole part of the story just didn't ring true to me, honestly. I get being concerned for Dustfinger, but not obsessed to the point of stalkerishness with him. Creepy. 
 Meggie finds a new, completely random and weird, love interest. It actually ties into the story decently with Fenoglio remembering that he'd written a short story about that particular character but it was never published. But it's still random and weird. And the love interest character never feels like a part of the integral cast. 
 Mo's character was probably the least disappointing here. He went through a pretty awesomely harrowing torture sequence with Orpheus near the end. But even then, the ending felt odd and kind of disjointed. And totally not what I expected. 
 So, I'm glad I read Inkdeath because yay closure! But at the same time, I think I would have preferred a different ending like the one that was good in my head. I also would have liked to know the baby's name, just because I'm curious like that.

I loved this final installment. What a great book. It had me pulled in right at the start. She is such a great writer. I felt like I was in the Inkworld with Mo and Meggie. I can absolutely not believe that it took me four weeks to read this book---I'm usually a fast reader! I think actually that the length of time it took me to read this book may actually have hindered my appreciation of it; it was full of suspenseful events and impossible situations and yet I had to force myself to keep reading it. It wasn't the plot that was problematic, but the writing style that I found hard to get through---yet I've not had that problem with the first two books of the series. I think perhaps my timing was off---when I'm grading student papers every week, I should maybe stick to quicker reads. 
 In any case, I do recommend Inkdeath to those who have read the rest of the series. The first book is still my favorite, for its sense of mystery and the wonder of books, yet all the favorite characters are still here, in some form or another. I prefer Mo as the mild-mannered, albeit Silver-tongued bookbinder than as the Bluejay, even though daring bandit-types are usually my thing. There's a bit of a change in the relationship between Meggie and Farid, and I found myself wishing how old Meggie was supposed to be by now. One thing I really appreciate about Funke's books is how complex her characters are; there are the good guys, and there are the bad guys, but there are plenty who fall in between,who exhibit qualities both good and bad, or who change over time. Elinor, for example, was somewhat unpleasant when we first met her, but has become delightfully curmudgeonly by book number 3. Funke is willing to let her good characters disagree, and does not pull any punches when it comes to dealing with sad and serious matters, which is why I would recommend the series for mature middle schoolers and above.

Inkdeath, buku terakhir dari trilogi Inkspell. 
 Mungkin ini buku fantasi yang terbagus yang pernah saya baca, selain Bartimaeus Trilogi. Dan Cornelia Funke menutup kisah Mo, Meggie, Resa, Staubfinger, Fegnolio, Pangeran Hitam, dan Pangeran Perak dengan cantik. 
 Antara buku kesatu, kedua, dan ketiga...cerita kian berkembang.Memang di buku ketiga ini muncul tokoh-tokoh baru tetapi kemunculan mereka gak memusingkan, melainkan semakin memperkaya cerita ini. 
 Petualangan Mo sebagai si Gagak Biru kian seru di sini. Ia benar-benar telah jatuh hati dengan negeri Tintenwelt, sementara istrinya Resa dan anaknya Meggie kian mengkhawatirkan keselamatannya. Sebagai Gagak Biru, Mo merampok yang kaya untuk memberi makan yang miskin bersama sahabatnya, Pangeran Hitam dan komplotan perampoknya. Kayak Robin Hood gitu deh. Karena aksinya yang kerap menantang bahaya, Resa istrinya malah melakukan pengkhianatan. 
 Sementara Orpheus yang dimunculkan Meggie melalui tulisan Fegnolio malah bertingkah. Wataknya yang memang licik dan serakah berusaha membolak balikan cerita di negeri Tintenwelt semau dia. Fegnolio sendiri terpuruk menjadi pemabuk tua setelah gagal dengan rencananya. Sebenarnya Orpheus didatangkan dari dunia nyata untuk bisa merangkai kata yang bisa mendatangkan kembali Staubfinger dari pelukan kematian. Farid, murid Staubfinger pun merelakan dirinya menjadi budak Orpheus. Ugh, pokoknya Orpehus ini ngeselin banget. Dia gak mau mengakui kalau dia gak sehebat Mo dan Fegnolio, wong dia cuma copycat ajah. 
 Sementara, anak pangeran perak,Violente memiliki rencana sendiri. Ia yang hatinya dipenuhi kesedihan dan kepahitan berusaha untuk mencari peluang merebut tahta Ombra dengan memanfaatkan Gagak Biru. 
 Sementara ayah Violente, Natternkopf, mengejar Mo alias Gagak Biru karena merasa diperdaya oleh Buku Putih yang dibuat Mo. Buku tersebut membuat hidup Natternkopft abadi, tetapii..ia malah jadi monster hidup. 
 Plot yang enak dibaca dan penuh dengan kejutan membuat buku ini enak dibaca. Kalau bisa selesai sehari deh membaca buku 700-an halaman ini biar ga penasaran..hehehe.. 
 Sebenarnya, sempet gak yakin juga sih sama trilogi ini..tapi beneran, Cornelia Funke benar-benar jago meracik crita ini dan tidak membuatnya basi di akhir trilogi... 
 Bintang empat buat Inkdeath!

reference_books.title: The Disaster Artist: My Life Inside The Room, the Greatest Bad Movie Ever Made
reference_books.review_text: This was a fascinating book about the making of the worst movie I have ever seen, The Room. And in reading this book I learned that The Room was made with all seriousness and not as, like, a parody of a bad movie. At the center of the narrative is Tommy Wiseau, a man who is secretive about his past, and everything in his life but who also wants to be a star, who wants, like all of us, to be seen and understood and loved. This book is fucking hilarious, told through the eyes of Tommy's friend and an actor in The Room, Greg Sestero (and his co-writer). Greg is a little smug but given the travails he shares throughout, that's kind of understandable. But this book is also heartbreaking and I found myself filled with tenderness for Tommy who is so misguided, and so deluded but who is, also, incredibly committed to an artistic vision he has little control of. Really, this is a story about loneliness and earnestness and The American Dream.

sample_reviews.review_text: This is just not my kind of book. There were times that I stopped and thought "wow" and parts that left me unsettled and thinking, but overall I felt very unconnected to the stories. The short story format made it hard for me to get to know any of the characters and there was so much military jargon that I felt confused a lot of the time.
I have no interest in the military and this book just makes them look super uncool.
Don't know how close to reality the stories are. The more real they are, the more amazing they'd be.

My dad was in the navy, my brother in the army, my stepfather was in the Marines, and I myself worked on Lackland Airforce Base for almost 6 months in 2006. I read this book because I know very little about the military outside of the discipline and physical routines of a trainee as that's the only insight I've had into the world. This book focuses on the Marines but is told in 12 stories from 12 different perspectives. The book is not a political piece and does not focus on whether war in Afghanistan and Iraq was a good or bad decision. Instead, it focuses on individuals and their personal experiences with the war. I had to read only one story per day because I found it to me a very heart wrenching journey and I appreciate what the author tried to accomplish. I think it's an important read for anyone wanting to look at the war from the perspective of those that have been involved. And while it is fiction, it feels incredibly real and raw. This is not my typical read, but I'm glad that I read the book, and I would recommend the book to anyone trying to look at the war from the perspective of people who have served or worked overseas during the conflict.
Mixed bag.

Maybe the best way to get at the truth about war is to read fiction. Klay's collection of stories shows us just how that might be true, for he comes at aspects of the Iraq war from unique angles: PsyOps, Chaplain, corpse corps, infantry, artillery. He must fuse the experience of many into these snapshots, giving us both an unreal picture, but one that is strangely more real than any other. What cannot be clearer is that we have to be very sure of our motives when we place men and women in harm's way. Otherwise the bargain--one life for the many--is off. 
 Klay has a remarkable gift. I felt completely in his hands and he turned me this way and that, one moment laughing, the next cringing. My opportunity scanner for critical comment felt disabled. 
 I don't really know why I read so much about war. Perhaps because it is the thing that tears away all coverings and reveals us as we really are. Lots of people experience war but not that many can convey that moment when it changes one. Klay is able to capture those moments. Those moments are mined, for they are deeply stored and not often held to the light. Most folks can't even find those moments, let alone articulate them. So Klay's got a bit of PsyOps happening there. I'm not sure I envy him that skill, that knowledge. 
 It is difficult to pick a favorite story but the relief I got from the funny one in the middle, "Money As a Weapons System," makes me choose that one. In it, our narrator is a Foreign Service officer in charge of reconstruction. He confronts the absurd both in the abstract and in the flesh: a strange collection of folks have been assembled to fulfill head office policy directives and they are doing it...to the letter. The policies sounded good, but when confronted with the realities on the ground, they maybe don't work so well. 
 In "OIF," the economy of abbreviations gives a racing, manic, wild feel to the story...and we are running headlong off a cliff. For a mere seven pages we are not just reading, but immersed in the hyper atmosphere and not-completely-clear thinking of folks who get shot at every day. 
 In the very first story, "Redeployment," is a quote that had me gulping in recognition: "And glad as I was to be in the States, and even though I hated the past seven months and the only thing that kept me going was the Marines I served with and the thought of coming come, I started feeling like I wanted to go back. Because fuck all this." To tell the truth, this isn't war-talk. This is leaving-home-talk. It's real and it cinches our connection with the author. He's got the goods, tells the truth, and we understand that. 
 In "Bodies," Klay writes "there are two ways to tell the story. Funny or sad. Guys like it funny, with lots of gore and a grin on your face when you get to the end. Girls like it sad, with a thousand-yard stare out to the distance as you gaze upon the horrors of war they can't quite see. Either way, it's the same story." Klay gives us both in this collection, sometimes both in the same story. Our nineteen-year-old narrator comes home and visits his girlfriend still living in her parent's basement. The inchoate longing for connection is physically painful. 
 Klay has the talent to write about anything at all. In one of his stories, "Unless It's a Sucking Chest Wound," when he writes about school and banking and law in NYC, we believe him. We believe in him. I am curious what he will do next.

I started this book for book club months ago but had a hard time getting through these stories. Perhaps at the time I wanted to escape the brutal realities of all the terrible happenings in the world right now and reading is often my escape. The constant news about shootings, police brutality, kidnapping of girls in Africa, and the seeming hopelessness of the conflicts in the Middle East seemed everywhere. As my son turned 18 and had to register for Selective Service, I realized how naive I am and how truly blessed to not have experienced war firsthand (although just one generation ago, my parents survived Japanese occupation of Korea, WWII and the Korean conflict before making their way to the suburban Midwest). I hope and pray that my children and grandchildren do not have to experience it either. This book is not easy to get through but a necessary read. 
 The most memorable parts for me were the ones when the protagonist of the story returns to "normal" life back in the states and can't reconcile what he has experienced and has an even harder time accepting Americans going about their daily life. 
 "Gluttonous, fat, oversexed, over consuming, materialist home where we're too lazy to see our own faults" 
 The stories do tend to blend together and there aren't many distinguishing characteristics for each of the protagonists but you do feel that you are getting a firsthand report of what this war did to the minds and souls of many of our young men. Especially a war that was fought by only a few people and is not truly reflected upon by the majority of Americans. 
 The most uplifting residual of this book is that despite the horror and confusion, the characters and in essence the real men who served believe at least they did something bigger than the average person. 
 "The weird thing with being a veteran, at least for me, is that you do feel better than most people," one of Klay's characters says. "You risked your life for something bigger than yourself. How many people can say that? You chose to serve. Maybe you didn't understand American foreign policy or why we were at war. Maybe you never will. But it doesn't matter. You held up your hand and said, 'I'm willing to die for these worthless civilians.' "

There is a lot of anguish contained in Phil Kay's 12 short stories chronicling the Iraq War and the resulting emotional aftermath of its various characters. Klay's prose is lean, visceral and uncompromising all at once and every tale become a tone poem of sorts in a different shade of blue or gray. Some might balk initially at the frequent utilization of military jargon/acronyms that are rarely explained but when combined together with its raw and organic dialogue there is a magnified sense of presence established that gives each story added punch. Where this collection deserves merit however, is the pitch-perfect notes that Klay superbly manages to end each tale with. Regardless of whether or not I enjoyed a particular story each one stayed in my thoughts for quite some time.

I REALLY did not like this book. Considered giving it 1 star, but there was one or two stories I liked. First off, I do not like short stories and had I know that this was a collection of sad "war is hell" stories that were unrelated and poorly written, I wouldn't of wasted my time. Thankfully it was a short book. 
 Now I have read a lot of military books, but there were a few chapters where the acronyms use was beyond overboard. I know in one story this was done on purpose, but crap was it distracting that I had to find a website page devoted to explaining the acronyms in this stupid book. 
 How did this end up being so highly reviewed? What am I missing here? There are SO many more worthwhile Iraq war books out there that are NONFICTION that are way way better than this. 
 I would NOT recommend this book.
First 5-star book I've read in a long time that has me at a loss for words. Heavy emotional impact.

 Lucy is a temp working at Hamilton Industries. She has a crush on this tall, handsome stranger. She makes sure to arrive on time everyday to ride the elevator with him. One day, while they are both alone in the elevator, he hits the "stop" button and they get naughty. She finds out that day that the man she has a major crush on is Jeremiah Hamiliton...the CEO of the company. 
 Jeremiah is surprised that Lucy had no idea who he was and is intrigued. He makes her a deal...he will give her a better job...his personal assistant (where she has to do EVERYTHING he wants, if you know what I mean). She takes him up on his offer since she is in a bad place right now and they have already been physical.

Jeremiah was betrayed by his brother, Lucas, has not so nice parents, and works really hard at anything he does. Lucas is interesting. He is older than Jeremiah but acts younger, he is the outcast of the family, and enjoys ruffling his brother's feathers....what better way to do that then to pursue Lucy.

Shey's review posted on Guilty Pleasures Book Reviews> 
 3 Stars 
 Lucy Delacourt, is someone who thinks of herself as invisible, at work and in life. Plain Jane if you will. Losing her parents while in college and then losing her family home as well. Working minimal jobs to get by and payoff her college debt she takes a temp job at Hamilton Industries. 
 Every morning Lucy rides the elevator at the same time just to get a glimpse of the tall, dark, mysterious stranger. She knows he's out of her league but she can't help be attracted to the handsome man. When it's just the two of them and he seduces her in a mind blowing encounter. Then again after work in the parking garage, Lucy doesn't know what to do, this isn't like her she doesn't understand why she is compelled to follow his orders. 
 She finally finds out who her mystery stranger is, her boss, Jeremiah Hamilton, CEO. He offers her a full time position as his personal assistant. When asked what kind, of course his answer was "anything I want". With the generous offer he makes her she can get out of debt and go back to school, Lucy takes the offer. 
 Jeremiah Hamilton was not an easy man to connect with, he is very jaded and complex. He is very dominating and possessive and Lucy is submissive however she doesn't understand these feelings and it's never explained to her. There is light bondage in a few places and also minimal after care, I had a hard time with that not being in place. He did showed he cared in his own way when she was poisoned, he took her to in home in the Hamptons, although she wasn't allowed to leave and he would never give her any answers as to what was going on, he was protecting her. Then after she was kidnapped he came to rescue her himself. 
 Lucas Hamilton, Jeremiahs older brother, there is no love lost among those two. However, Lucas he was witty and sarcastic, even when he was causing trouble. When Lucy meets Lucas they have an easy banter back and forth. She also can see that Lucas is using her to manipulate his brother. 
 However in the end, Lucy committed the ultimate sin and told Jeremiah she loved him of course he dismisses her and walks away. 
 I felt like the author rushed to get as much information as she could into the last chapter of the book, although I have to say it was my favorite. Left with a cliffhanger and unanswered questions it's good to know that there will be another book.

2 stars - OK, I guess. A few things did not sit well with me. 
 Hmmm...I'm having a deja lu (as opposed to deja vu) moment. Have I read this book before? Or something very much like it? I really wanted to like this book; I had high hopes. Unfortunately, this book read very much like a fan fiction. 
 Anything He Wants: Dominated by the Millionaire is the story of Lucy Delacourt, a young temp. Every morning she rides the elevator with a very handsome stranger. He notices her, and is attracted to her, and things get hot and steamy. Later that day, she once again hooks up with the gorgeous stranger and has another hot and heavy encounter in the building's parking lot. 
 The next day, Lucy is summoned to the company CEO's office. Guess who the handsome stranger is? Jeremiah Hamilton. CEO of Hamilton Industries. Big surprise. Jeremiah tells her that his company is laying off all temp workers, but he makes her an offer she can't refuse. Jeremiah proceeds to interview her bent over his desk for a well-paying "personal assistant" position. 
 *Facepalm* OK, this is so wrong on many levels. Here, we have a subordinate female employee (in a very subordinate position) in financial difficulties basically backed into an "agreement" with the boss to do anything he wants. Sexual harassment lawsuit, anyone? The reality is that Lucy really had no choice - she needed a job. 
 I found the sex kind of boring. Jeremiah kind of likes his sex the same way. Sure, there were a few added toys here and there, but really, it kind of lacked the spark you see in other novels. 
 With regards to the story, it was just OK for me. Nothing really stood out. There was an exciting story line about an assassination attempt and Jeremiah comes to the rescue. Apparently our billionaire CEO was also an army ranger sniper a few years back. Quite handy. I did like Jeremiah's brother Lucas. 
 I must say that publishing a serialized novel should entail a little more editing in order to make all the parts of the serial more cohesive. I found the ending to be quite abrupt - it felt like the story was somehow incomplete. 
 Anything He Wants did not work for me. Readers who like serialized novels may enjoy this more than I did. 
 Thank you to NetGalley and St. Martin's Griffin for a review copy of this book.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I originally reviewed this book on my blog - The Cosy Dragon. For more recent reviews by me, please hop over there. 
 Callie doesn't talk about what she does. In fact, Callie doesn't talk at all. At Sea Pines she is expected to reveal all about what she does. What she does should be obvious to you! The book title says it all. 
 So this is yet another angsty teen novel I have read lately. And sadly, I found it lacking in a couple of ways. The storyline was very predictable, thin and unsatisfying. There wasn't enough fleshing out even of the environment. I couldn't imagine anything except the laundry and the bathroom, and even then there wasn't enough detail to satisfy me. 
 In a way, I found it pathetic. Each of the characters, although they tried to support each other, I just found it a bit lacking. Especially Amanda. Her character is so much in opposition to everything that is trying to be achieved by Callie and the other girls. I wanted to know more behind each of them! Just giving them problems and names wasn't enough. 
 Yes, this book did touch me. I felt some shivers. It did disturb me a little. For a book written by someone who has never cut, it's not bad. I guess I'm comparing this book to Scars (Cheryl Rainfield) and The Burn Journals (Brent Runyon). Those books are built on true stories, and the sincerity really shines through to make a well-rounded and developed character. 
 Some things I find absurd, such as the therapist visits. I find it hard to believe that the therapist could lie so blatantly to Callie about Becca. Also, the whole thing about her scars fading - that's something that Callie could have worked out for herself - no they won't fade completely, but there is makeup! I guess for a 13 year old girl willing to believe anything she is told, it's ok. 
 This book is very female biased. There are no men, except Callie's brother, Sam, who is very sick and so understandably sympathetically portrayed. In contrast is Callie's father, who she doesn't talk about. It seems like there is a deeper issue there - I was hanging out for it to be rape, or something serious - but it was simply something else. Callie did a great job with the situation she found herself. I can't give too much away, or I'll ruin the little suspense the book had. 
 There is something about the show Rescue 911. I've never watched it. But apparently everybody loves it! And of course it has relevance to Callie's situation. It's not a subtle reference, and I guess that ruined it for me. This book is going to be dated within a couple of years for sure, and it doesn't even make any attempt to be universal (not that it necessarily should, just an observation). 
 I was particularly dissatisfied with the ending. Arg! Would it have killed McCormick to give Callie a decent ending? Sorry, but I know how cutting works, and a on eoff idea that you're going to stop isn't necessarily going to carry on. And I didn't have much faith in talk therapy like that (with no cognitive behvioural therapy) fixing a problem. No wonder some of the girls were still sick. 
 The bonus of this book was that it was short and cheap! So I don't feel like I wasted too much on it. I've ripped it apart, but surely there are other people that like it. The cover is surprisingly attractive to my mind. 
 I'd recommend this book for teens. It's not a great insight into how Callie's mind works (and certainly not how all cutters' minds work), and I think maybe it could be negative for some other people who have never thought of the idea of cutting before. The idea of a residential facility fixing all mental problems is absurd, and out of reach of most people anyway - they'll never be able to relate.

I had heard a lot about this book before I read it, even before I had heard of booktube/goodreads and equivalent sites. One half of my dual major is psychology, so I was hoping for a good explanation on the mental health topics covered in it; also coming from a perspective of going through some of the things in this book as well, and I wanted a book to relate to in some way shape or form. I heard about some of the author's statements on why she wrote them, but since I heard so much about this small volume, I decided to overlook it. 
 And BOY... do I wish I hadn't made that choice. The thing is, what happens in this book? Cause I am damn sure I must have missed something somehow because this small volume packed zero punch, just a whole lot of words and the ability to waste my time.No characters grew, it was about a recovery center with no recoveries and seemingly barely any good, consistent help for the characters. On the topic of the characters,they were forgettable. I'd say that is the last thing you want to hear about book characters, especially ones meant to have any sort of impact on the reader. There was potential, that was not utilized and I can leave it at that... like wishing I left this book back on the shelf.
Honest and well-written. I read this in one sitting with tears streaming down my face for the kids who deal with cutting.
it's okay. I read it in one day, gave me a new light on why people cut!

This was the second time of me reading this book and it was good. I like the characters and the story line but I had to give it only 4 out of 5 stars because it could have gone deeper. I feel like you didn't really get callies story. But other then that it was a good look into some of those types of places. She is a great writer and very easy to follow!

** spoiler alert ** 
 I was not at all impressed with this book, at least after the expectations that had been set up for me. It was too short and too shallow. There was only one part I liked, in which the psychologist suggested to the girl that perhaps she cuts herself because she blames herself for all the painful things around her. But even that is cliche, and kind of obvious. 
 I guess it was a decent story, but the writing was just very average. Oh and the ending was not only stupid, but also anticlimactic and nonsensical. [Possible spoiler below] I mean, she ends the book saying that she wants help - that she wants to get better - but I, at least, was under the impression that by the end of the book she has already IMMENSELY improved from her previous self and probably doesn't even need to live in the rehabilitation center anymore.

I do not like this book. Mostly because I read it when I was struggling with self-injury and hiding it and this book played on one of my worst fears: If your self-injury is discovered you will be thrown into an institution against your will. This is not true. You go to an institution if you're a danger to yourself or others or if you feel you can't solve your problem in outpatient therapy. Plus you'd need to get a referral from a physiologist or a doctor to get the insurance company to even think about paying for long tern inpatient care. Insurance companies really, really don't like paying for inpatient care. Since cutting is not a suicide attempt and Callie wasn't doing anything that could unintentionally lead to death (cutting really deep, attempting to break bones, drinking and cutting . . . .) she would have gone to psychologist or physiatrist after school or whatever- so this whole book could have been avoided.

It was an interesting book. Patricia McCormick is very good at letting you see whats going on inside the main characters head. She has a very good writing style. It was, however a little too depressing for me. I'm going to try her other book, "Sold" next... heard it's really good.

This book made me want to start a "books that left me feeling hollow" shelf. I agree with another reviewer who said it was shallow and flimsy. There was build up and build up and build up and then .... nothing. 
 I'm left with unanswered questions. I'm left feeling, well, hollow. While I'm "okay" with the resolution Callie came up with on her own, I'm not happy with the resolution I was left with as a reader. 
 I was liking the book enough until the end. I kept waiting to figure it all out, but I felt like I kept reading the same scenes over and over. 
 It wasn't a horrible book, but I'm not sure how much I could recommend it to others. If you want to read it, though, it should only take you a short afternoon to read it.

This book was horrible and did not portray what it feels like to self harm or any of the reasons behind it. Unfortunately, I used to cut and continued to for 12 years, up until about one year ago, and this book does NOT convey anything realistic whatsoever. This book really bother me...do not waste your time.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Review courtesy of Dark Faerie Tales 
 Quick & Dirty: This book had an interesting plot but it was defiantly not a book for me. 
 Opening Sentence: "Well, boy," the ringmaster said. "What can you do?" 
 The Review: 
 Micah Grey has just recently run away from home. He has wondered the streets for a time and he decides to spend his last bit of money on the Circus. The Circus is magical and he decides that he would love to be a part of it. He ends up getting a chance to join as a trainee for the trapeze act. The circus life is hard, he gets hazed for being new and most people are very unwelcoming. As time goes by he starts to fit in and really become part of the strange group that makes up a circus. But Micah has some dark secrets from his past and he can't run forever. 
 Iphigenia Laurus, more commonly known as Gene has grown up with a very privileged life. Her family is very wealthy and she is expected to always behave like a proper girl, but she loves to do boyish things. She loves to hang out with her older brother and friends much more than she enjoys the company of girls. She loves to climb trees, play in the mud, and go swimming, everything that is improper for a young lady. Gene is nearing the age of coming out, and it is time for her to start excepting suitors. She is very nervous about courting and possibly getting married one day, because she has a secret that very few people know and she fears that no one will accept her when they find out. 
 Micah's life in the circus is very interesting. He is very determined to make it in the circus which is an admirable quality. He is very secretive and seems to be lost for most of the story. He has a really hard time opening up to people because he has been hurt in the past. I had a really hard time connecting with him, I found him to be a boring character. Nothing about him really stood out and the more I read his story, the more I found myself just not caring what happened to him.

 I admit, I was blown away by this book. I absolutely loved it. All of it. The summary does exactly what it is supposed to do, describe the story. And it does that well. But when you begin reading Pantomime, you are pleasantly shocked with a pretty big secret that you would never guess from reading that summary. I honestly don't know to write up a good review without giving anything away! 
 The world slightly confuses me. It never actually gives you a date for when all of this takes place. It seems to be a mixture of historical (think nobles, big dresses & Lords and Ladies) and the future. There is magic and tales of ancient people who vanished. An odd combination, but it works! The descriptions of the world painted a lovely picture inside my mind. 
 This was my first "circus" book. I've never read about anything that had to do with circus acts. I loved it. You could picture the acts in your head like you were really there watching them. I can't wait to dive into more circus themes now! 
 I'm not sure if there is plans for a second, but I hope and pray there will be. Pantomime leaves you wanting more. It ends with a cliffhanger! I can't wait to find out what happens next. The anticipation just may be to much to handle.. 
 If you love the circus, magic and unfolding mysteries, then this is the book for you! I highly recommend it to anyone and everyone!

This review won't really discuss the book. Just saying. Not that I wouldn't talk about it, but I won't ruin it by sharing, well, much of anything. 
 Okay, if I'm being honest, I was slightly disappointed by this book. No, it wasn't bad. It wasn't even just so-so. It just wasn't as fabulous (to me) as the publisher's other books. 
 At first I thought I didn't like it. Really, the back-and-forth between what's happening "now" and what happened "before" just drove me out of my mind. Until about a quarter of the way in, when I loved both story lines, and it made the reading go faster because I was constantly looking forward to finding out what happened in two different stories. 
 Turns out, when the book ended, I was annoyed. Which means I liked it more than I realized. 
 I have to say, things felt kind of slow. I could feel/see the story leading toward some great things I was looking forward to, but they never happened. Not that they won't, just not in this book. A lot of time was spent dawdling, IMHO. Of course, we were getting to know our main character, and that counts for a lot. Just don't expect a fast-paced story.

Micah Grey runs away from his life as a privileged aristocrat and joins R.H. Ragona's Circus of Magic. He wants the chance to discover who he is, rather than who his parents expect him to be, especially after learning something rather unexpected about his past and unwelcome about his future right before running. 
 He doesn't fit into the circus immediately. He might be an outsider and an outcast, but he has to endure the other performers' hazing in order to prove it. He must work hard at grunt work and train to be an aerialist. He starts a relationship with Aenea Harper, one of the circus's experienced aerialists, and feels a strange attraction to Drystan, the circus's head clown. But it's difficult for Micah to keep his secrets and gain the trust of the performers. 
 PANTOMIME is also the story of Iphigenia Laurus, who wants to be called Gene, though only her brother bothers. She's old enough to make her debut, but she's not interested in courting and being a lady. She'd rather climb trees and hang with her brother's friends, just like she did as a little kid. She chafes under society's expectations and lives in fear of being married off to some dolt, because a clever man would discover her secrets rather quickly. 
 The fantasy elements of PANTOMIME are subtle. Most of Ellada's magic is relics, rare and losing power. But not all magic is gone. Micah might have a connection to those vanished Civilizations, though he's often too busy trying to conceal it than to bother trying to discover how. 
 I rather enjoyed PANTOMIME and its examination of class, society, and gender combined with the classic stories of a boy running away to join the circus and a girl avoiding an unpleasant marriage. Some of the story's reveals are obvious, but other twists are very surprising. And it all builds to a sudden, violent conclusion. PANTOMIME is only the beginning of the story. It's a lovely, quiet story but I expect the sequel will be more explosive, given everything that happens. 
 I recommend PANTOMIME for fantasy fans looking for something slightly offbeat and full of subtle magics, as well as for people looking for something to follow the bestselling THE NIGHT CIRCUS. It's a magical, romantic tale and I think Laura Lam is an author to watch.

Knowing that the two characters portrayed in the story are really one character is an important aspect to the story that is not shared until the story is read. It should be a key factor in marketing, though the cover is phenomenal and the reason I picked it up. 
 I, however, stopped reading and started skimming the story because it became a little long-winded trying to unravel the story, the characters, and the setting. I want to find someone who appreciates it and find out why they liked it to be able to sell, I cannot do it on my own rather than facing it cover-out and letting someone just pick it up.

In short: Pantomime by Laura Lam is a highly original and profound read with a shocking twist. 
 What a bizarre and yet completely fascinating and original read Pantomime was. One with an utterly shocking twist that is sure to leave you reeling. And unfortunately, it's that twist that is going to make Pantomime so hard to review because I don't want to ruin the surprise. So let's keep it simple and vague: Iphigenia, or Gene as she likes to be called, is a tomboy who wants no part leading the life of a lady, but is being heavily pressured by her marriage-obsessed mother. Micah is a vagrant of noble upbringing who runs away and finds a new home in the circus. Gene and Micah have a secret - a MAJOR one. Chapters alternate between Gene and Micah, but again, I can't say how the two are connected. 
 Pantomime is a fantasy though it's a very subtle one - the story reads like a Victorian Era novel with some added magical realism and a hint of fantastical mythology and history. I liked that a lot. It grounded the story and allowed the reader to focus more on the issues Gene and Micah have to deal with while maintaining a certain level of intrigue and fascination with the world. The circus atmosphere was great; debut author Laura Lam describes with perfect clarity an old-fashioned circus complete with clowns and acrobats and freaks. 
 I felt a heart-wrenching sympathy for Gene and Micah as they deal with the pressure to be normal and fit in, but also pride for their nerve and courage to not give in to that pressure and not want to change who they were born to be. Both Gene and Micah reach some pretty low points in Pantomime and my heart broke for them, but both demonstrate some serious chutzpah when dealing with their situations. There is some romance in Pantomime and it's of the LGBT variety. It was exciting to me, having LGBT issues brought up in a fantasy book, because it's usually contemporary reads or nothing and I applaud Laura Lam for bringing the topic to the forefront in Pantomime. 
 The pacing in Pantomime is a little slow and there's not much in the way of action - with the exception of the ending - but I found I didn't mind too much because I was so involved in the story and characters. I would have liked a bit more development in the mythology and history of the world as I was left with quite a few questions in the end. Overall though, I appreciated Pantomime for its originality and Laura Lam for choosing to write a book that deals with complicated and sensitive issues regarding gender identity.

 Like many others I was expecting a book full of doodles and brainstorms and a guide to the inner workings of Cassandra Clare. Thats what I wanted. I want to know how she came up with such a magical world, right under our noses. How she created the demons, shadow hunters, valentine. WHY she did that to poor simon. 
 But.....thats not what we got. What this reader actually is, is a collection of essays (something I expect to find written on a literature degree, not in a book about a book) by some very well known authors about different aspects of the stories. But they are then edited by Clare, so if anyone actually said anything bad about the books, then we wouldn't know because its all nice, nice, nice. 
 I struggled with this, I REALLY did. I wanted to get through it as when I'm given an ARC or galley I don't want to give up, I feel that my pain is expected in exchange for the free book. This was painful. Some essays more than others. 
 Michelle Hodkin stole the show, her essay about Simon and his Jewish faith was brilliant, I learnt a lot about jewish history, the links to vampirism and it just FLOWED. But it was the only one that was worth noting. 
 None of the others really stood out for good reasons, Blake's Brotherly Love section was justifying Clare's Incest storyline, saying it was ok because they didn't grow up together. Now I don't object to the storyline, I think its a good twist, but its NOT OK. Its incest -its illegal in most countries for a reason. Milford's ramblings about New York lost me completely. I could go on, but they were all a little self-indulgent (or at least clare-indulgent), and they add nothing to the story world for the reader. 
 Its a shame because a good reader can be great fun, but this just isn't hitting the mark for me.

I liked this one much more than the first book, or maybe I should say I liked Beauty much more in this one. Here, we see her exhibit some spirit, occasionally rebelling in order to be given harsher punishments. I could relate more to this side of her. She decided not to always be obedient, perhaps knowing that by pushing back she would reach a greater level of submission than if she meekly obeyed every order. This fascinated me as much as it disturbed me, yet ultimately made me adore her more for it. 
 We also get to see the pov of male slave Tristan, who was also disobedient, but for very different reasons: Tristan longed for a firmer hand, the guidance of someone who could and would truly master him with decisiveness and confidence. Once he found what he sought, he began to find peace and contentment in his position as a slave. 
 Overall this story was more fulfilling, and I found a deeper understanding of the mind and soul of a true submissive.  Another emotional whirlwind from Sylvia Day! After dropping off a bit in book 2 Sylvia Day makes a huge come back in Entiwined with You!! 
 Description: 
 The worldwide phenomenon continues as Eva and Gideon face the demons of their pasts, and accept the consequences of their obsessive desires... 
 From the moment I first met Gideon Cross, I recognized something in him that I needed. Something I couldn't resist. I saw the dangerous and damaged soul inside-so much like my own. I was drawn to it. I needed him as surely as I needed my heart to beat. 
 No one knows how much he risked for me. How much I'd been threatened, or just how dark and desperate the shadow of our pasts would become. 
 Entwined by our secrets, we tried to defy the odds. We made our own rules and surrendered completely to the exquisite power of possession... 
 My Thoughts: 
 I unlike some other actually did like book two, it showed how our characters grew and start defining themselves as a couple. Yes it was full of heartbreak and uncertainty but it did put us in the perfect mindset for Entiwined. 
 We start this book off with our characters dealing with the death of Nathan and worried about the ongoing investigation. Eva's Mom gets more into her business and of course Corrine is a shadow over the couple reuniting. These are all givens and I don't want to go into detail about what happened because you really do need to read the book to ascertain what is going on. I will say that no one creates a plotline like Sylvia Day with her ups and happiness and her drastic downs and questioning feelings. So much happens in the book that you just can't put it down. I tried saying to myself that I would stop at the next chapter, then said one more...til finally at 3:45am I finished the book. 
 Then I knashed my teeth, cursed and threatened to kick my ereader out of bed. It is seems this trilogy continues and that there will be a fourth book. I can see how SD was going to end the series but she has extended the plot and is taking us on Gideon and Eva's journey and has already foreshadowed events that are going to happen in the next novel. I had to wonder if the publisher's got to SD and "encouraged" her to keep writing them since they are so popular and making them a bunch of money. Did Sylvia sell out or will the writing of a fourth novel give us even more pleasure than finishing it at book 3. 
 I guess we will need to wait another year to find out. I have given this novel a 4.5 stars and hope that all those who gave up after book 2 gets swayed into giving book 3 a try. Things are good but still the outside interference hampers their every decision. Looking forward to book 4 and hoping it will be the last book focusing on these two lovebirds.

reference_books.review_text:
Imperial Bedrooms or, a small pile of shit. 
 Before I get into this book I feel I should just say: I have always wanted to be a Bret Easton Ellis fan. I loved the edgy subject matter and controversial publicity, but you know what? His books are not good. They are simply NOT good.

reference_books.review_text: This book was interesting at first but I soon grew pretty tired of Frank. I felt that he had sugar coated much of his story in that he made himself out to be a much better person than he in fact was. Frank was simply an addict who was hooked on money, women, danger, and thievery. There were very few moral principles and I suppose that is how this book is intended, but there really wasn't that much to frank. I know I'm not judging the subject, but the book, and for me, the book was shitty. Easy reading to excite ignorant people.

reference_books.title: The Screwtape Letters
reference_books.review_text: I had this book for two years and just got around to reading it. I've started at least seven other books and haven't finished them. Long books like Pynchon's Gravity's Rainbow, and DFW's broom of the system. Good books, but marathons of prose nonetheless. This book was a different kind of marathon. It puts you in front of letters written by an administrative demon to his nephew and pupil regarding the possession of a human soul. I say that it was a marathon for me because every chapter was chalked full of satirical religious stuff that almost made me feel anxious. Now, I'm not a religious person, but it can get creepy as fuck listening to someone with diabolically evil intentions speak. I enjoyed a lot of parts, there wasn't enough of a story in my opinion. I would have liked to of known more about the human. I think there could have been a deviation from the strictly letters format. I know, that's the point. It was all intended to be unique and it honestly is. 3 stars means i thought it was a good book, not great.

book_a.title: The Stranger
book_a.user_review:
I guess this is a book where you take what you want from it. What I got is a classic frustrating story about a man who shoots another man and is sentenced to the death penalty. Some would say that because he is unable to express himself, this is his true undoing. He can't bother to speak up for himself, because he just doesn't see the point in it. I guess there is a lot to be said about it, but I've read enough literature to get the point. The world is shitty, we don't know why, and we are screwed if we don't conform to the 'norm'. 
 I didn't hate this book, but I didn't see much to like. The disconnected central character just doesn't do it for me. Which is why I wouldn't NOT recommend this book to somebody. There is a definite possibility that others will like it, but it just isn't my type of book. I like heart, this book has none. Granted, Meursault finally breaks down at the end of the book, arguably the best part of the book in a tirade that is aimed at a priest, but for me it was all 'too little too late'. I couldn't stop from thinking while everything was going on, that I didn't care at all about him. This was obviously the point that Camus was making and was admittedly great at it. However, I've noticed in other reviews of this novel that people regularly bring attention to the fact that this book was written in 1941 and express the point of it being before its time or ground-breaking in relation to its peers. I never let that kind of hype affect my judgement of a book. If I don't like something, I don't like it. It has nothing to do with common reception, nor do I let reviews dictate my conclusions. I hope that none of you will do the same. Read it for yourself, and do not let my review alter your perception of its quality. Please. 
 The bright side for me is that it is was very short book that I finished in a little over two hours. I know my review sounds negative, but like I said, many people will enjoy this book and it may have just been a not my taste of style.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Prior to The Stranger Camus received a BA in philosophy, an MA in Christian Thought and wrote a number of non-fiction pieces. This was his first work of fiction and...I think it reads like that, as a philosophical idea with characters and plot built around it. I enjoyed it because I like literature that makes me think but if the idea was "life has no meaning so how should we proceed" I think he might have done better with a protagonist that tried even a teeny bit to find some meaning. In the same way, I don't believe the protagonist's "epiphany" at the end of the story that he had 'been happy' and that he would have realized that earlier if only he had opened his heart to "the indifference of the universe". Huh? 
 First of all, this was not a happy man. In fact, the dullness of his interactions throughout the first half of the book made me think maybe he was mildly depressed. He takes buses, he smokes cigarettes, he views the landscape and carries on short conversations but never does he engage in a way that an even mildly happy person might engage with the people around him. He sees his mother's "fiancee" have a fainting fit but offers no help. When a good friend of his mother's cries at the funeral, he says "I wanted her to stop crying, but dared not speak to her". Yet what a surprise when later accused of callousness! Is it really the universe that is indifferent or is it indifferent people that make it seem that way? 
 Throughout the first half, also, the protagonist claims that things "have no importance". He could marry Marie or not, he could accept his employer's offer to move to Paris or not. "I didn't care much one way or the other" he says because "one life was as good as another". Does this sound like a happy person? Does this sound like the universe being indifferent? Or does it sound like the kind of B.S. a moody teenager might spout. 
 This phrase (near the end) got me too: "...supposing she were dead, her memory would mean nothing; I couldn't feel interest in a dead girl". This just confirms that all the protagonist feels are physical sensations: the desire to touch Marie, the heat of the sun or the coolness of the evenings. If death only means the cessation of physical sensation then - sure - the protagonist is right that who cares if death occurs at 40 or 80, by guillotine or by old age? It's all the same. Yet most people's lives have motive, a reason for doing something that creates value to our lives that the protagonist neither has nor understands. (The word motive sprang to mind when mulling over Mersualt's crime since he, predictably, has none). 
 Sorry - if you shoot someone 4 times at close range and then feel "less regret than a kind of vexation", I will have to argue that you've either got a psychological problem or you are a creation of a philosopher's active imagination.

Honest - I know that this book is like a wet dream for existentialism and what have you. Maybe because of my psychology background but it felt like reading a book where the main character has some variant of autism. So his behaviour wasn't that surprising from that angle.

The protagonist of this story is a 'stranger' indeed, in the way he reacts to events in his life. He seems impassionate with regard to everything and without deep moral feelings. In the view of his and each man's destiny, death, nothing matters for him anymore. This presentation of the character of this man tastes a bit artificial too me, too theoretically philosophical. Also, the trial seems rather absurd in the argumentations used (or is it only outdated?). The description of the thoughts of Meursault when he approaches the Arab he is about to shoot are very effectful as are the last pages of the novel.
This was a quick and powerful read, revelatory of social issues, existence and death. Albert Camus is a master writer to pack so much philosophy so casually in this short, simple book.

***Spoiler alert 
 Mersault was a sociopath. He was friends with shady characters. He had no problem with women being beaten. He was strangely okay when his mother died. And he shot and killed a man with the only explanation being "It was because of the sun." It struck me when, during his trial, the prosecutor placed much emphasis on premeditation and intention and Mersault thought to himself, "He was right though." The tone that Camus used throughout to tell the story left me, the reader, just as detached as the character himself. And the result of that was losing sight of terrible crime he committed. Mersault didn't show much feeling. And by much, I mean that he didn't show any at all. In fact, his negative reaction to his execution was almost too much emotion for him and a detraction from his apathetic character. 
 I know this book was supposed to make me "question my existence" or something of that nature. But reading it didn't make me feel any more or less human. I felt exactly how I should feel about the particular story - disgusted. I did not feel this disgust because society told me it is appropriate to feel it when a man is killed by another man. I felt disgusted because killing a man is a disgusting crime. The only thing Camus accomplished with this novel in my opinion was giving us readers insight into the mind of a puzzling character. A character who has no control over what he does and doesn't care how he feels about it. In other words, a sociopath.
