book_b.title: Sometimes a Great Notion
book_b.user_review:
This book is so good because it portrays a realistic American family. There is much to dislike and like about every character. It doesn't attempt to shine a positive light, nor a negative light on any character. It just leaves it for you to judge without caking on any opinion or over emphasizing the impact of any character's particular action or unfortunate tragedy. This book allows you to draw from your own experience and relate it to the stories it tells. There is absolutely no point in describing the details in a review. It's not about what happens, but what happens to the people and what happens to their family. Much like the Godfather, Sometimes a Great Notion is really about family. 
 Combine that with being able to feel like you are in the Pacific Northwest through the quality of writing and this book is not to be slept on. I one day hope to read it again.

sample_reviews.review_text: It had some interesting parts, but I just couldn't ever get into this book. I gave it up after slogging through a bit over half the book.

Kesey's masterful novel about a logging family in the Pacific Northwest and the impact of a strike in collision with their never-say-die attitude towards the world, has been somewhat overshadowed by the success of One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, and that is unfortunate, for it is one of the best novels written about the west and the western mindset. Belongs on the shelf with Stegner's Big Rock Candy Mountain, Denis Johnson's Dead Again, and Steinbeck's East of Eden. A movie was made from it with Michael Sarrazin, also Paul Newman, Henry Fonda and Lee Remick--why do I only remember Sarrazin? Damned good.

This book takes a bit of work to read. I read it in the 70's, and didn't really get what all the fuss was about. This time, I did the work and it was worth it. The writing is fantastic. There is poetry in places - especially where he describes nature*, which is extra fun for me because he's describing the northwest. 
 Another great thing about the writing was that he switches voice mid-paragraph and sometimes mid-sentence. It's as if the characters are bursting to say their piece, and can't wait their turn. Lee's sub-conscious is a separate voice. 
 The book's one flaw (IMO) was that, for the most part, the women are gray and one-dimensional at best, and at worst.. how do I put this? Here's an example of the worst: Indian Jenny was a prostitute and a dirt poor Native American, so what does she spend her declining years thinking about? Why, wishing that Hank Stamper would have gone to bed with her, of course! 
 The male characters are complex. I still don't know how I feel about Lee.. So, overlook the woman problem. This book is well worth reading, or re-reading. 
 *I love his description of the Oregon rain: "The same old rain, and, even if not welcomed, at least accepted - an old gray aunt who came to visit every winter and stayed till spring. You learn to live with her. You learn to reconcile yourself to the little inconveniences and not get annoyed. You remember she is seldom angry or vicious and nothing to get in a stew about, and if she is a bore or stays overlong you can train yourself not to notice her."

I know it's a "masterpiece," but like many of them (Thackeray, anyone?), I couldn't stay with it. I was skimming too early in the story, and that's always a warning sign. I wish the rest of you well with this one.

If you intend on reading this book or are somewhat curious about doing so, its best to read Tom Wolfe's The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test, as it gives a very good picture of the lifestyle Kesey was living in during the time he wrote and finished this novel. In other words, he was on acid. A LOT. 
 Also, this book is very dense narratively, shifting from first to third and person to person between paragraphs. If you're into that sort of thing this book is great. If not, then go elsewhere. At times this style does provide a neat picture, but honestly the book holds to plot far too long and this thick zig-zag style after a while becomes tedious and long-winded. I have read in other reviews that the book could have easily been 300 pages less, but i would play it fair and say 200. There is this intention of attempting to be an epic in the novel that simply doesn't work to a degree, especially in those last hundred pages. 
 But it is overall worth the ride. Kesey truly was a good writer, i enjoyed One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest much more than this but it's still very well written. The dialogue and much of the narration are rich in this Oregon-area folk language. 
 The book is also worth rereading. While reading the book i tended to go back and look at where i've been and begun connecting ideas previously that seemed vague or obscure at first. At any rate, it helped me realize that this book doesn't give everything away very easily. 
 I'm also curious about the theatrical version and will probably attempt to see it in the near future.

Though it took me ages to finish, and parts of it just were too much, the last 200 or so pages are some of the finest writing I've read in a long time. To get mood and tension right in stream of consciousness with constantly changing narrators and points of view is at the heart of the art of literature... If you're patient for 400 pages or so, you'll get to the jewel that drives the novel. Many metaphors -- not least of which is the American dichotomy between self sufficiency and reliance on community -- make it a layered, complex work clearly worth a read... Better yet, worth a read on one of those weekends where you can read, mainly undisturbed, in a single stretch, so that the setting and mood isn't jagged, but a continuous brushstroke over the 600 pages. You won't be disappointed.

A phenomenal, gritty, rich, innovative, astonishing book full of suppressed passions (often the best kind in literature), the great Northwest, familial tensions, politics and economic polarities, indeed a kind of mythology. 
 While most people know ONE FLEW OVER THE CUCKOO'S NEST much better, this is Kesey's masterpiece. How I wish he'd written more. This is the book he'll be remembered for. It will draw out every emotion you have, including grief the size of a of sequoia, and you will never forget these characters. If you haven't read it, read it. If you have read it, read it again. 
 Some people shy away from Kesey because of his involvement in the Merry Pranksters, the drug-riddled 60s and Timothy Leary. And yes, it's a shame that his acid trips seem to have altered him to such an extent he never wrote anything nearly as good again. Cautionary tale, there, young writers. 
 There's quite an interesting article in the LATimes about the two books, and about Kesey: http://www.latimes.com/style/la-bkw-p... 
 And Neil Griffiths gives a lovely, inspiring chat about it here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HMCw_...

I'm going to divide my review of this into 2 sections: me as a reader, and me as a writer: 
 I love reading books that straddle that line between profundity and enjoyment. In "Notion", Kesey tackles some difficult themes--union busting, technology infringing upon humans involvement with the means of production, sex and family politics/roles, revenge, alcoholism, social stigmas--yet the book never feels didactic or preachy. He avoids this because of the tone with which he wrote the book: it's fun to read. Not to oversimplify things, but too often I think we muddle things up as we dissect or deconstruct literature. Some times, maybe it's better to write a fun, kick ass, hilarious, vivid, sad, confusing, all-encompassing messy book! There's a vitality and life in this narrative; it almost feels conversational, like someone's whispering it in your ear. And so it engages the reader on a personal level, lures us into the complex story with its relaxed, self assured style. 
 The writer side of me: Kesey is doing things with point-of-view that are/were groundbreaking: his willingness to have multiple characters talk in the "I" voice all in the same paragraph is an incredible risk. I admire his confidence to write in this wild way, seemingly not to worry (or care) whether or not the reader gets confused (he does give clues as to the speakers' identities, but it's still bemusing). He's asking a lot of his audience, in terms of active participation with the narrative, but if you're willing to do the work, this novel is amazing. But if you don't like "working" a bit to decode what's happening on the page, this one probably isn't for you. 
 Definitely in my top five all time...

reference_books.title: Wonderbook: The Illustrated Guide to Creating Imaginative Fiction
reference_books.review_text: jam-packed with wisdom & perspective, this is the writing book I wish I had a decade ago when I was taking creative writing classes and my prof thought my fiction was inappropriately weird for an undergrad workshop. (blah blah blah "learn the rules before you break them" blah blah blah) anyhoo, what I particularly liked about this was the general attitude when talking about an approach (and I'm paraphrasing) "this works for me, here's what works for some other people, this other way works for others" -- which is a crap load more helpful than what you get from lots of other sources, which often dribble out some pathetic non-advice like "everyone must find their own way." also appreciated how the author name-checked some of my favorite authors (Samuel Beckett, China Mieville, etc) and introduced me to interesting authors I'd never heard of (like Amos Tutuola).

I read the book, then watched the BBC series and I must say that I liked the series a little better. It seems that this story really does better with the visuals then the bare text. 
 The basic plot has an Alice in Wonderland quality with typical, understated British humor. The main character, Richard Mayhew, begins the story as a listless man who, despite having the 'good-life' finds something lacking in his existence. A chance encounter with one of the denizens of 'London Below' (Lady Door) pulls him into a shadowy and magical world that coexists with, and is invisible to, our real "London Above.' What follows is a typical journey of self-discovery ... Only Richard doesn't really stop being a putz until the end. 
 London Below appears to be the stomping ground for our dreams and nightmares where everything is surreal ... It also brings to mind the homeless within our cities in that when were aren't ignoring them (ie. not invisible), it is not uncommon to see them displaying symptoms of mental illness (talking to other invisible persons, rats, etc.). Add this up with a touch of word play and you get a very humorous trip into what seems to be a mental breakdown, trapping Richard within his unconscious or primitive mind where he can discover and become the hero that was denied him in the real world. Gaiman never really exploits the potential questions which arise from his brief foray into insanity, but then I don't think this was intended to be that serious a story either ... It was supposed to be fun and I did enjoy it much like I enjoyed Monty Python's Holy Grail.
Awesome Gaiman novel, not one for everybody, though - it's more like a twisted Wizard of Oz journey, but great entertainment.

I don't know how he does it, butNeil Gaiman paints the most amazing stories with his words. Neverwhere is the story of Richard, a young man who is reasonably content with his predictable job and his predictable fiancee and his predictable London life. Until one evening when he notices a girl in trouble on the side of the road and stops to help her. This act of kindness turns his world completely upside down, tearing him from his London Above world and dropping him into the world of those who have fallen through the cracks of society, to London Below. No longer visible to his former friends and colleagues, Richard joins forces with Door, the girl he saved, as she embarks on a quest to find out who orchestrated the murder of her family. As wonderfully drawn as Richard is, the secondary characters are quite amazing: the deliciously evil Mr. Croup and Mr. Vandemar, the self-invented Marquis de Carabas, and Hunter, the beautiful bodyguard who longs to defeat the Beast that prowls through London's underbelly. Although Richard spends much of his time in this new world questioning his own sanity, he slowly comes into his own and is ultimately a key to the quest's success, learning quite a bit about himself in the process. Delightful, delicious, multi-layered, and never, ever dull.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Neverwhere by Neil Gaiman is touted on the back of the book as "A dark contemporary 'Alice in Wonderland.'" That's pretty accurate, but it reminded me more of The Wizard of Oz. 
 Neverwhere makes use of a fairly standard trope: an ordinary schlub is drawn into an extraordinary situation and forced to call upon hidden strengths he never knew he had. 
 In this case, the unassuming Kansas farmgirl is London resident Richard Mayhew. He is the very caricature of a boring nobody. With an office job, an apartment, and a fiancee, there is nothing interesting about his life until he stops to help a strange girl he finds bleeding on the sidewalk, brings her back to his apartment to clean her up, and sends her on her way. 
 A few days later, he finds that no one in his world can see him anymore: now he is a part of her world, the Land of Oz, the shadowy and mysterious "London Below." 
 He locates the girl he helped (who I imagine as the Scarecrow) in this filthy world that exists like an alternate dimension of the subways and sewers beneath "London Above." She is the Lady Door, eldest daughter of a murdered nobleman, and is being pursued by the grossest, most evil guys ever. Their motley crew is soon rounded out by an appropriate Cowardly Lion and Tin Man: a fierce lesbian huntress Door hires as her bodyguard and a seedy Lemmy-from-Motorhead type who calls himself the Marquis de Carabas. 
 They go in search of the Wonderful Wizard and encounter plenty of spooks, flying monkeys, and horses of a different color along the way. 
 My main beef with Neverwhere is that its plot and characters are really nothing new. I like my stories that have a certain moral ambiguity to them. Pure good vs. pure evil doesn't do much to excite me, and fifty pages into the book, I knew that if Richard succeeded in using his ruby slippers to get his old life back, there is no way he would want it anymore. 
 Also, I generally prefer science fiction to fantasy so it bothered me slightly that the oddities in this book were never given a logical explanation. Why can Richard and Jessica see Door at the beginning of the book when those from London Below are usually invisible? Why will breaking an egg with a toasting fork bring someone back to life? I realize that this was a fantasy book and the whys of things aren't as important in this genre, but this was a new approach for me. 
 That said, I still quite enjoyed reading it. Gaiman's style was easy to read and engaging. It had a lot of very interesting and memorable imagery, including the bad guys chomping on raw rats and birds. I will be interested to check out more of Neil Gaiman's work to see if moral ambiguity enters the picture at some point. If so, hurrah!

I am glad to see that other readers loved it as I paid good money for the book and now I will pass the book onto my older son to see if he finds some enjoyment out of it. Great cover!

The front of this book boasts a quote from Ray Bradbury: "This guy can write!" I'm afraid, no. 
 Garrison Keillor - can write. Isaac Asimov - can write. Annie Dillard - can write. Even Mr. Bradbury himself - can write. 
 Ben Loory - can publicize. How many of us got this book after seeing this stuff in the New Yorker or hearing it on This American Life? Granted, he had two pretty good stories on TAL, but if you're looking for a book of pretty good stories, you might preview this one in the bookstore before committing. 
 Each story in this collection uses the same voice which sounds like a high schooler with a deadline. Some of the stories don't seem to have a point, or are too cryptic to make me care to investigate. Many of them just live to provide a "ha-ha, got you" punchline in the last few sentences. But the journey there is not enjoyable. 
 The book has such a cute name. It's a shame it can't be judged by its cover.

This is a handsome book, smooth, textured pages, and with a UFO and an octopus tentacle on the cover I was instantly captured. The short form of the stories was intriguing to me, the breif sections were ambitious- they could have ended up really helping or hurting the stories. I think it ended up hurting most of them. Hardly any of the charcters have names, the anonymity really begins to wear around the thirtieth story. Attatching even an arbitrary name would have helped the significance of the characters if only a little. In some of the stories the absurtity seems forced, as with a few of the endings. A lot of the concepts are likeable, cool, or cute. An Octopus that drinks tea, a walking tree, a lightswitch that controls the weather, but the stories are ultimately hindered by the terse form. A little bit more would have gone a long way. Some of the details were also lazy and began to become boring, mostly because the same format was repeated too many times- ex: We walked, and walked, and walked, and walked, and walked some more. There were three stories that I loved and thought the short form was successful, The Swimming Pool, The Rope and the Sea, and Hadely. The last story which did not follow the short form like the rest was good as well, it had more meat to it, I would like to see meatier stories from Ben Loory.

I wanted to like this book SO badly. The cover is gorgeous, and the format of the short stories are right up my alley. Unfortunately, this was a huge disappointment. There was only one story that I semi-enjoyed. The stories started off with good premises and a lot of potential, but the endings were a complete let-down. It felt like the last paragraph or even the last sentence of every story ruined them. I only finished this because it was a quick-read, but I was hoping for something scary (because of the title!). Maybe I just went in with the wrong expectations, since a lot of people seemed to enjoy this. I honestly didn't understand the point of any story in this collection.

A couple of months ago, a guy named Ben "liked" one of my reviews here on Goodreads. Curious, I clicked on Ben and discovered he was an author. Again curious, I checked out his book Stories for Nighttime and Some for the Day at my local library (which also happens to be my place of employment). I was pleasantly surprised to discover a wonderful collection of odd little stories. From an octopus living in an apartment in the city to a television that writes an opera about Winston Churchill, I loved the weird mix of totally bizarre and completely ordinary. Thanks, Goodreads, for helping me find this unique writer.

Someone is going to start a cult based around this book. In less than a generation its followers will outnumber the Mormons and have a greater impact on the media than the Scientologists. There will be schisms, heresies and wars. It is entirely possible that I will rise to power as a Torquemada like figure in the Loory-following theocracy that the Western US shall become. I shall spend my every waking moment rooting out and torturing those who have not read this tome. 
 It would be for the best if you just read it now.

This is an amazing book. When Ben Loory read a small piece of it in Denver, my girlfriend and I both cried. When Ben Loory sent me the manuscript for a blurb, I held it in my heart each night for a summer while my girlfriend was in Taiwan. Oh, to get through the day and have stories from this book awaiting you!! 
 Here's the blurb I wrote: 
 Stories for Nighttime and Some for the Day is a book that comes alive when you read it. It will stand on its own, pet your hair while you sleep, and hold the umbrella over your head in the rain.

I am not usually a fan of short stories but when I heard about this book, I knew I had to give it a try. I am so glad that I did. Stories for Nightime and Some for the Day is a fun, kooky, entertaining collection of short stories. 
 So of the stories I liked better than others. For example: The Book, a story that teaches you to use your imagination. The Octopus, a story that shows you that you can always return home. Also there was the story, The End of It All, about a husband and a wife, where the wife is taken by an alien. The man searches all over to find her to no end. Though, the man never finds his wife, he would not trade anything in the world for the time that he did get to spend with her. Of course, there were some stories that I did not like as well. Than there were the dark stories. Stories for Nighttime and Some for the Day has a little bit of everything for everyone to enjoy. Don't be fooled by the title of this collection of stories and the stories can be read any time of the day or night. I plan to check out more of Mr. Ben Loory's work.

I don't necessarily seek out books by savvy GR-reviewers, but if I happen to run into their work in the wild, as it were, I'm often automatically intrigued. I have a Eugene Lim novel that I snatched at Unnameable Books around here somewhere. I may have clutched at a Ben Spivey at that amazing new d.i.y. library in East Williamsburg. And so this popped up outside Book Thug and I grabbed it immediately. Naturally. 
 Loory's concern here is with the basic ground zero storytelling forms: the fable, the fairytale, the myth. Each has been pared down to the bare essentials of its action, floating in short motions of words that twist and shift with or against the reader-expectactions of the form. Thematically, there's an elemental quality to the simplicity. Without echoing, exactly, the archetypal examples -- in fact, these often veer into wildly unexpected places -- Loory constructs arcs that seem inherently archtypal. New archteypes, at best. At worst, a casting about for startling developments that have no reflection in the story that leads up to them. 
 However, also, the extreme streamlining, the simplicity, the archtypalness -- they're perfect when they're perfect, but dicey when not quite. The elegant oddity of something like "The Women and the Basement" seems like it will stick with me. But sometimes austere simplicity of word and plot can just be an emptiness, a void impossible to fill from the reader's side of the page. Sometimes lack of detail can just be lack of imagery, lack of memorable flesh. Without the slight breath of words needed to give a story an atmosphere of its own, we risk suffocation.

reference_books.title: Traitor to the Throne (Rebel of the Sands, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
The first book was really good, but this one was AWESOME! I loved it. 
 Review to come next year...next year!? 
 I feel sorry for you who have to wait so long for this sequel, but let me tell you: it won't disappoint.

reference_books.title: Night Film
reference_books.review_text:
This physically heavy book (623 grams, I weighed it) of 600 pages is surprisingly exciting all the way through. There is not a dull moment. The short, but many chapters where not only absolutely necessary for a moment to breathe, but also gave me a chance to put the book down to, you know, eat and sleep. Yes it was that hard to put away. It was exciting, dark, mysterious, hitchcock-ish and dream-ish, in a nightmare kind of way. At one point I remember thinking of the opening to Queen's song, The Bohemian Rhapsody - Is this the real life? Or is this just fantasy? Because that's how it felt like reading this book, I started to doubt what was real and not. And so did our hero, Scott McGrath. 
 Why is that middle aged journalists, reporters or detectives of some sorts are always made from the same mold? I feel like I've never read about an investigator with a happy private life, nope, they are always divorced, have difficult relationships with their children and drink in the daytime. McGrath is no exception. He is not an original character at all, but a good guy to have as our eyes and ears. As an experienced journalist he helps us out on the way putting things together and processing information. 
 But, for the first time, at least for me, I am not only reading about the investigation, I am actually part of it. Because what made this book truly unique was that it contained more than just words and chapters. Never before have I been such a part of the investigation, because instead of being told of the emails that are sent, the articles that are read or the pictures that are shown, I actually get to see them for myself. 
 What Pessl succeeded the most with was building up a story that felt both so real, and at the same time not. The way she built up the legend of the famous director Cordova made me forget that he was pure fiction and not a real person. She would also, very cleverly, mix up his name with very real and non fictional people like Tarantino, Marlo Brando and other famous people that made it feel like he was alive. His name was mentioned so often that it now feels like he is an actual director. 
 "Life had been a suit I'd only put on for special occasions. Most of the time I kept it in the back of my closet, forgetting it was there. We were meant to die when it was barely stitched anymore, when the elbows and knees were stained with grass and mud, shoulder pads uneven from people hugging you all the time, downpours and blistering sun, the fabric faded, buttons gone." 
 Without mentioning the ending, I have to mention the ending. During the book I am with McGrath all the way, working closely together him. But at some point towards the end, the already high tempo goes into ultra speed and I got a bit confused about what was unraveling. I don't know if it was intentional, that I should be just as confused as McGrath was, or if I was perhaps to excited and read to quickly to really understand all the little details. 
 This is definitely a book I need to re-read in the future. I think it's the kind of book that might even benefit for it. Anyhoo, it was a really good and exciting book. Now I can't wait to get my hands on her first book - Special Topics in Calamity Physics which I hope to do soon.

reference_books.title: Rebel of the Sands (Rebel of the Sands, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
There are a lot of typical things in this YA fantasy book. A young girl who wants to break free, a handsome stranger, a land in revolution, magic and of course love. But, it didn't feel typical. 
 This world is fascinating. There's kingdoms and rebelling princes, scary creatures, politics, intrigues and a whole lot of sand. It has an interesting setting that seems to be the new jam in YA, which is this sort of middle eastern/wild wide west vibe, which I'm digging actually. It feels new and untouched. 
 Our main heroine Amani is easy to like. She manages to be both very rational, and a day dreamer at the same time, and no wonder she wants to break free. She lives with her aunt and uncle (since her dad (who wasn't really her dad) and her mom are dead) and they are like most aunts and uncles in fiction - evil. Well maybe not evil, but they're not the kindest people. Her uncle, who already has more than one wife, is considering marrying Amani (because why not? He's already feeding her, he might as well get something out of it) and that is plain horrifying. Ew. Also, there's a creep neighbor who doesn't hesitate threatening to basically rape Amani so she will become his by default (because a woman once ruined doesn't have the choice to refuse marriage, right?). Double ew. 
 As you can detect from this, the attitude towards women in this world is crap, and that's a huge part of this book. Again and again Amani's sex stands in her way and to escape it some what, she sometimes dresses like a boy to hide it. There was a particular line in the book that caught me - "But I'd lost my authority with my gender" - and that resonated so much with me since I've said something along those lines myself before. Amani is a fantastic shooter and a skill shouldn't have anything to do with gender, and although I've only shot people in the photographic sense, I've definitely been undermined because of my gender working with my expertise that has nothing to do with it. So I felt connected to Amani. 
 Also, it's a very exciting book! There's shootings and kidnappings and train chases and battles. Its very fast paced and it's such an easy and enjoyable read. It also had a lovely language with a magical and poetic feel that never went overboard, but balanced nicely with the rational mind of Amani. 
 Oh, and there are also other characters in this book! There is the handsome stranger, that I kind of liked but also found kind of annoying. There are some other interesting people they meet along their way that I'm exicted to get to know more in following books. And another thing I appreciated was the fact that no one was safe. People died, unexpectedly and more than once. People also got hurt and it was unpredictable. 
 So yeah, it's a bit typical at its core and it has a traditional build, but so have many books. I really liked it and I definitely want to read more from Hamilton.

reference_books.title: The Dark Days Club (Lady Helen, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
It has taken me some time to write this review, not because I'm lazy, but because I had to think about feelings toward it. And I've come to a conclusion. I think. 
 Some books are better as a series than just on their own, and after some thinking, I'm sure this is going to be one of those. Even though it was almost 500 pages the adventure has only just begun and there is a lot more to get explored in the future. 
 In many ways it follows a classic story - a young woman discovers she has powers from a dark handsome stranger and now she must save the world. Kind of. Which doesn't sound very exciting, or original, and even though at it's core it's that kind of story, it didn't feel typical or silly. 
 Lady Helen is a great heroine and was portrayed so well. She was the reason I kept flipping the pages and she felt so real. She's intelligent, she analyzes things and thinks through. She has depth and a sincerity in her actions that I loved. 
 But I questioned her relationships. Supposedly she had a best friend, but she was barely in this story (even though she was mentioned often) and therefore I think she might as well not even have been in it. Also, her relationship with her maid was a bit odd and I rather think she could have taken the best friend role instead. The relationship with her brother and family though was entirely believable and I've read enough historical books to understand and be grateful of not living in a time where a woman's worth and independence were so frightfully low. I'm also grateful for the lack of evil uncles looming over my shoulder. 
 And of course there is the relationship of the big love interest in this book - The Earl of Carlston. As a lover of the dark broody handsome stranger, I'm of course going to like him, and I did like him, but I didn't feel tension between Helen and him until the last couple of chapters - and I was craving that. He has an interesting backstory and I'm sure we're going to know more of it in books to come. 
 Strangely enough the fantasy elements weren't the most exciting parts of the story for me, the mystery was what carried me until the end. It might have started a bit slow, but it ended very dramatically and thrillingly. 
 Something else I really appreciated was the fact that Helen's powers were a choice. So often in books like these powers are thrust upon heroes and heroines and it's become a tiresome trope. But this was far more complex that I initially thought and I really liked that. 
 This is a great start and I enjoyed this book, but I'm certain that as a series, it's going to be something I will love.

reference_books.title: Uprooted
reference_books.review_text:
I wanted to like this book so much, but I didn't. I just liked it, without the so much. I read somewhere that this bok is like a lost Brothers Grimm tale and I definitely felt the same. But remember how the original fairytales are, not so damn cosy. So yes there is a fairytale vibe going on but if you're expecting Disney, you'll be disappointed. 
 I heard an interview with the author and she said the story was inspired by a Polish fairytale she used to hear as a child, and that definitely seeps through. So here's what going on. Our heroine Agnieszka lives in a small village within a magical world where every ten years The Dragon, a wizard who protects her village, takes a price for his protection in the form of a young woman who has to serve him. Agnieszka is convinced that her beautiful bestie Kasia is going to get chosen, but hear and behold, our heroine gets chosen instead. So just like Belle in Beauty and The Beast, she is thrown into an unknown world where adventure and love ensues. 
 So love stories doesn't have to be lovey dovey all the time, definitely not, but by god, it has to be something. I just didn't feel the relationship between The Dragon and Agnieszka at all, I thought he was dick throughout the book. There was no twinkle in his eyes, or affection behind his mean actions and words, no sweet moments and he felt like a brat. Besides the momentarily sexual attraction, I could not see how our cool and competent heroine could fall for him. So that was a downer. 
 But there were two things I really liked, the concept of the woods and our heroine's best friend, Kasia. 
 So the woods made for an interesting villain and I loved the creepy and eerie feeling that came from it. I thought the backstory with how it became The Woods and where it ended up by the end of this book, was fascinating. And Kasia is a person that should have gotten so much more space in this book because I thought her story and character development was the most interesting of all! She had prepared all her life to be taken by The Dragon and when she isn't, she does the most amazing turn around and becomes this kick ass warrior. I want a book about her! 
 Mostly this book lacked feel and even though I kept turning the pages and it was exciting at times, I felt emotionally disconnected and felt no sense of wonder, which is what a fairytale should do in my mind. But the language was lovely.

book_a.title: Eleanor Oliphant is Completely Fine
book_a.user_review:
This book was somehow boring and interesting at the same time. I mean, I did finish it and found it to be an ok read but there was just something missing. I kept wavering back and forth while reading, loosing attention and wondering where the story was going. 
 I did however appreciate the way Honeyman combined light-hearted comedy and dark mental health issues, but I just couldn't connect to our heroine. And if I can't connect and feel for my main character the book will always be lost for me, however well written it might be.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Reese Witherspoon (Book Club), you've done me wrong. Actually, Reese playing Eleanor might be the only thing that can save this story. This was one of the worst books I've read this year. The characters in this book, especially Eleanor, were not believable at all. The first-person narrative style didn't help and actually took me out of the story instead of helping me see Eleanor's perspective. The first chapter was an information dump, and the story didn't improve from there. I think Eleanor is supposed to be some sort of lovable misfit or grump, but she came across as obnoxious and mean-spirited. Her behavior just didn't ring true as being the result of abuse or a traumatic incident. Also, as other reviewers have noted, she works in accounting, but she's scared to turn on a computer? I don't think so. 
 Overall, super disappointing book. Eleanor Oliphant is not completely fine.

"If someone asks you how you are, you are meant to say FINE. You are not meant to say that you cried yourself to sleep last night because you hadn't spoken to another person for two consecutive days. FINE is what you say." 
 Eleanor Oliphant may very well be my favorite character from a book, ever. Unfortunately, just about every time I try to say her name, I say "Elephant Olinor", instead. 
 I can't say enough good things about this book. It's simply perfect.

Thank you Netgalley for an advanced copy of this book. 
 I made a mistake. Before picking up this book I looked at a few quick snippets of reviews - you know, those taglines that claim a book is like "such and such" a book. And that kind of decreased my enjoyment of the book. You see, I read that Eleanor was the female version of Ove (from A Man Called Ove) (whom I absolutely adore) and so I had that in mind ... and she wasn't really that. At least not to me. 
 I also started reading this book when I was pretty exhausted and so I can't say that I committed to reading it as well as I should have from the beginning: it did take me a minute to warm up to Eleanor and her story. 
 That said. 
 3.5 stars. 
 Eleanor is wonderful in that she remains true to herself; smart, comfortable with who she is, unapologetic for being honest. She made me smile a number of times thanks to her social interactions - she never felt awkward, even though as a reader you know that perhaps she had messed up or misread a situation. So it's especially lovely to meet Raymond and Sammy and Bob and a handful of other characters who accept her for who she is. Aware that perhaps she won't do what is socially acceptable, but that she has a kind heart and means well. 
 This is a story about a woman who is coming to terms with her past, who is welcoming other people into her life, and adapting to what comes her way. It's a really lovely story that will give you all the feels - just like Ove did (oops... I guess I do see the resemblance). I have to say that the ending was especially nice; I liked that Gail Honeyman didn't try to turn Eleanor into someone she isn't; what you see is what you get. She grew as a person without changing who she really is. 
 Recommended read. 
 ps. And because I can't help myself ... If I were writing a tag line for this book it would be that Eleanor is the female Don Tillman from The Rosie Project ... and that Raymond is her Rosie.
Stopped at page 86. Eleanor annoyed me. I only found a few parts mildly funny. Otherwise I decided since I read over 1/4 of the book and still didn't like her, I was done.

What an original and engrossing story! The book got better as it went along. A young woman grows into who she is meant to be from having had a difficult childhood. It was so heartwarming to see that growth in who she is and her personality. Funny in places and tear-jerking in others. So glad that I read this.
A delightful, quirky book that makes you think about how you treat people without knowing their entire story. Love the characters and their relationships!

Eleanor ist eine Soziopathin, deren Geschichte sehr episodenhaft erzahlt wird. Grosse Teile der Story haben uberhaupt keine Auswirkungen auf ihre Entwicklung und am Ende ist es - Hallo Klischee - eine Therapeutin, die ihr Leben verandert. 
 Ich verstehe den Hype um dieses Buch nicht.

Loved this book and the main character . She was easy to relate to in some aspects. I liked that this book had a humorous tone to it , and that I was able to visualize the characters in various circumstances. Some of Eleanor's remarks reminded me of either something I would think or say. I liked that she had a what you see is what you get type of personality.
So much potential, yet such a predictable ending.

22 books into 2017 and I may have awarded my book of the year!!! 
 I actually get concerned when I read a book I really really love as I know my review will not do it justice. I think the last time I felt like this was when I read A Man Called Ove which has rocketed to one of my all time favourite books ever. 
 Eleanor Oliphant is a similar character to Ove, in that, she is not immediately likeable or easy to relate to. The author slowly feeds you bits of Eleanor's past and present and you can't help but absorb her, and accept her and begin to like her...alot! And by the end, I felt quite bereft at losing Eleanor Oliphant and her closest friend Raymond from my life. 
 When I started this book I didn't really know what it was about. My sister told me that she doesn't read the blurb again after purchasing a book, and she certainly doesn't read reviews before reading, so I thought I would give it a go. I had no idea what the story was about - so I am not going to tell you the plot line, just incase you are reading this before purchase and want to go in blind like I did. I will say that the first few pages read a little bit like a high quality chick lit novel, which would not have sat well with me as I don't really enjoy chick lit. However I soon realised there was so much more depth, beauty and sorrow in Eleanor Oliphant than any chick lit I had read. 
 If I were to summarise the story, I would say it is about a young woman, perhaps on the edge of the Autism spectrum, perhaps just scarred in more ways than one by her past, who learns to truly live for herself and love herself. It is beautifully charactersised, every one of the 'players' in the book could be sat next to you whist you are reading. It is is perfectly paced - nothing is left out or rushed, however there was not one page where I found my attention drifting. It is also the perfect balance of heart wrenchingly sad and soul warmingly happy. Without a doubt my best book of this year. And probably moved into my top twenty books of all times. Along with Ove, Eleanor Oliphant has a permanent place in my heart .

book_b.title: The Girl with Seven Names: A North Korean Defector’s Story
book_b.user_review:
North Korea escape stories are very "hot" at the moment and I've read a few of them. This is the best one so far. It was not only interesting and horrifying, but also super exciting. Every time I said to myself, only one more chapter, I always ended up reading about 5 more because I couldn't put it down. 
 It is one of the most well written autobiographies I've ever read and the pace was perfect. The only thing lacking for me was in fact North Korea. I wanted to know more about the everyday life there, instead a lot of the book is spent in China and South Korea. 
 Many things surprised me in this book and I thought Lee did a great job of explaining the meaning behind it all, both politically and in society, and also the significance of different customs taking place. All of these of course astounded me and the more I read about this very strange country, the more horrified I become. 
 Lee also writes loads about her feelings and it felt very personal. I thought at times that she was a bit harsh on herself, taking blame when it wasn't necessarily hers to take, but her life took extraordinary turns when she was young and not yet an adult, so its bound to happen. 
 So. I learned loads of things, got to know an amazingly strong woman and had a great, interesting read.

sample_reviews.review_text: One of the best books I have ever read. A true story of a girl who escapes across the river and her amazing story.

Fascinating read about the internal workings of North Korea and one young woman's struggle to leave and to help her family escape. While we may never completely understand North Korea, this book provides a riveting insight. Ms. Lee's perseverance is inspirational. The book is well written and the author's guile, and sometimes foolhardiness, kept me turning the pages. Recommended.

I did enjoy this but I also feel like she made a lot of really incredibly dumb choices that really made no sense. For example she stayed with relatives in China for 2 whole years (!!!) and didn't think of maybe using that time to get a job to save money, or to learn a vocation? Then she runs away penniless on the spur of the moment and has no plan of what to do. You had 2 years to think about it and relied on the kindness of distant relatives to support you, but you didn't think ahead of what to do next?? 
 She seemed really naive in general, especially when she constantly turned to brokers for help, even though she clearly says again and again she didn't trust them. She was incredibly lucky and fortunate to have people around her who had a lot of money to constantly bail her out and those connections clearly helped her. 
 Also the fact that she didn't even know at first that people were starving in the 90s in N. Korea and she was eating meat daily, makes it clear that she lived a very insulated life there, and probably had a very different experience from the average N. Korean. I'd really love to know her mother's story, because to be honest, she sounds like a much tougher cookie than her daughter, cleverly supporting her 2 children and getting them through famine as a single mother. Wow, hats off to her! 
 I did enjoy this book because I'm fascinated with any books from N. Korean defectors in general, but my sympathies with her were limited. I'm glad she got out, and that she was able to help her family as well, but this is probably not the experience of most N. Korean defectors. I do wish her all the best and hope more people learn about what is going on in N. Korea.
excellent read. i have read a few books about north korea. it makes me appreciate Canada all the more. the rights and freedoms that we take for granted. north koreans do not even know they exist.

The story of Hyeonseo and her family's escape from North Korea is fascinating and moving. The style itself is very matter-of-fact, and the writing isn't emotional. It doesn't have to be. The stories she tells are powerful enough on its own. Just when you think that Hyeonseo catches a break, something else terrible happens. But what really sets this book apart for me is the nuance - the fact that life is as difficult for a North Korean defector in China or South Korea as it is to remain in North Korea. For Hyeonseo, this is because she had a remarkably "normal" and happy childhood. The totalitarian regime infects every part of life, causing neighbors to inform on each other and kindergarteners to have to go through self-criticism sessions, and there is no concept of human rights. Even with all of that, though, what struck me is that Hyeonseo's family was actually reasonably well-off and happy. Not every North Korean experiences this privilege, of course, but it casts the struggles in China and South Korea in a very different light. Life was not automatically better for them when they defected. There are significant emotional scars from growing up in a place where every action could be considered suspect, and these are things that they will always struggle with.
After I finished the book I watched the TED special by the author, highly recommend both. Read the book first as the special will spoil it.
Nevjerojatna prica!

I couldn't put this book down. I was fascinated by her stories of what life in North Korea was like, but also found myself curious about how she would survive once she made it out. I found myself sympathizing with her emotions, even at times when she wanted to return to North Korea. I would recommend this book to everyone!

This is a truly inspiring story. Some reviewers point out that the author has had many opportunities opened to her because she comes from a higher social class in North Korea. While that is true, her struggles were not any less real. Her defection required a lot of quick thinking on her part, a bit of luck, and a lot of secrecy. She could literally trust no one. 
 This book was an eye opener for me. I was unaware of how dire things really were/still are in North Korea. I would recommend this to anyone and everyone. I plan to talk it up a lot.

The Girl with Seven Names by Hyeonseo Lee is an inspiring story of courage and bravery as one woman struggles to keep her family together after separation that included varying periods of incarceration for each of the three-member family. It is an incredible (as in hard to believe) story but if a reader wanted to check the authenticity of some of the incidents cited, it could be easily done by examining public media reports. Imagine a Korean woman (Hyeonseo) meeting a western traveler in Laos who voluntarily gives money to Hyeonseo to aid in paying corruption money to get Hyeonseo's mother and brother out of a Lao prison. There was not an exchange of favors for money and the traveler had no assurances of ever being repaid. The incident happened, the traveler was repaid, and the story was reported by the Australian press. 
 Hyeonseo was 17 years old when she decided to cross the border between North Korea and China. It was illegal but because she was under 18 years old, her punishment would be a slap on the wrist. If over 18, it would be jail time. She decided to take the risk because she thought it would be her last chance to see the town across the river, a town that seemed to always have electricity, far different than her own. She crossed the river, met a trading partner colleague of her mother and asked for help to make a trip to Shenyang to see a distant relative. While there she received a call from her mother. A day after crossing the river, the North Korean government began a census. It was noted that she was missing; her mother reported her as missing in an attempt to cover up the illegal crossing. She could not go home to North Korea; her eighteenth birthday had come and gone, she was stuck in China 
 Hyeonseo was stateless, she had no identification papers in China. She stayed for such a long period of time with her relatives that there was thought of marriage just to get an ID and avoid repatriation by China. Hyeonseo thought marriage was just another type of incarceration. She had escaped, even if unintentionally, from North Korea; now she would escape from marriage. Leaving her relatives secretly, she went to another Chinese city with a Korean expatriate community where she fell into a trap set by human traffickers. Escaping from that, she went to yet another Chinese city where she purchased false ID and settled into an acceptable job. However, she felt she would never be accepted by the Chinese, she had false identification papers, and she missed her family. How could she reunite with them or even communicate with them without putting them in danger from the north Korean government 
 Each time she changed location in China, she changed names. She would continue to do this in an attempt to avoid capture by an increasingly more efficient bureaucratic surveillance system. Missing her family and feeling unaccepted by China, she finally resolved to go to South Korea. She felt she would better fit into that society. But entry to South Korea would also have to be done illegally. Once she arrived in South Korea, she could claim political asylum, but getting there would involve subterfuge. 
 She got to South Korea, she got her mother and sister out of North Korea, the three of them eventually got to the United States. This is not a spoiler. The excitement in the novel is with the tricks and subterfuges necessary to make the many, many escapes. 
 The first one-third of the book Hyeonseo writes of her childhood in North Korea. She writes of struggles to survive hunger on the parts of most of the population. After the death of her father, she writes of her mother's successful attempts to establish herself as a black market trader and a government official willing to accept bribes and gifts that were at the heart of North Korean bureaucracy. Her success allowed Hyeonseo to escape much of the hunger that the general population endured. 
 While in China she discovered some of the horrible truths about life under the North Korean regime. Things she considered normal everyday coping strategies to deal with an authoritarian regime were deplored by every country outside North Korea. Her former government and leaders were laughing stocks to the rest of the world. She asked herself a question. How could such a world exist? She answered the question and it is an answer that fits for all corrupt and authoritarian governments in the world today. What is the answer? I won't reveal it. That would be a spoiler. Read the book. 
 I read this book in preparation for a writer and reader convention I will attend in Bali, Indonesia at the end of October 2016. One of the authors I will meet is a Korean lady who went undercover as an investigative journalist in North Korea. It would be nice if I could ask an intelligent question. Hyeonseo also gave A TED talk. Google to find it; it is an inspiring twelve-minute talk.

Premise: Sookie is a waitress; she mostly keeps to herself. She sort of has to, otherwise she ends up reading people's minds and knowing things she'd rather not. She's intrigued when the first vampire shows up openly in their small town, which quickly turns to worried when her new friend is suspected of murder. 
 This was....fine. Nothing special. It's cute, I guess, and the writing is competent and I was curious enough to get to the end, but in the end I just thought it was fine. 
 My main problem with the book was Sookie. Laying aside her annoyingly cutsie-pie name, she's irritatingly dense. Why are you surprised when something paranormal happens? YOU CAN READ MINDS! You ARE paranormal! And then, why are you surprised the next time something paranormal or scary happens? And the time after that? And the time after THAT? I know it's a lot to take in, but she is really incapable of rolling with a situation, and I find that off-putting in a heroine. 
 The rest of the supporting cast is fine, the twist of the end of the mystery was okay but nothing amazing. The other intended twist maybe was a surprise in 2001, but at this point my reaction as a reader was: "of course that is the case, I knew from page two. That's how these books work."

 That is, if you're a reader of sci-fi/fantasy/urban fantasy/mystery/etc. If you're primarily a romance reader, I can see coming at this from a totally different angle and seeing it as new and different. However, I don't think the romance adds much to the book from the angle of a genre reader.

 Everything else is filler and pointless and only offers different locations to have sex. There's no drama, no unexpected plot twists, no nothing. Like... really???? That's it??? Three books to tell a story that shouldn't take more than 10 lines?? 
 And the sex... Oh, man... Being an erotica book of sorts, you would at least expect a decently written sex scene. Well, guess again. All of the scenes are not only badly written, they're all the same (with MINOR changes here and there). The S&M is poorly portrayed (obviously the author doesn't know enough of this practice), looks like something only a depraved and insane person would do (which is not), does not sound healthy, fun or sexy (which SHOULD be) and it's just boring. Sex. Boring. I can't believe I'm putting those two words together. And yet, it got an overall rating of 3.92??? I weep for mankind... 
 If there's anyone out there, reading this rant: Please, don't waste your time on this crap, don't do what I did. There are millions of books out there, and I'd bet the shittiest one of them is still better and more entertaining than this shit.

Stupidest fucking thing I've ever read. There's literature, bad literature, 50 feet of shit, and then this book. Everything about it is horrendous: the writing, the "plot", the pacing, the characters. I mean, the first two books were terrible in their own right, but the "relationship" between Ana and Christian in this book goes to a whole new level of unhealthy and pathetic. 
 And James has absolutely no concept how to build a plot. Things happen without any precedent and then an out-of-nowhere infodump explains it away between the crappily written gratuitous sex scenes. And the epilogue is even more nauseating than the Harry Potter one, and that's saying something. 
 I know they say people have a right to enjoy what they want but I have the right to judge anyone who actually likes this garbage.

Yuck. Thank God this mess of a series is over.

reference_books.title: Night Owls
reference_books.review_text:
"Night Owls" focuses on the relationship between 18-year-old Beatrix and Jake as they get to know each other and get through personal issues at the same time. 
 Beatrix is an average girl with a pretty average life, she pretty much just gets through life in a normal way. What makes her special is her talent and her passion for anatomical art. She looks at corpses and draws them anatomically. In the ya literature world it's really - and sadly - rare for a person this young to be passionate about something, let alone being passionate about such a "weird" branch of art. But imagine a character who knows she wants to make a job out of her passion. It's incredible and incredibly refreshing, as well as a strong message to young people: pursue your dreams, don't let anyone tell you your passion can't become your job in the future and specifically don't let people tell you art is not economic enough to be followed. 
 Jake, also a young boy, has a complicated life. His family is famous and rich, someone he cares about is dealing with mental health problems and he does all he can to help. On the same path as Beatrix, he has his own interests: he's a Buddhist, he's all about the zen life, he's into street art. Jenn Bennett is clearly very good at portraying that side of young adults which rarely gets portrayed: young people with passions and spirituality. 
 Something else worth mentioning is the characters' relationship with their respective siblings. I really enjoyed the way Beatrix and Jake relate to their brother and sister, especially the latter. 
 As I said, the characters were good, the story kept me interested, the romance was nice and slow - it was more of a "let's know each other" kind of love story, never too cheesy -, but two things keep bothering me even weeks after I finished it. 
 The use of some tropes could have been done in a better way. A girl who's never done anything "wrong" meets a rich boy and suddenly starts telling lies to her mother and starts doing dangerous things with him. Most times I forgive the use of tropes if it's done well or if they are used as a plot device and then develops into something bigger, and this time it wasn't bad but in other books I've seen tropes taken to a whole new level in a way they don't look like tropes anymore. 
 The second thing I had issues with, which was what really made me lower the rating of this book, is the ending. The girl makes a decision that made me wonder whether she was really that determined to accomplish her goals. But I've made up my mind and decided that after all, we all make different decisions and even though what she chooses wouldn't definitely be what I'd choose, it doesn't mean she's any less determined. 
 Over all, I liked this book a lot, especially because of the representation of art and of two very different kinds of art and of teenagers with strong passions.

You'll find yourselfsurprised multiple times.If you get easily mad in front ofsocial injustice, you should consider reading this book twice: it's full of the worst injustice on earth.The main character is ascomplicated as she's simple, with a child's innocence and sweetness next to a sensible adult's intelligence.Usually I don't like happy endings, but when I read it I couldn't think of an ending that wasn't happy.The narrator is funny and creates alink with the reader in the very first pages, talking directly to them. I love it and I'm sure it's an efficient tecnique in children books.

reference_books.title: The Son of Neptune (The Heroes of Olympus, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
I open this review saying that I love where the series is going. I love the plot line with my whole heart of fantasy lover and I love Riordan's points, how he will unite (and already has, somehow) Romans and Greeks. And I love how their cultures meet. 
 Straight from the beginning, it's a strange feeling to see Percy remembering random things about his past; stranger than with Jason because we already have a connection with Percy while with Jason, at least at the beginning, we know as much about his past as he. I tremble when Percy mentions Annabeth, and it's a total joy when he remembers his brother and his goatly friend. 
 The new characters Riordan introduces are complicated with complicated pasts. Somehow, their life is even more complicated that the characters' introduced in The Lost Hero. But I think no demigod will ever claim to have a normal life. This is something clear right from the beginning of Percy Jackson and The Olympians series. 
 I like that all the heroes have common traits but each of them is differently characterized. 
 The relationships between the characters are never lame and never foregone. They are as complicated as the characters themselves. 
 Something I was meaning to say before, in this series there are no sexist barriers at all: crying doesn't make a man any less manly, and fighting doesn't make a woman any less of a woman. But it's not even stressed like in many books, it's just natural for the author to define a hero not by his gender but by their heart. 
 The real ability of Riordan is to make us feel as homesick for Camp Half-Blood as Percy is, but at the same time he makes us feel bounded to people at Camp Jupiter as much as Percy feels. Let's face it: we found a new family with Romans. And that's why I loved how the three of them got along, I found it truly moving, because just like Percy I would trust Hazel and Frank with my life. 
 I really missed Percy's sass and his character in general in TLH. He's truly one of the best male characters I've ever come across. 
 Now I have a little critic for the form. I love how in this series there are seven points of view, but while in The Lost Hero there were two chapters from one character's point of view, then two from the other and two from the other, now they are divided by four chapters per character in a row and it makes the book slow-paced. 
 Something I really appreciate about this series is how at the end you can find little anticipations about the next book and how you want to move on to the next book straight away. Multiple times, reading these books, I had a remote idea to take a break reading something else, something light, but when I reach the ending I look forward to continuing. So now, on to the next one!

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 One big fat disappointment. After hearing how great this trilogy was and reading a whole comparison to Tolkien, I was quite disturbed with how this ended. It wasn't so much as what happened as how this whole climax was built up throughout three books and it just fizzled to nothing. Apparently, Stephanie Meyer took the same instruction in writing as Philip Pullman, except her verse style is for people that don't read. 
 I don't like how Lyra was this strong female lead, but then she ended up being a submissive crier by the end. Was Pullman trying to say that females can't be strong enough without a man? Interesting when he spends a whole lot of time preaching about being more open-minded. 
 Father Gomez...what was the point of his character? That was the silliest character insertion I've ever seen. Mrs. Coulter, I thought her evilness was written very well...until the end. A strong willed woman becomes a blubbering fool as soon as she realizes her child is the main target, but didn't care for her when she was born? Or was she planning this all along? 
 Lord Asriel's departure was even worse, even if it was the same as Mrs. Coulter's. 
 It wasn't so much that the main characters had just fallen in love and then suddenly realized that they can never be with each other that was the disappointment. It was that I wasn't convinced enough. They fell in love when teenage cognition is sprouting and most likely came out of circumstance. 
 The book itself is twice as long as the first two, and I wasn't in much of a hurry to finish it. It seemed to drag on and on forever and I couldn't wait until it was over. This is very much the way I felt about the Sword of Truth series, except there weren't pages of review, so you actually had to pay attention to what you were reading. 
 What I liked was the different worlds. Yeah, that's about it.
The ending is anti-climactic and completely lame.

The Amber Spyglass left me with so many feels! Agh, my heart is tearing. It took me ages to finish this book but it was still pretty good. I'm so glad this is the last book but I want to know what happens to Will and Lyra. I guess I'll never know how they grow up. Such a wonderful series though! So happy I read it.
Pretty good, but the series falters and is disappointing.

Thank the Authority it's over. I've going to be honest with you. I didn't read it so much as I skimmed it because if I read it fully i was probably going to go meet the harpies. I got the general gist though because pretty much all you have to do is look for the new character and the dialogue that follows will summarize the last... 20 pages. 
 I'm being overly harsh. To be fair I liked the first book. I found it imaginative if a little overdone. The second was.... acceptable. This one was just so long. 
 Mrs Coulter has drugged Lyra and kept her in a cave, understanding every mother has wanted to do this to their daughter Mrs Coulter is doing it to protect Lyra from the Magisterium who want to kill her. Because Lyra is going to be the new Eve and bring about the fall of man. 
 Will is working with a couple angels to find and rescue Lyra while an assassin follows the scientist Mary Malone... i.e. the serpent.... hoping she will find Lyra. Mary enters into another world where she meets mulefa and she uses tree sap to construct a spy glass that allows her to see Dust. 
 Meanwhile Will meets Iorek and destroys Iorek's helmet with the knife and Iorek is like oh cool power and joins will on his crusade to reduce Lyra (while also avenging the aeronauts death) 
 Pretty much everybody in every universe minus Mary find Mrs Coulter's cave and Will wakes up Lyra with the help of a servant and tries to escape, accidentally shattering the knife. They manage to escape into another world with two dragonfly kinda creatures called Gallivespains and Iorek repairs the knife while giving will a cryptic warning. They (minus Iorek) travel to the world of the dead to find Rodger and have to leave their daemons behind. Will all of a sudden kinda conjures one when he's in the boat with Lyra. It's painful. The harpies attack them before they find the kids and on their way back they strike a deal with the harpies. The harpies are nourished by truth but hate lies and they will escort the newly dead through the underworld in exchange for their stories. When the dead are lead through they dissolve because they are reunited with the universe (and by extension their daemon) 
 Mrs Coulter who has been flip flopping as much as our president elect and with about as much integrity now allies herself with Asriel and Metraton the guy who has been the acting authority while keeping the real authority in a cage attacks Mrs Coulter and Asriel. All three fall into an abyss and die. Will and Lyra release the Authority from his crystal prison and he resolves into the atmosphere, seemingly with relief. 
 So they find Mary who says she stopped being a nun so she could hard core make out and grind. Will and Lyra decide to do the same. Apparently the American version is censored. I guess this is the way Lyra became Eve? I'm still really unclear on this part but it's the only time Mary and Lyra communicate in this book and Mary I guess was the serpent who told Lyra of how awesome sex is and so Lyra was like hey okay i'm going to give it a shot. I dunno folks. 
 We are then kinda told out of the blue that instead of an angel getting its wings everytime there is a bell a specter gets it's goulish nature every time will uses the knife. I guess it's because dust escapes and forms? But we also learned earlier that angels are made from dust too so I'm not really sure why one is good the other other bad. Maybe it's a bit like people. 
 Will and Lyra have to return to their own worlds because they'll die in the others. (Not really sure why John Perry made it so long) They make this "same time next year" type promise where they'll go to a bench in their respective oxfords and think of each other. Will and Mary return they break the knife and Lyra returns to Jordan college. She decides to study alethiometry after considering living with the bear of the witches. Her main life goal however is to rebuild the kingdom of heaven.

 Sermon quotes on grace and kingdom of God in this world.

Ever seen the third movie of the matrix? Ruined the entire series in my humble opinion. Well, this book offered the same favor as the final book in His Dark Materials series. A real stinker.
