book_b.title: Soundless
book_b.user_review:
Actual rating: 3.5/5 
 "Soundless" focuses on the life of a village at the top of a mountain where every inhabitant has been deaf for ages. No one can go up and no one can go down. They don't have any contact with the outside except for a township at the base, who sends up food through a zip line as long as they send down the metals they mine. The story picks up when the main character, Fei, starts getting her hearing back and people are going blind. Since the miners can provide less metals, Fei is the only one that can save her village from starvation and death. 
 Reading the premise you wouldn't classify this book as a fantasy novel, but rather as a dystopian. This book definitely is a fantasy novel because the author throws in a magic element at the end of the book which conveniently helps saving the situation. However, I don't agree with people that say this fantasy element was sudden and unexpected. The "thingy" is hinted at throughout the book, as slight as it may be, and I enjoyed the way things turned out. 
 The main character is a heroine, although she isn't a rebel. She accepts her condition and she accepts the organisation of the society she lives in, as unfair as it may be. There aren't many other characters that are fairly important to the plot, and the few we meet aren't as well characterised as I wished. 
 That is due to the rush Richelle Mead seems to have been in while writing the book. The plot could have been developed in a better way, and had she spent more time on it, it could have been a very nice fantasy novel with interesting plot twists. All the wasted potential left a bittersweet taste in my mouth. This is the reason why I can't rate this book more than 3.5/5 stars. 
 What I really liked is the romance Fei is involved in. It's not the main thing in the book, but it's nice and heart-warming.

sample_reviews.review_text:
While this was an easy and enjoyable read, for the bigger part, I can't give this more than 2,5 stars total. 
 Mead's world building is completely non-existent (I mean seriously, where's the background story?) there's little to no action and whatever action there is, isn't very exciting. Oh and it's only within the last 20 pages that the mythical creatures alluded to in the beginning of the book appear to make a far too convenient ending for this story... 
 As quick as I was able to go through this book, and as much as I liked the concept of deafness, I was a little disappointed.

So, with this book came the moment I fully accepted that for me Richelle's writing has gone from mindblowingly good to frustratingly bland. 
 I was epically disappointed in the last three books of the Bloodlines series, because I felt that both the characters suddenly gave up their unique personalities and became just another generic lovestruck couple from a poorly edited romance book. But I still had some hope that if I read something non-Adrian-and-Sydney related from Richelle I would let go of the bad memories and go back to worshipping her writing. 
 Unfortunately, this book is the epitome of bad characterization. I wasn't even a chapter in when I knew I would not care for the protagonist and her robotic personality. The male lead was just as bad, and as a couple they did even less for me than they did individually. With every new supporting character or "twist" to the story, I just felt more and more that if I were to change the names and locations this would pretty much end up being the exact same story of every cliched "adventure" you have ever read. 
 Given that this is a standalone novel, another major problem is that the plot was not giver enough room to unfold; in some instances you read about rather meaningless things for a while, but when the actual plot came around, a ton of things just went down in two pages worth of space. 
 The social structure and "rules" of this dystopian society didn't feel well established and never managed to pull me in, the way they did in the Hunger Games for example; you are supposed to feel horrified and to root for the heroes trying to change things, but I just rooted for this book to finally be over instead. 
 To add to that failure of worldbuilding, I feel sort of insulted as a reader when Richelle just pulled a random deus ex machina move out of a completely different genre than the one I had been reading about up to that point. And never bothered to explain shit about it. 
 I will probably be a sucker and give her another chance by reading her new series, but I feel that if someone wants to understand the hype that surrounds her writing, they better stick to the Vampire Academy and adult book series and form an opinion based on them, instead of anything she has written lately.

This one unfortunately, whilst the concept was unique and intriguing, didn't live up to its full potential. There was practically no world building or dimension. Being 250+ pages, there was plenty of room to flesh things out and paint a more vivid picture of the story world, but for the most part it just wasn't there. 
 I will say that I love Richelle's writing, and her books are such a breeze to read. I just wish there had been more of the story and world to enjoy.

My feelings towards 'Soundless' are very mixed even 3 weeks after reading it. It has so many flaws that I still don't know if I even enjoyed it or not. The plot was interesting enough and the characters were pretty average and typical for YA but overall I felt it was quite badly written, which I didn't really understand as I've read other Mead books in the past that were written decently. 
 I think my main problem overall was the world-building; supposedly inspired by Chinese mythology, besides the Chinese sounding names nothing about 'Soundless' struck me as being heavily inspired by China. The random inclusion of supernatural creatures at the end was also quite jarring as up until that point the book hadn't given any real hint of being that sort of fantasy novel. 
 So yeah, very mixed feelings but I suppose I enjoyed it enough for it to be at least a 3 star read. 
 3 / 5

what can I say .... 2 Stars ... it was just OK, I think I had like 50 pages left and someone asked me what I thought of it and all I could say was that it was ok, I wasn't invested in any of the characters yet and I just had a few pages left. Kinda a disappointment from one of my favorite authors

Not strong writing, wish this had started off as strong as The Vampire Academy series. Nothing interesting, nothing different, nothing new. Got through two chapters, it just wasn't something I wanted to read when I have so little time to read.

Really interesting read. Has some seriously unique elements to it with a world I personally would not have been bold enough to venture into as a writer. The story is well-paced and the characters are compelling. It's also a quick read so I'd certainly recommend it to anyone looking for a short, entertaining read.

I try to read the Vampire Academy series at least once a year because it was one of my first (and favorite) YA series. I've also enjoyed the spin-off Bloodlines although I still have to read the last two books. Needless to say, I had high hopes for SOUNDLESS. Sadly, they were not entirely met. 
 This one has a much different feel than VA and Bloodlines had, and I think that was due to the author really branching out and trying new things. Everyone is deaf in this novel and there is technically no dialogue (spoken, at least). People communicate in sign language and I applaud the author for taking on such a challenging task. However, I do have to say that this did lead to some pacing issues, as this book was full of paragraphs that dialogue usually breaks up. 
 SOUNDLESS seemed to be lacking development in both world-building, characterization, and plot, because I wish we had gotten more explanation to why things the way they were. This style of writing also contributed to some confusion in general. 
 I thought the characters not being able to speak verbally would allow the reader to get to know them on a deeper level but that did not happen. Because of this, I had trouble caring about Fei and the others, especially when it came to the romance which seemed to randomly intensify from bitterness. 
 Overall, I think SOUNDLESS lacked the complexity of what I have come to expect from Richelle Mead and it didn't deliver what I have come to expect from a fantasy book either, although the concept was intriguing and the reveal compelling.
It was ok.... A bit slow for me and you are left wanting more till almost the very end. I'm sure a lot of people will love it but for me it just took to long to answer anything.

I'm still finding it incredibly hard to believe that Richelle Mead wrote this book. 
 When this book was first announced, I was super excited about it. A Deaf community? Chinese folklore? A fantasy stand-alone by someone whose books I really enjoy? How could I not be excited? 
 But then the book came out and reviewers whose opinions I trust were giving it... less than favourable reviews. And still I decided to give it a shot. Because a) Richelle Mead and b) Tastes are subjective. Maybe this will be one of those books I love but they hate. 
 Aaaaaand this is why I gave up on blind optimism a looong time ago. 
 I mean, this book was so bad, that I don't think I can even give it a full review. I'm pretty sure the only reason I even finished it was because I was hoping it would get better. And even then, I skim-read after I hit 53%. That's it - hope. That was my only motivation. I wasn't even curious about the big mystery. 
 And on that note, here's the best review I can give you guys. 
 THE PREMISE: 
 Great on paper. Great in theory. In execution, not so much. But this is also a writing issue, so I'll get back to this. 
 THE PLOT: 
 Boring. They climbed down a mountain, discovered The Big Thing, and then climbed back up the mountain. There was also some junk about magical, flying, glittery kitties . More on this later. 
 THE CHARACTERS: 
 Again, boring. I've seen cardboard cereal boxes with more personality than these characters. Honestly, I don't even remember their names. And I remember shit, okay? That's, like, my thing. I remember stuff. And if I can't remember something as simple as the main characters' names, you know you have a problem. 
 THE WORLD-BUILDING: 
 Nonexistent. Pull up a map of the world. Close your eyes. Point to some random place on the map. Even if you point to a spot somewhere in the middle of the pacific ocean, it could still be the setting for this story. There was nothing remotely Chinese about this place, or the people in it. There was nothing Chinese about the culture. At one point the MC even walked around the school while sipping a cup of tea, and it seemed so... rude. Like, I've never seen anyone do that. And the only reason I even remember this was because I texted a friend to ask if I was crazy for finding that weird. 
 THE WRITING: 
 Flat. Boring. Monotonous. Tell-not-show. Boring. Dry. Boring. Did I say boring? When you write a book about Deaf people, you have the opportunity to go crazy with the other senses. Mead did none of that. Everything, from the MC's thoughts, to the movements and actions of the people around her, was so lifeless and robotic. There was almost no use of scent, and she barely scratched the surface with sight. I am not joking when I tell you that I can't believe Richelle Mead wrote this. I've seen 14 year old fanfic writers who've written more compelling, believable stories than this. 
 THE FANTASY: 
 Ridiculous. I mean, can you even call this fantasy? The whole thing with whats-her-face regaining her hearing was weak. There was just one or two breadcrumbs leading up the big reveal at the end. The entire fantasy element (the giant, glittery, flying kitty cats) was so random and dumb, it felt like it had just been tacked on to the end of the book at the last minute because the author couldn't think of anything else. 
 Bottom line? This book was an utter disappointment and a bloody waste of my time. I would not recommend it to anyone. If I could go back in time and stop myself from reading it, I would. Save myself from feeling as upset as I am right now. 
 Richelle Mead. What happened?

sample_reviews.review_text: I usually love Laura Lippmann's books. This one didn't work well for me for two reasons: I did not find myself able to develop sympathy for the protagonist, and I found the ending too contrived and almost by-the-numbers in execution. The protagonist is a single mother who is also a madam running her prostitution ring from her home in an upscale suburban neighbourhood. Given that Lippmann has written many novels with characters who are not automatically sympathetic, I'd expect that she could create someone whose life choices and outlook would be compelling, but from the start of the book, she just left me cold. Usually, I tear through mysteries, but I wasn't invested enough in this character to reach for the book very often. Lippmann is as always a competent writer, but this one doesn't work for me.
I have loved so many Laura Lippman books, so it makes me pretty sad that she's been phoning it in these last two times. Pick up the pace, lippman!

Got through disc 3 of this on CD and just didn't have any desire to start disc 4. I have really enjoyed the other Lippman books I've read, but this one is just not interesting enough for me. I need more bite and intrigue and action.

This book is kind of difficult to categorize. I enjoyed the read and Lippman's writing is always eloquent, but I kept wondering what kind of a story it was. I had a hard time sympathizing with the character of a modern madam, and the suspense element didn't come into play until the last half of the book. I enjoy Laura Lippman's books enough that I will always read them, but this was not my favorite. I miss her mystery series.

This was a waste of time! I listened to the audio at work and that is the only reason I finished this one! It was more like a bad first draft. It jumped all over the place. I didn't feel anything for any of the characters.

"SUBURBAN MADAM DEAD IN APPARENT SUICIDE." 
 With this startling opening line, we are plunged into the world of Heloise. A world of secrets, fear, a son to protect, and a long history that led to this place in her life. 
 Once upon a time she was Helen with a "nothing face." Or so that's what her father told her. His verbal abuse set her up for a whole chain of events leading to this moment, this life. 
 Narrated in alternate chapters in the voices of "Heloise" and "Helen," "And When She Was Good: A Novel" held my interest from the first page to the end. Just when I thought I knew what would happen next, Lippman would surprise me. 
 How can one feel such a strong connection to a character like Helen/Heloise? Certainly many might argue that Helen made wrong choices and kept making them until it was too late. But is there a chance for someone like Heloise to redeem herself? Can we feel for her plight? 
 I certainly did, because the author reveals the inner thoughts of a woman who, like all women, has felt the pain of betrayal and the insecurity of not belonging. A woman who feels the need to be in control when life doesn't often offer the opportunity to control things. 
 This was definitely a story about finding oneself and learning from the past. It's a story about forgiveness and second chances. It is unforgettable, and thus earned five stars from me.

Lippman presents an interesting story about a "madam" and how she became a madam. The story does not go into vivid description of the murder scenes, or into Helen/Heloise's fall from grace. The story follows Helen's life in all the sadness and triumph. The story misses the depth of degradation and hopelessness that is shown in the books of Tess Gerritsen. Lippmann presents a Technicolor movie version minus the grit.

I think Perrotta really wanted to write an "issue novel," but knew that he had to disguise it as being "really about the characters," which it wasn't. This was my first Perrotta book, but I got the same impression from this that I did the two movies of his I've seen: a story driven more by condescension than anything else.

The story unfolds...It sounds like such a cliche but that truly is the best way to describe this absorbing read. Perrota does an excellent job of reeling the reader in, slowly disclosing background information and details about the main characters, all the while allowing the story to be told. Perrota never hints at his own personal position on the controversial issues raised by this novel (i.e. educating high school students about abstinence, public prayer, Christianity.) Both of the main characters are deeply flawed so there is no clean cut division of good and evil. Instead, the players are wholly believable and human, the issues cloudy and multi-faceted. The story begins slowly, alternating its focus between Ruth and Tim. As the tempo picks up the passages about each character become increasingly brief, almost as though the two are pitted against each other in a boxing ring. Two caveats: First, Perrota is overly fond of the hyphen to the point where I found it distracted my reading of the novel. The second problem is that the story seems to end so abruptly. There is a terrific build-up, a crescendo, then bam! it's over. Huh? This is not to say that some of the loose ends weren't tied up. they were, it is just that the rapid ending did not jive with the style and pacing of the rest of the novel. Overall, engrossing and well-executed.

While the theme might be interesting, this book did not live up to my expectations. The changes the main characters underwent seemed rough and somewhat arbitrary, as if they were changing because the author wanted them to change for the purposes of the plot rather than through their own internal motivation. Tom Perrotta's writing style does nothing to rescue me from this plot-driven drivel. Don't get me wrong: this book has its moments; they are just few and far between. 
 The Abstinence Teacher begins by introducing us to Ruth, a divorced mom who's the sexual education teacher at the high school in this small, conservative town. She's under siege at school for wanting to teach safe sex instead of just abstinence. Meanwhile, she picks fights with her younger daughter's soccer coach, a born-again evangelical Christian, for leading the team in a prayer after a game. And she neglects her older daughter, which drives that daughter to seek meaning through--you guessed it--Christianity. Oh, and she wants to find a man. And she's friends with a gay couple. 
 I'm not making this up. 
 See, that's my problem with this novel: it's too contrived. I say too contrived because I realize that most novels, especially ones with overt thematic agendas like this one, need to be contrived to an extent. Perrotta has gone further than that, however, because he weaves sexuality into every aspect of the book and uses stereotypes like "the gay couple" to advance his theme. Others may not have a problem with this, but I found it awkward and artificial. 
 After getting to know Ruth, suddenly the book switches cameras to follow her daughter's soccer coach, Tim. Tim has problems: a former drug addict and reformed alcoholic, he credits Jesus with his salvation. Good so far--pretty believable. But he just can't shake Ruth from his mind, and eventually temptation rears its ugly head (heads?), forcing him to take advice from the spirited evangelical pastor of their local uber-conservative church. 
 Pastor Dennis is a great character, actually. Perrotta makes it clear that Dennis has a radical agenda on his mind and isn't above using radical means to advance it. It also helps set Pastor Dennis up as the real antagonist, thus allowing us to sympathize with Tim and his struggle to discern some sort of "truth" from the mess of life. 
 We experience a major portion, if not the majority of the book, following Tim's perspective before jumping back to Ruth, and then ultimately interspersing Ruth- and Tim-centric chapters. This works well, allowing us to see how each perceives the other and how each interprets shared experiences. 
 Unfortunately, Perrotta has certain other idiosyncrasies that made it hard for me to enjoy his writing. He has a tendency to introduce every single minor character with an appositive that sums them up in a trite little stereotype. I started noticing this about halfway through, and then it annoyed me for the rest of the book. Sometimes minor characters are just minor characters, Tom. We don't need to know about their favourite sexual positions.... 
 Alas, it's an interesting concept, and one that is apparently relevant in contemporary American society. Yet I just could not enjoy it. I suspect, however, that others may like the book for the very reason I disliked it, so your mileage may vary.

This book would have received five stars if there had been just one more chapter in it. I felt that Perrotta ended the book in a very weird place. Yes, it is right at that precipice where so many different things could happen, but instead of feeling postmodern in that regard, it just feels unfinished. So, so close to being a really amazing book.

In many ways, I feel like the last bookseller in the country to read this book, but now that I have, I must add my voice to those that have given this beautiful book such a glowing reception. 
 Set in Jackson, Mississippi in the early 1960s, The Help gives voice to a group of women from both very similar yet different backgrounds and experience, who find themselves drawn together in a combined effort to shine light on something that affects them all. 
 The world in which The Help is set seems very far removed from the world we now live in, and in many ways, thankfully it is. The world in which we now live does not have the same strict lines of division concerning race, class and so forth, and that is truly a good thing. However, in the time that has passed it seems we have forgotten how far we have come in a relatively short time. Not to mention how hard the journey was for so many, and what they risked to pave the way for those who would follow. 
 The Help introduces us to wise, regal and caring Aibileen, a woman who has raised seventeen white children- the most recent one after losing her own beloved son to a tragic accident. Aibileen is alone in the world, except for the children under her charge, and her best friend, Minny. Although they share a close friendship, Minny and Aibileen are very different. Aibileen is quietly resolute, choosing to teach the children in her charge a different way of seeing the world while she suffers the indignities of a bigoted society. Minny, on the other hand is daring and outspoken in her opinion towards her white employers. When we meet her, she is on the brink of losing yet another job due to her inability to appear in any way subservient to her employer's daughter. When that same daughter uses her influence to ensure Minny is unable to get another position, Minny exacts revenge on this woman in a manner so daring and outrageous (while at the same time so comically just) that you can't help but cheer at her audacity. Ironically, for all her flash and fire, Minny lives in fear of how her husband Leroy will react to her losing another job. In fact, contrary to her outwardly bold nature, Leroy seems to be the one thing Minny truly fears. 
 The woman who, in her own unwitting way, brings Minny, Aibileen and eventually many others together is young Eugenia, or Skeeter, as everyone knows her. Skeeter has returned home from college, with a degree and a desire to write professionally- but to her mother's consternation, without a husband. The person Skeeter is most looking forward to seeing is Constantine, the woman who raised her in much the same way that Aibileen raised her 'children'. However, when she arrives home, she finds that Constantine is gone. The fact that Constantine, who has been a source of continuity and support throughout Skeeter's life is gone without any word is unacceptable to her and she sets out to find the truth about what happened. 
 In the course of trying to resolve the mystery of Constantine's abrupt departure, Skeeter slowly befriends Aibileen, who is also her best friend Elizabeth's housekeeper. The more the friendship between Skeeter and Aibileen evolves, the more Skeeter sees the injustice and wrongdoing that her life-long friends see as perfectly acceptable behavior. When Skeeter asks Aibileen at one point if she wishes things could change, the seed of an idea is born. This idea evolves into a book documenting the stories of a collection of women who have served generations of white families. They have cooked, cleaned and tended to them. They have held their confidences, soothed them in time of illness, and raised their children when they were unwilling or unable. These women were treated like trusted confidants or with crass indifference and cruelty- sometimes both. 
 As Skeeter collects the stories of the women Aibileen brings to her, all of them becoming partners in this project, her view of the world she has always known is altered with almost brutal clarity, and she is forced to reevaluate whom she can and cannot trust. 
 In The Help, we see events both large and small in the context of how it affects the lives of these women. We see these women grow and trust one another regardless of their differences. We witness both their combined and individual strength. The Help chronicles both the amazing kindness and love that humans are capable of, as well as their careless and deliberate cruelty. Stockett does this with an amazingly deft hand, creating every character in the novel in fine multi-layered detail. Each story, from each woman's perspective, draws you in and holds you. You cheer for them, cry with them, and feel both their pain and joy. The Help is an unforgettable joy to read.

I want to say, right up front, that I hadn't planned to read this book because those of us who read the entire Twilight Saga already know that things don't turn out well for Bree Tanner. She played a very, very minor role in the book, Eclipse - I don't even think she appeared in more than 2 pages - so, why read something about a character I cared very little about and already knew the outcome of? 
 The first 50 pages seemed rather ho-hum to me, and I've decided that's because I began this book dreading the outcome. Once I wrapped my mind around reading this for the story as it related to Victoria's army of newborn vampires, I couldn't put it down. I'm not going to go into the plot, because frankly, if you've read Eclipse you won't need details, and if you haven't read Eclipse, you'll not understand what the point of this book is, and it would take way too long to explain. 
 What stands out most to me about Bree's story is how all of the newborns were manipulated. It made me think of charismatic leaders around the world -- political, religious, corporate or yes, even vampire -- and how much influence they have over the people who are dependent on them, because if you can convince someone or some group that they need you, that you're only looking out for their best interest and that life without you as their leader would be filled with pain and anguish, possibly even death... you'd have absolute control over them. 
 Such was the case with the newborn vampires, and when looking at them in this light - as people violently torn from humanity and forced into a new way of life which they nothing about - were literally newborns and dependent on someone else for their survival. I started wondering about the families who are missing them, what kind of people they would have been had they lived out their human lives. So what started out as an excited hype for me left me with a disappointment.
I can't make any headway on this. It's horrible. DNF

** spoiler alert ** 
 I had high hopes for this one and I was very disappointed. I was really hoping the book would start about Bree being human and how she meets Riley and so on. That didn't happen so right from the start I was disappointed but then I thought "okay maybe the rest will be better and she won't have a love interest."......WHY WAS A LOVE INTEREST NECESSARY?!? I don't understand! It seemed so rushed and pointless to me especially how it ends! I'm pretty sad that I didn't like this book very much. Like I said would've liked to know more about her when she was human and how she met Riley and how she felt after getting bitten. Yeah. 2 stars.

I was actually pleasantly surprised with this book. I was unsure how successful Stephenie Meyer would be, pursuing what seemed to me to be the story of one random vampire that died within five minutes of meeting Bella. But what I found was a lovable, independent young woman who was dealt the wrong cards, but still got to make a difference in the end. (To say a lot without spoilers.) 
 The story was smooth, and even though it was short, I was so enraptured in the world of Bree, that fact didn't matter. This book was worth picking up and reading. Especially because every book you buy donates one dollar to the Red Cross.
Sure to be enjoyed by Twilight fans, although there is very, very little of Bella and Edward in it.

I understand wanting to give readers thorough detail but there are ways of doing it that work and Meyer's tactics do not. The sections that are good were vivid and atmospheric, the same as the previous three but unfortunately the bad elements were not enough to save it from the series two star curse.

Argh I don't know what I was expecting from this book, but it couldn't have been much. I was still frustrated reading it. This newborn vampire girl is pretty much Bella but the only difference is she's a vampire and 15. She loves to read? She strays away from other people? I don't think Stephenie Meyer knows how to write new characters. It's as though since Twilight has become so popular, she can just do whatever and people will read it; she doesn't need to put too much effort into it. I also felt like I was reading an amalgamation of people's posts on "My Life is Average" with all the talk of BFFs and ninjas; perhaps it's just because I don't fit that demographic. Overall, I think this was just an obvious attempt to make more money before the Eclipse movie came out.

sample_reviews.review_text:
4.5 wonderful stars... 
 Okay. So I finally broke down and read it. 
 Generally, I'm not a big fan of girl drooling over cute guy w/bad attitude books. But surprisingly, Obsidian turned out to be quite the opposite. And then a funny thing happened...I found myself reading it in one sitting. I mean, I put everything aside for the next six hours and 
 plowed through Ms. Armentrouts charming tale of an alien guy and his human girlfriend. This is something that's hard for me to do given my super cluttered lifestyle. 
 Things I adored: there were no sparkly vampires. No girl trying to commit 
 suicide because drool-worthy cute guy acted like a douche. There were no epic 
 battles with names I couldn't pronounce. The single mother in the book wasn't portrayed as sex crazed, drunk, or dumb. She had a profession and her daughter was the first priority. It was quite simply, a quick and fun read. 
 Things I didn't adore. There really was only one...Daemon. He was a jerk for so long that 
 when he started to reveal some of his motivations for being a douche that I had to work hard 
 to feel for him the way Katy did. I was about ready to start getting my 3.5 wings ready 
 until Katy held her ground against this guy. Go Katy! 
 There were some epic get-even scenes in here, I thought. Without getting spoilery, there's this one cafeteria scene that you will remember and re-read again and again. I did. I LOVE that Katy was so strong. But she was also soft at just the right moments. 
 All in all this was a very good read. I happily give it 4.5 wings in hopes that Daemon will work harder and charm me even more in the next installment...Onyx. From what I've seen of the reviews I have no doubt that he will. I'd recommend this one to paranormal romance lovers who enjoy fast, fun reads.

I want to believe. 
 I really do. Just following the news these days is enough to make one lose faith in humanity. I really want to believe that there is something out there, god, gods, whatever. Aliens. ANYTHING. I want to feel like there are other creatures out there in this vast universe of ours, with greater knowledge, greater intelligence, and maybe one day they'll grace us with their presence and bestow on us their superior intellect. 
 I certainly hope those future aliens are more intelligent than the dumb-as-dirt creatures in Obsidian. 
 Seriously, how stupid can you get? I've never been on the run, I've never had to hide, but if there's some things I've gleaned, it's how NOT to stick out like a sore freaking thumb. 
 First, you find a HUGE goddamn city, like San Francisco, where nobody will even blink if you step out into the street in rainbow-colored pantyhose and an accompanying beard. You do not find a backwoods town where it's likely you're considered outsiders if your grandparents were born the next town over. 
 Secondly, you BLEND IN. 2 pairs of triplets move into town within days of each other? That is not blending in. Supernatural beauty? Not blending in. Names like Daemon? NO. NOT BLENDING IN. 
 Thirdly, you FIT IN. You make friends, you're friendly to people. You do not act like everyone is your enemy and warn off the friendly girl next door just because she wants to know where the closest store is. 
 I just don't understand how this book got so many positive reviews. I get that this is fantasy/sci-fi YA fiction, but there's gotta be a limit to willing suspension of disbelief. For me, there's very little to like about this book. The heroine is all right, but I kind of rolled my eyes at the "I'm a BOOK BLOGGER. I'M SO HIPSTER. I'M A ZOOEY DESCHANEL GEEK GIRL" bit. That's how she seemed to me. She's a fair bit more intelligent than some of the YA fiction heroines I've read, but considering there exists Luce/Bella/etc...that's not saying much. The spaghetti scene was kick-ass, though. 
 I found Daemon to be an enormous asshat for most of the novel. He's hot, sure, but that's it. He's such an unbelievable jerk, and I found Dee to be like the patient wife of an abusive husband, sniveling and simpering and constantly making excuses for her brother's rude, boorish, borderline abusive behavior. 
 And Ms. Armentrout, enough with the 100000x random alien references/foreshadowing in the book already. It's called subtlety.

I LOVE IT SO SO MUCH!! 
 one of my favorite books :)) this is great! and hilarious.

This book is so awesome! I love the chemistry between Daemon and Katy is so damn hot. I can't help but really compare some parts of this novel with twilight. But well i love both books so it doesn't matter. Overall this is a must read book, definitely!! Love it so so much ~ I can't wait to read the rest of the series. 5 stars on this first book!

4.5 stars 
 Mon avis sur le blog: http://read-listen-feel.skyrock.com/ 
 Sincerement, je ne tiens meme plus le compte du nombre de livres que j'ai lu de J. Lynn ou Jennifer L. Armentrout depuis le debut de l'annee 2014. Peu importe le style de roman, je suis toujours en admiration devant son style d'ecriture et c'est pour cette raison que je voulais commencer cette serie. En plus, elle sortira en VF cet automne! Je suis toujours heureuse de voir que le livre d'un auteur que j'adore sera lu par un plus grand nombre de personnes. 
 Mais parlons-en de ce livre! Il est evidemment inutile de vous dire que j'ai adore. Je n'avais jamais lu de livres sur des aliens et c'est hyper interessant comme sujet. Ca change des histoires de vampires, loup-garous, anges et compagnie. Evidemment, on a droit au scenario classique YA avec un bad boy sexy et la jeune fille fragile qui deviendra irremediablement forte et independante au fil de l'histoire. Si, de votre cote, vous vous en etes lasse, ce livre n'est peut-etre pas pour vous. Sinon, jetez-vous dessus. Le concept est tres intriguant. 
 L'heroine, Katy, est la plus merveilleuse des jeunes femmes dans tous les livres reunis. C'est une accro des livres et elle possede un blog, fait des videos IMM. Tout ce qu'on peut imaginer. Elle est juste captivante, non? Non?!? Dans tous les cas, c'est un personnage auquel nous pouvons tous nous identifier et je crois que JLA a voulu faire un petit clin d'oeil a ses lecteurs. Je ne l'en aime que plus pour cette raison. 
 Quant a Daemon, on ne peut faire autrement que de tomber sous son charme. La premier fois qu'on le voit, on se dit: "Mais il se prend pour qui?!" Il est la, inebranlable, croyant etre le centre de l'univers. Mais au fil de l'histoire, on le decouvre de plus en plus. Malgre ses (frequentes) sautes d'humeur, Daemon est tres attachant et on ne peut que l'aimer. Je trouve tres drole que ce soit grace a sa soeur que Katy apprend a connaitre Daemon. Et elle a recours a des techniques assez particulieres. 
 Ce qui m'amene a parler de Dee. C'est la soeur jumelle de Daemon. Alors que son frere est maussade, Dee est une vraie petite boule d'energie. Elle a une de ces joies de vivre contagieuse. Elle est drole et jolie, mais elle est aussi tres seule dans son petit monde. C'est pour cette raison qu'elle va s'attacher immediatement a Katy. Comme elle est nouvelle en ville, elle n'a pas entendu parler de toutes les histoires concernant la famille de Dee et Daemon et lorsque ca arrive, il est deja trop tard : Dee et Katy sont inseparables. 
 La relation entre Katy et Daemon est assez particuliere puisque c'est la que les choses prennent une tournure inattendue. Ils se detestent! Vous vous souvenez lorsque j'ai dit que Katy n'etait qu'une jeune fille fragile? Mon erreur... Elle peut resister au charme de Daemon ET passer une journee complete sans succomber a la tentation de l'etrangler. Ce qui fait d'elle une fille incroyablement forte. C'est la ou la relation amoureuse classique n'est plus. 
 En somme, je suis totalement tombee sous le charme de cette histoire. Elle a tout pour plaire : une heroine bad ass, un bad boy sexy et sensible, une intrigue intrigante (est-ce que j'ai le droit de dire ca...?), de l'action a revendre et des ALIENS !!! Je vous conseille cette lecture x1000. Ca se lit tout seul et on veut immediatement connaitre la suite puisqu'on nous laisse sur une fin renversante. Katy sera definitivement plus bad ass dans le deuxieme tome. C'est definitivement un must read.

Read my interview with Jennifer L. Armentrout HERE. 
 Read my full review at The Fairytale Nerd. 
 LOVE: 
 I was just on the first chapter and I was already laughing the life out of me. Only Jennifer Armentrout can do that. This book was unbelievably addicting. Usually, I finish a book in one day. I have other things to do that I consider more important. But I finished this book in 5 hours straight. I just could not let go of it. At that time, Daemon and Katy became the center of my world. Their banter is just so funny and witty and sarcastic, that I just can't get enough. And hours after I finished the book, I find myself thinking (or swooning, even) about a certain alien with hypnotic green eyes. There's not much kissing in this book - a few scenes. But the sexual tension between the main characters is undeniable. Their chemistry is sizzling even when they are fighting and shouting at each other. I also love the fact that Daemon is very protective of Dee (Daemon's sister). Dee is the only one he has in his life, and he would gladly give up his life to protect her. I love Dee too! She's friendly and bubbly, and it's not a surprise that she instantly became Katy's best friend. I also love the whole "alien marking" thing, and something new to me and I want to know more about it. 
 NO LOVE: 
 Daemon - that obnoxious a$$hole. I hated him most of the time. He was mean to Katy. But then again, I love him for it. Am I confusing you now? 
 FAVORITE CHARACTER: 
 My letter to the hottest alien on earth: Dear Daemon, Oh Daemon! I don't know what I feel about you. Sometimes I dislike you, sometimes I like you. But most of the time I despise you. But then you smile your sexy smile and you walk around half naked and let me ogle at your sculpted body, and my anger just... fades away. You charm me with sarcasm. You protect me with your life.You exhaust me, and I love you for it. I'm yours. Always and forever, JoAnne 
 MUSINGS: 
 This is the first alien book I have ever read. (Nope, I haven't read I Am Number Four, and I have no plans on picking it up.) This book changed my notion that aliens cannot be sexy. In fact, they can be the sexiest creatures in the YA book world, and Daemon is on top of this "sexy" list.

DNF @ 50% 
 Half audiobook/half ARC. 
 I JUST COULDN'T DO IT ANYMORE, OKAY. 
 Originally, I started reading this book around mid-November, when the lovely ladies at Abrams Children sent me an ARC to read and review. Due to work and other adult life things, I had to put it down around the 100 page mark, and tried to return to it today. 
 Don't kid yourself. If I'd been enjoying this book, I wouldn't have sacrificed precious reading time in the name of work. But I did, because I was bored, and I thought I just wasn't in the mood for it, and it was me, not the book, etcetera. 
 When I saw the audiobook on Audible today, I couldn't help myself: I downloaded it. And after listening for a good eight hours or so, I just couldn't do it anymore. 
 RoseBlood, it's you. Not me. Sorry, buddy. 
 In summary: Rune is a special snowflake with a special past (she could hum opera when she was a toddler, kids), going to a special super goff school, has special dreams about a special boy she's pretty sure is dead, and every time she sings, it almost kills her. 
 EVERYTHING about this book revolves around the characters being as flat as pancakes, with only one person being even remotely interesting, and the interest I had was quickly dashed in the first four hours of the audiobook. Thorn is a thorn in this book's side. He is drowning in his own angst, in his own special-ness, fancying himself in love with Rune because their dreams are CONNECTED. They've known each other their whole lives because they dream of each other. Of course, he lived a terrible life as a child (which I found incredibly unbelievable due to the fact he was born in the modern century and not, you know, the 1800s) and now, to pay his 'father' back for all the kindness, he needs to... trap Rune? Kill her? Or something. I'm not too sure. I think I stopped listening after the 30% mark. 
 This is the first negative review I've written in over a year, and although writing negative reviews used to be cathartic, I literally do not feel a thing towards this novel except for apathy and boredom. I can't deal with how goth RoseBlood Academy is. 
 Let's talk about that for a second, shall we? 
 Rune is sent to RoseBlood to work on her music and, one day hopefully, become some sort of musical start. Rune, however, is less than ecstatic about this, which made me roll my eyes. Bad, considering we're only five pages in at this point. 
 Why on earth, out of all the romantic, gothic, dark names provided by literature, is the academy called RoseBlood? Why? Why?! I don't get it. Is it supposed to be symbolic? Because at the beginning of the book, Rune is describing a painting she has at home about roses that bleed or something, and then later on she's given a bouquet of bleeding roses, so it has to be symbolic, right? But it's still stupid. I don't get it. Why not call it THIS IS WHERE YOU COME TO DIE Academy? 
 I also don't understand how things work at the academy. So they have class in the morning then... chores in the afternoon? WHY? If you're paying thousands of PSPSPS to send your kid to an academy called RoseBlood, don't you want your kid to learn something except for how much soap to put in the dishwasher? I mean, it's cool that they're learning real life things they'll need to know as adults, but in that case teach them about taxes and how to not be a dick! 
 Speaking of, of course we have the Mean Girls clique who torment Rune left, right and centre and even though I stopped listening at this point, I'm pretty sure one of the Mean Girls is in love with her twin brother or something and constantly try to sabotage her chances, because how else are we going to feel all the feels for her? Spoiler: I felt nothing. 
 My review is all over the place. I apologize. I can't even turn my brain on long enough to write this thing because I'm that bored. I'm so bored I'm practically asleep. 
 The only Phantom of the Opera-ish thing this book has is that the original phantom is still lurking around. That's it. Oh, and he signs his name as "OG" which, to my disbelief, does not stand for Original Gangster, or even Oppa Gangnam-style (thanks, Natalie!) but for "Opera Ghost." Barf. 
 From what I've gathered: Rune likes wandering the gardens and feeling all emo-like and misunderstood; Thorn is a weirdo who peeks at girls (specifically Rune) through the air vents in her bedroom and tells her how they're "destined to be lovers"; Thorn and Rune have glowing fairy blob things that transfer from one to the other called heart chakras (what even?!); Eric the OG is very much just a backdrop so that Rune and Thorn can wile away the time talking about how much they are destined for things. And that's it. That's all I've got. 
 For now, I'm outie.

-POTENTIAL SPOILERS- 
 This was unexpected. While I knew I wouldn't consider this to be an amazing masterpiece, I did find parts of it to be unique and original. 
 I liked the heavy gothic atmosphere surrounding this book, as well as the ties to the original novel., like the stuff with the Persian and Christine. 
 I also really liked the side characters in this novel. I actually found them more interesting than the main characters, and wished I could just have a novel focusing on them. 
 Plus the writing in this book is really good! This author can write! Even people who don't like her novels have to at least admit that. 
 Aside from that, literally the first two hundred pages of this book were a huge slog to get through. They were just so boring, and nothing much happened in them. Plus the first few chapters were just major info-dumps. I don't mind info-dumps at the best of times, but this was just annoying. 
 Plus I hated the whole twist with the Phantom and Christine's baby. It just seemed....creepy and really out-of-place. It reminded me way too much of that terrible musical Love Never Dies, and the less we talk about that, the better. 
 Plus, why do people find that cover pretty? It looks weird to me, and misleading. When I first saw it, I got all excited because I thought it was a genderswapped retelling of Phantom of the Opera, which I'd be all for. But it's not. At least that model looks like the main character. 
 Overall, a fairly decent book that I was highly anticipated and was mildly disappointed by.
A Gif List of Thoughts and Feelings:

I read about 100 pages of this book before finally quitting. I couldn't get into it. I'm a huge Phantom of the Opera fan, so it really shouldn't have been that hard for me. But I felt like the (verb) tenses kept changing, and so many things were left unexplained. What exactly where the Phantom and his "son"? I realize if I had kept reading I might have gotten those answers, but the descriptions were just enough to be vague and leave more questions that I just didn't care if they got answered. Also it seemed as if they were some sort of vampire that needed to "feed" on a specific type of person or songstress but never explained how or what it would do or anything. I felt like there needed to be way more information given when it came to the Phantom and his son. 
 Also, it makes NO SENSE that Rune would ONLY have to sing female arias. When a song is written it doesn't have a gender. And the key can be changed to fit any voice type, male or female. So for the author to put forth that she only HAD to sing "female" arias just didn't sit well with me. 
 I wanted to like this book. I did. I wanted to fall in love with. But the truth was that I hated it.

It troubles me when authors fall back on racial/ ethnic stereotypes in an effort to show diversity. I won't even get into the offensiveness of the superstitious, mystical "gypsy" culture of the protagonist. We also have the single Hispanic character described as "the only one who's ever actually had to work for [her costly French boarding school tuition]. Working two jobs. Fundraisers. Babysitting. No inheritance to throw away like the rest of us." Of course the one Asian kid excels in science and his parents want him to become a doctor. 
 I might have been able to enjoy some of the nonsensical plot of this book had the author nor committed this common, unforgivable error. As it was, I only finished reading the book because it came in my Owlcrate box, and I can only justify that subscription if I read all of the books they send me. Too bad - this book could have been so much better.

sample_reviews.review_text: Jack Reacher is awesome. This book is a thrilling suspense novel.

I appreciate this is fiction, but it's so far beyond belief that it becomes stupid. And it's really rather dull. In fact for a thriller it's REALLY dull, with very little thrilling about it all. The second Reacher I've read, and I doubt they'll be a third.

The good, and there isn't much, includes the action sequences and the description of Reacher's tight squeeze, near death experience in the tunnels he must navigate to escape from a locked room. But that is it. 
 This second Jack Reacher novel was simply too full of holes and convenient circumstances and good luck in Jack Reacher's favor that by halfway through the book, I wanted it to be over. I don't mind if the hero is given a second chance by the bad guy to make a comeback, (you know, the bad guy talks too much about his plans and rather than kill the protagonist he elects to torture him, but the hero escapes...that kind of jazz) but Reacher is captured, wreaks havoc upon his captors, is given a couple chances to say he is sorry, kills some more bad guys, is told to play nice, destroys munitions and supplies, is released into the wild (yeah, RELEASED) so then he can come back and put the bad guys down. WHAT? The actions of this paramilitary group that wants to become independent of the USA are so asinine and backwards that they deserve their own country...in a mental institution. Seriously, who allows this outsider, Reacher, to do what he does then hands him a sniper rifle to show what he can do, then, upon realizing how deadly accurate he is, basically lets him go. I haven't even mentioned the incredible luck he has in figuring out the bad guys' plan based on a couple things Mr. HeadBadGuy, a 400 pound fat ass by the way, has said. With time ticking against him, Reacher correctly guesses which way the bomb was headed on a hunch. Just too unbelievable for me.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Synopsis: "Mary Shelley began writing Frankenstein when she was only eighteen. At once a Gothic thriller, a passionate romance, and a cautionary tale about the dangers of science, Frankenstein tells the story of committed science student Victor Frankenstein. Obsessed with discovering the cause of generation and life and bestowing animation upon lifeless matter, Frankenstein assembles a human being from stolen body parts but; upon bringing it to life, he recoils in horror at the creature's hideousness. Tormented by isolation and loneliness, the once-innocent creature turns to evil and unleashes a campaign of murderous revenge against his creator, Frankenstein. 
 Frankenstein, an instant bestseller and an important ancestor of both the horror and science fiction genres, not only tells a terrifying story, but also raises profound, disturbing questions about the very nature of life and the place of humankind within the cosmos: What does it mean to be human? What responsibilities do we have to each other? How far can we go in tampering with Nature? In our age, filled with news of organ donation genetic engineering, and bio-terrorism, these questions are more relevant than ever." 
 My Review: I ranked this as my top favorite book after reading it in high school. It was assigned reading and once starting it I could not put it down (I snuck it into my calculus class). It has been some time since I last read it and have considered other books might take the top spot. So this month I decided to re-read it but got the audio version instead. There is now no doubt what so ever that this book will remain my #1 favorite book, especially after listening to the audio book. I don't feel that this is a horror book, to me it is beautiful and an emotional drama. I can't help but become teary eyed and choked up when the creature confronts his creator in the mountains and I must admit that I am totally on the creature's side. This is a classic and really one that everyone should at least try and it could become an instant and forever favorite!
See my full review at hlgibsonauthor.com

I HATE THIS. There I said it. I hate Frankenstein with a passion. I read a hundred pages of this book but it was just SO BORING I couldn't finish it. I only read it because I heard it was better than Dracula and I adored Dracula. This one however... It is boring, it is awful, I detested the writing style, there was no action, the characters had extremely long conversations talking in an unrealistic way, why the fuck is this a classic? I'm glad I've read Frankenstein but goodness gracious such a burden it was. I cannot believe this edition was under 300 pages but felt way much longer. 
 Wouldn't it have been much more uncomplicated to instead write an essay about wrong and right, about not standing above God and other morally-aimed subjects? At least it was better than Dracula.
This has to be the most tedious thing I have ever read in my life.

Frankenstein was published the same year as Jane Austen's last novel Persuasion. What a contrast between the rule-bound manner in which Austen's characters work toward their goals, making the best of the roles that society has assigned them, and the overwrought way in which Shelley's characters agonize over the vicissitudes of fate, seeming almost to believe that they have no control over their actions. 
 How can I give such a low score to a classic? I found it hard to immerse myself in the story with a number of unrealistic elements. I don't mean the idea of Victor Frankenstein creating life -- that's the premise that I must accept as the basis of the story. Nor do I mean the unlikely coincidences of repeatedly meeting the right (or wrong) person at the right (or wrong) time -- that's to be expected in early 19th century fiction. Nor even that we're expected to believe the characters would orally relate such absurdly lengthy and detailed accounts, and that Capt Walton would write them down verbatim in what must have been very thick letters to his sister -- that's also a convention of literature of the time. 
 What keeps me from getting involved in the story is how the more mundane things that happen don't seem as though the author quite thought them through. How does the creature learn to read and write peering through a gap in a wall for hours each day, for months on end, with nobody suspecting he is there? Even in ideal conditions, how can he learn enough in these months to read Paradise Lost? Why would the creature scratch lengthy, complete sentences on a rock instead of something shorter and more like a telegram? 
 Frankenstein's travels to far-flung locations for various reasons remind me of a 1980s James Bond movie.

Very interesting and disturbing. I think it is amazing but also telling that Mary Shelley was about 18 when she first wrote it. It reminded me of Wuthering Heights with its over-the-top angst and drama, but still I liked it. The questions that came up over a creator's responsibility to his creations as well as the references to Adam and Eve and the theme of choice, make for a great discussion. I'm a happy-ending sort of gal, so I'll probably never read it again, but I'm glad I did.

Heartbreakingly sad and very surprising. 
 As well known as the idea of Frankenstein is, I was surprised to learn that I really had no idea what the story was, and it was beautiful and haunting and very, very sad. The monster was so human and so misunderstood. I was amazed the entire time of Mary Shelley's poetic words and just her mind in general.

This will go down in history as one of the very few books I have ever rage quit. Victor is just too whiny of a narrator to hold my attention or keep patience with. My first clue that I would end up disliking this book was that there is no version of the movie I have come close to liking, unless you count Young Frankenstein, which, lets face it, is a spoof, which is probably why I do love that movie. I am just glad that my rage-quitting the book did not evoke a bad grade on the report I had to write on it.

reference_books.title: The Egypt Game (Game, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
A slightly dated tale of kids who invent a harmless game, the Egypt Game in the backlot of an urban store. Their neighborhood reels from a kidnap-murder, and the kids game is interrupted for a short while. In the end, an adult they mistrust the most turns out to be the one who saves them. 
 Wonderful description of the neighborhood, really captures the look, the feel, and the attitudes of the people in it. The kidnapping and child predator were startling when this was first published, and makes for good classroom discussions today.

book_a.title: Al Capone Does My Shirts (Al Capone at Alcatraz, #1)
book_a.user_review: Family and friendships and innocent schemes, taking place at 1935 Alcatraz, a very compelling setting. Moose is 12 and moves to Alcatraz island with his family when his dad takes a job at the prison. He and the other kids at school are fascinated by stories of the prison's most famous con, Al Capone. The best part of this story for me was how Moose cares for his sister Natalie who is autistic--actually, the whole plot is about perceiving differently, giving insights into "Natalie's world" from Moose's view. Great read.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Alcatraz in the 1930s is the setting here, but the story is more about living with a sister who has autism and a mother who has a daughter with autism. More questions are asked than answered and the depth and humanity of the characters are developed at the expense of preaching any deep moral or wrapping the story up in a tidy bundle at the end. 
 Highly recommended for anyone who likes stories with believable characters and is OK with loose ends being left to dangle.
I read this with my son when he was around 10. It is a favorite of his and a good read for kids--especially read aloud with a parent as we did.

4/5 I really don't know why I bought this book. There are just times when you buy enter a bookstore and go out with a book in hand not knowing what happened inside and why you have that book on hand. 
 The best reason that I can think of why I bought the book is because it has an appealing title. "Al Capone Does My Shirts", how appealing is that with the map of Alcatraz on the cover plus it has the Newberry Honor seal too. Well, I guess those thing got me buying this book. 
 I am glad I did. 
 Alcatraz Island is located in the San Francisco Bay, 1.5 miles offshore from San Francisco, California. It is where the Alcatraz prison is located where the most notorious and hardened of criminals are imprisoned. The author added map of Alcatraz inside the book for the readers to better visualize the setting. 
 Alphonse Gabriel "Al" Capone was an American gangster known for his brutal acts of violence. He was imprisoned in Alcatraz island during the period that Moose's family lived there. 
 The novel is a work of fiction but it is historically correct. 
 The books follows the story of a 12-year old boy named Matthew "Moose" Flanagan who lived with his family (along with 60 other families where one or two of the heads of the family work in the prison) on Alcatraz in the 1930s. This was his adventure to stay out of trouble and be wary with the watchful eye of the warden. This was Moose's story learning the ropes and keeping up with the changes made by their transfer to Alcatraz island. This was also Moose's family's story keeping up with the changes around them and how they deal with it. 
 Moose live's with his father, who works two jobs (as prison guard and electrician) at the island to keep with the family's financial dealings and whom Moose share the love of baseball. He also lives with his mother, whose unconditional love to his children, especially with Natalie, is oftentimes misunderstood even by his own family. And lastly, his "ten-year old" sister, Natalie, who has mental issues. (Autism was not yet named as such during those times). 
 The readers will be taken to how their mother would do everything to try to even at least have Natalie live a decent normal life like the others but always ending up failing, starting by trying to get her into a special school which along the way hurts, in many other ways, all the family members affecting their connection and bond as a family. 
 The novel also narrated how Moose kept up with his sister Natalie. How he, at his young age, sometimes question the decisions his parents made and how he was able to cope with school and his friends in the island with Natalie always beside him. 
 The central theme of the book is about the complications of loving someone. Sometimes we do things that we might associate with loving but others may not understand. It also depicts how we sometimes have to forget ourselves just to deal with things that we know we should understand but at times already too much for us to handle. Moreover, it also discusses the uniqueness in everyone and how we, sometimes, just needs to accept it rather than enforce the thing that we want them to be. 
 The author was able to use the characters in an effective way making one feel the unique and in-depth replationship of each of the characters. I like how the author was able to connect the characters to its readers and how the emotional connection was so present. 
 The novel is unique in its own way (with added plus for its originality of setting ;) ). It was a fast-read and simple. I like how short the chapters are making it very easy to read. The narration was good, same as with character and world building. The author was able to write like an adolescent going througn the mind of Moose for the writing was so youthful. This book is intended for middle grade readers but it definitely transcended beyond that. Topics of jails and autism were discussed in a way that were light but with depth. 
 Two-thirds in reading the book and I haven't had a glimpsed yet of Al Capone interacting with any of the characters and it will only be until the end that I got a glimpse of him as he was exchangign correspondence with Moose. The ending was well executed. 
 Well, so how did the book got its title? Let's just say a little rat came up with this idea to make money by advertising that prisoners can wash your clothes. Who would definitely not brag if Al Capone did wash your clothes? ;) 
 Overall, it was a good and sweet, well researched, light and funny read. Great historical fiction. 
 4/5

Moose moves to Alcatraz for his father's guard position. He doesn't like it, but he's busy with the warden's daughter's manipulations, his sister's undiagnosed autism, never seeing his father, and having to fit in in school.

Moose Flanagan and his family have just moved to a new home. He's had to leave his friends, his grandmother, and the house he loved to start a new life on...Alcatraz. 
 Twelve year old Moose, his real name is Matthew, but everyone calls him Moose, is not at all pleased about his family's relocation. Sure, now he lives on the same island as legends like "Machine Gun Kelly" and Al Capone himself, but he doesn't get to see them or anything. Moose spends most of his time playing baseball (or wanting to), reading, and watching out for his sister, Natalie. 
 Life is anything but dull when you live on an island with the world's most dangerous cons and Moose is only just finding out how interesting his life is becoming. 
 I originally picked this book up for two reasons, it was nominated for the Rebecca Caudill award last year and I couldn't imagine what it would be about. At first I thought boy who helped Al Capone when he was in prison or maybe boy who had some sort of relationship with him post prison. The actual story of Al Capone Does My Shirts was much deeper then I expected, and funnier too. 
 Moose is an incredibly sympathetic character. He genuinely loves his family. He admires his dad, cares about his mom, and is very close with his autistic sister, Natalie. Natalie and Moose's relationship is one of the strongest in the novel. He loves her and wants to protect her, but he also feels angry with her because he just doesn't understand everything she's thinking. I loved how careful Moose is with Natalie and how much he wants her to have the best life possible. 
 The secondary characters in this novel are interesting contrasts to Moose. My absolute favorite character was Theresa, a young girl who lives in the apartment next to the Flanagans. She throws herself right in Moose's path from the moment he moves to the island, showing him around and nudging her way into a friendship with him. She is outspoken, but kind. Outside of the Flanagan family, she was the one character who really understood Natalie the best. 
 This is a wonderful story, but don't skip out on the author's note at the end of the novel! I thought it was fascinating. I never realized that there really were families living on Alcatraz during the years that it was a working prison. Gennifer Choldenko interviewed people who grew up on the island and provides some great historical insight that will fully flesh out the story for readers. 
 Already read Al Capone Does My Shirts? Check out Al Capone Shines My Shoes, the newly published sequel. I know I'm going to!

it's a shame the scandal that surrounded the author, pennies for peace and the central Asia institute. but at the and time their accomplishments far pay the poor management, maybe? I didn't realize at first this was the junior adaptation, but the point is there. It reminds me of Charlie Wilson's War where the US pulls troops and leaves a country to pick up on their own. one of the things suggested to get them back on their feet was schools. being the main purpose of the CAI is commendable at least. just a pity.

3rd grade book club. seems too intense for 7-8 year olds. First two chapters I spent more time defining words, themes and rewording what he'd said than actually reading it. Honestly, who picked this book :( 
 ** update, she and I just are not going to make it through this. I'm going to stop "forcing" her to read it. too much for my 7 year old.

This is a worthwhile book for young people to read, but I have one minor quibble. On p21, a reference to Mortenson's sister's death at an early age is attributed to vaccination. Perpetuating this type of ignorant myth-making is entirely inappropriate for readers too young to be aware that the claim is highly contentious and dangerous if people take it seriously. 
 http://lisahillschoolstuff.wordpress....

If I had been reading this for myself, I would have wanted more detail. There were stories that I thought, "Wait... that can't be all of what happened?!" But, I wasn't reading this really for myself. I was reading it for my 11 year old. And I thought it was a great book for him and well written for his level. 
 I did have one complaint and it's a small one... for a man who is so embarrassed by being the center of attention so much... he sure threw himself into it often. I know he had to do it to up to a certain point to let people know about the schools and try to raise money, but if he hated it so much, why not try to find others to go to some of the meetings? or take on other responsibilities? I get that he was passionate about what he was doing but I think he likes the attention even though he said MANY TIMES that he didn't.
good book

Pedantic in the extreme and an indulgently self-congratulatory book (self-observation that he [Greg:] deserves the Nobel Peace Prize for his work. But, I suppose, if a school can be built because someone is inept at mountain-climbing, then it's a Good Thing. 
 The Intent of this work is decent, the Reason seems quite shallow. 
 I've compared some chapters between the "adult" and "young readers" versions, and find Mortenson is no less pedantic towards his "adult" readers, although the glossary seems to be slightly less packed with holding-you-by-the-hand-and-coddling-you-because-Greg-Mortenson-thinks-you're-ignorant definitions.

This is probably heresy, but I didn't really like this book (to be more specific, I didn't like this version of the book). It is clearly written to promote the Higher Purpose of the Work rather than telling the story of Greg Mortenson, his schools and the CAI. Unlike some of the other remade-for-a-YA-audience books I've read, this just doesn't feel as real as the original did. 
 I'm also very unclear what age group "young readers" encompasses. At times, I thought perhaps 4/5 graders and at other times perhaps a little older. The glossary at the back is almost haphazard, defining words like "glacier" while leaving "clambering" alone. A better strategy would have been to only highlight those words that were not in English. 
 It's a pity that Mr. Mortenson's book didn't get a better adaptation.

Well that was a rollercoaster of a ride. And not the fun kind of rollercoaster...this was just a hot mess. I almost didn't finish and I skipped out on most of the ending which felt very dragged on. The whole novel felt very dragged on and SO MUCH happened within such a short period of time. 
 I really hated Jaxson. I mean the description of the book says it all..."arrogant, angry, and aggressive". He literally threatened multiple women in the book and we were supposed to like him? No matter how mad someone makes you, you can't just tell threaten to kill them...and his crazy outbursts were so dramatic and eye-roll worthy. And Julia...she was the PERFECT example of a Mary-Sue. 
 Also, I think I could have done without Wyatt completely. It just felt so dramatic and unnecessary. I could have thrived on Jaxson and Julia's drama alone and all the back and forth and back and forth (and back and forth and back and forth....) which was dramatic enough but then the author has to randomly throw in a murderer? As I said above, it was a rollercoaster.

Mhmm... where to start...? I don't know whether to rant or review this book. Maybe 
 BOTH 
 . :/ 
 Alright I'll do this: I'm one who likes to hear the bad news first, then the good news to sort of cheer me up afterwards... 
 CONS 
 - Everyone seemed too perfect (mostly the main characters). 
 - She cried at EVERYTHING and ANYTHING. 
 - I have never rolled my eyes so many times at a book in 45 second intervals the whole way from start to finish. 
 - Cringed a lot. 
 - Blew angry, frustrated sighs every time. 
 - Julia made it hard for me to like, especially in the middle of the book. I would have liked her to be a bit stronger than she was. There were times she would cry and I thought it was very unnecessary. She tried to have that backbone... but no. 
 - Jaxson: that's my favourite name for a guy tbh. But he was angry about EVERYTHING and ANYTHING. Like chill dude. #NoChill 
 In terms of characters they did become annoying. Mainly Julia and Kayla. The just overreacted either waaaayyyyy too much or came across self-absorbed. 
 I liked Cooper though. :) He seemed the more sensible and most believable character in the entire book. 
 PROS 
 - The writing wasn't bad. It kept me wanting to read. 
 - The author did a good job with building the world and the surrounding characters that follow on later in the other series. 
 - Everything was obvious and I figured out who, what, why, how before it was later revealed in the chapters much later on. 
 - I can totally see where the author was heading with the characters. So not a bad effort. 
 Overall... not a bad storyline but the thing that brought it down for me were the CHARACTERS and their reactions/personalities. They just ended up getting on my nerves and that took a little of my attention away from the storyline.

5 Love Always Lasts Stars 
 What can I say about Jax and Julia that hasn't already been said? They're a couple that's destined to be together even if takes a few years to get there. Their story is truly a second-chance romance. The chemistry between them could start a fire and most importantly, they are each other's best friend. 
 It's not an easy path for these two that's for sure. There's Julia's family that doesn't think he's good enough, Jax's own insecurities given his family background and a romantic rival that just thinks he's all that and a bag of chips...he's not though!!! 
 I devoured this book. I felt like I was living in their small town and could see and feel in person the angst, irritation, romance and passion Jax and Julia have. And when Jax breaks her heart because he thinks they can't hold onto their friendship, my heart broke with her. But when he comes back a few years later, I was rooting for them with everything I had. 
 KC Lynn is one of those authors that once she brings you into her story, she gives you a storyline that resonates with you for the rest of your life. Her characters are so well developed, the pace of her writing is stellar and because of this she allows the reader to really feel like we're right there with our H/h. 
 I'm a huge fan of KC's and I'm so excited to see what she has in store for us in the future!

sample_reviews.review_text: This book seemed to forget what its plot was supposed to be at a pork. It started off well but then just veered off course.

Ending was way too neat and tidy. There are holes in this - some very significant, but largely this is engaging and fun. Tone is my kind of book, irreverent and sarcastic. 
 Excellent reader.

"The Rook" is a quick read. I wasn't entirely convinced by the setting--the language choices were off the mark a bit, which challenged my suspension of disbelief. (It's set in the U.K.; I grew up in London.) 
 It wasn't easy to put down, but when I finished it my reaction was 80% "meh", 15% "well, that was fun", and 5% "I want some tea". Make of that what you will.

I have two observations: 
 1. I do NOT like the Checquy. (Okay, I like the Grafters less but...) 
 2. As if the blatant sexism, male domination, childhood indoctrination, forceable removal of a child from their family weren't enough to hate the Checquy, we find that once again white people steal other ethnicities babies for their own purposes. Nasty, that should have died with the death of colonialism, but apparently not. 
 And it hasn't passed me by that there are only two out of eight leaders are women, one of which was a mouse and easily bullied. (I suppose Eliza sort of counts as a third but her other three parts - the ones that attend meetings and interrogations- are male) 
 And much to his credit, O'Malley does address these issues brilliantly. The Rook is well written, fast paced and only has a few moments when I wondered if the writer was just padding his word count. Both personalities of Myfanwy are well drawn and extremely sympathetic. The other character are equally well written and even the minor characters stepped off the page inso far as their participation in the plot. 
 Some of his notions on "special" powers were to say the least icky and I thought "why?" but the major characters were intriguing in their powers and themselves. I do wish he had done more with Gestalt, because the implications of one brain controlling four bodies, each with it's own behaviors and quirks, are like a grand farce schizophrenia and should have been explored further. 
 Minor spoiler: I knew the villian early on because he had the same name as the villian in one of my favorite mysteries. Whether that was coincidence or not, I do not know.

reference_books.title: The Pact
reference_books.review_text:
The friendship between the Hartes and the Golds started to change when a tragedy happened to both their children, Chris Hartes and Emily Golds. Emily Golds was found dead one midnight and the only sole witness at that time was Chris Hartes, who later confessed that they both were actually in a suicide pact. But the police however had a doubt on Chris's statements and this is where readers learned the truth. 
 The story alternates between the Now and Then. The Now was about the investigation, the ongoing trial for the case, where Chris was accused of being the murderer. Then, where the readers get the insight on their lives -the Hartes and Golds - particularly on Chris and Emily. I like the alternate timeline style, especially because more exposure was given on Emily's parts. 
 I see how Picoult's styles now. I've read her books - My Sister's Keeper, Plain Truth, Perfect Match - and I think these went basically almost the same - something tragic happened, the characters then were put on trial - except this time I think Picoult put more exposure in the jail scene instead of just the trial or the outside world. 
 I would not say this is a romance book. I see it more than that. It's about family, friendship, and depression - how to handle them - in this case, I would say, poorly. 
 I really wanted to like Emily's character but I just can't stop thinking how selfish she was. It's not okay to put someone you love in that kind of situation. You cannot say 'if you really love me, you must keep the secret that I am suicidal.' Heck, if you really really love me, why don't you help me with it? Oh what the hell, come join me instead. 
 Do you really love someone so much that you would literally do anything for them? Well, in this case, Chris does but then see where it got him. 
 Anyway, despite my hectic life right now, I cannot put this book down. I just want to keep reading it, really wanted to know what will happened. The way Picoult writes her characters are very interesting, especially in this book, the character of Jordan, the defense attorney. I always find reading ongoing trial is boring, with all the terms and too complicated thinking. But this time I find it enjoyable and the character Jordan put some humor in those tense moments.
