sample_reviews.review_text: Life after Will Traynor has left Louisa Clark in a rut. After touring Europe, she's stuck in a dead-end job, fell off a roof, and got herself involved in a therapy group whose sessions she attends half-heartedly encouraged only by her parents who thought she is trying to kill herself out of her grief. On top of these, she meets Lily, a delinquent teenager who claims to be Will's daughter. She also met Sam, a paramedic who rescued her after she fell from the roof who offers her a relationship she is too afraid to take part for fear of being left alone again. This story is her journey in trying to find a life for herself after Will. She is still supported by her family although they are also confronted with issues of their own. She introduces Lily to Will's parents whose shock in learning that they have a granddaughter is interpreted by her as their refusal to accept her as family. Emphatic soul that she is, she looks after Lily as if she is her own daughter and gets entangled in her own problems leaving Lou forgetting about herself. Sam feels left out because of her constantly bringing Will into their conversations creating a wedge in a premature relationship. This story is about what Louis did next. Her struggle in her depression and her longing for Will. I love how this story turned out for everybody. I read this right after finishing the first book because I cannot get over the story and I wanted to find out what happened to Louisa. I love how the events turned out in her favor. I am at peace for her. :)

sample_reviews.review_text:
Read my review of 
 Into the Wild 
 .

"In April 1992 a young man from a well-to-do family hitchhiked to Alaska and walked alone into the wilderness north of Mt. McKinley. His name was Christopher Johnson McCandless. Four months later, his decomposed body was found by a moose hunter. How McCandless came to die is the unforgettable story of Into the Wild." 
 I will start out with saying that the 5* rating given to this book is for the story and not for the book. I don't know if that makes sense but I have always connected with this story. 
 The reason the 5* rating isn't for the book is because it isn't always about Christopher McCandless, for several chapters the author just talks about himself or other people who have hitchhiked in the past, and personally these are the chapters I didn't want to read. 
 I know it must be hard to write a book like this, having to hunt down people to interview and the author is able to make an image as to what happened on Chris's travels. The thing I think the movie did well was talking about the conversations Chris had with the other hitchhikers he met, because in the book it is simply "Chris met ...... and then he left. Bye" 
 I can't talk to much about this because its sad but I suggest you read up on this guy/story.

I DID NOT like this book. In fact, reading it made me angry. I only finished this because we had to read it over the summer before my junior year of high school for our AP Language class. Otherwise, I would have never picked it up and I would never have finished it if I had. 
 I remember on the first day of school when I walked in and threw the book on my desk and when the teacher asked what we thought about it, I had some of the strongest feelings and opinions about it (most likely because I was one of the ones who had actually finished the book). When she heard me say how much I despised it, she said I better have some good reasons to back it up. Of course I do. I love books and I always try to find something good about them. I rarely come across one that brings out such feelings of distaste. But being me, of course I had strong opinions and reasons as to why I hated this so much. Here they are: 
 1. I hated the way this book was written. Trust me, I studied and analyzed this in depth and know why Krakauer did this stylistically. But I couldn't stand it. He would retell the same story about four times in the hopes that his audience would get something new out of the anecdote each time. Nope. I didn't. I thought it was completely boring and the way that it jumped around all over the place just annoyed me. Next time, stick with chronological order and just tell each individual part one time. 
 2. The content killed me. Everyone sees Chris as this adventurer and great guy who would give up everything to go find himself. Just no. Can we please see through this and realize that he came from a very privileged family (who had pretty much everything, which is what most people strive for their entire lives but never achieve)and Chris was just a bored rich boy who wanted to rebel, try something different, and then failed miserably. He died because of his own stupidity and he has no sympathy from me. Many find it brave what he did, but I don't see anything brave in going through a phase that you want to just live on the road for a while and then make a bunch of mistakes that lead to your death. That's just plain idiotic. 
 I could rant more, but I highly doubt anyone is still reading and I'm probably only typing for my own therapeutic reasons. But don't read this book. I couldn't stand the way it was written OR what was being written. A very deadly combination for a book.

I have always been fascinated by tales of survival, in whatever form they take. This book was a little different than most, however. 
 Chris McCandless wandered into the wilderness in Alaska and he died there 4 months later. This traces his steps during the last couple of years of his life, and examines his early life, his background, his interactions with friends, fellow employees and family. You get a good picture of what made him tick but there is no doubt he was a very complex man and a bit of an over-confident one as well. 
 It would be nice to leave the suburbs behind and survive purely by your wits, which is what he ended up doing, not only in Alaska but in other places as well - albeit in less spectacular fashion. 
 This book seems to be dividing people, although the author is firmly in Chris McCandless' corner. Jon Krakauer has personal experience of pushing himself to his limits on mountains and he understands the restlessness that young people can get, to prove themselves, to explore, to pull away from how they were brought up. 
 Personally, I can see it from both sides. There are young people everyday who break away from their parents and live their lives in an entirely different way. There is nothing intrinsically wrong with that, but unless your parents were severely abusive, it is a good idea to at least let them know that you are ok. Since I am a parent myself now, the thought of what Chris' parents went through when they had no clue where he was, hurts my heart. On the other hand, how amazing would it be to live in the wilderness and truly see the wonder of nature in its rawest of forms and be as self-sufficient as you can. 
 I found the book was written in a bit of an odd format, and the actual story of how Chris came to found, dead, in the middle of the Alaskan wilderness, is only a small part of the book. I did enjoy, however, the stories of others who had gone on similar journeys. The font of the book I read was ridiculously small though! 
 Anyway, I give this book a solid 3.5 stars.

This is a very interesting look at why Chris McCandless, a young well educated man, walked into the bush in Alaska and starved to death. It is important to teach children the value of life, to teach them not to cause harm to others or themselves and also not to be selfish. With that said I recommend not to buy or read this book.

What makes me even more angry that this spoiled rich kid, who has more than millions of poor people in this world will ever have, commits suicide. What a moron. Smotrel fil'm, no audioknigu tozhe bylo interesno slushat', tak kak avtor poroi dobavliaet svoi mysli i interpritatsii proiskhodiashchego, osobenno v kontse on analiziruet prichiny i sledstviia proizoshedshego, a tak zhe privodit fakty o kotorykh v fil'me ne upominaetsia. 
 Mne v koei-to mere imponiruet glavnyi geroi, tak kak menia chasto tianet k odinochestvu i na prirodu. No konechno zhe pered tem kak vykhodit' vyzhivat' v prirodu nado uchit' matchast', chtoby ne povtorit' sud'bu Kristofera i Igoria Grudtsinova.

Krakauer does a phenomenal job in this book as he attempts to flesh out the story of a young man who essentially flips the bird to everyone who loves him, refuses to form lasting bonds with people (other than a couple of pen pals), and wanders off into the Alaska wilderness to have a solitary adventure while he accidentally starves to death. I love the way Krakauer blended his painstaking research of McCandless' life, interviews with the McCandless family, historical accounts of other nature-enchanted loners, and an emotional and revelatory story of his own McCandless-style expedition as a troubled young man. Ultimately, though, I still despise the way McCandless treated people. I enjoy interpersonal relationships, and to see this intelligent young man throw away so much love - it seems that nearly everyone he met instantly wanted to give him a home and a friend - was nauseating. If I were geared more like Krakauer and McCandless, this book would approach perfection for me. But because I remain so disgusted by the actions of the protagonist, I can only give the book two stars for a valiant effort by the author.

While it does not change my opinion much of McCandless as selfish and reckless, the book is very a good read as it is a biography of both McCandless and Krakauer. The author explores the common points and impetus of their own dangerous outdoor adventures without seeking to endow McCandless with a false nobility.

I'm a lark. At 5.00am in the morning I can read anything. In fact I'm up for a challenge. But as the day wears on I flag. Come 11pm at night my brain is mush, and my bedtime reading has to be easy, soothing and happy. Stodge for the eyes. It has to go down like my favourite pudding. 
 "Dewey - The small-town library-cat who touched the world" was in this vein. It should have appealed to bedtime me - I am completely besotted with cats, and with libraries for that matter..... but it didn't. The book was deeply earnest in tone. There were two dissonant threads, firstly, a story about a wonderful cat, and secondly, the story of the sad life (blighted by various tragedies), of the woman who ran the library, and looked after Dewey. This librarian was fantastically brave throughout all her negative experiences, but they pealed like a gong throughout the book. For me her distresses detracted from Dewey's story. (I know that's an awful thing to say, but they did....) 
 I was also let down in that Dewey the cat didn't really come alive for me. There were several occasions where I could have found myself dabbing my eyes with tissues and aww-ing at Dewey's adorableness, but this didn't happen. Instead we were given lots of statistics to prove his lovability (e.g. when people were asked to choose a name for him, hundreds responded, and when he died the librarian received more than a thousand emails conveying sympathy), but this was proof from the outside. I wanted proof in my heart, and it never happened. I never experienced Dewey's wonderfulness for myself. Judging by the statistics, and descriptions of Dewey's behaviour, he really was a very exceptional cat, loved by many people...but I never really felt it for myself. 
 I feel a mean and horrible person for not liking this book more. 25,689 people have rated it here at Goodreads (now that is a phenomenal number of people!) with an average rating of 3.77.... but it just didn't turn me on.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I have to say that I loathed this book. 
 I gave it 2 stars instead of 1 because I did enjoy some aspects of the story. The world-building was excellent and Winston's complex character traits were created very well and kept me interested in what he would say and do next. The thought police and the totalitarian society was well done and quite realistically alarming. You could see a future like this and that's scary. 
 1984 was very hopeless, dry and dark. Things that you expect from a dystopian novel. But I certainly didn't expect to be bored, which I was by the recounting of the passages in "the book". 
 I was very excited when Winston received "the book" and to find out what was in this mysterious tome. Well an unbelievably dry political system description filled with theories and random musings. Very few surprises and secrets were discovered about Big Brother in the book. And at that, ones I had already guessed (the war being a machine for the manufacture and destruction of goods, Oceania dropping bombs on it's own people). I haven't read a book in a long time where I have been so bored I skipped pages and I skipped A LOT in this section. 
 Portions of the story felt contrived, especially Julia's sudden, dangerous love for Winston. And the shop owner being a secret thought police leader. Why observe Winston's infractions for 7 years before arresting him? Ultimate de-humanization maybe? Maybe they were waiting until he was finally happy? This book left me with a bunch of questions and no answers. It was not poorly written or anything like that I just really personally disliked it.

The ideology behind this book has always fascinated me. I first read 1984 when I was in university, and now, decided to read it again. 
 I recall the concepts that I walked away with after having read the book as a young adult. Orwell presented a totalitarian, dystopian society. I remember Big Brother and the surveillance. I recall the sensory deprivation that existed in the everyday lives of the society as a whole, and how it played into the brainwashing. The citizens were like the walking dead. 
 After having read 1984 for the second time, it is Orwell's ability to stay in character while discussing such abstract, complex and opposing political ideologies that most impresses me, along with his creation of the cognitive dissonance that he realized the members of society had to experience. 
 We often hear about actors having to stay in characters in order to be believable, but authors have to stay in character as well in order to create realistic characters. Authors are always asking the question, "What would this character do or say in a given situation?" Authors are like profilers when it comes to character development. 
 George Orwell comes across as a genius in this book.

This is just one of those must read classics. You may have read it in school and didn't fully appreciate it and if that is the case I would urge you to read it again. Orwell's writing is beautiful and descriptive. Once you put down the book lines will be ringing in your head. 
 "War is Peace, Freedom is Slavery, Ignorance is Strength." 
 With the advancement, of technology it makes this dystopian novel even more frightening. I was sucked in after the first chapter and simple devoured the book. This is one of those books I believe everyone need to read except maybe people who are paranoid that the government is constantly watching. 
 Haunting, thought-provoking, terrific

sample_reviews.review_text: One of the strangest books I have ever read. I have never read any Kurt Vonnegut so I wasn't sure what to expect. What I'd read was that it was an anti war novel concentrating on the bombing of Dresden. What I got was a tale of Billy Pilgrim, a soldier and err, time traveler and alien abductee. There were some good insights in to the inevitability of war and death but it was just mostly ludicrous. It's satire apparently, but I didn't get it.

An interesting, quirky book... The amusing, humorous sections make the World War 2 sections of Pilgrim's life all the more horrifyingly frank... It's the comedy that puts the tragedy in gruesome, exaggerated light.

'There are almost no characters in this story, and almost no dramatic confrontations, because most of the people in it are so sick and so much the listless playthings of enormous forces.' 
 Slaughterhouse 5 is basically a novel about the Second World War, and aliens. What's surprising is how seamlessly Vonnegut manages to weave them together. As factual and realistic the descriptions of Dresden and the war are, the science fiction elements just seem to fit right in. 
 The sci-fi subplot is Vonnegut's way of exploring the depths PTSD has on people. A coping mechanism of fragmenting reality and completely removing yourself (and in Billy's case -literally) from the situation (or current world) to feel in control. This is apparent even in the narrative style. Any sentence which the reader cannot shy away from is immediately followed with 'so it goes', immediately creating distance. 
 'It was the next night that about one hundred and thirty thousand people in Dresden would die. So it goes.' 
 I really enjoyed this short novel, a very interesting read. A 20th century classic I highly recommend!

 It's a shame - I have heard lots of good things about this book. Maybe I shouldn't have tried reading it at the same time as The Hunger Games which was like literary crack. You can't compete with literary crack.

Hailed as one of the greatest anti-war books. It seems like it wants to ridicule the war. But to me it ends up ridiculing everything including itself. Novel idea but not the most powerful anti-war book out there. Preferred the author's Breakfast of Champions.

Memorable Quotes (there's several) 
 "It is so short and jumbled and jangled, Sam, because there is nothing intelligent to say about a massacre. Everybody is supposed to be dead, to never say anything or want anything ever again. Everything is supposed to be very quiet after a massacre, and it always is, except for the birds. And what do the birds say? All there is to say about a massacre, things like "Poo-tee-weet?"" 
 "There are no characters in this story and almost no dramatic confrontations, because most of the people in it are so sick and so much the listless playthings of enormous forces. One of the main effects of war, after all, is that people are discouraged from being characters. But old Derby was a character now." 
 "He is in a constant state of stage fright, he says, because he never knows what part of his life he is going to have to act in next." 
 "We went to the New York World's Fair, saw what the past had been like, according to the Ford Motor Car Company and Walt Disney, saw what the future would be like, according to General Motors. And I asked myself about the present: how wide it was, how deep it was, how much was mine to keep." 
 "Like so many Americans, she was trying to construct a life that made sense from things she found in gift shops." 
 "And Lot's wife, of course, was told not to look back where all those people and their homes had been. But she did look back, and I love her for that, because it was so human. 
 So she was turned into a pillar of salt. So it goes." 
 ""He was a funny-looking child who became a funny-looking youth - tall and weak and shaped like a bottle of Coca-Cola." 
 "'The most important thing I learned on Tralfamadore was that when a person dies he only appears to die. He is still very much alive in the past, so it is very silly for people to cry at his funeral. All moments, past, present and future, always have existed, always will exist. The Tralfamadorians can look at all the different moments just that way we can look at a stretch of the Rocky Mountains, for instance. They can see how permanent all the moments are, and they can look at any moment that interests them. It is just an illusion we have here on Earth that one moment follows another one, like beads on a string, and that once a moment is gone it is gone forever. '" 
 "He ate a pear. It was a hard one. It fought back against his grinding teeth. It snapped in juicy protest." 
 "If what Billy Pilgrim learned from the Tralfamadorians is true, that we will all live forever, no matter how dead we may sometimes seem to be, I am not overjoyed. Still--if I am going to spend eternity visiting this moment and that, I'm grateful that so many of those moments are nice."

reference_books.title: Chronicle of a Death Foretold
reference_books.review_text:
Awal baca buku ini: Tidak bisa berhenti. 
 Di tengah-tengah: Mendadak bingung. Banyak sekali tokoh di dalam novella ini. 
 Di akhir: Ohh, jadi gitu kejadiannya. Jadi itu alasan kenapa mereka membunuh si Santiago Nasar. tapi kan si Angela... tapi terus di bagian paling akhir sendiri kok gitu... kok pembunuhnya tampaknya tidak membunuh... jadi... 
 Nah, hingga di kalimat terakhir aku masih bingung dengan buku ini. 
 Meski tipis, aku butuh waktu ekstra buat baca buku ini. Faktor utamanya karena faktor bingung tadi. Bahasa Inggrisnya nggak susah. Aku juga jarang buka kamus. Yang paling aku suka adalah gaya penceritaannya. Gaya penceritaan di buku ini baru bagiku, Menggunak 1st POV tapi terasa 3rd POV. Jadi naratornya ini tidak diperkenalkan siapa. Pokoknya dia itu temannya Santiago. Dan ini yang unik, naratornya tidak pernah ngomong aka omongannya tidak pernah ditulis dalam bentuk kalimat langsung! 
 Unik banget, kan? 
 ================ 
 Icip-icip Chronicle of Death Foretold 
 Tampan, mapan, punya tunangan yang cantik. Mungkin itulah sosok Santiago Nasar yang, pada pagi hari sebuah perayaan penyambutan seorang tokoh penting, dibunuh oleh tetangganya sendiri. 
 Bagaimana kejadiannya? Siapa saja nama pembunuh Santiago Nasar? Kenapa dia dibunuh? 
 Yak, sebenarya ketiga pertanyaan itu telah terjawab dalam sinopsis bukunya. 
 Jadi, apa sisi menarik buku Chronicle of Death Foretold kalau hampir semua hal telah dibeberkan di sinopsis? 
 Yang pertama adalah, kasus pembunuhan Santiago yang dibiarkan terjadi oleh penduduknya. Ya, semua penduduknya tahu Santiago bakal... tapi tidak ada yang berusaha mencegah para pembunuhnya. 
 Cita rasa Chronicle of Death Foretold 
 Gigitan-gigitan awal, wah, tampaknya menjanjikan kenikmatan hingga akhir. Apalagi aku belum pernah baca novel dengan gaya bercerita unik kayak Chronicle of Death Foretold ini. 
 Menuju ke pertengahan hidangan, lidahku kesulitan mendeskripsikan rasa yang sedang dikecapnya. Manis enggak. Asin enggak. Asam juga enggak. Nggak pahit juga. Mungkinkah umami? Tapi umami kan adanya di ajinomoto #eh #malahsebutmerkpenyedapmasakan :lol: Oke, paragraf sinestesia ini akan berlanjut dan arti untuk paragraf dua itu adalah aku bingung. Mau dibawa kemana kisah ini. Maksudku, penjahatnya sudah ketahuan dan mengaku kalau mereka-lah yang membunuh Santiago Nasar. Lalu, kenapa halamannya masih banyak? *aku membaca buku ini tanpa membaca dulu sinopsisnya. 
 Gigitan-gigitan akhir, yak, tentu saja aku... masih bingung. Tapi mulai paham sedikit-sedikit. Dan ternyata... *sengaja dipotong demi tidak berubah jadi sop iler. 
 Entah sengaja atau tidak, Opa Marquez membuat pembaca berspekulasi apa benar penjahat yang itu yang membunuh Santiago? Masalahnya... *beee-* tampaknya... *-eeeeeep*. Belum lagi masalah alasannya. Orang-orang terlalu sibuk... Shock kayaknya, atau bersukacita secara kebetulan pembunuhan itu terjadi pada sebuah perayaan. Hingga alasan itu tidak digali kebenarannya. 
 Yang aku suka dari hidangan yang diberi judul Chronicle of Death Foretold ini adalah, gaya penyajiannya yang tidak biasa. Sudut pandang orang pertama tapi terasa seperti sudut pandang orang ketiga terbatas. Naratornya adalah teman Santiago, dan uniknya, tidak pernah ada kalimat langsung yang terucap dari "mulutnya." 
 Sebenarnya buku ini adalah bacaanku buat proyek baca bareng bulan Oktober. Tapi karena aku nggak kelar bacanya tepat waktu jadinya molor hingga November dan baru posting reviewnya bulan Desember.

..bought of out of curiosity. thank God it's Thai, a backpacker and a tattoo artist, otherwise it would be a very boring book.

A popular Indonesian novel. I read the prequel of this trilogy (?). I cant remember much from the previous one. I am quite sure I had a good time and was impressed reading it. I remember an expression "badai serotonin", the serotonin storm! Not bad! 
 Having said that, I found it difficult to enter the realm of this novel until I changed my attitude to the one I use when I read a scifi/fantasy novel. The striking quality of this novel is its inovative creativity, sometimes bordering ambitious. It is like the author wants to say a lot of things - covering a lot of grounds, achieving universal grandeur - at the same time. 
 The use of analogy and metaphors is, though naughtily creative, sometimes weird. "Menatap rambutnya seperti makan bubur ketan hitam: gelap, padat, wangi", "Perbukitan hijau itu tampak seperti meja bilyar diseraki butiran Nutrisari". I tried hard to imagine what kind of effect or images intended to arise in the reader's mind. 
 Description of tattoing process, a wushu style called chang quan (which I happened to practice a long time ago), or Bodhi as a character are some of the achievements of this work. 
 If I were the author, I wouldn't be too generous with foreign words.
Reading this book is a proof to me that u can live many lives from reading a story.

reference_books.title: Born to Run: A Hidden Tribe, Superathletes, and the Greatest Race the World Has Never Seen
reference_books.review_text: This book makes running as interesting as J.K. Rowling makes Quidditch--which is to say, VERY. I expected a self-help book, but what I got was a laugh-out-loud adventure story that's already caused me a few awkward moments on the train when I snort laughter over my Kindle next to a dignified business man. I won't even get into how this is already revolutionizing my approach to running (saving those enchanted musings for later), but this book ROCKS and I want to shove it in everyone's hands.

reference_books.title: The Sweetest Dark (The Sweetest Dark, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I read this in manuscript and LOVED it. The Libba Bray comparison is dead on, except that Lora is a much more spunky, nuanced heroine than Gemma. Her rough past growing up in an orphanage makes her a tougher girl lead than I've seen in a long time in a YA novel--you can trust that, when Lora gets bullied at her new, mysterious school, she's will NOT be afraid to fight back hard. 
 My favorite part about this book is two-fold: 1) the writing is FANTASTIC and 2) the magical element is a highly original twist on an old fantasy concept. I've gotten very tired of clunky, poorly written YA novels that all seem to be about the same thing. Though the set-up of this novel seems like standard boarding school magical drama, I was constantly surprised by the original twists it took. 
 Did I mention the crazy romantic tension between Lora and her two love interests? Shiver-worthy, I tell you!

reference_books.title: Belong to Me
reference_books.review_text:
Loved it. Belong to Me, in my opinion, was even better than the first book, Love Walked In. Marisa de los Santos just effortlessly nails certain things about life, love, women, friendships, families, and many other difficult subjects. It's the kind of book that makes me shy after reading it--like I want to put it away in a dark corner for a while because it knew too much about me and poked at too many tender parts. 
 The one drawback of the book, in my mind, was that it was at times overwritten. Marisa's a gorgeous writer, but I hate it when I can almost feel a writer being dazzled by her own skill. It's distracting! Let me read your brilliant book and stop trying to wow me!

reference_books.title: The Death Cure (Maze Runner, #3)
reference_books.review_text: I loved Maze Runner, but the conclusion was lackluster. After a while, I got tired of wondering whether something was real or a trick by WICKED. That twist got old very quickly. Once this book started mentioning plot points and memorable moments from within the Maze, all I could think was, "Man, I wish I was reading that book instead because it really was incredible." This one, however, was a poor conclusion. I hope James Dashner's next effort will showcase his talent more.

reference_books.title: My Life Next Door
reference_books.review_text: Awesome YA. I was a little frustrated with some of the unresolved issues with side characters, but overall I liked this book a lot. It had just the right amount of scope and tackled everything seamlessly--family drama, first love, politics, sibling dynamics, moral dilemmas big and small, and more. I'd recommend this to anyone looking for solid contemporary YA--nothing earth shattering, but thoroughly enjoyable.

book_a.title: Cloud Atlas
book_a.user_review: It's rare, I think, for a novel to be this intellectually stimulating while being so emotionally challenging. I love that in particular about Mitchell--how, despite writing high-brow fiction, he manages to create such full-fledged, sympathetic characters. This book is mind-blowing and beautiful, and I'm happy to say it lived up to its ambitious, high-concept promise. I found The Thousand Autumns of Jacob de Zoet more reader-friendly, but Cloud Atlas is one of those books you look back upon with, "HOW did he do it?!" It's indisputably brilliant yet immensely satisfying. I can't wait to read the rest of his backlist!

sample_reviews.review_text:
Cloud Atlas was an uneven book for me. On the one hand, I thought the structure was brilliant. Loved how he told an interconnecting story across time, spanning 19th century slavers all the way to post-apocalyptic Hawaii and then going all the way back. I thought this technique of bookending the narrative lent itself well to telling stories within a larger story. 
 Some of these stories, I loved. Essentially, the middle 4 stories in the book worked for me. Hawaii, Korea, Cavendish and Seaboard are all fantastic, containing intertwining themes about politics, consumerism and family. And the characters really are kindred souls drifting across time, as the book jacket suggests. 
 Unfortunately, the two "bookends," or the first and second story are dull and seem completely disconnected from the rest of the book, save for a cursory connection. (A discovered book, a penpal across the ocean.) I found myself so bored for the first 140 or so pages that I contemplated giving up. Then, when the book had delighted me and I hit those storylines again, I withheld judgement, hoping I'd appreciate the 2nd half of each of these stories given the context of the middle. I didn't. The opening and the ending left me with a general sour taste in my mouth, even though I liked the middle bits. 
 Mitchell does do a phenomenal job mastering different voices and genres. The beginning feels very much like a tale from the old masters (Robinson Crusoe, etc.), while the end dips into solid sci-fi territory with dystopian themes. But even that can't save the dullness or how flat the first and last 150 pages of the book feels. I'm interested to watch the movie now, to see how they pulled it off. Like the book, I could see it being brilliant, but I could also see it being a failure.

I give this book most-unjustifiably-boring cover award! Seriously, the cover isn't actively ugly or embarrassing, but it would never have intrigued me into picking up this book. I only read it because it was the selection for this month's Post-Apocalyptic book club meeting - and it turned out to be my favorite of all the books we've read so far. 
 I'm not sure the six stories in the book (which are linked thematically and through a bit of structural gimmickry) really needed to be presented as one work, but since all of them were interesting, and a couple of them were excellent, I didn't mind. 
 Update: I've belatedly decided to up my review to 5 stars, from my initial 4 - because this is a book I find myself repeatedly thinking about, and recommending to people. It holds up to consideration.

This book was amazing and deeply philosophical--and a bit religious, although not the kind of religious I tend to avoid. 
 I will start with some notes about how I came to read it. I watched the movie for the first time years ago (when it came out in theaters) and have seen it a few times since. I didn't know it was a book until after having seen it perhaps twice. I put it on my list, where many books go but do not get removed from quickly. As was my luck, I won a contest where a book from my TBR was chosen as a prize for me, and this was the one. Naturally, it was then sent to the TBR that is my bookshelf (along with several hundred unread others) where it lingered for months. Then I decided to pick it up and read it, entirely on a whim, which is an unusual thing to happen to such a long, philosophical book. To tell you the truth, the only thing that really kept me reading was the fact that it made sense because I had seen the movie first. 
 And as I read, the book illuminated the finer aspects of the movie that were perhaps missed or left out entirely. So both I would say are necessary to understand the story, but definitely do watch the movie first, read the book, and then watch it again. I described it to my friend as "fitting together the pieces of a puzzle," which is quite satisfying and the best way to describe the book as a whole. I understood the theme the movie was trying to illustrate, but it really clicked while I read the book, and that made the experience all the more enjoyable and meaningful. 
 These were my thoughts early on in the book. I reached page 200, and I read on, happy that the movie was becoming so clear with the help of the book and the book was comprehensible after having seen the movie several times (it doesn't help that Ewing's story, written in the most old-fashioned style, is first), but there was a growing nagging sensation in my mind. I was worried about missing the point. 
 Yes, there are connections, these people's lives are entwined in ways unexpected, but after the initial realization, what had once seemed so groundbreaking now appeared mundane. So what? It's an easy concept to grasp now, easy to apply to everyday life. Why are there five hundred pages, six such different stories devoted to this idea? For, truly, each story could be its own book, but presented in this way, they lacked inherent meaning. Typically, stories are praised and considered based on their substance and individual meaning, not--not meaningful only in terms of how they connect to other stories. So what IS that underlying factor connecting them all that is so important? Could it really be just that our lives influence or are present in others' lives in ways unfathomable to us while we live? I looked for more clues, and I noticed that the order mattered--each story mentioned the one before it, until halfway, where it peaked and then the stories mentioned the ones after it (but the same stories were mentioned in the same ones; it was consistent in that). But after that, the similarities were few. But why take the time to flesh out such unique stories? The concept of connections could be explained in a much simpler collection. I couldn't help but search for meaning in the individual stories, detailed as they are. Nothing seems to be an accident. I kept looking. 
 As I read on, it hit me at around page 480 (nearly the end) that perhaps one of the greater themes is the rise and fall of civilizations, because that's a big theme in the stories of Adam Ewing, Sonmi, and Zachry. I wasn't sure how it played into the stories of Robert Frobisher, Luisa Rey, and Timothy Cavendish, but it occurred to me that perhaps they are simply examples of civilizations that have risen and fallen. Those three are the ones with the most in common--they can't span more than a century, maybe a century and a half. But Adam Ewing's story is the earliest, maybe a half-century earlier--I confess I do not recall any exact dates, but it is around the time of the California gold rush, which is in the 1850s, so indeed a half-century is not so far off. Frobisher's letters are around the 1930s and Rey's adventure is around the 1970s. I haven't any solid idea of when Cavendish's story was, although I might if I had paid better attention. Perhaps in the 20th century. Events in Europe usually tend to take place in a more modern time than I assume they do. [Note: I wrote this before reading the synopsis. I'm pleased that I was dead-on, although Cavendish's is present-day.] 
 Anyway, I had assumed such about the big theme until it was elaborated on in the last couple pages, and thankful I was for it. Yes, the rise & fall of civilizations was mentioned, but it went on. Adam Ewing mentioned belief and its power; how we perceive the world will determine its outcome. If we give way to the predatory types, believing that the world is for the strong and so letting them have their way, then that is how it shall be. Predators shall reduce society to extinction. Of course the power of belief in a better world is at most a fantasy in our realistic times. As Ewing says, "It is the hardest of worlds to make real" (page 508). It is difficult to get enough of the world on board with this idealist viewpoint to make a significant difference. I am not blind to the difficulty, although Ewing has hope. As the Star Wars rebels say, "a rebellion is built on hope," and I think Sonmi would agree, no matter how eloquently she tries to rephrase it into oblivion. I just think it's funny how accurately Ewing, the earliest of the narrators, predicted the fall of civilization (that would occur more than once, it seems) resulting in the story of Zachry (the last story, chronologically), whose form of civilization will surely not be the last. 
 It truly is interesting, though, how expertly Mitchell wove the stories together. There were borrowed names, identical metaphors, and of course that telltale comet birthmark. It was exciting to come across the ways the title cropped up--"cloud atlas" meant nothing to me before, but in reading the book you understand it (at least somewhat; it's still a bit of a vague concept). A few stories mention it, but not all (that I can recall). I don't believe I knew it in the movie, although Zachry may have said it (as he did in the book). I honestly could not tell what anyone in his story was saying most of the time. The book, while still a bit difficult to understand, makes it easier. 
 It's also fascinating how different the stories are. They are told in different ways. Ewing's is a journal, published by his son. Frobisher's is a series of letters, all written by him. Rey's is a story told in 3rd person omniscient, present tense no less, later to become a book. Cavendish's is a memoir, I believe, later to become a movie. (What I love best about his story is that there is movieception; he publishes a book made into a movie, which I'm sure makes it into the movie about his own life based on his memoir, which is part of the book Cloud Atlas which also becomes a movie.) Sonmi's story is an interview of sorts. Zachry's is in the form of a story he is telling to youngsters around a campfire, or whatever his equivalent is. Each narrator has a unique voice (and unique writing quirks). It's like reading several different books by different authors in one. Each story is split in half to make room for the other stories and then resumed later, but is impossible to not get attached and invested. It is impossible to forget the events. It is also difficult to predict the outcomes; some have it luckier than others. But it is a tale you can't stop reading until the end. Definitely one for those who like books with philosophical themes presented in such a puzzle-piece format. 
 After this lengthy review, I have no choice but to recommend this book. Again, watch the movie first and after. It's a beautiful movie. And the music. That's one thing you can never experience the beauty of in the book. I can play the Cloud Atlas March (not the famous Sextet, for I am no orchestra) on the piano, and it sends me back into the story every time. It is definitely something that stays with you. 
 P. S. I realize I did not say much on how it was religious. There is the obvious theme of reincarnation. Then there are the various religious beliefs of the characters. Sonmi's story has a lot of religious undertones. The other things are subtle, but appealing. It's not a preachy book. It is more a book for figuring what you want to get out of life. 
 P. P. S. This review is a fantastic companion to reading & understanding the book and its themes better. 
 See the full review (yes, there's more!) on my blog, Awesome Book Assessment.

reference_books.review_text:
It took me over a month to read this book. That almost never happens, especially for YA books. This book just didn't hold my interest until I hit chapter 18. And then I was interested, for about four more chapters and the. I was just interested in finishing. 
 Okay, so I loved the Abhorsen trilogy. But, I also read it a long, long time ago. In fairness to this story, perhaps I should have re-read them prior to reading Clariel because, well, I couldn't remember who the heck she was supposed to become. Obviously a bad guy. Obviously a necromancer. But...hm....just can't remember and that took out some of the pleasure away from reading an origin story. I fully recognized that this is my experience, and not the fault of the author. (However, what if someone was just picking up this book and not starting with the trilogy? I think showing the descent into evil would have been much stronger.)

reference_books.title: That Summer
reference_books.review_text:
At the end of this book in the notes section Willig wrote that some books just flow off the pen and some don't and this book was the latter. I think that I could tell that because this book was just tedious to get through. An easy and enjoyable kind of tedious but still... 
 This is a dual timeline story, which is Willig's specialty. It was a more serious read over her Pink Carnation series, which I was glad to see. But it was surprisingly undeveloped in places. In the modern story you have Julia who inherits a house from her great aunt that she didn't know existed. Julia just wasn't much of a character and what little personality she did have, I simply didn't like. 
 In the past you have a painter/a love story/and a murder mystery. How can that story line be tedious? Well...because it just didn't go anywhere. And I love a good historical tragedy, this one was left with gaps in the narrative. I get that it's history. I get that some things you never know. But the point of the past/present storylines is that you DO get to know. 
 This one just wasn't my favorite Willig book

Probably not. She still has feelings for Alcide - even though she killed his fiance, watched his father die in the packmaster race so that put a damper on that relationship - but can she trust him? Eric is a secondary character in this book and we know how Sookie feels about him. And then there is the witch she meets in New Orleans who moves in with Sookie in Bon Temps. Anyone else think all of these factors are a disaster waiting to happen?

sample_reviews.review_text: Once I began reading this series, I could not stop. After finishing one I picked up the next.

If I didn't already own these books I wouldn't bother with them. They are so frustratingly stupid.

Charlaine Harris is back in the saddle again after her last series title Dead as a Doornail left a little to be desired. Sookie is packing her bags to go to New Orleans to collect her dead vamp cousin Hadley's belongings and clear her apartment by order of the Queen of Louisianna...yah I know...that wasn't really explained anywhere in the current novel. A side note about that is the back story for most of this novel is from a short story published by Harris. Odd, but at any rate the novel is still enjoyable. This story is chock full of the supernatural and in it we meet the queen's lawyer and his driver, both demons, Sookie's new love interest Quinn ( a hunka hunka burinin were-tiger) a witch that's a landlord and a vampire-were and lots of other interesting supes. Most intriguing is the vamp queen of Louisianna Sophie Le-Clerq and her entourage. Wow! Harris includes some great action sequences, plot and character twists that will make the reader gasp and Sookie's usual sense of humor and street smarts. Sexy, smart, funny and well written you can't ask for much more. Well Done!
Another good one, I'll have to read more of this series.

I liked Definitely Dead better than the previous novel in the series. Having said that, I think I need to take a break from Sookie Stackhouse and her many suitors for a while. 
 In Definitely Dead Charlaine Harris adds a new paramour in Sookie's stable of suitors: Quinn, a tall bronze-skinned Were-Lion, a Supernatural Events Coordinator that Sookie met during the Were Leader's Challenge in the previous story. So, now the list includes: Vampire Bill, Vampire Eric, Alcide a Were, one or two Were panthers from Hotshot, Sam her shifter boss, and Quinn. The only males not interested in bedding Sookie are Jason, her brother, and Claude, a gay fairy. 
 It's wonderful to watch Ms Harris juggle this growing cast of would-be lovers, making sure they all make an appearance and have some role to play in the story, but frankly, she needs to start rounding up some shifters for the Bon Temps Zoo and/or staking a couple of vamps. By the time Ms Harris has recapped the story lines, introduced new characters, and added some descriptive detail, there isn't much room left for new plot elements. 
 Having said that, in Definitely Dead the reader is introduced to more vampire politics, and learns of Queen Sophie-Anne's history. Sookie once again attacked and beaten up (three or four times), and Eric, Bill, and Quinn come to her rescue, sometimes all at once. 
 If you've stayed with the series this long, you might as well continue. On the plus side, there is more sensuality in this story, so that might garner Ms Harris new readers. But as for me, I think I'll let a few full moons pass before picking up another one of her novels.

I loved plunging into a history and a culture that are unfamiliar to me. The book relates two parallel love stories during two periods of political unrest in Egypt nearly a century apart. I couldn't stop reading because the history, politics, and the earlier love story pulled me in. All the same, I thought the book was rather poorly executed with an excess of complexity and historical details in dialogue. Nor was the later love story compelling; indeed it felt contrived.

2.5* 
 The book started as 4* but ended as a 2*. When I read the synopsis I thought I was going to love it. It ticked all the right boxes : a love story set in Egypt, a country I really wanted to know more about, the use of letters and diaries to tell the story, two parallel stories set at different points in time. 
 I loved Anna's story up to the point she got married and moved together with Layla and Sharif's mother. I was hopping for a more passionate relationship and I thought the romance story was not developed enough. Also, i believe that it is impossible for Anna to be so great friends with everybody from the Harem( from Layla to Sharif's mother). No cultural clashes whatsoever...Hard to believe that. Also, there was no difficulty for Anna to adapt to the life in Egypt with her husband. I would have liked the book to discuss more about the cultural aspects of relationship. 
 After the middle of the book I felt that all the dialog and all the new characters were there only to introduce a political idea/problem. Although I enjoyed to learn more about the Egyptian history I did not fell that I got a clear idea of the events that happened during the time the two stories were set. I though the romance-history lesson was structured quite poorly and I did not clearly understand the message of the book. 
 The transition from one time to another was sometimes messy. There were too many narrators: Anna, Isabel, Amal, Layla and Sharif. It made me fail to care for any of the characters. 
 Some of the plot twists, such as the unresolved possible incest and the love interest of Amal were unnecessary an somewhat bizarre. 
 As a result, despite of an interesting format, the story did not succeed to engage me emotionally and I did not care about the characters' evolution and relationships. I was bored many times and the last 200 pages were a pain to finish.

reference_books.title: Go Set a Watchman
reference_books.review_text: I really wanted to love this book, but I finished it feeling disappointed. I had to force myself to finish it, which is never a good sign. Overall - the writing felt dated and the storyline was just ... blah. I think Harper Lee was effective in conveying issues surrounding equality and racial tension of the South in 1955, but I was personally disappointed in how Atticus' character thought about and approached things. Several reviews discuss how his decisions and actions in this novel made him more human, but I personally preferred his saintly-like character in "To Kill a Mockingbird." Similarly, I loved the spunk and tenacity of Scout in Lee's earlier work, but she grew up to become an intolerable, opinionated, entitled young woman - the epic fight she has with Atticus at the end of the novel was painful to read through - painful because I wanted to smack her in the face. Ugh. She was just SO ANNOYING. The other characters in the book didn't grab me, either - Dr. Finch was loony tunes and Henry (Hank) was kind of pathetic. This was a book I had to read, but now that it's over I'm ready to move onto something more interesting.

reference_books.title: Sweet Lamb of Heaven
reference_books.review_text: Interesting read but not sure I completely understood what was going on. This book presents two intertwined story lines - the first a very real, very tangible story about a young mother, Anna, trying to escape her manipulative, sociopathic husband who has designs about keeping her in his life for the benefit of his political campaign; and the second a very esoteric, unrealistic plot about a supernatural and paranormal auditory hallucination that Anna (and others) suffer from. I just couldn't reconcile the two story lines together to make sense of what was going on. Strange read.

reference_books.title: Life After Life
reference_books.review_text: I was really intrigued by the premise of this novel, which is quite simply about having second chances in life. It explores how subtle decisions or actions can change the course of a person's life, or on a larger scale, can change history. I am fascinated by the Buddhist concept of rebirth, and as a yogi I have studied reincarnation as part of the Hindu philosophy. This has led me to develop my own notions about the possibility of having endless chances to live one's life, and I've entertained the idea of being able to come back and live my life "more perfectly." So, given all that, I enjoyed Kate Atkinson's book "Life After Life," which begins in 1910 and continues post WWII. I liked the English perspective on the war, and I started developing connections with Ursula (the protagonist) and her family. I also earned to better understand how Ursula took experiences from a previous life and somehow, miraculously and subconsciously would apply them to her subsequent life. At times the book moved a bit slowly for me (particularly in the beginning), and I was kind of perplexed with the ending. But that said, Atkinson wove an interesting and thought-provoking yarn with this one. It's a likely candidate for re-reading.

reference_books.title: My Life on the Road
reference_books.review_text: This was the first book by Gloria Steinem that I read. When I finished the book I felt appreciative of the groundwork that she laid for women's rights and diversity, and inspired by her methods of listening, learning and being open to the wisdom she found on the road. She was a truly amazing and fearless political activist and leader. This is a recommended read for anyone who is passionate about equality, and who is interested in learning about how to be an effective organizer.

reference_books.title: The Heart Goes Last
reference_books.review_text: This book was a quick and entertaining read. It was an imaginative, whimsical and thought-provoking examination of human desire. It was my first time reading Margaret Atwood, and I thought she created a salacious dystopia for her protagonists, Stan and Charmaine. S & C survived a tragic economic downfall only to become almost jobless, nearly homeless and desperate for happier times. They live in their car, constantly scared of being robbed or raped, and not surprisingly their marriage is crumbling. They see an opportunity to change their fortune by joining a new community that promises them employment, housing and access to basic needs (Food without maggots! Underwear without skid marks! Little to no chance of being killed (they think)!). It sounds like heaven ... but like all things that seem too good to be true, there are strings attached. Stan and Charmaine get to spend one month living worry-free in the retro town of Consilience and in exchange, spend one month in (wait for it ...) prison! Yay! While they are in prison, their home in Consilience will be inhabited by their "alternates," who quickly become intriguing objects of kinky desire and temptation for Stan and Charmaine. The bulk of the novel takes place in the twin town & prison community, and, it turns out that four walls and a roof are not enough to save this relationship. The rest of the story is a number of twists and turns, and touches on wonderfully strange topics (Lobotomies to program human desire! Organ farming of the scum of the earth in order to prolong life for the rich! Sex with robots AND chickens!) while constantly weaving in icons of the 1950s that are reflective of a perfect human community. It was a book that sparked numerous conversations for me and one I would recommend for fans of speculative fiction.

book_a.title: My Absolute Darling
book_a.user_review: This story is beautifully written but incredibly hard to read; there were parts of the book where I cringed and had to take a breather before I could finish a chapter. The novel is graphic, disturbing, emotionally draining ... and the subject matter is not for the faint of heart. However it is a true page-turner that I mowed through. Gabriel Tallent captures the natural beauty of the Mendocino landscape and creates a true survivor in Turtle, as well as a disgusting villain in Martin. Just thinking about him ... I feel like I need to shower, and possibly figure out a way to punch him hard in the face. Ugh.

 I had to push myself to finish this one, and I give it this rating only due to the last quarter of the book, which really sucked me in. Descriptions were all too lengthy and I found myself skimming over Martin's dialogue. 
 However, I do feel that this book shows the deep complexities that come with abuse. Martin was extremely abusive, threatening Turtle with knives and guns and constantly raping her, but would turn around and tell her how much he loves her and how he can't live without her. People had made it known that they would help Turtle if she needed it, but she really thought she could fix her father.

I really liked the storyline and the insight into how the main protagonist Turtle thinks was well thought through, but the language was a bit too flowery for me. 
 The author is super descriptive and writes rather poetically, but there was so much detail and words that I'd never heard before in relation to flora and technical jargon. 
 I thought that I'd get used to it, but it just became a bit of a headache to plough through, so I'm only giving the book 3 stars.
Too much graphic violence without the benefit of good writing or interesting characters

I realized that I hated this book at the end of the first chapter. I'm not entirely sure why I continued to read it, but I did. I guess we all have to live with our choices. Fair warning: there will be many, many spoilers. 
 Turtle Alveston is a 14-year old girl living outside of Mendocino, California, with her abusive father, Martin. Martin physically and sexually abuses Turtle, and has for a very long time. Turtle's mother is dead, she went solo abalone diving one day when Turtle was very young and never returned. Or at least that's Martin's story. When we finally hear the story behind the death of Turtle's mother it is so loaded with heavy-handed uncertainty that I spent the rest of the novel waiting for her to either turn up alive after all, or for the revelation that Martin had murdered her after she'd caught him raping their daughter. But nothing ever came of it and ultimately Tallent wasted a lot of time imbuing the passage with ambiguity for no reason. 
 For all the mountains of praise being heaped upon this book, I am fantastically disappointed in the quality of Tallent's writing. He is the worst writer of dialogue I have encountered in years. Characters incessantly repeat themselves, there is far too much artless cursing, and no one - save Grandpa - sounds authentic. Jacob and Brett sound like caricatures of teenagers, and nothing from Turtle's inner monologue suggests that she'd be able to interact socially with them as easily as she seems to. 
 Tallent depends on the dialogue to help readers understand the characters and their motivations, which is largely why the character development is also poor. Martin attempts to blame his damaged psyche on his own father, accusing him of a level of hate and abuse that seems completely contrary to the way grandpa is depicted in the novel. Yes, Grandpa is clearly an alcoholic, but compared to Martin he comes off like an angel of mercy. Martin's accusations against his father fly in the face of the scenes where he and Turtle play cribbage, where he gives Turtle his beloved bowie knife, and encourages her to ask Martin to take her dress shopping and ask a boy to the dance. This is not the same man that Martin describes as hideously abusive. Is this meant to demonstrate how off-his-rocker Martin really is? Or is it a serious accusation of intense abuse, the legacy of which is now passed down to another generation? Perhaps it is neither of these? It is impossible to tell. 
 Tallent also goes way overboard on the description of the natural environment. We get it already, they're in the wilderness of the Pacific Northwest! It's verdant and wild and dangerous - JUST LIKE LIFE YOU GUYS. But by far the element of his style that I found the most grating was his tendency to turn nouns into verbs. At one point a man's arm is "sleeved with tattoos," at another point rain comes "sheeting off the roof." No. No no no no no. This is lazy writing. Not only are the lengthy descriptions of everything excessive and burdensome, but readers also have to suffer through the tortuous twisting of nouns into verbs because Tallent is too lazy to choose his words more carefully. BOO! 
 Speaking of choosing his words carefully, someone needs to ask Gabriel Tallent why he chose to write scenes of unimaginably horrible sexual abuse by a father against his teenage daughter with a tone of eroticism that is usually reserved for descriptions of consensual love. The first encounter they had I thought, "That was.... really weird," but thought that, perhaps, his intent was to demonstrate that while it's obvious to the reader that what Turtle is experiencing is extreme sexual abuse, she herself believes that when her father has sex with her it is him expressing his love for her. I found myself trying to remember Lolita, and how disquieting Humbert Humbert's feelings toward young Dolores Haze are; but then I recalled that in Lolita Humbert Humbert is the (very) unreliable narrator from whose point of view the story is told. This novel is not told from Martin's point of view, it's told from Turtle's, a 14-year old child who is being repeatedly raped by her own father. The tone Tallent chooses for these passages is, frankly, reprehensible. 
 This book is an orgy of weapons, especially guns. So. Many. Guns. Martin and Turtle bond over the weapons as he teaches her to use them, and then a rift forms over the very same weapons as her caution and knowledge surpasses his own. Notably, Turtle has a Sig Sauer pistol that she carries pretty much at all times, somehow - inexplicably - even to and from school without being caught, and she cleans it approximately 72 million times. It's clearly therapeutic for her, she has something important and powerful to take care of, but Tallent belabors the point until it ceases to carry any symbolic meaning before the novel is even half over. There is also a bowie knife which is given to Turtle and has great meaning and significance - a knife that sticks around and plays a very important role at the end of the novel - but somehow Turtle also carries that to school with her, along with her Sig Sauer, and remains - unbelievably - under the radar. 
 There are many, many other small details about this novel that are infuriatingly stupid. Her teacher, Anna, clumsily confronts Turtle about the abuse she suspects and while Turtle does her best to deny it NO TEACHER ALIVE that was alert enough to suspect an issue in the first place would be convinced by her insistence that everything is fine. Then a week after this conversation happens Turtle arrives at school, limping and black-eyed from her father beating her with a hot iron fire poker, and THERE IS NO POSSIBLE WAY that Anna wouldn't notice her injuries and contact social services - they JUST had a breakthrough conversation about it. Plus teachers are mandatory reporters! Also, when Turtle and Jacob are swept out to sea by the tide and she suffers compound fractures to three of her fingers, they just somehow magically heal in like, a week? With no residual problems with her dexterity or anything. Martin kidnaps another little girl later on in the plot and her whole entrance into the drama serves no real purpose that I can figure out. And the scene with the scorpions actually made me dry heave. And her name is Julia, but some people call her Julia, and her dad calls her Kibble, and she calls herself Turtle. Where did she get all of her names? Character names are usually kind of important. 
 In the end, I have nothing good to say about this book. I found it offensive, and the writing was terrible, and I'm angry that I wasted hours of my life reading it, and disappointed in all the authors that I admire who are heaping praise upon it. Do yourself a favor and skip it.

"The Widow" by Fiona Barton. 
 This was considered a Thriller? 
 The next "Gone Girl"? 
 Seriously???

I liked The Widow although it had a much slower pace than other psychological suspense novels I've recently read. I thought the dynamic between Jean and Glen was interesting and I found the novel interesting as a character study and how complex marriages can be when one of the partners is accused of a heinous crime. 
 Jean was an unreliable narrator, but I found her chapters to be a little boring. The author seemed to purposefully make her flat in order to give nothing about the plot away. The chapters from the point of view of the reporter and the detective working the case was much more engaging. However, I did like the flashbacks to Glen and Jean's courtship and subsequent marriage to get a better understanding of why she stood by him as she saw the signs of the seemingly double life he was living. 
 There are some disturbing parts of The Widow that were really hard to stomach. As Jean and the police find out more about Glen's porn addiction and how it relates to a missing child investigation, I felt truly revolted. Jean became increasingly frustrating as a character and I really couldn't find any sympathy for the situation she finds herself in after Glen's death. 
 There were a few twists that I didn't see coming, but a few reveals were pretty obvious early on. I guess I was waiting for a big shocker to blow me away, but that never really happened. But despite my few issues, I did overall enjoy the book and finished reading the entire book within a couple days.

*2.5 stars 
 By now I've read quite a few reviews of Carve the Mark. Many early reviewers really liked this book. Later reviewers found the book problematic. 
 I'm some where in the middle. 
 It's not as problematic to me as it is with some other people. I really don't see the overt racism that other reviewers have pointed out, nor do I think that Ms. Roth had that in mind while writing this book. 
 Both the Thuvhe and Shotet people have citizens who have of various shades of light and dark skin. Comments have been made about how the Shotet people are described as a savage race and are darker skinned,. Cyra, one of the main protagonist, is described as having darker skin,but it's very clear in the book that the leader of the Shotet people, Cyra's brother, has very pale white skin. 
 And as far as the Shotet people being a savage race, that is a stereotype that has spread throughout the Thuvhite people, but which Akos, our other main protagonist, can clearly see is untrue after being thrust into Cyra's world. The Shotet people themselves are not a savage race, only the man who rules them, and even then he has his reasons for being this way. Amos learns not to judge an entire group of people based on the beliefs of their leader. As far as their ritual of carving marks into their skin to remember those they have killed, Akos also transitions from seeing this as a barbaric tradition into one of remembrance and respect. 
 If you simply view carving marks into someone's arm as an example of self-harm, you are not respecting the rituals and traditions of a lot of indigenous and aboriginal people who do not see this as a form of self harm at all, but an important part of their history and heritage. The story shows that you can't judge a group of people from the outside unless you have lived in their shoes. 
 My major complaint was with the world-building. I actually enjoyed a lot of the aspects of the world-building. My problem is that I just wanted a lot more of it. It created such an interesting world and universe, but it often felt like background setting for the relationship developing between Cyra and Akos. Many parts of this book when unexplained and felt very shallow, which was very disappointing. I also was disappointed in some of the character motivations and developments of the minor characters. 
 I will probably read the sequel because I am interested if Roth will be able to resolve those problems in the final book. If she doesn't, I don't think I will be reading any more of her books. I wasn't a big fan of the Divergent trilogy, especially the last book, so I was hoping for more with this duo logy.

 -Okay, so I had heard a lot of mixed reviews about this book so was really unsure what to expect. Some people love it and some hate it- it seems to be the marmite of the YA Fantasy world. I know there was a massive hype for this book when it first came out but somehow I missed that so I didn't have any prejudgements of the book itself which is always a good sign. But I was hoping it was going to be good. 
 The plot follows two witches, Safi who is a rare Truthwitch and Iseult who is Threadwitch meaning she can see others emotions/feelings and their connection to the world. So basically the coolest witch. Can you tell I am biased? Safi and Iseult are both Threadsisters and I found it interesting because Safi is much higher in terms of her status whereas Iseult seems to be very low. The book follows them being chased by various bad guys around a world which seems very medieval. You can tell this book is meant to be a set up for a series for sure but it also does a great job of that. 
 At first I found it really hard to get around the world building because there seemed to be a lot of words but not a lot of explanation. You really are shoved at the forefront of all the action as a reader. But I really did love this world! I just had to give it some time. I think this is because everything is very unclear to begin with such as the types of witches, who Safi and Iseult actually are and an impending war (I still don't know how it began). 
 However, I think which really made the novel was after the first 200 pages everything really started to come together and when Safi and Iseult are both separated there is real development within their characters. I liked that romance wasn't the forefront of the novel either- you don't often get a girl/girl friendship being the main vocal point of any novel never mind fantasy. 
 The one POV which I really enjoyed because there was a lot of POV's was of Aeduan. He is the Bloodwitch and plays the 'bad guy'. We all love a bad guy. His witchery was also totally badass. He quickly became my favourite character and I just wanted to know more about him. I was left with so many questions at the end of the book. It wasn't fair! 
 All in all, I did enjoy this book and will be getting the sequel, Windwitch, soon. So a big thank you to Anna and Sakina for recommending it to me!

 --- [07.08.13] Updated with review. 
 Firstly, thanks to HarperCollins Australia for this review copy <3 
 "Who can fight fate, really?" 
 Earthbound held a very promising concept to me and I had this preconceived idea of what it would be like - something of a cross between Hodkin's Mara Dyer and Brennan's Unspoken. What I got instead was almost a mix of Twilight and Fallen. Everything felt so forced and coincidental, it was all a bit too much and by the end I was just sceptical of the previous 350 pages. I'm sort of at a loss as to what to say about my experience with Earthbound. There were times when I liked It, but the majority was me thinking "Wait, slow down, WHY is this happening?!"I got frustrated a lot. 
 The story commences months after the accident that killed our MC's parents and the whole plane, save for our protagonist, Tavia, who's the lone survivor. She's on the road to recovery and attending therapy when she starts seeing this boy - well actually it's one occurrence when she's in the car and then he appears in her backyard at 2am the next morning and when he disappears? Well she misses him. This was the yellow light to me that something was slightly off, but I kept reading because in Tavia's defence, she does freak out. This was chapter three. Everything went downhill in chapter four. He feels special to her. Makes her feel all warm and frothy inside. Based on one chance encounter and one where he appears at her BEDROOM window and BECKONS her outside. And then he disappears. So they haven't spoken a word and even though Tavia's mind is saying maybe he's a stalker, it's acceptable because he's her age and she feels he won't hurt her. Oh my fucking goodness everything is just wrong with that. On every bloody level. Don't worry, I'm not spoiling anything, this is only page 31. Her reactions are supposedly off because she suffered brain damage. Tavia thinks her initial reaction to vision-boy is because of her brain... I'm not sure if Pike is trying to play off that insta-love/obsession thing as something to do with Tavia's brain or not. But either way, Tavia decides her feelings are true. Or something. And she seems to react to this perfectly FINE. She wants to get to know him. NEEDS to. At this point I'm just going "Nuh qurrrlllll, just no, no matter how yummy he looks". Her priorities are all over the place. When revelations are made about certain events and situations I just felt her initial thoughts and reactions were wrong - she'd think about less important things when something else was screaming at her in the face and she'd only see this later. I also hated how EASY everything came to her. Such a freaking coincidence really. 
 "I don't even know his name, but he feels special somehow. My secret. Not the kind of secret that makes you feel guilty and empty inside; he's a cappuccino secret - something sweet and frothy that warms me from the middle out." 
 Usually this paragraph is reserved for my commenting on the male MC - cue my gushing and lip biting over how gorgeous he is and how much I love him. So you'll excuse me if I don't, except to say that I actually don't know what to say about vision-boy. He just pops in and out and there's a hug here, a kiss there, and I just got sort of bored even though there's all this enigma surrounding him. And best friend Benson? By god this guy was ANNOYING as hell. In my eyes he tried too hard, was too perfect and understanding and to me that just screams that something is wrong. Everything between Benson and Tavia felt so forced. The crush, the chemistry(?), everything. I. Did. Not. Feel. A. Thing. Horrible, forced, unrelatable love triangle. And this is coming from someone who saw the devotion Jacob Black and Edward Cullen had to Bella Swan, wrong as it was. Ick. 
 All the secondary characters were so full of crap ugh. Elizabeth her therapist, Jay and Reese her step-uncle and step-aunt. All the same bland characters. Accepting and kind, encouraging, all unbelievably giving her the space she needs and supporting her. I had raised eyebrows every time I read them. And just the way everybody seemed to be ok with everything that was going on with Tavia. I mean, hello WARNING bells when your therapist says it's completely normal to be seeing things and encourages it, not asking WHY Tavia thinks she sees the things she sees. It wasn't the kind of inquisitive psychology where the other party sees how the person thinks, there was no attempt at understanding. 
 "You've made so much progress lately that I've actually been expecting you to start experiencing some... some changes." 
 "And Tavia, you might have more strange things happen. Unexplainable things. And that's okay." 
 The actual plot? It was all over the place! Pike was trying to do everything at once, packing too many ideas into one story. It got so convoluted I kept questioning "why here", "why him", "why her". I got so confused I didn't know if there were plot holes or not. It was all a jumble of science-fiction, paranormal, history, mythology and Pike tried to tie everything so it seemed connected but I just got this information dump. By the end I got the feeling Pike was trying for a conspiracy theory type feel with roots from deep within mythology and I was meant to be blown away by all this. But I just wasn't. 
 "It's the reason you see things the rest of us can't." 
 If my review didn't make sense it's because I don't really know what went on with most of the book. I got the whole story in the space of five chapters through information dumps basically. Forgive me if I feel slightly overwhelmed. 
 This book held so much potential. It was a quick read and I could see Pike trying to pull everything together. But sadly the fragments failed to give Earthbound the integrity it strived to achieve. I think there are many people out there that would enjoy this, but Earthbound just wasn't my thing. 
 "He needs me. And the world needs us."

 Update 8/4/13: 
 Okay...I had a difficult time rating this book, and kept going between 3 and 4 stars. I decided to round up because I do want to read the next one, and there were just a couple things that I didn't really like about this new novel by Aprilynne Pike. 
 So to start, the overall story was interesting and new. I thought the paranormal/supernatural element was unique and very creative on Ms. Pike's part. I was left guessing about the type of supernatural the characters were until everything was revealed. I had some thoughts about where this book was going, but it is entirely new, which is something I liked. The other thing that I really enjoyed about this novel was that it was a giant mystery. I've always enjoyed books where the characters have to put the clues together, and basically are going on a kind of "treasure hunt" to reveal the final mystery. The story keeps you on your toes, with some action sequences throughout the novel, but I'll get to why this was also a problem later in my review. I found this to be a marked improvement over the last Aprilynne Pike book, Life After Theft, and this was more on par with how I remembered her writing in her Wings series. While I definitely didn't like this novel as much as I liked Wings, I still think this is an interesting premise to a start of a series. 
 This leads me to the things I didn't like about the book (or just kind of felt eh about). This is a 
 major 
 set up book. I mean the story doesn't really even start till the end. And as soon as it really gets good, the next thing you know, the story's over and you want the next one (which is slated for Summer 2014). It's not terrible in ways of set up books... in fact, it's quite good. However, I felt there was a lot of times the book dragged, and scenes could have been cut out. 
 Another thing I didn't like was the love triangle. I know I shouldn't compare books, but since the books are by the same author, I think it's okay in this situation. In Wings, the love triangle was thrilling and I loved/hated it. The love triangle here is just blah. I wasn't anything special or anything to become excited about. While I understand the insta-love with Quinn (and it'll be okay for you too after reading why there's that insta-love later in the story), I still wasn't totally sold on it. Also, there's kind of an insta-love with Benson. It literally goes from zero to sixty in the course of a sentence or two, and I just couldn't buy it. It just all seemed very forced to me, and I couldn't get into it. However, I will give major credit to Ms. Pike...I have no idea who Tavia is going to end up with in the end. Usually, there's a pretty clear winner from the very beginning of a series, but that's not really the case in this novel. In this way, I'm interested in seeing where the love triangle goes. I just hope it gets better in the following books. 
 Finally, I didn't like the reveal of everything. This is more of a personal preference, but I don't like when all of the information is dumped on the reader over the course of a scene/chapter. I like when the information is slowly revealed throughout the novel, and then by the end, everything makes sense. You (and the characters) have a better sense of where the story will go and what exactly is going on in the world you were introduced to during the novel. With this novel, everything is just dumped on the reader, and since this is a new concept/world, I got a little confused. After re-reading a couple sentences, I understood everything better. However, I wish that the information could have been relayed over the course of the novel, or even just over a couple of chapters that were spread out. There was just too much at once. 
 Overall, this is a promising start to a new series. While it won't be as good as the Wings series, I have high hopes for it. Aprilynne Pike knows how to write a great, thrilling story. I'm looking forward to learning more about the world and how it develops in the next book. I would recommend reading it, but I think the next book will be the ultimate test of how good this series will be. Happy reading!
