Picking uo a book from a author I know and love, she has never failed me. This time around, she took my breathe away, taking me on a unexpected journey of truth and lies. 
 1. Plot. The plot of the book is brilliant. I love how in an instant, the reader is moving with the plot, feeling every depth of emotion. The story really moves with the reader and I can appreciate that. I enjoyed being out of the loop and overcoming every single plot twist and turn with Tavia. 
 2. Build Up. The author did a great job in building up tension, trust, secrets, etc. GAH! I want to explode and tell you everything!!! I will not. Trust me when I say that I thought I had it all figured out....I was wrong. 
 3. Love interest. This too was also done extremely well. With the turn of event at the end of the book, I'm VERY interested in seeing where this love interest will go. At this point, I think it can go either way. Tavia is a very strong person for all that she went through. I admired her determination to see thing through. 
 4. Secret society. Yes, there is one and I really loved how well it was written. The reader is given piece by piece and able to make connections at the right time. I really enjoyed the back round to the society. It's gives the story much more depth and information to look forward too. I'm anxious to see exactly how it will all played out now that certain secrets where exposed. 
 5. Excitement. This story brings enough excitement to make your heart race! I really loved the world building, the setting and breaking of trust. Towards the end of the book, I didn't even know who to trust anymore. I was getting so caught up in the book that every decision that Tavia made, made ME nervous!! 
 An excellent start in series that I know will impress me, Earthbound is unstoppable. Jam-packed with on the run action, intense love and secrets, Earthbound serves up everything you want in a story. An effective thrill ride from start to finish, Earthbound rocks!

reference_books.title: The Slap
reference_books.review_text:
Lazy. My major problem is this: it is apparently narrated by eight separate people... but they all sound exactly the same. 
 Briefly, The Slap begins as an extended family gathers for a suburban barbeque. One of the children gets out of hand and one of the other parents gives it a slap. There is uproar and the novel explores the ripples afterwards. 
 The narration is close third person, so although the 'I' pronoun isn't used we're following the thoughts and feelings of each individual. Eight sections, eight narrators. But they all sound exactly the same. 
 The characters' dialogue, both quoted and internal, sounds like it was written by one person. No effort has been made to create different people with their own vocabulary, thought patterns, speech rhythms or values. 
 You could argue that this similarity might come from culture and social milieu. After all, they are at the same barbecue. But even so, there would be individual variation from the characters' different natures. In the simplest terms, some would be introvert and some extravert, yet they all have similar levels of aggression and introspection - ie the emotions and urges behind their speech and thoughts are the same. 
 Indeed, characters in The Slap have many reasons not to be similar. They have an assortment of occupations, which form their daily environments - a TV scriptwriter, a vet, a civil servant, a businessman. They're different ages too: narrators span the generations from schoolkids to grandparents. Just these life situations alone should mean they have different thought processes and vocabulary. 
 Also, the cast is culturally diverse - we have Indian-Australian, Greek, Greek-Australian, Aboriginal-Muslim. Indeed the book has been praised for this, which can only have been an idiotic political knee-jerk because their provenance makes no difference to their internal identity - and internal identity is what we see in a novel. 
 In The Slap, all the characters speak with one voice and default to one pattern of behaviour. 
 When upset, which they are a lot, they express it in exactly the same language. They have the same reactions. They want to smash things or people. They often think back over incidents and arguments and wish they had hit the offending person, pummelled their faces, grabbed them by the hair and shouted obscenities at them. 
 This similarity especially shows in cursing, which they all do plenty of, and with the same words. Readers really notice when all the characters have the same curse personality. 
 When husbands are getting annoyed about something, the wives all dismiss it with a smile. All of them. These women aren't identical twins or even ethnically similar; the reaction doesn't have a cultural reason. It's just what they all do. 
 A lot of the men react to outrage by becoming sexually aroused. This might be an interesting way to characterise one individual, but when all of them do it it looks as though the author can't imagine any other reaction. 
 Thankfully, all those stiffening members get some exercise. When the characters do have sex, which happens a lot, it proceeds in exactly the same way - same emotional tone, same preferences, same sequence of manoeuvres. A few characters break the pattern here: the teenagers and the grandfather don't get a roll in the hay, but if they did we can guess how it would go. 
 Sequences of anger, sex and other kinds of extremis should tear the characters' masks off. They should show us who they really are. 
 The same goes for habits when in private. Quite often in The Slap, a character looks at their reflection or a body part and thinks about themselves - an amateurish, stagey cliche. They gaze in the mirror and muse. Or look at a pregnant belly and think. What they do in privacy should be ways to differentiate their souls, even if their backgrounds are similar. 
 Perhaps characterisation wasn't the author's priority. Maybe he was most interested in his themes - which are family, friendship, relationships, society, parenthood, maturity, violence, anger. If so, this was an unfortunate way to do it, as we have eight puppets operated by the author, which adds up to a shallow read.

reference_books.title: The Teleportation Accident
reference_books.review_text:
I'll declare from the outset: I couldn't get more than a few pages in. Neither could my husband, who is more tolerant of difficult beginnings than I am. But I can't understand how this got published, nor how the writer appears to have won several prizes for fiction. Normally I wouldn't think it fair to review under such circumstances, but it's the prizes that tipped me over the brink. 
 It begins with a meandering account of a man who's building a teleportation machine, inspired by a similar machine that was built some centuries earlier. Our hero has a name that rhymes with 'Loser', which probably demonstrates how he's a SYMBOL in thin disguise. 'Symbol in thin disguise' is one of this book's problems - the writer doesn't care one iota about his characters as people, and doesn't want us to make the mistake of being curious about them as anything more than puppets for his ideas. And they're not terribly interesting ideas either - two people making daft devices, but somehow narrated in a style that lacks all warmth and humanity. 
 Which brings me to the writing style. You could forgive a lot (especially of a prizewinning author) if his prose was beguiling. Beauman's is unpleasantly smug, haranguing his characters for not being as clever as he is (and enjoying the fact). 
 But as I said, I read only the beginning. It could be that once you get past this stinker of an opening, you find a clever, rewarding book. I couldn't get there; but if you did, do tell me why it was worthwhile.

reference_books.title: The Mountain Story
reference_books.review_text:
Nothing about this especially grabbed me. It does have its good points, however it wasn't the special read that I expected from the blurb. 
 In summary, the situation is this. The narrator is harking back to a time when he went up a mountain to commit suicide, ran into a group of people, and one of them didn't survive. Now clearly he did, or he wouldn't be telling the tale, so the main piece of curiosity is who died instead of him. And there's certainly nothing wrong with that scenario. 
 The author deftly sets up expectations and keeps us guessing. There are reasons why most of the characters could die, though I thought the actual death wasn't very plausible. It seemed to be one of those situations where a character has to behave in a stupid way. 
 Also I found a lot of the action was quite repetitive, and could have been streamlined to make a tighter read. I confess I ended up skimming because my attention wasn't sufficiently held. There's also a back story plot about the narrator's friend who had an accident, and that seems pretty average and a bit strung out. 
 But something I did enjoy is the way the ordeal changes the narrator's three companions. They're three generations of one family, and during the story they rub their rough edges off, bare their secrets and come to a new understanding.

reference_books.title: Fates and Furies
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I read this as part of a book club. If I hadn't been committed to a podcast about it, I wouldn't have finished it. 
 It's beautifully written. Ms Groff has a remarkable facility with language. Her prose is dense and intimate; she turns emotions inside out and puts you right into the truth of a moment. But for a large part of the book, this was not backed up by substance. 
 Fates and Furies is the story of a marriage, seen from two perspectives. The first 60% focusses on Lotto (short for Lancelot), a beautiful young man who marries an enigmatic woman called Mathilde. The language certainly enthralled me in the early chapters; every page was a delight. But gradually I began to suspect there was nothing else. I felt no pull, no curiosity. Lancelot seemed dull; hardly worth so much attention. He seems not to have an interesting personality, or an interesting problem that makes us eager to spy on him. 
 Some of our group felt his was deliberate; indeed a delicious irony. I felt it was misjudged. 
 One of our group countered that 'not all books have to have car chases'. I agree - but they do need something. Plot doesn't have to be a hooligan or an explosion. Action can be very tiny. 'Interior' books can be spellbinding, but they must keep you curious. Look at Steinbeck and East of Eden - it's a long voyage through several characters' lives and lacks a conventional 'goal' or 'purpose', but their actions and psychology keep us fascinated to follow them. Fates and Furies didn't keep me fascinated. 
 Groff certainly seems to indicate we shouldn't take everything at face value. She uses an interesting technique of head-hopping. Within one paragraph we might have several points of view - a friend, then another, then even the neighbour's cat. This creates a state of detachment, telling us to view some of the action like an account of a period of history rather than a series of events we engage with. At other times, she pulls us into Lotto's experience so that we feel what he feels. 
 She also indulges in asides to the reader, breaking the fourth wall. After a character quotes the Robert Frost poemabout the world ending in ice or fire, Groff adds, in square brackets [fire]. I liked this occasional spark from the author. but at other times, I found it intrusive - after relating something that Lotto did, she adds [glutton]. To me, that was a clear sign that she was indulging Lotto too too much. Possibly it accounts for why we saw so much of him. 
 Then there are the dramas. Lotto becomes a renowned playwright and Groff treats us to some of his work. There's a big problem with plays-within-plays, or books-within-books. We know they're fake. So what we look for is illumination of things we're curious about in the story's 'real' world. By the time the plays appeared, I was very uninterested in Lotto's inner state, his family or hopes and fears, so the plays were an ordeal to read. Especially as one of them goes on for a considerable number of pages. Later, when Mathilde takes over the narrative we see that she massaged them without Lotto's knowledge, but that still doesn't excuse them occupying so much of the book. Again, it seemed to confirm my impression that the author was indulging her character Lotto. But others in the book group felt that the direness of the plays was an ironic joke - though they all admitted they found them gruelling. My feeling was that the irony could have been achieved with much less text. 
 At about the 60% mark, Lotto dies and the narrative switches to Mathilde. Here we have a more conventional plot - Mathilde is a strange and twisted girl and she does odd things. We revisit certain moments from Lotto's life and see what he was blind to. There are some truly memorable and affecting moments such as an abortion sequence, and a scene where Mathilde finds Lotto dead at his desk. These were beautifully done. Mathilde's voyage through absolute grief is truthful and harrowing with standout moments. I just wish she hadn't spent so long on Lotto. 
 Ultimately, I found this to be a book that coasts mainly on writing style. Strip that away and it becomes like a high-dazzle movie with astonishing special effects but little substance. The characters are not especially unusual or remarkable; and certainly they are not worth the close scrutiny this book gives them. I saw several reviews that suggested it could have been a lot better with a thorough edit - and I have to agree.

Wow, such positive reviews on this book...I'm still baffled as to why I didn't like it. I love time travel books but I could not get into this one at all. I found this story very hard to rate. 
 It was a very up and down reading experience for me for three fourths of the book. And for pretty much the last fourth of the book I just wanted it to be over with already. 
 The writing style was just ok for me. Pretty straightforward, barebones writing style; nothing beautiful about the way the prose was constructed. I've read plenty of books where the writing wasn't as strong that I still really enjoyed, but this book just didn't capture my attention. 
 There were plot devices and clever choices the author made that I really appreciated, but for me, it was a story that didn't hold my attention well. 
 Definitely not a bad book, but not one I would recommend.

I've been ambivalent about some of Powers' work, finding some of his later books not as immediately accessible as I'd like, but this early classic gets it right, perfectly blending big ideas and the near-poetic references to myth and history with all the virtues of the thriller format. 
 Summary: Brendan Doyle, expert in English Literature, is hired by a rich but eccentric man and offered a rare chance to see his subject matter in person, by acting as a tour guide to the period itself. His patron has discovered the means of traveling backward through time and is offering tours for the very rich to jaunt centuries back and witness historical events firsthand. 
 As an expert on Samuel Coleridge, Doyl is tasked to walk the paying guests through a lecture and reading by the poet himself on one of his historically documented presentations. 
 While doing so, however, he runs afoul of the minions of an undead Egyptian sorcerer, plotting to bring about the end of England and a resurged Egyptian empire. 
 From there, things only get better. 
 The thriller format fits the subject matter, giving readers a breakneck pace of action and unexpected plot twists. There are a number of nods to historical mysteries, such as an explanation for Lord Byron's early and unexpected presence in both the east and England, as well as some creative and fantastic answers to events surrounding some of the great literary figures of the age and their influences. 
 Particularly interesting was seeing how Powers manages to refer to documented historical events, while inserting his adventure story in the background, then showing the impact of one on the other. The central conceit: these time travelers aren't changing history, they were there all along and their actions contributed. 
 There were moments of casual revelation about a mystery or a character's secret that made me want to flip back and re-read earlier sections with that in mind, even as I wanted to hurry ahead and keep up with the excitement of the pace. There were comic pratfalls and grotesqueries and profound moments, and it's not every book that can combine obscure serial killers, an evil clown, a werewolf, Egyptian myth, famous poets and the Beatles all in less than 400 pages. 
 The only flaws were toward the end, when loose ends were tied up a little too neatly, but even that has its place, since things had to happen as history recorded them. 
 Overall: a great historical fantasy and definitely worth reading through again.

I have had this on my to be read shelf forever, it ended up being an okay read. It really wasn't what I was expecting. This book is supposed to be one of the main books that started the steampunk genre and it really doesn't have that much steampunk at all in it. It is more about time travel, Dickinson era London, literature, and the preservation of Egyptian supremacy. 
 This may have been better if I hadn't listened to it on audiobook. The book switches POV a lot and the narrator of the audiobook didn't really pause between POV changes. So it would take me a few sentences before I had figured out that we had switched characters; it made the book very confusing to follow at points. 
 I have also heard this called a YA book...it is absolutely not a YA read. The main character is a middle aged man and there are topics of torture, abuse, and rape. Although nothing gets too explicit, this does seem more geared toward adults. 
 Some parts of this book were very slow...part of that is because there are just too many different character points of view we read from. There is a lot in here that didn't actually seem to add much to the plot. 
 Like all time travel stories things get a bit twisted and turned, and there are places where things don't quite match up or make sense. There is some interesting irony in this book, especially towards the end and I enjoyed that quite a bit. 
 There were a few times when I almost stopped listening to this audiobook because I just could not pay attention to what was going on, it was just boring and not all that engaging. 
 Overall parts of this were okay but most of it was boring. There are some interesting twists and turns that the book takes which were enjoyable. I didn't really enjoy the characters all that much; there were just too many of them and the story switched between all their POVs too abruptly. If you are really into time travel stories you might enjoy this book. Otherwise I would look elsewhere. This is not a steampunk read.

Storyline: 1/5 
 Characters: 1/5 
 Writing Style: 3/5 
 World: 2/5 
 --Below information added approximately two years after original reading-- 
 I had a hard time getting into this. It always seemed like a case of telling a story for the sake of telling a story. I was never impacted by or involved with a character or storyline. I never found the world full, intriguing, or even interesting. Everything fit together in haphazard and fumbling ways. In the end it was just too dependent on spectacle and genre devices. 
 There was one fabulously described and constructed scene, however, that still sticks with me Monsters in the sewers of Jacky . Still, it wasn't enough to make this even mildly palatable.

I really wanted to love this book but once again I face a story that is filled with lots cool ideas that don't mix very well with each other. 
 You see, there's a little bit of everything in The Anubis Gates: Time Travel, Magic, Egyptian Gods, Secret Societies, Poetry, Historical Fiction, Werewolves, Body Snatchers. All of that is cool but there's like a thousand moments where each of those elements feel like they shouldn't be where they are. 
 Powers writing style doesn't help either. It gets confusing more than once. He just feel the need to tell you how things almost are but never how things actually are. So everything is vague and sketchy. He also needs to introduce a and finish a subplot in almost every paragraph. I found it annoying. 
 Another classic that didn't live up to the hype (For me). But It's fine.

Well, you certainly have to admire a guy who can pull this off. It's enough of a challenge to resolve the conundrums faced with time travel, but add in a body-switching werewolf, a deformed clown lord of beggars, 
 sorcerers, poets, and enough surrealism to make Felini proud, and you can't help but feel obligated to keep reading. I was 20 pages into The Anubis Gates when I decided it wasn't for me. I went out and picked up 
 a Ruth Rendell novel, came home and after checking out the Amazon reader reviews again, I decided to give it another 10 pages or so to see if it would take. It did, and 100 pages later I was certain I was reading the 
 best novel I'd read all year. 
 Unfortunately, the outrageousness overtook what momentum the novel had for me. The last 100 pages were somewhat of a struggle to get through and it got to the point where I just wanted to get it finished. However, 
 don't let this dissuade you from giving it a whirl. The first 200 pages are marvelous, and a brilliant effort. I'm sure there are many of you who will feed off the frenzy for the entire ride, so give The Anubis Gates a try.

** spoiler alert ** 
 The premise of this book is that time travel is possible if one knows where certain "gaps" in the flow of time are. The main character gets taken back with a group, then gets stuck in the past by a group of people trying to restore the power of the ancient Egyptian gods. While I think this premise has great potential, I didn't think this book fulfilled it in the way I would like to have seen. Once the main character gets stuck back in 1800's England, the plot becomes really convoluted. He goes from one life-threatening situation to another, and then even from one body to another, with little or no time spent by the author on emotional development or plot building. I couldn't finish it.

book_b.title: Cloud Atlas
book_b.user_review: Beautiful writing, ambitious concept that didn't really work. In fact it looked like several short stories strung together and to me didn't add up to any coherent whole.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Thisbook is very clever and is a compelling read. 
 The stories failed to engage me so i dont care about the chars, which is a big flaw in my mind. 
 I will be looking out for more from this author as he is clearly a master storyteller.

It's rare, I think, for a novel to be this intellectually stimulating while being so emotionally challenging. I love that in particular about Mitchell--how, despite writing high-brow fiction, he manages to create such full-fledged, sympathetic characters. This book is mind-blowing and beautiful, and I'm happy to say it lived up to its ambitious, high-concept promise. I found The Thousand Autumns of Jacob de Zoet more reader-friendly, but Cloud Atlas is one of those books you look back upon with, "HOW did he do it?!" It's indisputably brilliant yet immensely satisfying. I can't wait to read the rest of his backlist!

An amazing read! Will admit at first I wasn't sure I would stick with it, I'm glad I did, because it was rewarding. I loved how all the stories built on each other both forward and back, the different styles Mitchell used to deepen your relationship with characters. The only probably I have now is I'm not sure I want to see the movie. Because the casting (or at least what I know of it) doesn't mesh with the characters I grew fond of.
Read about 1/3 of book. Could not follow. Slept a lot.
Not enjoyable at all. Way too difficultly written and not entertaining

I'm giving this book 4 stars because it is extremely well written. The author is kind of amazing at character development, and writing in each character's voice. He makes them all unique, and each one tells a different story. That's a pretty amazing trait. Of course, I didn't love all the characters, but then, I don't love every person either, so it makes sense. It's a very interesting read and I like the over-arching themes of treating races the same, appreciating art, and developing compassion throughout the book.

Oooooooooooookay, so, needless to say, I started reading this book cause I absolutely fell in love with the movie. And well, I was warned............this book is nooooooooooooooooothing at all like the movie. I mean, oh, it is, but it goes into waaaaaaaaay more detail for faaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaar longer than the movie did and honestly, that lost my interest for me. I'm not sure when or if I'll ever be able to pick it up again. Hopefully I'll try, just can't say when. 
 So! If this sounds like the book for you, then go ahead, the detail was amazing and the characters really came alive, I just couldn't get into it. :)
Enjoyed the stories on their own standing, but as a whole book? Baffling!!

Ok, so I have to be honest on this one. I have tried several times to pick up this book but the way that David Mitchell writes is simply and utterly tedious. 
 Several short stories that are so weak and I am not going to review each and one of them. The "linking" of the stories, I simply did not get it and at the end trying to make a point of things that is completely and utterly nonsensical! 
 I have never in my life felt so disappointed. I really do not recommend this book.

Spinta dai positivissimi commenti al film ricevuto da amici e vari siti internet, mi sono cimentata nella lettura delle seicento pagine di Atlante delle Nuvole e, ahime, piu procedevo nella lettura piu mi sembrava di non vederne mai la fine. 
 Veramente ammirabile la tecnica di Mitchell, il racconto a matrioska con sei storie che si aprono l'una sull'altra per poi richiudersi su se stesse, tecnica che mi ha colpito e inizialmente non mi ha lasciato staccare gli occhi dal libro. Poi arrivano le storie: sei narrazioni tra loro differenti per stile ed ambientazioni che inevitabilmente portano il lettore a preferire il diario di di Edwing o l'intervista a Sonmi ma che tutto sommato riescono ad attirare l'attenzione del lettore perche ogni volta interrotte per poter introdurre il nuovo racconto. 
 Cio che piu mi ha lasciata interdetta e la linea sottile che dovrebbe collegare i vari protagonisti delle diverse narrazioni, i labili legami che dovrebbero essere i fili conduttori dell'intera storia e dell'intero romanzo: il bene o il male, la reincarnazione o il karma o piu prosaicamente il chi lo sa. 
 Non so se e stata solo un'impressione personale ma seicento pagine che ti trascinano sempre piu lentamente verso la fine per poi lasciarti con queste domande e questi dubbi non ti invogliano di certo a ricominciare la lettura per risolverli. Mi vien facile pensare che forse i dettagli cosi labili sarebbero dovuti essere maggiormente sottolineati in un romanzo cosi lungo e in un certo modo anche complesso. E' raro che dica una cosa del genere ma a questo punto spero nella trasposizione cinematografica e confido nella speranza di veder almeno risolto qualche mio dubbio esistenziale. 
 Una cosa e certa: a Mitchell daro una seconda possibilita con un altro romanzo ma questa volta non mi dovra deludere.

sample_reviews.review_text: This book was OK. It wasn't GREAT for me for several reasons...I felt Williams evil-ness was clearly established, and his evil deeds were redundant. I also felt that they kept building Ellen up... But never fully created her character. The book was unnecessarily long for me. However, Ken Follet is clearly very talented and I absolutely respect his work.

The unrelenting mindless smashing of women and their spirits just wore me out. Yes yes medieval times, I get it I get it. But this book does not leave me with a heroic soaring sense of the masterful creation of gothic cathedrals, it leaves me spitting mud out of my mouth. Wore. Me. Out.

Loved the character development, but didn't love the cathedral descriptors. Can't picture that in my head...some parts were very slow, but overall a good book. 
 Ok, after some time away from the book I was able to reflect with more love for Pillars. Very well written, I may even attempt World Without End.

Anachronistically strong female characters. The male charcters are are all evil, useless/bumbling, pathetically impotent due their faith, or accomplished only insofar as they have been supported by a woman. That's probably why this appeals so widely, reaching even the "Oprah's Picks" types.

I kinda hated this book. Ludicrous plot lines dependent on both ridiculously melodramatic behaviour and startling coincidences. I read historical fiction in part because it offers a entertaining way to learn more about the past, but the detail was actually pretty scant. And the main female character was rarely mentioned without an explanation as the current state of her boobs (firm or dropping, swaying, bouncing or restricted. Yes really). Which was at least pretty funny, albeit unintentionally so.

*SPOILERS* 
 Very good. I had watched the mini-series so I already had an idea about who the characters were and what was going to happen, but I wasn't prepared for the details of the cathedral building and monastic life that people led back then, and it brought back a lot of memories from my elementary Catholic school days. I was really impressed by the narrator of this book (whose name escapes me now) and was deeply relieved to find that he kept me attuned and attentive throughout, even when I thought I should have been bored to tears but wasn't. I was able to easily keep track of all of the characters of the story, even when they showed up later, I was able to remember them, so that also can be attributed to Follett's style of writing. When Jonathan finds out about his parents, I actually cried, it was so moving...When Phillip would scream at William to leave (i.e. the Fleece Fair), I was enraged along with him. There is a lot of historical significance in this book, which talked about Henry II and Thomas Beckett, of which I read a lot about while in Catholic school many years ago....Anyway, I really enjoyed this book and would recommend it to anyone who enjoys historical fiction, especially dealing with old England. :)
I feel like I should get an award for finishing. Alternately fascinating and weird. Very very long. So much detail. So much.
At long last I've finished it!
GREAT book. I actually bought a copy just to lend to friends. It's THAT good.

book_b.title: Blood Meridian, or the Evening Redness in the West
book_b.user_review: I really wanted to quit this book. But I promised a fellow quitter that I'd be the one to stick it out. Never got any better and I love me some Cormac, usually. The constant carnage was too much and I never cared much for any characters, since they all pretty much die. Boo.

sample_reviews.review_text: Blah.

A travelogue gallery of old west horrors. 
 There are things present in this book that made me - on multiple occasions - have to put the book down and regain my wits. There are wanton acts of grotesque and depraved violence throughout. To say that this book is not for the faint of heart is a massive understatement. 
 As far as the plot goes, it follows the tried and true literary path of meandering across its setting in various states of meditation and philosophizing. It rarely moves quick, but when it does, you'd rather it didn't. Any time the book began to mount for a major action sequence, my stomach would clench and my palms would sweat - afraid of what was about to be inflicted upon me. 
 But of course, much, much more time is spent weathering McCarthy's dusty, electrified wilderness. Some may find his prose rambling, like a delirious old man alone on his porch. But indeed there was a maddening quality to his prose and though at times it came as an avalanche of step-by-step nothings, it was layered with such profound discoveries of metaphor and poetry that I was often moved to tears or frisson. 
 Finally, regarding the ending - If you felt that No Country for Old Men's ending left much to be desired, you will not be satisfied here. 
 The story truly begins to take shape about two thirds of the way through the novel, and much before the ending you realize who this book has really been about all along.

OK, so I thought that being forced to read All the Pretty Horses for an American Lit class in college nigh on 20 years ago was why I absolutely haaaated that book. 
 Nope. 
 McCarthy's writing reaches a level of irritating only matched by scrubbing my ass on a mile-long strip of traffic spikes. 
 I can't explain it, and I don't have to. 1 star.

I listened to Blood Meridian. That might have been a mistake because I found myself drifting in and out of it. Not always knowing what was going on. It is beautifully written and I loved both No Country for Old Men and The Road but this one didn't hit home in the same manner. Maybe I need to pick up a copy and read it.

After 50%, I had it with this book. As some of the other low star reviewers pointed out, a lot of staring over yonder, while spitting and sweating in the heat of the merciless sun is being done. It seems to suggest some deep thinking in the minds of the raw and raucous souls that walk this book, but I don't get it.

Far and away the most gruesome and harrowing book I have ever read. Nothing remotely comes close. There are an alarming number of characters who do not survive the page on which they are introduced. Several perish in their introductory sentence. The Judge is one of the most terrifying characters you'll ever encounter. And as the story accumulates, you become more and more hardened to what is happening before you. The protagonist seems secondary for large sections of this novel, so it is as if you somehow become the protagonist, the mute witness to all of the horrors that take place. And you learn not to make attachments to anyone or anything. 
 The prose is excellent. Evocative and fluid. And that McCarthy manages to get in some sincerely funny lines (no funny scenes in this novel, at least not for the well adjusted) in what might be the darkest book I will ever read, that's a statement to his skill as well. 
 And it has been a long time since a book has insinuated itself so thoroughly into my thoughts, my life, while I was reading it. Isn't this the whole point of reading? To look forward so much to being able to see where the story goes? To be shaken out of our own thoughts and patterns? 
 Bleak and ghastly, but a truly excellent work.

A dark western that has several memorable characters. The historical roots of such episodes serves to accentuate the dark nature of those involved. The different writing style does take some getting used to.

It's not often that I give up on a book but I did with this one. I managed 3 of the 13 hours (audio book) before throwing in the towel. The book comes with some incredible reviews but for me, quite simply, I was bored. The Kid not nothing about him to care about, he had no objectives, no purpose, nothing even interesting. Things that did happen seemed meaningless. I'm sure that things did become relevant later on but I realised I just didn't care enough to listen any longer, I was just getting annoyed by it. 
 I regularly tell kids at school that life is too short to battle on with a book you don't like, so I took my own advice. 3.5 hrs of my life I'll never get back (the extra 30 mins due to re-listening to 2 sections early on because I thought I'd missed something as they didn't make sense. After re-listening I realised that my first impression was correct and they didn't in fact make sense!)

The language is beautiful and it grips you. It's clean and spare and yet filled with some of the most wonderful words I've read. At the same time I found it unrelentingly male, which is all right but I got a bit tired by the end of the book. As I did with some of his descriptions of the desert, probably because I grew up there and it is terrible and beautiful but he somehow makes it 'other' as well, when it slipped into that I confess it grated. My favourite lizard is the horny toad, we used to catch them and if you flip them over and stroke their bellies their bones turn to water and they lie in deepest content in the palm of your hand. So I must also confess I laughed out loud when he called it the basilisk of the desert spurting blood from its eyes -- everything in those paragraphs was demonic, possessed, hateful in a way the desert is not. But this is true of so many westerns, as though the landscape itself in the eyes of strangers somehow becomes the mirror image of their hearts bent on rapine and plunder. Indians are used the same way, every evil from the hearts of the white men is projected onto them, while they also somehow remain remote and unknowable. 
 Horny toads can certainly squirt blood from their eyes, but how cool is that?

This is the fourth McCarthy novel I have read and by far this is the most challenging. Critics have cited its magnificent language and its close representation of a defining period in American history. This is no easy read with its depictions of violence with a cast of characters who appear less than human. The prose is haunting and the desert descriptions are truly beautiful in contrast to the graphic torture scenes.

reference_books.title: Homesick for Another World
reference_books.review_text: Not sure why everyone loves this...this book was just not for me. Most of these characters are unbelievable. What's up with the constant fat shaming as well?

reference_books.title: Fates and Furies
reference_books.review_text: This book is told in two parts. Almost reading as in Two sides of a story. A husband and wife. Two sides of a relationship/marriage. Fates & Furies. Hence, the title. Fates is told mostly from Lancelot (Lotto) perception. It was decent until about mid-way I had to struggle through. I almost quit several times but didn't because I bought this instead of borrowing from my library. I had read other reviews of people who said Furies picked up the pace. I pushed through to Furies-which was told from Mathilde's point of view. It really picked up the pace and I found I didn't want to put it down. It was a decent read but I hate that I had to push myself so hard to get to that end result. I have very mixed emotions on this, as I'm sure you will read from others reviews.

reference_books.title: The Little Stranger
reference_books.review_text:
Very slow starting. I was told this was a great horror story but I found it to be more of a love story. I was frustrated throughout because Waters spent the majority of the time trying to have the main narrator rationalize the activities of the house and this was a relevant theme. It was redundant. 
 I think it had potential but it never quite got there for me.

reference_books.title: Eligible (The Austen Project, #4)
reference_books.review_text:
I must preface this review with: I am a HUGE fan of Pride and Prejudice. I have read SO many knock offs and re-imagined versions. I am a hard sell. This book is EVERYWHERE! I keep running into it. It was in EW, it was all over instagram, in my book circle of friends, it was even featured on Book of The Month club. I finally decided to give this a go. I had read Ms. Sittenfeld's Sisterland a few years back and I liked it so I was expecting great things. 
 I liked this novel. It was a quick read and funny. Again, I am a huge Pride and Prejudice fan so some things didn't sit well with me. Elizabeth seemed a little too bitchy for my taste (she is and has been my hero for my entire life) and Mr. Darcy wasn't as romantic as he turns out to be in P&P. 
 I think my disdain come purely from a die hard P&P, unwilling to change perspective. If you are more open to retelling of a wonderful classic or if you are not familiar with P&P you may love this book. I liked it but I didn't love it as much as all of the fanatics are posting all over social media.
