reference_books.review_text: BIzarre

book_a.title: Modern Lovers
book_a.user_review: This was an easy-to-get-caught-up in read but I hated every character. I did enjoy the read but I really wanted at least one character that I could side with but they were all kind of pompous and self centered. Andrew and Ruby were probably the worst.

sample_reviews.review_text: I liked this one. It was a quick and easy read. I liked the story and the characters. The writing was good. It was witty and had relatable characters. And I loved the modern take on love and marriage, and the choices we make.
Really enjoyed this. Bit of a slow burn interest wise but well developed characters and engaging family dramas.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I can't believe I finished this book! I really like The Vacationers, but this plotless novel nearly killed me. The big climax was that someone got arrested for selling unlicensed kombucha? Seriously? I'm so mad I read this; I kept waiting for a pay-off, trusting the author to give us one, and there wasn't. I don't think plot should be everything, but it needs some sort of conflict/resolution, besides hippie-man getting busted.
I wanted to like this book, having enjoyed Straub's work before, but the lack of a meaningful plot became numbing. Some interesting characters and situations, but not enough story.

In a more charitable moment, right after I finished reading this book, I conceded that Modern Lovers was a competently assembled novel and gave it two stars. There was a plot that went from A to B to C, although clearly nothing was ever at stake for any of the characters, and the sentences were mostly fine, etc. It is set in a paper-thin and blinkered New York City, in a neighborhood called Ditmas Park, where, incidentally, I lived for four years. Ditmas Park, as it really exists, is not reflected in this book at all, though clearly Emma Straub had a little map of the neighborhood taped to her writing desk, so she could get all the street intersections correct. But she does one very clever thing, which is to make one main character a real estate agent. This real estate agent's approach to the city- what a price a piece of property can fetch, how 'desirable' (read: rich) the residents are, what 'amenities' (read: expensive restaurants, yoga studios) are nearby, is reflected neatly in this novel, where all the plot points, except for the one about two teenagers having sex, revolve around the real estate issues of people who have inherited a great deal of family wealth. What a sad, shallow, lame version of New York this is. 
 Now, a few days later, I think about how boring it was, how shocking that someone like Straub can live in Brooklyn and still gesture the concept of 'hipster' by its most played-out signifier- ironic facial hair, and do so more than once- in a novel where someone squanders a hundred grand with nary a consequence, and I feel less charitable, it is a one star novel for sure.

Back in college, Zoe, Andrew, and Elizabeth were in a punk band together with another member, Lydia--an oddly untalented musician who got famous after releasing a song Elizabeth wrote for the band as her breakout single. Elizabeth and Andrew have been living off of royalty checks, Lizzie's real estate career, and sometimes Andrew's family money (cuz he's technically filthy rich). Years earlier, Lydia passed away from a drug overdose and now, a production company out in Hollywood wants to make a biopic about Lydia's time in college, the time just before she made it big as a rock star. Elizabeth is ready almost immediately to sign over her life rights and be represented by a young actress on screen. She doesn't have anything to hide, to be ashamed about. Andrew on the other hand, does have a secret that he is not ready to reveal to his wife because he thought he would never have to tell her. But when Elizabeth makes that impossible, he has to tell her the truth at last. 
 Elizabeth and Andrew have been married since they were fresh out of college, and now they have a well-behaved teen aged son, Henry. Elizabeth sees the way her best friend Zoe's relationship is failing and starts to question her own. Andrew is going through his own midlife crisis, he's never held down a career and now he just wants to figure out what to do next. He starts working with a yogi who may or may not be running an illegal business in the neighborhood. Andrew is desperately trying to find somewhere he can fit in, but that desperation causes him to make a few bad decisions. 
 Read my full review here: https://ladykatiereads.wordpress.com/...
Pampered, upper middle class Brooklynites meandering through middle age.

If I read another book by Emma Straub, it'll be her describing how she convinced the NYT to feature her book in this summer reading list. 
 http://www.nytimes.com/2016/05/27/boo...

Funny, smart, and a little twisty. An interesting look at what happens 20 years into marriage, when you realize you're not married to the person you thought you were -- and that you're not the person you wanted to be.

Modern Lovers by Emma Stroub tells the story of two families living within three houses of each other in Brooklyn. A lesbian couple, Jane and Zoe have a daughter, Ruby, who is just graduating from high school, while Andrew and Elizabeth have a son, Harry, who is between his junior and senior year in high school. Jane and Zoe have their own restaurant, Elizabeth is a very successful real estate agent and Andrew is between jobs. 
 The back story involves a band that Zoe, Andrew, and Elizabeth were in together in college, Kitty's Mustache. The drummer for this band, Lydia took Elizabeth's song, "Mistress of Myself" and made a career off of it. Although Elizabeth wrote the lyrics and most of the music, the band took joint credit for the music. After a brief, meteoric career, Lydia died young and now Hollywood has come knocking, looking to make a biopic of Lydia's story. 
 The book is engaging enough to keep a reader involved, but I was never totally taken by the characters. Although I enjoyed the two teens, Ruby and Harry, I found it extremely difficult to care about what happened to the adults. There was nothing so compelling that I couldn't have put it down at any point with no regrets. 
 There were really two major issues. First, I didn't really care about the characters. I was not emotionally involved in any way and that is a key to this book being successful. You have to care about them and if you don't, then you'll be somewhat disappointed in the end. Speaking of the end, that is also a major disappointment. Andrew makes an error that costs he and Elizabeth around $150,000 and he never tells her until the end. When he does, she blows it off like it doesn't even matter. Maybe these people should be forced to live in a Third World country with no money for a while. 
 Anyway, every characters is totally self-absorbed and prove to be a non-entity. Very disappointing. Not recommended.

book_b.title: The Art of Fielding
book_b.user_review: Found an awesome review of this book in Entertainment weekly and I rented the book from library. First couple chapters I was unsure. I couldn't put the book down and after three months I find myself still thinking about this book!! Give it a shot.

sample_reviews.review_text: The book was much better than I had expected, given that I was not the most interested in a book about baseball, but the book ended up being much more about the relationships between the characters rather than their contextual sports/academia. Overall it was a good read. Apparently more meaningful if you read Moby Dick first, but I enjoyed it nonetheless. It gets docked a star for having no strong female characters; the one female featured in the book ends up being solely defined by her relationships with the males, never as a standalone person.

To gather my thoughts before reviewing The Art of Fielding, I started reading other reader reviews. I quickly realized that was a mistake. I don't want to know about the literary community of young writers Harbach comes from, how much of an advance he got, or how jealous other first-time novelists are of his success. I returned to this blank page, where I will now write my own review with a clear mind. 
 I loved The Art of Fielding. It's a straightforward story, centering on five main characters, told in a refreshingly old-fashioned linear fashion, moving from A to B and on to C. No flashbacks, no flashforwards, no sudden jumps into parallel story lines filled with people you haven't met before. Reading Harbach's novel, I thought of Philip Hensher and The Northern Clemency. I thought of Jonathan Franzen and Freedom. But mostly I tried not to make comparisons and just enjoy the story. 
 I'm a sucker for colleges, liberal arts, and literary references, so I loved everything about Westish College and its affable president, Guert Affenlight, a Melville scholar (I especially loved the Melville references). I believed, almost to the end of the novel, that there really was a major league shortstop named Arapacio Rodriguez, and that he had written a Zen-like book titled The Art of Fielding. I did believe ... and still do ... in Henry, Mike, Owen, Pella, and Guert. Well, maybe not so much in Owen, who is essentially a foil for the stories of Henry and Guert. I was enthralled. I hung on every element of the story. I cared about what was happening and what might happen. I whispered mental advice to every character, trying to help them along. 
 Some parts of the novel were less than perfect. Guert's sudden death was too convenient, almost as if Harbach decided to cut off one of the most interesting subplots rather than take it to its conclusion. Henry's worsening inability to throw and his fall into incapacitating depression was believable; his unasked-for return to the team during a championship game, not to mention his game-winning hit, was not. But I forgave these sins, because I bought everything else; and hell, if they ever make a movie out of this novel, those cinematic bits will fit right in. 
 A comment from one of the reviews I tore myself away from keeps coming back to me. That reviewer said you need to love baseball to love this novel. Before I started reading The Art of Fielding, that was in fact a concern of mine. I was a lousy athlete in elementary and high school, and a particularly lousy baseball player. By the time I got to college I had resolved never to think about baseball again. Until I started reading this novel, I had stuck with that resolve. And now I'm here to tell you this: you don't have to love baseball to love this novel.
I didn't think I'd like this book but it surprised me. It wasn't what I thought it would be in the best way possible. Filled with Memorable characters.
My book club read this book and it was so brutal getting through it. Not my taste in a read. Didn't really enjoy any of it.
So satisfying.

I read this for my book club - it's not something I would have picked up otherwise given my complete lack of interest in baseball. So, it was okay. But I know absolutely nothing about baseball/playing team sports or Herman Melville, and I can only assume that this made a difference. I didn't understand any of the characters, much less identify with them. That said, it was a quick enough read and certainly not unpleasant. I just don't know if this one will stick with me in the long term.

4 stars 
 This is one of the rare ones where I race to the finish the first time, just to find out what happens, and then immediately go back and start sections again, just to savor the prose. Understand me: I wouldn't call this "literary fiction," exactly--it's too real-world and action-y for that label, I think. But the language SINGS in places, sailing a high, hard one past you at times or giving you a low, dirty slider at others. Beautiful, beautiful book. I can't believe it's a debut novel. (The 1 star off is because the midsection of the book drags just the teeniest bit, and some of the goings on are a little over-the-top.) 
 This is the story of: 
 --Henry Skrimshander, a shortstop with infinite potential who's recruited by a small private Divison III college that has never won a championship 
 --Mike Schwartz, team captain, informal scout, and leader of men, who thinks he's going to apply for law school 
 --Guert Affenlight, president of the college, an academic who's struck by love late in life 
 --Pella Affenlight, Guert's daughter, who's returned home after a failed marriage and is now a bit adrift 
 --Owen Dunne (the Buddha), Henry's gay roommate, teammate, and partner in crime, who Has a Secret 
 For the first third of the book, Henry is becoming the best shortstop who's ever played the game, tying his idol's record for error-free games and getting scouted by the big leagues. It all goes wrong with one throw, though, and the rest of the book covers the fallout as the team heads for the playoffs for the first time in the college's history. 
 This book works on many levels: the classic everything-hangs-on-the-last-game sports story; the small-town isolated college pressure cooker; young adults learning about themselves in relationships; the stamina required in the drive to be the best; academic bullshit; and sports politics, among others. I'd heartily recommend this book for baseball junkies (male AND female), those who root for underdogs, fans of small towns (especially in the Midwest), and those nostalgic for their college days. This book hits all these bases, and more. Home run.
this just wasn't for me. it wasn't awful but the writing and subject material just didn't interest me. I was interested enough to finish the book, though.

For me, this was one of those books that you want to begin reading again the moment you've finished the last page. I suspect it would get better and reveal more with each reading. 
 Despite the hype for this book, I resisted picking it up because I'm no fan of the game of baseball. So glad I finally did though. It's a dense, but easy read and it's about so much more than just baseball. 
 I would have given it an additional star, but even as I came to the end of the story, I still felt like I didn't have a handle on the inner workings of the main character, Henry Skrimshander. A bit of opaqueness seems in keeping with his personality though, so I tend to think that unreadable quality was intended by the author. I'll have to give it more thought when I sit down to read it again. 
 Highly recommended.

I have not liked characters this much in a long time! 
 I have always loved the movie A League of Their Own, and I think this book gave me the same warm and fuzzy feeling. You find yourself caring about the outcome of the game, but caring even more for the lives of the members that make up this misfit team. 
 A new favorite for sure -- I'm going to start my next book and find myself missing Henry and Schwartz...

reference_books.title: The Peach Keeper
reference_books.review_text: Sarah Addison Allen creates worlds in which I wish I lived. Another great story, beautifully told

reference_books.title: When She Woke
reference_books.review_text: This is a very hesitant 3 stars. I was intrigued by the premise of this book: an up-dated version of the American classic "The Scarlet Letter". This modern version tells the story of Hannah Prynne and is set in a future where the far right evangelical Christian sects have convinced the government to save money and relieve the over-crowded prision system by letting people convicted of crimes back into society. These convicted persons have been genetically altered so that their skin pigment "matches" their crimes. People who have committed drug related crimes are "chromed" and re-enter society with yellow skin; blue for offenses against children; red for murder or attempted murder. It is immediately obvious which people have been convicted of a crime. Those who've been convicted can also be "looked up" on the internet...information about their crimes, conviction and even real-time location is available to the public at large. Hannah, who comes from a very religiously conservative family, has been convicted of aborting a child...one she conceived while having an affair with her married pastor. All told, this book asks difficult questions...similar to it's inspiration. However, this book does not stand up as well as the original. The original was less about whether it is right or wrong to bear an illigitimate child and more about personal responsibility and how petty people, blind to their own mistakes and failings, feel justified in treating badly and judging someone with more obvious sins. As Hester protects the identity of the father of her child we are able to compare how different people individually deal with guilt (when guilt is hidden, secret or unknown versus known by an entire community). This book tries to ask similar questions but gets very side-tracked...by abortion, ultra-conservative Christian sects, vigilantism. It reads more as a cautionary tale than as an invitation to think about how we deal with each other (all told, I'd rather read "Handmaiden's Tale" to fill my cautionary tale quota). It could have been much better...

reference_books.title: Oryx and Crake (MaddAddam, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I am usually a fan of science fiction...but sometimes authors write science fiction badly. This story, while intriguing, had so many holes: I understand the need to leave the reader slightly uninformed, thus creating a feeling of unease and angst, but leaving out so many important details makes the story entirely meaningless. The idea of a rampant and ravaging virus, destroying almost all of mankind (except for Crake's creation...) in intriguing, but all the other "futuristic" advances were weird and laughable.

reference_books.title: Shiver (The Wolves of Mercy Falls, #1)
reference_books.review_text: easy read. Not too different from all the other paranormal teenage angst-ridden love stories, but the writing is a little more poetic and pretty (if only just...and that's mostly because she quotes Rilke and I really like Rilke). It must be nice to have such clueless, absent and ineffective parents ;)

reference_books.title: If I Stay (If I Stay, #1)
reference_books.review_text: An amazing book...Mia, a high school senior and Julliard aspiring cellist, is in a horrible car accident with her family. She hovers between life and death, aware of what is happening around her comatose body. She realizes that she must choose between living and dieing. Each chapter is organized in real time but intercepted with flashbacks highlighting Mia's life and the things she weighs as she decides if she should stay. This is an intriguing read...a great description of what music is like, what making music is like, for a musician and how a love for creating and experiencing beauty color the whole of your life. I may have to buy this one...

book_a.title: Trapped
book_a.user_review: This is a fairly good YA novel about kids being trapped in their high school during a freak, multiple day blizzard. It details how they survived (well, most of them...)and how they thought differently about themselves and each other (the group includes three boys who are good friends, two girls who are good friends, a "loner" kid and a kid who is perpetually in detention or other trouble. It was an easy read...it would provide a great platform for discussion about taking care of yourself when the adults are gone (the one teacher assigned to make sure the kids waiting for rides after the majority of the student body and staff have left also leaves the building early on when they think they see a snow plow...) and how easy it is to judge other kids based on who they associate with or where they sit at lunch.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 Trapped has a premise that would catch any reader's attention -- a group of students get trapped alone at school when a disastrous snowstorm hits the area. Anyone would be intrigued, and start thinking of what these teens would do in order to survive. Unfortunately, readers won't be given much of anything. 
 There was really no attempt to connect the readers with the characters, to get them involved in the plight. The idea of the story can only carry someone so far, and when there is practically nothing happening, no step to move forward, the reader will quickly grow bored. 
 Similarly, the ending isn't any better. Although the main character is rescued, the only sense of relief anyone would feel is that the book is finished. There is no word on the other students who were trapped, no sense of what's been happening in the outside world, nothing. As a result, the ending, like the rest of the story, falls completely flat. 
 A real let-down.

I was kind of excited about this book when I read the summary of it but was kind of left disappointed in the end. I had never heard of another book taking on this topic and I thought it would be really good. The beginning was good especially when the snow kept falling and falling and wasn't going to stop anytime soon. But towards the middle and right before the climax (snow coming through the roof of the school) and then at the end I kept wanting to read more to figure out if the kids would be saved. 
 Didn't really like Scott (main character), thought he was kind of annoying and acted like a girl rather than a strong male character. Also the other students weren't very well developed and I felt like I still really didn't know them at the end of the story. Also I felt like the kids weren't really smart with trying to stay warm too. 
 Also, what happened to the teacher that left? I'm assuming he died but I dunno. 
 I thought this book had a lot of potential but kind of fell.

If I could give 0 stars I would. 
 The plot interested me - a group of teens stuck in their high school during a storm and conditions get worse and worse. However, Absolutely nothing happens in this story. Nothing. It was cold, the kids ate food, then they slept. Over and over for 220+ pages. 
 What's worse was the writing. The author clearly hasn't been a teenager in a very long time. His attempts to be "cool" were awkward and so annoying I got too angry to keep reading. I toughed it out to see what happens at the end, where it abruptly ends with the character saying something irrelevant. What a waste of time.

Bored now. Information in this book is relayed in first-person format and is rather like a cross between a novel and a shopping list. There are scattered foreshadowings which are probably supposed to be teasers but instead are annoying reminders of what hasn't happened yet. I kept hoping the pace would pick up and someone would go "rogue cannibal". Alas, life is too short to read dull books.

The central premise is great, but the execution is a little lacking. While trapped in their school under an ever-increasing pile of snow, seven high-school students try to stay warm and fed while they wait for rescue. Some characters are well-developed, but others are left with little to do. And it always felt like there should have been more drama than there was.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Notes 
 High School Students become trapped after a blizzard...some parts are really interesting - tricks to adapt, survival skills 
 The book added a "competition" element when students are not rescued after the "normal disaster relief period" Alliances are formed and enemies are made 
 *i didn't like the storyline of girls attaching themselves to guys for protection or others receiving unwanted attention 
 The concept was good but some side stories were weak...for example 
 food & supples (general mysteriously airlifted to them & unceremoniously dropped inside)

Totally totally riveting. I read this during breaks at work, and had to tear myself away everytime my breaks were over. I'd come out and rave to my coworkers. This is a slim volume of just 232 pages, and the chapters are really really short. There's a dramatic sense of suspense, as Northrop foreshadows how horrible the trauma will be from the very beginning. 
 Seven teens are "trapped" in a high school during the mother of all snowstorms. As the snow piles up, the power and water goes out, and after a while, the snow covers the whole first floor, where the cafeteria and other niceties are. The kids are stuck in a classroom in the second story. Interpersonal struggles don't make things any easier. 
 I definitely agree with those who say the ending is abrupt, but the rest of this is good enough that it's ok.
Interesting at times but could have been shorter. The ending was too abrupt.

It was just ok for me. 
 Rating: 5/10 
 Full review at Unraveling Books
So much wasted potential! This story could and should have been a fun read, but the kids lack imagination, and ultimately it's mostly about acne and frozen pudding. Very disappointing.

book_b.title: Wicked: The Life and Times of the Wicked Witch of the West (The Wicked Years, #1)
book_b.user_review:
yeah...what's up with this book?! 
 The musical is very, very loosely based on this...

sample_reviews.review_text: The stage adaptation is fantastic, the book...not so much. Sadly, I would not recommend this book. Go see the show instead! I mustered up two stars because the basic story is fantastic.

I was really diappointed with this book.A few of my friends have read it and seen the play.They thought it was great.I on the other hand found it just a little too far fetched for my liking.I read the Oz books by L.Frank Baum and loved them.I understand that those were far fetched as well.And I also knew when I began reading this book that it was not A continuation of Oz.It is about the Wicked Witch and her life.It fell completely short of my expectations.I applaud Gregory Maguire for his efforts but I will not be reading the next book in the set.I won't say I won't try to read some of his other work,but I'm done with this set.

I'm apparently one of few who didn't gush over this book. 
 I do like the idea of the story about the side story... 
 I would not have made it through the reading - but sometimes audio is not the best way to receive a story.

It's come up a lot in my life recently. There's the musical... There's the sequel... Rebs bought it and despised the beginning so heartily she took it back to her bookstore... Di liked it enough to IM an endorsement. And I've been listening to a podcast version of The Road to Oz over the course of the last few months. 
 If your only experience with Oz is the movie, you may not enjoy the book as much as if you have read some of the Frank L. Baum stories the movie is based on. But having said that, I thought that most of the book was very clever, thorougly drawing on Baum's world as it does -- from the characteristics of the various inhabitants of the nation to the types of characters he peopled his books with to the small details that changed between the book and the movie (those slippers aren't really ruby in the stories, for instance). 
 Maguire enjoys playing with language and includes a number of Word Wealth words. My friend Amani was so taken with his vocabulary she started writing down words she wanted to learn. 
 Maguire also began an interesting discussion on the role and/or nature of evil. Is there such a thing? If so, what makes a character evil or makes them do evil things -- free will, destiny, some combination? Is collateral worth the price of eliminating evil? Is it cut-and-dried? And are there always two legitimate sides or perspectives to things? 
 Unfortunately, something happened toward the end of the novel and for whatever reason he rushed around trying to squeeze the end of the story in before the book got too long. My head reeled as he bounced from one scene to another and as he tried to wrap Elphaba's (the witch's real name) story up as neatly as possible. But in his hurry to close the curtain, he undermined the importance of the questions he raised earlier, leaving me a little disappointed in what was otherwise a terrific novel.
I love the music, I want to see the musical, so I read the book, and was really bugged by how it dragged on and ended not the way I wanted it to.
This book bored me to tears and I really don't understand what all the fuss was about. I found it irritating to read and I can't even remember if I finished it or not!

I know it's hugely popular and has a show and all but....ugh. Book was terrible and misogynistic. Play was great. All the changes they made in the play were one that should have been in this book. I couldn't even muster interest in the ending...I kept skimming pages in the last quarter just to finish the darn thing.

I thought that this was one of the most cleverly written books i've ever read. the idea of the story of the wicked witch of the west from her point of view...growing up...giving us the reasons behind her bitchyness...just genius. i loved that she was not a bad person...but was turned into one by misunderstanding and society.
I wanted to love this book more than I did, based on its premise. Still entertaining. Wish I had seen the musical.

I cannot understand it. 
 Really.

reference_books.title: The Maze Runner (Maze Runner, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I seem to be the last person to read this book, but as the film's out next year, I decided to jump on the bandwagon! And this was a great, intense read. James Dashner literally drops the reader in the middle of the action as Thomas wakes up in a strange place called the Glade, unable to remember anything except his own name. He and the other teens there seem to be part of some kind of experiment, trapped in the middle of a maze populated by horrific monsters. Thomas determines to get to the bottom of what's going on. 
 Needless to say, this is a gripping read. The action is frantic and the mystery of Thomas and the others' situation is suspenseful. Dashner sure knows how to keep up the suspense, and the monsters are wonderfully creepy. Definitely recommended!

reference_books.title: Dinner with a Vampire (The Dark Heroine, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I first saw this book in my local newspaper. The author, Abigail Gibbs, originally began posting the story on Wattpad at the age of 15, and gained millions of readers, ending up scoring a six-figure deal with Harpercollins before she'd even started university! Pretty impressive! 
 When Violet witnesses a horrifying mass-murder in the middle of London, the last thing she expects is to be kidnapped by the murderers, who are actually vampires, and held prisoner in their grand house. She swiftly discovers that she's been dragged into a sinister vampire-ruled underworld in which her position as the daughter of the city's Defence Minister makes her an unwilling pawn in a power play between the vampires and the slayers trained to kill them, and the subject of a prophecy. Now she has to choose between life and undeath, with the fate of humans and vampires alike potentially hanging in the balance. 
 It's certainly an action-packed plot, and even though the book is fairly long, I didn't find myself tuning out. The thing that bothered me at first is that Violet, the protagonist, doesn't talk like a 21st century teenager. Her narrative voice is a bit too formal, and this didn't completely gel with the modern setting and dialogue. This bothered me less as I read further, however, at least there isn't as much angst as you find in a lot of vampire fiction. This might be because it isn't YA - there's a lot of violence and gruesome moments, and the vampires are a genuine threat. 
 This isn't a bad book, but it suffers from an overlong, convoluted plot which is a tad predictable in places. I felt some situations were a bit contrived, and I didn't take to Kaspar, the main 'love interest' - he never quite lost the creepy factor for me. I thought the editing was a bit rough in places, and there were a few awkward sentences and clumsy wording which drew me out of the story. But overall I did enjoy the read, and I think this young author is at the start of a very promising career.

reference_books.title: A Court of Thorns and Roses (A Court of Thorns and Roses, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I'm a fan of Sarah J. Maas's Throne of Glass series, and I was excited to read ACOTR! I admit I don't always like fairytale retellings if they stay too close to the original. Luckily, this wasn't the case with ACOTR, in which Maas creates a stunning new world populated by three-dimensional characters and some genuinely terrifying villains. The opening is action-packed, but as I'm not a huge fan of romance-centric plots, I felt the pace lagged a bit in places until the 2/3 mark, when all hell broke loose. From then on, I was riveted! Feyre is a great heroine, strong yet vulnerable amongst the dangerous faeries. The worldbuilding is vivid and when the overarching conflict comes in, the pace is relentless. An engrossing dark fairytale with excellent characterisation!

reference_books.title: The Fiery Heart (Bloodlines, #4)
reference_books.review_text:
I couldn't wait to read the fourth in Richelle Mead's addictive Bloodlines series, and I wasn't disappointed. Sydney and Adrian's relationship gets more development as they risk everything to be together, and Sydney's decision to learn magic also puts her at risk from the Alchemists she once trusted. But now she's working to undermine them completely. 
 I liked the alternating POV's as we got Adrian's perspective as well as he struggles against the unstable mood swings brought on by using spirit magic. I like how he and Sydney both mature and how each considers the other's feelings, and the development of their relationship takes centre stage in the story. The plot wasn't as evident and I did get a bit bored with some of the recapping and tangents which dragged out the romance sub-plot but did nothing to advance the main plot. That said, I still love the characters, and this instalment brings more of the passion and drama that make this series so addictive!

reference_books.title: The Unbound (The Archived, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Oh, wow. You know there are some books which are THAT good you have trouble finding the words to express it? The kind of books you get totally lost in and are surprised when you look up and four hours have disappeared? The kind of books which worm their way into your head and you wander around in a book-haze for a few days after finishing? Just like The Archived, Victoria Schwab's sequel The Unbound totally blew me away. 
 Three weeks after the events of The Archived, Mackenzie Bishop is struggling to come to terms with what happened. As a Keeper, it's her job to prevent stray Histories from escaping from the Archive into our world, but after nearly being killed by one, she's haunted (possibly literally) by his violent presence. Worse, people are vanishing, and she starts to suspect someone is trying to frame her. 
 The Unbound has the same spellbinding combination of gripping mystery, action, romance and emotion as The Archived. I loved that we got more of an insight into the Archive, the Crew and Keepers, particularly the darker side (with the threat of Mackenzie losing her memories and consequently her identity if she fails the Archive's tests). Mackenzie herself goes through some seriously tough times. She's a great character - both tough and vulnerable, and I loved how Victoria made Mackenzie's and Wesley's relationship believably complex. 
 Oh, and the writing is beautiful. I had the dilemma of wanting to read slowly to absorb every word, but being too gripped by the plot to put the book down! All I can say is: read this series. You will not be disappointed.

book_a.title: Marked (Servants of Fate, #1)
book_a.user_review: An engaging, character-driven paranormal romance set in a future world post-environmental collapse. I really liked the twist on afterlife mythology. Cecy and Eli are strong lead characters and the chemistry between them is well-written. I did wish there was a little more focus on the plot rather than on the romance.

sample_reviews.review_text:
DNF: finished 70% 
 Nah. 
 Either I'm in a reading slump or I've been unlucky lately, cause nothing I've read recently has done it for me. 
 This is just your typical fantasy romance. The characters are generic. The plot is generic. The world building - a Boston flooded into an almost Venetian-like, disease-filled city full of reapers and ferries fighting for dominance - could be very cool but the book does it no favors.

If you like plots that are completely free of logic*, AND you enjoy characters that become instantly obsessed with one another, then I definitely recommend this book. 
 * Spoiler alert: mortals die! How does it benefit the reaping community to have mortals die young, before they have the chance to make as many babies as possible who will also eventually die?
I mean, I finished it, so I guess it wasn't terrible? but really, it kind of was.... a trainwreck in terms of the plot, characters, and romance, but somehow interesting enough to keep reading....
I tried, I really did. But the overemphasis on the romance (i.e. "He's sex on a stick" "she's so hot") overshadowed what was an interesting plot and world building. Too bad.

This book was OK, but I'm not going to read any more by this author. The basic story line was OK, but the basis for the story was a fractured mess. One race of creatures/gods who are responsible for deciding who on earth is going to die and then marks them. A group of modified humans use an electronic/magical device to find the spirits of the dead people and conduct them to the afterlife. And for each person that they mark/conduct they're paid in gold, which is then used to establish financial empires on earth? This first book in a new series ends in an unfinished plot line leading you into the next book. Sorry. I don't even care enough to read the second book.

***This review has also been posted on The Social Potato 
 This is the first adult book by Sarah Fine. I repeat. IT'S THE FIRST ADULT BOOK BY SARAH FINE. When I first heard about it, all I could think of was how much I wanted to read it and about how awesome I thought it would be and I wasn't let down. But then again, it IS Sarah Fine. When has she ever really let me down? 
 What first drew me to the book, aside from it being written by Sarah Fine, was the concept. The blurb doesn't give you much of a look into the world this book is set in but it's definitely original. It's not that no one has ever written a book about death or afterlife, hell, Sarah Fine's YA series deals with those things too, but this book, or I should say this series, has a take on it that I personally haven't read about. The basis of this world is in myth but at the same time, this book is also set in the future. 
 They live in a world where the rich people are the only lucky ones. Everyone else doesn't even have full time running water. Chocolate is so rare that even it's substitute, Mockolate, is way too expensive (this is your cue to gasp chocolate lovers). The waters are disease ridden and people don't have much prevention against diseases. Eli's sister, Galena, is looking to change that. She wants to invent a way for vaccines to mutate along with the diseases they are supposes to prevent. It would decrease the death rates by a third, but it would also become a huge drawback in the business of death, the business the Kers and the Ferrys deal in. 
 This book however, doesn't dwell too much into that, we are instead introduced into the world, like we would be at the beginning of any series. Fine helps us settle into this world she has created so that when we get around to reading the following books, we can be submerged into the world with more ease. 
 This book, is more about the characters, Eli and Cacy. They are both formidable characters to say the least. On their own, they are strong, a little bullheaded but ready to do what they can for the ones' they love but together, they are a team, they are in sync and are always there for each other to fall back on. Isn't that beautiful? 
 Like a lot of Fine's romances, this one definitely has the insta-vibes to it but Fine always crafts her romances wonderfully and we get to see how these two work together as as a team. We see how they make each other better people. They may be a little afraid to lean on one another but that's part of the process. They have feelings for one another but they need to learn to trust one another. It is a wonderful journey. The deep stuff said, this book is HAWT. With capitals. If you've read her YA books and remember how well she writes sexual tension, I am sure you'll have a vague idea as to just how hawt this book will get. 
 The main characters aside, we also have an entourage of wonderful secondary ones, my personal favorite being Moros ;) (please keep your hands off). They are developed but our main characters remain in the spotlight. I like that none of the characters are just there though. They all serve a purpose and all play an intricate part in what is going to happen in the future books aside from the fact that they will star in them. 
 This book also has a tendency to keep you on your toes. There is plenty of action and Sarah knows just how to punch you in the feels (if you don't believe me ask Nick... she had to deal with some of the aftermath.. no one heard the weird noises I was making though). None of what she does every feels unnecessary though. Things happen, but it all serves a larger plot line. Nothing can ever be perfect can it? You cannot gain one thing without losing the other and such is life. 
 I have to say though, I was a little surprised by the twist. I am not sure if it was the fact that I purposefully chose to blind myself to the possibility but I was taken off guard by the identity of the traitor. I didn't even have a specific person in mind but I was surprised that it turned out to be that person. 
 On the whole, this is a book I'd recommend to everyone who likes a good romance but also likes it when there is something interesting happening that isn't in the background.

Lily Proctor deals with life-threatening allergies every day until one day she is suddenly taken from her world into a frightening, alternate world similar to Earth but with many terrifying changes. This Salem is full of terrifying creatures and alternate versions of her former friends--and even an alternate version of herself, a girl called Lilian who is threatening the future of the world and wants Lily's help to do it. With the help of Rowan, this world's version of Lily's former ex-boyfriend, Lily discovers that she is the most powerful witch the world has seen. With her powers, she and Rowan try to stop this world's Lilian from killing lots of innocent people and find her way back home to her world. During the final battle, she and Rowan escape to another world. 
 In many ways, this book is a mess of underdeveloped, unclear ideas. Lily is a Mary Sue: perfect, self-sacrificing, almost an orphan, delicate, hated by everyone in the beginning, and incredibly beautiful but doesn't realize it. In her world, Lily is sick and weak. In this world, without spending the years it is required for natives of the world, she is incredibly powerful and her sickness is a manifestation of her power. This treatment of disease as power makes light of real issues that aren't cured by magically being transported to another world. The love triangle is forced and awkward. When they first meet, Rowan tries to kill her, and then the relationships goes from hating each other to being crazy about each other with no transition. Tristan has no real value to the plot and is only there to play the part as a male best friend, part of a love triangle, and to make sure there are lots of attractive guys. The world is confusing, with some parts fantasy, some parts historical, and some parts science fiction. The book ends with many things that are not explained, like why Lilian wants Lily in this world so badly. There is never any real tension because the reader knows that Lily will make it out unharmed because of her amazing powers. Overall, there were so many weaknesses that enjoying the book may be difficult for some people.

This is maybe more like a 2.5, but I rounded down because even though the premise was really cool, I had some major issues with it. The basic idea is that a girl from Salem, MA in our world travels to an alternate version of Salem. In this version, witchcraft is normal and accepted, and scientists are persecuted. I love alternate universe stories, and there were lots of little references to The Crucible, which was fun. But the protagonist was way too annoying for me to really like. 
 In some ways, it's just the way that maybe I have a hard time relating to a teenager. But I read a lot of YA, and I don't always have this problem. Basically, Lily is a super self-righteous vegan, who won't eat animals even to save her own life and the lives of others, which is just beyond stupid, especially when she quotes unethical farming as one of her reasons for being vegan, which is completely irrelevant in the alternate universe she goes to. There are a few other sort of issue-y rants she goes on, but those at least made sense with the character. 
 The other sort of issue I had was with the portrayal of Indians (Native Americans). Early in the book, Lily says she doesn't think there are an Algonquins left in her world. Allow me to quote the first sentences of the Wikipedia page on Algonquin: "The Algonquian are one of the most populous and widespread North American native language groups, with tribes originally numbering in the hundreds of thousands. Today, thousands of individuals identify with various Algonquian peoples." So she's wrong and also Algonquin isn't a tribal name. You can make the argument that maybe the character wouldn't know this, but I think if that's true, then that assumption should be challenged at some point. There are already so many misconceptions about Native Americans, and the author does nothing to counter those. 
 There is also a group of people in the alternate Salem that are basically Indians, although they simply refer to themselves as "outlanders." They do, however share tribal names with actual existing tribes, so I think it's safe to assume they are strongly based on the Native Americans in our universe. Or, at least, the stereotypes about them. The outlanders are, more or less, the "good guys," but they are still described in old-fashioned ways: braves, "guttural" language, painted savages, etc. So I think the author really could have done better here. 
 The narrator of the audiobook is the same narrator who did the Divergent series, and something about her voice is a little grating, but I think it suited the character well. It threw me off a little when she used the New England sland "bubbler" (meaning drinking fountain) but she pronounced the 'r' at the end of it pretty hard. I know, I know, that's a small nit to pick. 
 Anyway, this book ends on, not a cliffhanger exactly, but kind of, and I don't feel I have any reason to pick up the next one.

The more time passes since I read this book, the worse it seems. As I was reading, I didn't pay any attention to the characters whatsoever (the first sign pointing to the fact that the book is crap), choosing instead to focus on the magic system which is, to pay the book it's due, original and interesting, so I considered it a four star read. Once I finished it and had a moment to think, however, I noticed how flat and uninteresting all the characters were, and decided to give it three stars. By the time I opened it's Goodreads page, I couldn't stomach rating it more than two. And finally, while writing this review, I couldn't see any reason not to give it one star and be done with it, hopefully banishing it to dark corner of my mind from which it'll never return.

reference_books.review_text:
Good writing style, I usually don't read these kind of books, but it was good. Bella plays too much of a damsel in distress, and I would've liked it more if they played in the vampire element a bit more. 
 Stephanie Meyer definitely got into a teenage girl's head. Although I don't know if that's a good thing. Bella was just stupid. And it seemed to me that Edward was a little...what's the word, insane. 
 But shivers go down your spine every time they kiss. Or you envision Edward. Or you hear his name. She definitely did well at turning Edward into a fictional character that every girl has a crush on. Although he is insane and a vampire. 
 I wonder what Stephanie Meyer's husband thinks of Edward... 
 Okay, my opinion keeps changing about this book and the rest in the saga. First I think it's stupid, then I think it's awesome, then I think it's a combination of both. But I think Meyer captured what it's like being a teenager. Of course, she could've made all the vampires seem less cool, have less fun, whatever, but that may have made it too depressing. I think that this would be a very complicated and difficult book to write, and I think that Meyer did pretty well.

reference_books.title: The Time Traveler's Wife
reference_books.review_text:
I can't decide on this one. 
 On one hand, the language was often beautiful, with tasty phrases to turn over in your mouth. 
 For the last hundred pages or so it's impossible to put down, 
 and the love seems very real between the time traveler and his wife. 
 On the other: 
 There was way too much profanity. It wasn't creative at all, and every time I read the 'f' word or 's' word, I thought, "here she goes again..." because after she wrote one, she had to have at least five on the entire page. It could've been a good book even though she swore so often if it weren't for: 
 the...ahem, sex scenes. There were about sixteen in the entire book. It was annoying. You would read this absolutely awesome paragraph, and then you'd come to a sentence like, "She slipped her dress over her head," or something like that. Plus, there were a lot of swear words in those scenes. 
 Those last two paragraphs are going to make me seem immature, that I'm just not old enough to handle stuff like that. But I want to tell you that's not really the case. She really could've done without all that, I think. It was very explicit, even more explicit than some of the similar scenes in Wicked! 
 Another thing: 
 During the first 200 pages or so, I couldn't put it down. It was so intense and I couldn't wait to see what would happen next. The last one hundred pages were also really intense. But the pages between then were undeniably BO-RING. That's why it took me over a month to read it, I kept starting all these books in between. 
 And the Name Dropping! It was like she was attempting to advertise every single thing she liked in the course of 500 pages, but make it good enough so it would get reviewed on TV, and then it could get broadcasted even more! She would start in with this really beautiful sentence, and then follow it up with this mention of the Violent Femmes (great band by the way, I'm not a hater, but gosh, couldn't she have name dropped during her numerous interviews instead of in her novel?), and then I would think, Oh No! Because after she did that, she would get really sloppy. 
 And of course there are too many characters. There were so many small ones that came back later, and I found myself wondering, "Who. the. Heck. Is. Ben?!?!?!" 
 I also felt that towards the end she was trying to hurry. She could've cut out a good one hundred pages, and it still would've been a great story, but at the end, where as in the rest of the book it was just ambling along, nice and slow, here she decided to take up one paragraph to describe the most shocking thing in the entire book! 
 And the ending! Oh my gosh I hated it! 
 Well, I guess it was incredibly well written and all her foreshadowing wouldn't have worked before then, but I just felt so...cheated! I think most people either love or hate the ending, from the reviews I read, but I hate it, to be completely honest. 
 (I knew it was coming, because of all teh glorious people whose reviews contain spoilers that DIDN'T CHECK THE 'THIS REVIEW CONTAINS SPOILERS' box) 
 So, here's my mixed review: 
 Grammar: 3 stars. It would've been better read aloud, but the run on sentences kind of drove me crazy. 
 Language: 5 for the poetic-ness, 2 for the swearing and explicit info. 
 Plot: 4 for first 200 pages, 2 for the next 200 pages, and 5 for the last one hundred. 
 Characters: 5, they were all realistic and hateable (it's harder to make a character hateable than loveable), some a little overly so. Here's a rant, you can skip over it if you want: 
 So neither of the main characters have 'real jobs', yet they still make enough money to buy a studio and crap? COME ON! Too many small characters and they were all a little racially stereotyped, or stereotyped in other ways. 
 Description: 5. She ALWAYS described really well, no matter how crazy it drove me. 
 In conclusion (gosh, this review is long), I'd like to say that in parts Niffenegger is a genius. In others, I wanted to throw the book across the room. 
 It's well worth a read, maybe a reread once I get older, but after that, never again. 
 *I also highly recommend you wait until you're over fifteen to read it, maybe then you won't be as annoyed about some parts as I was*

It's a fucking tragedy that I should feel the need to write this, but this book - about Melinda, a 13-year-old girl who is raped at a party but after a year of misery comes out the other side - should probably be handed to every girl in her first year or two at high school.

I reread SPEAK in honor of Banned Book Week. More than ever, this book has a place in every high school. I would even go so far as it belongs in middle school because current middle schools have students who have experienced the same experience as Melinda. The book describes Melinda's experience at her first high school party. She spends her 9th grade year suffering inside when she needed to voice her disgust and find the necessary help she needed. Her suffering exposed itself in her attitude, her grades, her lack of friends, her feelings of poor self esteem, in other words, her entire life. The reader goes with her through that ninth grade year.

LAURIE HALSE ANDERSON, PRINTZ HONOR BOOK 
 Anderson's Printz Honor Book explores Melinda Sordino's freshman year of high school as she deals with the aftermath of being raped at a summer party. Because her peers believe that she called the cops about the party (and not about the rape) she becomes completely ostracized. The title of the book hearkens to Melinda's inability to reach out to her parents, peers, best friend, teachers, etc. to get help. Depression, anxiety, self-harm, abuse, and relationships are all themes explored throughout Anderson's book. I absolutely loved this book. I felt that Melinda's voice was so authentic, the problems in the book were so applicable to young adults, and the tie-in of Melinda's art class and teacher helping her to come to terms with her experience was so significant. In her art class, Melinda is assigned 'tree' as her year-long subject--she is supposed to master the image of the tree. This assignment comes full circle as, at the end of the novel, one of the trees outside of Melinda's home rots, and a man comes to cut the rotten branches away. The reader learns that by cutting away at the rotten parts of a tree, the tree is able to flourish--and similarly, by the end of the novel Melinda learns to cut the rotten pieces of her life away. I would absolutely recommend this book to any upper level junior high school or any high school student.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I can see why people have challenged this book, and I can see why it might make some uncomfortable. But that said, I loved it. It's original, creative, intelligent and witty. Lucky is living in "the real world" with the rest of us where things are not ideal or necessarily filtered and tidied for our safety. Grown ups with grown up issues make no sense and her internal process of trying to make sense of them, along with her own fears and issues, are touching and funny. 
 The book starts out with her hiding behind a dumpster listening to people in an AA meeting tell their "rock bottom" stories. The involvement of alcohol has caused the book to be challenged, along with a story a man tells about passing out and waking up when his dog is bit by a rattlesnake on the scrotum (see, if you neuter your pets...). Lucky doesn't know what a scrotum is, except it's bad to have one and they're only on boys, and therefore she's glad she doesn't have one...it also sounds like something you hack up when you have the flu... She thinks she might like to see one to find out what it looks like, but at the same time she's also VERY sure she would not like to see one at all. 
 These little back and forth internal deliberations, dilemmas and growing pains are brilliant. Maybe not pretty, maybe not entirely appropriate for all audiences, but definitely honest & therefore I loved it.

I read this book for my Newbery class and fell in love with the characters. I love how Susan Patron is able to so eloquently capture what it feels like to be 10. Also, it's such a smart book, with literary references (HMS Beagle, "Are You My Mother?" etc). I love the whole debate over "Slow Children At Play." Highly recommended for ages 10 and up.

My current delve into children's literature has come up smelling like roses. Susan Patron creates a unique and compelling story about a girl named Lucky who is trying to find her "higher power," a term she learned from spying on AA meetings. She hopes that once she finds her higher power she will know how to deal with a mother who has passed away and a father who doesn't want her. Sometimes it takes seeing life from a child's perspective to give you a fresh one.

This review also appears on my blog, Read-at-Home Mom. 
 I'll start by saying I am a big fan of realistic fiction, and a really big fan of books set in small hard luck towns. So the fact that Lucky lives in a town with only 42 people in it, where the majority of those people attend multiple twelve-step programs predisposed me to loving the book before I even really got into the story.But even beyond just the appealing set-up, there's lots to like about Lucky. 
 She's scientifically minded and unafraid of bugs and snakes. She's kindhearted at the core, but has flaws, including her exasperation with her clingy five-year-old neighbor Miles, and her underlying suspicion that Brigitte, her guardian, is secretly planning an escape. Lucky also eavesdrops on twelve step program meetings, looking for hints on how to find her higher power, and, still mourning the accidental death of her mother, maintains a survival backpack, filled with everything a person would need in case of emergency. She doesn't quite trust her new life without her mother, and copes by being constantly prepared for the next disaster to strike. 
 I think what truly won me over about this book was the writing itself, and the amazingly detailed characterization of each person, and of the town of Hard Pan. There are lots of books out there where kids have to overcome some obstacle in order to grow and change and become more mature, but I don't think many of them are written this well, or with this same style. 
 I also think Susan Patron has a really good sense of how children observe the world, and of what is important to them. For example, Lincoln, Lucky's friend, takes offense to the SLOW CHILDREN AT PLAY sign in their neighborhood, because without proper punctuation, it's insulting to the children. In an act that Lucky calls "presidential," Lincoln makes the necessary changes: 
 Lincoln did something brilliant. Next to SLOW, he drew two neat perfect-size dots, one like a period and the other a little above it. Lucky knew it was a colon and it made the sign mean, "You must drive slow. There are children at play" (p. 24). 
 I also loved the little things, like the phrase "brain crevices," and the fact that Lucky's dog's name is HMS Beagle. I enjoyed the stories Lucky tells Miles about Chesterfield the Burro in the Olden Days of Hard Pan, and Short Sammy's efforts to cook with government cheese, about which he says, "...nobody can figure out what to do with it to make it something you'd want to eat." Best of all is Brigitte's exclamation of "Oh, la-la, la-LA, la-LA, la-LA" whenever her anxiety or anger level rises. So many very specific details went into Susan Patron's portrayal of Hard Pan and its people, and I eagerly ate up every single one. 
 One final bonus was the references to other children's books, namely Are You My Mother? by P.D. Eastman, and Peter Sis's The Tree of Life. I especially love the fact that the author took the time to cite them in the acknowledgments, along with the serenity prayer, which most young readers would probably not know on their own. 
 This book represents exactly the kind of contemporary, realistic fiction I love, and of which I wish there was much, much more. I'm sure my bias toward realism contributed to my positive review, and I'm not 100% sure that kids would love this book, but I still say it's excellent, and I'll probably become one of those adults who wants to give it to a kid "for his own good."

I didn't like this one. I really didn't. This is the first children's lit book that I have given just a one star rating. I can't say exactly why I didn't like it, but I can give a few reasons. 
 1- 'Scrotum' - If you know anything of the hubbub of this book this word will surface. Going into the book I was expecting the reference and really was prepared to laugh at the silly people who made this such a big deal. However, it was just wrong to me. First of all the man who initially said the word is basically a hobo living in a tin can. This man would use the official term and not the crass one? Not so much. Obviously, it was put in for the shock factor. I like shock value - but it can also be a cheap trick. I just didn't buy it. Then, to have the main character reminisce about what a real scrotum would look like? Some people call this honest. Maybe it is, but if a ten year old wants to contemplate genitals - unless it is imperative to the plot - I'm not really interested. This set the tone for the rest of the book . . . 
 2- The story seemed 'off'. I can't explain this other than the characters seemed plastic and unreal. I'm sure I was already bent from trying to understand the above reference, but I was not able to connect with any of the characters. It felt choppy and unpolished. I never felt that Lucky actually cared for anyone but herself - and this showed in her descriptions of even her guardian. It was filled with her musings of everything - yet nothing. 
 I don't read a lot of children's lit typically - This year I have decided to read all of the Newbery Award winners - and if I had read this book and didn't expect Award quality it most likely would be sitting with 2 stars. I get that Children's lit is harder to get amazing - but isn't that why we have the award in the first place? It has been done, however, and to have this book sitting on the shelf with Holes and Bridge to Teribithia and the Hero and the Crown - it just isn't right. 
 The end.

IF YOU LIKED THIS TRY... 
 This is one of those kids books that feels a little too precious for its own good. Sure addiction, death, and identity are tough concepts to expect any 9 year old (older kids won't touch this book, trust me) to grasp, but that's not my problem. It's more that I felt the story spoke to me as an adult. The best kids books speak to the kid in me, or speak to the adult AND the kid in me, or uh, something like that. Anyway the big moment of the book, when Lucky thanks the townsfolk for coming to her mother's impromptu memorial, is just not a moment made for children. I'll be interested in talking to the kids I teach who've read it to see if I'm dead wrong.
I read this book because it was a Newbury winner, but I thought it was pretty unoriginal.

This book will have readers looking for a Higher Power to end this novel. The story is about a ten-year old girl named Lucky who lives in a disfunctional town in the middle of nowhere in California. A series of unrealistic, unfortunate events brings Brigitte (BrigEET) from France to be Lucky's guardian. Lucky has a job cleaning up after the members of various addicts anonymous meetings. This is where she begins her search for her higher power, which ultimatley leads to her running away. This book has no actual plot and unrelatable charachters that never really develop. I'm not really sure how this book won The Newberry. What I am sure of though is that Lucky is an ungrateful little girl that does not know how good she has it in life. In short, the lack of a story line and unrelatable charachters will leave readers scratching their heads and wishing for an end to this book!

 A V I SO en esta resena (o intento de resena) hay demasiados spoilers, lee bajo tu responsabilidad. 
 Lo mio con Kiera Cass se llama amor-odio a su escritura. Algo con lo que sin duda a veces se disfruta pero en otras ocasiones se detesta. Con The Crown lamentablemente me ha pasado con The Elite, un libro que me resulto una carcasa salvo por dos sorpresas; y aqui con The Crown ha pasado lo mismo, he sentido rapidez e inconclusion. Algo con lo que sin duda tras leer The Heir no esperaba encontrarme. 
 Vale, lo admito, en la vida de nina disfrute con las peliculas Disney, unas que a lo maximo que aspiraban sus protagonistas en la vida era con sonar con el dia de su boda, con la perfeccion de un hombre que no existe y con el deseo de encontrar un amor perfecto que nada tenia que ver con la realidad. Asi pues ?como nos vendieron La Seleccion? Pues como eso mismo pero con el anadido distopico tan maravillado que vino acompanado tras el exito de Los Juegos del Hambre. Con eso sobre la mesa nacio lo que nadie en su momento esperaba: un exito desmesurado con el que anos mas tarde se vendieron otras novelas, comparandolas a esta misma. Fijaros como nos vendieron The Red Queen (the Selection meets... blah blah blah). 
 La trilogia acabo, y vimos un cuento de hadas con tintes politicos, que no distopico, cuidado. Asi pues pienso que tras vender los derechos para pelicula Kiera penso en hacer una continuacion que siguiera con el estigma de exito que habia tenido su principal trilogia. Y asi empezo The Heir, con una protagonista que nada tenia que ver con su madre, y que sin duda disfrute porque si se apreciaban preocupaciones e inquietudes politicas que sin duda habian sido tapadas mas de la cuenta para elevar el nivel de escenas amorosas. 
 The Heir mostro un aumento de "originalidad" de Kiera y logro gustarme, cosa por la que no apostaba. ?Que paso entonces? Pues que las expectativas para este libro fueron bastante elevadas. Bastante. 
 Vale. Primero empiezo por lo positivo. Que es poco y luego os justifico mi descontento. Lo mejor de la novela son dos sorpresillas. Primero que Lady no se que resulta ser la tia de Ead, cosa que supongo que algunos sabiais y otros desconociamos. Resulta que la amante del padre de Maxon le solto tras llamarle zorra... 
 Ya le dire a tu hermana que le envias saludos 
 Imaginaros con la cara con la que me quede. ?Que era su tia? Pues eso, nuevo miembro para la familia real. Toma, ya. 
 Y la segunda, pues la relacion homosexual de dos de los Seleccionados. Es un cliche que decidas poner al que le gusta la moda como homosexual, ?pero que le vamos ha hacer? La cosa es que el que le gustaba la moda se enamoro de otro Seleccionado. Uno del que no sabemos mucho de el, salvo que es encantador, carismatico.... Vamos que una cosa llevo a la otra y ahi florecio el amor. Ead decide dejarles ir como enamorados que son y ella prosigue con su Seleccion. 
 A partir de aqui no hay mas sorpresas. Asi que solo me queda lo negativo. 
 Primero: ?Os acordarais como Ead leia la prensa informativa en The Heir, y bueno nos hacia participes de los descontentos de los ProCastas? ?Si? Pues vale. Olvidadaros de esas informaciones Kiera las tira por tierra, y si hace falta de hace un rebozado de croquetas con ello. Asi pues la buena de Ead, que era una chica aplicada por la politica de su pais pasa de preocuparse de ese tipo de prensa a preocuparse y contentar a la prensa amarillista de Illea. Si senoras y senores, todas las decisiones de Ead (la mayoria de ellas) son en base a contentar a la prensa del cotilleo de su propio pais. Ole tu, Ead por tu involucion. Ole tu. 
 La segunda: Unica meta en doscientas y pico paginas: El matrimonio. No se cuantas veces he leido la palabra matrimonio. Si, ya lo se, no os echeis encima, que ya se de que va la Seleccion: de matrimonio. Pero os aseguro que si me vendes esto como una distopia, algo mas que solo matrimonio tendra ?no? Pues no, ya os lo digo yo. ?Os acordais de como he empezado la resena? ?Con lo de Disney? Pues eso. 
 La tercera: Eikko/Erik/Ahora me doy cuenta que suspiro por ti. Antes que nada, os aviso que yo apostaba por Erik como interes romantico de Ead, solo que no asi de mal desarrollado. Vamos, que resulta que en el anterior libro, en la famosilla pelea de la cocina, te das cuenta que te gusta el susodicho y Kiera no decide contarnos que empieza a sentir algo desde ese momento. No que va. Nada de nada. Eso no lo intuimos hasta que se miran un par de veces, se intentan besar otro par de veces y poco mas. El amor es de TOMA, PUM, ME GUSTA. Y nada, tenemos que conformarnos con creernos la historia, porque claro (aqui va otra expresion que se repite hasta la sociedad) su historia puede ser como la de sus padres: un cuento de hadas... 
 La cuarta: La incongruencia. Si, si, la incongruencia ?que quereis que os diga? Hace unos instantes os he comentado que Ead nos dice que se enamoro de Erik en la pelea de las cocinas. ?Os acordais? ?Si? Pues vale. En un escenario un poco distinto uno de los pretendientes se declara a Ead (!que romantico es todo aqui eh!) Cosa que la deja pasmada y que no tarda en compartir con Neena, que la informa de que le parece raro que le dijera el hombrecillo que justo se habia enamorado de ella en las cocinas, que todo eso le olia a chamusquina... 
 Creo que lo que me hace dudar --empece-- es el hecho de que empezara a sentir algo especial por mi justo la noche de la pelea en las cocinas 
 Vamos, no me jodas. ?Que la protagonista si puede enamorarse en una cocina y el hombrecillo de la Seleccion, no? ?Pero que me estais vendiendo? 
 Vale, ya paro. Si os soy sincera pienso que Kiera apoderara los genes de Casandra Clare y nos dara mil versiones de su mundo?Por que? Por el hermano de Ead que dice que nunca se saltaria las normas, pensando en Kiera, seguro que ya le tiene una historia prohibida para el. Fijo. 
 ?Que ha supuesto para mi este ultimo libro? Poco, la verdad, la idea de casarte porque te hace femenina delante de la nacion y no masculina no me gusta. Pienso que Ead tenia mas capacidades para gustar a su gente, que no centrarse solo en eso. Pero bueno ?que mas da? 
 Otra cosa que he echado a faltar: explicaciones. ?Que ha pasado con los rebeldes de Cristina/Cristine? Aquellos de los de la cruz ?os acordais? Por que yo si. Como aquellos diarios de Gregor, que nadie ha echado a faltar. Me falta informacion ?Aun existen rebeldes en Illea que repudian lo que suponen las clases sociales? 
 Bah mas cosas, incongruntes. Os acodais como les echan en cara a los del pueblo que deciden hablar con Ead, que Ead ha diferencia del pueblo no podia elegir su profesion, que practicamente eran unos dioses por poder elegir. Vale con esto en la mano ?que pasa con esa mujer que te esta lavando el retrete? ?Tambien ha tenido eleccion como el resto? O como Ead ?no ha podido elegir, porque debia atender a una familia a una unidad de personas que necesitaban de una persona trabajando mas que formando ?. Que se interpongan cosas asi sin sentido alguno me asquea. ?Pero que mas da? 
 Ya esta. Seguro que pocos coincidireis conmigo. Aun asi quiero expresar que ha significado para mi: una perdida.

La traduccion espanola salvaba algo al primer tomo, la diferencia con Red Queen es que en este los hechos ocurren rapido y sin ningun tipo de orden. No acaba de pasar algo y !pum! nos plantan otra trama, asi por que si, metida con calzador; el resultado al fin y al cabo queda confuso e incloncluso. 
 Os sere sincera, si ya de por si ya me cuesta entenender el ingles con Victoria me cuesta todavia mas. Aun asi y todo... Bueno, debo agradecerle el giro final en su novela que sin duda llego a compensar en gran medida los fallos que le vi. 
 Coriane como protagonista no me gusta, pero bueno, eso es porque su personalidad no encaja con la mia. La chica esta se lamenta por todo. Y bueno el libro gira a traves de esos sentimientos, nos cuentan como subio y llego a ser la reina que nos contaron en Red Queen. 
 Siguiendo con el hilo de pesimismo de Coriane, sus "todos estan contra mi" y sus multiples "no soy feliz" vienen por el hecho de simplemente es una adolescente, una que al fin y al cabo se esta descubriendo, y que anhela todo lo que es ajeno a ella. Concretando, Coriane esta en la edad del pavo; vive en una pelicula Disney cuyo compositor pricipal es Kurt Covain.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Summary: 
 America Singer is chosen to be one of the Selected, a handful of teenage girls who will compete to win the affections of the crown prince and become his future Queen. America, whose "true love" is from a lower cast, has no interest in gaining the affections of the prince, but eventually the two start to become friends as the competition is narrowed down. 
 Review: 
 Not every book is for every reader, and that is probably why I put off reading this one. This was a book group pick so I felt obligated to read it. I know how popular this book is, but it never held much appeal for me--just not my thing. 
 Essentially this book is "The Bachelor" for teens. I think my biggest problem with the book is the predictability--it is all so cliche. Of course America doesn't want to be chosen to be the future queen, she has no interest in that. Of course the prince would be intrigued by American who just wants to be his friend. Of course they will begin to fall in love. Sorry, but there is nothing original here--it is very stereotypical. 
 Despite that teens love these books, and apparently quite a few adults do too (judging from the reactions of most of the members of my book group). I think the appeal is that the everyday girl gets the unattainable and then there is the happily ever after. Entertaining fluff, but that is sometimes what people want. I may pick up book two someday when I am looking for something light and entertaining, but that's for another day. 
 Overall: 
 Light and entertaining, but lacking depth. Perhaps the sequels will have more meat to them, but this didn't really hook me. It was okay, but it wasn't a favorite. Still, I might pick up book two someday should I feel the need for something light. 
 Cautions for Sensitive Readers: 
 Language: Mild--I don't remember anything graphic. 
 Violence: Some, though mostly off in another part of the palace from the narrator. 
 Sex: Some kissing and groping, but nothing explicit. She is informed that she must be a virgin to compete in the Selection and that the prince may ask anything of her. 
 Drugs/Alcohol: Some alcohol consumption.

I'm not entirely sure what to say when the majority of you have nothing but positive comments... How should I put this...? I feel like I spent the whole time reading this book, idly flipping through pages (clicking actually, because I read it on my Kindle) and I was always WAITING. I was waiting for more, for something that would finally snap my attention fully into The Selection. I was waiting for the story to get set and finally take off. 
 But it never did. 
 And I so, so wanted it to! I kept giving it another chance to blow my mind. And besides a few make out sessions and Maxon's and America's first meeting, there was nothing too exciting about The Selection. No cliffhangers or climaxes. Not even in the end. 
 Southern and Northern gangs ambushed the palace at times, and a few mean girls played dirty tricks. For me, some of the most boring parts of the book were the raids made by the rebels. No one ever got hurt...I don't even think much damage was done! 
 I am told that the dystopia world in The Selection will be more firmly developed in book 2. Well, I sincerely hope so! Because right now it is a little unclear where things are, why they are this way, and why the history of this world isn't written down anywhere. There were also a few remarks about the rebels searching for something during their raids. These aspects were surely compelling, but I don't think Miss Cass should wait so long to dive into them. Don't make us wait until book 2 to actually get our thrilling excitement! Why would you put those things in the book if they had no purpose being there? You either wanted this book to be the 'Bachelor' or 'The Hunger Games," but you tried to make it both. It can't be both! Because it is nowhere near as exciting as the Games, and it is very cheesy like the Bachelor. It was a nice idea, but couldn't you have thought it out a little longer? 
 Even when Aspen reappeared on the scene from out of nowhere (literally) there was a very tiny climatic moment. Nothing that took my breath away. Nothing that begged of me to turn the next page. Nothing that made me stop, pause, and read the paragraph over again because I was so in awe. 
 The one and only thing that propelled me through this story was the hype and the hope that -- around the corner -- I would find a reason for why I paid that seven bucks. 
 *Sighs* Oh well.

This book is stunningly beautiful.From the writing and characters to the flawless blending of myth and reality, it is perfect. Not to mention the gorgeous cover, I mean, really, what girl doesn't dream of a dress like that? 
 What caught me most was the writing. It was dramatic and completely character-centric. No unnecessary words or long, rambling paragraphs. Yet it never felt rushed and flowed naturally throughout. I loved how the author managed to portray such intense emotions with such subtlety. I also truly love what she did with two of my favorite myths, Orpheus and Eurydics and Hades and Persephone. 
 Nikki is wonderful. She's so quiet that you don't always notice, but she has a will of steel. Knowing that she has little time before she is lost to torment and death, her greatest wish is to make it easier on the people she leaves behind. Especially for Jack. 
 Ah, Jack. My favorite character. He's a really, really nice guy with hints of a rebel that sneak out with an eyebrow piercing. He doesn't know where Nikki has been for so long, but he knows that she's been hurt. So he is what she needs most; a friend. He never pushes too hard, but he never gives up. He may take a step back at certain revelations, but never for more than a moment. 
 Cole is an entirely different kettle of fish. He's dark through and through, and has undoubtedly done terrible things, but is he completely irredeemable? Perhaps, perhaps not. It should be...interesting. 
 I would recommend this book to just about anyone, but especially lovers of mythology and beautiful, beautiful romance. And to people who don't mind shedding a few tears over a magnificent ending. 
 I received an advance copy of this book through the author in exchange for a fair and honest review.
