4,5 stars 
 I'll be strictly honest here: The first and main reason why I own this book is it's georgeus cover. 
 When I first opened account here on goodreads, back in 2013, I couldn't help but notice it and a material girl in me wanted to have it on her shelf. 
 Only recently I learned that Everneath is a reteling of a greek myth about Persephone. 
 You have my premission to judge me! 
 In the first few chapters I was little afraid this would be one of those ya books that have so many similarities with Twilight. I was little annoyed how Nikki went in Return and all she was thinking about was Jack. The main reason why that annoyed me was that she didn't spend that much time with her brother and dad. She claimed she wanted to spend her last days in Return with people she loved, but it seemed to me that for a first few months she spend them alone. 
 I know her dad was busy and had elections, so that explains his absence, but why there was no more scenes with her little brother? 
 I had a feeling that in the first half of the book we only get to know about him when Cole mentions him, and Nikki's afraid Cole would hurt him, but we don't get actual scenes with Nikki and little Tommy. 
 After I got over that I actually started to enjoy the story.

 At first I wasn't a fan of Jack but somewhere in the third third of the story I fell for him. I am Team Jack all the way! 
 Cole was an interesting charater but I never precieved him as a love interest. Despise that, I'm looking forward to read more about him. 
 I never paid much attention to Jules. She was just there. I know she had a reason to be in the story, but I didn't feel interested enough to connect with her. 
 The most ineresting person in this book was Meredith. 
 The writing style in not unique but it is not as ussual eather. 
 As we read we go back and forward from past to present.

 I guess that's what happens when the book is good!

What worked: 
 Greek Mythology is a one way ticket to Fangirl Kingdom. It's not like I know a lot about the different myths and legends but there's something about them that I just can't get enough of. Brodi Ashton's new twist on the Persephone myth (which is something I've read a LOT of) is very intriguing and I liked the hierarchy of the Greek system. 
 What irked: 
 Have I been reading the same book as everybody else? My good friend, Brooke, really enjoyed it and normally our taste in books is spot on but with Everneath it wasn't happening. I actually did a buddy read with Hollie from Music, Books and Tea and the only thing that kept me sane is that she felt the same way about it. Everything about it was a disappointment. 
 Nikki is so frustrating and drab in a way that reminded me of Bella Swann. The whole reason she fought so hard to come back home was so she could put things right when actually she spends her time ignoring issues and focusing on the stupidest of tasks instead of the people she cares about. She jumps to conclusions and as for her pathetic excuse for going to the Everneath with Cole, don't get me started. I don't even see the appeal for this leading man. He's boring, he's kinda obsessive and he's a bit creepy and as for the other part of the "love triangle", I'm reserving judgement on Jack for now. He's a forgettable character to me and actually I have a question. Nikki creeps into his room at night (because obviously some YA characters have a blindspot for the creep factor) and he puts on some glasses. Hold on, did he already have glasses? Does he wear contacts the rest of the time? Because right now the image in my head is changing drastically with this sudden piece of information. Before she'd even climbed through his window I was already wondering about the logistics of it because Nikki looks through his window. It's 2am people, does he have blinds? Does he have curtains? If so, why aren't they CLOSED?! If I had a bedroom on the ground floor at the front of the house, I'd be gripping onto every bit of privacy I could, especially with riff raff clambering through my window when I'm sleeping.

3.5 
 Really it was just what I expected it to be: a little mindless entertainment. It was pretty well done for its kind - not too many annoyances and pet peeves - but it does stick to a typical romance and "special" girl who always thought she was normal storyline.

Sooo...Everneath. If you checked out my other reviews or know anything about me, you would know I love Greek mythology. Like LOVE it. LOVE LOVE LOVE it!(Seriously, it's a problem)So, when I hear about a possible retelling of a myth, especially of Persephone and Hades, I get all: 
 And when I started Everneath, I was like: 
 And then I read it. 
 And then I was all: 
 Seriously, WHAT HAPPENED EVERNEATH!!?? 
 I wanted to like the story. I wanted to be nice and say, "Well, it's just the first book", but then I remembered other retellings I've read recently (I'm looking at you Goddess Test and Abandon) and I was like, "No, this rage monster is gonna live!" 
 So, if you actually like this book, you may want to leave, because it just goes downhill from here. 
 This book had a lot of potential - the idea of the Everneath, Cole and his demon buds, the whole "Daughters of Persephone" thing, what it costs to be immortal, etc. However, all of that potential was wasted by the inexplicably boring characters and underwhelming story. 
 Nikki and Jack...what can I say about them? Nikki is so beyond pointless, I can't even pretend to like her. She does nothing in the novel and, due to her time in the Everneath, feels nothing. This combination makes for a very boring read. I understand what Ashton was going for, but after a while I got tired of hearing about how she couldn't smile or laugh or feel period. I mean I've been depressed and sad before and felt numb and empty, but, eventually, that passes and I can't connect with a character who is nothing but emptiness. However, my dislike of Nikki extends beyond her hollow interior. Throughout the story, she exhibits a very Bella Swan logic. When she sees something dangerous or potentially so, what does she do? She sallies forth right into it, even though she clearly lacks intelligence or physical strength or any other form of protection other than the fact that she didn't turn into a grandma when she got back to Earth. Seriously, throughout the book, constant, CONSTANT references are made to Persephone or Eurydice and it's the eleventh hour before anything clicks in her pointless skull! 
 Of course, by that point, I was like: 
 So I no longer cared if she went to the Tunnels or not. Honestly, the most reaction this novel got out of me was when Jack took her place in the Tunnels. That reaction went something like, "No, you blithering moron! You don't need her! Save yourself! Or at least save the rest of us from her stupidity!!!" 
 Aside from Nikki's character individually, the relationship between her and Jack, which was supposed to be uplifting and make you go "awww...", was almost as hollow as Nikki herself. Seriously, you love each other soooo much, but you trust some guy you've never met who reveals himself to be one crazy mofo (eating your emotions and shiz) more than the guy you've been friends with for years? I can't even... Just no. 
 What makes their relationship even more frustrating is how easily Nikki gets off the hook. Oh, you made a deal with devil because you ASSUMED I was cheating on you? Oh, you've damned yourself to life as a battery and I'm supposed to save you, even though I have done NOTHING wrong? I am all for chivalry in a guy, but, as I said before, idiocy is something different. There is no reason Jack should do what he does to save Nikki. There isn't. But he will and does because god forbid Nikki should have to deal with the consequences of her actions or figure out how to fix her own problems. No, prince charming swoops in and saves her and she goes back to being a pretty doll on a shelf. 
 Aside from Dumb and Dumber (or because of them), Everneath's story was absolutely boring. The entire novel revolves around their love story, which, fine, I can understand why, but the mythology Ashton is trying to build ends up getting put on the backburner. For most of the novel, Everneath and its society are mentioned, but nothing ever gets explained. To some extent, I can understand this (Nikki's experience of the world is very limited), but after a while this failure to deal with part of the narrative becomes inexcusable. Why is it so important Nikki doesn't grow old after leaving Everneath? It is never really explained other than that it is a sign she could replace the current queen. But why? Or there is the whole "eating emotions" thing. We get some explanation on how that works, but it comes very late in the novel and remains kind of slippery. The Everliving consume emotion because, to be immortal, they have to remove their hearts? Why would you remove the seat of emotion (the heart) to live forever if you have to regain them somehow anyway? I don't understand the fail of logic at play other than as a symptom of being ignored in favor of a love story or something else. I don't know, maybe it makes sense in a twisted way, but, as I've said before, after a while I just stopped trying and just wanted to finish the book and be done with it. 
 So, once again, I was baited with the promise of a modern retelling of one of my favorite myths and I was let down. Badly. Maybe the most out of all the crappy retellings I've gone through because this book has received a lot of praise, especially for its depiction of addiction (to which I respond, WHAT? What addiction?...Do you mean the three times she wanted jump Cole? Cuz I read that as sexual tension, not as the experience of a recovering addict!) 
 After reading Everneath, I found myself huddling in a corner with a mythology book clutched to my chest, muttering,

I'm not really sure what to make of this book, I enjoyed it but Nikki irritated me she spends quite a lot of time being depressed and feeling a sorry for herself and she does have a decent reason but I kind of feel like I've read this character enough already. She also has a massive choice to make and I felt like she made the wrong one If she has such a big problem with humans being taken to the everneath she could become queen and . . . stop it happening!!!

This is a book that had the potential to be wonderfully amazing. I'm not one to obsess over covers because I really honestly don't care, but the cover for this was gorgeous. The main factor in my picking this up though was the premise. I read the back of the book and I was digging the whole Everneath concept. I'm a sucker for mythology and I was interested to see what kind of spin the author would take on the Persephone tale. Sadly, I have to say that I was super disappointed. It had all the components to be a fun book, but I felt a little let down. The characters were bland and I didn't connect to any of them. It also seemed liked nothing much happened, which was surprising for a book where the main character is on a time limit to save her soul. It was pretty much Nikki hanging out knitting and awkwardly staring at her ex, Jack. It wasn't until a great deal in the book where things started happening and even then, it was a lot of back and forth. Of course, the whole time Nikki was determined to damn her soul to the Tunnels of the Everneath. I was like, 'Is she serious?!'. Sure, Cole's kind of freaky, but the guy is nowhere bad enough for her to be so resistant to his offer. I'm sorry but if I had the choice between eternal life and being buried alive in hell, I'd for sure be running off with Cole. Just saying. Her doing what she was doing was just stubborn and stupid. The longer I read, I just wanted her to throw herself into the Tunnels already and end the book. The ending itself was a little lackluster. I have a feeling I was supposed to be heartbroken by how things played out, but I wasn't. 
 The main character Nikki was boring personified. Gahh, I swear that she had no personality whatsoever. I could get through a slightly underwhelming book plot if the characters are realistic and have some life to them. Nikki was the type of protagonist I hate reading about. She came off as a lethargic blob of a person who wandered about wasting time. Not that every protagonist has to be a kickass pillar of strength, but at least make them have some kind of spark. I have no clue what Nikki even looks like, which shouldn't be such a big deal, but I also have no insight whatsoever into her as a person. Looking back, I honestly have no clue what things she likes or dislikes, what she wants to do in her life, etc. Aside from the car accident thing, I virtually knew nothing about her. She was just some cardboard person bumbling about the storyline. 
 As for the two guys Jack and Cole, I didn't feel either of them. They didn't have much of a personality either. I'll admit I kind of liked the two of them in the flashbacks Nikki had, but any life the characters had were thrown out in the present part of the book. Nikki had these two guys fighting over her and I couldn't understand it. Cole I could kind of love because he had ulterior motives for the things he was saying and doing. He's not a nice guy really. I mean, the guy feeds off people's souls. However, the author had to ruin things by making Cole some obsessive, love-struck boy. I would much rather Cole didn't like Nikki and was just using her for his whole power ploy. Jack also was a bit cardboard. He was just there. I didn't feel the connection between him and Nikki either. All the words were being said, but it didn't feel real to me. The two of them were made to seem 'so in love', whirlwind romance or whatever and it wasn't to me. Jack and Jules should have hooked up because they seemed better together than him and Nikki. 
 Overall, I didn't really like this at all. I don't want to bash because it wasn't even close to being the worst thing I've ever read. That goes to 'Personal Demons' by Lisa Desrochers. However, it was sort of disappointing. The premise itself sounded interesting, but the execution was kind of terrible. I hate to be mean, but I feel like this would have been a lot better if someone other than the author would have written it. The concept was there, but the characters needed to developed more and just in general I wanted more depth. I want to read a book that makes me fall in love with all the characters, both good and bad. I want to care about what's happening and this book was lacking all that for me. It seems like a ton of people are in love with this book and good for them, but it just wasn't for me and I'm defintely not going to read the next one.

reference_books.title: The Marriage of Opposites
reference_books.review_text: Once again I am in the minority. While everyone seems to have enjoyed the story of the mother of painter Camille Pissarro, I found it dull. It started out fairly well, but soon lapsed into plodding pace, uninspired dialogue, and characters whose motivations made little sense. Since I also disliked Hoffman's Museum of Extraordinary Things, this was my last Hoffman read. I listened to this as an audio book and although it was read oddly, I kept with it because I had to take several long walks and had nothing else handy to listen to. Ugh.

reference_books.title: Pride and Prejudice
reference_books.review_text: Who can fail do love Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy? Jane Austen is so good at making engaging characters, an interesting story (romance), but mainly at making the most astute, universal, timeless, funny, witty observations about people, relationships, and society. This may be from the early 19th century, but it is also astonishingly "modern".

reference_books.title: Both Ways is the Only Way I Want It
reference_books.review_text: This is simply a stellar collection of stories. I enjoyed every one, although the term bittersweet is definitely an apt way to describe them. The stories felt deftly related in their exploration of similar themes of love and desire, of the complexity and vulnerability of loving relationships ... and then they are wonderfully related by a strong sense of place (Montana). The language is nuanced, but not overly wrought and the stories end well (so often not the case, I think). Brava!

reference_books.title: The Cove
reference_books.review_text:
If I could give a more nuanced rating, this would probably be a 3.6, but I am rounding up because Rash is just such a good story-teller. 
 This small story is made up of a love story intertwined with a bit of mystery, and it is moody and sad and moving. I wanted the story to continue -- not stop where it did -- so that I could follow the characters some more, perhaps out of their harsh Appalachian life. And I also felt that a bit early on that made Walter's love for Laurel more credible was missing, but this is a minor complaint. 
 Rash describes landscape so beautifully, his characters are people who you care about (or despise) and his effortless narrative makes you eager to read the unfolding story.

reference_books.title: The Beautiful Things That Heaven Bears
reference_books.review_text:
I was moved by this first-person narrative of Sepha, an Ethiopian man who owns a shop, has few friends, and who befriends a neighbor and her daughter. His perspective on the U.S., on Washington, D.C., and on his own rapidly-gentrifying neighborhood, is unique and seem drawn from a life lived. His perspective is also poignant, memorable, nostalgic and -- for me, at times -- terribly melancholy. 
 Mengestu (who we heard speak at our local library about this book and his approach to writing it) presents not so much a story of immigration as a loving portrait of a lovely man. I found Sepha so charming, so sincere, so worthy of (and able to enjoy and appreciate) a less lonely life. But personality, past, race, alienation and loss combine to direct his life on a lonely path ... despite himself. 
 I found the relationship between Sepha and the neighbor's daughter Naomi wonderful and I loved the Mengetu's comment (at our library) when asked why Naomi chooses to have Sepha read her The Brothers Karamazov. Answer: because she wanted a long book so that he will have to read to her for a very long time. It is such a tender relationship between these two characters and it underscores the almost palpable sense of loss and nostalgia that permeates this beautiful little novel. I am quite sure that this will be one of those books that stays with me for a while.

book_a.title: The Wife
book_a.user_review: What a fabulous read this insightful, ironic, entirely believable novel was, and what a sharp portrait it is of a marriage. It beautifully written, perfectly paced, and devoid of cliches, despite the fact that it deals with a story that could be hard to make fresh. It reminded me a bit of Richard Yate's Revolutionary Road, but with a frank, specifically female point-of-view, that of the memorable and eloquent voice of the wife. I couldn't put it down.

sample_reviews.review_text: I didn't particularly *feel* anything while reading the first 2/3 of this book. However, as it picked up towards the end, I began to to enjoy and appreciate it for what it was. It seemed like the first parts were overly and unnecessarily sexual. The flashbacks into the past were not always helpful, and often confused rather than shed light on Joan and Joe's relationship. Wolitzer's writing skill did, however, shine through towards the end.

The Wife is a sad chronicle of a woman's life from her early college years to the end of her marriage. Her insecurities and doubts allowed her to feed the enormous appetite of a narcissistic, self-absorbed man. She chose to subjugate her talents, her self respect and her instincts as a mother to a man whose selfish egotism knew no boundaries. He was despicable and she enabled him. The ending is a fitting tribute to their fifty-year marriage.

I could not get interested in this book. The author was trying to be too clever with her prose instead of just telling the damn story already. I couldn't connect to the wife. She seemed emotionally distant and all the crude language felt like the author was trying to prove her hipness when it was like adding cud to a soup. Unpalatable and off-putting. This isn't The Catcher in the Rye.
My favorite's of Wolitzer's.

Love this author, and in the beginning, I laughed so hard. She paints such fun images---LOL stuff. About marriage--about marriage of my era--early 60's. He's a writer, she was his college student.... 
 However, at the end, I was very let down. The humor went away, the honesty seemed to go away---well, it's hard when a story doesn't end as a reader thinks it should. Perhaps it was good...but not to me.

Joan and Joe Castleman are visiting Finland for Joe to receive a literature price. Many people would no doubt envy Joan to be married to Joe, the famous author, but it turns out that their marriage is flawed, to say the least, and that Joan has sacrificed much to be with a man who is narcissistic and self-centered. 
 Meg Wolitzer alters between present day and earlier years. The reader learns about how the two of them met and that the power balance was askew right from the start. It is a portrayal of a couple that many people probably recognize, and the book has a certain feminist vibe to it. Sometimes the writing is wonderful, like when Joe is hilariously stupid at a party, or when the children see through their parents facade. However, I would have liked more of these events. Sometimes, I think the book is repetitive and tedious. It is as if Meg Wolitzer relies on the theme of the book, which is indeed very interesting and a little feminist, but it is not enough to build a book upon it without more strong moments.
I didn't care for this book, I found it to be boring. It didn't hold my interest and I wouldn't recommend it to anyone.
Couldn't get into it.

Wow! Bitingly sharp, funny and tragic at the same time. The twist at the end is breath-taking and strangely sad. An homage to feminism and the inexorable ties of marriage (not for the faint-of-heart!).

Not as interesting as The Interestings. This book offered insight on the role of a traditional wife (I have wished for a wife when I was busy with work and parenting), but the story was unfortunately pretty dull. The most interesting character was their troubled son, whom we hear little of.

book_b.title: The Power of Habit: Why We Do What We Do in Life and Business
book_b.user_review: Half way through, I abandoned this. Although the premise is a good one (the power of replacing triggers for bad habits with positive triggers), this felt unbelievably repetitive and downright boring. It could be of more interest to those who want to know how these practices can be applied in the business world, but it is a topic that I find of little interest.

sample_reviews.review_text: The first half and appendix of the book are worth a read. The second half lags...and the notes are a bit strange.

An interesting if slightly unsatisfying read. The author explores what habits are, how they form and how they can be modified. The author defines a behavioural cycle consisting of a Cue, a Routine and a Payoff - all of which constitute a Habit. Using this cycle as a framework the author explores how individuals and organisations big and small form habits and how one could modify a potentially toxic habit. 
 The book has many interesting anecdotes and the author offers examples as diverse as the marketing of Pepsodent toothpaste and the evolution of the Civil Rights movement in America to explain how habits are formed and how they can be manipulated. This is not a self help book and is more like a popular science book and should be read as such. The book comes with copious notes and the clear "self help" section is relegated to an appendix. 
 I found this book an easy and rewarding read. I wish the author would have focused more on individual habits and perhaps less on anecdotes. I would still recommend this book to anyone who enjoys reading about what makes us tick as well as those who are looking for some "management" tips.

I read the first half and skim read the second. There seemed to be some big leaps in the some of the science behind this book and I didn't find much helpful in it. I couldn't stand the way the author would interrupt a story in the chapter to draw out the suspense. That seemed like a silly thing to do in a non-fiction book.

The sections on personal habits were fairly interesting, particularly the bits about habit loops, the ripple effect of certain types of habits (like exercise), and also the depths to which our habits take hold (beyond consciousness and memory, for example). The sections on social and business habits were less exciting. I found myself doing a lot of skimming toward the end. 
 Perhaps my biggest issue, however, was the organization of the book. It didn't feel cohesive. It was a stylistic choice, I'm sure, to present the larger stories in sections, intertwining them and breaking them up across a chapter, but the transitions weren't smooth. Instead, I felt like I'd finished a part of the story only to say five pages later, "Oh, we're back to Tony Dungy again?" Didn't work for me.

Have you ever gotten into the car to go to destination A and a few turns later realized you're going to destination B and have to turn around? 
 If so, you've experienced the power of habit. 
 Have you ever told yourself you will NOT eat the cookies sitting out on the counter and two minutes later pick one up and eat it? Or perhaps it was the cigarette. Or the drink. 
 Habit. 
 Did you know that the genius behind the methods of Tom Dungy-the only coach in the NFL history to reach the play-offs ten years in a row and the one who turned a troubled Colts team around and three years later took them to win the Super Bowl in 2007-was to teach his players to be faster than everyone else. But they wouldn't be faster because they would focus on increasing their physical speed. They would be faster because they would learn habits that would make their moves instinct. When his strategy worked, Dungy's players could move with a speed that was impossible to overcome. 
 According to some research, more than 40% of the actions we perform each day are not actual decisions, but habits. And habits that we didn't always consciously choose to start. We have sleeping habits, shopping habits, exercise habits, eating habits. Habits at work, at home, at school. Habits of the mind. 
 Companies have a huge interest in changing our shopping habits. Coaches have an interest in changing the habits we use when we play. Teachers have an interest in the habits of their classroom. Families and communities have habitual ways of interacting. We all have personal habits we'd like to adopt and others we'd like to give away. But unless you know what you're doing, habits can be extremely intransigent and slippery things. 
 The good news is that a lot of research has been done in the last few decades, and we now know how habits work. When we arm ourselves with this knowledge, we'll have a much better chance of changing. Luckily for us, we don't have to track all that information down. In The Power of Habit: Why We Do What We Do In Life and Business, Charles Duhigg draws on hundreds of academic studies, interviews with more than three hundred scientists and executives, and research conducted at dozens of companies in his book and distills all this knowledge to its essence. 
 The title might sound boring, but Duhigg follows the style of Malcom Gladwell (Outliers, Blink, The Tipping Point), and the Heath brothers (Made to Stick), and has written a book that I couldn't put down. For example, I couldn't stop reading about coach Tom Dungy, or Target as it predicts who is pregnant and how far along they are, or the scientists who couldn't figure out why Alcoholics Anonymous works, or how bad organizational habits led to thirty-one people being burned alive in London's King's Cross subway stop. I couldn't stop reading about why Rosa Parks, not the first African American to refuse to give up her bus seat, could pivot the civil rights movement. I couldn't stop reading the stories of individuals losing bad habits, others picking up good ones, and others who lost their minds but not their habits. Duhigg uses these and many other examples and studies to illustrate the key principles underlying how habits work. In the appendix, he gives us a guide for examining and forming our own habits. 
 I personally know the power of changing habits of the mind (which I've already written about). And teeth. A few years ago, I flossed once a week. It was such a pain. Now it's a habit that I almost crave each night. I look back at how I made those changes and see it all laid out in Duhigg's book. Can I actually change my habit of going to bed late? Stay tuned. 
 If you're interested in forming the habits of a class, team, company, or family; if you want to change some of your own habits; if you're interested in knowing why we do what we do and enjoy the style of Malcom Gladwell and Dan and Chip Heath, then I think you'll love this book. Let me suggest you watch the video below. Then go to http://charlesduhigg.com/the-power-of... and click on the "Additional Resources" to watch and read more. Then just get the dang book.

I enjoyed the book and the clear explanation and illustration of how the habit loop works. While I found the anecdotes interesting and helped to reinforce the premise, I felt that the book dragged it out quite a bit. If you've ever wanted to understand habits and why they are so hard to break or if you want to stop a bad habit or start a new one, this is worth reading.
Very Gladwellian. A good and easy read, with a few useful tips. I found the examples about Alcoa and the Montgomery Bus Boycott the most interesting.
One of the most important books I have ever read. It is the only book that I have read again immediately after finishing it the first time.
Loved it.

It is a fascinating book on how people, businesses and organizations develop habits, for good and bad. He writes about some interesting case studies of how habits shape everything and everybody. Basically he shows how a cue, a routine (habit), reward becomes a habit loop. If you want to change a habit than substitute it with another using the same cue and reward. Of course the problem is there is not a formula for a rapid change. Each person and habit are different and each habit is driven by a different craving. The basics are: 1. Identify the routine 2. Experiment with rewards 3. Isolate the cue 4. Have a plan 
 The real value of the book for a reader is how it changes their life in some way. So we will see.

reference_books.title: The Ocean at the End of the Lane
reference_books.review_text: OK, the guy writes well and has good imagination. But the book is infantile. A boy growing up, young love, troubled relationship with parents, mysterious stuff, fears - a perfect recipe for a bestseller. Yet...I am not a teenager...and got bored quite fast. I forced myself to read it.

reference_books.title: Modern Romance
reference_books.review_text:
I liked "Master of None", so when I came across this one, I thought "Why not?" 
 It doesn't really say much more than we already know, namely - technology has changed dating forever and makes getting in a serious relationship harder and cheating easier. Still a pleasant and mildly amusing audio-book to listen to in the metro :)

reference_books.title: Franny and Zooey
reference_books.review_text:
Lovely language, indeed. 
 But I would've probably be more thrilled, if I had read it some 15 years ago as a teenage girl. 
 Alas, you cannot catch-up with reading what you've missed without any consequences :)

reference_books.title: The Fault in Our Stars
reference_books.review_text: Mislia, che e vazhno da se pishat knigi za sm'rtta. Osobeno za sm'rtta v tazi v'zrast i ot tazi gledna tochka. Kato tsialo obache knigata e banalna - geroite praviat i govoriat tochno neshchata, koito chovek bi ochakval. Za p'rva sreshcha na tiineidzh'ri s temiata obache, predpolagam e dobre.

reference_books.title: The God of Small Things
reference_books.review_text:
The book is as heavy as a monsoon rain and equally beautiful. Very Indian. 
 It is one of these books that I guess u need to re-read to understand fully.

book_a.title: Reading Lolita in Tehran
book_a.user_review:
As much as I wanted, I could not like this book and barely managed to finish the first part. 
 I am angry that a potentially interesting topic and point of view did not unravel in a piece of engaging literature but ended up as a rather dull book. 
 On the positive side I can outline Nafisi's extensive knowledge on literature and the parallels she tries to make between the fate of fictional characters and her student's lives in oppressed Iran. 
 Well, that's about all I found for myself. 
 A fundamental problem with this book is that it lacks structure and plot. It is a series of accounts about a literary group discussions on "forbidden" books, alternated by almost random stories and comments on the lack of freedom in every aspect of daily life in the Islamic republic of Iran. 
 I found the book quite boring. It reminded me of the literary critics texts that I had to read in High School to be able to form my opinion about a certain author. While discussing a book in a face to face meeting might be a really exciting adventure, it is a rather tedious task to write about such discussion (unless you are truly a brilliant writer). 
 What I think might have saved this book - if the author chose to drop the biographical narrative and imagine an event that could create some action and turbulence and showcase the stark contrast between the world of dark reality and the life-saving universe of fiction. 
 Alas, Nafisi chose to pile up facts, which, while helping to create a certain ambience, did not manage to make the book captivating enough and prove the point that reading literally saves lives.

sample_reviews.review_text: Though I dont agree with few things that were mentioned, and strongly believe it comes out as a reaction, overall its a good book to read despite the in depth details of literature that some might find boring
I felt "Reading Lolita in Tehran" was very disconnected, not to mention poorly written. What teacher of English doesn't use quotation marks?

They can translate it in 220 languages, it will remain a lost opportunity to take a stand for real. It's herself to say she was vile in the book. Be cool and have fun in the USA, Azar. Because real Italians write great books about those horrors, but they stay and fight.
I thought this was a wonderful book. It was nicely written and I found the descriptions of life in Tehran fascinating. It was a pleasant surprise.

I couldn't say it better than one of the book's reviewers quoted in the front material: "Certain books by our most talented essayists...carry inside their covers the heat and struggle of a life's central choice being made and the price being paid, while the writer tells us about other matters, and leaves behind a path of sadness and sparkling loss. 'Reading Lolita in Tehran' is such a book." (Mona Simpson, Atlantic Monthly) The style of the book (and Nafisi's wistful revelation of detail) reminds me somewhat of de Botton's "Art of Travel" in that art is used to illuminate personal journey (and inspires a desire for deeper understanding of and engagement in both). A special element of this book (for me) is that it brought Iran into my heart, which for an American is not a straightforward matter. The memoir challenges a nuanced understanding of people, places, and society -- one where you dare to be touched by people instead of ideas of people.
never finished it because it was so tedious, but is good for someone with a greater interest or concern for the "scarved" woman.
Inspirational.

I was a bit disappointed by this book. I had read so many good things about it, but for me it just didn't live up to it's hype. I found it to be disjointed as it careened between literary essays, tales of oppression in Iran and stories about many of the author's Iranian students. 
 I did learn a lot about the background and ongoing affects of the Iranian Revolution; especially it's horrifying affects on the women in that society. It also made we want to go reread 'Pride and Prejudice' which isn't a bad thing. But I found myself making deals with myself to get through the book. Things like, "Just read 25 more pages and you can read more of that fun summer read you've started." 
 I'm glad I finished it, and I think it did get better towards the end as many of the threads and storylines were wrapped up. It did shed new light on the hurdles faced by Iranians in protesting the latest election issues.

After reading this book I realized how lacking my education was in the field of literature....of course that was not my major either. For those who are majoring in literature and have read "Lolita" I think this book will be extremely interesting. For me, not so much. Lots of references to other works but if you haven't read those works, well, you're left wondering the intended connections the author is trying to make. I did create a list of classics I should read so it was worth it to me. I also got a new insight into the women of Tehran.

At first, I wanted so badly to like this book. Like many others who've reviewed before me, I found the premise to be very interesting. Hence, I started reading. The first few chapters were engaging. Each girl had her own story to tell. 
 But then the book no longer seemed to be about this book group. The members faded into the background as the story turned into the author's personal struggle during the Iranian Revolution. Now don't get me wrong, that story certainly has its own merits. And I certainly expected the girls' story to be framed in its proper historical and social context (it is nonfiction, after all). But I suddenly found myself reading a very different book than I had started with. In essence, Nafisi betrayed her readers, tricking them into reading an unintentional story and alienating them in the process. I went from wanting to like the book to just wanting to finish it. 
 In the end, I couldn't justify the time and effort put into reading a book that I already knew I wouldn't enjoy. And so I didn't. It's really too bad.

book_b.title: David and Goliath: Underdogs, Misfits, and the Art of Battling Giants
book_b.user_review: S'zhaliavam, che triabva da go kazha...no s vsiaka prochetena kniga Gladuel mi stava po-skuchen.

sample_reviews.review_text: Interesting Concept. Over generalized.
Great for identifying your perceived weaknesses and using them as strengths

Good storytelling but some of the stories don't really fit the underdog theme (having your parents die when you are a child doesn't make you an underdog). The data to back up some of his conclusions was lacking. The dyslexia chapter was pretty specious and the characterization of the British Army in Northern Ireland as being there to help but going too far in enforcing the law to maintain the peace really glosses over a complex historical and political situation.

Malcolm Gladwells books are all of similar nature where he focus on the extreme data. His books on Outliers, tipping point and David vs Goliath all focus on extreme values and imo, he is quite biased towards the Outliers (David) and neglect many other factors that determine success. 
 I also do not like the negative nature of his books. He always talk about the negative nature of small classes, elite schools and completely bashed them without talking much about the merits. One can easily disagree with his small class size (<18 students) vs large class size argument. 
 Also, other than a few tips, I don't think people are so interested in dyslexia or 3 strikes unless these affect them.

This was just so much less compelling than other Gladwell books I've read. I'd say enjoy it for what it is: popular non-fiction, an easy, quick read. You'll have some new dinner party conversation points, though they may be a bit shallow and trite. I have a newborn, that's my excuse.
Amazing, like everything else Malcolm Gladwell has ever written.

Another great book from Malcome Gladwell, taking the biblical story of David v Goliath to illustrate why the underdog is not always the loser and why in life we perceive disadvantages perhaps too negatively, and how we can, in fact turns these, if they don't destroy us in the process, in the winning card.

I have read, and enjoyed, several of Gladwell's books, but was quite disappointed with this one. I finished it to see if it would improve or come to a good conclusion, but sadly it did not. I would not recommend it for several reasons: 
 1) Unlike several of his books, this one does not seem to come to a "so what?" conclusion. It presents many stories and opinions, but doesn't bring them together to a meaningful lesson or conclusion. 
 2) This book seemed to make the jump from correlation to causation too quickly. He uses the example that a few people who had tough beginnings (e.g. dyslexia or losing a parent)but overcame and succeeded to justify the idea that to really succeed you have to have overcome something tragic. I think you would find far more examples of people who succeeded because they had positive upbringings. 
 3) In several of the examples, Gladwell seems to suggest that if you are the underdog, it is okay to lie a little or cheat a little, because that is how you win. I don't think being at a disadvantage justifies being dishonest or unethical by itself. 
 Overall, I was very disappointed.

Easy to read

sample_reviews.review_text: If you're not sure whether or not to read the Covenant series, this will help you decide. This is a prequel and what starts everything. It is a great preview to the action and romance that is definitely worth a read.

Daimon es el abrebocas que nos permite dar una probadita de lo que podemos esperar encontrar en Mestiza. 
 Aqui es donde conocemos a Alex, su situacion, su vida, y sobre todo la vida que dejo atras -antes de que su madre decidiera abandonar el Covenant. 
 La historia pinta muy bien, y despues de leer esta precuela es segurisimo que leere Mestiza. Me llama mucho el hecho de que sospecho, habra un hombre sexy -pura sangre- con ojos grises por alli ^^ 
 Como siempre, Jennifer Armentrout tiene un estilo muy sencillo de leer. Las paginas se van pasando practicamente por voluntad propia, y cuando menos te enteras ya terminaste el libro. Los personajes tienen esa personalidad marcada- que aunque en este libro corto no se pudo apreciar del todo bien- sospecho se vera resaltada en Mestiza. 
 Y las situaciones estan llenas de accion, cosa que hace te metas mas en el libro, y no lo quieras soltar rapido. 
 Resena completa

Wow! This is just a short novella, but it is awesome. If this is awesome, I know Half-Blood is going to be freakin awesome! Daimon was full of action. I didn't want it to end. Some parts were totally creepy and others terribly sad. I enjoyed every second of it. I like Alex already. She's the "don't mess with me" type of girl. She's strong and can kick butt. This novella will leave you wanting more. I can't wait to read Half-Blood for I know it's going to be great.

Daimon is the prequel to Half Blood. In the description of it, it says that it is Covenant 0.5. The story starts out with Alexandria Andros remembering when she was examined by Hematoi ministers. They do this because Alex is a half-blood and they determine what she will be in life. Then Alex is pulled out of her memory by Matt Richardson, the boy that she is out with at the time. While they were on the beach, a few guys came over to them and started some trouble. Alex, having been trained, defended her and Matt from the guys only to have Matt get mad at her for it because he didn't condone violence. 
 When Alex gets home, she is greeted by her mother who talks to her about sneaking out at night in Miami. She relates the events of the evening and gets that off her chest before going to bed. The next morning, she was supposed to be up "bright and early" cleaning up the balcony. After waking up at noon, she quickly got dressed and then proceeded to go out to the balcony to begin cleaning it. What she discovered when she was out there, was alarming. She saw the very thing she was trained at the Covenant to fight - a Daimon. Daimons feed on aether, the essence of the gods or the life force running through pure-bloods and less concentrated in half-bloods. What happens when she encounters the Daimon is where this story really starts. 
 This is the second book by Jennifer L. Arementrout that I have read and I really like it. She is quickly becoming one of my favorite authors. I liked this book because it gave you a good background into the Covenant series. Daimon leaves a lot of questions and I hope that they will be answered as the series progresses. 
 I Like: 
 *Alex. She has a good personality that is easily likeable. She doesn't know the reasoning behind her mom and her leaving the Covenant but doesn't question this decision outright. I also like the fact that she is a take charge kind of girl. 
 *Alex's mom. You can tell that she has given up a lot for Alex. Being a pure blood, they believe that half bloods, such as Alex, are beneath them. Alex's mom doesn't show this belief. She genuinely cares about Alex. 
 I Didn't Like: 
 *Matt. The guy that she is out with on the beach. He doesn't like it when Alex defends her and him. He seems like a nice guy, but he makes Alex feel like a freak afterwards. 
 *Daimons. They are aether-loving, weird looking with bad teeth, evil people. 
 Cover 
 On the cover it shows a green tulip. This picture reminds me of pictures that I have seen before where they took x-rays of flowers. Only this particular flower has a green smoke-like substance rising out of it. The cover is very pretty, although it doesn't tell me anything about the story.

Daimon is an excellent prequel to Covenant series! It was short but very enjoyable and eventfull story. My only regret is that I read it after the first book. If I read this before Half-Blood, I would probably enjoy it better. Thanks to this prequel, I respect Alexandria even more since it made me understand better what she had to go through in human world.

Won't be a long review since this was a short story. With me, prequels are either hits or misses. And I guess it depends if you actually read it before the first book or not. This one, it was ok nothing special to me. No new information, just when the daimon had found Alex and her mom, with Alex on the run. I'm sure I probably feel differently about it if I had read it before the first book. If you haven't read Half-Blood, then I would recommend reading this first. It leaves you wanting more. I do kind of wish it went back to right before Alex's mom pulled her from the covenant and ran for it. I would love to see Alex in those days.
Actual rating: 4.5 stars

This is a prequel to the first book in the Covenant series called Half-Blood. I am glad that we get the great glimpses of the main character Alex, I especially liked the scenes with her mother. There was a lot of action in this one, Alex is not a tea and crumpets kind of girl and I loved that about her. 
 I like that Alex already knows that she is not exactly human. Don't get me wrong, there are some great books about discovering new powers but I love it when the story is about more than that. In Daimon, Alex knows what she can do and has to be careful to hold back. I do have my suspicions however that she is more than even she knows. 
 This novella serves as a wonderful ambassador for Jennifer Armentrouts upcoming Covenant series. The first chapter of book 1, Half-Blood, is included with Daimon and I can tell you that you are not going to want to wait to see what happens next! It is in that chapter that we are given the first glimpse of Aiden. I can feel an inappropriate crush on a literary character happening. I can not wait! 
 BOTTOM LINE: MAKES ME EVEN MORE EXCITED TO READ BOOK ONE!

Pretty good introduction to the series. I will probably keep reading since most of the series is out. 
 I still prefer and are more infatuated/in love with "LUX SERIES"

Ughhh...yet another weepy, lame YA book where the heroine gets weepy and lusts after the good looking guys for no real reason. First major Fail. 
 Preview is somewhat un-fulfilling. I don't exactly feel the urge to continue reading the actual series after the sneak-preview ebook. The mythical background leaves much to be desired. Blah blah blah, long story short, a bunch of demigods (half god/half human) mate with one another, gets pureblood kids (2 demigod parents) or halfbloods (half demigod, half human = just mostly human). There's a bit of a contradiction in the story where the good purebloods apparently can't do shit and are just there for eye candy, strut around like they're all that, provide the background story and yet the evil purebloods (daimons) have epic god-mode/hackz and can pwn most anyone except the halfbloods (who again apparently are supposed to protect the purebloods against their evil daimon cousins). 
 General Fantasy logic dictates that diluting the blood of any supernatural, all-powerful critter with inferior species results in weaker, far less powerful offspring. Apparently the author superseded that logic and created her own where critters with less strength than the originals can apparently pwn and hunt down the far superior creatures who control the elements and do...demi-godly things. Wow. Strike two. 
 Some (well most) of the reviews here apparently think the Hematoi are Gods. Check again peeps, they're purebloods aka the undiluted offspring of demigods, hence they're demigods. I mean COME ON. It's in the fricking plot summary. Major reading comprehension fail. It makes me wonder whether their Twilight eyes just glazed over most of the story and just thought "Omigod, hot spunky chick with some powers (relatively unknown at this point what they are) and some cute guys and evil 'scary' bastards to fight!!!" Jeez. The fanbase fail is strike three for me.

It's 11:55pm in London, U.K. And I've just finished reading the second book in the series of "Miss Peregrine's children" -> "Hollow City" 
 I was so desperate to finish the book tonight i sacrificed some precious hours of my sleep, as often happen to us readers.

I'm flying threw it and really enjoying the ride, but I still feel it drags on too long. It becomes clear what's about to happen but there's like, 40 steps between now and the Event. (I don't mean one single instance of something happening, I mean between the 'boring' parts and every single conflict). I like the 'boring' parts where everything feels very real, I LOVE in particular the description of London during the Blitz and the people they meet (and the implicit discussion of morality of time travel and survival) but the three pages before every single conflict is...too many pages. Get ON with it already! Jacob realizes things too slow. Which, I mean, he is a fairly-inexperienced 16 year old but still. Also, Enoch is the most annoying ever! But realistically so. Anyway. This all sounds like a lot of critique but I really did enjoy the book!

reference_books.title: Shockaholic
reference_books.review_text:
I love Carrie Fisher, I really do. She is very special to me, as she is for many people around the world. 
 I listened to her reading of this book between last afternoon and this morning, and I have to say I found myself forced to take breaks because my cheekbones hurt a lot of laughing too much. Despite that, in this book she talks more about stuff that I found difficult to laugh about: it really hit me when she said that if anyone would have known how she really felt during her Wishful Drinking tour, she would have won an Oscar for Best Actress because all that she could think of at that time was that her daughter hated her. She mentions that she failed her and that's why she began the ECT treatment to her bipolar disorder. That's something really painful to talk about and I really respect her for doing so, and not even trying to be funny. 
 I was shocked about her talking about her experience with Evan Chandler, the dentist that launched the first child molestation acusation against Michael Jackson. Not about she talked about it, but the things she knew and what kind of man Chandler was: I can't believe that are people so awful walking on Earth. But then again, fucking Donald Trump is president so... 
 Her memories about her late father, Eddie Fisher, and the relationship they shared during the years was something I was looking forward to when I read the synopsis of this book: we all know how close Debbie and Carrie were, but not so much about Eddie.
