reference_books.title: Forbidden
reference_books.review_text:
Ese momento en el que todo el mundo parece adorar un libro, entonces llegas tu lo lees y... Te sientes rara porque te guste tan poco. 
 Desde que lei la descripcion del libro supe que era un libro que muy raramente me iba a gustar, pero es que puedo catalogarlo facilmente como el peor libro que he leido en mi vida. No por la forma en la que esta escrito - he leido una traduccion de fan, asi que no puedo juzgar en ese sentido -, sino por todo el argumento en si: no solo la trama de Lochan y Maya sino por el contexto en el que la historia se desarrolla. 
 No se, la verdad es que soy muy poco fan de los libros "desagradables" - en el sentido de que te hacen sufrir de verdad -, y este en particular si lo tuviera que definir con una palabra seria "disturbing" - no encuentro un termino en castellano apropiado para ello -. 
 De hecho, me lo he leido rapidisimo porque queria terminarlo y pasar a otra cosa - no me gusta dejar los libros a medias, siempre acabo volviendo a ellos -. 
 Es muy libro muy muy duro, desde luego no para cualquier persona - no lo ha sido para mi, desde luego -... Y que quereis que os diga: yo no pienso volver a leerlo ni mucho recomendarlo a nadie.

book_a.title: Donde los árboles cantan
book_a.user_review:
Maravilloso, precioso, todo lo que diga de este libro es poco. 
 Ahora que acabo de terminarlo, me he quedado con la sensacion de haber podido vivir (si, este es uno de esos libros que te lleva a otro mundo mientras lo lees) una de las historias de amor mas bonitas que puedo recordar: de cabeza a mi top 10. 
 El personaje de Viana es muy especial: como la vemos evolucionar de ser todo lo que se espera de una dama noble a toparse con que la vida no siempre suele ser lo que uno espera de ella, y que aun asi uno debe seguir adelante, encontrando su propio lugar en el mundo y convirtiendose en su verdadero yo. 
 Si estas pensando en leerlo, no lo dudes ni por un solo instante, y un ultimo consejo: mucho mejor leerlo al aire libre, en un lugar donde haya muchos arboles :).

sample_reviews.review_text:
Cuando lo agarre por primera vez dudaba sobre si me iba a gustar, ya que algunos libros de esta autora se me hacian un poco aburridos, y me habian dicho que lo unico bueno del libro era el final. 
 Si alguien les dijo eso yo les digo lo contrario. Este es un libro que no pude (ni quise) soltar en dos semanas. Tiene personajes entranables, como Lobo, que es el que mas piensa en todo el libro, como Viana, que la llegas a odiar por no hacerle caso a Lobo nunca, como Uri, que es sin duda uno de mis personajes favoritos en toda la literatura. 
 Tiene la declaracion de amor mas hermosa que haya leido nunca, y las criticas feministas mas apropiadas. Las dudas que se le generan a Viana sobre como debe ser una mujer, son las que nos deberiamos generar nosotros ahora mismo. Porque si, ya no usamos corset, ni tampoco nos pasamos el dia bordando o cociendo, ni tampoco tenemos por que quedarnos en la cocina, pero hay muchos cambios por hacer y libros asi son el primer paso! 
 Completamente recomendable y hermoso!

El comienzo me parecio algo flojo. Si hay algo que me encanta de Laura es la fantasia que rara vez falta en sus historias, y durante los primeros capitulos la eche muchisimo de menos. 
 Sin embargo, la historia fue cogiendo vuelo y me atrapo; la lei en un viaje en bus de casi siete horas y la verdad es que solo solte el libro para ir al bano y detenerme a comer algo en una parada. Vamos, que el viaje se me hizo la nada misma (y creo que mi companera de asiento se debe de haber reido bastante con mis caras mientras leia, ahahah). 
 La relacion entre los protagonistas se me hizo muy rara siempre, pero muy tierna. Quizas sea como se presenta al segundo que hace que su relacion luego no me cuadre, pero bueno. De todas formas estuve a punto de llorar al final, y si no lo hice fue porque mi orgullo me impidio hacerlo en un bus lleno de gente. 
 Me gusto como jugo con lo de la historia de como Lobo perdio su oreja, aunque la autentica me decepciono un poco, a decir verdad. 
 En general me gusto bastante y supera por mucho al ultimo de Laura que me habia leido (La Emperatriz de los Etereos), asi que he quedado muy satisfecha.

Tengo muchas palabras para este libro, pero quiero decir solo una: HERMOSO. La historia que nos cuenta Donde los arboles cantan es tan linda que te llega inmediatamente al corazon. Fantasia, amistad y un romance muy especial hacen de este libro una de las mejores lecturas que he tenido en lo que va del ano. Muy recomendada. 
 Resena: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vCehh...

4.5/5 en realidad. 
 Donde los arboles cantan es un libro que en general me ha gustado mucho, que me ha hecho pensar y viajar a lugares magicos e inolvidables, a traves de personajes que parecian muy reales y que sin duda han dejado huella en mi, por unas u otras cosas. 
 Resena completa aqui: http://somuchmorethanpaper.blogspot.c...

Al contrario que todas las buenas criticas que tiene el libro en la contraportada, a mi no me ha parecido un libro tan maravilloso como nos lo querian vender. 
 La historia es bonita, tanto la de superacion como la de amor. Esta llena de esas cosas que le gusta poner a Laura Gallego en sus libros: una chica fuerte que supera las barreras impuestas por la sociedad (que suelen ser machistas) y esa idea de que tenemos que proteger la Naturaleza. 
 Pero no considero que sea una GRAN historia escrita maravillosamente. Es un libro normal. Para leertelo y pasar un buen rato, pero ya esta. La portada y el resto de la edicion del libro hacen creer al lector que la historia va a ser la bomba, pero a mi parecer no es para tanto. Aunque eso si es verdad, el formato fisico esta muy trabajado y es precioso. 
 En resumen, no es uno de los mejores libros de Laura Gallego pero es pasable.

No me parecio tan entretenido como otros de los libros de esta autora.. Aunque si me gusto todo el proceso por el que paso Viana cuando los barbaros invadieron el reino en donde vivia y como tuvo que adaptarse a una nueva forma de vida.. dejando atras a la doncella que solia ser para volverse una habil cazadora capaz de sobrevivir en el bosque.. 
 En la parte del amor..es una pena lo que paso con Uri.. pero bueno.. desde mucho antes ya se podia anticipar lo que era y lo que pasaria.. 
 Y claro.. adore a Lobo con todas sus anecdotas de como perdio su oreja y como en cada ocasion saco dos ensenanzas.. y claro.. su ingenio y sabiduria en varias ocasiones :p..
AMO a Laura Gallego, todos sus libros me enamoran...
Me encanta como escribe Laura Gallego. Sus historias son increibles. Es el segundo libro que leo de ella, y estoy deseando seguir con mas. Me enamore de los dos personajes principales, Viana y Uri.

Me gusto mucho la historia!!!, de principio a fin. Recomendado a gente que le gusten las historias sobre damiselas en apuros, lugares magicos, caballeros y reinos medievales. Me parecio una historia muy bonita y la disfrute mucho :)

** spoiler alert ** 
 Siceramente, me esperaba mas de Laura Gallego. Con ese curriculum de exitos literarios, no solo por las ventas sino por su particular forma de crear un sentimiento de intriga y placer al leer sus historias que muchos han fallado a resolver, esta historia me deja indiferente. 
 Para empezar, ha querido hacer una novela de caballeria con sus escenas de aventuras y sus romances imposibles que ha quedado en un folletin pseudofantastico que no llega a crear ni un minimo de interes ya que las escenas estan faltas de dialogos trabajados y de elementos sorpresa. 
 Es una historia totalmente predecible, con personajes tipicos y abordados anteriormente y maravillosamente por otros autores de renombre, en la que se ha gastado demasiado papel haciendo florituras e imagenes y poca literatura. Mucho ruido y pocas nueces que se dice. 
 Esta historia deberia haber ocupado 100 paginas a lo sumo, no las casi 500 que tiene. Para mi, una decepcion absoluta. La imaginacion ha brillado por su ausencia, menudos personajuchos, que historieta mas sosa y aburrida y menudo final mas odioso como queriendo compensar la falta de trabajo de todo el libro en las ultimas diez paginas. La tipica historia de amor imposible y los finales tristes narrados por personajes supuestamente enigmaticos han pasado a ser un intento de novela. 
 Espero que su proximo libro no traiga mas de lo mismo, porque ultimamente sus obras son una decepcion para mi. Que buenos tiempos los de "La leyenda del rey errante" o "El coleccionista de relojes extraordinarios" incluso "Cronicas de la Torre" y el primero de Idhun. En aquellos tiempos disfrutaba del placer de leer a Laura Gallego, pero ayer cuando termine el libro me recorrio una sensacion de engano. Haber estado esperando tanto tiempo este libro para que resulte ser un folletin rosa malo.

book_b.title: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child - Parts One and Two (Harry Potter, #8)
book_b.user_review:
Todo lo que habia leido sobre el es verdad: parece un badfic en toda regla, el famoso My Immortal hecho canon. 
 Hay unos agujeros en la trama bestiales, incoherencias con asuntos planteados a lo largo de la saga, personajes totalmente fuera de su caracter (por Dios, Ron llega a dar verguenza ajena) y la sensacion perenne de que estas leyendo un fic mas bien cutrecillo. 
 Toda la storyline de Delphi (no anadire mas para no spoilear al personal) es de reir por no llorar: cuesta creer que JK Rowling haya tenido que ver con nada de esto. Y tambien me cuesta mucho creer lo que dicen que hubiera sido de Cedric Diggory si no hubiera muerto: es mi personaje favorito y por ahi no paso. 
 Pero me han gustado cosas, sobre todo lo concerniente a la familia Malfoy: la relacion de Draco y Astoria, el personaje de Scorpius en si... 
 Todo lo demas... Puf, es que me lo llegan a ensenar diciendo que lo han encontrado en FanFiction.net y me lo creo a pies juntillas. Muy mal, Rowling: tus personajes merecian algo mejor que esto.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I feel now how I felt such a long time ago...when I finished the Deathly Hallows. It was so nice to be back in the world and those characters--old and new. 
 However, the writing was clearly not J.K. Rowling's and it didn't genuinely feel like a Harry Potter book...at least not like how I had expected it to feel. It just feels more like someone paying homage to her and her work instead of staying true to the real writing? I don't know if that necessarily makes sense... 
 All-in-all, I think my enjoyment was still genuine because I missed (SO MUCH) reading Harry Potter and of the wizarding world. 
 Final rating: 2.75/5 stars
For me, this is not canon.

Oh dear. I should have listened to my gut, and simply borrowed this from the library versus buying it. This was ok. Barely ok. And only because I simply loved Harry Potter, and with the play/screenplay format, could envision my beloved characters once again. 
 So disappointing.
I expected nothing and I am still disappointed.
I loved it - I did not expect the story line it followed but it was perfect and I wanted to shed a tear when it finished

Aggressive eye roll. Some moments in this really sing, but for the most part it's overly convoluted, has lots of your favs acting very out of character, and has no regard for subtlety. A+ for lots of Ron and Hermione being cute though.

Muddled thoughts on this one, what can I truly say except for what is in my heart? Tbh, it reads like a piece of simple fanfic, and that's the bottom line. I could add that I think Rowling might have sold out but that is speculation on my part. I have my reasons to think it however. 
 So, I give it two stars - It was ok.
Good if you want Doctor Who-ish meets Harry Potter fan fiction but don't want to search for it.

Gaah I never thought I'd ever give anything related to Harry Potter 1 star and yet here I am. 
 SPOILERS BELOW 
 Now if you go in expecting another Harry Potter book, you will be sorely disappointed. If you go in expecting a play which borrows your favourite characters for a story, you'll probably still be disappointed considering JK Rowling's name is attached to this and you expect a certain level of clever writing from her. Alright so she didn't write the whole thing, she did give her stamp of approval. 
 Firstly, no one is in character. Yeah, sure 19 years have passed but there is so much incongruence it's just making my head hurt. I love Ron. I have always loved Ron. But it seems like they forgot how to write Ron. It reads like movie Ron and not book Ron. Do you not remember Ron Weasley who shared his family and home with Harry after only a year of knowing him? Do you not remember Ron who told Sirius that he would have to go through him before killing Harry, when he thought Sirius was a mass murderer? Do you not remember Ron who Hermione fell in love with because he remembered the house elves and went to warn them during the Battle of Hogwarts? But you know, whatever. Let's have Ron only for comic relief, who only thought about food and wore a gravy-stained napkin when his best friend's son went missing. Fuck you. 
 I get Albus. I get it, it can't have been easy being Harry Potter's son and living up to his name. I can understand his frustration and his anger. What I can't get is Harry's reaction to his son. Really, you really think Harry is going to tell him he wished Albus wasn't his son?? Are we basing Harry on his 5th year when he got mad at everything? It's so out of character for him. And don't give me the bullshit that JK Rowling obviously knows her own characters better, because if she did, no way would she treat Cedric like that. 
 Which brings me to Cedric. Cedric Diggory, the boy who was kind above all, became a Death Eater because he was humiliated during the Triwizard Tournament? Is this the same Cedric Diggory we are talking about who wanted a rematch because Hufflepuff won only because Harry fell off his broom? The one who wanted to be fair so told Harry about the Second Task? The one who wanted Harry to take the cup because he felt Harry deserved it more?? Okay, as long as we're clear. This is especially shitty, considering Hufflepuff has almost no other heroes. 
 What about how the only reason Ron and Hermione are together is because Ron got jealous about Krum?? What are you even on about?? 
 Yes, completely murder Draco's character, why don't you?? 
 The worst of all was the plot. The really weird bizzaro plot. Time- Turner? Is this even a plot? It sounds like those memes where people keep suggesting why didn't they just go kill Voldemort when he was a kid? The wacky plot had so many loopholes it'll make you laugh. 
 The only good thing was Harry confronting Dumbledore about leaving him in an abusive household for ten years. 
 Scorpius as a character was really good. He was funny and smart. 
 But the plot. Ugh. 
 My head hurts from all the bullshit. 
 tl;dr I've read fanfics by 15 years old with tighter plots and better characterisation.
ga terlalu rame....ceritanya bisa ketebak

reference_books.title: The Devil in the White City: Murder, Magic, and Madness at the Fair That Changed America
reference_books.review_text: The story is interesting, certainly. However, the structure of the book makes it entirely anti-climactic. I couldn't imagine how much more I could read about the landscaping, the plans for the architecture and even the serial killer's mad behavior. I truly wish the book had been structured differently to keep the story engaging.

reference_books.title: The Group
reference_books.review_text: Others' reviews make me feel like I missed something tremendous with this book. Initially I found an intriguing look at an earlier generation of women's experiences but as the novel continued, I lost interest. I felt frustrated by the characters, their slim connections, in some cases, within the group, and the lack of voice of many of the women. I understand it's a different era and the inherent differences between then and now but general self-worth wasn't entirely absent then was it?

reference_books.title: The Versions of Us
reference_books.review_text:
Perhaps because I read this on an e-reader, the pattern of the "versions" of the story were not immediately obvious because I didn't see the words "version one" (or two and three) at the top of the chapter. I assume that's easier to see on a print version. 
 In the end, I really enjoyed the stories of Eva and Jim- the ways in which their lives intertwined in each version of the story. Eva and Jim meet one afternoon in college and then their blossoming romance is tested by circumstances that lead to choices that give us three versions of their two lives. Familiar faces populate each version- Eva's parents and brother, friends they have known since college or soon there after- all providing continuity to these stories no matter how the relationship of Eva and Jim varies. 
 The novel takes the reader from Jim's and Eva's college years to their later years and as a result, the book has an emotional resonance and the natural bittersweet reality that comes with love and loss of loved ones and friends over the course of a lifetime.

reference_books.title: War Brides
reference_books.review_text: I agree with reviews I've read about War Brides- the beginning and end feel rushed and tacked on but the portion of the story set during WWII is good. I'd actually like to read more about Churchill's SOE and Aux groups now. Decent book but a little too fluffy for my tastes.

reference_books.title: The Greater Journey: Americans in Paris
reference_books.review_text: I haven't read other McCullough books but this one was a slog. Parts were so uplifting and fascinating- so many writers and artists are covered in this book. But the Franco-Prussian War sucked all of the energy out of the book. I nearly gave up but am glad I didn't.

book_a.title: Life Itself
book_a.user_review: What a wonderful book. Parts are a bit too detailed but overall, it's an honest, painstaking look at his experiences and the realities of his life sans voice. Audio book with Edward Hermann narrating was very engaging.

sample_reviews.review_text:
If you are interested in the most insignificant details of Roger Ebert's early years, this book is for you. There are the riveting details of his breakfast order in a restaurant in 1965 and similarly fascinating details of his life. 
 I wanted to hear about his struggles with illness and his courage to overcome physical limitations. 
 I'm sure this book gets better and I believe he has lead an interesting life but I'm about half way through and just can't hang in there to see.
I got up to the third chapter and quit. His style of writing bored me and I just couldn't get into it. There's also editing problems and spelling errors.

Roger Ebert is one of my favorite writers, and I looked forward to this autobiography with tremendous anticipation. But although well-written, I found it fragmented. Rather than telling the story of his life, the book consists of a series of standalone chapters, each talking about one specific topic, and several of which originally began life as posts on his blog. I was surprised how little of his book was devoted to his life as a film critic; instead, we get (often wonderful) stories about his wife and his extensive travels in Europe, especially his beloved London. But I found myself bored by enormous sections of the book, in which Ebert waxes poetic about people the vast majority of his readers will not know. That's his right, of course... but considering his friendship with Studs Terkel is given about the same amount of coverage as his partnership with Gene Siskel, you'll understand why something seems off in the way the topics are organized. My problems with the book are more the result of my incorrect expectations than the book itself. If you want to read a collection of disjointed personal essays about a wide variety of topics that Mr. Ebert finds interesting, you'll enjoy this book. If you want to learn the story of how Ebert became the most famous film critic in the world, this isn't it.

I bought this the day after Roger Ebert died. After having read the book, I'm sorry I didn't know the man in person. Yet I'm thankful for getting to know him, to the extent that that's possible, through these, his memoirs. 
 What emerges is a deeply sympathetic man, who was essentially conservative (especially in his relationship to place and to the past), but who lived quite an exciting life. He was an unashamed liberal, but he cherished tradition - his non-theological devotion to Catholicism being the most touching instance of this fusion. The book is funny, it's touching and like so much of Ebert's other writing, it's poignant in its observations on human nature and experience. Some of my favourite parts are his memories of other people, some famous like Lee ("F...ing") Marvin and John Wayne, some not so much like Chaz, his wife. 
 It's bittersweet to read a book about the life of a man so recently departed. Especially one as alive as Ebert was. But somehow that makes the book and the life partly contained within its pages that more precious. Ebert was a good man. He lived a good life. And this was a good book.

Roger Ebert was and always will be the definitive movie critic. I don't care what anyone else says. I have wanted to read his collections of essays and reviews for a long time now; instead, I found myself downloading the audio version of his memoir. I don't regret that decision. This is extremely well-written, proving that Ebert was a born scribe and had a gift with words. Ebert's life is quite extraordinary, though I felt some sections should have been fleshed out a bit more. Overall, though, this was a very good memoir, one that made me miss the man tremendously.

I've been a Roger Ebert fan for many years. When Ebert and Siskel reviewed movies I usually favored Ebert's take. I admired his opinion enough that I sought out and read his books. He had a unique knack of connecting with the reader. I've been looking forward to reading his autobiography because I hoped to learn more about him and what got his into the movie review racket. I was pleased to get that and surprised when I got so much more. Besides a riveting and very personal account of his life, he shared a few tips on writing. I'd been commissioned to write a book review and applied his technique. It made writing the article a lot easier, and I got a compliment from my copy editor on the piece. I've no doubt that Ebert's mortality was very present in his mind as he penned this autobiography. He professional career was successful because he described what he saw through his lens. His autobiography was a chance, probably he last one, to describe to us the lens itself. He did a very admirable job.

Not a straightforward biography, but more of a memoir. Ebert has an easy-to-read writing style and looks back on his past with nostalgia and humor. Much of this I had read previously in his blog posts. 
 My favorite sections were the ones on his surgery, his wife and Gene Siskel. I also enjoyed his memories of his childhood, which reminded me of Ray Bradbury in content. (They both grew up in Illinois.) 
 If you like Ebert's reviews, you may enjoy this book.

This is a powerful and well-written memoir. I thoroughly enjoyed Roger Ebert's reflections on travel, especially London. He perfectly captures the thrill of being overseas. His examples of the new journalism--profiles of Robert Mitchum and Lee Marvin--were so humorous that I was laughing as I was reading them. Most of all, his recollections of bohemian Chicago (the news rooms, O'Rourke's tavern) is a lost bit of Chicago history. Roger, you are an inspiration, and I am glad you were a Chicagoan. Rest in peace.

Picked it up hoping to learn more about his career as a movie critic. Instead, it focuses on his memories with his family and his various stories attempting to portray him as a "ladies man" (nice try, I'm not buying it). Also, much of the content is repetitive from chapter to chapter -- not sure if this was intended to be written as a series of essays, rather than chapters, or if it was a technique. Either way, it was annoying.

Pulitzer prize winner Ebert is the only film critic to have a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. I first started noticing him on TV in the late 1970's. He was cohost of Siskel & Ebert and Ebert & Roeper on TV for 33 years. Unfortunately, his most recent show, Ebert Presents At the Movies, went off the air about a year ago, giving him some time to finish this autobiography. I was quite surprised to find that this is the 22nd book for which he has been either author or co-author. 
 Most revealing aspects of Ebert's life include alcoholism, his marriage, and especially his long relationship with Gene Siskel. Then finally his cancer diagnosis and treatment, ending with his loss of the ability to eat, drink, or speak. 
 Although Ebert is about five years older than me, many aspects of his youth are very familiar to me, such as growing up with books about Tarzan, the Hardy Boys, and Tom Corbett, Space Cadet. As I did, Roger attended Catholic grade school at which the teachers were Dominican nuns who required the memorization of the Baltimore Catechism. Recesses were filled with games of softball, dodgeball, marbles, and hopscotch. 
 As I did, the youngster Ebert attended Sunday Mass, had a paper route and was a voracious reader who fell in love with Science Fiction. Philip K. Dick, Arthur Clarke, and Ted Sturgeon. Ace Doubles. We both collected stamps, rode our bicycles all over, and marveled at Jayne Mansfield. Both of us bought sky-blue Fords, his a 1954 model, mine a 1973 Maverick. 
 A great read by a cultural icon!

book_b.title: Before the Fall
book_b.user_review:
A private jet carrying eleven people crashes into the ocean on its way from Martha's Vineyard to New York. In addition to the crew, a family of four, a couple and another man make up the party on the plane. Only the single man, Scott Burroughs, and the four-year-old child of the family survive the crash and make it back to shore. What follows is author Hawley's reflections on the modern state of media and the inevitable circus that results when a media mogul and another wealthy man die inI that crash. That Scott should survive and want no attention for his heroism under dire circumstances is viewed as suspect by one media outlet that sounds remarkably similar to Fox News. Scott must rely on his wits to withstand the scrutiny of the media and those who would take advantage of knowing him. 
 Thriller of the summer? I'm not sure I would agree with that assessment. Most of the drama lies in Scott's remarkable swim to shore. The rest is a mixed bag of not altogether unexpected events and a not entirely surprising reveal of the cause of the plane crash. Before the Fall has a great premise and starts with energy but soon slows and loses that sense of purpose. Enjoyable but not my idea of a thriller. 
 I received a free e-ARC from NetGalley in exchange for an honest review.

sample_reviews.review_text: Really enjoyed this book but found the ending somewhat disappointing.
It was only ok for me. I really wanted to like it but I was underwhelmed.

I can't for the life of me begin to describe how poorly written this book is. There seemed to be missing words, and sentences that made no sense. I had to read and reread some parts just to attempt to piece everything together. 
 There didn't seem to be any order either, while I'm a huge fan of the past/present writing style that leads to a huge revolution, it was just too confusing in Before the Fall. You would be in the present one second, and the past the next. 
 I struggled to keep up with whose thoughts we were reading and placing them in context. 
 The idea of espionage, money laundering, and possible terrorism is thrilling and can be wildly entertaining in fictional writing. However, that just doesn't happen in this book.

The first half of this book was riveting. As the book progressed, however, I became frustrated with the direction of the conflict between privacy and the public's need for easy answers. The chief antagonist, news personality Bill Cunningham, was very one-dimensional. The author could have given him a much more interesting motivation of greed, jealousy - something other than being a mean-spirited news-hack. The ending of this story missed the boat for me.

I really enjoyed this book. It was a suspenseful, heartbreaking, edge-of-my-seat kinda book that really has me thinking about our news outlets, especially those that seem more interested in ratings than the truth. I didn't know the truth until almost the end of the book. I don't keep many books, but I will be keeping this one! 4 1/2 stars. I hope to read more from this author.

I believe this will be one of the must read books of this year. One of those books that everyone is talking about. Noah Hawley has crafted a masterpiece in the mystery/thriller genre. One thing that most readers crave is character development, and Hawley definitely delivers that in this book. Each character is thoroughly profiled, including background, common threads, and the events leading up to them boarding the plane. Vivid descriptions immerse you in the story with the characters. There is a depth and richness in these pages that is far superior to most books found on the bestseller lists. The ending seems abrupt and leaves you wanting more, but you do not come away disappointed. I would recommend this book to all fans of mysteries and thrillers. I received this as a free ARC from Grand Central Publishing on NetGalley in exchange for an honest review.

This is a story of the aftermath of a plane crash, the best part of which is an examination of how the 24-hour news cycle and politically-motivated "journalism" distort events and judge people for shock value rather than elucidation. I found the main character to be particularly interesting because he has a rich inner life but his ability to articulate that life is poor, so he usually sounds shallow or caught off-guard when speaking, even when his interior monologue is much richer.

I read this on holiday and it was perfect for that - easy to read, short sections, very well-plotted. There were a few red herrings that I nearly fell for but he kept me guessing to the end. The ending was a bit "made for TV" I thought. much as I wanted it to turn out that way.
Not too interesting.
Great story! Loved everything about this mystery/drama.

reference_books.title: Fingersmith
reference_books.review_text:
I loved the first part of this, until the switcheroo, which felt like a total break of the author-reader contract. But I did keep reading, even though I hated Maud -- and to be fair, it is extremely difficult to write an interesting and engaging passive character -- because I knew there was something more at stake here, a reason for the initial switcheroo. And a glance at other reviews showed that one of the characters was going to have a comeuppance, and I was curious how that would finally unfold. 
 I dind't get to that comeuppance. When I got to the second switcheroo, which came in the guise of a Big Secret, I rolled my eyes and shut the book. 
 I admire Waters for taking chances and pushing boundaries, especially because that's one of the things I'm seeking in my pleasure reading these days. But this didn't do it for me, and I can't say why. Maybe because as soon as each switch happened, I could see clearly how we'd been set up for it - and after the first, I was looking for the second, so I watched it unfold and was therefore not surprised. Maybe it's just not a storyline that grabs me; I was certainly more interested in the initial life we are shown for Sue and her band of fingersmiths than I was with what came after. (And again, some of that is due to the passivity of Maud and her blank and boring life.) Maybe it was simply that Maud and her life at Briar simply WERE too passive and boring to hold my interest, capture my imagination, and engage my emotions. 
 At any rate, I wound up taking this back to the library as fast as I could.

reference_books.title: Sweet Ache (Driven, #6)
reference_books.review_text:
DNF at less than 25% -- not something I do lightly. 
 But here's the thing. This is supposed to be a standalone, yet chapter 2, which opens at a race, doesn't set the scene for anyone new to this world. It wasn't until someone pulled into pit row that I realized we weren't at an Ironman event or something, yes despite the series title. DRIVEN can be taken many ways, after all - and this is supposed to be a standalone. That means no assuming the reader understands the world this is set in. 
 So then we meet Quin, who's got major issues with the men around her. Luke can't take NO for no -- and Quin just sighs and goes about her life. She tells us she's a grad student who is behind in her thesis work (clearly, she's not DRIVEN), to the point that I have to wonder what she's even doing in grad school at all, if she's not doing the work. 
 She tells us she's caught a number of her ex-boyfriends having sex with other women. Seems to be a problem for Quin, which is a bit alarming that the heroine's instincts are THIS BAD. Is there something wrong with her that even though she says she's going to be more careful, she simply can't be, especially when Hawkin Play, our rocker, enters the scene. He all but molests her, again -- like Luke -- not listening when she says no. And of course, he knows her own will better than she does because he doesn't stop and then she gives in and it's the best kiss ever and... 
 This shit is how rape culture is perpetuated. She said NO to Luke. She said NO to Hawkin. 
 NO MEANS NO. 
 Period. 
 End of discussion. 
 And don't give me that, "But it's realistic..." whiny line. Yes, it is. Because we're fed a normalization of abuse and rape culture. It's a cycle that spins and spins -- and it's time for it to end. 
 So, yeah. DNF. 
 Oh, and the editing in this book is terrible. Misplaced modifiers, missing commas that change the entire meaning of a sentence and often leave me with a "What the fuck is this even trying to say?" - and I'm an editor. I have clients who care enough to pay me to figure it out. The fact that no one did for this novel is an insult to the reader -- and, given that this was published by Signet, the author. She deserves better. So do readers.

reference_books.title: Sweet as Sin (Bad Habit, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
There is often a fine line between alpha male and abuser. Maybe it's not that fine a line, come to think of it. After all, the sexiest alpha males have respect for their women or partners. Abusers? Not even close. 
 In Sweet as Sin, narrator Kat tells us she's been in abusive relationships before and she knows what they look like. Yet she lets Nico manhandle her and even use non-consensual sex as a punishment. In fact, it turns her on. 
 This isn't a character who is sincere that she's done being abused. This is a character who gets off on it. 
 And so Nico pays off her mortgage without discussing it with Kat. He shows up uninvited. He ignores her when she says no. 
 And Kat loves it. 
 This is a kind of depravity that's not for me. It's not love; it's abuse. 
 There's nothing that can ever convince me that a story about an abusive man and the woman who loves to be abused is worth my time. Abuse shouldn't be normed like this; the carnage left in its wake is too expansive and runs too deep. Of course, that's not on the page. Carnage isn't romantic. 
 But apparently, according to some, the abuse itself is.

reference_books.title: Laid Bare (Brown Family, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 When I talk to people about erotica, erotic fiction, erotic romance, Lauren Dane is one of my go-to authors. I met Lauren a number of years ago and we ocassionally Tweet to each other. I admire her. 
 But for some reason, Laid Bare didn't do it for me. I wanted it to. 
 Oh, it's hot. And it's hot in the right way: the sex advances the story. It advances the character development. Oh, sure, some may say there's too much sex, but to each his or her own and I think that the sex lives of Todd, Ben, and Erin just lead to the fun of the story. These people are hot for each other! 
 But I had other problems. Often, dialogue felt forced. The storyline was HUGE, maybe too big for its book. We had the issue of Erin's losing her daughter, Erin no longer on stage, Erin the cafe owner, Todd and his sexual tastes, Ben and his sexual tastes, Erin's employee, who was stalked by her ex, how the family reacts to a triad... There's a LOT going on, so much so that it's next to impossible to boil this down into the usual formula: This is a story about ____ who wants ____. And that creates problems because when you don't know what motivates a character, it's hard to watch them grow. 
 Yet Erin does grow. Is it because of her love for Todd and Ben? Is it because time has passed and she's ready to face her past? Is it because Ben and Todd are men who work in security and that gives her the feeling of security that she's been lacking? 
 Impossible to say. 
 So it's a messy plot, and sure, you can argue that life is messy and so fiction should be as well, but again, it's hard to say exactly WHAT the story is. Romance? Women's fiction? I won't even go near the derogatory terms, as I don't buy into them in a story like this, when the erotic portions are integrated so well into the story and characters. 
 Overall, I'd call it a good read, not a great one. I wouldn't classify it as Rock Fiction, either, because Erin could really have any other job, and in fact, seems to identify more as a cafe owner than as a musician. I'd have liked to have seen more focus on how the tragedy of her daughter's death affected her rocker self and how that changed her. 
 Still, I'm always glad I read it because Lauren Dane's got the chops to show someone the truths of erotica and erotic fiction. I love that she didn't take the easy route with the threesome sex, that she let the characters have boundaries that each respected. And I love that there's no magic cocks; Erin has to follow her own path to heal. The intimacy forged through sex is what gives her a sense of security in which that healing can take place, and that's an important, empowering way to use sex and intimacy in a meaningful relationship. I wish there were more books featuring this sort of healthy sex and intimacy on the market.

reference_books.title: A Visit from the Goon Squad
reference_books.review_text:
It figures that Jennifer Egan's A Visit from the Goon Squad just won the Pulitzer Prize for fiction. The judge found it to be emotionally satisfying. 
 Before the prize was handed out, I sat down with a copy, freshly downloaded from my local library. And... I hated it. I didn't finish it. I couldn't make myself do it. (That's why it figures that it won the Pulitzer! I've seen this happen waaaay too many times.) 
 To be honest, I found the book boring. I found it emotionally flat, the same way I react to way too many short stories I've read in my time. The stories may have been about rock and roll -- and they were, since they featured an aging record exec and his young employee -- but they failed to strike that chord with me. You know the chord I'm talking about: the one that resonates and makes the book breathe. The one that transcends words and makes everything come alive. 
 Goon Squad felt too much like I was back in graduate school, bored and yearning for something different. (Of course, I feel the need to point out that my fellow students felt similar loathings toward me -- only they wished I'd conform and write something they could relate to. Needless to say, workshops could be difficult. You grow a thick skin FAST in those environments.) 
 I'm not surprised this book won the Pulitzer. The only award-winning books I seem to like are the Printz award winners, and I've only read a couple of them. (They're for Young Adult, in case you aren't familiar with it, and one of my all-time-favorite books, Fat Kid Rules the World, was the first Printz winner I encountered. Yep, another work of Rock Fiction.)

book_a.title: Spider's Bite (Elemental Assassin, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Originally posted at http://rockread.westofmars.com 
 When I'd heard that Jennifer Estep had a new series in the works, a darker series that was going to feature an assassin, I was conflicted. First was the sorrow at the end of the Bigtime series. It's a fun series, full of humor and a fictional world so vivid, I'd move to Bigtime if I could. After only three books, I wanted more. The potential characters were there. They just had to get a book contract so they could come to life. 
 It's okay, I ws told. Just wait, I was promised. The Elemental series will kick Bigtime's butt. 
 It does. It is darker, as promised, and the delicious absurdities of Bigtime have been smoothed out. Yet names still have matching initials, Fiona Fine makes an appearance in passing, and Estep's narrative voice -- this time in the guise of Gin Blanco, aka the Spider -- still rocks. 
 The plot's pretty standard: the bad guys tie our heroine up in a double-cross and she's got to untangle it. Important people die. There's a love interest. 
 But, as happens in all the best books, nothing is this easy. Gin may be an assassin, but she's got a conscience. Our romantic interest has got one, too -- only his gives him trouble (and really, when was the last time we saw this happen? A man? Really? A lot of fiction would have you believe men lack consciences.) and gets in the way of romance. 
 That's okay, though. Gin's too busy to be swooning over the good detective. Much. It's a good balance our girl gets going, and it all makes sense at the time. Decisions that would seem stupid if I wrote them here work. 
 A couple of things truly impress me with this series-starter. One is the world-building. Estep knocked it out of the park with Bigtime, and she takes it a step further with Ashland. We've got dwarves, vamps, giants -- and people who can control the elements: air, fire, water, and stone -- an interesting twist on the familiar Earth magic. It is this magic of Gin's that provides a low, humming resonance to the book. 
 Gin's got an unusual hobby, as well. Part of her cover is as a college student, so she amuses herself by taking, among other things, cooking classes. Our heroine rises above the stereotype of the working woman (always with a completely empty refrigerator) and has her place stashed. Not only is her larder full, so's her knowledge of what to do with those foods. It fits, as the other part of her cover is a part-time employee of the Pork Pit (note those repeating initials!). While she may not whip up barbecue at home, she's comfortable with a kitchen. And with knives (that's her joke, not mine). 
 Again, this is a series starter that I could go on and on about. Estep gets how sleazy the true forces behind a city's scenes can be, and she puts that on display. Mab Monroe is a character with huge potential; I hope Gin interacts on a more direct scale with her as the series progresses. I hope Ashland continues to evolve and become a character in its own right. 
 I hope... I hope... I hope. 
 I hope I can make it to March and the release of Web of Lies.

"My name is Gin and I kill people." 
 And so Gin's tale of loneliness and murder begins. Gin, herself is as blunt as her opening statement. Her views are as rigid and unyielding as the stone magic she wields. However, while Gin can use ice magic, she is as not as cold as she'd lead most people to believe. Her assassination assignments (trying saying that five times fast!) are governed by strict rules: no children, no pets, no innocents. The motivations that drive her through the events of Spider's Bite are linked to the love and loyalty that she shows her chosen family. 
 That being said, I found it hard to identify and truly care about her struggles and this definitely coloured my enjoyment of the book. What made up for this was the intricate web (ahem) of plot lines woven throughout the story. Estep has sewn lots of hints at further conflicts and mysteries in following novels. I love this kind of forethought, as it really adds depth to the characters and their world. As there are far more intriguing questions raised than answered, I will be picking up Web of Lies soon!

Spider's Bite by Jennifer Estep Gin Blanco is a stone elemental and an assassin known as the Spider. She also works part time at the Pork Pit in Ashland, at the junction of North Carolina, Tennessee, and Virginia. A job goes south when she discovers she has been set up and now an air elemental is after her, along with the local police. With her handler dead and her base of operations currently unsafe, her resources are limited. However, she does gain a temporary ally - Detective Donovan Caine. The stage is set for Gin to fail spectacularly - and she knows it. The knowledge that the cards are stacked against her won't stop her from taking out those that set her up. 
 This was a fun addition to the urban fantasy genre! I liked that it was more action and character development than romance, though there is a touch of that sprinkled in here. The story starts off in a mental health asylum. Gin is there undercover as that is the only feasible way of getting to her target. I had a lot of fun with this opening as it was not what I was expecting. Gin's limited morals make her an interesting character right from the start. I like that she doesn't go all emo when it comes to killing people. She's already figured out what her limits are and where the lines are drawn for her in the matter of killing humans. 
 Her adoptive family trained her and now act as her partners in the business. Fletcher Lane is her handler, setting up the jobs and keeping her from direct contact with those that require her services. Fletcher's son, Finn, is really good with documents and can make nearly anything that Gin might need for her jobs. They've been working together for years, and with the Pork Pit as their base of operations, they have a really good thing going. That is until someone set's the Spider up for assassination herself. 
 So I wasn't expecting things to get personal for Gin in the first book, with her adoptive family targeted along with her. That made this story much more exciting! As the injuries occur and the body count increases, we meet other magical misfits that have worked with Gin and her family for years. Jojo is a Dwarf beautician and a healer. Gin definitely needs access to a healer. Regularly. Sometimes desperately. Jojo's Goth sister, Sophia, is good at disposing of bodies; another must for the assassination business. I really enjoyed Sophia and her usually monosyllable responses to queries. The image of a grunting, aloof Goth Sophia is awesome! 
 Then we have the problem of Donovan Caine. He's a straight arrow detective and he has a personal beef with the Spider; his partner was killed several months back by the Spider and now he wants this assassin behind bars or dead. Yet Gin saved his life even as she was busy taking out targets that were there to set her up. So now he owes her and agrees to help her on this one case. Pretty soon it becomes clear there is an undercurrent of attraction between the two, even if it is an unwelcome distraction for Gin and an undeniable fact for Detective Caine. Gin had very good reasons for killing Donovan's partner but she holds off on telling him. After all, she doesn't have to defend her actions to this detective! Part of me wants Donovan to ask and learn all the facts and part of me wanted Donovan to figure it out on his own - he's a detective after all! This situation added a delicious dollop of tension to the book. 
 In the end, I really enjoyed this story. It was a fun mix of magic and mystery. The romance was an undercurrent and didn't become the main feature - which is just how I like it! Gin is a very interesting character that already has a strong sense of who she is and what she will and will not do. I liked that we learned some keys things about her past but the book wasn't flooded with flashbacks. Over all, a most enjoyable urban fantasy romp! 
 I won a physical copy of this book from AudioGals (thanks!). As always, my opinion is my own. 
 Narration: Lauren Fortgang was great with her southern twang for the Spider. She had distinct voices for all the characters and her male character voices were masculine. She did read the one sex scene in a kind of monotone, like she was bored with it, but that is my only criticism.

This is the kind of book which seems good on the surface, but underneath there lie a whole heap of glaring flaws which totally spoil it (for me, anyway). 
 The story has promise: Gin is a magical assassin who gets framed and has to find out who framed her. Gin is kick ass and hard as nails, which doesn't give you a whole lot to identify with but I liked how tough she was. 
 But the flaws- arggggh! 
 The opening scene seems cool on the face of it- Gin has infiltrated a mental asylum so she can kill one of the counselors there. Why go to all the trouble of masquerading as a patient? Why didn't she just snag the woman when she was on her way home? The reason given is that people often get killed in asylums so the murder will attract less attention. But wait- after she kills the woman, Gin (the supposed patient) disappears. So what you have now is a murderous lunatic escaped from an asylum, which would cause far more uproar than just quietly offing the woman and dumping her body. Basically, I think the author thought of a cool opening scene (which it is) and decided to use it, plausibility be damned. 
 Gin is an elemental- as in earth, air, fire, and...ice? The book says that water is a derivative of ice, but surely it's the other way round? 
 Then there's the way Gin gets caught out by another assassin when she's on a job, because she's busy ogling a dude. She's supposed to be a super-assassin, the Spider, but she lets someone creep up on her with a gun cos she's checking out a guy. Apparently she's only kick ass when there aren't hot guys around. 
 The writing is also desperately repetitious: over and over Gin thinks about how hot the Detective is, how her family was burned, how she has grey eyes, and how she's sad about Fletcher- gah, we get it, already. She looks at things with her 'grey eyes'- who thinks of themselves like that? Then every time her gaze meets the detective's, its 'grey on gold'- or should that be hazel? There's some inconsistency there. And the detective is constantly moving his eyes from her breasts to her legs and back again, like some kind of crazy bobble-head perve. Over and over. It made me want to throw my Kindle out the window. 
 The most original and interesting thing about this book in my opinion is that they use condoms during sex and the detective comes too quickly the first time. 
 I wouldn't go as far as to say the book isn't entertaining at all, but by the end I didn't really care what happened or about any of the characters. 
 It's a real shame because it seems like it's going to be really good, but the holes. repetitions and errors in detail let it down. I've given it 2 stars rather than 1 because if you aren't the kind of person who pays a great deal of attention to detail, or plausibility, the book is probably quite enjoyable.

sample_reviews.review_text: Lynsand Sands has a way of creating a world of normal people slipping into a different world, which still seems normal. As an author myself, I wish I'd come up with the idea myself! Once reading one you've already fallen in love with all the characters needing to hear their stories too. The pages are full of passion, drama, friendship, laughter and comedy - some scenes have you laughing out loud. All read page turners.

For the purposes of disclosure, I must admit that had I known that Love Bites was a paranormal romance, I never would have agreed to read this book. I am normally not a fan of paranormal romance, and try to avoid the genre altogether. That said, I must admit that I kind of liked the book. Yes, it had the usual boy meets girl, girl runs away from boy, and boy and girl get together storyline. It was extremely predictable for a lot of the book, but I still found it entertaining and when it comes to reading anything, the ability to hold my attention is extremely important. Unlike many paranormal romance books, I didn't find myself stopping because doing laundry seemed more interesting than reading this book. 
 I suppose I should give you a little background now. Etienne is a three hundred year old vampire who suddenly shows up in Rachel's morgue with a gunshot directly to his heart. Immediately Rachel finds herself attracted to the corpse however she calms herself when she realizes that what she is thinking about actually amounts to necrophilia. Rachel is sick with the flu and when Etienne sits up and begins to speak to her, she believes that she is having a fever induced hallucination and promptly passes out. Days later when he arrives in her morgue yet again he burned from head to toe but this time, a man intent on finishing the job actually mortally wounds Rachel when she attempts to save Etienne from having his head shopped off. To be clear, she intervened because she thought she sensed a heart beat coming from him. 
 When she awakes next she is in Etienne's home and he is faced with task of telling her that he has made her vampire rather than letting her die. What follows is one of the most humorous exchange that I have read in a paranormal romance book ever. With references to neck sucking and Buffy the Vampire Slayer, Rachel attempts to understand what has happened to her. Next comes a series of interchanges with Etienne's vampire family and I can tell you that in between the mushy lovey dovey vanilla sex, that the laughs keep coming. 
 I really wanted to like Etienne, but I found his attempts to force Rachel to stay with him to be extremely manipulative. Rather than to help her take blood on her own he actually fed her spoiled blood so that she was be forced to rely on him for intravenous feeding. I also didn't like the fact that Etienne's cousin gave Rachel drug laced blood to encourage sex between Etienne and Rachel. When we consider how often women are slipped date rape drugs, this was uncomfortable to say the least. Even though Rachel did consent and consent enthusiastically to sex the degree to which she influenced by the drugs bothered me. When it comes to consent and sexual activity, there should never be any murky water.

 Tame vampire love story with a lot of sex 
 The story: 
 In theory, a vampire is pretty darn close to indestructible. But Etienne Argenau finds out the hard way that all it really takes is a determined self-proclaimed vampire hunter with the means to stack up on weapons and gadgets. During Etienne's second involuntary trip to the morgue (once shot, once burnt), the hunter barges in to finish the job - and the confused young doctor in attendance, Rachel Garrett, throws herself between the madman and the miraculously recovered "corpse" and gets an axe in the chest for her troubles. 
 There is only one way to save her: Etienne is allowed to turn ONE single person in his endless life. Just one. And if she doesn't turn out to be his soulmate, he's in for an eternity of loneliness. 
 Pros: 
 I liked the basic idea of the story: what happens when a Vamp lands himself in the morgue more than once? That's bound to be a sticky situation! And what happens when he turns a woman who didn't ask for it and who might not thank him for it, either? 
 The novel is easy to read and entertaining for an evening or two of light reading - if you don't expect too much. 
 Cons: 
 In large parts of the story, I didn't like Rachel much. She's described as a "firecracker" and "prickly", but to me she often sounded like a rude, whiny teenager. I didn't feel any real connection between Rachel and Etienne, either; it felt forced because they *had* to fall in love for the story to work. 
 The "villain" is introduced on the very first page, and from there, the story pretty much follows a tired old pattern: two people who were thrown together by fate get to know each other, fall in love, face some minor obstacles and a few misunderstandings... Then there's the showdown with the villain and they live happily ever after. There absolutely nothing surprising or new in this novel. 
 There were some hints that the villain has a tragic backstory, but he's mostly portrayed rather one-dimensional. 
 It also doesn't really make sense that Etienne doesn't stop him - vampire, mind control? The big show-down at the end was just unbelievable - it was like watching a B-movie. 
 The sex scenes are numerous, but mostly not very exciting, more like filler to eke out the plot - except for that one scene where Rachel starts thinking about how biting Etienne would be just like biting into a juicy sausage... (You can guess what she's doing at the time. It doesn't end well for him.) That one was memorable, but not necessarily in a good way! 
 Summary: 
 I'm sorry if my review sounds mean... I honestly wanted to love the book, but it left me feeling like I'd just eaten a huge helping of cotton candy - sweet and fluffy, but without much substance. Don't get me wrong, sometimes I'm in the mood for cotton candy! I just wish the novel had a bit more of a bite (pun intended). 
 Zahme Vampirgeschichte mit viel Standard-Sex 
 Die Geschichte: 
 Eigentlich ist ein Vampir ja so ziemlich unverwundbar. Theoretisch. Aber Etienne Argenau findet auf die harte Tour heraus, dass das leider nicht immer stimmt - ein entschlossener, selbsternannter Vampirjager (mit genug Geld fur Waffen und technischen Schnickschnack) kann das ganz leicht andern. 
 Bei Etiennes zweitem Besuch in der Leichenhalle (einmal wurde er erschossen, einmal verbrannt), sturmt der Jager schwerbewaffnet herein, um dem Vampir den Rest zu geben. Die vollig verwirrte Arztin, die in dieser Nacht Dienst hat, sturzt sich todesmutig zwischen den Verruckten und sein Opfer - die Leiche, die irgendwie keine Leiche mehr ist - und bekommt zum Dank eine Axt in die Brust. 
 Fur Menschen ist das eher ungesund. Etienne bleibt nur eine Moglichkeit, sie zu retten - er darf EINE einzige Person in seinem schier endlosen Leben zum Vampir (oder zur vampirin) machen. Und wenn sich dann herausstellen sollte, dass sie leider NICHT seine Seelengefahrtin ist, steht im eine einsame Ewigkeit bevor. 
 Pro: 
 Mir gefiel die grundlegende Idee: was passiert eigentlich, wenn ein Vampir gleich mehrmals in der Leichenhalle landet? Das muss doch Probleme geben! Und was passiert, wenn er eine Frau zum Vamp macht, die nicht darum gebeten hat und ihm womoglich nicht dafur danken wird? 
 Das Buch liest sich locker runter und ist recht unterhaltsam fur ein oder zwei Abende leichter Lekture - wenn man nicht zuviel erwartet. 
 Kontra: 
 Streckenweise war mir Rachel nicht sehr sympathisch. Sie wird als feurig und kratzburstig beschrieben, aber mir kam sie oft mehr vor wie ein unhoflicher, weinerlicher Teenager. Da war auch irgendwie kein rechter Funke zwischen Etienne und Rachel; es fuhlte sich mehr so an wie: "Die Beiden mussen sich jetzt verlieben, sonst gibt's keine Story." 
 Der "Bosewicht" wird schon auf der ersten Seite vorgestellt, und von dem Moment an folgt die Handlung einem alten, oft benutzten SChema: zwei Menschen, die vom Schicksal zusammengefuhrt werden, lernen sich besser kennen, verlieben sich, mussen ein paar Hindernisse uberwinden, haben ein paar Missverstandnisse... Dann gibt's das Showdown mit dem Bosen, und danach leben sie glucklich bis an ihr... Oh. Glucklich fur immer. 
 Hier ist absolut gar nichts neu oder uberraschend, leider. 
 Es wird ein paarmal angedeutet, dass der Bose eine tragische Hintergrundgeschichte hat, aber ansonsten wird er eher eindimensional portraitiert. Es macht auch nicht wirklich Sinn, dass Etienne ihn nicht direkt am Anfang aufhalt - da hatte ein bisschen Gedankenkontrolle doch noch wirken mussen? Das grosse Showdown am Schluss ist total uberzogen und nicht sehr glaubwurdig - das las sich so, wie sich ein schlechter Actionfilm guckt. 
 Die Sexszenen waren zahlreich, aber nicht sehr spannend. Mehr so wie Fullmaterial, um die Handlung zu strecken. Ok, da gab es diese eine Szene, wo eine hungrige Rachel beim Sex beginnt, daruber nachzudenken, Etienne an einer gewissen Stelle zu beissen, und dass sich das sicher anfuhlt, als wurde sie ihre Zahne in ein saftiges Wurstchen schlagen... Nicht sehr sexy, und es geht auch nicht gut aus fur den Armen. Die Szene werd ich sicher nicht vergessen, aber das ist nicht unbedingt ein Pluspunkt! 
 Zusammenfassung: 
 Es tut mir leid, wenn meine Kritik ubermassig gemein klingt... Ich wollte das Buch ja lieben, aber nach der Lekture fuhlte ich mich so, als hatte ich tonnenweise Zuckerwatte gegessen - klebrig suss, locker-flockig, aber ohne viel Substanz. Versteht mich nicht falsch, ich hab nichts gegen Zuckerwatte... Aber meine Vampirromane mag ich mit mehr Biss.

There is supposed to be a certain amount of sucking in vampire stories but Smith has picked the wrong kind entirely. 
 Elena has gone from being a high school prom queen to some sort of living angel creature who is described in ever increasingly nauseating terms. At one point she is described as 'the crowning jewel in humanity'. At least 200 of these pages are tireless descriptions of how perfect Elena is, and in depth descriptions of her many outfits.  The plot is also completely incomprehensible. At several points I was forced to re-read passages (torture indeed) to try to work out who was talking to who, and just what the hell was going on. If this book was read by an editor before hitting the bookshelves they ought to be fired immediately. 
 This book is essentially an Elena-Damon adventure, which I had looked forward to, but it's a total train wreck. I'm hugely dissapointed with this, and I don't think I'll be reading the final book when it comes out. Life's too short.
