"Get a room you two" 
 This was so funny with all their comments!! I loved the discussion questions where they would never take them seriously. And clary would wonder why she let Simon write in the book anyway. All in all, really interesting and SIMON I LOVE YOU!
E muuuiito bom e bem divertido, mas eu deveria ter lido depois de alguns livro de Os Instrumentos Mortais e antes da trilogia As Pecas Infernais. Acontece.

Anything that isn't written in the form of a story goes right over my head, including this book, hence the four out of five stars. 
 Other than that, it was the cutest thing ever! I'll forever use it as a reference book for The Mortal Instruments and The Infernal Devices because I'm so easily confused. 
 The art was incredible; both Clary's doodles and the ones already in the codex. 
 But, c'mon. The conversations Simon, Jace, and Clary had while reading was the best part. I feel like I know them more! I was even tempted to leave comments in the Codex myself.
I got through it. it was much like reading a textbook, and the only reasons I stuck with it were the notes and drawings and some of it was interesting as Shadowhunter history and background.

I really enjoyed this book! I was expecting that with the absence of an actual plot, I would have been frequently bored. Thankfully, this was not at all the case. I was completely intrigued and couldn't put this book down!:) (First completed book of the Booktubeathon!)

This book was so much better than I thought it was going to be. One of the most exciting things was the notes scribbled throughout it from Clary, Simon and Jace. Before I bought it, I didn't know they were going to be in it so it was a nice surprise. It really made this book. Another thing that made this book was that it was full of drawings, and I love pictures in my books. The last pages are full of character sketches and there is even a great small poster tucked into the back. 
 We get to learn everything a new Shadowhunter learns. We learn about Jonathan Shadowhunter, the first Shadowhunter, and how Shadowhunter's came into being, as well as other significant events in Shadowhunter history. There is an in depth look at Shadowhunter weapons, demons, downworlders, the Silent Brothers and the Iron Sisters. I found it all very interesting, and if you love the world of the Shadowhunters, I'm sure you will too. 
 The Shadowhunter's Codex is a must read for all Shadowhunter fans.

Rating: 3/5 
 This book basically gives us all we need to know about the universe in The Mortal Instruments and The Infernal Devices. It contains information on everything from Shadowhunter origin, to the Accords, to Downworlders, and weapons. If you recall from The Infernal Devices, this book was given to Tessa in order to learn more about the Shadow World, and that is essentially the purpose of this book. 
 Reading this was pretty interesting. I did find that a lot of the information in here I already knew, obviously because I already completed both TMI and it's prequel, TID. However there is some things that I didn't already know that was cool to learn. The origin story was especially interesting. I also found it enjoyable to connect the Shadowhunter history to characters which we already know of from reading TID. Henry Branwell's name pops up often as the inventor of several things. To think everyone thought nothing he made was useful! 
 I must say, the most enjoyable thing about this book was the little comments made by the characters. Throughout the book, you can read comments about the contents written by Clary, Simon, and Jace. At times when I was somewhat bored with the contents, these would cheer me up. 
 Overall, this was an interesting companion to TMI universe. Of course, it isn't necessary by any means, and a lot of the information provided in it you would have already learned by reading the other two series. However, if you're a fan of either or both series, this book is a good read. I wouldn't recommend it if you have not finished The Mortal Instruments series, as it contains some huge spoilers for it. However, if you haven't finished The Infernal Devices sereis then the threat of spoilers is not as high.

reference_books.title: The Drawing of the Three
reference_books.review_text: It does get better in the second book. Still some discomfort with all the characters that I can't quite name right now. Freaky imagery, though, and it dragged out a long time. Half the book takes place on a beach. I was really bothered by King having Roland travel North on a beach he had first traveled west to get to, but he continues to describe the ocean as being on his right. I don't know how that works, and I know it's silly, but it bugged me. I am willing to buy that this was an upside down world of fantasy, but this book could have used a sharper editor all around. The whole thing felt sloppy. But it was enthralling and I kept reading well past bedtime.

reference_books.title: Sharp Objects
reference_books.review_text: Flynn really, really must enjoy writing about horrible women. There's all kinds of little tidbits dropped throughout her books creating a theme of self-disgust, victim blaming and just distrust of all females. Her women are complicated, psychotic and always sabotaging themselves and hurting others casually. Her men are always two dimensional and witless wonders who stand there helpless at the evils around them. This was her most opaque book, slow and obvious and brutal. I enjoyed it but I found myself rolling my eyes with the merciless repetition of punishing her characters. Her subsequent two books were more realized in my opinion but I would love to see her really break away from her themes and try something new.

reference_books.title: Being Mortal: Medicine and What Matters in the End
reference_books.review_text: Truly one of the greatest books I have ever read. It's so important, and so relevant that I feel like everyone should read it. It's so refreshing to hear someone talk about aging and dying with frankness as well as compassion. This book will make you want to run out and be a hospice nurse or gerontologist.

reference_books.title: The Other Queen (The Plantagenet and Tudor Novels, #16)
reference_books.review_text: I've seen Philippa give several lectures and Q&A sessions on book tours here in Dallas, and at the last one she gave out xeroxed copies of the first three chapters of The Other Queen, several months before it was published. I was a little disappointed she decided to write about Mary Stuart, and she herself was extremely hesitant because there had been so many books written about her from various angles. I agree. I think Philippa's main strength lies in telling the story of the unsung heroines of history, the ones like Mary Boleyn and (even fictional) Hannah Green. It's when she tackles the big divas like Mary and Elizabeth that it becomes disappointing. So much is already known about them that Philippa the Historian takes over as opposed to Philippa the creative writer. I think that this book became so repetitive at times, and anti-climatic. Enjoyable escapism, still, just not her best. I know she can do better.

reference_books.title: The Bear and the Nightingale (The Winternight Trilogy #1)
reference_books.review_text: FABULOUS. This book was everything I wanted it to be.

book_a.title: Uprooted
book_a.user_review: This one was a struggle. The first half was fantastic and very well paced. There is a strong mythological architecture and I enjoy the Eastern European fairy tale theme. But somewhere in the middle, the story got sloppy. I love reading fantasy for so many reasons but I am immediately turned off when a fantasy writer commits the most stereotypical offense of constantly repeating phrasing and language. And also I began to get really annoyed with the strange relationship the heroine and her mentor, this 900 year old wizard dude, have. It smacked of Twilight and 50 Shades, honestly. I was disappointed and about 85% of the way through, when I should have been itching to finish- I just had to stop.

sample_reviews.review_text:
"They come and go like seasons, the winter that gives no thought to the spring." 
 I went into this one thinking it would be about a girl who was led to a man donned 'The Dragon', about her growth and journeys and adventures. Then I started thinking it would be about their relationship. I was wrong. 
 I found out it was a story of magic, about an ancient twist in the path that had gone horribly twisted, that it was up to a handful of characters to brave it out and try to set the paths straight again. The story isn't about the protagonist as much as it is about the larger picture looming in a horizon. 
 The story starts simply enough before it branches into unique complexity; she is chosen instead of Kasia, the beautiful one who everyone had always assumed would be taken instead. At first the reader will pause in confusion along with the protagonist and the villagers, but it eventually becomes clear why she must be the chosen, and then the story erupts from there. 
 Uprooted is one of those stories where the back blurb and the first quarter make it seem easier and simpler than it looks, but it's a deceptive surface covering something much deeper and more sinister. She doesn't stay in the castle, and the magic grows and grows to involve others, political struggles, kingdoms and heartbreaks, magic and battles, discovery and illusion. 
 The protagonist is fun at first because she's awkward, clumsy, a true tomboy who cares little for appearance. As her friend Kasia remarks, it's almost as if the magic inside her demands she dirties everything she wears, swearing one time that she even saw a branch reach out to soil her clothing when she was leaving the woods. The Dragon is definitely not a charming man - he is a reclusive, irritable wizard who has lost his hold on his own humanity while he battles to keep the humanity in the village from losing itself to the Wood. 
 The Wood is the biggest player for the story, a creatively woven and structured backbone that raises the story out of mediocre territory into richer, fertile imagination. There's violence and surprising twists, sadness and despair, but as with most dark fairy tales - light can exist at the end of these tunnels. 
 I applaud the author for her imagination - the story keeps getting more complex as it grows and it's not possible to guess all of the conclusions and wrap-ups. She writes differently - simply and easy to comprehend but not with elementary, stilted words. The pacing is sluggish sometimes, hence the four star rating, but it did plant itself firmly enough inside my reader zone that I couldn't help but continue following the trail. 
 A fantasy definitely worth reading.
It was a decent book. It didn't blow me away, but it was just enough fluffy fantasy for me to enjoy once in awhile.

I loved it! And just because out there are writers like Brandon Sanderson, George martin or Patrick Rothfuss , i didn't give it stars, because those are reserved for them. 
 But i really enjoyed this book and it was refreshing for me, not being part of a serial but just a standalone book. The writing, the word building, the characterization and the story- i liked it all. I recommend it warmly to everyone who likes a good fantasy with a drop of romance ;)
4.5/5 stars

Update: Re-read this in conjunction with the notes I'm taking from Structuring Your Novel by KM Weildand and this book is actually perfect in terms of the plot structure and pacing. Reading it as a writer rather than a reader has given me a greater appreciation of how Novik is able to keep cranking up the conflict. This book kept me on the edge of my seat, even as a re-read! I purchased the audiobook for this exercise...these factors have led me to change my rating from 4 to 5 stars. 
 What a perfect book, and I cannot say THANK YOU enough to Naomi Novik for writing a standalone fantasy in the era of series that authors do not finish in a timely manner! There's so much to love here. The magic system/spells were reminiscent of those found in Harry Potter, Agnieszka was a plucky heroine, the Dragon was a curmudgeon that you couldn't help but admire, the evil Wood was scary as hell. The only reason I didn't give it 5 stars is that I wish it had a little more in the way of romance. Nonetheless I really enjoyed this book and the patrons of my library are about to be bombarded with recommendations to read this if they haven't already.

For someone who doesn't read high fantasy, being me, I read and loved this book so that says a ton. I'm always pro girl power 110% but this book had me falling for the heroine's counterpart...who was a guy. Great magic concept and I loved watching the heroine develop and grow and react as the story went on. I hope so badly for a sequel because I did not want to leave this world! The imaginary was spot on and was not over detailed or dragged out like how I felt in a Tolken book. The ending totally blindsided me which I love because usually I foreshadow correctly in books and it left me guessing. beautiful cover and story and it makes me even more want to become a tree more than I ever had before. This is one of those books you read by a new to you author then you crave ALL their books which I will begin to collect as soon as I find them! loved it!

I plan on posting a lengthier review to my blog, but for now, suffice it to say that I haven't devoured a book like that in a year. It had everything that I look for in a book: a relatable main character with a backbone, an intriguing world, a kick-ass magic system, fantastic secondary characters, and romance. Added bonus for awesome action scenes, a real page-turner plot, and a complex and touching look at female friendship. It's basically a fairytale that's all grown up, with a body count and a bit of sexual tension. I can't recommend it strongly enough. Grab a copy as soon as possible!
Freaking fantastic. Also, I learned the word profligate.

This book was very promising at the start. I loved the premise and I liked the narrating voice and the magic was very interesting but the story developed quite slowly and somehow, I lost interest along the way. What seemed quite magical at the start became dull, as if it was too convoluted and I was anxious for a resolution. It felt like a missed opportunity, I don't know why since the book was well written and imaginative, but it fell a bit short for me. *shrugs*

This book has been generating a lot of buzz, but I wanted to add my little shout into the void because I really loved this book! 
 Every ten years, the Dragon takes a village girl into his castle. After the decade is up, he lets them go, but they are never the same. Of course, the Dragon isn't an ordinary dragon but, in fact, a wizard. With that Novik takes this well known trope in a new direction. The whole village believes Kasia, beautiful and talented Kasia, will be taken; however, the Dragon takes Agnieszka. 
 The beauty of Uprooted is that it covers well-trod territory in fantasy, but it makes it feel lovely and new. Have you ever read a book and thought, "This author and I, we have loved the same books"? Many people have made these comparisons, but there were elements of my favorite fantasy stories, such as the Sevenwaters series or Tamora Pierce's books. Agnieszka's sheer determination to save the people and home she loves reminds me so much of the women of Sevenwaters. Her determination is interesting to me because, unlike the other wizards and witches in the story, she seems to wield magic through sheer will. Much of her strength comes not from her skill or learning but her belief in herself to make it happen. I loved how Agnieszka discovers other past witches from the valley who, like her, use intuitive and outdoorsy magic but aren't taken serious by learned wizards because they just help their villages survive and don't write down spells. The romance is slow and isn't really a main point to the story. It might turn a few people off if they don't like huge age differences (I think it's a bit complicated because of the whole live for hundreds of years thing, and I also cut my teeth on romances like Daine and Numair's in Wild Magic) and if the "bicker until they kiss, then bicker some more" things grates on the nerves (I personally love relationships with lots of bickering). 
 The most important relationship in the story, in my opinion, is that of Kasia and Agnieszka. I wish more stories showed how powerful female friendships can be, and this book places a high priority on this one. It is very clear how much the girls love each other; however, this relationship is complicated by being raised knowing one was going to be taken by the Dragon, and the fears and jealousies that came with that. It is a complex relationship, and the novel doesn't shy away from the complexities, making the friendship even more poignant.

book_b.title: The Warded Man (Demon Cycle, #1)
book_b.user_review: I've been repeatedly resorting to fantasy novels lately, most likely to not have to think of the truly unbelievable election happening right now, and this book certainly did what I needed it to do! It's a Solid hero's journey, horror-fantasy tale with an inventive take on a mediaeval feudal society world with Demons! Yay Demons! The demons are more like wicked elemental spirits than traditional biblical interpretations but the rest of the dystopia's premise is extremely Christian -infused. I got a bit tired of the huge time jumps in the story and the main Hero's complete change of personality/identity about 70% of the way through the book, I felt like that could have been better thought out. But I'm definitely going to read the continuations in the series and I recommend it if you want an exciting, gory adventure tale.

sample_reviews.review_text: Awesome ending but I took away 1 star for a slow start and the villains could also have been more intelligent. Leesha's story was also very sad towards the end but the events that came afterward felt unnatural and forced. Otherwise it was a good read

I have a problem with this book. I am going to attempt to explain my problem clearly and calmly. My previous attempts at writing a review have all lapsed into inarticulate rage. I will admit that, as I did not finish reading the book, it is possible that Peter V. Brett redeems himself later on. I do not consider this likely. 
 Here is the problem: 
 The sun goes down, and demons overrun the earth. Protection is provided by defensive wards which get drawn on houses, barns, fence posts, etc. If a living creature is outside of these protections when night falls, that creature will be ripped apart and eaten. There is no way to fight the demons. 
 Eleven-year-old Arlen lives in a village with his parents. A messenger from the city shows up, carrying mail and salt. Arlen gets the job of showing this man around, and during the tour the man tells Arlen about a country far away in which young men train to fight and then go out at night in the hope of finding a way to defeat the demons. They all die, but the point is that it is not in man's nature to cower in safety while demons walk the earth. Men want to fight, and when deprived of that opportunity they become weak, depressed, and suicidal. The messenger's argument is supported when, during the tour, they come across a man from a nearby town who has hanged himself to death from a tree limb. 
 So Arlen takes this putrid idea to heart, and starts haranguing his father about how cowardly it is to stay safely inside the wards when there are demons to fight. I think this is very stupid, because if every man took Arlen's advice humans would have died out long ago. At this point, though, I am willing to give the author the benefit of the doubt. Arlen is only eleven, so it would be a bit much for me to expect him to act sensibly for the entire book. Perhaps he will learn the error of his ways. 
 Arlen is living with his mother, father, and a woman who recently lost her family in a demon attack. One afternoon, the sun sets more quickly than they were expecting because some clouds moved in. The adults and Arlen scramble to move the animals to safety. They run back to the porch, and then realize that the dog is still chained to a post in the back yard. Demons are about to start sprouting from the earth, and the dog will suffer a horrible, agonizing death. The guest runs out and unchains the dog, which bolts to the porch. The woman moves more slowly, and as a result gets a chunk ripped out of her leg by one of the first demons to spawn. Seeing this, Arlen's mother runs out into the yard to help the woman back to the house. Demons start attacking the mother, and drag the guest away to be eaten. 
 Arlen looks at his father. He realizes with disgust that his father is too afraid to move, so he jumps off the porch, beans a couple demons over the head with a nearby bucket, and drags his mother to the safety of the pigpen. They hang there till morning, when Arlen's father comes out to help them. Arlen gives his father a cold shoulder, and goes on and on about how cowardly he was, etc, etc. 
 I was filled with disgust, and stopped reading soon after. Why? 
 Because it became obvious that the author agreed with everything Arlen was saying. Not only that, but in his pursuit of setting Arlen up as The One (or whatever), he had to stack the deck in the kid's favor and kill/injure a few women to make the point. 
 Problem one: 
 A preteen farm kid should not have had any more success at fighting/surviving/staging a rescue from demons than two grown women. 
 Problem two: 
 Who demonstrated the most courage during the demon attack: the woman who risked death to save a dog, the mother who risked her life to save a woman who wasn't even part of her family, or the kid who risked his life only when his own mother was in danger? I think the answer is obvious. 
 Who demonstrated the most common sense during the demon attack: the kid who ran out into a yard full of hungry sprites to attempt a rescue that two adults had just failed at, or the father who stayed on the porch instead of running out there and leaving his kid an orphan? Also obvious. 
 Arlen is the loser by both metrics. If the author treated him the same as everyone else, he should have been eaten. And yet he lives so that he might make his father's life miserable. He lives, but not once does he say, Father, why couldn't you have been brave like Mom? 
 After that, I was afraid of what bits of blindness and idiocy the rest of the book might contain.

I found this book kind of annoying. The exposition was very obviously exposition-y (hey, person who has travelled a lot, tell me about the world in which I live! Hey, storyteller, tell us a story about the history of our world!), which dragged on the story a bit. I also found the plot to be a little too obvious, and the characters too generic (gee, I wonder if this exceptionally smart and beautiful female character will choose to stay with her abusive mother and marry her dumb and sexist boyfriend, OR leap at the chance to become an apprentice to the town's gruff-yet-secretly-kind healer, for whose trade she has a surprising and natural talent...). The final thing that bugged me was the seemingly arbitrary decision to create a dialect that differs from conventional English only in that the words "are" and "have" are reversed in usage/meaning. So people are constantly saying "we've" where you would normally say "we're" (We've going into town!") or "they've" for "they're" ("They've all in that building over there."). There seemed to be no logical reason to do this, and since it was the only apparent attempt at creating a "unique" language for the story, it grated on my grammatical nerves every time I saw it.

This book had potential, but the preoccupation with sex and sexual innuendo (including group rape, sexual encounters, humor and comments in dialogue and internal monologue) detracted drastically from the overall narrative.

Read this as an arc shortly before it came out, saw it come across my dash. I honestly don't remember much except the horrible taste it left in my mouth. Lots of 'we're building a historically accurate fantasy world because every woman gets brutalized' So YMMV, but for me it was a sexist mess in a potentially interesting world.

The beginning of a series that's already up to 4 giant novels and 4 shorter entries. I kept hearing good things about it, so decided to check it out. 
 Well... it's a start. A slow start, however. 
 The largest part of the book really moved too slowly for me, as it shows us three young people who are bored of life in their small, backward, restrictive towns. 
 Admittedly, I guess the point is that their lives are restricted and boring... but it got to the point where reading about them was boring, too. And oh, the stereotypes. 
 The reason that life is so very restrictive and boring here is that, for the last few hundred years, a plague of bloodthirsty demons comes out every night. Anyone caught outside a warded area will be quickly and viciously killed. Whenever it's dark, both the residents of rural villages and the inhabitants of walled cities huddle inside buildings protected by the magical symbols drawn or carved into their boundaries. 
 It's a war that people are losing, too, by a slow, drawn-out process of attrition. 
 Understandably, travel is avoided. Villages communicate mainly through traveling duos of Messenger and Jongleur who facilitate news, trade and entertainment. It's a glamorous job, but a dangerous one. 
 One of the aforementioned bored young people, Arlen, wants nothing more than to be a Messenger. He's got a talent for drawing Wards, and when his family situation goes south, he runs off to try to pursue his dream. 
 Meanwhile, orphaned Rojer is taken in by a Jongleur and brought to one of the walled cities. While grieving his family, he also learns the trade - and discovers a special talent for the fiddle. 
 Leesha also has a horrible family situation. An unloving mother and a thuggish fiance cause her to end up with her reputation destroyed. However, she finds new direction in life when she apprentices to the local Herb Gatherer and begins to learn healing arts. 
 It's not really a surprise to find that eventually, these three stories might merge and, in that convergence, turn out to have something to do with fighting the demons... 
 It takes a while to get there though, and, as I said, there are just so many stereotypes along the way. The backwards villages with sexist attitudes and uneducated inhabitants are utterly familiar. The walled cities with craftspeople, apprentices, public performers, &c also seem right out of any number of fantasy novels. Then of course, there's the OTHER walled city a few days' ride away that's inexplicably inhabited by a Middle Eastern culture full of every trope about the Middle East you could pull out of a hat. Of course, the countryside is dotted with ancient ruins full of the forgotten Knowledge of the Elders. And that's not even touching on the archetypical behavior that the individual characters exhibit. 
 I also had a couple of basic logical issues with the setup. First, if the demon plague has been the situation for as long as the narrative says, people would've learned to deal with it a lot better. You just WOULDN'T go running outside your wards after a stray animal, for example. Not doing that would've been beaten into every single person from babyhood. It would be unthinkable. 
 Second, the concept of painting or tattooing wards on your person just isn't an unthinkable idea. You'd think nearly everyone would've thought to try it. And once one person figured it out and tales started spreading about the Warded Man painted or tattooed with protective symbols - you'd think that tattoos would very quickly become the hottest new trend for everyone. 
 However, if you're OK with the familiar... the book isn't terrible. The pace does eventually pick up, and ends with a big ol' climactic action scene. Having just finished it... I do have these criticisms, and I think they're valid... but I have hope that it might get better as it goes on. I may just go on to the next book in the series and find out what's happening next.
Writing style. A quickie - little description, little or none expression, lots of conversation.
A solid 3.5 start to this series.

I didn't get very far into this book. The world was very dark and the relationships were all very messed up. Shortly into it I decided it wasn't anything that was good for my spirit. It may have gotten better but I wasn't willing to dig deeper into the mire to find out

Decent writing, good word building and had me hooked till the first 10-12%. 
 Then it all fell apart, the rampant misogyny and the ridiculously skewed gender bias is just a buzz killer. 
 Men are supposed to be the hunters and protectors while women are just used to procreate? Really? 
 I get that the post apocalyptical world created by the author may have needed such a view on gender politics but it was particularly unbearable for me. I still tried to read and power through but the sexual violence and child marriage was the straw that broke the camel's back. 
 Stay away if you are as sensitive as I am about such topics

reference_books.title: The Angel (The Original Sinners, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 Reviewed at http://scorchingbookreviews.blogspot.... 
 Review edited for GR 
 The Siren introduced us to the world of Nora Sutherland, erotic writer extraordinaire. In the Angel, we are introduced to Eleanor, the woman who created her. Do NOT read this book without reading The Siren. In fact, don't read this review...go read The Siren. 
 Nora has been a permanent fixture in Soren's bed ever since the departure of Wes at the end of The Siren. She craves the pain that he gives her and he, in turn, craves her. When a reporter starts to investigate him upon his nomination for Bishop, it becomes apparent that all they hold dear is under threat. If they find out about Soren, they find out about the two people whose secrets he holds close to his heart; Nora and Michael. 
 Unperturbed at the risk to himself, but finding the risk to the others unacceptable, he sends them both to the home of Griffin Fiske, a favourite Dom of Nora's from time ago. Whilst there she has instructions to train young Michael to be a sub, but playboy Griffin is not allowed to touch. Griffin is a bisexual Dom who parties hard and gives his heart to nearly nobody; Soren doesn't want him anywhere near someone as vulnerable as Michael. But the vulnerability that Michael exudes is hard for any Dom to resist and the "no-touching" rule makes him harder to resist. When Griffin finds out he is also a Masochistic, Bisexual bottom, it seems that someone has cooked up his ideal man. But Michael has been hurt so many times he bears physical scars and Griffin can offer nothing to him but eventual pain. It clearly will be a long long summer for them all whilst they try to sit on their hands. 
 Meanwhile, Soren has to deal with the reporter sure that he is hiding a secret. Allowing her prejudice to cloud her judgement she decides that he must be a paedophile and she vows to dig until she finds some dirt to punish him with. In keeping his heart protected, Soren must tell her more than he's told many other people before; he must tell her about his past. In baring the secrets of his past, can he keep the secrets of his heart safe? 
 I don't know what the end will be; I don't know what ending I'm even hoping for. There is only one thing that I am sure of; I am team Nora. I am not team Soren, I am not team Wes. I care not who she ends up with as long as it's the right decision for her and right now I don't know that living without either of them will be the right decision. They both heal a part of her, both needed in their individual way. She needs the healing pain from Soren as much as the unconditional love from Wes. Fair notice, I may get fan-girlie in this review and try to implement some shit reasoning onto a character that isn't mine to reason for (sorry Tiffany!) 
 This series elicits a personal reaction in everyone who reads it. It doesn't deal with middle of the road feelings or situations; it deals with the extreme edges of emotions. It deals with the slightly obsessive, possessive edge of love, not the warm and cuddly bits. It doesn't deal with happy as a warm and comfortable feeling, it deals with happy as a visceral need. It deals with emotions that you can't control, needs that you can't suppress and situations that leave you uncomfortable with your individual response. I was never imagining myself in Nora's shoes. I was never thinking that any of the men in this book could be added to my book boyfriend list. I was reading Nora's story, what she wanted and needed, and that made this book addictive and compelling. 
 I could go on and on about the Nora and Soren but they aren't together for the most of the book. They are the driving force of the series, the reason behind all of the actions, but they weren't the focal point. The main plot points of this story are Michael and Griffin's developing relationship, Nora's feelings for Wes and Soren's past. I loved every single one of them. 
 Michael and Griffin were beautiful and hot and amazing. Seriously, I don't think I've read anything more perfect. I promised no spoilers but read the tattoo scene and come back to me. I cried. Michael needed protecting, Griffin needed to be needed.... they fit. 
 Nora's feelings for Wes were hard to read. They were made harder for the fact that I liked Soren, that I could see that she was hurting him. There is a scene right at the end where Soren makes a choice and I cried again. The only reason I didn't want to slap her silly was that I knew she wasn't playing fast and loose with either mans feelings; it was as hard for her as it was for me to read. 
 Reading about Soren's past was quite hard in places. It made me understand a little bit more, but it didn't make me like him anymore. As I say, I don't judge a character on what makes him up, but it was interesting to read the history behind him. His childhood was horrific. Truly, no one would come out of that without some sort of damage. My heart bled for him but I didn't like that he was sharing something so personal with that reporter. I know it was unfair of me to see her as a threat to Nora/Soren's relationship, and hate her for it, even though Wes is a massive threat too. However, I draw your attention to my previous comments; I am team Nora and Wes is not a threat to her, this bint is. I think I should also mention here that some of the events in The Siren are explained in this book with reference to Soren's past. One of the many issues I had with the man was his part in the scene between Michael and Nora. The reasoning behind it is explained in this book and it is this, along with the scene with the reporter, showed me just how good a man Soren is. Yes, he is kinky. Yes, he is manipulative. Yes, he is a priest having a S & M relationship, but he is a man who will reveal parts of his soul to try to help another. I am hooked. 
 This is a book that can't be summed up in one sentence. It's kinky, twisted, heart-breaking, heart-warming, controversial, beautiful, hot and many other things in-between. I can't tell you if you'll like it, I can only tell you that I adored it. It will remain on my keeper shelf, it will be read over and over again and it will be on the favourites list for 2012. If you can cope with a priest having sex, a woman who needs pain and the notion that these are normal people who just happen to be kinky, try this book. I can't wait for book three.

reference_books.title: Always on My Mind (Lucky Harbor, #8)
reference_books.review_text:
FTC: I requested this book as a mammoth fan of the series. I got the book for an honest review but it may be a little biased due to how good the other books are. 
 I love this series. It is sweet, sexy and fulfilling; I read each one with a big dopey grin on my face. The way Jill Shalvis writes romance is something that everyone should experience; I truly recommend it. Although I loved Leah and Jack together, separately I had some issues. Together they completed each other, seemed to give each other some peace. It was sweet which is why Leah frustrated me so darn much! 
 Jack, I adored. Leah was the only woman to remain consistent in his life and their current ploy put that at risk. Although they had laid the rules down, he knew that she had always been the one too close to his heart and he feared that they did not truly appreciate the risks that they had taken. I loved the way he transitioned into his role from playboy to boyfriend in a split second, giving up his many dates without a quibble. It was like he had been in a holding pattern before and now was back on track. His concern for his mother was admirable (and obviously made him that more attractive) but, honestly, it was the way he was with Leah that made me adore him. He knew her so well, treated her so fairly, and he was so damn sexy with her. If a sexy fire-fighter paid that much attention to me, I think I'd become a juddering mess. 
 Leah was a pain in the ass to be honest. I get that her life was up in the air, I get that she didn't stay anywhere long but I just couldn't get why. Her childhood was shocking but she fully understood the ramifications of her actions on other people and did them anyway. Maybe I am a little protective over Jack, but I thought she was pretty awful with him. She was only willing to give him a small portion of herself but allowed him to give her everything knowing full well that she was going to break his heart. I just thought she wore her past like an excuse to do whatever the hell she wanted and she didn't really want to face up to the consequences of her actions. Whenever she made arrangements that would affect her relationship with Jack, she wouldn't tell him. He'd find out by accident and be left reeling; I have no idea why he bothered with her. I may be being a little unfeeling towards her past but I can't help it; she wasn't blind to her actions and she selfishly did them anyway. Together, I loved them. The chemistry was sizzling and the history between them only made it that more satisfying to read about. It was clear that their arrangement would fail from the second it began. 
 The same shenanigans go on in Lucky Harbor as in the rest of the series and the small town antics made me chuckle and get all warm and fuzzy because they are comfortable to read about. They fleshed out this story but they didn't really add to the love plot in this one. 
 Overall, it has all the hallmarks of a lucky harbor book and that made me enjoy it. Jack may be in my top three Shalvis heroes (number one will ever be the good doctor I think) but I'm afraid Leah isn't on my heroine list. A good installment and I cannot WAIT for Ben...

reference_books.title: To Command and Collar (Masters of the Shadowlands, #6)
reference_books.review_text:
Determined to break apart the slave-ring that has been preying on the Shadowlands submissives, Master Raoul snags himself an invite into a viewing of some "bargain-basement" slaves. His mission from the FBI is to reject all the slaves with the hopes of being invited into the auction which would allow them to finally arrest the leaders of the evil Harvest Association. Unfortunately, Raoul finds it hard not to "buy" one of the cheaper slaves when she turns out to be the best friend of Gabi (from Make Me Sir). Potentially blowing months of hard work for the FBI, his Dom instincts sneak up on him and soon the pretty brunette is in his home. A lucky break means that there may be other opportunity for the imposing Dom to attend the auction, but first he must make his ownership of Kim look real. Can he impose his collar onto someone who is not only is unwilling but is also damaged to the core from her previous "Master" 
 Kim wants out of the nightmare that her life has become. Kidnapped, tortured, raped and forced into slavery, this is not the life that any little girl dreams of. When she finds herself back on the market after her previous owner returns her as "damaged goods", she doesn't believe that the man who promises her safety can keep to his word. After hearing proclamations from both her friends and the authorities that he isn't one of the bad guys, she resigns herself to playing the role of his slave in order to try to help the other girls. Unfortunately for her, the Harvester Association check on their sales and want to see her perform in her role as slave. Can she really ever trust a Dom again? When her submissive nature starts to rise to the surface, she finds herself fighting against the one relationship that has ever felt right. Can she really let herself trust him enough to become his slave? 
 First of all I need to warn you of a couple of things. 
 1)These books are a series. You can read them individually but you won't appreciate the characters and their relationships. This would be a shame as they are all amazing 
 2)I have an immediate bias towards anything with the name "Cherise Sinclair" on the front of it (sorry!) 
 Now that that's out of the way I can start to rave with a clear conscience. This story had the potential to be an incredibly dark story with very little light at the end of the tunnel. The background setting was truly horrific and a very brave choice for a Romance story. In Make Me Sir, we began our journey into the sick and twisted world of the slave traders. The situation wasn't resolved in one book, nor should it have been. I appreciated that Ms Sinclair took the time to show the aftermath of these events for the victims rather than using it as a nifty plot device and then finishing with it when the HEA occurs. Kim was so damaged she made me cry. Raped, tortured, verbally abuse, kept in a cage.....honestly, I don't think I've read more abuse in a Romance. When Raoul "buys" her, she struggles to adjust to real life, struggles not be scared of what's around each corner, struggles to trust the people around her. I thought she was the strongest character I have met in a while, as she has a choice to just go home, but instead she put herself under the control of a stranger to try to save her friends. I didn't know if her sanity would hold up in the face of some very tough situations, but I was ever hopeful. Some people may take issue with the fact that she went from one form of slavery to the other but, to me, that was the point. Kimberly was submissive to the core; she would always be in a relationship where the lifestyle infringed on her life, rather than sticking to the bedroom. The choice was taken away from her by the cretins that kidnapped her but, although she was somewhat cornered into the M/s relationship with Raoul, it was still her choice to enter such a contract. 
 Raoul was dreamy. Raoul took this story and made it a little sweeter because he was just so caring. The other Dom's in the Shadowland series all have their inner sappy side, but Raoul's is pretty much out there for everyone to see. He nurtures Kim, whilst giving her the control that she needs. With any other type of Dom this story would be in danger of heading towards the darker, twisted side of BDSM, but he lightened up every page that he appeared on. I loved them together and thought he was the ideal Dom to heal her. On a side note I want to bitch slap his ex-wife....with a bat. Was he my favourite Shadowland's Dom? Nope, that will always be Nolan. Are they my favourite couple? Yes, I think they were! The sex scenes were pant-worthy and you need to look out for a fire play scene.....mega hot!!! 
 There were a lot of other things going on in this story. We get to see Galen and Vance work as a team whilst attempting to intimidate little Sally (Seriously, shivers people!) I've wanted Sally to get a book in forever and am glad that it seems to be en route. We also get to see Sadist Sam in action in this one. I think I want his book the most and this shocks me a little. I have read many books involving a Sadist but never enjoyed any of them because it's not my kink. I think Ms Sinclair has been very clever in leaving his book until the end because he is now so far beneath my skin, there is no way I couldn't enjoy his story and I think this will be the same for anyone who is dubious about true S/M! We got to see the whole gang again too; Kari and Dan have some news, there is a big event for Nolan and Beth and once again Gabi gets the best lines! 
 Another fabulous addition to the Shadowlands series. With a damaged heroine and a dreamy Dom, this book made me laugh, cry and hope. A brave book that I thoroughly enjoyed.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This is one of my all time favorite Gibson books. Everyone talks about her other hockey books, but this one gets overlooked far too often. I adore John and Georgie both. 
 The heroine isn't shown in a very flattering light at the beginning of the novel. She's getting ready to marry a man 50yrs her senior for his money, can barely read and looks like a centerfold pinup. Gibson really makes her a truly sympathetic character, though. She isn't the type to feel sorry for herself, or wallow in her misery. She puts on a positive attitude and tries to make the best of whatever bad situation she finds herself in. Because of the way she was raised the reader can really relate to her, even though it doesn't seem like it in the beginning. 
 John has his own demons to face. He's struggling with the pain of losing his wife. He drinks too much in the beginning, and is selfish and rude a lot of the time. But he grows a lot over the course of the novel, too. He puts his life back together and deals with his issues as best he can. 
 The secret baby plot is one I enjoy but only if it's done well. It isn't done well very often. Gibson is one of the few who can make it work well. Which she did here. I completely understood Georgeanne's reasons for not telling John about their baby. Even though I hurt for him, knowing he missed so much of his daughter's life, I couldn't be angry at Georgie for not telling him. 
 This is Gibson at her best.

I have been on a hockey-romance kick for the past week, and after finishing Toni Aleo's Assassins Series? I wanted to continue on the love. So I turned first to Goodreads (Hockey Romance list) and second to my library for what was available. Rachel Gibson's Chinooks Series was on the shelf in it's entirety, so I grabbed it! 
 I wanted to love this one, I really really did. Maybe it's suffering from book hangover, maybe it's something else. I'm not sure what, but despite really enjoying the story? I didn't just love it. This book had it's moments where it was super sweet, those where I was rolling with laughter and those where the sex scenes were so steamy you blushed! And I loved those parts, but there was just something that nagged at me. 
 John was the sort of hero that I've grown incredibly fond of. Hot, Athletic and brooding over his past. (Although his repeated references to his second wife, DeeDee Delight, sort of annoyed me.) But when he finds out about Lexie, his daughter with Georgeanne, this is where he hooks me! His instant devotion to her - I just love a doting dad!! 
 Georgeanne is what bugs me. First, I hate when women hide their children for long periods of time (occasionally the romance is hot enough that I can overlook it - but 7 years when you're in the same damn town???? Nope. Not acceptable.) So I think this is where my hold up lies. That and her odd propensity for lying. She tells some really REALLY odd whoppers that make no sense to me at all. So I just kind of rolled my eyes. 
 All in all? This was my first foray into Rachel Gibson's writing, and I loved her style. (And I realize that this book is a) really old - way back to the "1990's" **LOL** and b) her first book published, so I give it some wiggle room for that!) I'm still excited to continue the Chinooks series, and hoping that they get better with time! (And possibly have a bit more humor tossed in!)

This was the first book I've read of this author and I liked the writing very much. I also enjoyed the storyline and loved that John is a hockey player. (I'm a big sports fan.) But I struggled with liking John and understanding what Georgianne saw in him besides their physical attraction. The only times he was endearing was when he was with Lexie. Even in discovering his love for Georgianne, he never truly stated what he loved about her, only that he couldn't live without her. 
 I did enjoy the author's writing, however, and am going to continue reading the Chinooks Hockey Team series. I just didn't connect with this particular main character.

sample_reviews.review_text: I liked the idea of a cross-breed human/vampire child but for the most part it is 700 pages of nothing. A bland conclusion for a series that started with great promise.

Seriously, what kind of story is this. 
 I read the first book because I was curious. I read the second book because I didn't want to judge a series by the first book. I read the third because I wanted to see how bad it could get. I read the fourth because the mindfuck had officially drawn me in and I couldn't help myself. It's like a car accident, you know you shouldn't look, but you can't help it. I don't even want to remember the things I've read.

I loved Twilight, New Moon and Eclipse but this last book of the saga I didn't like very much. There were moments when I felt disgusted while reading it, like at the moment of Renesmee's birth. There was something that I didn't enjoy at all that was when the narrator changed. I was too used to be like inside Bella's mind and when I read Jacob's side of the story... It was really weird for me. Despite that, I think it went ok.

** spoiler alert ** 
 It appeared as though the first three books had some conflict. Some actual conflict. Sacrifices were going to have to be made. In the end, Bella wouldn't be able to have everything she wanted, nor would Edward, nor would Jacob. And with the added peril of the Volturi coming, it seemed as though someone we cared about might actually die. 
 But, in the end... everyone gets everything they'd ever wanted and nobody we care about dies. What is this, Disney? The intended audience is not the problem - I'm sure we can all think of a well known series for young adults that deals with conflict, sacrifice, and death, and deals with these things for real. 
 It seems the drama of the entire series centers around characters being afraid of what might happen, even though none of it ever does. I think the final "battle" scene sums it all up (I accidentally just typed "scums it all up," which would be apt as well). They've been anticipating all possible outcomes of this battle for a good chunk of the book. They're prepared for casualties. They're prepared for orphans. They're making a stand against oppression with their very lives. 
 And then... nothing happens! All conversations go according to plan. They convince the right people of the right things. The bad guys leave without a fight! The Cullens' extended "family" all survive with nary a scratch. 
 Happily ever after blah blah blah. If it weren't such a quick read, I'd say it was a waste of my time. Maybe it still is.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This was not my favorite book out of the four Twilight books, but I did enjoy it. It seemed like most of Meyer's books, reading with fits and starts. There were parts where I couldn't put the book down, especially the end (once Alice saw the Volturi coming) and the section narrated by Jacob. But there were parts I could've done without. The long wedding/honeymoon section. Bella's new adventures as a vampire. I just wasn't that into it. I don't know how many times Meyer wrote "through my new eyes" "with my sharp senses," probably as many as she wrote about Edward having cold, hard, marble, sparkling skin. Yeah. I don't think these are books I will reread.
The redemption for this book that honestly has the weakest plot of anything I've ever seen published was the snippets from Jacob's point of view. I think he's a really funny narrator.

Well. Bella always wanted to be with Jacob, and now she got her wish. Pffft. 
 I actually enjoyed the series and reading more about the other vampires. Too bad though, I think Marcus would have wanted to die already.

Zero stars! Zero f***ing stars!! This is seriously must be the worst thing ever written. Meyer's prose hasn't improved even a little since the first book, she contradicts her own mythology, the plot is filled with logical holes, and it all culminates in a giant epic battle that never actually happens. Really, its a thousand pages of nothing. Crappily written nothing. I won't even get in to the disturbing, violent implied sex and the equally disturbing, violent pregnancy. Not to mention the horrendous mangling of basic human reproductive biology.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Good lord...talk about your lame ass everything wrapped up in a neat little package ending...She should have died...then she could have stopped boring the world with her plain obsessive BORING whinyness.

Although I sort of enjoyed the first book, as the series went on, I became less and less happy with the content. Although I did like the character of Jacob Black, I did not like the way the books were heading, and by the middle of the 4th book, Breaking Dawn, I quit. Things were a little too personal for me, although I was glad that they did get married, and the language was hard to ignore any more. I'm sorry it had to be this way, but I couldn't really continue.

book_b.title: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings
book_b.user_review:
This book started off really well, but things kinda fell apart for me as I neared the end. 
 The first half of the book is told in a linear fashion with events unfolding without big gaps of time in between. The author's recollections of that time in her life seemed to build upon her previous experiences whereas by the end, events seemed more random. The ending itself was quite abrupt and leaves the reader confused as to what the point of the whole story was. 
 In addition to Maya's story, I found her mother quite inspiring.

sample_reviews.review_text:
"Words mean more than what is set down on paper. It takes the human voice to infuse them with shades of deeper meaning." 
 We all know how amazing Maya Angelou was, right? That's not even at issue. So no one should be surprised that this book is amazing. 
 I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings is Angelou's autobiography, which covers her childhood through parenthood, with the birth of her son shortly after graduating high school. I read this book myself for the first time while I was in high school, after being lucky enough to hear her speak. Now this was before the Oprah years, and she was still amazing then, but a little less internationally reknown, and I thought I had discovered a hidden treasure then. I devoured everything I could of hers, and read this particular book perhaps four or five times then, the last time when I was a freshman in college. 
 After that, I hadn't re-read it until now, and oh, the differences. 
 When I read this as a girl, I related to the story of the girl. I saw through her eyes, and lived her hardships with her, and felt for her in the way that you do for your friends. As an adult, my heart wrenched more for the little girl she was once, and I wanted to take care of her as a mother, as an adult. I was even more gutted by the violence and the abrupt end to her innocence, the lackadaisical parenting, the disregard that would allow her to live in a car as a teen or be treated with such callousness by her family members. I got angry. 
 Maya Angelou's story is not an easy one. It is a story of poverty. 
 "I find it interesting that the meanest life, the poorest existence, is attributed to God's will, but as human beings become more affluent, as their living standard and style begin to ascend the material scale, God descends the scale of responsibility at a commensurate speed." 
 It is a story of racism in the south. 
 "If growing up is painful for the Southern Black girl, being aware of her displacement is the rust on the razor that threatens the throat. It is an unnecessary insult." 
 It is a story of parental neglect and disregard. It is a story of children falling through the cracks in this world, and what it does to them. It is full of pain and misery and anguish. 
 But it is also full of hope. It is a story of overcoming odds. It is a story of wrenching every drop of good out of life, out of educational opportunities, out of what you're given in this world. And if you aren't given very much? Well, it's about balling all of that up tight as you can and climbing up on top of it anyway. It's about triumph. 
 This is one of those books that everyone should read. It's one of those books that can help people with privilege learn empathy, and those without learn that there are ways out. It's about those labeled "victim" changing the word to "survivor". I am eternally glad that I read this when I was very young, because it changed the way I looked at the world. I am also glad that I re-read it now, as it took me back to a place of understanding, a place of standing up and fighting for others, and a place where I believe anyone can do anything. 
 "The caged bird sings with a fearful trill, 
 of things unknown, but longed for still, 
 and his tune is heard on the distant hill, 
 for the caged bird sings of freedom."

I didn't know about Maya Angelou's life before reading this book, I know of the author and have read some of her beautiful poetry so I was very intrigued by her first autobiography. This part of the story focuses on her childhood up to age sixteen. During this time Maya suffered through racial tensions, rape, getting to know her long lost parents and through it all she conquered obstacles, these experiences made her into what she is today. 
 The only thing that bugs me about the book is that the California and Baja geography is all wrong, not sure if that's how she remembers it or maybe some cities got mentioned instead of others. Other than that this book is great!
Not a fan. Get over yourself, Maya. Get over yourself. (I concede that you are pretty cool for the whole conductorette thing but still. Your tone infuriates me.)
Beautiful, honest, textured, deep ... simply, wow.

Caged Bird 
 A free bird leaps 
 on the back of the wind 
 and floats downstream 
 till the current ends 
 and dips his wing 
 in the orange sun rays 
 and dares to claim the sky. 
 But a bird that stalks 
 down his narrow cage 
 can seldom see through 
 his bars of rage 
 his wings are clipped and 
 his feet are tied 
 so he opens his throat to sing. 
 The caged bird sings 
 with a fearful trill 
 of things unknown 
 but longed for still 
 and his tune is heard 
 on the distant hill 
 for the caged bird 
 sings of freedom. 
 The above poem by Maya Angelou (not from this book, BTW) encapsulates in a few lines why the voices of protest are the loudest, and the literature the most powerful when it is forcefully suppressed. Because the only thing the caged bird can do is sing, he will keep on doing it, lest he go mad. Poetry will keep on flowing out of the decapitated head of Orpheus. 
 I understand that this book has been banned multiple times. Not surprising, considering that the words of the poet have more power than swords or bullets, as proved time and again by history. 
 ---------------------------------------------------------- 
 Maya Angelou (born Marguerite Johnson) and her brother Bailey were sent to live with their paternal grandmother in Stamps, Arkansas when their parents' marriage fell apart. It was the early thirties, and the North and the South of USA were poles apart as far as coloured people were concerned; in the North, they were part of the society (albeit an insular one) while in the South, they were the despised 'niggers'. 
 Maya spent most of the formative part of her childhood down south. Her grandmother ('Momma') was a singularly resourceful woman who owned a store: they managed to live in relative comfort even during the Depression era. However, this material comfort was offset by the fact that they were always the hated 'other' - the 'whitefolk' who lived apart (almost a mythical race, in Maya's young mind) were powerful and whimsical gods who could visit death and destruction any time on any black man or woman. Even the 'powhitetrash', the drifters and squatters who had the fortune to be born into the Anglo-Saxon race, could insult even the propertied black people with impunity. 
 When she was eight years old, Maya's father took her brother and herself to their mother, Vivian Baxter, in St. Louis. Here the incident which was to become the turning point of her life happened. The eight-year old girl was raped by her mother's current boyfriend, Mr. Freeman: he managed to wiggle out of jail only to be murdered, presumably by Maya's maternal uncles who were also the town toughs. As a result of this, she became a virtual mute for almost five years. 
 Sent back to Stamps, Maya continued her zombie-like existence until she was brought back into the world of the living by Bertha Flowers, a teacher and family friend - she did this by the expedient of introducing the girl to books. Maya found refuge in the world of imagination, and slowly came back to normal. 
 She again went to live with her mother in California when she was 15. During this sojourn, she visited her father in Southern California where another traumatic even in her life took place. After a frightening journey across the border into Mexico along with her father (when she was forced to drive a car back to the US in the night with him passed out in the back - even though she was not a qualified driver!), Maya was attacked and stabbed by her father's girlfriend. She quit home and lived for a month in a junkyard, with similar social drop-outs, before returning to her mother. 
 A month of living in the rough had emboldened the shy and withdrawn girl. Maya decided to get a job as a streetcar conductor, even though the occupation was closed to blacks, and succeeded: the activist and rebel were just emerging. The first instalment of this extended autobiography ends with the picture of Maya as a teen mother, of a child conceived out of a casual sexual encounter which she had just to satisfy that she was 'normal' (that is, heterosexual)! 
 ---------------------------------------------------------- 
 Maya writes with a disarming honesty and a genuine sense of humour. Even the most distressing events are discussed casually - the child's eye view is done really well. The book is eminently readable. Still, is this a great book? I would not say so. Good, yes: genuinely great, no. 
 The causal tone, for me, took away most of the poignancy. Even the extremely distressing rape incident - though described in gory detail - fails to really make an impact. My personal feeling is that this is the author's way of coping with personal trauma: you take the emotion out of it. However, it might come across to people that her mother never cared much (I have found this view expressed on one or two of the one-star reviews for this book on this site). 
 However, I salute Maya's courage in writing this explicit memoir. Being a black woman, she feels disadvantaged thrice, as she says: 
 The Black female is assaulted in her tender years by all those common forces of nature at the same time that she is caught in the tripartite crossfire of masculine prejudice, white illogical hate and Black lack of power. 
 So maybe, the best defence is to attack. Throw the hypocrisy of society back in its face. Say: "This is I. Accept me for what I am, whether you like what you see or not!"

This book ended right as I was getting into it. As a result of reading this book, I have decided something about my life. I don't want to give people an autobiography of my life thus far, which has been messy and dull, but rather short stories of the interesting parts or discombobulated poems that allude to parts that were just as puzzling to me as they would be to the reader. But I certainly don't want to waste anyone's time with the dull uninteresting parts of my life. Perhaps if I must write an autobiography of myself, I must live an adventurous life. 
 I felt like this book had a lot of dry moments in it, which was why it took me longer than a month to drudge through. I will admit the merit, though, of this book. An autobiography must be a really difficult and draining to write; I'm not sure if I want to remember everything of my life. If I was to read this book again, I would read only the ending.
I was disappointed in this book. Her poetry is better.

I read Maya Angelou's classic autobiography I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings as a part of the "Read Harder Challenge" in the category "Read a book that is frequently banned or challenged." Angelou is thought by many to be the most banned and/or challenged author in the United States. 
 Her book is magnificent, a study of personal psychology, philosophy, and culture as well as a critique of American society. I can see where Angelou got her determination not to be marginalized either as a person of color or a woman.

I don't think this, or any book, should be banned from a school or public library. I do however understand why it't not taught. I feel like it's unnecessary to teach a book with this kind of content if it isn't of amazing quality. I feel like I might be alone on this, but I think it wasn't very well written and felt really boring through most of the book. Wish I had something better to say about it. =\

This book is beautifully written about Maya Angelou's life memoir narrated in her 3rd person girlhood. Her account of America's deep seated racism, Black history, rape, has made this a "banned book" but I am of the opinion that Americans don't like a powerful Black force/voice reminding them about their oppressive ancestry rather than the raw sexual content, which was often cited as inappropriate for youth as if life is full of only roses. 
 Life is ugly and Maya wasn't afraid to paint it so but what was most dazzling about this book is how Maya/Marguerite found her compassionate voice and how brutal her honesty to her vulnerabilities growing up that we can understand...and how beautiful education can support, knowledge to inspire and books to the imagination can build a person.

reference_books.title: The Death of Bunny Munro
reference_books.review_text: Hmmm. Mr. Cave has a knack for writing about the wretched among us. The topics that I love in his music can be a hit or miss when he's writing prose. I deeply loved his first novel, "And the Ass Saw the Angel" even though it was profoundly disturbing and a total bummerfest. Cave's protagonist Bunny Munro is a traveling salesman of beauty products, serial womanizer, and terrible father. I often have difficulty enjoying a book when I can't stand the main character, and that was definitely the case with this one. Bunny's son, the aptly named Bunny Jr; is a beautiful and intelligent child who has drawn the short stick in the bundle when it comes to family. His mother commits suicide while his dad is out on sales calls, leaving Bunny Jr. to fend for himself for a day or two before his dad comes home. When his dad returns to a trashed house and his wife hanging in their bedroom, he takes his son out on the road to "learn the ropes." Thus begins chapter after chapter of sex with strangers, poor parenting, and general misery. There are some beautiful lines tossed around in this novel, and it was definitely readable, but I expect more from the amazing Mr. Cave and this book ultimately let me down.

I particularly liked Turtle and Chris, two smart kids, each with issues that set them outside of the socially accepted circle. A rollicking read... I am looking forward to reading more of Raskin's work.

I had been recommended this book probably the longest ever. My teacher in 2nd grade had asked me to read it, and although I had checked it out of the library I never did read it. Every year since then I would get recommended this book at least twice a year from numerous friends, teachers, colleagues, and peers. Every time I would go to the library and find their busted up much-loved copy of The Westing Game, and every time I wouldn't read it. Finally a year ago I decided the only way I was ever going to read this book is if I owned it. So I bought it off Thriftbooks for something like $2, and still I waited a year to read it. 
 I finally read it, and let me tell you the overhype of the book definitely depleted its stars, and I found some parts extremely boring, especially the middle. In addition to that, the characters seemed 2-dimensional and not well rounded, but this is a middle grade "children's" book so I eased up and that being so negative. 
 To tell you the truth I almost abandoned this book. I was UPSET! Why wasn't the book as good as everyone said it would be? Why haven't I connected to it? Why don't I love this? 
 Then I read the solving of the mystery and ultimately the end. I was speechless honestly. But mostly I felt sad at myself for not reading this book when I was younger and needed it. I was mad that I had waited so long so that my brain would age and wouldn't be able to connect with this book as a young child of Turtle's or Chris's age would have. I'm 19 years old now and it took me a total of 12 years to finally read this book, and I'm happy I finally read it, but it saddens me knowing I couldn't connect with it fully. It also makes me tremendously sad that I totally would have connected with it when I was 7 years old and lonely. I guess this could count as one of my few regrets in life, not reading The Westing Game sooner. 
 The ending is probably one of my favorite endings to a book, but sadly I'm just to old I guess to fully appreciate the whole novel. I'll probably give it another go in the future, and it will stay on my shelf for the rest of my life. Maybe one day if I ever have kids I'll read them The Westing Game so they could appreciate it and let it shape their lives. It just didn't do that for me, and man oh man I wish it had.

Sehirde gecen fantastik hikayeleri seviyorsaniz, cok fazla buyu olmasin diyenlerdenseniz ve kara filmler hosunuza gidiyorsa cok basarili bir roman.
