book_b.title: These Shallow Graves
book_b.user_review:
3.5/5 I received an ARC for review from Random House. This was a good read but it took me awhile to get into it. 
 These Shallow Graves is a historical fiction mystery about a young high society girl Jo who wants to be a reporter and be free from society's constraints on her for being from a good family and being a women. When her father is killed in a accident this triggers a series of events that lead to the realization that it was no accident. To find the truth Jo allies herself with a young reporter and puts her reputation on the line (which was a big deal) to find the truth. 
 It was sadly very predictable for me and I guessed many plot reveals but it was still a good read. Donnelly has very descriptive writing and I like her style. I didn't connect very well with the characters but Ioved the side of New York we get to see where the upper and lower class are so drastically contrasted and explored.

sample_reviews.review_text: By the third chapter, I wanted to just toss the novel out a window. Just too much dialogue and not enough narrative to make this a good read.

Compared to Jennifer Donnelly's other YA novels, These Shallow Graves was a large disappointment, full of stereotypical characters, an uneventful mystery, anachronistic dialogue, and obnoxious cliffhanger endings. 
 There was no finesse or depth to any part of this novel, which is a shame since A Northern Light and Revolution were both so brilliant. I definitely skimmed the last 150 pages and feel that I missed out on nothing.

3.5 
 This had so much awesomeness. I loved the ideas and deeper arguments presented. 
 That said, there was a bit of a shaky start but I pressed on because I really liked Revolution and I trust Jennifer Donnelly to give me material to feel emotional and passionate about. I felt she did in this work. I liked the plot and mystery. I also liked the characters.

3.5 Stars 
 If there is one thing you can count on with me, is that I love to read about the 19th century. I have said it many times before but there is just something to be said about a strong minded, strong willed feisty girl living in a time when she wasn't suppose to be anything but quiet, well bread, and demure. 
 Throw in a irresistible murder mystery, a handsome rogue and it was a story that was doubly hard for me to say no to. 
 I'm so glad I read this. I really did enjoy every single thing about it but especially Jo herself. She was everything I was hoping she would be from the synopsis, strong, fierce, brave, feisty, determined, and a woman that wasn't to be shunted and locked away. 
 And while this wasn't quite the creepy read I was seriously hoping it would be based on the cover, it did have it's suspenseful moments and I did thoroughly enjoy it. 
 This was well written, easy paced, character and mystery driven and just enough romance to keep you interested. I do wish the ending hadn't been quite so open ended with a few things left to the imagination but it also left it open to a possible sequel, which I truly would love to see and read. 
 *An ARC Copy of this is provided by the publisher in exchange for an honest review.*

Here's a not so good book by a wonderful writer. 
 First off, this is mostly very, very predictable. The bad guy is obvious early on, and everything fits neatly and perfectly together. Too neatly. 
 Now for Jo. While I find her incredible naivete a lot more believable than a lot of readers, who apparently don't know enough about turn of the century New York to believe that rich girls of this period could be this sheltered and childlike--they really were--I find her managing to walk in and out of danger throughout the book and getting a lucky rescue EVERY SINGLE TIME to be totally unbelievable. The "romance" is also too nice and neat and more a plot point than a true relationship. The end is tidy as can be, and again, too perfect. I was expecting a (believable) unhappy ending for one character, and instead Donnelly makes everyone happy. 
 I will note that this particular character seems to be a reader favorite judging by reviews here. But the plot devices Donnelly used with her made me want to scream--one of the worst plot twists of all. 
 The pity is that Donnelly does great research and writes well enough for me to keep on reading. But apparently most modern editors let best selling authors write messes like this, knowing that they will make lots of sales regardless of the quality. That's a sad thing.

Source: Netgalley in exchange for a review. 
 For a change, the female protagonist didn't need a man to set her life right. Were men/love interests present? Absolutely. Did the love interests overshadow the plot? Absolutely not. This was a great mystery with plot twists that some would never see coming. Ultimately all loose ends were tied up and all the secrets were laid to rest in their own graves.

"...I've buried quite a few...and I can bury you, too." 
 This book and I were supposed to get married and have 2.5 kids and live in the suburbs together happily ever after. (HEAs stopped working out for me a very long time ago, though.) 
 These Shallow Graves 
 's premise was a truly interesting one. The whole setting had a very Downton Abbey-feel to it; plus, it's not every day you find an author who handles feminism in Historical Fiction as well as Cat Winters does. 
 I find the nineteenth century a fascinating time, though this makes me come across as a romantic and a somewhat starry-eyed little kid, I like this era despite its patriarchy, none-too-comfortable fashion and prejudices. This book takes us to the streets of 1890's New York, inside the slumps, brothels and docks of the city and the secrets lurking in there. 
 The good of this book is these things: it's setting, for one, which is well done. It's fast-paced, and its characters feel full of life. And God, the first half is more or less a shitload of upperclassmen angst, but it's fun to read. There's plenty of feminism and great character development, especially our protagonist's. It's all very likable. But I wasn't completely swayed by it, despite the most perfect ending of all time and the writing's pleasing aesthetic excellence. 
 What's the worst thing about it? Well, I might be in the minority this time, but I knew from the seventh chapter who it was. Reader's intuition, or whatever, but I knew who was the culprit and that lessened my enjoyment of its climax. Conclusion: the mystery was predictable. And giving me predictable mysteries is more or less a recipe for disaster. Next problem, its Main Character, Jo Montfort, though develops in time to a wonderful person you'd have liked to be friends with in real life as you journey with her, fell flat for me because of only one thing: she's got something of a damsel-in-distress complex. Sure, I don't expect every single character of my books turning out to be badass Katnisses or Penryns, but she is saved from one dilemma or another every single time by someone or another, most notably by Fay. I'm all for girl-power, and dude, Fay's an awesome character, but you need to save yourself at least once in order to gain my respect. Another thing, this book ends almost every chapter with a cliff-hanger. I don't have anything against them, Rick Riordan has made them terribly lame for me with time. But the thing is, this takes it to another not-new, pretentious-punchline- 
 Looking for Alaska 
 -level. It annoyed me, sure, and I thought the romance was kind of insta-love-ish? I totally shipped that ship and it's balanced well--doesn't make the plot completely revolve around it, but its beginning seemed kind of...gimmicky? 
 Despite the, err, poor quality of its mystery aspects, I must say, it never once felt like the characters investigating were being handed clues on silver platters at every twist and turn of the road, which has become quite a recurring theme in YA. They worked for it, fought for it, and you know what, it has never once felt easy. Plus, how easy it was for a woman to be considered insane during this time really creeped me out. 
 Did you read 
 A Madness So Discreet 
 and felt like punching walls because of its mystery? Then 
 These Shallow Graves 
 's will probably soothe your angry soul. Is this book life-changing? For some, perhaps. For me, no, but it was an enjoyable read, though I kept losing interest due to thirteen tests and vivas I suffered through this October. Do I recommend it? Yes, I do. But I'd say don't go into it with expectations as high as mine had been. It was a good book, but not to a satisfying extent for me. 
 "Dead people always make me hungry." 
 It's fun, captivating despite the shitty mystery; carries a great message. You're guaranteed to be hooked. 
 Thank You, Random House Delacorte, for providing me with an Advanced Reader's Copy
A marvelous Victorian mystery. I enjoyed the action, the romance, and the head-strong leading lady quite a bit.

I don't exactly know where this book and I went wrong. I really wanted to like it, and in a sense there were parts in the book that I did enjoy, but overall this was a big disappointment with me. Which sadness me because so many of my friends loved it, and I was so eager to read it myself, that it just turned into an absolute failure. 
 First, when I read the opening chapter I was excited. Grave digging, my imagination ran wild, I had all kinds of hopes for this book that ended up not only disappointing me but it fell completely flat. 
 Where do I start? 
 Jo. I honestly kind of hate her. She is a 17-year old that acts like she is younger, much, much, younger. Not only does she appear obtuse sometimes, but she is also naive, childish, melodramatic, too trusting, and overall not the smartest crayon in the box. Like in one scene while she is in Brooklyn, after facing so much danger already and learning the dark side of New York City, she goes ahead and thrusts some out of the mill older woman who offers her a ride back home, not even contemplating what kind of danger might be facing her trusting this woman and her husband. Now let me tell you something. I was raised in NYC and if some random older woman and her husband offered me a ride home while I was alone in a neighborhood I am not familiar with, I would run the other direction screaming fire. I guess it might just be me, but as an ex-New Yorker, I actually learned how to not trust people - an issue my husband and I choose to agree and disagree on. 
 Conveniently for Jo though there is always someone there to rescue her from her bad decisions, most notably Fay. 
 The romance was lame and honestly felt a little forced and fake. There were a few scenes that left me questioning if Eddie was actually using her for a story like her uncle has mentioned. Which in itself was never explained. When Eddie was confronted about it, he denied ever saying it, but the author never explained how Jo's uncle pulled that one out of thin air. There wasn't any tension and felt kind of instant. 
 I don't understand why the book was over 400 pages long. It dragged a bit at times. I found myself wanting to finish it in hopes of a better ending, but everything I predicted at the beginning of the story came true, which actually only disappointed me more because it was that damn predictable. There had been parts that also felt a bit rushed and not only that but oddly written. In example, this scene, just found weird the way it was written: 
 "Oh, look!" Jo said. "The man sitting next to her just stood up. He knocked her gloves off the counter. Go return them to her, Oscar!" 
 "He's crazy about her," Eddie said as he watched his friend go. 
 Jo smiled. "I never would have guessed. Is she really a medical student?" 
 Maybe I would have to backtrack a little more for it to make sense on here, but stuff happened conveniently and the actions kind of felt odd? 
 There was mostly just the bad side of NYC at that time and good part. Not much in between. 
 I wanted to know more about the Tailor, he seemed kind of creepy. 
 I only really liked Fay in this book. 
 And the prologue or whatever it was that gave us a glimpse into what is happening later in the book, did not really reflect what happened later. It didn't match. I can't go too much into it, but the feelings and actions of the moment just did not match. 
 I also thought this would be more creepy due to the cover, but it really wasn't. I was surprised Jo could not see the answers in front of her as the evidence continued to pile on, since I myself already figured who done it right after it happened. 
 Also, in one chapter her mother sucks.This review was originally posted on Night Owl Book Cafe

4.5 stars 
 These Shallow Graves is the first book I have read by Jennifer Donnelly and I mean it when I say, it will not be the last. I loved everything about this book. The cover and the actual pages are beautiful (There's a MAP), the characters are fantastic, and the mystery...while I guessed what was going on, I didn't care. Donnelly created a story that yanked me in from page one and wouldn't let me go until I finished and knew what was going to happen. 
 Jo Montfort comes from a well-known family and has grown up surrounded by riches and rules. As a member of the elite society of New York City, the only thing that is expected of her is that she not embarrass her family name and she marry well. The thing about Jo is she wants more than that...one of the things she wants is to be able to write - preferably a newspaper reporter like Nellie Bly. 
 When tragedy strikes her family, Jo is thrown into a situation she never expected to face. As she digs more and more into the death of her father, Jo is introduced to people and danger both of which would get her into a lot of trouble if her mother and uncle knew what she was up to. I loved seeing her do what she wanted to in order to find out more. I have read many books about this time in our history and every time I hear how condescending men were to women (they couldn't possibly have a brain or want to use it for more than discussion about weather and parties) it makes me cringe and appreciate the things I am able to do. 
 As Jo digs, she meets a guy named Eddie. At first it was clear he saw her as an opportunity to advance at the paper but when he learns more about Jo, he finds himself drawn to her. The challenge for these two as they start to have feelings for each other, is that they are from different classes in society and definitely not allowed to do any of the things they have been up to. Both romantically as well as journalists. I liked Eddie - he has a past and as his secrets are revealed he becomes more than just the guy who will help Jo. 
 Coming from different classes, it was interesting to see the way they viewed each other and how they came to realize just how different they really were. From a relationship perspective, I loved seeing them realize the differences and try to figure out how they could even make their relationship work...or if they should. 
 There are a number of secondary characters that add to the story and I have to say, the timeframe that Donnelly set the story in was the perfect framework for this book. If you are looking for a good mystery with solid characters and a page-turning story, definitely check this book out when you can. 
 Thank you to the publisher and NetGalley for the review copy!

reference_books.review_text:
I heard many good reviews of this book but honestly, I couldn't get past the rest of 50%. How the story took its turn from crime investigation to spiritual was something hard for me to grasp within my belief system. Even if I were a Christian, I wouldn't buy the fact that you're sad after losing your child and one day you get a letter from God and visit the same place where your kid died. Then you meet a black-African lady who happens to be God (and is making pan cakes), and then you meet Jesus (who's busy gardening) and then another woman who is a Holy Spirit. 
 Umm... seriously? 
 There are lots of people who suffer from this grief but I don't think anyone would encounter God in a shack dY$?" 
 I still wonder if Matt (the main character) found who killed his child? Will figure out later! 
 ***3-stars*** hard to believe spirituality

sample_reviews.review_text: I liked this book from the start. It is a very dark and mysterious book. There was something about the main character Libby that I loved reading- I think it was her no nonsense/sarcastic attitude. I enjoyed reading the books from the various perspectives of Libby, her brother Ben, her mom Patty, etc. I also liked how it went back and forth in time. It made things interesting. It kept my interest also because the entire book is talking about the night Libby's family was murdered except she and Ben and who did it and what the town thought, etc. It kept me guessing. It was a bit weird all the talk of devil worshipping and drug use - a little scary. I also didn't love how quickly the ending wrapped up- I always feel like books I read lately end too abruptly or easily. Maybe it's just me.... Overall good and interesting book and I'm excited to see the movie.
It's hard when there is not one character to remotely like. Dark, violent.

What a dark but delightful read. I picked up this book on vacation, thinking it was a new release, and then realizing this was published before the oh so popular, Gone Girl. Really had no expectations when I opened the cover. The story was engaging - dark, yes - and exciting to go back and forth between now and 1985 as the story unfolded from three perspectives. The ending was good...not fantastic...but good and it wrapped it all up with no loose ends. Definitely worth the read!

I'm working Gillian Flynn in reverse - first Gone Girl, sensational bestelling movie-adapted third novel; then Dark Places, second coming of a newly-started author, apparently living up to the expectation of her debut, Sharp Objects - which I'm planning on reading ASAP, because few authors get me like Flynn can. 
 I think it's all about the characters and points of view, to be honest. Flynn has the best kind of writing style - one that doesn't pressure the reader, doesn't make the narrator a looming presence impossible to ignore. She also writes about horrible people in a sympathetic way, but without putting them on a pedestal. I love this. There's way to many authors (and readers, sic!) excusing and/or romantizing terrible behaviours just because of some sappy backstories. Which, nope. I'm sorry for your loss, but they don't excuse you being an abusive person, or a murder, or ehi! even an ordinary bastard. 
 Gillian Flynn doens't make heroes out of ordinary bastards. She leads you into their minds and makes you understand what made them the monsters they are, but she never forgets to showcase them for what they are - monsters. Gone Girl is a great example of what I mean: you can't escape the twisted magic of that book, the one that makes you symphatize with both Nick and Amy. But never once the book stops from showing you how toxic and sick and 100% NOT-TO-DO their love is. 
 It works the same in Dark Places. You've got the main girl, Libby Day, only survivor of domestic massacre. When she was seven, her older brother Ben murdered their mother and two sisters, then was condamed to life sentence thanks to Libby's shaky witnessing. Grown-up Libby is a mean, selfish, weak young woman with not will to either live or die, who gets roped back in the murderous mess that was her past by young, lost causes obsessed Lyle and his little club of Murders Solvers. 
 Libby is a bad person, and her family is made out of some hugely messed-up persons - and I loved each one of them. I loved twisted, scared Ben and his surrander to a mean world. I loved mama Patty and her desperate love for her children. I loved Libby, messy, mean Libby, a survivor with no sugar coating her emotional scars. It was hard to take in all their emotions, because Flynn is a merciless writer, when it comes to emotions. But that's her charm; and the raw, intense, yet never over-the-top way she describes her characters' journies leads the reader in some of the most compelling, twisted and terryfing plots I've ever read, with just the right amount of tension and details to never make it too much.

Just have to fair, because she wrote this book before Gone Girl, Gone Girl was much better in style and writing, sometimes I need to stop a bit before I can continue to read. Good thriller, but the plot and the story background was not my cup of tea (don't want to include spoiler here). Can't wait to see the movie adaptation to see if I like it better or not.

Very twisty. Gillian Flynn is a masterful writer, she made me care about a character I didn't like and felt absolutely no personal connection to. The twists she made along the way were fascinating and the ending was unexpected. There were a few spots that didn't sit right with me just a tiny bit, but not enough to dislike the book. She more than made up for it. Next, Sharp Objects.

A HUGE thank you to House Party, Forever Publishing and Jodi Ellen Malas for the oportunity to read, review and chat about this book! 
 Chatter Box 
 As mentioned, I received a copy of This Man as a Chatter Box from HouseParty.com! (I also received a coy for a friend - which I gifted to a fellow book lover!) I hadn't heard much about this series, but I devoured Fifty Shades and the Crossfire Series. (I saw as many technical errors and other annoying facts as everyone else, but for some reason I couldn't put them down!) This series is much the same. 
 Is the editing perfect? Nope. Are there things that I hate about the stories? You bet. Are there things that don't make sense? Yep. Too many questions left after reading? Yep. But for some reason, these books are absolutely intoxicating. 
 This Man was a one day read for me. (At 470 pages? That's quite the feat too!) And it's definitely one of those books that I love to hate. I seriously could not put it down (and I'm anxious to finish writing this review so I can start reading book two!) But I hated it. I hated the instalove. I hated that Jesse has ZERO redeeming facts. That there's no real relationship beyond the sex. I hate how controlling Jesse is - let's face it, he's an asshole. And Ava is equally annoying for just caving to his whims. 
 And the predictability factor? It's gag-inducing. (Seriously; I picture myself in the late 80's - "Like, totally! Gag me with a spoon!" ) 
 But? I couldn't quit. I just couldn't. I can't tell you what it is about this story that has me coming back. But there is definitely something that has me hooked. (I'm going with it being that Sam and Katie - the best friend - have me hooked. Because otherwise? I just can't figure it out!) 
 I know this isn't much of a review - it's more a confusing reason why I shouldn't like this book. But I just can't stop reading it! (And seriously, I will be up most of the night going on book two - so stay tuned for that review too!)

book_a.title: Tampa
book_a.user_review: I knew, more or less, what I'd be getting into here. But there's nothing at all redeeming to recommend it -- pacing, style, characterization. Try though it may to substitute shock value for these things, and pass itself off as a character study of a psychopathic pedophile.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I really, really wanted to like Tampa. Lolita is one of my all time favorite books, so I think I was trying to relive the magic of Nabokov by delving into Tampa. I enjoy books that deal with the moral compass of sexual deviants. I studied sexuality and gender in college, and find these books a fascinating character study. However, I found Tampa to be boring. Echoing other reviewers, I felt the characters fell flat. Perhaps this was part of Nutting's plan, to make the character one dimensional in an effort to showcase how much her desires overwhelmed her other personality traits and actions. Regardless, it didn't work for me. 
 While I think the story is a two-star, I think the writing was exquisite. Nutting is a fantastic writer. Her talent for being descriptive cannot be emphasized enough.

Update - I found this book so offensive, not in subject matter but in how poorly it was written, that I couldn't stop thinking about it. So I did some digging. I wanted to know what would possess someone to write a book this bad. 
 Was the author trying to be shocking? Was this supposed to be satire? It seemed very campy, and the protagonist seemed more like a comic book villain than an actual human person. 
 Turns out, this book was inspired by a real woman, who the author went to high school with. I watched an interview with the woman, an English teacher who had an affair with a 14-year-old student in Tampa. She was a very beautiful blond white lady, and her lawyer actually did make the "too pretty for jail" argument, and she did end up just getting house arrest & probation. She could've maybe got more, but the parents dropped the case to protect their son's identity. 
 But the woman was very lost, suffering from rape at around the age of her victim, and probably still stuck at that age herself, as victims of childhood trauma often are. She struggled with an eating disorder and depression, her big sister died, her husband was unsympathetic (I know this as fact, because he wrote a bitchy book about how she moped around the house). She said in the interview that at the time she felt like the boy was her peer, and I absolutely believe her. 
 Then I read Alissa Nutting's interview about why she wrote this book in such a way, with a flat & unbelievable character, who has no thoughts or feelings outside of wanting to fuck & victimize teen boys. She REALLY wants us to believe that all women who sleep with teens are heartless, dangerous, calculating sociopaths, because she thinks WE - her audience - believe that about men. This entire book was written so she could go, "See, women can be big bad predators too!" 
 Um, sorry Alissa, but nobody has ever denied that. 
 She admitted that it angers her when people want to know "why" women would do things like this - as if us trying to understand why is letting them off the hook. No, we are literally asking WTF. 
 Here's why people aren't shocked when men sleep with teen girls - that's what society teaches us from the time we're born. Women are supposed to be youthful and demure and innocent. The entire cosmetics and fashion industries, plastic surgery, and entertainment industry teach us that. Women spend their entire lives trying to look like they did as teenagers, and there are even vaginal rejuvenation surgeries to make them like virgins again. 
 Society doesn't elevate teen boys. Not at all. Women are taught from birth - and Disney movies - to like manly men, men of power and wealth who can provide for us. 
 Also, biologically, these are the things we're wired to want. I think all men find teen girls attractive, whether they be 19 or a developed 14, but they have the morals to not act on it. And not all who do are sociopaths or sexual deviants who can't have healthy relationships with people their own age. Sometimes, good people just do bad things. 
 And it's not looked down on by everyone. Khloe Kardashian has said she lost her virginity at 14 to a grown man, and she doesn't today as a woman see the experience as wrong or negative. If SHE doesn't feel victimized, then she wasn't a victim. Nobody can make that call for her. Sure, the guy was a scumbag, but that doesn't mean her entire life was ruined just because we think it should mean that. It used to be a perfectly normal thing for girls that age to marry men, and in some places it still is. 
 THATS why we asked why a gorgeous woman who could have any man she wanted would mess with a kid. Not because we're coddling her, but because we as a society find that odd, so our reaction is "Eww.. Why?" and a few icky people respond "Lucky boy." Was he harmed by this? That depends on him, and if he feels like he was or not. Plenty of men had a similar experience and think nothing of it, they're married with kids now. Others were traumatized from it. It's a case-by-case basis. Just like with the adults who do this, and why they do it. You can't generalize such a personal experience for all people. 
 I would've loved reading a book that truly answers why a woman would do something like this. But unfortunately, this author didn't dig deep or reveal any truths or answer any questions. She just wrote a ridiculous moral story, like those in the Bible. Read it if you want to be preached to, and have no real interest in human psychology and sexuality whatsoever. 
 *** 
 Could not finish more than the first 15 pages. Never has a book made me physically sick before, but I really felt like I was going to vomit with this one. It's not just the subject matter - the main character is not likable at all. I could tell she would never gain my sympathy, even if I read the whole thing. And if you can't ever see it from the narrator's point of view, there's no point in reading a book. This was over written as well, very purple prose.
It's a well-written novel on a revolting subject. Nutting creates nuanced characters and the story was all too believable.
Creepy but well written.

I think Nutting was trying really hard to create a character in the tradition of Patrick Bateman but, instead, she created a ridiculous caricature. This subject matter has been handled much more successfully in books such as WHAT WAS SHE THINKING? by Zoe Heller, KINGDOM OF CHILDHOOD by Rebecca Coleman, and even LOLITA by Vladimir Nabokov. Heller and Coleman gave their characters depth and complexity. Nutting's character was a cardboard cutout. Not only was she unbelievable but readers must have a huge suspension of disbelief to believe that not one single person saw any signs into the true nature of her character. As I worked my way through the story, I found that it got incredibly tedious. While the subject matter is certainly distasteful and disturbing, I think Nutting relied too heavily on shock value to give her book any impact. 
 I think many people who enjoyed this book were probably drawn in by what they saw as the author's clever handling of a difficult subject. However, these same people may not have encountered this same subject matter handled much more deftly in other books. My issue is not a knee-jerk reaction to the subject matter but more a reaction to what I think is inadequate writing. I simply don't believe you should be given kudos just because you chose a controversial topic. 
 Overall, a pretty disappointing offering.

I was so dissapointed, the concept is a clever one, something a little bit different, but as the story took place, i found it dull, lacking and just no were near as shocking as it was claimed to be. Maybe thats just me, i just found it moved too quickly, with a pace that seemed unnatural , and overall - unenjoyable. Just holy crap. This book is crazy but I couldn't stop listening. The audiobook makes the sound of the young boys even more cringeworthy.

I've always felt there is a fine line between transgressive lit, and generally 'shocking for the sake of being shocking' pulp. I feel this book definitely crossed that line and became an empty read, there was no depth and it just seemed to be begging for notoriety. 
 You really won't find anything interesting here. 
 I will however take a leaf out of another reviewers review, and simply suggest you read 'Notes On A Scandal' instead. Same story, so much more. 
 One Star for Tampa.

I really wanted to like this book. I really liked what the book wanted to be. I really liked what the book was trying to say. I really liked what the book was trying to do. But I didn't really like the book. 
 Tampa is about Celeste, a young, beautiful, eighth-grade English teacher who is sexually attracted to 14-year-old boys, boys who are on the cusp of puberty, only just beginning to grow into men. And Celeste plans to use her position as a teacher to do exactly what you think she's going to do -- get some teenage D up in her vajayjay. 
 It's based on an actual case of a teacher sexually assaulting students in, you guessed it, Tampa, Florida. The true-life case involved a woman that author Alissa Nutting had gone to school with, which inspired this book. And I think it's an idea worthy to explore. 
 There's an interesting difference in attitudes between when a woman sexually assaults a minor and when a man does. If it's a man, he's quickly labelled a predator, a rapist, a sexual deviant. And yet when a woman sexually assaults a minor, there's this weird sort of wink-wink, lucky him, kind of attitude. Like we should be high-fiving the victim, buying him a drink, slapping him on the back. He got to fuck a hot teacher -- what male student wouldn't want to do that? 
 But that's fucked up. He's the victim. He was taken advantage of. He was exploited. He was assaulted. And we forget that. 
 So I think a book that would dig into that kind of thing, about the attitude differences, or about how it really is an assault, might have been interesting. Unfortunately, nothing like that happens here. And I think it's probably because the characters never get to be much more than cardboard cutout cliches. There's not a single interesting or 3-dimensional character in Tampa, which gives the proceedings of the book very little weight. It's hard to care about people who don't really seem real. 
 So it's too bad. There was a lot of potential here that was unfortunately wasted, a great idea but an author who wasn't quite up to the task of pulling it off.

book_b.title: The Cuckoo's Calling (Cormoran Strike, #1)

sample_reviews.review_text: I really enjoy mysteries, so it is no surprise I liked this one. I hadn't heard of it before the news of JK Rowling being the author came out so I did come to it with that knowledge in tow. Regardless of that, I think I still would have really loved it. The mystery kept me guessing til the end. I also enjoyed Cormoran and Robin. I look forward to reading more in this series.
This surprised me because several of my friends loved this book, but I could not get into the characters and could not finish this book.

After starting (and abandoning) The Casual Vacancy, and then reading this, I can definitely say that while I am an unashamed fangirl for Harry Potter, the same can't be said for J.K. Rowling herself. 
 This completely underwhelmed me. Harry Potter has such complex & incredible characterisation, and I felt resonance with even the most evil of characters. With this, none of the characters resonated with me at all, and that was a huge disappointment. I had hoped at least to feel some warmth for either Cormoron or Robin, but ... eh. 
 It seemed rushed in parts, and slow in others, and I just didn't find it gripping or compelling. I feel like a lot of the bad language was forced as well, as a device to really separate herself from her children's author alter ego. It didn't feel natural. 
 This was ok, it was certainly readable, but even knowing who it was that wrote it, I can't believe it was written by the same person who wrote Harry. I'm so diappointed. I really wanted to love this, and have more books by her to read. Oh well.

I really enjoyed this book. Initially wasn't too keen to read due to knowing Author's pseudonym. Not my usual choice but persevered and enjoyed plot evolving. Well worth reading, have ordered next in series.
This was great! Like, seriously, Kate-Atkinson-good. Who would have thought that J.K. Rowling would be my new favorite mystery author? A happy surprise. I can't wait for the next one.

This is the first serious mystery novel that I've read since Agatha Christie's "And Then There Were None." 
 The victim, of course, is Lula Landry, a supermodel...because of course she is. Cormoran Strike is hired by her brother find out if the suicide was really a murder. And of course it was a murder. 
 TCC involves a lot of subtle clue gathering, and I'll be honest and say I didn't follow much of it. I've said it before, I'm not a huge fan of novels where the main characters basically stand around and talk. That's most of this novel. 
 Still, it shows Rowling's immense strength when it comes to making small details turn out to be important. 
 There's not a lot of action in this story, it's basically for a single page at the very end. The characters are diverse and fairly well drawn. There's a fair amount of drama in Lula's family that is, of course, the central reason for the murder. 
 There's plenty of drama on Strike's end as well, mostly due to his twat of an ex-girlfriend. 
 The reveal of the killer at the end is somewhat typical, considering their relationship to Strike. They always strive to make it the person you least expect. 
 I have the sequel to the story, The Silkworm. I'm going to read it sometime in the future, but not for a while. 
 I wish I could review the book with more passion, instead of the blaah I'm giving you. But it took me about a year and a half to read through this, because of the issue I mentioned. I think Rowling is a great writer with great talent, so there is that.

While I did thoroughly enjoy the story, it was a bit slow at parts. Couldn't hold my attention for long stretches most of the time, and I read a bit here or there, put it down, and come back to it. But all in all, I did enjoy the story when I was able to sit down and read it.

This was an okay novel, full stop. This was also a detective novel, full stop. Those two clauses are mutually exclusive. I think the art of a good detective novel, or even an okay one, is giving the reader everything they need to solve the mystery, and either doing it in a way that they feel good about solving it and continuing reading, or in a way that brilliantly masks the truth from them. 
 Cuckoo's calling does neither of those things. It witholds clues to prevent the reader from solving the mystery, which I consider to be quite lazy. Our author, whatever name you wish to call her by, even goes so far as to have the main character, Cormorant Strike- who is otherwise pretty likeable, taunt the audience with the clue one would need to solve the mystery. 
 So, my review in a word? Awful.

3.5. The first thing you should know going into this book is that you must read Delirium first and that it is much better to have recently read Delirium. This book is definitely for the series junkies. Pandemonium picks up where Delirium left off. It took me a little bit to get back into the swing of things and although I didn't feel too lost to finish the book and really enjoy it, I do wish that I had re-read Delirium recently. Oh well, now I know that I need to re-read both Delirium and Pandemonium before I tackle the third book whenever it comes out. 
 Anyhow, this book covers two times in Lena's life. One in the Wilds (which is the part that I liked more) and one when she is back in civilization. The two times are denoted as then and now. I wish that we would have had a little bit more insight into how far apart the two times were but there isn't a good indication until they converge. It was a little bit confusing. 
 I really liked the description of the Wilds and how the people there formed their own society. While I don't feel like we learn much about what makes Lena tick in this book, we are introduced to some cool characters. I especially liked Raven. She's tough and knows how to get everyone to do their assigned jobs, which is necessary to make sure that their society continues to run the way that it was supposed to run. 
 Fans of the first book in this trilogy, Delirium, will really like this book. I think that personally I liked Delirium a little bit better than Pandemonium. Pandemonium is good but it sort of feels like a bridge between Delirium and the last book in the trilogy. What I did like is that there is a good cliffhanger at the end and while usually I don't like cliffhangers, this was a really good one that ignited my excitement for the third book!

Pandemonium is written in 2 parts (Now and Then). In "now" part, we can see Lena's life 1,5 years after Delirium and in "then" part we can see Lena's life right after Delirium. At first, it's confusing but it's really help to build the story. After what happened in Delirium, Lena has to go to the wild without Alex. In the wild, she meets Raven, the leader of an invalid group. In the wild, the invalids are haunted by the bomb, sickness and scavenger, and Lena has to learn how to survive from it all. 
 In "now" part, Lena is working with Raven and Tack in Manhattan to gather information about DFA, a group of people who believe in the cure. Lena has to keep an eye on Julian, the son of DFA leader. In one of DFA meetings, Lena and Julian are kidnapped by the scavenger and lock up in a room together. During their time as the prisoners, they are getting to know each other. When there's a chance, they are escaping together. During the process, Julian is taken back by his father and Lena is reunited with Raven and Tack. What would Lena do when she learns that the kidnapping is an arrangement? Would she save Julian from the procedure? What about Alex? 
 When I read the book, I can feel how hard to live in the wild. I often find the moment where I want to cry. The author sure to know how to bring out the reader's emotion. In Pandemonium, we can find more action than the previous book. The book is full of tension, I often hold my breath when I read the book. We can also see how different the old Lena with the new Lena. She's stronger and more exciting. We also meet with new characters like Julian, Raven and Tack. 
 Before I read the book, I hear that we wouldn't find Alex in the book. It's a surprise for me because that's one of the reason why I can't wait to read the book. But after I read the book, I think it's great. The ending is really a big surprise for me. It's totally an evil cliffhanger and it kills me to wait for the next book. It's definitely better than Delirium. If you haven't read Delirium yet, you should do it now. 
 I give Pandemonium 5 out of 5 stars.

I may be in the minority, but I didn't love it. I LOVED Delirium. But I didn't even really like this one until the end. I kept reading and holding out hope and finally, I had what I wanted and that's the only reason I'll read #3.

So. Delirium made me stabby, and yet I really like Lauren Oliver's writing, and I couldn't stop myself from nabbing this off the library shelf. I'm glad I gave it a chance, because I enjoyed it more than its predecessor. Much like Days of Blood & Starlight, it is far more about war than love. It improves upon the much-abhorred (by me anyway!) trilogy format of the second book being nothing but a bridge between the action of the first and last books. There is action here, and for the most part it doesn't feel like danger just for danger's sake. Ultimately, I wasn't crazy about the pacing, the end went exactly where I was praying it wouldn't go, and the plot as a whole just feels SO derivative. I enjoyed it enough to put myself on the waiting list for Requiem, so I suppose that means I'm invested now, but I think the concept as a whole could use some work. 
 In Delirium, Oliver introduces the concept of a cure for the disease of love. At age 18, everyone must submit to the procedure, which somehow removes their ability to love, or really feel any strong emotions. Apparently this is better for society, since as we all know, love makes you do the wacky. What never made sense to me is the idea that human emotions can just be turned off. Even the people we see who are actually cured still seem capable of some amount of feeling, and Lena even mentions that the cured live in fear of an uncured revolution. Last time I checked, fear was an emotion! The cured also seem to be passionate about, well, the cure itself. Lena mentions crowds being stirred into fervor over hearing Fineman speak -- again, if people truly feel NO emotion, once you are cured, why would you care at all what happens to anyone else? Lena mentions that the officers who show up at DFA (Deliria Free America) rallies will go home having killed revolutionaries and not think twice about the corpses they left behind. Okay, but why do they care at all about those rebels? If they are truly emotionless, why does it matter what other people do or want? There's talk of Julian's father being abusive...isn't anger also an emotion? Wouldn't having the cure make you incapable of getting angry? It's sort of an inherently illogical concept, and as yet, Oliver hasn't provided a satisfactory explanation on how it works, or why it seems to deaden only certain emotions (positive ones like caring and affection and happiness). I get that this is quasi-science fiction, and I'm not asking for a plausible medical explanation of the cure, but as I'm constantly harping in reviews of dystopian novels, the rules of the universe you create need to make sense within that universe. 
 Anyway. We pick up with Lena in the Wilds -- she and Alex escaped from Portland, but Alex was shot and though Lena tries to convince herself otherwise, she truly believes he is dead. And while there's a bit of Bella Swan-style moping near the beginning, Lena earns my respect by putting on her big girl pants and sucking it up. She doesn't immediately get over Alex, and she's constantly thinking about him and wishing he were with her (and as much as their insta-love bothered me in Delirium, this feels authentic. He's her first love, after all). Lena is rescued by a woman named Raven and a group of Invalids (uncured) who live in the Wilds, constantly on the run. The group makes a dangerous journey south for the winter, and as they do, Lena grows stronger and more determined to fight back. It's a good blend of character development with action, and we learn a bit more about the world outside the walls of Portland. 
 These chapters constitute the "then" portion of the novel -- the chapters cycle back and forth between present day Lena (living in New York and working for the resistance, posing as a cured teenager), and Lena as she was when she first escaped. Although I liked the structure at first, the inherent problem is that, knowing Lena is living in New York with Raven and Tack in the "now" chapters eliminates a lot of the suspense of the "then" chapters. There's a point when everyone believes Tack has died on a scouting mission, and I knew he'd eventually come back, since he and Lena and Raven all lived together in the "now" portion. I also assumed that "then" would eventually take us up to Lena's involvement with the resistance, the three of them settling in New York, and perhaps even the specifics of their actual mission. But "then" cuts off long before that point, and "now" opens with Lena already having lived in the city for a few months. I didn't like that weird gap in both narratives. 
 Present-day Lena's job with the resistance is to tail Julian Fineman, the teenaged face of the DFA. Having suffered seizures for most of his young life, the cure could most likely be fatal for Julian, but he's bravely choosing to have the procedure done anyway. Lena tails him on the day of a rally when all hell breaks lose and revolutionaries known as Scavengers (who are uncured, but apparently different from Invalids like Lena and co. in ways that are never fully explained) show up like ninjas and wreak havoc. Lena catches a group taking Julian into the abandoned subway tunnels, and when she follows them, she ends up captured herself. She and Julian spend several days locked in an underground cell, and obviously end up growing attracted to one another. I can kind of buy this attraction at first -- in an extreme situation, you aren't sure how much time you have left, but you're lucky enough to have an ally of sorts, of course you're going to latch onto one another. And for her part, although Lena cops to feeling attracted to Julian, it seems like she's mostly using him as a crutch because she misses Alex. Of course by the end she's decided she's actually in love with him, just in time for obviously not-dead Alex to show up. Blah. Have I mentioned how much I hate unnecessary love triangles? The question "who will she choose?" has never compelled me in any story, ever. I didn't care if Katniss ended up with Gale or Peeta, because hello? bigger problems to be solved. It's the same issue here. The world is in absolute chaos and clearly on the brink of a revolution. I could give a shit about who Lena chooses in the end. One of the reasons I enjoyed Days of Blood & Starlight so much was the fact that Karou clearly realized that other factors outweighed her angst over whether or not to trust Akiva. She was a little busy building an army of monsters and trying not to get assaulted by Thiago to worry about having a boyfriend. Arg. End of rant 
 Overall, this just felt so derivative (much in the way Divergent did). If I tried to read this series back-to-back with the Matched trilogy, I'm not confident I could tell the two apart. And both are borrowing far too much from the far superiorThe Giver anyway. The scenes in the Homestead with the Invalids reminded me a LOT of the Colony in The Passage and The Twelve. The deformed people living in the subway reminded me of the wretches in Pure and Fuse (and also a little of the mutants of Old New York from Futurama). In short, there was very little about the plot itself that felt fresh. There's nothing wrong with using a familiar plot, but you have to put your own spin on it. I can honestly say that I still really like Lauren Oliver's writing, and I just wish she would have stretched a little more with this series.

book_b.user_review: I'm going through this whole thing of I don't know what to read - and this is my go to - so I read it again.

sample_reviews.review_text: Okay, so I knew the book was going to be about sex. "Fifty Shades of Grey" I hoped that meant an older woman with grey hair was going to have great sex. But no, I was disappointed. Anyway, there was lots of sex but I would have told Mr. Grey to go F*** himself from the beginning and then there would be no story.
Utter drivel.

The success of Fifty Shades of Grey is the very definition of viral marketing. A book that was originally self-published as an eBook and a print-on-demand paperback, it somehow caught the imagination of women everywhere and it's said that a copy now sells every sixty seconds. Amazing. There are three books in the series and they are numbers 1, 2 and 3 on the New York Times best seller list, and have been for months. 
 I have three words for this phenomenon: WTF?? I mean really...have you read this thing? 
 I bought a Kindle version ($9.99), just to see what all the hoopla was about, and got through about 1/3 of it (31% according to my Kindle), rolling my eyes and saying, "Oh, please," on every other page. With one exception (from Jessica Reaves of the Chicago Tribune) it seems to be immune to criticism of any kind (because it's made a boatload of money?), and as an author it's probably bad form to say this (you know that won't stop me), but it's crap. I don't mind the concept of it or the genre of eroticism itself, but something that's selling like the latest iPad release should at least be...well, good. 
 Fifty Shades of Grey is not good. That's not hurting sales in the least. It doesn't seem to matter that the writing stinks, the characters are unappealing and not engaging, the storyline is non-existent and, worst of all, the sex isn't even good, just lots of murmuring and moaning and gasping, and heartbeats quickening and racing. Kinda trite. At least be original. 
 The protagonist, Anastasia Steele, is a 21 year old virgin, and the narrative (told from her point of view) is sprinkled with lots of italics: holy crap! holy fuck! holy shit! jeez! and so on. And her inner goddess talks to her, and does "merengue with some salsa moves." Need I say more? Now, you can't argue with that kind of success - it's phenomenal - and good for E.L. James. She seems as amazed by this as everyone else. But seriously...what are you people thinking? Whatever it is, could you please transfer it to my book? And when mine becomes a runaway best seller it won't bother me a bit when E.L. James trashes it on her blog.

The author will be the first to tell you she isn't a great writer, and it's evident in Fifty Shades. The gratuitous sex scenes got ridiculous and tired very quickly, the language used was very asinine, especially in the everyday conversations of the characters, and the main character's thought process was like a balloon with the helium slowly leaking out. 
 At first the sex scenes were fun and thrilling, and then they never stopped happening and I began skimming through them in order to get to more of the story-- which was, sadly, lacking. There isn't much to this book other than a whole lot of sex. 
 If you've never read a sexually explicit romance novel before, then this might float your boat. I've read my share of romance novels (ones that actually had characters you could care about and plots with mysterious twists that make you want to keep reading), and this one was so ridiculously bad, in my opinion, that it was hard to finish reading.
Did not finish.

Before Fifty Shades of Grey, the only experience with the BDSM genre I had was Vishous' book in the Black Dagger Brotherhood series, Lover Unbound, by J.R. Ward. (And I suppose if you count the cult classic movie, Manos: Hands of Fate, which I in fact do) While it's a pretty epic book (my favorite in the series), I was not completely prepared for what was in store for me from Mr. Grey. I had my expectation, and this book certainly exceeded them. But as much as there were some hot, steamy moments, there were a lot of things that left me cold. 
 Check out the rest of My review for this novel, posted on my Romance Novel Rview Blog, Reading Until I Fall Asleep. Check it out here: 
 http://www.readinguntilifallasleep.co...
