sample_reviews.review_text: I think my reading of this book suffered from all the hype. I had read a number of glowing reviews, and I think those set my expectations higher than was reasonable.
I picked this up on a whim. Not at all in my usual wheelhouse but I really liked it. The mystery was pretty good and the characters were even better.

This book was not for me. The thug life, with gangster rap and life on the streets, just doesn't interest me. Plus, I'm not a fan of profanity, so this book really did nothing for me. None of the characters were the least bit interesting, to me. The mystery/case had little appeal either. I appreciate what the author was trying to do with the main character, setting him up as a potential recurring character in a series of books, but it is just not a character or setting that I enjoy at all. Thugs and gang bangers, rappers and music executives really hold zero appeal to me. It is just not my area of interest. If it is for you, then this book might really interest you.

Not your typical detective novel. Isaiah Quintabe, known as IQ, is a quiet, unassuming and brilliant high school dropout who works as an under-the-radar investigator. His heartbreaking past and his vow to make amends for his mistakes makes him a fascinating character. 
 The language, dialogue and rap music scene characters sound and feel very real. Joe Ide hit it out of the park with his debut novel. I hope he's a fast writer. I want more!

** spoiler alert ** 
 IQ - Isaiah Quintabe - Smart - Sherlock Holmes smart; drops out of HS when older brother (who is raising him, who loves him, who sees the best in him and the world) is randomly killed in a hit and run... we get Isaiah's story bit by bit when 10 years later, a neighborhood detective, he is rejoined by Juanell Dodson, his post brother roommate (to help make ends meet - he wasn't going into foster care), drug dealer, fellow thief... 
 Dodson wants to work with him to solve an attempted murder on a rapper... 
 IQ is charming, is human, is indifferent to threats, and still hears his brother's words and wisdom as he confronts his life... 
 convoluted path to solve the mystery, but he does...

Interesting read for his first book. the character has possibilities for the future. He only gives us glimpse of his talents. Puts way to much association with Holme's reasoning. Be it inductive or deductive.

I received a free ARC of this from NetGalley. 
 There's no shortage of Sherlocks these days. Both CBS's Elementary and the BBC's Sherlock are doing fun modern day twists on Holmes. When Robert Downey Jr. can tear himself away from his duties as Iron Man he's been known to play Sherlock as a steampunkish action hero in the movies. Plus, there always new novels featuring the detective being published. Countless other stories inspired by the character are also always circulating like the medical mysteries that Hugh Laurie solved for years on House. So you wouldn't think that we need yet another variation of Sherlock Holmes. 
 Thankfully, Joe Ide disagreed and came up with a fresh new take on the world's most famous consulting detective that is a helluva of a good story and a welcome addition to Sherlockian style books. 
 Isaiah Quintabe (a/k/a IQ) is a brilliant young man living in a rough area of Los Angeles where he acts as a kind of public service oriented detective for the community. Unfortunately, his services usually only net him baked goods, and Isaiah has a serious need for some cash. That's when his old roommate Dodson shows up with the offer to figure out who tried to kill a famous rapper for a big payday. Dodson is a hustler that Isaiah doesn't really trust, but he reluctantly takes the case. His only lead is a security video of a monstrous attack dog who was let loose on the rapper in his own kitchen, but the trail will lead him to a professional killer who loves his work. 
 The Sherlock influences are pretty obvious from the start. Isaiah is self-contained guy who can make instinctive leaps of logic based on what he observes whose persona can seem cold and off-putting to others. His partner on the case is Dodson which rhymes with Watson if you didn't notice. There's an oversized dog that immediately brings to mind The Hound of the Baskervilles. If that's all there was then this could have been just a Holmes homage without much else going for it. 
 However, Ide prevents that by coming up with ways to play off the Sherlock tropes. Instead of Dodson being a kiss ass who marvels at IQ's brilliance their relationship is a contentious one with a troubled history that we get in a parallel plot that also functions as Isaiah's origin story. I also liked that IQ's detective skills don't come from having obscure knowledge like being able to identify the tobacco of Belgian cigarette. Instead he depends on his ability to reason through LA traffic patterns or researching police alarm times as well as applying a common sense rationality to the way people behave to make his deductions, and it comes across as impressive as well as realistic. The backstory of IQ's life as well and his history with Dodson makes him far more sympathetic as well as giving him legitimate reasons for what he does than Sherlock ever had. 
 Aside from the Sherlock connections this is also a fast paced mystery/thriller in its own right. We get the hit man character's perspective, and he's also built up as being both a very dangerous threat as well as believable. The way that we're introduced to IQ and Dodson and then get their backstory delivered in installments dovetails nicely with the main story. It's all got a logical progression and a clever solution that is very satisfying. 
 Maybe best of all is that IQ is an interesting character that I want to spend more time getting to know. Hopefully, Joe Ide will again follow the example of Arthur Conan Doyle and give us many more stories with this fascinating detective.
1.5 stars

Sherlock Holmes updates are a plenty in the early 21st century. Guy Ritchie's take has RDJ as a bare-fisted fighter. Steven Moffat's Sherlock, like any Millennial, is glued to his Smartphone while Watson is married to a superspy. Then comes author Joe Ide whose eponymous character is a young, black man in LA solving crimes for the poor folk of the 'hood for payments of blueberry muffins. IQ drives a maxed out Audi while Watson, this time going with the rhyming handle Dodson, is a Tupac-loving, ex-drug dealer. And brother it works. 
 Hardly your typical noir LA PI, Isaiah Quintabe is a quiet man who has the gift of observation. As a means of absolution, he simply wishes to help, while his former roommate, Dodson, who sets himself up as IQ's business manager, gets him involved in a case involving a rapper targeted by a hitman who specializes in breeding pit bulls. Ide provides a hip-hop soundtrack as the unlikely duo works the case while the b-plot reveals the friends' former criminal ways that breaks IQ away from the genre and into an untapped realm. 
 Ide's dialogue is fresh and, typical of the Sherlock genre, revealing as IQ proves himself, distances himself, from mundane, particularly those in his community who see happiness by way of Benjamins and bling. The plot is fast and fun if even the solution runs on the convenient side. Best yet, Ide has a follow-up planned. Having more IQ is always a good thing.

(2) This author has a world of potential. There are parts of this book that just hum along, flowing and fun. Other parts are totally self indulgent in Ide trying to show us how hip he is and delivering one cliche scene after another. Isiah, the protagonist, is part wonderful and part way too sappy in his creation, but in the end, he is still a worthwhile character and I would enjoy seeing more of him. The premise here is mostly solid, some of the rough edges need to be smoothed out.

book_b.title: Smarter Faster Better: The Secrets of Being Productive in Life and Business
book_b.user_review:
I'm not impressed. 'The Power of Habit' was fine; this isn't. There are some neat stories of various scenarios where someone did something admirable and succeeded in some way. E.g. Disney, worker factories, West Side Story, airplane accidents and so on. Those are fine, but no enough. The 'secrets' of being productive are pretty lame and on the whole this book feels like 'The Power of Habit 2', the bad sequel that should never have been made. 
 There are thousands of productivity books out there. You should get one of those instead of this one.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Smarter Faster Better by Yale & Harv Bus School grad Charles Duhigg is surprisingly uneven, breezy and journalistic, and lacking in the quantitative, scholarly analytic rigor one might expect of a Pulitzer Prize winning author. 
 This is not to say the book is entirely without merit. There are some interesting points made here and there, albeit they are raised willy nilly out of nowhere in disconnected fashion erupting out of the midst of an altogether unrelated discussion, like Mt. Aetna or Mt. Vesuvius. 
 Let me focus for a moment on the problems with this book. 
 First, the chapter on poker and Annie Duke is inaccurate, out of date and betrays a complete and total misunderstanding of what Bayesian probability is. Either you explain fully, or don't discuss it at all. What the author does instead is mis-explain it, and dumb it down. Second, Annie Duke dropped out of her doctoral program eons ago. It's not relevant to the here and now. Third, the author suggests that she has been cured of anxiety disorder by becoming a millionaire. Four marriages and divorces, not mentioned in the book, and the fact that she is hell on wheels, suggest otherwise. In fact, one might speculate that she might have been dropped from her PhD program rather than she quit. 
 Next, the footnotes do not support or properly cite the studies touted in the text. And, to the extent they are cited, they are old and out of date. Thus this is not the cutting edge book you might expect--rather, it has the feel of older profile pieces cobbled together into a second book and unified into a snappy sounding current sounding title. 
 Next, the interview process at Google has been covered to death, and the issues covered in this book are already out of date. 
 Finally, the author notes that he refuses to make known many of his sources and many of his interviews for the book on the grounds of "privacy". that makes no sense. if you publish, the right is waived. and, it's an academic work, not journalism or reporting. 
 if we dont know the sources, how do we know the author is telling the truth? who can fact check a book? to the extent he wrote about things i know about, 75-80% of what he says is flat wrong. 
 for example, the author writes that most people would not be familiar with actuarial life expectancy tables. 
 but in fact, all law students study those as part of estates law, and again in income tax law. That's 3 million people. And so do CPAs, actuaries, life insurance industry workers, bankers, finance people, the tobacco industry, etc. in fact, probably 100 million Americans know those tables and read them. 
 so that's just a wrong statement, without a footnote. 
 this book is not utterly without merit. it has good points, and is even entertaining in spots, but it suffers from not being fully researched up to date, fails to list internet sources, does not cite market performance, lacks analytical and statistical analysis, and in general, is just not sufficiently math driven.

Charles Duhigg reports for the Wall St. Journal, and, because of this, he is a master of compelling anecdotes. He uses this skill to give examples of how a number of specific tools can enhance people's productivity. For me, this book offered some snippets of immediately relevant information in a universally compelling package.

I read this after loving The Power of Habit: Why We Do What We Do in Life and Business. A book that I loved and gave 5 stars to. This one was as far as day and night. 
 This book was not as well written, and did not wrap the topics well, but that is the least of the problems. Even the story about Frozen wasn't engaging (and I have read about Pixar in so many other books already). I think the main thing about this book that it feels like the advice you get for your diet. You already know what you need to do, so the advice is pretty useless. And the number of people that can live up to this advice (especially if they need it) is so small. And as the diet advice, it brings nothing knew. Nothing at all! 
 But moreover, I had a huge problem with the book. The book mostly went around two topics that I personally know well: Google's culture and Yom Kipur war. I found so many wrong examples and stories there, that I couldn't stand the book at all. How much time did Duhigg actually spend with the relevant people before writing this book? I am not sure, except not enough. And I don't feel that I will read his next book with the trust I had on the first one. 
 Personally, I would say that the leader role in the open team collaboration and developing people is a strong one, more than most books empathize (and here there is no exception). We need to work on better leadership, that will groom the people, and coach them upwards. And we need to work on self leadership, that will allow people to take the empowerment and do something good with it. (And this is all outside this book, there are many others that explain that more clearly and simply and a great example is Ken Blanchard). 
 For better book about Google's culture, you should read Mr. Penumbra's 24-Hour Bookstore (it is also wrong, but at least very funny and doesn't try to be right). For better books about teams read Patrick Lencioni's books (The Five Dysfunctions of a Team: A Leadership Fable and The Three Signs of a Miserable Job: A Management Fable About Helping Employees Find Fulfillment in Their Work). And for good management read Kenneth H. Blanchard (he is too simplistic, but the best that I found. and they are concise and give the right message. e.g. Empowerment Takes More Than a Minute and The One Minute Manager). And of course Good to Great: Why Some Companies Make the Leap... and Others Don't, the book about better (that does talk about leadership and successors) and makes an amazing work related to research (unlike the above). 
 2 stars, and I feel so super generous.
Not nearly as good as the power of habit but still a book to help you improve in 8 key areas of your life. The chapters on motivation, focus, abd problem solving were especially insightful.

this guy should have read his own book. 
 it is a loser.

"The Power of Habit" was quite a fundamental research and while I see now how it had the similar pattern of issues that I disliked in the "Smarter Faster Better", it was still a coherent narrative. The problem with this book is that it's mostly a collection of anecdotes and there's pretty much no connective tissue between them. In fact, the Appendix where the author tells the story of how he applied some of the principles and techniques he's describing while he was writing this book, seems the most coherent part. But the rest of the book lacks that and many times I couldn't follow why I'm reading some particular anecdote and how it connects to the previous ones. 
 Also, most of the stories are split up in two or three sections and interleaved with other stories in the same way as they do in many reality TV shows (think, Mythbusters), so you have to keep 2 or 3 storylines in your head. Why? Hell if I know. I don't like that on TV, I like it even less in the book form. 
 Now, while majority of the material is not new and have been described in many other books, I enjoyed parts about probabilistic thinking, Bayesian logic and such. Yes, if you're really interested in this type of stuff you should read LessWrong and Nassim Taleb, but still it's an interesting topic. 
 But overall the book is pretty bad.

If you read only one Charles Duhigg book, don't pick this one. His book The Power of Habit: Why We Do What We Do in Life and Business should be on everyone's reading list. This one -- not so much. Not that it is bad, it just compares poorly to The Power of Habit. If you are a Duhigg fan, you will still enjoy this book, just be prepared to be underwhelmed.

More like 2.5 stars. 
 Eh. This was alright. 
 I found The Power of Habit to be much more interesting and much more helpful for day to day living. I really appreciate the author's usage of anecdotes to make the subject matter interesting (something so many people seemed to NOT like), but I felt like he was really stretching with some of them. 
 All in all, I would definitely suggest The Power of Habit because I think it's a good enough primer to better understanding how and why we get into certain behavioral patterns and ways to change them. I was expecting to really hit the ground running with this book and come away with a lot of advice on how to be a lot more productive, but I only came away with a few tidbits of advice. Which is a shame. High hopes, and all. 
 I was also a little annoyed with how so many of the anecdotes meandered aimlessly. I sat there thinking, "okay, but this is important because...?" It goes back to what I said about stretching a bit too much. Give this one a pass but check out The Power of Habit.

I picked up this book because "The Power of Habit" was so good. This is a lesser effort. There are some good concepts in this book, but they really are a coherent big idea, more of eight loosely related pieces. For example, the chapter on Baysean reasoning feels out of place. Still a worthwhile book, but temper the expectations.

Read it cover to cover as the end notes had gems in them too. Though some of the subject matter covered was familiar to me (SMART goals, Lean thinking, team dynamics), Duhigg offers history on the genesis of these standard productivity tools as well as a host of new insights. His skill in weaving them together through the stories of people and organizations that have been improved through their implementation is on full display and highly enjoyable. Not to be missed is the Appendix where the author shares his own application of this productivity tool box to the writing process. If you liked The Power of Habit, you will not be disappointed by this book.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This novel takes an old , overly used idea and spruces it up a bit to make it more modern and exciting . It was fun to read about the different fey creatures and the iron knights that were so deadly to them. 
 However , to really enjoy a novel , you have to appreciate the main characters. 
 Unfortunately for me , I found Meghan and Ash insufferable. 
 Meghan is deeply in love with Ash , and that would be okay if there were any solid reasons why she would feel this way. As it stood , she obsessed over him constantly,mourned the absence of his presence for half the novel , and generally annoyed me. She strung along her poor friend Puck into believing they had a relationship even though she knew she was unsure of him , dismissing the option of treating his thoughts and feelings with care ,and thought of another man while kissing him. 
 She was constantly in tears with longing over Ash , a man who has the personality of a houseplant and is only half as charming. 
 I honestly tried very hard to understand what was so appealing about him . 
 This is what I know about him 
 1. He's the winter prince 
 2. He is mostly sullen and morose. It takes half the novel for him to even crack a smile. 
 3.He loved a girl named Ariella , who was killed ... by a scorpion monster...or something ? 
 4. Whenever he is upset he shuts down emotionally, which is JUST LOVELY. I can't count how many times he gets broody when Puck even dares to stand in Meghan's general proximity. 
 5. While Meghan is stringing Puck along , Ash is stringing along Meghan , breaking up with her and then saying things like ," You are different from any other girl I've met before BECAUSE OF REASONS , and oh yeah let's totally have a snog before I stamp your heart beneath my heels repeatedly. Honestly , did what he think those things would do except fan the flames of their relationship? 
 5. He hates Puck. It's the only time I actually feel any emotion from him , So there's that. 
 6. He has the looks of a J crew model morphed with a Greek god. I'm surprised Meghan ever gets anything done , she ogles him so much. 
 7.He has ice powers , which are never fully explained.Seriously , don't ask about them , I have no idea how they work. Does ice shoot out of his hands ? Does he have freeze breath ? I don't know , but that would be cool. 
 8. He's perfect. He literally has no flaws , and that's just boring. I'm not saying I wanted him to have a drug habit , but some character depth wouldn't have killed me. 
 9. Did I mention how pretty he is ? What am I even saying ... His eyes are so blue I'M GONNA RIOT. 
 So that's it . 
 Despite my dislike of the main characters , I did enjoy reading about Iron horse and Grimalkin. I can't believed what happened to one of them actually happened. Darn it , Julie Kagawa , don't do something like that to one of your only good characters! Oh , I also really started to love Puck. I thought he was a flat character in the first one , but in this one he shines bright. I love the way he grins viciously before going into battle and how he made me laugh several times. I hope he gets out of the unhealthy relationship he has going on with Meghan. 
 Would I recommend this series ? 
 Well , its clean , and some parts are vaguely amusing. If you like hormonal teenage girls who think they are in love , enough romantic angst to make you want to swear off dating until college , and a love triangle so generic and obvious you wonder how the author got away with selling it in print , then this is the book for you.

After Struggling to finish this one I DNFed it. :( 
 Full review to come!

The Iron Daughter is the second book in The Iron Fey series by Julie Kagawa. I absolutely loved the first book in this series so I was excited to finally get the second book and start reading it. 
 The first book ended with the defeat and death of the Iron King. So what else could go wrong? Well, it seems like that even thought the Iron King was defeated, the Iron Fey are still around and they have a new leader! Before the iron fey come back though, there is some court drama between Meghan and Mab, the Queen of the Winter court. The drama basically revolves around Winter-Summer fey drama and Meghan's feelings for Prince Ash. It is forbidden for a fey from the Winter Court to be with a fey from the Summer Court so this gives us a little tragic Romeo-Juliet esque story. 
 In this book, Meghan and the gang have to leave the fey world and make a trip to Earth. To be honest, while this was a nice break from fey world drama, I found myself skipping some parts here; namely the prom scene. 
 Really though, the fey court drama and the fight with the new foe, iron fey, are my favorite parts of this series. I don't care about Meghan's school drama. :p 
 Another interesting thing that happened in The Iron Daughter is that we learn about Puck's feelings and thus the love triangle is introduced! I have to say though, although the love triangle plot device is overused in YA literature, I think it works with the Iron Fey series. It makes sense and I do not feel like Puck's feelings are so out of place that they are completely unrealistic. They were friends for a while and he spent enough time around her to maybe develop feelings. 
 I am still not a fan of Ash and would much rather see Meghan with Puck or no one. Ash treated her like crap throughout the whole book until the end and even in the end he is not that nice and loving. He gets jealous over some guy at Meghan's high school trying to flirt with her. I just don't see the appeal in a guy who is a jerk to you then gets jealous at everything. He's not worth it, Meghan! 
 Ironhorse and Grim are still the best characters though. but I think Ironhorse needs to go to a day spa and learn to relax! He keeps yelling (ALL CAPS). 
 Over all, I loved this book and was not disappointed. The writing flows together nicely and there was no part in the book where I felt like things were dragging on so much that it made me want to put the book down. Also, the cover art is still so beautiful.

Meghan begins her stay in the Winter Court, hostage to the Unseelie Queen, Mab, and seemingly friendless, especially as Prince Ash turns cold towards her in the unforgiving environment of Tir Na Nog. 
 But The Iron Fey have not stopped their plotting just because their king is dead. A new monarch has arisen and he has sent his agents to steal the Sceptre of the Seasons, the powerful artefact passed between the courts to signify their changing power - and the changing seasons. Mab instantly accuses the Summer court and the two great courts of faerie march to war - leaving them vulnerable to the Iron fae's attack 
 Only Ash and Meghan know who truly took the sceptre - and no-one believes them. It's down to them to find the sceptre and save the fae. And the world - because while the sceptre is out of the court's hands, the weather will rage out of control. 
 I said in the review of the last book that, while I found the romance and budding love triangle annoying and fast tracked, they were properly second to the main plot and while they were a little irritating, they were ignorable. 
 Which is why, when this book started there was a moment when I nearly put the book down and refused to pick it up again. 
 They're heading to Tir Na Nog and Ash reminds Meghan that any display of fluffy emotion will mean that Mab & co will see it as weakness and promptly exploit it to the doom of them both. We even get a vast copy and paste from The Winter Passage to drive the point home. So when we get Meghan in the same room as Mab and Ash? 
 Meghan: *soulful puppy eyes at Ash* 
 Ash: uh... hide emotions... remember 
 Meghan: love me Ash! Love me! ZOMG WHY ARE YOU NOT LOVING ME!? 
 Ash:... y'know, Mab is RIGHT THERE watching us 
 Evil prince: Hey human-princess I loathe and despise - want to eat this totally innocent apple? 
 Meghan: Fairy food in fairy land offered by an obvious enemy? WHY THAT SOUNDS DELICIOUS! Clearly there can be no catch to this 
 Ash: Meghan... 
 Meghan: And IIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIII WILL ALWAYS LOOOOOOOOOOOOOVE YOU!!!!!!!!! 
 Ash: *sigh* Of course we do not love each other, that is only banned by all our laws and would get us both banished or executed *hint hint* so no, I don't love you. *icey angry eyes* 
 Meghan: ICY EYES! Zomg he hates and despises me! It was all a lie! He clearly isn't acting and he must totally mean he hates me! Oh woe is me! WOOOOOE! WOE!!!!!! 
 Later: 
 Ash: Come Meghan we must go! 
 Meghan: NO! You hate and despise me! 
 Ash: uh - secret remember? Showing emotion is weakness? We did explain all this - did you hit your head or something? 
 Meghan: NOOOO! Clearly you only pretended to be in love with me and it was all a trick to get me to Tir Na Nog! 
 Ash: Yes, that makes sense. You had no power, no magic and can't fight - I could have dragged you to Tir Na Nog by your hair if I wanted to. Why would I even bother to trick you? 
 Meghan: You did it all to mess with my head and break my heart like you do to mortal girls! 
 Ash: Yes, I went to a land that poisoned me with its very air, burned me with acid rain and nearly killed me so I could screw with some girl's head. That makes perfect sense. 
 Sadly, while Meghan's lines are a heavily paraphrased version of her position, Ash did not respond with that snark, but he really should have. From here we move to Robin telling Meghan he loves her - this would be the same Robin who has watched her since she was a baby to her current age of 16 but for some reason absolutely no-one thinks that's severely creepy. And Ash catches them in a semi-compromising position and huffs off to more angst and drama. 
 Which leaves me wondering what happened? Did someone slap a CW label on the book or something? 
 Thankfully, after Ash slopes off, the romance stops clogging the gears and we return to the same kind of story that made The Iron King such a good book. We have an excellent story with lots of action which is really well written and exciting. We have the rich world that draws heavily from a lot of research of different fae myths (and non-fae myths at that) brought together really smoothly that really draws me in. While at the same time there's that excellent balance of description - just enough to give everything its full worth, but not so much that we feel like we're being pulled on a guided tour of faerie land. Throughout the story rarely loses its sense of epic - of grand forces in balance and dire consequences awaiting failure - and I've got a soft spot for epic. 
 Read More

The fact that I kept stopping to check my facebook should of been a clue. I finally gave up about halfway through. The Iron Daughter just wasn't able to keep my attention. It almost seemed like the same story. Unseelie and the Iron fey are both after her, Puck and Ash risk themselves to save her, and none of it is very exciting. I have too many books I want to read, and no time to force myself to finish one that I don't want to read.

The Iron Daughter definitely feels like Romeo and Juliet in some ways. Girl and boy from rival groups meet at a party. They dance and fall immediately in forbidden love and passion. They manage to spend time together and begin a forbidden, star-crossed relationship. Her friends and family want him dead; his want nothing more than to see her frozen alive or killed. Of course, this doesn't happen, because the book series would have to end. 
 When the story diverges from it's star-crossed inspiration, boy leaves girl, trying not to get them both killed. Girl feels betrayed even though he warned her eighty-five bajillion times what was going to happen. Girl decides to lead on/flirt with her best male friend who is in love with her too. She does this while continuing to want nothing more than forbidden boy. Seriously? This story is supposed to be really romantic, but how can I want this obnoxious girl to end up with any of these guys (except maybe the jackass from her high school who she still finds attractive) when she clearly will go with whoever happens to be there at any given moment? This little side plot is just what was needed to make the whole forbidden love angle even better. 
 Meghan has not improved much as a main character, mostly for the reason above. She continues to save herself and others sometimes, which is nice, but she generally expects the menfolk to save her, which is less nice. The other really frustrating thing about her is that she continues to be an airhead. So-called plot twists are obvious, but she never sees them coming (i.e. Ash being all ice prince-y to her in front of his mom). Smaller things baffle her as well. For example, she tries on a dress that has just been finished for her to wear to a prom-like event (at her high school that she no longer really attends) and observes that "it fit perfectly, sliding over my skin as if made for me." Umm, yeah, hon, that's because they made it for you! Also, don't get me started on the whole the-only-way-to-heal-the-faery-prince's-injuries-is-to-go-to-a-school-dance-thing.

I enjoyed this sequel to The Iron King and I found the development of the Iron Fey to be particularly interesting and well handled. 
 On the other hand, Meghan's character continued to annoy me - I found many of her responses to be predictable, despite the obviousness of her situation and her emotions trite. I do like it when the center of the love triangle is at least interesting enough to hold the attention of the boys in question and Meghan, like many of her predecessors, does not strike me as convincingly appealing to capture the hearts of those who love her. 
 Is it too much to ask for both good story and good characterization? Does it have to be one or the other?

I really enjoyed this book. I am definitely liking the whole series, and each book just gets better. Meghan is growing into her own, and doing a really good job of overcoming seemingly insurmountable odds. 
 We get to see more of Faery, Queen Mab, King Oberon, Puck, Ash, Rowan, Sage, Grimalkin, Ironhorse and all the rest of the characters in this story that just wouldn't be the same without them. 
 Leanansidhe is probably one of my most favorite characters, with all her "darling" and "pet" talk - it just cracks me up. Even though she seems formidable and dangerous at first, I can tell she is really a great person to have in your corner if you are lucky enough to befriend her. 
 I really like how Kagawa explains and shows all the differences of Winter vs Summer and why Ash & Meghan shouldn't be together. It has a very star-crossed lovers feel, like Romeo and Juliet. 
 This series is great and keeps getting better!

Meghan is back at the winter court....the court of her enemies or at least her not so friendly neighbors, the courts are in times of uneasy peace but peace all the same. She is a "guest" so no Calvary can arrive to save her from winter's wrath. 
 She is in over her head and despite her caution things don't go as planned for her she finds her self in hotter water every time she opens her mouth like the simple sixteen year old we met at the beginning of the series though she has learnt some it's not enough. 
 it's not long before the courts are at war for all the wrong reasons, she is whisked away by ash but he's just taking her home, which set's off the typical "omg i will die without him" reactions teen books are famous for but despite that this is a decent story on how they have so much more to deal with now that there's a new kind of fey in town. 
 With the ever changing world she's been thrown into, she must now save the courts from waring, while being hunted down for treason and stealing the youngest prince and killing the oldest. 
 They finds they have a common enemy and must work together though they are supposed to be sworn enemies, to defeat a new threat that may just destroy everything for all fey 
 my little annoyance: her constant whining, crying and becoming a puddle over ash. I know ya books are this way a lot but doesn't make it any easier to deal with when it's a constant through out the book. 
 I feel kinda bad for puck i mean he puts his heart on the line and she acts like it's nothing...harsh 
 I think that the whole L bomb going off all over the place was a little soon but i understand the need to establish more than interest from a writing perspective, and the end result was super she could have ended the series there and though i would have been sad to see it end i would have been happy for the turn of events in some sense and sad in others. 
 i love the boys in this book series even the cat, the dynamics between ash and puck. They hate each other only sometimes but they want to kill each other the rest of the time and i am sure this isn't about to get any better considering the plot bombs going off in this installment. i think the below quote sums them up perfectly. 
 "those two they are either the best of friends or the worst of enemies which i can't tell" 
 a few more quotes i like: 
 "So, we're at war. Perfect. Shall we save time and kill each other now, or did you want to wait until later?" 
 -Puck" 
 "Wow, icy reception here. And to think I came back from the dead for this." - Puck" 
 "From the moment you stepped into the nevernever, you've been my undoing. I should never have agreed to that contract." 
 -Ash" 
 "I could have taken a nap instead of waiting for you to finally show up. What took you so long human? Did you walk?" 
 -Grimalkin" 
 A solid story despite all the whiny annoying girly behavior from our dear Meghan but i will cut her some slack cause she's only 16 and she's not been around many boys, much less hot boys from another realm. The other little bombs lead you to believe where the story will go but i guess i will have to read the next one and see if i am right.

She almost reminds me a an Anita Blake type characters, she's also short and excoticlly pretty.Her job is a FBI behavior analyst and profiler. 1st TO DIE REVIEW 
 BOOK: 1ST TO DIE (WOMEN'S MURDER CLUB)

 I have to admit this was not my first time reading this series (I stopped reading it around 8th or 9th, maybe 10th) but I seemed to enjoy it more the first time around then I did this time. It might be because it was the first mystery novels outside Nancy Drew and the Hardy Boys I read but it left an impression on me and I decided to reread it when I saw it at the library to borrow. 
 Again I read this years ago but I barely remembered anything except for the characters: Lindsey a bad-ass Homicide Cop, Claire a funny and witty Medical Examiner, Cindy a resourceful and stubborn, and Jill a hard-ass prosecutor. Together they work to solve the case of the Honeymoon killer. 
 It may be because I subconsciously remembered the plot as I went along but it was an easy-to-see through mystery with barely any twists and turns to keep me on the edge of my seat in anticipation. 
 What I liked: the characters- they were funny resourceful and skilled, including Sweet Martha. 
 What I did not like: the mystery needed a little work and the romance part seemed a bit force.

sample_reviews.review_text: Fanfic, this book is pure 100% fanfiction. And not even GOOD fanfiction which is why I loved it so much. It was just enough to keep me reading (I love reading bad fanfic) and just good enough to keep me loving it. I've always been a sucker for Harry/Draco stories and this just led right into it. I'd kill to know what fandom name Rainbow Rowell wrote under, because there is no way she wasn't one of us!

I'd give this a 2.5-3 It was...ok....I'm just disappointed. 
 I really wanted to like this book because it has so many things I normally enjoy. Vampires, Wizards, romance & LGBT romance to boot. The book starts off strange like I picked it up in the middle of a series and I am supposed to really care about these characters already. I spent the whole book telling myself to care about these characters but it just felt forced. I think maybe if this was the 3rd book in a series and there was some kind of build up and back story I might care...or not. As it was all these characters felt as empty as a bag of potato chips. 
 I struggled to get past the heavy Harry Potter influence and had trouble not seeing these characters as Harry Potter characters. I think I started thinking of them as Harry Potter characters to help me get through the book easier. 
 On the topic of the romance let me start by saying I am a romance sap, I love romance in books, movies, TV even ultra sappy romance. The romance in this book felt so ???? unfounded and forced like it felt like it was just a romance to have 2 hot guys make out woohoo!!! I feel like I might of bought the romance if there was more build up to it but there wasn't. One day Simon wants to murder Baz for going after "his girl" then the next minute it's like oh hey they are kissing & now they are in love ok yeah that makes sense. 
 The characters really needed more fleshing out. Simon is total boring jerk with like no redeeming qualities. However to be fair to Simon there was no connection for me to any of the characters, at all. They were all just so boring. This book just came off as flat which is a shame because it had so much potential to be a book I could totally love. I managed to get through it fairly easily and quickly which was nice. It wasn't the worst book I've ever read but it wasn't good. It was just ok. 
 P.S. I'm thinking about it more & did this book have a plot? like did it? Where was the plot??? Who fucking knows!! the plot was was a mess. I've read better one shot fanfictions than this entire book. That was mean I'm sorry but it's true!! 
 P.P.S All of this is really a shame because I really enjoy Rainbow's books and I think she is a good writer this just wasn't what I was expecting.

Again, like Fangirl, I just don't see it. This one was overhyped and was too overhyped by booktuber katytastic. It was interesting enough for me to power through it (the harry potter x fanfic similarities we're gripping) but it just didn't wow or intrigue me at all.

** spoiler alert ** 
 What happened to Rainbow Rowell? Don't get me wrong the story was cute and I got heart warming moments, but what happened to that thing that made her books so damn amazing?! No I'm not bothered by the gay thing or the cheese spells or the weird world that is a copy of Harry Potter and Vampire Academy. Honestly this book read more like Carth's fanfiction than a Rainbow Rowell book. Where was the depth in the characters? Where were the unique moments that made her book so heart warming? Where was the author that wrote Fangirl and Eleanor and Park? This characters are flat and boring and, my god, could they be any more corny? Disappointed in this book. Maybe Rainbow Rowell should stick to real life fiction.

There are a handful of reasons why I did not enjoy this book: 
 1. I read it as I was rereading Half-Blood Prince and it helped highlight what a pale imitation of the world created by J. K. Rowling this is. 
 2. Having just finished Jodi Picoult's Small Great Things, the idea of creating a superior being--which I compared to race--made me uncomfortable. 
 3. I did not appreciate being parachuted onto the end of a saga. 
 4. I read other things to escape, but I look for substance in my YA and I found it lacking. 
 5. It was not good writing.
Did not like it at all. I did finish hoping something original would happen. It reminded me of Eregon where the author cherry picked from other books.

Carry On is a Harry Potter-style spin off. It's an expansion of the book series first referenced in Rowell's novel about fanfiction, Fangirl. It's basically, give or take a lot of worldbuilding and character development, a Harry/Draco Seventh Year fic. This is a very similar concept to A HERO AT THE END OF THE WORLD, which was one of my favourite books of last year. I personally enjoyed that more, but this was a very fun read. 
 It picked up a lot of speed near the end - the start had a little too much info-dumping for my taste. I did come to love Simon and Baz by the end, and found Baz's candidness about his sexuality particularly refreshing for a fantasy novel ("Are you gay?" "Completely."). His queerness is a huge part of his self expression in a way that's never usually seen in fantasy and science fiction. 
 In fact, Simon and Baz are a brilliant pairing, above and beyond the Harry Potter connection. It's a very long book, but I flew through it, and would happily read more about this world. Penelope in particular was a really great character, and I want to read a sequel about her and Micah. 
 Huge kudos for Rainbow Rowell for writing and publishing a straight up Harry/Draco fic though (life goals right there.)

After reading and loving Fangirl, this book was everything I wanted it to be. The story of Simon Snow was fun and snarky with characters who acted and spoke like real teenagers (with the addition of magic).

This book was so much fun !!! I will definetely read it again someday. 
 The only thing is... I was a bit surprised by some of the elements at the end, more than any other Rainbow Rowel's books. The last few pages reminded me that it's supposed to be a fanfiction, which I had completely forgotten

 You know, I normally don't read books that has a same sex relationship as a lead -- (nothing personally against the LBGT+ community, the thing is.... I just don't care *shrugs*)-- but I decide to give this a try, and I've also read other books that have the same theme, but it's a no go.

It was like I knew more about everyone else in the story than I did about her. Not very impressed and I won't be reading the rest in the series.

I thoroughly enjoyed Kerstin Gier's Ruby Red, so I was excited about reading another of her books. This story was similar in that the main character travels outside of her reality. In this story, however, Olivia is able to enter other people's dreams. At first, she thinks she is just having imaginative dreams but soon realizes that there is something must more sinister at work.

The dog was snuffling at my bag. 
 Liv and her sister have moved around a lot with their professor mother. Their latest move takes them to London, where there are several surprises waiting for them. The move has also caused Liv to begin having strangely vivid dreams, including one about four boys from her school engaged in a strange ritual in a graveyard at night. What is even more worrisome is that the boys know what happened in the dream. What is dream and what is real? And more importantly, what is the purpose of the ritual the boys were performing in the graveyard? 
 I really enjoyed the Ruby Red series by this author and hoped to enjoy this one as well. I did like it but felt, much like other firsts in a series, that it was just a super-long prologue. I also felt the 11th hour solving of the mystery came out of left field and just did not flow well with the rest of the narrative. With that being said, I did find the characters in the book to be fascinating and cannot wait to see what happens next. Gier does a great job giving each character unique features and making them feel real and relatable. The story was unique in the world of paranormal romance and I will be interested to see where things go from here. 
 I recommend this to those who are fans of Gier and those who are looking for something new and unique.

I was excited to read this book too.

Blah. I did end up really liking this, but I had some issues! I was very disappointed with how Easton's mental illness and past were dealt with. OCD is SERIOUS and is not a fucking cute quirk that makes characters more interesting. This seems to happen especially for OCD in books, and it needs to stop being a thing. It should not have been treated so lightly, and this book needed to stay away from the 'love cures all' message, because that's not how it works. ALSO Tyler's arrogance and ~alpha maleness~ was not endearing to me, but I did end up liking him, though I still think his character was underdeveloped. But I LOVED Easton, even if she pissed me off a few times. She felt very real to me, with her insecurities and her cold shoulder, and with her need for control in her life. It all ties into her past, and it's something that she ends up being able to balance by the end (BUT that still felt way too believable and perfect, this girl needed some goddamn therapy, not a magic dick). Anyway! Pretty much one major gripe, but other than that, I enjoyed the second half way more than the first. And I'm happy with how the forbidden romance storyline went. Low on drama, high on maturity. Very much liked that! It was handled much smoother than I would have expected in a Penelope Douglas book. And omg Christian was awesome. I liked this one okay - but there were many things that bothered me that kept me from loving. 
 I recant that statement because the more I think about this book, the angrier I get. 
 ***** Full Review ***** 
 My thoughts 
 First thought after finishing 
 *Tosses kindle.* 
 Misconduct came highly recommend to me from one of my blogger friends - here's lookin at you Kim- and just the taboo aspect alone had me adding this to my TBR. I was beyond excited when it popped up on my kindle as a Christmas gift. (Thanks, Jess!) Sadly, as much as I was hoping to love this one, I just could not. The more I think about it, the angrier and more annoyed I get. 
 Honestly, the taboo aspect was by far the only part of Misconduct I really liked. There was a 12 year age different between the two characters and Easton was one of Christian's teachers, which happened to be Tyler's son. It adds an extra oomph to the story and makes all the scenes hotter. 
 And some scenes, were hot. 
 Easton was a hard character to like at times. She is smart, witty and I understand and related to her insecurities and need for control. But I felt like her brazenness was an act, and I could never take it, or her, seriously. Granted, I understand the need to keep people are arms length but... I don't know. I didn't buy it.. As for Tyler, well. 
 Straight to the point - he was a dick. I am this close *pinches thump and forefinger* to stating I hated him. I KNOW he is trying to redeem himself when it comes to the mistakes he made with his son, but again, didn't buy it. The alpha male persona was a major turn off. There was one scene in particular that had me raging They were having sex she kept saying, "please stop" or "we can't." Her body may have wanted it but never the less, he should have stopped and he didn't. It angered me so much I saw red. Could it have been part of their game? Absolutely. But just, no. 
 I also really, really disliked the sheer lack of seriousness with regards to her OCD. It was mocked throughout the entire book and coming from someone who has an up close and personal relationship with it, it was insulting. This isn't a curable condition, and it's especially not curable with a fucking dick. Yes, one can feel safe by being around another, but those "little quirks" do NOT go away. 
 The resolution was sub par, and convenient, I might add. The little added "mystery" part to the story line was in my opinion, ridiculous and not needed in the slightest, especially because again, convenient. This whole book felt under developed. And fucking mocking. 
 Will I read more from Ms. Douglas? I can't answer that. But I know for sure Misconduct is a very difficult one for me to recommend at this point.

Original Review @ Naomi's Reading Palace 
 I snapped up The Deal for just 99c, but I swear I've been eager to read it for twelve months or more, and now I'm kicking myself that I didn't do so sooner, because it was just what I needed. A New Adult read, with broken characters, who are fiery and passionate, with a good amount of humour entwined throughout. 
 Hannah... I loved her from the beginning. I knew what happened to her immediately, but all the details aren't disclosed until later in the book. She grew a lot throughout this story and was able to face her fears and found someone to open up to. I liked how she was strong enough to keep rejecting Garrett in regards to tutoring him. But, like any guy who wants something bad enough, he chases after it. 
 Garrett appeared to be a cocky guy in the beginning, but he soon won my heart over! I could see that he was struggling with his work, but he was a smart guy too. He was almost stalking Hannah, which I thought was hilarious! He doesn't have a filter and says exactly what he was thinking. 
 These two were fantastic together. They seem to be from different worlds, but due to issues outside their control, they find a deep connection. They were strong, passionate and hot together. I loved meeting Garrett's friends too - Logan, Tucker and Dean - they are all close and play ice hockey together. 
 This was the first book in the series, and I'm eager to jump into the next book. Elle has found an instant fan in me, with her alternating perspectives and easy writing style. The characters feel real and I love the world of hockey!

Oh man, the title makes me mad. It's like the author attempted to write a cosy mystery/ romance novel but thought by adding in Jane Austen's name a few times, she could market it as some sort of tribute. The protag goes on a vacation to a place which is never properly explained, where people sort of act like it's the 1800s, and a romance may or may not have been set up for her. Unfortunately, this setting feels nothing like "Austenland", provides no insight into Austen's work and fails to impact in any way. The romance is one of those one's where the characters' declarations of love, though completely predictable, are almost unexpected because absolutely nothing romantic has happened.

This is a girl book. And its fantastic. 
 Its simple, which I like. Its about a girl whose been unlucky in love, recently divorced. She heads to Austenland to find herself and learn to feel again. 
 Its got all the silly things we love about Austen--corsets, elaborate dinners, turns around the room and around the park, gentility, manners, and--of course--a fantastic ball ending with a declaration of love. 
 And its super clever--mimicing the satirical style of Northanger Abbey with a few twists of its own. 
 What I like most about this books is the main character--Charlotte. Charlotte travels to Austenland to release the difficulties of divorce and teenager children for a short time. What makes her stick out to me is that she does everything for her kids. And she wants to move on with her life. She wants to feel again. 
 In this story, Charlotte initially thinks she has done something wrong or that she is not worth it. That's the reason for divorce. But as she continues through her Austenland experience, she discovers that she has control of her life and her out look. She is a strong and dedicated woman. 
 She even gets the handsome gentry gentleman at the end.

This was an easy read but it was engaging, heartwarming, funny, and tragic. This was my first time reading John Green so I wasn't sure what to expect, but it was well done!
A very highly rated and publicised work. This a YA and I don't love YA much. But a good read. A must read if you are in YA genre.
Full of truths, the way only John Green can write. But writing about cancer is tricky, and by the end I found it a little too sentimental. Still a good book.

Once again, I've tried to read it. First time, I made it to about page seven. I didn't even get to the bit on America's Next Top Model. This time, I made it to page nineteen. See, I made progress? To me, from what I read of the book so far and what friends have gushed about to me, Green writes perfect prose -- and he does, the quotes I've read from this book are amazing -- and his characters are teenagers. Teenagers that don't exist. I know that these guys speak and think differently than I do because they had cancer, but I still grew up with teens. Not even the ones who read Green speak like his characters do.

After all the hype, I expected more. I was not impressed by this book. A bit too "teen" for me. I've read books like this before that are better. Yes, it was sad in the end, but it's like everything was okay in it's separate parts and didn't quite come together.

This is the first book by John green I've ever read. I was hesitant to read it because I try to stay away from hyped books and best sellers, and also because I knew it was YA and its not really my genre. However I enjoyed this book. It is fast paced, easy to read, funny and sad, and very complete. I liked the characters, they were very real and relatable. But the thing I enjoyed most in this book was the approach of cancer and death and life. It does not turn the characters into victims, it does not make you feel sorry or pity any of the characters. It celebrates life and the message of living the life you are dealt comes across very strongly. 
 It's pretty deep for a YA book. And although I did find the whole romance thing a bit cheesy, It made me be very grateful for being healthy and alive, and also I think that people who have struggled or are currently fighting cancer would appreciate it, I people treated them like regular people, and see far beyond their illness, because cancer does not define you. 
 I recommend it widely and I'm also curious to read more of this author.

book_a.user_review: Too deep for me. Colorful at times. Often vulgar. Some good weed smoked by all the critics who raved.

sample_reviews.review_text:
...because it was onced banned. 
 Unfortunately banning this book only fueled interest and in a sense landed Tropic of Cancer as a masterpiece. Upon reading this exhausting story it is anything but a masterpiece. 
 Tropic of Cancer is basically the meandering thoughts of a tortured soul, oversexed, often poor and homeless man (Henry Miller) who fancies himself as a writer. He often shares company with not only various prostitutes, but other men who are in the field of the arts and who dole out money to support him in his time of need - or habit, which is quite often. Henry Miller as the author uses vulger and obscene language which at first I was startled by but after a while I realized that it was his way of writing without editing and using words that you don't normally see. Basically shock value. However, shock value has no value in my opinion. 
 "I have made a silent compact with myself not to change a line of what I write. I am not interested in perfecting my thoughts, nor my actions." 
 "...Now we shall have a vessel in which to pour the vital fluid, a bomb which, when we throw it, will set off the world. We shall put into it enough to give the writers of tomorrow their plots, their dramas, their poems, their myths, their sciences. The world will be able to feed on it for a thousand years to come. It is colossal in its pretentiousness." 
 Give me a break! Henry Miller comes across as such an ass that the one word that he uses quite liberally is really what I think of him. He has such a blantant disregard for women that not only can he not live without them and sex for hire, but upon looking at the female anatomy he ponders life and the "cancer" that is eating at our society. WOW - that's deep?! (no pun intended) However, Henry Miller has a chance to change his life and "start over" but just can't give up women and his cunning ways.
Meh. I was expecting an exotic masterpiece but found the ramblings of a dickhead.

Okay I finally finished this sucker. Although sprinkled with patches of brilliant writing I considered abandoning this random string of thoughts about a hundred times. Although the patches in a quilt can be bright and beautiful the value of the quilt is in the pattern in which these random patches are sewn together. I'm not sure if my one star rating is due to the fact that I thought the content of this book was pure crapola or if it is a result of the dark funk I was left in after meeting these low life characters so brilliantly defined. If you're going to read this pile of fly puke despite my warning you can at least look forward to learning about the apple trick and catch a glimpse of what it might have been like to be and "be with" Marilyn Monroe. book_b.title: The Secret Speech (Leo Demidov, #2)
book_b.user_review: Good. But nowhere near as good as Smith's first one.

sample_reviews.review_text: This started out really well, but the end was just confusing and really felt like it should have been some other book.

I read Smith's first book, Child 44, and fell in love with it. The book was gripping and kept me wanting more. I felt that Secret Speech lacked some of the luster that 44 had. This is a follow up to Child 44, with Leo Demidov as the main character. The book picks three years after Child 44 and Leo is running the state homicide division. Through a sequence of events, Leo is thrust into the horrors both he and his country perpetrated under the rule of Stalin. 
 Speech was a bit slow. I found some of the parts really engaging, while others left me flat. I found that this was almost three different stories, that converged together into one book. When one finished, I was satisfied with the climax, but then the book seemed to start over, which detracted from the read. 
 Overall it's a good read.

My interest in this book rapidly plummeted down, down, down. 
 I was intrigued by the creation of Moscow's first homicide department with former-MGB Agent Leo Demidov at the helm, since the Soviet State officially considered murder to be a product confined to the decadent and capitalist West. The homicide department -controlled by the militia - was to be kept secret from the Russian people and investigations could not be openly pursued. 
 What a rich and unique set-up, a Moscow police procedural in post-Stalinist USSR! 
 I wanted to be a fly on the wall as Demidov created from scratch a department that did not officially exist! 
 I wanted a "First 48" look into the details of a murder investigation, Soviet-style! 
 But, no. 
 Unfortunately for me, the book I wanted to read is not the book that Smith wrote. It quickly devolved into a frenzied and completely unbelievable revenge fantasy. 
 I couldn't read another page.
the better of his two books in my opinion
I'm really happy with this series. It's messed up and terrifying; and the hero is no one's hero. All the suffering makes it real - and no one is spared.

A good novel 
 but not as good as "child 44"
Excruciating.
The book is a mess. All the stylistic flaws from Child 44 writ large, but this time with a boring, incoherent plot that mistakes contortion and coincidence for cleverness.

I truly enjoyed Tom Robb Smith's Child 44 and have no idea why it took me so long to read the second in Smith's Leo Demidov series, but I am glad I did. The Secret Speech is fast-paced, full of intrigue and I personally enjoy reading about the former Soviet Union. I would definitely recommend The Secret Speech, but I do suggest reading Child 44 first.

The sequel to Child 44, a mystery set in Soviet Russia. Except The Secret Speech isn't a mystery: it's a thriller, and not a particularly good one. Smith should have stuck with mysteries, because he just isn't good enough at maintaining suspense or interest to write, you know, SUSPENSE. 
 Recommended for: Skip it.

The first book in the series was amazing, the second was good but seemed a bit like a repeat in many ways, but without the arena atmosphere and game element of the Hunger Games, I thought that Mockingjay buckled under the war story. I also thought that a large portion of this book suffered from Collins telling us what was happening with blocks of text of Katniss summarizing for the reader instead of letting us observe the story take place.

book_a.user_review:

Went to Shteyngart's reading/signing and it was hilarious! He's a bit like a stand-up comic looking for an audience, so he trolls bookstores. I'm going to read this on vacation next week. 
 ______________ 
 I'm baaack. I'm also terrified of giving this book 3-stars. After reading the scathing reviews here on Goodreads, it appears all the cool kids hate this book. Fine. I've only ever been the opposite of cool. And that's hot. 
 Here's the thing: I don't think Shteyngart's witty, super fast, referential humor comes across in written form very well. Like I said above, the book reading had the whole audience in stitches. Not just the banter introduction, or even his self-deprecating way he'd answer all the lame questions he must get at every reading ("What's your typical work day like?"). The reading itself - you know, the actual words in the printed book - was really, really funny. He did voices, he had comedic timing, it all made sense. So I was reading Lenny Abramov's diaries in Steyngart's voice, and it was pretty funny. In parts. 
 It just wasn't anywhere near as funny as when he read the book out loud. 
 Also, I got the strong impression that as a minimum, the target audience for this book should be well acquainted with New York City. More appropriately, the designated reader should belong to one of the immigrant classes described in the book. I don't think I was part of the target audience, and just like when I watch Seinfeld, I miss a huge part of the joke. Not unlike this philosophy class I took in college where the prof would make a Yiddish joke every 15 minutes, and a huge question mark would appear above my blonde shiksa head. 
 Nonetheless, I thought the characters were interesting and fleshed-out. They certainly weren't like characters I've encountered before, so that was new. The future Shteyngart paints is impressionistic and not particularly believable, which is a shame. The story was silly, but it kept me entertained. I don't know about it being Super or True, but I'll grant that it's a Sad Love Story. And... that's why I gave it 3 stars. 
 I'll never get into the cool kid clique now, will I?

My first abandon from the Tournament of Books lineup. I've seen others say it's a slow starter, but MAN I hated this book. HATED. "Comic" novel? WTF? Not funny. Not even a tiny bit. 
 The final straw was when I found myself reading my alumni newsletter obituaries to avoid this book. Back to the library it went. 
 I think a fellow TofB reader summed up Shteyngart well (although he was talking about Absurdistan, which is now crossed off the to-read list): "a pretentious, unfunny mess." 
 Thank goodness it lost. I would have had to ban The Morning News from my feed reader. http://themorningnews.org/tob/

But, since being in a book club -- at least for me -- is all about going outside of your reading comfort zone and forcing yourself to try new things, I tried it. I read the first two pages and put it down. Having felt like that was not giving it enough of a chance, I tried a few more times to read it. Each time I was able to muddle through a few pages.  I need to stick to a 100 page rule or something, there's so many books I really want to read that I shouldn't just be sticking with a book I'm not enjoying.

I will steal a term I read in another review here on goodreads to sum up what I think of this book: pretentious fuckery. 
 That is all.

I genuinely don't know how to quantify my feelings on this book. I didn't dislike it, but i didn't love it, so I'm putting my star rating squarely in the middle. It took me a long time to get into it, due in part to the wannabe Blade Runner cyber/consumer punk jargon, but mostly due to the obsessive sexualization of race and youth. Towards the middle I began to find myself invested in the relationship, but the point which broke it for me is when Eunice cries about how she can't shop online. I realize we live in a society based around conspicuous consumption, but the blithe references to massive conglomerations like BarnesNobleTimeWarnerMcDonalds (made up) actually served to diminish the effect of the potential future economic collapse. But in the end, it was both entertaining and funny, and maybe could have been excellent if it dialed things back just a tad.

I'm sorry, but I just don't get it. I know this book has been picked for nearly every critic's "Best of 2010" list, but I think it's been way overpraised. This is a satire about a technology-obsessed world in which people rarely "verbal" with each other, books are no longer read, and real human connections are a thing of the past. The two main characters are Lenny, a Russian Jew who can't get past his Mommy and Daddy issues, and Eunice, an unlikable, self-hating Korean with Mommy and Daddy issues. It really doesn't progress much beyond that, and I primarily finished the book in the hopes of finally figuring out what everyone is raving about. Maybe I'm not "literary" enough for this, and the themes and metaphors and DEEPER MEANINGS blah blah blah are going over my head, but I'd rather read a book I enjoy any day over this pretentious, highfalutin crap.

I tried, I really did. I wanted to love this book, I thought the plot sounded wonderful! I just could not get into it. I didn't really care about any of the characters to want to read to the end to find out what happens. I did enjoy the descriptions of the places.

Again, I judged a book by its cover. I thought the cover was pretty cool (stupid me) so I picked it up. Ugh! I am on page 37 and I can't take it anymore. Seriously, it is so boring. We have twin sisters who love each other but who have not seen each other in twenty something years, are not talking because of something bad in the past AND are separated by an ocean. Then there is the OCD neighbor, the wife of the OCD neighbor who left him, a man who suffers the loss of one of the twins and who works as a tour guide at a cemetery, and two young mirror-twins who are just plain odd. What girls in their twenties watch back-to-back episodes of This old House every Saturday? Whew, I am bored just typing that out. 
 Book, back you go to the store. Be gone I say. In your place I shall get another book, one I will hopefully love more than you!

I was so looking forward to this book. It looked spooky and scary...about cemeteries and ghosts...things I normally do not enjoy reading about as I am a HUGE chicken and get creeped out very easily... that said it still looked like a good read. Throw in the fact that it arrived in the mail as a surprise from my husband...even better. 
 The book starts out fantastic...let's start with the title (I love William Blake), the sad death of the aunt with a mysterious background, the setting in London near spooky Highgate Cemetery, the inheritance of the strange twins. I nestled right down for a good read. But then things took a turn...and not for the better. 
 Unlike Dan Brown, Niffenegger's writing is wonderful...her prose elegant and beautiful. On the other hand, like Brown, her plot is mysterious and intriguing and unfortunately like Dan Brown her ending was a letdown...wait...let me take it a step further. It was laughable. The last third of the book had me rolling my eyes and saying "You've GOT to be kidding me!!" By the ending I was saying "What the @#$%?" Not to give anything away but crows people? Then I was left saying "ridiculous". 
 This "twisty tale" turns out to be another instance of a book that started out great and then by the end it felt like the author had no idea how to end this crazy tale or redeem any of it's unlikeable and dull characters. You are left with more questions than answers...the history of Elsbeth and Edie for one. I feel like this tale could have gone in many other more interesting directions and I wish that it did so because there was a much more interesting tale that could have been told. 
 Things I liked...writing style, setting, Martin (the one character worth rooting for), and Highgate Cemetery. 
 My rating: A BIG disappointment.

reference_books.title: Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion
reference_books.review_text:
Robert Chaildini "Psikhologiia vliianiia" 
 Etu knigu mne posovetoval kandidat na odnu iz IT vakansii, za chto ia iskrenne priznatel'na emu. 
 Ee dolzhen prochitat' kazhdyi. Ne kazhdyi psikholog, ili kazhdyi HR, ili kazhdyi prodavets, a voobshche kazhdyi chelovek. Vse my v uskoriaiushchemsia mire ekonomim sily na analiz situatsii i priniatie reshenii, dovodia mnogie resheniia do avtomatizma. Kniga imenno o takikh situatsiiakh, kogda "shchelk, zazhuzhzhalo", i o tom, v chem ikh pol'za, a v chem vred. 
 Edinstvennoe, s chem ia ne sovsem soglasna v etoi knige - eto nazvanie. Chitaia na oblozhke "Psikhologiia vliianiia" ozhidaesh', chto kniga - sbornik "retseptov" vliianiia na liudei, rukovodstvo k deistviiu dlia tekh, kogo Chaildini nazyvaet "professionaly ustupchivosti" (torgovtsy, reklamshchiki, peregovorshchiki, etc). Na samom dele kniga khot' i soderzhit real'nye tekhniki, ona v bol'shei stepeni o tom, kak rabotaet nash mozg v rezhime "avtopilot", i o tom, kak raspoznat' i zashchitit'sia ot nasil'stvennogo vliianiia drugikh na nashi avtomaticheskie skhemy. Vse tekhniki, opisannye Chaildini, pomogut izbezhat' nepriiatnykh situatsii tipa "ia-sam-ne-ponial-kak-soglasilsia", pochti vse pomogut ne potratit' lishnie den'gi, a nekotorye dazhe mogut spasti Vam zhizn' (bez preuvelichenii!). 
 Studentam-psikhologam kniga ponravitsia eshche i detal'nym opisaniem psikhologicheskikh eksperimentov, kotorymi Chaildini podtverzhdaet kazhdoe svoe zaiavlenie. Ser'eznaia, nauchnaia kniga v luchshikh traditsiiakh eksperimental'noi psikhologii, kotoruiu, tem ne menee, ochen' interesno chitat'.

reference_books.title: The English Patient
reference_books.review_text:
Moei osnovnoi oshibkoi bylo vziat' etu knigu v otpusk. Ona daleko ne legkoe i priiatnoe chtivo. I sovershenno neodnorodnaia. Menia periodicheski zatiagival siuzhet i bylo liubopytno, chto budet dal'she, no v osnovnom ia probiralas' skvoz' stranitsy kak cherez pustyniu, tiazhelo i o-o-ochen' medlenno. Istoriia liubvi Patsienta tak sil'no kontrastirovala s izmuchennoi voinoi Italiei i iskalechennymi dushami obitatelei villy, chto poslednie kazalis' eshche grustnee i pechal'nee. 
 Kniga pravil'naia, khoroshaia, napisannaia krasivym iazykom, no dlia menia okazalas' chereschur tiazheloi. Potomu rekomenduiu chitat' kholodnymi zimnimi vecherami i v periody zhalosti k samoi sebe, kategoricheski ne rekomenduiu kak knigu v otpusk. 
 Odnoimenny fil'm eshche ne videla. Posmotriu, dopolniu otzyv.

reference_books.title: The Curious Case of Benjamin Button
reference_books.review_text:
Prekrasnaia malen'kaia povest' (ili dlinnyi rasskaz). Sovershenno otlichnaia po siuzhetu ot odnoimennogo fil'ma. Obshchego tol'ko imia geroia i to, chto on rodilsia starym i molodel s kazhdym godom zhizni, vse ostal'noe sovershenno po-drugomu. Chitaetsia na odnom dykhanii. Chitat' stoit khotia by radi prekrasnogo ironichnogo stilia povestvovaniia: 
 "Oni vpervye reshilis' otdat' dan' ocharovatel'noi staroi traditsii -- obzavestis' rebenkom, i mister Batton, vpolne estestvenno, nervnichal. On nadeialsia, chto roditsia mal'chik i on smozhet opredelit' ego v iel'skii kolledzh, shtat Konnektikut, gde sam mister Batton tselykh chetyre goda byl izvesten pod nedvusmyslennym prozvishchem <<Petukh>>".

Kha! Pervye stranits 30 ia plevalas' ot chereschur primitivnogo (v sravnenii so Shcheglom) iazyka, potom vtianulas', v itoge ne smogla otlozhit' na noch', rydala v kontse i do trekh nochi ne mogla usnut', obdumyvaia prochitannoe. 
 Khotite uznat' mnogo o zhizni invalidov i evtanazii - vam siuda! Chik-lit s kheppi-endom na drugoi polke.

book_b.title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
book_b.user_review:
Odna iz nemnogikh knig, kotoruiu ia brosila, ne dochitav i poloviny. Odna iz nemnogikh knig, o kotoroi nichego khoroshego i skazat' ne mogu. Vozmozhno, delo v tom, chto moi ozhidaniia byli zavysheny, ved' sobiralas' chitat' ee let piat', esli ne bol'she. Vozmozhno delo ne v knige, a v moei otvratitel'noi pamiati na imena. A tut - tol'ko nachinaesh' otlichat' geroia po imeni, on ischezaet ili poiavliaetsia drugoi s takim zhe imenem ili s pokhozhim, i nikakoi sily voli ne khvataet, chtoby probrat'sia cherez takoe kolichestvo odnoimennykh rodstvennikov. 
 Ponravilis' tol'ko otdel'nye personazhi, kak propisany ikh kharaktery. Neskol'ko liubopytnykh istorii bylo opisano. Chem bol'she pishu ob etoi knige, tem bol'she prikhozhu k vyvodu, chto otsenila by ee v vide otdel'nykh rasskazov.

reference_books.title: The Hunger Games (The Hunger Games, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I'm so glad that I stopped listening to this book after 7 chapters and just picked it up and read it. It was so much more engrossing when I was actually reading it. I also get the hype. Like many others have said it's very well-written, perfectly-paced, and has lovable, believable characters. 
 There is only one thing I didn't like. This book stinks of Bella in the main character's tendency to be self-deprecating. She goes on for more than 100 pages thinking that Peeta couldn't possibly actually "like" her. In the beginning it's understandable, but after a time it just gets old and it makes me dislike her. Of course, her naivety is Collins' invention, and hence, her fault. As someone who works with 11-14 year old girls on a regular basis, I just wish that some of the good (or popular) YA fiction out there would show-case a strong, intelligent girl who actually LIKES herself and believes that others could too.

reference_books.title: The Palace of Illusions
reference_books.review_text:
This wasn't my favorite Divakaruni book... and I kind of knew that going in. Although it's based on some very interesting cultural stories that Indian children may grow up with, I found it hard to follow because I had zero knowledge of said stories going in. There were a lot of characters to keep track of. She helps by giving you a family tree and also a list of important characters in the beginning of the book, but there were still points when I was reading and would be like, "Oh! That's the girl who blah-blah-blah earlier.. now this makes more sense." You almost have to read it two or even three times to "get" all of it. 
 That being said, it was very well-written (as always), excellent plot with lots of unexpected goings-on, and a you-don't-guess-it-until-there's-only-5-pages-left ending. All in all, still a great read.

reference_books.title: The Pleasure of My Company
reference_books.review_text:
I picked up this book on a whim, from the clearance rack of Barnes & Noble, for several reasons. One, it actually has a reasonable synopsis on the inside flap; two, it was only $4; three, it reminds me of a very good friend of mine. A LOT. Said friend will be receiving this book in the mail as soon as another friend of mine finishes reading it. 
 It's called The Pleasure of my Company and it's by Steve Martin - yes, the actor. The style is fairly stream-of-consciousness and full of beautiful profundities. If you can pick it up - DO! 
 Some of my favorite quotes: 
 "I have a tough time just being myself, you know, at parties and such. I start talking to someone and suddenly I know I am no longer myself, that some other self has taken over" (4). 
 "I see something that describes her more clearly. It occurs in the pauses in her speech when her eyes fix on an air spot roughly waist-high and she seems to be in a trance. And then suddenly it's as if her mind races, trying to catch up to real time, and she continues right where she left off... her mind is being overwhelmed by two processes that must simultaneously proceed at full steam. One is to deal with and live in the present world. The other is to re-experience and mourn something that happened long ago. It is as though her lightness pulls her toward heaven, but the extra gravity around her keeps her earthbound" (13). 
 "When an endeavor is special in a person's life, others discern it intuitively and appreciate it more... and as ordinary as such an event might be, it can be instilled with uncommon power" (58). 
 "In the deeper hours of the night I began to look at myself, to consider myself and my condition, to measure the life I'd led so far. I did not know what made me this way. I did not know of any other way I could be. I did not know what was inside me or how I could redeem what was hidden there. There must be a key or person or thing, or song or poem or belief, or old saw that could access it, but they all seemed so far away, and after I drifted further and further into self-absorption, I closed the evening with this desolate thought: There are few takers for the quiet heart" (80).
