Easily this reader's least-favorite of all four books in the series, New Moon does show a degree of style growth as we're introduced to a storytelling shift from the first book: Dual-POV. Not only are we given Bella's first-person perspective, but also Jacob's. Edward features little throughout most of the story (aside from Bella's semi-hallucinating moments brought on by self-inflicted danger--in which some semblance of her own conscience/common-sense seems to manifest as Edward, with the request that she STOP risking her safety.) Sound a little insane? Well, to be fair to realism, I've known few teenagers in love who weren't leaning pretty far over the cliff-o-craziness... 
 I digress. 
 At a base level, New Moon is a highly emotional YA urban fantasy continuation revolving around an inadvertent love-triangle--and a girl who deals with her relational co-dependency in less than healthy ways. Readers are also allowed inside the head of a somewhat whiny male protagonist, who happens to be going through some physiological changes that make puberty look like a hormonal walk in the park. The world-building expands to encompass both vampires and shapeshifters, rounding out a far broader sense of conflict than was conveyed in the 'star-crossed lovers' plot of the first book. 
 While some have contended that Bella's period of depression was overly dramatic, there are many who may find her response entirely believable. For this reader, the primary detraction to enjoyment was spending too much time in Jacob's head. Purely subjective, to be sure, but the guy annoyed me. If this reader wanted to end up in any male's head, it would have been Edward's. (16-year-old male mind vs. 100-year-old male mind? Not really a contest, there. Just sayin'.) 
 I did appreciate the vampire socio-political aspects that came into play toward the end. The book managed to stand well on its own, while hinting more at future issues that would likely need to be faced.

One thing I need in a series is character progression - things happen, they change you, your outlook, mark you in some way. Sure Bella might have a scar on her hand, but she's still the same, still feels inferior. And then comes the breakup and I wanted to throw something. I disliked that Bella was so weak. I get being sad, I get loss, but I can't approve of letting go of life entirely. And she's wishy-washy. I liked the werewolves though - an interesting take on the mythology (and better than the sparkly vampires IMO).

I do not like this book. Mostly because I read it when I was struggling with self-injury and hiding it and this book played on one of my worst fears: If your self-injury is discovered you will be thrown into an institution against your will. This is not true. You go to an institution if you're a danger to yourself or others or if you feel you can't solve your problem in outpatient therapy. Plus you'd need to get a referral from a physiologist or a doctor to get the insurance company to even think about paying for long tern inpatient care. Insurance companies really, really don't like paying for inpatient care. Since cutting is not a suicide attempt and Callie wasn't doing anything that could unintentionally lead to death (cutting really deep, attempting to break bones, drinking and cutting . . . .) she would have gone to psychologist or physiatrist after school or whatever- so this whole book could have been avoided.
Callie was difficult to relate to for much of the book. I also didn't like the narrative devices used by the author.

A very thin but not superficial book. I felt the author drew her teenage characters very accurately: sometimes confident, sometimes insecure, always questioning. Deals with an adolescent girl who feels guilty about her brother's asthma and so begins injuring herself through small cuts. When she arrives at the institution she refuses to speak and this reader just kept urging her to talk so that she could arrive sooner at some type of solution, even if it didn't solve everything hunky-dory; at least it would make things somewhat better. Ends well with the character growing through some very mature and independent decisions.

This book was horrible and did not portray what it feels like to self harm or any of the reasons behind it. Unfortunately, I used to cut and continued to for 12 years, up until about one year ago, and this book does NOT convey anything realistic whatsoever. This book really bother me...do not waste your time.

reference_books.title: Fury (The Fury Trilogy, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Okay, so this book... The pitch was amazing, the cover was amazing, and I was so happy to finally get my hands on it! 
 Then I started reading it. This is only the second book I have ever posted a DNF on in my entire life. (DNF = Did Not Finish). I made it to about page 60 before I gave up and tossed this one back onto my shelf. 
 What bothered me about this book? I mean, the pitch made it sound like it was going to be this amazing novel. But then I was introduced to Em and Chase. *SPOILERS AHEAD* 
 Em: The quiet girl who likes to study, who is best friends with a loud, bubbly, boy-crazy girl. The first chapter is all about how Em has a crush on this guy who HAPPENS to be her BFF's BF. And her voice is so whiny and all "I hate my best friend because she's too happy and bubbly and dating the boy I love" and then they throw in a random "I love my best friend" so she doesn't seem so whiny. Only it doesn't work, and she's still annoying as heck. 
 Then there's Chase. 
 Chase: The poor kid who only wanted to be popular, because DUH, that's what's most important in life! So he pretends to be something he isn't, sleeps around, and is an ass. He finds out a girl committed suicide and gets pissed off because everyone is acting sad. He thinks everyone should forget her and PARTY! Cause that's the right way to celebrate someone you've bullied trying to kill herself, of course. Then all he can think about is finding a "hot chick" to take to a banquet thing with him. 
 Basically, the characters were so ARGH! that I couldn't even pay attention to the story. Since, someone has told me that the characters are supposed to grate on your nerves, but who sticks around to finish a book like that? At this point, I think they both deserve what is coming to them, but that doesn't mean I want to stick around for another 300 pages in their whiny brains. I'd rather make my own ending to this one and move on to something that won't make me want to slap someone.

Girl is moved to a new place because father (whose name starts with C) is transferred in his job. book_a.title: Hereafter (Hereafter, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Hereafter was a great read. I loved the love story aspect, the ghostly otherworld was very original, and there were just a lot of interesting pieces to this book. I loved that the boy was a little socially awkward, but he still had friends. Not everyone is popular, so this really touched that nerdy side of me. Definitely a must read for anyone who loves a good ghost story. 
 Basically, Hereafter is the story of a girl named Amelia who doesn't remember anything about her human life. She only knows that she is dead. One night, while walking along the river she always finds herself drawn to, she wanders onto the scene of a terrible accident. She sees a boy drowning in the river and for some reason she acts, trying to save him, and manages to "will" him to live even though she can't touch him. After this, he becomes the only human who can see, hear, and touch her. 
 From there the story branches off in all kinds of directions. Another ghost named Eli who has already "passed on" and found his place in the after life comes to Amelia claiming he wants her as his apprentice. There are secrets revealed about Joshua's family and it's basically just a really original and enticing idea. I don't want to give everything away. 
 For me, the writing was good. It was simple where it needed to be, the dialogue was natural (as natural as dialogue between a human and a ghost can be, anyway) and the characters were well developed. I loved the pieces of Amelia's memories as they came back and her reactions to them. Not to mention the descriptions were amazing, if not sometimes a little bit overdone. I didn't really care to know every detail about the outside of Joshua's home, but to a ghost who hadn't seen houses in a while, or anything other than her river, it was okay. I'll definitely be picking up Arise, the sequel, as 
 soon as I can. 
 CHARACTERS: 
 For me, the characters were great. Do you ever get tired of the gorgeous, popular, smart, witty boys that plague YA literature and make you want to shoot yourself because those boys don't exist? Me too. And I loved Joshua. Sure, he was attractive, and he was funny. But he wasn't a genius, and he wasn't "popular" in the "every girl swoons, every boy fist bumps" kind of way. In fact, he was really withdrawn throughout the book and only really "socialized" when his younger sister made him. He had two really close guy friends that stuck by him and an entourage of one overly flirty, highly annoying blonde. I liked that, and how different it was from most YA literature that exists these days. 
 As for the female MC, Amelia, she was different. She wasn't all "I'm not pretty enough for his attention." In fact, she had no idea what she looked like, as she was dead and cast no reflection. She was smart, but she had to slowly learn that she was smart (another side effect of not remembering anything). Turns out she was pretty, but she wasn't over confident. She was still a bit shy; that happens when many years pass without any interaction with ghosts or humans. To me, these characters were the exact opposites of what has taken over the YA world, and I seriously loved them. 
 Then there's Eli, the other ghost of the story. Charming, seductive, gorgeous; what do you expect from a used-to-be rockstar? He was the entire YA male package, cast as the bad guy. It was pretty much perfect to contradict the other characters. I couldn't help but feel for him as the story went on, but he makes it hard to like him, which I loved. 
 PLOT: 
 As I said before, the plot in this book really hit all the right notes for me. It was so different from the other ghost novel that I read, and it kept me entertained throughout. I think I read this one in about two days. I couldn't put it down. "One more chapter" lead to three more chapters because each chapter ended on a cliff hanger or with a new twist that I had to find out about. And when Eli showed up, the story took even more twists that I wasn't expecting. Something different and exciting happens every step of the way with this one. 
 OVERALL: 
 Basically, what it all comes down to is that I loved this book! It wasn't one of those books that I will read over and over again, so I gave it four and a half stars instead of five. Really, it's a four and a half star novel, at least. It stuck with me, and I can't wait to get my hands on the sequel to see what happens next with Joshua and Amelia. Especially after Hereafter's epic ending.

This book was such a pain to read. I don't understand how anyone can like it because it is so boring and underdeveloped. I honestly have no interest in any further sequels. 
 Premise: Girl Ghost falls for human boy and together they must face the evils that want to consume her and take her away from him. 
 Yeah. It's pretty lame. Save yourself the time and energy and don't read it.

Amelia's dead which kind of sucks, but it mostly consists of walking around feeling nothing and nightmares. Her ghostly existence vastly improves when a hottie, Joshua, nearly drowns in the same place she drowned. It's love at first sight for both of them. But can a boy and a ghost really make it work? 
 Oh my god. This book. I just. Aaaaaaahhhh! To begin and explain simply, this book is definitely capitalizing off of the Twilight school of YA popularity. The writing and the plot are ridiculous. Even more ridiculous is the insta-love (just add water! - Get it?) between the main characters. In my last top ten list about the most obnoxious YA heroines, I mentioned Bianca from Evernight for the trait of immediate obsessive, ridiculously gooey love, but definitely would steal this crown from her without a contest. 
 Ghosts are tricky heroines. For one thing, they're insubstantial, so what they can do is a bit limited. Of course, with any other paranormal thing, there are ways to play with the legend and make them a bit more interesting. Hudson has devised her own, rather inconsistent ghost lore. Amelia mostly can't do anything. She can't open doors or move things or go through them. Apparently though, she can cry and bleed and breathe and have a racing heartbeat. Well, I lied. She does get to touch one thing (well, a couple others too, but pretty much only in conjunction with this one): super smexy Joshua, whose life she saved. Yeah, they can touch all they want and he can see her because of his ghost-seeing and exorcism powers. Convenient that. 
 Joshua couldn't actually see ghosts until he died just a lil bit in the water that night. He sees Amelia and thinks she's the prettiest thing in the world and goes back to the scene of the accident to ask her to meet with him the next day. Amelia hesitates but "stunningly, impossibly" agrees to go (32). She worries he will not like her when she learns she's a ghost, because, well, she's dead and no one else can see her. Instead, when he learns, he's like "Sweet! Let's make out!" No one should react to this news so happily. Getting over it would be one thing, but thinking it's the best? No freakin' way. 
 Although I have to say that imagining Joshua out on a date with her was about the only thing I enjoyed in the book. I mean, even though she's invisible to pretty much everyone else, he talks to her in public, he holds hands with her in public, kisses her in public. He must look so incredibly cray cray. Just picture it. Oh, also, the second and third things he does after she tells him about being a ghost: invite her to calculus class with him and to dinner with his family. Lol, whut? Oh, and apparently, ghosts smell like peaches, or nectarines. 
 The plot, with its number of villains, none of which I cared too much about, was not interesting whatsoever. However, what really makes this book so incredibly awful for any but Twilight fans is the writing, especially the writing about any scene that features Joshua and Amelia. Here's a sampling of quotes to illustrate what reading Hereafter is like: 
 "The moment his skin brushed mine, a current shot through my entire body, from my scalp to the tips of my fingers. The current made the ache in my chest, and the tingles that races along my spine each time he looked at me, seem like low-burning cinders. My heart, my brain, my skin--all of it was momentarily engulfed in flame, a flame lit only by the spark on my cheek." (51) 
 "The kiss sent a jolt through my entire body. The sensation was more intense than any I'd felt until now--a pure shock wave rushing along my spine and down each of my limbs. I gasped from the strength of it, dragging in a near-shriek of air." (115) 
 "I simply nodded, too befuddled by his proximity to say anything even remotely clever." (140) 
 "The heat of the little kiss spread across my lips, turning them into two smoldering coals." (155) 
 So, if you like these quotes, you'll love Hereafter. If not, leave it to that first set of folks. This a story for people who believe that love can overcome any obstacle, even death and the fact that one of the beings involved will never age.

Cuando vi que este libro habia sido recomendado por Becca Fitzpatrick, pense que iba a gustarme. Despues de todo, yo amo Hush, Hush. Lo primero que vi al abrir este arc fue una nota de la editora de Harper Collins, alabando la historia y justo tenia otros arc's de la misma editorial sin esa "nota". No pude evitar pensar que algo no marchaba bien. No. Sin embargo, no podia dejarlo sin leer, es parte de un book tour y me empuje a hacerlo y oh, desilusion. 
 ...PUEDE CONTENER SPOILERS MENORES... 
 Hasta los primeros 3 capitulos la cosa no iba tan mal. Amelia es un fantasma, que no recuerda como murio, ni su edad, ni algo remotamente util, por decir algo. Un dia mientras hacia nada productivo, salva a Joshua de morir ahogado en "su rio". Momentos antes o despues o entre la muerte de Joshua (vayan ustedes a saber), el la ve, la toca y finalmente logra escapar de su carro, salir a la superficie y salvarse. Dias despues, nuestra aburrida protagonista no puede olvidarlo y zaz! Joshua aparece buscando a la chica que le salvo. 
 Por aqui hay una escena divertida porque Meli sale huyendo de el. Disculpenme, pero yo me rei mares. Es decir, ella es la fantasma y el el humano!! 
 Despues de eso, todo va peor. Porque lo dire de nuevo, ELLA ES EL FANTASMA. Y recordemos que nadie, salvo Joshua, puede verla. Entonces imaginemos una escena (que las hay varias), donde nuestros protagonistas se encuentran en lugares publicos y se besan!! YO no lo podia creer. Es absurdo. ?Ellos pensaban que nadie los veria? Pues nadie los ve, pero como lector, me tenian con el jesus en la boca y luego enojada con su estupidez. ?Recuerdan aquella pelicula de Ghost, con Demi Moore? Tenemos ahi escenas donde parece que la medium habla con el aire y la VEN! Pues aqui nuestros tortolos ni eso consiguen. BORING... 
 Tenemos un malo-malo que termina siendo un tonto. Ni dire en que escena pero ?EN SERIO? 
 Me queda claro que este libro tenia todo para ser bueno. La idea es estupenda, pero creo que la autora no pudo darle vida a sus personajes. Josh (y eso es otra cosa que me fastidio. Era Joshua para ella y Josh para todos, porque el asi se lo pidio Uuh?) y amelia eran dos personajes sin sustancia, que aburrian a mas no poder. Sin contar el hecho de que amelia recibiera sus flashes en los momentos mas oportunos, pero con cosas que solo me tenian poniendo los ojos en blanco. 
 Definitivamente puede que este libro guste a alguien, pero conmigo no lo consiguio.

Yes Juliette is annoying, she is weepy, winey and faints all the time but if she wasn't would you have the same feelings throughout the book? I don't think so. Juliette is a character that that needs protecting and that is what Adam is there for. 
 At the moment paranormal romance and dystopian books are my favourite and Shatter Me combines all of this and more. The writing style was unique, I have never seen another author use strike through like Mafi did to express Juliette's emotions. 
 The one character I wasn't keen on was the villain which is a surprise because I normally love the bad guy but this villain reminded me of the little blond annoying king from games of thrones. I felt a little bit like someone should just push him over and it was hard to understand why everyone was doing what he is saying. I think that this is maybe part of his "Charm" though and obviously people are not supposed to like him. 
 I enjoyed how this book ended it makes me want to continue to see Adam and Juliette grow as character. 
 The physical book was very floppy even for a paperback and this I didn't like. 
 Tahereh Mafi is a young author and applaud her for success of this series of books.

I wanted to love this book so much. IT'S A DYSTOPIA, THEY SAID. IT'S AWESOME, THEY SAID. 
 My gawd, I liked only two things about it. First one, the idea of a government wanting to erase our past (which made me go all "aksjdkasjdkasjdkasd" at first... If only this was portrayed in the book, oh God). Second... Finishing this book. 
 The writing 
 I could put up with the first 100 pages or so. It seemed original, different, and I liked that. But then it was... Uhh, it was awful. Metaphors had no sense at all and I found myself like this 
 Like, WTF DID I JUST READ? Does -that- actually mean something? Endless paragraphs to express something that could have been said in two lines. The fact that she wanted so hard to sound smart and poetic showed off through the entire book. She wanted it, yet so didn't accomplish it. 
 Besides, the repetitions... It was, was, was all like this, this, this. All. The. Time. The punctuation ended up being weird and I was about to stop reading this book because I couldn't bear with it. Not to mention the strike throughs. But I hate not finishing books. 
 The plot 
 Dystopia? What dystopia? This is one of the most crappiest romances ever, set on a dystopian environment. But this ain't about a dystopia, that I can say. 
 So, in a sum up, is the story of a kinda psycho girl that's been in reclusion for almost 300 days that can't touch people because of her special power. If doing so, she drains people's lives, and that's the main reason of being locked up alone. Then she meets Adam, the super hot guy she knew since they were kids and starts "falling in love". And, I don't know how, from one moment to the other, everybody's in love with her and/or wants to bang her. And she wants that as well, but yet so can't get laid. The end. 
 Overall, this story was so boring and frustrating. The idea first shown about the government caught my eye and I thought it was kickass and then all I got to read was about Juliette complaining once, twice, a third time... COMPLAINTS EVERYFUCKINWHERE. An emo yabba-dabba that will make you want to rip your eyes off. And, in spite of this "oh gosh, I can't touch people, I can't be touched, oh, oh, sadness, pouty, pout, pout", she appears to think each guy she meets is incredibly handsome and beautiful and... HORMONES ATTACK! 
 And the ending... Seriously? SERIOUSLY? The fact that it was a copy of X-Men that had no sense at all in the story made me want to punch my PC. Not cool. 
 So, nope. Not an interesting plot. Not a real, clear plot, either. 
 Characters 
 Juliette 
 Whiny, whiny little biatch... So, she's been in reclusion, without seeing the sun, without eating properly, in totally unhealthy conditions. Instead of being mentally and physically f*cked up, everybody think she's the most beatiful and sexy girl ever. Really? To be sincere, all I got from this character was a hormone overdoze. 
 Here you go, Juliette. Cool yourself a bit before you jump over any of the guys surrounding you. 
 Adam 
 Err... Such convenient that he can touch Juliette! Oh, that must be real love guys. That must be! 
 Typical YA guy. Supermodel outside, somehow broken inside. It's the bad guy that it's not bad. Woot, woot, props on the originality. 
 Warner 
 Psycho with no limits, he's obsessed with Juliette (and not to mention the scene of both making out... She was grossed out but at the same time enjoying it. Like, wit, what?) and wants her by his side, no matter the costs. Bad guy. Bad, bad guy with mental issues. Oh, and guess what? He can touch Juliette too without being affected! Boyaah, that's having lots of luck dude! 
 Overall 
 Why this has to be a series? I don't want to go through the next books, yet so I don't want to leave the series unfinished. But, by now, for me it's over.

reference_books.title: The Silent Sister (Riley MacPherson, #1)

reference_books.title: You Should Have Known
reference_books.review_text: Despite the recommendation on the cover claiming the reader will be 'in its thrall from page one' I found nothing really happened until page 205, even then it wasn't exactly a page turner. I found it very hard to sympathise with the protagonist and didn't feel like there was very much interaction between her and other characters (not what You would expect in a book that is 440 pages (tediously) long) was very bored reading it and couldn't wait to finish! Don't get the hype I'm afraid. Dull.

reference_books.title: Disclaimer
reference_books.review_text: Meh. 2.5 stars. Maybe I have just read one too many of these samey phycological thrillers and so am not shocked by them anymore. I was very disappointed considering the hype surrounding this book, I found it mediocre at best. reference_books.title: The Girl on the Train
reference_books.review_text: I found this to be a very enjoyable and accomplished debut novel. I love thrillers when You're not sure whether the narrator is 100% reliable or not...this is definitely one of those books. Although the story leaps back between the present and the previous year with 3 different voices, I found it very coherent very easy to follow. I did however guess the ending about 50 pages from the end but I still found myself turning those pages just as quick. A must for psychological thriller fans!

reference_books.title: The Shock of the Fall
reference_books.review_text: I don't understand the hype around this one. I'll admit I struggled for such a small book, I just couldn't engage with it at all. I found the narrative very confusing (I don't think it's beautifully written' either(!)) and the characters were not endearing in any way. Am I the only one who didn't enjoy this book?

book_a.title: The Ocean at the End of the Lane
book_a.user_review: This was not my cup of tea at all. The main character whose name we don't discover, really relies completely on other the other characters of the story. He has no control over his surroundings or fate, and thus there is no sense of adventure, only the sickening horror of watching events unfold like a nightmare. I can't say that it's a great insight into grief or how the mind can adapt to protect You from memories of your past as there are no profound revelations. The story at times reads like a children's book as some of the adult themes are witnessed through seemingly innocent eyes, yet I wouldn't recommend this to anyone under 16, it's hard to pigeon hole this one! But apparently many love it!

sample_reviews.review_text:
My first experience with a Gaiman novel and I'm still trying to sort through it in my head. I did really enjoy the story, and the story telling style he has. I'll definitely be reading more of his works, when I want something a bit more challenging and emotional than my usual escapist fare. 
 All the feels are present in this book and at the end I found myself with more questions than answers. But I suppose that was the point of the story all along, and in that it succeeded mightily. I was uncomfortable with the narrative for a short bit (child endangerment trigger) but thankfully that part was short lived, even if the resolution (erasing the incident as though it never happened) left me uncomfortable as well.

2.5 stars. Do you ever read a book that's good, on a technical level, but which you kind of hate anyway? I feel like that's what just happened to me. 
 You know what the problem is? I knew all the themes and the places this book would go. Do you know how I knew everything? Because it's the exact same themes as The Graveyard Book. And Coraline. And probably some of his other books too. It's about letting go of your childhood. Which is cool. It's a good theme. But I can't read an entire book with no other appeal. 
 I can acknowledge Gaiman is a great author. His imagery is pitch-perfect. Unfortunately, I don't know if that's really a good thing. If you've read this book, you know I'm talking body horror. The whole worm thing genuinely brought me one inch from DNFing this. Or dying, whichever came first. Don't read this if you're not a fan of body horror. Genuinely, do not. 
 The whole thing honestly just felt like a repeat of The Graveyard Book, but with less compelling characters. Yes, there were some nifty twists, but I somehow didn't care about any of it. This just felt so mediocre and angering to me, as a book. I felt like I should have loved it and I just didn't. 
 audiobook began: June 24th, 2017 
 Blog | Goodreads| Twitter | Youtube

This was my first book from Neil Gaiman (although I've watchedCoraline but as we all know, the movie may not be anything like the book, so I don't know if that's a true representation). I don't know what type of writing this is--I'd say a dark fairy tale? I'd give a 3.5 rounded down, it might be very good for its genre, but I don't read too many so I don't know. 
 It's a little disturbing to realize that we may have other lives being lived without our knowledge at any one time and that our world may just be a piece of canvas that covers something else. 
 The quote at the end of Saving Private Ryan--"earn it"--is very similar to the ending here, but I thought it was very realistic when the boy (Does he have a name? Even the cat has a name, Fluffy, but not the main character?) felt the weigh of the future guilt he might have. 
 I picked a hardcopy of this at a local bookstore, but the inside is stamped "no longer property of the Seattle public library"! Wonder how it got from Seattle to Northern Virginia!

Sometimes books come at just the right time. Another time, I might have been put off by the fanciful story in "The Ocean and the End of the Lane", but this week in November, days darkening and nostalgic, it was a tale in which I didn't mind getting lost.

The essential fairy tale has returned. 
 Great short book - set up is quick and efficient, no worries with all the background information on every character - it just dives right in. We are again brought back to the essential - the imaginative - the simple in order to tell and retell a story. Complete with heroes, heroines, evil doers, and a twist here and there. 
 I dare not go into details - what fun would that be? Go, and discover for yourself (and I bet you only need a day or two to in fact discover). Instead, I'll just leave with a few favorite quotes from the book - it gives a great snapshot of the tone of this little treasure. 
 "Adults follow paths. Children explore. Adults are content to walk the same way, hundreds of times, or thousands; perhaps it never occurs to adults to step off the paths, to creep beneath rhododendrons, to find the spaces between fences." 
 "Nobody actually looks like what they really are on the inside. You don't. People are much more complicated than that. It's true of everybody." 
 "When I left, I went with Lettie Hempstock and her mother out of the front door, and the moon was a thin white smile, high in a cloudy sky, and the night was gusty with sudden, undecided spring breezes coming first from one direction, then from another; every now and again a gust of wind would contain a sprinkling of rain that never amounted to anything more than that."

I have to be honest. I didn't like this book at all. I felt like I was duped based on the synopsis of the book. Although I appreciate that others liked it, I have to tell you that not one person liked it ... AT ALL. If it was going for fantasy, it missed and just became silly. One person in my BC said that they felt that it was written to become a movie. I think hey were probably right. But there's a reason why authors aren't screen writers! It's a different style completely. I'm glad that so many others liked it, but this was a major fail for me.

The opening chapter drew me in straight away and I settled into my armchair with a cup of tea and the anticipation of losing myself in the story - but sadly it just got too weird for me pretty quickly.

As someone who is only vaguely familiar with Gaiman's work, I have to say I wasn't overly impressed. An emotional story, but it sort of toes the genre line between adult and YA. I feel like the overarching plot is a tired one. It was a strange, short read. It was just okay for me. I didn't find his passages as profound as other readers seemed to. The book was too short to dig deep and resonate with me, but at the same time, I was so indifferent about the book that had it been much longer, I would have given up on it.

I feel like I missed the point of this book... I get some of the likely nuances, but otherwise, I definitely feel like I missed something. The story was definitely interesting, but again, I definitely feel like I'm missing something. However, I don't feel all that inclined to figure it out, which is unlike me, but I don't think I'm going to question it in this case... too many things to do and too many books left to read! Still, enjoyable book but not one I think I will be revisiting. 
 Note (added later 8/17/16): I feel the need to add that I've thought about this book for a little while now and I've come to a conclusion as for why I don't really care to dissect this book.... I found it somewhat depressing. The writing was terrific, as is the case with all of the writing I've read by Neil Gaiman, but ultimately this was not a book that made me feel all that good about myself and the world in the end. It was an interesting commentary on adulthood (yay! I think I figured out a little bit of the point of this book...), but ultimately it isn't something that I'm dying to reread or recommend. Still, if you are interested in a fantastical commentary on real life... this is the book for you.

Although I feel like I didn't completely understand this book, I was completely enchanted by it. It's been a while since I cringed or had nightmares about creatures from books, but that's what happened with this book. It was beautifully written, and I was so happy that Gaiman wrote this great addition to the genre of magical realism!

 I'll probably take a break from these. I get more excited about books that don't follow a pattern and break out of the mold.

This book checked off all my must haves in a favorite book - interesting characters, well written and a memorable plot. I don't have to agree with or like everything that each character does but I want the story to support why they made those choices. I adore how each character was inter-woven into the next. The pacing is spot-on and I made my self savor this story and not race thru it. The story is interesting but the way that Moriarty spins it makes this one of my favorite books this year.
I don't know...it was just ok...nothing special.

sample_reviews.review_text: Love cliffhangers and this one has heaps!

Amazon kept suggesting that I read this book, and I kept putting it off until I saw that it was going to be made into a TV series (mini-series?). At that point, I tossed it into my reading queue, and finally got around to reading it a while later. I wish I had read it a lot sooner, as it was a great trilogy! 
 It's hard to mention very much about this set of books because there is so much, that once revealed, spoils the storyline for people who haven't read it yet. 
 When I started the book, I assumed that I was going to be in for a Koontzesque book, and though quite a bit of the first book is definitely in that vein of writing, I'd definitely have to classify this as a science fiction novel, rather than a thriller/suspense. 
 The ending of the first book made me feel like there was not going to be any story left to tell for the second and third books. Everything was wrapped up nice and neat, even though there were a few unanswered questions, they weren't quite burning in my mind. I could have stopped after that book, and been very happy with the story. It makes me wonder if the author had planned on only writing the one, and expanded it into a trilogy later on. The first book was quite an amazing read for me. It's been a while since I really got into a book as much as I did with this one! 
 The second book took everything I knew about the Wayward Pines world and turned it on its head - and it answered almost every unanswered question I had. There were a few plot points that I didn't agree with until I later read the third book. I had to read the third book after the second because the second book has this giant cliffhanger that forces you to continue - even though I had planned to do so anyway! 
 The conclusion to the series in book three had me slapping my forehead with the realization that 'I should have known!' but I was so into the book, I didn't even think about it. Again, there is a few trailing ideas that could be expanded upon into another book, but I doubt that it would be worthwhile to add onto the story's end. As with the ending of book one, it's a great place to stop! 
 I think anyone who likes thrillers and/or sci-fi would enjoy this trilogy.

Perhaps with some serious editing, the Wayward Pines trilogy could have been made into one excellent book instead, rather than three "meh, they're ok" books. I just found it hard to connect with the story. It seemed too general, like there was too much fluff.
To be continued.... It IS interesting, but doesn't grab me. Still, on to The Last Town.

Reading the series after watching the TV show, you can tell the show is just "based" on it. The first season is really the only one that stayed true to the books and that was only up to a point. Good series though! It was hard to not just start the new one this morning after I finished the last.

The second book of the Wayward Pines series picks up right where the first book left off, and continues in the same delightful prose and fast paced story. And the more I read, the more disappointed I am in the TV series, which appears to have done little more than take the names of characters and the basic plot, and then clunkily plod through story arcs that have barely any resemblance to the books. These books are delightfully fun, quick reads and it breaks my heart to see them treated poorly on the silver screen.

The first book in this trilogy was intriguing and exciting but Wayward felt like a deconstruction of everything I enjoyed about Pines. 
 This book was so slow paced and uninteresting. I caught myself skimming just to get through it, whereas the previous novel constantly had me on the edge of my seat and quickly reading to see what happened next. 
 The supporting characters were flat and irrelevant while Ethan became increasingly annoying. 
 My biggest issue with this book was that the plot was entirely illogical. Why did Pilcher continue to trust Ethan? Why did he keep giving him more power? Why would he have him investigate a murder that he committed? Pilcher could have easily averted Ethan's attention from Alyssa's presumed murder. He could have easily staged her death as an abby attack for crying out loud. 
 As another reviewer pointed out, why would the cameras be attuned to the chips rather than be motion sensored? 
 And then we have the annoying, cliche love triangles. The ending with Adam "Tobias" Hassler had me rolling my eyes so damn hard. 
 I decided to cut the author some slack and give this book two stars instead of one. Maybe the reason I disliked this book so much was because the series has shifted into a dystopian rather than mystery. 
 This book simply proved that I am exhausted of the dystopian genre.

A fun series, though I wish we could have done away with the antagonist more quickly to explore the world. While I would have preferred a faster pace, I felt the premise was really interesting despite a few scientific inconsistencies.
Blake really knows how to write a fast paced, thriller. Each chapter ended and I had to start the next.

Part whodunnit part Sci Fi. The sequel to the earlier story of the agent waking up in a strange town populated by odd characters under surveillance by a strange shadowy organisation cranks up the paranoia as everyone tries to overpower one another as they vie for political supremacy. 
 Some answers come too easily as the investigation maintains a breakneck pace until the town revolts and the owner retaliates in shocking fashion, leaving the story on a cliffhanger. Guess they're forcing us to complete the trilogy.

I listened to this on audio book last night and it was surprisingly good. Overall it added a bit to the story arc and was just enjoyable to listen to, recommend if you've read Steelheart and can't wait for Firefight!

I have to confess, while I love most things that Brandon Sanderson writes, the Reckoners stuff just isn't my favorite. Oh, I enjoy reading the terrible metaphor-spouting hero as much as the next guy, and seeing the superhero genre get turned on its head brings me particular pleasure. But I just can't get into them like I want. They feel too young. I want a grittier take on the world--it certainly deserves one. 
 As for this particular story, it was cute and breezy fun without costing me too much time or brain cells. Unfortunately, it kind of had a "so what" feel to it, even though Sanderson tried to hint at something bigger toward the end. So, it was fun and enjoyable, if not particularly thrilling. 
 In the end, if you liked Steelheart, you'll probably like this one, too. If you thought Steelheart was only so-so, expect more of the same, just shorter.

This review has been crossposted from my blog at The Cosy Dragon . Please head there for more in-depth reviews by me, which appear on a timely schedule. 
 This tiny (#1.5) short story occurred in between the first and second novels of the Reckoner's series (Steelheart and Fireflight respectively). 
 I remind astounded by the sheer number of convincing magic systems Sanderson can create. There are so many interesting novels about superheroes, it's hard to stand out. 
 It's almost too short to write a review, you don't really get that much story. It is where David first gets his insights into how the epics work, so it's valuable in that way. 
 Since it is a Brandon Sanderson, I'll give it five stars by default , but it's just too hard to come up with that much of an opinion. I wasn't that excited about the extra material in the novel (having read the second one already), but it would be worth it if you're just starting and reading the novels in series.
A good way to keep my appetite sated until Calamity arrives in February.
A quick and entertaining story that reads pretty much as an intro to the next book in this series. If you liked Steelheart and can't wait for Firefight, this one will serve as a nice little teaser.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Over the course of one sleep-deprived, but laugh-filled, week, I devoured Penny Reid's Knitting in the City series, thus starting a (perfectly healthy) obsession with her writing. Reading a book by Penny Reid is like being inducted into a world of adorably quirky characters and writing that is both intelligent and humorous. She injects an unparalleled zaniness into each of her books and I'm thrilled to say that her newest release, Truth or Beard, follows suit. Charming, refreshing, lively, and entertaining - any and all of these words can be used to describe Truth or Beard. It's undoubtedly the kind of book you read from the comfort of your own home, unless, of course, you're perfectly fine with people giving you strange looks as a result of your frequent and loud bouts of laughter. 
 What's not to love about the pairing of a math teacher whose Halloween costume of choice is a sexed up Gandalf the Grey and a mechanic whose unrequited crush prompts him to pretend to be his own twin? In case you're wondering, the answer is nothing. Every minute of the love/hate relationship between protagonists, Jessica James and Duane Winston, is just plain fun, from their whip smart conversations to their heated intimate encounters, and everything in between. When I read a book, I tend to gravitate more towards either the hero or the heroine, yet with Truth or Beard, I was equally enamored with both Duane and Jessica. Their unabashed honesty and genuineness made me feel as though I got to know all aspects of their characters; there was no mystery with them because they each laid everything out for the other to see. 
 ...Having said that, I will admit that I'm a tad bit enamored with Duane Winston. A guy who reads book, acts like a gentleman and has a dirty mind is pretty much my idea of perfection. The fact that he could say something inconspicuously sensual like "you're a siren who doesn't need to sing" in reference to Jessica's effect on him and not induce an eye roll speaks volumes to his level of charisma. Duane is so amazingly sweet and sexy, I couldn't help but swoon over his words and actions during his and Jessica's every interaction. I'm well aware this guy is a fictional character but that didn't stop me from giggling like a schoolgirl and fanning my face every time he opened his mouth. Did I mention he's a redhead? There just aren't enough redheaded heroes and I, for one, am glad Penny Reid is taking it upon herself to fill the void. 
 With its large cast of eclectic characters, the budding romance between Duane and Jessica, and a subplot to add a bit of action and suspense, there is never a dull moment in Truth or Beard. Like the Knitting in the City series, the Winston Brothers series is made up of interconnected standalones - a fact that fills me with immeasurable amounts of joy because, after reading Truth or Beard, I am more than anxious to become better acquainted with the remaining Winston brothers. There are six Winston brothers in total, which means there are five books in the series I have to look forward to. Five! If I could, I would set up camp in Penny Reid's mind so I could witness every story as it springs into existence. Until then, I think multiple re-readings of Truth or Beard are in order...

I really liked that Reid gave us POVs for both Duane and Jessica, and knowing what they were thinking and feeling heightened the emotional level and the steam level too. 
 I would never have imagined from our first introduction to the Winston brothers in Beauty and the Mustache that any of them would make a great leading man, but I truly loved Duane - and I am prepared to fall for his brothers as well.

reference_books.title: A Court of Wings and Ruin (A Court of Thorns and Roses, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
I WANT MORE I WANT MORE I WANT MORE I WANT MORE I WANT MORE I WANT MORE I WANT MORE I WANT MORE I WANT MORE I WANT MORE I WANT MORE I WANT MORE I WANT MORE I WANT MORE I WANT MORE 
 Driven by hatred and vengeance, Feyre learned to don a mask well, to deceive Tamlin and his court, to turn his people against him, to spy and to ruin. 
 BAD NEWS FIRST 
 The world created by Sarah J. Maas is riveting and the characters are so damn lovable. The plot is extraordinary but I think it was executed poortly in the ending, full of disorganized elements that are all over the place. Sometimes Part Three: High Lady felt so rushed and compressed, I can almost see the holes poking out of the pages. 
 *sighs in disappointment* 
 For instance, when Feyre finally decided to look into the Ouroboros , an important decision and unfolding, where she saw what she was, what happened, what she's become after everything she did, Sarah J. Maas only portrayed the first beast Feyre saw without her detailed thoughts on the matter. Without her telling us how, specifically, she'd conquered the overwhelming truth shown by the mirror that damaged everyone who looked. That even with all the darkness inside her, the monsters lurking in her soul, her ugly... she still thrived and owned the mirror, to be summoned by her whenever she wished, that she now believed that she was still worthy even when the world broke her. I felt like this was an important part of the story, especially that the story's almost ending. This scene felt skipped, along with other scenes, and I didn't like it. 
 Moreover, after that sliver of Rhysand POV in the previous book, and especially that Feyre and Rhys are separated in the first part, I would have loved it if there are as many Rhys POVs as Feyre POVs. I really like and admire Feyre. I think she's an amazing heroine. But I am disappointed that so much focus was on her while almost all the characters deserve their own spotlight. There are story lines I would have died to explore more (i.e. Nesta-Cassian, Lucien-Elain, Lucien-Tamlin, Azriel-Mor, Amren-Varian) that in the end, even if Feyre's finally wearing her red lacy underthings, it still felt unresolved. 
 I also did not like the parts where the others' stories are told through Feyre's visions - when she went to Lucien's mind that first time he conversed with Elain in the library, when she went to Rhys's mind to see what he was doing during their first battle (the fact that Rhys allowed her in his mind that might distract her should an unpredictable danger presented itself in front of her is beyond me), and when she was gripping the Cauldron and viewing the war from its perspective. I can't help but compare the writing to Cassandra Clare's where most of her characters' feelings are shown to us. Since the characters in the ACOTAR series had their own special tasks - Rhys and Feyre as High Lord and Lady, Cassian as commander of the Illyrian Legion, Azriel as shadowsinger, Mor as second-in-command, Amren in perusing the Book of Breathings, Nesta as emissary to the humans, Elain as seer, Lucien in finding Vassa, Tamlin in saving his court, even Jurian in his turncloaking... , and their own important self-discoveries, I think this series would have been better if it was written in the Cassandra Clare way I know and love. Who knows, though? I heard more Prythian stories are coming in 2018 so I'll probably get what I desperately wish for! 
 GOOD NEWS 
 Some deemed most of the book boring but I did not think so at all and looking at the whole book's picture, I loved it! The main characters are also warriors but they are generals and leaders first. It is their job to strategize - form alliances, spy on enemy territory, bargain with mercenaries, research in libraries for all advantages they can gain, and gamble with what they have. Sure it isn't as action packed as the bloody fights in the battlefield but the power plays and their dirty consequences have their own allure and I was madly intrigued, as much as I would have been attentive in detailed and amazing fight scenes.

 [Warning for the spoiler sensitive] 
 It's such a feel-good book! It reminds me of all the good vibes I had when I was watching Weightlifting Fairy Kim Bok Joo, that Korean drama starring Lee Sung-kyung and Nam Joo-hyuk. The conflicts weren't so hardcore, and they are resolved immediately. 
 I have to admit that as the chapters progressed and it still felt like fan service, I felt like in the end Jenny Han would kill us all by having Peter get in a car accident or something else terrible. And I am so glad my paranoia didn't come true. 
 I also feel like a hypocrite right now, since I've always felt that books 2-3 weren't necessary at all and To All the Boys I've Loved Before could have thrived as a standalone. I WANT TO KNOW IF THEY BREAK UP ANYWAY BECAUSE STATISTICALLY SPEAKING THEY PROBABLY WOULD DESPITE THE HINTS STATING OTHERWISE DURING THE END CHAPTERS. I WANT TO WATCH KITTY GROW. I SRSLY SRSLY SRLSY WANT MORE SO MUCH I'M GOING TO CRY. 
 This book is the happiest book I've read I'm not ready to let go of it just yet. (Especially that the next book in my RL is fantasy and I'm certain there'd be people dying and hearts breaking)

sample_reviews.review_text: I am so happy I got to read this trilogy after they were all out! When I finished the second one I was okay with the thought of that one be the last one but I was so happy it wasn't! This one was a way better ending for sure! So many emotions and finding yourself and doing what is best for you before your relationship no matter how hard it is. It was so great. I loved Lara Jean and Peter's little story and their character arc throughout the three books. They definitely went from clearly a teenager to young adults only wanting the best for each other. SO GOOD! Like I said before I'm so happy that this was the end that we got so see. While the second one's ending was sweet I would have always wondered and now I don't have to!
Like nothing actually....happens?

Oh boy! This was just beautiful. Peter is my favorite of all times. Every time that I read something that he wrote or said to Lara Jean I was just dying inside. He's just perfect. 
 I love the way Jenny Han writes, it's so easy to read and light and you just feel love in every single word. 
 The problem with this book is that I just want, no, I need to know more. LOL! But I think it's a fair way to ending this amazing and beautiful story. 
 I finished this trilogy with so much love and happiness!

I'm so sad to be done with Lara Jean's story. Her regular little story of love and decision making as a high school senior is so refreshing in the YA world. This book and the 2 before it would be a great mother/daughter read for anyone with a middle or high school daughter. I'm thinking that Lara Jean is such a great role model, I wish she'd been around when I was 15 or so. There's nothing life or death about these books and reading them as an adult definitely drives home the memories of the things you stressed over as a teen that really weren't such a big deal. It's so nice to live in Lara Jean's world. I'd recommend if you need a light quick read in between thrillers or dramas.

4.5* 
 Truly loved it. It had such a nostalgic feel to it for some reason but I just wanted a teeny tiny bit more. Was an epilogue too much to expect?

This is the third and final book in the To All The Boys I've Loved Before series. Lara Jean is now a senior in high school. She is on the cusp of graduating, her future is uncertain. She isn't sure what school she will go to in the fall and she's not sure where that leaves her relationship with Peter. 
 I absolutely love this series. This is my go to perfect summer contemporary. Lara Jean loves staying home, baking, spending time with her family, and loves her boyfriend. She loves a great love story. She is has an amazing family that we get to spend so much time with. The book is filled with so many wonderful family moments. 
 The romance is so adorable and just a little too good to be true. Peter is such an understanding boyfriend. He truly cares about Lara Jean and her family. These two have come such a long way since the first book. I really like how Jenny Han tackled all the insecurities couple go through when they are stuck in the in between of high school and college. 
 This book captured such a pivotal time frame that we don't oddly see enough of in young adult books. 
 I give this book a B+.

There's something about the Lara Jean novels that make me feel very young and very old at the same time. The novels show me what I think the sweetest kind of young love might feel like. At the same time, it also reminds me how much older I am and how unrealistic it is, but I cannot help but like it all the same. 
 Of the three novels, I would say this is the weakest of them, but I love Peter, and I love Lara Jean, so I can't help myself loving their story. I'm truly glad they got their happy ending, even though nothing substantial happens in this novel other than Lara Jean talking about their relationship and deliberating on choices for college. While I understand that this is very important to a young girl leaving high school, it's the kind of thing that I just can't relate to anymore because I am no longer at that stage in life. 
 Still, it put a smile on my face and I'm glad Jenny Han decided to write a finale for Lara Jean. The novels are exactly like the kind of cupcake covers they have... light, frothy, but in the end, not all that profound. Then again, they've never pretended to be.
Es tan hermoso, Lara Jean es un personaje tan percioso.

 The plot of story are stepward and backward. But it is still easy to be understood. I love the point how we make a choice and influence our life or how life make a choice for us. And in the end it doesnt matter at all. It is very normally how we always do sacrifices for someone we loved. There is no regret.
This made me cry. And the Adam in the book reminded me of Adam Lambert- both of their personalities fit almost perfectly! :P

I hadn't heard of this book until the previews for the movie started playing. As with most movies that started as books, I wanted read it first. Turns out that was a really good idea as I didn't care for the movie. 
 I really enjoyed the family dynamic that our main character, Mia, had. Her parents were everything that I dreamed mine were. Cool, calm, and progressive. They loved their two children with every fiber of their being without smothering them. This family lived for music. Mia's father was once in a very popular local band when she was born and a few years after she came along, he decided it was time to get a more steady job. His daughter ended up showing great interest in the cello and although he knew little about the world of classical music, he and his wife were thrilled at Mia's interest and encouraged her to keep learning. 
 I was one of those band kids growing up. I remember the last newsletter of my senior year me fellow bandsmen voted me most likely to end up a music teacher. That didn't exactly happen, but 10 years later, I'm still playing on a professional level (which is kinda cool!). My parents, like Mia's, encouraged me to keep playing, and I found my own little niche of friends in the world of fine arts. But enough about me, back to Mia. 
 Most of this story is told in the past tense. The accident that ends up claiming the lives of Mia's family happens at the very beginning of the book. We are reliving the best memories with Mia while she tries to decide if she wants to linger in this world or to join her family across that mysterious beyond. 
 She methodically picks through her life, trying to weigh the options. She has a wonderful boyfriend who, like her father, is a rock star in band that is on the cusp of fame. He falls for Mia after watching her in a practice room. The connection she has with music is so vastly different from his own that he is drawn to her. To learn more about her and her passions. Then there is her future. She is a candidate for Julliard and if we are to believe the people around her, is a guaranteed to get in. 
 So here we have this young girl with the world at her feet. But the pain of everything she has lost is so fresh and so much that I couldn't help feel that the decision was an impossible one. One that I don't know if I could make. The most beautiful gesture in this book, for me, was when her grandfather was alone with her and he tells her that it's ok if she wants to let go. As much as he wants his last grandchild to live, he understands that waking will be more painful than letting go. 
 I really enjoyed this book. The movie was ok, but I felt that the emotions that are evoked in this book were just too difficult to translate on to the Silver Screen. I thought it was a wonderful story that was told very well.
It was a good book- I just thought that it could have been better, especially with such a good concept.

After seeing the preview for the movie and tearing up, I decided to read the book. I finished it in an afternoon and thoroughly enjoyed it. It wasn't amazing or incredibly well-written but I'm looking forward to crying at the movie.

4.5 stars. Oh the feels with this one! The last 20% or so, I was a blubbering idiot. Ugly Cry Central!! 
 My only complaint is that the Kindle version ended at 80%. It was a bit of a shock really. It ended a bit abruptly too. I kept flipping back and forth trying to figure out if I was missing a part.

This was such a well-written book. The emotions completely drew me and I found myself invested in the characters and the story. The premise is devastating enough: a young girl who loses everything and must make the decision of whether to live, but the story that was told through this girl's voice was remarkable. It is a story of hope, of facing tragedy and letting it strengthen you, of realizing the "family" we have all around us, of choices to make. I liked how the book wasn't predictable, and the ending was up in the air until the last page! I definitely recommend this!

This is a beautiful story about a teenage girl who loses her entire family in a tragic car accident. She literally watches herself being taken into the ICU, her remaining relatives and friends gathering around her and it becomes clear that she must make a choice. Should she stay or go? Dotted within the story are her memories of her family, her best friend and her musician boyfriend who is fighting to see her, to save her. I was most affected by the fact that she finds out that her brother did not survive and prayed that the angels went to look after him so that he wasn't alone and left her to deal with this herself. A lovely story that proves that teenage stories do not have to be about vampires to have impact.
Seriously, who would read something like this???

reference_books.title: We'll Always Have Summer (Summer, #3)
reference_books.review_text: I'm torn between 4 and 4.5 stars, so I'll settle for 4.25 lol.... I breezed through the last of this series because I just wanted to see who Belly ends up with already. This time around she's in college and has been with Jeremiah for the last two years. She is convinced that they are each others only true loves and that Conrad was just that first love that she will never forget. But as soon as Belly is near Conrad you see the effect he has on her. I don't want to give too much away for all of the readers that want to enjoy the surprises, but I will say that I'm happy with the way things turned out. The first book is still my favorite of the three because to me it was the one that really captured the magic of summer at the Cousins beach house and of Belly becoming pretty and Conrad finally seeing her as more than just a tag-along young brat. I look forward to what comes next from Ms. Jenny Han - I love her writing and her books. :)

reference_books.title: The Next Best Thing
reference_books.review_text: Disappointed, was not entertained as much as previous Weiner reads. I'm a huge Golden Girls fan and I live in So Cal, and I noticed inconsistencies throughout and straight-up exaggerations. Dorothy never had a gay son (Blanche had a gay brother) and not everyone has orange trees in their backyard in LA and some of the descriptions were totally glamorized. I know, I know, it's fiction and it's Hollywood, but it was just meh.

reference_books.title: If I Stay (If I Stay, #1)
reference_books.review_text: In under 200 pages this book packs a punch - I was seriously bawling. The story takes place in about 24 hours. On a snow day Mia and her family make plans for the day and head out, but there is a terrible accident. Mia is forced to make a decision and while this is happening there are flashbacks of Mia's life and other decisions that have shaped it and that will shape it. There is a love story that is very touching as well as many well-developed characters that surprisingly are not lacking in anything despite the length of the book. The author does an excellent job of only presenting was is necessary and drawing you into Mia's world immediately. Although there is much sorrow and pain, there is also hope and love in this story.

reference_books.title: The Dark Divine (The Dark Divine, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I really comtemplated giving this 5 stars, but I think 4.5 is what I'm settling on. I thought the story, although reminiscent of this whole werewolf/supernatural trend, was very well written, paced, and the characterizations were excellent. It kept my interest the whole way through, and it kept me guessing. Grace Divine is a pastor's daughter who three years earlier lost a "brother". Daniel was taken in as a son and brother to the Divine household because his father was violent and because he had always been Grace, and her brother Jude's, best friend. But one night Jude comes back covered in blood and Daniel is gone. Grace is left with no answers and no one seems to want to give her any even after Daniel mysteriously returns. There is love, action, history, legend, and even religion in the story. I liked how everything was woven together and there was a door left open at the end for a follow up book. I enjoyed this book much more than Shiver and I think fans of other vampire/werewolf/fairy books will also enjoy this one.
