Full review: https://mackenziesmountain.wordpress.... 
 This was my favourite book in the Shopaholic series. I actually sat on it for about a month before reading because I detested the previous book and was worried it would ruin the series for me if I disliked to the Rescue as well, but once I started, I couldn't put it down. Cue laughing out loud on page one. Not to mention staying up til 3am to finish. Shhhh, let's not share that particular point, okay? 
 I think what set this one apart from the others is that the focus wasn't on the trouble Becky finds for herself. Although she blames herself for the problems, she isn't to blame and after seven books fixing her mistakes, it is refreshing to see Becky has grown into a more mature and responsible version of her youthful self, and that sometimes that "perfect" friend can dig herself into a real doozy of a hole. 
 It almost felt as if Kinsella was closing the series on this one, but I feel like there is one story left to tell. Hopefully we'll get to read it.
Later installments in this series haven't been as good, but this one is better than the last one. Readable, but Becky has lost some of her charm/flair by this point.
Parts of this series can be annoying, but they are still fun to read for entertainment.

As ever, Becky's in trouble with everyone! A funny , easy to read, romp from LA. To Vegas to Sedona in an RV with the entire family and friends searching for lost fathers and husbands. See Becky lose and get her shopping mojo back.
Although I have loved the Shopaholic series from the start, Kinsella's latest Becky story was just okay. The plot was very thin, but it did make for good 'fluff' reading for summertime.
It's lost it's quirkiness.

I'll read anything she writes as Sophie Kinsella. And the Shopaholic has been one of my favorite series. 
 I was disappointed with the last book as I felt it was just a stepping stone to this one. I was afraid with all the "mystery" surrounding Becky's Dad's Secret and the whole built up (it was going on till almost 60% of this book and I guess 30% of the previous one) , I'd be left disappointed. 
 And in way I was. It would have been a normal plot but the amount of clue searching and importance everything was given, the final reveal felt flat. 
 Becky wasn't even the crazy spender, story maker and good natured woman that we have grown to love. I think this was more of a transformation to an adult Becky Sophie Kinsella wanted. But it didn't work out well because she just stopped wanting to shop at one moment. And the actual why and struggles weren't addressed until much later in the book. 
 But this book did bring along ALL the characters at one go. I thought that would make it a real fun fest. And in the start it did give me some giggles. The book had some typical Sophie Kinsella laugh moments through out, but not too many. I did wish there was more. 
 There were so many mature issues to be considered with Suze and Tarkie's marital issues. Becky's parents relationship. Seeing both Becky's Dad and Tarkie left without saying a word and then doing it for the whole book. The reasoning why they did it didn't even fit. 
 Also, this wasn't Becky's story as much as it was of her Dad and some random people. Becky and Luke were just there along with the other characters. While Becky's Dad story unfolded. (where Becky's Dad wasn't even in present) 
 Every book in the Shopaholic series was centered around Becky and how she messed up and then did it again and again and how she saved the day. This wasn't like it. This was about everyone and Becky just seemed to be narrating it. 
 I feel the series has to end because now it's not the funny fluffy read it used to be. The plots are done, there is not much story left to tell. The end of this book with all the characters and the whole philosophy of friends and family being important -I felt it was a goodbye of sorts. But who knows? 
 If another book comes out, I'll definitely read it. Who am I kidding? But I really hope we get the authenticity of the Shopaholic series back. :)

Better than Shopaholic to the Stars (which I still think I sort of hated just because of the awful narrator in the audio book...) but not at all as enjoyable as the first few books in the series. It made for a fairly entertaining, easy read during a recent trip.

I absolutely loved the early shopaholic books. The first one was hilarious. The next few were very readable, and funny. Sadly they've just gone past their best. It still made me laugh out loud a couple of times though.
This book is as far away from how this book series started out. I don't like this development at all...

book_b.title: Burn for Burn (Burn for Burn, #1)
book_b.user_review: 3.5 stars. I can only assume that the ending was set up in the way that it is because there is another book that will follow, but if it is not, then I am baffled. I also did read an advance copy, so there may be that. This book is about three girls who have been wronged or feel that they were wronged by former friends and even by current best friends. They all live on a small island and attend the same high school. Lillia was having a great summer until one fateful night, and as the new school year begins, she is determined not to let her little sister fall in the trappings of the popular life. Kat used to be friends with Lillia and Rennie, but now she is just the butt of their jokes, especially of Rennie's cruel words. And Mary is back after being gone for the past 4 years. She is no longer the outcast fat girl and she wants to see the reaction of those that tortured her before. These three girls come together to teach everyone that wronged them a lesson - burn for burn, but is revenge truly sweet? That's what had me questioning the book the entire time. I get it. When you are the butt of someone's joke all you want is to get them back for it. But in the end, that isn't the healthy thing to do. Part of me did enjoy when certain retributions were made, this is fiction after all, but I don't agree that this behavior should be imitated and I hope that it will not be in real life. The writing was good, choppy at times which may be revealing of how the book has two authors. I liked that there were characters of a different ethnic background and most of the characterizations were definitely 'teen' in nature, although some characters spoke in a younger voice than they actually were in the story. I was not happy about the abrupt ending or the unnecessary supernatural twist that was thrown in, but I do hope that we can find out what happens in a sequel.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Book 2 in this series haunted me last night and I couldn't sleep because I keep thinking about all the small tips the authors gave us during the books that I did not notice before. I got that as a sign that I needed to write a review today. 
 Honestly, I went to this book expecting so little after being really disapppointed with The Summer I Turned Pretty by Jenny Han but now I'm so happy I gave her another chance because WOW, really, WOW this series is turning into one of my favorite things. 
 This is how to make me interested in your contemporary book: mix a little of Mean Girls, girls seeking revenge, girls turning into great friends because of revenge, teenagers acting like real teenagers, add a lot of Pretty Little Liars, just a tiny little bit of a supernatural mistery and A BIG cliffhanger at the end of each book. 
 If you think this is just another book about 3 girls playing around with small traps you are so wrong. At the end of book 2 it's closer to a thriller than anything else and I spent the last pages screaming: HOW IS THIS BOOK DOING THIS TO ME I'M SO SCARED. Then when I found out the next book is still going to take a few months to get out I freaked out a little bit, because honestly, you can just throw me this giant revelation and not expect me to be so curious. 
 Anyway, it's so hard to talk about this book because everything that makes it so good is a spoiler! Basically a story about 3 girls that found each other looking for revenge but end up getting in a big mess where they can't know who to trust anymore. Even if you don't get into the story in the beginning you should really try to stay till the last pages. 
 TW: drugs, alcohol, rape, suicide.

Since this was marked as a DNF read at Pg. 119, 
 this review only reflects the portion that I got through. 
 Unfortunately, I have nothing good to say about Burn for Burn, so if you're an avid fan of this novel, I suggest you leave now. Or else you're going to want to suckerpunch me in the end. Burn for Burn was an absolute catastrophe. It is my reason, embodied, for not reading contemporary novels. However, the premise and the gorgeous cover were impossible to resist. Three girls seeking revenge on the people who wronged them? I mean, come on, who could resist that. Sounds a bit like modernized Furies, does it not? But even though this novel had oodles and oodles of potential, as well as an absolutely gorgeous cover to support that potential, it unfortunately fell flat and made me want to chuck it into a fire and take off running. 
 So this novel takes place in a teensy, tiny island called Jar Island. Kat, Mary, and Lillia are three girls who are supposedly completely different from each other, yet strive towards the same goal. Sweet, sweet revenge. Yeah, no. Even though I saw what the author was trying to do, making three completely different characters by putting them in different social circles; The Outcast, The Popular, and The Runaway, they all seemed the same to me. Completely shallow. I would've expected the popular one to be conceited and annoying, but the outcast and the runaway? They were all immature, frivolous, stupid, superficial, brats. These people kept on jumping to conclusions when they should've just asked for the truth in the first place. The levels of irritation I'm experiencing right now astounds me. 
 Well, this is probably one of the shortest regular reviews I've ever written. There really is nothing else to write about, because nothing was memorable to me. Perhaps, their stupidity, but I already covered that in the last paragraph. There was no action, no suspense. Just frequent moments of facepalms, headbangs, and chucking books at walls. Overall, I'm definitely not going to be finishing this novel anytime in the future. In fact, I probably won't be picking up any contemporary novels for a while either. If you're already a huge fan of contemporary, unlike me, perhaps you will enjoy this novel more. However, if you're iffy about contemporary reads, run far, far away. 
 Heroines- 1/5 
 Action- 1/5 
 Romance- 1/5 
 Writing- 1.5/5 
 Overall- 1/5

Wow. 
 As cliche and unrealistic as this was, it was still really enjoyable!! This series will definitely be a guilty pleasure. (But I'm not gonna feel so guilty because it's really great.) The only other con is that the writing styles of both of these authors could be depicted when it comes to who wrote what. 
 Also, that ending??? I NEED BOOK 2 AND 3 NOW!!!!!!

In a quick summation 
 Burn for Burn was a book about three girls all unlikely brought together by their one common passion which at the moment was revenge. They each aid each other in getting revenge on the people they loathed most and in return they built a tight friendship, a ring of trust, and a feeling of righteousness- or at least that is until one of their plans on their chosen prey goes horribly and unexpectedly wrong and they are the ones in the crossfire of will they get caught, when will they get caught, and can they ever be the same again? 
 Burn for Burn teaches young adults that it's okay to screw up people's lives, as long as it's well justified, and as long as you can get away with it. Not only was the writing horribly un-descriptive, it was also premature and flat. 
 The pranks that these girls pulled gave me some giggles and chuckles here and there, but over all I really didn't like the story as a whole and I didn't like the message. 
 Revenge is sweet. 
 I get that. 
 You just got dumped or you just caught your boy friend cheating and you find satisfaction in slashing his tires or cementing his tooth brush-- or you work out and you bring that boy to his knees, making him realize he just lost the greatest girl he was ever going to get. 
 Whatever- point blank, revenge can be pretty awesome. 
 But also it can be stupid. Revenge can be like swallowing poison and anxiously and excitedly waiting for the other one to die. 
 Honestly, I felt that these three girls in Burn for Burn had no reason to try and get revenge. For the actions that they did, and what happened to them to fuel their reasons FOR those actions-- well it was all poorly justified. 
 AND THEN 
 what gets weirder is the more introverted of the three girls, Mary, she suddenly has some psychological power of telekinesis. This girl who should be in rehab or a mental institution, NOT back at her house where she tried to kill herself, and NOT back at her house alone with her depressed aunt, she suddenly becomes determined that when she screams she can slam locker doors shut instantly, she can break all the light fixtures in a gym, and she can make a girl fall off a cheerleading pyramid just with her gaze and her thoughts... 
 Not only did the author write this matter in a contemporary YA novel, a matter more falling under "psychological powers" NOT "summer friendships on a secluded island" but the authors also put this matter of Mary's new "powers" in the book- RANDOMLY. 
 When I first read that Mary was determined she was the reason why people were falling off of cheerleading pyramids, that she did it with her mind, I had to drop the book and look around for a second before asking "now where the hell did this just come from?" There was no initial referencing towards Mary having telekinetic powers- but also, the idea of it stuck out like a big ugly sore thumb. 
 Along with the ending not even being an ending- more like at the climax of this novel, someone just ripped the last pages out, this book was also 
 completely and absolutely predictable. 
 And then when it wasn't predictable- my predictions would have been better for the story than the actual story. 
 As for the sequel, Fire with Fire where the three girls are at it again but now their plan is to make Reeve fall in love with Mary (predicted that too-- saw the whole "John Tucker Must Die" blase thing) I'm not sure I'm going to be too anxious to pick up that book any time soon. 
 But who knows. 
 Maybe. Or maybe not. 
 Maybe I'll want revenge on myself, and reading that will be the perfect solution.

Honestly this book didn't live up to the hype. It was more boring than I imagined. Until the very end. And then it was over. Sigh. I hate that with series books. It's like you read the whole book just to wait another year. I was most interested in the relationship between Mary & Reeve. I hope there's more of that later. It was a fine book. I don't know. I guess I never felt overly invested in anything or anyone. 2.5 stars

In late middle school/early high school, my small class went through a transition period. This is the one point in time I look back and can pinpoint exactly when it became clear there was a hierarchy of popularity. Claws came out and some girls became mean while others remained innocent and naive. I was among the naive, not really understanding the social ladder. I wanted to be friends with everyone. 
 It didn't really make sense to me when gym clothes were stripped away from one of my friends while the native mean girls proceeded to use them as skates on the locker room floor and glide around on them. A group of about four girls tossed the clothes over our heads and played keep away. To this day, I'm not really sure where the desire for that kind of behavior comes from, but this experience made Burn for Burn more understandable for me. 
 Three girls, Lillia, Kat, and Mary all have some issue or event they want revenge for. They've individually experienced something that causes these three very different characters to forge together and promise to help one another out. These girls aren't in the same social circle; they have to learn how to trust one another as they become more deceptive and their revenge becomes more intense. 
 While I wasn't directly targeted in the above scenario, I do understand that it would have been nice for the bullies to receive payback for the torture they put my friend through. I could relate to Lillia, Kat, and Mary's pain, but the extremes they went to seemed a bit vindictive at times. I worried about all they had to lose as their plans got bigger and riskier. I was a mixed bag of emotions because I knew that the girls wanted closure for the pain they had suffered. However, I'm also a girl that doesn't necessarily believe in "eye for an eye" behavior -- it's nice to take the high road and resolve issues in less forceful ways. 
 Han and Vivian did an incredible job of seamlessly writing the story - I felt that each girl (since it was told from all of their POVs) was unique and I couldn't tell which sections were written by either author. The build-up was fantastic and there was an interesting dynamic between the three girls. I do hope in the upcoming books of the trilogy that we'll see each of the relationships explored a bit more - both with the team of three revengeful friends and the people they are out to burn. 
 Within the last fifteen percent of the book, there is a lot of explosive action. My heart raced and the crazy action made the end pass by quickly. I was left with a few particular questions about Mary and definitely have questions regarding the serious cliffhanger of an ending. I can promise you will be very "OH MY GOSH! WHAT JUST HAPPENED?!" as you close the book. Brace yourselves. 
 I'm very excited to see where Vivian and Han take this story in the upcoming books. For two authors I admire very much, I'm sure the message they'll be sending will be on pointe, even if I have a few lingering questions right now. 
 Review originally posted on Rather Be Reading.

Another book rather the last book, from the Heroes Of Olympus series. The blood of Olympus by Author Rick Riordon. ISBN 978-0-141-33925-2 Publisher Puffin Books 
 Seven half-bloods shall answer the call 
 To the storm or fire the world must fall 
 An oath to keep with a final breathe 
 And foes bear arms to the Doors of Death 
 The earth goddess has been rising through the past four books, Her minions the giants, the monster, the dead and the cursed all out there. this is the final battle for demigods. The Greeks and Romans, the Hunters of Artemis and warriors of Amazon. 
 The series has slowly lost its focus with the mark of Athena. It appears as though the book starts abruptly without following the flow from the previous book. This becomes more important since the roman and Greek demigods go on a joint quest beginning with the Mark of Athena. 
 The prophecy talks of seven on the quest, looks like Rick Riordon got his math wrong and he has not accounted for Reyna and Nicco who turn the quest to nine. 
 The book lacks the pace of the earlier series. And ambles along. With Leo finally going to Calypso to fulfil his promise, while the remaining eight put the earth back to sleep. 
 Athena Pantheons is supposed to heal the bridge between the Romans and Greeks, here we are introduced to Nikes the goddess of victory. She is in conflict with her Roman form Victoria. Then there is the Roman goddess Belladonna, of course she is also the goddess of strategy.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Giving this book 2 stars when I gave the rest of the series 3 gives the impression that I consider this book to be a step down in quality from the rest of the series and, although I found it to be disappointing as an epic conclusion to the series (the blood of Olympus was Percy's nosebleed, seriously?), I'm not sure if that's really the case. In reality I've probably been a bit too generous to the rest of the series in comparison to this book. 
 I've had issues with this series throughout however there has always been elements that I liked enough in every book to give it that extra star. When I read the first book, The Lost Hero, I found the central premise of the Gods having Greek and Roman aspects to be nonsensical & the 3 central narrators failed to engage me the way Percy's narration always has. However the story itself was as enjoyable as anything from the PJO series and I was prepared to go with it. The Son of Neptune was probably my favourite in this series. I don't know whether it was because we were back with Percy but I definitely found the story the most enjoyable overall and the setting of Camp Jupiter and all its internal politics was interesting and different enough that it convinced me this series might be worthwhile. 
 It was really with The Mark of Athena that things started to go downhill. Once 'The Seven' united I felt like the series devolved into a sequence of mediocre and unconnected side quests that all kind of merge together in my mind. The last 3 books all have elements in them that I appreciate: the spotlight on Annabeth in 'The Mark of Athena', Nico's development & Hazel's pivotal role in The House of Hades, getting Reyna's point of view in The Blood of Olympus. However I mostly found these books to be insubstantial, aimless and underdeveloped. Elements that have the potential to be interesting introduced and then dropped with no further development (Dark Percy, anyone?) and because of this the series lacks in emotional weight. 
 No one could ever accuse Riordan's books of being heavy. They are exclusively light, fun and humorous reads. The problem with HoO though is that it is so lightweight it feels like it could blow away at any moment and yet is simultaneously lacking in the humour that characterises the PJO series & the new Trials of Apollo which I am currently reading. (A side note: It's a weird thing to say because the consensus is that third person is almost always superior to first person but I think this series suffered from being written in third person - Rick's humour just simply works better in first.) You only have to compare The Last Olympian to this book to see the difference; The Last Olympian succeeds where this book fails at being an epic finale with actual emotional weight (I felt more for the death of Silena Beauregard who is a very minor character than I did for Leo who is a main, just as an example) AND manages to be the funnier book. 
 According to Goodreads, 2 stars indicates the reader's view on the book was that 'it was okay' and this is how I feel about the Heroes of Olympus series overall: it was okay. I appreciate it for introducing me to new characters that I love (although in all honesty Reyna is the only character introduced in HoO that I'm as attached to as the original PJO set) and for giving me more of my old favourites (I particularly love it whenever Thalia makes a cameo). I also appreciate Riordan's efforts in making this series more diverse than PJO by making 5 of the 9 characters who get a point of view non white and revealing Nico to be gay. Other than that, however, I'm struggling to think of what the point of this series even is.
What an explosive ending to such a great series. Rick Riordan is the man!

4.5 Stars. Definitely didn't like it as much as Me and Earl... But it's still written in that same humor and word vomit that I loved from MAEATDG, so yes!!!! 
 Wes and Corey are high school kids from Pittsburgh going to jazz camp in New Jersey for 2 weeks. Upon arrival, it's not turning out to be all that great. It's 99.9% boys (really really annoying boys), and after a try-out, they get put in the least talented jazz group. 
 During a brutal rehearsal, a scene erupts, leaving the pair sticking up for Ash- one of the only girls in the camp. The three feel like outcasts, and after an inspired jam-session, they decide to ditch the camp and go on their own adventure.... a road trip and an impromptu tour!! 
 My Thoughts: 
 Me and Earl and the Dying Girl was one of the funniest books I've read. It was one of those books that captivated me from the first page and had me laughing out loud in public places. To say that I was excited to read another book by Mr. Andrews is a severe understatement. I was DYING to read something else from him!! 
 First things: The cover!! I love it! It's so simple and eye-catching and cute. I also think the color is good for standing out. I also love a road trip book. This one follows 3 teenagers who form a spontaneous band and go on an unscheduled tour. Basically just driving to random cities and begging people to let them play... even if it's in backyards. There's something so fun about the idea of not having any responsibilities or technology (they turned off their phones). Just driving with friends and making memories without even being aware how awesome these memories are. Just living in the moment. 
 What I loved: I loved that even though the characters in this book were different from the characters in Me and Earl, the humor was similar. Now, I don't want you thinking that I was LOLing all over the place like I was with Earl. No, this book had it's moments, but I didn't think the humor was as off-the-wall as his first book was. Either that, or I've started to grow immune to immature teenage boy humor.... but I highly doubt that. 
 The three main characters are very hard to get to know. At first it seems like they all mesh and that they're all just your run-of-the-mill teenagers, but quite soon it's clear that they've got all kind of twisty issues within them. Wes is our main character, and his story-telling abilities are a bit out-there. There's major over-sharing and word vomit going on. But I found that's what is fun about Jesse Andrew's books. His characters over-share. They like to talk about their dicks (this character likes to talk about harming his dick). They like to have freak outs over things that wouldn't bother normal people. 
 What I didn't love: The humor was not as strong as I had hoped for. The LOL moments were minimal compared to my other experience with this author (although maybe it isn't all that fair to be comparing SO hard). Beyond that, there were some parts that got overly gross for me. And yeah, we get you like to joke about your nether regions, but after a while it's like no more please. Also, it was frustrating to read about people who didn't know what the heck was going on. Were they really a band? Were they any good? Did they suck? Were they friends? More than friends? What was the plan? Was the plan to have no plan? None of them knew. Which is FINE if that's the point... but I don't think it was. I think they wanted to know what they were doing, but could literally just not get it together enough to actually plan. At least that's the what Wes had going on, and he's our narrator, so..... 
 What I've learned after 2 of Jesse Andrews' books: This author is not going to write characters that you can put in a box with a bow around it. They aren't going to have massive "coming of age" moments and make HUGE realizations about life. They are prickly on the outside and you aren't going to pull back the layers and find that they have this glorious shining heart of gold underneath. That's just NOT what he does. His characters aren't here to teach you lessons, act the way you expect them to, or change. They are who they are, and I kind of love that about them. 
 OVERALL: I enjoyed this road trip book!! I liked the strong voice, the adventure, and the awkward teenage feel. Not as strong as the author's debut novel, but still worth reading if you liked that book.

Watched Me & Earl & the Dying Girl with my daughter and found it underwhelming in relation to all of the critical love it received. Didn't read it in book form and picked this up not fully realizing that it was the sophomore offering from the same writer. This book is all over the place and comes off as if the author had a great idea and then didn't really know how to execute that idea.

I've been trying to break out of my comfort zone and try more books that I wouldn't normally pick. And with such high praise for this author's first book I thought I would give this one a try. While I did like some aspects of this book, I ultimately think it was just okay for me. 
 One of the things I did like about the book is the humor and honesty. I think that Andrews definitely captures that whole teenage rebellion thing but he does it in a real way. There is a lot of swearing, inappropriate jokes, and even more inappropriate actions. It was rude and crude and I liked that. 
 But unfortunately that didn't really reflect very well in the characterization. I never really connected with these characters. They felt a little flat to me and were not at all likable. That's not a dealbreaker for me but when you have a character-driven book you kind of need good characters. I was hoping for an interesting book about friends forged and made stronger by shared experiences but this honestly was just people treating each other like crap and then realizing at the very end that they were being jerks. It didn't work on that level. 
 But the general plot development I think was the part that didn't work for me. I'm not a fan of road trip stories. For me that's not a plot point I enjoy and that was the basis for the story. And I think I would have liked it a little bit more if there had been some more self-actualizations and epiphanies on their travels but I didn't get that vibe. It was just people driving around and getting up to some shenanigans. Those aren't the kind of books that I like. 
 I don't think this was a bad book. I just think it isn't my kind of read. If you like road trips and crude kind of humor then definitely check this one. It's a fast and fun contemporary that I think big fans of the genre may enjoy.

Part travel story, part music story, part story of friendship, and part story of family. I liked it better than "Me and Earl and the Dying Girl." It was funny in places, but I think I am just too old to appreciate it.

Nope. Just nope. I can't do it. 
 I loved Me & Earl & The Dying Girl SO MUCH, but I can not stand this book. There's only so many dick jokes that I can take and it turns out that 100 pages worth is my limit. 
 Also, for those readers that miraculously made it to the part with the hotel sink incident...just UGGGGH. *shudders*

Here, Jesse Andrews settles hard into the niche he carved with Me and Earl and the Dying Girl. I can't say this is a bad thing though, as his boos manage well the things they attempt, and these things aren't just boring cliches that have been done thousands of times before. 
 In particular Jesse Andrews has a way of writing flawed, immature, and even grating characters that inspires more empathy than contempt. This is great, because for readers like myself who have been flawed, immature, and grating in similar ways are encouraged to think of our past-selves with an attitude of gentleness, rather than hating them or cringing away from the topic completely. So, his books are actually kind of therapeutic. 
 Other highlights include vivid and extremely fun descriptions, strong but non-idealized highschool friendships, people being interested in making art without necessarily being amazing at it, and a sneaky idealism hiding behind a disdain for the trite. 
 In the end there are a lot of great things here, but somehow I don't want to give this more than three stars. I enjoyed everything well enough, but I don't really expect it to stick with me. Maybe, like Me, Earl, and the Dying Girl, it will make a bigger impression as a movie.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This was an incredible read. Bella Aurora did a fantastic job creating this beautiful, emotional and funny story. The whole plot and characters were just simply captivating and original. The main characters are so unique I never read about such a pure pairing yet. 
 Mina is in a unique situation, she is homeless for a while now and her survival depends on a constant fight. Strangely despite her position she stayed positive and kind didn't become a bitter and evil personality. However in the beginning of the book she is an already desperate situation and makes a life changing decision. Lucky for her everything turns out fine and her life starts on a brighter path. She is really strong, hard working, honest, has a positive view of things a stayed surprisingly pure after 7 years on the streets. She throws herself into work and willing to do anything to better her life. I liked how she established a connection with Lev and his family. She just fits into their dynamics. After a while she opens up and blossoms out into a beautiful and kind woman. 
 Lev, I absolutely loved. His way of thinking and he stole my heart. He is a special cookie. He has all of the characteristics I require in a book hero. He is kind, funny, protective, hot and his 'mental situation' gives him an aloof kind of removed aura, way of thinking. I loved it. How he acted around his family, how he simplified thing most people usually over complicate. He became my favorite book boyfriend of this year. 
 Together he and Mia have an amazing connection, intensive chemistry and their relationship is so cute. Sometimes it felt like they lived in a bubble as either of them let the negativity and others opinion affect them. They remove themselves from the crowd, sometimes even the population. I really liked the way they worked together. Their pairing is a unique one and the idea behind their characters is really original. 
 What else? The supportive characters are so good to. Each one of them has a defined and strong personality and they all work so well together. They create the kind of family dynamic that I love in books. They all have really interesting background so I'm looking forward all of their individual books. 
 The plot is full of surprises and shocking revelations especially regarding Mia past. There isn't one boring moment in the book. The author created fantastic satiations and enjoyable dialogues. It's fanny, eventful and so sweet but has a darker side, too. The storyline is flowing seamlessly and the writing style is wonderful. This story is a truly marvelous read and highly recommended to contemporary and NA lovers. Believe me Mia and Lev sensual love story is going to sweep you off your feet. 
 Other reviews from me, here:FantasyRaiders

Mina is truly the epitome of strength, determination and fierceness. She didn't let homelessness or hunger make her a thief and she wasn't hardened by her circumstances. This is what made her perfect for Lev. 
 Lev, wow, just freaking wow! I already had some strong feelings right from the start, but before I knew it I was head over heels all tingly inside for him! Lev is different from any other alpha male (I should just come out and say bbf ) I have come across. Its the way he is, his honesty, his matter of factness his feelings. The suffering he went through as a child brought me to tears, no child should ever suffer because they are different from what their parent or any other person. Everything that Lev is though is what makes him so much more! 
 This was an amazing story. I loved the mixture of other characters and the multiple pov's. Everything ebbed and flowed very well!
4.5 I love Lev stars!!!!

3.5

OH. My. GER! I freaking LOVE Lev so much! I really enjoyed this book, it was a little awkward at times, but that was the best part! If I were to choose between chocolate and this book? I would totally choose chocolate. It's inevitable. But Lev would definitely come into a close second. *Taps finger against lips* I guess the best thing about this book was that it was unpredictable. I couldn't really guess what was going to happen (a very common concept within Belle Aurora books). 
 Everything between Lev and Mina was different than anything I've ever read before. Which of course, was wonderful because so many books are very similar in many ways. I mean this wasn't the first Belle Aurora book I've ever read, nor was it the first romance book. So it could've been girl falls in love blah blah blah. The thing is, it held the element of surprise. Some of these scenes were so Uber stressful, because I had no idea if they were going to be together or if she was just going to end up out on the streets again. I think part of the reason it was so surprising is because the characters were different. Lev took broody to another level. He was VERY different from any character I've read about. I can't really describe it (it's one of those you need to read it to see it moments) but he was different, in my opinion. 
 Mina was also a surprise. I always thought that the best part of Belle Aurora's books is that she always adds that sugar with that spice. None of the characters are the same and the girls especially all have that spunk with that spoonful of sugar mixed in. To me, I love characters like that. In other words, she brings out the best in her characters and doesn't muddle their personality because of the problems they face. 
 All of her side characters were also such a plus! I loved Sasha the most oooh and I can't forget Mina's brother! He was sooo adorbs even though he was such a butt at first! They gave this book that extra oomph that it needed and I LOVED IT!!! Like seriously! I AM IN LOVE!

sample_reviews.review_text: Julia Quinn hits another one out of the park. She gives us a feisty heroine in Billie Bridgerton and a somewhat pompous hero with George Rokesby. These two neighbors have known each other all of their lives but don't appear to have anything besides proximity in common. Billie is a tomboy who grew up getting into one escapade after another with George's younger brothers. As the heir to an earldom, George has had to maintain more dignity and assume more responsibility than his siblings. The book opens on a hilarious note. Billie (who is now 23 years old but not exactly an adult) has climbed a tree to save a stray cat. She falls onto the roof of an isolated building, spraining her ankle in the process. It appears that she is stranded there until someone comes to her rescue. And, of course, the first person to pass her way is George. I had assumed, based on the title, that this was another entry into the Bridgerton series. I was delighted to discover when I logged the book into Goodreads that it is actually the first one in a new series about the Rokesbys. I look forward to reading about the further adventures of George's brothers.

4.5 Stars 
 You can never go wrong with a Bridgerton book (even though it's a Rokesby series). 
 I read the whole book in one sitting, and thoroughly enjoyed it! I just felt it was a bit too short; maybe because I just wished it'd keep continuing. Oh well, I guess all good things come to an end. 
 I have to agree with most of the reviews given - it ended abruptly. I was just left thinking: "So... now what's next?" 
 The answer to which is kinda obvious... gotta wait for the next book to come out. To that, may I just say: ugh! Hate the waiting game. 
 I'm so in love with all the characters introduced in the book (especially the lead characters' mothers - hahahahaha, I so totally saw that coming! I had them figured! Love it!). At times like these, I wish I could read minds, that way I'd know what all my fave authors have coming up next in the series they write. Sigh.

This is a typical Bridgerton story - as promised, it is fun to read because as promised, it does have lots of witty repartee which is so reminiscent of the earlier Bridgerton books, there's an unconventional and smart heroine and a classy hero and there are some really awkward and sweet moments between them. Also, lots of noisy, close-knit family members getting in each other's business. And....we get to find out the history of The Mallet of Death. However, unlike many JQ stories, this one has a cliff-hanger ending (although the MCs get their HEA) 
 There's probably going to be lots of books on the other unmarried Rokesby and Bridgerton siblings: Edward, Andrew & Nicholas Rokesby and then Edmund and Georgina Bridgerton, although Edmund already has a story of sorts (he married Violet, right?). 
 Can't wait for the next one....

I absolutely adored Billie Bridgerton! It was nice to get back into that world and learn of the creation of the "Mallet of Death"! George had me the moment he went weak in the knees! Off to re-read the Bridgerton series!

Guys, I REALLY enjoyed this one. I'm not quite sure exactly why, but it REALLY worked for me. I liked that Billie wasn't typical, but she wasn't really one-sided either. She was mainly confident in herself and her abilities, but was still fragile about things that she knew she didn't do well. I just really dug this one.

Very nice story of an unconventional heroine who runs her parent's estate, is reckless, but smart. She has always been friends with 2 neighbor boys but, in this story, she falls for their dependable older brother. It was a sweet story.

Writing: 4.5 Star 
 Plot: 2 Stars 
 Characters: 3 Stars

 Read again? No 
 Total: 2.5 Stars 
 I loved the entire Bridgerton series by Julia Quinn, so when the new book came out featuring the next generation of Bridgertons, I was thrilled. The book started of well. We (the readers) had a spunky heroine reminiscent of Elizabeth Bennet and a hero of Mr. Darcy's potential. Perfect! 
 However, soon after the first few chapters this story fell apart. There was no question that these two would end up together. We know that they will end up together, because it is a Romance Novel, but there always has to be a question, a struggle to that ultimate happy ending. This book had no such struggle. Everything was very pleasant and civilised and, well, boring. There was a lot of talking with little substance. I still think that Julia Quinn is a great writer, but this book had no plot, or if it did it completely passed me by. There was an incident with one of the family members, but even that went nowhere. As a consequence, the characters had little to do, and ended up rather flat. There was not a single problem that the characters had to solve, that brought them closer together and made them realise they were perfect for each other. The hero had no heroic moments, the heroine did not save him... There were no villains! 
 Where was the nasty Miss Bingley? There was a potential Miss Bingley, but she was not that nasty and she was not the hero's friend. The heroine who was showcased as a tomboy did not even have a humiliating social moment, but was instead triumphant through and through! All the potential for a great romantic comedy that went nowhere. 
 This novel was a disappointment. I would like Ms. Quinn to rewrite it -- to create a better plot with villains and conflicts, because there are none.
Not as smooth a read as other Julia Quinn books.

I cannot believe that I am saying this about one of the lovely Julia Quinn's books, but I am decidedly underwhelmed. With barely any plot or character development to speak of, I do not understand how this "book" was conceived by the same author who gave us Romancing Mister Bridgerton. 
 Though I usually love it when authors revisit favorite characters, I think the Bridgerton series was fairly well tied up and did not need a prequel series. In fact, people who pick up this book with the original series in mind will be confused by the tenuous family connection to the seven boisterous siblings. I thought Julia Quinn was doing a wonderful job of expanding her universe by fleshing out the Smythe-Smith quartet, and I was hoping she would continue in the same vein. 
 All in all, a disappointing read. I would rather have seen a Pleinsworth Sisters series.
