book_b.user_review: This one's going to take a while ...

sample_reviews.review_text: I could not finish this book because I could get into it. Not as funny as the other Stephenson's. Too dry maybe. First time in a long time that I give up on a book.

I can see why this book was nominated for a Hugo, but I almost didn't make it through the first hundred pages. The pace is glacial. The expositions and the dialogs go on and on. And the characters not particularly engaging. Once it gets moving, the story is quite engaging. But it was 500 pages of story crammed into 800 pages. 
 Still, you've got to give Stephenson credit for finishing his story: an increasingly rare accomplishment these days. 
 Unlike many SF authors, Stephenson correctly identifies the difference between the apparent "gravity" of centrifugal force inside a rotating space habitat and real gravity. 
 Quibbles: On a planet apparently near Earth size, people travel about 4000 miles across the North Pole, occasionally at a walking pace, in about a week. He seems to confuse "fissionable" and "thermonuclear" once. "Consciousness" is "nonspatiotemporal"? If the Abre air is only partially breathable, what did Durant do for water? Since the geometers can travel (backwards) in time as well as hop between cosmic, saying that a particular event happened 100 years ago--or last week--is almost meaningless. 
 The ending was so predictable as to be a letdown.

This book made me want to add a new shelf - "shouldn't have finished". How can this be the same guy that wrote -Snow Crash- and -Diamond Age-? The story doesn't even really start until about 250 pages in and even after that there's hardly any action. No cool new devices, no 5 new ideas on every page. It was just really lame. 800+ pages of lameness, about 200 of which are philosophical exposition. 
 That said, the world building was good and the writing was fine, all that was needed was a story. I would have never finished this if it wasn't on audio and maybe that would have been a good thing. I was just too lazy to upload another book to my mp3 player. 
 The Baroque Cycle was starting to look good but now I'm totally put off of Stephenson. Can anyone tell me if it's similar to this?

I read 120 pages of this. That's plenty far enough for some sort of plot to develop, right? Well. Not that I could see. It's interesting on one level as Stephenson lays out his world. But nothing really happened . Moving along . . .

In writing this review, I'm faced with the fact that this is the 991st review of Anathem on Goodreads. It isn't the 991st detailed review, nor is it the 991st long review, but somewhere in those 990 other reviews, I'm sure other people have said anything I'm going to say, and probably better. (How Lorite of me.) Yes, the book is long, and yes, it's a dense philosophical exploration of our universe disguised as a philosophical exploration of an alternate universe. But how did it affect me? 
 It just worked out that I read Anathem while beginning two philosophy courses: Philosophy of Science Fiction and Philosophy of Science & Technology. The serendipity of this will be apparent to anyone who has read Anathem, for the book is very much a philosophy text, and much of its philosophy has to deal with science and how people should go about doing science. As a mathematician myself, I have to admit I sometimes wonder what it would be like if we had "mainstream" monasteries consisting of nothing but academics. On that level, Anathem is an interesting thought experiment. 
 Also, Anathem reminded me of the importance of keeping the notions of "science" and "technology" separate. There is an intriguing scene between Erasmas and Cord while they are travelling toward an Arctic sledge post in pursuit of Orolo: 
 "I guess because I live in a place with almost zero praxis, it never occurs to me to think about such things," I said. "But at times like this, the absurdity hits me between the eyes. There's no reason to put up with junk like this. A stove with dangerous, unreliable chemical fuel. With orifices that clog. In four thousand years we could have made a better stove." 
 "Would I be able to take that stove apart and fix it?" 
 "You wouldn't have to, because it would never break." 
 "But I want to know if I could understand such a stove." 
 "You're the kind of person who could probably understand just about anything if you set your mind to it." 
 "Nice flattery, Raz, but you keep dodging the question." 
 "All right, I take your point. You're really asking if the average person could understand the workings of such a thing . . ." 
 There are two points here. The first is very relevant to our current society: many of us walk around with computers in our pocket that are more powerful than those that took us to the moon (looking at it from that perspective, the moon-landing becomes an even more impressive achievement, but I digress). Nevertheless, how many of us can take apart an electronic device and say, "Aha, this is so simple! I understand how this works!" I couldn't, and I'm a pretty smart guy. I'm not saying that such technology is bad, but as Erasmas and Cord discover, it leads to a dependence on the type of people who do understand it. And we, as a society, need to understand this dependence lest it lead to the sort of problems that Arbre experienced in its past. 
 The second point is relevant to all times: technology advances regardless of science. The scientists on Arbre are all sequestered in maths, but the extras keep developing new technology and new formats (the speelycaptor is a good example of this trend). The science remains nearly static, four thousand years stale . . . but the technology changes. While it's true that scientific and technological innovations can go hand in hand, that isn't always the case. 
 I went through three "stages" with regards to how I felt about the world of Arbre. In the first stage, I was fascinated but bored. I was interested in learning how the avout/Saecular dichotomy worked and figuring out more of the rules of Arbran society. Yet much of the description and exposition is tedious at times. In the second stage, which arrived much later in the book, I became disenchanted with Arbre because of the blatancy of the parallels between it and Earth, especially in the development of theorems in the mathic world. Finally, by the end of the book, I reached the third stage: acceptance. The parallel nature of Arbre is probably the cleverest way that Stephenson could have accomplished what he set out to do. It has flaws, but no narrative approach is perfect. 
 The world of Arbre is well-defined, but it was not immersive. The sheer amount of terminology Stephenson introduces is dazzling to the point of blinding. Part of the trouble is that I'm in that unhappy middle portion of the population of readers, where I recognize most of the concept's he is duplicating in Arbre, but I can't readily put an Earth philosopher/scientist name to the Arbran one. Anathem makes it evident that there is a point at which, if you introduce more terminology, you will start getting diminishing returns. 
 I'm not so certain Anathem is really a "philosophical primer" or even a "philosophical text" so much as it is an exercise in thinking philosophically. As the story opens, Fraa Erasmas is already a philosopher, but his way of thinking matures throughout the book. Each digression into a Dialog about some form of philosophy isn't as much a way to teach us the philosophy as it is an opportunity for the reader to stop and just think differently. Most books, even if they have moving, poignant themes, simply don't do this. 
 Although impressed by the deftness of Stephenson's world-building, I can't manage to feel very enthusiastic about the result. My feeling about Anathem, which is one reason this review took so long to write, is a distinctly apathetic, "So what?" Yes, it's philosophical. Yes, it's challenging at times. In the end, however, I don't feel like Anathem changed the way I think about anything, and I don't feel like the story itself moved me. 
 So this is where I talk about Anathem's length--or rather, its complexity. There's no question that the sheer physical presence of the book will scare away some people. Even I questioned my desire to read it now, at the beginning of a new school term, as my third book of a new year. Now I feel dreadfully behind! And at times, it is slow going. Yet I can only think of two alternatives: make the book shorter or turn it into a series, and neither seems appropriate in this case. Oh, I do think some parts could have been edited out, but removing some of Anathem's complexity runs the risk of destroying the fragile truce it has achieved with the amount of philosophy and physics Stephenson has packed into the text. On the other hand, I can only see Anathem as a standalone book. It is a self-contained narrative. 
 Hence, Anathem's complexity is inherent in the story Stephenson wants to tell. There is no way the book could work like it does without this complexity. Yet the same complexity that enables the book also seems to make it fall short of its goal. Anathem never captured my imagination so much as it held my imagination at gunpoint while it read a lengthy list of demands.

I'd like more plot to go along with the speculative dialogues. In some ways it reminds me of Tolkien: creation of an alternate universe, a group of friends begin a quest and find help along the way from a variety of others, a lot of linguistic play, and in the end good seems to win.

I could have tagged this book with almost every one in the list. It's just shy of 1000 pages and densely packed with ideas, most of them at least moderately interesting. I'm not sure it's a book I could recommend to everyone - it's not exactly fast-moving, and some days I realize that my reading speed makes some books engaging that would be plain boring at a more sane pace, but it's overall a fascinating work and I'll be chewing over bits of it for a long, long time.

Reading this book was a surreal experience. Not only did I fight my way through the first part, filled with back story, world building,nonsensical words and set up, the pages themselves would fall out and flutter away. It didn't even matter if I stuck them back in whatever way, nothing made sense and there wasn't a compelling story either. I don't even know what made me keep reading. My style is to skim over "filler" stuff so I skimmed a lot and just picked out what story there was. 
 Now, after reading all that, you're wondering why I gave this book 4 stars, right? Well, around page 170 (I kid you not) suddenly, out of no where, we have a story, we have a sense of humour, we have intriguing ideas explored in intriguing ways, we have drama,adventure, emotion-even a romance. And then it's compelling reading all the way to the end. I even made sure to read the pages that fell out. I didn't want to miss anything. 
 So hang in there. Honestly, it's worth slogging through the first (170!) bit.

This was hard for me to get into, but it was worth it. I'll be reading it over again after I let it percolate in my brain for a while; Stephenson did a good job of presenting the math, science, and philosophy theoroms and whatnot clearly, but it's still a stretch for me. The first 100 pages or so were slow going for me - took me a couple of weeks. The remaining 700 pages went much faster; around the 500 page mark I started getting annoyed if traffic wasn't heavy during my bus commute.

I must admit that at the end of this book my reaction was "finally". I'd been pretty much ready for it to end for some time...probably before encounter. 
 The book is (in my opinion) more of an "experience" than a story. It's an intricate exercise in world building that takes things from "the world" and altering them just a bit sets up a layered society. 
 The best part of the book in many ways is/are probably the the dialogs based on the logician debates. I haven't spent a lot of time reading philosophy in recent years and don't have the advanced math that a lot of the views here are based in, still aside from the frequent use of the "straw man" fallacy the set piece debates carry some interest. 
 The story follows it's arc through intro of the "Concents", their more or less monastic thinkers or intellectuals and their relations with the seculem those who live in the secular world (interestingly of course the monastic orders are largely irreligious, but those who who live outside are still the secular world.) The story is of the society and the gathering of evidence of an "extra-Arbreian" intelligent life form (Arbre being the planet) and what appears to be a UFO. 
 More of course would be "spoilerish". 
 I wasn't really taken with the book, I didn't hate it nor did I enjoy most of it overly. I would have preferred to put the time into reading some of the other books I have waiting. So..to you who enjoy this I'm happy for you. I don't plan at this time to run down further works by this author.

sample_reviews.review_text: Kills and I mean kills to rate a KA book lower than 5 stars but I needed more drama!!! I needed something to go down with Benito... Kidnapping.. SOMETHING I liked this story but it honestly fell a little short and that makes me sad because I LOVE KA so hard.... What's coming next.. I am feeling some love for Jed and I seriously hope it's more along a dream man or Colorado mountain book... This was a little soft for me... :(

The only thing that kept this from being a four star read was... Kids and repetition. 
 Story line was easy to understand and the sex scenes were of the vanilla kind. A classic Kristen Ashley, bad ass tough biker falls for hot crazy "straight" woman. 
 I realize that most people after 30 usually have kids, but it seems that ALL of the kids in these books are too perfect and too willing to let the step-mom or step-dad in. But, I am not the writer and this is really fiction! 
 The repetition comes from cross over phrases that I have read in other story lines. 
 I do like this Chaos story line and will read another.

Lanie is Tyra's best friend, so therefore she's part of the Chaos family. It's been several years since her fiance's connections with the mob almost got her and Ty killed, and did get him killed. She's still not over losing the Elliot, or the nightmare of how she lost him. So when she approaches Hopper 'Hop' Kincaid for a no-strings, one night stand, he knows there will be complications. He just can't resist her. 
 ***Spoilers*** 
 Lanie and Hop fall for each other quick, and hard. They both have their own baggage and several times try to walk away. Neither of them let on to their friends what's going on. The story falls in line with Tabby and Shy's story, some overlap there. Her parents are nuts, mom is an alcoholic who can't get over the only man she has ever loved has been seeing another woman for the last couple of decades, and her dad is too much of a coward to break it off. She knew Elliot wasn't her knight in shining armor, but she did know he wouldn't ever cheat on her. I think I would rather be cheated on, than become his personal shield against the mafia.. Hop has his own baggage, his psycho ex wife, and the son that no one knows isn't really his. Tack loses his shit when he finds out about another brother sleeping with one of the women close to his family. They explain the situation, and everyone is cool. Lanie finds out she is pregnant, but doesn't want to get married. Hop takes it that she doesn't want to get married, not that she doesn't want to be married. So naturally he kidnaps her and takes her to Vegas. With no plans, no dress, etc. it's all totally different than Elliot, and just what she needed. Chaos is not officially at war with Benito, since he drew Chaos blood. The guys were called in to rescue Natalie, Tabby's bff when her dealer demands she work off her debt on one of his porn sets.

eARC provided Grand Central Publishing and NetGalley 
 I could NOT wait to read this next installment in this series and again Kristen Ashley knocked it out of the park once again but this book did have a different feel than her others. 
 I love how this book was happening in a parallel time frame as Shy and Tabby's book making the build up of what to come with Benito into quite the angst. The only downfall to parallel time frames was there was very little Shy in this one but the good news was there was loads of Tack. 
 I wasn't sure if I was going to love Hop from his indiscretion from Motorcycle Man 
 As well as Lanie's loving but poor decisions in her past. 
 But together 
 For Lanie she was guarding her heart 
 For Hop he wasn't looking for love 
 But Lanie put up road blocks where ever she could 
 Hop felt once he had class he couldn't let go. He knew what he had and didn't want to let go. 
 As soon as Hop and Lanie got together you almost forgot about their pasts and just wanted them to break through their shit together even though there were a lot of internal and external interferences that were going against them. 
 Hop changed Lanie's world by letting her finally live. 
 When rules didn't apply, only feelings did. 
 You went with your gut, you led with your heart, you did what you wanted and you didn't think of consequences. 
 You lived. 
 You were free 
 I did really enjoy Lanie and Hop the only thing I didn't feel was her nickname 'Lady' I loved the sentiment about it but throughout the whole book every time I read it, it seemed to grind on me a bit but other than that I loved it and can't wait to find out about the shit storm that is brewing in Denver.

Rating this book 5 stars is just so wrong but its the highest option I have I LOVED LOVED LOVED LOVED LOVED LOVED this book yes it was that good. What is there to say but that I loved this book, but then again any book from Kristen Ashley is bound to be excellent. I waited and waited for this book the wait was torture I thought I would never get to read it. I craved this book, every other book seemed to fall by the way side when I thought of Fire Inside BUT(yes thats a big but) the wait was so worth it. 
 So here's the given if the book is written by Kristen Ashley it will be filled and over flowing with hot, possessive, strong, domineering, demanding, did I say hot men, a great heroine that I wish was my friend (and friends with her friends as well) a great story line, great dialogue (that is uniquely Kristen Ashley) and a book that I finish way to soon. So some questions you may ask, would I read this book again? psh absofreakingloutly. Would I recommend this book? why are you asking these crazy questions, I can't even dignify this crazy question with an answer. Was it KA greatness? most defiantly. Did my life revolve around Hop and Lanie? oh yes it did, and did it stand up to book one Own the Wind? and the answer to that is a 100% positive most defiantly. 
 Fire Inside starts in the same Time Frame as Own the Wind, after seven years of holding herself back from living Lanie has decided that it is time to make a step forward and that step will be to sleep with someone and Lanie has the perfect person in mind. She knows Hop would never demand or want more than one night so when Hop agrees Lanie knows this is the perfect time to start to heal herself. Lanie and Hop jump head first into their one night together, when Hop wakes up he knows that he hasn't had enough of Lanie and he isn't ready to walk away till he has. 
 With Hop and Lanie agreeing to continue in their physical relationship only, Hop and lanie soon find out that there is so much more to the other than they ever thought and that keeping everything hidden and uncommitted is growing harder and harder. Soon Lanie is pressured to start dating by those who love her and she and hop will have to decide what is really brewing in this unrelationship that is growing in more ways than one into a very real relationship. All the while Hop is having to deal with trouble coming at not only the club but at his brothers and his self as well. But as everyone soon finds out in life secrets can't be hidden for long. 
 So yes I loved this book, yes I love Hop, he completely redeemed himself or I should say his story was finally told so that I don't think he is a horrible person, I think Hop is an awesome person, father, man and friend. I think Hop and Lanie are perfect for one another he was just what she needed, he protected her, he had her back, and he was soft place to fall, he respected her and loved her more than any woman ever. And Lanie was made just for Hop and the love she had for not only him but his kids was beautiful. So why am I sad( and yes I am so so sad) and that my friend is because I am now in the throws of KA withdraw and no matter how many of her books I read and no matter how many times I go through this I'm still never prepared for feeling at a loss when I finish her books, and I know nothing will help till I have my next Kristen Ashley book in my hands. 
 **Thank you NetGallery for this ARC copy of Fire Inside** 
 **and just a side note I pre-ordered this book the second it was available for pre-order and even though NetGallery and Hachette Book Groups so graciously gave me an ARC copy I am still keeping my pre-order because I love KA so much and think this book is so great I want to show her my support, so yes this book was that good**

 Ready for book 2.

This book has an amazing over-all rating so I was very intrigued. Unfortunately this book could not hold my attention. I couldnt get on board with the main character and her near constant need to screw over the people around her.

Ellie Watt is the daughter of grifters -- con artists that began using her at a young age to help them get what they wanted. She's had a rough life, to say the least. After being deserted by her parents and left to struggle through her high school years in the home of her Uncle, Ellie takes off and starts her own life as a con artist. After years of perfecting her craft, twenty-six years old now, she is on the run from a con gone wrong, which is nothing new for her, and ready to take back her real identity. 
 "I was used to running and always kept a spare life in the trunk. Spare clothes, spare driver's licenses, spare Social Security numbers, and a spare tire." 
 Ellie has played the role of many different people through the years and she wants nothing more than to go back to her home town with her Uncle and start over - totally legit. When she arrives back in Palm Valley, though, her plans to head down a straight and narrow path go right in the crapper, and it all starts with smokin' hot Camden McQueen. Of course, it doesn't end there. It's not nearly as simple as just a guy from her past. There's another guy, from a time between her past and present, loads of dirty money, and a stolen car. 
 Sins & Needles is ... WOW. I don't even know where to start with this one. There's simply not a significant enough way to express how well written this book is, how gritty and intense the plot is, how vibrant the characters are portrayed. The story flows so perfectly, even the flashbacks to Ellie's high school years, when the relationship between she and Camden first developed, is seamless. This book is not for the faint of heart. It's raw and real, no sugar coating involved, and at times very steamy. 
 My feelings for Ellie Watt flip flopped a few times. At first I thought, "Yeah, this chick is totally bad ass!" She's tough, clever and freaking hilarious, she doesn't put up with any shit from anyone. After meeting Camden.. oh, Camden.. I became so angry with Ellie. I didn't understand why she was scheming again so quickly after declaring her plan to change her ways. I really wanted to punch her. Why does she have to screw everyone over? I felt protective of Camden, which is strange because he is this beautiful, blue-eyed, muscular, tall drink of water, obviously not in need of my help, but still. Throughout the story my feelings for several characters alternated, which was extremely interesting to me. It was incredible how much I felt like a part of this story, as if I was watching it unfold with my own two eyes. And then the way it ended.. GAH! I wanted to immediately begin reading On Every Street, the prequel/backstory on Javier -- oh, you'll meet him, too, the evil, sexy bastard -- but I had a NetGalley to Kindle issue and just about screamed and woke up my family in the middle of the night when I realized it was missing. I really want to read that one before moving on to Shooting Scars! 
 Anyway, Sins & Needles is freaking phenomenal and I highly recommend it to all fans of adult contemporary (dark, twisted, sexy) romantic thrillers. This is a fast-paced book full of intense action, heartache, and an extremely dangerous road to redemption mixed with steamy romance. I may just have to set aside a few weeks to do nothing other than read Karina Halle books.

"I'm not bad. The world is bad and I'm just trying to survive in it." 
 An kai ekhoun perasei polles meres pou ekho oloklerosei to proto biblio tes trilogias "Sins & Needles" akoma duskoleuomai na grapso ten kritike mou. Den exera ti akribos na perimeno xekinontas to. Eikha akousei oti einai polu diaphoretiko apo alla tou eidous alla eniotha pos den tha mporeso na sundetho mazi tou. Terastio lathos! To agapesa. Agapesa kathe sunaisthema pou mou edose. Prote phora diabazo kati tes Karina Halle kai to mono sigouro einai pos den tha einai e teleutaia...! 
 "Beautiful, sad, wounded, and lost... A freak, a work of art, a liar, and a lover." 
 E Ellie Watt megalose me duo goneis apateones. Megalonontas iskhorei kai e idia se auto ton tropo zoes. Oi goneis tes omos ten egkataleipoun otan mia apate paei polu askhema me apotelesma na trekhei oloi tes ten zoe. Kourasmene pia apo ola auta thelei na zesei mia ereme kai nomime zoe. Gurnaei piso ston topo opou megalose me ten elpida pos den tha ten thumatai kaneis. Kanei aitese se ena kaphe otan pephtei pano se enan palio philo tes apo to gumnasio. O Camden pou apo to phrikio goth agori tou skholeiou einai pleon enas sexy kallitekhnes tatouaz. 
 "I have to live with my mistakes, but I dont have to regret them. I regret my actions but I can't regret the consequences. We all make our own paths in life. Everyone we meet, everything we do, it changes us. It makes us who we are. And, if we're lucky, we're given the chance to make things right again." 
 Latrepsa ten isorropia pou uperkhe anamesa sto romantismo, ten drase, ten agonia kai to khioumor. Epises e enallage ton POV se kratouse se egregorse. Eno khares auta mporesame na sundethoume kai bathutera me to backstory tes istorias mas. 
 Apo ten alle pleura agapesa kai misesa ten idia stigme olous tous kharakteres tou. Thelo na skholiaso tosa pragmata pano se auto alla tautokhrona den thelo na sas kano kapoio spoiler kai na makregoro. To biblio einai skoteino kai terma realistiko. Oloi oi kharakteres, kathenas apo autous einai elattomatikos. Den uparkhoun pragmatika kale e kake. O Camden einai enas orgismenos anthropos, pragmatika sparaze e kardia mou otan diabaza gia ta ephebika tou khronia. Eikhe merikes polu treles stigmes alla pragmatika ton agapesa. Eikhe tose diastase. Ten mia stigme etan alazonikos kai sexi, ten alle sokaristika tromakhtika ekphobistikos kai telos omos kai romantikos. Apo ten alle e Ellie mou pere polu khrono na ten sunethiso kai na ten katanoeso. Antitheta me alles paromoies istories edo den uparkhei pragmatika bad boys alla bad girl. Autarkhike, paizei me ton kinduno kai tous anthropous. 
 "Do you think because you can't see my scars that they don't exist? That's the trouble with pain, Ellie. If you're lucky, you can wear it for all the world to see. Most people have their pain deep inside them, in places no one ever goes. Not until its too late." 
 To oikopedo etan phobera dunato kai exupno. Me sunepere kai me sugklonise para polles phores. E skhese metaxu tes Ellie kai tou Camden oi anatropes kai ta nemata me ekane na anarotiemai sunekheia gia to ti ginetai pragmatika ti einai aletheia kai ti psema. 
 "Someone who was asking me out on a date, to see his show. And I was thinking two things: 1) I can't afford to befriend anyone, let alone someone I wouldn't mind seeing naked and 2) how much cash could I take from him before I hated myself" 
 Gemato drase, romantismo kai apsoga grammeno. Ena biblio prototupo okhi mono logo tes istorias tou alla kai tes proseggises tou. To telos mporei na men etan akribos aprosmeno alla etan toso iskhuro pou se sunepairne! To sunisto anepiphulakhta. 
 "I hope I'm always a part of you, Eden. You'll forever be a part of me. A world without you in it is a song without the music. You need both to make it whole."

reference_books.title: Throne of the Crescent Moon (The Crescent Moon Kingdoms, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
The book was not bad for me, but it was not overly good either. It took me a week to finish the last 50 pages: though it was about the major good vs evil battle, it failed to keep me captivated, and the ending was predictable - just like Chechov's gun. 
 In addition, I think, there is not enough language and style consistency to the Middle East atmosphere. 
 One of the strong sides is the variety of so called "every-day moral dilemmas" that our heroes need to resolve. 
 I would recommend it to the genre lovers only.

reference_books.title: Death Comes to Pemberley
reference_books.review_text:
This was really disappointing, both as a homage to Jane Austen and as a murder thriller. Apart from rather Austen-ish prologue and few more lines that are actually a P&P rewritten this book is simply very weak. 
 If you look at it as a P&P sequel then the style and characters are completely wrong. There is very little interaction between Elizabeth and Darcy, and it seems that Darcy suffers from a severe amnesia - after six years of marriage he has completely forgotten all the mistakes he made prior to it. Elizabeth looks too weak and lifeless to suit me. 
 If you look at it as the murder thriller, then the plot is really weak and somewhat illogical, there is no investigation to speak about, no thrill and no tension are built and the resolution comes in a rather illogical and unreasonable way. 
 BBC 2013 series change the plot a little, add some colour to the characters and overall improve the story significantly.

book_a.title: Gentleman Jole and the Red Queen
book_a.user_review:
It's complicated. 
 Bujold is one of my favorite authors and yet this probably is going to be my least favorite book in the series. I say probably, because I've finished the eARC in less than two days and will re-read it in a short while to get a better grasp on the finer details. 
 Based on this first and very fast reading I'd say the book lacks a prominent plot, the conflict implied is solved too easily and too many heroes are mentioned often enough to become part of the story but fall short on the in-depth development. 
 On the strong side, I love Cordelia moving on after Aral's death, and I like the direction her life is taking. It's good to see Miles growing up even more and it's reasonable enough to understand that his life with Ekaterin isn't all roses. And of course, all the social - genetic and moral - issues are the very high bar set for the reader to ponder at. 
 So far I don't like the book as a whole, but I lover the bits and pieces - I had things to mull about and plenty of fun while reading.

sample_reviews.review_text:
How the mighty have fallen. 
 That was my first reaction after reading this book. But still, I feel I can't dole out such harsh commentary about a book from a beloved series without expanding my thoughts. I have a long history and sentimental attachment to the Miles Vorkosigan series. 
 Around the ages of 13-14, I devoured the majority of the series (barring the last two novels). I witnessed it all: the days of sacrifices, pride and glory; then Miles' attempts to find his place under the sun; his numerous nail-biting adventures; his eventual faux-pas and major career change, up until the chronologically last Cryoburn. I grew fond of the novels, and especially Miles. I also admired how Bujold crafted the series. As a series which spans such a long period of time, it's only normal that Miles evolved during the time, along with the inevitable transformations in his family. Consequentially, changes of pace and genres in the later novels are expected and welcome occurrences. Heck, I've enjoyed entertaining romps like A Civil Campaign and more recently, Captain Vorpatril's alliance quite a bit. 
 Before Gentleman Jole and the Red Queen was out, I expected a more quiet, subdued book. After all, it takes place after Cryoburn and it would star Cordelia as the protagonist, so I imagined it would be... not quite a sombre affair, but certainly different in tone than Shards of Honor. 
 And I got a more quiet book - I can't complain. But - and there's a huge but - there were other things that were not to my liking. 
 As the majority of other readers and reviewers have noticed, there is a revelation in the very first chapters of the novel. Some people may find it disturbing, some may find it amusing, but I think it's safe to say it's a bolt out of the blue. So much a bolt out of the blue, my dear friends, kind neighbours, that I can only agree with the majority and call it a retcon. Frankly, I still can't believe it. Maybe it's that 13-year old kid talking out of me, that kid who imagined Aral and Cordelia as a prototype of a powerhouse couple. They were so cool and right for each other that I could never imagine a third person there. That hypothetical third person - or third wheel, whichever you prefer - would only break the symmetry, the beauty of their yin and yang. It simply does not compute to have a third person there! But let's put aside the personal feelings of that kid here. Let's talk about facts. 
 The majority of the books from The Warrior's apprentice onwards were from Miles' POV. Some may argue that, during those books, he spent most of his time away from Barrayar, getting himself in all sorts of scrapes, and getting himself (and the Empire) out of them. I agree with that, but darn it, isn't Miles an intelligent, perceptive guy? Wouldn't he have noticed something? Heck, he figured out about lady Alys and Illyan sooner than anyone else ! This is what offends me the most - Miles being relegated as some sort of bumbling Homer Simpson who can't put two and two together. 
 But okay. Let's say that Miles is some sort of bumbling Homer Simpson who can't put two and two together. However, he's not the only character who gets his POV. In the later books, we are privy to other people's thoughts, like Mark, Ekaterin and Ivan. Is Mark an idiot who can't put two and two together? For heaven's sake, he was programmed to kill Aral, wasn't he supposed to notice things about his target ? Also, I recall a conversation Mark had with Cordelia in The Mirror Dance, where he directly asked her about Aral's orientation. Wasn't he supposed to sniff out her lie? . Even that idiot Ivan may have had a chance discovery. But no, in an assortment of other characters who have their own POV, no one suspects a thing. To top it off, not one of Aral's and Cordelia's enemies, folks whose job is to dig dirt, has suspected a thing! So what's this, a miracle? Or a retcon? I'll let you decide. 
 Apart from my essential disagreement with the retcon this novel introduces, I don't have much to say about it. I have fully expected it to be an introspective book, but there is too little action going on, even for me. Regardless of how much I like Cordelia, there was not enough material here for a full-fledged novel, more so because she doesn't face any real obstacles. Shards of Honor and Barrayar were all the more interesting precisely because Cordelia had so many challenges and difficulties to overcome. In this novel, she is a powerful Vicereine who is always right, and it never takes her much to convince everyone else that she is right, whether it's Sergyar politics or her own personal decision of siring more children. I'm sorry, but that's not the way things work. 
 As for Jole and his falling for Cordelia - ever since I heard the title of the novel, I figured that was supposed to happen. For me, that is totally okay . However, that development was shot in the foot thanks to the retcon. I would have found it much more natural - and more challenging - if there wasn't that silly menage a trois thing . Without the retcon and the "secret history", we would have the privilege of watching how Jole and Cordelia surpass the bounds of their secretary-admiral/employer-Vicereine relationship, which would have been professional and friendly, into a romantic one. But unfortunately, since they already have a common history, that is already taken away from us . Furthermore, Cordelia's gift of genetic material to Jole in the beginning, which started the ball rolling, would have worked even without the menage a trois. Actually, it would have been a fitting gift to Jole after so many years of hard graft alongside Aral, without any romantic involvement . But no, why make things more challenging for the characters... 
 Miles doesn't make a huge appearance in the novel, which is a minus. This story would have benefitted from more Miles and his antics. 
 To summarize this long-winded review: 
 In the glorious Miles Vorkosigan series, Gentleman Jole and the Red Queen is the dud of all duds. There is not much happening here; it's almost all talk, very little action, and very few memorable events. Character development is a thing of the past, because of the non-existent plot and lack of challenges the characters face. However, the novel is not a complete fiasco thanks to Bujold's writing style and flashes of humor that manage to shine through in critical moments. Nonetheless, that was not enough to redeem this book. If anything, this is an example of what happens when you milk a book series for all its worth. It comes awfully close to beating-a-dead-horse territory. In my mind, this is borderline fanfiction and not a part of the Miles Vorkosigan series. The Vorkosigan series ends with Cryoburn, which makes a full circle. 
 I grant it two stars because, despite all its shortcomings, it's still incomparably better than... *drumroll* 
 Logan's run 
 .

This was probably the least eventful book of the series. While I liked the introduction of some new characters, and I naturally relate to a lot of the "dad stuff", there just wasn't much to invest me in the story.
the author has lost touch with Vorkosigan's world
Excellent, as always. It's nice to see the family going on and getting up to its usual shenanigans, and I'm so glad Cordelia seems like she's going to have a good next chapter of her life.

I love Bujold, but this might have been the weakest book she's written. It's become clear that her personal life often colors her novels, and I find myself (selfishly) hoping that something horrible will happen to inspire her to greatness again!

Hardly a stand-alone novel, this addition to the Vorkosigan saga knits a bundle of story-lines together while creating the potential for an entirely new web of possibilities. The Bujold facility for writing very human characters is on display and though the story on the whole is not compelling, is familiar and comfortable to long time readers. The door may be open to new stories and new Vorkosigans, I wonder if this isn't rather a signal the series may be at an end. 
 A pity, if so - I had hoped for a prequel of sorts of Count Piotr's war, perhaps part of the history Duv Galeni has written.

I really wanted more character development and talk about the relationships between the characters. I got what I wished for and regretted it. 
 The best thing I can say about this book is that I'm happy for Cordelia and I hope these plans go well for her. And I'm happy that there was a stable polyamorous relationship represented despite, you know, Barrayar. But the book itself wasn't that interesting, which is a shame.

Yeah so... that's going to be book #2 that I do not finish this year. I stopped about halfway through, after ruminating for a few days. What a dangerous precedent to set! 
 The why is sort of spoilery. Read below at your peril, though I will try to limit the amount of information to a minimum. 
 The main problem I have with this new Vorkosigan book is that it isn't really science fiction, and it even hardly qualifies as space opera anymore. What it is, is a romantic comedy slash social commentary, variously touching on: the joys and mysteries of parenthood, unconventional romantic structures, sexuality of the not-so-young anymore, etc. This all comes packaged in what is really a rather tame delivery, which really increasingly appears more as a vehicle to carry the "message", such as it may be, than a real fiction writing exercise. 
 The treatment of beloved characters does not help. Cordelia used to be this kick-ass spaceship captain who more than earned respect through her actions and words and didn't let elevation to the Nobility slow her down. Even though she still figuratively dominates her entourage in this book, I think she deserved better than this... middle-age projection. Miles shows up about mid-way through, raising my hopes for something interesting to happen and upend the whole thing, but that is not to be (I read a few spoilers to make sure). He is a much tamed and edulcorated version of himself, in what may actually be the scariest development in the book as a commentary on the effects of aging. 
 So what's to salvage? The writing is still brilliant in places, with good dialogue and wittiness. It's kind of nice to visit the old Vorkosigan stomping grounds again... I think that's really about it. Everything else about this book is really not what I set out to be reading. :(

Gush gush gush. Cordelia is my favourite Bujold character (maybe one of my favourite characters full stop). Shards of Honour is one of my favourite books. This book stars Cordelia and is set on Sergyar, where much of Shards of Honour took place. I've been wanting to read more about Cordelia being Vicereine. I only wish we'd seen Mark. 
 This book was an absolute delight. I will be reading it again and again. Visiting with all the characters and hanging out with them? So fabulous.
ACTUAL RATING: DNF

book_b.title: Mr. Darcy's Diary (Jane Austen Heroes, #1)
book_b.user_review: Disappointing in every possible way.

sample_reviews.review_text: Ya lo sabia pero con esto lo confirmo: Amo al Sr. Darcy.

I was a bit worried about starting this Mr. Darcy's Diary. The only other book in this collection that I had read was Captain Wentworth's Diary and at the time I was less than impressed with it. Sometimes you form an idea, on your head, about a character and it's not always that the author can match that idea. 
 Fortunately I had no such problem here. This Darcy maybe not be the Darcy that Austen wrote but he is close enough for us to get a glimpse of that world and, even if we don't learn anything new, we leave entertained and wishing to revisit the original Pride and Prejudice. 
 The events are pretty much the ones described in P&P but from Mr. Darcy's perspective, this means we get a few more scenes, just over or mentioned but not seen in the original story. We follow the change in Darcy from being the arrogant pretender to the man deeply in love and for fans of the original I guess it is a nice way to spend more time with your favourite characters. I found it a fun and entertaining read. 
 Grade: 4/5
Sometimes a girl just needs a good romance. This was a pretty interesting take on a classic, although the writing style left a little bit to be desired.

The author recreates Pride and Prejudice in the pages of Mr Darcy's Diary very well - so well that they sound just like...I mean - oh, hey, wait a minute! That's directly quoted from the book. Most of this diary was directly from the book. 
 Sadly, I didn't find much depth to Mister Darcy, which I was hoping for, and not much explanation to the motives for his actions, which I was really hoping for. I like P&P, and I can read fanfic till the cows come home, but that's kind of what this seemed to me: fanfic with a good agent and a shiny cover.
I might have enjoyed this more if I hadn't already read Pamela Aidan's similar - but far superior - series.

Read in one sitting. Lots of repeated material from P&P, which I find kind of cheating. Not very deep into the language of the time, but clear enough. One part or two that made me laugh out loud at the humor. A nice quick read.
Really liked this retelling. Nicely done.

After reading Pamela Aiden's "Fitzwilliam Darcy, Gentleman" trilogy a few months ago, I found this to be merely a much simpler version. Grange doesn't go much beyond the events we already know of from the original novel, and Darcy himself doesn't seem to have much depth at all. He switches from being determined to stop thinking about Elizabeth to suddenly proposing without almost any explanation at all. His feelings seem to flip flop to quickly throughout the novel with no basis. Overall, I knew exactly what was going to happen - there were no surprises. Nothing happens to Darcy that we don't already know about to some degree. 
 The book was enjoyable for the story itself, and of course I found myself smiling when Elizabeth finally accepted. The glimpses of their life after marriage were cute too. If you really want an in-depth look at Darcy, I recommend the Pamela Aiden trilogy. Although it can be a little far-fetched a times, she adds a slew of new characters for Darcy to interact with, and really shows the way his mind works.

I wish I had read Clarissa's review before I wasted my time on this one! Barely able to hold my interest long enough to finish it. Some of the writing was so bad I thought I probably could have done better with imitating Regency style.

reference_books.title: Between the Lines (Between the Lines, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Reviewed at http://www.mandikayereads.com/archive... (6/29/12) 
 This is one where I really had no idea what to expect. Jodi Picoult is very genre-oriented - and fairy-tale/fantasy isn't her usual genre. 
 That being said, I was very pleasantly surprised. This one turned out to be three stories in one: we get Delilah's life, we get Oliver's life, and we get the fairy tale that Oliver was written into. That last part was the most surprising - I didn't expect it to be included. But it was the middle part that I thought was most inventive. 
 The idea that the characters in a book exist outside of the story when the book is closed is a fascinating one to me. Especially since in this world they are, for the most part, completely independent from their characters (excluding Seraphima, of course). The book characters are simply roles they play when there is a Reader. When there is no Reader and the book is closed, they go about their own daily lives. 
 There have been so many books where I have wished the characters were real and were actually my friends - and for Delilah, this came true. I found myself envious of her as I read the story. Some of my best friends can be found between the pages of a book - but they don't talk back to me. 
 I definitely recommend this one - especially if you like a good fairy tale.

reference_books.title: New Girl
reference_books.review_text:
Reviewed at http://www.mandikayereads.com/archive... 
 I finished this one a few hours ago, and I'm still not sure how I feel about it. I never read Rebecca by Daphne du Maurier, so I can't comment on any similarities - as such, the story was completely new to me. 
 I liked the main character - it startled me at the end when someone said her name. I hadn't realized that for the entire book she'd only been called "New Girl." I liked that she figured out pretty quickly that she was worth far more than what her classmates made her out to be. I liked that she stood up for herself. 
 I pretty much hated the rest of the characters, even Max. Yes, even Max. 
 They all treated her so horribly - as if she were trying to steal Becca's identity - when all she was trying to do was live her own life. They were mean to her. They were petty. 
 I think that's why the book left me so unsettled - I couldn't find a redeeming quality in most of the characters I met. Max managed to redeem himself - somewhat - but no one else did. 
 While I didn't care for the characters so much, I can't deny that the writing was high quality - that's why I gave it 3.5 stars. If Harbison hadn't written such descriptive characters, I wouldn't have ended up feeling the way I did - and I wouldn't have been so eager to find out what happened to Becca and how things would end up for everyone.

book_a.title: Brightest Kind of Darkness (Brightest Kind of Darkness, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Reviewed at http://www.mandikayereads.com/archive... (2/13/12) 
 I really need to start paying more attention to the books I read. I don't mean to the story. I had no idea this was a self-published novel until just now, when I had to look up the publisher. And knowing that makes all the difference - and added half a star to the rating because I found myself more forgiving of the technical issues. 
 This story is some strange hybrid of Final Destination and something else that I haven't yet figured out yet. Quite frankly, I think it's brilliant. I was hooked from page one and didn't stop until I finished it. I adore books where I don't figure it out from the start. This one is far from predictable. 
 The chemistry between Nara and Ethan blew me away. It's pretty close to what I remember feeling between Mac and Barrons in Karen Marie Moning's Shadowfever series. For that reason alone, I'd recommend the book. They get pretty steamy - without there even being any sex! 
 But I digress. 
 I mentioned some technical issues above. They were not major things, mostly grammatical issues or typos. The one thing that really gave me pause about the book was that there were a few scenes where something was referenced that the reader had no prior knowledge of it. It was confusing. The book moved back and forth between dreams and reality and also the past, present, and future. It made it somewhat difficult to keep up. 
 An example: Inara has a dream early in the book where she has trouble with the zipper on her jeans and vows to destroy them (this was such a minor detail that I had to go back and find it because the later part confused me). Several chapters later, after many - important - things have happened, Inara's mom finds the destroyed jeans in the trash. I had no memory of the previous incident because it was so minor, and the zipper incident wasn't mentioned again, nor did we get to see Inara destroy them. It may seem like a small thing, but when I read it I was confused and ended up flipping back through the story until I figured out what the heck was going on. 
 But those technical issues are minor enough, in the context of a self-published book, that I added a half star back into my rating. 
 The book as a whole is really just that good.

sample_reviews.review_text:
4.5 Stars 
 "You know that feeling of deja vu people talk about? I live it. Every. Single. Day." 
 This book is about a 16 year-old girl who can predict her next day through dreams. Nara Collins lives her day twice and she finds it boring. One night before she went to sleep she wished for just one "surprising" day... she woke up the next day regretting her wish and decided to do something to prevent her dream to happen. 
 I read this book for a reading challenge that I joined and I wasn't expecting much about it. I thought it was just another YA paranormal book, but I was wrong! I had a hard time putting it down. It sucked me in after reading a couple of chapters. I loved the plot, the writing style, the pacing, the characters... I think I liked almost everything about it, LOL! 
 Nara isn't your typical YA heroine. She's tough, independent and athletic. She's not perfect though. When she stopped dreaming her future we learned that she's misusing her gift...she started failing her classes, not performing well as a soccer goalie, and to top it off, her relationship with her best friend became shaky. Through all of that stuff, there's one guy who unexpectedly became her ally. Ethan Harris is a mystery to everyone. He has a bad reputation and keeps to himself until she met Nara. They became good friends and later developed into something more. The chemistry between this two is undeniable, they are just perfect for each other! *sigh* As they get to know each other, their secrets are revealed one by one. 
 The mystery is one of the best things in this book...*note: AVOID READING SPOILERS!* it will make you want to read more. Also, the twists in the plot and the action will keep you on the edge of your seat! There's one thing I didn't like on this book though --- Nara's friends, including Lainey. I think I'm more hurt and annoyed than Nara when Lainey believed Sophia about the whole Jared thing. The way they turned their backs on her when she wasn't performing well on their soccer games made my blood boil. And the pranks...arrgh, thank God for Ethan Harris! 
 Anyway, I am so glad that I have a copy of book 2 handy because the book ended abruptly, there were a lot of questions left unanswered. I immediately jumped to Lucid as soon as I hit the last page of The Brightest Kind of Darkness. I had to find out what happens next! If you plan on reading this, make sure you buy Lucid too. =) 
 This book is highly recommended to readers who like action romance and mystery on their YA books. =)

At first, I was really into this book. I couldn't put it down. But as the book progressed, I felt myself wishing that it would hurry up and end. Yeah, there was a interesting storyline but I felt like it was dragged out for too long. Nothing really stood out to me. At first, I felt that I was really going to like Ethan but halfway through the book I lost interest. It wasn't anything about his personality, the protagonist, or the story in general, per se, but I just couldn't get into it. Still, it wasn't a bad book and I did enjoy it to a certain extent, just couldn't get emotionally attached. 
 3/5 stars seems rather reasonable considering my lack of emotional investment. The cover was beautiful, and the writing was written well for the most part.

Very cliched with cliched romance and damsel in distress bah:{ {starts vomiting and gagging} Quite painful took me four days to read.

Originally reviewed on Hello, Chelly. 
 The good: What drew me to the book was the concept - the idea that this girl knows her entire day ahead of time and how she deals with it. It was interesting to read how Nara used that knowledge to her advantage with school, sports, relationships and how that same knowledge also crippled her at times. 
 (Major) reservations: Aside from the concept, I just didn't like the book or the protagonist very much. The concept was great; the execution was not. There was so much to explore and instead the author focused too much on a romance that felt extremely rushed. It was a bad case of instant "falling in love" and overly dramatized moments of professing their feelings, which I didn't find compelling at all (and I love a good romance!). The language also felt too juvenile and I'm pretty sure I caught some grammatical errors (it's self-published so that might explain why). 
 Do I recommend?: No. I really wanted to like this because I've seen so many positive ratings but I could not get into it. Now, that makes two books in a row that I haven't liked - wish me luck on my next one. I need something good!

Brightest Kind of Darkness is soo good! Seriously, I loved this book. The premise is fresh and such a cool idea! Plus it is more complex than it initially seemed. I still have no idea what is going on with Ethan. You get answers in layers, and I want more, more, more. All I know is that I LOVED him. I just started reading book 2, Lucid because I need to know what is going to happen next. 
 Nara dreams her whole next day. How different and awesome/scary is that? I can't decide for the life of me if I would love or hate this gift. I think I would like it, no matter how creepy it might be, because I always like knowing things over not knowing. I applaud her willpower too. She normally always stays out of things. Meaning, she lets life take its natural course. But then one day, she steps in to save some lives and that is when the book takes off from. It is action right from page 1. I was so engrossed in the story the whole time. Ethan is so freakin' perfect for Nara it is crazy. I love seeing the two of them interact. 
 The writing is excellent, the plot is so intriguing, and the characters are awesome! I had to think long and hard before even coming up with anything critical to say about Brightest Kind of Darkness because I really enjoyed the book. I got sucked in right from the start and I just kept reading until I was done. But I did finally come up with something- Lainey. She was so quick to give up and turn her back on her best friend. She eventually came around and realized how uncool and rude she was, but it still bugged me to see Nara isolated like that. 
 I can't wait to get back to Lucid and see what is going on with Ethan, Nara and the whole gang. I have a feeling that way more is going on with Ethan than even he knows about. If you are looking for a mysterious paranormal, the Brightest Kind of Darkness series is one that I would wholeheartedly recommend for you to check out! I have fallen in love with it.

Book Review: Brightest Kind Of Darkness 
 By: P.T Michelle 
 Truly a captivating mysterious paranormal book. I recommend this book to all lovers of paranormal, mystery, and love stories. This book has a creative story plot and great writing style. Which keeps the reader wanting more. 
 There are a few great life lessons in this book. Which is to appreciate what you have because you never know when or if it will be taken away. Also that true love will undergo anything together no matter what. The two main characters remind me that no matter how odd you think you are, you are perfectly normal to someone else. They also remind me that no matter how useless or unimportant you think you are, someone out there needs every bit of you. 
 Written by: Jesenia Sanabia

As I said in my review for Ethan, I had pretty high expectations going into Brightest Kind of Darkness that weren't really met. It was more the writing style than anything else as I think Michelle has likely become a stronger writer since she originally wrote Brightest Kind of Darkness. I felt like Ethan was not characterized properly and I became confused because it seemed like events in Ethan contradicted events in Brightest, like when Ethan starts at the animal shelter and what happens on his first day. 
 It was also a little more 'woo woo' than I wanted, what with personified forces of nature and whatnot. However, that might be a result of my post-BEA fatigue as Brightest Kind of Darkness encourages the reader to mull over the concept of Fate vs free will and that was more thinking than I wanted to do. 
 I'll read the next book in the series, Lucid, eventually, especially since the reviews of that title seem to support my theory that Michelle gets better with each book. Actually, I might pick it up sooner rather than later because I'm curious if you could get away with going from Ethan to Lucid and skipping Brightest all together.

Sadly, I skimmed through most of this book, so I don't remember some of it. But what do remember wasn't very good. When I read the synopsis for Brightest Kind of Darkness, I was immediately intrigued. It reminded of Final Destination and this television show I used to watch called Tru Calling. Most of the book involved Nara obsessing over Ethan or being total doormat to her best friend (I use the term "friend" loosely because no real friend would behave the way Nara's did). The supernatural bits that were there were decent, but not as exciting as I was hoping for. I don't really remember the other characters because they were all kind of bland. Overall just not what I was expecting

book_b.title: Cleaving: A Story of Marriage, Meat, and Obsession
book_b.user_review:
This book had so much potential. Julie Powell's first memoir, Julie and Julia, was a book that I absolutely adored. The movie version was even fairly well done. When I heard that she'd written a second book, I was thrilled! When I saw the fairly epic subtitle (A story of marriage, meat, and obsession) my hopes for this book grew to epic proportions. 
 Sadly, it fell flat. 
 The first part of the book wasn't so bad. In fact, the parts where Julie talked about butchering and how she apprenticed at a quaint shop were absolutely fascinating. Those parts left me actually wanting to experience what she did. I don't know that I actually wanted to butcher any meat... but I certainly wanted to watch. 
 But the primary focus of the book was the affair that Julie had with "D." The vast majority of the book was filled with insipid whining about the fact that he had decided he could no longer be with her because she was married and it was too hard for them to have a relationship when she was still so attached. 
 She whined about the loss of her lover. She whined about the strain on her marriage (she carried this affair on for two years while her husband knew about it). 
 Once she moved on from talking about her apprenticeship, I quickly grew bored and actually put the book down for a few weeks because I simply couldn't stomach the whining any longer. 
 Bottom line? The title and subtitle are far more entertaining and well written than the rest of the book.

sample_reviews.review_text: I was curious to read a book by Julie Powell after seeing the movie "Julie and Julia." I was disappointed in both the story and the writing. (One sentence began this way, "Seams seem (seams seem heh)...") The book is by turns gratuitous and mind-numbingly boring. Couldn't finish it.

This book is one giant ode to one woman's monsterous ego. Julie Powell's insane opinion of herself is like some awful version of a sentient bacteria that eats everything it touches. Between the extra marital affairs, the self indulgent rants, the whinning, the sheer entitlement that she oozes, I often found myself wondering if the same person had actually written 'Julie and Julia', it just didn't seem possible. But, alas, it is. To say that my rosy image of all things related to 'Julie and Julia' took a nosedive is an epic understatement. 
 Oh, if you think you ought to feel bad for Julie Powell's husband... don't. He's just as much of a snot and he's having an affair too. By the time these two are done going around and around on a revenge merry go round with each other, you wish they both would just shut up already and get a divorce. Not that I can possibly imagine ANYONE, EVER, being romantically happy with these two dipshits.

I read the whole "Julie/Julia Project" blog. I loved the movie. I even found it inspiring. However, this Julie Powell is a real asshole. I'm kind of appalled at the callous way she describes her affair, pretty much constantly rubbing her husband's nose in it the entire time it's going on (never mind the things she says and the acts she describes in the book - I think being with someone for over a decade and then reading those things would be extremely damaging). How unfeeling... 
 The writing is less than stellar. She tries to be one of the boys and a tough butcher lady, she really thinks she is pretty awesome and sexy and everyone wants her, etc... but through the whole book she whines, she lets the men in her life define her, and then she leaves to go "find herself" in a few other countries. I was over it after she left the butcher shop. I skimmed the last few chapters. I don't like this Julie Powell and the way she has no regard for anyone who is close to her. And I get the suspicion this is the "real her". She definitely didn't hold back talking about any aspect of her sex life. You like it rough, wooo you're a revolutionary! TMI, dude. 
 I'm kind of mad that I bought this book. Should have borrowed it from the library.
This has to be the most boring book I have yet to read. Sorry Julie because I loved Julia and Julia. I just did not care for this sequel and what you did to the characters.

I wish I hadn't read this book. I think I liked the persona Julie Powell created in Julie and Julia......the charming goofball ala "I Love Lucy" who dreams big, makes a mess sometimes, but always wins our heart. So, this book is an account of Julie's new project, a six month apprenticeship as a butcher (which does have some interesting writing), but nearly every page is devoted to not getting over a love affair with another man and the problems this makes for her ever loyal husband. 
 At the end of the book, the writer acknowledges the helpfulness of her editor's comment that there is never too much information. I beg to differ.

This was a big disappointment after Julie and Julia. The premise seemed cool - woman about my age decides to learn all she can about cutting meat by taking an internship at a butcher shop. This is cool. I would like to do that someday. The personal side of the memoir, however, was a bit too personal for my taste. I felt bad for this couple. I didn't want to know so many of their problems and was left feeling sad for them both.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Powell didn't quite hold up to the par she set with her first book. Maybe it's because I'm not a huge fan of meat so I had trouble getting past the butchering part but I think I struggled more with the collapse of her marriage. Either way, Julie & Julia was way better.

Be warned that the (failing) marriage and obsession part far outweigh the meat of the story, no pun intended. I picked this up because I was very inspired by the idea of a woman who just up and decides to learn the art of butchery. It started out swell, but the meat soon takes a backseat in a horrific and, at times, gut-wrenching ride through Julie's personal life. I have to admit, I admire her bravery. This is the one (and only) redeeming quality of this book. She puts it all out there for the world, knowing fully well that they will moan and wail and gnash their teeth at her. How she does it I don't quite know, but I can respect her for it. In the end, I give this book a 1 star because this was not the ride I signed up for. You never truly know what the ride is going to be like, but this was just too much for my heart. 
 P.S. DO NOT pick this for book club.

I didn't read Julie and Julia, however I did see the movie and thought it was enjoyable. So going in, I didn't have any expectations or the prejudice of reading the first book like many other readers. Basically there are two stories happening in the book - Julie Powell is having an affair and she is learning to be a butcher. Overall, I thought this book was disjointed and that it was trying way too hard. The passages describing her butchery are tedious, confusing, and for someone who doesn't have any problem eating meat, kind of disgusting. Powell tries way too hard to metaphorically connect what's happening in the chop shop to the even bigger mess of her personal life. I'll give her credit for being very honest to the point of basically casting herself as an unlikeable character throughout the story, but at some points I felt like I was reading a diary instead of a memoir. She agonizes over these two men in her life during the entire book, then near the end, she takes a trip to three places - Argentina, Ukraine, and Africa. I felt like this part of the book read like a poor man's version of Eat, Pray, Love. Then the book wraps up without any real closure, as both relationships are still up in the air - I can't really fault her for this, but the ending seemed hasty after such a long first part of the book. I was disappointed in this memoir and though Powell may have thought she was being edgy and showing a different side to herself from Julie and Julia, this book needed to be more cohesive to really pack a punch.
Butchery, adultery, travel, recipes .... an unfocused and self-indulgent book. I couldn't read more than a chapter or two.

reference_books.title: A Court of Thorns and Roses (A Court of Thorns and Roses, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Still my absolute favourite 
 -first read 03.09.15- 
 *SPOILERS BELOW* 
 *NO BUT SERIOUSLY. DON'T READ THIS UNLESS YOU WANT TO KNOW THE PLOT OF THE ENTIRE BOOK* 
 *WARNING - THIS BOOK IS BRUTAL AND WILL DESTROY YOU EMOTIONALLY* 
 So it seems my TBR jar is blessing me with really good books this year! That and authors are publishing the first book in amazing series this year! 
 I'd like to start by saying that I hated Feyre, like really hated her. I got a Katniss-like vibe from her. You know the one, "I hate you all. Even though you're being nice to me I really hate you. I don't care what you say or do, I will never not hate you!" And then she kind of redeemed herself when she actually got over herself. I still don't get why she took a liking to Lucien before Tamlin though when Tam was never anything but nice to her. So everything was going along nicely and I thought "you know what Feyre, you're actually not that bad" and then when she found out the truth about the curse I thought she was going to do a major 360 and decide to hate Tam for lying to her, because lets be realistic, Tam didn't spare her life, he dragged her back to Prythian in the hopes she'd break the curse, and in fairness he did send her away because he truly did love her and it wasn't about the curse anymore, but seeing as Feyre was such a Debbie-Downer about everything at the beginning it seemed like a betrayal of her character that she overlooked this MAJOR transgression and forgave all. Which to be honest I was glad she did because I couldn't handle anymore of her whining and I actually ended up really liking her. UNTIL... She killed those faeries under the mountain. Because now I'm getting some serious Katniss vibes from her again, we all know all is forgiven that she killed the faeries because she did it for the greater good and essentially saved the world so nobody is going to hold it against her, but I'm worried that throughout the second book she will be all "Oh I wanted the world to change, and I made it change, I am essentially a hero right now and I have everything I ever wanted but I'm going to wallow in my own misery forever." Let us all pray she lightens up and sees the bigger picture. 
 Also speaking of the end of the book, I feel there was no wrap up with Tamlin. He should have at least apologised for just sitting there and doing nothing while she was tortured. I know his reasons were totally noble and I understand why he did it but I feel some of this should have been explained on paper. Like at least half a paragraph where he tells her how much it killed him inside watching her tortured and humiliated and begs for her forgiveness in that adorably noble manner of his *fangirls* I feel that after the Spring Court were dragged Under the Mountain we lost a lot of the Tamlin/Feyre romance and at the end, where this should have been revisited, it was overshadowed by Rhysand which I'm assuming will be the setup for the next book. 
 Which brings me to my next point. Please don't make Feyre go to the Night Court. PLEASE. If Rhysand becomes a love interest I will lose it. I am so bored of love triangles and second book breakups. So so bored. Why does she have to go anyway? Rhysand confessed that he was only toying with her to make Tamlin really really mad so he'd rip Amarantha apart, so surely he should just release her from their deal so they can both go their seperate ways. I got the feeling he was pretty much going to do that anyway until she reminded him of it. Don't get me wrong, I like Rhysand quite a lot, but I feel like ACOTAR could have been a standalone or the series could divert in a different direction and Rhysand would maybe be better explored in a spin-off because let's face it, we're all going to fall in love with him and then Feyre's going to end up with Tam in the end and all of our hearts will break. 
 Final point - Lucien is the sassmaster and I love him.

reference_books.title: Tiny Pretty Things (Tiny Pretty Things, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I've read many reviews on this book, most of them good but I have to say that I didn't really enjoy it. I didn't really like any of the characters, Bette is egocentric and vain, Gigi is immature and naive and I get the impression she acts like a 5 year old. June was my favourite of the 3 although I didn't connect with her either. I think I like her more because she was less whiny and irritating than the other two. 
 As for the content of the story, I've read a lot that readers like the ethnic diversity and exploration of sensitive issues in the book but I hated it. I felt like it was put in there for the sake of it and it was trying to hard to be a culturally diverse and gritty novel. There were far too many cliches and stereotypes and they didn't mesh together enough for them not to be glaringly obvious. It practically screamed "look how edgy and unique I'm trying to be." On the topic of the sensitive issues in particular, it was just too much. One or two issues that were properly developed would have been enough instead throwing in the amalgamation of every problem ever experienced by any teen ever. 
 So those of you who have read this will know about the plot twist towards the end of the book and I thought it was excellent. I really didn't see it coming. However the aftermath of this was dealt with by the author very badly. Naturally there were people pointing fingers towards an innocent party. But the thing that really winds me up is that Alec claimed he saw the real culprit. If this is the case why hasn't he spoken up? Why don't we know who really did it? The ending of this book and the failure to wrap up loose ends is what downgraded it from 3 to 2 stars for me. 
 I don't know, despite everything I did like this book and it will be interesting to read the sequel. There were just too many faults and it was far to contrived for my liking.

book_a.user_review:

 The thing I liked most about this is that, unlike any series of novellas I've read, they all combine to make one whole story.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I was torn over whether I should write a book review for this, because, on the one hand it really is just a series of novellas, but on the other, it has the length and feel of a full on novel. In the end I decided I needed to say something... so here it goes! 
 Basically my two major thoughts were: one, how the hell did Celaena ever become a notorious assassin? I mean seriously, I have yet to see her successfully assassinate a single target. While at the same time I have seen her make stupid mistakes, get caught tailing someone, completely misjudge people, and almost die. I believe in her ability as an assassin even less than I did during Throne of Glass--and that's saying something. 
 My second thought was: this is just too long. Normally novellas are just a short break from the main story, not an entire novel in themselves. And, I found that I could do without having read most of it. 
 Don't get me wrong. I absolutely adored learning more about Celaena and Sam's romance. In fact I think I may like Sam more than either Chaol or Dorian. He was just so sweet and kind and wonderful all while still being a bad-ass assassin. In fact, I believed Sam as an assassin way more than I ever did Celaena. What happened to him was also totally heart wrenching and nearly brought me to tears. 
 I also liked getting a bit more context for Celeana's life in the assassin's guild. Although, I now have a newfound and intense hatred for Arobynn. 
 Really, this book is almost worth reading just for the Chaol and Dorian cameo in The Assassin and the Underworld. 
 But, I basically could have done without everything else. I hated The Assassin and the Desert. It was just completely cliched and predictable and did little to advance the story. (I mean really? an exotic master that teaches her a fighting style based on animals? Now where have I seen that before?! Not to mention the impossible-jump-on-horseback and the-sword-so-close-it-cuts-her-hair scenes). The Assassin and the Healer also added very little, but at least that one was short. I think if I were to read it again. I would skip those two entirely. 
 In the end, I'm still happy to know more of Celaena's background. I just wish it didn't take 400 pages to do it.

4.75/5 
 I LOVED those five novellas. I expected to like them since I love this series so much and Sarah J. Maas' writing is so great, but I just loved it. I don't even think I have the right words for it. 
 I really enjoyed that all the stories were connected, but somehow felt comlete. I mostly enjoyed "The Assassin and the Pirate Lord" and "The Assassin and the Underworld". The fifth one was just painful, though I still liked it a lot. 
 And Sam... This is such cruel fate. I'm so team Sam, JFC. I love him, love him so much that I hurt me to see what they've done to him. 
 And I hate Arobynn. I hated him from pretty much the first book, but this... UGH.

Many of my friends have recommended me to read assassin's blade before tog so I finished this book and all I want to do is curl up in my bed and cry. Ahh!! The five stories were amazing! Celaena is such a kickass female and I totally admire her. She is such a strong person. Where do I start about Sam *sobs* I loved sam through out the stories. He is just too good and I just LOVE HIM SO MUCH. Sam I'm still rooting fr u tho u..why did you do this Sarah??
already read all 4 novellas
Amazing read!!! This set of novellas had me hooked from the get go!! I loved the characters and the plots. It's a constant page turner, I couldn't put it down!

These novellas are a must-read for any fan of Throne of Glass. They give some background information on how Celaena became who she is when we meet her at the start of Throne of Glass, and fill in interesting info about some characters who return again later in the series. Each novella was solidly written and fun to read, though I found I liked some (The Assassin and the Pirate Lord) way more than others (The Assassin and the Empire). The huge story of what happens between Celaena and Sam at the end, which has a tremendous impact on her and who she eventually becomes, just felt like a little bit of a let-down compared to how I'd built this up in my mind. But that might be my own fault. Overall, these are awesome. Read them!
