this is the best star wars fanfiction i've ever read.

This is one of those books that I didn't find particularly engrossing or compelling, but by the end of it, I was glad I had read it, and I can say it was a good book. As the first in a series, I don't know that I will go on to book #2. 
 First off, let me say that placing a book in the sci-fi category does not represent any form of appeal to me. However, as I was reading this book, I did not think of it as a sci-fi book. It was only after it was over, and the author was discussing how the book came to pass that I really recognized that it was sci-fi. 
 What this book was to me was the operationalization of an idea...what if in future society the government has to select future military leaders at the age of 6, and train them as they grow up while en route to some far off interstellar battle... what might that look like? Well, that is what Ender's game is, and with that core of an idea, the author did a decent job of wrapping a story around it. There are the seeds of subsequent books in the series, no doubt, but the ideas and concepts presented in this book were enough to entertain me for now, and I can say, "That was fun. What good history book should I pick up next?"

I seldom read sci-fi. I'm more of a fantasy girl myself, as for some reason I can imagine magical worlds better than futuristic ones. I find sci-fi worlds a bit cold and lackluster, and the idea of aliens is just too farfetched for me. But elves and wizards and fairies aren't. Weird, I know. 
 But this book just blew me away. I can't help but empathize with its main characters, as alien as their world might be to me. And by the time I reached the ultimate twist, all I could think of was "What the WHAT?!?" I almost threw away my kindle in surprise. 
 So Ender's Game certainly changed my outlook, and I can't wait to get my hands on the next book! And the next sci-fi series!! I've got a lot to catch up on.

book_b.title: The Friday Society
book_b.user_review: Meh. I was very excited about reading this book but my enthusiasm waned as I continued reading. I only kept reading because I paid for this book. So many problems from the modern slang, uninteresting characters, a "big reveal" that was very anticlimactic to me. This was just a very disappointing read for me.

sample_reviews.review_text:
The Gist: It's 1900 in London, England and we are introduced to 3 very different young women: Cora Bell, an ex-street urchin, she was plucked off the street as a child and raised in a Lord White's house and now is his right hand woman and inventor extraodinaire; Nellie Harrison, formerly of Ireland, she was rescued from a life of burlesque by the Great Raheem and has become his invaluable magician's assistant; Michiko Takeda, who gave up nearly everything to become a Samurai warrior, she was tricked by a con-man into leaving Japan to help him train young English women in the art of self-defense and now finds herself in a strange land with no allies. 
 These three young ladies find themselves thrown together in random turns of events, trying to uncover a mysterious society with plans of anarchy, as well discover the identify of a serial murderer. 
 Vopinion: I liked this one - it was fast, the three characters took turns narrating the story and as result there were numerous sub-plots that kept the story quite engaging. Honestly, the book had a little bit of everything - mystery, suspense, sword fights, chases, crazy inventions (steampunk, people!), humour, explosions, and a dash of romance. The three young women - I think they're all 18-ish, if I recall - each come from such different lives that it's quite enjoyable reading each character on their own and then reading the next chapter and seeing how the other characters react to her actions and words. A very complete story. 
 It seems that this is the first book in what is to be a series - I look forward to reading what happens next!

It's been a while since I read this book, so I don't remember many details. I remember that it started off really good, but then they brought in the whole floating rock thing and everything just got kind of silly. I didn't like the ending, and I found the whole plot to be unrealistic and a bit absurd. However, I can definitely appreciate that it takes a lot of work to write a novel, and The Friday Society was very well-paced, with an intricate and intriguing plot basis. It just didn't quite deliver, in my opinion. I do think that Ms. Kress definitely has talent. Ooh, and I love the cover.
Very Fun!

Mostly enjoyed this book. The three main characters each had interesting histories. 
 Since this book was aimed a the younger crowd I shall not be too hard on it, but it did have a few flaws. I believe if a book is taking place in a certain time, the language should be of that time. 
 Nothing drives me crazier than to have characters using words, phrases and even sentences that are so obviously taken out of todays jargon. 
 The plot was well written and flowed nicely.

Thoughts on the Overall Book: Oh where to begin? So, this is one of those books that I had been wanting to try for a while, but kept putting off for reasons that ended up being correct. It really didn't look like the kind of book I'd like, but I have known books, covers and descriptions to be deceiving and I thought, well, it's steampunk and an adventure, so it will be worth the try, right? Well, it turned out that all my suspicions were proved correct and worse, because not only were the story line and characters lame, the writing style itself was horrible and childish. In fact, after the first page, I knew this book was going to be torture. And I quote, from the book, the first few lines that sealed The Friday Society's doom: 
 And then there was an explosion. 
 It was loud. It was bright. It was very explosion-y. 
 That's right folks. "explosion-y". 
 Cover--Yea or Nay: No, this is exactly the kind of cover that turns me off a book. The only thing interesting about it is that it is steampunk. A lot of times though, covers are deceiving. This time, it wasn't. The cover portrays exactly what you are going to get from this story. 
 Characters: Okay, so I do love strong female heroines. For example Mackenzie from Victoria Schwab's The Archived and Cinder and Scarlet from Marissa Meyer's books, but these girls in The Friday Society seem to be the typical kick-butt female heroines teen girls love to read about for what ever reason, but in actuality they give real women a bad name because they are simply stupid and there was nothing in this book that convinced me they knew what they were doing and were capable of it. All I saw was stupid teenage girls going out to do things they couldn't and somehow surviving. If this had been real life these girls would be dead 20 times over. They were all your typical man-haters too, and the men in this book just had to be idiots as well, obviously, because these kinds of books can never have intelligent male characters, even though their female characters are no more intelligent. The only male character who was remotely supposed to be smart was still degraded because the girls were always telling him what he needed to do as if he didn't know and simply called him "cute". Demeaning. 
 I will admit that of the three girls I really didn't have a problem with Michiko, in fact I felt really bad for her. She couldn't speak English well so the other girls, who professed to be her friends didn't seem to really care whether she understood or not, and gave me the impression they thought she was stupid. She was actually the smartest of them. 
 Cora was your typical female heroine in these types of books. She thought she was better than everyone, especially men because she was soo smart, which she wasn't really, and the author tried to make her seem modest when she obviously wasn't. 
 Nellie was just pretty much, to use a common Victorian term, a tart. She was silly, and flighty and not cute or adorable like I'm sure the author thought she would be. 
 There was one character I really liked and that was Hayao, who was the young boy Michiko was training. He was cute, and I liked him, and as I said, I didn't really mind Michiko either, she wasn't nearly as annoying as the other girls, and seemed to think they were silly too. Why Hayao had to die when the girls obviously couldn't even kill off the baddies, though, made me so angry. I hate it when authors kill of kid characters, especially when there was no reason for it! And then Michiko couldn't even kill the person who did it? Come on! 
 The Romance: Surprisingly, or not, there really wasn't all that much romance. The whole bloody story line of Andrew and Cora was stupid and totally unnecessary. I mean, seriously unnecessary. The guy had no reason to be in the book, I don't even know why he was written in it was a total red herring and a very poorly executed one with him being the murderer of the flower girls. Why? I ask. It had NOTHING to do with the plot. I think it was just all about trying to be a poorly disguised red herring that failed epically 
 After that, we have Nellie and the police officer, Murphy. Murphy was sweet, but he let himself get kicked around by the girls too much. Making it seem, as all the other male characters in this book that he was an idiot and obviously, the only gender who could think rationally are the females. 
 However, one thing about this book was that there is a line that literally sums up every stupid YA romance and I will put it here: 
 He was standing behind her and leaned down, placing his cheek against hers, wrapping his arms around her. 
 Why did it feel like he was holding her prisoner and not just being affectionate? 
 Still...he smelled nice. (Pg 285) 
 Because that obviously makes everything better. 
 Oh yeah, and it was totally all insta-love. Like seriously. 
 Writing Style: Here's where this story got even worse. Even if there are annoying characters, and annoying plot, if the writing style is good, I can forgive a bit. But as I have probably already made clear, the writing style sounds like it was written by an 8-year-old and that would be insulting the 8-year-old. Or maybe written for one, and even then, I never believe in writing down to children. Anyway, it was juvenile. There was way too much mundane description, too much of the characters explaining things for the reader to understand which always makes one feel like an idiot. About a third of this book is actual plot, the rest is random junk thrown in, probably to be entertaining but is just stupid and annoying. The author is obviously trying to be funny, but there is nothing funny or witty about this book. In a battle of wits, Ms. Kress, you come unarmed. I'm sorry, but it's the honest truth. 
 There was this weird thing she does where she mentions something in the description and then reiterates it in dialogue which was annoying and just sounded so lame. Here's a couple examples: 
 Then she pulled her pistol from her purse and placed it firmly between the fifteenth and sixteenth vertebrae of the stranger standing in the middle of the room. 
 "Is that a pistol you've got placed firmly between my fifteenth and sixteenth vertebrae?" (Pg 23) 
 Looking at how well they were dressed, she imagines it might even be one of those new expensive steam cabs. Nellie sighed wistfully. 
 "Are you sighing wistfully?" asked the Magician. (Pg 36) 
 See how annoying and unnecessary that is? 
 And another thing, the chapter headings were so dumb. Like the rest of the book they were obviously trying to be funny but they weren't. And I don't understand why we had to have a Chapter 10, 10 1/2, and 10 3/4 
 There was also several times that perspectives changed in a chapter without a break and made it very confusing to figure out which girl's head I was in. 
 Accuracy/ Believability: Um, well, let's just say that there is absolutely nothing accurate about this book. This is a disgrace to steampunk genre. Steampunk authors usually do a ton of research into the actual Victorian time period. It's totally obvious the author either ignored or had no clue as to what Victorian society was like. Social classes mean little to nothing in this book, women run rampant and do all kinds of stuff and yet somehow still complain for their rights, even though they have WAY more than any Victorian women would have even imagined and it had no feel of Victorian London at all. No feel of England at all. It was terrible. And the language is all completely modern, even down to the terminology and that drove me up the wall. Here is a list of some of the modern words and phrases that made it into this book: 
 Freaked 
 Get High 
 Make out session 
 Wow 
 Smokin' 
 Among more that I didn't write down. 
 I could say more, but I think I'll address the rest of my problems in the next section. 
 Problems/What bothered me: The whole book bothered me. But let me try to explain why. I know this review is harsh, but I think it's necessary to say what I really felt about it. And I suffered through this book so I should get to, and also leave this so like-minded people can see this and not have to suffer through this book. 
 Okay, first off, let's talk about the girls. It states more than once that they obviously think they are hot. Like actually, they say that. Let me direct you to some more parts taken directly from the book. 
 See Cora Angry. 
 See Cora Tired. 
 See Cora in a bright red dress that makes her look super hot but not giving a ****. (Pg 67) 
 Very attractive. And this: 
 But the fact was she did look charming. She looked smokin'.(...) She knew his lordship had ordered her an outfit that would make her stand out like crazy in a crowd. She was a representation of his awesomeness. His beacon. And there would be no missing her tonight. (Pg 68) 
 So yeah, we get it, the girls are hot and they know it. And furthermore, they continually flaunt it unabashedly. So then, tell me this, why do they get so uppity when men look at them and leer and get grabby. If you don't want to have to deal with grabby men, ladies, then bloody well dress modest for heaven's sake! If you're out there acting like a tart, then that is the kind of treatment you're going to get and you don't have anyone to blame but yourselves. 
 And the slumber party. Oh my gosh, I didn't realize I hated them so much. Why on earth did we need a slumber party scene? And then to make it worse, we have a game of truth or dare, which ends up in Nellie almost kissing a dead guy who has been lying in her parlor since earlier which, by the way, no one really cared to call the police about. 
 And that was another thing. This book was so pedestrian, nothing seemed to be a big deal at all, even when it should have been. There were murders happening all over. And why on earth was the magician Nellie worked with letting her go out, and actually telling her to go out and investigate? Seriously the girl is a ditz, and obviously didn't know what she was doing because she kept almost getting caught! And when the guy dies after bringing a message to their house, do they call the police? No, they go to their show and leave the body there until morning like it's nothing! 
 And then there's the case itself. Someone is murdering scientists, and flower girls, but wait, are they connected? And then someone blows up a cathedral, but does anyone do anything about it? Nope, everyone seems to just go on living. I think that's taking the Keep Calm and Carry On a little too seriously. I mean, you think the government would have someone on it. And let me tell you the truth about the whole thing: The baddie is a woman who is only doing this because she wasn't allowed to join the all boys club at the scientific society. Boo hoo, sorry your feelings have been hurt, princess. La di da di da. It was the stupidest villain excuse I have read in a long time. I don't even want to call her a villain. And she was totally going to blow up the entirety of London just because she wasn't allowed to play with the boys. Dang, I guess it's true what they say about a woman scorned. And she was a character who we only saw twice and had no reason to think about. It wasn't a surprise, it was just lame, and here is how it was revealed: 
 The woman placed her sword to one side and leaned back in her seat. "Well, isn't that typical. I thought maybe someone of my own gender might notice me. But clearly I was wrong." 
 "Stop pouting and tell us who you are," Cora said sharply. 
 The woman looked at her and gave her a wry smile. "My name is Jane Webb. And I work the front desk at the Medical and Scientific Institute." (Pg 395) 
 Dum Dum Dum!!!! Shocking beyond reason. 
 There were also randomly gory bits, and, oh, I must also make mention of the Franken-Zombies that randomly showed up and were quickly destroyed. 
 There was also the girls' inability to kill anyone. Yeah, I know that sounds bloodthirsty, but they went off to stop the baddies, they needed to have a grasp of the duty they might have to perform to keep England safe. If they wanted to be heroes, they should have realized that killing might be necessary. They brought heavy duty weapons. But yet they still balked at the thought of killing the gross baddies even when their lives and the lives of their friends were threatened. 
 So here's another thing that made me want to hit my head against the wall. Nellie was probably my least favorite of the girls. First of all, she's totally devoid of modesty. There is a part in this book where she has to scale a wall, but instead of putting on trousers as one would expect, she just takes her dress off and does it in her underwear! 
 Of course, because of her history working in a burlesque house (yes, seriously and since she's only seventeen or so in this book how old was she then???) this is only to be expected. But that's not even the most annoying thing about her. No, her "weapon of choice" is poisonous glitter. I'll let that sink in. Yeah. And when they were coming up with fake identities, hers was "Lady Sparkle" 
 And here are just a few things that I picked out at random just to show why I disliked this book so much, and to prove it is poorly written. To do this properly, I would love to simply copy the entire book out and comment on each part, but because I don't have time, I'll leave you with a few that I found particularly rediculous: 
 This part is one where poor Nichiko is trying to explain what happened to her to the other girls and they're being stupid about it: 
 Michiko appeared to calm down then. "Not asleep. Un...con...shus." 
 Cora glanced up at Nellie and Nellie gave a small smile. They were on the same page at last. (Pg. 108) 
 They always were on the same page, eedjits! Just because she can't speak English well doesn't mean she didn't know what was going on! 
 Here's Nellie and her glitter obsession: 
 She turned around...only to find herself looking into Dr. Mantis's beady eyes again. She had no glitter this time to aid in her escape. Note to self: Never leave home without glitter. (Pg. 331) 
 And I will add here that Dr Mantis was a total psychopath who collected eyeballs and other body parts. But yet in the end Nellie just couldn't abide the thought of getting rid of him! 
 Later when Cora is asking at the post office to see if they could find who ordered the package that led to the bomb (You know, by this time, the plot was such a mess, I honestly don't couldn't keep a clear thought as to what was what and why they were doing what they were doing) this is how helpful the girl there was. I picked this out simply because it was silly: 
 The note was plain, with little more than Lord White's address written on it, but the symbol embossed at the top was familiar. 
 "You've got to be kidding me," Cora said. 
 "Not kidding, that's the paper. I like to collect interesting stationary," explained Lucy. (Pg. 336) 
 And here's an example of how the humor in this book falls flat when Cora is looking for the grave robbers who have captured Nellie: 
 There was a moment in which the woman was clearly deciding between pretending she had no idea what Cora was talking about and just answering the question. Finally, she let out a sigh and said, "Graveyards, obviously." 
 "Obviously. Do they have a particular...haunt?" The choice of the word had been unintentional, but was actually rather appropriate. (Pg. 338) 
 Here's a part that I found particularly stupid, leading from the subject of how the girls couldn't seem to get rid of anyone. I think the author did it because she was afraid it would be a 'bad influence' on readers. Well, the YA genre is allowed to do what they want. This is what Cora says after Nellie actually takes the initiative and whacks three guys over the head with a shovel: 
 "You know, that's actually rather dangerous. You could give them serious brain damage, even kill them like that," said Cora as she watched Dr. Mantis fall to the side. (Pg 344) 
 Another example of silly writing: 
 A watched Kettle never boils. So why was Cora staring at it so intently? She needed to fixate her mind on something else, something other than the frustrated thoughts and feelings she was thinking and...feeling. (Pg. 346) 
 Wow. And yeah, the author loves ellipses. And this part is little better: 
 Cora nodded and did her best to look thoughtful. "We do have our bosses' reputations to think of. And we're pretty well known in society as it is. What we need are...disguises." 
 Nellie, who was now sitting with her arms folded across her chest and a heavy frown on her face, glanced up at Cora. "Disguises?" 
 "Yes." 
 Cora waited. It was best when trying to convince someone of something to let the person think. To figure things out for themselves and let them speak first. 
 Which is what happened a moment later: "As in...costumes?" (Pg. 356) 
 *Epic eye roll* And I'll leave you with the bit from the back cover which I don't know why I didn't read at first because then I would have known what I was getting into: 
 Why did he underestimate her like that? I mean, who threatens someone without a backup plan? Honestly, Cora removed the knife from its sheath at her waist and placed it at the young man's throat as he came at her in some kind of attack. He froze in place. 
 "Ah, well, now I know for certain you've got a knife to my throat because I saw it," he said, tensing his neck against the blade pushing into his skin. "And can feel it. Very bladelike." 
 "No mistaking it for a finger now, is there?" Okay, so now she was kind of having fun with this. 
 "No indeed. Very well played." 
 "I'm good at games. I always win." 
 There is so much more that I could say here, but honestly, this review is long enough, and I'm tired of writing it. 
 Conclusion: 1 star. Worst book I have read this year. 
 Recommended Audience: I think it can be deduced by the previous review that I wouldn't recommend this book to anyone. 
 Oh yes, and there was also this bit at the end of the book that is supposed to be their add to get business for their little society of helping people out. This is it directly from the book: 
 To the citizens of London and its surrounding Burroughs: 
 Are you being blackmailed? Does a loved one's untimely demise seem suspiciously tied to a brother's new bank account? Are you receiving threats of a personal and/or physically painful nature? Fear not, salvation is at hand. 
 We are a trio of lady heroes. If you need us, we will be there. Respond to this advertisement by post, and we shall come to your aid. 
 We have many talents and skills. But above all things, we know how to assist. 
 Yours sincerely, 
 Hyde, the Silver Heart, and Lady Sparkle 
 AKA 
 The Friday Society 
 So yeah. I'm going with Nathan Ford at Leverage:

I'm not sure if this should be 1 or 2 stars - it feels closer to a 1 star than a 2 star. 
 It's a book that has the potential to be interesting: extremely capable women in a patriarchal society working together! Michiko is an immigrant samurai from Japan, Cora a trained inventor/mechanic under the apprenticeship of Lord White, and Nellie is a stage magician. They decide to work together to solve a series of murders. 
 This is when it falls apart. I have no idea why they start working together - it seems like they just coincidentally decide to check things out and keep meeting each other? - and their joint decision to actually work together comes late in the book. Things felt like they were happening because the author wanted events/relationships to form - but not because it was natural for the characters to behave that way. I couldn't get immersed in the world the author was building. 
 The good includes: I like the steampunk descriptions (though I felt the explanations were more only the lines of "just there for decoration" rather than anything else) and the prose could be quite funny at times. I loved the description of Nellie flirting with Officer Murphy - it's very sweet. 
 The bad: the execution. I dragged myself through the book. 
 Because the worldbuilding was poor/below average, and the execution was bad, this is properly a 1 star.

A cover alone can draw a reader into a book. Of course, everyone says to not judge a book by its cover, but how can you resist with THE FRIDAY SOCIETY? It has three very strong-looking girls from different backgrounds, including a person of color. And while the story inside isn't exactly what I was expecting - and unexpectedly was filled with anachronisms galore - I found myself really enjoying the ride. With a few minor reservations. 
 GIRL POWER 
 This is the reason you should read this book. The main reason. The biggest reason I am going to harp about this book to everyone who will listen. 
 A main character ditches her controlling, demanding, drunk love interest and finishes the novel without a boyfriend. In YA, it's super refreshing, especially because in the majority of YA novels, the girl will take him back or, even worse, will think that a boy demanding sex and kissing her without her consent or getting drunk and trying to grab her is ROMANTIC. Ms. Kress, thank you for doing the logical thing and presenting a heroine who is strong without needing a boy to complete her, especially when the boy is quite frankly crazy. 
 On top of this, our heroines do not need boys to help them. They are strong and take matters onto their own shoulders in an era where modesty, subservience, and loyalty to their male caretakers wasn't only expected but frankly demanded. Cora, Nellie, and Michiko are some of the fiercest, most determined girls in 2012's YA offerings, and in this YA debut, we are treated to three girls who blew the boys out of the water in their quest to prove their worth, their skills, and their strength of mind. 
 Despite their differences - intelligent, powerful inventor Cora; giddy and hyper magician's assistant Nellie; strong-willed and quiet former Samurai student Michiko - they make a wonderful team. And their cast of characters around them for the most part is well thought out, even if there are SO many characters that several get lost. 
 VICTORIAN STEAMPUNK WITHOUT THE VICTORIAN STEAMPUNK 
 Even though I quite frankly loved the characters in this, there were some other issues that need to be mentioned - particularly the fact that this was pitched as a Victorian-era steampunk novel when in fact the steampunk aspects got lost. Of course there were mentions of steampunk devices and other anachronisms you expect to see in novels of this sort. The problem was that, for a steampunk novel, the details that I desired were never there, only found in brief mentions. What's the point of a steampunk novel without the steampunk goodness? 
 Another issue I had was the dialogue. Instead of going for a traditional Victorian-era way of speaking, we end up with three girls that sound like they could be from now - a Cockney girl, a Cockney girl pretending to be a prim and proper Englishwoman, and a Japanese girl that speaks about much English as I speak Japanese (note - have I told you that my minor from college is Japanese?). While this is nice to read, it doesn't really pull you into the time period, once again losing the time. 
 CUTE, ACTION-PACKED, AND EXPLOSIVE 
 Looking past the anachronisms and wonderful kick butt girl power, THE FRIDAY SOCIETY has a lot going for it. It's action-packed, fast-paced for being almost 450 pages long, and EXPLOSIVE. Like seriously, things blow up, there is a serial killer, evil scientists, grave robbing, and magic. I could easily overlook the timeline flaws when I was served a heaping platter of fun on a bun. 
 So am I recommending that you go and pick up a copy of THE FRIDAY SOCIETY right now? Yes. Now. This book might have flaws, but it is going to go down as one of my favorite reads of early 2013 most likely, even if I wish maybe it had stayed true to the time period. 
 VERDICT: A story with amazing YA heroines kicking butt and kicking bad love interests to the curb automatically is awesome. Pair it with explosions, adorkableness, and intrigue, and you have a winner. THE FRIDAY SOCIETY wins. Period. 
 - FOUR HEARTS

Found the treatment of girls refreshing. They are friends rather than competitors, their lives do not revolve around men or boys, except as their three respective employers, and most of the book involves the mystery and/or their own views of what is occurring rather than talking about men. Set in Victorian London but with very modern viewpoints.

Eh. This was OK, but i was hoping for a bit more Gail Carriger and a bit less modern-day girls dropped in a steampunk-lite setting. The language was extremely modern, so it was hard to get into a suitably Victorian mood. It wasn't terrible, but I wouldn't seek out more like it either.
The writing style is not for me.

reference_books.title: Into the Water
reference_books.review_text:
One to avoid. I rarely give bad reviews because life is too short to struggle with bad books but this was shockingly bad and had so much hype! 
 There's a lot happening here, and none of it is executed well at all. Lots of poorly drawn characters, terrible dialogue (personal favourite moment is a character unprepared for questioning who says "When I thought about that later on I concluded it must have been a lie, because I'd seen a photograph of Nel moving into her first flat in Brooklyn, her t-shirt stretched tight over her already pregnant belly". Has anyone ever spoken in casual conversation like that? Ever?), reams of internal monologue - often the same points repeated by different characters but with nothing new added at all - and little action. 
 I was particularly annoyed about the LS lighter, an on going mystery/clue but the audience is never given a fair shot at understanding it because the character it refers to has a different name up until the reveal. 
 Also Erin has a secret that is literally never mentioned until the last 15% of the book when it is used against her by other characters. What's the point? Why do I care about that if I have no idea what the stakes are or what's on the line? 
 There's a mini-mystery in the first few pages of the book as to the whereabouts of one character in particular, don't get interested in it because it's completely irrelevant and won't be referred to again. 
 Personal gripe: this book seems to be set in the North-East of England, which is where I grew up, and I was super annoyed that all Hawkins did about this was randomly name drop towns. It could have been set anywhere at all, there is so little feeling of the setting in a book that is ostensibly ABOUT A PHYSICAL GEOGRAPHICAL FEATURE, there's nothing in it apart from cliched descriptions of the river (it's constant, it moves, it has dark water). Totally missed a chance on this one. 
 It's just not a good book, recommend to avoid.

reference_books.title: The Elephant Vanishes
reference_books.review_text: I guess I just don't "get" Murkami. All of these stories were dull and colourless featuring indistinguishable characters listening to music and reading books. "Sleep" was the high point for me, but saying it was a high point isn't really saying much at all.

reference_books.title: If on a Winter's Night a Traveler
reference_books.review_text: I wanted to like this book, I really did. As many others have noted, it starts really strong, and there's no way you could say that the author isn't immensely talented but... ugh. Reading this was in turns frustrating and boring. I understand the premise but by the end everything began to grate on me. I really struggled to finish this and did it purely out of bloody minded determination, but as soon as I put it down I thought "thank God that's over."

reference_books.title: How to Be a Woman
reference_books.review_text:
Thie first half of this book is really great, really funny and makes interesting points relating the author's experiences to certain feminist issues quite successfully. And then the second half of the book happens and it drags everything down. The second half feels far more rushed and careless and that's when the writing style goes from humorous and fun to grating and annoyingly twee. With her many italicised and caps locked proclamations of "GOD!" I felt a bit like she was co-writing with a brattier Napoleon Dynamite. 
 I also found it to be annoyingly preachy and prescriptive, a lot of "this is what I think and you should think it too because I have decided that I am terribly clever and also this one time I met Lady Gaga". Which is particularly good as she also mentions that many people find feminism hard to understand and overly academic, so rather than make coherent arguments, she's just sort of pushed a viewpoint on the reader presumably because she assumes her readers aren't very good at that whole thinking and understanding for themselves thing. 
 Had this just been a memoir (and better edited to take the grating edge away), I'd have given it a much higher rating. Unfortunately, it was pushing too hard to be something it's not; useful and insightful.

reference_books.title: The Secret Place (Dublin Murder Squad, #5)
reference_books.review_text: my first reads copy of this never emerged, so I went out excitedly on release day to buy it. Overall, I'm disappointed. A lot of this reads like then YA, which is a genre I usually love, but it's not what I expected or wanted from this. The whole 450 page book takes place in one day with a lot of it being focused on interviews with teen girls saying "everyone knew they were seeing each other because we saw them snogging!" etc, which was wearing and boring and repetitive. I'm going with 3 stars because everything aside, French is still a great writer, I just can't get over how dull a lot of the first half of this book was. Also, the side plot with magic is just... Yeah.

book_a.title: The Icarus Girl
book_a.user_review:
Review should be more like 2.5 stars. 
 This book was ok. It took a while to get remotely interesting but later it did improve. I really wanted to like it more but it all felt flat and it was hard to care. 
 It wasn't bad or anything but not one I'd recommend. I do want to read the authors later books though, to see how her work has evolved as she grew up.

sample_reviews.review_text: As an English teacher, I spend a lot of time being told to tell teenagers that the "only" important West African author is Chinua Achebe. Having long believed that Benjamin Oke and Sole Woyinka prove that wrong, I was delighted to find The Icarus Girl, and in it, a lovely, slightly scary story about a Nigerian/British girl. It is more Western than most "Africa" books; more African than most English books. In all, it is a delight, and I look forward to reading more from the same author.

Well, this was a bit of a surprise. The Icarus Girl is definitely my least favorite book by Oyeyemi, though the story is not at fault here. This is the most conventionally suspenseful book in her repertoire, it just so happened that I failed to engage with any of the principal characters, and the sudden bursts of lingual glory that I've come to expect also largely fails to make an appearance here. No sentences that really made me sit back and marvel, no descriptions that give me those chills of recognition. 
 But, if you read the first 100 pages and find yourself engrossed in the characters of The Icarus Girl, then I have no doubt the suspense of the story will carry you through and leave you thrilled.

Helen Oyeyemi's first novel is the story of a precocious, gifted, lonely eight-year-old girl named Jessamy Harrison. Jess doesn't seem to belong anywhere. She is half Nigerian, half English. She has been moved up a year in school due to her exceptional intelligence. She doesn't relate to other children, and her parents and teachers are wary of her too. Her parents take her to Nigeria to visit family where Jess finds doesn't fit in either. While there Jess meets a strange, magical girl she names TillyTilly. Things are not all they seem and TillyTilly is no ordinary young Nigerian girl who mysteriously moves to England when Jess returns home. As Jess becomes more attached to TillyTilly, she becomes ill, and the people she cares about experience unexplained accidents. The descriptions are haunting and a sense of dread builds throughout the novel. It's an eerie tale that doesn't quite fulfill it's promise.
Waste of time. Terrible characterization, horrible dialogue, nonsensical content. This read like really bad young adult fiction.
I love the detail.

As a precocious 19-year-old studying for her A-levels, Nigerian-born Helen Oyeyemi earns points for writing a thematically ambitious novel. The Icarus Girl depicts an equally precocious eight-year-old girl, Jessamy, or Jess, daughter of a Nigerian mother and English father, who is wildly imaginative, bright, rebellious, and full of dreams and fantasies typical of many girls her age. But Oyeyemi loses points, big time, for being unable to devise a story that can sustain her literary ambitions. 
 Jess has behavioral problems - fits of screaming - that lead her parents to visit the family estate in Ibadan, Nigeria, where Oyeyemi wonderfully evokes an extended Yoruba household (and knocks down a number of cliches and popular images of Africans in the process). Jess meets her austere but loving grandfather, but more ominously, she encounters Titiola, or TillyTilly, a young girl who appears to be half spirit, half witch. 
 Oyeyemi's plan is to tackle one of the oldest the literary devices, that of the double, the shadow, the doppelganger - and she does so with a vengeance: TillyTilly's appearances, in Ibadan and back in London, and her impact on Jess, drive the book's plot. Initially, TillyTilly is a wonderful secret and magical friend for Jess, but soon her actions grow ominous, motivated by jealousy for Jess's relationships with her friends, and even her parents. 
 Jess's behavioral problems grow worse, often caused by TillyTilly's machinations, and Icarus Girl becomes a kind of horror story as both the reader, and Jessamy begin to dread TillyTilly's next appearance and increasingly destructive actions: terrorizing Jess's friends, smashing computers and bathroom mirrors, and possibly even causing her father's mysterious illness and depression. 
 The problem for the reader becomes one of storytelling. The Icarus Girl is not a YA novel, and the daily life of an eight-year-old - no matter how precocious and troubled - becomes an uninteresting routine of school and home where not much happens until TillyTilly decides to show up. And even then, Jess and Tilly sometimes seem both bored and wary of each other, as Jess exacts promises that TillyTilly will behave - only to have Tilly ignore her a moment later and cause trouble large and small. 
 Matters finally escalate, and TillyTilly reveals the critical information that, yes, indeed, she is somehow not a living being, but wants to live by "trading places" with Jess and possessing her. This sets off the final battles between the two , which results in serious injury to one of Jess's sleepover friends. 
 Parents, teachers, and psychiatrists finally become aware of TillyTilly as well, although Jess continues to insist that Tilly is an independent spirit and not simply a projection of her own fears. 
 Resolution can only come the old-fashioned way: with a return to Ibadan, and a dose of African witchcraft to give Jess the strength and insight to finally confront and defeat TillyTilly on her own ground. 
 In the end, I think TillyTilly is a more frightening figure that Oyeyemi gives her credit for. The story might have worked much better as a novella that embraced the horror element from the beginning, modeled more as a "Turn of the Screw" story than a family drama.

Reading this book, I kept questioning the relationship between liminality and doubling. Common motifs in Gothic fiction, these themes are actually connected quite strongly. Liminality, that is, being caught on the borders, being caught between one thing and another, almost always causes this 'doubling'. One must be both things, be one thing more than the other, be neither. This causes a split, a fracture, a schism. And thus, doubles occur: mirror images, split selves. 
 In Oyeyemi's 'The Icarus Girl', Jessamy is caught on the fringes. These include: English/Nigerian (the narrative itself is also split in this way, with sections I - II - III taking place in separate parts of the world), Well/Unwell, Awake/Dreaming. Coupling this sense of bordering is a deep loneliness. A loneliness that is remnant of, and yet surpasses, traditional adolescent alienation. These things isolate Jessamy and make her feel like she does not 'fit' anywhere, a 'half-and'half' girl. Naturally, magical realism dictates that these circumstances birth a double. Jessamy's double is a frighteningly cruel yet soothingly understanding little girl who she calls 'TillyTilly'. TillyTilly understands Jess's perpetual fear and why she has to scream and scream and scream. But TillyTilly also makes it difficult for Jess to feel 'really real' by pulling her into her supernatural games. Jess must keep TillyTilly a secret, which leads to an extraordinary double existence between one world and the next. Again, Jess becomes caught between borders, or even realms. She splits and doubles again, and this time, a twin is unearthed. This process of bordering and doubling creates a wonderfully rich psychological atmosphere. And one that could be analysed and analysed from a variety of angles (especially considering that ambiguously ambiguous ending). 
 Of course, 'The Icarus Girl' is about more than liminal spaces and not-so alter egos. It is about myth, and about childhood. Critics pointed out it was about cultural identity and modern day alienation. It is also, in my opinion, primarily a book about good and bad, right and wrong. It is about wanting to be good, always, but finding out that this is impossible (even for the nicest of nice people). 
 I personally loved this book. I love anything thematically rich, magical and frightening, so this ticked all the right boxes for me. It astounds me that Oyeyemi wrote this when she was studying for her A Levels. I think all I did when studying for my A Levels was read comic books and eat pringles. And he writing is so damn evocative and brave and haunting. None of it feels clunky or awkward. I think I'll be singing this lady's praises for a long, long time.
This was depressing. But well-written and thought provoking. But not as good as the other things I've read by her. -\_(tsu)_/-

Beautifully written, but had a very slow build. Not much happens in the first 100 pages, and after that things start to get confusing and jump around a good bit. I think the story could have been better if it started further in, if the author had just skipped the first 70 pages or so and made things more active. I think, that the fact that it's from a 9 year old's confused perspective, makes the whole story confusing. Which means that you learn things only as a child learns them. Which works for people who like suspense and mystery, but that kind of confusion just frustrates me.

Jessamy Harrison is a somber, contemplative child who keeps to herself. She loses herself in her world and her imagination. Her mother, a writer originally from Nigeria, decides to take her family (which includes Jess and her English husband) to her home country where Jess learns about her mother's roots for the first time from her mother's family. There Jess meets a little girl named TillyTilly who becomes one of Jess' closest friends despite the fact that there's something a little strange about TillyTilly. As the story progresses, Jess realizes there's something disturbing about TillyTilly as strange things begin to occur in her world that makes the reader questions what's real and what's part of Jess' imagination. 
 Part myth and part horror story, this was certainly an engrossing read. I don't think this story will surprise too many people, especially if you read much horror. However, that's true of most horror, and it's more about the atmospheric quality of the story than anything. There's not creepier than children interacting with ghosts/monsters in horror stories because of the innocence that most children bring to the story and the helplessness they can pull from the reader because they're a child involved in something that's much bigger and scarier than they can truly comprehend. Jess is no exception, and it's quite a harrowing ride to follow her as TillyTilly firmly plants herself in Jess' world. 
 Bahni Turpin narrated this story. I'd forgotten that I had this book when I reviewed Unholy Ghosts, which is narrated by Turpin as well, and I didn't have to get that one to sample her work. However, the style she used for the books couldn't have been more different. I was much more moved by her narration of this book, but her narration of Unholy Ghosts is nothing to laugh at either. She's a talented narrator, and her range and depth of character and emotion is amazing. I did think this story went on way too long. It felt like it would've been a great short story. If it had been tight and concise this would've probably resonated with me a little longer and the ending would've had a great impact. I'm floundering on how I feel about the ending a bit, but I think, if this had cut out much of the story, it would've been more fitting. Still, this was a lyrical, haunting story that certainly left me mulling over for quite some time after I listened to it.

book_b.title: Far From You
book_b.user_review:
Updated review: 
 3.5 stars 
 I received this book by winning a Goodreads First Reads competition. 
 Far From You is a tense and bittersweet YA whodunit/romance following the story of Sophie's recovery from crippling car accidents and addiction, and her attempts to find out who killed her best friend. The book alternates chapters between the past and the present, reining memories of the girls' friendship and Sophie's various struggles. 
 The strength of this book lay very strongly in the romance aspect. The love triangle, Sophie and Mina's relationship, even the little we see about Mina's boyfriends, all of this was clearly drawn and well realised. The build up to the reveal with Sophie and Mina was slow and natural, and the issues surrounding bisexuality and lesbianism were handled very gracefully. 
 Unfortunately, the book falls down with regards to the murder mystery. There were definitely some echoes of Veronica Mars for me, and I was disappointed that this book didn't quite reach those heights. As mentioned above, the book flips back and forth between the present; a device which I thought could have been better used to give more red herrings about who the murderer was and what their motive was. As it is, those flashbacks only really touch on Sophie's feelings about Mina. While this really helped the romance plot, it did little for the mystery storyline and the big reveal is actually kind of a let down because there was almost no foreshadowing or surprise or shock. 
 This brings me to the other big issue I had with this book, which is that the main characters (Sophie, Mina, Trev) are excellent. They're flawed, complicated characters, with nuances and all that good stuff. However, it's as if all the detail was saved for these three only, and supporting characters show far less personality and distinction. I found myself wishing that Rachel and Kyle were allowed a bigger part of the action rather than relegated to convenient sidekicks, and of course, that lack of characterisation really hurts the chances of caring about the killer because we know nothing about him/her! 
 The style flows well enough, the story is absorbing enough, and the romance is touching enough to forgive these aspects and that's why I've leaned towards 4 stars. By the last chapters of the book, I felt genuinely emotional and invested in the relationships and found the finals very moving and enjoyable (especially when Sophie leaves Trev and wonders how things would have turned out with Mina - if they would even have made it without their relationship being secret ). I would happily have traded the addiction side of things for more mystery, and if that had been the case, I think this probably would have been a long time favourite of mine.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Scrawling out of review because this book actually filled a major void caused by another book with that literally in all ways was trying to be this book, but failed in all aspects. 
 That is to say that if you have to choose between Vanishing Girls and this, my vote is this. Because it did everything better. The genre, the love triangle between siblings, the mental health/rebel teen edge, it was all handled much, much better in this book, and tackled issues of sexuality, drug addiction, and grief in a much less smoke-and-mirrors way. 
 This book was really hard. 
 I went in knowing that this book was going to be hella gay. And it delivered. I am so happy that we finally have a bisexual character choosing between two love interests that have factors outside of gender that make the choice complicated. I still didn't like the implication of her having to choose to begin with, but her choice is the one who's kinda dead (not a spoiler it's the first thing you find out in the book), and instead it shapes her arc around recovery from addiction and letting go of the people she's mourning. 
 At first I found Mina to be the biggest, most annoying bitch in that typical "she was the exciting one and I was the quiet one" stereotype, but honestly, for someone as angry and closeted as Mina I sort of forgave her for it These were two real, well rounded queer characters. 
 It is very high stakes drama 24/7. There's not a lot to cuddle into and savor, but our MC is high on Oxy for most of the flashbacks, so there's not a lot of spare joy to be found. But it's there. I definitely will keep my mind rolling this one around for a while.

This review from my blog: http://lostinstory.weebly.com/home/re... 
 Young adult book about Sophie who is leaving rehab and mourning the loss of her best friend when the book opens. The incident that landed in her in rehab resulted in the death of her friend Mina. Mina told her they were going to meet someone in the woods and this man shoots Mina and plants drugs on Sophie. But Sophie knows she was clean, even though no one (deservedly) believes her. As soon as she's out of rehab, she sets out to find Sophie's killer which leads to a much larger mystery. 
 What I liked: 
 This book does a good job of showing complex relationships. I feel like in a lot of YA, the dead character is flawless and amazing and everyone loved them. That really isn't the case here and it's refreshing. Mina could be really manipulative and emotionally cruel, but Sophie and her were extremely close and there are a lot of good things about her as well. Also, while people are still mourning Mina, the whole town hasn't shut down on her behalf, which is far more realistic. 
 Sophie is a complex character who truly struggles with addiction and has to deal with the consequences of her decisions. 
 Sophie also has very really disfigurement from a car accident and struggles with disability that results from this accident throughout the book. 
 There is a central LGBTQ+ romance which I thought had a good amount of complexity as well. 
 What I didn't like: 
 The book had a lot of points that just were too convenient or improbable. Not beyond what you would usually see in a YA book, but as an adult reader it was noticeable. 
 There's a tragic love triangle that I understand but didn't really like. I felt like it didn't add to the central relationship of the book in any way and seemed to mostly serve to show Sophie was desirable. 
 I thought the solution to the big mystery of the book was completely out of left field. A big part of the book is Sophie trying to solve the mystery of Mina's death and another mystery that lead to her being killed. I didn't feel like any of the things she did to try to find the killer actually had any impact on the plot. The killer chooses to out himself by attacking her for getting "too close" when she wasn't really close at all.

When I first picked this book in the library, I thought I will read about an exciting YA thriller. I was wrong. There is nothing interesting in this book. The plot twist was horrible and I can't consider it a plot twist any way. It is more of "the author lied to the readers for her silly plot". WHY! I kept on reading to see if the ending would make me like the book. NOPE! This book is not a thriller and not a crime and a mystery book. It is just a trick to force the readers to the boring love story. Next time, be honost and state in the cover the true story, not lie for the plot!

** spoiler alert ** 
 A student gave me this book, although she herself had not read it. I really liked the way the story jumps around in time, it kept me on the edge of my seat as I wanted to solve the mystery right along with Sophie. I was totally shocked when I found out who Mina's killer was, I did not see that coming! I didn't mind the drug addiction aspect of this book, it was interesting to get into the head of someone who's using and who's try to stay clean. I could have done without the sex scenes though, at least they weren't too graphic! This is why I read YA books... I can't take that, lol!

Sophie is released from rehab- for the second time. Seriously hurt after her best friend Mina was killed, no one believes that the drugs found on Sophie were not the reason the two were in a remote area known for drug dealers. Even her close friend and Mina's brother, Trev, doesn't believe. Especially her parents do not believe her. Now Sophie finds solace and obsession in finding Mina's killer, who of course, knows she is out and searching. 
 Starting with flashbacks, the story moves from the present to the past, four months ago, to the present, to the past, eleven months ago, to the present, but 3 months into the future, to the.... You get the idea. It is very annoying and disconcerting. They do however, allow us to slowly realize that Sophie and Mina were more than best friends. The flashbacks allow us to understand the depth of Sophie's addiction and her struggle even now. They do not allow us to be a mystery reader and see clues about the killer. The ending surprises even good mystery readers. 
 All that said, this is a very enjoyable read. It is heartbreaker and thriller, with well-written characters and a fierce and tenacious heroine. First novel from Tess Sharpe, an author to be watched.

I really enjoyed reading this book, it was definitely different than I thought it would be. I liked how it flicked back and forth between the past and the present, so you were following two different aspects of Sophie's life at once. I liked Sophie's character, she wasn't your typical main character, and i found her really intriguing - she was grieving for the loss of her best friend, she was a recovering drug addict, keeping secrets, etc. Her personality was made up by all these things that had happened to her which for me made her a more interesting character. 
 I didn't predict the relationship between Mina and Sophie, but I thought the bisexuality was handled really well. I also didn't predict the murderer, so i thought the mystery aspect was really good. 
 I'll definitely be reading more of Tess Sharpe's books in the future.

** spoiler alert ** 
 What can I say? I know a lot of people praise this book for its representation of an openly bisexual character, but as I found said character utterly unlikeable and at times even deplorable the book crumbled around her for me. The murder mystery was sloppily executed, the previous drug addiction felt like it was forced into the plot and its consequences were badly portrayed. Both Sophie and Trev were very superficial and the only reason I even finished the book was because I adored Mina. That being said, the Sophie-Mina sex scene, however short, was steamy and amazing. Just for that and for Mina's character, I am giving 2 stars instead of 1.

Everyone, from the detective to her own parents, know that it was Sophie's fault that Mina was killed. After all, Sophie is the one who's hooked on Oxy, not Mina. Booker's Point is not a place you go without wanting to score. And when a container of Oxy is found in Sophie's pocket, everything assumes that Sophie is just lying like she always does. Trouble is, they've all got it wrong. 
 But as Sophie starts to piece together that fateful night, things don't seem to be adding up. And since the police seem to be reluctant to believe Sophie's side of the story, it is up to her to try to find the killer. 
 Part mystery, part coming-of-age tale, Far From You has so many nooks and crannies where little tidbits of story are hidden, just waiting to be discovered. Chapters shift back and forth from different time periods, adding a richness and a depth to this ballad of innocence lost, pain and honesty. The mystery is so well-enveloped into the rest of the story that you almost don't see it coming. 
 The relationships in this book are fabulously drawn - so real. Frequently lovely, mostly heartbreaking, it's a drumbeat of what-ifs, what-could-have-beens, and some hopeful what-can-bes. 
 Far From You by Tess Sharpe was published by Disney Hyperion on March 27, 2014. A free copy of this book was given to Ink and Page in return for an honest review. Big thanks to NetGalley/the Publisher/the Author.

reference_books.title: Shades of Milk and Honey (Glamourist Histories, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I had read the third book in this series first, because it was on the new book shelves at the library, and liked it well enough to want to go start from the beginning. This one isn't so involved with the war and spying - it's a pretty standard Regency about class and station and marrying off daughters and such, nicely done - plus the magic, which I like because it's quite different - no wizards, no witches, just a particular sort of magic that is an art, like playing the violin - many can learn to do a little, some can make a living at it, a very few can travel the world as professionals at it. 
 A few pros - as I said, the magic is different, and nicely integrated. Our heroine and hero are not ideal characters, they have flaws. Also, our heroine is rather more the rescuer of others than the hero is. 
 A few cons - boy, the younger sister is an unpleasant, whiny brat. And man, the part of the plot with the evil guy was obvious from miles ahead. But there, it resolved nicely nonetheless, and I'm quite ready to go on to the next volume.
