reference_books.title: Neptune's Brood (Freyaverse #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Warning: even a one-sentence summary of this book is a spoiler if you have any idea what I'm talking about in the first place. So let me preface that spoiler sentence with this: if you find the financial industries (roughly, banking, insurance, accounting, economics) interesting, then the rest of this is spoilers, and if you /don't find the financial industries interesting, then you're going to find large chunks of this book tedious, even though they are very funny, unless you are so enamoured of Stross's writing style that you plan to read everything he writes whether you like it or not. 
 OK, here's the SPOILER: 
 Post-Singularity deep space accounting fraud, with mad priests, zombies, and pirates. Chiropteroid space pirate insurance adjusters, to be precise. (Chiropteroid means bat-like, for those of you who don't have a biology background, and yes, our space pirate insurance branch office is headed by Count Rudi, a giant fruit bat.) 
 There are lots of references to other things in the science fiction canon, as with any of Stross's books, and some of them are to his own books. Certainly, if the Gravid Mother doesn't make you stop and reminisce about the first time you read John Wyndham's "Consider Her Ways," then you haven't read nearly enough classic science fiction. Go find it - if it's not in your local library in a collection of classics, well, it's available used online for less than a dollar. 
 As far as Stross's style - it's one of those things where you either find it amusing, or you find it irritating. Let's see which you find this paragraph: 
 "They call it piracy, you call it hijacking; I call it taking advantage of an unscheduled rendezvous to audit the undeclared cargo of a suspicious long-haul vehicle and order put options on the raw materials prior to its arrival on the commodities market at its destination." 
 Or consider the place-names within the Dojima system where we are travelling: 
 "...from Taj Beacon to the glass-windowed spinning baubles of the Leading and Trailing Pretties, the Shiny! Asteroids, the colonies on the moons of Zeus and Chronos, the zeppelin-castles of Mira and the hundred warring laminar republics of Shin-Tethys." 
 OK, I have a sense of humor enough influenced by geek culture to find naming an asteroid belt Shiny! (with the exclamation point) amusing. If you don't hang out with people who say "Ooooooh, shiny!" at new things, then you might not be as amused. 
 If you have read "Saturn's Children" - which was an homage to Heinlein as much as anything, then consider that Freya's generation of androids is a few thousand years earlier than Krina's, since Freya's generation was considering whether to revive the human species from extinction the first time, and this book refers to humans as having been revived several times in the past. And if you have read "Accelerando" than you have an inkling of Stross's take on capitalism. (Remember the uploaded lobsters? I loved the uploaded lobsters.) You don't have to have read either of those; although they're in the same universe, they are not necessary prequels at all.

book_a.title: Karen Memory
book_a.user_review: Elizabeth Bear isn't always my cup of tea - though by choice of topics and plots she should be, her writing style just doesn't happen to be to my personal tastes, most of the time. This is one of the exceptions. This book is a hoot and a half! Very funny, with all the gadgets you could possibly want, and a few you wouldn't. I enjoyed both concept and execution.

sample_reviews.review_text:
So, I find this book very upsetting. I was told it was a Seattle Steampunk, jack-the-ripper novel. What I got was wild-west, name a harbor town on the Pacific Ocean made up city, with a slave-trade mystery going on. Other then a side character of a serial killer (not knifing rapist), who only gets apprehended as a side note of the main story line, there was no jack-the-ripper angle. I can't really blame the author on this, I was told by other people that that was what the story was about. 
 It did have steam-punk moments, things that clearly couldn't have happened in the wild-west, but overall because my expectations were different it was very hard for me to enjoy this novel.

A fun, action packed steampunk western! A wide diverse cast of characters, it makes you wish the West really was like that. It was a quick read for me because it kept my attention and told its story well. Recommended.

Karen is trying to make the best of her orphaned status by working at Madame Damnable's high-quality bordello, along with a group of resourceful women, in an alternate pre-underground Seattle Underground. One night an injured girl arrives needing sanctuary and followed by the man who holds her indenture, and this man has a machine that can control people's minds and bodies. If that wasn't enough, they find the body of a brutally murdered streetwalker in their rubbish heap the next night. 
 Elizabeth Bear's Karen Memory has a little bit of something for everyone. It's a pulpy western sci-fi steampunk alternate history thriller with a dash of romance and featuring a memorable and diverse cast of characters. Karen, our narrator, has a distinct, honest voice and she carries this Jack-the-Ripper-esque story well. Even though Karen is such a great character, my favorite is easily Bass Reeves; he totally makes the story for me. If you are unfamiliar with the real-life Bass Reeves, I recommend you look him up. Overall, this new standalone adventure from Elizabeth Bear turns stereotypes on their head and is well worth your time.

I really didn't enjoy this book. Primarily, I think, because I found Karen's voice grating as hell. If you're going to write a particular dialect, you need to commit to that dialect---just because a bunch sentences are all ungrammatical, that doesn't mean they make sense as part of a single dialect. For example, sometimes Karen "knowed" things, sometimes she "knew" things, but there was no rhyme or reason for either choice. It was just so . . . jarring. 
 Also, the characters were pretty flat. There were the Good Guys, the Bad Guys, and not a single shade of grey to be found. The characters were diverse, yes, but it felt as if the author thought that diversity meant she no longer had to bother actually drawing fully-fleshed characters. 
 As the book progressed, I ended up skimming more than actually reading. Other people might enjoy this, but I definitely did not.
The reader did a great job, but her lovely accent made the whole book sound so Western that it felt much less steampunk. There were some cool inventions too.

It took a while for me to get into this book. I almost considered not finishing it. Not sure where the turning point was, but it finally caught my attention. I would have to say it was enjoyable, but predictable. Steam punk isn't really my thing. Chose it for one of the prompts of a reading challenge I'm doing.

Not much about this book impressed me. Neither the world nor the plot were very interesting (though both were passable). I found the prose distracting. The things I wanted to see the most of - the steam machines - were featured infrequently and in too little detail. Neither one of which is a real dealbreaker, but I found the combination of all these things to be... not boring, but not awfully interesting. Passable.

This book was frustrating, because it had so many good elements that simply didn't gel. The whole is less than the sum of the parts. 
 The concept is fun, the ideas are neat, and I appreciate how rare it is to find a steampunk story that is Science Fiction rather than Fantasy. I even enjoyed the patois the book was written in. 
 But the problems overwhelm the good bits. 
 Let's start with the main character, Karen Memery (why it's changed for the title, I don't know. "Memory" as a concept or plot device never comes into play). She's a 16-year-old orphaned rancher's daughter who becomes a prostitute. Give her ranch-hand background and her clear lesbian tendencies, I didn't buy that she would choose that profession. I also didn't buy that she was 16. Her voice comes across as distinctly adult. I was actually thinking she was in her late 20s by the end of the tale. She's also very bright and reads a lot, which makes me wonder why her grammar is so messed up. It certainly gives you the flavor of the era and class of folks the book is about, but a smart girl who can read both English and French isn't likely to use "must of" instead of "must've." 
 The only thing that really marked her as a teen was the fact she developed an instant crush on a strange girl who comes to the brothel. But that was so at odds with the rest of her character that it was a poor fit. 
 Then there's the plot. This is a mash-up of Jack the Ripper and a Western, which is fine, but there are so many preposterous coincidences and deus ex machina moments that the plot becomes a mess by the end. It seemed like the main characters confronted the main bad guys a half-dozen times at the end, yet never explained how they A) kept turning up after having been apparently dynamited/drowned/shot, and B) why they behaved so inconsistently. At one point Karen and her crush are taken aboard The Octopus, a Jules Verne-inspired version of The Nautilus, and are kept alive by ruthless murderers. If it were just the serial killer who felt compelled to keep them around in order to torture them later, that would make sense, but it's the cut-throat mercenaries who have the girls. Then they show off their submarine's abilities. Why? Bragging, sure, but the whole point of their submarine is to keep their activity secret. Yes, the girls were prisoners aboad the sub and the submariners were confident they couldn't escape and were planning on murdering them. No, it still makes no sense. 
 Karen becoms an epic version of the Action Girl trope, but it's too much. By the end she's ranging out into Mary Sue territory. 
 I could go on, but all in all I just didn't buy into the story. I really liked the diversity of the characters, but none of them ever felt like real people, instead of constructs designed to move the plot along.

I received an ARC of this from tor.com, and had a lot of fun with it. Sadly, ARCs usually don't have the cover art, so I'm missing that FANTASTIC cover. I'm considering getting a real copy simply because that cover is so pretty. 
 But wait! We're not supposed to judge books by their covers. This one's a steampunk pacific northwest (what is it about Seattle and Steampunk, anyway?), where our protagonist and her pals work in a brothel, "sewing". But the action doesn't revolve around tricks --- it's just that a (properly run) brothel is a likely location to find women who can (and do!) think on their own and take the power they need to accomplish their goals. So no sex scenes. (And they're *not* missed.) 
 The cast of characters here is fantastically diverse; many points of view and wildly varying personalities. The inner dialog of our first-person protagonist was a dream to read; her language and word choice just oozes attitude. 
 The city itself was odd, Bear had posited a city where rising waters were a worry, so all the city-owned properties were raised. (In other words, the streets.) The buildings between the streets were the problem of the owners, so they tend (especially in the poorer parts of town) to still be nestled on the ground. So there are ladders from the ground up to the street. And some jumping from upper story windows to the roadway. It's quite a strange bit of world, and I'm not sure it really works for the story at all. 
 The "tecnhology" in this steampunk setting is also more farfetched than other steampunk-style stories I've read. The transformation of a sewing machine into an armored exoskeleton was the most farfetched (mostly because it wasn't ever described; it just sort of changed at some point). I haven't really read enough steampunk to know if this is the norm or not, but it rubbed me wrong. 
 Still. Lots of stars for strong, independent, smart women characters! 
 4 of 5 stars.

Cute YA fiction. I feel it is well done, with a good voice and good story. Easy reading, easy to like the characters and hate the villains. You know exactly what's going to happen, but that's okay; it's cliche in all the good ways. Best of all, NO LOVE TRIANGLE! That's right, a teen book with a gay love story that is well done, positive, and does NOT have a love triangle. Why can't more novels follow this pattern?

book_b.title: The Enchantment Emporium (Gale Women, #1)
book_b.user_review: Eh. I like Tanya Huff, but this isn't one of her most exciting or even one of her funnier ones.

sample_reviews.review_text: I read this book over a year ago when I was on a Tanya Huff kick. I loved the humor of the main charecter and her interactions with her family. When she took over her Grandma's store, the people she meets are fantastic. The complete story is really great!! I couldn't reccommend this book fast enough if asked what my favorite Huff book is. Only drawback is she didn't write a sequel. =;[

I'd have given this book 5 stars for plot and creativity if it weren't for the profanity and innuendo woven throughout. I would not recommend this book to the morally sensitive and I won't likely read another Tanya Huff book. But I say that with regret because I so thoroughly enjoyed her humor and writing style, and I couldn't put the book down until I'd finished it.

The book deserves more than two stars, but I can't get past my unmet expectations. I'm not sure why, but I expected a Diana Wynne Jones style magic for adults. The Enchantment Emporium has its own style. If it suits you, the book is definitely more than two stars. It has a sharp edge, pop culture references, tangled loyalties and coherent world building.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This review deals with all three (thus far) books in the series. It contains spoilers. It's not really a review so much a commentary/observation. 
 I don't know if Ms. Huff intended it this way, but what I took away from this book was this: This is what a traditional fantasy series would look like if the gender roles were reversed. 
 Think about it. The Gale girls are high-handed, arrogant, they sleep with whom the choose, they mostly ignore issues of consent, they do all the real work, and while boys are sometimes let in, they really don't play a big role. The women are most of the characters, they have complex relationships with one another and to the world, they take action. The Gale men are tied to a place, generally pursued rather than pursuing, seen as passive, and they have exactly one power: "to choose." 
 It's not a full-on reversal. If it were, the men would be two-dimensional and have no distinguishing characteristics other than their gender. And there would be far fewer of them, they would speak and do less, and they wouldn't have any voice at all. Ms. Tuff is too good a writer to turn her men into cardboard cut outs. 
 I adore this series, even if it's a little ... odd in places. (The semi-incestuous thing was a more than a little strange until I decided/grasped that it's a big clan and you can certain date your fifth cousin without any issues.) I love the old-school 70s hippie ethos of a matriarchal clan of kitchen witches engaging in free-love and Mists of Avalon-type rituals. 
 I hope there are more books to come.

DNF. Too many characters introduced in the first few chapters- all of the same family so hard to keep track of who's who. Very muddled and confusing storyline. 
 I hoped it might settle down and resolve into an enjoyable story but it didn't.

I didn't realize that there is now a genre called "urban fantasy" but with all the vampire lit out there these days, I'm not surprised. This book is about a family of witches but that is never actually stated. The rituals and organization of the family into "circles" is never explained very well, nor is the role of all the implied sex in those rituals. The plot is really, really weak as are the characters.
Interesting fantasy book that was written in such a way that the magic felt that the magic is natural.

I really like Tanya's work, she's one of the few authors that got me to read actual Fantasy, I do enjoy her Valor series a lot, but my true love always was with her Vicky Nelson novels and so it was with great anticipation that I awaited her return to Urban Fantasy. 
 Ah, but what a disappointment this book is. 
 After a hundred+ pages I'm still not sure what the main protagonist is supposed to be. Other than some variety of magic user that is. 
 All that Tanya cares to tell us about her is that she comes from a family that is very free about using incest as a means to keep "the power" within the family and doesn't mind sexual encounters between siblings. This and that they feel strongly drawn to power. Other than that she's strangely vague about what the Gale's are. The fact that male Gale's grow horns probably means some sort of fairy folk. 
 And while their enormous, barely controllable sex-drive explains why for example main protagonist Alysha's closest friend and lover Charlie is bound to evaluate each and everything by his or her worth as potential sex partner, and to hump them at the drop of a hat, it leaves us guessing, when the author tells us that Charlie's hair is blue if she means dyed blue or by nature... and that's just the minor unexplained stuff ging on. 
 A very personal thing I minded was the use of text messaging in the book without any translation. Given, we do come upon a passage written in French, only shortly after, but that's something I've come to expect from Canadian authors, same as American ones are liable to drop some Spanish phrases and past century ones to use Latin phrases without translation. 
 The difference here is that French is a language, which I'm willing to look up if need be, while text messaging is only a abbreviation system without agreed rules. But as I say that's a personal thing. 
 Btw. I still don't know what- "Spnt nght cxng A Ruby off H2O twr." -is supposed to mean, but water seems to have something to do with it. 
 I'm not saying by that, that this is a entirely bad novel, but it's certainly not a good book to start a series on. It's written for people that either read a lot more straight fantasy novels than I do, and by that are better at reading the hidden clues, or that just don't mind a game of guess the character race and are willing to take random magical occurrences at face value. However, I'm just not ready yet again to trust a novel against better judgment to perhaps make some more sense down the road. As it stands I have to say, sorry, but this one goes to the did not finish staple.
I really enjoy Tanya Huff. I especially liked how accessible these characters were and how the story focused on independent women.

I want to be clear that this review is based on the audiobook of this novel. This is an important distinction because I suspect I would have liked the book. The Gales are different. Powerful. And mostly women. When Gale girls have babies, they become Aunties. When Gale boys become adults, they have to choose. If this sounds confusing, it was made even more so by ambiguous names and a reader who didn't have enough vocal variation to create effectively male or female characters. Take Charley. A girl. Or Gran (short for Grandmother) and Graham (pronounced in this audo as Gram) making it impossible to figure out what was happening. The gist is that Gran dies and leaves her Enchantment Emporium to Ally. She takes it over and discovers a leprechaun, a sorcerer, a dragon king and an assassin. And that's only in her first week. I suspect the book itself has greater depth. Huff has a deft talent for dialogue and pop culture which kept me listening but there were too many characters for the reader to give this book the quality it deserved.

reference_books.title: Alex + Ada, Vol. 2
reference_books.review_text:
I really liked the first installment of this graphic novel series, but volume two fell a little flat for me. In volume two, Ada is struggling with her place and purpose in the world now that she has consciousness and can make her own decisions. The two become closer, but understandably, Alex wants to give Ada enough space to figure out who she is. Ada does not take well to Alex's imposed distancing and decides to venture out into the world on her own. 
 I'm still trying to understand why this volume didn't resonate as strongly for me. Part of it is definitely that the single issues within volume two are less cohesive than they were in volume one. One of my biggest issues with graphic novels is that they can tend to feel choppy and disjointed. The other issue I have with this installment is that I don't really agree morally with how the conflict panned out. 
 In the end, Ada and Alex do get together romantically and I just can't buy into that at this point. I totally agree with Alex at the beginning when he rejects her romantic advances because she's basically a child at this point. She might have more knowledge than a child, but she has very little in the way of lived experience. It just seems wrong to jump into something like that before living a little.

reference_books.title: The Last Policeman (The Last Policeman, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I've been completely spoiled by Tana French who manages to make even the most basic characters interesting. One could even argue that her mystery plots aren't all that complex or interesting and yet, I'm always enthralled. 
 This book squandered a super interesting premise on a garbage character. 
 The Last Policeman takes place as the world is falling apart. An asteroid is due to hit the earth in just a few months, killing most or all life. The impending doom causes major disruption in the basic running of the world as people decide to quit working and live out their dreams. Some people are sticking it out however, including Hank Palace. Palace works as a detective for the Concord Police Department. Many are killing themselves before the impending doom so when he gets called out to a body that looks like a suicide, the department laughs at him calling it a suspicious death. He's convinced that it could be a murder though so he follows the nonexistent leads. 
 If this character were a woman he'd be called a Mary Sue. He made the dumbest decisions on the basis of no logic and then was time and time again rewarded for it. His gut is the strongest and truest of guts.

reference_books.title: The Cartel
reference_books.review_text:
Full disclosure: I didn't actually finish this book. However, I did read about 300 pages of this bloated novel, so I feel pretty comfortable writing a review. It was so tempting to finish The Cartel after reading so much of it but I just couldn't bring myself to do it. Those are hours of my life I could be reading The Babysitter's Club fanfiction or watching cat videos on youtube. 
 I put this book on my TBR list after hearing a great interview Don Winslow had with Terry Gross on Fresh Air. He wrote The Cartel as a fictionalized version of El Chapo, the famous head of the Mexican Sinaloa cartel. Winslow's two main characters are Art Keller, a DEA agent who has been struggling for thirty years to rid the world of Adan Barrera, the head of the El Federacion cartel. After Barrera just walks out of a prison, Keller comes out of retirement to help track him down. 
 This book was fundamentally incompatible with my tastes. Obviously a book about cartels is going to be chock-a-block full of unsavory deeds, but there's a fine line between being realistic and being gratuitous. The way Winslow writes about violence, murder, and rape falls on the wrong side of that line. There's no nuance or humanity in the way he lays out disgusting deed after disgusting deed. And the male gazey way he writes about women is gross. Instead of being realistically drawn, his characters felt two-dimensional and cartoonish. Keller is a nothingburger and Barrera is a Hollywood villain. Maybe it would have been less noticeable if Winslow had written a fast-moving plot to keep the reader engaged in the story. Instead, he hops to and from random characters in different parts of Mexico that have very little to do with the main plot. 
 I gave this book my best shot, but it didn't pull its weight.

reference_books.title: The Heiress of Winterwood (Whispers on the Moors, #1)
reference_books.review_text: This book started out really well. It promised to be fun regency romance, but kind of turned into a moralizing, religious story. Which is fine if that's your thing. I would recommend it to someone who wanted to read a romantic story about people finding faith in God.

reference_books.title: The Language of Flowers
reference_books.review_text:
2.5 stars. I'm trying to figure out if this book really did have serious flaws or if it was just wasn't a fit for me and my tastes. It's very possible that it's a mixture of both. Obviously I made it through to the end and it wasn't a hate read so it wasn't a terrible book, but I found it to be an incredibly frustrating read. The beginning was almost magical in the way it drew me in. By two-thirds of the way through though, I was debating whether I could continue. 
 The main character, Victoria, has had a really difficult life. She grew up in foster care dealing with various levels of abuse and neglect all the way through. When she's ten, she gets placed with a single woman running a vineyard who is determined to have Victoria be a part of her family despite Victoria's insistence that she hates everyone and everything. Flash forward to Victoria's 18th birthday when she's leaving her foster group home into transitional housing. All she cares about is growing flowers and she literally thinks of nothing else, even though she should be looking for a job so she doesn't become homeless. 
 The book jumps between her life at ten and eighteen. I've read many books that jump between times or narratives that were well done, but The Language of Flowers was a little uneven. I get that Diffenbaugh was trying to draw out the parallels between the storylines and create a little mystery, it just didn't always work. I'm sure this was a good representation of what it's like to be in foster care because the author works with foster kids. While I appreciate that, I had a hard time connecting to the character. I generally like hard-to-like female characters so I couldn't figure out why Victoria was different. After some thought, I think it's that Victoria is a really closed off person who can't communicate or trust anyone with her secrets and yet, the author chose to tell this story with first person narration. So Victoria's pouring her guts to the reader while supposedly being closed off to human connection. In my mind, the disconnect was huge. The fact that I listened to the audiobook version probably compounded that issue. 
 I didn't know that this book would be so relentlessly grim, so know that going into it. Looking at the reviews on goodreads it seems like many people liked it more than me, so if it sounds interesting, give it a try.

book_a.title: Out
book_a.user_review:
Ugh. 
 I was so excited to read this book and had heard good things about it, but I just hated it. HATED it. The only reason it's getting two stars instead of one is because the translator handled the prose magnificently. Too bad the story stunk. 
 Out centers on four women who work the night shift making boxed lunches. Masako is the smart one, Yoshi is the kind one, Kuniko is the selfish one, and Yayoi is the innocent one. One night Yayoi gets fed up with her abusive asshat of a husband and strangles him to death in their living room. Unsure of where to turn, she asks her friends from work for help in getting rid of the body. From there, everything starts to spiral out of control. 
 Part of my loathing lies in my expectations. I thought it was going to be some real "Earl had to die" story about women showing their terrible husbands what's what and banding together to start a body disappearing business. On paper, that's kind of what happened, but the tone is very, very grim and there is zero joy to this book. The closest book I'd compare it to would be Crime and Punishment. Even if I'd been prepared for that level of awful, I still wouldn't have loved Out. There are some weird sexual undertones about women enjoying abuse that I just couldn't stomach. I kept expecting it to get better, but it just got worse and worse, climaxing in a brutal, nonsensical scene.

sample_reviews.review_text: This is why bookclubs are great: This is so not a book that I would have chosen on my own. But after having read (and loved) The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle, along with my love of all things Japanese, I was really looking forward to this. Totally worth it. Definitely dark and disturbing at times, but the characters are real enough that you want to know more about them and see how everything turns out for them.
Un thriller japonais et une reflexion sur la condition de la femme.

This book is from the author of grotesque; its a japanese dark thriller suspense type book. Everyone in the book has jobs that are on the edge of everything - part time night shift factory workers, a loan shark, a club owner, etc. Everyone is so isolated and lonely and sad.. The book is about a group of women who work the night shift who help their coworker when she murders her husband. But it goes way beyond that. This is a super dark book, kind of depressing, but very interesting. It's horror but not your usual type of horror. It's not a fast read - it forced me to slow down my voracious scarfing down of novels and read at a more normalish pace. It's really twisted. I enjoyed it a lot. I recommend that you go read this book. If it seems slow at the very beginning, stick with it, because it quickly sucks you in thereafter. I hope to read more of her books.

I loved this book from beginning to end. You cant put it down without finishing it. It's an absorbing thriller about what a simple person, a housewife is capable of, how people could do unnatural things for money. But its very gruesome and could be disturbing!

Really facinating book. Dark and interesting from the perspective of a group of downtrodden women who work in a factory. Interesting angle on murder and friendship from a female point of view. Enjoyable
Utterly engrossing, compelling characters and a fine story about the darkness that resides within one self.

I didn't like this book as much as I did with her other books. Her characters didn't really appeal to me this time, I couldn't sympathize with them, not when their principal motivation seemed to be selfishness. Add greed and money into the equation and the plot seems almost predictable. Since Natsuo's character developments were my favourite part of her books, I thought the development here was weak, in favor for the plot, which I must admit was better than her other books. 
 So I guess I was disappointed this time, because I was hoping to be creeped out by her book again, only to be disgusted by it instead.

Gloomy characters with monotonous life? Check 
 Identity crisis? Check 
 Brave protagonist who does not hesitate to defend herself and does not entirely live in the 'white side'? Check 
 Blood and murder? Check 
 Sadomasochism? Check 
 All of the factors I'd love to see in a book can be seen in Out. One thing it lacks is comedy, but it doesn't really matter given that I've hold my breath in suspense several times when I read this. This book is intense, and while it actually could've been better, it is satisfying enough.
Poludiaphemismeno, alla kata ten apopse mou "ligo". Bermpalismos, perigraphes pou tha mporousan na eikhan apopheukhthei. Den mou arese idiaitera.

This is another book I gave up on halfway through. In fairness, the climactic ending of a thriller is probably pretty important to your sense of how good the book is and having not read that part, maybe I am missing out on the brilliance somehow. But leading up to that finale, I thought the writing was pretty terrible. 
 In theory, it should be exactly the sort of thing I'm really into. A feminist, Japanese crime novel? Sounds great, right? And for some reason a lot of the major mainstream critics have given this book rave reviews. 
 It's possible a lot is being lost in translation here. The brilliance of noir writing is how basic, ordinary language is carefully placed to read like a knife. I can easily imagine how the crispness of a crime novel like this could have been translated into a plodding, overly basic dud. The fact remains though, as the book is translated, it really aggravated me. 
 First, Kirino adopts an omniscient point of view, jumping into all the different characters' heads, which is incredibly difficult to pull off successfully. I felt like her fooling around with the perspective failed pretty dramatically and almost all the characters were one-dimensional and wooden. I got annoyed with all the other characters fawning endlessly over the main character, Masako, as "mysteriously strong and composed." Her character's back story annoys me in the first place; she is the hard-working female office worker constantly passed over for promotions because of her gender and ultimately forced out of her company when she tries to assert her value. I don't know the state of feminism in Japan right now and I know this is something that continues to happen in America every day, but it's just such a beyond obvious, blunt way to make her sympathetic to readers and to flag the book as feminist. 
 Secondly, the book is clearly trying to profit from a certain amount of shock value. Good Japanese working women from the suburbs murdering their husbands and dismembering the corpse! Described in graphic detail! And doing it in a very matter-of-fact way! What could be more shocking! The stereotypes about women it rests on to create it's shock value are offensive to begin with and the fact that she is in turn using her subversion of those stereotypes to be shocking? At the very least it annoys me, at most it's pretty offensive in it's own right. 
 The book also uses rumors of sexual predators attacking women at the factory where the characters work, a stalker-ish character who tries to rape the main character, and the ultimate villain character to create a weird atmosphere of sexual tension in the novel that really bothers me too. The sexual tension mixes with a heavy handed attempt to evoke a sinister mood that all teeters way too close on the brink of melodrama. 
 As I mentioned before, the key to any great crime novel or thriller is simplicity and understatement. Out feels like an overworked attempt to achieve that effect through a basic, 101 Women's Studies lens that may be unique and intriguing to the average person, but that bothers the fuck out of me as someone overly invested in feminism and all it's much more interesting and under-examined complexities. And even putting the feminist stuff aside, I still don't think it's particularly well-written. The characters just plod the fuck along without ever feeling real because they lack all subtlety. Bleck.

book_b.title: The Storied Life of A.J. Fikry
book_b.user_review: A complete joy to read. From the description, I didn't think I'd like it as much as I did. Anyone in a life long love affair with books should give this one a go.

sample_reviews.review_text: This is a great book about life!
Every one of us who's dreamed of running a bookstore or having a family of their own will cheer for A. J. Fikrey.

I liked this book, more than I thought I would, in fact, very quickly I bought into the characters and read the entire book in two sittings. 
 An interesting format and the a deftly handled switch between characters throughout the book helped to move the story along. 
 There is more to this story and Zevin seemed to come near the end, tire of the characters and wrapped it up rather quickly - that was a little disappointing. 
 Worth pondering: "No one who travels without purpose. Those who are lost wish to be lost."

"No Man is an Island; Every Book is a World" 
 So reads the motto on the sign of Island Books. Owner A. J. Fikry, a recent widower, is the owner of Island Books on Alice Island. Slow sales, few friends and grief are taking a toll on A. J.'s enjoyment of life and love of books. After the theft of one of his prized possessions and a mysterious appearance of a small but important gift, A. J.'s life begins to change but not in a way that he would ever have expected. 
 Each chapter begins with a reference to a short story and becomes a sort of love letter to his daughter, Maya. We see how books, reading them and writing them can change your life and transform what you expect the future has in store for you. 
 This is a must read.
Just didn't connect with this one. I can see why people liked it though.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Why, Goodreads, why can't I give a book zero stars?! Because this garbage book certainly deserves zero stars. 
 Sometimes, the library opens my eyes to enjoyable books with the book club selections (not specific group, just a title which is segregated into an area where many copies are available for patron's consumption). "Fikry," which sounds a bit like a swear and which I may begin using as such given the increase in my bile due to reading this waste of paper, however, is not one of those books. Have you guessed that I didn't find the novel "a page-turning delight," "marvelously optimistic," or "a reader's paradise of the first order?" The only delight in turning pages was to finish this heap of trash. 
 Let me explain why before continuing with further metaphors. The characterization is nowhere; there are just cardboard cutouts propped up everywhere. 
 And the plot. My Lord, what a mess. The "charming" device of using a memoir about a widower to eventually connect the curmudgeonly middle-aged bookstore owner and publisher's rep was soooo ham-fisted. And what's the name of the publishing house of this magical tome? KNIGHTLEY. Good gravy, save me from bad Jane Austen allusions. Let's just tack a bunch of stories together about a stolen, prized book, an unfaithful author husband, a surprise baby, adoption, and suicide. Of course, the baby transforms the curmudgeon (who, let's face it, is unsurprisingly falling apart after the sudden death of his beloved wife). And he suddenly becomes beloved by the entire town. OF COURSE. Mind you, I love old movies, but this Fikry thing is like a really bad movie from the '30s or '40s, all saccharin and nonsense. I'm surprised the author didn't throw in a dance number or something. 
 This book doesn't even have decent writing to tie together the mess of a plot. Goodreads won't let me quote the exact problems with the book BECAUSE I'D HAVE TO TYPE IN THE ENTIRE CONTENTS. I will state that the chapter intros describing short stories to Maya were soooo stupid. 
 Okay, I'm all worked up. It's time for wine to cleanse my pallet of this terrible taste.

This is the story of one man. His life is the life of an ordinary man. At the same time it is a remarkable book about a remarkable life. Like George Bailey, A J Fikrey influences more than he knows in ways he doesn't recognize. Loved the book

A true testament to the bibliophile. For what other reason do we gather not just to talk about but to at times dissect books? The author wove the story together so subtly I hardly noticed where it was really headed. I started out not caring much for Mr. Fikry only to realize, at some indistinguishable point, that I'd totally fallen in love with him, mourning the fact that he of all people wound up at such an incredulous end. I loved Maya for her unique "nerdy" mind and Amelia for her fortitude and total love for the bookseller. 
 Just a lovely, lovely read.

Charming novel that is a paean to books and reading and book stores. Grumpy widowed book store owner on a thinly disguised Martha's Vineyard loses his most valuable possession, a rare E. A. Poe manuscript, but receives a much more valuable package left in the book store by a distraught woman, thereby changing his life forevermore.
I've read as much as I can. It's just not keeping my interest, & after almost finishing, I just can't get to the end.

sample_reviews.review_text: This was recommended to me by several visitors to my site, but I'm sorry folks, I simply couldn't finish it. Cardboard, cliched characters and a monster on a rampage in a museum don't quite add up to a great read. I gave it a good effort, the quick readability of it got me halfway through it but I don't care how it ends or who lives or dies. I'm moving on.

I had to work hard to read this to the end. The worst book I have read in a long time. One dimensional characters, familiar plot, ham-fisted storytelling. Two ending twists: both so over explicated (sp?) that my brain was screaming at my hands to throw the Kindle down. I can imagine the two authors faxing chapters back and forth trying to write something gripping, thrilling or mildly entertaining: "you think that's scary (gross, weird, etc)? Try this!!" There were some great unintended funny lines, but finding them would require I pick up this book again, so...not gonna happen. This kind of book has to be a page turner and this particular one is not. I have read and enjoyed supermarket thrillers before. The Relic doesn't do it for me. 
 Finally, it's way too long.

This was my go-to audiobook for working out. Cheesy, classic monster story, but so much fun! The reader on the audiobook was just excellent, all full of accents and different personalities. Glad I dl'd this one. Now, to find something as equally exciting and interesting to motivate my workouts...

Most of this book is very boring. Margo Green is far from being an awesome character; really she's just what makes the book so boring in the first place. I cannot find anything about her character that makes her stand out from any other chick working at a museum. She's not witty, or weird, or especially clever, just bleh. The only reason to read this book is to get your first introduction to Pendergast and his badassery. They don't even tell you his first name in this book. That's just a sign of how awesome and unMargo-y he is.

4.5 stars creepy mystery 
 When there are three grisly murders at the New York Natural History Museum An FBI agent partners with a NYC cop to try and find the killer as scientists at the museum begin to suspect that an ancient curse may be at play.

Here is the short and long of it. 
 For characters you love to hate, read this book. 
 For characters you root for from the start, read this book. 
 For an old fashioned type of horror, read this book. 
 I listened to this on audible and I have to say I adore the narrator, he made Pendergast and Augusta come alive for me and those who moaned and and and I felt I could strangle them. 
 For entertainment level alone, this is well worth the read and I will most assuredly be investing in more books written by these authors. 
 WaAr

5/5. 
 Positive: A teenage favourite. 
 Negative: 
 Need to re-read.

Well I've watched the film & thought I'd see what the book was like. It is better (isn't it always?). I enjoyed it and there is a lovely lead into the next book; which I'll also look to listen to. Good fun...

Interesting reading the first book in the Pendergast series! I have listened to some of these on audio book out of order and fallen in love with them (in no small part due to the titles that are narrated by Rene Auberjonois...I love that guy, and his voice for Pendergast is just perfect). It was a little different for me hearing the original narrator, but I decided that these are so entertaining to listen to on long drives that I needed to start from the beginning and really get the full story of Pendergast and D'Agosta. I read these like some people read crappy romances or eat chocolate candy...I have to pace myself lest I gorge. :)

This book was just ok for me. It was a fun thriller, but it takes a long time to even meet the main detective Pendergast and i thought it was a little bit clunky in parts. The epilogue saved some of it for me cause it just seemed so obvious. I think this would have been better had it been a shorter novel.

book_b.title: Crazy Little Thing (Bell Harbor, #1)
book_b.user_review: This book kept catching my eye on Amazon and finally I just had to try it. I'm so glad that I did.... it was a nice funny story about a woman starting over. I can't wait to read the next Bell Harbor story.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Do you like turkey sandwiches? I do. In fact I LOVE turkey sandwiches. And while it is true that all turkey sandwiches have the same components (turkey, bread, and optional toppings/sauces) not all turkey sandwiches are the same. I could eat a turkey sandwich just about every day and be happy. Toasted turkey and gruyere on sourdough with cranberry chutney, oven roasted turkey on farm white with lettuce and bacon, thinly sliced deli pepper turkey with Hawiian ham and pepperjack, are all good choices. Do you know what I don't like? MUSTARD! A tiny bit of spicy brown mustard is okay on some things but yellow mustard is without any redeeming qualities (besides as an ingredient used sparingly). Do not ruin a good sandwich with mustard! 
 I know what you're thinking, 'Nobody cares about your dietary preferences Jim.' or even 'No sandwich is complete without mustard.' My point is that there are things that can ruin things we like. 
 I like romances. Crazy Little Thing is a cookie cutter romance. It has all the parts in the right order. The writing is not completely to my taste but is not bad either. The humor is good. The hero is likable with a good backstory and completely believable reason for being there. That's all straight 3 star territory. Some of the humor and the hero are even possible 4 star candidates. So what's the problem? The heroine (our narrator) is PURE MUSTARD. 
 She is bitter, judgmental, and whinier than a middle school goth wannabe. She's just plain old unpleasant. And as far as I can see, she never really recovers throughout the book. 
 Would I read another Bell Harbor book? Probably - after all I like turkey sandwiches. But if this author spreads any more mustard on it she's dead to me.
A quick, funny, easy lil read. It had me laughing out loud more than once.

This book was way too vanilla and campy for me. I got about 65-75% done and it fell flat with the love scenes. like the chapter ends with kissing and the next one starts "when we woke up the next morning". The relationship built up reeeeeally slow just to end with fizzle. Also, I don't understand how Sadie even got with Des because she was so flaky and childish when she got mad and overthought things.

sample_reviews.review_text: As an author I love Emma Chase's book, particularly the Legal Briefs Series. Essentially porn without plot. The actual storyline didn't feel properly developed at all. None of the characters were given proper depth and I didn't fall in love with any of them. 
 I think part of the reason for this is because the book is just too short overall. I knocked this over in an afternoon and a decent length romance usually takes me a day of two. 
 The plot felt way too rushed as well and felt like it was just trying to get the smut as quickly as possible. I was looking forward to seeing Nicholas have to put in a good woo to get Olivia to finally go out with him but it happened after only one day of "I'll make him work for it." which didn't feel like the tough as nails character that she was being portrayed as before Nicholas walked in the door. 
 Also I got so fucking sick of reading about his cock especially because it was so explicit all the time. Every sex scene in a book doesn't need to be detailed. "I felt all his hard lines pressed up against me" tells me the exact same thing as "I could feel his huge cock" or whatever other ridiculous lines I had to put up with while reading this. 
 This book was a huge let down. I love the Tangles series. For me they are that perfect mix of sweet, funny and sexy. I've only read the first of the Legal Briefs series but also really enjoyed it and do plan to get my hands on the others when I can. Royally Screwed felt rushed. It felt like someone was standing behind Ms Chase and prodding her until she finished a novel. It doesn't feel like it was given a very good look over by an editor for adjustments before it was released. 
 I'm so frustrated that I didn'y enjoy this because there is alot of potential to this idea and story that just wasn't given the time to develop. I would rather quality not quantity from authors. You don't need to be releasing books every year (sometimes even every few months) and not everything needs to be a series where you set up the next books characters in the current one. I'm fucking sick of this trend. Take your time and write a good standalone story with no pressure of follow ups. 
 I won't be reading the others in this series. And to be honest I'm not sure when I'll pick up a new Emma Chase book after this.

First, a funny side note. This is the first book I've ever read that features a shirtless guy on the cover. I don't know why, but I find that funny, especially considering it's not the first romance I've read. Ok, moving on now... 
 The reason I picked this book up in the first place was because I saw the sequel being advertised recently. I read the synopsis for that book and thought it sounded interesting. But then I saw that it was a series, and I figured since I was only one book behind, I'd give the first one a go. 
 Where to start. It was... okay. I didn't really care all that much for either Nicholas or Olivia. I thought Nicholas was brash, disrespectful, and self-centered. Which, in the book, he is described as being and knows he is. But for some reason, Olivia likes it? She even says that she likes her guys to be a bit jerky.... uhhhhh ok. There is a difference between being confident and being an arrogant jerk. Be as confident as you like, but please, leave the arrogance at home. I think no matter your status, celebrity or regular joe, rich or poor, royal or commoner, you don't have to be arrogant. 
 Olivia fell flat for me. We got some details and a peek into her somewhat difficult relationship with her alcoholic father, but all the discussion she and Nick had about their pasts or their difficulties were summarized or glazed over. There wasn't anything I could sink my teeth into pertaining these two. Honestly, I was much more intrigued and interested in Henry's story, the brief glimpse we got of his troubled time in the military, than anything to do with Nick and Olivia. 
 I really wanted to know what legislation Nicholas and his grandmother, The Queen, were trying to pass in Parliament. All we got was that it was something to do with wages and jobs, but nothing else. I'm a smart girl who happens to like reading romance books. But I want those romance books to not undermine my intelligence. I was genuinely interested in the specifics of the legislation. I wish the author would have given her readers more credit, and written more about it. It is possible to want a love story but also want some brain food to go along with it. 
 I love the Royals. Ask anyone who knows me well, and they will tell you I love the British Royal Family. I had high hopes going into this that it would give me a royal fix. Unfortunately, it just didn't do it for me. 
 I'm giving it two stars because, I mean, I didn't hate it. I just didn't really care for it. If you want something easy, steamy, and fluffy that doesn't require you to think too much, then Royally Screwed is for you. If you like your books with more depth, then you probably should go to the next book on your to-read list.

One of my all time favorite books. Great world building and characters. Sucked me in right away!

I read the book, then watched the BBC series and I must say that I liked the series a little better. It seems that this story really does better with the visuals then the bare text. 
 The basic plot has an Alice in Wonderland quality with typical, understated British humor. The main character, Richard Mayhew, begins the story as a listless man who, despite having the 'good-life' finds something lacking in his existence. A chance encounter with one of the denizens of 'London Below' (Lady Door) pulls him into a shadowy and magical world that coexists with, and is invisible to, our real "London Above.' What follows is a typical journey of self-discovery ... Only Richard doesn't really stop being a putz until the end. 
 London Below appears to be the stomping ground for our dreams and nightmares where everything is surreal ... It also brings to mind the homeless within our cities in that when were aren't ignoring them (ie. not invisible), it is not uncommon to see them displaying symptoms of mental illness (talking to other invisible persons, rats, etc.). Add this up with a touch of word play and you get a very humorous trip into what seems to be a mental breakdown, trapping Richard within his unconscious or primitive mind where he can discover and become the hero that was denied him in the real world. Gaiman never really exploits the potential questions which arise from his brief foray into insanity, but then I don't think this was intended to be that serious a story either ... It was supposed to be fun and I did enjoy it much like I enjoyed Monty Python's Holy Grail.
Awesome Gaiman novel, not one for everybody, though - it's more like a twisted Wizard of Oz journey, but great entertainment.

I don't know how he does it, butNeil Gaiman paints the most amazing stories with his words. Neverwhere is the story of Richard, a young man who is reasonably content with his predictable job and his predictable fiancee and his predictable London life. Until one evening when he notices a girl in trouble on the side of the road and stops to help her. This act of kindness turns his world completely upside down, tearing him from his London Above world and dropping him into the world of those who have fallen through the cracks of society, to London Below. No longer visible to his former friends and colleagues, Richard joins forces with Door, the girl he saved, as she embarks on a quest to find out who orchestrated the murder of her family. As wonderfully drawn as Richard is, the secondary characters are quite amazing: the deliciously evil Mr. Croup and Mr. Vandemar, the self-invented Marquis de Carabas, and Hunter, the beautiful bodyguard who longs to defeat the Beast that prowls through London's underbelly. Although Richard spends much of his time in this new world questioning his own sanity, he slowly comes into his own and is ultimately a key to the quest's success, learning quite a bit about himself in the process. Delightful, delicious, multi-layered, and never, ever dull.

I really enjoy Neil Gaiman's novels, so the low-ish ranking is probably unfairly due to my higher-than-usual expectations for Gaiman's work. It was a fine and quite readable novel. I enjoyed it. But I didn't find it particularly exciting or compelling, unlike American Gods, Anansi Boys, or Good Omens.

I'm dumb and accidentally deleted this from my shelves, so i'm reposting my review now!

 I have always been intimidated by historical fiction. Yet, I've always wanted to get my hands on a Ruta Sepetys book. Being partly German and currently attempting to learn the language, reading about WWII sparks my interest. But, a common element in Ruta Sepetys' books is that it's hidden history. Salt to the Sea is about four individual characters: a young Polish girl, a German sailor, a Lithuanian nurse and a Prussian art thief. Seeing the different perspectives all going through similar situations blew me away. They all aboard the Wilhelm Gustloff. The story shows how they got themselves there and how they deal with it. If you're not informed about this ship before reading it, the journey through out it all will amaze you even more. We were also introduced to some precious side characters such as: the shoe poet and the blind girl. All these beautiful stories and people intertwine in such a heart breaking way, yet, I left the story with a sense of positive closure. Throughout each chapter, the story kept me gripping onto where I didn't want to let it go near the end. I'm definitely going to be reading her other novels as i'm sure they're just as wonderful. But, i'm so glad that this was my introduction to historical fiction. If you like historical fiction and haven't read a Ruta Sepetys book, what are you doing with your life? I even mentioned this book to my current history teacher and he enjoyed it just as much. I read this book entirely in a day, on a school day. I barely ever reading after school because i'm so exhausted but I forced myself to stay awake and binge read this book. The heartache and day long binge were entirely worth it.

reference_books.review_text:
lola and the boy next door 
 "I know you aren't perfect. But it's a person's imperfections that make them perfect for someone else." 
 Lola and the Boy Next Door by Stephanie Perkins was everything I've ever wanted in a contemporary romance. From the boy next door aspect to the lgtbq+ accepting family, I was swooning the entire time. I wasn't exactly so sure how I was going to feel about this before reading, though. I know Stephanie Perkins is titled as the contemporary romance queen to some. I've read Anna and the French Kiss but I didn't have such strong feelings about it. It didn't disappoint me, but I didn't feel enough depth to it. It was just another cute romance to me. But, I was entirely fulfilled when finishing this one! The story follows a quirky teenager and her difficult relationships between her strict dads, her so obviously punk boyfriend, and her fascinating neighbors. 
 Our main character, Lola Nolan is out of the ordinary. She doesn't believe in outfit, she believes in costume. Lola is a costume designer living in the marvelous San Francisco. Due to how quirky she is, of course I'm going to love her. 
 Throughout the novel, I truly could picture myself in her shoes, as if I was going through the same situations she was in. Although, I felt as if she was naive when it came to her older boyfriend, Max. Considering what happened to their relationship, I can tell it was necessary. He was incredibly rude and ignorant, even in the beginning of the book. I knew it wasn't going to end well with him and i'm glad it ended the way it did. Lola's approach on it was so heartfelt and real. Despite how he treated her, she still showed emotion and mourning. I feel like that's important in books, to have the emotional depth as Stephanie Perkins gave her. There were a few chapters after the entire conflict with Max that just tore my heart into pieces. I felt goosebumps reading those scenes, as I could relate. 
 Soon enough, Calliope and Cricket were put into the picture. They'd lived next to each other before, but because of Calliope's career in iceskating, they had to move. By the way, Calliope's entire character nearly drove me crazy. Even near the end where you were supposed to forgive her, I couldn't let myself. But when they do move back, I think it was love at first read when Cricket was introduced. A tall, handsome yet dorky boy who she has known all her life. I live for the neighbor aspect. I think a part of me died when they'd talk to each other through their windows. I know I definitely died when he mentioned the Physics project he had made for them to talk to each other through the windows. 
 Did I mention he's an absolute Physics nerd? I'm currently taking Physics and I just loved being able to relate to his interest in inventing. Although Cricket wasn't extremely confident in his ability, i'm glad Lola comforted him and tried to make him realize that just because his sister is successful doesn't mean he can't be too. God, I loved this book entirely. Lola and Cricket had a wonderful relationship. I mean, I can't help but say it was just absolutely perfect. 
 Another significant point in the novel was her family. I feel like both her dad's relationships with Lola's mother gave the book so much more depth. It really pulled the novel together. Her mother was distant due to her drinking and personality. She just needed to get her life together and in a better place. But, no matter what, Lola's parents were there to help her. They'd give her the support she needed. Lola was obviously bothered by it, but it was clear she understood the point. 
 Not to mention, Anna and St. Clair were brought into this novel and they were just lovely! They were that couple who've clearly been dating awhile and are so annoyingly too cute. 
 To conclude this book review, Stephanie Perkins actually made me feel several emotions while reading this book (which I did in one sitting, actually.) I believe she wanted to make a point on how we see ourselves, separately. As Rupaul says, "if you can't love yourself, how in the hell you gonna love somebody else?" Our main conflict in this story is Lola dealing with who she wants to be. She was aware that she's empty but she wants to fix this on her own. She doesn't want to use a mask to cover it up forever, she wants to become her own person and to know herself well. I love that there wasn't an instant solution to this problem. When she realized this, my heart ached. I realized how I feel the same and how I need to fix it by myself. Overall, I absolutely adored this book from start to finish. It's so important what Stephanie conveys through each character in this book. I would recommend this to anyone looking for depth in a contemporary romance, love between neighbors, or simply where the protagonist has been in love with another character for such a long time. I was beyond impressed and fulfilled after finishing this novel! I just wish I could experience it once again. I know i'll pick up the next companion novel. Fingers crossed that Lola and Cricket make a cameo!

 The book did do a wonderful job discussing both mental illness and physical disability. Amy and her CP was written fantastically and it motivated me to do more research on the disability. Meet Amy and Mathew, two teens with different types of disabilities who somehow find one another and become best friends. When Amy leaves for college, they both need to realize their limitations or abilities, and learn to adapt to life without one another. I definitely recommend this book to anyone who is a fan of recently popular teen fiction. This book explores people with disabilities in an unexpected way and succeeds in helping the reader understand people with disabilities as more normal than you would expect. On a basic level, I could relate with most of the characters of the book and understand their struggles. The book is not only well written, it keeps your attention with its witty dialog, and deep introspection on love and life. Really worth picking up!

When I first started Say What You Will, I didn't know what to expect. I've read plenty of stories about growing up/finding yourself, friendships, and romance but what makes this novel unique is that it blends in all of those aspects and is narrated by two characters who have to deal with everything that comes along with being a teenager and their disorders. 
 Amy is born with cerebral palsy, which means she cannot walk long distances without a walker, needs to use a voice box, and cannot control certain parts of her body. I really liked Amy at first, I love how positive she was in her situation and how despite not having control over her own body, she fought to have control in her own life. She stood up to her mother without being disrespectful, and instead of choosing the easy route-enjoying her senior year of high school with adult aids-she decided she wanted to try and be normal and hire peer helpers. Although most of optimism is a bit forced, there's no denying the fact that she knows she's different but she accepts it and that frame of mind is both beautiful and liberating. 
 For Matthew, he has an extreme case of OCD where a voice in his head tells him horrible things will happen to the people he loves if he doesn't do things like tap all the lockers he passes by or go to the bathroom to wash his hands. I feel like everyone always says they have some case of OCD, "Oh I have to color coordinate all my pens from lightest to darkest" or "I can't go to sleep without cleaning my desk." Most of the time, these cases aren't that severe, and reading Matthew's chapter I've learned how severe OCD can be and how it can take over your life in ways I've never imagined possible. 
 Unlike a lot of people who say that Amy is too bossy and Matthew is too compliance, I did really like their friendship. Amy is obviously more outgoing than Matthew and takes more risks than him, but he always supported her. He didn't treat her as an invalid thinking all she should do is sit at home and try not to be noticed, which is what she needed-someone who fully supported and believed in her. For Matthew it was that his disorder made him nervous around people, and I like the tasks that she made him do. Were some of them too much? I don't think so. I don't know his disorder personally, but I felt like little things like asking Sarah out to lunch or getting a job is both useful for the task and for the future. 
 What I didn't care for was the romance. This story could have been amazing if it focuses on the individuals and their friendship, but once they started to have feelings for one another was where the author lost me. Especially when Amy confesses to Matthew that she had sex with Sanjay, just so she could "know what to expect" with him was ridiculous. Granted they weren't official but they basically were, and cheating on someone and trying to make it seem like she was doing it for him was awful. Especially since Amy said she kind of did it because she thought he was having sex with Sarah was beyond stupid, where did the girl from the first half of the book go? Matthew had every right to be piss off, hell I know I would be! 
 Also, after graduation I felt as if the story dragged on a bit too much and took twists and turns that really made no sense. Come on, getting pregnant after having sex once? So Amy didn't think to use a condom? I don't believe that. Also, her just dropping out of school to live with Sarah's dad? That didn't make sense either, and when she finally wrote Matthew a message it was just her basically needing him to be there. All the drama with the baby made me feel like I was reading a completely different book than the one I had originally started, and I don't mean that in a good way. She basically pushed Matthew away, and only came back when she was depressed or lonely and expected him to come back whenever she called. That really annoyed me, and I lost all sympathy I had towards her. If having and later on giving up her baby was suppose to be a big story line, then how come towards the end of the novel it ended with her being so invested in her theater class that she stopped thinking about her child? I don't understand... 
 I still stand by my point that this story would have been stronger if Matthew and Amy stayed friends because I wasn't feeling the romance. I felt as if Matthew deserved someone better than Amy, who didn't push him away and pulled him back whenever she felt like it. It was really good in the first half of the book, but the second part really dragged on and was a bit too much for me. The writing was great, and I can see a distinct difference between Amy's narrative versus Matthew's which was great. I'm actually looking forward to reading more works by this author, despite my problems with this book. I have to admit I'm intrigued to see what this author has to offer.

I pretty much despised this book. I almost didn't finish it. There were countless times of displaced drama in the book, or decisions of the characters that I hated, it all really made me want to put the book down. 
 It looked really promising, which frustrated me. The girl named Amy, the outcast that talks through a computer and has to use a wheelchair. The outcast whose mouth is open, and she sometimes drools (without meaning to of course). She decides that since she is in her senior year, she is ready to make friends. That was prompted by the rant of a student in her grade, Matthew, who brings her to reality. 
 It had soooo much potential. It could have maybe been an Eleanor and Park type romance. It really could. 
 But then... it wasn't. 
 I mainly hated the fact that Amy won't just have what she has with Matthew- friendship. From the minute Amy and Matthew finally start really knowing each other, Amy starts prompting Matthew to admit he loves her and it got REALLY annoying. Like almost every time Matthew and Amy talked, Amy would set up conversation situations to get Matthew to admit he loved her. 
 She didn't want him to kiss her, she wanted more than that, she wanted to have sex which I didn't like because Matthew did not want to do that and she was always pressuring him for more. 
 I didn't feel like the main characters should have been seniors, I would have liked it better if they were freshmen or sophomores and acted accordingly. Nothing in the book felt like it truly flowed together, definitely not the ages and the personalities of the characters. 
 I'm sorry. I probably would have liked it better if I didn't expect so much from it beforehand. 
 Never judge a book by its description.

3.5 stars, I think this would have been a 4 star of even 4.5 star book for me if it weren't for the plot twist.

It's really more of a personal preference, the story went in a direction that I really didn't like, it used a plot point that I just really don't like, especially in YA. I won't say what it is because spoilers, but it's a plot line that whenever I see it I just get kind of uncomfortable, it's not something I enjoy reading about. 
 Other than that this book was great.

Nalini Singh nails it again with the second installment in her Rock Kiss series. "Rock Hard" stars Charlotte Baird, best friend of Molly from "Rock Addiction" and Gabriel Bishop, Charlotte's new boss and former professional rugby player. In fact, this story overlaps with "Rock Addiction" so you also get scenes with Molly that correlate events between the books. 
 On the surface, the novel involves Charlotte and Gabriel forming a close bond, becoming a couple, and hopefully living every after. But underneath the cover is a much more complex story. 
 Charlotte was a victim of a horrible crime, one that almost took her sanity and self-confidence. Now she battles everyday just to get out of bed and go to work. 
 Gabriel comes from a broken home with an abusive, alcoholic father who he never forgave. 
 This is a story about personal growth, about redemption and forgiveness, about learning to accept the past without tainting the future. I found myself cheering for Charlie and T-Rex (her nickname for Gabriel), watching them as they changed, hoping for their connection to turn into a friendship and then a romance. 
 I recommend "Rock Hard" to anyone who needs a bit of sunshine and redemption in their life.

If you caught my review for 
 Hero 
 a few weeks ago, you noticed how much I disliked that book, which is about a personal assistant and her boss getting together. Well, shortly after that I came across Rock Hard by Nalini Singh on Jennifer's blog. Jennifer loves this author, and she really liked this book, so I decided to give it a go, even though it was another book about a personal assistant and her boss. And friends, I absolutely LOVED Rock Hard - it obliterated all my negative feelings for this trope from the bad experience of Hero. 
 I liked Charlotte from the very first page. It's clear that she's had something very traumatic happen to her in the past, and even now she's still struggling with overcoming her fears. Her first meeting with Gabriel, the new CEO of the company Charlotte works for, is shocking for Charlotte, and a lot of her fears pop up. Gabriel's huge size doesn't help matters (he's a former pro-Rugby player). 
 But, even though Charlotte is scared a lot of the time, she's also so strong. Once she gets a little more used to Gabriel, she doesn't let him walk all over her. I really loved that about Charlotte. She wants to not be afraid all the time, but knowing this and actually making it happen are not the same thing. She never gives up and I just love that about her. 
 And Gabriel - he's a SWOONFEST, my friends. This is the type of hero I love. He's really nice and supportive and understanding of Charlotte's issues. He's not afraid of commitment, and he really wants to be with Charlotte. But he knows that she's scared of a lot of things, so he has to take things slowly. That's not to say that Gabriel doesn't get frustrated some times, but he calms himself down and he does understand that things are going to be slow. Their romance is just so sweet and wonderful. 
 And of my gosh, I adored the setting of Rock Hard. It's set in New Zealand (where Nalini Singh lives) and oh my gosh I want to go there right this very minute! I absolutely, truly loved Rock Hard and it will not be my last Nalini Singh book. Rock Hard is perfect for fans of contemporary romance with some deeper issues.

4,5 
 Alala finally the much anticipated adventures of the famous T-Rex and the cute Mouse =D 
 Shy and unsure of herself, Charlotte leads a quiet life trying to make as little fuss as possible. But the arrival of Gabriel Bishop her new boss changes her life. Between indecent proposals, more or less innocent flirtations and tasty pastries, Charlotte feels herself melting in front of the determination of the T-Rex. But Charlotte's demons are far from belonging only to the past ... 
 So much humor, laughs, thrills, twists and a huge desire to leave to New Zealand and never come back x) 
 I loved every moment of this book that I preferred to the first book, the titles of chapters so funny, the story (even if it lacked a bit of twists sometimes), the author's style (I have always been a huge fan of Nalini Singh style anyway ><) and the construction of the relationship between Gabriel and Charlotte =) 
 The characters are amazing and absolutely not cliche =) Gabriel is soooo smexy and handsome, intelligent, with humor, protective, romantic, stubborn, playful while Charlotte is more gentle, smart, pretty, fun, so strong yet so frightened by her past, a box full of secrets =) 
 In short, a Must-Read I totally LOVE and I hope that Nalini Singh will wrote another book in the same vein =)
