reference_books.title: The Children's Book
reference_books.review_text:
The slow pace of this very long novel perhaps reflects the pace of the age in which the bulk of it is set - late Victorian and Edwardian. 
 I liked it, even if I don't quite share the raptures of many of its fans. Pottery, politics, fairy tales, marionettes and the arts generally season this meander through the lives of the intriguing, sometimes secretive, Romney and London Wellwoods and their friends and acquaintances. It is the richly detailed background of an extraordinary time that fascinates. Early in the book, the Anglo-Boer war is being fought, with both jingoistic support and opposition in England. Further in, Fabians and suffragettes clash with reactionaries from all walks of life. Historical personalities cross paths with the mostly youthful characters (the children of the title) - Oscar Wilde, Marie Stopes, James Barrie, Rupert Brooke and many more. 
 With the last two sections - The Silver Age and The Age of Lead, the pace picks up. Now adult, the characters are preoccupied with themselves, with no idea of the horror that is to come in the form of the First World War. I found these latter parts of the book the most poignant. 
 If you're a fast reader or you have the luxury of great chunks of reading time available to you, go for it! 
 The cover is beautiful.

reference_books.title: The White Princess (The Plantagenet and Tudor Novels, #5)
reference_books.review_text: In a way, one of the saddest of The Cousins' War series. Poor Henry Tudor's awareness that he cannot compete with the York charm and gift for winning hearts and commanding loyalty feeds his escalating fear of York claimants to the throne.

reference_books.title: We Were Liars
reference_books.review_text:
The Sinclairs are a golden family. Their lives seem idyllic, especially their summers which all three generations spend on the family-owned Beechwood Island. 
 Cadence Sinclair Eastman revels in these summers shared with her beloved cousins and with Gat, her Gat, the outsider, the politically and socially aware boy she loves so passionately. 
 Yet she cannot remember more than scraps of images from one of these summers. Questions about her accident that summer torment her in tandem with agonising migraines, but no one is giving her clear answers. 
 The mystery at the heart of this amazing YA novel grabs you and holds on. The heart-piercing emotional content is skilfully handled. 
 We Were Liars is about family, love, privilege, prejudice and greedy, needy adults behaving badly - and how the four main characters, all teens, respond to the ugliness that seeps into their little piece of paradise. 
 Cadence, Gat, Mirren and Johnny are beautifully realised, and utterly believable. 
 Insightful, deft and clever, with an ending to stop your breath, We Were Liars is set above much other contemporary YA by its spare, poetic writing. Stunning.

reference_books.title: Who Fears Death
reference_books.review_text: What a bold and creative writer Okorafor is, unafraid to mix issues of gender, including female circumcision, cultural tradition and identity into her dystopian fantasy. The prose is wonderfully direct in this story of Onyesonwu, who is Ewu, the angry child of rape, struggling to understand and control her remarkable abilities as she grows up and begins a journey across desert Africa.

reference_books.title: Hausfrau
reference_books.review_text:
You don't have to like a novel's protagonist to appreciate the book. 
 Her name is Anna. She is an American expat living in Zurich. She has a husband (Swiss) and children, but she doesn't have her own bank account; nor does she drive. She is afflicted by a strange passivity. There's an absence or a lack in her; she seems incomplete, and perhaps this is part of the signal she sends out, as men somehow sense that she's open to an affair. 
 Details of life in Zurich supply background and become a theme, as well as serving as the excuse for Anna's adultery, at least in her own mind. Her domestic existence and infidelities are interspersed with brief excerpts from her sessions with a psychiatrist who has a penchant for metaphor (the heart as a leaking bucket). 
 The author is a poet, and this novel is also about the beautiful and dangerous subtlety of language - English, German and Swiss-German.

book_a.title: Trash
book_a.user_review:
You never know what you'll find ... 
 What a superb children's book, gripping and fast-paced, with a very clever plot. Best of all, you get three utterly engaging characters, Raphael, Gardo and Rat, to fall in love with. They're dumpsite boys who spend their lives sorting through the trash among which they live. You fear for them in their flight from a mercilessly brutal police force, and you cheer their every breakthrough in understanding the puzzle they have set themselves to solve after an astonishing find among the city's mountains of rubbish - the dumpsite being based on a real one in Manila. 
 Wonderful, moving and very satisfying.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Before reading this book, I vacuumed the house, gave my dog a bath, memorised jabberwocky, did a 5000 piece puzzle, coloured in my homework book and spent time with my family being social *shivers*. Anything to not read this book. 
 0.5 
 Terrible. 
 This book, was simply a task to finish. It didn't draw me in. Writing average. I hoped for the 3 boys to die in the end, anything to stop the misery story. Like the title says, it simply belongs in the 'Trash'. 
 Even if you have 2 hours to waste, I'm more than sure you have better things to do.

This book is aimed at around 7-14 year olds but it is a cute story nonetheless. The english in the book is purposefully very poor and usually I would've found it extremely difficult to read, but this one was not as difficult, maybe because it was coming from children. 
 The story was fast moving, maybe a little hard to focus on at times but that was mainly my zoning out while reading, rather than the words or plot being difficult to understand. 
 Overall, I enjoyed the book and would recommend it to 7-14 year olds.

The book centers around three dumpster boys, those who make a living scavenging from huge mountains of trash. One day, Raphael finds something in the trash-something that might be worth money to his destitute family. When the police scour his neighborhood looking for it, Raphael hopes to turn this trash into even more treasure. Gordo and Rat, two other orphans, are his partners in crime as they try to unravel the mystery of these papers and why the police are so interested. Their adventure takes them from the trash heap to a prison to one of the wealthiest and most powerful men in their city and, finally, to a graveyard where the mystery is finally unravelled. 
 It is a futuristic novel, but not really dystopian which made it a little confusing for me. In this future, most of the world is a third-world nation--overdeveloped, poor, corrupt with too many orphaned children. There is absolutely no explanation of how this came to be. So, why not just set the novel in a third-world present day setting? The futuristic setting just didn't make sense and wasn't explained. 
 I did like a lot of things about this book. The mystery and story within the story was captivating; the characters were likable and well-developed; the plot was realistic and exciting. I did like that a variety of people told the story in different chapters. It added to the depth and was different. In short, I liked it okay. I just didn't love it.
The title describes the writing. I only finished this book because it was required summer reading. Why it was required summer reading for a high school senior, I have no idea.

Trash is a fast-paced adventure story as well as a fascinating glimpse into the world of extreme poverty and child labor in third-world countries. The plot revolves around 3 "dumpsite" boys who unexpectedly find something very valuable mixed in with all the trash they sort through daily. The boys embark on a quest to solve the mystery behind what they've found, and must ultimately decide how to deal with the information they uncover. 
 I found the 3 main characters very likeable and endearing, and I was quite caught up in their predicament. The settings are vividly described and evoke images much like those in the Slumdog Millionaire movie. Beyond the action and suspense, the multicultural elements and moral dilemmas in this book are quite thought-provoking. It is told from multiple points of view, and the plot gets a bit complex, so I would recommend this for sophisticated 7th and 8th grade readers. 
 Asked on his website what he hopes readers take away from his book, Andy Mulligan says, "I hope they get involved with the boys, and live closely with them. I hope they enjoy the thrill of the chase, and I hope their adrenalin pumps. I hope they find the ending rewarding, and I hope they think - because we all need to think." I certainly did all those things.

The parts of the book that dealt with life in Behala were fascinating and were my favorite parts of the book. I wish the book had been more about the people who lived in this rubbish town. I have a feeling that a book that focused on their lives would have appealed to me much more. The look at other parts of this unnamed city - the bus station, the police station, & the prison, in particular - were okay, but I really just wanted the author to take us back to Behala. 
 I am ambivalent about books with chapters narrated by different characters. When done well, I really love it and see how useful it can be to advancing the story. This book did not do that well. To be honest, I often couldn't tell the difference between the characters' narration. They weren't well-defined enough for me to be able to "hear" each character clearly in his/her narration. And a couple of the characters pop up so seldom that I wondered why the author even bothered to include their point of view at all. 
 I'm a big lover of mystery, but the mystery of this book just wasn't interesting to me. I often felt impatient and just wanted the boys to solve the darn thing and get the book over with. 
 I like the idea of this book quite a lot, but in the end it just wasn't a compelling read for me.

Really enjoyed this book. My daughter has to read it for 6th grade and I'm so happy they chose this tale of corruption and deceit. At times it made me tear up to read about the unrelenting poverty and sometimes it gave me chills. Loved the ending.
http://librarianaut.com/2012/05/18/bo...

author Andy Mulligan is a white English man who tried to write of the experieces of three very poor boys (race not specified) living in an "unnamed Third World country" (quoted from the back of the book). the currency is pesos, there is a mission school and a volunteer from England, they're somewhere near a sea, and there is talk of typhoon season. other Goodreads reviewers have noted the place names are identical or close to places in the Philippines. 
 there are many harmful paths a novelist from a privileged background can travel down when he writes beyond his direct lived experience: cultural appropriation, exploitation, stereotyping, tokenization, speaking over/for marginalized people, normalizing or whitewashing systems of oppression... the list goes on. i think Trash is guilty of several of these. i don't think any amount of volunteering, tourism, or voluntourism would make Mulligan qualify as having direct lived experience similar to his protagonists. 
 i would not recommend this book for anyone. should you ignore that advice and read it anyway, be warned that there are graphic descriptions of police brutality and police torture of a child.

I found this book to be really dark. I felt sad about boys making a living picking trash and living amongst it. When Raphael was tortured by the police I was aghast at corrupt law but I know it exists. I found it a good story with some intriguing twists. I did like the ending.

book_b.title: The Marriage Plot
book_b.user_review:
Late in The Marriage Plot, there's a paragraph about working through the pages on agrarian reform in Anna Karenina, until you get to a good part again. This novel itself is a bit like that. 
 Perseverance is needed here. There are sections where the temptation is to abandon the book unfinished, where you're wondering what the point is. Set in the nineteen-eighties, with three central and young characters. One seems to be longing to hear 'the still, small voice', another is what in those days was still called manic-depressive, and then there's Madeleine who 'had always liked air fresheners' we're told on page 118 of the edition I read. Oh, and she writes her senior thesis on Jane Austen. 
 Interesting in parts, but still a disappointment, possibly due to unfairly high expectations prompted by the author's previous two novels.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I listened to the audio version of this book. I have read the other books written by Jeffrey Eugenides. While they're not my favorite books, they were okay. This was my least favorite of what he's written. 
 The idea of a main character who loves reading (Victorian, marriage plot novels) is always appealing to me. However, the characters were unlikeable for the most part. I didn't find any of them to be that relatable, and I didn't ever feel like "rooting" for any of them. There are always complaints of this writer being pretentious. I'd say that was one of my main complaints with this book. The audio version also had a reader I didn't particularly enjoy either. The voices he used for women were horrible and left me feeling like he was reading them with a mocking tone. Perhaps they were written that way. 
 The last 1/3 of the book was enjoyable enough. The drawback is that one must get through the first 2/3 of the book to get there. I won't be rereading this book or recommending it to anyone.
This book was surprisingly dry, particularly for a writer like Eugenides. I will continue to recommend Middlesex and Virgin Suicides, but will suggest a pass on this one.

I had high hopes for this book, but finished it feeling disappointed. The writing was good, the characters were complex and interesting, but there was something missing. I'm not sure what it was, but towards the end I was just hoping it would be over.

Meh. It's one of the only books I've read in which I felt NOTHING for any of the major characters. Not hate, not dislike--but I didn't like any of them, didn't root for any of them, did not care about any of them. This was hard for me to even finish. If you like history of Victorian literature you might get something out of it.

Eugenides is a genius. Enough said. 
 Seriously though, this book was so humorous and thoughtful. I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys a good joke and a good romance plot. If you like Austen, you will like this too.

Readers should just sit back and enjoy this compelling novel, without worrying so much about grumpy-puss reviews comparing it to Middlesex. You'll connect with the characters, their struggles, and complex relations. I think you can also find some deeper threads that will warrant reflection. After reading, I've been thinking about the limits of empathy in modern society. Is the cost of our expanded social freedoms paid with a reduction in the capacity to feeI connected? I think the author has a sad message for us under this compelling romance. The characters' personal struggles (Madeleine-romantic love, Leonard-mental sanity, and Mitchell-religious faith) are pre-determined and remain elusive to each. The human truth of these struggles make the book stand out.

Oh man has this book sucked me in right from the beginning. It's simultaneously making me miss the days of college when everyone is philosophizing on the experience of living and thinking our ideas are so big and important while at the same time making me happy I'm past that stage. This is also a book lovers book with tons of literary references and criticism. This is going to be a quick read. Now that I'm done I really loved it. I absolutely couldn't put it down. Eugenides captured the feelings of finishing college and starting life so well. I feel like I related so much, being a bookish girl who was attracted to the brooding academic myself at that age. In the end there is nothing overly special about this book. It is not a great work or literature nor does it really have a new take on "the marriage plot," but I still thoroughly enjoyed it.

I'm wondering why Eugenides felt he had to write THIS novel. Won't change anyone's lives and not as provocative as Virgin Suicides and Middlesex. I was done thinking about it about 15 minutes after I finished it.

I finished this book late the night before packing my husband, our two kids, my Vita-Mix, and ten days' worth of stuff into our VW Jetta for an ambitious road trip around Lake Erie and then back to New England. I thought about writing a review right then, but the desire for sleep won out. As a result, I've been mulling this book over for the past couple of weeks, and my view of it has shifted a fair amount in that time. 
 At first, four things stood out for me: 
 1) I did not like Madeleine. Beautiful, sought-after, wealthy, part of a loving family, intelligent: just the kind of woman I seek to befriend and then feel inferior to for the duration of our friendship. 
 2) My opinion of Leonard changed as his mental illness developed/was revealed. I discovered a wellspring of empathy for him even as I felt a vicarious need to just escape him and all of the assistance and guidance he required. 
 3) I felt incredibly jealous of the reading lists of the characters. Their reading lists included books I read in college, books I was assigned in college but didn't really read, and books I'd never even heard of but which sounded absolutely intriguing. They made me want to go back to undergrad and just immerse myself in reading and writing again. 
 4) I liked Mitchell---with all of his confusion and whining and searching---the best. 
 But during my two-weeks-plus of thinking about what to say about The Marriage Plot, I discovered something funny: I kept mixing it up with Jonathan Franzen's 
 The Corrections 
 . Why on earth is that? Is it the mental confusion or the depression or the sex? Is it because Eugenides' style is similar to Franzen's? I'm not sure, but my opinion of a book tends to fall if I confuse it with another book. 
 But then I began reading two books about spiritual practice, 
 The Sacred Way 
 by Tony Jones and 
 The Pen and the Bell 
 by Holly Hughes and Brenda Miller. Reading these, I finally recognized that Mitchell was on a spiritual quest. Here he was reciting the Jesus Prayer and attempting to experience spiritual awakening through service and making pilgrimages and engaging in lectio divina. He went about it in a rather haphazard manner and much of it centered around either trying to forget Madeleine or trying to gain divine assistance to bring her to him, but it was clearly a spiritual quest. In my thinking of the book, all of the other characters have sort of faded into the background and Mitchell has moved to the forefront. 
 I almost want to read The Marriage Plot again to see if I can spot more of Mitchell's spiritual quest. I don't think I will, though, at least not right now. Mostly, like with the books I didn't read or don't remember from college, I wish I'd paid more attention when I read The Marriage Plot the first time. I still don't like it as much as I liked 
 Middlesex 
 or 
 The Virgin Suicides 
 , but this realization about Mitchell has bumped it up a few notches in my esteem.
I loved his other books but this one was disappointing.

One thing that bothered me was how Grandma spoke - far more intelligent than the other characters but it really just seemed like all of her "smart" words came from the thesaurus. reference_books.title: So You Want to Be a Wizard (Young Wizards, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
So my great Uncle Bob bought this for me when I was the appropriate age to read it. But guess what? It was never touched except when I sold it, which probably led to his untimely death. Or not, since it was rather timely. Either way, adulthood is no better a time than never especially since I heard it is something similar to Harry Potter but NOT a rip off since it was written before. 
 Let me let you in on a secret. JK Rowling read this book. So did Christopher Paolini (author of Eragon) and so did the guy that wrote the Percy Jackson series. I guess it must be hard to come up with new ideas. 
 Okay, the only character I liked was Fred who is a white hole. The two main kids are bland as all get out. I did like the way the characters had specialties they could control and I really hope that when I find out I'm a wizard, my specialty will be nature like Nita's. Relax, that's not a spoiler. But this book was definitely written for children (duh) so the plot was constructed for such an audience and like I said, there was little character development. I secretly enjoyed it nonetheless but I really need to start reading things around my age group.

Ok, at least one good thing came out of this. I learned that a book written for an elementary school student is not going to be for me. But even for an elementary school student, THIS WAS AWFUL.  This book is bad and I would not recommend it to anybody of any age. However, there is nothing obnoxious or offensive in this book. This book was okay. It couldn't really hold my attention too well but it wasn't horrible. At times the writing was a bit irritating because it was so repetitive but you get used to it after a while.

I heard this as a book on tape when I was about 14 on a family road trip. I remember thinking about some of the events in this story for weeks afterwards, which can be backed up by the fact that I even remembered what this story was when I saw the title a moment ago. I don't remember feeling bored while listening to this as others have mentioned, but I was also in a car for several hours which in and of itself is one of the most boring settings of anyone's life. book_b.title: Mockingjay (The Hunger Games, #3)
book_b.user_review: Incredible last installment to one of my all time favorite series. I'm always searching for entertainment in my books, HP, Eragon. Anything with a plot that won't let me put it down (as you can tell, it doesn't necessarily have to be that well written...). This was so satisfying. Thank you Suzanne!

sample_reviews.review_text:
I loved this book. I loved the plot, plot twists, and character development. It was a very satisfying end to a trilogy. 
 I feel like I can add a little more without spoiling anything for people who haven't read it yet. This is the conclusion of a sci-fi dystopian trilogy for young adults, readers 12 and up as recommended by the publisher. It is not a fantasy or teen romance trilogy. 
 Collins is in part writing about the effects of war and violence on humanity. Unlike the news or popular media, she takes current and recent events from history and writes them in a way that the reader can feel and understand and consider that maybe there is more cost than 'just' loss of life in war and revolution. 
 Collins is graphic, but I think it is age appropriate and I believe it is not anything that you can't find in the news, or be taught in a history class or the Holocaust museum and it doesn't have that titillating, rubbernecking feel to it that the news does. The Hunger Games trilogy is a very thought-provoking series that poses the right scenarios and questions for teens and readers to evaluate their own beliefs and opinions without being preachy, cliche, unrealistic or poorly written. 
 Also, I cannot believe that so many people are referencing Twilight in their reviews and critique of Mockingjay, as if it's acceptable to compare teen vampire romance with dystopian YA literature.
Such an unsatisfying ending.

I have to agree with many other people that have read the entire series and agree that it goes downhill after book 1. 
 Mockingjay was an okay book but not fabulous. 
 My official stance on the Hunger Games series is as follows: 
 The Hunger Games Book One is a must read novel, it's an exciting adventure story. I would stop reading the series after book one. 
 If you venture into reading Catching Fire you might as well read Mockingjay to finish out the series. But overall I think The Hunger Games Trilogy, much like The Matrix trilogy is better off with one fantastic story and the sequels are unnecessary and actually cheapen the original story.
I... I dont get why this is so popular. Just not for me I guess. I kept waiting for something. Meh.

Overall, I think this book was a great way for people to understand alls fair in love and war. Theres no sugar coating things, this isn't a complete happy ending, it's more realistic, despite tahat they are letting a 17 year old calling shots in the last parts of the book. While your happy some characters still live, there are other favorites that die you wish hadnt or continue living that you wish had died. It's a heartbreaking yet bittersweet wnd, and each factor that occurs has a purpose to why it happened.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I had always hopped Peeta and Katniss would get together. It was a great book/series.

The last book in the Hunger Games trilogy and it doesn't disappoint. 
 Katniss, her mother, sister, Gale and a few others from District 12 are in District 13 where everything is regimented, down to when to eat, when to exercise and when to sleep. 
 A revolution is happening and the leaders of the rebels need Katniss to become 'The Mockingjay'. However she doesn't feel up to being the spokeswoman for the revolution, until she sees Peeta alive and being paraded by President Snow on TV. 
 A rescue attempt is made and an assault on the Capitol is planned. 
 The ending seemed to be a little rushed to me, but I didn't want this story to end. 
 Warning: There are a lot more deaths in this book, each more vivid than the other.

My theory that the third book in a trilogy can never be as good as the first two is in full effect in this series. 
 Without the adventure/anxiety/thrill of the games, the book was completely separated from anything resembling the first two novels. Instead, Mockingjay became a long-winded story of preparing for war, only to FINALLY reach the battle and be completely underwhelmed. 
 The entire time spent in district 13 was a complete bore and Peeta being brainwashed seemed so far fetched and a desperate attempt on Collins' part to make this book exciting. It was so cheesy and something out of a bad 80s Sci-fi movie. 
 I finished the book because I simply can't start a series and not know how it ends, but the ending went far from reaching my expectations. I've just had it with "corrupt government" plots. Thats all there ever seems to be in these dystopian novels! 
 That said, overall I enjoyed the series and the first two books were good enough for me to forgive the misfortunes of this one.

Where to start... I devoured this book as quickly as possible. I had to know what happened after the cliffhanger ending in Catching Fire. However, I was mildly disappointed. When the actual Hunger Games ended, there seemed to be something lacking from the plot. I had a hard time getting into the complicated political overthrow plot. This book also had some new characters that seemed a little out of place. Maybe out of place isn't the right term. They were there, but I couldn't figure out what purpose they served. It was hard to connect to any of them because there wasn't much depth. It was as if they were there for the purpose of the plot's subterfuge only. I really felt like there was no attempt to grow the new characters at all, except for maybe Boggs. 
 ** Spoiler alert** 
 Then there is the problem with Katniss herself. In the other books I thought she was so strong and defiant. Now, she seems so weak. In the aftermath of the events in Catching Fire, it makes sense. Her mental breakdowns and nightmares are acceptable and one hundred percent justifiable. What annoys me, however, is her constant pity party. Everyone knows that bad crap happens (that was obvious in the first two books), but to keep harping on it drove me nuts. It's as if we needed a constant reminder of how crappy life could be for her. Complete over kill. 
 I hate to say it, but this time around my favorite character was Finnick. He had the most depths out of all of the characters in this book. Oh, the secrets he has to share! Holy smokes. That was a dark turn I didn't expect. But then he gets killed off. That irritated me. I really wanted him to survive. It's not the fact that he died, either, that bothers me so much. It's the manner in which he died. What a waste. That entire scene seemed so rushed and out of place. I didn't even realize so many people died until two or three pages later. One of the major deaths in the book didn't even stand out to me. I knew she died because of the massive bombing that occurred, but what was the purpose? 
 I will say that there was one surprise that caught me off guard. Peeta. Wow. I didn't see that one coming. Poor, sweet Peeta. 
 No review would be complete if I didn't talk about the ending. WTH?! I am so unhappy with how things ended. I'm all for Peeta, don't get me wrong, but the way things were left with Gale seemed so wrong. No closure. I know there is supposed to be some great message about war and the roles we play--whether knowingly or not--but still... I felt so invested him that love triangle. I wanted a better solution. I don't care so much who Katniss ended up with, it's just the why that bothers me. It's like she didn't have a choice in the matter at all. She gets sent back to District 12 alone under the impression that no one will come for her. But then someone does... Only, it seems like he's there because he has nowhere else to be. Did anyone else get that feeling? Obviously Peeta wouldn't stay in the Capitol after what happened, so it only seemed natural that he would return to his home. With Katniss being there, of course they would end up together eventually. They are the only ones who can fully understand what it's like to be a survivor of The Hunger Games. But does that mean he wants to be there with her or she with him? Not necessarily. It felt like they were both going with the hand life dealt them because they didn't know what else to do. 
 ** End spoiler alert ** 
 I guess there was some sense of closure after the epilogue, but I still don't know how satisfied I am with it. The pieces do fit together and there is plenty to think about afterwards, that's for sure. Leaving the series with this book unread would be wrong. Be forewarned, though, it's a rollercoaster ride of emotions, and how you feel at the end really depends on whose side you're on.

Ninety percent of me LOVED this book. Over the series, I liked the transition of Games to full out rebellion. I like the changes in Katniss and the struggle for Peeta. It moved fast, introduced new roles - soldiers vs survivors, members of a new community, Katniss as political pawn - and those transitions were believable and I was glad for them. And OF COURSE, I loved the ending. I was so worried about how it would all turn out. 
 SPOILER SECTION 
 To me, stories where someone is destined to destroy an evil regime because they were somehow born special are boring. The only prophecy of greatness story I like is Arthur. It's a personal thing, I know. I like The Hunger Games series because Katniss is not born special, she's a good hunter and a hurt individual trying to make her way in the world. The fact that she is used as a pawn and is not a born leader (not to me anyway), makes it more intriguing and captivating to read. 
 I also love how, at the end, Katniss is damaged. Peeta is damaged. They are not magically happy. This is what the Games and war will do. It is not glossed over. I appreciate that aspect greatly. And I was so happy Peeta lived and he and Katniss stayed together. That made my day. It's brilliant when you can be happy for fictional characters. 
 Now, to the ten percent that I wasn't fond of in the novel. A lot was covered in this novel and at times, the triangle romance was hard to take seriously with the backdrop of revolution and war. Also, through all three books, I felt like the reader never got to know Gale well, so it was hard to root for him. I was a Peeta girl from the beginning. 
 I felt like too much time was covered and therefor not everything was as developed as I would have liked. I would have loved to see the moment where Katniss and Peeta were finally able to hold each other again. It seemed like Peeta, through most of the novel, was shoved off to a corner because there wasn't time to discuss how he was getting better. I also would have loved a revisit with Annie to see how she adjusted to Finn and an actual moment together with Katniss and her mother after Prim's death. 
 My last little gripe, and I fully believe this could be my own limitation, was I had a difficult time visualizing the pods in the Capital and I had a hard time understanding why they had booby-trapped their entire city. There are so many things that can go wrong with booby-traps and so many ways to injure/enrage your own citizens. It made it seem not as real to me, more like "how can I up the anty now?". I may be the only one bothered by this and if it were changed I doubt the novel would be better, just different. 
 Overall, yay!!!! Loved the entire series.

3.5 stars. this novel told in a memoir style tells that story of young Isabella and how her love of dragons and natural history developed from childhood into young adulthood. we see how her path in life followed her love for dragons. her passion lead to her meeting her husband and going on a life changing expedition to study dragons.

I found this book very charming. I really enjoyed the Jane Austin-feel of the novel, splashed with a fantasy element. Despite being set in that period and style, it didn't feel slow or excessively drawn out. I loved the relationships in the novels, and I enjoyed Isabella as a character and would be interested in reading more about her adventures. She is a strong female character who still has humanity and weaknesses, and struggles with the gender roles appropriately for the setting and time period. 
 The memoir aspect I had mixed feelings about. It gave the book a very distinct feel and character, but sometimes became distracting from the story, particularly when alluding to events in future novels. Sometimes in places where you would just experience her undergoing character growth, it felt like those moments were truncated and you would just be told she grew out of that habit or became more self-aware. However, the memoir style felt different from a lot of other things I had read, which is always a plus. 
 I think it's an interesting world with great starting characters. I think the novels have a lot of potential to grow as she ages as a character, and with the different dragon settings that are yet to be explored. Hopefully the next books will build on the foundations this book lays and keeps it up!

I had a lot of delight in reading this pseudo Victorian memoir of a famous scientist who is as renown for her discoveries about dragons as much as for being a female scientist explorer. She apparently has had a life similar to the fictional Indiana Jones, but lived under the restraints of Victorian manners and mores imposed on upper class women. It is as if the now Lady Trent, who used to be Isabella Hendemore before her marriage to Jacob Camherst, was requested by an adoring public to recount her popular adventures. So she modestly acquiesces, beginning with this book describing her birth, childhood and early adulthood. This part one of her 'autobiography' satisfies the public's interest in how she overcame the expectations of society and her mother and became the famous scientist she is currently. 
 The book cover is gorgeous, as are several included plates of the 'Lady Trent's' pencil drawings of dragons. The story is a faithful depiction of our own popularized Victorian period, only in this imagined universe, there be dragons. They are exotic animals enjoying the same fascination by the civilized people of 'Scirland' as did our universe's African fauna. The dragons are Isabella's speciality in the book, and they have excited her curiosity since she was a child. A series of incidents and in fortuitously marrying a gentleman who supports her in her explorations sets the stage for her future career and famous discoveries. 
 If it not were for an unexpected and sad ending, this would be an entirely fun cozy. The book's tone is of a scientific memoir, as advertised, but written in the voice of a cozy genre heroine with some realistic adult steel in her backbone. However, the novel loses energy in the last half, and then there is that rather horrific ending which is truly a bucket of cold water on what was otherwise a fun read. 
 I liked it very much, but I wish things had concluded more happily.
Still coming to terms with why I didnt like it even though it sounds like something right up my alley...

A Minute Review: 
 5 Stars: 
 Be warned, then: the collected volumes of this series will contain frozen mountains, fetid swamps, hostile foreigners, hostile fellow countrymen, the occasional hostile family member, bad decisions, misadventures in orienteering, diseases of an unromantic sort, and a plenitude of mud. 
 There is a lot I could say about this book because I loved it so much, but I'm going to keep things short (it is a minute review, after all). This is a wonderfully written memoir from the perspective of a woman who has become a household name in the study of dragons. Her world is very much like ours was a hundred years ago, except with the existence of dragons as a poorly understood force in the animal kingdom. The story is full of Lady Trent's wisdom, snark, and crazy life experiences, and I can't wait to start book 2, The Tropic of Serpents. 
 Recommendation: 
 Read this if you enjoy biographies, dragons, natural history, subtle but momentous romances (think Young Victoria), and/or women who follow their passions and change the world.

(This review may contain spoilers). 
 It's been a while since I read the first book in this trilogy, but I did find this book easy to read and pick up the storyline on. 
 I really liked Fox and Layla together, but I kept getting confused with the other two sets of characters. It was interesting to see the abilities each of the characters had and how their abilities complemented each other. 
 It was interesting to see hints of the past and what happened to each of their ancestors. What I found the most intriguing was the idea about sacrifice. It's a nice change-up to see the idea that the good guys still have to do bad things, even if the reasons are good. 
 I'm not sure 'liked' is the right word, but I thought the atmosphere in the book was really intense, considering it was building up to the next Seven. I wasn't very clear on what rules there were for the demon, though, as I assumed that its power was stronger on the actual night. 
 I found it interesting to see the history of the characters and the town and how Layla, Quinn and Cybil were fitting in there. I liked the fact that I could see Layla and Cybil's issues, even if Quinn did seem to settle in with Cal very quickly. 
 There were some quite creepy moments in this book, especially when it came to them each experiencing the things that had negative effects on them in their pasts or what they feared. It was also scary to see how commonplace some of those things were, to the point that Fox wasn't even startled by the sight of the boy. 
 I also liked being able to see glimpses of not only Fox's past, but also Gage's. It was good to see something of what made them the way they were, even though I felt that Fox didn't really seem like he had that secret in his past. The effects weren't really that clear before he had the dream. 
 I also liked seeing the relationship between Fox and his family and there were a few amusing moments involving them and Layla. It was also really nice to see glimpses of Fox's relationship with his sister and Paula.

Maybe it's just me but I didn't really like this book. So those of you who did like it I'll advice you not to read this review. For those of you who want to know why I didnt really like this review : 
 Yelena is a young woman when she kills the son of a General and is scheduled for execution. 
 After almost a year in the dungeon she is summoned, only to be given an option. Either she could become the Commander's new food taster or she'll hang. 
 The General still wants her dead and while she's trying to avoid inevitable death, someone is plotting against the Commander. Gaining friends and skill, Yelena's life is getting more complicated by the hour. Will she survive the nightmares that haunt her? 
 "This may work out better than I'd planned. Yelena, I'm offering you a choice. You can either be executed, or you can be Commander Ambrose's new food taster. His last taster died recently, and we need to fill the position." 
 After killing the son of her old benefactor, Yelena is awaiting the moment she'll be executed. However her future is altered when someone close to the Commander, Valek, offers her another path; to be the new food taster of the Commander. Yelena is not foolish enough to let this pass and so she accepts the position, knowing that every day might be her last. Not only is she in danger of dying by tasting the possible poisoned food for the Commander, she's also poisoned so that she needs an antidote every morning, or else she'll die. 
 With escape being out of the question, Yelena sets to learning everything about every possible poison, Valek even lets her taste some particular poisons before she's appointed official food taster. 
 However this does not change the feeling of pure hatred of General Brazell, who still wants her death because she murdered his son. He keeps haunting her in every way he can and he even sends a magician after her. And the nasty housekeeper Margg is not being a great help either by acting so hostile towards Yelena. With death on her heels, Yelena needs all the help she can find and so, slowly, she makes friends and gains skill to defend herself. But will that be enough to keep her alive? To prevent her from being murdered even now? 
 Next to her own troubles, she's something else to deal with. When it becomes obvious that something is wrong with the Commander, she has to put everything she has to protect him and the future of her country. 
 But the ghost haunting her doesn't make her life any easier either. She needs to believe in herself and she has to keep herself together, otherwise it would definitely be the end of her life. 
 This was how I felt trying to read this book. 
 I wanted to like it, I really did and I really tried. But after a while, some things start to get old real quick. This book in the nutshell: 
 1. Everyone wants Yelena dead for one reason or another. 
 2. When things tend to go towards ok, something comes along to make it horrible again. 
 3. The last few years were hard and she is a really scarred person. Yes, that's something that gets very obvious after about... O I don't know... 500 times. 
 Let me explain why I was feeling like hitting someone while reading this. 
 Firstly there is a problem I encounter more often but one that doesn't always bother me as much as it did now: the first person way of writing. This time it really got to me because all she was thinking of, or at least so it seemed to me, was how hard her life had been and still was and how she wanted to escape but that it wasn't possible because she would die. Also instead of giving some information about, O I don't know, the surroundings or the castle or the way things were living in that country/kingdom, the only pieces of information you get are: the castle is not symmetrical and build in something that looks like building blocks, the country is divided into military districts, there is an enemy country on the southern border and there is some sort of hierarchy consisting of the commander, generals, advisers, soldiers, normal people/servants and magicians. 
 Another thing that bothered me was that Snyder could have done so much more with the history of that country and the border conflict! But all she did was tell a little about the point of the takeover when the Commander came to seize power and killed the old King. Now, I know that while reading this you'll only know what Yelena knows but at some point she gets to a library and the place where she's staying has a lot of books as well so why isn't there a moment of a little history? Or some sort environmental/orientation part in this story? That would make everything so much more alive! Instead all we know in the end is: There are trees/forests , the castle looks like it's been built by a three year old, the only animals in this country are probably dogs, rats, snow cats and sometimes there is an owl. Oh and there are five seasons instead of four. Nothing to go on really. There's even some point where Yelena finds a map and copies it into her diary, but information about the layout of the castle? Nope. 
 Now you may wonder: Was there anything you did like in this book? Anything at all?! Well... yes... there were some things that I could appreciate in this story. Snyder did depict how things are like when one power falls and another takes its place. I appreciate that because not in every Young Adult book this is obvious. Snyder did a good job in mentioning that the inside of the castle changed after the Commander took his residence there, she also mentioned the disappearance of some supplies when the borders closed between the two countries and also she did a good job in depicting the change in how the country was ruled. 
 So I fear that this is it. This is the conclusion of my review about Poison Study. I didn't like it much. There was too much missing for me to really enjoy this book and there were too many things that annoyed me from the very start. It's really hard to say but I'll give this book two starts because I don't know if I can handle this...

I tried to like it, I swear! This probably would have been better if I had read the book. The audio-book gave certain characters odd voices and unexplainable accents. And there were already too many questions without answers. 
 The author's use of English really bothered me in this book. She chose words that felt anachronistic in her pseudo-feudal setting; "networking" came into use in 1980s, for example, and why would she say she went about her day like a "zombie" without any description of what zombies are in this world? Also, if she didn't know the difference between "protege" and "prodigy," her editor should have. 
 It's just that there wasn't really anything special about this book. It was colorless, formulaic, forgettable. If you feel that makes me a literary snob, so be it. 
 It's just that some books set in invented places do have fascinating and colorful yet reasonable histories, though we can't all be Scott Westerfeld. And some books have diction so carefully chosen that the pages sing with poetry, though we can't all be Maggie Stiefvater. And there do exist some books with characters so lifelike and lovable that you feel not only like you could meet them, but as though they are parts of yourself; although we can't all be Shannon Hale. 
 But when you know these books exist, you can't go back to stories that are poorly edited and poorly executed.

sample_reviews.review_text: The tale of one foolish young man's growing love for the eponymous tenant, a widow with a child and a very solemn disposition. The main character is a foolish prig and his beloved is little better; if we could average out their bloodless piety with Wuthering Heights's overwrought passions, perhaps we'd reach a happy medium. That Helen's husband had been a brute is unquestionable, but read what she thinks about him: "And I had been looking forward to this season with the fond, delusive hope that we should enjoy it so sweetly together; and that, with God's help and my exertions, it would be the means of elevating his mind, and refining his taste to a due appreciation of the salutary and pure delights of nature, and peace, and holy love." Oh noes, he doesn't want to "refine" his tastes in "due appreciation of...holy love." I uh, don't blame him. Tangentially, here's a passage that amused me greatly, in which Gilbert writes of Helen's brother Mr. Lawrence, "...the increasing pleasure I found in his society--partly from his increased cordiality to me, but chiefly on account of his close connection, both in blood and in affection, with my adored Helen. I loved him for it better than I liked to express; and I took a secret delight in pressing those slender white fingers, so marvelously like her own, considering he was not a woman, and in watching the passing changes in his fair pale features, and observing the intonations of his voice, detecting resemblances which I wondered had never struck me before." Hee!
I love the Bronte sisters.

A traditional Victorian novel this is NOT. No polite company or tight lipped tea parties. Instead you get: Immorality, brave female characters, love triangles and ultra modern switching narratives. I loved this. I rooted for the main character, loathed others and sunk into stunning description. This book was scandalous when written and is often thought of as the first feminist novel. Well worth the departure from more traditional novels of the time.

I'm a Bronte fan in general, but found this book to be a tougher going than expected. It revolves around two characters and their relationship, although a bulk of the book is given to a diary account of the recent life of Helen, the central woman in the book. 
 It contains the usual good writing in terms of well crafted sentences, but I'm never convinced of the love between the two main characters. Plus, the diary makes Helen a bit unsympathetic as you see her ignore everyone's advice and make a poor decision in terms of agreeing to marry a rich brat. 
 Still, Anne Bronte pulls it off. So I liked it, but am not likely to reread it.

Fabulous Bronte book. Better than Wuthering Heights. On par with Jane Eyre. The copy I had said that it was scandalous when it first came out and that it "still has the ability to shock." Couldn't have said it better myself.
Good.. I mean, nice way of showing how foolish it is to think that you can actually change a person.. and the male protagonist kind of seemed immature .. but, o.k

This novel gave me a real sense of frustration: For god's sake just say how you feel!!! Save a hundred pages of "well I wonder...surely not!...could it be?" This is not to blame the author as much as the stifling social conventions of the era. You can still see this mechanic in modern movies and (especially) TV shows where the entire plot hinges on things left unsaid (no matter how obvious to the viewer!)Perhaps it's having the omniscient view of all parties that things appear obvious. I suppose most of us can relate to being reluctant or afraid to tell someone of our feelings...aaaanyway..the novel is well written and captures the settings very well. The oppression of living with a drunkard is invoked well and I felt a great affinity with the Tenant. Her suitor was a bit of an ass in my opinion but I think he grew up by the end and was deserving of her heart.

I had never read this and really enjoyed it. It is surprising that this story of a strong willed and capable woman was written so long ago. It still has timely messages to share and I recommend it to readers of literary fiction.

Partway through chapter 22, and I quit. Dear Goodreads, why do you keep recommending me books that are first-person narratives of women who decide to fall in love with the wrong person? I despise romances. It's Pride & Prejudice, isn't it? Maybe Emma? Look, two exceptions do not make a basis for recommendations, goddammit, and to slog my way through I Capture the Castle because you claim I'll like it, hate that, and then try to follow up with *this*... you hate me, don't you Goodreads? I've done something or said something to make you despise me. Well, recommend me one more book with an insufferable prig of a young woman heroine and the hate will be mutual. Don't get me wrong, I was actually somewhat interested, while the story was from Gilbert's point of view (though I don't know why Anne bothered to pretend he's writing to a friend when the second 'letter' reads nothing like a letter, certainly not like a letter from an uneducated farmer. 
 Anyway, as I was saying, Gilbert's story was interesting - reading a romance from the POV of a man (albeit written by a woman) was something new. But as soon as Helen's diary began I started to see how it would be. There was little attempt to hide how it would go - Helen starts out proud and bragging about how good a judge of character she was, and I admit, I was somewhat hoping she really would turn out to be that good judge of character. Maybe be pushed into a marriage and make the best of it. Whatever. But no, the twit runs screaming into the arms of the first relatively good looking man to give her a second glance, ignores hints the size of freight trains about what sort of man he's going to be, and really, they're not even married yet and I already despise her for what sort of wife I know very well she's going to be. And, noting that I am not even halfway through the novel yet, I'm not even remotely interested in suffering through her self-imposed suffering. So I chose, in the middle of a ridiculously long history of Helen's fiance's corruption of one of his friends, to read the wiki summary instead. And surprise surprise, it pretty much reads exactly as I foresaw the moment the diary portion started.

I wish I hadn't put off reading this for so long because it was a great read. It intrigued me from the start and told a story that still seems relevant today. Vivid characters and a plot that moves along nicely.

book_a.title: Dead Wake: The Last Crossing of the Lusitania
book_a.user_review: Very well researched and detailed, just not my cup of tea.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I did not think it would be possible, but "Dead Wake" has replaced "The Devil in the White City" as my favorite Erik Larson book. (Can I take a second to brag that my copy of the former is signed by the author?!) If you have not read any of this guy's books, you need to. Like now. 
 In "Dead Wake," Larson explores the events during the weeks leading up to the sinking of the luxury ocean liner the Lusitania on May 7, 1915. Many people have heard of this World War I disaster, but few know the minute details, the ill-fated set of conditions that culminated in the deaths of hundreds of passengers. In his characteristic compelling biographical style, Larson educates readers on this maritime catastrophe. 
 First, let's talk basics. The Lusitania was a Cunard transatlantic liner that navigated between New York City and Liverpool. In response to competition, it was designed in 1907 to be one of the biggest, fastest, most luxurious and most modern ships around. It was the first of Cunard's "grand trio" of four-funneled ships. This "Greyhound" was cruising from NYC to Liverpool in seas recently declared by Germany to be a war zone when it was attacked by a German U-boat, or submarine. On its final excursion, the Lusitania was captained by William Thomas Turner and contained passengers both regal and humble, as well as numerous children. Remarkably, as Larson demonstrates, the passengers were relatively calm sailing into submarine-infested waters during the tenth month of the war, likely an effect of the widespread expectation that civilian ships were to be kept safe from attack. But as luck would have it (and by luck I mean an array of circumstances that melded juuust so), Unterseeboot-20, the German submarine captained by Walther Schweiger, torpedoed the Lusitania, effectively ending its nautical reign, as well as forcing America's participation in the war. 
 That summary of the Lusitania is truly just the beginning. It is tempting to detail all the interesting components Larson compiles in his newest nonfiction tale, but not only would that spoil the story, it would take ages. Larson unearths the myriad facets, both large and small, that led to this calamity, and he describes how the interrelation between them resulted in such an outcome. Weather, politics, ship design, cryptanalysis and more--all are important pieces of the story, and Larson presents them eloquently and effortlessly. He paints a vivid picture. Readers will walk away feeling quite familiar with the Lusitania, its history and its peripheral contexts. 
 Larson chose to present the overarching narrative by alternating two discrete storylines and merging them. One gives the background of the Lusitania, the other that of U-20. The back and forth between prey and predator creates tension, tension that escalates with Larson's depiction of the actual sinking event and its sobering aftermath. The people involved will get under your skin, and their fates just as much so. Be prepared for tons of emotion... 
 Visit Book Nook Reviews to read my full review of Erik Larson's "Dead Wake." Happy reading! http://booknookrevs.com/nook/review-d...
I think this would have worked better as a print book for me - I found myself not paying attention to the audio version. I do think that Erik Larson is a popular nonfiction writer that is overrated.
Couldn't get through this one. You might like it, but I found it very tedious.

Larson's latest book details the time before and the aftermath of the sinking of the Lusitania, an event that would be the first volley into tempting the United States into entering World War I. The action shifts from the ship itself, to the White House, to Great Britain and to U-20, the German submarine which would sink what was at the time the fastest and most luxurious passenger liner in the world. I admit I didn't know a lot about the incident, other than it led to the loss of a lot of people and that it sorely tested America's neutral stance. America would be drawn into the war a couple years later, of course, after an even more incendiary incident: the interception of a message from Germany to Mexico, asking for an alliance and offering up a part of the United States as a prize. The author, as is his style, not only goes over the facts and figures, but highlights various people affected by the infamous event. All the small pieces that led up to this incident -- the delays in launching, the fog, the slower speed the ship made -- resulted in more than a thousand dead-- many of the victims women and children. Indeed, it's a miracle in some ways that there were any survivors at all- the one stroke of luck was that the weather was calm. Chilling is the ruthless and efficient Schwieger, who seemed to have no reservation in taking out a passenger ship filled with civilians. More chilling still is Germany's exuberant reaction and the escalation of U-boat attacks. But perhaps the most chilling is the theory that the British government back then may have wanted the attack to happen, to entice American to join the Allies. This is not just an idle conspiracy theory, either. For if there was no plan to dangle an unprotected Lusitania in front of the nose of U-20 like a rich sweet, then the failure of British intelligence was colossal.

I loved this book. It grabbed my attention immediately and filled in some gaps in my understating of the events leading to the American entrance to the war. Larson has once again proven his standing as one of the leading non-fiction writers in this decade. 
 The way Larson wove the passenger's personal lives into the larger war environment was compelling and enjoyable. I loved the chapters he wrote from the perspective of German submarine captains and crew, humanizing them in a way that no other book I have read has had the courage to do. And while some non-fiction writers bog their stories in details, Larson provides a perfect amount of information so that readers still learn something without feeling like they are reading a textbook. 
 I didn't want this book to end. 
 Highly recommended.

I really enjoyed this book. It mixed history with an essence of creative writing that made a story so engrossing that it was hard to put down. I would highly recommend reading this even for people who aren't interested in nonfiction. It does not read like nonfiction and keeps the readers interest to the last page.
Not as riveting when you already know the ending but still full of interesting stuff

Every 10 pages or so, I wondered if I would not just put back the book on my shelves. While the Lusitania was about to sink, the author was drowning his readers with too much information. I am in awe with the amount of work and involvement Erik Larson put in this book. As a French who had 2 great-grand-uncles who died during WWI (one in the Battle of the Somme, near Peronne and the other on the Hospital-ship Le Provence), I have always had a great interest for this war and like many of us, always had thought the torpedoing of the Lusitania had prompted the Americans to join the war. In fact, it took them 2 more years. While I had adored the light and beautifully poetic 'Everyman for Himself' by Beryl Brainbridge that had its story set on board the Titanic, I could not help expecting such identical angle for the book by Erik Larson. Instead I had a story hard to swallow, but that I could not stop devouring because I was frustrated. The people are treated like events, so you don't get attached.What is left then is an accumulation of details of more or less importance treated on equal footing. I am glad I read it though because it made me reflect on our times. Yesterday 700 migrants from Lybia lost their lives in the sinking of the ship they had boarded to escape poverty, war and religious persecutions, and while the UN are calling for global concern and reaction, nothing so far has been done to stop this inhuman tragedy. Like the US who waited for 2 more years to help put an end to ww1 hecatomb, our nations seem to be at a standstill. History repeats itself.

Another good one from Larson in the tradition of Devil in the White City and In the Garden of the Beasts. I've had to do a lot of research for my own books, non-fiction and novels, but Larson is in a class by himself.

I had always thought we entered WWI b/c of the Lusitania. But we actually didn't get involved until 2 years later. I wonder how this became such a common misconception. 
 Those submarine captains seem pretty heartless, watching helpless people panic and drown and such. 
 I never had any opinion of Winston Churchill before, but now I dislike him.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Summary: 
 America Singer is chosen to be one of the Selected, a handful of teenage girls who will compete to win the affections of the crown prince and become his future Queen. America, whose "true love" is from a lower cast, has no interest in gaining the affections of the prince, but eventually the two start to become friends as the competition is narrowed down. 
 Review: 
 Not every book is for every reader, and that is probably why I put off reading this one. This was a book group pick so I felt obligated to read it. I know how popular this book is, but it never held much appeal for me--just not my thing. 
 Essentially this book is "The Bachelor" for teens. I think my biggest problem with the book is the predictability--it is all so cliche. Of course America doesn't want to be chosen to be the future queen, she has no interest in that. Of course the prince would be intrigued by American who just wants to be his friend. Of course they will begin to fall in love. Sorry, but there is nothing original here--it is very stereotypical. 
 Despite that teens love these books, and apparently quite a few adults do too (judging from the reactions of most of the members of my book group). I think the appeal is that the everyday girl gets the unattainable and then there is the happily ever after. Entertaining fluff, but that is sometimes what people want. I may pick up book two someday when I am looking for something light and entertaining, but that's for another day. 
 Overall: 
 Light and entertaining, but lacking depth. Perhaps the sequels will have more meat to them, but this didn't really hook me. It was okay, but it wasn't a favorite. Still, I might pick up book two someday should I feel the need for something light. 
 Cautions for Sensitive Readers: 
 Language: Mild--I don't remember anything graphic. 
 Violence: Some, though mostly off in another part of the palace from the narrator. 
 Sex: Some kissing and groping, but nothing explicit. She is informed that she must be a virgin to compete in the Selection and that the prince may ask anything of her. 
 Drugs/Alcohol: Some alcohol consumption.

Hi, I'm baack! And here's my first book finished in 2015. The first book in The Selection series which I finally start due to curiosity and I'm a sucker for long pretty dresses I could never wear nor own, not a good reason to start a book, but it's something. 
 Anyway, The Selection is about a selection, thirty-five girls competing to win the heart of seventeen year old Prince Maxon of Illea. The heroine, America Singer, is, yes, a singer. And here are a few things I thought of the book: 
 The start of the book is slow, I'm so close to give it up, but I held on and finished it. Entertaining read, yes, but it left me with a lot of unaswered questions. 
 Like, I still fail to see the need of a monarchy heir to marry a true daughter of the country, as it was put in the book, unless there was a written agreement to do as such or else the people will overthrow the crown. It seems like Illea is a weak, developing kingdom, unsettled in their international relation (past princesses sent off to marry foreigners) and also its own internal matters, I mean, weekly televised report? 
 And the rebel attacks. While, Maxon's theory on North and South rebels is interesting and I expect it to be explored more, I still wonder, how the rebels even get past the gate? I mean, this is the royal palace, the king and the royal family live there, the current king is not its first monarch, so I assume the palace has been around for a long time, and rebels get past the gate and into the property. HOW in the world? What are the guards doing? The rebels got in to their bedrooms, for god's sake. While the purpose might be to emphasis the danger and threats these rebels posses, that's plain ridiculous. I expect a much, much better security measure for a royal palace. Like, invest in a impenetrable wall as high as you can build, a strong, defendable gate, a new security head. It doesn't matter how many of them are, they should be well prepared. People like these rebels just can't be allowed to go waltz into a royal palace like it's a freaking open-for-all shopping mall. 
 And on the second attack, the king himself was also in the safe room along with the Selection ladies. Oh my God. And Maxon was also there. As the palace was attacked. Perhapts Kiera Cass was trying to be unconventional, the monarch's life is important, I know, but having him in that safety room looks even more ridiculous. (I thought the king, and the prince, would be out there leading the fight back? His kingdom needs a more than an administrative, doing-office-works king in its current state, it needs a king and heir who could also defend it in actual fights.) 
 And our dear girl America saw this situation as the king defending the palace like a ship captain. Then she just kind of remind me of Bella Swan. Average, but kind of okay, wanted by two men, uncertain whom she wanted to be with. (The start of The Elite has even got me disliking her character.) 
 Oh and the whole China invading USA and got labor instead... wait, China actually needs more labor force? Their population is much bigger than USA's, unless it declined drastically for some unknown reason, they don't need any more people to do anything for them. And the American State of China, what kind of a state was that? Is it like the Dutch East Indies? 
 What I'm trying to say is while the story idea is good, its base is not. For a universe to be believable, it needs a strong base for the whole thing to grow on. This lack of strong base might be due to America Singer's own lack of knowledge regarding her own country's history and current affair. But, still, when you dig deeper as reading the book, there is nothing much. 
 As I previously said, it's an enough entertaining read, but nothing more. I don't expect much as I begin reading, but even it still fell short of what I expect to find. 
 I'm not sure if I'll finish the second book, I'll give it a few more chapters.

No one told me this is "Hunger Games and Tiaras". 
 But yeah, I'll read the next book anyway.

book_a.title: The Art of Racing in the Rain
book_a.user_review: I'm not a dog lover, but I did enjoy reading a book from a dog's perspective.

sample_reviews.review_text: If you like car racing or dogs, you will enjoy this book. I knew this book was from a dog's point of view, but it was still not what I expected. I guess I didn't expect the canine narrator to have such a wide vocabulary and brilliant command of the English language. Not that it was a bad thing. Enzo the dog was actually very insightful and sometimes prophetic. The main plot was intriguing as well, exploring such virtues as patience, perseverance, humility, and love. There were some villains in the story who I had hoped would get their just rewards, but didn't. And the aging of Enzo was rather sudden towards the later parts of the book. But overall, I liked it. Once I hit the 55% point, it was a race to the finish as I couldn't put it down.

** spoiler alert ** 
 So I half-read/half-skimmed through this last night. I actually think telling a story from the dog's point of view could be an interesting idea. One of the big problems here is that this is not the dog's story; it's the story of his master-- not only that, but it really makes no sense to have the dog narrate this when the dog is not witness to crucial bits of the plot. Instead of accepting the narrator's limitations, the author forges ahead and tries to wedge those scenes in anyway. It's jarring and it derails the read. 
 The other problem I have here is the plot. 
 *********SPOILERS AHEAD****************** 
 Look, the goal of writing is not to play whack-a-mole with the world's most emotional plot points. We start out with a dying dog. Oh, that's sad. Then we quickly move to his owner's whirlwind romance (which we never really feel, since it's from the dog's POV), the arrival of the baby (AW!), the wife's illness and tragic early demise from brain cancer (BOOHOO!), the evil in-laws (GRRRR!) trying to gain custody of his little girl (NOOOO!), the rape charge (GASP!) by the Lolita that loved him (WHORE!), the reunion with the estranged parents (YAY!) after they disowned him (BOO!) for abandoning the care of his blind mother (BLIND?! HOW AWFUL!) and the family farm; finally, the confession that the charge was a lie-- justice, custody, and the career chance of a lifetime (YAAAAAAAAAAAAY!) all come barreling down on the conclusion like an avalanche of Karma. Oh, wait, did I say finally? Because I meant penultimately-- the dog dies (BOOHOOHOOHOOHOO!) but reincarnates as a little Italian boy (AWWWWYAAAYBOOHOOHOO!) whom Dennis meets, recognizes, and agrees to teach how to race cars (GRAZIEBOOHOOHOO!). 
 *sigh* I just want to smack this book on the nose with a rolled-up newspaper. 
 These elements, when used sparingly, can provide an emotional core to a story, and allow for exploration of character, or show personal growth and change. This book uses all of these elements to develop no character whatsoever. Nobody seems to change, and all of the characters, including our narrator, are flat. Flatness is not necessarily a bad thing, but in a book like this where it's basically an emotional plot point gang-bang, you'd better damn well have a round character or two in there that is capable of surprising me in a convincing way. They didn't-- everyone behaved exactly as their archetype was supposed to. 
 It's effective at tear-jerking... you know, if you're game for that sort of thing. Otherwise you'll probably just walk away feeling a trifle insulted. 
 Finally, I have a big problem with the theme. 
 "The Art of Racing in the Rain", the book tells us, is about making your own destiny, never remembering your past mistakes, and living solely in the moment. This actually means that having the dog be the narrator is not a bad choice: most animals seem to live very much in the moment, and many of them don't seem to have decent short-term memories, much less long-term ones. Even the intelligent ones that are trainable will forget (or "forget") things like not to go rooting through the trash for food, or they'll wind up with a major stomachache. 
 Why, then, is the book primarily narrated by the dog in the past tense? It's bookended in two present-tense narrations, but the majority of it is reminiscence. 
 There's a lot of discussion of racing as a metaphor for life, and a lot of it just seems to fall flat, or doesn't really get supported by the elements of the story.
I really enjoyed this....I see my Daisy in a whole new light!

It had quite a few emotional moments that warranted a sporadic reading of it. If there are dog lovers out there, this book is for you. I think it validates the importance of a dog's like and makes us wonder even more what's going on between the big eyes and wagging tail. After all, they only have gestures to share with us.

The racing and life analogies are good. However, I didn't like it. Too close to life and too many skipped-over racing analogies. However, there were some poignant moments and quotes you could take out of the book.

I have a really bad habit of marking my books. Passages that speak to me or interesting facts, it doesn't matter. This is a fabulous but tough book to read. finished it flying home from Calgary. Not a book to read in public, especially towards the end. I highlighted 16 different passages that I found were truly gifted thoughts. It is very well written and I hope to find something else by this author in the future. The ending was stupendous.

After years of people telling me to read this book because I love dogs I finally relented. Woof. I'm sorry I did. A dog (but really an unimaginative curmudgeonly old man character) narrates a flat and contrived plot that takes place in some sort of misogynistic fantasy land where men are honorable, young women are liars, and life can be described in endless metaphors to car racing. Also, don't market a book to dog lovers and then add a scene where the owner strikes the dog. Not cool. No dog lover I've ever met is okay with that.
Great first chapter, but for me it became less credible and less interesting as it progressed. Skimnmed to the end.

More like 3.5 stars. I didn't like the racing/life metaphor, but I loved Enzo, the narrator. As a dog lover, his wise observations goes along with my belief that animals have souls and are more human than we realize.

A must read - especially for any dog lover. Amazing how he captures the thoughts of a dog in such a believable way. I found myself thinking of my own dog, who has since passed, and how he reacted to my moods and different situations.

sample_reviews.review_text: Beautifully written with a clever plot. Just a great read.

That said, I bet the movie will pick up on her descriptions of the circus tents quite nicely I am sure... Since rights have already been optioned, etc... 
 http://www.goodreads.com/review/show/...... Fantastic review!
I loved this book!

I wanted to like this book more than I ended up liking it. The beginning hooked me, but the end left me wanting a little more. No, that's not the right thing to say. The love story. That's what got me. It just wasn't very believable to me. The world is fantastical though, and I wouldn't mind checking this circus out.

I just couldn't get into this book. I made it to page 257 (of 391) by the time the book club was due to meet. I'm not one to stop reading a book and am curious where it went, but am not interested in continuing with it. 
 I need more narrative to keep me engaged and fewer scene descriptions. Magic and fantasy also don't interest me, so those were additional obstacles.

Because I'm in school, I read a lot to just acquaint myself with as many different authors, styles and genres as possible. That's why The Night Circus was such a delight. I read it just for fun. The story swept me up into it completely. I spent the entire day in bed just wondering, "What is going to happen next?!" And that is the best reason to read ever.
Wonderfully written. Full of creative imagination and fantasy. A little long, well worth the read.

Though well written and imaginative, this was a bit too "out there" for my tastes. The story is unique and sometimes fascinating, but the writing style (great descriptions) and the setting are probably the book's greatest strengths. In its defense, I'm not much of a fantasy fan.
It bothers me when a book is supposed to be amazing, then, two pages in, it says the f-word. I don't want to read that. So I was only two or so pages in when I put the book down. Such a downer!

The only thing that kept me from giving 5 stars was the fairytale romance element, which doesn't resonate with me. Setting that aside this book is magical and mysterious in ways that no other book I've read is. I think this writer has a very bright future ahead and I'm very much looking forward to what she comes up with next.
