reference_books.title: Across a Star-Swept Sea (For Darkness Shows the Stars, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
I highly advise for a third installment of this books. 
 Please. 
 With a twisty, complicated plot, with some For Darkness Shows the Stars people, the return of the Wild Poppy, technology like never before seen & lots of Justen & Persis. 
 Plus Persis & Justen. 
 PLEASE? 
 I kid you not, this book heart attacked the shit out of me. I read it up to pieces & loved the fuck out of it! For starters, it has everything I like about a book; from the complicated not-love relationships to confusing friendships all the way to kickassery & action. 
 So, here's the thing. This will be a non-review, where I will point out real, fair, not-made-up reasons of why there. Must. Be. A sequel. 
 Okay? 
 Okay. 
 First things first. Oh my god, you, Persis! There is no doubt that she's my hero. I loved Persis determination to hide her real identity & be the most acclaimed air head on Albion's court so she could become the most acclaimed spy & savior of New Pacifica. 
 Yes, yes, this was amazing! 
 By day she's Persis Flake, court's shallow, stupid & uninterested girl, while by night *evil smile* she becomes the Wild Poppy, mastermind & responsible of saving aristos & enemies of the galatean revolution. 
 Beautiful, brilliant, resourceful, she got it. 
 Then again, if someone will cross the sea to risk her life like that, you can only expect it to worth something. Sure, she's saving lots of lives, but hey, the extreme amounts of action she gets in every scene is the real deal breaker. & for me too!! 
 The missions Persis carried away as the Wild Poppy in Galatea were total nail biters. & here's where I present to you, 
 Reason #1 of why a sequel is needed 
 I need MORE. More action! 
 More badass spy scenes! 
 More intrigue & conspiracy theories & fights with the bitch!! 
 Right. 
 It's a fact that I'm all over Persis political mind, cleverness & sarcastic comments. She's great, the kind of character you wish were real, & that's perhaps why her disguise as the sweetest stupid bothered me at times. 
 Is the best cover the Wild Poppy could yet, yes. 
 You need wit to play dumb, fine. 
 Still... Persis is the the Princess Regent closest friend. Isla doesn't have it easy, trying to rule over such macho society, what kind of help is Persis Flake? NONE, I tell you! 
 On the other hand, Persis fucking Blake could have been a great social influence that could have helped her friend in her first months as regent of Albion. 
 Ow, Isla... Ah, Isla was wonderful as ruler! (I shall whoosh about her later). 
 The act also affected Persis' life too much. 
 Clearly she was set to make some sacrifices in order to save people in Galatea, so hurt her reputation is not much in exchange. But what about her parents? 
 Her relationship with her father was very damaged. & why must this happen when her mom was... sick. 
 Anyway. Regardless of my feeling about Persis act, she was amazing at it. 
 Now, lets see. 
 Schemes & blindsides, consorting with the enemy in order to benefit your interests (as a spy!), help the princess legitimate her rule through deception; a lie of a romance that ends in unexpected something (love)...? 
 OMG, WHAT ARE YOU WAITING FOR!! 
 That is exactly the kind of love development I like! 
 & man, does this book deliver. Beyond the fact that Persis & Justen are perfect for each other (& that Isla mentions it several times to nag Persis) is the fact that they deny it AND/or are to busy regarding the plot to realize. 
 The major peeve I had with For Darkness Shows the Stars is that I wanted TENSION, but I got tension instead. 
 & Elliot's passive-hysteric manners,too, but I just realized about that... 
 Hell, Across a Star Swept Sea is made up of great, pointy, hurtful splinters of TENSION!! 
 Never mind my craziness, I loved that. 
 Persis is neck deep with the Wild Poppy, & she can't trust Justen by any means because he's the enemy. That she has to fake a romance with him is bad enough; that he'd be her dream boy (smart, handsome & all that) makes it all kinds of worse. 
 But she wouldn't let all those confusing feelings distract her. Instead she sails south to Galatea to save some galateans. 
 Because she's badass like that. 
 Justen, well, as a good revolutionary, he has too many prejudices against aristos. He brushed Persis as shallow & stupid all too quickly... the better for Persis & her act. 
 Yet, when he was beginning to trust her & reach out of his revolutionary guilt & loneliness, BUM! 
 You are dealing with an SPY, Justen! 
 Not that he realizes. 
 Then he kisses her to prove something, but that's not the point. Persis played some interesting psychological games with his head, driving his revolutionary guilt to the point that he feared his actions would hurt his sister, the person he loved the most. 
 *happy sigh* 
 Isn't it romantic? 
 Oh, the confusion! 
 Oh, the doubt! 
 Oh my heart, this was so good. 
 Is not just the circumstances of how they met or that there were lies upon lies. Persis' little heart & personal issues beyond the Wild Poppy affected her take on liking Justen when she shouldn't. 
 Couldn't. Love was magma, shooting from the Earth. It had the potential to form pillars of rock that would last for a thousand years or plumes of ash that choked the sky. She would never love like her father, never let herself be loved like her mother.Our girl has kind of closed herself about the idea of love. She thinks that there's no boy alive who can love her because what she is & not in spite of it; because of her brilliance & not just her pretty face. 
 Considering she's a little crazy, she might have been right. 
 But then HE COMES AROUND & AAAH... 
 Reason #2 of why a sequel is needed 
 This is how I like my romances to happen. 
 & just that. 
 It was perfect. 
 I want more of this (the contradictions) & more of them (the unexplored passion). The end was so very sweet, after that roller coaster of stuff they did & thought about each other, it was amazing. 
 But I also need... more. Something more. I need to see, er, read them go beyond "this kiss I will give you is real". To finally see each other as they are, without the masks & with the secrets on the table. 
 The sequel's plot should unite them AND challenge them as a couple. 
 OH, YES! 
 PLEASE, somebody hear this, I am begging you!!! 
 Talking about Justen, he was my great dilemma. 
 One moment I was reaching for the darts to knock him out, the next I was loving him. 
 What. 
 I know, I didn't get it. & he bought Persis act too easily, he SHOULD have known better, so I kind of wanted to slap him, too. 
 Anyway, I think that in this regard, one of the best parts of the book is when it hits him that he may have been more interested in her than he pretended to be. That he cared! Vania's visit had proved that. After all, she'd as good as threatened Persis yesterday. 
 And Justen had almost bitten her head of for it. Dude, the realization made him want to slam his head on a wall. 
 Now. 
 Reason #3 of why a sequel is needed 
 The women in this book are pure kickass material! They are so badass, & the boys... well, they used their brain, which is good, too! 
 So Justen is a genius & Persis is badass as shit, okay. 
 But Isla, OMG! Princess Regent Isla (along with Andrine, who is a total lady) was a master of regal shut-the-fuck-up faces. 
 I LOVED how she managed her precarious situation on the power, given that the neighboring country had killed its queen & that the Councilman in her nation didn't respect her or acknowledge her as ruler because she is a woman. 
 & she kicked some ass, too! 
 In her very royal, queenly way, of course. "You think they like you because you're soft on them. But all you're teaching them is that you're soft." 
 Now Isla did turn, and fixed Councilman Shift with her most royal glare. "And if I let your insult pass unpunished, sir? What am I teaching you?" 
 Shift's mouth snapped shut. In her defense, Councilman Shift was a total asshole. 
 Also, it was her idea that Persis & Justen faked a relationship, so he could stay in Albion & do his anti-revolutionary investigation, while Persis could collect information from the enemy. 
 Considering all the above, that can never be a bad idea. 
 I see what you did there, Diana Peterfreund. 
 In one hand we have Galatea, currently under a revolutionary rule of terror, previously ruled by a queen for hundreds of years. Where the problem is class inequality. 
 On the other we have Albion, an almost paradise, ruled by kings since recently. Where the problem is gender inequality, & where the diseased King's daughter can't do more than wait for her baby brother to grow up & take the throne. 
 *slow clapping* 
 That. 
 Reason #4 of why a sequel is needed 
 Just imagine all the social, political & ideological things a sequel could deal with! That's be wonderful (specially if the darlings are involved). 
 Plus some Andromeda's guilt, *muajajaja* 
 Please! 
 *sigh* It was everything I love in a romantic development & action, just bring another book & my year will be complete. 
 No joke. 
 I'll be waiting.

book_a.title: Gameboard of the Gods (Age of X, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Oh my god. 
 Now, every time I say that, I snicker to myself & do a metaphorical head shake because I'm not particularly religious. But believe me when I say: 
 Oh my god!! 
 This book is everything I ever wanted to be true about religion! A world where religion is strictly regulated & believers are zealots created by one of my favorite authors. 
 What? My favorite books are Religious Conspiracies, okay? Religion is a conspiracy.Now, don't take it wrong. I respect all religions all around this world & their beliefs. Everyone. No discrimination & stuff. 
 I even think there is a GOD, universal energy, omnipresent/omnipotent force (whatever you call it) something out there. 
 I just think religions are a kind of imperfect social institutions & am really pissed at the fact that my parents hosted a Baptism party when I was less than 1 year old & I didn't know & nobody asked. 
 As I was saying, the world is what I liked the most about this book. But not just because of the religious aspect. There is a lot more to be interested about. 
 In a short & sweet resume: 
 Tech stuff is advanced; 
 Social & political aspects are a critical mirror of what actually happens; 
 & what remains of Mexico is a strong dictatorial force(!) *tear* (I couldn't be happier). 
 So, the RUNA is The Jewel of the World. 
 Gemmans its citizens. 
 Aside what you'd think, it receives this name because after genetic outbreak, there were groups rich & privileged that maintained the, say, genetic purity. So there you have patricians (or castals) Nipponese, African, Mediterranean, & so on to the Nordic (in which Mae belongs). 
 Everyone else is a plebeian. They are not less privileged or poor, just genetically mixed up. 
 After this plague hit the world, some would have some secondary effects named Cain (marks, poor hair & skin & asthma). Castals are more prone to Cain because of their poor genes, so the way to measure that probability is with an Genetic Resistance number 1-9, nine being a Cain free person. 
 Oh, yes. About their beliefs; 
 Everyone is a cynical bastard, because yeah, religion is bad & not many practice, all right, for they don't venerate a mythical god but they go in all fours to venerate & mystify a country & a system. 
 RUNA is their religion. 
 At the beginning Justin comes as a cross of bitter & cynical. I didn't dislike him, I was just skeptical about him, IDK... 
 I was just frowning down at him when he turned out to be the most self absorbed & arrogant bastard around the place,& yep, I liked that on him. 
 Plus the fact that he's an exile of the RUNA in Panama, hmhmhm! 
 Still. It wasn't until he proved himself as someone smart & capable that I began to understand him. What, I like smart men. Still, his vices & wasted attitude could be frustrating at times. "I can't shut my brain off. It's like a hamster wheel." So, you think too much? Oh, poor you, let me slap you unconscious, yes? At points he would come as a washed version of Adrian, but then I'd realize that Adrian at least has his spirit thing issue as a excuse. Justin doesn't have one as strong. 
 So, which excuses could he have to be so... like that? 
 Deals with the gods. 
 That'd drive anyone crazy. 
 He also has had faith issues. 
 The point of his job is not to have faith at all; yet, he's seen things many people hasn't & those things got him kicked out of the RUNA. 
 The gods, I mean, the real mythological gods that come to claim people as their own kind of gods, can be bastards, in Justin's case, a cunning bastard god wants him. 
 So they made a deal... when Justin was about to die, so I think it was totally unfair & tricky. 
 Damn it unknown god. You'll know her by a crown of stars and flowers, and then when you take her to your bed and claim her, you will swear your loyalty to me. Well, he promised Justin the love of his life (plus salvation), can we really blame him? 
 So far, Justin had managed to avoid any links with the god, aside with the ravens (the god's pets) that live in his head. 
 Those... cunning bastards. Just like their god. I was SO sure I had discovered who the god was because of them but they misled me, damn it. 
 So, Horatio & Magnus. 
 I liked their presence because of reasons beyond the purpose of this review. They gave Justin's thoughts kind of an edge, since he's always thinking & over-thinking but guarding himself all the same, it'd have been hard to follow without another couple of perspectives along the ride. 
 Here's where Mae enters. 
 She's the kind of strong, elegant woman I like to read about (she kind of reminded me of Gwyneth Paltrow), with her castal upbringings & being a deadly praetorian elite soldier, I loved her. 
 She's perfect. Too perfect. 
 Oh Mae *hugs* For her this wasn't the best moment to meet Justin, even if they are perfect together, by all means, he does NOT want to seal the deal with the god, so all that chemistry & sexual attraction can go down the toilet. 
 Frustrating much? I know. 
 I think this star-crossed point of their non-existent relationship (one that can't exist anyway) was too stressed out, to the point where the central point of the book was left to the side. 
 Granted, if they ever sleep together (again) Justin will be forever-bound to this god, whoever he is, & that'd be a problem. 
 Still, she's a strong praetorian & she's awesome. I am a soldier of the Republic. I do not serve my own will but that of my country. & talking about the plot. 
 They only have 4 weeks to solve a series of murders in Castal grants. As I said before, Justin is exceptionally intelligent, regardless of what messed up aspect he may have. Plus his experience he could solve the case... when the murder is black smoke. 
 *X-files intro here* 
 I was SO ready to start the murders investigation right away. 
 Seriously, sexy Sherlock Holmes outfit & all. 
 It was really frustrating to have to wait for the guys to be up & ready to start figuring out what the hell with the murders. 
 Oh, but we have a month. 
 Right. NO. 
 The first two weeks are for Justin to settle back in his old life. 
 To grow into Mae's mysteries. 
 & for Tessa to accept & follow her new life at the RUNA. (Oh, Tessa! okay, later...) 
 Then, once they were ready (& I was desperate, hooked & murderous), they... traveled all the way to Mazatlan!! What? That was great; there's where the fun began. 
 They nearly died!! 
 & was right then when I formed this totally coherent theory in my head about the murder & the gods involved... it was proven half right *proud self love* 
 Yeah, it was solved in their last two weeks in a bunch of pages, but it all came together beautifully & I just am in love with the case... & the seeds! 
 There are some unsolved questions & I need to know... 
 So, I nearly forgot about Tessa. 
 She's great & is in the pat to become my best friend. 
 She is Justin's niece of sorts, & he brought her back to RUNA from Panama because, why not? He claims she's as smart as him, so obviously she's a prodigy & must study in the best place on earth. 
 I liked that he relies on her to be a fresh POV in solving the murders, as the fact that while he & Mae were busy solving non-relates murder issues, Tessa would be the one putting 1+1 together. 
 & how her actions would lead to greater plot threads. 
 Well, Panama is considered a province, so Tessa is a provincial, from a high class, old fashioned family. & a religious mom (ugh!). 
 The provinces are not all messed up places (like Panama), though there are some really bad ones. 
 The thing is, people in RUNA regard her just as provincial & discriminate her as such. 
 Do you know how to read? 
 This. Thing. Is. Technology. TECHNOLOGY, okay? 
 Do you know silverware at the provinces, do you dear? 
 Dude, people can be so stupid. 
 I felt very identified with Tessa because, being Mexican, I know what is like to be asked such stupid questions. From the usual Hey, taco, rico, right? question to this person who was all too surprised to know that there were cars & an hell of traffic in Tijuana. & one who asked how we'd travel outside the country since airports are all modern, & do donkeys fly, anyway? True story. 
 I feel you Tessa. 
 *sigh* 
 Now, the gods aspect. 
 To talk about religion & deities is very different. 
 In the RUNA there are many different religions you can follow as long as people like Justin don't find ways to shut them down. The thing is, most of this religions are based in random stuff & almost all the time the priests or administrators are just a fraud. 
 About the real I-will-mind-fuck-you gods... I liked them. Specially the one responsible of the murders. 
 Also the mythology like & polytheistic approach given to the unknown. *Win* 
 Still, the real deal about this deities choosing followers & reddening themselves... "We're all pieces on a game board, Dr. March, and some of us are more powerful than others. You. Me. Her. We're the ones the gods want. We're the ones they're fighting over." 
 Yep, I am hooked & I can't wait to see the War between GODS. 
 & their followers. 
 That's it; I loved the gods, I loved the mystery & I love Richelle Mead.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Wow, what a bizarre world. I'm still undecided as to whether or not I absolutely loved it or not. So, let me give the basics using the language I know and not the futuristic terms given in the book. To start, this book is told from three people's point of views: Justin, Mae, and Tessa. It's set sometime in the future where a disease has destroyed most of the population. And to avoid conflict and prevent more diseases, religion has kind of been monitored and slightly stripped from the world. But when humans deny the Gods, they do tend to come back with a vengeance. (Okay, so that last sentence came from my grasp of the theme of this series, not what happens in this book.) 
 Justin, a guy who's probably in his early thirties (or late twenties) returns to the RUNA to investigate a murder mystery. He's kind of like a detective who helps regulate religious activity. Oh, and there's a God keeping his eye on him. 
 Mae, a 28-year-old girl who has enlisted in the military and is one of the most lethal kind of soldiers in the RUNA. She basically has an implant that gives her body a boost in adrenaline when needed. Basically, don't bet against her when trying to determine who will win in a fight. 
 Tessa, a 16-year-old immigrant who has been given the chance to make something of herself in the RUNA. Trying to mesh where she was raised and where she is now into who she will become is interesting to see. 
 I enjoyed this book. Richelle Mead is very good at asking all of the right questions and giving you just enough answers to want to keep going. I did have a big "aha" moment in the middle of the book and figured out the plot. But the bigger plot (what the series is about) was only beginning to form. And we do get one major question answered, but you want to keep going at that point. 
 Overall, this was a really good introduction to a new series. It is definitely not a standalone novel, and I wouldn't recommend people expect it to be. This book introduces its readers to a new world, new characters, and a new kind of mythology. All I can say is: it's going to get addictive...
wtf was this? Vampire Academy was awesome, bloodlines was amazing and this was horrible. Why did Richelle Mead try changing her writing style?
This was a fantastic read. Gripped me right from the start.

For a futuristic society, Gameboard of the Gods is definitely not progressive. 
 In a world of religious extremists, RUNA (Republic of United North America) have established themselves as the superior state where their attitude, technology and lifestyle is clearly 'better' than others. Here, you'd encounter extreme castal segregation between the plebians (residents of RUNA) and patricians who are blonde hair and blue eyed and clearly different. All plebians look the same and have been conceived in a petrie dish whereas patricians are more superior because they've clung onto their cultural heritage. The plebians despise the patricians who live on old money and the patricians look down at disdain at the plebians who are the 'lowly' class. And then there are genmans who live in the rural areas, who are looked down upon by the plebians. It's just a book full of cultural and race segregation and snobbery. 
 If you haven't noticed already, there's a lot of confusing, brand new concepts introduced here. This is only a small sample of what's to come. Gameboard of the Gods is not an easy book to digest and read, and if you're a fan of Richelle Mead's previous paranormal books, this is on a league of its own in complex world building and new concepts. 
 If I didn't read the blurb and hadn't known the society was meant to be set in the future, I would have forgiven a lot of things. Despite the advanced technology, these people live like they're back in Ancient Rome with the segregation and the punishing people for the worship of the Gods and slight hint of magic existing. 
 Continued on the Happy Indulgence Book Blog.
Wanted to love it, but couldn't

I've actually not read any of her other books, this one was at the dollar store and I totally loved it (And have to order the next in series from amazon.) 
 I picture the main female character as charlize theron, esp her prometheus character....cold, stiff, tall and very soldier like!!

There's no easy way to say it, I didn't like this book. 
 I read through some other reviews while trying to put my thoughts together to write my own and mostly it seemed like people were confused by the "world building" and disappointed that Mead was doing something different than she normally does. This really didn't seem that different or new to me. Mae, the "heroine" was basically an amalgamation of all the things I disliked about Rose from VA and Georgina from Succubus Blues and Justin, the "hero", was a less charming, less likeable version of Robert Downey Jr before he got clean. But I'll get to them later. 
 Speaking of Succubus Blues, the world building in this followed a similar theme...i.e. there was none. Oh sure, you're fire-bombed with the random names for objects, places and peoples that Mead seemed to pick out of a hat and assign via the use of a complicated dart board system but you're given no explanation of the meanings behind these things until nearly a hundred pages in. 
 I suppose I should talk about the world building as far as I was able to comprehend it. Nearly the first hundred pages take place outside of the country that now seems to rule the western world. It's called RUNA. Want to know what the letters stand for? You'll have to wait until page 79. 
 Whaaaaa??? 
 Yup, for 78 pages and 46 mentions of the word RUNA, Mead keeps you guessing. No, I don't know why. While reading it I was convinced it was some new literary mechanism designed to stress test a reader's cardiovascular health but that seems a little farfetched in retrospect. 
 The people that live in RUNA are called Gemmas and while you might suspect this before it's spelled out (on page 82), you might, like me, be so confused by all the other mysteries that you begin to think they could very well be alien overlords instead. 
 Before you can get to RUNA--which we're led to believe is some sort of utopian paradise--you have to first bear witness to the near complete breakdown of society as you know it in one of RUNA's provinces, Panama. Its here you learn about the complicated and overtly racist caste system of the "modern" society in this world. Every citizen of RUNA is even forced to go through genetic testing and assigned a number 1-10 based on how attractive they are and it seems that race directly ties into that. 
 No, I'm not fucking kidding. 
 We're told that at some time in the past RUNA and the EA (Eastern Alliance--basically Asia) swapped large parts of their populations in order to genetically mix humanity. If you refused to participate you were fined and imprisoned, so a lot of people fled to the provinces to avoid these punishments and have kids with the people they loved instead of those they were assigned to or however it worked. I only read to page 240 before giving up so if it's explained why later, I missed it. 
 The people that descend from this western-eastern mix are called Plebians (no not plebeian, thank you Google) and as in the ancient Roman society RUNA is modeled after, they're pretty much second class citizens. 
 People whose genetics are less diverse are called castals or Patricians but more specifically Nordic, Welsh, etc etc. Like in ancient Rome, they're the elite. They even live on their own land grants together with their borders on lock down to keep out those interloping Plebs. 
 Oh hello segregation, welcome back. No one but these guys missed you: 
 Curious about how after all this forced genetic mixing there is still a population of genetically "purer" humans around with enough numbers to have their own land? And also how they escaped the forced mixing? You'll find out 159 pages in and be both irritated and reminded of The Selection. 
 In Panama you also learn that classism is still in full swing in the provinces but instead of being in its current state or a more evolved form, it has devolved to closely resemble that of 18th century European aristocracy. Women of "good breeding" don't go out in public alone, they don't wear their hair down or don *gasp* pants, and when they reach marriageable age their parents expend large amounts of money to buy them a trousseau and send them off to society functions to find a husband. They're poorly educated, relegated to second class citizenship and are basically only good for breeding. This would be the first point that I nearly quit. 
 When you finally do get to RUNA, aka utopia, you learn of a society built on religious intolerance, racism and consumerism gone wild. Paradise? Hmmm, not mine. 
 Now on to the characters. The story is primarily told through three perspectives. Mae is a cold, detached, semi-sociopathic, racist Robocop. Justin is a drug addicted, womanizing label whore and lastly there is Tessa, whose sole reason for existence (at least in the first 240 pages) seemed to be to make Justin seem like less of a self centered asshole. I'm not even going to get into Justin and Mae's "relationship" other than to say that it was completely childish and if I wrote any more about it everyone would have to start an f-bomb count. 
 Oh, also...gods are interested in them. I don't know why because they couldn't even hold MY attention or interest long enough for me to finish the book and so I have no idea what type of redeeming qualities a deity found within them. 
 Like the world in which they live, you only get snippets of their pasts as the book progresses. This is dangerous for a number of reasons. I feel that if an author waits too long to show the reader the reasons behind a character's behavior they run the risk of their audience passing some critical "I don't give a shit, this character is a douche" point. 
 If your main characters act like spoiled, selfish children for the first two hundred pages then I (the reader) begin to believe that's all they are. I formed a seriously negative opinion of them and when I finally DID begin to get some of their back stories it was too late because I'd already judged them and written them off. 
 Lastly I'd like to talk about the Frankenscience in this book. With the entire interwebs at your fingertips there is no need for it anymore. Not when a simple Google search can tell you things like why the human body needs sleep or how the brain, liver and your body's metabolism function. I'm no science geek and even I noticed how many inconsistencies there were. Why are they there? They were unnecessary. There were so many ways that the same information could have been explained to make the science at least plausible. Ugh. 
 In short, this book could have been great. It really could have. The plot was there, the world had potential and the mystery was good too. What killed this book for me was the way in which it was executed, the way in which petty, high-school style drama was introduced into nearly every scene. If there was no romantic element or if Mead had created more mature characters I could have loved it, I think. Sadly, I didn't. 
 But hey, this is just my opinion. 
 This review can also be found at The Book Eaters.

No. Such disappointment. 
 Honestly, I loved Richelle Mead's Vampire Academy series, so I thought I'd love this...but I couldn't even finish it. I tried to twice - but it just wasn't doing it for me. I didn't like the main character and the story didn't interest me.

Whew. I don't even know what to say, but okay here it goes. The first 100 or so pages I was confused. Then the next 200 pages I was still confused. After that I just stopped caring. 
 If I didn't read the synopsis I wouldn't have known what this RUNA the characters were talking about. It stands for the Republic of United North America. There is very little world building and no explanations of it whatsoever. Just random words that you literally have to assume what they mean. It was called the Decline and people died. No mention of it was a disease or virus or war. Just that Vancouver is the capital of the world now. And the city is clean and bright and civilized. Outside of RUNA, it's not. People breed like bunnies and have religions where in RUNA, you have mythological cults that are shut down by servitors if they're doing illegal things. Um what?! Then there's the crazy rating system of how genetically perfect someone's genes and looks are, that they base them on a scale of 1-10. Talk about the craziest caste system I have ever read in a book. Oh and did I mention the plot? Two main characters have to figure out who is murdering these beautiful blessed people by the end of four weeks. And add in the random conversations of three RAVEN GODS talking to one of our main characters in his head. UM WHAT?! Lol I didn't even bother wanting to find out about that.. 
 Yep I couldn't take it anymore. Dropped it halfway through and couldn't even fathom this was written by Richelle. It was boring so boring. SO MUCH DIALOGUE. I just couldn't keep going. I gave if a shot but I just don't want to bother. 
 RATING 1/5 
 QUOTES 
 "You don't like people making assumptions about you, but you don't want to show them the truth either." (46) 
 "Men like him get that self-assured because they know they're good in bed." (47) 
 "You like to be in control. And you're afraid for me or anyone--to see you lose it. To see your emotions inbound. To see your soul." (49) 
 "Revealing her ignorance would be a weakness." (109) 
 "My stunning good looks are ruined. How will I get by in the world now?" (141) 
 "Don't listen to the promises of men, even ones who mean well. Take care of yourself." (168)

What can I say? I love Richelle Mead. She is one of my favourite authors and I think everything she writes is pure genius. 
 This is no different. IT was such a great story and I loved that it was written in 3rd person. It's so different from her usual 3rd person perspective, but she did it so well. 
 However, the reason I didn't rate it 5 stars is for several reasons. 
 1. It was quite a slow book. There was a lot of world building in it and some of the different terms got a bit confusing after a while. For instance, I didn't realise until halfway through the book that Castal and Patrician meant the same thing. Castal is considered more derogatory, though. 
 2. The characters reminded me a bit of Vampire Academy. Mae was Rose, Justin was Adrian, and Tessa was Jill. Obviously, there are a few difference (Adrian is nowhere near as perceptive as Justin), but the comparison was still there. 
 Overall, though, I loved it. I can't wait to read the next book, because that's when things get REALLY messy. I can't wait to see what Richelle does with this series, because it looks like it's gonna be good :)

book_b.title: Tiger's Destiny (The Tiger Saga, #4)
book_b.user_review:
This is not going to be a review. This is a shit where I'll express how much this book disappointed me & where I point out how it wouldn't have done such thing. 
 Therefore, consider yourself warned. 
 I'm gonna rage & I'm gonna do it spoilerishly right. 
 *Deep, resigned, damned sigh* 
 Okay. Here's the thing; since the very first book, this saga has been a Guilty Pleasure. 
 A Guilty Pleasure. 
 This means it is NOT excellent or awesome, but has something (good enough) that made me obsess over it. 
 Now, ALL along the way, my biggest problem was *drum rolls* yep, KELSEY! 
 Yes, yes. 
 Before, she was way too naive & stupid, but there was one point where she wasn't THAT bad 'cause she improved... until she hit the ceiling in her way up & fell LOWER than ever. 
 & that's because in this 4th & last book, she wasn't just stupid (MORE stupid than you could ever believe possible), she took a PhD on DRAMA, too!! 
 & what do we think about dramatic people? NOT today~ 
 I really wouldn't like to do it, but I will make a recap since book one 'cause I'm upset & I'm just this contreras. 
 First of, Tiger's Curse had me at the edge of HATE until half the book passed & I ended up loving it. Specially the end; OMG, The End of Tiger's Curse is GREAT in a very particular, bittersweet way. 
 Shortly after, I started Tiger's Quest & please! Somebody hold me! Just remembering how & why I loved it is worth the rave. 
 Because Kelsey loved Ren & Ren loved kelsey, & destiny was like Why, fuck you two, so BITTER-SWEET. Bitter-sweetness Everywhere. 
 THEN, I painfully waited for Tiger's Voyage... & everything got screwed up. Half screwed, because I THOUGHT I got it, but still, WTF. (& I'm not talking about the Amnesia thing, but about the Oh, but... I did a promise part. *RAGE*). 
 Tiger's Voyage is where the whole saga went downhill, because HERE enters the Love Triangle. 
 You ask, How's possible there's a Love Triangle if Kelsey & Ren so obviously love each other. Even a blind foe could see how that way the story line is perfect. RIGHT? 
 Well, I tell you, Kishan is a very interesting character... 'CAUSE HE's THE ONLY OE WHO DOESN't SEE IT. 
 & wants the chick for himself, too. 
 So, here's where I start with Tiger's Destiny. 
 As messed up as their love life is, the Curse is still unbroken. 
 The Rope of Fire is the last of Durga's gift & the world-to-visit is Fire themed, obviously. 
 Again, the mythology, the world, the everything else but Kelsey (& now Kishan's attitude. You'll see) was awesome. 
 If anything, this book lacked sarcasm. I remember i started liking Kelsey (In Tiger's Curse) because she & Ren fought all the time & she would throw some great arrogantly-sarcasticly answers. 
 If just this would had happened again... *sad sigh* 
 This book was a tad faster than the others, mainly because the quest was completed pretty quick & the other half of the book consisted on Time Travel to the past to defeat Lokesh. 
 *sigh* Those Indiana Jones adventures. 
 So good. I'm gonna miss them. 
 They hold most of my love for the series. Is the LOVE part in our love/hate relationship. 
 But, self-pity, selfishness, stupidity? Gee, NO! Those are the HATE part. 
 & that's what I want to talk about. & I won't talk about the Love part because too complex & way too spoiler-ish. 
 Is the Curse. If you want to know about that, read the book. 
 NOW, brace yourself. 
 I have to say it. I am the Relationship Runner kind of girl. Specially if I don't feel like... um, you know, Golden Light from heaven & that shit. 
 Why would I have a hollow relationship? Fuck off, no! 
 But I WANT to think that even with the Light showering you, when you know you're in love, is fair to run, as long as are clear with the other person & you return whenever your self-issues are healed. 
 For instance, Kelsey had already run from Ren once; truck-loaded with self issues. Her pain; loneliness; fear; etc. 
 But she returned to him. 
 Good. 
 Then, both got fucked by destiny & she wasn't confident enough to hold on & the self issues returned stronger & screwed up. Even when Ren returned to her (& you know he didn't go because of Self Issues), she just couldn't. 
 That's NOT fair. Shouldn't be legal. 
 & even MORE illegal, to be with other guy (Kishan) because that seems "safer"... NO! 
 What's wrong with you, Kelsey?? 
 She says Ren has a Super Hero complex, so (maybe) trying to save her (or, yeah, any other worthless soul, why not?) he would put himself in risk & (probably) DIE. So, if she is NOT with him, if she is with a guy who meh, is okay & nice, he won't die. 
 *Here, use THIS spot to snort ALL you want. Take the time you need* 
 ...*More time needed? Sure. I'll hold on*... 
 (...) 
 Well, as I was saying, Kelsey fills the pages with self-pity because the people around her (her parents, her grandma... & just people in general), have the tendency to die. 
 Gee, Kells, BREAKING NEWS, People DIE. All the TIME! 
 &, as the Phoenix says, living a life where you fear the loss of your loved ones is a particularly wasted life. 
 Specially if you parade yourself with your boyfriend in front of the man you love. 
 In Tiger's Destiny, the Self Issues created by Ren's Amnesia should have had time to HEAL. Kelsey needed time to recover (ALONE) & then decide what to do with Ren or Kishan. 
 YEAH! 
 She doesn't do that! 
 Such thing NEVER happens!! (& I blame Colleen Houck). 
 That's just WRONG!!! 
 Because Kishan's like Hey, are we a couple now? At Tiger's Voyage, & Kelsey is all *shrug* Yes. Ren's gone, anyway. 
 Ren comes back & yeah, she was issued-up, fine. Be conflicted between the guys, you can; pero no te pases(!). 
 Try to heal, dear. Is called character improvement. 
 AND THEN, comes malefic Lokesh & kidnaps her. 
 Talk about self issues. 
 She was about to start a Long Life of suffering by Lokesh's side, & when the guys rescue her, she's just like, Nailed. Now, where were we? Oh, yeah, about mess up the whole saga. 
 She doesn't heal. 
 & that's why the characters in this book will need a date with the mans on white. 
 Now, even if Ren & Anamika would never burn each other, I liked how they spent time together. 
 Don't take me wrong. I mean that things were really unfair for Ren here. He was really HURT, & I think he had some time of relaxation staying with Anamika all that time. 
 Good for him. 
 On the other hand, I LOVED younger Durga. She's not just the goddess known as India's Mother, but also used to be a warrior badass. 
 Since Tiger's Quest it was very obvious that Kishan was hers... we just didn't know how such thing would happen. So, whenever they meet in the past, it was GREAT the fact that they disliked each other(!) 
 Cheers for it, I loved their fights! 
 I just wish there would have been MORE fights & MORE time for them to develop together. Whenever it turned out Anamika needed a tiger, it just seemed forced. 
 You couldn't really expect them to have a happily ever after together. 
 Though, I loved how natural Kishan flowed at the usual meeting with Durga at the beginning. 
 She's sure a smart chick. 
 But, but, but... Kishan, dear, you are DEAD to me. 
 DEAD. 
 So, we already stated Kishan has vision problems, but really, how can he do THAT to his brother? 
 That's just plain selfish! 
 He KNOWS how Ren has loved Kelsey since... always. But oh, no. HE's the one who's been lusting over her since ALWAYS, & the one Yesubay (she was named Yesubay, right?) deceived, so sure enough HE MUST deserve Kelsey more than his brother, RIGHT? 
 Not really. 
 "Ren CAN get over it". (Kishan Actually says that. A trillion times). 
 He knows Kelsey has been in a radish-metaphor Love with Ren since ALWAYS too, but oh, no! Hey gorgeous, I'm desperately looking for the meaning of life. & this is my chance, feel sorry for me & be with this guy! 
 REN HAS TO ACCEPT IT. *Bangs soul against imaginary wall* 
 Bitch. Please. 
 & you know which the worst part it? KELSEY DOES SO! 
 Oh, no! I PROMISED Kishan he would get a Happy ending & he MUST. Even if I have to spend the rest of my worthless life doing SO. 
 Also, Kishan was the Perfect Bad Boy. Perfect. But he changed his behavior & put himself at Kelsey-level. 
 Fuck it, that's why I hated him the most. He lost himself for someone else. 
 That's disturbing. 
 That means he could never be his true self around Kelsey or the Spell would break. 
 You guys, my head spins. This is too much. 
 So, to finish it up, THAT End. Not really what I'd have expected. Of course, was due to happen sooner than later but... er. Well. 
 I just can't believe Kelsey didn't want the henna tattoo because that brought SAD Memories. *Bitch slap* 
 Fini. I'm DONE. 
 Oh, no, WAIT. 
 Obviously, in this book I HATED Kishan. But one thing really, REALLY unfair for him is that he & Kelsey never had The Talk. The one that says I don't really love you THAT way. See ya! 
 Kishan stays in the past & he's like Yeah, I know you feel tiny butterflies with Ren, Kelsey, I KNOW. So kiss me Good Bye. 
 Kelsey NEVER had the mind-fuck guts to go & be HONEST with him (whether he deserved it or not, because he KNEW & didn't want to face it.) 
 The Love-Triangle was awful, yes. But This book would have had at least 4*'s if, like, at the middle, Kelsey would had dumped Kishan, er, I mean, if by the middle Kelsey would had been honest with Kishan, Ren & Herself. 
 By this I mean that if she stayed SINGLE the rest of the 4th quest (I mean, if she had said NO to Kishan's marriage proposal, for bitch's sake), focused in the Curse, coming to terms with the insides of her heart later (probably in the past, when they are about to defeat Lockeh hand-by-hand, with Anamika as judge of her action), I wouldn't have raged THIS BAD, because, at least, there wouldn't had been so much Oh, no! drama & self-pity.

sample_reviews.review_text: This was a fantastic finish to the series! Loved it from beginning to end!
a nice ending to the series

Just finished Tiger's Destiny by Colleen Houck (4th book in the Tiger's Curse series) - it was amazing! Just as much action and adventure as the first three books and the twists and turns in the love triangle between Kelsey, Ren, and Kishan had me in tears at times. Colleen really knows how to keep a reader engaged and takes you places that you never dream possible. 5 stars for this book!

Like all the other books from this series, I LOVED this book. I just love the adventure. I love that there is never a dull moment when you are just reading to get to the next exciting thing. Its action packed from the beginning to the end, whether is part of their quest or Kelsey fighting to decide what to do about her feelings toward the brothers. At the same time, this book was hard emotionally for me to read. I have grown so attached to these characters and to know the end has possibly come for some of them, it definitely hurt my heart. I definitely shed some tears on this one! 
 In the beginning of this book, Kelsey of coarse has been kidnapped by Lokesh. He is holding her at a far off location, hoping that the princes will not be able to find her. He wants her to become his wife and have a heir for him, a son that will be strong and posses both of their powers. Kelsey plays along, pretending that she was only using the tigers. Stringing them along on her quest for power. Though, we all know this isn't true. What we know, is that she has a tracker embedded in her hand, and her princes are on their way to her. But it seems they are on their own. Mr. Kadam and Nilima have been lost somehow during their war with Lokesh on the yacht. There is not even a blimp for them on their tracking device. They of coarse show up just in time to save Kelsey from her ruse of a wedding and whisk her off to the safety of their home. 
 When they get home, it isn't long before Mr. Kadam and Nilima return as well. It seems the family is all back together again. Except something is different about Mr. Kadam. He isn't his normal self and seems sad. He stresses how important it is for them to get started on their quest as soon as possible and they head off to the temple for Durga's blessing. Though it quickly becomes apparent after they leave that this quest will be different than the others. Lokesh will stop at nothing to get his hands on Kelsey and gain her piece of the amulet. 
 As it turns out, that is not the only difference in this quest and the others. Mr. Kadam will not be able to aid them on this quest. He has helped prepare them as best he can, but this is a journey he will not be able to take with them. He sends Nilima in his place, but she as well can only go so far. They will have to trust what they have learned and their instincts and do they best they can with what they have. 
 The first part of their quest leads them down into a volcano, where they must go below into the "Pit of Hell" in search of the Rope of Fire. They come upon many obstacles here, but Kelsey also feels very connected to her surroundings here. The trees can sense the fire within her and literally reach out lovingly to brush against her as she walks by. It isn't long before they come upon their first test. This is one for Kelsey and the one who will test her is none other than a phoenix. She must become a sati wife in order to pass the test. She must cross burning coals without succumbing to their damning heat, but in order to do that, she has to answer some questions as she crosses. Her honestly will be the difference between making it across alive and dying there on the coals. But to do that, she has to be honest not only with the phoenix, but also with herself about feelings that she has tried so hard to lock away. How can she admit them now and keep them locked inside? If she is honest, the phoenix will save her, not only from the coals, but from herself. He will give her a chance to start over. A chance to live her life and not waist anymore of it. But will she heed his warning, or will she be as good as dead? 
 There is so much more to this book, but I can't just give it all away, so I must stop here. But I promise you that you will love this one. It takes us on a action packed emotional roller coaster that ends all too soon. There is one more book to come for this series, but it seems we will have to be patient because we have a while. This book ended pretty well and tied up lots of loose ends, so I really have no idea what will come in the next book. But it doesn't mean I want to read it any less than the ones I already have. I can't wait to get my hands on a copy. It will definitely be interesting to see where this story goes now that the quests are all complete. I am praying that Tiger's Dream will be a book that leads to a spin off series. I guess only time will tell!

Sometimes it's really hard when it is the last book of a series. You're sad that it's over and you really don't want it to be. This however was not the case for this book. I really enjoyed this series but I was glad to read the last book. I think it was time for it to end and I think over-all it ended well. I think the author really tied everything together well and you really felt like you understood everything. A few complaints are: 
 I really couldn't stand how she strung both of the brothers along until the very end. I just found it hard to read. I mean they were both in love with her and she kept being with one of them and yet still being completly in love with the other. I also thought it was sad that Kishan was left behind. I know it all turns out well for him, but somehow I just felt sad. 
 Her books are just TOO WORDY! Almost every single one of her books I end up skimming pages. I can't stand how detailed she gets. It's too much. 
 I will say though that the story was thoughtful and it really did end well. All the "i's" were dotted and all the "t's" were crossed. 
 Over-all good series. The second book is still my favorite!!

PLEASE GIVE ME THE LAST BOOK NOWWWWWWW 
 ***Editing my review because I feel so empty....I will never look at tigers the same way again...now i have to go and cry in a corner because i feel so lonely without this series
A beautiful conclusion. Very satisfying.

I'll never get enough of Ren (or Kishan) but ESPECIALLY Ren. My favorite characteristic of Kelsey is the fact that she is willing to go above & beyond for the ones she cares about. I badly want to get my hands on Tiger's Destiny!
Ending was boring.
GREAT ending to a pretty cool series. Made me cry...AGAIN.

sample_reviews.review_text: I tried very hard to enjoy this...it's an absolutely fascinating subject and something that really should be common knowledge. But dear god, it was boring. I lost track of the characters after a while, couldn't remember who was who....and it was just dry...dull...boring.

Pretty boring. I became interested in this book because of the new motion picture. For me, it read too much like a history textbook. It was more a chronological line of events without a good story line. I wouldn't recommend this one.

I did not finish, first time that has happened in a very long time. I am a huge fan of history, the space program, biographies about strong women, etc but I just could not get into it at all. It is very dry and did not flow as much as I would like.

I read this for book club and didn't realize until I was over half way through it that I had the youth edition. It had less pages and less interesting stories. My version also had a timeline and glossary. Not a hit with my book club members - they wanted to read this version.

I really struggle in my rating of this novel. Margot Shetterly is clearly a researcher and it comes across in her novel. This is not a fiction story, it isn't fictionalized, and it isn't an easy read. This is a challenging collection of biographical insights interspersed with historical events tied in a beautiful ribbon of mathematics and science. It reads like an event biography (as opposed to an individual person) where many people's stories are told, but in a very factual way. I was not as drawn in by this as I was with Unbroken, and found myself slowed heavily by the minute and repeated details that the author has presented. I was delighted at the people being discussed and several moments captured me fully, but at other times I felt like I was wading in the deep end without my floats. Many of the people in my reading group agreed that the information was wonderful to behold, but it is easy to get lost in the details. And if you aren't a science and mathematics person, as some of my reading group aren't, it is possible to find yourself so lost as to skim your way out. I didn't like that aspect of it at all. I didn't skim, but it was a challenge to get through some sections. Therefore, I will refer to this as a 'chewy' book for those who enjoy history and want to know more about the history of NASA and the women (and men) behind the scenes. This was a good read.

More encompassing in scope: more women's contributions over a longer period of time. Covers from women's wartime jobs in World War II to the moon landing and even into the end of NASA's most notable epoch, the book covers so many more women and advancements, if you watched the movie before reading the book.

I've been wanting to read this book for some time. Lately, I've been on this reading kick where I pick up non-fiction books about female scientists and space missions and this one feels like the perfect way to close the loop on those two subjects. Granted, the actual writing is a bit dry for me, but the topic and the women were so interesting that I can kind of forgive this.

Anhand einzelner Lebensgeschichten umfasst die Autorin die Geschichte der NACA, die spater die NASA wurde. Faszinierend ist dabei nicht nur, dass die ausgewahlten historischen Figuren allesamt Frauen sind, sondern auch Afroamerikanerinnen. In einer Zeit, in der die Schulen und Bussitzplatze nach Hautfarben getrennt waren, leisteten diese Frauen die Rechenarbeit fur das Langley Memorial Aeronautical Laboratory, die Flugzeugentwicklung und spater die Raumfahrt. 
 Ich habe den Film, zu dem dieses Buch inspiriert hat, noch nicht gesehen. Allerdings muss ich gestehen, dass ich beim ersten Blick in das Buch sehr verwundert war. Statt einer Geschichte fand ich viele kleine, die mal auseinandergezogen wurde, mal als kurze Episoden daher kamen. Dazwischen aber zeigte das Buch sein wahres Gesicht. Ein erzahlendes Sachbuch vielleicht, aber eindeutig ein Sachbuch. Eines, das geschichtliche Veranderungen zeigt, ohne sich zu sehr in einer Geschichte zu verlieren. Am Anfang war ich kurz irritiert. 
 Das Buch zeigt gleich mehrere hochinteressante Entwicklungen in den USA auf. Zum einen die unterschiedlichen Ausgangspunkte fur Weisse und Schwarze, ehe der zweite Weltkrieg auch in Amerika Frauen als Arbeitskrafte entdecken liess. Statt kleinburgerlicher Hausfrauen waren die meisten Frauen, die Margot Lee Shetterly fokussiert, erwerbstatig und gleichzeitig Mutter. Fasziniert bin ich vor allem daruber, dass die Frage nach Vereinbarkeit in keinem Moment angesprochen wird. Selbst wenn die Frauen keine Grosseltern oder einen Ehemann an ihrer Seite hatten, haben sie ihre Karriere verfolgt. Unschlussig bin ich aber, ob das Buch sich hier einfach mehr auf die Arbeit der ,,schwarzen Computer" konzentriert und andere Probleme einfach ausser Acht lasst, oder (was irgendwie unwahrscheinlich ist) es keine gab. 
 Dabei ist die Geschichte der afroamerikanischen Rechnerinnen der verbindende Handlungsstrang. Die einzelnen Schicksale sind hier miteinander verbunden. Und uber diese Gemeinsamkeit blickt das Buch weiter, in die Geschichte der Burgerrechtsbewegung hinein. Diskriminierungen und Entwicklungen fur die schwarze Bevolkerung Amerikas werden aufgezeigt. Manchmal ist dabei nicht ganz klar, wo der eigentliche Fokus des Buches ist. Hidden Figures will Frauenbewegung, Burgerrechtsbewegung und die technischen Entwicklungsschritte in Einklang bringen. Auf weiten Strecken schafft das Buch das, aber eben nicht immer. Dann schweift es ab und muss sich wieder - fast sprunghaft - konzentriere, was denn eigentlich das Thema ist. 
 Dass Margot Lee Shetterly Hidden Figures dazu noch in ihre eigene Biografie einwebt und einen zusatzlichen Rahmen gibt, ist eigentlich unnotig. Es weckt den Anschein, begrunden zu mussen, warum gerade sie sich diesen Themas angenommen hat. Das muss ein Autor nicht. Stattdessen wirkt es unsicher und impliziert, dass sie dieses Buch nur schreiben konnte, weil sie auch schwarz ist und darum die Geschichte der Hidden Figures kennt. Damit erreicht sie, was das Buch genau nicht will. Eine kunstliche Grenze zwischen Schwarz und Weiss zu ziehen. Schade finde ich gerade hierbei auch, dass Hidden Figures die Erfolge der Burgerrechtsbewegung und Emanzipation zeigt, aber nicht zugibt, dass in beiden Feldern noch jede Menge aufzuholen ist.

These women are amazing, and Shetterly has done a mind-blowing amount of research, but a lot of the writing pertaining to the women's home lives was speculative, and I wish she had told the story in a more linear fashion rather than circling back multiple times to re-introduce certain people. I kept having flashes of deja vu thinking we'd already covered a period of time when really it was like "AND THERE GOES BLANCHE" or "HERE COMES MARY." 
 Would still recommend tho.

Wow, I couldn't have predicted how much I would dislike this book. The magic was great, the characters were well-drawn and they evolved through the book, and there was just the right amount of plot progression, tension, and resolution. Yet, I found myself strangely hating the whole story and by the end I couldn't wait to put it down. 
 Maybe my disappointment was in the simple predictability of the story, or perhaps because I knew from the beginning that this was only the first book in a series. I knew there would be a cliff-hanger ending, which there was, and yet there were just so many *words* to slog through before getting to that unsatisfying ending. But I think the real issue was the drabness and ordinariness of the words themselves. For all the imagination put into the story, the words used to describe it seemed plain. I know that Young Adult books are *in* right now, and maybe the author was afraid that big, colorful words would put the book beyond the reach of a mass audience. But for me, reading this book was the visual equivalent of listening to Gregorian chants ... I got the point but found the experience wanting.

Good read with a few nice twists for the ending. I liked this even better than his Night Angel Trilogy. You can see his growth as a writer. I'm excited to read the next two books that are out. I already bought them.

I made what I think was probably a grave mistake with this one and listened to the audiobook rather than reading it. I got maybe 1/3 of the way through and then realized there was absolutely no way that I was going to be able to suffer through the whole thing. The audiobook production itself is fine. The narrator is good, the pacing was nice, there weren't any weird effects or anything like that...this just isn't a book that you can listen to on audio. It needs to be read and probably read somewhat slowly. 
 The magic system was really, really hard for me to get into. I just couldn't visualize anything that was happening. I got the colors (obv) but I never quite understood what the magic itself (the luxin) actually looked like. The characters were mostly enjoyable--almost everyone was nice and complex, just the way I like them in my fantasy novels. But, like, I didn't care very much about any of them? Kip was annoying as hell, Gavin was interesting but was seriously lacking something, Kip's mother was idiotic, we're told rather than shown why the White deserves everyone's allegiance...the only character I gave half a damn about was Karris and it wasn't enough to make me keep reading. 
 The worst thing about this book was the plot. Basically nothing happens, at least not in the first 1/3 of the book that I managed to get through. I heard before picking this up that this series is more plot based than character based. While I usually enjoy character driven stories, I can let that go if the plot is awesome. That is not the case here. Maybe things pick up in the second half of the novel-I don't know. You'd have to suffer through endless inconsequential scenes featuring boring characters to find out and I just couldn't do it. 
 All of that said, I do plan to revisit this book. This series has been on my TBR for years. Literally. I'm going to try reading rather than listening and hope that changing formats saves this series for me.

This is one of those classics that I have gone throughout the years without picking up. Don't ask me why, because I don't understand it myself. It is magical and filled with supernatural elements. Completely engrossing. It's not just a book for the younger generations, this goes with everyone that loves to read. The characters are eccentric, off-putting, and loving at the same time. And can we talk about how impressive of a character Charles Wallace is? 
 "I mean like in biology,' Calvin said suspiciously. 
 'A change in gene,' Charles Wallace quoted, 'resulting in the appearance in the offspring of a character which is not present in the parents but which is potentially transmissible to its offspring.' 
 'What gives around here?' Calvin asked. 'I was told you couldn't talk.' 
 'Thinking I'm a moron gives people something to feel smug about,' Charles Wallace said. 'Why should I disillusion them?" 
 Then enter three elderly characters that are extraordinarily mysterious and unearthly. Catching our attentions right as they make their entrances into this realm that Madeleine L'Engle has created for us. Mrs. Whatsit, Mrs. Who, and Mrs. Which, whom you are going to want to get to know. They're not at all what I expected when first introduced to them. Their stories run much further than imagined. If Charles Wallace says they're ok, then they must be. 
 "Suddenly the three of them were there, Mrs Whatsit with her pink stole askew; Mrs Who with her spectacles gleaming; Mrs Which still little more than a shimmer. Delicate multicolored butterflies were fluttering about them, as though in greeting." 
 As I come to know Charles more and the three traveling companions, Meg's character grows more stronger and is brought to the forefront of the book as the pages are read. She, at first, seems angry, complicated, but is more than that. A misunderstood character with so much to give. She doesn't have any desire to prove herself to anyone and has plenty of strength and courage to become who she wants to be. And what is there to fit into when you're that awesome of a person. She is bold and strong and smart with a plethora of zany qualities. 
 There are copious amount of ah moments and hair-raising tales of the darkness that resides outside of our world. Answers that come when most needed. Adventures that commence once Charles, Meg, and Calvin agree to go on a rescue mission that will test all their wits and either make them better for it or keep them fearful of the unknown. 
 "She knew that her own puny little brain was no match for this great, bodiless, pulsing, writhing mass on the round dais. She shuddered as she looked at it." 
 "But now she thought that if only she had a dissecting knife she would slash at IT, cutting ruthlessly through cerebrum, cerebellum." 
 A tesseract is not needed to travel within this novel. Just a love for books and a childlike imagination that will keep all of us reading for many more years to come.

I read this book as my son had it as a school novel. Although I wasn't sure what to expect, it was a totally different book and style than expected. It is what I would call, Junior Science Fiction. For someone who had never read any of this style before, it was quite puzzling. The main characters were children, an older sister and a young brother, and their friend who they just happened across in the nearby forest. The book plunged right into the characters and used terminology which was not real. Even so, I even found the first half of the book quite slow, and only put the pieces back together during the last chapter or so. Overall, not the style of book that I am used to. Don't think I would read the rest of the series.

Ugh. I really really hated this book. It started out with so much promise, but then just fell flat. I wonder if I would have liked it better as a child. The ending leaves way for more books (which there are), and I'm kinda curious as to what the Mrs Ws were about to say... but not enough to slog through another book. This was just painful.

i remember liking this as a kid (i was probably around 7 or 8 when i read it) and moving on to the other books in the series. it probably says something, though, that nothing from this book stuck in my memory - definitely not the bludgeoning God-stuff. (the book that i do recall is "a swiftly tilting planet.") decided to pick this up when i saw it used and give it a reread, mostly gearing up to get to the third book. 
 well. what can i say about this? the pacing kept me moving through the book, but there's a lot going wrong here. stilted dialogue, bland characters, unimaginative places - how does a book about interplanetary time travel manage to be so dull?! perhaps this book is a necessary step in the evolution of the genre, but it does not stand up to the test of time. nearly fifty years on, it has simply been eclipsed. the child prodigy is better written by Orson Scott Card (ok, not at this age level, but still); Sherman Alexie has captured the misfit voice in young adult writing brilliantly; Judy Blume's female characters are much more sympathetic... you get the picture. 
 i reread this hoping it would be something i'd pass on to my friends' kids, but really, no. the breaking point for me was the notion that the communal kills the individual and is evil, just rankles me. sure, kids should learn that blind conformity leads to awful things (like, hey, just pick up a newspaper for evidence of blind following leading to disaster) but as a detractor of the western cult of the individual, i find the oversimplification here unacceptable. i'd like to hope that we're past this and can begin to model ways of community building. again, perhaps just a product of the book being thoroughly outdated now. nostalgia couldn't save it, and shouldn't.

sample_reviews.review_text: Carino, si. La fiera dei buoni sentimenti.

What's this book about? 
 There's not much to say, most of you have heard about Shiver so I'm keeping it very short. A girl,Grace, who's been bitten, a sad and emotional werewolf, Sam, with scars on his body, mind and soul . A heartbreaking love story. 
 If you want a more in-depth book description check out the one on Goodreads. 
 My thoughts: 
 It's only been a couple of hours since I closed Shiver but I just had to sit down and write a review while the story was still fresh in mind. 
 The novel starts off with Grace thinking back to the time when the wolves attacked her. And with that the story pulled me in. Grace is a very lonely girl, she has friends and family(though her parents are very distant) but still she carries a longing in her heart that no one can cure. She has an obsession for the wolves that lives in the forest behind her house, not every one is too happy about that. A boy has disappeared and people want to get rid of the wolves. 
 The characters were nicely written and I would characterize this as a story with a character driven plot. You want to know everything that goes on with Grace and Sam. 
 Maggie Stiefvater's writing kept me spellbound, glued to the pages. I read one sentence which pulled me to the next and the next(you get my drift), in a blink of an eye I had finished the entire book. Maggie can take the most trivial thing and describe it like it is one of the wonders of the world. Here's an example from the book: 
 I always loved going to the post office with Beck; it was a treasure cave with rows and rows of little locked boxes holding secrets and surprises only for those with the proper key. 
 It's almost too much but at the same time it isn't really, it is just outright beautiful. Can I share one of my favorite passages before I end this review? 
 'Sam released all of me but my hand, and tugged me deeper into the shop. "Come on. Now the hard part. What do you want? Pick something. Anything. I'll get it for you." I want you. Feeling the grip of his hand in mine, the brush of his skin on mine, seeing the way he moved in front of me, equal parts human and wolf, and remembering his smell - I ached with wanting to kiss him.' 
 I would recommend this novel to anyone who likes a great paranormal love story!
it was a really good read
Some people would like this a lot! Just wasn't my thing.

Unfortunately the whole book just felt flat to me, with only a few scenes of heightened tension that came and went quickly. I liked their characters well enough, but Sam and Grace's instalove relationship didn't ring true, and I was more interested in the lives of the supporting characters (Beck and Isabel in particular). I'll be trying Maggie's other novels - she has some wonderful ideas - but won't continue with this series.
It was not the best series I have read. Some people may enjoy it but I wasn't too fond of the series.

A little embarrassed by my current book selection. But like I said, this book had a pretty cover and I'm too busy to feed my brain with complicated plots. Haha. Interesting turn of events towards the end. It's like all the action happened too late in the book. And now I'm just left with so many questions. Off to grab the sequel! :)

Shiver has two major problems: 1. non-sufficient character development and 2. a plot that suffers from not only too little action but also action that lacks suspense. 
 Grace and Sam, while I actually like the idea of there being a relationship of some kind between the two while he is a wolf, it toes the line of creepiness with the idea that she is actually physically attracted to the wolf. The story never really gives us a reason why we want these two to be together so much. Both are static and never have any motives beyond keeping the other safe. Sam especially seems to have little personality beyond his reading, and while his background story manages to add some depth, I think if it really was so dark and tragic he needed to be more affected by it. Grace who is described by Sam as "stoic" is "stoic" to the point that I feel I know nothing about her beyond her obsession with wolves and negligent parents. 
 Any secondary characters are so flat and 2D that they stand out no more than the scenery. Isabel Culpeper is the only one who I found at all intriguing and, even her character seems completely underdeveloped. 
 It is surprising that this book is the first one in a trilogy because the ending really does not leave us with huge untied strings. It is vaguely hopeful, but in no way left me dying to know what happened. Also, the story failed to establish who exactly the villain is. At certain points, it is Jack, but Jack is dismissed quickly and we really know little about him besides the fact that people thought he was a "jerk". He certainly shows some selfish actions but they all can be dismissed by his emotions over becoming a wolf. 
 Really I think the story needs a more developed, alluring Sam, a 3D villain, more internal conflict with Grace, and a hell of a lot more secondary characters who have more than one specific character trait. 
 Just to end on a positive note, it does have sweet moments and while you probably will not find yourself drawn to any character, I think anyone who says they were not hoping for Sam to stay human is a liar.

9.2.2009 
 So far at only about 115 pages or so into the book I am not so impressed. I think I may have gone into this book with too high of expectations based off reviews and the description. 
 So far the characters, especially the main ones, are just so completely one sided. I cannot really understand either of their sudden attachment to one another at the beginning or Grace's way of just 'knowing' who Sam is. It's as if there is this great possibility of characterization and depth but the author just continuously skims the surface. 
 Furthermore, the time line of this book is confusing me so much, and the constantly changing perspective isn't helping at all. From the first few chapters on I got lost as to when exactly during the year this story was occurring, and now I am wondering if maybe more than 1 year passed between chapters without ever realizing it. I mean Sam saw Grace in the book store one chapter, but was a wolf the next time she saw him, then he was shot in September but doesn't remember if it was the summer of that same her he changed or the one before. 
 9.6.09 
 I just finished and I was totally trying to prepare myself for a horrible ending to this book up until the last second. 
 I finally got used to the temperatures being used as a time setting, and understood it a bit more. The plot picked up a lot more as the book continued thankfully although I was still hoping for a bit more depth in the characters. 
 All in all I think I will read the sequel just to see what happens, but I am sad that this book never really grabbed me like most books do. I knew I would finish it, but most of the time I will read until the dead of night or totally blow off doing my laundry if it means I can finish a book. Sadly enough this book just never hooked me like that. 
 The temperatures were a pretty inventive concept for moving time along, but not knowing Minnesota personally it is hard for me to match up the temperature with a time.

This book was okay, but I don't think I'll read it a second time. Also, I'm not sure if I'll finnish the series out either. The main character ,Grace (That's her name right?) I just could not connect with her in any way, shape, or form. She just seemed too uptight to the point where I was saying "Girl, you need to get that stick outta your butt!" 
 Also, I didn't really sense the chemistry between the two characters. I just kept waiting for a turning point in there relationship and it never seemed to happen.

3.3 stars. I don't know. This was like a slick hollywood film that is one of the studio's few "quality" films for the year, released in november so it's closer to awards season. I was certainly hooked by the plot, following the good guys through one close shave after the next, complete with flashbacks, tender moments, and even the occaisional light instant of humor before you're thrown back down into the infinite degradation of the post-apocalyptic hell-world. 
 I might have even given it 4 stars, except that every so often you have to put up with McCarthy deciding that he cannot just write a story, but simply must craft some arresting, ethereal prose for our benefit. Sadly, it sticks out like a sore thumb among the blood and guts surrounding it. It comes right off some dumb "ethereal-prose-crafting checklist":1. use a noun as a verb. 2. add "en-" to some noun to make a cool new verb. 3. have a character say something which no human being would ever, ever, ever say in the course of any conversation, ever. 
 viz., 
 1. "Borrowed time and borrowed world and borrowed eyes with which to sorrow it." 
 2. "Ten thousand dreams ensepulchred within their crozzled hearts." 
 3. a stressed-out woman actually says to her husband in the course of an argument: "A person who had no one would be well advised to cobble together some passable ghost. Breathe it into being and coax it along with words of love. Offer it each phantom crumb and shield it from harm with your body. As for me my only hope is eternal nothingness and I hope it with all my heart." i mean come on. 
 but it is a pretty good story. a page-turner.
A beautiful ode to the heroic nature of parenting (and canned food).

I am not quite finished with the book, but so far, I've found it an absolute masterpiece of modern literature. I got the audio book from the library, because I'd read so many comments about how readers were distracted by McCarthy's minimalist prose. If you are planning on reading this book and think that his style will bother you, I recommend the audio version. Tom Stechschulte reads it and does a wonderful job. 
 The book is dark. It is dark in a soul-wrenching way. I found myself tearing up at some of the simplest passages, because McCarthy taps into very real human emotion and thought. How many of us haven't wondered about a post-apocalyptic world? McCarthy makes it real and understandable, even if we don't know exactly how it happened, how many years it is post disaster, or even the characters names. It's easy to envision the gray world that McCarthy paints with his words. The contrasts of the two main characters makes for some interesting comparisons. The boy knows nothing but a post-apocalyptic world - the man remembers what once was and what's been lost. They have two opposite perspectives, and that sets the book up for real introspection. The rambling journey they take is as aimless and purposeless of a post-apocalyptic life. 
 There are some real moments of terror that might not be suitable for younger readers.

Ehh, it was okay, if I hadn't needed to have read it for school, I would've DNFed after the first forty pages. It wasn't really something I like to read in books though the last few pages were good but to get to that point... -_- 
 It was literally like a road, the book structure and just in general - flat and boring. It just went on and on and on and on of nothing. Okay, just a few hills were thrown in here and there to keep it interesting. But not much else besides walking and trying to find food and occasionally killing someone. 
 I know it's post apocalyptic, and not a world I would ever want to live in, but it's hard to connect to and even characterize characters with no names, barely any descriptions, and morals that are slightly askew. 
 I know I'm in the minority because my whole class loved it and it was one, huge, stupid, boring, chore for me to read. Like I said - last five pages: Great! Everything else...didn't hold my attention. 1.5 stars because of the last five pages.
Cormac McCarthy, the greatest living American writer, as far as I'm concerned.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I hate the way this book was written. A reviewer compared Cormac's writing style to a grocery list and I kind of agree. It's so dull I wanted to cry while reading it. I read on simply because some reviewers online said some of the details in the story would be shocking but cannibalism (on books) isn't exactly something new for me. Maybe if I read the book when I was younger, I would have loved it. I also hate the way the author ended the book.... It felt almost lazy to me. I just didn't find this book rewarding at all and regret buying it.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I know that a lot of people love this book and find it worthy of high minded literary praise. If that is you, that's ok we can just agree to disagree on this one. I am just going to list the things that I think are wrong with this book. I am guessing that some of these things might be why certain readers like it, but to my mind these things are lacking. 
 Things wrong with this book. 
 1.) There are no apostrophe marks in the words couldn't, didn't, wouldn't, shouldn't. Yet there ARE apostrophe marks in It's, They're and We're. I am sorry but if you have the guts to wipe out apostrophe marks in the first place, be bold enought to wipe them all out. 
 2.) I have never read a book with more flowery descriptions in as many ways as possible about what someone is eating. I couldn't count the number of times I had to read that the boy wiped bean juice off his chin and licked the can. It was the same basic description over and over and over. The food did change occasionally and then he licked the can of peaches instead. 
 3.) There are no names given besides papa and the boy. I get that it's not supposed to matter what their names are, we are supposed to care about the characters anyway. But I found it very hard to grow attached to someone whose name I don't know. How many friends do you have who you don't know their names? Would you care more that one whose name you didn't know got eaten by a cannibal or would you care more about the one that was eaten whose name you did know? Me too.
