 4.) We keep being told that things happened "before the world burned" but not enought to know what made it burn or how or why. I wanted an explanation and I don't think that is too much to ask for in a story. 
 5.) This is about the extent of the boy's dialougue. "Are we still the good guys papa? Okay." Oh, and I ADDED the quotation marks because apparently after the world burns another thing you lose besides random apostrophes is quotation marks. 
 6.) There are pages and pages and pages and pages and pages of nothing happening. I suppose you could argue this is what it might really be like after an apocalyptic event and that the day to day events might be dull. But that sure as hell doesn't mean I want to read about that part. Then there are short sections of something kind of exciting happening and then straight back to pitching a tent, maiking a fire, eating some food. 
 7.) If these two people could find enough food for themselves all this time, why does everyone else have to be a cannibal? That just plain didn't make sense. And is again where an EXPLANATION could have come in handy. 
 8.) The dad, far from being a heroic protector most of the time seemed to me to mostly be an idiot. He is constantly getting out the map but at the same time realizing he has no idea where he is. He perpetually leaves the kid alone, even when that is just stupid. He always runs from trouble which I understand but then doesn't seem to think very much before going into say an abandoned house and opening up a cellar. Idiot. 
 9.) After going through the whole plot, slogginly, slowly, wondering if anything of note will ever happen, the dad finally dies. I didn't really care that he died. But more irritating than that was that a page and a half later the "good guys" show up and rescue the boy. They also seem to indicate they had been following them for a while so why didn't they help the dad. 
 10.) Okay last one, the whole time I kept feeling like something had to happen to make this more interesting. It never did, it was just dull, dull, dull, dull, dull, dull.

Eh. Took me about a month to read this. Honestly, I was sort of uninterested. It MIGHT have been because I'd just finish playing the Last of Us. Quite frankly, I think that the story works better in video game form.

I'm about 50 pages in and don't like this book. I never like Oprah's book club selections though, so I'm not really suprised. Going to try to stick to it... 
 I finished the book (barely, and just because I HATE not to finish a book). I didn't like it. What can I say, I want to be entertained and uplifted. This book makes you think and I just wanted something to take my mind off of my troubles. If you want to cry/be depressed/worry about the future, this book is for you. If you want a good, entertaining read, then look elsewhere.

book_b.title: The Curiosity
book_b.user_review: Way too predictable. Doesn't challenge the reader enough.

sample_reviews.review_text: I am willing to accept for purposes of this book that a man flash frozen a century ago in Arctic ice has been reanimated by scientists. But, after accepting that, the characters and plot should proceed in a normal and logical fashion. There is something off about this novel that keeps it from seeming true to life. For instance, the scientists don't seem to follow scientific protocol. There appear to be only four or five employees in the whole big corporation. Despite the internet, no one does any research about the frozen man's life. Also, what the author shows about the frozen man's discovery of modern life is not very insightful. It really does not make one think. And, it is boring.

I finished this book, but it was not necessarily enjoyable. I read all the blurbs on the back cover from authors I really admire, so that in part explains why I kept going with it, but I found most of the narrators to be unbearably annoying (Kate) or reprehensible (Dixon). The end was alright, but in all I thought this was a good idea, just sloppy execution.

Though a debut novel, this is not Kiernan's first publication - and his polish definitely shows! He successfully juggles four perspectives - each written in their own distinct styles that nicely reflect the characters' disparate personalities. There's Dr. Kate Philo, the scientist/love interest, Dixon the old-school-reporter, Dr. Carthage the Pompous (his chapters are even written in the second-person to further augment his alienating and genuinely awful personality) and the Honorable Jeremiah Rice - originally born in 1886. What should be cheesy (after all, the entire book revolves around the reanimation of a man found frozen in a glacier for over a century!) never feels that way. The book - despite its science fiction-like premise - feels well-researched... and somehow, plausible. The story feels surprisingly fresh, too. 
 But despite the strength of the writing and the balance of perspectives, the overall plot drags a bit. The "great love story" never feels actualized and not that much really takes place. The book requires a certain suspension of disbelief, and the potential for the book to be more powerful definitely is there. Unfortunately, by the end, the books falls a little flat. I just want more than what is actually delivered.

In The Curiosity by Stephen R. Kiernan, Dr. Kate Philo is aboard a research vessel in the Arctic when a man is found frozen in an iceberg. Her mission had been to find small frozen life forms to bring back for testing rejuvenation techniques developed by a cutting-edge institute run by Erastus Carthage. While their successes had revived frozen krill and shrimp, there was no sense that it would work for such a large specimen. But to flinch from a groundbreaking task was not the way Carthage saw the world. 
 In addition to the journey of the frozen man through the world of scientific research, the book explores many ideas. Among them are: whether cryogenics is a successful plan for fatally ill people waiting for a cure; the ethical gray areas of whether a human can be considered property in scientific research; and whether the notion that we must let our deeds be our ambassadors does us service as a viable way to move through the world. (432 p.) 
 Highly recommended.

Actually 4.5/5 
 The Curiosity by Stephen Kiernan is not the type of book I would think to pick up or that I would enjoy, but I am very glad I did because I enjoyed it immensely. Kiernan is a brilliant writer and it is quite possible this literary thriller will be one of the most talked about books of the summer. Kiernan takes the reader through a full range of emotions as an Artic expedition team makes a find that could change scientific thinking and challenges each members of the team on varying levels both scientifically and morally. The curiosity is told through various voices allowing the reader a much deeper look into the "find" and to challenge the reader as well as keep the reader on their toes. I highly recommend The Curiosity by Stephen Kiernan, especially to book discussion groups, this choice will definitely keep the debates lively and running long.

The story of the reanimation of a man believed to have died in 1906 in the frozen arctic waters is a masterful combination of science thriller and love story. Told from four different perspectives; the journalist covering the story, the scientist who discovered the body in the ice, the egotistical genius at the head of the project and the reanimated man himself, Jeremiah Rice, this novel explores the very human side of science and those involved in its study. The voice of Jeremiah Rice is written with such a fine hand, giving the character the formality and substance that make him so believable as a man that has come from the early 20th century. His insight into modern day life is powerful without being preachy. Although the ending is foreshadowed at the beginning of the novel the path that takes you to that end is one that is filled with beautiful, thought-provoking style that keeps you turning the pages to the inevitable ending. "

I don't know if any of you have payed attention to this before, but see that last paragraph, the one just before this one, I normally don't include those when I'm typing up the synopsis. Partly because I find it to be part of an opinion by someone who is not me, rather than being an actual part of the synopsis. And partly because, it's just too much typing for me. I already take up more than my share of blog space, so why add to your reading. Of course there are those who have claimed I'm lazy for not writing my own, but quite frankly, I think my thoughts belong in the review itself. 
 But I'm digressing, so let me get back to the point I was trying to make to begin with. The reason why I chose to include that last paragraph, was pretty damn simple. I won't go as far as saying it's a big fat lie, but I will say it's a little grandiose for what the book actually read to me. I'm not sure where the thriller part comes in, unless they are talking about the last few pages where Kate and Jeremiah are running away from the paparazzi. And while I may agree that the book does touch on the themes of medical ethics, faith, what it means to be alive, and the state of our media driven culture; I can't say as if they seemed to be overarching themes that the author was trying to explore. Instead the felt as if they were a small part of the story, a story of a man brought back to life and those around him who for various reasons are trying to exploit him in one way or another. And it's a story of two people, who despite the obvious differences find themselves connecting in ways they didn't see coming, nor fully act upon that connection. 
 I don't want you guys to think I'm critiquing the book, because I'm not. The book itself, despite a slow start, was an engaging read that once it got a hold of me, I was hooked. I fell in love with Jeremiah. Of all the characters in the book, he was the one that felt the most real to me. He is one of those characters that had I a huge Edwardian country home, he would be a frequent guest. He was a man who came of age in a period of time where everything was new, where his contemporaries were exploring far flung lands and new inventions seemed to spring up all over the place. His was a time of true human expansion and progress was achieved by brave men and women who put their blood, sweat, and tears into everything they did. He was one of the youngest district court judges in history, and his intellect is one to be admired. Add in the fact that he is gorgeous, kind, and a truly good person, and you almost have the perfect man. And despite all that, he never seemed to be the stereotypical romantic hero, there was something grounded and real about him as a character. 
 I could go on and on about Kate as well, but at this point in time, I think I'm taking up way too much of your time already. She is the perfect instrument for Jeremiah to see this new world through. She is a truly interesting character, that while I may not have fallen for her in the way I did Jeremiah, I was never bored when it was her turn to tell the story. She had her own voice, and it was one that I found myself respecting and in many ways admiring. 
 My love affair with the character ends there though. The other two characters who narrate this story are one dimensional bores that I could have done without. Dr. Carthage is what he is described to be in the synopsis. There really isn't much more to say about him, other than I felt as if the whole reference to his father felt a little forced and seemed a bit out of place. The sleazy reporter, was like Dr. Carthage, a one dimensional character that despite his good nature, I never liked, and I just wanted him to shut up. And it's in how we get to know these character that I think this book did have one major flaw. 
 The book is told, after the events are already over, from the viewpoints of those four characters. So while I may have loved half of the chapters, the other half were just flat out annoying to read. I think this story, and these characters, would have been served better by having the story told by a third person narrator. It would have allowed more page time for the two characters I loved, but wouldn't have fragmented the story itself in such a way that I found myself annoyed with certain chapters and truly enjoying others. 
 My last quibble, and then I promise to shut up, I've been trying to convince myself to be happy with the ending, and I just can't be. It felt a little rushed, and despite some of the differences Kate has made in her life by then, it just doesn't satisfy me. I can't tell you what I wanted, without telling you what didn't happen, so I'm sorry about that. I didn't hate the ending, but I think I could have liked it so much better had it been closed a bit differently, though I think the actual end result would have been the same. And now that I'm done talking in circles, and if you are still reading at this point, please take the time to get this book. I'm almost positive, and while I won't name names, I'm pretty sure I know which of you would fall for Jeremiah just as hard as I did.

Hm. Engaging read, and I liked the alternating viewpoints. 
 Unfortunately, though, early on there is a description of Jeremiah and his big bushy sideburns. Which made me picture Wolverine. Which led to my mental casting of Hugh Jackman in the role. Which led, of course, to remembering that movie he was in several years ago with Meg Ryan- the one where she was a modern gal and he had travelled through time (I can't remember the name of it). It fit perfectly, especially all those scenes of Kate showing Jeremiah the modern world and his stiff, naive formality with everything, and because I thought that movie was so silly, it made this story feel a little silly, too. So there you have it.

Halfway through I was thinking, Get on with it already! I read the end of each chapter because I got really bored. My major complaint....we keep getting told that Kate is a super genius, but we never see her being genius-y.

A brilliant page turner of a book that questions the boundaries of science, the essence of humanity, and the tenderness of memory. I hardly know how to categorize this book as it combines so many genres - science fiction, literary fiction, and part thriller and love story. Book clubs will find much to discuss in this updated "Frankenstein" story. There is currently so much media attention on the anti-science activities of the Christian right that this book is sure to generate a hot debate about bio-ethics and the quest for scientific knowledge. 
 The multiple narrative style of the story is absolutely riveting as each chapter peels back another layer of the story and the truth is finally revealed. In THE CURIOSITY, the reader finds that the past often reveals the mysteries of the future and that love has no scientific measure. 
 This well crafted novel is a definite "must buy" for any serious bibliophile.

reference_books.title: The Burning Sky (The Elemental Trilogy, #1)
reference_books.review_text: SO I didn't immediately love this book. If anything I found myself put off by the writing, the setting and the slow pacing. I was not immediately gripped about the characters, if anything I was a bit indifferent to them. I gradually began to enjoy the book, but again I was not enthralled. Then I got to the last quarter and I was fully absorbed and could appreciate why this book is so highly rated. I only wish I had picked it up sooner

reference_books.title: A Little Something Different
reference_books.review_text:
This book was everything I wanted it to be. It was sweet and it was simple. There were romance without it being ridiculous, it was cute and sweet without being cloying and it represented people in a very real way. 
 I think I related to this book a lot becasue the characters are shy and you got that and it was nice. It was endearing but also showed how debilitating shyness can be at times and how it can stop you from being more. There was just something great about it. 
 I admit that the different view points often made this book feel like it was something done for a school assignment. An author showing their ability to write in different voices and show different perspectives of the same events. I enjoyed it, but it did get to you atimes as narratives switched. It worked in this book but it's certainly not something you would want all the time, but maybe that is what made this book so good, it was different.

reference_books.title: The Coldest Girl in Coldtown
reference_books.review_text:
I loved this and I don't know why I always wait to read books I'm obviously going to enjoy. This book did an excellent job of being a love letter to the vampire genre without romanticising vampires too much. It was a sharp dose of reality about vampires a lot of the time and didn't fall into the Twilight trap. This is the book I'd want to give to teenage girls thinking of reading Twilight. 
 It is an excellent YA book but I'd expect no less from Hollu Black. More importantly it's a good book outside of the YA genre. It hooked practically from the start and I was constantly thinking about reading. It reminded me that I don't read anywhere near enough vampire or paranormal books and that it's not hard to make me fall in love with secondary characters.

reference_books.title: The Cuckoo's Calling (Cormoran Strike, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I probably reread this far too a on after watching the BBC adaptation so I knew the majority of twists and turns anyway. I enjoyed reading this again though. It was a good mystery and I was totally hooked even knowing what was happening which is a sign of a good mystery. I would expect no less though really.

reference_books.title: Thief's Magic (Millennium’s Rule, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I wasn't sure what to expect going into this book. Canavan wrote another series I've been dying to read, so I knew when I saw this on offer on Book Depository I had to give it a chance, but it was still an author I had no experience with. 
 The premise is quite original, a book that used to be a person talking to whoever holds it? A girl who has magic but is terrified to use it in fear of offending the angels? This all sounded like a story that could get confusing or be really awesome. Thankfully I enjoyed it. 
 The writing was excellent, although sometimes I got a bit confused with the detail and lengthy descriptions or the more specific detailed things which happened, but I think that was more my attention span than anything else. I also wished for a map during a lot of the travelling, I couldn't grasp what was happening, I normally welcome the inclusion of a world map in fantasy novels, but this had none. I think I can guess as to why it didn't, but still it would have been nice. 
 I am not normally a huge fan of switching stories within the book, where you follow multiple characters lives, I find myself growing more attached to one character's story than the other. This wasn't the case with Thief's Magic, instead I'd find myself fully involved with both, and whilst when the story switched character I was still a little hung up on the other's story, I could easily get back into the story for the other. This shows how good Canavan is at both her story development, but at writing the characters themselves. I think if I hadn't become so attached to them when they were first introduced this wouldn't have been the case. I think it helped that initially you spent several chapters with either Tyen or Rielle before the story shift, it was only later on you got more frequent switching. That was smart of Canavan because it meant the she had plenty of time to develop the story to begun with, and then at the end as the pacing increased so did the perspective switch. 
 As a whole, I really enjoyed the book. I wanted to give it 5 stars, but there is something holding me back from giving it. I loved the story, but it isn't the crazed love I get from some books. I'm convinced that is because I'm holding out for the rest of the series being just as good. There is every chance once I've read it all my rating could change. I think the fact there is still so much story left untold is what prevents me from giving it that extra star, and there is nothing that can be done about that except wait for the next book in the series.

book_a.title: Attachments
book_a.user_review:
This book is difficult for me to review. I enjoyed it, don't get me wrong, but it was very much a slow build book, which is something Rainbow Rowell is wonderful at. She really builds up the characters, slowly develops relationships. Allows characters to slowly grow, age, develop in such a real and fantastic way. And that is probably why this book got a 4-star rating off of me. That, and the actual premise of the book, this guy falling in love with someone based simply off of the words that she has written, is just so unique and wonderful. 
 From the premise I was so ready to fall in love with this book and devour it in a day, just as I have with so many other books. But that just did not happen. I really struggled to be gripped by the characters' struggles. I liked everyone in the book, but I didn't love them. I was interested in their stories, but I wasn't gripped by them. And I wanted to know what was going to happen, but honestly, I was only interested, and was almost prepared to google and find out the ending. It was that kind of book. 
 I think maybe the storyline and character development was a bit too slow for my liking. It just didn't happen quite as quickly as I wanted. And honestly, I didn't see how it was going to work out. After such a huge breach of privacy at the start, how were they ever expected to comeback from that and form an actual working relationship? I don't know. Maybe I'm taking it too far and being far too practical, but that was something that continually nagged at me and probably contributed to some of my struggle with my book. I just found it too difficult to believe, and that's a difficult thing to overcome when you're reading anything.

sample_reviews.review_text:
All the feels, man. 
 This book should be creepy, and in places it was, but the characters were so charming and well-formed that it wasn't hard to forgive them their really weird intrusive behavior. 
 Also, funny. 
 (Second read) STILL AMAZING.

I feel like many people probably thought this was romantic, but it wasn't to me. Honestly I would have abandoned it if I hadn't been hoping for a last minute tone change. The premise was stalkerish and creepy. It would have been a better idea for a thriller or horror story. Several times I was shivering and thinking, surely the stalker stuff will be addressed? 
 Nope. I can only hope or think that this is a first novel, with all the pitfalls such things can have. I decided to read it after I read another thing I really loved by this author and wanted to see her debut book. I guess people are complicated, and can change. The newer things by this author were good and interesting but this still gives me the shivers.
Boring. At least not for a grown up.

This is one of my favorite books of all time. 
 If you like Rainbow Rowell you will LOVE this. It's so Rainbow it hurts, but in the best way possible. 
 I read this back in July but just now realized I never actually wrote a review. 
 This is such a feel good book and it describes romance and relationships in such an honest way. I love the narrative and adore every character. It's very rare when I actually enjoy reading a characters inner thoughts, because sometimes they are just so unbelievable, but these characters are very human and it's such a fresh experience. 
 I would reread this book all the time if I could.

[SPOILERS] 
 I can't believe Lincoln barely got any crap for his gross invasion of privacy and even got the girl he liked in the end. It felt creepy and unsatisfying to see him just get away with it. This is a romance book but I ended up rooting against Lincoln and definitely not shipping him with anyone.
Sweet and charming summer read

** spoiler alert ** 
 This book bothered me a bit. It was fine while I was reading it, though I admit that Lincoln's character hit a little too close to home in some ways - but I was very very very frustrated with the ending. Like, it's okay that you've been cyber stalking me & stalking my ex-boyfriend and you are obsessive and kind of a weirdo with no friends, because you are cute, so we can get married! yay the end. 
 I much preferred the other two works I've read by Rowell (fangirl and eleanor & park) - while not necessarily realistic, they felt much more plausible and only slightly less wish-fulfillment-y than this.
Cute.
une histoire sympa mais un peu trop chick lit pour moi. la legerete fait du bien quand meme!

I love Rainbow Rowell's YA books. 
 Eleanor & Park 
 Fangirl 
 Carry On 
 Love, love, love! 
 I tolerate Rainbow Rowell's adult contemporary romance books. 
 Landline 
 and now my completion of the Rowell library, Attachments. 
 The characters are a little juvenile and the protagonists unrealized view of himself is more fitting for a 15 or 16 year-old, not a fully grown adult. 
 Stick with teenagers, Rainbow. 
 Story: 3 stars 
 Character Dev: 2 stars 
 Prose/Language: 3 stars

book_b.title: The Perks of Being a Wallflower
book_b.user_review:
I had high expectations for this book. I think it's because of that I'm left feeling a bit disappointed now that I've finished it. It was good, I defenitely enjoyed it, that I cannot deny. It wasn't amazing though. Maybe it's because I'm British and now 21 and so it is a bit more difficult to relate to Charlie and everything he experienced. Maybe it's because everytime Charlie cried I was just left a bit confused because mostly he sounded like a little girl I wanted to smack upside the head and tell to grow a pair. I don't know, but something just didn't click for me with this book. 
 At the same time I finished the book in a twenty-four hour period so I definitely didn't hate it or anything, it's not like I can claim I didn't enjoy reading, I just found it difficult to relate to. I didn't finish the book and have that satisfied feeling of finishing a great book. 
 I think it's a book that people should read, it's a decent read, but I think my reading of it was marred by expectations. Don't go in with any proconceived notions of what the book is a bout and you'll be fine.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This book was a quick read, but it felt very much like an after school special gone wrong. The main character was likeable at times, but he often acted/thought/wrote like a 10 or 11 year old instead of a freshman in high school. The author puts this very young character through some really horrible things. The book deals with some very mature subject matter including rape, abortion, suicide, homosexual encounters, drug use, and even pedophilia. This was a book that left me feeling the need to take a shower once I had finished it. I was glad it was a quick read, but I still regret wasting even a couple of hours on it. 
 Just an example of the ick factor for me: the main character learns about masturbation at one point in the book and describes his experience. I could have done without that (and a lot of other things in this book).
Definitely not what I was expecting when I read this book. There were some great lines.
infinitely good!!

By reading this book, I wish I would like it more than I actually did. In fact, I saw the movie last year and I quite liked it, but I didn't expect this book to be the way it was, especially written exclusively with letters (which I got used to with time). 
 Also, there are so details that disturbed me, and things in Charlie's behaviour that made me confused. But it was still a quick and entertaining reading. 
 Of course, I am going to watch the movie adaptation again soon!

** spoiler alert ** 
 Its taken me a long time to write a review for this book and this is mostly because I have a very unpopular opinion about it. This book has such cult following and a hype surrounding it that I felt a peer pressure to read it. Do you know what I mean? Its like when someone says they've never watched The Breakfast Club or Ferris Bueller's Day Off and you all give that person the side eye and crazy look cause they are like generational shaping classics. Anyways I felt compelled that I read this book before the end of 2016 since this year has been fantastic for me in terms of my reading, reviewing and activeness on Goodreads. 
 I went into this book not knowing anything about it expect how life changing it was suppose to be but the thing I just hated about it was that it was soooooo pretentious. It is a novel written all in journal form and it talked about all the mundane things that happen in the life of 15 year old Charlie during 1991 to 1992. These letters were all observations of events in Charlie's life in his first year of high school and I felt like some of these observations weren't written well enough to be understood. He would use flowery prose to talk about or describe a tree or a car ride through a tunnel. Talking about how it felt infinite. Other times he will be talking about things at home and then he is at a party and then he is lying in the snow outside and at the end of the chapter he is like "Im never taking LSD again". WTF when did that happen? Supposedly he got it from a guy named Bob but were not introduced to Bob until page 142 which is after the event mentioned above. Things like this irritate me cause the plot could have been straightforward but the author chose to complicate it unnecessarily. 
 Charlie as a character seemed like a nice person but his total lack of knowing wrong from right was infuriating. The kids that came into his room during a party his brother was having where the guy raped the girl and he saw the whole thing but never said anything is disturbing. The guy that hit his sister and he saw it and only told a teacher when said teacher asked how his weekend went like it something that needed to be checked off on a to-do-list is not normal. Now its implied that Charlie had some mental instability but we don't know what his condition was. We know that he goes to a psychiatrist and takes medication but this story is trying to pass this stuff off as teenage awkwardness instead of a mental health issue. If the author wanted to write a book about mental health than he should have just done one and done it tastefully. 
 The only thing that I found interesting in this book was the quote " We accept the love we think we deserve". This I thought was thought provoking. Other than that I didn't find this book life changing at all and I feel like it puts contemporary books in a bad light. Just random drivel for 200+ pages and with a holier than though feel. This totally reminded me of those books your teacher in school would make you read for English because it was part of the course syllabus and you asked yourself how on Earth did this get to be part of the curriculum. This book has left a sour taste in my mouth for the genre and I may take a break from it for a bit to recuperate. 
 P.S. I did watch the movie after I read this book to see if things were better explained and/or flushed out now that the author/director had a different medium to try and express this supposedly life changing work but it still missed the mark. I think it missed it even further because it didn't show all the drug use Charlie was doing. The scene I was describing with the LSD happened in the movie as he was taking a wafer from the priest in mass. This was strange because if you'd never read the book then, based of the movie , you would have never thought Charlie would try recreational drugs. Then with Charlie accepting the wafer and laying it on his tongue you get transported to this party with flashing lights and heavy music. I almost thought the priest had given it to him. This convolution happens when artistry tries to supersede storytelling. Examples of beautiful artistry with fantastic storytelling: Romeo and Juliet (1996) directed by Baz Luhrmann and Upside Down (2012) by Juan Solanas. Both of theses movies were quirky and unique in their own way and managed to use flowery prose without losing the story being told. None of the writing in either was unnecessary and both conveyed a message that was important and could be understood. 
 P.P.S. adding this part in Jan 3 2017. Today I learned how to use the link function on Goodreads. So I wanted to use it to link to a great review from another book lover who also gave it a 1 star rating but gave additional points I didn't mention in my own review.

I know that lots of people love this book. I understand why they do. It made me angry. When I got to the end, I closed the book and was just mad that I read it. I am not doing a longer more thorough review because to talk about the specifics of why I hated it would ruin the reading experience for others and I don't want to do that.
I don't know why but I just couldn't get into this book. The boy its about is suppose to be 15 but I felt like he was much younger. I think someone else might enjoy the book but I just didn't.

I thought it was a very intriguing writing style and a very well written book. I had issues really connecting with the characters but discussing it with my mom and sister helped me appreciate the book more. Mostly how traumatic events really do shape people. I also enjoyed how the family dynamics really impacted people and it made me so grateful for my family.

I really wish i hadn't just got round to reading this book now, and wish i had found it before the film was even beginning to be discussed. I think the fact that i have already seen the film before reading this (i only ended up watching the film a couple of weeks ago- i was extremely late to the party) ruined it a bit for me, as reading something without knowing anything is a massive part of the reading experience, but i already knew how the story turned out, so it did ruin it a bit for me. 
 Nonetheless, this is a brilliant book. Books written through letters have always interested me and the writing style instantly pulls you into the story. Although i already knew the characters and the story, i still found myself being drawn into it the same way as if i didn't and i become unable to put the book down (shown in how i finished it a day after i started- something unusual for me), needing to know everything the book had to offer as quickly as i possibly could. I do not feel like i need to persuade people to pick this book up, as i'm sure the majority of people have already done so, like i said, i'm extremely late to the party. However, i do have to say how this book spoke to me in such a beautiful way, i really related to the characters and (some) of their issues and i believe this book to really connect with people who are wallflowers. Although there are many of "coming of age" books out there, i think this one peaks right at the top with how honest and brilliant it is. A must read for teens out there who can relate to introverted, socially awkward Charlie.

reference_books.title: Presumed Innocent
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 What a mess. It was unnecessarily racist, and unjustifiably long. 
 I opened this book expecting to be gripped, suprised, and excited. Instead, I was disppointed. 
 It was a far too long blow-by-blow account of unimportant details. I guess who the killer was halfway through the book, and it somehow managed to further disappoint me, in the process of revealing the killer to me at the end. 
 I'm not even sure whether or not I should go into the mess of a sub-plot. Becuase the killer is, suprise surpise, his wife, and because he wanted to avoid having to end with her confessing her crime to the courtroom, Turow decided to end the trial abruplty, through the use of that infamous 'B-file'. Judge Larren was once involved in bribery, and through fear of all of his dirt being brought to light in the courtroom, he dismisses the trial, and sets dusty free. No one cared in the slighest. Practically every one knew, but not one single character cared. Why, then should I have cared? I didn't. It was sloppy tactic. It's as if Scott Turow sat at his desk scratching away with his pencil in a 'got to have a twist, got to have a twist' frenzy, and was prepared to jot down ANYTHING, to deliver that god damned twist. 
 I can't remember being gripped by the story, once, and the highest point, was the second to last trial. 
 I gave it two stars instead of one, because although a drag it's written well (linguistically), and the facts pumped behind all of the law, and forensics, were interesting (if you like that sort of thing). 
 All in all, it was nothing out of the ordinary, and am quite miffed that the reviews on the back claimed that this book would take over my life for a while. Maybe I should be blaming them.

reference_books.title: Beloved
reference_books.review_text: This one wasn't for me. I just couldn't get into the story.

reference_books.title: An Abundance of Katherines
reference_books.review_text:
I can't finish this book. Torture. 
 I'm done.

reference_books.title: Paper Towns
reference_books.review_text:
I had such goddamned high hopes for this title, purely because it is from the same man who gave me 'Looking For Alaska', and for a short while, this made him god. I must say, I was sorely disappointed with it; it's almost as if John Green took everything that made LFA incredible and mangled it. 
 Paper Towns is the story of teenage Quentin named 'Q' by his friends Radar and Ben, Lacey and Margo Roth Spiegleman. They all have stupidly grating names. The story itself comprises of three parts, the first of which sees Q and Margo set off on a short, mischevious adventure, presumably for the purpose of highlighting the depth of their relationship and to give us a sense of why Q loves her so much. It doesn't. After this all-nighter, Margo rushes off and disappears, quite abruplty, and the rest of the story focuses on Q's plight to discover her whereabouts, for he fears that she is dead. He locates her by rounding up a host of enigmatic clues, he believes she has left for him, and these clues take him on various road trips across the Eastern states of America - mainly on school nights. 
 Q seems to be the only one who cares very much about the fact that Margo is missing, and his search to find her is bordering what it means to be 'obsessive'. There are times where he is angry at his friends, his best friends, for not dropping everything and their lives to help him pursue this girl he's infatuated with, and I couldn't, for the life of me figure out why he would expect them to. 
 Paper Towns is an incredibly over-thought, overly metaphorically indulged 'mystery', which lacks suspense, a legitimate plot and intellence, which makes it not much of a mystery at all. It tries ridiculously hard to live up to the legacy of 'Looking For Alaska' and where lacking in plot, is soiled with paragraph after paragraph of John Green trying to draw emotional relevance out of every tiny thing imaginable. The language is corny and the character interactions, at times, unforgivably embarrassing to read. 
 I had high hopes for Looking for Margo, sorry, Paper Towns and it's an awful shame that it did nothing but deflate me. I understand what John Green was trying to achieve but unfortanetely, he picked the wrong set-up and he picked the wrong crowd.

reference_books.title: The Hunger Games (The Hunger Games, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I'm never going to finish this.

book_a.title: The Island
book_a.user_review: Got abut 50 pages in and I just couldn't continue this one. The writing style isn't for me.

sample_reviews.review_text: Through three women's generations, we discover the life of a community of sick people affected by the leprosy exiled on the island of Spinalonga in Crete.

I adore Greece so this novel being set on Crete and the leper colony of Spinalonga (where I've visited) appealed to me. It's the story of Anna and Maria, their parents and eventually husbands and significant others. It was a historical read in part, with world events happening and the island of Crete and Spinalonga's reaction to them. It's a multi-generational tale told from multiply points of view, which did get confusing at times. I did enjoy the book but felt I didn't know the characters quite as well as I could have and the last part of the book felt rushed. I would have liked to have seen a little more of Maria and Anna's father and some loose ends tied up with Manoli. It held my interest, for the most part, and the descriptions of Crete brought the setting to life.

Interesting story, especially the history of the leper colony on Spinalonga. Something about the writing style that I just didn't get on with, though I can't put my finger on what it is. An enjoyable book, but for me, not a page turner.

I am a Victoria Hislop fan and I do think this is her best novel. 
 When I read The Island - I was moved by the struggle of the Cretans during the German occupation. I found it well researched with powerful descriptions of leprosy and the discrimination, illness and prejudice that came with it. 
 Her writing style appears effortless. It's well structured and behind it all is the moral that things will come right in the end which is always uplifting and a positive way to end a novel. 
 For me Spinalonga became a place that I would like to visit and it is now on my list. I will imagine being transported there, as an outcast...

The story of Spinalonga, an island off the coast of Crete, that was used as a leper colony from 1903-1957. The novel follows the Petrakis family. Eleni Petrakis was sent to Spinalonga in 1939, leaving behind her husband and two daughters. One of the daughters, Maria, was also sent in 1951. Even through tragedy, the family perseveres.
One of the most poignant books I have read. It is profoundly moving, especially if you ever sit in a restaurant in Plaka, looking at the former leper colony.

A very interesting backdrop for a story (leper colony off the coast of Greece) but I did not care for the writing style. Way too simplistic for me. I felt like I was reading a book written at the 4th grade level and kept hoping for more dialogue for some point of interest, but it was rare, and even that wasn't good.

So badly written and predictable. The only reason I gave it two stars was because I found the setting and the time period interesting, the characters were very black and white ( good or bad) and I only finished this book because I was reading it for my book group. Not a good book for a book group as it is seriously lacking in anything interesting we can talk about. Really disappointing.

I just couldn't get into this at all. The prose is awfully breathless and romantic, in a way which borders on parody - except it's a parody without any jokes. 
 After about sixty pages I was forced to conclude this wasn't a book for me.

** spoiler alert ** 
 If this were made into a movie it might look a bit like Titanic, with its book-ends structure, and the old woman relaying a sad tale through romanticised lenses to a younger person who's new on the scene. 
 I liked the bits about the lepers. Every time someone was struck down with leprosy I sat up a bit straighter, hoping for some sort of insight into what it's really like to be afflicted with such a terrible disease and ostricised from friends and family. But the author's choice to write in distant omniscient third person meant I never really learnt what that feels like. 
 This is meant to be a quick read, so everything is given to us on a plate. It's one of those books where we're not painted a scene and left to work things out for ourselves; we're given both the scene and the narrator's judgement on it. 
 I found the judgement of Anna particularly harsh. The contrast of two sisters, one good, one bad, was too reminiscent of fairy-telling to offer much to the thinking adult reader. I found Anna the more interesting of the two. Maria was a hopeless, doe-eyed wet-dream of a character. The image of the beautiful, pious, meek and obedient Maria, standing on the shores of that island looking at the doctor will stay with me as an especially overdone romantic cliche. (In my mind there is wind. Blowing. Through her silky but unpretentiously adorned hair.) 
 I was feeling more positive about this book until after she got shot by her husband in a fit of (completely out-of-character) rage. When a fictional character stews on something and then acts like a mad person for five minutes it doesn't work. Well, authors do it, but it's been done so many times before. I'm not a huge fan of such melodrama. 
 These days I find it harder and harder to enjoy a light-hearted story about women who are basically chattels, as Cretan women were in those days. As I blossom into a curmudgeonly middle-aged woman, I frequently need to remind myself that we can't rewrite history; that's how things really were, and some women must've been happy, so why not write about them? But I got increasingly frustrated with this narrator. On page 426 she took the cake with the bit about what Giorgis was thinking after his daughter was murdered by her husband for sleeping with the husband's cousin: 'Though [Giorgis] wanted justice for Anna, he was never in any doubt that it was his daughter's behaviour that had triggered Andreas's violent reaction.' 
 Having recently read a book by Geraldine Brooks, this statement was far too reminiscent of the honor killings that still take place around this sorry world, and I felt pissed off that this book forms a sort of endorsement. The not-so-subtext message is: 'Well, you'll have to go to prison if you shoot your wife dead, but it's completely understandable that you killed her. After all, she was having sex with another *man*!!!!! That's YOUR honor she's taken off with, right there!!!!' 
 I hate that shit. 
 Yet many, many readers do so love this book. My mother borrowed someone else's copy on a cruise. She liked the story so much that she kindly bought a new copy and sent it straight to me, which is why I made it all the way to page 426 in the first place.

book_b.title: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (Harry Potter, #3)
book_b.user_review: Probably the one I enjoyed the most as a child. (Note, my rating is of how much I enjoyed it about 12 years ago).

sample_reviews.review_text: My favorite HP book forever!

A wizard criminal named Sirius Black has escaped from the top-security prison, Azkaban, and all signs point to him targeting Harry Potter. The soul-sucking guardians of the prison, the Dementors, are installed at Hogwarts to protect the students, but they're much more of a disruption than a comfort. Harry, Hermione, and Ron experience speed bumps in their friendship due to squabbles over whether Hermione's cat ate Ron's rat and Hermione reporting a mysterious gift that Harry received (presumably for his own protection). But the trio are all united in trying to save Buckbeak, Hagrid's hippogriff, who is due to be executed because he hurt a nasty student who provoked him. But when Ron's rat does turn out to be somewhere--and someONE--that he'd never suspected, other old friends come out of the woodwork, including Sirius Black himself. But exactly whose side is Sirius on--and who are his allies? It could very well be that Harry may finally learn a few things about his family. 
 The Dementors are a horrifying idea. They were expertly handled as an eerie presence in the book, though I had trouble imagining any grand wizarding society would accept their widespread use for the cause of order when they can suck people's souls out. I liked the switcharoo of loyalties and the way the characters' pets figured in, but I again got frustrated at how nobody tells Harry anything for the sake of a nifty reveal at the end. The red herrings are kind of out of control sometimes.

This book is magical. Joanne's writing and style is amazing 
 she's an awesome writer , each page fits perfectly with the others, it is like everything was thought perfectly. the plot you know, is like OMG, incredibly, the growth characters and the time travel part.. we see our characters older and how they start thinking more like as an adult, hermione being so smart and nice, in this book you find love, emotions, wisdom, action and a huge plot. Harry Potter is just wonderful, once you start reading you can't stop and you want to live in there, being in Hogwarts and stuff. Haha :') 
 No doubt, This is one of my favourite books of the series if it is not my favourite.
The Harry Potter series is beginning to grow on me. In this book the reader is introduced to Sirius Black, and more layers are added to the story.
Awesome!

I love the scene in the shack when Sirius reveals himself and forces Peter Pettigrew to do the same. Rowling at her very, very best. I was very disappointed when the film version glossed over this scene in about 2 minutes.
Expecto patronum! This is the first one that makes me weepy!

I found myself getting really annoyed with Harry's "special one" treatment in this book. I get that he's the main character and he has to be special, but everyone treats him like he's the Second Coming, and it started to get old in this book. I actually thought Snape made some good points, that Harry thinks he can get away with anything and the rules don't apply to him. It's totally true. Even Dumbledore makes a fool of Snape in front of Harry. It seemed very unprofessional of him to me. If he doesn't want Snape teaching there, he shouldn't have hired him! I really didn't like how everyone catered to Harry, and how, yet again, Harry manages to ditch his friends to be the lone hero and defeat the bad guys all by himself at the end. It would be nice if his friends could contribute to the climactic fight scene in ONE of the books and show some themes about friendship and such. Just my two cents. I didn't love this one at all.

Como fallos, lo mismo que el anterior: sigue volviendo a explicar cosas que ya sabemos y abusa de la exageracion para enfatizar emociones. 
 Sin embargo la trama ha ganado mucha complejidad y me parece increible como J.K. Rowling ha creado una historia tan redonda. Por ahora es el libro que mas me ha gustado de la saga.
So far my favorite of the series. J. K. Rowling really fleshes out the whole wizardry world and manages to address some politically and morally relevant issues at the same time.

reference_books.title: The Haunting of Sunshine Girl (The Haunting of Sunshine Girl, #1)
reference_books.review_text: This is the first time I have ever read a book based on a YouTube web series but I have to say that it works in print just as much as it did on video. Sunshine and her mother are relocated from sunny Austin to the dreary damp Northwest as her mom begins a new position at a hospital. Sunshine's first reaction to the house they are renting is that it is creepy which her mom dismisses along with her daughter's photos and evidence of a ghost. After some pretty shocking surprises and items in her room being moved, Sunshine does find a fellow ghost hunter in Nolan a boy she meets at school. Turns out that Sunshine might be a bit of a ghost whisperer. Together they must find out who the ghost is, what does she want and what is going on with Sunshine's mom? For fans of classic ghost stories, this one will have you leaving the lights on and having a sudden urge to play Monopoly.

reference_books.title: Hungry
reference_books.review_text: Imagine a world where food is a fond memory - except one day Thalia hears a strange sound. It is her stomach gurgling and suddenly the protein she drinks every day doesn't satisfy the hunger. Her grandmother applauds her rebel spirit but the rest of the family doesn't understand her love of all things retro from her clothes to her attention to the relics of the past. This story gives a whole new meaning to "Hunger Games" and will delight fans of dystopic world-gone-wrong thrillers.

reference_books.title: The Dog Stars
reference_books.review_text: I enjoyed the storyline but the format it is written in made the book not work for me. The world is messed up and almost everyone has died from a horrible flu. Hig is living out in the middle of nowhere with one other guy whom he really doesn't trust not to shoot him in the back one of these days. Hig is very useful because he can fly his plane around and survey the area to alert the two of them against intruders. He will meet a woman who will change his view of this new world and give him hope for the future. The book is written in short journalistic passages which work considering the starkness of this future world and the grimness of their situation but I felt it did not make it easy to read.

reference_books.title: Red Rain
reference_books.review_text: Just in time for Halloween R.L. Stine gives adults a real scare in his new book, Red Rain. A nice couple living in the northeast has to deal with a not so nice addition to the family when the wife, an adventure travel writer, goes down to a voodoo island off the coast of South Carolina only to find herself in the middle of a horrible hurricane that wipes out the entire island. She is traumatized by the destruction and adopts twin boys whom she sees walking alone along the beach. Her husband, a child psychologist and writer, along with the son and daughter at home do not share her glee at the new additions but try to adjust for her sake. The twins have a very old fashioned air about them in their mannerisms and speech and try to charm those around them. When that fails they have others ways to "rule the school" and their new home. This will keep you up at night and make you study your kid's friends.

reference_books.title: Every Heart a Doorway (Wayward Children, #1)
reference_books.review_text: This book forces you to think differently about kids who don't fit in. Eleanor West's Home for Wayward Children is a front for a place where kids who have fallen down the rabbit hole and come back can fit in. Ms. West was once one of these kids and now pretends to "straighten" out wayward kids but really she tries to help them understand the world they find themselves in. It doesn't matter what gender you are , your social skills or pedigree , at the home everyone is welcome and left to find their way. Nancy is one of these kids after coming back from the land of the dead and finding the world of the living less than satisfactory. Soon after Nancy arrives at the school her classmates begin to be murdered and it is left to the kids to find the killer before the killer finds them. I enjoyed the first part of the story and would have liked a smoother segue to the second half and the murders. The diverse cast of characters really makes this story unique. My thanks to the publisher for the advance copy.

book_a.title: And Every Morning the Way Home Gets Longer and Longer
book_a.user_review: Fredrik Backman is magical and he takes ordinary characters that we would pass on the street and shares their thoughts, hopes and dreams with us. Such is this new novella where a grandfather sits trying to make sense of his last days and searching for a way to explain it to his grandson. The days get more confusing for him and we see how the faces blur as he forgets if it is his grandson or his son sitting next to him. He also tries to make sense of where things went wrong with his relationship to his son and so right with his grandson. We get all the emotion, confusion and love of a life well lived and the desire to get it right. Thank you, Mr. Backman for getting it right. My thanks to the publisher for the advance copy.

sample_reviews.review_text:
i love fredrik backman. like....a lot. this novella did NOT do it for me. missing were the quirks of his longer novels. missing is the beauty of his writing. the humor, the nuance. 
 to me, this book was random and really just sappy.

This may be a short novella, but the impact is tremendous. Told through the eyes of his "numbers" grandpa, a little boy - Noah, who is more like his grandfather than his own "words" father Ted, learns the stories and fears of holding on to life's most precious memories. How the square is getting smaller and smaller and how Grandpa's family is both struggling to hold on to help him and to gently guide and let go at the same time. 
 The way home does not talk specifically about a place, but more of the comfort and memories that home entails. It is the people and the places. The stories and memories. The things that get lost over time and yet we try harder and harder to hold on to. 
 This is a story of compassion - surprising compassion from the most unlikely person. Sometimes we are too close to our own parents and it takes a grandchild to see through the blurred frustration that parents and children hold on to. The next generation is more open and willing to sit and listen to the stories and see both the hope and lament that is just below the surface. 
 As I said, this is a short novella that reads like a full-blown novel. Fredrik Backman is a master storyteller that knows just the right amounts to include without bogging down the reader with unnecessary drivel. The reader knows the amount of time that has passed and how the relationship between Noah and Grandpa has changed without going in depth with timekeeping and medical analyses. This book is not about a disease, it is about relationships, compassion, and wanting to spend as much time with a person that you love no matter what you are talking about or how many rocks you have to put under an anchor so you can always remember a child as a child. 
 I have underlined so much in this story that out of fear of quoting the whole book, I have not including any quotes. You will want to keep this novella close so you can read it frequently and I will guarantee that each time you do, you will get something different from the telling and take away a better understanding.
Beautiful short story about love

This is really a short story - very quick read. I am a seriously cynical person and was worried I would hate this story. I pretty much did, but I thought the author's vision of the inside of the mind of someone suffering from Alzheimer's disease was clever.

Actual rating: 4.5 stars 
 A sweet, thought provoking novella about a grandfather living with Alzheimer's. The story really hit close to home for me. Especially when the grandfather says; "No, sometimes I remember that I've forgotten. That's the worst kind of forgetting." As someone who has endured brain damage, I can concur with that statement. He described it as being locked out in a storm. I'm not stuck outside in raging weather. It's nice outside; I've simply misplaced my key. 
 It's heartbreaking to see someone you love slip away from you and Backman really shows that in his writing. It's sadder still when you know Backman has endured this loss. 
 Going from the square to the real world was jarring. I understand it's from the perspective of a man with Alzheimer's and it makes complete sense why it was written that way. It makes the story believable and all the more heartbreaking. It was just tough to read from my perspective; which is why I took off a half star.
This tiny little book will absolutely break your heart. It's beautifully written and moving. A story full of grief and love. There is so much said in so few pages.

I had to clean the muck out of my mind after the last junky book I read so I turned to this novella by Fredrik Backman. This book, which had less than 90 pages and took only an hour or so to read, had me sobbing through all it's beautiful, heartbreaking emotion. Even in such a short little book, the author manages to perfectly develop his characters and clearly and gorgeously define their relationships. Such a touching work of writing. Grabbed it on impulse at the library - will be purchasing a copy to keep for myself.
A short story that proves that sometimes less is more.Just the right length as it shows a man's shrinking world as he loses his memory.Sad and touching.
Beautifully written story that shpuld be required reading for everyone!!

Do you have 30 minutes? Then take 60 and go slow. Take your time with this 76 page novella and absorb it. Go someplace quiet where no person and no thing can disturb your time with this book. 
 This MAY have hit me because several months ago we buried our 88 year old dad. A man who was loosing the sharpness of thoughts and ideas he always had. He had been taught by a journalism teacher to always carry a pen because you never knew when there would be something to record. He almost always had a pen with him, cap clasped to his shirt and the pen dangling in front. He spent the last 10 years of his life missing the love of his life and spending many mornings by her grave site with his coffee and newspaper. So, yes, this maybe, just might have had something to do with my tears starting on page 10 of And Every Morning The Way Home Gets Longer and Longer. 
 Good byes are hard ~ we all loose someone, sometimes when they are still here. It is a different sadness ~at a different age ~ for different reasons for each of us. Sadness stinks! 
 But nonetheless ~ there is a lot of beauty in the messages contained within this 76 page book. So go buy it - don't get it from the library - you will want to keep it - share it - and remember who you shared it with because you will want it back! 
 And now - I am going to share this review with my husband (who he fondly says "my 90 year old mom is always in the now."), my 3 daughters, 9 siblings and their families - because THAT is who I really wrote this review for.

book_b.title: The Water Castle
book_b.user_review: Sweet story of a family that moves to a small town "castle" so their father can recover from a stroke. The three children must try to fit into a town where everyone seems to excel and it seems to have something to do with the underground springs. Easy pick for the younger group but I did miss some of the violence and drama of many other books for this age group.

sample_reviews.review_text: An enjoyable middle grade read, original but with a feeling of familiarity, but not in a bad way. An old-fashioned, Lake Wobegon (where all the children are above average), comfortable way. The kids are smart and likeable, there's enough conflict and mystery and hints of fantasy to make you want to jet ahead, the settings are a nicely juxtaposed blend of contemporary and historical, and the writing is solid. If you read and liked THE PENDERWICKS or THE MYSTERIOUS BENEDICT SOCIETY, you'll be in your element with THE WATER CASTLE.
I loved this book, as did my 9- and 11-year-old children.

Ephraim and his family move to a small town in Maine to take over a long neglected family home. His father, an artist, has had a debilitating stroke and his mother, a doctor, thinks that the house (once the site of a sanitorium utilizing the water, which seems to have healing properties) will make him better, and there is also a doctor nearby who specializes in this sort of problem. Ephraim manages to get settled in and makes friends with Mallory, whose mother's family were caretakers of the house for years. Since her mother has left, her father has stepped in to take care of it. He also befriends Will, whose family wants nothing to do with Ephraim's. The three learn some secrets of the house while preparing their explorers research project from school, and Ephraim hopes that he can uncover the secret to the fountain of youth and use it to cure his father. 
 Strengths: There is a lot going on in this book. There's science, there are racial issues, there are family issues, there's some more science. It has a nice ensemble cast and and features boys and girls AND a character of color. 
 Weaknesses: This just didn't grab me. The cover was blah, and the whole book had an older vibe, like I Capture the Castle meets Miracles on Maple Hill. I should have liked it, but I felt really bad that Ephraim thought the water would cure his father. I was also a bit confused about whether or not this was fantasy. 
 This seems to be one of those divisive books that people either love or they don't, and it hit me at a time when I didn't.

Ooooohhhhh! I dare you to put this book down! After their father's debilitating stroke, siblings Price, Ephraim, and Brynn head up to their mother's family's mysterious house in Crystal Springs, ME. The house has been in the Appledore family for generations and has all sorts of secret tunnels and laboratories that ancestors used in their quest to find the Fountain of Youth. 
 Meanwhile, Ephraim struggles to fit into to the town where every student is a star pupil and he's judged before he even arrives on the basis of his name. Ties run deep between the Appledores, the Wylies and the Darlings. The Wylies hate the Appledores because both families were vying for the same treasure: the Fountain of Youth. The Darlings have also been in service to the Appledores, but when Ephraim befriends a descendent of both families their elders aren't pleased. 
 This story is part science fiction, part fantasy, and part historical fiction. It's a gem of a balanced piece of literature as the characters are well developed and the story is told in both the past and present with an exciting plot focus on the expedition to the North Pole lead by Peary and Henson. This is one of the best books I've read this year! Recommended for grades 5-8.

Touted as a possible Newberry contender I read this for my Mock Newberry Club. Many of my friends raved about this story, and I hate that I didn't LOVE it. It had a difficult, slow start. Because I am always reading with students in mind, I think I would find many of my readers handing it back to me after a week saying: "I don't get what is going on". This book had a slew of characters from several different generations. In addition the premise of the book is a mystery, so there is built in confusion already. 
 The story does steadily pick up speed and by the end I was following with greater interest. Which brings me to my second complaint, and that is that it left everything unanswered. I assume that is because there will be a sequel. I am beginning to feel manipulated by publishers and authors making every story a series. 
 As the story grew, I did like the 3 main characters and their respective family issues. Although the mystery portion seemed incomplete, the character's personal development and their improved self-awareness was nicely rounded out by the author. 
 Will it hit the "distinguished" mark necessary for the Newberry? I am not totally won over. It will depend on the quality of the competition.
This sweet story about family rivalries, science, and the fountain of youth reminds me a little of Natalie Babbitt's Tuck Everlasting.
Uuuuuuuggggghhhhh. This was a slog, and then the ending kind of stunk. Yuck.
Did not come together

4.5 stars. I wanted a LITTLE more out of the ending (or maybe I was just tired when reading this), but overall, such a lovely, lovely book. 
 This one felt like The Penderwicks meets The Apothecary meets Tuck Everlasting. SO GOOD, FRIENDS! 
 I also loved that this was written by a fellow librarian super hero. She totally sneaked wonderful library references in this book (Let's use online and print resources for our report! The school librarian is nice and helpful and the library is bright and lovely to be in!) without it being super awkward, which is pretty hard to do. 
 I'll probably try to booktalk this one at Summer Reading school visits and I absolutely can't wait :)

I was looking forward to reading The Water Castle more than any other title on Sam's list. I am all about spooky old houses and baroque, intertwining plots. The intersection of fantasy, mystery, and science fiction is also an exciting place for me as a reader. 
 Sigh. 
 I'm afraid I'm with Nina Lindsay here. I just can't see any distinguished elements in this book. 
 Sam extolled the character development, but I disagree. The three main characters - Ephraim, Mallory, and Will - are reasonably well-developed, but they certainly don't measure up well beside Delphine of P.S. Be Eleven, Oscar of The Real Boy, or Billy Miller. The secondary characters, on the other hand, are either vague outlines (Ephraim's mother, Brynn, Mallory's dad) or caricatures meant to advance the plot (Price, Will's dad, Orlando Appledore). I agree with whoever said that Price seems to exist only to provide a foil for Ephraim's immaturity and ineptitude. Ditto Winifred Wylie, who's a total Nellie Oleson. 
 I can't find a lot to admire in the plot either. The multiple threads are handled clumsily, and a lot of the events feel forced. I was particularly disappointed in the sudden resolution of the conflict among Ephraim, Mallory, and Will. One minute they're enemies, and the next they're friends, and this is brought about by... what? A walk down a tunnel? That's a failing of both character and plot, actually. 
 Sam also admired the ambiguous ending, and the way the author doesn't spell out the solutions to the various mysteries. I actually agree with him on that, but it feels disingenuous after the reader has been bashed with the foreshadowing stick for the preceding 275 pages. You can't give a Dickens novel a Virginia Woolf ending. Or you can, I guess, but it makes for a jarring reading experience. 
 Some of the prose is well-crafted, stylistically, but that's not enough to save The Water Castle for me.

reference_books.title: Boomerang (Boomerang, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
My Thoughts: 
 Boomerang was such a cute, fun, humorous, and romantic love story. It's the story of Mia and Ethan, and told from their dual perspectives. These two applied for an internship at Boomerang, an up and coming matchmaking site. The night they both go out to celebrate, they end up drunk, making out, and Mia's naked in Ethan's bed naked the next morning. Neither really remembers what happenned, but one thing is obvious, and that is the sizzling chemistry and undeniable attraction that they share. As the story unfolds, both Mia and Ethan remember bits and pieces of their steamy night together. The next morning, they are shocked when they both end up at the Boomerang office. They learn that the internships that they thought they had earned, have been turned in to a competition of sorts. There is only one position available, and it's all a matter of who does a better job at the end of the summer. They will be setting up the Boomerang booth at a huge match making conference in Las Vegas. Things between Mia and Ethan are now very complicated. Not only are they competitors, but there is also a strict no dating co-workers policy at Boomerang. As their attraction for one another grows, they are expected to sit side by side at work daily, and even date applicants at Boomerang to go through the process. Will Mia and Ethan be able to stay away from each other? What do you do when you have to choose between your dream job, and your dream mate? 
 Boomerang was such a fun story! I could see it being made in to a romantic comedy for the big screen! It was a very light hearted, feel good, laugh out loud funny, great time story. I felt like I was right their with Mia and Ethan as they lived this romantic adventure with one another. They were both great characters! I thought that they were both very likable and fun. I could see myself being friends with both of them. The secondary characters were great as well. I loved Mia's best friends, Beth and Skylar, as well as Ethan's roommates, Jason and Isis. Their co-workers at Boomerang added a great dynamic to the story as well. All of these characters made for an amazing supporting cast. 
 I highly recommend Boomerang! It was an extremely fast-paced story. If you are looking for a light, fun, entertaining, feel good read, this one is a great choice for a Bookish Escape. I can't wait to continue this series and see what happens next. When you put Veronica Rossi and Lorin Oberweger together, you get pure magic! This team sure knows how to create a sweet, sizzling hot, and beautiful romance together. You will love the characters, and the twists and turns in the plot will keep you hooked!!! I give Boomerang by Noelle August, 4 Fun, Adventurous, Sexy, Funny, "Falling In Love," Filled Stars! This story is a great addition to any romance lover's library, and is sure to be a hit!!!

reference_books.title: Wallbanger (Cocktail, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
My Thoughts: 
 Wallbanger by Alice Clayton was a very entertaining, "laugh out loud" read that grabbed my attention right away. The story is told exclusively from the main character, Caroline's, point of view. Caroline is frustrated because she's been "O less" for months now. Her last sexual encounter was horrible, and since then her "O" has disappeared. She's tried many different ways to bring it back, but nothing has worked. So, she decides to go on a dating hiatus, and just focus on her career as an interior designer, her friendships were her two best friends, Sophia and Mimi, and enjoying her brand new apartment that she is renting from her awesome boss and good friend, Jillian. 
 Caroline enjoys living in San Francisco, and her new apartment is like a dream come true. To top it off, Sophia and Mimi buy her a Kitchen Aide Mixer as a housewarming gift, which is the perfect gift for her considering that she has a passion for baking. Then, her first night there, she has a sleepless night, when her next door neighbor's headboard is banging against her bedroom wall. To top it off, her wall hanging comes crashing down and hits her in the head. Exhaustion sets in when night after night she is subjected to her neighbor's wall banging, and the main screams, spanks, meows, and giggles of the women that he's sleeping with. She tells Sophia, Mimi, and Jillian about the dreaded "Wallbanger" that is costing her precious sleep, and the ladies think it's hilarious. Eventually, when Caroline has had enough, she pounds on her neighbors door to yell at him about his incessant wall banging. This scene was hilarious, as Caroline didn't realize she was in her sexy pink nightie when she ran next door to confront him, and he just winks at her. 
 Once Caroline see's how sexy Simon is with his dark hair, beautiful deep blue eyes, strong jaw, and knockout body, she can't get him out of her mind. She quickly finds herself fantasizing and dreaming about him, which makes her angry because she doesn't want to be added to his "harem" of girls. Caroline and Simon's lives quickly become intersected as well as that of their close friends. They decide to call a "truce," and try to become friends. I loved how Caroline and Simons friendship developed at a good pace. They really got to know each other, and I loved the way these two characters interacted with one another. There sarcastic, flirty, and teasing banter had me laughing throughout the book, as did Caroline's inner dialogue. The chemistry between these two really built up, with all of the sexual tension. They really were compatible, had fun with one another, and their relationship was believable. I loved being the outsider looking in and seeing how these two were falling for one another, no matter how much they tried to deny it to themselves, and their best friends. 
 Ms. Clayton used so many beautiful settings in this story. I could picture San Francisco, Lake Tahoe, and Nerja, Spain. The descriptions were perfection, and I felt like I was traveling right along with Caroline and Simon. I loved all of the characters. They each had their own distinct and unique personalities. The friendships and conversations felt genuine, and reminded me of the good times I have had with my own girlfriends talking about everything, and anything, and being silly at times. What I loved the most about this story was that is was an amazing escape. It was lighthearted, funny, and a happy story that didn't deal with serious issues, and angst. Wallbanger is the perfect story if you just want to sit back, relax, laugh out loud, and have a good time! 
 My Rating: 
 I give Wallbanger by Alice Clayton 4 hilarious, sexy, fun, flirty, and passionate stars! Read this story if you are in the mood to be surprised, amused, entertained, and swooned by a hot, and sexy male lead. Simon will rock your world, and you'll be ready for round two! I would love to read a sequel that included this cast of colorful, fun, and phenomenal characters!

reference_books.title: Sweet Little Thing (Sweet Thing, #1.5)
reference_books.review_text:
Lindy's Thoughts: 
 Sweet Little Thing, by Renee Carlino, was the perfect little follow up novella! I loved this story so much, and can't get enough of Will and Mia's love story. This novella was told from Will's perspective, and it was such a pleasure being privy to Will's thoughts. The deep love that these two shared was palpable in every page. Will adored Mia, and she in turn loved him with all of her heart. 
 In this installment, Will and Mia are getting married, and while Mia wanted to elope, her parents wanted to be there, so Will gave in. As Mia is planning her upcoming nuptials, and things are going fairly smoothly at their music studio, life has other plans for them! "The Sweetest Little Thing," has come their way, and life will never be the same again! 
 Sweet Little Thing was a beautiful story. It had a colorful cast of characters in Martha, the sweet and wise woman that always had the right advice, Jenny, Mia's sassy best friend, and Tyler, a hilarious jokester, and Will's partner in crime! I grew very attached to all of these characters, and all that they brought to Will and Mia's lives. 
 Ladies, Will is as sweet and sexy as ever! Boy is that man smooth! His words and actions towards Mia gave me the swoons at times, and goosebumps at other times! He has such a way with words, music, and expressing his love. I fell in love with Will Ryan all over again! I just can't put in to words how sexy, attractive, and amazing his character is. Also, he had many moments that had me laughing! I got to see a different side of Will in this sequel, and it made me smile and chuckle a whole lot! 
 Many times in Romance stories, I don't like the leading ladies as much as the leading men. This series, is one huge exception to that rule! I adore Mia! She's sweet, loving, caring, and she doesn't take any crap! She knows how to put Will in his place with just one look! Mia is a very strong, independent, talented, and an entertaining character. 
 My Rating: 
 I give, Sweet Little Thing, by Renee Carlino, 5 Romantic, Hilarious, Touching, and "Sweet Little Stars!" Fans of Sweet Thing will not be disappointed! If you haven't read Sweet Thing, I highly, highly, recommend it! This series is absolutely amazing, and one of my favorites! Don't miss out on this feel good, deeply romantic, one of a kind series! 
 My Favorite Quote: 
 "Sometimes we're just along for the ride," she said over my shoulder. We can't control everything; we can only do our best to control our reactions when life doesn't go our way." (eARC, Loc. 225) 
 ~Martha
