reference_books.title: Drew + Fable Forever (One Week Girlfriend, #3.5)
reference_books.review_text:
My Thoughts: 
 Drew + Fable Forever by Monica Murphy was a beautiful continuation of an epic love story. I have been following this series from the very beginning, and my love for these characters just continues to grow. These two beloved characters have faced so many challenges in their lives and in their relationship. Yet, together they are strong, unbreakable, and have proven that their love will get them through any adversity put in their paths. 
 In this novella, we get a beautiful glimpse in to the future of Drew and Fable. Drew has become a quarterback for the Forty-Niners and is financially well off. Owen (Fable's brother) is in high school, and is being taken care of by Drew and Fable. Drew wants to get married before the football season begins, and whisks Fable off to Hawaii for a very romantic and beautiful wedding. Once the football season begins, Drew is required to travel regularly, and while Fable travels with him at times, she also needs to keep any eye on Owen also. Drew and Fable get lonely for one another. Pretty soon, Fable is thinking about starting a family, but Drew is not ready. As their marriage progresses, they have ups and downs, go through trial and error as they learn how to communicate effectively and compromise with one another. Their story is all about what happens after the wedding. 
 I loved this novella! It was a real treat, and I know all of the other Drew and Fable fans out there are going to love it as well. Drew made me fall in love with him all over again as he supported Fable, wrote her beautiful poetry, always made her feel special and beautiful, and loved her unconditionally. Fable went through times of self doubt and insecurity, where she questioned whether she was good enough for Drew and worried that he might get tired of her. Yet, Drew always knew how to reassure her. Fable was a great wife to Drew and a wonderful sister to Owen. Drew & Fable was a beautiful story. It made me smile, and feel sentimental. There were so many sweet and heartwarming moments, as well as sexy and swoon worthy moments. I give Drew + Fable Forever by Monica Murphy, 5 Touching, and Beautifully Romantic Stars! 
 My Favorite Quotes: 
 "She's no longer a girl anymore. The jaded, angry, and defiant girl who was so determined to fight the world is gone, though shades of her still shine through. I loved that girl. Fiercely. And I love the woman she is now, just as fiercely. She's my fiancee, my future wife, the future mother of my children. Fable is the woman who will always stand by my side. Forever." (eARC, Loc. 164) 
 ~Drew 
 "When you struggle for something so good, so right, you cherish it more. You hold it close, nurture it, protect it, make sure you never, ever let your guard down." (eARC, Loc. 181) 
 ~Fable 
 "I'll always be the one to rescue you, Fable. You never have to worry about that." (eARC, Loc. 534) 
 ~Drew

reference_books.title: Nocte (The Nocte Trilogy, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
My Thoughts: 
 Wow! Bravo Ms. Cole! You have completely floored me! Nocte was an amazing psychological suspense story! It had mystery, intrigue, darkness, complexity, and was a huge puzzle, that I still haven't solved! I loved every moment of Nocte. I was pulled in to Calla's world from the very beginning, and an intricate and multi-layered world it was... 
 In Nocte, we meet Calla Price and her twin brother Finn Price. These two are extremely close and protective of one another. Finn is mentally unstable, and Calla takes it upon herself to keep him functioning in a healthy manner. Then, there is the delicious, sexy, Brittish love interest, Dare DuBray. He has a sexy accent, and I know every woman who reads this story will go gaga for him! Dare is mysterious, and harbors a secret, one in which Calla is determined to figure out! 
 Nocte is one of those stories in which you try to dissect every single clue to figure out what is going on. You know that there is a lot more to the story than meets the eye, but it's not all laid out in front of you. This mystery, had me turning pages like a crazy woman. By the time I got to the end of the story, I was dying to learn the secret. I had many different theories in the works, and yet, I was still left in complete surprise by the ending! I will say that even though you learn the secret, the ending leaves you with even more questions, and a major cliffhanger. Nocte is going to be a trilogy, along with a Novella included. I'm glad I got some answers, but my curiosity is still piqued, and I can't wait to see what Ms. Cole still has up her sleeve. 
 My Rating: 
 I highly recommend Nocte. If you are like me and enjoy stories full of mystery, suspense, layers, and intensity; this is one book that you don't want to miss out on. I give Nocte, by Courtney Cole, 4.5 Dark, Chilling, Intricate, and Addictive Stars!!! Be prepared for this story to take you on one heck of a crazy roller coaster ride!!!

book_a.title: A Christmas to Remember (Lucky Harbor, #8.5; Chaos, #2.5; Last Chance, #6.5; Everson, Texas, #0.5; Tallgrass, #1.5)
book_a.user_review:
My Thoughts: 
 Christmas time is my favorite time of year! So as I'm getting ready for the holidays, I was 
 really excited to add Christmas themed reads to my reading list! I have read stories by Jill Shalvis and absolutely love her, but haven't previously read anything by Kristen Ashley, Hope Ramsay, Molly Cannon, or Marilyn Pappano. A Christmas to Remember was such a great sampling of these authors, and now I've added a few more series to my TBR! 
 The first story in the christmas anthology was, Dream a Little Dream by Jill Shalvis! This little story was fabulous!!! It is a Lucky Harbor story, yet you do not have to be familiar with the series to read this story. It is about Melissa, and Ian. Melissa (Mel) has never done long term relationships, and is a bit of a serial monogamist. The moment things started getting too serious with Ian, and she realized that she was falling in love with him, she left him. The two of them never stopped loving or thinking about each other as they went their separate ways. Then, 6 months later Melissa's apartment catches on fire and she is trapped in the building. Ian is the firefighter on scene. Melissa's near-death experience completely changes her. She realizes that life is too short, and she wants Ian back. She sets a plan in place to win him back, but will Ian risk a broken heart again? This second chance at love story was sweet, emotional, heartfelt, and made me fall in love with the Lucky Harbor Series, and Jill Shalvis all over again. Even though this was a short story, it felt complete, and like nothing was missing. It was well developed, and I felt like I really got to know Melissa and Ian well. This was a great holiday story about love, healing, and second chances. 
 The second story in this anthology was, Every Year, by Kristen Ashley. This is the first story that I've read of Kristen Ashley's and I absolutely loved it! Tabby is spending Christmas with her father, "Tack," stepmother, Tyra, older brother, Rush, and two little half brothers, Rider and Cutter. This is Tabby's first christmas with her boyfriend "Shy," and he is celebrating the holiday with her family, along with his brother, Landon. Shy and Landon had a sad childhood being raised by an aunt that didn't want them, after their parents were murdered when they were young. This story was heartwarming and made me cry, as I read how Shy and Landon got to experience their first happy christmas in years. I really loved this story. Ms. Ashley has a beautiful way with words, and made me feel so much emotion. Even though I had never read any of the books in this series, I was able to jump right in, and didn't feel lost at all. She recapped all the names and relationships as she told the story, and got me to love and become attached to these characters fairly quickly. After reading this, I immediately downloaded the first two stories in the Chaos series! 
 The third story in this anthology was, Silent Night, by Hope Ramsay. It is the story of a young and single mother, Maryanne, and her three month old baby, Joshua. She has no home or money to her name, and runs out of gas, as she leaves the woman's shelter she was staying in to travel to South Carolina in search of her older cousin, Jennifer, who she hasn't seen since she was a young child. When nobody answers the door, she takes her baby in to the barn to get warm as she waits for her cousin to return. However, instead of her seeing her cousin, she ends up meeting a good looking lawyer, Daniel. Maryanne and Daniel end up having a magical christmas, filled with miracles and hope. This story was very sweet. I loved how Ms. Ramsay intertwined fate, miracles, the magical quality of Christmas,and new beginnings in her story. 
 The fourth story in this anthology was, Have Yourself a Messy Little Christmas, by Molly Cannon. Lincoln (Linc) is a hardworking accountant who started living in his parents old home, when they retired and moved away. One day, Linc is surprised and aggravated when he learns that his mother hired him an early Christmas present, Dinah, to organize his home in preparation for the holidays. Dinah is a sweet, young woman, who has a very bright personality, but Linc is resistant to the idea of anyone touching and rearranging all of his belongings. However, as Linc and Dinah get to know one another better, their mutual attraction grows and affections toward each other deepens. This story was very sweet, fast paced, and a real, "feel good" type of story. I think it was a great addition to this anthology, and really enjoyed it! 
 The last story in this anthology was, A Family For Christmas, by Marilyn Pappano. It was a story about a young widow named Ilena. She had lost her husband in the war while she was pregnant. Then, a handsome and sweet doctor, named Jared, moves from New York to Tallgrass Oklahoma. Attraction is instant between Ilena and Jared, and as the two of them get to know each other, they start to fall in love. However, Jared had planned on his move to Tallgrass being temporary, and Ilena isn't willing to move. This was such a sweet story, that I didn't want to end. The characters had great chemistry and passion together. I loved how Jared got attached to the baby, as well as Illena. After reading, A Family For Christmas, I am really am excited to see what other stories Marilyn Pappano has written! 
 A Christmas to Remember was such a great anthology, filled with memorable and touching stories about the magic and miracles that happen during Christmas time. It is the perfect book to read by the fire, with hot chocolate or coffee in hand, during the holiday season, and really got me in the christmas spirit! My favorite stories in the anthology were, Dream a Little Dream by Jill Shalvis, and Every year by Kristen Ashley. However, I enjoyed all of the stories in the anthology for different reasons. I give, A Christmas to Remember, 4 Bright, Hopeful, and Magic Filled Stars!

 4 star rating

 Maryanne is a single mother to a 3 month old baby named Joshua who is just trying to do right by her baby. She has idealized her one summer in Last Chance and is heading to Cousin Jennifer's as a result of being unemployed and now homeless. She runs out of gas approximately two miles short of her destination. She wraps up the baby and begins to walk. As the weather deteriorates, she seeks shelter in a barn, believing she has made it to her destination. Little did Maryanne know that she ended up at the property of Daniel Jessup. When Daniel comes back to his familial home after a quick shopping excursion (he is here to clean out the home and prepare it for sale following the death of his parents) he is surprised to find Maryanne and Joshua holed up in the barn, seeking shelter. 
 I really enjoyed the slow growth of the relationship between Maryanne and Daniel (well - as slow as it can be given this is a short story). An entertaining and engaging story. 
 5 star rating 
 Have Yourself a Messy Little Christmas: 
 Lincoln is your classic bachelor with the attitude that he can do everything himself. His mother sent a professional organizer to his home as an early Christmas present, to ready the home for his mother and father's return for the holidays. In walks Dinah, the professional organizer dressed as a Christmas elf. And humpf goes Lincoln. You just know there will be sparks. And the story does not disappoint. The slow "ish" progression from hired organizer to two people interacting in a steamy way was well told and kept my interest throughout. 
 This is the first writing of this author I have read but I will search out more of her stories! 
 4 star rating 
 A Family for Christmas: 
 Jared, a pediatrician who just moved to Tallgrass, a small town in Oklahoma has volunteered to work for a local charity Prairie Elf Foundation. It is here that he meets for the first time Ilena Gomez, a diminutive woman dressed as an elf. Ilena is a single parent (a war widow) and very passionate about the Prairie Elf Foundation. While Ilena is not Jared's typical type, he does indeed invite her for a beverage after their first meeting. A few days later, Ilena runs into Jared at the local Walmart. Jared is looking for a Christmas tree and decorations for his doctor's office. With Ilena's assistance, both in transporting the tree and with decorating the tree, their relationship blossoms. I got the sense that Jared's upbringing in a wealthy, upstate New York family was anything but warm and fuzzy. And that is exactly what Ilena brings to their budding relationship. The scene where Jared feeds baby John is quite moving. 
 This story definitely pulls at the heartstrings more than any other in this book. All in all, an enjoyable love story. 
 *OBS would like to thank the publisher for supplying a free copy of this title in exchange for an honest review*

Usually anthologies are a mixed bag, but in this one, I enjoyed all of the stories. Several of them featured insta-love (the Hope Ramsey, Molly Cannon and Marilyn Pappano stories), so they weren't too believable, but they were all sweet stories, filled with likable lead characters who you were rooting for by the end. I wish they had been longer so that the time period didn't have to be quite so compressed. I thought the Jill Shalvis story was the best in the book (no surprise there since I'm familiar with Lucky Harbor and love the series), but even though I personally enjoyed Kristen Ashley's story and I'm a big fan of hers, I thought her contribution was the least successful one in the anthology. To me, that story is really more of a gift to fans that have already read the books featuring Chaos, It doesn't work well as a stand-alone, whereas all of the others did. I enjoyed it very much since I was already familiar with the characters but I think it would be much harder to enjoy if you weren't. I also liked the excerpts from each author's work and I plan on keeping an eye out for at least one or two of the authors that I wasn't familiar with, so all in all, this anthology was a successful one for me.
I'll be honest, I liked the novel excerpts better than the short stories, but it was still okay.

book_b.title: Dragon's Lair (Wind Dragons MC, #1)
book_b.user_review:
My Thoughts: 
 It's always such a fun adventure reading about MC Clubs, their lifestyle, brotherhood, and the rules they live by. When I saw Dragon's Lair, I was intrigued. I love forbidden romance, and this one definitely caught my eye. 
 In Dragon's Lair, we get Faye's story. She grew up in a cold family environment, with a mother that was never satisfied, and an apathetic father who let his wife make all of the decisions. Faye is a "good" girl. She's a rule follower, and has always been a stellar student. Growing up next to the Black brothers, she always had a crush on, bad boy older brother Dex. He has always been good and kind to her. However, she doesn't see him for several years, when he has a falling out with his family. 
 Faye gets in to a serious and monogamous relationship with Eric Black, the younger of the two brothers. In college, they are both practicing law, and are at the top of their class. Faye has her future all planned out. She will marry Eric, practice law with him, have children, and live happily ever after. When Faye discovers Eric having sex with a woman that she thought was her friend, all of her dreams are crushed. Eric begs her to give him another chance, but she refuses to be with him ever again. Her life takes are dramatic turn when she runs in to older brother Dex Black at a bar. The chemistry between them sizzles, and they both give in to delicious temptation. The one night they are together changes both of their lives forever. 
 Dragon's Lair was fast-paced, entertaining, and easy-reading. Faye was a hilarious character who added a lot of fun and laughter to the story. Dex oozed sex appeal, but I would have liked to see more sex scenes, and detail to them, between him and Faye. There were few, they were short, and not very detailed. The story had a lot of cliches, common themes that are done in MC Biker stories, and was for the most part on the surface. Yet, I read it quickly, was very entertained, and am looking forward to the next book in the series. One of my favorite aspects of the story was Faye's relationship with the various MC brothers. She forged a special bond with many of them, and I was excited to get to learn about Arrow, Track, Rake, Jim, Vinnie, and Irish. I felt like I really got to know the different characters personalities. 
 My Rating: 
 I give, Dragons Lair, by Chantel Fernando, 3 Fun, Fast-Paced, Funny, and Entertaining Stars!!!

I kean if the author had made the story longer and made the relationship between Dex and Faye more realistic as the auther never actually delves into their relationship

book_a.title: Happier at Home: Kiss More, Jump More, Abandon a Project, Read Samuel Johnson, and My Other Experiments in the Practice of Everyday Life
book_a.user_review: Gretchen Rubin's books may restate the obvious but she does so in the most thoughtful and encouraging way. Her writing is a constant reminder that happiness is a choice and that we can all lead happier, more thoughtful, lives. This should be required reading!

sample_reviews.review_text:
As someone who had never given a single self-help book more than a pitying glance before, I was surprised by how much I liked -- how helpful I found -- The Happiness Project: Or Why I Spent a Year Trying to Sing in the Morning, Clean My Closets, Fight Right, Read Aristotle, and Generally Have More Fun. But with that and now Happier at Home under my belt, I'm starting to understand. A good self-help title (though, fairly, Rubin prefers the term "moralist" or life essayist, in the more researched and philosophical vein of Benjamin Franklin or Thoreau than say, Steve Harvey) is like a sensible diet: deceptively simple. Exercise and eat healthy, lose weight; Be honest about who you are and what want, be kind to yourself and others, be happier. In a nutshell. Sometimes you just need a reminder. 
 Rubin's presentation, and her project as a whole, is straightforward and easy to understand. She makes simple, clear statements and she repeats them a lot, but it's not to condescend; it's because she's learning these things about herself and life at the same time that she's writing about them. As easy as her manner is though, being happy -- even trying to define "happiness" -- is hard. As she makes evident through her repeated "Secret of Adulthood" to constantly "be Gretchen", what might sound easy is not always easy to do. Rubin has many profound truths/rules, but I think her rule to "be Gretchen" is the one that brings her the most happiness and success in both of her Happiness Projects. She shows, through her own life experiences, that it's a struggle not just to do what you want, or to behave in accordance with your own nature, but just to figure out what that is. But when you really look at the patterns that reemerge in your life, you can better understand who you really are, rather than who you wish you were. 
 I carry many of Rubin's "splendid truths" with me. In particular, I find resonance with "be Gretchen" (be Nicole), and motivation in the reminders that "happiness does not always make me feel happy" and that I can influence others, but ultimately I cannot *make* anyone else happy, and no one else can *make* me be happy. Seems obvious enough, I know, but sometimes something has to be plainly stated, or seen in action, to click. That's what Happier at Home is. It's putting obvious truths into action and measuring results. And for me, it clicks. 
 I had to pace myself reading this. I find Rubin so likeable and relatable, that I could have whipped right through the whole book in a couple sittings, but it resonates more if you give yourself some time to think between chapters and reflect on your own home and relationships. That said, I found Happier at Home less of a home run (a triple?) than The Happiness Project. In many ways, Happier at Home was strangely similar to my own life. I don't have Rubin's income, for sure, but embracing my love of children's literature has likewise brought immense happiness to my life; learning to drive is on every New Year's Resolutions list and my inability to cross it off said list gives me more anxiety than actual driving would; we've lived in the same city and we can both be pretty... uptight? But there is a lot of talk about her relationships with her two daughters and parenting -- and naturally, her relationship with her children must be huge element of her happiness at home -- so while I don't begrudge her those chapters, I just didn't find them as useful as the one on organizing your house and the importance of possessions, for example. 
 Reading about Rubin's perpetual awareness of her own happiness takes me to my zen place -- like collecting favorite quotes does for many a Pinterest-user, I suppose -- but one detractor I found what that, though subtly, this companion book often reads like an addendum to her self descriptions in The Happiness Project. 
 I can't blame a person for wanting to be understood (especially in their own work), but anytime someone says "I'm not a ______, BUT _____" all they really do is describe the ways in which they are EXACTLY that way. Rubin sweetens any mention of familial discontent in a similar fashion. Of course it may only be a happiness booster, reminding herself to be grateful even as she mentions a negative trait about her husband or parenthood, and I did find her repetitiveness a good way to drive other points home... or maybe I just can't relate because I don't have to deal with the harsh critiquing of other parents... but stated so often (at one point she even addresses a reader comment from her blog about the accusation that she is selfish), it read like a constant arrow pointing toward her own virtue. And I like Gretchen Rubin just fine without asides or apologies! Sure, she's a workaholic sometimes-stick-in-the-mud. But she's also a woman trying blatantly to help others, who puts her own damn e-mail address at the back of the book so that you can connect with her, and sets goals for herself that involve Wednesday afternoon dates with her daughter. She's no monster, and need not worry that we all think otherwise. 
 I hope that in future titles, Rubin will feel better able to be confessional without so much sugary justification, because I really do appreciate it when she's honest about her less attractive traits -- whether she's admitting how much of a nag she can be, or being truthful about how tiring or irritating other people, even the one's you love, can be, about how she loves her children but they aren't and can't be the only thing she loves. If she wasn't honest about the drains on her happiness and her own imperfections., how would her project resonate? How would anyone relate? But I do relate. And that's what I love about Happier at Home, and The Happiness Project. Write another one and I'll read that too.

I'm not sure what I think of this book. In a way it doesn't seem like the "work" the author says it is to put together. She is on a quest to find happiness, and some good ideas are generated for everyday living, but there's almost too much detail for what she discovers. The writer is often self-absorbed, self indulgent and whiny. On the other hand, finishing this book made me begin writing of some of the things that are keeping me from embracing happiness.

I really enjoyed The Happiness Project so I was excited at the prospect of spending more time with a continuation of the ideas presented in that book, but I wasn't as blown away this time. I love Rubin's writing style and voice, the careful research she puts into her writing, and her detail, but the content of this book just wasn't as powerful for me as in The Happiness Project. I still had my "Gretchen you're a genius moments," but sadly, I had a few moments where I rolled my eyes. 
 For me, the goals this time around were a little weaker and sometimes I was overwhelmed by the amount of detail used to describe a very simple task. I like this author enough that I will be intrigued by future books she produces, but I have to say for this subject stick with The Happiness Project.

Not as good as The Happiness Project (seemed to drag at times, maybe because it was at points too rambly and detailed) but still plenty of good insights. 
 Random quotes: 
 To "Be Gretchen" was the way to happiness, but there was also a sadness to this resolution--the sadness that comes from admitting my limitations, my indifferences, all the things that I wish I were that I will never be. To cram my days full of the things I loved, I had to acknowledge the things that played no part in my happiness. 
 Robert Louis Stevenson remarked, "The habit of being happy enables one to be freed, or largely freed, from the dominance of outward conditions," 
 Elias Canetti observed, "One lives in the naive notion that later there will be more room than in the entire past." 
 Throughout my life--during college, during my clerkship with Justice O'Connor, during Eleanor's pre-school years, during my books' publishing cycles, even at our wedding--I've experienced a ... skipping, a feeling of jumping from prologue to epilogue without ever feeling that I'm at the center of time. "It's too soon for that," "I have plenty of time to get to that," or "I'm too young to do that," I'd think, then suddenly, overnight, "It's too late for that," "It's almost over," or "I'm too old for that." In Saki's short story "Reginald at the Carlton," a character remarks, "Hors d'oeuvres have always a pathetic interest for me.... They remind me of one's childhood that one goes through, wondering what the next course is going to be like--and during the rest of the menu one wishes one had eaten more of the hors d'oeuvres." I didn't want to come to the end of my life and wish I'd paid more attention along the way.
Super fast read.

I was hoping she would be less annoying in her second book, but I was wrong. She comes off as quite know it all and I sometimes struggle to take her seriously. I persevered and I am glad I did because she does have some very good points on happiness.

Happier at Home is definitely a feel good type of book. My husband and I have very stressful jobs and three special needs kids - I was definitely looking forward to reading Happier at Home. So far, I have read it one time through without implementing anything. I just couldn't put it down. Now I plan to read it again - one chapter at a time and work towards implementation. I will say much of what is in here though is common sense - but how many things in life do we ignore, regardless of how common sense-like they are. We are busy, lots to do, places to be and responsibilities to meet. I am glad I took the time to read this book. Even if I (or you) don't take what she says to heart - the manner in which the book is broken down is a great place to start with your own "prescription" for a happier home. All in all I give this book 4 stars.

I really loved The Happiness Project and I really admired Gretchen Rubin for wanting to appreciate her life more. And I cleaned my closet as a result! But Happier at Home just irritated me. sample_reviews.review_text: Definitely a lengthy book, and it was hard for me to follow sometimes, especially w/all the names of people and the heavy foreign politics. I loved the family history and being able to see into the president's personal life. And I really enjoyed all the pictures. Great to see the behind the scenes part of the presidency. Learned alot, especially about Katrina and 9/11.
I didn't like this as much as Robert Gates' memoir, "Duty."
Stopped reading in Chapter 3

The surprise best-seller from Chimpy McHitlerburton. This is sort of a memoir, but rather than tell his tale chronologically, Bush organizes his book around 14 "decision points" - crucial moments that left him with a choice with profound consequences. Obviously, a lot of this material covers 9/11, Afghanistan, and Iraq, but Bush delves into areas both well known (Katrina) and not so well known (his AIDS initiatives in Africa). His prose is forceful and unadorned with occasional touches of emotion. He seems to take a certain delight in quoting prominent Democrats who initially supported the Iraq War, which only underscores what a bunch of a**holes Bush had to deal with in his 8 years in office. Unlike the other chapters, his one on Katrina is full of harsh criticism, both of himself and of the others involved in the mess in New Orleans. You don't have to agree with Bush to know that he was a fundamentally decent man who took his job seriously, and who dealt with a seemingly endless series of disasters with cool competence. Worthwhile.
glib. too glib. v. depressing.

A really amazing snapshot of the Bush Presidency. Covers in detail the main issues President Bush had to deal with, letting us see what was going through his head at the time and why each decision was arrived at. Also very valuable to both casual readers and historians will be the candid responses to most of the partisan attacks, especially those coming from the media and celebrity camps. 
 President Bush not only comes across as a convincing statesman, but also puts to rest any allegations that he is lacking in intellect. If anything he is way smarter than his detractors, some of whom may confuse the man's humble nature and honest belief in his religion for naivete. A big mistake, as many found out along the way. 
 This book is definitely one that should be read by those in favor and opposed to President Bush. It will be an eye opener for both camps. 
 It will be a valued part of my library, more so because it is an autographed copy.

I enjoyed this book. I've always liked Bush and I like him a little more after reading this. I personally thought that it was a little long and repetitive at times, but the title makes no bones about it. This book is literally all "decision points" that defined Bush's presidency. I also enjoyed all of the pictures scattered throughout the book!

This is my first presidential memoir. It is not my type of book, as a rule, but I felt compelled to read it. While I tend to fall on the conservative side of the fence on financial issues, I'm socially moderate. I voted for Bush in both elections, but I don't think he's made all of the right decisions. In reading his book, I was pleased to find that he doesn't, either. In fact, I think it will be decades until we can legitimately assess the impacts of his presidency without the bias we all feel after living the issues he describes in Decision Points. 
 Specifically, I enjoyed the format of the book--a chronological approach would have felt too overwhelming and potentially have lost my interest. I enjoyed the personal aspects of the story, and the former president's candor. The book reinforced what I've always thought about him--he made the decisions he thought were best based on the information he had. Right or wrong, he was resolute and confident. 
 Reading this book has inspired me to seek out more presidential memoirs.

Throughout the entire book, I felt as if Bush was sitting right in front of me telling me all the sordid details of his presidency. It is well written, and the topics covered are incredibly interesting (even to someone who isn't so fascinated by politics in general). As a New Yorker whose husband works across from the WTC site, I've always been especially grateful to Bush for doing everything he could to keep this country safe. This book makes it abundantly clear that that was his focus during his presidency. I can only hope that future presidents will have the courage to do what it takes to keep this nation safe, even at the expense of public opinion.

Pretty much a waste of hard earned money and precious time. I started reading with the stereotypical image of George W as a privileged son, with little experience of running anything other than a baseball team, and a Bible junkie and pretty much finished with nothing seriously challenging my initial assumptions. George W has a very black and white view of just about everything in life, there is the good (white obviously) and the bad. Its funny how desperate he seemed to leave his mark on history as one of the great leaders of the first world without actually knowing much about history himself. 
 I am beginning to question democracy as the best system to choose the most cleverest and ablest people to lead any country with its heavy reliance on public speaking. How could such an average guy lead a first world country for eight years?

sample_reviews.review_text: This autobiography had the horrific fascination of a train wreck. I read it for a book group and I couldn't put it down.

There are families and there are families... 
 p. 25 "When Dad wasn't telling us about all the amazing things he had already done, he was telling us about the wondrous things he was going to do. Like build the Glass Castle." 
 p. 96...I had a personal connection with Jeannette's sister, Lori, when she got her first pair of eye glasses--"I cannot only see that tree, I can see the individual leaves on it....Can you see them? " 
 Christmas Tree story on page 115--"....we all had our own ways of shutting down and closing off..." 
 On p. 144, Mom taught compassion, even in the face of cruelty. 
 p. 168, I loved the comment about books...."They transport you to a different world." Books saved these kids in many ways. 
 When Jeannette told her mom she was fine--comfortable, her mom replied that it was exactly that, that had her worried... 
 For all the apparent sadness, poverty, and danger, somehow, this group survived it all, and created an energy that I still cannot name. There was love, but it was more than that...a spirit of some kind. 
 Tho disturbing for me, I saw the hopefulness in the children, and they did grow to be successful. Respecting the choices their parents made for themselves in later life, was in my humble opinion, an ultimate act of love. That expression, "what doesn't kill us makes us stronger," certainly held true for the Walls Children.
I know I'm in the minority here but I just didn't latch onto this book the way many others have.

Wow....what an incredible story. Definitely makes you appreciate what you have. Really opened my eyes to the fact that there is real poverty here in the U.S., and yet it is written in a way that isn't meant to make you feel sad or to persuade you to do something about it. It's literally just an unassumin, amazing tale of this woman's life and I'm so glad she found the courage to write it.

There are two main reasons I doubt I'll ever write a memoir of my childhood. First, I would be afraid of what my mom would say if I aired our dirty laundry. And second, I hesitate to put into print just one version of the story of my growing-up. For while it was just the one childhood I lived, there are so many different ways to frame the same events, and I would rather not tie myself into just one interpretation. 
 Even though The Glass Castle was largely a laundry-list account of the events of Walls's childhood, it still reflects a specific interpretation of the events. I'm not saying the events didn't happen, but rather that they would look different if viewed from a different angle or through a different filter. Walls's parents certainly saw the events she describes differently than she did. What they saw as a series of adventures and parenting choices that fostered independence and strength of character, Walls saw as trauma and neglect as a result of her parents' selfishness. I tend to side with Walls's perspective on this one, but I'm not certain it's any more valid a perspective than her mother's. 
 What amazes me about this story is that the family managed to stay together, for the most part. Or, seen in a different light, of course they stayed together because they were all locked to one another by codependency. It's a lucky thing Walls's parents moved the family around so much when they were younger. If she'd been born and raised in Welch, I doubt she would have ever left. Moving away from home takes a certain mindset, and the fact that Walls was accustomed to moving from place to place I think made it easier for her to leave when the time came. This was my favorite part of the book, actually, Walls and her sister planning their escape. Up until then it was just this depressing reminder of how dependent children are on their families. 
 So, there were things I liked about this book, but there was also plenty I didn't like. I've already mentioned the "first this happened, then that happened" style of the book, which made it feel repetitive. It was also difficult to keep track of what age she was at each place, and although I didn't write down a timeline, I suspect that the anecdotes don't fit together in time quite right. Walls didn't age uniformly in comparison with her siblings, and years passed in fits and starts that left me feeling disoriented. The repetition of language heightened this feeling---more than once Walls mentions that her mother "didn't drink anything stronger than tea," in those same words. 
 I just prefer a little more art in a memoir. And I prefer Half Broke Horses (although I do think that title needs a hyphen).
Couldn't put this down. Exquisitely written and with such a gentle touch on such tragic scenes that one smiles through the tears. Humanity is so resilient at times.
There's something both heartening and disheartening about memoirs of people growing up with awful parents. She made it out, so I guess that's good.
Made me grateful for the parents I had. Kudo's to the Walls kids for overcoming what they did.
I really loved this book. It's a must read.

I wanted more in the coming-of-age/young-adult part of the story. I wanted to know more about the process of living through that childhood and figuring out how to come to terms with what had happened to her.

book_b.title: Ruby
book_b.user_review: It was very well written. A lot of darkness to it but wonderfully written.

sample_reviews.review_text: I'm sorry, but every book I have read that Opra recommends is so dark and depressing. The content and language and over all book is one I wish I had put down immediately instead of reading it to completion. And that is all I want to say about Ruby!

"Ruby Bell was a constant reminder of what could befall a woman whose shoe heels were too high." 
 These are the intriguing words that start off Cynthia Bond's new book Ruby. It is also a tale that caught the eye of Oprah Winfrey and made it to her esteemed Oprah Book Club. And, it's easy to see why: rift with tension from racial conflicts to dark forces that reign over humanity, the book is a cross between a Stephen King thriller and a historical narrative. Yes, there is even a symbolic crow that makes an appearance in the book. 
 The book is as disturbing as it is powerful. It gets into your being and resonates long after the last pages have been turned. Definitely not for the faint of heart, or for the young at heart, Ruby has content that is evocative and grown up. 
 Full Review at sukasareads.com | http://sukasareads.blogspot.com/2015/...

This book was beautifully written, but wow is it intense and rips your insides out. 
 Proceed with caution.

It seems many people have given this book one or two stars because they hate the experiences that are related. There's no question it is dark, and many passages are difficult to bear, but to paraphrase Ephraim, if there are women out there who have experienced this kind of abuse as children, I should be able to read about it. The more that we whitewash the world, the harder it is for people to talk about, not to mention, get help for the horrible pain inflicted upon them physically and psychologically. 
 Cynthia Bond's prose is just amazing --several articulately-drawn character stories -- both beautiful and gut-wrenching. It was a painful book to read, but certainly redemptive. I'm not always a fan of magical realism, but Bond made it work for me.

There's no question to me that this is a good book--I can't find anything wrong with it. I just, for some reason, couldn't get into it, but it's beautifully written and poignant and I'm not sure what's wrong with me. dY~!
WOW, WOW, WOW! The books Oprah recommends never disappoints :) Both Ruby and Ephram are unique characters that you build deep empathy for and so glad that their paths cross to find one another.

I have incredibly mixed feelings about this book. Between Oprah's recommendation, and the description of the story, I was really excited to pick this up and dive into it. What I thought was going to be a story of love, empathy, and redemption, turned out to be a story about some of the most painful and horrific things an individual can experience. It is true that there is love, empathy, and redemption in this story, but it was overshadowed by the terrible aforementioned events. It would be easy for someone to have vicarious trauma from reading this book. 
 When I finished it, I was prepared to give a completely negative review, but after listening to the author in an interview, and reconsidering the craft of writing in this story, I have reconsidered. So my dichotomous review is this - if you are sensitive to abuse and the terrors of the world, if you are unable to listen to someone's terrifying story and let it go, this is not the book for you. Don't read it, you will struggle to get out of your head and sleep at night. However, if you want to read something that is well-written and speaks to how someone can rise like a phoenix from the ashes, and you can handle traumatic information, then you may very well love this story. I now understand why the author wrote it. I carries a message indeed. However, I am too sensitive for this stuff. It took me over 3 months to finish it because I was afraid to see what horrors would happen next. No one wants to hear about this stuff, but then again, there needs to be an awareness that things have happened, and do still happen.

I was so excited for this book as I love most of Oprah's choices, but I was disappointed...it was nicely written, a bit over-descriptive at times where it became a distraction to the picture she was trying to paint. The two main characters are hard to get to know as the author relies entirely on flashbacks and ghosts. It ends with the same questions you had at the beginning that are never resolved leaving the reader wondering and left to draw their own conclusions which is rather annoying to me. Apart from that, the book has a vibrant Satanic element that was quite unsettling and rather disturbing. The bottom line? She tried too hard and overshot it with this one...

I went back and forth, between a three and a four, before deciding to rate this book a four. Despite describing Liberty as a place of "devastating violence," I was not anticipating a novel as disturbing as this one. There are a few scenes where I found myself thinking about them the next day, asking "Did I really read that?" The hatred, racism, and sexual violence in this book are strong, and frightening. It makes you question the nature of human beings, and how people can treat others in such inhumane ways. Ruby paints a picture of the Southern States, during a time that should never be allowed to be forgotten. 
 Despite the disturbing nature of this book, the writing is beautiful and powerful. There's a love story at the heart of this book that kept me reading. The characters are multi-faceted and well-developed. It's a surprising read, as you find it difficult to like everything even about one character - compared with most books where you are strongly fond of or connect with a character. This may very well be because it's historical fiction, and so far removed from anything I've ever experienced. 
 It's funny, now I've written a fairly lengthy review for what feels like the first time - now I'm questioning whether I should've given this book a five for provoking so much thought... I would encourage you to read this book, but warn you of the descriptive sexual violence.

Ruby is not quite what I was expecting. This was not my kind of book, and I was not able to discern this from the book's description, otherwise I would not have requested to read it. Since Ruby contains material that is both disturbing and far outside of my comfort zone, I have decided to discontinue reading it. I especially do not feel comfortable reading books that contain voodoo and the occult. I am also not particularly interested in reading long, detailed accounts of sexual abuse because I find it depressing. If this were non-fiction I might be a little more inclined to stick it out because it would be someone's actual experience and you can't sugarcoat facts; it is what it is. However, I don't find it necessary or desirable to sit through a fictional account of sexual depravity and such. I feel that my time would be better spent reading something more desirable. This book can be mentally draining which is not desirable to me. 
 I received a copy of this book from Blogging for Books in exchange for an honest review.

 Major Depressive Disorder; 
 its silent, malicious, and stealthy way of creeping into someone's life and taking it away, without people around being able to notice, no matter how close they were. 
 * The story also pictures the lives of relatives and friends to people who had committed suicide, grieving them, consoling them, telling them that it was not their fault, for the fault had always been the disease's. 
 *I didn't like the personality of the main character "Cody". 
 and I think that looking for a person whom helped her friend in her suicidal mission just to go to his place of residence to "talk to him, and let him know that someone knows" was so dumb. 
 * It was also terrible for romance, annoying, and encourages skipping paragraphs. 
 In General: 
 it is the meaning behind the story that made me like it -kind of- enough to read it all.

reference_books.title: Cinder (The Lunar Chronicles, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I made the mistake of ( 
 judging a book by its cover 
 ); 
 The book title, the shoe on the cover... were a little discouraging. 
 I thought it was some kind of lame fairytale story, that involves a weak naive girl awaiting a prince to save her from her misery. 
 I only read it because I was curious that it has a high rate on Goodreads, and I'm glad I did !. 
 Yes, the first chapter was a little confusing, I was thinking: "am I missing something? is it me that is misunderstanding?", and when I had finally comprehended, I was worried that it is one of those poor novels. 
 But, turns out it's not ! 
 No weak girl, raised to be a "housewife". 
 No pathetic dreams of wanting a prince to give her a "happily ever after". 
 No sickening, unreal romance. 
 No "the good always wins", or "people never die", or "worlds full of glitter and rainbows" 
 but rather, an independent, strong, fearless girl. 
 That strives for freedom; and ready to fight front row, not hiding behind a man. 
 And although roses may grow amidst thorns; People are full of hatred towards each other, Evil may win, people die, and the world is a dreadful place. (convincing enough) 
 An impressive build of a human-machinery world. 
 A Total page turner ! 
 I have only finished it now at 9:08 am. couldn't sleep without reading it all. 
 unfortunately, I found out that although I had finished reading the book, the story did not finish. 
 This was my first Lunar Chronicles novel to read, and I am excited to read the rest. 
 I would love to see this made into a movie !

reference_books.title: The Tales of Beedle the Bard
reference_books.review_text:

 I am fascinated by the limitless imagination of Rowling's. 
 some people thought the book is not suitable for children for different reasons -which can all be found on Disney movies-, but I find 4 of these stories -excluding hairy heart- suitable for children, & I do want to read them for my future kids-if I ever had any-. 
 Those stories teach the consequences of decieving, lying, power, selfishness, preferring shallow life choices to those wiser ones. & teach Independence, strength, courage, helping others, feeling others' pains, & thinking wisely. 
 It's a light, small book, I read the first story with its Dumbledore notes in 20 minuts. & completed the rest of the book the next day in 2 hours (may be you will take less if you're a native English speaker or if your English is better than mine.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Found this while picking up my book club book. I wasn't all that interested in the movie but the back cover caught my attention. 
 I liked this book, although I was a little put off by some of the scenes. At first, I thought that the many characters and POVs were disjointed. I understood how they were connected but I had been under the impression the story would be more about Oskar and the vampire, Eli. Of course, their story was complicated. 
 The last twenty pages or so had me on the edge of my seat as everything came to a climax. Not to say that the rest of the novel wasn't a page-turner, the last chapter was the most action-packed. 
 I did find the way the dialogue was written a little distracting. There were a lot of pauses and trailing off. I know people speak like but every single character did. Of course, I'm extra sensitve to things like that with my own novel in the process of publication. 
 I would recommend "Let Me In" with the disclaimer that there are some disturbing scenes. Europeans are just more liberal with sexual and abuse themes, and I had to keep telling myself that.

"Are you OLD?" 
 "No. I'm only twelve. But I've been that for a long time." 
 Let Me In is definitely one people need to talk about in the horror and/or dark novel community. This story does way more than tell a vampire story- it explores the darkness of humanity in, most of the time, unsettling ways that make your stomach turn. I personally don't think this is done enough in horror novels or films and I wish more would explore these themes as well. I think it could be more than just a scary monster chasing you- horror or "scary"can be the things that we as humans see in other humans such as murderers, pedophiles, rapists; self-harm and mutilation. The friendship between Oskar and Eli, while not a normal one, will stick with me for sure. This novel is definitely more literary horror (does this genre exist? It does now!) as it's scenery, environment heavy with sparse and blunt dialogue.

This is the story of a young boy named Oskar who becomes friends with a seemingly androgynous child vampire named Eli. Prior to befriending Eli, Oskar's oddities had prevented him from having many friends. To name a few, he is plagued with the inability to maintain control of his bladder, and he also possesses some rather morbid fantasies. As a result of his loner status, Oskar is bullied in horrific ways at school by a group of lecherous boys. Oskar believes that Eli is a girl (and a potential girlfriend) when he meets her, but actually Eli was a boy before becoming a vampire and being castrated 200 years prior. 
 Eli moves into Oskar's apartment building with an older man named Hakan who is supposedly his father, but is actually a disgusting pedophile who is obsessedly in love with the child vamp. Because Eli needs living blood to survive, Hakan takes responsibility for the necessary murders to keep him strong. Haken targets children for the killings because they put up less of a fight and therefore less chance of mistakes. Eventually Hakan is caught in the midst of a botched murder attempt and has to take drastic action to keep Eli's secret. There are subplots in the book that revolve around the locals who are trying to solve the sudden spike in gruesome murders in their community. 
 In the end, Oskar finally stands up to the bullies who have been torturing him throughout the story. Instead of keeping those kids away however, an older brother gets involved and is on the verge of killing Oskar - until Eli saves Oskar in his own unique way. 
 I like scary books, I like vampire and supernatural books, I even like violent books... But I just could not like this book. It was my mistake that I bought the book thinking it was a Paranormal book and it is not. This book is Horror, no question about it. With that said, it wasn't the blood and gore that caused me to dislike it. I was actually okay with that part of the book. What I couldn't stomach was the violence specifically toward children throughout the entire book. There was more than one scene that would be any parent's worst nightmare. 
 Besides the fact that Oskar is bullied by older and stronger boys in torturous ways that made me sick to my stomach, there were other scenes that absolutely horrified me. Early on in the book, Hakan (the pedophile) hires a 9 yr old boy for oral sex. This boy had all of his teeth knocked out by his pimp so he could be sold for oral sex without his teeth getting in the way. Further in the story, a boy wakes up after being gassed to find that he has been strung upside down by his feet and is about to be drained of his blood while still alive. These are examples, but certainly not the only instances of horrid violence toward children. 
 If the same book had been written about adults, I may have been able to be more objective about the writing. I just simply could not get past the graphic depiction of violence against kids. We all have lines that we don't like to cross, and this is mine. This was horror in its most evil and ugly form. 
 My poor rating of this book has nothing to do with the creativity or the quality of writing. My poor rating is only because I personally did not like the book. It made me sick to my stomach literally. Read at your own risk.

After having seen both films I found the book every bit at fascinating but existing within it's own energy. I found the comparison between book and films interesting: how Oskar is a rather ungainly and not particularly attractive in the book but is portrayed by two pretty boys in both films, who dies and when, and the license taken with what is omitted in both films. Lindqvist's prose is succint and what my BiL Richard called the 'Swedish Weirdness' in the film Let Me In plays better in prose, gives the story more depth. 
 I don't really see the comparisons with Anne Rice that are claimed in the cover reviews because I find Lindqvist's writing more honest and not as affected. 
 I look forward to reading more of his work.
The details and extra characters ruined this one for me. I was enjoying it at first but then it just got boring.

An anti-Twilight vampire romance/horror novel? My curiosity thus piqued, I began the ultimate descent into a Swedish vampire nightmare. 
 The book begins with introducing a young boy Oskar, who is a loner and frequently bullied at his school. One day he meets a young girl, Eli, at his apartment whom he befriends and falls in love with; even as he becomes more aware of her increasingly bizarre habits and behaviors. Peppered in with the central story are other characters within the town. There's a group of poor alcoholic peers dealing with their own issues and the mysterious murder of one of their friends, the bully's point of view, and a teenage boy living in Oskar's apartment complex. Eli's "father" is given his own storyline as well. I am still deciding whether or not I like this tactic. On one hand, using multiple characters and perspectives, Lindqvist transforms the novel from a simple bloody horror fest to a sort of social commentary on the poor and overlooked population in Sweden. However, I found myself caring more about Oskar and Eli and wished their relationship and plot line had been more flushed out. 
 This is a heavy, dark book, and not just because of the vampire aspect. Pedophilia, genital mutilation, violence, alcoholism, poverty, and loneliness are all equally prominent themes which together create a sense of pure dread. I took longer to read this book than I expected because I needed to take frequent breaks and watch something funny on Netflix to mitigate the effects this story had on me. 
 On the other hand, this book is very well written and fans of the horror genre will not be disappointed. It's creepy in a way that it sneaks up on you, making you feel like you're walking down a dark street and are positive someone is following you, even though you keep turning around and see nothing. 
 As people have said before, this is the ultimate anti-Twilight book. It's a vampire love story, but it's not sparkly skin and Robert Pattinson's pouty expression. It takes the erotic themes associated with vampires and twists them in a way that is satisfyingly disturbing to a horror fan like me. 
 Curl up in a blanket, and invite this book in.

Sometimes I wish books came with trigger warnings. 
 I didn't know anything about the story beyond the vaguest outline or I probably would have skipped it entirely. 
 Don't get me wrong, this is a well written book, no argument about that. 
 I do understand that the humans being the real monsters is pretty much the whole point, but holy crap. 
 With the exception of Virginia -who was actually somewhat likeable- and Eli, who was just flat and quite uninteresting, my reaction to the characters ranged from dislike to outright repulsion. 
 To me the book wasn't scary or gripping, just depressing and upsetting.

I've been trying to write a worthy review of this one, but I keep falling short. This one was excellent. Kept me up nights, like a horror story should. Got into my head. I really liked it. Do it again!
Ugh! I could not get into this book

book_b.user_review: Boring.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I used to love Patricia Cornwell. Her Scarpetta books were my absolute favorite, but now, things are going awry. 
 I found Predator very difficult to get into. It felt disjointed. I didn't feel that I knew much about the characters (old and new) and what I did read about them confused me. They seemed to evolve to different people that they have been in the past. I know people change, but the characters are changing too much and too quickly. 
 I also found the ending very unsatisfying. I had too many questions to answer that I know won't get answered in the next book. I still have questions from previous books that haven't been answered!
got to page 310 of 405. It was awful. I cared so little about the characters and the story, that I was able to leave the book unfinished.

All the usual characters are present but each of them are sad, angry and bitter with little interaction between them. A most unusual book. By the way, what happened at the end? Scarpetta is strangled one minute, then riding along happily in a car the next, no explanation. All in all an unhappy book about twisted people

Credit where credit is due: I hate books written in the present tense AND I went into this book expecting a forensic mystery. 
 That being said, the pacing was terrible, the book was so overstuffed that at one point, in the middle of discussing a crime scene we get step by step details of the main character cooking a risotto and the most minute of characters (characters who were mentioned on less than two pages) were given names and personalities. The ending was the most trite thing imaginable and several plot holes were left unfilled. 
 By far, the best thing about this book was the forensics -- full of luminol and superglue fuming; however, forensics took a far back seat to the life details of every minor character.

Remember when you could actually read and enjoy the Kay Scarpetta books from Patricia Cornwell? 
 Back when the series started, Kay was human, had a sense of humor, enjoyed cooking, did things normal people do. As the series has gone on, it has gotten darker, weirder (not a word, I know), more ominous, just...horrid. 
 The characters have degenerated into caricatures of their worst selves. The world has become sinister and evil. Honestly, there isn't anything enjoyable about reading these books. Who wants to read an extended description of torture? 
 It makes me remember why I quit reading them a while back.
I have enjoyed all the other Scarpetta books but I had to got myself to finish this one.
The early ones were better -- but I'm still going to read the next one.

Where have Scarpetta, Benton, Marino and Lucy gone? This book feels like a poor science fiction novel where the intelligent and likable characters were all abducted by aliens and replaced with cartoonish alien beings who are trying to mimic the originals. On top of that the story is complicated -- but not complex and surprising. The mysterious bits are not shocking and surprising and interesting, they are just confusing. 
 I miss the people from the first ten books of the series who allowed us to understand their friendships, love and mutual respect. I miss the people who had things they loved to do -- like Scarpetta's love of cooking. I miss the people who worked together to solve crime and although they got on each others' nerves, they never treated each other with disdain. 
 My hope is that this book was written by a ghost writer, an apprentice, a person who doesn't know and love the characters the way Cornwell did and I did.
What a crock of shit! I'm done!! No plot, nothing!
I hated it. I couldn't make it past the second chapter. This author's style is not my cup o' tea.

reference_books.title: The Dream Lover: A Novel of George Sand
reference_books.review_text:
I'm a huge fan of Elizabeth Berg, and was intrigued when you announced that she was going to writer her first historical fiction. The Dream Lover is a fictionalized autobiography of Aurore Dupin Dudevant, better known as George Sand, the flamboyant French nineteenth-century novelist who is probably best-known today for her intimate associations with most of the leading artistic names of her era, most notably her affairs with Frederic Chopin and Alfred de Musset and friendships with people like Gustave Flaubert and Franz Lizst. I attended the spring luncheon to hear Elizabeth speak and read from her book. 
 This is her first foray into historical fiction and Elizabeth Berg does not disappoint. I knew little about George Sand prior to reading the book, and Ms. Berg certainly put a "face" on her persona, allowing us a glimpse into this interesting and admirable woman!

reference_books.title: Circling the Sun
reference_books.review_text: Very disappointed in this book. What I thought was going to be a wonderful heroic story of Beryl Markman was more a book about wealthy British expats in Africa in the early 1900's. Everyone has too much time on their hands, relationships revolve around drinking and bed hopping and everyone has horses. This could have been a wonderful book about a woman far ahead of her time, and her aspirations involving aviation. I really enjoyed The Paris Wife. This book fell flat.

reference_books.title: The Valley of Amazement
reference_books.review_text:
Can't believe I got through this book! I should not have picked it up while packing and organizing a home move. However, I wanted this book to "take we away" for respite during this crazy time in my life, and house! No could do.... 
 This book is too similar to Tan's other books, and in fact most of the books I read about generational females from China. The book was WAY too long, too disjointed, too predictable. 
 I felt no emapthy for the characters, the women all headstrong and made very poor decisions, the men either wimps or con artists. 
 I'm so sad that I wasted my time on this book. Can't believe this is the same author that I loved!

reference_books.title: The Ashford Affair
reference_books.review_text:
I had high hopes for the generational novel The Ashford Affair by bestselling author Lauren Willig. The career lawyer with no social life, a grandmother with a secret, while enticing, failed to live up to the mystery that "kept me up late into the night". From Ashford Park in the early twentieth century to present day Manhattan, with a brief interlude in Kenya, the book had the makings of a fascinating tale reminiscent of Downton Abbey, but failed to deliver. I found few if any characters inspiring or likable. From other reviews it appears that this author, whom I've never read before, has lots of followers and they truly enjoyed this book. 
 Things I did like about the book was the movement from different timelines throughout history and the present day. I enjoyed the descriptions of Kenya, and the author wrote with a richness of the country which was appreciated. It was to me, more of a romance novel rather than a historical fiction. I'm a character driven reader, and the characters to me, were rather distasteful. 
 I can think of several people that I know that will really enjoy this book, so I'm now going to pass it on! I think one of them has read a series of books by this author as well, so that will be a plus.

book_a.title: To Kill a Mockingbird
book_a.user_review:
Last month a book club I belong to read this book, and Go Set a Watchman together. I hadn't read TKAM since I was a young teen. I'm glad I read this again. I have agonized over how to rate and review this book for several weeks. I'm not going to mince words. In my opinion, this book is not good. Most people in my book club did not really enjoy it either. Many of us thought that while we enjoyed it in our youth, truly, it wasn't very good. I'm not even going to go into why I didn't like the book except to say, personally, I think the writing was terrible. The fact that this is considered an "American classic", makes me feel ill. Because of all the hoopla regarding her other book, more people were talking about Harper Lee, her writing, and what was so glaring for me is how many people liked the book, but LOVED the movie, and perhaps interchanged the characters. I don't know how many times I've read or heard that Gregory Peck WAS Atticus or vice versa. 
 I also was surprised how long and boring the book seemed to be. And Boo Radley? My word, the book was mostly about him wasn't it? lol 
 Can't wait for all the bashing now this review will get!

With all of the publicity surrounding Lee's new release, I decided to re-read To Kill a Mockingbird. What a great book full of messages people should take to heart. The language used is gorgeous. I loved it even more as an adult!

This was a re-read in conjunction with reading Go Set a Watchman. Like many others, I think Mockingbird is the far superior novel. 
 The writing of To Kill a Mockingbird is nothing special overall. It doesn't require a graduate level English course or Cliffs Notes to decipher. But the beauty is certainly in the simplicity. It's a quaint novel, telling the childhood of the Finch kids and the various characters who inhabit their world - small town Maycomb, Alabama. 
 Much of the story is typical kids stuff - fisticuffs on the playground and sibling dynamics. But things take a turn when their father has to defend a black man accused of raping a white woman. Scout and her brother Jem must contend with heavy issues that force them to grow up and see their world in a new - and not better - way. 
 I appreciated the story from Scout's point of view. It lent so much color and humor to the the book. I also liked the world that Harper Lee created. It felt real, from the descriptions of the town square to the townspeople's varied personalities. And its message of kindness and justice for all is necessary and accessible to both young people and adults. I think it's a must read for everyone.
I've read this book twice and loved it both times. :)

4.5/5

R- I thought I was a very good book. Although I didn't really choose to read this book, I thought it was very good. I developed a strong connection with the characters and the writing style was good. For forced read it was great.

I was fifteen or sixteen when I first read To Kill a Mockingbird. It was high school, that great bastion of superficial drama that I still can't seem to rid myself of eighteen years after graduation, where I first heard of Harper Lee's novel. I was much closer to Jem and Scout's age then than I am now. I can't truthfully recall, but I was much less jaded back in the tenth grade than I am now. I probably would have believed then that Tom Robinson wouldn't be convicted. Ah, the delusions of the young. Now if you will permit me one quick Harry Potter quote: "Fear of a name increases fear of the thing itself." While we cannot take Dumbledore at his literal word, for Lord Voldemort does not exist in Maycomb, Alabama, we can still extrapolate from it: that which is avoided, is that which is feared even more. That, dear readers, is applicable to Mockingbird. That being said, I think that this is still a novel of hope. It if were not for the children, there would be no hope for anything. 
 Classical novels are classic for a reason. They are well written and usually quite accessible (though I would argue the contrary point if we're discussing Russian literature). Mockingbird is an easy, if uncomfortable, read, told from the point of view of Scout Finch, a young girl. If newspapers are still to be believed, this is a prequel to Lee's recently published Go Set A Watchman. If true, it makes Mockingbird all the more remarkable. Such a powerful novel written on request? Impressive. 
 The children are the key to this story because of their lack of cynicism and hypocrisy. Why, poor Dill got physically sick at now the prosecutor was treating Tom Robinson. None of the adults, except perhaps his own neighbours, even batted an eye at Tom's treatment. They shunned Mr. Raymond, with his alcohol filled coke bottle, him and his 'nigger-wife.' What did Dill do when he discovered Raymond's secret? Not faint. He laughed. He and Scout did not run crazily up and down the streets when they learned the truth that Mr. Raymond put on an act that he was drunk to help the townspeople accept that he chose to be with a coloured woman. What a perfect example of the occupational malleability of children, and that hate is a learned and not innate response to difference. 
 I have only yesterday started reading Go Set a Watchman, and will have comments on that later, but I have read that Atticus is depicted as a racist. This is disappointing on the surface, however it made me wonder about how he was not depicted as a racist in this novel. Assuming this wasn't an error, and I have confidence in Lee as a writer that it was not, I can see one of two reasons for this apparent discrepancy, and they could each be true in part. Atticus was a man of great character and morals. Perhaps he was racist, but when called on to defend Tom Robinson, he did it to the best of his ability because he knew no other means. Setting a good example for his children would come of that. The other option, and certainly could overlap, was that he chose to act the way he did to help better his children. Kids learn by example, if he realized that his own beliefs were wrong but could not change them, he at least had the ability to show his children a better way to act. They say you can't teach an old dog new tricks, but a puppy is no problem. Atticus at one point tells his children that he got started late, perhaps too late to change his ways, but still able to provide a better path for the kids? 
 Way back in 1935 they could feel that change was coming, with the jury being out as long as it was, and not just convicting right away. We also see that it does not come only with the ebb and flow of the tide. We are able to effect change. When the mob shows up at the jail to kill Tom, Atticus is there to fend them off, but so are his children. Jem refuses to leave. Scout, for her part, singles out someone she knew and started talking to him, eventually breaking mob mentality and sending everyone home. Perhaps she is a psychologist in her adult life, because she certainly got through the anonymity thing. 
 I wrote elsewhere about fear, and repeat myself enough already to not want to do it again, but I think the same thing applies here. There is a reason they say fearful dogs are the most dangerous: fear is a great motivator but can cause us to act rashly and irrationally. And in the deep south, circa mid-20th century, fear of the 'coloureds' was high. Fear and hatred. The black people were great scapegoats for all manner of crimes. They were looked down on as savages, inhuman, trash, animals, you name it, what happened when Tom Robinson made the mistake of saying he felt sorry for Mayella Ewell? Outrage. How dare a nigger feel sorry for his betters, even if that white woman entrapped him? Disgusting. 
 Robinson represents the African American people as a whole, and the unjust system that they had to endure, are still having to endure. it is disgusting to think that fifty, nearly sixty years on from To Kill A Mockingbird, progress in many respects is going backwards. #blacklivesmatter is an important and sadly necessary movement. I am even more revolted by the ignorant asses who start the while lives matter, too whine. Not the point at all, you arrogant fucking pricks. Millenia of history have shown that white lives matter, and we still live it every minute of every day. Perhaps if we would take our heads out of our asses long enough to look around we would see that we are not the only people on this earth. 
 Unfortunately, justice for the likes of Tom Robinson and Boo Radley only come in fiction. 
 What angers me most is the total, TOTAL hypocrisy of the Maycomb residents. Scout's teacher in one scene is lamenting the terrible fate of the Jews who were being persecuted by Hitler, but could not recognize just as bad an injustice in her own town? The Ewells were only white trash when they were talked about by other white folk. If a colored even 'felt sorry' for her, he was guilty. 
 'Mr. Underwood simply figured it was a sin to kill cripples, be they standing, sitting or escaping. he likened Tom's death to the senseless slaughter of songbirds by hunters and children . . . " (p. 275). 
 And it is. It really is!

It took me a good few chapters to get properly interested in this book but I'm glad I did! Such a lovely story and from the view point of a child makes it so endearing. This book illustrates that racism is a learned behaviour and children see people for themselves rather than what they look like, until society ruins them. I will definately lend my book to family to read.
