I don't even know why they teach it in schools because you can't even learn a lesson other than "Gosh nobody likes an over-dramatic spoiled brat who thinks they have the worst life ever." Thank goodness its a short book because if it were any longer I probably wouldn't have been able to finish it.

Watched the J D Salinger documentary on PBS this week and am going to read this again. 
 It is still a fail. I don't understand why this book is listed as a classic nor do I understand how three people felt compelled to shoot innocent people ( hinkley ronald reagan and tom bradley, campbell john lennon and the guy who shot the rising star actress of the series " my sister sam)after reading this book? 
 after watching the documentary, people fell in love with this book because the main character, Holden, points people out as phoneys and all these teenagers and young adults appaulded this character insight. I miss be missing something because HOLDEN IS THE PHONEY! He gets kicked out of an elite school ( his fourth) and instead of facing his parents knowing that the dean sent his termination letter to his parents and thinks he has 3 days before his parents will receive said letter, so he goes to New York City, lie about himself, his name and puts himself in these situations that are stupid. He just your typical angry kid who thinks he knows more than adults ( like most young adults), won't listen to anybody and believes he has it all figured out. 
 I can see why this book was not required reading at my high school in the 80's in KCK because of the swearing in the book as well as his analogies are violently themed i.e page 106 he describes how a guy really likes a girl as " cutting his throat over her." 
 Yes, I understand Salinger was in WW 2 when he carried 6 chapters of this book with him and wrote this book during WW2 and he spent over 200 days in horrific war battles until the war ended on V day, but jeesh, this book is loaded with violent references and what is sad the main character can't fight! Holden is always running his mouth and when push come to shove, he can't fight, cannot stick up for himself so he couldn't help anyone else ( i.e. damsel in distress) and yet he feels he is so powerful great guy when in fact HE IS THE PHONEY! 
 I think this book is overrated. Maybe this was the first book of its kind that came out in which described what young males were feeling in the 50's and 60's and now years later television, movies, music have taken this step further with depicting young adult's move from child to adulthood, realizations one's parents aren't the all and powerful but human, and people make mistakes and one has to make one's way in the world, I will give this book credit for that. 
 This book was difficult to like and while I was reading this, I kept thinking, " So what" and " what is the big deal about this book?" since it still sells over 250,000 copies each year. 
 well, I read it again and no I am not going to read the detailed books of the HOlden life up to his suicide prior to him searching for God which is suppose to come out between 2015 and 2020 as the documentary teased at the end that Salinger gave permission to have this and two other books released after his death ( which is what he was working on all these years). 
 I think salinger was like any other writer/artist: don't change my stuff, what I create is personal and his tantrums when editors changed the title or this that and the other is a part of publishing. ask any writer and i think salinger was just too sensitive about his work and was over dramatic just like any eccentric artist. so to me, he wasn't any different than Warhol or Monroe etc. He just chose to remove himself from the public ( when he chose to come out he did) and do what he loved to do and deal with his demons from war. Why people blew him up to be this false god of the publishing industry is beyond me. Sorry did get it and found his documentary interesting as most artist are.

I guess I can understand why the adolescent male really connects with this book. Just a whole lot of immaturity and bad language all rolled into about 200 pages. I want to tell Holden to "get over yourself, already". I don't understand why this is considered a classic. Blah.
Hated this book! Is there even a storyline? I kept waiting for it to come to life, but it never did.

I don't like this book for two reasons. 1. Holden is a whiny, obnoxious, self-centered baby and I find reading about him unpleasant. 2. I don't like the style of Salinger's writing. 
 In high school this was one book I refused to read. I had to teach it a few years ago, and my students had the same reaction to it that I did.
As good as teen angst gets!

I really tried to enjoy this. But it was way too much rambling and I didn't quite understand the significance of the storyline. Holden constantly repeats himself and then rambles on about something random for a few pages. The book could easily be summed up in 5 pages if you took away the rambling. Holden was not a lovable character, I found him too arrogant.

reference_books.review_text:
The first time I read this book was over six years ago..maybe seven, and I hated it. When it became this huge phenomenon I couldn't understand what all the hype was about, but I decided to give it another try. I'm so glad I did because this book is definitely worth reading. reference_books.review_text:
Ugh! When someone puts a collection of short stories out, the stories should be short! Some of the stories were really novellas. I could only read one, however, because the characters were sooooo boring, and all I could think of was how uninteresting the story actually was. reference_books.title: The Historian
reference_books.review_text:
I got so excited when I read the back cover of this book. I love reading about dark points in history and was intrigued that someone was going to write a vampire story with the motivator for the character of Dracula as one the main characters, and then I began the book. 
 I know I have marked this in my list of books I've read, but halfway through I just couldn't swallow any more of this trollop. Between the painfully boring descriptions of everything encountered to the meandering quest of the main character, I just couldn't take it anymore, and I believe I gave it a fair shot. I read over 300 pages before I threw in the towel. I kept telling myself that it would pick up, but you can only fool yourself for so long. 
 Brutally, horrid book.

reference_books.title: A Million Little Pieces
reference_books.review_text: At first I enjoyed this book even if it did seem a bit extreme at times to believe. Then I was told that the whole thing was a lie. I finished the book anyway and then immediately ripped it into pieces as I was so disgusted with a person who would fill so many pages with lies that I didn't want it sullying my house any longer.

book_a.user_review: I think I could have liked this book if I had been able to interpret more than 10% of the slang. Most pages were read with a vague sense of knowing how the plot was moving. The slang was so heavy that even the context couldn't help me because the context was more slang. I finished this book feeling very frustrated.

sample_reviews.review_text: Couldn't get through the whole thing.

I had somewhat high expectations for this book, as it is so well known... 
 I hated it. 
 Don't get me wrong, the writing was good, often poetic, to the extent that even though I didn't understand a lot of the words, you could still get the gist, which makes for a clever author. 
 But the STORY, urgh. Yes, themes are all there, I understand the moral, but the story? It was grim. It was hard not to wince at some parts of this book. Maybe it's my gender speaking for me, but it was so uncomfortable to read. 
 I forced myself to the end of this book in the hopes that there would be some light at the end of the tunnel but I was wrong. I just felt empty, angry and deflated. 
 Would I put this book in my top 100? No. Would I recommend it to someone else? Probably. Just because I feel liked it was a learning curve for me. 
 However, I would not ever read it again and I most definitely won't be watching the film.

Not sure how I feel about this book. The vocabulary made it quite hard to understand, although easier to stomach some of the super violent scenes, especially early on. I would agree that the last chapter, omitted in the American version, ends on a note of optimism that I don't think the story ever merits. 
 Alex's remorse under reconditioning is not true remorse; it's merely classical conditioning at its finest. As the chaplain put it, "a man who cannot choose ceases to be a man." And when he can choose, he chooses violence again, which says a lot about the human condition. Others in the story show little or no remorse either, as his victims turn around to brutalize him just as easily. 
 There were some salient points about the government however, especially regarding the cycle of violence and power and how violence maintains power. Still mulling over the story though. Might be good for a revisit later.

What can I say...this was one of the strangest books I have ever read. I was a little nervous to read it considering I had heard about the movie when I was in college and all that was entailed in it...but I was curious and wanted to know more. Boy...I'm glad they have an introduction to this book to help explain what in the heck is going on here. The language is something else..."nasdat".....the talk of teenagers at that time. It does help to soften the reading of the gross violence that Alex bestows upon his many victims by sounding it out in "nasdat talk"...but it is still so strange and foreign. I could not entirely enjoy this book...I suppose it kept my interest...I did not find it boring...but I did not find myself wanting to race through my daily routine to get back to it. But hey...now I can finally say I actually read it!

There is only one thought that comes to mind after reading this book: 
 Jesus wept.
I get why this book is a classic but I hated it so there you go!
Amazing.

I had to watch the Kubrick film of Clockwork several times for a couple of film studies classes I took, and every time I did I hated it. There was always an eye roll and a "oh not this again!" mental note. So when we got around to writing papers I completely ignored this film. 
 So now.. approximately 2 years later, I am going back and actually reading the books to the films we studied (it wasn't encouraged in class to avoid comparisons or bias, the film should stand alone we were told). At any rate, I am so very glad I read this, and so very glad I read it after I saw the movie! My mental scenes were so vivid, it was like watching a better and more intricate version of the film. Also I was surprised at how easily I could pick up on his language and the meanings to the words. 
 I also noticed that the book was very efficient at removing the reader from the violence through the use of the Nadsat slang language of the droogs. I kept commenting to myself repeatedly throughout the book, how much reading the violent passages in plain talk would have been highly disturbing to me, and yet reading it in Nadsat, it wasn't. The film did not have this effect at all. The weird language did nothing to alter the sharpness of the violence. 
 I also very much love the 21st chapter. Perhaps one of the reasons I hated the film so much is because Alex did not learn or grow, it was as if his whole crazy journey was pointless because nothing changed in the end. I was pleased and surprised to see that Burgess actually wrote a last chapter that the US publishers had removed. It gave me a closure that the film could not. 
 And lastly, of course, the unavoidable philosophical questions that repeatedly surface throughout the book. The age old question of free will. If free will is what ultimately makes us human, and distinguishes us from machines, robots, or AI, then conditioning free will out of someone would whittle them down to just a machine, or a puppet. So although Alex is really quite an awful person, the reader cannot help but to subtly root for him, and hope for a cure to his conditioning. 
 I really have no critiques for this book. I thought it was excellently composed for all of the reasons stated above.

Excellent book. There was a period where the last chapter was actually edited out and banned in the 60's but rereleased in the 80's if I remember correctly. Get the unedited version and you'll laugh at why it was banned. There is a version that also has the slang dictionary, after reading this book, I had to catch myself from saying some of these terms. This is one of those books that is epic and has a cult following, I highly recommend it.

I was kind of worried that I was going to find this boring or hard to understand but it ended up being a very interesting read. I listened to the audiobook narrated by Tom Hollander and it was a great experience. His performance of Alex was spot on and he nailed the voices each and every character. There's quite a bit of made up language in this book but listening to the audio helped me catch on quickly. I eventually found myself thinking with Nadsat words, haha. 
 I really appreciated the brevity of this book - it was just long enough to explore the theme of good vs. evil. It was extremely interesting (and kind of horrifying) to read from the perspective of a completely immoral narrator. I wasn't sold on what happens in the last chapter but I kind of liked the conclusion anyway. 
 ...I wish I could write a more insightful review about this classic, but I'm terrible at Goodreads reviews.

book_b.title: The Last Lecture
book_b.user_review:
Excellently written. I really needed to read something uplifting as I'm embarking on a new chapter in my life and feeling quite a bit of trepidation. Although I am not terminally ill there is no reason that this book wouldn't inspire anyone who picked it up to continue to shoot for the stars and keep after the things you want until you get them. I have always felt that I have led a charmed life because I have pushed and pushed and pushed for the things in my life until I have gotten them. Sometimes it takes months, sometimes only days, and sometimes it takes decades, but I have always led a rich life filled with things I have always wanted. I completely believe in the power of karma and positive thinking. 
 I recommend this to anyone that already thinks like the author or just needs a reminder that you aren't alone and that you can do anything with a little bit of optimism and good faith.

A few years ago I spent about 10 months writing a blog that wasn't about anything in particular. It was meandering and unfocused and, ultimately, useless (as a lot of blogs tend to be). I gave up on it without much thought, regretting only that I didn't make more of the opportunity. You see, blogs are almost universally panned at this stage of the game, but I'm one of the few (as you seem to be) that sees the value inherent in being given the chance to lay your thoughts out, completely uninhibited, for the whole world to read. There's something refreshingly intimate yet communal about blogging, and I was disappointed that I'd swung and missed (or, more accurately, I wished I'd at least taken the bat off my shoulder). 
 A year or two later I started flirting with the idea of writing another blog, but I wanted something of substance, something with meaning, something that would have a practical application for someone other than myself. What I ultimately wanted to do was share a bit about who I was and how I thought. I wanted a written record of me in my 20s, not so much for my friends and my family, but for my theoretical children. 
 I don't have kids. But I desperately want them some day, and I want them to know what their dad was like, especially in those prime, formative years. In a way I never knew my birth father, and I was damn sure to not let that happen to them. 
 Regrettably, I never set out on that particular quest. To this day I'm not quite sure why. But I still believe in the concept, which is, in part, why I was initially drawn to Randy Pausch's The Last Lecture. 
 Back in 2008, Pausch, a computer science professor at Carnegie Mellon, was asked to give a "Last Lecture", in which he was asked to consider his own demise and ruminate on what mattered most to him. This concept is a common one, for professors have been giving "last lectures" all over the country for years. But with Pausch, he didn't have to imagine it as his last, since he had recently been diagnosed with terminal cancer. 
 The lecture he gave, entitled "Really Achieving Your Childhood Dreams", wasn't about dying. It was about the importance of overcoming obstacles, of enabling the dreams of others, of seizing every moment (because "time is all you have...and you may find one day that you have less than you think"). It was a summation of everything Randy had come to believe, but more than anything, it was a time capsule of Randy himself, one that he wanted to leave for his three young children (ages 6, 3, and 1). 
 Randy, like myself, was asking the questions, What wisdom do I want to impart on my children, before I no longer have the chance to do so? If I vanish tomorrow, what would I want as my legacy? 
 What resulted from those questions was a subtly unique piece of writing. 
 On the face of it, The Last Lecture is a not-all-that well-written series of anecdotes that are at times self-serving and schmaltzy. Pausch was an arrogant man (he freely admits this a dozen times) and he sometimes writes like one. He doesn't dole out life lessons as learned through others so much as he imparts self-evident truisms that seem to have been gifted to him from on high. For the most part, these lessons are important because Pausch tells us so, and we ought to treat them as gospel. 
 It's anecdote after anecdote in which Pausch, himself, is the star. 
 But that doesn't diminish the fact that there are many valuable pearls of wisdom in here. It's clear that Pausch was a smart man who'd learned a lot since 1961, and even if his lessons are aren't all that unique, they're true nonetheless (for the most part). 
 This is an emotional book. It's touching, at times beautiful, but also a bit of a mess, which is kind of the point. I ended up really enjoying the book because of what it represents. 
 I think the idea behind The Last Lecture is stronger than the inevitable result. I think the contents of this book are fantastic, but I don't think Randy Pausch is a writer (he wasn't). Had someone more equipped than Pausch written this material I think it might have had more gravitas and impact. Someone else would have written a quote/unquote "better" book, but what Pausch ended up producing is a more appropriate one. 
 When Pausch sat down to write this he had a few scant months left to live. What's great about this book is that you can tell. The whole thing is written with an immediacy and pace that befits someone who's about to die. It reads almost like a first draft or an overview, where each chapter is almost hurriedly accomplished in order to get everything out before the ideas fade away into those irretrievable vaults in his brain. Pausch doesn't wax poetic or deliver his final thoughts in flowery prose, he simply tells it as it is, because he doesn't have time for anything else. The result was a worse piece of writing, but a more affecting one, without doubt. 
 I loved that. 
 For the first half of the book my one complaint was the impatience of the thing. Randy, just slow the fuck down and let these lessons breathe a bit, I'd think. But once I understood what exactly was going on, I wouldn't have changed a thing. The Last Lecture reads almost like a stream-of-consciousness exercise written by someone with an extremely organized, mathematical mind. It's fascinating. 
 Like the lecture, the book is earnest and straightforward. Randy tells a story, then gives us the moral in case we missed it. What is extremely evident is his deep affection for his wife and children who he knew he would be leaving behind. It's impossible not to feel like you know Randy Pausch when this book is done. He seems like a genuinely good man who perhaps could use a little tact, but he sure made a fine teacher and mentor. He's a smart man who learned to never give up on what he really wanted ... but he also beats us over the head with that fact. 
 He has a lot of good things to say without a unique way of saying it. As a cathartic reading for families dealing with terminal illness this book would no doubt provide a salve, but as a sermon of wisdom this book offers many of the same chestnuts one would find in any self-help essay. This is a wonderful capsule of Randy and his family, but did it need to become a book? Maybe, maybe not. It's helped millions of people, so it's hard to argue to the contrary. It all depends on whether or not you can take something valuable from it. 
 The great thing about these types of books is that if the reader can find even one platitude that truly and powerfully speaks to him/her, then the purchase was worth it. For me, there are a handful of those in the book, and one in particular that will give me strength in the coming days. A few of my favorites: 
 "When you're screwing up and nobody says anything to you anymore, that means they've given up on you." (p. 37) 
 "Experience is what you get when you didn't get what you wanted." (p. 148) 
 "She's probably confused and scared to death. If she doesn't really love you, then it's over. And if she does love you, then love will win out." (p. 78) 
 "Brick walls are there for a reason. They give us a chance to show how badly we want something." (p. 79) 
 Near the end of the book Pausch talks about cliches and their inherent value. After all, they've become cliches for a reason. He references one I find particularly applicable here. It's a quote that goes, "Other than that, Mrs. Lincoln, how was the play?" It's a reminder not to focus on the little issues and to instead focus on the effectiveness of the whole. 
 The Last Lecture has its fair share of problems, but the whole is so much more than the sum of its parts. This is a work that's intensely personal and undeniably affecting. This is a book that truly has value and that's more than I can say for most of the shit that clutters the shelves. This was a labor of love ... a labor about love, in so many ways. 
 After his lecture was finished Pausch invited his wife, Jai, onto the stage with him. They embraced, kissed, and unable to think of anything else to say, Jai whispered in his ear, "Please don't die." 
 Find me a more touching, powerful moment than that and I'll call you a liar. 
 Randy Pausch will be missed by millions of people, but the good thing is that he's taken a piece of all of us with him. Wherever he is.

At Carnegie Mellon University there is a lecture series about life lessons that use to be titled "The Last Lecture" series. The name of the lecture series has changed since but the idea is the same - for professors and others to share their wisdom with students in an hour long lecture. For Randy Pausch the term "Last Lecture" is poignantly appropriate - he has terminal cancer and doctors had given him only 3-6 months to live. Pausch agreed to give his last lecture and it was filmed and uploaded to the internet. As often happens, things got a bit crazy after that. That video was watched by millions. It was passed around via social networks and email, word of mouth, featured on TV news programs and prime time shows. This book grew out of Pausch's lecture and perhaps as a result of all that popularity. 
 The book is not merely a rehashing of Pausch's lecture - though it does reiterate some of the points. It expands on the lecture and gives a more intimate look at Pausch's life, and his family following that devastating diagnosis. This book is Pausch's love note to his kids, trying to tell them about himself, about their lives together, about achieving dreams and living a good life and all those things he'll never be able to tell them. It's really inspiring and you have to admire Pausch's strength, conviction, honesty and positive attitude. I wish I'd had him as professor when I was in college. I bet he was phenomenal. 
 I appreciated that Pausch was honest about how hard things are as well. While he focused on positive things, on a life well lived and how to grab on to your dreams, he also talked about the fact that he and his wife attend therapy, that they've clung together and cried over the unfairness of it all. But the overwhelming message in this book is to live your life the best you can and to dream big. We can do more than we think we can and enjoy one hell of a ride along the way.

I think this was a great story. Yes a feel good story but with a twist the book is "supposedly" not written for money, for the kids he was giving the lecture to or anything but is actually for his kids who will never get to hear all these things, and all these wise words he has to say. I think that is what was so special about this book. Yeah ok so he probably made a fat load of money after the book was released and promoted on Oprah and whatever else, but ultimately it is what seems like a really good guys attempts to give something to his kids something that shows his nature, his life, his wisdom, his love, amongst other things. 
 I felt really strongly for Randy right through this book and even after the book was finished. He begins by "pointing out the elephant in the room" and straight away combatting any nerves or sympathy people had for him (and I had to look the AMAZING video up on you tube after reading the book and sat through the whole thing that way as well and Man, I can't do press ups!!) And then he talks to appealingly to his life, to what he's learnt, to things that he's noticed about people and about moving yourself forward, about his growth and about his struggles and stuff. 
 Perhaps not the best story in terms of a "story" but definately a great read if you read it KNOWING that it was delivered not as a book originally but as a man dying talking for the last time to his students and to his kids. THAT is what this book is. THAT is what this book should be reviewed as. 
 It gives you a lift in life and it talks about the potential for humananity to be decent to each other once more. It's almost as if he's left the most amazing gift to civilisation and that perhaps he really means the book to be about bettering yourself and the world we live in. A big ask, but like I say if this book is read as a last LECTURE and not just a money making scheme, then MAYBE hearts could be opened enough to go oh yeah maybe I can love my neighbour, help my neighbour, be grateful for my neighbour. You know what I mean?? Maybe not.

I feel like such a churl, disliking this book so much. Yes, it is a moving and sad story, but it is also a cliche riddled and dull book. The author is diagnosed with terminal cancer at the very young age of 46 and shares his life lessons. But the lessons range from the banal ("Work hard!") to the inane ("Never carry less than 200 dollars cash!"). I imagine that the lecture that led to the publication of this book was much more inspirational and interesting.

Lots of gems about how to live life to its fullest with the knowledge that life is short - much shorter than anticipated. The writing is honest, strong and vulnerable at the same time. This one's worth a second read.

I actually prefer Randy Pausch's actual lecture (available on youtube), but this book does provide many ideas to think about. I think he was an amazing man that truly exemplified a "pollyanna" attitude.
This book is escentially the things a dying man wants his children to know. I think insights from someone's final evaluations of life are invaluable. The tone wasn't sad, but light and fun.

How To Live Your Life 
 This book was loaned to me. I will return it to its rightful owner, however, I will also buy my own copy. It's the kind of book I want sitting on my nightstand--not in the massive "to-be-read" pile, but with the others I know I'll pick up again and again, just to be reminded of the wisdom. I will also pass it onto my daughters, as it's filled with a lot of parenting. 
 The Last Lecture, based on computer science Professor Randy Pausch's now famous "Last Lecture" given at Carnegie Mellon University shortly before pancreatic cancer took his life, is primarily a message to the three young children he knew he'd be leaving behind. When Pausch's diagnosis became terminal, this otherwise upbeat, dream-driven man dedicated his remaining months to recording everything he deemed important his children know about him. It's deeply affecting, and often brought tears to my eyes--not only because of his sad fate, but also because of his clear passion for living. One doesn't feel like an intruder while reading this highly personal memoir and collection of anecdotal essays about lessons learned. Instead, it's more like being a student in a class called "How to Life Your Life." 
 The Last Lecture is a beautiful gift to those who knew him, and those who will never have the opportunity to meet him. I highly recommend it for all readers.

Amulet #6 continues to follow the journey of the stone keepers and Navin. 
 The book is filled with action and adventures to keep young audiences engaged.

 Rating 4 out of 5 
 Read@Book

Every time these books start to show improvement, the next volume manages to dash all those rising hopes. How is it possible that this one is the worst yet? The pacing in this volume was absolutely terrible - characters jumped from dramatic moment to dramatic moment with very little linking them, and rather than pursuing character development for the existing cast, the author once again introduces another set of new folks for the readers to attempt forming a connection with. Max's storyline, like that of Trellis's brother in an earlier installment, made absolutely no sense in the context of his previous actions. Navin's status as "Commander" is ludicrous and even less deserved than Emily's stonekeeper skills: he skips and fails his classes and is constantly saved by those around him, while somehow being sold as a competent pilot and hero. There's a certain suspension of disbelief involved in stories where kids are the heroes, but there isn't even to grab onto to make this possible. I'm continually exasperated by how quickly characters' roles shift to fit the plot, a plot which changes at its author's whim, following no logical progression that I can find. I don't know why I'm even bothering to continue reading these books, other than the fact that I hate to leave things unfinished. This series is, overall, really not worth the effort.
Such a great series

This is probably the favorite graphic novel of my students. It's visually stunning with characters to which just about every kid can relate even if some of them fall a little flat at times. That mom is ... extremely trusting. Waaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaay more trusting than I would be of bunny robots and anyone who lives in a Cloud City. 
 The full page spreads in this volume outdo the other five. They are just gorgeous. Chronos, man. Chronos is awesome. I'm not a huge fan of portal fantasy, but this series is really delightful and one I would recommend to get young readers into the genre or as a fun fantasy for any comic fans. The main issue is it took so very long for vol. 6 to be released and who knows when we'll have vol. 7. Write, Kazu, write like the wind.
Not my favorite volume, but still really good! Super excited for the next volume to come out!
[2.5] This was not AS GOOD as the previous ones but still looking forward to reading the next book soon.
Trellis is basically Zuko from Avatar: The Last Airbender - with the scar and everything (and that's not a bad thing).

Book blurb: Emily, Navin, and their friends continue to battle the Elf King in hopes of destroying him forever, but one of his most loyal followers, Max, isn't making it easy for them. The crew journeys to Lucien, a city that's been ravaged by the war. Emily has more enemies there than she realizes -- and it'll take everything she's got to get herself and her friends out of the city alive. 
 I've said it before and I'll say it again, the best young adult graphic novels work really well for adults as well. Our heroes face new dangers on many fronts. Will they survive? This story will not make any sense unless you read the books in order, and I plan to revisit the entire collection once the story concludes. The art only is worth the price of admission.

When I heard there was a new Amulet book being released, I was ecstatic. I'd read the graphic novels as they were released and was eager to get my hands on a new one. However, because Volume 5 had been released so long ago, and I read it when it was first published, I couldn't recall a lot of the characters and what was happening. It was tough to read because I was like 'Who is she? Wait what? Where's Emily?' However, I still enjoyed the characters and plot, and mostly the gorgeous designs! My suggestion is to recap or re-read the previous volumes before reading this one.

 Things have definitely been brought up a notch in BREAKING POINT. We get to meet a ton of new interesting people and learn more about people we already know. The world building is just as fantastic as ARTICLE 5 and we get to see more of the landscape. There is a ton of action from start to finish. Chase and Ember's relationship is once again slow moving and a bit frustrating at times but you can definitely see their feelings in the way they describe their looks and those stolen unfiltered interactions with each other. They are both madly and deeply in love with each other and they are starting to open up again. There is great growth all around and I';m excited where things are headed.

"I'm sorry Article 5 (the series). 
 But I think we need to part ways. After getting to know you better via Breaking Point, I don't think we can stick in a relationship that will make both of us happy. 
 So it's best that we cut our losses and stop seeing each other." 
 That pretty much describes my reaction to reading Breaking Point. When I first read Article 5 I initially was quite enamored by it. There were some major flaws in it (like I can't stand the main character, Chase can be kind of bland and the lack of purpose towards the end of the book really really got to me) but just like anyone who gets into a new relationship, you get all these fluffy feels (and I did get them with article 5 I'll admit to that) and you either ignore or are blind to their initial flaws. But as the dust settles and realities come into play, these flaws start rearing it's ugly head and than there's screaming, the ranting, the rolling of eyes and you're hoping that at some point it'll change (It just gets better you tell yourself) but nothing happens and you're left right at the end contemplating what exactly happened and how did it end up like this? 
 First of all, I couldn't stand Ember as a main character (that should have been the deal breaker in my relationship with Article 5 but no I decided to be stubborn and continuously ignore it). In Article 5, she's quite tolerable but in Breaking Point she's melancholicly emo to the point that it gets downright annoying. She's also back to strange sense of justice and morals which we saw snippets of in Article 5 but get blown to full proportion here. Because of this her chemistry (or lack of chemistry to be honest) with Chase really suffers which brings me to my next point: 
 Chase Jennings is possibly the blandest character I've ever read in fiction... ever. Seriously, he makes grass growing an exciting hobby. His sole purpose in the book is to be a love interest and protector to Ember, when he's not doing that he's as interesting as watching paint dry! There's absolutely nothing to him in Breaking Point which is a pity because he had a lot of potential in Article 5. Due to the exciting plot twists and points in Article 5, you don't realize how bland a character he is until Breaking Point where the action is not as fast paced as it was in Article 5. Heck, if the 'antagonist' Tucker is more interesting and has BETTER chemistry with Ember than your main love interest than you have a problem. 
 I guess I didn't realize all these flaws because the plot in Article 5 was fast paced and interesting enough but in Breaking Point the plot isn't as interesting and a bit slow at times so the cracks began to show. 
 Anyway I don't think I'd continue this series at all and would probably recommend against starting it (even if Article 5 was a pretty decent book)

Breaking Point is the second in the much acclaimed Article 5 series. Ember Miller has escaped from the reformatory where she had been placed after being arrested for being born out of wedlock. The not too distant future has a post war government ruling the country with an iron fist, exchanging the Bill of Rights for "Moral statutes". 
 Ember is on the run with her neighbor and first crush, Chase, who was one of her arresting officers when they came to get Ember and her mother. Chase can never go back after betraying his post so he and Ember join the resistance to fight the government and take it back. 
 Ember's journey has been tough and this book is very gritty, not for pre-teens, but certainly for teens, young adults and adults. Thought the heroine is only seventeen she is forced to take on an adult role as she finds herself on her own. 
 Romance, fear, self-discovery and injustice all follow Ember on her journey as she now is on the most wanted list and becomes a liability for even the resistance. 
 This is an amazing book, very much worth the praise and hype it's gotten in the media. The characters seem so real you find your heart racing as you travel with them through the story, feeling their every move, every mood, every turn. Kristen Simmons is an amazing YA author with a wonderful writer's voice. I highly recommend this book, and series.

Goodreads calls this series fast-paced and gripping, and that is no exaggeration. These books are epic! Something about the characters and the action is just so awesome and addicting. I really loved 'Article 5', and in my review I mentioned how it sticks out from other dystopians because of its characters and its heart. This continues to be true in 'Breaking Point', where we get to know new characters from the rebellion, and fall even more in love with characters from the first novel. 
 As you can tell, the characters, and the relationships between those characters, is one main reason why I love this series so much. In 'Article 5' Ember was naive and pretty sheltered, but in 'Breaking Point' we get to know a whole new Ember. She's been through so much and seen so many things that she can't help but be changed in certain ways. Even though it took some horrible events for this stronger Ember to emerge I really loved how she stepped up to the plate and was so brave in situations where it would have been easier to just hide away. And then there's Chase. I've described Chase as "the best type of boy, fiercely loyal to and in love with Ember," and this, of course, remains the same. Chase has also been through some incredibly tough times, but he stays strong when it's needed, especially when it comes to taking care of Ember. These two together are one of my favourite YA couples: they take care of each other, always stick together, and they have years and years of history between them. They seem to understand and "get" each other, which makes them a perfect fit. 
 The other main reason why I love this series so much is the action. Holy moly, the action! No second book syndrome here, not at all. Sometimes in books, especially dystopians where the characters have to physically journey somewhere, it can take forever for characters to complete their mission. I'm so grateful that this isn't the case here. Even when different circumstances pop up, the characters are always still aware of their original goal. There are different journeys that get completed throughout the book, but the characters are never sidetracked from Sean and Ember's plan to rescue Rebecca. 
 What else can I say about this book and this series?! Fabulous characters, incredible action, and just so many awesome aspects in general. I loved how we got to know more about the resistance and about how the present government came to be. I loved how there were hints about the centre of the resistance movement, which I suspect will be a big part of the third book. I also loved how even when there was success, nothing came easily for the main characters. There's nothing worse than when characters skip easily from task to task, getting by on technicalities that seem completely fake. These books feel like they have real danger and real consequences, and I really appreciate that about them. 
 Basically: do yourself a favour and check out 'Breaking Point', or pick up 'Article 5' if you haven't already.

"Being in love is a birthmark?" 
 "It's something that never comes off, no matter how much you might want it too." 
 This is a story of a girl on a journey to find direction, love and herself. Allyson is a nice girl. She doesn't drink, she doesn't party, she sticks to the itinerary, she collects vintage alarm clocks and she wants to be a doctor someday. But maybe that's not what she truly wants. Maybe she wants to be reckless? Maybe she wants to be bold and spontaneous? Maybe she wants to be someone else? And a day is all it takes for her to turn her back in all that she has known her entire life. And it's all because of Willem. 
 Willem gave her a new name. He gave her company. He gave her a chance to fall in love. But he won't give her another day. 
 I heard good things about Just One Day and moi, being totally in love with Forman's If I Stay and Where She Went, was eager to read another novel of hers. I was really unsure about the first part, about how hopelessly romantic it is that it is border-lining stupidity. In the literary world, meeting someone new, going with him and trusting him with your life, and then falling in love in a span of 24 hours is romantic but in the real world? I like to call it naive, not for the lack of a better term. 
 Things picked up at the second part. I was literally hungry for more pages. I traded precious sleep time for me to be able to finish the last 100 page stretch of the novel. I was eager to learn how they would find each other and what will happen if they do but imagine my anxiety when I'm down to the last 20 pages and still they haven't faced each other. 
 I love Gayle Forman, I really do, and maybe this book is not just about finding love but instead it is as much as finding oneself. But the hopeless romantic part me wants to have closure, not just for me but for Allyson as well. The book ended with so much unanswered questions that even with my eyes heavy with sleep after reading I couldn't sleep right away and just had to take a teeny tiny peek of the sequel.

 The main character fall in love at first sight and then after just 24 hours she's depressed and annoying ! Then when she finally getting better she decided to go on a trip to find her lost love(r)... I actually love the travel but seriously how can a girl be so naive and so work up for a guy she barely know. She spent one year moping/trying to forget about a guy she barely know. I can't try to understand that. I just wanted to slap her and tell her to wake up life is not a fairy tale!

What this book taught me: 
 If you meet some hot guy during a tour of Europe and he invites you to run off to Paris with you for a day even though you've known each other for less than 24 hours, you should totally say yes. And if he asks you on the train to Paris if you're a virgin (because that's so totally not a creepy question) you have no reason to be freaked out. And if at some point during your time in Paris you're being chased by men who throw glass at you, that's okay because Paris is soooo romantic. And if at the end of the night this guy who hasn't even asked what your first name is wants to have sex you in some dirty abandoned building you should TOTALLY go for it because PARIS IS SO ROMANTIC. 
 Wow, this guy is just Prince Charming! 
 The rest of the book is about the main character being mopey and depressed because she misses this guy who had sex with her then mysteriously disappeared. The whole time I just wanted to scream, "Get a hold of yourself!" 
 Some other ridiculous parts of this story: 
 The name of the college the main character attended was "University College." Yeah. 
 Also, she takes a French I class and is magically fluent. Which, as someone who has been taking French for two years as opposed to her 6 weeks, I can guarantee is not possible. 
 So annoying. So ridiculous. The ending killed all possibility of redemption. Ughhhhhh. No.

Either I am becoming more picky when it comes to YA books or I just haven't read anything spectacular lately, but yeah, this book is nothing more than "okay" in my eyes. Will post a better review when it's not 5:00am and my brain is a bit more awake!

sample_reviews.review_text: Such a fun read! Love reading about big families and the dynamic between them. Especially when it's 8 hot brothers! Can't wait to read the next one!

I am a huge believer in fate and destiny so Badd MotherFer was right up my street. 
 Dru faces the worst day of her life when she finds her groom in a compromising position minutes before their wedding. Drowning her sorrows with the only family she has, her dad and his police buddies, Dru impulsively decides to escape her life on the next plane she comes across, no matter where it leads her. Still in her wedding dress with little money and no belongings, Dru lands in a tourist port in Alaska and straight into the nearest dive bar run by the broody mountain aka Sebastian Badd. 
 Sebastian (Bast) has cultivated his player image as a way of keeping everyone at arms length. Losing his mother at an early age and his father behind a bottle and his bar, Sebastian has taken responsibility for his younger brothers. The oldest of eight, Bast, embraced the role of parent to his younger siblings ensuring they got to live their dreams while forgoing his own. Lingering issues present themselves when his brothers leave to fulfill their dreams leaving Bast to manage the family bar by himself. Bast is clearly weighted down by unresolved emotions of grief and loss since his father's death and his brother's departure. He combats his deep-seated loneliness with alcohol and random hook-ups, only exasperating the problem. Until it is taken out of his hands by the terms of his father's will, whereby his brothers have to return to the bar for a period of a year. Not only does Bast have to come to terms with reuniting with his brothers but also the attraction he feels to the bedraggled beauty in a wedding dress that stumbles into his bar. 
 Sparks fly as soon as Dru and Sebastian meet, neither can deny their physical attraction and very quickly are unable to, lol. However, neither are prepared for the deeper connection they feel or the way in which they fit perfectly together without compromising who they are as individuals. 
 The character development is the fundamental basis of the story, with both Dru and Sebastian coming to terms with who they are, where they belong and who they belong with. 
 The repercussions of losing a parent whether by them leaving or passing away can have devastating and long-lasting emotional damage on the children they leave behind. Dru, in particular, has to face the fact that she lost herself as an individual when with her douch-ex in an attempt to fit into a role she subconsciously thought she wanted, the elusive 'normal' family. It isn't until she slots so seamlessly into the Badd family that she realizes her own worth 
 Badd MotherFer introduces us to all of the Badd boys setting the groundwork for the rest of the series; they are certainly a unique bunch and my curiosity to see how their year together is going to work out is at a very high level.

reference_books.review_text: This was a good book but not a great book. I must agree with other reviewers on how they rated this book. reference_books.title: The Great Gatsby
reference_books.review_text:
Gatsby, the man, is a mystery. Everything about him inspires envy. People want to be him and are in awe of him. He's a man that flaunts charisma and is in demand by others who live their lives just being around him. 
 Now to the book. The book seemed, in my view, to jump around quite a bit. It often seemed that you were envisioning a snap shot of single moment before jumping to the next, and then trying to put them together as a puzzle in order to make the story clear. The book at times seemed to be at slow pace and it didn't seem to draw me in until the last 60 or so pages. I fully aware that this is a classic and it speaks to the time of the reckless jazz age, with the liquor flowing parties and sexual interludes that were often noticed but not spoken about. 
 Overall, I'm glad I read it but like other classics it just didn't resonate with me.

sample_reviews.review_text: Two thumbs up. Great ending to an amazing trilogy.
Omg- this book... Yes. Yes.

Let it go down in history that I have never cried this hard over a book. Ever. This book destroyed me. 
 THAT is how you end a trilogy. Yes, its controversial but there is something for everyone. Beautifully written. Honestly has to be only ending of a trilogy that I've loved this much. 
 And I'm so, so surprised that when people said how much this affected them - I always thought it had something to do with major deaths. It turns out it was better/worse. I cannot even comprehend... 
 Oh, my poor smol babies...from Legend, they've come so far. They've suffered so much and they've been - I literally cannot even talk about it. 
 I can't think of two people more perfect for each other than June and Day. from this day on, I will always be salty about those 10 years. 
 LOVED that we got the whole detail about the global scale - I'm always SO fascinated by the way things are affected in dystopias and something that bugged me in THG was that it was so constricted. I wanted to know about the global scale and the info dump was so good. Marie Lu has a way of writing that's just...amazing. 
 Also!! The plot twists. Never saw them coming gtg 
 Loved the extra mentions of Eden, Anden and Tess. They grew so much and I'm so glad. 
 I love how they use logic and just pure knowledge TBH it's so brilliant ...like . Thank gods. This isn't just a dystopia novel where the ending is just lots of explosions but something that is strategized and actually very realistic. 
 still bitter about Juneday. I can't. I cried when they had sex the first time and when Day was in June's arms I was sure he was going to die and I sobbed my eyes out. Then it got worse. I just kept thinking of how June deserved Day and vice versa but that goddamn brilliant amazing girl decided to walk out and let him live. 
 * June Iparis is currently #2 on my top 10 female characters in books right now but it'll prob change.. But she'll still be in the top 10. This I can guarantee. 
 Thank you to Marie Lu for writing this wonderful series and I look forward to reading more of her work :) esp cos the characters are so diverse.

No se que hacer mas que llorar. 
 Antes de leer el primer libro Legend, yo estaba segura que iba amar esta trilogia, porque es del estilo que me atrae; creo que si no lo hubiera amado, me hubiera sentido tan desilusionada, pero por suerte lo ame.?Vieron cuando te enamoras de los personajes, la historia y el mundo creado? Bueno yo estoy asi, y la verdad que no lo puedo superar. Hacia mucho tiempo que no me sentia asi completamente al leer un libro, pero Marie Lu junto a su trilogia hizo que lo vuelva a sentir, y no hay nada tan lindo como eso. 
 No tengo nada mas que decir que me encanto todo, y creo que es una trilogia que es un must read si te gustan los libros distopicos y con accion. Desde la primera pagina de Legend que me engancho y asi me tuvo hasta la ultima pagina de Champion, nunca me aburri con estos libros, y Champion me lo hubiera terminado es menos sentadas, si no me hubiera propuesto hacerlo durar porque no queria que terminara la trilogia. 
 Los POV alternados, fueron fantasticos, nunca tuve duda de a quien estaba leyendo, y le dieron tanto a la historia, creo que fue algo totalmente acertado e hizo que la historia fuera como es. Ademas, los personajes, ni hablar de June y Day, realmente me encantaron, y los personajes secundarios tambien me gustaron como aportaron a la historia. 
 Aparte, los giros que va dando la historia que, personalmente, nunca te imaginas en donde va a terminar todo, es algo que le da mas suspenso, y te deja ansioso pasando las paginas para averiguar que va a suceder ahora. 
 De verdad que es una trilogia que se le recomendaria a todo el mundo porque realmente me encanto, pero es un must read, como ya dije, para aquellos que aman el genero como yo. No se porque no la lei antes, y eso que no me faltaban ganas para leerla. Si tenes esta trilogia en tu tbr pile, te recomiendo que la leas YA, ni lo dudes. 
 Hablando un poco de Champion... 
 Cada uno de los libros de Marie Lu en esta trilogia, se supero a si mismo y a los anteriores, y Champion no se quedo atras. 
 INCREIBLE. EPICO. ESE FINAL. Mis cuatro palabras para resumir todo lo que siento. 
 La verdad que considero que podria haber tenido un poquito mas de accion en algunas partes del libro, but el final desde que June dice "The final fight for the Republic has begun.", AMIGO, RECOMPENSO EL POQUITO DE ACCION QUE ME FALTO EN ALGUNAS PARTES. 
 Despues, lo unico que me vine venir en todas las paginas de los tres libros de la trilogia Legend fue que cuando Day se desperto pense en mi interior, seguro no se acuerda de June, y bueno sucedio eso , pero igual, me encanto, y aunque me esperaba eso, lo sufri un monton, despues de tanto, no se merecian eso. 
 YYY EL FINAAAAL!!! ****SPOILERS DE ACA EN ADELANTE DEL FINAL**** 
 MENTIRA SI QUE QUIERO HABLAR. Les juro que crei que se repetia lo que pasa en Allegiant, cuando Day 'hablaba' con la mama. Como llore como una desgraciada. 
 Y despues el epilogo, me siguieron quedando lagrimas para el. Me encanto que June vaya a visitar la tumba de Metias, y le contara sobre su vida, y dijera que ese ano en adelante no seria mas su hermanita menor, fue como un lindo cierre que nos dio Marie Lu sobre su relacion, me emociono. 
 Y obviamente fue super tierno que despues de tanto tiempo Day y June se hayan reencontrado, y que ella todavia no supiera si se acordaba de todo lo que les habia pasado. ESE TOQUE PARA TERMINAR LA TRILOGIA FUE MAS QUE TIERNO Y ME SACO MAS DE UN PAR DE LAGRIMAS: 
 "Hi", he says. "I'm Daniel". 
 "Hi", I reply. "I'm June". 
 Recordando: 
 "I wonder what things would be like if I just... met you one day. Like normal people do. If I just walked by you on some street one sunny morning and thought you were cute, stopped, shook your hand, and said, 'Hi, I'm Daniel.'" 
 ..."If only," I whisper". 
 Por mas que quisiera saber como ellos estan en el futuro y de la vida de los demas, entre mas cosas, ese simple detalle, fue tan pero tan hermoso, y le dio el final perfecto sin lugar a dudas. 
 Sin mas comentarios, me gustaria volver a la primera pagina de Legend y revivir todo de nuevo. Increible.

Champion supero mis expectativas. Marie Lu concluyo la historia de una forma magnifica. No me quejo de nada fue un absoluto deleite leer cada capitulo. 
 **ALTAMENTE RECOMENDADO **

reference_books.title: What I Talk About When I Talk About Running
reference_books.review_text:
Buf. A mi me parecio tremendamente soporifero. Es el primer libro que me leo de Murakami, pero me consuela saber por opiniones de otros que su estilo literario es bastante mas entretenido y emocionante. A caballo entre el ensayo y unas memorias, nuestro querido amigo Haruki comparte con sus lectores sus pensamientos acerca de actividades que han ocupado su vida durante ya varios anos: correr y escribir. 
 Lo que no daria para mas de 50 paginas se ve completado con reflexiones personales sobre la edad, la creatividad, la vida, y en general todo lo que Murakami ha ido aprendiendo a base de esfuerzo y constancia. ?Su problema? (en mi opinion) Que es un libro bastante irrelevante. Son recuerdos de un hombre que se ha dedicado a correr y a pensar cada meticuloso detalle de su existencia mientras tanto. Dicho de otro modo: si lo hubiera escrito yo, tendria el trastero lleno de copias. 
 Supongo que para los muy-fans y los que se dediquen a correr activamente hay varias reflexiones que les llegaran muy hondo. Pero yo, desgraciadamente, no encontre ninguna. A ver si el siguiente que pille tiene una trama de esas que hipnotizan...

reference_books.title: The Catcher in the Rye
reference_books.review_text:
No pude con este libro, y no entiendo como puede ser considerado un clasico de la literatura. Quizas fue rompedor cuando se publico por el vocabulario y el caracter del protagonista, pero a mi me ha parecido, en pocas palabras, infumable. 
 La historia trata sobre nuestro queridisimo amigo Holden Caulfield. Adolescente estereotipado. Vamos, que nadie le comprende, que lo sabe todo todito, que se deprime y se anima en cuestion de segundos, que quiere huir de todo. VALE. LO HEMOS COGIDO, Salinger. A medida que el libro avanza el personaje no hace mas que hilar pensamientos de este tipo con otros un poco mas aleatorios, mientras desfilan variopintos personajes que no anaden nada a la historia. 
 Al estar escrito en primera persona, Holden no es presentado ni bueno ni malo, simplemente es asi. Exasperante y repetitivo. Es una lectura amena, si, que representa la indecision y el hedonismo adolescente, pero ya esta. Un personaje que no para de quejarse de lo falso e hipocrita que es el mundo. Un chico que no puede hacerse amigo de un chico por unas maletas de baja categoria. 
 Ya se lo dice su propia hermana: "No te gusta nada de nada". Pues eso.

reference_books.title: Seeds of Yesterday (Dollanganger, #4)
reference_books.review_text: De nuevo el personaje raro que viene a meter cizana. Mas situaciones sacadas de la mejor telenovela que hayas visto. Mas dramatismo gratuito y por fin, el final. No puede superar a las idas de olla de los dos primeros libros, pero desde luego, es mucho mejor que el anterior.
