reference_books.title: Alex + Ada, Vol. 1
reference_books.review_text:
I picked this one because I've heard fairly positive reviews on it and they were right one point. This is a good graphic novel with average art and a solid story. Our story centers around Alex, an incredibly lonely professional, who robotically lives his lives despite being very human. There's a definite sense of loneliness in this novel, the art is purposefully alienating and you can see where he reaches out to anything and anyone. 
 Alex's rich grandma gets him Ada, a fully functioning cyborg and unlike the cyborgs found in the Lunar Chronicles, which were simply humans with mechanical parts much the way a wounded soldier might get a high-tech leg. The cyborgs in this world are machine-made with artificial intelligence and some of them have become sentient. The story takes off from there as the plot reveals itself as Alex finds himself connecting to Ada. It gave me the same creep factors as that movie Lars and the Real Girl. 
 Honestly, I'm not sure if this one is for me and I feel like I'm saying that of a lot of graphic novels lately. However this one is only 3 volumes and I think I will finish the series despite not being overall intrigued with the premise. I think it's OK. Points for originality and nice flow of the story plus the true sense of loneliness they were able to capture.

reference_books.title: Since You've Been Gone
reference_books.review_text:
In this coming of age story Matson presents us with Emily - a shy and awkward girl who has been the perpetual shadow of her best friend, Sloane - the outgoing one. I think this book is for the audience it intends it to be - a teen girl who can identify with our main character. However, I don't think this book translates well to the adult palette. 
 I had a really hard time with this book, I came to DNFing it almost 5 times but I kept going because I was able to download the audiobook. My dislike for this book can be attributed to 2 things: 
 1 - I am way to old to enjoy Emily's awkwardness. Usually I can appreciate the teen angst but the extreme of Emily's shyness left me frustrated. I lost my patience with her and the way she's written and hence I had a really hard time continuing this journey with her. It took me a full 4 days to finish a book that would've normally take me 2. 
 2- The pacing of this story is ridiculous. I don't think I can comprehend how a YA contemporary sits at 450 pages, most especially when while reading I felt like taking a red pen and crossing out chunks of this book that served as extra fluff or run-on descriptions of Emily's shyness like a sledge hammer over and over to the reader. (a classic example of a lot of telling not showing) 
 I would divide this book in 2 parts - the first 60-70% of this book could've have been reduced in nearly half. There's scene after scene that could have been deleted to employ a more cohesive narrative. There's also a lack of urgency in the general plot despite Emily claiming to be desperate for her best friend. Now, I don't need all plots to be urgent but I truly felt like chunk of the book were rather stagnant. 
 The last 40% of the book really picked up for me and I enjoyed most of it, Emily has changed in her journey, she became more a much more appetizing character and I was willing to go through this journey with her. The 2 stars are entirely for the last half of this book. Despite the pick-up at the end, I felt this book was very... vanilla. Tame and lacking in excitement. I felt like I was reading diary entries "today I woke up, went to work, was shy, spoke to someone, but it consisted of one word answers and long pauses and I didn't know what to do with my hands so I didn't do one of the things in my list, I miss my friend, end of day." 
 Despite the blatant flaws I found, I think this is a great teen book, I think they will enjoy it far more than I would and for that I will be gifting it to my friend's teen daughter. I think she will love this to pieces because she's the right audience for it.

reference_books.title: All the Missing Girls
reference_books.review_text:
This book follows the story of Nicolette 'Nic' who is in her late 20s and has to go back home to a small town in the middle of fucking nowhere to sort out her father's home now that his health is declining. This book is told in a backwards to front format for the period of 14 days. So you start out with her going to this small down and arriving to her childhood home and then we go to the future and tell the story backwards. 
 There are a slew of problems with this novel and I will attempt to delineate because I don't like to slap a one star on a book without cause or explaining. These are things that for me destroyed what could've been a really awesome story. From now there will be SPOILERS! 
 1. Format: while I appreciate the concept of backwards to forward it doesn't work in this story because the fact is that Day 14 Nic details the events as if she didn't know what happened in Day 1. Does this make sense? So though we're telling the story backwards it's as if Nic didn't know what happened in the past. Information is withheld from days until the end which defeats the purpose of the backwards storytelling. This made the story extremely confusing. 
 2. The Unreliable Narrator Trope from Hell: It's not that I do not like an unreliable narrator, I very much enjoy it but the problem here is that there are 2 types of unreliable narrators: the ones you don't know they're unreliable until the end and it blows you away because it was so well crafted that you almost want to read the story again to see what you missed, those are the awesome ones. Then there's this one. The ones you KNOW the entire time that they're holding shit back, that you can't trust anything they say, etc. There's a serious lack of elegance to this narration, Nic is a complete mess and you know it and it's frustrating because she's so sloppy in her narration. She's repetitive, unlikable, selfish, lying, weak, jumbled - she's everything that I dislike. She believes in the justification of her actions but at the same time condemns them. Also, the entire world view presented is that everyone is like her, deep inside, we're all just nasty people. 
 3. The Lack of Likable Characters: When I tell you that not one of these motherfuckers are likable, I don't think I've ever experienced this before. In all books/movies there's always that one sympathetic character which you need, you need it to contrast the rest. In this narration not ONE is likable and mostly it's because you don't know anything about them. The characters in this story are just dimensions, they're interchangeable, they lack deep quirks and roots and things that make them come alive. Because our story is told by the hateful and bland Nic we see everyone through her eyes and thus they are reflective of her blandness. 
 4. So Predictable: About 10% into this book I knew that A: all the chicks were dead and 2 that it was one of the 5 main characters. Now, this format has been done well before - for example Clue, the movie. If you've watched it you know one of the characters killed Mr. Body, maybe even more than one of them but it's done so flawlessly that by the end you love them all, even the killer(s). This book was the opposite. You wish they were all the killers and you wish they would all die. 
 5. The Reader is an Idiot Trope: Oh, you know that book - the book that decides that you as a reader are a moron and you need to repeatedly be told plot points. This book is incredibly repetitive, you can literally skip from Day 10 to Day 4 and you'll be fine. 
 6. The Nothing Happens Trope: Oh yes. Nothing actually happens except the last 50 pages and by then you would like to join in on the murder spree. 
 Needless to say, I don't recommend this book.

reference_books.title: Sleeping Giants (Themis Files, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
The premise of this story is that we get informed, in a series of case files, the events that led to the United States finding a giant alien robot which had been buried underneath the earth thousands upon thousands of years ago. They put the robot together and thus begins political pandemonium as you can imagine seeing as humans see anything as a weapon. I had previously read dossier-style books before - they seem to be the 'letter writing' style of the late 1800s (The Time Machine, Dracula, etc) as many authors today choose to do their books as such however despite some succeeding (Illuminae is a great example), Sleeping Giants missed the mark by a mile. This book is a quick read as it feels like you're reading a movie script, if you've ever read a script or a play you understand the general gist. We are presented with a series of interviews done by an unnamed man who seems to be the puppet master of the rest of the group. 
 The main issue that I had with this book was the utter lack of the human element. The point of a book is usually a connection between the reader and the writer; the writer attempts to make the reader feel something and the reader accepts this and internalizes it. However this book was so disconnected, the format made it even worse given that the characters were so stereotypical and lacking in dimension. The bad people were all bad, the clever people were always clever and you do not get to understand the why behind the decisions. There needs to be a balance between characters and plot and here the scale tipped drastically. 
 So we follow 2 pilots of the giant statue/weapon and these characters were absolutely painful to read. The plot of this book is ridiculous, which is fine, this is sci-fi, plots are meant to be ridiculous but it was all plot, plot, plot, the entire time and the human element was not woven throughout the novel which left the reader alienated. I cannot tell you how incredibly let down I felt, the disappointment was palpable because the premise held such promise and I was so excited to read this. I believe this is a debut novel so I can see how Mr. Neuvel will grow, he knows how to do plots, he just needs to learn to bring the reader to his characters. I also think this format does him no favors; this is truly better suited for a big blockbuster script than a piece of literature.

book_a.title: Anna and the French Kiss (Anna and the French Kiss, #1)
book_a.user_review:
I might simply be the wrong audience for this book but this book was not the dream most people said it was, at least for me. That's not to say that it did not have its highlights. For me, especially, was the vivid description of Parisian life - the boulangeries and patisseries. That absolutely saved me from giving it a 1 star review. 
 Essentially I have a few irreconcilable problems with this particular book. The first is the fact that the love story centers around cheating. Despite the fact that Anna and Etienne do not kiss until the end, the emotional cheating is there from the moment Etienne meets Anna (not to mention hand-holding, the tally of how many nights together, the sleeping in the same bed). This is essentially the reason why none of the romance in this book was swoon-worthy to me. I do not like books which have affairs in them, I find cheating inexcusable and for that I really could care less about Anna and Etienne. 
 Moving on to the main heroine Anna who is by definition #whitepeopleproblems - her dismay at being sent to study in Paris for a year and her essential tantrum that she throws made me side-eye her something fierce. Without doubt, a seventeen year old would be petrified at the prospect of being alone but this chick cries because she wont have prom. You know who will have prom? Nearly every teen in America. You know who might never get to go to Paris for A WHOLE FUCKING YEAR? Not even a few thousand. I found her immature and whiny and it sucked because I really really wanted to love this book. Being a Francophile myself I jumped at this book and it was such a let down. 
 The other thing I had serious issues with was the pacing in this book. At 372 pages this story could have used with about 50-75 pages less than what it got. Many scenes did not move the plot forward and it felt stagnant at many times and I admit to scanning forward to get to the juice of it. 
 As for our love interest, Mr. Etienne St. Clair. Oh Etienne... I just did not like him whatsoever. I found him confusing and he was always sending mixed messages to Anna embodying the nerdy BFF with bad-boy issues, like a combination of all bad YA love interest cliches. I just...no. It was all emotionally unhealthy. All of it. 
 I also felt that the bullying issue was so poorly handled by Perkins, I did not like the message that someone bullied should not say anything to the adult authority about the situation (most especially when the subject of the bullying is pertaining to sexuality and slut shamming!!). Anna kept quiet and took the bullying giving all the power to the stereotypical pretty mean girl and the adults were wallpaper. Seeing as this book is aimed at teens I do not think I would recommend it. Usually YA books that I find 'too young' for my taste I pass them on to my best friend's daughter - she's 13 but I would hate for her to read this. 
 Romanticizing cheating, badly handling bullying and slut shamming when it came to Etienne's girlfriend (the nurse Halloween costume) who was naturally the bad one in the relationship despite her lack of presence in the novel since it's told from Anna's perspective made me overall dislike the book.

sample_reviews.review_text:
"The more you know who you are, and what you want, the less you let things upset you." 
 I'm usually not a fan of contemporary books, so me giving this book 5 stars is HUGE! 
 Anna and the French Kiss is one of the cutest and most perfect books I've ever read. It honestly spoke to me in such volumes, I could relate to the main character and I really admire the author's writing. 
 Anna is sent (against her wishes) to an American School in France. Having to give up her best friend, her crush, and her favourite brother. When Anna makes friends with the girl across the hall, Meredith, she invites Anna to join her and her friend. Etienne is one of a kind, he's handsome, American with a British accent, and flirty beyond compare. The only problem is that Etienne has a girlfriend, and Meredith has had a crush on him for years. 
 The romance in this story is absolutely perfect. I loved how Anna was described as a fairly average girl, yet she still managed to catch Etienne's eye. Even though there was a bit of insta-love, the romance in this book was fairly realistic, usually when you fall in love there is something stopping you from being together, and Etienne's relationship was the biggest reason, as well as other smaller reasons. 
 My favourite part of this book was the travel aspect. It was so wonderful to read about Anna coming out of her shell and exploring France. The settings were described so well, I could feel as if I was standing in Paris myself. The feelings Anna had, brought me back to my travels throughout Europe, at first feeling that difference crashing around you, but then you start getting used to the new area and falling in love with the city. Ugh it was absolutely perfect. 
 The only thing that I didn't love about this book, was near the end when Etienne still hasn't broken up with Ellie. While I loved it at the beginning, near the end it was being clear that he did not love Ellie anymore and it was just horrible to watch him drag on his relationship with Ellie. 
 Overall, I would highly recommend this book to anyone who loves YA contemporary, or just loves to travel throughout Europe and would like to be taken on a trip back. 
 Happy Reading, 
 Aneta

** spoiler alert ** 
 This book makes your heart throb. The characters are vivid and really artsy, perfect for the setting...Paris (said in an exquisite French accent) 
 I think the reason why I loved this book so much is because I am fully bilingual and understand French perfectly. So the little bits in French got me really excited! 
 I've never actually been to Paris, but I'm always reminded of how "European" everything is because of the little boutiques and cobblestone roads, just like my hometown (Montreal=New France hahaha) 
 Some reactions I got from the book include that I was satisfied that Rashmi and Josh broke up. Rashmi is very independent and a great friend to Anna toward the end and Josh is more reserved, the really shy version of Etienne. And oh my stars Etienne....tu es le garcon de mes reves [?][?][?] 
 I feel bad for Meredith, I really do...who hasn't been in the same/similar situation, but I admire St.Clair for telling her exactly how he feels...However...The kiss scene between Anna and Etienne was so satisfying only because things were building up to it from the start. St.Clair and Ellie probably started having problems in their relationship the moment the summer came along and then when Anna got to Paris and expressed her interests and values (non-verbally and orally), I can see why Etienne was attracted to her. And it is hard, I'd imagine, loving someone so much and then someone else comes into your life who gives you a another even bigger reason to live. 
 I'm interested to see how Anna and Etienne adjust in San Francisco and what becomes of Josh at SOAP. I'd like to know if Anna and Bridge ever truly make up, or if Anna, Rashmi and Meredith stay really close friends. 
 Final verdict: 9.5/10 
 Favourite Character: Etienne St.Clair 
 Favourite Scene: Anna and Etienne at the top of Notre Dame Cathedral

MY HEART CAN'T TAKE IT. This book is a dream and I wish I was Anna with every ounce of my being. I wish I could read it over and over and over again for the very first time. I love it. I love it. I love it. Anna, may I be you? And may I find my own Etienne?

I finished it yesterday evening and I had to send everyone who wanted to come into my room out because I wanted to enjoy the ending. I just had to let out all the feels :) 
 This was just the right amount of cheesy and I loved it! I will be checking out other books Stephanie Perkins wrote because I want 100 more of those kind of stories <3

I started this young adult novel with high expectations, and not that far into the book I got bored with all the cliches and teenage drama. I was prepared for the teenage drama, I just didn't think it would be that bad or that boring. Perfectly well written scenes were ruined with "Seriously? MORE STAIRS?" and I shook my head, wanting it all to be over. Stephanie Perkins writes well, but I miss reading about teenagers and smiling about it, and not rolling mye eyes.

Why didn't I read this book sooner?! Ack! For so long people have been saying they really liked this book and I loved it. It's been awhile since I have been the girl who read under the table. Anna and the French Kiss brought that right back. I devoured this in about 2 days. Yeah, that's how good it was. It was funny, romantic, and so relatable. I loved it, loved it, loved it. 
 Ahhhh I loved the characters. Anna, St. Clair, Josh, Bridge, Mere, AND JUST EVERYONE. Yes yes I may have disliked some of them but this book wouldn't even be as good without them! Anna, the main character is just pretty realistic. She is in a country where the language they speak is something she can't understand, let alone speak it. From the beginning of the book to the ending, Anna grows so much and it is awesome to see that growth. For one, she can now understand French. She is has gone through so much drama, this girl knows how to deal with it. I really enjoyed reading from her and definitely will miss her perspectives in the next books. St. Clair, the only other person in the synopsis (therefore I can talk a little more about him) is great! He made a pretty good impression for me when I first read about him. This guy is someone that can easily be your best friend. He is funny, easy to talk to, and just the guy you jokingly insult 24/7. St. Clair is someone I would definitely want by my side as a best friend. 
 I enjoyed reading the plot very much. Yes even if it does sound super cliche it's still a worthwhile read. I loved the fact that St. Clair has a girlfriend. I love how Anna is basically the new girl. I love how this book takes place in Paris because there are so many things I didn't know about the city. The basic plot may sound super "fluffy" but it's these small details that just made the plot so good and addicting to read. Every chapter left me wanting more and I couldn't put it down. 
 I gave this book 5 stars because I loved the character and the plot and just everything about it! 
 Full review: http://next-page-please.blogspot.com/... 
 Update; 12/27/16: Went to Paris and got feels for this book and decided to reread. Just as great as I remember it to be!

I really enjoyed this one. I loved the characters and the setting. Ofc, im obsessed with paris now. I loved Josh and Etienne and rashimi. Some negative thoughts: Dave annoyed the crap out of me and Anna was a little dumb sometimes, but i still liked her.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Paris. Teenage angst. Romance. 
 It will not surprise anyone familiar with the story to hear that it is romantic - 'Anna and the French Kiss' is renowned in the YA community for its romance - but what struck me most was how relatable the characters were. 
 We've all experienced annoyance at our parents, awkwardness around our peers, desire, anger and betrayal by a friend. We may also have experienced heartbreak and getting what we want. The strength of this book is how it accurately depicts the emotions of the average teenager and the highs and lows of first love. 
 I won't go into much more detail about 'Anna and the French Kiss' because I think it's a story you'll know if you'd like or not from reading the blurb. It's not the most well written novel, but if you like romance, I'd recommend it. If you don't, then I wouldn't.

"Niggas in Paris" is playing in the background. 
 Just... no. I'd love to punch Anna and Etienne (or whatever his name is). Ellie should do that for me.

I wasn't a fan of this book. I found Anna to be extremely whiny and self centered and overall not a fun character to read about. I love the concept behind this book, and it could have been a great YA read had the story been more than 400 pages of two people not admitting they liked each other from the beginning. 
 1 stars.

book_b.title: Unravel Me (Shatter Me, #2)
book_b.user_review:
Finishing this book like: 
 Oh man, oh man oh man oh man. You know what gentle readers? I TRIED. I need fucking giant sized cookies for trying because this book is just awful. There came a point that I decided I was just going to laugh at it and once I made that decision I enjoyed it quite immensely. And, in order to bring forth a review more entertaining I have decided to use GIFS!! 
 Meet Juliette - expert moper, suffering from acute teenage angstatitis. The entire world is at war but Juliette is very busy trying to mope until she can't mope anymore. Spoiler alert: she ends the book moping. 
 You think she got better from book 1? That is not so! She will share with you her angsty poor-me, whoe-me mental diatribe for about all 460 pages! Can I get a hell to the yes for that one? To add sprinkles to that cupcake we're going to convey said feelings in a purely metaphoric manner! Throw in a few similes and voila! Instant bestseller!! By page 150 I was basically like this: 
 Let's not forget the boy troubles because there is a serious problem with the ecosystem and Juliette and Adam are acting out a poor man's Chuck and Blair. 
 We get ZERO world-building, zero adult involvement other than Castle who ended book 1 holding promise but here he walks about like a concerned professor of the history of genetic theory swimming in helplessness. It builds no tension, we don't have a clear picture of the structure of the story and meanwhile there's tons of pages dedicated to Juliette and Warner dancing the attraction dance. 
 Somewhere around this point I decided to simply laugh at this toasted bowl of lunacy and just fucking go with it all the while enjoying the hell out of Kenji who is, without doubt, the best character Mafi has created in her life. 
 Some more metaphor, metaphor, simile, simile, metaphor, metaphor - blah blah over and over and caving in, shatter, splat, splat, blah blah. 
 Did you know that in this book Juliette either cries or 'blinks back tears' a total of 21 times? 
 A few more hundred pages of plot without a plot ANNNDDD we have a novel!! And how does it end you may ask? WE HAVE A CLIFFHANGER, of course we do. The popular ploy of those with not much to say but really want you to buy the next book! 
 This book made me want to watch Adam Sandler movies so I can remember something more awful. 
 But let's be serious for a minute here. I've mentioned before that some YA books translate very well to an adult palette (Lunar Chronicles, The Winner's Trilogy) and others are specifically written to only be loved by their contemporaries and that's the younger than 20 crowd that will in all likelihood identify with Juliette. She suffers from the Bella syndrome and unfortunately nothing can save her from being so utterly helpless and unsure. She just is what she is and I will gift the entire trilogy to a young teen I know that might completely love the books. If you're an adult I urge you to skip this, actually run to the other side of the bookstore. 
 Worst line of the book: 
 "I am falling to pieces in his arms. 
 My fists are full of unlucky pennies and my heart is a jukebox demanding a few nickels and my head is flipping quarters heads or tails heads or tails heads or tails heads or tails" 
 rinse and repeat 436 times.

sample_reviews.review_text: 4.5 stars

Things I never want to read about again: 
 1. Juliette's tortured soul. 
 2. Her inability to breathe. 
 3. Her breaking bones and collapsing organs.

I'm... confused. Why is it that every time I finish reading a full length book from Tahereh Mafi, I feel confused after. Again I have felt that the ending was not right. Well, not really, It felt right and at the same time it didn't felt right. So see, I'm really confused right there. 
 Unravel me, told from Juliette's perspective took off after Kenji led Juliette, Adam and James to Omega Point's hideout. The first part of the book is spent dwelling on how much Juliette pities herself. Basically, it's being trapped inside the head of a depressed, pessimistic girl who hates herself too much. Though, this is the case, Kenji is there to lighten up the mood but of course Juliette, being the pessimistic girl that she is, will turn all the scenes that is all sunshine and daisies into a scene that will make you feel that you hold all the problems in the world on your shoulders. 
 I don't know why everyone's going on Team Warner and Team Adam, when evidently, Kenji's gonna beat Adam and Warner's team wagon to a pulp. Yep, i'm Team Kenji. Team Kenji all the way. hahaha! Forget Adam and Warner, I'm going to line up for Kenji. I am going to throw a fit if Tahereh Mafi kills off Kenji in the succeeding books. 
 Anyways, though at first, Juliette made my eye roll a thousand times,the development of her character was pretty good. Along the way, you find Juliette developing somehow of a split personality (and yes she acknowledges the existence of this split personality) which I think is very well done to show the readers how confused Juliette is. Although, it took a long time, and seriously a very long time for Juliette to get over herself and to lessen her tendencies of being the drama queen in this book, the descriptions Tahereh Mafi was just on the spot. (though sometimes the metaphors go overboard, but yea.) As always, Tahereh managed to make me believe that Juliette is really messed up and I believe at some point I managed to see Juliette as bat shit crazy. I mean literally bat shit crazy. For a moment in that book, I was scared of Juliette, and that was something that doesn't happen often. haha. 
 Anyways, Adam, I didn't really feel Adam that much in this book, it was like he was just there. After the scene where in Juliette inevitably and stupidly thinks that they can't work it out and Adam blurts out this speech about how he can't love any other girl which made me turn into a puddle of goo for a moment, after that he slowly disappeared. haha! Now I'm quite curious as to what is happening in his head at this time. So yep, give me some Adam POV goodness, I just wish he was not being a drama king during these times because as of now, I am assuming that he is in fact being a drama king during these times. Tahereh Mafi prove me wrong. haha. 
 So yea, basically the focus of this book is Juliette's character development and more Warner and Juliette interaction. Now, Warner. I am so fascinated with his character, Warner really is a very complicated character. He knows exactly who he is and what he is capable of. He knows what things he can live and live without and he does not pretend that he cares about everything. He's one messed up kid. I don't blame him for this, I blame his father for everything that is wrong with him. Anderson is a horrible, horrible, and really horrible person. He's like the very personification of everything that is horrible. He's like the guy version of Professor Umbridge. yea, PURE EVIL. 
 Now, let's talk about that the JuliettexWarner pairing shall we, Warner and Juliette. I don't know how to feel about this pairing. At some point, yes I think they are basically meant and perfect for each other but there's also a part of me that says, NO, they will clash and it will not turn out good. Choosing between Adam and Warner is like choosing from the split personality Juliette was able to develop midway into this book. I am still on Team Warner for Juliette but there's a part of me that doubts this. I'm confused about the love aspect of this story. So I'm going to let things play out as how they're supposed to play out and just go and line up behind Kenji, because Kenji is the most awesome person in this book. 
 Now the writing, the writing as always is full of metaphors and intricate descriptions that some will leave you hanging because of awe and some will sometimes make you laugh because of it's ridiculousness but despite that you can't help but feel amazed because even though it sounds ridiculous, it just felt right. :) 
 Anyways, giving this book another 3.5 :D

I was more than disappointed with this book. I thought the first book in the series was good, minus the psychotic period in the very beginning. The first half of this book was fine, then it went down hill. Quickly. I want to go as far as stating it's an amateur novel, but Mafi being a traditionally published author crosses out the title of "amateur author". 
 I hoped for more, but received less. There were multiple things I didn't like, but I will only name a few. First of all, if you like love triangles that don't make sense and are so stupidly cheesy, then this book might be good for you. The first novel continues in a strong way with Juliet finding her knight in shining armor (Adam) and professing her love for him, and vice-versa. He loves her back. They have a passionate, hot relationship and they seem to get along more than just alright. Well, throw that shit out the window for book two. You remember the guy that helped keep Juliet imprisoned for nearly a year, the guy who knew all along that she wasn't getting much food? Warren? Yeah, she trips head over heels for him. AND, just after breaking up with Adam for "physical incompatibility", she starts getting handsy with her new "muscular" boy toy. She says she still emotional over Adam and still loves him, but then nearly sleeps with Warren. Uh, okay? Warren, the same guy who had Adam bound and beaten until bloody in an old factory above a conveyor belt, which Juliet know's of, still gets the girl... Not only that, but she keeps secrets and lies to Adam about Warren. That's a real acute love triangle if you ask me. 
 Also, I didn't like Juliette's "I should've said that, but I didn't", "I don't know why I said that", "I don't know why I just did that", etc, etc. That is a VERY annoying repetitive problem throughout the book and it gets worse as the book progresses. The characters are shallow, all seeming very similar with only slight attitude variances, and the dialogue is a bit stiff. Juliette supposedly "grows" as a stronger woman throughout book two, but it's not as much of a progressive growth as some readers perceive it to be. 
 I could go on... 
 I would only recommend to those who like very cheesy YA mainstream fiction. I'm talking something lower than Divergent (I'm not judging that one, I promise), or even the Maze Runner prequel (yep, that one IS me judging). 2/5 is generous.
I didn't finish this. I couldn't. it was torture to read more of this sorry excuse of a novel.

If you couldn't tell by the two-star rating, I did not like this book. This series doesn't feel like a dystopian. There's hardly any action with a weak plot and not nearly enough world building *sigh*. 
 First things first, Juliette. In my review of Shatter Me, I did a quick rant on how annoying she is. Well, she got worse. I hate hate hate Juliette so much. She just bothers me and gets on my nerves. Honestly, I'm not entirely sure why I hate her so much. You know how you just have those people you just don't like for really no reason? I feel that way towards Juliette. There was some character development (yay!!! I love character development) so I'm happy that was there. 
 But, Juliette is still super whiny and a bit insecure (not as much as before, thankfully). She comes across as kind of selfish with the way she acts towards people and how she has to complain when someone won't tell her every single detail. New flash, the world doesn't revolve around you, Juliette. 
 Energy is coursing through me with a vigor I've never felt before and I'm not even thinking but I have to do something I have to touch something and I'm curling my fingers and bending my knees and pulling back my arm and 
 punching 
 my 
 fist 
 right 
 through 
 the 
 floor. 
 See, here we have the really annoying writing style of this book mixed with Juliette being super annoying and needy. 
 Then we have Adam, who, yes, I still don't like. He's just so desperate for Juliette. Adam comes across as kind of creepy and I totally don't trust him at all. Like Juliette, he also enjoys whining and complaining in his free time. Whenever they go like five minutes without seeing each other they start going on and on about how there's no privacy and they never see each other. I mean, that's like half the book right there. 
 Adam is also super ungrateful. Like he acts moody and depressed half the time and can't even act somewhat grateful for his so-called best friend Kenji who came and rescued him. So yes, I hate this guy. He and Juliette both need to learn the world doesn't revolve just around themselves. 
 I actually really like Warner a lot more than before though. I have the same feelings towards him as I do with the Darkling from the Grisha trilogy. He's a villain, but also a potential love interest, and I just love that! I don't know, I just really like when the main character has a romantic relationship with the villain. 
 One thing I hate in books: love-triangles. And what did this one have? A love triangle. UGH. Okay, but there's no chance Juliette could even end up with Adam anyways. like she's going to have to see the annoyingness in him at some point. Thankfully, she kind of does, but sadly, she kind of doesn't. 
 What I want to know is how there is even a Team Adam. Then again, this is just my opinion of him and I can't think of any reasons why people would like him, but that's just me! (So many people love this book. I'm definitely in the minority here with these opinions) 
 For a dystopian, this book (as I said before) doesn't seem like one. Where's the world building?! Sure, we get some, but not enough. There are a few details added in about the Reestablishment here and there, but I want to know how and why most of this is all happening. I also really want an explanation on these abilities everyone has. Is that too much to ask? I want someone to figure out why this is all happening and how people ended up with these abilities. But there never is any explanation. 
 And then, we have the writing, which is just weird, by the way. There's less of the crossing out in this book, but more weird metaphors. Especially in the beginning. I honestly felt like this book started off really weird but the writing got more normal, like the author just got tired of adding in all these metaphors here and there. I could do without the weird comparisons, so I'm kind of glad it was more frequent in the first half. 
 The world might be sunny-side up today. 
 The big ball of yellow might be spilling out into the clouds, runny and yolky and blurring into the bluest sky with cold hope and promises about fond memories, real families, heart breakfasts, stacks of pancakes drizzled in maple syrup sitting on a plate in a world that doesn't exist anymore. 
 That was only the first paragraph. I don't know about you, but I found that to be really quite odd. 
 There wasn't enough action or plot either. Majority of this book is spent at Omega Point with a few points here and there, but they were all really rushed and felt crammed in there. I like books with action and a good plot! The action and plot here was mostly nonexistent. It was just terrible romance 85% of the book. 
 If you couldn't tell, I really didn't like this book. The two star rating was because I like Warner, and that's pretty much all. I didn't hate this book enough to give it one star though.

3.2/5 
 I continue to love Mafi's writing style, it's very lyrical and poetic. I had a lot of trouble relating to the main character in this book (even more than the first book believe it or not). I found Juliette to be very frustrating, annoying and naive to the point of stupidity. I did enjoy this book but it was often more due to all of the other characters and not because of the protagonist. That being said the last few chapters we saw extensive character development for her so I'm actually looking forward to the final book. 
 One more grip I have in this book is WHERE ARE THE LADIES? Aside from Juliette we have meet four other female characters in this book and two of them didn't even speak?! I need more female representation in this series.

I can't believe how terribly impressed I am with Tahereh Mafi's sophomore effort considering the fact that I wasn't all that into her debut book Shatter me. While I thought Shatter Me's content was sorta kinda interesting, the plot while fast paced wasn't all together all that interesting, the characters were kinda lacking in some ways (I could never really get deep into them, there was some sort of glass that was separating me from actually emotionally connecting with any of them) and really the writing wasn't spectacular and the style was borderline annoying (do we really need to repeat our words? our words? our words?). So what changed here??? 
 Well first of all, the writing voice has changed somewhat. Juliette's narrative isn't as teenage melodramatic as it was in Shatter Me and I guess this is largely contributed by her character growth too. While I get where she's coming from (she was stuck alone in an asylum for a year) but I think in Shatter me, Juliette was just frankly over killing it. I love the fact the other characters are actually calling her out on this fact that she's so self-centered and has a penchant for drama. 
 You're not with your shitty parents anymore. You're not in that shitty asylum, and you're no longer stuck being Warner's shitty little experiment so make a choice. Make a choice and stop wasting everyone's time. Stop wasting your own time Okay?" 
 Thank you very much for that line! That was EXACTLY what Juliette needed to hear so she would stop being so 'omg my life sucks, my touch kills people, it's always about me, myself and I... me me me me me me me'. So yes the narrative is a lot more palatable than it was in Shatter me and stylistically I'm glad Tahereh Mafi decided to do away with the repeats (but instead has replaced them with strike text but hey I prefer strikes over repeats any day!). 
 The second thing that really stood out for me was the characters. In Shatter me I always felt that the characters were just very surface (especially Warner who was just this caricature of a bad guy) but was I pleasantly surprised when Tahereh Mafi starts revealing her characters and you really start to get to know them. Adam to me isn't a very deep character but I'm glad to see he has grown and wasn't the 2D he was in Shatter Me but who took me on a 180 spin was definitely Warner. Never in a million years would I have EVER found myself attracted to let alone root for a character like Warner until I finally got to know him. In Shatter me he was pretty much painted as megalomaniac psychopath but than as you get to know Warner, he's hardly a megalomaniac psychopath at all and instead eerily similar to Juliette. 
 Yes there is a love triangle here but surprisingly I have no qualms with this love triangle (because it makes sense, it really does) and for once I am actually not sure who she's going to end up with. Both boys frankly at this point in time have an equal chance with Juliette (esp Warner's actions in the last chapter definitely pushes him as a strong if not equal contender as Adam). Just for the record I am definitely on TeamWarner. I just feel he is a better match for Juliette than Adam is. While Adam and Juliette do make a sweet couple, I feel that Juliette doesn't grow as a character with Adam. She surprisingly grows so much with Warner because he's always challenging her and vice versa and they become better people as a result of their interactions. But that's just me trying to wave m TeamWarner flag. :P Plus seriously Warner beats Adam in the hotness meter any day! 
 So yes overall, Tahereh Mafi's sophomore effort is a more polished and well fleshed out book that her debut book. So if you've read Shatter Me and liked the premise but weren't particularly impressed with the writing or the characterization, you may want to give Unravel me a try and see how you like it. You may be in for a pleasant surprise. :) 
 PS I would read Destroy Me the novella before this book. It's Warner's story about what happens in between the first and second book and it such a LOVELY insight into his character. Honestly I was absolutely charmed by him after Destroy me and he firmly wormed his way into my heart at the end of Unravel me. 
 PPS What is with these counter culture bad boys... First the Darkling from Shadow and Bone and now Warner. Yummmm ;)

I would give this a million stars if I could. That's how amazing Tahereh Mafi's writing is. I can't even begin to explain the vast amount of feelings this book brings as you read it. And the second one comes out in a year. Noooooooo.

Kenji, contigo al fin del mundo 
 Warner, te quiero... un poco. 
 De resto, meh con todos, especificamente con Juliette. 
 En serio que crei que este libro mejoraria lo leido en Shatter Me porque me dijeron que habia "evolucion". ?Y con que me encuentro? 
 Con nada... Absolutamente nada relevante y adicional al primer libro. Todo es tan "lo mismo" ?Donde esta la accion? ?Donde esta el desarrollo de los personajes? Por favor, necesito algo mas que no sea a Juliette quejandose por todo: tocame, pero no me toques, amame, pero no me ames. 
 Pseudo romance, ah... Y detesto el triangulo amoroso de aqui. 
 La escritura de Taheren no es mala, al principio la tenia tomada contra ella, pero ahora noto que mi espinita es la protagonista, no se como Warner, que es tan increible, puede si quiera verla. 
 Lo importante es que a pesar de todo no quise dejar de leer y que incluso espero leer el tercero, sufriendo y todo. 
 Sip, mi puntuacion es porque lo salvable de este libro es Kenji, su manera de ser, de actuar y ser directo me enamoraron. Cien puntos para ti. 
 Warner tambien me ayuda a no pensar que todo esta perdido. 
 Adam, tu eres un cero a la izquierda... SorryNotSorry.

reference_books.title: This Is How You Lose Her
reference_books.review_text:
I was disappointed in this short story collection. After being enchanted by "The Brief and Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao," I expected "This is How You Lose Her," to be equally impressive. While Diaz maintains his signature, pop culture-laden style (think poetry slam), the characters seem less human and relatable. Perhaps it's because the stories lack strong female characters like his mother and his sister Lola and the men, including the incorrigible but normally charismatic Yunior, are entirely unsympathetic. 
 That being said, I won't let this book sour me to Diaz. I still look forward to his future work.

reference_books.title: The Shambling Guide to New York City (The Shambling Guides, #1)
reference_books.review_text: The Shambling Guide to New York City is a wonky, fun read that's creative in its world-building--the author was an RPG writer for years and I wonder if creating those interactive narratives aided in her ability to create this underground world. At times, the plot felt a bit forced, but I have to give it props for the ingenuity and the plucky heroine Zoe Norris.

reference_books.title: A Confederacy of Dunces
reference_books.review_text:
This posthumous Pulitzer winner is the all-time favorite of a former coworker who lent me his original copy. He had lived in New Orleans and still makes an annual pilgrimage to participate in his 'krewe' for Mardi Gras. 'A Confederacy' will certainly not be added to my list of favorites, but I am glad I've read it. 
 Ignatius J. Reilly is possibly the most unlikeable protagonist you will ever encounter. He's 30, fat, slovenly, lazy, arrogant, and judgmental. Having spent his 20s working on various graduate degrees, he now finds himself back in New Orleans, jobless, friendless, and living with his mother whom he seems to desperately need but constantly criticizes. Following some unfortunate property damage, his mother finally demands that her son gets a job. As you can imagine, chaos--involving everything from labor protests to hot dog cart shenanigans to strip shows with parrots--ensues. 
 Enduring Ignatius's never-ending diatribes made the novel slow and tedious for me at times. The real highlights came in the cast of zany characters: the hapless Patrolman Mancuso, whose sincere attempts to do the right thing turn him into a laughing stock; Burma Jones, who despite being underestimated for his color and background is probably the smartest person in the novel; the confused yet feisty Miss Trixie, who actually reminds me of a different coworker; and Myrna Minkoff, at once Ignatius's only friend and greatest foil. 
 O'Toole doesn't pretty up New Orleans, but rather he stitches in its unsightly features. It's the same for the characters. And the fact that I can easily imagine encountering many of them today (Myrna is a shoo-in for 'Girls') makes it a somewhat timeless read.

reference_books.title: The Summer Prince
reference_books.review_text:
NPR had featured this book when it first debuted, and the review was enough to pique my interest after becoming a bit disenchanted by the Hunger Games trilogy (only the first book was worth reading) and the Divergent books (the first was good, but not enough to entice me to continue with the other two). 
 Indeed 'The Summer Prince' has fresh elements. Like the aforementioned series, it is set in a future dystopian world where violence (often involving teens) is part of the new order. However, this YA is not set in the U.S., but in Palmares Tres (formerly Rio de Janeiro), and the romance is not a rivalry between newly elected Summer King, Enki, and the would-be heroine's best friend Gil, but rather a triangle in which Enki is interested in both Gil and protagonist June Costa. 
 Beyond attraction, the book explores themes of friendship, family, and revolution. I loved how June's art helped flame the fires of discontent while also exorcising her own inner demons. 
 I really can't criticize this book, but nevertheless I did not feel a connection to the characters or place. Despite how lushly described Palmares Tres was and how three-dimensional June, Gil, and Enki were, it felt superficial, as if Johnson only showed us the tip of the iceberg. Or perhaps, I've simply grown weary of YA dystopia.

reference_books.title: The Interestings
reference_books.review_text:
I had some strong likes and some strong dislikes with The Interestings, so the rating stands as is. 
 The overarching theme was strong and thought-provoking. However, it could best be summarized by the opening quote from Mary Robinson: "to own only a little talent ... was an awful, plaguing thing ... being only a little special meant you expected too much, most of the time." 
 Wolitzer explores what happens when talent (and life) divides a group of camp friends as they age. It's an intriguing premise, and many of us can relate to the protagonist Jules in feeling that she has fallen short of her friends. Unfortunately the chemistry between characters feels artificial. What is so appealing about Ash and Goodman anyway? Is Jules as miserable as she often seems or are we the readers just seeing her darker spells? 
 I appreciate that the story explores the possible twists and turns that come in life; if only I felt compelled by the characters taking that path. At the very least, Wolitzer raises the question of artistic ability and success and self-worth-- two months later, I'm still pondering those themes.

You know it's bad when you're sitting in front of a blank screen, trying to figure out what to say about a book. This is how I feel about Her Fearful Symmetry, Audrey Niffenegger's long awaited follow-up to her fantastic debut The Time Traveler's Wife. It has taken me a full six days to slog through the meager 400 pages of this story. Never once in almost a week, did I experience that "can't wait to get that book open" moment that makes for a good read. I had to force myself through the entire thing. 
 Her Fearful Symmetry begins with such promise, but the story quickly goes downhill. I thought I'd be really interested in the twins, Julia and Valentina, but I just couldn't make myself care about them. Up to about page 275, I was just bored. Then the story took a dark turn (involving an innocent kitten) and I was disgusted. Valentina's plan to live as an individual away from her sister is not only incredibly selfish and horrifying, but also ridiculous. Whatever small redeeming quality the story had, it lost somewhere between the incident with the kitten and Valentina's plan. 
 I kept reading, hoping at least for a satisfactory ending. Not a "happy ending" - there was no way that was going to happen - but at least an ending that made the reading worth while. I did not get it. The ending was pointless and without any kind of tangible meaning. I was completely let down. 
 I am so surprised at the good reviews I have read about this book. The prose is really beautiful, but that is not enough to make for a good story. In finishing the book, my world is neither better or worse for the reading (unless you take into consideration almost a week lost within it's covers.) I will not recommend Her Fearful Symmetry to you. It definitely lacked the magic of The Time Traveler's Wife, and has nothing really redeeming - no interesting characters, no captivating setting, no fascinating plot line. I am really disappointed.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I wanted to like this book, but anything that takes me this long to read is never going to be on my list of great books. The things I had read likened this to an adult Harry Potter. That, it is not. More like a re-vamped (pardon the pun) Twilight. Before I realized what kind of turn this book was going to take, I was enjoying it. And then somewhere between 250-300, I let out an audible groan. This trend of sudden, undying love for someone so quickly after they meet, especially in relationships where the male is so controlling and the female allows it, is getting to be beyond ridiculous.

I couldn't finish this. The multiple-page info dump that chronicled the main character's life story within the first 1% of the books should've been a big enough red flag to save me from wasting several more hours of my life, but I pressed on, hoping for an improvement. There wasn't. After trudging through to the half-way point, at which I'd endured more conversations about wine, tea and yoga than I thought possible, I gave up. It's clear the author did her research -- that's great, but it doesn't mean we have to wade through her notes. Part of effective story-telling is to weave the research into the story without dragging it down. Harkness missed the mark there. 
 I also saw no good reason for the alternate POV's, other than to give the author a chance to over-explain and suck all the tension out of the book. It was like a glaring neon sign -- "Hey, just letting you know...there's no danger from Matthew...'cause he loves her. Already. After two days. Two days of drinking wine and tea and hanging out in the library." His entire first POV chapter is pointless -- multiple scenes where he and his friend blather on about nothing, in the form of 'as you know, Bob' dialogue, and we get more information on how to play various games of pool than necessary in anything other than a book about how to play pool. 
 I'm incredibly grateful for this site, because I considered trying to go back and finish, but after coming here and seeing this is only the beginning of a series I know stopping is the right decision. Had I forced myself to read through the rest only to find a million hanging threads I would've thrown the book at the wall. Which would've been a problem, because I have it on my kindle.

I've read this same story, told by better writers.

Enter a world, no THREE worlds each with their own version of London. The only ones with the ability to move between worlds are the Antari, or those born with the strongest form of magic. Kell is one of the few with the ability to move between worlds. There are four Londons: Red London, Grey London, White London, and Black London (but no one ever talks about that one). When Kell is tricked into smuggling an old relic into his world he finds himself inadvertently setting loose a dark and powerful force into his world. In his quest to rid the worlds of the darkness he runs into a pickpocket and thief named Lila. She is fierce and desperate with nothing to lose. Despite being magicless her quick wits and determination end up helping Kell in more ways than he could have imagined. When she forces him to let her help he is left with no choice but to accept, and together the two struggle to bring balance to the power hungry worlds. 
 This story was a shade darker than the stories I typically read. (Yes, I know its called A Darker Shade of Magic). The story contains some inappropriate content and swearing, so it is definitely geared towards an older audience. Still, I found it good enough to finish so that says something. Honestly I finished this book in two days. I was about to return it to the library, but I wanted to know what happened to Kell and I ended up staying up until to 2am to finish it. 
 Pros: 
 The characters are entertaining. They do not grow or change significantly throughout the book, however I loved the characters to begin with so this was not as much of a problem. I was just thinking to myself the other day about how the guy characters are always the ones who are witty, one-step ahead and think of the awesome comebacks. I asked myself -why aren't there any girl characters as sassy and hilarious as say, Eugenides from the Thief? Lila is almost like a girl version of Eugenides....but different. She is smart, sassy and just a little too weapon crazy. Her desperation drives her, yet beneath her cutthroat bravado she genuinely cares about the people around her. 
 Kell on the other hand has a very intense, wry personality. He struggles with his loyalties and identity throughout the story but never comes to a conclusion on who he is necessarily. The book is written as a trilogy and so I assume the following two books explore both Kell and Lila's characters in greater depth. 
 The storytelling is excellent. I enjoyed Schwab's descriptions immensely and the plot was compelling and full of twists and turns. 
 Cons: 
 The story claims that magic = power. The story further claims that either too much or too little power is bad. While the story does an excellent job of showing how too much power is bad, I never felt convinced that too little power was bad. In the story, one of the characters Rhy doesn't have much power and yet he is a wonderful ruler. This theme wasn't explored enough for me. I wish the pros and cons of power would have been talked about more in depth. 
 The darkness is pervasive. This book left me with an eery, oppressive feeling. However I will say that I'm glad I finished it. There are a few lighthearted moments as well as dark ones, but it ultimately ended on a good note. 
 A Darker Shade of Magic is captivating. Literally. Read it and you'll understand why I chose that word specifically.

Actually I want to give this one a 4.5 star.

I was intrigued by A Darker Shade of Magic, but it wasn't really on my radar for a book I had to pick up the second it came out. I recieved a brand-spanking-new fresh copy in my Owlcrate and it peeked my interest even more. I haven't read anything by Schwab before this, but figured if Owlcrate was choosing to feature this book in their first book, it must be something special. 
 Likes: 
 I am a huge advocate for world-building. When a story is set in a newly created world, I want to be able to understand what the world looks like, how society operates and how the world really works. Schwab did an amazing job creating the Londons. There is a lot of detail given to the history of the worlds, along with creating multiple Londons and characters. 
 Kell. He stuck with you from the beginning. The beginning of the story starts with Kell's jacket and you are immediately intrigued. "Kell wore a very peculiar coat. It had neither one side, which would be conventional, nor two, which would be unexpected, but several, which was, of course, impossible. The first thing he did whenever he stepped out of one London and into another was take off the coat and turn it inside out once or twice (or even three times) until he found the side he needed." 
 Once I met Lila, I could not get enough of her. I wanted every chapter to feature Lila and when it was just Kell, I felt like I almost wanted to rush through to get to Lila. I am not sure why I loved her character so much, but she felt like a best friend that I could go on some crazy adventures with. 
 The whole concept of magic or the lack of magic in the Londons was really unique. I felt like it was fresh, new fantasy and enjoyed that I couldn't predict the plot. 
 Gripes: 
 The only thing that really frustrated me, in the beginning of the book, was that there was no real plot. I was reading about this amazing world, traveling between the Londons, meeting new people and enjoying the characters, but I felt like I was reading a story with no purpose. It was about 100 pages in when we had a clear purpose and path. I needed that. I love the characters and the world-building, but I feel like I am floundering when a story doesn't have a direction. 
 Victoria wrote this post on Twitter. As much as I agree with her, I did realize that plot was important to me. It didn't really matter what the plot in the story exactly was, but I just needed a purpose

The protagonist with manufactured angst ("who am I? why am I a captive if I am so powerful?") couldn't inspire me to root for him. The duoprotagonist/non-romantic secondary lead had no moral grounding ("I'm gonna be a pirate and victimize people and have no empathy for anyone I have stolen from even though I've strangely bonded with an innkeeper who would otherwise have no place in my life but who mysteriously takes me in when I need a place to hide from the law"). The royal "brother" had an inner life as deep as a piece of tissue paper. Kell's role and duties and privileges in that society were ridiculous. The technology of Redworld made no sense (with flashing electronic billboards but 1800's society and naval capacities).

sample_reviews.review_text: Main characters Noa and Peter are engaging older teens, each with problems, Noa's with being parentless in a system tough on anyone in that state, and Peter, with successful parents who bring a severe group of challenges into his life. Both have suffered personal losses, and both are very talented with computers (to the enormous jealousy of this reader!). Through different paths, they come face to face with a callous business conducting heinous testing of abducted runaways. The story line focuses on how Noa and Peter attack this enterprise after their connecting, an obvious must from early on in the book when they begin separately. This is the first of a trilogy. I will read the second part when I can either borrow it in eBook format from the library or its price goes down. It's good enough to read more, but not to stretch for. That makes it hard to figure out how many stars to give it, so make this a three-plus. Noa and Peter are very easy to root for, and the bad guys are truly horrible. I can see how a teen, particularly one feeling some angst and idealism, and who is good with computers would enjoy this a lot.

Don't Turn Around by Michelle Gagnon was one of those books that had potential to become something great but just failed to deliver it. At least, that was my first thought after finishing the book. This was also the kind of book that made me spend ages just deliberating over, because I didn't know whether to give it three or four stars. 
 What I liked the most about Don't Turn Around was the overall idea. It was original, full of fast-paced action, and definitely managed to keep me hooked. The title was one that made sense, too! Unfortunately, there were also many other things didn't work out as well as the story. 
 For one, I couldn't connect with any of the characters. I didn't feel drawn to them at all. Not even Noa or Peter, who are the main characters of the book. That was probably why I couldn't feel much of the emotion either. I knew what the characters were feeling, but I couldn't exactly feel it. 
 Another thing I didn't quite understand was the whole point of this book. Once I was finished done with it, I didn't know what it was actually about, because it isn't what the synopsis says it is at all! I felt that the real plot was only revealed at the very end, and by that time, it left me feeling like I'd gained nothing out of the book. 
 Readers who are expecting romance from this book will also be very disappointed. I was not particularly affected by the lack of romance, because then there wasn't any insta-love. Of course, there were hints dropped here and there that Peter and Noa would become more than just friends later on, but to tell you the truth, I'm not really pleased about that. I think the author tried to induce a teensy bit of chemistry between them, but it just didn't work. 
 Overall, Don't Turn Around was a bit of a disappointment to me. Though I loved the whole idea of this, Michelle Gagnon wasn't able to make a lasting impression on me. However, I am hooked enough that I'll probably read the sequel and hope that it'll be much better than the first book! 
 3 stars.
