Honestly, fuck this book and fuck its historical inaccuracies. 
 Warning: This is basically me being all annoyed and comparing how the book made shit up to actual historical truths. 
 1. Historical Alexander was hella gay so often; it was ridiculous to the point that sometimes I need to set down whatever material I was reading on him and just gape. 
 I mean, a) he kissed a boy and he liked it, to misquote Katy Perry. 
 So there was a dance that Bagoas performed that was apparently so damn fine he agreed to kiss him in front of everyone (his soldiers weren't that much of a help, they were all like 'pls go get a piece of dat ass') 
 b) Him and Hephaestion !_! 
 - Aside from how he compared themselves as Achilles and Patroclus respectively (which fyi people at that time were already debating if the latter two were bangin' in the Iliad or not), they decided it was cool to go visit their graves and run naked (after rubbing oil all over each other) on a beach. 
 - Then there is the infamous "He too is Alexander" quote after a queen accidentally mistook Hephaestion for Alexander. 
 - Oh yeah, also the philosopher Diogenes (this man is the ultimate sass master btw) sent a letter that was basically "dude man up stop yielding to Hephaestion's thighs" could you even believe 
 - "Without me, you would be nothing" 
 - OR PERSEPOLIS THIS FUCKER GAVE HEPHAESTION A 1.5 BILLION POUND FUNERAL I SHIT YOU NOT 
 Yeah this is way too long just to make a point but you get? 
 So when the novel erases this side of him and makes A straighter than a ruler it just makes me so pissed. Because?? He is no longer Alexander?? And I don't care that it's fiction or fantasy because what is the point of saying that he is Alexander the Great when you change him to fit into a typical heterosexual YA male protagonist? 
 2. Also let me be clear that this sympathetic Alexander bullshit in the novel is -10000/10 true. 
 He is, for a lack of better word, a dickhead to everybody aside from Hephaestion (and others currently in favour but v. rare). Like he was really shit on how he treated his men (he sent his army on a death march though Gedrosia where supposedly three quarters died in the desert, on purpose, for Christ's sake). 
 He gave exactly zero fucks on planning or governing or economics or even common sense. Guess what he did to get rid of Macedonia's debt and to finance his army?? Oh just casually starting a war with the possibly most powerful empire that existed on earth bc why not?? And the thing was that it actually worked????? 
 Like. Yeah. Who the hell is so obsessed with his own success that he can actually pull of this sort of thing? 
 So this Alexander (who does not deserve 'the Great' in this novel) is absolutely foreign to me. He named a city after himself when he was 16 for fuck's sake. 
 3. The first chapter, which the lovely Emily May clearly compares it to The Hunger Games so I'll just skip that. 
 However, just some stuff to add: The Blood Tournament happening in an arena. 
 The Blood Tournament is a single free-for-all held in a large arena with a simulated landscape made to increase difficulty, featuring added natural challenges like quicksand or cliffs. It is hot, bloody, and chaotic, with fighting taking place all over the stadium until the crowd--and the king--approve a single victor. 
 Correct me if I am wrong, but I am 95% sure arenas didn't exist in Greece. Hell, the idea of the gladiator games, where people fought with weapons with one another didn't exist until several hundred years later where the Romans popularised it and brought it over (and even then it didn't really catch on-- the Greeks decided that they were too cultured to consider bloodshed as entertainment). 
 I don't even want to talk about how the everloving fuck was the quicksand transported into the arena. 
 Anyway, the very existence of the Tournament is to me rather unbelievable. If you were King, how would you choose your elite unit of warriors? 
 Soldiers that had already served in your army for years for you to observe their quality, skill and obedience or people like seventeen year old boys, "Olympic athletes, professional wrestlers, and soldiers" that are just going to battle it out and be chosen if they win? Historically, Phillip agrees with me that the Hypaspists should be a position awarded based on merit, but for plot's sake why not suspend common sense. 
 4. I don't know much about names, but Lucy makes an interesting point that a character (Jacob?) has a Hebrew name. It's the small things that nags me so much, because even though I may have not recognised the flaw I had placed my trust in the author, expecting that they took time to do their research.

I'm growing obsessed with this all over again! 
 Since the Fallen Star series made its debut here on Goodreads, I've been an ardent fan of the world Sorenson created. I loved the characters, the plot, the world-building. All of it. But this reimagining of the original series is, in my opinion, WAY better. 
 The events that seemed so stretched out in the Fallen Star series have been condensed to only the most pertinent, pulse-pounding events, and things go at a much faster pace. The characters are older, more mature, and better developed than their teenage counterparts. Plus, we really get more into the inner workings of Gemma's emotions - or lack thereof - in this book. Her relationship with Alex in this series is FAR more complicated than it was in Fallen Star, and she constantly battles with the issue of trusting him. 
 In this series, at least so far anyway, Aislin and Laylen kind of take the back seat to Gemma and Alex. I'm interested to see how this is going to continue what with the new pacing and plot trajectory! 
 Highly recommended for an audience that enjoys New Adult lit and fantasy!

This book had a really strong start. It had me hooked... until the reader got to know the characters really well and it started to go downhill. 
 The MC - Gemma - is the shy, responsible college student. And I liked how she started off been emotionless - due to her past which was slowly revealed throughout the book. Then she started to get her "feelings/emotions" back and it came across as feeling every emotion all at once. It got really annoying. Fast. 
 There were unnecessary reactions that didn't need to be expressed and things that didn't need to be said as the book progressed. 
 The story itself was interesting but for me it was like too much going on. 
 The reader learns of what type of supernatural being the character is and then in the next chapter we have a character who is a vampire. Then another character who is a witch. 
 Another chapter and character a Fairy. 
 Another chapter and character a Wolf. 
 Another chapter and character an Angel. 
 Another chapter and character the underworld. 
 Another chapter and char - you get the point. 
 Personally I'm not a fan of too many supernatural beings in one. My limit is two. So for me this had too much going on at different turns and I saw it as random placement in the story just... because. 
 Less is more in this case... 
 The romance was weird for me. It started off with the MC making the reader believe that Alex was 
 one 
 and nothing could change that and then half way through the book we hear of another character and she makes it look like Alex who...?. Totally forgets Alex and all the sudden it's only and all about this Laylen guy (vampire btw). He was probably the only character that didn't frustrate me as much as all the others. I would read his backstory. 
 I could see the author's potential in trying to tell this story with the characters she created and I won't hold this book against her. I will definitely try her other 'non-supernatural' series though and see how they are. 
 Happy reading! :)

I enjoyed this novel. I found the concept new and interesting. I am having a hard time with Gemma's behavior and actions, considering how she was raised. I read her shifting emotions but I don't feel them. I picture someone a great deal more standoffish. Someone who wouldn't touch a complete stranger so readily no matter how drawn to him she is. And I think she would be acutely aware of people more than she is. 
 We come into the story with Gemma as a senior in college, so she has had at least three years out of her "grandparents" home, which is probably how she is much more social than she should be for all the emphasis placed on her being unloved, untouched, unseen, having had her soul detached, and someone who has cut themselves off from the world because of how she was raised, but since we aren't told/shown this, her behavior in so many ways contradicts the character Sorensen is trying to create. 
 Alex is the same in ways. He is extreme in his behavior. He is either all over Gemma or completely ignoring her. There is very little in between. The wave of emotion makes it hard for me to relate to him or feel their relationship. In order to understand him more, I think Sorenson should have switched points of view--some scenes in hers and some in his--so we get a better idea of what kind of person he is. 
 At this point, I'm not really invested in their relationship. I see her attraction to Laylen as much hotter and emotional, and would prefer them together. 
 One last note, I'm all for rough sex, but the biting and scratching to bring blood is just not appealing. It doesn't fit Gemma, and should have been explained.

This is my opinion and note to self. 
 Putting this one on hold. I think it would have been better if I read this book instead of started it by listening to it. The narrator, Erin Bennett, is just one step above Suri (iPhone). She sounded so mechanical. No emotion. The heroine is supposed to having these horrific nightmares and Erin Bennett just reads it like she is reading a manual. She ruined it for me. Anyone who listens to books knows that SOMETIMES, no always, the narrator can kill the book for a reader. I may go back to this book when I have the narrator's voice out of my head. 
 I think she did Alex's voice pretty well and that is probably because she had to put some effort into it.

Originally posted on my blog!! :) :) 
 As it states this is a reimagining of her YA series The Fallen Star. I absolutely love the fact that she's started doing this for a couple of her YA series. While I'm not saying that there's something wrong with them I really enjoy those for the genre that they're in. They're great! But it's also just as fun to hear these stories on a bit of a higher level. Instead of being in high school, they're in college so the age level is different. The situations are different. More mature. Some parts are the same along with the dialogue which is cool but there is still quite a bit of a difference between the two enough to make it feel like a different series. (To me..) 
 I love the characters. They're so full of life and emotions, struggles, wants, needs, desires. Gemma just struggles with emotions in general having not felt a thing for 17 years. Nothing. No happiness, sorrow, anger...anything. And her reactions to situations are very fitting for someone in her position. She really grows emotionally as the story goes on, with everything she has to deal with. And Alex, as he is described by Gemma in the book as being hot one minute and cold the next, as if he were bipolar, it's kind of how I feel about him. There are times I'm rooting for him and times when I just wanna scream at Gemma to just run! *sigh* and then of course I have a major soft spot in my heart for Laylen :) Maybe it's the whole vampire thing, but I simply adore him. 
 This book has the perfect ending. I know if you've read it you're probably saying to yourself right now "what on earth is she talking about?!" Trust me I'm right there with you. Cliffhangers 
 suck 
 ! They drive me crazy. All this build up and then you're left at the end thinking, "are you kidding me? You stop there???" But that's just the point. It leaves you dying for the next book. Which I so very much am. And the thing that sucks is... this one JUST CAME OUT. Fractured Souls, the next book in the series is expected to publish in June...that's like...SO LONG. *Siiiiiiiiiiiiigh* Oh well that just gives me extra motivation to finish the YA version of this story line :D 
 Truth be told, the whole reason I started reading the Fallen Star series was due to a teaser that Jessica Sorensen put up from this book back around the beginning of February, you can find that teaser here to avoid spoilers if you don't want them, but it was the first teaser I had seen for Shattered Promises and I was quite literally needing to fan myself after seeing that. I had Fallen Star in my NOOK already for a while, but other books kept getting put in front of it...it kept getting shoved to the back of my pile. But once I read that teaser, even though it was going to be a YA version and a bit tamer than this one, I immediately started reading it. And even though I haven't finished, yet, I'm totally loving both of these series. I mean I know basically they're the same thing plot wise but they're both told in a very different way and are equally satisfying. June cannot get here fast enough!!
Uuuugggghhhhhh I could not finish this book.

reference_books.title: Inherent Vice
reference_books.review_text: awful

reference_books.title: The Precious One
reference_books.review_text: Again this was an Audible. I liked the book and the characters were great but the reader was my issue, the reader pronounced each word with deliberateness to the point of irritation. It was beyond exaggeration to the point of annoying.

reference_books.title: Britt-Marie Was Here
reference_books.review_text: At first I didn't know if I could read this but it ended up the best book. It's great to see that "old dogs" can learn new tricks. Britt-Marie just wants someone to know she's here. She is 63 with major life changes, not use to being out of the norm. Not every thing goes as planned, you want to yell at her, cry with her, stomp your feet but you don't have to because all the characters do that.

reference_books.title: Life After Life
reference_books.review_text: Had a hard time understanding what was happening in this book. Guess I should have read the previews prior to starting the book. Once I caught on, I loved the book. Looking at how life could be or was is amazing and creative. The wrap up of what actually happened made it all tie together.

reference_books.title: The Mill River Recluse
reference_books.review_text: Forgiveness is the strongest word alive. While some look to excuse their present lives because of the past experiences, others use those past experiences to be what they needed to receive.

book_a.title: The Girl You Left Behind
book_a.user_review: Another great read by Jojo Moyes. I thought this was well written without the emphasis being on the violence. There was just enough to be realistic for the time but not an emphasis. This is a great testament for faith, believing in the humanity of man, reminding that not all actions of the German soldiers were cruel and inhuman. There are several who will leap on those nuggets of humanity to save and be with someone they desperately love.

sample_reviews.review_text: The parts about Sophie were more interesting to me than those about Liv.
I gave up on this book! Disappointed because I loved her other one me before you.

I liked this book - i wasn't crazy about Liz, the main character. Liv has lost her husband and is living in a permanent state of mourning. She has a painting from her husband in her home and it is her favorite thing. It is her lifelike to her husband. Cut to Sophie 1917 - the subject of the painting. Sophie is trying to survive German-occupied France during WWI. The beginning of the book is Sophie's story and then we hear Liv's story as she sues to retain the painting that is deemed a stolen artifact from the Great War. I enjoyed this story but I am starting to see a pattern in Moyes' female protagonist and their love interest. The women are independent but somehow need to rescued by the male protagonist. I enjoy her writing and her stories however so I am sure I will continue to read and enjoy future works of hers.
3.5* algumas partes da historia sao um pouco cansativas, muito descritivas...

I absolutely LOVED "Me Before You" by Jojo Moyes which is why I was thrilled to win a copy of her new book via the Good Reads give away. The Girl You Left Behind is an interesting story but it took me quite a long time to get into it. For me, the voice in the first half of the book felt awkward which made it difficult to care about the main character, Sophie. I persevered and am glad I did as the second half of the book is stronger. Ms. Moyes excels at romantic stories with strong contemporary male/female characters and the second half didn't disappoint.If you liked Tatiana de Rosnay's Sarah's Key, you should enjoy this.
3.5 star read
I would give 2 stars to the first section and three to the last part so I guess it really evens out to 2.5. This book is fine, but nothing to get really excited about.
Jojo Moyes continues to be one of my favorite authors. I enjoyed this book as much as her other ones.
I couldn't get into this book.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Compelling read, until the end. It was tied up a little too neatly. In an effort to force a happy ending, the author sacrificed believability. I found it difficult to believe that the character best known for digging up information missed not one, but two leads until the last five days of the trial. I also find it impossible to believe that Liv, who waited so many years to date after the death of her husband, would so readily forgive Paul.

book_b.title: Barbarian Days: A Surfing Life
book_b.user_review: I know nothing about surfing and didn't even know that was the subject until I started reading. William is a good writer, smart individual, and fine surfer. He makes you understand the life, the yearning to be out i8n the waves, even though sometimes you think he has to be crazy.

sample_reviews.review_text: Shortly into this book I began madly texting others to read this book. This is exactly as promised by a few of the reviews, a classic must read. He follows his iconoclastic lifestyle with full out passion and still emerges as almost sage like voice. You will hold your breath until he surfaces from the churn, you will long to shove a suit and towel in a backpack and take out, and you will enjoy the lyrical way he writes. I will definitely re-read...and probably soon!

There was a movie " Endless Summer" about surfing. This book like that movie about the surfing life was endless. I understand that some have a fixation that blocks everything else out. That author fixated on the minutiae of surfing and a 100 page book would have covered the subject more than adequately as I see it. To try to stay involved in the subject matter was beyond tedious and I ended up skimming the book. I could not stay involved in the story about the next great wave but this book might resonate with those who love something to the exclusion of all else
Misspent youth. Not Finnegan's. Mine. An outstanding read. I don't understand much of the surfing lingo, but I know passion and great writing. I am prone to neither envy nor regret. And yet......

In what world is this not a vanity project or just a diary of every wave Mr. Finnegan has ever, ever surfed? 
 I will summarize: "I really liked surfing. Then I was good at it. I was a lot better than most people, though of course I was really humble. I had this girlfriend who was brilliant and I made her follow me around for a while. She didn't mind that I hung out a lot with my friend who had a subtle, limber surfing style and was, by the way, also brilliant. We decided to go on a trip and because we were upper middle class white kids in the 70s, we could easily finance it. I'm going to describe eighty-seven waves. I fell down a couple times. I'm still a really good surfer. My girlfriend and I broke up. I made new friends who had easy, lithe surfing styles and who said that I was a good surfer still. My new girlfriend tolerated us. My part-time job allowed us to pay for lots of international travel. Later, I did additional surfing in other places and was really good at it, and even though my friends all said I was really good I still sometimes didn't feel that good, but deep down I knew I was really good."

This surprising memoir was on my list because it was President Obama's reading list last year. This book pulled me into the story right from the beginning. Finnegan's story begins in the 60s as a young boy starting out, the fights at school, surfing and the lure of the waves. He surfed first in California, then Hawaii and from there around the world. I have to admit this was one of the best memoirs I've ever read. Finnegan's writing was stunning, and his story brutally honest, reaching such depths, I couldn't put the book down. I loved reading about surfing around the world and his bare bones traveling, though even he admits in retrospect that he was careless with his health and took some big risks surfing. Adrenaline junkies will love his descriptions of ferocious waves and getting sucked out by riptides and the poundings he took all too often. This book stuck to the "surfing life," the main characters changed in the end and it was a great story all the way through.

If Finnegan wasn't a staff writer at the New Yorker, I wonder if this would have been a Pulitzer winner. Memoirs are navel-gazing at their core but this one felt especially so. I tried not to compare it to this year's Pulitzer winner for the same category - The Return: Fathers, Sons, and the Land in Between - and failed. I'm looking forward to discussing this with book club this weekend, but this one was Not For Me.
Amo este libro.

The review that got me to read this (my 3rd non-fiction book of the year) came from Green Apple and said this: The Chronicle review put it best: "Were I given unlimited space to review this book, I would simply reproduce it here, with a quotation mark at the beginning and another at the end." 
 That's pretty glowing, right? And I really like surf documentaries (like Riding Giants, and Step into Liquid), so I dove in. Some of the writing is quite lovely. And sometimes it is overdone. There is no teaching of surfing or surfing terms....you just have to read through and get the gist of it - oh. the wave was big. or fast. or hard to catch. or all of those things. That didn't bother me. I did finally get the gist of it more and more. And when he got to the part about Ocean Beach here in San Francisco, I really began enjoying myself. And further, when I read a dozen or so pages outloud to my husband while we were driving, I appreciated the prose even more. He is a gifted writer, and not one that you can/should skim over. Even when he taking a lot of words to tell you that the wave was big.

I listened to all 20+ hours of this, and I feel waterlogged :)! The author has written for the New Yorker and other publications and has a wonderful writing style that translates into beautiful prose with an excellent, learned vocabulary. Saying that, I wish I had read this book instead of listening to it so I could have skimmed some of his endless wave riding. Boy, he knew what he wanted to do and he did it! He will never be able to say, "if only I had-----"; he did it his way for sure!!!! If you are drawn to the "endless summer", you will love this narrative travel saga!

Exceptionally well written - a literary masterpiece by a credible author/surfer. 
 When I heard about Mr. Finnegan's memoir, chronicling his lifetime of surfing adventures intertwined with his journey as a writer, I knew it would be one of the best books I've read. Readers who have never surfed a wave or had any interest in the surfing lifestyle will still find this work well worth reading. Finnegan has a knack for smooth beautiful writing that will evoke emotions both familiar and otherwise. 
 This memoir is more than a story of one man's life's journeys and adventures. It is an exploration of what it means to be devoted, almost entirely to a way of life. With Barbarian Days, Finnegan created an avenue for the non-surfer to become immersed in what a relationship with the ocean is all about. As a surfer, William Finnegan could likely be counted among the very few who have surfed many of the best, challenging waves that the world's most exotic locales have to offer. 
 One of the later chapters that I found captivating was the author's experiences with San Francisco's "Ocean Beach". Having grown up surfing on that stretch of coast, the winter swells at VFWs, Noriega, Sloat, and Fleishackers, is still considered something a surfer must work up to. These aren't places a casual surfer can handle, even in perfect conditions. Finnegan offers an honest, unblemished portrait of the Ocean Beach experience without any need for embellishment. Conquering the winter waves at Ocean Beach is an extremely difficult endeavor that only an author with Finnegan's experience and credibility can illustrate with integrity. 
 As a reputable writer, William Finnegan is proof positive that it is indeed within the art of the possible that a great surfer can at the same time be a great writer.

reference_books.title: Hidden Figures: The American Dream and the Untold Story of the Black Women Mathematicians Who Helped Win the Space Race
reference_books.review_text: Pretty boring. I became interested in this book because of the new motion picture. For me, it read too much like a history textbook. It was more a chronological line of events without a good story line. I wouldn't recommend this one.

reference_books.title: Extremely Loud and Incredibly Close
reference_books.review_text: I really tried to like this book, but at the end it just fell flat. "Extremely Loud and Incredibly Close" is a novel about a little boy who explores New York City in the hope of learning more about this father's death. Some parts were really powerful, but overall it didn't have a clear and interesting story line to keep me engaged. It was one of those books that about I kept thinking, "God get on with it already" and "I'm really ready for this book to be over." This book has gotten such good reviews and it was recommended to me by multiple people, which means it could be a classic case of being over-sold to me. People with eccentric reading styles might appreciate this book, but I definitely would not recommend it everyone.

reference_books.title: My Grandmother Asked Me to Tell You She's Sorry
reference_books.review_text: This book was really disappointing. "My Grandmother Asked Me to Tell You She's Sorry" is the story of young, charismatic Elsa who is sent on a quest by her mother after she passes. I initially really enjoyed the book and loved the spirit and magic of Elsa and her grandmother. However that intrigue died quickly for me and I totally lost interest in this book, which is unfortunate considering Bachman's "A Man Called Ove" is one of my all time favorites. 1.5 stars

reference_books.title: The Roanoke Girls
reference_books.review_text: I wanted to like this book. It was just too predictable and stupid.

reference_books.title: Simon vs. the Homo Sapiens Agenda
reference_books.review_text: This is one of those books that I knew would be a "5 out of 5" after the first chapter. "Simon vs the Homo sapiens Agenda" is about an "in the closet" high schooler being black mailed by a schoolmate with his own agenda. This book has everything I'm looking for when it comes to YA books: a weird yet normal and relatable main character, a romantic and unique story line that keeps you guessing until the end, and an overall warm and pleasant undertone. My first 5 out of 5 rating for 2016 :)

book_a.title: You're Never Weird on the Internet
book_a.user_review: This book is a funny, easy memoir to read. I honestly had no idea who the author was, and although we have little in common I still found myself relating to her. Good book, but nothing special.

sample_reviews.review_text: A funny and gut wrenching romp through the world of Felicia Day.
Oh soooo love it!

Deciding to read this book was kind of a risk because first, I didn't know much about Felicia Day before I actually started reading it, and second, I'm not a gamer and I don't consider myself a huge 'nerdy' person, so there were a lot of chances that this was not going to be the book for me. But I surprisingly liked it! It is funny and full of great advice, and being an eighteen year old girl who is trying to figure what to do with her life right now, I cherished it a lot. I don't think it was necessarily an important or special book to me, or at least at this moment in my life, but I'd definitely recommend it to people who are trying to start their own thing on the internet.

I liked this a lot. I'm hovering between four and five stars on it - it was well written, engaging & interesting. I love Felicia's work and have been a fan for many years. She's frank, open and unashamedly herself - even when she's anxious about it. 
 The parts about her anxiety really resonated with me. It's not easy being open about your mental health issues, and I find it incredibly brave when a public figure admits to having a problem. 
 I'm really glad that I read this - it's a really enjoyable read.

This book was cute - I am a huge fan of The Guild so was delighted for this opportunity to hear from Ms Day. The message is important, especially for younger women/girls who are still trying to find their community. I liked it.

Must read for any fan of Felicia. If you're not yet a fan after reading this book you'll be part of Team Hooman for life. :) 
 I strongly recommend the audiobook.

Absolutely fantastic, geeky perfection. Felicia Day is my hero. she's beautiful and fragile and real. She had me laughing hysterically, reconsidering my life choices, and reminiscing about the good ole days. Wonderfully written!

As for as biographies go, this wasn't my favorite. There were a few chapters I was more interested in than others. Maybe die-hard fans of Felicia Day love this, but there wasn't much that kept me involved, unfortunately.

This book was great and l could put this book down. Felicia Day shows the reader that you can do anything as long as you put your mind to it. 
 She starts with her homeschooled days to being in college at 16 as a violin prodigy then her acting career and her startup of The Guild and much more. 
 I am a geek and think that even non geek people would enjoy her memoir. She tells us all the hoops that she jumped through to get where she is today a SuperStar. 
 She did wake me up in her book that you should do something you love
It was a fun and inspiring read. And I totally read it in Felicia's voice. Read it. Now.

book_b.title: Fates and Furies
book_b.user_review: I don't really know what to say about this book. It started off so slow, to the point where I almost gave up on it. I liked the twist at towards the middle, but just not quite entertaining enough for me. 1.5 out of 2 stars

sample_reviews.review_text: I was so underwhelmed by this book that so many people loved. I finished it, so it wasn't horrible, but none of the characters felt like real people. It was like an indie movie where the characters were clearly a work of fiction and not anyone you could ever expect to know in real life. And I didn't come to know or care about any of them. A disappointment.
Finished today (9/11/17), and I'll have to say the best novel I have read in five years. Excellent. Many plot twists and character development continues until the last page.
An incredibly talented writer. I wasn't amazed by the 1st half but once the narrative switches to Mathilde I was captivated. Can see how Obama called this his favorite book of 2015.
A beautifully-written story I didn't care about as much as I wanted to. The writing, though. Very few moments that felt overwrought, and many, many lovely bits.

A 24 year hetero marriage told from two perspectives. First there is Lotto, short for Lancelot, the golden son with so much promise. Then there is the complicated Mathilde, renamed from her original French Auriel. An exploration of love, artistry, mistrust, secrets, pain. What does family mean? What does independence mean? I thought I would like this so much more then I did - a love story set in the land of theatre in NYC. However it just felt so melancholy and cynical that I was not enchanted.

An interesting portrait of a marriage. And then it takes a twist. And becomes just heartbreaking. 
 But it goes on a bit.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Really interesting book that I got on Audible. First half is Lotto: okay actor, great playwright, madly in love with his icy wife, Mathilde. Disowned by his rich mother for marrying Mathilde at age 22, Lotto paints a picture of his wife as a goddess and a saint. Second half is Mathilde: we learn of an evil streak in her that Lotto never saw. Her version of their 24 year marriage is very, very different from Lotto's and made the story far more haunting.

I liked it more than 3 stars, but not quite 4...on one hand I loved the writing and felt like every word Lauren Groff used was perfect. On the other hand, sometimes I'd need to read and reread passages and I'd still feel like I didn't quite get it.

Good book, slow at times. It's about an unconventional marriage between Lotto, a charismatic man who women adore & Mathilda, a cold calculating woman. It's love at first site and through out the first part of the book which focuses on Lotto's life, you learn everything you think you should know about these two who are devoted to each other. But the 2nd half makes everything more clear and the story really picks up. I slowly read the first half & raced through the second half.

See "Emily" 's post from June 2015. 
 That says it all. 
 I am not sure how this book became so "famous"....I don't get it. 
 It was so boring....

reference_books.title: Dumplin' (Dumplin', #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I am not sure what I was expecting from this book, but it sure was a lot more than this. 
 There are several reasons that this book just did not work for me: 
 1. It is supposed to be a body-positive book, but yet 90 % of its content is the total opposite. First, Willowdean is not at all that happy in her body, which is made clear throughout the whole story. In addition, she spends most of her time judging other people and feels sorry for people who does not need anyone to feel sorry for them. Futhermore, she keeps rambling on about how she cannot be in a relationship with Bo because she knows that people will laugh at them and make fun of them being together. How is that supposed to make anyone feel good about themself and his/her body? 
 2. Willowdean is a horrible person. I feel like I am supposed to love her because she is "brave and a fighter" but I simply cannot stand her. She uses people (especially Mitch) and does not even apologize to him 
 3. There is a love triangle. (For NO reason!) Do I need to say more? 
 4. Bo. The typical kinda-bad boy who is "handsome, perfect, good-looking, flawless...." but is SO boring because he has NO personality!! 
 5. There is way too much drama EVERYWHERE and it is completely unnecesarry. 
 6. The whole story is so predictable. There were no surprises (at least not any good ones). 
 7. A lot of the lines were so cheesy and unoriginal that it made me want to vomit. 
 8. Most importantly, I wanted to read this book because I liked that it has an obese main character since most YA does not have that. However, it left me feeling very disappointed. What I want is books where the main character, or some of the side characters, just happen to be overweight without it being the main theme of the book. A lot of people are overweight, and they have completely normal lives and PERSONALITIES that are independent of their weight. However, Willowdean's whole identity is based on the fact that she is overweight. I am left with a feeling that I do not really know anything about her except that she is overweight, has an annoying best friend, has problems with her mom and that she likes Dolly Parton. She is not interesting and her personality feels really flat to me. Therefore, it is really hard for me to sympathize with her. That she is overweight does not make her interesting, neither would she be interesting if she were underweight. Yes, she is flawed but I need her to feel like an actual person if I should sympathize with her. 
 In addition,she says that she is okay with being overweight, but clearly she is not. She lets her weight hold her back (right until the last 10 pages, in my oppinion). Yes, I get that people do not treat her fairly, but everyone in this book is so judgmental towards each other that no one has it easy, and Willowdean is just as horrible to other people around her. While I expected the book to be body-positive and show that your weight does not really mean all that much, it did neither of those things. When the main theme is weight and "being fat" it is almost impossible to feel that your weight does not matter. 
 The books intentions were good, I guess, but the author has failed miserably. 
 Why can a book not have diverse characters without it needing to be mentioned all the time how different and outsider-y these characters are? Yes, this book shows how overweight people can enter beauty-pageants but why should that make anyone feel good? It is so focused on looks, and no one seems to realize that life is about so much more than that. 
 9. She is 16 and keeps whining about how hard it is for her because her car has broke and that she now needs to borrow her mom's car. I mean, seriously, how am I supposed to feel sorry for a person because she has no car? She could get a bike or walk to work since the town she lives in is so small. I have a really hard time accepting that she thinks of that as an actual problem.. 
 The only reason that I give this book 1 star is that Goodreads sadly will not let me rate it zero, and that there were a few paragraphs that had some sense in them.

reference_books.title: Wintergirls
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I didn't like this book and here is why: 
 -The writing. I did especially NOT enjoy the crossed out words, the italic font and the whole way the story was told. For the first 3/4 of the book I just couldn't make myself sympathize with either Lia, Cassie or anyone else in the book. The characters didn't feel real to me, and that's the biggest reason that this book didn't work out for me. 
 -The plot. A lot of things in this story make no sense. Firstly, Lia and Cassie were fighting about something stupid and stopped talking, then Cassie kills herself after she tried to call Lia 33 times in one night. 
 Seriously. 33 times? That is so many times, that I ended up agreeing with Lia that she should feel guilty about not picking up the phone. It seems so unrealistic and also selfish that she didn't just pick up the damn phone once. 
 I just can't sympathize with Lia. The whole book she talks about how much she hates herself and how she wants to loose more weight. We hear about her family who is sort of messed up, and how she was hospitalized and now tries to loose weight again. When Cassie dies because of anorexia, it doesn't change anything for Lia. She doesn't learn anything from it, and that annoys me. As a character she doesn't develop at all throughout the first 3/4 of the book, and even though her family tries to help her she refuses to be helped. She doesn't feel that they are seeing her for who she is, and she clearly doesn't feel good at all, but she doesn't ask for help either. She is misserable, but I don't think her family could have done a lot of things differently when she didn't even want to get help. 
 Then suddenly in the last 30 pages she suddenly decides that she wants to live and she is hospitalized again and everything ends nicely. She made peace with Cassie and the ghost-thing is apparently not a problem anymore. Her relationship with food changes from one page to another, and I just didn't buy it. 
 It took her way too long to get to that place where everything could get better, and it felt really annoying. 
 I guess it's good that books like this one are written to put the whole anorexia subject into focus, even though I didn't learn anything from it at all.

reference_books.title: The Rest of Us Just Live Here
reference_books.review_text: So I reached page 150 and I'm gonna DNF this now. Not that it's a terribly written book, it's just not for me. I personally find it really boring, and I don't like any of the characters that much, so I'm just gonna go read something good instead.

reference_books.title: Dark Places
reference_books.review_text:
2.5 stars. 
 I cannot help feeling disappointed after finishing this book. It didn't get very suspenseful until I was more than halfway through the book, and that made me expect some sort of plot twist that would make the ending less predictable. However, that didn't happen, and therefore it just didn't feel very much like a crime fiction novel. It definitely was depressing and disturbing, though, and I must admit that I had to skip reading some parts of it since it was just too brutal and detailed (which didn't feel good). 
 Also, I felt as if I was supposed to like Libby or at least sympathize with her, but she did some terrible things to people (and animals) which made it impossible for me to feel anything for her. I don't know what the author's intention was, but I felt weird about it. 
 However, I did like that it focuses on some of the problems in the (American, mainly) justice system and it's consequences. But I don't think I'll read anything by Gillian Flynn in the future.

reference_books.title: Eleanor & Park
reference_books.review_text:
I will write a review for this book when I know how to describe what I feel about it in words. 
 This was something else.

book_a.title: The Ocean at the End of the Lane
book_a.user_review: I don't know why I haven't read anything by Neil Gaiman up until now, but I'm definitely going to in the future. This was amazing.

sample_reviews.review_text: The story of Lettie's ocean is a long rambling dream, which makes little sense and rouses little interest. I hate leaving novels unfinished. But Neil Gaiman leaves me with no choice.

I'd never read any of Gaiman's novels before but had a passing familiarity with some of his other work. 
 Honestly, I'm mystified by the huge popularity of this book. The writing style felt clunky and it wasn't particularly original. The first half had me mildly intrigued and occasionally summoned up some nice imagery, but in the end it all felt pretty lightweight and disposable.

*3.5-ish stars (I don't even know) 
 This is the kind of book that makes me hate rating books. 
 This is an extremely hyped-up book and even though I did like it, I must admit that I am a bit disapointing. This is a story about childhood, magic and monsters and it is absolutely like nothing I have ever read before which I must credit Gaiman for. I think it's most fun to go into this novel pretty blind like I did, and discover this higly ambitious, imaginative story for yourself. It's the kind of story that I think everyone will take different things from. I found the actual plot to not really be my cup of tea. I can't explain it but I just didn't personally connect to it even though Gaiman is clearly a talented author. It is very unique but something about the plot just had me wanting more. I was though, I big fan of the themes that were presented and the last 50 pages were just amazing but I just wished that there had been more of those big "life-universe" questions and less of the "spooky monsters" elements in this book. But as I said, the acutal "life-universe" questions presented were amazing to read about and the whole mystery about the ocean and the conflict between childhood-adulthood really intrigued me. 
 As you can see, I am very torned between different opinions when it comes to this book. I did like it, but I can definately not say that I loved it as much as most people seem to love it. I would recommend it because I think that it can offer people something but for me, it could have been better.

I really did love this novel. It really hit home with me, I was feeling tears in my eyes by the first chapter because it just was something that I could strongly relate with. 
 To describe this novel and to do it justice, I really do not think I can. However it made me feel a lot of things. I felt not alone, that someone actually understood me. It made me feel moments joy, happiness and moments of genuine terror and fear. 
 Something about reading this novel felt so deeply personal, that I was getting a secret glimpse into this wonderful secret story, that was for nobody else, but I was privileged enough to have read. 
 I also found this wonderful novel a sensory experience. Rather than necessarily have strongly depicted characters or surroundings, Gaiman beautiful describes to us how are protagonist felt towards characters, surroundings, or events. The moments of joy, made me feel warm, and when he felt terror my heart what race alongside our protagonist. This is element that I think I loved most about the books. 
 Within the novel I think a truly beautiful message was also conveyed. Joy and happiness may be taken as quickly as they come, but pushing through and overcoming darkness, something better will meet you at the end if you work hard to stay strong to survive. Each moment should be cherished and that really our existence is just a small little dot amongst many, and so we appreciate everyday, relish every moment, absorb all knowledge that we can, but appreciate so much more exist that we may never know. 
 A brilliant Book by a brilliant, amazingly talented Author. 
 Neil Gaiman has done it again !

There are some books that stick with you for the rest of your life. Whether it be in memories in your head, or in your heart. This is definitely one of them for me. 
 Have you ever read a book that was so beautiful? Not just in the happenings of the story, but also the way it was written? The way it made you feel? 
 I finished this book approximately ten minutes ago, and I still have little tears running down my face because of how beautiful it was. I have no idea why exactly I'm crying, but I absolutely adore this book. 
 WHY AM I CRYING?! 
 I borrowed this from the library, but I'm ordering my own copy straight after I finish writing this. 
 I'm going to read more of Gaiman's works soon.

After the suicide of his parents' lodger opens up a tear in the universe where all manner of nasties and nightmares can creep out, our boy finds himself on a bewildering adventure with his enigmatic neighbour Lettie Hempstock, who is determined to sew up the gaping hole and defend her friend's small world. In a tale that falls far closer to the horror of an original Grimm Fairy Tale than expected, our boy is infiltrated and inhabited by a shapeshifting worm that finally materialises in his home and life as the terrifying (yet thoroughly respectable looking) babysitter Ursula Monkton. Under the guise of 'giving people what they want', this netherworld monster shakes the narrator's cosy world until we can stand it no longer, given only rare respite in the Hempstock's farmstead kitchen, lushly gobbling up honeycomb and ice cream. 
 I adored this magical little book and devoured it in little over a day and, you know what book groupers (and everyone else), I don't care if it doesn't quite match up to his other work, because I haven't read any of it! Following my terrifying foray into previously unseen sections of Waterstones to retrieve this book I discovered a fairytale with a literary heart, something I could really believe in. Did it matter that my imagination struggled to visualise some aspects of the story? (such as the huge monster supposedly made out of something resembling a massive, pinky-grey tent...) Not one bit. I believed in this little boy's world and his fantastical adventure (or even perhaps - as one smart book-grouper pointed out - an imagined nightmare of the child's own making in reaction to distressing events in 'real life'). This is an oddly comforting novel, transporting us back to the magic of childhood and the sinister forces lying in wait for us that make the joys and simplicities of life all the more precious. 
 Read full review at: http://relishreads.com/2013/11/18/the...
At times, I felt like I was reliving discussions from my masters in children's literature, but through a beautifully written fantastical story. Very quotable.

I was not sure what to expect when i sat down to read this book, if it would be like Coraline or closer to American Gods. What then suprised me was a wonderful mix of the two with something... different to it. 
 This book spoke to me in a way i was not prepared for. Gaiman is a true artist when it comes to painting a mental landscape as well as an emotional one. 
 This book is worth a read for no other reason than that it is a good one. If you need more reasons than that, i could list hundreds, but i have dinner cooking and no time for that. I recomend you give it a read and find your own reasons for liking it. My reasons are my own. As yours are your own.

I raced through this intriguing book, far too eager to see why everyone seems to love Neil Gaiman so much. 
 These kinds if books just aren't my cup of tea, in terms of the story and narrative, but that doesn't mean I didn't like it. Gaiman truly has a delightfully impressive writing style but sadly he still failed to totally excite me with this book. 
 I think this is just a matter of personal preference, and my preference is zombie apocalypse novels. (I'm sort of kidding but I'm also sort of not.) This book was a refreshing change nevertheless.

I don't know where to start of with this book. 
 It was a great book to read so much mystical adventure part, that I throughly enjoyed. 
 It has a great writing style that I love. 
 Heart griping moments that I would love to read over and over again. 
 Sadly it not one my favourite books, I just overalled enjoy the whole plot story. 
 It also one of my first Neil Gaiman books.

book_b.title: Paperweight
book_b.user_review:
2 stars. 
 First of all, I don't feel good about giving this book a bad rating, but I just didn't enjoy reading this. At first, I was pretty sure that it was going to be good, but it didn't take long for me to start feeling frustrated. 
 I think it's great that books about eating disorders are written, and I think those stories are important. Therefore, I really wanted to be able to sympathise with Stevie, but I just couldn't. I wanted her to get better and everything, but she never really came alive as a character. Also, I saw her as a really selfish person who didn't treat other people as they deserved. I get that she had family problems and everything, but I think she handled them in the worst possible way. I just didn't like her at any point, and I think she made some stupid decisions. Also, if she was feeling so miserable I don't understand why she chose to spend a whole year planning her death. It just didn't seem realistic to me. It made it come across as some sort of thing she just wanted to do for attention or something. 
 I can't really say a lot without spoiling anything, but this book just wasn't for me. It reminded me too much of Wintergirls and Unspeakable which was frustrating. It was just exhausting to read many times, and I couldn't wait to finish it.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Here we go again... 
 These mental disorder books are easily predictable. The main characters are usually described as angst-ridden, spoiled teens and the doctor(s) is always right, bar-none. When they put on their lab coats and crack their fingers on their expensive desks, holding out a bottle of meds, well, you just know that the book is about to get preachy about the psychiatry practice. 
 Paperweight was slightly different from the norm, mostly in that the main character was so self-entitled, snarky and annoying that by the time the book was halfway through I was thinking, "jesus christ just do it already so you'll shut up and a better narrator can take your place!" I can see why she doesn't want to be at a treatment center full of self-righteous doctors and shrinks and quacks, places like that are definitely not fun. But planning to kill herself just to spite the world because she's full of herself and convinced she has all the answers?!? Kids these days can get away with the nastiest behavior, it seems. 
 The text was choppy, dragged on, and quickly became lifeless and dreary as it went on. I donated this book to the Salvation Army and I highly doubt I'll ever read it again.
Meh. Not a bad meh...just meh.

This was a beautifully written story. Stevie was a likeable character and her development was great. I actually started to feel proud of her near the end. I have a friend with an ED so this was a good read for me it was true to the issues that come with having an ED and all the emotions you go through and it also helped me get into the mind of someone with an ED and has helped me understand my friend even more.

I don't even know how to write a review for this one. Honestly, it was not much of anything. I did not particularly like it, but that does not mean that I hated it either. It was just one of those bleh book that does not make you feel any sort of emotions.

3.5 stars 
 It would really come in handy half stars. 3 stars don't feel right but 4 stars also don't feel true to how much I enjoyed this book. I can't really say I enjoyed the story because who can when it's such a heavy and serious theme. What can I say is that the description of the disorder felt so real and relatable. I think the characters were well done and built, it could have been better. Major trigger warning because despite having a nice cover etc it's not a light reading. It talks eating disorders, suicide and real struggles that need to be talked about more and not romanticised like they are so often, especially on TV or in other YA books.

A dark and emotional book about a girl struggling with an eating disorder, I thought this was such an important story that all young girls need to read. It was confronting and made me feel uncomfortable at times, but I'm so glad this book is out there in the world. 
 The characters were so genuine and relatable to all young girls (and boys) who are currently living in a society that promotes the thin ideal and poor body image. This is a story that I think all readers could learn something from, either about themselves or about eating disorders.

I wanted to like this but like....there was something about it that I couldn't get into. It's obvious that the author knows what she's talking about when it comes to eating disorders, but I couldn't put myself into the place of Stevie. I didn't understand her. I didn't understand why she thought it was HER fault that her brother died. To me, I thought hearing Ashley's story would have been interesting. Another thing: I thought there were too many side characters that really didn't matter. Who the fuck is Hannah and why do I have to care about her? I just kept seeing names and maybe it's because I couldn't get into the book, but I'm just thinking....wait, who is that again?

*I received this book from Edelweiss in exchange for an honest review* 
 I read this book entirely in one sitting, and it absolutely consumed me and dragged me into Stevie's world. I'm not joking, my husband talked to me for 5 minutes before I realized that he was talking to me (it might have helped if he'd said my name). Stevie and her tragic story were just engrossing from beginning to end, this story doesn't pull any punches from the beginning and I can't remember the last time a Young Adult story this series came across as sincere. Most of the time these stories are full of cliche's and the characters don't feel real. 
 Stevie felt real to me, her illogical thought process are exactly the kind of thing that is so hard to argue with when you have a mental illness. You can recognize its not necessarily true, but it's true to you and that's all that matters and you will do anything that you think is right. I thought the process of showing how slowly Stevie came to her decision about investing in treatment was perfect. I'm not sure that I would have picked up this book if I had really understood how it was going to be written, but I'm glad I did. I would give it 4 out of 5 stars. 
 *This review was first posted on Moonlight Gleam Reviews http://moonlightgleam.com/2016/05/pap...*

Stevie is in treatment for bulimia, which is just another way she has failed in life. For the last eleven months, she has been starving herself with the goal of suicide, but she weighed in too heavy for an anorexia diagnosis. For Stevie, whose only feeling of control comes from not eating, bulimic, with all its bingeing and weakness, is a shameful label. 
 Stevie's life started going off the tracks more than a year ago: her mother left them and Stevie is sure it was her fault. Stevie started drinking, staying out late, spending time with Eden (who she later describes as a virus creeping through her mind and soul), and not eating. The only person brave enough to confront her is Josh, Stevie's older brother. Josh's calling her out only makes her furious with him--Stevie does not want to look at her self-destructive spiral. And then he dies. We don't find out how until later in the book (so I won't spoil it), but we know that Stevie is sure she killed him. She has decided that the best way to redeem herself is to die on the anniversary of Josh's death. 
 With twenty-eight days of treatment ahead, Stevie is determined not to get well. Slowly, the counselors, the other patients, and her memories of Josh, begin to change her mind. Flashbacks don't help. Letters from Eden don't help. Getting well is almost as hard as forcing yourself to die. What will Stevie choose? 
 While reading Paperweight, I realized I haven't read that many novels with an eating disorder focus. I don't know how this compares, but I thought it was very well done. It offered a keen look inside the brain of someone with bulimia or anorexia: the feelings felt accurate, authentic, and showcased the reasons why someone might choose to not eat. It's a sad and hard book, which you'd expect, but has short chapters and language that still makes for a fast and easy read. Definitely recommend.

Originally posted on citygirlscapes.com 
 Paperweight by Meg Haston is anything but light. Focusing on the obsessive addiction with weight and eating disorders, delving deeper into the disease as a way to control your guilt and pain, using it as a form of self harm, this book takes heavy to a whole other level. Man, is it ever powerful. 
 I have never struggled with a disease like this, but the way Haston writes about it makes it so familiar, so understandable. The way she describes everything is so vivid, the disease becomes its own character and you can't help but be charmed by it. She really brings the ugliness and pain to life and I can't properly describe how moved and affected I was by this. 
 Most of the story takes place in a rehab facility where girls struggling with weight issues go to recover. I loved Stevie as a character, she was so strong willed, so complex, she really resonated with me and I was really rooting for her through this whole thing, encouraging her recovery. 
 I read this in one sitting; it was such an enthralling and interesting story that is probably, sadly, all too real for so many people. I can't say enough good things about this book. Wow.

reference_books.title: The Girls
reference_books.review_text: How did a twenty something writer capture the life of a teen in the 1960s so well? The Girls is a coming of age story of a teenager who is desperately trying to belong somewhere and the plot of her following the murderous cult is secondary. Although the graphic depiction of their activities I could have done without.

reference_books.title: The Execution of Noa P. Singleton
reference_books.review_text: Very disappointing. So much did not make sense. The character of the victim was not at all developed which made the "crime"too puzzling to care about the perpetrator. The device of the mother writing a letter to her dead daughter was a ridiculous way to add details to the plot. Also way over- blown prose and out-of-conrol metaphors!

reference_books.title: Sister
reference_books.review_text: Good exploration of the sister relationship, but the scientific aspect was a tad suspect...

reference_books.title: The Hand That Feeds You
reference_books.review_text: I can't say I was disappointed, because from the beginning I had little hope. We knew from the outset that the murdered man was not who he claimed to be and that could have been a fun surprise. There were no other surprises especially not the identity of the real killer. And the cup holder paragraph? Ridiculous!

reference_books.title: The Art Forger
reference_books.review_text: I am surprized that this is featured in so many lists of "bests," including indie booksellers. The writing is very sophomoric and the plot improbable and full of holes. Also, portrayed a great artist (Degas) as kind of creepy with no historical justification that I know of. I gave it one star because I finished it and I don't always do that!

book_a.title: The Sleepwalker
book_a.user_review: Chris Bohjalian is a good storyteller and this is a good story. It is written as a true mystery, not just a story that happens to have a mystery around it. A little more graphic in the sex-department than I remember in others of his books. The two sisters are good characters and his depiction of his home state of Vermont is very evocative.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I received an Advance Copy of this book in exchange for an honest review. 
 Having come relatively recently to the works of Chris Bohjalian via The Guest Room, I was excited to be able to jump in to another of his books. I'm sorry to say that I didn't connect with these characters nor get very much out of this story. 
 A brief summation of the plot is that we are introduced to a family where sleepwalking is prevalent. The maternal character is missing and the eldest daughter narrates. I found the narrating stilted and awkward. The mother is frequently referred to by her first and last name, even though the mother-daughter relationship is described as close. I found that strange as I read it over and over. It was as if the daughter was describing someone who had been gone for years rather than weeks. 
 The element of suspense never built up for me, and the big reveal felt very anticlimactic. 
 I haven't given up on Mr. Bohjalian however, and will try again.
Wow. Didn't see THAT coming

What a downer. Yipes! This was a very depressing story - a horrible story, even. 
 Being a Bohjalian fan of many years, I wasn't expecting "Rebecca of Sunny Brook Farm," but neither was I expecting the tragedy that it was. 
 I can not recommend this to anyone.
I read this in a weekend-what can I say except that Bohjalian's writing is infectious. His books are definitely those you can't put down!
I have read several books by Chris Bohjanlian and really liked them. This one was so-so. The one thing I got out of it is that I learned a lot about different kinds of sleepwalking.

Chris Bohjalian is a disappointment. It is my second book of his, and I find him mostly boring. It is especially funny when I find him trying to be mind blowing. The effort made me smile a couple of times, but the main conclusion is that I will refrain from his books in the future. 
 Bohjalian tries to spice his books with the topic sex as much as possible, it happened in The Guest Room and it happens here. In both cases, it is failing to bring much interest to the book. 
 A mother goes missing, no one knows where she is or what has happened to her, except that she is a sleepwalker. The daughter that tells most the story and the police raise a bunch of irrelevant and not even reasonable theories of what happened. In addition to the police being extremely unprofessional. Most of the book is a mumble jumble of talking about the mother's sleepwalking, and what she is doing while doing so. The end is supposed to be a surprise, but exists in other books already. 
 Maybe he was trying to put all of us to sleep, together with the book main characters. In that he succeeded. Less than 2 stars. 
 Reminded me at some points of Arrowood, which is a much better book than this one.

This book kept me going and interested, but it didn't make me want to drop everything and read. I liked that it was told from the point of view of Lianna remembering the events that occurred at the time of her mother's disappearance when she was 21. The author created some light suspense which is what kept me coming back though I never felt truly worried for the characters.

While the plot of "The Sleepwalker" is interesting, the narrative is quite boring, soporific in fact. The prose is sleep inducing, and the story doesn't pick up until after Annalee's body is found. I have to admit to skimming parts of the story, but being none the worse for it, as I didn't feel lost at any point in the book. 
 The characters were just OK. No one person really stood out. For me, the most intriguing question was what exactly was the nature of the relationship between Annalee and Gavin, given the type of relationship Gavin and Lianna were conducting. 
 I applaud the author for not presenting a definitive answer as to Paige's parentage. As her father and Gavin pointed out, Warren Ahlberg 
 is 
 Paige's father, period. It takes more than biology to make a parent. 
 But, overall, the book didn't live up the promise in the synopsis. I was unimpressed with the narrative, dialogue, and characters.

Another well-written, fine novel by one of my favorite authors. Each of the major characters will remain etched in my brain for a long time. And a mystery, to boot! Icing on the cake is a big intro for me to somnambulism and its ramifications....
Tried this twice and decided it's just reeaaalllyyyy sllloooooowww... Disappointing!

book_b.title: My Name Is Lucy Barton
book_b.user_review: I loved Olive Kitteridge and I loved the recent Fresh Air interview with Elizabeth Strout, but I didn't love this book. I didn't care for the story (there really was none) and frankly did not care for the writing. Seemed like notes for a book...maybe I would like that book better.

sample_reviews.review_text: There was something about the stream-of-consciousness style of this novel that made it feel like reading a poem. It was beautiful, and moving, and left me wanting more.
This book was like a poorly written diary. It skipped around and the author would share random thoughts. Glad it was so short...

Although I am a fan of the author's past work, I did not care for this book in the least. As Seinfeld is a show about "nothing", My Name is Lucy Barton is a book of the same, minus any thread of humor, or investment of the character's lives. 
 Lucy, a grown woman who is married with children finds her self in a hospital for a mystery illness for several weeks. Her mother, whom she has not talked to in multiple years due to her tumultuous childhood appears at her bed side and stays with her around the clock for five or so days. The book is about the gentle gossip, and stories (that go no where) that are told between them. 
 What I especially disliked about this book was the narrator (I listened to this book on CD), who over emoted and read like her audience was a tribe of either illiterates or very small children whom she needed to read over slow to capture their attention. 
 Perhaps there was a poignant story in here somewhere, but if so it was sketchily told.

I was browsing my local Waterstones, and a bubbly and enthusiastic bookseller recommended it as an awesome read so I bought a copy. How could I resist? 
 It was superbly written as expected with a very strong start. And I was hooked until I reached a certain point in the book and realised it wasn't really a story per se, more a fictional biography of musings. At that point it lost my interest and I took me about six months before I decided I needed to finish it. 
 At first I thought it was a relationship between a character and her mother (in my opinion the blurb fooled me too), but then it broadened into life. So I guess it's just a book about a woman's life during a certain period in her life. However Elizabeth Strout's strength is in her powerful subtext. In summary, Lucy Barton goes up in rural poverty, escapes it and marries well. However she marries a man her family hates, and in the end she divorces him for those reasons. 
 There are strong themes of lack of understanding, procrastination and lack of reconciliation. Like Lucy Barton's parents loved her very much but couldn't reconcile the fact to who she married there for making her estranged from them. She didn't understand that until very later in the book, and for the same reason divorced the man . It's interesting because what haunted her father, came to also haunt Lucy. And is a twisted parallel of modern times, also ended her daughter's childhood phase. 
 So a very powerful book where it's not only about love but also being able to live with one's self and conscious while loving. Sometimes love isn't enough.

Not what I was expecting. I think my rating leans more towards 3.5 stars though. We get bits and pieces of Lucy's life, & in turn thoughts and personality, at different points in Lucy's life as she thinks about them. I feel like I still some unanswered questions....

I read Olive Kittridge and liked enough that I decided to try another by Elizabeth Strout and picked up My Name is Lucy Barton from the library. 
 I am really glad the book was as short as it was. A rambling meandering mess of a book. Lucy is an older adult looking back at a time when she was sick in the hospital for an extended period. Then, she was married with kids but her husband was a wuss afraid of hospitals and she had been estranged from the rest of her family for years. Her husband arranged for her mom to fly in and come see her in the big city in the hospital and they had this ...totally non-bonding .. time. They talked about everything, except the important stuff, about random people you never meet or hear about again in the book. The visit is so surreal, at one point I wondered if it really happened. I thought perhaps she had a high fever in the hospital and hallucinated her mother being there. 
 This episode is spliced between Lucy's current life as a writer and her childhood, which she remembers as abusive and poverty stricken. The poverty is the truth. The abuse seems pretty ordinary coming from a generation in which kids were pretty regularly told to go pick a switch from tree for a whipping. Not that I am agreeing with it, I am just saying that it is not something extraordinary that the book was exploring. It was just boring. There was no big reveal. She never really reached any understanding of her mother or herself. She didn't resolve the conflict with her father. There was no resolution or even understanding reached. On top of that, Lucy wasn't even that likeable. A disappointing read from an author that I hear great things about.

The story is written in a conversational manner, skipping around many events and times in the life of Lucy Barton. As the reader learns throughout the book, she comes from a poor, abusive and dysfunctional family. The author has some very thought provoking thoughts, especially concerning what children hold tight to in their memories. I found the whole book very sad as Lucy yearns for her mother to say she loves her even after these many years. It seems she successfully has a family and career she never seems to have any joy which is what some people never get I suppose. I am not judging as Lucy might think but the author seems to leave no room for hope.
I think with the style of this novel that it would have been better to read rather than listen to. This novel explores the complexities of mother-daughter relationships over time.
I did not get this one. I have no idea what Strout was trying to do or why this strange story was being told.

This is a reflection of Lucy Barton's life. The vast majority of the novella occurs while Lucy is undergoing a lengthy hospital recovery after a surgery. Her husband, William, has asked Lucy's mother, whom Lucy hasn't seen in years, to stay with Lucy. She does. The two visit, gossip, catch up on family, etc. all of which allows lugubrious life to unfold for the reader. If Lucy expected their reunion to end in rapprochement she was mistaken. Her mother seems wholly incapable of a nurturing relationship. 
 Don't be fooled by the three stars. This is a solid piece of work. I just never really connected with Lucy even though I can empathize with her. I'm a bit perplexed as to why because our lives have some interesting parallels. I also liked Stout's writing style. It may be a bit prosaic but it is simple and straight-forward. For some reason it was just a bit underwhelming.

reference_books.title: Rhett Butler's People
reference_books.review_text: The book does not offer much insight into Rhett. In fact there is little insight to the main characters with the exception of Melanie. From a literary aspect the writing is pretty sophomoric.

reference_books.title: Cry Wolf (Alpha & Omega, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Read this one for BookClub. This is related to the Mercy Thompson series we read last year, only this has the other brother werewolf Charles Cornick. I found it kind of confusing story line, but it is probably because I'm not that interested in werewolf culture.

reference_books.title: Left Behind (Left Behind, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I liked the story line, but the dialogue is very hokey.

reference_books.title: Turbo Twenty-Three (Stephanie Plum, #23)
