book_b.title: The Goddess Legacy (Goddess Test, #2.5)
book_b.user_review:
See this review and more on The Moonlight Library! 
 The Goddess Legacy is a collection of five novellas about several of the more important Olympus deities in the Goddess Test series. They were originally released as five separate short stories/novellas in ebook format but bundled together as a paperback release. Clever marketing there. 
 Hera's story was awesome. It really showcased a lot mroe of her character and led her to being quite sympathetic in my eyes. I'm not falling for Carter's vilifying of her in the novels, especially not after this novella. It was all about how she was the strongest of the gods yet she was basically pushed back into the kitchen where women belong because Zeus is a treacherous selfish man whore. Also, Hades doesn't love her and that's her problem, not his. 
 Aphrodite's story was incredibly sweet, and showed how she could be married to one man and still have her flings. It was a nice story for the free love concept and I think she's a lovely little character, even if all the other characters slut shame her all the time. HELLO, GODDESS OF SEXUAL LOVE. Commitment has nothing to do with it, and anyway, she was committed to her husband. She always came back to him. More importantly, he entered into the arrangement fully aware of her situation. 
 Persephone's story was also really good. It detailed her life of misery with Hades and her happiness with Adonis. Of course there's a heap of slut shaming towards Aphrodite who even though she is married can't keep her hands to herself. And Persephone not being in love with Hades is her fault, not Hades', and Persephone's a giant slut for cheating on him and then leaving him miserable in the Underworld because apparently Persephone's happiness comes second to what the other gods want - namely someone to hurt Hera by marrying Hades. Also, Demeter is a bitch. 
 Hermes' story sucked. It was the story of why the gods change their names. And it has something to do with having the people still recognise the gods because now they're all modern. BUT IF THEY CHANGE THEIR NAMES HOW DOES ANYONE KNOW WHO THEY ARE? The old names are the ones still used. Hell, they're the ones I use when I discuss this book. This was a waste of time and basically showcased Hermes crying a lot because the other gods blamed him for having an affair with Persephone which led to her leaving Hades because Adonis totally had nothing to do with it /sarcasm. 
 Hades' story is so forgettable. I think it had some pedo-stalking in it. It was so blah and boring and utterly pointless. Just remember, Hades is the good guy, so the only myth in the whole world that was ever a great big fat lie is the myth that he kidnapped Persephone. How it got so distorted, no one knows. In the original myth, winter comes about because while Persephone is away Demeter refuses to fertilise the earth and help the people grow their crops. With Persephone never being kidnapped, Demeter never had the gods come begging to her to please keep their humans alive. She just eagerly pushes Persephone into this marriage she never wanted. 
 Overall this novella was entertaining - except for the boys' stories. The subtext, however, is completely abhorrent. Women are evil sluts who obsess over men and have absolutely no power of their own. It's pretty disgusting to think about it that way, but that's what the three goddess stories are basically about.

sample_reviews.review_text: What happened to the greek gods in current YA literature, they're not meant to be puncy and whiny, they're meant to be damn gods. Really dissapointed with this one, the only character who had a bit of attitude was Hera.

All of the stories were pretty good, but my favorites wwere James (Hermes) and Henry (Hades). Ava (Aphrodite) was probably my next favorite. It helps you understand them better :) Persephone's story makes her seem a little less like a bitch since we find out that Calliope (Hera) didn't actually bless the marriage, but put up a wall between them to prevent Persephone from ever loving Hades if she got over her resentment of her predicament. Still like Kate better than her though.

"The goddess legacy" e una raccolta di racconti basata sui personaggi secondari della serie incentrata sulle avventure di Kate. La Carter, osannata persino dalla Clare che mi ha indotta a leggere il primo libro, e assolutamente eccezionale nel prendere i miti classici della tradizione greca e a riscriverli per perseguire i suoi scopi e adattarli alla sua rivisitazione. Una raccolta bellissima e estremamente interessante che inganna l'attesa per l'ultimo volume della trilogia. 
 Il primo racconto e incentrato sulla figura di Era. Si e appena conclusa la guerra con i Titani e i sei figli devono riorganizzare il regno e dividersi le responsabilita. Era ci illustra come diventa la moglie di Zeus e perche inizia a covare uno spaventoso desiderio di vendetta. 
 Poi e la volta di Afrodite che ci svela la verita sul suo compito e la sua capacita di amare piu persone contemporaneamente, come sia la preferita di Zeusdw e come inevitabilmente finisce per sposare Efesto. 
 Ermes ci racconta perche cambiano nomi e come ha trovato il vero amore solo per essere tradito inconsapevolmente. 
 Segue poi il racconto della regina dell'oltretomba. Chi e Persefone e perche non ama Ade e perche rinuncia alla sua immortalita? 
 E infine proprio Ade che ci spiega perche vuole scomparire e rinunciare al suo regno. 
 Il libro tiene fede al titolo in ogni senso. "The goddess legacy" significa "il lascito della dea" e in qualche modo tutto cio che viene narrato concorre alla storia di Kate, come la ragazza viene al mondo, perche e qual e il suo compito in una somma senza fine di piccole occorrenze. Tutto e perfettamente calcolato e tutto va a sommarsi per costruire una storia intrigante e affascinante. 
 Una delle cose che mi ha piacevolmente colpita e che mi ha convinta a proseguire la lettura e proprio la capacita della Carter di partire da storie che noi in qualche modo conosciamo gia, chi in un modo o nell'altro non e mai venuto in contatto con l'antica Grecia?, e le abbia reinterpretate in modo da creare i suoi racconti in una organicita impressionante. La mitologia e una di quelle cose che mi hanno sempre interessato, come l'astronomia e l'antico Egitto, fin da ragazzina e non dico mai di no ad un libro che coniuga piu punti di vista. Siamo sempre affascinati da cio che non conosciamo e da cio che non possiamo vedere e la storia della creazione del mondo ha sempre interessato tutti da scienziati a pittori. Tutti ci siamo domandati da dove veniamo e in qualche modo tutti cerchiamo della risposte. I miti sono le risposte degli antichi e continuano a creare meraviglia in chi li legge. 
 Tornando al libro della Carter posso affermare che io non amo particolarmente i racconti ma in questo caso il tutto forma un'unita congeniale e armonica che permette al lettore di capire il perche di determinate situazioni. Un prequel azzeccato ed estremamente interessante. Non posso che fare i complimenti alla Carter che e stata capace di una fantasia senza fine. 
 Era e sicuramente il personaggio piu affascinante e non solo perche la sua e la storia piu tragica ma anche perche e lei che muove le fila di tutto in modi che non avrei mai preventivato. Ogni divinita ha il suo compito nell'esacerbare una situazione al limite e basta poco per far saltare equilibri vecchi di millenni. Sembra che in un lungo periodo di tempo non cambi niente e poi basta un secondo per sconvolgere tutto in maniera definitiva. 
 Non voglio scrivere di piu non perche non avrei da commentare i singoli personaggi ma perche mai come in questo caso finirei per spoilerare tutto e non voglio. 
 Il particolare da non dimenticare? Un salto, un pendente, un'isola, una foto... 
 Il libro e uscito a fine agosto 2012 e vi aspetta per regalarvi una serie di storie affascinanti e istruttive, estremamente importanti per capire i fatti che avvengono nella trilogia. La Carter svolge un ottimo lavoro ed e in grado di tenere tutto sotto controllo in modo unico. 
 Questo prequel precede l'uscita di "The Goddess Inheritance" prevista per marzo 2013 e io non vedo l'ora di metterci le mani sopra. come si concludera l'avventura di Kate e di Henry? 
 Buona lettura guys! 
 Ringrazio infinitamente Netgalley e Harlequin per avermi concesso l'onore di leggere questo libro in cambio della mia recensione. Thank you very much. 
 Recensione anche sul mio blog: 
 http://pleaseanotherbook.tumblr.com/p...

I really didn't enjoy this book. I've picked it up several times and am just unable to read it. I have no idea why, except that I really didn't like them. I don't like the people (gods) that they are & reading this book just made me angry.

What to say about this piece of crap? How the author has tweaked the Greek myths in this book is almost as blasphemous as Disney's Hercules movie. Um, hello, Adonis wanted to be with Aphrodite not Persephone, for one, and for another, just as long as I'm bitching about Adonis, Aphrodite hid Adonis in a box after she decided he was the most gorgeous mortal she had ever seen and entrusted the box to Persephone; she then told Persephone to not look in the box, which she did, and decided that she didn't want to give him back. After much argument, they went to Zeus who decreed that Persephone would get Adonis for four months, then Aprhodite would get him for four months, and then the remaining four months of the year, he would go where he wanted, and he decided that he would stay with Aphrodite. 
 Oh, and another thing: while yes, you could say that the marriage of Persephone and Hades was an arranged marriage, Demeter knew nothing about the agreement made between Zeus and Hades. I feel the need to complain further about how the myths were tweaked in this book. Hera was never relieved of her duties as Queen, EVER! (Though I will admit, the author did a fine job getting Hera's personality down.) And in all the research I've done regarding the Greek myths, not once have I heard about Persephone having an affair with Hermes. (And I have done quite a bit of research on the subject.) 
 By telling the myths in this matter, people who read this book are going to think that this is the correct telling of these myths. While I do admit, there are different versions of the myths, what she has written here are too far off from the accepted versions of the tales. 
 My other huge complaint about this book centers around point of view. With the exception of the section centered around Hades, she wrote the book in first person. Then she decides that she need to switch to third person to tell Hades' side of the story. 
 Now while I loathed how the author tweaked the myths, I thought that with how she tweaked everything, she came up with a fine story. I give her credit for bringing up the correct elements of the myths. This is one of the reasons I'm giving it two stars and not one. The other reason I'm giving this book two stars and not one, I've recently read a book that I thought was much, much worse.
Just no....no no no no no! This is horrible. WHAT HAVE YOU DONE TO MYTHOLOGY! WHY!! DX

3.5/5 
 For those who love The Goddess Test series, well, this novella is certainly a treat. And for those who are curious (like myself although I do love the TGT series) and like to find out the backstory of the gods featured in the books you're also in for a treat. The Goddess Legacy is a novella composed of five stories--stories that will help us understand the gods more. Like, why is Hera acted that way? Or about Hades/Henry and his desire to just fade. I got the answer and more in this novella. 
 I'm not really that keen at first about the other gods since I didn't have that much interest on them. But this novella does certainly help me understood the situation more. Like Hera's (Calliope), we all know she did awful things to Kate (and for the poor eleven girls before her) but she didn't become what she is now out of nowhere. There's a reason behind her behavior and it is heavily rooted with her relationship with Zeus. Then there's Aphrodite's story which thinking about it didn't leave anything on me. I mean, I know she's the goddess of love but oh boy did she love. She loves a lot. 
 One story though that caught me off guard was Persephone. I didn't expect to kinda like her story. We all know what happened with her relationship with Hades (Henry). Why she got herself married with Hades expecting things will work out (and we all know it didn't). She hoped for the best, she didn't even doubted Hades (Henry) of his love for her. She was sure of it. She had expected to love him while married to him. She hoped that love will naturally emerge while they're together. She didn't even ask for extremes, she just wanted something that feels...right. Less suffocating. Something natural. But she didn't get that while she was with him. While I don't exactly like how she got what she really wanted, or rather 
 who 
 she really wanted. But I must say, I kinda impressed that she followed what her heart really longed. 
 And finally, I was more interested (heavily I must add) with Henry. While I find him sometimes weak because of his decisions and his lack of enthusiasm at the beginning but I understand him better now. After loving Persephone so much, more than his existence itself. And his life all alone after that (plus the atmosphere of underworld) will surely dampen even the most enthusiastic spirit. He had been longed to be more than just a shadow. He wanted to have his own happiness too. But eons had passed and it is still the same, the guy has limits as well. Consider the loneliness and the betrayal he had experienced, I understand now why he wished to fade. So I'm glad that despite how he arrived where he is now (how bumpy and perfidious the path was), I'm glad he has Kate now. The guy deserves happiness which before he only gets in his dreams. Though their (Kate and Henry) relationship is far from perfect (bordering annoying) he has someone who truly loves him. 
 To sum up, I really enjoyed The Goddess Legacy; the stories are wonderful. Like I said earlier I'm not into the gods (Calliope, Walter, James, etc.) before I read this (I initially only wanted Henry's story) but their stories quite interesting and it served some background to the gods. Before I was detached, very indifferent to them. Well, I finally got to see them in a different light. All thanks to this novella. Though I still hate Hera. :angry: 
 I received an eARC from Harlequin Teen via Netgalley. Thank you.
couldn't read it. I didnt really want to read another point a view of what we already knew. since it was not furthering the original story not interested.

This review also appears on my blog at http://www.thegoldenruleof666.blogspo... 
 Absolutely brilliant! I feel like I know the characters so much better now. I wondered whether this would be worth reading in regards to the series and, after reading it, I would definitely urge any fans of the series to read The Goddess Legacy. Not only is it interesting, but it also clarifies a few things that weren't touched on in the first two books. 
 The story about Calliope/Hera explained how jealous Hera became insane Calliope. It shows how she turned her affections to Hades/Henry and became obsessed. I actually understand her insanity now, why she would go to such great lengths to have Henry for herself. I can't say that I like her any better, but I do understand her much better now. 
 The Ava/Aphrodite story was sweet. This one was about how she developed her relationship with Hephaestus. In the myths, of course, that marriage was arranged and devoid of love. In Goddess Interrupted, we find that their relationship is actually a loving one. This story explains how that came to be. It also gives a good explanation as to why Ava has more lovers than the ocean has drops of water. It made me like Ava a lot more because that tendency of her's tended to get on my nerves in the first two books. Getting a reasonable explanation fixed that for me and now I can actually like her. 
 Persephone's story was...enlightening to say the least. It describes her time with Hades, from the moment they took their vows to Persephone giving up her immortality for Adonis. There were times in this story when I wanted to wring her neck-like the many times she hurt poor Henry. But I do understand why their relationship never seemed to work. It doesn't say it outright, but it can be assumed from the many hints. Let's just say that their relationship wasn't meant to be, and someone made sure to keep it that way. After finding out that the debacle of Hades and Persephone's relationship wasn't entirely her fault, I can't hate her anymore. I still don't particularly like her-I think she's selfish and a witch for hurting Henry-but at least I understand her actions. But I'm still beyond glad that she's out of the picture. 
 James/Hermes' story was probably one of the most informative. And it was adorable. In this one, Hermes gets to know a few mortals while trying to find out why so many gods are fading. He is, as always, charming and adorable. But, most importantly, we find out why the gods changed their names. I didn't understand the necessity before, but the explanation given in this story was thoroughly believable. It actually makes perfect sense that the gods would change their names-and their relationship with mortals-after reading this explanation. This story, along with Persephone's, also gives light to the animosity between James and Henry. I know it's touched on in the previous books, but this made it much more understandable. 
 And finally, Henry's story. Ah, Henry...I didn't know it was even possible to love you even more, but I seemed to have managed it. This one chronicles how Henry decided to give up and fade, and the subsequent tests on the potential goddesses. This actually includes a condensed version of the first scene in the first book. And, a little surprise into how Kate and Henry first met, and I don't mean when Ava "died." The way they actually met was so adorable. I swear, in the moment that I found out how they really met, my conviction in their relationship quadrupled. And if you're panting to know how they first met, I'll let you stew in the agony and find out for yourself. But this story gives light to how Henry felt watching all the girl die during the tests. And how he felt after meeting Kate. And we get the explanation as to how Henry got that reflection of Kate and her mom that he gave to her for Christmas in the first book. A little add on about Henry in general: During each story, it was stressed how Henry was the best of all the gods, the only one not corrupted. That truly made me lose my heart to the tormented god and it gave a reason as to why Henry is so different from the other gods. All I have to say to him at this point is: Henry, I love you! 
 Along with all this, we also understand the origin of each of the god and goddesses' new names. In each story, we get a look into how that character chose their name. All of this gave light to the characters, allowed me to understand them so much better. 
 The Goddess Legacy is wonderful and, if you like the series, you'll love this book. 
 Definitely 5/5 
 Thanks to Netgalley for a copy!

The novellas for The Goddess Legacy were intriguing and informative, giving insight to several different characters in The Goddess Test series. I loved learning what occurred in each of the five gods' lives before Kate Winters joined the group. My favorites were Hermes and Hades. Their stories were the most heartwarming and heart wrenching of them all. 
 However, I wish there was a little more consistency in the style throughout the book. Where Hera, Persephone, and Hermes are first person, past tense, Aphrodite is in first person, present tense, and Hades is in third person, past tense. And considering these novellas together form a single storyline, the inconsistency made it a bit confusing. 
 Additionally, I would actually classify the book as a prequel (i.e. Goddess Test #.5) rather than Goddess Test #2.5, since all of the stories occurred before Kate Winters appeared as the main character of The Goddess Test. And with that stated, I would recommend reading this book before starting the actual Goddess Test Series. 
 For more book reviews, you can also visit my website over at Ketch's Book Nook. Thank you.

reference_books.title: Zen in the Art of Writing
reference_books.review_text:
As others have said in reviews of this book, it is not a 'how-to' guide, it will not teach you how to write best sellers, it will not give you the top ten ways to reach a publisher... it is a look into the writing process of Ray Bradbury, a writer with a keen mind and a brilliant turn of phrase. 
 This book is made up of a series of essays, each with a different focus. There are certainly a few excellent tips contained within these pages, and and aspiring writer would I think glean a few kernels of truth and hope from it. I know that I have started to write down the prospective titles that pop into my head without plots for them, for future reference. As well, i think for me the two most valuable ideas are to examine what scares you, and to give experiences time to bubble in your subconscious and not force them. 
 I was however left feeling a little sullied by the self-indulgence of the last few essays. Rather self-congratulatory, but then, I guess the man did achieve an awful lot, and obviously put in a lot of work. He deserved to be a little smug.

reference_books.title: Grave Sight (Harper Connelly, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Really enjoyed this. As a True Blood fan, and a Southern Vampire series fan, i was a little apprehensive about trying another one of Charlaine Harris's series. What if I hated them and it coloured how I felt about Sookie et al.? I'm so glad that I tried it though, because Harper Connolly is a wonderful character. 
 Harper is no Sookie clone, she has her own voice, and a wonderful brother who is nothing at all like Jason Stackhouse! The book was a quick read, an easy read. The mystery was suitably intriguing, and the clues just twisty enough that solving them is tricky. I look forward to reading the next one.

reference_books.title: A Visit from the Goon Squad
reference_books.review_text: This book is hard for me to describe... a series of intertwined vignettes that explores relationships, regrets, secrets, desires, and over-arching-ly Music... I enjoyed this greatly. I think I will have to reread it to make it clear in my head what I have got out of it though. there are some beautiful passages, some stunning descriptions within. Some of the characters are so beautifully drawn. Sometimes the large cast and the intertwinings were hard to keep straight in my head, though that may have been more my fault than a fault with the book. Really glad to have read this, and I know a couple of people I'll be recommending this too, as well as putting it back on my to read list for a second go around in a couple of months. Definitely worth the effort.

reference_books.title: The Eyes of the Dragon
reference_books.review_text:
Wow, when I started reading this book I had to double check who the author was. It is so very different from Stephen King's normal genre. And yet, looking back at it having finished it, it's not too far a leap. 
 A fantasy tale involving two princes, a rather boorish king, and an advisor who keeps to the shadows and deals in poison. Pretty classic really in a swords and sourcery way (and there is plenty of both). And a nice little tale about good versus evil, about justice and truth conquering all, and even the weakling gets to redeem himself in the end against a clearly defined evil. Nicely done, voiced by an interesting unidentified narrator. Reading about the links to the Dark Tower series by King made me smile; I like it when an author grounds a tale in their universe, something that King manages to do quite well generally. 
 All in all an easy read that was enjoyable. If I had come across this when I was younger I might have loved it passionately, or perhaps have disliked it for its cliched subject matter, but right now I can appreciate it for a good fun story, well voiced, that shows a deft hand at storytelling. All that I generally expect (and receive for the most part) from Stephen King.

reference_books.title: Infinite Jest
reference_books.review_text:
This book is very hard to capture... it is at turns funny, horrifying, utterly depressing, and mesmerisingly involving. Some parts are hard going, taking great effort to plow through; other parts read comparitively easily. This is not an accident at all, but a carefully orchestrated build-up, giving a literary conclusion that is all the more satisfying for the work that went into getting there. 
 I belong to the camp that belives that literature should be challenging to read, who revels in (occasionally, at least) wrestling with prose, plot and characters. Infinite Jest fits into this category very, very well. I enjoyed reading it, even when it was hard reading. And though I got a lot out of it, I feel like I need to read it again to grasp it more fully. And that is a very unusual position for me to be in. I will tackle it again, in, say, 6 months time?!

book_a.title: Shutter Island
book_a.user_review: Unfortunately I had been spoiled for the twist by a movie review, but despite that I still found myself engaged, and raced trhough it in one sitting, unusual for me. Intriguing and creative... I enjoyed the psychologist characters, and the visual imagery. Well worth a read. Now to watch the movie and see how it measures up.

sample_reviews.review_text:
In 1954, widower U.S. Marshal Teddy Daniels and his new partner Chuck Aule go to Shutter Island, home of Ashecliffe Hospital for the criminally insane, to investigate the disappearance of a patient, Rachel Solando (who was incarcerated for drowning her three children). She has escaped the hospital and apparently the desolate island, despite being kept in a locked cell under constant supervision. 
 Teddy reveals that he wants to avenge the death of his wife Dolores, who was murdered two years prior by a man called Andrew Laeddis, who he believes is an inmate in Ashecliffe Hospital. During a hurricane Teddy ends up in Ward C to investigate what he assumes in wrong doing. While separated from Chuck for a short while in Ward C, Teddy meets a patient called George Noyce, who tells him that everything is an elaborate game designed for him, and that Chuck is not to be trusted. 
 Teddy and Chuck are separated again after leaving ward C and Teddy heads down to the beach where he discovers a woman who says she is the real Rachel Solando. She tells him she was actually a psychiatrist at Ashecliffe, and when she discovered the illegal experiments being run by them, she was incarcerated as a patient. She escaped and has been hiding in different places on the island. 
 In an attempt to do right he climbs to the top of a light house to save Chuck and finds hospital administrator Dr. Cawley seated at a desk. Cawley tells Teddy that he himself is in fact Andrew Laeddis (an anagram of Edward Daniels) and that he has been a patient at Shutter Island for two years for murdering his wife, Dolores Chanal (an anagram of Rachel Solando), after she murdered their three children. 
 Andrew/Teddy refuses to believe this and takes extreme measures to disprove it, grabbing what he thinks is his gun and tries to shoot Dr. Cawley; but the weapon is a toy water pistol. Chuck then enters, revealing that he is actually Andrew's psychiatrist, Dr. Lester Sheehan. He is told that Dr. Cawley and Chuck/Sheehan have devised this treatment to allow him to live out his elaborate fantasy, in order to confront the truth, or else undergo a radical lobotomy treatment. Teddy/Andrew finally realizes that he killed his wife and his service as a US Marshal was a long time ago. 
 The ending of the novel is unclear as to which "reality" is true: the recovery or the investigation. It is also unclear whether Teddy has truly regressed, or if he wishes to "die" (at the very least, lose his ability for conscious thought, through lobotomy) in order to avoid living with the knowledge that his wife murdered their children and he is her murderer. 
 Meeeeeh. I wanted to like this book. I really really did. But it was hard to get into and I felt zero investment in the characters. I also really despise stories where I don't know what the "real" ending is. If Teddy is a good guy or bad. Glad I read it once.....Won't read it again.

Dennis Lehane's "Shutter Island" is a damn good creepy psychological thriller. Lehane proves that he is one of the best writers of suspense-thrillers working today. The Scorsese movie starring Leonardo DiCaprio is merely okay. Read the book.

An eerie read. But Lehane can definitely write beautifully. Has some things that the movie didn't (obviously) and was just as good, if not a little better. Although I gave it 4 stars it kind of left a sour taste in my mouth. A somber ending to say the least. In all, a strong read but not one with a happy or even resolute ending. The final words sting. Any lover of King or Poe would dig it.
Nicely done thriller/noirish type mystery. Big WTF moment late in the book - WOW. Enjoyed it.
a book good for reading on the beach, a current Leo movie, a twisty ending, a fast read that will not change your life. I won't watch the movie..
I learned that my brain can't keep up with others. This book completely lost me at times. At the same time I couldn't put it down. Probably ones of the strangest books I have ever read.
It's maybe cheating to read the book of a movie I know and love, but to me, it just enriched the experience because the adaptation to film was so well done.
I think I would have found this book very good if I had not seen the movie twice and knew already all the plot twists coming. Still it was enjoyable.

God awful book, I cannot believe they have made the movie of this rubbish. 
 In the movie Adaptation one character describes his plot for a serial killer film called "the 3" he may aswel have described Shutter Island.
Had to DNF this... almost 100 pages in and really slow paced and wordy. Not keen at all! Shame because I loved the film!! Just hate the writing style.

book_b.title: The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle
book_b.user_review: Most intriguing... putting straight on my re-read pile...

sample_reviews.review_text: After slogging through the first 400 pages of this pseudo-philosophical treatise, I still couldn't explain what it was about or bring myself to care about any of the characters. The third "book" did finally pique my interest enough to get me through to the end, but barely. I walked away with no real sense of resolution or even a sense that the lack of resolution was on purpose. The only reason this warrants two stars is because my book club had a fantastic conversation about it. We didn't resolve anything either, but our general inability to describe or agree on any one point was interesting in itself.

The Wind-up Bird Chronicle is a wildly imaginative tale straddling the known and apparent world and a shadow world where strange, malevolent and sometimes inexplicable forces are at work. On its face, the tale concerns a jilted, cuckolded husband whose cat and then his wife disappear. Trying to understand and regain her, he encounters a series of very odd women, some of whom he sleeps with. His attempt to reconnect with his wife is punctuated by long stories of the pre-World War II occupation of Manchuria related in part by one of the strange women and in part by an old soldier of the war. Much of the book is spent in the bottom of a literal well. 
 It is a nonlinear tale, a pastiche of news accounts, real-time narrative, old war stories, letters, and personal histories. A number of disparate themes present themselves throughout: fate, water, birds, baseball, skin, men without faces. None is really tied up in a neat way; unfinished threads hang from this book's pages. While many of the individual war stories would themselves make fine stand alone narratives full of doomed and evil men and driven by strong narrative force, the tale of the main character's search for his wife is far more slack. 
 What drives this slackness is the fact that the main narrator, the husband, is by far and away the least interesting character in the novel. Females full of character and drive and ambition surround and dote on him, but he is completely acted upon rather than acting as an agent himself. He largely obeys their direction. We learn a lot about the sandwiches he prepares and the cigarette varieties he does not smoke. When the going gets tough, he disappears down a well for days to think. I kept hoping he would disappear from the novel and let the more interesting characters have more room on the stage.

I can't keep doing this to myself 
 File this one under a new Goodread tag: books-i-gave-up-reading. 
 I did not hate this novel, but I could not finish this novel. I'll tell you why: 
 My general rule for reading novels is to give it 50 pages. If by that time the novel isn't doing anything for me--the style of writing, the characters, the story development--I'll stop. I mean: *something* the author is doing must make me want to read. Rarely have I put a book down. Rarely is there nothing--style, characters, story--to make me *not* want to read. 
 Well, I gave The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle much much more than 50 pages. But I can't go on. 
 As I've mentioned in other reviews, novelists give themselves away in their novels. It can't be helped; it's part of the creative process. What also can't be helped is that novelists tell you about their novel *within* the novel. With the best writers--in the best novels--this is very subtle. It's almost non-existent, or transparent, because it's so much a fabric of the novel itself. But it's always there. It's always there. 
 And here it is in The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle: Mr. Murakami warns us what kind of novel he's writing on p. 82. It's free form literature. He mentions three "free jazz" musicians on p. 82. Albert Ayler. Ah, I thought. I see where he's going with this, and I'm not liking it. On the next page, p. 83, Mr. Murakami reviews the main portions of the "story," such as it was up to that point, for us. Thank you, I wanted to say, because I don't remember! And don't really care anymore! 
 I plodded on. 
 By page 180 I felt like the narrator when he says to himself: "I had to move my body, to begin working toward some goal." The next page stopped me cold: "I felt as if I had become part of a badly written novel....." 
 I put the book down and thought: I wouldn't say "badly written." I would say "poorly constructed." To this point in the book it was like reading a Bukowski "slice of life" novel; or, watching Andy Warhol's 45-minute epic "Eat". It's idiotic. 
 As a writer and reader, I find nothing of value to continue reading this book. I take that back. I find things of value in how *not* to write. But I can't go on. 
 I'll leave my review of The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle at that and close this book and place it back up on my shelf where it will remain likely unread for the remainder of my days.

Any book with a torture scene automatically gets a "one star" from me. And war was a significant sub-plot so there were a couple mass murders and plenty of personal violence. ugh. 
 And then, I just never cared about the main character. He is completely un-interesting to me. This book has so many people recommending it, I thought for sure something interesting must happen at the end. But nope. *shrugs* oh well.

This is a book that made me completely absorbed when I first picked it up. However, towards the end, the story seemed to close rather abruptly that I wasn't sure what I was reading. It is unlike many other books I have read and there is a rare appeal to it.

I have to mull this one over a bit. I very much enjoyed the writing style. The content requires suspension of disbelief in places. It is surreal. At the same time, it's not so much a stretch to believe the cruelties of war. The war stories are the most grounded in reality and that makes them all the more difficult to read. The writing is explicit and this is not for anyone who is easily uncomfortable with sex, violence, and the mythical. But again the writing is designed to pry you out of your place of comfort and force you to confront reality. 
 May was my favorite character. If you're looking for a realistic, well-written teenager, she's it.

I feel guilty for not liking this book more than I did. I finally concluded it is just not my cup of tea, though I admit there's a lingering memory of the characters and events and most of all the atmosphere that still stays with me, like a dream. It was recommended to me by a friend based on my love of Ishiguro, but it turns out Murakami is just too subtle for my taste. So sue me.
He's really not that great of a writer, but I think this plot is so interesting. It's a big book, but it doesn't feel like it when you're reading. I didn't want to put it down.
a lot of side stories that makes it a little dragging...

I can't with the author. Maybe one day I'll return to this book when I'm in more of a mood for it. But I cannot stand the way this author writes about women, rape, and extremely violent or sexual scenes.

reference_books.title: Atlas Shrugged
reference_books.review_text:
NO spoilers, not to get too detailed. 
 Been on my TBR forever, until my brother final convinced me to tackle this. 
 Essentially how does one describe this mammoth of a book, for me the following: 
 First the negatives - it is way too long, and was in need of an editor. Some of passages a very long especially John Gault's speech. 
 On the flip side this is a great story that has predicted everything that has occurred up to this point (2016) in the USA and other parts of the world, then taking it beyond, with additional government control of business and everyday life that is absolutely scary. 
 The story takes place in an alternate North America of the 1930's or 40's. With industrialist, inventors etc. and the talents that these people bring to society, then turns sour with government control and the ruination of free trade, thought etc. 
 If one has a good deal of time to devote to this book and are interested in industry and politics go for it. This is a book that makes you think about life and our world.

reference_books.title: Rat Queens, Vol. 1: Sass & Sorcery
reference_books.review_text:
Since getting back into graphic novels as of the last I have come across some very good stories. I must say this one falls short. The dialogue is a bit childish for the mature nature of the book, characters are very wooden, and the illustrations are average. 
 I will not be continuing this story, as it has not peaked my interest.

reference_books.title: Mightier Than the Sword (The Clifton Chronicles, #5)
reference_books.review_text:
This is book five in a series , that I had originally thought that was to be a trilogy. Therefore, I am compelled to see where Archer concludes the story, certainly not in book five. 
 Not a great deal occurs in this book to move the story along, and much is predictable in many of the plot arcs, which has been done before. We have some new antagonists introduced, and one finally meets an end. 
 With all that said I still enjoyed this story as it is truly a forbidden desert, with all the melodramatic scenes, that occasionally take you away, as in the sense as a reading of the Enquirer newspaper in the US. You pick it up and before you know it you read several pages.

reference_books.title: Prince of Thorns (The Broken Empire, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I have to go with 2.5 stars here. 
 This book knocked me for a loop. 
 This fantasy is dark I mean really dark. 
 The story line was ok, revenge is the theme, with killing upon killing among other heinous acts. Narrated by the main character Jorg, who has to be the worst anti-hero I have ever come across. How can you like him, I have tried, but detested him and his whole band of men, and funny I am curious where this story will go. Will Jorg change at all? 
 With that, since this trilogy is on my TBR, and reading the reviews of book 2, I am going for forge on ahead. 
 I will keep my fingers crossed.

reference_books.title: The Ocean at the End of the Lane
reference_books.review_text:
Gaiman takes us back forty years, as the main character returns home for a funeral, and remembers his childhood, and the magic that surrounded his young life with a neighborhood girl. 
 Here Gaiman I'm sure has used his childhood as a guide through these times. 
 A quick read, but not one of his best.

book_a.title: Winter of the World (The Century Trilogy #2)
book_a.user_review:
No Spoilers. 
 I must say that I enjoyed this book, but not as much as I did the first installment in this series. While we discovered the characters for the first time in the Fall of Giants, the history covered was more of a compacted period. I found that with the expansion of characters into their children's lives, Follett did not give enough attention to the historical events, with this story stretching over 16 years, and half the world. There was too much time lapse at certain moments, and volume one characters were dropped off, with very little written on. 
 While I did enjoy the history, and its' accuracy, I would have enjoyed if Follett spent more time concentrated on the war, had fewer characters, and left the after wards with Volume three, however then I'm sure that would have led to a book four, which publishing perhaps would not permit?? 
 Still to this date the best historical fiction on this period is Wouk's Winds of War and War and Remebrance.

sample_reviews.review_text: Loved this book in the Century Trilogy. This book takes place from 1933 to 1947, and encompasses the war from the points of view of the Americans, Germans, British and Russians. We cannot know, just how lucky we really are, and how much we need to make sure that another world war never happens again. I am looking forward to book three. Thanks Ken Follett for sharing your book with us!

I love Ken Follett's writing. His characters are very intriguing and I feel invested in their experiences. His mastery of history woven into stories is what keeps me so engaged I can't tear myself away.

I really wanted to like this book, but did Follett phone this in, or what? Character development was non-existent. People were props for historical scenes and nothing more. I gave up after about 300 pages.

What can I say? Couldn't put it down. Excellent character development. Excellent story line with WWII. Excellent integration of the story lines (a little pushed on the realism of the overlap between characters. Ken Follett is a gifted story teller. The sections on Pearl Harbor did a great job capturing the naivete (and perhaps arrogance) that American had before the bombing and also the chaotic realism of the attack. Also, love the way that the rise of Nazism was handled because it showed how a beaten down population can follow a mad man without realizing until its too late.

What a disappointing follow-up to Fall of Giants. I enjoyed this as first, but I was listening to it in audio, and the reader was charmingly British and did a bunch of cool accents. But as it wore on, I realized that the historical facts were a thin backdrop to a soap opera, rather than acting as the story's backbone. 
 Most of the characters from the first novel returned, but their children became the focus as they randomly fell in love with eachother. I'm talking "love" creepy old man style - there is no reasonable explanation or backstory for the relationships, just a lot of pervy descriptions of boobs. Sometimes Follett describes clothes, but boobs are definitely his preferred subject matter. 
 Pass.

There is a danger of social and political historical fiction like the Century Trilogy. People already have a connection to the events and a sloppy author can simply trade on that knowledge to hold a reader's interest without allowing the reader to uncover something new.Historical fiction is often centered outside the experiences of the reader. When Gone with the Wind, hit the best sellers list in 1936, there were both living veterans of the Civil War and many children of those veterans. GWTW reinforced much of the moonlight and magnolias myth of the Ante-Bellum South to such an extent that those myths still resonate one hundred fifty years after the War. 
 Fortunately Ken Follett is an uncommon author. Covering the period from the end of the War to End All Wars to the end of the second such war, most readers are close enough to those events. However, Follett lets readers uncover new perspectives on these events. 
 Many have written about the rise of Fascism in Europe and but few demonstrated how close the British aristocracy came to embracing it themselves. It is one thing to write about the Holocaust on a grand scale and something else altogether to witness the forced evacuation of the ill and insane from Jewish hospitals on trucks bound for extermination camps. The stupidity of American isolationism, the cruelty of Stalinism, idealism of the expatriate fighters in Spain, gay soldiers,and the bravery of the French and German resistance are all subjects within the reach of Follett's pen. 
 Sit back, settle in and enjoy this part of what will be considered, for a long time to come, a contemporary gem.
Long on information. Short on inspiration. Well researched, a wealth of story but it lacks literary content. History buffs will love it I suppose.
I did not enjoy this book at all. It felt a lot different than the first book.
This is such a great picture of WWII It really takes you there Not in a buried in facts way either It's long so take your time but it's worth the effort

For me, Ken Follett is a guilty pleasure. His books are big, entertaining page-turners -- no more, no less -- and sometimes, that's exactly what I need. "Winter of the World" is Part 2 of his Century Trilogy, in which he follows several intertwined families on two countries through landmark events of the 20th Century. With the turn of every page, you can practically hear the sound of the mini-series contracts being written and signed. While much of this book is utterly predictable, that doesn't lessen the pleasure of reading it. Follett knows how to tell a story. Don't let the weight of this tome scare you off (nearly 1000 pages!); it's a quick read. I look forward to Volume 3 of the trilogy, scheduled for publication next year.

book_b.title: Red Rising (Red Rising, #1)
book_b.user_review:
No spoilers here. 
 I must say that I read several blurbs on this one, and was intrigued. I must says that I give this 4.5 stars. It was a good story, and definitely in my opinion not a young adult novel by any means. Yes the main character is young, but all the themes dealt with are adult and told from an adult point of view. 
 A portion of the story has parallels to The Hunger Games, although much more complex. Wonderful world building as well, and great memorable characters. 
 I highly recommend this book, and am looking forward to the next one in January, shame I have to wait until then to find out what Mr. Brown has in store for Darrow!!!

sample_reviews.review_text: Wow, Red Rising was just spectacular. It was brutal and like nothing I've ever read before. I really really liked it. The action was intense and it was a roller coaster of emotions. I will definitely read the next book. Also, I hope Darrow and Cassius resolve their differences in the end.

I have never DNFed a book so quickly. I didn't even make it to fifty pages. I don't care if this book gets better. I was absolutely loathing it so why should I bother? 
 The writing style aggravates the crap out of me, especially the slang for this society. It's just so awkward to read. And because of that the book was incredibly emotionless. 
 Darrow already annoys me. He's so damn perfect. He's The Chosen One I can tell. 
 I feel like Brown just changed the names of The Hunger Games' first few chapters. It is just way too damn similar. 
 But what made me throw the book across the room was the killing off of a female character to further the rage and plot of a male character. I didn't even like her but I don't care. That's bullshit. 
 I'm sorry. I know a lot of people love this book but I was seething with rage (as well as bored to tears) and I hadn't even hit page fifty yet.

I bought the book because of the positive reviews. I also happen to like Katniss and Ender so I didn't see why I shouldn't give Darrow a go. 
 By chapter 2 I can see why they referenced The Hunger Games and Ender's Game. 
 I would not say that this is a must-read book because the premise is mostly cheesy. I didn't feel any love coming from Darrow when he talks about how he absolutely loved his wife. Just didn't buy it. The writing is quite tight in the beginning. You'll want to devour it whole. But it kinda lost its momentum after 15% of the way. I had to let the book stew for several days because I was quite frustrated where it was going. It has so many things going on but took a predictable formula of YA dystopian book. No matter how high and mighty Darrow is, he can't escape his predecessors' shadows. 
 I already bought the second book and will start today. Don't disappoint me, Darrow.
I got about a third of the way through and couldn't continue. I couldn't connect with any of the characters or get into the plot or world building. Interesting concept but boring execution.

Red Rising is most interesting for its portrayal of the reluctant resistance fighter and its impeccable character development. A member of the lowborn mining class colonized on Mars, Darrow and his fellow Reds have been fed propaganda for generations regarding their role as pioneers preparing an uninhabitable planet for those desperate to flee the dying Earth. Proud and loyal, Darrow believes his work is noble and accepts his lot in life. His reckless young wife, however, has other plans for him. Sentenced to hang for forbidden acts, Darrow resigns himself to following his beloved wife to the grave, yet is confused to find he has survived his execution. For his death is a hoax and he has been secreted away by underground rebels in order to be groomed for infiltrating the elite, as our reluctant, bitter hero is meant to serve a purpose greater than himself. Brown's literary debut was a hard sell in the initial chapters with an abrupt start and complex world with distinct jargon, but the action and intrigue quickly builds and doesn't let up. Red Rising is complex and honest, heart-wrenching and violent, as it mines the tricky depths of the human soul.

Super good. It's all those things others have said much better than I. A great book that borrows from lots of other great stories and series in an awesome not stealing but complimentary yet still original kind of way. I realize that makes no sense so how about this, Red Rising is like taking Cap'n Crunch, Lucky Charms, both types of Pebbles, Fruit Loops, and Frosted Mini Wheats, and mixing them all with something healthy like a big bowl of bran flakes, and creating something wholly new, amazing, and delicious. It is the best damn bowl of cereal you've ever eaten.
4.5 Very good, quite different from other things I have read

So, this was a disappointment. The first fourth of the book is wonderful. The characters and relationships drew me in and I was crying bitterly a few chapters in. It was beautiful, moving, well-written and interesting. 
 Then the book loses it. It's basically another Hunger Games with weird names, a male lead who should be called Gary Stu of MarySueness and that reads like a strategy game, not a novel. There's a reason I don't play video games, don't give me the same structure in a book. The only good thing about the rest of book after the first fourth is Mustang. She still doesn't make it worth it. 
 I would say make a pass on this one.

3.5- it was good. I did get a bit bogged down in the military tactics. I can see this becoming the next dystopian movie series! I will go see it;) 
 It ended in such a way that I do think I will continue with the series, just not right away.
A MILLION STARS!!! This is now up there as one of my favourite books. I can't even begin to explain how amazingly this story is written, it really is just next level.

reference_books.title: Animal Farm
reference_books.review_text:
If you've been thinking you should read this, do so. 
 If you haven't been thinking you should read this, do so. 
 It's mind-blowingly well done. Orwell is a marvel and I am just so impressed by his work. 
 Listen to the audiobook on 1.25x speed and you can get through it in the length of a couple of podcasts.

reference_books.title: A Wrinkle in Time (A Wrinkle in Time Quintet, #1)
reference_books.review_text: It was fun for me to re-read this as an adult. I read it a lot as a kid and it brought back great memories. That said, a) I didn't remember it being so god focused, and I always find that distracting/annoying b) I couldn't help but notice SO MANY THINGS that reminded me of Harry Potter and it gave me sort of a sour feeling toward JK Rowling (bc this book came 30+ years before HP), deserved or not. The evil man with red eyes! Good vs. evil! Protagonist saved people bc the one thing they had that the enemy didn't was love! Tesseract/apparting. There were other things but I'm forgetting. Anyway, I still liked the book but inevitably not as much as when I was a kid.

reference_books.title: The Storied Life of A.J. Fikry
reference_books.review_text:
What a lovely, quirky, unexpected little book. 
 We all lead storied lives and I love how this book showcases how beautifully imperfect life can be. It was a perfect mix of realism, fantasy, bibliophilia, twists and turns, and a somewhat unconventional format. Just. I just really enjoyed it. 
 Why four instead of five stars? Something was juuuuust missing for me but I can't put my finger on it. If I can name it, I'll edit my review. Doesn't matter though. You should pick this up.

reference_books.title: The City of Mirrors (The Passage, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
I have mixed feelings about this book. 3.5 stars? As with the rest of the books in this trilogy, it is a TOME. 
 There are parts I FLEW through, like Zero's background and the battle scenes, and parts that I got so bored with, but I kept trudging because I knew it would eventually get good again. The story, overall, was good, and the payoff was pretty good. 
 Aside from needing some editing, though, I actually rolled my eyes several times at some of the sexist undertones. A few examples that come to mind: 1) rape as a plot device. Alicia was a strong, resilient character and her being raped was a cheap ploy to move her story along. 2) Several times things and/or people being called "bitch" at the height of someone's anger 3) There was a comment during the battle about how women wanted to help fight along the wall, and that was okay, whomever was in charge should let them. GIGANTIC EYE ROLL. 
 In a trilogy with strong female characters, a trilogy which is LITERALLY about a girl saving the world, do we need women to be raped as a plot device, and for them to be given permission to fight when there was a shortage of fighters? Cronin can't seem to decide how he feels about women. 
 Additionally, while I liked the ending, are we really supposed to believe that Logan went from someone who couldn't detect a joke to falling in love with someone and becoming a completely different, emotionally open person...in less than two weeks? 
 You know what, never mind. Three stars.

reference_books.title: Born Standing Up: A Comic's Life
reference_books.review_text:
Two stars is generous. [Which is why I edited this review and am giving it one star. I normally don't finish a one star book, but this was the audiobook and it was short, which is why I stuck it out.] The audiobook is only four hours but I spent most of it being mad. I finished it because it was so short and I kept hoping it would get better. What's the saying? Don't meet your heroes? Admittedly I didn't know much about Steve Martin's standup, so shame on me, but I've always liked Steve Martin and I thought this would be an interesting and fun read, especially as he reads the audiobook himself. 
 Unfortunately, reading this book is like listening to self-indulgent, creepy, self-aggrandizing drivel and corny dadjokes from your drunk uncle at Thanksgiving who wants everyone to know about his accomplishments and is very pleased with himself while everyone else rolls their eyes behind his back. Every female in the book seems to exist solely for decoration: they are almost all, to a person, described by their looks and whether or not Steve Martin had sex with them. The one exception I can think of is Gilda Radner and another woman from SNL, who are described in passing and in terms of what their voices sound like. He skips pivotal plot points-like mentioning a divorce even though he never mentioned the marriage-and comes dangerously close to whining about being misunderstood. Perhaps the worst part is that despite reading/performing his own memoir (about comedy!), his tone is flat and rather than bring the material to life he manages to make it more boring. I laughed exactly once in this book about comedy, and smiled fewer times than I have fingers on one hand. Yes, I counted. It was that bad. Did I mention I spent a lot of this book feeling angry and gross? 
 F-. I will never be able to watch Father of the Bride the same way again. Thanks a lot, Steve Martin!

book_a.title: The Alchemist
book_a.user_review: I wanted so badly for this book to live up to the hype. I gave up with an hour or so left of the audio. I'll have to settle for loving a few of the quotes.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I'm not sure about how to review this novel. I always feel terrible when I have to give a novel or book less than three stars. I'm too empathetic in that sense; I just think about all the effort the author must've put in their novel, like coordinating and constructing the proper structure for their plot, how to arrange the dialogues and finding the proper words to express what they want their characters to say, finding ways to develop their emotions and conveying a believable synergy to the reader among other things. When I think about all these things I feel both bad and amazed, the prime because I didn't like the novel and the author put effort into it and I feel bad for disliking it, the latter because, well, the effort must've been big. However, I cannot force myself to like a novel, and I just didn't like this one. 
 The spiritual and metaphysical basis of "The Alchemist" seems to be a combination of Christianity, Pantheism, Mysticism and every speech any public motivator would want to deliver an audience. The novel sums up in the following words: " 
 Follow your dreams and do not give up, no matter what the circumstances are. 
 " 
 I almost feel as if Darth Vader was trying to say in the most polite and protracted way possible: " 
 Use the force, Luke! 
 " 
 Unfortunately, I consider this novel to be filled with the trite, over-used and hypersensitive phrases we have all heard before: "Don't give up!" "Follow your dreams!" "You can do anything you want!", and that's simply not my cup of tea. I like cold, hard truths and different point of views, not recycled phrases I can read on-line. Now, with all that being said, I'm not certain if Coelho's objective was to help his readers grow and feel more confident about themselves, or if he simply wanted to use demagogy at its finest to win his readers and have a larger audience for his next novels. Quite frankly, this novel is both demagogic and boringly trite, so in short words: I didn't like this novel. One star.
that's so stupid. sure not "everything is one"!!

The Alchemist is a story about a boy who was a shepherd, found out his Personal Fortune was to find a treasure in Egypt, and had to decide whether to follow this Personal Fortune or stay where he was comfortable. The book was written like a YA book with simple language, proselytizing, and mercifully short. Everyone except for one character was unnamed, the main character was "the boy", which made me wonder how old he was. No character is fully developed, everyone is rather flat. The section with the boy and the alchemist was the worst part. It was boring, drawn out, and the "God" talk and "turning yourself into the wind" was ridiculous. The ending was okay, but the rest of the book was so bad, it didn't shore up.

0.5 stars 
 It's a fucking sad excuse for a book. 
 It's tedious. It's a drag. It's annoying. It's full of an incredulous amount of statements that just made me roll my eyes and say "ugh, duh??". It's taken (I would use the term stolen but I'm trying to be a little polite here) several stories from everywhere else that it lacks originality. It's basically another version of the Bible, with less blabs and a more modernized tone to it. 
 This book is just so goddamn awful that I don't understand why several people (peers included) liked it a lot. This isn't a self-help book. If anything, it's preachy and leads people into thinking that if they want something hard enough, the universe will fucking conspire for them to get it. And all that without lifting a finger. 
 Also, what is up with this only think about and focus on your present shit?? Why are you telling me to forget about my past or not worry about my future?? What the hell is the fucking matter with you??

book_b.title: Plum Island (John Corey, #1)
book_b.user_review: It was entertaining. But it was also far longer than it needed to be - some of that length would have been better served going toward thickening the plot and developing the characters rather than serving for the misogynist main character to be tickled with himself at every turn. Admitting you're a total pig doesn't absolve you from being one. It's not as cute and charming as he thinks it is. And when I say he, I'm not even sure if I'm talking about the character or DeMille himself. This was my first Nelson DeMille book, and all I could think was that to write that way, you have to think it's okay, and it's not. As such, I think this is going to be my last DeMille book. I began to realize as the book went on that there was not one single female character - whether part of the plot or incidental, such as a waitress - that the main character didn't leer at and sexually evaluate almost instantly. Any smarts or anything else she brought to the table remained a firm second to how badly the main character wanted go screw her. So gross, so unnecessary, not at all charming, and totally distracting from the plot. D minus, DeMille. And that's being generous.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Although a lot of people complained about the main character, I thought he was really the only thing that made the story interesting. I love the concept of a mystery on Plum Island, a biohazard zone that works with deadly viruses. However, it makes absolutely no sense that people would be able to take their own boats there and do random archaeological digs. I also didn't really understand why they made such a huge deal out of certain characters at the beginning of the book when they really didn't have anything to do with the rest of the story. 
 Anyway, I was waiting for some great big twist, but it never really came. Instead it just dragged on and on to the point that I didn't even really care anymore. I won't be trying any more DeMille.
Detective John Carey is convalseces in a quiet Long Island town. He becomes involved in investigating the murders of two biologosts who west researching aninal diseases at an offshore site.

Could have skipped this one. Although I really enjoy mystery, Mr. Demille has an uncanny ability to stretch through a description of a scene that is truly intensifyingly long. So much so that at the end of the book I found myself skimming through paragraph after paragraph.
The first in the John Corey series. Almost 5 stars, but the ending could have been better.

The first 2/3 of the novel are like a guidebook to Long Island and it's very interesting. 
 Too bad at the end DeMille pulled a terribly nasty trick to justify the hero's violence to follow. 
 very disappointing.

The timing of my reading, coming just after the Weinstein story broke, couldn't have been worse. When you're in John Corey's head, his behavior toward women comes off as inappropriate but mildly amusing, but when you pause to put yourself in the position of the female characters, it's downright creepy. Interestingly, the two gorgeous female characters fall for him, despite his assholery and the fact that it's said on several occasions that he looks like hell, as seems to generally be the case in detective novels written by men. 
 The story itself was absolutely ridiculous, but it was compelling enough to keep me reading, hence the two stars.

reference_books.title: Revenge of the Girl with the Great Personality
reference_books.review_text: Though the book possesses good themes and messages for girls, I found it to be too predictable and therefore unremarkable. If you have time to kill, then go read it. However, it is not a book that must be on a person's must read list.

reference_books.title: Lady Renegades (Rebel Belle, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
I am from the South and I cannot tell you how many times I laughed out loud with some of the mannerisms characters had and social commentary that is found within this series. However, I think it was only that connection that I had to the world that kept me coming back to the series. Otherwise, I wouldn't have continued because every book fell just a little more for me plot wise. 
 For the ending of this series, I needed some scenes more fleshed out ( you will know what I mean when you get to those last 40 pages or so). I wanted to feel more for the Harper and the impossible situation David put her in after the last book. However, instead I simply skimmed most pages because there was little action or emotion to help me connect to her. After reading more ya books than most people, I am aware of what those last 40 pages could have been when it comes to the level of angst and pain I could feel ( you know the angst that makes you want to put down the book because it is painful and yet you can't stop reading because it is that good...) and I didn't get it from this book. Yes, I am aware that this series is supposed to be a fast and entertaining read, but I still want more from that ending... Though that last page with him asking if he could call her "Pres" definitely had me smiling to myself . 
 I still adore Rachel Hawkins ( Hex Hall is a fav series of mine and one I have found myself re reading on more than a few occasions), and I look forward to what she has next for us! It just seems that Rebel Belle wasn't truly for me.

reference_books.title: A Court of Thorns and Roses (A Court of Thorns and Roses, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I have read a lot of reviews about this book about Tamlin an Feyre and how amazing their love story is. And these reviews were correct. Throughout the book, we glimpse multiple occasions when either one will do whatever it takes for the other. 
 However, almost none of the reviews really mention the character of Rhys... and truth to be told I will be reading the next book because of him. I find him to be such an interesting character And I really want to know why he was so shocked/scared of Feyre in their last conversation .

reference_books.title: Dearly, Departed (Gone With the Respiration, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This book is freaking hilarious! Forget the Hangover( well, no, better not), this book brings sarcastic quips to another level. 
 Nora, is your typical head strong heroine, who lost her father a year ago and is better for it, in the sense that because of that loss, she is independent and mature and can handle her self. Which is shot to hell when she is kidnapped, but actually rescued by the oh-so charming-zombies, who are a secret weapon of the army to help eradicate the "Punks" or Grays(Punks/Grays are the bad zombies with an extra dose of psycho). 
 The zombies were created by a lethal virus called The Laz which made sure that once one was infected with it, they would have five years to retain themselves before becoming completely crazy, like the Grays. One particular zombie, Bram, you fall absolutely in love with, way before Nora gets the memo. 
 Though, at first it took a while to come to terms with the fact that instead of dealing with vampires or angels, this was a zombie. A skin peeling away from the face and have to repair body parts and OH! I like human flesh, but I'm not going to eat you, zombie. As the book develops and we are thrown into the war against bad and good zombies, the book gets better when it follows Bram and Nora's story( the book branches off into multiple POV's) it becomes pretty adorable. Bram, has been dead for two years and is the captain of the Laz army, and is head over heels for Nora within a few days of knowing her. And it also helps that after they saved her, she encloses herself in his room for days and only wants to speak to him. 
 And as for Nora, Bram is one hot piece of Zombie flesh. He's cute in an old fashioned I-never-had-a-girlfriend-but-I-really-really-like-you kind of boy who is one of the worthy candidates to have awesome lines. As for the other quotes, they belong to Brams friends and fellow zombies. They make this book hard to put down.Of course, there is more going on in the book besides the love aspect, there is betrayal and war, but mostly, this book is filled to the brim of ridiculousness.

reference_books.title: The Here and Now
reference_books.review_text:
ARC from Netgalley 
 Actual rating is 2.5 
 I am not sure how to write this review. The story had many interesting ideas and definitely makes you want to "go green" if that means saving the world and future generations from the "future" in this book. Furthermore, it makes one appreciate the technology we have today and also realize just how ridiculous some of the inventions we now possess. 
 However, the world building is rushed. Indeed, there are many times I wish we could read more about the future these people escaped from by traveling to the past. Also, how did the ability to time travel become available? I also want to read more about Andrew and how he was able to travel back on his own as well as Poppy. 
 Then there is the relationship between Ethan and Prenna. I honestly do not know if Ethan actually loves Prenna or if he simply loves the idea that she is from the future. Furthermore, their relationship simply seems rushed. Prenna went from rarely talking to the boy outside of class to declaring her love for him while on an adventure. If the author had delved into their relationship in a more deeper level, I would have believed their love. 
 I suppose one can simply say my biggest problem with the book is that it was not long enough because the author did not build the world. 
 Also, that ending... Is there a sequel?

book_a.title: Sanctum (Guards of the Shadowlands, #1)
book_a.user_review:
This book won't change your life or be considered one of the best books you have ever read. However, it is pretty entertaining. 
 It does need some help in the world building (still don't really understand why the enemy race is inhabiting people in the city and how they somehow found a way into our world) . Yet, the characters had some good lines- Malachi had a good speech here and there. Now the mc was a lesser version of Rose Hathaway. In fact, the relationship between Malachi and her felt like a watered down version of Rose and Dimitri. Then there was the insta love which can be tiring after a while. 
 At the end of the day, the book did its job of entertaining me while I am waiting for my more anticipated books to be released.

People I follow on Goodreads with similar taste to mine looooved this book, but I almost didn't make it through. Perhaps I'm lacking in compassion, but I spent much of the story wanting to strangle Nadia for refusing to do anything at all to help herself and not caring whom she hurt (yes, that's common with depression, but that doesn't make it less exasperating). Lela irritated me nearly as much while she repeatedly put everyone at risk by trying to save someone who didn't want to be saved, while proclaiming "I'm so sorry I got you maimed, it's all my fault" and then doing it over and over again. 
 I did enjoy the author's take on the afterlife, and I liked the ending enough to go on to read the next book in the series.

Maybe 3.5? I need to think about this more but I'm super bummed that this didn't work better for me. I loved the setup and idea of the dark city filled with lost people. It was creepy and fascinating in a horrible way. I loved Malachi and the slow burn romance was delicious. But I quickly lost any interest in Nadia, which slowly eroded my connection to Lela. I admire Lela's determination to rescue her friend, but it got to be a little bit too much when Lela was neglecting everything else, including reason, and putting herself and others into danger for a cause that I had ceased to care about. I also didn't really understand the Mazikin or the mythology around them. They seem sort of random to add chaos. 
 I do desperately want Malachi to be happy, and I would like to see a lot of growth from Lela. But the idea of 2 more books is kind of daunting. Especially with what I know is coming in two. 
 Does the mythology get stronger? Will Lela grow on me? Help!

Loved the worldbuilding, Lela is a great character, and the story is well-paced. I don't think I've read much else of this genre (is it paranormal romance? urban fantasy? there are so many fantasy subgenres these days, I can't keep up with them), so I don't know how it compares to others of its type, but I enjoyed it. 
 I had just a few nitpicks with it, the same sorts of things I always complain about when YA stuff gets too afterschool special-y. Also, did it have to be Auschwitz? It would have felt more authentic if she hadn't gone for the most famous concentration camp for Malachi's past, in my opinion. I suspect lots of readers won't mind this, however, as it does make for some pretty high drama.

I think probably 3.5 stars. 
 Lela, a foster kid, has had her fair share of trouble growing up, but it has only served to make her tougher. When she stands up for the most popular girl in school, she unexpected gains a best friend. When this best friend, Nadia, then commits suicide, Lela knows she must try to save her from Suicide City, a place she's already familiar with. 
 Unfortunately, this didn't work for me as much as I expected. Malachi's feelings for Lela developed straight away, and this doesn't appeal to me. After one meeting with her, he's willing to step completely out of character, and risk his life for her. 
 I enjoyed the plot, and Malachi was quite awesome, but at times, this felt a little too romance based for me. (Very unusual for me to make this statement). Lela was a character who quite annoyed me at times, and I didn't know whether I should admire her for her dedication to helping her friend, or hate her for how her actions were hurting Malachy and the others. So, I was frustrated with her for most of this book. 
 The ending worked well for me though, even if it was a little too good to be true. But it makes and interesting setting for book 2 :)

I don't know what is happening lately, every book I pick up starts off really nicely with a strong lead character and a great plot that slowly loses balance as cliches seep in and the main protagonist starts to annoy me.

You guys, I adored Sanctum! I've always been partial to paranormal books and this one was fantastic! 
 Lela Santos knows that she needs to rescue her best friend Nadia from hell. So she willingly walks through the Suicide Gates to go looking for Nadia. I loved the way that this city was described. It's desolate and reeks of despair. Every single person there is there because they've taken their own life and now that they're in that city, they become consumed with their own personal demons. Lela, having gone in willingly, is not like the others and goes on a search for Nadia. This mission is easier said than done. The city is humongous and there are those in the city that prey on the human souls there. Lela has to get out of there alive and rescue Nadia at the same time. 
 This was such an amazing story of friendship. When she was alive, Nadia was the best friend that Lela needed. Nadia helped Lela be able to dream of a future that had previously seemed impossible, especially after the terrible things that Lela has gone through in her past. While Nadia was the thread that lifted Lela up before, now Lela has to be the one to lift her out of hell. 
 Lela is one of those sassy, independent, strong headed characters that you just love right off the bat. The fact that she is choosing hell for her best friend just gives a testament to her character and how strongly she loves her friend. Lela is completely badass (I mean, she snuck into hell, how much more badass can you get?) and I loved how strong she was despite what she's gone through. 
 As Lela goes on her mission, she meets Malachi who is Captain of the Guard. The Guard consists of soldiers essentially protecting those in the city. Malachi is this quietly strong leader that is SO swoon worthy. He decides to help Lela on her journey and lends his crazy awesome fighting skills because they definitely need those on their side. I loved Malachi. He has such an interesting past and I can't help but admire him and his selflessness. Loved this guy. He kind of exudes safety and somehow I'm always drawn to guards, captains, people in uniform? Read it, you'll love Malachi too. =) 
 The world building of this city was detailed and just fantastic. Everything was described really well and at the right pace. I loved seeing Lela's journey. Sanctum not only explores how deeply the bounds of friendship can go but also the little nuances of life and death, love and sacrifice. I was glued to this book and could not put it down!
