An exciting, quick paced read

As we all know by now, I'm all about the girls in dresses covers. Combine that with the comparison to THE DA VINCI CODE (which I read in a single afternoon back in the day), and I knew I had to read this one. 
 The mystery in this book was the main thing that kept me turning pages, since it moved super fast and I loved how the history of Alexander the Great and the Diadochi were incorporated. That being said, preparation to suspend your disbelief going into this book is important, since the main character, Avery, makes some decisions I couldn't quite understand. Number one being, running off to Europe with two boys she barely knows, one of which followed her around town and brandished a weapon at her. I understand that she wanted answers about her father, but jumping on a plane without bothering to try talking to her mother first? That was a little far-fetched, for me. But once I set that aside, I was able to get really into the story. 
 There is a love triangle in this book. I happen to love love triangles, as long as they're done well, and this one was done well. I could understand Avery's attraction to both of them, and while I found Stellan to be a slightly more compelling character because of his motivation for working for the Dauphins (and also because he broods and is morally ambiguous, really), I think either boy would be a solid choice. I really appreciated that, while they kept warning Avery she had no idea what she'd gotten herself into (which is fair, since she didn't), they also didn't underestimate her, and she also played an equal part in solving the mystery. Additionally, it's not actually that clear which boy Avery is going to end up with, which should make the romance aspect of the next book really interesting. (I mean, it's clear which direction Avery is leaning, but there's also room for that to change. CONFLICT.) 
 Finally, the setting is fantastic right from the beginning. Avery starts out in a small town in Minnesota and ends up visiting Paris and Istanbul, and each setting felt unique thanks to Hall's use of details that grounded us in each setting. At the same time, the use of detail didn't feel overwhelming. I think Hall did a great job balancing the exposition with the action in the story. 
 Overall, THE CONSPIRACY OF US is a fun mystery with wanderlust-inducing settings and a fast pace that just takes some suspension of disbelief to get really invested in.

I read this book because it was on a list of YA books with LGBT themes. I read this entire book for one sentence describing a secondary character. One sentence! 
 Also, sadly, the book wasn't that good. Sure there's a female lead and that's great. But besides her mom and one very small supporting character, everyone else was male. We need equal representation. The mystery wasn't that good. The leaps of logic to follow it through were too much to ask.

A good AU YA. Love all the travel! It reminded me of several others like it, but I tend to like these types of series so I didn't mind. But I am over the whole "bad boys are more interesting and understand me more" relationship trope. But I immediately got the sequel!

**You can see this full review and more at Book Briefs: http://bookbriefs.net**YA ReviewMy ThoughtsHave you ever picked up a book and by the time you were finished, you were convinced that the author crafted the book just for you? That was what happened to be with The Conspiracy of Us by Maggie Hall. It was like the author poked around in my head, and pulled out a bunch of winning elements for me, mashed them all together and popped out a story that was sure to make me fall in love with it. Everyone is comparing The Conspiracy of Us to The DaVinci Code, and I get that comparison, but I feel like it was even more than that. It felt like The DaVinci Code mixed with Tomb Raider mixed with the biggest international secret society of all. Plus the focus was on Alexander the Great, who I think is a fascinating historical figure. (and yes, I do know that a ton of "facts" surrounding Alexander have been fictionalized and sensationalized throughout history, but that just makes him all the more interesting in my opinion.) The Conspiracy of Us will leave you wanting more. 
 I was immediately swept up in the Circle of Twelve and everything that has to do with them. Personally, I really enjoyed a majority of the characters in this book. I know some readers biggest complaint was that they didn't feel a connection to Avery, but I did. I got that she so badly wanted to know more about her father, because she thought it would fill something in her. She was constantly on the move, and constantly stuck in surface level relationships. She wanted something more, something deeper. I think that was her driving motivation throughout the whole story. Avery's mom was my only annoyance in The Conspiracy of Us. I don't like the whole Parents keeping their kids in the dark about some huge part of them or their lives. (but it does happen a lot.) However, as Avery was brought into the mystery and intrigue of the Circle of Twelve, I soon forgot about that roadblock, and I was quickly swept up in the Mandate. I couldn't read this book fast enough. I kept wanting to get to more clues. 
 There is a dash of romance thrown in, to satisfy that romantic sweet tooth, and I think there will be even more to come. Honestly, I just can't wait to get my hands on the next book. Maggie Hall does such a great job making you want more, that while I am kicking myself for waiting so long to read The Conspiracy of Us, I am also happy that I did wait, because book two- The Map of Fates comes out in only 2 months. The Conspiracy of Us ends on a cliffhanger, so if you are smart, you will grab books 1 and 2 at the same time and start on a wonderful binge read. You will thank me. 
 Bottom line: If you are a fan of The Davinci Code, of secret societies, of history and of tomb raider this book is a match made in heaven for you. There isn't much to NOT love. I loved this book so much. It is a favorite of mine for sure. 
 This review was originally posted on Book Briefs

I don't entirely hate this book, but I'm not in love with it either. I think I'm more annoyed by this book. It's just... I can't even.... I don't know anymore. 
 It starts off with Avery wanting to go to prom with hot guy #1 but can't because she has to move with her mom in two days. She sneaks out and goes anyways. There, hot guy #1 and hot guy #2 start fighting over her. (Seriously, this seems like some wishful thinking here) And Avery decides to leave with hot guy #2 who pulls a knife on her only a minute before. That's right, this girl who snuck out of the house decides to go with someone who threatened her life moments before and they happen to go out of the country. Because that's the most logical answer! 
 Honestly, it would have been nice if Avery decided to go home or let her mom know or pack or something before just leaving. Or even thought about it more than, he's hot and mysterious. 
 Whatever. She's in Paris. Which you can tell by the constant mentioning of the Eiffel Tower. Over and over again. How she can see it from her room. From the plane. From landing. From this, from that. I got it. Eiffel Tower is in Paris and saying that relates more to Pairs. But come on! You don't need to mention it over and over! 
 Now there's some "mystery" going on and Avery wonders who this family is that she's suddenly related to now. Oh, turns out, it's the circle. And there's a prophecy, because what awesome book doesn't have a prophecy in it? And guess what? Avery happens to be in said prophecy with her stupid special eyes. Only a girl with purple eyes will something or another. And this family only has guys with purple eyes, but no girls. (Except the pregnant lady who is going to have twins and one is a girl with purple eyes. Is that even possible to know before they're born what color eyes they have?) And special special Mary Sue has to fit this prophecy and is the ONLY girl who has purple eyes!!! OMG!!! Ugh, fail already. 
 Then there's all this history, which I'm up for. I love history. But it annoyed me about this history. Apparently these families are responsible for every major event in history including WWI and WWII. No. Just no. It didn't work. 
 But the things that do need explaining are not explained. Like how do these families get in power and stay in power? No idea. 
 Also, how in the world would some teenage girl know who the most famous golfer is and the French President is? Oh, yeah, and the VP of the US? I don't know that and I'm older than Avery is. But no, Avery knows everyone. Yay her... 
 But Avery is so smart, yet she can't figure things out. She has no common sense at all. Things that should be obvious are not to her. 
 Then, there's the forbidden romance! She's in love with hot guy #1 and he loves her, but it's so forbidden! If anyone finds out, he'll die! Blah, blah, blah. Find something new people. Can we have something original for a change? 
 And love triangle. Just no. It's not surprising, but it's frustrating. Even more when both guys are described as hot guys and "mysterious". They're not. They're pathetic losers and one should be locked up. 
 Then again, there's no real characterization. None of the characters are developed more than how hot they are. How "smart" they are. How rich they are. That's about it. I want to read more than he's so hot. That doesn't make me like a character. 
 The "twists" in this book are so predictable. I knew what was going to happen before they mentioned it, it was disappointing when I was right. And it just ends. Nothing is solved or resolved. It ends because gotta do a trilogy! That's the new thing to make money. Seriously, half the boring crap could have been taken out, developed other things more and you could be done. The pacing was so bad too. If it was fixed, it would be better. I'm so frustrated with this book. It had potential but lost it. Thought about giving this two stars, but more I write here, more I'm annoyed and less motivated to give it two. One it is.

When I first picked this book up, after reading a couple chapters, I honestly thought it was a joke. It's so bizarre, and there was so much info-dumping going on, that I really couldn't take it seriously. But once I realized that it actually wasn't supposed to be a super serious book, and that there are just these ridiculous circumstances that take place and you kind of just have to roll with it...I started to actually really enjoy it. The Conspiracy of Us is basically a YA version of The Da Vinci Code, except not quite as well written or mind boggling. 
 The idea of it is actually quite cool, though. And very unique! Have you ever heard of the conspiracy theory that there's actually a coalition of powerful families who, together, are the people who truly run the world? The Conspiracy of Us takes that theory and runs with it. Avery West has moved from one town to another her whole life. She was always told that her father had left the family as a baby, and they had to constantly relocate because of Avery's mom's job with the Army. But when two strangers show up at her prom, Avery learns that there's quite a few family secrets she was never told about. 
 Once I got into the rhythm of suspending my disbelief and enjoying the ride the book was taking me on, I realized that The Conspiracy of Us is actually wildly entertaining and it really became a story that I was having a lot of fun reading. I definitely didn't want it to end! I'm kind of disappointed that it's actually not a standalone like I thought it was, but now that I know there's going to be another book, I sort can't wait to read it! Especially after that cliffhanger! 
 Overall, The Conspiray of Us was a unique, fun, and action-packed read that I would recommend to fans of the Something Strange and Deadly trilogy by Susan Dennard (it's not paranormal or historical fiction like those books, but the writing style, tone, and plot really reminded me of them) and people who are more into plot-focused stories vs. character-focused ones. The characters in this book are likable, but lack depth. They could've been any characters from a million other YA books I've read; they didn't stand out or connect with me in the way that I look for in my favorite books. But the plot was surprisingly decent and well-thought-out, and while there was a touch of romance, it didn't overpower the story. 
 So, even though I didn't love this one, I'm pretty excited for the next book!

reference_books.title: We Were Liars
reference_books.review_text:
"We were liars. We are beautiful and privileged. We are cracked and broken." 
 I did not like this book at all. The beginning started off really good but then it just got boring. I was very confused all throughout the book, but I forced myself to continue. The pace was really slow and it never picked up until I read the ending. I definitely did not see the ending coming. I understood why the summary of the book says, "And if anyone asks about the ending...just lie.." I don't understand what the point of this book was. The romance was lame. The writing style was not for me. It was a quick read but not enjoyable. 
 I wish I had more to say, but to be honest, I don't. The story didn't have any 'major' plot twists, other than the ending. 
 Maybe you will end up liking the book, but I certainly didn't.

reference_books.title: Matched (Matched, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
"I'm falling in love. I am in love. And it's not with Xander, though I do love him. I'm sure of that, as sure as I am of the fact what I feel for Ky is something different." 
 I hated this book. Especially the romance. Damn. The romance was bad. This book was as bad as Twilight. (I'm sorry if this sounds rude, but I'm just stating my opinions.) 
 When I first heard about this book, it sounded amazing, but I hesitated because my friends said it was really bad. About a year later, I decided to give it a shot. Yup. They were right. It took me forever to read this book. It kept going on and on about the same thing. The whole book was basically the main character trying to decide between Xander and Ky. I guarantee you that she wouldn't of been intrigued by Ky if he hadn't of showed up on her results. The whole book was so boring. I wanted to put it down multiple times, but I like to finish books even if they are really bad. 
 I am going to compare the main character to Bella in Twilight. Cause they are so alike in my opinion. Cassia is so desperate for a guy. I would've been happy with either Xander or Ky. Don't string them along, don't kiss Xander one day, and flirt with Ky another day. 
 I don't even know if I am going to read the series. The way the book ended was terrible, there was no cliffhanger, no amazing ended, all there was, was the fact that I was going to have to read through, two more painful books. 
 I heard the Matched is going to become a movie. Who knows, maybe the movie will be better.

reference_books.review_text: RTC

reference_books.title: Twilight (Twilight, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I read this book a very long time ago, back when I was /obsessed/ with Twilight. I had only seen the movies and I loved them. (Don't judge me xD It was a very long time ago) 
 I loved the books and movies when I first read/saw them. But, the only reason why I loved them back then, was because I didn't read much, I had never read anything close to what I read these days. 
 These are just some main points that I would like to point out real quick; 
 Vampires being sparkly? Really? C'mon they are supposed to be blood-sucking, badass, evil creatures. 
 Did anyone else think that Bella was very whiny? She complained about /everything/. I hated her character because she acted like it was the end of the world when Edward left her. Seriously? Is she that desperate for a man in her life? It's time to move on already. 
 Love triangle between a vampire and werewolf? Smhh never heard that one before. 
 I still laugh so hard at myself for being /in love/ with Edward Collins. I used to watch the movies non-stop, it was my life. It's funny how your opinion on something can change that much.

reference_books.title: The Last Star (The 5th Wave, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
This book was the worst in the series. I HATED THE ENDING! Why!? Why did it end like that?! It didn't even explain the purpose of the 5 waves. The only reason I continued after I read the second book, was to find out the ending. Well, that was a disappointment. 
 More points of views? Really? There was enough in the second book. Now you add points of views from characters that aren't needed. I was fine with Evan's point of view, Ben's point of view and Cassie's point of view. Not everyone's point of view. 
 I thought that the ending could've gone wayyyyyyyy better than it did. I wasn't even sad, I was disappointed and shocked. 
 I will watch the movie, because I feel like the movie will be better. The book was slow paced, but the movie definitely speeds things along.

book_a.title: Burning Glass (Burning Glass, #1)
book_a.user_review:
(I am extremely honest in all of my reviews, I am not trying to be mean to the author. Also if you liked the book, that's totally fine, shoot me a message and we can talk about it!) 
 Wow this book took forever to get through :/ 
 Hate love triangles? Hate annoying characters? Well this is the book for you! 
 Warning: No plot whatsoever & basically the Red Queen except Red Queen was actually good ;) 
 One of the biggest problem was...duh..duh...duhhhhhhh 
 1. The length of the book. This book was around 500 pages... 500 pages!!! For a love triangle. NO PLOT. I am not kidding. I probably would have liked it a lot more if it was shorter. This book dragged on and 500 pages was not necessary. It kept going over the same things over and over. Yeah, yeah, we get it. Sonya can't decide between Valko and Anton, but no need to keep saying it.This book was about a girl named Sonya who was an Auraseer. Auraseers are basically people that can sense another persons emotions. Auraseers are captured and trained until it's their turn to serve the empire. Sonya's turn is up and when Valko sees her, he's determined to make her his. Valko is the emperor who has 'daddy' issues. He has mood swings all the time and he's very abusive. But, get this!!! Sonya still falls for him!! HAHA! It's the best. Though, to be honest, I like Valko a lot better than Anton. Maybe I just have a thing for guys like that :/ The good thing about Valko though, is he understands Sonya. He trusts her. Hopefully Valko will get better in the next book. Anyways, back to why this book has no plot. Sonya basically just has to walk around with Valko all day and watch out for anyone that might harm the emperor. Now, here is the best part. The rest of the book, is all about, Anton, Sonya and Valko falling for each other! Well, not Valko and Anton, that would be weird. That's all the book has to it. And that's why there is no need for it to be that long. 
 Sonya was a really annoying character. In the beginning of the book she was about to cry, no wait, I think she did cry. Should would get mad when Anton ignored her, yet she was playing around with the other brother. She would act like she wanted nothing to do with Valko, but she kept coming back to him. Sonya also kept trying to get involved in everything that was going on. She would always get mad if Anton or Valko kept something from her. 
 I really didn't like this book, but I'm hoping the next one is better.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Before we get to the insides of this book, can we please discuss how gorgeous the outside of it is? It does have significance to the story, but again, STUNNING. Anyways, to the actual story...Sonya has the power to feel people's moods and intentions. However, she is not very good at this in the beginning, like at all. However a great tragedy happens where she is the oldest auraseer in the empire and is called to serve the emperor with her gift. She has a hard time meandering through court life and trying to hone her powers. One mess up from her can mean the death of the emperor - or hers. Meanwhile there is something mysterious going on with the emperor's brother, Anton, that she is determined to get to the bottom of the plot. I will say at first I did have some difficulty understanding Sonya and her powers (that could totally be my fault) but I did thoroughly enjoy her journey of not only understanding other people's feelings but her own. Sometimes she struggled with that fact that if her feelings were her own or if they belonged to someone else. She eventually learns that she is capable of so much more than she ever realized and that empathy has a lot to do with that. This book was a wonderful journey of watching Sonya become stronger and more aware of her growth. I think this book is very relatable through Sonya's struggle. You will keep guessing about certain characters and be heartbroken for others. I loved this debut novel and loved the teaser for the next book (can I read that now, please). Seriously, the story couldn't be more perfect! Make sure you give this book a shot when it releases next week. 
 I received an advance copy of this book for an honest review.

I had mixed feelings about this book. There were parts I like and there were parts I hated. So, I'll split this review into what I liked and what I didn't like. 
 Starting on a good note, what I liked: 
 Big one for me - character growth. I could see a steady progression of growth in Sonya throughout the book. 
 Revolution theme. Seeing the rising of a revolution and the problems that arose with it. 
 World building. I really got a sense of the countries and cultures. 
 What I didn't like: 
 The inconsistentness of Sonya's 6th sense. For example, in the beginning Sonya feels the anger/hunger of the peasants at the gate of her convent and it controls her to the point that she ultimately kills her friends. Then later she has no (mostly but I'll get to that later) problem controlling her emotions in just as high emotional situations. 
 The only time she can't control her emotion 6th sense is when the emperor feels any passionate/lusty type emotion toward her. She's then all over him later blaming her 6th sense for the lack of resistance. 
 The books focus was much more on her love interests then it was on revolutionary plot or that there were starving people in the world. 
 Lastly, for Sonya having killed her friends in the beginning of the book, she got over it pretty fast. She "punished" herself by holding a statue with her friend's blood on it (she can feel the pain of her dead friend through the blood). But that stopped even before a quarter of the book was done. 
 Aesthetic note: For me the book was really a three part book. The first part was between the convent and arriving at the castle, the second was arriving at castle and finishing reading the poetry book, and the third part was between finishing the poetry book and the end of the book. I had an ARC so maybe there was a page that said part 1, part 2, and part 3, but if not, it would have been a nice physical transitional between the growth of the character. 
 *Thank you to Edelweiss and Katherine Tegen Books for providing this book.

This book has one of the most darkly captivating opening chapters I've ever read, and the book only gets more intense from there! 
 I loved reading about an empath. This is the first time I've read a novel that included that particular power, and it was so fascinating. Purdie did such a phenomenal job of crafting this magic system. I really enjoyed the fact that having this power does not make Sonya's life easy. There are some very serious drawbacks and consequences to it. So while it absolutely makes her a powerful character, the road to her harnessing that power and being able to use it in the way she needs to is full of bumps and pitfalls. 
 The dynamic between Sonya, Anton, and Valko is absolutely captivating and so much more interesting than a love triangle. 
 The romance in this book is super swoony and there's definitely an element of danger to it that kept me on the edge of my seat. 
 This is a stunning debut novel for Kathryn Purdie and the beginning of a phenomenal trilogy.

Started out jumbled and confusing, no real plot for much of the novel, tepid romance, uncomfortable victim blaming and relationship with the abuser (I get that her power confuses her as to whether what Valko does is wanted or not but NO. NO TO ALL OF THAT ), no real worldbuilding, bland cliched characters and it laaaags. 
 RTC.

-I'll say this: The book was very well written. BUT it lacked the proper character and plot development. Both were missing though there was a lot of potential. I would say if you are looking for a book along the lines of 'The Orphan Queen' and 'Red Queen' this is a great addition. 
 -So yes, let's start with the characters. In case you were wondering--it is a love triangle. In case you didn't know--it's a sucky one. 
 So here's the thing. I love love triangles. But it annoys me to no end when a love triangle is used for angst and does not properly explore the characters. And to be quite honest, neither of the romances worked because none of the characters were fully fleshed. 
 We have an abusive emperor who is a terrible leader and essentially abuses the main character. And then we have the alternate prince Anton, who is quiet and mysterious. Except, he really isn't. He was always avoiding the heroine and plotting things. But the way he did it made it seem as if he really wasn't interested in the heroine. Plus, the only hints we get that he cares are the flashes of sorrow in his eyes. And the MC swoons over this. Rather, he seemed a little moody. There was nothing intriguing about him and when we did find out more the idealism was well...painful. It was the stupidest plan ever and came together for a very cliche ending. 
 Okay, back to the abusive emperor Valko. There were mentions of how he felt he had to prove himself because everyone thought he was a changeling. That was good. I would have loved for us to explore more about why he did what he did what he did. But instead, those scenes were rare and not really moving. 
 Our main character was especially annoying at first with her curse ability. However, she slowly learns to control it and becomes more involved with palace life. I thoroughly enjoyed her relationship with Pia. Her downfalls came with the weird obsession she had with Anton. It was unnecessary and annoying. I just couldn't see why they liked each other. 
 Oh, and the ending was very choppy at best. Anton's big reveal made me cringe and I was a little saddened by how easily Sonya was willing to be used.

Sonya is an Auraseer - that's aura-see-er. As in she sees and reads people's auras. I don't know why they couldn't just outright say that. It took me longer than you'd think( 91% of the way through the book, ahem, )to figure it out. In my head I was pronouncing it a-roar-sear. I don't know why. Anyway... 
 So Sonya is an orphan. In Riaznin any auraseers belong to the Emperor, and must serve as his protector. As someone who can read auras Sonya can sense emotions, and thus identify potential assassins, as you would imagine they would be quite angry/ hateful/ dark as they are about to do the deed. 
 Sonya's parents wanted her to be free so they entrusted her to a tribe of travellers called Romska, to keep her safe from the Empire; they were then murdered for disobeying the law. 
 Eventually Sonya was found and given to the Convent where auraseers are trained. Even amongst her peers Sonya's powers are strange and powerful; she can sense the auras and emotions of animals and dead people. Yeah, that's sounds delightful. 
 Because she was taken and hidden amongst the Romska, Sonya has never been trained to control her powers; she takes on the feelings of others as if they were her own emotions, and gets into some awful scrapes (understatement) from becoming carried away by said emotions. 
 After a terrible "accident" leads to Sonya becoming the oldest auraseer, Sonya must leave the convent to become Emperor Valko's protector. The previous Sovereign Auraseer( a fancy title that comes with room, board, fancy robes and the penalty of death if you don't spot assassins )has been executed for failing to prevent an assassination attempt which took out the Dowager Empress instead of the emperor. No pressure then. 
 The Crown Prince, Anton, brings Sonya to the palace, and immediately expresses doubt in her ability to do her job to protect his brother. Sonya is untrained, wild and reckless. Despite this there is a mutual attraction between them. Can Sonya prevent the emperor from being assassinated and learn to control her powers? 
 This was an okay novel; the concept was interesting and I liked the fictional world in which the story took place. The downside? I really didn't like Sonya. The "accidents" which took place could have been easily avoided by her using a bit of common sense. She knows she gets carried away by the feelings of others, would it have been too much to stop and think, hmm, do I really want to do this? 
 I also really hated the love triangle. Anton is nice if a bit too concerned with not taking advantage of Sonya's empathy abilities. Valko( excuse my language )is a knob. Sonya doesn't like him, she knows she doesn't like him. She knows he manipulates people, especially women. Does she still fall for his crap? Every. Damn. Time. It's like Fifty Shades for teenagers with better writing and slightly less abuse. 
 I'm not sure if this is the end of the story or if there will be a sequel. If there is a sequel I'm torn as to whether or not to give it a chance. The romance aspect just became so tiresome, and Sonya turns herself into a complete victim, beats herself up( metaphorically )for causing so many problems, but at the same time doesn't seem to take responsibility for her actions or change her behaviour. It's almost as if she is just saying bad things about herself so that everyone will go "oh no, you're fabulous, we love you". What's even more annoying is that they do! Anton tells her she's brilliant. Really??? Do you know what she's done??? Not buying it, sorry. 
 The kindle version is PS8.99 at the time of this review and I think the hardback is PS12.99 from Harper Collins.

This book is not what it appears to be. 
 It's shelved in Fantasy and Adventure, but could easily, if not more appropriately, fit in Young Adult Romance. A love triangle literally is the only driving force behind the plot. The concept was really interesting: it was told by a girl named Sonya who was an auraseer, someone with the "gift" to feel the emotions of all those around her. This makes it difficult for her to discern what she is actually feeling from what she is absorbing from others, a fact that was literally nailed into our brains over and over and over and over again. 
 I wanted to like Sonya, but she was kind of boring, and had very little personality and lacked in her own convictions. I understand that she spends most of the time feeling other people's auras, but she would surely have some opinions of her own? She doesn't. 
 She is then forced into a life of slavery, which was offensive in many ways as getting to live in a lavish room with fancy clothing and feasts does not equal slavery. Yes, her freedom of choice was taken away, but to equate that with slavery was a bit distasteful. She is supposed to protect the Emperor from threats and in doing so, becomes involved with him and his equally attractive but much more docile brother. 
 Anton was annoying in his overabundant self-righteousness. I get it, you want everyone to be equal and for no blood to be shed, but with the state of things currently, he never acknowledges that it isn't realistic. And then the way he toys with Sonya... 
 The Emperor is meant to be the third point in this triangle but he is nothing short of abusive. Physically, emotionally and mentally. Granted he is not held in a good light towards the end, but just reading about him made me angry. 
 There was definitely potential here for a great story. And who knows? Maybe I'll end up reading the sequel. But, for sure not a favorite.

Lacking in action and highly predictable, this was a long and kind of "eh" *shrugs shoulders* novel. Probably will not be reading the rest of the trilogy, but this book did have a couple of fairly good moments, which is why I gave it 3 stars.

Love triangle - LTs are generally ok for me but I didn't like how she was juggling between two guys? At the same time? Like, get a grip woman! I feel like I ONLY like a special kind of love triangle.. Like if h is inlove with another man who doesn't like her back, that's when she sees the worth of our H. Idk idk idk. 
 Heroine is OK? Like some of her decisions especially from the beginning of the book were a bit.. stupid. She killed half of her sisters because of what she did? 
 I didn't like both main male characters too. The emperor could have been ok but 30% of the book, I nope-d out. 
 The redeeming thing about this book was that the writing was so gorgeous! :)
I really enjoyed this book. I thought it was written very well and the concept was very interesting. It read like a stand alone.

reference_books.title: The Road of Lost Innocence: The True Story of a Cambodian Heroine
reference_books.review_text: Somaly Mam's book is one of courage and determination. A survivor of sex trafficking, Somaly Mam now works to rescue others. The stories she shares are devestating. There were times when what I read made me want to scream and cry. The injustice and devestation of what so many girls face around the world is heartwrenching. I think anyone who read this book would be spurred into wanting to act in the anti-slavery movement, but that's one thing this book lacked - practical suggestions to those who wanted to become more involved in the abolitionist movement. Somaly Mam fails to point out that trafficking is prevalent in countries around the world including Western regions like Europe and North America. While I understand that her book and experiences focus on slavery in Cambodia, I wish Somaly Mam would have provided more recognition that sex trafficking is a global issue and provided some suggestions on how to be an abolitionist in your home country. The book provided a perfect platform to spur others into action; it details horrific stories that move peoples' hearts, but then fails to use the opportunity to direct the reader's compassion and desire to act.

reference_books.title: It Was Me All Along
reference_books.review_text:
As I've mentioned before when reviewing other memoirs or personal accounts, I really feel uncomfortable assigning stars and critiquing the books. No matter my feelings of a book, it takes a lot of vulnerability and bravery to expose oneself through mass publication. I don't want to come across as judgmental or appear to minimize the experiences of another person... But in this case, I feel like I need to use this reviewing process to unpack some of my feelings of this book; I'm still digesting (no pun intended). 
 I listened to the audio version of this book. I find myself often getting bored with biographies and memoirs, having started and not completed many books in the past (and I'm fairly certain I wouldn't have made it through this book if I had been reading it). But with audiobooks, I find I am more captivated or maybe more willing to invest myself in the story while washing dishes or driving. As I first started listening to It Was Me All Along, I thought perhaps it would be a solid 4 stars (though maybe I came into it with high expectations after hearing rave reviews by a friend). As I kept listening, I found myself liking it less and less (even now as I write this, I am torn between 1 and 2 stars). 
 At times, Mitchell's beautifully descriptive writing really adds to the book. At other times, it is overwritten and just too much. Her introduction, with the description of the richness of the cake and icing, is an example of her ability to appeal to all of the readers' senses. But other times Mitchell goes a little overboard with a flowery writing or overdoing it on the details (the part about meeting Mark Ruffalo and Leonardo ("Leo") DiCaprio was just way. too. much.). I am often skeptical when memoirs or biographies include an abundance of details; detailed dialogues from years past, quantifying things too much, etc. The credibility of the story (whether the details are supposed to be taken literally or not) dwindles for me... An example of this in It Was Me All Along: at the end of the book, Mitchell describes the times that her mother goes into her bedroom and "cries for two hours" after Mitchell pierces her nose, loses weight, etc. Though perhaps not meant to be taken literally - the exact amount of time her mother cried each time - I got hung up on this detail and it just frustrated me). In other sections, Mitchell goes into elaborate details about what she ate in comparison to others, often referring to childhood meals of hers and her friends. These sections bothered me, not only because of the level of detail I just mentioned (over emphasizing calories, contents of each meal, etc.), but because this constant comparison of eating habits was incredibly triggering for me. For a book that was supposed to emphasize her transition to acceptance of her body, I found the parts that dwelled on who ate what, how many calories each meal was and the frequent comparison to others to be unhelpful. I would find these sections more justified if Mitchell then focused more attention on how it was that she was finally able to come to terms with her eating disorder and obsessive compulsive tendencies. By the time she got to this, I found it fairly shallow and rushed. 
 I was also disappointed with the instances that warranted more critique of our society's way of approaching food. She had mentioned that her father's side of the family tended to be on the larger boned and heavier weight side of things, so I expected her to elaborate more on the fact that genetics play a crucial role in our bodies' various shapes and sizes. She mentioned that the culture of eating was vastly different for her in Italy than in the U.S., so I expected her to elaborate more on the way fast food (not just restaurants, but in the way we shop for food in stores too) plays a role in obesity rates in North America. She mentioned that when she returned to college she found it more difficult to eat healthily on campus, so I expected her to elaborate on how the university years impact young adults' health and habits. There were so many opportunities for Mitchell to reflect beyond the personal and dive into a larger critique of how other systemic factors play a role in health and obesity, and I was left disappointed with her lack of depth on the issues. 
 Lastly, I felt really uncomfortable with (what I saw as) fat shaming through the book. Despite supposedly being a book about acceptance and positive body image, Mitchell only seemed to dwell on the need to accept her new body, to come to terms with the fact that she was still the same person skinny as she was fat. But the way that Mitchell talked about this transition was alarming: she talked about feeling like she was finally "beginning her life" and finally being able to move with "grace." I don't feel like this left a positive message for those who are overweight anyone. Regardless of your size, your weight, your shape: your life is yours to live in abundance, with grace and in fullness. 
 Admittedly, as one who has struggled with low body image and compulsive eating behaviours, I found this book to be really quite triggering. Which was really disappointing for me because I was really looking for something that I would find more empowering and motivating. Despite my critiques of the book, I found myself identifying with Mitchell many times, and I empathized with her struggles and desire for healthy change. 
 Other reviewers who have also given this book lower ratings have mentioned that her blog is quite different than her book, so I would like to follow that and give it a chance. I bet Mitchell is a wonderful person, and I wish her all the best.

I am a little divided on this book: On the one hand, it is one heck of a page turner. I had to really struggle to put it down and go to bed on time while I was reading it. On the other hand, it's not particularly well-written or fresh. 
 - So when is the whole teenage death contest trend going to be over? I mean, I know the initiation doesn't actually have them fighting to the death, but close enough. I've read Stephen King's The Long Walk, why do we need 3,000 more stories where teenagers die for some shadowy adult purpose? 
 - The best part of the book is the last 20%. Before that, while Tris is doing the whole initiation thing, I was really kind of waiting for the real book to start. 
 - Why are some of the factions named after nouns, and some after adjectives? This doesn't make any sense to me, and it nagged me through the whole book. 
 - Speaking of the whole faction thing - it's not a workable idea. I don't know how long this system is supposed to have been in place (Though long enough for Tris's mother to have grown up in a different faction) but in the real world, I suspect it would have lasted no more than 6 months before it fell apart. Violently. This idea of segregating people by their strongest traits and eliminating people who aren't conformist enough... it's a recipe for groupthink, and groupthink leads to genocide. And fast. 
 - Why does every YA book have to be a romance? Especially since this one isn't working for me. Also, I don't care whether or not Four is a virgin (though why is she so surprised? He's 18 not 40) While we're at it, the skinny girl who doesn't think she's attractive and the handsome boy with the tortured past get together... Yawn. 
 - In what universe would Eric be a faction leader? I don't care how well he serves the shadowy conspiracy, or how democratic Dauntless is supposed to be. He is 18, it's only been 2 years since he was initiated, he wouldn't even have the hang of being an adult yet. 
 - Of course... daredevils wear black, have tattoos and body piercings. Of course they do. 
 What the heck, read it for fun. It's a fast read and fun brain candy. But don't try to think to critically about it, it doesn't hold up to the scrutiny.

I was really excited for this book. It had been recommended to me a few times and I was excited to read it, but, after plowing through it in just a few days, I don't get the hype. 
 The story is interesting, sure, but there's a lot to be desired in this book. It could have done with another round of editing to bolster character development and enrich the plot. 
 Here are my main issues with this book: 
 1. World development: A quick scan through other less-than-stellar reviews shows I'm not alone in finding the world building lacking. Where's the history? How did Chicago get to this state? How were the factions formed? What happened to Lake Michigan? I wanted scenery painted and a history created and it just never came. I kept wondering, while reading the book, what the background story was and the lack of it left me distracted for much of the book. 
 2. Icky Love Stuff: I get it - it's a YA novel, but COME ON! It reads, at times, like soft-core paperback novel. I wanted to stick my head in the sand each time things got mushy. It seemed like the book would get interesting, only to wind back to more icky love stuff in the heat of the moment. 
 3. Lack of depth: This applies to everything - the characters, the world, the things that happen, all of it. It just didn't have the sense of honesty or realness that something like the Hunger Games had. 
 4. It's kind of boring: There are quick and short bursts of action, but they fade too fast, leaving me frustrated that things ended so quickly. The build-up to any action takes far too long and most of the best stuff is squished into the last 50-70 pages of the book. I didn't feel like anything happened until the very end, and even then I was left feeling like I'd just read 400 pages about nothing. 
 All that said, it's a quick easy read. It's not mind-blowing, nothing on the caliber of the Hunger Games, but it did mostly hold my attention.
Watch my review on YouTube: http://youtu.be/30SZc0ASfyg

I feel like there should have been more backstory. For example, WHY is there apparently just a few hundred people left on earth and HOW did it ever make sense to anyone to divide people in this manner. I mean it logically follows that the serum was invented prior to dividing into factions, otherwise how did they ever decide? But why would such a serum be invented in a world without factions? Or maybe it was invented and caused the factions? I mean I just don't really follow. 
 Doesn't it make more sense to divide them by other, more intuitive means? Is anyone really that easy to pigeonhole into one personality type? and depending how long this situation has been in place, wouldn't the faction less at some point have become their own faction? Perhaps leaving Chicago and starting anew? 
 And if the erudite are so smart don't they realize their slanderous articles would go much further with overthrowing the abnegation than oh I don't know, ruthless bloody slaughter? I mean maybe you'd get the other factions to reassess power structure if you exposed corruption, real or imagined. But I do not see everyone jumping on board with an abnegation holocaust. 
 Aaaand finally. Stupid love story involving an oft underestimated (especially by herself) girl and a powerful but aloof hottie with a mysterious side. Oh and did I mention they're in LOVE?? Like hardcore, die-for-you love. At 16. Sound familiar? #TwilightHungerGamesEveryYAEver.

The Light in the Ruins tells the reader a story from 1943, in the midst of WWII and the German occupation of Italy, to 1955 and a young female detective working to solve a series of gruesome murders that seem to be targeting one family. Cristina is 18 years old and has spent much of her life sheltered on her family's villa. Normally at her age she should be debuting into society, however the war has come to Europe. One of her brothers is in the military, and another is working at a museum, trying to keep the Nazi's from absconding with the art. Cristina ends up falling in love with one of the German officers, much to her family's despair. Serafina is the directive in 1955 trying to determine who is seemingly targeting Cristina' s family. I was struck by the differences in the two and how the war affected each of them. 
 I have read a few of Chris Bohjalian' s books,this is the first one I would consider a mystery. I would recommend this to anyone who enjoys mysteries and historical fiction as it was a nice mix of the two.
I love Bohjalian and this is, easily, his best yet. Thrilling and compelling even as it examines the little discussed end of the Second World War in Italy and it's aftermath. Loved it!

Review first posted on my blog: http://memoriesfrombooks.blogspot.com... 
 The Light in the Ruins is a story of World War II as it comes to Italy and a story of a war vendetta carried out about ten year later. The story moves back and forth between the two time periods, slowly revealing bits and pieces about the characters and the events that transpired. 
 The story centers around the Rosati family. During the war, the Rosatis live on their estate, the Villa Chimera near Florence. Two brothers, Vittore and Marco, serve in the war. Eighteen year old Cristina, along with her parents and Marco's wife and children, live at Villa Chimera. The hope is that the war will end before it truly reaches them. Unfortunately, that is not to be. Italy becomes a battleground, as the Allies reach near, Germany makes a stand, and the Italian partisans fight in the nearby hills. The Rosatis are caught up in the fighting, becoming host to both the Nazis and the partisans. 
 Ten years later, Francesca, Marco's wife is found brutally murdered in Florence. The police investigate. One of the investigators, Serafina Bettina, was one of the partisans during the war and discovers her own link to the Rosatis. 
 The book continues with the story from both time periods. Interspersed throughout the thoughts or words of the killer, possibly to provide hints as to the killer's identity and motive. The suspense builds in both time periods throughout the book as the killings and the investigation continue, and as the war comes closer and touches Villa Chimera. Chris Bohjalian's writing brings both time periods and the characters to life. 
 Most of Chris Bohjalian's books have an unexpected ending, one that makes you look back through the book to see if you could have seen it coming. With this book, the unfortunate thing is that you could not have seen it coming. The ending and the resolution was almost tangential to the main story built throughout the book. As a reader, that takes some of the fun out of it. It's one thing to be surprised. It's quite another to feel that it was almost unrelated. Still, the writing is enjoyable.

Sigh! Ah, what a tale and so superbly expressed. Can he write! And lo and behold, here is the two different time periods switch technique ONCE AGAIN. Every other author seems to be going this route. Switching time periods in every other chapter or so is endemic right now. And yet in this book it actually works well. 
 In this long tale with endless intriguing complications, the structure does not admit constant redundancy or break the tension- neither- as most others do who use the time switch writing style. In fact, it increases the tension by the subtle hints of their "futures" while also giving full foreknowledge of certain death for others of the characters. Beyond that fatalism, it results in a subtle immersion in character, place and context of the emotions and core values. An inch at a time. Before, and after. 
 I was not a big fan of Bohjalian before, despite his well earned reputation. Found most of his writing too dark and traumatic. Like looking only upon the murky negative end of the universe's color spectrum. And this one was very dark as well. No happy tale here. 
 But also like an operatic drama, very similar. A tragedy. The depth of love, tension, loyalty and family connection! And the ill fated romance/love story between the "impossibles"! To me, that couple- the Italian woman and the German man- and in those circumstances, it held more attraction, connection and pure pull of need than Romeo and Juliet. Far more. They were just a couple of teen-agers with high hormones in comparison. 
 Excellent read. And so superb in the detail of nuance in understanding the psychology of vitriol within the conflicts of a war when it becomes A CIVIL WAR. The worst kind of war, a Civil War. As it absolutely did in Italy during the final years of WWII.
Solid 3.5 stars

Bohjalian captures the moral complexity of wartime in scenes of anger, fear and love. Italy is exquisitely beautiful, timeless in its beauty until the war intrudes and destroys all 
 --Ashland Mystery

 The Princess and the Goblin is a cute, fairy tale-esque story about a princess named Irene. With some help from her mysterious magical grandmother, she saves a miner boy who is being held captive by goblins. I've heard that this is a classic that inspired Tolkien and C.S. A pleasant story in the style of all great Victorian children's novels: sweet, a tad moralizing, and chock full of tongue-in-cheek humor. This is, of course, unsurprising, given that a Victorian children's novel is exactly what George MacDonald's The Princess and the Goblin is. MacDonald sets up the Princess Irene and the miner's son Curdie as exemplars of "good" children--they are kind, they are friendly, they are dutiful--but they do make mistakes, which they quickly understand and work to rectify. When Curdie does not believe Irene about the magic aid she receives which, in turn, saves Curdie from the goblins he then feels very bad for hastily deciding he couldn't believe her and MacDonald says, Here I should like to remark, for the sake of princes and princesses in general, that it is a low and contemptible thing to refuse to confess a fault or even an error. If a true princess has done wrong, she is always uneasy until she has had an opportunity of throwing the wrongness away from her by saying: "I did it; and I wish I had not; and I am sorry for having done it." So you see there is some ground for supposing that Curdie was not a miner only, but a prince as well. Elsewhere these injunctions of manners and behavior are lightened with humor--and always presented with a kindly expectation of the of course you know how to behave yourself variety:That the princess was a real princess you might see now quite plainly; for she didn't hang on to the handle of the door, and stare without moving, as I have known some do who ought to have been princesses but were only rather vulgar little girls. 
 All this lesson-making is then wrapped up in a bright and rollicking adventure where a Princess has a magic ring that can lead her places, and the goblins a plotting to take back the above-ground lands that they lost so very long ago, and a boy with no fear and a quick mind for rhymes can frighten the goblins away from him--and if it doesn't work, he can stomp on their soft square toeless feet to get rid of them. The toe thing is actually one of the most clever pieces of humor in the book--the goblins and their beasts are to look like horrible misshapen versions of people and domestic animals, respectively, but the goblins do not think themselves ugly. In fact, they think toes are the most horribly disgusting attribute that any person could have and that humans wear shoes because they cannot bear the sight of their own toes. As Curdie and Irene work to discover and stop the goblins' plots and save the day, the story whisks off to a cozy fireside and a Medieval castle all at once, making for a lovely and gentle read.

My first impression when reading this book was: "Ah finally a Victorian children's book that's actually written for children." But then I had to study it for a week, and that ruined it haha. There are a lot of deep elements to this story that might be missed on an initial read; MacDonald has a lot to say about faith and imagination. It was okay, not really one of my top children's book, and I wouldn't recommend it to anyone in this day and age, but it's not terrible either.

Like a cousin to The Maze Runner (book one) set in space, Scott Reintgen's extremely fun Nyxia (also book one!) is quite the page-turner! Reintgen has created an adventure story packed with mystery, adrenaline, and a diverse cast to be celebrated. A sharp, short, and funny little book by Gillian Flynn. Not exactly what I expected, but ultimately a satisfying read. There is something familiar in the twist, which might be a staple of Flynn's work but having not read Dark Places or Sharp Objects I can't really say for sure. I will say that if you're looking for a "traditional" ghost story, this probably isn't for you, but if you're looking to read a short story by a fantastic writer then I can't recommend it enough. 
 On top of that, The Grownup has what is easily my favourite literary quote of all time: 
 "I would rather be a librarian but I worry about job security. Books may be temporary; dicks are forever"
Good writing but very graphic.

book_b.title: Trans-Sister Radio
book_b.user_review:
Several years ago, a dear queer friend gifted me this novel, Chris Bohjalian's Trans-Sister Radio. I don't remember if she'd already read it, or was just hoping I'd let her know if it was any good. But anyhow, the book trickled down to me around 13 years after original publication in 1998. 
 Bohjalian is a prolific author, with tons of books and swarms of adoring fans. I've never read any of his other works, but I assume and I hope this one is not his best. The story choices here are painfully contrived, so convenient you can practically hear the plot cogs churning. I think some readers love such satisfyingly easy books - and I do, too, sometimes! But the thing is, trans* stories - even in 1998 - deserved better than this. 
 There's certainly something to be appreciated about a mainstream transgender novel being as... ordinary as the next summer paperback. Yet there's something dangerous about it as well. With so little representation in media, each instance garners that much more importance. And trans experiences aren't something to be researched and displayed like Jodi Picoult might do with organ donation. Most importantly, trans awareness deserves better than barely scratching the surface beyond the decision of sex reassignment surgery. 
 Trans-Sister Radio makes for an interesting review to write. I don't hate the book - instead I just find it average. If not for the problematic choice of topic, I probably would've forgotten it by now. I guess all this is to say: if you're looking for a great trans fiction novel (or a great novel, period), look beyond this fluffy Transgender Surgeries 101 piece.

sample_reviews.review_text:
First of all, take my review with a grain of salt. I didn't really go into the book wanting to read it. A friend gave it to me and said it's a good psychological read. I thought it sounded interesting, as it obviously pondered ideas surrounding transgender people. 
 I did like the way the book was structured and how it shifted points of view, but the ideas in the book were rather elementary. Everything related back to sex, basically the females of the story thought about sex 70% of the time they were thinking. Many key decisions in the novel came down to sex. For characters who are supposed to be of intellectual rank to be questioning and acting upon ideas of gender and sexuality it seems like they think about nothing else. 
 The plot was kind linear, flat and boring. It is one of those books which follows a basic line without twists or anything. Which is perfectly fine as long as you put some substance or meaning in the book. I didn't find symbolic or direct meaning aside from the main moral, kind of like Beauty and the Beast only the Prince is reversing his metamorphosis and the Beauty has to cope. 
 I only got halfway through it before putting it down. After getting through the introduction/plot set-up each chapter feels like it rehashes the last, the ideas repeat over and over. At first it is an interesting book and has some cool stuff, but you might as well read the first few chapters because they all become the same. The plot is so linear and predictable it is not worth reading after getting the ideas from it. 
 That's what I thought, if you decide to read it, I hope you enjoy it more than I did.

When my mother in law mentioned Bohjalian as an author "everyone has read" except apparently for me...he became of interest to me. My mom had this book on her bookshelf (neglected and unread, sadly) so I jumped at the opportunity to finally read something by an author I should've (according to my mother in law) read before. Here's my take: Bohjalian had me turning pages, which I guess is a win no matter what. But I was annoyed the whole time. Way too much of the novel is dedicated to discussion of the issue rather than developing character. I had no sympathy for Allie. (And I can't *believe* we didn't hear her reaction to the denouement and twist at the end!!) It's written in four different voices, yet they ALL sounded the same, with slight effeminate variation for the trannie (and that seemed forced). I was interested in the surprising ending but so disappointed we didn't hear from Allie that it pissed me right off. Sorry, mom in law, but I don't think I'll be picking up another from this author "everyone has read."
Haha. "Amusing" "twist" at the end.

 Chris Bohjalian you touched my heart & soul when you wrote: 
 "Or walk with me a few generations into the future. You're a short man. You're barely 5 feet. And you are sick to death of being treated as...small. Especially since you are so big inside. So tall. You know it. You sense it. You feel it." 
 Chris, my Husband is 4'4" a Dwarf/Little Person. Yes, he is sick to death of being treated as different, a freak...not Normal! What the hell is normal?!! We have learned to live with the stares & the snickers & the outright rudeness.

After 13 years together, thank god the internet chatrooms were around in 1995 when... of all the chatrooms... in all the world, we both ended up in a chatroom called 40-Friends(us both being 40 at the time) & FATE stepped in and for 6 months we talked online & the phone before SteffieStar flew from Ketchikan, Alaska to Santa Monica, California on Feburary 14, 1996 to meet in person the man she fell in love with and who had fallen in love with her...Fairly Tales Do Come True!!

This was the first time I have read anything by this author - but I can assure you that it won't be the last. I thoroughly enjoyed this book and would compare the style of this author to that of Jodi Picoult - another one of my favourite authors. 
 This particular story is about a modern family - told through the eyes of it's four members: the ex-husband, the ex-wife, the ex- wife's new transsexual partner, and the ex's daughter. 
 Allison, and elementary school teacher, meets a professor - Mr. Dana Stevens - and they fall in love quickly. She knows there is something "special" about Dana - but she doesn't delive into thoughts - rather, she allows herself to become wrapped up in this new, incredible relationship she's found. Eventually, Dana describes to Allison who he really is - basically, a woman trapped inside a man's body. He admits he wants the surgery - so he can once and for all, be happy in his own body. Allison is angry at first, but once she begins to question what love is - she decides she will be open to the possibilities of a future with Dana even after his surgery. 
 The story is essentially just that - the trials and tribulations of their relationship, after Dana has had a major surgery and returned to a small town... a town where people are for the most part, extremely conservative, religious, and love to gossip. 
 Not unlike Picoult, Bohjalian loves to give his readers a little surprise at the ending.

I had read books by Chris Bohjalian before and liked them so I picked this up as a used book not knowing anything about it but the author's named. 
 It was an interesting book and a very interesting topic. The author did present it in a impartial way. I liked how he presented using reports or interviews from NPR radio and that he used all the different voices in his book to express the different views of the topic. 
 The book explored gender dysphoria: the condition of feeling one's emotional and psychological identity as male or female to be opposite to one's biological sex. 
 Transvestite (a person, typically a man, who derives pleasure from dressing in clothes appropriate to the opposite sex.) versus transsexual (a person who emotionally and psychologically feels that they belong to the opposite sex.). 
 I did like the point that the author made that people's soul's were either male or female but I disagree that when the souls were put in the body--they were mixed up? 
 The book was very well written on the subject; it is a little graphic in parts. It has a twist at the end. 
 https://www.nytimes.com/books/00/06/0...

I think the author had a good idea, but the execution fell a little flat. Too much of the story remained focused on the sexual reassignment surgery, and failed to allow the characters to have lives and stories outside of that context. 
 Also- no transsexual or gender queer individual would use the word "trannie". It's derogatory, and seen as an insult in the community. I cannot believe no one in the editorial process noticed that in the 16 years of reprints.

book_a.user_review:
I think I am one of the few people left that has not read the Twilight series. I am also one of a growing minority of people that have not seen any of the movies. I actually have avoided the films intentionally. Normally if I see a movie trailer or hear of a movie that sounds interesting, I bypass the film and go straight to the book. 
 So what can I say about this book that hasn't already been said (at least a dozen times)? Not much. I must say that I did enjoy this book. It is my first foray into the world of YA literature, and I was pleasantly surprised. I must admit I was a bit skeptical. I wasn't sure this book could live up to all of the momentum and hype I have witnessed. To be perfectly honest, I thought the first 300 pages were really drawn-out. The last 200 pages though were very good. I think that Ms. Meyer found her flow. I had a hard time identifying with the characters, but I am chalking that up to the fact that I am not a teen, nor have I been one for several years! This book was very easy to read and it is easy to see why this book has appealed to both young and old, readers and non-readers alike. I was shocked at how many people stopped me when they saw what I was reading simply to tell me what a good book it was. Even when I went out to breakfast alone on Sunday the waitress was compelled to tell me how she hadn't read at all since high school but once she read this book, she polished off the entire series in two weeks! 
 This book was a simple, entertaining read. And let's face it, any book that can inspire an entire generation of non-readers (and then some) to dive into a book, especially one of this length, is worthy of praise!

sample_reviews.review_text:
I didn't really like A Reliable Wife, but I had hoped this one might be better. No, I'm not just looking for punishment - both books were read for my library book group! 
 Unfortunately, it wasn't - this one has the same problems that bothered me before. What bothered me most was the pretentious, and sometimes ridiculous, descriptions that added nothing and simply sounded like he was following the rules from a writing class - "be sure to add a lot of metaphoric language so your book will sound deep." 
 One that caught my attention as being particularly absurd was a long description of the main character walking home at night. "A shimmering and a stillness, all at once. Charlie moves across the land, humming a song, but compared to the landscape itself, he is still and mute as a rock. Compared to the animals that, unseen, surround him, moving, feeding, breeding, he is a statue." Sorry - I don't find that evocative, just pretentious and meaningless. 
 A couple paragraphs later, he tells us that Charlie is in the Blue Ridge Mountains, and that he is "cradled in the palm of the valley as a mother holds an egg." What is that supposed to mean? Offhand, I can't think of any species that reproduce by external eggs and that also has hands with which to cradle those eggs. Or, if we're just referring to a human mom getting out eggs to make breakfast - well, not a very sentimental thought, since she's presumably getting ready to crack and cook those eggs............ 
 I never could get terribly interested in any of the characters - there seemed to be a real distance, and much telling, rather than showing. I just didn't see anything to evoke the supposed compelling passion that Charlie felt for Sylvan, nor did I find in the book anything that made the ending seem convincing. 
 There were also a number of things tossed in for no apparent reason and that didn't seem based on any particular plot purposes or character development, and facts that didn't make a lot of sense and were never explained. 
 Really, I felt the same way I did about his first book - Goolrick just throws out a lot of characters who do melodramatic things for no good reason, and then tosses in lots of pretentious descriptions and metaphors to make the book appear "literary."

I loved this book! Here was my Amazon review:

sample_reviews.review_text:
Good sci-fi ideas, but lacks character development. Not enough showing. It drags. 
 OPINION ON THE ENTIRE SERIES: 
 There are five titles in the series. They are not complete stories. They are sections of one long story. The author published as he wrote. I suggest you buy the Omnibus Edition instead of the individual titles, which will save you $1, as of the date of this review. The Omnibus includes all five titles. 
 At the end of some of the titles I was angry or frustrated at the cliffhanger endings. For example, not knowing if the main character is dead or alive. But the ending of title 5 is very good. It's a happy ending for the group and one main character. 
 The overall plot concept is good. Neat ideas and events in a dystopian world. People live in an underground silo. The air outside causes immediate death. 
 But, I was not entertained. I wanted to read fast to get through it. The author doesn't do characters well. He names a bunch of people, has things happen to them, but I don't get to know them. At one point a guy does a complete turn around in the story, but I never see it. I don't see what led to it, why he changed, how he changed, or what he did after. Another guy is killed at the end. I assume I know who the guy was but the author didn't say. And the author didn't show conversations and actions leading to that killing. The author needs some John Grisham influence. I get to know John's characters. I'm pulled in emotionally. That is missing here. 
 Too many parts of the book are told and not shown. Like reading a newspaper it can be interesting, but you are not living it. For example, there are two battle/fight scenes. In one, we hear there is gunfire and two are dead - but no details prior to or during. Where are the emotions of a guy during battle? Of seeing, fearing, reacting? In the second battle, some guys are on the run, and I hear attackers are after them. But no details at all. 
 THIS SERIES: 
 Wool (Wool #1) 
 Proper Gauge (Wool #2) 
 Casting Off (Wool #3) 
 The Unraveling (Wool #4) 
 The Stranded (Wool #5) 
 SUBSEQUENT TITLES: 
 Wool #6, 7, and 8 are a prequel trilogy telling what happened a hundred (or more) years earlier to create the silo and toxic environment. I started to read it, but I lost interest. 
 DATA: 
 Narrative mode: 3rd person. Swearing language: strong but rarely used. Sexual content: none. Setting: in the future, Georgia, U.S. Copyright: 2011 and 2012. Genre: dystopian sci fi.

This novella was less "stand alone" than the other novellas in this series. Loose threads from previous stories are clarified,new ideas are introduced but essentially one knows this book is just the prequel to the much more interesting Wool #4
These novellas/books/shorts/whatever have been a wonderful reading surprise. The writing is top-notch, the story is compelling, and I'm onto the next!
brilliant.

In the wake of the recent deaths of Sheriff Holston and Mayor Jahns , Juliette finds herself far from the Mechanical floors of the down deep that she considers home and trying to get her bearing as she takes over the role of silo sheriff. But she can't get over her curiosity about what led to Holston's death. Or her suspicions over the recent murder that still blankets the silo in a pall of tragedy. Yet asking too many questions is what seems to lead to the inevitability of death by cleaning. 
 Juliette is a great character. This third story continues the highly enjoyable, tension-filled pace of the previous two in the Wool series. I also have to take a few moments to gush over how much I love Howey's series and story titles. Wool, the title of the series and of the first installment, has several meanings in and of itself. Wool is used for cleaning. It signifies the wool pulled over the eyes of the silo residents--an obscuring of the truth. And yet it is also used to clean the camera lenses, to reveal and expose truth. It also supports the knitting metaphor of the titles of the other installments. And, being a knitter myself, I just love that.

 And deeper into the intrigue.
