book_b.title: Winter of the World (The Century Trilogy #2)
book_b.user_review:
I was amazed reading so many positive reviews of this book. Not that it is a bad work of fiction - it's a fairly decent work of FICTION. It is just so biased and European Unionized that reading it was painful, mostly because it pretends to be based in history of the 20-th century, and as a matter of fact skews it and rewrites it in a truly disgusting way. 
 I find that presenting WWII as kind of a big misunderstanding where everybody was equally at fault, and totally omitting most of the facts that would be damaging to the pushed here, and unrealistic picture of Germany is despicable. The truth is this - 99.99% Germans supported Hitler in 1939 and that only changed when Germany started loosing war. Then and only then certain elements tried to minimize the costs to Germany by eliminating it's crazy leader. Not a moment sooner those good Germans tried to prevent the mass extermination of Jews and Slavs in the Eastern Europe. 
 So in fact we would have 99.99% chance that Mr. Ulrich would join Gestapo and have a nice position in Warsaw, rooting out Polish underground army, by any bestial means available, torture, killing, maiming, public executions. Eric would most likely end up on concentration camp train ramp working hard at selection for the gas chamber, as he had basic medical training, and could spot weak and sick and ill, from whom no work could be had. Maybe he would even be able to study medicine further, under the expert tutelage of Dr. Josef Mengele. And his sister would proudly adopt "orphaned" children from Zamosc (of course only those with blond hair and blue eyes). Her and her mother would run a nice German household with a help of slave labor maid and cook. And they all will be proud serving their Fuehrer and Fatherland. 
 As it stands now this plot line is a pure fantasy, more in line with the works of Harry Turtledove. What, Eric went with German army to Paris and back, and then to Eastern Front and he only figured 50 miles from Moscow that Nazis kill civilians?? I mean REALLY???!!! Never saw a street execution in all that time??? No inclining of mass executions in the forests and mass graves all over the occupied territory?? No sight of burned villages with corpses of shoot villagers near the smoking ruins of their houses? No destroyed cities with dead civilians shoot in the streets?? Be still, my bleeding heart, for when he finds out the shock almost kills him, poor soul. Oh, what a joke. Basically the only brutality shown in this book is a brutal behavior of Germans toward their own and Soviets toward Germans. Not that that was not true, but well, you live by the sword, you die by the sword. In my opinion it would be of far greater value, not to mention closer to some sort of objective historical truth to show how Germans behaved towards people of Polish, Russian, Jewish nationalities, and stress that they were merciless, brutal and inhuman. They EXTERMINATED nations for the greater good of their own nation. THEY WERE NOT THE VICTIMS HERE. 
 And so what if Germans killed, maimed and tortured their own on their way to world dominance? What percentage of maimed, tortured, shoot, gassed and exterminated in other ways during WWII by Germans were German? 0.001%? Less? Why then only this aspect was portrayed time and time again, over and over? Making hero out of any German, when there were real heroes (albeit unsung by Mr. Follett) in abundance, is beyond disingenuous. RAF targeted civilian areas? Oh, how beyond belief, considering how careful Germans were to avoid civilian casualties - just take a look at Warsaw in 1945 - that should tell you all what you need to know how careful they were. 
 Well, despite Mr. Follett's best efforts, I just don't feel a slightest twinge of sympathy for those horribly, horribly suffering Germans. They chose their own poison - and on their way to hell poisoned the world and send it to hell. This is history that should be remembered, and no amount of whitewashing should change it. 
 Books like this one are dangerous in their dis-ingenuity and bias - younger readers and the ones that are not interested in history might 
 just take Mr. Follett's fantasy for a reality. This is certainly a good read, and much easier than any serious work on the subject, so it is very effective at brainwashing. And then we hear Obama mentioning "POLISH concentration camps", and see him brushing it off instead of apologizing. Ta-da, bygones, why dwell on it? What's a couple of million of people, who cares who killed them? That just couldn't be Germans, they were such a nice people... Just read Winter of The World if you don't believe me... However I bet Obama knows that the BMW, Mercedes and Audi are GERMAN cars... 
 Reading this book I has wondering - European Union stipend? Or literary award in Germany? 
 Other plot lines were sketchy, maybe it's understandable considering the scope of the work, however I got the distinct impression that the Soviets in Spain and later Germany were horrible, inhuman criminals, thieves, rapists, ruling by brutality and terror (pretty much like German themselves) however the same Soviets all over Eastern Europe were hardly worth a mention. Actually, they were not worth a mention at all. It was so bad that Germany was occupied by them, that there was simply no room for the fact that thanks to the same Germany all of the democratic Eastern European countries were occupied by Soviets for 50 years. For West Germany war ended in 1945. For everybody east of that privileged country only in 1990's. 
 Bias runs amok and whitewash is laid out in with a shovel and is about as subtle as Hitler's speech. This book got on my nerves so badly that I could hardly wait to be finished, and the last 100 pages or so was a pure torture. What did we have in there? Total omission of the fact that Allies allowed hundreds of millions of people suffer under Soviet occupation for 50 years, at the same time doing what they could to help suffering Germans. 
 I have had it with the whitewashing, bias, quarter-truths (or .1% truths, I should say), suffering in Germany, Soviets who did not participate in WWII until they were invaded (a small matter of Soviet invasion on Poland on 9/17/1939 is hardly worth mentioning, as it would put England and France in an even worse light for not actually fulfilling the duties as per signed international treaties) and Marshall plan. Guess what - Marshall Plan was disallowed by Soviets in Eastern Europe, most ruined and savaged, even though we were not aggressors in this war. We have GERMANY to thank for that. 
 Since I don't think Mr. Follett is going to come back from his La-La Land anytime soon, this will be the last book I read by him. I am overjoyed that I had gotten this one from the library. Paying (other than taxes) for this hogwash would just about cause me a heart attack. If I could give it -5 stars I would.

sample_reviews.review_text: Loved this book in the Century Trilogy. This book takes place from 1933 to 1947, and encompasses the war from the points of view of the Americans, Germans, British and Russians. We cannot know, just how lucky we really are, and how much we need to make sure that another world war never happens again. I am looking forward to book three. Thanks Ken Follett for sharing your book with us!

I love Ken Follett's writing. His characters are very intriguing and I feel invested in their experiences. His mastery of history woven into stories is what keeps me so engaged I can't tear myself away.

I really wanted to like this book, but did Follett phone this in, or what? Character development was non-existent. People were props for historical scenes and nothing more. I gave up after about 300 pages.

What can I say? Couldn't put it down. Excellent character development. Excellent story line with WWII. Excellent integration of the story lines (a little pushed on the realism of the overlap between characters. Ken Follett is a gifted story teller. The sections on Pearl Harbor did a great job capturing the naivete (and perhaps arrogance) that American had before the bombing and also the chaotic realism of the attack. Also, love the way that the rise of Nazism was handled because it showed how a beaten down population can follow a mad man without realizing until its too late.

What a disappointing follow-up to Fall of Giants. I enjoyed this as first, but I was listening to it in audio, and the reader was charmingly British and did a bunch of cool accents. But as it wore on, I realized that the historical facts were a thin backdrop to a soap opera, rather than acting as the story's backbone. 
 Most of the characters from the first novel returned, but their children became the focus as they randomly fell in love with eachother. I'm talking "love" creepy old man style - there is no reasonable explanation or backstory for the relationships, just a lot of pervy descriptions of boobs. Sometimes Follett describes clothes, but boobs are definitely his preferred subject matter. 
 Pass.

There is a danger of social and political historical fiction like the Century Trilogy. People already have a connection to the events and a sloppy author can simply trade on that knowledge to hold a reader's interest without allowing the reader to uncover something new.Historical fiction is often centered outside the experiences of the reader. When Gone with the Wind, hit the best sellers list in 1936, there were both living veterans of the Civil War and many children of those veterans. GWTW reinforced much of the moonlight and magnolias myth of the Ante-Bellum South to such an extent that those myths still resonate one hundred fifty years after the War. 
 Fortunately Ken Follett is an uncommon author. Covering the period from the end of the War to End All Wars to the end of the second such war, most readers are close enough to those events. However, Follett lets readers uncover new perspectives on these events. 
 Many have written about the rise of Fascism in Europe and but few demonstrated how close the British aristocracy came to embracing it themselves. It is one thing to write about the Holocaust on a grand scale and something else altogether to witness the forced evacuation of the ill and insane from Jewish hospitals on trucks bound for extermination camps. The stupidity of American isolationism, the cruelty of Stalinism, idealism of the expatriate fighters in Spain, gay soldiers,and the bravery of the French and German resistance are all subjects within the reach of Follett's pen. 
 Sit back, settle in and enjoy this part of what will be considered, for a long time to come, a contemporary gem.

When I finished book 1 of the century trilogy (Fall of Giants) I opined that Follett was mailing it in and taking advantage of his well-earned reputation but a mailed-in Follett was still better than most other authors' best work. But, there is a limit and Book 2 just had me counting the pages until the end. We have the requisite star-crossed lovers subplot, the requisite "Nazis sure are evil!" subplot and the requisite "Communists sure are stupid and almost as evil as the nazis" subplot. I just couldn't get excited about such cardboard characters, to be frank. I won't be reading the third instalment, I'm afraid.

A somewhat enjoyable read which falls short of the first episode in the series. I do believe the author gets paid by the word. These books are massive and the amount of content is overwhelming. While Folett does a solid job at explaining history from different perspectives, the unbelievable circumstances get out of hand. We have the one cousin that assists in building the atom bomb and the other steals it. There is a character who decodes the attack on Pearl Harbor, the day his family arrives for a visit, confirms Midway for the American trap and is on the deck of the Yorktown for the battle. 
 The books strength lies with the German characters and the price National Socialism extracted from their nation. The rise if the secret police is described in great detail along with the treatment of the German women by Soviet soldiers.
This is such a great picture of WWII It really takes you there Not in a buried in facts way either It's long so take your time but it's worth the effort

For me, Ken Follett is a guilty pleasure. His books are big, entertaining page-turners -- no more, no less -- and sometimes, that's exactly what I need. "Winter of the World" is Part 2 of his Century Trilogy, in which he follows several intertwined families on two countries through landmark events of the 20th Century. With the turn of every page, you can practically hear the sound of the mini-series contracts being written and signed. While much of this book is utterly predictable, that doesn't lessen the pleasure of reading it. Follett knows how to tell a story. Don't let the weight of this tome scare you off (nearly 1000 pages!); it's a quick read. I look forward to Volume 3 of the trilogy, scheduled for publication next year.

reference_books.title: Broken Promise (Promise Falls Trilogy, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Promise Falls is a town of 30,000, and it's dying. On David Harwood's first day at the local newspaper, it closes down. He's forced to move in with his parents until he can find another job. There are many characters in this novel, and each has a problem. David's cousin Marley's problem is that she has lost touch with reality since losing her newborn baby. Suddenly she has a baby she claims an angel gave her. The baby's mother is dead, and David investigates, not wanting to accept that Marley could be capable of murder. 
 Connections and red herrings carry us along, as chapters alternate between David's first person viewpoint and the third person viewpoints of others. Who is guilty? Who is innocent? Excitement builds and brings us a surprising but satisfying ending. The main strings are tied, but other strings point to other mysteries that will become major in book two of this trilogy. Barclay is a master of intrigue. He gives us a sense of reality in his use of character and conversation. I want to read more by this author.

reference_books.title: Sandstorm (Sigma Force, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
A mysterious explosion wipes out an antiquities exhibit in a London museum. Thus begins a quest for an unholy power that draws two teams to the Arabian peninsula, one that hopes to use the power to benefit the world, the other to control it. The power, itself, is unstable and might explode with devastating effects at any moment. 
 Five view-point characters lead the action. Every one has personal issues, apart from the quest. Consequently the individuals have depth, so we can see what drives them. Each receives equal time, but I feel the curator, Safia, is the female lead. Her ex-fiance is an Indian Jones style adventurer, who may be selected as the male lead. He seems constantly in trouble, perhaps so we can see him as an adventurer. I couldn't help but feel however that some of his run-ins were contrived, and I lacked the patience to get caught up in them. Despite his larger than life aspects, he is upstaged by Painter Crowe, American operative and scientist. This is my favorite character, and I was pleased to see he appears in another novel. 
 It can be noted that Rollins must have delighted in naming his characters. Kara, Safia, Omaha, Painter, Cassandra...Wonderful names. Not a Dick or Jane among them. 
 We have great atmosphere as the drama unfolds during a sandstorm. The storm threatens the survival of both the good and the bad guys. The writing is vivid, but at times jars, as when a noun is used as a verb, such as "clotheslining." Uh, what? Or the overuse of water tickling. Should I smile? 
 The surprises and the mystery plunge us into what appears as fantasy. Turns out, most of it is science backed by proof. At the story's end, the author lets us know which is science and which is fancy. The combination makes for a delicious thriller.

reference_books.title: The Winter People
reference_books.review_text:
Ruthie is nineteen and eager to leave home and enter college. She's tired of being poor and living off the grid with her mother and younger sister. Tired of living in the country near a forest she must not enter. In the forest, within view of their ancient house, stands a spooky collection of rocks suggestive of an open hand. 
 From time to time, people disappear. When her mother disappears, Ruthie and her sister search the house with all its secret places. They come across a copy of Sara Harrison Shea's diary, written in 1908. Somehow this diary holds clues to their mother's whereabouts. It is a tale of ghosts, craziness, and murder. It leads Ruthie on an odd journey of revelation about her own roots and why her mother insisted on living off the grid. 
 Each chapter follows a particular individual, mostly in third person. Some take us to 1908, and some take us to the present. As the story unfolds, we view the situation from different viewpoints. It leads us to some surprising truths. If you like Stephen King's novel, you'll like The Winter People.

reference_books.title: The City
reference_books.review_text:
One of Koontz's greatest works. A masterpiece. Well deserving of its best seller status. 
 This is a story of Jonah Ellington Basie Hines Eldridge Wilson Hampton Armstrong Kirk's coming of age. It is also a story of goodness and love. 
 It begins inside Jonah's point of view as he chats with the reader. In his breezy and witty style, we meet lovable characters who are unique from one another. We'd like to invite them to lunch. The tailor upstairs, the lady downstairs, his mother and grandfather, Jonah and his best friend. And then there is the mysterious lady who calls herself The City. The City represents all the goodness that exists beyond the bad news. At crucial times she connects with Jonah and places him on the path to salvation and gratification, without removing his sense of responsibility. 
 Bad times begin for Jonah when his father leaves and becomes involved with wrong-doers. These wrong-doers soon have reason to kill Jonah and all those he loves. The tension keeps us reading as we worry about the good guys. Will each one survive? 
 When evil strikes, our heroes rise above adversity in a realistic and gratifying way. Jonah learns that no matter how bad things seem, if you have the right attitude, everything works out in the end. His mother, the tailor upstairs, and the mysterious lady who calls herself The City teach him this lesson. The attitude of the wrong-doers leads them to darkness and despair while the attitude of the righteous raises them to a brighter future. 
 The love, wisdom, and beauty of Koontz's writing shines into my heart. Here is a story to relish and to share. It's an easy read, a gripping adventure, and inspiring.

reference_books.title: Tortilla Flat
reference_books.review_text:
I've heard of Tortilla Flat and seen places named after it, so when I came across the story, I felt it was something I should read. 
 Tortilla Flat isn't really flat. It's a mountainous place with forest. The characters in this humorous story are ne'er-do-wells who join together and eventually disband. Their main reason for existence seems to be the consumption of vast quantities of wine. Nevertheless each man has his adventures, which impact on the entire group. I guess one could describe the characters as cute and rascally with good hearts. They are not the type of people whose company I would seek out. The only character I felt any fondness for was Pirate, a not so smart guy who slept with his dogs and had the gumption to collect and sell firewood for 30 cents a day. 
 My opinion does not reflect on the quality and value of the story. Steinbeck's writing is magnificent in its aptness and simplicity. The humor was wonderful. And one gets a look at a subculture that existed in the early part of the 20th century.

book_a.title: Major Pettigrew's Last Stand
book_a.user_review:
This isn't the type of book I usually choose to read, but it was among the books my sister lent me. I was prepared to be bored, but as I got into the story, its charm captivated me. Major Pettigrew is a delightful character among more or less delightful but interesting characters. He's caught up with obligations to family, class, and community that he would just as soon ignore. Nevertheless he is a man of honor and diplomacy. And we're on his side as he struggles to do the right thing in as inoffensive a way as possible. How can he keep the heirloom rifles in his family when his son wants to sell them? How can he stop the development that threatens the beauty of his community when he must support the lord who is forced to sell his estate to be developed? And how can he pursue the relationship he desires with a woman who is considered an outsider because of her ethnic background? These and other knotty problems find their resolution in amusing, interesting, and satisfying ways. For much of the novel, the pace is leisurely. Toward the end, however, the pace picks up for a surprising conclusion. 
 As I read this witty novel, I saw it as a movie of great appeal.

sample_reviews.review_text: I agree that this book was Austenian, but it was also thoroughly modern. I LOVED reading it. In fact, I didn't want it to end. The characters are rich and loveable, and the pacing was just right.

Sometimes love doesn't respect 'respectability'. An older widower, a man guided by 'what is right' finds himself falling in love with a Pakistani woman from the village. His finds that his attraction to her is often at odds with what others and he himself regard as proper behavior. 
 For fans of Alexander McCall Smith, Elegance of the Hedgehog

I loved this book. The characters were amazing especially the Major. I would love to know him. The writing was vibrant and perfectly descriptive. When I read it again I will pick out the lines I particularly love from Major. I found the situations realistic and the characters real life warts made the book all the better. It is one of my favorite books of late!

A comfortable read 
 So much happens in this book, yet nothing happens. 
 That is such an odd statement that I'd better explain. 
 The characters, and their interactions, and the landscape in which they operate, are very well developed as the story progresses. The principal character, Ernest Pettigrew, lives in a village in the south of England. He is universally known as "Major." The events in his life, and in those of the people who surround him, take on enormous significance: for him. Those events would not even figure in the local newspapers and would probably mean nothing to anyone at all a few years later. 
 What the story shows is that something which may dominate our thoughts, our lives, may mean absolutely nothing in the greater scheme of things. 
 For the Major, the two most important things in his life are a gun which, for many years, has been in the possession of his dear, recently departed brother, and the owner of the village shop, Mrs Ali. 
 For about three-quarters of the book, nothing really happens, but one feels compelled to keep reading. Then the action commences and runs right up until the final pages. At the end, I was left wondering what it was all about. 
 This is what I would call a comfortable read. For some, I can imagine that it would provide a nostalgic look at Little England. However, for me, as somebody who lives in South East England, there were flaws which did not ring true. For example, the Major drives home past the "twin airports of London." There are no twin airports of London. There are hardly any similarities between any of the airports around London, any more than you could compare, say, JFK and New Dehli airports. 
 Still, it is a pleasant read, and this is a book which I would recommend to friends who long for the nostalgia of "the Old Country."

The first third of this book seemed like a pleasant story about a crotchedy Englishman figuring out his life after the death of his younger brother. Then the middle third gets a lot more complicated. Suddenly it's a book about race and class, honor, ethics and proper behavior. It loops back around to being about a crotchedy man who has a new leaf on life.

I was shocked that this book got so many rapturous reviews. Major Pettigrew is packed full of ridiculously awful characters -- the kind of characters who only exist as foils because nobody in real life is that selfish, that rude, that racist, without paying social consequences. I never enjoy books or movies that concoct the most ridiculously awful characters so that the audience is invited to feel smugly superior to them. And yet I love things like E.F. Benson's Lucia series -- which is also full of awful people. Benson's awful people, however, are very recognizable and relatable; he's encouraging us to laugh at our own least likable traits, not to sneer at THOSE terrible people who aren't like US. 
 Also, for a supposed comedy, Major Pettigrew is entirely unfunny.

It was a very sweet love story between two people of advancing years, going to show that love isn't only for the young. It had some lovely similies in the writing but there was rather too much detail in the description for me. I like just a suggestion and then for my imagination to do the rest. The pace was a little slow but I think that matched the slow burning romance. On the whole I enjoyed it, it was very endearing and I'd recommend it.Song of the Phoenix
A lovely story.
Loved the writing. Great character development and writing.

Major Pettigrew's Last Stand is a beautiful novel about loneliness and love, fustiness and openness, racism and classism, the elder and the young. Major Pettigrew is a retired military officer, a widower, at times, was more concerned that his sister-in-law wouldn't get his parents' 'second-best china' than he was of experiencing the world and people around him. Mrs. Ali, a widowed shopkeeper, was chafing against the strict familial rules of how "older" widows should behave. She has a love of Kipling, as does he, and despite obstacles of prejudice, racism, and the selfishness of their family members, they're drawn together. 
 Some of the sentences were so evocative that I copied them down to read aloud. I found the novel thoroughly engrossing; I had great affection for both the Major and Mrs. Ali, and I marvelled at the descriptions of the English countryside and landscapes. A beautifully written novel.

book_b.title: Gone with the Wind
book_b.user_review:
Not being into romance, I was prepared to not like this book. Nevertheless, I felt I should read it when the opportunity arose, so I could see what all the praise was about. 
 Scarlett and Rhet are not particularly likeable characters, and as we follow them and the others through the novel, I realize the book is more than a romance; it is a literary feat. It is a character study. Pick any vain, empty-headed, boy-crazy teenager, plop her into the 1860s, and you have someone seemingly similar to Scarlett. But for all her narrowness, she grows on the reader. She is a survivor, stating repeatedly that she'll never be hungry again, and tomorrow is another day. Events that bowl others over add to her determination to win. She has talent unbecoming a lady of her day but necessary for her survival--a business sense, drive, a sense of obligation. 
 Her fantasy concerning Ashley eventually fades when reality glares through, but again we see this as idolization similar to what has been seen in more modern gentler times with fans of Rudolph Valentino, or Elvis.... 
 In the end, when she has destroyed her dreams of happiness, her stubbornness refuses to allow her to surrender to defeat. She resolves to piece together the dream she has shattered. 
 We get a look through Southern eyes at the Civil War and Reconstruction Eras. We may not agree with their views or solutions but we can understand, based on the author's words.

sample_reviews.review_text:
To explain why I only gave this one star, the book is probably a really good book, but when this was "required reading" at school, it was a bit much. I grew up in the south, all you learned about in history class was the Civil War. Everything before it was just a prelude and everything after was just a result from it. We barely finished studying WWII and that was because we rushed it. 
 Now another reason I don't like this book: if you grew up in Atlanta as I did, Gone With the Wind was an almost every week discussion. There is a whole culture surrounding the book and the movie. I guess I just grew too tired of it to appreciate the work itself. 
 Now, having said all that, I do rather admire Margaret Mitchell. She seemed to be a bit of a "trailblazer" for southern women of the time. Flounting conventialities (sp)and expectations of "proper" women of the time. Plus she defied expectations and never wrote a sequel, when she was pressured to do so. 
 But truly, to never hear of Scarlett O'Hara and Rhett Butler again would be so very peaceful.

Almost a year later, and I finally finished Gone With The Wind. While I can see why it's a classic, there's another part of me that thinks it's vastly overrated. I don't see why people would want to read it more than once. Margaret did a great job making Scarlett a spoiled brat. She ended up having four kids, but only one mattered. For the second half of the book I kept wondering what about the other kids? It was only about Bonnie. There wasn't any characters that I found myself attached to. It was meh.
Another one of my favorite books ever. Good to have a different perspective of the Civil War. Second time reading.
Its one of the books that tell the life and story of one girl as she faces dissappointed love, war, hunger and lost innocence
Read this a hundred years ago I swear. I actually am amazed as I look through book lists and remember reading them and my feelings on the book at the time I read them.

Didn't like the prose - too slow and boring. Scarlett got on my nerves from the start. There was so much overt racism and nastiness from characters who thought nothing of killing black people. I did not like it at all and cannot understand the fuss.

Gone With the Wind is pretty cool, except for all the racism! 
 Of course, you could say that about the Old South in general, and look where that got them. Spoiler, it got their asses kicked because they were hateful fucks who absolutely refused to stop enslaving millions of people and 70 years later in 1936 here's Margaret Mitchell whining about it for a thousand pages. If you'd like to hear why slavery was terrific and black people are inferior to whites and they liked being slaves, here is your epic. If that sounds unpleasant, you're not going to like Gone With the Wind. 
 A non-racist book can have racist characters, and all the characters in this book are racist. Is the book itself necessarily racist? Yes. It has an omniscient narrator, and many long, racist passages that are clearly not from any character's perspective; they feel like the nonfiction interludes in War & Peace. Is it possible Mitchell means for us to disagree with her omniscient narrator? No. There's no evidence whatsoever of that, and the passages that defend the South and slavery are written with passion and supported by racist scenes in the story. This book intends to be racist; Margaret Mitchell believes what she says; she was a racist person who wrote a hateful book. I can prove it and I'm about to. 
 We start off in the glory days of the Old South, as a young, callow, beautiful Scarlett O'Hara flirts with everyone's boyfriends. Happy slaves bustle around: 
 "The house negroes of the County considered themselves superior to white trash...they were well-fed, well-clothed and looked after in sickness and old age. They were proud of the good names of their owners and, for the most part, proud to belong to people who were quality." 
 We meet some of them, Scarlett's "small white hand disappearing into their huge black paws and the four capered with delight at the meeting and with pride at displaying before their comrades what a pretty Young Miss they had." 
 Faithful slave Mammy is introduced, with her "kind face, sad with the uncomprehending sadness of a monkey's face" - "the mottled wise old eyes saw deeply, saw clearly, with the directness of the savage and the child, undeterred by conscience when danger threatened her pet." Mammy is one of the few morally pure characters in the book, but it's always that noble savage quality. 
 Luckily Scarlett stays away from the slave quarters, where "the faint niggery smell which crept from the cabin increased her nausea." 
 But then war comes. Here's noble and boring Ashley, the limpest point of the oncoming love triangle, describing what the war is about. Notice that his vision of the South is indivisible from slavery: 
 I hear the darkies coming home across the fields at dusk, tired and singing and ready for supper, and the sound of the windlass as the bucket goes down into the cool well. And there's the long view down the road to the river, across the cotton fields, and the mist rising from the bottom lands in the twilight. And that is why I'm here who have no love of death or misery or glory and no hatred for anyone. Perhaps that is what is called patriotism. 
 After the War and during Reconstruction, things get really dark (get it? lol) as Northerners ruin black people: "Some of the free negroes were getting quite insolent. This last [Scarlett] could hardly believe, for she had never seen an insolent negro in her life." 
 But "The [Freedmen's] Bureau fed them while they loafed and poisoned their minds against their former masters." And here's much more from the omniscient narrator: 
 [They] furthermore told the negroes they were as good as the whites in every way and soon white and negro marriages would be permitted, soon the estates of their former owners would be divided and every negro would be given forty acres and a mule for his own. They kept the negroes stirred up with tales of cruelty perpetrated by the whites and, in a section long famed for the affectionate relations between slaves and slave owners, hate and suspicion began to grow. 
 [Now Southerners] were looking on the state they loved, seeing it trampled by the enemy, rascals making a mock of the law, their former slaves a menace, their men disenfranchised, their women insulted. 
 This eventually leads to the formation of the noble Ku Klux Klan, who merely attempt to protect Southern women from being raped by uppity former slaves. Here's a Klan member now: 
 "'Wilkerson had gone a bit too far with his nigger-equality business. Oh yes, he talks it to those black fools by the hour. He had the gall - the - ' Tony sputtered helplessly, 'to say niggers had a right to - to - white women.'" 
 "The negroes were on top and behind them were the Yankee bayonets," thinks Scarlett: "She could be killed, she could be raped and, very probably, nothing would ever be done about it." 
 And here's the omniscient narrator summing it up: 
 It was the large number of outrages on women and the ever-present fear for the safety of their wives and daughters that drove Southern men to cold and trembling fury and caused the Ku Klux Klan to spring up overnight. And it was against this nocturnal organization that the newspapers of the North cried out most loudly, never realizing the tragic necessity that brought it into being. 
 This is all demonstrated in the action. Scarlett O'Hara's headstrong ways nearly get every man in town hung. Her foolish habit of driving alone through the worst parts of town almost gets her raped by a freed slave, forcing the Klan to take action and lynch him, and they all almost get caught. Her second husband is killed. Divorced from its context, this is a brilliant scene. It's done entirely from Scarlett's point of view, so the actual gun fight is totally off page. What we see instead is the wives, with Northern soldiers in their living rooms waiting for the men to return - surrounded by enemies, their faces frozen into nonchalant expressions, desperately and silently scheming to save their husbands' lives. It's great stuff, as long as you can forget that you're being asked to root for the KKK to get away with lynching a man. 
 And here's a pretty long series of quotes. Again, they're all from the omniscient narrator - that is, from the book itself. 
 The South had been tilted as by a giant malicious hand, and those who had once ruled were now more helpless than their former slaves had ever been. 
 The former slaves were now the lords of creation and, with the aid of the Yankees, the lowest and most ignorant ones were on top. The better class of them, scorning freedom, were suffering as severely as their white masters...Many loyal field hands also refused to avail themselves of the new freedom, but the hordes of 'trashy free issue niggers,' who were causing most of the trouble, were drawn largely from the field-hand class. 
 In slave days, these lowly blacks had been despised by the house negroes and yard negroes as creatures of small worth...Plantation mistresses had put the pickaninnies through courses of training and elimination to select the best of them for the positions of greater responsibility. Those consigned to the fields were the ones least willing or able to learn, the least energetic, the least honest and trustworthy, the most vicious and brutish...[but now] the former field hands found themselves suddenly elevated to the seats of the mighty. There they conducted themselves as creatures of small intelligence might naturally be expected to do. Like monkeys or small children turned loose among treasured objects whose value is beyond their comprehension, they ran wild - either from perverse pleasure in destruction or simply because of their ignorance. 
 To the credit of the negroes, including the least intelligent of them, few were actuated by malice and those few had usually been "mean niggers" even in slave days. But they were, as a class, childlike in mentality, easily led and from long habit accustomed to taking orders. 
 ... 
 Here was the astonishing spectacle of half a nation attempting, at the point of bayonet, to force upon the other half the rule of negroes, many of them scarcely one generation out of the African jungles. 
 ... 
 Thanks to the negro vote, the Republicans and their allies were firmly entrenched and they were riding roughshod over the powerless but still protesting minority. 
 Man, just read that last sentence again. Wow. 
 Anyway, this is all very difficult for poor Scarlett: "The more I see of emancipation the more criminal I think it is. It's just ruined the darkies. Thousands of them aren't working at all and the ones we can get to work at the mill are so lazy and shiftless they aren't worth having. and if you so much as swear at them, much less hit them a few licks for the good of their souls, the Freedmen's Bureau is down on you like a duck on a June bug." 
 She complains that Northerners "Did not know that negroes had to be handled gently, as though they were children, directed, praised, petted, scolded...How could anyone get any work done with free niggers quitting all the time?...[It's] too dear a homeland to be turned over to ignorant negroes drunk with whiskey and freedom." 
 And with the final word, here's a former slave himself, Big Sam, who "galloped over to the buggy,his eyes rolling with joy and his white teeth flashing, and clutched her outsretched hand with two big hands as big as hams. His watermelon-pink tongue lapped out, his whole body wiggled and his joyful contortions were as ludicrous as the gambolings of a mastiff. ... 'Ah done had nuff freedom. Ah wants somebody ter eed me good vittles reg'lar, and tell me whut ter do an' whut not ter do.'" 
 Okay, is that enough? That was gross to type out. And don't think I'm cherry-picking the only racist passages; this book is soaked in racism. God's nightgown, this book is fuckin' racist. Pat Conroy, in a despicably fawning introduction, sees fit to mention that "No black man or woman can read this book and be sorry that this particular wind is gone," and what the hell kind of thing is that to say? "White people, on the other hand...you gotta be a little bummed out, right?" Is that what you meant, Pat? 
 And look, yes, it's too bad that this book has destroyed itself with hatred, because it's got a lot going for it. It certainly has Scarlett O'Hara going for it. She's fuckin' terrific, a towering antiheroine, amoral, selfish and brave - somewhat like the South itself. Rhett Butler, her swarthy and cynical love interest, is pretty good too, although he can't stop mansplaining amorality and he might have some kind of social learning disability. (He's also a murderer, by the way: "I did kill the nigger. He was uppity to a lady, and what else could a Southern gentleman do?") They have sortof a proto-50 Shades thing going on, including a fairly kinky love scene that's not explicitly described but Scarlett was definitely into it. Third love triangle corner Ashley sucks, no one cares about him. 
 It also taught me the phrase "God's nightgown!" which is certainly a great thing to yell. 
 But it is totally, irredeemably ruined by its racism. Look, I'm not trying to be "politically correct" here. That's not even a thing; it's a term made up by haters to excuse hate. Gone With The Wind angered me. I don't like hearing black people described as stupid monkeys over and over again. I didn't enjoy reading the book because I was constantly pissed off by how ignorant and hateful it is. 
 Books matter. We use stories to describe and define society. If we allow this book to become part of the foundation of our past - if we call it a classic, as some people have - we're basing our past on a terrible lie. And it is a terrible lie, in case we need to say that out loud: Slavery was bad, black people didn't like it, almost everyone else didn't either, and the South were the bad guys in the Civil War. 
 And books are also our companions. When we choose to read, we're spending significant amounts of time - hours and hours - deep in their worlds. This companion is full of hate. These hours and hours will be spent listening to her yell about insolent niggers. If you find it unpleasant to hang out with viciously hateful racists, you won't like this book. It's the most racist book I've ever read. I didn't like it.

I like the book a lot better then the movie. You get a much better picture of how it was to live in the south during the civil war and also Scarlett is a much less sympathetic character (if you can imagine that) just in the way she treats her older children.

This was very much a "meh" book for me. It wasn't the worst book I've read in the series but it certainly wasn't the best. But it clearly signalled the end of Sookie and Eric's relationship (which I know everyone is up in arms about) but I haven't been a fan of them together the whole way through.

Not that I enjoyed her relationship with Bill any better and every other Supernatural male that comes into contact with her finds some attraction but I haven't met anyone I'd like to see her end up with. 
 Does she have to "end up" with anyone? 
 But of course she does. This is why it's dragged out for thirteen books, just to see who Sookie has as a boyfriend at the end! 
 Obviously I can't wait to find out.

You can read this entire review and others at Pages & Prose 
 Okay, I know I need to review this, but I'm not sure where to start. I'm giving Deadlocked a 2/5 only because it did get better toward the end. 
 I suppose I should say that I've been readying the Sookie Stackhouse books for a few years and many of them I've loved. However, when I picked up this one I realized that I couldn't even remember what had happened in the previous two or three books. Everything blended together in this huge mish-mash of jumbled ideas. I felt kind of lost when I first started reading Deadlocked, but I soon figured out everything that was going on, which was a lot of 
 nothing 
 . Honestly, it would have been better if I hadn't even read this one. 
 I don't recommend this to fans and especially not to those new to the series. I suggest y'all just skip this one and call it a night. Read Ms. Harris's Harper Connelly series if you want a southern style paranormal story that's well written.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I hate to say it, but the Sookie series has reached that point where it does need to end. Sure, this book had its fun moments, but the big reveal just left me going "waa? Huh? That makes NO sense at all!" and the explanations to back it up just weren't sufficient enough. Beyond that, a lot of the story seems like ground we've already covered. Bill still loves Sookie. Sookie and Eric have a troublesome relationship. There are vampire politics, were politics, and Sookie has a horrible, no good birthday that outdoes a few of Buffy's. At least the fairy storyline does get wrapped up, and Harris has started the rest of the plotlines down their final paths. 
 At this point, the series just feels old, and a lot of the fun and magic it had in the beginning has gotten lost along the way. The fairies overstayed their welcome, and somewhere along the way, Sookie seems to have lost her edge. Hopefully, the final book will end with her getting a bit of control over everything and making some firm decisions. It's also looking like it will end with her riding off into the sunset with Sam....

Sookie has never had great luck, but her luck seems to be all bad lately. She was invited to a vampire party, only to walk in on her husband, Eric, in a rather erotic sucking of blood from another woman. She finds out she was told a wrong time to be there in the first place, which, had she gotten there on time Eric would have fed from her instead of another woman. Later in the night that same woman is found dead in Eric's yard! Who would kill her? Did Eric or Pam do it while Sookie was collecting her thoughts in the bathroom? The police have been brought in, which is never good when it involves vampires in any way, much less when a dead girl has been found in a vampire's yard. Sookie teams up with Bill to find the answer to this murder before someone is wrongly accused. Can they figure it out in time? Also on her plate is the mess of things in her Fae family. There is something going on with them that is not good at all, but does Sookie really have time to figure that out too? She has a lot on her plate right now; the dead girl in Eric's yard, Sam's relationship with his Were girlfriend, helping with the bar that she is part owner of now, her brother Jason's relationship, Fae family problems, and her best friend Tara having her twins. How can she spread herself all over like is needed? They say what doesn't kill you makes you stronger, but will it be too much for Sookie? 
 This book was much better than the last one I read in this series. The action and mystery of it all started much quicker and drew me into the book much faster than the previous book did. So much always happens in Harris' books I never know how to really describe them to people without giving spoilers away, which is why I usually just comment on the writing and the plot and the characters for her books. This book is no different, which is why I love her writing style. She writes so much into the book, and yet, it never feels overwhelming to the reader. There may always be a few side plots, but they never seem to muddle the main one and they add to the main plot. Between the characters and the plots of the book they make up a fantastic tale. I simply love the characters Harris has created and I love how they have grown so much over the course of the series. As the series comes to an end (only one more book in the series after this one) I can't help but wonder what will come of all the characters and how Harris plans to bring that "end" to the series and the lives of Sookie and her family and friends. This book kind of starts to wrap some things up, such as the surrounding characters relationships and such. Once again I am left with a great curiosity and want to read on in the series and see how it all turns out. Harris is a very talented author and that is shown again and again in all the books of this series. If you have read any of the series, you really need to read this book, I thought it was just great! So much mystery and mayhem! 
 5/5 Stars!

FULL REVIEW ON Talk Supe 
 All good things must come to an end... 
 And I'm glad that Deadlocked is the second to the last installment in Charlaine Harris' Sookie Stackhouse series because I'm not sure how much more disappointment I could suffer from this series. Sookie Stackhouse has and will always have a special place in my heart but the last few books in this series has left me so utterly disappointed and deflated. Harris had me hooked on the after reading Dead Until Dark and things were great up until book nine. Since Dead and Gone, the series has taken a nose dive (in my humble opinion). Everything that I loved about the series from the very beginning has faded away and we're left with little hints of what the main characters used to be.

I gave it 3 stars, but it could and should be a 1 or a 2. Formulaic compared to the earlier books. Am going to go back and start rereading Sookie from the beginning and then re-assess my ratings. Will I keep buying them? Yes, because I love what they've done with the characters in True Blood and hope that Ms. Harris will bring that level of writing back to the series.

Intriguing in concept, lackluster in execution. This book is ideally suited, I believe, for those who've never read Pride and Prejudice. For someone like me---who has not only read the book, but seen the miniseries, dabbled in fanfiction, read other interpretations of the same story, and inadvertently memorized whole passages---this was rather tedious than entertaining. Despite the inclusion of zombies, nothing changes. Certainly a handful of details are different, but the book remains in essentials unchanged. Which is a little hard to believe when you have zombies running around. 
 Add to this that the editor, or perhaps the writer, cared so little for continuity that they allowed "Bennet" to occasionally gain an extra T; "Kilkenny" to shift back and forth from "Kilkerry;" and characters to consistently reference statements they don't actually make in this version of the classic (e.g., Elizabeth refers to Darcy saying his temper is "resentful"---a statement he makes in the original but not in this book), and it's hardly any wonder that by the last third of the book I was desperate for the end. 
 If you've been meaning to read Pride and Prejudice, but can't quite bring yourself to struggle through early nineteenth century prose, this is the book for you. But if you already have a strong background in the book, you'd be far better off skimming this version for the zombie bits and paging through for the pictures.

I am a huge fan of JA. I have read some fun knock offs so I thought I would give this one a try. It was pretty bad. The author took the original and threw in some blood, fighting and grossness to appeal to teenage boys. I am a glutton for punishment though....and I plan to go see the movie.

I am not a zombie fan and when Walking Dead is playing in my house, I avoid the room with the television. What I am is a Jane Austen fan and especially a Pride and Prejudice fan. I love the story more as time goes on. 
 So, when our library offered the opportunity to watch the movie one week and discuss the book the next, I decided it was time to check out this book. 
 It was a pleasant surprise to find out that the original text is preserved and the zombie parts added into the plot. In my opinion, Grahame-Smith did an excellent job of combining his zombie excerpts with Austen's original text. Hence, the four stars. 
 Now, a brief word about the movie. Worth watching, for sure. Don't expect the plot to follow P&P as closely as the BBC mini-series. They take a rather large detour and some rather creative plot points. With the exception of Darcy, the casting gets high marks. Colin Firth has spoiled me for eternity and no one else measure up. reference_books.title: The Shock of the Fall
reference_books.review_text: I have had this book sitting on my bedside table for approximately a year now and on top of it I have just piled more and more books as I buy them, meaning that it was taking a while to get down to this one; it appears that for every book I read, two more I buy. Then a few weeks ago my class in tutor period was dedicated to books and my tutor, a psychology teacher, recommended The Shock of the Fall. When I bought the book I didn't have much idea what it was about except for the fact that a character, Simon, was going to die and I saw that it had won an award. So, at my teacher's recommendation I rearranged my stack of books, ensuring that The Shock of the Fall was going to be read this month. This book did not disappoint. I love the, well, messiness of the narration as it skips from one point in time to another and from one place to another, and I enjoyed how the font changed every now and then so that you can identify when he's at a computer, or using his typewriter, or someone has written him a letter. The format is beautiful, though this is hardly surprising coming from someone who loves epistolary novels. It was also intriguing, every now and then Filer would release more details and we'd see characters for a small section, not really expecting their return, but then there they are again. Furthermore, I love books which are aware of mental illnesses because nowadays I know so many people that suffer from one thing or another while other people remain completely oblivious to how other people are suffering. On this subject, whenever I do read books in which characters have mental illnesses, it is usually focused on depression, so it is lovely to have a more unique perspective into mental illness as there are so many different types. I definitely recommend this book to basically anyone.

reference_books.title: Nirvana (Nirvana #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I received a digital copy of Nirvana from NetGalley to read and review. The expected publication for this book is November 10th. 
 Nirvana is set in the future where life is very different. The title of this book refers to a virtual world where people can visit, if they've earned it or paid for it, and here they can return to life as it used to be. The book is set six months after Larissa's husband, Andrew, supposedly died. Larissa doesn't believe that he is dead and searches for him, trying to uncover the mystery of what happened. 
 My first thought on this book was that it sounded very interesting with great potential. However, as I begun reading it I found it difficult to get into. After the first half of the book I began to just skim read because I wasn't interested enough and at parts became confused. 
 The story would often change character perspectives as well as time periods. This can make it temporarily confusing every now and again which didn't make the experience of reading this very pleasant. This is because it wasn't clear when perspectives were changing or when the author was going to transport us back to a past event or conversation. 
 I also felt that the world this story was set in had a lot of potential, but we weren't given a lot. Technology is extremely advanced while loads of animals and stuff are extinct, the whole world is pretty artificial, so no wonder people were escaping into Nirvana whenever they could. There are places like the Farm, the Barracks, the Bubble in this world, but the descriptions weren't vivid and didn't make me interested enough to find out more about them and when we are given information it's a lot at once and I can't really retain what is happening. 
 Halfway through the book I became rather disappointed because the mystery aspect was taken away. While Larissa doesn't know what has become of Andrew, the reader does and in some circumstances this can work for a book, but in this case it didn't encourage me to keep reading. This also meant that when Larissa came to the conclusion at the end, the reader hasn't really learnt any more about where he is. 
 However, I have spoken very negatively of this book so far. When I finished this book I must admit that the cliffhanger left me wanting more. Despite my opinions on the writing, I can say that I quite enjoyed the characters and the concept of the book. Larissa was the most interesting and I much preferred reading from her perspective. 
 Overall, the story feels disorganised and doesn't flow. The world sounds like it would be interesting, but to read about it wasn't very much and I only kept reading because of the sympathy I felt for Larissa and the fact that I felt I could only review this book honestly if I had read the whole thing. As a result of this, I rate it 1/5.

book_a.title: Sharp Objects
book_a.user_review:
After reading Gone Girl by Gillian Flynn last year and loving it, I knew I had to read some of her other books. I never used to read many crime books, but I absolutely love them and definitely need to buy more. Sharp Objects is a thriller, it has mystery and suspense and this is what I love about crime books because you want to try and beat the narrator at uncovering who committed the crime, but in the end they throw in a big twist and you can't stop reading until you have all the details of how and why everything occurred. 
 Sharp Objects follows Camille who returns to her home town as a reporter in order to write an article on a murder that took place the previous August and a girl who recently went missing. As well as the mystery of what happened to these girls, the reader is left wondering about the strange and unique relationship between Camille and her mother. 
 I am going to start here with what I didn't like about the book because there wasn't that much. In the whole novel there wasn't a single character I can say I really liked. The whole town appears to have a rather unhealthy diet of alcohol, so it is rare to see many characters sober. In fact, our narrator is very rarely sober herself. So while I may have felt some sympathy for certain characters, I wasn't very attached to any of them. However, this can be hard to achieve in stand alone books as you only get roughly three hundred pages with a character unlike a series wherein you will read about them for several books. 
 Now, onto what I liked. While I didn't like the characters as people, Flynn created some very complex characters. I hated Amma, but I also pitied her and by the end of the novel you can kind of understand why she is the way she is. Amma is rather terrifying and creepy and the control she wields for a thirteen year old is astonishing. Despite everything she did, part of me just wanted to wrap her in a hug to remind her that she is loved and wanted and she had such potential for a good life. 
 The ending of the novel was not a happy ending, but I was very pleased with it. As someone who reads plenty of young adult books, there is an abundance of the theme of love. In this novel there was a possibility that Camille may find love, but the sole purpose of the book always remained fixed on the mystery of the murders. As a result of this, I was glad that the book didn't end with the murderer in prison and Camille going home to Chicago where her career really took off with the love of her life. That ending would have been too unrealistic given everything Camille has gone through. I am very happy with the fact though, that she's not on her own and she does have people who care about her and will look after her despite everything. I may not have liked Frank at the beginning, but he would probably be my favourite character if I had to pick one because he obviously wanted the best for her and at the end of the day him and Eileen were the most genuine people in her life. 
 I really liked this book and rate it 4/5. I would recommend it to those with an interest in crime, thrillers, mystery and psychology. Beware that there is some disturbing content including self-harm and sexual abuse, but it is a very gripping book and you won't want to put it down. I shall definitely be purchasing Dark Places by Gillian Flynn and any other novels she may release in the future.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Read this review @ my blog Wonderless Reviews 
 Thank you to Penguin and Netgalley for providing me with a free copy of this book in exchange for an honest review. 
 Trigger warnings: suicide, homophobia, abuse, bipolar 
 Pitched as the Breakfast Club feat. Murder One of Us is Lying had all my checkmarks for a potential new favourite book: 
 * Thriller 
 * Multi POV 
 * Misfit characters 
 * MURDER MYSTERY 
 Unfortunately, it fell short. 
 In my opinion, what this book did get right is the multiple points of view. Each character being defined to a single trope could spell disaster, but I think Karen M. McManus delivered it perfectly. Whilst I did enjoy certain characters more than others (Ads was my favourite) each one was more than just their main attribution. 
 One of Us is Lying is very fast paced and I found it so hard to put down. Every time a chapter ended I instantly wanted to keep reading the next one. I did guess the "twist" early on, but I was still kept interested enough to want to see how it all ended. 
 I had quite a few issues though. There was a ton of misogony - the words "slut" and "bitch" are mentioned a lot and not in a reclaimed positive context. One of the character's mother also has bipolar and whilst I'm not bipolar I felt like it was handled really poorly. There was no real education on bipolar and the mother was given so many negative traits. 
 I can't sit here listening to her promises and hoping it'll all work out. That she'll stay sober, stay employed, stay sane. 
 I like when less "socially acceptable" traits of mental illness are included in fiction and I know that some people must have hard childhoods growing up with a mentally ill parent, but it just felt like such a cop out and an insult to people with bipolar who are genuinely trying to be a good parent or family member. There was also some ableism: 
 He got a workman's comp settlement and wound up disabled enough to collect social security. 
 What kind of rehab-speak is she spewing? 
 There was also terms like "whack job" used and some casually mentioned "slitting your wrists". A character's sexuality was also somewhat used as a plot twist which also never sit rights. 
 One of the things I think this book did get right was the portrayal of an abusive relationship. It's why Ads is my favourite character from this book. It really shows just how much an absuive relationship can affect you. At first Ads can't see the abuse which is the case for a lot of people in abusive relationships, but then she eventually realises what is happening and she removes herself from the situation. I was so proud of her. I know this can't always happen in abusive relationships, but the situation wasn't glorified. She also had a fantastic relationship with her older sister. 
 The main problem I had with this book would be considered a "spoiler" even though I think it's something that should be talked about in reviews because it really made me feel awful. I'll try and keep it as vague as possible, but ultimately this glorified suicide so much. This was one of the biggest cases of "suicide revenge" that I've seen. It's not even that the character didn't display "typical" symptoms because I appreciated that. It was the fact that it made people who are suicidal or who have committed suicide into a "villain". I know this isn't a book about mental illness so it's not going to be the focus, but it was all just used as a negative character trait and it made me so uncomfortable. I'm so over the "mentally ill people are dangerous to society" trope. So. So. Over it. 
 I realise my opinion on this book is really unpopular to most others, but even though it was fast paced and kept me reading it missed the mark on so many elements. I just couldn't get past the fact that mental illness was so awfully represented.
*3.5 Stars*

 Some twists were surprises, others not so much. In the end, the resolution wasn't really a surprise (the thought actually crossed my mind at the beginning) but it was nice to read. I don't really feel like the plot is waterproof but at least it was enjoyable & I wasn't bothered by the writing.

Actual rating 4.5/5 
 "everyone's got their secrets" 
 The Breakfast Club meets Gossip Girl with a murdery twist! Five kids get sent to detention but only four walk out alive. 
 One of Us is Lying by Karen M. McManus is a detention-turned-murder with four unreliable teen narrators who have made mistakes they'd rather not admit to. 
 Who killed Simon, the creator of the schools most notorious gossip app? 
 I really enjoyed reading this! I think my favourite thing about this book was realising how real and flawed the characters were, and seeing how hard they worked to make themselves better people. 
 The thing that kept me hooked though, was not knowing who to trust, and pretty quickly realising that not only can you not trust anyone, but nothing is what it seems. 
 Would definitely recommend if this sounds up your alley!

Ooh, I am finally writing a new review. 
 So, I picked up One Of Us Is Lying a few weeks ago from Waterstones Piccadilly, breaking my great YA book buying ban. I've been carrying it around for about a week, and then, today, I read most of it (and finished it, yay!). 
 This is a murder mystery that is essentially Pretty Little Liars meets Gossip Girl meets The Breakfast Club. Our four main characters (and we see from each of their perspectives throughout the novel) are all forced into detention with Simon, the school's Gossip Girl - he runs a gossip app that has never failed to be true. Suddenly, he drops dead. Our main characters are the main suspects in a murder enquiry, and he had dirt on each of them - dirt none of them wants getting out. Our characters deal with the fallout of Simon's death each in their own way, whilst trying to figure out who dunnit. 
 This book did take me a while to get into, but once I did, I couldn't stop reading. I also didn't guess the ending, but it wasn't a horrible shock (cough Pretty Little Liars cough) and it felt believable. I liked the use of technology in this book that other authors shy away from, and although the characters did feel cliche at times, that's because they are cliches (geek, jock, stoner, princess) but they did start to feel more rounded as we went through the novel. 
 All the characters had believable back stories, parents, families and hobbies, which I really liked - the characters felt fleshed out. I also felt this book was the perfect length at 360 pages, and kept me guessing until the very end! 
 This is one beautiful book (with foil title and red sprayed pages) that I'm really glad I picked up.

I've got issues with a few things in this book (mental illness as a throwaway plot device, some of characters doing shitty things with no real consequences, bad boy cliches, one major plot hole) but cannot fault it as a whodunnit. 
 Kept me guessing until the very end and I can't think of too many YA mysteries who manage this. Would go as far as saying the plot and resolution are a bit Agatha Christie-esque. Will definitely be reading her next book

Do you love a good mystery that has you gripped from the start? If so then you need this book. 
 Five students walk into detention at the end of the school day but only four make it out alive. Simon, the school's biggest gossip and owner of a scandalous website exposing students' secrets, is murdered. Are one of the other four guilty? Did someone kill him to prevent him exposing their biggest secret? Can any of them be trusted? 
 I was absolutely hooked on this story from the start. We have perspectives from each of the four students: Bronwyn, the smart girl who earns straight A's. Cooper, the star athlete. Addy, the popular girl. And Nate, the bad boy. There's more than what first meets the eye to these stereotypical personas, and as the story develops we quickly learn that each of them has secrets and issues. It quickly becomes apparent that any one of them could have had motive to kill Simon. 
 I guessed the big reveal quite early on in the story and even though I was right, it didn't detract from my enjoyment of the story. I still really enjoyed getting to that reveal and there were still a few surprises thrown in along the way to keep me entertained. 
 One Of Us is Lying is a completely unputdownable whodunnit that mystery and contemporary fans will love. The mystery isn't all that hard to figure out but the story is entertaining and the characters interesting enough to keep you engrossed throughout.

This was an okay read. Initially from the blurb I was convinced it was going to be a sort of murder mystery version of The Breakfast Club, which it was at first. However, detention didn't last very long. How inconvenient that someone should die so soon during detention and spoil my fun. 
 I found the beginning of the book exciting and intriguing, but I soon found myself losing interest. I know that I can be hit-and-miss with Young Adult fiction, and unfortunately on this occasion it was more miss than hit. I found myself going through the motions, but not really connecting with any of the characters. 
 What is a coincidence is that a few days ago I started watching Pretty Little Liars for the first time. I'm hooked, and I do think this may have reduced my enjoyment of this book, as it definitely reminds me of the series, but I'm enjoying watching the series far more than I enjoyed reading this book. 
 There's nothing specifically wrong with this story, it just wasn't for me. I think I just prefer this genre of book to be darker and more tense. However, I'm sure there are lots of others who will love it, so don't just base your decision on my review alone.

This is my review of "One of Us Is Lying" by Karen M. McManus. All thoughts and opinions expressed are my own, and this review will not contain spoilers. 
 This book features five main characters, Bronwyn the Yale hopeful, Cooper the sports star, Nate the criminal, Addy the popular girl and Simon the outsider. One day they all end up in detention together, and then Simon dies. But who killed him? 
 This book was a lot better than I expected, and kept me hooked until the end. I liked the various twists and turns that popped up throughout the book, many of which I never saw coming. 
 I also liked the characters in this book. As the book progressed and we learned more about them, each character became more realistic and lifelike. 
 Finally, I liked the plot of this book. It was the breakfast club meets a murder mystery, fast paced and exciting. It kept me guessing throughout! 
 Overall, this has been one of the best YA books I've read so far this year, and it fully deserves a rating of five out of five stars. I hope to see more books from this author in the future.

reference_books.title: East of Eden
reference_books.review_text: This was my first Steinbeck. And when I read the prologue, I was hesitant to continue on to the actual story because it sounded very ... serious and Biblical because of its association with the tale of Cain and Abel. But East of Eden is so much more than an allegory in that sense. It's amazing how much complexity and humanness the protagonists of Eden are handed by Steinbeck; and I went through all the emotions of extreme hatred for certain characters (ahem, Cathy/Kate), while feeling the utmost respect and love and admiration for others; and defending the thoughts, actions and feelings of one while trying to contain the apprehension that one feels for someone they're concerned for because they're obviously marked and ALLLLL the emotions there are that a person can feel! (Well, excepting Kate I should say.) But yeah, I loved it. And it's the kind of book with so many things to offer, lessons that you could learn from laid out with such simplicity at times and without the sort of pretentious, sanctimonious stance that some writers take. Good god I'm rambling. Okay, in conclusion, this I'm certain of: I'll be visiting East of Eden again.

reference_books.title: Utopia
reference_books.review_text:
So once upon a time, Thomas More says to Raphael Hythloday, "Yo man, tell me more about this place, this Utopia." And so Hythloday's like: 
 "Oh my god, Utopia's like the coolest, most awesomest country in the Universe ever. Me and my friends crashed there for like some time and we had such a bomb time getting to know the rad Utopians and how they did what they did, the way they lived and cool shit like that. The things they do are like soooo different from what the rest of us are used to! Oh like, for example, did you know the Utopians don't, like, own stuff? Like, they LITERALLY don't own shit, they share everything. Every single thing. You might think that's kinda sad and shitty but you'd be surprised how many problems getting rid of private property and money and things like that can solve! They like, don't have anything to worry about when they don't have anything in the first place to worry about, you know what I mean? 
 And oh my god, like the Utopians have this crazy tradition of eating together in a communal way. Like, it's totes similar to a boarding school or something. Everyone eats together and instead of prayers, the old people at the table, they like talk about wise things, and shit like that to the kids so they grow up just like them. And they try to let the kids know how, like, gold and money and all those bling-bling are actually worthless. Oh man, listen, this is gonna sound batshit crazy to you but it's true - the Utopians make their toilet out of gold. I kid you not, they make golden toilets. And it's not a metaphor, I checked off 'Shit on gold' on my list when I was in Utopia. That's how they teach the people not to put too much value on glitter, you know, it's mad but it's cool too, know what I mean? 
 I'm telling you, dude, Utopia's the shit. You should go check it out. Matter of fact, the rest of the world should go check it out and learn a thing or two. They've got cuckoo stuff going on like shit pots made of gold and getting girls and boys to look at each other naked before they get married so that no weird surprise presents itself when they're on their honeymoon, you know? *nudge nudge, wink wink* But it's mad cool, ya dig? 
 Kthanksbye."

reference_books.title: The Spirit Catches You and You Fall Down: A Hmong Child, Her American Doctors, and the Collision of Two Cultures
reference_books.review_text: I was not expecting to be drawn in as much as I was by this book, being primarily a medical account of a Hmong child and her family's travails in dealing with the Western doctors in California and the cultural chasms that make it difficult for both sides with the little girl suffering its consequences. But I found it to be a very moving, heartbreaking story that every cultural or religious minority living in the West could relate to in some ways. But it is first and foremost, I think, a testament to parental love. It was truly amazing to learn that Lia Lee lived for as long as she did in her vegetative condition, and that she died only a few months ago, a month before I started this book actually. It is a great book in short. And very well written as well. Something everyone in the medical field should try to read for a better understanding of the significance of culture and religion.
