book_a.title: Bring Up the Bodies (Thomas Cromwell, #2)
book_a.user_review:
Thoughts: 
 - Oh to be a woman in the royal Tudor court and inadvertently catch the fancy of the mercurial, murderous king. You'd think you were the most fortunate of women at first, but after marriages number 1, 2 and 3, I would expect no sane woman to wish to even pass across Henry's line of vision, even by mistake. 
 "Queen? No thanks. I prefer my head on my shoulders. What's a crown sans tete, AMIRITE?" 
 - I've read a lot of reviews that say the same; the last pages of Bring Up the Bodies are so very good, they're the kind that makes your breath run faster, shallower, even if you know what to anticipate. The way Cromwell gets to each of the condemned persons, ticking off each enemy of his previous master as he goes, to the last few pages that see Anne Boleyn, for whose favour the whole of England was compromised, is killed, the pages claim your entire attention. 
 - So, Mantel should be tried for witchcraft. Because of her writing. It's too well done. Oh okay, it's because she turned me into a newt. I just got better. 
 - So many good metaphors. So many excellent lines, paragraphs. Like this one that closes the book; 
 "There are no endings. If you think so you are deceived as to their nature. They are all beginnings. Here is one."

sample_reviews.review_text: I'm not a huge fan of historical fiction, but this is about as good as it gets. Mantel began her account of the (almost) incredible saga of Henry VIII and his parade of wives with "Wolf Hall," and while I found that hard going at times, it was hard to resist the way Mantel imagined conversations that sound exactly like what would have taken place. That craft is even more in evidence in this one (the second of a planned trilogy). We get it all here--Henry's massive ego, which demands a male heir that none of this wives can seem to produce; the heightened political maneuvering of his circle of confidantes and aides, all more than aware that any perceived misplaced allegiance could cost them their heads; and the sorry lot of the women themselves. In this one, Katharine of Aragon dies in disgrace and exile; Anne Boleyn struggles against her fall from favor, and Jane Seymour resigns herself to the fate of becoming the next in line. It's all high-class soap opera, sweetened by Mantel's prose and the realization that it is all completely true.
Meh!

i really really like this writing, though i know it is maybe not for everyone; also, know the next volume covers seymour to cromwell's execution, but i'd love to know more about his early days in venice and the low countries; his remeniscences are some of the most interesting parts to me 
 haven't read anything else by mantel (besides wolf hall) and i'm pretty sure it's very different style and tone but will definitely pick up some of her other work because this is how it's done
Imagine you are Thomas Cromwell .Set in the Tudor era.Live through the politics of what everyone is thinking and doing !

Same problem as Wolf Hall. Dull writing throughout. Very workaday stuff that anyone would find in a national newspaper. Story may be good but the quality of writing on display was not high, or deliberately set at a mediocre level.

Second book in the series by Hilary Mantel (of course I never read the first one, because that is how I roll) around King Henry VIII and his court. This book takes the story up from when Katherine is in prison, the new Queen, Anne, has officially taken over the throne and all the trappings...and has yet to provide the one thing the King asks: a son. 
 Told through the viewpoint of William Cromwell, King Henry's go-to man, Mantel weaves a good picture of how the politics of the day were used to push Henry's agenda through. The current agenda, to kill his second wife, and annul the marriage (best to leave no questions of who should be next on the throne, those silly silly daughters he keeps having). Cromwell is up for the task. 
 I'm not a huge historical fiction person--and I have a hard time when real people are given a primary place in a fiction novel (how do we know they would say that phrase?). But overall a good read. Historical fiction readers will eat this up and ask for more.

A dangerous confusion of historical fact and fiction. I found it difficult to get into due to the odd style of writing, but once I persuaded myself that 'he' is almost always the voice of Thomas Cromwell, it became easier. It is about his character and influence, as affected by his upbringing. It was obviously very easy in those days to become convicted on a whim or a rumour and the book conveys this readily . There is a powerful acceleration at the end (the executions ) and overall, the book left me with a feeling of more insight into a black area of or history. But is it true or false, this is the dangerous confusion.

I was SHOCKED that I liked this sequel even MORE than Wolf Hall... Perhaps it's just because this period is about the fall of Anne Boleyn which is full of drama, but I also found Cromwell more engaging and relatable in this book. If you have ANY interest in the time period, do not miss this spellbinding read.
I usually like books about the Henry XIII era, but even though this one is well-written it's pretty slow moving.

Solid, extremely well done follow up to Wolf Hall. Excellent for the gray-ish, near winter sort of weather. Covers 8 months leading up to Anne Boleyn's execution from the main POV of Thomas Cromwell. 
 Completely unrelated, I wonder how annoyed Thomas Cromwell would have been if people tried to call him Tommy. Or Tom-Tom. Tom-Tom Cromwell. Ok I'm done.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I thoroughly enjoyed this book. I can see what all the hype is about. It was truly amazing. It did take me a liitle long to finish it because it is my first adult novel and it is a little tougher to read than a young adult. 
 The story line is very unique and extremely unpredictable. I absolutely loved it and I can't wait to read the next on.

I have never read high or epic fantasy like this before. 
 When I started to read this, a lot of friends responded with, "I'm sorry." Their main reason, apparently, was Martin's brutality toward his own characters; a LOT of people die. However, I'd already seen the whole first season of the HBO show, so I was prepared for all the deaths, and STILL wanted to read the book... so I knew that, while it was still going to hurt, it would be worth it. I did genuinely love it. 
 Martin does not go the route that contemporary fantasy authors go; there are no knights in shining armor, there are no true heroes who always win. Shit happens. Sometimes evil wins over good. The fact of the matter is that he does not pull his punches, things happen realistically because his characters are crafted like real people, not tropes painted on cardboard cut-outs. 
 His characters are lovely; his setting superbly crafted; his battle scenes do not make you want to skip over reading them. This is by far one of the best books I have ever read.

This book is a classic of high fantasy literature. There's not much I can say about it that hasn't been said already. I was moved to buy this book, and the other three books in this series, by watching the HBO series upon which it is based. (Yes, I know, there is a fifth book out now. I will probably buy it when I'm done with these.) 
 In this first book of the Song of Fire and Ice series we meet all the major factions in the coming succession war in the Seven Kingdoms. The Starks are the lords of Winterfell who command the entire northern half of the realm. The Lannisters, the wealthiest, and most devious, of the great houses. The Baratheons, who hold the Iron Throne as the book opens, now must defend their claim. Meanwhile, beyond The Wall, a great barrier of ice built by the First Men to keep the terrors of Winter at bay, the Others are stirring once again. Also, across the narrow sea the last remaining heir of the Targaryons, deposed ruling house of the Seven Kingdoms, marshals the Dothraki barbarians in a bid to regain what was taken from them by the usurper Baratheons. 
 There can be no doubt, Mr. Martin is a master of his genre. His characters are memorable and readily identifiable. His descriptive world building passages are particularly effective and evocative. The battle scenes are entirely convincing. (I most enjoyed witnessing the fog of war through Tyrion's eyes.) 
 One thing I did find rather unique about this book was the very low key nature of the magical elements. There were no super powerful wizards/sorceresses, no flashy spells and little by way of fantastical creatures. There were hints of more to come, but that was all, just hints. This is not necessarily a bad thing. It simply sets this series apart from many others in the Fantasy genre. I have a feeling, though, that as things ramp up in the next few books, there will be more magical happenings.

I can't put to words what I felt when I was reading this book, but I can tell you that what you've seen on the TV adaptation of this marvelous novel is exquisitely true-to-the-book. 
 Ok, I guess somehow I have to say a little something about this read. First of all, this is an epic fantasy book. I can't fathom Martin's imagination; zombies, frozen wastelands, a cunning queen with a cruel son, a twisted plot, a smart dwarf, a young fighter, dragons; everything's here. Though it's a long read and it will really take all your time to finish through the end, it is worth it. 
 I especially love Daenerys' flow of story. Every time I near through the end of a character's POV, I almost always wish that it's Daenerys' turn. I love how her life turned upside down. She's becoming stronger as each page past, even Viserys can't contain how huge her authority had grown. I was just saddened that Drogo had that fate (though I already knew what will happen). She's my favorite character in the book. 
 Another character I fancy is Tyrion Lannister, the imp. He's wise and can't be fooled and those are the features that make him stand out. I adored the moment when he was about to be executed on the Eyrie by Lysa. Thinking about that trial by combat - wow. I look forward for more interesting scenes of Tyrion when I read the second book soon. 
 Although Arya is headstrong and naughty, I also liked her character, because unlike Sansa, her eyes weren't blinded by the truth. She was smart, too, having to escape the castle when Lord Eddard was captured by Lannister men. 
 Overall, the flow of the book wasn't confusing at all. It was well written and the story was just divine. It's a masterpiece that the author should be really proud of. I can't wait to read the second book, A Clash of Kings, and I can't wait for the season 3 of its TV adaptation. 
 This is seriously a 5 out of 5 stars for me.

"When you play a game of thrones you win or you die." -- Cersei Lannister 
 I read the series before there was a TV-show and I loved the story. I think there are many great things about the A Song of Ice and Fire series. But since this review should be about A Game of Thrones, I've narrowed it down to these: 
 1. The world-building is great. Westeros is kind of based on the medieval times, and that may be a little predictable in epic fantasy ... BUT, the world of Essos is amazing! I love the Dothraki and their culture. The kind of simple, dark, gritty lives they live was very compelling to read. 
 2. The language is masterful, beautiful, effortless to read. 
 3. There is a great deal of political shit in this book, which is pretty much like the politics in our own world (perhaps without all the killing...) and that's actually one of the reasons I like the story. It's all about being a master-manipulator, and whomever is best is probably the one that will survive the longest. And all the manipulations going on, it's just great entertainment! 
 4. The shock-value! You never know what's going to happen. Seriously! And that's why I fucking love it!! 
 5. Even the most unlikely person can gain power, which only adds to my testament in the previous point. 
 6. Tyrion! He is, seriously, the funniest character in this book, and he alone is a reason why everyone should read this book! 
 7. Dragons! Do I really have to add anything to that?

The trees pressed close and shut out the light of the setting sun. A thin crust of snow cracked beneath the hooves of their horses, with a sound like breaking bones. When the wind set the leaves to rustling, it was like a chilly finger tracing a path up Jon's spine. The wall was at their backs, and only the gods knew what lay ahead."

I read about 30 pages of this like a year ago and hated it because I thought it was a rip off of Lord of the Rings. Martin's writing style is pretty similar to Tolkien's but I'm glad I gave this book a second chance. It was pretty amazing.
I said earlier that I was not likely to read the rest of the books in this series. Yeah, um, about that......

There was nothing original that stood out in this book. Everything was oversexed and unpleasantly obnoxious. I understand that sex will always be a part of anything, but that doesn't mean that every two pages some old wheezy slimebag has to start fingering little girls. But ugh if I sat here and talked about everything I detested in this book, I'd be here until next year. 
 However, I would not be honest if I wasn't being just a little sarcastic. There were parts of the book that I really enjoyed. Martin does a good job of building some entertaining characters, and that's hard to do, so kudos to him. The world he crafted is not without its intrigue. Some of the fight scenes are pretty cool, and the whole bizarreness o Dany was what really kept me reading despite my overall negative attitude towards this text. 
 I was somewhat disappointed, yes, but there are worse things out there. I have low expectations for the rest of the series, but we shall see.

book_a.title: Looking for Alaska
book_a.user_review: This book truly touched my heart and I think everyone should read it. John Green has a way of getting you attached to the characters and making each one of them have their own special characteristics. Yes, the book is sad but it was an utterly wonderful story.

sample_reviews.review_text: The Fault in Our Stars (which I loved) transcended the conventions of the angsty teen story as well as the cancer love story. This didn't transcend anything. The whole book felt like it was written overnight. The characters fall flat, the plot does not rise above its premise, and I guess I just didn't care about anything that happened. Now there are moments that do shine here or there where John Green shows promise (which he has further developed at this point in his career). There are some great passages, strongly executed scenes, and some interesting plotting, but for me it felt vastly overshadowed by the overly angsty teens and cliche dialogue and characterization. There are some strong similarities between this and TFIOS, and he pulls them off much better in that novel than in Looking for Alaska. Read The Fault in Our Stars first, or else the aftertaste of this commendable but underdone novel might take away some of that magic.

Although I enjoy John Green's writing, this book reminded me too much of "Paper Towns". I thought that the character development of Alaska could have been better, and I wish the ending were different.

This is probably a great book, but I just couldn't see it. 
 Miles is a junior in his first year at Culver Creek High School in Alabama, following in the footsteps of his father who graduated from there. Miles has a unique hobby--memorizing the final words of famous people--and in the words of Francois Rabelais, he is off "to seek a great perhaps." Miles' roommate, Chip "the Colonel", introduces Miles to his nickname (Pudge), and his friends Alaska and Takumi. From the start, Miles is obsessed with Alaska, who reads biographies and is searching for the meaning of Simon Bolivar's last words: "Damn it! How will I ever get out of this labyrinth!" In true boarding school fashion, Miles finds himself caught up in drama and escalating pranks that resulted from Alaska reporting on an incident that contributed to the expulsion of another student. Miles and the reader find that Alaska is emotionally unstable, which drives the plot of the rest of the book. 
 I wanted to love this book but I couldn't. First, I did not like the characters: Miles reminded me of the famous literary whiner Holden Caulfield, moping about his situation rather than seeking to remedy it, a character who let others propel him forward. Alaska was damaged, yes, and I felt pity for her, but she did nothing to help herself that I could see. Seeing her through Miles eyes, we are presented with just another hot girl with emotional problems. Second, the story seemed campy to me. Right away, what impressed me about The Fault in Our Stars was the stark truth of the story he was telling--there was no sugar coating. While there was no sugar coating of the events in this novel either, the story seemed to take boarding school tropes (drinking, pranks, cliques, sex, etc.) to tell the same story you always read. 
 That being said, Green's writing style did not disappoint. Unfortunately, that wasn't enough to keep me engaged enough to care about Miles and his friends.

I simply love this. I may be a nerdfighter but I know that even if I'm not I will still love this book. Finished it in just one sitting, and it was just made of awesome. The characters are real, pure and raw. It shows that no one, really, is ever perfect. The hero himself is not at all perfect. All those REAL teenage issues where tackled as it is with a twist here and there, that happens in real time. Losing your innocence and realizing that it's not half-bad even if it is really bad. 
 Escape from the labyrinth. It's all about that. But in it's own accord, it is indeed full of methods of how to escape even though it clearly states that the characters where all seeking it until the very end. 
 The ending was unexpected, the climax was unbelievable. A conflict that you will never, ever expect in a genre like this. It's unbelievable. Love Green's imagination, reality from his view is very compelling. The smoke will definitely get in your eyes. A must-read.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This book was a good blend of hilarity and seriousness. I like that about John Green's novels-like the old TV show MASH. Anywho, this is the 2nd books of Mr. Green's that I have read and when I started it, I figured that it was going to be pretty much the same as Paper Towns. A boy likes a girl. The girl is mysterious and unattainable. Yada yada yada... been there done that. And the book kinda is a 'been there, done that,' age-old story, but there is something special in the characters, especially in the "After" part of the book. It took me a while to read this book because 1. it was my book I carry around to read in spare moments and 2. I was reading other books at the same time which, well frankly, were just more captivating (and belonged to the library). I think that once I got to the end of "before" I really began to relate a little more to the story. There was a kid in my high school who died in a car accident. I'm pretty sure it was not due to intoxication, if it was they didn't tell us. I didn't actually know the boy, I was a grade ahead of him, and honestly didn't socialise much. I was surprisingly more affected by his death than I thought I would be. On a completely different note: OMG! a stripper! ha ha that was amazing! I was laughing so hard while I read. Anyway bottom line: good book, bit predictable, very interesting, and looking forward to reading more John Green books, especially Will Grayson, Will Grayson.

When sixteen year old Miles Halter leaves his home to go to a boarding school in Birmingham, Alabama he had no idea how his life would change. He left a minor life in Florida, one that had little friends and little significance.... Miles own words. He first meets his roommate Chip who what he lacks in statute he makes up for in attitude. Instantly Miles is dubbed the nickname "Pudge" even though he is quite the opposite and Chip asks to be called Colonel. While things seem to be off to a good start in Miles, errr... Pudge's new adventure, he was unprepared to meet Chips, best friend Alaska Young. 
 Alaska is a free spirit, she is smart, beautiful, witty and reckless. She has books everywhere called her life books, the books she hopes to read in her life time. She smokes on campus which is strictly taboo, and drinks in her room long after lights out. Miles is instantly infatuated with all that she is. 
 That was 136 days before.... 
 In Looking For Alaska, Miles is looking for something more. He is a huge fan of "famous last words" and wants to make sure his own life has some sort of significance worthy of his own last words. 
 I am stopping here to say, I really like Miles. He is just the level of geek that I can appreciate because I am one too. He is looking for the meaning of his life, in fact, due to an assignment he is given by a teacher regarding the after life, this is a small background theme in the book, so small and smoke screen like, you can easily miss that it is there at all. 
 Anyhoo.... as much as I enjoyed Miles/Pudge's straight-laced life.... I just as much enjoyed Alaska's free will "lets try anything" attitude. I think... some of both live in me. 
 As you may have picked up, our story starts out 136 days before. You may be wondering "before what?" and that... I can not share as that is really a huge part of the story... as the book counts down, you can have a sense of the foreboding... what are we counting down to. Is it good? Is it bad? What happens at day 0? Is there an after? That is the beauty of John Green. 
 I loved this book on audio. The narration by Jeff Woodman was good.... really good and captures the teen voices well. 
 I really enjoyed this book and had a hard time shutting it off as I wondered what would happen and where do they go from there? I highly count this read/audio as gush worthy and recommend if you have not yet experienced the greatness of John Green please do so soon so you can gush with me.... we will chat on-line, drink coffee or iced tea and gush Green!

First of all, may I say, John Green is my favourite author. Every book he writes, it has a meaning to it. A point. I love his books, they always make my day better with his truthful, influential words for readers to remember and share. 
 Looking For Alaska was.. I'm speechless here. It was stunningly, fantasticly, PERFECT! I can drone on and on about how much I love it, but I won't. The plot, characters and meaning were astonishing. From Miles' point of view, everything seemed to have its ups and downs, but he was smart enough to fight them and look beyond the clouds. 
 Alaska. Alaska Young was a perfect female heroine. She's sexy, in her own way, funny, clever, and different. You can see her bright side of things, and with her bad girl style, makes readers feel even more connected to her. I couldn't believe it when what happened to her happened, and her story is a mystery for readers to overcome. 
 Miles/Pudge. Miles was different, in a great way. I loved him, with his awkwardness, that shone to impress readers with his love for Alaska, and for his passion for finding the ladybrinth of life. He got his girl, in a way, and didn't need help to find what he wants in reality. 
 Overall, Looking For Alaska changed my life, as well as The Fault In Our Stars. I learnt that you need to find out what life has in store for you, and we have to enjoy things while they last. 
 Thank you, John Green, for writing this book. You are my inspiration. -Michelle
loved this book!

I am majorly disappointed in this book. I liked Green's novel, The Fault in Our Stars so was excited to read Looking For Alaska. I started reading and I just had to put it down. It was immensely boring and had to stop half way through because the storyline was dreadful.

John Green has once again taken me away with his words. Looking for Alaska is beautifully sad and humorous. its set in a boarding school, we get to see the world through this average boy (Miles/Pudge) eyes. the nicknames they all give each other a great i love how they reflect each character. Alaska and the others changes the way he view things, he opens up more about his quirks and he remains me of Charlie from the perks of being a wallflower. Looking for Alaska is personally my favorite john green book. It talks about real problems that everyday teen go though. The context may be a little mature for younger teens but its realistic and honest and i don't think you should stop young teens from reading this. i love Alaska and everything she stands for, its strange how much i related to her, i really liked the idea of the labyrinth and how their may never be no escape but we have to keep moving. i especially love that the book continues, it doesn't just stop because of one event (no spoilers) it keeps going just like life.

sample_reviews.review_text: Very topical subject matter win all the incidents of racial shootings lately in the media. Told from multiple perspectives, friends, alleged gang members, witnesses, and family members, what exactly happened to the victim seems to keep changing. Much like real life where there are so many sides to a story. Interesting book, really enjoyed it.

Okay, so here's the plan: Let's give this one and Lies We Tell Ourselves Printz awards or honours or whatever, and fuck every other book in the universe. 
 No, seriously, this book is awesome. A devourable book, with complex characters and a ripped-from-the-headlines storyline that never feels forced. Kekla Magoon effortlessly sets up a dozen inconsistent narratives and gives each of them the life necessary to be believable explanations for how it went down...if only there weren't all the other affected parties to consider. The real heartbreakers are Vernesha, Redeema, and Tina, Tariq's mother, grandmother, and baby sister, but there wasn't a single voice I disliked. Every character has an interesting angle on the two enigmatic figures at the center of the shooting of Tariq Johnson, as well as the culture that made his death possible. 
 The only reason I'm not giving it five stars is...well, kind of petty, but here goes. I was really thinking that either Tyrell or Jennica was going to end up not being straight. I was disappointed that it wasn't the case for either of them--or anyone else in this book. You can definitely read both of them as potentially super closeted, but it's subtext at best, and some of the actual text disagrees with it. I guess I shouldn't have gotten my hopes up, but right to the end, I was hoping Magoon was going in that direction. No dice.

This book felt about ten thousand pages long. 
 There were WAY too many alternating perspectives, and I couldn't keep any of the characters straight in my mind. 
 Interesting subject matter somehow became an incredibly dull book.

I could immediately tell that the author, Kekla Magoon, was very influenced by the events surrounding Trayvon Martin's death, too many overlaps with his death to dispute this. This fictional tale of Tariq Johnson's death, of the many perspectives of those who see the event and those who are impacted by it, of the wider impact brought about by the national media. It's a hard story - one without clear right and wrong, good and bad, truth and lies. The reader is forced to grapple with the fact that he or she might never know the full story. Sure, the reader can see how it went down in that particular moment but even that moment is fuzzy depending on whose perspective, whose lens you're looking through. 
 Stylistically, I wondered if it would be difficult to follow the various perspectives that Magoon uses to tell this story. There are more than 20 different voices. But, Magoon accomplishes this task rather seamlessly. The short snippets quickly introduced me to each character and it was easy to distinguish one voice from the next when I continued reading. 
 I found this to be one of my best reads of this year. My country, the USA, is desperately struggling with issues of race, of the power and purpose of police, and of media involvement in traumatic events. It's going to be a book that I recommend to students as well as to my own peers, no matter nationality.

Someone needs to explain to me why this book is getting all the buzz it is. Other than a book that might work as a great spark for discussion in a classroom, I didn't find it buzz-worthy. Just average.

Definitely an interesting & current concept for a book. My biggest issue with this book was the amount of characters. A multi-layered account of an incident that is all too common, and all too tragic nowadays..My Urban Fiction requirement and a story that is loosely and very closely based on the sad Trayvon Martin shooting where an unarmed black youth was killed by an armed white man and ends up getting off with no punishment. Questions and perspectives come up in this book through everyone's point of view and opinions and thoughts on the victim: sixteen year old Tariq. Every other page or so and rather disjointedly and kinda confusingly a new voice is introduced from eyewitnesses, people directly involved, the clerk at the last store he visited, his family: mom, sister, grandmother, neighbors, those who loved and hated him and others indirectly affected by the tragedy that shakes their community. With so many conflicting sides of this one boy what was the truth--did he actually have a gun and does it matter?--was he a gang member and if he was does that matter? How should you feel about a boy shot down in the street who may or may not have had a gun with no real criminal past and how does the community heal from senseless tragedies like this whose effects resonate far beyond the shooter and victim...One of the most interesting points of view was from a minister seeking political gain who travels to the community to shed attention on their tragedy and while there reflecting on his purpose, his wish for a national situation and regret on having brought so much media to their grief. This book ends sadly like many other stories in the news highlighted by the BLM (Black Lives Matter Movement) whose names and sad stories we now know, whose protests and movements we have joined and watched online but whose lives never get the validation or vindication they deserve as there was never any punishment for their murderers and the ending of a life just swept under the evil rug of hidden racism, systematized poverty and despair from the oppressed. Life is hard and not being heard or understood is just another stigma young African American youths must bear as they travel through life prejudged and presumed to be violent and destructive..Realistic look at a community's response to violence and cautionary tale for those who think that life goes on after a child is murdered in the street.
Timely and well-written. A powerful story for many marginalized voices.

Moderately paced urban tale about the events surrounding the shooting of a unarmed young black man by a white man who thought (of course!) that the Snickers bar he carried in his pocket was a gun. It's a powerful and relevant story, and the two stars I'm giving it have nothing to do with its message or its sense of importance in today's society. 
 I just didn't like the way this story was written. There are too many perspectives (the victim, the shooter, the shooter's friend, bystanders, the victim's family members, the victim's friends, a minister, etc) ---everybody has a 'say' in this story and it was far too confusing for me to keep track of who is saying or doing what. There are labels at the top of each section before each character speaks, but with over a dozen people 'speaking,' it was just too much. About a third of the way in I tossed my hands in the air and didn't finish. Would not recommend.

There are those who dislike violence for teens but in order to challenge the mind strong actions and extreme behaviors are needed. It's the role of a good smart science fiction story and there is no better audience then our modern teens overexposed to meaningless violence stories on screen. This book has also a male central character, which is good after all the teen female leads. The subject is hard, thee was a chapter that was very difficult for me to read/listen but the story is great. Special thanks to our dedicated librarian for her recommendation. The biggest problem I had with When Day Breaks is the almost total lack of action and suspense that made the first four KGI books great and the next four tolerable. It was a brilliant move pairing Swanny, scars and baggage and all, with a world-famous supermodel, but other than Swanny's insecurity about his body and Eden's constant attempts to cure him of that, we don't get any romantic growth from them. It's an insta-love situation drowning in melodrama. There's no suspense, no building, and not really any opposition from anyone or anything until the very end. 
 When I found out that Swanny was getting his own story, I was so excited. I've had a crush on him since we first met him and Nathan in that cave in Afghanistan. Swanny's quiet, reserved, and contemplative--which if you've read any KGI or even any romantic suspense, you'll find is a pretty rare breed of hero. But throughout the story, Swanny's pensive moments were dragged out and repetitive. I don't mind characters constantly being lost in thought, but when it's about the same few things over and over again, it gets old pretty fast. And it wasn't just the moments lost in thought--so much got repeated and re-summarized and restated when it was already obvious that I started skimming whole pages. 
 One reason Nathan's story (Whispers in the Dark) worked so well for me was because Banks imbued the writing with his frustrations and setbacks while recovering from the torture and imprisonment he and Swanny faced. Even though in When Day Breaks we're told that Swanny is still fighting the night terrors and anxiety, we never see any of his struggle on the page, so changes that could've been really moving and meaningful--Swanny's ability to sleep when he was with Eden, not averting the scarred side of his face around her, his growing confidence--fell flat. 
 Honestly, I probably wouldn't have finished reading When Day Breaks if I'd had it in ebook, but since I have the rest of the KGI series in physical book form, I bought the paperback to finish off the collection. I'll probably give the next KGI book a chance (especially if it turns out to be Joe's story)--I've come this far and there's always the hope that the quality of writing will spike back up to what Banks started out the series with--but I'll be going into the next book pretty skeptical.
