reference_books.title: Chess Story
reference_books.review_text:
This is one of those wonderful little books by authors who make you think, like D.H. Lawrence, Tolstoy, Twain, and others. It's a story within a story, with the narrator the link between the two. 
 Zweig begins with an ocean voyage from New York to Buenos Aires and his discovery that the world champion chess player is on board. The man is notorious for his abrasive behavior to people, not least of all his opponents. The narrator hopes to entice him into one game during the voyage. To do so, he and his wife set up the chess board and play (badly). The champion sees them, but doesn't stop. The narrator won't give up and finds others on the voyage who also play. When he mentions to one, a rather strident personality, that the chess champion is on board, that gentleman determines he will do whatever it takes to get the champion to play. 
 The real story is Dr. B and his detention during WWII. As part of a rather clandestine law firm in Vienna, which quietly took care of business for the royal family and the church, Dr. B is swept up when Austria is "annexed" to Germany. Because he is not a criminal as such, nor a Jew, or any of the common categories, he is put in seclusion in a hotel room. There is nothing there but furniture: no pens, paper, newspapers, books. All day and all night, he suffers. No stimulation at all. No talking. No reading. No scribbling. No stinking cell, but he begins to be jealous of anyone who might be in a concentration camp instead. At least they see a variety of things during the day. Ever so often he is taken out for interrogation. He is never physically tortured. But the agony of the solitude eats at him. 
 One day while he is waiting to be called into the interrogation room, he notices that the pocket on one of the coats the officers hang in the anteroom has a bulge in it. A book!!!!! He manages to extract the book and successfully conceal it through the interview and back to the room. He takes his time to discover what it actually is - a novel? a romance? a book of poetry? philosopy? history? 
 When he finally looks, he is stunned. It's a book of 50 chess games by champion chessplayers. He has never been interested in chess. But it gives him stimulation. So he begins to teach himself the notations and the moves behind them, first using his checkered bedspread and "chessmen" made of bread crumbs from his meals and ultimately in his head. Eventually he can play every game through in his head alone. 
 When that is no longer stimulation enough, he begins to play games against himself. He divides himself into a Mr. Black and a Mr. White and mentally visualizes himself stepping around the chessboard as each side plays. He becomes so entangled in this mental world that, when the Germans release him because of the occupation of Czechoslovakia, he needs to spend time in a mental hospital before he can return home. 
 He is now going to Buenos Aires and sees a game between the chess champion and the rest of the chess players. (Rather than playing individual simultaneous games, the champion has allowed the other players to agree on a move and play him as a team). Can he resist? Can he actually play on a board since he has always played in his head? Would he know what to do? 
 It sounds simple but it isn't. The characters are well drawn: the champion is more or less an idiot savant - he was taken in as an orphan and literally could not learn anything. It was amazing to the clergyman who took him in that he had a talent for chess and that after only ever watching games. McConnor, the man who decides that he will do anything to draw the champion into a game, is a sort of blustery British colonial officer. The narrator is invisible, only the conduit through which the story is told. 
 There is no O.Henry here or Roald Dahl where the ending is surprising and unsuspected. It's very quiet. 
 "'Pity,' [the chess champion] said generously. 'The attack was not at all poorly conceived. For am amateur, this gentleman is really extraordinarily talented.'" 
 And the story grows on you. It's one of those.

reference_books.title: Batman: The Dark Knight Returns (The Dark Knight Saga, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I really expected to like this since I like Batman and the Dark Knight series. But something didn't sit right with this one. I had trouble following the panels and it almost seemed in the chapters that pages had been left out because I couldn't figure out why the next page started like it did. 
 I like noir but his didn't seem noir, it seemed just plain black. The actions didn't always make sense to me, I felt that the Harvey Dent subplot was not completed and that the Joker subplot did not show the true sneakiness of that villain. The addition of a young girl as the new Robin was good and I did enjoy Batman trying to understand the younger generation's proficiency in technology. 
 But overall, it just didn't seem to me the polished work that I expect from Frank Miller. 
 If you enjoy the Dark Knight series, you should certainly read this. Perhaps you will get more out of it than I did.

reference_books.title: Where'd You Go, Bernadette
reference_books.review_text:
I was looking forward to this book and its "critique" of Seattle. The critique turned out to be only partly "right." And the characters and the plot weren't really good enough to hold my interest. 
 Three women are leading stupid lives and finally come to realize it. I know you're not supposed to judge other people, but I had a hard time getting interested in these women's lives. Not that I haven't done stupid things myself, but I haven't strung them together to form a lifestyle like they do. 
 Part of the problem is that Semple doesn't draw a good picture of her main character, Bernadette. We see her past success as an architect and the personality traits that will guide the rest of the plot are touched on but not brought out enough. Much of the book consists of emails, documents, etc. that her daughter has collected to try to understand why her mother disappeared and where she might be. 
 And boy does Bernadette have reason to leave. First of all, she has neglected the house they live in. It was a former "girls' school" - read unwed mothers' home - and had been badly kept up before they bought it. Due to several miscarriages, Bernadette has lost interest in her architecture and quits doing any work on it. She's become agorophobic. She doesn't get along with the neighbors and manages to nearly destroy a neighbor's house in a fit of pique. But worst of all, she has given nearly all the family's financial information to a scam run by the Russian mafia. 
 Her husband, a Microsoft genius, and her daughter are sympathetic characters. But I didn't find the rest of the cast of characters so. None of them were really developed well enough to determine whether they SHOULD be sympathized with. 
 The one thing I liked VERY much was the near destruction of the neighbor's house. The neighbor has demanded that Bernadette remove the blackberry bushes from the hill next to the neighbor's house. So she does. Bernadette then has a huge 8ft. sign made and placed right next to the boundary line. During a brunch to encourage new enrollments to the school both women's children attend, a rainstorm causes a mudslide (remember, all the blackberry bushes have been removed from that hill......) and carries the sign right smack into the house. 
 Now that part wasn't what I really enjoyed. It was the reaction afterwards. The two kindergarden classes from the school were on site to play marimbas as entertainment and, of course, they got muddified and had to run from the falling wall. HOWEVER, none of the children showed any signs of distress over it. HOWEVER, one of the attendees from the school was a counselor with Swedish Medical and she sends what must have been a three-page letter to the parents of the kindergardners describing the complete incident and warning them to watch for signs of PTSD, which may not appears for years yet, but could still be connected with this incident. She explains how she triend very must to "listen, express curiosity, and simply 'be' with each child" and observe them for symptoms. At the end of the letter she expresses that she thinks that some sort of forum - entire school, kindergarden only, or parents only - should be held to "process this traumatic event." 
 THAT'S what gets me most about Seattle. People here (and I suppose I should include myself but I'm not this way) are WAY too sensitive to what might possibly make another person or group upset. (I won't get started on this because I'll never stop.) 
 The novel I was promised in the writeups and reviews just wasn't here. And although I can usually say of a book I didn't particularly like that it's still worth reading, I can't say that in this case....

reference_books.title: A Game of Thrones (A Song of Ice and Fire, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I don't like fantasy. Let me repeat that. I don't like fantasy. But I LOVE this book! I really don't like to put it in the fantasy category, but I guess it belongs there if that is where Lord of the Rings is shelved. 
 I'm on my second time through. After watching the first season of the HBO series (we don't have cable TV, so I had to wait), I decided to go back and re-read GOT. I'm catching SO much more this time and I'm sure I'll catch more every time I read it. To me, that is the sign of a fantastic book. 
 Sure, there are fantasy creatures beyond The Wall and across the Narrow Sea, but the characters do not interact with them like Tolkein's hobbits, dwarves and so on. They WILL interact at later times (real dragons are hatched from supposedly petrified eggs that had been given to a woman of the Dragon clan), but the focus is not on that interaction. It's on the development of the characters. As the book progresses you find that Martin allows characters to develop, sometimes even change gears. He also believes in real life, not fantasy life. As one of the characters from the HBO series said in an interview "just when you think you have it figured out, it changes!" Villains have good sides, virtuous people do not always flourish, people are as blind to obvious clues as we are. 
 This IS a book to read again, and again. It's as complex as real life and just as easy to get lost in.

reference_books.title: Wayward (Wayward Pines, #2)
reference_books.review_text: I liked this book in the series better than the first one. The action seemed to move better, the plot hung together better and the twists and turns twisted and turned better. It makes me glad that I didn't give up after the first book. Crouch has also introduced a couple of complications that I'm really looking forward "resolving" in the next part.

book_a.title: The Possessed: Adventures With Russian Books and the People Who Read Them
book_a.user_review: I was expecting more on the people who read Russian books, not realizing Batuman was going to talk about academics. It does have some interesting autobiographical parts to it. Plus the fact that, instead of cats to keep the rodents down, Tolstoy used snakes!

sample_reviews.review_text: Read about 50 pages and I couldn't get into it. The writing was OK, but the subject wasn't that interesting. Definitely did not match the fun cover!

Nancy Pearl recommendation: 
 http://www.npr.org/templates/story/st... 
 OK, I did not actually read it. I could not even get through the introduction. You must feel passionately about Russian literature to appreciate this treatment of it. 
 I credit Batuman with that passion. Good luck with that.

This is one of those baffling books that one just doesn't know what to do with. The prose is engaging and the author's voice is funny, yet I just couldn't enjoy this. 
 I think it's because it was mis-sold to me and the subject is just a little too specified to really pounce on. Lots of people read books by Russian writers, but that in itself does not a book make. Rather than telling the story of fans of such novels, as I had originally assumed, Possessed rambles through vignettes of the author's life, smatterings of facts about each author, long soliloquies on grad school, and on and on and on... 
 It does a disservice to Bautman to complain so much, because I really do think she's a fine writer and could be a fabulous one - with a different subject. I hope she changes gears and gets on something else!

Fantastic. Especially the first half which induced in me a sustained sense of surrealism. At times laugh out loud funny, with very well written prose and a surprising number of thoughtful insights sprinkled throughout.

An excellent and highly readable mash-up of the author's experience reading Russian books, and living in the area studying them. Her stories of living in Uzbekistan are particularly interesting, though perhaps just because one doesn't read much about day-to-day life in that country. Anyway! The book wants to be many things-a memoir of trying to find beauty, a history of Russian literature, and a critique of the same-and thus it can be unfocused. One minute you're reading about her obsession with a narcissistic fellow student, and then he's being compared to the philosophy behind Dostoevsky's Demons, and then there's something about mimetic theory, and it kind of works, but it's preceded by musings on why Uzbek literature is ultimately uninteresting, and why she grew beyond her college boyfriend, and it all doesn't quite hang together. Still, there were passages that arrested me so greatly, I just had to stop and read them over and over. All in all, time very well spent.

Quirky...not what I expected in an essay. 
 Batuman does entertain....but not enlighten.

Some is great, some really feels like filler, some seems too closely adapted from either journalism or academic papers. Rather disjointed as a book. And all that detail about Uzbek culture, oy vey (was a bit like ten pages of Levin on agricultural techniques... But a bit more eye-glazey). I love her voice and the memoirier this was the better. And then it just ends with, oh I'd still choose literature tidy sentiment. The Tolstoy conference was wonderfully done. Stars for that, and for generally being interesting *enough*. I would give her next book a go... Or read more articles in the New Yorker.

I wish I read Russian and new as much about Russian Literature as the author. Reading this book is to enter a whirlwind which whips as fast as Batuman's high-velocity mind. Fatiguing, more than enjoyable.

Taken from the articles found in journals like n+1, The New Yorker, Harper's Magazine, and the London Review of Books, Elif Batuman combines them into this memoir. The Possessed may be a collection journal articles, but combined together it forms more of a memoir of Batuman's academic life. Starting with a conference she was involved with at Stanford University about Isaac Babel in the first article "Babel in California". 
 I mention the first article "Babel in California" because I think it represented everything I did not like about this book. On the surface this book sounds right up my alley. The misleading subtitle for this book is "Adventures with Russian Books and the People Who Read Them" and that is the expectation I had when going into this book. However going by the first article about one conference, I got a very padded book with no real structure. It seems like Elif Batuman has edited her articles in a way to fit into a book, but she turned articles into sixty page chapters that are so drawn out that it is boring. 
 There is some interesting sections within this book but I feel the major problem is this book has no structure. If this was a collection of essays, I would expect a theme. If this was a memoir, I would expect more focus on her life. The Possessed sits somewhere in the middle, each chapter is very different; about a conference, her travels, her studies or just reading Russian lit. Each chapter does not seem to connect to the previous chapter, which just made it too clunky. 
 I wanted a book about Russian literature, but The Possessed did not give me that. In fact any literary criticism was never explained properly, so made it hard to understand how she draw her conclusions. I am looking for a good book about Russian literature, like a literary exploration or a journey into these books. If you know of a book like this that you would recommend, please let me know. 
 This book originally appeared on my blog; http://www.knowledgelost.org/book-rev...

I loved this book! Batuman's graduate school experiences studying linguistics and Russian literature are fascinating and so relatable. I laughed out loud in places and also learned much about the Russian novels and novelists that I love. I especially liked contemplating the obscure topics studied and researched by the author and her colleagues. As a former literature student and lover of literature today, I agree wholeheartedly with Batuman's final words in this book: "If I could start over today, I would choose literature again. If the answers exist in the world or in the universe, I still think that's where we're going to find them." Yes! 
 And I can't wait to read Elif Batuman's new novel!

book_b.title: The Ballad of Black Tom
book_b.user_review:
This is another of those books that are so highly acclaimed that I find not at all worth all the hype. This is supposed to be a Lovecraft-type horror book but I didn't find either Lovecraft or horror in it. I'm not a Lovecraft fan, but I have read several of his stories so I understand what the critics mean. But it didn't find what they did. 
 Tommy Tester is a young black male living in Harlem (NYC) in the 1920s. He does odd jobs. One job entails delivering a small, yellow book to an old woman who lives in Queens, a place a "black fella" really stands out. The woman who has purchased the book barely opens the door. When the book passes from hand to hand, the book sizzles a bit in the sun. 
 Moving through the first section quickly, Tommy is "discovered" by a man who wants him to play guitar at a meeting of his. Two policemen (one a private detective) are surveilling this man. The picture window in the man's library seems to be a huge projection screen. When Tommy tries to leave the library, he opens the door and sees a lobby, not the hallway, in which the policeman Malone stands..... 
 It's complicated to describe as Lovecraft usually is. Suffice it to say that Tommy becomes Black Tom after the horrid death of his father. Black Tom can make entire plots of land, along with their houses, disappear. He can appear and disappear at will. And the policeman Malone plays a large part in the whole story. 
 The story is supposed to revolve around the Supreme Alphabet, but the alphabet seems to be made of words instead of letters. This alphabet is used in the plot when it's convenient, but it's not the focus it should be to connect the story. So although the idea that the alphabet controls something unworldly and evil hangs in the air, it's not clear what and how to summon it or what that evil actually is. 
 If you like Lovecraft you'll probably like this.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This novella is basically a rewrite of "The Horror At Red Hook" by H. P. Lovecraft. Victor Lavalle took Lovecraft's story and added just enough to make it truly his own, while keeping the larger story intact. Both stories stand alone, you do not need to read the Lovecraft to enjoy this and vice-versa. 
 I did enjoy this story by Victor Lavalle, and will be looking for more by him. I especially enjoyed how he ended this one.
More like 3.5.
I have several notes on this. Not all of them are clear or ledge-able at the moment....full review to come soon.

Recently received this book from Tor through a Goodreads giveaway. 
 First off, I rarely give 5 star reviews, I like to save that rating for truly exceptional books, and this one certainly qualifies. 
 As a fan of the Lovecraft mythos in it's variety of forms for a great many years, it isn't often something comes along like The Ballad of Black Tom, and adds extra layers of depth and characterization to a sometimes stale genre. 
 At least for me, the most uncomfortable part about being a Lovecraft fan was the obvious and blatant racism present in some of his works. LaValle deftly turn this on it's head by making one of the worst of Lovecraft's tainted screeds, The Horror at Red Hook, into a taut story of escalating horror. Effortlessly mixed into this tale is the backdrop of racial injustice in 1920's New York that never takes you out of the story, and in fact enhances the motives of various characters and their motivations. 
 Whether or not you find it to be a condemnation or a paean to H.P. Lovecraft, the fact is it's a briskly paced and plotted novella worthy of the best of the mythos tales.
An ode to H. P. Lovecraft.

Interesting, but a bit too disturbing for my tastes in the end. I didn't like how the end of the book was told through Malone's eyes, after you get attached to Tommy in the beginning. I understand why he did this, and that there was more at play in this story (criticism of racism in Lovecraft's work), so maybe someone who has more of a background in that will appreciate it more. It's portrayal of the impact of racism and police brutality was poignant though, and well done.

When I started it, I had no idea what it was about, just that someone whose reading taste I trust recommended it. So good! Warning: racially charged language and scenes. If you are uncomfortable with that, get over it. This novella is too good to miss.

(Added addendum concerning 2017 Hugo finalists.) 
 "Mankind didn't make messes; mankind was the mess." 
 Fantasy historical fiction. I wouldn't have finished this once I realized what kind of story it was, but felt constrained to read it all if I was to vote on it for the 2017 Hugo Awards. Can't conceive why it was nominated, much less a finalist. 
 "He thought of himself as an entertainer. Others ... called him a scammer, a swindler, a con, but he never thought of himself this way. No charlatan ever did." 
 Good storytelling, good character development and good voice. Good sense of time and place, which gradually--then with increasing speed--veers into the horrible. Shifting away from the main character propelled the story, but diluted the impact. Not my kind of story. Can't imagine recommending anyone read it. Yuck. If this is set in the Lovecraft universe, LaValle has done me a favor by warning me away forever. 
 "Walking through Harlem first thing in the morning was like being a single drop of blood inside an enormous body that was waking up." 
 I don't normally post negative reviews on my blog, but I am reviewing all the 2017 Hugo novella finalists. Not fair to the others to pass over this one just because I don't recommend anyone read it, let alone vote for it. 
 "There was more to this world than what we touch to taste or see. His time as a detective made him sure of this."

Really loved this novella and will DEFINITELY be reading more by LaValle. You can easily read this in a couple hours and I'd suggest doing just that. It's a great lovecraftian modernization and the plot feels more genuine because it is devoid of the racism endemic to Lovecrafts writing. The writing obviously isn't as good as Lovecrafts because....come on, the guy was a fucking genius, but it definitely gets the feel and LaValle makes it his own. I'd love to read more stuff just like this!

I really liked the beginning of this but need to pay better attention to what I'm reading, because I don't generally like horror and once this went to the horror place I was a lot less interested. That isn't the book's fault, though! It was well written and engaging, just not my genre.

reference_books.title: The Bad Beginning (A Series of Unfortunate Events, #1)
The First Phone Call from Heaven
reference_books.review_text:
To be fair, this is most definitely not my type of book. I read it for a book club and likely would not have finished it if I didn't have a sense of obligation to them, as the organizer. Inspirational fiction does not find any ground in my skeptical (though I would argue warm and at times overly sentimental) little heart, and Albom's story was just dripping with feel-good sweetness. Faith is confirmed or returned to lost souls, lives are changed forever, etc. 
 Like I said - just not my thing. 
 The real issue I take with the story, though, and the reason I am only giving it one measly star, comes down to setting. The book is set in a real town, Coldwater, MI, which just so happens to be a short drive from where I live and work. The issue is that Albom repeatedly refers to the area as "northern Michigan," even though the town is not even remotely in northern Michigan. (Coldwater is closer to Indiana than it is to anything resembling northern Michigan.) He also mentions the town being established in a specific year (I believe 1898), though it was actually established in 1861. This probably would not bother anyone else, but as far as I am concerned if you are going to set your story in a real town you damn well better get the basic facts right, or just leave them out entirely. This was totally unnecessary and in no way added to the story. There was no need to mention the town's founding date or repeatedly comment on the northern Michigan climate. 
 Coldwater. isn't. in. northern. Michigan. 
 I do believe this will be my first and last Albom outing.

reference_books.title: Homer & Langley
reference_books.review_text: A book about such interesting real-life characters has no excuse for being this unbearably dull.

reference_books.title: The Butterfly and the Violin (Hidden Masterpiece, #1)
reference_books.review_text: An interesting story, drowned in cheesy romance and heavy-handed religion. As another reviewer put it, this is Christian Harlequin romance meets the Holocaust. Cambron is not a bad writer, but this book features the worst of both romance and inspirational fiction writing, set against a backdrop that deserves more weight. Definitely not recommended as a work of historical fiction, but I'm giving it one star for having a measure of historical accuracy (the orchestra and artwork of Auschwitz are both true to history and I might seek out other books on those topics).

reference_books.title: Colorless Tsukuru Tazaki and His Years of Pilgrimage
reference_books.review_text: My first Murakami read, and I'm stuck between a 3 and 4 on this. Even though I could attribute some awkward dialogue to the translation, in the end I found the character's behaviors pretty consistently unbelievable. That being said, I still felt compelled to read on, and the musings on loss and grief, the rough transitions that take place growing up and finding your way in the world, were worth the read.

book_a.title: S.
book_a.user_review:
How to Get Chelsea to Want to Read a Book: 
 state in the review that it was "as if Franz Kafka had written an episode of "Lost."" 
 ----- 
 For me, this falls somewhere between 4 and 5 stars. 
 Like so many things J.J. Abrams, how much you like this is going to depend wholly on what kind of reader/viewer you are. Do loose ends drive you crazy? Do you prefer not having to use an EOTVOS Wheel to decipher codes yourself? Then you probably won't like this book as much as someone who wants to gleefully follow Abrams and Dorst down the rabbit hole and find themselves on SoT-themed subreddits at 1 a.m. 
 I am the latter kind of person (here's looking at you, /r/Westworld), and I still had a hard time sticking with some parts of this book. So, a couple suggestions if you decide this is a book you want to tackle: 
 - Read the margin conversations in order by color (black and blue, green and orange, red and purple, black and black). They aren't written in chronological order even within the color, so it can be hard to figure out what's going on anyway. Don't make it harder on yourself. (Unless you like that sort of thing, in which case you should love juggling five conversations over 450+ pages.) 
 - I'd recommend trying to read the margin notes in as few sittings as possible. Hell, that would probably be a good idea for the whole book. There's just so much going on that I imagine it would be easy to forget details if you spread it out over weeks. 
 - Prepare to keep reading after the first ending. It took me nearly as long to read the margins and ephemera as it did to read SoT. 
 All in all, this was a fun read. It didn't exactly go where I thought it would, but I really liked what it had to say about identity, and got a kick out of the more speculative fiction elements. I'm still not totally convinced the simple version of the story is the "right" one. There is a lot of room for deeper analysis and conspiracy theories with this book. And that makes me one very satisfied reader.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Very disappointing. S. initially seemed like it was going to be bit of fun escapism wrapped in a striking package. Instead, the more I read, the more I was forced to admit that all of the beautiful production and design concealed an awful, awful book. 
 Two main texts comprise S.: the novel Ship of Theseus, by a fictional writer named V.M. Straka, and the annotations, written in the margins and across various inserts, being shared by two students as they are drawn further and further into the mystery of Straka's "true" identity. Theoretically, this should be interesting and fun and exciting to read, but it isn't. Why? Well, firstly because the actual novel Ship of Theseus is bad. It's so bad that it is painful to read. Secondly, as a result, it is literally impossible to believe that Straka is a giant of Western literature (no matter how many breathless student annotations profess it to be so). So why would anyone care about the "true" identity of the author of such a bad book? Why should I, as the reader of S. care? I mean, I can hardly believe that we are supposed to believe that Ship of Theseus was "published," let alone that it's supposed to be an important piece of literature! Thirdly, no one in academia reads literature to get "clues" as to the identity of the author. That's not how academic scholarship works! Even with an author like Shakespeare, no serious scholar actually cares about his "true" identity. That question is the sole preserve of old-fashioned cranks and weirdos at the margins of academia, who seem to have missed Barthes' memo about the death of the author. And that's Shakespeare, ffs! And finally, those marginalia... embarrassing. I can't believe two grown adults (Dorst and Abrams) wrote such sophomoric rubbish, most of which boil down to trite cliches like "be true to yourself!" and "love is all you need!" At one point I was cringing so much that I developed a cramp. 
 The layers of interwoven text mean that S. demands a serious investment of time and effort. Unfortunately the reward is incommensurate with that effort. As a physical object, S. is gorgeous. It's a pity that the actual text(s) contained therein are so bad. 
 [edit] Maybe my review sounds a bit harsh. It's clear that S. is a labour of love for Dorst and Abrams, a book about books and reading. It's just not a good book. Oh, and to all the people saying that this is a "smart" book: no, it isn't. It's dumb as a bag of rocks.

Spoilers in this review. 
 This book read like a less coherent Da Vinci Code for art majors, and I am unimpressed with both the fake-novel (if the foreword prepares the reader to experience one of the most fascinating books ever written by an incredibly genius author, the book to follow should probably actually be at least close to fascinating and genius), and the fake-meta-commentary of the fake-novel. Though at first I enjoyed the novelty of the story's main conceit - that the two main characters have to communicate with each other almost solely by writing in the book's margins over the course of a year - there was a point at which I ceased to be convinced by it; it felt contrived and unnecessary. Around the same point or maybe slightly after that I completely stopped caring about the panicky, trivial girl with standard daddy issues and the surly, damaged boy who just needed to find the right girl to plumb his secret sensitive depths. I may have groaned out loud when they both reach their epiphanies about how important love is and what their really real identities are and how they should let go of the past etc etc etc. I felt like the beginning of the novel unintentionally(?) prepares the reader for a much more epic and convoluted mystery than the college-age romance that eventually unfolds. 
 In short: this was a solid concept with really great, but squandered, potential. "House of Leaves" used the ergodic lit approach far more effectively, creating layers within layers within layers of narrative all referring to each other in a way that drew the reader deep into its eerie, monstrous world. It was, like S., essentially a mystery story, but it allowed the reader to discover and interpret the mystery independently. In contrast, "S." felt like it was using all of its two layers as nothing more than a cheap marketing gag, and while its narrative is intended to be a puzzle, the reader merely watches other people solve it instead of participating in the solution. 
 Also, not that this affects my overall enjoyment of the content, but this book is annoying as SH*T to read in the bath with all those freaking inserts.

Elsker du ogsa den gode, gammeldags, stoflige bog, som man bade kan maerke og lugte? Sa skynd dig ned til din lokale bogpusher med virkelige mennesker bag disken og kob dette forrygende pragtvaerk af en bog. Gor det med det samme! Det er ikke sikkert, at du orker at laese den, og du gar i sa fald nok heller ikke glip af sa meget. Men du MA eje den! 
 Jeg indrommer med det samme, at denne anmeldelse er noget forudindtaget pa den made, at jeg allerede, da jeg stod med bogen mellem haenderne i min boghandler, havde besluttet mig for at vaere vild med denne bog, og at den ikke kunne fa mindre end fem stjerner. Alene pa grund af den laekre og originale udforelse, som er helt uden for kategori. 
 S. er en bog i en bog... i en bog. Eller rettere sagt: Den er mindre en bog i traditionel forstand, end den er en ide eller et projekt fort igennem som en bog. Dette er sa ogsa dens svaghed, men det kommer jeg tilbage til. 
 Laes hele anmeldelsen pa min K's bognoter.

This has to be the most challengin book I have ever read. With at least four different plot lines running simultaneously, trying to decipher codes and jumping around in time , it was a nightmare to keep track of everything. I'm proud that I finished it, but I am sure that I misssed huge chunks of important plot line simply becuase I couldn't juggle it all in my mind at the same time.
Excellent concept! Really original! The "real" book wasn't the best, I definately loveddddd the margins though! I fell in love with Jen and Eric. Definately worth a try!!

I absolutely loved this book!!! The whole point of it is 2 show how reading a book is a singular experience, unlike anything else. The 2 authors make it look like a library book with all the familiar stamps. They create an author, named V.S. STRAKA, who has written a book called, THE SHIP OF THESEUS. Now, the story is real the author is not. It is a fabulous story of the high-seas and derring-do, filled w intrigue, exotic locations + femme fatales - like a BOYS OWN adventure. As well, there are apparently, 2 people corresponding in the margins who love this book + its author. There is also various artifacts contained in the book itself - postcards, letters, pictures, maps, etc. This is all 2 heighten the reading experience + it really does. This book is a truly a SINGULAR experience for all + highly-recommended for ages 14-140.

Well, I don't know what kind of sorcery this is, or how one even begins to write a book like this. Just reading it requires a decision: in what order will you read this book? I read it from beginning to end, but I think at some point in the future, I will reread it in chronological order: SoT, then the notes in chronological order. I think this book will reward multiple readings, and I am impressed by a book that can live up to such an ambitious concept. SoT itself is a great read, even without the mystery. 
 Finally, I am certain that Eric and Jen did not figure out al of the ciphers in SoT, and on a future pass, I intend to.

Like House of Leaves this incredibly meh story is saved by the execution. Written by the writer/producer/director/allaroundlegend JJ Abrams it adds a lil summinsummin to the standard book formula. The majority of this story is told by the notes written in the margin between two students. 
 Gotta respect a man who puts effort into making coffee stains look real. 
 It comes like this!

Back when the Kindle first came out (and before I read most of my books in e-format!), I predicted that people would write books that *needed* to be in paper, that wouldn't work as an ebook. This is one such book. The story is told through the main book, the footnotes of the book, and the marginalia written by two readers, trying to find out more about the enigmatic author. There are also some documents/ephemera included. This is definitely a spiritual successor to Pale Fire; if you like that you would almost certainly like this. I think, or really, know, there are a few puzzles within this book I haven't solved. 
 It also has a lot of re-read value. As a reader, you get a rough idea of when the notes inside the book were written... basically two readers are going back and forth writing notes to each other on subsequent readings, and so going through, knowing a little more about the end of their story and having more context for the "later" notes would be an enjoyable second read.

After it was found out that the video teasers J.J. Abrams had released were actually about a book, and that the premise of the book had to deal with two people finding each other in the margins of a novel, I was beyond excited about getting it. I love novels that have unconventional structure or design, and I bought this one on the day it came out. This is a complex novel, but I'll try and keep this review brief. We'll discuss the three main categories at play: 1) the design and inserts, 2) Jen & Eric's margin notes, and 3) the main story entitled "Ship of Theseus." 
 Let's talk about design and inserts first because that is the first thing that one notices. The authors and the design company that the authors partnered with truly deserve all of the book design awards there are for this year. The design makes everything feel very genuine: everything from the handwriting in the margins, to the drawings, to the various fades and stains on the paper, to the library sticker and stamps in the back making it feel like a real library book that's been handled by many over time, all of the inserts the book has throughout it like letters, postcards, pictures and the like, and finally to the packaging the book comes in. Again, all of it is top notch and you can tell a ton of time and hard work was spent on getting the designs right. Some of the inserts fall out of the book from time to time, and some reviewers have suggested taking them all out and putting a post it note on them so you know where they are supposed to be, but I didn't really have that much trouble with them. The design aspect of this book deserves 5 out of 5 stars. 
 Let's talk about the margin notes. Essentially, you have a boy named Eric who read Ship of Theseus, loved it, and became obsessed with trying to figure out who the author was/is, writing out some of this thoughts in pencil in the margins. A girl named Jen later found the book and his notes and wrote her own thoughts in response, and the two began to communicate through the book in the margins. Reading the margin notes can sometimes be confusing as Jen and Eric use different color inks for different times that they are reading and rereading through the book. All of these different color inks are mixed in together, making a chronological read of the book confusing and a little tedious. When I began reading this story, I read everything on each page before moving on to the next page. This turned out to be very cumbersome, and I found the best way for me personally to read the novel was to read the story for the whole chapter, and then read the margin notes for the whole chapter. The exchanges between Jen and Eric feel very realistic, and it can really make you feel as if these are real people. (It is kind of crazy to think about how many times Jen and Eric would have to take the book back and get it out again to write each and every line at the library though.) My favorite parts about their writing in the margins to each other was actually not the mystery of them trying to figure out who the author was, in fact I felt that part could get very repetitive and confusing. Also, I thought the paranoia they developed that people were following them etc. felt very over dramatic (why would anyone care that they were discussing who the author was that much/how would they even know?) My favorite parts were when they talked about things that had affected them emotionally growing up, such as when Jen ran away. I also enjoyed the love story that grows slowly between them, although when they first meet felt very anticlimactic for me. The notes can be complicated but I enjoyed them, and the unique characters and dialogue between Jen and Eric. I would rate this section a 3 out of 5 stars. 
 But let's talk about Ship of Theseus, the main story, because to match the great design, there needs to be a fantastic story supporting it. While I felt the overall story of Ship of Theseus was entertaining, I felt that there were a number of things that turned me off from the story. So many things go unexplained, including, and maybe most importantly, who our main character "S" really is. In the beginning, we (and he) know absolutely nothing of his past, or who he is, and that really never changes all the way through the book. This becomes a flaw in the story as it becomes hard to care about S and what he's going through when we know almost nothing about him. I really wanted to be enraptured by this book and not be able to put it down, but for a long time, I couldn't get through more than a couple pages at a time. Here is a list of just a couple of the many things that go unexplained: why have all the sailors on the ship had their mouth sewn shut? Why does he seem to age faster on the ship than he does on land? Why is he on the ship repeatedly at all? Why is S constantly writing random words on the walls and on paper if it never factors into the actual story at all? Why does S seem to always be losing his memory, and just appear at random places with new skills and supplies, having no idea how he got there and who told him what to do? Why is the mission never truly explained? Why is Sola never truly explained? Again, I thought the story had entertainment value, but I felt there were a number of things that could've made it better. I would give the story a 2 out of 5 Stars. 
 Who knows, maybe if I had gotten more into the codes that are apparently throughout the book, maybe I would've gotten some more answers (I never used the code wheel that's in the back for example.) The cool parts about this book are enough that I would recommend it to others.

book_b.title: The Light Between Oceans
book_b.user_review: Decent enough for a book club read, but spent the last third of the book irritated and infuriated with the characters, in equal measure.

sample_reviews.review_text: Really good plot and some standout passages but the pace was too slow for me to rate it more than 2 stars.

It's very "good for a book club"--esque, plus its set in a faraway land in the olden days, which is normally sooo not my jam, so the fact that I'm giving this 4 stars and debated giving it 5 should tell you something. it drags a bit in the first third, but it really steps on the gas later, and the ending made me cry real tears.

The characters were written beautifully. It says something that I was rooting for characters whose interests were in complete conflict. Parts of the plot were like watching a train wreck - you knew what was going to happen but you still felt compelled to keep reading.

This book was tough for me to get through and the only reason I finished it was for my book club. It was dull and dragged on and on. It picked up a little by part three, but not enough to redeem the book for me.

This book was predictable, boring and melodramatic. Unfortunately, it starts off very strong and thus tricks you into reading further, with Tom being an interesting and mysterious character, Isabel tough and a little unorthodox, and Janus' secluded and hostile setting. If you're entering this book hoping to read about two people surviving on the island, dealing with the issues that arise and overcoming them, you've picked up the wrong book. This novel is 5% about living on a secluded island and 95% melodramatic boring drivel. 
 The last hundred pages are near insufferable. The only "heartbreaking" thing about it was that I read to the end, and that's only because I had to read this book for a Book Club. Honestly, not only did I want to wring everyone character's neck, but the author insisted on giving Lucy dialogue, which was utterly painful to read. 
 Maybe this novel just isn't for me, because I found it insulting how it suggests that women go completely bonkers regarding children and conception. There are many many women/couples who can't conceive and they don't go around stealing babies. But apparently all Isabel can think about is having a kid so she loses it. Granted, she was stuck on that island so maybe that drove her a little crazy, but then in the same novel you have Hannah, another women who, when faced with the presumed death of her child, becomes a mentally unstable women who is basically unable to function in society. Give me a break.

 j'avais commence le livre en anglais et puis apres quelques dizaines de pages j'ai change pour la version francaise car j'ai eu du mal avec le style de l'auteur. Il y a beaucoup de termes techniques sur la marine, le phare, la guerre je n'ai pas toujours tres bien compris le sens en anglais. 
 Passee cette difficulte il a fallu que je m'adapte au rythme tres lent du recit. Il y a quelques flash backs, la vie de chaque personnage et ce qui les a marque est tres detaillee. Cependant je n'ai pas accroche avec les personnages principaux, je n'ai pas trouve leur romance tres profonde, Isabel est capricieuse, egoiste et avec peu de morale et Tom souffre d'une sorte de syndrome post-traumatique de la Premiere Guerre Mondiale mais je trouve que cela a ete mal aborde, mal developpe...Il est froid, sans sentiments. 
 Je n'ai pas non plus beaucoup aime les references a la 1GM car elles eludaient beaucoup l'intrigue principale du roman. Il y a egalement beaucoup de references religieuses mais les personnages semblent s'en preoccuper seulement quand cela leur est favorable. 
 J'attendais beaucoup de ce livre et finalement l'histoire est basique, cela m'a tres peu emue. J'espere que le film rattrapera toutes ces petites choses que je n'ai pas apprecie dans le livre.

This book came highly recommended and I did like it, but I have to admit I felt it was too slow paced for me. After suffering miscarriages, Tom and Isabel save a baby that washes ashore beside a dead man and they decide to keep her, passing her off as their own child. I enjoyed that Isabel brings life back into Tom's being after suffering through war and the way she changes through the novel is true to life. As it turns out, little baby happens to have a mother still searching for her. The reader is torn between understanding why Isabel and Tom kept the child to feeling disgust that they could allow the real mother to suffer. A strange story. I am also interested in the fact that the author keeps a low profile and prefers for readers to enjoy her story and not poke around into her life, claiming 'it wouldn't shed any details on her writing.' A fresh approach to be sure :)

IT IS NOT OFTEN THAT I HAVE NO WAY OF FIGURING OUT HOW A STORY IS POSSIBLY GOING TO HAVE AN HAPPY ENDING FOR ALL THE CHARACTERS I LOVE, but this book was a very happy exception to that. 
 To learn more, check out: addypolet.com/2017/01/30/the-light-be...

My heart is still in my throat and tears are still drying in the corners of my eyes. 
 I wanted to stop reading several times. I only kept on because of the encouragement of my friends, whose judgement I trusted. I know why I needed to now. 
 Life is definitely not easy after a war. Love can come so unexpectedly. That is what happened to Tom. Isabel was the love of his life and Tom never allowed himself to give that up, no matter what else happened. 
 The fairy existence of living on a small island 100 miles off the coast of Australia and being a Lighthouse Keeper was such an enormous attraction for wanting to read this story for me. I wanted to know what it was like. I found out. 
 Life and death and love and loss and love. That is what I found out.

The Light Between Oceans is a beautifully written book about moral choices made and the consequences of those choices. Each decision made in life becomes part of the fabric of that life. The setting ,which takes place at an isolated lighthouse post in Australia, adds to the beauty and atmosphere of the book.

reference_books.title: Crown of Midnight (Throne of Glass, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
For someone not in the target demographic, I thought this book was good, if juvenile, until about 2/3 of the way through. There are issues that I tried to ignore, including characters that are too black and white, especially Celaena, who is too good to be a believable assassin. While this book is more complex and overall more satisfying than the first one, it still feels like a YA novel for girls. There are a few twists, but nothing really surprising. And then came the part I mentioned that just angered me. I started hating Celaena for her idiotic reaction. That part nearly ruined the whole book for me. 
 Yet for some reason, I'm reading book 3. I guess I'm just masochistic.

reference_books.title: Ivanhoe
reference_books.review_text: For a book called Ivanhoe, there's very little of him in it. And the end was pretty anticlimatic. It was more interesting for the history than for the adventure.

reference_books.title: City of Stairs (The Divine Cities, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I have some mixed feelings on this book. For the most part I liked it, but some things didn't work so well for me. So I'm going to do a pro vs con list. 
 Pros 
 The setting is different from most fantasies. Set in a semi modern analogue to Russia, conquered by an analogue to India, it makes things a bit more diverse, especially when the heroine is a little brown girl with big glasses. 
 It has an air of mystery and wonder to it throughout the whole novel, juxtaposed to the aforementioned setting. 
 It has a rich mythology. 
 Cons 
 Shara, the heroine, feels like a Mary Sue. She seems just a little too smart. Her companion, Sigrud, is a Gary Stu when it comes to fighting. Between them, there isn't much suspense when they get to the action. 
 There are some parts that go deep into exposition, especially one part where Shara explains everything while cooking. While there was a lot of stuff to explain, some of it should have been parsed out more. 
 Along with telling too much, there was some showing too much. One time when a monster attacks, we see several viewpoints telling us basically the same thing, just how powerful it was. After the second or third, I was like, "I get it already." 
 Some of the mythology seems to be a critique on organized religion, especially religions like Catholicism and Judaism. It seemed like the message was, "You don't need God, nor should you follow any rules religions proscribed." It kind of rubbed me wrong. 
 I see that this is book number one of The Divine Cities, but the ending pretty much wrapped itself up, so I don't know where any other books would go with it. Not that I wouldn't mind returning, but the way it ended, I don't know how much more there is to explore. We'll see.

reference_books.title: Hyperion (Hyperion Cantos, #1)
reference_books.review_text: This book was a little hard to get into, as I had no frame of reference for this universe. But once I got through a few stories, things started to make a little more sense, although I'm still not sure I understand all the factions. Each of the six stories tackles different aspects of interstellar life in some 700-800 years from now. Simmons tackles topics like religion in that time, artificial intelligence, time travel, poetry, and small town life versus globalization (galactification?). For the most part, especially once I figured some things out, I liked it, but some things still took me out of suspended belief. Apparently, everyone in the future is obsessed with John Keats, and almost all the quotes are from the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, of which there are many. And then, of course, there's the cliffhanger, complete with the Wizard of Oz reference. I'm still deciding whether to let myself get sucked into the sequel. But it was a good book.

reference_books.title: Dracula
reference_books.review_text: Dracula, the most famous vampire in history, no matter how much Edward wants to beat him. Due to a slip up by Bram Stoker, the book was not covered under copyright here, so writers and movie makers had a party using the character in every way possible, from silly to sensual to scary. A few years back, Stoker's great nephew or something like that came out with a sequel that turned the villian into an antihero, pitting him against a vampiress Elizabeth Bathony in attempt to regain control of the character, but it was too little, too late. Anyway, I decided to read this book, to see what the original story was really like. Was the reason Dracula was so popular because he was so scary? Turns out he isn't. His popularity probably had more to do with the copyright issue than the book itself. Dracula is so bound by every little thing, from garlic to crosses, to light of day, that he makes a wimpy enemy. A normal serial killer would be scarier, because you can't ward him off with some strange ritual. The book basically has Dracula bite one of the character's fiancee, and he and his friends turn to a vampire expert, and old guy name Van Helsing, who says they need to kill Dracula or she'll turn into a vampire herself and lose her soul. So they go off chasing him, with Helsing explaining vampire lore on the way. They are never in any real danger because they are so protected against vampires, it's kind of pathetic. There was hardly a scary moment in the book. If you want something creepy, read Frankenstein, also overused, but the actual novel is really interesting.

book_a.title: City of Bones (The Mortal Instruments, #1)
book_a.user_review: I read this book as I heard that there would be a movie coming out, and it seemed to be pretty popular. It felt like a mashup between Percy Jackson and Twilight, with some Star Wars family drama thrown in. It is an easy read, targeted towards teenagers, especially girls, I presumed just from the cover. The protagonist, Clary (notice how the author's last name is Clare, although that itself is actually just a pen name), is not particulary strong in this book, at least. She pretty much just reacts to everything, and sometimes convinces Jace, her hunky shadowhunter demonslayer guy, to do stuff for her. The problem I always have with a supernatural urban setting is this: it starts out normally, then the main character starts seeing strange things, and then finds out there is a whole world of magical creatures like vampires and werewolves living among humans, but no one is smart enough to figure it out except this teenager. Even if magic is involved, you'd think that all the stuff getting destroyed by their fights would rouse people to attention. Then there is the infodump, where some wise character explains detail by detail how they hid themselves for thousands of years, and is about to explain some vital secret when they get interrupted by demons or something and once things calm down, the character conveniently forgets to continue explaining until later. Again, like in Percy Jackson, I never felt like the characters were in much danger. There's such a limited cast that I doubt anyone's going to die. There's a fight with a greater demon and they kill him with some sunlight. Still, plenty of revelations, although many were obvious. Not the most sophisticated read, but if you don't have high expectations, it's fine, goes quickly.

sample_reviews.review_text: I'm way behind on this, but I decided not to watch the current tv show - Shadow Hunters - or watch the movie with Lily Collins. Oddly enough I needed to pass the time on my commute in/out of Boston for the week and this did the job. On some days, I whipped it out during my lunch break because I wanted to see how it would end. I'm giving this 3 stars because I think there were portions of this book that could have been paired down -- did we really need the fight scene with the vampires or the Hodge betrayal to take up 4 chapters? Otherwise, I thought was a great escape.
There were parts of this book when I could not put it down, and then other parts where I felt it was obvious and dull. It is a good book if you want a pulpy distraction. It would be a fun beach read.

I'm told the City of Bones is being made into a summer movie. That saddens me. The City of Bones is yet another example of a weak female character. 
 Clary is a typical damsel in distress waiting for a boy to rescue her. The only thing she is good at is making biting, sometimes cruel remarks to those who are trying to help her. She also excels at not staying where she's told to wait. When confronted with danger, she freezes, too petrified to think. She is so ineffectual, I sometimes forgot she was there. Throughout this rather long book, Clary never picks up a weapon to defend herself or to help her friends. She never runs away to find help for those fighting in her defense. She never even uses her brain to work out a puzzle. I kept waiting for her to obtain magical powers or do something to justify her presence in this book. She is dead weight. Yet the story is about her. 
 At the end, Clary and her friend Luke, enter a castle belonging to the main bad guy. Luke warns his werewolf friend not to follow because it's too dangerous and instead charges him with leading the fight outside. Yet he takes Clary, a fifteen-year-old girl, with him. During the final battle scene, Clary runs to the weapons room to arm herself. Finally, I thought, she is showing some gumption. But the author, in her wisdom, affixed all the weapons to the walls so Clary couldn't get one if she wanted to. 
 What should future generations glean from this behavior? Should we all be mindless and passive, like Snow White waiting for her prince to come? 
 City of Bones joins the ranks of a long string of immensely popular stories about shallow, self-absorbed women. THIS IS A STEP BACKWARD! I implore all young readers to stand up and say Yes I can! Yes, I can fight back in my own defense. Yes, I can think for myself. And yes, I can pick up another book that is more worthy of my attention.

City of Bones by Cassandra Clare - no spoilers, well...not really. 
 Last week I "found" another wonderful writer - Cassandra Clare. Actually she was recommended by a lot of fellow book lovers from Goodreads.com. I love her style and the actual ability to write (unlike some other published writers). I had high expectations when I started reading City of Bones - the first book from Mortal Instruments series. It is a young adult urban fantasy book set in New York. The story is about Nephilim or demon-fighting Shadowhunters, werewolves, vampires, angels and fairies. And I wasn't dissatisfied. The teenagers actually sound like teenagers, the plot is well done, most of the characters are developed really good (I would work on Alec a bit more but that's a minor complaint) and there are enough twists and turns to keep a reader totally engrossed in the book. The romance between the main characters is subtle but well defined. I'm blessed with a vivid imagination but for those who are not, Cassandra Clare provides fantastic sensory descriptions. 
 There are only a couple of things that I wasn't crazy about. I was disappointed how Jace's and Clary's relationship turned out to be. Also I didn't care much about teenage drinking scene with Isabelle getting wasted. 
 Check out the Mortal Instruments webpage: http://www.mortalinstruments.com/mort... 
 The next two volumes in the series are: City of Ashes and City of Glass. 
 Happy reading!
I didn't like it very much! Kind of bored me. But I will reread...some day.

It seems that most people either love or hate this book. Well, last night I finished City of Bones. I didn't hate it, nor can I say I LOVED it; however, I did really enoy it. Actually, my feelings fall somewhere between the Goodreads 3 and 4 star rating, so I gave it 4, even though I think it fall slightly short of that. 
 City of Bones is HEAVILY plot driven, more akin to a thriller than most YA novels out there, which tend to put character first.Some people really enjoy plot driven novels. I do too, but it took me 2/3rds of the book to really begin to care about some of the characters. And in the end, I'm a character reader. I read books because of characters first and plot a distant second. With that said, the plot is exciting, different, and weird enough to have pushed me through the book until I reached the point where I began to care about ALL of the characters. And the more I think about it, the more I believe the reason I didn't care for some of the characters is because the reader isn't supposed to care. Mostly, this book is from Clary's POV, and she thinks half the characters are shallow jerks, and so do we. It's an interesting approach that one doesn't see very often in YA. So kudos to the author for doing something not done very often. 
 It has some great twists -- yes, I suppose a few are obvious, but so what? And to be honest, one of the twists I really didn't see coming, or I figured out just a few pages before the reveal. That's actually the sign of good writer. If we figure things out 60 pages before, that's not good. If we don't figure it out until the moment of the reveal, that's really just shock and awe, and means the author didn't leave clues for us to figure things out. Having that Ah ha moment just before -- that's good writing. 
 Yes, the book does follow some common tropes, but again, EVERY book does this, so what? If you enjoy it, who cares. This is certainly not a John Green novel, nor is it trying to be. It's not Hunger Games, either. It is a little bit Buffy, mixed with a little Harry Dresden, mixed with a little slasher Horror. 
 Which brings me to one point -- I was surprised how uber-violent the book is. I mean, we're talking almost Terry Goodkind violence here. Not quite, but pretty darn close. So if this is something that bothers you, you have your warning. Other than that, I definitely enjoyed it. The last 50 pages were extremely good, and pulled the story together in a way that made me care about what was happening. I'm definitely going to read book 2 as I think the series can only get better!

It's practically impossible to be around the bookish community without having encountered Cassandra Clare titles. I mean, the books are everywhere, the fans are everywhere, and the haters are everywhere. 
 Personally, I wanted to stay a good mile-radius away because of Clare's plagiarism-spotted history and the infamous incest plots (are those even spoilers anymore?), but I say again, they're impossible to avoid. 
 Eventually, curiosity got the best of me and I picked up City of Bones. My friends swore on our friendships that it would be amazing and the best thing I've ever read. 
 And that was how our friendships went to trash. 
 Nah, jk jk. But yeah, when I finally turned over the last page, "awe-inspired" was hardly what I felt. More like "asdfghjkl", and not the good "asdfghjkl" either. Just "asdfghjkl; thank god I'm done and aw crap did I really just waste that much of my life on this thing??". 
 The writing was horrible, the characters annoying, and the romance bleh (for lack of a better word). The plot... I suppose it was there, but most of it was drowned by the writing. 
 Because oh gosh, the writing. Thank you, Cassandra Clare, for feeding us paragraph-long metaphors that don't even tie in with the mood or setting. After the first five ridiculously lengthy and oddly placed descriptions about this moon or that decrepit building, I was ready to toss the book at the wall. It was so painfully obvious how hard she was trying to assert and reinforce the fact that Clary likes art, just as it was painfully obvious how important Clare thinks it is for the reader to know the exact hue and saturation of Jace's hair and eyes. 
 (Jace, by the way, was not impressive. At least, not impressive enough to have his pecs and abs plastered on to the front cover.) 
 And the romance? Seriously? The point of the forbidden love plot device is to get readers rooting for the two tragically star-crossed lovers. I'm a personal sucker for LGBT+ characters and characters on opposite ends of the socioeconomic spectrum, but incest? Hell no. I'm not here to watch siblings have that sort of attraction towards each other. That's just plain disgusting. 
 I mean, if they'd just been long-lost siblings that had a short fling before realizing the truth, I'd be willing to label that "Awkward" and move on with the story. From what I've heard, however, this story, was not willing to move on, so we're back again at "plain disgusting". And Sebastian...? Wow, I guess Clare really wanted to drive the incest thing in. 
 There's more I can rant on about, but I won't. I think I've done my fair share of ranting, and there are plenty of other reviews here with reviewers who, unlike me, actually took time to pull quotes and scrutinize everything that was done wrong in this book (which, if you can't tell already, is a buttload). 
 I do trust that this series does get better later on, at least in terms of the writing (The Infernal Devices trilogy was pretty decent), but I really lack any incentive whatsoever, despite neverending pestering from my friends (whose statuses remain questionable... jk <3). It's been a few months since I finished City of Bones and I still have enough yucky feeling ingrained into my head to write this review. That says something, doesn't it?

I don't even know where to begin. There was just so much wrong with this book, it's hard to remember every bit of the wrongness and put it in a coherent review. I'll try, but I can't guarantee it will be in any particular order. 
 First, the title of the book. What's wrong with it? you ask. What's wrong with it is that it's taken from a scene that probably doesn't even need to be in the book because it doesn't advance the storyline, which appears in the book a whole once, doesn't capture the story, and quite frankly doesn't make any sense whatsoever in context. I imagine the author chose the title because it seemed "kewl." 
 Next, we have the scene in question that prompted the title. It could have been completely eliminated from the book altogether, and the book probably would have been better for it. Nothing happened, it didn't advance the storyline, and essentially has no place in the story whatsoever. 
 This is reminiscent of the great big vampire/werewolf fight scene. Again, we have a scene that doesn't advance the storyline, and appears to have only been written so that vampires and werewolves could be introduced into the author's world. This is a really lame reason to write a scene. 
 Then we have the one scene that just WILL NOT stop bugging the crap out of me, because it is so horribly unrealistic. Clary is making her way to her room, then suddenly wakes up in bed. She doesn't know how she got to bed, but Jace is there to explain they found her asleep in the hallway. Clary is apparently ok with that and asks no more questions. 
 What's wrong with this? Well, I wasn't aware that passing out in a hallway was considered normal human behavior. I mean, I don't know about anyone else, but I've never been walking to my bedroom and just fallen over asleep, only to wake up the next day and not see anything wrong with the fact that I passed out in a hallway. Not to mention if she'd actually dropped from exhaustion, she would, at the very least, have ended up with some bruises or soreness, if not a concussion (seriously, you try just flopping headfirst into the floor and see how well you come out of that experience). 
 Metaphors are abused, badly. Most of the time, it's like the author writes a paragraph, realizes the paragraph is crappy, then adds this incredibly crazy, colorful imagery to the end to somehow right the fact that the paragraph was horrible to begin with. Yes, the writing is that bad, and no, Ms. Clare, the horrible metaphors at the end of a paragraph don't make it better. 
 Clary herself has no personality. At any given moment, you can't predict how she'll react to something, because her reactions are all over the spectrum. If she was a real person, I'd suspect her of either having severe bi-polar or possibly schizophrenia, given how she can't seem to stick with a set of behaviors and reactions that would define who she is as a person. As far as I'm concerned, Clary isn't a main character, she's a story prop who reacts to any given situation in the manner the author finds most dramatic. 
 Jace is supposed to be this badass sexy meanie, only he comes across as a very bad amalgamation of Draco Malfoy and some other random male leads. Ok, scratch that, he's just a really horrible version of Draco Malfoy, like if you tried to make Draco Malfoy this evil-yet-good person but were too bad of a writer to pull it off well. 
 There's even a horrible attempt at a love quadrangle among Jace, Clary, Alec, and Simon, with an especially ICKY result, especially given this is supposed to be YA. The ICKINESS stems from the fact that Jace and Clary make out like mad fiends, only to find out they are siblings. Not only is the Star Wars ripoff evident, but EWWWWW. 
 Not to mention the at-least 30 something-year-old warlock who hits on a 15 year-old boy. I'm assuming this was to hint at the fact Alec is gay (which we, the readers, already realized long before the scene in question), but it comes off as another EWWWWW moment in the book. 
 All the revelations were empty, as the author has no ability to foreshadow anything to save her life, and you've got the whole thing figured out LONG before the "big reveal" in the story. 
 There is no actual plotline. Really, there isn't. Clary's mom gets abducted, and Clary is ok with that for the whole story until she realizes how she can save her mom. Prior to that, Clary is more concerned with Jace and Simon's affections for her--except that she forgets completely about Simon at least half of the time. So, her mom is a non-issue until Clary figures out how she can save her, then all of a sudden, Clary gives a crap about what's happening to dear old mom. 
 Luke = Lupin from Harry Potter, ripoff so blatant I almost groaned when I saw it. 
 Other characters completely unremarkable, flat, stupid, and not worth commenting on. 
 So, in a nutshell--writing is horrible, plot is non-existent, characters are flat and I wouldn't be the least put out if they all died, storyline continually jerks you around without telling you it's jerking you around, making it all the more horrible to read, and the storyline wanders down scenes that make no sense and really, have no function in the plot whatsoever. Plus the incest and grown-man-hitting-on-boy parts. 
 This book is awful. I will most certainly not be watching the movie, because I don't have faith that even with Hollywood's "artistic license," that they could make something watchable out of this load of awfulness.

DNF AT 160 
 Ok what is going on with you Sarah J. Mass? Your first books were soooo good and this one is garbage. I'm done with this series :(

** spoiler alert ** 
 I thought it was kind of slow initially and I was honestly kind of annoyed with Manon's chapters (because I wanted to hear from Aelin, Dorian, Chaol, and Aedion) but then the book picked up and it was SO CRAZY (AWESOME). So much happens in this book, there was SO much amazing character growth and it happens to be a GREAT setup for the next. The new characters Rowan and Aedion are wonderful and it's nice getting to know who Ren is a little bit better. Sorscha also turned out to be incredibly brave even though I did NOT like her relationship with Dorian. I still ship Celaena and Dorian for the end! They'd SERIOUSLY be this incredible power couple. They could unite their kingdoms. She has fire and he has ice! Not to mention the dialogue between Rowan and Celaena when he said, "'Sometimes, mates can be together intimately before the actual bond snaps into place.' 'It's a useless hope to cling to, anyway.' 'Do you want the truth?' She tucked her chin into her tunic and closed her eyes. 'Not tonight.'" Dorian and Celaena have been together intimately in some ways and maybe the REAL bond just hasn't happened yet. There was a connection between them though and they're like a present day Elena and Gavin. I REALLY hope they happen... UGH... it's all so great! I'm really looking forward to the Aelin and Aedion reunion that will hopefully happen and I really really really want Dorian to be freed of his dad's dark collar. That was one of the craziest parts of the book and I totally didn't see it coming. On the bright side he isn't dead and all hope isn't totally lost. I think Celana cares enough about him to try to redeem who he used to be. All in all, I'm anticipating the next book to read how this plays out.This series is arguably THE BEST YA FICTION I've ever read. Like I said in another review its a great mix of action, adventure, romance, fantasy and mystery. And on a side note... this book slightly reminds me of LOTR because she wants to retrieve the Wyrdkeys and put them into the gate in order to keep their power from access like Frodo and Sam wanted to bring the ring to Mordor.

Is it just me or do we suddenly have a bunch of characters to keep track of now? 
 When I started Heir of Fire I didn't realize that only a fraction of this book would actually follow Celaena...it's a bit of a jarring switch from the roller coaster ride that was Crown of Midnight. As such it took me way longer than I anticipated to finish this book -- I think this was due in part to the fact that it took me a loooong time to care about Manon, Aedion, Sorscha, and Rowan (who's character was really only developed when Celaena's was). Now that I'm at the end of the book I think I like some of the characters enough to see what happens to them in Queen of Shadows...it just took a while to figure that out...ok, like 500 pages to figure that out. 
 I'm hopeful Queen of Shadows builds on the momentum that started in the last few chapters of this book -- I have a feeling I will read the next book and realize that everything in Heir of Fire had a distinct purpose...I just have to be patient to see how it all plays out.

I can't. I just don't even know what to say. I mean my initial thought when I could form one was "What the heck did I just read???". No joke I sat on a super uncomfortable concrete bench for like 2 minutes with my eyes wide and my mouth hanging open because...WHAT THE HECK DID I JUST READ???!!! 
 I'm not going to go into a description this book. What I say wouldn't really give it any justice. But what I will tell you is that Heir of Fire is very different from the other two books and I had a whole host of emotions going through me when reading it. I had read Throne of Glass and Crown of Midnight pretty close to reading Heir of Fire so I expected something similar to the two. But that is not what Heir of Fire was. As one of my blogging friends said to me, this is Celaena's book. And I couldn't agree more. But because of that I had trouble when I first started reading this one. It was on the verge of being 4 stars. I know, GASP! But as I progressed further into the book, the book was pushed up to 4.5 stars level. And then when I read the last heart pounding 60 pages it was cemented as a solid 5 star read. Let me tell you why: 
 4 Stars: The new characters flustered me. After reading Throne of Glass and Crown of Midnight pretty much back to back, I was used to a certain setting with certain people. Heir of Fire threw that comfort out the window. There was more magic than I expected, an added level of enemies that was hinted at in Crown of Midnight, and just plain more people. I had trouble connecting to the newbies when I craved my trio. 
 4.5 Stars: Celaena started to grow and not be so mopey and whiny. In the first two books Celaena was this powerhouse that had no fear. She was so strong. But she was changed in Crown of Midnight and that change carried over into the beginning of Heir of Fire. At first it was not a change I liked. And then the book started to grow and take shape and Celaena started to find herself again. She stopped being stuck in her land of self-pity and became the warrior, the champion, we all love her to be. 
 5 Stars: THE END. The fantastic flipping ending! That is really all I have to say. This book could have been a 2 star read throughout the whole story and I would give it 5 stars because of that freaking ending! I can't even comprehend that ending. Maas blew all her other books out of the water with that ending. (Hmm...how many times can I say ending in one paragraph???) 
 So basically all I can really say about Heir of Fire is that it is an amazing roller-coaster of emotions and growth and action and heartbreak. I cannot stress enough to not go into this book expecting things to be the same as they were in Crown of Midnight. Now that I am removed from the book I can see why things changed and why Heir of Fire was different. It's because life changes. There are always new obstacles and we have to deal and move on and Maas clearly got her point across on this one. As it was said in a discussion with two other book bloggers, Heir of Fire is very much Celaena's book and I now feel closer to her after reading it. 
 Give me more Ms. Maas, GIVE ME MORE!
Obviously it was awesome but I didn't like it as much as Crown of Midnight or Throne of Glass. I felt there was little action. I dunno. Maybe I'll change my mind someday.

It was a bit more fragmented than the previous books, but thus more encompassing. We got to follow three different threads and six different people. The evil has to be more evil to let the good side stay good even if they make decisions that aren't pure good.

I'm falling on live with this series as it is so far beyond my expectations of it. 
 Celeana has really come into her own in these past two books and it's glorious. 
 "She was the heir of ash and fire, and she would bow to no one...." 
 She's so broken I can feel her slipping away and am never truly sure that she's ever coming back, and yet her spirit is ever healing, changing and growing.
