reference_books.title: Red Queen (Red Queen, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Ever since the Hunger Games, we've seen the rise of a character I like to call the Super Special Revolution Girl. 
 The SSRG narrates in the first person, but does not spend a lot of time on introspection. She has mad crazy awesome abilities, but not a lot of time is spent on how she got them. She is in every way a cool girl, stabbing and bashing and brawling with the boys and never asking for stuff she has every right to demand. She is thrust into the spotlight in an unlikely way. She is white and ordinary looking. Every boy is in love with her. As is, in fact, the whole country. She is leading the revolution seemingly without effort - despite having no charisma, not being particularly bright, and lacking formal combat training, she is the one the world looks to for guidance. She is 16. 
 She is Tris in Divergent. She is Cinder in Cinder. She is Marguerite in that stupid time travel book I will not name because why give it traction and also I have forgotten what it is called. She is Lilac in these broken stars (post some initial character development). And she is utterly, in every way, Mare in Red Queen. 
 Don't get me wrong, I have no particular beef with the SSRG. I adored the original, Katniss, who managed to avoid most of the below tropes, and I devoured the entire Cinder series. But I feel we're reaching the peak of the character, and I have thoughts: 
 1/ Working hard for stuff is a cool and good thing to do 
 When I was a teenager, Tamora Pierce and her army of girl knights and mages were my idols. And while some of them do share traits with the super special revolution girl, there is a key difference between the two groups of characters. 
 An SSRG doesn't work for the power she has. With the exception of Katniss, who spent years avoiding starvation by hunting, they kind of all just...are. Even Cinder, who initially seemed like she knew some kind of useful crap, turns out to be a good mechanic because she has a computer screen in her brain. 
 While it can be boring to write, training for stuff is cool and good and I don't see how some of these characters are supposed to have gotten good at fighting with seemingly about ten minutes of instruction 
 2/ You can just ask people why they're white 
 WHY ARE ALL THESE GIRLS STRAIGHT AND WHITE? End of point 
 3/ Why do none of you have (legitimate) emotions? 
 Your village blew up, your parents are dead, you're stranded on a deserted planet, you're about to kill 1,000 people to save 10,000 lives. You and I would have feels/mental health issues about such things. But not that SSRG! She's just worried about which member of her love quadrangle gets to bang her when this is all over. 
 There's nothing wrong with feeling feelings, authors. Where are all the feelings? The ones not about boys, I mean. 
 In summation, Red Queen may be the most derivative yet of the SSRG genre. It's most interesting elements go literally nowhere and we spend all our time with it's most boring plot points. Forced child marriage? Ancient families with magic powers? A dad with a completely unique homemade machine keeping him alive? A secret underground organisation? Sounds great but let's spend the entire time talking about how boring balls are and deciding which prince I like more. 
 Two stars though for Mare's killer snark about Evangeline, the semi-interesting premise, and for straight up copying the character of Gail, who deserved more love from Katniss and frankly, from the world.

reference_books.title: Anna Karenina
reference_books.review_text:
I do honestly feel that for some people, the size of a book is an indicator of greatness - they'll give good reviews to anything over 600 or so pages because they feel so damned distinguished for having gotten through it all. And some writers seem to feel the same way about their work. 
 Somewhere, buried within this brick of a book is the greatest novel ever written. Unfortunately, it's so caked in Tolstoy's thoughts on the minutae of Russian agriculture and foreign policy that I couldn't find it. 
 There's so much beautiful language here, and the sections that centre around Anna's betrayal and its direct consequences to those around her were almost always fascinating. I flew through huge sections of it, only to come up against a hundred or more pages of debate about what to do about the muzhik problem because we're all soooo rich but somehow have more debt than the average Sydney homeowner. 
 Loved the characters, loved the symbolism, loved the story - but Tolstoy should really have just started a blog* and let his poor editor ditch some of his farm-based rants. 
 *Yeah, I'm not an idiot. Whatever the contemporary equivalent was

Jesus a fifth of the way through and I couldn't stand it anymore. I hate him/her but oh they're so pretty. The voices of the characters doesn't match their dialogue and Tarver definitely doesn't sound like the Tarver being debriefed/interrogated (whatever is going on between chapters). And everything happens so slowly, the parts with "action/suspense" not even quickening the pace of the plot. This just makes me want to stray from YA even more.

This book would have been a five star read for me if it wasn't for something that happened near the end. 
 Firstly I want to talk about how much I loved Lilac and Tarver both separately, and together. I found both to be entertaining, and although both did annoy me at certain bits, I understood where their choices and decisions came from. I loved the chemistry the pair had, and I like the slow burning romance at first ( although I wasn't too sold at the end with how much they depended on each other). 
 I loved the alien planet in the novel, and I loved how intriguing the mystery around it was, however I found the reveal to be a bit meh, and I'm still confused about a certain event that occurred near the ending of the novel. 
 Overall it was a pretty special book, and although I kinda fell into a slump for a week, I'm glad I stuck through it till the end.

What in the heck did I just read, and when can I read the next one?

What happens when you mix the wealthiest heiress in town with a handsome major who has been stationed on another base and doesn't know that she is off limits? Trouble and even more so when there is an accident that forces the two of them to flee a spaceship in distress and find a terra-formed planet where they appear to be the only survivors. The plot is very inventive and we have the budding romance that can't happen with the very real possibility that they may be the only people there for each other. Lilac LaRoux proves to be much more capable than we think a spoiled teen would be and Major Tarver Merendsen feels much more likeable and vunarable than we think he will be. The book is broken up with sections of Tarver's testimony so their survival seems a forgone conclusion. There is a paranormal link as well with Lilac's ability to hear whisperings that guide them but pull them into something they may not want to discover. Not for the preteens as there are adult situations but they are handled well. I was fortunate to get an advance of this book which is due to be published in early December.

What a wonderful, wonderful sci-fi book. Definitely one of my new favorites. I would rather give this a 4.8 for the typical "survival, stranded with a lover" plot but I love the eeriness of it. Very suspenseful and thrilling!

I'm hoping that books taking place "in space" will become the new IT thing to do in YA literature because I am a sci-fi girl at heart (and I'm kind of sick of dystopian novels). True, much of this book takes place after the main pair -- Tarver and Lilac -- have crash landed on a mysterious planet, so they're not exactly in space, as it were, but still. Yay for space books. 
 This book is extremely engrossing. There are so many mysteries to be solved: what are "the whispers" that keep tormenting Lilac? Why was the planet terraformed and then abandoned? What happened to the Icarus (the ship)? Some of your questions will be answered by book's end, but that only succeeds in raising more. I'm terribly curious as to the society in which these two belong. There is mention of colonies, and Tarver is in the military -- are the colonists revolting? Are colonies at war with each other? None of this information is deemed important in the grand scheme of things, and it's certainly not something with which Tarver and Lilac care to concern themselves, considering the circumstances, but I would like to know. 
 I'm quite enamored of Lilac, who seems to be a very complex character. She's not pigeon-holed into one particular category, as most female characters tend to be. Right off the bat we learn that she plays a role, acting like a spoiled princess in public and secretly fascinated by mechanical things. I appreciated that Tarver's surprise at her mechanical knowledge wasn't down to her being a girl, or even a pretty girl, but rather that she is such a public figure it didn't occur to him that she could have a hidden side. I also appreciated that Lilac's mechanical knowledge didn't make her into some perfect character -- she still had flaws and little to no survival knowledge, but she developed as they went along. 
 I wasn't quite as in love with Tarver. He's a fine person, I like him well enough, but he seems to be a fairly straightfoward character, which made him not quite as interesting to read about. As the book progresses, you can see him changing his opinions, going against preconceptions, and that was great. I like that he trusted Lilac enough to do the things he didn't have the knowledge for, and it was nice that he still treated her civilly after she humiliated him on the observation deck of the ship at the beginning. 
 Their relationship was, I thought, nicely done. It didn't feel shoe-horned in, as a lot of relationships in YA novels tend to be. They found each other attractive at first, which is why he approached her on the ship, but they didn't experience inexplicable feelings of attachment after only one glance. Instead, their relationship grew out of their circumstances -- thrown together in a harsh environment and dependent on each other for survival, their relationship naturally progressed. Granted, it progressed at a more accelerated timeline than normal, but I think that's down again to their circumstances. 
 I enjoyed this book immensely and am eagerly anticipating the next book in the series. Also, as a side note, the cover is GORGEOUS. Even if I hadn't heard so many good things about this book before purchasing, I probably would have picked it up based on the cover alone.

Well paced and well rendered, but I found myself skimming through a lot of the internal stuff after a while -- OK WE GET IT YOU'RE IN LOVE WITH HIM/HER BUT YOU'RE NOT SURE HOW HE/SHE FEELS IN RETURN. Also, those little scenelets of interrogation got super old super fast. But, all told, it was good. I like Lilac and Tarver. Yay.

** spoiler alert ** 
 The cover of this novel is gorgeous. I was tempted to buy a hardcover just because it's so pretty. I'm glad I didn't!! The cover and the first couple chapters are pretty much the only good thing about this novel. I was excited going in, but disappointed and annoyed by the end. 
 I don't think I've ever seen such shoddy world building. And I'm not a stickler about world building. Just give me something. If there are a few holes, I'll fill in the blanks. But there were so many things in this book that just didn't make any sense at all, and they seemed to be there for no apparent reason except the authors decided it was so. I'm going to try not to get too in depth with this, because I could go on for awhile, but an example or two... 
 The upper class apparently have balls and wear corsets and big ball gowns and tails and top hats. They have rooms that are replicas of early 1900 architecture and even lighting. The Icarus was essentially the Titanic in space. But they have tons of money and electricity and hover trays and all kinds of technology. So why is there wardrobe and way of interacting with each other reversed back to over a hundred years ago? No one knows. Meanwhile the peasants wear like jeans and stuff but they have no electricity and live very primitively. Except like Tarver's mom and dad who were a poet and a college professor by trade. If they were as rural and "backwoods" as Tarver portrayed them wouldn't they have been small farmers or laborers? Anyway, basically nothing added up. I couldn't ever figure out why the lower class would have no electricity. They didn't seem to be all that poor and certainly weren't downtrodden or starving. I also couldn't figure out if the upper and lower classes even shared the same planets. 
 On the planet that Tarver and Lilac crash on, there is ONE mountain lion and that's it? If the planet was abandoned and mountain lions are the only predator wouldn't it be overrun? Or wouldn't they have all died off because there is no mention of any other kind of animal except "small burrowing things" that didn't sound like they'd be enough to sustain mountain lions long term? Okay, two examples is enough. But there were a lot more. 
 After the big crash, which happens fairly quickly, the book is just Tarver and Lilac wandering alone on this abandoned planet. Nothing else really happens to them. It's not even an interesting, unique planet. They could have been wandering through any random forest down here on regular old earth, except they probably would have run across more predators. Up until about half way through I was interested and even intrigued. Then things started to get a little weird and ridiculous. There was so much potential for Tarver and Lilac to interact, bicker, learn from each other, grow as characters. But instead they just started to seem more and more flat the more time we spent with them. There was more chemistry between them in their first meeting than there was in the rest of the novel, in my opinion. I wouldn't classify their romance as a "slow burn" because really nothing was happening until almost the end when they finally decided "hey I found you attractive before and we've been alone for so long, now we're about to be rescued and split up again, let's get together while we can!" 
 I didn't like the way the "relationship" was handled at all. It all seemed so weird and arbitrary. They were attracted to each other for seemingly no reason. They had absolutely nothing in common. Neither one really had much of a personality at all. And if it was such a huge deal that no one think Tarver was involved with Lilac (like it could cost him his LIFE) why did they find it necessary to sleep together? Gonna be hard to hide the fact that they were together when she ends up pregnant with his child. None of that was even addressed. And frankly after the 'big twist' the only thing that saved the book from a trip across the room was the fact that it was on my Kindle. The whole thing was beyond ridiculous at that point. And was I the only one uncomfortable with the fact that the post explosion Lilac wasn't really Lilac at all? It bugged me SO much that Tarver held on to her so hard knowing that she was really just an imitation. I'm not even going to go into how little sense all that made. I only finished this book because I was seemingly so close to the end by the time I'd had enough. I wanted to see how it ended. It was a real struggle to get through the last quarter of the book though. Promising start that ended in a convoluted mess. 
 www.wanderingthepages.tumblr.com

3,5

In prima jumatate se repeta scenele la nesfarsit (mergem, suntem obositi, ridicam tabara, nu ne suportam, nu te poti apropia de mine), dar pe urma a devenit mai alert si interesant, dar nu suficient cat sa ma faca sa astept cu nerabdare urmatorul volum. love it so far

Easily this reader's least-favorite of all four books in the series, New Moon does show a degree of style growth as we're introduced to a storytelling shift from the first book: Dual-POV. Not only are we given Bella's first-person perspective, but also Jacob's. Edward features little throughout most of the story (aside from Bella's semi-hallucinating moments brought on by self-inflicted danger--in which some semblance of her own conscience/common-sense seems to manifest as Edward, with the request that she STOP risking her safety.) Sound a little insane? Well, to be fair to realism, I've known few teenagers in love who weren't leaning pretty far over the cliff-o-craziness... 
 I digress. 
 At a base level, New Moon is a highly emotional YA urban fantasy continuation revolving around an inadvertent love-triangle--and a girl who deals with her relational co-dependency in less than healthy ways. Readers are also allowed inside the head of a somewhat whiny male protagonist, who happens to be going through some physiological changes that make puberty look like a hormonal walk in the park. The world-building expands to encompass both vampires and shapeshifters, rounding out a far broader sense of conflict than was conveyed in the 'star-crossed lovers' plot of the first book. 
 While some have contended that Bella's period of depression was overly dramatic, there are many who may find her response entirely believable. For this reader, the primary detraction to enjoyment was spending too much time in Jacob's head. Purely subjective, to be sure, but the guy annoyed me. If this reader wanted to end up in any male's head, it would have been Edward's. (16-year-old male mind vs. 100-year-old male mind? Not really a contest, there. Just sayin'.) 
 I did appreciate the vampire socio-political aspects that came into play toward the end. The book managed to stand well on its own, while hinting more at future issues that would likely need to be faced.

One thing I need in a series is character progression - things happen, they change you, your outlook, mark you in some way. Sure Bella might have a scar on her hand, but she's still the same, still feels inferior. And then comes the breakup and I wanted to throw something. I disliked that Bella was so weak. I get being sad, I get loss, but I can't approve of letting go of life entirely. And she's wishy-washy. I liked the werewolves though - an interesting take on the mythology (and better than the sparkly vampires IMO).

reference_books.title: Looking for Alaska
reference_books.review_text:
This is the 2nd book I've read by John Green, the first being "The Fault in Our Stars" and though I didn't like that book very much, I thought I'd give Green another try. Sadly, I was disappointed with this book as well. 
 For some reason that I can't exactly put my finger on, I dislike this book. It was just...okay. This kid named Miles with a penchant for knowing famous people's last words moves from Florida to Alabama to attend a private high school. Although he didn't make many friends in Florida, he made a handful at Culver Creek, one most notable being Alaska Young, beautiful and mysterious. 
 [SPOILERS. READ AT YOUR OWN RISK.] 
 Miles, or now nicknamed Pudge, desires to find the Great Perhaps. What that is I have no idea and still don't know at the end of the book. I also had a feeling that someone would die and I suppose it had to be Alaska. She wasn't a very concrete character and maybe that was the point. I don't see why Pudge said he fell in love with her. I think he fell in love with the idea of her rather than who she was because she wasn't really someone you could figure out. 
 I didn't care for any of the characters in this book. I felt no attachment, nothing to make me actually keep turning the pages outside of "I want to finish this book so I can read another one." 
 I suppose the one thing I did appreciate was the friendship between Alaska, the Colonel, Pudge, Takumi, and even slightly Lara. They cared enough about her to come to a conclusion about Alaska's death (although I'm a quite obsessive way).

reference_books.title: Royal Bastards (Royal Bastards, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Thank you to NetGalley and Disney-Hyperion for giving me a free, digital copy in exchange for an honest review. 
 This book has been on my radar since I first heard about it. While I felt the synopsis gave a lot away, IaEUR(tm)m always up for a YA fantasy, and thankfully, this book didnaEUR(tm)t let me down. It was a near perfect read for me. It was a quick and easy read, too. Nothing too complicated, and nothing that felt like info-dumping either. I finished this book in a matter of days, and already I hope thereaEUR(tm)s a sequel planned. While reading this book, I had a funny thought though: I had heard next to nothing about this book, whether it be on the #bookstagram community or Twitter, which is really sad because if you enjoy fantasy, youaEUR(tm)ll enjoy this book. 
 There isnaEUR(tm)t anything too complex about this novel. The world-building is good, and there may have been times I became confused but I think itaEUR(tm)s mainly because there was no map in the eARC version. (Was there one in the physical ARC? Can someone help me out there?) The protagonists are all enjoyable characters, and I liked the internal conflict Tilla, the main character, felt as the story progressed. 
 What started as a group of unknowns bastards quickly became a tight-knit group of friends (despite the plot twist, which I didnaEUR(tm)t see coming! IaEUR(tm)m horrible at guessing those). I also wasnaEUR(tm)t expecting the amount of feels when Zell, the Zitochi warrior, shared his story. But I think IaEUR(tm)ve found another OTP so heyyyyy, IaEUR(tm)m not complaining! dY~%0 Princess Lyriana came to be one of my favorite characters, too. Despite being only fifteen and a bit childish in the beginning, it becomes obvious she hasnaEUR(tm)t seen a lot of hardship and of course has lived a fairly pampered life. n the beginning, I wasnaEUR(tm)t sure how I felt about Princess Lyriana, but IaEUR(tm)m glad she came to prove her own. In her case, I loved the magical aspect of this book, the idea of mages, rings, and different types of magical schools. This is why IaEUR(tm)m hoping for a sequel because IaEUR(tm)d love to see this explored in later books. 
 Some might say this book is predictable, and while we see the good guys persevere as usual, as I said before, IaEUR(tm)m horrible at predicting things or looking out for plot twists, so I found myself unable to put this book down. However, I did wish there was a bit more descriptions, not in terms of world-building but just in terms of everyday things: buildings, the outdoors, etc. 
 I enjoyed the action, too, and author did well putting obstacles into the characters way. When I felt like something dragged, an event or scene came to change my mind and rile me up again. IaEUR(tm)ll definitely add this book to my own library when itaEUR(tm)s released!

reference_books.title: Gone Girl
reference_books.review_text:
I'm pretty sure I have a love/hate relationship with this book. About 25 pages in, I was ready to put it down because the relationship between Go and Nick was just plain weird to me. 
 Nick and Amy Dunne have been married for five years and on the morning of their 5th anniversary, Amy disappears. Nick is absolutely flabbergasted and even more so as the strange events keep happening. Each year for their anniversary, Amy puts in a treasure hunt, leaving clues for Nick, clues that have something to do with their past, but this is one treasure hunt and one anniversary that Nick, and Amy, will most likely never forget. 
 Let's just say, this book reminded me why I don't like to read generic fiction books. 
 [POSSIBLE SPOILERS. READ AT YOUR OWN RISK.] 
 I have to admit that I sort of guessed where the whole treasure hunt thing would lead, especially after I really thought there was no clear evidence that Nick did in fact kill Amy. And for a moment, I did feel sorry for Amy and then more so for Nick. Nick isn't actually the crazy one, it's really Amy. And Amy isn't just crazy, she has a serious psychological problem. Nick is just absolutely normal. 
 After all the big stuff blew over, I kept thinking, "So because Nick and Amy have two different stories, a lie detector isn't going to be brought in at all?" I thought, "HOW STUPID." 
 What's even more idiotic is that Nick and Amy resume life like nothing even happened. Nick becomes a weak man, afraid of his wife (for good reasons) and they just go on pretending to live like before her disappearance. I didn't know who to root for. 
 I have never read such a twisted book before. I was taught in creative writing classes, never to connect the author and the characters in the story but for this, I just can't even help it. Who would write stuff like this? (This probably sounds extremely snobbish.) And then in the acknowledgements, Flynn says hello to her kid and basically tells him to not read this book until he's older. I can't even deal with that. 
 I didn't like the ending because I really didn't think there was enough closure. There was a lot of action throughout the book and then it died for me...just sort of kaput with no great ending. I wouldn't recommend this book to anyone, and I'll just stay out of general fiction for a very long time.

reference_books.title: The Star-Touched Queen (The Star-Touched Queen, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
You can read a spoiler-free review on my blog! :) 
 Actual rating: 3.5 stars 
 This book was one of my most anticipated releases for April. I was very excited to start reading this and truthfully, I wasn't wholly disappointed. The magic and fantasy elements in this novel were amazing. The writing was splendid, poetic even, weaving magic through my mind. Yet I still think... I don't know. That maybe it is missing something. Maybe it's just because I know this is a debut novel from a debut author... Regardless, this is a lush, fantastical story, tying together mythology and fantasy to create a gorgeous setting and decent cast of characters. 
 Possible spoilers below. Read at your own risk. 
 I cannot brag enough about the magic and the setting of this novel. It's gorgeous and Chokshi did an amazing job tying in mythology with real world (historical world?) settings. It reminded of Alice in Wonderland and the Chronicles of Narnia with like Harry Potter too. I was enthralled and loved every minute of it. 
 The few things I did have problems with were the characters. I felt like there was a deep lack of character development and familial relationships between Maya and her family, Maya and Amar, and even Maya and Nritti. I didn't think there was enough to make me feel anything for the characters. The moment I did was the moment Maya was whisked away to another place. This time with Amar. 
 I appreciated Maya's quick thinking but her naivety irked me. How could she so easily believe Nritti? I understand that she struggled to love Amar and I even appreciated her pull to Amar since he was a means for her to escape her fate with her father. I was also able to better understand their connection once the story progressed and the readers learn they are connected on deeper level. 
 I loved Kamala though! Talking animals are always fun. I wished there was more time with Maya and Gauri, I think then I would connect more with the meeting they had years later. 
 I also liked that Maya had what I would call a journey of self-discovery. She was stripped of almost everything so she had to find herself, disassociate herself with Nritti and Amar and revisit her old life though no one knew who she was. It helped shaped her as a stronger character, giving her a better belief in herself and I think, overall, the power to conquer Nritti and regain Amar. 
 It'll be interesting to see what else Chokshi writes.

reference_books.title: Uprooted
reference_books.review_text:
Ugh. If I see a book with a nice synopsis, I'm just going to stop reading reviews on it...or SOMETHING. 
 Step 1: See pleasant book sitting in the "new" section of the bookstore. 
 Step 2: Check Goodreads for ratings and reviews. 
 Step 3: Check out book from library because I'm INDECISIVE. 
 Step 4: Start reading. Quiet unsure of things. Don't like main character. Or ANYTHING for that matter. 
 Step 5: Stop reading at chapter 18 because I. Just. Can't. Do It. Anymore. 
 It's true, guys. I picked up this book after reading and seeing some of my favorite reviewers give it a great rating with a nice review. So I started and I thought, "Okay, maybe this just takes a bit." 
 Halfway into it, I realize, as I have many times before, that life is wasted reading books you can't get into. For DAYS I've struggled to like this book, to relate to the characters, to be CAPTIVATED by the writing. 
 Alas, no. Just no no no. 
 I've never read anything by Novik before so I did some research and saw that she wrote a nicely rated and reviewed series. Okay, cool, I can dig that. 
 Sadly, I can't dig the book. Sure, I like descriptions. But I need words, too. I need the characters to speak. I don't need to be reminded in nearly every chapter that the main character always seems to get dirty. I don't like that I don't even understand how magic works in this place. I can't even bring myself to like the Dragon. I mean, I'm more than halfway in, he should have some sort of redeeming quality, right? 
 The quick scene between the main character and Dragon, their brief kiss and his hands flying up her skirts, didn't even get me excited. You know why? Because where in the world is this romance even based? The two practically hate each other. UGHHHHHH. 
 So I'm done now. I'm not motivated at all to find out what happens simply because I just don't care. Actually, I never cared. So there.

book_a.title: Longbourn
book_a.user_review:
There was a small debate within myself for maybe a brief second as to whether or not to give this book 2 stars instead of 1. What would I tell people if they asked me about? Sure, it was okay, but I still didn't like it. I can't tell people, "If you like Pride and Prejudice, then read this book" because that's certainly not the case. I know there are novels that explore further into the main characters of Pride and Prejudice and nothing that says anything about the servants or the like. But despite that, I think this book could have been written about any servants/household staff in any other middle-class family such as the Bennets. Using Austen's beloved characters as a selling point--perhaps that's what happened. 
 I admit that I was excited to get my hands on this book, considering its' contents and that it explored the world of the servants. Lately, servant life from this time era and on has intrigued me. Sadly, this novel was in no way what I expected it to be. I was not thrilled or enthralled while reading the story of Mrs. Hill, her husband Mr. Hill, or of Sarah and Polly the housemaids. Even the footman, James's mysterious entrance into the household staff held no enticement for me. I thought Sarah's suspicions of him held no ground or merit. In all honesty, I wanted to know a bit more of what the servants thought about their mistress' situation and there was but a smidgeon of that. 
 [Possible spoilers. Read at your own risk.] 
 I know that things for servants of this era weren't exactly fine and dandy, and that even for the Bennets, it certainly wasn't fine and dandy either. But Miss Baker showed the characters in such a harsh light. I mean, what happened between Mr. Bennet and Mrs. Hill in their younger days most likely happened in real life to many men and women. I didn't care that Mr. Bennet was tainted in that way. I didn't like Baker's portrayal of Elizabeth. She seemed harsh, especially after she married and went to Pemberly. I understand that Lizzy was scared and nervous but she didn't handle it nearly as well as Austen's Lizzy would have. Even though Wickham isn't a great person anyway with great character, he was shown in such a harsh light that I grew to dislike him even more. 
 Anyways, off point because it's not necessarily about the Bennets. I was confused in some parts because of the time. It went back in time and it took me a while to realize that they spoke of James the footman instead of some random other character. And then I realized it was telling back story. And maybe that's the problem, there was a lot of "telling" instead of "showing." I like descriptions, don't get me wrong, but I also love dialogue and I certainly felt this story lacked dialogue. 
 Nonetheless, I won't recommend this book to a friend, and I'm quite glad that I checked it out from the library instead of buying it like I had originally wanted.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This review and others posted over at 
 my blog. 
 While the Bennet family worries about who will marry whom and how their estate will be entailed, should Mr. Bennet pass away, the running of the household is left to Mrs. Hill and the young maids, Polly and Sarah. The washing, the cooking, the cleaning, all go unnoticed throughout Pride and Prejudice, but realistically those who lived to serve did not have an easy life. 
 From page one of this book, where Baker is disgustingly describes laundry day, I was interested. This book sheds a new light on the life of one of my favorite heroines, Elizabeth Bennet, and that of her family. Never once did I think about the work involved in running the Bennet household or preparing their many daughters for the ball. While they are portrayed as "poor" (especially in comparison to the Bingleys and Darcys), they still employ several servants to cook and clean for them and tend to their whims. While Hill and Sarah and Polly are not abused or starved, they do not live free, comfortable lives. Sarah chafes against her lifestyle - no moment of the day is her own. 
 I especially enjoyed how Baker fleshed out Mary and Mr. and Mrs. Bennet. The love story between Elizabeth and Darcy and Jane and Bingley takes a backseat, while readers are given insight into the daily lives of a family of their station. Mary is given a bit more of a personality, and Mr. Bennet has quite a backstory. 
 I certainly see one of my favorite books in a new light after reading this book. It was thoroughly engrossing and an excellent companion novel for fans of Pride and Prejudice. If you've never read the novel, the plot does contain some spoilers, but the story does focus on the life the servants, and if you're interested in historical fiction, I would recommend this.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I honestly considered giving this just one star, but there were some really beautiful bits so, it earned one back. 
 The first half of Longbourn was really enjoyable. I loved seeing the play between upstairs/downstairs in a story I love so much. But after about that first half, the book takes a big departure. It goes back in time, explains back stories and relationships and... I think I wouldn't have minded that so much if it'd been introduced sooner. I felt like the book went from being Sarah's story to being a lot less focused. I REALLY wish the flashbacks to pre-Pride And Prejudice storyline had started waaaay earlier in the book. They felt like a departure from the tone/style of the first half. 
 The ending was enormously unsatisfying, and actually pretty hard for me to buy in to. 
 It's unfair to compare any author to Jane Austen - but if you're going to set your book in the world of a Jane Austen book, it would make sense to me to at least try and capture some of the tone and humor of her world. The occasions when the servants of Longbourn interact with any of the Bennet sisters feels *shrug* kind of fake. Like, THESE aren't the characters I know and love. Who are these people? I didn't feel like many of Austen's characters were captured accurately here. Mr. Bennet's wry humor/annoyance wasn't there. Lizzy's spirit was boiled down to "she's really pretty". 
 There was also just TOO much information. The slave trade? The war in spain? Mr. Bennet's dallyings with the housekeeper? Illegitimate Bennets? It was all over the place. 
 I also failed to understand Sarah's motivations towards the end. She definitely grows as a character - you see her go from sort of punky late teen to decisive woman. That's great. But, (and here be spoilers) I did NOT understand why she decided to leave Pemberley at the end. It would have been so dangerous and foolish to just be a woman living on the road with a knapsack at that time. Like... unimaginable. And she just walks away from a comfortable, safe situation and then just happens to track James down on a road? I just... gah. It doesn't make sense in the time and place.

Loved every single second of this book, fully, completely. Found it to be a brilliant, and well written, counterpoint to the many Austen "fandom" titles. Longbourn is a rich tapestry of the life beneath the pages of the beloved Pride and Prejudice, where the ladies have monthlies, laundry must be done weekly, and the business of the bathroom must be disposed with in the morning. Highly recommended.

I'm a huge Austen fan and I am always open to trying tributes/retellings/sequels. I am usually disappointed. 
 Not so in the case of Longbourn. The premise is interesting (although I must also admit that I love alternate viewpoints) and it seemed to be well researched. 
 I felt the author fit the major P&P plot points into the story well. Some fan favorite characters suffer from their plotlines and one undergoes a last-chapter personality change but the book is not really about them. 
 The two main quibbles I have with the book are: 
 -The lengthy and tedious detailing of James' back story. Yawn. 
 -Random cursing that seemed out of place and threw me out of the story to wonder if that was a phrase commonly used at that time. 
 I received an advanced reader copy of this book from the publisher in exchange for my honest review.

I love Jane Austin and find myself compelled to read every deriviative book that comes down the pike. Most of this copycat genre are really bad books - poorly written and trying to hard to capture Austin's magic. Jo Baker's book is an exception. She did a nice job of creating unique characters you care about, while successfully incorporating the original Pride and Prejudice characters we all know love. She created interesting story lines. Further, she obviously did her homework in regards to what life of servants would be like during this time period - her attention to detail was remarkable. 
 So why the 3 stars? Beware of spoilers*** 
 I really did not buy her two main plot twists. First, it seems inconceivalbe that Mr. Bennet would continue to hide a male heir after having five daughters. Surely, he would have had enough residual care for his wife and single daughters than to leave them to the whims of Mr. Collins. Second, when Sarah was departing from Elizabeth, I find it hard to beleive that neither Darcy asked Sarah why she was leaving. With Mr. Darcy's resources, it would be a simple matter to track down James. This contrivance really took away from the overall novel.

It has a kind of interesting story. It doesn't feel like the time period and that may be because the author is depicting a part of the time period that is so different than the feel of Pride and Prejudice. The only similarity to Pride and Prejudice is the names of the characters. I know the author is giving another side to the story, and perhaps because the story of "below stairs" is so different, it isn't at all reminiscent of Pride and Prejudice. I waited a couple of months for this to be available through the library. I just didn't enjoy it at all and had a hard time getting through to the end.

Read for our book club. I enjoyed what it added to the Pride and Prejudice story, though I felt like the it took sometime for the novel to hit it's stride. It was honest and a little graphic, and because of that I was a little disappointed by it's clean ending. The romance didn't do a lot for me, though I did enjoy that the love triangle was never a full out brawl that other media tends to make those situations.

For starters I really liked the premise of this book, it offered a different perspective on a story anyone interested in Austen already knows intimately. Unfortunately there were a few thnigs I believe could have been sorted out better. 
 I liked that Longbourne has its own narrative- It doesn't waste time repeating events from Pride (except for a phrase or two at the beginning of each chapter, so as to guide the reader on what was happening with the Bennets) and instead focuses solely on what happens to its own characters, which I really appreciated since I wasn't really looking for a recycled version of the novel. 
 Characterization-wise, some were more interesting than others, although to me the main couple happened to be the blandest during most of the story. I found it difficult to connect with Sarah and had the same issue with James, although that changed by the second half. On the other hand, Mrs. Hill was one of the most interesting, tragic creatures I have read in a while. I loved how the author managed to develop a storyline for her that felt as believable as it was compelling. 
 As to the plot, there were some things I found quite refreshing but didn't feel completely necessary for the storyline. The main couple's development felt quite modern as to pacing and while that usually has consequences, in this case nothing changed because for their actions. Because I was expecting those events to happen, I found it odd but fresh when they did not, although the lack of events made the general pacing in the second half feel a bit slower. 
 There were a few wasted opportunities as well: the whole chain of events that lead to James discovery at the end seemed a bit too luck-dependant for my taste. I would have preferred Sarah to get on with it and make some detective work instead of sitting on her hands and expecting some information to fall on her lap (which it did, eventually). There was little character development as well on her part during the final stretch- no self-discovery or catharsis-, which I found disappointing because I felt that there could have been a more evident maturing process for her, some change in her after what she lived through. 
 All in all, it is intended to be viewed as a 'b side' of the original novel and it delivers perfectly on that part, but on a personal level I think it wasted a chance to go a bit further and offer the reader some development of its own characters, especially during the final chapters which are set after Austen's ending and are a point in which the reader is already emotionally invested in most of the characters.

It's a charming idea - a look at the harsh realities behind the gilded lives of the Bennetts (no matter how badly done by they may think they are, they are of course remarkably privileged) and the prose is quite lovely. It does sometimes get bogged down in the detail - you feel the author has done so much research she's keen to show it off - so it's slightly more slow moving than it could be. Definitely worth reading though.

The title Pride and Prejudice could literally translate to "Rich People Problems." If you find your hand reaching up to clutch your pearls at that statement, please go re-read "Darcy and Lizzie Make Out In a Barouche, vol. 152." Because Jo Baker is a badass, and not for you. 
 Listened to the audiobook, mostly while preparing for Thanksgiving. Good company while dealing with domestic concerns, especially if you want to feel thankful for indoor plumbing and recognizable meat products. I would love to see this made into a Downton Abbeyesque mini-series, because it deals so beautifully with characters who tend not to get their due in adaptations - Mary Bennett, Mrs. Bennett, and Mr. Collins in particular. Perfect antidote to all of the cloying Jane Austen fanfic out there, and a good reminder that it takes an army of servants, a ton of beauty privilege, and the mother-effin' slave trade to create the world Austen fans have so romanticized.

book_b.title: Traveling Mercies: Some Thoughts on Faith
book_b.user_review:
I feel as if I must say a few things before I write this review. This is the first book I've ready by Anne Lamott and only had it in hoes to back of my mind since I heard it somewhere a few years back. Perhaps mentioned by Donald Miller ("Blue Like Jazz") or something mentioned by the organization, To Write Love on Her Arms. Either way, I don't know what I was expecting when I read this and considering I don't read a lot of memoirs, I suppose I really wasn't expecting much. 
 Lamott writes about many things I've never dealt with personally (granted I'm only 25), but considering what little I know about the time she grew up in, her childhood seemed common among her peers and when she found something radically different, she clung to it, like her childhood friend's mother. But she has a family who is dysfunctional without realizing it and perhaps we can say the same for our own families. Lamott's younger days were a whirlwind of drugs, pills, and booze, and in a sense, I really don't think she began life until her son, Sam, was born. Admitingly, there were struggles and we all have them. 
 As for her faith, I was just a bit confused. Some of the things she said were great, and I could relate to them, but she says God is either "her/him" and yet she mentions Jesus and I just feel maybe Miss Lamott is confused. I really wouldn't necessarily agree with the subtitle of "Some Thoughts on Faith" as much as this is really a commentary in her life. Laugh, I know, because that's what memoirs are in a sense, but the faith... I understand how it worked in her own way (as faith does individually) and I really do like her God In Box idea. And perhaps I say this because it's somewhat different from the faith I have. I'm not overly religious but. God and Jesus play an essential role in my life. 
 I guess I can say, "Whatever works for you" or "Whatever makes you feel better" but I sort of feel that to be a cop-out, sadly. I suppose, too, that this book isn't for me.. I hate to say that somehow I can't relate because that just sounds ridiculous and prudish, but I felt as I had to be a somewhat older audience to appreciate the book more. However, this does not mean I will give up on Lamott. I will just read something else.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Would recommend: Yes 
 A really interesting view on a faith journey. A short, introspective read.
Great stories.
This book came highly recommended and everyone I know enjoyed it, I for some reason, had difficulty getting through it.
This book reminds me of what I said about my mom's church: it's like a song I enjoy, but it's not the song of my heart. Her chapter on grace was my favorite.
What's not to love about Anne Lamott. She gives us permission to be human while we seek and fall and get back on our feet again.

This is a memoir in a way, but each chapter is a separate autobiographical story. In each chapter some spiritual aspect connected to faith comes up. 
 It seems that the stories are kind of chronological. The book starts with the time before the author became a Christian when she had lots of problems with addiction. She becomes a single mother and there is a church where she is accepted and loved in her messed up state and she's slowly transformed. By the end of the book her son Sam is eight years old and of course he's part of many of the stories. 
 I liked the book. She's definitely not the "perfect Christian", but her struggles and the humor and insight with which she writes about her experiences are refreshing (after she overcomes her addictions) although sometimes I had the urge to shout a warning at her. Don't expect any really deep insights, but her experiences are kind of interesting.

I love the review on the cover of this book that says "Anne Lamott is walking proof that a person can be both reverent and irreverent in the same lifetime. Sometimes even in the same breath." (San Francisco Examiner and Chronicle). EXACTLY. 
 This is essentially an examination of Anne's journey to spirituality and religion, but made colorful and interesting by her interweaving of life stories including her own addiction and eating disorder history, watching her best friend die of cancer, etc. Sounds dreary but in addition to making me shed a tear or two, this book is laugh-out-loud funny. And wise. I think she's a great writer.
I could have done without the strong language early in the book, but the reflections were amusing aside from that.
Such a beautiful memoir about life and faith! I have passed this along as gift to many..

Okay, look. I know it's basically blasphemy to claim a progressive Christian identity and say this, but I don't like Anne Lamott's writing. I like some of her blog posts and quotes but I just cannot get into her books. I find them to be annoying. I tried to read Some Assembly Required when I was in high school and I could not get through it. I let a few years pass and thought, hey, I just need to get into her writing that centers more on faith, since that's what all my friends recommend anyway. But I'm calling it, I can't get through this one either. I'll try Anne again in a few years but I think she's just not my taste.

Mixed feelings about this book. 
 My stars are based on: 
 1) The story. The essence of it- I liked it.. VERY MUCH. 
 2) The change in the main male character. The initial innocence of Elder is so fresh compared to most YA novels bad-boy prototype, it kept marveling me D: 
 2/5) THE UNIVEEEEERSE! (I'm a Space Freak, can't really help it, so I'm just adding a 0.5) 
 3) The scenario in general. The way the ship works, the technology, and it's levels, kept my mind racing a bazillion light years away. 
 Those are my 3.5 stars to it. It leaves the other 1.5 to: 
 *THE FREXING AGES! Ugh.. 
 *The romantic development between Amy and Elder- or whatever it's called. I mean, HOW CAN YOU ALREADY LOVE EACH OTHER WHEN SHE'S JUST BEEN KHBGKHBGK- stupid. I think it all comes back to the ages. Like, 16 and in love? Really? 
 Overall, it was well written and I enjoyed going through both their versions of the story (: Even if I kinda hated the fact that my favorite character almost always isn't likable to others, or gets killed in books, including this one.
Ok I give up on this one too. I've read the first five chapters and I can't take it any more. I love Sci-Fi so I thought I'd like the whole space thing but I can't take it any more. Sorry.

I had read a lot about this book, so I was expecting a lot. Was I disappointed? Yes, a little. Was it good? Yes, it was. The story is well written. The plot is interesting. I may not usually like science fiction, but this one caught my attention. I found it hard at first to get into the book. Once I did, I couldn't put it down. 
 You end up liking Elder and Amy, hating Eldest, and feeling confused about other characters. I don't want to give any spoiler, so I will be short. This book is worth reading, even if you don't really enjoy science fiction. Why? Because it is easy to forget that it is. It is about figuring out the truth. This is what matters (and of course, finding if something will happen between Elder and Amy.) 
 One of the thing that slightly annoyed me was that there are two narrator. I don't know why, but it bugged me. Still, once I got over that, I really enjoyed reading it. 
 I would totally recommend it. Good book, good story. It is to add to your list, because it probably isn't the last time you will hear about Beth Revis.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Amy is a strong, vibrant character. Immediately, I sympathized with her and wanted her to be able to run under an open sky. Because of this, it got REALLY hard to read through the middle and end of the book--especially when I realized that the situation was going to get worse without relief. It was gut wrenching to watch it all go down in the end. A bit of a depressing ending. 
 It didn't have to be a happy ending--but I think some smaller victories for the character I loved so much would have helped. I'll have to read the next book to find out.
This book was really inappropriate an should be rated R.

Review 7 out of 5 
 Seventeen-year-old Amy and her family leave Earth to colonise a planet which is 300 years away. But she is brutally woken fifty years before she was supposed to be. Amy feels so alone, but there is someone who wants to protect her. Elder is sixteen, but he is to be the new leader of "Godspeed" when it's his time. 
 Can Amy and Elder unravel the secrets and lies and get to the truth? Can they find the killer before more lives are lost? 
 I absolutely LOVED this book! Those who know me know I very rarely, if ever, swear. BUT - O.M.G. - This book is fantastic! 
 I had heard on the review grapevine that it was good, but to me it's an understatement! This is one of the most exciting science fiction novels I have read in a long time! The characters are so life-like, that I couldn't believe that they only existed in the author's imagination. This book is told from both Amy's and Elder's point of view. 
 Amy is a typical teen, but she has to make a hard decision whether or not to join her parents on a 300 year journey to a new planet. She is very brave, because if I was in her position, I don't think I would go through with it. After being woken, she has to cope with her new reality. 
 Elder is a not so typical teen. He has been raised on ship to be the next leader. When Amy is woken up, he takes her under his wing, trying to protect her from an unknown murderer. 
 There are some other great characters in this book too. I especially liked Harley, Elder's friend. There are some disturbing issues brought up in this book, but I think that they (the issues) need to be examined and are quite relevant today, as I'm sure they were in the past and will be in the future. After I finished reading, I sat for a bit thinking "WOW, that's some story!". 
 Beth Revis has found a new fan in me, and I'm now looking forward to reading the sequel, A Million Suns. I highly recommend this book if you love YA/science fiction/adventure/action/mystery.

Actual rating 1.5 stars. 
 This was poorly written but the worst part was that she was a seven year old, not a teenager. It creeped me out, how can someone miss so bad in targeting the age?

Liked the premise, didn't care for the structure. Was engaged in the initial story, but lost interest after the jump ahead. 
 First in a trilogy I won't be reading.

This was an okay book. For my first YA Sci-Fi Novel, I was really expecting more... 
 Not to spoil it for anyone else, but I saw EVERYTHING that happened at the end of the book within the first half of the book. All of it. The revelations, the secrets, the reasons everything. It was kinda disappointing. 
 CHARACTERS: 
 Amy and Elder are the main characters and the novel jumps back and forth from their perspectives. Honestly, I didn't see much difference between their viewpoints. Both of them had the same narrative style, they just had better insight into some area of the story (which is fine, it just made it a little confusing resuming the read half-way through a chapter). 
 I was more than a little disappointed that neither character showed much development or change by the end of the story. Amy was still upset, and Elder was still confused and torn. The romance felt a little one-sided to me, and forced. 
 STORY: 
 A really novel (ha-ha) idea. I was really expecting more of a star-trek feel to the book, but was surprised when it kept reminding me of the Giver (dystopian, a ban on emotions and free thought, a single individual chosen to carry on duties as ruler, love interest with flaming red hair, etc.). The Giver freaked me out, but still, I pressed on. 
 There's a few moments that made me antsy in reguards to the sci-fi/YA world. The whole 'season' thing, I could have done without and I don't think the story would have suffered for it. And for those of you who have read it, i don' think Amy needed to go through what she did in the cornfield for the novel. I really didn't see the point. You traumatized her, and them moved on. Not realistic. 
 Finally, I should mention that there's and awful lot of characters talking about death and suicide. I mean, a lot. There's at least two characters who were referenced as having killed themselves, and it plays a big part in the story in two places. 
 OVERALL: 
 Worth it, but know what you're getting into. It's a good read. I'd say it's the giver in space. It's definitely not for the younger YA readers. I'd say 17+ for some of the subjects in it... I might read the next book. I haven't decided yet.

I was so hype for this book because everyone else seemed to be saying how great it was. While it was in fact great, it wasn't as enjoyable as I thought it would be. I still really liked it though :) 
 This is the story of Steffi, a 17 year-old high school girl with selective mutism and anxiety. On the first day of school, Steffi was introduced to Rhys, a new guy at school who was deaf. The school staff thought it would be great to pair them up, only because Steffi could speak BSL and therefore could help Rhys settled in. What started out as annoyance on Steffi's part quickly turned into happiness because Rhys is actually a really great and adorable guy. 
 From the very first chapter, I instantly connected with Steffi. Not because I share her condition, but simply because she's a very relatable person. That, and the fact that she has a really sarcastic sense of humor really charmed me. I loved how Sara Barnard explored Steffi's condition as a selective mute and as a person with anxiety, and how no matter how much she wants to get better, there's the fear of losing her sense of self if she suddenly be able to talk all the time. The way she described her anxiety, it was so easy to understand for someone like me. Between AQKOT and Queens of Geek, the book I just finished recently, books are doing really good job explaining anxiety. 
 Rhys is downright adorable, but I've said that before. He's so friendly, sweet, patient, and genuine, but now without his angsty side. Just like how it is with Steffi, being deaf plays a hugeee part of Rhys' life. It's not all he is, but it is a central part. I love seeing how he navigates between both worlds, the hearing world and the deaf world, and how sometimes everything just frustrates him beyond belief. It was all so real. Reading about Rhys also made me realize that as a hearie, there are so many offensive things I could do without realizing that they are in fact, offensive. Things like raising my voice when talking to a deaf person, talking too fast, or not looking at them while talking. This is all so important and I'm glad the book managed to touch these issues effortlessly. 
 Their relationship is both simple yet complicated at the same time. The way they understand each other? It was effortless. But there's also the barriers, starting from the most basic one like how Rhys can't hear and Steffi can't talk, to the usual couple problems of miscommunication. I love reading their texts, super adorable and I really think texting is one of the most exciting element of a new relationship. It's also nice to see that although they bonded over their limitation in communication, it's not the reason why they are in love with each other. 
 And I think... every couple can relate to their problems, because their problems aren't exclusive to deaf, selective mute, and anxious people. Misunderstanding, insecurity, saying things we don't actually mean, it could happen to every couple. It does, actually, so it's kind of nice to see that even if Steffi and Rhys have their own situation, it doesn't always have to be the source of the problems. Obviously, I'm not trying to downplay their struggles and say that it's not a big deal, because it is. 
 Let's not forget that friendship and family also play a big role in Steffi's life. I love her relationship with Tem and the conflicts within it. It's wonderful and multi-dimensional. And her family, albeit far from perfect, is a realistic portrayal of family life. I love Steffi's dad, Lucy, and her mum, though she's definitely not my favorite person in the book. Also, also, cheers to how much animal appreciation there is in the book! I feel like I love Rita <3 
 I also appreciate that being with Rhys doesn't automatically cure Steffi from her anxiety nor selective mutism. I admit, I was so worried that there would be some romantic cure but as far as can tell, that's not what happened. Steffi gets better, but it's not only because of Rhys. Like the book said, it was a combination of medication, Rhys, and being 'forced' to go to school without Tem. I like how comprehensive it is because as far as I know, that's what actually happens in real life. A combination of things. 
 ALL IN ALL, A Quiet Kind of Thunder is a wonderful, quick read that effortlessly handles so many important issues. Deafness, selective mutism, anxiety, family, and friendship, among other things. On top of it all, this book is also incredibly sweet and adorable it would make you giddy with happiness. Highly recommended for a fan of realistic fiction contemporary :)

This books was everything everyone told me it would be. Cute, funny, SO MUCH character growth, romantic, diverse, and about learning how to work in a world that doesn't always make room for you.

There's a chance I'll change this to a five-star rating . . . Can't quite decide. I already know I want to read it again, and I'm thrilled to see that Goodreads has given it a series page, meaning at least one sequel will be happening. These are characters we needed--Hannah, Millie, Amanda, Ellen, even Bo--and especially Willowdean. 
 I found some of the more popular Goodreads reviews totally confusing on this front, because to me, Willowdean was a realistic and highly relatable character. She doesn't always act the way she should, even when she knows she's wrong, and if you're telling me that's never been true of you, I'm pretty sure you're lying. (Example: Objectively, what she said to Ellen about the pageant wasn't fair. But life isn't objective, and though I think Ellen was right in her response, I also think she should have been able to understand where Willowdean was coming from.) 
 Everyone thinks Will is more confident than she is, because she doesn't believe in making herself invisible to make others comfortable--but knowing something in your head doesn't mean your gut doesn't still struggle with it, and that internal voice was my favorite thing about her. When I say I want to read it again, it's because I think Julie Murphy really nailed those thought processes, the conversations Will has with herself when she's freaked out by a boy touching her backfat or whatever. I wasn't fat as a teenager, but I genuinely thought I was. Whether you're "actually" fat or not--whatever that even means, since it's a subjective concept anyway--most people can probably relate to that feeling, and the idea of being able to read along with someone else who's figuring it out is what makes this book fantastic.

OH MY WORD, THIS BOOK WAS A STRUGGLE TO GET THROUGH. Usually I don't actually finish one-star reads, but this one started out so good. So good. And somewhere along the way it all fell apart, though I can't quite peg where. This book was supposed to be about Willowdean, a beauty pageant, her fight with her best friend, and her clandestine sort-of relationship with her crush. That's what it started out as and that's what the blurb led me to believe it would be. BUT INSTEAD. Instead, the book meandered around, and not in a good way. Certain plots seemed to be dropped unceremoniously, only to be picked up many chapters later, once it seemed that the story was on a completely different course and I had nearly forgotten about the first plot completely. 
 I literally FORCED myself to make it through this book. I don't know why I did that.

This review is also on my blog, The Library Canary. 
 ***I received a free copy of this book from the publisher in exchange for an honest review. This has in no way influenced my opinion. The review below reflects my open and honest thoughts.*** 
 Do you ever stare into the mirror and nitpick every piece of your body? Do you ever wonder what other people see when they look at you? Do you ever get self-conscious when someone touches a part of you that you're not happy with? Do you hold yourself back from doing things that you want to because of body image issues? Like strutting around in a swimsuit? Or walking into a particular clothing store in the mall? Or even entering a beauty pageant? Who hasn't done all of these things at some point in their life? 
 I'm going to let you in on a secret. I'm not always the most confident person when it comes to my body. During college I put on some weight (who doesn't?) and I'm still slowly trying to take it back off. And sometimes I look in the mirror and am really unhappy. And Willowdean gets that. I was instantly able to connect with her. I've never been overweight like Will is, but I've had the same insecurities she does. And that's what I think people connect with in this book. The feeling of not being good enough. Will is actually pretty comfortable in her skin which was refreshing to read about. But once she starts dating hot guy Bo, she starts to question whether or not she's good enough for him. Which leads her to question whether or not she's good enough to compete in the beauty pageant. She is fighting against the knowledge that she should be comfortable in her own skin and the thought of Bo discovering all her imperfections. The internal struggle that Will goes through is something that everyone will be able to relate to and that's why I loved this book. 
 Julie Murphy made me laugh, made me cringe, made me clench my fists and made me cry during this book. There were so many different facets to Dumplin' that I enjoyed. There was a heart-breaking mother-daughter relationship that brought me to tears. Will's mom is not nice. I couldn't stand her for the whole book. But I could see her mom's own insecurities and they felt like kindred spirits to me. I knew that eventually they would get to an okay place with a lot of hard work because Will's mom understands her better than she thinks. There was a relationship between Will and her best friend, Ellen that was complicated and messy. Ellen is skinny and beautiful and Will feels like she's living in her shadow and slowly being left behind. I loved watching Will slowly realize that maybe she can't blame everything on Ellen. Maybe she has to shoulder some of the blame herself. 
 And then there was the Will and Bo relationship. I loved these two together. I loved how they both had to learn about relationships and the importance of fostering those relationships. Neither of them were perfect, far from it, and their relationship has a really rocky start. But the journey was fantastic and I got all the feels watching them slowly figure things out. 
 The pageant is actually not a huge focus of this book. We barely get any pageant stuff and I was happy with that. The focus is on Will and how her choice to participate is changing her entire outlook on herself and on others. The lessons she learns from competing are amazing and her transformation is a thing of beauty. I highly recommend this to anyone looking for a contemporary that will make you laugh and cry at the same time. If you want to learn how to accept yourself as you are, Willowdean can teach you a few lessons.

Quand j'ai decide l'annee derniere de relire ma petite collection que je possedais (qui depuis a grandit, c'est devenu un beau bebe de plus de 300 livres... hum), la saga des vampires vegetariens ne pouvait pas passer a travers les mailles du filet: elle aussi, je vais la relire. Sachant que le jour de ma premiere lecture, j'avais beaucoup apprecie cette saga, ma relecture cinq ans apres me semble amere, parce qu'aujourd'hui je n'aime plus cette saga. Je n'ai pas flanche face aux detracteurs qui n'ont vu que les films (et je vous comprends...), mais j'ai juste eu un oeil plus mature sur une saga que je n'aurais meme pas pris la peine de continuer a lire si elle etait sortie cette annee. 
 Reprenons l'histoire, et ce deuxieme tome qui annonce le triangle amoureux que nous aurons par la suite (et donc la gueguerre qu'on avait eu, team Edward ou team Jacob, guerre que je trouvais puerile a l'epoque). Un tome ou Bella va se faire larguer par son vampire, et qui va vivre pendant quatre mois en depression, et va tenter de s'accrocher a Jacob pour sortir la tete de l'eau. Mais ce n'est qu'une fois que ca va mieux, que Jacob devient un loup-garou et devient donc distant avec elle, pour se rapprocher ensuite de l'humaine, qui filera avec Alice pour retrouver Edward. Oui. Bon. Vu comme ca, c'est negatif. 
 Ce que je n'ai pas aime, c'est Bella. Se taper une depression parce qu'on se fait larguer apres six/sept mois de relation, faut pas exagerer non plus. Elle realise par la suite que si elle se met dans des situations quasi-suicidaires, elle entend la voix d'Edward, telle une hallucination, qui lui dit de ne pas faire de betises. Quelqu'un de normal fuirait ces hallucinations auditives, Bella les traquent, quitte a filer aux urgences ou etre sur le point de mourir. Et je trouve ca egoiste. Egoiste pour son pere, pour ses amis, sa famille, mais surtout hypocrite pour Jacob, qui n'est en faite que la roue de secours de l'humaine. Bella au final joue avec les sentiments de son pote loup-garou pour ne pas le perdre, comme la scene ou ils se revoient apres sa transformation et qu'il l'envoie bouler puissance x1000, et qu'elle lui fait le coup qu'elle peut essayer de tomber (en gros) amoureuse de lui pour qu'ils puissent continuer a se voir. Bon, Jacob tombe dans le panneau, mais c'est debile. Quant a sa relation avec les vampires, les prendre de haut comme elle fait (sauf avec les Volturi, dommage d'ailleurs...), alors que ce sont juste des betes assoiffees de sang qui peuvent la tuer, je ne m'y fait toujours pas. Sa volonte a devenir un vampire avant la menace m'enerve egalement, limite elle est avec lui juste pour se faire transformer, et ca je ne comprends pas. 
 Ce que je ne comprends pas surtout, c'est que l'auteur ecris tres bien. Elle a un vocabulaire riche (j'ai appris pas mal de mots en lisant Twilight, si, si, je vous assure), elle raconte bien son histoire, c'est poetise, c'est coherent, tous les autres personnages sont logiques et interessants, mais ses deux personnages principaux sont plats et detestables comme ce n'est pas permis. Et autre point incomprehensible pour moi, dans Midnight Sun (Twilight vu par Edward, jamais publie, mais trouvable sur internet), Edward ne me parait pas detestable, et est presente comme un etre torture, qui fait moins vampire-guimauve... Donc, je ne comprends pas pourquoi il me parait comme ca dans Twilight vu par Bella... 
 En bref, je n'aime plus cette saga, et je crois que je continuerais ma relecture uniquement si on me demande de les sortir de ma PaL. Sinon bah... Ils y resteront.

Continuing from my review of Twilight, I'm going to refute points that claim that Twilight is better than Harry Potter. 
 I repeat, I'm only posting this because I read this article. I'm literally only refuting the points mentioned in this, nothing else. I don't like comparison, but if the other party does it, be sure that I will respond. 
 REBUTTAL POINTS 11-20: 
 11. In harry potter all they do is fly around on brooms and kill people with magic sticks (wands) I mean, really? 
 In Twilight, all they do is lust after each other and play baseball. I mean, really? 
 In defence of Harry Potter, though, they also learn magic, give exams, celebrate Christmas and Halloween, deal with loss, deal with horrible teachers, plan their careers, protect the downtrodden (remember SPEW), participate in duels, watch Quidditch, play Quidditch, go to Hogsmeade, learn to make potions, and more importantly, learn of the importance of human relationships. I could go on, but I'm sure you get the gist. 
 12. Edward wasn't a dork. Yeah, sometimes, dorks are cute. However, Harry was a bit too dorky and I can't see why girls even liked him.

Easily this reader's least-favorite of all four books in the series, New Moon does show a degree of style growth as we're introduced to a storytelling shift from the first book: Dual-POV. Not only are we given Bella's first-person perspective, but also Jacob's. Edward features little throughout most of the story (aside from Bella's semi-hallucinating moments brought on by self-inflicted danger--in which some semblance of her own conscience/common-sense seems to manifest as Edward, with the request that she STOP risking her safety.) Sound a little insane? Well, to be fair to realism, I've known few teenagers in love who weren't leaning pretty far over the cliff-o-craziness... 
 I digress. 
 At a base level, New Moon is a highly emotional YA urban fantasy continuation revolving around an inadvertent love-triangle--and a girl who deals with her relational co-dependency in less than healthy ways. Readers are also allowed inside the head of a somewhat whiny male protagonist, who happens to be going through some physiological changes that make puberty look like a hormonal walk in the park. The world-building expands to encompass both vampires and shapeshifters, rounding out a far broader sense of conflict than was conveyed in the 'star-crossed lovers' plot of the first book. 
 While some have contended that Bella's period of depression was overly dramatic, there are many who may find her response entirely believable. For this reader, the primary detraction to enjoyment was spending too much time in Jacob's head. Purely subjective, to be sure, but the guy annoyed me. If this reader wanted to end up in any male's head, it would have been Edward's. (16-year-old male mind vs. 100-year-old male mind? Not really a contest, there. Just sayin'.) 
 I did appreciate the vampire socio-political aspects that came into play toward the end. The book managed to stand well on its own, while hinting more at future issues that would likely need to be faced.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 To be honest, about 1/4 of the way through the book, I began to lose interest. It seemed to veer off the mystery too far as Heat's love life was called into question and then fast-as-lightning resolved. If you're going to build up tension, why resolve it within half a page? The exploration/investigation of the case also was just a bunch of fact pouring. There was not enough of the work done. Instead, most of the findings of the investigation was handed to Nikki by other detectives. The last 1/4 of the book really picked up as the investigation (and not Rook & Heat's sex life) took center stage. Surprise twists, great wrap ups, and a bit of a cliff-hanger to end with! I really liked the way it came together. I guessed the (SPOILER) dirty cops but not who was at the top of it all. I liked the twist of the money stash. I just wish the rest of the book was like this last piece. It was driven by the mystery, it was intense, focused, and it had good humor -- just like the best Castle episodes. The "writer" has also improved on the description of places and tracking character movements. This book felt more poetic in its setting observations than the previous two books. I look forward to the next book and hope there's more foot investigation and less romantic details. This book could have filled another 100 pages if there was more of the mystery involved as well as Nikki's test results and her exploration of that aspect.

What's to say? Honestly the review should be very short. If you like the Castle TV series (which I do..one of my favorite shows) then this book should be right up your alley.. 
 I've said it in previous 'Richard Castle' reviews I've written that this is really a brilliant tie in idea on ABC's part.. 
 Fictitious writer Rick Castle is to Jameson Rook as Kate Beckett is to Nikki Heat and 'Castle' does a great job of using his 'experiences' from his ride alongs with the 12th precinct in NYC to write fun and fast paced thrillers. Some threads from the TV series are used, hinted at and fleshed out in the books but it doesn't feel as if you're reading the TV series, although the characters are very familiar to their TV counterparts...as is expected..but Castle uses good creative license to weave a new story that leave you guessing.. 
 The 'roguishly handsome' Rook and Heat work well together and their banter is fun when it needs to be, playful when it should be and serious when it must be. 
 A local parish priest is found dead in a S&M torture chamber in NYC. Heat is tasked with the case but it seems as if Captain Montrose is hamstringing her investigation at every corner. It also doesn't help that Montrose is under scrutiny from the upper brass and hasn't been acting himself lately. There's much more to this story than a priest who lost his way though. This is actually a pretty complex mystery using come of Castle's 'experiences' from his time with Beckett and company and well as introducing new characters and many red herrings..all from the brilliant mind of master wordsmith Rick Castle ;) And the ending..the ending was well crafted, had a big impact and wasn't telegraphed at all..very well done.. 
 So, as long as Castle keeps writing books based on his working relationship with Kate Beckett, I'll keep reading his Nikki Heat series. Kudos to the cast and creative team at ABC for a very fun literary tie in to a great TV series

I was lost in Yelena's world once again. Snyder did it again, she sucked me right in. Books with characters who have to go through a drastic growth process - be it literal with things like magic training or figurative like overcoming an internal struggle - are right up my alley. However, not all authors do a good job at that. Snyder did it wonderfully. I loved reading about Yelena's training at the Citadel and how much she was learning about her own powers. 
 My favourite part about this book was the drastic clash of cultures between Ixia and Sitia that we get to learn more about - Snyder masterfully points out the flaws and beauty of both cultures but never sways you to think one's more evil than the other - She leaves it to you to decide. We get heroes and villains from both countries. 
 We also get to meet Yelena's family which is hinted at in Poison study. I liked this one more than the first book - I didn't think I would especially because Valek was absent from a good chunk of the book and I loved him in the first one. He does appear in the second half though. I didn't mind because this is Yelena's story after all, not Valek's. 
 I definitely recommend this book to anyone who likes YA high fantasy with a little romance on the side.
