This is the second book in Maria Snyder's ...Study trilogy. 
 I didn't like this book as much as I did the first one. This book had the potential to be just as wonderful as the first one, but it really fell short. I thought the first book was very elegant in prose, set up and execution. It told a great story with much of the character development and plot unfolding organically. This one could have been the same, but I felt it got hijacked by the completely unnecessary soul-stealer-serial-killer plotline. 
 There was enough material to make this story the simple counterpoint to the first one. Yelena's struggle to fit back within her family, her need to learn and control her magic, the discovery of Cahil's existence, her interaction with the all the different suspicious people -- all that and the juxtapositions of how different the Ixian and Sitian societies were from each other would have been just enough for this story. I actually felt the above things got short-changed in the attention paid to Yelena haring off and looking for a killer. I wanted more depth and richness to her interactions with her family. As it was, Leif was just angry and hateful and her parents were just...nice. I wanted there to be more in depth exploration of her family coming to grips with understanding what she had been through during her abduction. There was no real mention of it except for a couple of "You don't know what I've been through's" 
 And the serial killer plot also had the unpleasant side effect of making me exasperated with Yelena. In the first book, she was quick and smart and thought through her actions. And when she made decisions they were generally the result of some logical follow through. She was a true victim of her circumstances and you really cheered when she triumphed. In this book she just ran off and did stuff without real motivation (of course she always came out the victor). But it seemed like she was put in contrived situations that made her the victim who had to work her way out of a pickle so we could nod and say how resourceful she is still. 
 The book picks up a bit when the Northern delegation comes to town on a diplomatic mission that includes Janco, Ari and Valek (in disguise). They added a much needed jolt of familiarity and more of a link to the first book. I think Yelena is more much interesting around her Northern people than she is around the Southern people. 
 I recommend if you liked the first one.

I just have one question. If the Ixians are all pale and the Setians are brown, then how the heck did no one notice Brazell's orphanage full of brown children?! Really though. I do not understand! 
 Beyond that little detail, I'm not buying the talking horses thing. Kiki is adorable and she saves me from disliking this aspect of the story. Their relationship is so cute! 
 Speaking of relationships, Valek now and forever has an English accent in my head! So much "love" usage! I'm only going to excuse it by justifying that Yelena obviously unlocked his personality with love. Because fiction. I can live with that. 
 Overall, I'm not necessarily disappointed in this book. I do feel like a lot just happened in 400+ pages and I'm not sure I liked all of it. Mostly, I just don't feel like anything surprised me. I do have hopes for the next one though.

My feelings for this book can be summed up into a big ball of WTF? 
 I miss the intelligent and resourceful Yelena. Here, she constantly gets herself stuck in dangerous situations that could have been avoided if she bothered using her brain. She gets captured too many times for a supposedly strong magician like herself. I was hoping it was all a terrible mistake, but Yelena as it turns out, is a lost cause. 
 The truly annoying part was that no matter what she would always, somehow, end up saving the day. Even when things were supposedly rough, it didn't affect her like it should have. It's like Yelena could be stuck in the middle of nowhere with a sword through her heart but you can count on a hospital - and help suddenly sprouting out of nowhere. 
 Valek is no longer my sexy assassin from Poison Study. He's a lovesick puppy who is more than ready to do anything Yelena asks him to. He's just her go-to person whenever she's in trouble or feeling particularly hony. I mean, the last time we checked, their feelings for each other just about bloomed and now their conversations can be condensed to: 
 Valek: You flow in my veins like poison, love!!! 
 Yelena: Awww, you're ma one and only 
 Valek: let's fly off into the sunset on a unicorn ily, love 
 Yelena: ya, oki ily2 but you be naked pls 
 Valek: you da one for me, love 
 Yelena: ily get in ma pants 
 Valek: ok, love 
 As if the story wasn't bad enough, Yelena starts talking to horses. Yes, I'm not kidding. This book is now Yelena the Horse talker, the sequel to Dora the Explorer. Weirdly enough, Kiki the horse was the only character I could bear. Even the "power twins" failed to impress me. 
 The plot was the only that stood between this book and me throwing it against a wall. The continuous rescue missions were annoying, yes, but the magic was as intriguing as ever.

reference_books.title: A Shade of Vampire (A Shade of Vampire, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Let me first say that I misjudged this book. I figured based on the title and the author's pen name, that this would be Twilight meets 50 Shades of Grey. While there are some Twilight overtones, the 50 Shades aspect is missing, making this safely a YA book (I was a bit worried at first, but teens can read this). 
 Here, we have a pretty wallflower, Sophia (who's never thought of herself as pretty) kidnapped by a band of bloodthirsty vampires. These guys aren't trying to restrain their thirst for blood and they use teen humans (male and female) as blood donors and slaves. They live on this really cool island where it is always night (thanks to a witch's spell) and have palaces in the tree tops. I liked this world a lot and could imagine it well thanks to the author's descriptions. 
 All of the vampires, save for the newly-awakened prince, Derek, are grade A jerks. You will love to hate these guys, especially Derek's older brother, Lucas. But Derek slowly wins Sophia's affections through his protection of her, his understanding, and his willingness to change for her. For Sophia's part, she wins Derek's heart by being considerate to the other slaves, telling him like it is, and being pretty brave considering her circumstances. 
 This isn't a very long read and I would have given it 5 stars if we had gotten a little more development at the end. I don't want to give anything away, but towards the end, something drives a rift between Sophia and Derek and I would have liked to see their relationship go down hill a little more before they mended things. (I also didn't love the prologue.) Other than these two things though, the book was entertaining and kept me turning the pages while I sat waiting to be called for jury duty. 
 This is the start of Sophia and Derek's tale and it is apparent that they have many obstacles to overcome ahead of them. I would definitely check out the second book. 
 ** Note: I was provided a free copy of the book in exchange for an honest review. **

reference_books.title: Wanderlove
reference_books.review_text:
I absolutely love the premise of this novel. I have some wanderlust myself (but was never brave enough to backpack anywhere), so everything about this novel called to me. I loved how Bria thought she was going to be part of this group of beautiful young people and ended up on a tour filled with old people. Can't you totally imagine this happening? Isn't that like one of our worst fears about a tour like that? 
 Anyway, I also loved how we gradually unraveled the pain Bria carries with her. And her mistakes. Bria grows so much during her two weeks abroad, but in a very realistic way. We gradually see her forced out of her protective wall and learn to take control of her own life (and fate). 
 Better yet, her adventures along the way are awesome and authentic. Having read this after I just returned from Belize, I recognized so many of the placed described in the novel. And the author's/Bria's illustrations (like a sketch book), just add to the feeling that you're really on this trip with Bria. 
 Last, I enjoyed the slowly-developing relationship between Bria and Rowan. This novel was not your typical girl and boy are instantly drawn to each other the moment they lock eyes love story. Their relationship happened organically and believably. 
 If you enjoy realistic contemporary fiction, with a bit of travel and self-discovery, I highly recommend Wanderlove. Enjoy!!

The book started out pretty good, and I was really interested to know what happened. Then, the characters started to frustrate me...and then things got a little strange... and then there was a cliffhanger at the end. 
 So. Definitely better than the first two, although the ending kinda ruined it for me. I'll probably finish reading the series because: 1.) I want to know what happens to the characters and 2.) The covers are so pretty! ;)

I was really disappointed with this book. I had a hard time even finishing it. By about 2/3 of the way through, I seriously disliked all the characters. Keenan is... ugh. Donia has always been a jerk, but in this book she really takes it to an extreme. I can tell that the author wants us to feel sympathetic to Don, because of her "tragic circumstances", but every major character in this book is dealing with as much or more than Don, and her judgemental and horrible behavior towards them killed any pity I may have felt for her. She needs to get over herself already. And ditto for Niall, which is sad because I liked him in the first 2 books. I get his dislike for Keenan, but his treatment of Ash is inexcusable. My favorite irony is that he tells Ash that Leslie was hurt because of her stupidity (which is apparently why he hates her... strange because he was in a position to enlighten her about that and didn't, but its still all her fault, right?), and then he tells Seth that Sorcha can make him faery, with no thought as to the consequences. Well, thank you Mr. Genius. The best part is that he is hateful towards Ash because Seth went to Sorcha. Its cool, continue to blame everyone else for your actions, but castigate them for theirs. It doesn't make you hateful or hypocritical at all. 
 And then there is Ash. Though she is the only one I still had sympathy for, I really struggled to not dislike her. Both because she kept repeating the same mistakes again and again (really, what is it going to take for her to stop blindly trusting Keenan? ), and because she just sat there and took all this shit from Don and Niall. Spit all their mistakes back at them! Or hell, just spit on them! I would have taken ANY display of self-respect by the end of this book. But no. Ash is a dumping ground. She takes it from Don, from Niall, and in the end even from Seth (I wont even get into my opinion of him in this book, except to say that I have a hard time believing that something that "special" comes in a package that stupid - sure, War, lets traipse off together, I trust you implicitly). 
 Very disappointed.

Anybody else get slightly weirded out by Seth in this book? I admired his mature handling of the whole Ash-Keenan situation in Wicked Lovely, so the whole green eyed thing he has going on in Fragile Eternity was annoying. 
 It's strange but even in Wicked Lovely I sensed something about Seth was a little off; he could come across as pretty strange and even kinda sinister at times. The creepy factor shoots up in this book; I have a feeling he could turn into a bit of a badass, especially since Niall wants him to join with the Dark Court and become his successor. 
 Weirdly, I think I'd like the dude more if that happened; I find myself hoping he does succeed Niall and take the throne in the Dark Court, which would result in a lot of trouble for Ash & Keenan, and then his character could properly develop. Seth's always came across to me as the long-suffering boyfriend who has to put up with Aisling's faery crap because he loves her so much, an admirable trait, and it'd be nice to see him get out from under her feet & become his own character. His friendship with Niall and weird mother-son thing with the queen of Faerie made him more interesting to me, and instead of becoming a bit of a psycho (which I could see happening) I do hope he goes to the Dark side and becomes the Dark King. 
 Ash is just annoying here; she spends all her time moping over Seth, while poor Keenan has to deal with her. I felt way more sympathy for him in FE, he showed a different side to the arrogant guy we saw in WL. And he seems to really care about Ash and keeps getting knocked back, but I'm never sure whether he really does want her or is just using her as a replacement for Donia. Who, by the way, turned a bit psycho here. Stabbing Ash? With ice? One of the best bits in the book IMO, but a little melodramatic. However I also find myself hoping she becomes a bit more of a baddie; Ash & Keenan are so self sacrificing and 'good', it'd be nice to see their attitudes challenged by having feelings for their enemies. 
 I really hope the next one moves the story along a lot more - I want to see substantial character development and the plot to become a little more interesting. Radiant Shadows with Ani seems promising - I liked Ink Exchange way more than Wicked Lovely, but I'm hoping RS has a happier ending than IE. I mean, I'm not someone who always complains when there isn't a nice ending, but the characters in MArr's books seem to get a bad deal most of the time. 
 So, I shall still read the next book, if only to see whether my Seth predictions are right, in which case my interest in this series will increase dramatically =)

sample_reviews.review_text:
While Dawn Treader is a single, self-contained novel in the Narnian series, it seems like a collection of wonderful stories in itself. The "voyage" takes the characters all over, into and through many different countries: various and distinct.

 At first thought I would say, even as an adult, that this is very possibly my most favorite work of fiction. Lewis's depictions of the rim of the world found within "Dawn Treader" are, I believe, strikingly similar to his imagined heaven in "The Great Divorce". Inspiring and hopeful.

C(harlatan of) S(atan) Lewis continues his demonic brainwashing of our youth with his tale of this "quite gay and jolly" cruise ship full of jaunty "sailor-types" and lusty teenagers. There's even a talking hamster on board, but I won't go into those satanic undertones. This smut recounts the "coming out" of this ship from harbor and voyaging "east" towards the "end" of the world, read: sodomy. The lion-soul devourer Asslan makes an appearance during one of the anti-Christian rituals which pepper this book. Definitely not recommended.
Read in 2009

Lucy and Edmund gets to go back to Narnia, and with them they have their annoying cousin Edmund who can't stop complaining. They suddenly find themselves on the ship Dawn Treader. Prince Caspian have left Narnia to go and search for 7 knights who left long ago. On this journey they will meet dragons, utter darkness, sea people and slave traders. It's a new adventure. 
 I was with my boyfriend at his parents over the weekend. I had two books with me and to my horror I realised that both was so not for me. What to do, I had this urge to read so I looked trough the house for something fast and easy to read, something I could finish there. This is what I found, and I have actually never read a Narnia book. 
 This is just going to be a short review. Some thoughts here and there. The book was really short and I finished it in now time, such an easy read and it was ok. Little too simple though for me, I am getting old. I have watched some miniseries long ago, and of course the two movies. The first one was ok, and the second cool, dark. This one, well it has an annoying brat, and the two kids that I least cared for in the movies. I did not care for that. Some exiting things happened, and all in all it was ok I guess. 
 But there was the end, I know that Lewis has a lot of Christianity in these books, but I didn't see that in the movies (ok, but hello, fantasy, we can pretend whatever we want.) This one had such an obvious end that it felt like preaching, if the use that in the movie, no, I will not like that. It destroyed it for me. There is a reason why I don't like people fall into other worlds books. They take their baggage with them. I want a world where anything is possible, a new world, with new ideas. Not something from this world. It actually made me not want to watch the movie when it comes out cos I know it will annoy me. He could have hidden it a bit more, and made us look, or made those who didn't get it don't see it.The fantasy lost it's appeal.

I don't like the cousin near as much as Peter and Susan. He's whiney at times. I did like the mouse though.

I enjoyed parts of the story and shenanigans they got in to. This one just had Lucy and Edmund, the two older children were off doing something else. Lucy and Edmund were told they would never come back because they were getting too old. Since C.S. Lewis is famous for the religious allegory in these books, does that imply that the children are growing out of their religion? Interesting. Aslan intervened in the adventure and treated the adventurers like children to save them from themselves a little too much. I really like the dufflepods! That was kind of cute, but the way they treated them was like Aslan treats the main characters. Patronizing. Some of the adventure was okay, but the suspense is missing since we know nothing bad will happen.
My second favorite of Narnia books. As I remember, because it has "feeling".

I have to say that this is my absolute favorite book of the Narnia series. There is just something so rich and imaginative about it that I fall in love with it each time that I read it. In fact, I've held off watching the movie just because I'm afraid I'll be disappointed. While you could almost read this one as a stand alone, I would highly advise that you read the other books that come before it, especially The Lion The Witch and The Wardrobe and Prince Caspian. For those not familiar with the series, the Pevensie children (and others) have the ability to visit a magical world called Narnia. Here in this world are talking animals, mythical creatures, and stately people, but as well there are evil witches and people who inhabit the world. Most important of all is a lion named Aslan who is the great lion and holds the world together with his wisdom. 
 The Voyage of the Dawn Treader takes place one year later by Pevensie time, and three years later by Narnian time. The younger Pevensie children, Lucy and Edmund, along with their horrible cousin Eustace find themselves sucked through a picture and into the sea next to a magnificent ship. On this ship is none other than Prince Caspian himself and he is taking a journey east by sea to see what happened to seven lords who were sent years ago on a journey, and also to see what is in the utter East. Along the way they have many adventures and meet several strange folk. They feel like turning back sometimes (and Eustace can get quite annoying, but they know they have to go on. 
 The characters are interesting. Lewis did a very good job making Eustace highly unlikable from the beginning, yet letting him grow throughout the novel. Lucy and Edmund actually took a backseat to him in this novel. I did like Caspian better in this book than the last. I thought he had more personality. They meet several interesting characters along the way too and they are all unique in their own way. 
 The writing while fast, is still very good and this is one of the more descriptive books. It is appropriate for children (although there are a few minor curse words) although they may not understand the finer nuances of the novel. I just loved all the adventures that Lewis sent his characters on in this novel and each time I read its like reading them anew. 
 Definitely the best book of the series for me. If I didn't read any of the other books, I would surely read this one many times over. 
 The Voyage of the Dawn Treader 
 Copyright 1952 
 271 pages 
 Review by M. Reynard 2011

reference_books.review_text:
****4 STARS**** 
 This was my first book by K.L. Kreig and I will be picking up more of her books for sure. Have mercy on my soul, this was a really good book, now let me tell you why.... 
 The book starts with Maverick marrying her childhood bestfriend, Kael. Now, Maverick is not in love with Kael, she's in love with his brother, Killian. But....Killian is married to her sister, Jillian. Yeah, I know, crazy. 
 Kael knows that Maverick is not in love with him. He knows that she loves his brother, but he doesn't give a rats ass. He's like, "I love her and she can learn to love me." God bless his heart for that because unrequited love is a b**ch. 
 Let me tell you what I love about Kael.... 
 1. He likes his girls with some meat on their bones. No stick figures. 
 2. He marries Maverick knowing that she is not in love with him - now, normally that is a huge turn off for me but it works in this story. But trust me, WHEN you read this book (because you will) you will see what I mean. 
 3. His self control is amazing considering the fact that he his loved her since they were kids. He was willing to wait until she was ready to at least try to love him. 
 4. Maverick's temper is sexy to him. (I can get a little crazy from time to time so I love a man who loves the crazy.) 
 5. He never pushes her into falling in love with him, he waits for it to become natural. For her to decide whether or not she can love him as more than a friend. 
 6. He's willing to give her up if she decides she can't ever love him and wants to be with his brother. 
 7. And my #1 thing....he sees her love as a gift. 
 K.L. Kreig was able to portray a story where there was no physical cheating but some may view it as emotional cheating. I may be in minority but when you marry someone who isn't in love with you, you have to accept that their emotions are still tied to someone else, you don't have their heart. Now add to that that it's your brother and you are going to be around him....you knew what you signed up for. But Kael handles it like a man, so I have to give him props for that. Side not - Maverick does kiss Killian at one point but I don't really see that as cheating. It was circumstantial. 
 All that being said, Kael is not a pushover either. He can get a little but alpha on her ass when he needs to and that is so sexy. 
 Maverick does work as hard as she can on her marriage. She really wants it to work. But it's not easy to turn off your feeling for a man you've loved for almost 20 years. To make matters worse, Killian still loves her too and is not letting go that easy. But how do you get over a man who is still holding on to you? 
 I enjoyed this book very much! Plus no one died, yes! Thank f**k for that, I didn't know how many more I could take where someone dies. I started to feel like I needed therapy. 
 There is a HEA and everything is cleared up in the end. 
 I recommend this book for sure! :)

book_a.user_review:

sample_reviews.review_text:
Paxton Wilder is a dare devil, he's rich and sexy and the best kind of bad boy that leaving you swooning and drooling. Paxton is a student as well as a stunt man along with his 2 closest friends. He's a part of a cruise that has a study abroad program. He has a sexy little tutor that has to help him pass his classes or else he won't be able to graduate. Wilder is all about the stunts, he's the worst kind of student and poor Leah, his sexy tutor has her hands full. Will Leah be able to tame the wild and addictive Wilder? 
 "Just moving you out of the faceable category in my brain. I'm going to need a minute." 
 Rebecca Yarros has done it again! She's created such an amazing story that sucked me in from the very beginning. Wilder is adventurous, wild and keeps you on the edge of your seat. It's one of those books that has you screaming at the characters to just bang already ecause you know they want to and the sexual chemistry is off the charts between Leah and Wilder. Leah is going through the motions of everyday life. She's been through something horrible and my heart hurt reading her story. While this story is adventurous and addicting, it's also suspenseful as it keeps you trying to figure out who the prick behind all the mishaps is. Like I said, this is a page turner that keeps you guessing and wondering what the hell is going to happen next. And let's just talk about this cover.... HOLY SHIT! I absolutely love it. Wilder is wickedly hot in every possible way. You just need to read it for yourself to see. 4.5 Wildly Sexy stars!

'Wilder', the first of the extreme sports series has so much crazy in it and I'm still wondering if that's a good thing. 
 I struggled immediately with the entire setting which was just...way too batty to swallow without a vat of salt--a cruise ship with a work/study option sounded like a huge excuse for a frat party with equally trashy people around vying for bed-warming spots with every opportunity to film an extreme act after another. 
 Well, if anything, it's a glimpse into the problems of the rich and privileged, aka, The Renegades, a group of extreme athletes who live hard and fast with everything. 
 But it simply seems that beneath the hot glow of the camera lights and the adrenaline thrill, we're back to several tired tropes that seem stereotypical of this genre: extreme sports that engender extreme acts of behaviour, the apparent license to be a manwhore(s) given the privileged background of the romantic and the potential romantic leads, the sudden, inexplicable instant love and the constant mooning over why the heroine is different from other women and the ultimate twist that seemingly decides the fate of a relationship that seems to be based on arousal and heavy attraction. 
 The writing is good though; Yarros handles YA and the first person POV with a kind of deftness that helps flesh out the irksome and daft thinking of the self-indulgent characters who have their own issues to deal with in the stupidest of ways, which ironically, failed to endear me to any of them at all. I understood and even empathised with Leah's fear of heights and her traumatic past, but couldn't get past Wilder's and Landon's self-destructive, reckless behaviours and incredibly selfish ways of dealing with them. In fact, the latter felt like immature juveniles who needed to be managed by everyone around them because they couldn't handle themselves at all, which made it increasingly difficult to see Leah and Wilder as equals in a relationship of respect and trust. I couldn't see Wilder's personal growth matching Leah's own tentative steps into taking chances since her accident and that lack of sacrifice or compromise that he didn't make for her (along with the instant lust) made both of them an unconvincing pairing. 
 My ranting skepticism here however, stems from my own personal hang-ups of overused tropes and cliched characters that significantly lower the enjoyment of a book for me. 'Wilder' would generally be--and has already been--a hit for those who adore YA writing (and possibly over the top characters), so clearly it's just me here.

I enjoyed this book from start to finish.

 If you're looking for an amazing charming adventurous man, amazing woman and mix it with amazing friends.. You'll enjoy this story!

I have been so anxious to read this book. I wasn't sure if I was going to like this series as much as her last one but I was wrong. I LOVED this book! Paxton is a guy who has absolutely no fear doing stunts that make my heart skip a beat from fear. Leah is a woman who is not willing to take chances as she has survived a horrible accident. 
 These two are really complete opposites but the attraction between them is something they both can't walk away from. I loved everything about this book. The whole renegade life, the amazing and descriptive places they visited to the love they share.

apparently i have a thing for romances on cruise ships (Caribbean Cruising was my lifeblood growing up) so i couldn't resist picking this up after seeing it on book barista's instagram. i felt it was a bit cheesy and over-the-top at times and felt kinda "ehh" about paxton but i LOVED leah. i picked it up because i thought it would be more of a sports romance (it isn't), but i still enjoyed it - it's really more of a travel situation. i couldn't stop comparing it to Caribbean Cruising which in my memory was better (though less steamy), but that does seem unfair as i probably haven't read that one in 8+ years. for me this was a very middle-of-the-road romance that was nothing special, but not bad either. if the premise/setting/characters intrigue you, pick it up - if not, give it a pass.

I'm sitting here trying to wrap my head around what exactly to say about Wilder. Words simply won't do it any justice. I, just wow!!! That about sums it up. But anyways here I really go. I don't need a synopsis to know I'll one click anything Rebecca Yarros writes. I just know. I have that feeling it's going to be everything I want it to and more. And Wilder didn't disappoint! Instead, it blew me away even more! Paxton Wilder is your typical boy with an image to uphold. He doesn't do relationships and his next adrenaline rush or trick is what concerns him the most. Then walks in Leah Baxter and let's just say, neither one will ever be the same. They each have their own demons and pasts they have to work through but with the help of each other life keeps going. I don't know what it is about Rebecca's men but Paxton Wilder is now on the top of my list of book boyfriends! Josh Walker first stole my heart in her first book and Paxton Wilder now currently holds it! And Leah, she's just she's one strong woman who can do anything she sets her mind to! And I love that about her! Penna and Landon are two pretty important friends that I would love to have my back and they do just that for these two. I don't want to say much more and want to keep this as spoiler free as possible. But if you read ONE book the rest of this year, Wilder has to be it!
A bit long but pretty good read!

I really liked this story about Paxton Wilder, one of the original Renegades. He's a daredevil, looking for a new thrill when he meets Leah. She's his tutor on a nine month cruise around the world. There's a bit of an instant spark between these two, and a definite rough start, but I really did enjoy their falling in love. This is a storyline that Rebecca Yarros does best -- I just love how hard Paxton falls for her. 
 There's some intrigue from a mysterious perpetrator who sabatogues their rigs which provided some nice tension and provided the needed breaks from the romance. I have to admit, I sometimes found Pax too good to be true, and his continued use of the word "exquisite" got on my nerves a bit. I also liked that Leah was a lot stronger than she thought she was, and really came through when she needed to and got angry in the right spots too. 
 Overall, Rebecca Yarros does a nice job with this NA romance. The characters don't come off as too young or too seasoned and I found the backdrop of the cruise and the Renegades fresh. I did have a few problems in spots that had to do with pacing. The middle was a bit slow, and the ending seemed rushed. It would have been nice to have some balance there. These are the reasons I'm giving this four stars. 
 Looking forward to rest of The Renegades! 
 ARC provided for review.

I loved this book! Pax stole my heart right alongside Leah's. The stunts, craziness, plus the bond between these friends, known as the Renegades, was awesome to read about. Paxton Wilder, the leader of the Renegades, lives his life doing crazy stunts and living for the next adrenaline high. 
 Leah, after being in a tragic accident, lives her life safely. She doesn't do anything crazy and has just begun to actually live again. When she's assigned as Pax tutor on the study at sea program, she's thrust into his crazy world and is forced to do things she never thought she'd do again. 
 Pax makes her live and Leah has taught Pax to love. He didn't think he was capable, he never had a good show of love in his life until Leah shows him what it's like to love and be loved. Can these two opposites make it work or are they destined to be apart despite the love they share? 
 I can't wait for more of this series, I sincerely hope there is more coming! I loved all the Renegades and want to read their stories. I loved everything about this book and hope to see more from them and this author!

sample_reviews.review_text:
THE EPILOGUE KILLED THIS FOR ME. 
 IT WAS SO UNNECESSARY. 
 WAS THE BOOK ITSELF GREAT? NO. IT WAS GOOD. I WAS CONTENT. 
 AND THEN 
 THE EPILOGUE. 
 GIRL, BYE. WHO ARE YOU KIDDING?

"Moments come and go; quick flickers in time. Yet those moments can have the profoundest impact on our lives. Either we seize them, and wield them to our needs, or we let them go. It's the moments we let go that, I believe, remain with us strongest--because regret is something that never leaves us." 
 This story will leave you in a mess.. and I meant that in a really good way. It is a story of love, family, relationship, lesson in life and how we cope up. 
 Charlotte, view her life as a wasted case since her brother Axel died in a motorcycle crash 6 years ago. She is ready to end her life when a someone stopped her from doing so. The problem is.... He is a soul. Yep, Charlotte can see dead people who can't crossover since they have unfinished business in this world. She's been helping this dead people for the past 6 years. But she never thought this soul who just saved her, will be part of her life forever. 
 Ike, the soldier who saved Charlotte's life from killing herself has been wandering since he died in Afghanistan. When he tried to saved her, little did he know that Charlotte can see her. 
 "You can see me?" I shake my head in disbelief. 
 She clenches her eyes closed and groans. "You're dead." It's not a question, but more of a statement... 
 "You can really see me?" I ask again, convinced I'm going mad. 
 "Dead and stupid," she mumbles. "Obviously I can see and hear you." 
 That's when Ike realizes that his unfinished business can be resolved anyway by the help of this girl. And little did he know that she will be forever part of his journey as they solved his twin brother, George. 
 George, is a mess like literally a mess since his brother Ike died in Afghanistan. He tries to cope up but in all the wrong ways. "drugs, alcohol, sex.... " But then he met Charlotte, who he felt is different and will be a part of him and his brother Ike's life forever. 
 Be astonished with this beautifully written book by B.N Toler. How will you not love the twin brothers who gave their love to charlotte. And how to cope up with Ike leaving. 
 "It's an odd bond. I'm fighting to give her and my brother life, while she's fighting to help me let go. Somehow we've become tethered to one another, even though we both know our time is limited." 
 Charlotte's connection to the two brothers was very different. While with Ike, their connection came easily and they bonded very strongly early on, George had a lot of issues to work through before his relationship with Char was able to develop all the way so they had quite an interesting hot/cold dynamic. 
 Charlotte and Ike had the ultimate forbidden romance. They both knew they had no chance at any real future, but their emotional connection was no less strong. It was both beautiful and heart-breaking. 
 So have your kleenex ready as this will give you heartbreak in all the beautiful ways.

AMAZING!!! BN Toler is fast becoming one of my favourite writers. This was such a beautiful, heartbreaking, funny, moving book. Loved the characters and it's one of my top faves for 2015!!! Such a unique story and I wish it could be turned into a film. It would be incredible on the big screen!! 5 stars are not enough!!

Where One Goes is a sweet story about healing and acceptance. 
 Charlotte is a medium of sorts who can communicate with the dead stuck in limbo. She helps them by assisting them in settling unfinished business with their loved ones so that they can cross over. Dealing with her own grief caused by the loss of her brother and the rejection of her family she has been drifting from place to place helping those souls in need. Overwhelmed by her loneliness and sorrow she feels that there is only one way to escape those feelings, until she is saved by Ike; a soul trapped in limbo, asking for her help. 
 This chance encounter sets in motion a series of events that is heartbreaking, and at times difficult to read through tears. While parts of Charlotte's story were overwhelmingly emotional, those poignant and tear-jerking moments were well balanced with characters who brought vibrancy and liveliness that left me crying and laughing, at times even in the same paragraph. 
 Some of the interactions between Charlotte and Ike felt dubious and I found myself questioning the believability of it all. Ultimately I understand the motives behind them and appreciate the authors fortitude in including them in their story.

I could not put this book down. I ran the battery out of my phone and then ran it out on the iPad just to finish it. I am completely gutted. So many tears, laughter and love flows from this book. I cried for most of it, laughed at Charlotte's sassiness and completely fell in love with Ike and George. This is an outstanding book and I highly recommend it.
3.5/5 estrelas

Wow... I loved every single second of this beautiful book. This was very different then I thought it would be and turned out to be a very pleasant surprise. This is one of my new favorite authors and books for this year.

3.5 
 The story of one woman falling in love with brothers, twin brothers in fact, one alive but not really living and the other a spirit stuck in limbo, was a really intriguing idea. In so many ways it could have gone so horribly wrong but B.N. Toler handled it with a lot of care and it worked really well. I will say that as a fan of The Ghost Whisper, it definitely had a lot of that same feel and I'm not sure if that was a good thing or a bad thing that it made me constantly think of that as I was reading. 
 Charlotte "Char" Acres is at a crossroads in her life where the future seems pretty dismal at best. She's lost and alone and isn't so sure, despite the people she's helped, that her gift is really a gift at all. In a moment of complete despair she meets Ike McDermott, he convinces her to help him in exchange for him helping get her back on her feet. This is the first time any spirit has sought out her help but offered some in exchange, putting her needs with theirs. This agreement pulls her into small town living where she befriends some genuinely nice people that help her out without question or expectations of reciprocation. Not only does she begin to fall for Ike as she gets to know him while trying to help him cross over, she begins to fall in love with his brother, George, who is what is keeping Ike in limbo. As she gets to know both Ike and George I was never "team" anyone. Obviously she could never be with Ike but it made sense that there were feelings there. Her falling for both McDermott men made sense and was both heartwarming and heart breaking. There are definitely some obstacles in the way of Ike moving on and George and Char being together. There is a lot for them all to overcome including a drug habit, an unsupportive family, ex bed buddy and her pissed off boyfriend, police and a murder investigation. 
 I was a little lost in the time line of things. Some moments would out right say it had only been days but imply it had been longer. I got a little confused here and there. It made the time line of the feelings evolving between the three main characters a little hazy at times. There were also times I would have liked to see a little more development in the story as George and Char opened up to each other while they were getting to know and fall for one another. Some stuff felt rushed and there was so much else going on it took away from the focus of Char, George and Ike's story. There were, for me anyway, a couple missed opportunities for some really amazing moments and a few too many secondary stories that distracted from the main focus. 
 As a whole I enjoyed this story and despite any issues I may have had along the way, the ending was so beautiful that none of that really mattered...then the Epilogue happened. It ruined the journey up to that point for me. For me that was one of the missed opportunities. It was short and didn't really give a lot of after the HEA. It left me feeling a little cheated. I can't even say what Char decides to do because I don't want to give any spoilers but for some reason it just pissed me off. Not the helping part but the other part. Obviously that won't make sense if you haven't read it but I really don't want to give it away.

Million IKE stars!!! 
 Such a beautiful, beautiful tear-jerking love story! I love every word of it! Thank you B.N. Toler for creating such an amazing book! XO 
 Reread again on Dec 13, 2016.
4.5 star read for me. This was a beautifully told story that made me cry more than once. I loved how different this book was from everything I've read lately.

reference_books.title: Blindness
reference_books.review_text:
Blindness really hooked me at first. The premise was interesting, but also scary; it really kept me on edge and wondering what would happen next. However, I have to say that about 3/4 of the way through the book, I lost interest. 
 SPOILERS AHEAD: As soon as our 'merry' troupe escapes the hospital, the story got progressively less interesting and more laced with pretentious bullshit. The author became more concerned with trying to moralize the blindness and the subsequent events of the book than with telling a story. That can work in some circumstances, but I felt that in this case, it did not. The pages became peppered with the characters' self-aggrandizing crap and weak symbolism. Also, though I recognize what he was trying to achieve, on some level I feel as though the story would have been stronger for leaving the characters blind. That may just be a personal interpretation, though.

reference_books.title: The Circle
reference_books.review_text: I found this book incredibly boring. It was a shallow indictment of millenials and their perceived apathy (look, we made democracy viable to young people through the magic of ~~social media~~) and completely ignored the reasons why people might not feel threatened by certain invasions of their privacy, and also what it is about social media and interconnectedness that appeals to people in the first place. The Circle is comprised entirely of shallow, uninteresting and useless characters who can't think for themselves and while the book tries to delve into a few deeper ideas (violation of privacy, monopolization, democracy, crime) it ultimately fails by shoving them all through this pseudo-tyrannical organization that we're supposed to believe billions of people mindlessly buy into. The only character I even remotely liked was Mercer (and if you've read the book you'll know why this is ridiculous.) This book was written by an older generation, for a younger generation, in order to condescendingly warn them of the evils of their naivety and use of technology. Yawn.

reference_books.title: All the Single Ladies
reference_books.review_text:
I'm not familiar with any of Dorothea Benton Frank's books, but based on this one I don't know that I'd read any more. Not my cup of tea - though I doubt I'm the target audience. 
 Spoilers below. 
 It was cute enough, a really light and easy read with kind of a faux-mystery, but as a 25-year old this book just felt like someone was trying to jam a largely humorless Golden Girls-slash-mystery down my throat. It was easy to tell right off the bat that this was a book about older women becoming friends and ultimately finding husbands because, what else in life is fulfilling, right? Eesh. The characters were mostly lacking in any kind of distinguishing characteristics (even by the end, Paul, Mike and Harry were interchangeable), and the sort of witty southern banter just wasn't enough to redeem the weak and predictable plot. I will say that I did enjoy Miss Trudie, and I thought she was a nice break from the overall pace of the book. 
 But my biggest complaint with this book, by far, was Lisa's relationship with her daughter, Marianne. Oh my god, is this actually how older women who are mothers think? That they're perfect and anything that their children do that they disagree with in the slightest is misguided and horrible? I didn't mind Lisa as a character until it became clear what her big issue was with her estranged daughter - which was just that they didn't see eye to eye on something! Sure, marijuana is a divisive issue but for goodness sake it's legal in Colorado, which is where Marianne sets up her business in the book. Lisa's holier-than-thou attitude to the entire situation made her eminently dis-likeable, and I was thoroughly unimpressed when the author set up the ending so that Lisa was ultimately right, but just refraining from saying anything because her daughter was hurting. I'm sorry, what a load of crock. Lisa was being not just a terrible friend to her ADULT daughter, but a meddling nuisance with a god complex. And the story rewarded her behaviour! Not impressed with this aspect of the book. 
 All said, I didn't mind "All the Single Ladies" and it was at least a quick read. I obviously wasn't the target demographic here, so to each their own, but I won't be reading any more of Dorothea Benton Frank's books.

reference_books.title: America Again: Re-becoming the Greatness We Never Weren't
reference_books.review_text: While this book had me giggling and obnoxiously telling family at Christmas what I was laughing at, I lost interest about halfway through. The writing style, while amusing, critiques American society to some extent but then leaves you mostly unfulfilled as it never quite drives the point home. I know, I know, it's satire; it's only meant to make you think! I simply felt that much of this book pointed out obvious flaws in American or other contemporary societies' rhetoric (immigrants bad! guns good!) while never truly criticizing anything. That being said, this book had me laughing out loud at times, and if you leave it in the bathroom this book may prove to be a solid read. Ultimately, however, as a lover of Stephen Colbert's show, I have to say that reading the book left something to be desired; namely, the opinion of whoever he would be interviewing.

reference_books.title: Rant
reference_books.review_text: This was a great book, and in true Palahniuk style, left me often dazed and confused. Written through testimonies of characters that knew or interacted with Rant Casey, this book is at times difficult to follow, but the ideas are relatively clear and the writing, as always, is graphic, perverse, and superb.

sample_reviews.review_text: Get past the first 100 pages and you'll love it; I promise!
This book is amazing. Can't wait to read the other 2.

The acclaim for The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo has circled the globe a couple of times over and, personally, I don't see what all the fuss is about. The first half of the book is boring as Larsson takes forever to set up the characters, then when the book does finally get going there are so many twists and turns that I was like who was doing with the what with the where? Then round and round it went. The character of Lisbeth is interesting, but completely unbelievable. She seemed so cold that I could never really understand where she was coming from and was so bogged down in conspiracy that it lost a bit of the humanity. For me with all the expectation around it, I was incredibly disappointed. On the other hand, I've heard the next book is better...we'll see if I get suckered in.

I wanted to read this book to see what all the hype was all about - and no, just because I read this book for that reason doesn't mean I will read Twilight. I was pleasantly surprised with The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo; it feels like a modern twist on the classic trapped-on-a-island murder mystery format. Basically the story is about an investigative journalist and a researcher employed by a millionaire to try and solve a mystery in his family that has been plaguing him for many, many years; the disappearance of his niece, on a day when only about 40 people were on the island. 
 The characters are flawed and feel so real because of those flaws, well except for the fact that Lisbeth only weighs 40 kilograms. I couldn't help enjoying these characters and the way they interacted with each other. I'm glad I chose to read this book. Its nice to have a good murder mystery style book and even better to have a modern take on a classic format. I will read the rest of the books in this series at some point in time and hope they are just as enjoyable. 
 Word of warning; there is a bit of graphic violence and sexual abuse towards Lisbeth.

I started reading this on the advise of one of my brothers, I simply could not get into this, too much family history,blah blah..... last night I rented the movie it was absolutely mesmerizing,superb photography, a bit raw in certain parts, but a very worthwhile story.

I really wanted to like this book as so many people recommended it to me- but I just didn't. The twist and turns of the story were seductive but the writing seemed flat to me- plus I am squeamish about issues of violence and women. This book was just not for me.

If not for you, my Goodreads pals, I would feel like the only person on the planet who didn't love this book - left standing in a public square, gaping and utterly alone, while legions of Larsson fans point at me and shriek in an alien, unified voice. That might have been an exaggeration. But it's hard, I tell you, to be a bookseller who doesn't love whatever publishing darling is huge at the moment. You'd think I'd be good at it by now, having hated my way through Dan Brown, 'The Secret', and the collected works of Stephenie Meyer. And really, it's unfair to lump Larsson in with any of the above, because this book didn't completely suck - it just wasn't great, veering between boring and distasteful, like sitting through a lame documentary into which a snuff film has been spliced.

Brilliant writing, Steig Larsson has edited the book to perfection. Characters are well developed and are easy to hate/love. The plot kept me guessing right up until the end. 
 One of those rare books that everybody says you must read and one that I actually agree with.

I don't know if I was confused because I was losing something in translation or what....also, there were a lot of characters and not sure who I needed to know, but I did suspect some people that were indeed guilty!
I hated this book. I think the author was sonewhat of a perve.

book_b.title: No Logo
book_b.user_review: Klein's analysis and criticism of corporate culture and what she calls the "brand bullies" is certainly poignant, well-timed and almost increasingly relevant. I agree with a previous commenter, however, that the way the book is written leaves something to be desired - Klein has portrayed what is a very important phenomenon through a pseudo-scientific approach, accompanied by numerous personal stories that, while providing entertainment in what is predominantly a bleak story, mainly distract from the generally somewhat academic nature of her research. As well, the book certainly could have been shorter while making similarly powerful arguments - much could have been left to the footnotes. Her depiction of global corporatism and the co-opting of culture for brand promotion is ultimately well-executed, provides varied examples and makes her point well.

sample_reviews.review_text: I loved This Changes Everything: Capitalism vs. The Climate, but couldn't finish this one. Naomi Klein's writing style changed a lot between the two books, written about 15 years apart. This one is full of the over-confidence of youth and an obsession with brands which I just found too irritating to read. Part of the problem is that I just don't know some of the brands she is talking about, but I also find the whole topic of marketing depressing. I am sure I would have learnt more by getting past the third chapter, but I just had no motivation to do so.

An interesting subject but handled in such a religious manifesto manner that this is unreadable. I toiled at it for 6 months but kept putting it down due to the firebrand comments, lack of real description, constant moralizing and quoting of her friends. A good book gone bad through the religious zealotery of a manifesto.

While reading, I could split the book into two parts: the first one, which describes how the brands became the center of today's marketing and capitalism, how they entered the our public and private lifes and what werethe main consequences of the change of thinking of MNC's, and the second one, which provides the thoughts on the such anti-corporational movement. Whereas the first part delivers at almost all aspects of my liking, the second one is quite sloppy and way too negative to be enjoyed, i.e. the negative tone is exaggerated with respect to the problems identified. 
 Klein outlines a painful issue, which may not be as obvious for us as the consumers, therefore the book is highly recommended for both, people, who consider themselves as socially responsible, and for the other one, who do not practice that consciously. 
 Book is not just well researched - it provides millions of facts, cases and other examples regarding the issue of branding (and the consequences thereof - no choice for customers, no places untouched, limited number of jobs in the developed world due to transfer of capital/outsourcing to the developing world). I would just keep my expectations in check as the second part of the book did not deliver (at least for me) as much as Shock Doctrine.
Seems to be only about the^ disadvantages about brands. I sympathize with many of the points, but this seems to be a bit one-sided...

What an appauling book. 15years after it was written it became obvious how her predictions were pretentious and misleding. But wat strikes me even more is that people took it as a kind of revelation. Bad. Bas.

It is iteresting to read a book like this in 2014. By the end of the book you can't help to imagine how does it compare the damage that it is already being done by the actual big players of capitalism like Apple and Samsung vs the titans of the 90's like Wallmart and Nike. 
 In itself the book reads a little bit dated, and i think that is normal, like many books of its kind NO LOGO fails to offer a real solution to the problem of workers in the third world.

Slightly outdated with pronounced anti-business bias, Naomi Klein's book is nevertheless an incisive, well-argued expose' on the forces and abuses of corporate branding. Professionals working in companies with outsided identitites and brands cannot afford to ignore this book.

A must-read for anyone interested in the background of globalisation and brand impact. It's a little out of date - several additional things have happened since publication and it is very North American-centric but as that is where 90% of the brands referenced come from, that is understandable.

An enjoyable read at the start, but I got bogged down in esoteric grammatical mistakes and references to seemingly nonexistent images later in the book. The second half was kind of a slog; I considered not finishing it. Much of it seemed a bit repetitive. 
 The occasional turn of phrase struck me as odd (I'd never thought to myself that I should "suck back" a latte--my dislike for coffee aside), but the real intrigue was in the references to tables in the Appendix. Every reference I found in the text gave a page number that was wrong, the table in question located exactly 12 pages later than specified. (While I'm on the subject: Most of those "tables" aren't tables at all, but figures. But I quibble over semantics.) 
 My original hypothesis was that 12 pages of notes were added at the last minute and the references were never updated (something I've run across a few times when compiling documents in LaTeX, which often requires multiple passes to get all the references right). But when I looked at the Afterword and discovered that it was precisely 12 pages long, I realized what had happened. The page numbers were quite likely taken from the first edition, which having no Afterword put the Appendix 12 pages earlier, and updating them was probably overlooked in the preparation of this edition. Oops.

Esta lectura la bote, la verdad tiene una redaccion tan casual que parece mas un cuaderno de chismes que un libro de divulgacion, quiza su intencion sea hacer una lectura amena para cualquier tipo de lector, sin embargo esto le quita mucha seriedad, por lo que termine abandonando la lectura despues de 4 sesiones

Thank you to NetGalley and Bloomsbury for an advanced reading copy in exchange for an honest review. 
 I am going to look at The Mime Order through the lens of my brief goodreads review of The Bone Season. 
 This is probably actually closer to a 2 1/2 for me, and I'll probably check out the next installment. 
 Well here we are. 
 However, this one took me a while to get through despite how fast of a read it is when you get going. I never felt really immersed in the world, and didn't really feel all the stakes. 
 The Mime Order felt like it took forever to get through despite the fact it's a fairly standard length at 528 pages. Nothing crazy. However, the prose weighs these narratives down so much. It just feels heavy and plodding. It takes any urgency out of what is going on. 
 An example--Keep in mind this may change by publication, and this is the worst sentence I found. Most of the sentences are perfectly serviceable. But: 
 It was into one of these that I walked, heading for the single doss-house it housed. 
 The idea of who we're fighting or why is not something I feel extremely invested in at this point 
 I felt like Shannon did a much better job at establishing the world this go round even if some things still feel murky. Unfortunately, she didn't necessarily make it exciting for me. I need to feel the vibrancy and the sinister nature of this world, and it's just not happening. A lot of this can be blamed again on the heavy narrative. The why we're fighting still really hasn't been shown. Additionally, things that are supposed to be twists were not that surprising, when the world wasn't still somewhat muddled that is. 
 For the length of the book, I don't really have an ending sensation of all that much happening. 
 There was more forward momentum in this installment, even if the amount of action could have been encapsulated in a just as, if not more, compelling way in a shorter page count. 
 Neither did I feel like I really had a handle on Paige before going on this adventure with her. 
 I know Paige better. I'm kind of "meh" about her most of the time, because she's not really giving me anything interesting to work with. She has to save the world or whatever, but we don't really see how bad it is right now for the average person. She's kind of going through the motions of a protagonist somewhat. But she's tough enough. 
 I lost all concept of passage of time within the novel; the end listed much longer than I thought the events had set up. 
 The passage of time was handled much smoother this go around. If I'm not sure how much calendar time has passed, there are concrete events referred to throughout that I can use as measuring tools. 
 Maybe the publisher's hype played into what I was expecting from this novel, but for something that had so much promotion power behind it, I was expecting a very specific and clear world. The potential is there, and that potential will carry me over to the next book. 
 The hype for this installment has seemed less, although there is another month until publication. But I feel like I had the Bone Season on my radar for ever. The potential got me here. Last I heard this was a 7 book deal. If that is still the case, this narrative is being drug out unnecessarily and it is not doing the overall story any favors. I appreciate an attempt at a longer series, but would much rather read a more concentrated novel that moves well. I just want to feel some more forward motion in these books. Even with events progressing somewhat I feel stalled. 
 I wanted to see how this series would build on itself, and now I know. Again, I'm leaving a little disappointed. Although I do feel like this was better than the first. 
 If you've been looking forward to finding out what happens to Paige and the gang (And Warden. You know you wanna know about Warden, 'cause while the Stockholm Syndrome is legit and creepy, he might be the most intriguing character in the book.) next, pick up The Mime Order on Jan. 27th.

sample_reviews.review_text: This book continues the story from Maus I and details the main character's experience in Auschwitz and finding his way back to Poland after his liberation. Very moving.

** spoiler alert ** 
 "Saved": More brilliance from Spielgeman - an ambitious and fitting sequel to his masterpiece 
 For me, the pivotal moment comes when the narrator - Artie -and his father, Vladek, an Auschwitz survivor - argue about breakfast cereal. That may sound trite, but it isn't: it's the culmination of the idea that those who survived are ordinary people. They have faults - Vladek is mean, something explained by his terrible internment but also by his character, one is told - and those faults survive the terrible experiences they have been through. 
 As such, there is a corollary to Arendt's 'banality of evil' - only Vladek and others like him represent a 'banality of survival'. They are like you and me, prey to all those petty idiosyncrasies, foibles and fragilities. Later, when they pick up a hitchhiker, the difficulties in the substance of humanity are fully exposed. 
 In a sense, the subtext of this book (that is, the narrative outside the main one, of the catastrophic inhumanity of the concentration camps) it's a triumph of spirit that the contents of a cereal box still matter, and the everyday legacy of the Nazi's ambition: 'Ever since Hitler, I don't like to throw out even a crumb'.

In Maus II, Art Spiegelman continues his father's horrific story of persecution and imprisonment in Auschwitz during WWII. Spiegelman has an enviable talent for simple drawings that convey complex ideas and feelings. Scenes with his father seem all too real - both amusing and a bit sad. Great series, I'd recommend it to anyone.

ACESSE: http://becoliterario.com/resenha-maus... 
 E dificil caracterizar a qualidade deste segundo volume. 
 Quero dizer que ele e melhor que o primeiro, mas logo me lembro de que o primeiro foi muito bom tambem e fico num impasse. Sendo melhor ou nao, em Maus II tudo parece ser intensificado, essa e a sensacao que se tem ao se le-lo. Voce se pergunta intensificado como? O tom sombrio se intensifica, o sofrimento se intensifica, a crueza se intensifica. 
 Na primeira parte tivemos contato com a realidade dos judeus durante a Segunda Guerra Mundial do lado de fora dos campos de concentracao, vivendo em guetos e se escondendo sob condicoes incrivelmente precarias. Na segunda parte em vez de dizer que mergulhamos em Auschwitz, prefiro dizer que somos empurrados, empurrados junto com Vladek e os outros muitos judeus que tiveram esse triste destino. 
 O que mais me impressionou foi o olhar interno que Art Spiegelman nos proporciona atraves das historias de seu pai. E realmente impressionante saber de algo como o pequeno comercio que rolava entre os prisioneiros e ate alguns guardas corruptos. O leitor passa todas as paginas num estado de torpor e o queixo cai com frequencia na sequencia de cenas tornada eletrizante pelo traco rustico de Spiegelman. 
 Em termos de enredo, temos muito mais cenas dos tempos "atuais" e conhecemos melhor a esposa de Art, que eu nem me lembrava do primeiro volume. Pelo fato de termos mais cenas do pos-Auschwitz, temos muito mais nocao da personalidade de Vladek, se no primeiro volume voce achava que ele estava rabugento, chato e implicante, voce nao tem ideia do que te espera em "And Here My Troubles Began". Mas ao mesmo tempo voce le o porque disso, voce entende mais profundamente porque alguem vive assim, depois de uma experiencia tao traumatica, alias, a rainha das experiencias dramaticas. Porem, ve-se tambem que saber a razao nao ajuda tanto aqueles que tem de conviver com a pessoa traumatizada: Mala, a segunda esposa de Vladek, vai embora por nao aguentar mais. 
 Por fim, deixo aqui minha indicacao: e uma leitura engrandecedora, esse seria o ultimo livro que alguem poderia dizer que "e um perda de tempo".

Kako oceniti velicani Maus Arta Spigelmana, prvog stripa dobitnika Pulicerove nagrade, konstantno hvaljenog kao jednog od najboljih i najvaznijih grafickih novela? Ulazeci s takvim preporukama u citanje stripa uvek je prevrtljiva stvar i, barem u mom slucaju, rezultat je blago razocaravajuci. Prvo, Maus nije los strip; daleko od toga, ima naravno svojih dobrih strana. Prica je poprilicno jednostavna, otac prica sinu o svojim dogadjajima za vreme holokausta, ali ona je toliko puta vec ispricana u raznim medijima, koji ipak bolje to prenose. U tom prenosu svakako da odmaze Spigelmanov svesno amaterski crtez, koji ne ostavlja prostora izrazima lica preko kojih bi mnogo licnije i jace doziveli previranja u likovima i njihove reakcije na vidjene uzase rata, sta vise, crtez je nekad toliko "zamuljan" da je tesko razaznati sta se dogadja na slici. Lep ukras je nehronolosko i retrospektivno pripovedanje, gde Vladek prica svoju pricu o ratu ali i u njoj skace na prosle dogadjaje, kao i dvostruka prica, ona o ratu i hororu prozivljenog i druga o odnosu oca i sina, Vladeka i Artija, njihove ocigledne razlike i nemogucnost istinskog razumevanja izmedju njih. Jedan od problema kod mene je bio nedostatak saosecajnosti prema likovima jer, za jednu pricu o Drugom svetskom ratu, bilo je premalo osecajnosti, empatije, "krvi i mesa". Pisanje je jasno, kratko, sazeto i vise se oslanja na fakte, a manje na neko dozivljavanje katarze, sto smatram da je vazno za ovakvu pricu; cinjenice o ovom dogadjaju svi toliko dobro znamo. Kako bi se zacinio poprilicno realisticki i "suvi" narativni tok, Spigelman je pribegao jasnoj i lako shvatljivoj metafori o zivotinjama- svaka rasa je odredjena zivotinjska vrsta, onako kako su nacisti dozivljavali to. Fin postupak ali nedovoljan kako bi se ceo dozivljaj izdigao od prosecnog i ravnodusnog shvatanja. Sve u svemu, Maus nije los strip, ima dovoljno u svojoj prici da barem nakratko zaintirigira citaoca, ali gledajuci ocigledne primere dela koja su se bavila ovom tematikom i vec ispricali i izneli ovaj teskobni period u ljudskoj istoriji, sa mnogo vise srca i osecaja, uvek pod ogromnim pritiskom nagrada i priznanja koja je dobio, smatram da strip ne donosi nista toliko revolucionarno i novo u svet devete umetnosti, niti prozivodi katarzicni efekat kod nas da bi bio na tom mestu gde je danas a to je, neshvatljivo, sam vrh stripske umetnosti.

reference_books.title: Along for the Ride
reference_books.review_text:
Even more than John Green, Sarah Dessen repeats the same plot elements over and over again: 
 1. ONE SUMMER, 
 2. AN OLDER TEENAGE GIRL WHO IS REPRESSED IN SOME WAY -- family secrets, personal secrets, others' expectations, her own cynicism or need for control 
 3. MEETS A WACKY GROUP OF PEOPLE -- long-distant family, a rock band, coworkers, a new group of friends 
 4. INCLUDING ONE UNUSUAL BOY -- usually artistic in some way 
 5. SHE DOES SOMETHING UNCHARACTERISTIC OF HER THAT STARTS OR DEEPENS HER RELATIONSHIP WITH THEM -- like confess a secret, or kiss the boy, or take on a job -- something that exposes her for a moment 
 6. AND THINGS GO ALONG SWIMMINGLY FOR A WHILE as she gets to know the boy and has her original assumptions about the people challenged and develops new skills through her association with them 
 7. But then, about 1/3 to 1/4 of the way from the end, SOMETHING HAPPENS TO SCREW THINGS UP, usually causing the girl's retreating for some reason into her original repressions/assumptions 
 8. A CONFRONTATION INVOLVING/REGARDING THE CAUSE OF THE GIRL'S REPRESSION OCCURS. 
 9. GIRL REUNITES WITH BOY; HAPPINESS INTO FORESEEABLE FUTURE. 
 There is no doubt Ms. Dessen works and reworks this material very, very well -- she has wonderful, fully developed image systems (in this one, the idea of what being a girl means, and riding a bike); the prose flows gorgeously; her supporting characters are consistently marvelous; the dialogue is terrific and realistic, particularly when it's teenagers sitting around b.s.'ing; every i is dotted and t crossed writingwise. I love the way she weaves all her characters into one large world. And I adored this plot the first time I read it, in THIS LULLABY, and also greatly enjoyed THE TRUTH ABOUT FOREVER and JUST LISTEN. 
 (Also, she creates great store names -- someone should hire her as a brander.) 
 But by this one, I was feeling a bit of diminishing returns in the familiarity of everything, chiefly in the fact that all her narrators sound the same, the same hiddenness, the same neatness. I'd love to see her do a book from the point of view of one of the supporting characters, or the boy . . . someone a little more scattered, more unpredictable and passionate, where the voice and the story wouldn't tie up in a neat bow. I do not know that this wish is fair to Ms. Dessen; when you know your material, you should own it and work it, and she's doing that, and I'm delighted that it's paying off for her. (Such a pleasure to see a GOOD writer of teenage romances on the Times bestseller list!) But all the supporting characters here felt more interesting than Auden to me, and the few changes she rung here just too familiar; and I'd love for Ms. Dessen to break some new ground in both structure and protagonist.
