I recently came to the conclusion of why I didn't like the Twilight series. 
 For the first three books, the obstacles that Bella would have to face if she were to become a vampire were constantly brought up (to name a few): Insatiable human blood thirst, risking breaking the treaty, losing her family, and losing her friends. 
 Apparently, if you spend enough time fearing that you will become a monster, then you just magically won't become one according to Stephanie Meyers. I thought that we would get to see Bella's struggle to keep her humanity, but instead the writer waved her magic pen and decided that nope, it wasn't going to be a big deal after all. Check. If one of the pack imprints on a person, no one from the pack was allowed to harm that person, so Jake imprinting on Renesme nicely got rid of the problem of that pesky little treaty violation. Check. I guess Charley was okay with the changes, but didn't want to know what they were. After spending three books terribly concerned about her, he suddenly seemed not to care. What kind of self-respecting, over-protective father wouldn't ask what was going on? Check. Her so-called friends weren't even mentioned after the wedding. Not that she really cared about them anyway, seeing as how she completely forgot about them in New Moon for a few months. Check. If you're building something up for three previous books, you should at least have some sort of struggle in the last book. But no, these were wrapped up all nice and neat with a little bow. 
 Throughout New Moon and Eclipse, she literally could not decide between Edward and Jacob. She said that she loved both. Ultimately, she went with Edward. So there was this huge build up of Bella being attracted to both for two entire books, and then suddenly when she changed into a vampire, *poof* it was neatly taken care of. As a vampire, she found Jacob's scent repulsive and he was no longer pleasantly warm but too hot. Also, after the birth of Renesme, she no longer loved him or was attracted to him in any way, because apparently the part of her that was like that was now Renesme. Then, Jacob found Bella repulsive because she smelled like a disgusting vampire. He was no longer attracted to her, because he imprinted on Renesme. Well, that love triangle was tied up nicely, don't you think? Completely realistic, no? I didn't think so either. I guess the lesson here that girls were supposed to learn is that if you're having a tough time deciding between a guy you'd have to change to be with and the one you wouldn't, go with the one that you have to change yourself for because those feelings for the one you didn't have to change to be with will just evaporate the second you change. It's like magic, don't you know? I seem to be saying that quite a bit... 
 Then there were the two main love interests themselves, and their relationships with Bella. First is Edward. He found her fascinating because he couldn't read her mind and he wanted to know what was going on inside there. Understandable, but then he creeped on her by watching her sleep. Personally, if someone admitted to doing that to me, I'd call the police. Then he's controlling. He not only told her she can't do something, he went out of his way to make sure she complied. He took some sort of plug out of her truck so she couldn't drive to the reservation to see Jacob. Then there was the time that he broke up with her because he felt he was putting her in danger. She said she didn't care, and really it should have been her choice. He left her suffering from depression for months while he was away. He forced her to marry him, even though she didn't want to. Edward was an unrealistic ideal that no boy could possibly live up to when dating a girl Twihard. He was beautiful, he won't age, he won't gain weight, was incredibly wealthy, and refused to have sex until after marriage. Second is Jacob, who had much more personality. He let her make the choice of whether or not to use the bikes (until it becomes clear that she's not quite right in the head). He also urged her to not abandon Charley, or her friends. He was there to pick up the pieces Edward left behind when they had broken up. He was more realistic, because he wasn't doting on her every second of every day. He had a bond with his pack, and his friends whom he hung out with when Bella was not around. Jacob also worked on his Rabbit and various vehicles, at the same time as going to school to learn things he didn't all ready know for decades. He was impulsive, passionate, and loyal. He tried to push Bella away for her own safety when he first phased, but soon realised that the decision of whether or not they should hang out was not his to make so he let her choose, and was fine with the decision. He didn't constantly whinge about it. Some Team Edward supporters would say "But Jacob was controlling too, he told Charley about the bikes so that he'd punish Bella." Put yourself in Jake's shoes. He despised Edward. When Edward broke up with Bella, she fell apart and went into a depression for several months. He spent that time trying to put Humpty Dumpty together again. Then, when Charley and the people on the Reservation (who were kind and friendly to Bella during her depression) needed her the most, she left witthout a second thought to save Edward from his own selfishness (aka suicide... did he not think of his family at all?) Wouldn't you be even a tiny bit angry or hurt? Jacob was 15 at this point. He was a teenager, he's allowed to act a little immature like tattling on her to get her in trouble, unlike Edward who after 100 years should know better. 
 I know it seems as though I'm on Team Jacob, but I'm truthfully not any more. It would have been much better for the books (and Bella would have therefore been a good role model) if she said, "You know what? My entire sense of self-worth is based upon whether or not these two boys like me. It's unhealthy. I need to base it on something else, so I'm not emotionally crippled if one of them leaves/falls for someone else. Being alone is a scary thought right now, but it's what I need to do for me." That's why I like Tamora Pierce's heroines, not all of them who have romantic interests in the books end up with someone by the end of the novels. If they do end up with someone, they don't just settle for the first one that comes along, either. 
 Bella was the worst role model ever. She spent all her time worrying about whether first Edward, then Jacob liked her. She ditched her own friends the minute she and Edward started to date. When they broke up, she was reduced to a suicidal schizophrenic (jumping off cliffs just to see/hear Edward). Teenagers don't take that long to get over a relationship, especially one that was for only a few months. I could see depression and whatnot taking over for that long if it was a married couple because they had more invested in the relationship... Bella also worried too much about what other people thought about her, which was her reason for not wanting to marry the vampire she supposedly loved. She also fell to pieces again when she went for a while without Jacob speaking to her. Then, magically once she turned into a vampire (read: changed everything about herself to be with Edward), all her problems just disappeared. Tell me if I'm wrong about this, but that's a horrible message to send to young girls (change yourself to be with your man, and you'll live happily ever after). 
 There was also the problem of the Volturi. From the end of New Moon on, there was this build up to a big battle with them, which was over in just a few minutes, with only one casualty which we had no emotional investment in. It was nothing like the heart-wrenching battle for Hogwarts at the end of Deathly Hallows, where we lost Colin Creevey, Tonks, Remus, Fred,and even Harry for a time... I was expecting both Edward and Bella to die, and Jacob to raise Renesme (which is wrong on a few levels) based on the lead up (and repeated allusions to Romeo and Juliet) but no, it was a perfectly happy ending and everyone except the Volturi were perfectly happy at the end of the perfect little story. Bella didn't become the queen instead of a pawn, like Meyers wanted the cover of Breaking Dawn to suggest. She just became even more of a Mary-Sue than she all ready was (I took the Original Fiction Litmus Test for Bella, she's an Uber-Sue). 
 Just because you have an idea of the end of a story (in this case, Bella, Edward, and Renesme) when you first go to write, doesn't mean you have to keep it that way even after the first draft is done. I thought that was Writing/Revision 101. The only reason I kept reading the books was because I hoped Bella would smarten up and decide not to be with Edward.When that didn't happen, I kept reading in the hope that at least it would end like Romeo and Juliet because of all the allusions... but no such luck there. I did like learning about the other vampires and their pasts, as well as all the Quileute legends. Too bad the secondary characters were so under-used, as they were the most interesting. 
 This book is filled with plot lines with tons of build up which were wrapped up much too quickly and easily, a Mary-Sue for a main character, a love interest that is too high of an expectation to live up to for any guy, under-used secondary characters, and just shoddy writing overall. I doubt I'll be picking up "The Host" or any other book written by her any time soon.

book_b.title: Eat, Pray, Love
book_b.user_review:
I liked this book. Much of the criticism of it seems to have revolved around the author's self-absorption and privilege, and certainly she has both of those things in spades. Indeed, that is the very point of the book -- to focus on herself for a year while she was paid to write a book about focusing on herself for a year, all in three locales exotic to Americans. 
 But I feel less resentful of that than "You go, girl!" -- that she said "I want to do this," and then did what she wanted. And through that experience of focusing on herself, she seems to have come to a place of genuine happiness, first spiritually, then romantically; and those also seem like things worth celebrating and emulating, so far as possible, more so than snarking at. (Though I have to admit that if that romance had been in a novel I was editing, I would have asked the author if she didn't think she was going a touch over-the-top.) 
 Most importantly, her writing is smart, thoughtful, and thought-provoking about the ways in which present American culture doesn't promote eating, praying, or loving (so to speak). I enjoyed spending time in Elizabeth Gilbert's company, and I'd read more of her work.

I'm having feelings
Welcome to Shadowhunter Academy doesn't really feel like Cassandra Clare, but more like fanfiction. It was nice to read about these characters again, however, the characterization felt wrong.

The Review: I have suffered for theses characters. I've cried myself to sleep for them. I've laughed with them, got mad at them, and now Cassandra Clare, I'm having to repeat the frustration and feels of Simon and Isabelle. 
 WTF Cassie, I thought this would be done. Ended. No more angst for this pairing, but no you had to throw them under the bus AGAIN! 
 WELCOME TO SHADOWHUNTER ACADEMY takes place a few weeks after CITY OF HEAVENLY FIRE ended. So Spoilers will be in this review, so be warned. 
 Our hero Simon is confused, conflicted, fearful, and trying to remember what life was like before he lost his memories. He wants to be the hero every claims him to be. His journey begins with him going to the Academy to learn how to be a Shadowhunter. Where he'll be Ascended-if he survives the Ascend that is and that's where in that time he will have all his memories fully restored. Instead of the frustrating spurts of memories that make absolutely no logical sense to him. 
 The hype for this book was major. I waited months for some other Shadowhunter book to come out for the long wait of Lady Midnight, that's coming out in March of next year. To my dismay, I ended up hating this book more then I liked it. In fact the only funny part was when Isabelle came to the academy to claim Simon as hers. Only for him to break-up with her because he, I quote "I cant be your boyfriend, I'm not him-that guy who was your boyfriend. That guy you want." 
 Ouch, you could of put it a bit more gently? Like we need a break? Or can we wait until after I get my memories back? No, you had to break her heart, and squash it until she became cold again and say "Have it your way." NOOOOOO. NOOOOOO. Screw you Simon, Screw You. I felt bad for you but you ruined it, like big time. You have a lot of redeeming to do. 
 I am totally, utterly, done with this series. I will not be reading the next book of Tales from the Shadowhunter Academy. I will wait for Lady Midnight without further reading for this series.

Spellbound was an entrancing read. I'm sketchy about romance in YA these days, especially when it involves paranormal elements, because it seems like every other one I read lets me down and annoys me. So, I was excited when this one really was different. The romance was great, both Emma and Brendan had to give up something, had to struggle to keep things going, to keep from dying (literally). There were still the typical ups and downs, but when they decided they wanted to be together towards the end, it finally all worked out and I went YAY inside. 
 I like the story behind this pairing, how it's a curse that needs to be broken and who actually ends up breaking it in the end. And to be honest, the side characters really made this novel for me. There's two supporting characters that really put themselves out there for Emma, one is a witch and the other is a gay guy. They were so colorful and had a larger role than normal side characters do and I just loved seeing them in the book. I definitely think that this wasn't the perfect novel, the action was lacking for me, but it was nice to have a normal bad guy for once (besides the curse).

Spellbound was a beautiful tale of tragic love and selfishness, redemption and selflessness all in one. This is probably the 4th young adult story I have read, this month alone, that deals with love through lifetimes, soul mates, and reincarnation. Despite the fact that I have read so many with similar themes, this story had a very fresh take on things. It was a fast paced read that I finished in a few hours (I devour well written fiction - sometimes too quickly for my own good). 
 Spellbound was yet another fantastic YA paranormal romance that I highly recommend to readers of the genre. I already added the follow up to Spellbound to my TBR list for 2012. I can't wait to see what Shultz does with the next story.

It's okay to not like every book. I won't be able to like every book. 
 I have to tell myself this when I read a book I thought I was going to like and it turns out the book is horrible. The premise sounds so interesting! "Meeting The One means she's cursed to die a horrible death." WHOA, mega interesting. 
 Too bad the characters are annoying. 
 Emma, the main character, can't stand up for herself. I like girls to be strong and able to kick ass if they have to. Breakdowns are fine because it happens. But when Emma picks a fight, gets cornered, and Brendan has to save her? 
 Oh hell no. I was done there. 
 And Brendan. I think the author tried to make him hot while sometimes being a jerk, but holy hell, he pissed me off. Especially when he and Emma figured out their fairytale and destiny and Emma's all "Oh, I had a dream this would happen!" and Brendan gets mad at her for not telling him sooner. 
 Jesus. They've been going out for like a week. Chill the hell out. Let Emma take care of herself. 
 And the most annoying thing? Emma's a witch. I don't see why the author made her a witch -- there's no reason for Emma to be a witch. It doesn't matter for this story, unless it comes in handy in a sequel (I don't know if there is one. Spellbound is a standalone story, and I will. Never. Read. A. Sequel.) 
 In my status updated, I whined about the dialogue. I was about to break my iPad during one dialogue conversation. Besides the dialogue being so freaking stilted, the characters are always addressing each other, so it's like this: "Conversation, Emma, blah blah blah!" "Brendan, blah blah blah!" 
 All. The. Freaking. Time. 0.o 
 I could nitpick over everything that annoyed me, but I'm going to stop here. I really don't recommend you reading this book, BUT it's up to you. Please don't let my negative review make your decision if you really want to read this book. I suggest reading a sample before buying it. For me, it didn't get *really* interesting until page 175, and then it sorta lost its interesting-ness, then got it back around page 300, then nothing. 
 Yeah.

Spellbound has quite a few good traits. The protagonist is witty and lovable. There is no love triangle (whew!). The paranormal aspects are intriguing (strange dreams of past lives and supernatural warnings? Oh my!) but there was something distracting about the narration. 
 There were times that I felt as though Emma was just giving me a list of the things she did and then what she did next. There were also times where she spun the tale so tightly that I couldn't help but admire the characters on the pages as opposed to parsing through the words. 
 The conflict of the story felt a little forced and I kept wondering, why they characters were acting the way they were. Perhaps it's their life of privilege but there had to be some other reason for their behavior, however, I seemed to have missed that reason. 
 There were times when I loved Brendan (the love interest) and times that he felt overbearing and to me. I understand that this might be due to the circumstances surrounding his relationship with Emma, but sometimes it felt stifling. There wasn't subtly to the sweetness, but it was super sweet and this doesn't work for my particular taste. 
 The resolution left me feeling a little confused. Perhaps this will be taken up in another story, but it felt as though one of the antagonists disappeared in the end, lost in the narrative. However, I enjoyed the little extra from Angelique's point of view and would be curious to see how Cara Lynn Shultz explores this character and that story.

First I have to start off by saying that I LOVE the way the author wrote her characters. The fact that I'm an adult and I found myself thinking how I would have definitely said something Emma thought in her head. Or at least have the same thoughts too. For example, Emma and a few of her friends were out one night and Brendan (Emma's love interest) asked Emma what would she like? And in her head she thought "Um how about you, shirtless?" Now how many times have we thought that about some sexy guy. I know I'm guilty of it. The author had me laughing out loud quite a few times, and there's not many books that have done that. I had requested "Spellbound" from Netgalley and had it on my TBR pile due to numerous requests, until one day I responded to someone's retweet on Twitter about 90's music. And we hit it off immediately so when Cara started to follow me, I checked her out and found out she was the author of "Spellbound". So I bumped it to the top and I'm glad I did because I enjoyed every single word I read. 
 Poor Emma has lost almost everyone in her life and is left stuck with someone who isn't responsible. And one last event made her leave the place she called home to begin a new life in NYC. I have to say I really loved Emma's personality. She's funny, sarcastic and she stands up for what she believes in even if it means practically getting herself beaten up in front of the whole school. But there were other great characters in this book, they all were very well written and fit perfectly in the book. For one you have to have your hot guy that everyone wants, in which in this book his name is Brenden. I would have loved a Brenden in my days. Then you have sweet and naive Ashley, so innocent full of hope and dreams. Then you have your new friends and your spoiled rich girls.Overall there is a diversity of different characters, which make the book the success it is. 
 In "Spellbound" Emma is having a difficult time in her life and new school. Lucky for her, she's made a few friends and she has her cousin at her corner. But of course being new at a school, you have your "popular" girls and her followers who want to put you down. And never mind if you happen to fancy the interest of the most wanted boy in school. Oh war would start with the "popular" girls. Basically nothing comes easy to Emma. Her new life in NYC isn't all that its cracked up to be. 
 Basically this story is surrounds itself around Emma's pendant and the history behind it. Her twin brother who had passed away came across a pendant at a yard sale and bought it for his twin sister. No longer having her twin brother with her, she wears the pendant and cherishes it. But one day Brendan takes an interest on the pendant and proceeds to ask Emma about it and the history of it. To which she has no knowledge of, because it was a gift. Together Emma and her new bff search the history of the pendant and discover the mystery behind it. Little did she know that her special pendant is alot more than just a pendant. It's a door to her previous lives. 
 I wish I could say more, without giving any spoilers. Which I feel like I did already. But all I know is that I really really loved this book. I finished it in like two days. Spellbound has a little of everything. It has humor, sarcasm, love, magic and physical attraction. Her writing and characters pull you in so much you actually do feel like you're "Spellbound". I give this book a 5 stars and a definite "Good Choice for Reading" A must buy! Must read! You will NOT be disappointed.

I don't give a book such a low rating unless I just cannot finish it. This book had a lot of things that I had issues with. The first was that Emma isn't a very interesting character. It has the cliche idea of having there always be one girl in school who hates the main girl's guts. It can work if used correctly, and here, it's just plain silly. The love interest thing is boring, and really? I'm supposed to like this girl who goes out to parties that she's too young to go to and drinks just to look good? No. This book is not for me.

Spellbound is a mix of fairy tale and mystery that will keep readers guessing. This unique story is a entertaining and eventful read. Keep readers attention through the last pages this promises to be a success for the debut author. Noticeable a new author there is much potential hidden in this 300 pages, and the future of this author looks to be very promising. Emma and Brendan are great characters, and the attraction presented in this new story is spellbinding in itself. Emma has lived a life of tragedy, and the need to sympathize with her character is strong. Brendan is the fairy tale prince; that would grab readers through his protective nature throughout the pages. I look forward to see what is to come in the future for Shultz, but I am also wondering by the conclusion if there will be a possible sequel to this lovely read.

Love Abbi Glines!!

3.75 stars 
 HARDCOVER book to be released May 25, 2015 
 ~~ 
 ABOUT THE BOOK: Release Date April 1, 2014 
 Innocence was never meant for the addictive... 
 Addiction was something Krit Corbin accepted as part of his nature a long time ago. He decided to embrace it and flip his finger at the rules. Women had always been the number one thing on his list of addictions. He couldn't get enough. Being the lead singer in a rock band had only made access to his favorite addiction that much easier. 
 Being alone was the only thing Blythe Denton understood. The small town minister's family that raised her hadn't accepted her as their own. The minister's wife had always made sure Blythe understood just how unworthy she was of love. When Blythe is sent away to college and given a chance to finally be free of living as an unwanted burden, she looks forward to having peace in her life. Being alone isn't something that bothers her. She escapes reality in the stories she writes. 
 However, the ridiculously sexy tattooed guy who keeps throwing parties in the apartment above hers is driving her crazy. For starters, he doesn't treat her like she would expect a guy with a different woman always hanging on his arm to treat someone as uninteresting as her. She looks nothing like the gorgeous women she sees parading in and out of his apartment, but for some strange reason he keeps showing up at her door. 
 During a party at his apartment, Krit's new neighbor comes to the door with her long brown hair pulled up in a messy knot and a pair of glasses perched on her cute little nose. She wants him to turn down the music, but he convinces her to stay. 
 ~~ 
 REVIEW: 3.75 stars--BAD FOR YOU is the seventh installment in Abbi Glines's contemporary, new adult Sea Breeze romance series focusing on the residents of Sea Breeze. This is bad boy, lead singer for the rock group Jackdown Krit Corbin, and college freshman Blythe Denton's storyline. BAD FOR YOU can be read as a standalone without any difficulty. Any important information from previous storylines is revealed where necessary. 
 Told from alternating first person points of view (Blythe and Krit) BAD FOR YOU follows the building relationship between naive, young virgin Blythe Denton, and manwh*re rock star Krit Corbin. Blythe has led a sheltered life-orphaned as a new born, Blythe was raised by an emotionally absent pastor and his abusive wife. When the pastor's wife died, Blythe at nineteen years of age, was sent on her way to start a new life in the town of Sea Breeze. Enter Krit Corbin-Blythe's upstairs neighbor and the man who would literally rock her world. 
 The relationship between our couple is one of immediate attraction but Blythe is naive to the world of dating, love and sex. As Krit befriends our heroine, a parade of women come and go from his bedroom and backstage. Blythe's heart continues to break as she becomes all too aware, that she will always remain in the friend's category as far as Krit is concerned. Krit is a player; a manwh*re with a reputation with the ladies; but a man who will lose his heart to Blythe Denton. 
 BAD FOR YOU is an emotional storyline wherein our heroine's self esteem is so low that she places the blame for everything that goes wrong upon herself. Blythe's ego has been destroyed and at every opportunity, Blythe's continues to debase herself with a constant stream of negative attitude and self fulfilling prophecy. There were moments when a single tissue wasn't enough to contain the tears I let flow. Although the storyline is predictable, I believe if an author can bring me to tears, there is something to be said for the emotional factor of the writing. 
 Copy supplied by Edelweiss

"Just maybe I was worthy of love." 
 OMG Abbi Glines... how do you do it?! I have not read a book by Abbi yet that I have not loved! Bad for You was no exception to my I love Abbi Glines rule! 
 I have to start off by saying that almost the entire Sea Breeze collection is sitting on my kindle patiently waiting for me to read them (along with way too many other books). When I received Bad For You for review I decided to read it anyway knowing that this was a companion novel and it could be read by itself. Although I felt a little lost when past characters appeared, it really did not hinder the experience for me at all. 
 One thing I have to say about Abbi is that the girl knows how to write and create a real man! And I mean a sexy, manly, protective, loving, kiss the ground you walk on man... in other words MY kind of guy! Krit fit this profile perfectly! Of course he had many flaws, a typical rocker with a cocky attitude, addiction tendencies and way too many notches on his bed post. But as I have said before, I love my characters flawed and Krit just did it for me. Then there is Blythe, sweet, naive and pure. She is trying to move on with her life and start over after escaping a very abusive household. Abbi has a way of making me empathize and truly care for each of her heroin's and Blythe really captured my heart with her sweet personality. I wanted to take care of her myself and punch the people who had hurt her! 
 This book was told from both Krit and Blythe's POV's. I love that Glines does this, seeing both sides of the story builds each character so well for me. I really got to know and love each of these characters. I also loved Krit's sister Tricia and his BFF Green. I am really hoping that we see Green get his own story. Law student by day... rocker by night... oh boy what a story!! 
 "You don't just fit into my world, Blythe. You are my world" 
 This story was a slow burn romance, Blythe and Krit start a friendship and enjoy having dinner and just talking. Blythe too afraid and insecure to start a relationship and Krit holding back because Blythe is too sweet and not his usual "type." They are just too cute! Krit teaches her how to make sweet tea and Blythe is so happy to have a friend in this new place. I love that this story started off slow and built up to a steaminess that Abbi Glines has perfected! She can do no wrong in my eyes and all I can say is.. 
 This was my first Abbi audiobook and I loved the experience! I was not the biggest fan of Shayna Thibodeaux, her voice came across slightly nasally and she took a lot of audible breaths. I know it sounds weird... but it totally bugged me! I eventually got used to it and got over it. Then there is Sebastian York... *sighs and swoons* that voice! He had me eating out of the palm of his hand! His voice sounds like it is honey coated and dipped in chocolate.... whatever it sounded good in my head. From now on I will listen to anything that he narrates! 
 Check out this review and more on my blog!

Uhg, Krit is such an utter jackass. Addict, man'ho, posessive...double uhg. And, of course, the girl he's wooing (while still doing others) is a virginal innocent. Nope. Done.

It was ok. The story line is basic. Not particularly well written. Lots of sexual content for a ya, which is fine with me, but I didn't find it well done. Over all I'm not sure I was in the mood for this type of read and I listened to this one and found the readers to be awful. So... maybe I'll pick up another some time and try reading it to see if that makes a difference, but probably not. I feel like I get what these books are and could sell them to someone who was looking for this type of read. So I'm probably done.

Well there goes my money. To think I had hope because Misbehaving was actually bearable. 
 I'm kind of upset about the time I wasted on this book but at the same time I got a few good laughs out of it. I'm not sure if it was things I was supposed to be laughing out but oh well, right? 
 Spoiler Alert! 
 Oh my god, how I hate Blythe. She puts Bella Swan and Anastasia Steele's straight up ignorance to shame. How can one character be so naive and stupid? I get it, she lived in a sheltered home her whole life and abuse played a role in her development but I really don't think anyone is that stupid. Speaking of abuse, why did we briefly cover some scene where Blythe is obviously molested and it's never addressed again? Isn't molestation a pretty traumatic event? If you want to add some depth to your novel, and you decide to go this route, don't make it some nonchalant topic that is discussed in one paragraph and then move on. 
 Next we have Krit. We have met Krit in past novels. We know what he is like, we know he is a total douche towards women and that he is probably suffering from sex addiction. He is literally just like almost every other male character in the Sea Breeze series. Original, amirite? Now rest easy ladies, he eventually changes for Blythe because of his deep love and addiction for her. Swoooooon . Man, if this story doesn't give you hope that you can change that one guy down the street that you are totally in love with and possibly close to stalking, I don't know what will. 
 I may be way off with this idea but as I was reading this book, I felt like we were dealing with huge daddy issues. I felt that Krit was acting like a daddy figure in Blythe's life and that Blythe was looking for just someone, anyone, to love her since her own dad didn't. I may be reading into this too much and those few psych classes I took a couple years ago could be influencing me, but I just felt this huge ick factor with the Krit and Blythe's relationship. 
 And the sex scenes! Oh my god. No one talks like that! Well, maybe some people do but is it really fantasy material? The adjectives used in these scenes were cringe worthy. If you or anyone you know, tastes like sunshine, please get medical attention right away because chances are, you need it! 
 You can also find the review here 
 http://www.thereaderinmereviews.blogs...

I don't know what to say, maybe I am too old to appreciate Abbie Glines books. I think she is sending young girls the wrong message, you need a guy to help make you whole. I am so sick of broken innocent girls falling for the player it is beyond cliche. Maybe that is why she writes Young Adult books. I am sorry but seriously, grown ups don't fall in love with the guy they heard having sex with at least 20 different girls.

 This final book in the Rock Chick series was, to quote Ally, righteous! It was the perfect ending to a series that is one of my all-time favorites. It's been quite a ride and I've loved every second of it. 
 Thank you, Kristen Ashley, for introducing me to "a motley crew of cops and crooks, bounty hunters and baristas, PI's and rock stars, hot guys and Rock Chicks." You've made them my people. My family. :)

Read it. Loved it. Wish there was another RC book but know KA is already working on her next fab-you-las book in Colorado Mountain Men series. Hoping she someday writes Deck's story. Also hoping for an LA Hot Bunch Brigade series. :)

4.5*

 But the great thing about this book is the self-deprecating humor by KA. In a matter of fiction imitating life, the author of the Rock Chick books in the book (named Kristen Ashley) is picked apart by the Rock Chicks. It's absolutely hilarious! 
 The other memorable thing about this book is the epilogue, in which we learn about what happens to the couples and their families.

Beyond better !!!!!!! 
 N I hate to see it end

So, I've noticed there's those who either love the end of the Rock Chick series or hated it. I'm raising my hand up as one who actually really enjoyed it. 
 But those who have read the previous books and plan on reading this one, I will let you know, straight up, it's totally different to the others. And in a way I'm kind of happy it was. While it worked for the others, it was nice that the finishing book held its own. Because you'll always remember the first in the serious, and I think its important to remember the last one in a different tone. If there is one thing that prevented me giving this a five star, is that (like most people thought) I didn't feel like there was enough Ren. Ally was up front and centre in this book, and I really feel like Ren got sidelined a bit too often. 
 Ren was still able to make an impression, but the fiery, heated and dominating arguments which usually occur in the other books didn't happen that often. And while sometimes I found that particular fights went on for too long in others, I found in this one there wasn't quite enough. I know right... damned if you do, damned if you dont.... 
 Besides those pointers, what I DID like about this book was how Ally was pretty much on a journey on figuring who she was and what she wanted to do with her life. While all the other Rock Chicks had a place in their life, knew who they were and had their Hot Bunch Hottie there to help them through a a series of unfortunate events, which in turn brought us the hi jinx and their HEA, which provided much source of entertainment. This was more a book of self discovery for Ally and that once she figured that out it, it was up to the men in her life on if they could accept that about her or not. 
 I'm sad to see this series end, cause I loved the ride it took me on, and I know that I'll definitely have to do a re-read of the series, and my favourite book may change from time to time, but I don't think I'll ever stop reading them. 
 Rock on! 
 My casting: 
 Ally (seriously... how could I not. She practically threw it at me in neon lights!!) 
 Ren

One of my pet peeves, is for a writer, to make the love interest of a love triangle in a previous book, who lost the hero/heroine to their competition, fall in love with another character in the next book. This is something Kristen Ashley does a lot, and in many of her books I could pretend the character was a new character. Not in this one. There was no escaping the fact that Ren had been in love with Ava. Even though I rarely can tolerate, much less like love triangles, I loved Ren in Ava's book, because he contributed to the story, in depth, emotion and yes the exact correct amount of angst. Throughout this series Ally has been a favourite secondary character and I had very high hopes for her. I never wanted her to be a second choice of anyone, even hot, swoon-worthy Ren. I much rather she had found another hero. Because even though we are asked to believe that Ren isn't in love with Ava anymore, and has moved on, would you like a guy who CAN move on so quickly from his first love to his second love? And even if, say, we are asked to consider that he wasn't in love with Ava after all, then wouldn't that make Ren, the man-about-town, bad ass, suave, sophisticated Ren, seem stupid and clueless? Also cool, laid back Alley was portrayed as a caricature of the person we had been led to believe she'd turn out to be. She is angsty, needy and desperate. Whereas we, or at least I had been led to expect a smooth operator, with her own set of connections, contacts and dealings in both the underbelly of society and above, say in secret service or something. (Lol eye roll, but seriously!) I was very disappointed for both Alley and Ren, and sorry for this book to have been the finale of a very enjoyable series.

reference_books.title: The Friday Society
reference_books.review_text:
Decent idea: Uber-competent women witness a murder, get together to change things. Exceedingly bright in inventing, fighting, and more, they use their wiles to do good. On the surface, this sounded like a great plan for a novel. 
 In reality, the length of the novel, the repetitive writing, the pacing--leaden in some areas and I wondered when things would start popping--and dialogue that sounds as 'Old Style' London as Valley Girl speak did it in. Really cool cover, though. But that wasn't enough. 
 Would not recommend. Had it been edited better and shortened somewhat, it would have made for a better read. As it is, it's a collection of bits and pieces and not all of them fit.

reference_books.title: Halo (Halo, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
The cover is gorgeous. 
 The writing is less so. I admire Ms. Adornetto for attempting to write a full-length novel at such a young age, but Halo suffers from a number of faults which caused me not to finish it...I got about halfway before I gave up. This is one of the few times I've never finished a book. 
 The descriptions of people and places tend to be very lush in spots, and I certainly got a solid image of where the angels were sent. That was about it. Everything else, though, was offset by a lot of info dumping, the slow pace, the two-dimensionality of the characters--everyone is either a Mary Sue or a Gary Lou or a total moron only interested in shopping or guys or...you get the idea. I know fantasies deal in asking readers to suspend credibility, but this verged on the "please believe me when I write this, it could happen and aren't all people like this?" kind of deal. 
 So...no. Adverbs, the plague of many a fledgling writer, are overused, and the dialogue verges on corny to unbelievably bad. I won't get into the religious aspect of it, mainly because I know it appeals to those who believe (which I respect) but I found it incredibly preachy. 
 I think that if it had been edited and considerably shortened, it would have worked a whole lot better. Bestseller or not, it was a great disappointment to me.

reference_books.title: The Running Man
reference_books.review_text:
I read this novel a long time ago, and recently pulled it out of the shelf and gave it a quick reread. Like the first time, I enjoyed the concept and the actions resulting from the conflict. Our protagonist, Ben R. needs money. He's poor, he's desperate, and his daughter is sick. So he signs up for The Running Man, a game show where if you can evade your assigned assassin for a period of time, you get money and fame and... 
 So Ben goes through all these thrilling adventures and finally ends up going out in a blaze of glory. And while it was a fast-paced read, it had a few issues. One, the character of Ben isn't given that much depth. We get his reasons for doing this killer show and that's about it. He's rude, not very likable, and if I can't like the guy in some way, what's the point? 
 The assassin I expected to be a real killer/psycho/whack job...sorta ordinary. 
 In fact, the only person with depth was Killian, the game show host. (Having seen the movie, I can say that casting Richard Dawson was a great choice). 
 The Running Man is a decent dystopian read, but nothing more than that, although I can well understand where other dystopian novels might have taken a few cues from.

reference_books.title: Hades (Halo, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
I'd always promised myself that after suffering through Ms. Adornetto's other novels in the trilogy, I wouldn't subject myself to more masochism. However, as a famous villain once said "I'm a man of my worrrrrd." 
 And so, I began reading this novel. I lost it at the motorcycle. All respect, all the possibilities that the dark inferno has to offer, and is Bethany the stupidest angel around? She has to be. Her depiction as a naive shnook in the eyes of the deity above...I'm surprised said deity doesn't hurl HER into the pit. She deserves it. Burn, Bethany, BURN!!!!!!!!!!!!! 
 The other characters are just as shallow and unconvincing, and the novel, like the first and third, could have been edited better and cut down about thirty pages. Still, "I'm a man of my worrrrrd." I'd always promised myself I'd finish this trilogy and sure enough, I did. 
 I should have broken my promise. One star, only because Goodreads doesn't give out half stars or allow us into the negative integer zone.

reference_books.title: The Alchemist
reference_books.review_text:
I started this novel in August, put it down for a spell, and then picked it up again. 
 Sorry I did. I'm always willing to give any book a shot, and foolish me, when I saw "bestseller" I figured it had to be decent. Then again, some downright rotten novels have achieved bestseller status, so perhaps I was being naive. 
 This novel just didn't do it for me. I found it slow, pretentious, and incredibly preachy. I, too, would love to follow my dreams, only doing so in my case--and I suspect, other cases as well--would lead to rack and ruin. Every other page was filled with drivel about self-enhancement and self-fulfillment. It was slow and dull, and no, I would not recommend it. I simply couldn't get into it. At all. 
 Meh.

book_a.title: 172 Hours on the Moon
book_a.user_review:
I love S/F. I love fantasy. I write about both. 
 And this falls into neither category. First, the premise is unbelievable. You have NASA sending up teenagers from different countries to the Moon. THE moon. Not Mars or Venus or anywhere else, because A) we haven't made it to those planets yet and B) we've been to the Moon so it has to be safe, right? 
 Not. You have NASA, an organization that is supposed to train young men and women (i.e. adults) for at LEAST a few years to man a spacecraft and all its controls and pilot it to a celestial orb and back. And they've decided to suspend protocol as well as common sense and send up some teens. 
 Riiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiighht. 
 Then some scary stuff happens up there which, to me, wasn't so scary at all. What I disliked outside of the premise was the fact that I didn't feel ANYTHING for any of the characters. They were all shallowly developed, the suspense was pretty much nil, and the ending sort of does away with the revelation. 
 I know this novel won some awards and all that, but quite honestly, to me, I hated every page of it. I usually recommend the novels I review because they have something to offer, imperfect though they may be. This book was slow--especially the beginning and buildup to the flight--and doesn't offer me anything to recommend to readers, outside of a nice cover. One star, and if I could dole out a half star I would.

sample_reviews.review_text: Good premise, but it had too many places that just seemed ill-conceived or contradictory.

Passei metade do livro angustiada e assustada, nao estou brincando. E esse final? Ainda estou sem acreditar! Gostei desse livro, foi bem diferente dos outros do mesmo genero. Alem de ter sido uma leitura leve e que fluiu rapido.

This book is a crazy sci-fi romp that I would have eaten with a spoon when I was 13. It's not great literature, but it is unputdownable and thrilling. Reminded me of my childhood favorite, Christopher Pike.

Oh my god what. 
 I think maybe this was actually written by an alien rather than a Norwegian. At first I just assumed the peculiarly flavorless dialogue was a result of the translation process, but the way that no character at any time behaves the way an actual human would--there's just no other explanation. 
 Alien wrote this. 
 The end. 
 (the end, by the way, I did enjoy since everyone dies . Yay!)

To celebrate the anniversary of the moon landing, NASA decides on a major publicity stunt to win back the world's waning interest. They're going to send teens to the moon. Chosen at random, three teens from around the world win a special trip into outer space, but there's something darker going on with in the walls of NASA. There is another reason for this trip, a more sinister reason, one that may just cost them their lives. 
 The premise of this book was interesting, and the mystery of the moon had potential, but nothing comes of it. Things just happen. There were so many points where this story could have been great, but whenever it came time to take action, it felt like the characters had taken a lethal dose of stupid. 
 At one point, a pair of astronauts had to fix a malfunctioning generator and were running low on oxygen, one of them wanted to stay behind and keep working on it but they were out of time, and then they find themselves trapped with no escape. So, what did they do? Work on the generator until their dying breathe? No. They took off their helmets and just gave in. It's moments like that that really grate on me and made this book hard to finish. It happened so often that by the end I just didn't care anymore. 
 The number of plot holes and irrelevant info dumps really just hurt this book. It's clear that the author had done plenty of research, unfortunately it wasn't on any of the areas that actually count. In one chapter, there is an unnecessarily detailed account of the Kuchisake-Onna myth that had very little payoff and even less relevance. 
 The ending itself seemed to go out of its way to avoid making sense. There were several times when the story could have taken a turn and ended with some actual meaning, instead it finished with evil!Mia strangling a homeless man and taking over a New York hotel . 
 The story tries to be too many things at once; at some points it wants to be a scifi thriller like Alien, at others a ghastly horror story like Blair Witch, elsewhere a teen drama or an action adventure, and just ends up feeling like a mess. While it wasn't so bad as to make me stop reading, it did end up feeling like a waste of a perfectly good premise. 
 I begrudgingly give this book 2 stars.
Terrifying!

This book... Was just stupid. I went in expecting to be terrified, and all I could think about reading this book was "meh". 
 Gave it 2 stars because of the ending got me like "lol wut". Total waste of my reading time. Oh well!
It was just about scraping three stars, the ending pushed it down to two. Promising start but fizzled out.

My daughter told me to read this book, that it started slow but got really good, really scary. I never found it so. The characters were card board cutouts: the Norwegian toughy, the French romantic, the Japanese fashionista. They never expanded beyond that. I think the biggest problem I had was I could not suspend my disbelief enough to follow along. They were supposed to have three months of training but this is never described and then when they are on the spaceship/space station they sound like they don't know what they're supposed to do. I don't know if this is a problem with the translation (the original is in Norwegian) or just lazy, not-bothering-to-research writing. I suspect the latter because even in the original Norwegian whole chapters aren't going to suddenly appear. Also, or, at least, if not describing the technical details of astronaut training the characters might have been delved into in more depth, especially their relationships with each other. The story jumps from them arriving at the training facility to they're on a rocket to the moon and the relationships haven't changed from their first meeting. I believe they would have spent so much time together training that strong bonds would have formed, good or bad. 
 I guess I sound a little harsh but it's because the book had such promise. The plot is good. I'm not mad, just disappointed.

Wow. This book was very creepy and I thoroughly enjoyed it. At times, especially the beginning, it seemed slow but it definitely picks up and keeps a great pace from there. I definitely recommend this book.

book_b.title: The Velveteen Rabbit
book_b.user_review:
I first read this story as a young child, loved it, and have continued to love it all these years. A simple story about toys coming to life when no one's around--gee, what a novel concept Pixar had!--it's a moving tale about love, pure and simple by a young child for his toy. Nothing deep or earth shattering, just a simple belief that love makes all things real for us. 
 This puts The Velveteen Rabbit in a category all its own. Yes, it's schmaltzy and manipulative in a way, and sure, it's old-fashioned, but only in the best sense of the word. Worth buying and worth reading time and again by someone who's five to eighty-five.

sample_reviews.review_text: What the hell

Cute short little read even for adults. A friend of mine posted the best quote from the book. 
 "He said, "You become!". It takes a long time. That's why it doesn't happen often to people who break easily or have sharp edges or who have to be carefully kept. Generally, by the time you are Real, most of your hair has been loved off, and your eyes drop out and you get loose in the joints and very shabby. but these things don't matter at all, because once you are Real, you can't be ugly, except to people who don't understand." 
 And that is why I picked up this beautiful little read, my first by Margery Williams, and finished it in 20 minutes. It was a break from the heavy-duty stuff I read, and a message I needed to hear. A message that is relevant to so much of life and what we are experiencing, for me it's the path to creating a business and staying humble on the Ashtanga journey, and for you, it may be something else, but it is entirely applicable to an aspect of your life. 
 All the same, I am reserving my 5-stars for books I love-adore-inhale so this is a 4-star.

I'm afraid I will never like this book the way that so many people I know seem to. I found it horribly traumatic when I was small because the message I got was that all of my toys were self-aware and completely and utterly doomed if I didn't love them well enough. I had no idea how to do that but knew I had to try. I still felt vaguely guilty about it into my teens. And I never figured out what I could do about all of the doomed toys I didn't have any access to. 
 All the way through elementary school, we read the book and watched the movie pretty much every year, and it upset me every time. I think it's important to be aware that there are likely to be some children who react the way I did and see not love saving one toy but lack of love dooming all the others.
