sample_reviews.review_text: My favorite Virginia Woolf. How could she describe the waves and sky in so many precise and elegant ways??? I think this book accomplished her project in writing better than any other.

This is a book I will want to read again and I expect will move up in "stars" and appreciation when I do. For more: 
 http://satiasreviews.blogspot.com/201...
With a little more structure I could have enjoyed this book without wondering what on earth was going on.
Beautiful...gorgeous...pure writing in that fantastic stream of consciousness vein of going about putting it down...only better. Love it.

It's possible that I've found a book more boring than this one, but if so, I can't recall which book it was. I don't know why I didn't give it one star; probably because at the beginning, I was mildly curious to see whether this thing was actually going to go anywhere. (It didn't.)

Phew! I finished it...I was tempted to quit more than once but curious...as VW herself states that she was "writing to a rhythm not a plot" and even fears that it may be "fundamentally unreadable"...yet she was proud of it and claims it as the "first work in her own style." 
 The Introduction in this Wordsworth Classics edition is very helpful but the reader advised to read it AFTER enjoying the book. 
 The stream of consciousness style is ...difficult for me. I struggled with The Sound and the Fury in the same way and yet, I find in both cases that there is something there that I keep thinking about...sections of prose that I must re-read, ideas expressed in ways that are unusual and thought provoking. 
 You can read more well written summaries but I will just say that it starts with six youngsters and through monologues of their thoughts the reader follows each of them to maturity and old age. 
 I liked Jinny's thoughts as a young girl embarking on college and growing up. 
 "I tremble, I quiver, like the leaf in the hedge, as I sit dangling my feet, on the edge of the bed, with a new day to break open. I have fifty years, I have sixty years to spend. I have not yet broken into my hoard. This is the beginning." 
 So I can't say I didn't like it -I'd say 2+ for now... Next I crave a straight-forward 'story' as relief....Reading can be hard work.

** spoiler alert ** 
 First reading: got about 20% of the whole thing. Plot is slippery. Names are confused. It demanded undivided attention just to keep up with the stream. 
 Second re-read: got about 60% more, magically. Plot becomes a deliciously smooth stream of consciousness. Can identify characters now. Highlighted almost half of the book because the passages are just too good.
This isn't writing. It's word-shaped blobs of ink placed randomly on a page

"The secret story is the one we'll never know, although we're living it from day to day, thinking we're alive, thinking we've got it all under control and the stuff we overlook doesn't matter." - Roberto Bolano 
 Woolf's novel is about the overlooked life, the life buried and forgotten in the living. It is an exploration of our greater, unborn life, through the prism of her six characters, each of which represents a different way of standing in relation to, and of finding personal meaning in the inscrutable world. To me, the secret to her work, to her narrative technique, to revealing the underlying unity of the many themes that seem to most capture her imagination, and to her overall philosophy alike is this overriding interest in giving us, her readers, the expressive tools with which we can come to bring to awareness the secret story of our lives, the story that is to be found in the things uncommunicated and overlooked. The novel reflects our own attempts to relate more fully to one another, to our own buried, unlived life within, and to The Inscrutable, the irreducibly Other, pre-personal world that haunts our every moment of consciousness, as its inescapable background. 
 Much of the dramatic force of her novel is built up from the ironic tension that results from the clash between our surface, consciously affirmed, constructed selves on the one hand (represented by how the characters appear to others), and our unborn, unknown and unformed inner lives on the other (represented by how they reveal themselves to be, in the fullness of solitude). So much of her work is a wake-up call that seeks to rouse us to this ironic, and all-but-total neglect of the central thread of our lives, which ever remains uncommunicated and unknown, even as we immerse ourselves in the self-forgetful ritual of void-content social exchanges. Reading Woolf is learning once again the forgotten meaning of true communication, and of communion, with ourselves, with others, and more importantly still, with the world. 
 It is also a story about the making of stories. Her novel is thus about the forming of form and the making of meaning. Her narrative method seems to re-enact the forming of form and meaning by which we build up our life stories out of the experienced flow of life. Her narrative method thus mirrors the making of self, and the processes by which we seek to know -and to evade - our selves. 
 Time and time again, the story shows how all the storying we do to try and give substance, shape, and direction to our lives is a mere embroidering around an emptiness. When we tell stories, we do so under the following bit of pretense, assumed at the outset by the narrative act: 
 "Let us again pretend that life is a solid substance, shaped like a globe, which we turn about in our fingers. Let us pretend that we can make out a plain and logical story, so that when one matter is despatched--love for instance--we go on, in an orderly manner, to the next. " 
 This postulated globular substance is the key ontological fiction that all our narratives project. Woolf invites us to follow her as she starts her story from outside this postulate in order to show us how the magic occurs and the events come together into a meaningful structure. 
 Here we can see ourselves reflected as creatures that spin their webs of symbols in order to beguile themselves into thinking their lives have knowable foundations that can be described in a tidy plot structure: 
 "I have made up thousands of stories; I have filled innumerable notebooks with phrases to be used when I have found the true story, the one story to which all these phrases refer. But I have never yet found the story. And I begin to ask, Are there stories?" 
 Maybe this is the question of questions. Woolf's story is that strange story that would ask us about the ground and source of all stories. It takes us back to dwell at the beginnings of life, where meaning always dwells. 
 Talking to people, it seems that one of the most baffling things about Woolf's unique approach to story-telling for them is her overall figure-ground reversal of perspective. This reversal lies at the heart of her lyrical mode of story-telling, which weaves its narrative thread around radiant, elusive images that somehow manage to speak of an underlying unity immanent in things. These images, which she often characterizes as "globed wholes," seem to represent moments in which the characters experience a fullness of being. These are moments in which characters somehow manage to reach a level of unity of perspective and of being that otherwise eludes them in the self-forgetful flow of their everyday lives. Oftentimes, in such epiphanic passages, the background is allowed to "speak" more loudly than the characters are, as are the silent peripheries of events, which reveal for us the reverberations of the characters' actions. As an example: 
 "The roar of the traffic, the passage of undifferentiated faces, this way and that way, drugs me into dreams; rubs the features from faces. People might walk through me. And what is this moment of time, this particular day in which I have found myself caught? The growl of traffic might be any uproar - forest trees or the roar of wild beasts. Time has whizzed back an inch or two on its reel; our short progress has been cancelled. I think also that our bodies are in truth naked. We are only lightly covered with buttoned cloth; and beneath these pavements are shells, bones and silence." 
 In this powerful image, the familiar, quotidian bubble-world of traffic and of commerce is embedded in the larger context of a suppressed, background deep-time awareness of everything that came before: the bones below the pavement. This passage, and countless others like this, represents those moments of fully realized being and awareness, which are like islands in the great sea of unconsciousness in which we have our lives as the culturally-programmed automata that we are. Condensed imagistic passages like this give us, the readers, potential access to epiphanic moments in which the characters reveal their unique relation to being. Images manage to somehow replace other more usual means of plot and character development, and to ground the unfolding of most of the narrative. 
 This figure-ground reversal informs Woolf's redefinitions of character, of what counts as an "event", and of where to look for dramatic loci in the characters' lives. These redefinitions also seem to be confusing for readers trained by pre-modern patterns of characterization and plot-patterning. And yet, they are not incidental to her meaning - i.e., "mere" stylistic experimentation. To me, they reveal her underlying immanent ontological sensibility. 
 A character, for instance, is something formed and enacted. It is not a pre-given unity, as was the case in the classic novel where the point of description was to faithfully get at the essential structure and drives of a personality (think Dostoyevsky or Dickens). And, above all, perhaps, characters make themselves up from their words, which express their efforts to give form to their indefinite experience. "When I cannot see words curling like rings of smoke round me I am in darkness--I am nothing." Each character brings to our awareness the various ways that we construct, and ultimately, counterfeit ourselves. 
 The story shows how every word has a certain irrevocable fatality to it. We see how every haphazard attempt characters make at fixing an interpretation cements for them the beginnings of a pattern to which they ultimately become bound. Each seeks to ever more closely approximate the form of reality by their tentative, fumbling efforts at collating descriptions of events out of available fragments. This effort at articulation, at self-begetting and self-forming, begins with the characters in their infancy as they strive to individuate into objects a blob of purple from a blob of yellow hung above their cribs. The effort to get at the object has thus been with us since the dawn of our consciousness; the novel brings home how we (at least as we know ourselves to be) are merely the sum of our countless, largely unconscious, improvisational efforts at description and interpretation which seek to define how we stand in relation to the fundamental datum: the inscrutable, faceless world. 
 "'Like' and 'like' and 'like'--but what is the thing that lies beneath the semblance of the thing?" This is perhaps the primordial question of consciousness: What is the unity that grounds all our made-up unities? A novel that would ask this question can't structure plot and character by the traditional means. 
 Thus, word by word we make, willy-nilly, the story of our lives. And we are also made by others: "I am made and remade continually. Different people draw different words from me." The web of words, giving shape to our life story, determines where we stand, what we see, and what we remain blind to. The accretion of words in the end forms for us the semblance of a unitary self by abstracting from the mass of detail that we're immersed in in experience. It is only at rare moments of lucidity that we can stand apart from the pattern we have ourselves spun around our solitude and see: 
 "There is no stability in this world. Who is to say what meaning there is in anything? Who is to foretell the flight of a word? It is a balloon that sails over tree-tops. To speak of knowledge is futile. All is experiment and adventure. We are forever mixing ourselves with unknown quantities. What is to come? I know not. But, as I put down my glass I remember; I am engaged to be married. I am to dine with my friends tonight. I am Bernard." 
 A novel cannot reflect a pre-given, "nuclear" self since there is no such thing. Such a self as there is is merely the end-product of the larger forming of self out of scraps of conversations that Woolf charts in her six sustained soliloquies. To focus on form is to focus on the end product of life; it is to miss describing the process - the forming of form - that is life itself. 
 Ultimately, it is the background which connects the islands of form and meaning that the characters inhabit. Thus, it is the background which turns out to be the main character of the story. It is the underlying, yet elusive unity that bridges the void of the incommunicable. In the end, each character is defined by its unique way of giving a personally relatable face to the inscrutable background. Compare, say, Rhoda's tortured otherworldliness with Susan's vigorous yet progressively disenchanted earthiness. Each of the six has established its own unique line of communication with the world, which defines its exclusive way of drawing meaning out of life. Many of Woolf's most poignant, epiphanic passages are narrative gestures to just this elusive and unknown (unknowable?) ultimate source of action, driving the characters' lives from the background: "that unfeeling universe that sleeps when we are at our quickest and burns red when we lie asleep." She manages to give voice to those moments at the threshold of awareness where we define our stance to the real, and which determine our personalities more than any superficial psychological facts could. 
 By this indirect gesturing to an active yet unknown background, Woolf manages to make room for the unrepresentable, and to give it a real place in the story, as the hole in left in the center of so much Islamic arabesque art, which acts as a powerful reminder of the incompleteness of all human efforts at representing the Real. Somehow Woolf manages to bring this background context in which the characters' (and our) lives transpire into active awareness, yet without specifying its content in a definite image. The closest she comes to condensing its meaning into an image is, of course, through the pervasive image of waves, which embodies the whole elusive grounding for the forming of form that is the theme of the story. The image of the waves also helps weave into the narrative thread subtler, more impressionistic moments of awareness that would otherwise escape characterization. In so doing, it brings to awareness the irreducible open-endedness of life, its supersaturation with irreducible detail, without striving to fix it or fossilize it into a tidy and inert structure. After all, fixity and closure of structure is necessarily built on the basis of an abstraction from life: 
 "But for ourselves, we resent teachers. Let a man get up and say, 'Behold, this is the truth,' and instantly I perceive a sandy cat filching a piece of fish in the background. Look, you have forgotten the cat, I say." 
 As for her redefinitions of event and of dramatic locus (i.e., of where the real action and value to be found, in life), I get the sense, reading her works, that it is, ironically, the unnoticed sedimentation of those things scattered about and gathering dust in the background and at the periphery of our lives which forms the real foundation on which we stand in life. It is these half-formed, unclaimed inklings of insight into our true relationship with The Inscrutable, and which we let fall back into latency as swiftly as they emerge, that form the true fabric of our lives. Woolf thus gives a fuller account of the meaning of events by not merely sketching the exchange of words, but also by drawing into the picture the reverberations left in the recently emptied room by the passage of people into yet other rooms. We follow the whole arc of the characters' movement: from stillness, to attempts at exchange, and back into unfulfilled, unbridgeable stillness: 
 "How much better is silence; the coffee cup, the table. How much better to sit by myself like the solitary sea-bird that opens its wings on the stake. Let me sit here for ever with bare things, this coffee cup, this knife, this fork, things in themselves, myself being myself." 
 The light waning on a wall turns out to be an event in their life brimming with uncharted, untapped significance. If we could but tell it, get at the heart of it, instead of ever skirting its peripheries, you get the feeling that everything would change. 
 Woolf takes the time to sketch out the margins and the background within which our deepest connections to life form. It helps me, at least, be more aware of these "interstitial" events in my life in which my true relations to things are revealed. Isn't it true that hearing the chaos of a city's rumblings coalescing into transient harmonies at night through an open window can be an event more pregnant with revelatory fullness than many of the sort of dramatically supercharged events that novelists generally lavish their attention on? As she put it more explicitly in "A Room of One's Own": 
 "What is meant by "reality"? It would seem to be something very erratic, very undependable--now to be found in a dusty road, now in a scrap of newspaper in the street, now a daffodil in the sun. It lights up a group in a room and stamps some casual saying. It overwhelms one walking home beneath the stars and makes the silent world more real than the world of speech--and then there it is again in an omnibus in the uproar of Piccadilly. Sometimes, too, it seems to dwell in shapes too far away for us to discern what their nature is. But whatever it touches, it fixes and makes permanent. That is what remains over when the skin of the day has been cast into the hedge; that is what is left of past time and of our loves and hates." 
 The moments in which we come closest to reality can be unspeakably trivial, so insignificant as to barely cross the threshold of awareness. Nobody has so well demonstrated, to me, that a newspaper coiling itself in the wind on the street such that we register some nascent -gesture- in it can be a closer sign of the real than can a dramatic conflict of character purposes. The truth we live by is as trivial, as quotidian, as intimate, as fragmentary a thing as these images. It turns out that truth is not "out there." It is the most frightfully intimate thing that we all instinctively flee from in order to preserve our bubbles of meaning. And yet, it is also the sustenance that we cannot live without. "The great change never does occur, only matches struck unexpectedly in the dark. Here was one." A chance bridging over the void. Such are our revelations. 
 Woolf's narrative captures such moments of awareness in which events come to reveal an intenser meaning for us. It captures also how the scrim of meaning suddenly falls off events, while the inscrutable moment itself remains, flashing mutely, and staring at us blindly. Then we ask, -do- these events mean? How do they come to mean, and what? How is it that meaning flickers in and out? And how do we hold on to the trick that permanently makes all things (including ourselves) seem part of a greater, homey unity? 
 All that we and the characters know is that we stand in some as-yet-unspecified relation to these happenings, and that we are held together in a temporary coalescence that overfills us with something we'd almost baptize with the honorific word "meaning." There is some temporary lifting of an age-old barrier between mind and world so that the two temporarily come to make up one reality, one conflictless, overfull moment of realization that forms the stable point in the unfolding pattern of our lives. Woolf persuades that attention to what we are accustomed to think of as the margins of our life takes us directly to the heart of our life. These transient imagistic microcosms often remind me of Whitehead's thought: "The foundation of reverence is this perception, that the present holds within itself the complete sum of existence, backwards and forwards, that whole amplitude of time, which is eternity." The beauty of these moments of chance coalescence that Woolf patterns her narratives around almost make me believe that the spiritual language of immanence can fully make up for the loss of every metaphysic of transcendence, of every cosmic framework for the alienated selves cast adrift. 
 On the one hand, the self stands outside all unities conceivable. Even amidst the warmest circle of friendship, a part of us still stands apart: 
 "The circle is unbroken; the harmony complete. Here is the central rhythm; here the common mainspring. I watch it expand, contract; and then expand again. Yet I am not included." 
 On the other, in "To the Lighthouse," she offered us something like the promise of uncovering at the culminating epiphany to be found at the end of this creative self-reflexive process, i.e., something like the image of a non-counterfeit unity: 
 "There is a coherence in things, a stability; something... is immune from change and shines out... in the face of the flowing, the fleeting, the spectral, like a ruby. " 
 If this is true in "The Waves," and there is still a basis of coherence in things, then the irony is that these counterfeit foundations we make with our stories is that by the process of constructing unities, we inexorably postpone our encounter with our true basis for experiencing unity. I am not sure if the escape hatch that was offered in "To the Lighthouse" is available here. "The Waves" really does seem to dissolve all substantial ordering grounds out of existence, and leave us with pure process, with the endless forming of form itself. There is only the question left: "Are there stories?" Is there a great story of stories in which our partial and haphazardly formed stories can find their completion? There is only the longing, not the fulfillment, in the end. 
 Ultimately, Woolf's work convinces that, if the most ordinary person could be given the means to tell the truth about the most ordinary event of their life - to see it and to describe its true form - everything would change.

This is one of the most exquisitely written books I have ever read. It felt like poetry for all 297 pages. Every single sentence has the ability to make you marvel over the complexities of the English language. That being said, this book took me nearly six months to read, and it wasn't for lack of time or anything. This novel is narrated by six voices of six friends (the book is not told as a normal story, but rather each character takes turns soliloquizing throughout the book). Despite the characters changing, the tone of the book remained consistent, which made it difficult for me to remember which character was which. Obviously it is meant to be experimental and not straightforward, but I think it may have gone a tad too far. This book is complex and beautiful, but there is no doubt it is confusing, even to the point of frustration sometimes.

book_b.title: And the Mountains Echoed
book_b.user_review: A good read but not quite as wonderful as KH's two previous novels. The Afghanistani background was very enjoyable.

sample_reviews.review_text: Although this book was well written, and at times pulled me in. It just didn't grab me the way Khaled Hosseini's other books have. It's more like a collection of short stories, that while are linked, really don't come together in the end.

It's been a few days since I finished this book and I can't figure out why it was on some of the best of 2013 lists. I enjoyed the story, Hosseini is a really beautiful writer, but the plot fell short. The entire book revolves around reuniting brother and sister torn apart as children. Their story is told through lives of a slew of other characters you meet during the novels duration. Unfortunately, while it was a great idea, this is where the book falls short. Hosseini introduces new characters for a chapter or two at a time, spends a lot of time getting the reader invested in them, and then never mentions them again. These characters were important for the overall story but about a third of the detail was needed describing these people so when they are pulled away, the reader wasn't left confused. I honestly couldn't tell you why many of these details were even shared, since they had no overall investment in the plot. It weighed the book down immensely. I would've like some more character development in the correct direction. In the end, the novels two protagonists still felt like strangers while you were very well acquainted with minor players in this whole story. I finished the book feeling it wasn't complete and not because Hosseini meant for it to be this way, but simply because he didn't finish writing the book the way it needed to be written. 
 I would still recommend this novel because Hosseini's writing style is always a joy to read, but do not expect it to be of the same caliber as his past books.

Khaled Hosseini writes a good story, the style of this book though did not suit my style of reading. 
 As always Hosseini has a way with words and what I did read was enjoyable and would recommend this book to his followers.

The writing in this book was beautiful but the plot was confusing muddled with characters whose stories went nowhere and had little bearing to what I felt was the main story, that of Abdullah and Pari. The side stories of Markos and Thalia, the Bashiri cousins and Iqbal and the commander and his son were never developed and had little to no bearing when it came to the central story of Abdullah and Pari. There were minor connections but sometimes the connections were allusive. I kept thinking that Hosseini would tie them all together at one point but he never did. There were also sudden jumps from past to present with no warning which at times made the book hard to follow. I found the book wandered from idea to idea without any real clarity of plot. I am not sorry I read it but it was not as well done as Hosseini's other works. It almost would have better served as a collection of stories rather than a novel but maybe I missed something. Overall rating: disappointed.
Another beautiful book by Hosseini. Like many others, this was my least favorite of all his books but still a pleasure to read. The opening story alone was incredible!
I loved Hosseini's first two books but I had a hard time keeping up with which character the chapters switched to. I probably need to reread this book.

Many layers of time and place enrich this story of family relationships and inter-connections. As with all Hosseini's work, I also appreciate the window he opens into Afghanistan that transcends today's news headlines and clips. I recommend this one for serious readers and also anyone who just enjoys a good read!

The writing is beautiful, in the typical Hosseini narrative style I first encountered in The Kite Runner. However, I did find the book terribly melodramatic, often unnecessarily so to provoke reaction from the audience (sympathy? empathy? I know not, definitely not introspective). Reading it feels like having a dull cramp. Maybe it's just not for me.
Multi stranded story, gripping & hart warming in places but not sure I'd be in a hurry to read any of his others.
Took me a awhile to get into this, but once I did it turned out really great.

reference_books.title: Anna Dressed in Blood (Anna, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
There will be bloody fucking spoilers in this review. 
 Sentence: I sentence Kendare Blake to a Supernatural and possibly some classic Japanese horror movies marathon. Also, writing something that is not teen. 
 Review: When I first saw this title in stores I thought Shit, this author knows how to hook you in with the dramatics. And then I thought, I hope this isn't a teen version of Carrie. While keeping it fairly dramatic, Anna Dressed in Blood did not disappoint me. 
 This series is a reminder of why I bother with teen at all. I had sworn off teen for three months and failed because sometimes it just doesn't feel like teen. It's something more than that stupid, superficial crap or the very depressing "everything is about me and it's all life and death" stuff. Don't get me wrong, some of those books turn out very good, but they are all very overdone. 
 Well written horror teen is pretty hard to find and Blake's novel is just that. Readers start off with a lonely Cas and his mother travelling around the world and freeing the ghosts tethered to certain areas; causing mayhem and death. You end up with Cas trying to figure out how he can keep Anna in his life, even if she isn't alive. 
 I'll admit at first the way Cas wielded the athame reminded me of Supernatural, but then the story started to create its own character. Cas turns out to be a compassionate young man just trying to save people and ghosts alike. And there is certainly Something About Mary Anna. 
 If possible, there is a more sinister creature than Anna haunting Thunder Bay. Familiar bite marks are discovered on the bodies and Cas is suddenly facing his ultimate ghosty; the one that killed his father. 
 From the setting in Thunder Bay (Canada, ftw) to the overly expressive cat (and even the touch of voodoo), Blake weaves a story about love, friendship and haunting histories. 
 This book bled into a seat of favour on my bookshelves.

reference_books.title: Darkness Becomes Her (Gods & Monsters, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Normally, I don't bother with reviewing books, but this one really deserves some explanation. I picked up this book expecting it to be one of the worst reads ever. Surprisingly, it moved fast and it really was engaging...except things just didn't make sense. And even the world of fiction and fantasy have rules. 
 Firstly, it's awesome that she's got kick-ass skills and a healthy dose of potty-mouth, but then things turned unexpectedly sour. While I was excited by the prospects of "New 2", I didn't expect anything beyond weird-looking people. That really wasn't the problem, however. Despite the book's abrupt dive into mythology and voodoo, the story had potential. 
 Until I realized she was practically in love with Sebastian (dark, tall, hunky and obvious) within her FIRST DAY in New 2. Seriously? And I know she doesn't think she's going to be preggo anytime soon, but at the rate she's going, she'll have three young'ins before she finds her father. After Athena was introduced, the rest was too easy for me to predict, though I didn't guess she was Medusa's descendant directly, because, well, she's not exactly a gorgon. She conveniently doesn't react to the curse until she turns 21. I'm not particularly sure why, but I think it's because it works better for the story. 
 I'm not quite sure how the silver hair and teal eyes play into everything either. Medusa, in later mythology was characterized as a beautiful, mortal maiden raped by Poseidon in the temple of Athena (versus early classical mythology regarding her as one of three gorgon sisters born to a sea god and goddess). No one said anything about a girl straight out of a magic-girl anime. 
 In the end, while the story could have been really fun, there was just too much going on. It was like reading Twilight crossed over with Percy Jackson and a bit of adult humour/language. It was terrifying.

reference_books.title: The Wolf Gift (The Wolf Gift Chronicles, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I couldn't get through this book. It was too much I-don't-give-a-shit and oh-god-why-do-these-characters-breathe? 
 I've stopped and I plan to never continue; something Anne Rice should have considered as well.

reference_books.title: Level 2 (The Memory Chronicles, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I really tried investing into this book, but all I got out of it was a lousy explanation (as well as a lousy "dark past") and more questions than answers. But seriously, I had no idea what was going on. I don't know if all that unspoken shit was hacker speak...or maybe it was godspeak, I don't know. But whatever I just read was real goddamn weird. Like a dream about trying to get to heaven but it takes seven levels, and in your dream it's like a freaking seven-level parking structure. And each of these levels take an entire book journey to figure out. Yes, no sense at all. 
 I also found it hard to like any characters. They all seems to have ulterior motives. Even poor Autumn--I couldn't pity her because of her initial "dibs" call and self-serving denial about everything. Julian was...well, controlling and an ass. Neil had this weird "I-could-be-a-closet-serial-killer" vibe going for him whenever he surprised you with anger. Felicia was apparently the subject of everyone's desires and jealousy. 
 I liked Beckah. She seemed cool, until she died...again. 
 I'm definitely not continuing this series. There's too much preaching and Christian-y stuff I don't know about, and not enough deliverance and relatability.

reference_books.title: Insignia (Insignia, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Note: I tried to keep spoilers to a minimum. I only reveal the ending (just a brief point about something that is not really important for the plot...yet), so I still feel pretty evil about it. :D 
 Keywords: School, tactics, military, teen, young adult, cyber-tactics, corporations, power, corruption, government, economic collapse, globalization, alliances, war, technology, stocks, investments, future, enterprises, friendship, education, video games, gaming, neural processor, brain invasion, viruses, hacking. 
 Rating: 
 Sentence: I sentence S. J. Kincaid to an across-the-US-road-trip (or across the UK would be ten times better) where all we listen to is the Harry Potter audio books, as read by the brilliant Stephen Fry. It's only torture if you let it be. We can even stop for bathroom breaks and food, but I'll be blasting the speakers, I swear it on my first edition UK copy of Howl's Moving Castle. 
 Review: If I could love this book more I would [Note: I initially gave this book four plums before I had read the ending]. There was just something so fantastic about the entire premise, plot and even info-dumping. Those who read and loved Dan Wells' Partials will recognize this form of info-dumping and explanation as a valuable introduction to what appears to be a totally new world (but not quite). Kincaid gives it to us easy in the form of education through the classroom. 
 At first the thought about having to read about how these countries (corporations) formed alliances and the entire globalization process made me want to sleep. But once I started reading about this fictional future of our world I just couldn't seem to get enough of it. 
 This entire dystopian-esque setting revolves around one of my favourite and most feared possibilities in the future of this planet, after zombies and the earth being destroyed by some space-shit of course: corporations taking over the government completely. We are an economy-driven world and power now lies in the politics of the economy. 
 I do not want to reveal much about the book, except that the little blurb on the jacket does not do it justice at all. In fact, I put off reading it because it didn't sound like something I'd want to read. I am so glad I decided to pick it up anyway. This is a soft version of science fiction, for sure, but that isn't necessarily a bad thing, as it lacks the intense cheesiness of much of SFF. This leaves room to appreciate Kincaid's actual humour and some of her more serious topics and themes in the book. 
 So, if you're like me and all you got from the jacket blurb was BAD FATHER and GAMBLING, I am here to tell you ignore all that crap. Instead take this away from the book: CHIPS IN YOUR BRAINS, VIRUSES MAKING PEOPLE ACT LIKE DOGS, GAMING IN MYTHOLOGY, and JACKASS COVERED IN SEWAGE. And if you began this book thinking it was like The Hunger Games due to representation of certain companies/countries through these teens, you are sorely mistaken (and I am glad for it). 
 I'll be honest though, I couldn't give Kincaid a full five stars out of hesitation (at first). The feel of the book was like a really elaborate fan-fiction sometimes, because of the eerie similarities I could draw to some Harry Potter characters (and situations). But that is my own feeling about it and I may just be in an HP frame of mind right now. 
 If Kincaid did borrow some things from pop culture today (who doesn't?), she sure is goddamn classy about it. My only concerns with the borrowing, really, were some of the character developments and personalities (I love HP characters, even evil, so I am biased to begin with). Beamer resembles Ron Weasley (and sometimes Marvin the Paranoid Android) a little, especially being a ginger and having a younger sister that reminded me of Ginny from the first book. Tom and his sadly unstable home life resembles Harry Potter and his non-home-home situation, including that feeling of sympathy when it's the day that parents come to visit their kids and all he's [Tom] got is an asshole company man representing his absent mother. Blackburn is like a weird hybrid of Moody and Snape (keen on torturing Potter Tom, but in a way that'll help him defend himself against the unforgiveable curses and legilimency neural viruses). Elliot is a dead ringer for Gilderoy Lockhart, in my opinion, except somehow Elliot comes off more legitimate if that's possible. And also likeable. 
 It left me with a bit of a hollow feeling at first, because I didn't see any parallels to the Weasley twins or Dumbledore (my favourites). Kincaid, WHERE IS DUMBLEDORE?! It certainly is not Marsh. I refuse to believe it! Okay, so I should probably just feed my need for HP through fan-fiction, but alternate universe versions of it. Like HP Arthurian Legend or HP Nancy Drew 
 or HP Steve Jobs' biography. Why am I so off topic? 
 I really loved this book because I couldn't always see where it was going. Much of the characters' actions were a surprise for me and I appreciated it. In fact, when Tom was asking about seeing what Medusa looked like physically, I felt a heavy burden that comes with disappointment. This had happened before, after all, in books like Ready Player One, where the main love interest turns out to be normal looking or absolutely gorgeous (although Cline countered that with his unexpected best friend IRL being a robust black chick in an RV--AMAZING). As soon as Tom said something about girls being prettier IRL when they say they aren't, I was in agreement with him, thinking "this is so typical". And then Kincaid hits you with the big one. 
 Medusa is not pretty at all. Well, she might be pretty under all the burns or whatever is going on, on her face, but Tom still really likes her even though his expectations have been shattered. And that is the main reason I changed my mind about this book. I will give it 4.5 for giving the middle finger to conventional expectations of what the main love interest should look like. This is something, I hope, cannot be fixed. It's not that I want her to suffer from the judgment of society and perhaps Tom (we shall have to see in the next book); I want her to rise above that. And Tom too. 
 But seriously, where is Dumbledore?

book_a.title: The Vampire Stalker
book_a.user_review:
This was a hilarious read, and I don't think it was on purpose. It was like reading what a Twilight fan would write about Twilight coming to life to spite the "haters". It's petty, unimaginative, but certainly easy to read as there is really not much to take in. 
 It's definitely fast-paced, but leaves you wondering why the author seems to think she understands string theory in the least. 
 It feels like the story is rushed so it can be written, rather than written so it can be felt and related to. It's definitely something for the fangirls' hearts. Junk teen fiction. Nothing to really enjoy or think about. It's written more to satisfy a fantasy. 
 For an author that talks loads about professional writing, I see very little evidence of it.

sample_reviews.review_text:
So I was at my local indie bookstore talking with two of the booksellers, when one of them stopped and said, "Oh, I have a book you have to read. You'll appreciate it." She then picked up The Vampire Stalker and said, "Ignore the title, and the cover," and then explained the book to me. 
 It was a quick fun read, and is good for anyone who likes fanfiction or has ever been too into a fictional character. 
 Amy and her friends are excited to get their hands on the next book in the popular Otherworld Vampire trilogy. While her two best friends are in love with the book's James character, Amy has always loved Alexander, the dark brooding vampire hunter, the best. Imagine her surprise when after a school dance she is attacked by a vampire, and the real Alexander saves her. 
 It turns out that the Otherworld books are the product of what is called 'literary physics', which is the idea that there are multiple different demensions, and that some books are the product of authors who can simply see into other demensions. 
 Now Amy and Alexander have to team up to save Chicago from one of the Otherworld vampires that is terrorizing the city.

** spoiler alert ** 
 It was not bad...I liked it, I think. It was not exactly what I was expecting which is why I'm on the fence about it. It was also written strangely. It seemed that these were some pretty mature and self sufficient kids! It seemed that sometimes the author couldn't make up her mind as to whether these were teenagers or adults. I had a job when I was in high school but taking a boy on a shopping spree just wasn't on the cards, and heavens KNOWS my mom would never have allowed me leniency to come and go the way Amy does in this story! 
 The writing was also not so great. Sometimes it took me a minute to get through the sentences because they felt a bit short and stilted. For some reason, it just didn't flow well for me. It kind of felt like the sentences were almost too simplistic if that makes sense. 
 The story was cute and was what drew me to this book in the first place. I've had characters in books that I just loved and would love to meet so that's why I picked this one up. I did think it was way too convenient that the only cool adult had been a physicist who just happened to work on the very theory which brought Alexander to our world. Uh, yeah, okay, sure I'll go with that... 
 Also, the story seemed a bit fast. It was shorter than I thought when I bought it and I think it actually would have benefited from some more time. Amy and Alexander immediately fall in love and he chooses to stay with her...yikes, move fast much? 
 Don't get me wrong, it wasn't bad. I do wish Amy had been an adult though, or closer to one. Maybe I could've bought it more if she were 18 or 19 and in college but just happened to still live at home. Maybe that would have helped.

I wanted to like this book more then I actually did. The concept was cool, the writing wasn't bad and for the most part, the characters were interesting. However, I felt like the fake author and fake book series and fandom was based loosely off of Twilight. Which was kinda lame and annoying. And the ending felt like a complete cop-out. Total let down. I doubt if there is a second one, that I'll be reading it.

This book was a short and easy read, but had right to the point detail which I liked. I really enjoyed it. I enjoyed the buildup from Alexander and Amy. I enjoyed the idea of the author bringing a book to life inside a book. Hmm, if only I could find a portal to some of the books I've read, lol. It was fast paced and nothing dragged. I enjoyed the characters and the plot. I look forward to reading more from this author.

I REALLY wanted to love this book! I was so excited to read it, but it was disappointing. :( It started out so slow that I had to push myself through most of it. Even then I ended up skimming through some chapters just to finish the book. I wouldnt purchase this book.

To be honest I wasn't that impressed with this book. It was good, and the concept was interesting, but I found myself more fascinated in the book that Alexander came from (Otherworld) then the story about him coming out of a book. I loved the ending, especially the last line. I thought it was sweet. 
 In my opinion there doesn't need to be a sequel, and I hope this is just a stand alone novel. Not a lot of authors write stand alone novels any more it seems. The author wrapped everything up nicely and it will hopefully just be left alone. It seems like it will be.
Quick, fun read about a girl who meets her favorite character from a popular vampire novel.

You know the kinds of book series that you are thinking about constantly? The ones that you would not mind at all waiting in a line forever to be the first to get the new installment or to get your book signed? Series like The Twilight Saga, Harry Potter, The Mortal Instruments, The Hunger Games (which I still have yet to read...). Now imagine Edward Cullen (because Jacob is a sorry excuse for a point on a love triangle), Harry Potter, Jace Wayland, or your favorite Hunger Games character appeared in the real world. The Vampire Stalker is the story of what happens. 
 Amy is utterly obsessed with the Otherworld trilogy and wouldn't mind marrying it's tortured protagonist, the vampire hunter Alexander Banks. When Amy comes face to face with Alexander, her whole world changes. Not only is the extremely good-looking Alexander Banks talking to her, but she also has to come to terms with either she's crazy, Alexander is a fake, or there is some weird science going into novel writing. Oh, and Alexander's existence also means that the villain, evil vampire Vigo is also in town. And that is bad. Really bad. 
 I really enjoyed this book. With the influx of fandoms surrounding book series, The Vampire Stalker is being released at prime time. So many people can relate to Amy, and it is actually kind of funny to see your own obsession from the outside, see how ridiculous you seem (but still wouldn't change a thing). 
 Another thing that I really appreciated was the science behind Alexander's existence in modern day Chicago. It isn't just explained as "magic", it is explained in a way that seems somewhat possible. No, I'm not expecting Edward to appear down the block any time soon, but Allison Van Diepen makes it seem less impossible. 
 This book is pretty straight forward, but I would recommend it. it is a really fun, quick read that any book obsessed person would enjoy. It is your secret dream come true - until your realize that is just might not be what you thought it was. The Vampire Stalker is a must read for anyone who's ever talked about a book series for hours, dreamed about the characters, stood in lines at midnight, and decorated their walls with posters upon posters movie adaption actors.

This is the second books with vampires I read this year and it's definitely not the best, but it was cute. I loved the idea of a fictional character coming in our world and fighting off vampires from his dimension while trying to stay under the radar. 
 FULL REVIEW COMING SOON!

Oh my goodness it is such a cute and sweet book !! I've always dreamt of the guy coming from the book and falling in love (I'm a dork) and it was just that this book was that. And the story line was so awesome it was a book within a book. And how the story line all connected. It was epic !!!

book_b.title: The Windup Girl
book_b.user_review:
The Windup Girl by Paolo Bacigalupi is a science-fiction or steampunk novel following the story of Anderson Lake, a "Calorie Man." The planet is in a state of disarray, where food we take for granted today, have gone extinct. This is a result of genetically engineered diseases, which mutate faster than vaccinations are created, infecting crops (and people). The value of calories are equivalent to currency and corporations have a hand in mostly genetics (reminds me of Repo! The Genetic Opera), especially to manipulate them into a food capable of resisting diseases. Lake is a genetic engineer who works for one of these Midwestern calorie companies, and his research has landed him in Thailand, which seems even more chaotic than the rest of the planet due to the staggering caste system and dissatisfaction with society. 
 The windups are a lower-level caste group, because they are genetically engineered with superior traits to humans (hearing, eyesight, beauty, etc.)--basically treated like trash. Lake is intrigued by Emiko, a windup from Japan who is rather resistant to authority and smart-mouthed, despite her precarious situation (sex slave). And their adventure takes off from there. 
 This story is great because it manages to take different points of view and shape the story with ease. The build up is intense and full of action, easily keeping the reader at the edge of their seat. The story itself seems incredible and yet so familiar and possible, especially with a near wipe-out of an entire species of banana (see Panama disease and Gros Michel). The idea of a planet torn by science is also not a new idea, but definitely one people like to read and talk about. It's also a very easy world to picture, especially because of the effortless way Bacigalupi sets the scene. 
 Unfortunately, while this story is fascinating, it is also lacking. There was a lot of build up and potential, but things were never properly fleshed out, such as the fate of the New People, and a proper idea of the Green Headbands (he mentions really enticing tidbits and then cuts himself off). And honestly, the story doesn't quite pick up steam until almost halfway through, and even then the ending is a little deflated (unless this will have a sequel). 
 The Windup Girl is on its way to predicting the future of agricultural profit and genetic manipulation/biotech today (see Monsanto monocultures and patent rights).

sample_reviews.review_text: Addresses ecological and industrial issues deserving attention, but details lack a certain practical plausibility I found too distracting, despite any literary purpose the nonsense serves.

Horrible! I couldn't finish it. The characters are terribly blah! The windup girl has the personality of a blow-up doll. And really I have no investment in what is going on. The author had some very cool ideas but just could not pull them off, in my opinion.

I was curious to see how this book compared to "The City and The City", since these novels shared the Hugo in their year. It was very good, but lacked an emotional center, something or someone I cared about beyond "what's going to happen next/in the end". I liked "City" better, but that's not to say that there weren't some very strong parts in this book: the street fighting, the conspiracies, the technology and the backstory were great, and of course the Megodonts! I didn't like Anderson, the initial "main character" at all, didn't like Kanya talking to Jaidee's ghost all the time, that took the book somewhere it didn't need to go. Overall, deserving of a Hugo, certainly, but not in Mieville's year :)
Life is too short to read books that don't excite me. This book put me off; preachy and disconnected, arrogant and disconnected. I couldn't get through the first chapter without feeling irritated.
I'm proud of myself for finishing this. Blech.

Originally reviewed on A Reader of Fictions. 
 For years, I have been looking forward to reading this book. I did check it out from the library once and read a couple of pages, but I gave up and moved on to something else. I hoped that now, with a broader experience of dystopias, I might get into the story and appreciate its marvelousness. Sadly, I did not. Were I not incredibly stubborn, I would have DNFed this early on. 
 Tons of brilliant people that I have the utmost respect for love this novel. Honestly, they're smarter than I am, I expect, so it could be that I just don't have what it takes to fully appreciate The Windup Girl. That said, I can appreciate the depth and breadth of Bacigalupi's world building. Many novels feel sort of slapdash, as though some things have not really been though out at all, but every bit of this has obviously been fine-tuned and worked out with precision. 
 In fact, there is such focus on the world building that I occasionally felt rather like I was reading a newspaper or a text book on that period of history. The whole book was a description overload for me. Perhaps if I had an interest in science, I would apprecciate all of those details, but, with science always having been my least favorite subject, I had trouble focusing or caring. 
 In The Windup Girl, mankind has, through the constant genetic modification of food, created new diseases and is having difficulty producing food. Conglomerates that produce new disease-free strains essentially run the world. The Windup Girl takes place in Thailand, where Anderson Lake has been sent to investigate the appearance of fruits previously disappeared. They are hiding a seedbank and his company wants access. In addition to the science, there's a ton of politics, which also really is not my thing. 
 The Windup Girl follows a fairly significant cast of main characters, not a single one of whom I cared a fig about. In fact, I'm not even entirely sure whether I was supposed to like them or not. Were some of them protagonists and some antagonists? Other than Emiko, the windup girl, being a protagonist, I'm really not sure. One of the characters dies fairly early on and I had absolutely no reaction to his death. Was I supposed to feel sad? Was I supposed to be glad? I legitimately have no clue. 
 The title character, the windup girl, proved most interesting, but even her sections got more boring for me as the novel went on. Actually, I think the only reason I cared what happened to her was that I felt pity for her. As she gained in power, she seemed to need my sympathy less and I was able to focus on just how little personality she really has. Admittedly, this is not her fault, considering that she is an engineered human, made to obey. 
 While I have no doubt of Bacigalupi's great talent, this novel, at least, was not for me. I failed to have any sort of emotional reaction to this book whatsoever; I was just bored. I hope that his young adult dystopia, Ship Breaker, is more accessible. The Windup Girl will appeal to readers who delight in detailed world building.

The most depressing book I read this year. 
 A dystopian story, focusing on Thailand in the future. This time the destruction of the world is brought by bio-engineered plague causing the plants and animals (and human beings) die. Thereafter, the world is controlled by global calorie companies producing genehacked carbohydrate sources, fruits, vegetables. Add to that the extinction of fossil fuels. I am shuddered thinking of the possibility that this might also happen to us in reality. 
 The idea itself is very interesting. But I can't say that the story-telling is exciting. The author also tends to say the same thing over-and-over-and-over. I had to struggle until at least 3/4 of the book to get to the part interesting enough to wake me up. Finally I know why the windup girl is in the story. And I am not happy at all.
Audiobook. Literal-wise one of the best science/speculative fiction books I've read. Fantastic writing! The plot is good, characters are interesting but the technology is somewhat unconvincing.
Bacigalupi's stuff is dense and brilliant.

The first two thirds of the book is mainly world building, which is long and somewhat dry. The windup girl is an interesting character who is barely in the story till near the end. Definitely a different mixture of genres - bio punk? I also have a problem with a world in which they can manufacture new life - plants and animals but are unable to produce solar or wind power and even have difficulties with radio cranks. I also have a hard believing that countries would adhere to carbon limits or taxes when their people are starving and the country is on the verge of collapse.

reference_books.title: The Wrath and the Dawn (The Wrath and the Dawn, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 DNFed at about 70% 
 Life is too damn short. 
 But this rage fueled review won't be. 
 There is and always will be a big problem with writing about romance (or even friendship) between captor and captive. The line between "Hey I understand why you did this and I acknowledge that you're actually a decent person" and full on Stockholm syndrome is pretty damn thin. Some authors handle this problem really well. I recently read another retelling of One Thousand and One Nights- A Thousand Nights by E.K. Johnston and the whole issue (you know, him killing his wives and all) was handled pretty well. 
 That can't be said about this book. 
 So, the main character Sharzard (because Scheherazade is just not cool enough?) wants to get revenge on Khalid because he killed her best friend. So she's all like, yeah I'll volunteer to be his wife and ruin that bitch. And... That's pretty much where the problems start. 
 First off, she literally has no plan. She is just like "Oh yeah! He married me! Time to kill him! Uh... Wait a second... How the hell am I gonna do that?" Maybe it's just me, but if I wanted to kill a king, I think I would at least try to form a plan. It's just plain stupid. How would she do it anyway? Poison? He sure as hell has someone tasting his food and drink? Knife? Please. She wouldn't get in 5 feet radius before she would be decapitated. 
 The main character is such an idiot that she shows her secret weapon to everyone , including the man she wants to kill. She goes to archery grounds (I don't know what it's really called. They shoot arrows and shit there. You know what I'm talking about). There she can't control her burning desire to show off and shows everyone she is incredibly good with an arrow. What did she think? That the guards would think "Hmmm, this girl volunteered to die and now showed that she had some amazing secret training. Also, she is always around our king. Ha ha, totally safe." 
 The second and my biggest issue with this book is the relationship itself. For the first 20 pages or so Sharzard is all business- she is going to avenge her best friend. She is going to kill the monster. Then she sees his pretty face and after spending two fucking days with him she decides that, hey, sitting on his face would be much nicer. 
 Are you fucking kidding me? 
 They haven't had one meaningful conversation. It wasn't like he said to her "Hey I have to kill 100 girls or my entire country will die. So I kind of have to kill you too. Lol sorry bye girl. Xoxo, Khalid." Nothing. All that happened was her telling him a story of Aladdin and... That's it. I would maybe kind of understand why she would feel sorry for him if he explained the situation or she figured it out or she had been a hit over the head really hard. But. 
 But. 
 But excuse the fuck out of me . Since when does any sane human being prioritize cute guy over her dead best friend? I'll repeat myself- she didn't know anything. To her he was still a crazy beast who murdered his wives for fun. And. She. Still. Wanted. To. Make. Out. With. Him. 
 This makes me feel fucking disgusted. I keep seeing this shit happen in plenty of books- he is dick/asshole/abuser/fucking murderer but he's got a pretty face so that makes everything okay! He insults and humiliates heroine but damn girl those eyes! He shoves her around and treats her like an imbecile but my gosh those arms! He thinks she is no better than scum and walks all over her but jeez that bronze tan! He kills girls and he killed a woman who was practically her sister but my god what a killer smile! 
 Seriously. Where do we draw a line? 
 Imagine if Edward Cullen looked like that guy who followed you home from store one night. Imagine if Patch looked like that old drunk who yelled at you on the bus while you were on your way home. Imagine if Khalid looked like those sleazebags who keep coming by the coffee shop you work in and who, despite being closer to your grandfather's years than yours, keep making those disgusting comments. 
 You all know what I'm all talking about. Those creepy old men who make you feel like running 40 miles in other direction and taking a long shower to fucking feel clean again. Now imagine if each one of your golden blue eyed chestnut haired hunk looked like that. Their behavior doesn't seem so cute anymore, does it now? 
 Okay, we sympathize with shitty things people do. When we see a guy who stole because he couldn't pay his bills, a girl who kills her boyfriend for abusing her, it makes you feel for them because you know that not every situation is the same. The world is not black and white. Circumstances matter. But going "Oh you kills girls for fun, let's make out."? No. Fuck no. 
 I can't fucking stand this book and what it stands for. 
 Also it's super dull and pretty badly written. But who gives a shit, really? If it was the best thing ever written, I would still give it one star.

book_a.user_review:
How I wanted to feel after reading this book: 
 How I actually felt: 
 This book did not live up to my expectations. At all. 
 I expected wanted it to be beautiful, exciting, life-changing (like the movie was), but... It wasn't. 
 Don't get me wrong, it's not a bad book, but, for me, it's also not particularly great. 
 It took me a while to get into the book, thanks to the writing style, which really annoyed me at the beginning. It was so painfully simple. 
 "Today I met John. John is tall. He doesn't like football. He likes basketball. He likes horror movies. He doesn't like ketchup." 
 Come on. Give me similies. Give me metaphors. Give me something. 
 After I did get used to it, I kinda enjoyed reading the book. The writing improved and I can't say that the plot wasn't interesting. 
 However, there was one thing that really, really bothered me. It was the fact that we never got an answer to this question(s): What the hell is wrong with Charlie? 
 What mental disease does he have? Because he was pretty... Unstable. During the whole book. He also always seemed to be kind of detached, unconnected from rest of the world. 
 Does he have PTSD? Autism? Some other mental illnes? 
 Because the writer never told me and it's really fucking frustrating. 
 The Perks does have some great quotes such as: "We accept the love we think we deserve" and "Things change. Friends leave. Life doesn't stop for anybody." 
 It's not a bad summer read but there are so many better coming-of-age stories that deserve to be read.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Its taken me a long time to write a review for this book and this is mostly because I have a very unpopular opinion about it. This book has such cult following and a hype surrounding it that I felt a peer pressure to read it. Do you know what I mean? Its like when someone says they've never watched The Breakfast Club or Ferris Bueller's Day Off and you all give that person the side eye and crazy look cause they are like generational shaping classics. Anyways I felt compelled that I read this book before the end of 2016 since this year has been fantastic for me in terms of my reading, reviewing and activeness on Goodreads. 
 I went into this book not knowing anything about it expect how life changing it was suppose to be but the thing I just hated about it was that it was soooooo pretentious. It is a novel written all in journal form and it talked about all the mundane things that happen in the life of 15 year old Charlie during 1991 to 1992. These letters were all observations of events in Charlie's life in his first year of high school and I felt like some of these observations weren't written well enough to be understood. He would use flowery prose to talk about or describe a tree or a car ride through a tunnel. Talking about how it felt infinite. Other times he will be talking about things at home and then he is at a party and then he is lying in the snow outside and at the end of the chapter he is like "Im never taking LSD again". WTF when did that happen? Supposedly he got it from a guy named Bob but were not introduced to Bob until page 142 which is after the event mentioned above. Things like this irritate me cause the plot could have been straightforward but the author chose to complicate it unnecessarily. 
 Charlie as a character seemed like a nice person but his total lack of knowing wrong from right was infuriating. The kids that came into his room during a party his brother was having where the guy raped the girl and he saw the whole thing but never said anything is disturbing. The guy that hit his sister and he saw it and only told a teacher when said teacher asked how his weekend went like it something that needed to be checked off on a to-do-list is not normal. Now its implied that Charlie had some mental instability but we don't know what his condition was. We know that he goes to a psychiatrist and takes medication but this story is trying to pass this stuff off as teenage awkwardness instead of a mental health issue. If the author wanted to write a book about mental health than he should have just done one and done it tastefully. 
 The only thing that I found interesting in this book was the quote " We accept the love we think we deserve". This I thought was thought provoking. Other than that I didn't find this book life changing at all and I feel like it puts contemporary books in a bad light. Just random drivel for 200+ pages and with a holier than though feel. This totally reminded me of those books your teacher in school would make you read for English because it was part of the course syllabus and you asked yourself how on Earth did this get to be part of the curriculum. This book has left a sour taste in my mouth for the genre and I may take a break from it for a bit to recuperate. 
 P.S. I did watch the movie after I read this book to see if things were better explained and/or flushed out now that the author/director had a different medium to try and express this supposedly life changing work but it still missed the mark. I think it missed it even further because it didn't show all the drug use Charlie was doing. The scene I was describing with the LSD happened in the movie as he was taking a wafer from the priest in mass. This was strange because if you'd never read the book then, based of the movie , you would have never thought Charlie would try recreational drugs. Then with Charlie accepting the wafer and laying it on his tongue you get transported to this party with flashing lights and heavy music. I almost thought the priest had given it to him. This convolution happens when artistry tries to supersede storytelling. Examples of beautiful artistry with fantastic storytelling: Romeo and Juliet (1996) directed by Baz Luhrmann and Upside Down (2012) by Juan Solanas. Both of theses movies were quirky and unique in their own way and managed to use flowery prose without losing the story being told. None of the writing in either was unnecessary and both conveyed a message that was important and could be understood. 
 P.P.S. adding this part in Jan 3 2017. Today I learned how to use the link function on Goodreads. So I wanted to use it to link to a great review from another book lover who also gave it a 1 star rating but gave additional points I didn't mention in my own review.

book_b.title: The Fault in Our Stars
book_b.user_review:
Actual rating: 
 2.5 
 Okay, let's do this. *cracks knuckles* 
 How I wanted to feel after reading this book: 
 How I actually felt: 
 {Or, as I like to call them: 
 Phase 1: Annoyed. 
 Phase 2: Slightly less annoyed. 
 Phase 3: Not bad/meh. 
 Phase 4: Kinda good actually. 
 Phase 5: You just had to ruin it all with that metaphor, didn't you? 
 Wash, rinse, repeat.} 
 Now, let me get one thing straight; it doesn't take a lot to make me cry. I cried on Up, I cried when Marley died and I cried approximately 3 times during Les Miserables (don't judge me). So, when I bought this book, I thought I was going to cry for days. Why? Because, well, everyone kept going on and on how sad this book is, how tragic and deep and beautiful the story is. 
 And you know what? I don't see. I don't see some sensational beauty, I don't see the deeper meaning. I don't know, maybe I just expected too much from the book? Or is it just my cold, dead heart? 
 What bothered me the most (a.k.a. the big bad): 
 Writing 
 It is so... Pretentious. It sounds awkward, fake and every metaphor in this book is ridiculously over the top. The way the characters talk, dear God, the way these people talk. They sound like they're reading directly off a script: 
 "I am," he said. He was staring at me, and I could see the corners of his eyes crinkling. "I'm in love with you, and I'm not in the business of denying myself the simple pleasure of saying true things. I'm in love with you, and I know that love is just a shout into the void, and that oblivion is inevitable, and that we're all doomed and that there will come a day when all our labor has been returned to dust, and I know the sun will swallow the only earth we'll ever have, and I am in love with you." 
 "My thoughts are stars I cannot fathom into constellations." 
 "That's the thing about pain, it demands to be felt." 
 I mean, who talks like that? I'll tell you who: nobody. Not even Shakespeare went around saying things like that. 
 The characterization of Hazel Grace: 
 Okay, right, even though I never had cancer I know what's like to live with someone who has cancer. 
 I know that, once you get it, you can't forget about it, you can't put aside the thought that you may die. You can't escape from the realization of how mortal you actually are, you can't stop thinking about what will happen to you in a day, a week, a month. 
 Wow, that was poetic as shit. 
 So, yeah, I don't think that Hazel's entire life revolving around her cancer is a bad thing. That's normal. However, I just felt like there wasn't much to Hazel beside her disease. I didn't know anything about her (beside the fact that she liked reading An Imperial Affliction and that she loved Gus). There was one thing Hazel was lacking and that was a personality. 
 I just think people should be more than just their disability; that they shouldn't be defined by their disease. 
 Van Houten: 
 I'm just going to say this: a sad story doesn't excuse someone's truly revolting behavior. Okay? Okay. Accidental book reference is accidental. 
 The love story: 
 When I started reading this story, I wanted their love to be something great and beautiful, something that will inspire people. Cheesy, I am. I wanted it to be that kind of love that starts slow but lasts for a really long time. I wanted a YA book where it takes longer than 50 pages for characters to fall in love. 
 I thought this was going to be it. I thought it was finally going to be a book where there's actual love instead of instalust/instaluv. 
 I was wrong. It takes them 50 pages to say that they love each other. 50. Pages. I don't know, maybe author did it on purpose to show that love can happen suddenly or some shit like that. Idk man. Still, would 50 or 100 more pages of relationship development really be that bad? 
 Now, for the good: 
 Augustus Waters (occasionally): 
 Let me explain that occasionally part; you see, when Gus wasn't reciting ridiculous metaphors or giving even more ridiculous speeches, he was a good character. He was far more fleshed out than Hazel, he was fun and I liked reading about his last days . Don't get me wrong, I didn't like what was happening to him; I liked the way his character acted in that situation. It was realistic. 
 Writing (again, occasionally): 
 When you ignore annoying metaphors and cringeworthy dialogue (and couple of other things, but those are minor faults), the writing wasn't that bad. It was actually kind of good and I remember that there were 3 or 4 pages that completely blew me away. 
 Hazel's parents: 
 Finally, some good parents in YA book. They were amazing. They took great care of Hazel Grace, they were fun to read about and they were really good characters. Two thumbs up for them, John Green. 
 Overall: 
 I wanted life-changing and I got mediocre. 
 Oh well.

Originally posted on my blog: www.book-scents.com 
 The Fault in Our Stars is something I've put off reading for forever. The subject matter scared me! Kids and cancer. That is a recipe for heart aching disaster for me and for my heart's sake, I put it off. However, with the movie coming out and all, I wanted to read it before watching it. I mentally braced myself. I started reading, preparing to have my heart ripped out. 
 Now, I don't know if it was the hype or the fact that everyone touts it as a masterpiece, amazing, life changing and all that but... I feel like I didn't have that same connection with it that everyone else did. Which is kind of disappointing to me. I feel like I need to inform: I cry easily. Very easily. I get emotionally invested in all books or movies and I cry during them all the time. I expected to cry. I teared up but I didn't have the gut wrenching sobs I thought I'd go through. I'm not heartless I swear!! The story was sad and touching but I felt disconnected from it. 
 I think one of the main things that made me feel the disconnect was the dialogue. I realize that Augustus Waters is supposed to be witty and funny and clever and everything but I just can't imagine a 17 year old boy talking the way he does. 17 year olds just don't spout eloquent monologues on the spot! Or even craft them ahead of time as beautifully as he did! It just didn't seem plausible and sometimes Augustus and Hazel's dialogue just came off as pretentious to me. Don't get me wrong, Hazel's snark made me smile but most of the time I found myself tilting my head to one side and thinking, "really? did this speech just happen?" 
 I can practically see the mob coming for me now. *hides* Granted, there are amazing quotes from this book. They're poignant and insightful and I love it -- but it really didn't seem natural coming out of a 16 and 17 year old. 
 Maybe the dialogue was what took me out of the story enough that I didn't cry. I'm not sure. I don't know what it is. The story was sad to be sure but this book didn't leave the lasting impression on me that I expected it too.

Once again, I've tried to read it. First time, I made it to about page seven. I didn't even get to the bit on America's Next Top Model. This time, I made it to page nineteen. See, I made progress? To me, from what I read of the book so far and what friends have gushed about to me, Green writes perfect prose -- and he does, the quotes I've read from this book are amazing -- and his characters are teenagers. Teenagers that don't exist. I know that these guys speak and think differently than I do because they had cancer, but I still grew up with teens. Not even the ones who read Green speak like his characters do.

After all the hype, I expected more. I was not impressed by this book. A bit too "teen" for me. I've read books like this before that are better. Yes, it was sad in the end, but it's like everything was okay in it's separate parts and didn't quite come together.
I didn't cry, what's wrong with me? I wasn't as connected as most of you, I guess. I liked it...but maybe being a nurse made me relate and understand on a different level. First JG book.

I hope you won't ever read a simplified version of this book. Simplified books are parodies and caricatures, good for nothing. Even people trying to learn a new language had much better plunge in the deep end. 
 If you haven't read this book yet, and are skimming the reviews to see what it's like, and if you happen on mine then this is my advice, don't read any more reviews and read the book at least twice. And then come back and read about how other people have experienced it. 
 If you have read the book, then you may be among a large group of brilliant people who hate it, or join the other group of equally brilliant people who love it. Though using the word love may not be the correct term! There won't be any ambiguity. And right there, is one of the charms of this work of art. 
 For second time readers, for what it's worth this is my suggestion if I may, don't think much while you're reading and don't try to analyse, just let your emotions come to the surface and observe your Self. Not the book. You will see you are drawn in and are experiencing the emotions and life lessons of souls who only ever existed in Emily Bronte's chest, and then in the book she wrote. Who knows how she did this? My mind can't fathom how she and other prodigies and creators of any great work of art in any field did it. But no matter if you love or hate it, this book shall leave you a bit changed. The hours you spend reading it will somehow amount to years of experiencing life. I hope you will have, indeed, read it even before you read my review. Because that way, I wouldn't have set your expectations in anyway, or clouded your eyes. Or your feelings.

I can appreciate Bronte's (perhaps rather realistic) depiction of how humans really work, and the ending with the graves were rather touching all the same, but I just couldn't bring myself to like this book.

This is not a love story. Stories like this contribute too much to why people have such a skewed version of what love is supposed to be, and why so many girls think abuse in a relationship is acceptable and normal (Do you hear me Stephenie Meyer!?!). 
 Synopsis: A guy with reactive attachment disorder meets one of the most narcissistic chicks in all of literature. When he's the only game in town she'll "love" him because hey, narcissism has to be fed, but he'll never get the fulfilling love out of the relationship that he needs. And he'll never know how to "love" anyone else because he thinks that obsession is love and is incapable of forming any other attachments-- Lord help you if you do anything that smells like abandonment (she does). So they blithely go about wrecking havoc on the lives of everyone around them, even their children and the one or two truly decent people they know... all in the name of "Love" (selfishness). 
 It's a train wreck. I can see someone enjoying it for it's literary merit. I can see enjoying it as a horror story or psychological thriller. But as the ultimate end-all and be-all of love stories, or even a love story at all? No thank you. 
 Blech.
