Let me start off by saying that I love books about troubled people, especially if they feel like they are written by the main character and have a distinct voice. I love them. 
 BUT: 
 I decided to read The Catcher in the Rye because it seems to be one of those "essential" reads, and about 13% through I realized why it is essential. People either love this book or despise it, which I think is the reason it's so important. Holden is either relatable or he isn't, and I cannot relate to him whatsoever. 
 The thing is, I probably would have loved this book if I would have read it when I was thirteen, still painting my eyelids red and putting the letter "x" on either side of every username, but right now, at the tail end of age twenty, I absolutely could not stand it. Even the rebellious thirteen-year-old in me wanted to smack the hell out of Holden. In my opinion, he wasn't even a well-rounded character, because he had absolutely zero likable characteristics and that makes for a very flat characterization. 
 I asked my boyfriend a little ways into the novel if Holden ever shoots somebody or something interesting like that happens because I found myself completely bored with the monotony of his vapid existence. I'm fine with annoying characters like him if they have some sort of eye-opening experience or at least one likable quality, but he lacks any of that. There weren't even secondary characters that were at least mildly interesting. 
 Needless to say, I'm going to spend my time reading about worthwhile protagonists (who do not have catchphrases that make me want to knock them out) rather than repetitive, annoying, pointless, unchanging ones like Holden Caulfield. 
 He's got a great name, though.

My teacher actually managed to convince me it deserved more than 1 measly star - so 2, but with a lot of reservations. 
 BONUS TIME! 
 Counting of catch phrases! 
 And all - 338 times. 
 Goddam - 237 times. 
 Killed me/her/him - 50 times. 
 Phony - 45 times. 
 Hate/drive him crazy/pisses him off - 51 times. 
 Boy - 74 times. 
 Repetitive? It is repetitive, it really is, if you want to know the truth.
I think I'm the only person I know who hated this book, found it incredibly overrated....

I heard so many good things about this book that I thought to myself "I refused to read it in high school, hell why not read it now!". I should have just stuck with not reading it. This book SUCKED! 
 The book starts on some random day & ends on some random day. There is no beginning middle or end. It's like spending 2 days with some kid that hates school - in a TON of details - and then it ends. I was the kid that hated school and I've lived 27 years. My life is much more interesting than this crap! 
 UGH! Glad I bought this book at borders at 80% off. Had I read this crap in school instead of hang out with my friends I would have been pissed off!
Augh - What are people thinking? This was a horrible book. I felt like I was reading some very very bad high school writing project. No story, no point, bad grammar. A total waste of time.

What's all the hubub, Bub? Maybe it's a coming-of-age thing from '60s nostalgia of a time past, but I don't get it. Holden was annoying, but it was not just that. I expected so much more, and sometimes hyped expectations are disappointing. Maybe I should have read it earlier in my life to appreciate the angst. 
 I need to re-approach this book some other time in hopes my disappointment was about timing.

I decided to read Catcher in the Rye for Banned Books Week. At first I was intrigued by it b/c it was referenced in a movie (Conspiracy Theories), so I wanted to know what it was all about. About halfway through I was annoyed by the incessant whining, exaggerations, and swearing. To be fair, it's pretty on par with teenagers, at least today. The only part I really liked was the last couple of chapters. Now that I've read it, I don't ever have to pick up this book again.

I feel like there's something wrong with me. I don't find this book as entertaining as some others did. It's basically just about a guy expressing random thoughts in different chapters, the end. Couldn't find the spark to it... help!

I don't know if it holds up when you're an adult, but it's rather life-changing to read as a teen or college student. Salinger's profane Holden Caufield was the first kid of his kind I'd ever experienced on the page, then I looked around and saw dozens of him in the hallways at school.

reference_books.title: Frankenstein
reference_books.review_text:
I can't say I disliked this novel but I was also hugely underwhelmed - this would've made a great short story but the endless whining of Frankenstein and his depression just drove me to boredom on far too many an occasion when reading this. 
 To begin with, the book is written in an interesting style, with letters from a sea captain to his partner describing an encounter with an odd man near the Arctic Circle whilst on an expedition. Thus unfolds the story of Frankenstein and the creation of the monster and a final act (which I won't explain in depth because it's a bit of a spoiler). It's an interesting tale of a scientist acting without thought for his actions and the hideous consequences, as well as a suspenseful thriller as we await the monster's reaction to mankind, and indeed his creator, shunning him. Unfortunately Dr Frankenstein is such a dismal character I found myself not caring a damn what befell him or indeed his monster, his family or anything at all!

reference_books.title: Never Let Me Go
reference_books.review_text:
This is such an emotional book - I read the whole thing in almost a state of shock at the content. I encourage everyone to read this book with as little prior knowledge of the storyline as possible - the book unfolds in such a shocking and gripping way that it's a pleasure to turn the pages. 
 Without giving away too much, the story is told by Kathy, a girl in a private school where they are encouraged to keep away from the outside world. They realise something is not completely sound with the situation but never rebel against it. I found myself screaming at the characters to turn away and run from their lives but their total submission to their lives is the most shocking theme in this book. An absolutely classic.

reference_books.title: Rabbit, Run (Rabbit Angstrom #1)
reference_books.review_text:
It's so hard to review a book like this - it's seen in many polls as one of the 'classics' of literature but how can you enjoy a book where the protagonist is so disdainful - I have nothing but contempt for Rabbit. 
 Set in a sleepy suburban town in 50's America, this is a very well written novel but reminds me of the equally hard-to-read Revolutionary Road and the bleak, depressing mood these post-war novels evoke. 
 Deciding he cannot live with his family anymore, Rabbit runs away and tries again at setting up his life, oblivious to the damage he does to everyone he meets. The problem I had was trying to understand if we're supposed to like, or even relate to Rabbit? Perhaps 50's men could but to me he's an insipid and insufferable chauvinist with no obvious redeeming qualities, and his character made this book hard for me to enjoy at all.

reference_books.title: Ubik
reference_books.review_text:
A big fat 5 stars for this, I'm amazed I've never heard of it before and that PKD is known for 'Electric Sheep' so much more! 
 This extremely intricate sci-fi treasure opens in 1992, a future for when the novel was written that now includes people with psi-abilities, but also anti-psi abilities, as one character explains it, like privacy police. I still can't work out the overall tone of the book as PKD does a wonderful job of bringing quasi-futuristic concepts, technology and even fashion (the description of the characters' clothes is wonderful) but also a distinctly anti-consumerism feel to all this. For example, everything is coin-operated in this somewhat dystopian future, a nice plot device for later on but also a fantastic way to introduce a Douglas-Adams-esque talking door which won't let our poor protagonist leave his apartment because he's so in debt. The wry, acerbic humour throughout the novel really surprised me, but lifts this book into a new level of enjoyment for me. 
 The characters are sufficiently larger than life to fit into this backdrop and their abilities and anti-abilities all dealt with subtly enough to fit in perfectly. Finally, we're given the concept of reanimated dead people through moratoriums, a macabre concept that puts one more tick in the box for this novel. 
 Suffering from boredom? Try one Ubik and all your worries will disappear. Take as directed, once daily.

reference_books.title: Fanny Hill, or Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure
reference_books.review_text:
Oo - definitely not a book I would've thought to have read but a naughty pleasure indeed! I picked this up in the library just before Christmas and found myself laughing out loud at the baudiness and sheer graphic nature of the novel. 
 The language is fascinating (especially as I'm not an avid reader of the period) and enthralling - what a joy :)

book_a.title: Dark Force Rising (Star Wars: The Thrawn Trilogy, #2)
book_a.user_review:
Following on immediately from the Heir to the Empire, this novel is a different beast to the first - perhaps because some of the surprises have been revealed and we're down to the detail now, but the beginning reminds me of the lull in excitement which the original Star Wars films all suffer from. It's interesting finding out about Mars Jade's past as the Emperor's Hand and C'baoth's deception of Luke but it's not quite as well paced or enthralling as the first in the trilogy. The book spends perhaps a little too much time dashing between one destination and another making it all seem a bit rushed and cluttered. 
 All things considered though, this is an enjoyable sequel - the Noghri storyline is clever and the action scenes are well played, I'm just hoping the concluding novel ups the ante a little.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I'd been reading children's stories I should have read when I was eleven: Sherlock Holmes, Jules Verne's adventures - when I came across, in storage, the books I was reading when I was eleven. In fact, Timothy Zahn's Thrawn Trilogy, appeared the year I turned eleven, and at that age I thought it excellent - so much so I kept buying Star Wars novel right through until 1996, hoping each time that they would be as good as Zahn's original trilogy. They never were. They say you should never go back: and it is true. Zahn's Thrawn trilogy is fun, and this, the first volume gets things off to a cracking start: it reintroduces us to the classic figures, Luke Skywalker, Princess Leia, Han Solo et al, and some minor characters, and gives us a menacing new villain, yet the writing is never as strong as I recall, and all the nods to the classic films becomes a little tiring. 
 I did, however, plough through all three novels with such speed, and enjoyed them immensely while reading them, that I can see what eleven year old me enjoyed in them, and why fans of the Star Wars world still read them today. Interestingly it is not the main characters that shine in this series, but the new ones: smuggler Talon Karrde, and his secretive companion, Mara Jade, who has one subconscious command: Kill Luke Skywalker. The Grand Admiral Thrawn is an enigmatic and genius villain - he learns a species flaws by studying their art. Then there is the insane Dark Jedi, Joruus C'Boath, whose megalomania threatens to engulf the universe as a new Emperor. I kept wondering: would these adventures be better without the need to conform to George Lucas's original vision? Perhaps Luke et al should have just been background. 
 Nevertheless, Timothy Zahn is a great writer for these sorts of things, and he sows seeds that he surprises us with later - the true nature of Delta Source, the secret behind Mara Jade's desire, and he makes parents of Han Solo and Princess Leia - and that is the right ending for the love story that begun way back in 1977 with Star Wars.

Just gets better and better. Zahn continues to amaze and keep you on the edge of your seat with his continuing Star Wars saga. The characters have to face political enemies, personal enemies and the Empire itself. There is not one page, one paragraph, one sentence where your attention strays. The characters are all struggling with the insecurity of it all and you want so desperately for this long war to be over and for them to finally have some peace. 4.6/5

The first half of this book was a bit of a slog, but it got much better (action-wise) near the end. There are far too many references to the original Star Wars trilogy planted throughout to remind the reader again and again that he/she is reading a Star Wars book. Famous lines from the movies are used repeatedly, as if the characters are talking toys with pull-strings. This is really a 2.5 star book. I'll read the final book in the series to how it all wraps up, but am in no hurry to do so.

"Right." "Right." "RIGHT." It's been some time since I've encountered a writer who repeated the same pattern of dialogue with nearly every character. This is similar to all of Steven Erikson's characters, shrugging and nodding as a response to nearly everything. Even as I'm writing this, I think I'm going to lower it to two stars. Honestly, it wasn't bad by any means. It's just very soft, predictable, and often repetitive. I'm pretty excited to finish the final installment so I can move on.
STAR WAAAARS

So what happened after The Return of the Jedi? This series answers the question. If you are a Star Wars fan, you will want to pick this up. The writing won't win any literary awards, much in the same way that the movies were not nominated for Best Picture at the Oscars, but who cares? It's action with all those characters that we have come to know and love. The series consists of : 
 Heir to the Empire 
 Dark Force Rising 
 The Last Command 
 http://www.books.rosboch.net/?p=1520

One of the best Star Wars novels out there. Many people wish that Lucas had changed these books into episodes 7,8 and 9. Yes, they are that good. Timothy Zahn is a very good author and helps bring the feel of the original movies into a novel form.

As with any book written as a spin off from Star Wars (or Star Trek, Battlestar Galactica, etc.), this book runs the risk of contradicting future installments of the franchise. Since episodes seven through nine of the Star Wars Saga have not been made, this hasn't happened yet. This was a good read, regardless. Just make sure to read the first of the three books in this series, Heir to the Empire, before reading this book.
Loved this trilogy when I was 12- again, Zahn really is the best Star Wars book writer, with the possible exception of Aaron Allston, but that's just 'cause he's funnier.

book_b.title: Contact
book_b.user_review:
I don't think I can possibly give this less than four stars because although the book has its shortcomings, Sagan does an amazing job of taking his suppositions for our future and the history of the universe from his factual books and turning them into such an intriguing read. 
 I loved Sagan's Pale Blue Dot so I was fascinated (and more than a little surprised) to find out he'd written Contact. I remember going to watch the film when it came out and being impressed by the concepts but feeling they'd been diluted too much. Lo and behold Sagan put a huge amount more into the book, going into tremendous detail explaining the science behind his characters' beliefs and chronicling how politics is so likely to get in the way should (when?!) we make contact. 
 Sagan's seemingly simple way of explaining complex concepts is wondrous, well suited early on in the book to demonstrate Ellie's initial grasping of huge ideas as a child and used throughout the novel to make important but complicated topics easier to read about. 
 The novel isn't without its flaws; it's clear Sagan is a scientist at heart and some of the character interactions are a little clunky. It's also been well edited to get down to this length but there are still some sections which seem overlong. I found those small issues easy to overlook when treating the book as a whole though because ultimately even the overlong sections add depth to the story and its characters and Sagan is first and foremost an eminent scientist. Whereas the film jumps from finding a message to decoding it and using the contents in a remarkably short span, Sagan's original novel delights in pointing out that even intercepting the whole message would be a gargantuan task requiring international effort and months if not years of collaboration. 
 Sagan treats how a find of this magnitude would affect society (in particular those who are religious) in a sensitive way, making his protagonist vehemently athiest whilst forcing her into interacting with religious leaders and realising the shortcomings of being intentionally antagonistic. Again, how the filmmakers treated this so heavy-handedly and decided to shoe-horn a love story in (when only the merest of hint of romantic interest is hinted at) is beyond me. 
 Brilliant - a real thought provoking book that is also a highly enjoyable read.

sample_reviews.review_text: I was debating between 4 and 5... 2/3rds through it was a solid 5 but then I struggled with some choices but this is a hard book to have a satisfactory ending for... and then in the last moments I very much enjoyed the imagery so back up to 5 it went! I very much enjoyed which types of technology Sagan could envisage when this was written (he almost nailed DVR!) and which ones he couldn't. I also loved how much depth he gave the main character and through her addressed the sexism in science that women have had to endure. I am also hopeful that there has been progress since its writing. Also the themes of knowing, and how practitioners of science & religion needlessly talk past each other were very good. I highly recommend this book.

Not bad but I think I expected more. To much preparations for the journey, to short second part. I think it woyld be good if I read it 10 years earlier. Now I would like a book much more progressive than that.

A Gone Bookserk Perspective 
 This has been a book long overdue to read. I have been meaning to read it for years, and finally the time is here, and I have read it. Actually, it's been quite a while since I have read a book lately. It's been some tough times lately, but reading hasn't failed me and so here I am again! 'Contact' has been an amazing journey. 
 This is a very dense and complex book, to say the least. It is DENSE. It's hard-writing as well. It sort of gave me the feeling that I sometimes get after reading 3-4 research scientific articles - a pounding headache from the overload of information at the top of my right temple. Nevertheless, nothing worth knowing or having comes easy, and so is the case with this book. It really covers a whole spectrum of topics - childhood, coming of age through wonderment and questioning, being a female in a male dominated science field, having a passion for the universe, battle between science and religion and whether we are alone or not in the Universe, and if we are not alone who else is out there with us, and topics of religions all over the world and the parallel stories they share between one another (this subject in particular flew over my head most of the time). Then there are the topics of physics and mathematics. Not only are there quite a large number of topics being covered, but all are of multidimentional aspect. They involve cultural notions, individual voices, the human soul, ancestry and the future, the planet and our universe...etc. And on top of everything this is not a short read, it is 448pages! 
 So what if it's dense, complex, and long? For me, this was one of the most enlightening but most challenging books - intellectually, spiritually, and scientifically. There's not doubt, I will have to revisit this book if I can take away even 25% of the whole message or even a small portion of the debates between science and religion. As a science fiction, it is an acquired taste, and more so because of the topics of universe and religious arguments and history, you have to be a little familiar with the two to get a good chunk of what's going on. Even against the fact that I am quite ignorant of many things, including religious beliefs around the world and even astronomy, this book was very fulfilling because it still maintained a consistent human element throughout the book. And that, THAT, is the key to any great book - a consistent human presence in the voice of the writing. Carl Sagan didn't get the Pulitzer Prize for the Cosmo out of thin air. 
 This book has changed me a little bit, and a book that can do that is a powerful book. I look up at the sky multiple times every day, and for the first time in my life I really look up at the sky and, one, remember very profoundly that I live on a very special planet, and two, realize that it's very likely that we are not alone. I believe we are not alone, but we have no proof of it, and as a scientist I have to hold a level of skepticism until the proof is confirmed, but as a spiritual person I believe we are not alone! This book has also opened up my eyes to our past and our future, our religious beliefs-where they come from-and where we are and where we are going in terms of religion, and most importantly ask 'WHY' just like the main character in the book did. For a while now, I have felt the urge to look at the interconnectedness of the world, and this book pushed me further to delve into different aspects of our existences and maybe link different things together form religion, to science, to the Universe, and most important to learn as much as I can about our own planet because there is enough on this planet, right in front of our eyes, to teach us all we need to now about ourselves, our ancestors, our future, and possibly our place in the Universe. 
 It's about that time in the world when 'Contact' is probably more relevant than ever before! Maybe this comment will make more sense in the near future, just mark my words. We are not alone! I say this not just from reading 'Contact,' but from other reputable sources, but since the topic here is about 'Contact' I'll stick to stating that the book did in fact have a part in it too. 'Contact' opens an avenue for discourse at least, and I have always believed that a platform for discussion is the first step toward getting closer to the truth.

This was an amazing book. After watching the movie of the same name several times in the past, what struck me as incomprehensible was how the makers made such a hash of it. The book is a bit complicated in places with its science but it is about a message from outer space that includes the building of an interstellar space craft. But inside this message is another message and it is quite profound. The story is well written and anyone with a mind that contimplates life beyond the end of their nose will be awed by it. I don't know of another book that makes what Sagan does in this book more believable or more plausible than him. From the concepts, to the stories, to the plotline, to the human interactions, to the philosophical implications of a message being received from outer space.

Not my usual genre, but amazing book. I thoroughly enjoyed it and will place this on my "read every couple of years" shelf!

It starts with two of the friends, Stephanie and Linden, make a pact to be married at 30 if not in a serious relationship. As the years pass, you learn how neither are finding what they want in the people they are dating, but see exactly what they crave when looking at each other. Around two months later, a near fatal accident sends them all running back to the friendship and love they ran from.

Hace algun tiempo, estuve enamorada de quien solia ser mi mejor amigo. 
 Sera por eso que no puedo evitar leer libros como este, que no puedo evitar reir, llorar y entender a los personajes como nadie. 
 Lamentablemente para mi, mi vida no esta basada en un libro, y las cosas obviamente no terminaron como me hubiera gustado que terminaran. Es por eso que siempre caigo por los protagonistas masculinos de estos libros, esos que tienen el coraje de admitir sus sentimientos y de seguir a su corazon. 
 Linden McGregor no fue diferente. Lo ame desde el primer momento, bueno, tal vez desde que me entere que era escoces *y no pude evitar imaginarmelo como Jamie Fraser diciendome "sassenach" al oido* *babas* jaja 
 Hablando en serio... 
 Karina, te amo. Siempre admire tu forma de escribir, pero con este libro me robaste totalmente el corazon. Tal vez es porque me llego mas profundo, o tal vez es porque Linden es irresistiblemente sexy, dulce y divertido. 
 Y porque no hay ningun enano maldito interponiendose en el medio *ejem Javier ejem*. 
 Quizas haya algun proyecto de Legolas, que es mas un Bilbo Bolson que otra cosa, o un modelo cabeza hueca, o una pelirroja loca e histerica, o un amigo que puede parecer un villano pero al que, a pesar de todo, pude entender totalmente. Aun asi, este libro es hermoso, y me alegra haberlo elegido como mi primera lectura (terminada) del 2015. 
 Tal vez, con mucha suerte, este ano pueda encontrar un Linden para mi.

Too many grand speeches - not gonna lie, I skimmed over a bunch of this. For how slow and drawn out the first half is, the second half has a lot of activity, but it feels rushed/unearned.

The Pact was free on Amazon and I was so excited to finally get a chance to read anything by Karina Halle. Wrong choice of book I guess, since her other series have stellar reviews and this was underwhelming and disappointing, and I wasn't even impressed by the writing style either. It wasn't exactly what I had in mind when I read the blurb. Linden and Steph, in their mid twenties decide to form this pact to get married on their 30s because of course in your early 20s you guess you're going to be alone a decade later and you want to secure a marriage. 
 Years later the MCs are still single and going through boyfriends and girlfriends like there's no tomorrow, even though the hero is kind of in love with her but what the hell let's wait a decade for her to come to her senses and the heroine is seriously worshipping this dude with long, boring descriptions that were supposed to make me as a reader love him, it didn't. The story bored me to death, and so did the characters, immaturity at it's best! 
 He's your typical rich guy that has endless hooks up while he's waiting for his dream girl to wake up and she is a miserable woman who has no idea what she's doing with her life and dates losers while occasionally eye fucking the MC and of course there's the mutual best friend that kinda has a thing for her and they dated unsuccessfully at some point and now they might hook up because why not. Also he kinda hates The Pact they have formed. Needless to say the entire plot had no point, the characters were just doing random things that made no sense given their age. 
 And just to clarify, I'm totally on board with people dating whomever they want and however many people they want, as long as those relationships don't make you more miserable than happy. 
 Moving on. 
 If the story didn't have a timeline I'd bet they were in freaking high school and made a pinky swear. There even was a big slap from the hero's current girlfriend to the heroine when the two kissed during a game of Truth or Dare; again, what's their age? Two stars only because it had a few good moments and it's still free so you might as well get it if you want to.

I really am confused about this book. 
 it's not right to say I expected something more from this because I did not have expectation. 
 But the idea, the plot was something intriguing. I started this book thinking there was a good start with a good story to begin with. I thought "This is something refreshing". And reading that this was considered a "funny" book was something I was happy about. 
 I love funny romances book. Sorry. My mistake. I love story with humour, and a little sass. 
 But let me start from the beginning. 
 THE PLOT 
 There is this girl Violet that goes to the hockey match of his stepbrother and then meets his teammate: the beautiful famous hot captain Alex Waters. And all goes from there. 
 MY FIRST IMPRESSION 
 Since the beginning I noticed there was a lot of lets call it "stream of conciousness" of Violet. In the first moments I thought it was just to introduce the heroine. But then I understood that the book would have been all like this. 
 GOING ON WITH THE STORY 
 going on with that her thoughs and the narration by Violet became really annoying. And then I understood that what she thought and what she said out loud was supposed to be funny. 
 LET ME EXPLAIN 
 I'm not an hater. I don't like write bad reviews and I'm not here to destroy anything. I'm here to share and express my opinion and feelings about a book. I appreciate the effort of every work. 
 But I think that the mistake in this book was the desperate persuit of a funny story that wasn't reached. I think that all the situations where Violets is are too forced. Too much. And I think the reader can pick up easily when something is made with effort and not just comes with the flow. it's not spontaneous. 
 And this -i'm sorry- did not make me laugh. 
 WHAT I MEAN AND WHAT I THINK 
 A lot of situationS made me think that Violet was stupid and I felt a sense of shame for her and not for a minute I smiled.I found some things- not to say voulgar- not very classy. 
 AGAIN- it's not that i'm picky and snob. It's not that I don't like the dirty talks -because believe me, in other context I love them- or that I can't easily smile. It's that this was a kind of funny that I did not really appreciate. 
 RECOMMENDATIONS 
 So for people who enjoyed humour like the one on The Deal or A Perfect Ten I don't recommend it. 
 If you enjoy a more easy humour like the one Cocky Bastard maybe this is something for you. 
 IN the END..THE SEQUEL??? 
 The story wasn't bad. It could have potential. But some dialogues and moments really turned me off. 
 I don't know if I'll read the second book in this seriesPucked Up. 
 Should I give another try?

 So I have to preface this with I own Dream for an Insomniac on VHS and we wore that movie out in college, so I had good vibes for this author before every reading the book. Loved the writing style. Quirky, witty, insightful characters like Jacob and "Trixie" are right up my alley. You are told what's going to happen from the beginning. Yet as the book comes to a close part of me was hoping that it wouldn't happen. Fate would be wrong; divine intervention would occur. Unfortunately, exactly what was said would happen, happened. This review is going to be a complete anomaly from me. I'm going to do several things I've never done nor ever thought I would do. First and foremost I'm about to get real. More real that I've ever been on this site. 
 Sometimes I think (and probably unfairly) that there are two kinds of writers. I guess you could break it down to followers vs. leaders. It seems like some write because they are following a trend, be it vampires, angels, dystopias, what have you. Then there are those writers who seem to only write a book because they have a story in their mind that needs to be told. I think it's safe to say Tiffanie DeBartolo falls in the "leaders" category. I've now read both of her books and they are both amazing. I'm just blown away by how talented she is, and I don't mean to sound like an entitled reader but it pains me to think that she hasn't written more. If I ever had the chance to speak to Ms. DeBartolo, I don't think I'd be able to stop myself from quoting Magneto and exclaiming: 
 So, have you ever heard the phrase "the human condition"? I have, and to be honest, I've never really bothered to find out exactly what it means; I've just come up with my own assumption. And to me, Tiffanie DeBartolo gets it. There are so many lines from this book that so utterly rang true to me. For instance: 
 "I always felt like that myself, that I didn't marry into the landscape of the human world like others did, that I was on the outside looking in." 
 Or: 
 "As long as I can remember being conscious of existence, I've been conscious of death. Eternal rest isn't some abstract concept for me. It's real. It chases me down like a dog behind a bicycle. I'm faster than it is, for the moment, but I might pop a tire any second and it'll sink its teeth into my heel. Or worse, into the heels of someone I love." 
 And then there's this: 
 "I like to say I don't believe in mystics. I don't believe in fate. I don't believe in destiny or kismet. I don't believe in God. I don't believe in anything. 
 But I believe in the possibility of everything." 
 There are many more but they would seriously require copying pages of text. I had a note where I would write down a page with a quote I liked, and part of it says 57, 58, 59. She's just one of those rare authors who it feels like is writing things that exist in my head, only far more eloquently than I ever could. 
 If your intentions are pure 
 I'm seeking a friend for the end of the world. 
 I mean the woman wrote a personal ad using a Chris Cornell song. And I kid you not, a few days before reading this, I was in the mood to listen to Audioslave, and found myself googling Chris Cornell, telling myself I need more of his music. 
 I don't intend to talk about anything too spoilerific, but I'm using a spoiler tag just to be safe. 
 There are so many books out there with numerous gif-heavy, 5-star reviews. And when I read them myself, I'm either left indifferent, or baffled because often all I felt was contrived angst. Just when I start to question how picky I am when it comes to star ratings, a book like this comes along and completely validates my position. It is just in a completely different stratosphere. THIS is heartache. THIS is anguish. This is worthy of the expression "it feels like my still beating heart was ripped out of my chest." 
 I realize this is not the opinion of a well-adjusted 30 year old, but I've always thought the phrase "'Tis better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all" to be...well kind of a crock of shit. Now, this is where the whole "writing things that exist in my head" comes to play. It's as if this entire book was like her literary version of my own wildest dream and worst nightmare, all in one. Rather cryptic, but it makes sense to anyone who's read it. Obviously I felt the aforementioned heartache. After finishing, I would drift off to sleep only to suddenly remember what happened and feel that punch in my gut. But the strange thing is, instead of falling into a dark, despondent place where I feel righteously withdrawn from the world, I actually feel a sliver of hope. That maybe there is something to that quote above. After all, "Fear won't keep you safe from being hurt." 
 So there we have it. A highly opinionated, quote laden, image macro included, spoiler tag containing review--a first by yours truly. There's so much more I wish I could say about this book, and How to Kill a Rock Star for that matter, but skilled with words I am not. I will end this by saying I sincerely hope this is not the last book I read by this author.

** spoiler alert ** 
 An interesting tale of how a girl finds her true love (although very weird and excessively intense) and how she loses him. Sad, but not quite enough to make one cry as you somehow see it coming.

Ugh. This book was a workout. First off, its cover is misleading. The front talks about how a gypsy predicted main character's true love would die young and leave her alone. Spoiler Alert: This happens. Yet, the gypsy and all that is more like an after thought that gets brought up in prologue and last chapter as a sort of deus ex machina. 
 The work is an obvious first novel from DeBartolo, who is trying to channel the struggling writer story and rocky love life into a novelized version. Her main character Beatrice and her love interest Jacob are vain, selfish, boring people who have kinky sex at almost every opportunity. Jacob has some misogynistic tendencies that come into the light in a disturbing "sexy rape" scene that still makes me shudder. Beatrice is a poor, basic white girl who makes a great living selling her uncomplicated jewelry. She gets her kicks making fun of everyone who isn't as deep as she is, and she hates her doting and supportive parents almost as much as she hates when Jacob supports her. 
 This book...(shakes head sadly, knows she must go on just a little further to spread the truth) 
 Plus, there's enough subplots within one-half of the book to sink it. There's a dead dad, and a missing dad, and a new life plot, and a relationship, and another death, and ex boyfriends and girlfriends all over the damn place. 
 Painfully, I admit, that I wrote something similarly emo when I was in college. At least, I self published and kept the majority of the world from my diary-esque ramblings. 
 #2StarRead

4Stars 
 Genre: Contemporary Romance 
 Type: Standalone 
 POV: First Person - Female 
 "If your intentions are pure I'm seeking a friend for the end of the world." 
 Beatrice aka "Trixie" Jordan was a free spirit kind of person; an artist at heart. She occupied her time making and designing her own jewelry and she made it from the heart. They were precious to her. Her talent was well known and very fast her business bloom big time. Trixie loved music and wasn't the type of person that could deal with peoples crap. She just didn't feel that she had time to deal with people if she didn't have to and so she focus on what she liked best, books, music, making jewelry and having sex. The essentials of course (my type of girl) hehe. 
 Jacob Grace was a writer with dreams and super cool character. He was simple yet complicated because he knew what he liked and he was extremely honest. He spoke his mind and heart and that's why his circle of friends adored him. He was also a free spirit that loved to live in the moment making memories. 
 One silly newspaper add changed both of these two forever. They knew from the first day they met that they were meant for each other; they have found their soul mates in each other. Their relationship was super cool, fun, hot, real, and adventurous. 
 "Here's the thing. I feel like we grew in the same womb or something. Like we've been connected from the beginning by blood and veins. Someone soul lovers, if there could ever be such a thing." 
 I really liked all the side characters from heroine best friend who was hilarious and hero's circle of friends. Jacob struggle internally for not growing up with a father; things happened and he felt he couldn't opened up so he leaves Trixie for few weeks without telling her. Oh boy was she angry and was I pissed off?! Hell to the yes. I was so angry at him it really upset me. However when he comes back it was hard not to forgive him, still he left a sour taste in my mouth because I don't forget easily haha. The words he said; the things he did though made him so unique and special. 
 "We're all searching for something to fill up what I like to call that big, God-shaped hole in our souls." 
 The end; well ever since the beginning and based on blurb and title I already knew how this was going to end. So when it happened I didn't cry; however the aftershocks effects were painful, the memories, what could have been gutted me till no end. I kid you not I cried in the shower for an hour, I cried myself to sleep that night and I'm crying as I'm typing this right now...but Shhh don't judge whatever. Haha! 
 "Everyone feels that void. Everyone who has the balls to look inside themselves, anyway. It's what life's all about...A search." 
 This book is unique, the writing is phenomenal, the characters are awesome, there are sexy times, hilarious stuff I laughed so hard reading this book. I can honestly say it is not for everyone though because if you are looking for a "HEA" you best stay away from this book. One thing I know for sure is that this story will stay with me forever.

There really needs to be an official name for the genre of books about cranky old men redeemed. "A Man Called Ove","The Hundred-Year-Old Man Who Climbed Out the Window and Disappeared" and now "The Unlikely Pilgrimage of Harold Fry" have all (at least in the UK) been wildly popular in recent years. If you enjoyed one, you'll probably like the others. Overall, I liked this book, and it improves as it goes along, becoming unexpectedly thoughtful in the last few pages. I probably wouldn't recommend anyone to rush out and buy it, but you could do worse.

At the age of 65, Harold Fry takes on a journey on foot across England to search for himself and to come to terms with all his internal demons. Harold's touching journey is that of introspection and faith , and the story is suffocatingly sentimental.

This book is - on the outset - a seemingly light hearted, somewhat odd tale of a retired man who decides to walk the length of England for a woman he once knew (Spoiler! He wasn't - and isn't - in love with her!). Harold Fry is an unassuming man, quietly getting on with being retired, doing little, and having non-conversations with his wife. 
 He gets a letter, he starts a journey, and as he travels, we learn so much more about him. Harold has lost so much, and behind his tall, persistently stooping exterior, is a man who needs to make this journey as much as the woman waiting for him on the other end needs him to make it. 
 So many books that deal with the kind of topics this book deals with tend toward either sugar coating or sentimentality. This does neither. It is a simple, well written, well plotted story, and I found my heart travelling with Harold, thinking about his journey even when I wasn't actively reading it.

 I haven't been kept up at night by a book for a good few years (and I read constantly) but Harold Fry gripped me and kept me turning the pages into the wee small hours. 
 I would say that Rachel Joyce is an accomplished writer much in the style of Anne Tyler who is my favourite female author. 
 I cannot wait to read Joyce's next book. 
 Bravo to Harold Fry

It's almost unfair to give this book one star because the writing is refreshing (see phrase "vehicular awesomeness"), but the narrator is a male high school senior, and thus talks and thinks like one. Not exactly the sort of mind I want to dip in and out of. I read about 50 pages before the swearing was too much for me.

Quentin "Q" Jacobsen is about to graduate high school when the girl across the street, who he's loved from across the street, takes him on a night of adventure and then disappears. Q knows there is more to it than she just left town and he enlists the help of his friends and her friends to try to find her: dead or alive. 
 This is the third John Green book I have read and I am noticing a pattern. As I've noted before, Green has a way of making characters fun, unique, and interesting and does so again in this book. However, I am noticing that its his supporting characters that I wind up being fascinated by and that his main characters tend to be cut from the same mold from book to book. Green likes for his main female characters to be "manic pixie dream girls". This is a movie term that has been coined to describe female characters that are so quirky and cute and strange yet sexy and alluring. Think Ellen Page in Juno. Think Natalie Portman in Garden State. Think Zooey Deschanel in anything. Our main female in Paper Towns, Margo Roth Spiegelman, is this character. In Looking for Alaska, it was the titular Alaska. In An Abundance of Katherines, it was Lindsey Lee Wells. For me, this makes the story itself less interesting because these female characters are all so similar. In Paper Towns, even the popular girls become this way towards the end. Lacey Pemberton, who is a popular slightly bitchy friend of Margos, ends up dating the nerdy friend of our main character. It just feels convenient. Our male main characters are similar as well. They are nerdy, outsiders who lust after these manic girls. 
 Now for a high school novel, which all of these are, this plot is not absurd or even outlandish. But it takes something away from what could be a better story. In Paper Towns, I am much more interested in Radar and his black Santa collecting parents than Q and his obsession with Margo. Actually, I would rather read about any character besides Margo. 
 This is not to say that the book wasn't enjoyable. It was, even if it reminded me a lot of Looking for Alaska (Alaska is superior). I'm just hoping that all of Greens books aren't going to turn out this way.
Meh. It was an ok story. The over use of Margo was unbearable. I wasn't a fan of her in the book at all. The side characters were just ok as well.

Hated it. I don't even get how this is such a success and even has an upcoming movie. The story to me seemed nothing but an excuse to write smutty sex. 
 edit 2017: i couldn't remember if i had read the book or just read half way, still can't remember lol

sample_reviews.review_text: Okay, so I knew the book was going to be about sex. "Fifty Shades of Grey" I hoped that meant an older woman with grey hair was going to have great sex. But no, I was disappointed. Anyway, there was lots of sex but I would have told Mr. Grey to go F*** himself from the beginning and then there would be no story.
Utter drivel.

The success of Fifty Shades of Grey is the very definition of viral marketing. A book that was originally self-published as an eBook and a print-on-demand paperback, it somehow caught the imagination of women everywhere and it's said that a copy now sells every sixty seconds. Amazing. There are three books in the series and they are numbers 1, 2 and 3 on the New York Times best seller list, and have been for months. 
 I have three words for this phenomenon: WTF?? I mean really...have you read this thing? 
 I bought a Kindle version ($9.99), just to see what all the hoopla was about, and got through about 1/3 of it (31% according to my Kindle), rolling my eyes and saying, "Oh, please," on every other page. With one exception (from Jessica Reaves of the Chicago Tribune) it seems to be immune to criticism of any kind (because it's made a boatload of money?), and as an author it's probably bad form to say this (you know that won't stop me), but it's crap. I don't mind the concept of it or the genre of eroticism itself, but something that's selling like the latest iPad release should at least be...well, good. 
 Fifty Shades of Grey is not good. That's not hurting sales in the least. It doesn't seem to matter that the writing stinks, the characters are unappealing and not engaging, the storyline is non-existent and, worst of all, the sex isn't even good, just lots of murmuring and moaning and gasping, and heartbeats quickening and racing. Kinda trite. At least be original. 
 The protagonist, Anastasia Steele, is a 21 year old virgin, and the narrative (told from her point of view) is sprinkled with lots of italics: holy crap! holy fuck! holy shit! jeez! and so on. And her inner goddess talks to her, and does "merengue with some salsa moves." Need I say more? Now, you can't argue with that kind of success - it's phenomenal - and good for E.L. James. She seems as amazed by this as everyone else. But seriously...what are you people thinking? Whatever it is, could you please transfer it to my book? And when mine becomes a runaway best seller it won't bother me a bit when E.L. James trashes it on her blog.

The author will be the first to tell you she isn't a great writer, and it's evident in Fifty Shades. The gratuitous sex scenes got ridiculous and tired very quickly, the language used was very asinine, especially in the everyday conversations of the characters, and the main character's thought process was like a balloon with the helium slowly leaking out. 
 At first the sex scenes were fun and thrilling, and then they never stopped happening and I began skimming through them in order to get to more of the story-- which was, sadly, lacking. There isn't much to this book other than a whole lot of sex. 
 If you've never read a sexually explicit romance novel before, then this might float your boat. I've read my share of romance novels (ones that actually had characters you could care about and plots with mysterious twists that make you want to keep reading), and this one was so ridiculously bad, in my opinion, that it was hard to finish reading.

The story, I've gathered, seems to about a girl called Anna and her absolutely perfectly damaged hunk, Christian. 
 Anna seems to act like a bratty 16 year old. Well that was my first impression anyway. 
 But no, Anna is actually in her mid 20's who happens to be the most childish virgin in history! 
 I've known puritans less repressed than this lady! 
 Anyway, when her friend commits the horrific crime of asking Anna to do her interview for her, Anna stomps her feet a bit but ultimately accepts the proposition. She travels to a very big hard........office and meets Christian. The manliest man that ever maned. 
 A manly man so completely manly, in fact, that he can make you drop your panties with a single smile. What a virile bastard! 
 With some schoolyard flirtation and some encouragement from the crazy voices er I mean her inner Goddess, Anna decides that he is absolutely dreamy. A conclusion many people who've read this book, seem to be agreed upon. 
 What follows is some heavy petting, with some kind of awkward sex scenes and some strange metaphors. Oh and lets not forget consultation from the crazy voices/the Inner Goddess and lip biting. Lot's of lip biting. 
 The writing style is not terrible, but I personally didn't find it appealing. Then again, I hated Anna from the first page and this is in first person, so perhaps it's all her fault. As a 21 year old, I found the portrayal of Anna weird and unrealistic. I felt she was nothing but walking hormones ie a teenager. I also found broken but otherwise "perfect" Christian a little bit creepy and a control freak. I haven't even gotten to the infamous "tampon scene" either. 
 It just seems like Twilight attempted to grow up, but kept it's teen angst. 
 Sorry, this is one bandwagon I just cannot climb aboard.

Everyone probably knows what this fan-fiction novel is about already, but I'll just summarize it briefly. One day when Ana's friend falls ill and calls in a favour, requesting Ana to interview one of the richest, successful men in Seattle in her place. Although it should it was indeed a formal interview, Christian and Ana both realize that this encounter was anything but ordinary. They start to form a curiosity and fatal attraction for one another. But as all businessmen know, sometimes the only way to keep something is by signing a contract... 
 I read this book because there were so many people raving about it, and of course it was also because it made it onto the top 20 list of best sellers on Indigo etc. If you ever watch or read the Vampire Diaries, Twilight or any other similar television shows or books, it is a definite possibility that you will enjoy this novel. I think the most captivating part about this novel is Mr. Grey himself. What kind of girl does not have an attraction to a bad boy? A handsome bruting one? A mysterious, rich, powerful and charming one? When you combine all of these aspects into one character, it becomes irresistible to desire more information, and the only way to gain more information is by blazing through the pages! 
 So why do I give this three stars? As explicit as the sexual content in the novel is, there is quite a bit of repetition. Not only in vocabulary, but also events in the story. The higher the predictability, the less enjoyable it is (excluding fairy tales, the ones where we watch because we expect the feel-good happy endings).

Ok, I'm just going to start this with an apology to my friends who really enjoyed this book. You are entitled to your own opinion and I respect that. However, I wholeheartedly disagree with you. I went into it with zero expectations, and somehow it fell beneath zero into a negative WTF wasteland. 
 I know this whole thing got started as Twilight fan fiction, but after it got popular shouldn't she have changed some more details? This is just barely skimming the edges of plagiarism and if I were Stephenie Meyer I would be very pissed off. It was set in the same city, with similar characters--down to the zany scatter-brained mother, all-adopted siblings, and clumsy inexperienced main character. Take Twilight, change the names and remove the vampire aspect and you have 50 Shades of Utter Crapola. 
 I'm not even going to get into the bad writing. It speaks for itself. 
 The storyline was DEEPLY disturbing and I'm sure it had domestic violence counselors cringing across the world. Anastasia literally called him a control freak, said she felt smothered, and actively worried that he was going to hit her again if she made him mad. Her eating was controlled by him, who she could hang out with, her behaviors--everything. He would randomly show up where she was and somehow even after she told him he was a "stalker" she was in the same breath talking about her feelings for him and how much she loved him. She just knew he was damaged and complicated and SHE would be the one to change him! Ignoring the fact that he'd had over a dozen other women in the same situation and none of them had ever changed him. 
 Sound familiar? That's because it was an ABUSIVE relationship with a ton of mixed messages. He'd tell her he was incapable of love and didn't want her to touch him, and then later that night he'd be excited about introducing her to his mother. Um... no. It doesn't work that way. To quote He's Just Not That Into You--"you are not the exception, you are the rule." 
 (I'm going to ignore the obviously incredible things--like that the main character was in her 20's and had never had sex or been drunk at all in her life.) 
 I'm just extremely confused as to why all of this is considered hot to some people. I was revolted all the way through the book and for a lack of a better term, I can't get it up for someone who is a fucking psycho. I agree with the memes out that there that say if he wasn't hot and rich the book would go nowhere because women would see it for the garbage it is. 
 Honestly I'm terrified that women are going to take this to heart and stay in an abusive relationship because they are trying to save their abuser from his own mental issues. Please please please realize this is a STORY that was written by a woman and in no way mirrors your situation because it is a completely ridiculous piece of FICTION. 
 If you are looking for erotica that is not full psycho-stalkers, try Anne Rice's Sleeping Beauty series. It is WAY better and doesn't contribute to the dumbing-down of women everywhere. 
 One star. 
 I've had better.
An insight into intelligent, artistic, and original writing.

I'm about as confused as much as Miss Steel about this book. I really hated this book....I loathed it, and 1/2 way through it I set it down and didn't pick it back up for months, but I wanted it cleared off my night stand so I finished, and ...........I hate, hate, hate to admit......I liked the ending. It went from a 1 star to a 3....Just for the ending.
This has to be a joke.

Sans paroles... or then again: 
 The most beautiful love story I have ever read.

"...there are two types of people in the world: those who prefer to be sad among others, and those who prefer to be sad alone." 
 It is perhaps unfortunate that I read this book so soon after reading Extremely Loud and Incredibly Close, which happens to be written by the author's husband. Some of the themes are so similar that I cannot help but compare, and most of the time this book is the one coming up short. While it is in some ways an easier read, I did not find it as moving or as satisfying. (One thing I did like better about History of Love was that some of the characters and especially the young people were portrayed a bit more realistically.) 
 Trying to review it for itself without comparing: I liked the main character Leo Gursky, the old, lonely man afraid of dying without anyone noticing. (At the beginning we are told that he goes out of his way to make himself seen, but aside from the few examples given at the outset I didn't see him really acting this way through the rest of the book.) 
 The unusual ways the story is told (like Alma's story being written out in lists) just didn't work for me. The mysteries of the novel within the novel and how all the characters were connected frustrated me instead of just keeping me interested. And one point revealed at the end (no spoilers) made me feel cheated. 
 There's a writer with some talent here. The book is not bad. But it's not great, either.
Funny, I have read this book. It was written by her husband, Jonathan Safran Foer. Oh, and the title was Extremely Loud and Incredibly Close. Yeah. Her writing is a sad rip off.
I didn't want to read a book called "The History of Love." It sat on my shelf for over a year. I ended up loving the beautiful, lyrical pose and original story. Lovely.
over reaching but done in a way that wasn't too pretentious.

reference_books.title: Lover Eternal (Black Dagger Brotherhood, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Eternally Lovin' it Bada ba-ba-ba 
 Lover Eternal sucks us deeper into Black Dagger Brotherhood. The story of Rhage, the impossibly gorgeous warrior who is known as Hollywood, is revealed to us. We learn what makes him tick. Rhage is living proof of the reason why you shouldn't judge a book by its cover. 
 The brotherhood makes some new acquaintances, Mary Luce, John Matthew and Bella. Mary Luce is a warrior in human form, in her own right. 
 Mary meets John Matthew, a 20 something year old guy who looks like a fragile boy. He is a mystery to himself and finds himself having strange and terrifying dreams about blood, fangs, and the creepy ghostly looking, soulless people who are after him. 
 Bella is a civilian vampire and Mary's neighbour. Not to mention she is incredibly jaw dropping beautiful (which blood sucker isn't?). She ends up meeting John Matthew through Mary and recognizes signs that he isn't just your regular human. Bella, John and Bella get pulled into the brotherhood for a whirlwind of an adventure into the unknown. 
 Mary and Rhage become intertwined in an unusual way. Mary feels like she is just your average woman, especially when she compares herself to the league that Rhage is in. She and Rhage get tangled up in a fierce relationship full of angst, passion and uncertainty. How will things unravel between them and will Rhage be able to protect Mary from all the evil in the world? 
 This full of angst and thrilling story will be a bumpy, wet and exhilarating ride for any fan of vampire reads. You will get glimpses into a few of the other brothers. There's just enough to keep you tingly below the waist and in anticipation for the rest of the brothers' stories and futures. Keep a box of tissues handy and maybe a mop for any other spills. There won't be a dry seat in the house whether it is for the raw emotion that zings between the tight knit characters or the legs drenching, breath taking love scenes.

reference_books.title: Hourglass (Evernight, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
Star crossed lovers stuck in Paranormal Tug-a-War 
 **Third book in the series so its spoilers galore for the first two books.** 
 Bianca and Lucas are the star crossed lovers of the Evernight series. This love story that I've come to love has grown into something much more complex than any other Romeo and Juliet stylized story. 
 Hourglass takes off right where Stargazer left off. Bianca and her Evernight school room mate, Raquel have joined forces with the Black Cross. As we learned before, the Black Cross is a team of Vampire hunters and view all vampires to be the all the same cold blooded killers. In return the vampires think the same about them. The motto seems to be kill first, ask later. This bothers Bianca more than ever before now that she has her nose being rubbed in it, and is being trained to do the exact same thing to beings of her own kind. Bianca's true identity is still hidden from everyone in the Black Cross and even from Raquel. With everyone having such black and white opinions on everything, Bianca stands no chance of ever being accepted for what and who she really is. On the bright side, Bianca and Lucas finally get to be together. Although with this new soldier life style they see less of each other than when they were sneaking around and separated by many miles instead of under the same roof. 
 Their star crossed lover issues are far from over though. The vampires of Evernight, the wraiths, and Charity and her tribe are all after them with deadly force. People Bianca and Lucas may have trusted in the beginning will fail them at some point in the most surprising ways. With all the danger, there's a natural magnetic sexual tension that burns hot and long between Bianca and Lucas. It makes you root for them every step of the way of their dramatic adventure. Even at the most heartbreaking times and when you think its impossible for them to be in the same place at the same time, hope stays alive. Hope drives their love and makes it burn stronger. 
 I was frustrated at points of the book, mainly because you're so wrapped up in Lucas and Bianca's raw emotions. To balance it out you have the light hearted and charming Vic with his vampire sidekick, Ranulf. I think everyone could use a Vic in their lives. He sees in shades of gray instead of just black and white. He's laid back and accepting of everything thrown his way and not everyone has such grace under pressure. 
 Everything got very intense near the end and it really makes you beg for more. What a great read. This is a series in which you start out slow and you might be not all that impressed with the pace at the beginning, but you will not be the least disappointed if you keep reading. Its hitting its own level of greatness with each coming book. Great for all YA paranormal romance readers. Trust me, you'll love it long time.

book_a.title: Shadow Kiss (Vampire Academy, #3)
book_a.user_review:
Wow.. Intense installment to the Vampire Academy series. Everyone probably knows or has written about the story line already so i'll let that go as usual and skip to my impressions on the events. 
 **Spoilers may occur..** Finally Rose is stepping out on her own two feet. About time. The Chrisian and Rose bro sis dynamic is highly amusing and pleasurable to me. Since rose gets to be Christians guardian this time.. it really allows Rose to get out of the mind of Lissa and worry more about herself. Her choices in her career, life, love relations. Plus she has enough to deal with; the ghosts, people around her being one step away from putting her in a straight jacket, locking her in a padded room and throwing away the key. You'd think in a world with magic and vampire, it wouldn't be so crazy to be seeing your dead friend's ghost. 
 I loved all the intense action and fighting off the bad guys in this. And i would have been perfectly happy if all the good guys won and all the bad guys burst in flames. But no no.. not in the Vamp Academy novels. I must say Richelle throws out the rules of happy endings. The people who do die, never should actually die. It really just rips your heart out cuz you're seeing it through the eyes of the loved ones. I know it takes the story in a different direction now.. but come on.. this is like the Buffy having to kill Angelus all over again. Only the damage is already done and she has to kill ensouled Angel anyways. Harsh. Sorry about the buffy reference. All i wanna say is.. why Dimitri.. why him. So upsetting. The last line of the book is just so heartbreaking.. bah.. Let's hope our spirit users can re-ensoul him. He and Rose belong together. And if not.. even fictional world is a cruel cruel world. 
 Go read it you'll love it and feel it all. Bring on the next. And i pray for a happy ending in the near future.

sample_reviews.review_text: Ftw! out of all the first three books, this one os by far the hardest to read.. oh my gosh, I just can't believe what had happened to Dimitri.. I was crying until the last page of this book! and the end drove me nuts! I'll go insane if I didn't start it soon. fudge! I was happy that they got together but so devastated the way things turned! Dimitri being a Strigoi changes everything.. I don't know how Mead turned the story.

World-building: A 
 Girl Power: A 
 Guy Hero: A 
 Suspense: A 
 Plot-Twists: A++ 
 Feels: A++ 
 The two previous books in this series were good but this one seriously WOWED me!! 
 For you clean-readers: this one does NOT have mature content. There is kissing, a glossed over sex-scene (NOT explicit), and scary fight scenes as well.

I have one word for you: Amazing. Shadow Kiss was such a thrill ride that I read all 440 pages in one night... I just couldn't stop. Now after that one amazing word, I think I may have a few other words for Richelle Mead because of how she made me feel at the end of this heart breaker. I'm only joking, Shadow Kiss has further put me in awe of Mead's talented storytelling and superb writing. I know I normally do spoiler free reviews and I can assure you I will not be giving away any huge plot twists, but be cautious in reading this review as I feel like I need to get some things off my chest that may spoil some mystery to the series. 
 Shadow Kiss starts with our characters cooping with the events of the past and they must deal with the death of their friend. As this semester begins, the senior novices must begin their field training and they are each assigned a Moroi to protect. Rose believes everything is goign according to her plan: Lissa will be her Moroi, she's trying to make peace with her nonexistent relationship with Dimitri and she's coming to terms with her interaction with the Strigoi, but of course when things seem to be going their best, it's the the calm before the storm. 
 Now as I said before, I went and saw Richelle Mead speak at her launch party for The Golden Lily and I had not read any of her books yet. She sympathized with her readers, not quite apologizing, for the ending of book three and in my head, I thought wow, these people are nuts. With all their whining and grumbling you'd think Mead had gone and kicked everyone's puppy. Now, I feel like she really did kick my puppy. 
 This lady has a special way of ripping your heart out and stepping on it, while you still appreciate her writing and her big plot twist. Obviously I won't be giving away what happened at the end, but while I was beyond devastated (I may or may not have cried in my bed for a little bit at 1 am) I appreciated what she did. I've been reading a great deal of paranormal romances lately and they all end the same, something bad happens but then things right themselves and the couple snuggle but look forward to further evil in the next installment. While this makes me happy (obviously) it doesn't make for a very interesting story. In Shadow Kiss, I felt as though Mead turned my world upside down, which while sad, is a good thing! It kept things interesting and I am scrambling to get my hands on book 4. 
 The story was actually longer than the other two in the series but i found it much easier to get through and I really enjoyed the story. After the devastation that occurred on their ski trip, our main characters have changed. They are more cautious, wiser and have a different out look on life than their fellow students at St. Vladimir's. I welcomed this change in personalities and it made fore a much more interesting read. 
 Rose has a lot to deal with in this book as she finds out more about her relationship with Lissa and she has to come to terms with what's really inside of her. Is being a guardian and putting her Moroi's every need before hers something she wants? Rose questions a lot of her deeprooted beliefs in this story and she has to make the hard decisions, which is one of the things I love most about Rose. I said in a previous reveiw that she's working her way up to one of my favorite heroines in YA fiction and I think she made it up to the top five. She is kick ass and I love her. 
 We also get to see more of her relationship with Dimitri. While I won't talk about this too much for fear of more heartbreak, I love him, plain and simple. I sense that Adrian is going to be moving into the spotlight a little more and I can't decide if I like him or not. While I love his charming whit and the bad ass air he exudes, I'm still stuck on Dimitri and I don't know if I'll be able to give Adrian a chance. Are you listening to me right now? What did Richelle Mead do to me?! On to book four... 
 9 out of 10 
 Happy Reading (keep tissues handy) 
 Allison 
 imabibliophobic.blogspot.com

book_b.title: Gone Girl
book_b.user_review: This book is batshit crazy in so many weirdly wonderful, yet disturbing ways. I'm usually a romance/young adult/urban fantasy reader, so this is the book to read if you're looking for a change. The characters are delightfully unhinged and the plot is filled with some mind-fucking "what!?!?!??!?!" twists, crazy inside voice type humor, and some frighteningly close to realistic crimes that will leave your mind reeling long after you've finished this book. Warning: your views on marriage might change a little after this fuckedupness of a tale.

sample_reviews.review_text: One of the best books I've read. I was completely hooked and couldn't stop thinking about the plot when I had to put it down.

I was so keen to read this..but found it an enormous let down. Kind of clever, but in a self-conscious and showy off kind of way. Kind of unpredictable but in a kind of predictable way because of the alternating narrative viewpoints. Characterisation is unconvincing. Awful Amy is odious and nasty Nick is a good pupil. Desi and the supporting cast are transparent and insubstantial. Little literary merit and even less narrative tension. But... Couldn't give up on it!
What was with the last quarter of that book?
Sick, twisted, disturbing, delicious.

What do you get when you take one type A anal retentive person and marry them to a self absorbed Mama's boy??? Amy and Nick Dunne. Amy is the only child of writer parents who have made a fortune on the Amazing Amy books. Amazing Amy is the perfect little girl who always does the right thing. The Real Amy is always trying to live up to this fictional persona. Through out her life, she has discarded people who have made her feel less than perfect. And along with discarding these people, she ruins their lives forever. When she meets Nick...small town boy made good, she thinks she has found Mr Right. But after several years of marriage, just as things are beginning to unravel in their relationship, Nick and Amy lose their tony NYC jobs and must move to Carthage, Missouri, Nick's home town. Things go from bad to worse and on the morning of Nick and Amy's fifth wedding anniversary, Amy disappears from their home. Police and Public opinion quickly decide that Nick is her murderer. But is he? This book had more twists and turns than a corn maze. The ending will leave you shaking your head and saying,"WHAT?"
It's a sneaky page-turner, and now I wonder why did I let it steal any of my time.

This book was brilliantly written. It probably deserves a 5 star review. But it won't get one. Why? Because fuck Amy. And Gillian... well you're on my list with George R.R. Martin, Nicholas Sparks, and Karin Slaughter for robbing me of my happy endings. Hell I'll just take a satisfying ending. So one star is all you get from me.

I ordered this from the library after reading a lot of glowing reviews on Goodreads. I did enjoy it, was gripped by it and in some ways I think it's really exceptional. The characterisation especially is brilliant, and so is the sense of 'trial by media' that seems to be taking over, especially in the USA. But I felt it was patchy and there were some things I didn't like which are major spoilers so I'll put them in a tag. 
 I thought the actual ending was very clever but some of the steps on the way were hard to believe. She just lets that couple in the mountains take all her money? Just shrugs and drives away? Doesn't plot any kind of revenge? AMY? Then there's Desi ... so obviously NOT the person she should have contacted. I thought for a while maybe she was only good at planning in advance and couldn't cope when anything threw her plans out. But then she handled things so well with Nick at the end...? 
 The other point, more general, is the way that women are portrayed in the book. Being a complete bitch pays: all of the most vicious women get what they want, including minor characters like the TV presenters or Greta; while the good, apparently resourceful women like Go and Boney fail. Perhaps it's as realistic as the media domination, but it seemed a pity there was so little hope for the nice girl.

Sometimes there are times where I wish I could quit a book half way through, and not finish the rest. However, when you're already half way through the book you want to finish reading it and see what the ending is like. With Gone Girl, I wish I quit the book for good. I am going to try and write up this review because I haven't read a book in a long time where it just makes me so mad. 
 Gone Girl is a story of Nick Dunne whose wife goes missing on their 5th wedding anniversary. It was a who did it type of novel, and what made it different is that you saw the events from his point of view and you were able to read journal entries from Amy's point of view leading up to her disappearance. 
 The first half of this book was great. It kept me on my toes, and I want to read more. I wanted to find out what was going to happen to Nick. Will Amy ever be found? Nick became their first suspect. I can see where people were finding this sexist, but in a way it was like all other major crime stories. It goes to the person you think is the most accountable. Nick had holes in his story from the start, and he was hiding things from the police. It's no wonder they suspected him. I first started rolling my eyes when the affair was announced. How predictable. Then, once we found out that Amy's personality was just crazy is when I really started getting mad. I don't know why it just infuriated me. This also goes with Nick. He was starting to get on my wrong side. 
 The book continues on. You find out about Amy's past, and how she has framed people before. Nick tries to use it against her. The only sum what redeemable thing was Tanner and his wife. The rest just I can't even. 
 I stopped reading the book fully at about 88% left in the book where the rest of it I just scanned. I couldn't handle it any more. The sad thing was I have read more enjoyable young adult fiction books then this book. The ending made me even madder. You sit there and want to frame your wife, your wife uses you for a pregnancy so you are trapped, and yet you stay with her?! Worst ending in a novel since Jacob and Bella's baby became soul mates in Twilight. I apologize now for those that I recommended this book originally too in the beginning. The first half was great, but ugh.
I'm torn on what to rate this, I really loved it as I was reading, total page turner, but the ending fell so flat, all that building and then nothing. So liked the book, hated the ending.

Much like many of the reviews I've read since I finished this book, I picked it up without any real expectations. It was available for free and looked mildly interesting, but it definitely surprised me and made me incredibly glad I took that chance. 
 Neil Josten has been running from his past for as long as he can remember. When his skill in a sport known as Exy get the attention of a recruiter at Palmetto State University, however, he has a decision to make: keep running or take some time to pursue playing the sport he loves. And the fact that the team's new star player is someone that he knew in his past seems like a point in the favor of either decision. 
 The way Nora Sakavic builds the world and slowly introduces the characters is something that really keeps the reader engaged (at one point, I sat down to read a chapter and got up nearly 10 chapters later) and demonstrates a skill in storytelling that I haven't seen in a while. One has to suspend some disbelief to accept aspects of the story (I just settled on the idea that it takes place in the near future to explain some of the differences in societal norms and regulations), but Sakavic makes it very easy to do so. For a book that is touted as having m/m romance elements, it is a bit light on that front (they're mostly hinted at in this book), but I expect they will continue to build in the future books in the series.

November 4, 2017 -- Amazon freebie! 
 -------- 
 Nothing prepared me for THE FOXHOLE COURT. I thought I knew what I was getting into (some kind of weird character driven [ala the Raven Cycle series] made-up-sportsy college story with shades of hidden identities and mafia and an m/m romance) and instead I got some of what I expected and a lot of what I didn't. 
 First of all, this team is basically made up of a cast ala the movie The Losers except.. maybe more psychotic? Misfits galore. They play a made up sport that is some weird amalgamation of lacrosse and hockey. Then we have mafia families, characters with histories of abuse, japanese gangsters, violence and drugs strewn all throughout the narrative. It makes it sound even more interesting, if you're into that and can suspend your disbelief a bit (especially when it comes to the depiction of mood stabilizing medication, and, you know.. lots of other shit), but it's also just a weird experience. 
 The second half of the book feels much stronger with our characters more fleshed out and some issues settling down, while others take the express bus to crazytown, but at this point this book (series?) feels like it should be treated more like fantasy based on it's creative license on most of the above-mentioned items. It's definitely an extreme setting for an extreme group of characters in extreme situations. Which makes it very compelling at times and really fascinating. 
 I'm surprised by all the four and five star ratings as I did find the beginning not only weaker but also confusing at times but I'm excited for more character arc development and to see more of where the romance might go (ps there's pretty much zero in book one). 
 Post-series-read spoiler : this series takes offff so don't let this three star review scare you away. Sakavic's series is complete crack.

 - Exy. Literally created twenty years ago and is a worldwide phenomena, amazing. It's... literally just violent lacrosse? Okay? Why does it have THAT name.
