 - especially since Neil thinks they would be genuinely good if they weren't so dysfunctional like what is the point 
 - WHY DO THEY HAVE TEN PEOPLE ON THEIR TEAM AND EVERYONE ELSE HAS LIKE OVER TWENTY??? why are they selective??? if they're so selective they could certainly have screened everyone for compatibility. college sports teams recruit like.... worldwide. and selecting kids from troubled backgrounds is very very odd, especially for COLLEGE SPORTS BECAUSE COLLEGE SPORTS ARE BASICALLY PROFESSIONAL???????????????????????????????? im losing it on this point honestly

I feel like I just spent the past two hours reading a mermaid-related version of Real Housewives of Orange County. So much bitchiness. So much bickering. So much name-calling. So little combined intelligence in one single book. Apparently, daughters of men and daughters of Greek gods have one thing in common: idiocy. 
 Putting aside the unrealistic premise of mermaids this book, the whole story and the characters' actions are pretty lacking in credibility. I'm not talking about the fact that mermaids do not exist in real life. Come on, it's not like anyone reads YA paranormal and fantasy expecting realism and actually believing that there are actually really well-hidden unicorns in our world. The credibility factor to which I'm referring does not refer to the fact that the book's premise relies on the fact that the reader suspends his or her disbelief and believe in the existence of paranormal creatures, but that the plot twists are entirely too easily solved, the characters' actions are irrational beyond the limits of common sense, and the behavior of the ancient siren sisters are so fraught with back-stabbing and fighting that the reader doubts that they can exist together for a week without shedding blood, much less thousands of years. 
 This is the third book in the Watersong trilogy. So far, Gemma has been turned into a siren, resisted being a siren, and now is trying to break the curse of being a siren, despite the fact that she might kill herself and her siren "sisters" while she's at it. The plot is simple, the characters forgettable, the writing is elementary, the pacing and resolution of the mystery is incredible and unrealistic. 
 The main focus of this trilogy has so far been the plot, and not the characters, and the book does poorly on both fronts. In a good book, the mystery unwinds gradually, the writing should slowly unveil subtle hints that the reader can follow and be involved in the eventual resolution, the clues should not (since we're continuing with a nautical theme here) a) land like a big fat fish in the reader's lap or b) make the reader feel like they're getting slapped in the head with a swordfish. There is zero subtlety here in the revealing and eventual solving of the big mystery, things just fall into place too easily for it to be a compelling mystery. 
 Example: Gemma needs a clue, how do I stop being a siren? Oh, I'll ask my sister's coworker. Sister's coworkers shocking knows someone who is willing to believe in mythological creatures and fairies and sirens, and also shockingly happens to own an esoteric book shop and knows all about breaking the curse!!!!!!!!! 
 "...the point is, I was talking to this old friend of mine. I'd completely lost touch with her, but it turns out she owns a bookstore up in Sundham. She'd definitely have some books that might help you out with the sirens. Plus, she's pretty knowledgeable on all that kind of stuff." 
 Weeeeeeell, isn't that just terribly convenient. I probably know someone who knows someone who knows about the esoteric and ancient myth surrounding sirens, too, if I bothered to ask around, I'm sure. 
 Random flashbacks attempt to give insight into the siren's characters and previous lives fail to add anything to the harebrained plot. The only serve to further instill in the reader the fact that it is utterly incredible that these sisters have existed and lived together for all this time, hating and fighting among each other so much that it took this long for one of them to attempt to kill the other. I am not kidding about the fighting. 
 "Lexi!" Penn growled. "You are annoying! I'm gonna pull this car over if you don't shut the hell up!" 
 "No! I will not shut up!" Lexi shouted at her. "You are annoying me...you're being a total---" 
 ...and 
 "You stupid wench!" Penn shouted, and Lexi cringed. "Thea's right! You are the biggest mistake I have ever made! You are so dumb and useless!" 
 ...and on, and on, and on. You think I was kidding about the fighting and the reference to the Real Housewives franchise? There is so much bitchiness and cattiness among the sirens that I imagine living with four siren sisters is like living in a sorority house, with more backstabbing and poorly-concealed vitriol, and a whole lot more hair-pulling, and by hair pulling, I mean hair pulling. 
 "She climbed on top of her, grabbing Lexi's silky hair to keep her from pulling away, and she hit her in the face over and over again. Lexi squealed and clawed at Penn's hand, but she never really fought back." 
 Sigh. 
 As bitchy as they are, the sirens have more personality than the two other main characters, Gemma and Harper. The entire series is supposed to be about them, and we see their point of view more than that of any other characters, but the personality is just not there. It's Gemma does this. Harper does that. They are very, very dull characters. For a siren, Gemma is severely lacking in charm and confidence. She is quiet, reticent, and in complete denial of her new nature. I am so sick of characters who just completely fight what they are. Get used to it, make the best of the situation, if you must kill, then take your siren sisters' advice and feed upon the douchebags of the world. There are plenty of those to go around. 
 Gemma is also a severe hypocrite. She doesn't want to hurt anyone, she is in denial of her true nature, but she uses her siren song anyway, multiple times, with disastrous consequences. Take her actions with Alex after she made him hate her in the previous book: 
 "It doesn't matter what you meant!" he shouted, and she flinched. "Did you ask me if I wanted this? Did you even talk with me about this before you did it?" 
 "No, I knew what you would say." 
 He scoffed. "You knew what I would say, and you did it anyway?" 
 Yes, give someone no choice when changing their entire essence of character. Their entire being. Does that sound familiar to what happened to you, Gemma? 
 And Harper, her sister, the 18-year old going on 40. As her own boyfriend says, "You act like her mom." She is a martyr to the nth degree. She has to do everything. She is fucking Atlas with the world on her shoulders. She has a dad, but certainly the man who's been single-handedly responsible for raising the two of them can't possibly handle things without her help. Neither can Gemma. Harper has no personality and seems incapable of anything but worry. She worries about her dad, she worries about her friend's ability to manage the shop, she worries about Daniel, she worries about Gemma. Never mind that Daniel can get by and has done so on his own for years, never mind that Gemma is a freaking sea monster who can kill at the blink of an eye. Nooooooo...Harper needs to be there for her helpless siren of a sister. Right. She is so utterly blind to what Gemma is capable of, too. "She didn't think Gemma had hurt anybody. Gemma would do whatever she needed to do to survive, but not at the expense of somebody else." Yes, because sirens just sing happy songs and sit on rocks looking pretty, never hurting or eating people or anything. Harper is such a sainted soul that it hurts. 
 This is a terrible book, and the only positive thing I can say about it is that it approaches the end of a poor series, which I kept reading due to my masochistic tendencies.

Aaaaaand the game has been upped, folks. I thought book one was utterly fantastic. A little heavy on the fighting, but that's something marginal that didn't take away from the entertainment. 
 Then came this one. Pretty sure there's a form of perfection of how great a plot can be. Characters are smart, capable. hilarious. 
 The plot was on point. Political intrigue, romance, fighting, hilarity. Everything that makes a book or even a tv show perfect, was introduced in pretty much perfect doses. Which creates enjoyment. Just saying. 
 I mean, I was thrown off a little upon realizing that the book took place two years later, but it actually worked. Obviously. I enjoyed seeing the characters growth, their relationships to each other. 
 Amara and Bernard? Oh, good grief yes. Their marriage vows seriously reminded me of Pirates of the Caribbean. Getting hitched in the middle of battle and all. *sigh with happiness* 
 Tavi and Kitai? They kind of came out of left field like that, but ohhhh I can't wait to see where they go. It's gonna be good, guaranteed. 
 But my favorite favorite absolute favorite part of this book was Doroga's and Kitai's commentary on the somewhat "unusual" behaviors of the other characters. What is perceived as normal for everyone is just absurd to them. I can't wait to see what else they have to say on certain matters.
Not as good as the first in the series. He was trying to put too much into it. There were what...4 or 5, maybe even 6 badguys, depending on how you count. It was cluttered.

While I really, really like these books, I don't like their similarity. Tavi is fighting giant spiders under the castle as page for the First Lord, and these spiders have taken over wolf- like Canim bipeds who are Aleran enemies. Bernard and Amara are fighting the giant spiders from their garrison, against overwhelming odds, with one Marat's help, Doroga. Doroga's daughter, Kitai has gone to the capital to help Tavi. While Steadholder Isana has gone to the capital to ask for help, and because the prince invited her to come, she has been taken prisoner, essentially, but no one will see her, so she accepts help from her enemy, Aquitane.

This was a book with good and bad bits in it. I liked the action, and the development of Tavi and Kitai, and some of the newly introduced characters. All in all, it was a fun read. But, the surprises(?) in the story are hinted at with all the subtlety of a 400 piece brass band. I probably shouldn't complain when the author spoon feeds me a big slice of obvious pie since I eagerly consume it because I enjoy the story so much. I am going to give the third volume a read, even though I think that anyone reading this series already knows how it is going to end.

Butcher delivers on the action, and keeps an interesting story line going strong. He more or less hooked me when I read "The Aeronaut's Windlass," and these older stories, while not quite as strong, have great characters and dialogue. 
 Kate Redding, of course, is a fabulous story teller.

5 stars 
 After Furies of Calderon succesfully blown me away, the next installment of the Codex Alera series, Academ's Fury apparently did the same. This book, despite its thick and tasty length, able to awake me from my reading slump for almost 2 months. As expected from Jim Butcher, with his vivid story telling and his story crafting that feel like magic, more than any fury crafting that happen in this book. 
 Two years after the event in Furies of Calderon, Second Battle of Calderon Valley that happen between Aleran and their barbarian enemy, The Marat, Tavi of Calderon now become a page for First Lord of Alera, Gaius Sextus. While he also pursue his career as Cursor (aka First Lord's Messenger) in Academ. Don't worry, the story didn't fall in Harry Potteresque story type. Quite opposite in fact, since Tavi's study just shown a little and he already in his final phase. Since he's furyless, aka can't conjure his own fury. Tavi considered as freak and have enemy that remind me of Draco Malfoy &co. Just meanier. Lucky for Tavi, he also have his comrade that remind me of Ron and Hermione in Ehren and Gaelle. Afraid not, this doesn't mean Jim Butcher copy Rowling blatantly, because Tavi also befriend Antillar Maximus who will help Tavi in so many problems that the boy manage. 
 Like usual, Butcher told story in this book from so many person narative. Beside Tavi, there are Bernard and Amara's who know didn't shy away to show affection to each other despite Amara's worry that she didn't suitable to be Bernard's wife. Quite romantic, and I never mind romance subplot. I'm glad that Butcher insert it so it make the story make sense. Then, there was Gaius Sextus himself with his loyal captain, Miles. Butcher also told story from Isana, Bernard's sister that from the latest event now become a first woman steadholder. A fact that endanger Isana, since women still considered as second class citizen in Alera. Isana herself think that Gaius decision to make her steadholder more like politic and she hate that Gaius took Tavi from her. But Isana can't run from her destiny and sooner or later, she must go to the Imperial Capital to walk between a snake nest that is High Lords and their cohorts. While she must choose, who she must allied with. Even with enemy itself. 
 The problem is now bigger than the first book, because while Aleran kinda have peace with the Marat, now a sinister malice crept and tend to threat Aleran's peace. The Marat warn that the Vord, a parasitic creature have escape from their hide and ready to take all Aleran, Marat or any living alike. They are dangerous, since people who possessed by the Vord will be like zombies. The threat begin in Calderon, and Bernard, Amara and the Marat chieftain, Doroga must join force to drive the Vord from reaching further while their resources are limited. 
 Meanwhile, Tavi also have big problem because Gaius health faltering and he must cover his Lord's condition if he didn't want the Empire in uproar and some High Lords that already conspired to coup d'etat will attack Imperial when they see a chance. Isana is frantic to reach Gaius, but she almost assassinated and the result is make her somehow a traitor. On the other side, the Canim, a beast man clan that have thin peace with Aleran have strange moves toward Alera, even their Ambassador already warn Tavi about that. And without Tavi realize, the Vord already reach Imperial and prepare the next move. 
 Such a busy event that happen in Academ's Fury! No wonder this book is 700 pages long! But, Butcher's writing style able to make me impatient to read pages after pages. Make me want to end this book in one sitting. Sure there some part that Butcher like to prolong, like war between the Vord and Calderon. The despair is apparent and make me want to pull my hair because I want Bernard and Amara to win while their source are limited. I want Gaius just wake up and send forces to help Calderon and finish the war, because yeah, the battle with the Vord is frustated to read. Frustated but still I enjoy it nonetheless. 
 What I love is how Butcher portrayed women in this book. He write them not as secondary characters, but as individual that strong and standing in their own feet. From Amara, Isana, then Serai, a courtesan that more that it seems. I really like Serai because she help Isana to understand how the politic in Imperial work. How to thread carefully between the thread of lies and deceits. Even Tavi have his own match in Kitai, the Marat girl that also daughter of Doroga. There is also High Lady Placida Aria who have high authority and charisma, provide a useful help for Tavi when he's in problem. And then, there is Lady Invidia Aquitaine, a lady that also cunning like her husband who become enemy to First Lord, or even more cunning and calculated. Her power is so great and her tactic is delightful to read. Butcher sure know how to write women characters. Not place them as victim, but as a character and that a plus for this book. 
 I can go on and on about this book, but I think I already write too long. I just wanna said that if you love epic fantasy, you must read this. If you like a zero to hero kind of story, you must read this. If You like fantasy with a bunch of ass kicking heroines, you must read this. 
 Now, into book #3!!

I admit it, I was hesitant to start reading the Codex Alera series. The description I read of them online made them out to be basically your typical fantasy series. I didn't want that, it bugs me when books play a little too far into the cliche, but I should have known better. 
 Like in the Dresden Files, Jim Butcher has taken something old and turned it into something new. With a different magic system, and a world where the power hangs in politics, instead of spells, the Codex Alera appears to me to be something good for everyone. Also, I enjoy the similarities to books I've read about Rome.

The world of "Codex Alera" is not a pleasant one. I wouldn't want to visit, let alone live there! As the shape of the political and external threats became apparent in the first portion of this book I considered abandoning it based purely on the bleakness of the outlook. I in no way demand happy-happy stories, but I do want Some sort of payoff if I am going to wade through a bunch of gore and nastiness... 
 Anyway, I am glad I stuck with it. The character development is actually pretty good and the plot worked out better than I'd hoped. :}

I feel apologetic when I don't like a book someone has lent me to read. Normally a voracious reader and someone who rarely quits in the middle of a book, I had to put this one down after struggling to progress over weeks. Maybe I'll try again some other time, I see Goodreads' folks really liked this series.

book_b.title: The Trespasser (Dublin Murder Squad #6)
book_b.user_review: It was a good detective/crime book.

sample_reviews.review_text: I had this mystery figured out early on and it was very long winded getting to the end but still a pretty good read.

I'm a HUGE fan of Tana French, but this installment in her Dublin Murder Squad series just didn't do it for me. Both the central mystery and the detective lacked the usual French sparkle. However, a 'meh' Tana French book is still head and shoulders above most mystery writers, which is why I'm refraining from giving it an actual star-rating. Really, Tana French deserves her own ratings system.

I absolutely loved this one! The Dublin murder squad books are some of the best...broken harbour is still my favorite but this is a close second now. The Audible versions are my fave way to read these they are done very well. Tana French is just amazing at writing 10/10
I want the 3-4 days I wasted reading this book back. So tedious and drawn out and excessive. I found myself flipping through 2-3 pages at a time Bc it was literally the same stuff over and over.

Great read. My only wish with this book is that the main character would've been a tad more likeable. She was just such a wench.... Or maybe a little romance? I know, it's not really Tana French's style and I appreciate her raw characters... They are all broken people and that's a big part of the story. Anyway, great twist in this one. I've read all her books and I think this is my second favorite after The Likeness.

SPOILER ALERT: There was something missing from this book. French's previous books involving the Dublin Murder Squad had such lovely, mysterious and eerie twists and turns. This one just didn't have the same depth. True, French does delve into the Squad's personalities, Conway and Moran, in particular. However, I grew tired of Conway's constant defensiveness and bitter take on her colleagues. I would have cut at least 50% of that part of the plot. It didn't serve the plot well and was frankly distracting. The murder itself was rather mundane. Sorry, I like murder mysteries that shock the living daylights. French's decision to focus on the psychological aspect of the victim might have been more powerful if the motive fit the crime. Just didn't do it for me. I'm also not buying that the perp did not recognize the victim right from the get-go. He had to know it was the daughter of Des Murray. I kept flipping back in the pages to see if I'd missed that part. This fact ruined it a bit for me. I'm still a big fan of French, though. I know she'll come up with something amazing next time.

I normally don't review my "guilty pleasures," but I have 'em just like anyone else, and during the past year, recovering from surgery, I've tried dozens of books and authors I wouldn't normally give a second glance. 
 Ms. French is a clever writer who puts most of her effort into Irish urban slang and nonstop dialog, both outer and inner, both of which become tedious in the extreme. What she doesn't seem to care much about is setting, ambiance, or character development. I'm aware that Irish cities tend to be pretty dismal places, so maybe her failure to evoke them is a blessing in disguise! But her protagonist could do with a life - Detective Conway has got to be one of the most boring, selfish, one-dimensional characters I've ever encountered. She has no style, no passions or interests other than the case she's working on, and even that seems to be more of a nuisance or an annoyance than a passion. She despises nature and spends almost all her time in a state of anger or paranoia. Let's hope she doesn't become the subject of a series....

Tana French is brilliant. Her characters are so true - they leap off the page, so as a reader, you are so vested in them! Then she adds these wonderful mysteries which twist and turn and leap, so that you are even questioning your own thinking. THEN she adds the subtle nuance of deeper meaning - what role do your parents play? How do you become independent? When does self-reliance turn into destructive isolation? Who do we trust and why? How can we let an obsession derail a life? Fascinating. Please tell me the next one is out... please.

This is back to the one voice style which I much prefer. French is a great writer and draws unexpected characters with skills few current writers have. She takes her time so you know it's time to settle in for the ride.

This is my least favorite of the series so far. I knew the outcome 30 pages in. The character development is poor. The parallels between the detective and the victim lack subtlety. The pacing was painful. The only reason I didn't give it one star is French is a talented writer. This book feels like it was thrown together the meet a publishing obligation.

reference_books.title: Sparrow Hill Road (Ghost Stories, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
2.5 stars...rounding down. Oh, I had high hopes for this book. High hopes that were thrown off a cliff and dashed on the rocks until they were tiny little mangled pieces not even resembling hopes. Let me tell you why this book didn't work. 
 The biggest problem is the storytelling format. For the first half of the book, there are just random ghost stories about Rose. They start and stop randomly. Granted, they're ghost stories told from the ghost's point of view, but they're still ghost stories. There's very little rhyme or reason to the sequence in which they are told. Sure, you get to understand Rose through those stories, but you never really connect with her. 
 I'm fine with a non-linear story line, but there needs to be some kind of plot. There's absolutely no plot until you're more than 150 pages into the book. None. Just the little vignettes. Then, finally when there is some form of plot, it's far too little. Too little. Too late. 
 Here's the plot. Rose wants to kill the big bad guy who killed her and is still killing others. The end. That's the whole plot. Stuff happens, but there's no clear plan...from Rose or McGuire. Even when Rose faces down the guy who killed her, nothing happens. The story, what little there is, doesn't reach a conclusion. 
 Another issue is the repetitiveness. Enough already! I get it! She's only corporeal when someone gives her a jacket. She's hungry and can only eat when she's corporeal. She can use her super nose to know what's going to happen. She's always freezing. I got it the first million times you said it!! Sheesh. 
 I'm not sure a placeholder book is the right direction to take, when it's the first book in the series.

reference_books.title: Shadowfell (Shadowfell, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I've read Marillier's Daughter of the Forest. It was so very beautifully written and so very tragic. It was a little too depressing for me. I was hoping that Marillier's YA fantasy wouldn't be quite as heart-breaking. It's not that bad, so far. 
 This is a pretty standard fantasy story with the heroine on a journey discovering her magical gifts while going through trials that relate to a prophecy. The fact that it's a standard fantasy is the biggest issue I had with this book. That says more about me than the book. 
 All of the traveling, finding shelter, and scrounging for food reminded me why I started reading urban fantasy instead of traditional fantasy. It just starts to get old quickly. They walk here. Find shelter. Eat some of their meager supplies. Walk again. Find more shelter. Eat more of their dwindling supplies. Complete a trial. More walking. Find some other shelter. Eat the last of their provisions. Just repeat that over and over again for the complete book. 
 Now, let's talk characters. This is where the book really shines. The characters have a lot of depth and are wonderfully developed. Flint is everything you'd want in a tortured hero. He's brave, confident, patient, and self sacrificing. Neryn isn't nearly as much fun as Flint. She felt fairly naive for an independent sixteen year old. Her trust issues are really annoying, too. If I continue reading this series, it'll be for Flint alone.

reference_books.title: The Governess Affair (Brothers Sinister, #0.5)
reference_books.review_text: I was concerned about reading this short story when I realized the basis for the conflict. But, I think Milan pulls it off. Once you get over the lack of clear information about the heroine, the story is really sweet. It's actually very impressive that we get such a cohesive tale from a short story.

reference_books.title: Succubus Blues (Georgina Kincaid, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I'll admit I was hesitant to read a series with a succubus as the heroine. My chief concern was lots of promiscuous sex without any plot. But, Mead pulls it off by placing her heroine in a strictly grey moral area. I'll try and explain. 
 After years of succubus indentured servitude, Georgina just craves normalcy, which is something a succubus can't have. Georgina has a cat, a job in a bookstore, and a tight knit group of paranormal buddies. Fine, she has to have sex to survive and fill a quota, but that doesn't mean she has to like it. As a subversive act, Georgina won't sleep with good guys. Instead, she feeds off of men whose souls are already tainted. The problem is that Georgina can't have a normal relationship with a guy without taking years off his life if they even kiss. 
 Ok, so there's not a lot of depth to the book or the characters, but it's a book about a succubus. How much depth was I expecting? Georgina's group of friends ranging from humans, imps, angels, demons, and vampires are what really glue the story together. They're funny and endearing. But, on the downside, there is an annoying love triangle. However, with Georgina being a succubus, a certain amount of appeal to many males is to be expected. The mystery was well done with enough red herrings to keep me guessing through a good bit of the book.

reference_books.title: To Sir Phillip, With Love (Bridgertons, #5)
reference_books.review_text:
Ugh. There's just something about the men in this series that make me dislike them all. Well, Colin is an exception. But, all the other heroes are just jerks. 
 Here, the hero's particular jerkiness is based on wanting to con a woman into marrying him so his children can have a mother. Even by the end, I wasn't sure that Phillip wanted Eloise as anything other than a free babysitter. 
 This series is such a disappointment. I'm really not sure why I keep reading it...at least it's almost over!

book_a.title: Bitten (Women of the Otherworld, #1)
book_a.user_review: Ok. Can I just start complaining now? This book just didn't work for me. First, I don't like love triangles. This was one giant love triangle where the heroine couldn't make up her mind between her live-in boyfriend and her ex. Her whishy-washy back and forth infidelity was so very irritating. Second, the writing style was very descriptive without enough dialogue. We're in the heroine's head almost the entire time and that's not a good thing. The heroine isn't engaging enough to spend nine million hours in her head. Yeah, reading this book felt like it took nine million hours to end. Third, it moved so slowly. I had been reading for forevers and thought the book was wrapping up soon. Nope. I was wrong. I was so wrong. The book was only 46% done. Sigh. The only positive is that I did appreciate how the author was willing to kill off her characters.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I started this on an airplane, and if the book were a bit shorter or the flight a bit longer, I might have knocked it up a star. But as it is, the setup's a lot more interesting than the conflict/climax, and the outcome of the romaance plot had me going -- uhh, really? Okay, then. 
 I've read some later books in the series and I know the plotting and characters get better but this one, after an interesting beginning, ran out of steam before it was over.
I loved this book and I'm normally not into werewolves. It was definitely a page turner and kept me up all night.

I thought this book was going to be a winner when I bought it, but alas, it wasn't all that great. A lot of people seem to love it, though. I just found the characters to be predictable and not very interesting or engaging. Blah.

[Spoiler warning] Elena Michaels was easy for me to like. Smart, feisty, independent, taking charge of her life... except that getting turned werewolf understandably complicated that. Especially since she had been in love with Clay, who not only turned out to be a werewolf, but in biting her, ruined her life. He betrayed her. She still feels attracted to him, but it's Philip she wants to spend her life with: a good man she can trust.She questions herself: "In love? Was I in love with Philip? Damn it, that was such a trite, overworked cop-out. I loved him. There was no "in love." There was "in lust," "infatuated," and "in heat," three ultimately destructive emotions that had nothing to do with real, lasting love." This distinction made sense to me. I've wrestled for so many years with the fact that I was never "in love" with the man I married. With how our culture stresses being in love as the basis for a committed relationship. I've eventually decided it's crazy. That romantic fascination is hormonal, and doesn't last. Cultures throughout history, throughout the world, have achieved happy marriages based on other factors

Not for me. I need to stop trying to like these urban fantasy/paranormal books. I was hoping because the main female character in this book is a werewolf that it would be different, but there's still lots of gender-based power dynamic stuff that just squicks me out.

The first book I read in this series was Living with the Dead - my local bookshop only had this paperback copy - yes those days before I discovered the magic world of eBooks!!!! - and whilst I liked that story, I did find it a bit difficult to get into. 
 Now, I wasn't exactly uber-lover of werewolves/shape shifters before, but something about that book had me wanting to read more books by Kelley Armstrong. 
 I decided to read the books in order to be able to get into the world that the author created. 
 Bitten is the 1st book in the Women of the Otherworld Series and though the writing style is somewhat different from what I usually read, it still pulled me in from the first page. And being a debut book is truly amazing. 
 A thrilling and tight plot, fast paced paranormal romance filled with action, mystery in a world inhabited by werewolves, demons, half-demons, ghosts, witches and lots of other supernaturals and humans too of course, that is both convincing and believable. 
 Strong and memorable characters, my favorites being Elena & Clay (the one who BITES her!!!!). 
 Elena is not the delicate and swooning heroine and though it took me a while to warm to her, she does in the end show that she's more than just a sexy and pretty woman. 
 Clay - wow this is some hardass guy...werewolf. He's something wicked, hates humans and is totally obsessed over Elena. This werewolf is beyond alpha-male - super macho. 
 Great character development and such an interesting world building. 
 Great series and I'm onto No 2 next.
Not what I expected from reading her other books, but just as great! I can't wait to read the whole series.

Sent to me by Random House, I quite enjoyed this book and look forward to reading more in the series. Kelley Armstrong has created a very strong female character which I loved! Found this book hard to put down because I wanted to know how they got rid of the threat of the mutts.

Maybe a 3.5 I liked this, but the main character was frustrating at times. I will probably give the next book in the series a try sometime, but it's not at the top of my "must" read list. There are a lot of other werewolf series I enjoy more. Personally, I would recommend Patricia Briggs Alpha and Omega series first.
No way..could not get into it at all..moving on

book_b.title: The Sweetness at the Bottom of the Pie (Flavia de Luce, #1)
book_b.user_review: Cozy mysteries are not my usual stomping ground, but a friend recommended this book to me. She was right in her assessment. I loved the narrator. Flavia's charm is what holds the story together. Flavia is a precocious 11 year old with a love of poisons. As a person with a fascination with an unusual topic, I completely identified with Flavia's quirky obsession. Her plotting and planning of revenge upon her sister sealed the deal for me. Often overlooked, Flavia takes on the mantle of proving her father's innocence in a murder that occurs in her yard. The mystery didn't really hook me in, but Flavia's personality is well worth the read.

sample_reviews.review_text: An awesome read! It was hilarious, sinister and whimsical all at the same time. What a character Alan Bradley has created in Flavia. I loved the way he was able to transport me into her 11 year-old mind and realistically relate the reasonings and rationalizations that she makes at every turn.
A modern day Nancy Drew, told from the perspective of an 11-year-old brat. About 30 pages of actual story with about 343 pages of fluff.

Cutesy, strange writing. I did not love Flavia, but resolved to finish the book and solve the mystery. It took some time to get used to his writing style. I can most certainly say I didn't love it. Meh.

I'm not usually a fan of mysteries but the narrator of this book, 11 year old Flavia de Luce, made this entertaining. Flavia is bright and precocious and obsessed with chemistry (most specifically poison.) When a dead bird is found on her family's step and then a dead body in their garden Flavia sets out to solve the mystery. 
 I can't say that I cared so much about who was the murderer but Flavia herself kept me reading. I especially loved when she seeks revenge on her older sister by melting down her lipstick and combining it with oil she extracted from poison ivy and then waiting for the symptoms to appear.

This is a cute, enjoyable book. The cuteness factor comes in the form of the narrator, Flavia, a stupendously precocious 10 going on 11 young girl living with her father, two sisters, caretaker and cook on an estate in rural England around 1950. Based on the display of her knowledge at 10, she should have won the Nobel Prize at 12, 15 at most. Besides being bright, she has a wry sense of humor and is clever enough to connect the dots to solve a murder committed in their garden. The book is essentially about Flavia who happens to be involved in a murder mystery. That say, it is fairly well constructed, enjoyable, and moderately satisfying as a mild work of fiction. No straining of the brain here. Flavia is a character whose energy, innocence and pointed observations regarding the world around her make the novel enjoyable and worth reading, more to some than others but definitely worthwhile.

As an Anne of Green Gables fan for life, I am always going to be a fan of a book with a fearless, precocious young girl protagonist. Especially one who is a science nerd to boot! So this was a fun mystery for sure. The sheer density of similes/metaphors can be a bit overwhelming and tiresome, but I try to see it as consistent with the voice of the narrator, and they don't come across as serious attempt at literary prowess and more the way a kid who's just learning about literary devices might overuse them. Even still, it's a bit grating.

Flavia is a girl after my own heart! Chemistry, books, mysteries... all right up my alley! While I, at times, felt like this story was drowning in allegory, it was brief and the characters more than made up for it. Can't wait to see what Flavia is up to in the next book!
Delightful!

I liked the idea of this book enough that when I couldn't get into the audio book I tried just reading it. and nope. couldn't do that either. Flavias leaps in logic and deduction just seemed too great. Not the series for me.
I really hated this book. So much hype over what really is a Nancy Drew mystery? An eleven year old heroine who has to register at least a genius? No thanks. I did this many years ago.

reference_books.title: Wideacre  (The Wideacre Trilogy, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I read this after The Other Boleyn girl... It was a mistake. One word: incest. Lesson learned: Just because you like a book by an author does not mean that you should go out and read all other books by that author.

book_a.title: The Readers of Broken Wheel Recommend

sample_reviews.review_text:
This book should come with a warning. If you are listening as an audio book, be sure to not listen while driving, may cause drowsiness. 
 That should explain enough how I felt about this one. This started with such potential. A book about a couple of people who love books!!! I mean all books! Also about opening a little bookshop in a small town. I imagined a cast of colorful characters coming in a out of the bookstore perhaps carrying exciting stories to tell of their own lives etc. what I got was a tedious, ever so dull book about a lot of forgettable people. I mean you forgot about them the minute they were out of the scene. 
 Besides the mind numbing boredom, I wasn't real keen on our protagonist trying to decide whether books were a place to hide from experience. How life and living and blah blah is so much better. As a reader and a liver of life, I don't think you have to compare one to the other. Reading is a hobby like knitting is to some people and No one says those things about knitters! 
 Also, I felt the author was trying to be too much like Jane Austen and the whole Darcy thing with tom and Sarah. I mean really this was just barely a notch above chick lit. If you want a nice, safe, vanilla bean of a story, by all means, read this.

Sara comes from Sweden to visit an old friend in a small, broken Iowan town only to find her recently deceased. What's a quirkily and painfully shy bookworm to do? Why, despite the fact that she is a foreigner traveling under a tourist visa, try to revive the town by opening up a bookstore with her friend's used books! In this day of online ordering, the bookstore, sans business plan, registration, and tax number, is a wonderful success. Perhaps it is the charming walls painted yellow, or the smelly used armchair in the window, or quirkily arranged titles arranged under clever subject headings like "Books for a Friday Night" or "Books With Happy Endings" that make the magic happen! Apparently, the town's requisite group of quirky citizens join forces to embrace Sara and at the same time tidy up the loose ends of the town's eligible but reticent bachelor. 
 You know how it ends by the close of the first chapter, so all that's left is to try to endure the uber-quirkiness oozing from every page. In Sara's bookshop, this title might be arranged under "Formulaic Books for When Wanting to Be Annoyed by Characters." 
 This book did earn an extra star for its questionably effective but earnest promotion of reading. Book lovers weary of over-played charm will be carried through the pages by the many references to modern and classic literature found within.
2.5 stars. I thought it would be quirkier and not as cliched.

I wasn't quite sure how to rate this book. On one hand, I couldn't put it down. It was exactly what I needed to read at the time (high stress in real life and a cozy read to take a break from life). I read this book in the bath, while eating dinner, while sitting and waiting to pick up my kids after school. I had to know if Sara was going to stay in America, if the book store was going to succeed, and if George would be reunited with his daughter. 
 However, the writing style was really choppy and sometimes threw me out of the story. There was an element I didn't like (the casual attitude toward sex). But even with those two objections, I couldn't put it down. I guess that means it deserves a four star rating, though this book isn't a favorite and I wouldn't reread it. 
 I loved this particular thought because it so describes me! "She had thrown herself into one ambitious reading project after another, but things had rarely gone according to plan. It was boring to think of books as something you should read just because others had, and besides, she was much too easily distracted. There were far too many books out there to stick to any kind of theme" (167). Yes! I will read one book and then come across another recommendation and veer off into a completely different genre. My mantra - "So many books. So little time!" 
 There was also a small description of George cleaning a neighbor's house as a pleasant surprise. I really liked the way he described it. "With satisfaction, he saw the dirty pile grow smaller with each glass he washed. The kitchen seemed to grow before his very eyes. It became bigger and airier and much more pleasant... it was nice being able to do something when you could so clearly see your progress" (237). I really struggle with this. Dishes are a never ending job, same with laundry. But if I could turn it around and see our home becoming so much more pleasant with each chore I do, maybe it would be easier to tackle the daily chores.

Stopped around page 30-ish. It felt so unnatural, a small Iowa town of less than 700 people with no industry or jobs, but everyone has money, there's a town bar and diner and public internet, and the characters socialize like an EU town/village not like folks would here in the US. Too "off" to continue. :(

2.5 Stars 
 Got ARC from Net Galley. 
 This was an odd yet cute book that had some spoilers in it but since I have the brain of a goldfish they will just slip right out before I read the books that were mentioned. I think there should have been a warning about that since you can't expect every reader to have read every single book they want to read yet. In my case the list just gets longer and longer so I found that a bit annoying although it did fit in with this book since Sara is a book lover. 
 This will appeal to people who absolutely love books and might even prefer them to people. You know who you are. I would love to have a pen pal/book buddy that I could write letters to and send books to and vice versa. Sara and Amy bond over their love of books over a period of two years before Sara decides to come all the way from Sweden to Iowa. When Sara gets there she gets some news. I liked this book but it was kind of odd because I don't think anything close to this could happen in reality. The people in the small town of Broken Wheel were all interesting but not really realistic since I don't think what happened would ever happen in reality.

This was a sweet story about a Swedish bibliophile named Sara who travels to Broken Wheel, Iowa, to meet her pen pal, Amy, only to arrive the day of Amy's funeral. Instead of returning home as you'd expect, Sara decides to stay a couple of months in Amy's house. 
 Broken Wheel has fallen on hard times, but that doesn't stop the townspeople from taking care of Sara as Amy would have done. To repay their kindness, Sara decides to open a bookstore, and maybe give them just a little ray of hope through reading. The author was spot on in capturing the feeling of a dying Midwestern town. 
 This is a book about books and book lovers (Sara and Amy), and literary references abound. It was fun getting to live the dream of opening a small town bookshop through Sara. She's a shy and timid young woman, but seems to have found a place to belong in Broken Wheel. Of course, Sara's travel visa will eventually expire, so the folks of Broken Wheel come up with a plan for her to stay. 
 No big surprises in this book, and the plot seemed to drag in a few spots, but overall this was a fun book. A perfect read for chick lit fans. 
 Disclosure: I received a copy of this book from the publisher through NetGalley in exchange for an honest review.

I have never been so bored reading a book in all my life! And someone had the nerve to make this into a movie!!? That must be the worst movie ever. I might watch it just to see if they make it any better than this book. The author is from Poland, so maybe something was lost in the translation that would have made it more engaging, but I doubt it. One star for you, Solaris! I need to give SF a break for a while. So glad I'm finally finished!

An astronaut arrives on a distant planet...a very odd one, made entirely from a thick gelid ocean. Almost immediately, odd things start to happen... 
 This was a tough and very dull book to wade through, as short as it was. The planet Solaris consists of a large sentient (or possibly not) ocean. For an uncounted score of years, humanity has been trying to contact it, or even discover if the ocean is alive in any meaningful sense of the word, but Solaris doesn't want to play. It ignores all attempts at contacting it and defies definition, something which apparently drives scientists to distraction and increasingly esoteric and more subtle divisions. 
 The lead character, Kelvin, says that Solaris denies definition, and that humanity shouldn't try. Pity the author didn't think so; fully two-thirds of the book is exposition on what Solaris might be, quoting fictional sources as though the reader knew who they were. ("Barian's theory was the predominant position until Kilkowsy's day", that sort of stuff). 
 As a result, we don't really care about the characters, or what they're going through. Dialogue is stilted and wooden, characters are two dimensional and we have very little understanding of them. 
 It only merits another star for the descriptions of the world beneath them, particularly of the sunsets and sunrises.

This book was a real exercise in stamina for me. It's not even very long - only 204 pages - but the lines of print are smooshed close together so there is a lot of text per page. 
 The basic concept of this book is fascinating... but the rare moments of "plot" were broken up by huge sections detailing the previous theories and scholarship on the planet Solaris and its "inhabitant." I am not against creating a detailed history for a work of fiction; Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell did this admirably via footnotes. But in this case, it was just a snoozefest. I felt like I was fighting to get through each page. 
 I'm slightly tempted to watch the movie, although my husband describes it as "Sphere without the action." 
 As I was reading, I attributed some of the awkward, dense feel of the prose to the translation. It FELT translated, which some translators are able to avoid. I don't know if I'd attempt another Stanislaw Lem novel, but who knows...

I have often wondered myself why people are so interested in life on other planets. What are we looking for? Isn't the search for life on Mars, an asteroid, or exoplanets just an excuse for us? We can't face our own humanity so we look for it outside and miss the mark. Lem really hits this point home in his book, where all of those on this mystery planet must face their own conscience, their own memories, their own brain, and their own emotion. The search for extraterrestrial life is just a search for human life within us, and reaching out to communicate with what is not seen, as he mentions, is a cheap substitute for connecting with God. I really dug this book! It was psychological sci-fi, creepy, fun, and interesting. There were a couple of chapters that went off the deep end of too much alien trivia, but the rest was a great ride. I liked the ambience, the spooky vibe, and especially the undertones of "Why?"
A tragic love story wrapped in a space station of horrors and questions. It explored the limitless expanse of imagination and the limited trapped feeling of humanity.

Interesting Sci-fi book. Group of guys on another world gets visited by beings who take the form of difficult items from their past. For the main character, his visitor is his wife - the woman he killed once before.

An obviously hugely influential work of science fiction. The imagery is particularly rich and atmospheric, and echoes can be found in later classics like Neon Genesis Evangelion, and Blade Runner. Furthermore, Lem's philosophical approach is ground-breaking and still relevant. Who today in science fiction questions the worth and possibility of "contact"? Not many authors seriously treat the topic. 
 While the literary merits of Solaris earn it a home on my bookshelf, it cannot gain a perfect score in my opinion because of its tiresome racism and sexism. I never fail to feel disappointed that for all their imagination and creativity, the scifi writers of generations past could not look beyond the flimsy confines of race, gender, and social stratification.

I didn't always like the main character but I related to her, I understood where she was coming from but I didn't always understand her actions. I liked Will though and I'm quite happy that he got the girl :3 Makes me happy when the nerd/geek/general outcast gets the girl in the end.

sample_reviews.review_text: It was alright, but personally, I think I could of written it better myself.

Not nearly as awesome as Elsewhere was. It wasn't bad, it just wasn't...interesting. It didn't feel complete. I wish we could have had an idea of what Naomi was like before she lost her memory - she seemed pretty decent after, if confused about certain relationships, and there was very little, if any change, in her after she regained her memories, despite the allusions that she had been pretty bitchy. It bugged me a bit that her original boyfriend kept telling her that she loved tennis, but she couldn't remember why she liked tennis at all, and then she got her memory back, and 100 pages later, when she had a chance to play tennis again, there's this random line about how she had missed tennis and really had loved it. Hello, show me that, damn it. LOL It came out of nowhere and disappeared. A lot of her pre-fall likes and dislikes were randomly mentioned every now and again, and it just didn't fit together well. 
 But I did like Naomi, she did have an interesting story, and it wasn't bad at all. Just could have been better.

The worst book I have read by Gabrielle Zevin. Nothing about this story is appealing nor do I understand how it held anyone's attention. I started skimming the pages because it was so damn boring and I could not have cared less about any of the unlikable characters. Had this been the first book I had ever read of Gabrielle Zevins, I would never pick up another one again.

4/5 I really enjoyed this book! I enjoyed seeing through the main character's eyes as we went through her life with her without her memories. I also enjoyed that this story was extremely realistic when it came to teenage relationships. No insta-love or soul mate stuff, just honest to goodness real first love stuff. Highly recommend in the plot intrigues your interest.

I was disappointed. I really expected to like this book, my expectations weren't sky high, but the concept seemed to be to my taste and heard great things from reviewers with whom I normally agree. 
 I didn't dislike this book. I didn't hate it. It was simply okay. I found it rather slow paced and not a lot happened. I don't even mind when not a lot happens in a book if I'm invested enough in the characters, but I just didn't feel anything but annoyed. I was annoyed with the MC. I found her selfish and judgmental, and not in the "they're flawed but that's what makes me love them" kind of way either. Everyone really tried to accommodate her, but she really didn't appreciate it. I didn't really feel like she grew as a person very much throughout the book. She came to a few realizations and acceptances at the end, but nothing that really showed her growth of character. I found her love interest horribly annoying to the point where I tried to read faster so I could get to a scene that didn't involve him. 
 That being said. I liked Will. I liked Mr. Porter. Her father and Ace might have been my favorite characters despite their small parts. I found them real. These are people I feel could be your dad, my dad. Ace could be a boy I went to high school with and could date or know. There were some very honest and real moments to this book, and those were the parts I genuinely enjoyed. Those were the parts that made me enjoy it as much as I did. 
 So to sum it up again. It was just okay. Probably not one I will reread.

I didn't enjoy this book as much as I thought I would. I've had high expectations for it, but I was disappointed on how bland it was for my taste. 
 I've expected to read about the hardships of being an amnesiac; it was sad how little of that I got to read. 
 It is true that there were some struggles on Naomi's part as she tries to cope with her memory loss, but the storyline lacked emotional substance. The story just jumped from one part to another. 
 Even with the love interests, there was absolutely no chemistry between the characters; it all seemed superficial to me. 
 Probably I've set very high expectations on this book, which actually lead to my disappointment from head start. If I did not have such high hopes, I migh have liked it. 
 Overall, it was ok, as there were parts that made me smile.

I am glad I bought it and I read it, if only to bring closure to the series.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Alisha: The fan who is neither crazy, nor entitled rants 
 Update: 
 So I've been on Amazon, watching the reactions. Lots of sock puppets and rabid Charlaine fans giving this turd 5 stars. Even Anne Rice is weighing in! I'm uber suspicious of all reviews that say, "She tied this up nicely, way to go Ms. Harris! and I look forward to reading the Coda in October!" Gotta hand it to Penguin, they are on top of this. 
 "Hey everyone! Look over here! Disregard the bad reviews. Those people are CRAZY!" 
 There's been a lot said about this final installment of Sookie. There have been angry fans, sad fans, furious bloggers, and Charlaine sheeple. Fans of Charlaine and maybe free speech? are calling the upset masses entitled and crazy. If you didn't like the book, you are a crazy Eric/Sookie shipper. Just check out the Wall Street Journal's crap article, How to Kill a Vampire Series if you don't believe me. 
 It's a mess. In the end, this will sell plenty of books, but a good portion of readers will remember that their emotional trust was broken. Say what you will, that is a legitimate feeling. There is a relationship between reader and writer and that is built on trust. When a writer chooses not to just add a twist, but to twist a knife into the reader, it's sometimes permanent. 
 The world of Sookie has changed. I've thought a lot about why Harris would write an arc that heavily favored Eric, then dismantle the entire work in three books. My guess is that Harris, being tired of Sookie isn't in the same frame of mind she once was when writing the frisky waitress/telepath. Of course she isn't in the same place she once was. We change. What once was exciting and fresh, can become dull and stale. Likewise, with Sookie, Harris' ability to do what she wanted in light of True Blood, crazed fans, and simple boredom all took their toll on the work. 
 I've read books 1-9 at least five times each. 10-12? Why bother? 
 I'm not a whiny girl who didn't get her way. 
 I did not read this final installment and I don't plan to, but not for the reasons that you might think. I'm not an entitled douche bag. I don't want to make Harris my bitch. I've been known to read a book or two, and despite what Harris' PR camp is spinning, I won't be attempting suicide or threatening the author any time soon. Most likely, I'll just read something else. 
 Here's my complaints, since I know the ending and I've read all the reviews on Amazon. 
 Bad Plot Devices 
 Alisha takes offense. Harris thinks that rape is a appropriate plot device, selling Eric into sex slavery for the next 200 years. Lets salt that and add that Pam is forbidden to go with him. What's troubling is that I doubt she would have made the same choice for a female character, because RAPE! Holy crap! . Try saying that out loud to someone who hasn't read the books and see if they don't laugh at the absurdity of that particular choice. "She did WHAT to Eric?!?" 
 1. I waffle between thinking that Harris hates her fame or or fans or the book. I can't tell which one. Then I think, no, she's just tired of it. But after her choices for DEA, I am back to thinking that she's a bit vindictive. Why? I haven't a clue. It could be the fans, or True Blood/Alan Ball hate. I can't say. I do feel her choices for Eric were vindictive. Let me restate that. I feel this. YOU are free to feel other stuff. 
 But Alisha! Wait! Harris can do whatever she sees fit. See my last comment, but also... 
 Sure, she can and she did. I ask you though, how did Moning conclude the Fever series? How has Gabaldon treated Fraser and Claire? How did Mead conclude Vampire Academy? You can literally insert any couple into this example and get a similar outcome. That outcome being that not everyone is satisfied with conclusions, but the readership did not freak the fuck out. 
 2. Harris wrote the love between Eric and Sookie. Eric always had Sookie's back even when she didn't realize it. He graveled her drive, and replaced her coat. He called her brave and self-less. He tried to protect her from a bond with Andre. Harris also wrote Sookie saving Eric. In those books, many of us became invested readers. 
 3. Harris wrote the friend/boss/big brother relationship between Sam and Sookie. There was a kiss here and there, but we READ that it could never work because Sookie could hear his thoughts unless he was actively blocking her. But now, it's all good. Thoughts, shmoughts, is what I always say! 
 4. Harris wrote that Sookie was worried (annoyingly concerned) that the bond between her and Eric was influencing her feelings of love, so much so that she broke the blood bond. And yet, Sookie is willing to overlook the use of the Culivial Dor on Sam because...we don't know. Sookie decided that reading Sam's thoughts didn't matter, so maybe it a new life choices/attitude thing. Maybe her clock is ticking? Settling worked well for Tara, right? After all, Tara has twins! 
 5. Harris wrote Sookie as brave in the beginning and accepting of other supes because people had always treated her like crap. She was open to others, but now, to live a happy life she must shun other supes and try to live as humanly as possible? 
 6. I'm not okay with the way it ended for Eric. Rape happens and so does sex slavery. I know it's just a book, but it leaves a horrible taste in my mouth. CH wouldn't make this choice for a female character, but it's okay for a man? *face palm* Just kill him off! This choice is cruel and the sex slavery is icky. We know what happened between Eric and his maker and we know he was abused sexually. That was sad. Now it's full circle? Jesus. I just can't... 
 My hard-hearted husband laughed up when I told him what Harris did to Eric. He said I ought to charge Harris with committing a McMurtry in the first degree. If you don't know what I'm referring to, see Lonesome Dove and the sequel, The Streets of Laredo. 
 But wait! There's more weird plots! Why would Sookie's gay cousin, Claude want to kidnap and rape Sookie? He was foiled by homophobes? Right wingers save the day! Again, I didn't read this, but there are some heated rants of tumblr that are discussing this peculiar plot device. 
 If you don't want to end up a spinster, it's time to settle! 
 Back to my point. I'm not reading the book because Sookie isn't fun anymore. That character I loved has devolved into a bigoted old woman, hell bent on nitpicking every aspect of her life. Sookie settled! She settle for line dancing, kids, and casseroles. That is NOT BRAVE. Remember ladies, when a woman nears thirty, it's time to quit being picky. The music is about to stop, so pick a chair! Charlaine wrote that too. 
 SVM books once involved a mystery, some witty banter, a bit of fantasy with a smidgen of lust. When it worked, it was magic. 
 Sadly, the magic is gone. Luckily, there are other books in the sea, err...library.

This final books starts out rather different than the rest of the series which gave me some reservations but Charlaine Harris is a master story teller and I should never for a moment have doubted her skills. 
 While I am not sure this is how I would have wanted the series to end, I can not truthfully say I'm unhappy. 
 Kudos for Ms. Harris staying true to her world and her books and not bowing to fans which (whether they know it or not) would have not done Sookie a service. On the contrary, I think any other ending would have felt false and completely ruined the entire series.

I have read a lot of book over the years. I know you don't always get the "Happy Ever After" you think the character(s) should have. Heck, sometimes your favorite character gets killed off... or everyone does. But I have NEVER read a book where the author so blatantly gave all of her readers the proverbial finger. I said I'd go into this book with an open mind and a heavy heart, but I know I will never again read anything she writes. Dead Ever After was as horrible as we were all told and I now wish I had just slept instead of reading it. 
 FULL review coming soon.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Honestly the major things that happened in the book were not very surprising, especially with Sookie ending up with Sam. It was all wrapped up with a bow, and I'm sure I would have been mad if it wasn't.

Better than I thought it would be. I had a bit of a time getting into it. I think because this book has more viewpoints to it. I am use to Sookie. What worked really well for me was that the author seemed to go back to her earlier story. The characters were more like the people I knew and loved or hated. I disliked the feeling I got towards the end that Ms Harris was trying too hard to wrap up the story while leaving enough open for another book. After all this was suppose to be the final book but we were fooled. I am not so certain Sookie ended up with anyone. I do think the ending was a typical Sookie man action with a lesson learned aspect. I missed Pam. She is my favorite, (and I totally would be psyched with a Pam spin off), and was just not in this book enough. I wasn't as satisfied with the ending as I would have been if this were the final book, but I am giving it 4 stars. It is more in line with the first books.

I have been a fan of this series since a friend of mine recommended them to me, so I am sad to see it end! There are things that I did not particularly agree on in this last book, but I was not comepletely disappointed nonetheless. All loose ends were tied up, and although I would have preferred Sookie to end up with someone else, I was still happy with the way things played out. I recommend this series to anyone who is interested in this genre. I agree that the first ones in the series were much better, but I still had a difficult time putting even this one down.

Ok i haven't had the courage to open DEA. I pre-ordered it a while ago and it's been there compelling me to read it. 
 On Tuesday 7th I was reading on my iPad (Game of Thrones, excellent book so far, I highly recommend it) and all of the sudden the reminder of the book release appears in the center of my iPad screen, anxiety and excitement cursed through me as I pressed the "library" button on the top right corner of the screen, and after so many months and 13$ less (I thought the book was really expensive BTW), there it is, the arrow that tells me that I can start downloading my new book, and I just....couldn't do it. It was like something was telling me to wait, and weirdly enough not for the right reasons; so I decided to finish GoT before I start DEA. it's so disappointing to see so many bad reviews after all this years of loyal reading and readers. It literally pains me knowing that I will not like the book and that I, as my fellow readers and companions in my sadness; will end up being extremely disappointed with it. I've read literally hundreds of different reviews in hopes that maybe, just maybe the book its not as bad as everybody says, but no and I'm still shocked to see how bad they are. Some of them are really enraged towards Harris, which I admire (haven't read the book yet, so give me time) and I mean, as a writer she has the right to do whatever she wants to do with her characters, I think you become a writer to tell a story and create whatever a world you want, the perfect world as u see it, in a way you become God. You have the power to do whatever you like in this world who actually owes YOU, it's existence. I'm a big fan of the TV Show True Blood, and I just think, if Harris wouldn't had dared to create this world we wouldn't had have Alexander Skarsgard as Eric Northman (such a beautiful sight can't be denied to the world) or Joe Manganiello as Alcide (another gorgeous man) or Bill Moyer...but I'm babbling, what I'm trying to say is that I hope we are not being to hard on Harris, after all we have to respect everybody's work, but I as I stated before I haven't start the book, (give me two min after I'm done with this review) and I just hope that the disappointment and unfairness that I hear and read in other people reviews isn't as bad for me as it is for them. 
 Wish me luck!

Wow. What happened? Harris' books used to be fun, and at least competently written. This one was no fun at all (Could it have been any more boring? ENDLESS paragraphs about Sookie cleaning, Sookie dressing, Sookie moisturizing her legs) and the writing was atrocious. It was like the worst fan fiction ever written. I'm so relieved this is the last book, because now I won't be faced with the difficult decision on whether or not to give another of her books a try. I definitely will not be. 
 The only bright spot was that she ends up with Sam . Of course she did; that ending was broadcast loud and clear from the very beginning. And he is absolutely right for her. I'm just sorry that their relationship had to resolve itself in this particular book. Worst sex scene ever in the history of bad sex scenes. Well, okay. Maybe not the worst, but I do feel the need to scrub out my brain.

Oh. My. Goodness. 
 I have spent years loving the Sookie Stakhouse novels and waiting patiently for them to be released one after another. Though I didn't find them until after 2005 (the first was published in 1999) I became a big fan of Sookie and have enjoyed the Sookie Stackhouse saga. 
 I was not disappointed with this last book necessarily. Well, not at all... as you can see I gave it a 5/5. It was a great ending to a phenomenal series. I'm just not 100% positive I gel with the person she ended up with. Not that I don't like the character the ends up being "The One" for Sookie. He's great! I just don't feel like Ms. Harris got you warmed up enough to the idea before throwing you in to it. 
 Needless to say, I consider Sookie Stackhouse to be one of my best literary friends and I wish her fictional-future to be nothing but happy! 
 Dead Ever After was a great final book. Not only does Ms. Harris tie up a BUNCH of loose ends that were just blowin' in the wind there for a while... she does so with enough finality to make the readers comfortable with leaving Sookie alone. There's hope for her having a happy life after all. 
 I was surprised by (though shouldn't have been) by the sheriff swap. I wasn't sure what was going to happen in that department but it came together nicely. 
 Also... WHAT THE HECK, NIALL!? 
 Alright. Anyway. Ms. Harris uses her last book as an opportunity to reintroduce characters that the reader hadn't heard from in a while... she also takes great care in making sure that each of Sookie's love-interests are either "off-limits" enough or "out-of-mind" enough for there never to be any future requited love issues going on there. Which is good... because Sookie sure did know how to fall for some pretty dangerous guys! Yoiks! 
 In the series Sookie dated 2 vampires, a werewolf, a were tiger, and a shape-shifter. She was also pursued by multiple other-creatures including fairies. I mean, yikes. This girl had an interesting love-life and, honestly, I'm going to miss hearing about it! 
 Sookie Stackhouse was a brave, unique, sassy, and out-of-the-norm heroine. Not only is she a SOUTHERN girl... she's also been described as being a size 10 with a healthy appetite. I could go on and on about how I appreciate a book with a main character that isn't "slim waisted", "waiflike" or "athletic". 
 Ms. Harris managed to create a female character that could stand up for herself without coming off too cold or bitchy. She made Sookie juuuussst vulnerable enough to make us feel like we weren't reading about a stone-cold, emotionless female. However, I never felt like Sookie was the "Rescue me" damsel in distress, either. She knew how to take care of herself and when to let others help take care of her. 
 The entire LGBT underline was well done and perfectly displayed. Though these books were romance/action/mystery/supernatural all woven together in a harmonious saga of awesome... they were also a commentary on today's human rights movements. 
 Anyway... I'm sad that the series has ended but I'm happy that I got a chance to enjoy it for 13 full books. Also, I'm happy to hear that Ms. Harris will be releasing a book with information about the fates of many of her characters after the end of the series. 
 This book is called "AFTER DEAD" and will be released October 29, 2013. 
 If you're a fan of supernatural books and you HAVEN'T read any of the Sookie Stackhouse books then you need to GET ON IT! NOW! But, if you're like me and thousands of other Sookie fans you'll be anxiously awaiting the next Charlaine Harris book... whatever its topic may be. I'll help pass the time by reading her Aurora Teagarden mysteries for now!
I thought it was a good book. Sorry that it had to end. I think her choice for Sookie to be with Sam was a good way to end the book. I'm glad also that Pam got to be the new sheriff for the vampires.

book_b.title: After Alice
book_b.user_review: This was awful. I just did not enjoy the style, the characters, or the story. I was really looking forward to this but sadly it was just not a book that worked for me.

sample_reviews.review_text: I did not like this book at all. The writing was not well done and I didn't like any of the characters.
Not really in the right mood for a silly, ridiculous book like this.

I would like to preface this by saying that Gregory Maguire is one of my favorite authors. His adaptations of classic fairytales have always tickled my fancy and seeing as this is a reimagining of one of my favorite fairytales, I was extremely excited to read it. "After Alice," does not really retell the story in a new and interesting way. Instead, it tells the tale of Alice's neighbor who accidentally falls down the rabbit hole also and the shear panic that occurs among the adults above ground who want to know where their children disappeared to. I found it wholly unenchanting.
It was a good book. There was a lot of information in it that I felt was randomly put together making it hard to follow at times. But over all it was a good Alice in wonderland book

I gave up after 75%, too uninterested to keep going. This is the most boring heap of drivel I've ever encountered. I don't believe MaGuire gave two hoots about the actual story supposedly being told here, he'd just struck a bet with the demons of bad writing to see how many inane large words he could sneak into a manuscript and still dupe some poor, witless editor into publishing it. The only Alice-like nonsense to be found was the fact that reading a book in my native tongue should never feel this much like translating as I go. All this is very disappointing after reading Egg and Spoon earlier this year, and loving it. After that book, I had hoped MaGuire was actually writing things I'd want to read now, but apparently Egg and Spoon was just a fluke. One measly star to After Alice and it's ridiculously unreadable word gymnastics.

I have enjoyed other books by Gregory Maguire and kept reading this one expecting it to get better, but sadly, no. 
 One pet peeve of mine is when authors use $25 dollar words when a 10 cent word will work just fine. Not that that means I disapprove of the use of big words, but this book was liberally sprinkled with words I'd never heard before. Here's just a few: rubicund, gammon-pink, janissary, termagants, quern, colloquy; and these were just from a handful of chapters. Please, I don't mind one or two words I have to look up, but really? one or two in each chapter is just too much. I read for pleasure and that pleasure suffers (not to mention the flow of the plot) when I have to stop and consult the dictionary every page or two. 
 Rant over. 
 Otherwise, the book seems to completely miss the whimsy of the original Alice and instead is dismal without relief. There are a lot of references to death and the afterlife and for some reason Mr. Darwin becomes a character of major influence. There is also a young American slave boy who becomes a major character and even at the end of the story I had no idea what his purpose was or why he was in the narrative. 
 If there was some moral take-away the author was trying to convey, I confess that I completely missed it.

I didn't understand the ending. I assume someone was dreaming, but I don't know who. If anyone who's read this knows the answer, please tell me. What happened with Ada? Did she shed that contraption she had to wear or was that just her imagination in the end? I'm unsure how I feel about the book. It was easier to get through after the first few pages which had way too many fancy words and phrases, which I decided weren't worth trying to understand. Once it got down to an actual story I could understand I enjoyed it to some degree. I liked reading about Alice and Ada's family and what they were experiencing while the children were awol in wonderland. I wish the ending was more clear.

Couldn't make the fifty page rule and quit after 35. Maguire is trying to create a dreamlike prose in the Victorian style and ends up as unreadable. I got to the White Rabbit and the Walrus and the Carpenter, and they weren't reimagined at all as I had hoped.

I tried to enjoy this book, but I just couldn't get into it. The prose was hard to read, and there wasn't a very logical flow to the story; it meandered all over the place. I get that it was trying to be like the original writing in Alice in Wonderland, but it just didn't work for me.
Too wordy and not a bit interesting to read. Gave up after 31% and decided to try something else instead...

reference_books.title: The Scourge (Brilliant Darkness, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
My enjoyment level of The Scourge was 5 stars, but as I was left with too many questions at the end, I went with a 4 star rating. 
 The Scourge was a truly unique story. It is dystopian but hardly feels like it as the people live in the forest and are more primitive than most dystopian novels. I liked that a lot. Reading from the perspective of a blind girl was also a nice change, and AG Henley did it very well. There was plenty of action, but the characters also had depth, and Fennel's perspective was a good one. I didn't like how her and Peree created a bond only after a couple of days. It seemed rushed, and they didn't have that much conversation before setting off to find the hidden waters. For me the first half of the book could have been longer and more detailed, also because things were not clear right away. 
 The middle of the book was well done, I liked Koolkuna a lot. Again, I think it could have benefited from some more detail, but it was fine. 
 The end was really the part that needs work. Everything was happening and then suddenly, nothing was. The past few days was just recapped and then that was it, boom, done. Meanwhile the reader is left with questions, especially about Peree and Fennel. How can they just suddenly be together, in front of people? It doesn't' make any sense. The end just didn't feel concluded well enough. I know that more will happen in The Defiance, but still. 
 I know it seems like there were a lot of problems from this book, but it really was excellent. 100% worth reading, it is truly different and creative, nothing else is like it.

reference_books.title: These Broken Stars (Starbound, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I loved it. Going in I thought it would be around a 3-star, just knowing what it was about, but it was so much more than that. Right off the bat we were thrown in, lots of action, but deep characters too. It was a perfect balance, really. The character development mixed with the fast pace could not have been better. I was never bored, in fact I only put it down out of necessity. One of my favorite things was that the relationship between Tarver and Lilac was not insta-love. They were on the rocks for quite awhile, and the slow build felt more realistic, and reminded me of Under the Never Sky in that it took it slow and was worth more in the end. 
 As for the overall premise, it was very unique and well done. I was expecting more of a space story, but what I got was just as interesting. There were so many plot twists I never could really predict what was going to happen. I also liked that it wasn't as "fluffy" as expected. There were many serious moments thrown in. 
 The one thing stopping me from giving These Broken Stars a perfect rating is that there was no real explanation on the world view. It wasn't confusing to understand it, but I think more history of how the people's universe got to be the way it is would have added so much more, because i really am curious. Hopefully in books to come this will be addressed. 
 Definitely reccomend this.
