reference_books.title: Twilight / Life and Death (Twilight, #1, 1.75)
reference_books.review_text:
I will be honest: when I first heard of this I was actually kind of excited about it. Skeptical, of course. I was a big fan of Twilight in high school oh - 9 years ago, right after it was published. But then I grew up and I've never looked back (okay so maybe I've seen the movie once or 10 times...guilty!). As far as the books go, once the saga wrapped up I was left disappointed and completely over Edward and Bella's story. 
 But then Stephenie Meyer had to come out with Life and Death and once again I was 15 years old and excited about vampires again. *sigh* What intrigued me the most was of course, the gender swapping. Meyer is right in that many people critique Twilight based on the portrayal of Bella as a weak woman, a total no-no. And those people are right, to be completely honest. So for me it was very interesting that she would take that and try to prove that it didn't have to necessarily be a woman in Bella's shoes: it could also be a man. A very exciting prospect. So, let's dig in. 
 I was pretty disappointed that ALL of the characters were gender swapped, except for Charlie and Renee, in Life and Death. While it does make sense, for me it was more confusing to re-learn who everyone was meant to be. It was distracting from the actual point of this retelling: the gender swap of Edward and Bella. I was not so much interested in seeing how it would be if all of them were swapped, but how the two main characters would function within the same world. This fell extremely short and I wish she would not have done this. 
 Meyer failed in a few ways in proving her point with the gender swapping. For example, in Twilight, Jane Austen novels are amongst some of Bella's favorites. In Life and Death, it's 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea. Why the change, Meyer? You are shooting yourself in the foot with this! Why isn't Beau allowed to call Pride and Prejudice or Sense and Sensibility favorites? That to me proved that she wasn't fully grasping what her gender swapped story should actually be like. If you want the reader, and ultimately, your critics, to back down and admit that anyone could be in Bella's shoes, then you need to stop with the "traditional gender roles" nonsense. 
 It's been quite awhile since I've read Twilight, so it's hard for me to say if Life and Death really is just a lacking retelling (social issues aside) or if both of the stories really are just not that interesting. 
 I did re-learn that Meyer's writing is not as great as I once would have thought (9 years and 900 books ago). In the beginning it was very choppy and I felt that I was stumbling through her too short and uninteresting sentences. 
 All-around Life and Death did not live up to my expectations. I wish it would have been more true to Twilight, with just subtle changes here and there to fit Edyth and Beau. While I enjoyed the alternate ending, and found it to be very satisfying in its own way, I think it ultimately failed in backing up the entire point of changing all of the characters genders. If you are a die-hard fan or have some time on your hands, feel free to pick this up. I wouldn't go out of my way to get my hands on it, though.

book_a.title: Anna and the French Kiss (Anna and the French Kiss, #1)
book_a.user_review:
file under: Adorable. Perfect. Fun. Relatable. Must-Read. 
 I literally cannot believe it took me so long to read this. This is not a joke. 
 I see this book everyone. On top YA and Teen lists, on Amazon, on Goodreads, on blogs. Everyone raves about it. 
 I guess the title and old cover design just turned me off. It seemed juvenile and cheesy, cliche and overdone. Boarding school boy. Reluctant and angry girl about going to school so far from home. 
 Yeah yeah, we've heard that story before. 
 Unless you haven't read Anna and the French Kiss. Then you have absolutely no idea. 
 The very beginning we start with Anna just arriving in Paris. Her parents are leaving her, she's all alone, in a country she doesn't know, surrounded by people who speak a language she doesn't speak. 
 Instantly I'm drawn to this character. Not only am I already liking this, but it seems familiar . Because everyone who's ever went to college or boarding school, or traveled internationally, knows this feeling. So right then it was easy for me to fall in Anna's shoes, and know what she was feeling. 
 But then, she meets Etienne St. Clair, by chance in the hallway outside her room. And then we are all swept off our feet. This is not hyperbole. I don't know how anyone could read this and not become completely charmed by Etienne St. Clair as a character. He is suave, funny, romantic, a great friend, charismatic, and he will talk his way out of anything. From then on, we are goners. That's it. Etienne St. Clair is the star of the show, and we are all Anna. 
 It doesn't hurt that this book is set in Paris and Stephanie Perkins does a phenomenal job at weaving the city into this book. It's not done in an obvious or deadpan way: Hey we're walking around the Eiffel Tower. We're in Paris. She just sets the scene and city so casually and effortlessly. I've been to Paris. I liked it a lot, but the picture she paints makes me aching to revisit the city I haven't seen in 6 years. I need to see this place again, stand on the Kilometer Zero point, wander the Latin Quarter, visit some of the small charming movie theaters that are so revered. There could not have been a better setting for this book. 
 Anna is such a great protagonist. She is down to earth, she isn't vain, she has just the right humor and sarcastic tendencies, with a touch of self-deprecation. I respond to her character so well, she reminds me of myself a lot. But Anna does get jealous, and sometimes she says stuff she doesn't mean, or takes things out of context. She gets mad at Etienne, sometimes. She's far from perfect, but that's why she's so great. She is perfectly realistic. I highly enjoyed reading in her viewpoint. Between that, the setting, and the surrounding characters, this book was just so. dang. good. 
 Probably everyone's favorite aspect of this book, mine included, is the relationship between Anna and Etienne (mostly called St. Clair throughout the book). They are quite the pair. And while they are friends for most of the book, due to his having a girlfriend, there is just so much undeniable chemistry between them. Their personalities fit so well, they are an ebb and flow that just can't be contained. By the end of the middle I was at the edge of my seat rooting for these two. They are quite the emotional rollercoaster. So. Many. Feelings. 
 This is the relationship every reader wants to read about, and every writer wants to write. They actually fit together, and their relationship has time to build. They learn about each other, there is humor, there is angst, there is so much chemistry. But most of all: they're friends. They don't rush, nothing feels forced. Utter perfection. 
 I could hardly stop thinking about this book all weekend. I finished this Friday night, it is now Monday and here I am, still reeling. I even purchased myself a copy because I just have this feeling that I won't be able to read this just once. A+, 100%, 5 Gold Stars to Stephanie Perkins. You nailed it.

Definitely not as good as Lola and the Boy Next Door I thought. It didn't have much substance to it and I didn't get the warm cuddly feelings I did with Lola's story. I suppose it's because there wasn't much of a story to it. Boy meets girl, girl falls in love, boy already has a girlfriend...oh no. Anna isn't a bad character though, but Etienne was a bit 'meh' in my opinion. It was okay all in all.

Ohmygosh I love this book so much! I must have first read it shortly after it was published, and it was one of those books I could have just started over immediately after finishing. Since I've been wanting to read it again for so long, I made it my book group pick. What a fun excuse for a light read! Anna's voice is so fabulous right from the beginning: "At least the people in my new school speak English. It was founded for pretentious Americans who don't like the company of their own children. I mean, really. Who sends their kid to boarding school? It's so Hogwarts. Only mine doesn't have cute boy wizards or magic candy or flying lessons." I love her wit and poignant observations. I love that she was written like a high-schooler - she has many emotions, some surprising to her, and at times she acts annoying and overdramatic, which makes the plot realistic. I love the setting (I wish I had found Paris as magical as Anna does) and her descriptions of it - the cinemas, the first time she visits the Notre-Dame cathedral and the Pantheon, their visit to the creperie. I love when she first stands on the star at Point Zero and says, "I wish for the thing that is best for me." And I love the idea that home can be a person instead of a place.

I was so excited to read this book and I hate giving it a bad review but I didn't enjoy this as much as I wanted to. I thought the plot was a little crazy but bland at the same time. I didn't like how the end of chapters were so clipped and I didn't have a good understanding of little things. I wish there was more of a connection to specific detail. But I give it a 3.5 stars. I will try to continue of to the other companion books.
Good time filler. I did love it. But I have read other books that I loved more.

This was a ridiculously cute story and if was very well written. I felt I could identify with what Anna was feeling at every step in the story. And not only that, I felt what St. Clair was also struggling with. This novel perfectly relays that overwhelmed unbelievable feeling everyone has the first time they fall in love. It was truly a perfect account of those feelings.

Loved this book and maturing with Anna. She handled living in Paris in her senior year of high school with great maturity and attitude. I would have liked to have been friends with Anna in Paris. She was a wonderful character and was surrounded by an awesome circle of friends. Highly recommend this read. I am looking forward to the companion book, Lola and the Boy Next Door.

*** Read on 12/12/2010. Re-read from 08/09/2012 to 08/13/2012. Review written in 2010. *** 
 Let me tell you: There is nothing too special about the storyline: 
 Seventeen years old girl is sent to attend a posh American boarding school in Paris against her will, gets included in a circle of close-knit friends she would not have befriended under different circumstances and falls for a nice boy of the sexy variety who isn't really available, supposedly out of her league and who has a waiting line of interested parties - including one of the heroine's new friends - queued up should a miracle aka break-up occur. 
 In addition I usually despise unimaginative titles beginning with FIRST NAME AND. I have wanted to read it very badly inspite of that since I had read the two-lines-review author Laini Taylor wrote on her Goodreads page in October 2009. Good for me, because although the story is pretty "normal" for a contemporary young adult novel, the excecution is not. The writing is not fluffy, but cute, realistic, but not depressing or grey. As the author writes in her blog, Anna and the French Kiss is "serious and fun". 
 I have to re-read "Anna" soon to get the gist of it, but Stephanie Perkins' skill in displaying the miraculously realistic actions, reactions, emotions and thoughts is so masterful you cannot help investing your whole heart into the characters and their lives. 
 Confession time: I am neither Anna, nor Etienne (I really do not like calling people by their last name only, b.t.w. and ... I immediately played the 80s' hit Etienne by Guesch Patti in my head when he was introduced to Anna and to me), nor Meredith, but a lot of scences and a lot of Anna's inner turmoil triggered good and bad memories of my own - which perhaps enhanced the powerful impact the book had on me. 
 - There are these scenes in which Anna and Etienne share a bed or in which Etienne bumps into Anna on her first evening in the dorm. Anna is so very self-conscious and has difficulties to remember how to breathe. She berates herself for the silly things she said because she was so flustered. They made me remember the tiny moment it took me to recognise ,,This is it: We are going to kiss. Oh, my God" or my futile efforts to subtly get the attention of the boy of my dreams each Saturday at a church group, who seldom noticed my presence; but when he did, I turned tongue-tied and had to look away. Shaking his hand when making the round at the beginning switched off all my life-supporting organs. And ... holding hands in secret at the cinema? I've been there! Hasn't everybody? 
 - The infatuated giddyness Anna is drenched in when she spends time with Etienne and she notices that he seems to enjoy her presence, too. It took me back to uncountable points in my life: Teasing a boy I liked as a ten-years-old, behaving like a drunk without a drop of alcohol working on my system ... I almost cannot believe that my husband, back whe he still was my boyfriend ripped out a PAGE out of his PASSPORT to write down his home address for me when he went home for the holidays, which has caused us several awkward discussions with airport officers since. Or that I wasn't shocked or angry when in the middle of a makeout session at night next to a beltway I found my own naked butt exposed to the world, because that impossibly naughty guy wanted to test if I'd notice that he pulled my jeans - and panties down. Imagine: I just laughed happily and rearranged my clothes. 
 - Etienne's reluctance to finally split up with Ellie and his guilt when he comes back after his first non-date with Anna: I have to admit: After six years with a former boyfriend I took flight and selected an internship in a far away city telling him that I rather did not want him to visit instead of making a clean cut at home. There were the good times still fixed in my head and a tiny pull to make it right and maybe also the fear to be alone again. Like Anna, who accepted the admiration of Dave and its consequences up to a certain point, I took to cuddling up with at least a handful of boys in my dorm for TV or board games. 
 - Anna is hurt by the reactions of her little brother when she returns home at Christmas. She deems him fickle, because in her absence he transferred his affections to Anna's best friend Bridge. Oh, how I missed MY seven-year-old brother when I left home for university at nineteen. We were really close whe he was in Kindergarden and now at 23 - and ravishing - in my eyes he is still the cute kid grinning his cheeky grin at me, begging for a story. 
 - Meredith is in love with her friend's boyfriend. So she settles for being a good friend to him, but hopes he will somehow see her worth and change his mind. I've been in love once with a friend from a very pious family. I tried to convince his familiy of my purely "friendly" intentions by behaving chummy, because I knew I would have been banned from the house otherwise. But in secret I always hoped he would say "Screw my parents and their strange views on sex. I want to be with you." I am sure if they would have looked at my face closely, I would have been as easy to read as Meredith is. 
 - The Anna-Bridge-Toph thing. I also almost lost a very good friend, because my former boyfriend told me he fell in love with her, which made me behave distanced toward her. Silly me. 
 - Anna feeling uncomfortable because of her friends' public dispay of affections (Rashmi and Josh), but when she is the one kissing in the park she doesn't care what happens around her. Oh, I remember not knowing where to look when my best friend from school acquired her first boyfriend and spent the whole evening of a garage party on a mattress in a corner with him. We arrived together and I thought "How can she do this to me?" But later, when I had my first boyfriend I got thrown out of a church in Taize (hey, I WAS a teenager), because my kissing offended the congregation (said the orderly). 
 - The whole dorm life. In spite of the noise and the gritty kitchen and the mold growing inside the waste bins, I loved it!!!! 
 Powerful memories like that stay with you always, but time takes away their luster and their thrill. Reading Anna polished the dust from the emotions that came with them. Thank you, Stephanie Perkins, for the roller-coaster-ride and the memory trip. How did you do that? Where did you buy your magic wand?

A new paranormal romance series by Gena Showalter. WAs originally going to be a trilogy, but has now plans for 6 at least in the series. It is darker than most of her books on theme and the use of pain and pleasure. Interesting idea with the Titans and Greek gods. I love the new take on Pandora's box. Each Lord of the Underworld is a warrior that was punished for defying the gods by being cursed to "house" the demons they released. For this specific tale, we have Maddox who is possessed by the demon/spirit of Violence. He is also cursed to die each night with the assistance of Pain and Death (other demon lords of course). 
 Ashlynn is an innocent female who enters into their world seeking a way to control the voices that she can never silence. She knows no peace and is hoping that the "angels" or "demons" that these strange warrior men are referred to by the citizens of Buda can help her. Much to her surprise, they are not what she expected and things get weird fast. 
 Overall, the story seemed very chaotic. A lot of world building and set up forced the "romance" to almost take second stage. There were so many introductions it was hard to keep up at first with who housed what. Plus, it was hard to see the "beast" side being tamed so easily considering these are supposed to be "Evil" spirits to begin with. I guess the "evils" from Pandora's box weren't that evil afterall. I was a tad disappointed with that, but willing to let it go. The book itself was a fun romance that by the ending had me wanting to read the next to find out what happens with each guy. We kept having so many elements being introduced it was hard to relax into the story. The men are definitely alpha men with the whole "mine" possessive attitude that Christine Feehan does in her Carpathian series. The meet their potential mate (hard to say loved ones considering) and become obsessed despite themselves. I had mixed feelings about that. It seems such a cop out to have a couple meet and instantly "fall in love" without knowing each other or speaking. Falling lust I can understand. But terming it love? Nah. 
 It was an interesting, unique story. Nice to pass the time with. The second book read easier and flowed better than this one. Like I said, it was more set up for the whole series I think. Still good for fans of Showalter or paranormal romances that like J.R. Ward and Feehan's books. They are definitely set up to get more complicated with each book so I will be sticking with it though I don't think I will keep the books.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I moved my mouse back and forth between "2 stars" and "3 stars" 5 or 6 times before I finally settled on 2. It's because 3 stars said "liked it" and I felt like that was maybe too strong, although I've given 2 stars to worse books in the past. I guess 2.5 is maybe the best rating for this, but I've been really trying not to give half stars since they don't really count. I'm trying to work within the system that Goodreads has given us. 
 So anyway. 2 stars. 
 I had two main problems with this book. 
 1: It was such a blatant rip off of the movie Shelter I couldn't believe it. I'm not going to go so far as to say the author did it on purpose, but if he didn't... wow. It's not just the basic premise. It is character for character. Some details were changed (it's the mom that runs off and leaves him with his brother, not his sister leaving him with his nephew. He wants to be a writer, not an artist. The boyfriend is a photographer, not a writer. It takes place in Oregon, not California) and the timing was different (this takes place 3 years after the mom leaves, unlike Shelter where that event happens at the end. The kid is a little bit older, etc.) But really, these differing details can be glossed over. At its heart, it is the same story. This was sort of a double edged sword, in that on one hand, the glaring similarities bothered me. Like hello, be original! I only listed a few differences - I could go on for pages about the things that were exactly the same. But on the other hand, the fact that it was so much like a movie that I adore so much probably helped it. It kept me interested when I don't if I would have been otherwise. And it certainly helped the visualization. I already knew what all the characters looked like, and the house and the grocery store... So I'm conflicted about whether or not the similarity to Shelter is a bad thing, but it certainly had a huge impact on how I approached this story. I couldn't stop thinking about it. 
 2. Early on in the book, our main character Bear throws up after experiencing a traumatic life event. "Oh no..." I thought. But I kept reading. A little bit later on, the other hero, Otter, throws up after a much less traumatic life event and I thought "Oh, great. How did I get roped into this?" Because I stopped reading Amy Lane books for a reason. This book really felt like maybe Amy Lane had written it under a different name. All the things that drive me crazy about her books were present here: namely, the two leads are characterized as these perfect, selfless guys to whom life has dealt a Raw Deal and we are meant to Feel Sorry For Them. Everyone around them thinks they walk on water, are willing to drop everything, put their own lives on hold, sacrifice whatever to help these two guys for whom life is So Hard. But these two guys really give nothing back to these other characters. They're just self-absorbed, self-involved whiny bitches. I really do not like when characters are portrayed as being so perfect and I'm just supposed to feel sorry for them because of the raw deal life handed them, but then they go creating all their own drama instead of putting on their big girl panties and dealing with it. All of the conflict in this book is based on lack of communication which drives me CRAZY. Any other events that acted as catalysts seemed so contrived, just incredibly convenient little moments that kept the main characters from talking to each other but then never went anywhere. So frustrating. 
 Despite that, there were things that I liked. I obviously kept reading for a reason. I liked that the sex scenes, while not exactly "fade to black" also weren't incredibly descriptive. They stuck more to how Bear experienced them and not so much of a step by step description of the mechanics, like a lot of sex scenes in the genre seem to be. It made them that much more effective in my opinion. There was definitely chemistry between Bear and Otter (god, those names!) and I did want to see them work their shit out. 
 I liked the character of "the Kid", although Jimmy Hanson had a good point in her review when she said "as cute and enchanting as Ty [aka. the Kid] was, by the end his insight seemed a bit over the top. He was like the voice of reason and while it worked decently for the first half of the novel [it was interspersed fairly well with kid-language], but the end he seemed nothing more than a mini-psychologist unable to let go of the psych chair and intone to everything what they should and should not be doing or feeling." I agree completely. 
 And like I said, its similarity to Shelter made me feel somewhat more invested in it. I felt like I already knew these characters and it was just a new way to spend time with them, so that was good. 
 Unfortunately, the needless, self-created, contrived angst ruined what could have been a good book. Characters whose only purpose was to stir up jealousy and stupidity, the whole "we can't be together for some stupid reason invented only to create drama so I'm going to lie to you and pretend I don't want you" trope, the "even though I changed my mind and I do want to be with you I'm going to wait to tell you for no apparent reason, just so that the moment I do choose to tell you can be the moment your ex-boyfriend shows up" thing... need I go on? 
 So yeah. Two stars. I think maybe I'll watch Shelter over the weekend.

For the past three years Derrick McKenna--"Bear" to his friends--has been raising his 9-yo prodigy brother with the help of his friend Creed and off-and-on girlfriend in the 3 years since his mother abandoned them. But now Otter, Creed's older brother, has returned to town, and Bear must work through the awkwardness between them and face the feelings that lie underneath--but just as everything seems possible, events conspire to threaten it all. 
 Remarkably good m/m romance, with some themes that seem more YA (Bear is 18-21 during the events of the book). The characters are fully fleshed out, including the female characters. The Kid's quirks are interesting--he's vegetarian, a PETA activist wannabe, but also insightful about human emotions--and impatient with teacher mistakes in a way that seems very typical for gifted children. The dialogue is often cracking, and the prose is entertaining as hell, with many giggle-out-loud moments. On the other hand, Bear's excessive internal agonizing about his life and sexuality, along with a extensive use of flashbacks, broke the flow of the story somewhat. 
 I finished this book and then I sat down and read it again, which only happens when a book touches me deeply. This is apparently Klune's first novel, and I look forward to reading his other work.
Little too melodramatic for me. Probably would've given it 3 stars if it wasn't a rip off of Shelter.

Damn. Looks like this is an uncredited rip-off of the Movie Shelter, hell the movie blurb is pretty much the book blurb. *sigh* I have waffled back and forth on this, because I've not seen the movie, but the blurb is just too close for MY comfort, so I'm keeping the 3 stars I originally gave it along with this caveat. 
 So... Bear, Otter and the Kid. One of the most popular books of the past year. Everyone loved it. Well, I kinda wish we had the ability to award half stars, because this at times was a 3 1/2 star book for me. Young love, gay for you, love conquers all - it was all here. 
 Of the title characters, I loved Otter and I loved the Kid - Bear, not so much. I wanted to smack him far too many times for me to love him. Good Lord, talk about getting in your own way! Sheesh! I think he was just a little TOO ... whatever he was supposed to be - neurotic, damaged, paranoid. And a lot of it was the same stuff over and over. Not a great student, our Bear. :) In retrospect, maybe giving a couple of Bear's flaws to Otter might have been a good thing. 
 I found myself wishing that Bear would pick one metaphor for his inner feelings and stick with it - be it the ocean or the earthquakes. (I really liked the whole bathtub for safety thing.) I also wished he'd stop hitting us over the head with them so often. Introspection is good, but too much of it just makes the character seem selfish, self-absorbed and not sympathetic at all - at least to me. 
 That being said, I did enjoy the actual scenes between the characters. Bear and Otter were sweetly sexy and hot. Bear and Tyson were adorable and made me laugh out loud more than once. Creed, Anna, Mrs. Paquin - I enjoyed their appearances as well. I think that was the strongest part of the book for me - the characters interacting. 
 The huge stumbling block that was thrown in for the last quarter of the book seemed unnecessary to me. I think the conflict between the characters could have carried us through to the end and the 'twist' felt a little like 'deus ex machina' to me. I still don't get the motivation behind that one character's actions. 
 I did enjoy the choice to write the book using the 1st person POV and present tense. It was different and refreshing for the most part and the author did it quite well. :) 
 If I'm honest, Bear, Otter and the Kid felt like to me as if the author was trying to write their own story in Amy Lane's Promises series and for me, it doesn't quite measure up. 
 Would I recommend it? Yes, I would. Would I read something else by T.J. Klune? Yes, I would.

 My Series Rating: 5 of 5 Stars 
 I think I had the good sense to read this series when all three were all already out and I had the misfortune of having power outages. I took to the first book and fell in love, inhaled the second and grinned myself silly, then broke my heart on the third. The past two days have been a roller coaster ride of emotions coupled with the heat of anticipated storms and ended up dreaming of Bear, Otter and Kid. 
 Bear, Otter, and the Kid is a story of abandonment, heartbreak, making it out there in the world and learning to accept that not all family are genetically connected. It is a story of survival and enduring strength based on love and acceptance. 
 It all begins with Bear. He was handed a bad hand early on in life and ended up having to raise his younger brother, Kid, all by himself. First with his mother around but not much and finally all on his own when said mother disappeared with his savings. He had a girlfriend who was a very good friend, he had a best friend who had a brother and whose parents loved them all. And then there was Mrs. Paquinn. As his world fell apart around him, this non-related family rallied around him and gave him the boost to make it through. It gets complicated when his best friend's brother, Otter, that older and hunky brother, gives him a kiss then disappears for three years. When they reunite, his relationship with this new family is threatened. His love affair with Otter may just be the key to give him that family life he always wanted, but it could also be the same one that would make him loose everybody else, excepting Kid. And what about his girlfriend, Anna? 
 The second book opens to Bear and Otter raising Kid on their own, but of course the rest of the unrelated family members are all there, ready to lend a helping hand and thought, solicited and unsolicited. Complications had risen with the reappearance of the un-mother so not only are they both stressed from life itself, they have to be stressed out dealing with things like lawyers, therapists, judges (the one sitting and the those who know nothing but everything), and all other things. Bear is nearly losing it, but thanks to Otter and Kid, he does make it. He gets his strength from the two men in his life and no one, not even a sexy teacher ex-anything of Otter can get in his way. Life is as it should be for this incredible three complete with all the panic attacks, hilarious misconceptions and imagery that can be a bit incredible in their lack of logic. All in all a fun book that gives readers that feeling they are reading a fairy tale and the dragon is sure to be slain. 
 As the third book begins, the point of view shifts and instead of Bear on the forefront, we have Kid. He is a young man now who dares to dream. And to love. We go through his heartaches, his earthquakes and his misconceptions. For all his logic and knowledge, he is truly an immature young man who can fall victim to his own lack of wisdom. We are shown a story of how he slowly matures into that promise we were hinted to in the first two books and we are also shown how his future will look like, especially with Dom and Ben at his side. Is his story parallel to Bear's and Otter's? In some ways it does but mostly it does not. It is Kid's story and it is an incredible journey seeing him grow in so many ways. 
 Bear, Otter, and the Kid, the series, is a beautiful read, especially the way I read it, back to back. There was no chance of losing track to what was going on and it was truly an incredible journey. If I had read this as they were released, I would probably have been confused and made it a point to read the first two again just to keep track. It is quite a verbose work and can be confusing. Read the way I did, and it is enjoyable, heartbreaking, real and yet fairy tale like and simply a must read. Now I know what the hype was all about.

sample_reviews.review_text: A delightful, fun and sizzling read! This is a great series!

Nine Rules to Break When Romancing a Rake (Love By Numbers #1) Review 
 Oh, Sarah MacLean. No one does fluffy, sweet, adorable Regency Romance like you. 
 Ok, I actually wouldn't really know if that were true or not, because she's really the only Regency Romance author I've read. Suggestions are welcome for future readings. 
 Ten Ways to Be Adored is actually a bit more outside plot driven than it's predecessor Nine Rules to Break When Romancing a Rake. Ten Ways follows Lady Isabel Townsend, a woman who has been gambled away by her father multiple times (though she vigilantly remains unmarried), and who is keeping the house together after his death. They have very little but the house and whatever is part of the entail for her ten-year old brother, the current earl. But with no money, and no income, they are alone in the house, no servants, no one to help them. Until Isabel starts taking in battered women, running from whatever situation they came from, looking for respite. The Duke of Leighton's sister finds her way to this Minerva House, as they call it, and Nicholas St. John comes looking for her. 
 What he finds, is Isabel, a woman who repairs her own roof, wanders about in men's clothes, and has a house full of female servants. Not to mention that Georgiana, Leighton's sister is currently acting as governess to the young earl. Nick takes it upon himself to help Isabel, and though he desperately doesn't want to, thanks to miserable events in his past, he falls in love with her. 
 Isabel is quite a damsel in distress. She's making a go of it, certainly, trying to repair her own roof and such, but especially in this time period, she needs a protector. And Nick is willing to provide that protection. Their relationship is adorable, as are all of MacLean's romances. There is misunderstanding, secret keeping, stubbornness, and entertaining shenanigans around every corner. I really enjoyed the plot about Minerva House, and all the women Isabel is helping, as well as James, the young earl, needing a grown man as a mentor and finding one in Nick. 
 I quite enjoyed the little pieces of the article "Rules for Landing a Lord" at the beginning of each chapter as well. It was funny to see the advice and then how opposite Isabel acted. Nick's annoyance with being named a top Lord to Land was always very entertaining. 
 All in all, another excellent regency romance from Sarah MacLean. I always know going into her books that I will be highly entertained. They are like candy, quick reads and very enjoyable. 
 Content: Language, graphic sex. Recommended for 18+.

I hated that they "fell in love" in 72 hours with very little to justify it. I am afraid to try the next one Eleven Scandals to Start to Win a Duke's Heart
Very good. But Isabel was driving me crazy........she needed to accept his love sooner.
review to come

Lord Nicholas St. John may not be titled, but he's as rich and handsome as his Marquis brother, and they can be told apart by the scar Nick has on his cheek, which he sustained thanks to a treacherous lady during a campaign in Turkey. A seasoned solidier, adventurer and trained archeologist and scholar, Nick is desperate to escape London after a popular ladies' magazine votes him one of the city's most eligible bachelors. When his old school friend, the imperious Duke of Leighton, asks him to use the skills he learned in the army to track down the whereabouts of his younger sister, Lady Georgiana, who's gone missing. Happy to avoid the grasping clutches of the young ladies of the ton and their match-making mamas, Nick agrees, and sets off to the north of England accompanied by Rock, his huge Turkish former comrade-in-arms. 
 In a crumbling manor house in Yorkshire, Lady Isabel Townsend has just been told that her father, the wastrel Earl, has died, leaving her and her younger brother, the new Earl, completely penniless. Isabel has to find the money to fix the leaky roof, send her brother to Eton and feed and clothe the two dozen women under her roof. Isabel wants her ten-year-old brother to have a proper education so he can become a proper gentleman and raise himself and the Earldom above the reputation their father left. She is also running Minerva House, a refuge for abused, battered and helpless women from all over the country. Their newest arrival, Lady Georgiana, is pregnant and desperate, and despite the warnings from her various members of staff (all former Minerva House refugees) about this likely leading to trouble, Isabel determines that the young lady gets to stay. 
 In order to get money, Isabel resolves to sell off the large collection of marble statues she inherited from her mother. Though she loves the collection, her need for money is greater. Imagine her luck when famous archeologist and expert in antiquities, Nicholas St. John turns up in her village in Yorkshire, saving her from being trampled by a carriage and offering to appraise her valuables for her. 
 Nick is less than impressed with the willful and stubborn Lady Isabel, who while very pretty, insists on courting danger by stepping in front of speeding carriages and balancing on crumbling manor roofs. As the village near her manor is the last place Lady Georgiana was seen, he figures that he may as well use the excuse of the marbles to gain entry into her house. Little does he know that while he though he'd escaped match-making, Isabel's all-female staff are avidly reading ladies' magazines and feel that Isabel marrying the rich and handsome lord would be a much better solution than selling her beloved marbles.

I know this is horrible, but I have to stop reading three pages after the h/h meeting. I can tell from the short dialogue, she is going to be a ridiculously stubborn woman who won't listen to a thing. I mean come on, she almost gets hit by workhorses and is all in a tiff that he saved her life? Get a grip. From the other reviews I have read, it looks like she gets even worse.

reference_books.title: The Small Backs of Children

reference_books.title: The Most Magnificent Thing
reference_books.review_text:
Loved this book...the only one I can think of that covers having a great idea, making all kinds of mistakes, feeling frustrated by how things aren't coming together (really frustrated!!!) and then, taking a new look at the work that has been done and finding a path to completing that great idea.

reference_books.title: Hidden: A Child's Story of the Holocaust
reference_books.review_text: After just visiting the Holocaust Museum in Washington, DC, this book strikes a chord. For young audiences, this book does not gloss over the experience of one young girl forced into hiding whose parents were taken away to camps outside of Paris. She must change her identity and call another woman (a friendly neighbor) "mama", all while desperately wishing to be reunited with her real parents.

book_a.title: Brown Girl Dreaming
book_a.user_review: Stunning. Beautiful. An essential read, especially considering current events. Read Betsy Bird's review for more.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Sometimes it was the words she used and sometimes it was the memory itself that made me choke up about fifty times while reading this. How did she have these stories in her head and heart and not share them until now? I loved it. 
 There's so much to talk about here - family, racism, regionalism, history, being a writer. I can picture this in the hands of a 5th-grade book club. But would the parts about religion be a problem in a school?
Exceptional memoir from one of my favorite authors of all time!
I struggle with appreciating books in prose and poetry. Great award winning book. I read it so I could book talk it to the middle schoolers at my library for summer reading.

This was just so good. I knew it would be, and I was still surprised by how powerful the poems were (this is how a verse novel should be: actual poetry; more than just language arranged in lines). I felt it was accessible for younger kids who could appreciate the simple, vivid language about friendship, family, loss, and moving, and it offers multiple layers for older readers who can catch the political unrest of the time, the primer of African American history that is offered, the blossoming of Jackie's ambition, her questioning of her faith. I caught the haikus that seemed to mark each time she learned anew "how to listen." I looked up Angela Davis and Shirley Chisolm. I feel like this is a book to re-read. 
 Favorite parts: 
 p. 62 the beginning 
 p. 145 
 p. 227 Stevie and me 
 p. 249
Amazing!!

Wow, this is a beautifully written account of Jacqueline Woodson's childhood, written in verse. As a fan of her writing, I consider it a gift to allow us a view into her world and show us how she became the writer she is. I loved reading her notes at the end and viewing her family pictures.

Gosh, I feel absolutely awful about this, but I have to be honest...I was not a huge fan of this book. I'd heard amazing things about it, and after recently discovering that I love Ellen Hopkins-style poetry books, I figured that I would give this one a shot. 
 But I just didn't really get into it. Some of the poems were beautiful, but many of them were extraordinarily mediocre. So, once I realized that I thought the poetry was not that great, I tried to judge it solely as a memoir in general, but I still couldn't find a whole lot to like about it. It's not that her story wasn't "good," because who I am to judge somebody's life experiences? I just...didn't really think many of the details in the memoir were interesting. Not a lot happened. 
 I also thought that it was going to be much more race-focused, considering the title, but although a few of her memories bring up things like Rosa Parks, etc., to me, it didn't come across that her race was something that really defined her as a person or affected her a lot as a young child. I have no idea whether or not that's the case, but I did feel that many of her poems discussing race read a lot more forced and unnatural than the others. And they were far outnumbered by the ones about things that a child of any race might've experienced -- so I think that the title was a bit misleading in that sense. 
 Unfortunately, this one just wasn't for me. But I do appreciate it in the sense that it's obviously a very personal work of poetry that feels honest and real, and clearly has a lot of effort and heart behind every word.
Mother from the South, father from the North means this girl is caught between two ways of life. When her parents get divorced and she moves South with her mother and siblings, she has to adapt.
gorgeous gorgeous language. and to top it off, the audiobook is read by the author herself!

This was a beautifully written autobiography expressed through verse. This book has gotten plenty of Newbery buzz. I do think it was wonderful, however, I think it was much more appreciated by the adult audience than the child audience. It would be excellent to read as part of a unit after reading some of Jacqueline Woodson's other literature. A full study of her writing, the time period of her childhood and then this autobiography would be a great package.

book_b.user_review:

sample_reviews.review_text:

Great insight into the raw grief that Sheryl continues to live with like so many. I lived how candid she is and the steps that she is taking to help others with their own grief. 
 I was expecting more insight into developing resilience outside of the death of a loved one so I was somewhat disappointed.

I understand this is a way to get rid of the burden and apply a kind of mass logo therapy in order to smoother your pain but as a book I can only describe it as something that I didnt need to read. This read more like a memoir than a self-help.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Sheryl husband's Dave died suddenly because of cardiac arrest during their holiday. Noone is prepared for death, and there she was grief striken for life loss of her dear husband. As much as this is a story of sadness, it is also her way of healing. This book is her honest struggle and lesson learnt we all can get lessons from.
A great 3.5.

Skimmed over the passages about raising resilient children because I felt didn't apply to me. Liked how the author acknowledged some of the shortcomings of Lean In while moving forward with this book. Would have liked the anecdotes and stories to have more directly related to the psychology info.

This was my non fiction book this week (I alternate fiction and non fiction books). It is a must read for everyone. It is not only about how to deal with dramatic events, like Sandberg did with the tragic death of her husband, but rather how to take a better approach to moving ahead with some of the bad things that happen to us. Sandberg had to go to Option B and rebuild her life and family. The book shares her insight about what happened to her but there are so many little stories about others and how they dealt with a loss, relationship issue, or even job issues. I particularly liked these little stories and took away some coping strategies. One of my favorites was the story about a friend from Google and how they shared their "Whoops" or the struggles or mistakes they made at work. The winner was awarded a Whoops monkey that sat on their desk all week. This resinated with me that sometimes we need to learn from our mistakes in order to move forward at work or with personal relationships. As a friend told Sandberg, "Option A is not available. So let's just kick the shit out of Option B." Everyone will take away lots of ways to deal with life's struggles from this book. And, the proceeds, I read on the back cover 100% go to OptionB.org to help people deal with adversity.

reference_books.title: Everything, Everything
reference_books.review_text: If you like "The Fault in Our Stars" type stories (and I TOTALLY DO) then this one is a great read for you as well. Kind of mad at myself that this one sat on my TBR shelf as long as it did. Young love between Maddy and Olly creates passion and adventure for both, with a nice plot twist at the end that I did not see coming. Fun and quick YA reading that hits the spot.

reference_books.title: The Princess Diarist
reference_books.review_text: Carrie Fisher is well known for her honesty and candor about her life, and this book lives up to the same expectations. Her secret relationship with Harrison Ford during their three months shooting "New Hope" is outlined in this book along with the rest of her time on set and the impact it had on her life for decades to come. Ms. Fisher is funny, emotional, and honest about that time in her life and it helped give me a greater understanding of what she encountered personally and professionally after playing such an iconic character. Her voice and talent will be greatly missed.

reference_books.title: Before the Fall
reference_books.review_text: Scott is a struggling artist who manages to snag a seat on a private jet owned by a "Fox News-Like" cable news channel, ALC. The short flight from Martha's Vineyard to NYC marks the start of gallery meetings to show his recent work. However, just minutes into the flight, it crashes, killing nearly everyone aboard: The head of ALC and his wife, Maggie, who invited Scott onto the plane after showing her his work, along with one of their two children and bodyguard; a big time Wall Streeter, who just found out he will be indicted on money laundering, and his wife; and the pilot, co-pilot and flight attendant. The only two survivors? Scott and the youngest child, JJ. Scott manages to swim miles to shore, saving himself and the boy, and finding his private life suddenly turned upside down, both for the positive and the negative. An interesting look at the role the media plays in shaping the public's perception of a news story and how the people directly affected by tragedy have to deal with the lifelong repercussions of a life defining event.

reference_books.title: Crosstalk
reference_books.review_text: This book was a roller coaster ride of emotions. Dealing with the very timely concept of what is communication and when can it get to be too much and too overwhelming. I love near future science fiction such as this because you can completely see this situation becoming a reality. Will we get to the point that in order to continue, we have to be in constant communication with each other, not trusting our own instincts on love and emotion, but needing actual data to back these feelings up? Fun, page turning, and just the right amount of romance building to a very satisfying conclusion!

reference_books.title: Sense and Sensibility
reference_books.review_text: I love revisiting the classics on audio. Makes the work day so much faster. Like an old friend in your ear.

book_a.title: The Wanderers
book_a.user_review: This book has been compared to "The Martian" but I don't think that description does it any justice. This is a highly introspective look at what it actually takes in order to survive the solitude, isolation, conflict, boredom and stress of a deep space mission. I loved how all three of the main characters, Helen, Yoshi, and Sergei, deal with their own personal journeys as they participate in a mock mission to Mars. Their relationships with each other, their families, and their own minds are front and center in this novel, allowing you to put yourself into their shoes and try to understand how you would handle an adventure like this. I also enjoyed how the story explored how far the astronauts were willing to go in order to achieve their dreams of the "Gofer".

sample_reviews.review_text: Fantastic concept that didn't quite deliver. Chalk this up to a failure in advertising - marketing this as a mashup between Station Eleven and The Martian doesn't to the book or the author justice. Too slow for my taste, with pinballing character development that doesn't follow a coherent arc.

As I read this book, it struck me as a mashup between "Westworld" (the tv show) and "The Martian" (the movie), with more just a soupcon of 1984. The premise (three people participating in a test in Utah for an actual Mars landing) was troubling, and then I had serious questions, such as 
 -would these people would give up twice the number of years for a trip that they might not even take? 
 -would their families agree to the scrutiny and scripting during the test? 
 -would decent human beings even impose those burdens on their families? 
 It might have helped if I had connected with any of the characters. I came closest to connecting - or, being interested in - the wife of the Japanese astronaut, mostly because she was given the richest inner life. However, the book is not about her. 
 Disappointing. 
 I received this book as an ARC from Goodreads and NetGalley, and this is an honest review.

DNF at 50% 
 I saw a lot of people comparing this book to The Martian which is ridiculous, because The Martian is amazing and this is anything but. Holy shit, this book is so boring. I barlely made it to the halfway point before giving up. All the characters are so flat and boring and one dimensional and there are so many characters it's hard to keep track of them all (especially when they are all equally uninteresting). Sorry, this one just wasn't for me.
I liked this. I think I would have rated it higher if I'd read it in larger chunks.

When approaching The Wanderers by Meg Howrey, remember to check your expectations. What are you hoping to get out of this book? Because let me tell you, this is a kind of novel that might not appeal to everyone. It's a very well-written character study, similar to The Long Way to a Small, Angry Planet, but with a realistic setting, so if you are looking for an action-driven space adventure, this is not the book to satisfy that itch. 
 The story follows three astronauts and a small number of their family members, as they go through a highly realistic simulation of the very first voyage to Mars. During this test they get to learn more about themselves, their relationships with their loved ones, their fears about Mars, and the psychological challenges of co-existing with each other in close quarters under stressful situations. There are lengthy philosophical monologues about life, love, and space travel. So basically there is no plot. It's a thoughtful, smart read, but not an easy one. There is also very little payoff in the end, as the final pages are very much open ended. 
 I loved the meticulousness with which the author described the life of astronauts and the beautiful language that swept me off my feet. To read this book is to float in infinite space and to reflect. If you prefer your novels slow and character-driven, I guarantee you'll be right at home.

The premise, cover, and marketing led me to read The Wanderers by Meg Howrey. Unfortunately, the book suffers from two things. First because of the number perspectives, it becomes difficult to track the different storylines or to fully vest in any of the characters. Second, this book described as Station Eleven meets The Martian suffers from its own marketing. It is like neither book, and sadly, I end up not the right reader for this book. 
 Read my complete review at http://www.memoriesfrombooks.com/2017... 
 Reviewed for NetGalley & Penguin First to Read

Thanks to First to Read for the ARC in an exchange for an honest review. The Wanderers by Meg Howrey seemed like a book that was going to be right up my alley. Unfortunately, it was a slow-paced novel with too many perspectives. The novel focuses on three astronauts that are spending 17 months in a simulation of a Mars exploration. The rest of the novel shows the psychological effects of the astronauts and their families while they are in simulation and, for me, it just dragged on and on. Overall, it was not a bad book but will probably not be one that I pick up again.

I received an advanced copy of this novel from the publisher via Netgalley for an honest review. 
 This is one of those novels that I just could not finish. It says something when the novel I am reading literally puts me to sleep absolutely every time I pick it up! It's just so unfortunate because this novel sounded really good and it was advertised for people who loved Peter Weir's The Martian! This was a very wrong demographic to aim for. The Martian, for starters, is actually on Mars and about Mars and is an action/adventure/thriller that keeps you on the edge of your seat. This novel is none of those. 
 The idea of this novel sounded interesting, essentially testing people psychologically BEFORE sending them to Mars...but this wasn't that interesting. These people aren't that deep and don't have some crazy, weird shit happen to them. It felt like reading a boring school book about a psych experiment that led to no real findings. This novel also reminded me of a really AWFUL Syfy movie I watched, but I cannot remember the name for the life of me. The movie was about putting 4 astronauts in a time capsule 'spaceship' underground for one year to test how they would manage (again, the same concept, test before we send to space) except someone breaks into their time capsule thing before the year is up and so they leave early to find that the world is now dark and either the moon crashed into the Earth or the moon exploded and moon dust is on the Earth....but it's never fully explained, everyone is killed to be eaten and it makes no sense at all. I wanted those two hours of my life back. That is how I felt reading this novel. Maybe this is a good sort of psychological novel to look at, but it's not even a psychological thriller, it is very distinctly NOT thrilling. Just a sad situation because I was very excited about this novel and even more excited when I was given an advanced copy. Not so much my cup of tea.

This was a weird one, and I'm having a hard time figuring out if I liked it or not. I think marketing was a bit of an issue, personally I think it would have done better with the VanderMeer treatment and been pushed with the literary side of fiction rather than the SFF. Or as much as I hated it, Faber's The Book of Strange New Things. 
 It reads like a literary novel, in that it's purely a character study of three astronauts and their families preparing for a long mission to Mars, and honestly I just didn't care about any of them. When your book is solely based on character and not plot, you have to make your characters...interesting. 
 I've come to find these types of genre mashups just typically aren't for me. I find myself wanting to know more about the plot in the background than the characters random thoughts. Just when this book got interesting with the questioning of whether or not it was a sim, or more exploration into this paranoia it ended. I realize I am the type who needs resolution in my endings, so naturally this one was aggravating for me. However, as much as I wasn't really into it, I couldn't seem to give up and DNF it. I kept slogging through, hoping for a payoff that never came, unfortunately. 
 TLDR; If you like a good character study with a SFF setting, give this a try. If you like a bit more plot with your SFF, this probably won't float your boat.

book_b.title: Hogwarts: An Incomplete and Unreliable Guide (Pottermore Presents, #3)
book_b.user_review: Quick fun blurbs and commentary on the sights, sounds, and spirits at Hogwarts. Was able to read this in one hour and enjoyed the added detail about my favorite school of Witchcraft and Wizardry.

sample_reviews.review_text: I loved reading this short overview of all of the secrets of Hogwarts. Made me smile a lot. J.K. Rowling is so amazing and I loved reading about her thought process in creating the Harry Potter series. Recommended for all Potterheads!
The Hufflepuff common room finally revealed to be as lame as we always assumed.

I enjoyed the extra info, but felt it could have been so much more. Also not wholly convinced on the style, where it's partly in the story, but then partly looking at it from the outside e.g. "in the Harry Potter books", and with extra info from JK Rowling herself. I was kind of hoping it was going to be written by someone from the HP universe, in character. Same applies to all three of the newly released books.

Estos libros son oro. 
 Durante los ultimos anos habia disfrutado mucho al leer algunos fragmentos desde Pottermore (nunca alcance a leerlos todos) y lo que mas me llamaba (y me llama) la atencion es la complejidad de este mundo, la capacidad de Rowling de expandir y crear. 
 Leer desde su punto de vista, acerca de todo el proceso de creacion, siempre me ha fascinado. El pensar que hubo una mente que dudo, recreo, borro, combino, busco, que existieron decenas de bosquejos, cientos de borradores, el lugar o persona de donde salieron esas ideas es simplemente genial. 
 Ademas, leer de nombres y lugares que algunos estuvieron alli y al mismo tiempo no lo hicieron, o de sucesos de Hogwarts que tal vez no te habias detenido a pensar, se convierte en un juego, donde por cada pregunta que te responden, te crean unas tres mas. Junto a la forma semi jocosa y honesta en la que esta narrada, hace a la lectura aun mas amena. 
 Todavia me asombro con esta saga y eso es lo que mas me gusta, porque entre mas informacion, mas real es.

I love this background knowledge to the wizarding world. It is just this deep background that makes Jo's writing so alive and it is wonderful to get a peek at it! 
 Another fun read to share with my #hpchapteraday peeps dY~S I dY'oe feeling like I know Hogwarts just a little bit better & am ready to go exploring to discover even more of its treasures, secrets, & maybe a few dangers (just little ones though dY~oe)
Love love love this one the best.. well obviously I'm pretty biased because it's all about Hogwarts and its secrets. This is must-read for all Harry Potter fans!
Underwhelming.

Very short to be honest. I would have loved if this was Hogwarts, a history as most of the things that are presented in here we already knew. A fun read and very insightful. I love the bits about ghosts and portraits. I think she chooses to write these short passages and her thoughts about them because she knows she can never top the image we, the readers, have about Hogwarts. I think that is very powerful. Our imaginations are infinite and we can imagine every little detail about the castle of the magic school that made us fall in love with Harry Potter.

Kaum was Neues fur den aufmerksamen Harry Potter Leser. Ich fand ca 90% waren bereits bekannte Dinge aus den Buchern. Einzig JKs Beweggrunde und Hintergedanken zu einigen Dingen waren spannend. Aber leider viel zu kurz, manche bestanden quasi nur aus 2 - 3 Satzen. 
 Nett, muss aber wirklich nicht sein.
Fun, quick read. Especially if you are a Harry Potter fanatic!

reference_books.title: Babe in Boyland
reference_books.review_text:
For anyone who saw Amanda Bynes' 2006 movie She's the Man, you can probably skip this book altogether as it runs pretty much in the same vein not to say this wasn't a fun, fast-paced read. 
 Natalie is an under-appreciated writer on the school paper who just wants to prove her worth to the student editor and get some answers for the female population of her high school about what really goes on inside boys heads when they say they'll call but never actually do and other questions girls have pondered for years. Natalie takes it one step further than most by going undercover at the local all-boys school where she is forced to wear a mustache, share a dorm with the irresistible, Emilio and hide in the costume closet for hours on end. 
 I really enjoyed the backdrop of high school theatre and of course, there is the regular mention of a great set of best friends and the usual meanie also rears her head quite a few times throughtout the book but what bothered me overall is the fact that Natalie's escapades at the boys school didn't result in any real answers making her time spent in the boys dorm seem like a waste. 
 Jody Gehrman's novel has all the elements of a class act but something about it just didn't click with me, it may have to do with the fact that I recently read The Lonely Hearts Club by Elizabeth Eulberg which poses some similarities in my mind and goes above and beyond this book with it's many Beatles references among other things.

reference_books.title: Guardian of the Dead
reference_books.review_text:
Definately not my type of book, I now know why I have been avoiding fantasy stories for so long. 
 Part One (a good 200 pages) focuses on Ellie's life as a New Zealand University student, she is then offered a position to help out the theatre's fighting scenes and this is all quite enjoyable but the hints of fantasy start taking over the book slowly but surely and I did not move much past Part Two due to disinterest. 
 I'm really loving the Australian cover much more than the popular mask cover.

reference_books.title: Deadline
reference_books.review_text:
Unfortunately, I just couldn't get into this one as I felt it was purely aimed at the teen male reader especially with so many references to football. I was also bothered by the authors efforts to showcase psychology in the best light, it almost felt like he had set out with an agenda to do so and it just didn't sit right with me. 
 Overall, I just could not relate to the protag from the outset with his choice to ignore medical treatment and forego telling his friends and family of his recent news. An interesting idea for a book but ultimately failed to win me over within the first 50 or so pages.

reference_books.title: The Moon and More
reference_books.review_text: MUST-HAVE!

reference_books.title: Eve & Adam (Eve & Adam, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Eve and Adam is a fairly enjoyable dystopian novel, I only wish the story was a little bit more developed as I often found myself questioning the motives of certain characters. If you're looking for something similar in style to The Hunger Games or Divergent, you may find it here but with slightly less believable content.

book_a.title: Deadly Little Secret (Touch, #1)
book_a.user_review: I usually stay away from fantasy books, but this one is different. The story is fast-paced, but not rushed and the plot is entirely captivating. I'm glad I finally picked up this book!

sample_reviews.review_text:
Even though Deadly Little Secret is just over 250 pages, it took me almost a week to get through it because it was so incredibly flat and boring. I had to force myself to finish it just so I could find out who the villain was and even that payoff wasn't worth the trouble. 
 Deadly Little Secret lacks interesting characters you want to root for, a truly suspenseful plot, and the romance between Ben and Camelia is stale and unbelievable. The first half of the book is a clear ripoff of Twilight, from Ben saving Camelia getting crushed by a car to the two of them having to be partners in a science class, and the second half's potential was killed by Camelia's utter stupidity regarding her stalker and the half-assed plot device that kept her from telling her parents about it. Girl, someone is invading your home, leaving your threatening messages, and clearly intends to hurt you - tell your damn parents about it and call the cops, don't rely on some stupid boy who "accidentally" killed his last girlfriend and doesn't trust authorities, okay? By the time the stalker was revealed, I was so fed up with Camelia that I was skimmed the last 40 pages or so. 
 I will not be continuing on with this series.
Strangely enough, I don't remember who Ben was. Guess he isn't that memorable...
I was looking forward to reading this but was a little disappointed. I didn't connect to the characters as much as I would have liked to. It was an okay read.

I wanted to like this book, but unfortunately, that was not to be. The premise was what piqued my interest in the book. I mean, I had never heard of pschometry - the ability to sense things through touch - and, given the dearth of vampire and now fallen angel books that are populating bookshelves, I was looking for something new. 
 Unfortunately, I didn't really care about the principle characters Camelia and Ben, and the supporting characters were basically set-props - very two-dimensional. But what really irked me was how this story was the basic rewriting of Twighlight: from the near death first encounter, to Ben's seeming aversion to Camelia, to Ben's fear of "losing control" with Camelia. Not to mention the settings of some of the pivotal incidences mirror those of Twiligh (c'mon, can we at least get a different class subject for Camelia and Ben to share). AND, without giving too much away, the ending of the book was very reminiscent of the beginning of New Moon. Honestly, if I wanted to re-read Twilight, I would have done just that.

Camelia Hammond is starting her last year of school, but instead of looking forward she can't help but look back, to three months ago at the end of the last school year when her life was saved by a beautiful boy who then disappeared. She still tingles from where he touched her. 
 Yet when, on the first day of school, she sees him, Ben Carter, the new boy with a bad reputation and an even darker history, he pretends he doesn't recognise her and insists he never saved her life. He avoids her until one day in Chemistry class when he accidentally touches her - and all hell breaks loose. 
 Her infatuation with Ben isn't the real problem, though: her unknown stalker has made himself known and is becoming scarier with each photo put in her mailbox, each gift left by her window. Ben insists she's in danger and that he can help her, but who can she trust? Who is fixating on her? 
 I think, if I'd known this book was going to be a stalker book, I probably wouldn't have picked it up. I'm not a big fan of the genre. The suspense here was dealt with well, with good pacing and plenty of tense, even scary moments - especially as, while I knew the stalker wasn't Ben from the beginning, there was quite a large number of boys/men to choose from and that does make you rather edgy. 
 It's very dialogue-driven, which, when not taken advantage of, allows the characters to be under-developed: as they were here. You don't get to know Camelia all that well, even though she narrates - there's not much going on in her head aside from describing what she sees. Very disappointing. Ben's an intriguing character but you don't get close to him either. I'm wondering if he's the link that will pop up in the other books in the series (not yet written), especially considering they're called "Touch" novels. (Can't explain that without giving the only cool element of the book away.) 
 It's a stupidly quick read, tells a simple enough story and doesn't delve into the teenage psyche much. I quite liked Camelia's friend Kimmie. Part of my problem with these suspense books, is that so often supporting characters are set up: they're fodder for our mistrust, our suspicions, and turn out to be nothing more than plot devices. If the prose offers something more, if the main character/s offer more, then this could be overlooked, but when, as in Deadly Little Secret, the prose and main characters are superficial, the entire book becomes bland and disappointing. 
 That said, I did find it engrossing - perhaps against my better judgement - so I need to be fair in my rating. 
 Oh, and Ben reminded me of Edward from the Twilight books. Cashing in much?

The Moody Reader

I'm almost definitely sure that I'd give this book a 2 stars rating because of the two characters. Camelia, dear god, woman. She can't stop thinking about ben because of blah blah blah cliche cliche and there's this I-like-you-but-for-some-reasons-it's-like-we-can't-be-together-but-hey-i-like-you thing going on and it was annoying. 
 What saved this book from me giving it a 2 freaking stars rating was, Camelia's friends, Kimmie and Wes, they are hilarious and of course the suspense and mystery that's surrounding it. There's these extra entries between chapters written by the stalker, it was creepy as fuck and it will leave you guessing. When I found out who the stalker is, I was shocked. Honestly, it never even crossed my mind. 
 Well, over all, it was a good read. Even though there were times when I wanted to punch Camelia and Ben on the face. The suspense and mystery were really engrossing, it will keep you on turning the pages even more.

The school year starts and low a be hold her hero is at her school. She walks up to say thank u for saving her life and he acts very cold and denies saving her. She learns his name is Ben but rumor has it he is at their school after a big legal battle over killing his girlfriend in his old town. Camilla starts getting these weird and scary pictures and messages, she isn't sure if it is Ben or some other crazy. I like it enough that I'm starting the 2nd book when I done here. Also I LOVE pretty covers and this whole series has gorgeous covers!!!!

sample_reviews.review_text:
I hope you won't ever read a simplified version of this book. Simplified books are parodies and caricatures, good for nothing. Even people trying to learn a new language had much better plunge in the deep end. 
 If you haven't read this book yet, and are skimming the reviews to see what it's like, and if you happen on mine then this is my advice, don't read any more reviews and read the book at least twice. And then come back and read about how other people have experienced it. 
 If you have read the book, then you may be among a large group of brilliant people who hate it, or join the other group of equally brilliant people who love it. Though using the word love may not be the correct term! There won't be any ambiguity. And right there, is one of the charms of this work of art. 
 For second time readers, for what it's worth this is my suggestion if I may, don't think much while you're reading and don't try to analyse, just let your emotions come to the surface and observe your Self. Not the book. You will see you are drawn in and are experiencing the emotions and life lessons of souls who only ever existed in Emily Bronte's chest, and then in the book she wrote. Who knows how she did this? My mind can't fathom how she and other prodigies and creators of any great work of art in any field did it. But no matter if you love or hate it, this book shall leave you a bit changed. The hours you spend reading it will somehow amount to years of experiencing life. I hope you will have, indeed, read it even before you read my review. Because that way, I wouldn't have set your expectations in anyway, or clouded your eyes. Or your feelings.

Their relationships verging on pathology... I think this book to be highly overrated. Whether I was just in the mood or it was so well written, I don't know, but I didn't mind that fancy, descriptive language I usually have only loathsome feelings for. Additionally, it rekindled my longing for solitary heights and munros of the north, thus I could not grade it any lower.

I read this book as several books I've read recently have quoted from it and I realized that I didn't really have any idea of the storyline. I'm still not sure what I think of it. I can see how English teachers could have a field day with essay questions from this book but I'm not sure if I see it as something that I would recommend for recreational reading. Heathcliff is so evil, and Catherine is such a flighty witch, yet they're both also somewhat justified in their initial reactions that ultimately formed their adult selves. I'm glad that everything ended reasonably well in the last ten pages, which was totally unexpected, but I don't really think I'll be reading this again any time in the forseeable future. It was nice to see where the various quotes I mentioned came from in context.

I'm changing my rating on Wuthering Heights. Every 10 years or so, I try to love this book because all women love it, and because I haven't met a 19th-century book that I didn't enjoy so of course I enjoy this classic. Right? GACK, wrong. My last attempt was to listen to the book on Libri Vox. These recordings are not always good because they rely on volunteer readers, but for WH they actually got someone who reads well. She put drama and expertise into the voices of the various characters. The end result is I finally admitted to myself that I hate these characters and their twisted obsessions. They whine and whine. Heathcliff needs a therapist. At best, the book is a critique of 19th-century sexual repression and bad child rearing. But that's not enough to garner my enthusiasm. These characters are waaaaay too emo for me.

Frankly, I hated the book! I've never been one for tragic love stories, and the characters in this book were so extremely unlovable. Selfish, self-obsessed and extremely weak in different ways, it left me rather disgusted. I can appreciate Bronte's (perhaps rather realistic) depiction of how humans really work, and the ending with the graves were rather touching all the same, but I just couldn't bring myself to like this book.

This is not a love story. Stories like this contribute too much to why people have such a skewed version of what love is supposed to be, and why so many girls think abuse in a relationship is acceptable and normal (Do you hear me Stephenie Meyer!?!). 
 Synopsis: A guy with reactive attachment disorder meets one of the most narcissistic chicks in all of literature. When he's the only game in town she'll "love" him because hey, narcissism has to be fed, but he'll never get the fulfilling love out of the relationship that he needs. And he'll never know how to "love" anyone else because he thinks that obsession is love and is incapable of forming any other attachments-- Lord help you if you do anything that smells like abandonment (she does). So they blithely go about wrecking havoc on the lives of everyone around them, even their children and the one or two truly decent people they know... all in the name of "Love" (selfishness). 
 It's a train wreck. I can see someone enjoying it for it's literary merit. I can see enjoying it as a horror story or psychological thriller. But as the ultimate end-all and be-all of love stories, or even a love story at all? No thank you. 
 Blech.
