sample_reviews.review_text: Bring your hankies when you read Violet's story!

Each story is an epilogue of sorts, updating readers on what is happening with their favorite characters after each of their books. That being said, readers who have not read all the books in the Bridgerton series would not fully appreciate the events and stories in this novel. I highly recommended starting with book one, to experience the magic that Quinn has created. 
 Before each story, Quinn pens a quick note on what the vignette is about and particularly why she decided to write the story. It's great insight into the mind of the author and will have fans rejoicing as they return to the crazy family antics that have made this series so well-loved. 
 Lastly, Quinn gives readers a treat! Violet in Bloom is a short novella featuring the author's most favorite Bridgerton. Violet is the mother to all the heroes and heroines we've met but for the first time, we meet Edmund Bridgerton, her husband. For me, this was an exclusive I had to have my hands on! 
 THE BRIDGERTONS: HAPPILY EVER AFTER is an exceptionally well-written collection of stories. As an avid fan, I found myself returning to the first time I read the books and wishing I could read them again. Quinn brings back fond memories and creates new ones that show how family and love can conquer all. 
 Read this review in its entirety at Fresh Fiction
I'm a Bridgerton fangirl. And I knew what I was getting into - a book intended ONLY for the most devoted of Bridgerton fangirls. I was still disappointed. Just reread the Bridgerton series instead!

Honestly, I can objectively see that this book isn't going to be 5 stars for everybody - it's a collection of novella-length "second-epilogues" for Quinn's Bridgerton novels, for one thing, so anyone who hasn't read those books would be lost; and, objectively, a lot of these stories don't have really strong plot structures - they're more about the much-loved characters just hanging out together in later life, sharing lovely small successions of events together... 
 ...but ohhhhhhh did I love this book, personally. Julia Quinn is one of those authors who has become an auto-buy for me because her books just always, always make me happy, whether I have logical nits to pick with them or not. (Starting with the second Bridgerton book, chronologically, and from then on in her career - I think the second Bridgerton book was when she really found her tone as a writer, and that's when her books started really working for me.) I love the humor, I love the characters, I love the sheer comfort and pleasure in her writing...and getting to hang out with all the Bridgertons again in this collection of novellas made me really, really happy. 
 My pre-ordered copy arrived yesterday, in the middle of a Very Bad Day, and oh, it was just exactly what I needed. I curled up with the book and a cup of hot chocolate and felt so deeply comforted as I read. I finished it that night, and felt sooooo much better for having read it. 
 So for me, how could it not be a five-star book?

Treacherous betrayals, secret alliances, unforseen murders, and forbidden love--the world of Mytica will hold you captive: 
 Auranos: Privileged princess Cleo is forced to confront violence for the first time in her life when a shocking murder sets her kingdom on a path to collapse. 
 Limeros: The king's son, Magnus, must plan each footstep with shrewd, sharp guile if he is to earn his powerful father's trust, while his sister, Lucia, discovers a terrifying secret about her heritage that will change everything. 
 Paelsia: Rebellious Jonas lashes out against the forces of oppression that have kept his country cruelly impoverished--and finds himself the leader of a people's rebellion centuries in the making. 
 Witches, if found, are put to death, and Watchers, immortal beings who take the shape of hawks to visit the human world, have been almost entirely forgotten. A vicious power struggle quickly escalates to war, and four young people collide against one another and the rise of elementia, the magic that can topple kingdoms and crown a ruler on the same day. 
 3.5 stars!! 
 I liked this book, don't get me wrong. It was intriguing and it did a good job of keeping me interested. There were a few things I had problems with though. 
 First of all, why did everyone have to have a secret? Seriously, it felt like every other chapter, one character or another would have to stop themselves so they wouldn't give away their "big" secret. I could understand Lucia's need to keep her secret, especially since she didn't really even understand what was happening to her. But Cleo's secret? So what, she made a stupid mistake. Who hasn't? You don't sit there and lament over your mistake, you learn from it and move on. 
 Then there's Magnus's secret. I can understand him wanting to hide it at first, that kind of thing wasn't usually popular. Although, considering the direction most people's thoughts went, he might have wanted to come up with some sort of reason for not being interested in eligible maidens. Then of course, you find out that Lucia's not really his sister which means his feelings could come out in the open. She still retains the option to say no, just like anyone. I can see her opinion as well, brother through genetics or not, she's always seen him as her brother and nothing more. Even knowing that they're not really siblings, I don't think her feelings could change just like that. 
 Moving on. 
 I felt that the romance between Cleo and Theon was way too rushed. They went from being princess and bodyguard to love-of-my-life so fast it almost made my head spin. Not that they shouldn't have fallen in love, I just think there should have been a bit more of a build up with their relationship. I can see where the thought process was coming from, considering that Theon dies almost immediately after he and Cleo declare their feelings, but I still feel the relationship could have maybe started a little earlier or been a little more gradual 
 I also had a hard time really getting to like Cleo. For a lot of the book, she came across as a spoiled princess who was so used to getting her way. I did enjoy her a lot more when her spunk came through and she was standing up for herself, Theon, or even defending her father. However, that spunk didn't show up until much later in the book. 
 The secondary characters were great. In some ways, it felt like they were more developed than the main characters. 
 I can understand Jonas wanting revenge for Tomas, but why was he focusing on Cleo? Yes, she was there when it happened, but so were like 8 other people. No matter what happens, right or wrong (and just for the record, I think Aron was completely at fault), the chain of events that led to Tomas's death happened to quickly for anyone to stop. I'll admit an argument could be made that you could have predicted that something was going to happen, but I think most people would lean towards some sort of a fist fight. Personally, I would have focused on going after Aron, but that's just me. Either way, Jonas got his revenge all screwed up, especially when he allied himself with Chief Basilius and King Gaius.

Bah bah black sheep. 
 It's sad when a potentially good book gets overhyped but it's tragic when a terrible book is overhyped. I would like to say that I may have rated Falling Kingdoms '2-stars' if not for the fact that it's marketing as Game of Thrones for YA, but thinking about it, I don't think even that would have helped. When they say GOT for YA, I think what the marketing team really means is that the book minces up the characters in GOT, strips off their personalities and threw in the gasp factor for extra measure because every one of the characters we meet are so one-dimensional and predictable. I could tick off the different characters they are emulating from GOT (unsuccessfully to say the least) and there was a WHOLE lot of show and tell going on. 
 Honestly, I could go on about why I hated this but there are a few other amazing reviews out there which put my thoughts to words in a pretty impeccable manner. Here's all you need to know.

reference_books.review_text: I loved this book. His audio version of it was good. I wouldn't tell other people to spend more money to get it (than to purchase the book or rent it) but if you can get it for the same price I'd say do it. It was a good story that I wasn't familiar with in a lot of ways. I had lots of Asian friends growing up and was a regular fixture in their homes so I was familiar with a lot of parts of the culture Huang talks about. What I was unfamiliar with was Florida in the 90s, especially through the eyes of a Taiwanese family. That was new and very interesting to listen to. Huang does a great job chronicling his life; he keeps it interesting and detailed and really hooks the listener/reader in via his passionate explanations and interpretations on parts of his life. He's a good storyteller and I found myself interested in each story. Though I will admit, when he talks about food it's really wonderful and you can hear the love and appreciation in his voice. Great book for those that love bios, food, pop culture, and just decently written books in general.  When I finished it, I thought, "Aw, frig. Now there's going to be fifth one, and I'll have to read that one too." 
 It's weird being so anti Odd, being a life long Koontz fan.

I should've checked first before reading this, because once again, I'm reading a series backwards. Grrr. Anyway, I'm looking forward to reading the previous books in the series because I really like the character whose name is "Odd". I was gripped the web of his tale and finished this book in 24 hours, it was such an interesting read. Sometimes, a little too descriptive for my tastes, because I like to get to the next main event. So, admittedly I did do some skim reading. I might reread it so that I can savor the words next time. :) The plot twists and subject matter were compelling and the ending was slightly baffling. I actually had to have a moment of silent reflection.

I couldn't even finish this book. This is not paranormal, just supernatural, really, it's just an allegory of God vs the Devil and he ain't subtle about it. I liked this when it was more about Odd and his struggles, but as he has become really the stand in for the Seeker trying to get ever closer to God so that he might more fully fulfill God's will and therefore abide in the peace that comes from submitting to God's plan for him- you know what? I don't read that kind of crap. I hate it. So, no more Odd Thomas for me.
This book was different and mysterious, in a good way:) I feel sorry for Odd, for the things he must do and endure. And to be without Elvis! I really miss Elvis.
This was disappointing compared to the first few in the series. Repetitious and lacking in suspense. A bunch of stuff was left open, however, so I'll most likely read the next one.
So far the least engaging of the series.
I do think Koontz should have stopped at book #3 in this series. It gets at least 2 stars from me just for having Odd in it - love that character!
Although cryptic and leaving some things unexplained, it was Odd at his best, making me laugh even while holding my breath in suspense.

book_b.title: Dad Is Fat
book_b.user_review: It's rare I drop a book, but this was just so so boring and not funny that I couldn't make it through. I rented this through my library as an audio file, and it's read by Gaffigan himself, so you'd figure if anyone had a chance of making this interesting and funny it's the author and stand up comedian himself, right? Just too boring, not interesting stories about his life before and with kids. Meh.

sample_reviews.review_text: Hear it all before. Some minor laughs, but he has almost nothing new to say on the topic.

I am a fan of Gaffigan. I like his stand-up a lot, so I found myself quite disappointed that he couldn't be bothered to come up with new material for this book. Now, much of it was, but there were enough recycled jokes in here to make me a little upset. 
 Overall though, I still enjoyed the book and found it funny with some very prescient observations about the realities of being a parent. I also can't get over how they survive in such a small apartment with 7 people. Also, when on earth do the parents sleep? He has a night job, which she helps with, and you know the kids aren't sleeping in. It makes me tired just thinking about it.
It just wasn't funny.

Any one who has ever had children can relate to this book. Jim Gaffigan reveals all about the ups and downs of raising five young children n a two bedroom apartment in New York City. Gaffigan first began tweeting about his experiences with his children, but his wife encouraged him to expand the idea into a book. And I'm glad that she did. Written in sixty short chapters that read like stand-up routines, Gaffigan explores such topics as why he and his wife opted for home births instead of utilizing the medical expertise of nearby hospitals, why they are raising five children in a small apartment in the Bowery section of Manhattan, the inherent horrors of a Disney vacation with a gaggle of children in tow, and the strange world of children's literature. A really fun read, especially if taken in small doses.

I really wanted to like this book but I realized half of what makes Gaffigan funny is his facial expressions & mannerisms. I just thought it was boring hearing about his life with babies & toddlers. Been there, done that, glad I'm no longer doing that. Someone with younger children might enjoy it more.
Some parts are really funny and other really annoying. All together it's mostly enjoyable and listening to the audio version read by the author made it better!

Jim Gaffigan is one of my favorite stand up comedians, but unfortunately his humor does not transfer to the pages of a book very well. 
 I'm not sure who his intended audience is, but this book tends to fall flat no matter who it is aimed at. If you're a parent, then Gaffigan is telling you things you already know. If you're not a parent, then you really don't want to hear about all the trivial complaints Jim has about his kids. If you're a fan of his stand up shows, you'll be disappointed because a lot of his material has been recycled within this book. 
 I'm also not sure if the point of this book is to complain about his kids, because that's really all he seems to be doing. Hey, you know what would probably cause less complaining? NOT having five kids within a tiny two bedroom apartment in NYC. I'm not saying he shouldn't have that many kids or whatever, but maybe he shouldn't have had that many if he needs to write a book about all the grief they give him. 
 When Jim's not complaining, he's kind of on a soapbox. People always seem to be asking him if he's done having kids, and in this book he's taken the liberty of telling those people to stop asking. But, it doesn't come across as funny--you can tell he's beyond irritated, but hey, it's just a fact that people will be asking you these questions no matter how many kids you have. People are just nosy. 
 I wish I would have enjoyed this book or gotten at least a few laughs out of it, but happily it was a short read...I'll stick to Jim's stand up from now on. 
 I received this book from Blogging for Books for this review.
I did not finish it. I did about 97 pages and realized I was bored.

I only made it eighty pages in, but I just couldn't appreciate his style--and no, not because I don't have kids. The writing style didn't work for me neither did his tone on family. Although he is known to be a clean comedian, I found some of his humor distasteful and crude. I was really looking forward to this so I am sadly disappointed.

I liked this book. I expected something a little different, but I'm not sure why. I think the title is appropriate as it's more a book for dads than anyone else. I enjoyed listening to Gaffigan read the audio version and found lots of humorous stories to enjoy, but I think my husband would like it more than I did.

reference_books.review_text: I enjoyed this book. For some reason, it did not appeal to my son, so I didn't continue the series (switched to Hardy Boys, I believe). This is a good book to read to an older child at night if you are a read-alouder. Clear, clean format with easy to understand language.

book_a.title: The Old Man and the Sea
book_a.user_review: I read this for the first time in high school when I was in detention. Read it four times because I had nothing else to read. At the time, I enjoyed it quite a bit. I think my later readings of Hemingway were sometimes biased because I knew of his misogynist views.

sample_reviews.review_text: I have to admit the middle of the book nearly bored the hell out of me, but in the end I came to appreciate Hemingway's style of writing, the concept of man versus nature, and the emphasis of human relationships.

Ernest Hemingway published his novella The Old Man and the Sea in 1952, but it still reads well today, owing to that terse style that won him many a prestigious award. I'm not a big fan of fishing and that kind of lifestyle, so reading this one was a bit of a trudge. However, the book was short, so I'd be damned if I wasn't going to see it through. 
 Which is kind of the point of The Old Man and the Sea. 
 Thematically and symbolically, the book is a goldmine. First, it deals with life as an endurance test, overcoming obstacles. (DiMaggio's bone spur, anyone?) If you don't catch a fish for months, the other fisherman deem you too old to be in the game any longer. But the human spirit can defy these declarations. He is not just the "old man," but rather the great fisherman and arm-wrestling champion Santiago, and he aims to conquer the age discrimination against him by capturing a truly great fish in the sea. 
 The Old Man and The Sea also describes the loneliness endured in this quest for survival, not just physical survival but the survival of one's dignity in the face of these judgments. Above all, though, perseverance is king, and Hemingway expertly demonstrates that, if at first you don't succeed, try again. You are never too old to do so. 
 So, while I didn't like the book all that much, its brevity was a plus, and it can be interpreted widely and greatly. I wouldn't recommend it, but if any of the above interests you, then maybe it's the book for you.
It's a classic piece of literature, but it's also incredibly lengthy. I'd add it to my list of classic literatures to read.
Boring man and the sea.

Okay, I know my fellow readers are going to hate me when I say this...but I just couldn't get into this book. Now, I realize that Hemingway is a huge icon in American Literature but his novel didn't grab my attention like Salinger's or Steinbeck's did. (At least I'm honest)

I read this book in high school and hated it ... but I don't remember why, so I'm going to tackle it again 
 OK ... finished it again. And this time I had to admit it wasn't horrible. I'm sure I didn't get all the symbolism and theme messages that were there, but it was definitely a story of the struggle between life and death, between man and nature, between success and failure. I don't know that I benefited from reading the book; the religious imagery didn't impress me (though the bleeding hands, reference to a man "who had nailes driven in his hands", carrying the mast up the hill and falling beneath the load ... were fairly obvious). I doubt I'd read it again .. however had to give it a moderate rating, because once I picked it up to read, I didn't put it down until I was finished! 
 And I did notice that I missed a lot when I read it years ago in school!
Hemingway at his best. Old man and the sea is a story of grace under fire, life's little struggle, and dealing with loss all in one novella. Old man is a story that I will read time and time again.
This book was short, and I know it's a classic, but it didn't really "grab" me. It's about an aging Cuban fisherman who wants so much to get this one really exceptional fish. I say, "Who cares?"
Symbolic and thought-provoking short read. If you like thinking deeply and the idea of Hemingway, read this.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This was quite possibly the WORST book I have ever read. It was all about a man..... going fishing..... getting the fish...... losing the fish...... then sleeping..... NO

book_b.title: The Bell Jar
book_b.user_review: Sad and moving--foreshadows Plath's life in many ways.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I missed the cutoff for totally relating this book by about two years. If you read it when you're older than say, 18, then you just want to tell the main character to wait it out and stop moping. Or possibly that's just my own asshole reaction. The first page is amazing, then as she "descends into madness" or however you'd have it described, it gets...possibly boring, possibly just unrelatable. Something. 
 Anyway, the main thing is it's not cool Sylvia Plath's life sucked so bad.

At a few points early on I considered not finishing this book, since the first half read like a more articulate Holden Caulfield (those who know me know I can't stand Catcher in the Rye). The second half, where Esther undergoes psychiatric treatment, was much more interesting, and I came to enjoy and appreciate the narrator's wry sense of humor. It pulls no punches in its candid look at someone wrestling with inner demons, but stops just short of true self-reflection (which I suppose is true of most people). That particular observation is especially interesting knowing that the author herself failed to escape her own "bell jar" in the end. The unresolved ending is especially poignant in that context.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This book hit a little too close to home which made the shock therapy scenes so disturbing. I was fidgety witnessing Esther's mental unraveling, especially when I realized exactly how unreliable she was the narrator. My thoughts on that realization...I'm still not quite sure of. I have a lot of thoughts on the book that I'm still trying to make sense. I will definitely revisit the book.
Well written. Loved the sentences and the prose ... And the story too....

This book is very anticlimactic. I was expecting to delve deep in the psyche of a young, educated and privileged girl who slowly slips away from reality. Instead I got a series of events and I'm not sure which ones happened or were simply part of her inevitable madness. The book offers more disappointment and confusion than closure.

No matter how many times I read this semi autobiographical novel, there is a freshness, an originality in the voice of Esther which is thoroughly convincing and engaging. Plath is disarmingly honest about the alienation and frustrations endured by her protagonist in pre feminist USA. It is funny, ironic, moving and of course, in its depiction of the treatment of mental illness, harrowing in the extreme.

Having heard this was the next closest thing to Salinger's The Catcher in the Rye, I had incredibly high expectations for this book. In that regard, it was a let down. By itself, however, appreciating Plath's voice and that it's unfair to hope her book could compare to one of my all time favorites, it was a quick and satisfying read. I can understand why it became a phenomenon, especially with everything Plath was going through in her own life.

3.5-4 stars. 
 I finished this book surprisingly quickly given its contents, and I'm not sure if I can leave a review for it. There're so many people that say The Bell Jar is representative of this or that big theme or issue, but to me reading Plath's only novel didn't feel like reading a book at all. It felt like reading someone's journal. Without permission, might I add. 
 The entire book just felt so personal; I don't see Esther as someone that I'd have liked if I'd ever crossed paths with her, but I can't...hate on her on I would do with unsavory characters in other books because I understand exactly where she's coming from, and all the things that make her both a good and bad person are just so heart-rendingly clear. She-and the book itself-is just so real to me that I can't approach this as I would any other book: good plot, or good setting, meaningful blah or good blahblahblah. 
 If I could, I wouldn't give this book a rating at all. 
 I will say this though, there's something beautiful about how Plath writes. All of her words just leave me with this heavy, sinking feeling.
My sister recommended this highly but I could not get into it one bit.

I've been readings this Indo version, the translation was ok - for general translate ... but for me something 'missing', maybe because this is not just ordinary novel, but more like poems, so the feeling when I read those pages with translation and the original , so different, those poems or more like 'prosa' was so beautiful and captured the sadness she wrote, and when I read the translation just got really bored feeling ... 
 For this I read ( the translate edition ) I only give 2 star, never want to read it again, ever ... 
 For you who wants to know a little about this book, please visit my blog on : 
 http://my-classic-books.blogspot.com/...

reference_books.review_text:
DNF. 
 I sloughed through Chapter 4 and gave up. The characters didn't hook me, and the writing was awkward and clunky. Just not a writing style that engages me, though clearly, other people love her.

reference_books.title: The Casual Vacancy
reference_books.review_text:
DNF. 
 Yep, I got taken in by the hype. Boy, was it wrong. 
 I think if you like stories about small English villages and lots of backstory and no real conflict and lots of nattering about the politics of English villages, this will fascinate you. 
 It did not fascinate me. With so many character hurriedly introduced and not any of them especially likeable or compelling, I had no reason to keep going. 
 It may just be her writing style doesn't appeal; I never got through even three chapters of the first Harry Potter. FWIW.

reference_books.title: The Almost Moon
reference_books.review_text:
Like others, I wasn't able to get past the subject matter and the unlikeable main character. The time jumps were confusing, and the presence of a mini-flashback in most every single scene felt irritating. 
 I got to about page 30 and gave up. DNF.

reference_books.title: The Road to Woodbury (The Walking Dead #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Compared to Rise of the Governor, this book isn't nearly as strong. I've not read the comics and know the universe only from the television show, so I'm not an uber fangeek, but this one wasn't as compelling as the first novel tie-in. 
 Lots of chum and spewage and guts flying around, of course. And mucusy? One, maybe not a real word and; two, used too often. :) 
 I did like that more female characters were on the page and the focus of the main storyline, something completely devoid in the governor novel. Not all of them were heroines, and that's a good thing. I think books and culture should be able to show women being just as weak and ineffective as men, and we can just let it go. We need to be able to fail and fail just as spectacularly as some men have. 
 If you're a WD fan, you'll like this. If you're not, I don't think this will turn you (heh heh heh) as quickly as the first book would.

reference_books.title: Lord of Misrule
reference_books.review_text:
An interesting, if at times inaccessible, take on racetrack life. Told from alternating first-person POVs, it makes the reader have to stop in their tracks, and figure out which character is speaking. This technique has been done more effectively by Maggie Estep, who often writes around the same settings. 
 Ultimately, I couldn't figure out what the big conflict was, but then, this is litfic so conflict, action, and drama don't have to be on the page. (They can be in a character's head, though. But if you ask me to be in a character's head for a long period of time, you'd better make damn sure the character is somewhat interesting and/or appealing.) 
 I know this was an award winner, but it confounded me. Not a keeper, gave it to my local library.

book_a.title: Wild: From Lost to Found on the Pacific Crest Trail
book_a.user_review:
DNF. 
 I got past the hike-the-trail-completely-unprepared in any way, shape, or form scenario. I got past the mother's death and life spiraling downward after that scenes. Most of us have lost someone dear, and most of us have some empathy for that pain. 
 I did not get the frothy experimentation with heroin and the endless self-destructiveness and the rest of it because, well, I just don't get it. And I *really* did not get the inept, drawn-out, and incredibly inhumane shooting of her mother's elderly horse because no one could be bothered to, you know, pay for a phucking vet and needle. Sorry, but one can borrow money from *somewhere*. You don't you have to blast a horse's brains only partly out with four bad shots and let her die slowly. Strayed lost me there, and lost me permanently. I closed the book. 
 No sympathy, no empathy, and no more reading of this crap. 
 If no stars were allowed, I'd rate with none.

sample_reviews.review_text: I really enjoyed reading about some of Cheryl's experiences on the trail, would have liked to have read more about the trail itself. Far to often I found myself saying "is this girl for real?"which is why I only gave it 3 stars.

In her mid twenties Cheryl Strayed's life seem to be falling apart due to the unexpected death of her mother, a broken dysfunctional family and just poor life choices. There are times in the book when you just want to reach out and stop her from her self distracting impulses, but then again, it was these personal disasters that led the author to an eleven-hundred-mile solo hike across the Pacific Coast Trail. 
 Wild is the the PCT experience that broke down the author once reeling from catastrophe--and built her back up again. 
 One of those books that had me torn between savoring slowly or consuming the pages at record speed-I chose the latter.

I was really looking forward to reading this book - which I naively expected to be in the tradition of "Into the Wild" or "Eat Pray Love" where there would be an introspection of her life, with a vivid description of an inward journey that coincided with her outward one. Instead, it is a memoir of a self-absorbed, immature, spoiled, ignorant "woman" who is utterly unprepared for this trek of a lifetime. Much of the drama of her hike along the Pacific Coast trail was completely self-created by her lack of planning (she doesn't even bother to learn how to use a compass, measure how heavy her backpack is, get decent shoes, or even sleep in the outdoors once), and really quite dangerous. It spoke little to the rigors of the actual trail, and after the long journey and hundreds of pages later, she was still emotionally unstable, shallow, and exactly the same place where she had started from. Not to mention her purely sexual relationships, her constant seek for affirmation by men, her obsessive grieving, and her nonchalant feelings over, what should be, very serious matters in her life was extremely grating. The fact that this author is, in fact, a college graduate stuns me and she acts like a bratty teenager throughout the entire book. The only thing saving this book is the few details about the journey. I kept reading, hoping the author would redeem herself, and bitterly disappointed that, even when she had completed the journey, she was still an unlikable character to the end.

Queen of the PCT... definitely not. What idiot would take on such an endeavour without any experience. I spent alot of time just shaking my head and in the end did she find herself- I think not. The only redeeming quality was that the writing flows well.

I'm not an unfeeling person and there were times when I read some passages in this book that I felt the author's pain but it's really a self-absorbed bit of writing i could have missed. I flipped through a lot of it quickly because of that. I have little patience and tolerance listening to people's problems when they are self-created problems and not true bad circumstances.

Love, love, love, if you like "Into the Wild," this book is a great addition to your reading repertoire. It made me so happy, will be one of my favorite reads from 2013. Definitely a good granola crunchy tale of nature, hiking and finding oneself in the beautiful wild of it all. 
 One favorite quote... 
 "Small cool black frogs jumping all over me. Each one was the approximate size of a potato chip. They were an amphibious army, a damp smooth-sinned militia, a great web-footed migration, and I was in their path as they hopped, scrambled, leapt, and hurled their tiny, pudgy, bent-legged bodies from the reservoir and onto the scrim of dirt they no doubt considered their private beach."

Aside from being amazingly well written, Wild is just a compelling story. When Cheryl was 22 her mother died of cancer and a few years later her marriage fell apart and ended in divorce. Throw in some self destructive behaviour including drugs and cheating and cross it with a chance run in with a tour book on the Pacific Crest Trail at a local store and you have all the makings for the soul searching adventure that became Wild: From Lost To Found On The Pacific Crest Trail. 
 At 26 Cheryl Strayed found herself newly divorced and self admittedly devastated with her life and feeling lost, so she decided to embark on an 1100 mile hike through the PCT, from the Mojave Desert through California and Oregon to the border with Washington State. Alone. 
 Cheryl writes about her personal demons in a way that doesn't make you feel sorry for her because she fully owns the fact that most of her decisions were bad, but it also makes you understand why a woman who absolutely no hiking experience would decided to embark on this sort of trip long. But the more I read the more I wanted to hear about her adventures and misadventures and about her hiking boots and her poor, destroyed feet and all the people she met along the way. And you wonder why you end up liking her when she makes such vapid and poor decisions, and writes about them with little remorse. Sometimes I was surprised by her candidness about her generally selfish and self destructive behaviour, but it also made her a bit more real to me. No one is perfect, and we can often excuse our life mistakes but for the most part Cheryl owns hers. 
 I think I loved this book the most because I felt that I could relate to Cheryl. Not that our lives are even remotely similar, and I've never done heroin nor have I ever cheated on my husband, but who wouldn't want to just pack up and leave everything behind and see what you can learn about yourself when it's just you and your wits for a few months? Most of us could do with a bit more self-discovery in our lives. 
 I really, really loved this book and I'm looking forward to seeing the movie.
Fantastic story. Anybody who has ever grieved or hiked could relate.

Well, I'm not a fan. I understood that the author was broken, hopeless and making incredibly bad choices. What I didn't understand was why she didn't move from regret (sorry, there were consequences to my actions) to repentance (my character is flawed and I need redemption). Hiking the trail may have brought her out of her lopsided misery but it didn't seem to transform her morality.
It was very interesting to read about the PCT and about Cheryl's journey! She inspired me.

book_b.title: Hater (Hater, #1)
book_b.user_review:
Didn't hate it, but didn't love it either. 
 The prose is pretty flat and repetitive. Because there's no resolution or explanation, this fails as a classic horror tale. There's apparently a sequel, but it won't be something I'll be reading. This was just too nihilistic for me.

sample_reviews.review_text: There isn't one character in this book that is likeable. The author created a world where everybody acts self centered and one dimensional. So, you can't and won't care for the characters. When the world starts to fall apart, you don't care. You might be able to place yourself into the situation with some imagination, but the author doesn't connect you to a character so you will enter the world he created. The husband, the wife, the kids, the boss, and the step father are all characters that you won't have any rapport with. So, you don't care what happens to them. If the author would have built some charm or likeable traits into the characters, the story would have had more impact, and the reader would want more at the end of the story. Instead, the reader will just be happy the story is over. A whiny loser husband, a whiny loser wife, a whiny father in law, and whiny kids don't make a good story.

This had a ton of potential. Random people wake up thinking everyone is out to get them - strangers, friends, family. They react violently. No one is immune and the violence continues to spread. 
 The author does a good job of describing the terror the Haters, and their victims, feel. But the book felt like it was written for the sole purpose of having a sequel. In my opinion, it would have been better if it was a self-contained book. I'm not sure if I'll pick up the other two books of the trilogy.

I read it all, which means some part of it captivated me, but by books end I was irritated. Halfway through the point had been hammered home by the main character, they are different but no one knows why. The difference equals an automatic death sentence. I'd say fully 1/5th of the book could have been chopped and I wouldn't have had to keep reading about this senseless violence that can't be explained and did we mention that no one understands why and in case you were worried that it might happen to you, well you should be worried, cause no one knows why it happens ... etc. etc. etc. It's senseless violence because it lacks sense ... we get it. I'm getting grumpy just recalling this book and the frustration I felt by the end. And then I read that there are going to be sequels, and then I laughed.

No me cabe duda que 'Odio' de Moody resultara una lectura de lo mas interesante para muchos lectores. No es mi caso; tuve que abandonar la novela por pura desesperacion. 
 Buena parte de culpa la tiene el narrador protagonista, probablemente uno de los padres de familia mas cargantes que me he topado en toda la literatura. El argumento no esta mal, consigue transmitir esa sensacion de repulsion y hartazgo que a veces asfixia nuestra sociedad. Pero pasar cada pagina es una prueba de fuerza de voluntad. 
 No obstante, si el argumento te interesa no me hagas caso y empieza el libro. Tan solo recuerda que no eres el unico/a si te rindes a la mitad.
Not so much into zombies.

Giant waste of time, thy name is Hater. 
 The first half of this book follows [Protagonist] (No, I can't remember the name of the main character of the book I just finished. And I can't be bothered to turn 90 degrees to my right, reach out and pick up the book to find out.) as he complains about his shitty job and his shitty family. Frankly, it reads like some of my more tedious "friends'" Facebook statuses. This is literally the first 120 pages of a 281 page book. 
 The second half replaces boring whining with boring, senseless violence. You see, people are turning into Haters and are mindlessly murdering anyone left Unchanged. Why are people becoming Haters? Who knows. How do you recognize a Hater? Who knows. What is the government doing with the Haters they round up? Who knows. Even when it's revealed that [Protagonist] is a Hater himself, the reader still doesn't get the satisfaction of any additional information. [Protagonist] is a Hater, he loves being a Hater, he doesn't question how he became a Hater or what that means in the larger scheme of things. But he still manages to whine a lot, but now instead of whining about his shitty job and family, he whines about how the Unchanged are the real haters and about standing for a long time. 
 So if I wasn't planning on mailing this book out to one of the 14 schmucks currently wish-listing it on paperbackswap.com, I would have thrown it against the wall. I still feel somewhat dirty, sending this book out to be read by the unsuspecting masses. But, hey, I need the credit. Maybe I should include a warning note or something... 
 For a few minutes, I was curious enough about what happens in the next two books in this serious to look them up on Wikipedia. When it turned out there isn't an article on them there, I decided I certainly wasn't curious enough to actually read the next two books. Heck no.

WOW..... What a book ! A fantastic apocalyptic vision of Britain, to me a classic to be put on the shelves with the 70's British classics , Survivors, Doomwatch etc.... A really good twist, it's like a zombie apocalypse but without zombies. People just violently turn on anyone for no reason. This book fills you with paranoia... Will you be next, will the person sitting next to you, your wife, your child???????????????? I really enjoyed this book, have to get the rest now !!!! Can highly recommend this book
Ever read a book and weren't sure how you felt about it? Yeah. That's me with this one.

Ok, this was some seriously weak writing. I can enjoy a good suspense book as much as I enjoy a literary masterpiece, but "Hater" was neither. 
 The characters were underdeveloped, the writing awful and the publicity info had already given away 2/3 of the plot. Even the violence was not interesting, imaginative or graphic enough to be enjoyable in any way. 
 I admit that a part of me wanted to keep reading, the part that was certain that if I put the book down I would never bother finishing it. Ok, I did want the plot to improve - give me a twist, even a predictable one. But no, nothing. 
 Yes, I know that it's part of a trilogy, but guess what, even then there has to be some sort of ending, some sort of closure, something interesting at the end of each of the books. At least a cliffhanger? This just felt like I was watching a movie that cut into commercial break abruptly and never resumed.
I feel like I have read this book but not sure we'll see!

I really enjoyed this book it was vey informative
I really enjoyed this book! I'm a sucker for birth stories and these are some of the best! The show definitely follows the book pretty well, though I did miss the relationships the show develops.

I do not normally read memoirs so I was surprised how much I enjoyed this one. Worth wrote in an engaging manner that drew you into the lives of her patients. Having given birth to a child with all of the modern conveniences available to me it's hard to imagine how these women and children back in the 50s managed to survive. I can't imagine what it would be like going through what they went through. I also have to give credit to the midwives of Nonnatus house for their dedication. I would highly recommend this book to anyone who is a mother. It is definitely an eye-opening account.

This was a very interesting look at a young midwife's experiences in the slums of London after World War II. She shares stories of all kinds of deliveries, from the perfectly normal to one that is fraught with such complications that both the mother and the baby are in jeopardy. We also get a glimpse of her life as she learns to be a midwife in the company of a group of nuns whose calling is to provide just these services to the poor. I quite enjoyed this and I think if you have any interest you should certainly pick it up. I hope this will make for a good discussion when my book club meets!

Love the way the author didn't sugar coat anything. She tells us about life, birth and deth in 1950's East London without using one single euphemism. The series was great. The book was a 'titch' better.

sample_reviews.review_text: Loved the Shakespeare play. Loved 10 things I hate about you. This is probably the worst adaptation I've experienced as it seems to celebrate all that is chauvinistic about the source material while missing out on some of the fun of it.

For many women, The Taming of the Shrew is just not amusing, even when wrapped up in the gossamer gloss of an MGM musical. What damn fool of a man thinks he will humiliate a headstrong woman and, as a consequence, make her think he's wonderful? 
 There is an interpretation of the play -- that instead of being played as a comedy, this is supposed to be an example of what women were expected to be in Shakespeare's time and, as such, is a portrayal that champions women's rights. That doesn't explain Kate's turnabout. Her long speech at the end advising wives to be gentle with their husbands does not speak of women's rights or an individual's rights, a speech given for her husband to win a wager about whose wife is most obedient. 
 There also is an interpretation that Petruchio doesn't know how to handle the attraction he feels for Kate any more than he understands how to fit into society. It still doesn't explain the cruelty. Inept and boorish are not synonyms. And if he is lashing out at her because she stands up to him, out of pride, how can that be a character worth falling for? 
 The latest version of the play is Anne Tyler's Vinegar Girl, part of the Hogarth series of novelizations of the plays. 
 In this modern-day setting, Kate's research scientist father is still the one who decides she will marry. But this time it's his Russian orphan assistant whose visa is running out. So now we've got both The Taming of the Shrew and the old marriage of convenience plot. 
 Her father is clumsy going about this. He's so obvious that Kate is at first oblivious, then aghast, at the idea. Pyotr is no better. He's introduced as a well-meaning, hapless sort, more the secondary male lead that Cary Grant gets the better of. No one except Kate even pronounces his name correctly. But Pyotr believes in her father's work and wants to stay there. 
 Kate decides might as well marry Pyotr so he can get a green card. She's not doing much beyond running her father's house as he wishes (including the weekly making of a meat mash that is served for the entire week) and working as a preschool assistant (where she tells the four-year-olds that the tomato sauce and pasta lunch smells like wet dog). She's prickly and unfulfilled. 
 The plot takes on screwball comedy tropes, including little sister's endless stream of tutors and her habit of ending sentences with question marks when men are near. The end goes full would-be Preston Sturges. 
 The tack Tyler takes is that this Kate is a "vinegar girl", that instead of trying to attract more flies with honey than vinegar, she doesn't know why anyone would want to attract flies. Her Kate also has an "aha" moment about her husband-to-be when she decides he is trying to fit in, just like she is trying to fit in, and neither one has been very good about it until they try to fit together. 
 That could be a nice enough sentiment, but it's a hard slog to get there with the green card marriage of convenience, a daft father who thinks he can control others' lives -- and then gets away with it, and a would-be hero who remains unformed. 
 Other titles in the Hogarth series include The Gap of Time by Jeanette Winterson, a retelling of The Winter's Tale, and My Name is Shylock by Howard Jacobson, who has co-written Shakespeare's Magnanimity: Four Tragic Heroes, Their Friends and Families. Margaret Atwood is contributing Hag-seed, a retelling of The Tempest. 
 Vinegar Girl doesn't work. Its source material has a great deal to do with that. Even the ad campaign for this novel that asks "if a thoroughly modern woman like Kate can ever be tamed", which shows that no matter how a story gets updated, if its core is rotten it remains rotten.

This a charming, bingeable romance, great for reading all at once while on vacation when exhausted from sightseeing (one could imagine). Often falls short in its examination of gender politics and social norms around marriage, which is really all I want from a Taming of the Shrew retelling, but truly a sweet story nonetheless!
Wonderful retelling.

Oh my, I think I hated almost every minute of this book? I did not like the main character and I found the plot to be insanely mundane and dull. I've never read The Taming of the Shrew so possible could be something that took away from my reading experience. I found Kate to be an incredibly unlikeable character. Pyotr is honestly the only character that I enjoyed because had some funny lines. Most of the characters were extremely one dimensional and almost like caricatures of real people. Ugh, I was so annoyed the. whole. time. For some reason I thought this was going to be a thought provoking read and it was essentially lame chick lit. If anything, I think it was the opposite of thoughtful and relied on a lot of gender stereotyping. Ugh, I want a refund on the time I spent on this book.
This is supposed to be a modern interpretation of The Taming of the Shrew. I didn't really enjoy it. The plot seemed thin and the characters - and character development - unbelievable.

I was really excited to read this title, as I love Shakespeare and had not read any Anne Tyler and was looking forward to reading my first. However, Vinegar Girl was somewhat disappointing - it felt unsatisfying and unfinished, as if Anne Tyler had gotten the commission and then just phoned it in. I understand that Anne Tyler is purported to be a master of the internal and middle-class family tension, and indeed, a lot of Kate's internal monologues were stellar; however, in the rest of the book, it seemed like she was bogged down by the framework of Taming of the Shrew, and was more focused on preserving those parallels than crafting her own interpretation of the story. The ending in particularly came completely out of left field and fell flat (it can be argued that the ending of Shrew does the same thing, but isn't the point of adaptation to make the story your own?) I am still looking forward to the rest of the Hogarth Shakespeare series, but this one in particular was just not for me - although I am sure that Anne Tyler fans will find a lot to love in it.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Cute book, expected the ending

Intelligent young woman goes from being controlled by her father to being controlled by some goofball she marries in order for him to get a green card and continue working for her father. After her initial resistance, she ends up in love with him. Faithful-ish to the Shakespeare, I guess, but is this really a theme for the twenty-first century?

I normally adore Anne Tyler but this one just didn't do it for me. The book was plot-driven and thus lacked Tyler's usual wonderful character development. Bunny and the father were just annoying, and I didn't really care for Kate--she seemed malleable for someone who was supposed to be strong-willed. Her last minute speech on how hard things are for men was a little abrupt and off-putting too. I did like Pyotr, and the symbolism of Kate and Pyotr standing side-by-side in the end was nice, but I was disappointed that those warm, interesting moments were few and far between.

reference_books.title: Mad About the Boy (Bridget Jones, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
To all of those who refuse to read this book due to the fact that Mark Darcy is gone....you're missing out on a great story. 
 Bridget Jones is older, a mother and a widow. However, she is still Bridget Jones, in a reassuring way. New dating dilemmas abound since she has new methods of communication to obsess over--texting, email, dating websites, but the story doesn't feel like a re-write of her previous books, nor is it simply an "I Don't Know How She Does It". There are laugh out loud moments, cry your heart out moments, high-five Bridget! moments. I am glad my old friend is back.

reference_books.title: Eleanor & Park
reference_books.review_text:
Literally could not stop until finished. 
 Magnificent. 
 If you are an adult and feeling sick and jaded by our world, step back into the 80's with a pair of teenagers and their all-consuming love. Their lives aren't perfect (Eleanor's is far, far, far, from perfect) but it seems their powerful bond will make everything all right. Be reassured that good people exist out there, and some of them happen to be teenagers.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I can no longer read this crap! I was beginning to think this was an inspirational story centered around a person overcoming adversity with hard work and determination until I reached pages 194 and 199 on my Kindle. What a joke!! JD can't even see his own hillbilly luck! Or should I say HANDOUTS! 
 On pg 194 he can't understand why working class whites have the lowest expectations and outlooks on life by citing a PEW Economic Mobility Project study. Then on page 199 he goes on to brag about how his POVERTY allowed him to goto a TOP University for literally NO COST!! Wake up JD...I lost ALL respect for you. Yeah, its us HARD WORKING MIDDLE CLASS WHITES who didn't have the benefit of a DRUG ADDICTED mother with 10 husbands who DONT get the same opportunity as YOU and the other classes mentioned in that PEW survey. 
 Those two pages discounted everything you think you've achieved thru hard work in my mind. I'd love to have a chat with YOU about real life and struggles. I can't even finish your book now...
What a great and timely read. Anyone upset and/or affected by the election NEEDS to read this book!! Provides great insight into a much overlooked group of people.
I really liked this book. It was not what I expected when I decked it out from the library. I recommend it to anyone!

J.D. Vance is a hillbilly. He is thirty something, writing a memoir of his very difficult and disturbing life. He is one of the fortunate ones, joining the Marines, going to college, graduating from Harvard Law and marrying a wonderful woman. However the story itself does not tell us anything we are not already aware of. These trial and tribulations that he faced can be descriptive of any minority In the same socio economic situations. He does admit he has no answers or solutions to the problems these people face. I just don't know what the author is trying to accomplish with this book, we all are aware of the poor in America and none of us have an answer.

"We didn't live a peaceful life in a small nuclear family. We lived a chaotic life in big groups of aunts, uncles, grandparents, and cousins. This was the life I'd been given, and I was a pretty happy kid." 
 This book, which purports to be part memoir and part socio-anthropoligical treatise on hillbilly culture falls unfortunately flat on the latter. J.D. Vance's stories of his own family helped me to put into words some things I've long struggled to understand and express about my own family, but I don't see how it helps us as a society fix any problems. 
 He states, 'Whenever people ask me what I'd most like to change about the white working class, I say, "The feeling that our choices don't matter,"' but offers no plan for making this change. For him, the change came when he learned that his choices did matter, in part through his military service and in part through his acceptance to and attendance at Yale Law, and I suppose it's good that he doesn't attempt to simplify the issue and state that this path will work the same for everyone, but I had hoped for some thoughts about a way forward. And although J.D. and I had roughly the same conversation with our dads about applying to Ivy League schools ("I don't care if got into Notre Dame. You can get a fine, cheap education at the community college."), when, as he rightly says, 'the irony is that for poor people like us, and education at Notre Dame is both cheaper and finer,' I came to no solutions about why he felt empowered to commit to Yale while I allowed the attitude that the Ivy League was overpriced and nothing all that special to dissuade me from even applying. 
 Overall, his story left me feeling no more hopeful or empowered to help make a substantive societal change.

While it was an interesting book, it read sort of like a series of essays written by a high-schooler. Anecdotes flow awkwardly into analysis with occasional clunky interruptions by social history passages that barely scratch the surface of the subject matter.

I throughly enjoyed the memoir aspects of this book. It's a compelling story of triumphing over the obstacles. I loved his portrayal of his beloved grandmother Mamaw. 
 But as a window into why folks from the rust belt went for Trump -- that was a task too large for a 268 page book. I got some idea of the isolation people in that area live in. And a window into the suspicion that some evangelical religions view the rest of the world. 
 I thought the author painted with too broad a brush his thoughts for why his hometown was failing and what/ if anything big G government could do to help. 
 I think he would have been much better off just sticking to memoir. This is not a fix it manual and the fixes he offers seem too specific for a government agency to enact given that those agencies have to service the entire county both rural and urban and every kind of family in between. Although maybe there is a way for the people who work in to agencies to be able to pivot or work in a grey area to keep a family together. 
 PS by definition what is a hillbilly? Is it universally a pejorative term? That term made me very uncomfortable.

First of all, I'd like to say that J.D. Vance seems like a fairly self-aware individual now. He's worked hard for his success, and I congratulate him for a) working so damn hard for his accomplishments and b) not preaching the "pull yourself up by your bootstraps" ethos for everyone (though he's obviously a conservative). It's not his fault that his memoir is marketed as an insight into the rise of the fringe Republican party in Middle America. However, when you peel away that layer, what you're left with is the life story of someone who hasn't really accomplished anything extraordinary enough to merit reading hundreds of pages about his life. 
 I grew up in Appalachia as well, and I'm only a few years younger than Vance. There are plenty of "hillbillies" in my family, and yes, some are dirt poor. I also worked hard to afford college and move elsewhere. Vance seems torn between wanting to explain the disadvantages of his youth without condemning his family. His beloved grandparents were remarkably abusive, hostile, and aggressive, but he frames that in a sort of childishly devoted way. Though his grandparents and mother made middle class wages, he doesn't draw a clear link between the financial good times and how he ended up growing up "poor" (though I assume it was due to his mother's prescription drug addiction). He seems to have a lot of excuses for why his family members are the way they are, though he's quick to condemn anyone who he perceives as abusing government assistance. His own temper and ill behavior are brought up again and again, but he rarely contextualizes or offers up remorse. It left me wondering what kind of a teenager he was to those around him. 
 There are precious few citations throughout this, and it's really not a cultural study. It's just a memoir. However, I was incredibly put off by Vance trying to explain why people he knew distrusted President Obama. He claimed it was due to Obama's education, poise, and urban background and not racism or rumored/patently false "Muslim" ties. However, just a few pages before, he excused a Kentucky native for not knowing what Catholicism was because he grew up around a single sort of religion. I think that failing to address the lack of diversity in these communities (and, yes, the condemnation of anything "different" and some good old fashioned bigotry) left a horrible taste in my mouth. 
 Vance's background certainly doesn't represent the "hillbilly" nature of my youth, and I mourn the fact that so many will read this book and assume it applies to so very many of us.

So True 
 This book should be required reading for every high school freshman, and earlier if possible. On the other hand, it would be beneficial to anyone, young or old. I found the belief in the possibilities of our phenomenal country to be encouraging. Be involved!

This is the book everyone is reading, because it's being pitched as a window into the apparently hidden world of Americans that came out of nowhere and elected Donald Trump to be the next president. If you want to know why Donald Trump was elected president, it probably has more to do with the fact that those who can't fathom the possibility of his presidency thought reading a book about the phenomenon would be the best way to understand it. I imagine most of the people reading this book are a lot like Victorian Britons reading Heart of Darkness in an effort to understand Africa.
