reference_books.title: Dorothy Must Die (Dorothy Must Die, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Talk about crumbling infrastructure! The state of Oz is in terribly disarray, as noted by Amy Gumm, yet another Kansas teen blown there by a monster of a tornado. The land is decimated, she soon learns, by the monstrous magic-draining activities of none other than the famous Dorothy, whose inhuman power plays allowed her to install herself as Oz's despotic princess-ruler. Amy's arrival and compassionate actions soon bring her to the attention of Dorothy and a sure sentence of death but she is saved by a renegade band of Witches formerly known as Wicked, who train Amy to bring about the downfall of Dorothy. 
 Have we yet mentioned the Violently Bullying Lion, the Twisted Experimenter Scarecrow, or the Slavishly Devoted Tin Man, all Dorothy Protectors and Partners-In-Crime? 
 What could have been sacrilege to legions of Wizard of Oz fans instead becomes its own version of the literary and film legend by convincingly creating an entirely new spin that is still firmly grounded in the old. Amy is an immediately likable character (whose last name, Gumm, is a nice nod of the hat to Dorothy's famous portrayer, Judy Garland, whose birth name was Gumm), and the transition from her miserable life in Kansas to a fantastical one in Oz is completely believable due to the honestly of the emotions and reactions expressed by Amy. Because this new world is created so convincingly, the reader easily jumps on board this (yellow-brick) road leading to plenty of intrigue, suspense, and action. The ending leaves one breathless for the next book in the series. Thank heavens I waited to read the first till AFTER the others were published - three clicks of my heels later, and the next one is off the library shelves and into my greedy hands!

reference_books.title: Etiquette & Espionage (Finishing School, #1)
reference_books.review_text: What a very interesting semester spent at a decidedly different sort of finishing school for the daughters of Britsh gentry! Sephronia soon finds out that her new boarding school teaches, along with posture and dancing, espionage and assassination. The fun for the reader is not so much the mystery Sephronia must solve but the revealing of the particulars of this steampunk world: airdinghies, an entire school that floats, and a charming and contraband mechanimal that Sephronia hides under her bed. Readers should eagerly reach for the other volumes in the series.

reference_books.title: Popular: Vintage Wisdom for a Modern Geek
reference_books.review_text: Advice books and memoirs for young teens don't come any more awesome than this one! Loved author Maya's year-long attempt to become popular at her middle school by following the advice in an advice book from the 1950s. Wish I had this when I was 12. Scratch that...I believe I'll use some of Maya's advice the next time I brave the faculty room!

reference_books.title: A Man Called Ove
reference_books.review_text: This formulaic novel about the redemption of a grumpy old man has all the usual suspects - a recently deceased wife, intrusive yet quirky neighbors, youth of various ages needing attention, and even a homeless, abused cat. Although this cloyingly written story was obviously not my cup of tea (I don't take saccharine, after all), I am obviously in the minority - this Swedish import has taken the publishing world by storm. So if you are looking for a sweet, feel-good, predictable take on human nature, by all means, set yourself up in a comfy chair, put on your "Best of Lawrence Welk" playlist for background enhancement, and enjoy bringing Ove into your life!

reference_books.title: Victoria
reference_books.review_text: Closely following the Masterpiece presentation (no surprise as the author is also the screenwriter of the series), this title explores the early years of the reign of Queen Victoria. Navigating her complicated relationships with her mother and her mother's advisor, and that of her own advisor in Lord Melbourne, the story makes it abundantly clear the immaturity and inexperience of the young Queen, and the pressures of politics, influence, and expected marriage. Long live the Queen! ...as well as the future titles that are sure to follow after the success of this first one.

book_a.title: Confessions
book_a.user_review: "Revenge is a dish best served cold," or at least lukewarm, as is the case found in this tale of a Japanese middle school teacher who discovers her young daughter was murdered by two of her students. The outlandish tale sometimes requires a dedication to suspending disbelief, but the twisted motives of the characters, nicely given voice by each of the characters themselves, more than makes up for the plot stretches. Fiendishly delightful!

sample_reviews.review_text: For the first half of the book I was mildly interested, and wanted to believe that what I found unconvincing in the story was due to my ignorance of Japanese society. By the end, I was thoroughly bored by it. I'm prepared to believe that there are children who are evil, or simply so desperate for attention they'll kill anyone to get it, but this novel throws no light on why there are kids like that, or how to cope with them. Minato makes the mistake or having the story told in turn by various participants from their own perspective. What's wrong with that is her plot being too convoluted for its own good, it becomes less and less plausible with each retelling. This is just a silly shocker, with pretensions to High Art status clumsily advanced through references to Dostoevsky and Camus. Please!
A stark and grim story that I am happy to be done with.

This is more of a 2.5 for me. 
 First off, the good(ish): Confessions called up in my mind a vivid image of a Japanese junior high. I found myself wondering if the author had actually described the old desks with bags clipped on the sides, the wall of windows over a dirt courtyard, the staffroom students apologized for entering...or if I was just remembering all that myself? Her description of the students listening to sensei, cleaning up around the school, and having teachers reprimand them for out of school behavior was all spot-on and so Japanese chugakko. I appreciated the way in which the story unfolded: separate chapters by different protagonists who provide a contrasting perspective to the central story. Most chapters read like a monologue to a specific audience with the narrator responding to the listener's reaction. 
 While the book is about a murder and "punishing" the murders, much of the content feels like Japanese horror rather than straight up crime. Lots of bullying/ijime which just makes me hate everything. My greatest issue though was the treatment of HIV and AIDS (shocked that's even in there, aren't you? I mean, right?? This book is not even supposed to be about that! What the heck?) In the book, contracting HIV is depicted as end-of-the-world devastating and, in all cases, viewed as a punishment for bad behavior. Granted, most characters' horrific reaction to those who are or might be HIV+ show the ignorance of students (who display fear that simply touching someone will result in you contracting the disease. Small rant: Is this pre-Google? I mean why doesn't Naoki just look up how it spreads instead of bleaching his whole house, omg). At the same time, this builds on the general perception of HIV and AIDS in Japanese society. It is horrific that any teacher would torture children with the threat of exposing them to any harmful agent -- one reason I view Confessions as horror -- but it is exceptionally telling and offensive that HIV is presented as the worst of all possibilities. It just made me want to punch Japanese news. So, I recognize I come into this with lots of bias. Overall, the story is a very Japanese horror/crime novel set in a school. Full of horrible people doing horrible things. The structure and unraveling is intriguing, and those who like crime or mysteries set in school situations should likely be entertained.

Not bad for a book that cost me less than $1! It was also interesting reading a book set in Japan (and written by a Japanese author), which was something a bit different for me. 
 A very suspenseful book, I found it to be a page turner. Some awful things happen over the course of the book but it's not hugely graphic. Interesting to think about what makes people-and especially children- commit crimes; and the effects of revenge.

I received this book as part of a Goodreads giveaway. 
 A fantastic and gripping book with unexpected twist after twist. I couldn't put it down. Great suspense and I loved how it was narrated in alternating voices. Very well crafted.

I expected an overly sensational thriller but the narrative choices were interesting and the plot tight. It got slightly carried away towards the end but it is still a very assured debut novel and I await the translation of her other books.
This one definitely kept my attention.

4 out of 5 stars -- Judgment and revenge... 
 Yuko Moriguchi is a middle school teacher when her 4-year-old daughter, Manami, drowns in the swimming pool nearby. Consumed with grief, she retires from teaching -- but leaves her class with one last lecture. While giving the students a little background of her life, Yuko shocks them all by declaring that she now knows that her daughter did not die in an accident, but was murdered! And that the two killers are right in that very room! Then she tells the students that she has decided not to go to the police and turn them in, but will punish them herself -- and has already set her plan in motion. She leaves the students to do what they will with this knowledge and information. 
 What follows is a point of view shift by chapter as a significant person attempts to give rationalizations, explanations or interpretations of both the murder and what follows. The climax is both shocking and horrible -- TWISTED! The reader will not be able to put this short book down until finishing the very last page. Be sure to allow yourself a couple of uninterrupted hours! 
 I'd recommend this to anyone who likes chills and suspense full of characters who are mostly completely unlikeable (for many reasons), and a great, unpredictable story! 
 Thank you to NetGalley and Mulholland Books for the e-book ARC.

Dark, melodramatic candy. I tore through it, even though I don't think it's particularly well-written (which could be the translation). I liked getting new viewpoints as the chapters switched narrators. Pretty much everyone is a bit socio- or psychopathic. It's over the top*, but definitely had some chilling passages. 
 * I know people do commit crimes like the ones in the book, so I'm not saying stuff like this doesn't happen. But all contained within this one narrative the constant dramatic events create a feeling more kabuki than real.

I would never have heard of this book if it were not for the book review section of "The Week", which is a super informative magazine. The tag line was that this story was "Gone Girl" meets "Lord of the Flies" in Japan and since I liked "Gone Girl", had previously read books set in Japanese schools, and generally had been really pleased with previous recommendations from "The Week" got this from the library. book_b.title: The Boy on the Porch
book_b.user_review: Sweet fable about a childless couple whose life changes with the appearance if a young boy on their porch. The contrived (was it meant to be?) dialogue between the two, which comprised much if the text, seemed too sweetly and simply annoying to me, though....

sample_reviews.review_text:
First line: The young couple found the child asleep in an old cushioned chair on the front porch, p. 1. 
 The Boy on the Porch won the 2016 WAW award grades 3-5, but I didn't enjoy it. The adults in the story are the least competent people who should be watching over children. Marta and John, the protagonists, are described as being a young couple, but how young? The way they spoke they seemed much older. 
 "How come he doesn't remember, Marta? How come I have to keep reminding him? Should I be hollering at him?" 
 "Oh, no, you shouldn't do that." 
 "Well, that's what my father did when I forgot to do something." 
 "And did his hollering help you remember?"- p. 67. 
 Is this contemporary or 1950s? I'm just so confused about this book.

This beautifully written book reads like an adult short story. The child, Jacob, in the story is mute and the point-of-view comes strictly from the adults. Jacob plays, draws, and interacts with the people and animals, but he never speaks out loud. It reminds me of the book, "The Prince Who Fell from the Sky," that has a boy who has no dialogue in the story. This technique makes me identify with the adult voice and seems off-kilter for the target audience of children. I liked the adult perspective on the uncertainties of being a parent, but will young readers connect with the characters and plot? I'm not sure. The pacing might be slow for some young readers, but oh-my, I do like how Sharon Creech puts sentences together. Just as Jacob taps out songs and sounds on any object he can find, Creech has a rhythm to her sentences that makes me want to sing. My only question is the audience and what students will think of the book. 
 John and Marta find a six or seven-year old boy, Jacob, abandoned on their porch with a note asking them to look after him. The note says the person will come back and get him, but as time passes it seems very unlikely. Because Jacob can't speak, John and Marta cannot find out any information from him about his past and who wrote the note. Months go by and they come to love the boy like their own child making them fearful of him being taken back and marring their happiness as a family. A nice message regarding what makes a family. 
 This story is about the transformation of John and Marta from a childless couple to learning what it means to love and care for a young boy. John is worried Jacob isn't boyish enough while Marta worries about him not having friends. They nurture his talent for music and painting and do not bully or criticize him. In return, he loves them unconditionally. The two struggle with telling the authorities about the lost boy because they don't really want him to be found by the person who left the note. They eventually do the right thing, but almost lose the boy over their choice. Creech shows how their decision was from a good heart, even if misguided. The story also shows the lack of laws in place to protect children from parents who don't know how to parent. In this regard, it might be a good book for a book club with grade 5 students. The story is only 150 pages so it is a quick read. The plot is well organized and the tension from wondering when or if the parents will come back for the boy kept me turning the pages. Like I said, I just don't know if students will take interest.
Heartwarming story I enjoyed. My friend, Cindy, will be getting a copy. She has been Marta, for over 30 years.

Synopsis: A boy arrives on the porch of a childless farming couple (who don't seem to do much farming, but they have two cows). He's about six or so, and he's mute. There's a letter with him, barely literate, that says his name is Jacob, and 'we'll be back for him'. 
 A forewarning of my bias: Diana Wynne Jones was my hero, and the hero of my childhood. Stories where the abused/neglected kid doesn't achieve some form of escape or acknowledgement of this neglect gets my caw. Neglected or disabled or abused kids as life lessons to someone else? ARGH. (By the way, Jacob is all three of these.) 
 I remember reading Bloomability and Walk Two Moons when I was in the appropriate age bracket, and seeking out Sharon Creech in bookshops (Aiken - Creech - Jones - Pratchett... My own bookshelves were alphabetised, too.) 
 I have a plot problem with The Boy on the Porch. In that it sucks. And tells neglected kids there is no recourse because a father has the right to his boy. Kids are possessions. They belong to someone. And no matter what the kids feel about it, and the legal authorities and whatever nice people they meet along the way will not help them. 
 Stylistically, it's halfway to a fairytale. The town has no name, but is all American farming towns, where you can barter for jellybeans in the single store. There's an echo of the Depression, perhaps, with transient workers and having to get in contact via mail. It certainly doesn't allow any development of all the twists and difficulties modernity would give it. The Sheriff is by the law, but the law is whatever he determines is alright, and there isn't much of a structure which is enforced by a wider social, legal, or governmental framework. It is a Republican's one-horse dream town. 
 Which would be fine, except it *isn't* set in the Depression. 
 It's now-ish, or at least not too far behind now. There's an organised system for becoming a foster parent, and a lot of kids who need fostering, and there isn't an orphanage system. Kids from families with very few prospects and learning difficulties come back as college grads, because this is, to give it a very generous date, sometime in the last 40 years. 
 Let's talk about Jacob. Jacob is a child who is mute (reasons unknown, and not investigated), but loves painting and making rhythms and making music. Unfortunately, for a titular character, Jacob is not the lead of anything. John and Marta, his quasi-foster parents who find him on their porch, are the leads. The story is from their point of view. Their struggles to communicate with Jacob are discussed between the two of them. Jacob's fears, dreams, feelings, passions, interests, and friendships are only background. Jacob teaches them, the adults with names, that they can love kids, that art and music are valid forms of expression, that communication can take on many forms. 
 Think I'm saying Jacob too often in this review? It's because Jacob's almost always referred to as 'the boy', by everyone. In description, in dialogue, in reminiscing. 
 This is literally and metaphorically a story about a child without a voice! And the story took away his voice, and his name, and let him be abandoned and taken away because 'a father has the right to his boy'. 
 When Jacob's father finally comes back to collect him, a few months have passed. They've found where Jacob used to live, and know his family skipped out on the rent in the middle of the night. A single man comes to collect Jacob, and waves around a birth certificate. Not childhood photos of Jacob - nothing which says this certificate belongs to this child. Jacob doesn't want to go with this man. He attempts to communicate - he has tapping signals which father-dearest doesn't attempt to translate for him. 
 The Sheriff shows up, looks at the birth certificate, says 'a man has the right to his boy', and this man who left a false address takes Jacob away and leaves. Jacob was *physically left on a porch*, and that isn't enough to bring in social services? Be a case for severe neglect and child endangerment? Jacob being mute a red flag for other abuses? Really? WTF, Sheriff? 
 And *then* Marta and John get legal about it. They miss having a kid around, so they foster others legally, and suddenly this fairytale Depression farming town has modern social services. They've learnt that families of choice are awesome, and they want to bring stability to cute little kids in the foster system who only need short term placements and don't have a pile of abused kids issues. 
 I was ranting to a writer friend who doesn't know kid lit, and she asked who a child reader is meant to be identifying with, and I really don't want the answer to be Jacob. For a kid who fantases about being left behind and found by someone who loves him and wants to raise him, this book kicks that escapism in the face, and then grinds it in cowpats. Because you will not be rescued, the police won't help you, and your parents have the right to you, whatever they do.
Nice little story, quick read, but it seems like it's more for adults than children. Hm.

The Boy on the Porch features a young mute boy, known only as Jacob, who gets dropped off on the porch of an older married couple. Ms. Creech crafts a unique story about family and foster care. Jacob breezes into the life of this couple and changes their perception of what it means to be a parent.

** spoiler alert ** 
 John and Marta find a young boy asleep on their front porch with a misspelled and cryptic note saying that someone will be back for him. The boy doesn't speak, but the note indicates his name is Jacob. He seems to have a way of communicating through tapping, but John and Marta don't understand. The two are leery of contacting the local law enforcement, because they are mean, so just get him clothes and try to do the best they can to raise him. Jacob shows an affinity for music, loves the dog, and seems frightened of his past. The law is eventually involved, the father shows up, and Jacob is wrenched from John and Marta, who are devastated but soon start to take in foster children. 
 Strengths: Creech writes beautifully, and this would be great for teachers who love her work or that of Patricia MacLachlan. The tie in with foster care could be used if a group were making blankets for My Very Own Blanket. 
 Weaknesses: This struck me more as a book mothers would read in a book discussion group. Jacob, since he is mute, is not very engaging, so most of the perspective is from John and Martha. It is very slow paced. I also wish that a clear date had been given for the setting, since I had concerns about Children's Services not being notified. It seems to take place in the 1930s or 1940s, but this is never delineated.

Amazing book! 
 If you are a Maeve Binchy fan, then sit down and enjoy this feast for the eyes and senses! Seriously, I sound crazy but this book is awesome.

I became a big fan of Maeve Binchy when I first read Circle of Friends years ago. And Binchy's early books remain my favourites. I was very disappointed with more recent books like Nights of Rain and Stars and Whitethorn Woods. Minding Frankie is not as good as her early works but I did enjoy it and raced through it in a day. Set in the working class neighbourhood of St. Jarlath's Crescent, Dublin, the novel is filled with a large and varied cast of characters, some of whom have featured in Binchy's previous novels. Noel Lynch is an alcoholic in a dead-end job, living with his pious parents, when his middle-aged cousin Emily arrives from America for a visit. Emily arrives as a breath of fresh air, a catalyst for change, and one soon wonders how this community functioned without her. When a dying, pregnant woman, Stella, claims that her unborn child is Noel's, Emily steps in to help Noel rise to the challenge of raising his child. And the whole community takes part - all striving to keep ahead of social worker Moira who is every ready to catch them wrong-footed. At times I had to stop to remind myself who a particular character was, and occasionally, I wanted to give some characters a good shake (Lisa!) but overall this novel abounded with life, its hopes, its failures, its kindnesses, its losses, its follies, and I couldn't help but get caught up in the whole thing.

Maeve Binchy has always been a favorite author of mine, as I tend to prefer novels set in Ireland and the UK (the Old Country is so much more romantic somehow). However, my fondness for Binchy is wearing thin, and I much prefer her earlier works. I have read all her books, so I was familiar with the characters from her previous novels who showed up here, and there are a lot to keep track of. I'm beginning to find it irritating how she flits from one character to the next, lightly touching down before flying off to the next one. She only grazes the surface, and I don't feel there's any real character depth. I also find it exceedingly unlikely that one of the major characters, Emily, a New Yorker visiting relatives she's never met, manages to transform their lives and every thing she touches, even giving life-long Dubliners directions on where and how to find anything. She's some kind of miracle worker, intervening and solving problems and becoming so essential that everybody becomes dependent on her, but we really know nothing about her character. I think as nice as she seems to be that I would find her to be an interloper who's just a tad annoying. Funny that none of the characters think this, because she's too perfect, and everyone adores her. (To be realistic, aren't fictional characters supposed to have some flaws?) And I also found it unbelievable when she becomes romantically linked with a character who's barely mentioned. That could have been a wonderful part of the story, but it comes totally out of left field, with no development at all. As in Binchy's other recent novels, characters' lives are magically transformed, the hard-working deserving lower class receive financial windfalls, the demons of addiction are easily dispensed with, better jobs always await those who show initiative, family issues are happily resolved, and nearly everyone finds the right romantic partner. It's a reassuring world Binchy creates, but her slice-of-life stories resemble more of a fairy tale than real life. I like happy endings but I don't like feeling manipulated. Still, I enjoy the pleasant diversion of spending time in Binchy's world, even if it does have a rosy tint.

My only gripe about this story is that the American character spoke and thought exactly like the Irish characters, which I found a tad hard to believe. I myself have been accused of wrapping things up too neatly as an author, but I love happy endings and Binchy always provides them.

Over the last few years, Jonathan Tropper has asserted himself something of a master of the genre I like to call Novels About Middle-Aged Suburban Men Whose Lives Aren't Awful, Just Unsatisfying. His latest, though, was surprisingly satisfying. I was a little underwhelmed by This is Where I Leave You, but I think that was mostly because of where I was in my life more than anything about the book itself. With that in mind, I did approach this with a small amount of skepticism but ultimately I came away with a nice, healthy dose of the feels. 
 The set-up here is just a little darker. Drew Silver is a washed-up one-hit-wonder playing the wedding-and-mitzvah circuit. His ex-wife Denise is getting remarried to a guy Silver can't bring himself to hate, and his teenage daughter Casey has just announced she's pregnant. He lives in an apartment building with a bunch of other middle-aged men whose wives have left them and together they make weekly trips to sell their semen to medical research. He cruises through life more or less on autopilot, not really noticing the hurt caused by his lack of engagement. 
 Then Silver has a ministroke and an aneurysm, diagnosed by his ex-wife's new fiancee Rich. Equal parts pride and surrender prevent him from allowing Rich to repair the tear in his aorta, meaning that Silver could literally die at any second. He's okay with that, because he's lost everything that's ever meant anything to him and he doesn't see how life is ever going to have meaning again. Then Casey reveals her pregnancy, admitting that she's telling Silver before her mother because she's less concerned about letting him down. So Silver decides that in the time he has left, he needs to make up for eighteen years of crummy fathering. 
 The first chunk of the book is a little too full of hyperbole and testosterone for my taste -- Silver and his fortysomething buddies ogling young women with perfectly taut everythings while exchanging excessively witty one-liners. After a while, though, Tropper finds his groove and the book finds the right balance between poignant and schmaltzy. You start to sympathize with Silver, genuinely root for this man who has never proven to be anything but an apathetic fuck-up. And yet he's anything but unlikable. There's maybe a little flash of George Bailey here, as Silver learns what he means to the people in his life, yet it never quite falls over into excessive sentiment.

Read this hoping it was going to be similar to "This is where I leave you" and it wasn't as funny to me. The book overall was just okay, story line was a little dragging and I wish the ending was different.

Jonathan Tropper is a great writer - one of my all-time favorites - but this is not his best work. The plot line about a one-hit musical wonder past his prime who needs surgery but refuses to have it because of familial angst was not plausible and did not excite me, nor did the subplot of having a pregnant teenage daughter. Tropper usually does well with stories of family dysfunction (please read This Is Where I Leave You!) but this novel does not rise to the level of humor, wit and insight I'm used to from him.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Beyond 5 Magical Stars 
 "That could go on forever, but we both know that mystery is better than the truth. So why not live with the magic? Be a kid again and believe in the fantastical. Life is more fun with a little smoke and mirrors." 
 This book must have taken one hell of an outline. It's a pretty simple story on the surface but once you add in the character's, the plot, the romance, and the background stories it get a lot complex... which makes it genius. I was unsure when I first picked it up, the prologue was odd, and the two pages of the first chapter were odder but then I met Jay, and now I am mentally berating myself for not reading this sooner. I'm not going to bother making my own synopsis for this book considering the fact that I love L.H. Cosway's synopsis so I'm just going to jump straight into characters, romance, and basic plot. 
 "Better to disillusion the illusionist from the get-go... There. The outfit says, This is me. Take it or leave it." 
 Matilda Brandon aka Watson is the narrator for this story and the main heroine and boy was just amazing. Watson (as I think of her in my head) was cheeky, sarcastic, nerdy, smart, cute, and down-right goofy. I loved her after reading her monologue in the first chapter with the internet dating? Oh man I was a goner and a part of me desperately wants to be friends with her. Watson knows her faults and is misguided in her attributes, she doesn't see herself as pretty, unique, or fun and a part of it makes sense I mean if you are twenty-three and are struggling for a date of course some people are going to have some self-conscious issues. But trust me when I say she gets over them with a good healthy does off Jay Fields! 
 "Jay is godlike, and that god would be Loki, the trickster." 
 Jay Fields aka Holmes is an illusionist for a living and our hero, and when I place him under the shelf of: angel's weep for these hero's, you can bet your ass I mean it. Jay is everything charming, gorgeous, intelligent, and he even get's down with some of Watson's geeky jokes. He also has one of the biggest heart's and is the most kindest and generous person I have ever had the pleasure of reading. He truly made this book. 
 " We fall for the person as a whole. We fall for their souls. 
 The romance was breathtaking, it had me sweating from the chemistry, laughing at the friendship, and crying over the love. It was a good slow build-up that allowed me to see how exactly they both fell for each other and why. 
 "Curiouser and curiouser:" is literally how I felt moving along with the story. The reader's already have a pretty good assumption as to what to make of the mystery aspect in the book because of the Prologue. However because it is all in Watson's POV you learn with her, and Jay is very adamant in keeping her in the dark, so the reader's don't find out the whole story until close to the end. Yes, I will be honest and say I wish we all learned sooner than near the 90% mark, but it still didn't feel all that rushed because the readers weren't completely in the shadows like Watson was. 
 At the end of the day I would never change anything about this novel, and wish that I could mentally erase it from my membrane so that I could enjoy the magic all over again.

POV: 1st person, Matilda 
 Ages: early/mid 20's 
 Setting:Ireland or Scotland (I can't remember) 
 Heat:3.75 out of 5 
 This was awesome. I absolutely loved the characters-they were unique, fun, and relatable. The writing flowed and had a brilliant unique style to it. The romance wasn't rushed; meaning that it had time to develop and feel more realistic to the reader. I thought that the plot was very interesting- that, plus the writing and characters kept me turning the page. over all, this was an A+ book. L.H. Cosway, you are now one of my favorite authors.

5+ Wickedly Smart Stars! 
 Jay Fields is an Illusionist, blurring the lines of reality. But he wasn't always a trickster, he used to be a scared little boy. One that lost everything in one night. Now his whole life has been one quest to right the wrongs of those he loved. Returning home, Jay seeks the assistance of Hugh, the small time solicitor to assist him battling the paper that is dragging his name through the mud.... but nothing is as simple as it seems. 
 Matilda is a little awkward and even more shy, but there is something about Jay that pulls her in. Beyond the mystery of the man and the smooth confidence, she finds her attraction growing. But there are secrets that Jay isn't quite ready to reveal just yet. As these two grow closer and Jay approaches the end of his goal, Matilda can't help but falling for the man that has more than one trick up his sleeve. 
 When you open a L.H. Cosway book you are guaranteed to be taken on a magical journey. There is just something about this author's ability to create such a vivid story. From the opening of this story I was grinning ear to ear. Jay and Matilda's interactions were perfection. I could have read another hundred pages of just their witty banter and not grown bored for even a second. 
 When you fall into one of her stories, you are pulled into this mix of fiction and fantasy you just can't escape. As Matilda slowly came out of her shell and became captivated by the smoke and mirrors, you fell in love right alongside of her. There was not one moment of this story that did not hit the mark. 
 Jay's drive to right the wrongs of the past was such a captivating part of this story. Although you know the connection these two share from the prologue, the build up for Matilda to realize their connection was done masterfully. Even knowing where this story was heading, the author threw in enough that you were still surprised by some of the revelations. 
 I've read two prior books by this author, Painted Faces and Still Life in Strings and I can honestly say these are stories that will stick with me for years to come. There is something so unique about the style of this author and how she paints the picture for you. I've read a lot of books and yet, nothing else out there has had this little touch of magic to it. If you have not yet picked up a book by this author, you need to. Seriously, you will not be sorry.

Six of Hearts foi uma leitura incrivel. 
 Achei a heroina um doce. Ela acredita no amor epico, mas de um modo real e tocante. Seus criterios para musicas, filmes, hobbys e beleza masculina, entre outros, combinam em unissono com o meu gosto pessoal. Amei isso. Nao foi a toa que ri absurdamente quando numa determinada cena o filme O Casamento de Muriel e mencionado. Nao poderia deixar de registrar que eu ja o assisti dezenas de vezes e mantenho sob protecao e cuidado absoluto um DVD, que nao e HD, com o status de intocavel. E a musica do ABBA, Dancing Queen! Absolutamente nostalgico e cativante. Esses pequenos detalhares ja me cativaram. E olha que eu ainda nao mencionei um prologo arrepiante em homenagem ao Conde de Monte Cristo. 
 Agora, Jay, o heroi, merece uma mencao honrosa. Inteligente, carismatico, charmoso, sexy, engracado, misterioso e absurdamente lindo. E um pacote completo de beleza masculina com direito a olhar hipnotizante. 
 Nem preciso mencionar que ele e um ilusionista. Sim, essa e a grande sacada da autora, o que singulariza este livro, diferenciando-o de muitos. Jay conquista o leitor assim como ele conquista seu publico. E apaixonante e surreal. 
 Mas nada disso faria sentido se nao fosse a trama bem amarrada, dificil de ser descoberta em todas as suas nuances. Significa dizer que a autora consegue a proeza de manter a tensao e o segredo ate 95% do livro e nada acontece por acaso. 
 O heroi esta determinado a colocar e executar um plano de vinganca sem falhas, que nem mesmo Sherlock Holmes descobriria. 
 Faltou muito pouco para o livro ser perfeito. Acho que houve um preciosismo no inicio do romance, um quero nao quero desnecessario, mas posso garantir que nao falta aquela quimica gostosa regada a uma tensao sexual de retirar o folego. 
 Mais do que recomendado. 4/5/5

This book had its fair share of issues. But guess what? 
 I really advise going into this book pretty blind. The only part of the plot I knew came from the blurb. Of course, within a few chapters, I pretty much had an idea of how the book was going to go (minus a few details and a reveal or two along the way). All you need to know is that Jay Fields is a magician illusionist and that he is determined to have the heroine's father as his lawyer in a defamation lawsuit. Except it isn't just simple. What in life is that simple? Jay is out for revenge. Revenge for himself, and revenge for those he cares about. He has a master plan and no one is really privy to it until the time is right. Honestly, the mystery of it all was one of my favorite parts of this book. While some things were fairly easy to piece together, others really weren't. That would normally bug the hell out of me. Unless it's a mystery novel, I don't really enjoy spending most of a book in the dark. I mean, I'm not one of those people that read the ending first or anything, I just like to have a decent idea of where a book is going. I made an exception for this book and I loved it. I loved it all. 
 There were so many times that Jay came off as just...too much. I didn't care. There is a reason I stopped reading contemporary romance for so long. I really enjoy super intense romance and when it's just run of the mill contemporary I feel like it comes off as either entirely forced or really really stalkerish. This book was such a great example of doing that all so well. Jay had a lot of traits that only work in a romance novel. He was super possessive, manipulative, really intense, jealous, and had secrets galore. I mean, he actually admitted to following her. He was pretty much a walking red flag. Didn't matter, I'd let him call me "darlin'" any day. Jay and Matilda's relationship bordered on mate-like. Like paranormal romance mate kinda thing. Their romance was instant and all-consuming. Jay had already decided that she was his and he would never change his mind on that. 
 He leans his face in agonizingly slowly, then tells me in a gravelly, possessive, stomach flipping voice, "Because you're mine." 
 In the real world? Run Forest, run. In this book? 
 Bloody hell, it was just so damn hot. Sure, Matilda had a moment or two of complete stupidity but once again, it did nothing to lessen my enjoyment of this book. I'm not really sure anything could have. 
 I realize this is basically me explaining in a million different ways that regardless of any issues I had I loved every minute of it, but I just can't help it. This book is a pure guilty pleasure that I would happily read again and again. So yeah, just read it. Read it and enjoy it and try not to pick apart every little thing that might not work if it were in any other book. It just worked. 
 "We both know that mystery is better than the truth. So why not live with the magic? Be a kid again and believe in the fantastical. Life is more fun with a little smoke and mirrors." 
 Yes, yes it is.

Seriously?!?! Seriously, LH Cosway?!?! You blow my mind every. Single. Time! 
 Jay Fields is an illusionist with a well laid out plan. Matilde is just trying to get through the workday as an assistant in her dad's office, then get home and work on the clothing she sells on the side. When Jay walks into her dad's office and ends up becoming their 'roommate', things start to get interesting. She starts falling, how can she not! The only issue is that the more time she spends with him the more she realizes he's hiding too much. 
 I know I'm always in for a treat when reading an LH Cosway book. The banter is always hilarious. The men are always sexy. The story is always unique.

I didn't have high hopes for this after the miserable failure that Painted Faces was for me. However, in some respects, it did surpass that book. For example, Jay didn't press his junk up against Matilda's rear mere hours after they met. Also, Matilda had a habit of calling out Jay's crappy behavior. 
 That's where the good stuff stops, and it isn't much to recommend a book anyway. 
 The author seems fond of "knowing" what the reader is thinking. Yet every single time she does this in the text, she's wrong. She never knows what I'm thinking or what I want to know in the story. 
 These last couple of weeks I've been making my debut into the hazardous world of online dating, and right now I'm staring at my computer screen, trying to figure out if this latest "suitor" is serious or just seriously taking the piss. What does he look like? I hear you ask? 
 Um... I wasn't at all curious about what he looks like. I want to know why you think he might be taking the piss, obviously. 
 A track starts up, blasting through the speakers, and I immediately recognise the song: "Till I Collapse" by Eminem. What? I had a rap phase. 
 So? Am I supposed to think it's weird that she knows an Eminem song? Am I supposed to assume that Matilda would never listen to rap? 
 Dad calls "hello" to him and continues on his way downstairs, none the wiser about his daughter hiding within and her slatternly ways. Yeah, I'm bringing back the word "slattern." Deal with it. 
 Please, just stop. No one cares. 
 Now, on to the characters. I found Matilda to be kind of an idiot, prone to stunning observations such as each card in blackjack has "its own numerical value" and that a drawing on the sidewalk is done in "some sort of chalky substance" (like, maybe, chalk?). She also freaks out when Jay walks into the room "topless." Also, when she was getting ready to go see Jay perform, he told her not to wear her earrings (a request which she never even questioned, like a man telling her not to wear earrings on a night out is totally normal). Later, at the show, Jay does a trick where the key to handcuffs ends up in Matilda's ear like an earring. Her reaction? 
 "You told me not to wear earrings. You planned this," I whisper in reply. 
 BRILLIANT DEDUCTION, WATSON. 
 And then: 
 "Can I come visit you later?" 
 "You mean like how you visited me last night?" I ask, one eyebrow raised, a half smirk on the go. 
 "Kind of like that. Perhaps there'll be a little more activity this time." 
 Well, I don't need to be a sex addict to know what that means. 
 What the hell does sex addiction have to do with anything? I mean... 
 Matilda wasn't perfect, but my issues with her pale in comparison to my issues with Jay. He was SUCH a douche. Immature too, in a way that's not appealing or cute, even though that's clearly how the author intended him. He's repeatedly described as charming, when he's actually obnoxious. 
 "Well, it's not like I'd mind if there was sex involved. It's just that i never seems to get that far. Michelle says it's because I don't give out vibes of availability. I give out 'stay away from me' vibes." I laugh lightheartedly. 
 "Nothing wrong with that," says Jay. "Your friend sounds like she wants you to act like a slut." 
 I scowl. "Uh, no. That's not it at all. Michelle is very supportive of me." 
 "If you say so." 
 Yeah. So charming. 
 At one point, Matilda chooses to ignore what Jay is talking about in regards to women calling him Jason in the bedroom. 
 "You want women to call you by your full name while they clean out your underwear drawer? That is a strange fetish, Jason." 
 "Nope. I clean out my own underwear drawer, Watson. This is what I'm talking about." He puts on a breathless, heaving voice several notes higher than his actual one, "Oh, Jason, you're a god. Fuck me harder, Jason. Jason, you're the biggest I've ever had. Make me come, Jason." 
 Brb, swooning. 
 Jay's flirting technique: 
 "Sometimes I go with: 'Do you know what you're doing later? No? That's funny, 'cos I do.'" 
 A burst of laughter escapes me. "You're joking! That works?" 
 He nods his head. "Yup. Like a charm." 
 Texts from Jay when Matilda is going on a date with a guy she met online: 
 Jay: Oh come on, Watson. Don't leave me hanging. 
 Jay: Still waiting... 
 Jay: He better not try to touch your boobies. 
 Jay: Fine. I know when I'm not wanted. 
 Jay: Only joking. Everybody wants me. ;-) 
 He calls Matilda's perfectly nice date a douche for no apparent reason other than he's jealous. Hello, pot kettle black. Besides, jealousy isn't an attractive quality. 
 But enough about Jay. The book itself just sucked. It was so clumsily put together, with a bunch of pointless scenes in the beginning and Jay's court trial tacked on at the end. The book would have been served much better to stretch the trial out over the course of the book, interspersed with scenes furthering the romance. Not to mention it would have been more interesting that way, because damn, was this boring at times. The romance was just so dull, with dumb drama and dumb excuses to get the leads in the same room. So dumb. There are also random fucking scenes that served no purpose whatsoever. Like when Jay and Matilda have to leave having drinks in order to rescue Jay's friend Jessie from a potentially dangerous situation, they stop by Matilda's house so she can change from her dress into "some jeans, a T-shirt, and plimsolls." They go rescue Jessie, then everyone goes home. Matilda never got out of the car. What is the effing point of making a stop so she can change, when someone needs their help? 
 UGGGGHHHHHH I just disliked this so much. I really wanted to DNF but I was curious about Jay's whole plan (which he went about in a really stupid way, and stupidly jeopardized it by running his mouth during mediation). It was kind of interesting to see how it all came together, but at the same time, it was annoying to read how he and Matilda judged the shit out of Una Harris based on her appearance and choice to have plastic surgery. Judge her for being a piece of shit, not because she's a "desperate" older woman who dresses nicely and gets Botox. Fuck. 
 I didn't even get to talk about the fact that Jay was an annoying magician along the lines of Criss Angel or David Blaine. Or that he stalked Matilda and got a tattoo in her honor before even talking to her. There was just so much nope in this book. 
 1 star.

4 Stars!!! 
 I finally found a New Adult/Adult book that hooked me from the start, original, creative and different! Lately I wasn't having so much luck with this genre... 
 Jay Fields. That was my favorite part of the book. The man was just amazing. I loved the way he's looking for revenge, and I totally adored the way she acted towards Matilda. 
 She was a nice heroine too, she didn't get on my nerves and I respected her character and personality a lot. The chemistry between Jay and her was so obvious, but not in a bad way. Even though she was attracted to him, she still looked for someone else for herself. I found amazing the way her relationship with Jay develops. They take the time to know each other and create a friendship before anything else, and the rest just felt natural to me, nothing forced. 
 There were some things from Jay that I didn't understand, but he was so full of mystery and we get to understand everything towards the end. 
 And yeah, maybe it was almost predictable from the start, but there were still some facts that surprised me and I didn't expect. I really liked the way the story ends, everything makes sense and I felt so much respect and admiration for Jay. It was so good. 
 This was my first book by L.H. Cosway, and it won't be the last one for sure. The sex scenes were awesome, so well written, and the sexual tension was palpable and exciting. A good and sexy read that I recommend and you'll definitely enjoy.

This book has a lot of potentials. I love how J.A. Redmerski created something different compared to other romantic and contemporary novels. At first, I expected the story to be quite dull and boring. Two strangers traveling together? It sounds cool but I don't think it encourages romance between the two characters, yet I was wrong because all the while, the romantic development between Camry and Andrew was fascinating. 
 The first portions of the book was quite slow and a bit tedious but during the middle part, the real picture of the love story was clearer, so somehow I was able to determine the real sense of the plot. 
 The interesting part of the story is how the author introduced the characters. Camryn, a 20 year-old girl, is in a soul-searching mission and she needed to get away from home and travel alone to find her share of happiness after dealing with difficult circumstances of her life. Andrew, on the other hand, is also in the same boat with Camryn. So it's not at all difficult to make a connection for the two characters. 
 Actually, I love Camryn and Andrew. Their chemistry is very evident and I think they're perfect together. They share the same passion most especially when it comes to music. Their story isn't also an "insta-love" kind of thing since they first got along each other before they actually fell in love. 
 What serves as a drawback here is that there are scenes that are way too hard to believe. I understand that this is a work of fiction but I also get the point that it's also based on reality. But I rather found some scenes quite overly exaggerated. It's also hard to believe that Andrew or Camryn will instantly trust each other after what, two days of being together at the bus? 
 Their friendship-turned-into-relationship thing is special, yet their emotional and sexual dependence to each didn't sit well on me. I also think there's an emotional obsession between them and for me, it's not at all healthy. I can't imagine how Camryn could not breathe without Andrew. It seems to me like she really can't survive the rest of her trip without him. I don't think that's a good character development. 
 Anyways, the book is great. One thing I do appreciate about it is the fact that it's VERY WELL WRITTEN. There's humor to it and most parts are entertaining. And also, the romance is scorching hot you will definitely be carried away. I also didn't expect the twist at the near-end chapter. Whoa, didn't expect that coming! 
 This book, by the way, is the first book of the sequel so there's a second book waiting, The Edge of Always - which is the thing that I'm going to read anytime real soon. :)

sample_reviews.review_text: I went into this book kinda skeptically because I had heard it wasn't that great by a few people. It was hard to get into. It took 4-5 chapters before I wasn't totally confused by what was going on. After that, the story really picked up for me. I know that lots of people don't like this as much as Twilight, but to me, it is like comparing apples to oranges... I totally loved this book. I was amazed that she could keep the ending in suspense until right at the very end. I knew it would go one of two ways, but I didn't know which way she would go. I also knew that I could totally hate the book or love it depending on how she ended it. I was happy with the way she ended the book although there were some things I would change but it was a good enough ending to make me like the book overall. I would love to discuss this with anyone else who has read it, but I don't want to give any spoilers in this review.

All right. On the one hand, Stephenie Meyer drives me crazy. On the other hand, even though the premise isn't original, I think we all have to admit that she can write an exciting story. I know non-readers who've gone through hundreds of pages of her books in just a couple days, and you have to appreciate that. 
 But back to the first hand, on which I will ask this question: Am I the only one who is sick to death of reading female protagonists who are so self-deprecating that they honestly cannot process the idea that someone could care about them? As soon as I started this book I was regretting that I'd read Twilight first, because I knew that having read Bella Swan for four books was going to make me have less patience with Wanderer. I just get so tired of reading characters who say things like this: 
 "It bothered me that someone else had suffered for my silence--even someone who had once tried to kill me. This was not how torture was supposed to work." Page 182, when the man she's in love with has just tried to punch her but hit another man instead, because the second man (who once tried to kill her himself, actually choking her until she almost passed out) got in the way. She's upset that the guy who'd tried to kill her got hurt. 
 "My legs felt hollow, numb. Did it have to be Jared? It would be so much easier for Jamie if Kyle were the one to kill me." Page 273, when--once again--she thinks the man she loves is about to kill her, and is only worried about how it will affect her younger brother Jamie if Jared is the one to kill her. Our protagonist is always trying to literally sacrifice herself to avoid bringing anyone else pain. 
 "He grinned again. 'I feel silly standing here with my arms empty while you lug these around. Chalk it up to gallantry.' His words troubled me, and I followed him in silence. Why should gallantry apply to me?" Page 284, when she's been with the group of humans for long enough that most of them are friendly with her now. 
 "Maybe I should have run the other way. But no one was holding me back now, and though his voice was cold and angry, Jared was calling to me." Page 290, when she thinks Jared has finally come to kill her--and just after she's been telling someone that wouldn't it be better for Jamie if they just killed her now, because won't it be harder for him the longer she's alive? 
 The parts about saving the lives of her enemies (which she does at least three times) are made fairly understandable by the fact that she's a member of a peaceful, incredibly gentle alien race. The parts about her standing in front of a man who's literally on his way to kill her and only being able to think about how beautiful he is, not so much. 
 Then there's the fact that to Stephenie Meyer, the ideal man appears to be one who: 
 --is several years older than his teenage love interest, 
 --struggles against his overwhelming desire to kill her, and 
 --uses his physical strength to control her against her will (because he loves her so much and is concerned for her safety)(which actually makes sense in Meyer's twisted world because we've already established that the protagonist has literally not one single instinct to save her own life). I just think these books are giving us a really disturbing insight into the author's mind. 
 Basically, don't bother with this unless you already love Twilight, in which case you'll probably love The Host, too. Otherwise, it's not worth the number of times you'll want to smash your head against a wall.
"Science fiction for people who don't like science fiction"...but not for people who like complex fiction.

I read The Host after reading the Twilight series - I actually really enjoyed it in comparison. While it still won't make my list of favourite books, I'm willing to re-read it, and that's what matters to me. 
 Reread 17/11/2012 
 While absolutely not even close to the best science fiction I've ever read, I nonetheless enjoy The Host as a simple, casual read. I'll start with the cons I listed in my notebook, as they outweigh the pros IMO: 
 Romance really annoys me, no matter what the setting is. There's very few exceptions to this. Granted, I can appreciate it if it's well done, but I don't necessarily enjoy it or search for it in a story. The Host reminded me very much why I don't really like it - the initial romance between Mel and Jared, for example, pops up out of pretty much nowhere. It was a 'hey you're a woman, hey I'm a man LET'S MAKE OUT NOW' sort of deal, and it never felt authentic to me. Just really choppy and awkward. 
 It sort of carries through when Wanderer inhabits Mel's body and she also begins to have these feelings forced upon her. I was (and still sort of am) kind of confused about how the whole emotions affecting the soul thing was working, and the whole thing felt really...just thin, or at least underdeveloped. 
 Mel (while inhabited by Wanderer) also couldn't settle on any sort of opinion about Jared once they joined the rebels - one minute she was doe-eyed, insisting he could do no wrong, the next minute calling him out for being a 'pig' and totally wrong about something. Uh? It was both confusing and incredibly irritating, and I found myself sighing and reading through the bits that Mel pops up when Jared is around quickly, just to get it over and done with. 
 The introduction of the fellow rebel caste right at the end of the book is so sudden and rushed that it felt like a last minute addition, maybe as some sort of plot-turn to hook people into thinking they'll be a sequel, just in case. It seemed pointless to me. 
 All in all, I found the majority of the characters as flat as hell. Nothing stood out about the three main guys - Jamie, Jared, Ian - and Mel/Wanderer were both just kind of boring. Mel's hot temper was a nice balance for her character, but of course, we never really got to see it in anything more than her shouting at Wanda for one reason or another. It would've been nicer to see what sort of trouble it could've gotten them into, if only to push along some sort of character development for somebody. The only character I can truly say I really enjoyed was Jeb, and he seemed to just melt away into the background in the second half of the book. 
 And one more, minor little thing that made me want to pull my hair out - Jamie's infection, when his leg gets cut. They're so busy going on and on about not having antibiotics to treat it, yet it's mentioned not even pages before that they have honey. Which is antiseptic and antibacterial and great for treating wounds. I don't want to assume they had salt as well - another way to treat an infection. Doc should've known this, and it annoyed the hell out of me for the rest of the book. It isn't hard to take a minute to Google 'home remedies for an infection' - if only to rule such easy options out. 
 As for the pros: 
 The quality of writing was neither good nor bad in my opinion - it was just writing to convey a story, which is not necessarily a good thing. Sometimes I felt like I was reading someone's homework essay instead of a book. Though, despite the flatness of it, I didn't feel it tried too hard to be something it wasn't. Instead of trying to write absolutely amazingly (and likely fail horribly in the process), the author stuck with her comfort zone and tried to make the best of it. It won't ever be in the top ten of great writing examples, but it had that at least. 
 It was interesting to see Wanderer learning more about humans as the story progressed. Again, it's not a super detailed in-depth analysis of the human nature, but it's interesting enough to see things written from a different perspective. Though she seemed to get a little extreme at times (bouncing between 'her' humans being monsters or not) it was probably what I enjoyed most about the book. 
 All in all, it was an okay read. Nothing special. If you're hardcore into sci-fi, you probably won't like it at all - but everyone is different! 
 The Host is definitely leagues ahead of the Twilight series though.

I couldn't do it. I made it 32 pages into the book and had to stop. Maybe it gets better as the book goes on and the 18 year old writer protagonist matures. But I didn't find it worth going through the beginning to get there. It reads like a teenager wrote it, and maybe Scott Westerfeld intended it that way. The descriptions are bland, the interactions over the top cheesy and the dialogue painfully to the point or cliche. 
 My impression is that it's meant to encourage young writers to participate in NaNoWriMo, and give them hope that their novel will one day be published. (Which I support, as long as the author does a lot of self-editing before submitting it anywhere) But if this is the writing style that he's claiming will be picked up by big New York publishers, then I worry about the future of YA publishing. If fact, I cringe that this book is being published and will do well just because it has Scott Westerfeld's name on the cover.

El padre le dice: "pero, podes escribir en tu tiempo libre y aun ir a college" "No, escribi la novela en un mes y casi me mata" (WTF!!!???) 3.5/5 
 This book took me almost a month to get through. A month! Now, it wasn't because I didn't enjoy it or anything (I really did enjoy it!), but I think just the mere size of it was so daunting, that it was constantly putting me off from reading, and thus I landed in quite a reading slump. Not wanting to give up on a book half-way through, I managed to sit myself down and push my way through. 
 Afterworlds is unlike anything else that I've ever read before. It's basically two stories in one. One of the stories is about Darcy Patel, who has put her life and college on hold in order to move to New York and focus on publishing her first novel, Afterworlds. The second story is that of Lizzie Scofield. Lizzie is the protagonist of Darcy's novel, who after surviving a terrorist attack, develops the ability to see and interact with ghosts, and travel to the 'Flipside'. 
 Each chapter alternates between Darcy's and Lizzie's stories, so at the end of each chapter, you are just kind of hungry for more and want to know what happens next! So for me, once I sat myself down to read it, it became a real page-turner, and I managed to get through it a lot faster. 
 I absolutely adored Lizzie's story. I wish that it had been a whole book on it's own. I would love to read more about her, and know what happens next. Darcy, on the other hand, could be quite rather annoying at times, but I still enjoyed her story all the same, despite how unrealistic the publishing side of the story is. But hey, that didn't really bother me so much. 
 All-in-all, this was an enjoyable book, and I would recommend it to those that want something a little different, with a light paranormal tone. Just maybe don't go in with high expectations, especially if (from what I've heard) you're a fan of Scott Westerfeld's other work. But hey, don't listen to me. This is the first of his books that I've read before, and I hope to pick up another someday soon!

A disappointing book written by a usually reliable author, Afterworlds is actually two full-length novels inter-cut with each other. The first is a tiresome wish-fulfillment fantasy for wannabe writers, depicting an 18 year-old author, Darcy Patel, who moves to New York City after selling her first manuscript. The second is the novel Darcy has written - a bland supernatural romance about a girl who discovers the ability to see ghosts. 
 Let's start with Darcy. Darcy's story is totally devoid of conflict and therefore the most boring story I have ever read. She gets everything she wants without any effort whatsoever. She gets $300,000 dollars for a crappy first draft she wrote in a month, she moves to NYC and finds the perfect apartment, everyone loves her books - from her instant girlfriend to distinguished authors she barely knows, she goes on an amazingly successfully pre-publicity tour, blah, blah, blah, blah. Honestly, the only obstacle that Darcy ever faces is the occasional slight insecurity which she quickly overcomes. She's the most boring character of all time! She never faces any hurdles; she never has to try particularly hard. This fact is made ever more deeply ironic because at one point in the story Darcy tries to convince a crowd that conflict is the most important element in any story! Maybe the author should have listened to his own advice and actually included some conflict in Darcy's story. 
 I appreciate that Westerfeld has tried to show what "real" YA writing is like - the pressure from editors to make books marketable, the long delay before publication, the pressure to write sequels, the total necessity of publicity and networking. All that is great. But without any conflict, Darcy's story is just a series of unengaging events. By the end, I was actively irritated by her for getting everything she ever dreamed of without any cost or consequence. 
 In addition, while I appreciate the gesture of a 50 year-old straight white man deciding to write a teen lesbian romance about a woman of colour, I was utterly underwhelmed by Darcy and Imogen's romance. Most everything about their relationship was unconvincing, inauthentic and unmoving. I don't want to criticise Westerfeld for attempting to write a YA lesbian romance - the world most definitely needs more of them - but I honestly wished he cared enough to make the romance real, not some ridiculously diluted-down version of lesbian romance written by a straight man for a presumably straight audience. 
 And as for the story Darcy writes... Well, that's a whole different level of atrocious. Darcy's novel about Lizzie Scofield, a teenage girl who survives a terrorist attack and acquires the ability to see ghosts, has got to be the most horrendously generic supernatural romance I have ever read in my entire life. Lizzie's love interest has no personality whatsoever - he's a hot guy who shows up and Lizzie falls instantly in love with him. There's no substance whatsoever to their relationship, just PG-rated kisses. Lizzie's relationship with him isn't even that relevant to the plot and plays such a minor role it could easily be dropped entirely. 
 Lizzie's friendship with the ghost of a murdered girl takes up much more time and it's also more emotionally engaging and actually drives events. Except that Lizzie's story is so shapeless! She gains the ability to see ghosts and then hangs out in her house for a while. Every time she gets into a problematic situation she just summons her hot boyfriend to save her instead of solving things herself. Lizzie appears to have a few plot goals involving a serial killer and a ghost collector, but even those plot lines turn out to be too brief and insubstantial to amount to much. And THIS is the story that all the characters in Darcy's story are crazy about!? It's absurd! 
 The worst part is that Westerfeld is very obviously aware of the shortcomings of his book, but he just doesn't care. The book features a lot of meta-commentary about YA writing in general and, in particular, about cultural appropriation. Darcy wonders if it's okay to include a Hindu god in her story "for the purposes of YA hotness." But the book never properly resolves this issue, nor acknowledges that it's actually 
 Scott Westerfeld 
 who has appropriated a Hindu god into his story for the purposes of YA hotness. Lampshading a trope doesn't suddenly make it okay. Lampshading is not a get-out-of-jail-free card. 
 And what's more, there's very little point to inter-cutting the two stories. They never really influence each other; they never intertwine; they are always merely the sum of their substandard parts. I was longing for the moment that the two stories would mesh together and become some mind-bendingly post-modern self-parody of YA literature. That was honestly the only thing that could have saved this book. Alas, Scott Westerfeld is not so self-aware. 
 This book has totally changed my opinion on Scott Westerfeld. Previously I saw him as a solid, varied writer who occasionally misses the mark. Now I see him as a mediocre, generic writer who occasionally finds a decent idea. This is definitely one of Westerfeld's worst.

book_b.user_review: This story is beautiful it shall stay with you forever. THIS IS LITERATURE!

sample_reviews.review_text:
I'm not sure about how to review this novel. I always feel terrible when I have to give a novel or book less than three stars. I'm too empathetic in that sense; I just think about all the effort the author must've put in their novel, like coordinating and constructing the proper structure for their plot, how to arrange the dialogues and finding the proper words to express what they want their characters to say, finding ways to develop their emotions and conveying a believable synergy to the reader among other things. When I think about all these things I feel both bad and amazed, the prime because I didn't like the novel and the author put effort into it and I feel bad for disliking it, the latter because, well, the effort must've been big. However, I cannot force myself to like a novel, and I just didn't like this one. 
 The spiritual and metaphysical basis of "The Alchemist" seems to be a combination of Christianity, Pantheism, Mysticism and every speech any public motivator would want to deliver an audience. The novel sums up in the following words: " 
 Follow your dreams and do not give up, no matter what the circumstances are. 
 " 
 I almost feel as if Darth Vader was trying to say in the most polite and protracted way possible: " 
 Use the force, Luke! 
 " 
 Unfortunately, I consider this novel to be filled with the trite, over-used and hypersensitive phrases we have all heard before: "Don't give up!" "Follow your dreams!" "You can do anything you want!", and that's simply not my cup of tea. I like cold, hard truths and different point of views, not recycled phrases I can read on-line. Now, with all that being said, I'm not certain if Coelho's objective was to help his readers grow and feel more confident about themselves, or if he simply wanted to use demagogy at its finest to win his readers and have a larger audience for his next novels. Quite frankly, this novel is both demagogic and boringly trite, so in short words: I didn't like this novel. One star.

Not sure I get the hang of this book or interpret the message Paulo Coelho is trying to make her. 
 Follow your destiny? Never give up? Do what you love? Clueless!!

The Alchemist is a story about a boy who was a shepherd, found out his Personal Fortune was to find a treasure in Egypt, and had to decide whether to follow this Personal Fortune or stay where he was comfortable. The book was written like a YA book with simple language, proselytizing, and mercifully short. Everyone except for one character was unnamed, the main character was "the boy", which made me wonder how old he was. No character is fully developed, everyone is rather flat. The section with the boy and the alchemist was the worst part. It was boring, drawn out, and the "God" talk and "turning yourself into the wind" was ridiculous. The ending was okay, but the rest of the book was so bad, it didn't shore up.

Madeline is a fearless little girl living in what appears to be an orphanage in Paris. One night Madeline has an emergency appendectomy and all of the other girls are envious that Madeline has had such an adventure. This story grew on me, because I wasn't sure that I liked it the first time that I read it. Even though it is a Caldecott Honor book I don't really like the pictures. They feel sloppy to me.
One of my much loved picture books as a child.... Beautiful and bright illustrations.

This is a charming story told in rhyme about little Madeline who has to have her appendix out. My son likes the rhythm and rhyme of the book. Some of the pictures are rather bland, but what makes the illustrations unique are the depictions of Paris (where the story takes place) and the key at the back of the book identifying famous landmarks. If you love Paris, you will thoroughly enjoy teaching your children about it's sites. 
 As Madeline is living in a Paris boarding school for girls (making all the main characters girls), the subject matter may be more appealing for girls than boys. It should also be noted that while it is not elaborated upon (at least not in this work), both the boarding school and hospital where Madeline is tended appear to be run by nuns, indicating a Catholic influence. Kids may have questions about how/ why the women are dressed in habits.
An old standby when I can't find anything else that I feel like reading to K-2 classes.

Hace mucho tiempo encontre este libro cuando estaba buscando por libros del estilo de Dr Seuss y otros grandes de literatura infantil. Este libro aparecio pero no lo pude encontrar en pdf y no persevere.

 Lo lei entero y la verdad es que no me gusto nada. Cero moraleja y cero ensenanza. 
 Le daria una estrella pero los dibujos eran hermosos y es lo que mas destaco. 
 Cero recomendable.

Ah Madeline, how I remember you. I'm probably biased because I adored the TV show as a kid but I never got to read the books. There is a whole series of these books where Madeline goes on adventures but this one is very sweet on its own. It is a rhyming book which is always a plus and the illustrations are very nice too. 
 The first story of Madeline introduced us to the old house in Paris that is covered in vines and we get a nice introduction to the 12 little girls and their world. Madeline is shown as a strong and independent little girl and she is very brave compared to those around her. But poor Madeline is not immune to everything as the story shows. 
 If you want to take anything out of this story it is a bit hard besides showing a strong character, the rest of the series bring in new events and people to interact with that probably can show lessons and morals if you needed them, but for now this is just a great story about a dear little girl. 
 The Madeline books are a great and you do want to keep reading about all the other adventures they have and the introduction of even more characters. For kids this would be a great book, as would the remainder of the set, and as an adult it still brings a smile to my face as we watch Miss Clavel get flustered and panicked whenever Madeline tries to have any fun.

On a recent morning the grandmothers got into a contest: who can remember more of Madeline by heart. They both did very well. My wife and I are getting there. Madeline means a lot to us, partly because we grew up with it, and partly because on our kid's stomach is also a scar - his guts were like all in the wrong place or whatever - so it has Special Meaning for us. 
 I'm the one on the left. I know it's hard to tell. 
 But also it means a lot to our kid, who if you show him Madeline and any other book in the world will definitely pick Madeline, and if you show him two different books he may very well just complain until you go get Madeline. He loves this book, and we don't know why. He doesn't speak English and he's never been to Paris. Maybe he likes that Joanne and I collapse in hysterics every time we get to the doctor dialing DAN-ton ten six, which by the way is also the name of our imaginary children's band, but this is far from the only children's book that makes us collapse in hysterics. We think he has an eye for design - he also likes Charley Harper and Andy Warhol, don't ask, or go ahead and ask, what do I care, the answer is we're pretentious - so maybe it's just those terrific evocative scribbles of Bemelmans'. They're incredible, right? This one is my favorite, Notre Dame in rain. 
 Who cares why, anyway, this is Nathan's very first favorite book and he has impeccable taste so far. Some day maybe he'll read it to his kid, and he'll know it by heart too.
