reference_books.title: Rock Me (Ross Siblings, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
So on the advice of numerous people, I skipped the first book in the series and went straight to rock me. And I have to say that I liked it a lot. Brian is awesome. Hard and pierced and tattooed on the outside, sweet and kind and insecure on the inside. He always knew the right words to say to make everything better for everyone, and though he and his family seem to have a tumultuous relationship, he is so independent and strong it didn't really phase him. Now for most of the book I thought Candance was a typical female lead, she was innocent, naive, and in my opinion wanting attention, but then again like I said, typical. But for the last 25% I thought she wanted too much from Brian, he kept having to give, and give, and give, and without really getting anything in return. Now I think that there should be some kind of middle ground in relationships. That said the sex, was HOTT, every interaction between these two in the first 75% of this book, was had me on fire. Brian was just to good at what he does, and on top of that the descriptions of the piercing (which I had to look up) and what they do, had me drooling over one of these guys in ways that I never thought I would. 
 Overall for a quick, SMUTTY read, sure give it a go

reference_books.title: Witness in Death (In Death, #10)
reference_books.review_text:
Another amazing book in this series, I love every moment I spend with this cast. Roarke and Eve are not officially my fave couple in the contemporary literature world. They are just so real, in all their imperfections and flaws, and I love that they still stumble in their relationship, and even the amazing Roarke still stumbles. They make this series so damn additive. 
 I also love how the secondary characters are taking on their own life in this book. Peabody is becoming just as awesome as Eve, and I love that her love life is this complicated, and fun. I also like that Eve is opening up so much to the people around her, her character development is great, its clear the the author has planned this is series with the utmost care. 
 I listened to the audiobook, and I am addicted to these audiobooks!

reference_books.title: Covet (Covet, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Covet is a magnificent book. It is a moving, emotion-driven story about what can happen to normal people under what is sadly becoming normal circumstances. But at its very core, I believe that Covet is a book about love. And how the lack of showing love for each other can have some terrible consequences. I think that Ms. Garvis-Graves has another masterpiece on her hands. She has crafted the kind of characters that are all heroes and all villains, and it really does push your ethical and moral boundaries, but in the end, I think it tells such a realistic story, there are no fantasy endings, its just so honest, and real and raw, and I loved that about this book. 
 There were some really unique attributes to this book. But I think the one thing that really stood out for me was the fact that there were three points-of view. I think that aspect really set this books apart from others with a similar theme. The multiple POVs ensured that there was no villain and no hero. This is a story about how things can go wrong in marriage, and how much work it can take to make it all got right. I think knowing what all the different characters were thinking all the time, really helped me to understand why they were making the decisions that they were. It made this book feel more well rounded, because you knew what everyone was thinking and feeling, and I think thats one of the reasons this book is so unique. 
 My buddy who I was reading with (yes Angie you!) said that I had to read carefully, because the emotions were more important than that dialogue and I totally agree with that evaluation. The truth is that the characters were hardly ever upfront about what they were feeling. And I think that is true about most people, we are afraid that by being honest, we will hurt the other person, when in fact if we are honest, it will make the relationship so much easier. I think TGG is very good at pointing out these universal character defects in most of us. But the emotions, the inner dialogue is so amazing in this book. I felt for each character. i understood where they were coming from, and where they wanted to go. 
 Funny moments: the masseuse, i'm worried santa won't bring me presents 
 Supporting cast: I think the supporting characters were so well put together in this book. And the plot really supported the way the reader and Claire got to know the truth about the relationships of her neighbours. I loved Elise and I loved how honest she was about all the things that she and her husband went through. She really was such a great friend to Claire. Then there was Julia and Justin, who on the surface seemed to have it all, but we quickly found out that there is more to it than what meets the eye. Sam and Bridget, I thought had the most visible issues, and even they put on a front a lot of the times. But I really liked how everything worked out, and how we got to learn about the secrets behind those doors. 
 Daniel: So if Daniel was a police officer here, I'm sure he'd not be giving out very many tickets lol. He is super hot, and for most of the book I kept wondering why the hell he was single. But I liked him alot. I thought he was just such a great guy. He was so caring, and kind, and compassionate, he really cared about what went on in Claire's life on an everyday basis. I think he needed someone like Claire, to know that he could be in a relationship again. That he didn't need to be hooking up all the time. That he could love someone, and they could love him back. It sucks that he had to fall for Claire, but I think part of his attraction to Claire had to do with the fact that she reminded him of his ex. Overall though, I feel in love with Daniel just like Claire did. And I saw that there was real chemistry between them. 
 Chris: Chris was a great father. I want to say that first because truth be known thats one of the best things about him. He was a provider, in his mind in order to be happy, he had to be providing every want and need for his family. And that is what made Chris a broken man when we first meet him in the book. He is very broken. And he can't seem to be able to put himself together. I think even more than Claire, Chris was one who we knew had good intentions, but did not know how to go about showing his love for his wife in a tangible manner. But he loves her, as much as he loves his kids, I think that Chris just wanted things to go back to how they were before. And he was so focused on that, he couldn't see how much more damage he was causing. 
 Claire: This is a woman I admire. I think Claire was so strong in all that went down. She was resilient and adaptable, and she let nothing get her down. I think that is what Daniel and Chris saw in her. She was this person who could walk through fire, get burnt, and was willing to do it all over again the next day. She was a good wife, and she tried to be there for Chris in his time of need, but I think I wish she'd pushed him more to talk about what was going on with him. Instead she left things, and then when things got really bad only then did she speak up. I think she should've tried harder to keep the lines of communication open between the two of them. There is no doubt that she loved Chris, but I think Daniel was more open with her, and that attracted her to him. I have to say I don't envy her position, but thought Claire was not always honest with others, she was very honest with herself. And her inner dialogue really helped me understand why she made some of her decisions. 
 Another 5 stars for TGG. I don't think I've read a book about cheating like this before, it takes such skill to be able to tell a story this well. I can't wait to see what topic she tackles next!

reference_books.title: Something About You (FBI/US Attorney, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Loved this book, loved the main character they were so funny, and real. The only thing I didn't like was the fact that the villain was revealed from the get-go. I thought the story would've been better if we didn't know who it was. Other than that, I really liked this book I think it would make it into my re-readables for sure. Quick-paced, and racy, and I love how the relationship bloomed between Cameron and Jack.

reference_books.title: Lovely Trigger (Tristan & Danika, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
No two characters have ever deserved an HEA more. This book was not as hard to read as the last I will admit that. I think RK Lilley has a unique talent to weave stories that are emotionally driven, but have lots of sex in there. Seeing glimpses of Danika and Tristan through the six years they were apart was heart wrenching. It was so clear from their internal dialogue that they were both in so much pain. But still they found the strength to at least attempt to move out with their lives. It was just a great story. 
 Tristan stole my heart from the moment he first reached out to Danika and asked her to be friends. It was clear that he just wanted to have some kind of connection to her. And that he was willing to do whatever it took to make that happen. I love that he gave her time, he was patient, and kind, and jealous as hell. Tristan's love for Danika never faltered, he never questioned whether they should be together, but instead, he tried his damnedest to become a part of her life in any way he could, even if it was being a father figure to her nephew. I think that Tristan above all showed me hope, the kind that survives beyond all shadow of a doubt. And I loved LOVED LOVED his response to Danika's secret, it was by far the best ever. 
 Danika is so different from the carefree young woman I came to know and love in the first two books. She no longer has this 'hell with it' attitude, and instead, she's so careful, and calculating in everything she's done. But once Tristan reenters her life, she becomes Danika again, it was literally impossible for her to say no to him, and she did try, but when they were together, it was like nothing else matter in the universe. I have to say I really loved Danika's strength her ability to try to move on from a really difficult situation. And her forgiving and giving attitude with Tristan. She clearly never wanted to hurt him. 
 I honestly never thought that this book would end with a happy ending that these characters deserves after so much pain and suffering, but the end was better than I could ever dream. I'm so happy they are finally happy.

book_a.title: Lady Luck (Colorado Mountain, #3)
book_a.user_review: Wow this book got waaaaaaaaaaaay serious, and maybe its because Ty is so serious, but it isn't as light hearted as the previous two in the series. That said, it is y favorite so far, i felt that the emotions, conflict and plot were very very real, and I really enjoyed the book. Ty and Lexi both have some seriously tragic lives, and that is felt from the moment u meet them with Ty walking out of a prison after serving 5 years for manslaughter and the first thing he says to her is "Shift knows two kinds of women whores and junkies, you a junkie?" that's the first real conversation that they have, and two days later they are married, so can i just say excellent set up for a wonderful story. Now while tate had a temper, Ty is the kind who does speak often, so when he does speak its very very intense and he cuts deep and hurts. But he cut up a lot of people, but he's also has the sweetest heart ever, and he was the first time that a guy says I love you first, and the moment he does was so beautiful. I also loved the fact that all the characters from the previous books (including my beautiful nina) are part of this book, its wonderful that tho Ty has had a hard life, he has these wonderful people around him.

sample_reviews.review_text: I think this might be one of the better stories by Ashley that I've read.
I'd pick Ty up from the big house any day!

So far Colorado Mountain series has been one of my favorite series. Lady Luck has had more interaction with the other books than any other book so far in the series and I really like getting a dose of the other characters and where they are at in their respective lives and how they intermingle with the story line, Hello- Max and Nina!! (Loved The Gamble). 
 This book starts with Lexi doing a favor for a seedy individual that she is tied to from her dealings with her boyfriend who is deceased. Lexi must pick someone up at a correctional facility in California. Out walks, hotness Ty Walker. Queue- angels singing and porn music at the same time, because KA describes him like a god of yummy hotness. 
 So begins the road trip to Colorado with a stop over to Las Vegas as we find out that Lexi was only given partial information on her "favor" to Shift. Ty needs more from her and she agrees and so starts the web of vengence that Ty is looking to enact as he was wrongly imprisoned for someone else's crime. 
 As the story progresses, the characters fall for each other and who wouldn't fall for Ty. While he remains a man of few words, he dotes on Lexi and it is so hot. Seriously swooning over Ty. The intermingling of other Colorado stories comes into play with Tate, Laurie, Woods, Pops, Stella, The Carnal Police Dept., Max, Nina, and more... 
 Lexi goes to Tate and the others and asks for help for Ty so he doesn't go down the road of revenge but rather the road of legal redemption and restitution. This of course sends Ty over the edge as he trusted her with this information and Ty has major trust issues, i.e. MISTY KEATON and her lying ass. Hence begins Ty and Lexi's seperation and hurt. 
 In swoops Julius to play both of them and bring them back together, all of this while drama is unfolding in California, Texas, and Colorado. 
 In the end, I couldn't be happier with the way the story progressed and my my my, does TY do things for me that are soooo... hot. I also loved the set up with Chase and the beginning of his story. Awesome job KA.

Kids, next vacation... Colorado!

4.5/5.0

book_b.title: Defying the Odds (Battered Hearts, #1)
book_b.user_review: Now this was a really fast, fun, HOTT, sexy read. The two main characters are two people who are both broken (my kind of set up) and this chance meeting where Melody is a waitress working on Thanksgiving who buys a slice of pumpkin pie for the lonely male patron, Clay (love that name btw) who is at the diner where is works, assuming that he has no where else to be much like her. That said tho, I liked the story, but the supporting cast namely Jules and Wyatt were too mean, and too aggressive to a certain extent but I guess since their stories are next it was only an introduction, but I am interested in reading the next book in teh series so overall it was a fun read, just wanted a lil bit more.

sample_reviews.review_text: This was just not my cup of tea. I really didn't connect with any of the characters. On top of that I was so annoyed by Melody and how she was portrayed. Instead of being seen as sheltered and abused she seemed uneducated and plain dumb. There was no angst or real issues in the book. What was the problem or climax? If it was the ex husband then that lasted all of two seconds. Not what I expected.

a very sweet love story.. 
 simple, nice and sweet... 
 looking forward to read star crossed, romeo and juliet...:)

** spoiler alert ** 
 I have a million reasons to complain about this book. Alas, I will stick with the insurmountable issues. 1) the book spans Thanksgiving to Christmas Eve of the same year, so about one month. Within two weeks they were soul mates that swore they always knew they were waiting for the other. I can't even say the romance developed quickly, just one day they were making eye contact and the next she was asking him to spend the night. 
 2) most formulaic plot line ever. Girl leaves husband because he's abusive. Meets someone stronger and bigger and better than ex-husband. Ex hunts her down and tried to kill her, larger-new-better man physically assaults the other man. 
 Aside from the fact that the male lead is only described as white with a MMA build, and she's larger, with glasses covering her green eyes, and she has blonde hair, they are never described in any detail. I don't know how tall they are or anything else. 
 She makes these awkward jokes about how her ex used to rape her, and he responds by mentally wanting to kill him. The entire one month relationship is pathetic. He of course has more money than her, which makes him good enough to build a shelter for battered women, but she continues working as a waitress at a diner
Loved this book. Clay was the perfect hero. Can't wait for the other Battered Hearts books.

***This book was provided by Netgalley in exchange for an honest review.*** 
 I'm sad to say this book didn't do it for me. I just couldn't connect with the characters in this one. Clay and Melody were incredibly naive for the life experiences they'd had, and the supporting characters, Jules and Wyatt, weren't very likable. 
 The descriptions of the love scenes were pretty good, but the dialogue ruined it for me. There's something about a woman saying 'help me' when she's turned on that's a mood killer for me. 
 I thought the 'big showdown' at the end with Melody's ex-husband felt more like an attempt to set things up for the next book than an actual resolution to the story. 
 I just didn't feel invested in the story. This one was a miss. :(

This was a short and sweet book. 
 Loved the underlying themes of abuse and loneliness and it did a good job tackling them and how love can appear in the most unexpected of places. 
 The story was actually good and I loved that the love story was not rushed or anything. Clay and Mel spent a lot of time in each others' orbits before actually entering a relationship and this was really refreshing to read in the era of insta-love. 
 Apart from that, nothing really stood out, but I guess that's a good thing.

I did find myself skipping & skimming over some parts because I started to get bored with it. I was hoping for more of a MMA plot line but it just fell flat. It was a really quick read which was good.
After all the hipe I was extremely disappointed with this book

This book had a really good beginning I was really into it, and then it just lost its momentum for me.

reference_books.title: A Darkness Absolute (Casey Duncan, #2)
reference_books.review_text: According to the author, the first book in this series, City Of The Lost, was originally meant to be a stand alone novel. Boy, am I glad that there will be more! Book 2 was a thrilling read. With interesting characters that I definitely want to read more about. The mystery was a bit dark and gruesome. A very well done and entertaining book.

reference_books.title: The Bear and the Nightingale (The Winternight Trilogy #1)
reference_books.review_text: With all the buzz about this book, I thought I'd give it a try. But unfortunately, I couldn't get into this story. It was too slow, predictable and not very exciting for me. I started skimming after awhile. I just think this wasn't my type of book. If you enjoy a slow burn fairy tale/fantasy type of story, you will probably like this book.

reference_books.title: A Court of Thorns and Roses (A Court of Thorns and Roses, #1)
reference_books.review_text: This book was not what I was expecting at all. The pace was way too slow for me and focused mainly on the romance between Feyre and Tamlin. The writing was good enough, though, to keep me reading. It drew me in enough to want to know what happened. But the book felt long. The last quarter of the book did get more interesting and exciting for me. But I am on the fence about whether I will continue this series.

reference_books.title: Turtles All the Way Down
reference_books.review_text: It took some time for me to get into this book. Aza has crippling anxiety and her thoughts often spiral out of control. It wasn't always easy going down these spirals with her. It was exhausting and mind boggling at times. Her friend Daisy was much needed comic relief. She was funny, loyal and a die hard Star Wars fan, and writer of fan fiction. The part of the story that kept me from putting the book down, were the moments where Aza and Davis were connecting. There were some really great, inspirational quotes, and real feelings bared between these two. This wasn't an easy book to read. But the author did a good job at shining a light on mental illness and first love.

reference_books.title: Camino Island
reference_books.review_text: This was a quick, easy read. I love books about books and/or writers. And this one had both. There was plenty of information about classics, rare books, and famous authors like F. Scott Fitzgerald and Hemingway. This was a pretty straightforward story. Not a lot of suspense or thrill. But it was enjoyable. A good summer read.

book_a.title: Illuminae (The Illuminae Files, #1)
book_a.user_review: I knew this book was different. But decided to give it a try anyway. I listened to this on audiobook. It was a real production with different narrators for each character and sound effects. But this did not help me to enjoy it. It was difficult to follow at first. I missed the details I'd get from a traditional writing style. Some parts were humorous, but I did not get invested in the characters. I am not likely to read anymore. Glad I gave it a try, though. And that I got this from my library!

3.5 stars.

I'm giving it a 3 stars really, but the .5 extra is for the cool visual aspects of the physical book. It kind of translated to the audiobook but it definitely lent itself better to the visual format. 
 And since Gemina isn't really a continuation and from a different point of view, I don't really have any interest in picking it up. I would have if there was more Ezra in Gemina tbh.

DNF 10% 
 I can't with these idiot teenagers.

The format of the book was so different from usual and unlike any i've seen so it was very refreshing. The plot of the story is very interesting, twisting and thrilling, I think it was a great starter for the series and look forward to the sequel.

The hardcover version of Illuminae is stunning, the audio version of Illuminae is stunning, so it should come as no surprise then that the paperback version that just released this week is equally as incredible! For those of you who haven't read this book yet, DO IT! Illuminae is a reading experience unlike any other. 
 I am so thrilled to be participating in the blog tour for the paperback release of Illuminae. Not only because this is one of my very favorite book series, but also because these books have the most innovative approach to storytelling that I've ever experienced, and I was dying to see what the paperback version would be like. 
 I fell in love with the hardcover and getting to visually see the different forms of media this story was told through was just so cool. The audiobook made me cry, and it wasn't even during a super emotional scene in the book. It was just because of how beautifully the story was told. And now this paperback is the perfect addition to the collection for us Illuminae lovers. It would also be a great way to get started in the series if you haven't already. 
 The story that's told within these pages, is every bit as gorgeous and captivating as its exterior. There is a large cast of dynamic characters, and the way that Kristoff and Kaufman switch between the various POVs is expertly done. Reading this book feels like watching a movie, a really, REALLY beautiful movie. 
 The plot is fast-paced, high-stakes, and utterly addictive. There is an awesome romance that actually feels like an authentic teen romance. And the world-building is just on a level of its own. 
 This is probably the only book that I've ever read that I would say readers NEED to experience in multiple formats. I would definitely recommend grabbing a copy of this new paperback and then immediately listening to the audio version afterwards. I have never experienced an audiobook like Illuminae before, nor have I seen a physical book like Illuminae before, and believe me, you don't want to miss out on either version.

3.5 stars 
 Ok, I might be victim of all the hype surrounding this book, but I'm disappointed. I was expecting more. The first 100 pages or so were too confusing, and the following ones were at some points very boring (i.e. too much military strategy, too many detailed descriptions). It was still a pretty good read (I loved the format), but it was not as mind-blowing as I was expecting.

I swear, AIDAN seems to be the male lead in this book, I kid you not. It somehow stole the spotlight from my beloved Ezra in the final chapters. Still, damn, for a lunatic AI, he made me feel a lot of emotions throughout with his poetic binary persona 
 Also, cheers Kady. You are BRILLIANT

Space, Artificial intelligence, warships, romance, action, suspense, deadly virus, zombies, all packed in one book. what else can you really ask for? 
 With the peculiar style of this book, the authors took a risk, and it really paid off. I literally had to turn the book upside down at times to read. it's simply the most gorgeous, creative and unique book I have ever read. It basically is a dossier- a detailed report of events that took place during the battle of karenza, which means you learn about everything through files, reports, emails, cam feeds etc. The book is filled with twists and turns that you will never see coming, and that will keep you on the edge of your seat. 
 "Are you afraid?" 
 "Yes" 
 "The energy never stops, remember. It changes forms." 
 "I am still afraid." 
 The conversation between the AI and our protagonist were so astonishing it melted my heart and made me feel warm, like the words were hugging me tight. 
 "In a time of universal deceit, telling the truth is a revolutionary act." 
 In 2575, the planet Kerenza recieves a surprise visit from a corporation called Beitech, who brings missiles and bombs for the planet where our protagonist, kady and her boyfriend ezra, lives. Kady and Ezra had no idea that their relationship wasn't the only thing that was ending, but their entire planet was on the verge of destruction, the moment the first BieTech warship flew over their head. when the first bomb drops, kady and ezra make a run for their lives and ends up on different space crafts, owned by two different groups. 
 The spacecraft (Alexander) ezra ends up in has a very sophisticated artificial intelligence. It recieves critical damage during Alexander's encounter with BieTech's warships, and when the AI wakes up again, it goes rogue, takes control of the ship and kill a bunch of people who were infected by the virus the bombs had unleashed. For the AI it was mercy killing not a massacre. 
 "Am I not merciful? " 
 In Kady's spacecraft no one has any idea what's going on with Alexander. Kady uses her hacking skills to figure out what her superiors weren't revealing. When she finds out about the virus and AI's malfunction, she decides to help. And That's how the adventure begins my friends. 
 "At the apex of callousness she found zeros and ones. " 
 It took me 3 sittings to finish 600 pages. I have never read anything this fast before. Loved everything about this book and can't wait for next.

Holy Smokes! This was the best book I've listened to, quite possibly, ever! Everyone with a love for sci-fi young adult must (absolutely must) listen to this full production. What does it mean to alive? Who or what can live? And then what happens with death? I can not wait to listen to the second one, Gemina.

This book is definitely very different from the books I'm used to reading. Told through recovered emails, government files, and other documents, this book is essentially 2001: A Space Odyssey meets 28 Days Later meets Star Wars. Illuminae follows Kady and Ezra, two survivors of an attack on their planet, as they race through space away from enemy ships. The book has hackers, space soldiers, conspiracies, zombies, and everything in between. 
 I'm trying not to give too much away here, because I think it's best to go into this book without knowing much. I was looking for a fun and quick read, and I found it. I'm looking forward to the sequel!

Merriam-Webster: 
 CONTRARIAN 
 -a person who takes an opposite or different position or attitude from other people 
 I have always been the unpopular, contrarian, black sheep in the blogosphere. When everybody has been raving about how they freaking loved Eveything Everything, I was sourpussing in the corner. When everybody was held spellbound on Ridge's swoon worthy moves on Maybe Someday, I was eye-rolling the whole time. When everybody has been complimenting The Heartbreakers as the cutest YA contemporary to date, I was posing a facepalm worthy of Asgard. This time, I know I will be put again at the top 10 most unpopular-crummy-pathetic reviews in the blogosphere. Sometimes, I wonder if I'm making any sense at all; but that's perfectly okay for me! :) 
 The first question would be: 
 Am I reading a different book? 
 So why 2 stars? Why not 3, 4, or 5? 
 I ask myself. In the absence of all the alluring graphics and diagrams, look at the story alone. Did I really enjoy the content? Was the twist really mind-blowing? Was this a rereading material for me? Will I be willing to go through an exhausting narration of 2575 interstellar war between the two battlecarriers? Who knows? Perhaps, knowing the fact that Class Alpha Zero Pathogen was not your ordinary common cold or knowing the enemy warship Copernicus was in hot pursuits, would somehow put me in a psychedelic journey of reading. Knowing all the political scandals committed by notoriously-corrupt-think-skinned politicians here in our country is far more interesting than this. Oh boy, I am not going to pretend to like this book just because it was a freaking science fiction that even my cerebrospinal fluid has gone dry after processing all the video footages, military files, hacked documents; including the two megacorporations hand-to-hand fleet to fleet combat. Nope. Not a chance. 
 Second question: 
 Did I love the story? I certainly could have. But... 
 THE UNPOPULAR OPINION 
 This book had been such a huge letdown for me. Imagine I was supposed to read Jojo Moyes's Me Before You and Patrick Ness's The Rest of Us Just Live Here but I decided to pick up this book instead only to get disappointed pages after pages. I have been patiently waiting for that final moment where the story would otherwise change my opposite stance. Because of such a beautiful writing format, nothing could have prepared me for the impending doom and slap-in-the-face disinclination for a certain book told in an unconventional manner. 
 The inherent antagonism in me, again, dysfunctions my cortex that resulted in a blurry vision. It was a compulsive habit of mine not to settle for anything that I didn't enjoy. Nonetheless, I don't normally leave books halfway no matter how much I dislike it, so finishing the story is my way of showing respect for this book. 
 There are a lot of books where you wish there "could have been more." But in this case, it's the other way around: I wish "it could have been less." Less on embellishments but more on character development and world building. 608 f*cking pages and I got a world building & character development so paper thin! If I was looking for a brilliant graphics, I should have read an aesthetically appealing graphic novel filled with a riveting story. 
 PLOTLINE 
 I could actually narrow the story down into bulleted formats with less adjectives and unnecessary ornamentations: 
 1. Kady Grant and Ezra Mason broke up. 
 2. When Keneza was attacked, the old couple manage to escape and find themselves aboard two separate battlecarriers: Alexander and Hypatia. 
 3. Lincoln/Copernicus was in hot pursuits. 
 4. A deadly virus/plague in the middle of interstellar war. 
 5. IMs: Kady and Ezra's illegal ship-to-ship communication like cheesy old love letters. 
 6. Someone died. Actually the entire people in the fleet died because of the PHOBOS (virus). 
 7. AIDAN (Atificial Intelligence controlling the fleet) played an important role in the story. 
 8. The girl with a pink hair will save the world and win the boy over. 
 9. The twist. 
 10. Another radical change in the story. 
 11. Reversal of motive to surprise the audience. 
 12. Boom!! 
 13. End of story. 
 Reading it halfway through, I found myself bored to death. Enough of artwork please, I want the full story. For me, there's just too many unnecessary dialogues when they could have come straight to the point. 
 Types of weapons 
 and 
 cyclone drones 
 and 
 Alpha Zero Pathogens 
 and 
 wartime espionage 
 and 
 court-martialing offense 
 and 
 hyperspatial chromodynamics held in stasis 
 and 
 keyboards //ubEWdcfhug0i8jugiov//[[{g898231# 
 are so damn interesting, wooo! Common, please tell me some more!!! 
 (*insert sarcasm here*) 
 How could something so rich in detail fell way too flat for me? 
 Main problem: Brilliant idea but poor execution. 
 For me, I think the artworks failed to beautify the entire story but they're rather deliberately misleading. Yes, every reader would want a story told in an unconventional way, but I prefer a simple book with a gratifying delivery. Take the Aristotle & Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universeas an example, the plot was no extraordinary. No hallucinatory plot twists. No fascinating dossiers. No diagrams. No illustrations. But the author was still able to enmeshed its readers to a painful but liberating reality none of us would want to admit. 
 Illuminae 
 is nothing but another clever attempt to masquerade the fact that books can be taken at face value. All those false beautification and other visual improvements do not make up to the fact that the book lacks substance and are nothing but deceptive markings. Seriously, I have less interest in flamboyance. 
 STYLE OVER SUBSTANCE LOGICAL FALLACY: 
 This fallacy assumes that: "good delivery equals good content." For me, the book didn't make good points and it failed to produce a captivating storyline but the book still left us with good impressions anyway. Why? Because the author embellishes the story with compelling language and copious visual aesthetics. It metamorphosed a "normal story" into a "competitive plot" and diverts reader's attention through the substitution of style over substance. Presenting something in a beautiful way, makes it more good. WOW the readers with visual graphics and they may not notice that the plot was not so marvelous. 
 This, in a nutshell, is a prototype of disillusionment. I was so engrossed with the graphics that I failed to focus on the actual story. 
 Much to my utter dismay, everything seems like a series of isolated events told through the use of annoying dossiers of hacked documents, emails, schematics, military files, IMs, medical reports and interviews instead of pieces of evidence that could form a linear story. Bottomline, it didn't appeal to me at all. 
 When a certain book is inserted with "some" fascinating graphics and diagrams the result would be: COOL! But when an entire book was bombarded with these dossiers, it became less and less interesting and annoying at some point. Some parts didn't even make any sense to me and it turned out that I was forcing myself to keep on and it was not because it was poorly written, the writing style was actually good but there was something lacking in the content. Much to my distaste, were all the interplanetary cussing that were comically marked out. The romance, on one hand, was indeed cute but it was nothing exceptional. 
 "Perhaps, bravery is simply the face humanity wraps around it collective madness." 
 OVERALL 
 Boring and confusing as f*ck. Again, this book wasn't bad, it's a pretty decent book and obviously it was purely a product of hard work and intense brainstorming. It was visually entertaining, yes, but plot-wise, it was a NO for me. The twist alone was enough to like and trust this book but I just couldn't bring myself to love the entire book when I didn't even enjoy it to the full extent. The story didn't blow me away to outer space. Everthing failed to hold my attention. Regardless, this book will probably be a good movie to watch but not to read. 
 So tell me folks, I was f*cking ready to love this book but where have I gone wrong? 
 Expected Publication Date: October 20, 2015

sample_reviews.review_text: Completely overdone, indulgent and boring. Incredibly long passages that were full of waffle and unlikeable protagonists.
Made it through 300 of the 525 pages before giving up. She's a fine writer, with a gift for description, but ultimately the story never grabbed me.
This was a great read- I listened to it and the performance was A++++++. You can't beat a book that contains- and I'm not kidding- a game of strip Chutes and Ladders.
The middle of the book was engaging - the beginning and end were slow and unnecessarily drawn out. Would have been much better if they cut at least 100 pages.

There is so much to admire about this book that I feel almost guilty that I didn't love it. And I feel I might struggle to explain why without losing sight of the fact that it is a great book and beautifully written in places. 
 As you'd expect from Waters, The Paying Guests inhabits a very specific historical moment. In this case, she takes is to the social upheaval of the 1920s and the interbellum years. The aftermath of The Great War looms over the novel: a generation of men have been lost; soldiers returning have found themselves unemployed and unsupported; the division between the gentry and clerk classes are dissolving. Again, as you'd expect of Waters, the historical details are utterly convincing; her language never jars you from that period; her dialogue feels completely authentic. The voices of her characters and the way that their language is almost insufficient to reflect the depth of the emotions, passions and pain her characters feel is wonderfully evocative. It somehow recalls my grandmother. 
 Waters locates the writing in a traditional grand house in Champion Hill, London - a house used to a team of servants and a family of five before the war, but which now houses only our main character, Frances Wray, and her mother. Saddled with debts, the Wrays take in a married couple - Ken and Lillian Barber - as lodgers in order to maintain the cost of the house upkeep. The novel opens with the Barbers arrival and the tension created by that arrival: the hesitation over whether to offer or even drink tea with the Barbers on their arrival; the awkward maneuverings and negotiations between two families finding a space between cool civility, pragmatic commerce, resentment and an uncomfortable enforced intimacy. 
 It comes as no surprise to those who have read Waters before that the awkward intimacy between Francis Wray and Lillian Barber becomes something more romantic and passionate. 
 And Waters is just as fabulous writing about emotions as she is in capturing a voice. Just read the following extract: 
 It is one of the most beautiful and natural analogies of the quickening of love that I have read. Domestic. Sensuous. Gorgeous. And the contrast between the narrator's lyricism and the characters' almost inarticulate and gauche attempts to communicate those feelings was exquisitely painful. 
 Locating the story firmly within the Champion Hill house also worked wonderfully. It became claustrophobic and enclosing... reflecting the limitations and restrictions imposed on the characters by society and morality and family. The house almost became a character in its own right and a reflection of Francis' own psychological state. 
 It is the second half of the novel, however, that lost me a little. The novel shifts from the drama of Francis and Lillian' love to a more plot driven crime thriller. The turning point is quite horrific to read but something gets lost. 
 I stopped liking either of the two characters. 
 Their inability to communicate, which in the first part of the novel, was endearing and overcome through their contact, became frankly irritating. Their lack of agency</em, of control, became tedious. I'm sure that it was a realistic portrait of the lack of agency women had in the 1920s and the way the patriarchal machinery of society robbed women of exactly that self determinism. 
 However, as a novel, it alienated me. 
 I didn't find their actions and reactions credible in the second half of the novel... even though I know that Waters is a writer for whom credibility and authenticity are paramount. 
 It is odd though that this is the second lesbian novel I've read in a row, following on from Eleanor Catton's The Rehearsal . The comparison is interesting: where Catton's novel is arch and self-aware and overtly literary, Waters is real and - I keep coming back to this word - authentic. Thinking about the two books together, and being fully aware of the subjectivity of this, it crystallises what it is in books that really grips me: it is the artfulness, the language games, the twisting of not just the plot but the very relationship I have - as reader - with the writer and his or her creations.
Claustrophobic melodrama
wish I hadn't wasted the time on over 200 pages of this book
Long book that started off very slow. Put it down a few times to read other things. Enjoyed it once the story picked up a bit, but I almost put it down for good a couple times.

It is 1922, and London is tense. In South London, in a genteel Camberwell villa -- a large, silent house now bereft of brothers, husband, and even servants -- life is about to be transformed as impoverished widow Mrs. Wray and her spinster daughter, Frances, are obliged to take in lodgers. 
 With the arrival of Lilian and Leonard Barber, a modern young couple of the "clerk class," the routines of the house will be shaken up in unexpected ways. 
 I was expecting more from this book. I saw this book in a bookstore and it was number 1 as a best seller so I grabbed it off the shelf excitedly. It was a very sloooow start, the first 75 pages I just didn't think anything was going to happen. After that, the book became better and I was intrigued. Sarah Waters is a very good writer, reminds me an old soul writer. 
 I just wish the book wasn't so long, after awhile I just wanted the book to end, not caring what happened to the characters.

I appreciate peeling back the onion to reveal characters and building tension, in this case, between Mrs. Wray and Frances (the landlords) and Leonard and Lillian, the paying guests, and in particular between Frances and the guests. That said, the story has to move faster. I stopped reading at 33% - was not invested in the characters, either to cheer for them or to loathe them, much less to learn what happens to them. DNF

reference_books.review_text: It took me a while to get through this book, but I did like the ending. I would recommend to mature readers as (spoiler alert) the mom gets diagnosed with breast cancer, and it may generate conversations. book_a.title: Pax
book_a.user_review: This book will appeal to certain readers, possibly fans of the Warriors series, or kids who love wildlife. A good story, just didn't do it for me.

sample_reviews.review_text: Saying that this one didn't do it for me would be an understatement, and I wasn't sure I'd even make it to the end. I'm going to hold off on saying anything else because I know there are some people out there still very excited to read it.

This is a beautiful little book. It's a book that will speak to adults and children alike about important, big things. I took my time getting through it...savoring a Pax or Peter chapter a few times a week. My favorite thing was how Pennypacker addresses the idea of oneness and community throughout the text: "Oneness is always growing in the world...two but not two. It's always there, connecting its roots, humming...you can be with its heartbeat. You be be on your own. But you don't be alone." Sigh. 
 After spending weeks with these characters and loving the compelling, emotionally complicated plot, the ending was too terribly abrupt.

This book had good intentions, and based on its high rating, has touched the hearts of many. It's a book about a boy and his pet fox, what do you expect? But to me (and my kids, 10 & 7), it was slow and anti-climactic, even down to the end. I enjoyed the chapter rotation - one chapter focusing on the boy, Peter, and the next focusing on his fox, Pax, as they worked their way back to one another. It was also interesting to read things from a fox's perspective and to see how fiercely loyal Pax was to Peter. Overall, the book had a clever and tender plot, but I was bored through most of it.

This book started out with a lot of promise to me. I had been eyeing it on the self of my local library for a long time, but finally decided to pick it up this last week because that is a beautiful cover, and the first chapter is beautifully written. I'd say any time we are in the fox's POV it is beautifully written, honestly, and there are places in the boy's POV that are good too ... but the further I got into this story the more frustrated I got. The message is pretty heavy handed, and it's not a hard or subtle message. The "war is bad," "humans are destructive" thing is not a new lesson to be learned, and it tends to be treated with a lot more nuance by other authors. 
 It's going to be hard to break down my major issues without touching on the ending a lot, so I'm going to put spoiler tags after this point. 
 First off, I never got a handle on the setting/time frame. I spent the first half of the book trying to figure out where this was taking place and if the rumored war was historical or a made up war in the not so distant future. I'm leaning towards the second, but it's odd because the story is really grounded in our real world, but has a very old fashioned feel to it. It doesn't feel like the modern world, but it also doesn't really feel like any place I know. I think the author was going for "timeless" but the choice to use an obviously American setting was, I think, a mistake to achieve this. 
 The realization that war was on American soil (over water, apparently? It seemed like the author couldn't decide between realism or making the war sort of a vague idea that represents war generally rather than a real war so she kind of fell in a weird place that gave me just enough details to make me question the reality and "how" this is happening without giving me any eventual answers ... would've worked better if they'd kept everything a lot more vague.). Also, the war is happening about 200 miles from where people appear to be living very normal lives (with no fear of bombings or airstrikes ... which again, messed with my impressions of this being a modern era/futuristic/realistic war). The author didn't really commit to the dystopian future needed to pull of the realism of a modern war on American soil ... but the attempts to provide real world details kept pulling me out of the fantasy of a made up war in an unknown land ... 
 K, now the rest of my problems circle around the ending: 
 the ending is abrupt and unhappy but completely unearned and doesn't fit the rest of the story very well. 
 1. The boy letting the fox go back to the wild was actually completely expected because that is how 90% of these stories end, and we've been seeing the fox get comfy in his new wildness throughout the story ... HOWEVER, the boy just got through thinking how dangerous this area he's releasing the fox into was and he just sends him off into it with no attempts to move him to a safer area, knowing full well he can't stop the advancing war. It doesn't make sense to the character's internal logic. 
 2. The boy never really deals with his father. The father is a strawman for an unloving (maybe abusive? The story never commits to him being abusive, so it was hard for me to hate him the way the ending appeared to want me to hate him.) parent who never gets a chance to speak for himself or explain his choices. And in the end rather than resolve the father/son relationship, to try and heal it, the ending is the boy determining to be not like his father and turning his back on him rather than trying to heal. Honestly, other than being willing to fight to defend his home from an invading force (which we are supposed to believe is a bad thing in this world) and making the boy give up the fox because it will be hard on the grandfather ... we're only really give vague hints that the father is anything but a sad, lost man who doesn't know how to handle life and fatherhood after the death of his wife, and I was really disappointed in the approach of "it's okay to throw away your father because you don't approve of his choices" that the ending seemed to indicate. 
 There is a clue given in a newspaper clipping that the father intentionally let the fox fall into danger, but the idea that the father masterminded the fox potentially dying doesn't really work to make him a "villain" because we're not given any motive why he would do this or explanation of his side of things. 
 but rather than approach his character with understanding, the end wants the reader to turn away from him and those of his ilk (called "war-sick.") which is really annoying to me especially as a military spouse who knows that men who have gone through these sorts of experiences don't need condemnation and "hollier than thou" judgments about how "broken" they are. There's a reason veterans have a high rate of suicide and substance abuse, and dang, this story is like, "well, that's okay, because they're broken beyond fixing and we don't need to bother to love them, just learn from their mistakes and move on." 
 In fairness, the broken but healing character of former soldier Vola is probably meant to show that they can be fixed, but it does this by showing that she's so broken she has to live in the woods for two decades to redeem herself. 
 So veterans are either disposable because broken 
 or 
 so broken that they can't lead normal lives and therefore must go into the woods for a 20 year penance. 
 Honestly, when I read the book my first thought was, "well, that's just not a good ending" but the more I think back about it, the more this book goes from, "Not a good ending" to "this is actually making me a little angry."
A quick read, but poignant and heartfelt. Loved it so much
A very enjoyable, suspenseful animal story that I will be recommending at my library often. But dang, that ending was a little too abrupt and sad! This book made me really want a pet fox, though. :)

The story is told in two voices, that of Peter who strikes out on his own to find the fox that he had raised from a kit, and that of Pax, who is certain that his boy will come back for him. The story stirs many emotions, including love, loyalty, grief, and the effects of war. I found this to be a very moving story that stays with you long after you've finished reading.

I liked this one a lot and it's getting a lot of buzz for the next Newbery. I'm ALWAYS wrong about those, so I won't weigh in on that part. Even though I really liked it, I'm not sure the kids will. There were several things that made me go "Huh?", like how the main character could run away from home, break his foot, and end up with adult he's never met before and stay with her for an extended period of time with out there being a BIG problem. Or how analytical a fox could be... Like I said, I DID like it. Just not sure the kids will.

Great book. If you like "a boy and his dog survival stories", this is a must read for you. (Only the dog is a fox!) Vola is my favorite character. I too have a collection of quotes, love the meaning of her name, and seek to find the true purpose of my life which is in line with my core beliefs.
This book was ok. Not thrilled about it. My son was like oh, Pax.

book_b.title: Some Kind of Courage
book_b.user_review: An amazing western adventure starring a boy in a quest to get his beloved horse back. Dan Gemeinhart is my new teacher librarian author hero. I will be buying multiple copies of this 2016/17 Great Stone Face nominee!

sample_reviews.review_text: Amazing.

Welp. I'm not the target audience. 
 Too many things happened - bear attacks, Indian horse races, riding the rapids, shootings. The parents' remembered platitudes were annoying. The conversation with Caleb was unbelievable. The "he 'weren't's" were super annnoying until I watched an episode of "Vera" and heard people in the north of England using the same bad grammar. Finally, if he called Sarah "sweet" one more time, I was going to throw the book across the room. They should just get married. 
 That being said, I'll probably buy for my kids who like "adventure."
Well written, but so sweet you'll get a toothache.

I found this really preachy, the "survival" to be far too easily overcome, and so many adults way too pure good or evil. And the ending? Put a bow on top. C'mon, if you're going to write a "dead dog" book at this point in time, you've got to make it dynamic. This wasn't. 
 And don't even get me started on the racism. Oh, good job making mom conveniently empathetic enough to teach this kid that "Chinaman" is a slur and that peoples is peoples, but then maybe don't portray the Chinese character as a stereotype good at everything and quiet with his little charm. Not to mention the portrayal of the Natives... "growling like a wolf," multiple references to "the Indian" and the Chief of no-name-nation being GEORGE. Ugh.

Whoa, I...LOVED this. Why?! It's a western! Have I ever in my life enjoyed anything set in the Wild West? (aside from like DOS Oregon Trail) But it's soooooooooooooo good and it made me cry, like the sucker I am. gr. 4-7
I started this back in January and then slipped into a slump. It's not this books fault but I just couldn't get into it. Which is a shame since I loved Dan Gemeinhart's first book.

Joseph Johnson doesn't have much left in the world, but he has his horse Sarah. That is, until it is sold out from under him. This starts his adventure to get her back. This is an amazing story of hope, courage, and love. I loved this book for many reasons, but especially its connection between a boy and his horse. I know my other horse loving friends will find it just was wonderful. I can't wait to read it aloud to my class.

Another sad one, folks. There has to be a novel published in 2016 that isn't about death and/or other bummers, right? I did really (I mean really, really) like this one. But I'm still and ever weary of this theme. 
 Set in the late 19th century, this is historical fiction at its most exciting. Our 12-year-old hero Joseph is tragically orphaned and alone in rural Washington State. He goes on a quest with one goal: to get his horse, Sarah, back. She's all he has left in the world. Along the way, Joseph faces danger and forges a bond with another lost boy. In some ways this is very different from Gemeinhart's first book (The Honest Truth) but both books have a strong emotional core and riveting (and, if I'm putting on my critic hat, kinda over-the-top) plots. 
 I grew very attached to Ah-Kee, the Chinese boy who, like Joseph, is all alone in the world. It says something about an author's abilities when they can create a fully realized character with no dialogue. Ah-Kee doesn't speak English and the story is told from Joseph's POV, so the reader doesn't know exactly what Ah-Kee is saying. (Just now, though, I'm realizing that Gemeinhart also does this with his animal characters. No dialogue, but lovable and well-drawn through action and description.) This book explores communication without a common language in a way that's both funny and meaningful.

Oh, man, I'm soooooo in the minority here! But this book made me roll my eyes a LOT. It all just felt so contrived! Every single time someone told the main character, "watch out for so-and-so," what did he IMMEDIATELY encounter? Yup. I just couldn't quite buy much about this at all. I liked Joseph's friendship with Ah-Kee, but it didn't feel real to me, and just...everything is so convenient, you know? Everyone he interacts with seems to behave in ways that seem...exaggerated or unbelievable, and despite Joseph's internal moping about how everything is getting in his way and nothing's working out, he always seems to have these moments right after something has magically worked out. And I got really tired of all the "my sweet Sarah"s. 
 Great voice, though, and I love the cover...

I am not a historical anything reader. Seriously, I am not. I read biographical literary non-fiction picture books because my readers need exposure to this genre and some of them enjoy it so I want to be able to procure and recommend the best out there. But...on my own I wouldn't pick up anything historical. I gritted my teeth when I started listening to Some Kind of Courage by Dan Gemeinhart, because it's a cowboy story. It is also a title on the 2018 Texas Bluebonnet Master List, as a librarian I read through most if not all of the list, I want to be able to BookTalk all the titles and get kids excited about reading these stories, it's what makes the love of reading take hold and grow roots in my readers' hearts. So although I started listening with skepticism it didn't take long for the story to take a hold of my heart. I warn you, there will be some crying, maybe a lot of it, if you read Joseph's story. If you are the type of reader that gets wrapped up in a story like if it's your own, the crying WILL get ugly. But, I assure you it will be worth it, you will come out of the experience thinking about so many of the kids you know and how they have greatness and nobility in them, the Joseph kind, even when their circumstances are unbelievably harsh, just like Joseph's were. This book is worth the 3-5 hours you will invest in reading it, I do not say this lightly, as a reader with a TBR pile that will certainly outlive me, I take the investment of reading time very seriously.
