reference_books.title: Croak (Croak, #1)
reference_books.review_text: 3.5/5 Stars This was a fast, easy read. I first picked up this book because of my love for the TV show Dead Like Me. It wasn't as amazing as the show and lacked the comedy I was expecting to lighten up the dark subject matter, but I still very much enjoyed it. It was an interesting concept and the fast paced writing really kept me into the book. The characters were somewhat stereotypical, but enjoyable none the less. I liked how the book wasn't the typical happy ending YA and I'm looking forward to the rest of the series.

book_a.title: Vampire Academy (Vampire Academy, #1)
book_a.user_review: I'm looking forward to continuing this series solely because of the mythology. I found it interesting enough and if it's developed well, could make for a very interesting series. I've heard that this series has a bit of a slow start, which I hope is true because I did not care to much about this book. It was entertaining enough, but honestly wasn't that good. I have the next to books, so I'll be reading those soon.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Vampires. Deadly, blood-sucking monsters. They kill and cannot be killed. Yet what if they needed protection? In this vampires are known as Morio a mortal vampire with an unbreakable bond to the earth's magic. Dhampir are the Morio's protection from the Strigio a used to be Morio but now an immortal Strigio out to feast on Morios. 
 This is how Lissa Dragomir and Rose Hathaway story comes into play. Lissa is a Morio princess and Rose is her Dhampir protection. They live and go to St. Vladimir an academy for the Morio to learn how to use their magic, and the dhampir to learn how to protect them. Yet Rose and Lissa share a special bond that no one has heard of in forever. Rose can feel Lissa's feelings as if they were her own. This special bond formed right after the accident. Because of that accident and other things Rose broke most of the school's rules by taking Lissa out. 
 After two years of illicit freedom they get caught and dragged back to the academy. The academy filled with royals, classes and more drama Rose and Lissa have to readjusts to their new old life and learns the ways of the Academy again. Yet there is new trouble unfolding for Rose with her not right love life; and Lissa's magic. Morios specializes in magic by the four elements: fire, wind, water and earth. Yet Lissa has not specialized yet. There are a few rare who never specialize, but maintain a low hold on all four. Could Lissa do that? 
 Richelle Mead writing is magical. It pulls you in and never let you out. The book is feature around Rose, but always gives you a glimpse of Lissa's life. The first book in a series of six follow Rose's adventure as she protects Lissa from the unknown. This book is also being made into a movie releasing in theaters in February of 2014. This unlike twilight and Dracula will give you a whole new view on vampires.

I originally picked up this book while awaiting the next book in the Sookie Stackhouse series to be released. I was on a vampire kick at the time and thought that I'd give this series a shot, even though it is YA. While not a literary masterpiece, I was intrigued by the different take on the vampire social scheme (dhampirs, vampires and strigoi) and the excluded society that they live in, with humans oblivious to them. 
 The writing style was aimed at a younger audience so I read through this novel very quickly despite it being a few hundred pages. 
 While I do enjoy the character development of the main characters, there is a distinct "Twilight" vibe throughout this (and subsequent novels) that diminishes the story. Very wishy-washy in the "love you but can't be with you" department. Its Bella and Edward all over again, just with a quicker pace. 
 Overall it was a quick read that filled in my Sookie hiatus and it got me into a new vamp series that while I won't run to the stores on release day, I will eventually get around to reading when my favourite series are all caught up.
This book is really good! I really liked the interesting part towards the end. The only thing I didn't like is that Dimitrie didn't end up with Rose!!! But there is still more books so I don't know.

The story line was fun. Definitely a teen vampire series. I always love when authors come up with new ideas. In this book there are mortal and immortal vampires which I think is awesome. It almost gave a zombie hue to the vampire world. Love the main character. Her attitude is appealing yet badass, someone you probably wouldn't want to piss off but wouldn't mind being. Dimitri is sexy and I couldn't help developing a bit of a crush. Excited to read the next one. 
 I feel like editing could have been more thorough. Noticed quite a few grammar mistakes.

I absolutely adored this series! From the start of the first book all the way to the last, I was hooked. These Vampire Academy had a mix of successes and failures. It was filled with happiness and heartache. There were moments when I found myself sobbing relentlessly and other times when I was so excited that I had to put the book down to do a little "happy dance." This series has the obvious similarities to the Twilight books (i.e. vampires and impossible love connections) but that is where the similarities end. This series is much more relatable and a must read for any vampire loving reader!

Okay, some things about me before I write this. I am really good at mysteries. I figure them out pretty easily. Secondly, I've been trained to read as a writer, which I've had to do a lot lately for class, but it's starting to affect everything I've been reading. I'm not sure if I can slip back into reading as reader. So what does that mean? All I see are the writing flaws and the plotlines and the characters and the purpose of things. 
 So here's the actual review. SPOILERS AHEAD 
 I really hoped when I started reading this book that it was as good as everyone said it was. I highly doubted it, but after Amazon offered all six books for less than $20, I figured I'd give it a try. Unfortunately, I tried reading the book four times before I actually started the book. But I finally did. It wasn't anything special, but it wasn't horrible...so I kept reading until I hit this little gem: 
 "As it was, things didn't look good for our heroes--or heroines, rather." -page 12 
 Can you say stupid? Like really stupid. First of all, the story is in first person point of view. This one little line comes out of that into third person point of view, and it reads like a comic book joke. It especially reads like the author talking to the reader--which big no no. 
 There was so much info dumping and random moments. I'm sorry when you are running for your life, don't stop to describe how hot the guy who is beating you up is, especially when the guy will be appearing in the book in the future. You can describe him on the plane, in the car, anything after the fight. 
 The mythology is...complicated. Three types of vampires: Moroi--the royal, stuck-up class of living vampires who do magic; Dhampir--the Moroi's half-human children who can only procreate with the Moroi; and the Strigoi who are undead vampires who are mostly previous Moroi who killed someone during feeding. They are hunting the Moroi because it makes them strong, but the Dhampirs need the Moroi to procreate, so they agree to live their lives to protect the Moroi because the Moroi are weak and the dhampirs are stronger and faster. 
 And all I could think is why the hell are these people allowing the Moroi to treat them like lower class citizens just because they need the Moroi to procreate. The Moroi need the dhampirs to survive because their so "weak." It should be a symbiotic relationship, but no. Dhampirs are treated like dirt. Moroi royals run the place. Like please, someone stand up to these jackasses instead of letting your race die young just for the possibility of procreating. 
 I guessed the entire plot on page 89. I got one detail wrong. One. 
 The thing is, though, throughout the entire book we are told how dangerous Strigoi are, how they are everywhere, how they are after the Moroi and can't control themselves. Except...we don't see a single one in the book until there is only 13 pages left in the entire book, and it was really for nothing. Please. How am I supposed to believe they are so dangerous and everywhere as they are said to be is they aren't anywhere and Dimitri, coming out of nowhere, easily dispatches the one at the end. 
 And then the ending was like a wrap up. Telling up all the things that she didn't bother to answer before in one giant info dump. Can we say talking to the reader much? 
 About characters: 
 Rose Hathaway: 
 I did not like Rose for most of the story. I did not sympathize with her. I think she is a terrible friend and person. First of all, all she talks about is how much hotter she is than her friends and the other Moroi, how hot the guys are or aren't, and sex. BUT SHE'S A VIRGIN. But she practically talks about sex ALL THE TIME, and then gets upset when people imply that she's had sex. It's a reputation that she's put forward practically, but when they reputation goes one step further (SHOCK) people believe it, and she becomes upset. All she cares about is looks. For instance: 
 "Fighting and training and always being outdoors--they aren't pretty anymore...This...this life, it destroys them. Their looks, I mean." 
 Yeah cause looks are everything, Rose. You might want to reconsider the life you've chosen. Oh wait. It's this or being a blood whore. I forgot. RME. But that is not why I didn't like her. It was annoying, but whatever. 
 What bothered me was how she acted toward Lissa, her best friend and Moroi charge. She was like an overbearing, overcontrolling, jealous boyfriend or girlfriend. Telling Lissa who she can hang out with. Telling Lissa who she needs to date. Getting jealous when Lissa had to feed. AND WHAT WAS COMPLETELY UNFORGIVABLE TO ME: Rose lied to Christian about Lissa, interfering in her romance with the boy just because Rose didn't like him. Like what the fuck? 
 And then she also utters this little gem: 
 "Back in my room, I had my own crash. The fear and excitement had worn me out too, and for an instant, I wished I could have a normal life and a normal best friend. Immediately, I cast that thought out. No one was normal, not really. And I'd never have a better friend than Lissa...but man, it was so hard sometimes." -page 164 
 This is how I read that statement: My princess best friend who I obsess over and try to control is special and someone is trying to kill her and is leaving dead animals in her room to freak her out to the point that she is now cutting herself. I wish I had a better friend, one who isn't so much hassle. Oh woe is me. 
 SELFISH PRAT. SERIOUSLY! 
 She was very inconsistent too. I mean she pushes and pushes to always be at Lissa's side, but when Lissa gets kidnapped and she leads Dimitri and the other guardians to the cabin in the woods, she tries to go with them on the rescue attempt and Dimitri says no, that he needs her safe, and she just complies. AND DECIDES TO TAKE A NAP! Of course, her nap is rudely interrupted by Lissa's escape attempt, and because of Lissa'a stupidity for not believing Rose was on the way to save her, Rose has to go save her. OF ALL THE NERVE! 
 She's also kind of dense. We're supposed to figure things out with Rose. That's the whole point, but she was so slow. The author kind of pounded the answers at us, and Rose took forever just to get where I was already at. It's not like I got to view other things going on that she didn't. 
 Lissa Dragomir 
 Cool name. Crappy character. I liked that she was going against what Rose said about Christian, but she was just kinda there for most of the story. I almost forgot about her, until she went all dark side, and then she just freaked me out. I feel like she'll be a bad guy or someone I shouldn't really trust. 
 ALSO IF YOU ARE GOING TO BE MAD AT ROSE, LISSA, DON'T BE MAD BECAUSE SHE TOLD ON YOU FOR YOU CUTTING YOUR WRISTS. BE MAD AT HER FOR BEING A OVERBEARING, OVER-CONTROLLING CRAPPY ASS FRIEND AND GETTING IN YOUR RELATIONSHIP WITH CHRISTIAN. 
 I just hope this gets better.

I really enjoyed this and although it treads pretty similar ground to many other YA vampire stores, particularly House of Night, I think Rose's character is more endearing as she's a much more a true to life teenage girl. She's wrong sometimes when she thinks she's right and she's moody and tempestuous often. Some of the things she said or did were downright cruel, particularly her verbal slap to Christian. However, they are no more despicable than the average teenager might do whilst trying to protect themselves and their friends, and she is certainly loyal, protective and kind overall. I appreciated her rounded character, and the book as whole, more for this.

Another series that I absolutely must finish. 
 Loved this.

Finally, a YA novel with characters that act like teenagers - they drink, they swear, they have sex and yet they aren't considered the scum of the universe and looked down upon by the pious, untouched main character who can't contemplate doing anything wrong without having a panic attack. Absolutely awesome. I can't wait to read the next one.

3.5 stars 
 Before I start with the review, I just want to pause for a second and address the elephant in the room; was it just me or were there A LOT of similarities between this book and Jennifer Armentrout's Covenant series!? Seriously, WTF?! I was massively shocked by the parallels between the two, I could dedicate an entire post to my rants about this. I know, I KNOW, that I can't blame the Vampire Academy for these similarities because it was published before the other book but it still really bothered me and took my focus away from the story and the characters. If VA hadn't been published before the Covenant series I probably wouldn't have finished it because I don't like reading stories that are so damn similar! I get that this is clearly a kick-ass idea that sells a lot of books and that they aren't exactly the same, but there are enough similarities for it to really annoy me. 
 Anyways moving on. 
 I'm so glad that people convinced me to give this book a go! Seriously SO GLAD. OK, yes, this book has flaws but overall I really liked it and can see why people are so addicted to this series!! 
 I found that at times the writing could be quite confusing. It would sort of assume that I had knowledge of the story that hadn't been mentioned before and wouldn't be clarified until much later. I often found myself going "who the hell is [insert name here]?" or "what the heck is this or that?" because suddenly they're just being casually mentioned in the narrative but won't really be properly introduced until a chapter later. I think the idea was to create mystery and intrigue but it was a bit of a flop. There were moments when that worked, for example I liked that they just jumped straight into the story and described this supernatural world slowly. But there was too much of that happening and it was frustrating. However the appeal of the characters and the plot made up for it. 
 Characters like Rose. I adore Rose! She is snarky, flirty, sarcastic and pretty kick-ass. She doesn't take shit from anybody and doesn't give a damn what other people think of her. While she is overly protective of her best friend, Lissa, they're friendship also felt very real to me. My one dilemma is the budding relationship between Dimitri and Rose. I have conflicted feeling about this one. She's 17 and he's 24... that's not even legal in some parts of America! I don't really like the whole idea and I hate it when anyone says "oh bust she's so mature for her age." The rational part of me thinks it's too pedo-y and creepy. But my rational brain can be such a loser sometimes! When Dimitri basically agrees with me, I was all "NOO you can make it work! Just give it a go and please for the love of God - KISS HER NOW." I am seriously conflicted about this one but as you can probably tell I'm already addicted to this forbidden romance! 
 There is just something about this story that drew me in! I couldn't put the book down. The book is not perfect but it has a very addictive quality to it as well! The plot is intriguing and the characters are fresh and fun to read about. I finished the first book in about 24 hours and immediately started the second. Plus I've already gone out and bought myself the entire series. I think it's fair to say I'm a little obsessed!

book_b.title: Not That Kind of Girl: A Young Woman Tells You What She's "Learned"
book_b.user_review:
I went into this book actually liking Lena Dunham. I have watched all of Girls so far, and for the most part found it eccentric and enjoyable. 
 I was truly disappointed to find out that the character of Hannah is essentially Lena Dunham. Hannah is so self involved, messed up in the head, and is so self entitled that everything thing she does is self serving in some way. Lena Dunham comes off the exact same way in her book. It comes off so pretentious and arrogant that reading it became truly difficult. I concidered giving up on it and looked up some reviews to she how other people received it. Many people were saying that people who give it low ratings must not have finished the book, because it was obviously so amazing. Well, I call bullshit. It was horrible.

sample_reviews.review_text: I tend to like books written by strong women, but I struggled to get into this one. I got through the first few chapters and then it became more work than enjoyment to finish reading it. I'm not sure what they want the takeaway to be? If you decide to crack it open you can expect lots of real and unfiltered stories, but no real point or conclusion to any of the conversations that are started.

Nope. Got about 70 pages in and gave up. Picked this up because I like her show, but this is self-indulgent p.o.s. is pretty worthless despite its myriad attempts to seem self-aware or insightful. Could do it. Abandoned.

SUCH A DISSAPOINTMENT! I love Lena Dunham and her show "Girls" so I had high hopes for this book. Unfortunately, it was a total let down. I couldn't even finish it because I could no longer stand her trivial essays. One essay, recalling her online relationship with a Russian boy named Igor was particularly dreadful. Most of her essays seemed to have no real impact her life, just non-funny experiences she had growing up. I could not relate to anything Lena had to say, which is sad because I look up to her as a feminist. But this book was just no good in my eyes. 
 Again, I am so sad to give this book such a poor review. Maybe one day I'll give it another shot... But for now, 1 star :/

I had to change my review to "2" stars after I asked myself: if I had no prior knowledge of a Lena Dunham, never watched Girls, and picked up this book purely as a book to read, what would I think? While this book fits nicely into the Lena Dunham brand that I appreciate: quirky, wry and narcissistic, as a stand alone piece of literature it doesn't really add up. 
 The author has no real struggle beyond the issues in her own head. She even says as one point, if she had been molested as a child it would explain all her mental health problems. She was raised in privilege. So, for me, I don't understand or sympathise with her on that level. It's like her persona had to make up mental health issues because she was dealt such an easy life and she needed something to set her apart. 
 When she describes wild nights out and thrift shop clothes I like it. Her nerdy obsessions with music and books are relatable. Her very brief insights to people in Hollywood were entertaining, as was most of the sexual encounters she describes. Her voice is amusing, but as I said, is it funny because I read her as Hannah in Girls, or funny because it's an original voice in literature? 
 Miss Dunham is only three years younger than I and maybe I'm a narcissist but I think I could put a spin on my own life's adventures just as well as her. There is nothing unique about her life as described in this book, despite having a TV show, which she doesn't really detail getting or working on. 
 As much as I like her, I have realised in the future when someone picks up this book with no prior knowledge of who she was, they won't find this book particularly illuminating in any way. Unless you grew up privileged in Manhattan with artist parents and attended private schools and summer camps, the vast majority of people will not be able relate.

Bad. Just really bad. Written by a self-important, self-absorbed woman who loves drama and does everything in her power to surround herself with it. A lot of strange stories, about her sexual experiences and her weird family, that go nowhere and seem to have no purpose or meaning other than to illustrate her own lack of proper upbringing, confidence and self-respect. Really, really bad.

Review in English: Soon to be translated. 
 Review in Portuguese (BR): Vou ser sincera com voces: Eu nao queria ter de fazer essa resenha. Eu sei que ela vai ser extremamente controversa porque a Lena Dunham e uma atriz muito querida por varias pessoas por aqui, principalmente por causa de seus pensamentos feministas e no quanto que ela se tornou inspiracao para muitas sobre a liberdade profissional e sexual da mulher moderna, junto com varias outras pessoas que existem por ai. 
 Mas ao mesmo tempo eu to me cocando para falar o que eu achei a respeito desse livro, e ja peco desculpas de antemao se eu ofender alguem. Mas eu particularmente eu acho que a plataforma que foi utilizada para a venda do material que tem dentro do livro foi... Na minha opiniao, nao a mais certeira. 
 Como outros livros de nao-ficcao que eu li no ultimo ano, eu dou preferencia para o formato de audiobook sempre que e, no caso, o proprio autor que narra, porque eu acho que essa experiencia de leitura um pouco mais up close and personal com ele, mas em varios momentos enquanto eu escutava Not That Kind of Girl eu me senti extremamente entediada e desconfortavel. 
 O principal motivo do meu desconforto com esse livro foi o fato dela contar constantemente - em aproximadamente 60 a 70% do livro - sobre as suas frustracoes e dilemas com homens e a sua sexualidade, o que eu acho que nao tem nada de errado em falar nisso, de forma alguma, mas quando se isso se torna a grande massa do seu livro isso pode chegar a pontos que podem causar isso mesmo, isso quando eu nao tava extremamente entediada. Eu acho que nunca demorei tanto pra escutar um audio livro de apenas sete horas que nem eu demorei com esse aqui. 
 Acho que a escolha do formato para falar sobre isso foi um pouco infeliz. Eu acho que se fosse em formato de videos curtos que nem esses do Ask Lena que rolam na internet ou como um seriado com pintadas de humor funcionaria muito melhor do que de fato como um livro. 
 De fato nao me levem a mal quando eu falo isso, por favor! Eu acho a Lena Dunham como uma atriz e como pessoa alguem incrivel, mas acho que o livro dela deixou muito a desejar no fator de se tornar de fato algo inspirador para o publico no geral, principalmente o feminino. Se voce e fa dela de fato eu imagino que voce vai gostar ainda mais desse livro, mas infelizmente eu nao consegui gostar dele, por mais que eu gostaria muito. :/ Eu acho que nesse aspecto existem outros livros que sao melhores para inspirar as pessoas, inclusive um deles eu pretendo falar por aqui em breve.

PLEASE DO NOT READ THIS BOOK. 
 Okay, I got that out of the way. 
 Lena Dunham is a smart chick. She knows how to spin a good story and make people laugh. However, this is the most self-indulgent piece of garbage I have ever read. I disliked almost every one of her anecdotes. She isn't old enough (and hasn't experienced enough) to write something of substance. While she has had a few struggles in her life--the account of her rape had chills running down my spine, and was the only thing in the entire book that struck a chord with me--for the most part, she comes off as a whiney, narcissistic, upper-middle-class, privileged girl (yes, EXACTLY THAT KIND OF GIRL). Reading this was like watching a train wreck; I couldn't put it down because I was waiting to see what new horror was around the next corner. 
 In retrospect, I am not surprised that everyone who recommended this book to me was under the age of 21. I am not knocking the younger generation; they just haven't had the life experience to know that this kind of "memoir" doesn't have much to it.
I don't get it
I liked the last chapter...THAT... IS...IT!

I am saddened that I can't give this book a -100 star rating. It's horrible. Lena Dunham sounds like a horrible human being who tortured her parents from the time she learned to speak, and sexually abused her sister. I now understand why hamsters sometimes eat their babies. If Dunham was a hamster her mother's instincts would have kicked in and she would have realized that there was something terribly wrong with her baby and chomped her head off immediately. Aside from being a sexual predator, she slept with any man that would have her, pretended to sleep with some who wouldn't (like her imaginary internet boyfriend who had to fake death to get away from her.), she is a hypochondriac...or the most sickly person in the world..., and an obsessive compulsive. I can only hope that young women out there don't think that she is a good example to look up to. The only saving grace I found in this book is that she (in graphic detail) told of her tilted uterus, and regaled us with the story of how she may never have children. It's pretty obvious that her genetic makeup should not be carried on. Don't waste your time, or your money on this piece of crap book!

reference_books.review_text:
2.5 out of 5 stars 
 I read this a very long time ago, but I don't remember being overwhelmed with joy when reading it. From what I can remember, this book had a good foundation. The characters were likable and I enjoyed the movie quite a bit. The themes were a stronger point in this story, more so than most books I was reading at the time. This book just wasn't enough to be a favorite and it wasn't very memorable.

reference_books.title: A Thousand Pieces of You (Firebird, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
lawl edited my review after 5 minutes because I felt bad 
 Alright, this was dandy. It was a quick read which I appreciated like no other. And alas, when I finished reading this little book about dimensional travel - I was rather impressed. But I still had some issues with it. 
 Here's a list of small-ish hangups I had: 
 + The main character, let's call her Meg because I don't have time to spell out her full name, was actually a complete moron 80% of this book. I had no problem with her until after the Russian dimension. She came to terms with being stuck in Russia for three weeks WAY too fast. Like are you joking? That's three weeks in which she did virtually nothing but daydream about her love interest and hang around with the professor. Why was she not more proactive? 
 + There were four different dimensions and none of them were that fascinating. I'm glad everything stayed action packed and new information was almost always being thrown at us, but really - a London with high tech gadgets, Romanov ruled Russia (which I loved in theory because Russian history is my life so naturally I thought this section would be amazing), a world basically the same as Meg's own dimension, and one involving oceanic/under the water type living. Sounds cool, right? Well, it was but it wasn't. I feel like there was a boat load of potential with these settings but they weren't blowing me away. 
 + The under the water setting was by far my least fav and the last few chapters were meh. The beginning and middle were much more interesting. 
 + Theo became another Dorian. I liked him at first, then I just wanted him to waltz on out of my life. Sorry bud. 
 + Why the fuck was Meg so upset about Russian Paul dying? IT WASN'T EVEN HER PAUL AND SHE ONLY KNEW RUSSIAN PAUL FOR THREE WEEKS!! Then she proceeded to "punish" regular Paul for not being as wonderful as Russian Paul even though she frick fracking knew regular Paul longer! THE HELL, MEG?! This was part of the reason I thought she was such a dumbass. The girl barely knew Russian Paul so it seemed really selfish of her to say stuff such as, "I loved Lieutenant Markov" like bitch, you aren't even the Russian princess Meg that, oh I don't know, knew him in Russia! Also, she slept with Russian Paul in the middle of a crisis - umm okay??? 
 Other than the things listed above, the last one being the most frustrating for me, I enjoyed this book. The writing wasn't stellar but I breezed through quite a few chapters at a time so that's saying something. I really enjoyed when Meg talked about growing up with her parents, sister, and the grad students. I thought that was a special piece of the story, especially when she described the rainbow table because when I think about this book, I think of small details like that now. Her life was different than a lot of other kids and I'm glad that there was an emphasis on that because it showed that it's okay to grow up with a "not so typical" family. I do wish I would have known in advance that this was going to be more of a romance than sci-fi, but eh, whatever. I would still recommend this to friends and family!

reference_books.title: The Heart of Betrayal (The Remnant Chronicles, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Review was originally posted on my blog Hungover Fiction Lover 
 Real Rating: 4.25 
 For being the second book in a trilogy, The Heart of Betrayal sure refused to show signs of second book syndrome. I suppose I should focus my thoughts in a linear fashion, starting with the beginning. The first book left off with a cliffhanger and the second book jumps right in to the resulting consequences - and it was chaotic. Beautifully chaotic. 
 Lia is immediately thrown into the Vendan way of life, along with Rafe, but he fares much better thanks to his quick stitched fibbing. Kaden on the other hand is trying to act as a savior when truly, he's a borderline traitor. Then, only moments into the book, we meet his boss man. The Komizar. Holy shamwow, this dude was a brilliant bad guy. I'll admit he felt oddly familiar and I want to say it's because his demeanor reminded me of Klaus from The Vampire Diaries - but hey, that's a good thing. Throughout the whole book I wanted to hate his guts, yet I found myself waiting for scenes involving him. I NEEDED TO KNOW MORE EVEN THOUGH HE'S AWFUL?! ARGHH! So yeah, I wanted more Komizar fun facts every five seconds. 
 Moving right along, we were introduced to Calantha and Aster in this book. To put it lightly, Calantha was a beezy for 75% of the book and Aster was cute though rather boring. I hate using the word 'boring' to describe anything in these books but sometimes the characters really slow down the story for me; how ironic since they usually push it forward. Anyway, aside from the new additions, there were a few familiar faces and I was on the fence about most of them. Pauline annoyed the heck out of me. I adored her in the first book, but only one word came to my mind whenever she spoke this time around: naive. The best example I can provide is her last chapter. She just doesn't get it. Oh and Gwenyth was there to drop a bombshell that will obviously come into play in the final book. 
 Those two were what I call "Lia's girls" and sadly, they didn't do a whole lot. Thank goodness, we had "Rafe's guys" and ugh, can we take a moment to appreciate Jeb? I feel a strong affinity toward him which has everything to do with the way Mary E. Pearson wrote his character because he's only in a few chapters. Like what. I loved him. Can he be featured more often? Okay, I'll stop fangirling now because lastly, we have to talk about Lia's brothers - Regan and Bryn. I have two complaints. The first is that I didn't learn anything about them and the second is that they can't possibly be serious near the end. I mean, are you joking? I know you're grieving but do you realize you still have a sister who could kind of use your help? 
 As much as I make it sound like I wanted to slap the crap out of the secondary characters [which I did], this book was solid and I enjoyed it. I think the problems I had were minor in comparison to The Kiss of Deception which I reviewed last month. The larger problems I had - though they weren't that problematic - were rooted with the main characters, such as the constant deception [no pun intended]. I understand that it's an important part of survival in this book, but I think Lia takes it too far sometimes. She's always pushing and it bothers me. I love reasonable rebellion, but she completely disregards Kaden's feelings, even after she learns about his past. The romance she had with Rafe earned a few eye rolls from me because I can't grasp why she throws herself at Rafe but refuses to give Kaden a chance. Also, I was weirdly not surprised by any of the large plot twists but some of the smaller moments left me stunned. 
 At the end of the day, I enjoyed The Heart of Betrayal much more than its predecessor. It kept my attention for a longer period of time. I felt heavily invested. Slowly but surely I have been immersed within this historical world and I'm sad that it's coming to a close next summer.

My mini review will be posted at http://hungoverfictionlover.blogspot.com in a few days! 
 I went into this book with high hopes. I needed something lighthearted with wit and I heard this was that type of book, which it was for the first half. I quite enjoyed the characters, mainly Alexia, Ivy, and Lord Akeldama - and occasionally Professor Lyall. Lord Maccon was alright but he was similar to many other male leads. Yawn. The only problem I had with Alexia was her self deprecation, I mean come on, you're a 26 year old curvy Italian: GET OVER IT! 
 To get back to the story itself, the beginning was much more enjoyable to me than the second half. Then around the middle, everything started to get muddled. The descriptions were tedious and too long, almost pretentious. Also, the things the characters were talking about were just plain boring. I think the very end was ruined for me because of what ruined most of Allegiant: the bullshit science. It felt like an afterthought. Oh and I almost chucked this book at the wall solely because the word manacle(d) showed up way too freaking often in the last half of the book. Honestly though, there are other words - use them. 
 In the end, I wanted to love this book but alas, I did not. I think there was a lot more potential that could have been worked with to make the overall storyline stronger. I think I'm going to continue on with this series but it won't be for quite some time.

Full of truths, the way only John Green can write. But writing about cancer is tricky, and by the end I found it a little too sentimental. Still a good book.

Once again, I've tried to read it. First time, I made it to about page seven. I didn't even get to the bit on America's Next Top Model. This time, I made it to page nineteen. See, I made progress? To me, from what I read of the book so far and what friends have gushed about to me, Green writes perfect prose -- and he does, the quotes I've read from this book are amazing -- and his characters are teenagers. Teenagers that don't exist. I know that these guys speak and think differently than I do because they had cancer, but I still grew up with teens. Not even the ones who read Green speak like his characters do.

After all the hype, I expected more. I was not impressed by this book. A bit too "teen" for me. I've read books like this before that are better. Yes, it was sad in the end, but it's like everything was okay in it's separate parts and didn't quite come together.

This is the first book by John green I've ever read. I was hesitant to read it because I try to stay away from hyped books and best sellers, and also because I knew it was YA and its not really my genre. However I enjoyed this book. It is fast paced, easy to read, funny and sad, and very complete. I liked the characters, they were very real and relatable. But the thing I enjoyed most in this book was the approach of cancer and death and life. It does not turn the characters into victims, it does not make you feel sorry or pity any of the characters. It celebrates life and the message of living the life you are dealt comes across very strongly. 
 It's pretty deep for a YA book. And although I did find the whole romance thing a bit cheesy, It made me be very grateful for being healthy and alive, and also I think that people who have struggled or are currently fighting cancer would appreciate it, I people treated them like regular people, and see far beyond their illness, because cancer does not define you. 
 I recommend it widely and I'm also curious to read more of this author.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This is a very thought provoking book, challenging in a way, because of its subtle complexity. Often, it reminded me of the bible. Not only was Buck's prose reminiscent of the King James', but the characters behaved much like some of the old prophets and kings in the bible, and the gods were just as whimsical. The book was occasionally difficult for me to digest because, on the one hand, it told a tale of a Chinese family and described Chinese culture and history, but on the other hand, it was written by an American 'missionary'. It felt sometimes like a Ragged Dick story, but, to be fair, it wasn't too overtly moralistic or didactic. 
 This book leaves me wondering so many things, but that is often the reward of great literature. The plot was engrossing, but I felt the narrative voice maintained distance between me and the characters. Buck was very matter of fact about many aspects of Chinese society, and she spared us any editorializations, so some of the book was shocking and slightly off putting for a modern-day Westerner. But, nonetheless, it was compelling and interesting, encouraging and poignant.
Depressing

I read this book in high school and I want to read it again because this book is the first book I read that I did not choose myself and I loved it. It made me look at the world differently as though there are many more worlds to explore and the possibilities are infinate. Thank you High School Literature Teacher!!! You made a reader out of me.

This is the second time I have read this book. It was one of the few books I didn't resent being assigned to read in High school. I thought about giving it 5 stars but I just can't quite get there, however, I really do like this book a lot. 
 It is the story of Wang Lung who in the beginning is satisfied with his life and his land and only desires to have children. As the story progresses he is changed in many ways and easily loses sight of what was important to him. 
 Throughout the book the one thing he always clings to is his land. It continually renews him whether times are good or bad. His fortunes change frequently for the better and worse in different ways and while I read it I found that the moments that stood out to me the first time I read it still strike vividly in my mind. I have never been able to think about pearls in the same way since reading The Good Earth. 
 Wang Lung has intense moments of cruelty and fleeting moments of regret but I think had he made different choices he would have been essentially a good man. Some things can feel unresolved at the end of this book (I haven't read the sequels to know if they ever do get resolved) but I think that is so often like life that I was ok with it. Occasionally, I like a story where you can say well, that is life and what's to be done? I know the author could mold the story any way she wants but to give everything in it a solid conclusion and to give everyone in it exactly what they need (O-lan's retribution, Wang Lung's realization that he is mirroring the hated old lord he buys land from) would be false and less fulfilling to me. 
 The language can indeed feel slow but I think it has it's own beauty to it and paints a vivid picture of life in China at the time it is set in. I am going to get around to the sequels sometime although I never really cared for any of Wang Lung's sons as people in the book. Still, it will be interesting to find out what does happen to the family after the revolution. In the end, though, I feel like The Good Earth is good enough to stand on its own without the need for sequels. If the sequels are written as well as this one, I am sure I will enjoy those too.

reference_books.title: Naamah's Kiss (Naamah Trilogy, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This book was a very solid return to the world of the D'Angelines that brought Jacqueline Carey to her place as one of the fresh voices of fantasy. The first trilogy was nigh flawless, and the second trilogy was pretty uneven, with the second book being a near-total mess. This book picks up a lot of the unresolved messes of that second book and crafts a coherent story out of them. 
 I have been skeptical each time Carey returned to this world, but it frankly works for her. Far, far better than the Banewreaker books, which I couldn't even get through. 
 This book was a worthy successor to the first trilogy, and I am looking forward to the next book!

book_a.title: Prized (Birthmarked, #2)
book_a.user_review:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I enjoyed this book very much, and there was a point in reading it that I got annoyed that I had to put it down at the end of lunch/breaks at work. For me, that's the real test of if a book has hooked me properly: if I don't want the immersion of a story to END, the book is doing something right. 
 There's a lot in this story that's right, and my hat is off to O'Brien for daring to broach the subject of deliberately-induced miscarriage and some of the reasons a woman might wish to terminate a pregnancy. There are complicated, muddy issues all over this novel, and Gaia reacts to them in ways that feels realistic. She is, after all, a sixteen-year old girl. She makes mistakes, and she learns from them. The stakes are high, and sometimes Gaia blows it. I gather from some of the other reviews I am reading that people didn't like this about the book, but I fall on the other side of the argument. I like that she screws up sometimes, and that she has to apologize for it. 
 I think a lot of the bad ratings for this novel are motivated by people's political feelings about the induced miscarriage storyline and not on the merits of the book itself, and that's a shame.

This one started as slow as the first and then about 40% picked up pace. I want a book to grab me from the start and neither the first book or this one has done that. I'm hugely disappointed in the pace of the book.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Review to come!I have to say, I think that "Prized" is far better than its predecessor ("Birthmarked", the first book in the trilogy) and definitely on my best of 2011 list. Why? Because this book takes some pretty big risks. Love triangles? Try love rombuses. You thought the politics were crazy in the first book? The issues introduced in this book blow the ones established in the first way out of the water (or should I say Unlake?). I absolutely ADORE O'Brien for taking these risks, knowing how sensitive (in particular) American audiences are to issues like these. This woman has a uterus of steel. Or maybe titanium. Either way, it's absolutely awesome. 
 Now, spoiler alert: this book delves very, very deeply into the issue of abortion rights. If that makes you uncomfortable, or if you're really pro-life, you might want to avoid this one (though I urge you not to, and listen to what Gaia and O'Brien have to say on the matter). 
 I think the reason why this book worked so very well in terms of discussing reproductive politics is because O'Brien really amped up Gaia's voice, making it the voice of a professional midwife despite her age, and not O'Brien's own opinions (though they may be her own). She does not preach at us, but urges the reader to look at the issue from both Olivia Matarc's side, and from Gaia's side -- that of the female body. In a situation like you have both in Sylum and in the Enclave/Wall, and the goal is to keep the human species alive and reproducing no matter what, to whom does the female body belong? Both sides make really good cases, echoing years and years of debate in current American (and Western) society. She does not preach at us, she does not just blast us with her opinion, but opens it up for discussion. In a time where girls are starting to mature earlier and earlier, this is a very important subject that needs to be talked about, especially within non-contemporary YA lit. 
 Why not contemp YA lit? Because so much of the time, there's a spin for either side. A girl has an abortion because she has no other choice, regrets it, and so forth. Oh, and finds a man by the end of the story to whom she can sob/find love again. Or the reverse - she keeps the baby because of the same reasons. But in the contemp YA lit that I've read that has broached the subject, there's far too much of an emphasis on either side, and not a fair presentation of the entire case as a whole. Couching the ideas within sci-fi/dystopian YA lit helps release the matter to be contemplated as a whole, where you can see cause and effect for both sides without (as much of) the bias. O'Brien makes "Prized" her best book yet because she opens this subject up so very well, and made it so easy to digest. It had me thinking and rethinking my own opinions on the matter, and I hope that other YA gals who read it do the same. While the end of the book does end favoring one side over the other, the message is still the same - discussion is important, and without it, you have a dystopia. Without discussion, you have the end of research and thus, growth. And finally, the biggest punch in the gut of all (which O'Brien did so wonderfully) -- without growth, there is only death. The end of evolution. The end, period. 
 And then there's a love rhombus thrown in, but that too makes perfect sense when you look at how Sylum is populated in a female to male ratio. I enjoyed that, and chuckled quite a bit when Gaia herself brings it up in one of her POV asides. 
 This may be one of the best YA dystopia books for girls yet in terms of discussing gender and reproductive rights. I urge everyone to read it, despite whatever side of the matter you're on. "Prized" is definitely one of the best of 2011, and I can't wait to read the final book in the trilogy whenever it does get announced/released.

This series went from being interesting to me practically despising the characters and their attitudes. I didn't like any of them at all.

3.5 stars 
 Prized picks up right were Birthmarked ends, with Gaia and her new born baby sister alone in the wildness, on the run from the Enclave. With little supplies and not much to protect them against danger, both Gaia and her sister aren't in the best condition when they run into a stranger who helps/kidnaps them and takes them to safety. Once there, Gaia realizes she's in a whole new society and one that ties her to her Grandmother and family, but this society isn't blissful, in fact it gets Gaia in a lot of trouble, changes her, opens her eyes a bit and takes her sister away from her. 
 Much like Birthmarked, Caragh again creates a vivid dystopian world that was so easy to imagine as the story goes on. I liked the fresh take on a new society which allowed Caragh to tie Sylum with Gaia's family, specifically her Grandmother that was mentioned through Birthmarked. Her Grandmother is no longer here, but her ruling this society and the clues she leaves behind plays a role in what Gaia uncovers as the story goes. Unlike Enclave, this society is ruled by women, which make up a very minor percentage of the mostly male population. There's strict rules in this society, women and men are forbidden to touch unless married, and the women is the one who chooses who she marries. Women are required to have many children to help not only a declining society, but help try and boost the dwindling female population. 
 I liked the introduction to some new characters, despite being frustrated with how narrow minded some of them were. I liked the possibilities of new relationships for Gaia, and loved getting to know Will and Peter. I was extremely excited when Leon enters the picture and the friction and chemistry that once again develops between he and Gaia was fabulously drawn out. Unfortunately for me Gaia herself wasn't the girl I had excepted her to be, at all. I really felt like she regressed as a character for much of this story. She was this lively, stubborn, strong willed, independent girl who wouldn't bend to anyone's whim and yet in this new society she becomes opposite of all that. While I tried to understand how a new society would change her, I didn't really buy into her changing so much. I felt like I got a completely different character than Birthmarked and I missed the old Gaia. I liked that Caragh even had Leon questioning Gaia and how much she changed since being in Sylum. It isn't until close to the every end did I see a flicker of the old Gaia. 
 While I didn't love this book as much as I loved Birthmarked, it's still a great addition to this series. I'm very eager to find out what's in store for the third and last book in this trilogy. I'm hoping that Prized doesn't change Gaia and that with the next storyline she'll become that inspiring character she was before. I think this story line's purpose was to place Gaia in the position she ends up in at the end of the book for the sole reason of helping bring change to a society in desperate need of it. I'll definitely be picking up the final installment to this series when it's out.

 Wow just wow. I can't even wrap my head around that book, particularly that ending. I adore Oliver's writing style and extra points because Hana was awesome but seriously I felt like Oliver must have said "I'm tired of this series so I'm just going to write a bunch of pretty fluff with no conclusion because I can't be bothered to figure out an ending." 
 Lets get to the meat of the problem: 
 First off probably the WORST love triangle ever. EVER! I hated the way Lena treated both of them. She used Julian and flip flopped on Alex. I knew this crap was coming when I finished book two but that was in a league of its own Second nothing actually happens on Lena's side of the story. There's no more anything except her being whinny and cruel. You do learn more and get into some great sociatal issues in Hana's story, she really was the redeeming factory of the book. 
 Finally WTF KIND OF ENDING WAS THAT. It was so unsatisfying, so nonexistent it was ridiculous. I didn't even read Alex's story because the ending was that off putting. And it wasn't even the emotional, gut wrenching, heart stabbing, desire to know more that was cultivated in the Hunger Games. I don't even care at this point what happened I'm just passed that she thought that was an acceptable way to end a book.

reference_books.title: Sophie's Choice
reference_books.review_text:
I am disappointed by this book. I had great expectations considering the contents of this story and I was upset that William Styron used "Sophie's Choice" as it's climax all the while filling the middle pages with fluff. And I use the word climax lightly. 
 What the hell?! 
 Sophie's Choice is about a Polish woman, Sophie, who is imprisioned at Auschwitz along with her two children. Upon arrival, she is forced to make a crushing choice that will forever plague her. However, you don't find out about this "choice" until 529 pages later with only 33 pages left. All the while, you learn about her life leading up to Auschwitz and her crazy and bizzare love for Nathan, her lover. 
 Yes, a heart-wrenching story and one that I had placed off reading for some time due to the nature of the book, but it could have been something more. It SHOULD HAVE been something more. I expected it to be something more...more moving...more emotional. However, by the time our author developed the characters and allowed the reader to associate with each character, I found myself, not only loathing Sophie, but hoping the book would end a certain way so she would finally be placed out of her misery and mine as well. 
 William Styron filled the pages in between with such adolescent bullshit that I often thought I was reading Playboy forum or something of the sort. An oversexed Polish woman, a drugged-out sadomasochistic Jewish lover, and a wet-dream of a 22 year old virgin friend...now couple that with Auschwitz, NO THANKS! 
 I just changed my star rating from 3 to 2!

reference_books.title: Tropic of Cancer
reference_books.review_text:
...because it was onced banned. 
 Unfortunately banning this book only fueled interest and in a sense landed Tropic of Cancer as a masterpiece. Upon reading this exhausting story it is anything but a masterpiece. 
 Tropic of Cancer is basically the meandering thoughts of a tortured soul, oversexed, often poor and homeless man (Henry Miller) who fancies himself as a writer. He often shares company with not only various prostitutes, but other men who are in the field of the arts and who dole out money to support him in his time of need - or habit, which is quite often. Henry Miller as the author uses vulger and obscene language which at first I was startled by but after a while I realized that it was his way of writing without editing and using words that you don't normally see. Basically shock value. However, shock value has no value in my opinion. 
 "I have made a silent compact with myself not to change a line of what I write. I am not interested in perfecting my thoughts, nor my actions." 
 "...Now we shall have a vessel in which to pour the vital fluid, a bomb which, when we throw it, will set off the world. We shall put into it enough to give the writers of tomorrow their plots, their dramas, their poems, their myths, their sciences. The world will be able to feed on it for a thousand years to come. It is colossal in its pretentiousness." 
 Give me a break! Henry Miller comes across as such an ass that the one word that he uses quite liberally is really what I think of him. He has such a blantant disregard for women that not only can he not live without them and sex for hire, but upon looking at the female anatomy he ponders life and the "cancer" that is eating at our society. WOW - that's deep?! (no pun intended) However, Henry Miller has a chance to change his life and "start over" but just can't give up women and his cunning ways.

reference_books.title: Beloved
reference_books.review_text:
UGH! This was a difficult read for me. Not only did the story track back and forth from past to present, but the story was extremely depressing. 
 Beloved is about an African American woman, Sethe, who is bought, sold, and traded to various farms. It's about her fight for freedom, the lost of her children, the reuniting of her children, and the unforgetable act Sethe does to protect her children from slavery. 
 I gave Beloved 4 stars because it was difficult to follow. I know this was made into a movie, however, I won't be renting it. 
 This book was a 1988 Pulitzer Prize winner for fiction. I believe it's probably due to the acute story telling of slavery and the misuse/mistreatment and degrading of African Americans in our time.

reference_books.review_text:

 Unfortunately, I think the author, Edna O'Brien, used the Little Red Chairs title to capture the reader and included a snibit commemorating the 20th anniversary of the siege of Sarajevo, misleading the reader completely. 
 I was totally irate reading this because she placed women in such a bad light. Fawning over a good looking man who comes to town, asking for sexual favors like women had no moral compass. Shame on her!! And then tossing in Sarajevo as an after thought and peppering it with a rape. Really? 
 Pass!

book_a.title: Lolita
book_a.user_review:
** spoiler alert ** 
 One of the most annoying books I've read in a long time. I read this book because it is one of Amy Tan's favorite authors and she spoke of this book often. I wanted to know what the hoop-la was all about. It's a love-hate book for me. 
 H.H. is shockenly stricken by a very young Lolita. He describes her beauty in great detail and his thoughts are very well laid out. However, the only way to get to this young girl is the marry the mother. However, now the mother is in the way between H.H. and Lolita. One afternoon while cleaning H.H's study Lolita's mother reads a journal with very private and explict details about her daughter's sexual being and how much H.H. is in love with her. She confronts him and threatens to leave taking Loltia with her. So of course, he decides to murder the mother while Lolita is a camp. 
 However H.H. doesn't tell Lolita that her mother is dead he instead tells her that they are going on a trip. They have their first sexual encounter and Lolita is very relaxed about it. So relaxed that it's very unnerving. H.H.'s raw emotional feelings and very over-powering and soon Lolita learns to control H.H. by either giving him what he wants or holding out. And so the story continues... 
 Vladimir Nabokov does a fabulous job and showcasing all sides of the story. The torrid love affair and the raw all- to consuming sexual emotions that we had with our first real loves. He reminds us what it was like to feel everything for the first time; the mix emotions, the can't breathe, eat, sleep, and how sexual emotions can take over our lives. But then he shows us the side of the unwanted attention. The ugly side of brutality, the side that shows us what some people will do in order to get that. A side that is almost common place in some parts of the country. And just when you think you might have it figured out...Vladimir Nobokov shows us the side of Lolita who uses that raw sexuality to make men do things. And ultimately destroying a man.

I can't say I'm glad that I've read this book. I can say that I'm glad to be able to mark it off as read, both here and on my mental 'to-read' list. But I wish I had never read it. 
 Oh sweet Jesus. I absolutely loathed this book. 
 The subject matter was, of course, vile. I feel like I need to go and have a bath in disinfectant, bleach my brain - anything to get this filth off me. But, subject matter aside, this was the most pretentious piece of crap I've read in a long time. Long-winded, at times completely pointless, and God, the parts in French - enough already! The narration style was (to me) absolutely irritating - his incessant talking of himself in the third person (Humbert Humbert), as well as his ridiculous nicknames for *himself*. 
 It was obvious that he was a complete lunatic. He really did not appear to have any remorse for what he had done, or indeed any real acknowledgement that he had done anything 'wrong'. He was obviously trying to endear himself to his 'readers'. Nabokov was obviously very skilled - he's an incredibly memorable character, and quite possibly the only character I despise even more than Joffrey from Game of Thrones. Absolutely no redeeming features or qualities whatsoever. 
 I can't remember a book ever making me feel like this before. That in itself is worth something, I suppose, but I just don't know how to rate this book. I am wavering between one star - because I truly detested it like nothing else - and five stars, because it's clearly a masterful piece of literature. 
 So three stars it is - I'll split the difference. And I would never, never, never recommend this book to anyone. Ever.

book_a.title: Uninvited (Uninvited, #1)
book_a.user_review:
** spoiler alert ** 
 This is a pretty spoilertastic review, considering that I feel like if you're going to give a book one star, you need to say why and explicitly. So, just, caution. 
 Let's be clear, first of all, that I was incredibly excited by the concept here. I think this is one of the better concepts to filter out of the YA sci-fi zeitgeist happening (tho this one remains decidedly non-post-apocalyptic, which I think is a good choice - in fact, it takes place in 2021, which sounds interesting but actually is not). I think the idea of a "kill gene" is exciting and opens up a lot of room for discussion and real-world parallels of the obvious variety. The descriptions of this book make it sound like a gamechanger, like something that could be huge in YA. 
 HOWEVER - UNINVITED was a huge, massive disappointment to me on every level. It is not a gamechanger. In fact, I would say this was the most disappointing book I've read in a long time. 
 The title itself, UNINVITED, refers to Davy's expulsion from her expensive prep school, and literally nothing else. I suppose you could draw conclusions about how she's been "uninvited from her former life" and that sort of thing, but I really find that doesn't work as well here, especially since Jordan clarifies that "uninvited" specifically refers to being expelled from school and is a term that characters are familiar with. That said, I could deal with a bad/irrelevant title if the rest of the book was good. 
 Davy herself is literally perfect as a person, or, like, I guess what Sophie Jordan thinks a perfect teen girl is. She's flawless in every way, as well as being tall, model thin, and blonde. She has the most desired boyfriend in school, who loves her pretty much unconditionally (until she's diagnosed). If that weren't enough, she's the ultimate virtuoso - from infancy, basically, she could play any instrument and sing like an angel. You know, because only perfect people are really hurt when their lives are ruined. Normal people just have to suck it up. Davy is a privileged asshole, really, and I actually don't feel that bad for her. I mean, I do, that sucks, but like...it's really hard to feel sorry for people who revel in privilege. 
 Anyway, Davy's life is ~~~over~~~~ when she's found to have the gene, because suddenly she has to go to public school (which is made out to be like having to daily go to the pits of hell for education). She's segregated with other carriers of the gene, her boyfriend breaks up with her, and her best friends dump her. After her boyfriend publicly dumps her at a party where her "best friend in the world" is furious that he brought her, a carrier, to this fancy prep school party, she slaps him and then is tattooed with the carrier symbol on her neck, like the "truly dangerous ones." Also, you know, the only other girl (also one of the only POC in the book) in her "class" at school is sleeping with their gross supervisor to "protect herself", although that literally has no meaning because there doesn't seem to be any real danger other than embarrassment at this time. Apparently being attacked by the other students is an issue, but, like...is it? Really? Fine. 
 ANYWAY, then the book takes a direct turn into "book two", in which carriers are rounded up and put in internment camps. But because Davy is sooooo special, she's chosen to possibly be a leader and is put into a special training program. And it's not just because she's a genius and musical - she's also chosen because of her breeding and gentility. YES, Jordan uses those two words verbatim in that conversation. I cannot. Did I mention that she has love feelings for one of her fellow carriers from that nasty public school? Anyway, he's there, too, and I guess it's good that one or two things carry over from the first half of the book to the next. You'll never see Davy's family again, I don't think. She has world-saving to do! 
 So she's being trained with other carriers (insert training montage from Divergent, basically), and when it becomes clear that they aren't being trained for anything except actually killing, she and her friends decide it's time to escape. So, uh...they do. Like, super easily. You know, because it's super easy to escape from an internment camp. A guy picks them up in a truck (???) and they go to plan their next adventure. I can't. 
 Oh, and spoiler alert: Davy does kill someone, because the supervisors at the camp make her do it by threatening to kill her bf (after a Hunger Games-lite game of capture the flag, where the flag is a carrier who tried to escape). I was sure she was going to kill someone, because that's what happens when you're diagnosed with the kill gene in a good story, but wow, this was a cop-out and not great. 
 And, for having inserted conversations with authority figures every twenty pages, they literally never explain HTS (the kill gene), its history, how they found it, how they use it, how they determine anything. It's literally nothing. If I were queen, I would say that this is a massive social experiment used to see how people react to a form of segregation (hi, Divergent), but I guess we'll see. There's just no explanation of how they determine that you will kill - just that you have the capacity, and it does get interesting when there are HTS carriers who take their diagnosis and do get violent, but it feels hollow. 
 The other major bone I have to pick is that any parallel to our world is unclear. I have no idea who the marginalized group is supposed to be. It draws from bad government treatment of almost all marginalized groups over the last hundred years or so (primarily in the US) in a way that makes HTS carriers seem like they could be any one of those groups. That's not necessarily a bad idea, but the carriers are so general and vague that it makes the plot muddled and unclear. I love the idea of the fall of the empire happening before our eyes, but it just...it never quite hits here. Ever. 
 So, to sum up: This contains every bad trope of the present YA trend, it's poorly written, the characters are flat and uninteresting, the main character is the worst, and it's literally split into two books. Two! I was shocked when the book turned in the middle to another book, especially since this is allegedly a series. Maybe Jordan couldn't fill up the pages, I don't know. But I was much more interested in Davy's navigation of her old life when she's been branded as a killer, and that never really happened. It's like Jordan was too excited to get to the second book of her new YA trilogy, so she quit writing the first one and put the second one in as well. 
 Overall, I thought this book was bad. One star for creativity in concept, zero stars for everything else. I hope you like it more than I did.

 Full review can be found here: https://agingerlyreview.wordpress.com... 
 This book has intrigued me for a while now, but I never brought myself to actually read it until very recently. I just get too distracted by shiny books and also the worry that a book is going to disappoint me. This, I'm sad to say, was a book that disappointed me. 
 This story opens with teenager Davy Hamilton finding out that her test results have come back saying that she is a carried for the Homicidal Tendency Syndrome (HTS) - the killer gene. Davy's life is forever changed as her boyfriend dumped her, she had to register as an HTS Carrier, she was sent to a more 'common' school, one that teaches HTS carriers, and her dreams of attending Julliard are shattered forever. She has to learn quickly that people will see her has a threat now, even if she never acts out, but genes never lie and she will kill someone one day. 
 I really was hoping for something more from this book. I never connected with Davy at all. She came across as a truly spoiled brat that had everything in life handed to her. She whined all of the time and was impossibly naive. "This cannot possibly be happening to me! I have not ever done anything wrong!", said every person diagnosed with this killer gene. Davy thought she could convince everyone she was truly innocent if she acted innocent. Give me a break.She thought she was perfect and wanted the world to know how perfect she was. "I have a natural talent with music. I can sign in perfect pitch and play about every musical instrument imaginable." Uh, ok. We get it. Just stop already. I did not like any of the other characters either. There are too many to name but believe me when I say they all range from typical to predictable. 
 Now let's talk about a lack of background. The entire premise of this story is around this special mystery DNA gene called Homicidal Tendency Syndrome (HTS) and the fact that it is never truly explained. The background behind this is still a mystery! How did scientists discover it? How is it tested? (A simple blood test, apparently.) Has it been proven that people with HTS actually commit crime/murder? The world may never know because it is not discussed. 
 I know this story is labeled a dystopian but this did not feel dystopian at all. Was this an apocalyptic future? Nope. Has society crumbled beyond repair? Don't believe so. This felt more sci-fi than anything simply based on this killer gene. It does remind me of very similar story that came out earlier this year - Flawed - but that did not involve a killer gene. It felt like heavy topics were covered - social injustice and judging. Anyone with this gene was automatically treated different in the eyes of the law and eyes of society. 
 Oh, there is also a bit of a love story involved but it's not truly worth going in to. Shawn, the male Davy meets after being put into the special school for HTS students, is the dreamy bad guy who has a softer side. The romance didn't feel believable or real. 
 In the end, I really expected more from this one. I didn't like how totally and completely naive the MC was. I don't feel she grew or developed at all. I'm not sad I picked up this book to finally read, but I am sure I don't want to pick up the second book to find out how it ends. I didn't DNF it so maybe I was just holding out for the ending to deliver me a huge punch but alas, it did not. I did not hate this book, but I did not love it either.

Uninvited was a very unique kind of Dystopian book. It's set in the near-future in which people are tested for the "kill-gene" and ostracized for having it. This book brought up a ton of questions about psychology and prejudice. It's a book that can make a good discussion. Uninvited was so different from the Firelight series, but Sophie's writing style is still the same with it. 
 I love getting to read in first-person present tense. It makes the story so much more thrilling and really brings out the main character's voice. Davy was a unique character, but somewhat similar to Jacinda in some ways. Rather than being a shape-shifter, Davy is a musical prodigy. She can play any instrument without having to be taught. She can sing songs from memory. She never expected that she'd have the kill-gene. 
 Davy does not seem like a psychopath at all. Psychopaths don't feel remorse or guilt. They're manipulative and like to hurt people and things. Davy's not like that at all. It's a major surprise that she has this gene. It brings up the idea of nature vs. nurture. Davy was nurtured and cared for. She has a brother that looks out for her, a mother and father who adore her. She was accepted Julliard, she's got serious talent, and a boyfriend named Zac. She has no built up anger. She has everything going for her. Then she loses everything. She's uninvited from her private school, sent to public school to be in a caged classroom with five other carriers. 
 I think that being labeled as a carrier is what causes most carriers to become violent. There are real sociopaths out there, and then there are people who got stuck with bad genetics. Go and ruin those people's lives by taking away everything they want to do and they're bound to become violent. These people clearly don't understand that it's the situation that's causing their actions and not their genes. 
 I liked Sean. He was very protective of Davy. He was gentle and silent and sometime a bit broody, but not a dangerous as he looked. He only beat up the guys who mean to Davy. There's a little romance here and there, but it's just enough and sure to grow throughout the series. I also liked Gil. He's a computer geek and a carrier. He's not violent. He's a wimp, but a really nice guy. He becomes a good friend to Davy. 
 This story took a twist when Davy is sent to a training camp. This camp made me think of the Dauntless faction in Divergent. Davy trains hard in hopes of having a chance to be something more, and get her mark removed. She doesn't want to kill. She wants her old life, but that won't happen. This story is full of action toward the end. I recommend it if you enjoyed Divergent, Blackout by Robison Wells, Shatter Me and other dystopian books.

 ~Haley G

This book was nothing like what I expected and that was a great thing. I went into this book not really sure what I was expecting out of it but the premise intrigued me and made me want to read this one. I can't even imagine this world that Davy was living in. I mean imagine being a teen on top with everything you could want and you are also talented and a great student and then it is all snatched away from you because of what you may become. I loved that the author touched on such a topic because it really made you think what happens when people already expect you to become a horrible person. I loved that despite what Davy was labeled as she refused to become what they wanted her to be. I loved her spirit and positive attitude throughout this book and was rooting for her to come out on top. As we get deeper into the book we soon learn that things may not be what they seem and you start not being able to tell the good guys from the bad and I loved every minute of it. 
 Davy soon learns her normal life and all that she knew is going to change in major ways. I think the world the author created is one that terrified but yet intrigued me at the same time as I loved finding out everything about how they tested for the kill gene. On the other hand I hated that they were basically willing to write people off as killers and not even give them to chance to prove they could be better. I hated to see how Davy was treated and I have to say it made me not like her parents that much because they really didn't fight for her at all. I loved that Davy was strong enough to endure everything that was being thrown her way but I think I liked it better once she made some friends like her and started to realize that just maybe she would be ok. I have to say that I am loving the friendship that is building between Sean and Davy and I really want to know more about who Sean is. I love the mystery behind him and can't wait to see what will become of him and Davy. I love that the author isn't pushing a instalove romance on us and are letting them slowly become a person the other one can count on. 
 Overall this was an awesome read and I am already waiting on the next book as I have to know what happens next in Davy's world. The author created a great and terrifying world full of complex characters that I felt connected to and wanted to learn more about. I loved seeing the side of normal people without the HTS gene also because it showed how some people treat those they think are criminals. This book was full of plenty of action and the author wrote with such ease that you get sucked into this book and don't even realize it. This book truly sucked me in and I was sad to see it all end. I am anxiously awaiting the next book. I highly recommend this one to readers of a great story full of great characters and a fast moving plot.

Future dystopia where people with homicidal tendencies can be identified by a test. Davy - musically gifted, good student, a good girl from a good family - tests positive and her life changes. There's lots of discrimination against her, people (including her own family) treat her differently and her future is taken away from her. Increasing governmental restrictions on people with HTS culminate in her being taken to a detention center, where she slowly discovers she's being groomed to be a double agent. (it's pretty obvious to the reader). 
 Fairly mediocre, very obvious in parts, but I just couldn't enjoy it.

reference_books.title: Six-Gun Snow White
reference_books.review_text:
This was a bit of a let down. 
 I like it when they give an original spin on a classic tale, I like it when they incorporate fairy tales and lore in stories (The Book of All Lost Things is a good example). Snow White, retold as a western, sounded like a cool idea; and done by a respected author is an even bigger plus. 
 But somehow it doesn't really translate well to the page. 
 I liked the take, I liked the racial issues, I liked that the story between Snow White and the witch was extended, I liked the narrative structure of the first halve. 
 Then Snow White leaves the castle, and the whole thing spins out of control. 
 The narrator changes, which is weird to say the least. 
 The 'dwarves' are a total let down. 
 But most of all, I just feel as if Valente is trying to incorporate too many items in too few chapters and then tries to be artistic with the ending. It spoilt a perfectly fine book. 
 2 Stars, grab something else when possible.

reference_books.title: Daughter of Smoke & Bone (Daughter of Smoke & Bone, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
The same gathered crappy-ness most teenage fiction seems to exist of. Put in some lore of any kind, a girl who is stronger than she thinks and an impossible love. Really?! Haven't we had enough of this? 
 And, no, I don't think there is anything wrong with reading novels like these. Really, if someone enjoys a particular genre, please read it. But I can't help but saying that this one is not particularly well done (if not plain and uninspired). 
 It starts of nicely and sets the tone of the mystery life and hidden worlds, but then the author decides this is to hard to keep up and it is easier to just bring everything in the open, rehash the plot through past lives and then end it on a big 'oh no will they ever get back together' (something that is probably going to happen anyway, or else the fans will rage). 
 Don't. Just don't. There are so many good books out there, leave this one for a cold winter day, but use it to feed the fireplace.

reference_books.title: Fourth of July Creek
reference_books.review_text:
This book is astonishing in its bleakness. From the onset it paints a world in which hope kindles and is immediately stomped out again. I read this in the Tirolean mountains surround by friends, family and warmth, which caused such an antithesis that I didn't fully appreciate the story and setting. Now a week or two later, I must admit feeling this book grow on me as time passes. I think that in a couple of years I dive back into it for a re-read. 
 3.5 stars and rising.
