reference_books.title: The Enchantress (The Secrets of the Immortal Nicholas Flamel, #6)
reference_books.review_text:
I wish I could say that I found this a great ending to a series and a splendid book in itself, but I really can't. 
 Where I sort of liked the previous novel, which had a good cliffhanger and some interesting twists, this part is just a simple clash between good and evil. All of the good ones are honourable (even ready to die for a cause), whilst those who are bad are overconfident and scurry away like rats when they are no longer winning. 
 Granted, I did not see the final reveal coming and I was pleasantly surprised by that. But then again, how can you see anything coming when you are constantly switching between storylines, timelines, shadowrealms, prophecy-forks and what not. And this is one of this books major flaws: It is overly complex, whilst trying to stay simple, making everything feel cramped in or heaped up in a hurry and most of all wrong (I'm not going to discuss the everlasting problems with time-travel, but let's just say this is also far from perfect/believable). 
 I have the feeling that in stead of maturing the books along with the audience, Michael Scott 'immatured' into b-type fiction, giving me that empty 3-star feeling.

book_a.title: NOS4A2
book_a.user_review:
NOS4A2, just doesn't do it for me, but it shows promise. 
 Joe Hill's first novel shows that he is a story teller, albeit an immature one. 
 The story is fun and there are aspects that are fresh, new and terribly scary. Sadly, every time I started to really enjoy this book there was some weird phrasing, an awkward paragraph, or an unneeded section that jarringly pulled me right out of the book. Sometimes badly enough that I stopped reading for a while. 
 Which is sad because there is a properly fun thriller in here somewhere. 
 Even though I cannot give this book a high rating and won't recommend it, I look forward to see Joe Hill's next novels and his progress in becoming a great storyteller. 
 2 stars.

Full Review at http://wp.me/p2s3sT-y5 
 In Joe Hill's new novel, NOS4A2, we're introduced to a girl nicknamed "The Brat," and, as heroines go, Vic McQueen has shot to the top of my list, in large part because she's a complete mess. Looking to escape the painfully slow degradation of her parent's marriage, Vic takes to her bike and rides as hard and fast as she can away from her father's anger and her mother's misery. She wants to fix things, and discovers a way to manifest a crumbling covered bridge that takes her to other places to find lost items. When she takes one more pass across the bridge to escape the reality of her family finally shattering, she stumbles upon Charles Talent Manx, an elegant, venomous man who kidnaps children. Vic manages to escape, and in doing so leads Manx to be captured. Vic uses the trauma of the events to brush over the magical way she came across Manx, and as he ended up in a coma during his capture she looks to finally put the strange, horrible events behind her. 
 But, as Hill covered so well in Heart Shaped Box, the past is never really gone. Victoria has a child of her own, and struggles with a screaming sense she shouldn't be a mother and a fierce love for her son. She wants not to fail, and so inevitably stumbles constantly as a parent, as one does when you focus so intently on trying not to screw up. The fact she has more baggage than she can possibly carry doesn't help, nor do the strange calls by the children of Christmasland who taunt her and threaten her son. Then Manx escapes his prison hospital, and comes looking for Vic. By the way, he escapes after being declared dead, autopsied, and sent to the morgue. 
 All of this is built out of the creepiest of parts, with the kind of electrifying tension that makes turning the pages so damn easy. But this is only the build up, the prelude and introduction that sets the scene and puts the pieces in place. Because once Vic's son Wayne is taken by Manx, Vic sets out after him. She is a wreck emotionally, right on the edge of madness, and beat to hell by her encounter with Manx and Bing, but she's also fiercely determined. True, she's going after her son, but she's also going after Manx for herself. Hill has developed a fantastic character type across much of his work; men and women who lurch forward into the horror rather than recoiling. Whether it's the Locke kids, Wayne Coyne, or Ig Perrish in Horns, his characters aren't frightened and cowering when they encounter evil. Yes they're scared and disturbed, but they accept their lot and put their shoulder right into the conflict. They might prefer to cower, but there are things that need doing, and no one else to do them. If you haven't read Hill yet (brief aside as I ask what the hell's wrong with you?), think of Vic McQueen as an incarnation of Ripley in Aliens. She knows the evil's out there, sees those around her don't understand how deep in shit they now find themselves, so she steps up to take care of things herself. 
 There definitely seems to be something magical about the number three. After all, A Fistful of Dollars was Sergio Leone's third film, while Born to Run was Springsteen's third album. There may be a bit of overstatement in saying Joe Hill's NOS4A2 is exactly on the same level, but man is it up there.

I hate to say it but I hated this book. I loved Heart Shaped Box and liked Horns. The only reason I kept reading is because I felt like I had to finish it. The only character that was likeable throughout the book was Lou. The story was about 300 pages too long and I found myself skimming pages. 
 Heart Shape Box scared me but other than give me nightmares about little kids this one did nothing for me.

I saw this book a while ago at Half Price books, and thought about getting it...just like I thought about getting Heart Shaped Box, or Horns a while before that. In all cases, I passed. However, when I saw it again a month or so back, I went...hmmm...that is a very creative cover, with the license plate spelling out what could be Nosforatu. I wasn't sure who Joe Hill was, but had heard some positive things about him, so decided to pick it up. When I looked at the back cover plate of the author, I took a double take, and thought...he looks a bit like a younger Stephen King. Anyway, picked up the book, looked up Joe Hill when I got home (the internet is an amazing thing, eh Constant Reader?), and was not surprised to find out his name is really Joseph Hillstrom King...the son of none other than Stephen and Tabitha King. Yes, THE Stephen King. Wow. So the writing gene apparently passed from both parents to the son. After finishing the book. Wow. Brings me back to early King days in one sense, but also it's clear Joe has his own voice and writing style. I loved the parts in the book where a lot was happening over a short period of time, and each chapter ended by going into 
 The title of the next chapter. 
 Very cool. The characters were well laid out, and likeable, or hateable as the case may be. The inscapes of America was interesting of itself, but the icing on the cake were small comments like this road led to Pennywise's Circus, or Mid-World...I guess you can take subtle references to his dad's creations, and darn but they fit very well, and make sense. My only issue was what I would call a Star Trek the Next Generation ending. When I finally got to Christmasland, I wanted to read a lot about it, but alas, I think there was only 30 or so pages from arrival to the end of the book. Makes me wonder if for some reason the editors suggested a lot of cuts from there due to the lengthy amount of words in the book. Nothing like his dad's 900+ pages or Under the Dome or The Stand behemoths (or the Dark Tower as a whole). I plan to track the other books down now, ASAP, to add to my soon bigger collection of Joe Hill. He's a very good writer. You might even say a chip of the old block.

i'm sort of glad i read this in that it helped me decide to give up on joe hill's books. he has such creative ideas, but for some reason the actual stories themselves fall flat for me. i think maybe just a bit more character development with a few less fight scenes make horror really enjoyable for me, but something with too much action and really quirky, unreal characters makes me feel like i'm reading a comic book. i read heart-shaped box and enjoyed it less than i did this book, but i think i will skip horns, which also has an amazing-sounding concept. 
 i love stephen king and this guy totally looks like his dad, it is just so funny, so i really want to love his stuff. and i do think it is dramatically improving. i would just love him to dwell on the stuff that puts you into a story a bit more without propelling its action forward.

I really like Joe Hill's writing. This book really packs a lot into its 600+ pages. It's the story of a girl who finds things. She grows up, and she hears the voices of children.... It's the story of a very old serial killer who steals children and takes them to a place where they will always be innocent and always be happy, and where it's always Christmas-Christmasland. It's the story of a small town librarian who has magical Scrabble tiles. It's a story about love and the power of family. It's a horror story. It's violent. It's gruesome. It's like Stephen King, but with a contemporary twist. (ha!) I loved the cultural references, and I loved how the story moved.

NOS4A2 by Joe Hill puts the creep in creepy! I borrowed this one from the library but intend to add it to my wishlist because it was that good. Manx is the type of villain that leaves you looking under the bed at night and Vic is the sort of unexpected hero that proves you don't have to be rich or strong to save someone, you just have to be determined. Excellent spine chilling read.

Listened to the audio version via audible w Kate Mulgrew narrating. Such a delicious experience. She made the book & characters come alive. She's an amazing talent. Also great b/c Joe Hill talks about the genesis of his idea for the book at the end and perhaps he does the same in the afterword? Loved the dialogue Hill creates as well as the librarian, especially in that he creates such a complex character with Maggie Lee going beyond typical librarian stereotypes. but Vic and Lou are fantastic and I also love Manx's rather naive evilness. Such a rich book this is Hills best yet.

I enjoyed this one. I can't say it was one of my favorites - I enjoyed The Heart-Shaped Box much more. But with all the hype I've seen about this one, I had to give it a shot. Although not one I would rave about, it was an interesting read, and I will most certainly read more by Joe Hill.

I really enjoy Joe Hill's books - which makes sense cause I'm a huge fan of his dad and they have similar writing styles. 
 This book was fun and engaging, the characters felt real and I could connect and empathize with them. The plot didn't drag and the story kept you interested until the very end. 
 Only problem is that it might mess up Christmas music for you hah.

Mid-to-good quality horror. As I've said, almost indistinguishable from a mid-range SK novel, but I think that's understandable and even OK. I enjoyed myself (a super-creepy book to be reading this time of year), and will read the rest of Hill's stuff too, I'm sure.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Not a book for me. Again, the plot sounded interesting, a group of friends playing Caverns & Creatures roll some magic dice and get trapped in the fantasy world, with the same rules applying (leveling up, all the constraints on when they can use their spells etc) except if they die, they stay dead. The problem for me is that all these people are the folks you would immediately put on ignore if you met them in a game online. They would be the ninja pullers, the rager in a BG, the asshole spewing racist stuff in trade (and the race thing in this book I also found odd). 
 Their only repartee involves 3 things: 
 1) Your mom jokes 
 2) Calling each other fags (sometimes with a combo of 1--accusing each other of having fags for mothers) 
 3) vomitting or shitting themselves in random moments 
 So it's pretty juvenile. There are a few jokes, but everything is very overexplained. I know there's a bunch of these and hopefully there's some character development, but everyone in this book, including the raven, were braying jackasses to me.

I made it three chapters into this book and turned it in for a refund. The casual gay-bashing and sexism, total lack of any female characters whatsoever, and the stereotypical idiotic characters killed it for me completely. I love Lit RPG, but I'd rather have read the back of a cereal box than kept going with this one.

Interesting idea, decently executed. 
 A group of Dungeons and Dragons like gamers get trapped in their gameworld after severely annoying/ insulting their Game Master. A GM who just happens to be in the possession of magical dice that trap in the gameworld he creates. 
 The stories is a quick read and quite funny. The idea of real world people in a fantasy game world is an interesting one and overall quite well executed. The adventure is interesting and the characters reasonably well done. 
 A good novel overall, but not an outstanding one. 
 [Reader note: This book contains copious amounts of strong language throughout. Not recommended for children

I love stories where people are stuck in a game world. I LOVE fart jokes. What could go wrong here? A book about people thrust into a D&D-esque world, full of crude humor - this should be amazing! 
 Only it's not. Call me a fuddy duddy, call me a feminist killjoy or a social justice warrior if you want, but this book is about a bunch of assholes. These guys are calling each other vaginas and using gay and faggy as pejoratives. (Faggy? Really?) 
 Ugh. Just so much ugh here. 
 That being said, if it sounds like something you would like and you aren't offended by homophobia, pick it up. There are some pretty funny scenes and a talking bird to redeem it, sort of.

This book is based on a good idea. I've read other books based on this idea. I've liked books based on this idea. The plot idea of modern gamers being unexpectedly thrust into a fantasy world is an excellent one. 
 Sadly this particular book is crap. 
 I know there are players like the ones pictured in this book...there have to be. Every group no matter what, political, religious, sports, people who live in a given area or region, MMORPG players or table-top players has to have it's idiots. The ones who give us all a bad name. The ones on which everyone else likes to base their negative stereo-types. 
 That's these cretins. They apparently get together occasionally to drink, tell fart jokes and attempt to play their game (obviously based on D&D). Had I ever had the misfortune of being invited to game with these imbeciles I'd have been gone before the "CM" (DM, game master etc.) had gone through with his reaction to their nonsense. 
 Look I see that this part of the book doesn't bother some readers. Personally I couldn't get past these characters. I have been gaming since 1978 (I also raised a family, had a career etc.). If these morons are how you picture table top gamers...or worse yet your experience of gamers then I'm sorry. 
 This book is as I said, crap. Not only that, it's annoying crap. I not only didn't finish it, I got rid of it. I not only can't recommend it, I recommend you avoid it.

I could start by saying this isn't the kind of book I might usually go for, which is true, but I don't read in only one genre and reading Bevan's blog I thought I'd try his books. 
 I loved it. Its bonkers, rude, crude and eminently enjoyable, an adventure story not unlike the D&D cartoons I loved as a kid, but with foul-mouthed adults in the place of too-good-to-be-true kids, or like the adventure role-play books, but with a sense of humour. 
 If you're easily offended, I wouldn't bother, but if you're happy to try something a bit different, go for it. I'm getting the second book to continue the story. 
 Funny, bonkers, crude and yet with characters who I found myself genuinely attached to, I thought it was a most entertaining read.

Posting the review here because I've read part I and II, This adventure is classic. The story flows like a David Eddings's story but for adults. Wickedly funny, pissing myself and crying. Histerical laughter. Very good, must read the conclusion.

I was not expecting this book to be so much fun. It never stops being ridiculous all the way through. I would definitely recommend for a fun run. I listened to the Audible edition and the narrator did a fabulous job.

This is a fun romp with irreverent and believable characters in an unreal setting of a D&Desque game world. They are placed there by a GM who isn't amused by teenaged boys jokes and goofs. But things get real very quickly. This isn't for the polite or those who turn up their nose on foul language...but if it is for you and you have a role playing background you will find this amusing and entertaining
terrible. offensive. boring.

 My heart.

sample_reviews.review_text:
A cute story about middle school age kids who still play with dolls....but one of those dolls is made out of human remains and haunted by a little girl's ghost. 
 Zach, Poppy, and Alice have been friends for many years, bonding over the elaborate adventures they construct with their favorite action figures and dolls. Even the creepy antique porcelain doll in the china cabinet in Poppy's house has been incorporated into their stories as the magnificent queen trapped in her glass tower. But though Zach truly enjoys playing as William the Blade, a noble pirate attempting to save the kingdom, he is troubled by the knowledge that boys his age aren't supposed to play with dolls. (Although, honestly, all these kids play in a very DnD-like way, and if someone had just introduced them to the slightly more socially acceptable concept of RPGs, half the drama in this story could have been avoided.) When Zach's father misguidedly throws away his dolls and the two girls begin acting strange and giggly, Zach worries that it may be time to leave his childhood behind and give up on his beloved games. But when Poppy comes to his window in the middle of the night, she has one last adventure for the three of them--only this one isn't pretend. 
 Poppy has been haunted by dreams of a little girl named Eleanor, whose ashes are hidden inside the Queen and whose bones were made into her porcelain. The girl died under mysterious circumstances and now she wants her remains to be buried with the rest of her family in a cemetery several towns away. As the three friends embark on this real life quest, their bonds of friendship and trust are tested like never before. 
 Though ostensibly a ghost story, Doll Bones focuses more on the trials and tribulations of friendship and growing up than it does on hauntings, mysterious deaths, and angry spirits--though there's still a bit of each. It is not entirely clear by the end of the book whether the ghost is real, or the product of the children's especially active imaginations. But that ambiguity only adds to the story. 
 For more of my thoughts, see my review for The Gothic Library: http://www.thegothiclibrary.com/doll-...

I did not really want to read this book, as I do not care for the spiderWick Chronicles books. However, Holly Black weaved a tale that was sufficiently creepy about three friends who are 12 years old, Zack, Poppy and Alice, trying to return a porcelain doll to a grave, believing a dead girl's ashes are inside. Read pgs. 64-65 to hook kids.

Doll Bones by Holly Black 
 Publisher: Margaret K. McElderry Books 
 Release Date: May 7, 2013 
 Pages: 256 
 Buy the Book: Amazon | B&N | Book Depository 
 A copy of this book was provided for free by Simon & Schuster. 
 Doll Bones by Holly Black is a spooky ghost story. This is the type of book that I think kids will be clamoring for. Holly Black writes with a style that creates a spooky atmosphere. The story is that three children Polly, Zach and Alice are all best friends. They have been playing a make believe game with figures and dolls for years. When it seems like the game might end forever, the trio embark on a quest, one last game. Polly says she had a vision of a ghost possessing the doll they had dubbed the Queen. Now they are on a quest to bury her with her family. 
 This book is aimed at the upper elementary level ( grades 4 and up). As far as ghost stories goes this book is good for that level. It is spooky but not extremely scary. I think that the story is more interesting than the typical Goosebumps book. This book differs from a Goosebumps book because it is well written. The characters are developed and you care about all of them. None of the three main characters seem like cardboard cutouts. I would recommend it to very imaginative children between grades 4 and 6 because they would appreciate the game that the characters play. 
 I rate this book 5 stars for being a spooky well written ghost story.

"I thought you needed to be tougher. But I've been thinking that protecting somebody by hurting them before someone else gets the chance isn't the kind of protecting that anybody wants." 
 A middle grade horror novel, Doll Bones tells a story about adventures and friendship that gets mixed with creepy events and different emotions. This was very age appropriate and even though it was horror story, there wasn't much scary things about it except the old china doll. 
 Friendship that was presented between Zach, Poppy, and Alice was incredible. It's that kind of friendship that you have with people who you've known since you were 5 and probably will be going to each other's kids birthdays. Their emotions and feelings were very well portrayed. With Zach being 12, it was interesting to see his confusion about girls and anger about his dad leaving their family and then coming back. 
 I did think that adventure aspect of it could have been more intensified and not so much left to the imagination. The bus ride, the park, and even the boat - give me something more creepier! But overall it was a good story line, except I wasn't much a fan of writing and didn't connect with the story as much as I wanted to.

A blend of charmingly creative kids, intense emotions, and spooky ghost-like elements that just might be "only a story". The parent/child relationships, friendship struggles, and internal character emotions ring true throughout, while the writing itself was splendid. Example: "That past summer, the mysterious thing that stretched other boys like taffy had started to happen to Zach. He'd always been tall, but now he'd almost reached his father's height, with hands so big that..." You get the idea. 
 Well-suited to kids who adore, inhale, obsess over fantasy-adventure stories, with many reflections within the story on their own obsessions with the genre.

Loved this book. Three friends on the verge of adolescence must confront the fact that they are getting too old to play pretend. The problem, of course, is that they still really love their created worlds and characters. What unfolds is a great adventure that involves midnight bus trips, sailing down the Ohio river, breaking into a library, and ultimately searching for the graveyard where a creepy doll can be buried and the spirit of a little girl laid to rest. I love this book as both a coming-of-age story and as an adventure. I'm also personally drawn to and fascinated by these characters who love to imagine and create but who know that they are expected to give it up. I'm still working out exactly how to respond to this issue eloquently. 
 My one and only complaint is that I think that the spooky factor of this book was oversold. Yes, the doll is creepy. But I didn't at any point feel the need to hide under a blanket. Still, this is probably a good dose of creepy for those who don't want a lot of scary.
I bought this for myself at the book fair and I loved it!!! 4 1/2 stars

A creepy story without being scary. Three friends on the cusp of out growing their imaginative play, embark on a quest, across western PA and Eastern OH, to put a ghost to rest. Include an antique china doll that seems to move on her own ant Holly Black has once again penned a chilling story that keeps you up. I have yet to find a book by Black I am not wowed by!
This is a book of the loss of childhood more than a ghost story. Probably excellent if you're twelve rather than a jaded and overly cynical 35-year old.
Meh.. had to really suspend reality. Kids would not have been able to get away with this.

Love the cover art so far 
 ____________________________ 
 As someone who grew up in the country away from pop culture, I had a hard time relating to the topics and rants. The writing style was enjoyable, but I just couldn't care about the material.

Sex, Drugs and Cocoa Puffs by Chuck Klosterman seemed to be a good book. Its a good idea but it was just a major rant. And of nothing in particular either lol. What ever popped in his head at the time he was writing is what he ranted about. Couldnt stand it, sounded like a kid whining the whole time i was reading it

I started out loving this book - I thought the first few essays were interesting, insightful without being too serious, and funny. Then I hit the middle of the book and found myself alternately bored and out-of-sync with Klosterman's perspective. By the end of the book I despised him. It was a long way to travel in the course of a short 250 pages. I think I would have liked many of the essays better if they had been one-offs; but Klosterman in large doses is irritating. I think the problem is that his aggressive arrogance worked when I agreed with or thought his points made sense but when what he was saying seemed forced or was outside my realm of knowledge, I just found him grating. As this is as much a problem with me as it is him, it's hard to know whether to recommend the book; I think I would recommend reading it, but not sticking with the essays that don't catch your interest right away; or maybe, better yet, don't read this book in consecutive sessions - I think I would have liked the collection way better overall if I'd sat down every so often over the course of a long period and read a single essay at a time.

A good friend of mine let me borrow this book, thinking that it was up my alley - which normally, based on its subject matter, it would be. I usually find sociological/philosophical examinations of things like pop culture fascinating, or at the very least entertaining. Unfortunately, this book fell flat in many ways. 
 The writer's style and ideas reminds me of a young, male college student who is incredibly smug and self-satisfied, who thinks he knows better than 99% of society and makes blanket statements that fall apart upon even the tiniest bit of close critical examination. The author is a self-admitted cheater in romantic relationships, for example, and then claims that he can't ever find true love because "no one can" in this society, that the media has built up such high expectations that we are all doomed. And yes, there is absolutely a Disneyification of romantic ideals that can make being realistic about your relationships difficult, but the essay comes off as so bitter and borderline misogynistic ('my girlfriend would rather go see Coldplay sing whinily about fake love and nonsense than stay in an expensive New York hotel with me, bwaaaah') that it makes me roll my eyes even when he comes close to making valid points. 
 His essays are chock-full of hyperbole, often devolving into rambles that I can't imagine anyone would care to read about, like how everyone he meets is a 'type' of person based on someone from MTV's The Real World, which the show somehow "caused"...which is a stupid essay because 1. There are a ton of people who have never watched that show, even if they grew up in that era and 2. He keeps referencing specific cast members, which just made me want to skip the essay altogether. In fact, I *did* skip another long essay about basketball players I'd never heard of. (Which brings me to another point, which he actually voices as a concern at the beginning of the book: A book about pop culture, which references contemporary celebrities before you know who is going to "stick" in the collective consciousness, is doomed to become horribly dated. I had a lot of moments where I didn't know who the hell he was talking about, and occasionally was like "ohhh, right, that person who was briefly famous in the mid-90s." This wouldn't matter so much if he more skillfully wove them into his essays, but he leans fairly heavily on people knowing who these specific individuals are.) 
 Don't even get me started on the book's closing essay, in which he repeatedly claims that born again Christians are "cool" because they don't back down on judging people and view every conversation as an opportunity to save someone from hell. I don't know if he is just trying to be edgy at this point (another thing that seems very sophomoric to me, but whatever), but as a former victim of that community who has seen up close the psychological damage that kind of uncompromising attitude can do, it seriously rubs me the wrong way. He talks a lot of shit about things he has no idea about, which, as he claims in one essay, is "what journalism is all about." Ugh. 
 Despite these issues, I didn't completely hate this book, and I found a handful of the essays sufficiently entertaining, with some genuinely interesting points. It just wasn't enough to save it from being a rare one-star read.
rants, complaints. Not all that entertaining, but was a decent read during train travel.
I've tried multiple times to read this one, but I just can't get into it.

Klosterman is pretty funny. These essays are generally entertaining, even though he comes off as a complete bore you probably wouldn't want to meet in person. His analysis of computer games and consumerism in the essay on "The Sims," and his discussion of the merits of Billy Joel, were the strongest essays, IMO. The sports essays didn't interest me much, but that owes more to my lack of interest in sports than his writing. If I were a college freshman I would have probably loved the iconoclasm and offhand mockery of everything, but I couldn't help thinking that he thinks he's a lot smarter than he actually is, and though he makes some disparaging remarks about hipsters, this is very much a hipster manifesto, for better or worse (mostly worse).

Before I forget, I tried to read a Chuck Klosterman book of pop essays called Sex and Drugs and Cocoa Puffs. I made it through two essays that I liked. But when he started to analyze The Real World season by season, I just lost interest. Granted, I'm not a fan of reality TV in general, so it's possible this book was just not meant to be read by me.

I couldn't disagree with the author more. His opinions on pop culture were on one end of the spectrum, and I was on the other so needless to say, I've decided that this book is not deserving of my attention. Nonetheless, I felt that it lacked innovation on a number of levels, the least of which was author intelligence. One might say that the book itself is low culture.

book_a.user_review: This started as just a fun read and then I got really really into it and almost couldn't put it down. sample_reviews.review_text:
This book makes you think. Not the kind of contemplating thinking, but the one that makes you piece the puzzle together. 
 I love its mysterious and magical atmosphere, how the plot unfolds little by little to reveal the true core of the story which, in my opinion, is not as captivating as I thought it would be. The ending is also somewhat dissatisfying to me. 
 However, I am usually not into too descriptive narration, but the one in this book is sort of blowing my mind. I surprisingly enjoyed its beautifully crafted magical illusion.

Weird 
 I think I liked the book, but I need the author to sit me down and explain it to me.

So many people have said the beautiful descriptions of the circus are what drew them into this book. Many reviewers have noted how they found the timing confusion, but it is not such a major issue to disrupt your reading. Although I am a cynic and find love-at-first-sight stories too far fetched, I've read many people's comments saying they loved that aspect of this book. 
 My attraction was the characters and their interaction with each other, and that's not to say they were all likable. I loved the innocence of the young characters, the development of the circus structure, and how the author intertwined all the characters for the plot "twists." 
 I can understand why this title is so popular right now and am still digesting the details of the story lines several weeks later.

What I liked most about the book was the whole commentary and subtext on love as competition. I thought she did a lot of interesting takes on that. It is so prevalent now in youth culture for relationships to be about who is better looking, who is smarter, more money, etc. In fact, this often carries over into adult relationships. She does an admirable job as an author of addressing this then sending it up. Props also given for the sheer inventiveness. Brilliant set up and construction. Brilliant handling of the material and author savvy in knowing just how much of the circus to reveal and how much to remain a mystery. I dont really get though why its a YA novel. These characters are far more mature and responsible than most teenagers. Perhaps due to the era in which the book is set teenagers often assumed adult responsibilities earlier. Kudos again for remaining true to the time period. Favorite characters are definitely Widget and Poppet. Well drawn and endearing.

The lush and descriptive writing really draws you in, and the core concept is imaginative and unique. 
 Pointless time-jumping helps to obscure the weak progression and pacing. While the author seems to have a clear picture of the "competition" it is never compellingly portrayed to the reader, and the reason/logic behind the competition feels weak and wholly inadequate to justify a life/death contest. 
 I would have preferred fewer, well-drawn characters to the dozen or so lightly-sketched primary actors interwoven throughout the narrative, but each did have an actual function within the story. 
 All in all, I am not sorry I read it, but would not be likely to read another by this author.

This was such a fantastic read. 
 I never would have picked up this book if it weren't for a bookclub I participate in, but I am so glad that November's read was this book. 
 What I liked most about the book was Morgenstern's descriptive writing. The images I have of the circus in my head are beautiful... Years from now I'll probably forget about everything to do with this book excluding those wonderful images of the night circus. 
 So different and beautiful.

almost 4 stars... I'm so nitpicky these days, though - I did not like the use of present tense throughout the book even as it flip-flopped its way through the late 1800's & early 1900's; it just got tedious to read after awhile, for me. And it seemed to take a long time to get to the point, to the end - I found myself skimming the last few pages just to get done... felt it went overly long, too much blah, blah, blah at the end. Again, I'm getting so nitpicky about my reading. 
 It was a very different read, though - like a Tim Burton film on pages.
Two magicians have a contest using real individuals who create a magical circus.

I coudln't finish this book. Not saying it was horrible. I just don't think it was a book for me. 
 The character switches were too confusing. There were multiple names for people and I couldn't get them all straight. 
 I read probably about 20% of the book and most of what I read just seemed like a set up. Not much happened we just keep getting introduced to new characters. And I don't see the point in meeting them, Other than that, the two kids are practicing their magic. That's all that's happening. 
 To me, this book is boring. Maybe I'll pick it back up and finish in the future - I hate to give up - but who knows.

I really wanted to like this book, I really did, but I'm quite sad that unfortunately, it did nothing for me. Nothing at all. 
 I think I've been the victim of an over-marketed book frenzy. The hype that came with it was enormous. But to me the story is pretentious and rather too proud of itself to be genuinely good. It tries to be more interesting than it is, and it did nothing to keep me engaged. The blurb may catch your attention, your hopes for a few magical hours of reading might have soared. But sadly, this is merely very clever advertising of what it is, for me, an empty vessel. It has left me sorely disappointed. Nothing that is hinted at and promised in the blurb comes to be. It is full of lies that never materialise inside the book. Yet again, the hype of advertising......! 
 However, as much as I detested it, it surely must have some literary merit, some paragraphs perked me a bit, my interest rose for a little while to be crushed again, and I am reluctant to give it one star. Perhaps just because by comparison, my "one star" shelf is full of utter crap, the rejects that make me furious, and I cannot bring myself to give The Night Circus just one star. But it is close. 
 The impact that this book has had on me, is that instead of loving the time that I can dedicate to my reading, I was dreading it. Reading felt like a chore for the duration, and to me that's possibly the most heinous crime against the pleasure of reading. I procrastinated, I played lots of solitaire (even Candy Crush, how embarrassing), I watched lots of TV, which I hardly ever do, I even started and finished about 10 other books before I managed to force myself to return to this one. Basically, I felt cheated, patronised and ultimately taken for a ride by this book. 
 The pace is off, the structure is off, the content is off. It took me the best part of two weeks to finish it and I only did because it was part of my reading challenge. Otherwise, it would have been added to my "I couldn't care less" pile. 
 Overly descriptive, the story, which is as boring as watching paint dry, unfolds over many years. It seems that nothing happens for ages, and I found myself often mumbling "So, what?"....... "Do I care about this?" ........Sadly, I didn't. The story caught up a bit after the 75% mark, but then, only briefly and timidly, and by then, I just wanted to finish the bloody book to fulfil my challenge, not because I really gave a damn about the resolution. I could not have cared less! And this, mostly because I could not make myself feel anything for the characters. I did not manage to develop any investment in them or their journey. This book is definitely not character-driven. 
 The book has even spoiled one of my favourite literary structural devices. The plot jumps forwards and backwards in time. While I typically love this type of non-linear book structure, in this case it was gratuitous and unnecessary. Here it only served to confuse me, and I'd like to think that I am not particularly thick! It does not flow easily and there is no reason for it. It adds nothing to the story, but detracts a lot. I had to keep trying to use my math to work out how old the characters were at any particular time and really, really there is no good reason to make the plot jump forwards and backwards in time in with no rhyme or reason. In my opinion, it simply contributes to make it even more pretentious. It is fake mysteriousness. 
 Just to end, I will give it something positive, though: it is a very visual book and I'm sure that with the right director (Tim Burton, perhaps?), it definitely has the potential to be translated into a visually stunning movie. I'll probably even go to watch it. 
 As for the book, I'm going to give it the Rotten Tomatoes award: greatest disappointment of the year! 
 Popsugar Reading Challenge 2015: #39. A book with magic.

book_b.title: You Will Know Me
book_b.user_review: Terrible writing. Goes no where. Not much mystery. Did I mention terrible writing? Avoid this book.

sample_reviews.review_text:
**** 1/2 
 Really fun, dark read and my favorite so far from Megan Abbott. The plot was mostly predictable but no less compelling. It did feel like Ryan's connection to the group was somewhat implausible and forced; surely there were stronger ways to tie him to the group? Anyway, a really fun one that I've been recommending to people all week.

A suspense novel centered around young gymnasts and their families, putting everything on the line to reach the Olympics. There's lots of detail about the sacrifices of family members, about the cattiness and ambitions of parents, the intentions of the girls, etc. It feels as though Abbot's spent time either as a gymnast or as a mom of a gymnast. The mystery--how a young man associated with the gym was killed in an apparent hit-and-run--is a twisty one. There are enough poorly-turned phrases that I could never quite trust the language, and the claustrophobic closeness of the protagonist's viewpoint meant that other characters always felt distorted by her current perception. In the end, it was probably the elite-gymnast aspect that soured me on the book--a world I personally condemn, so I don't sympathize enough with the various characters.

This book just wasn't my style. It did keep you guessing until the end but it also had me questioning what in the world was going on for the first 1/3 of the book...and not in a good way. 
 I really didn't like the authors style of writing, just very disjointed and really I honestly thought, "What in the world am I reading about here?" I guess maybe it's meant to be clever or something, I don't know but really just not my cup of tea.
I don't know why, maybe the French translation was not that good, but I did not enjoy it at all but ended up speed-reading it. Didn't get better at the end.

My first thought upon finishing this book was "THANK GOD IT'S OVER." 
 To be fair, this is not the kind of book I usually like. I was sold on a novel about gymnastics, but that's not what this is. Gymnastics just happens to be how all these characters know each other. Otherwise, it's a typical "small community is rocked by tragic thing and now clueless main character is figuring out that people have Secrets and she doesn't actually know anything." Filled out with enough purple prose to choke an elephant. Rare is the sentence that doesn't include a simile, excess adjectives, or ties to random memories. And listening to it as an audiobook made it worse, the reader emoting carefully at every flowery description. 
 Also, wow, so many borderline creepy descriptions of the bodies of little girls. Yes, we get it, gymnast girls have different bodies from typical little girls, you can stop describing their chests and legs and butts ANY time now. Please. 
 I'm so glad I got this one from my library, so I didn't spend any actual money on it. And now it's over! Hooray!

Beautifully written suspense novel about teenage girl and family dynamics. Devon Knox is a talented young gymnast with the potential to be an Olympic contender. Her parents, Katie and Eric, have turned their lives around to focus everything - time, energy, money that they don't have - on Devon and her training. Shortly after the start of the book, Ryan, a good looking young man who is dating the beloved niece of Devon's coach, is murdered in a hit and run. As the police investigate, Katie begins to discover dark truths about her husband and daughter. 
 I really enjoy Abbott's writing style; it is very atmospheric and psychological penetrating. She expertly creates an unsettled yet familiar atmosphere. The ending wasn't that shocking - there were clues sprinkled throughout the book but Katie's realization of what happened and how she reacts marks this as literary suspense.

Picked it up because it sounded interesting, kept reading because I wanted to know what happened, but I hated it after I put it down. There is no justice in this book, no good morals, and I ended up hating all of the characters. It got a little gross too. I just pretty much think that if you have any sort of similar taste in books as me you should skip this one.
1.5 stars. Nothing was specifically wrong with this book, but I didn't find it interesting.

I really hated almost all of the characters, especially the protagonist, Katie. Conceited, annoying, a really bad mother for her second child, clueless...I really cannot find anything good about her. Only Drew was a nice enough kid, which was growing up ignored by his whole family and feeling alone all the time. I finished the book waiting for a redeeming quality of Katie or Devon or Eric, but tough luck, it never happened. Selfish people without any morals. 
 Also, the plot was nothing much, It failed to keep you invested.

Roxane Gay reviewed it best and I'm in complete agreement: 
 No one writes about the intersections between teenage girls, ambition, bodies, and obsession better than Megan Abbott. Her voice is distinct throughout this novel. Tight, taut, tense, terrifying. You Will Know Me is both a portrait of a family who put their talented gymnast daughter at the center of their world, and how ambition is the thing that holds them together and tears them apart. The words in this novel are like weapons and Abbott wields them very well.

reference_books.title: Red Seas Under Red Skies (Gentleman Bastard, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Oh forget about being polite: FANTASY SEQUEL FAIL. 
 Lynch's impressive debut was probably embarassed when this one hit the shelves, as it reads more like a poorly planned Dungeons and Dragons game than a novel. The same tricks used several times over and over again eventually wear on the reader, as do the characters who have a knack (like Roleplaying characters) of figuring everything out just in the nick of time. 
 Worse still--the plot takes a completely irrelevant sidetrip, to the tune of 400 pages, placing the characters in a ridiculous (and ridiculously boring) quest away from the main action. It's almost as if the Dungeon Master didn't wrap up loose ends before sending his players on a wild goose chase for a few weeks.... 
 If you can find a way to skip the nautical middle section, the novel is pleasant, but not as exciting as its predecessor. Certainly nothing new; I daresay a step backward for the author.

reference_books.title: A Fire Upon the Deep (Zones of Thought, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Only made it about 20% through this one. Very hard science fiction, with underdeveloped characters and a meagre plot. Perhaps it's dated, as I didn't find the books central conceit all that inspiring.

reference_books.title: Between the World and Me
reference_books.review_text:
An instant classic. Will be read alongside Frederick Douglas, Booker T. Washington, Malcolm X, James Baldwin, and Toni Morrison. Not since Alexis De Toucqueville's Democracy in America has an author pulled back the veil on American Exceptionalism and rendered it naked and plain. 
 This book is necessary reading for every American, in particular people who believe themselves to be white Americans. Coates writes a deeply personal and revealing account of growing up in a black body within a society that destroys black bodies. I was shocked at how direct he was, but there was nothing to argue with. He is a masterful writer and a truth-teller. If there is any hope that this country can ever live up to the lofty promises of its nationalist rhetoric, one must grapple with the ugly nasty truth that Coates lays bare. 
 Five stars. Highly recommended.

reference_books.title: Dream Country (The Sandman #3)
reference_books.review_text:
This volume contains four short vignettes that lack purpose, individually,and focus, collectively. The alleged highlight of the volume--Gaiman's riff on A Midsummer's Night Dream--amounted to parading around a clever central conceit without any conflict or plot to contextualize it. 
 This is my ultimate problem with Gaiman: he has wonderful ideas but lacks follow through. His series lacks the quintessential element of a good graphic novel--an intricate plot. A plot where the revelations compel the reader to continue on; a series of delights and defeats that make navigating the complex setting worthwhile. On this front, volume 3 completely failed to deliver.

reference_books.title: A Dance with Dragons (A Song of Ice and Fire, #5)
reference_books.review_text:
Martin has lost control of his creation, as evidenced by this massive, meandering, pointless book. What started out as a fun, fast-paced story has become a chore as we see characters slog around doing nothing for damn near 1000 pages. The book's various plots are not resolved and everything is left on a cliffhanger. The editor herself was disappointed the climaxes were left until the next volume. It's anyone's guess when--and even if--we ever see that. 
 My advice: watch the HBO show. It's much better than this, and actually will be completed. Can't say the same for ASOIAF

book_a.title: Wizard's First Rule (Sword of Truth, #1)
book_a.user_review: This was a dreadful book I read years ago. For anyone who cares to listen: it's awful. Not worth the paper it was printed on. It takes the most predictable, common tropes from fantasy and makes them even more boring, and pushes an antisocial, libertarian political philosophy in such a ham fisted way it was transparent to me even as a 14 year old. Pure garbage.

sample_reviews.review_text: Eh, very mediocre writing. Way more words than necessary. The story was okay, and I did finish it, but there were way too many flaws to make it worth reading. I don't want to be too mean though, there were fun parts. I'm sure his writing has improved.

I really wanted to like this, but I had to give up at page 70. Horrible dialogue, even worse inner-dialogue, the two main characters are so average and stereotyped it makes me want to kill kittens. 
 If you're into fantasy, avoid Terry Goodkind. 
 Mind you, I read "The Law Of Nines" before trying this putrid pile, and guess what? I found it to be one of the biggest pieces of crap I ever stumbled upon, but I had been told that it was Goodkind's worst offering so I was like "let's give the bastard another chance". Seriously: if "Wizard's First Rule" is supposed to be Goodkind's best book, I don't even want to know what's inside his other novels. 
 Sorry, Terry... I don't like your shit.

This book was legitimately terrible through much of it, especially the early parts. Goodkind just writes the least believable characters. The hero's progression was compelling enough to get me up to 2 stars, and I remember liking this when I was young, but dang, this book sucked.

Shmeh. It was okay. Another reviewer called Goodkind a "grossly inept writer," and I think that's probably on target, but you know what? For a fun, fantastical read, it was worth the time it took to read the 600 pages. If you're looking for hard-hitting literature, look elsewhere; if you're looking to read something absorbing and fun, half-tongue-in-cheek and half actual interest, go for it.

This was my first experience with Goodkind, and I started reading the book because I really been enjoying the series based from it, "Legend of the Seeker." I loved the book, and look forward to reading subsequent volumes in the Sword of Truth series. 
 I had heard negative things about Goodkind's tendency to use rape and violence against women in his books. At least in this volume, I didn't find that to be pervasive. It is violent at times, and Kahlan almost almost gets raped by a D'Haran quad. Essentially, though, most of the extreme violence is done by the antagonists. 
 Nevertheless, the story was gripping. I found this 800+ page book to be a much more entertaining read than Martin's Fire and Ice series (not to be misunderstood, I enjoy that series, too).

To excuse all of the logic flaws, anachronisms, abysmally poor characterization, weird pacing, and extremely surreal flow because "it's just fiction" is the same as saying "it's just a kid's book" which is a huge peeve point of mine. In either case, this fact remains: if you are made to suspend not only disbelief but also your intelligence in order to enjoy a book, "it's just" poorly written. 
 If you enjoy this book, author, or series I am glad for you. You obviously clued into something I could not. Please continue to enjoy them without me.

First, I love fantasy novels as a general rule. In fact, I will overlook a lot of bad writing for a great story. 
 This story wasn't great. It was formulaic AND I finished the book with this uneasy feeling that Terry Goodkind may actually hate women. The scenes of torture and pain were far more extensive than those of love and redemption. 
 Some parts were entertaining although I saw the big twists at the end coming for about 500 pages. Generally dissatisfied though.
KILL WITH FIRE. Seriously, stay away from this book. The story is bad, the characters have the depth of a paper sheet, and writing is juvenile at best.

I just... I wanted to like it, but the dialogues were stiff, the characters bland, I... I don't know what to say, I'm really disappointed. I wanted something Tolkien-ish but it ended up being like "Anhar".

Overall rating 2 stars. 
 I am so happy to be done with this book. It took me over a month to finish it, but it felt like longer. I suppose I should explain my rating a little bit. I am going to break my rating down into 3 categories: story, length, and narrator. 
 First, lets start with story. I probably would give it about 3 stars. There was nothing that great about the story, but there was nothing that bad about the story either. The word I kept thinking about that best describes this story while reading it was simplistic. Not too long ago, I went to a website that broke down the different kinds of fiction (Epic, Heroic, High, low, quest, young adult, sword and sorcery, military, urban, etc.) I had never thought there could be so many different types of Fantasy out there. After reading the list, I found that the type of fantasy books I like to read the most is Hard Fantasy. What is Hard Fantasy? 
 " Logic and reason rule the pages of Hard Fantasy and attention to detail is a writer's best gift. Hard Fantasy is the Fantasy version of Hard Science Fiction, but the two aren't completely analogous--Hard Fantasy is not just Fantasy that treats magic like science. Fantasy is 'hard,' when it is concerned with how and why things work. 
 Hard Fantasy also does not pull away from the traditions of the genre, as Mundane Fantasy does, but instead offers a detailed explanation for the existence of magic itself, magical creatures, and seemingly fantastical settings. For example, dragons with an evolutionary past, rather than legendary. Hard Fantasy takes fantasy's traditions and the mundane details and uses them to create a complex and meaningful story--an enchanted sword is not taken for granted, it has ramifications within the story the justify the detail needed to explain how and why it has been enchanted." from website http://bestfantasybooks.com/hard-fant... 
 This book is as far from hard fantasy as you can get. There were wizards in this story, but there was not much discussion about the amount and extent of their powers. The main character is Richard who has been identified as the Seeker. A position that is very respected and feared because of how much power this position holds. However, I never got the impression the position or the character was that powerful. The Seeker is also known as the Seeker of the Truth, because the overriding characteristic of this position is that they seek out truth. He is given a sword which has magic that apparently can cut through almost anything, but there is a price for each time he uses the sword. Other characters in the book were shocked at how Richard could figure out the truth behind a situation, but for me everything that Richard said and did was common sense. Some of the things that he "figured out" were obvious from the start, but all the other characters in the story were amazed at what he had done. Here is an example. Early on in the story the enemy placed a spell on a cloud that constantly followed Richard around, so he could always be found. So, Richard asked a wizard if magic was used on the cloud to follow him around, could magic be used to solve the problem? The wizard was astonished at how creative and intelligent Richard was for coming up with that answer. WTF? All the characters were pretty simplistic as well. Richard was either the most laid back, thoughtful person who was always trying to figure things out, or he was furious with rage were he could not think. He was either one extreme or the other. There are two other main characters in the story: Kaylan and Zed, but I don't care enough about either of them to spend time writing about them except to say they were similarly written characters in term of there emotions. Kaylan was either completely emotional, or very stoic. This might of been a good story for me to read when I was much younger, but the fact that I have read so much very well written Fantasy books before reading this book, I was hoping for so much more. I watched the first season of the television series that this book was based on and I had almost the same feeling while watching the show. I always felt that there could be something there, but it never really developed for me. I stopped watching after the first season. I didn't really dislike it, I just couldn't bring myself to care that much. I never thought that what Richard said or did was that impressive. The bad guy in the story is, of course, the worst person anyone could ever think about. There was no complexity to him at all (I think they tried to make him complex but I did not really believe it). The pace of the story was also very slow, spending too much time talking about insignificant points. The author also used way to many hard adjectives (incredible, immense, intense). This leads us right into the next category: length of the story. 
 I listened to the audiobook instead of reading. I usually have one book for listening and one book for reading at the same time. This book was 34 hours long. Halfway through the book, I was begging for it to be over. Because of the simplistic story, I pretty much knew what was going to happen by the end. It was excruciating knowing what is going to happen and having to wait that long for it to come to pass. If this book was 8-12 hours long, I would have probably rated it a little higher, but the length of the book brought the rating down. I have to give it 1.5 stars for the length. There was a point in the book where Richard is being tortured and the pain is excruciating (see another power adjective). This goes on for 3 hours. I am not saying that he is tortured for 3 hours, I am saying that I listened to him being tortured for 3 hours. I understand the reasoning later in the story, but couldn't the author have gotten his point across in 30 minutes? It was somewhat painful (torturous?) to listen to this book. 
 Since this is an audiobook, I also have to talk about the narrator. Sometimes a narrator can make a mediocre story great or a great story mediocre. This narrator made a mediocre story bad. I compare this narrator's style to that of an old time BARD from England. It felt like he was reciting something to a group of 1000 people in a theatre; he was being so over-dramatic. He was the type of person that over-pronounces every syllable. I got annoyed with the narrator from the very beginning because he had over exaggerated his "S" sounds into the microphone, causing a little bit of feedback. His volume control was off as well. I had the volume way up most of the time so I could hear appropriately most of the time, but then he was whisper so I could barely hear, or raise his voice so loud it almost hurt. I did not like this narrator much at all. Some of the voices he used for some of the peripheral characters were terrible too. I would have to rate the narrator as a 1 out of 5. I still think I would have liked this story better if I read it instead of listening to it. 
 Based on those 3 criteria is how I arrived at the overall rating of 2. I think the worst thing about this book is that is was not bad enough for me to stop listening. If it were just a bad book, I would have turned it off and never thought twice. The fact that it was not that bad made me stick with it till the end. I have to admit around the halfway point of the story I gave serious thought into throwing in the towel. I am glad that I finished the story. The last 5 hours of the book went the fastest and were the most interesting (which I knew it would be).

book_b.title: The Way of Shadows (Night Angel, #1)
book_b.user_review:
A somewhat awful page-turner: 
 A page-turner I'm embarrassed to have finished. The plot in this exciting thriller rolls along, almost too swiftly, but ultimately left me unfulfilled. The author never fleshes out his world or the characters inhabiting it. They often lack motivation for their actions and are little more than mere vehicles for the plot, whose elements fit *too well* together. The central love story is so trite its laugh-out-loud funny, and while I realize Mr. Weeks met his wife at a very young age, we'd need a little more explanation for our hero's affection for a girl than that they knew each other when they were young. This element ruined the ending for me, and Weeks showed absolutely no capability of handling complex emotions. The book reads like a role-playing game with very maudlin moments thrown in to give it a depth which is beyond this author's reach. 
 This is one of those books where everything falls into place nicely, the characters find out what they need to find out at exactly the precise time for the plot to progress, and every single character introduced ends up being central to the plot if not biologically related to the other characters. 
 I will say there were a few wonderful scenes, especially in the first half, but Weeks needs to learn to linger, slow down, and build these scenes up for a greater payoff. We're barely ever asked to consider something momentous before rushed along to the next bright, shiny plot-object. 
 Very similar to Mistborn in its strengths and weaknesses, but much worse. The hype surrounding this debut obscures what a petty project it is, and while there are some great authors out there, I hope this sort of trilogy isn't indicative of the direction in which the fantasy genre is moving. 
 Read only if you want a *very* light, fun fantasy that clunks along at times but keeps you turning pages and rolling your eyes.

sample_reviews.review_text: Eh, just not that into it.

I'm roughly 25% into this book, and it hasn't grabbed me yet. I keep hearing good things about this, so I'm begging you guys to maybe motivate me or confirm my initial thoughts. 
 So far, the writing is fine. There's nothing good or bad about it, which is just fine with me for a funtasy book. One minor quirk: Durzo is a badass, I get it, no need to keep repeating that Durzo is the greatest-most-bestest-awesomest assassin. It cheapens the character. I swear at one point the narration actually points out that he's the best assassin, as if "best assassin" is some plaque Durzo received. 
 Okay, that rant aside, the rest of it is fine. That's kind of the problem. There's nothing GREAT about it. The characters don't stand out at all. You get the baddestass assassin and a protege who's lived a really harsh life, but 25% into it, and I've yet to gain any sense of motivation from these characters. I don't know why Durzo does what he does, and that's fine, but shouldn't I WANT to know why he's doing what he's doing? Where's the intrigue, or foreshadowing, or hints of characteristics that will make me want to know more about this uber assassin? 
 With Kylar, at least I'm interested enough to root for him to survive. His relationship with the girl is downright heart-breaking, and it definitely makes me want to know more about him. 
 Anyway, I'm not sure I can keep reading this. If any of you LOVE this or HATE this, please comment. I hope I'm not missing out on an amazing book just because I decided to stop. 
 Side note: I forced myself to finish book 1 of the Mistborn trilogy, and I'm glad I did. I was bored of that book in a somewhat similar manner as this one.
DNF at 120 pages. I feel like I've seen this story before countless times, and better written as well.

The friend who recommended it to me called it the Mary Sue Assassin novel. It totally is, but not necessarily in a way that diminishes the book. A bit cliche and melodramatic, but the author gets some things right, namely his depictions of nobility and street rat life. The villains are still totally mwa-ha-ha evil but his women seem to have sense and intellect. Total trashy plane reading in the best way.

I liked the book, there were some pretty brutal parts to the story but was a ok read. This book is sort of the book series you read when your in between series and you can't decide what to read next. Definetly not for children to read, there are some pretty graphic things in this novel. I really like the world he created and have bought the remaining two books in the series, not something I will probably read again but don't think I have wasted my time in doing so. One interesting this in this novel was how children are treated. I have NEVER read a novel that contained that sort of content, except from possibly George R. Martin. Which is what made me this novel stand out for me. Anyways, not something I recommend other people read, but if you do you won't regret it but your life won't be changed for reading it.
Took me a while to finish, parts felt liked it dragged. The pacing was just too slow for my liking.

My biggest complaint with this book was I was not invested at all in the world. Big things seemed to be happening, but I didn't really care beyond the main character. A bit of humor might have been nice too. Overall I was intrigued by the magic system, I'm a fan of the assassin set-up, and I'm interested to see what will happen in the next books.

I got quite a few chapters into this book--far more than I was really comfortable with--when I found myself sitting there and watching this character doing horrible, immoral stuff with absolute callousness (and I'm not even talking about the assassination gig!). And I pulled away and sat there watching myself watching him, and I thought, "What am doing? Is there any way in which I can justify what I am exposing myself to right now?" And I realized I couldn't. So I left it unfinished. 
 Rating: Extra R. Also, I didn't even get to the worst stuff. Violence, deviant sexual attitudes, yada yada yada. Did I mention I couldn't finish it?

Unfortunately not my thing. I stopped reading at the 9% mark.
