Whats not to love about this novel? 
 A orphan raised in the gutter as a thief and scavenger, who triumphs over adversity to become an assassins apprentice. And add a touch of magic near the end of the book (that's the essence to the next two) Okay that the simplistic view, and a lot more's happening here than solely that. 
 Azoth who is an orphan who lives in the Warrens of Cenaria City. He has two friends, Jarl and Doll Girl. Then there's Rat who rises to be the leader of the guild and hates Azoth and his friends to the point of murder and buggery. We see his life in the warrens and his struggles to over come that life. He wants become Durzo Blint's apprentice but has to prove himself. - okay any more here adds spoilers. 
 Meanwhile the cities ruler is Duke Gyre and his heir Logan Gyre. Duke Gyre leaves the city to fight invaders leaving his son behind. Add to this a travelling mage Solon Tofusin who seems to be following a prophesy involving Lord Gyre but isn't sure if its the Duke or his son. 
 Once Azoth, now known as Kylar Stern has become Blints apprentice we get to witness some training and grooming that's addictive in the telling. He becomes a blade master and we learn he has a wealth of magical mojo, but the connection to it is broken. However a "kakari" would bridge the connection but is a very powerful weapon and only 7 are in existence. 
 Kylar eventually gets the black kakari which has some unusual qualities including defying death at a dire cost to Kylar. 
 The book then goes into overdrive with a fight between Kylar and Blint and Khalidorans invasion arrives by sea with vurdmeisters (powerful mages) and amongst the chaos Logan Gyre becomes King and hides in a most unusual place. This end part of the book had me on tender hooks the entire time, and I refused to put the book down until I had finished it. 
 Its an old story of waif to assassin but it has a whole new feel here. The Black kakiri and the vurdmeisters magic are a new twist on magic as we normally perceive it in these books. Told in a new and ruthless manner this book is simply addictive. The characters are endearing. And the ending climatic.

reference_books.title: Wide Sargasso Sea
reference_books.review_text: I'd heard lots of praise for this and I love Jane Eyre, so naturally I decided to try it. I was disappointed. It's not bad, exactly, but I feel it has been over rated. Rochester's role is reasonably small and not in keeping with his character in Jane Eyre. Given the material, Rhys could have done so much more...

reference_books.title: The Distant Hours
reference_books.review_text: My main problem with this book was it wasn't as good as Morton's first two. The opening, with the story of "The Mud Man", was great and the ending is also good: building the tension, giving a shock and then tying things up in a satisfying conclusion. But the middle - and there is a LOT of middle - is just a bit saggy. I really got the feeling the book hadn't been edited; so much pointless stuff that didn't have any bearing later. It isn't bad, but it became a bit of a chore to read before finally gripping me again at the end. You can do better, Kate!

reference_books.title: The Taxidermist's Daughter
reference_books.review_text: Enjoyable read with lovely descriptions and an interesting idea for a killer. I'd hoped for a really shocking twist at the end but sadly it didn't happen - even though it was just beginning to be done! Still a good reading experience, though.

reference_books.title: Pure
reference_books.review_text: Miller's writing is just superb. This is so easy to read, yet so elegant at the same time. The story is about an engineer who has to clear a festering graveyard in the centre of Paris on the brink of revolution. A very original idea and perfectly executed. Loved the characters, the plot, the period detail - in short, just loved it. *goes off to search for more books by Andrew Miller*

reference_books.title: The Historian
reference_books.review_text: I only listened to this on an abridged audiobook so I'm not sure if the pros and cons are the same with actual book. I enjoyed parts of the story and some of the vampire scenes were very exciting. However, I found myself bogged down in the detail. The endless searching and trying to unravel the mystery wasn't as thrilling as it could have been - I was mainly bored and wanted them to get on with it. Some nice pieces of writing, I just wish it was consistent.

book_a.title: The Taming of the Queen (The Plantagenet and Tudor Novels, #12)
book_a.user_review:
To be honest I was dubious about this book. I love Katherine Parr's story and I love Philippa Gregory's writing, but the blurb about serial killers made me think it was going to be wildly over the top. I was pleasantly surprised to find this was one of the best Philippa Gregory books in years! 
 Henry VIII is portrayed in all his old, stinking wreckage of glory, but we also get glimpses of the better side of the man who became a tyrant king. Katherine feels affection for him and it is made quite clear that his actions are not necessarily all his fault - while he is selfish, he is clearly also suffering from mental illness or trauma. 
 To complete a character arc, Katherine starts off with little interest in religious reform or being queen, but comes to find her purpose in her position. With a great grasp of the religious issues at the time,and of theology in general, Gregory explores the arguments of reform from both sides of the Tudor church and gets to the crux of a deeply spiritual woman. Being religious myself, I particularly enjoyed this aspect of the story but I think everyone will be able to appreciate Katherine's bravery for her faith and the significance of her early scholarship. 
 I attended a talk by Gregory where she mentioned the narrative did not follow Katherine all the way to her death. Knowing the history, I was worried that Gregory was 'wimping out' by ignoring some of Katherine's later struggles. But actually, there is enough foreshadowing in the book that we understand our heroine may not necessarily get such a happy ending as she deserves. 
 For a very different, but equally enjoyable, take on Katherine Parr I would recommend fans of his book also read Queen's Gambit by Elizabeth Fremantle.

sample_reviews.review_text: Although Catherine Parr was an interesting queen, this book was too long, and not as suspenseful as Gregory's other Tudor novels.

I don't know if I finished this book because I was moved by the writing or if I just wanted King Henry to DIE already. I enjoyed the theological debates and that KP was a scholar who enjoyed writing. The way she lost herself in learning and writing was refreshing from the unending, ridiculous political intrigue of that maniac's court. I'm glad it's done. I'm sorry she died in childbirth later.
I need to just stop reading these, they have gotten so bad - think your history book meets EL James,

Philippa Gregory knows her history and she knows how to tell a great story within the confines of a historical setting. Although there are a few factual inaccuracies (remember that this is a piece of fiction set within the Tudor reality and such things are to be expected), the story moves very well. We see Tudor times through the eyes of King Henry VIII's last wife. We see The King through her eyes. We see the events through her eyes. We feel her fear and her joy as she lives each of her days. 
 If you are looking for factually accurate tales of history, then move on. But if you are looking for an excellent read, a riveting tale, and a constant page turner - well, this is the book for you!

The Taming of the Queen is the story of the last wife of Henry VIII, the one who united all his children and is known for nursing the sick king. Certainly history has painted a rather dull portrait of Kateryn Parr, the thirty year old widow chosen by Henry after his disastrous marriage to Kitty Howard. She was the wife I knew least of, a patient nurse, loving step-mother, and deeply religious woman. Philippa Gregory illuminates the lifeless image, creating a flesh and blood character that touched me more than any of the other women. Married for dynastic reason, once to a very young then an older man, she finds the love of her life in adventurous Thomas Seymour, uncle to the prince. When she catches the king's lecherous eye, she is forced once again to marry to advance her family. After all, Henry has made her a offer she cannot refuse. Gregory's Kateryn is smart, passionate in her convictions, whether it's the budding reformation, or the challenge of keeping the ferocious king 
 stated and happy. She embraces her responsibilities with both loyalty and conviction to make a difference. I loved reading about her. Instead of a matronly nursemaid to the king, I enjoyed her scholarship, dignity, and savvy way she handled queenship. As her star wanes, with the same arc as her predecessors, Gregory was able to make the reader feel her panic as she realizes her life is in danger, as well as the shame when she debases herself to a monster to save her life. This is a rich history, one that explains the deep schism that fractured Europe as the different churches evolved. Kateryn is a learned woman, a representation of the spirit of the Renaissance. A model for her step daughter, Elizabeth to aspire as a framework for her own court. 
 Of all Philippa Gregory's books about Henry VIII's wives, this one had to be my favorite. She captured the rising fear of the glittering court as the wheel of fortune made it's slow spin. Henry was a Machiavellian prince who pitted rival factions in a court turned into a bloodbath, playing them against each other to smoke out insurrection, leaving him standing victorious over their smoking bones.
I always enjoy Philippa Gregory, but this was one of my favorites. I love history and Henry the VIII is definitely an interesting character to explore.

This was bad. Really BAD. 
 When you make it through 50% of the novel and still nothing has happened it is not worth your time. And when I say nothing I mean zilch, squat, zero. Kateryn Parr (the author for that matter) never shuts up about translating the bible for the people of the England and that gets old real fast. It is literally the only thing happening in the plot. 
 And I just cannot fully express how disappointing this was. Philippa Gregory hadn't let me down yet, but this novel was not worth the pages it was printed on.

Another good book about the life and times of the wives of Henry VIII. Since seeing The Six Wives of Henry VIII on PBS when I was a teenager, I have been intrigued by this king and his wives. I really enjoyed this book about Katherine Parr because she seems to have been quite different than the other wives. While her beauty drew the king, I think he enjoyed her bright mind as well. And while she did run into trouble, she was able to escape with her life. She was fortunate that Henry's ill health caused his death before he could cause the death of his sixth wife.

Having read all of Philippa's previous tudor books I was really looking forward to this new one and it didnt disappoint. I think its one of her strongest actually. Like I think many people I knew very little about the last wife of Henry VII, but now I am curious to know more she was a fascinating woman and Philippas portrayal of her is compelling and intriguing. She seemed to be an brave and intelligent women. Philippa's book brings the tudor court and the tyranny of HenryVII to life vividly. Would highly recommend this book to readers of Philippas other books and new readers alike.

Let me start by saying that Philippa Gregory is one of my guilty pleasures because she gives readers a visceral reaction to her stories. You've heard of the advice "show, don't tell"? PG shows better than most. That said, as a long-term Tudor fan with my own beliefs as to the events of the time, I had an issue with some of her choices and my issues grew over the course of the book. I was fine that she had KP sleeping with Tom Seymour before she married Henry (I don't count that as a spoiler - it happens on page two!), I also accepted her portrayal of KP as not very learned before she married Henry (again, this is quite early in the book and helpful to give us a context for the religious issues) but things went downhill from there. 
 You want to read this book? Come at it as you would alternative history. Suspend your disbelief and you'll enjoy the story.

book_b.title: The Roanoke Girls
book_b.user_review: 3 1/2. Enjoyed this book, it was twisty and dark with a strong pace. The sense of place was well done. Couldn't rate higher because I struggled to like any of the characters, but I do understand that was kind of the point with this story.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Warning: this book deals with sexual assault and incest. 
 I don't even know what this was. An American Gothic novel with the strangest premise of the most dysfunctional family I have ever read. I get that these girls had no father figure, but to have all of them turn out like this was just tragic. And it was too predictable. I called it from the very beginning because the simple clues were all there. I hated how they each had such a grand form of superiority of their beauty and bodies that put all the others to shame. The sexual predator was obviously the most disgusting despicable one of all. I would cringe every time he appeared. The only relationship that was a highlight for me was between Allegra and Laney. Engel writes with ease, and I found myself just wanting to know what happened to Allegra, and the twist that happened, well I saw that coming too. I pretty much skimmed most of the book because it was so long and I couldn't really stand reading the incest scenes (if there were some.) It felt a little like FLOWERS IN THE ATTIC, but this one had a murder mystery feel to it. Just be wary of this since I'm sure it can trigger a lot of people.

Content warning: childhood sexual abuse, rape, incest 
 When Lane was a teenager living in New York, her mother committed suicide, and Lane went to live with her grandparents and cousin Allegra in rural Kansas. Her mother never told her much about their family, so Lane has no idea what to expect. After one summer, Lane flees Kansas, and then spends the next decade of her life descending into alcoholism and depression. When she receives a cryptic email from Allegra, she ignores it, until she gets a call from her grandfather to say that Allegra has gone missing. So begrudgingly, she returns. "But it also means facing the secret that made her flee, the one she may not be strong enough to run from again." 
 Can YOU guess what the secret is? 
 If you guessed childhood sexual abuse, DING DING DING! Tell them what they've won, Bob!! Well, I made a mistake and decided to give this book a chance, imagining that the secret could be anything other than what the secret ALWAYS is when a woman has fled her hometown, has to return for some reason, and then ends up Confronting Her Past. 
 I blame Gillian Flynn for this recent resurgence of faux-literary "noir" books. Her success makes everyone think they can do it too. It is very clear that Engel's intention is to be considered literary with sentences like, "But one long summer here at Roanoke is somehow imprinted beneath my skin like a tattoo of memories running through my veins" and "I run my fingers over the eye shadow, golden glitter sticking to my skin, and like a blind person reading braille, I feel the bumps and ridges of letters under my fingertips." Ugh. She definitely missed the mark there. 
 It's also VERY clear that Engel is a former YA author. There is a subset of YA authors who--much like a child star who decides to take an oversexualized role to show everyone they're a grown up now--decides to go with the most personally upsetting and appalling situation they can imagine and make a book out of it. Sensationalism for sensationalism's sake is just that. It is not inventive, it is not new, it doesn't add anything to the literary landscape. It's not titillating, it's just exploitative. 
 The first part of the "big reveal" is clumsily hinted at throughout the beginning of the book until it is hamfistedly revealed on page 32. After all, the conceit of the story is not about leaving the abuse a mystery. The second part of the "big reveal"--that not only has Lane and Allegra's grandfather been sleeping with his granddaughter, he actually started by sleeping with his sister, and every one of the so-called Roanoke girls is not only his victim but his daughter as well--doesn't come until a bit later. At that point, you pretty well know it's coming. It is also not a surprise. 
 However, rather than representing these girls as the victimized, brainwashed, Stockholm Syndrome sufferers that they are, the toxic, incestuous relationship with their grandfather/father is portrayed in an incredibly romanticized manner. This could have been a study in the psychological power of someone with charm, the strength of isolation and insulation on developing young minds, and the manner in which cult survivors are inured to a certain lifestyle. But instead, we see people who were not abused by this man continue to support and maintain this secrecy, including his wife, the housekeeper, and the ranch hand. His wife especially, who is the mother and grandmother of the girls, has been letting this happen under her own roof for decades, and believes that THE GIRLS ARE GUILTY BECAUSE THEY ARE SEDUCING THE DAD/GRANDFATHER. 
 Even Lane, who is "the one who got away," BARELY makes an attempt to call out the abuse, and feels almost jealous of her grandfather picking Allegra to abuse. Lane recalls one of her most vivid memories of her mother: "We'd been lying on her bed in our apartment, on our sides, facing each other. I was ten. She was tracing my face with her fingertips, and I remember being happy. Happy she was paying attention to me, focusing solely on me without tears or trepidation. 'Right now,' she whispered, 'you look exactly like your father. I loved him so much.' I thought maybe she was finally going to tell me some detail about him, but before I could ask a single question her hand trailed lower, around my neck. She squeezed. Gently at first, so that I didn't wrench away as fast as I should have, then harder, her nails digging into my skin." (45) She loved him? Her dad who raped her, and she fled with Lane, her child, to prevent the same thing happening to her, and she loved him? Nope. 
 Allegra, the missing cousin, is used as a plot device and as a method of character development for Lane, in much the same way that rape in a female character's background is often used as a lazy means of showing how "strong" she is. Allegra exists purely in relation to others and not to be even the brainwashed, psychologically damaged representation of her own person. 
 Of course, despite over a decade of descent into alcoholism and general disconnectedness, Lane is saved from it all by the love of a good man, her teenage sweetheart. Isn't that easy and nice? Even the fact that she had an abortion that she never told him about barely provides two minutes of conflict, and doesn't hinder or even slow down the happy ending that Lane gets after her cousin is confirmed dead. 
 The Chicago Review of Books summed it up pretty well: "Ultimately, The Roanoke Girls is a tale of violence against women paired with victim shaming. This cheapens the characters, the descriptions, and the tale itself. Engel writes masterfully manipulative men, but the women are consistently framed as villainous, weak, or stupid enough to be abused. The ending is frustrating, because the implication we are left with is that since a single woman escaped the violence, it is acceptable, despite the cost of the generations before her." (The Kirkus Review also said it was "sordid, unrealistic, and unredeemed.") 
 I say, avoid at all costs. Especially if, like me, you may be a survivor of childhood sexual abuse who had no warning before you started the book, and for whom panic attacks ensued. 
 My Absolute Darling 
 Although I finished this book over a month ago, I was moved to come back and review it in earnest following a conversation that is currently happening around a new release book, My Absolute Darling. It is admittedly a slightly different situation because one of the major points of contention with that book is that it's written by a male author about a female character who is sexually abused by her dad. But the similarities were too striking, with the incest and the romanticization of that situation, it brought Roanoke Girls right back to the forefront of my mind. 
 I first heard rumblings about issues with the book on Twitter. I follow a number of people in publishing, because it's something in which I have a great deal of interest and curiosity. 
 This was the Tweet that started it for me. 
 Can we just talk about how many men seem to be writing revenge fantasies about female rape survivors and how grotesque that feels? 
 -- Jim McCarthy (@JimMcCarthy528) September 5, 2017 
 Then there was this thread about the topic of men writing about female sexual assault survivors: 
 I think a lot about why male writers feel so comfortable writing about the sexual assault of women and girls. 
 -- Tess Sharpe (@sharpegirl) September 5, 2017 
 This piece of the thread was striking to me, and stuck with me: 
 And ask yourself "Why do I want to tell this story?" and "Am I the person to tell this story?" and "Who might I hurt if I tell this story?" 
 -- Tess Sharpe (@sharpegirl) September 5, 2017 
 In the replies to Jim McCarthy's Tweet, he gave hints about the book he was referring to, including that it was going to be on the Best Seller list the following week. 
 The thing that really struck me was that, when I searched for reviews, EVERY SINGLE ONE on the first page of results in Google was glowingly positive, saying that the book was "difficult" and "challenging" and "hard to read" but a "remarkable debut." 
 Then Roxane Gay was reading it: 
 Y'all hyped this book I just bought buuuut so far it isn't ummmm. Yeah. 
 -- roxane gay (@rgay) September 6, 2017 
 Men writing about sexual abuse like it's romantic. Ok. Ok. 
 -- roxane gay (@rgay) September 6, 2017 
 And she reviewed it on Goodreads, even still giving it three stars despite the problems she readily admits exist. Which was interesting to me. 
 So I've curiously, and with an ever increasing rage, been watching how this develops. I have yet to see a truly critical review from a mainstream source. 
 The questions surrounding representation, writing characters that have experienced things that you as an author have not experienced, and especially men writing female characters who have survived abuse (and the romanticization of that abuse that often accompanies the past), are questions that I consider quite regularly. I don't know that there's an answer. But I DO know that there's an overabundance of men who are INCREDIBLY quick to throw rape into their lead female's backstory as a means of fleshing her out, often without ever even trying to deal with the ramifications or aftermath that past abuse might cause. 
 Originally posted at Musings of An Incurable Bookworm

Not for the faint of heart. 
 (Full disclosure: I received a free electronic ARC for review through Netgalley. Trigger warning for child abuse and violence against women, including rape, as well as suicide. This review contains clearly marked spoilers, but I tried to keep it as vague as possible.) 
 "'Roanoke girls never last long around here.' She skipped along the hall, her voice growing fainter as she moved, like we were standing at opposite ends of a tunnel. 'In the end, we either run or we die.'" 
 "My feelings for Allegra were never complicated. It didn't matter if she acted crazy or made me angry or smothered me with devotion. In my whole life, she was the only person I simply loved. And I left her anyway." 
 THEN 
 Camilla Roanoke's suicide doesn't come as a surprise to her fifteen-year-old daughter Lane. For as long as she can remember, her mother has struggled with depression - not to mention alcoholism, mood swings, and blinding bouts of rage. Some days the tears come so fast and thick that they threaten to drown them both. So when she's found dead in their NYC bathroom, bathrobe belt wrapped around her neck, Lane is more or less numb. Yet the cryptic note Camilla left behind - I tried to wait. I'm sorry. - puzzles Lane. The news that she has family - her mother's parents, Yates and Lillian Roanoke - who aren't merely willing to take Lane, but actually want her? Well, that's the biggest shock of all. 
 Camilla rarely spoke of her life on the family estate, Roanoke, situated among the prairies and wheat fields of Osage Flats, Kansas. And there's a damn good reason for it - one that Lane will discover during summer she turns sixteen. One hundred days of being a "Roanoke Girl" was all she could take before she fled Kansas - hopefully for good. 
 NOW 
 Eleven years later, a late-night phone call from her grandfather summons Lane back to Roanoke. Back home. Her cousin Allegra is missing, and Lane is determined to find out what happened. It's the least she can do, for leaving Allegra behind all those years ago. 
 There's no way to sugar-coat it: this is a seriously fucked-up story. Between the synopsis and early reviews, I had a pretty good idea of what I was getting into. Even so, Amy Engel still managed to shock me - mostly through the sheer extent of it all. I don't want to give anything away, so I'll try to be as vague as possible. But if you'd rather go in completely ignorant of the plot, maybe stop reading now? 
 ** Caution: Spoilers ahead! ** 
 There is rape, and incest, and mostly the two are not mutually exclusive. The relationship that started it all is a little murky, since both kids were, well, kids, but it becomes less so from there. Think: Josef Fritzl, but one whose prisons consist of kind words and loving gestures, instead of steel bars and locked doors. Or: an even more warped, inter-generational version of that genetic sexual attraction episode of Law & Order: SVU. The Roanoke Girls actually feels a lot like an episode of SVU, but with a gothic, down on the prairie spin (and more skillful writing, too). 
 My feelings about this book are complicated. On the one hand, I feel really icky about consuming a rape-fueled story line like so much entertainment. (Pretty similar to the feeling I get while watching SVU, fwiw.) And this one is really over-the-top and out there. Yet Engel handles it with surprising sensitivity and keen insight; The Roanoke Girls isn't just a portrait of a highly dysfunctional and damaged family, but a window into rape culture, victim blaming, and male privilege and narcissism. In particular: her exploration of the way women turn on one another - rather than the men who do them wrong - is so on point. I mean, look no further than the hate-fueled dumpster fire that was the 2016 election season. 
 Thankfully, the rape is mostly hinted at, skirted around, approached from the margins, rather than described in graphic detail. Yet I don't think this diminishes its impact at all; rather, it allows us to focus our attention where it belongs, on the victims, rather than dwelling on the more sensational aspects of the story. And in Lane - and Allegra, Camilla, Eleanor, Penelope, Sophia, and Jane - we see and feel the very real impact sexual abuse can have on young women. This is done especially well through Camilla, who initially comes off as a rather unlikable figure - emotionally and sometimes physically abusive toward Lane - yet by story's end, we understand why. With Lane, we find understanding and even empathy. 
 I picked this book up on Halloween, thinking that it would be a scary read. It is, but not quite in the way I'd anticipated. It's tense and horrifying, dark and twisted, and all but guaranteed to turn your stomach.

Received this from Netgalley in exchange for an honest review. Thank you to the author and publisher for passing it along. 
 This book focuses on the lives of The Roanoke Girls a family that lives in Kansas and the fact that the lot have either died or fled as a result. The novel introduces us to Lane who returns to the Kansas home, after leaving ten years ago, after hearing news of her cousin Allegra's disappearance. 
 This book wasn't very long but I found myself wanting to put it down when I got to the "secret" reveal. Other reviews make note that this book has disturbing subject matter so it's definitely not a light read but it just wasn't one that kept my interest after that.

A family where it seems all the females either die or leave, even the ones that try to escape the pull of the old Roanoke homestead. 
 Drawn back when her cousin disappears, can Lane again stay out of trouble that threatened to de-rail her life as a teenager? Will they find her cousin alive? 
 As you gradually follow various time lines & find out the mystery surrounding the Roanoke girls, you see how truly sinister the real story is.

While the storyline was tolerable, the writing style was amateurish. Early on she mentions a house owned by an abortionist that had architectural features similar to the one her family lives in. I was expecting some sort of tie in later on but it never came.

I received a copy of this book from Blogging for Books in exchange for a fair review. 
 I initially felt this book might have potential, even if it was Oprah's Book Club potential, but the novel quickly sunk into trite dribble at best. The big "secret" of the novel is revealed very early on and dominates the remainder of the novel to the exclusion of all else. The story, which could have been somewhat believable, gets more and more stretched to the limits of depravity as the novel progresses to its highly predictable conclusion as to be beyond any glimmer of realism whatsoever. The ending is a farce and feels like a pathetic cheat. The subject matter is tired, the writing uninspired, and the conclusion ridiculous. I lost a night of my reading life to this novel and cannot recommend it to any reader who expects more than a cheap imitation of a bad Lifetime movie (oxymoron most definitely intended) on paper.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Lane Roanoke's mother committed suicide when she was sixteen years old. She was then sent to live with her wealthy, but unknown to her, Grandparents in their rural Kansas farm. She also meets her cousin Allegra who is like the sister she never met. It doesn't take Lane long to realize why her mother ran away to New York City to have her and suffered from depression. What is the curse of the Roanoke Girls? 
 The novel also flashes forward to the future where cousin Allegra has gone missing. Lane returns to Roanoke to help to solve the mystery of her disappearance. She also has to battle past demons and the feelings she still has for her high school boyfriend, Cooper. Tommy, Allegra's high school flame, is now a married cop and works with Lane to help to solve the mystery. What happened to Allegra? 
 I liked the parallel story lines of the past and future working together to tell the entire story of the Roanoke girls. Unfortunately, part of the mystery was a deal breaker to me and I couldn't really enjoy the rest of the book. 
 SPOILER ALERT 
 Near the beginning of the novel I suspected the secret of The Roanoke Girls and then it was blatantly laid bare for the readers pretty early in the story so I wrestle whether this is really a spoiler alert. The secret is the story is really a story of incest in one family with Grandpa as Dad/Uncle/Grandpa/Brother lover. I am not keen at all on incest stories with every female member of the family sleeping with Grandpa including his daughters by his daughters and sisters. It reminded me a bit of A Thousand Acres by Jane Smiley, but not as in depth of a story. I didn't like A Thousand Acres. It also reminded me of VC Andrews's books that I used to read as a teenager. The difference is that the VC Andrews characters were so well developed in their love story with one central love story that I could almost be convinced that it was a justified romance. In the Roanoke Girls, there are a lot of different girls through the decades and some only get a brief chapter that tells of their love and demise. Grandpa is also not well developed, I wanted to know why he had this problem with incest. It really made no sense to me at all, and frankly disgusted me. 
 SPOILER END 
 If I would have known the secret of The Roanoke Girls before I read this novel, I wouldn't have read it. I liked the style of writing and the characters, but the topic disgusted me and I didn't feel convinced by the novel why the Roanoke girls would have all went along with this. 
 Book Source: Review Copy as part of the TLC Book Tour 
 This review was first posted on my blog at: http://lauragerold.blogspot.com/2017/...

I loved this book. It was quite different from my normal read and was quite dark and disturbing but thoroughly enjoyable. I certainly wasn't expecting it! I look forward to reading more by this author.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Ready? This book gets a good ol-fashioned NOPE from me. 
 I wish that could be it. I wish that could be the beginning and the end of the review. Just, NOPE. It isn't though because this book has caused me to feel so much rage while reading that it has to come out. So, here we go (spoilers discussed below). 
 This book is terrible. It wants to be something more than it is and it feels like author desperately wants to build a reputation as a dark gritty author (see: Gillian Flynn) but it fails. It's basically sex, incest, sex, incest, sex, oh, and more sex. Of course, there is alcoholism, self-hatred, and tons of mental anguish mixed in but the general tone of the book is that incest and sex causes mental anguish in victimized women who then either tun to sex as a cure (#irony), alcoholism, or suicide. 
 So, here are a few things about that: 
 1 - I'm so, so, so sick of sexual abuse being used as the motivation behind women's actions in books. WE ARE MOTIVATED BY MORE THAN THAT #thankyouverymuch. It's lazy writing and it's pathetically presented in The Roanoke Girls. Not to mention, literally everyone turns a blind eye to what's going on? Family members? Hired help? Townsfolk. Yep, move right along. Nothing to see here. Just granddad gettin' it on with every female in the family. 
 2 - Women combat trauma by doing more than running away, becoming alcoholics, and destroying their lives. When did this become such a common literary trope? It gets all the eye rolls from me. Literally, there are chapters in The Roanoke Girls dedicated entirely to brief descriptions of how a woman just cannot handle being rejected and replaced by her abuser so she throws herself into suicide because that'll show him. There's not a strong woman in the book, not even Lane. I know other reviews disagree with me but, again, NOPE. 
 3 - It can't just be sexual abuse...no...it has to be incestuous sexual abuse! Over the course of 3 generations. Literally...the same dude abusing all of the women in his family, including his own daughters and grand-daughters, yet no one says a thing. Have we reached a point where sexual abuse in a book is so common that authors feel the need to push the envelope even further to earn head pats and fame for being the one willing to go there. 
 4 - Oh, and of course this incestuously abusive dude has to be depicted as THE GREATEST THING TO EVER HAPPEN TO WOMEN because the women are basically throwing themselves at him, practically pleading to be manipulated and abused, then kill themselves or run away when he moves on to someone else. PLEASE! That's just disgusting. If I had to read one more time about how handsome granddad is or what a soothing voice he had, I was going to take this book to the backyard and burn it. Can we not romanticize sexual predators, please? 
 Oh, yeah, and there's a cousin missing in all of this. Allegra (the cousin) disappeared so Lane (the main character) gets a call from dear old granddad saying she needs to come home. Right. Lane fled to California to escape the family but yup, she's going to come home to try to find her cousin. The police are on the case but no, Lane has to come back to this horrific place full of sex and abuse to solve the case. Only she finds herself hooking up with an old boyfriend because, sex. 
 I read to the end and was just glad it was over. This was an epic waste of time and doesn't deserve nearly the praise it's been receiving. It's try-hard and pathetic. There are way better books out there more deserving of your time.

reference_books.title: In the Country We Love: My Family Divided
reference_books.review_text:
I am very critical of biographies written by people so young and unaccomplished. Having gone through the same situation with immigration and deportation I felt an extreme victimization angle was overly politicizing the book. And clearly the book is solely political because again no one would ever read without that hook and that hook would not be pushed if not for the new political trends. 
 Forgive the honesty but this girl is a useless idiot. Which any respectable person should of been suspecting by her short list of TV credits. 
 The issue with this book is that she pushes for the adaptation of a dangerous criminal memology that rationalizes the parents' crime by taking a mindset the crime is acceptable and so any punishment unreasonable. I experienced a lot of this obfuscation surviving in the grey market, as a child I always just considered it hypocrisy, but it the tough guy mindset of being bigger than the system and above the other players of the game, who manipulates it to their advantage by perverting and abusing unintended schemes. 
 This book is interesting in examining the memology of a criminal's children. 
 I will take the bold stance now to say that this is a crime story. That is why this is interesting to me. 
 Without getting into details her situation with immigration is very similar to mine, and for a long time I felt the exact same way. That changed when I accepted the reality that my parents had made errors. I accepted these mistakes and that is when I really started to take ownership and responsibility for my life. You can't grow up and go on thinking it was the fault of immigration officials only doing their job or with hate towards a nation by blaming national policy. 
 I might add to the review at a later time with a character profile of the subject.

book_a.user_review:
WORST BOOK OF 2016 - cast advocates serial rape and are unabashed racist

 just a really self serving praise of their effort to put on a play- which they rank as equal with sacrifice of the founding fathers but still better than them

sample_reviews.review_text: This one is probably my bad - I don't know what I expected from what is ostensibly "The Ultimate Fan's Guide to Hamilton", but it never stops FAWNING over itself long enough to actually share anything interesting. It reads like an extended acknowledgements section "thanks to brilliant input from _____, when they saw ________ audition they knew they had lightning in a bottle". This was a real boring drag.

This does not have the music or details about Hamilton. It's just the history of the show and it's success. The have a woman narrator for 80% of the book. Without her, you'd see this as a very boastful book, which it is. The author is high on himself, and you can see it through the writing. However, the show was successful so it's not really overconfidence when you can back it up. Still annoying though. The parts that were read by the author were the annotations on the songs and the purpose. Overall I found this book to be interesting but not all that entertaining. Perhaps I may have enjoyed it more if I actually learned something about Hamilton or had send the show on Broadway.

This. Was. Amazing. 
 First off, this book looks and feels incredible. It's bound with a leather-like spine, so it looks like a giant old-fashioned tome you'd find in some grand castle's library. The pages are thick stock and have those unfinished edges, giving the book so much weight and life to it. It's awesome. 
 It was fun being able to read all the behind the scenes and making of the musical. I knew a lot of the stuff already, but it was great reading it in chronological order and having it all laid out like that. I kinda knew somewhere in the back of my head that a song had gotten cut from the cast album, but this was the first time I really got proof of it. 
 Overall, I'd really recommend this book.

Queue up the soundtrack on Spotify and read along - it's almost as good as being there! Okay, not really. But the "Hamiltome" is a delightful gift for Hamilton groupies. Beautiful full color pics, lyrics to all the songs, fascinating profiles of the actors and behind-the-scenes movers & shakers. Plus extensive footnotes from Lin-Manuel describing his writing process and offering details on the history behind the hottest musical around.

Lin-Manuel Miranda is a genius. If you didn't already know that, this book will show you why. Highly recommended for theater fans, hip hop fans, and lovers of Hamilton the music. The book is positively sumptuous, rich with pictures and information about the show and small details about the songwriting. It makes me appreciate the show as well as namesake Alexander Hamilton. The book is a joy to hold, truly a delightful reading experience. Having previously read the special hardcovers about Wicked and Book of Mormon musicals, I can confidently say that #Hamiltome does not waste its shot and blows them all away.

April 5th, 2017. 
 I finally finished the Hamilton-Tome! Hamiltome! I love this so much! Behind the scenes stuff is my absolute favorite and since falling in love with Lin-Manuel Miranda's writing, I knew this was a book to be owned. So many feels, so much good, insightful articles and those pictures. Epic. 
 Why not give it a five star?
I was crying like a baby reading the final pages of this book. Amazing to see the creative decisions that went into putting this story together.

As a major musical fan, Hamilton already had a special place in my heart before reading this. However this book has truly changed my perspective on not only this show, but all Broadway shows in general. It is incredibly interesting to learn about the process behind possibly one of the most successful shows. This is a must-read for not only musical theatre fans, but also for anyone interested in art and creativity, because this show is full of that.
I loved this book so much! It made laugh and cry (there where lots of tears). It was so cool to read about how Hamilton got started and how it became what it is today.

I'd probably give this 3.5 stars if I could. It's a beautiful looking book, and I found reading Lin's annotations of the songs interesting. But the majority of the book was written by the co-writer, whose perspective I wasn't as interested in. I was disappointed at how little Lin Manuel actually contributed to the book: his insights were great and it would have been nice to have seen more of them.

reference_books.title: Inferno (Robert Langdon, #4)
reference_books.review_text:
This book really, really stinks and is really, really formulaic and stupid. Don't bother to read it, it is a massive waste of time. If you want a tour guide of Florence, Venice and Istanbul, just save yourself the pain and buy a tour guide. I liked The DaVinci Code and sort of liked Angels and Demons despite the fact the latter book and some major flaws. Inferno is just one flaw after another - waaaaay too many coincidences; waaaaay too much stupid, predictable dialogue; far, far too many hidden passageways, secret doors and unexpected stairs that show up just at the moment they are needed so that Robert and Sienna can sneak out just steps ahead of the 'bad guys'. 
 If I could give zero stars, I would. We have been duped into buying an expensive book. I want my money back!

reference_books.title: Escape
reference_books.review_text: This book is very interesting. Carolyn Jessop was born into the FLDS cult in Colorado City, Utah. At the age of 18 she was "chosen" to marry a man of 51. She was his fourth wife. She bore him 8 children before she finally escaped the cult. Her story of life in the cult under Warren Jeffs is simply too amazing. It would be like living under Taliban rule. It is very, very difficult to get away from the FLDS because they hunt a person down; threaten them with taking their children; threaten them with never seeing any of their family members again; leave them penniless and with no where to go. Carolyn was (and still is) a very brave woman.

book_a.title: The Glass Castle
book_a.user_review: Jeannette Walls tells the story of her childhood in this book, and what a strange, dysfunctional childhood it was. Some would say her parents were eccentric and others would classify them as demented and abusive. Through it all Jeannette tells the story with humor and with no shred of self-pity. If she had told the story any other way it would have been too much of a downer. As it is, I found myself laughing from time to time. Her parents were well educated and highly intelligent but completely incapable of providing stability to the lives of their four children. The family often went without food, moved around constantly until the very end, when they hit absolute rock bottom, and lived in a series of places which, by anyone else, would have been considered completely uninhabitable. No matter what your upbringing, you owe it to yourself to read this book just for the opportunity to see life from an entirely different perspective for awhile.

sample_reviews.review_text: I really enjoyed this one. I found the authors storytelling style easy to get sucked into. I actually forgot for awhile that it was a memoir. What a real picture the author paints of her childhood! Would definitely recommend this--especially for those who don't read non-ficton often. And for those who need to put everything in perspective a little.

I had ordered this book based on reviews I had read but did not pick it up until a co-worker urged me to read it. 
 While I think the story was interesting and sad I just did not believe it. Jeannette starts out with memories going back to when she was three or so, and while I do remember a few details from that far back, I can not narrate them as she has done... so I was immediately turned off. I think if she had tried to release this book after James Frey was busted she would have been denied.

I couldn't bring myself to care that horrible things were happening to these kids. Didn't spend the time to finish because there are so many other things I want to read. Things that don't put me to sleep!
I don't know why, but I have a thing for memoirs. Y'all need to read this one.

I thought this was both horrifying and wonderful at the same time. I wouldn't recommend it to people who may be easily offended. It had some really disturbing parts -and I found it difficult to keep reading occasionally because it was just too dang depressing...and yet, the whole time you are thinking Wow, This woman made it! It gives you hope for all of the under-privileged, abused children there are floating around in America.

See my Full review on my blog 
 https://betweenfoldedpages.wordpress.... 
 Why did I wait so long to read this?! Iv'e been told by so many people to read this book, I saw it on sale at Chapters a few week's back and decided to finally buy it. A million stars!!! I LOVED this book! The chapters are short and direct, and I flew through the book. I wanted to savour the story but also needed to know how it would end. Beautiful, heartbreaking story of a girl growing up in poverty.

I enjoyed this book well enough, and I think Jeannette Walls is a good writer (unlike so many memoir writers). However, there were two issues that leaped out at me: 
 1) Though she didn't mind providing a detailed story of her childhood, she really skimped on her adult life. She didn't need to give us every sordid detail of her life to date, but giving at least a reasonably full picture of life as an adult would have made the book more well rounded to me. 
 2) The book ended very abruptly. I felt there were still a few things that needed to be said in order to end it with a satisfying conclusion. Perhaps providing an epilogue with a brief update to tie up some of the loose ends (i.e. Maureen visiting or not, the current situation regarding her mother's apartment building, etc.) would have helped. 
 Overall it was a fairly good book & decently written. It didn't affect me as negatively as other memoirs of this nature have (Angela's Ashes, for example), so I suppose that's a good thing. It has its flaws, but I've come to believe that the majority of memoir writing will by its nature have flaws. I'm not sure perfection is attainable within this genre, because it's so wide open in terms of structure & style. To be able to write a good but flawed personal account of one's life that people want to read is a goal worthy of achieving, and Walls has done that.
Loved the beginning, but then. It seemed to just keep sounding the same note.

After seeing so many accolades for Walls' "The Glass Castle", I decided to pick it up to see for myself how great this memoir was. Walls' tale of growing up in abject poverty with an absentee yet well-meaning alcoholic father and flighty, artistic mother was quite an eye-opening experience. The material ranges from hilarious, to sad, to heartbreaking, sometimes in the blink of an eye. It is clear that Walls memoir is a testament to her great love for her terribly dysfunctional family, even after all the shame she endured at the hands of peers and all the years that (as a child) she had to assume the role of parent to her siblings (and mother/father) due to her mother's refusal to parent and her father's horrific struggles with alcohol addiction. It would be easy for one to throw in the towel after the childhood that Walls experienced, but her story proves triumphant as she mustered up the courage and scrappiness to rise above her ineffective parents and turbulent childhood. It is sad that her parents could not (or would not) escape the throes of addiction, malaise and chaotic lifestyle resulting in them remaining homeless after their children's careers took off. Highly recommended.
While I appreciated the struggle and thought the writing was great, it made me so angry/sad I couldn't wait for it to be over.

book_b.title: Shift (Shift, #1-3; Silo, #2)
book_b.user_review: Wool is my favorite dystopian future book of all time. The whole time I was reading it I kept asking myself, "How on earth did humanity ever get to this place?" Shift provides those answers. I really did not like it as we'll as Wool because the characters aren't as likable, but if you have read Wool, you pretty much have to read Shift.

sample_reviews.review_text: Ponderous, boring, poorly written with weak character development and a plot that has gigantic holes in logic. Desperately needed a skilled editor.

This is an interesting prequel to Wool, though definitely meant to be read after it. I liked the story and pacing a lot, but I wasn't as engaged with the characters. I missed having some of the strong female leads that Wool had, and felt our main actors here were flat and uninteresting. I liked getting some back story on what the silos were, where they came from, and where they were in the US. I'm looking forward to Dust to get the last installment!

As a followup to 3.5star "Silo", "Shift" was a major disappoint. I struggled thru the 1st quarter and excused the slow & confusing pace as needed background. By 50% it hadn't improved and I set it aside for awhile. Picked up again and only got worse so I finally gave up. I can suspend reality with the best of them but this was beyond my limits. "Silo" may have been a one trick pony

I am 130+ pages in and I have to say this is one of the most boring, disjointed books I have read in a long time. The timeline keeps switching back and forth and so far it has not advanced past the point where they are designing and building the silo and where it is complete and some people are living in it. If he would cut about two thirds of it out and get on with the storyline, I would probably read it to the end but as it stands, I' m done. I'm not wasting any more time on it. There are too many entertaining books out there to read and not enough time to be wasting it reading this. It is going in my trade box along with "Dust".

Hugh Howey has created a gripping and original premise in the underground silos that are the key set piece of his Wool series. In the original Wool (omnibus), there was much mystery over how it came to be that everyone lived in the silos. That made it very engaging to look over the shoulder of the people trying to find answers. 
 In Shift, the second in the series, we have a better idea of what's going on from the start. As a result, it's not as much of a page turner. Rather than moving the story forward, Howey takes a step back and explains how the silos came to be. Then he takes a step to the side and fleshes out material from the first book that had been in the background, such as minor characters and the people on the other ends of conversations. 
 Maybe in part because of the above, it felt harder to relate to the characters in Shift than it did in Wool. I found myself passively watching them do things without ever really feeling invested or emotionally concerned about what happened to them. 
 In the end, Shift is interesting from a world-building perspective, but some of the momentum from the original has been lost. With the next book Dust taking place after the events of Wool rather than before/concurrently, I am hoping things pick up.

Probably about a 3.75 read for me. I still was really engaged with the concept, but as other reviewers have said, I was not as invested in the characters as I was in the previous book. I'm still looking forward to reading the third book and think these books would make an interesting movie.
While still fun, didn't find it quite up to the level of wool

As the sequel/prequel to Wool, I was ready to settle in for a committed read as this is another thick read. Unfortunately, I had a difficult time following, or wanting to follow the story. It's difficult to stick with a long read when there isn't a character of interest or one if relatability. Donald? Too weak. Thurman? Too brutal? Anna? Too annoying? Mission? Too what? Don't know, but he annoyed me also. I might have liked Helen if she had been around long enough to develop a personality. 
 Truthfully, I lost interest two-thirds through and skimmed to the end. I don't think I missed much. I did like Wool and recommend it. I doubt I will move on to Dust. And I applaud the author for setting the publishing world on its ear.

Again, really enjoyable although I'm not sure quite as good as the last one but think that's more to do with the lack of revelations compared to the first. I think the writing style has matured although some minor typos in there. Still deserves the 5/5 though and I'm looking forward to the final book. 
 Enjoyed it more second time around. Time for Dust! Just a little bit excited!
You should be reading this.

book_a.user_review: I have enjoyed all of mrs. George's books. I like how she can combine fairy tales together. She is great at it.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Fabulous! Just what one would expect frkm Jessica Day George. From the first book, to the second, up to the last, the author has managed to captivate me with her retelling of the classic fairytales. My only complain is that she left out Beauty and the Beast and Sleeping Beauty, 2 of my favorite tales. 
 Poppy, however, is still my favorite princess. I like her spunk and her self-assurance. I wish the author made a story for Jonquil, the most vain princess. She could have been Beauty and one of the Shadow princes the beast, perhaps? I think it would have been nice if at least one of the princes from the Kingdom Under Stone was reformed. Yes, indeed, it would have been so romatic. 
 I am definitely looking forward into reading more of Ms George's works. It was a lot of fun.

In this continuation of the twelve sisters doomed to dance with and marry the princes of a dark underworld, the focus is on the youngest daughter, Petunis. The King Under Stone's son has taken the throne and the evil is trying to break out into the world again. I generally like Jessica Day George's writing, with the fairy-tale retellings, but felt this one was a bit less quality than the others. The story also was a bit more edgy than usual, since the topic of nine sisters all bearing children to the (spoiler here) King Under Stone and giving birth on the same night was covered. However, there was no more detail than simple statements like that. An occasional use of "bastard" as well.
Clean read. Fun.
Not my very favorite of this series, but it was fun to read, and I love all this author's catalog!
I'm sure this would have been a lot better had I read the first two novels (didn't realize it was part of a series until I was half way through), but as a stand alone it didn't do much for me.

Another in the 12 dancing princesses series begun several books ago. Lots of evil nasty princes, magic good and bad, and, of course, fairy tale romance. Still sweet and nice narrative for young and younger adults who like this genre.
I really liked these books. Good clean stories with plenty to keep you involved.

This book made me happy and sad at the same time. Happy because I loved it. It was a great addition to George's other two "Princess" books. Sad because it's the last one. I want more! While I feel the first two books stand alone fairly well, I feel like this one might not have as much impact or make as much sense if one hasn't at least read Princess of the Midnight Ball first, especially since they share villains.  Note: I read this as a free eARC from Netgalley

book_b.title: Swann's Way (In Search of Lost Time, #1)
book_b.user_review: I read this in college in my French literature class. I know everyone loves this book, but I hated it. If I read it in English it will be the same.

sample_reviews.review_text: This is just the introduction to the Search of lost time in so many ways. This is a book to be be enjoyed in the moment and revisited. Beautifully done in audio by recorded books if you have a hard time keeping up with reading alone. Like Ulysses, it is a work to let wash over you and relate to as you will at the time. Coming back again to the writing is part of the cycle of discovering something different with every reading at different stages of life.

If I pushed myself, I'd be able to finish this, you know. It's surprisingly readable. 
 My problem was the plot. I got as far as the part where the narrator (whose name I still don't know!) - where the narrator's mother stays the night in his room and they read a book together, before I gave up. That far, and nothing happened, not counting countless memories and feelings (it's called In Search of Lost Time, but it doesn't seem to me like he's lost a lot of time - he remembers so much I got underwhelmed). 
 I'm aware that this is a masterpiece, and nearly 30k+ people will disagree with my rating and my opinion on this - but let me remind you that you are not me. I am probably being tastelessly blasphemous in my choice of literature, but know that I never read every word of LOTR either (although I did finish that one, even if it took a ridiculously long time). 
 So no, I didn't finish this, and I am sorry, if only because of its fame and charming writing.

Does Proust translate well to today? Is Proust the Charlie Parker of Modernism? 
 The answer to the first question, is 'No' in my opinion. Proust's needlessly verbose description of the Combray countryside failed to create meaningful mental imagery for this reader and his description of his family was pointlessly overdone. I searched in vain for any wisdom from the narrator, his thoughts, or his actions. As we move into Swann's ridiculous mid-life crisis, Proust ought to be illuminating French bourgeois society for us. He does, to a degree, but it is too stuck in its time and place. If Swann were modern, he would have bought a Porsche. That Swann is stuck between aristocratic society where he is accepted but does not belong and bourgeois society where the opposite is true, comes through. Surely that's not the cause of teenage love saga with Odette. 
 If we accept Proust as Modernism's founder and Charlie Parker as bebop's founder, then can we also accept that their disciples have done and are doing it better than their elders? 
 Yes, we can. Charlie Parker's disciples, let's use Jackie Maclean, had passed him by the early 1960's. Parker is difficult to listen to today. You'd rather listen to Swing, Swang, Swingin' as you'd rather read Christ Stopped at Eboli. Levi's work is timeless but still of the time. He puts you in a rural Italy that's real on a plausible premise. It works and he did it better than Proust. Why are we, did I, suffer through this Proust novel?!

The first two sections of this novel are unlike anything I have ever read. Proust describes the most ordinary occasions of life in detail and with intensity, imbuing everything from a hawthorn bud to an old woman's naps with a sense of extraordinary sacredness. His descriptive language seems to explore perception itself, and his examinations of consciousness and cognition are done in equal depth. He uses his superlative gift for figurative language to range far afield for a metaphor, but always finds the one that opens a door to a new yet recognizable view of the thing compared. 
 I withheld one star because I don't find the section titled "Swann in Love" to reach the same level as the rest of the novel. It may have been groundbreaking at its date of publication, but the obsessive nature of romantic love has by now been so thoroughly explored that poor Swann's musings seemed repetitive from the start.

 All the stars!! I'm crying.. Review coming soon. I need a moment now 
 SPOILERS! SPOILERS! My entire review contains massive spoilers so please do not read unless you finished EoS!! I would hate to ruin the book for anyone 
 I finished Empire of Storms a few days ago and I still cannot stop thinking about it. Sarah did it again. She blew my mind and took the series in a direction I never expected it to go. 
 First of all can we talk about the scene with Manon and her grandmother and Asterin? I cried during all Manon chapters following this one because I was so scared she would not make it. But Abraxos oh our dear Abraxos he saved her and knew exactly where to take her and I was so glad when she finally arrived and our two female bad ass characters started working together. 
 Furthermore, I completely fell in love with Asterin's character when we got to know her secret and we began to understand why she acts the way she does, and when Asterin put her arm around Elide in the end I wanted to scream from happiness. 
 Elide is such a strong character not in a way that she brought much to the story but her development was amazing. When we first met her in Queen of Shadows she was weak and scared but on the road with Lorcan something in her clicked and she became that independent, confident woman who knows exactly what she wants and even though she was still scared and weak at some points I learned to love her and to enjoy her point of view. 
 Anyway, as much as I love Elide I still did not trust Lorcan and I was right. What he did to all of them was stupid and reckless. His intention to save Elide was completely crude. He knew Maeve and he knew what she would have done to the girl. 
 I have to admit that I was not the biggest fan of Dorian's until this book, but throughout Empire of Storms I learned to love Dorian and I got the feeling that I understood his voice much better than in the first four books. 
 I loved his scenes with Manon (you know exactly what I am talking about) and with Rowan in Skull's Bay. 
 And can we please just appreciate this quote from the very end, when Rowan thinks about losing Aelin: 
 ''His Fireheart. 
 His equal, his friend, his lover, his wife. 
 His mate.'' 
 But that leads us to another point. The mate thing. I was convinced from the moment Rowan appeared in Rifthold in Queen of Shadows that he and Aelin were mates. With their scents so woven together that Aedion noticed and the bond between Aelin and Rowan. I just knew. I am not sure if it was that obvious for a reason or if it was the feeling in my tummy saying 'YES THAT'S IT!' 
 It still surprised me how Sarah explained the whole Rowan already had a mate thing and I don't know about you but I feel like the mating bond between Rowan and Aelin feels like something Sarah added in afterwards and now she had to find a way out. 
 I still really like the idea that it was all Maeve's plan but it did not feel right, it did not flow into the story quite as easily as everything else. 
 All in all, this book was exactly what I hoped it would be and I cannot wait to find out what happens in the last book and if it really will break all our hearts.
I'm disappointed. I don't really know if I want to continue this series anymore.

 Review by Tina 
 This is going to be a gush/pro/con piece. 
 What an emotional journey. I feel like I went from high to low in 0.2 seconds. 
 Gush 
 First of all, this is the best book in the entire series. It is humorous, exciting, epic. Each moment is impactful. 
 Second, Aelin doesn't have it easy. I like that she has to go through so many obstacles to get to the final point. 
 Third, this book is info intensive. Without a good knowledge of the entire country and its people, you can get lost. 
 Fourth, love love love! she called in all her "old debts" ah that Celaena charm. Love her maginifient bad self. I feel like my anticipation is fulfilled. 
 Fifth, this is completely a book about awesome heroine characters. It's like she collects queens. Sailor Moon much? 
 Sixth, her writing style changed. I think it's due to the fact SJM gained confidence because each word is so powerful. Her writing also consists of threes. That's a little new for me. Like an urgent request. 
 Seventh, you can easily tell how much fun she's having in writing this book. 
 Pro 
 -Absolutely no fillers 
 -Went quickly from scene to scene to scene 
 -Each word written is refreshing and quoteable; staggeringly impressed 
 -It explained everything I questioned in book 1, on that aspect this story can end here 
 -Favorite character of the book goes to Elide 
 -Manon is so much more exciting and interesting 
 -Aelin is back to being a badass 
 -Dorian is no longer a whining child but now a cold dark adult 
 -Really like the other Faes in the cadre ~ gives me a desire to reread Heir of Fire 
 -It is dropping to the floor funny; her one liners 
 -The Speak is hilarious. Male not men. Semantics. 
 -All the main characters in Assassin's Blade appears in this book (as SJM has mentioned) 
 -It still takes me by surprise when I start sobbing; I forget the feels and remember that's why I read her books; it still gets to me 
 Con 
 -There are often lines that make me do a double take - did she plaguarize herself? 
 -Sometimes the story stops being TOG and becomes ACOMAF 
 -Less human and more fae (thoroughly dislike this) 
 -The dramatic scenes and final outcome of the story is so much like ACOMAF that I can place the book side by side and they are same scenes 
 -Some parts in the "feelings" and "words" such as mate, bond, consort, the collection of queens, the males fussing and doting, the males inferior to females - I felt were too similar to Daughter of the Blood (cringe) 
 I really really love this book. I enjoy it so much my heart is full. 
 Out of that 100%, 1% the originality irks me. I have to force myself to overlook some scenes where my mind starts to compare to another story.
