book_b.title: The Age of Miracles
book_b.user_review: I feel like the entire time I was reading the book I was waiting for something big to happen... But then the book ended. Good book but kind of disappointing

sample_reviews.review_text: Depressingly beautiful. Makes me remember all the heartaches and painful stuff I endured when I was growing up.
I pushed through and finished this book. It was a chunk of my life I will never get back. The premise of this book had so much potential. Unfortunately it never lived up to that potential.

This is the way the world ends 
 This is the way the world ends 
 This is the way the world ends 
 Not with a bang but a whimper. 
 I kept thinking of the Eliot poem while reading this. It almost seems like it could be its thesis. 
 Even a couple weeks after finishing it, I am so torn on this book. In some ways, I LOVED it. It was sweet and magical, and pretty mind-blowing. I cannot get the slow, terrifying death of the earth out of my mind. So scary. I think about The Age of Miracles a lot, and find myself talking to people about it. So I definitely think it's worth reading. 
 But it's a very internal book. Besides life unraveling in every way while people try to carry on with everyday things...not much happens. But it is such a beautiful, slow story. 
 It's told from the perspective of Julia, a normal 11 year-old growing up in California--and I could really relate to the glories and humiliations and insecurities of being that age. How vulnerable we all are at the bus stop, and when we fall in love with someone who never seems to realize we exist, and when we realize our parents are human, and that we ourselves are mortal. It's so utterly beautiful in this way. Thompson Walker captures it perfectly. 
 And it has the added layer of an almost science-fiction-y doomsday scenario making it so fascinating. I will literally never get this book out of my head. 
 My only gripe is that it's quite negative. It's a downer. I mean, that's to be expected-it's about the end of the earth. Things are falling apart, people--and our planet--are dying. But, there are plenty of great works that treat serious themes with levity and optimism. I think The Age of Miracles could have used a little more of these. I think if it was a little less depressing it would be perfect.

I enjoyed this book for its new interesting earth ending event. It's less post apocalyptic and more just apocalyptic as it's based during the catastrophic planet event. So what would happen if earths rotation slowed down and days and nights got longer? We get to find out through the eyes of an 11 year old. This also ends up being a kind of coming of age story. While the premise I thought was great and the writing is beautiful, do have to say it does fizzle toward the end. But not enough for me to put the book down. I recommend it!

I had read some very laudatory reviews, so thought I would give this book a try. On the good side, the author has a very good writing style. She gives good descriptions without being excessively detailed and did a nice job of creating a mood. She has a good eye for details as she diaries the changes in this average middle schoolers life. 
 However,she does not write about much and does not explore the emotional life of any of her characters. Why does the relationship change between the girl and her friends? What is going on with the mother? How does the girl change as a result of the world changing? How does she feel when she see the status of life at the camps? The book is more like reading a diary than a story. 
 SPOILER: 
 The most frustrating part of this emotionless book is the lack of any sort of closure. We never learn what happens to the neighbor. We know the schools and hospitals are still operating, but never get a sense of how other aspects of life differ. Then the book jumps from the girl at age 12 to the girl at age 23, with no explanation as to what has happened to her during the intervening years. Typically, when you find an adult character looking back, there is a degree of insight and growth. Here there is nothing. 
 A very disappointing read.

Finished reading this book, The Age or Miracles, in less than a day! I read a review that said this book is "science fiction, but not" and that really sums it up well. Julia, an 11 year old California girl, narrates this story of the end of the innocence and blind faith of childhood against the background of our world on the edge of extinction. As the world begins to fail and deteriorate around us, so does Julia's childhood. If this book has a major flaw, it is in the ending.

I picked this up because I had seen some good reviews, but didn't find this an enjoyable read. The characters were not likable in any way, and the novel itself moved from one depressing scene to another. I think the author shows promise, but did not find this to be a good read for me.
Inventive, thought provoking, touching- A must read

When the Earth's rotation suddenly starts slowing down, and days become progressively longer, everything changes--the way normal society operates, the things we take for granted, down to the interpersonal relationships we all have. Karen Thompson Walker lets the reader experience events through the eyes of a middle-school age girl, an interesting choice because of the innocence of the age, but not an interesting choice because her life is kind of boring--even with major global change happening around her. Walker's novel is a word of warning of things that could come to pass if the world's population stays on its course of greenhouse gases, etc., but I didn't find the novel terribly enjoyable. It's under 300 pages and should have been a quick read, but it took me a long time to get through. It's kind of like eating your vegetables--they're good for you, but not much fun and you're left waiting for a dessert that never comes.
Beautiful coming of age story that happens to be set in a dystopian society. I've read a lot of dystopian society books and this one is one of the most unique. Loved it- highly recommend.

reference_books.title: Looking for Alaska
reference_books.review_text:
I'm not going to lie, I devoured Looking for Alaska by John Green. But, I had several quibbles with it. Okay, so Miles Halter is a kid with no friends who heads off to boarding school where he immediately makes two great friends. His roommate "Colonel", and Alaska, the beautiful troubled girl. And, in characteristic John Green fashion, they were all smart and immensely likable characters. The book also deals with faith and mortality in very thought provoking ways which I loved. My quibble...there was too much smoking, too much drinking and too much sex talk. And, this is a book directed towards teens and I felt like this smoking and drinking and sex was all part of the image of these likable characters and if a teenager is reading this and loving Miles/Colonel/Alaska then they might want to be like them. It just feels a little irresponsible to me even though objectively I can see how these were literary crutches to drive behavior and consequences. I think he handled all of these issues more responsibly and more beautifully in The Fault in Our Stars. 
 thisismybookblog.blogspot.com

reference_books.title: March: Book Three (March, #3)
reference_books.review_text: March: Book Three by John Lewis, Andrew Aydin and Nate Powell concludes the story of the Civil Rights Movement from Lewis' perspective. The third book starts with the infamous bombing of the black church in Birmingham, Alabama and follows the attempts of the movement to register black voters in Alabama and concludes with the Selma March and the eventual signing of the 1965 Voting Rights Act. Interspersed through all three books is Lewis' attendance at Barack Obama's inauguration in 2009. These graphic novels are such a powerful way to tell this story. Putting the words right in the mouths of the founders and key players in the movement with such incredible drawings is wonderfully impactful. I think it would be incredible to teach these books in a classroom. The idea for this project may have been perceived as "out there," but I think it was absolutely brilliant. I will recommend these to anyone and everyone and I think the United States could use this refresher right now.

reference_books.title: Kindred Spirits
reference_books.review_text: Kindred Spirits by Rainbow Rowell is a novella that was released in Great Britain for World Book Day. It's a sweet story about a teen girl waiting in line to see the new Star Wars movie. It was a perfect little taste of pop culture and the things we're willing to do for the things we love. It's also about feeling invisible and how things we feel are harmless can be hurtful to others. I enjoyed every minute of this story and I thought it had the perfect ending. Also, it has a mark on the cover that says "For Older Readers", I'm not sure why as there was nothing objectionable or beyond her YA audience. I'd even let my 11 year old read it.

reference_books.title: The Particular Sadness of Lemon Cake
reference_books.review_text: What the what? That's how I felt when I finished The Particular Sadness of Lemon Cake by Aimee Bender. I may have felt differently had I known the extent to which magical realism was going to be used in this book. And, I'm sure you're saying, duh, it's about a girl who can tastes peoples emotions when she eats the food they make. And, I was totally on board for that. But, I wasn't on board for how the magical realism was manifested in her brother, Joe. It just left me shaking my head, what? But, I liked Rose. I liked her dad. I liked Joe's best friend, George. Just overall, not a lot happened in this book and I didn't like the ending.

reference_books.title: A Voice in the Wind (Mark of the Lion, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I finally finished A Voice in the Wind by Francine Rivers. It took me awhile to get into this book and I enjoyed it for awhile, but then it started to wear on me. I appreciated the character of Haddasah and the struggles she was going through as a Christian in Ancient Rome. But, I felt that Rivers had a pretty heavy stroke with her 'sinners' brush on all the other characters. I'm not really interested in reading any of the other books in this trilogy.

book_a.title: Bad Feminist
book_a.user_review: I get why Roxane Gay has labeled herself with Bad Feminist, but I've got to respectfully disagree. If she wants to include bad in her feminist label, I think she should go with badass feminist instead. Because, if Gay is a bad feminist then I might be the worst feminist. I'm a stay-at-home mom who still has no idea what she wants to be when she grows up. I love a good rom-com and I watch some of the worst reality TV. I also read profusely and continue to educate myself everyday. I'm a work in progress. I also believe that women should be treated and paid as equals, that men shouldn't get to decide what we do with our bodies, and that we should get to forge our own paths. And, I'm hoping to someday release 4 badass feminists into the world. As for Gay's work, I found myself thoroughly engaged. She not only gives us her feminist perspective, but there is also a great deal of the book dedicated to race in pop culture. Gay opened my eyes to a lot of things I hadn't even considered with relation to some of the most popular things we have recently encountered in pop culture. Some of her opinions I was 100% on board for and some things I was 90% on board for, but I still appreciate everything she wrote. And there were a few things that she mentioned, that I thought, wow, I wish I could get her opinion on these things two years later, particularly Bill Cosby and Orange is the New Black. This year has been a year of getting educated for me both on feminism (though I've always considered myself a feminist) and race relations and this is a book not to be missed if you are interested in either subject. And, check out Roxane Gay's interview on Phoebe Robinson's podcast Sooo Many White Guys. And follow her on Twitter!

sample_reviews.review_text:
I picked up this book after watching Gay's TED talk, thinking it would have been an expansion on the topics she touches on in her lecture. It wasn't. 
 With no unifiying thesis, the collection of essays read more like someone's blog, than a book. As a result it was difficult for me to get through. It picked up in the later half, especially after the essay The Alienable Rights of Women.

I was looking forward to reading this book. However, I ended up a bit disappointed. I think the author is very bright and talented but some of these essays were way too drawn out. I respect the fact that she voiced her opinion on various issues but I often found myself thinking that she is over analyzing. It will be interesting to see what her thoughts are about some of these issues say 15 years from now. I did gain some insight from the book and it did make me think about the issues she discussed so I do feel like it is worth the read. I just didn't think that it was profound or anything new.

I feel like Bad Feminist in a lot of ways, has always been the voice inside of me, trying to make sense of how I can be me but feminist at the same time. 
 Roxane Gay's collection of essays is a mixture of topics, most notably race, but everything seems to connect itself in ways you may have subconsciously pieced together before but never really took the time to think out. I think she is a breath of fresh air because she is rational. She recognizes both sides of the story in many of her essays, and points out how damn difficult it is to be any one thing. How can we demonize the black kid just walking down the street, and blame him for his own murder, but creepily empathize with the "boy next door" kid responsible for the Boston bombings? These questions and points she makes are so well thought out in how she presents them. It's equal parts awe-inspiring and frustrating. 
 Parts of this book were not written for me. They were not written for the average, white privilege, white girl from the midwest. They weren't meant to speak to me on a personal level, because they are not me. But they did teach me a lot. 
 Because they point out the ludicriousy of white people and our failings to black people and how we marginalize in the smallest ways, ways we don't even realize, but happens to have big consequences. All these little thoughts people have about race, and how they're shared and presented, further perpetuates how we can literally put a black kid on trial for his own death, Gay points out. 
 At times these essays are baffling. You don't want to think of The Help as being detrimental, but quite frankly, now that I've read her perspective on this story, I can't help think it over and realize shes right. But it makes me a bad feminist because I still think its a good movie and a good book. 
 I like that she realizes shes a feminist but a bad one. It gives me hope, somehow. And, it's a relief.
I wanted to enjoy this collection of essays, but didn't for the most part. I'm glad that another voice is added to the discourse about feminism.
it wasn't as good as i wanted it to be, but it made me want to be friends with the author.

I agree with pretty much everything Roxane Gay argues in this book. But I don't feel like I got anything out of it. These are all arguments that others have made before. She never dug deeper into the issues she covers. There was never a moment where I said "huh, I've never thought about it like that before," which is one of the best things good feminist writing offers. 
 I am not sure who this book is supposed to be for. I don't think it is likely to convince anyone who sees feminist as a bad word to change their mind. And people who have read feminist writers may find that they have heard it all before. So I guess if you're looking for a beginner-level introduction to feminism this might be for you. But I don't think that a series of short pieces on pop culture or the author's experiences or both are the best way to learn about feminism. It isn't even a feel-good "I just want to retreat from the world and read someone who only agrees with me" kind of book, since Gay spends so much time rehashing the horrible statements of stupid politicians or celebrities. I finished the book feeling vaguely angry and completely adrift, without having gained a new perspective or having learned anything. 
 I honestly feel like a bad feminist for disliking this book as much as I did...Sorry!

I have a lot of opinions on this book, which has something good to say to Gay's work. 
 I was recommended to read Bad Feminist to get a wide point of view of intersectional feminism nowadays and indeed it has succeeded to give me that vision. The book spines around two big themes, feminism and race, but they are always connected with each other and also with loads of other issues like gender and sexuality, mass culture, class, beauty and weight bias, sexual problems and even bullying. Roxane Gay has a unique and diverse way to introduce those polemics, social problems or simply human conditions, making of this essay collection a deep insight to her inspiring thoughts without making those pages boring: there's a constant use of examples, personal experiences and of course movies, series and books reviews, which perhaps offer the most talented of Roxane's presentation of the issues I mentioned before. 
 But what I am most interested in is the fact that this is not only a bunch of essays about feminism, race, gender and every other fight she spots and analyses. This is a book that honestly, clearly talks about privilege, humanity, expectations, rebellion, bravery, election, being happy, relationships, mistakes, youngsters, communication, feelings, stereotypes, compassion and so many other things that truly matter and are directly affected by those different types of social inequality. She speaks about all those things seriously but keeping a usage of the language that make us feel connected, make us laugh and identify constantly with what she's saying, so we understand better. I have not read much feminist contemporary literature but I guess she is doing something really fine, she is being truly close to her readers. 
 Even if I thank Gay for this book as it will keep me thinking about multiple themes, it has shown me a new point of view on pop culture and it has made me laugh, identify and feel, I have two main objections (perhaps they are my own faults as I am a bad reader, see). 
 Firstly, I think the organization of the essays in the five blocks Gay divides them does not make much sense: if she is trying to show us the connection between issues it would have been better for me if she had not made the division, which is by the way unnecessary. 
 Secondly, and perhaps more important, I have a little problem with her automatic criticism over every author that writes or makes something let's say involving feminism and doesn't include special care for black women, non heterosexual women or lower class women. I completely agree that feminism should be intersectional and that we should all try to care more about the women that are oppressed in more ways, but that shouldn't mean writers, film makers or artists should be criticized just for making material that doesn't consider a view over every single condition a human being can have. I think specially talking about literature or cinema it's not fair to judge things this way because even when it would be nice to have a movie that would consider everything that wish is a bit unrealistic to me, as writers will still be closer to their own experiences and so they will make them appear in their oeuvres. Maybe the solution to this would be letting more diverse people enter the literature or cinema world and show their experiences instead of putting on other writers the responsibility of covering it all (of course I'm not talking about avoiding tropes or stereotypes, which I think is always crucial). 
 Finally, I think there's some irony in the way she kind of expects that people take into account women, other races and sexualities, and any other sort of people that could be discriminated but completely forgets about reality outside the US. Gay, as a lot of american authors, seem to live in a bubble where the rest of the world is just not enough important. She constantly talks about forgotten people entering the conversation, strongly criticizes superiority attitudes and claims that everyone should have a role model on TV with which they could identify, etc; but then forgets that us, non american human beings exist, and that the superiority she is against of is constantly suggested by the american apparently "more interesting" culture.

My review from Stories with Stephanie: 
 I wish everyone would read this book. I'd quote the whole thing at you if I could--I practically did over at my tumblr. Reading these essays was like sitting down with my best friend and having casual but heartfelt discussions about the problematic nature of pop culture and politics, or like delving into a series of the best blog posts ever written about feminism and entertainment. 
 But I don't want to put Gay on a "Feminist Pedestal," a position she intentionally tries to avoid by preemptively labelling herself as a bad feminist: "People who are placed on pedestals are expected to pose, perfectly. Then they get knocked off when they fuck it up. I regularly fuck it up. Consider me already knocked off." 
 Regardless, Gay has a lot to say--about more than just feminism--and she says it well. In 38 essays about gender, sexuality, race, politics, entertainment, and her own life, Gay covers topics ranging from Scrabble to The Hunger Games to Chris Brown to The Help. She's unapologetically candid in sharing her thoughts and experiences, even when it comes to opinions that might not be popular with all her readers (the chapter on trigger warnings comes to mind). 
 I'm sometimes nervous about reading nonfiction essays because I worry they'll be tediously academic or filled with technical jargon, but the beautiful thing about Bad Feminist is that it's so accessible. I hate to use such a cliche word, but it fits here. A lot of feminist texts might be daunting or turn readers off because they address the complex history of feminism and issues of sex and gender in such dry, scholarly language. That's not to say those writers aren't doing important work, but Gay shares her knowledge and experience in a way that turns a feminist text into an intimate reflection and conversation that anyone can join. 
 Part of the reason I loved Bad Feminist so much is because Gay puts into words everything I've felt about sexism in media and politics (see the chapters on 50 Shades of Gray, rape jokes, Chris Brown, and women's reproductive rights). And at the same time, she opened my eyes to so many other issues I'd been ignorant to, often because of my privilege; the essays on race and entertainment were especially enlightening. 
 I only had one issue with Bad Feminist. In her last essay, Gay says she is "failing as a feminist," and as proof she points to her desire to be taken care of, her affinity for the color pink, her appreciation for music with lyrics that degrade women, and so on. "If I take issue with the unrealistic standards of beauty women are held to, I shouldn't have a secret fondness for fashion and smooth calves, right?" Wrong. I think this is one of the biggest misconceptions about feminism (and feminists are, admittedly, partly to blame). 
 It's OK to shave your legs and like makeup, as long as you're doing it for yourself and not because the beauty industry tells you you should. It's OK to like movies or books that are problematic, as long as you understand and acknowledge why they're problematic. Being a "good feminist" doesn't mean hating men and babies, being totally independent, and not shaving your legs. 
 Being a good feminist means advocating for equal rights for men and women, calling out sexism when you see it, and being critical of media that promotes misogyny, rape culture, or domestic violence. In this sense, Roxane Gay is not a bad feminist--in fact, she's the complete opposite--and I think she knows that. But good or bad, she's still a feminist, and that's a wonderful thing to be.

(First, I must note that I was able to hear Roxane Gay speak and also have my book signed by her afterward!) This book was okay. Not bad. But it didn't really have the "wow" factor for me that I was rather expecting. It certainly has merit; Roxane Gay has a lot of important things to say and observations to note. I hope that people who do not consider themselves feminists read this book and learn from it. (Note that I already consider myself to be a feminist and decently aware of social/cultural issues.) Starting this book out, I was a bit disappointed. As I said, it didn't live up to my expectations based on its hype. I found myself getting "lost" in the middle of Gay's essays. I'd forget what the intent, or main topic, of the essay was. Now that I have finished the book, I do have a better appreciation for it, or perhaps specific essays. A lot of Gay's remarks are valuable. But perhaps they weren't all as groundbreaking for me since I already hold similar beliefs and knowledge. Some of my favorite essays were actually not feminist in nature, but rather, were about being a professor ("Typical First Year Professor") and Scrabble competitions ("To Scratch, Claw, or Grope Clumsily or Frantically"). A feminist essay I especially valued was, "The Careless Language of Sexual Violence." To contradict my previous statement about already holding similar beliefs and knowledge, I found her essays regarding race and entertainment especially eye-opening, thought-provoking, and strong: "The Solace of Preparing Fried Foods and Other Quaint Remembrances from 1960s Mississippi: Thoughts on The Help," "Surviving Django," "Beyond the Struggle Narrative," "The Morality of Tyler Perry," "The Last Day of a Young Black Man," and "When Less is More." These essays were the most groundbreaking and important for me. Perhaps it seems I am contradictory in this review, but Gay herself states that she is a contradictory person in her final essay, so I'll give myself some slack. In conclusion, this book is valuable. It states important observations and critiques. Yet, overall, I wasn't as impressed as I was expecting to be. But I was very impressed with her race and entertainment essays, which I found personally insightful. I suppose, then, that different people will find different essays in this collection particularly helpful, applicable, or insightful based on their preexisting beliefs, knowledge, and experiences, and those helpful essays will be different for each person. If anything, I am most grateful that perhaps this book has heightened the general public's awareness and knowledge of feminism and the various social issues it encompasses. [3.5 stars]

3.6 stars 
 I couldn't help but compare this book to Lena Dunham's (Not that Kind of Girl). Is that fair? No. But the pink, black, and white covers were begging for it. 
 Though annoyingly repetitive, the intro had me psyched. Especially compared to Lena's intro. Roxane Gay, thank you for not claiming to be perfect. For not claiming to know it all. 
 I struggled a bit as I read this, anticipating how I would talk about it with other people. I wanted to love it. But no one gets a free pass. Though they are arranged loosely by topic, the essays have a haphazard nature (I was entertained by the Scrabble one, but it definitely should have been cut!) and are often overstuffed with similar and repeated ideas. 
 And though I was on board for a more modest and grounded style of writing, I still often found myself confronted by a viewpoint that felt offensively narrow. It's okay and even laudatory (if not solipsistic) to write about your own experiences, but I was surprised to see how many times Roxane Gay discounted perspectives that differed from her own. (Skinny girls have body issues, too, please. And it's not just men who are guilty of reading almost only books written by men, and on and on). 
 So I'm conflicted... but that's okay. What's important is that we have these conversations.

book_b.title: Frankenstein
book_b.user_review: I just finished Frankenstein by Mary Shelley. And, there are so many things to ponder in this book. First, while this book is not particularly scary now, I'm sure the idea of it was really quite frightening when it was first written. And, though I was not scared by it at all, I could totally relate to that uneasy feeling in the stomach that Shelley described so frequently in the book in reference to Victor Frankensteins feelings towards the demon he created. Second, when the demon was describing his experience after being abandoned by Frankenstein, I thought a lot about children in the foster care system or orphanages who face abandonment from biological parents and then also feel shunned through the system. It's like they just need someone to see past the history and the baggage to see who they are on the inside. And, third, I thought about how sometimes science can be our best and our worst enemy. And, the idea of sometimes the things we create have the potential to destroy us. There is so much that could be said on the topic, but I will leave it at that. I was a little slow getting through this book, but ultimately I did really like it. And, I understand why it has been such a successful story.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Synopsis: "Mary Shelley began writing Frankenstein when she was only eighteen. At once a Gothic thriller, a passionate romance, and a cautionary tale about the dangers of science, Frankenstein tells the story of committed science student Victor Frankenstein. Obsessed with discovering the cause of generation and life and bestowing animation upon lifeless matter, Frankenstein assembles a human being from stolen body parts but; upon bringing it to life, he recoils in horror at the creature's hideousness. Tormented by isolation and loneliness, the once-innocent creature turns to evil and unleashes a campaign of murderous revenge against his creator, Frankenstein. 
 Frankenstein, an instant bestseller and an important ancestor of both the horror and science fiction genres, not only tells a terrifying story, but also raises profound, disturbing questions about the very nature of life and the place of humankind within the cosmos: What does it mean to be human? What responsibilities do we have to each other? How far can we go in tampering with Nature? In our age, filled with news of organ donation genetic engineering, and bio-terrorism, these questions are more relevant than ever." 
 My Review: I ranked this as my top favorite book after reading it in high school. It was assigned reading and once starting it I could not put it down (I snuck it into my calculus class). It has been some time since I last read it and have considered other books might take the top spot. So this month I decided to re-read it but got the audio version instead. There is now no doubt what so ever that this book will remain my #1 favorite book, especially after listening to the audio book. I don't feel that this is a horror book, to me it is beautiful and an emotional drama. I can't help but become teary eyed and choked up when the creature confronts his creator in the mountains and I must admit that I am totally on the creature's side. This is a classic and really one that everyone should at least try and it could become an instant and forever favorite!
See my full review at hlgibsonauthor.com
Couldn't wait for it to be over. Sounds like it was written by a teenage girl. Oh, because it was.

I HATE THIS. There I said it. I hate Frankenstein with a passion. I read a hundred pages of this book but it was just SO BORING I couldn't finish it. I only read it because I heard it was better than Dracula and I adored Dracula. This one however... It is boring, it is awful, I detested the writing style, there was no action, the characters had extremely long conversations talking in an unrealistic way, why the fuck is this a classic? Go to hell, Frankenstein.

I'm glad I've read Frankenstein but goodness gracious such a burden it was. I cannot believe this edition was under 300 pages but felt way much longer. 
 Wouldn't it have been much more uncomplicated to instead write an essay about wrong and right, about not standing above God and other morally-aimed subjects? At least it was better than Dracula.
This has to be the most tedious thing I have ever read in my life.

Frankenstein was published the same year as Jane Austen's last novel Persuasion. What a contrast between the rule-bound manner in which Austen's characters work toward their goals, making the best of the roles that society has assigned them, and the overwrought way in which Shelley's characters agonize over the vicissitudes of fate, seeming almost to believe that they have no control over their actions. 
 How can I give such a low score to a classic? I found it hard to immerse myself in the story with a number of unrealistic elements. I don't mean the idea of Victor Frankenstein creating life -- that's the premise that I must accept as the basis of the story. Nor do I mean the unlikely coincidences of repeatedly meeting the right (or wrong) person at the right (or wrong) time -- that's to be expected in early 19th century fiction. Nor even that we're expected to believe the characters would orally relate such absurdly lengthy and detailed accounts, and that Capt Walton would write them down verbatim in what must have been very thick letters to his sister -- that's also a convention of literature of the time. 
 What keeps me from getting involved in the story is how the more mundane things that happen don't seem as though the author quite thought them through. How does the creature learn to read and write peering through a gap in a wall for hours each day, for months on end, with nobody suspecting he is there? Even in ideal conditions, how can he learn enough in these months to read Paradise Lost? Why would the creature scratch lengthy, complete sentences on a rock instead of something shorter and more like a telegram? 
 Frankenstein's travels to far-flung locations for various reasons remind me of a 1980s James Bond movie.

Very interesting and disturbing. I think it is amazing but also telling that Mary Shelley was about 18 when she first wrote it. It reminded me of Wuthering Heights with its over-the-top angst and drama, but still I liked it. The questions that came up over a creator's responsibility to his creations as well as the references to Adam and Eve and the theme of choice, make for a great discussion. I'm a happy-ending sort of gal, so I'll probably never read it again, but I'm glad I did.

Heartbreakingly sad and very surprising. 
 As well known as the idea of Frankenstein is, I was surprised to learn that I really had no idea what the story was, and it was beautiful and haunting and very, very sad. The monster was so human and so misunderstood. I was amazed the entire time of Mary Shelley's poetic words and just her mind in general.

This will go down in history as one of the very few books I have ever rage quit. Victor is just too whiny of a narrator to hold my attention or keep patience with. My first clue that I would end up disliking this book was that there is no version of the movie I have come close to liking, unless you count Young Frankenstein, which, lets face it, is a spoof, which is probably why I do love that movie. I really wanted to love this book, because the idea of reanimating the dead is an interesting one, but I just could not find any emotion for it other than loathing. I am just glad that my rage-quitting the book did not evoke a bad grade on the report I had to write on it.

reference_books.review_text:
Kate could have tried using a little of the brains she was given and also, I had issues with Thorne. 
 What bugged the most was, that it came after Min and Collin's story which I absolutely loved! 
 A full review to follow once I have read the entire series.

reference_books.review_text: It has been two months and I have not been able to finish this book. Not even half of it is finished. At the suggestion of a friend I started it but it simply did not work for me. Not at all.

reference_books.title: Blue-Eyed Devil (Travises, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Hardy Cates, the man I formed a very negative image of in the previous book, and a naive Haven Travis find their happily ever after in this one. No, this is not a spoiler as the synopsis as good as says this. 
 Like the previous book, there is an instance that I am glossing over because it goes against something I staunchly believe in. And likewise a star is being socked off for that. 
 The thing that needs a mention is the strength of the woman in this scenario. The way she gets herself out of an abusive situation albeit a little late but that also depicts reality of the situation as from what I understand one needs to first come to terms with themselves and realise that they do not deserve what's being dished out to them. I applaud her for finding the courage to move on and getting to understand that she is not to blame! 
 As for Hardy, I will say he may have redeemed himself in this one but I am not ready to forgive him yet. It can be called a prejudice against this man or whatever but for me Haven is the star in this one. 
 My rating for the most part is for the way a very prominent social issue being highlighted in this story. 
 Domestic violence is a reality that the world is catching up on as it is not considered a family matter anymore that should not involve the forces or the state. The same is true for bullying. I have been on the receiving hand of it and I can so get how frustrating it can get as it erodes your self-worth and then self-respect.

sample_reviews.review_text: Did I say that the last book was my favorite in the series? Well, that's just because I hadn't read this one yet. When I first started this book I wondered at how well it would fit in with the rest of the series, since so little of it actually takes place in Spindle Cove. Despite being set mostly in London, this book fits perfectly with its predecessors. I'm a sucker for a less than perfect heroine, and Pauline was perfect in her imperfections (pun intended). And who could help but fall head over heels for Griff?

"Miss Simms," his mother said, "if you think you can trick me into repeating your vulgarities, you will be disappointed. Suffice it to say, slang, blasphemy, and cursing have no place in a lady's vocabulary. Much less a duchess's." 
 "Oh. I see. So your grace never curses." 
 "I do not." 
 "Words like cor . . . bollocks . . . damn . . . devil . . . blast . . . bloody hell . . ." She pronounced the words with relish, warming to her task. "They don't cross a duchess's lips?" 
 "No." 
 "Never?" 
 "Never." 
 Miss Simms's fair brow creased in thought. "What if a duchess steps on a tack? What if a gust of wind steals a duchess's best powdered wig? Not even then?" 
 "Not even when an impertinent farm girl provokes a duchess to a simmering rage," she replied evenly. "A duchess might contemplate all manner of cutting remarks and frustrated oaths. But even in the face of extreme annoyance, she stifles any such ejaculations." 
 "My," Miss Simms said, wide-eyed. "I do hope dukes aren't held to the same standard. Can't be healthy for a man, always stifling his ejaculations." 
 I was commuting and I just burst out laughing after reading this!!! All the people around me were looking at me like I was crazy! LMAO 
 This book is full of moments like this, but it's also full of very touching moments that brought tears in my eyes! 
 "You see," he said, "I brought Miss Simms to London to thwart my mother's matchmaking schemes. She was supposed to be a laughable failure. A hilarious joke." 
 One of the Misses Haughfells began to giggle. Her mother smacked her wrist with a folded fan. 
 "No, no," Griff said. "Do laugh, please. It's most amusing. A barmaid, receiving duchess lessons. Can you imagine? The best part was the diction training. My mother was forever drilling Miss Simms on her H' s." 
 "Is that so?" Lady Haughfell arched a brow. "I don't suppose she made much progress." 
 "Oh, but she did. Show them, Miss Simms." 
 Pauline smiled. "Hideous. Ham-faced. Hag." She looked to Griff. "There. How was that?" 
 "Brilliant." He beamed at her. 
 "Write it down?" 
 "Of course." As he scribbled the epithets on Miss Haughfell's dance card, he went on talking. "But you haven't heard the funniest bit, Lady Haughfell. See, I thought I was playing a trick on my mother --and all London--but it turns out, the joke was on me." 
 The matron stiffened. "Because you have lost what remained of your family's honor and society's good opinion?" 
 "No. Because I fell desperately in love with this barmaid and now cannot imagine happiness without her." He looked up and shrugged. "Whoops." 
 All three Haughfells stared at him in mute, slack-jawed horror. Pauline wished she could have a miniature of their expressions to keep in a drawer forever and pull out on dull, rainy days. 
 Griff sharpened the pencil stub with his thumbnail. "Let's make sure to have that down. It's important." He spoke the words slowly as he inscribed them. "Desperately . . . in . . . love." 
 "Don't forget the 'whoops,' " Pauline said, looking over his shoulder. "That was the best part." 
 I loved both Griff and Pauline. Both are very special persons. Griff has been living his life as a rake until a very tragic death hasn't woke him up. Pauline has been awake since she was a little girl while trying to protect her sister. 
 They are just perfect for each other! 
 Pauline is a very unusual heroine. She's a lower class (I hate this definition, but I suppose in that period it was an important issue with people...), but very intelligent and very straightforward. I loved how she handled the Duchess! She had wit and she had heart. It was wonderful to have insight in her feelings! 
 Griff is wonderful in his own right. But his being wonderful does not come out until later in the story. And it comes out thanks to Pauline. Great!!! 
 The secondary character of the (future) dowager Duchess with her knitting problems were endearing and very touching too. Her love for Griff, her only living child, was evident since the beginning, but it was masked by 
 phlegm 
 ... LOL 
 "Lastly," the duchess continued, "the most important quality any Duchess of Halford needs is this: phlegm." 
 "Phlegm?" Pauline echoed, choking down her food. "It's forbidden to speak of hunger at the dinner table, but it's fine to talk about phlegm?" She poked at a bit of ham. "If it's phlegm you want, I can give you that. I learned how to spit with the farm boys. The trick is to start far back in your throat and -" 
 The duchess halted, just as she was about to spoon some asparagus soup into her mouth. She looked at the rich green broth, then set down her spoon. 
 "Not that kind of phlegm, Miss Simms. I refer to self-assurance. Unflappability. Aplomb. The ability to remain calm, no matter what occurs. Never underestimate the power of phlegm." 
 I really hope Ms. Dare will continue with this series - it's just that WONDERFUL that it would be a shame if this were the last book!!!

I found it a bit boring, and I never really felt the connection between Griff and Pauline. Plus I personally hated the whole they fell in love in a week thing. It's just unbelievable, and I much prefer romances where they actually have time to get to know one another and spend more meaningful time together.

A sweet, funny romance that reads far more like a contemporary than a historical (which isn't really a good thing, since I like my historical romances to be historical in more than just superficial ways, but I was too charmed by this one to be much of a stickler about it).

This was written by someone who threw something together without any thought but sex. The Heroine was annoying. The Hero was dull. The only character I like was the mother. Wand what the heck was up with the "slang words" that were used in the book?
That's it. I'm moving to Spindle Cove.
While I liked the fact that it's essentially "My Fair Lady" at first, I didn't feel like the plot diverged enough from expectations to be really engaging. Writing is good, though.
The more books Dare writes, the more historical anachronisms take center stage. A duke marrying a barmaid? Only in someone's wildest dreams...

sample_reviews.review_text:
In Harlan Coben's, Promise Me, agent slash avenger, Myron Bolitar, inherits more than he bargained for when he asks a couple of teenage girls to promise and call him if they are ever in trouble. Coben delivers a plot full of action and misdirection that's sure to please mystery and suspense fans in this tale of suburban desperation. 
 I liked the book, though I foud the love scenes between Myron and his new girlfriend, Ali, to be a bit too cute. I also felt Myron's sidekick, Win, was an over-the-top hero. No matter what Myron needed, or when he needed it, Win was there to deliver. 
 That being said, Promise Me, has that hard to define Make-you-want-to-read-it quality going in full force. 
 Bob Avey, author of Beneath a Buried House
This is not my usual genre, but I think I might be addicted!!!

Long, fast paced, twisted narrative with lots of characters that flat lines. Very disappointing ending. First Myron Bolitar book. First time reading a Harlan Coben book. Don't think I'll revisit this series.

This is my second Myron Bolitar story by Coben that I found at the library. I still want to try to start reading this series at the beginning because this is a character that ages and goes through life changing events that need to build one on top of the other. Yes, I do love Bolitar and his 'gang'.

My only complaint is that the narrator (I listened to this series via audiobook) changed. I was used to the original voice and he did a stellar job, but in this book the Author (Harlan Coben) read it. He did an ok job, but I prefer the original voice. 
 The storyline in the book was kinda lacking for me, I still enjoyed it, but I am looking forward to his future Myron Bolitar books in the hopes that he gets back to what made this series great.

This is the book where Coben comes back to Myron after not writing him for a while and rather than pick up where he left off he basically says that Myron has been behaving himself for the last 6 years. A little different from most of his book as it doesn't involve a client. He finds his new girlfriends daughter and a friend in his old room and after hearing there discussion makes them promise to call him if they ever need a ride home. The other girl calls him later and after he drops her off she vanishes putting the heat on Myron as he once again falls into investigator mode to get to the end of it. OK read but little sports involvement which is one of the things I like about the series.
another book i couldn't get into.

Really interesting to read this book on September 11th, and seeing Coben tweet "Thinking today about those I love who lost so much 9 years ago. And only about them." This isn't exactly a 9/11 story, but there are definite overtones (not to mention clear plot points). 
 I still feel for Myron that he can't quite find the right person to settle down with. Ali is nice, but just not his long-term love. 
 On to Long Lost sometime this week. Wonder of Coben will come out with Myron #10?

Coben is a marvelous writer and I enjoy his stories quite a lot. I only gave Promise Me 3 stars because I had read it a few years ago and upon re-reading it there was only one scene that I actually remembered. I think a 5 star book should be memorable. Also the ending was a quick wrap-it-up-in-a-way-you-wouldn't-have-guessed type of ending. It was a bit contrived.

I am reading the books not in particular order, but depending on the mood and desire and description on the book cover. 
 It turns out that "Promise me" is the eighth in Myron Bolitar series. The basketball player who was injured at the age of 22, he founded an agency representing athletes, accompanied by a variety of bizarre characters. 
 This time he is asking his friends daughters to call him at any time if they needed help. he promise he will come to their rescue with no questions asked. After Amy had called, and Myron left her at 2 in the morning in a suburb Rig'oord without insisting ask questions, Myron discovers that she is gone. 
 This book is well written and interesting for young teenage parents. We all know how difficult adolescence and the social confrontations. 
 It also deals with troubling questions as to how much we really know our children to therefore go to protect them? 
 And deals with domestic violence which is another interesting aspect of the book. 
 The is not book nerve-wracking tension and is really suited me. Its rhythm and narrative suited mw. Except that Coben could give up the appalling scene of the biting, he did not need it to keep the plot.

sample_reviews.review_text:
3.5 Stars 
 My full review: http://coffeecookiesandchilipeppers.b... 
 The central character, Joanna, is a strong female, who has survived a terrible assault to become a reasonably normal adult. The book is written in the first person, so we get a great insight into her thoughts and feelings, and she is a generally sympathetic character, so I was invested in finding out more about her and her past. The other characters are mostly well drawn and there are some nice relationships: I especially liked her barbed sparring with Olivia's BFF, Cher. However, I felt like Chandra, as "the angry competitor for her role who hates her at first but then has to grudgingly admit that she's quite good" was more than a little generic, even down to the fact that Rachel mistook her for a man at first. 
 The world that Ms Pettersson builds is mostly believable, and quite well detailed. The zodiac theme feels a little forced and I would have liked some reason why the warriors are identified by the signs. There is talk of them being a separate race from humans, but some more details would have helped this to seem less random. I was also confused as to the true number of the warriors: it sometimes reads as if there is a set in each town or city, but then that makes Joanna's role as the Kairos seem a bit strange. Also, I really struggled with the instruction manuals for being an agent for either side being produced and kept in a comic store: this made very little sense and was almost reason for me to stop reading. This was just silly and was a major stumbling block. Hopefully, these problems will be addressed in the later books. One aspect that I really did like is the Light's use of cats as guardians because they can identify Shadow warriors: this is a nice way to incorporate our perception of cats and their supposedly supernatural powers . . . little Tiddles doesn't like that guy down the street because he is an agent of the Shadows! 
 My biggest issue with this book was the pacing. I almost gave up with it several times during the first two thirds because it was so heavy with exposition and so slowly plotted. Fortunately, the plot reaches a turning point, after which Joanna starts to kick some ass and the pace picks up nicely. I understand the need to establish the world, the characters, etc., but this was very hard going, and I spoke to several people who had given up before getting to the turning point. I hope, again, that this is not an issue in the later books. 
 This is not your traditional vamp-ridden urban fantasy, and that is refreshing. Plus, it is nice to have a heroine who is grumpy and paranoid, but has a really good reason to be like that: the assault robs her of her innocence, her mother and her boyfriend, so we can forgive her for being very defensive. It is a little rough around the edges, however, I am glad that I stuck with the book as it has great promise and it seems that this is her first published novel, so I can cut the author some slack: I am looking forward to reading the second book in the series.

I've read worse. 
 Not recently.
3.5 stars

The first part of the book was exciting and had me thinking that this could be an interesting superhuman book. 
 Then the clumsy writing, a bit of deus ex machina, and a deplorable hero got in the way. 
 After the first 20% I just wanted it to end, which it did, but unfortunately left the story open to sequels.
Currently I'd rate it 1.5. Maybe it'll get better but the writing is a little slow so far and we spent too much time analyzing heroine's feelings and motivations...

A heroine with a power-mad father, absent mother, and a past rape that tore her budding-but-true-love romance apart is enough drama for even the most demanding hanky-loving audience. Too bad, then, that Pettersson felt the need to pour still more on with adjective-laden, emotionally wrought hyperbole and descriptions as empty as they are florid. Add that the author manipulates her heroine to hesitate when she clearly shouldn't, apparently so that her loved-ones can suffer still more and you have a story I just can't credit even before you get to the hoky zodiac superpowers. 
 And somebody please inform Pettersson that killing someone with superpowers who has threatened to kill you and everyone you love at his earliest opportunity, after a long battle in which he actually *has* killed someone you love, doesn't constitute "killing in cold blood" even if he is unarmed at that particular instant.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Vicki Pettersson brings fresh ideas, deep psychology and Las Vegas's underbelly in this flashy first volume in the Signs of the Zodiac series. 
 Since her almost-deadly assault about nine years ago, Joanna Archer has been tough and hard, with an empty facade that keeps even her nearest and dearest away. A blind date ends in violence and death, and Jo's not just an innocent bystander. Turning twenty-five has awakened powers that have made her a target of the warring Zodiac factions, Light and Shadow. With a parent from each faction, Jo could go either way, and though she chooses to align with the Light, a traitor walks among the troop and exposes them all to the Shadow agents...including Jo's father. 
 Having become disenchanted with the genre of late, Vicki Pettersson's debut enlivened my passion with much needed originality (the Tulpa!), vibrant settings and intriguing psychology in a thrilling tome her urban fantasy peers can only dream of writing. Those fed up with vampires, psychics, witches, fae and whatnot will rejoice that superheroes take the stage here. Though the Australian publisher is marketing it towards fans of the TV series Heroes, the Signs of the Zodiac books seem more appealing than the show could ever be. (I don't watch Heroes, and don't intend to.) 
 At the start of the book, the writing itself makes me truly appreciate this. The flashy turns of phrase and such lessen as the action progresses, but science enforces the magic, there's deep character development, and it all comes together in a ripping yarn. 
 But what stands out is this could've been much worse, had the author and editor not been so cluey. With romance featuring early on, I feared this could've been about Jo and Ben Traina trying to have a relationship throughout all the life-and-death. But thankfully Vicki Pettersson and Diana Gill realised that for Jo to fully find herself she had to be alone. How many books in the genre would do that nowadays? 
 I highly recommend The Scent of Shadows, and I'm already onto Book 2. This is one series thriller fans should not miss.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This is getting three stars from me because I really liked most of the book and I love the tortured love interest. I'm tempted to read book 2 just for him, however, I doubt if I will because the end of the book just fell apart. The heroine has taken over her sister's identity after an attack which killed her sister but was aimed at her. The villain, who is head honcho of the paranormal bad guys and is also her father, wants her dead. He doesn't know he's her father but he does know he lived with her mother before she was born (and apparently he can't count to 9 and figure out he's her father). Her mother is one of the paranormal good guys who had infiltrated the bad guys. So at the end the heroine reveals to daddy dearest that she's half good and half bad (and thus is the object of a prophecy that makes her so dangerous.) Now really, he can't figure out who she is? Or who she's masquerading as? I can't stand when the villain is that stupid.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I loved this book at the start. A third of the way through I almost went out and bought the rest of the series. Now I'm glad I waited. An interesting premise, decent writing and good battles are ruined by the "bibmo transition" and waaay too much chat about heels and fashion. Maybe it's just my bad luck, but this is the THIRD book I've read in the past 6 months where a normal woman wakes up to find herself transformed into Barbie. Massive boobs, tiny waist, long flowing hair. If you want to write about Barbie then why not have one of these women just go for surgery? The involuntary "beautification" process is bad enough, but then these books invariably force the subject to dress like a hooker. Fighting and running in heels and miniskirts. I promised that I'd never again read one of these and here I was, fooled again. 
 And to make it worse she's transformed into her SISTER. The dead sister that she watched being terrorized, tortured with a knife, then flung out a penthouse window. I almost couldn't keep reading. 
 But the story kept me plugging along. I blew through more than half the book in a weekend and then it's taken me a week to drag through the rest of it. Every time she mentioned a designer or heel size I put it down. And it got worse as the book continued. When the heroes are in their sanctuary, after waht was supposed to be a training session, two of the women's "heels clicked as they went down the hall". OK, we've been told why our heroine is wearing heels. Why is the other fighter in heels? What kind of mortal danger are they in where they don't mind sounding like a machine gun as they walk? 
 And WHAT is the author's hangup with Chandra? I never did get a decent physical description, just that she "looks like a man", a "hermaphrodite", and the star of the book calls Chandra "She-Man" during an argument. WTH is that about? Am I reading a PR or the screenplay for "Mean Girls"? First we get the bimbo makeover, then she derides an unattractive female at every opportunity. Seems like someone has issues. 
 My favorite mess was the catsuit stuff towards the end. "Cotton / lycra" blend. Oh, thanks for filling me in! Just the info I needed to know as they're preparing for a suicide mission. Then when she drops Hunter and sticks one of his guns in the waistband. Lycra Catsuits have waistbands?? And the whole pile of stuff she lugs: her mini crossbow, his 2 guns, baton, and a 12 foot whip with barbs. And the WHIP went into her POCKET?? LOL. Who knew they made lowcut lycra catsuits with cargo pockets? 
 Lastly I didn't get the feeling that she's even been a comic book fan. The comic store folks were too superficial and were all stereotypes. As a lifelong SciFi/Fantasy fan and a veteran of dozens of conventions, I didn't appreciate the attitude. Or any of the attitudes: towards the comic folks, towards ugly women, and frankly towards sisters. I'd slaughter anyone that made me over into my dead sister. How could someone function under those circumstances? 
 Anyway. Interesting story. Good battles and writing. But too many off notes to make this an enjoyable read. I'm going to re-read a Showalter or Kresley Cole to clear my head.

I got this as a Kindle freebie and I was grinding along, hoping for something to click, perturbed that in a book where a more-or-less traditional super-hero trope was supposed to underlie the magic neither the author or her editor appeared to have ever actually held a comic book in their hands but could describe Louboutin stilettos down to their seaming. sample_reviews.review_text: Steampunk porno Love it.

I like most things Steampunk and I really like Katie MacAlister's Aisling Grey series. So when I saw that she had written a Steampunk romance I picked it up. 
 Let's start with the the book's classification - Paranormal Romance. There were no werewolves, vampires, or even ghosts in this story. Since when is being thrown into an alternate universe paranormal? How anyone can consider this novel a paranormal romance is beyond me. There are plenty of novels that take place in alt universes that are not classified as Paranormal. To be honest, I didn't even realize it was supposed to be a Paranormal Romance until I looked at the spine. And to be fair to Signet, I do not know what their definition of Paranormal Romance consists of. Perhaps I am the one that needs to update my definition of Paranormal Romance. 
 Moving on...the POV. I don't have problems reading 1st person narratives. But this one tried my patience to the extreme. The book starts with Jack's perspective which was fine, I have no problem following a male lead through a story. I actually liked Jack in the beginning. Then suddenly the perspective changed to Octavia's. It was jarring and not too pleasant. The change would have worked in third person I think, in the very least it wouldn't have been as jarring. I lost track of the the number of times I had to stop and think - Who is this "I" am reading? 
 The POV took a lot away from the characters and the story as well. I really liked Jack in the first chapters before the "accident". But the moment he opened his eyes in Octavia's world I felt that I was lied to about Jack's personality and I came to actually despise him. The elements of the story - the accident, the rescue, and even the romance would have all been better served and told in a different POV. 
 I was never given the opportunity to really connect with any of the characters and as I continued to read I found that I really didn't care what happened to either the hero or heroine. And to me that is a very bad sign. 
 All that aside though, I loved the details of Octavia's world. The steamships, the cabs, the disrupters, the clothes. There is even a small lexicon in the back of the book with definitions for terms - that I didn't realize was there until I finished the book and had worked everything out already. Unfortunately those details were the only thing I really liked about the novel. 
 From what I can tell this may turn into a series. I can only hope that subsequent books will be better.
Incidentally, the cover art is gorgeous.
This was a cute book. I loved that it was different. How many steampunk romances are there even out there? It was a great idea, unique and it made it a fun read.

It was hard to connect the two conflicting views. Our heroine was to be a strong fierce woman who defies convention and becomes the first woman to lead a ship.  I also had a problem with the narrative voice, the story was told from both the hero's and heroine point of view. It made it hard for me to connect with the novel Olivia seemed to 'talk' up all the novel.

 Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban is my favourite book in the Harry Potter series. The first time I read it I gave it a ten out of ten; that hasn't changed. I still love everything about this book. 
 This time I listened to the audiobook read by Stephen Fry. The audiobook was 11 hours and 42 minutes of genius. It was a wonderful experience! Stephen Fry brings the characters to life amazingly. I enjoyed every second!

 . 
 My Review of Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets 
 . 
 . 
 . 
 1st read in August 2014 
 /5 (10/10) 
 'Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban' is a novel full of turning points and surprises. Rowling has done it again! This novel is WOW. There is not a sufficient amount of adjectives to describe how this novel makes me feel and how it is to read this novel. 
 The novel is in one aspect very different from the previous novels: the difficulty with understanding the novel and figuring the characters out. The plot has more layers and is more twisted than what it seems on the surface. 
 People who were supposed to be the bad guys turned out to be the good guys. A rat, a dog and a wolf are supposedly just a rat, a dog and a wolf. NOT in this novel. In the Harry Potter universe, a rat is a villain who betrayed and fooled everyone. A dog is an innocent man who the whole world is looking for because he allegedly killed people. And a wolf is a good and kind teacher who once a month turns into a werewolf. 
 Rowling makes me believe in this world. She makes me root for the characters. When I open the novel, I am always happy to return to the Harry Potter universe and leave the Earth, that I know, behind. I grow with the characters and with the experiences they share. I learn from their mistakes. And I am excited when they are. Hogwarts feels surreal yet so real to me. It is a dream I never want to wake up from.

 Oh well. I'm off to my dreams of peace and starlight 
 2nd read in April 2015 
 9.75/10

 "Would you want to live forever," Brimstone had asked Madrigal once, "only to die again and again, in agony?" 
 1st read in November 2014 
 9.0/10 
 'Daughter of Smoke & Bone' is the second story that I have ever read that features angels. The story line is very interesting. It is mysterious and very good. Sometimes there are moments in the novel where the author gives hints about what's going to happen later on. Some events are foreshadowed, and others come as a huge surprise. 
 I love the main character, Karou. She is a very fierce and strong character. I also love the contrast between her normal school life, occupations and friends, and the errands she often has to do. The errands, her company, her past, all of it is very intriguing. 
 It certainly raised a lot of questions. These questions kept building up as new characters and new story arcs were introduced. The novel really became a page turner because of this. I couldn't just stop at the end of a chapter, I needed to know what was going to happen. So I finished the novel quite quickly. 
 The writing was outstanding. The descriptions of the places and people were fantastic. When I was reading the novel, I got lost in the world of seraphim, chimaeras and humans. It was all very palpable. It felt tangible. I could hear the conversations and taste the goulash soup. 
 I really loved the twists in the novel, they were executed amazingly. The novel ends with a cliffhanger, and I haven't got the second novel in the series yet. So I am going to order that one very soon, because I NEED to know what is going to happen next.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Daughter of Smoke and Bone is a magical story about fate, love, and battling for it all. Laini Taylor truly has a magic quality with her words, and was able to weave a story that left me wondering. 
 The beginning was a bit rocky for me, to be honest. I kept reading though, mainly because others had raved so much about this book. After a bit I finally got into the groove of things, and was pulled in. The main character Karou was very interesting, what with her blue hair, crazy battle skills and the fact that she was raised by chimeras. I couldn't help but wonder what the heck was going on with her, and what secrets her psuedo-father Brimstone, the teeth collector, was keeping from her. 
 Then you meet Akiva. An angel who at first is set out to stop Brimstone from his magical secrets. That is, until he meets Karou. Then everything changes. There is something about her that he can't resist. And now he finds he cannot bear to leave her. The reason why... is so much more than he expected. 
 Overall, the story was enchanting. Taylor created a world that was pretty believable, full of mystical creatures, battles of fate, and faithful friends. Many times I literally felt like I was there, in the story instead of reading it. 
 My issue with this read was that about three quarters of the way though, the story suddenly changed. I get why it did, and it does make sense. Still, I felt disoriented and am still unsure how much I do like that choice. Though everything does connect and make sense in the end (which might I add, leaves you with a complete, total cliff-hanger)... I can't say I fully enjoyed the switch up. I loved the story that was told. I really did. But... See? Even now I am all flustered. 
 Daughter of Smoke and Bone was a very enjoyable read. I do look forward to the next book in the series, though I might not be clambering to the bookshelves to get it as fast as I had hoped. I recommend this book to anyone looking for a quick magical outlet from their normal, mundane world.

book_b.title: Stitches
book_b.user_review: A moving memoir presented as a beautiful graphic novel.

sample_reviews.review_text: A beautiful, brilliant book--but so sad it was painful to read.
Wow! Crazy, crazy, crazy! Such disturbing artwork for such a depressing childhood.
Amongst the best graphic novel memoirs that I have ever read. David Small captures a horrific and loveless childhood in an easily digested, beautifully drawn, sparsely worded book.

I read an advanced reading copy of this new graphic memoir (to be released in September) and could hardly put it down. Small details his unhappy childhood, from the lack of affection in his family to mental illness of family members. He had throat cancer while in his teens, a result of x-ray treatments his father subjected him to, but his family never told him of his diagnosis. David left home at the age of sixteen, while still in high school, and found mentors that encouraged his talents. 
 This is a story of success through adversity, and I found David's straightforward honesty very engaging. He is already known for his successful picture books and I'm sure this new graphic memoir will be a hit as well.

This is another one that makes you turn over the book to look at the call number. Really, this is non-fiction? Someone actually grew up in such an unloving, destructive environment and not only turned out OK, but excellent? Shit. 
 David Small had two strikes against him at birth. This book illustrates the best possible outcome of a neglected child. Thank heavens he turned inward and not outward.

I'm probably too tired today to give this book the review it deserves. Nevertheless: graphic novel is the perfect format to present David Small's bildungsroman. He grew up in a household ruled by silence and withholding and he himself was silenced by a throat cancer surgery when he was 15. Small makes evocative use of the panels and page.
The art in this graphic novel is amazing it syncs up so nicely with the horribly tragic family story.

I found the ending to be a little too tidy (the "art gave me a voice" metaphor, although appropriate here, was almost too easy) but the book was tightly written (a common complaint I have with the few graphic novels I've read is that they don't seem well planned or edited) and the art was absolutely amazing. I will definitely be looking forward to his next book.
my first graphic novel - I loved it! It was terribly frightening and sad - just the way i like my books.

Small's autobiographical graphic novel - try saying that ten times fast - ranks up there on my list of the top ten graphic novels of 2009. His style strikes me as a combination of two of the medium's best -- Jules Feiffer and the late, great Will Eisner - as he recounts his childhood under two awkward and distant parents and the titular stitches from his early bout with throat cancer. Although certainly dark and frightening in places, Stitches comes across as Small's way of dealing with his childhood trauma, and the lingering effects of the emotional rift caused by unavailable parents. A dose of melancholy tinged with a ray hope.

Satanism is presented more as a philosophy than a religion and the main line is not to hate yourself for who you are but accept yourself flaws and all. 
 This books doesn't really stand alone as a cult bible. The first parts are mostly dedicated to show the hypocrisy of other religions. I would have assume that a church would have some more sophisticated guidelines about the philosophy it presents without having to go through pointing fingers at others. It mostly goes like this: This is human nature but other religions think it's bad because (generally attached an argument bringing said other religion a financial gain of some sort against followers, or hypocrisy, or stupidity) so you shouldn't listen to them but listen to what you want instead. 
 Personally, I totally see how that works and I totally see the all mess coming out of it if everyone listen. I mean the book is directed to smart people who have already learn to moderate themselves to give into indulgence instead of compulsion and even if the difference is clearly explained, we can see the compulsion in every human being all over. That being said the book also has a list of unacceptable behaviors. 
 I was expecting something more elaborated in term of cult and the only part that had any real interest in that sense was the Keys despite the lack of courses. 
 The other things that rang a bit off were the rituals. First it was said that the ritual should be performed at the time when the person you want to do witchcraft on is asleep and more accurately on the dream part. The example gives something like if the person goes to sleep at 11pm and wake up at 7am, do your ritual in his dream period around 5am. The little problem is that the dream period is usually not at the end of the period of sleep but at the end of every sleep cycle which last about 1hour 20 minutes, for about 20 minutes. 
 The use of the white candle in the ritual to symbolize the right-hand white-light magic hypocrisy also seems totally out of place. Why would anyone want to drag into their ritual something that has nothing to do with the task at hand? I mean yeah, the churches are filled with sinners who are forgiven and do the same sin over and over again as soon as they are out of the church, and the church doesn't care about anyone's well being but only create a vision of impossible perfection to be achieve and white-light magician call on powers they protect themselves from. They are all hypocrite. I get that, the End, get over it, you don't need to keep thinking about it all the time, especially during a ritual when you have to concentrate your energy on your desired out come. 
 Most of the things used in the ritual are just a different version of what is used during mass and other cult's ritual but is supposed to be more accurate and more true to nature. Personally I'm not entirely convinced. 
 There is also a huge part dealing with sex and acceptable sexual behavior. Basically do whatever you want as long as you do it between consenting adults which is totally how it should be. However there is a drag on and sex comes back is a lot of example and I can see why a lot of people associate satanism with depravation even if it's not meant to be. The book also treat sex magic and rituals to attract lust sex partners which to me seem to be contradictory with the consenting adults part. 
 The other problem I have with this book is that all there is to it is claims and no practical research. The Author has an opinion about other religions from his own observation but there is no real proof that his point of view can change something for the better of the human race. Would indulgence really make someone happy? I'm not sure to what extend. The narrative was also more turned toward the dismissal of the other religion system than toward the real progress given but satanism. 
 It was a good read and I think a lot more people should read this book and learn more about satanism. I don't like to see comments about certain topics from people who don't have a clue what they are talking about.

 The only reason I gave it an extra star is because it's so British AND I can't bring myself to give any Pride & Prejudice retelling 1 star. I'm glad so many people love these books & movies, but I'm just not a fan.
