I know two stars sounds harsh, but "it was okay" is just how I felt about this book. It was fine. Mildly entertaining, good pacing, and all ends happily. Plus, I read it in two days, which is exactly what I was looking for. That's one nice thing about chick-lit--you always know what you're getting. 
 So, a few thoughts: I didn't really get the whole diary thing. It didn't make sense as a real diary, because obviously no one is pausing in the middle of a dinner party disaster to make regular commentary about it in their diary. But, if it was meant to be read as her little internal monologue (more likely), only spoken to herself in "diary" form, then summarizations and updates that took place after the fact didn't really make sense. I know, pointless nitpicking, but I just couldn't get a handle on the form. 
 As far as content goes, I've read worse, but I don't think the story makes up for the questionable material, for those of you who are worried about that kind of thing. 
 Also, I found it amusing that Bridget was able to spell her faults out for us so clearly (recognizing that she's not a good friend because her bff's possible death sent her into fantasies about what she might wear to the funeral?) I just don't think anyone is that self-aware. For you die-hard fans of this book, I'm not talking about the New Year's Resolution type faults (I think pretty much everyone is THAT kind of self aware) I'm talking about the deeper things that we ignore about ourselves, and would refuse to see even when pointed out. 
 I was surprised at how closely the plot to this book followed Pride and Prejudice. Seriously, where would chick-lit be these days without Jane Austen? I hope she appreciates her contribution. 
 Anyway, not blindingly hilarious, or especially riveting, but a fun, easy read.

I'm still not really sure how I feel about this book... I guess confused...? I found myself wishing the book would just GET TO THE POINT, but it never did. It's not really a novel, but a compilation of complaints, bad behavior, and TERRIBLE characters. Why, why, WHY (hehe...ug) was EVERY SINGLE CHARACTER SO ANNOYING?!? The only likable character was Mark Darcy, and to my complete disappointment he was BARELY in the book. Why is this book such a hit? 
 I tried so hard to like this book. I was immediately turned off by the daily recordings and constant complaining, but I TRIED to convince myself that it was relatable because we're all quirky and a little crazy, right? 
 No. Just, no. 
 Seriously, Bridget is the WORST friend, and she has ZERO self control. I eat much healthier than most people, but I'm certainly not perfect, and I've had high calorie days on occasion. But SERIOUSLY, 5000 calories? 30 cigarettes? 22 smoothies?!? This is girl is BANANAS, but I'm sure the only time she's ever had a banana is if one accidentally made it into her smoothie. 
 I WILL give props where props are due, though. I chose to listen to the audio book, and thank goodness I did, because if I had tried reading the book there's no WAY I would have made it past the first page. I'd heard that the audio book was exceptional, and I was blown away by the skill and artistry that went into giving Bridget and her huge band of insane friends each their own voices and personalities. 
 I wish that I had only watched the movie, which was much sweeter and more fun than the book (also, only the FIRST movie). I found Bridget less crazy in the movie, and the men were much more present, as well as more charming. 
 Lastly, there ARE pronouns in MY diary, because I'm not a crazy person! And freaking "v.g." made me lose my mind... 
 *sigh* I think chick-lit is just not for me.

reference_books.title: Locke & Key, Vol. 1: Welcome to Lovecraft
reference_books.review_text:
"That was an admiring "fuck," not a "fuck you" fuck." 
 After the murder of their father, the rest of the Locke family moves to their summer house called the Lovecraft. While in this old house, some members of the family soon discover strange, mystical forces that make them question their sanity. Keys that can alter reality and a mysterious woman at the bottom of a well. And then there's the murderer. He's a man on a mission and somehow the Locke family is stuck right in the middle of it. Who will manage to escape their fates and who will die very miserable deaths? 
 Read this book. Then you'll find out. 
 All in all, it was amazing. The art here is so unique and incredible, I couldn't tear my eyes away from this graphic novel. And just like the art, the storyline was next level creative and intriguing. The whole concept about keys that can open different doors to make your spirit leave your body or to change your sex or to transport you anywhere is ingenious. I loved how interesting, relatable and sometimes amusing the characters were, especially when they were describing their social issues and mental well-beings. It was fantastic because the teenagers in this book didn't have perfect emotional states (relatable!). Yes, their dad just got murdered, but their reactions were very appropriate and I just felt like their reactions were very similar to what a real person's would possibly be if they had also witnessed a tragic event. 
 I recommend this graphic novel to lovers of fantasy and horror and keys. 4.75

reference_books.title: Dark Star (Dark Star, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Actually, I had really high expectations for this book (which might be why my rating is so low). The MC was boring and one-dimensional as were all the other characters. It just didn't "pull" me in like I wanted it to, and half way through, I realized that I was just reading it because I didn't really like giving up in the middle of books. Furthermore, the writing wasn't that impressive and gave me a bit of a "thrown together" feeling. The romance was also really forced -- Leon and Audrey randomly became an item at the end when throughout the entire book, they didn't even seem to like each other at all! It just confused me so much . To me, the MC didn't seem to have a big part in all the turmoil, even an unnamed person had more importance than her. From the back of the book, I got the feeling that the MC would be a super important and interesting person, but it was the complete opposite. The blurb from the book was totally misleading. I could probably go on and on and on about how disappointing Dark Star was, but basically, what I'm trying to say is that I wanted to throw it at a wall every step of the way.

reference_books.title: Siren (Siren, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Although I liked the general idea behind the siren concept, I think it wasn't incorporated into the story correctly and enough. 
 When I saw the cover of this book and read the summary, I thought it would be full of adventure, mystery, and, of course, sirens. However, I was seriously disappointed when I didn't even find out about the sirens until the last third of the book and even then it didn't seem thought out well. The ideas were there, but were jumbled up in an order that didn't make any sense. A huge chunk of the first half of the book was completely unrelated and unnecessary. 
 The characters, too, they were all uninteresting, dull, and predictable. At the beginning of the book, they weren't introduced well enough, and later, when more characters appear, they weren't fully explained. I had no idea what was going on more than half the time, and it really irritated me. 
 Another thing that really annoyed me was the fact that I had so many questions at the end of the book that were unanswered and unacknowledged. It felt as if the author didn't even consider the reader and how little we were left with. Such incompleteness made me think the author just gave up or didn't revise or something. 
 The only reason why it isn't a one star is because Simon is pretty decent and almost anything mermaids is always on my to-read list. However, I would still really not recommend this book.

reference_books.title: Ignite Me (Shatter Me, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
Dang. Tahereh Mafi has just blown my mind, and I think this is my new favorite trilogy. I loved Ignite Me, and I have to admit that after reading this, I am officially and forever Team Warner. 
 Honestly, throughout this entire novel, I just had this very strong urge to smack Adam in the face. Repeatedly. With a chair. Made of steel. He freaking pissed me off to the point of no return. 
 I really liked the character development that Tahereh Mafi incorporated. Juliette was totally boss in this book with the way she thought she could take over the entire country. It was a surprise when Juliette started to fall hard for Warner though because I honestly believed she and Adam were maybe going to get though it in the beginning. But I really liked the revelations she had about her and Adam's relationship and how she chose to get over her depressed-and-crying-and-emotional-all-the-time self. Warner become one of my favorite characters when he would just give up anything to make Juliette happy. It was beautiful. 
 Ignite Me definitely kept me more interested and on the edge of my seat than Shatter Me and Unravel Me. The plot line was great and I love that Tehereh Mafi didn't put too many cliffhangers! 
 Definitely 5 star worthy!!!

Please visit my blog at http://geobobspinelli.blogspot.com 
 OVERALL RATING: 4.5/5 
 My thoughts: 
 While I hate chick flicks, I adore Disney movies. And this book is definitely Disney material. It's like the Little Mermaid meets the Ugly Truth (if you haven't seen it, you should watch it). 
 Lily has been "in love" - and I quote because it's really more of obsession - with Brody for 3 years. They have a passing conversation here and there but for the most part he doesn't really notice her. Her arrogant neighbor, Quince, decides to help her to ask Brody to the dance and win his heart. But things don't go quite as she planned. I can't say what exactly without giving spoilers. But it's obvious from the start that Quince has a thing for Lily - he teases her and makes her life miserable (as she calls it). 
 Lily's infatuation with Brody reminds me of a crush I had in high school (for 3 years as well, coincidentally), so I really understand her position. But as the story progresses, she starts to get on my nerves a little because yes, she has a thing for Brody, but if she could just open her eyes she'd see what was right in front of her (Quince). Then, toward the end, the annoyance develops into me just wanting to smack the crap out of her. Um, hello? How can you be so blind? Poor guy. Hey Quince, forget about Lily because you won me over. 
 This book is totally unique in so many ways that it had me from the first page - hook, line, and sinker (hee hee!). Lily uses a lot of sea terms in her dialogue that really add to the story - terms such as "blowfish" for jerk, "carp" instead of crap, "damselfish" instead of damn, and "speak of the devilfish." Witty, right? 
 I don't want to say much more because of giving an unknown piece of the plot away, but I adored this book. A big factor of that is because she starts out hating Quince and slowly warms up to him. Like I've mentioned, I love that sort of thing. Is there a word for it? If not, there needs to be! Like stated in the book, "some people find beauty in chaos." 
 OVERALL ASSESSMENT 
 Plot: 5/5 
 Not something you read everyday! 
 Writing Style: 4/5 
 Characters: 4/5 
 The characters were realistic and made me feel like I was right in the story with them. 
 Pace: 4.5/5 
 Aside from a small bit at the beginning, I was totally hooked. 
 Cover: 4.5/5 
 This cover is beautiful to me because I love bright colors. The .5 docked is because her lipstick isn't on her lower lip all the way and it annoys me.

I don't know why authors think I want to hang out with a main character who is shallow, self-centered, abusive. This is supposedly a lighthearted YA Paranormal romance. It has a Mid-grade writing style, however, which makes it feel disjointed. Either way, it's aimed at readers from 11-16 which means that repetitive scenes of the heroine hitting people, throwing things at people and whining are not only obnoxious but also really bad examples of interpersonal conduct. The author wants to make Lily seem like a charming spitfire, I presume. Instead she comes off as a cantankerous brat. 
 The main reason I read books about mermaids is for the world-building. Here it was so sloppy, and consisted mostly of Lily using bad water-world puns and idioms. There is no explanation for why magical creatures would speak English. 
 At one point Lily says they can't take their clothes down to the kingdom. When they get to the kingdom 3 pages later her father greets her while wearing a coat. That right there should give you an idea of why I'm unimpressed with this book.

I'd never heard of this book when I went on Kobo to buy a certain YA book. After I bought it, I went back to the YA section and started skimming through the titles. I came across Forgive My Fins and immediately loved the cover. After reading the book blurb, I bought it. 
 Seriously, this is the best YA book I've read this year and in my top five books that I've read in 2010. 
 During the entire book, I felt the emotional intensity of Lily's situation, especially in the second half. Forgive My Fins is filled with engaging characters and captivating descriptions of Lily's home, Thalassinia. 
 When I thought I knew what was going to happen next, the plot took an unpredictable twist, not just once, but several times. I began to wonder if the ending I wanted would happen. I'm not going to spoil it for anyone though, but I'll just say I cried several times while reading the last few chapters. 
 Tera Lynn Childs also left the ending open for the next in the series, Fins Are Forever, and I plan on reading it as soon as it comes out.

Forgive my Fins is a painfully predictable novel, in which I guessed the plotline in less than 5 pages. It was an extremely fast read, in which nothing even had a bit of depth. Not even the main characters. 
 It's about a half-human/half-mermaid who lives on land and accidently gets "bonded" to the so-called obnoxious, arrogant boy next door who, SURPRISE, turns out to be her true love. A very common romance concept often daily applied to YA books. 
 Now straight onto the painfully unbearable characters: 
 Lily 
 Lily was an annoying heroine. She was just plain shallow and even though she's sixteen years old, still calls her father "Daddy", which most teenagers incidentally do not do in real life. Typically, she has a crush on a surfer boy, coincidentally the most popular boy in school, whom she has no chance of ever getting together because we're talking about high school here. Can it be more cliche? 
 Quince 
 Quince was frustrating as well,he never ever saw what Lily for she was for- an over-protected, bratty Daddy's princess who hurt him daily. Instead he just fell for her, goodness knows why, and daydreamed about her for THREE years. 
 Some of the characters were stereotypes stripped plain from society. Courtney for example, is the typical jealous, ex-girlfriend envious of the heroine. Brody- the typical, self-centered hottie who's the most popular boy. Dosinia- the spiteful, jealous cousin who despises the heroine. Very original. 
 Oh, and of course the puns. Oh my god, how many puns can you insert into a novel. It reached the point of inducing vomit-worthy feelings in me. All that fishy terminology was making my head ache. Don't mistake me, I have an obssessive love for puns, but there is a fine line between overusing the puns and rocking them. 
 All in all, I think this book could have used more angst, doesn't hurt you know, and the characters should have had a bit more depth. Not act like cardboard cut-outs.

2.7 stars I almost liked this book. . . . Almost. 
 This book had a lot of potential and there were parts I liked but I would never read it again and I have no desire to read any other books in the series. I really liked the concept of the curse and the difficulty to undo what had been done the middle of this story was really good and I got through it quickly. the problem is in the beginning I won't go into to much detail but you read the synopsis of what the book is about then you start reading and it takes forever to get to it. I was about 35% in before the real story started. it took me a long time to get through the book just because the beginning was so slow. There were also some very annoying moments near the end when the curse is broken and Sorcha still doesn't speak when she could and should. but maybe that's just me the idea that she stands there and let's her brothers speak for her and make choices about her life is beyond frustrating. oh well I don't regret reading this book but I'm happy to move on to something new. 
 One other thing there were a lot of major typos I usually don't find a lot of typos in books I read but it seems like whoever was proofreading this book just didn't finish it. All the typos I found were near the end and I don't know what to say about that.

The story is set in Britain and Ireland before the time of Christianity. The framework for Daughter of The Forest is a Germanic tale, The Six Swans, a wonderful story from the collection of the Grimm Brothers. Daughter of the Forest is a beautiful and tearful tale, and I find myself crying in many parts of the story. 
 Sorcha (pronounced: Sor-ra) is the youngest child and the only daughter of Lord Colum of Sevenwaters. After her mother's death, Sorcha and her six elder brothers live freely. Quiet abandoned by her father, the seven siblings become so dependent on each other. Together they learn the secrets about their forest and the mythic tale which surrounded it. 
 One day, their father comes and tells them that he brings a new mother for them. Lady Oonagh is a beautiful woman with proper manners, but all the siblings know that she is dangerous. She is not even human. The seven siblings try to destroy her dark power using the forest power, but Lady Oonagh knows what they try to do and catches them. Sorcha is able to escape, but her six brothers must suffer Lady Oonagh's curse. She turns them into six swans, and the only time they return to their true shape is on the day of midsummer and midwinter. 
 Sorcha, with help from mythical creature of the forest, knows that there is a way to break the spell. She has to sew six shirts, one for each brother. The shirts must be made from a thorn bush, and she has to suffer the thorns cutting through her hands while she sews the shirts. She must tell nobody about her brother's spell, and she has to sacrifice her voice until the curse is lifted. If she says even one word before the curse is undone, then her brothers will remain swans forever. 
 I find the story is really beautiful, and there are times I find myself drawn deeply into the story. The meeting of Sorcha with a guy from her enemy land plays a great part of the story. Red, the red-haired man who saves her when she is almost drowned, happens to be one of the leaders from her enemy land, Britain. The story of Sorcha and Red is really fun to read. I love most about the way Red protects Sorcha and understands her even though Sorcha can't say anything at all. 
 Daughter of the Forest is a really good book and I really recommend it, especially for people who loves remake of fairy tales. Sorcha is a wonderful heroine and she has my sympathy. I admire her dedication and love to her family and her land. Red is a suitable hero to balance Sorcha with his strength and his patience. In short, a must-read book! 
 Finally I fell asleep, still staring into the candle flame, curled up by small Alys for warmth, with my brothers' names sounding over and over in my head, as if by saying them I could keep them alive a little longer, just a little. Just long enough.

Cover Beauty Score: 5 out of 10 
 Goodreads Score: 4 out of 5 
 Plot Blurb: Sorcha is a young girl who lives in medieval Ireland, during a time when magic and the Fae Folk are still alive and well for the people of Erin. As the seventh daughter of a seventh son, she has always felt a disappointment, although she finds solace in her connection with the spirits of the earth and in her talents as a healer. When her father remarries a mysterious and evil woman, Sorcha and her six brothers are targeted by the woman and she turns all six brothers into swans. Sorcha is told by the Fae that in order to break this curse, she must complete seemingly impossible tasks and travel a path that will be the most difficult of them all. 
 My Reaction: This book, though. I can't even begin to describe the emotional roller coaster of this thing. I read this book because I thought it was in the YA category, although as I began to read I realized this was really a more classical fantasy than anything else. Despite Sorcha's initial age of 14, the book spans across 4-5 years so she the reader is able to see her mature and grow. 
 Speaking of growth, let's talk about the character development in this one. Out of this world. There is not a character who does not alter irrevocably throughout this tale. Marillier does an excellent job of plotting out the ways her characters will change on their journeys, particularly Sorcha. Once sheltered and naive, she is forced out of her comfort zone in the worst way imaginable and given some of the most horrendous hurdles to cross. My heart would break for her with each new challenge she faced. As she was given the task of remaining mute until her other tasks were complete, there were parts where as the reader I felt as though I should be just as silent. Her struggles transferred to me, as though I could help her somehow from my end. 
 That, my friends, is good writing. 
 And in regards to the writing as a whole, it was excellently done. Marillier obviously knows what she's doing with her words, weaving a tale that felt as reverent as the original Grimm stories. The writing flowed well with great dialogue, although due to the nature of Sorcha's task, there was understandably a lot of internal monologue. The nature of classic fantasy is that the story is long and in depth, which at times I found difficult to get through. The suspense was too much for me to remain patient enough to read a four page description of something. It was torture! 
 But should we touch on the love triangle here? We all know I despise love triangles... I was not a big fan of the one here, honestly. I didn't see it coming, and once our second hero Red was introduced, I knew he had to be the true choice for Sorcha. Simon would have been good for her, before her trials, but they grew in ways that took them away from their path together. This part was, perhaps, the most difficult for me. I did not feel as though Simon was given enough of a story - enough closure. 
 So we come to the part where I say this was a great book. However, upon finishing it I am reminded why I stay away from traditional fantasy. I read books to live in worlds that I would enjoy living in. The world in which Sorcha inhabits was dark and difficult and devoid of much laughter. I appreciate her journey and am still in awe of the tribulations she was forced to face, but I would not want to share this journey with her. Ever. 
 And so I will move on to something happier with my next book choice. Preferably something with less death. And heartache. And general emo-ness.

reference_books.title: The Last Chinese Chef
reference_books.review_text: A disappointment. The writing about the Chinese food is very interesting, but I just didn't buy into the story. There's very little character development into the writer, the love story is predictable, and there are some plot issues that really seem unresolved. This book felt really unfinished to me. And as someone who has actually worked as a professional cook and food writer, I find it extremely difficult to believe that Maggie spent her life writing about food and couldn't boil water. . . that's strange. I'm not saying every food writer has to go to culinary school but they should at least have picked up the basics. And I also didn't believe that Sam had all this time to talk to Maggie while he was cooking and preparing for one of the most important dinners of his life. Maybe I'm just too nitpicky.

book_a.user_review:
** spoiler alert ** 
 Started out great, got really over the top, the ending is pretty ridiculous. I really enjoyed all the medical/hospital aspects -- could have done away with the hitman plot altogether, and it would have been really interesting. Am I really supposed to believe this guy became a mafia hitman by killing four Russian mobsters singlehandedly at the age of 16???? And then became a doctor? Riiiiight. I'm getting a little tired of superhuman protagonists. After the shark tank, things got really bizarre, but the ending was just waaay over the top. 
 However, this didn't stop me from the reading the entire book in one night, and it is laugh-out-loud funny in parts. Also made me very scared of EVER going to a hospital! 
 I do wonder how this author had time to write a book -- and whether any of his colleagues will ever speak to him again.

sample_reviews.review_text: I found this book to be very odd. The use of footnotes to give more info irritates and I don't get why people write this way. I did like the main character, but the story was confusing with the flipping back and forth, sometimes it took a little bit to figure out if you were in the past or the present. I felt very let down with the ending. I want to know what more happened to this man.

Our hero is a resident at a scarily bad hospital in Manhattan, who turns out to have been a mob hitman before entering witness protection. I don't know which sections were more revolting: the hospital or the mob violence. 
 Crazy, darkly funny, and fairly un-put-downable. It starts out fast, and just keeps accelerating. Very violent, pretty earthy, but I thought it was great.
A great, fun read!
Boring at the beginning, interesting in the middle, boring again.

Another orignial writer with a fresh view of the world. The story was intriguing enough by itself and the 1st person narration gave it the flavor of our ex-mafia-hitman-turned-doctor, with intelligent yet tough commentaries throughout. The first page captured my funny bone right away and set the mood: 
 So I'm on my way to work and I stop to watch a pigeon fight a rat in the snow, and some fuckhead tries to mug me! Naturally there's a gun. He comes up behind me and sticks it into the base of my skull. It's cold and it actually feels sort of good, in an acu-pressure kind of way. "Take it easy, Doc," he says. 
 Which explains that, at least. Even at five in the morning, I'm not the kind of guy you mug. I look like an Easter Island scuplture of a longshoreman. But the fuckhead can see the blue scrub pants under my overcat and the ventilated green plastic clogs, so he thinks I've got drugs and money on me. And maybe that I've taken some kind of oath not to kick his fuckhead ass for trying to mug me.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Why did I finish this book? I hated it within the first two paragraphs (who says f***head that much?!). The main character did remind me a bit of Shadow from American Gods...for some reason, I see them as the same person. I don't know why. 
 Back to this book: Peter Brown is supposed to be a doctor in a NYC hospital. As you read, you discover that he's part of the Witness Protection Program because the mob is after him. The story jumps back and forth between his past and present...and I just kept losing interest. The only part I liked was about his girlfriend Magdalena, but he ruined that too. Then at the end when he cuts open his own leg and breaks his bone off...whatever! Not believable...I don't care if someone really can do that, only crazy people would try it!

A friend of mine recommended this boo (with much enthusiasm( back in 2010 and I was so excited to read. I have to say I was disappointed. Waaay too many footnotes, and a very simplistic parallel plot line. I thought the scene where he deploys kung-fu moves was very unoriginal. I give it one star for the one intersting scene in the whole book: where Bazell explained why and how the Mafia got its start in Sicily.
Pulp fun.FUN.

As funny as visiting a loved one in the hospital. As plausible as a generous insurance company. As unpredictable as the Indy 500. As outrageously cutting-edge as 
 Family Circus 
 . 
 People write and read books like this (meaning, containing heavy doses of sex, violence, and shallow opinion) thinking that it, and they, the writer and reader, are being outrageous and defying societal norms. Wanna really be outrageous and defy etc.? Try writing or reading something that is both actually funny AND features at least some characters who are one or more of the following: sincerely religious, gentle, and moral, i.e., resembling at least some people the real world. Boring? Too hard for you? Publishers don't print stuff like that? Worried that your so-called friends will think you are not sophisticated enough? 
 Yes, you're right. Why bother? This book got optioned as a movie vehicle for Leonardo DiCaprio. If that isn't success, what is? So what if your book does its little part to further metastasize the cancer of crudity, cynicism, and paranoia in the world. It probably doesn't make any difference. Besides, you can always live in a gated community with your new-found wealth. 
 If you listen to this book on a seven-hour audio download from Audible, it's not as big of a waste of time, because at least you can drive, exercise, etc., at the same time.

This book is the very definition of "a wild ride." It's totally outrageous (in a good way... most of the time), ridiculous, and very much a roller-coaster ride. It's a very quick, and very entertaining read. The gist of it is that this doctor runs into a patient that he knows... from his past days in the mafia. The mafia guy has cancer, and threatens the doctor with snitching if he doesn't cure the cancer. Thus begins the wild plot, involving the hospital, the curing attempts, the doctor being injected with awful things more than once (this is part of the outrageousness of the plot), and much about the doctor's sordid mafia past. It's ridiculous but very tongue-in-cheek. 
 Caveat: if you are offended by the f-bomb, do not read! It appears in the first sentence and in pretty much every sentence thereafter. I don't mind this but some others do. In this book though, it made perfect sense.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Read it, again. It's that good. 
 **Original review posted here. 
 My Review: 
 I love this book, and keep coming back to read it again and again. Everything about it screams perfection and excellence. 
 Giffin is such a creative writer and the humor and the dialogue is so spot on that you'll read Something Borrowed in no time at all and be begging for more. You want more? Well lucky for you, there is Something Blue, book # 2, and if you're up for it you can re-live Something Borrowed in the form of a movie! And trust me, while the movie is, well you know, an adaptation of the book, it's still totally worth the watch. 
 Something Borrowed is best read on a beach during summer or on vacation. Or curled up under a blanket on a cold winters evening. While the book focuses on the terrible acts of infidelity, you'll laugh, cry and picks sides. It's an easy book to fly through and you'll be glad you did. Rachel, Darcy, Dex and Ethan are characters that you can easily relate to some way or another and you'll find yourself picking them out in your own group of friends. 
 I can't say enough good things about Something Borrowed, and after reading this for the first time ages ago, Emily Giffin has become one of my favourite authors. Her chick-lit is a blast to read!
I found this book kind of boring, a bit silly, and completely unrealistic. Oh, and totally predictable.

This was fairly well-written as chick-lit goes (proven through dog-eared pages of underlined "difficult" words that apparently the book-swapper before me needed to look up). However, I could not get behind this story at all. I mean, I do realize that Shopaholic is even more ridiculous, but it knows it is being ridiculous. At least that character does all of her crazy sh*t out of good intentions. These people just suck. I'm sorry, but there is no "nuance" to the choices they made. They suck. Darcy sucked, Dex sucked, and Rachel sucked and also was pathetic (never should have gotten herself into that situation in the first place). I don't care if Darcy is a horrible girlfriend, friend, or person. They all made terrible choices, and I was annoyed almost the whole time. 
 I already bought Something Blue b/c I thought I might want to go straight into it, but I definitely don't. Made I'll read it eventually, when I'm no longer as annoyed! 
 I like easy reading for the summer, but I think I may be done w/chick lit for awhile. It just seems like such a waste when there are so many really good books out there and I'll never get to them all.
Waste of time. The main character is likable, but that's about all this book has going for it. You truly root for Rachel, but you just end up being disappointed.

Yikes. What can I say? I won this book through one of the goodreads contests. The blurb looked ok and I'd heard a million people talking about it so I registered to see if I'd win it. Surprisingly I did. I received it right before I left for Africa so it was one of the books I took with me. 
 The one good thing I can say about it is that it was a fast read. The rest of the things I have to say are not as good. I could tell the book was set up so that I would be on Rachel's side and through a series of rationalizations think it was ok that she was sleeping with her best friend's fiancee. Well, I never made the leap. No matter the circumstances, I think cheating is cheating and it is always wrong. So that was issue number one I had with the book. Issue number two is that the entire story was grossly anti-feminist. It took all the strength I had to plow through the story. All the waxing and waning and moping around about stereotypical love was nearly more than I could bear. I really wanted to just reach through the pages and slap Rachel silly. 
 I would not recommend this to any of my friends, mostly because I think most of them would feel the same way. If you are in to romance novels and think that cheating is ok under certain circumstances than go right ahead and knock yourself out.

Typically, I am not into chick-lit. But, when I entered to win this book (and win it, I did), I decided I was ready for something outside of my norm. As a former law student and a thirty something (and typical goody-two-shoes as I've been called), I thought HMMMM...... 
 I actually liked the book, though I wondered how I was feeling sympathetic for the Rachel when she was (essentially) stabbing her friend, Darcy, in the back by sleeping with her friend's fiance (Dex). Her unfaithfulness to her friend didn't stop there, she found she was drawn to Dex rather than walking away. I give kudos to the author for creating such true, conflicting emotion to Rachel and allowing us (the reader) to follow her as she deals with her guilt and her true feelings for her friend, Darcy, and for Dex. 
 I would recommend this book to a friend.

I find this book uninteresting. The event (early in the book) upon which the plot is based was rather uninteresting, which doesn't bode well for the rest of the book. So - I am not going to finish it. Also, I don't understand why the main character Rachel is even friends with her best friend Darcy - which provides the basis for the conflict. I think more could have been given to provide for the foundation of this relationship that is the crux of the plot.

rachel i have some advice fo you - if you stop whining maybe...just maybe you'll find a man. nobody likes a whiner. no one. i'm on page 8 or something and i just wanna grab this chick by her shoulders and shake some common sense into her. ugh. this book is truly a waste of paper.

Oh boy, where to begin? Why do I subject myself to these types of books? Why do women read these? Why doesn't it stop me from reading more? And how has this book gotten a 3.69 rating? So many questions...yet, no answers... 
 But, I can tell you what I hated about this book. I should not be wasting time and effort in writing a review, but I have to because I'm sick of reading books that have a smart (...typically illustrated by a stereotypical intellectual job, in this case, lawyer), yet poor self-esteem type of girl. It's normal to have insecurities, but when it's blatantly explicit throughout the book, it gets old real fast. With lines like "...wanting to please him, give him the right answer" or "I fall asleep hating myself" and so many more, it perpetuates the notion that "girl is dependent on man." 
 Most chick-lit books are mindless, but are pretty fun to read, especially when you just want to escape or read something that doesn't involve vampires. This book had no redeeming qualities. The plot, writing, characters, relationships, story, and denouement - these were just a few of the features I really despised. The book is about two best friends, one of which is pushy and the other is a push-over. The push-over has an affair with the pushy's fiancee and drama ensues! The author tries to make this a moral dilemma, while also trying to make the readers feel sympathetic for the push-over as well as the man who is cheating on his fiancee - but all you end up doing is hating both of them even more and not because of the infidelity or the immorality. I just hate when authors attempt to make these situations realistic, yet cast stereotypical characters who are not realistic but are entirely predictable. 
 Ughh, there's so much more to write, but I just don't feel like wasting my time.

reference_books.title: The Godwulf Manuscript (Spenser, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I've read a lot of Spenser but I really enjoyed reading the first in the series. It is interesting to see how the character has evolved. No Hawk, no Susan in this story. Lots of people complain about Parker's choppy style and the 'he said/she said' of the dialogue but to me, that is what makes Parker Parker. What I like about Parker are his descriptions. They are pithy, they are colorful and edgy and they are concise. With just a few well chosen words, you know exactly what he means--unless of course you don't understand the reference, in which case, you will be lost. 
 Since I listen to books, the narrator is an important part of the experience. I've heard a couple of different readers do Spenser. I'm glad that none so far has tried to imitate the Boston accent because IMHO, there is nothing worse than when it is poorly done. I enjoyed Michael Prichard's reading because he just read.

book_a.title: My Mother Was Nuts
book_a.user_review: Audio version read by Penny Marshall. A fun read but not five star writing.

sample_reviews.review_text: had to quit reading it.

This review is from: My Mother Was Nuts (Kindle Edition) 
 Penny Marshall manages to talk about her life and some really serious episodes in it, by finding humor in every thing and every day situations. I suppose that's what got her through it all so successfully. I wasn't sure I'd like the book, but I was pleasantly surprised :-)

I read this book because it was a free Kindle book. (Seriously, when will I ever learn that the Kindle Owners Lending Library is *not* a good resource for new books? Probably never. I'm too frugal to waste one aspect of my Prime membership.)But, I was attracted to this book because I find autobiographies interesting, and I like Penny Marshall's movies. 
 Penny Marshall has really led an interesting life, and I enjoyed discovering how it has intersected with so many other talented people's lives, such as Marvin Hamlish, Rob Reiner, River Phoenix's mom, Art Garfunkel, Carrie Fisher, John Belushi, etc. The book was a little heavy on the name-dropping, but given that's the reason I picked it up in the first place, I couldn't complain. 
 I particularly enjoyed the chapters describing her childhood and her crazy family. Like when she and her siblings were all at summer camp and her mother would write one original letter and send photocopies of it to the others. Or the time her grandfather died when she was at summer camp and her family didn't tell her because they didn't want to ruin her summer. Makes me feel like my family is more normal that it probably is. 
 I also enjoyed the chapters she dedicated to each of her movies. I always like the "behind the scenes" trivia from movies, and this book was great about that. I found it particularly interesting to hear her take on "Riding in Cars with Boys." I thought Drew Barrymore was terrible in it, and I have always wondered how she gets the parts she does. Well, now I know that it's because some studio executive calls up the director and forces them to use her, then allows her to run the show, despite the fact that she has no talent. 
 But, the book could have been much better. I kept asking myself throughout why Marshall felt compelled to write this. She showed little emotion during any part of it, which, in part, is just her personality. However, I came away from it feeling like she needed to write this stuff down because she felt like she was going to forget it soon. It was that blandly written. 
 Then I got to one of the last chapters and discovered she'd recently been diagnosed and treated for a brain tumor and lung cancer. Then I understood why she wrote it. She truly did want to get this on paper before it was too late. I wonder if she rushed through the writing. I think if she would have taken time to flesh out a few of the anecdotes and to tell us how she really felt about some things (like her abortion of Art Garfunkel's baby, the fact that her daughter was raised by her first husband's family for a large part of her life, the emotions she felt when Cindy Williams left Laverne and Shirley in such a weird way, how she felt when she and Rob Reiner fell out of love, etc.), then it could have gotten more stars.

Eh. What should I have expected when Amazon says, "Hey, buy this book for $3.99." This book was a self-indulgent, name-dropping, drug-laced trip down memory lane. And none of it was that interesting. The sad attempts at humor were not humorous. It made my opinion of celebrities go down significantly, considering they are all narcissistic babies. Dang. Get over yourself. Bah.

** spoiler alert ** 
 if you took out all the other peoples' names in this book it would be half as long. I can't tell if Penny Marshall is really this laid back about her life, or if she is still using drugs. She had a baby, let her mother and mother-in-law raise it, then we hear about the baby only a few times for the rest of the book, however she makes it out like she was so bogged down in motherhood that she didn't get to have any 'fun' while she was young. Her life in the '80's is basicly just parties and drugs, because she 'was a young mom'. Well, she may have been a mother, but she didn't raise the daughter, so if was confusing. I didn't care for this book, and I don't recomened it to anyone. Die hard fans of Penny's will be put off I think by her 'whatever' attitude about her child, her abortion, and her miscarrage, as well as her drug use and overuse of name dropping. After reading her book the only thing I left with was that Penny Marshall is irresponsable and not a strong female rolemodel or the trailblazer I had thought.
This was just OK. I've been a fan of Penny Marshall and I loved the pictures (that's why I'm giving it 2 stars) I did not like her portrayal of illegal drugs or the curse words.

My rating reflects the fact that I am an ignoramus when it comes to popular culture and showbiz. Many of the names Marshall writes about were unfamiliar to me, I don't think I've seen any of the movies she writes about (though I did recognize some of the titles) and I have not seen even a single episode of "Laverne and Shirley." Despite that lack of background, the book was well written and amusing, and Marshall told her story clearly and effectively.
Another story of a down and out kid who turns celebrity, does drugs, and turns to charity work. Was not a page turner. Liked her better when I knew less about her.

Very Good Book. My only problem with it was the use of some foul language. That is why I took off one star. It seemed to me that there was more in the second half of the book than there was in the first half. 
 I had some difficulty with her heavy accent in the beginning but adjusted fairly quickly.

I don't feel like I really know Penny Marshall after reading her 
 autobiography, except she was a lucky person who had a brother who 
 helped her get a life, and lots of famous "friends". Drugs, a couple marriages, ex-husbands she didn't say anything personal about, and 
 sex that only gets a mention because of the pregnancies, miscarriage, and abortion that results. Nice. 
 Oh, her mother seemed no more nuts than anyone else in her family. 
 The book got kind of boring when she told about her movie making. 
 I would have liked more details about her travels and more talk 
 about how she felt about events and experiences in her life. A book about her life by an outside source might be very interesting.

book_b.title: A Prayer for Owen Meany
book_b.user_review: Well done! I am definitely going to add more Irving to my reading list!

sample_reviews.review_text: Such a good book. And as much as you are prepared for the ending, you are not prepared for the ending.

I truly didn't enjoy this book. I think it has more to do with the time that I read it than the book, and I know its not fair to the story, but all the same. I do think there were some very well written parts, but over all it was sort of dull.

I received this book in a book exchange. It's not really my typical genre of choice. While I appreciated the social commentary, the symbolism, and the complexity of the storyline, I didn't appreciate the language and was left dissatisfied at the end. It's one of those books that pulls you along with the hope of justice finally coming in the end, but the reader is instead left with a feeling of disgust at the uselessness of it all. When I pick up a work of fiction I'm looking for an escape from reality, not a painful journey through someone's life that just ends with more pain & sorrow.

I really like John Irving... but this book took me all year to read. Great story, lots of food for thought. Still thinking about how to review this one, perhaps in a few days I will have some words to write.

I didn't really enjoy this book. The author is long-winded, the characters never grow, and the plot could have been well written in a book half the length. 
 There are a couple of decent twists that you don't expect, but overall the foreshadowing is so thick that you know what's going to happen to all the characters from the beginning.

Oh, for f*ck's sake - really? 
 Owen Meany's dialogue is printed in ALL CAPS all of the time... 
 Did any Christian reader truly miss that HUGE literary clue pointing to the custom of printing Jesus' dialogues in bright red in the New Testament portion of many of the Christian bible versions? 
 Vietnam was Buddhist, not Christian, by the way. Quite an ironic intersection of unthinking didactic beliefs on so many levels... 
 Whatever. What a bore this book is to read. 
 I thought after awhile the novel was masquerading as both an ironic fictionalized autobiography about growing up in eastern America in the 1950's, 1960's and 1970's, and an intelligent symbolic satire of the Christian Owen/Jesus's (and Buddhism too, perhaps) belief in predestiny/fate; which would end as a sad acknowledgement of the horrific meaninglessness of faith by religious believers (combining religion and killing/death always leads to deluded people, as usual, trusting in the efficacy of faith by providing hollow and juvenile meanings for dying). 
 Instead, this book is SO full of sincere treacly sentimentality, muddy plot architecture and dull endless exposition I skimmed the last 400 pages. I was quite sick of Owen and his best friend, the narrator John (3:16) after 543 pages of pseudo-biblical prophecy fulfillment. After all, we all already know the ending.
Forgive me. I've just finished the book, you see, and my heart is too full to write the review it deserves.

This is an interesting book. This is not for the faint of heart. There are some disturbing things, and it can also be kind of weird. That being said, I am glad I read it. I learned some things. That is an important criteria to me in regards to whether or not I liked the book.

I know I'm the minority in my less than favorable review of this book. This being said, I'm less than 100 pages from the end, but I can't finish this book. I've been trying for MONTHS to get through it, but it's like sticking needles underneath my fingernails. The first 150-200 pages were great, but then the author kind of went off the deep end with the whole Vietnam stuff and his feelings for America once he moved to Canada. It was if he just didn't know where to stop. I won't bother to pick up another John Irving book as long as I live. I had such high hopes for it, but I just can't finish it. 
 Surprisingly, I really enjoyed the movie "Simon Birch". Go figure!
I really didn't like this book. I thought the writing was boring and the characters dull. I didn't make it past 100 pages and had to give up reading it

reference_books.title: City of Stairs (The Divine Cities, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I received a copy of this book from Goodreads First Reads. This book started off slow for me, but I am so glad I stuck with it! It was a great book. Shara Thivani is sent to Bulikov to investigate the death of her friend and colleague. She finds so much more than the reason behind his death. The world-building is amazing. After I got used to the different names and started to get into the story, I couldn't put it down. Shara and Mulaghesh are great characters, but I have to say that Sigrud is my favorite! I would recommend this book to everyone. I hope their is more to come.
