sample_reviews.review_text: I couldn't quite get into the story. Too much story and not enough action for me. I actually stopped halfway through.
Not impressed. I found the main character boring, and the story moved slowly. This is the author's first book in a series; perhaps the subsequent ones are better.

An interesting premise for a police procedural - the fifth victim of a serial killer just does quite ring true so Maeve (the under appreciated token female in the team) is allowed to investigate as if the murder was a separate killing whilst it is still kept under the serial killer investigation. 
 Following Maeve around and learning about the murdered girl as she does was a great way to help the reader understand the case. 
 The real serial killer is caught during a sting operation and while it was mostly luck it did feel as if that was probably the way these things happen more often than not. 
 Unfortunately the book was let down on two levels. Both killers had to confess as there wasn't enough evidence and Maeve kept going on and on about how sexist the job was without there ever being any proof that it really was. If she was that concerned and determined to beat the sexists and prove herself as a great police woman sleeping with one of her colleagues wasn't the best way to go about it. 
 On the whole not a bad story and I would give the next Maeve mystery a go.

Brilliant British Thriller First, to get this out there, I love British police procedurals. They are normally crisp, compelling and well written. The Burning is a premier example of the best the genre has to offer. Written from the viewpoint of Detective Constable (DC) Maeve Kerrigan, the story focuses on the hunt for "The Burning Man" a serial killer terrorizing London. His crimes are horrific, and no young woman is safe. There have been four murders committed which can obviously be credited to the killer - but now a fifth murder has been committed. And Maeve questions whether this particular killing shouldn't be attributed to a copy-cat killer. 
 Maeve is an extremely likable heroine. She takes serious verbal abuse from her so-called colleagues as they make sexual and misogynist comments about her work style. Abuse that she handles with dignity - even when it comes from her own partner. As the story evolves Maeve becomes more and more involved with the fifth killing, following a trail of murder, drugs, deceit and violence that goes back several years to the victim's college days. Maeve is smart without being omniscient, funny and serious by turns, and is willing to put herself on the line for what she knows is right and true. 
 Filled by turns with violence and heartbreak, deceit and deep sociopathy, The Burning is a must read for anyone interested in police procedurals, thrillers and suspense novels, with a very light dose of romance to round things out. 
 I received this book from the publisher in return for an honest review. All comments and thoughts are my own.
This is the first in a series. I look forward to reading the rest of her works. Great first book.

Maeve Kerrigan is a 28-year-old Detective Constable with the Metropolitan Police in London, and along with her partner, Rob Langton, is involved in an intense investigation to find the serial killer nicknamed "The Burning Man" before he strikes again. He has been killing young women, burning them (along with any evidence) and dumping their bodies in parks around the city. A copycat killer is also on the loose. 
 Maeve is smart, gutsy and starry-eyed, and caring, and I look forward to the next book in the series. 
 Rating: 3.5/5

Picked up on the off-chance a couple of days ago and I haven't put it down since. Loved the characters, kind of guessed the ending (but didn't know *why*) and I'm looking forward to reading the rest of this series.

The Burning is the first book in the Maeve Kerrigan series. Kerrigan is a DC trying to impress in a man's world within her team. Based in South London, bodies are being found in remote areas, partially burned; the murders quickly turn into victims of 'The Burning Man.' The latest victim, a successful PR woman, Rebecca Haworth, seems to be woman with a fair few secrets and Kerrigan is assigned to her case to look more closely into it. On the surface she looks to be another victim of 'The Burning Man' but is she? 
 The book is told predominantly from Kerrigan's viewpoint and Louise, Rebecca's best friend. It's narrated in the first person from both counts which wasn't a problem for me. Just like being in their heads as they told their stories! I liked Kerrigan on the whole as a new detective (for me!) on the block. She's capable of holding her own without being too stubborn and taking stupid unnecessary risks like you sometimes come across in other books. You don't have to be superwoman to get the job done!! 
 The story itself is pretty good with a whodunnit weaving through though not completely a straighforward one. If I do have criticisms it's that I thought the ending didn't really meet with the calibre of what preceded it and I did come away a tad disappointed. That said I did like the laying out of characters and it did read with a feel of more to come. I'll definitely be reading more about DC Kerrigan to see how she develops. 
 This one sits at a 3.5 star rating for me.

Yeah this was a DNF for me. Maybe it would have turned out to be a decent book, but I was extremely bored with it and didn't have the patience to find out. It certainly wasn't bad, but I've read better.

DC Maeve Kerrigan is on a task force looking for a serial killer in London nicknamed "The Burning Man". Maeve is assigned to focus on the last victim who may or may not fit the profile of the killer. As Maeve delves into Rebecca's background, all is not what it seems. 
 The book is told from varying viewpoints, mostly Maeve and Louise who is Rebecca's best friend from Oxford days to the present. It is a great psychological thriller, well-written, and enjoyable to read. I really liked this crime drama and would recommend it. I plan to read the rest of the series. I read this book as an ARC for an honest review.

book_b.title: The Trouble with Goats and Sheep

sample_reviews.review_text: This was a delightful book. A missing person mystery told from the perspective of a 10 year old girl. It is set in an English village thick with lots of characters. The 10 year old and her little friend set out to find God thinking that the mystery would be solved then. It is funny and poignant. A very good mystery. Everyone seemed guilty at one time or another.

This book is a funny, witty, quirky little read peppered with references to the Midlands during the 1970s. 
 A coming of age story about two young girls, spending their summer finding more than they bargained for. Secrets and rumours abound, just what is the trouble with goats and sheep? 
 I thoroughly enjoyed the beginning of this book and I thought the ending was interesting too. I do unfortunately feel the middle of the book lost its sharp narrative a little and I skipped a few chapters. However, there were genuine moments of pure gold which made me smile and on occasion laugh out loud! 
 Overall, it's a lovely read. I'd definitely recommend it... it's hard to believe this is a debut!

I hate giving up on books. I HATE it! But this... This was booooorring. About 100 pages in and not a whole lot has happened, except we've been told it hot about 75 times and that Mrs. Creasy is missing. That's all. I could not make myself care about Grace or Tilly and all their adult neighbors and parents are pretty much the same character over and over. 
 I have much more interesting things to read.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Looks like I'm in the minority here, but I wasn't too impressed with this book. Part of that isn't even the author's fault but expectations triggered by hype and a misleading blurb. This gave the impression it was a detective story, which it really isn't. Any serious attempts to find out what became of Mrs Creasy fizzle out halfway through as they discover Jesus in the drainpipe instead. 
 There were some parts that were delightful. I liked the nostalgic use of products and 70s personalities - how Jesus could also look like Brian Clough. Grace and Tilly's friendship was well developed and realistic, not least Grace's crush on the local bad girl. Ultimately she needs Tilly just as much as Tilly needs her. 
 My main nitpick was the Walter Bishop storyline. This was disclosed far too early, and by the wrong people - it would have been more effective for the girls to uncover it and be horrified by their neighbours' actions. I worked out reasonably early on both who started the fire and who was responsible for taking Grace, meaning that the remaining hundred or so pages felt like unnecessary padding. It had the potential to be so much more, making it a frustrating reading experience.
What a fantastic debut novel. What I liked most about this story was the characterization. Very beautifully written which I would definitely recommend

This was a great mystery from the point of two girls who decide to look into the murder of their neighbor. I also liked that it showed the viewpoints of the other neighbors who lived on the street. Each person had their agenda and it wasn't clear right away who the killer was. I plan on reading more from this author in the future.
1.5 stars. A big WTF?!! So annoyed I finished reading it but I kept hoping it would get better because I started to like the first couple of chapters and then all down hill after that. Pointless
Will be talking about this book on Literary Roadhouse Podcast. I'll post the link here once it's live.

This is my pick for the most insipid novel I've read this year. It was just plain boring. The characters could have been spectacular with their proclivities and within this locale. 
 They weren't. They were dull and improbable to the point of it becoming perplexing why they were even seeking the missing Mrs. Creasy at all.
Contrived, self-conscious, trite.

reference_books.title: Seabiscuit: An American Legend
reference_books.review_text: Laura Hildebrand is such a brilliant story-teller that anything she chooses to write about will be nothing less than absolutely fascinating. As it is, Seabiscuit is an enthralling read that instantly became a favorite of mine. I can't recommend this book highly enough.

reference_books.title: Eleanor & Park
reference_books.review_text:
Eleanor & Park is a seemingly simple love story about two kids who can't quite fit in but somehow find each other and accidentally embark on that sort of romance you only read about in novels. 
 And for the for the most part, it works. 
 I am all for these two awkward kids. Eleanor and Park are both a breath of fresh air in a literary atmosphere polluted with cliche and unachievable ideals. They're clumsy and sweet and earnest and confused and wistful and perpetually uncool...which makes them both a bit frustrating, very likable, and extremely relatable. 
 Eleanor & Park also made me very, very grateful to be nearly thirty and well past the pangs of sappy, desperate teenage love, which Rainbow Rowell has managed to capture in all of its uncomfortable and clammy glory. Well done, but at times it was a little much for me. 
 Beyond the love story, Eleanor & Park takes on some pretty serious issues, and does it well. It's a book well worth reading.

reference_books.title: Sarah's Key
reference_books.review_text:
I so wanted to like this book. The history shared is so tragic and important, and Sarah's story is as captivating as it is devastating. 
 Unfortunately, even with such potential, this story was unforgivingly predictable. We start out with an intriguing heroine, but end up with a self-obsessed, confused, and annoying protagonist and her equally unlikable family in a crisis that would make Elizabeth Gilbert proud. Why?!!!!!!! 
 So much promise. Such a disappointment.

reference_books.title: David and Goliath: Underdogs, Misfits, and the Art of Battling Giants
reference_books.review_text: My first Malcolm Gladwell read; what a storyteller! Some of his arguments were a bit of a stretch, but the theory was intriguing and his presentation captivating. Well worth a read- and perhaps a second.

reference_books.title: Slaughterhouse-Five
reference_books.review_text: A note: this rating is not because this book isn't a masterpiece- I do believe it is. There is no contesting that Kurt Vonnegut is anything less than a genius. I couldn't figure out what was going on in this book, and the constant warping about gave me whiplash. I blame myself for my lack of literary prowess: if anyone can enlighten me on what I am missing, I would be grateful. Until then, I'll be honest: I didn't really enjoy this book.

book_a.title: Eat, Pray, Love
book_a.user_review:
Liz Gilbert whines, complains, and moans through this self indulgent biography detailing how she recovered from a failed marriage by running away on a paid vacation from life. If only we could all be so fortunate when times are tough! One star goes to the glimmers of actual insight and brilliance scattered throughout that just might make the read worth it- if you can withstand her self- congratulatory tone long enough. In truth, I am glad I read it: but I would never recommend it to anyone who was seriously interested in personal growth and development. Not that I am an expert- but even I know better than this. 
 As it is, I am embarrassed that women have been represented in such a disgusting way. When is a NY Times Bestseller going to portray a strong female protagonist? I'm sick of these spoiled, flakey, weepy adult women making it big. 
 Rent the movie; Julia Roberts is far more appealing, and the pasta in Italy looks amazing.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I read the eat+learn Italian part and was in love with the book but when I got to the Pray i just couldn't finish it and gave up on the book :| 
 India part was so slow and so "are you kidding me" that I put it aside and maybe someday, when I am really bored I will finish it. 
 I did like the writing style! very funny and easy to follow.

book club book! a woman gets divorced, breaks down, leaves her life for a year to travel to italy, india and bali. mostly everyone in the club loved it, said it changed their lives, rave rave. it was boring. bad writing style. too preachy and self promoting. the italy section grossed me out by her excess in food. i could never relate to this woman, i wouldn't get along with her at all. this is a memoir, true story.

The writing wasn't awful; she got a few things factually wrong, which was troubling, but I just couldn't get past her tone. Her self-deprecation seemed forced and she seemed to be charmed by herself and impressed with her own courage to travel the world (...on her publisher's dime.) 
 Not captivating enough to warrant finishing (and I am *love* fluff!), I ended up renting the movie to find out what happens in India and Indonesia.
I did not read this book. I just listened to a podcast discussing it and would just like to state publically: I never will. So don't ask me to.
Unenlightening whiny drivel.
I kind of enjoyed the first two parts but had got around to a state of extreme irritation with the narrator and her self-obsessiveness by the last part.
A disaster.

This was a waste of time. I almost finished reading the first third and then thought, "What's the point?" The author is a very skilled writer and I did truly enjoy her POV and style of writing, however, it was not enough to save this book. We all need to take care of ourselves and to fulfill the needs to grieve for lost relationships, youth, whatever... We don't need to spend a year whining and letting our past decisions control everything we do. Deal with it and move on. So, since the lowest rating I could give this book was one star, that is what Eat, Pray, Love earned from me.

the author begins by explaining the reasons why her journey of self discovery from Italy, to India and then to Indonesia was a necessary diversion from her fast paced life in New York City. Each country shall have a theme (thus the name of the book). I was intrigued...the narrator's voice was perfect for audiobook, it was easy listening. Italy--oh the raptures of Italy! I feel I could soliloquize on the abundance of luxurious food, rich romantic scenery, and the melodious language of the locals solely from having read this book. The first third of the book made me want desperately to pack a bag and set out for Rome. The rest of the book was boring. Probably just not a good choice for audiobook.
I ditched this book halfway through so i shouldn't say I've read it but i really tried to understand the point but i just couldn't. Maybe i am to young

I was 90 percent extremely excited to read this book; It was on my wishlist on Amazon for most of this year, and it was touted as being one of the best books of last year. If I hadn't saw that it was in at the library, I would have probably purchased it later this year. The 10 percent that wasn't excited was because I had attempted to read her previous book but found it to be pure chick lit. So I started this book, and realized that an author isn't going to do a complete 180 most of the time in their writing style. Is this a bad book? No. I consider it to be evolved chick lit, but at the core, the characters are shallow, the situations are silly and trite, and I didn't really root for any of the characters.
I liked it and it kept you reading. The parts about the weirdness of Seattle were my favorite.

Bernadette Fox has lost all interest in life. Her career as an architect failed. Her marriage is on the rocks. Her house is in shambles. She's hired Manjula Kapoor, an India woman she met on the Internet, to shop online for her, pay her bills, make her dinner reservations, and arrange for her family vacation to Antarctica. Bernadette is an artist who has stopped creating, a menace to society. She's become a recluse whose sole focus is her 15-year-old daughter, Bee. 
 Nothing about Where'd You Go Bernadette is conventional, including Semple's writing style. The novel is a compilation of documents--emails, handwritten notes, FBI documents, reports from a psychiatrist. Not to mention correspondence between helicoptering parents at Bee's school, the shallow women Bernadette calls gnats. Bernadette finds herself in the middle of one riotous crisis after another involving the gnats, yet she maintains her dignity while remaining true to herself. And to Bee. 
 Semple adds depth to her characters with funny antidotes of their past lives. Their voices are spot on. 
 Bee--On the verge of going off to boarding school, even though she is naive in her own charming way, Bee is intelligent beyond her years. Her loyalty to her mother is paramount. She even goes as far as to cheer her mother on in her battle against the gnats. The mother/daughter relationship is rock solid, which is why Bee refuses to believe the worst when her mother disappears off the planet. 
 LG--Bernadette's nerdy husband who is tolerant of his wife's eccentricity but too preoccupied with his career at Microsoft to notice she's falling apart. 
 Sue Lynn--gnat and administrative assistant for LG, who sets her sights on him when she senses trouble in his marriage. 
 Audry--gnat and neighbor, the focus of Bernadette's temper tantrums. 
 Where'd You Go Bernadette is imaginative, spunky, and oh so much fun.
I could not get into this book...
Very enjoyable quick read. I loved the format, alternating between emails, faxes, official documents, and narrative.

At once a comical critique and a love letter to the city of Seattle and it's inhabitants. As a Seattlite and Washingtonian, born and raised, I found the name dropping delightful and spot on. But I can admit my own bias in that regard. I doubt I would have enjoyed it quite as much without having lived here. 
 That said, the story itself is sweet, funny and engaging all it's own, and a worthy read even if you haven't lived in Queen Anne or breakfasted at Macrina or made secret fun of the North Face wearing tech wives shopping for specialty cheeses at the Whole Foods in Interbay.

reference_books.review_text:

The villain pretty much hands Kate a piece of paper telling her who the villain is (spoiler alert: him!) and explaining the mystery she is working on and she's like, "Hey that guy's creepy, not going to pay any attention to what he says". reference_books.title: Pride and Prejudice and Zombies (Pride and Prejudice and Zombies, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I hated this book with a passion. I never truly understood before reading this what it means to be a great writer and what it means to be a poor writer who throws a bunch of words together without creating anything of depth or meaning. 
 The one star is for an amazing idea, so poorly executed that it appears to not have been edited. There are thousands of fan-fics on the web that add something a little different to the original story. This is like a fan fic that takes the original, without properly understanding it, and randomly adds things that don't make sense to anyone else. Randomly inserting that Elizabeth was polishing her musket or is trained in martial arts does NOT make this a zombie, action or horror book. It's lazy, meaningless and poor writing. The zombie action scenes were few and far between, did not advance the action in any way and did not appear to be a metaphor for anything, which they should have. The jokes could barely be called jokes as none of them were funny. If it wasn't for Austen's original prose, the book would be unreadable. 
 Mainly though, this book just made me sad for its lost potential.

reference_books.title: Doubleblind (Sirantha Jax, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
"What do you think of Sirantha Jax representing your interests on Ithiss-Tor?" 
 "Well, it's a bit of a joke, isn't it?" 
 "In what way?" 
 "What kind of training has she had?" the girl demands. "They may as well have sent me. I saw her for years, showing her tits on the midnight bounce. Table dancing, amateur soft-porn vids, drunk-and-disorderly conduct, barroom brawls . . . how does any of that qualify her to be an ambassador? It's damn near the dumbest thing I've ever heard." 
 Yeah that's the thing, random girl interviewed in an annoying style-changing news report add-on. It is a dumb idea. It is also a dumb idea to go to a planet filled with aliens who want to kill you as an ambassador without any sort of security team or way to escape or a support team who actually know stuff about politics or the economy or anything. Also, not enough of the side characters and no one is any fun at all at any part of this boring story. I hope the next book is subtitled How Sirantha Got Her Groove Back cos she is lame-o right now, and I think she even knows it.

 But it was a fun read and I will for suresies be checking out any sequels.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This did very much not work for me. Let me count the ways: 
 1. This is much more Urban Horror than Urban Fantasy. Too much blood and gore for my taste. 
 2. That's why the humour does not work for me. A certain type of gallows humour would work, when people are being ripped to shreds, but that's not what we get here. The plot is very dark, but the way the characters interact with it is frivolous. That causes constant cognitive dissonance for me, which hurts my brain. 
 3. Throwing all possible paranormal creatures into a story would require solid backstory. This suffers from the same malaise Jim Butcher's Dresden Files suffers IMO; it's a mashup without structure. 
 4. SPI (Supernatural Protection and Investigation) apparently thinks its a good idea to throw a completely untrained new agent into melee situations. Its Supernatural Agency Amateur Hour! 
 5. While I don't require every UF heroine to kick butt, this one is just a wee bit too far on the girly side. There are moments when she takes no prisoners (the tractor!), but in between she can't even dress herself and falls over her own feet. Working too hard to create a non-Mary Sue? Because of course we know she'll hook up with her hunky partner. 
 6. The primary monsters, the grendels, are too powerful. And yet the humans prevail. 
 7. I don't care about anyone here. I know I am supposed to care because they're the heroes, but I just don't. Grendels can have them. 
 1 star seems cruel, it's not really sucky in the way truly bad books are sucky. But I didnot enjoy it one bit, and had to force myself to finish it at all.

I tried to give this a fair chance I really did. I HATED the mc. She was annoying and not the bad ass chick I was expecting. She always had to have someone else save her ass and the one chance she had to do something badassy she tumbles and her "arms shake too much" to do anything decent. She can't take care of herself and seriously her bark is way worse than her bite. She has no bite. She lets others bite for her. No thanks. I'm going to find something more worth my time to read. An mc that doesn't quake in her shoes as soon as she sees danger.

If the police are there to protect citizens from your run-of-the-mill bad guys, what happens when these bad guys are supernatural creatures? No need to invoke the famous Ghostbusters, because SPI exists precisely for this reason. Supernatural Protection and Investigations works to safeguard humans from scary creatures like vampires or ghouls or whatever, and to keep their existence as secret as possible. 
 Full review at SPACE and SORCERY BLOG

I love all Lisa's books and this is no exception here we a girl from the country learning to become a paranormal detective in the Big City. I think the story works very well and has a blend of action and humor that I enjoyed, I did get a bit bogged down near the end but that was more due to the Christmas hangover. I was hoping for a more paranormal love interest but I do like Ian so we will see how it goes.

This is a fantastic start to a new urban fantasy series! It has a fantastic cast of characters and plenty of action, but does not get sidetracked by stupid supposedly tough girl heroines, love triangles, or creatures that sparkle. 
 In fact, the main character, Mac, is anything but a tough girl. She is clumsy and unskilled, yet brave and smart. Thank goodness her partner, Ian, is a tough guy who is determined to protect her even going as far as teaching her skills to survive. They work for a supernatural agency whose mission it is to make life safe for humans and supernatural creatures alike, as well as keeping awareness of the supernatural away from humans. 
 In this particular book, someone has set grendels loose in Manhattan to create chaos on New Year's Eve. Yep, I said grendels, as in Beowulf. It was nice to see a different monster take the limelight. Don't get me wrong, this series is chock full of your typical supes: vamps, weres, fae, dragons, ghouls. But, it also throws in a few curveballs with a doppleganger and an as of yet unidentified mystery creature. 
 It is so nice to read a new UF book that doesn't have characters rushing into danger for no reason or that uses overreaction as a plot device in place of action. The characters in this book take risks, but they are calculated risks. It was also nice not to get bogged down with all of the characters lusting after each other from the moment their eyes meet. My only issue with this book was Mac's grammar. I get it, she's from Western NC. I LIVE in Western NC. Those with degrees in journalism know how to use proper grammar, even if they did not grow up doing so. Sheesh. 
 Regardless, this series is off to a great start. I've already started on the second book.

I know it's not fair to give a book four rather than five stars because as a reader I had such high expectations, but I haven't had my second morning coffee yet. Cue Ms Grump. 
 Lisa Shearin has a great style that I thoroughly enjoyed in her fantasy series with the heroine, Raine Benares. So when I heard of a new series, an urban fantasy one, I pre-ordered The Grendel Affair. 
 Unfortunately, the story is set in New York and Seanan McGuire has kind of created and cornered the market in a fictional, cryptid-infested New York in my mind. I kept wanting to meet her characters! (Discount Armageddon, if you're interested). 
 But once I made space for a different paranormal New York, The Grendel Affair has a nice line in monsters, a heroine with a lot of promise and a tough protective hero. 
 Oh, and for anyone who has ever thought their boss a dragon...

One of the cover blurbs describes the book as a mix of Stephanie Plum, the X-Files and tequila mixed in a blender; that's a fair description. Except that Mac is smarter than Stephanie and more on the ball and her family is, so far anyway, less dysfunctional than Stephanie's and her love life is decidedly less so. No love triangle! *happy dance!* :D 
 So, now that I've said what it isn't, what is it? A mix of standard urban fantasy elements, mystery, and delightful new elements - grendels and a nice uptake on mythology, a new take on seers, and a creative use of dragons. I'm a big fan of mystery blended with urban fantasy and I love mythology so this book appealed to me from the get-go. Shearin has humor, action, a sometimes overly twisty plot, and interesting characters. The story dragged a little, especially in the middle, but overall I enjoyed it. I liked that Mac wasn't a kick-ass, super-skilled heroine; she's untrained in defense and mostly untrained in weapons but she wants to learn and she's skilled in research. She's also quirky, funny, makes mistakes, smart, and unwilling to sit on the sidelines despite her job description. Ian, her partner, is more stoic and less developed but he has potential and I loved their draconic boss, Vivienne. SPI is an organization that also has potential; a secret, private organization that polices supernaturals and keeps knowledge of those same supernaturals from humans. It's a cross between Men in Black and the supernatural council in Kelley Armstrong's Women of the Otherworld. 
 The story doesn't take itself too seriously, there are several characters who are not white which makes for a nice change from many urban fantasy books, and potential for many mythological beings from around the world. "The Grendel Affair" is a good start to a new series and I'll be looking for the next book.

I am a big fan of Lisa Shearin's Raine Benares series. I was stoked to hear she had a new series, this time urban fantasy set in our world, coming out. That was ... three years ago. This is book one. What happened? 
 Life happened. The Grendel Affair came out during my last year teaching in England. No problem, I figured--I'll buy it when I move back in August. Then August came around, and I didn't. I was struggling to get through the backlog of books that had somehow shown up in my room in Canada while I was away. I'm still struggling to do that. (They're breeding, I think. Only explanation.) But when book three came out last week, I decided enough was enough. So I ordered all three books online, delivered right to my door. 
 That's right: I'm binge-reading this series the way others binge on Netflix. 
 The Grendel Affair starts the series with high stakes already: something or someone is planning to let some grendels loose on Times Square on New Year's, effectively exposing the supernatural world. Oh no! If only there were a secret organization of supernaturals and human, perhaps a Supernatural Protection & Investigation(s) outfit. Nah ... only a centuries-old dragon would be able to mastermind something like that. 
 Oh snap. 
 The use of grendels as monsters feels pretty original. I can't say I've run across those in urban fantasy yet. And Shearin spends a good amount of time establishing them as interesting monsters in their own right. They are mostly beast-like, but they've got a sense of strategy to them. The grendels and their offspring are formidable foes, but at the same time they aren't so powerful that defeating them feels like a deus ex machina. 
 Otherwise, The SPI Files is pretty standard fare: werewolves and vampires, goblins and elves (hmm, don't those sound familiar), ex-NYPD officers and seers and--oh, what? Yeah, our narrator, Makenna Fraser, is a human whose only powers include a nose for investigative journalism and the ability to see through the veils and glamours that let supernaturals hide in plain sight. Despite this ability, she is still technically a human. I appreciate that Shearin chooses to give us a protagonist with so few powers (at least for now). 
 Nevertheless, Mac might be the weakest thing about this book. Her lack of active power means she feels a bit like a reader surrogate protagonist-on-rails--always being dragged around by the other characters, reacting more than acting. Let's be clear: not every urban fantasy protagonist has to be an awesome fighter, and a woman doesn't have to be able to kick ass to be "strong" or progressive. But I want to see Mac do more than cringe and gripe at the various supernatural creatures around her. The tractor and the paintball gun were a nice start, but I hope she grows over the series into a more complex protagonist. 
 That's the key, I think: over the series. This is clearly the first book in an ongoing series, and Shearin does a lot of legwork. In some respects it's less subtle than I like--the opening chapter just showers us in exposition and backstory--and in other places it's more delightfully ambiguous. For instance, Mac is pretty clearly attracted to Ian, but will she act on it? Who knows? Shearin had an intense love triangle happening in her other series, so I wouldn't be surprised if a romance is on the books for these books--but maybe it's not the one that's being telegraphed so heavily here. 
 Now, despite laying ground for subsequent novels, The Grendel Affair is still a good standalone story. There is a sense of urgency to the plot, and it climaxes with a tense series of scenes and battle sequences that leave you breathless. I read this on a Saturday night (because I have especially exciting Saturday nights), curled up in a chair, just enjoying an action-packed story. 
 With six novels already, Shearin has a well-established style, and it's in play here. Her voice and approach to description and characterization remain the same. That being said, The SPI Files is definitely new ground, and Mac is by no means a carbon copy of Raine. I can't wait to read the next book--and unlike you scrubs who had to wait a whole year, I don't have to. Is this what the people just starting to read A Song of Ice and Fire feel like? Because it feels good.

book_b.user_review: Oh man, the title makes me mad. sample_reviews.review_text: I tend to like books written by strong women, but I struggled to get into this one. I got through the first few chapters and then it became more work than enjoyment to finish reading it. I'm not sure what they want the takeaway to be? If you decide to crack it open you can expect lots of real and unfiltered stories, but no real point or conclusion to any of the conversations that are started.

I was really disappointed by "Not That Kind of Girl". I loved books like "Bossypants", and I enjoy Dunham's HBO show "Girls", so I thought this would be a funny, interesting window into her life, creativity, and success. It ends up Dunham is either exactly like the main character of her show, Hannah Horvath, or she's not really ready to let down the curtain between her persona and her true person. The memoir's writing feels very contrived and studied, and yet at the same time the organization of the book makes no sense at all. She has it separated into parts like "Love & Sex", "Friendship", etc. but everything sort of seems to meld together, repeat, and ultimately make its way back to sex or bodily functions. If someone who did not know Dunham's real-life story read this memoir, they would assume she was a lazy, neurotic hipster who was self-indulgent and spoiled by her parents, and most likely still occupying her childhood bedroom and working at a coffee shop. They would not assume she was a successful young woman with her own popular TV show, feature films, multiple Emmys, and two Golden Globes. Dunham hardly mentions any of those parts of her and only flippantly mentions ambition once or twice. It's ultimately a puzzle to me why she would rather discuss her tonsil stones than, perhaps, her creative goals or development as a filmmaker and writer or really anything besides a bunch of stories that paint her in a fairly negative light. It's almost like she likes putting a certain group of people off, like there's a security in coming off as always self-deprecating and slightly inept. Read more at www.iwantmichikosjob.com.

Up until recently, I didn't even know who Lena Dunham is (nope, never seen her show, Girls). The only reason I picked up Not That Kind of Girl was because of the controversy surrounding it (the allegations that Lena sexually abused her younger sister, Grace). I wanted to read the book and form my own opinion. 
 Overall, I found the book boring. And while I didn't go into this book expecting anything, I am disappointed. Of course, I'm only disappointed because I've wasted my time and not because I expected this book to be something amazing.

I had to change my review to "2" stars after I asked myself: if I had no prior knowledge of a Lena Dunham, never watched Girls, and picked up this book purely as a book to read, what would I think? While this book fits nicely into the Lena Dunham brand that I appreciate: quirky, wry and narcissistic, as a stand alone piece of literature it doesn't really add up. 
 The author has no real struggle beyond the issues in her own head. She even says as one point, if she had been molested as a child it would explain all her mental health problems. She was raised in privilege. So, for me, I don't understand or sympathise with her on that level. It's like her persona had to make up mental health issues because she was dealt such an easy life and she needed something to set her apart. 
 When she describes wild nights out and thrift shop clothes I like it. Her nerdy obsessions with music and books are relatable. Her very brief insights to people in Hollywood were entertaining, as was most of the sexual encounters she describes. Her voice is amusing, but as I said, is it funny because I read her as Hannah in Girls, or funny because it's an original voice in literature? 
 Miss Dunham is only three years younger than I and maybe I'm a narcissist but I think I could put a spin on my own life's adventures just as well as her. There is nothing unique about her life as described in this book, despite having a TV show, which she doesn't really detail getting or working on. 
 As much as I like her, I have realised in the future when someone picks up this book with no prior knowledge of who she was, they won't find this book particularly illuminating in any way. Unless you grew up privileged in Manhattan with artist parents and attended private schools and summer camps, the vast majority of people will not be able relate.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This is one of the books that kept me reading on and on, always wondering what twists and turns might happen next. 
 We only get to know Sophie, the main character, through the eyes of all those who tell about her, and it is not always easy to like Sophie because of what she does. She can be rather brusque, and definitely causes hurt, but it seems most of this is because she is maybe too honest at times and does not always understand how she hurts others. 
 However, all in all she is a character that I thought was somewhere between fascinating and likable, and there are so many nuances to discover in her, and the other characters that tell about Sophie reveal so much about themselves too, that it is simply exciting to read on. Oh, and I also loved that Sophie's bisexuality is shown in a rather understated way, not like something you need to discuss, just like something normal. :) This is definitely a story I enjoyed a lot. 5 out of 5 stars.
I blew through this one. Really amazing, a must for any young artistic type this year.
Sophie Stark did not die soon enough.
I had little to no expectations going into this book (I think I found it abandoned on a shelf at work), and I was thrilled to find myself captivated throughout. Great characters, beautiful writing.

This book is difficult, much like Sophie herself. Everyone is an asshole- all flaws and prickliness, but there's beauty in it too. I liked Sophie even if she was infuriating and hard to understand. I wanted her to succeed or maybe even be more of an out and out villain. Instead, she was just a person who was trying her hardest even if that meant hurting people along the way. Her way of understanding and talking to people was through film, and it ultimately destroyed her and everything she touches. 
 This isn't a book to read quickly; you have to take the time to let it soak into your skin and settle there. Anna North has written an beautiful and intense character study of a "difficult" woman. 
 Thanks to NetGalley and the publisher for the ARC.

(I received a free copy of this book from Net Galley in exchange for an honest review.) 
 Who is the real Sophie Stark? 
 THE LIFE AND DEATH OF SOPHIE STARK is the story of an enigmatic film director, told by the six people who loved her most. Brilliant, infuriating, all-seeing and unknowable, Sophie Stark makes films said to be 'more like life than life itself'. But her genius comes at a terrible cost: to her husband, to the brother she left behind, and to the actress she can't forget. 
 This felt like it had so much potential for a cracking book but, for me, it really fell over itself and crashed to the ground. 
 The multiple POV's all started to sound the same; the problem Sophie had were all self-inflicted so it was hard to empathise with her; and there was so much in her personality that just made me dislike her - and, by extension, anyone who liked her. 
 Really hard for me to get into - I doubt I would try another by this author unless she drops the multiple POV approach. 
 Paul 
 ARH

I understand what Anna North's point was: with great art comes great human sacrifice; genius is isolating. This theme was interesting enough, but it was really blandly delivered. I had no sympathy for any of the characters, I didn't see anything particularly brilliant about Sophie, and the writing style was just "fine" at best. Maybe in better hands, this story would've been as fascinating as it promises. As it stands, I couldn't care less. 
 Nothing to see here.

I may bump down to a 4 but at the moment I still have that post-book tingly feeling. 
 Wondrous, addictive, unputdownable.

I loved this book. It idn't exactly your warm-and-fuzzy novel. The characters are easy to love and sometimes very hard to understand. Some are just hard to understand. But they are beautifully flawed and so very human.

The Life and Death of Sophie Stark is a captivating look at an unapologetic filmmaker, as told by the six people who loved her and knew her (arguably) the best. 
 Anna North has crafted a remarkable story about fictional director, Sophie Stark, a woman who openly admits to being difficult to get to know and connect with. She creates films out of the stories and lives of the people that she knows, and goes to any length to create the story she wants to tell. Her dedication to her craft comes at the expense of everything else in her life: family, friends, and potentially, herself. 
 Each part of Sophie's story is told by the people in her life - her brother, her girlfriend, her husband, etc. Some are told in a traditional narrative style, the stories forming entire chapters (no short chapters here, folks). Each story highlights one of the films that Sophie has crafted, and is then concluded by an article from a film critic who follows Sophie's career. 
 What I loved is how each narrator adds their own pieces to the puzzle that is Sophie - not one of them has her pinned down. She is all-consuming for them and yet she's dedicated only to her craft; to her art. 
 This is a great read, and a great way to spend an afternoon.

sample_reviews.review_text: I found this book highly readable but ultimately unsatisfying. Sullivan is a talented storyteller but there is little substance in her writing. I was thinking about how Jonathan Franzen (and many of his reviewers) were widely criticized. Why, people asked, do his books get so much attention when they are "just" domestic novels, not unlike so many similar novels written by women? But I believe Jonathan Franzen is a wonderful example of an author using the domestic setting to explore powerful ideas about modern life. Other examples that come to mind are Jennifer Haigh and Anna Quindlen. The world and characters created by Sullivan in Maine had potential for similar exploration but lack of analysis and cohesion left them meaningless. This lack of substance is particularly exemplified by the ending; I felt like Sullivan reached her desired word count and then stopped writing. Initially I planned to recommend this novel as I did enjoy much of the story. Unfortunately, the inconsistencies, loose ends and overall shallowness have caused it to sour in my mind.

This review first appeared on my blog: http://www.knittingandsundries.com/20... 
 Tara, whose husband Sam recently died in a car accident, teaches at Hunter High School, where her daughter Grace is also a student. Her best friends are Noelle, a midwife who also runs a babies-in-need program, and Emerson, whose daughter Jenny is also Grace's best friend. 
 The three women have been besties since college, and Noelle delivered Tara's baby. When Noelle commits suicide in the cottage she rents from Emerson, she leaves many more questions than answers. When Tara finds a box with thank you notes and baby pictures, she also finds an unfinished letter of apology with a shocking written confession. As she and Emerson try to puzzle out who the letter was meant for, more secrets will be revealed, and they find out that they didn't know their friend as well as they thought they did. Her secrets lead to an explosive and heartbreaking discovery, and the power of friendship and the idea of family is tested. 
 I was drawn in to the unraveling mysteries in this novel. Written around the themes of motherhood, friends, family, and loss, the multiple POV's and flashbacks help us unravel the story of Noelle, who for me was the most interesting character in the book. Even though what Noelle did was something that every mother fears, her reasons for it are complex and driven, and we find that she has lived with this guilt for so long because of the love she felt. Nothing can excuse what she's done, but as a reader, I could feel the pain that caused her to do so, and actually felt a few twists of my heart as I read about it. 
 A solid and intriguing read that will keep you turning pages until the wee hours of the morning, The Midwife's Confession is perfect for the reader who enjoys mystery, family drama, and friendship. 
 QUOTES 
 If you have a friend, I pondered, a good friend, a woman you love, and you learn she's done something abominable, do you stop loving her? 
 It was good she had done this, she thought. Yes, she'd betrayed on of her closest friends and she knew that would haunt her, but she'd needed to do it to let Sam go.

Each chapter switches perspective to a different character, and the story plays out through the actions and thoughts of the various characters. I really liked how the story unfolded. There were things in the story that I found really hard to believe, and some that were excruciatingly painful to imagine in reality. Good solid story, and I enjoyed getting sucked completely in.

This book is awful. As an English person, the dialogue, locations and situations do not ring true, but that is the least of its problems. 
 Readers are not in the nineteenth century any more, we are no longer satisfied with romances where the main couple barely speak to each other throughout the novel and then at the end conveniently realise they are in love even though they know nothing about each other and have been flirting with other people throughout the rest of the book.  Too many modern writers are jumping on the Austen bandwagon in order to sell fiction. They should stop. This book pales in comparison to 'Pride and Prejudice' and the Bridget Jones books which are guilty of popularising this trend. It is predictable, stupid and dull.

I know Shannon Hale's work as a young adult novelist, and so I was curious to see how she measured up as a writer of funny chick-lit for adults. I'm also reading a lot of Jane Austen-related books at the moment (did you guess?), and so I thought I'd give Austenland a whirl. The basic premise is our heroine Jane (subtle name choice) is obsessed with Mr Darcy as played by Colin Firth in the BBC production of Pride & Prejudice. No real man can ever measure up, so her obsession is ruining her love life. A wealthy great-aunt sends her off to Austenland so she can live out her fantasies pretending she lives in Regency times. She gets to wear Empire-line frocks and bonnets, dance at balls, and exchange witty repartee with men in skintight breeches and cravats. It's all meant to be good, clean fun, but Jane begins to have trouble distinguishing what's real and what's not ... all while getting tangled up in romance. Austenland is really chick-lit at its most frivolous and fantastical. All the pleasure comes from the dialogue and the situation; the characters are very one-dimensional and the plot as predictable as possible. It has been turned into a film directed by Stephanie Meyer and is due for release later this year, and I'll happily settle down with some popcorn to enjoy it again.

For Jane Austen fans, especially devotees of the 6-hour A&E "Pride and Prejudice," even the dedication of this book is pure enjoyment: 
 For Colin Firth 
 You're a really great guy, but I'm married, so I think we should just be friends. 
 This book also contains a line that almost made me burst into giggles on the bus and kept me smiling during my whole morning commute: 
 "Hooray for ham!" 
 Single, 30-something Jane is given a 3-week vacation to Regency England, where she must act, dress, converse, dance like a Jane Austen character. This concept in itself must have great appeal to Austen fans, but what made the book so entertaining for me was Shannon Hale's humor. Sure, Elizabeth Bennet may never have said, "Hooray for ham," but maybe Jane Austen did, when she was hungry and the serving of the meat course diverted her chatty table neighbor.

reference_books.title: The Vegetarian
reference_books.review_text: Devastating, quiet, exhilarating - this story of obsession and self, of agency and society, will stay with you well after the initial reading of it is over. Narrated through three characters close to "the vegetarian," the titular woman acts as a mechanism for explorations of self, morality, philosophy, and madness. The Vegetarian is beautifully sparse in its language, revealing an unsettling depth. Take your time with this short book.

reference_books.title: By the Time You Read This, I'll Be Dead
reference_books.review_text: You hope that she won't kill herself. She seems so determined. The character/narrator's muteness in life allows for interesting pseudo-dialog, and her struggle within herself to stay the course, despite personal and social growth, is compelling. An unexpected page-turner.

reference_books.review_text:
This review is based on the audiobook, so it does not reflect the experience of reading the text of the book. 
 A) whiny little rich bitches. I had to stop when the soon-to-be stepsister character pitched a fit that she wouldn't get to keep her roomS (plural) when the mc and her sister move in, and the mc failed to think her a spoiled brat either in narration or in dialog. 
 B) the actress who read the audiobook is clearly British. The story takes place in London so her accent is fine for the British characters, but the mc/narrator and her family are voiced with bad American accents. Don't make the characters "American," then use really European phrasing. Americans, especially snotty teenagers, are not typically eloquent. On this point I don't know exactly whose decision the accent thing was, because the dad is German, the nanny is German, and the mc and fam have moved around so much it would make sense for them to have garbled accents, kind of. So just don't make them have bad fake AMERICAN accents! Very jarring. 
 C) lost in translation. I think this was probably a very well written book in the original language, but the translation to English, combined with the phrasing part of point B, above, made the narration intolerable.

The Moor's Account - Owning the Story 
 The narrator of Leila Lalami's THE MOOR'S ACCOUNT, the Moroccan slave Mustafa (or as the Spanish rename him, Estebanico) is a lover of stories. As a boy he listens to his mother's stories and when he is older they come back to him as a source of comfort. As a man he learns to tell stories, first those of his mother and later his own. Lalami's novel is Mustafa's attempt to set the record straight and tell the true story of the Spanish expedition to "La Florida" in search of gold and to spread the King's empire as well as Catholicism. 
 In the beginning, chapters describing the expedition alternate with chapters about Mustafa's history starting with his birth. Eventually the two tales merge into the present. Mustafa wants to tell his version of the events because as a slave his account was not sought when the official record was drawn up. Only the three Castilian gentlemen, Dorantes, Castillo and Cabeza de Vaca, were required to make the Joint Report for the King. But as Mustafa listens to the story they tell, he notes all they omit and how they misrepresent certain aspects of their time among the Indians. Mustafa says, "What each of us wants, in the end, whether he is black or white, master or slave, rich or poor, man or woman, is to be remembered after his death." And so he sets down his account, hopefully for posterity, of "truth in the guise of entertainment." Here Lalami looks at the very nature of storytelling; its motivation and purpose. 
 A bit slow to start, the narration soon becomes riveting. The adventures that befall Mustafa are at once appalling and spell-binding. The reader witnesses the follies of the Spanish would-be conquerors who carelessly commit atrocities against the Indians whom they consider inferior savages and give "new names to everything around them, as though they were the All-knowing God in the Garden of Eden." One cannot help but draw parallels to the experiences of other attempts, both historical and current, of conquering nations. Mustapha says, "How strange, I remember thinking, how utterly strange were the ways of the Castilians - just by saying that something was so, they believed that it was. I know now that these conquerors, like many others before them, and no doubt like others after, gave speeches not to voice the truth, but to create it." 
 Lalami also looks at religion and identity. Mustafa, a Muslim, is forced to "convert" to Catholicism when he is enslaved and summarily christened and given a new name. Although the others now call him Estebanico, he never truly relinquishes his name as he says, "A name is precious; it carries inside it a language, a history, a set of traditions, a particular way of looking at the world." To the reader, he will always be Mustafa ibn Muhammad ibn Abdussalam al-Zamori. In the same respect, he never truly converts, keeping true to his faith throughout even if he cannot practice it openly. He muses, "Standing in that half-finished church, surrounded by statues of prophets and saints, I wondered why God created so many varieties of faiths in the world if He intended all of us to worship Him in the same fashion. This thought had never occurred to me when I was a young boy memorizing the Holy Qur'an, but as I spent time with the Indians I came to see how limiting the notion of one true faith really was. Was the diversity in our beliefs, not their unity, the lesson God wanted to impart? Surely it would have been in His power to make us of one faith if that had been His wish. Now the idea there was only one set of stories for all of mankind seemed strange to me." There is much food for thought in that one paragraph. 
 The writing is full of beautiful metaphors such as, "To overcome my fear, I shackled myself with hope, its links heavier than any metal known to man." And describing the feeling of finally being able to quench his thirst after days without water: "It was the same kind of pain I used to get when I broke the fast on the first night of Ramadan, a feeling of being at once satiated and yet still thirsty." The descriptions of nature and the Indians are also lovely. The reader is transported to these strange, exotic scenes, experiencing them through all the senses. 
 One of my favorite metaphors and one which exemplifies the novel's theme of storytelling is: "Telling a story is like sowing a seed - you always hope to see it become a beautiful tree, with firm roots and branches that soar up in the sky. But it is a peculiar sowing, for you will never know whether your seed sprouts or dies." For this reader, the seed that Lalami has sown blooms magnificently. 
 P.S. Here is a link to an interview with the author: 
 https://www.moroccoworldnews.com/2016...

A wonderful insightful story with a beautiful character about the early Spanish expeditions to the Americas. I enjoyed this book which contained a very different depiction from our high school history courses. It is well written and entertaining.

Ugh. This book was unbelievably boring. I don't how it made its way onto so many "best of" lists. It makes no sense to me. Maybe 1.5 stars because it picked up a bit around the end when the survivors travel to Spanish Mexico. 
 What's so ironically awful about this book is that storytelling is a central theme. And yet quality of storytelling is exactly what this book is lacking. It sort of just plods along with no sense of momentum or suspense, meandering in a manner as lost as the main characters, and with mind-numbingly simplistic prose. It's like reading an encyclopedia. There's not a single beautiful or profound line in the whole darn thing. 
 And the characters are all really monochromatic, especially the Spaniards and Native Americans, but even Estebanico/Mustafa is sort of one-dimensional. Oh, and boring. Omg is he boring. 
 The whole thing. Boring boring boring.
I guess I missed the boat yet again on another Booker prize. Great premise, but I couldn't get interested.
Just could not get into it.

I really wish this had a map, but then that gave it the extended feeling of being a parable, of being a myth. Excellent consequence since it is based on true events, however fictionalized or hypothesized. 
 Plus, I ended up pulling out my own map and determining for myself the track of the expedition and survivors... The sparse, clear storytelling makes that almost straightforward to figure out. 
 Still. A map would be nice. But the heart aching story was enough. This narrative questions what is humanity, what is authority in the face of equalizing hardship? And should force us to consider every single bit of history we learn and try to relearn it. It isn't enough to say history belongs to the victor.

Review: The Moor's Account (aka A Literary Sleep Aid) 
 You know what? Forget this. 
 This is so boring I can't put it into words. I could hardly stay awake. I had to reread several pages because I would zone out. The only part I was interested in was Mustafa's past. I gave zero craps for the genocidal Castilians. They got what they deserved, the greedy, stealing fucks.
Brilliant! I am overwhelmed by the novel's monumental power and grace.

book_b.title: We3
book_b.user_review: I get that this topic is relevant. We do test on animals; we do have flexible morals when it comes to technology and "lesser creatures" and military goals; we should examine the choices we make and the ethics thereof. But it was painful to read. Just animal torture and chaotic bloody animal violence and lack of agency and people being horrible. People. Being. Horrible. I just don't think this depicted a deep or critical enough lens to the story & theme to really justify the horror I felt looking at these things happening to these animals. They didn't even get to be angry and avenge themselves righteously... I had to hide the book from myself until I could return it to the library.

sample_reviews.review_text: Great story but way too graphic!
Short, sweet, and creepy

unning on the familiar sci-fi trope of science run amok of morality We3takes three household pets and turns them in to cybernetic killing machines designed to be used in the battefields. With enhanced intelligence and cybernetic suits the three animals, still at the core just simple animals, are equal parts terrifying and heartrending. Art duty rests on the shoulders of semi-frequent Morrison collaborator Frank Quietly. I'm not a huge fan of Quietly's art, it doesn't really mesh with my own expectations, but his style here (particularly with the humans being antagonists and our protagonists being animals) serves the story well and his attention to detail when it comes to the technology used in the three animals is nothing short of stunning. If you are an animal lover this is a story will definitely touch and definitely disturb you.

I've read a few GNs this year, but this was the worst one for me. It was very difficult to understand, the art was very scattered and non-chronological, and the story was not coherent. It seemed to just jump into things with no backstory or purpose. 
 I feel like with an idea like that, the author could have done so much more, but it just seemed to be throwing an idea together and not expounding on it at all. 
 Anyway, my least favorite GN I've read so far.

Quick review: 
 Extremely enjoyable book. Frank Quietly, the illustrator did exceptional work. His layouts are inventive and his points of view are dynamic. This is not my first encounter with Grant Morrison but it is by far the most satisfying and memorable. I always find it interesting to see how authors anthropomorphize pets and I was pleased with the job he did. The quirks that each of the 3 show serve only to make it easier to cheer them on and dampen the violence of their escape and flight. Screw Fly Away Home, I want a movie adaptation of We3.

This was wonderful, and so, so sad. I found myself tearing up on more than one occasion. Maybe it won't be as emotional for someone that doesn't absolutely love animals, or wasn't already a little sad in the first place. 
 When a friend handed this to me, I thought it would be silly. It certainly looks like something I would laugh at, if I just paid attention to the cover. But I'm amazed at how amazing this story was, considering it was only a little over 100 pages. Beautiful art and a beautiful, yet tragic story.. Definitely worth five stars and an add to the Wish-List.

Issue 1: Too gory for me. Not really interesting. 
 Issue 2: Still too gory. I really can't take comic book violence. It makes it so I can't concentrate on anything else in the story. I'm sure there's a lot of great stuff going on with the animals, but their language is too disjointed and the violence is too intense for me to concentrate correctly... 
 Issue 3: Better than the first two. The motivation of the animals and their fighting was interesting. Sort of get the ending, but it wasn't really a kick for me. 
 Overall: I like the message of the comics, but the comics themselves were too gory for me and a little hard to understand.
Just re-read this with my son. Must be one of my favourite stories ever.
Fantastic!!

Grant Morrison - Author 
 Frank Quietly - Illustrator 
 4.5/5 stars 
 Bandit the dog, Tinker the cat and Pirate the rabbit are all part of a top-secret government program to radically modify housepets into military killing machines. The three are decommissioned and scheduled for euthanization but the doctor who was in charge of the project cannot bear to put the animals down and instead helps them escape. The three housepets, horribly altered by human ingenuity, must find their way to the homes they were stolen from while evading the dogged pursuit of the U.S. military and the remnants of the program they left behind. 
 The story is fantastic; Mr. Morrison is perhaps the greatest writer of comic books working today. The art is powerful and emotionally evocative; Mr. Quietly shines in this collection. My only quibble would be with the length -- 3 issues is just too short for such a creative team working with such a promising premise. Highly recommended.

reference_books.title: Never Too Far (Rosemary Beach, #2; Too Far, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
"...you, Blaire Wynn, make my life complete. 
 Blaire is back in Alabama and she now has a secret of her own. 
 She goes to the graveyard to visit the graves of her mom and sister. She asks her mother for advice, even though she knows she won't get an answer. It simply makes her feel better. Then a car too fancy for her small hometown pulls up. It's Bethy. As Blaire and Bethy start to walk toward the car to go grab a bite to eat, Blaire hears a barely audible whisper saying, "There's your answer." 
 Bethy wants her to come back to Rosemary Beach, but Blaire knows she won't be able to face Rush. After Cain takes a trip down to Rosemary and gets himself punched in the face after questioning Rush, Blaire calls him to see where he is. She then asks Bethy to take her to Cain (who says he's in a hotel outside of Rosemary) so she can drive his truck back home. 
 She never planned on going to Rosemary Beach, but when she calls Cain again, she finds out he's actually in Sumit with Callie. Realizing it's wrong of Cain to string Callie along, Blaire asks Bethy if she can stay with her for the night. 
 Let me tell you how good this book is. I was reading it at work, at the end of my shift. When it was time to go, I did NOT want to put the book down. I have never not wanted to leave work and go home. Never Too Far has been a perpetual thought in my mind since the first sentence. 
 I was beginning to get annoyed with Blaire. I know why she wanted to stay away from Rush, I completely understand. But I was team Rush all the way and wanted Blaire to give in to him. Then Rush screws up a couple of times and I'm practically yelling at him to get it together. Any book that can make me feel that much frustration, is a keeper. 
 Near the ending, Grant seems to be the voice of reason and I was cheering him on, but then Abe (Blaire's dad) steps in and drops an unexpected truth bomb. I was glad he was finally being a man and telling Rush what he didn't know. The real story behind it all. 
 The last paragraph was a favorite of mine. I was overjoyed. Will Rush and Blaire get their HEA? We'll see.... 
 Recommended to everyone!

reference_books.title: White Hot Kiss (The Dark Elements, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I lost myself the moment I found you. 
 If you get to the part, in this book, where that quote is found and your head's not swirling with emotion? Then you're not human. That, or you're just not that into YA fiction or the paranormal. 
 It took a little while for me to really start feeling this book. Which is weird because, usually, anything that Jennifer L. Armentrout writes has me hooked within the first two chapters, three at the most. But....holy bat brains, batman! From somewhere around the time that Layla find out who her mom is, until the very last word on the last page, I could not stop reading! 
 Of course, any book that starts out with: 
 There was a demon in McDonald's. And it had a powerful hunger for Big Macs. 
 ....is probably going to be good. And this one exceeded my expectations. 
 Don't think that I didn't notice those little instances that paid homage to Supernatural, either. The 1969 Chevy Impala? (except Dean Winchester's is a 1967 Chevy Impala) The demon leaving a possessed body the same way? (except the smoke was red instead of black) Roth's favorite song being Paradise City? (everyone knows Dean loves the older music) Oh yeah, I noticed. Supernatural is even mentioned in the book. So thank you for that Mrs. Armentrout. I love that show and I love your book! 
 Now, as for the love triangle...at first, I didn't know if I liked Roth or Zayne better, but by the end, I was Team Roth all the way. What he did for Layla (well, the entire universe, actually) was something that any card-carrying demon would never do. If any of the Wardens wanted him dead after that selfless act, then...they should have their wings pulled off. (Ooh, was that too harsh? Good thing we are talking about fictional characters) :) 
 Recommended to: fans of Jennifer L. Armentrout, fans of YA fiction, fans of the paranormal, fans of Supernatural, or just everyone!

reference_books.title: Grave Witch (Alex Craft, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Alex Craft is a grave witch, meaning she deals with the dead. She has turned her talent into a career and reluctantly works along side Detective Falin Andrews. When she is attacked and a dark magic spell threatens her life, she realizes she is somehow connected to the case. 
 I am really glad I picked this book up. There were so many interesting and exciting aspects to this story that I never got bored with it. There was a perfect balance of magic and mystery. I thought I had Falin all figured out, but I was wrong. And Death...wow. I wish there would have been more of him in the book. Being all dark and mysterious just made me want to read more about him. I'm just as torn as Alex between the two of them. (Death and Falin) Maybe there will be more of Death in the second book. From what I've heard, it's even better than this one. Which means I will probably be purchasing it real soon.

book_a.user_review: I like it a lot, but I also like series really well on tv, so that helped!

sample_reviews.review_text: Loin d'etre un livre exceptionnel, cette premiere aventure de Vicki Nelson est sympathique. A lire quand on veut decompresser!!!

Okay, that may be borring but what' a coincidence: 
 "Although you know I enjoy talking to you, did you have an actual reason for calling?" 
 "Well, I was wondering if you might be coming down for Easter." 
 "Easter?" 
 "It's this weekend. I won't be working tomorrow or Monday, we could have four whole days together."
