I will admit that this lingering cold may be coloring my opinion of this book. Other reviewers are correct, there is nothing groundbreaking, earth shattering, or intellectual about this book. There are other much better vampire books out there. The characters were stereotypical and the plot rather blase with no surprise twists. What suspense Huff was trying to create failed due to the evident plot and its requirements. While Vicki may be a strong female character, her overly abrasive and defensive attitude dominated over her deductive capabilities which should have been developed more. As another reviewer mentioned, more emphasis on Henry's need to feed connected with sex would have made for a much darker and more interesting character. Celluci needs something evil to happen to him. Make him disappear. There was nothing attractive about his character. Evil little nerd was the epitome of all stereotypes. 
 On the upside, the little D&D scene made me laugh. 
 What is with editors these days? I need to research their actual process. Shouldn't they be catching all the grammar errors, incomplete sentences, etc? Yeesh. This is the second series I've delved into with consistent errors throughout the writing.

Blood Price is pretty fun urban fantasy. Victoria Nelson is an ex-cop -- due to a disability, even, which makes her unable to see at night, and has reduced her peripheral vision severely -- who is working as a private investigator. She stumbles onto a fresh crime scene, which is bad enough, and then gets caught up in trying to catch the culprit, something which quickly proves to be beyond anything she'd imagined, because the killers are supernatural in nature. And in the course of her investigation, she stumbles upon Henry Fitzroy -- a bastard son of King Henry VIII, supposedly dead since he was seventeen years old. He turns out to be a vampire. And a good guy. 
 It's not the most amazing prose in the world, but it is a good read if that's what you're interested in, and I promise Henry doesn't sparkle. It wasn't toe-curlingly tense or anything -- neither in terms of the mystery, nor in terms of the sexual tension -- but there were some reasonable dramatic scenes. 
 The geek stereotype killer didn't do much for me, though.

I heard about this book by a friend and because I have finished so many important series, I thought it would be a good idea to start with this one. Okay, the story is easy and short to explain. There is a student, who awake demons because he feel hurt by other students. There is a woman, who hunting him and a vampire, who helps her. Ok, there are some other things around but unfortunately not so many. So I have to say that the book was, well, ok but not very good. Some important things for a good story are missing. First, the author doesn't introduce the main character very well, so I don't know how Henry, the vampire, looks like? And Vicki? Yes, she has glasses (this was mentioned very very often) but other infos? No. 
 Then the story around the killing is without tension because you know very fast who is the murder of the people. And yeah, there is a ex-boyfriend from Vicki - Michael and some other not very important people. I don't know, maybe my standard is to high because I read so many very good books in the vampire genre. But this book wasn't good for me and I think I don't read the sequel 2-5.

This book is almost 20 years old - the first of one of the early urban fantasy series. It was good, but I had a really hard time with how dated it felt. A major component of the plot had to do with not being able to reach people who weren't at home. The lack of cell phones and PDAs made it seem dated to me, not contemporary, and I prefer contemporary urban fantasy. BUT I think there's a good chance that this series has kept going for the last 20 years (need to look it up), so it could have evolved into something I will love, like Hamilton's Anita Blake series did. Comments about the series progression would be great, goodreaders. 
 This story is about a former homocide detective in Toronto, Vicki Nelson, who quit the force a little while ago because she is losing her vision. She's a PI now, though not a very sucessful one. She happens to be near the scene of the first of a string of gruesome throat-ripped-out murders, and later is hired by the girlfriend of that first victim to investigate. Along the way, she meets Henry Fitzroy, a vampire, who is trying to find the killer because he doesn't want the media hype about vampires ultimately leading to his own death. His kind don't like attention, and seldom kill unless they are newly made without a mentor. The two team up. Along the way, you get to know the real culprit, so I suppose it's really not a mystery to the reader, just to the hero and heroine.

Tried so hard to like it -- but the characters are flat and the language is dreary. 
 Back in the Seventies, there was a classic TV movie called KOLCHAK: THE NIGHT STALKER about a wise guy reporter tracking down a vampire in modern Las Vegas. This story is EXACTLY the same -- except the heroine is a dead bore, and Toronto sure ain't Las Vegas! 
 Things improve a little when Henry Fitzroy shows up -- he's a vampire with a heart of gold, and a romantic past in the court of Henry VIII. But he can't save the story because the writing is so drab, and Vicky and her cop ex-boyfriend are so irritatingly bland. 
 I gave Tanya Huff a chance -- but this is the first and last BLOOD book I'm ever going to read!

I was thinking of this as a one and a half stars, but Vicky was pretty likable, so she got an extra half star all by herself. She was the only thing I found interesting, but I didn't find anything around her really caught my attention. It felt like I was reading an episode of Forever Knight.

Blood Price and Blood Trail made extremely interesting reads, with an engaging storyline and likeable host of characters. We've all seen female protagonists like Vicki Nelson before - tough, stubborn and independent, with a background in the social justice department, and otherwise fairly normal in modern urban fantasies. What made Vicki more likeable, or at least more believable, is her unique handicap, rentinitis pigmentosa. Whoever's heard of a female detective that wore chunky glasses and is virtually blind in the dark? I loved that aspect of her character; it made her so much more approachable because she has a very real weakness. 
 The "suitors" department is composed of Mike Celluci and Henry Fitzroy. While I was slightly irritated that Tanya Huff didn't veer away from giving the heroine multiple admirers, it did spice up the story a little to have some competition for her attentions, and the story never becomes wholy romance-centric (something which I'm glad of). Vicki does not become instantly attractive to every male she meets, nor does she pick up anymore suitors than that. Mike fills the requirement of "best buddy with benefits", but it was Henry that really grabbed my interest. 
 Henry, unlike many of the vampires that fill recent paranormal romances, is just what he is. He drinks blood, he doesn't go out into the sun, and he lives for ages. Rather than writing a revisionist version of vampires, Huff adds a sense of normality and realism to Henry's vampire. At some point, Henry is suffocated and simply tired of how many years he's lived for, but torn by his fear of dying at the same time. This is something that is rarely covered in vampire novels - vampires have super strength and longevity, but if you've lived for several centuries and have watched people you loved die around you repeatedly, it'd be surprising if there wasn't any mental stress involved. More than Celluci and Vicki, Henry's character has incredible depth, and his "vampire issues" make him more human, if possible. And really, who can resist the awesome idea that Henry Fitzroy, bastard son of Henry VIII, is a vampire and romance writer? Historical fans are guaranteed to get a kick out of that one. 
 The best thing about these books are the amazingly down-to-earth manner which Huff gives to all her characters, regardless of their race. Both Henry and the werewolves in Blood Trail are physically different from humans, but the way they act and talk are no different at times. The observations Vicki makes at the Heerkens' home draws many parallels between them and the way normal human families would operate.

INITIAL THOUGHTS 
 The only thing about this book that rises above mediocrity is the female protagonist Vicki Nelson; she is a great character and the sole reason I felt engaged throughout the run-of-the-mill story. It's also likely I will read the rest of the series on the strength of her character. 
 Although I've given it a "low" rating, I wouldn't discourage anyone from reading Blood Price as it is by no means terrible (I enjoyed it for the most part, it was never a chore to read so I breezed through it pretty quickly), it's just not a book that will live long in the memory. As for the contrived ending...I lost count of the number of times I rolled my eyes. 
 FULL REVIEW PENDING

book_b.title: The Grownup
book_b.user_review:
The Grownup is a short story from author Gillian Flynn who, once again, uses her skill for twists you didn't see coming. I was actually impressed with how much suspense she shoved into this book, which took me less than an hour to read. Not only does she add in a supernatural angle, but also introduces the reader to a few classic ghost stories. 
 One thing I wasn't much of a fan of was the ending. Only because I would've liked for it to more complete instead of leaving me guessing which scenario was true. With that being said, it was better than most of the short stories I've read recently. If you are a fan of Gillian Flynn's Gone Girl novel, or just want to grab a quick anticipatory read, you should definitely consider this one. 
 I received this book from Blogging For Books for this review.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I don't know what this book is supposed to be, but it just feels like something written for a little while and then the author suddenly lost interest in the story and so The End.

book_b.title: Mary, Mary (Alex Cross, #11)
book_b.user_review: This Alex Cross book was much better than the last couple in the series.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Mary Mary is an Alex Cross novel, and that normally would be a good thing, except that it isn't. Patterson started writing Cross novels in 1992, with Along Came a Spider, which instituted the forumla of pitting Alex against this week's serial killer. Along Came a Spider pitted Cross, a psychiatrist who doubles as a Washington D.C. homicide detective, against a copycat serial killer seeking to emulate the best work of others. Mary Mary is the next of the line; one hopes it's the last. 
 Having said that, if you've never read any of the Alex Cross novels, please read this one first. That way, you'll get the lousy one out of the way, and you can enjoy Kiss The Girls and even mediocre fare like The Big Bad Wolf that much more. But if you have read even one Alex Cross novel -- or any book more advanced than The Very Hungry Caterpillar, give Mary Mary a very wide berth. 
 Just to give the basics here very quickly, Alex Cross is an African-American detective -- now special assistant to the FBI director -- from the mean streets of Southeast D.C. He lives with his grandmother, the ancient Nana Mama, who is forever telling him to spend more time with his young family. His young family, Damon, Jannie, and Little Alex, are forever telling him to spend more time with them. His ex-girlfriend Christine, the mother of Little Alex, is trying to gain custody of the child on the grounds that Alex doesn't spend enough time at home with him. Alex feels continually guilty about chasing down serial killers all the time and not spending enough time with his family. Let me know if you begin to sense a trend here. 
 So, it should be no surprise that Patterson sends Alex and his family to Disneyland, where Alex is immediately called away to investigate the gruesome knifework of yet another serial killer. (Authors can be cruel that way.) And there is nothing wrong with this in theory, I suppose; having Alex miss his family humanizes him somewhat, makes him less of a bloodless superman, and provides counterpoint with the lives of the serial killers that he faces. 
 But Patterson has, I feel, beat this particular drum once too often, and beats it again and again until your ears pound. If you've never read an Alex Cross novel, it may not bother you; people who have read them all will cringe at every page. At one point, early on, Nana Mama expresses a desire to see Siberia, and the reader thinks, yes, that's a very good idea, let's send her, and forget her return ticket. 
 What you lose out of all of this, unfortunately, is Alex himself. By putting Alex mostly out on the West Coast, it separates him from Southeast, and we lose virtually every bit of local color or anything that makes the books interesting and true. All that's left is Alex clashing with bigoted LAPD officials and trying to track down the clues that will inevitably lead to the serial killer. 
 It is the serial killer -- known, unimaginitively, as the "Hollywood Stalker" -- who is terrorizing Los Angeles, doing away with high-priced starlets and local anchors and anyone that he (or she) disapproves of, or so it seems. It is the serial killers who make the Alex Cross books so interesting -- Patterson usually even allows them to narrate (in third person) about half of the books anyway. The last Alex Cross entry was The Wolf, a psychotic ex-KGB agent who enjoyed zamochit, which means breaking every single bone in the victim's body, even the tiny bones in your ear and those special bones that Ken Griffey breaks in his hand every so often. It would be hard to top that. 
 Patterson doesn't even try. This killer -- who calls himself "The Storyteller" is lame in the extreme. We know he's out there because -- wait for it -- he sends e-mails to a reporter at the L.A. Times announcing his kills, along with juicy little details that only the true killer would know. Which would be fine, just fine, if only Patterson hadn't used the exact same schtick in Kiss The Girls with "The Gentleman Caller". And he was a lot more romantic and literary and interesting than the Storyteller, who just hacks people up for giggles. 
 Does the Storyteller have a cunning plan? Sure he does! It was even original when Agatha Christie thought it up in 1936. (You may think I am kidding; I am not.) 
 Mary Mary is flat, uninteresting, and not worthy to be mentioned with the rest of the Alex Cross books. There is nothing in its pages to recommend it to anyone, so bad it is. I encourage you to read it only if you buy it used on Amazon (I am listing my copy as soon as I finish this review, really I am) or find some poor soul willing to give you his copy. 
 Why is it so bad? Well, if you look at James Patterson's Wikipedia page, it says that in 2005 he published a "Women's Murder Club" book, and three other books, and has another book coming out in February. If Mary Mary is bad, and it very deeply is, then it's because nobody has spent any time on it to make it better. Maybe it's time that Patterson took Nana Mama's advice. I'm sure his family would be glad to see him again.

reference_books.title: The Play
reference_books.review_text:
5 stars 
 I'm not sure if I'm going to be able to accurately tell how much I loved this book. It wasn't just the story that the characters were telling, but also the awareness that it's bringing to a subject that I'm very passionate about. 
 Lachlan McGregor isn't like his cousins. He's dark, mysterious, and broody. At least, that's how most perceive him. He has a past that constantly threatens to ruin everything he's worked for, everything he's worked to become. 
 Kayla Moore - forever the unattached fifth wheel. She's happy for her friends and the endless amount of joy that they've found, it's just not something that she wants. 
 These two both have their own secrets, some darker than others. When they finally get together it's like a firework stand went off. Lachlan is intense and passionate, and not just in the bedroom. He found a cause he cares about, one that seems to get all of the negative feedback these days. He wants to shed some light on it and make people see the positive in it. 
 Karina Halle isn't just writing about it. The amount of research she had to have put into this is amazing. She's not just researching to bring attention to it, she's donating to it, trying to do good and help change the way pit bulls are looked at by so many. I connected to this story on a deeper level because of it. 
 You will fall in love with Kayla and Lachlan. A deep, heartfelt story of finding love unexpectedly and having to make decisions that could change both of your lives. Make the smart choose? Or the reckless one? Reckless doesn't always mean wrong. 
 **Read and reviewed for FMR Book Grind**

reference_books.title: Wait (Bleeding Stars, #4)
reference_books.review_text:
5 stars 
 This is the kind of series that I love. Where it starts off amazing and with every book that is added they get better and better. You don't think it's possible, but somehow Ms. Jackson continues to completely blow me away. Wait is just another example of how phenomenal her writing is. 
 Austin and Edie both have their own demons that they have faced, each with their own set of hurdles they've had to endure. These are battles they fight daily. No one has been able to give them any reprieve from the nightmares, not until they find each other. There is this imaginary tether that holds them together. The pull they feel is tangible. Each night they're chasing away each other's demons just by being with each other. It's not about sex, but strengthening each other, having someone to share their fears with, someone to hold them when it all becomes too much. But one mistake changes it all and sends Edie running. It's years before they cross paths again. This time, Austin won't have her running away from him. 
 All of the emotions I experienced while reading mirrored that of the scene in the book. I could feel elated about a reunion that I could see the great possibilities in, fear when the past catapults into the present, and sadness when the horrors they've experienced haunt them each night. The strength they project into each other was beautiful, how just a hand to hold gave them everything they needed to battle it. A.L. Jackson creates the best heroes and heroines. While at times they can seem weak, they are anything but. They fight everyday just to continue living. I love when they find that one thing, that one person who lifts them up and makes it that much easier. When they realize that they're worth fighting for, when the battles aren't controlling their lives, that's the point that I really fall in love with them. From that point on, they keep going forward, moving up, and you'll see a continuous smile on my face. It's all here in Wait. Everything that makes a fabulous story is brought out, and I could not have loved it more. I say every new book in this series is my favorite because they get that much better with each one.

reference_books.title: Text 2 Lovers (2 Lovers, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
4 stars 
 This book was so much fun to read! I've never read a book by either of these authors, but after this I'll be going and finding more. These two authors wrote very well together. There was no place where I thought the writing was choppy or where the story didn't work. It was pretty much flawless! 
 Dani as she's known, is "too nice" as everyone around her puts it. Even the bartender they've known for a whole 5 seconds agrees with her best friend. After finding her boyfriend lip locked with his neighbor, she realizes that was 8 months of her life wasted. Did she call him names? Throw things? Burn his stuff? Nope. Just sat and stared and eventually turned around and left. After a few too many shots of tequila, and with the encouragement of her best friend and new bartender friend, she finds herself texting insult after insult full of expletives to her now ex. Until she finds out that it wasn't her ex she was texting, but yet a willing stranger. 
 Ram doesn't know who the number texting him is from, but he's enjoying the back and forth. Whoever her ex was must have deserved the lashing. Now, he's just trying to keep her talking. 
 I loved how the interaction went between Ram and Dani. They clicked on a whole other level, even just over text messages and then phone calls. When they do actually meet, it's fireworks. And continues to be that way until drama inserts her way into their lives. This story was so great. Witty banter, a heroine trying to grow a backbone and learn to say NO while having fun, and some best friends that are there to make things a little more entertaining and awkward. I couldn't put this book down. And you can bet that I was wearing a smile the entire time. That's how much fun it was. If you need a good romantic comedy with a little drama to keep things interesting, Text 2 Lovers has it covered. 
 **Read and reviewed for FMR Book Grind**

reference_books.title: Where Lightning Strikes (Bleeding Stars, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
5 Stars 
 A.L. Jackson somehow has a way of completely obliterating whatever expectations I have for a book of hers. The way she writes is beyond compare. The way she describes things paint the perfect picture that I can clearly envision in my head. 
 I thought I was ready for Lyrik's story. What I didn't expect was the way my heart would break for him and all that he's gone through. The men of Sunder have always had a bevy of women that would kill for one night with them. While it has always been great, Lyrik has had his eye set on one girl. The red-headed beauty at Charlie's bar. "Red", as he calls her, doesn't give him the time of day. She has up this front and dishes out sarcasm that usually keeps the boys at bay. Only, Lyrik isn't like most. He feels he should keep his distance, but he simply can't. 
 Tamar has a very hard exterior. She only lets a few select people see parts of her. She's been hidden behind her wall so long that she thought she was safe. She thought she was unbreakable. What she didn't expect was for Lyrik West to pick away at her until she broke. She reveals parts of herself that no one else knows about. He slowly becomes everything to her. Only, he's just as closed off as she is. 
 "And there you were, breaking up all the broken, brittle parts and making room for something different. For something better. Waking me up from the dead. Making me realize what it's like to feel again. Making me feel things I've never felt before. You were making room for you." 
 They both have this hard outer shell that they use as a shield. To shield themselves from getting to close to anyone, but when they find someone who is just as broken as they are, their souls seem to call out to each other. 
 The build-up that led up to the storm was palpable. It was as if I was standing in the middle of the storm itself. I felt the electricity building, the storm growing, and I knew that when the lightning struck, it would decimate me. Both of their stories are tragic, but Lyrik's past prevents him from allowing himself to feel, to even think "more" is possible. He helped Tamar overcome her fears and be brave. Now he just has to see that he too can be just as brave. 
 I cried because I was sad. I cried because I felt the gut-twisting pain that can cripple you. Last of all, I cried out of pure happiness. By the time all of Sunder has told their story, I feel like I'm going to be a complete wreck. When it comes to book boyfriends, it's hard to pick favorites for me, but these boys are making it easy. Lyrik is up high on that list with Baz. When it's all said and done, I have a feeling those first four spots will be reserved for all of the Sunder boys.

reference_books.review_text:
4 stars 
 These quick reads are just what's needed to get you in the holiday spirit. Nicholas is a very reclusive man. He's not one for socializing and tends to keep to himself, but when he's found the one his heart desires, he's willing to do whatever it takes to get her to come to him. 
 Christmas, her name is fitting for her. It's her favorite holiday, but not just that, she's always bright and cheerful. She has a way about her that attracts people to her and makes them smile. She loves the season and seeing all of it through children's eyes. There's nothing better to her. When she gets the message that she's wanted at Nicholas' house, she can't imagine what for. What she gets is an unexpected welcome. 
 Insanely sweet, over the top, and down right dirty, Alexa Riley knows just what we need. I've come to really love these novellas. They take me away from everything that is happening. They're just the distraction that I currently need.

book_a.title: The Way We Fall (The Story of Us, #1)
book_a.user_review:
*Reviewed for FMR Book Grind* 
 5 stars 
 I never truly know what to expect from Cassia Leo. She continually finds ways to give us books that completely annihilate me in the best of ways. 
 The Way We Fall is, in my opinion, her best work to date, which is saying a lot. It tells the story of two people who are so tightly intertwined that no matter what obstacles, what life throws their way, how many changes are made in their individual lives, they always find their way back to each other. 
 Rory is an aspiring writer. In the mean time, while she's slowly writing her first book, she works at a local grocery store. When a part of her history walks in the door, it's the last thing she expected. 
 Houston loved Rory. He really did. But secrets have a way of tearing apart everything that is and could be good. This secret that was thrusted upon him is one that could destroy everything, that already has in a sense. 
 I tried to predict what was going to happen, what the secret was. When I found out, it blew me away. It wasn't anything like what I expected. But that's the thing about Cassia Leo's stories, always expect the unexpected with her. She throws us curveballs that we never saw coming. She tears us apart, makes us feel everything these characters are going through and then slowly rebuilds us piece by piece. It's the sweetest torture. And I wouldn't want it any other way.

However, things didn't really start happening between them until after Haley her best friend and Houston sister killed herself. So as you can imagine this is a relationship built on a tragedy, the tragedy filled with lies and secrets. The book shifts between present and past and different POV, I have to say these are always my favorite books. Add in a little crazy, a lot of drama, a little passion, and I can't put the book down! And that ending, how could I not pick up the next book ASAP???

This is the first book in The Story of Us series and words cannot describe how much I loved this book. It is such a well-written story. When you read the last page, you will want to read it again. 
 It's hard to talk about the book without giving away spoilers, so I will just tell you about the characters. Such strong characters, you cant help but fall in love with them. This is a touching story of love, loss, sacrifices, and broken hearts. 
 Houston is such a beautiful soul, but he has a secret that is killing him on the inside. A secret that could shatter the heart of the one girl he truly loves. 
 Rory and Hallie are best friends, and they have such a strong bond. They share everything, but some things just cant be shared. 
 Rory has loved Houston forever, even when she thought he didn't notice her. Houston is Hallie's brother and he will do anything to protect her. 
 You will also meet some other characters who play a big part in this book, and their lives will be affected as this story unfolds. There were parts in this book that broke my heart, and then there were parts where I laughed out loud. This is what I love about this author. She brings all these different emotions out in you. 
 Amazing characters and a beautifully written story. Well done, Cassia Leo. 10/10

I have to say from the start this book contains an affair that is appears you should be hoping for and that is never I book I enjoy to read. Had it been the same story with out the man being married it would have been a good story but I would never recommend it to anybody because of that part of the plot line.

The Way We Fall was an interesting read, it was rather easy and I got through it within one sitting. The Way we Fall challenges subjects like suicide, affairs and [spoiler]abortions[/spoiler], that with all the negativity that seemed to seep from the pages put a bit of a downer on the storyline. I thought the ending would've been predictable but I was very shocked to find the complete opposite - it was refreshing for once to find a contemporary that will defy the laws of romance.

I'm a student. I live in a uni hall and I occasionally visit home when I can't afford food. Why is this relevant? It's relevant because when I go home, I immediately go to the kitchen in search for snacks. This book honestly felt like my parents left a bag of chicken chips in the pantry. And I, innocent and hungry, grab these chips, make myself a cup of tea -you know, getting all comfortable and shit- and park myself on the family couch like one of those French girls. And then I begin my usual decent into the bag, shovelling a hand full into my mouth, only to become an unsuspecting victim to god awful stale chips. 
 I was prepared for a good, nice, sweet, delicious story of young love but all I was given was an incredibly boring and disappointing love story. I wasn't even frustrated with this book. I just genuinely didn't care to finish it. 
 89% DNF do not understand why it has high ratings.

I did not finish it. I barely got through the first couple of chapters. There was nothing wrong with the writing itself or the story-line. The characters, right from the start just annoyed me. During the flash-back portion of the beginning of the book, they were irrational. 
 Maybe it was just that I wasn't in the mood. I usually love these types of books. This one just irritated me and I have no definitive answer as to why. I had also read two other books the same day that I started this and I loved them. This one did not compete with them.

I went into this book completely blind and I now have my eyes wide open thrilled at what I have seen. 
 This complicated yet at times very simple love story kept me riveted. The second chance romance of Houston and Rory, who find themselves seeing each other for the first time in 5 years, meeting by chance at her workplace. It's a shock to both their systems since neither of them truly moved on. Sure, Houston is married but the minute he is alone with her and has her scent firmly in his grasp, he knows he made a huge mistake ever letting her go. As they try to be 
 as cordial and unaffected as possible, simmering just below the surface is the love that never truly died. Both suffered an excruciating loss and although it led them to finding each other all those years ago after crushing on each other from afar, it was only a matter of time that they would both get their hearts broken. 
 As they attempt to put the pieces back together of their damaged souls, the threat of not only a desperate wife but a vital truth kept from Rory, it becomes a long hard climb to see if they can make their way back to each other. 
 What a wonderfully well written beginning to this gripping tale. I have such hope for our couple to find it in their hearts to forgive and move forward but I'm afraid it will be a very difficult journey for both of them. 
 I find both main characters extremely likeable with many of the secondary ones the perfect compliment to their whirlwind romance. 
 I look forward to book two and a satisfying conclusion. 
 Although not a fan of cliffhangers, I don't find myself wanting to throw my ereader in frustration. It will be worth the wait. 
 5 solid stars and highly recommended.

book_b.title: No Pants Required
book_b.user_review:
4 stars 
 This was another case of the "I'm scared to read this story because there is no way it can be better than her last book" -itis. 
 Kim Karr is one of my auto-click authors. Everything I've read is better than the last. Her books are original, humorous, attention grabbing storylines that you can't help but love. I never read the blurb for No Pants Required, but I had some ideas about what I was getting into when I started it. I was wrong on all levels. That's what I get for judging it by its cover. 
 Makayla is ready to make a change. She's stepping out of her comfort zone and moving all the way across the country to prove something to herself and everyone else that really knows her. 
 Camden is in a weird place in his life. The past year has been hectic and confusing. He's ready to get back home to his normal. He just doesn't expect to connect with his seat mate on his plane home. 
 When a chance to join the mile high club goes wrong, that changes the dynamic that you see. If Makayla can just get off of the plane she'll never have to see his face again. Apparently she forgot that life never goes the way you expect it to. 
 I loved everything about this story. Ms. Karr gives us everything. Humor, lots of sexy times that were capital H-O-T, and relationship that while started backwards built into something beautiful. I really didn't expect to love it as much as I did. My fears about new books from my favorite authors, while may be irrational, is very much real. I should know better that Ms. Karr would give us nothing but an exceptional story. 
 **Read and reviewed for FMR Book Grind**

sample_reviews.review_text: Had a tough time finishing this book. It didn't hold my interest long enough to keep reading and once I put it down, it was so damn difficult to muster up enough energy to pick it up again. It can only be described as fluff reading.

** spoiler alert ** 
 There's a couple of things that raise my hackles in books. First is too much co-incidence i.e. the bloke you witness getting a b.j in a nightclub happens to be the guy you sit next to on a plane from NY to Cali, that you try join the mile high club with. Who then turns out to be your bf's colleague and your next door neighbour. TOO MUCH! TOO CONTRIVED! 
 Second hate is when a character has a disastrous relationship with someone who commits an unforgivable sin but then allows that person to perform an intimate sex act on them. I just don't understand it - especially if it doesn't fit with everything else you find out about the character. 
 Regrettably and even whilst picturing the delightful Mitchell Wick as Camden this book didn't float my boat.

This was such a fun, sweet, and wistful story. Camden Waters and Makayla Alexander were wonderful characters to get to know. 
 Both were a bit lost. In a point in their lives where they knew change was needed. Makayla was ahead of game in her move across the country to start fresh. Can needed a gentle nudge, but together they were carefree, and fun. They had a great connection and built a strong friendship...amongst other things. *wink wink* 
 Everything moved at a great pace and I enjoyed their summer as much as they did.

'No Pants Required' by Kim Karr is the perfect summertime read! This absolutely fun and light hearted romantic comedy will completely whisk you away with its' witty and charming characters, laugh out loud moments, and sizzling escapades. I highly recommend you grab your favorite libation, prop up your feet, and dive right into this deliciously sweet and sexy summer read! 
 I would just like to start by saying that I just absolutely adored the characters in this book! 
 Makayla had such an intriguing and quirky personality, and I absolutely loved her inner dialogue. I also really admired that along with her insecurities, she also had great strength and confidence in trying to overcome them. It was quite surprising to me that she had so much sexual confidence, but that's one of the many things that made her relationship with Camden spontaneous and super-hot! Oh, and did I mention her checklist for finding her old self and how fantastic it was? Believe me, this isn't your ordinary checklist that I am speaking of, and Makayla showed great determination and courage in completing it to prove to herself that she could be the spontaneous person she once was! 
 I loved how Camden was strong and steadfast in his beliefs, although he struggled with his anger from his past issues and goals regarding his career. It made him more real and genuine, and it was very refreshing that he was so trustworthy and not wish-washy in his feelings for Makayla. He was so incredibly sweet, playful, and spontaneous which made his character even more charming, sexy, and totally dream worthy! 
 I also appreciated Makayla's and Camden's patience and respect for each other as they worked through their individual struggles within themselves. It ultimately allowed them to build a strong foundation of friendship with each other. Together, their passion was incredible and they made such a fun loving and absolutely adorable couple! 
 Kim Karr has such an impeccable ability in creating heartfelt and true to life characters and weaving them into unique storylines that consume you from beginning to end. The story moved along at a nice and steady pace, and combined with the beach setting made for a very refreshing romance. This is such a fun and enjoyable story that makes for the perfect summer reading escape! 
 *** 5 Stars for me!!***

3.5 Stars! 
 What would make a better beach read than a book set in California, complete with an adorable, dirty-talking lifeguard? No Pants Required hits the spot with its light-hearted humor that's also heavy on the heat, making it the perfect companion for summer holidays. 
 After the one-two punch of losing his brother and having a horrible falling out with his father, Camden Waters is drifting through life. He has moved to California to become a lifeguard instead of using his degree to go into the family business. While in New York to attend a memorial service, he unwittingly meets Makayla at a bar. 
 Makayla is also making changes to her life after being unceremoniously dumped by her fiance. She quits her job, decides to move to California to live with her best friend, and focuses on reinventing herself--or at least rediscovering who she used to be. While on the flight to California, things heat up between seatmates Makayla and Cam, leading to shenanigans at 35,000 feet. Let's just say, it doesn't end well. 
 I loved the chemistry between Makayla and Cam. They get hot and heavy quickly, while still trying to figure out where their lives are heading. Cam is a complete flirt and a total dirty-talking lover. However, there is a real tenderness between them that I wasn't expecting, but was a pleasant surprise. Seeing them navigate through the uncertainties was both frustrating and ultimately, heartwarming. 
 There were a couple of points in the story where it felt like it had 'multiple personalities' and didn't know exactly what it wanted to be. Also, a few of the plot points could have been more developed, especially where Cam and Makayla's family were concerned. I loved the last quarter of the book, though, and that's where I connected most with the characters. 
 Overall, it was a fun and hot read with quirky characters, funny supporting cast, and a sweet story. For my first book by Kim Karr, I'd say that I couldn't ask for anything more.

 Anyway - These two connect. Emotionally and physically. They have "relationship" stamped on them in spades but it's just a summer fling. Something to work out of their system. Right? Riiiiiight.

reference_books.title: The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society
reference_books.review_text:
This was an adorable little story, but I'm not going to say I love it like most people I know. I have a feeling that if this book hadn't been touted as so great by most of my friends that I probably would have liked it more. There is nothing worse than a book (or movie, etc) getting rave reviews and then falling flat for you. I expected too much and I just didn't quite find it in this book. 
 Don't get me wrong, this was a lovely read. The story of what happened on Guernsey during the war and to the people was definitely touching. I really enjoyed the letter format. It was a nice way to get to hear the stories from different perspectives. My least favorite parts were actually the letters back and forth from Juliet to Sophie and her publisher... I found most of them boring. 
 Ah, regardless... I'm glad I read it. It was cute and made me smile while reading it (as well as gasp and feel sad for some of it). I found myself rooting for some of the characters, while others I feel fell a bit short.

book_a.user_review: Okay, first off this edition of the book has a TON of errors, which made it extremely annoying to read through. Okay, now that I got that off my chest my rating is "eh". Nothing special. I didn't like or get any of the characters. Seemed to me yet another story of a bunch of wealthy well-do-to people playing by their own rules and doing whatever they want. I really didn't want to read this book just looking at the description as a "romantic thriller" as I am not into reading romance novels. That being said where exactly was the romance in this?? I read about hatred, jealousy, puppy love, loyalty, need, but not one single person was ever in love or romantic. Slow book to get into, decent middle part, but I was over it before I was halfway done. No thanks!

I picked this book up about 15 years ago after it was recommended to me and finally read it. I liked it but was left feeling unsatisfied when it ended.
What an annoying book.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I was left very non-plussed after reading this book. I had heard so many great things about it over the years and really didnt see how it merited them. It took me a long time to become even remotely interested in teh book. Probably around page 125 I finally didnt have to force myself to pick it back up. But it was never something that I looked forward to. 
 I thought the 'romance' was so contrived. Max was never once affectionate towards her (did she even have a name) in any way. Not before they were married, not when they were just back from their honeymoon and at Manderley for the first time, and not even AFTER he finally broke down and expressed his love for her. I just didnt buy it. 
 And the 2nd Mrs. de Winter (seriously, she didnt have a name) was so weak and pitiful that there was nothing to really like there. I hated her as a character. At least Rebecca has some spunk. 
 I really dont see what all the fuss was about. I'm giving it 3 stars because, while I was not a fan of it, I am also reading it long after it was written so am aware that I am bringing multiple biases to the table.

This is not only one of my all time favorite books by Daphne du Maurier, but it happens to be my number 1 book in a top ten list. 
 Rebecca is a suspense book that will keep you engaged the whole way through. Ms. du Maurier has a way with her writing that captivates her audience right up to the end. 
 "Last Night I Dreamt I Went To Manderley Again." This is the first lines in the book, which is told by the second Mrs. De Winters. Who seems to be living in the shadows of the first Mrs. De Winters, that everybody seemed to love and worship, including her maid, who now attends to the second Mrs. De Winters, who does not feel welcome in Rebecca's house. Your heart goes out to her as she tries to be a good wife to Maxium, her husband, who still carries a torch for Rebecca. Every where she goes on the estate, everything she tries to do to fit in at Manderly, she see Rebecca, not in a spiritual way or physical form, but by memories of people telling her, Rebecca loved this, or Rebecca did this, Rebecca would go here, do this, do that, and she feels she can't escape the past. 
 Until the night, Rebecca's little sailboat is found, and things will never be the same for the second Mrs. De Winters, Maxium, Manderly, and everyone else that Rebecca has touched their lives.

May be 3 and half stars....... 
 The reasons: 
 1. Daphne killed a powerful story by 'killing' Rebecca. I had the impression that Rebecca was one of the best women and Maxim was always living in the past, a person who can not come out of his emotional bond with the superb Rebecca. I expected this to be the course of the novel and that would have been a powerful analysis of characters. Instead it ended up like an usual romance in which one has to be bad for the justification of the other. I will never forgive Daphne for that. 
 Or was it my mistake expecting something different? Looking at the many responses and reviews I think my expectations are to be blamed. 
 2. To me, the story picked up its momentum only in the last ten chapters. 
 Final Remark: 
 I loved Rebecca even after Daphne had blackened her character. And may be that is the reason why I ended up hating the narrator and the author. Was it wrong for me to fall in love with Rebecca? I am in fact angry for making Rebecca black so that others could be perceived as white.

** spoiler alert ** 
 A good example of a rich person getting away with murder. I do not buy the book's theme ' oh, but she deserve it because she was a bitch'.

I'm not a big fan of romance usually, but this was a surprise to me. The characters were really well-drawn: the creepy housekeeper, the timid wallflower, the boorish "cousin". The story was also really suspenseful. I was sucked in to the very last page. 
 It's interesting that the book's title is the name of a character who dies before the story begin but who manages to totally dominate everyone even after she's dead. By contrast, the main character--who narrates the story--is never named. It's like she just doesn't think it's important to mention her name or show anyone calling her anything other than "Mrs. De Winter". 
 I saw the Hitchcock movie based on this book several years ago. I'm going to have to rent it again and compare.

2.5 stars. And that is strictly for the quality of writing. 
 I was told this was 'like' Jane Eyre...and it is in the fact that a young girl marries an older man with a phantom wife who causes grief. 
 Other than that, it's not at all like JE. 
 This book, while written well and having well turned words and beautiful descriptions had no charm whatsoever to me. 
 JE, with all the pain and hurt feelings had a bit of triumph over it all. You cheered for them at the end. 
 Rebecca, wow. I certainly didn't end that book happy for the couple. I admit I don't have much experience with 'gothic' - ish literature like this. But if this is a so-called masterpiece of Goth-lit, I'm done with it. Probably for the same reason I don't particularly like Poe.

You know that friend you have, the one who is quiet, shy, reserved, no self-esteem or confidence? No one knows why she is that way. She's very attractive. Not gorgeous, but attractive. She's smart and responsible. But for whatever reason she would rather be a wallflower then the center of attention. She can't look you in the eyes whenever she talks to you. She apologizes for everything. Most of her conversational responses are one word utterances. 
 Yep, we all have that friend. This type of person friend just happens to be the very ilk the protagonist in du Maurier's book Rebecca is made of. Received as a gift for Christmas from my mother-in-law (we buy each other books for xmas)and gushed over by her and my wife. Rebecca was exactly what I was expecting it to be. 
 Reading about the estate of Manderley was very entertaining. In somewhat of a stretch here, du Maurier writes of Manderley the way McCarthy writes of the land. Like I said, that is a MAJOR stretch, but I just want you to get the point that the house is a character in the book as well. 
 I will say this: Mrs. de Winter was infuriating. Many, many times I wanted to put the book down for I could not stand to read anymore of her self-loathing-woe-is-me-I-don't-deserve-this whining. So in that I guess du Maurier did a nice job in creating a character who pulls some emotions out of her readers. 
 There is a reason most of the reviewers of this book are women. It was written about a woman, for women.

book_b.title: Sent (The Missing, #2)
book_b.user_review: Not as great as the first one, however good enough that I will keep going with the series. I forgot how "young" this series reads. Honestly, I don't have much to say about the book other than it was a very quick, fun read about kids, history and time travel.

sample_reviews.review_text:
People tend to kvell about authors who have won major awards. Even if follow up books are uneven, somehow the concept that he/she is a great author seems to let them ignore less than stellar work. 
 I've managed to miss the first book in this series. I see that it garnered excellent reviews here. It is my hope that its plot is not as uneven and confusing as this one. 
 Obviously Haddix is planning more of the series,but unless one suddenly wins the Newberry and I am forced to purchase it for the library, I won't consider getting anything more than the paperback editions.
Meh. Not my favorite, the plot was sketchy, and I couldn't really follow why the characters where doing what they did. The history aspect was go though.

I liked the first in this series a lot. I LOVED the idea behind the following books in the series. But for some reason, I just wasn't enamored of the story in book 2. I think this might be one that doesn't quite translate as well to an adult. It felt like I'd like it better if I were a kid and it's intended audience.

Since the first book drew me in so much, I was excited to join in the suspense of book #2. Because the mystery of the adopted children was solved, I felt that this story didn't have as much suspense or intrigue. It was more historical fiction than science fiction, but still fast-paced and full of action. The book picks up exactly where the first one left off, with Jonah, Katherine, Chip and Alex traveling through time to the late 15th century, where Alex and Chip are the heirs to the English throne. The quad must adjust to the time period, figure out where in history they are and what is going on in the lives of their historical selves. Since Jonah and Katherine are not from that time period, they are responsible for fixing history and saving Chip and Alex. Character-wise, I felt that this book wasn't as strong as the first, especially because Alex was added as a new character but was barely a part of the story. Since the story ends with JB's plea for Jonah and Katherine to help another adopted tween fix their portion of history, I'm guessing that every book will contain a new historical time period to mend.

So far, I like the first book in this series better with its focus on adoption. The second book has Katherine and Jonah going back to the 1400s to rescue Chip and Alex, The Princes in the Tower. The plot took a long time to get going and the time travel explanations (until the end) was confusing. The last 50 pages or so (I won't spoil the climax) really saved the story, I was ready to put it down as it got very tedious. Can't wait to read the next part taking place in Roanoke, VA.
This is not only a good sci-fiction book, but one will also appreciate the good things of being able to know something about history.
I loved Found, the first in the Missing series. However, I couldn't get through this one. It took the kids 9 chapters to get out of one room. I don't know if kids will stick with it.

I really did like this one. I'm not sure what I expected, but I was pleasantly drawn into historical fiction which is one of my favorite genres.  Found picks up exactly where Sent left off, with Jonah, Katherine, Chip and Alex hurtling through a time warp toward 1483, where Chip and Alex were stolen from time. In their original lives, Chip and Alex were (respectively) the Princes Edward and Richard Plantaganet, sons of King Edward IV of England. 
 Since the story of the Princes in the Tower is one of the biggest mysteries in history, author Margaret Haddix has plenty of freedom to tell this story as she wants. I was interested to see where she'd take it. 
 Overall, I think Found was a better book. Sent seems to have a lot of downtime to me - when nothing is happening, when things are being explained. Perhaps I only felt that way because I'm so familiar with the historical aspect of the story, though. I absolutely enjoyed this book, and I'm looking forward to continuing the series.

This book started out sloooow. The writing and prose were excellent, but nothing seemed to happen for the first half of the book. Eva dances all the time, Nell wants to go to Harvard and reads encyclopedias. But later the book takes a much darker turn which I loved. Innocence is lost. Hopelessness and despair set in. The mysterious death scene of the father is finally revealed. But then as things get even more primal, I felt like the story veered off into the realm of not really feeling believable anymore. It actually felt uncomfortable. I love good writing and a good dark novel, but the strange turns and transformations seemed almost too shocking and actually verged on traumatic.

Nell and Eve are precocious teenagers living with their anti-establishment parents in the middle of a redwood forest. Their contact with the outside world is sporadic, so it takes them a while to realize that civilization is crumbling around them. Hegland is vague about the reasons--a far-off war, new strains of disease, terrorist attacks on US soil. (She wrote this in 1996, when all of this was less hackneyed.) But after a few seasons of this, the family is left without electricity, internet, telephones, mail, or gas. They are stranded in the woods, with nothing and no one to rely upon but themselves. 
 It sounds much more interesting than it is. The story is told through Nell's POV, and it would be hard to craft a generic character. Her sister Eve has a bit more personality, but that personality is so broadly drawn that it's hard to give much credit. Although the girls are alone with each other for most of the story, their relationship has only the trappings of intimacy, and none of the depth of it. This book has all the emotional intensity of a school essay--and reads like one, too. 
 OK, so the characters and emotional life are a bit lacking--surely their methods of survival would make up for it? Alas, no. Hegland is as vague about how to can or make acorn flour as she is on the intricacies of the girls' relationship. It's all very thinly sketched. 
 If you want to read about surviving amidst the ruins of Western civilization, I'd recommend reading how i live now or Parable of the Sower, or heck, even Hatchet before bothering with this. It's not a bad book--but it's not a good one.

reference_books.title: The Fountainhead
reference_books.review_text:
The Fountainhead by Ayan Rand 
 Howard Roark, Architect is an Objectivist. Objectivism is a philosophical ideal that was created by Rand herself. An objectivist is a person who achieves true happiness from his works, attitudes and behaviours. Rand opposed the theory of religion and faith and believed that her moral guidelines were based on reason and humanity as opposed to faith and emotions. Howard Roark was a very close visualization of Rand's philosophy but in human form. 
 Roark will not work with any client unless they agree to build on his terms, and his terms are that the building be built as he designed it with absolutely no change. His designs were more of a practical and less esthetic nature, modernistic as they called it. He wouldn't build for his clients he would build so that he could bring the buildings to life. People saw Howard Roark but Howard Roark saw no one. To him the streets were empty, the offices were empty. If he looked at you, you'd feel like he is looking right through you. His objectivism was largely confused to be selfishness (he did care but up to a certain point - ya whatever that means). His behavior was largely misunderstood as insolence. 
 The core of the story is Howard's career struggle to stand by his own morals and standards and to work by only them. Amidst all this, Howard had a twisted love affair with a beautiful woman who threatened to destroy him every step of the way. 
 Straight to the flaws: 
 I can never deny that Rand is a good writer. Her beautiful descriptive style makes you want to go back and re-read the lines she wrote. Her ideas are quite thought provoking and she definitely makes you look at life a lot more differently than before. But do I want to see this much philosophy in a novel? (that too 720 pages of it!) I don't think so. There are long endless passages of speeches made by characters that become over-bearing and quite honestly, boring. It's a thread bare story with hardly any fiction and purely a medium for Rand's own philosophical ramblings. Definitely overwrought. 
 There is a unique blend of characters in the story. There are creators, copy cats (second-handers) and power hungry animals. Characters like Dominque, were not plausible though. I don't get her reasoning and I don't entirely agree with her definition of love. Her motives to destroy Howard just didn't seem real. I don't know what this book is doing in the romance genre! 
 The philosophy: Objectivism sounds easy. Almost all humans are naturally individualistic because almost all of us put our happiness first; but it's ambiguous and self-contradictory even to this very day. She believes that there are creators that are heroic geniuses and the rest of the world are just second-handers (she sounds like she is saying that the rest the folk are fools!); that just sounds so morbid, bitter and in poor taste. So before you actually try and fully understand her theory you already hate it. Pity. 
 Is it ok to be selfish? Rand certainly thinks so. But I don't think that its' ok ALL the time. If we all became selfish will it be a nice place to live in? Objectivism believes that man should put his own happiness above all else, so how does this all fit in when we fall in love with someone? The difference between theoretical explanations and real life practical application is not so black and white as Rand says it is. 
 So use this book to give your life a different perspective. Remain firm to your principles, love your work but don't use this as a guide to life or you will end up very lonely and possibly without work (possibly).

reference_books.title: The Boy in the Striped Pajamas
reference_books.review_text:
Having just finished the Diary of Young Girl by Ann Frank and immediately picking this book (without reading the blurb) was a creepy coincidence. These two books are almost two sides of the same coin where the former is a Jewish girl's autobiography and the latter is a German boy's story. Where one is real the other is fiction. 
 Bruno is a 9 year old German boy who stayed in Berlin with his Father, Mother and Sister Gretel. Bruno's father is a high ranking army official. The story starts off with the family's hasty move from the comfort of their Berlin home to a new isolated place that is surrounded by an endless barbed fence. On the other side of this fence, Bruno sees people all dressed in the same striped pyjamas. Who are these people? Don't they have anything else to wear? Why do they all look so sad? 
 Ok, so despite all the blind spots/potholes I want to applaud the author for one thing, that he created a 9 year old character that actually thinks and acts his age...(a slow kid actually). If you compare him to other fictional over-smart kids like Anne of Green Gables, Oliver Twist etc Bruno is just a normal kid. Regardless of his innocent perspective, he makes all of our adult things seem silly and over-complicated. Quoting a few from the book: 
 "What exactly was the difference? he wondered to himself. And who decided which people wore the striped pajamas and which people wore the uniforms?" 
 "In his heart, he knew that there was no reason to be impolite to someone, even if they did work for you. There was such a thing as manners after all." 
 Now for the bashing; this book is over-rated, I could be wrong but these shiny stars look largely like "pity votes". Despite the plus points, the ending was poorly done, a bit too hasty. Almost like there might have been a better ending (because the book looked well spread out from the very beginning), but the author later decided to keep it short. 
 So don't read it for the ending. Definitely not. Also please don't expect that a 9 year old sheltered boy should have had a better understanding of this very troubled era of the Holocaust, because this was not the intention. Please refer to the History text books for that. 
 Read it because you just miss being a kid. Because you miss coming up with simpler reasons for things that happen around you. Read it in the hope that one day there will be a world with no fences and even if there are, you should at least get to choose which side you want to say on and not be judged for it. Once you're done, hold on to Bruno's simple but unique perspective of things because I'm dam sure we'll need it for the many more Hitler's to come.

Today I finished this book. Last week I had gone out of my way to grab a copy after stumbling across a review of the author and his blog. I was intrigued to know where in Dorset Ali Shaw came from, and a bit of digging led me to discover he was from Dorchester. Not that this impacts on his book at all. 
 So, the book. Two main characters: Ida and Midas. Midas Crook is the son of Midas Crook who was a hands-off father and husband who seemed to have brought much unhappiness to his family before finally committing suicide. 
 Ida is the daughter of a free spirit who was wooed by an academic who worked with Midas Crook senior. There is a lot of emphasis on the relationships between parents and children and the love affairs of said parents, which I did find a bit confusing now and again. A good premise for character development, but it got a bit laboured. 
 Loved the setting. Kept thinking it was somewhere in Scotland, and thought it was brave of Shaw to keep the geographical clues to a minimum. Loved Henry Fuwa and his landscape. 
 Shaw did pack a lot of story-weaving into this tale, with a few loose ends to foster the imagination. Don't know whether the book is better or worse for leaving these strands flying. Perhaps if every loose end had been tied-up, it would have been a contrite piece of work. Specifically, I wanted to know more about Fuwa and the Millionnaire/ hunting recluse; I wanted to know more about the condition itself, and the link to the environment, and why and how other people had been affected by it. 
 I loved the ending and Midas' development to overcome his past. Wished he hadn 't got rid of all his photos of her. 
 On reflection, I would look out for his second novel.

As I read this, my mind kept drifting over to Helprin's Winter's Tale: both are set in what feels like the real world, but the magic and wonder set them apart from the world we inhabit. 
 Shaw's book is about two very lonely people, Midas and Henry, who have made a fetish of being apart from the rest of us; it's also about Carl, who was in love with Freya (Ida's mother) and friends with Midas' father. And then there's Ida, seemingly normal but with this mysterious condition: her body is slowly turning to glass. The intersection of these four lives and how one deals with past loves, people in general and the wondrous things this world offers is what made this book one of my favorites.

book_b.title: The Miniaturist
book_b.user_review:
What can I say, except that I am on a good book streak. Lets begin. 
 It was in mid October 1686 that Patronella Oortman (Nella for short) knocked on her new husbands door in Amsterdam. She is eighteen years old and hales from a small village in the country side called Assendelft. 
 As she stands at the steps awaiting her fate, she recalls her 'blink of a wedding' a month ago to Johannes Brandt, a 39 year old wealthy VOC (East India Company) merchant. There was no garlands, no betrothal cup and no wedding bed. As the door is opened she is engulfed into a life that was far from normal, unlike anything her mother had ever imagined for her. 
 Nella's father was a drunk who owned several breweries. For a while, her family lived in every necessary comfort demanded by a respectable household. But over time the debts began to pile up. The soup thinned, the meat got scraggier and the servants began to fall away. It was not long before she eventually lost her father too. "You need to marry a man that can keep his guilder in his purse" her mother said as she sent her off. 
 11 days pass as a wife, longer than it took God to make the world and her husband had not so much as laid a finger on her. When one morning, Johannes presents her with a unique gift. A small wooden replica (cabinet) of her husbands house. The accuracy of the cabinet is eerie, as if the real house has been shrunk, its body sliced in two and its organs revealed. It begins to make her feel uneasy. Like each room are like eyes watching her... 
 For an escape and to occupy her now empty life she decided to furnish the cabinet, she goes through the Smits list, and there enclosed is an entry under M that catches her eye:MINIATURIST- Residing in Kalverstraat at the sign of the sun, ALL AND YET NOTHING. 
 Nella jumps to the opportunity and sends the miniaturist a list of the items she desires. She got them alright..but those were not the only items she got. This isn't correct! There must be some mistake! How could the miniaturist possibly know? Is someone watching me? Who is in the room with me? Questions cloud her mind but she is determined to have each one answered. 
 Will Nella ever find out the mystery behind the cabinet, the miniaturist and her strange husband? A household comprising of her secretive, cruel and unmarried sister-in-law Merin Brandt, her nosy Keyhole Queen maid Cornelia and the ever mysterious Negro manservant, Otto. 
 Beautifully written, gripping and one of the most unique books I have ever read.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Although The Miniaturist came with good recommendations, I overall couldn't decide if I liked the book or not. While I enjoyed some elements, others fell flat. 
 The setting is 1686 Amsterdam. We meet 18-year-old Nella Oortman, a girl from a smaller city, who is recently married in an arranged marriage to a rich merchant 20 years her senior, Johannes Brandt. The novel chronicles the first four months of her marriage to Johannes, where Nella lives with and gets to know Johannes, his unmarried sister, Marin, and their servants, Cornelia and Otto. As Nella slowly unravels the family's secrets, she keeps a few secrets of her own, which relate back to the craftsman she has hired to create miniature items for a cabinet house Johannes gifted her. The other major subplot features Johannes trying to sell a large amount of sugar on behalf of another rich merchant family. 
 The novel explores the themes of money, commerce, power, women's issues, family situations, sex and religion among the 1% of Amsterdam society at the time. 
 I enjoyed reading and learning about the historical context of some of those different issues, but I did not feel a deep connection to the characters. I had an especially hard time relating to Nella -- while I felt bad for her and the increasingly difficult events she faced in the book, she also came off to me as naive and spoiled, and it was not easy for me to like her as a character until closer to the end of the book. 
 I also thought that some of the dramatic plot developments seemed random and there just to shock, even though the suspense was built up before the developments quite well. Furthermore, one of the most major and mysterious subplots was left extremely open and ambiguous at the end of the novel, which felt very dissatisfying to me. 
 Overall, if you like historical fiction, I'd give The Miniaturist a go. However, while the plot is vast, historically interesting, and at times salacious, it didn't do much for me in terms of a truly satisfying story. 
 (p.s.: There are historical notes at both the beginning and the end of the book; I wish I had read both before the novel instead of reading the endnotes at, well, the end. It might be worth flipping to the back to check out the glossary and other info before you start reading.)

 She was independent in a world where she couldn't afford to be. At the beginning she appears as a very strict, closed up and pious woman but as the story progresses we get a totally different description of her personality. 
 Nella at the beginning of the book is (thanks to her mother) convinced that the only way to exist in her society is through marriage. Nonetheless she wish to find love is determined to be a good wife. But as the story unfolds she soon realizes how high her expectation were. Miserable and alone she takes confort in the deliveries the Miniaturist sends her. But soon she realizes that the miniatures she receives are more than perfect replicas. They tell stories and secrets. 
 I felt that Nella grew a lot in this book. She become strong to take control of the impossible situation she has to face. Furthermore faced with the existence of Marin she realizes that marriage does not make you valid as a woman. 
 Overall I enjoyed my read even though I wish to have known more about Marin and the Miniaturist. The mystery in itself was interesting but I was disappointed when it unfolded.
