 The story centres around Nella Orrtman. An uninteresting young woman who has married into the Brandt household. Her new husband is rather aloof and more interested in his work than her. In an attempt to show some interest in her, he presents her with a cabinet. An exact replica of the Brandt household for Nella to decorate as she pleases. 
 Nella contracts a miniaturist to begin crafting replica's to place in the cabinet. However she soon realizes that these pieces have more significance. Each piece seems to tell a tale of what is to become. I wanted more of this. More mystery and suspense but the books namesake never really takes her place in the story. 
 It's hard to really put a finger on what I didn't like about this book. It just didn't grab me. It was mundane. The characters are one dimensional and completely lack in emotional complexity. Nella and Johannes show no real interest in each other so I felt no emotion towards the end when the tides turn against him. 
 Nothing is ever really explained. Nothing was convincing, so nothing was believable
Just my kind of book.

I really enjoyed this book. I haven't read a lot of historical fiction, but this book is really great. The story might be a bit slow for some readers, but I liked how it made me feel like I can go at my own pace. I wasn't itching to finish the story and I didn't feel jittery when I couldn't keep reading because life. What a great thing this book does on top of that is the events that occur in this book feel overwhelming, but not rushed. This book made me really relaxed and it's what made me give it a four. 
 Nella is treated as kind of an outsider looking in. She's never fully introduced into the household or welcomed until near the end of the book, so most of the time she gives us a really objective view of the story. She asks the same questions I ask and, even though we never really found the answers, Nella felt extremely relatable because of it. 
 This book also touches on really heavy topics for Medieval Europe's setting. I'm not going to list them because spoilers, but I commend the author for putting it in. It gave the story a lot more depth and it showed the great hypocrisy that flourished around the time inside the church. 
 Another things some readers may not be happy about are the loose endings. Only a couple of the many questions in this novel are answered, but I personally enjoyed it. It left a really big open ending, but also it just added more to Nella's relatability because in life we don't get all of the answers right away or ever. 
 I definitely recommend this book to people who enjoy historical fiction, leisurely writing, and if they're looking for something that doesn't rush them or feel like too much is happening at once.

The Miniaturist was for me a very unpleasant read. I found myself baffled by the poorly drawn paper mache characters, unbelievable relationships between characters, a peculiar, inadequately described setting, and a crudely crafted plot that stumbles along to an unsatisfactory conclusion. Also I found the writing very uneven, which is to say not good. I'm frankly surprised this book was published. 
 An intriguing concept - a set of miniature figures replicating the book's actual characters that seem to control (in an inconsistent way) these people's lives - is an interesting one but has not been fully developed other than to lend an extreme oddness to the book. I kept reading till the end because I thought surely something interesting would be revealed, a compelling metaphor would appear, but, no such thing occurred. Ultimately the story is annoying and goes absolutely nowhere.

reference_books.title: Mr. Penumbra's 24-Hour Bookstore (Mr. Penumbra's 24-Hour Bookstore, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Clever and witty and fun to read. Had me visiting the Internet to find out is the Dragon Song Chronicles a real book series, is there such a thing as Geritszoon type among other questions. The power of Google (the company ) is shown in the book, but in the end, the human mind with its stupendous ability to make connections beats Google and who could not like that?

reference_books.title: Little Bee
reference_books.review_text: Little Bee started out with promise , but ultimately was somewhat disappointing. Little Bee and her sister escape from their Nigerian village following a massacre due to the oil discovered there. They run into a vacationing British couple on a beach and desperately seek their help. Two years later Little Bee shows up at the couple's home in England. The storyline is compelling, but there are flaws. Little Bee is an amazing girl, but often sounds much too wise for her 16 years. Sarah is supremely annoying and self centered. Perhaps this is intentional.? The ending of the story does not ring true. Sarah really returns to Nigeria after what she knows with her 4 year old son in tow? Seemed crazy to me...would you really place your child in such a potentially dangerous situation? Or maybe Sarah is just beyond arrogant...

reference_books.title: Yes Please
reference_books.review_text:
2.5 stars 
 The book starts out with Amy explaining that it is really, really hard to write a book. Yes, it is and I think Amy struggled mightily. The book didn't flow and there was too much fluff. No , I don't really care what Amy thinks about cell phones or the Internet. I do think she is funny, but she should stick with her day job.

reference_books.title: The Reader
reference_books.review_text: This was a tough read as I'm sure it was intended to be. I couldn't feel sympathy for either Michael or Hanna, but many interesting and unanswerable questions were raised. Particularly when Hanna asks the judge what he would have done in her situation and he has no easy answer. The writing style was not easy to read, yet suited the message of the novel. The story was told almost without emotion, evocative of the numbness Michael describes in the courtroom. The prose sounded like it was written by a lawyer, Michael's profession, so I supposed it did ring true. I just found it difficult.

reference_books.title: The Night Circus
reference_books.review_text: Different, had the potential to be a great one, but came up short.

book_a.title: Run
book_a.user_review: A little disappointed with this one as I loved Bel Canto. The writing was flat and the story was contrived. Just too many flaky conincidences. My breaking point was at the end when Fr. Sullivan knew Tennessee Moser.

sample_reviews.review_text:
interesting idea for a book but never went very deep and was pretty disappointing ... 
 the best book i've read by Ann Patchett is Truth & Beauty .... non-fiction book on friendship. HIGHLY recommend that book but not this !!!

I enjoyed Run. I liked that the story was compacted into a 24 hour period and that I learned the back stories of the characters by their thoughts and memories. It was interesting how we find out about Tennessee and Kenya. Totally unexpected! It was a quick read and I also liked how we learn of what happened to the family after that fateful day when all meet. I liked the support the family showed to each other and the acceptance they learn as each tries to become their own persons.

Maybe it was just that I listened to the audiobook version of this book--I usually like Ann Patchett, but found this audiobook to be tedious. Was sorry that I chose it to listen to on a long car trip.

I loved Bel Canto, and I'd really enjoyed her non-fiction work Truth and Beauty, so was eager to read another by this author. I wasn't disappointed. I really like the way she sees her characters and brings them into our vision. 
 What I particularly like about this book is how the straightforwardness of a child brings others into looking at the situation from a fresh point of view, or perhaps I mean into looking at the situation and themselves from a broader point of view than their usual. 
 I won't write any more. There are other reviews that talk about the book nicely.

I was disappointed in this book after being so blown away by the author's previous work (particularly Bel Canto). The story is slow, laborious, and I quit caring about halfway through but by then felt that I should finish.

This was an engaging read but really not a great book. According to the 'meet the author' section, it is supposed to be a book about American politics, race, class, and family. These topics do come up, but only superficially. So, I'd say it's a good read if you're at the beach or stranded at an airport, and want something that will keep you occupied but not make you think critically. But, if you're expecting another Bel Canto as I was this is likely to be a disappointment.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Just stay as far away from this book as possible. It's terrible, from start to finish. I cannot even begin to imagine why there are so many people who want to read this thing. 
 Imagine if you will the the following. A man adopts two black children in what has to be roughly the late 70s or early 80s and goes on to be Mayor of Boston. He wants to be governor but his son--the biological one--screws things up for him ala Kennedy, in a terribly written passage told for "the first time" without any reluctance to a perfect stranger. Now he lives for one of his sons to carry on the political legacy but they have no desire to do so. Suddenly a woman saves a life in our upper class family, and everyone's perspective changes as her ties to the family become known. What happens when a poor girl with a strong resemblance to the adopted boys is thrust into their lives? 
 This gets worse. 
 The two kids grow up with no desire at all to know who their biological mother was and all three children are drifting about--one steals drugs in Africa, one studies fish, and the other thinks he might want to be a priest. As the story progresses, switching from viewpoint to viewpoint so the author can tell us things we have to know about everyone, we add more characters than a Shakespeare history play--each of which gets to play narrator, jarring the reader all over the place. 
 As the story goes on it gets less and less believable--how could a man with the power of the mayor's office not know where the biological mother was? Just how bad are Boston hospitals that people can zip in and out of intensive care? How does a poor person afford going to concerts, political speeches, and other things that are barely affordable by a middle class person? 
 The book just gets progressively worse in terms of writing style. When a shocking--well, not to me because by this point I'm just reading to finish the book--secret about the girl's mother is revealed through a dream sequence, I lost any hope I had for this book to even claim to be mediocre. 
 The king of all "you've got to be kidding me" moments is saved for the end, when as a result of all this, and told several years into the future, when all of a sudden the father who wanted everything to work perfectly for his family--GETS EVERYTHING WE WERE TOLD HE WANTED. 
 Yes, 287 or so pages later, this book forces us into a happy ending for the one character in the book who up to that point had no compelling reason to be the one we give a shit about. 
 There's so much wrong with this book that I could go on for pages about it. Even without using spoilers, there's so much I can describe as being wrong. Let's start with the fact that people jump in and out of this book without comment--there are lots of white relatives at the start of the book who dislike the idea of the family having black relatives. Guess who we never see again after the opening pages? Of the characters we do have, they drop in and out seemingly at random. Sullivan the screw up son has no purpose at all, and his namesake uncle is about as needed as a third shoe. 
 Then there's the practical part of all this. Our patriarch is a former mayor, right? Has security guards, at least while being mayor, right? Yet he's had a stalker--there's no polite way to describe what happens in this book but stalking--for ALMOST 20 YEARS. Umm, either the security team hated him or they're more incompetent than the keystone cops. That's if you can believe that a powerful political figure wouldn't use his influence to find--and keep at bay--the mother of the boys if he were so worried about her, as well as the other problems I mentioned above. I could add more but that would require looking over the text again and I'd really prefer not to. 
 This book reads like a Hallmark movie, and if that's your thing, go for it. However, the only way to enjoy this one is to take the concept of suspension of disbelief and toss it off the side of the Empire State Building. I can do that in a comic book, but not in a real book. I'm willing to overlook some things in fiction, but this is like trying to ignore DNA, fingerprints, and a confession all in front of your face. Combined with the poor writing style that tells instead of shows for much of the novel, it leaves me as cold as the fish Tip should still be studying. 
 If you want a book that has believable characters, a plot that makes sense, and characters that logically progress from the book's beginning to the book's end, well, this one isn't it. (Library, 03/08)

I finished reading Run by Ann Patchett this afternoon. It tells the story of two brothers who are adopted into a political Irish family in Boston. Their whole life changes when one night, their real mother pushes one of them out of the path of an SUV. It was an interesting story, but I felt like there was a whole lot of the story that went untold and unexplored. I just didn't feel complete when I finished it.
No continuity in the story. And I didn't find the characters engaging at all.
I read this after Bel Canto, and while I did not find it as engrossing, I still enjoyed the book.

book_b.title: Bossypants
book_b.user_review: Nice summer read. Laugh out loud funny.

sample_reviews.review_text: i could be nit-picky and say that the last few chapters seemed tacked on. definitely not a "memoir", more like little funny essays. i like it best when she writes about SNL or improv, about babies, not so much.
Another great memoir and series of essays by a very funny lady. Her humor lands quite well with me, and it's great to continue hearing about the eventual success of female comedians.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Hmm, I'm sort of conflicted about this book. 
 What I expected: A laugh out loud book about a comedian's life and life in Hollywood. 
 What I got: A somewhat interesting left-leaning treatise that wasn't laugh out loud funny but made me smile in parts. 
 It's clear Tina Fey and I would likely not agree on anything political. She openly worships Alec Baldwin and his influence on her career which seems fine to be gracious but there's being gracious and groveling and the latter became evident. 
 Based on reading this book, if I had to guess I would say that Ms. Fey would come down on the side of the protesters against the police in these recent shootings and gun ownership. Against profiling. But then an interesting thing happens on page 49-50 of her book where she is describing advice from her father. 
 "Conversely, he would tell us things like 'If you see two black kids riding around on one bike, put your bike in the garage.' This wasn't racism; it was experience. Those kids were coming from West Philly to steal bikes. The social factors that caused their behavior were irrelevant to a Depression baby." 
 Hmm. Hmm. Hmm. Really? Because I'm pretty sure if a cop today said and did that she would not say the same thing. And, the chapter on her father, she only referred to him by his first and last name-- All. The. Time. That was just weird. 
 Some chapters I did find pretty endearing-- such as the one about her honeymoon. Also, the chapters on SNL and her impersonating Sarah Palin were interesting as well. I did appreciate the fact that she did try to protect Sarah Palin and give her a good experience on SNL. 
 What was most interesting but not really fully divulged was how she got the scar on her face which evidently happened when someone slashed her with a knife when she was five-years-old. She doesn't delve into the topic at all except to say that all the attention she got after that incident falsely inflated her ego to the point where she was willing to try anything and everything. It felt like a lot was missing from this autobiography not to talk more about that and the impact it had. 
 If you're left-leaning and enjoy all things Hollywood then I think you'll really like this book. All others, there are interesting parts but definitely get it from the library.
Hilarious! Seriously a great book. Easy and quick. Love love love!
FUNNY, FUNNY, FUNNNNNNNNNNNNNY!!!!!!!!!!!

I'm writing this on my iPad and it's hard to tell what the stars mean in the mobile version. Is 2 stars "it was pretty much exactly what I expected Tina Fey is a funny lady there are some funny parts good enough for the beach glad I didn't pay for it?" Because that's what I meant by 2 stars.

Autobiographies of comics are not expected to be completely truthful accounts of their life. All they need to do is be funny. Tina Fey remains one of the most consistently funny people associated with TV in any form. I have no idea whether her descriptions of her life bear any significant relationship to reality, but it doesn't matter. She's funny -- and her theories about management are a whole lot better than those subscribed to by most of the bosses I've had.

Listened to this in the car in a 7 hour trip (14 hours total to and from). While it wasn't long enough for the whole trip, it was entertaining and perfect for the ride. Not something I would have enjoyed reading, but something that was entertaining for a car ride. Basically about Tina Fey's life, about what you'd expect for a midwestern girl with both parents still married (so not really that exciting, but at least she's funny).
I'm putting this down halfway through. I just can't with it - it's so boring. Sorry, Tina.

As much as I enjoy Tina Fey and her wonderful show, 30 rock, I think she should stick to making scripts and shows. This book was in its own weird way, scattered. The good advice was drowned out by incoherence and random references. I know being self effacing is funny, but this . . . this was a bit too much. Sorry Tina Fey. I still think you are awesome. But not a very good author.

reference_books.title: The Glass Castle
reference_books.review_text: I had heard the title of the book somewhere but really had no idea what it was about. So when the book crossed my path I was quite interested and felt that it would be an interesting read. I found that it was quite engrossing and I felt quite saddened at the level of poverty experienced by this family but at the same time found them to be survivors - always resilient always bouncing back on their feet despite the setbacks. I was impressed that Jeannette found the courage to leave and move forwards in her life by getting an education and escaping her childhood. Now what was more interesting is that I was watching an episode of Oprah's Life class this morning and there was a segment on Jeannette Walls and it really put things into perspective for me. It was all about revealing secrets to overcome shame. It was eye-opening to hear Jeannette speak of her life - two-fold was her guilt that she was living a lifestyle of the rich and famous on Park Avenue as a her parents were still foraging and living life on the streets (albeit of their own choice) and embarrassment that if people were to find out about her childhood experience they would reject her - she decided that it was better to be truthful because in hiding she was living a lie - and as Oprah firmly believes - "the truth will set you free". Interesting book - an easy read about a family and their survival. I am now reading her other book and will review that one soon enough.

reference_books.title: The Lotus Eaters
reference_books.review_text: This was quite a book to read. It was intense and it was actually nerve-wracking to read!! It was quite an adventure and it did capture the sounds and the smells of the Vietnam War. Certainly brings to mind the documentaries on Tv about the rough and rugged life of a photojournalist and how everyone strives and takes huge risk to capture that cover photo!! Emotional and charged with a gamut of feelings about life, love, violence and just the whole concept of the purpose of war and the havoc it wreaks on human lives! Well done for a debut novel for this author!

reference_books.title: The Cookbook Collector
reference_books.review_text: It was a little challenging reading this book...really has nothing to do with cooking or as the title might hint at. But it was an interesting book with the many threads of the story all coming today in the end. A very contemporary sort of book - technology, political activism, juxtaposition of old and new, religion and family ties...but most of all about attempting to find one's self in the past and present with hope for the future.

reference_books.title: Catching Fire (The Hunger Games, #2)
reference_books.review_text: What can I say...loved it and even better that I have book 3 ready to be read because that cliff -hanging conclusion would have frustrated me if I had to wait for the conclusion. I thought that this was a pretty good second book. There was enough action and it was a very "smart" plot. Going to see the Hunger Games movie actually was great. It visually brought the two books together and it further enhanced my imagination and I enjoyed that greatly. The author does a good job with her imagery and makes her descriptions easy to translate onto the big screen. Book 2 certainly will have more special effects. Enough of this review - have to get a start on book 3!!!

reference_books.title: The Next Always (Inn BoonsBoro, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Always a sucker for a new Nora Roberts Trilogy...This book was alright. It did not captivate me as much as the Bridal quartet books did. I don't feel that I have to go and read Book 2 of this series. As always your characters are always strong-willed and always beautiful or handsome...and the villains are always sleaze-balls. She always writes books that are very descriptive and certainly easy to read without having to think too much.

book_a.title: Girl in Translation
book_a.user_review: An excellent debut novel portraying the American immigrant experience. The prose was easy to read and clearly described the situation, the gruelling experience, the deplorable living conditions and the challenges of making a life when in debt to family who are only supportive if it is to their benefit. The story is not unique but Kimberley's rise from poverty to a comfortable life is probably the experience and the dream of all asian/chinese immigrants. Education and hard work and maybe karma thrown in. The ending left me hanging a little - there was closure but did it truly tie up all the loose ends? Perhaps - we are meant to feel this way sometimes the choices that we make have to be what they are because nothing in life is ever that simple. There is an always an element of selfishness as to whether there is fairness for the other person who should have been involved in the ultimate decision-making process. All in all - a very quick and easy read - the story unfolded very smoothly and in no time I was making the book as finished!

sample_reviews.review_text:
For those of you who have never had a book resonate with your soul, let me describe it for you. It's like a tidal wave crashing over you on a warm, sandy beach. It's like hiding away in a warm blanket. The sun soaking into your skin. 
 In some ways, I've never had a book I'm pact me like Girl in Translation did. Something about Kimberly's narration struck a cord in my spirit and really connected. I think the last time I felt anything remotely close to what I'm feeling now (tears and everything) was when I finishedThe Fault in Our Stars. 
 At the moment, I think I'm still too out of whack to write a coherent review, but for now I guess my raw emotions will do.

Loved this book! It was interesting (particularly after reading about the immigrant experiences in How To Be An American Housewife last week), engaging, and thought provoking. I couldn't put it down, and I can already tell that I'll be mulling over the decisions made by the main character for a while. Highly recommended!

Every once in awhile I gravitate towards fiction about China, India, Africa or anyplace where the characters aren't white. I am also reading a non-fiction book about North Korea now just to round out the whole experience. Unfortunately, the experience with this book sucked. Nice back story, character development and lead in...to nothing. Another one of those books that sets a nice premise and then goes nowhere. Oh well, at least a non-fiction book about North Korea is better than this and that should let you know how poorly I regard this title.
read this review and others at http://readingforsanity.blogspot.com/...

interesting. really liked the way Jean Kwok created a realistic world, mirroring her life. She & her family moved from Hong Kong to a New York City slum and worked at a sweat shop. The mother/daughter dynamic was pretty well-written. the chinese idioms were great. But at the end I did not like it as much. 
 *spoiler alert* not just her choice to have sex at that time (before marriage, suddenly, impulsively, emotionally), but the final epilogue, "12 years later"... really ? she never married? she's still carrying a torch for him? they kiss? she thinks, " I had lived all these years for this kiss..." 
 the way it ties back to the flash forward of the bridal shop in the prologue is clever... but I found the rest to be overly dramatic.
Overall an interesting story, but some parts felt forced.

"Kimberley is eleven when she and her mother emigrate from Hong Kong to New York. They speak no English, live in abject poverty and work in near-slavery conditions in a sweatshop run by relatives. Yet Kimberley still manages to excell at school, win a scholarship for a prestigious private school and to go on to Yale. All the while she is forced to live a double life, poor and Chinese on the one hand, smart American student on the other. 
 I wanted to like this, I think it is an important story. However, the idea was better than it's execution. It reads for the most part like a YA novel, partly because of the subjects of growing up, fitting in etc, but also because of the writing. The use of Chinese idioms don't always work, and the same can be said for the occasional phonetic spelling of words that Kimberley doesn't understand as I sometimes had to stop and think what they are supposed to mean. I also didn't care for the ending. 
 This is a coming of age story with a difference, an interesting look at modern multi-cultural societies. Unfortunately, for me, it's not as compelling as it should be."

As a character/narrator, Kimberly seemed too amazing to be true, though I found her story interesting. I thought the writing was less than spectacular and especially was annoyed that Chinese idioms were always translated and in the same manner. I needed these translations at first, but after a while I was able to infer the meaning and the constant translation became pedantic and slowed the book down. I was engaged with the plot up until the end when it became overly maudlin.
This novel read like a memoir. I learned a few things about Chinese immigrant culture. It kept me hooked, but I wasn't a fan of the ending.
I enjoyed this one very much. Thoughtful.

book_b.title: Fifty Shades Freed (Fifty Shades, #3)
book_b.user_review: Well, the 3rd book is now complete...worth all the hype? Who knows...just another mindless romance book with just more risque descriptive scenes added to make it a little controversial and get it into the trending social media limelight. Have to finish what you start so all 3 books in the trilogy is done. When asked on The View if there would be a 4th book...the author did not deny anything so guess it depends on how much money she thinks she can reap in. Did the storyline get better? well...like all books you get to know all the characters involved and of course you are curious as to what happens to them...happily after? Hmm...life just does not work that way does it now??? On to better quality reading...the side track was good - it's always good to shock the mind and stir-up the imagination - a liberal mind is a healthy outlook when it comes to reading!!!

sample_reviews.review_text: What a poorly written terrible series. If I never hear/read the words gasp, ah, squirm, subconscious and inner goddess again it will be too soon. It seems these are the only words in the whole book. I would never have finished this series if I wasn't slightly OCD and need to finish everything I start. I honestly do not know what the fuss was all about. Annoying and weak characters and no plot. Sorry fans, there is much better mindless reading out there
well, i guess it could be worse. but i liked the "Meet Fifty Shades" part a lot, though - guess i like to look at both sides of the picture.

Third book seems pointless to me. The author is lost in a brainstorm of ideas about what to add into the story to make it more entretaining. She didn't polish the ideas and left them all unclear in the book because she got caught up on the kinky sex scenes. I suppose the author was just centered into covering sex fantasies, which were placed randomly across the text and the plots. The book just seems plain porn literature.
Maybe a somewhat sad admission, but I am much too cynical for book #3. I'm sure I rolled my eyes more than Ana.

I feel like I've read enough porn for a lifetime. Seriously. I feel dirty. 
 KILL E.L. JAMES BEFORE IT LAYS EGGS! 
 No, I'm sorry, I'm sorry. I know. I shouldn't be mean. I mean I'm not a writer and how would I know what it is to write a book and how would I know what it is to write about fucking all the time.. 
 No, I'm not a writer, but what I am is a professional reader and my professional opinion is that at the least this is one of the stupidest things ever published and at the most this is.. well.. the same thing. 
 Ok. Let's get started. 
 It's shitty, but I can understand why someone would like it. It has the handsome man, the shy girl, the kinky fuckery, the love, the family, the friends, the bad guys, the thrill. Fascinating. Just fucking fascinating. I do have to specify this, though : I would understand why someone WHO DOESN'T READ FOR A LIVING would like it. And even then I still have a thousand questions about this : why would you?? WHY? 
 There's many things in this book that I find completely stupid, many expressions that I can't get why an editor would let them pas through his hands. Was the editor who approved this book blind? Deaf? And with severe mental problems? (Mean, I know, but really now). 
 I did however pick two things I thought were out of this world in terms of how far bad writing can get. 
 One : Putting one arm around my waist and with his other hands tugging my lacy panties sideways, he IMPALES me in one swift move. I have to begin by saying that I live in Romania, and one of our national "heroes" is Vlad Tepes (also known as Dracula, Vlad Dracul), THE MAN THAT IMPALED HALF THE PEOPLE ALIVE BACK THEN. I really have a rich imagination, but by him sliding into her I really cannot think about the word "impaling" without laughing my ass off. It's just not good to use that kind of language - I know it was meant to sound tough , but all I could think of was Vlad Tepes and a pointy stick. 
 Two (and with this I have a real problem) : Many times across the book, I have stumbled across the expression "I open his buttons and he springs free ". I don't know if it's just me, but springing free makes me think of a happy bunny and a field of flowers, not in any case of a huge cuckoo and a sexual act. Every time (and I mean EVERY time) I read it, I'd burst out laughing , sometimes until tears, because it's just impossible to use this kind of language to express raw sex. He can't SPRING FREE, dear dear E.L. James, because his pants are not a jail and his penis is not a bunny! Oh Lord, again. 
 With these two issues talked about, I have to say this is not a book I recommend people to read. Yes, it has a lot of fucking in it, that's the reason we mad men and women read it in the first place. But apart from that, there is nothing good about it. Nothing different. Just another book for the masses, as a 2012 author should always give his/her readers (note the sarcasm).

Rating: 1.5 Stars 
 If you were thinking about whether or not to continue this series, let me tell you now: walk away. Seriously, Fifty Shades Freed isn't worth it. It's by far the worst book in this series. Ironically, it isn't even because of the sensual scenes (even though there are plenty of those), it's simply because this novel had no plot whatsoever! Christian and Ana are now married and...that's it. This is a story of their married life. The first quarter is all about their honeymoon, Ana complaining about having so much money, and her inner goddess looking up from her copy of The Complete Stories of Charles Dickens to make a face or some snide comment. The novel progresses in a similar manner: Ana and Christian buying a house, getting adjusted to being married, Ana's inner goddess appearing every so often, etc. The last quarter of this story was the only interesting bit and the last aspect of Christian's character growth that needed to occur finally happened. Still, after finishing this series I am unable to see why it has made such a huge splash in the book community. 
 I am constantly befuddled by why a woman would write this series and furthermore, why other women are extolling its virtues (non-existent virtues more like it). I understand that every woman probably has some crazy fantasy of seducing a man who can't be seduced by other women, of having a man be jealous of you and possessive, and even having a man who is romantic and completely besotted with you. Christian Grey is an extreme version of this Mr. Perfect though. He doesn't give Ana any freedom, any issues they have are resolved by sex, and they only seem to do what suits him. Of course, this is supposed to have changed by the end of the book, leaving you with an impression that their married life is all hunky-dory and that Ana and Christian have reached a state of equilibrium, balancing normalcy with their messed-up qualities, but that still doesn't explain Ana's characterization. Erotic content aside, this series could have been a lot better than it was if Ana showed more backbone. If she had stood up to Christian a little bit more, if she had had normal and realistic reactions to many of the uncommon situations she found herself in, if she had simply grown a backbone, this book would have been infinitely better. I know what you die-hard Fifty Shades Fans are going to say - Ana does stand up for herself! She's always fighting with Christian! That's why he loves her and not any of his ex-submissives! Yes, Ana brings up ideas that she disagrees with and argues with Christian, but none of these arguments are ever seen to their completion. Ana walks away in a puff of anger, she resolves not to talk to Christian, she finally sees him and then can't help but melt into his arms and do anything he asks of her. That isn't woman empowerment! It isn't even standing up for yourself! It's like starting an argument with a bully and then deciding half-way through it isn't worth it and giving in. E.L. James characterizes Ana in this same fashion and ultimately, the messages it's sending out to woman of today are bad. If James wanted to write Ana the way she did, she should have made this novel set in the 1800s or a little later. The fact that she didn't only fuels my anger towards this series. 
 I have to admit though that I did find one aspect of this novel interesting: the story with Ana's ex-boss and his connection with Christian. James explores the psychological situations that makes men revert to becoming Dominatrix's in the last few chapters of this novel, and that was extremely thought-provoking. Either than that though, this series simply is not worth the time and energy. 
 Unless you like mature, erotica content, this series is not for you. It will make you pull out your hair in frustration and bang your head against the wall - repeatedly! The only redeeming quality about this series is the fascinating psychological impact that these types of Dom-Sub relationships have on people. Either than that though, this series isn't worth spending time or money on. In some ways, I'm disappointed with the book community for giving a story like this so much popularity when there are dozens of literary gems which never get the recognition they deserve. Anyway, I won't be buying into the hype anymore - Twilight was bad, but this was just a nightmare. I don't think I've ever been this happy to finish a series and never have to read it again, but I am so glad I will never have to read about Ana or Christian again! There is only one thing I feel now: liberated.

"Tell me, little wolf. Do you want to punish those who have wronged you?" 
 3,5 stars. Now this is a story you don't read every day! How many writers can write about a protagonist who slowly turns into an anti-hero-possible-villain and still make the reader sympathize with her. Too bad the writing style wasn't as refreshing and the plot contained a lot of YA-fantasy cliches, but reading about a main character as unique as Adelina made up for a lot of things. 
 Let's start with that pesky first half, where you find a lot of familiar YA-tropes: we meet a teenage female protagonist who has had a hard childhood, one dead parent, and a younger sibling that she loves very much (well, not really...it's complicated). When the protagonist finds out she has mysterious powers she gets targeted by a hot villain, but luckily she gets saved by an equally hot hero and his cool band of misfits. Together they plan to overthrown the government, and...you can fill in the rest. 
 So although the second half gets a lot better, the overall plot is pretty average, the writing not anything special - fast paced without plenty of details - and for some reason the author decided to base the world on the Italian Renaissance (because it's romantic, I guess?). 
 However, the whole story has this dangerous atmosphere that always keeps you on your toes. This is because every character is this book is morally grey: you can't trust anyone to do the right thing. Not even our protagonist. 
 As I said, I found Adelina the most interesting thing of this book. Thanks to surviving a deadly fever that swept through the land of Kenterra, Adelina now has silver hair, only one eye, and powers that make her able to conjure dark illusions. Due to being raised by her abusive father kindness and trust don't come easy, but you can see that Adelina wants to be good - she's just constantly surrounded by people who rather want her to be ruthless and deadly. 
 How she struggled with her moral compass was fascinating and very tense, which made the ending of this book so heartbreaking. (I almost threw my book against the wall, I was so shocked). I had hoped for something more happy, but maybe this ending was inevitable. 
 The other characters sadly didn't have half the strength that Adelina had. Enzo was the mysterious handsome hero with fire-powers and a wish for revenge (oh how coool~! not) and most members of the Dagger Society never become more than a name. Also: what is it with gorgeous people having to wear masks? First ACOTAR and now this series. 
 Teren had more going for him - with his twisted mindset concerning the malfetto - but in this book he acted mostly as the Queen's doormat. Hopefully he becomes more his own person in the future. 
 There is some romance in this book, but I was the most invested in the friendship between Rafaelle and Adelina, and Adelina's relationship with her younger sister Violetta. The latter's time to shine came pretty late (at the end of the book) but Violetta's secret revealed a whole new side to her sister-bond with Adelina. I'm very curious to see how their relationship develops in the next book. 
 So even though the plot of this book isn't very original, the threatening mood of the story and its unpredictable (main) characters kept me reading until the shocking end. That wicked epilogue gave the final push, so I'll definitely pick up The Rose Society soon. I can't wait to see how things will get better...or worse.

I received The Young Elites by Marie Lu from Penguin's First to Read program. Adelina Amouteru survived a blood fever that ravaged the people of hers and surrounding cities. As a result of the fever, several survivors are forever marked with visible scars or differences, setting them apart from "normal" people. Some of the survivors even possess powers, making them "Young Elites". After escaping death not only once from the fever, but again from being burned at the stake, Adelina must decide whether to join Enzo Valenciano and The Daggers, a band of Young Elites, or to side with Teren Santoro and the Inquisition Axis, the King's effort to search out and destroy all Young Elites. Who will Adelina choose? Will she be blinded by the dark vengeance brewing inside her? 
 Let me say, I really enjoyed this book. If you follow my reviews, I don't think you'll find many fantasy novels in my repertoire. I like the occasional fantasy read, but it has to keep me interested. This book did just that. It kept me guessing. Just when I thought I knew what was going to happen, here comes another twist. Sometimes I wanted to cheer for Adelina, and other times I wanted to slap some sense into her. 
 The characters were developed very well. They were realistic and each had their own qualities that made them believable. Some I liked, some I didn't, but it's the same in life. The descriptions were very thorough and helped me bring the characters to life in my imagination. I could picture their costumes and the scenes clearly. All in all, a very entertaining read. My first Marie Lu book, and probably not my last. I give this book 4 out of 5 stars and recommend it to anyone who is a fan of Marie Lu, or likes a suspenseful fantasy novel with twists and turns at every page.

Ah, well. That was quite a read. 
 First I'll start with the things that I loved: 
 - I loved the world building. I've read some of the reviews before reading the book so that I can at least gain some insights, and I saw that some people thought the world that Adelina resided in was practically an alternative history for the years of the black plague. I saw that it rung true in the book, and while some got irked by that fact, I liked it. 
 - Their powers. Adelina's power reminded me of The Night Circus, seeing as the main protagonists and her have almost the same powers--Illusion to all the senses and shit. And it's imposing. So are the abilities of the others, like Enzos, Michael's and Lucent's, and Teren's. They were impressive. 
 - Teren and Enzo. I ship them. I know that it's unreasonable, that they practically stand on different sides of the court, that they're probably one another's enemies, and that Teren killed Enzo, BUT. I ship them. Yeah. Ain't nobody sinking my ship. 
 Now, the things that I half-liked: 
 - Adelina. I was waiting for the apparently strong as hell and bad ass anti-heroine that everyone talked about in their reviews. Alas, she never showed up. Or even if she did, it was only half-assed. I suppose she disappointed me, in a way. Some of her scenes in the book also reminded me of Cruel Beauty (I'm currently reading that book, and I'm on like, chapter two, and yet I've literally already cringed and banged my head on my desk a lot of times. So obviously, this fact was a minus for me), especially the beginning with her unnecessary resentment towards her little sister. And I might've expected something more from her. Oh well. 
 Aaaand. That's it. 
 This book didn't really disappoint me, except for Adelina's part, and yet I somewhat still liked her. The other characters were good enough. The multiple point of views was tolerable. And the plot was executed nicely. (I felt that it could've been better though. I'm sorry) The characters were also complex--they weren't sorted into the good and bad stereotype, and I loved that. That's what I want to see in books, because that's a sense of realism. Showing that people are neither good nor bad--they're merely in between. 
 So all in all, I liked the book. It interested me enough to want to read the next one. I give this three and a half stars.

 When I've finished reading it, I can't coerce myself to sleep because I want to know what's next and you want to relieve the moments you just have read, as if you were a part of it.

On the Jellicoe Road is a melodramatic and wearisome YA novel about a girl searching for her family. It's a joyless and jarring book, with all kinds of ill-fitting elements rammed in together. 
 The first half is mostly about school kids playing a trite game of "territory wars" in a small Australian town. The author treats the game with extreme seriousness and weight, but in reality it's a mere trifle. The "war" only lasts for 6 weeks each year, there are no real consequences for breaching territory, there's nothing at stake either externally or personally, the teens could easily seek help from their teachers at any time, and the main character, Taylor Markham, isn't even all that invested in the banal "war." Taylor's got other, more important things to worry about like having been abandoned by her drug addict mother as a child, and having witnessed a man kill himself via a rifle to the head (described with brain chunks and all. Ew!). 
 As a result, the so-called war is little more than a bunch of pathetic, foolish children having hammy, soap opera-style confrontations and saying "You can't go there, or else...!" for over a hundred pages. Oh, there's an occasional punch, but it's nothing to get worked up about. To make matters worse, eventually even the characters realise how pointless the "war" is and abandon the entire thing in an anticlimactic whimper. When even the characters think the central plot is boring and meaningless, that's a sure sign to the author that her book needs to go back to rewrite. 
 Apart from the so-called war, the book also features flashbacks to a group of teens 20 years ago, and explores Taylor's search for identity and family. The flashbacks aren't all that successful, chiefly because the past characters experience some serious, serious trauma that makes the present-day story seem even more lightweight and meaningless. For example, one repeated flashback depicts a girl surviving an horrific car crash and watching her mother getting decapitated right before her eyes. (Again, ew! Such exceedingly grotesque images are tonally jarring). How on earth are we supposed to care one iota about Taylor Markham's schoolyard rivalries after reading that? 
 Taylor Markham's search for identity is not particularly involving either. Taylor is obviously hurting from the separation from her mother and yearning for some sort of connection - that's fine. But Taylor is a histrionic drama queen who reacts to every minor problem in her life by screaming. Emotion-wise, there's no perceptible difference between Taylor being abandoned by her mother as a child and Taylor having a petty argument with her sorta, kinda boyfriend. Apart from making Taylor unlikeable, this strips all the impact from the actually serious, life-changing events in the book. Moreover, because so much of the book is taken up by the tiresome non-war, everything else is left rushed and underdeveloped. This book is unrealistically over-stuffed with some truly HEAVY topics. Apart from the traumatic car crash and suicide scenes, there's also paedophilia, child prostitution, homelessness, drug addiction, cancer, mental illness, attempted suicide, accidental death, a fire... But these big events aren't explored with much in the way of depth or subtlety. There simply isn't space in the book for that. Some of these events come across as exploitative, as though they were included simply to shock the reader. Others come across as excessively sentimental melodrama. 
 Not to mention, it's all incredibly predictable. Like, golly gosh, do you suppose there might be some sort of link between the present and past stories?! Golly gosh, could Taylor Markham's search for family possibly lead her to the group of teens featured in the flashbacks?! Every time a link is "revealed," I literally groaned in frustration because it was SO BLOODY OBVIOUS. I wouldn't usually complain about this, except that the author uses such flimsy, bald-faced plot devices to artificially extend Taylor's search for her family. Like, Taylor has been cared for by a woman who knows the whole story, but chosen not to say anything for positively no discernible reason. And Taylor discovers a manuscript depicting the events on the teens 20 years ago - but it is conveniently unfinished and then stolen before she can read it all. Not to mention that Taylor has conveniently forgotten or repressed the memory of every significant event in her life - until the opportune moment when her memory suddenly returns(!). And isn't it a tad unbelievable that 
 all 
 the characters were known by completely different names as teenagers? These contrivances had me rolling my eyes. I just couldn't become engaged with the story because the way it unfolds was so nonsensical. Oh, and there's also this totally random serial killer subplot that, unsurprisingly, goes nowhere. That sentence plainly has nothing to do with anything previously mentioned in this paragraph, but the serial killer subplot plainly has nothing to do with anything in this book. 
 The bottom line is this book was an absolute chore to read. I will gladly admit that there are some fleeting, isolated scenes that were dramatically effective and for that reason I can kinda understand why some readers absolutely love this book. For example, there's what might be the perfect teen sex scene - a scene that manages to be both emotionally intense but also painfully realistic. But for me there was just too much padding in this book for me to give it anything other than a 1 out of 5. With absolute honesty, when I finished this book I was downright relieved I didn't have to put up with any more of Taylor Markham's crap.

Whatever you think about this story, you have to admit that there's nothing simple or obvious about it, unlike other teen fiction offerings today. The story is unusual and complicated, and the two narratives are confusing for a very long time -- distractingly so. In fact, I suspect it will lose a lot of its targeted teen audience because it's "hard". 
 The italicized narrative is, in my opinion, the weak part of the book, and I wish that part of the story had been told in a different way. There are several things about it that bothered me. For instance, the writing is grandiose and overly dramatic to the point of being kind of ridiculous and annoying (Did she really count 132 minutes? Was that before or after Tate crawled over and held their hands? Did they all sit in the same spot for 2 hours and 12 minutes, counting the time? Before Fitz arrived? And then the cars blew up? After 132 + 10 or so minutes? Or was the dad still alive when Fitz dragged him out? Hmmm... ) Also, there is too much omniscient narration for a story told from one person's point of view. Definitely the weak part of the story. 
 However, the part of the book that deals with the day to day life of Taylor and her friends is fascinating and entertaining. I would have enjoyed more tales of the war between the different factions. The Australian setting is neat but negligible -- the story could have taken place in any remote place in any country. I also didn't think it was necessary to tie up every single loose end. Who cares who the serial killer is? Why state what happened to Webb when it's already heavily implied? Why make neat a story that is all about complicated messes? 
 Overall, an enjoyable, fresh read. I think adults who enjoy reading young adult fiction will like this more than teens.

3.5 stars--- 
 Katy Evans returns with a sexy novella, the final installment of the unforgettable love story that began in MANWHORE. 
 What lies ahead for Chicago's most envied couple, Malcolm Saint and Rachel Livingston? 
 Sparks flew between them in MANWHORE. 
 Separated by deception, the intensity and heat of their attraction turned up in MANWHORE +1. 
 Will Chicago's wealthiest and most notorious player finally settle down, or will one woman never be enough? 
 Find out in MS. MANWHORE, the ultimate conclusion to their electric, breathtaking story. 
 ************** 
 REVIEW: 3.5 stars---MS. MANWHORE is a novella and last installment in Katy Evans' contemporary adult MANWHORE erotic romance series focusing on billionaire Malcolm Saint and the woman he loves Rachel Livingston. Ms. Manwhore should not be read as a stand alone as the storyline is the culmination of the relationship between Malcolm and Rachel that began as a lie and ends with a destination wedding on a paradise island. 
 Told for first person point of view (Rachel) Ms Manwhore follows Rachel as she prepares for her upcoming nuptials-her friends Wynn and Gina, her mother, the dress and Malcolm's desire to give the woman he loves everything that she wants and needs. Rachel wants a small wedding without the over the top wedding hoopla, but her fiance needs to give her a wedding she will never forget. 
 A majority of the storyline looks at Rachel and Malcolm's sexual relationship. The imagery is detailed and graphic; Malcolm is a man who expresses his love with physical affection and $ex. When Rachel implements a 'no sex until the wedding night' policy, we watch as the sexual tension continues to build between our leading couple. The $ex scenes are erotic, provocative and hot. 
 There is the potential for a spin-off or continuation of the series (ala Katy's REAL series stylization) focusing on Malcolm's best friend Tahoe and Rachel's bestie Gina. Something has occurred between this couple or at the very least Tahoe knows something that the reader does not. 
 As per Katy Evans's style of writing there is some repetition. I found myself on the outside while the narrator (Rachel) told us about the events leading up to her wedding. I felt detached from the events as the narrator described what was happening and yet was reluctant to invite us into the action-I was on the outside looking in while the heroine relayed details. 
 If you are a fan of Katy Evans' MANWHORE series then Ms.Manwhore is a sweet, sexy conclusion to Rachel and Malcolm's love story. There are no anxious moments; no conflict and no threats from the outside (aside from Rachel's ex-boss Victoria making an uninvited appearance). MS. MANWHORE is a short story that looks at two people as they prepare for their wedding without the worry of financial hardship.

This beautifully written but self-indulgent memoir of a young woman stricken by grief at the death of her father did not 'hook' me initially much to my surprise. I have had a lifelong fascination with birds of prey and later in the story I became enthralled by the details of the training of her hawk, which she undertook as a form of grief therapy. Why did the story not immediately appeal to me? I believe it was the fact that the writing is complex; although the language is frequently poetic, especially in the author's descriptions of Nature and the English country landscape, there are sections where I felt she wrote to impress readers with her knowledge of falconry terminology and a narrative liberally scattered with words such as "annealed" and "accipitrine". 
 Her own story is intertwined with that of the sad life of T. H. White who wrote "The Goshawk" which she read in her youth, and to which she refers when training her hawk named Mabel. She condemns White's methods when training his hawk, but I found this rather hypocritical as some of her own methods were equally suspect - keeping a large hawk in the living room of a suburban home, overfeeding, walking the hawk through busy city streets. I acknowledge that people deal with grief in different ways, but I felt she merely acquired and trained Mabel as a romantic tool to assuage her overwhelming emotional state, although she had owned birds of prey previously. She began to endow the hawk with human qualities and to view the world through the eyes of Mabel, until she became wild herself, verging on madness. Her withdrawal from the world into solitude was not ultimately healing and her emotions could have possibly been brought to balance by earlier medical intervention; although in that case we may have been denied an interesting and unique story. 
 I was left with mixed feelings about the book, but my interest in T.H.White was piqued and I should now like to read the work of this tragically flawed writer.

book_b.title: The Little Prince
book_b.user_review: Kind of dumb.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Reading The Little Prince was such a strange experience. It's delightful. It's funny. It's adorable. The almost condescending attitude towards adults and the jokes at their expense makes this book appealing to kids since they can relate to being baffled by grown-ups. But as I'm laughing at the crazy adults and the crazy things they do, I had to stop for a second as it sank in that I do those crazy things, too. I found myself reflecting at the deeper story behind this prince and his cute travels to different planets. The little prince's complete bewilderment at the behavior of adults challenged the way I think in so many ways. And boy do I love a story that challenges my thinking. 
 Here's one that blew my mind - if sheep eat flowers with the thorns, then what good are thorns? I HAVE NO IDEA. My instinct is to explain evolution or genetics. But that's not the question. The thorns don't do any good and I hadn't realized that. Maybe as adults we simply stop questioning things because now we know science and math and stuff and we assume there's nothing left to learn. I do have a lot left to learn. I need to figure out why plants have thorns. 
 The little prince describes grown-ups as loving numbers and asking questions to get to know someone where the answers are numbers instead of questions about things that matter (like getting to know their personality). To prove the little prince is right, here's a numbered list of the types of adults he meets on each planet: 
 1. The King - talks about his control and power, but the little prince clearly sees that it's just an illusion since he commands things under the "science of government, until conditions are favorable. (pg 31)" Or, when they were going to do it anyway. 
 2. The Vain Man - wants nothing more than to be admired constantly. The little prince wonders "...what is there about my admiration that interests you so much? (pg 34)." 
 3. The Drunkard - the vicious cycle of shame. He's ashamed that he drinks so he drinks to forget his shame. The prince has literally nothing to say about that. 
 4. The Business Man - endlessly counts all the stars and says he owns them and they make him rich. The little prince sees that work should be a two-way street. "But you're not useful to the stars. (pg 40)" 
 5. The Lamp Lighter - stuck in the endless cycle of chores. He is a hard worker and the little prince likes him since his job is useful to others, but the little prince doesn't understand why he can't rest and enjoy the many joys (like sunsets) that his planet has. 
 6. The Geographer - never actually goes anywhere. He writes about places and discoveries that other people have made. He's the kind of adult that never fully lives their life. 
 7. Earth - the last planet he visits that has a combination of all these grown-ups (which he numbers to please the adults). 
 I think I relate the most to the lamp lighter. I get stuck in the daily grind of things. Who do you relate to the most? 
 My favorite thing about the little prince is his view of love. The time you spend caring for something is what makes it important to you. A huge rose garden is not as meaningful as the one rose you took care of. Like the fox said, don't forget this truth: 
 "One sees clearly only with the heart. Anything essential is invisible to the eyes." 
 -Antoine de Saint-Exupery, The Little Prince pg 63

 "I'm not perfect, Mia. And our relationship may not be perfect to you , but it is to me. You will never find one couple in this world without problems." He tossed his hands in the air. I stumbled across this gem while going through my Kindle feed late last night. The synopsis caught my attention and so I decided I would read a few chapters before going to bed but once I started I couldn't stop. This book was certainly all consuming! It made me remember just how much I loved discovering new-to-me authors especially magnificent ones like R.J.Lewis. 
 "Borden" is about a man from the wrong side of the tracks falling for a beautiful and privileged young woman named Kate. He knew just from their very first tryst that he was way out of his league. He was prepared to let her go, but Kate continued to push until it was much too late. Needless to say, his very first relationship was life changing. Heart-breaking. From then on, Borden vowed not to let anyone get that close to him ever again. Considering his dangerous lifestyle, this pledge would have been easy to keep yet once he reencounters a young woman way back from his past his vow is thrown out the window. 
 Early on Borden knew that Emma was different. She certainly was not like any woman that he had met before. She should have been terrified as everybody else was in Borden's presence, but Emma wasn't the sort that could be easily intimidated. She grew up in Borden's world and this was one of the many traits that earned the untouchable Borden's interest. 
 "I never wanted to be in this position again, but I can't get you out of my fucking head. I can't breathe without thinking about you, and I..I feel guilt over it." 
 Reading the first few chapters, I was convinced that Kate would be it for Borden. He cared for her wholeheartedly to the point where he did so many things just to earn her. I would never have thought that he would get over that immense love yet as soon as Emma comes into Borden's life it was as if she was the one. These two in all accounts fit together completely. It was as if she was specifically brought into this world just for him. This in my opinion was the strongest appeal of this entire story. Their chemistry, the passion and that inner connection between the couple was beyond spectacular. 
 That wasn't the only thing that was spectacular. Despite Borden's "crazy" his character development was remarkable. I appreciated how he channeled all the badness in his life and created something productive. Yes, he was still a thug but since the community benefited it seemed to have balanced everything out. If anything, he needed this power to protect those that he cared about. 
 I thought the story itself was striking - not like anything that I have read before. It was intense, gritty and enrapturing. The plot to me was outstanding. I loved that even if it is the first book in a two-part series that the author didn't leave us hanging. Instead, she ended it nicely and adequately prepped us for the next installment. 
 The negative part of "Borden" is the horrible formatting. This would normally have frustrated me, forcing me to shelve it, but the story was good enough to make me look past those issues. If spelling and grammatical errors are not a priority then I am certain that you will come to love this remarkable love story as much as I did.

I was torn over whether I should write a book review for this, because, on the one hand it really is just a series of novellas, but on the other, it has the length and feel of a full on novel. In the end I decided I needed to say something... so here it goes! 
 Basically my two major thoughts were: one, how the hell did Celaena ever become a notorious assassin? I mean seriously, I have yet to see her successfully assassinate a single target. While at the same time I have seen her make stupid mistakes, get caught tailing someone, completely misjudge people, and almost die. I believe in her ability as an assassin even less than I did during Throne of Glass--and that's saying something. 
 My second thought was: this is just too long. Normally novellas are just a short break from the main story, not an entire novel in themselves. And, I found that I could do without having read most of it. 
 Don't get me wrong. I absolutely adored learning more about Celaena and Sam's romance. In fact I think I may like Sam more than either Chaol or Dorian. He was just so sweet and kind and wonderful all while still being a bad-ass assassin. In fact, I believed Sam as an assassin way more than I ever did Celaena. What happened to him was also totally heart wrenching and nearly brought me to tears. 
 I also liked getting a bit more context for Celeana's life in the assassin's guild. Although, I now have a newfound and intense hatred for Arobynn. 
 Really, this book is almost worth reading just for the Chaol and Dorian cameo in The Assassin and the Underworld. 
 But, I basically could have done without everything else. I hated The Assassin and the Desert. It was just completely cliched and predictable and did little to advance the story. (I mean really? an exotic master that teaches her a fighting style based on animals? Now where have I seen that before?! Not to mention the impossible-jump-on-horseback and the-sword-so-close-it-cuts-her-hair scenes). The Assassin and the Healer also added very little, but at least that one was short. I think if I were to read it again. I would skip those two entirely. 
 In the end, I'm still happy to know more of Celaena's background. I just wish it didn't take 400 pages to do it.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I think 'read' is a generous term for what went down here. Merciful skipping and skimming. 
 I was eye rolls and exhaustion and boredom. Such boredom. Fires extinguished by the breadth of my yawns. 
 I can see why young adult audiences would thrive on this writing--it's overly effusive, sentimental, and dripping with soul mate love stories. The author attempts, I think, a kind of stream of consciousness approach, but it fails for a more .... self aware audience, I think. This book really could have been half as long. Limitless descriptions of every single thought do not make for enjoyable experience. Because the reader does not experience! We only hear, we are told over and over and over again from every single perspective about the magnitude of every single second. 
 That bores me. 
 Not to mention all my problems from the earlier novels: the recovery from a more or less genocide (even if souls can be refurbished) was too clean and simple; the instant love that is love for the sake of love being there (whenever their eyes meet!!!!) is meaningless--she tries to recover that by showing their discovery of each other's character in this novel, but it rings false all the way through; the storyline is convoluted, and the ending is just talking (not the epilogue); the idea that ripping through worlds creates traumas is straight out of Pullman (the idea of tithing it is unremarkable); akiva's all consuming and amazing powers again are made I think to try and make up for the fact that these people are all killers. They find a happy ending. Good for them. Abandon earth, and all is well. 
 Sigh. I didn't really read it halfway through. I found the prose too burdensome, especially with the constant longing and sexual tension that is dumped on us like a merciless avalanche. For me, the first half of the first book is stellar. The second book angers me bc of Karou's characterization, and this book was just unbearable to get through. 
 I am surely in the minority, but these are my thoughts.

More reviews available at my blog, Beauty and the Bookworm. 
 I was so excited to dive in to the last book of this trilogy, but also apprehensive, because the second book was not as magical as the first, and I was concerned about the third following in that path. And there's the rub: I was right to be apprehensive. 
 With seraphim invading the human world, our heroine Karou and hero Akiva find themselves trying to force the remaining Misbegotten seraphim and a paltry bunch of chimaera to get along long enough to save both Earth and Eretz. But here's the thing...Taylor can't seem to be satisfied with that as a plot. Instead, she starts throwing in new ones, like a looming cataclysm and a backstory that hasn't been mentioned until now and worlds-threatening monsters that don't ever actually end up getting resolved. And while some of this is cushioned by another burgeoning romance between Liraz and Ziri (THANK GOD, because I couldn't put up with any more of his pining) and of course Karou and Akiva trying to come together once again, it just felt like too much, especially because the story didn't really just end, it just kind of trailed off. 
 I'm not really sure there's that much more to say about this. There were some excellent moments in here--the confrontation in the Vatican comes to mind, Eliza's return to her true self, Mik and Zuze and the stormhunters as well--but overall I'm not sure they could really redeem a book that felt kind of scattered. It definitely didn't have the magic of the first book, the snap and sizzle and all of the tropes made over and new again; instead, it felt much more like a generic fantasy story, and one that didn't come to a soaring or even a crashing conclusion, but instead just sort of petered out. While Karou and Akiva were wonderful and even Liraz got some redemption (but what the heck was up with Haxaya? Something else that was never explained) there were just too many holes and dropped strings here to make me really like it as a book. Ultimately, the first book was the best of this series, and it was a bit of a downhill slide from there. I'm interested in Taylor's more recent book, but this series ultimately didn't deliver what I had really hoped it would. It read a lot like the upwards-of-a-million-word-long RP a friend and I have had going off and on for years--and while it might be fun to write your own melodrama and jump from plot to plot and have things dropped, there's the potential of it all coming back together again later. I kept hoping things would come together here, but they never did, and that was a disappointment. 
 2 stars out of 5.

Oh. Wow. This third book is the best of all. Well, no it isn't. All three are so good! But Taylor finished up her magnificent trilogy PERFECTLY. 
 I can't go into detail because, in all honesty, it would take me forever because there are SO many details to address! Let's just say that every doggone plot thread was brought to a clean and satisfying end, which is no small feat. This trilogy has ended up with a huge cast, and Taylor developed personal plot lines for, what, at least ten of them. I will say that the last fifth of the book starts to feel a little like somebody ticking items off a list: "Okay, this plot line is done, that one's done, this one's done," etc. But again, there's no other way to do it, really. It's THE END, and each character's personal adventure has to be addressed. 
 POSSIBLE SPOILER ALERT! 
 And Taylor had fun at the end. When Karou and Akiva can finally FINALLY get together, she throws in a monkey wrench that drives them apart again, just for a little while longer. It's perfectly logical, so even though I wanted to scream I couldn't really complain. The monkey wrench got worked out, and ta-dah! Our main heroes came together. 
 I can't wait for enough time to go by so that I can read them again!
I absolutely loved this series! I highly recommend it.

sample_reviews.review_text: A Thousand Splendid Suns by Khaled Hosseini. This book was excellent. In the same venue as The Kite Runner, this book is about two Afghani women, Laila and Marion, born in two different families and who went through the hell of the Soviet regime, the Mujahedeen, the Taliban and finally the Americans. As they go through their lives are destroyed, and brought together under the most awful of circumstances. I think that the author wanted to portray the plight of the Afghan women, with all the extreme difficulties (difficulty is such a wimpy word) that they had to go through, and in doing so the story rings a bit less true, less compelling. But in understanding why the author did this, you get such a vivid picture of the fabric of their lives, of the misery of their dashed hopes, their lives of forced ignorance, of total surrender to men.

Personally, I enjoyed The Kite Runner much more. I really love Hosseini as a writer, but couldn't find myself liking many of the characters in this book. The passion the Hosseini has for his country is clear and I love how he still sees the good in his people despite the amount of loss they have faced.
Throughout reading this book, I was dragging myself to wrap it up already, it was not until I reached halfway that I decided I could not put up with it anymore. It was exhaustively mundane.

What a wonderful book! Hosseini's talent, as he showed in The Kite Runner, is that he can make a totally foreign culture into an amazing read. He has such a gift in finding the human element that binds us all together.

I enjoy Khaled's writing, but found this darker than The Kite Runner...a bit too dark for my liking. I realize that the situation in Afghanistan has been/is grim, but the book could have used a little more hope

A Thousand Splendid Suns 
 -By Khaled Hosseini 
 Life is tough, not for everyone, but for some it really is. Mariam knew it is since her mother told her that you are nothing but a "harami" (Bastard). 
 Plot: 
 Penning down the story of Mariam and Laila's struggles comprising their husband's violence, loss of family, Afghan wars, Khaled Hosseini will make you sob and cry in this reading journey. 
 The story is divided into four parts. First part starts with the introduction of a Mariam, a harami, her mother Nana and Jalil (her biological father but a so called dad. Her hardships that she goes through while living in the small kolba, getting fake loved from Jalil then getting married to a man more than double her age are explained wonderfully. Though Nana behaves very rudely with her owing to the miseries she had faced in her life, she loves Mariam and say, "Like a compass needle that points north, a man's accusing finger always finds a woman". After her death, Jalil and his three wives marries her off to a man instead of consoling her of the grief she was going through only to erase, once and for all, the last trace of their husband's scandalous mistake. Her marriage brings no difference in her life and she keeps of craving for the love she never found. 
 The book takes a different turn with part two which has nothing to do with Mariam and her hardships. Instead it deals with the story of Laila, a happy-go-lucky, carefree girl who is in love with her one-legged-best-friend Tariq. Loved by her family, her life suddenly takes a different turn and leaves her pregnant with Tariq's child. Tariq on the other hand has left the country due to the ongoing wars. 
 Following the lives of these two girls, Part three and four dealt with how both of them meet and how this meeting brings a new era of suffering into their lives. After overcoming the feeling of hatred, a new bond of mother-daughter relationship grows between them which help them in fighting with their life's miseries. 
 In between, detailing the lives of people and a country during war, especially women, Hosseini is successful in visualizing his readers the destitutions both Marial and Laila suffer, the pain they go through, how their hatred with each other transforms into never ending love and how this love gifts Mariam the life she always desired. 
 But will they ever be able to come out of the troubles they are struck into? 
 Will they find a solution to their problems or will their troubles bring an end to their life?? 
 Will Marriam be able to find love in her life? 
 Will Laila and Tariq ever meet again? 
 Go through this emotional, heart breaking and brave drive which will make you feel pity, which will show you the life you have never dreamed of. I can bet once you start reading this, Mariam and Laila will not let you sleep till you complete their journey through 'A thousand splendid sons'. 
 My Opinion: 
 With perfect narration, simple language and world class visualizing ability, Hosseini has left no point of criticism in this read. All the characters are properly justified and all the scenes are wonderfully carved. With exceptional literature and visual appeal, he has been successful in winning his readers' heart. Right from the description of characters to that of the locations, his writing has made me his fan. This will make you cry, this will make you grieve for what his protagonists face. 
 Not only the life of his protagonists, but the consequences and sufferings people face during wars, the true life of Afghanis during the three decades of war in between the Soviet troops, Mujaheddin, Pashtuns and Hazaras and Tajiks and Uzbeks, this book details every minute details of a dying nation haunted with the impact and nightmares that war left on their lives. 
 Passing through the hardships, this is also a story of self-sacrifice, bravery and heroism which makes it dearer to its readers. 
 Final Rating: 
 Book Cover: 4/5 
 Plot, language and Literature: 5/5 
 Character Justification: 4/5 
 Final Rating: 4/5
